2026-10-02.title: UniWAM: Unified World-Action Model
2026-10-02.authors: Jiayi Chen , Wenxuan Song , Jingbo Wang , Shuai Zhou , Xicheng Gong , Zehua Fan , Ziyang Zhou , Junwu E , Haodong Yan , Fuhao Li , Qize Yu , Xu Huang , Pengwei Wang , Wen Chen , Shunbo Zhou , Haoang Li
2026-10-02.abstract:
Vision-language-action models benefit from the understanding and reasoning capabilities of pretrained vision-language models, but action-only supervision provides limited grounding in world dynamics. Conversely, world-action models inherit spatiotemporal priors from video generation models, yet remain limited in semantic understanding and reasoning under distribution shifts. We introduce UniWAM, a unified architecture that integrates a physical reasoner, a world generator, and an action predictor to jointly learn semantic understanding of the physical world, visual generation, and action prediction.
To ensure the quality of the training data, we developed a rigorous data cleaning and annotation pipeline for both human egocentric data and robot data.
To adapt the vision-language component to embodied tasks while preserving its inherited language capabilities, we represent low-level actions in natural language and introduce a pre-training recipe that assigns complementary supervision from visual question answering (VQA) data, human egocentric data, and robot demonstrations to the appropriate model components.
During post-training, future visual noise augmentation reduces reliance on precise future predictions, while history-conditioned flow matching uses encoded action history to initialize action generation. Together, these designs significantly reduce denoising steps while maintaining performance.
UniWAM achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance across multiple evaluations, including in-distribution performance, robustness, generalization, instruction following, and long-horizon task execution.
Furthermore, we uncover a log-linear scaling law of unified human-robot co-training, demonstrating the effectiveness of large-scale pre-training on a mixture of human and robot data.
2026-10-02.introduction:
In recent years, robot foundation models built upon Vision-Language Models (VLMs) ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Beyer et al., 2024 ; An et al., 2025 ) , namely Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) ( Black et al., 2025a ; Generalist Team, 2025 ; Bai et al., 2026 ) , have
demonstrated strong effectiveness, as they can effectively leverage the semantic understanding capabilities
acquired through large-scale VLM pre-training. However, using actions
alone as the supervision signal limits the model’s ability to
understand world dynamics. World-Action Models (WAMs) ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Bi et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026a ) inherit strong spatiotemporal
priors from Video-Generation Models (VGMs) ( Team Wan et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026d ) pre-trained on
large-scale video data, improving their understanding of dynamics through predicting the next
frame, but their understanding in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios
and reasoning capabilities for complex tasks remain limited. This paper
asks: How can we combine the strong reasoning and generalization capabilities of
VLMs with the strong dynamics understanding of WAMs,
thereby building a truly generalist robot?

To address this question, we introduce UniWAM, integrating a VLM-based physical reasoner,
a VGM-based world generator, and an action predictor
within a unified architecture, drawing inspiration from the idea of Mixture-of-Transformer (MoT) ( Liang et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2026a ) .
The hybrid model jointly supports semantic understanding, visual prediction, and action generation.
Figure 1 summarizes the training data, unified architecture,
and benchmark performance of UniWAM. Pre-training such a hybrid model presents three key challenges:
1) Adapting the VLM to embodied tasks ( Wang et al., 2026b ) requires updating its parameters to
acquire embodied knowledge. However, such adaptation must preserve
the language capabilities inherited from pretraining, which calls for supervision signals that
remain compatible with the VLM’s pretraining distribution. To
this end, we show that directly representing low-level robot actions
using natural language ( Zha et al., 2026 ) , thereby aligning the VLM’s action supervision with its pretraining
input-output distribution, provides an effective way to train
the VLM for embodied understanding while preserving its pretrained capabilities.
2) Another key challenge lies in designing appropriate supervision signals for each
expert using heterogeneous data, as differences in data
distributions and training objectives may lead to conflicts among the optimization processes
of different experts.
To this end, we construct a pretraining mixture consisting of Visual Question Answering (VQA), robot data, and human data, and
carefully assign their supervision to different components. Specifically, VQA data supervises the VLM to maintain its pretraining knowledge. Human data supervises both the VLM and VGM, thereby fully exploiting the physical knowledge contained in human videos while avoiding supervision from low-precision action
labels.
Since robot data exhibits the highest physical
consistency with downstream post-training and provides the most accurate action annotations, it
is used to supervise the VLM, VGM, and
action predictor, enabling the learning of precise action outputs.
3)
Large-scale training on heterogeneous data places stringent demands on data quality. We therefore developed a rigorous data cleaning pipeline. Since individual trajectories in human data often contain multiple actions, we further designed an automated pipeline for segmenting and annotating human trajectories.

During post-training , we continue the pre-training principle of maintaining unified capabilities and
jointly supervise the three experts
to adapt the model’s understanding, generation, and prediction capabilities to specific embodied
scenarios.
We additionally introduce future-visual noise augmentation and history-conditioned flow matching.
The former partially perturbs future visual latents while preserving the conditioning frames,
encouraging the action expert to extract control-relevant semantics
from coarse visual representations rather than rely on precise future predictions, thus
strengthening the interaction between visual generation and action
prediction.
Furthermore, the action expert leverages the dynamics and temporal continuity encoded in
historical sequences. It maps the action history into
a high-dimensional latent space and uses the resulting representation to initialize the
flow-matching process, thereby allowing historical motion information to
guide the generation of future action trajectories.
Together, these designs substantially reduce the number of denoising steps while maintaining
performance, improving inference efficiency.
Overall, at the architectural level, we build a MoT that connects language
reasoning, video generation, and action prediction through joint
attention.
Our contributions are summarized in four aspects.

For pre-training, we construct a three-source pre-training scheme comprising human data,
robot teleoperation data, and VQA data, and systematically
evaluate the contribution of each data source through source-level ablation studies.

For post-training, we explicitly formulate how recent action history and perturbed
future visual latents are incorporated into the joint
flow-matching process.

Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our UniWAM achieves SOTA performance across multiple dimensions,
including in-distribution performance, robustness, generalization, instruction following, and
long-horizon task execution.

We uncover a log-linear scaling law of unified human-robot co-training, demonstrating the effectiveness of large-scale pre-training on a mixture of human and robot data.

1. For pre-training, we construct a three-source pre-training scheme comprising human data,
robot teleoperation data, and VQA data, and systematically
evaluate the contribution of each data source through source-level ablation studies.

2. For post-training, we explicitly formulate how recent action history and perturbed
future visual latents are incorporated into the joint
flow-matching process.

3. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that our UniWAM achieves SOTA performance across multiple dimensions,
including in-distribution performance, robustness, generalization, instruction following, and
long-horizon task execution.

4. We uncover a log-linear scaling law of unified human-robot co-training, demonstrating the effectiveness of large-scale pre-training on a mixture of human and robot data.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Large-scale Pretraining for Robotics. Large-scale robotic pretraining has brought the field closer to generalist robots capable of performing a broad range of tasks across diverse environments.
RT-2 ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ) jointly trains on web
and robot data with tokenized actions, while
OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2025b ) adapts pretrained
vision–language representations to robot
demonstrations. π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2025b ) first combines a vision–language backbone with flow
matching. π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black et al., 2025a ) adds semantic subtask supervision and web data.
GEN-0 ( Generalist Team, 2025 ) leverages Unified Manipulation Interface (UMI) data to acquire physical sense towards scaling laws, while
Xiaomi-Robotics-1 ( Xiaomi Robotics Team et al., 2026 ) further constructs a two-state pretraining on UMI data for physical understanding and teleoperation data for embodiment-specific adaptation.
Galaxea G0.5 ( Liu et al., 2026a ) unifies reasoning and
action tokens through autoregressive training on
robot and visual question answering data.
Motus ( Bi et al., 2026a ) learns shared motion
information from heterogeneous data using
optical-flow-derived latent actions.
However, these approaches primarily emphasize either language–action or video–action joint modeling.
In contrast, our UniWAM’s pretraining framework unifies semantic understanding, dynamics prediction, and action generation through diverse data and complementary supervision.

World-action Models. World-action models (WAMs) are typically built
upon video generation backbones. They leverage the
physical dynamics priors of large-scale video
pretraining and obtain dense supervision by
predicting the future in diverse representation
spaces—including pixels, geometry, and
value—thereby facilitating the learning of
stronger action-generation policies.
DreamZero ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , Cosmos
Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) ,
Motus ( Bi et al., 2026a ) ,
MotuBrain ( MotuBrain Team et al., 2026 ) ,
LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026b ) , and
Dyna-2 ( Dyna Robotics, 2026 ) focus on modeling
visually grounded world dynamics and aligning
visual-state evolution with actions.
Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) ,
GigaWorld-Policy ( GigaWorld Team et al., 2026 ) ,
ImageWAM ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and
S-VAM ( Yan et al., 2026 ) further show that the
video-generation backbone can serve at inference
time as a representation encoder only, without
synthesizing complete future frames.
4D-WAM ( Yang et al., 2026a ) and
X-WAM ( Guo et al., 2026 ) extend the
representation domain of WAMs from pixel-temporal
features to four-dimensional spatiotemporal
geometry. MobileWAM ( Fan et al., 2026 ) and
ABot-M0.5 ( Chen et al., 2026 ) further push
WAMs toward more complex mobile manipulation.
Unlike these works, which primarily seek to unlock
the capabilities of video generation models, we
unify a vision–language model, a video generation
model, and an action expert within a single
framework and optimize it with complementary data
and supervision, enabling UniWAM to jointly
support multimodal understanding, visual
generation, and action prediction.

Learning from Egocentric Data. Egocentric videos provide a scalable source of
embodied experience beyond costly robot
demonstrations. Recorded from the actor’s
viewpoint, they capture diverse human–object
interactions and the resulting changes in the
physical world, while covering a broad range of
objects, environments, and long-horizon
activities. Recent datasets further enrich raw
videos with language, human motion, geometry, and
action-related signals, making them increasingly
suitable for large-scale embodied
pretraining ( Grauman et al., 2022 ; Damen et al., 2018 ; Hoque et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Punamiya et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026f ; Li et al., 2026e ; Deng and Zhou, 2026 ) . On the
modeling side, early efforts mainly focused on
representation learning, while later work
introduced more structured supervision through
latent actions, future prediction, and geometric
motion
cues ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026a ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026c ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . Moving closer to policy
learning, human motions and manipulation
trajectories are reconstructed and aligned with
robot action spaces for VLA
pretraining ( Kareer et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2026b ; Yoshida et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026b ) . Recent
embodied foundation models further unify human and
robot experience through shared action
representations and cross-embodiment pretraining,
allowing egocentric data to support both scalable
action learning and world
modeling ( Luo et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Zhong et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Sun et al., 2026 ) .

2026-10-02.title: H-SPAR: Hydrodynamic-aware Simulation for Particle Transport and Autonomous Robots
2026-10-02.authors: Navid Zarrabi , Nariman Yousefi , Sajad Saeedi
2026-10-02.abstract: Environmental robotic sampling requires considering the dual influence of water currents on robotic motion and particle transport. Existing marine robotics simulators generally model flow, autonomy, and sampling targets separately, limiting joint evaluation of mission cost and sampling performance. H-SPAR integrates spatially and temporally varying velocity fields, Lagrangian particle transport, probabilistic sampling, and ROS 2/Gazebo-based uncrewed surface vehicle (USV) autonomy. In this work, shared precomputed flow fields drive particle advection and current-induced forces during closed-loop vehicle execution. Path-planning experiments show that the existing current-aware planner SVF-RRT* achieves 69.4% lower upstream cost than conventional RRT* at the planning level, but this reduction falls to 41.7% during execution under time-varying currents, reflecting temporal flow variation, vehicle motion constraints, and path deviation omitted during planning. Coverage experiments show that sweep orientation changes the particle-sampling rate by up to 22.2% under the complete H-SPAR configuration. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating planning, vehicle execution, particle transport, and sampling together under consistent hydrodynamic conditions. 2026-10-02.title: BLT*: Informed Belief Localization Trees for Uncertainty-Aware Planning on Digital Twins
2026-10-02.authors: Elliot Preston-Krebs , Abhishek Goudar , Timothy D. Barfoot
2026-10-02.abstract:
We present Informed Belief Localization Trees* (Informed BLT*), a sampling-based belief space planning (BSP) algorithm that scales to large outdoor digital twins with point-cloud observations. We adapt RRT* and Informed RRT* to belief space using the 2 2 -Wasserstein ( W 2 W_{2} ) metric.
Assuming isotropic Gaussian beliefs, sampled belief states can be connected efficiently while accounting for available information and probabilistic collision constraints. This enables steering and rewiring without repeatedly propagating observations, and allows previously computed measurement information to be reused.
We present a framework to generate semantically labelled digital twins for planning in real-world environments with point-cloud-based localization. Experiments in simulated environments and digital twins show faster initial solution discovery in most maps with competitive cost convergence.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Autonomous unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) operating in large mapped environments must plan not only where they can travel, but also where they can reliably localize. A geometrically short path may traverse poorly observable regions, causing uncertainty to grow until probabilistic collision-avoidance or goal-reaching constraints are no longer satisfied. Belief space planning (BSP) addresses this coupling by planning over distributions of robot states and jointly accounting for motion and localization uncertainty.

Sampling-based BSP methods either propagate beliefs over nominal configuration-space graphs [ 1 , 2 ] or sample directly in belief space [ 3 ] . Although the 2 2 -Wasserstein ( W 2 W_{2} ) distance provides a suitable metric for Gaussian beliefs [ 4 ] , existing sampling-based methods use it primarily to define proximity while retaining a separate trajectory-cost objective. Other perception-aware planners incorporate spatial localizability or photometric information [ 5 , 6 ] ; however, sampling-based BSP is still commonly evaluated in low-dimensional environments with analytic or region-based observation models. Applying these methods to digital twins is more computationally demanding because localization quality must be inferred from local point-cloud geometry, while dynamic objects, vegetation, and reconstruction artifacts may provide unreliable observations.

We present Informed Belief Localization Trees* (Informed BLT*), which builds on RRT* [ 7 ] and Informed RRT* [ 8 ] to minimize accumulated W 2 W_{2} path length in an isotropic Gaussian belief space. Under a holonomic motion model, we derive a closed-form belief-reachability condition that supports direct belief-space steering and rewiring without sampling and propagating control sequences for each state. Point-cloud information evaluated at existing nodes can also be reused during subsequent connection and rewiring.
Our contributions are: (i) belief-space reachability, steering, rewiring, and informed sampling under a W 2 W_{2} path objective; (ii) a single prolate hyperspheroid outer approximation of the informed region induced by a convex goal set; and (iii) a digital-twin planning pipeline that uses semantic preprocessing to select localization-relevant geometry and the iterative closest point (ICP) Hessian as an information matrix for belief updates. We evaluate informed and uninformed variants of BLT* against three BSP baselines across 16 simulated and photogrammetry-reconstructed environments, comprising 8000 planner runs.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

Planning under uncertainty is commonly formulated as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) [ 9 ] , although exact solutions are generally intractable in continuous domains. BSP methods therefore employ various approximations. Censi et al. [ 10 ] discretize the configuration space, propagate uncertainty using Fisher information, and retain non-dominated beliefs at each configuration. Platt et al. [ 11 ] assume maximum-likelihood observations to obtain deterministic nominal belief trajectories amenable to linear-quadratic regulation, whereas Van den Berg et al. [ 12 ] use iterative linear-quadratic-Gaussian to optimize local trajectories and feedback policies without this assumption.

Graph-based approaches instead propagate uncertainty over sampled configuration-space structures. BRM [ 13 ] factors covariance propagation over a probabilistic roadmap [ 14 ] , while FIRM [ 15 ] associates graph edges with feedback controllers to recover edge independence and the optimal-substructure properties for a graph search. CS-BRM [ 16 ] connects sampled belief nodes into a roadmap using covariance steering with finite-time reachability guarantees. RRBT [ 1 ] bridges graph- and tree-based planning by incrementally constructing a graph of nominal trajectories and propagating non-dominated beliefs over its vertices; IBBT [ 2 ] extends this approach with batch sampling and an admissible cost-to-go heuristic.

More recent methods sample directly in belief space. Belief- 𝒜 \mathcal{A} [ 3 ] extends planners such as RRT [ 17 ] and SST [ 18 ] to belief space and has been extended to continuous-time belief propagation and safety verification [ 19 ] . Littlefield et al. [ 4 ] establish continuity properties that support the use of the W 2 W_{2} metric in optimal BSP. Whereas Belief- 𝒜 \mathcal{A} uses W 2 W_{2} for belief state proximity while retaining a separate trajectory cost, we use it as both the belief-space metric and path objective, enabling cost-informed sampling.

Environment-dependent localization has also been incorporated into planning via spatial localizability maps [ 5 ] and predicted photometric localization uncertainty [ 6 ] . Our work instead extracts localization information from map geometry and incorporates it directly into the belief dynamics and W 2 W_{2} objective for sampling-based planning in digital twins.

2026-10-02.title: Training-Free Diffusion Planning with Analytical Local Scores
2026-10-02.authors: Michael Y. Fatemi , Jinhao Liang , Ferdinando Fioretto
2026-10-02.comment: preprint - under review
2026-10-02.abstract:
Motion planning requires trajectories that are smooth, goal-directed, and collision-free in environments with complex geometric constraints. Recent diffusion-based planners have shown that trajectory generation can be cast as iterative denoising, which has opened the doors to learning-based approaches that can handle multi-modal trajectory distributions and refine entire trajectories.
However, such planners require training on large collections of feasible trajectories, rendering them map-specific, and difficult to deploy when high-quality demonstrations are unavailable. This paper introduces a training-free diffusion-based motion planner that replaces learned global trajectory scores with analytical local scores derived from obstacle, smoothness, velocity, and inter-agent feasibility terms. The proposed idea relies on a key observation: the trajectory score can be approximated from local interactions between neighboring waypoints and nearby constraints. This structure exploitation yields a decomposed denoising procedure that retains the optimization structure of classical optimization methods while inheriting the iterative refinement behavior of diffusion models. Experiments on a large collection of complex environments on multi-agent planning tasks show that the proposed analytical score produces smooth and feasible trajectories within very limited computational costs, for example in generating feasible paths for 300 agents in environments with 100 obstacles in under 6 seconds, while avoiding the data requirements of learned diffusion planners.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Motion planning is a fundamental problem in robotics and autonomous systems, where the goal is to compute trajectories that move a system from an initial state to a target state while avoiding collisions with obstacles ( LaValle, 2006 ) . In multi-agent settings, this problem becomes substantially more challenging: each robot must satisfy its own motion and safety constraints while also avoiding time-dependent collisions with other agents ( Sharon et al., 2015 ; Ma et al., 2018 ) . The spatio-temporal coupling and nonlinearity of these constraints make multi-agent path planning difficult to solve efficiently, especially as the number of agents and obstacles increases ( Liang et al., 2025 ) .

Sampling-based planners provide strong completeness properties under suitable assumptions and have been widely used for high-dimensional planning problems. However, they often produce paths in a coarse configuration space that require additional smoothing and can become inefficient in narrow passages or crawded spaces ( Kuffner and LaValle, 2000 ; LaValle, 2006 ) .
Optimization-based planners instead formulate motion planning as continuous trajectory optimization, making it possible to incorporate obstacle avoidance, smoothness, and kinematic constraints directly into the objective or feasible set ( Kalakrishnan et al., 2011 ; Mukadam et al., 2018b ) . However, these methods are often sensitive to initialization and can become expensive in multi-agent settings because collision constraints couple many agents across time.
More recently, diffusion models have shown promising results for motion planning by casting trajectory generation as an iterative denoising process that refines noise into trajectories ( Liang et al., 2026a ; Shaoul et al., 2025 ) . This perspective is attractive because diffusion models refine entire trajectories rather than committing to one waypoint at a time, and can represent multimodal distributions over possible plans ( Carvalho et al., 2023 ) . The key challenge, however, is that existing diffusion planners require learning a neural score model over high-dimensional trajectory distributions. This makes them expensive to train, dependent on large collections of feasible demonstrations, and often map- or distribution-specific. Moreover, learned diffusion planners may still fail to enforce safety constraints, a critical limitation for robotic planning ( Liang et al., 2025 ) . Projection-based refinement can improve constraint satisfaction, but it introduces additional computational cost ( Liang et al., 2026a ; Liang et al., 2025 ) .

To address these challenges, this paper develops a training-free diffusion-based planner with fully analytical local scores. The key idea is based on the observation that trajectory refinement has a strong locality of influence ( Pan et al., 2012 ) . Although the exact score of a full trajectory distribution can be globally coupled, the update of an individual waypoint is dominated by local temporal and spatial interactions: neighboring waypoints determine smoothness and velocity consistency, nearby obstacles determine collision avoidance, and nearby agents at the same time determine inter-robot separation ( Mukadam et al., 2018a ; Zucker et al., 2013 ) , as illustrated in Figure 1 (b).
Motivated by this structure, we introduce a decomposed local score formulation that constructs an analytical score surrogate directly from the planning constraints, rather than learning a neural approximation to the score of a high-dimensional distribution over complete trajectories. The resulting planner starts from a coarse trajectory initialization with fixed endpoints (Figure 1 (a)) and repeatedly applies analytical denoising updates under a decreasing noise schedule (Figure 1 (c)). Because each update depends only on local trajectory neighborhoods, nearby obstacles, and nearby agents, the method avoids dataset collection and neural-network training while remaining scalable to large multi-agent scenes. Contributions. The paper makes the following contributions: (1) It introduces a training-free diffusion planning framework that replaces learned global trajectory scores with analytical score surrogates derived from the structure of the motion planning problem. (2) It develops a decomposed local score formulation in which each waypoint is refined using smoothness, obstacle-avoidance, velocity-feasibility, and inter-agent collision-avoidance terms. (3) It demonstrates across multi-agent path planning benchmarks that the proposed planner achieves high feasibility and computational efficiency, obtaining high success on standard test configurations and scaling to scenes with 300 300 agents and 100 100 obstacles in just a few seconds.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Multi-agent path planning has a long history in robotics, with early methods largely built around sampling-based and optimization-based approaches. Sampling-based planners , approximate the feasible configuration space by drawing samples and connecting them through local steering procedures ( Kavraki et al., 1996 ; Kuffner and LaValle, 2000 ; LaValle, 2006 ) . These can scale to high-dimensional spaces better than exhaustive search methods, however, they often produce piecewise or fragmented paths that require post-processing, and their performance can degrade in narrow passages or settings where continuous kinodynamic constraints must be enforced along the entire trajectory.
A complementary line of work formulates motion planning as trajectory optimization problems ( Augugliaro et al., 2012 ; Park et al., 2020 ; Mellinger et al., 2012 ) . This gives these methods a direct mechanism for incorporating feasibility requirements, but the resulting optimization problems become increasingly difficult in multi-agent settings, where collision constraints couple agents across both space and time. To improve computational tractability, several optimization-based planners replace hard feasibility constraints with differentiable costs or penalty terms ( Ratliff et al., 2009 ; Kalakrishnan et al., 2011 ; Mukadam et al., 2018b ) , but they are often sensitive to initialization and can struggle in environments with many obstacles or agents. In contrast, our method formulates planning as an iterative denoising process driven by analytical local scores, avoiding dense state-space exploration while also avoiding repeated global trajectory optimization. Score-based Generative Models for Motion Planning .
Recent advancements in generative models offer have opened new avenues for solving motion planning problems by treating feasible trajectories as samples from a distribution and generating them through iterative denoising ( Song et al., 2020 ) . Diffusion planners are attractive because they refine whole trajectories at once and can represent multimodal plans in dense environments ( Carvalho et al., 2023 ; Shaoul et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) . However, they typically require learning a neural score over high-dimensional trajectory distributions, which depends on large collections of feasible demonstrations and does not guarantee constraint satisfaction. To improve feasibility, recent work has added gradient-based guidance during sampling, control barrier and Lyapunov functions, or projection-based refinement after denoising ( Carvalho et al., 2023 ; Mizuta and Leung, 2024 ; Shaoul et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2026a ; Liang et al., 2025 ; Christopher et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2026b ) . These Both retain learned generative models; TFDP constructs its refinement field directly from smoothness and feasibility factors.

The method proposed in this work, instead, replaces the learned global score with analytical local score components derived directly from smoothness, velocity, obstacle-avoidance, and collision constraints. This yields a training-free planner that preserves the iterative refinement behavior of diffusion models while making denoising updates fast and tied to the geometry of the environment.

2026-10-02.title: TouchTherm: Building Multimodal Digital Twins of Objects for Tactile and Thermal Rendering
2026-10-02.authors: Yitao Zhang (1), Hong Ying (1), Haoran Guo (1), Xiaoying Zhou (1), Guanyu Chen (1), Chenxi Xiao (1) ((1) ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, China)
2026-10-02.comment: . Project webpage: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract: Robotic simulation and virtual reality increasingly require object assets that capture not only visual geometry, but also the physical cues underlying tactile and thermal interaction. However, existing 3D datasets and reconstruction methods primarily represent object-scale geometry and visual appearance, overlooking the microscale surface structure needed for high-fidelity haptic rendering and the transient temperature dynamics required for temperature-aware interaction. We present TouchTherm , a framework for constructing simulation-ready visuo-tactile-thermal object assets from real-world objects. For visual and tactile reconstruction, we combine a high-fidelity handheld structured-light scanner with multiview normal maps obtained from photometric stereo. The normal maps are registered to the scanned geometry and transformed into tangent space to recover local micro-height fields, which are queried by an optical tactile renderer, while the coarse mesh handles collision detection. For thermal reconstruction, we capture synchronized multiview infrared videos of natural cooling following controlled heating and reconstruct a physics-regularized dynamic thermal field. These representations are integrated with the visual geometry into a unified, simulator-ready object asset. Experiments on 20 objects show that the reconstructed micro-height fields preserve dominant surface structures and recover higher-frequency details beyond the coarse geometry, while the dynamic thermal fields achieve held-out surface-temperature MAEs of 0.465 ∘ ​ C 0.465~^{\circ}\mathrm{C} and 0.592 ∘ ​ C 0.592~^{\circ}\mathrm{C} at 30 s and 45 s, respectively. The resulting tactile assets enable high-fidelity tactile simulation, including synthetic-to-real object recognition from tactile sensor observations, while a glove-based VR system demonstrates spatially and temporally varying thermal feedback. These results highlight the potential of TouchTherm for multimodal sensory simulation and temperature-aware virtual interaction.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Simulation has become a foundational tool for robot learning, but its effectiveness remains limited by the reality gap in contact-rich interactions [ 1 , 2 ] . One contributor to this gap is the limited range of sensory cues that virtual objects can provide during interaction. Existing digital assets generally supply object-scale geometry for visual rendering and force-based contact simulation, but often omit object-side representations of contact-scale tactile appearance and transient surface temperature [ 3 , 4 ] . These cues are relevant to robotic perception, human–robot interaction, virtual reality, and teleoperation [ 5 ] . We therefore seek to augment conventional geometric assets with spatially aligned tactile-rendering and thermal-feedback attributes. However, constructing such assets presents two primary challenges:

(1) Limitations of microgeometry acquisition and geometry representation tradeoffs. Existing acquisition methods provide accurate object-scale geometry and visual appearance [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] , but contact-relevant micro-structures such as shallow ridges, embossing, grooves, and anisotropic textures can be attenuated by finite scanning resolution and reconstruction artifacts despite their strong influence on optical tactile measurements [ 5 , 9 ] . Encoding such micro-relief directly as dense polygonal geometry would also increase storage and simulation costs [ 10 ] . We therefore seek to preserve contact-scale surface relief separately from object-scale collision geometry.

(2) Lack of object-level dynamic thermal field representations. Thermal cues contribute to material perception and can enhance thermal interaction in virtual and remote environments [ 11 , 12 ] . However, conventional visual assets do not encode how surface temperature varies across an object or evolves during heating and cooling [ 13 , 14 ] . These dynamics depend on object-specific material properties, geometry, and therefore cannot be represented only by a single temperature value or material label. A useful multimodal object asset should instead provide a spatially varying dynamic thermal field that supports surface-temperature queries over time.

To bridge these gaps, we introduce TouchTherm , a pipeline for constructing simulation-ready visuo-tactile-thermal object assets from real objects (Fig. 1 ). Visual object datasets primarily provide geometry and appearance [ 15 , 16 ] , whereas multisensory datasets typically contain partial, observation-only data [ 17 , 18 ] . In contrast, TouchTherm reconstructs spatially varying tactile fields and dynamic thermal fields at the object level. For tactile rendering, a coarse collision mesh is augmented with local tangent-space micro-height fields, preserving contact-scale relief without dense collision geometry. For thermal simulation, the reconstructed dynamic thermal field supports time-varying surface-temperature queries for robotic and virtual interactions.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows.

Multimodal object twins: We introduce a pipeline for constructing simulation-ready visuo-tactile-thermal object assets with registered visual geometry, tactile micro-height fields, and dynamic thermal fields.

Tactile rendering: We develop a contact-conditioned pipeline for rendering optical tactile observations from reconstructed micro-height fields.

Dynamic thermal field rendering: We reconstruct the field from multiview infrared cooling videos and identify effective thermal parameters for time-varying surface-temperature queries.

Validation and application: We validate the framework on 20 objects through tactile appearance, thermal prediction, and synthetic-to-real recognition, and demonstrate wearable thermal feedback in VR.

1. Multimodal object twins: We introduce a pipeline for constructing simulation-ready visuo-tactile-thermal object assets with registered visual geometry, tactile micro-height fields, and dynamic thermal fields.

2. Tactile rendering: We develop a contact-conditioned pipeline for rendering optical tactile observations from reconstructed micro-height fields.

3. Dynamic thermal field rendering: We reconstruct the field from multiview infrared cooling videos and identify effective thermal parameters for time-varying surface-temperature queries.

4. Validation and application: We validate the framework on 20 objects through tactile appearance, thermal prediction, and synthetic-to-real recognition, and demonstrate wearable thermal feedback in VR.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Multimodal Data Collection

Existing object reconstruction pipelines are largely vision-centric. Structured-light scanning and multi-view stereo recover metric geometry [ 6 ] , while NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting enable view synthesis and high-fidelity rendering [ 7 , 8 ] . However, these methods mainly capture object-scale geometry and appearance, overlooking the contact-scale surface relief and transient thermal properties needed for multimodal sensory rendering.

Non-visual sensing provides complementary physical information. Tactile sensors capture local surface geometry and contact responses [ 5 , 9 , 19 ] , while thermal sensors capture spatial temperature distributions and heat-transfer dynamics [ 13 ] . Yet, these measurements are typically localized observations rather than object-level representations registered to the object geometry. We therefore construct a unified representation that spatially registers visual, tactile, and thermal information as reusable simulation assets.

## II-B Datasets and Simulation Assets

Geometry and appearance assets. Existing robotics and embodied-AI datasets primarily provide object-scale geometry and visual appearance. YCB provides standardized physical objects with RGB-D scans [ 15 ] , Google Scanned Objects contains reconstructed household objects suitable for physics simulation [ 16 ] , and large-scale collections such as Objaverse and Digital Twin Catalog provide extensive 3D assets for learning and simulation [ 20 , 21 ] . These resources substantially expand the diversity of available digital objects, but generally lack spatially registered contact-scale tactile relief and dynamic surface-temperature information.

Multisensory object assets. ObjectFolder and its extensions associate objects with visual, acoustic, and tactile observations or implicit representations [ 17 , 18 , 22 ] , while X-Capture collects synchronized RGB-D, tactile, and impact-audio measurements of physical objects [ 23 ] . These datasets primarily support learning from existing multisensory observations. However, none combines registered tactile microgeometry with spatiotemporal thermal responses in a unified object asset.

Simulation-ready tactile and thermal assets. Tactile simulators synthesize contact observations from object geometry or height-field representations [ 3 , 10 , 24 , 4 ] . Coarse meshes are efficient for collision and contact simulation but may miss tactile-relevant surface details [ 25 , 6 ] , while dense geometric representations of microscale structures can be used for haptic rendering but increase simulation and rendering costs [ 10 , 4 ] . Beyond tactile-texture simulation, thermal simulation is less developed: prior work mainly uses thermal cues for material recognition or user feedback, rather than constructing object-level dynamic thermal fields. TouchTherm bridges these gaps by combining coarse collision geometry, registered tactile micro-height fields, and an object-specific dynamic thermal field within a shared object coordinate frame.

2026-10-02.title: Robot Learning on Discrete Surfaces: Theory and Applications
2026-10-02.authors: Matteo Dalle Vedove , Fares J. Abu-Dakka , Luigi Palopoli , Daniele Fontanelli , Matteo Saveriano
2026-10-02.abstract:
All the objects composing our world are enclosed within surfaces. Yet, most robot learning and motion generation frameworks treat surfaces as constraints ignoring their intrinsic geometry. This gap is acute for polyhedral meshes—the standard output of CAD and 3D reconstruction—whose discrete geometric structure remains unexploited.
In this paper, we propose a unified discrete Riemannian framework that enables robot learning directly on polyhedral surface meshes. Using discrete differential geometry, we define logarithmic and exponential maps, parallel transport, and ambient-space projections that remain well-defined across faces, edges, and vertices.
We instantiate the framework in three learning paradigms: ( i ) Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs), an improved exponential-map computation and a fixed-tangent-cone forcing-term encoding with parallel transport yield better cross-surface generalisation and stability over prior mesh-based approaches. ( ii ) Gaussian Process (GP), a geodesic-based kernel with practical admissibility control, enables regression at arbitrary mesh locations without smoothness assumptions. ( iii ) Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM), mesh-native operators improve generative quality over spectral baselines while reducing training time.
The framework is validated in simulation against state-of-the-art methods and demonstrated on two real-robot scenarios: generalising user-drawn trajectories across different surfaces and planning polishing motions on RGB-D-reconstructed surfaces.
2026-10-02.introduction:
In real applications, robots have to learn how to physically interact with objects and their environment. Sometimes this is required for manipulation purposes (e.g., grasping, pick-and-place, insertion), and sometimes for manufacturing operations (e.g., wiping, finishing, drawing, grinding, cutting, inspecting). A common trait of all these operations is that they are not executed in free space: in the vast majority of cases, they entail continuous contact with a surface enclosing the target object, where friction effects and geometric irregularities play a significant role. This raises a fundamental question: can a learning process for such tasks be truly effective if the geometric properties of the contact surface are ignored?
This issue has been often overlooked in the literature. Most existing Learning from Demonstration (LfD) and motion generation frameworks assume that skills evolve in flat Euclidean spaces and can be directly transferred to surfaces. When task complexity increases, surface constraints are typically recovered a posteriori through projection methods [ 1 ] , impedance control, or local parameterisation. While effective in structured and repeatable settings, treating surface geometry as an external constraint—rather than an intrinsic component of the learning process—often results in poor generalisation when the underlying structure changes.

In recent years, geometry-aware learning methods have been proposed for some classes of Riemannian manifolds, such as rotations or symmetric positive-definite matrices [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] , for which researchers have developed tools and methods to learn robot skills in non-Euclidean spaces. These formulations rely on differential operators—such as exponential and logarithmic maps, and parallel transport—that enable learning and control directly in the tangent space. However, extending these methods to surface-based skills remains an open issue, as surfaces encountered in real applications are rarely available as smooth manifolds. In most cases, surfaces are obtained from CAD models, perception pipelines, or 3D reconstruction tools [ 6 ] , for which the most natural representation is a 3D polyhedral mesh. Such discrete representations exhibit non-differentiable singularities at edges and vertices and do not admit the smooth structure assumed by classical Riemannian learning frameworks.

The absence of a smooth representation creates a significant gap between geometry-aware robot learning theory and its practical applicability to discrete manifolds. Although surfaces can be studied through the lens of differential geometry, constructing smooth representations for objects with arbitrary topology is generally intractable [ 7 ] . At the same time, naïve discretisation of smooth manifold operators on meshes either requires restrictive assumptions on surface smoothness or leads to inconsistencies and ill-defined behaviour at singularities. As a result, existing approaches often rely on local approximations, ad hoc embeddings, or spectral smoothness assumptions that limit robustness and hinder generalisation [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .

Paper Contribution. In this work, we take a more direct route to fill this gap by developing a discrete Riemannian framework for robot learning directly on polyhedral surface meshes. Starting from discrete differential geometry [ 11 ] , we construct
geometrically consistent approximations of key Riemannian
operators—including logarithmic and exponential maps, parallel
transport, geodesic distance, and ambient-space projections—that remain well-defined across faces, edges, and vertices of a mesh. Unlike prior mesh-based formulations [ 9 ] , which leave edge and vertex singularities unaddressed and rely on local approximations of the exponential map (valid only for small displacements), our operators are built on the straightest-geodesic principle [ 12 ] and are equipped with tangent-cone projections that handle all singular loci. Building on this geometric foundation, we show how three established learning frameworks can be naturally extended to discrete surfaces: ( i ) geometry-aware Dynamic Movement Primitives (DMPs) with a fixed-tangent-cone forcing-term encoding that replaces the local parameterisations used in [ 9 , 13 ] , ( ii ) geodesic-distance-based
Gaussian Processes (GPs) with controllable kernel admissibility, and ( iii ) Riemannian Flow Matching (RFM) with mesh-native operators replacing the spectral premetrics of [ 4 ] . These formulations yield motion and function representations that generalise across surfaces with different curvature, topology, and discretisation resolution, removing the need for smoothness or spectral assumptions.

To summarize, our main contributions are as follows:

A discrete Riemannian operator framework on polyhedral meshes—including tangent cones, straightest-geodesic exponential maps, and ambient-space projections—that explicitly handles edge and vertex singularities left unaddressed by existing mesh-based
methods [ 9 , 8 ] , enabling consistent geometric computations directly on discrete surface representations like polyhedral meshes.

A reformulation of geometry-aware DMPs on meshes that encodes forcing term in a fixed tangent cone and reconstructs it via parallel transport during execution, replacing the local, velocity-aligned parameterisation of [ 9 ] and eliminating the limit-cycle drift it induces on curved surfaces.

A geodesic-distance-based GP formulation on meshes that enables kernel regression at arbitrary surface locations—including face interiors—without smoothness or density requirements, overcoming the vertex-restriction and resolution-sensitivity of Laplace–Beltrami-based kernels [ 10 ] .

An extension of RFM to discrete polyhedral surfaces using geodesic premetrics, improving generative quality and reducing training time relative to the spectral baselines of [ 4 ] .

The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Section II analyses the state of the art. After a quick recall of foundation knowledge (Sec. III ), we present the unified approach for geometry-aware learning on discrete surfaces in Sec. IV . Section V provides simulation results and comparisons with the state-of-the-art, while Sec. VI provides experiments on a real robot highlighting the strengths of our approach. We conclude in Sec. VII with some limitations of the approach and final remarks.

1. A discrete Riemannian operator framework on polyhedral meshes—including tangent cones, straightest-geodesic exponential maps, and ambient-space projections—that explicitly handles edge and vertex singularities left unaddressed by existing mesh-based
methods [ 9 , 8 ] , enabling consistent geometric computations directly on discrete surface representations like polyhedral meshes.

2. A reformulation of geometry-aware DMPs on meshes that encodes forcing term in a fixed tangent cone and reconstructs it via parallel transport during execution, replacing the local, velocity-aligned parameterisation of [ 9 ] and eliminating the limit-cycle drift it induces on curved surfaces.

3. A geodesic-distance-based GP formulation on meshes that enables kernel regression at arbitrary surface locations—including face interiors—without smoothness or density requirements, overcoming the vertex-restriction and resolution-sensitivity of Laplace–Beltrami-based kernels [ 10 ] .

4. An extension of RFM to discrete polyhedral surfaces using geodesic premetrics, improving generative quality and reducing training time relative to the spectral baselines of [ 4 ] .
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related work

Learning from Demonstration (LfD) is a widely adopted paradigm for encoding human expertise and transferring it into robotic systems [ 14 ] . Classical LfD approaches—including DMPs [ 15 ] , Probabilistic MPs [ 16 ] , Kernelised MPs [ 17 ] , or Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) [ 18 ] —have been successfully applied to learn skills defined in Euclidean spaces. However, these methods do not account for the intrinsic geometry of constrained domains, and consequently fail when applied to data evolving on non-linear spaces such as rotations, stiffness matrices, or surfaces. To address this limitation, Lie-group-based formulations and Riemannian geometry have been introduced, with Lie-algebra approaches proving effective for specific spaces [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] , and Riemannian formulations offering greater flexibility by imposing fewer structural restrictions on the domain [ 23 , 3 , 2 , 4 , 24 ] . As a result, geometry-aware learning methods on smooth manifolds have been successfully applied to rotations, symmetric positive-definite matrices, and Grassmannian manifolds, where closed-form expressions of geometric operators are available. However, extending these results to surfaces remains largely an open problem, as real-world surface representations lack the fundamental structure that these methods rely on.

Several methods have been proposed to parameterise smooth surfaces using spline or subdivision representations [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] . While effective in computer graphics and geometric modelling, these approaches typically provide only local parameterisations or impose strong constraints on surface topology, restricting their applicability to robotic learning tasks involving complex or reconstructed environments. Working directly on polyhedral surface meshes has emerged as a promising alternative. Pantic et al. [ 8 ] proposed a mesh-manifold-based motion planning algorithm, framed as a Riemannian motion policy [ 24 ] , that uses isomorphic mappings to flatten meshes onto planar domains. However, this strategy requires restrictive topological assumptions and implicitly assumes sufficient mesh smoothness, avoiding the singularities arising at edges and vertices rather than addressing them.

The MeshDMP framework [ 9 ] represents the most direct prior reference for our approach, as it extends geometry-aware DMPs [ 23 ] to discrete surfaces. While MeshDMP removes topological restrictions on the mesh, it suffers from two important limitations. First, it relies on an approximate exponential map that is valid only under bounded face-angle conditions and does not explicitly address vertex singularities. Second, its forcing-term encoding is defined in a local, moving coordinate system, which can lead to instability and degraded generalisation, particularly for rhythmic motion patterns.

Our approach addresses both limitations of MeshDMP and, more broadly, establishes a geometrically consistent foundation for learning on discrete surfaces. By adopting a straightest-geodesic-based [ 12 ] exponential map and explicitly handling edge and vertex singularities, we obtain a more principled and consistent geometric formulation. Additionally, by encoding the forcing term in a fixed tangent space and transporting it during execution, we achieve substantially improved stability and transferability across surfaces, without relying on local parameterisations.

The Laplace-Beltrami operator (LBO) is the generalisation of the Laplacian to smooth Riemannian manifolds. Despite being initially developed for differentiable structures, its definition has been extended to discrete domains, including polyhedral meshes [ 28 , 29 ] . The LBO is a powerful tool for learning on surfaces, as its spectral decomposition can be used to approximate distances, kernels, and function spaces [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] . As an example, a pioneering work by Borovitskiy et al. [ 10 ] exploited the eigenfunction basis of the LBO to construct Matérn kernels on compact manifolds, effectively enabling Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) on meshes.

A key advantage of LBO-based methods is that they offer theoretical guarantees. However, they implicitly assume that the mesh is a sufficiently good approximation of a smooth surface and restrict function evaluation to mesh vertices. As a consequence, accurate GPR often requires dense meshes or additional interpolation steps, increasing computational cost and approximation error. Our approach, instead, relies directly on geodesic distance computation, enabling GPR at arbitrary surface locations—including points in the interior of faces—without any smoothness requirement. It is worth mentioning that geodesic-based kernels may lose positive definiteness beyond a critical lengthscale [ 33 ] . We address this limitation by treating it as a practical modelling trade-off and introduce criteria that ensure stable GPR in realistic scenarios.

Continuous Normalising Flows (CNFs) [ 34 ] are generative models that represent probability distributions by learning smooth, time-dependent vector fields whose integration defines a continuous transformation from a simple base distribution to a target data distribution. Despite their theoretical appeal and exact likelihood formulation, CNF-based architectures are computationally expensive to train, particularly in high-dimensional settings, and can suffer from numerical instability. Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) [ 35 , 36 ] addresses these limitations by replacing likelihood maximisation with a regression-based objective, substantially improving both training stability and efficiency.

Particularly relevant for geometric learning is the work by Chen et al. [ 4 ] , who extend CFM to Riemannian manifolds (RFM) by explicitly incorporating the geometric structure into the flow definition. By defining probability paths on manifolds, their approach trains a neural network to learn vector fields using exact differential operators on analytically defined manifolds (e.g., hyperspheres and tori), or approximate operators for discrete domains such as meshes, constructed via premetrics induced by the Laplace–Beltrami operator.

Our framework extends RFM to polyhedral meshes by introducing geometrically consistent operators tailored to mesh representations, enabling more stable and accurate vector field learning. As demonstrated in the evaluation below, the performance improvement is consistent across the tested baseline methods.

2026-10-02.title: Towards Physical Underwater Robotic Assistance for Scuba Diver Movement in Confined Spaces
2026-10-02.authors: Demetrious T. Kutzke , Junaed Sattar
2026-10-02.abstract:
Scuba divers are taught to control their depth to avoid rapid ascents and descents, which could result in serious injuries such as gas embolisms and barotrauma.
However, many underwater tasks necessitate lateral control, maintaining distance between subsea structures such as coral reefs, submerged drilling instrumentation, or unexploded ordnance.
In this work, we discuss a first-of-its-kind wearable robotic solution providing thruster-actuated directional guidance to a diver, as distinct from prior propulsive-assistance exoskeletons.
We introduce Robotic Assisted Diver Movement in Confined Spaces (RADMCS), a wearable robot that assists divers in maintaining a fixed distance from subsea structures by leveraging perception techniques in monocular depth estimation and force-feedback from submersible thrusters to provide haptic feedback. Its small and compact form factor creates a foundational platform that could be expanded to include more sophisticated control and navigation behaviors.
We present results from Institutional Review Board (IRB) in-water studies with eight human scuba diver participants on threshold sensitivity tests in both a closed-water swimming facility and ocean environments; distance-maintaining experiments in a closed-water facility; and form, fit, and function testing in the ocean.
We demonstrate that relatively low thrust values ( ≈ 10 \approx 10 % of maximum) allow robotic direction of a human’s movement using the physical sensation of the robot’s guidance.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Literature Review

This work draws from both wearable guidance in haptics, which is the study of navigation using physical perturbation, and physical underwater human-robot interaction.

Wearable Guidance and Assistive Technology .
Global positioning systems promise precise localization in areas where signals are present. Visual display of GPS navigation information is often inconvenient in instances where people must both navigate and maintain situational awareness of their environment, for example military personnel operating in war zones, visually impaired individuals navigating a busy city center, or individuals driving in unknown locations. An alternative to visual navigation displays are haptic feedback interfaces for wearable guidance.

Wearable guidance refers to a device affixed to the human body that provides some stimuli to assist the human in movement or navigation [ 7 ] . Often the type of stimulus used is vibrotactile [ 8 ] , where small motors or actuators can vibrate, effectively encoding messages about direction depending on body mounting positioning. Belt-style wearables arrange tactile actuators in an array, vibrating along specific positions to indicate direction [ 8 ] . Alternatively, in [ 9 ] the authors encode heading and distance in duration and rhythm of cell phone vibrations. Others have explored small handheld devices that provide auditory and vibrational feedback in response to receiver-transponder communication [ 10 , 11 ] .

Immersion protection and thermal layering of undergarments causes issues with vibrational feedback mechanisms, since waterproofing electrical components at the garment level to ensure user safety is critical and challenging. Movement assistance provided by wearable exoskeletons [ 12 ] , even under scuba diving drysuits, could be problematic since the power system and electrical components might fail if the suit floods. Although shape memory alloys (SMAs) and shape metal polymers (SMPs) have been shown to exhibit corrosion resistance and can be submersed for underwater applications [ 13 , 14 ] , to our knowledge, there have been no successful deployments of wearable SMAs or SMPs for submersible exoskeletons or rehabilitative robotics.

Some other locations discussed include limb mounting point wearables [ 15 ] , which assist in movement rehabilitation by providing muscular cues about object positioning and distance from the hand, for instance. Feedback is not limited to a single haptic modality. Some employ multiple, potentially interfering, haptic feedback sensors such as vibrotactile combined with compression for limb movement assistance [ 16 ] .

Exoskeletons Underwater .
Most of the work in physical underwater human-robot interaction has focused on exoskeleton style designs that tightly couple to the diver’s body or completely replace scuba diving equipment. These can be summarized as either “rigid,” in the sense that they use metal alloys for forming the external structure; or “soft,” that use cabling or flexible materials for the exoskeleton [ 17 ] .

Rigid Exoskeletons .
In [ 18 ] the authors introduce a conceptual rigid exoskeleton that assists in swimming for reducing metabolic energy consumption. Their suit uses a series of rotary actuators affixed to the diver’s legs to provide kicking assistance. They do not discuss the specific implementation of certain life support systems, such as breathing gas integration into the suit. The authors of [ 19 ] introduce a rigid, back-mounted swimming assistance robot that leverages hydraulic power to move the diver along. The back-mounted unit is sealed to prevent water intrusion. While they achieve good error with planned knee and hip trajectories, the unit occupies the volume of space where the diver’s tank would normally go, making it an unsuitable choice for movement assistance.

Other rigid exoskeletons include the atmospheric diving suit (ADS) and Deep Sea Expeditionary No Decompression (DSEND) suit [ 20 , 21 ] , which isolate the diver from the ambient water and pressure. These operate at depths of 300 300 – 600 600 m, without decompression obligations, since the suit maintains the diver at atmospheric pressure. These suits are not robotic, in that they do not have the ability to take action based on environmental observations alone. They are exposure protection suits that allow divers to achieve significant water depths, while maintaining human control via external actuation interfaces. These suits also cost significantly more than RADMCS, typically on the order of USD 100 100 K. By comparison, RADMCS costs USD 1 1 K assembled [ 22 ] .

Soft Exoskeletons .
The authors of [ 23 ] introduce a soft exoskeleton that uses a cable and pulley system for transferring rotational power to the swimmer’s ankle joints. However, the purpose of the exoskeleton is limited to rehabilitative swimming, since it occupies much of the diver’s lower limbs and upper torso. It is not clear how breathing gas would be provided to a scuba diver wearing their exoskeleton. The authors of [ 24 ] introduce a soft flexible exoskeleton that accommodates a diver’s regular buoyancy control vest and scuba tank, making it a more realistic alternative for actual scuba diving operations. They too use a cable system with two hip mounted actuator winches for cable movement. Their suit is meant for increasing swimming efficiency. Additional cabling and pulleys, while functional, often add additional pinch points or potential entanglement hazards for divers working in hazardous conditions. In contrast, the RADMCS robot integrates on a simple scuba breathing gas cylinder, which eliminates the issues with cable and pulley systems.

2026-10-02.title: ChunkVLA-AM: Parallel Action Chunking for Vision-Language-Action Robot Control in Additive Manufacturing
2026-10-02.authors: Zhugang Liu , Kaichuang Zhang , Jinman Zhang , Pu Sun , Martha Asare , Jose Hernandez , Maxim Ermolinsky , Efren Saenz , Qi Lu , Jinghao Yang
2026-10-02.abstract:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation, offering new opportunities for automation in additive manufacturing (AM).
However, deployment in AM remains challenging because adapting these models to unseen robot embodiments is costly, and performance can degrade under environment changes.
In this work, we present a framework for deploying OpenVLA-OFT on a FAIRINO FR3 robot in a fixed AM workcell.
A data pipeline converts monocular real-world demonstrations into OpenVLA-compatible TFDS/RLDS datasets to support adaptation to the FR3 embodiment. At runtime, each inference request predicts an eight-step chunk of 7-D actions. The FR3 executes each chunk open loop before capturing a new observation, providing closed-loop feedback between chunks. The system uses a cloud–edge architecture in which the FR3 client streams observations to a remote inference server through a FastAPI interface.
In 42 physical A-to-B object-transfer trials, evenly split between red and blue targets, the system succeeded in 39 (92.9%). All three failures occurred during final placement, when insufficient release-height control caused the object to topple. An illumination sweep identified a low-error luminance range of 85–125 on a 0–255 scale, with the lowest mean spatial error at 95.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Additive manufacturing (AM) has become an important production paradigm for rapid prototyping, customized medical devices, aerospace components, and high-value industrial parts [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Beyond deposition itself, practical AM workflows require inspection, part retrieval, build-plate handling, post-processing, and occasional intervention after process failures. These operations can expose human operators to process-specific risks: fused deposition modeling (FDM) may emit ultrafine particles and volatile organic compounds during heated thermoplastic extrusion [ 4 , 5 ] , while selective laser melting (SLM) involves fine metallic powders and particulate-matter hazards [ 6 ] . Robotic automation is therefore attractive for AM workcells because it can improve repeatability and reduce human exposure during inspection, transfer, and failure response. However, conventional rule-based robot programs are difficult to reuse across different printers, robot platforms, camera configurations, lighting conditions, object poses, and defect types such as FDM warping, inter-layer delamination, SLM porosity, lack-of-fusion holes, and cracks [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] .

Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a possible route toward more flexible AM robotic systems. By mapping visual observations and natural-language task descriptions directly to robot actions, VLA policies can represent tasks such as “retrieve the printed part,” “inspect the warped edge,” or “move the build-plate sample to the cooling area” without requiring a separate perception pipeline and a handcrafted state machine. Recent systems including RT-1, RT-2, Open X-Embodiment, and OpenVLA have shown that large-scale robot datasets, vision-language backbones, and action-token prediction can support general manipulation and transfer across tasks and embodiments [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . This capability is relevant to AM because the robot must interpret both the visual manufacturing context and the language instruction while generating manipulation commands within a constrained workspace.

Despite this potential, transferring a VLA model to an AM workcell is not a straightforward model-deployment problem. The first difficulty is migrating demonstrations and action interfaces across robot platforms. Robot datasets often differ in image resolution, observation structure, sampling rate, episode organization, coordinate frames, state definitions, and gripper conventions. Their action spaces may also represent joint positions, joint velocities, absolute Cartesian poses, or relative end-effector motion. Even when two platforms expose action vectors of the same dimension, the individual elements may have different physical meanings, units, ranges, or normalization rules. RLDS and TFDS provide a common structure for organizing episodic robot data, but they do not by themselves resolve these embodiment-specific differences [ 14 , 15 ] . As a result, transferring an existing VLA pipeline to a platform such as the FAIRINO FR3 requires more than renaming dataset fields. Coordinate transformations, action semantics, gripper commands, and normalization statistics must all be defined consistently before the model can be trained and safely deployed.

The second difficulty is robustness to changes between the demonstration environment and the deployed AM workcell. Lighting intensity, illumination direction, camera exposure, background clutter, camera viewpoint, and object pose may vary between data collection and execution. Reflective build plates, dark polymer parts, shadows cast by the robot, and changes in printer illumination can further alter the visual appearance of the part and the gripper. These variations are especially relevant when the model is adapted using demonstrations collected under a fixed camera and lighting configuration. Because a VLA policy predicts actions directly from image observations, it may associate the required motion with incidental visual features of the training environment instead of the task geometry. A policy that succeeds under the original lighting condition may therefore become less reliable when the workcell appearance changes, even though the physical task remains the same.

In this work, we present ChunkVLA-AM , a reproducible OpenVLA-OFT-based deployment pipeline for FR3-based AM post-print retrieval. To make embodiment adaptation explicit, we construct a conversion pipeline that transforms monocular FR3 demonstrations, Cartesian end-effector states, binary gripper commands, language instructions, and episode metadata into OpenVLA-compatible TFDS/RLDS episodes. The pipeline defines the coordinate frames, action semantics, and normalization procedure required by the target FR3 system, while LoRA is used to avoid full-parameter fine-tuning. For robot control, we adopt a horizon- H H action-chunk interface and use H = 8 H=8 in the reported physical tests, allowing the model to predict short-horizon motion sequences in a single request. The FR3 client then applies action denormalization, workspace clipping, unsafe-action rejection, and chunk-wise replanning after execution of the returned actions. This implementation focuses on the system-level adaptation and deployment required to use an action-chunked VLA policy in a fixed AM workcell and to evaluate its behavior under changes in lighting and object pose.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Models for Robot Control

Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged from the broader trend of connecting language, perception, and embodied decision making. Early generalist and language-conditioned robot systems, including Gato, SayCan, PaLM-E, and VIMA, showed that multimodal representations can support instruction following, planning, and interactive manipulation across diverse tasks [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . More recent VLA policies such as RT-1, RT-2, Open X-Embodiment, and OpenVLA further demonstrate that large-scale robot datasets and vision-language backbones can be used to predict robot actions directly from images and natural-language instructions [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . These studies provide the main methodological foundation for applying VLA models beyond household or tabletop manipulation. However, their evaluation settings are still largely centered on general manipulation benchmarks, leaving manufacturing-oriented scenarios comparatively underexplored.

## II-B Robotic Automation in Additive Manufacturing

Additive manufacturing (AM) has been widely studied as a flexible production technology for customized, lightweight, and high-value components [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Robotic systems have also been introduced into AM workflows for material handling, inspection, deposition assistance, post-processing, and large-scale or wire-arc manufacturing [ 20 ] . Compared with conventional automation, AM workcells pose distinctive perception and decision-making challenges because part geometry, surface appearance, thermal history, defect morphology, and process state can vary significantly across builds. Defects such as warping, delamination, porosity, lack of fusion, and cracking further require robots to reason over visual manufacturing evidence instead of simply replaying fixed trajectories [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . These characteristics make AM a natural application domain for VLA models: language can specify task intent, visual input can capture part and process context, and action prediction can support flexible intervention.

## II-C Challenges of Applying VLA Models to AM

Although VLA models are promising for AM, existing literature suggests two major barriers to practical use. The first is data and adaptation cost. AM tasks are weakly represented in large robot-learning datasets, while effective VLA adaptation requires demonstrations that align visual observations, language instructions, action labels, and episode structure in reusable formats such as TFDS/RLDS [ 14 , 15 ] . Full fine-tuning of large VLA models can be expensive and data-hungry, motivating parameter-efficient adaptation methods such as LoRA [ 21 ] . The second challenge is achieving temporally coherent motion. Single-step autoregressive prediction can accumulate covariate shift and produce open-loop drift during precise manipulation. Prior work on action chunking and horizon-based visuomotor policies shows that predicting multiple future actions as a structured sequence improves motion consistency [ 22 , 23 ] . In AM settings, such temporal coherence must be balanced against responsiveness and safety, because robot motions often occur near printed parts, build plates, tools, or process-sensitive regions. Therefore, the VLA–AM research gap is not only whether VLA models can represent AM tasks, but also how they can be adapted and executed with sufficient temporal stability for precise manufacturing intervention.
