# II Related Work

## II-A Spacecraft Planning, Language Grounding, and Trajectory Optimization

Classical spacecraft autonomy separates high-level mission planning from guidance, navigation, and control.
Onboard systems have demonstrated activity planning, scheduling, execution monitoring, and replanning from predefined goals [ 9 , 10 ] .
Autonomous decision-making based on discrete logic has also been developed for formation flying and rendezvous and proximity operations [ 5 , 11 , 12 ] .
In these systems, expert-defined activity models and transition logic specify high-level tasking and behavior sequencing, while waypoint and maneuver generation is generally handled by separate modules.

Trajectory optimization provides a principled mechanism for generating a state-control trajectory that enforces the underlying dynamics, waypoint conditions, and operational constraints [ 13 , 14 ] .
Learning-based methods can improve its numerical performance through warm-starting or approximation [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] .
These methods generally assume that the maneuver structure, waypoints, objectives, and constraints have already been specified based on the desired high-level spacecraft behaviors.

Recent work has explored the use of semantic reasoning for spacecraft operations [ 19 , 8 , 20 ] .
Parallel research translates natural-language safety requirements into mathematical representations, including explicit constraints and signal temporal logic formulas [ 21 , 22 ] .
Prior work by the authors learned language-conditioned trajectory warm starts from paired command–trajectory data and refined them through sequential convex programming (SCP) [ 23 ] .

Collectively, these approaches provide complementary capabilities for high-level spacecraft autonomy and continuous trajectory generation with potential for connection with semantics.
Their interface nevertheless remains dependent on expert-specified maneuver definitions or complete trajectory-level representations, leaving no structured mechanism for preserving partial operator intent, resolving unspecified mission decisions, and verifying the resulting behavior sequence under orbital dynamics and safety constraints, in a scalable manner.

## II-B Learning-Guided Task and Motion Planning

TAMP integrates discrete task-level decision-making with continuous motion generation [ 24 ] .
Classical TAMP evaluates symbolic choices through motion-level sampling or optimization [ 25 , 26 ] , whereas learning-guided approaches leverage data to prioritize task decisions, propose continuous parameters, or filter infeasible candidates [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] .
These methods provide a general framework for coupling behavior selection with trajectory generation.

Language-conditioned planning in robotics provides a complementary perspective by enabling high-level instructions to guide planning and control.
Existing approaches combine the reasoning capabilities of language models with learned affordances, executable programs, or external planners [ 3 , 30 , 31 ] .
Some use LLM to propose or prioritize skill-level plans under feasibility models [ 32 ] , while others translate instructions into a structured formal task specifications used by downstream planners [ 33 , 34 ] .

Collectively, these methods demonstrate how language-level reasoning can be connected to executable motion through structured planning abstractions.
However, their formulations generally seek a sufficiently specified symbolic problem or skill sequence and do not address the spacecraft-specific need to preserve operator underspecification while completing behavior, timing, and waypoint decisions within an admissible decision space for RPO missions.

Taken together, prior work in spacecraft mission planning, trajectory optimization, language grounding, and robotic TAMP provides complementary pieces towards language-driven spacecraft operations.
The proposed framework unifies these directions by representing language as a partial mission specification and systematically completing its unspecified decisions through a graph of admissible spacecraft behaviors, trajectory-aware evaluation, and final trajectory optimization.

2026-10-02.title: WBAG: A Whole-Body and Attached-Geometry Safety Framework for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation
2026-10-02.authors: Samuel Zhen , Siwon Jo , Yanze Zhang , Wenhao Luo
2026-10-02.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated impressive capabilities in generalizable robotic manipulation, but their deployment in the real world remains challenging due to potential collisions involving different parts of the robot, manipulated objects, and the surrounding environment. Existing inference-time VLA safety frameworks typically rely on simplified end-effector-centered representations that do not explicitly model the full articulated robot and attached-object geometry. In this paper, we present WBAG, a safety framework that models the robot’s whole-body and grasp-dependent attached geometry. WBAG constructs a grasp-conditioned safe set that adapts the protected geometry as objects are grasped, then converts this evolving geometry into differentiable CBF constraints that minimally modify the VLA’s native six-dimensional operational-space action for collision avoidance across robot, scene, and attached geometry. On the SafeLIBERO benchmark, a variant of LIBERO augmented with obstacles for safety evaluation, WBAG achieves the best overall safety and safe task success among the evaluated methods under a scene-level safety evaluator that monitors all eligible non-task objects, reaching 97.38% aggregate Scene Safety and 59.38% Safe Success.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language
instructions directly to robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks [ 1 ] , but their task-level generalization does not provide an explicit
geometric safety model to consistently safeguard robot motions. In cluttered environments, a VLA action may move the
end effector toward the target while causing an upstream link, wrist, gripper,
or manipulated object to collide. The relevant collision geometry spans the
articulated robot and changes when the robot grasps an object. Recent benchmark
evaluations further show that task completion alone can obscure physical safety
violations during manipulation [ 2 , 3 ] .

Control-theoretic safety methods, particularly control barrier functions (CBFs),
provide a principled mechanism for enforcing collision avoidance during robotic
control [ 4 ] . CBFs constrain control inputs to maintain forward invariance of a prescribed
safe set, but their effectiveness depends on how that set is represented. For
geometric collision avoidance, the safety function must capture separation
between the protected robot geometry and surrounding obstacles. The geometric
representation therefore determines which collision modes can be enforced.

Recent work on safety-critical control with VLA-based policies [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] spans both training-time and inference-time interventions.
SafeVLA [ 5 ] incorporates safety constraints during policy optimization through
constrained reinforcement learning. At inference time, AEGIS [ 6 ] combines perception-derived geometric information with CBF constraints to filter
a pretrained VLA, while KNOWS [ 7 ] combines VLA-based target
identification with online obstacle tracking. Other methods enforce safety directly within flow-matching action generation.
Recent work in [ 8 ] apply predictive
trajectory-level barrier constraints through minimum-norm corrections during
iterative denoising, while [ 9 ] modify the
flow-matching dynamics using an aggregate CBF over the generated action chunk.
However, existing
inference-time safety frameworks
typically enforce collision avoidance using simplified end-effector-centered
geometry [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Such end-effector-centered representations do
not explicitly model the full articulated robot or the rigid geometry of an
attached object: the end effector may remain
separated while an upstream link, wrist, or attached geometry collides with an
obstacle.

Geometric methods such as Bernstein-polynomial signed distance fields (BP-SDFs) [ 10 ] provide smooth, differentiable representations of object geometry, enabling efficient distance queries and gradients that are well suited for optimization-based control. For articulated robots, BP-SDFs can represent individual links, whose poses are determined by forward kinematics as a function of robot configuration. Recent work [ 11 ] employs BP-SDFs to construct geometry-aware CBFs from the minimum distance between robot and obstacle geometries and derive corresponding safety constraints on the robot control input. Applying such geometric safety constraints to VLA manipulation requires connecting perception, manipulation state, and the policy’s native action interface. In our setting, scene and target geometry are reconstructed from RGB-D observations rather than assumed known, while the protected geometry changes when the target becomes rigidly attached after grasping. At the same time, the resulting link- and object-level clearances are functions of robot configuration, whereas the frozen VLA produces six-dimensional operational-space actions. These factors must therefore be coupled so that perception-derived, grasp-conditioned geometric constraints can be enforced directly on the VLA action without retraining the VLA or modifying the operational-space controller.

In this paper, we introduce WBAG , a whole-body and attached-geometry safety framework for pretrained VLA policies. WBAG reconstructs scene and target geometry from RGB-D observations and constructs a grasp-conditioned safe set : before grasping, it protects the articulated robot; after grasping, the protected set expands to include the rigidly attached object. We represent robot, scene, and attached geometry with differentiable BP-SDFs and enforce the resulting CBF constraints directly on the VLA’s native six-dimensional operational-space action. WBAG minimally modifies the policy output while accounting for collisions involving the whole robot and attached geometry, without retraining the underlying VLA or modifying the operational-space controller. We evaluate WBAG on SafeLIBERO using a scene-level safety evaluator that monitors all eligible non-task scene objects. WBAG achieves the highest aggregate Scene Safety and Safe Success among the evaluated configurations, reaching 97.38 % 97.38\% and 59.38 % 59.38\% , respectively.
Our main contributions are summarized as the following:

We formulate a grasp-conditioned geometric CBF over articulated robot links and dynamically attached geometry, with the protected set adapting across pre- and post-grasp manipulation.

We develop WBAG , a novel perception-to-control safety framework that reconstructs scene and target geometry from visual observations, maintains grasp-conditioned protected geometry, and enforces the resulting constraints directly on the VLA’s native operational-space action without retraining the VLA or modifying the operational-space controller used to execute its actions.

We conduct a controlled SafeLIBERO evaluation with scene-level safety measurement that isolates the effects of scene coverage, whole-body protection, and attached-geometry modeling on safe VLA manipulation.

1. We formulate a grasp-conditioned geometric CBF over articulated robot links and dynamically attached geometry, with the protected set adapting across pre- and post-grasp manipulation.

2. We develop WBAG , a novel perception-to-control safety framework that reconstructs scene and target geometry from visual observations, maintains grasp-conditioned protected geometry, and enforces the resulting constraints directly on the VLA’s native operational-space action without retraining the VLA or modifying the operational-space controller used to execute its actions.

3. We conduct a controlled SafeLIBERO evaluation with scene-level safety measurement that isolates the effects of scene coverage, whole-body protection, and attached-geometry modeling on safe VLA manipulation.

2026-10-02.title: quARtet Marker: A 3D-Printable Multi-Tag Fiducial for Robust Near-Frontal Pose Estimation
2026-10-02.authors: Araki Wakiuchi , Hikaru Sasaki , Takamitsu Matsubara
2026-10-02.abstract: Robotic manipulation of labware is difficult when transparent or reflective objects must be identified and localized. Coded planar fiducials are a practical retrofit: easy to print, they leave the marked face flat and graspable. Yet a single planar tag is least reliable in near-frontal views, where perspective cues fade. Non-planar geometries restore those cues but intrude on the flat face that a parallel-jaw gripper must contact. Our idea is to tilt multiple tags within one compact footprint, so that each tag is seen at a non-frontal angle even when the marker faces the camera. We propose the quARtet marker, a 3D-printable fiducial embodying this idea: all detected corners of its four tilted AprilTags enter one Perspective-n-Point solve, and a shared configuration defines the fabricated geometry and the detector model. Because tilting consumes flat area, its three layouts trade pose-estimation consistency against graspability. In robot-referenced, same-setup fixed-camera experiments, all three layouts reduced the mean frontal orientation error from 2.18 ​ ° 2.18\tcdegree for a single planar tag to 0.24 0.24 – 0.47 ​ ° 0.47\tcdegree and the root-mean-square position error from 1.50 1.50 to 0.17 0.17 – 0.20 0.20 mm. A robot-mounted-camera pose-hold test confirmed this separation under closed-loop visual feedback. In swing-down trials under identical conditions, the two layouts with flat contact strips retained the object with about 2 2 mm of in-grasp slip, whereas the layout without flat strips slipped by roughly 100 100 mm. For the tested conditions, the results support a rule: the layout without flat strips when pose-estimation consistency dominates, a layout with flat strips when the marked face must remain graspable.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Laboratory automation can raise experimental throughput and keep experiments running for days with little human intervention Burger et al. (2020) ; Szymanski et al. (2023) , and it can spare people contact with hazardous materials Burger et al. (2020) , but it also places robots in visually difficult workspaces: transparent vessels challenge appearance and depth sensing Sajjan et al. (2020) ; Fang et al. (2022) , reflective or weakly textured tools provide few stable visual features, and visually identical containers may hold different materials. To manipulate such labware, a robot must know both which object is present and its six-degree-of-freedom (6-DOF) pose: its position and orientation. Manually taught positions and pre-calibrated placements can sidestep part of this perception problem, but the setup and re-teaching effort they demand works against the plug-and-play integration sought when existing laboratories are automated Wolf et al. (2023) . Printed coded fiducials, reference markers that a camera can both identify and localize, are therefore an attractive retrofit. Printed code tags already label chemical containers in laboratories Shukran et al. (2017) , marker tracking has been used to automate sensor registration in robot workspaces Gong et al. (2019) , and an ordinary camera decodes object identity and estimates pose from the same observation Romero-Ramirez et al. (2018) ; Wan et al. (2017) ; Rekimoto and Ayatsuka (2000) . The markers are also inexpensive to print and to replace after contamination. Figure 1 illustrates this application context and the four practical demands considered in this work (the marker proposed to meet them is introduced in Section 3 , Fig. 2 ). It is not a depiction of the validation experiments.

The remaining problem is the physical and geometric design of the marker itself. A single square tag estimates orientation from the perspective distortion of its outline. Near a frontal view that distortion becomes weak: a tag tilted slightly toward the camera projects to nearly the same image as one tilted equally away, so pixel-level image errors translate into large orientation changes Tanaka et al. (2012) ; Tanaka et al. (2014) , and the reported pose can flip between these two near-mirror solutions Schweighofer and Pinz (2006) ; Tanaka et al. (2014) . This near-frontal viewpoint matters in practice because a robot-mounted camera often approaches a target approximately along the marker normal. It is also the view in which a planar tag is easiest to detect and decode, because its image is largest and least foreshortened, so the pose is least reliable exactly where detection is most reliable. Adding more coplanar tags does not remove the ambiguity, because the enlarged array is still a single plane seen head-on, and enlarging a planar board is unattractive for small labware. Non-coplanar, multi-face marker geometries are an effective remedy Mateos (2020) ; García-Ruiz et al. (2023) , as discussed further in Section 2 . However, they raise structure above the marked face, and that face may be the only one available to a parallel-jaw gripper. Improving pose estimation through geometry can therefore cost exactly the flat surface that grasping requires.

A laboratory fiducial must therefore do more than estimate pose accurately: it must remain compatible with manipulation. When the marked face doubles as the gripper’s contact face, pose-estimation performance and graspability have to be designed together, alongside coded identification and low-cost fabrication paired with a detector model that matches the printed geometry. These are the four linked demands of Fig. 1 (c)–(f) . The problem addressed in this paper is thus to find a marker geometry that improves near-frontal pose estimation while preserving flat regions that a gripper can contact.

Our idea is to tilt multiple tags within one compact footprint. Even when the marker as a whole is viewed frontally, each tag is then observed at a non-frontal angle and supplies the perspective cues that a single planar tag loses near that view. At the same time, how the tags are tilted determines which flat regions of the face survive, so the tilt pattern itself becomes a design parameter that balances pose estimation against graspability.

Based on this insight, we propose the quARtet marker, a family of compact 3D-printable multi-tag fiducials. Four AprilTags are tilted within one square footprint, and all reliably detected corners are combined in a single Perspective-n-Point (PnP) solve, which recovers the marker pose from the correspondences between known 3D points and their 2D image projections Lepetit et al. (2009) and is computed with OpenCV Bradski (2000) . Three layouts use the same detection principle but expose different flat regions for gripper contact, and a shared configuration drives both marker fabrication and reconstruction of the detector-side 3D corner coordinates, avoiding manual measurement of inter-tag geometry. The experiments compare the three layouts and a single-tag control in near-frontal pose estimation and in a physical grasp-retention test, making the pose-estimation–graspability trade-off of the layouts explicit.

Throughout this paper, pose estimation is the umbrella term for estimating both orientation and position. The experiments report these two error components separately. The terminology does not denote two different estimation tasks.

The main contributions are:

A compact, configuration-driven multi-tag marker system. Four tilted tags retain non-coplanar perspective cues within the footprint of one planar tag and are solved jointly. One parameter file defines both the editable computer-aided design (CAD) model and the detector geometry, and the toolchain and data are publicly available.

A controlled evaluation of the consistency–graspability trade-off. Fixed-camera measurements under a common robot-referenced protocol and an independently re-grasped swing-down test separate the benefits and costs of the three layouts (Section 3 ) relative to the single-tag control. The layout whose four tags lean outward from a raised center is the most consistent across the tested viewpoints, whereas the two layouts whose tags tilt about their base edges keep flat contact strips for the gripper.

A closed-loop characterization under visual feedback. A robot-mounted-camera pose-hold test with five runs per marker type shows that the near-frontal separation persists under visual feedback: every quARtet layout holds the target with a significantly smaller orientation error and step-to-step reorientation than the single-tag control.

Section 2 positions the work relative to geometric and detection-side alternatives. Section 3 describes the marker and shared-parameter pipeline. Section 4 evaluates pose estimation and graspability against two research questions. Sections 5 and 6 interpret the trade-off, limitations, and practical layout choice.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Multi-Tag and 3D Marker Geometries

To overcome the limited geometric information of a single planar tag, several studies have enriched marker geometry with multi-tag and three-dimensional configurations. Multi-tag targets and marker maps have been used to obtain stronger geometric constraints for camera calibration Richardson et al. (2013) and for localization and visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) Wang et al. (2023) , while flexible tag layouts extend tag shape and data density beyond the standard square Krogius et al. (2019) . ChArUco boards combine marker coding with checkerboard geometry to support accurate calibration and surface estimation Hu et al. (2019) ; Puggelli et al. (2020) ; An et al. (2018) ; Lin et al. (2022) . However, the tags on any one such board remain coplanar, so from a single view the near-frontal ambiguity persists at the board level and can be mitigated only by enlarging the footprint, which small labware cannot afford. The quARtet marker instead obtains non-coplanar corner geometry within a single compact ( 35 35 mm) footprint.

Beyond planar arrays, multi-face and object-specific fiducials extend this idea to three-dimensional surfaces or custom-shaped substrates, including dynamic three-dimensional tag arrangements for swarm robotics in highly reflective environments Mateos (2020) , pen-shaped 6-DOF marker tools Le et al. (2022) , cylinder-specific designs based on projective invariants Wang et al. (2024) , and other application-tailored fiducial objects García-Ruiz et al. (2023) . These works show that spreading tags in space improves pose estimation across viewpoints.

Although effective, prior 3D and multi-tag designs typically pay a price in fabrication complexity, physical bulk, or application specificity. Volumetric and object-tailored markers often demand dedicated assembly or per-object redesign, which limits their reuse across heterogeneous laboratory targets and replaceable fixtures. The quARtet marker is intended to retain the geometric benefits of multi-tag/3D fiducials while remaining a compact, low-profile plate printable on standard fused-deposition-modeling (FDM) printers. Tiling four tilted AprilTags on a single compact plate-like base and exposing the geometry through a shared parameter set allows the marker geometry to be regenerated for different sizes and layouts without re-measuring inter-tag relationships, lowering the practical cost of adopting a multi-tag design.

## 2.2 Augmented Detection Process

A complementary line of work strengthens the detection process itself rather than the marker geometry, aiming to recover more reliable poses from challenging observations. On the algorithmic side, successive AprilTag systems have improved detection robustness and efficiency for the standard single planar tag Olson (2011) ; Wang and Olson (2016) , ArUco-based detectors have been accelerated for real-time use Romero-Ramirez et al. (2018) , and learning-based pipelines such as Deep ChArUco recover marker corners under low light and severe motion blur Hu et al. (2019) . On the hardware side, optical markers with lenticular (lens-array) or moiré (interference-pattern) structures provide increased sensitivity to tilt at the cost of specialized fabrication Tanaka et al. (2012) ; Tanaka et al. (2014) ; Tanaka et al. (2015) , while small fiducials combined with dynamic camera-parameter control such as zoom and focus can achieve high accuracy under demanding viewing conditions Haraguchi and Miyahara (2023) .

Effective as they are, these augmented detection schemes typically depend on specialized optical materials, tightly tuned acquisition control, or learned models that must be retrained for new targets. The quARtet system instead augments detection at a purely geometric level: corner correspondences from all reliably visible tags are pooled into a single PnP solve over the shared marker geometry. Because the same parameter set defines the fabricated geometry and the detection-side 3D corner coordinates, this joint solve operates with standard 2D camera input, requires no per-marker measurement of inter-tag geometry and no retraining, and falls back, by design, to the remaining tags when some become occluded or unreliable (Section 3.3 ).

2026-10-02.title: Online Planning for Sparse Ground Target Search from a High-Altitude UAV under Partial Observability
2026-10-02.authors: Ashik E Rasul , Hyung-Jin Yoon
2026-10-02.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) searching for ground targets from a high altitude face a unique challenge, particularly when the target is already within the field of view but effectively unobservable because of its small apparent scale. Standard object detectors often underperform in such scenarios because of resolution downscaling and limited context. In contrast, active object search frameworks address this challenge by directing the agent to a suitable pose to gather richer visual information. However, flight regulations in urban airspace often restrict such physical movements for UAVs. As an alternative active sensing approach, the UAV can leverage the pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) mechanism of the onboard camera to dynamically adjust its field of view and sequentially gather enhanced visual information from specific regions of interest. Once the candidate locations of the target are identified, it can deploy more expensive object detection schemes, such as an ensemble of multiple models, to get better reasoning at a fixed scale. In this work, we formulate the sequential exploration with PTZ operation as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which the agent maintains a belief state over the target’s true location. To solve the POMDP, we deploy partially observable Monte Carlo planning (POMCP), where we condition the sensing reliability on target object scale and deploy selective ensemble detection as an additional reasoning step.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Humans are particularly good at searching for relevant information in a cluttered environment through a spatial attention mechanism [ 1 , 2 ] . This capability allows us to detect small objects at a distance, even if they occupy a tiny area within our field of view (FOV). Emulating such adaptive perception capability is crucial for efficient object search and has been extensively studied in the computer vision community as human eye movement models [ 3 , 4 ] . However, these models assume that the object of interest is always present in the input image, that the image already contains sufficient features of the target object, and that the sensor has a high detection probability with negligible noise in the operating range.

In a real-world object search scenario, most images collected by a mobile robot may not contain the target object, the target object may be occluded or may not reveal sufficient features, and the detector itself may be noisy. There has been significant advancement in object search in indoor environments by the robotics community, where these challenges are handled by physically moving the agent to a suitable pose to gather enhanced visual information [ 5 , 6 ] . These works assume the observation uncertainty mostly arises from object occlusion or hidden features for the object’s relative pose, as the target object scale variation within the FOV is often negligible in indoor settings. For unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), searching for a sparse ground target from high altitude, such physical movement is not feasible due to flight regulations in urban airspace. Moreover, even if the target is visible within the FOV, it may be tiny, and the input image resolution may not be enough to reveal sufficient features. In this scenario, standard object detectors often struggle to produce reliable detections. Computer vision methods for tiny object detection also suffer in this case, as a higher-resolution version of the input image may not be available, and approaches such as slicing [ 7 ] , that attempts to enhance the size of the target by exhaustive slicing of the whole image with overlaps, or coarse-to-fine [ 8 ] detection, that runs a coarse detector to find the candidate regions and runs a fine detector on the candidate regions for finding the target, leads to significant resolution downscaling that produces uncalibrated confidence scores and a number of false positive detections. Though the detection accuracy can be further enhanced with more expensive ensemble methods [ 9 ] , which run inference with multiple models trained on a subset of data (bagging [ 10 ] ) or with random initialization [ 11 ] , they can still struggle under scale and resolution variation of the target image.

The UAV can leverage the pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) mechanism before capturing the images to selectively enhance the size, clarity, and position of the object of interest, while maintaining a fixed input resolution, as illustrated in Figure 1 . However, such selective enhancement can be expensive, and any exhaustive exploration may be limited by on-board computational resources and time-sensitive mission objectives. Conventional autonomous PTZ camera control follows a preloaded policy, often learned offline, that assumes complete environmental observability and focuses primarily on target tracking rather than ensuring detection reliability [ 12 , 13 ] . For the sparse target search scenario, these assumptions do not hold, as the UAV cannot access the full information about the environment simultaneously and can only receive noisy observations with variable uncertainty conditioned on the PTZ settings, environmental conditions, and the target’s relative pose. In other words, the environment is partially observable, and the UAV must maintain a belief state, which is an internal estimate of its surroundings, to effectively choose the next sequence of actions. At every time step, the UAV has to trade off between wide-scan exploration for quick area coverage to receive noisy observations and precise-scan exploration for slower area coverage to receive more reliable observations.

In this work, we formulate the sparse target search problem from a high altitude using camera PTZ functionality as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) [ 14 ] . In this setting, the control policy operates directly on the belief space to sequentially actuate the PTZ operation of the camera to optimize the long-term objective of finding the target with minimum steps. The belief gets updated as the UAV receives new observations. Unlike conventional approaches that assume complete knowledge of the environment (i.e., complete observability of the environment), assuming near-perfect sensors or fixed uncertainty across actions, we explicitly model the observation uncertainty conditioned on different object appearances within the FOV.
To solve the POMDP, we deploy Partially Observable Monte Carlo Planning (POMCP) [ 15 ] . To address the variation of the observation model in different deployment environments and UAV states, we formulate the detection reliability with a Beta-Bernoulli conjugate model that allows us to incorporate prior knowledge about the observation uncertainty as well as update the model iteratively as we gather more experiences from the deployment scenarios. Additionally, we selectively deploy an ensemble of DNNs at a fixed scale, conditioned on belief concentration, to improve prediction and enable successful target search.
Our proposed methodology is illustrated in Figure 2 .

To evaluate our approach, we use a simulation environment [ 16 ] built in Unreal Engine that models realistic aerial scenarios, including cluttered urban landscapes, varying altitudes, camera attributes (Field of view, focal length, and aperture control), and dynamic lighting. This environment enables thorough testing of the proposed framework, allowing us to study the effect of uncertainty, limited observability, and PTZ camera control against the baselines. Our key contributions are:

We formulate the PTZ camera operation, by a high-altitude UAV searching for a sparse ground target, as a POMDP.

We formulate the PTZ camera operation, by a high-altitude UAV searching for a sparse ground target, as a POMDP.

We formulate the observation model uncertainty as a Beta-Bernoulli conjugate model, conditioned on the object appearance, with a prior assignment.

We deploy POMCP to solve the POMDP that sequentially selects the informative actions for environmental exploration. Within the POMCP implementation, we integrate our defined observation model and selectively deploy ensemble detection to enhance reasoning when belief concentration is already high.

Finally, we validate our method in a photo-realistic simulation environment to show the confident discovery of the targets with significantly fewer steps, with minimal dependency on camera resolution, compared to traditional tiny-object detection methods.

2026-10-02.title: Divide-and-Remember: Recursive Action-Relevant Memory for Long-Horizon VLA Policies
2026-10-02.authors: Xuehui Yu , Eason Yu , Meiyi Wang , Haozhe Du , Stefano V. Albrecht , Harold Soh
2026-10-02.abstract:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models struggle on history-dependent manipulation tasks, where the current observation alone does not determine the action, and the policy needs a memory of the history.
Existing memory methods decide what to remember by design, for example, keeping frames with large pixel changes, and show inconsistent gains across tasks.
We view what to remember as an optimisation problem. From the POMDP formulation of imitation learning, we show that the optimal memory maximises the conditional mutual information I ⁡ ( a t ; m t ∣ o t ) I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) between the action and the memory given the current observation.
Intuitively, this means preserving the action-relevant information in the history that is not already contained in the current observation. Based on our analysis, we propose Divide-and-Remember (D&R), a recursive memory method that learns a memory function m t = ℳ ⁡ ( h t ) m_{t}=\mathcal{M}(h_{t}) and scales to long contexts while staying compute-light.
It involves two strategies: (1) the selection over the full history is divided recursively into subproblems of top- K K selection over 2 ​ K 2K tokens, so that fixed-size, lightweight selectors learned end-to-end support an unbounded history;
(2) all recursion blocks share one selector, which captures the selection rule common to every block and keeps the method efficient.
On RoboMME, a benchmark of 16 16 long-horizon manipulation tasks that require remembering when, where, what, and how to act, D&R achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate with consistent gains across all four suites under a budget of only 64 64 tokens; real-robot experiments show the same gain.
Code, checkpoints and more results are at dnr-memory.github.io .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) policies are visuomotor policies trained by imitation learning, a.k.a. learning from demonstrations (LfD): a policy is learned from a dataset 𝒟 \mathcal{D} of demonstrations, each an observation–action sequence { ( o t , a t ) } t = 1 T \{(o_{t},a_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T} . Powered by large-scale robotic datasets and pretrained vision–language models, VLAs have achieved remarkable progress in robotic manipulation.
However, many long-horizon tasks are partially observable, where the current observation o t o_{t} alone cannot determine the correct action. In Figure 1 (a), the robot must move a cube “in the same manner as before”, as shown in a video it has just watched; after either video it faces the same observation, and only the history tells it how to act.
When the task’s memory length, the shortest history the task requires, exceeds the policy’s context length (Definition 1 ), such ambiguity can only be resolved by the history h t = { ( o k , a k ) } k < t h_{t}=\{(o_{k},a_{k})\}_{k<t} . In this case, the policy needs memory , the ability to retain and reuse relevant information across time; we refer to this as the memory problem .

A growing body of research has integrated memory into VLAs, differing in what the memory encodes, from latent memory ( Koo et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) to perceptual memory ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Dai et al., 2026 ) , and alleviates the memory problem to some extent. However, what information the memory should carry remains fragmented.
Latent memory learns a dense compression of the history h t h_{t} , which tracks temporal facts well (e.g., a count of events) but aligns poorly with the pretrained token space of the VLA and loses spatial detail.
Perceptual memory keeps a subset of the history chosen by an inductive bias (e.g., the frames with the largest pixel change, or those picked by a VLM verifier); its verbatim snapshots preserve spatial facts (object locations and spatial relations) and object identity, but often miss some key robot behaviour, and the selection is not optimised for control.
This diversity reflects that existing work designs memory from task-specific ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) perspectives, yielding inconsistent gains and a limited understanding of what the optimal formulation of memory is.

Starting from information theory and POMDPs, we cast the memory problem of a visuomotor policy as an optimisation problem: the optimal memory maximises the conditional mutual information I ⁡ ( a t ; m t ∣ o t ) I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) between the action a t a_{t} and the memory m t m_{t} given the current observation o t o_{t} (formal definition in Section 4 ); intuitively, it keeps the key facts that o t o_{t} lacks but a t a_{t} depends on, such as the grasp pose in Figure 1 (b).
This objective gives a unified view of existing memories.
Perceptual heuristics keep the frames that differ most in pixels. This is a proxy for the conditional entropy H ⁡ ( o k ∣ o t ) H(o_{k}\mid o_{t}) , i.e., how much a candidate frame o k o_{k} differs from the current observation o t o_{t} . It is only a loose upper bound on what the frame adds, I ⁡ ( a t ; o k ∣ o t ) ≤ H ⁡ ( o k ∣ o t ) I(a_{t};\,o_{k}\mid o_{t})\leq H(o_{k}\mid o_{t}) , and spends the memory budget on information that does not help control, such as when the observation changes for reasons unrelated to the action (e.g., a lighting change).
Latent memory does optimise I ⁡ ( a t ; m t ∣ o t ) I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) through its variational lower bound; the action log-likelihood 𝔼 𝒟 ​ [ log ⁡ π θ ​ ( a t ∣ o t , m t ) ] \mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{D}}[\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid o_{t},m_{t})] is maximised jointly over the policy weights θ \theta and the memory m t m_{t} , but it learns m t m_{t} in a new latent space and loses the spatial detail that the pretrained tokens of the VLA carry.
Thus, we ask: Can a memory be trained to maximise I ⁡ ( a t ; m t ∣ o t ) I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) directly, without heuristics, while staying in the pretrained token space of the VLA, so that it is optimised for control and still keeps the spatial details?

We answer this question with Divide-and-Remember (D&R) , which optimises the memory against I ⁡ ( a t ; m t ∣ o t ) I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) in the pretrained token space of the VLA, so that choosing m t m_{t} becomes a discrete optimisation over the history tokens ℋ t \mathcal{H}_{t} . D&R is a recursive memory method, in which the full history is divided recursively into slices of 2 ​ K 2K tokens and a fixed-size, lightweight selector keeps K K tokens of each slice. The K K tokens kept from two neighbouring slices are merged into a new 2 ​ K 2K -token slice and selected again (see Figure 3 ), and the composition of these selections solves the memory selection over the full history. This design lets the history scale up while the learnable parameters stay light. The selector is trained end-to-end by the policy’s action loss, the variational lower bound of I ⁡ ( a t ; m t ∣ o t ) I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) .

We evaluate on RoboMME ( Dai et al., 2026 ) , a benchmark of 16 16 long-horizon manipulation tasks that each require a different fact from the past. Under a memory budget of only 64 64 tokens, D&R reaches a state-of-the-art average success rate of 38.6 % 38.6\% , against 32.2 % 32.2\% for the best latent memory and 17.9 % 17.9\% for the memoryless policy. D&R leads on every memory demand of the benchmark, whether the policy has to accumulate a count over repeated events, track an object after it is hidden, refer back to an earlier moment of the episode, or reproduce a demonstrated sequence.
We also evaluate D&R on a real robot over several long-run tasks, with a person intervening mid-task and under perception noise, where D&R achieved the highest success rate.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Memory-augmented VLAs. Existing memory methods for VLAs differ in what the memory encodes, and each fixes what to remember by design.
(1) Latent memory compresses the history into a compact representation, by merging each step into learnable moment tokens (HAMLET ( Koo et al., 2026 ) ) or by a recurrent belief state trained with world-model objectives (RB-VLA ( Bagaria et al., 2026 ) ); it tracks temporal facts well but loses spatial detail.
(2) Perceptual memory keeps a subset of the raw history chosen by a fixed selection rule: frames a VLM labels as events (EventVLA ( Yang et al., 2026 ) ), the patches with the largest pixel change (TokenDrop ( Dai et al., 2026 ) ), or uniformly sampled frames (FrameSamp ( Dai et al., 2026 ) ); the snapshots preserve spatial and object detail, but the rule is hand-designed and not optimised for control.
(3) Parametric memory folds the history into fast weights by test-time training (TTT) ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Dai et al., 2026 ) ; a fact stored in weights is written by gradient descent, which is slow, and is hard to read back exactly.

Routes to the optimal POMDP policy. Classical solutions differ in which statistic of the history the policy conditions on.
(1) The full history, π ( ⋅ ∣ o t , h t ) \pi(\cdot\mid o_{t},h_{t}) , by solving the associated dynamic decision network (Figure 2 (a)); the policy grows exponentially with the history’s length, so this works only for short histories ( Poole & Mackworth, 2023 ) .
(2) The belief state, the posterior over the current state and a sufficient statistic for prediction, as in RB-VLA ( Bagaria et al., 2026 ) ; its recurrent update makes compute and activation memory grow linearly with the episode length and cannot be parallelised over time, which is costly when every step runs a full forward pass of the VLA.

Our analysis gives all of these designs a common objective, I ⁡ ( a t ; m t ∣ o t ) I(a_{t};\,m_{t}\mid o_{t}) ; D&R is an approximation that optimises it in the pretrained token space, conditioning the policy on a bounded statistic, so that the memory stays small and the facts it keeps can be read back exactly.

2026-10-02.title: NarrativeFlow: Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Model Using Robot Velocity Fields
2026-10-02.authors: Shota Kobayashi , Koki Seno , Daichi Yashima , Komei Sugiura
2026-10-02.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-02.comment: Accepted at ACCV 2026
2026-10-02.abstract:
We focus on language-conditioned flow-based manipulation, where robot flows (robot velocity fields) serve as embodiment-agnostic, motion-centric representations for leveraging data collected from multiple robot platforms.
This task is crucial because language-conditioned manipulation is essential for practical robotic systems, yet scaling robot foundation models remains limited by the labor-intensive collection of embodiment-specific data. Existing methods either coarsely approximate robot flows with sparse keypoint displacements, or cannot handle language-conditioned manipulation.
To address this limitation, we propose NarrativeFlow, which models robot flows as continuous velocity fields using a flow-matching formulation conditioned on language.
Accordingly, NarrativeFlow generates robot flows that are physically consistent with real-world manipulation.
To validate NarrativeFlow, we have conducted experiments on standard datasets for language-conditioned manipulation.
The experimental results show that NarrativeFlow outperforms representative baseline methods on standard evaluation metrics.
Furthermore, through real-world experiments, we show that NarrativeFlow achieves higher success rates than baseline methods across multiple manipulation tasks.
The project page is available at https://shota0520.github.io/NarrativeFlow-project-page/
2026-10-02.introduction:
Labor shortages have increased demand for robotic systems that support workers and reduce physical burden in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare.
To meet this demand, such systems must perform diverse tasks across a wide range of real-world environments, while following natural language instructions.
In this direction, recent work has explored robot foundation models, which are often pretrained on large-scale data collected from multiple robot platforms [ 4 , 3 , 33 , 24 ] .
This line of work indicates that the scale and diversity of training data are critical to model performance, yet training these models still requires labor-intensive collection of embodiment-specific data [ 4 , 3 , 33 , 24 ] .

In this study, we focus on language-conditioned flow-based manipulation.
In this task, a model generates a robot flow (robot velocity field) conditioned on an instruction, and then a robot performs object manipulation based on the robot flow.
Robot flows serve as embodiment-agnostic intermediate representations that bridge visual observations and robot actions.
Because such flows can be extracted from arbitrary robot videos, flow-based approaches can leverage large-scale data collected from multiple robot platforms rather than relying on costly embodiment-specific data collection.
However, this task remains challenging: indeed, a representative method, Im2Flow2Act [ 49 ] , still underperforms a method using oracle robot flows by 21 percentage points in average success rate (see Table 4 ).

Many existing flow-based manipulation methods [ 13 , 49 , 2 ] do not formulate robot flows as dense velocity fields, but as displacements of sparse keypoints, even though robot manipulation is inherently a time-evolving physical process.
Specifically, these methods predict sparse keypoint coordinates and then derive robot flows from their displacements, yielding only a coarse approximation of continuous robot motion.
These formulations can be problematic because they assume that the displacements are deterministic, although such an assumption is rarely satisfied in practice.
By contrast, Flow as Flow [ 38 ] can model robot flows as dense velocity fields; however, it cannot handle language-conditioned settings.
Moreover, existing methods [ 13 , 49 , 2 , 38 ] typically rely only on primary flow-generation objectives during training, which provide no explicit supervision for capturing task-relevant semantics.
As a result, such models can be misled by task-irrelevant visual details, such as background appearance and lighting.

To address these limitations, we propose NarrativeFlow, a language-conditioned robot flow generation method that formulates robot flows as probability velocity fields within a flow-matching framework.
By modeling velocity fields, NarrativeFlow generates robot flows that are more physically consistent with real-world manipulation.
Moreover, we introduce an auxiliary loss that aligns the model’s intermediate representations with task-relevant scene changes, enabling the model to capture task-relevant semantics.

Fig. 1 shows an overview of our approach.
We first train our model on cross-embodiment datasets.
At deployment, given an instruction and an initial image, the model generates a robot flow that represents the robot motion required for the specified task (e.g., picking up the can and placing it on the table).
Subsequently, the robot executes the manipulation based on the generated flow to complete the task.

The contributions of this study are as follows:

We propose NarrativeFlow, a language-conditioned robot flow generation method that formulates robot flows as probability velocity fields within a flow-matching framework, enabling high-quality robot flow generation.

We introduce the Narrative Delta loss as an auxiliary objective that aligns the model’s intermediate representations with task-relevant scene changes. We further introduce two subtask tokens to mitigate interference between this auxiliary objective and the primary flow-generation objective.

We show that NarrativeFlow outperforms baseline methods across standard datasets.

Through real-world experiments, we show that NarrativeFlow achieves higher success rates than baseline methods across multiple manipulation tasks.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Language-Conditioned Manipulation. Robotic foundation models aim to address diverse tasks across varied environments and have been actively investigated [ 22 , 62 ] .
Recent language-conditioned manipulation policies build on pretrained foundation models such as multimodal large language models (MLLMs), adopting them as semantic backbones coupled with action heads that map language and observations to control [ 4 , 3 , 28 ] .
This design inherits semantic and perceptual priors from large-scale pretraining, which transfer to unseen tasks and objects [ 3 , 53 ] .

A separate line of work introduces an explicit intermediate representation between language and action [ 49 , 8 , 25 ] .
Such methods predict task- or scene-level targets, including 3D affordance maps (e.g., [ 18 , 25 ] ) and visual subgoals (e.g., [ 5 , 61 ] ), rather than conditioning the policies directly on latent features from the backbones.
Among such targets, robot flows represent task progress as point or end-effector motion, bridging language specifications and the low-level trajectories that execute them [ 52 , 49 , 13 , 19 ] .

Flow-Based Manipulation. Flow-based manipulation methods use robot flows as embodiment-agnostic motion representations that bridge vision and action [ 2 , 11 , 9 , 58 , 49 ] .
These representations can be extracted from heterogeneous robot videos (e.g., [ 43 , 47 ] ) and from web-scale human videos (e.g., [ 2 , 38 , 56 ] ).
Moreover, a large body of work has demonstrated the effectiveness of robot flows across diverse real-world tasks including rigid, articulated, and deformable object manipulation (e.g., [ 59 , 49 ] ).

Although earlier methods generate robot flows over the entire frame (e.g., [ 2 , 47 ] ), some studies use object-centric or hand-centric flows to further reduce the influence of embodiment-specific factors (e.g., [ 49 , 19 , 11 , 56 ] ).
Other approaches adopt flow-conditioned video generation to predict the future scene (e.g., [ 13 ] ), or extend 2D flows into 3D using depth estimation (e.g., [ 9 , 54 ] ).

These methods derive robot flows from the displacements of sparse keypoints. As an alternative, Flow as Flow [ 38 ] directly predicts robot velocity fields via flow matching, a framework that predicts probability velocity fields in a generation space.
However, this method is limited to goal-conditioned manipulation and hence it is unable to address language-conditioned settings.
In contrast, NarrativeFlow generates robot flows using the flow-matching formulation conditioned on language.

Learning Scene-Change Representations. To model temporal dynamics and task-relevant transformations, prior work has leveraged scene-change information in visual representation learning.
For example, procedure-planning methods predict sequences of high-level action labels from a current visual observation toward a visual goal in instructional video understanding [ 45 , 26 , 31 ] .
Other work has focused on scene changes for object-centric localization (e.g., [ 51 ] ), procedural modeling (e.g., [ 32 ] ), and fine-grained temporal modeling (e.g., [ 27 , 50 ] ).
In parallel, recent work has explored efficient temporal representations using video codecs, further leveraging temporal and scene-change cues (e.g., [ 55 ] ).

In manipulation tasks, goal images are often used to specify desired final scene configurations [ 40 , 5 ] .
These images provide fine-grained details of the scene change to be achieved, but are typically unavailable at inference time in language-conditioned settings.
To leverage this information for language-conditioned manipulation, GRIF [ 30 ] uses initial–goal image pairs during training to learn scene-change representations aligned with instructions.

In addition, world models and dynamics models predict how objects and scenes change conditioned on actions.
They model such changes through future observation prediction, learned physical dynamics, or dense geometric motion [ 5 , 12 , 17 ] .

2026-10-02.title: ShowerFlex: Achieving Pseudo-Static Balancing in a Continuum Shower Hose
2026-10-02.authors: Zhiyu Ren , Girish Krishnan
2026-10-02.comment: . Accepted to ASME IDETC/CIE 2026, Mechanisms and Robotics Conference
2026-10-02.abstract: With the global population rapidly aging, maintaining independence in Activities of Daily Living (ADLs)—particularly bathing or showering—has become a critical challenge. Older adults who sit while showering currently have limited options, often relying on rigid overhead showerheads or flexible hand-held hoses that require continuous gripping and precarious user maneuvers, increasing the risk of falls. To address this need, this paper introduces a highly articulated, pseudo-static balanced continuum mechanism designed specifically for accessible bathing assistance. The proposed mechanism features a modular continuum architecture composed of friction-locked ball-and-socket joints (loc-line), seamlessly integrated with a retractable spring-loaded reel for effective gravity compensation. This hybrid design achieves an intuitive “Push-and-Stay” interaction logic, maintaining an approximate static equilibrium with ergonomically low actuation force, without any external electronic power, while significantly minimizing the force needed for repositioning. Theoretically, we established a recursive forward kinematics framework to construct the geometric model of the structure, coupled with a comprehensive static equilibrium analysis to evaluate the system’s holding capacity across its 51-DOF structure. Numerical simulations utilizing Monte Carlo methods validate the system’s morphological adaptability and stability at various extreme positions within a standard bath space. Physical experiments further validate the prototype’s real-world performance, confirming its intrinsic static stability against gravity and ensuring that the actuation force remains well within the ergonomic capabilities of older adults. Ultimately, this research provides a low-cost, intrinsically safe showerhead design that reduces physical strain, restoring dignity and autonomy in personal hygiene.
2026-10-02.introduction:
The global community is rapidly aging. According to the latest projections from the World Health Organization (2025), the global population of individuals aged 60 and over is expected to double, reaching 2.1 billion by 2050 [ 13 ] [ 6 ] [ 14 ] . Within this demographic shift, maintaining independence in “Activities of Daily Living” (ADLs), and in particular maintaining personal hygiene through routine showering or bathing stands as a critical determinant of healthy aging. Independent bathing is often the most important physiological threshold where functional decline becomes apparent [ 3 ] [ 2 ] . The inability to perform this intimate task not only poses physical health risks but also precipitates a severe decline in psychological well-being, often leading to a loss of dignity and a heightened sense of institutional dependency [ 7 ] [ 9 ] .
For older adults who use wheelchairs or have trouble moving their legs, staying independent in the shower is difficult for two main reasons. First, moving from a wheelchair into the shower is physically demanding. To make this easier, homes often need structural changes, such as replacing traditional tubs with “walk-in” showers that have no curb or a very low entry point for a wheelchair to roll over. Second, for those who shower while sitting, ensuring that the shower reaches certain parts of the body like the back, head, and feet is often impossible [ 8 ] . Reaching the water temperature and flow controls can also be a struggle. This paper focuses on that second challenge: making it easier for older adults to reach their body and operate shower controls comfortably while seated.

Despite these well-documented challenges, shower hardware has remained largely stagnant for decades. Traditional fixed showerheads are reliable, but their rigid design cannot adapt to the human body’s shape. This forces users into risky physical movements just to reach their back or feet [ 8 ] . While adjustable showerheads from brands like Waterpik or Delta exist, they are designed for standing adults of different heights. They are ineffective for those who shower while seated, as the user typically sits three to four feet away from the water source. Handheld showerheads with flexible hoses are a common alternative, but they require the user to constantly hold and aim them. For frail older adults, this is a major safety risk: if one hand is busy holding a showerhead, they cannot use both hands to grip safety bars, significantly increasing the risk of a fall [ 16 ] .

To address these challenges, this paper presents “ShowerFlex: A friction and spring-balanced continuum hose with a showerhead at its distal end”. With ShowerFlex the showerhead can be positioned at any location and orientation within the bath space, and the hose holds its configuration without being continuously held or requiring external power supply. This allows for hands-free operation of the shower. Furthermore, our design allows the showerhead to be repositioned with little force, making critical areas such as the back and legs accessible to the shower. We refer to this hybrid strategy as pseudo-static balancing, a concept formally defined in Section 2.

Showerflex routes the hose through a Loc-Line® assembly, which is a series of hollow, friction‑locked ball‑and‑socket segments. One end of the Loc-Line connects to the water inlet, and the other attaches to a standard showerhead. A self‑locking retractable reel, anchored to a fixed support and connected to the showerhead, provides additional stability. The reel locks when stationary but allows smooth, user‑guided motion when slightly tensioned, while its internal springs help counteract the weight of the showerhead. Together, the Loc-Line and reel demonstrate the advantages of conventional static balancing, i.e. equilibrium at all configurations with minimal repositioning force.

The combination of friction locking and spring-loaded balancing is studied in this paper as a strategy to obtain the benefits of static balancing without actually requiring the forces to balance. To provide a theoretical basis for this behavior, we established a recursive forward kinematics model alongside a detailed static equilibrium analysis. These mathematical foundations enable numerical simulations, specifically using the Monte Carlo method to quantify the reachable workspace and verify the system’s stability for normal bathing tasks. Finally, we demonstrate the robustness by physical experimental validation, confirming the device’s intrinsic static stability and validating that the actuation force is well within the ergonomic capabilities of older adults.

# 2 RELATED WORK

Static balancing refers to maintaining a mechanical system in static equilibrium for all possible configurations by ensuring that all forces are balanced. A comprehensive theory for statically balancing linkages using zero‑length springs to exactly compensate end masses was presented by [ 4 ] . Static balancing offers two key practical design advantages: (i) stability, achieved through a constant potential energy leading to equilibrium in every configuration, and (ii) low actuation force, since only a small force is required to move the system. In practice, however, ideal balance, i.e. complete equilibrium combined with zero actuation force cannot be fully realized due to friction in the joints [ 10 ] . While joint friction contributes to stability by resisting unintended motion, it also increases the threshold actuation force required to move the mechanism [ 15 ] .

Static balancing has been applied to reduce the effective actuation stiffness of compliant mechanisms by incorporating members that exert forces in opposing directions [ 11 ] . By combining negative‑stiffness elements with constant‑force elements, designers can achieve a quasi‑static balance over a defined operating range of the compliant mechanism [ 5 ] . It is also noteworthy that compliant mechanisms inherently lack friction, as their motion arises from elastic deformation rather than discrete joints.

Continuum links such as a shower hose possess theoretically infinite degrees of freedom, making true static balancing practically impossible. Loc‑lines, which are friction‑locked hollow ball‑and‑socket joints, maintain equilibrium through friction generated at the press‑fit interfaces. Related design embodiments, often referred to as goosenecks [ 1 ] , use a hose tightly wrapped with a helical spring. Both of these commercially available mechanisms are highly effective in ”set-and-forget” applications—such as directing machine tool coolant or positioning medical monitors—where frequent adjustment is unnecessary. In these cases, the design goal is to prioritize equilibrium and rigid holding capacity over minimizing actuation force.

However, when adapted for heavy loads with long moment arms, such as a showerhead extended beyond two feet, a fundamental mechanical limitation emerges: increasing the joint friction extends the holding range, but it proportionally increases the force required to reposition the device. To the best of our knowledge, there is no passive continuum or articulated mechanism reported in the literature capable of simultaneously achieving a stable cantilever hold exceeding about 4 ft while maintaining an average actuation force below 3 N.

For a shower hose supporting a showerhead at its end, both stability through equilibrium and low actuation force are essential. However, friction‑locked ball‑and‑socket joints inherently involve a trade‑off. For instance, a 1.6 kg showerhead must remain in stable equilibrium without collapsing, even when positioned as far as 4 ft from the inlet. Achieving this requires substantial frictional resistance. The closest flexible shower using this concept could not hold its length beyond two feet [ 12 ] . Thus design also suffered from excessive force to reposition, but also suffered from noise. However, the user—often an older adult with limited upper‑body strength—may only be able to apply a modest actuation force to reposition the showerhead.

Consequently, the competing requirements of stable equilibrium and minimal actuation force highlight a critical research gap. Existing accessible showering solutions fundamentally fall short because they either (a) require continuous user grip, which increases fall risks, (b) rely on external power and mechatronics, which introduce waterproofing and cost barriers, or (c) utilize purely passive friction joints that cannot hold extended configurations under typical showerhead loads without requiring excessive manual force. ShowerFlex directly addresses this gap through our proposed pseudo-static balancing strategy. Unlike traditional static balancing which mathematically zeroes out potential energy differences, our approach uses a spring-loaded retractor to bear the bulk of the gravitational moment, while relying on intrinsic joint friction to counteract only the residual unbalanced torque. This synergistic design resolves the long-standing trade-off, achieving both robust hands-free positioning and an ergonomically low repositioning force suitable for older adults.

2026-10-02.title: A Survey on End-to-End Autonomous Driving Training from the Perspectives of Data, Strategy, and Platform
2026-10-02.authors: Chengkai Xu , Yiming Cui , Jiaqi Liu , Yicheng Guo , Cheng Qin , Geyuan Zhang , Xinwei Dong , Shiyu Fang , Peng Hang , Jian Sun
2026-10-02.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-02.comment: accepted by IEEE transactions on intelligent transportation systems
2026-10-02.abstract:
Autonomous driving is a cornerstone technology for the future of intelligent transportation, where end-to-end learning has emerged as a transformative paradigm that directly maps multimodal sensory inputs to driving actions through unified differentiable models. While offering advantages, the effectiveness of end-to-end autonomous driving (E2E-AD) is ultimately determined by the quality of its training ecosystem.
This paper provides a comprehensive review of training methods and ecosystem for E2E-AD. We introduce a Data-Strategy-Platform taxonomy that conceptualizes training as an interdependent system.
The data layer defines what can be learned, the strategy layer governs how learning aligns with driving objectives, and the platform layer supports scalability and continuous evolution. Within this framework, we survey recent advances across data-centric pipelines, learning paradigms, and training infrastructures, and analyze their interplay in shaping model performance, robustness, and deployability.
Finally, we reflect on current limitations and articulate a forward-looking vision that emphasizes a shift from data quantity to data value, from isolated optimization to foundation-driven generalization, and from static training to integrated training-testing loops, aiming toward robust, scalable, and trustworthy autonomous driving systems.
We maintain a continuously updated repository tracking cutting-edge literature and works at Our Project Page .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Autonomous driving has emerged as a strategic frontier in intelligent transportation systems, offering prospects for safer mobility, higher traffic efficiency, and new paradigms of urban transport [ 1 , 2 ] .
Traditional research has largely followed a modular pipeline architecture, where perception, prediction, planning, and control are separated into distinct subsystems.
Although this decomposition facilitates interpretability and engineering controllability, modular systems are prone to error accumulation across interfaces and struggle to achieve global optimization in highly interactive and mixed traffic environments [ 3 , 4 ] .

In response, end-to-end autonomous driving (E2E-AD) has attracted significant research attention.
By mapping multimodal sensory inputs directly to driving actions through unified differentiable models, E2E-AD reduces system coupling and allows joint optimization of perception, decision-making, and control [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
Such integration has demonstrated strong potential for handling complex interactions and long-horizon reasoning [ 8 ] .
Moreover, recent progress in large-scale representation learning, generative models, and foundation models further expands the capabilities of E2E-AD, pushing the research frontier from concept demonstrations toward practical deployment.

Despite these structural advantages, E2E-AD still faces challenges in large-scale real-world application, and its development bottleneck lies not only in model design but also in the training process itself.
As models become larger and more capable [ 9 ] , their effectiveness increasingly depends on whether the training ecosystem can provide: (i) data with sufficient coverage, quality, and governance to capture rare but safety-critical scenarios; (ii) strategies for optimization that can align multi-task objectives and stabilize long-horizon learning; and (iii) platforms with the computational scale and lifecycle management required for continuous model evolution. These three dimensions jointly define the performance boundary of E2E autonomous vehicles.

We clarify the positioning of this review against representative surveys in Table I . Existing studies provide valuable reviews of datasets [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , perception modules [ 13 , 14 ] , end-to-end architectures [ 8 , 7 ] , imitation learning [ 6 ] , and foundation models [ 9 , 15 , 16 ] . In contrast, this survey focuses on the training ecosystem and examines how data, learning strategies, and platforms jointly determine training effectiveness.

The main contributions of this survey are as follows:

A Data-Strategy-Platform taxonomy is introduced, which frames E2E-AD training as a system-level challenge rather than an isolated algorithmic problem.

A comprehensive review of recent advances is conducted, encompassing data, paradigms, and infrastructures, with particular emphasis on both the current state of the art and the dynamic interplay among these three dimensions.

Beyond surveying existing work, a future vision for training E2E-AD is proposed, where the shift from data quantity to data value, from task-specific learners to universal foundation models, and from static offline training to continuous training-testing integration is highlighted.

The overall logical structure of the review is shown in Fig. 1 . The Data Layer (Section III ) establishes the learnable information boundary through scenario coverage and governance, which supports the Strategy Layer (Section IV ), where paradigms ranging from imitation learning to world models are reviewed.
Finally, the Platform Layer (Section V ) provides the computational foundation for training and validation. Section VI discusses the cross-layer evolution shown in Fig. 1 .

1. A Data-Strategy-Platform taxonomy is introduced, which frames E2E-AD training as a system-level challenge rather than an isolated algorithmic problem.

2. A comprehensive review of recent advances is conducted, encompassing data, paradigms, and infrastructures, with particular emphasis on both the current state of the art and the dynamic interplay among these three dimensions.

3. Beyond surveying existing work, a future vision for training E2E-AD is proposed, where the shift from data quantity to data value, from task-specific learners to universal foundation models, and from static offline training to continuous training-testing integration is highlighted.

# II End-to-End Autonomous Driving

## II-A Development and Trends

Early autonomous driving systems largely relied on modular architectures, which offer interpretability and engineering modularity but suffer from error propagation and limited global optimization in complex mixed traffic.
With the advancement of deep learning and multimodal sensing, E2E-AD weakens information barriers between modules and enables integrated modeling of semantics, interaction, and control by mapping raw sensory inputs directly to driving actions through unified differentiable models [ 5 ] .
The earliest demonstrations, such as ALVINN and later NVIDIA’s DAVE-2 [ 19 , 20 ] , showed that neural networks could replace rule-based pipelines with data-driven control policies. While pioneering, these approaches relied on single networks with direct control outputs and struggled to cope with long-tail scenarios or domain transfer.

Subsequent work introduced more structured forms of end-to-end learning, often referred to as modular end-to-end approaches. Instead of discarding intermediate representations, they embedded them within a differentiable framework, allowing perception, prediction, and planning to be optimized under a shared objective. Systems such as MP3, UniAD, and DiffStack [ 21 , 4 , 22 ] exemplify this trend to integrate multimodal information and by incorporating differentiable planning modules to improve consistency between perception and control, which alleviates the interpretability issues associated with integrated networks while retaining the benefits of joint learning.

More recently, the field has increasingly embraced generative end-to-end paradigms that capitalize on advances in language models, diffusion models, and related approaches [ 15 , 23 , 9 ] .
These systems move beyond reactive mappings by anticipating long-horizon interactions and synthesizing counterfactual scenarios within latent space.
For example, frameworks such as LMDrive and OpenDriveVLA align vision, language, and action in a shared semantic space, thereby facilitating the natural integration of high-level instructions [ 24 , 25 ] .
Meanwhile, world models such as DriveDreamer and GAIA generate scene rollouts that capture rare or cross-domain conditions [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] .
These advances mark a transition from narrowly engineered control policies toward models with enhanced capacities for reasoning, generalization, and even imagination.

Alongside architectural evolution, research trends reveal deeper transformations in how E2E-AD is conceptualized.
The data paradigm is moving from scale expansion toward scenario prioritization, with increasing attention to rare, high-risk events and generative supplementation [ 30 , 31 , 10 ] .
Training objectives are shifting from perception accuracy to consistency with planning and safety, motivating the exploration of imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and generative models [ 32 , 33 , 34 ] .
Evaluation protocols are evolving from offline metrics to closed-loop benchmarks such as CARLA and nuPlan, which emphasize safety, comfort, and compliance under continuous deployment cycles [ 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 ] .
These trends illustrate that the progress of E2E-AD is not merely an architectural evolution but a systematic reconfiguration of training logic.

## II-B Core Training Challenges

As E2E-AD integrates perception, prediction, planning, and control into a unified framework, its success is determined less by any single algorithmic advance and more by the coherence of the training ecosystem. As illustrated in Fig. 2 , three dimensions emerge as decisive. The data layer defines the boundaries of what can be learned, yet the long-tail distribution of road events, the scarcity of high-quality annotations, and discrepancies between real and simulated data severely constrain generalization. The strategy layer governs how models optimize toward driving objectives, but multi-task conflicts, unstable convergence, and the misalignment between offline proxy metrics and online performance frequently undermine reliability. The platform layer provides the engineering foundation, where bottlenecks in data pipelines, distributed training, and continuous adaptation often limit scalability and reproducibility.

These challenges are not independent. Insufficient scenario coverage amplifies optimization instability; fragile optimization increases the burden on computational infrastructure; and platform inefficiencies in turn restrict the feasible scope of data and strategies. Well-known issues such as hallucinations, catastrophic forgetting, or cross-domain degradation often manifest when alignment breaks down across these three layers. Thus, the core challenges of E2E-AD are fundamentally systemic, arising from the need to coordinate data, strategies, and platforms into a closed-loop training process. This interdependence motivates the taxonomy adopted in the remainder of this review, which analyzes training methods along the axes of data, strategy, and platform to provide a unified perspective on the development of E2E-AD.
