# 2 Related Work

Object-centric methods retrieve and align CAD assets to observations ( Avetisyan et al., 2019 ; Kuo et al., 2020 ; Gao et al., 2024 ) , while neural representations
recover scene appearance and geometry ( Mildenhall et al., 2020 ; Kerbl et al., 2023 ; Ni et al., 2025 ) .
LiteReality ( Huang et al., 2025b ) and MetaScenes ( Yu et al., 2025 ) convert scans into asset-based environments. Video2Game ( Xia et al., 2024 ) ,
DRAWER ( Xia et al., 2025b ) , and HoloScene ( Xia et al., 2025a ) reconstruct
interactive worlds from video; DRAWER additionally recovers articulation.
FIRE3D ( Xia et al., 2026a ) predicts compositional scene assets with a feed-forward network.
For robot learning, Phone2Proc ( Deitke et al., 2023 ) generates procedural
environments from mobile captures, RialTo ( Torne et al., 2024 ) constructs digital twins
for policy refinement, and PolaRiS ( Jain et al., 2026 ) reconstructs environments
for policy evaluation. ACDC ( Dai et al., 2025 ) instead constructs digital cousins
using similar assets.

Image-to-3D methods range from multi-view synthesis ( Liu et al., 2023b ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2023a ; Long et al., 2024 ) to large reconstruction
and generative models ( Hong et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024 ; Xiang et al., 2026 ; Hunyuan3D et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) .
CAST ( Yao et al., 2025 ) aligns generated objects into a scene, while
URDFormer ( Chen et al., 2024 ) infers articulated simulation environments from images.
Real2Code ( Mandi et al., 2025 ) predicts articulation as code;
Articulate-Anything ( Le et al., 2025 ) iteratively generates and critiques
articulation programs. Articraft ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) couples programmatic asset
generation with a specialised SDK and validation harness.

LayoutGPT ( Feng et al., 2023 ) and Holodeck ( Yang et al., 2024 ) generate
layouts from language; FirePlace ( Huang et al., 2025a ) and
LayoutVLM ( Sun et al., 2025b ) refine placement through geometric or visual feedback.
3D-GPT ( Sun et al., 2025a ) , SceneCraft ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , and
LL3M ( Lu et al., 2025 ) use language models for programmatic 3D authoring.
The Scene Language ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) combines programs, words, and embeddings
to represent scene structure and appearance. SceneSmith ( Pfaff et al., 2026 ) ,
SAGE ( Xia et al., 2026b ) , and SceneWeaver ( Yang et al., 2025 ) organise agentic
scene-generation pipelines. BlenderAlchemy ( Huang et al., 2024 ) explores
visually guided editing, and BlenderGym ( Gu et al., 2025 ) benchmarks code-based
graphics editing.

SceneScript ( Avetisyan et al., 2024 ) and IG-LLM ( Kulits et al., 2024 ) infer structured scene descriptions from visual inputs. VIGA ( Yin et al., 2026 ) iterates through code, rendering, and inspection; Thinking in Blender ( He et al., 2026 ) refines scene factors in executable code from a single image.
HARMONY ( Sun et al., 2026 ) combines agentic placement with geometric refinement
for monocular scene reconstruction. Agentic Real2Sim ( Chen et al., 2026a ) uses vision-language agents to assemble physical simulations from interaction videos.
The AHa-3D research blog ( Xu et al., 2026 ) describes a closely related workflow
for video-to-simulation reconstruction with camera, measurement, and inspection tools.
LiteReality-Agent addresses metric RGB-D room reconstruction, combining articulated assets
and a persistent scene program with calibrated multi-view verification and explicit
collision and support checks.

2026-10-02.title: Finite-Data Safety Informativity Under Dynamic Asymmetric Actuation
2026-10-02.authors: Abhinav Sinha , Praveen Kumar Ranjan , Yongcan Cao
2026-10-02.subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Dynamical Systems (math.DS)
2026-10-02.abstract: When the system model is not fully known, measurement error and limited excitation can leave several models consistent with the same finite data. A command judged safe for one model may fail for another, while limited control authority can prevent the corrective action needed to preserve safety. To ensure safety under model uncertainty and asymmetric input limits, we develop a finite-data certificate that determines whether a command can enforce a prescribed safety inequality. For a linearly parameterized safety channel with exactly known regressors and bounded aggregate residual error, we derive a support formula for the worst-case safety contribution of all data-consistent models. The formula identifies the regressor directions that admit a finite bound, allowing rank-deficient records to contribute to safety certification. Using certified componentwise bounds on actuator tracking error yields an affine inequality with a necessary and sufficient test for pointwise command feasibility. The affine inequality reduces computation of the closest certified command to a scalar root-finding problem. It also yields a closed-form gate that selects the largest certified fraction of a prescribed command segment. The proposed certificate guarantees output safety within its operating domain, provided the feedback is locally Lipschitz and the uncertainty bounds remain valid. Domain retention and full-state continuation extend this guarantee to all time. A vehicle study demonstrates that output safety can be certified from finite measurements in a safety-critical setting with model and actuator uncertainty.
2026-10-02.introduction:
In many applications, a controller must meet a performance objective while respecting constraints that define safe operation. A vehicle, for example, may need to follow a reference trajectory while remaining inside a moving corridor. Near the corridor boundary, the controller must retain enough authority to counter disturbances without violating the input limits. When control decisions rely on finite measurements, the data must support the safety of a proposed correction, and the actuators must be able to realize it.

Set-invariance theory and control barrier functions provide conditions for selecting corrective inputs that keep trajectories within admissible sets [ 1 , 2 ] . Safety filters use these conditions to modify a nominal command through an instantaneous inequality [ 2 ] or predictive optimization [ 3 ] . Higher-order barrier designs address constraints of high relative degree [ 4 ] and the feasibility of corrective inputs under tight input bounds [ 5 ] . These safety guarantees depend on a model or uncertainty bounds that remain valid during operation. When a reliable model is unavailable, unknown contributions from the dynamics prevent direct evaluation of these conditions.

Measurements can be used to estimate the unknown terms and quantify the uncertainty relevant to safety certification. Gaussian-process methods use prediction bounds to account for uncertainty in barrier conditions [ 6 , 7 ] , while reinforcement learning can estimate corrections to the model terms entering safety constraints [ 8 ] . Conformal calibration connects learned models to probabilistic guarantees [ 9 ] . Robust adaptive and uncertainty-estimation methods combine estimates with certified error bounds [ 10 , 11 ] . However, accurate prediction and uncertainty quantification do not establish whether a given finite record is sufficient for safety certification under limited control authority. A deterministic certificate based on a finite record must establish that an admissible command satisfies the safety inequality for every model consistent with the measurements and their error bound.

Data informativity formalizes this question of sufficiency by assessing whether a record supports a specified task for all data-consistent systems [ 12 , 13 ] . In linear feedback synthesis, data parameterizations and matrix inequalities yield conditions for such sufficiency under bounded errors [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] . For nonlinear systems, set-membership and barrier-learning methods use structural and regularity assumptions to obtain deterministic guarantees from data [ 17 , 18 ] . A further challenge is to preserve the safety guarantee when the command is realized by a dynamic actuator. Tracking error can invalidate the safety inequality, while asymmetric limits restrict the corrective action available to maintain safety.

Actuator-aware barrier formulations address this challenge through optimization-based filters that account for dynamically generated inputs or unmodeled input dynamics [ 19 , 20 ] . Admissibility-preserving input realization (APIR) embeds asymmetric limits directly in a smooth actuator map, keeping the realized input admissible by construction [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] . Within this realization, certified tracking-error bounds quantify a margin in the safety inequality that accounts for the difference between commanded and realized inputs.

Output-safety certification from finite data still faces an obstacle in the sense that the corrective action required by the data-consistent models may exceed the authority available under actuator tracking error and asymmetric input limits. Addressing this problem requires bounding the safety contribution of the data-consistent models without full parameter identification and comparing that bound with the authority available under actuator tracking error. In such scenarios, a feasible certificate must be converted into command-selection rules with the regularity needed for trajectory safety. We address these requirements through the following contributions.

We characterize the minimum residual-error budget for data consistency and quantify the amplification of uncertainty at each queried regressor. For a consistent record and a nonzero safety functional, the result identifies the unmeasured regressor directions that make the worst-case model contribution unbounded.

We quantify the loss of certified control authority due to actuator tracking error as an additive reserve. Subtracting this reserve from the static finite-data authority characterizes pointwise feasibility for the chosen certificate and recovers the static certificate when the error bounds vanish.

For implementation, we derive the command projection and admission gate with sufficient conditions for local Lipschitz continuity. A counterexample establishes that pointwise certificate feasibility can hold even when no continuous feedback selector exists.

We validate the certificate numerically on a vehicle model by comparing coverage across equal-sized measurement records and against static and exact-parameter benchmarks. Closed-loop checks assess output and input constraint satisfaction, and halving the integration step preserves sampled certificate feasibility.

2026-10-02.title: Continuous Conditioning of VLAs with Augmenting EMG and Visual Task Descriptors
2026-10-02.authors: Edward W. Staley , Connor O. Pyles , Rahul Hingorani , Frank Camargo , Griffin Milsap , Jared Markowitz , Matthew S. Fifer , Michael Wolmetz
2026-10-02.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-02.comment: Presented at IROS WORLDS Workshop 2026. Four main pages double-column format plus references and appendices
2026-10-02.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models rely strongly on language for describing task information, despite having multimodal inputs. We hypothesize that other modalities in the state space may present opportunities for supplemental task conditioning, which may be particularly relevant in cluttered or otherwise ambiguous scenes. We introduce two tuned models to test this hypothesis: (1) an electrophysiology-conditioned VLA (EC-VLA) that incorporates 8-channel electromyography envelopes as continuous conditioning input concatenated to the proprioceptive vector, and (2) a visually-annotated VLA (VA-VLA) that incorporates visual segmentation annotations to the image inputs. On a cube-selection task evaluated across three participants, EC-VLA matches a language-prompted baseline in uncluttered, in-distribution conditions and substantially outperforms it in cluttered, out-of-distribution scenes. Similarly, VA-VLA shows modest improvements over a language-prompted baseline in in-distribution scenes with substantial improvement in cluttered, out-of-distribution trials. Together, these results provide strong evidence for the potential benefit of task-conditioning beyond language.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently gained significant traction as a means for generalized robotic control, and can serve as a base model to be tuned for a downstream task [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Such tuned policies inherit their high-level state structure from the base model: a low-level proprioceptive vector, one or more camera views, and a task description given as language. The majority of VLA parameters are often initialized from a large language model (LLM), forming the core backbone of the model. At deployment time, language is used to define what the robot needs to accomplish in the environment and is typically given as an up-front command that stays fixed during task execution.

However, as these systems continue to become more capable and take on increasingly complex tasks, there will be times in which language is insufficient as a task-defining condition. Cluttered scenes and nuanced tasks might require detailed explanation that a human would more naturally express with a gesture, picture, or gaze [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .

We explore tuning VLAs with tasks defined by continuous conditioning signals incorporated into state modalities beyond text. As shown in Figure 1 , we construct two experiments: one with task conditioning in the proprioceptive vector and one with conditioning in the image modality, with only generic task information given in the text input. We compare these to tuned models that use the more standard descriptive text inputs. We find that these alternative modalities for task conditioning, supplied as continuous state information, generally yield stronger performance than the baseline tuned policies, especially in cluttered scenes.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Background

## II-A Vision Language Action Models

In our experiments we utilize SmolVLA [ 6 ] and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 5 ] , which are both action-expert style VLAs that use a flow-matching [ 11 ] head on top of a VLM backbone. This architecture was first introduced in Octo [ 3 ] (using a diffusion policy head) and π 0 \pi_{0} [ 4 ] . It contrasts with earlier autoregressive techniques like OpenVLA [ 2 ] , which output discrete tokens that need to be converted into actions afterwards.

## II-B Electrophysiological Signals and Robot Policies

Many prior works explore shared control between a robotic system and user data collected through electromyography (EMG), (electroencephalogram) EEG, or brain-computer interface (BCI) signals. These inputs provide intent or feedback, often falling in the domain of assistive robotics. Xu et al. [ 12 ] use EEG signals to direct a robotic system towards grasping a target object. Akinola et al. [ 13 ] use EEG as a way for a human to note an incorrect action, a signal which is then used to further improve the policy.

More recent and relevant to this work, Lee et al. [ 14 ] combine EEG with an AI copilot, in a similar setup to our first experiment. M4Bench [ 8 ] explored eye tracking and EMG as input modalities in a multirobot pick-and-place problem. The extension by Douglas et al. [ 15 ] integrates EEG, EMG, and eye tracking in a system to control Franka arms in simulated kitchens with a focus on allocating control to either the human or policy. Our EC-VLA model is a robotic policy that directly receives EMG inputs as state information.

## II-C Visual Annotations and Robot Policies

Several prior works have examined visual prompting to describe tasks to a robotic policy. KITE [ 16 ] trains a policy that conditions on imagery and keypoints rather than language directly. MOKA [ 17 ] also annotates images with key points, asking a VLM to select among a set of key points to identify which are most useful. RT-Trajectory [ 18 ] uses 2D curves drawn over a scene that roughly depict how a robot should move.

Works similar to our second experiment include FOCA [ 19 ] , which uses segmentation masks from RoboCasa at training time to supervise predicted features, and RoboGround [ 20 ] , which uses segmentation-style masks to describe a target object and destination in RoboCasa. RoboGround conditions the policy on these masks and a language instruction, while in this work we explore omitting language when visual prompts are supplied. Also similar is MOO [ 9 ] , which directly describes a target object with a segmentation mask and omits this identity from language inputs to an RT-1 [ 1 ] -style policy. Gaze2Act [ 10 ] includes a human in the loop who provides conditioning signals to help select an object while the text prompt is underspecified. Its human focus aligns well with our first experiment, but its signal is supplied in a manner closer to our second experiment: a human gaze is first translated into a visual mask and then supplied as an image.

2026-10-02.title: 3DROID: A Renderable 3D Gaussian Dataset with Measured Per-Scene Reliability
2026-10-02.authors: Wonguen Cho , Junhoo Lee , Nojun Kwak
2026-10-02.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-02.abstract:
Robot manipulation models primarily reason from 2D observations while acting in the 3D physical world.
To bridge this gap, recent work has augmented robot data with geometric priors such as depth, point clouds, and 3D trajectories, while renderable 3D Gaussian representations provide another promising form of 3D supervision.
However, 3DGS representation is designed mainly for photometric fidelity and may not preserve real-world metric scale, particularly when the supplied camera extrinsics are unreliable.
We study the effect of extrinsic reliability and pose conditioning on feed-forward 3DGS, and propose a calibration-aware pipeline that anchors reconstructed scenes to the robot’s metric workspace.
Our experiments show that pose conditioning improves novel-view fidelity, while its geometric benefit depends on the reliability of the injected extrinsics.
Using this pipeline, we present a renderable, metric-pose-anchored dataset with scene-level reliability information for robot manipulation research. Our dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/wonguen/3DROID
2026-10-02.introduction:
Robot manipulation is inherently geometric: grasping and placement require
reasoning about objects, free space, and motion in 3D. Explicit 3D
representations improve spatial reasoning over 2D observations [ 10 , 16 , 17 , 21 ] , motivating recent 3D annotations and renderable robot scenes [ 3 , 13 , 22 ] .
Unlike point- or token-based annotations, renderable scenes provide a view-consistent appearance model from which observations and occlusions can be generated at new camera poses, enabling visual augmentation and simulation without additional data collection [ 22 ] .
Such novel-view augmentation has also been shown to improve policy robustness
to unseen camera poses [ 13 ] .

Constructing these representations at dataset scale favors feed-forward reconstruction.
Classical 3DGS optimizes each scene independently from its
available observations, making sparse robot views underconstrained and requiring repeated optimization over thousands of episodes [ 8 ] .
Feed-forward variants instead amortize reconstruction
across training scenes: their learned priors support inference from limited views, while a single forward pass avoids repeated per-scene optimization [ 7 , 11 , 18 , 19 ] .
This makes them a practical basis for constructing large-scale renderable robot datasets.

These advantages address sparsity and computational cost, but not physical reliability.
Both classical and feed-forward 3DGS are developed primarily for
photorealistic novel-view synthesis.
For manipulation, however, synthesized observations are useful only if they remain consistent with the metric workspace in which robot states and actions are defined [ 17 ] .
A reconstruction may preserve appearance while silently moving surfaces or changing scene scale.
Moreover, camera calibrations in real-world robot datasets are not uniformly reliable,
so shipped poses cannot simply be treated as ground truth.
Whether the resulting scenes preserve metric scale therefore remains unclear,
and calibration must be validated independently of the reconstructor.

Prior work addresses parts of this problem from complementary directions.
Geometry-aware Gaussian methods introduce surface constraints, stereo cues, or 3D priors to improve geometric stability [ 5 , 14 , 13 ] , while camera-refinement methods align visual observations with robot geometry [ 6 ] .
Yet these model- and calibration-level solutions do not by themselves specify how reliability should be communicated when reconstructions are released as data.
This leaves a dataset-level question: how can calibration suitability and reconstruction reliability be measured and exposed for each scene?

In this paper, we therefore build 3DROID by reconstructing DROID [ 9 ] with pose-conditioned feed-forward 3DGS and
separating photometric fidelity from physical consistency.
Building on robot–depth alignment used for camera refinement [ 6 ] , we validate calibration before reconstruction and separately assess geometric reliability afterward, together with measurement coverage.
This separates calibration suitability from reconstruction reliability.
We therefore release measured support rather than claim geometric ground truth or downstream policy gains.
Table 1 summarizes the scene-level assets added by 3DROID and the source modalities that remain in DROID.

Our contributions are threefold:

We release 3DROID , a DROID-derived dataset of renderable 3D Gaussian scenes with per-scene calibration and reconstruction-reliability metadata.

We empirically show that metric pose conditioning anchors reconstruction scale to the physical workspace and yields median per-scene PSNR gains of + 0.73 +0.73 to + 2.73 +2.73 dB at a fixed extrinsic source.

We repurpose robot–depth consistency as a coverage-aware reconstruction evaluation protocol that compares rendered 3DGS depth with classical stereo and kinematically localized robot geometry.

1. We release 3DROID , a DROID-derived dataset of renderable 3D Gaussian scenes with per-scene calibration and reconstruction-reliability metadata.

2. We empirically show that metric pose conditioning anchors reconstruction scale to the physical workspace and yields median per-scene PSNR gains of + 0.73 +0.73 to + 2.73 +2.73 dB at a fixed extrinsic source.

3. We repurpose robot–depth consistency as a coverage-aware reconstruction evaluation protocol that compares rendered 3DGS depth with classical stereo and kinematically localized robot geometry.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related works

Explicit 3D observations improve spatial reasoning for manipulation. DP3 demonstrated this with sparse point cloud, and FP3 scaled point-cloud pretraining to DROID [ 16 , 20 ] .
DROID-3D added depth and point clouds,
while 4D-VLA and Lift3D-VLA incorporated temporal geometry [ 3 , 10 , 21 ] .
PointWorld and Robo3R further improved calibration and robot-frame alignment [ 6 , 17 ] . Yet these point- or token-based outputs lack a view-consistent appearance model. Unlike point observations, renderable scenes can synthesize view-consistent observations from new camera poses, expose viewpoint-dependent visibility, and support data augmentation or visual simulation without recollecting demonstration.
RoboSnap builds layered mesh–Gaussian scenes from a single image, but does
not provide measured per-scene reconstruction reliability [ 22 ] .
This leaves open how to construct renderable robot scenes while explicitly measuring their metric alignment and reconstruction reliability.

Whereas per-scene 3DGS requires time-consuming optimization [ 8 ] ,
feed-forward methods leverage learned priors to reconstruct scenes from sparse views in a single pass [ 1 , 7 ] .
Regardless of reconstruction strategy, 3DGS is designed primarily for photorealistic novel-view rendering.
Yet photorealism and manipulation readiness are different objectives: novel-view fidelity does not guarantee metric scale, robot-frame alignment, or reliable geometry.
Pose-conditioned PixelSplat, MVSplat, and DepthSplat improve matching and depth estimation but assume reliable calibration [ 1 , 2 , 15 ] . NoPoSplat and AnySplat remove pose inputs, while YoNoSplat handles variable posed or unposed inputs and ZipSplat compresses the representation [ 7 , 11 , 18 , 19 ] . GenSplat applies this pose-free paradigm to robotic view augmentation, but evaluates DROID reconstruction only qualitatively without testing robot-frame alignment [ 13 ] . We instead audit calibration and evaluate rendering separately from stereo-supported geometry.

2026-10-02.title: Managing Context and Communication in Distributed Agentic UAV Swarms
2026-10-02.authors: Andrea Iannoli , Ivan Zyrianoff , Angelo Trotta , Lorenzo Gigli , Marco Di Felice
2026-10-02.subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-02.comment: . This paper has been accepted for presentation at the 24th IEEE Consumer Communications & Networking Conference 2027 (CCNC 2027)
2026-10-02.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms increasingly rely on language-model agents to provide adaptive mission-level reasoning in uncertain environments. Fully distributed control, in which each UAV hosts an independent Small Language Model (SLM), removes reliance on a centralized coordinator but introduces an information-management problem: long-running interaction histories can degrade the reasoning context, while indiscriminate information dissemination increases communication and inference overhead. We address these challenges with a distributed UAV-agent architecture that enables continuous local SLM control through an event-driven reason–act–observe lifecycle. Runtime knowledge is represented as structured atomic notes and organized into core, local, and peer-specific memory. A deterministic interest-aware gossip engine selectively disseminates these notes according to recipient-specific semantic novelty and recency. We evaluate the architecture using ten UAVs in a simulated search-and-rescue mission. Our approach completes all experimental runs, whereas unrestricted flooding messages completes only 70–85%, and delegating forwarding decisions to the SLM prevents mission completion in every run. Compared with unrestricted flooding, our approach approximately halves inference-token consumption, reduces transmitted data, and achieves lower survivor-count error.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms combine rapid deployment, parallel sensing, and wide-area coverage, making them attractive for search-and-rescue, disaster recovery, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure inspection. These missions are executed in uncertain environments in which predefined plans may become inadequate as hazards, observations, connectivity, and resource availability change [ 1 ] . Agentic AI can complement conventional perception and flight-control components with goal interpretation, contextual reasoning, and adaptive planning, enabling UAVs to revise mission-level decisions when unexpected conditions arise [ 2 ] .

Embedding such reasoning capabilities into continuous UAV swarm control, however, is challenging. Model decisions must be grounded in heterogeneous sensing and actuation interfaces, executed through a long-running closed loop, and constrained by safety requirements despite the non-determinism of language models [ 3 ] . To mitigate these difficulties, language-level reasoning in many existing systems remains centralized: a cloud, edge, or swarm-level agent maintains a global view and generates mission plans, while individual UAVs execute them through conventional controllers [ 4 , 3 ] . Such architectures depend on reliable connectivity to an external coordinator and introduce communication and computational bottlenecks as observations and control decisions are continuously exchanged and the swarm state grows [ 2 ] . Assigning an independent agent to each UAV instead enables local decision making, distributes the reasoning workload, and removes a central point of failure. Although distributed LLM-based UAV designs are beginning to emerge [ 5 ] , fully decentralized control introduces additional challenges: each agent reasons from partial observations, coordinates over bandwidth-constrained links, and operates under onboard memory, computation, energy, and latency constraints that favor smaller Small Language Models (SLMs) with more limited reasoning capabilities [ 2 ] . However, existing distributed agentic UAV architectures do not explicitly address how long-running local knowledge should be organized and selectively disseminated among resource-constrained agents.

Indeed, every action produces observations and execution feedback, while cooperation contributes a continuous stream of peer messages. As these records accumulate, replaying the complete transcript can bury mission-critical information among transient or redundant events. This degradation is commonly described as context rot , which refers to the model failing to use relevant information embedded in long inputs even before the context limit is reached [ 6 ] . In a UAV swarm, such degradation can directly affect mission safety and completion, e.g., an agent that overlooks a mandatory landing instruction may continue unsafe execution, potentially resulting in a collision, vehicle loss, or mission failure. Long-running control therefore requires a bounded and structured representation of accumulated knowledge that preserves mission-relevant information while separating it from transient history [ 7 , 8 ] . Regarding information dissemination, indiscriminately flooding observations wastes bandwidth and fills peer contexts with redundant information. Delegating each per-message, per-neighbor forwarding decision to the SLM can also introduce substantial reasoning overhead, enlarge the context, and interfere with the UAV control lifecycle.

We therefore propose a fully distributed architecture in which every UAV hosts an independent SLM-based agent, a Context Manager, and an Interest-Aware Gossip Engine. Each UAV continuously reasons over mission information, locally accumulated knowledge, execution feedback, and asynchronously received peer information, enabling its subsequent actions to adapt without a centralized coordinator. Knowledge produced during this process is represented as atomic notes , which are self-contained, metadata-enriched semantic units derived from the interaction history [ 8 ] . The Context Manager organizes these notes into a fixed Core Memory containing mission information, a Local Note Queue, and a peer-specific Neighbor Note Queue. The queues are token-bounded to prevent uncontrolled context growth while preserving information relevant to subsequent reasoning.

For information dissemination, we draw on a fundamental property of effective gossip: information should be forwarded only when it is novel to the recipient. Unlike conventional gossip mechanisms that are agnostic to message content, our approach evaluates forwarding decisions directly from the semantic content of the information being exchanged. For each one-hop neighbor, newly generated or received notes are compared with the peer-specific history using semantic similarity and recency. A strong match with recent information indicates that the peer likely already possesses equivalent knowledge, whereas semantic dissimilarity indicates greater novelty. Fixed thresholds map this novelty estimate to suppression, compact forwarding, or full forwarding. These decisions are performed deterministically rather than through additional SLM invocations, providing low-overhead and transparent information dissemination.

The main contributions of this work are:

Distributed agent lifecycle: mission-agnostic lifecycle for local UAV control by independent SLM-based agents, without a centralized coordinator;

Context organization: A bounded memory organization that structures mission, local, and peer-specific knowledge as semantic notes for long-running SLM control;

Interest-Aware Gossip Engine: A deterministic recipient-specific dissemination policy that combines semantic novelty and recency to suppress, compact, or fully forward information.

We evaluate the architecture using ten UAVs in a search-and-rescue mission involving 5, 10, or 20 moving survivors, with the objective of correctly identifying the total number of individuals. The proposed policy completes all experimental runs, whereas the evaluated SLM-based baselines exhibit mission failures. Compared with the most successful SLM baseline, the proposed approach uses approximately half the inference tokens and reduces transmitted data from approximately 6–7 MB to below 0.5 MB per mission, while achieving a lower survivor-count error.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. 2 reviews related work; Sec. 3 presents architecture; Sec. 4 and Sec. 5 describe context management and interest-aware gossip, respectively; Sec. 6 reports the evaluation; and Sec. 7 concludes the paper.

1. Distributed agent lifecycle: mission-agnostic lifecycle for local UAV control by independent SLM-based agents, without a centralized coordinator;

2. Context organization: A bounded memory organization that structures mission, local, and peer-specific knowledge as semantic notes for long-running SLM control;

3. Interest-Aware Gossip Engine: A deterministic recipient-specific dissemination policy that combines semantic novelty and recency to suppress, compact, or fully forward information.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Early work on embodied control focused on grounding language-model outputs into executable actions. For example, language-model skill scores have been combined with learned affordances to select feasible robot actions, while robot-specific language agents have been used for collaborative planning with centralized
motion planning [ 9 ] .
More recent UAV-oriented work has explored different ways of placing and using language models, including centralized language interpretation with distributed control, edge-assisted architectures with lightweight per-UAV reasoning, and separate language-model decision processes for individual UAVs [ 4 , 5 ] . In these systems, language models are mainly used for mission-level reasoning, task planning, or navigation decisions, while lower-level control is handled by conventional controllers.

When multiple agents cooperate, a key challenge is deciding whether, what, and with whom to communicate. Selective-communication methods address this by identifying decision-relevant neighbors, learning compact messages under communication budgets, or selecting human-readable state features for multi-robot coordination [ 10 , 11 ] . Despite different message representations, they share the goal of avoiding communication that does not aid coordination. Semantic and significance-aware communication follows the same principle by considering the value of information for a specific task, time, or receiver [ 12 ] .

Gossip and peer-to-peer protocols extend information sharing beyond direct agent pairs. Gossip research has mainly studied freshness, redundancy, topology,
and repeated local forwarding, while semantic and multi-objective dissemination has also been identified as an important research direction [ 13 ] .
Semantic peer-to-peer approaches have also combined embeddings and interest-based organization to route events toward relevant peers [ 14 ] . In UAV networks, adaptive gossip protocols have instead used packet-reception history to change forwarding probabilities
and neighbor selection [ 15 ] . These works show how multi-hop dissemination can reduce indiscriminate flooding through semantic routing, selective forwarding, and knowledge of previous transmissions.

These research lines provide main building blocks, but are addressed in isolation. In contrast, our work integrates fully distributed UAV control, semantic memory, and information dissemination into a unified multi-agent architecture in which each UAV hosts an independent SLM.

2026-10-02.title: FedCKA: Representation-Guided Layer Personalization for Federated 3D Perception Across Driving Domains
2026-10-02.authors: Jolle Verhoog , Ali Burak Ünal , Holger Caesar
2026-10-02.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-02.comment: . Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027
2026-10-02.abstract:
Robust perception in intelligent vehicles demands 3D object detectors that remain dependable under domain shifts, such as changes in time of day, location, or weather. However, due to costly annotation and rare shifts, some environments lack sufficient data to train a standalone detector. Federated learning offers a privacy-preserving framework for collaborative model training, enabling clients to benefit from shared learning across diverse environments. Yet, this framework traditionally relies on a single global consensus model, which struggles to perform across heterogeneous local data distributions. Local conditions are better captured by adapting a subset of the model, but many personalization approaches rely on predefined layer partitions or fixed personalization ratios, thereby limiting adaptation to client-specific divergence.
To reduce this rigidity, we propose FedCKA, a Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA)-based strategy that dynamically handles the personalization-globalization trade-off. Specifically, FedCKA computes layer-wise feature similarities between local client models and the global consensus model during training. By converting layer-wise similarity scores into client-specific aggregation masks, FedCKA selectively shares representation-consistent layers.
Evaluation on a unified multi-domain benchmark based on nuScenes shows that FedCKA outperforms established federated baselines, including FedBN, FedRep, and FedSelect, improving average NDS by 7 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The findings offer both a comparative benchmark and a promising direction for robust federated 3D perception across shifts in location, weather, and illumination. Code is available at https://github.com/j-verhoog/FedCKA .
2026-10-02.introduction:
3D Object Detection (3D-OD) is central to robotic perception in Intelligent Vehicles (IV), providing object poses and dimensions needed for planning and safe navigation.
However, domain shifts across vehicles, times of day, weather, and locations substantially degrade 3D detection performance [ 1 ] (see Fig. 1 ).
Because labeled data in niche or edge-case domains can be too scarce to support robust standalone training, a collaborative framework is desirable.
Yet, for IV applications, centrally collecting multimodal sensor data is constrained by privacy barriers and massive data volumes [ 2 ] , while naive localized retraining remains computationally expensive [ 3 ] .

These constraints motivate Federated Learning (FL), which enables privacy-preserving collaborative training for multi-domain adaptation without data centralization [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , by sharing only model updates. However, real-world deployment across heterogeneous data distributions introduces a central personalization-globalization trade-off: which model components should be globally shared versus locally personalized? Many personalization methods resolve this trade-off through static layer partitions or fixed personalization ratios, which may fail to capture client- and layer-wise representation divergence.
For multi-modal 3D-OD, this rigidity is particularly problematic because domain shifts can affect sensor backbones and fusion modules asymmetrically [ 7 ] .

Despite this need, FL for multimodal 3D-OD remains underexplored. While prior federated detection and, more recently, federated 3D-OD studies exist, they do not systematically isolate location-, weather-, and illumination-induced client heterogeneity.
This limits insight into whether personalization helps under these structured client-level domain shifts.
While recent federated 3D detection approaches, including FedM2Former [ 9 ] and FedPillarNet [ 10 ] , address client heterogeneity through personalized learning, they do not systematically isolate location-, weather-, and illumination-induced domains or compare representative FL personalization strategies within a unified 3D-OD benchmark.

To address this gap, we study how federated 3D-OD methods handle location-, weather-, and illumination-induced client heterogeneity, and whether representation consistency can determine which layers should be globally aggregated or locally personalized.
We isolate client-data heterogeneity by focusing on labeled, client-level domain adaptation across location, weather, and illumination, leaving system-level constraints such as client reliability and sensor-configuration variability to future work.
We make the following contributions:

Establish a unified multi-domain federated 3D object detection benchmark based on explicit location-, weather-, and illumination-induced client heterogeneity, enabling controlled evaluation under realistic domain shifts.

Establish a unified multi-domain federated 3D object detection benchmark based on explicit location-, weather-, and illumination-induced client heterogeneity, enabling controlled evaluation under realistic domain shifts.

Introduce FedCKA, a dynamic CKA-based layer masking strategy that uses layer-wise representation similarity to determine which model components should be globally aggregated versus locally personalized.

Demonstrate that FedCKA outperforms established federated baselines, including FedBN, FedRep, and FedSelect, improving average NDS by 7 percentage points over the strongest competitor by identifying domain-sensitive layers.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# II Related Work

3D Object Detection methods are commonly categorized by sensor modality: camera, LiDAR, or multimodal [ 11 ] .
While multimodal methods typically fuse LiDAR and camera data via Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) representations [ 12 ] , they struggle across varying domains like day, night, and adverse weather [ 13 ] .
This limitation motivates methods that can exploit multi-domain data, particularly when such data are distributed across clients and cannot be centrally pooled.

Federated Learning (FL) enables such collaborative training on decentralized data. It commonly operates under client data that is not independent and identically distributed (IID), not centrally shared, or not of equal size across clients [ 14 ] .
This statistical and system heterogeneity introduces challenges for convergence [ 5 ] and cross-domain generalization [ 15 ] .

The foundational FedAvg [ 2 ] algorithm aggregates independent local updates via weighted averaging. While effective under IID conditions, its performance degrades significantly under heterogeneous data distributions [ 16 ] .

Data heterogeneity in FL fundamentally shapes what client models should share and how the server should aggregate their updates. Approaches to managing this heterogeneity span data preprocessing, training objectives, and aggregation schemes [ 14 ] .
For all of these, the main distinction is the objective: aligning all clients toward one domain-invariant model, or producing multiple domain-adapted models.

To learn a more domain-invariant global model, methods such as FedProx [ 5 ] , FedDyn [ 17 ] , and SCAFFOLD [ 6 ] reduce client drift during training.
Other approaches use task arithmetic [ 18 ] to align client update gradients and estimate a less conflicting global update direction [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] .
However, a single global model may be suboptimal under strong client heterogeneity, and these methods require problem-specific manual parameter tuning.
Personalized FL addresses this by adapting models to client-specific domains while retaining shared knowledge.
Common approaches keep batch normalization or other targeted layers client-specific, as in FedBN [ 4 ] and FedRep [ 22 ] .
Because these methods require manually predefined global and domain-specific layer partitions, this static approach can be suboptimal when domain specificity varies across layers or clients.

Recent work addresses this rigidity by using model updates to infer which parameters to mask for personalization.
FedSelect [ 23 ] assumes the largest parameter updates are the most domain-significant and personalizes them.
FedMC [ 24 ] uses the Fisher information derived from gradient magnitudes to identify the most sensitive parameters for personalization.
Although these methods avoid manual partitioning, they still rely on parameter-space importance by implicitly assuming that same-index parameters across clients correspond to comparable functional components, which may not hold [ 25 ] . To overcome the limitations of parameter-space comparisons and manual layer selection, this work selects personalized layers based on representational consistency across clients.

2026-10-02.title: Supervise What Decides Success: Criterion-Aligned Auxiliary Losses for Latent World-Model Planning
2026-10-02.authors: Takumi Hara , Kanata Suzuki
2026-10-02.comment: . Under review
2026-10-02.abstract: Latent world models plan by scoring candidate action sequences with distances in latent space. However, task success is judged by physical quantities, which we call the success-criterion quantities. In all four latent world models we examine, the end-effector position is encoded in the latent state with an error larger than the success criterion allows. Such a latent state cannot separate successful candidates from failing ones. We propose an auxiliary loss that uses success-criterion quantities as training targets, whereas existing latent world models take them only as inputs. During training, a linear head on the encoder and predictor outputs regresses the success-criterion quantities, and the regression error is added to the training loss. The head is discarded after training, so the model, its cost, and its inputs at test time are unchanged. This loss alone improves the success rate on PushT and cube by 3.5% and 3.4% (absolute), respectively, and both improvements are statistically significant. A success criterion thus specifies what a world model must retain in its latent state, and we show that it can serve directly as a training target.
2026-10-02.introduction:
A world model predicts how actions change the world ( Hafner et al., 2019 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ) . A latent world model encodes the observation image into a low-dimensional latent state with an encoder and makes this prediction in latent space ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Assran et al., 2025 ; Maes et al., 2026 ) . Given a goal image of the scene the robot should reach, the planner selects the action sequence whose predicted latent state is closest to the latent state of the goal image. No pixels are reconstructed. The only quantity that ranks candidate action sequences is this latent distance.

Whether a trial succeeds is decided by the success criterion of each benchmark. A success criterion asks whether the positions of the hand and the objects lie within a tolerance of their values at the goal. Since the latent distance alone ranks the candidates, planning can succeed only if a candidate whose physical quantities used in the criterion, which we call the success-criterion quantities, lie within the tolerance is also the one with the smallest latent distance. Nothing in training asks for this condition. The training loss supervises only the next latent state; the success-criterion quantities appear nowhere in the loss. Indeed, in all four latent world models we examine, the hand position read out from the latent state by linear regression deviates from the true hand position by more than the tolerance of the success criterion. This deviation does not vanish with representation size or pretraining.

Prior work that uses physical quantities, including the success-criterion quantities, in training falls into two groups. DINO-WM ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) and V-JEPA 2-AC ( Assran et al., 2025 ) concatenate the proprioceptive state, such as the end-effector position, which we call the hand, to the input. Feeding a quantity as an input does not ask whether the latent state after the predictor retains it at the precision of the success criterion (Section 3.2 ). PhyLatent ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) and PSG-JEPA ( Yan et al., 2026 ) use physical quantities as training targets, but the designer chooses which quantities to supervise, and whether the targets correspond to the success criterion is never asked.

We propose an auxiliary loss that uses the success-criterion quantities as training targets. A linear head is applied to both the encoder output and the predictor output, and the error between its readout and the success-criterion quantities recorded in the demonstrations is added to the training loss (Figure 1 ). The head is discarded after training, so the model, its inputs, and the latent distance used for planning are identical to the baseline at test time, and the computation does not increase. What is supervised is fixed by the success criterion, not chosen by the designer.

The auxiliary loss, however, only drives down the readout error of the success-criterion quantities by one shared linear head from the encoder output and the predictor output. How much a difference in the success-criterion quantities between two candidates shows up as a difference in their latent distances enters the loss nowhere. A corrected readout therefore need not raise the planning success rate. Prior work reports cases where a proxy metric, such as video-prediction quality or linear-probe accuracy, improves while the success rate does not ( Tian et al., 2023 ; Burns et al., 2024 ) , and in our own experiments the frozen V-JEPA 2 shows a corrected readout together with a lower success rate. We therefore evaluate the auxiliary loss by the success rate, and use an ablation over which success-criterion quantities are supervised to determine in which trials the effect appears and which supervision avoids degradation.

Our contributions are threefold.

We propose an auxiliary loss that uses the success-criterion quantities as training targets. A linear head is applied to the encoder and predictor outputs only during training, so the model, its inputs, and the latent distance used for planning are unchanged at test time (Section 2 ).

On four manipulation tasks, a model supervised with the success-criterion quantities significantly improves the success rate over the baseline, and the improvement replicates on a world model with a frozen pretrained encoder (Section 3.2 ).

Through an ablation over which success-criterion quantities are supervised, we show that supervising all quantities in the criterion never significantly degrades the success rate on any task, for both a world model trained from scratch and one with a frozen pretrained encoder (Section 3.3 ).

A success criterion specifies what a world model must retain in its latent state. This work shows that the specification can be used directly as a training target, and delineates how far its effect reaches.

# 2 Method

## 2.1 Planning in latent space

A latent world model consists of an encoder and a predictor (Figure 1 (a), top). The encoder maps the observation image x t x_{t} to a latent state 𝒛 t = Enc ⁡ ( x t ) {\bm{z}}_{t}=\mathrm{Enc}(x_{t}) . The predictor predicts the next latent state 𝒛 ^ t + 1 = f ( 𝒛 t − H + 1 : t , a t − H + 1 : t ) \hat{{\bm{z}}}_{t+1}=f({\bm{z}}_{t-H+1:t},\,a_{t-H+1:t}) from the history of latent states and actions, where H H is the history length and a t a_{t} is the action. For planning, the latent state 𝒛 g {\bm{z}}_{g} of the goal image serves as the target, and candidate action sequences are evaluated as follows. For each candidate, the predictor is applied sequentially to obtain the terminal latent state 𝒛 ^ T \hat{{\bm{z}}}_{T} . The squared distance ‖ 𝒛 ^ T − 𝒛 g ‖ 2 \|\hat{{\bm{z}}}_{T}-{\bm{z}}_{g}\|^{2} between the terminal and the goal latent states is the cost, and the candidate that minimizes it is found by the cross-entropy method (CEM) ( Rubinstein, 1999 ) . CEM ranks candidates by this cost alone, so nothing but the latent distance decides the ranking.

## 2.2 Coarse readout of the success-criterion quantities

Because candidates are ranked by the latent distance alone, planning can succeed only if a candidate whose success-criterion quantities lie within the tolerance is also the one with the smallest latent distance (Section 1 ). At the least, this requires that two states whose success-criterion quantities differ by as little as the tolerance be separated by the latent distance near the goal; it does not require the latent distance to agree with physical distance everywhere. The simplest test of this requirement is to read the success-criterion quantities out of the latent state by linear regression. We use ridge regression, a linear regression that penalizes large coefficients, on frames not used for training ( Alain & Bengio, 2017 ) . On stack, the median error of the hand position read out this way is 3.2 cm for the baseline LeWM model, and 3.10 cm, 2.10 cm, and 4.02 cm for the image features of three frozen pretrained encoders (DINOv2-S, DINOv2-L, and V-JEPA 2; Section 3.1 ), all outside the 2 cm tolerance. We introduce the auxiliary loss to close this gap. Supervised with the hand, the error of the LeWM model falls to 0.14 cm (Figure 1 (b); Table 7 in Appendix D ).

## 2.3 Auxiliary loss supervised by the success-criterion quantities

The auxiliary loss corrects the coarse readout of Section 2.2 by restricting the targets to the success-criterion quantities 𝒑 t {\bm{p}}_{t} and adding only one linear head per quantity and one term to the training loss. For the k k -th success-criterion quantity 𝒑 t ( k ) {\bm{p}}^{(k)}_{t} we place a linear head 𝑾 k {\bm{W}}_{k} and apply it to both the encoder output 𝒛 t {\bm{z}}_{t} and the predictor output 𝒛 ^ t \hat{{\bm{z}}}_{t} . The squared error between the head’s output and 𝒑 t ( k ) {\bm{p}}^{(k)}_{t} is added to the training loss.

The second and third terms of Eq. (1) are the auxiliary loss; they correspond to the paths in Figure 1 (a) that are active only during training. The second term is the readout error from the encoder output and the third from the predictor output. ℒ wm \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{wm}} is the loss the world model has originally; for LeWM it consists of the latent prediction loss and a regularizer on the latent distribution. The auxiliary loss leaves it unchanged. A training sample is a clip of N f N_{f} consecutive frames cut from a demonstration. 𝒛 ^ t \hat{{\bm{z}}}_{t} is the one-step prediction of the latent state at frame t t from the frames before it, so a sample yields N f − 1 N_{f}-1 predictions. The second term averages over all N f N_{f} frames and the third over the N f − 1 N_{f}-1 predictions. d k d_{k} is the number of dimensions of the success-criterion quantity k k . k k indexes the success-criterion quantities and λ k \lambda_{k} is the weight on quantity k k ; the values are listed in the table in Appendix A .

When there are several success-criterion quantities, the heads 𝑾 k {\bm{W}}_{k} are independent across quantities. The same 𝑾 k {\bm{W}}_{k} , however, is applied to both the encoder output and the predictor output. The planning cost compares a latent state produced by the predictor with the latent state of the goal image, so unless both outputs hold the success-criterion quantities in a form the same linear head can read, a difference in the quantities does not enter the cost. Sharing the head builds this requirement into the loss.

Rather than using the readout as a planning cost, we discard the linear heads after training. We discard it so that the world model keeps planning from the goal image alone, with a cost over everything the latent state holds; the auxiliary loss only asks that the success-criterion quantities be among what it holds. Inference with the head removed is identical to the baseline: the planning cost, the computation, and the required inputs are unchanged, so no sensor for the success-criterion quantities is needed at test time. The only parameters added during training are those of the linear head.

The targets 𝒑 t {\bm{p}}_{t} are the physical quantities already recorded in the training data, so training needs no new sensor or measurement. We restrict the targets to the success-criterion quantities because the success criterion specifies what the latent state must retain for planning to succeed, and supervising a quantity outside the criterion does not move the success rate (Section 3.2 ).

2026-10-02.title: PhysicsLENS: Diagnosing Physical Property Blindness in Video Generation Models
2026-10-02.authors: Isaiah Milkey , Som Sagar , Aditya Taparia , Xinyuan Liu , Jiqing Wen , Ransalu Senanayake
2026-10-02.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-02.abstract:
Reliable video world models could provide scalable predictive environments for robot learning, planning, and evaluation. However, generated robot videos can violate physical principles and complete tasks through physically implausible behavior, limiting their reliability for robot learning and planning.
Current video-generation benchmarks exclude physics that are inherently hidden by visuals (e.g., weight, viscosity, friction). Due to this, video models are evaluated on the fidelity of physics, not the underlying accuracy of physics.
We introduce PhysicsLENS, a dataset and benchmark for evaluating plausibility of physical properties grounded in robotics. PhysicsLENS uses matched scenario pairs that hold the same conditioning frame and task, while varying underlying physics in the scene description. Scenarios are curated from public robot video sources and annotated across seven physical domains: collision, gravity, momentum, friction, deformation, fluid, and causality. We evaluate across four video generation models, producing over 400 human-annotated labels.
Results show that plausible-looking videos often ignore the stated property (34 of 47), and that stating the property lowers plausibility only slightly and not significantly.
2026-10-02.introduction:
Video generation models could provide scalable predictive environments for robot learning ( Yang et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA, 2025a ) , planning ( Du et al., 2023 ) , and evaluation ( Quevedo et al., 2025 ) . By generating diverse interactions without repeatedly collecting real-world data, these models could expose robots to rare events, unfamiliar objects, and changing physical conditions ( Jang et al., 2025 ) . However, increasing the volume of generated data is useful only if the videos reliably represent the physical consequences of actions. A video may appear realistic and depict successful task completion while violating friction, momentum, object permanence, or other physical constraints. Such violations undermine the usefulness of generated videos as predictive environments, yet may go undetected by benchmarks focused on visual realism and task success. We therefore require a benchmark that evaluates whether generated interactions respect the physical properties and constraints that govern them.

Existing video-generation benchmarks capture this reliability only partially. Most benchmarks focus on visual quality, temporal consistency, or motion plausibility. These criteria can identify obvious artifacts, but cannot determine whether a model correctly grounds the physical properties specified in its conditioning input. Properties such as weight, friction, viscosity, and deformability may not be observable from a single image. Consequently, visually identical scenes can require different outcomes: a robot should interact differently with a heavy object than with a light one, or with a slippery surface than with a rough one. A model can therefore generate a plausible video while producing behavior that is physically incorrect for the stated condition.

We introduce PhysicsLENS, a benchmark for evaluating both physical plausibility and physical-property grounding in robot video generation. The dataset comprises of curated image–text prompts, more than 400 clips generated by four video generation models, and structured human annotations for every clip. We construct prompts from public robot videos, grouping scenarios into seven physical domains: collision, gravity, momentum, friction, deformation, fluid, and causality. In unobservable scenarios, the text specifies a physical property that cannot be inferred from that frame. Matched unobservable prompts keep the visual context and task fixed while varying the specified property, allowing us to test whether generated interactions reflect the corresponding physical consequences. Figure 1 summarizes the benchmark workflow.

The benchmark evaluates generated clips through two complementary tracks. In the human evaluation track, annotators rate physical plausibility and task completion, describe and categorize visible physical violations, and assess whether interactions in unobservable scenarios reflect the stated property. In the automated evaluation track, a four-stage hierarchical pipeline screens each clip, localizes potential violations, verifies them through targeted vision-language model questions, and reports supporting evidence. Across four video-generation models and 439 generated clips, the results show that a video’s apparent physical plausibility does not guarantee correct grounding in a hidden property. Our contributions are:

We introduce PhysicsLENS, a robotics-focused benchmark covering seven physical domains and distinguishing physical plausibility from physical-property grounding.

We construct matched scenarios that preserve visual context while varying text-specified physical conditions, including properties that cannot be inferred from appearance alone.

We present a multi-stage evaluation procedure and benchmark four video-generation models with more than 400 human judgments, finding that plausible-looking videos often ignore the stated property.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Video world models are increasingly used as simulators and data sources for robot learning ( Yang et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA, 2025a ; Jang et al., 2025 ) , yet videos that look realistic can still break physics ( Kang et al., 2025 ; Motamed et al., 2026 ) . Distributional metrics and general benchmark suites mainly measure perceptual quality ( Unterthiner et al., 2018 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) , although VBench-2.0 adds physics dimensions ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Physics benchmarks score commonsense physics in generated videos ( Bansal et al., 2025 ; Bansal et al., 2026 ; Meng et al., 2025 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) , compare generations with real experiments or recorded outcomes ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Motamed et al., 2026 ) , or turn measured motion into verifiable rewards ( Le et al., 2025 ) . Physion-Eval and PQSG also localize failures, using expert reasoning traces and VLM-generated question graphs, respectively ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Pothiraj et al., 2026 ) . For robotics, WorldSimBench, EWMBench, RBench, and RoboWM-Bench evaluate generated manipulation videos on visual quality, motion, task adherence, or whether the motion can be executed as actions ( Qin et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . WorldModelBench scores instruction following and physics adherence across domains that include robotics ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and RoboGaze reports temporally localized glitches under a robotics-specific taxonomy ( Nguyen et al., 2026 ) . To our knowledge, none of these benchmarks separates properties that are visible in the conditioning frame from properties stated only in the prompt (Table 1 ), so a high score cannot show whether a model followed the stated physics or only what the scene looks like.

Inferring properties that appearance does not reveal is a classic test of physical understanding: Physion++ and ComPhy ask models to infer mass, friction, elasticity, or charge from observed interactions ( Tung et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2022 ) . PhysicsLENS reverses this flow of information: the property is stated in text, and the generator must turn it into motion. Controllable generators receive physical quantities as dedicated inputs, such as forces or mass and friction coefficients ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Gillman et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . T2V-CompBench tests whether prompt attributes bind to the right objects, but only for visible attributes such as color, shape, and motion direction ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . We instead test whether general-purpose image-to-video models follow a property given only in plain language, with the frame and task held fixed.

Automatic physics evaluation often relies on vision-language models (VLMs), either fine-tuned or prompted ( Bansal et al., 2025 ; Meng et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA, 2025b ) , but their reliability is limited. VLMs struggle with physical-world understanding ( Chow et al., 2025 ) , most models score near chance on intuitive-physics tests ( Bordes et al., 2025 ) , and plausible verbal explanations can hide wrong estimates of velocity and acceleration ( Puyin et al., 2026 ) . Multimodal judges also show biases and inconsistent judgments ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , and video VLMs have limited fine-grained motion and temporal grounding ( Hong et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Measured evidence helps: MASS adds depth, object grounding, and motion tracking to VLM reasoning ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , and GeoPhys finds that VLM judges detect physics violations near chance while a training-free score on frozen image-encoder features does better ( Internò et al., 2026 ) . PhysicsLENS follows this direction by combining tracked measurements with targeted VLM questions, and we test it directly against human annotations.

2026-10-02.title: FutureWorlds: Learning Robotic World Models from Alternative Futures
2026-10-02.authors: Hao Wu , Shengju Qian , Weiyan Wang , Fan Xu , Fan Zhang , Yuanpeng He , Qingsong Wen , Yuxuan Liang
2026-10-02.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-02.comment: including references and appendix. Code: this https URL
2026-10-02.abstract:
Robotic world models predict action-conditioned future scenes, providing a foundation for understanding action outcomes.
However, turning alternative predictions into useful learning signals remains challenging: similar candidates limit informative quality comparisons, while diverging trajectories require persistent maintenance of their individual histories.
We introduce FutureWorlds , a framework that unifies candidate construction, history maintenance, and learning from relative quality.
Built on a multimodal discrete autoregressive model, FutureWorlds uses diverse beam search during reinforcement learning to construct candidate futures that balance confidence and diversity.
Candidate-specific bounded memory preserves scene states and ensures that generation and policy scoring use matching histories.
We further propose MemSPO (Memory-Conditioned Search-Guided Policy Optimization), which converts video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages to optimize the world model.
On RT-1, BridgeV2, and RoboCasa, FutureWorlds reduces LPIPS for 32-frame predictions by 14.78%, 20.84%, and 9.12%, respectively, relative to the strongest baseline on each dataset.
Under fixed evaluation configurations, only 200 MemSPO updates further improve generation quality and support continued prediction beyond the training horizon.
Memory ablations, decoding sensitivity analysis, and optical-flow evaluation show that these gains extend beyond visual quality to more accurate motion prediction and more consistent object states.
Project page and code: https://github.com/Alexander-wu/FutureWorlds .
2026-10-02.introduction:
Robotic world models predict how scenes evolve in response to actions, providing a foundation for action-outcome prediction ( Finn et al., 2016 ) , visual planning ( Ebert et al., 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2019 ) , behavior learning ( Hafner et al., 2020 ) , and policy evaluation ( Yin et al., 2026 ; GigaWorld Team et al., 2026 ) . Given the same observations, action sequence, and instruction, a model can propose multiple predictions of the future. These alternative futures represent different hypotheses about the scene’s evolution, with varying robot motions, object states, and prediction quality. Their differences offer a learning opportunity: by constructing useful alternatives and comparing their outcomes against recorded observations, a world model can learn from the predictions it generates.

Most autoregressive world models learn from recorded trajectories through supervised training. Their reliance on ground-truth histories during training differs from the self-generated histories available at inference, allowing errors to accumulate along a rollout ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Bengio et al., 2015 ) . Token-level likelihood also does not directly optimize complete generated sequences ( Ranzato et al., 2016 ; Rennie et al., 2017 ) . Figure 1 illustrates this challenge: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can leave predictions with insufficient robot motion or inaccurate poses. Reinforcement learning (RL) connects generated outputs to sequence-level rewards ( Black et al., 2024 ) . In world modeling, RLVR-World uses decoded prediction metrics ( Wu et al., 2025a ) , while RLIR introduces inverse-dynamics rewards for action following ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . These advances enable learning from trajectory feedback, but the resulting learning signal also depends on which futures the model compares . More candidates alone do not guarantee useful comparative feedback. Effective post-training therefore requires informative candidate differences and history-consistent comparisons that turn alternative futures into reliable learning signals.

Learning from alternative futures requires coordinated candidate construction and history management. Candidate quality and diversity depend on the generation strategy ( Holtzman et al., 2020 ) : independent sampling does not explicitly coordinate these properties across candidates, while conventional beam search can concentrate on nearly identical sequences ( Vijayakumar et al., 2018 ) . A useful candidate set therefore needs to balance model confidence with distinct predictions. As these predictions unfold, each branch develops its own robot and object states. Retaining the corresponding history becomes especially important when prediction extends beyond the pretraining horizon, motivating bounded memory for sustained generation ( Dai et al., 2019 ; Wu et al., 2025b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Learning introduces a further requirement: policy scoring must condition on the same retained history that produces each candidate. These considerations connect three roles— constructing informative alternatives, maintaining their individual histories, and learning from their relative quality.

We introduce FutureWorlds , a framework that learns robotic world models by constructing, maintaining, and comparing alternative futures (Figure 2 ). We instantiate the framework with a multimodal discrete autoregressive model ( van den Oord et al., 2017 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) , whose token probabilities support candidate expansion and trajectory scoring under visual, action, and language conditioning. To construct alternatives , diverse beam search combines model likelihood with cross-candidate differences during RL training. To maintain their histories , candidate-specific memory retains scene and state anchors alongside rolling context, supporting longer predictions within a bounded memory budget. Search and memory operate together as each candidate evolves, and generation and policy scoring use matching histories. To compare and learn , MemSPO ( Mem ory-Conditioned S earch-Guided P olicy O ptimization) converts video trajectory rewards into group-relative advantages and updates the model through a search-guided surrogate based on GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and clipped policy optimization ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) . Candidate quality differences thus become feedback for improving the model that generates them.

Our evaluation covers RT-1 ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) , BridgeData V2 ( Walke et al., 2023 ) , and RoboCasa ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) . On 32-frame predictions, FutureWorlds reduces LPIPS by 14.78%, 20.84%, and 9.12% relative to the strongest baseline on each dataset. Under fixed evaluation configurations, only 200 MemSPO updates improve generation and support prediction beyond the training horizon. Memory ablations, decoding sensitivity analysis, and motion evaluation further assess historical context, robustness, and dynamic consistency. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

Learning from Alternative Futures. We introduce FutureWorlds , a framework that organizes model-generated futures into training experiences through coordinated candidate construction, history maintenance, and relative comparison.

Search-Guided, History-Consistent Learning. We propose MemSPO , a GRPO-based post-training algorithm that combines diverse candidate search with candidate-specific memory and matches the histories used for generation and policy scoring.

Experimental Evaluation. We evaluate generation quality and long-horizon prediction, analyze memory and decoding robustness, and assess motion consistency and inference resource requirements. LPIPS decreases by 9.12–20.84% versus the strongest baseline on each dataset.
2026-10-02.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Robotic World Models. Robotic world models predict action consequences for planning and policy learning. Early work uses action-conditioned video prediction for visual control ( Finn et al., 2016 ; Ebert et al., 2018 ) ; PlaNet ( Hafner et al., 2019 ) and Dreamer ( Hafner et al., 2020 ) learn latent dynamics. UniSim ( Yang et al., 2024 ) combines language and low-level controls for visual simulation, while Vid2World ( Huang et al., 2026 ) adapts video diffusion for interactive prediction. VideoGPT ( Yan et al., 2021 ) and iVideoGPT ( Wu et al., 2024 ) develop discrete autoregressive models, with iVideoGPT integrating observations, actions, and rewards through compressive tokenization. FutureWorlds uses discrete autoregression to construct and compare alternative futures under shared visual, action, and language conditions.

Memory for Long-Horizon World Modeling. Transformer-XL ( Dai et al., 2019 ) propagates segment-level history, while StreamingLLM ( Xiao et al., 2024 ) retains initial attention sinks and recent context. StreamingT2V ( Henschel et al., 2025 ) combines short- and long-term memory; FramePack ( Zhang & Agrawala, 2025 ) packs historical frames into a fixed context budget. Wu et al. (2025b) introduce geometry-grounded memory for scene revisits. Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2026 ) and Mem-World ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) retrieve robotic observations through pose conditioning and spatiotemporal surfel indexing, respectively. FutureWorlds maintains bounded, candidate-specific histories for long-horizon prediction and uses matching contexts for generation and policy scoring, preserving distinct conditioning as candidate futures diverge.

Search-Guided Reinforcement Learning for World Models. MIXER ( Ranzato et al., 2016 ) and SCST ( Rennie et al., 2017 ) optimize sequence metrics through policy gradients; DDPO ( Black et al., 2024 ) extends reward optimization to diffusion models. RLVR-World ( Wu et al., 2025a ) rewards decoded prediction quality, while RLIR ( Ye et al., 2025 ) evaluates action following through inverse dynamics. Candidate construction determines which predictions provide this feedback. Diverse Beam Search ( Vijayakumar et al., 2018 ) reduces redundancy, Expert Iteration ( Anthony et al., 2017 ) alternates search and policy learning, and BGRPO ( Lee et al., 2025 ) combines beam-generated candidates with rank-aware rewards for algebraic tasks. QWM ( Dong et al., 2026 ) searches predicted futures for robotic action selection and learns policies and values from real transitions. FutureWorlds instead searches futures under a fixed action sequence. MemSPO updates the video predictor from their relative quality using history-consistent scoring and a search-guided surrogate based on GRPO’s group-relative advantages and clipped updates ( Shao et al., 2024 ) .
