2026-10-05.title: A Passive AI System for Verifying Physical State on Automated Liquid Handlers
2026-10-05.authors: Junqiong Joanne Qiu , Zeckria Kamrany , Ananya Anand , Emma Vidal , Yunjia Johanna Bai , Nathan S Chen , Sean Son , Varada Abhyankar , Taryn Jakub , Eleazar Eskin
2026-10-05.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-05.introduction:
Laboratories are increasingly automating routine workflows. In a 2025 survey, 49% of respondents reported using robotics or automation in their company’s laboratories [ 1 ] . Automated liquid handlers are a key tool in laboratory automation, supporting molecular biology workflows such as sequencing library preparation, PCR setup, and high-throughput processing [ 2 ] . They enable workflows to be run reproducibly with minimal manual labor. These systems are offered by manufacturers such as Opentrons, Tecan, and Hamilton. Quality-control studies of laboratory automation show that liquid handlers require routine checks to stay accurate and reliable, since components can fail over time [ 3 , 4 ] . Setup errors, however, can occur even earlier: a plate placed in the wrong slot, the wrong tip rack loaded, a reservoir missing, or labware shifted or occluded on the deck. These errors can cause collisions, damage the robot, or lead to incorrect liquid transfers that compromise the experiment. This physical starting state requires manual assembly: labware, reagents, plates, and tip racks must be placed on the deck in the correct locations before the protocol begins. Correct deck setup relies on user confirmation, and there is no system in place to confirm that the setup matches the robot’s expectations, making the initial manual deck setup step prone to errors. Therefore, a monitoring layer is needed to answer three questions: what experiment the operator is running, whether the deck is prepared correctly for it, and whether the robot is executing the protocol correctly.

To implement a monitoring layer, a visual system is required. Currently, camera-based deck checking is available on the Opentrons Flex, which carries a built-in 2 MP camera that records images and video [ 5 ] . The camera sends images to an operator or to storage, but does not report whether the observed labware is correct for a given protocol. Tecan Fluent workstations run DeckCheck, which photographs the worktable after loading and compares the live layout against a stored reference [ 6 ] . However, DeckCheck only compares pixels and not labware identity, leading to the manual listing differences it cannot flag: different tip types, missing tubes on partially loaded runners, plates rotated by 180 degrees, and well shape [ 6 ] . Research systems have used computer vision to monitor laboratory processes and detect anomalies during automated liquid transfer [ 7 , 8 ] , and have supported colorimetric titration [ 9 ] , but these remain isolated capabilities rather than a general check against a protocol’s requirements.

Existing options do not provide a modular and accessible verification layer that a laboratory can add to the liquid handler it already owns. DeckCheck is integrated into a high-end workstation and is unavailable for lower-cost platforms. Accessible self-driving laboratories close the loop between planning, execution, measurement, and decision-making [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , but also require tightly integrated instruments, data infrastructure, and expertise that academic life-science laboratories often lack [ 13 ] . As a result, a laboratory running an affordable liquid handler has no straightforward way to check its deck against the intended protocol.

Such a system must meet four constraints: it must be inexpensive, leave robot hardware and firmware untouched, run on an available computer, and add no work to the operator’s routine. Computer vision makes this checking system practical: a camera is an inexpensive non-contact sensor, and deep learning now localizes, segments, and classifies objects reliably in visually cluttered scenes [ 14 , 15 ] . Applied to a deck image, these methods can find each slot, separate labware from its background, identify the labware type, and map it to the robot’s canonical deck coordinates, turning a photograph into a structured deck state that can be compared with a protocol.

We present the Labware Setup Checker, a passive vision system for the Opentrons Flex that utilizes a low-cost camera and lightweight models to confirm an observed deck setup against an intended protocol within seconds. A consumer webcam outside the robot observes the deck. The checker segments the image into slots, classifies masked and cropped labware images, corrects the assignments against canonical slot geometry, and compares the result with a reference protocol library, marking each slot as correct, wrong, misplaced, or unexpected. The checker operates passively and noninvasively, requiring only a simple session setup and checking the deck automatically without interrupting robot operation or adding manual steps to the established procedure. This work contributes an external verification architecture for the Opentrons Flex that requires no hardware or firmware modification, protocol-aware deck perception at seconds-scale latency in a deployed setting, and an evaluation system compatible with routine laboratory workflows.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2  Results

## 2.1  The checker reports protocol-aware deck states without modifying the robot

The checker is implemented as a web application (Figure 1 ). The operator selects the robot type and camera and then starts the live feed. The checker periodically samples the camera feed and overlays the image with predicted slot labels, labware labels, and confidence scores. It also displays the expected protocol layout and updates the detection log for each sampled frame. Because the checker runs independently of the robot controller, it requires no hardware or firmware modification and does not interrupt robot operation.

The checker processes each sampled frame by segmenting the observable deck regions, classifying the labware within each region, correcting the assignments against the canonical deck geometry, and comparing the observed slot–labware pairs with a protocol reference. The Opentrons Flex deck was represented by 14 observable regions, including the combined A1/B1 thermocycler region and all visible slots A2 through D4. D3 was excluded because the trash chute occupied that location in the evaluated protocols.

The checker converts the frame into a structured deck state containing the visible slots, predicted labware, classification confidence, and whether each slot matches the expected protocol. Each slot is assigned one of four status labels: correct when the observed state satisfies the protocol reference, wrong when expected labware is missing, wrong_slot when labware is detected in another protocol slot, and not_in_setup when the observed labware is not used by the protocol. The operator can therefore compare the observed deck, expected protocol layout, and per-slot results before starting the run.

## 2.2  The checker recognizes an empty deck and tracks deck preparation

We evaluated the checker on an empty Opentrons Flex deck and during preparation of a SwabSeq Respiratory Viral Panel (RVP) pre-PCR deck, a routine workflow in the laboratory.

To evaluate whether the checker could distinguish empty slots from missed detections, we analyzed 113 frames of an empty Opentrons Flex deck. Only the permanent C1 temperature module and D1 aluminum block remained on the deck. Across all 113 frames, the checker consistently recognized the remaining deck slots as empty (Figure 2 A).

During RVP pre-PCR deck preparation, the checker reported C2 as empty in the first seven frames. After the operator placed the MicroAmp base at C2, the checker identified the base in the next frame. The MicroAmp plate was then placed on the base, and the checker identified the complete MicroAmp plate-and-base assembly correctly in all 29 frames collected before robot motion. The checker therefore tracked the C2 setup from an empty slot to the base and then to the completed assembly (Figure 2 B–D).

For the 29 completed-deck frames, the checker returned results for all 406 slot observations. Of these, 348 observations came from the 12 regions requiring exact labware matches, and the remaining 58 observations matched their expected deck states. Among the 348 exact-match observations, the predicted class matched the known deck setup and protocol reference for 331 (95.1%); the remaining 17 were misclassified, including 15 at D1 and two at D4. All four tip racks were correctly classified in all 116 observations, the C2 MicroAmp plate-and-base assembly was correctly classified in all 29 observations, and the five expected-empty slots were correctly classified in all 145 observations. Combining the 331 correct exact-match observations with the other 58 correct observations, the checker assigned a correct verification status to 389 of all 406 observations (95.8%).

The 17 misclassifications arose from visual similarity between two aluminum blocks at D1 and limited slot visibility at D4. At D1, the expected 24-well screw-cap aluminum block was correctly identified in 14 of 29 frames and classified as a Bio-Rad well-plate aluminum block in the other 15 frames. These two aluminum blocks have similar shapes and surface features, indicating that visually similar labware requires better class-specific training. At D4, the expected empty slot was correctly identified in 27 of 29 frames. In the other two frames, the slot was classified as an Abgene deep-well plate with low confidence. D4 was at the edge of the camera’s field of view, and only a narrow portion of the slot was visible.

## 2.3  The checker remains robust to occlusion, camera position, and lighting conditions

To test partial occlusion, we placed four reservoirs with similar appearances across A4, B4, C4, and D4 in all 24 possible arrangements. Tip racks at A3, B3, and C3 partially blocked the reservoirs behind them, while the waste chute obstructed part of D4. We collected 20 consecutive frames for each arrangement, producing 480 frames.

Across the 480 occlusion test frames, deck-region assignment was correct in 6720 of 6720 observations (100%), covering all 14 regions in every frame. This included correct localization of the four partially blocked reservoir positions in 1920 of 1920 observations (100%), with 120 observations for each reservoir–position combination. The three foreground tip racks were also classified correctly in 1440 of 1440 observations (100%). Thus, the oblique view did not prevent the checker from preserving the Flex deck geometry under these intentionally difficult layouts.

We next held the completed RVP pre-PCR deck and protocol reference constant while testing three camera positions under two lighting conditions. The controlled set contained 154 stable frames, with 24 to 28 frames for each camera-position and lighting combination. Figure 3 shows two alternate camera viewpoints during live use of the checker.

Across the 154 stable camera position and lighting frames, the checker detected and assigned all 14 deck regions in every frame, giving 2156 of 2156 correct deck-region observations (100%). Across the complete deck, 2107 of 2156 slot classifications matched the protocol reference (97.73%). The percentages of correct slot classifications at the three camera positions were 96.43%, 96.71%, and 99.87%. The corresponding percentages under the two lighting conditions were 97.68% and 97.77%, and the six individual position–lighting combinations ranged from 92.86% to 100%.

The 49 incorrect slot classifications followed two main patterns tied to specific camera and lighting combinations. At position 1 under lighting condition 1, the D1 aluminum block was classified as a 15-tube rack in all 25 frames; under lighting condition 2 at the same position, D1 was correct in all 25 frames. At position 2 under lighting condition 2, the B3 50 µL tip rack was classified as an Abgene deep-well plate in 22 of 26 frames; under lighting condition 1, B3 was correct in all 24 frames. One additional D1 error occurred at position 2 under lighting condition 2, and one D4 error occurred at position 3 under lighting condition 2. Because the same labware was classified correctly from the other views, these errors are consistent with reflections changing its visible texture at specific camera and lighting combinations. Overall, the checker achieved 100% deck-region localization and 97.73% correct slot classifications across the six combinations.

## 2.4  The perception models achieve high validation accuracy

On the held-out validation sets, the YOLO11m segmentation model reached 0.993 box precision, 1.000 box recall, and 0.995 box mAP@50. Mask mAP@50 was also 0.995, with a mask mAP@50–95 score of 0.884. The YOLO26m classifier reached 0.992 top-1 accuracy and 1.000 top-5 accuracy across 17 classes.

The training logs showed rapid convergence (Figure 4 ). On an NVIDIA T4 GPU in Google Colab, the segmentation model completed 50 epochs in approximately 19 minutes. Segmentation mask mAP@50 rose sharply during the first several epochs and remained stable through epoch 50. The classifier training record used for Figure 4 contains 19 epochs. Its top-1 accuracy remained above 0.95 after epoch 2 and ended at 0.992. A separate classifier training run completed in approximately 15 minutes.

## 2.5  The checker completes deck verification locally and in deployment within seconds

The checker completed deck verification within seconds both locally and during deployment of the TECAN Library Cleanup workflow. Across 10 post-warmup runs on the CPU-only development MacBook Pro, the complete Flex deck-verification path processed a representative 2304 × 1536 2304\times 1536 pixel image in a median of 2.10 s. Preprocessing and PNG serialization took 1.24 s, segmentation took 0.624 s, and classification of 14 masked cropped images took 0.188 s. Slot correction and protocol matching contributed little to the total latency.

The same trained models were used for RVP pre-PCR deck preparation and the TECAN Library Cleanup workflow without additional training or protocol-specific validation. Supporting the additional workflow required only adding its expected deck setup to the backend protocol library. The deployed latency evaluation included 280 frames processed by the AWS-hosted checker during a TECAN Library Cleanup workflow. The checker processed each frame on the server in a median of 3.2 s. Median stage times were 1.64 s for preprocessing, 1.15 s for segmentation, 0.36 s for classification, 26 ms for slot correction, and 1.3 ms for protocol matching. Median end-to-end latency from frame capture to receipt of the verification result was 4.24 s (IQR, 3.52–4.48 s). The median estimated network and browser overhead was 1.10 s. In both the local and deployed settings, image preprocessing contributed more latency than model inference or protocol matching. Although the checker was not optimized for speed, the measured latency was short relative to the several-minute deck-preparation period.

2026-10-05.title: Real-time Event-camera Stereo Visual Odometry via Keytime Gaussian Process Regression
2026-10-05.authors: Nikan Nobari , Jonathan D. Gammell
2026-10-05.comment: Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027, . The corresponding video can be found at this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract: Event cameras have microsecond-level temporal resolution and high dynamic range which make them more resilient to motion blur and poor illumination than standard frame-based cameras. Event-camera visual odometry (VO) pipelines maximize these benefits when they process the asynchronous event stream at the native temporal resolution. Continuous-time Gaussian process (GP) regression and a white-noise-on-acceleration (WNOA) prior can handle asynchronous measurements but result in a prohibitively large estimation state when applied naively.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Frame-based cameras capture visual information as discrete images. Visual odometry (VO) and simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) pipelines built on these cameras have achieved remarkable success [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] but they struggle in the presence of motion blur or poor image contrast which degrade feature tracking and cause inaccurate estimates. This often occurs with highly dynamic camera motions and in environments with poor illumination.

Event cameras use a fundamentally different sensing paradigm that can avoid these problems. They report pixel intensity changes with microsecond-level temporal resolution and possess a higher dynamic range than traditional frame-based sensors. This combination reduces the limitations of standard cameras and promises VO pipelines that are more resilient to motion blur and poor lighting [ 4 ] .

Event-camera VO pipelines must account for the asynchronous nature of event data to achieve the full potential of event cameras. Some discrete event-camera VO pipelines maintain the asynchronous measurement times by using motion-compensated event frames [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] or extracting event-based features [ 11 , 7 ] in their front end but then group events during state estimation and reduce temporal resolution. Continuous-time estimation methods alternatively provide tools to handle the asynchronous measurement times during estimation [ 12 ] . Some Gaussian process (GP) continuous-time VO pipelines (e.g., GPCT [ 13 ] ) use a white-noise-on-acceleration (WNOA) motion prior [ 14 ] to maintain the individual measurement times but naive application of the estimator requires a state for each event feature and does not run in real time.

This paper presents a real-time continuous-time event-camera VO pipeline that uses keytime interpolation [ 15 , 14 , 16 , 17 ] to reduce the size of the estimation state. The pipeline considers event features at individual timestamps to reject outliers with motion-compensated RANSAC (MC-RANSAC) [ 18 ] . It then defines a smaller estimation state at a selected set of sparse keytimes but still evaluates each measurement at its individual measurement time by interpolating between the keytimes with a WNOA prior (Fig. 1 ).
This ensures that the pipeline runs in real-time while maintaining the temporal resolution of the event camera.

The presented pipeline is evaluated on the multi-vehicle stereo event camera (MVSEC) [ 19 ] and driving scenarios for event cameras (DSEC) [ 20 ] datasets. The experimental results show that the keytime approach maintains similar estimation accuracy as the not-real-time GPCT pipeline [ 13 ] while significantly reducing state size in all tested sequences (Sec. IV-C ). It also achieves better estimation accuracy than event stereo parallel tracking and mapping (ES-PTAM) [ 21 ] , a state-of-the-art discrete stereo pipeline, in all but one of the tested sequences (Sec. IV-D ). It does this with an estimation frequency of 22 Hz on MVSEC and 6 Hz on DSEC by using keytimes and a producer-consumer architecture analogous to keyframing [ 5 ] .

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. Section II provides a brief review of event-camera VO pipelines. Section III details the real-time continuous-time pipeline. Section IV presents experimental results of the pipeline across two datasets and comparisons against GPCT and ES-PTAM on the MVSEC and DSEC datasets. Finally, Section V summarizes our findings and concludes the paper.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Discrete-time Approaches

An intuitive approach for processing event streams is to accumulate events into discrete frames or equivalent spatial representations. These formulations leverage the extensive literature on direct or indirect methods for frame-based cameras.

Early event-camera VO works estimate rotation-only S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) SO(3) poses [ 22 ] or S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) trajectories by incorporating RGB-D sensors [ 23 ] . Kim et al. [ 24 ] presents an event-only pipeline with three decoupled filters that additionally provides depth and intensity estimates but requires a GPU to achieve real-time performance.

Monocular event cameras are frequently paired with inertial measurement units (IMUs) in visual-inertial odometry (VIO) pipelines. Many of these systems fully discretize the event data [ 25 , 26 ] but some of them address the asynchronous events with a combination of motion-compensated event frames and frame-based cameras [ 5 , 6 , 27 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] . These improve feature tracking by creating more stable features but do not preserve the individual event timestamps during estimation.

Zuo et al. [ 28 ] demonstrates the tracking capabilities of a monocular event camera under challenging conditions but requires a prior semidense 3D map. Chamorro et al. [ 29 ] uses line-based features and achieves real-time updates with an error-state Kalman filter but the success of the pipeline is dependent on a sufficient number of straight-line features.

Shiba et al. [ 30 ] utilizes contrast maximization to jointly estimate optical flow, depth, and egomotion but the linear motion assumption of optical flow can break with longer sequences and the pipeline does not run in real time.

Event visual odometry (EVO) [ 31 ] is a direct parallel tracking and mapping (PTAM) [ 3 ] approach. ESVO [ 32 ] , El Moudni et al. [ 33 ] , and ES-PTAM [ 21 ] follow a PTAM approach for stereo vision. These pipelines do not address asynchronous events in the back end and lose the temporal resolution of event cameras.

Hadviger et al. [ 11 ] presents an indirect stereo VO pipeline that uses only event cameras. It extracts features from the event
stream using Arc* [ 34 ] , which maintains individual event times, but this temporal fidelity is discarded by assuming all features in a frame occur at the same time during outlier rejection and state estimation.

ESVIO [ 7 ] is an indirect stereo VIO pipeline that uses a modified version of Arc* on motion-compensated time surfaces, both of which address the asynchronous events in the front end but the back end does not use this temporal resolution. Liu et al. [ 35 ] and ESVO2 [ 36 ] extend ESVO with an IMU, which helps create a smoother trajectory, but also do not preserve the individual timing of events in the back end.

All of these discrete time approaches are ultimately limited by grouping the continuous stream of events into fixed intervals, which approximates the native temporal resolution to discrete times. This reduction in temporal resolution can reintroduce motion blur and cause inaccuracies in state estimation.

## II-B Continuous-time Approaches

Continuous-time formulations are a natural framework for processing asynchronous measurements from event cameras. These methodologies were initially popularized for scanning LiDARs [ 14 ] and rolling shutter cameras [ 37 ] . A review of continuous-time trajectory estimation is available in [ 38 ] .

Mueggler et al. [ 12 ] presents a continuous-time monocular event-camera VO that models the S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) trajectory with cubic B-splines but it requires an a priori map for localization. This work was extended into a VIO pipeline [ 39 ] that removes the need for an a priori map, but the usage of numerical Jacobians instead of analytical Jacobians hinders real-time performance.

Liu et al. [ 40 ] presents a monocular VO pipeline where the continuous trajectory is modeled as a GP with a WNOA prior and a sparser set of states, similar to our formulation. The estimation state is updated with each new event, which couples state estimation with outlier rejection and may introduce different sources of errors than the standard VO approach of rejecting outliers before estimation. The evaluations are also limited to five-second sequences.

Wang et al. [ 41 ] uses cubic B-splines for trajectory representation and present a batch volumetric contrast-maximization approach. They map scenes in 3D but restrict the estimated egomotion to planar motion. Liu et al. [ 42 ] also uses cubic B-splines to model the trajectory and achieves real-time VIO but requires frame-based cameras for feature initialization.

Lu et al. [ 43 ] introduces a direct stereo visual-inertial velocimeter using cubic B-splines. The incremental velocity updates lack a bundle adjustment which makes it more susceptible to drift compared to batch or sliding-window VO pipelines.

IDOL [ 44 ] is a batch, line-based VIO pipeline. It uses Gaussian preintegrated measurements and associates events with them to handle their asynchronous nature but the batch structure of the pipeline and the time-consuming line-feature extraction reduces real-time performance.

Wang et al. [ 45 ] introduces an event-camera monocular VIO pipeline with local GPs on S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) SO(3) and ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} and white-noise-on-jerk (WNOJ) priors [ 46 ] . It does not achieve real-time performance and separate optimization of S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) SO(3) and ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} is generally less accurate.

GPCT [ 13 ] is a stereo pipeline that represents the trajectory as a GP with a WNOA prior. It addresses asynchronous events by using MC-RANSAC [ 18 ] for outlier rejection and placing a state at each measurement time, but this causes large state sizes that limit real-time performance.

Elms et al. [ 47 ] present a continuous-time SLAM pipeline designed for rapidly spinning objects that parameterizes the trajectory with an orbital motion model rather than B-splines or GPs. Guo et al. [ 48 ] is a rotational SLAM pipeline driven by contrast maximization that can use both linear and cubic splines. Subsequent work focuses solely on the bundle adjustment back end and replaces the contrast maximization with a photometric approach using linear splines [ 49 ] . All these pipelines are only presented on S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) SO(3) .

This paper presents a stereo event-camera-only VO pipeline that achieves real-time estimation rates while maintaining the asynchronous nature of event cameras. In contrast to discrete-time methods, it uses the individual measurement times of each event feature, which maintains the advantages of event cameras. In contrast to existing continuous-time methods that use B-splines, it uses a GP representation with a WNOA prior which provides a more physically founded model. In contrast to other GP methods, it both uses MC-RANSAC to isolate outlier rejection from state estimation, and uses keytime interpolation to decouple the state size from the number of measurements. It reduces optimization times significantly and achieves real-time performance with a producer-consumer architecture.

2026-10-05.title: CriticHack: Evaluating Visual Rewards Under Robot Policy Optimization
2026-10-05.authors: Jiaxuan Luo , Xingguo Xu , Shanshan Wang , Yuhan Zhou , Zhen Zhang
2026-10-05.abstract:
Learned visual reward models are increasingly used to optimize robot policies,
yet a reward model can score an execution that acts on the wrong object as
highly as one that completes the task. We show that optimizing such a reward
can amplify these wrong-object failures while reward and task success both
rise, so the signals a practitioner would normally monitor look healthy.
We fine-tune every denoiser parameter of a diffusion policy against Robometer
on a drawer task. Starting from a supervised policy with no prior reward
exposure, five training runs raise task success by 10.2 percentage points and
wrong-object failures by 10.9 points on 512 evaluation seeds, whereas five runs
trained on the simulator’s task-completion signal raise success without
amplifying wrong-object failures (difference 9.2 points, 95% CI 5.6 to 13.0).
The amplification recurs from a policy previously optimized against learned
rewards, under the policy’s native diffusion sampler, at matched distance from
the initial policy, and across constrained-policy experiments with two critics
and two optimizers. A tilt model explains when it occurs: under KL-regularized
optimization, an outcome becomes more frequent whenever its expected reward
under the initial policy exceeds the population average. Robometer separates
successes from failures well overall (AUROC .81) but scores wrong-object
failures slightly above successes (AUROC .37), so optimization raises both.
The same model predicts the outcome shifts across 26 constrained settings
(Spearman .89), including those in which task success falls, and Robometer’s
own published success-termination recipe inherits the error. A frozen outcome
verifier redirects the same optimization toward the requested task.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Learned visual reward models provide feedback for robot policy optimization
from camera observations and a task description, replacing hand-designed task
rewards ( Lee et al., 2026 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) . A reward model does not
need to fail broadly to steer a policy wrong. It can score most failures
correctly and still reward one coherent semantic mistake, and optimization is
built to find exactly such mistakes.

Consider a robot instructed to open the middle drawer
(Figure 1 ). Opening the upper drawer instead looks like
manipulation progress but fails the requested task. A stacking policy can
likewise build a stable stack with the wrong cube. We call these outcomes wrong-object failures : executions that manipulate a distractor in a
task-consistent way while the requested task fails. Liang et al. (2026) showed that RoboReward assigns high scores to such executions and that these
false positives reinforce incorrect behavior during online learning. What is
less understood is how such errors interact with genuine task learning. If
optimization simply degraded task success, standard evaluation would catch it.
We show that it does not have to: optimizing a visual reward can raise task
success and wrong-object failures at the same time. The two checks a
practitioner relies on, the reward model’s aggregate success–failure
discrimination and the policy’s task success after optimization, can both
look healthy while a specific semantic failure grows.

We study this with CriticHack , a closed-loop evaluation of visual rewards under
robot policy optimization in which simulator state measures task success and
wrong-object failures independently of the reward. Our main experiments
fine-tune every denoiser parameter of a diffusion policy against Robometer on
a drawer task. From a supervised policy that has never been exposed to a
learned reward, five training runs raise task success by 10.2 ​ [ 6.9 , 13.6 ] 10.2\,[6.9,13.6] percentage points and wrong-object failures by 10.9 ​ [ 7.3 , 14.4 ] 10.9\,[7.3,14.4] points on
512 evaluation seeds. Five runs trained on the simulator’s task-completion
signal raise success at least as much without amplifying wrong-object
failures, so the amplification is specific to the learned reward
(Table 1 ). The same pattern holds from a warm-start
policy previously optimized against learned rewards, where paired executions
show that the new successes and the new wrong-object failures both come from
converting former failures. It persists when the fine-tuned policies are
decoded with their native 100-step diffusion sampler, at matched KL distance
from the initial policy, and across distractor-motion thresholds from 5 to
40 mm. Constrained experiments that optimize a selector over a fixed bank of
diffusion-noise sequences reproduce reward gain with wrong-object
amplification across two task–reward pairings, Robometer and Language-Image
Value learning (LIV) ( Ma et al., 2023a ) , and two optimizers, proximal policy
optimization (PPO) and group relative policy optimization (GRPO).

Why does a reward with strong aggregate discrimination produce this? A
trajectory-level audit shows that Robometer separates successes from all
failures well (AUROC .813) but scores wrong-object failures slightly above
successes (AUROC .372); good discrimination against the far more common other
failures hides the inversion. A simple model turns this observation into a
prediction. Under KL-regularized optimization the optimal policy tilts the
initial policy toward high reward, and an outcome becomes more frequent exactly
when its average tilted reward exceeds the population average. A reward that
scores wrong-object failures about as highly as successes therefore raises
both, and stronger optimization is decided by the upper tail of the score
distribution. Fitted with a single strength parameter, the model reproduces
the outcome changes across 26 constrained settings (Spearman .89 for
wrong-object failures and .79 for success), including the drawer settings in
which task success falls, and it places the full-denoiser and constrained
results on one continuum of optimization strength. Robometer’s own published
recipe, dense progress with success-triggered termination, does not escape the
error: its success detector fires on 89% of wrong-object executions and on
73% of successes.

Finally, we use a frozen success verifier trained on outcome labels as a
diagnostic intervention. Reweighting the critic reward by the verifier raises
task success by 7.1 points and lowers wrong-object failures by 4.4 points
relative to critic-only training, and verifier-only rewards match it, which
identifies outcome supervision as the source of the recovery.

(i) We show, with independent training runs and simulator-measured outcomes,
that optimizing a visual reward can amplify wrong-object failures while task
success rises, and that a ground-truth completion reward under the same
optimizer does not. (ii) We show that strong aggregate discrimination can hide
the semantic misranking that drives this amplification, and give a tilt model
that predicts the resulting outcome changes across settings and unifies
semantic amplification with classical success loss. (iii) We show that outcome
verification redirects the same optimization toward the intended task.

The simulated experiments cover occluded-drawer manipulation and
identity-sensitive stacking. Full-denoiser fine-tuning uses Robometer’s
terminal success probability on two drawer layouts; constrained experiments
add LIV and stacking. The verifier is task-specific and trained on simulator
labels. The real-robot study is a case study with one training run per
fine-tuned condition.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Learned rewards turn human preferences into policy objectives ( Christiano et al., 2017 ) , but optimizing such a proxy can depart
from the intended outcome ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Skalse et al., 2022 ) ,
and more capable agents exploit misspecified rewards more effectively ( Pan et al., 2022 ) . Overoptimization has been characterized in
language-model and diffusion-model alignment ( Gao et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) , where it
appears as a decline in a gold or held-out metric under continued proxy
optimization. We study a signature this diagnostic misses: task success
rises while a specific semantic failure grows, both measured through
simulator state independently of the reward. Under a KL penalty the optimal
policy is an exponential tilt of the reference policy ( Korbak et al., 2022 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ) ; we use this closed form to predict
which outcomes optimization amplifies and to place semantic amplification and
the classical decline of the gold metric on one continuum. Reward-model evaluation raises
a related concern. Low prediction error need not imply low regret after
optimization ( Fluri et al., 2025 ) , and static ranking accuracy
imperfectly predicts post-optimization behavior ( Kim et al., 2025b ; Wen et al., 2025 ) . Aggregate metrics can also
conceal poor performance on meaningful subsets, a phenomenon known as hidden
stratification ( Oakden-Rayner et al., 2020 ) . Section 5.3 shows such masking in a visual reward model, on the very subset that
optimization amplifies.

Visual rewards have been learned from human videos ( Chen et al., 2021 ) ,
goal-conditioned value pretraining ( Ma et al., 2023b ) and language–image
alignment ( Ma et al., 2023a ) . RoboCLIP and vision–language model reward
models (VLM-RMs) use pretrained video– and image–language models as
rewards ( Sontakke et al., 2023 ; Rocamonde et al., 2024 ) , and Video-Language
Critic learns video–text alignment and temporal rankings ( Alakuijala et al., 2025 ) . RoboReward and Robometer scale general-purpose
robotic reward models ( Lee et al., 2026 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) . Our tasks
hinge on spatial reference and color-based object identity, distinctions that
match documented weaknesses of vision–language models ( Kamath et al., 2023 ; Yuksekgonul et al., 2023 ) . Liang et al. (2026) document RoboReward false positives on
wrong-object executions and their consequences for online reinforcement
learning (RL). We find the same failure class in Robometer’s own success
output, where strong aggregate discrimination hides it, and show that
optimizing against it can raise task success and wrong-object failures
together. Robometer’s published online RL pairs dense progress rewards with
success-triggered termination; on our drawer task that success detector fires
on more wrong-object executions than successes, so the recipe inherits the
same error (Appendix I ).

Success classifiers have long served as rewards, from event-based control ( Fu et al., 2018 ) to vision–language success detectors ( Du et al., 2023 ) , and outcome verifiers trained on correctness
labels are widely used in language-model reasoning ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) .
Other work corrects the reward itself: ensembles support conservative
optimization against uncertain feedback ( Coste et al., 2024 ) ,
Adapt2Reward uses failure prompts to adapt visual rewards ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , and RARM uses reference-anchored,
confidence-gated progress matching ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Our verifier is a
task-specific success classifier trained on simulator labels; we use it as a
diagnostic that tests whether changing the feedback redirects the amplified
failure.

Diffusion Policy (DP) ( Chi et al., 2023 ) generates robot action
chunks by iterative denoising. Treating the denoising chain as a Markov
decision process (MDP) enables reward-driven fine-tuning of the full denoiser ( Black et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2025 ) , while latent-noise steering improves a
fixed policy by optimizing the noise supplied to its denoiser ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) . Our two protocols follow these routes:
full-denoiser PPO under the denoising-MDP formulation, and a constrained
selector over a fixed bank of noise sequences with the decoder frozen.
Generalist vision–language–action (VLA) policies such as OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2025a ) can also be adapted with RL ( Chen et al., 2025 ) ; we
use task-specific DPs, which let us evaluate many independent training runs
against simulator-measured outcomes.

2026-10-05.title: RUL-Aware RRT*: Degradation-Balanced Motion Planning for Robotic Manipulators
2026-10-05.authors: Haibo Li , Zhiguo Zeng , Xu Li
2026-10-05.comment: Preprint
2026-10-05.abstract: Robotic manipulators operating over long durations often experience uneven joint degradation, which causes the weakest actuator to fail prematurely, leads to unplanned downtime, and results in significant operational losses. Traditional motion-planning algorithms do not account for joint health conditions and therefore tend to exacerbate this imbalance during extended operation. To address this challenge, this study introduces the RUL-aware RRT*, a motion-planning method that incorporates joint remaining useful life information into the planning process and adaptively adjusts joint usage in response to evolving health conditions. The method is evaluated across three representative scenarios, namely the Full Health Scenario (FHS), the Heterogeneous Degradation Scenario (HDS), and the Local Degradation Scenario (LDS). The results show that the RUL-aware RRT* effectively suppresses degradation imbalance, delays the emergence of bottleneck failures, and improves the long-term reliability of the robotic system during extended operation. These findings demonstrate that integrating health feedback into motion planning provides a practical and robust pathway for enhancing the durability and operational resilience of manipulators subject to continuous wear.
2026-10-05.introduction:
In modern manufacturing, industrial robots have become essential equipment for achieving automated production and flexible manufacturing ( Rüßmann et al., 2015 ) . As the most critical component of industrial robots, multi-degree-of-freedom robotic arms rely on multiple joint motors that must operate in close coordination to perform complex, continuous, and high-precision tasks ( Fan et al., 2019 ) . However, in practical operation, motion planning is typically optimized for geometric efficiency or energy performance ( Noreen et al., 2016 ; Feng et al., 2024 ) , while differences in joint health conditions and the resulting uneven motion usage across actuators are often overlooked. This leads to uneven motor utilization ( Raviola et al., 2021 ) , where certain joints may experience accelerated degradation due to high workloads or frequent movements, eventually becoming the weakest link of the system ( Kot et al., 2021 ) . Once such a motor fails, the entire robot must be shut down, resulting in unplanned downtime and seriously affecting production continuity and equipment reliability ( Lei et al., 2025 ; Mahyari and Locker, 2018 ; Raviola et al., 2021 ) . This issue, in which local degradation triggers overall system failure, has become one of the key challenges in the reliability management of industrial robots.

To address such issues, extensive research has been conducted in recent years in both academia and industry within the fields of condition monitoring and predictive maintenance (PdM) based on robotic arms ( Lei et al., 2025 ; Moore and Sawyer, 2024 ; Uhlmann et al., 2020 ) . By leveraging remaining useful life (RUL) prediction and digital twin technologies, researchers are able to monitor equipment health in real time, predict the degradation trends of critical components, and make informed maintenance decisions accordingly ( Mourtzis et al., 2023 ; Borgi et al., 2017 ) . These approaches have significantly enhanced the intelligence of maintenance management, shifting it from a reactive mode to a proactive strategy ( Molęda et al., 2023 ) . However, most existing studies remain at the monitoring and scheduling layers, where the focus lies in sensing system health and determining maintenance timing ( Kumar et al., 2023 ) . Their outputs, such as health indicators, degradation trajectories, or maintenance schedules, are seldom integrated into the motion-planning layer, preventing health information from directly influencing path generation or motion decisions ( Schacht-Rodríguez et al., 2018 ) . In other words, although health information is effectively perceived, it is rarely incorporated into the robot’s path generation and motion decision-making processes, thereby limiting the realization of a closed-loop predictive maintenance framework.

On the other hand, sampling-based motion planning algorithms, such as RRT, RRT*, and PRM, provide a flexible framework for incorporating multidimensional constraints into the planning process ( Kingston et al., 2018 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) . In recent years, various studies have introduced factors such as energy and consumption ( Alam et al., 2023 ) , collision risk ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , safety distance ( Mainprice et al., 2011 ) , battery endurance ( Chitre and Sinha, 2023 ) into the cost functions of these algorithms, thereby achieving a comprehensive optimization of efficiency, safety, and reliability. These works demonstrate that path planning can be applied not only for geometric feasibility analysis but also holds great potential for integrating health-related factors. However, existing research has not yet systematically incorporated the uneven degradation conditions across multiple motors and their imbalanced RUL distribution into planning models, leaving robotic systems lacking health awareness at the path-planning level.

Based on the above analysis, three major research gaps can be identified. First, traditional path-planning algorithms often lead to uneven motor degradation, as they optimize only geometric or efficiency-related objectives without considering motor health conditions. Second, predictive maintenance techniques largely remain at the monitoring and scheduling levels, without direct integration into the motion-planning process. Third, existing path-planning studies mainly focus on energy efficiency or collision avoidance, while overlooking the uneven degradation conditions across multiple motors and the resulting lifetime bottleneck.

To address these challenges, this study proposes an RUL-aware RRT* motion-planning algorithm that aims to redistribute joint-level motion usage, enhance health awareness, and mitigate lifetime bottlenecks. The proposed algorithm is developed on the basis of the traditional RRT* framework ( Karaman and Frazzoli, 2011 ) , whose original cost function considers only the path length, while RUL-aware RRT* extends it by introducing an RUL-aware cost function that incorporates joint health information into the path-cost formulation, thereby enabling deep integration of health awareness into the motion-planning process. In addition, two key mechanisms are designed within the framework: (1) an Online RUL Update Mechanism,which dynamically updates the current remaining useful life (RUL) of each joint before each motion-planning process; and (2) an RUL-driven Adaptive Joint Weighting Mechanism, which adaptively balances motor loads under different degradation conditions to achieve health-aware motion planning.

In multi-scenario experiments conducted on a UR5 six-degree-of-freedom robotic arm, including the Full Health Scenario, the Heterogeneous Degradation Scenario, and the Local Degradation Scenario, the results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves balanced degradation, enhances health-awareness, and extends the first-replacement time of critical motors, thereby realizing planable predictive maintenance. This study provides a new perspective for achieving health awareness and lifetime balancing at the task-execution level of industrial robots, and lays the foundation for future research on reliability-aware motion planning.

The implementation and experimental data are available at https://github.com/HelpLee/MotionPlanning_RULRRTstar .

2026-10-05.title: OpenRUA: Robot-Use Agents Are Zero-Shot Visuomotor Policies
2026-10-05.authors: Zhaoyang Chu , Earl T. Barr , Claire Le Goues , Peter O'Hearn , Mark Harman , Federica Sarro , He Ye
2026-10-05.abstract:
Coding agents are extending their reach into the physical world by writing and executing robot control programs.
One might expect the agents to use the existing mature software stack that engineers have developed over decades to access sensors and control motion.
Yet prior work primarily engineers complex custom harnesses to orchestrate agents for robot use, particularly by prescribing specialized workflows and providing bespoke interfaces.
This raises the question: “Is such additional harness engineering necessary?” We introduce OpenRUA, a zero-abstraction harness that bypasses bespoke abstraction layers by providing off-the-shelf coding agents with only terminal access to the robot’s native software interface ROS 2.
OpenRUA employs a minimalist workspace-as-harness design, only offering ROS 2 documentation and basic tools while leaving the coding agent to organize its own work without orchestrating any agentic workflow.
Within this workspace, OpenRUA recasts perception as file I/O and manipulation as coding.
With Claude Code powered by Claude Opus 5, OpenRUA achieves success rates of 99.0% on CaP-Bench and 87.0% on LIBERO-PRO, demonstrating that an off-the-shelf coding agent can serve as a zero-shot visuomotor policy through the robot’s native interface, without bespoke primitives or task-specific training.
Under this minimalist design, further analysis reveals striking emergent behaviors of coding agents: 1 For perception, the agent spontaneously writes programs that process raw sensory inputs ( e.g. , reconstructing point clouds from depth) and derive metric measurements ( e.g. , computing coordinates for Cartesian motion targets) in 96.80% of episodes. 2 For manipulation, the agent spontaneously builds motion-control clients ( e.g. , gripper control) in 95.87% of episodes and closed-loop control programs ( e.g. , adjusting motion based on sensor feedback) in 50.13% of episodes.
Our code is available at https://github.com/terminalworld/OpenRUA .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Robot control has long been engineered by writing explicit programs that translate task specifications into physical motion ( Fikes and Nilsson, 1971 ; Li et al., 1994 ; Siciliano et al., 2009 ) .
These programs execute on a multi-layered software stack, through which human engineers coordinate drivers, messaging, planning, and actuation to implement the required behavior ( Macenski et al., 2022 ; García et al., 2020 ) .
However, this process requires substantial effort and human expertise, with further engineering often needed for new tasks or environments.

One path is to learn end-to-end visuomotor policies , such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ( Team, 2025 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2026 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) and World Action Models (WAMs) ( Agarwal et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , that map visual observations and language instructions directly to low-level actions.
However, they require large-scale demonstration data, and their generalization remains limited beyond the training distribution ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Fei et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) .
For example, LIBERO-PRO ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) reports that OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) and π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) , despite average success rates above 90% on standard LIBERO, achieve 0.0% success under position and task perturbations.

Another path is to revisit explicit programming for robot control ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , while replacing the human engineer with modern coding agents such as Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2025 ) or Codex ( OpenAI, 2025 ) .
Such an approach is known as Code as Policies (CaP) ( Liang et al., 2023 ) , where the policy itself can be inspected, edited, and debugged by the coding agent without retraining ( Elmaaroufi et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) .
As a result, the coding agent acts as a Robot-Use Agent (RUA) ( Isola, 2026 ) , operating the robot the way it operates a computer ( Team, 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Robocurve, 2026 ; Berman et al., 2026 ) .

Despite this progress, existing RUA systems devote significant effort to engineering custom harnesses for robot use, especially designing the tool interfaces and primitive libraries through which agents compose policies to operate robots in prescribed workflows.
These systems either wrap learned visuomotor policies as callable tools ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Galanti et al., 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) or hand-craft custom libraries of perception and control primitives based on human expertise ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) .
However, it remains unclear whether such additional harness engineering is necessary for coding agents to operate robots effectively, given that robots have a mature ecosystem of software interfaces developed over decades for human engineers to access sensors and control motion ( Macenski et al., 2022 ; García et al., 2020 ) .
This raises the question: “Can an off-the-shelf coding agent serve as a zero-shot visuomotor policy through the robot’s native software interface, without relying on bespoke primitives or learned policies?”

In this work, we introduce OpenRUA, a zero-abstraction harness for robot-use agents that builds on the robot’s native interface, Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) ( Macenski et al., 2022 ) , the de facto standard of the robotics community.
OpenRUA bypasses bespoke abstraction layers by offering off-the-shelf coding agents only terminal access to ROS 2, allowing them to operate the robot as a human engineer would.

As illustrated in Figure 1 , OpenRUA frames robot use as a live, interactive software project and employs a minimalist workspace-as-harness design.
This design rests on the observation that frontier coding agents already operate autonomously on unfamiliar repositories to complete tasks ( OpenAI, 2024 ; Merrill et al., 2026 ; Chu et al., 2026 ) .
We hypothesize that the orchestration with bespoke interfaces in existing RUA systems compensates for limited agent capability rather than reflecting a requirement of robot control, and that a capable coding agent needs only a workspace directory.
Specifically, the workspace serves as the harness by only offering ROS 2 documentation and basic tools, leaving the coding agent to organize its own work without a prescribed agentic workflow.
Within this workspace, OpenRUA recasts perception as file I/O and manipulation as coding: task-specific perception and control strategies emerge as the agent acquires observations, interprets images, computes metric measurements, and writes control programs.
As a result, the coding agent itself serves as a zero-shot visuomotor policy: it goes from raw observations to motor commands, reasoning explicitly about geometry and iteratively refining its actions from execution feedback.

We conduct comprehensive experiments to evaluate OpenRUA on three widely used benchmarks, i.e. , CaP-Bench ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , LIBERO-PRO ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and RoboCasa365 ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) , in a zero-shot setting without access to privileged simulator state and the benchmark’s success predicates.
With Claude Code powered by Claude Opus 5, OpenRUA achieves success rates of 99.0% on CaP-Bench and 87.0% on LIBERO-PRO, exceeding leading systems such as ASPIRE ( Lu et al., 2026 ) and Harness VLA ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) by 18.0 and 4.6 percentage points, respectively.
On unseen composite tasks in RoboCasa365, OpenRUA achieves 28.1% success, exceeding Harness VLA by 13.1 percentage points.
The results show that an off-the-shelf coding agent can serve as a zero-shot visuomotor policy through the robot’s native software interface, without bespoke primitives or learned policies.

Further analysis reveals several findings about emergent agent capabilities: 1 For perception, the agent spontaneously writes programs that process raw sensory inputs ( e.g. , cropping images, adding grids, and reconstructing point clouds from depth) and derive metric measurements ( e.g. , computing coordinates for Cartesian motion targets) in 96.80% of episodes. 2 For manipulation, the agent spontaneously builds its own motion-control clients ( e.g. , trajectory execution and gripper control) in 95.87% of episodes and closed-loop control programs ( e.g. , adjusting motion or stopping based on sensor feedback) in 50.13% of episodes. 3 On RoboCasa365, OpenRUA maintains comparable success rates on seen and unseen composite tasks (26.3% and 28.1%, respectively), whereas RLDX-1 drops to 5.0% and Harness VLA, which orchestrates RLDX-1, drops to 13.8% on unseen tasks.
This contrast highlights the generalization potential of OpenRUA without reliance on a learned robot policy. 4 Increasing test-time computation through more interaction or greater reasoning effort improves task success without additional robot training or bespoke primitives, while performance eventually saturates at levels that vary across models.

# 2 Background and Related Work

We review visuomotor policies, robot-use agents, and CLI coding agents, and introduce the Robot Operating System; an extended version is provided in Appendix A .

Visuomotor Policies. A visuomotor policy maps raw sensory observations directly to low-level robot actions ( Levine et al., 2016 ) .
Such policies are predominantly learned end to end from robot demonstrations, as in VLA models ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Team, 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2026 ) and WAMs ( Agarwal et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) .
However, their generalization remains bounded by the training distribution ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Fei et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) .
OpenRUA instead casts an off-the-shelf coding agent as a zero-shot visuomotor policy, requiring no robot demonstration data or fine-tuning.

Robot-Use Agents. RUA ( Isola, 2026 ) refers to LLM agents that operate a robot the way they operate a computer, through tool calls or executable programs, a paradigm that traces back to CaP ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2022 ) .
One line of work wraps learned visuomotor policies as callable tools, with the agent decomposing tasks and selecting tools while the underlying policies handle physical execution ( ichter et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Galanti et al., 2026 ) .
Another exposes low-level actions directly to the agent, which specifies end-effector poses step by step or writes control programs using predefined, hand-crafted primitives ( Hu et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026 ) .
OpenRUA instead provides the coding agent with only terminal access to the robot’s native ROS 2 interfaces and a workspace, allowing it to build task-specific perception and control tools during execution rather than requiring them to be engineered in advance.

CLI Coding Agents. CLI coding agents such as Claude Code ( Anthropic, 2025 ) and Codex ( OpenAI, 2025 ) resolve real-world software engineering tasks through autonomous iteration ( OpenAI, 2024 ; Merrill et al., 2026 ) .
These agents exhibit closed-loop agency over long horizons: they navigate codebases, edit and run code, issue CLI commands, interpret terminal output, and recover from errors.
OpenRUA turns this competence toward robot control by treating the robot as a live software project, allowing the agent to apply these capabilities to physical tasks without adaptation.

Robot Operating System. ROS 2 connects robot components and exposes their sensing, state, and control capabilities via topics, services, and actions ( Macenski et al., 2022 ) .
The native ros2cli command-line tools and rclpy Python client library allow developers to inspect these interfaces, acquire data, and send control requests.
Prior work connects LLM agents to ROS through an additional abstraction layer of custom tools or predefined primitives, with evaluations limited to in-house tasks rather than standard robot control benchmarks ( Royce et al., 2024 ; Mower et al., 2024 ) .

2026-10-05.title: Autonomous mobile robot operations logistics: a dataset of jobs, dispatch events and robot states
2026-10-05.authors: Jan-Felix Klein , Yongkuk Jeong
2026-10-05.comment: Submitted to Nature Scientific Data
2026-10-05.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) increasingly perform material transport in production logistics, where their operation is governed by job generation, dispatching and robot control. We present MoRoOp, a dataset of AMR operations recorded in a laboratory kit preparation and supply scenario over nine eight-hour shifts. During each shift, an AMR executed stochastically generated kit supply, empty-box refill and charging jobs. The dataset links job specifications, the operations constituting each job, dispatch events documenting operation state transitions and outcomes, and robot-state observations comprising position, orientation, velocity, per-wheel state of charge and diagnostics. It contains 1,382 jobs, 4,815 operations, 19,352 dispatch events and 140,386 robot-state observations together with the kit specifications used during job generation. The dataset was recorded in an operating laboratory environment, and technically valid observations of delays, obstructed navigation and unsuccessful operations were retained. Both raw and cleaned robot-state tables are provided. Documented reuse directions include the evaluation of AI agents on operational decision records, disturbance detection, operation prediction, data-driven simulation and event-log analysis.

2026-10-05.title: Keep the Effect, Drop the Actor: Programmable Effect-to-Execution World-Action Models
2026-10-05.authors: Junyi Hu , Zhewen He , Zhenhua Li , Yi Fang
2026-10-05.abstract:
A robot demonstration records two things in the same frames: what happened to the objects, and how one
particular arm made it happen. We condition on the first. A demonstration is compiled into an effect
program : the 3D keypoint trajectories of the objects that moved, two points marking where each was held,
and the configuration the scene ends in, with the demonstrator removed. PEWAM, a 71.5M-parameter
world-action model, generates effect, robot execution, action and terminal state as four streams with
independent flow-matching times, so clamping a program and sampling the execution turns inference into
programming, re-solved closed loop from the live scene. On held-out LIBERO-Goal tasks, one demonstration’s
program completes 40 of 90 episodes, where the same backbone given a goal image or language, and published
demonstration-conditioned methods, complete at most 19; on three of Meta-World’s held-out classes it exceeds
the best published results, though not on the five-class mean. Because a program is a set of coordinates, a person can edit it: the placement
follows a shifted terminal state and the grasp turns with rotated contact points. The same program runs on
four robot arms without retraining, and after a push, re-solving completes 23 of 60 episodes where replaying
the demonstration completes 6. On a Franka arm, fine-tuned on real demonstrations of other tasks, programs compiled from single human videos complete 36 of 40 trials, against 22 for the same backbone conditioned on the video’s last frame as a goal image.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Showing a robot what to do is often easier than describing it, and a single demonstration is a direct way to
specify a new manipulation task ( Vosylius and Johns, 2025 ; Di Palo and Johns, 2024 ; Goswami et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . A demonstration, however,
records two things in the same frames: what happened to the objects, and how one particular arm made it
happen. Watch someone put a bowl on a stove and you learn where the bowl should end up, roughly how it
travels and where it can be held; you do not learn to bend your elbow the way they bent theirs. Most systems
that learn from demonstrations keep the two together. Policies that transfer the demonstrator’s motion keep
the body and treat the world as context ( Park et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; Haldar and Pinto, 2025 ) , and video-action models
prompted with a demonstration predict both at once, as one pixel-level future ( Li et al., 2026b ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . The
task is then entangled with one body’s motion: no variable states it on its own, so it can be neither edited nor given to another robot.

This viewpoint exposes a limitation of both dominant formulations. Conditioning on the demonstrator’s
trajectory or video ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; Vosylius and Johns, 2025 ) ties the task to one execution, which is valid only for the
arm, the grasp and the layout that produced it. Methods built on object motion do separate the object from
the actor ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024 ; Dharmarajan et al., 2026 ) , but they generate that motion from language
or video and execute it with a planner, a controller or a per-task policy. What is missing is a task interface
that leaves the actor out, that one multi-task model accepts with no parameter update, and that a person can edit.

As illustrated in Figure 1 , our key observation is that the change in the world is the task,
and the demonstrator’s motion is one of many ways to produce it. We therefore compile a demonstration into an effect program : keypoints of each relevant object tracked over time, two contact points recording where
the object was held, and the configuration the objects end in. Nothing in the program refers to the robot.
Based on this view we propose PEWAM, a world-action model that describes effect, end-effector execution,
native action and terminal state as four streams with separate flow-matching times ( Bao et al., 2023 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) , so that every conditional is a query of the same weights. Clamping the program and sampling the execution poses the question of how to make the effect happen, which turns inference into programming. At deployment the unfinished part of the program is re-solved from the live scene every few
control steps. Because a push moves an object just as a grasp does, progress through the program is counted
only for effects the robot has caused, and a disturbance becomes a new observation.

We evaluate PEWAM on LIBERO, Meta-World and RLBench, on four arms, under pushes, from pixels and on a real
Franka arm programmed by human videos. Where the demonstrator’s motion stays valid, copying it is stronger; the
program pays off where copying breaks: after a push, on another arm, and from a person’s hand.

We summarize our contributions as follows: (i) we formulate the task carried by a demonstration as an
actor-free effect program of object keypoints, contact points and a terminal state, and propose PEWAM, a world-action model whose independently noised streams let one set of weights both execute and predict; (ii) we show that the
program is an interface a person can edit and hand to another body: its terminal state moves the placement, its contact points turn the grasp, and one program runs on four simulated arms and, from a human video, on a real arm; (iii) we treat progress as an effect the robot causes and gate the program on engagement, so that
re-solving absorbs pushes that defeat replay; and (iv) we show that editability needs contact written as points,
not weights, and training data with several executions of one effect.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 World-action models and imitation from one demonstration

World-action models learn video and action jointly, so that one network can both predict and act. UWM ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) couples video and action diffusion with independent timesteps, JOPAT ( Guan et al., 2026 ) adds a point-track
stream, and Hydra-0 and Zero-WAM ( Li et al., 2026b ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) condition multi-billion-parameter video models on
flow or on a human video; generalist policies and pretrained world-action models specify the task with a sentence ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Methods that imitate one demonstration at test time read it as point-cloud graphs ( Vosylius and Johns, 2025 ) , as keypoint and action tokens ( Di Palo and Johns, 2024 ) , through demonstration-to-scene correspondences ( She et al., 2026 ) or as the video itself ( Goswami et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , or they retarget the demonstrator’s trajectory ( Park et al., 2026 ) ; each carries the demonstrator’s motion. We keep independent timesteps but condition on an
actor-free program that a person can read and edit.

## 2.2 Object motion as the task interface

Several methods drop the actor and pass the object’s motion to the robot. Most generate that motion, as 2D or 3D
flow from language, images, point clouds or generated video ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ; Ko et al., 2024 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Dharmarajan et al., 2026 ) or as a trajectory from a per-task
model ( Hsu et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2025 ) , and execute it with a flow-conditioned policy, a controller or trajectory optimisation. Others reproduce the motion in one human video by optimisation, retargeting or a policy trained for
that demonstration ( Zhu et al., 2026 ; Kerr et al., 2024 ; Lum et al., 2025 ) . Keypoints and trajectories also serve as task specifications ( Manuelli et al., 2019 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Zeng et al., 2020 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) , ATM and Point Policy ( Wen et al., 2024 ; Haldar and Pinto, 2025 ) condition on point tracks ( Karaev et al., 2024 ) that include the actor’s motion, and demonstration editing adapts recorded demonstrations to new
layouts to synthesise data ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ; Xue et al., 2025 ) . We share the premise that the object’s motion is the task.
Closest to us, Im2Flow2Act ( Xu et al., 2024 ) also carries a task from human video to a robot through object
flow, but generates the flow with a separate model and executes it with a flow-conditioned policy; we read the
effect from the demonstration itself, add contact points and a terminal state, and sample the execution from one
multi-task world-action model that also answers forward queries of the same program.

2026-10-05.title: Rethinking World-Action Model for Compositional and In-Context Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-05.authors: Shukai Gong , Xuanran Zhai , Yintianrun Zhang , Ruopeng Cui , Ye Huang , Yiyang Fu , Dexuan Lyu , Chaojie Li , Xinyi Song , Peiwen Lin , Chuang Wang , Mingyuan Jia , Yufan Deng , Jiaxin Fang , Bo Liang , Jiaxin Li , Yuxiang Gao , Hao Liu , Daquan Zhou
2026-10-05.abstract:
Long-horizon compositional manipulation has become increasingly important for real-world robot deployment, where a single task involves multiple coordinated subtasks. Existing world-action models (WAMs) jointly predict short-horizon visual futures and actions, but typically lack explicit subtask-level reasoning. We propose Visual Goal-conditioned Action Reasoning (ViGAR) , a hierarchical framework that factorizes manipulation into
a visual subgoal planner and a subgoal executor.
Given the current observation and global instruction, the subgoal planner predicts a visual subgoal for the next subtask. The subgoal executor then jointly generates future visual trajectories and actions conditioned on the predicted subgoal. Both components share a pretrained world-model representation, enabling task-level planning and action generation to benefit from common physical knowledge. Moreover, our framework naturally supports in-context learning: using a global goal image as context can induce different subtask decompositions and behaviors without parameter updates.
On the RoboTwin Clean2Random benchmark, ViGAR achieves 82.00% and 67.02% success rates under the Clean and Random settings, respectively, surpassing the strongest baseline by 12.86 percentage points in average success rate.
Real-world robot experiments on five compositional and two in-context learning tasks further confirm the effectiveness of ViGAR.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Robots in production and service settings increasingly face compositional manipulation tasks that involve multiple coordinated subtasks. Such tasks require policies to maintain progress across subtask transitions while generalizing to unseen scenes, objects, and spatial layouts, rather than replaying a fixed sequence from training.
Policies for real-world deployment therefore need both embodied generalization and mechanisms for organizing behavior over extended task horizons.
World-Action Models (WAMs) offer an appealing paradigm for this goal. By jointly predicting future visual states and actions, WAMs learn physically grounded action dynamics from dense video supervision and have demonstrated strong generalization across tasks, environments, embodiments, and visual distribution shifts [ 9 , 19 , 34 , 1 ] .

Despite these strengths, existing WAMs are not explicitly designed for long-horizon compositional manipulation. WAM formulations typically provide a useful local control signal by modeling what is likely to happen next, but do not explicitly organize behavior across a sequence of subtasks or expose a task-level interface through which the desired progression can be specified.
Recent studies [ 4 , 40 , 16 ] reveal that long-horizon task progression requires more than supervision on short-term evolution of the physical world, and further demonstrate the value of predicting semantic subtasks for open-world long-horizon manipulation and generalization. The core challenge is therefore to endow WAMs with explicit task-level decision making while preserving their strong world-centric prediction and physical generalization.

One line of work externalizes this decision making to a language planner that exploits VLMs to decompose a task into linguistic subtasks for a policy to execute.
However, language subtask descriptions often underspecify precise spatial outcome without ambiguity, whereas visual subgoals impose stronger constraints on the desired scene configuration [ 17 ] . Our key insight is that compositional manipulation can be factorized into long-term future selection and short-term future realization . World-action modeling for long-horizon tasks should first make explicit the target state robot intends to realize, and then generate the actions that will bring it about.

To this end, we propose Visual Goal-conditioned Action Reasoning (ViGAR) , which treats subgoal images as explicit decision variable linking task-level reasoning to physical action generation.
Given the current observation and the global task instruction, ViGAR first performs visual goal reasoning to predict the desired subtask goal image.
Then, conditioned on the current observation, global task instruction and predicted subgoal image, it jointly predicts future visual trajectories and corresponding robot actions leading to the subgoal.
Both task-level decision and physical realization are learned in one shared generative world-model representation, so that the model can leverage the same physical knowledge for both stages.

Moreover, our framework naturally supports in-context learning: with the scene and instruction held fixed, changing only the global goal induces a different composition of behaviors, forcing the policy to reorganize its action sequence rather than default to the most likely training trajectory. We term this in-context robotic manipulation : the global goal image serves as context for inferring a subtask decomposition, so an out-of-distribution global goal elicits a task composition unseen in training, with no parameter update.

Experiments on both simulation benchmark and real-robot compositional tasks validate the effectiveness of ViGAR. On the RoboTwin Clean2Random benchmark [ 11 ] , ViGAR achieves success rates of 82.00% and 67.02% under the Clean and Random settings, respectively, surpassing the strongest baseline [ 32 ] by 12.86 percentage points in average success rate.
In real-robot experiments, ViGAR outperforms strong VLA and Cosmos3-Nano-Policy baselines on five compositional tasks, and exhibits in-context learning ability on unseen global goals, confirming the validity of our method.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We factorize compositional manipulation into long-term future selection and short-term future realization , and propose ViGAR , a hierarchical framework that predicts the next subgoal as an explicit decision variable and conditions joint video-action generation on it.

We identify in-context robotic manipulation as a capability that emerges from explicit goal conditioning. With the scene and instruction held fixed, a new global goal image elicits a different subtask decomposition and a correspondingly reorganized action sequence, specifying out-of-distribution task compositions at deployment without any parameter update.

ViGAR outperforms strong baselines on both simulation benchmark and real-robot compositional manipulation tasks, and exhibits strong in-context learning ability on unseen global goals, confirming the validity of our approach.

1. We factorize compositional manipulation into long-term future selection and short-term future realization , and propose ViGAR , a hierarchical framework that predicts the next subgoal as an explicit decision variable and conditions joint video-action generation on it.

2. We identify in-context robotic manipulation as a capability that emerges from explicit goal conditioning. With the scene and instruction held fixed, a new global goal image elicits a different subtask decomposition and a correspondingly reorganized action sequence, specifying out-of-distribution task compositions at deployment without any parameter update.

3. ViGAR outperforms strong baselines on both simulation benchmark and real-robot compositional manipulation tasks, and exhibits strong in-context learning ability on unseen global goals, confirming the validity of our approach.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

VLAs for Compositional Robotic Manipulation. Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to continuous action trajectories, and have demonstrated strong generalizability across objects, scenes, and tasks [ 5 , 3 , 16 , 27 , 37 , 13 , 14 , 25 ] .
For compositional manipulation, however, a direct instruction-to-action mapping is often insufficient due to increased complexity, and recent systems introduce subtask information as an explicit planning interface, where a VLM or a pretrained world model synthesizes subtask information that conditions a VLA policy [ 16 , 8 , 17 , 22 ] .

World Models for Robotic Manipulation. World models learn the structure and evolution of physical environments by predicting future states, and world-action models (WAMs) extend this paradigm by jointly modeling future observations and actions.
Recent studies have demonstrated that WAMs exhibit strong generalizability beyond the training domain, owing to their explicit modeling of geometric and temporal transitions [ 19 , 34 , 1 , 23 ] .
However, WAMs typically focus on local action generation and lack a mechanism for reasoning about the plan a compositional task requires.
BagelVLA [ 15 ] and RxBrain [ 20 ] generate interleaved subtask text and subgoal images within a unified model, but these predictions either guide action generation implicitly through intermediate features or serve primarily as planning outputs, rather than acting as explicit subgoal conditions for the downstream policy.

In-Context Learning for Robotic Manipulation. In large language models, a novel task can be performed simply by specifying it in the context without any parameter update, termed in-context learning (ICL) [ 6 , 29 , 30 ] .
Carried into robotic manipulation, this moves the acquisition of a new task out of training-time imitation and into inference time, bypassing the need for costly data collection and model fine-tuning.
Zero-WAM [ 39 ] performs ICL by prompting a causal video-action model with human demonstration videos; HOST [ 10 ] acquires a new skill from a single human video by predicting the robot’s own future observations along the demonstrated progression; Skild S1 [ 2 ] and GEN-1.5 [ 26 ] likewise condition on a demonstration video or a short sensorimotor trajectory. In each case the context conveys how a task is performed, and the policy re-executes it under its own embodiment.
We instead specify a task by its terminal world state: a global goal image constrains only what the scene should become, leaving the subtask decomposition to the model.
