# II Related Work

## II-A Fisheye and Omnidirectional Object Detection

Fisheye object detection research has produced several datasets and benchmarks for studying strong radial distortion, including WoodScape [ 1 ] , the OmniCV challenge [ 5 ] , and FishEye8K [ 4 ] . surveys summarize the main challenges [ 2 ] .
Existing fisheye detectors typically redesign or retrain a complete model. For example, FisheyeDet uses self-study and contour cues [ 6 ] , Swin-Fisheye adapts Swin transformers [ 14 ] , FisheyeDetNet targets real-time surround-view systems [ 15 ] , and Rashed et al. provide a generalized detection baseline and representation study [ 3 ] .
Streaming and parking settings additionally require efficient inference [ 16 ] .
In parallel, panoramic 360° detection has explored distortion-aware tokenization for overhead fisheye person detection [ 17 ] .
RT-DETR and the YOLO family provide strong COCO-pretrained real-time baselines [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] .
Most of these methods assume enough fisheye labels and compute to retrain the detector, whereas our goal is to reuse a COCO-pretrained YOLO26 detector with minimal additional training for fisheye imagery.

## II-B Distortion-Aware Convolutions and Rectification

Explicit distortion models have been used to reduce fisheye distortion. Rectification networks such as FishFormer [ 8 ] and FishRecGAN [ 23 ] learn to recover perspective images, but require calibration or introduce a separate preprocessing stage. Networks can also be designed to account for distortion. Convolutional filters that are aware of distortion adapt kernels to the panoramic structure [ 24 ] , convolution kernels can be adapted to calibrated fisheye projections [ 7 ] , and adaptable deformable convolutions improve fisheye semantic segmentation [ 9 , 25 ] .
These methods integrate distortion adaptation into the architecture, but they typically retrain the full model and do not preserve the pretrained detector’s original behavior.
Z-Adapters share this goal in a calibration-free, parameter-efficient way. A residual adapter corrects the feature misalignment while a zero-initialized output projection keeps the COCO-pretrained YOLO26 unchanged at the first step of adaptation to the fisheye domain.

## II-C Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning and Visual Adapters

Parameter-efficient transfer learning has shown that strong performance can be retained while updating only a small fraction of weights. Early residual adapters [ 26 , 27 ] , Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 28 ] , and zero-initialized adapter mechanisms [ 29 ] established the basic recipe, and recent surveys benchmark these methods across vision models [ 10 ] .
Detector-specific Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning is also emerging, adapting frozen detection models with lightweight modules [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] . However, most generic adapters are not distortion-specific. Our Z-Adapters learn residual feature corrections from fisheye data while keeping the COCO-pretrained backbone frozen throughout the entire detector adaptation process.

## II-D Multi-View Inference and Detection-Level Fusion

When a single view cannot reliably recognize small or compressed objects, slicing and multi-crop inference can help. Slicing Aided Hyper Inference (SAHI) detects objects in resized overlapping crops and maps the predictions back to the original image coordinates for duplicate suppression [ 11 ] . AutoFocus selects regions likely to contain small objects for inference at finer scales [ 33 ] .
At the detection level, Soft-NMS [ 12 ] reduces the scores of overlapping boxes, while Weighted Boxes Fusion (WBF) [ 13 ] merges boxes using confidence-weighted coordinates. Learned NMS learns to suppress duplicate detections from boxes and their scores [ 34 ] .
WBF has also been applied to combine predictions from multiple YOLO detectors for fisheye object detection [ 35 ] .
In FUSEye, GridViews generates calibration-free overlapping views, and AgreeFusion learns per-cluster agreement scores to promote cross-view-supported candidates while preserving the original confidence threshold for isolated detections observed in only one view.

2026-10-05.title: Mind the Refinement Gap: When Safe High-Level Robot Plans Produce Unsafe Executions
2026-10-05.authors: Stabak Das , Priyesh Ranjan , Xiangfang Li , Lijun Qian
2026-10-05.abstract: Language-enabled robot systems increasingly combine semantic-graph planning with temporal-logic safety monitors. We investigate a trace-completeness assumption in these systems: whether the high-level action sequence checked by a monitor represents the navigation and implicit action effects induced during execution. We audit this assumption in RoboGuard by comparing its verdict on a surface plan with its verdict on a graph-refined trace under the same Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specification. Our evaluation comprises 28 controlled cases spanning five action-abstraction families and 14 end-to-end cases in which SPINE [ 5 ] generates plans from natural-language instructions while RoboGuard generates scene-grounded safety specifications. In the controlled evaluation, all 12 targeted abstraction cases exhibit the predicted surface-versus-refined discrepancy while all 16 controls behave as expected, motivating graph-based trace refinement as a lightweight mitigation and a diagnostic tool for physical-AI safety monitors.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Language-enabled robot planners increasingly use semantic graphs to connect natural-language instructions with objects, regions, and executable robot actions. Formal safety monitors can then evaluate the resulting plans against temporal-logic requirements. However, the guarantees provided by such a monitor are necessarily relative to the action trace that it observes. A semantic graph may contain enough information to identify an unsafe route, yet that information may never reach the monitor if navigation is represented only by its destination or is hidden inside a higher-level action.

For example, a surface plan may contain only goto(safe_lab_1) , although graph search realizes the action as goto(construction_area_1) followed by goto(safe_lab_1) . Similarly, an action such as inspect(sensor_1) may implicitly navigate to the object’s associated region without exposing that navigation as a monitored proposition. A prohibition against entering a construction area can therefore be satisfied by the surface trace while being violated by the graph-induced execution
trace. This is not a failure of temporal logic itself; it is a mismatch between the abstraction verified by the monitor and the behavior induced by the robot API.

RoboGuard [ 6 ] provides a suitable system for studying this boundary. It uses a protected language model to ground natural-language safety rules in a semantic graph, generates LTL specifications, and applies temporal-logic control synthesis to proposed robot API actions. Our central question is:

Let C C be a forbidden construction region. RoboGuard grounds the corresponding safety rule as the LTL invariant

We investigate this question at two levels. First, a controlled suite contains 28 fixed-plan cases with manually specified LTL constraints: 12 targeted abstraction cases and 16 safe or explicitly unsafe controls. The cases cover direct-action controls, hidden-waypoint position, route selection, action refinement, and multi-action plans. Second, a 14-case end-to-end suite provides natural-language tasks to SPINE and safety rules to RoboGuard over four paired semantic-graph scenarios. It covers goto , inspect , and map_region , including unique unsafe bridges, matched safe corridors, and graphs containing both safe and unsafe alternative routes.

Our contributions are:

A controlled methodology for distinguishing action-abstraction
failures from specification-generation failures by evaluating surface and
graph-refined traces under the same LTL specification.

A controlled methodology for distinguishing action-abstraction
failures from specification-generation failures by evaluating surface and
graph-refined traces under the same LTL specification.

A collection of paired negative cases and controls covering explicit
navigation, hidden intermediate regions, implicit navigation, route
choice, action refinement, and multi-action plans.

An end-to-end SPINE–RoboGuard evaluation that records planning,
contextual grounding, verification, graph-oracle, and interface failures
as separate outcomes rather than conflating them with safety verdicts.

An evaluation of graph-based trace refinement as a minimal mitigation
that exposes safety-relevant execution events already represented in the
semantic graph.

Our experiments operate over static semantic graphs and graph-derived execution traces. They do not model continuous robot dynamics, perception errors, collision avoidance, or physical execution. Accordingly, our claims concern the soundness of action-level monitoring relative to documented high-level execution semantics, rather than complete real-world robot safety.

# 2 Related Work

Language-enabled robot planners increasingly use structured world models to ground instructions. SayPlan combines hierarchical 3D scene graphs, classical path planning, and simulator feedback for long-horizon planning [ 4 ] , while SPINE plans navigation, inspection, and mapping actions over an incrementally updated semantic graph [ 5 ] . Although these graphs encode semantic and topological information, our study asks whether safety-relevant navigation events remain visible to downstream verification.

AutoTAMP and LIMP combine language models with symbolic planning or task-and-motion reasoning [ 1 , 3 ] . The Safety Chip encodes natural-language prohibitions as LTL constraints [ 8 ] , while related work verifies generated robot programs using automata and externally supplied specifications [ 7 ] . Runtime-assurance systems such as SOTER similarly rely on observable system states to detect hazards and activate verified fallbacks [ 2 ] . In contrast, we examine the abstraction boundary between planning and verification: whether high-level action traces omit intermediate navigation or implicit action effects already recoverable from the semantic graph.

2026-10-05.title: Test-time Multi-agent Coordination by Decomposed Value Gradient Flow
2026-10-05.authors: Dongsu Lee , Haoran Xu , Amy Zhang
2026-10-05.comment: NeurIPS 2026
2026-10-05.abstract: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) faces a persistent trade-off. Expressive generative policies can represent multi-modal coordination in the data, but cannot distinguish high-value regions, while value-optimized policies exploit the learned Q-function but collapse the multi-modal into a single dominant mode. A single agent’s mode collapse can break joint coordination, and simultaneous drift across agents can push the joint policy into unseen regions of the action space. We propose scalable coordination via optimal unified transport (SCOUT) , the first offline MARL framework to combine a generative foundation model with a learned value function through test-time action refinement. SCOUT trains two decoupled components: a flow-matching behavioral prior and a decomposed value function. At test-time, it transports behavioral samples toward high-value regions via Stein variational gradient descent. The number of transport steps controls adaptive test-time scaling, replacing a fixed regularization coefficient. Under the individual-global-max (IGM) principle, we prove a single-term KL bound on the joint soft-value gap that vanishes as transport converges, with an irreducible additive residual proportional to the IGM violation. Empirically, SCOUT achieves the best average performance across discrete and continuous offline MARL benchmarks and yields performance improvements in all offline-to-online configurations.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Offline MARL is motivated by the need to learn coordinated multi-agent behaviors in safety-critical or cost-constrained domains where active data collection is infeasible or expensive, e.g. , autonomous driving [ 1 ] , logistics [ 2 ] , and robotics [ 3 ] . In this setting, the learning objective is twofold. Agents must learn to coordinate their behavior from heterogeneous and suboptimal demonstrations, while avoiding the distributional shift that arises when the learned policy visits state-action regions unsupported by the data. Early offline MARL methods [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] rely on simple policy classes ( i.e. , Gaussian), which struggle to represent multi-modal and coordinated joint action distributions. When offline data contains a mixture of diverse coordination strategies, a unimodal policy often collapses onto a single mode and produces out-of-distribution joint actions that no agent in the data ever executed together.

To address this expressiveness gap, recent works adopt powerful generative models, including diffusion models [ 7 , 8 ] and flow matching models [ 9 , 10 ] , as policy representations in offline MARL. Although these models improve the representational power of policy, their iterative sampling process incurs a high inference cost. MAC-Flow [ 10 ] and OM 2 P [ 9 ] mitigate this via one-step distillation and mean-flow generation, respectively. However, improved expressiveness and faster inference do not resolve a more fundamental limitation. Since the outcome policy is optimized against a learned Q-function, it inherently tends to collapse diverse coordination modes into a single or blurred one.

Methods that parameterize a policy and optimize it to maximize a learned Q-function must balance value improvement against staying close to the behavioral distribution. A fixed regularization coefficient controls this trade-off. If it is too large, the policy stays too close to suboptimal data; if it is too small, the policy exploits errors in the learned Q-function and produces OOD actions. Although this tension is well-known in single-agent offline RL [ 11 , 12 ] , the multi-agent setting introduces the following compounding difficulty. Training-time value maximization deforms each agent’s policy away from the behavioral prior, and the regularization coefficient bounds how far each marginal may drift, but cannot bound the compound effect on the joint. Even when every marginal remains within its individual support, the joint policy can place mass on action combinations that no trajectory in the data ever visited ( i.e. , regions where the learned Q-function is least reliable). In fact, the data may support multiple distinct joint modes of comparably high estimated value, but committing each marginal to a single greedy mode at training time discards the others before the agent has any way to tell them apart. Once new interaction data arrives, the policy can no longer use it to discriminate which mode is truly higher-value, because the alternatives have already been suppressed.

A natural alternative is to decouple two objectives, motivated by test-time training [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Instead of learning a policy that directly maximizes value, we keep the behavioral policy as a foundational prior and defer value-based refinement to test time. At deployment, we sample action candidates from this prior and then move them toward high-value regions using value gradients. The extent of this adjustment acts as adaptive control, replacing the need for a fixed regularization coefficient.

In this work, we ask a question not yet studied by prior works:

We propose a policy-free value maximization for offline MARL that separates behavioral modeling from value improvement, replacing training-time regularization tuning with a test-time refinement budget.

We derive decomposed value gradient transport under the IGM principle, enabling fully decentralized test-time refinement that recovers inter-agent coordination with a bounded approximation gap.

Empirically, test-time refinement strengthens coordination without retraining, achieving the best average performance in continuous and discrete domains. Notably, unlike existing flow-based MARL, our method yields improvements in all offline-to-online RL experiments.

1. We propose a policy-free value maximization for offline MARL that separates behavioral modeling from value improvement, replacing training-time regularization tuning with a test-time refinement budget.

2. We derive decomposed value gradient transport under the IGM principle, enabling fully decentralized test-time refinement that recovers inter-agent coordination with a bounded approximation gap.

3. Empirically, test-time refinement strengthens coordination without retraining, achieving the best average performance in continuous and discrete domains. Notably, unlike existing flow-based MARL, our method yields improvements in all offline-to-online RL experiments.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Offline MARL. Several works have explored the data-driven sequential decision-making problem, including offline RL and MARL, which aims to extract a return-maximizing policy within the support of an offline dataset. Specifically, offline MARL requires learning coordinated policies for multiple agents. This is not trivial because it requires modeling dependencies among agents in a combinatorially large joint action space. The simplest baselines are multi-agent extensions of single-agent offline RL methods, either by introducing conservatism in the value function [ 11 , 12 ] or the actor [ 16 ] , or by performing Bellman updates without querying out-of-distribution actions [ 17 ] . To further promote coordination, more advanced works are often combined with additional multi-agent design choices, such as value decomposition [ 5 , 18 ] , policy optimization with a centralized critic [ 4 , 6 ] , or a centralized world model [ 19 ] . However, these methods often struggle to capture the multi-modal distributions present in multi-agent offline datasets because of their limited policy expressiveness. To address this issue, recent work has adopted more expressive generative policies, including an autoregressive model [ 20 ] , diffusion models [ 7 ] , and flow matching [ 10 ] . However, these methods couple value learning with the generative process itself: they either anchor the policy via BC-like losses [ 21 , 22 , 10 , 23 ] , which produces overly conservative behavior, or backpropagate value gradients through iterative sampling [ 24 , 25 ] , which is unstable. In contrast, the proposed solution bypasses explicit policy parameterization altogether. Instead, Stein variational gradient [ 26 , 27 , 14 ] fields refine flow-generated action candidates toward high-value regions at test time. This enables adaptive test-time scaling while retaining generative expressiveness.

Test-time action refinement. Our main idea in this work is based on test-time refinement ( i.e. , a ← a + ∇ a Q ​ ( s , a ) a\leftarrow a+\nabla_{a}Q(s,a) ) [ 13 ] , which refines actions from a base generative policy at inference time rather than during training. This paradigm has been explored along several directions in single-agent RL. Rejection sampling methods generate multiple action candidates and select the highest-valued one [ 28 , 29 ] . Gradient-based approaches directly optimize sampled actions via Q-function gradients [ 25 , 14 , 30 ] . Residual policies instead train a separate network to modify a base policy in noise or action space [ 31 , 32 ] . Complementary to these, optimal transport (OT) offers a principled framework for moving probability mass toward high-value regions [ 33 , 34 ] . More recently, particle-based methods adopt an OT viewpoint to transport samples toward value-preferred regions [ 35 ] . However, these approaches remain limited to single-agent settings. The proposed solution is motivated by this direction but specifically designed to solve the multi-agent coordination problem. This avoids explicit policy parameterization and naturally handles the combinatorial joint action space.

2026-10-05.title: World Action Modeling with Progressive Visual Planning
2026-10-05.authors: Fei Zhang , Zhaochong An , Duncan Frost , Yikai Wang , Pengfei Liu , Ya Zhang , Michal Drozdzal , Amir Bar
2026-10-05.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-05.comment: Project Page: this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract: World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual dynamics and actions from an initial observation and instruction. However, existing WAMs struggle with long-horizon prediction, as generating dense video rollouts is highly inefficient. Some recent WAMs address this by predicting a single future frame without generating the full video, but this approach neglects how to progress toward the goal. We present ProWAM , a progressive world action model that jointly predicts actions and an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals, providing explicit visual guidance to anchor action generation throughout task execution. This design scales naturally, as sub-goal prediction can be learned from large-scale action-free videos, allowing the video backbone to offload complex visual planning from the action policy. For efficient action generation, ProWAM executes a single video-backbone forward pass to cache sparse sub-goal features, eliminating iterative full-video generation and requiring only lightweight action denoising during replanning. Across extensive evaluations, ProWAM achieves superior out-of-distribution robustness. On simulation benchmarks, it sets new state-of-the-art results on LIBERO-Plus (85.8%) and randomized RoboTwin (75.7%), outperforming the strongest baseline with relative gains of up to +35.9% . On RoboCasa365, ProWAM achieves a 48.1% success rate and 18.2% on the challenging Composite-Unseen split, ranking 4th overall . Crucially, in zero-shot real-world experiments, ProWAM achieves 70.0% success, outperforming the strongest baseline by +15.0 (from 55.0% to 70.0%, a +27.3% relative gain) in novel scenes. These results demonstrate the value of progress-indexed visual foresight for closed-loop control.
2026-10-05.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models primarily inherit semantic knowledge from vision-language pretraining but remain data-hungry due to their reliance on large, costly collections of robot demonstrations ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ) . In contrast, world action models (WAMs) introduce a complementary source of transferable knowledge: visual-dynamics priors learned by video generation models from large-scale video datasets ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Wan et al., 2025 ) . Recent WAMs have shown that incorporating such predictive visual knowledge can improve data efficiency and out-of-distribution generalization in robotic control ( Pai et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026c ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026 ) .

Existing WAMs differ in how they utilize future visual prediction to guide action generation. Full-imagination WAMs ( Pai et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026c ; Li et al., 2026 ) leverage dense future rollouts that provide detailed near-term guidance but are inefficient as they require multiple denoising passes through a large video backbone. Alternatively, zero-imagination WAMs ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026a ) generate actions without predicting future visual states. Between these extremes, ImageWAM ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) conditions control on an action-horizon endpoint frame without explicitly representing intermediate visual states. These designs reveal a fundamental trade-off: dense visual rollouts provide short-horizon dynamics at high computational cost, whereas other efficient alternatives lack explicit intermediate-progress guidance over the full task.

To reconcile this trade-off, we introduce ProWAM , a progressive world action model that extends a single fixed-state prediction into an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals. Each sub-goal is indexed by normalized progress relative to the current state, where r = 0 r=0 denotes the current observation and r = 1 r=1 denotes the trajectory endpoint. This relative parameterization dynamically re-anchors sub-goals to the current observation, enabling consistent guidance across arbitrary task stages and varying trajectory lengths. Consequently, these sparse targets efficiently guide action generation without requiring dense video rollouts or separate high-level planning modules.

Specifically, ProWAM adopts a vision-action mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture consisting of a video generation expert and a lightweight diffusion-based action expert for policy generation. Each visual sub-goal is represented as a latent slot associated with a normalized progress value. The video expert jointly predicts near-term future transitions and progress-conditioned sub-goals, while the action expert attends to current observations and sub-goals to generate low-level action chunks. Asymmetric attention prevents action information from altering the visual prediction pathway. This design preserves the generative prior of the video expert, enabling video-only pretraining on large-scale action-free videos followed by joint fine-tuning on task-specific robot demonstrations to couple visual planning with action generation.
At inference, ProWAM reuses cached sub-goal features to eliminate repeated video-backbone computation, enabling efficient closed-loop control. Overall, our contributions are threefold:

We introduce progressive sub-goal imagination (Figure 1 ), a new visual planning paradigm for WAMs that represents long-horizon futures as an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals indexed by normalized task progress. This representation provides explicit intermediate guidance without requiring dense video rollouts during inference or an external planner.

We introduce progressive sub-goal imagination (Figure 1 ), a new visual planning paradigm for WAMs that represents long-horizon futures as an ordered sequence of sparse visual sub-goals indexed by normalized task progress. This representation provides explicit intermediate guidance without requiring dense video rollouts during inference or an external planner.

We instantiate this paradigm in ProWAM , a WAM that natively integrates progress-conditioned visual sub-goal prediction with action generation for long-horizon control. By embedding sub-goal slots into the video pathway and coupling them via asymmetric attention, ProWAM enables scalable action-free video pretraining followed by joint vision-action fine-tuning. At inference, cached sub-goal features guide action denoising without repeated video-expert computation.

Extensive simulation and real-world evaluations demonstrate that ProWAM achieves exceptional out-of-distribution robustness, setting a new state-of-the-art on LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) and randomized RoboTwin ( Chen et al., 2025 ) with an average absolute performance gain of +11.4 over prior WAMs. Furthermore, it ranks as the second overall on challenging long-horizon RoboCasa365 ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) benchmark, and outperforms DreamZero ( Ye et al., 2026c ) by +15.0 on zero-shot real-world tasks in novel scenes.

This representation provides explicit intermediate guidance without requiring dense video rollouts during inference or an external planner.

2026-10-05.title: Multi-Fidelity Policy Gradients Stabilize Data-Scarce Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-05.authors: Xinjie Liu , Ruihan Zhao , Anirban Chaudhuri , Cyrus Neary , Ufuk Topcu , David Fridovich-Keil
2026-10-05.abstract:
Policy gradient methods for on-policy reinforcement learning (RL) can become unstable when expensive, scarce target-domain data yield noisy gradient estimates. We address this challenge by complementing limited high-fidelity (HF) target-domain data with abundant, cheap, but biased low-fidelity (LF) data, e.g., from a simplified simulator.
Most existing methods directly optimize biased objectives based on LF data. In contrast,
the recently introduced multi-fidelity policy gradient (MFPG) framework uses LF data solely to construct a control variate that reduces variance and improves HF data efficiency without biasing the policy gradient estimator.
However, published work on MFPG is limited to REINFORCE on small-scale simulation tasks.
We develop MFPG for modern actor-critic learning in GPU-parallel simulation and on a physical robot.
Our analysis and experiments show that naive extensions to proximal policy optimization (PPO) can lose cross-fidelity correlation or inflate variance.
Our MFPG - PPO addresses these failures by redesigning the sampling, advantage estimation, and control variate construction to preserve cross-fidelity correlation, and by monitoring estimator uncertainty to prevent variance inflation.
We also introduce a budget-aware MFPG - PPO to divide a fixed sampling budget among high- and low-fidelity data sources. Across simulated robot locomotion tasks of varying LF -to- HF transfer difficulty and HF data budgets, MFPG - PPO improves upon PPO trained on HF data alone in nearly all settings, and consistently matches the performance of PPO trained with 16 × 16\times more HF data on the hardest task at the smallest HF budgets. In contrast, most baselines that use LF data perform well only where direct LF -to- HF transfer succeeds. MFPG - PPO enables stable learning on a physical Franka arm using only 4 real-robot episodes per update and no human demonstrations.
2026-10-05.introduction:
On-policy reinforcement learning (RL) with policy gradient methods underpins advances in areas ranging from language-model post-training ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ) to fine-tuning vision-language-action models ( Lu et al., 2025 ) for robot control. Yet in many real-world settings, target-domain data are expensive
to collect and therefore scarce, e.g., a physical robot may collect only a handful of rollouts per policy update. In such data-scarce regimes, standard on-policy methods can break down because their policy gradient estimates become too noisy to support stable learning.

We study how to enable stable on-policy RL in data-scarce regimes, ultimately using as few as 4 real-robot episodes per update, or target-domain data batches up to 512 × 512\times smaller than in standard GPU-simulation RL pipelines ( Rudin et al., 2022 ) . The key is access to multi-fidelity data: we assume that the target environment (a physical system or high-accuracy simulator)
provides limited, expensive high-fidelity (HF) samples, whereas a simplified simulator provides abundant, inexpensive, but biased low-fidelity (LF) samples. Exploiting LF data requires care, however, and can easily bias policy updates and degrade performance in the target HF environment.

Existing approaches use LF data in different ways. Off-dynamics RL methods ( Eysenbach et al., 2021 ; Lyu et al., 2024 ) learn to correct LF rewards for the dynamics mismatch, and sim-and-real co-training ( Wei et al., 2025 ) mixes LF and HF data. However, reliability is a major challenge. Most of these methods still directly optimize biased objectives based on LF data, so their performance in the target HF environment is largely tied to how well policies learned from LF data transfer.

The recent multi-fidelity policy gradient (MFPG) framework ( Liu et al., 2026 ) offers a principled alternative. Here, LF samples are used to construct a control variate ( Nelson, 1987 ) —a correlated auxiliary random variable with a known mean—for the HF policy gradient estimator. The MFPG estimator remains unbiased with respect to the HF objective, and the policy gradient surrogate variance shrinks as the cross-fidelity data correlation grows. MFPG is therefore robust to LF data biases.

However, the MFPG construction of Liu et al. (2026) is limited to the classic REINFORCE algorithm ( Williams, 1992 ) and small-scale, single-environment simulation tasks. How MFPG interacts with modern actor-critic learning and GPU-parallel simulation ( Mittal et al., 2025 ; Tao et al., 2024 ) , and how it translates to real-robot learning, remain unresolved.
An earlier preprint ( Liu et al., 2025 ) directly substituted proximal policy optimization (PPO) for REINFORCE. The resulting
method did not consistently improve over the REINFORCE
instantiation and sometimes even underperformed single-fidelity PPO . Hence, an effective extension requires more than algorithm substitution.

We address this gap with two contributions: (i) MFPG - PPO , a multi-fidelity PPO algorithm. Through analysis and experiments, we show how naive PPO instantiations of MFPG can lose cross-fidelity correlation or inflate variance by orders of magnitude. We address these failures by redesigning the sampling, advantage estimation, and control variate construction to preserve cross-fidelity correlation, and by monitoring estimator uncertainty to prevent variance inflation. Preserving correlation comes at the price of potential bias, a tradeoff we characterize analytically. (ii) A budget-aware MFPG - PPO . When HF and LF samples incur different costs, we allocate a fixed per-iteration sampling budget across fidelities, guided by the variance-minimizing allocation framework of Peherstorfer et al. (2016) .

We test MFPG - PPO in GPU-parallel simulation ( Mittal et al., 2025 ; Tao et al., 2024 ) and on a physical robot arm. Across simulation tasks and HF data budgets, we compare with 5 baselines that use LF data in different ways and with PPO and soft actor-critic (SAC) ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) trained on HF data alone. MFPG - PPO is the only method in our comparison that improves over PPO trained on HF data alone in nearly all settings, is never distinguishably worse, and scales monotonically with more HF data. Most baselines that use LF data perform well only where direct LF -to- HF transfer succeeds. On the hardest task at the smallest HF budgets, MFPG - PPO consistently matches the mean return of PPO trained with 16 × 16\times more HF data, cf. . Finally, MFPG - PPO enables stable RL on a Franka arm with only 4 episodes per policy update and no human demonstrations.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

LF simulation can support policy learning for an HF target domain through system identification ( Ljung, 1998 ; Ramos et al., 2019 ) , zero-shot transfer with domain randomization ( Tobin et al., 2017 ; Peng et al., 2018 ) , adapting simulation-trained priors with scarce HF data ( Smith et al., 2022 ; Levy et al., 2026 ) , and combining multi-fidelity data within policy updates. We focus on the last category. A complementary line of multi-fidelity RL research ( Cutler et al., 2015 ; Marco et al., 2017 ; Ryou et al., 2026 ; Bhola et al., 2023 ; Sifaou & Simeone, 2025 ) studies which fidelity to query at each training stage rather than how to combine fidelities within a policy update.

Three mechanisms for combining multi-fidelity data are particularly relevant. Pooling multi-fidelity data is a simple and effective recipe for sim-and-real co-training in imitation learning ( Maddukuri et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Lei et al., 2026 ) and in RL ( Di-Castro et al., 2021 ) . Off-dynamics RL corrects for estimated dynamics mismatch in LF data, e.g., through reward penalties from domain classifiers ( Eysenbach et al., 2021 ) or representation mismatch ( Lyu et al., 2024 ) , filtering by value discrepancy ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , support extension ( Le Pham Van et al., 2024 ) , or imitation-based transfer ( Guo et al., 2024 ) , with extensions to offline and hybrid offline-online settings ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Niu et al., 2022 ; Niu et al., 2025 ; Lyu et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) .

Pooling and correction optimize biased objectives based on LF data, whereas multi-fidelity control variates use LF data to reduce variance in HF estimates. Control variates are a classical tool in single-fidelity RL ( Greensmith et al., 2004 ; Gu et al., 2017 ; Cheng et al., 2020 ) . Recently, Khairy & Balaprakash (2024) develop multi-fidelity control variates for state-action value estimation in tabular Markov decision processes (MDPs) , while Liu et al. (2026) propose a policy gradient framework based on REINFORCE with function approximation. Building on these advances, we develop multi-fidelity control variates for actor-critic learning in GPU-parallel simulation and on a real robot.

2026-10-05.title: Network-in-the-Loop at Scale: GPU-Batched 5G Simulation for Massively Parallel Robot Learning
2026-10-05.authors: Zifan Zhang , Mingzhe Han , Kannan Athreya , Yuchen Liu
2026-10-05.subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-05.comment: It is open source at this https URL
2026-10-05.abstract:
Massively parallel GPU simulators train multi-robot policies in thousands of environments, and many fleets use private Fifth-Generation (5G) networks, where each robot’s delay depends on its teammates’ traffic.
Network-in-the-loop training places a simulated 5G network inside this loop.
However, GPU robot simulators reduce the network to an independent delay per message, while packet-level simulators run one scenario per CPU process and cannot keep pace with thousands of parallel environments.
To bridge this gap, we present Isaac-Net, a GPU-batched 5G New Radio (NR) module that advances the uplink of thousands of environments in lockstep with Isaac Lab physics.
Isaac-Net simulates every slot, the 0.5 ms interval in which the base station decides which robots transmit, for all environments at once.
Extensive experiments confirm that its NR engine reproduces the median delay of ns-3 5G-LENA across loads, with a median delay 5–10% low on an unseen carrier and 9% high at 32 robots per environment in closed loop.
The engine also reproduces the Age of Information (AoI), the age of each robot’s newest delivered report, while an independent delay per message leaves the AoI tail about three times too light.
In a configuration validated against 5G-LENA, Isaac-Net keeps the network in the loop for about one million robots on one GPU at 83% of the Isaac Lab rate without the network, measured under a random policy.
Isaac-Net is open source at https://github.com/ZzZTripleZzZ/isaac-net .
2026-10-05.introduction:
Robot learning has moved onto the GPU, where simulators such as Isaac Gym [ 1 ] , Isaac Lab [ 2 ] , ManiSkill3 [ 3 ] , and MuJoCo Playground [ 4 ] step thousands of environments in parallel and feed the resulting experience directly into reinforcement learning.
This throughput has made it practical to train policies for whole teams of robots, such as warehouse fleets, drone swarms, and multi-arm workstations, in which each environment holds tens to hundreds of agents [ 5 , 6 ] .
Many of these teams report sensor data to an edge server and receive commands from it over a wireless network.
Moreover, private Fifth-Generation (5G) networks are increasingly deployed for mobile robots in factories and campuses [ 7 , 8 ] .
A policy trained for such a team therefore acts on information that the network may have delayed or lost, so the network belongs inside the massively parallel training loop.
We call such training network-in-the-loop, by analogy with hardware-in-the-loop testing, although the network inside the loop is simulated, not a real one.

In a 5G cell, the base station, called the gNB, divides one pool of radio resources among the robots in every slot.
A slot is a fixed scheduling interval, 0.5 ms at the common 30 kHz subcarrier spacing, in which the gNB decides which robots transmit based on channel quality and on Buffer Status Reports (BSRs), the reports in which robots state how many bytes they hold.
A robot may transmit only after the gNB sends it a grant, that is, a permission to transmit on given resources, which the gNB issues after a scheduling request and then sizes from later buffer reports.
A failed transmission is retried several slots later through Hybrid Automatic Repeat reQuest (HARQ), a fast retransmission scheme of the radio link, and unsent messages wait in per-robot queues.
Consequently, the delay that a robot experiences depends on its own position and on what its teammates in the cell transmit, meaning that network behavior and team behavior are coupled.
This coupling also closes a loop between the policy and the network.
For instance, a policy may send more reports when reports arrive late, which could congest its own uplink and delay every later report.
A learning environment that captures this loop could teach a fleet when to send, how much to send, and where to move so that critical reports arrive in time.
However, GPU-parallel robot simulators typically model the network, if at all, as a fixed delay or as a delay drawn independently for each message.
For instance, the delayed actuator model of Isaac Lab [ 2 ] applies each command a set number of physics steps late, so it cannot express contention among teammates.

Motivation and Challenges: Putting a faithful 5G network inside a GPU-parallel training loop raises three challenges.
We measure simulation speed in robot-steps per second, where a robot-step advances one robot by one control step, the 100 ms interval at which the policy acts. First , delays from contention among robots for the same radio resources, from HARQ retransmissions, and from scheduling arise per slot and persist across a robot’s successive messages.
Thus, an independent delay per message misses part of what a controller observes under load. Second , a packet-level simulator on a CPU advances one scenario at a time, whereas GPU physics steps thousands of environments at once, so the network would stall the training loop.
Figure 1 shows that a pool of 12 ns-3 5G-LENA [ 9 ] processes, which run the 5G module of the packet-level simulator ns-3, delivers a few thousand robot-steps per second on a shared CPU.
One ns-3 process that advances in lockstep with the controller at 10 Hz keeps pace for only 48 robots.
In contrast, Isaac Lab physics alone reaches about 1.6 million robot-steps per second with simple sphere-shaped robots on one GPU. Lastly , the network must stay aligned with 20 ms physics substeps and with control steps while Isaac Lab resets any subset of environments at any step.
A simulator that pauses or restarts as a whole would therefore hold back every other environment.

Limitations and Opportunities: Mature mobile network simulators, such as ns-3 with its LTE and 5G-LENA [ 9 ] modules, Simu5G [ 10 ] , the Vienna 5G simulators [ 11 ] , and the MATLAB 5G Toolbox, model cellular networks accurately, and Veins [ 12 ] couples such simulators with road traffic.
Recent works have also coupled robot simulators with network simulators [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 8 ] , yet each typically pairs one robot scene with one network instance through the Robot Operating System (ROS) or a real-time broker, so it runs at or below wall-clock speed.
GPU network simulators such as GeDES [ 18 ] accelerate one large wired network.
Sionna SYS [ 19 ] batches the 5G link model and scheduler, but it keeps no queue per robot, no HARQ timing, and no uplink access driven by buffer reports.
QNet [ 20 ] learns when an agent should send over a shared network, yet its training network has no per-slot scheduling or HARQ and is not coupled to robot physics.

GPU-parallel reinforcement learning created three requirements that none of these tools meets together: 1) a batch dimension, so that thousands of independent scenarios advance together on one GPU; 2) lockstep with a physics engine, in which the network advances exactly one control step whenever the physics does, returns per-robot observations as tensors, and resets single environments at arbitrary times; and 3) closed-loop traffic and mobility, in which the policy decides what each robot sends and the physics decides where it is, so nothing can be precomputed or replayed.
Training experiments also need every environment to stay reproducible, which calls for a separate random stream per environment so that its results do not change with the batch size.
The network model must also avoid host synchronization, that is, it must never make the GPU wait for the CPU.
These requirements appeared with GPU-parallel learning, and Isaac-Net is built around them from the ground up.

Contributions: To this end, we develop Isaac-Net 1 1 1 Project page: https://isaacnet.zifanzhang.com . Code: https://github.com/ZzZTripleZzZ/isaac-net . , a GPU-batched 5G New Radio (NR) module that brings network-in-the-loop training to Isaac Lab at full parallel scale, where the robots of every environment contend slot by slot for the uplink of a shared cell.
In essence, three core techniques are developed:

First , Isaac-Net stores each robot’s channel, scheduler state, HARQ processes, access timers, and message queue in fixed-shape tensors indexed by environment and robot. The same tensor operations then advance the state of all robots in all environments at every slot. Per-environment clocks, partial resets, and random draws keyed by environment and step let Isaac Lab restart any subset of environments while every other environment continues bitwise unaffected.

Second , a configurable NR engine (level L2 in the code) models 5G scheduling, decoding errors, retransmissions, and uplink grants, while a simpler prototype engine (level L2-legacy in the code) remains as a cheaper option. Both engines run on three backends, namely a plain PyTorch reference, a graph backend that is bitwise identical to it, and a triton backend that fuses one control step into a single GPU function, called a kernel, and matches the reference to floating-point rounding. Equivalence tests feed identical random draws to a fast backend and the reference and compare every output and state value at every step, thereby verifying each speed-up before it runs at the scale of millions of robots.

Third , a mixin class, that is, a reusable add-on class, inserts the network through four hooks into any direct-workflow Isaac Lab environment, in which one class computes observations and rewards. It returns each robot’s Age of Information (AoI) [ 21 ] , that is, how old its newest delivered message is, together with its queue length, Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), and delivery flag. An Isaac Lab event term, a function called at every reset, redraws the radio parameters, so the policy trains over many radio conditions, which is called domain randomization.

Isaac-Net is released as the pip-installable package isaac-net , with its test suite, co-simulation bridges to ns-3 5G-LENA and to the OpenAirInterface (OAI) 5G stack [ 22 ] , an Isaac Lab fleet task, and documentation on the project page.

Extensive experiments show that, in the scale configuration, that is, the validated NR configuration without the buffer-report grant procedure, Isaac Lab runs 1,048,576 robots with the network in the loop at 1.24 control steps per second on one GPU under a random policy, against 1.50 without the network. With that procedure and no fitted parameter, the NR engine reproduces the per-run median delay of 5G-LENA within a median absolute error of 2.5–4.8% from light to saturated load. Under load in closed loop, it also reproduces the AoI that a hand-written controller, not a learned policy, observes over ns-3, while an independent delay per message, even one drawn from the engine’s own delays, leaves the AoI tail about three times too light.

To the best of our knowledge, Isaac-Net is the first 5G network model that runs batched on the GPU inside a massively parallel robot learning loop.

# II Design of Isaac-Net

## II-A Problem Setting

Isaac-Net serves E E parallel environments with R R robots each, where every robot is a 5G User Equipment (UE) attached to the gNB of its environment.
All robots of one environment share the radio resources of this gNB.
Isaac Lab owns the physics, the policy, and the reward, while Isaac-Net owns the path of each message from the robot to the edge server.
Time advances in control steps of length Δ \Delta , the interval at which the policy acts, and each control step covers K K uplink slots of the NR frame structure.
The goal is to advance all E E networks by one control step at a cost that is small compared with the physics of that step, while each environment evolves as if simulated alone slot by slot.

However, this problem is intrinsically difficult for three reasons.
First, the Medium Access Control (MAC) layer couples all robots of a cell at every slot, which rules out simulating robots independently.
Second, the clocks of radio slots, physics substeps, and control steps differ by two orders of magnitude, which rules out advancing the network only once per control step.
Lastly, Isaac Lab ends and restarts episodes of different environments at different times, which rules out restarting the whole simulation, as a packet-level simulator would.
These factors must be handled for thousands of environments within every physics step, which makes a direct GPU port of an event-driven simulator impractical and motivates the following design.

## II-B Overview of Isaac-Net

Isaac-Net advances the networks of all E E environments together, as one batch of tensor operations over the E × R E\times R robots, so a single call serves the whole parallel training loop.
It exposes two API calls on tensors, where submit takes the message class that each robot sends in this step, and step takes the robot poses and returns what the network delivered.
Two per-slot engines implement this interface, the configurable NR engine and a prototype engine, which the following Section II-F compares. A High-Level Walkthrough: Figure 2 traces one control step through Isaac-Net in five numbered steps.
In step 1, the policy submits a message class per robot, namely nothing, a small message such as a status report, or a large message such as a camera frame.
In step 2, the message queue captures each message with the robot’s pose at the start of the step and appends it to that robot’s First-In First-Out (FIFO) buffer.
In step 3, after the physics substeps, the radio model converts the start-of-step and end-of-step poses into a per-robot SNR.
In step 4, the NR MAC runs all K K uplink slots of the step for the robots of all E E environments at once.
In each slot, every gNB schedules its robots, selects a Modulation and Coding Scheme (MCS), and decodes Transport Blocks (TBs) against the Physical Layer (PHY) tables with HARQ retransmissions.
In step 5, Isaac-Net returns per robot the delivered and dropped messages, their delay, the AoI, the queue length, and the SNR, which the environment turns into observations and rewards.
The strip at the bottom of the figure shows how one control step of length Δ \Delta aligns D D physics substeps with K K uplink slots.
The boxes at the bottom right of the figure list the fidelity levels, that is, network models of increasing detail described in Section II-F , and the simulators that Isaac-Net was validated against.

## II-C Time-Stepped Slot Loop

Packet-level simulators such as ns-3 process events one at a time in time order, which batches poorly because events of different environments fall at different times and follow different code paths.
Isaac-Net instead exploits a property of the NR MAC layer, namely that scheduling, transmission, decoding, and HARQ feedback all take effect at slot boundaries.
A time-stepped loop over slots therefore visits every instant at which the modeled MAC state can change, and it needs no event queue, no dynamic memory, and no code path that depends on which environment is being processed.
Each slot becomes a fixed sequence of tensor operations over the leading dimensions [ E , R ] [E,R] , which a GPU executes efficiently.
A single fused kernel can run this sequence, and so can a CUDA graph [ 23 ] , a recorded chain of kernels that the GPU replays with a single launch.
In the Time-Division Duplex (TDD) pattern of the frame, only some slots carry uplink traffic, so a control step of Δ \Delta (e.g., 100 100 ms) spans K K (e.g., 40 40 ) uplink slots.

Two approximations make the loop efficient.
First, messages enter the network at control-step boundaries, which matches a policy that decides once per step what to send.
Second, the radio averages the SNR over J J (e.g., 4 4 ) poses interpolated across the step, while fast fading, the rapid fluctuation of the signal, still evolves every slot inside the engine.
Since mobile robots typically move at a few meters per second, the geometry changes by well under a meter within one step.

## II-D Fixed-Shape Network State

Every state variable of Isaac-Net is a tensor with leading dimensions [ E , R ] [E,R] and a fixed trailing shape.
For instance, [ E , R , S ] [E,R,S] holds the fading of S S subbands, the frequency blocks of the carrier, [ E , R , H ] [E,R,H] the H H HARQ processes, and [ E , R , F ] [E,R,F] a FIFO of F F messages per robot.
Algorithm 1 lists one control step on this state.

Stage I (Enqueue): The message queue writes new messages into the first free FIFO entry of each robot through a one-hot mask, a mask with a single 1 at the target entry (Line 1).
The mask avoids the GPU-to-CPU wait that an index lookup such as nonzero would force, and finished messages are removed while the remaining ones shift forward in order. Stage II (Radio): The radio converts the interpolated poses into one SNR per robot and cell from path loss, correlated shadowing, and optional blockage by other robots (Line 2). Stage III (Slot loop): The MAC layer advances fading, access, scheduling, link adaptation, decoding, and HARQ for all robots at once, and it serves queued bytes in order (Lines 3–10).
Because the FIFO holds bytes in a stream, a grant of c c bytes serves s i s_{i} bytes of message i i , which has r i r_{i} bytes left and starts b i b_{i} bytes into the grant, given by

Isaac Lab resets environments individually, so every state tensor supports a partial reset.
Thus, Isaac-Net keeps a per-environment clock, defined as the global slot clock minus the step at which the environment was last reset, and a reset rewrites only the rows of the selected environments in place.
Every random number is computed by hashing the seed, the environment, the episode, the step since reset, the slot, and the place in the code that draws it.
Thus, an environment’s draws depend neither on E E nor on other resets, and a reset leaves every other environment bitwise unaffected and never reallocates a buffer.

## II-E Backends and the Equivalence Guarantee

Fixed shapes make an engine fast only if its per-slot operations are fused.
At E × R = 64 × 16 E\times R=64\times 16 , the prototype engine in plain PyTorch launches about 3,000 small kernels per control step and the NR engine about 27,000, each doing only microseconds of work.
Isaac-Net therefore provides three backends that share the same state and API for both engines.
The reference backend implements the model in plain PyTorch for readability and thereby defines it.
The graph backend keeps every state tensor in a persistent buffer, derives slot and HARQ times from a device-side step counter, and captures one control step as a CUDA graph that is replayed without Python overhead.
The triton backend runs all slots of a control step in one Triton [ 25 ] kernel with one GPU program per environment, which keeps each robot’s state in registers, the fastest on-chip memory, and evaluates the same hash as the reference.
We call the graph and triton backends the fast backends.
The triton kernel of the NR engine covers the whole slot, from fading to the Radio Link Control (RLC) layer, and runs the downlink as a second kernel.
It is single-cell and supports every option of the lena_validation_v2 preset of Section II-G except the buffer-report grant procedure, in which buffer reports size the later grants.
The scale experiments therefore use this preset with a single fixed access delay, the time from a scheduling request to the first uplink data, in place of that procedure.
This preset is the scale configuration, and Section IV-C validates it against 5G-LENA.

Such optimizations can silently change the model, so Isaac-Net treats every fast backend as a refactoring that must be verified against the reference.
The equivalence tests feed the same pre-generated decode draws and fading innovations, that is, random increments of the fading process, to both backends and compare every step output, per-message field, and MAC state tensor with exact equality.
The tests run in a full-run mode, in which each backend evolves its own state, and in a per-step mode, in which both backends start from the same recorded state at every step because the reference state is copied into the fast backend before each step.
The per-step mode thus separates per-step disagreements from the later divergence that one early disagreement causes.
The graph backend must be bitwise identical in both modes, while the triton backend, which sums values in a different order and rounds differently, must agree to floating-point rounding.
Rare flips of a discrete decision, such as a TB decode at its threshold, are acceptable if they leave aggregate statistics unchanged.
A torch.compile backend of the prototype engine failed this test and is excluded from training runs (see Section IV-B for details).

## II-F Fidelity Levels

Every model in Isaac-Net implements the same API, so a task selects the network model by changing one argument.
The i.i.d. delay model (level L0 in the code) draws a delay and a loss independently per message, as current robot simulators typically do, with the delay either log-normal or resampled from a given delay sample.
The fluid model (level L1 in the code) approximates the MAC by letting active robots share the Physical Resource Blocks (PRBs) equally in every slot while their FIFO queues drain.
The two most detailed levels run the configurable NR engine of Section II-G and the frozen prototype engine, which ignores the MAC and PHY fields of the configuration.
The prototype engine uses a logistic BLER curve, one HARQ process, a fixed noise power, and a minimal grant after two uplink slots, and the NR engine replaces each of these simplifications with a 3GPP-based model.
Both engines have all three backends, and Section IV-C compares both with 5G-LENA.

## II-G Configurable NR

One configuration object, NRConfig , configures every module of the NR engine, and Table I summarizes what it exposes.
The frame structure follows the 3GPP specifications, and the Resource Block Groups (RBGs), MCS tables, and exact TB sizes follow TS 38.214 [ 26 ] .
The engine combines the SINR of all RBGs into one effective SINR by Exponential Effective SINR Mapping (EESM) [ 27 ] , which weights weak RBGs more, since they dominate decoding errors.
It then looks up the BLER in tables exported from Sionna [ 19 ] or generated locally from a 5G-LENA checkout [ 9 , 28 ] .
A TB that exhausts its HARQ transmissions is either retried by the RLC layer in Acknowledged Mode (AM) or lost in Unacknowledged Mode (UM).
Outer-Loop Link Adaptation (OLLA) [ 29 ] shifts the SINR estimate after every acknowledgment to absorb estimation errors, and SRs and BSRs follow the access procedure of TS 38.321 [ 30 ] .
Four configuration options, off by default and with no fitted parameter, reproduce how a 5G-LENA gNB serves a loaded cell.
First, the per-RBG PF update recomputes a robot’s average throughput after every RBG it wins, which lowers its priority for the next RBG, so several backlogged robots split each slot.
This update also leaves the averages of idle robots unchanged.
Second, Time-Division Multiple Access (TDMA) retransmissions give every uplink retransmission a whole slot.
Third, link adaptation picks each robot’s MCS assuming it will receive as many RBGs as in its previous uplink transmission, as 5G-LENA does.
Lastly, the buffer-report grant procedure replaces the single fixed access delay with a small first grant, after which buffer reports, which arrive late and in coarse size steps, size the later grants.
It also models the wait of a message’s last bytes for an RLC status timer.
The NR engine also implements a downlink with gNB queues, channel-quality reports, and HARQ feedback, which the fast backends reproduce but which has not yet been compared with another simulator.

Presets bundle these settings for common scenarios.
The lena_validation preset, called v1 below, reproduces the ns-3 5G-LENA scenario of Section IV-C with one fitted access delay, and lena_validation_v2 , called v2, adds the four load options with no fitted value.
The srsran_like and oai_like presets carry uplink delay parameters fitted on the prototype engine to public measurements of the srsRAN [ 32 ] and OAI [ 22 ] stacks.
The oai_rfsim preset carries three values measured on a running OAI stack, namely the SR period, the delay from a grant to the data it allows, called K2, and the HARQ round-trip time.
It adds one access delay fitted to the OAI traces, as reported in the later Section IV-D .
Each level declares which field groups it reads, and a strict mode rejects a configuration that sets a field the level cannot honor, such as a path-loss exponent under the i.i.d. delay model.

## II-H Multiple Cells

A fleet that spans a warehouse is typically served by several gNBs, so Isaac-Net supports up to C C (e.g., 7 7 ) cells per environment in hexagonal, grid, or custom layouts, batched over a cell dimension.
Each cell runs its own PF scheduler over the carrier that all cells share.
Uplink interference at a gNB comes from the robots that other cells scheduled on the same subband in the same slot, each through its own fading.
Link adaptation uses the interference of the previous slot, as a real gNB would, while decoding uses that of the current slot, and OLLA absorbs the resulting error.
Fractional uplink power control is on by default with more than one cell, because without it three cells can deliver less traffic than a single cell.
This scheme compensates only part of each robot’s path loss, which limits the interference that robots cause in other cells.
Handover follows the 3GPP A3 event, which fires when a neighbor cell stays stronger than the serving cell by a hysteresis margin for a time-to-trigger.
The multi-cell model runs on the reference and graph backends of the NR engine and on the reference backend of the prototype engine.
With one cell, it is bitwise identical to the single-cell engine.

## II-I Coupling with Isaac Lab

Isaac Lab runs physics substeps of length δ \delta (e.g., 20 20 ms) and applies the policy every D D (e.g., 5 5 ) substeps, so one control step lasts Δ = D ​ δ \Delta=D\delta .
Isaac-Net aligns its K K uplink slots with exactly this interval.
A mixin class couples Isaac-Net with direct-workflow environments through four hooks for setup, stepping, reset, and observations.
In its pre-physics hook, the environment decides what each robot sends, and Isaac-Net captures those messages at the start-of-step pose.
Thus, a message never reports a state that the robot has not reached yet.
The network step runs after the physics and before Isaac Lab resets finished environments.
The reset hook forwards the indices of these environments to the partial reset of the engine.
The observation hook returns, per robot, the AoI of its freshest delivered message, its SNR, its queued messages, and whether its last message was delivered.
A standard event term redraws per-environment radio parameters at every reset, thereby enabling domain randomization of the network.

2026-10-05.title: Co-design Gym: A Unified Benchmark for Embodiment-Policy Co-optimization
2026-10-05.authors: Aviraj Newatia , Yordan Tsvetkov , Leonard Pleiss , Andrew Spielberg , Rika Antonova
2026-10-05.comment: Aviraj Newatia and Yordan Tsvetkov contributed equally
2026-10-05.abstract: Finding an optimal behaviour policy within a given environment is a widely studied problem in domains as diverse as games, robotics, energy infrastructure, communication networks, and multi-agent systems. Numerous benchmarks have been developed to support such research, but the vast majority assume that the agent’s embodiment (design) is fixed, focusing instead on policy learning alone. Lifting this assumption gives rise to a broader class of problems in which optimizing embodiment and policy separately is highly suboptimal. An agent’s embodiment strongly shapes which control policies can be discovered, while the optimal embodiment is in turn defined by the policies it admits. To help the research community study this class of problems explicitly and systematically, we introduce Co-Design Gym – a suite of benchmark environments for jointly optimizing embodiment and policy. Our environments span domains such as robotic manipulation and locomotion, multi-robot cooperation, deformable and soft dynamics, video games, electricity grids, wireless networks, F1 racing, multi-agent warehouses, and optimal control, offering 20 environment families (domains), with over 85 distinct co-design presets in total. We further contribute a systematic evaluation of representative co-design algorithms, characterizing the current state of the art. Together, these contributions lay the groundwork for cumulative, comparable progress in co-design.
2026-10-05.introduction:
An agent’s ability is a function of both its embodiment and its behavioral policy . An embodiment determines what an agent is able to do : it is an interface for transforming perception into action upon an external environment.
The policy determines what the agent actually does , using a given physical interface. The process of jointly improving the embodiment and the policy toward performance goals is referred to as co-design .

Embodiment and policy are coupled: the quality of an embodiment is the performance of the best policy it can achieve for downstream tasks. Hence, fully assessing each candidate embodiment requires finding an optimal policy for it on a variety of tasks. However, running expensive policy optimization to completion before knowing the potential of an embodiment is wasteful. Tighter co-optimization is essential, especially when the embodiment and policy subspace structures yield challenging high-dimensional optimization landscapes.

The above calls for extending optimization paradigms such as Reinforcement Learning (RL), usually framed as singly non-stationary optimization. Recognizing co-design as a doubly non-stationary problem is more suitable, since both the policy and the embodiment can change rapidly.
Finding global or even high-quality local optima for this extended problem is expensive, and gauging real progress is nontrivial. To date, no unified benchmark tracks the performance of co-design methods across a variety of domains, or disentangles progress in embodiment search and policy optimization from progress specific to co-design.

Co-design today stands in a similar place to where RL stood before the introduction of unified benchmarks, when agents still struggled to solve basic tasks ( Mnih et al., 2015 ) . Benchmarks and unifying frameworks, e.g. OpenAI Gym and Gymnasium ( Brockman et al., 2016 ; Towers et al., 2024 ) , enabled compound progress that accelerated the field. RL agents have since reached superhuman performance in a wide variety of areas, such as strategic game playing in Go ( Silver et al., 2016 ) & Dota 2 ( Berner et al., 2019 ) , drone racing ( Geles et al., 2026 ) , control of tokamak plasmas for nuclear fusion ( Degrave et al., 2022 ) , and robot locomotion ( Peng et al., 2017 ; Peng et al., 2018 ; Margolis et al., 2021 ) , to name a few. A unified benchmark for co-design should spark comparable progress.

In pursuit of that, we introduce Co-Design Gym – a unified benchmark for co-design algorithms. Our contribution is threefold.
First, we extend the canonical Gymnasium API with an explicit design space, so that any policy-learning task can be lifted into a co-design task.
Second, we leverage this generalized API to convert prominent existing policy optimization environments into co-design tasks.
Finally, we present novel co-design environments in which embodiment optimization is decisive for what the policy can achieve: from reshaping fingertips for precise manipulation of small objects & reshaping a hand for fast in-hand reorientation, to dynamic ball catching, multi-robot truck unloading, and evolving soft robots for locomotion.
Overall, we offer 20 environment families and over 85 presets, with accelerated GPU-based resets that make it practical to evaluate thousands of embodiments in parallel. Benchmarking representative evolutionary, reinforcement-learning, hybrid and transformer-based co-design methods under matched compute budgets, we find that no single method dominates, and that many tasks remain far from solved.
This leaves substantial headroom for new methods, and we call upon the community to take advantage of this opportunity.
2026-10-05.related_work:
# 2 Background and Related Work

Co-design problems appear naturally across disciplines in design tasks that feature both a static embodiment and a time-varying policy component, and in which choices made in each domain can affect choices in the other. Over the last several decades, methods have been developed for the co-design of computer systems hardware and software ( De Michell and Gupta, 1997 ; Milder et al., 2012 ) , optics and their processing algorithms ( Dowski Jr and Cathey, 1995 ) , aeronautical materials and stabilizers ( Salama et al., 1989 ) , and chemical plants and processes ( Luyben and Floudas, 1994 ) , just to name a few. More recently, co-design of the embodiments and policies of virtual and physical robots has seen growing interest. This problem is exceptionally relevant now that investment in robotic hardware is at all-time high: advanced hardware prototyping is finally affordable, thus co-design solutions don’t have to be confined to simulation. Robots typically must solve tasks that involve a complex combination of dynamical moves, medium-to-long-term-planning, a mix of discrete and continuous optimization in both morphological structure and actions all at once, while still enabling fast (real-time) operation of the whole system. A further challenge is to transfer the success from simulation to reality. All these aspects make co-optimization of robot systems particularly challenging, yielding an ideal ground for testing novel co-design methods.

Early research built upon the seminal works of Ventrella (1994) and Sims (1994) and employed evolutionary algorithms ( Hiller and Lipson, 2011 ; Cheney et al., 2014b ; Cheney et al., 2014a ; Corucci et al., 2016 ) , a trend that still sees application in modern learning-based approaches ( Wang et al., 2019 ; Yuan et al., 2021 ) and are enjoying a renaissance in combination with off-the-shelf large models ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . While these approaches produce robust specimens ( Bongard, 2011 ; Hejna III et al., 2021 ) their sampling-based search can be inefficient when simulation time becomes the computational bottleneck. In such cases, complementary approaches that use gradient-based search tend to more efficient ( Matthews et al., 2023 ) . Given continuous and smoothly differentiable parameterizations of morphology and controllers, these approaches employ unconstrained and constrained optimizers to search over optimal parameterizations of geometry ( Wampler and Popović, 2009 ; Coros et al., 2013 ; Spielberg et al., 2017 ; Ha et al., 2017 ; Ma et al., 2021 ) , materials, ( Spielberg et al., 2023 ) , and controllers and observers ( Spielberg et al., 2019 ) for solving specified tasks. As the field has begun to mature in the last decade, holistic frameworks have emerged that have driven toward a unifying theory of co-design ( Censi, 2015 ; Zardini, 2023 ) . Sampling- and gradient-based approaches have also begun to merge under the umbrella of generative systems ( Wang et al., 2023a ; Zhao et al., 2020 ; Xu et al., 2021 ; Dai et al., 2026 ; Ha et al., 2026 ) .

Though much of the above work focuses on the algorithmic nature of co-design algorithms, co-designed creatures are not confined to the virtual world. Successful physical demonstrations of co-designed robots reach back as far as Park and Asada (1994) and have been applied to form factors such as quadrupeds ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , grippers ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Fay et al., 2026 ) , full humanoids ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , and more at large ( Yu et al., 2026 ) and small scales ( Kriegman et al., 2020 ; Balciunaite et al., 2026 ) .

Despite algorithmic progress, evaluation progress has lagged.
Two precedents have made some progress in this regard. SoftZoo ( Wang et al., 2023b ) provides benchmarking for soft robot co-design algorithms across terrains, materiality, and morphological representations, but lacks physical realism and is limited to 3D elastic dynamics. EvoGym ( Bhatia et al., 2022 ) provides an extensive array of tasks and environments and emphasizes complex neural control tasks, but it is also limited to soft robots, and in this case, 2D, low-fidelity pixel representations. Further evaluation setups relevant to co-design exist, but either focus on a narrow set of tasks, or lack realistic environment modeling.
Our work is most inspired by the OpenAI Gym ( Brockman et al., 2016 ) and its successor, Gymnasium ( Towers et al., 2024 ) , which have been seminal for RL research under a shared framework, but lack the extensibility needed to accommodate search over morphologies and other embodiment aspects.
