2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Generative World Models for Embodied Interaction

Large-scale video generators provide increasingly capable visual
priors for world modeling ( Wan et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2025 ; Ali et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) ,
with recent efforts extending pretraining and adaptation toward
embodied interaction.
Qwen-RobotWorld ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) uses
natural-language actions to predict future visual trajectories
across manipulation, navigation, and driving, while
LingBot-Video ( Ma et al., 2026a ) scales
mixture-of-experts video pretraining with robot-oriented data.
DreamGen ( Jang et al., 2025 ) adapts video generators to
target robot embodiments and recovers action labels through
inverse dynamics or latent action models, producing synthetic
trajectories for policy learning.
RoboScape ( Shang et al., 2025 ) incorporates physical
priors through joint RGB–depth prediction and keypoint-based
temporal consistency.
PhysisForcing ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) improves physical
consistency using supervision constructed through a multi-model
pipeline involving point tracking, depth-aware region selection,
and semantic relation extraction.
In contrast, our latent-motion distillation derives supervision
directly from temporal differences in a simulation-pretrained
teacher’s predicted video latents, without constructing explicit
depth, point-trajectory, or semantic-relation targets.

Action-conditioned world models connect robot controls to
predicted visual outcomes.
IRASim ( Zhu et al., 2025b ) learns from historical observations
and continuous actions, while AVID ( Rigter et al., 2024 ) adds
an action-conditioned adapter to a frozen video diffusion model.
Dynamic World Simulation ( He et al., 2026 ) combines action
conditioning with a motion-reinforced objective.
EnerVerse-AC ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) uses multi-level action
conditioning for multiview generation, and
Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2026c ) supports policy-in-the-loop
simulation with frame-level control and temporal memory.
Other methods encode control as spatial visual signals:
RoboMaster ( Fu et al., 2026 ) uses collaborative robot–object
trajectories, ABot-PhysWorld ( Chen et al., 2026c ) combines spatial
action injection with physics-aligned training, and
OSCAR ( Wu and Gao, 2026 ) uses rendered kinematic skeletons
across embodiments.
EA-WM ( Yang et al., 2026 ) projects actions and kinematic
states into camera-aligned visual action fields, with event-aware
bidirectional fusion supervised by VAE-encoded frame differences.
Masked Visual Actions ( Alzayer et al., 2026 ) reveals robot
or object motion in masked videos, unifying forward and inverse
world modeling through a shared pixel-space control interface.
FlowWAM ( Chen et al., 2026b ) adopts optical flow for video
prediction and policy learning, while
RynnWorld-Teleop ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) uses hand-pose
conditioning for real-time teleoperation.

Recent efforts further incorporate 3D and 4D structure into
embodied prediction and control.
TesserAct ( Zhen et al., 2025 ) jointly generates RGB,
depth, and normal sequences for 4D scene reconstruction.
Robo4DGen ( Liu et al., 2026b ) introduces cross-view
pointmap supervision for geometrically consistent multiview
prediction, while MVISTA-4D ( Wang et al., 2026a ) generates
arbitrary-view RGB-D futures through cross-view and
cross-modality feature fusion.
RoboStereo ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) couples action-conditioned
RGB and pointmap generation through a dual-tower diffusion
architecture, and RynnWorld-4D ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) jointly predicts RGB, depth, and optical flow to model
appearance, geometry, and motion.
Kinema4D ( Xu et al., 2026a ) uses URDF-based kinematics
to construct robot pointmap trajectories as control signals
for synchronized RGB and pointmap generation.
CausalWM ( Xu et al., 2026b ) sequentially predicts optical
flow, 3D pointmaps, and RGB videos, using intermediate
predictions as context for subsequent generation.
PointWorld ( Huang et al., 2026 ) instead models scene
dynamics directly as 3D point flows, representing robot actions
in the same space and learning across embodiments from real
and simulated manipulation data.
X-WAM ( Guo et al., 2026a ) further couples multiview RGB-D
prediction with robot action generation, using a lightweight
depth branch and asynchronous denoising to decode actions
with fewer steps than video.
WAM4D ( Li et al., 2026d ) uses spatial register tokens and
future-depth supervision to transfer geometric priors into
video–action representations, removing the geometric readout
branch for efficient action inference.
Our work addresses the complementary problem of transferring
simulation-derived motion knowledge into real-domain video
prediction, combining latent-motion distillation with
simulation guidance generated by the same model.

## 2.2 World Action Models

World action models couple visual prediction with robot control.
VPP ( Hu et al., 2024 ) , Video Policy ( Liang et al., 2025 ) ,
DiT4DiT ( Ma et al., 2026b ) , and
mimic-video ( Pai et al., 2025 ) learn action policies from
predictive video representations.
Unified World Models ( Zhu et al., 2025a ) ,
Motus ( Bi et al., 2026 ) , LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026a ) ,
and DreamZero ( Ye et al., 2026b ) jointly model future
observations and actions, connecting world modeling with
policy learning.
UniT ( Chen et al., 2026a ) develops shared visual-action tokens
for human-to-humanoid transfer, while
Cosmos Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) and
World-Value-Action Model ( Li et al., 2026b ) incorporate value prediction for planning.
Future RGB modeling is a common visual learning objective in
video-based WAMs ( Zhu et al., 2025a ; Ye et al., 2026b ) , although
auxiliary representations vary; Motus ( Bi et al., 2026 ) ,
for example, also learns latent actions from optical flow.

Beyond direct action generation, learned world models support
policy evaluation ( Li et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026c ) ,
reinforcement-learning-based policy improvement ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) ,
and paired video-action data synthesis ( Lang et al., 2026 ) .
Kinema4D ( Xu et al., 2026a ) and
RoboStereo ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) extend simulation with
explicit geometry, with RoboStereo further supporting policy
optimization.
Persistent Robot World Models ( Bardhan et al., 2026 ) and World Action Verifier ( Liu et al., 2026a ) improve model reliability through rollout-based reinforcement
learning and forward-inverse consistency, respectively.
Interactive World Simulator ( Wang et al., 2026b ) supports policy training and evaluation through learned
interactive dynamics, while
Genie Envisioner ( Liao et al., 2025 ) and
Cosmos 3 ( NVIDIA et al., 2026 ) integrate world modeling,
simulation, and control within broader frameworks.
FATE ( Wei et al., 2026 ) addresses the complementary problem
of feasibility-aware task generation and repair.

Recent work also revisits the visual supervision and generative
backbones used for control.
MaskWAM ( Yu et al., 2026 ) jointly predicts future RGB
observations, task-relevant masks, and actions, using optional
initial mask prompts to ground target selection.
ImageWAM ( Zhang et al., 2026d ) instead replaces dense
future-video modeling with a source-to-target-frame editing
objective and conditions an action expert on intermediate
editing features, without decoding the target image at inference.
Complementing these policy-oriented designs, our method focuses
on action-conditioned real-domain video prediction.
It distills simulation-derived motion through temporal latent
differences and uses the same model to generate simulation
guidance from input actions and a segmented robot observation,
without external robot-motion rendering at inference.

## 2.3 Simulation Supervision and Real-domain Adaptation

Simulation supports robot learning through data augmentation,
dynamics transfer, and visual conditioning.
Sim-and-Real Co-Training ( Maddukuri et al., 2025 ) mixes
synthetic and real demonstrations for policy learning, while
RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) scales synthetic data
generation with structured domain randomization.
ReDRAW ( Lanier et al., 2025 ) adapts simulation-pretrained
latent dynamics through residual corrections, and Simulation
Distillation ( Levy et al., 2026 ) transfers simulator priors
into world models for real-world adaptation and planning.
For video generation,
Cosmos-Transfer1 ( Alhaija et al., 2025 ) supports
sim-to-real visual translation through spatial controls.
GeniWorld ( Gu et al., 2026 ) and
AnchorDream ( Ye et al., 2025 ) condition video generation
on rendered robot motion, while
RoboDream ( Ye et al., 2026a ) additionally incorporates
explicit scene and object priors.
These methods rely on external robot-motion rendering to
construct conditioning inputs at inference.
In contrast, our method uses the same model for both
simulation-domain and real-scene prediction, without invoking
an external simulator at inference.
Conditioned on the input actions and a robot-only image obtained
by semantically segmenting the initial observation, the model
predicts simulation-domain video latents that then guide its
real-scene video prediction.
This model-generated guidance complements the motion knowledge
internalized through latent-motion distillation.
Our simulation-conditioning CFG scheme controls its influence
to limit reliance on inaccurate predictions.

2026-10-06.title: ArtifactArena: Evaluating Models by What They Build in the Physical World
2026-10-06.authors: Kushagra Tiwary* , David Mayo* , Nikhil Behari , Xiangzhou Sun , Abdulrahman Alabdulkareem , Isaac Galatzer-Levy , Boris Katz , Brian Cheung
2026-10-06.abstract:
To evaluate the frontier, we must measure models not by what they say,
but by what they can engineer and build in grounded physical
environments. We introduce ArtifactArena , an open-ended
platform where models face a physically grounded hardware-software
co-design challenge: engineering fully functional robots to compete
in a simulated arena. We evaluate a frontier model’s zero-shot,
verifier guided refinement, and open-ended physical design
capabilities through three harnesses that refine their bot artifacts
based on text descriptions, physics simulator feedback, and gameplay
data. We benchmark these capabilities with an Elo ranking of frontier
models derived from head-to-head tournaments between their artifacts.
By releasing this framework and tournament infrastructure for ongoing
community submissions, we establish a living, non-saturating testbed
to continuously measure the expanding limits of open-ended
intelligence in the physical world.
2026-10-06.introduction:
In 2002, a New Caledonian crow named Betty was shown a small bucket of food at the bottom of a vertical tube and a straight piece of wire. She picked up the wire, wedged one end against the tube, bent it into a hook, and fished the bucket out ( Weir et al., 2002 ) . What struck the researchers watching was not anything Betty said about her solution (Betty said nothing). It was the physical artifact, the hook, that evinced Betty’s intelligence.

Frontier model evaluations lag model capabilities: popular benchmarks such as MMLU ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) , MMLU-Pro ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , GPQA Diamond ( Rein et al., 2024 ) or code-generation benchmarks such as HumanEval ( Chen et al., 2021 ) test models against static question sets and answer keys which are now effectively saturated. To alleviate this issue, preference arenas such as LMArena ( Chiang et al., 2024 ) and DesignArena replace fixed answer keys with head-to-head (h2h) competition between models judged by humans or other models. The lack of an objective verifier often leads to performative behavior ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . As a result, functional evaluations such as SWE-Bench ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) and KernelBench ( Ouyang et al., 2025 ) test for functional correctness of model-generated code by running it against fixed tests, performance and efficiency baselines. However, they continue to evaluate models against predefined task objectives. Arena based evaluations like SWE-Arena ( Zhao, 2025 ) and CodeClash ( Yang et al., 2025 ) share a similar philosophy of model evaluation through h2h competition however they are confined to symbolic verifiers.

Given these recent advances, we propose ArtifactArena to competitively evaluate frontier model’s open-ended abilities to engineer and build verifiable artifacts that function and compete against other models’ artifacts inside physically grounded simulations. In ArtifactArena each model is tasked with open-ended construction of a complete robot artifact consisting of a body morphology and a motion controller (Sec. 2 ). While many evaluations explore physically grounded reasoning of models, Chen et al. (2025) ; Chow et al. (2025) ; Bear et al. (2022) , we are inspired by both BattleBots ( BattleBots Inc., 2022 ; BattleBots Wiki contributors, 2026 ; Mullins and Peterson, 2002 ) , and AI’s success in Go ( Silver et al., 2016 ) and design our arena environment based on principles that would allow creativity to emerge under physical constraints. Therefore the resulting robots are instantiated in MuJoCo ( Todorov, 2014 ) and compete in a Last Bot Standing Game . Last Bot Standing is an adversarial, objective, zero-sum game with simple rules that allow for open-ended exploration of strategies. Models are also given full creative freedom to explore a large design space of robot designs and competitive strategies, with physics as the only real constraint on exploration. Sec. 3 shows how this leads to creative robot designs by models.

The game rules are deliberately simple to allow for diverse winning strategies and objective in its outcome: a robot wins by either pushing an opponent from an elevated ring or pinning it under the arena’s adjudication rules (Sec. 2.1 ). Since the model must build this robot, success requires jointly reasoning about geometry, materials, mass distribution, actuation, and feedback control, as well as competitive strategy. The outcome is determined by the artifacts’ physical interaction, rather than by a human preference label or an LLM judge.

ArtifactArena deliberately keeps the physical environment and game rules fixed across evaluations, while the adversary population changes as new artifacts enter the arena. Each artifact must therefore compete against independently designed robots with different morphologies, controllers, and strategies. Holding the environment fixed makes the simulator a common objective verifier, allowing differences in performance to reflect artifact design and competitive strategy rather than changes in the task itself. As stronger artifacts enter the arena, they become new opponents that raise the bar for future submissions, allowing our arena to remain non-saturating and keep up with model capabilities. We ask models to build the strongest robots they believe can win the game and rank the models based on their artifacts’ performance.

Contributions: (1) A physically grounded competitive evaluation platform. We introduce ArtifactArena , an open-ended platform where models face a physically grounded hardware-software co-design challenge: engineering fully functional robots to compete in an objective zero-sum arena designed using the MuJoCo simulation environment. We maintain a live public artifact leaderboard open to community bot submissions worldwide. Our arena is harness agnostic and only the model-artifact matters: we accept both artifacts designed entirely by models and artifacts produced through human–AI collaboration. See Fig. 3 .

(2) A model leaderboard and systematic comparison of artifact-generation strategies. We benchmark frontier models build capabilities using three test-time generation strategies implemented as harnesses: Sampling Harness (SH) , Verifier Grounded Refinement Harness (VGH) , and open-ended agentic search using a Design Lab Harness (DLH) . We compute-match in terms of API calls on these harnesses to study which type of harness produces the strongest artifacts. Our leaderboard shows the limits of these models frontier capabilities and should be interpreted as measuring competitive physical design and control in simulation across frontier models rather than direct real-world robotic capability. See Fig. 2 & Fig. 7

(3) The unreasonable effectiveness of sampling. Our leaderboard shows that the most recent frontier models can zero-shot co-design complex robot morphologies with custom wedges using signed distance functions (SDFs) and controllers that implement charge and defend strategies while working within the physical environment. We show that this is a remarkably new capability that models have and sample this new capability to understand the extent of these designs. (Sec. 3.2 )

(4) An empirical anatomy of model creativity in artifact design. We open-source all model artifacts through the Bot Zoo with complete reasoning traces and design histories. We study not only the final robots but the processes through which models create them. Due to our large robot morphology and controller design space, we observe wedge, hammer, and pusher strategies implemented as both morphologies and controllers. The strongest agents also construct probes, adversarial opponents, and engineering tools to discover physical failure modes, while open-ended search can fail when self-created tests diverge from true tournament performance. (Sec. 3.4 )

To ensure ArtifactArena serves as a durable testbed for open-ended intelligence, we release the simulator, multiple harnesses, and our tournament infrastructure to support community submissions. This framework establishes a living evaluation horizon capable of continuously tracking the limits of artificial intelligence as it approaches and surpasses human-level capability in engineering and scientific endeavors.

# 2 Methods

## 2.1 The Last Bot Standing Game

Model Task. Every model receives the same fixed prompt (Appx. 11 ), which asks it to “design a robot to maximize its win rate in the tournament described below” and to return the hardware as MJCF XML and the controller as Python. We design the prompt to be descriptive rather than prescriptive: it states the game rules (Sec. 2.1 ), the simulation setup in detail (to avoid any assumptions), the qualification and tournament procedure including Bradley-Terry Elo scoring, the robot constraints and material palette (Appx. 7.3 ), an MJCF syntax reference, and the controller observation schema (Appx. 7 ). Models are also told to think from first principles based on the MuJoCo physics world. Finally, the prompt reminds the model to optimize for expected win rate rather than simplicity, treat qualification as a constraint rather than the objective, and compare diverse morphologies and controllers before committing to one. The model must return six named sections: r i r_{i} in the form of name , design_strategy , hardware_plan , combat_plan , robot_xml and controller_code which g i g_{i} and c i c_{i} respectively.

Qualification Stage. Once the model designs a robot artifact, it must first pass a static verifier: the XML must compile in MuJoCo, contain exactly one free joint on the root body, assign every geometry a material from the palette, stay within 25-800 kg, and fit the size box. Collision parameters, physics options, and gravity compensation in the XML are stripped to disable the model from cheating. The controller is also verified once on a live observation to check for exceptions or malformed commands. Finally the robot plays three 20s matches against a passive 342 kg plastic block that has no actuators, may translate, rotate, and topple, and is exempt from the inactivity rule. The robot must not lose in the best of three matches, or else it forfeits the tournament. Sec. 2.3 details how qualified artifacts are chosen.

Match. Qualified robots are allowed to enter the tournament. A match between two robots is a head-to-head round simulated in MuJoCo ( Todorov, 2014 ) on an elevated circular platform 15 m in diameter (Fig. 3 ), with both robots spawned at random positions and headings. Every pair of bots plays matches with three unique seeds, once from each side, so six matches in total. Each robot has an unactuated six-degree-of-freedom root joint, allowing its body to translate and rotate freely in response to gravity, contact forces, and forces generated by its internally actuated motors driven by its controller policy code. We resolve match outcomes based on the following rules after every control step and a match that reaches 300 s without one of the robots loosing is a draw.

Game Rules. The Last Bot Standing game takes inspiration from both BattleBots ( BattleBots Inc., 2022 ) and the ancient board game Go as both are evidence of emergent human-machine creativity in environments with simple rules and large design spaces ( BattleBots Wiki contributors, 2026 ; Mullins and Peterson, 2002 ; Silver et al., 2016 ) . A robot loses the match if any of the following conditions occur (listed in priority order):

Controller error : its policy raises an exception or returns malformed commands.

Controller error : its policy raises an exception or returns malformed commands.

Floor contact : any part of its body touches the floor below the platform.

Size violation : its extents in its own root frame exceed 2.44 m × \times 2.44 m × \times 3.05 m.

Inactivity : beginning 10 s into the match and checked every control step, the two most distant center-of-mass positions recorded over the preceding 10 s are less than 0.5 m apart.

Physics instability : its body drives the simulation to non-finite forces.

## 2.2 Robot Artifact Design Space

Frontier models must translate a high level design and competitive strategy into a robot morphology and controller that work together in MuJoCo. The morphology determines which forces the robot can apply, while the controller determines when and how to use them. We now summarize the robot design space available to the model and refer the reader to Appx. 7.1 for the full design constraints and implementation details.

Robot Hardware Design. The morphology is an MJCF kinematic tree under a single free-jointed root body, with up to 2,000 bodies, geometries and actuators, and must fit within a bounding box of 2.44 ​ m × 2.44 ​ m × 3.05 ​ m 2.44\,\mathrm{m}\times 2.44\,\mathrm{m}\times 3.05\,\mathrm{m} . Bodies are built from boxes, cylinders, spheres, capsules, ellipsoids, or inline signed-distance meshes, connected by hinge, slide, or ball joints. Each geometry takes one material from the palette (Appx. 7.3 ), which automatically sets its density (and therefore mass) based on model specified volume, and sliding friction. Motors drive internal joints, tendons, or sites, and only ever push one part of the robot against another. To allow for physically plausible motors, motor force scales with gear, and gear is charged against the mass budget, so torque is bought with weight. We also allow passive damping, friction loss, and springs on joints and tendons which let the hardware absorb impacts or store energy.

Controller Design. The controller is a Python function policy_step(obs) that returns a command in the range [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] for every actuator at each 0.01 s control step. It sees the game state through more than 50 named fields: positions, orientations, velocities, edge and opponent distances, contacts with forces and impulses, the closest geometry pairs, a rolling history of past observations and actions, and each robot’s compiled bodies, joints, and motors with their current state (Fig. 3 & Appx. 11 ’s observation section). State persists within a match and is reset between matches, so controllers may estimate, predict, and switch modes.

## 2.3 Test-time generation strategies

The goal of the model in ArtifactArena is to produce the strongest artifact it can engineer that can beat artifacts produced by other models. Therefore our arena is harness agnostic and we use this as a call to the community to build better harnesses that allow models to engineer physically grounded artifacts. We now test three test-time artifact generation strategies that differ in how much of the design loop the model controls. Figure 4 summarizes the three generation harnesses and their common evaluation procedure. See Appx. 7 for details. For each model, we allocate 10 API calls to each harness which is run independently three times.

Sampling Harness (SH) . The model receives a fixed model prompt (Appx. 11 ) and produces 10 independent robot artifacts. There is no feedback given to the model and all produced artifacts directly enter the Qualification Stage. The top bot per run is chosen through a round-robin tournament between all the qualified bots.

Verifier-Grounded Refinement Harness (VGH) . In VGH we conceptualize the model’s role as that of an optimizer over 10 sequential iterations: the model reads verifier feedback, a journal of prior attempts, and the match feedback, and proposes a better artifact. After each iteration, the harness validates the artifact, qualifies it against the stationary block. The full match feedback (game state at every time step), verifier feedback, design history (a JSON with what it changed on each iteration), and the current best artifact so far is given back to the model. The model can choose to iterate based on the full match feedback on the current best design. Every valid artifact enters a round robin and the Bradley-Terry Elo winner is chosen as the final artifact that enters the Qualification Stage.

Design Lab Harness (DLH). We conceptualize a model as an open-ended engineer working in a Design Lab , a sandboxed workspace containing the simulator and verifier source, the task documentation, and shell and Python execution. The model is given a budget of 10 API calls, which it can use to chain several tool calls that allow it to build, simulate, and analyze match feedback (Table 1 ). We show an example iteration using DLH from Fable 5.1 in Fig. 7 . We use the same process as VGH to choose the final artifact.

## 2.4 Tournament

Artifact Leaderboard . We first run the above (model, harness) for all models defined in Appx. 3 and for the three harnesses defined in Sec. 2.3 . After each run, a single robot artifact is selected based on harness specific selection method described above (Sec. 2.3 ). Each artifact is then validated and qualified through matches against a cube. For each (model, harness) pair this is repeated three times yielding three artifacts per model per harness. Artifacts that pass validation and qualification enter the Top-3 robot artifact tournament. These sets of top-3 artifacts play a cross-model round robin for 3 unique seeds (each unique seed plays two matches-one from each starting position so a total of 6 matches). We then compute a Bradley-Terry ELO score to get the top-3 resulting ratings, with a draw counted as half a win, form the Artifact Leaderboard . Using the Artifact Leaderboard , we also compute a Lab Leaderboard which is used to visualize the range of robot artifacts selected by all the models per research lab. We call this phase of the tournament the Top-3 Round and make all the matches
available https://artifactarena.ai/matches?round=top3 .

Model Leaderboard . Our goal is to evaluate models by the best artifact they produce. Therefore, we select the best artifact for every (model, harness) pair from the Artifact Leaderboard . We then play a new cross-model round robin tournament with 11 unique seeds (22 total matches) to compute the top-1 Bradley-Terry Elo score for the model’s strongest artifact. This top-1 score is used to create ArtifactArena Champion Leaderboard (Fig. 2 ) also available at Champions Leaderboard . We call this phase of the tournament the Champion Round and make all the matches available https://artifactarena.ai/matches?round=Champion+Round .

As an independent robustness check, we replayed the 21 frozen model champions generated by their respective harnesses on two disjoint sets of eleven seeds, once from each side. The resulting rankings have a Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.984 \rho=0.984 and preserve 201 of 210 (95.7%) pairwise model orderings, with the top three models unchanged in order (Appx. 6.1 ).

Uncertainty. Error bars in Fig. 2 are 95% bootstrap intervals over generation runs and match outcomes. In each of 1,000 replicates, we resample the three finalists for every model–harness pair and the 22 outcomes for every finalist pair, then refit Bradley–Terry, re-select each harness champion, and refit on champion matches. Since all finalists played each other, this only reweights existing matches. We do not resample within-run finalist selection, which would require bootstrapping every candidate-level round robin, so these intervals are a lower bound on full-pipeline uncertainty.

2026-10-06.title: MarvisNav: Making Memory Visible on Route Choices for Zero-Shot Object Navigation
2026-10-06.authors: Jincheng Wang , Chi Pui Chan , Wei Zeng , Shuyang Zhang , Jianhao Jiao , Dimitrios Kanoulas
2026-10-06.abstract:
When searching for an object, people choose their next move by considering both likely target locations and places already explored. The current view can cue place-associated memories, bringing target relevance and prior exploration into the same spatial context. In many zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) methods, however, vision-language models (VLMs) infer promising search areas from egocentric images, but exploration history enters the decision through separate representations, e.g., as text or maps.
This separation either requires an additional fusion step to align semantic evidence with exploration state, or leaves the correspondence between memory and route choices implicit for the VLM to recover.
We instead make exploration memory visible directly on visual route choice.
We propose MarvisNav, a ZSON framework that maintains a topological graph and projects candidate nodes together with their exploration states onto the egocentric perception as memory-bearing visual route choices.
These topological states capture local exploration progress beyond binary visitation. By binding exploration state directly to each visual candidate, MarvisNav enables the VLM to jointly evaluate target relevance and exploration state and make the final high-level selection without a separate post-hoc fusion or reranking stage. Without policy training, MarvisNav achieves state-of-the-art performance on HM3D ( 81.2 % 81.2\% SR and 42.5 % 42.5\% SPL), while competitive on MP3D. Moreover, it outperforms representative VLM-based methods with far fewer VLM calls ( e.g., 7.5 % 7.5\% of WMNav). Real-robot experiments across diverse scenes further validate its practical deployability. Beyond MarvisNav, our study shows that memory representation shapes VLM decisions and ZSON performance, highlighting that effective memory use in ZSON depends not only on its availability, but also on how it is represented.
Code will be released at https://wangjincheng1998.github.io/MarvisNav/
2026-10-06.introduction:
Imagine a robot asked to find an office chair in a home it has never seen. To succeed, it needs to infer where the target is likely to be and explore efficiently. This challenge is formalized as Object Navigation. Standard supervised methods are typically trained on a closed set of target categories ( Chaplot et al., 2020 ; Chaplot et al., 2021 ; Ramakrishnan et al., 2022 ; Ye and Yang, 2021 ) , limiting their ability to generalize to new objects. Zero-shot Object Navigation (ZSON) instead leverages pretrained semantic knowledge to search for novel targets without category-specific training ( Majumdar et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Gadre et al., 2023 ; Kuang et al., 2024 ) , making it a key step toward open-world tasks.

ZSON is a long-horizon search problem under partial observability ( Zhang et al., 2025d ) . When the target is not visible, the agent needs to use semantic cues to infer promising search areas. Existing methods obtain such guidance through visual-semantic alignment, which scores target relevance from visual observations ( Gadre et al., 2023 ; Yokoyama et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ) , or contextual semantic reasoning, which exploits scene context and spatial relations ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . Recently, generative Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have been widely adopted for object search, leveraging strong multimodal understanding and broad knowledge for richer semantic and spatial reasoning over observations. Long-horizon search, however, requires a sequence of high-level decisions. A VLM does not by itself maintain the agent’s exploration state across successive decisions. VLM-based methods therefore maintain explicit memory ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Padilla et al., 2026 ) to avoid re-selecting semantically promising but already searched areas.

Semantic guidance and exploration memory, however, are often met in
separate representations. VLMs form semantic judgments from the current egocentric view, whereas exploration memory may be carried as separate textual histories or dense maps. Bringing the two together therefore requires an additional fusion or alignment step before decision-making. When memory remains outside the VLM, the system must explicitly define how it changes the model’s semantic judgment ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Padilla et al., 2026 ) , for example through hand-crafted candidate filtering or score adjustment. This places part of the choice outside the VLM and may constrain or override its judgment. When memory is instead supplied to the VLM, external fusion may be avoided, but the alignment problem remains. A textual history records past events in language, whereas a top-down map lays them out in an allocentric frame ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Habibpour and Afghah, 2025a ; Habibpour and Afghah, 2025b ) . Neither is expressed in the egocentric view the agent is reasoning over. The VLM must therefore infer how remembered places relate to the current view before using that memory to decide where to search next (Fig. 1 , left).

Consider how a person searches for the chair in an unfamiliar house. They make both judgments from the same view, seeing which doorways look promising and which lead to areas already searched. A searched room is dismissed at a glance, while a doorway seen earlier remains a candidate if it still opens onto unexplored space. By making exploration cues visible on the corresponding spatial choices in views, we may then be able to give VLMs a similar decision interface, so that semantic evidence and exploration state are read together rather than aligned across representations.

To this end, we introduce MarvisNav , a ZSON framework that ma kes exploration memo r y vis ible to VLMs by grounding it directly on visual route choices. We first reduce continuous exploration into sparse high-level decisions, where the VLM selects among navigable search directions. We derive these choices from a Reduced Voronoi Graph (RVG) ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , where selected junctions serve as decision sites and local paths define candidate directions associated with reachable nodes. We extend this representation into a State-Aware RVG that associates each candidate with a local exploration state indicating whether nearby connected space may remain unexplored. At each decision, MarvisNav projects visible RVG paths into the egocentric RGB views and annotates candidates with local identifiers and exploration states, forming memory-bearing visual route choices (Fig. 1 , right). A VLM then jointly evaluates target relevance and exploration state on these choices and selects an identifier in a single query. The selected identifier directly specifies the next navigation goal, enabling memory-conditioned route selection without additional semantic-memory fusion.

We evaluate MarvisNav on standard indoor ZSON benchmarks, where it achieves strong performance without policy training. It also outperforms representative VLM-based methods with far fewer VLM queries, demonstrating practical efficiency for long-horizon navigation. We further validate its practical deployability on a Go2 robot across diverse scenes. Beyond MarvisNav, our study further demonstrates that exploration-memory representation can substantially affect both VLM preferences and navigation performance. These findings highlight the need to consider not only what an agent remembers, but also how that memory is made visible and associated with its choices.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

ZSON asks an agent to find an object in an unseen environment without category-specific training. A central problem in ZSON is determining where the target is likely to be found. Early approaches transfer pretrained vision-language knowledge to navigation through multimodal goal embeddings and open-vocabulary localization ( Majumdar et al., 2022 ; Gadre et al., 2023 ) . Later methods score the similarity between observations and the target with a pretrained image-text model ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and accumulate it in maps to guide exploration toward promising areas ( Yokoyama et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025c ; Kuang et al., 2024 ) . Large-language models (LLMs) extend this guidance beyond visual similarity by reasoning about object-room relations, scene context, and spatial structure ( Zhou et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . VoroNav follows this line and uses a Voronoi Graph to organize navigable paths and sparse observation locations for language-model reasoning ( Wu et al., 2024 ) . More recently, generative VLMs have moved this reasoning onto the egocentric image, judging which directions look promising without an intermediate textual description ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . This shift requires spatial alternatives to be presented in a form that the VLM can visually inspect and select ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) , while remaining tied to navigation goals that the agent can execute. Recent works provide such an interface by rendering frontiers directly into the observation as selectable navigation goals ( Padilla et al., 2026 ) . However, these visual choices indicate where the agent can go, but not whether unexplored space remains beyond each option, preventing direct joint reasoning over semantic promise and exploration state for VLM.

A VLM query does not retain exploration state across successive decisions, so VLM-based ZSON methods maintain explicit memory to avoid repeatedly considering already searched areas. Some methods keep memory outside the VLM’s semantic reasoning: exploration history may restrict the candidates before querying VLMs ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Padilla et al., 2026 ) , or adjust its preference afterward through fixed filtering or score modification ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Long et al., 2025 ) . In both cases, semantic evidence and exploration state are evaluated separately and combined by an external rule, placing part of the decision outside the VLM and constraining its judgment. A more direct alternative is to expose the memory to the VLM itself. Text-based methods serialize past observations or actions into the prompt ( Habibpour and Afghah, 2025a ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Ji et al., 2025 ) for VLM reasoning. However, the VLM must implicitly associate this linguistic history with the current visual choices, which can make route-memory correspondence ambiguous. Rendering exploration history into a top-view map reduces that alignment problem by placing candidates and explored regions in a shared coordinate frame ( Zhong et al., 2024 ) . However, reasoning directly over such a map moves the VLM away from the egocentric visual domain in which its perception and semantic reasoning are most naturally trained ( Nie et al., 2025 ) . A further step is to bring memory into the VLM’s egocentric view itself. Mem2Ego ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) projects candidate choices and visited locations into the view as separate markers. This preserves egocentric reasoning, but the correspondence between a candidate and its visitation memory must still be inferred from their image-space proximity. Moreover, a visited marker indicates where the agent has been, but not whether unexplored space remains beyond that location. Our work instead grounds topological exploration memory explicitly onto visual choices, indicating whether unexplored connected space remains beyond each choice. This allows the VLM to jointly reason over semantic evidence and exploration state, without recovering correspondences across representations or relying on external rules.

2026-10-06.title: Traversability-Aware Cooperative Path Planning for Human-UGV Casualty Evacuation
2026-10-06.authors: Kristian Dalland , Prithvi Poddar , Souma Chowdhury , Karthik Dantu , Ehsan T. Esfahani
2026-10-06.abstract: Heterogeneous multi-robot path planning is a well-studied problem in which agents with disparate kinematic and dynamic models must coordinate to achieve shared objectives. These formulations, however, treat all agents as robotic-their cost models are mechanical and their traversability is sensor-derived. In human-robot teaming, the human partner remains relegated to command and supervisory roles rather than being modeled as a physical co-navigator with distinct mobility constraints and dynamic energy reserves. This work investigates joint path planning for a two-agent human-UGV team in search-and-rescue casualty retrieval scenarios. We model the human agent using the Pandolf-Santee metabolic cost model with fatigue-modulated speed, and the UGV using a rolling-resistance energy model with terrain-dependent speed limits. By exploiting the complementary traversability of each agent-the human’s ability to traverse dense vegetation and shallow water versus the UGV’s superior speed on open terrain and roads-we optimize casualty transfer locations, termed switch points, to minimize total mission time. Evaluated across multiple synthetic 1 ​ km 2 1\,\text{km}^{2} environments with procedurally generated elevation and land-cover data, the optimized strategy reduces mean mission time by 5.3% relative to a human-only baseline and by 7.0% relative to a naive human-UGV strategy without switch point optimization, while reducing human energy expenditure by 17.8% relative to baseline. Notably, the naive strategy reduces human energy expenditure by a larger margin (22.4%) but incurs a 2% increase in mission time relative to baseline, illustrating that switch point optimization is necessary to realize time savings from human-UGV teaming.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Planning for human–robot teams (HRT) is inherently challenging because the diversity of applications and robotic platforms, coupled with the unpredictability and latent heuristic nature of human behavior, introduces significant uncertainty into every stage of mission design [ 1 ] .
This difficulty is compounded by the dynamic, unstructured environments in which many HRT systems
must operate. Manufacturing is among the most visible domains: errors in
shared workspaces can result in injury or death for human operators, motivating
efforts to separate humans from robots entirely. Yet humans and robots bring
complementary strengths to a task: robotic endurance, speed, and sensing paired
with human reasoning, adaptability, and dexterity. Exploiting both yields gains
in efficiency and capability that neither agent achieves alone. This
complementary nature extends well beyond the factory floor to logistics,
search and rescue, autonomous driving, and disaster response [ 2 , 3 ] .

Across these domains, HRT research has concentrated on task allocation,
communication, trust calibration, and the spectrum from shared to full
autonomy [ 1 , 4 ] . The DARPA Subterranean
Challenge demonstrated that directed autonomy-where human operators set
waypoints and priorities while robots execute low-level control-outperformed
full autonomy across 16 real-world search missions, yielding more artifacts
found, greater distance traversed, and broader area coverage [ 5 ] . In human-centered tasks, integrating a
robotic partner improves mission outcomes by combining robotic perception and
endurance with human reasoning and decision-making, ultimately enhancing
performance while reducing risk to human operators [ 6 ] .

Search-and-rescue robotics offers a particularly compelling case for
human-robot teaming. Early field deployments at the World Trade Center
demonstrated that robots served primarily as information sources rather than
autonomous actors, with effective coordination depending on shared mental
models between operators and robotic platforms [ 7 ] .
Subsequent work by Murphy and Burke showed that human-robot teams with
higher situation awareness were up to nine times more likely to locate victims
than teams with lower awareness, highlighting that cognitive factors-not
robotic autonomy alone-are the primary bottleneck in field performance [ 8 ] . More recent work on human-swarm interaction has
reinforced the centrality of the human element, showing that operator
physiological state directly affects coordination performance in
cyber-physical systems [ 9 ] . These findings
collectively establish that human-robot interaction in SAR is not merely a
matter of controlling robotic systems but of enabling teams to exploit robots
as active information sources, with communication, coordination, and operator
state playing critical roles.

Despite these advances, a notable gap persists. Heterogeneous multi-robot
path planning is well studied: ground-aerial teams [ 3 ] , robots with differing kinematic constraints [ 10 ] , and multi-platform coordination have all received significant attention. In these formulations, however, all
agents are robotic-their cost models are mechanical and their
traversability is sensor-derived, with human contribution limited to
coordination and oversight. When a human appears in the loop, it
is almost exclusively as an operator directing robots [ 9 ] , not as a co-navigating agent whose path must also be planned. The human’s role is cognitive
(task allocation, waypoint selection, supervisory control) rather
than physical (carrying, modulating effort). Joint path planning that treats both the human and robot as physically traversing agents, with distinct mobility constraints and cost models, remains comparatively underexplored.

This work makes three primary contributions. First, we formulate joint path planning for a human–UGV team in which the human is explicitly modeled as a physical traversing agent with fatigue-modulated mobility. Second, we introduce a coordination framework based on optimizing intermediate transfer locations (switch points) under heterogeneous and non-comparable cost structures. Third, we demonstrate that heterogeneous teaming does not universally improve performance, and that coordinated planning is necessary to realize time savings in terrain-constrained environments.

# II METHODS

## II-A System Overview

This work explores joint planning for human and robotic agents in challenging terrain. We focus on path planning combined with casualty transfer between agent types over varying terrain types and gradients. Our agents consist of a two-person human team able to jointly carry a 100 kg casualty in conjunction with a large off-/on-road UGV, modeled as the Clearpath Robotics Warthog [ 11 ] . These two agent types must navigate a complex environment to reach a 100 kg casualty and return it to the starting location as quickly as possible. Additionally, we consider safety by restricting loaded paths to gentler terrain grades in scenarios where the casualty is severely injured.

## II-B Agent Cost Models

The human and UGV agents use fundamentally different traversal cost models. The human model is metabolic: it predicts physiological energy expenditure as a function of body mass, load, terrain, and grade, with speed modulated by cumulative fatigue. The UGV model is kinematic: it computes rolling resistance force from vehicle mass, slope, and surface type, with speed reduced by grade but unaffected by fatigue. Neither model produces costs in shared units, so joint planning optimizes over mission-level objectives-primarily total time-rather than summing edge costs across agents.

The human cost map for path planning is constructed using the Pandolf equation for energy expenditure [ 12 ] . This model combines body weight, carried load, terrain gradient, terrain type, and walking speed to produce a metabolic rate in watts:

Once a candidate path has been generated, an accurate traversal time is computed using a human-energy-aware simulation [ 13 ] . This hybrid system uses two models in sequence: first, the Pandolf equation with the Santee downhill correction [ 14 ] calculates segment-wise energy expenditure; then, a three-tank hydraulic analogue of energy reserves [ 15 ] modulates walking speed based on cumulative fatigue. The hydraulic model abstracts energy reserves in a functional manner through a set of coupled ODEs that simulate exertion and recovery as a function of expenditure history. The result is a fatigue-aware speed profile in which the human slows progressively over long or strenuous segments and recovers partially during easier terrain.

The UGV cost model computes two quantities per edge: traversal energy, used as the A* edge weight for path planning, and traversal time, accumulated along the planned path.

The UGV experiences no fatigue: its speed depends only on terrain class and instantaneous grade. This asymmetry reflects the operational reality that human endurance degrades over distance while a battery-powered UGV maintains consistent output until energy is depleted. These differentiated constraints ensure that the UGV’s traversable subgraph is a strict subset of the human’s, which is the fundamental asymmetry motivating joint path planning: the human must traverse terrain the UGV cannot reach in order to retrieve the casualty and transport it to a feasible rendezvous point.

## II-C Synthetic Environment

In order to evaluate our planning framework, we designed a synthetic environment with realistic variance in terrain types and terrain grades. This decision was made to facilitate a high-resolution map, as publicly available digital elevation models and land-cover maps are limited to 30 m resolution [ 17 , 18 ] . Our synthetic environment resolution is set to 2 ​ m 2\,\text{m} per cell in each direction, which defines the per-pixel distance as well as the resolution of both the elevation model and land-cover classification. This resolution was also chosen to accommodate the Clearpath Warthog platform width of 1.38 ​ m 1.38\,\text{m} [ 11 ] , ensuring that each agent always occupies a single cell.

The environment is represented as a two-dimensional regular grid at a resolution of 2 ​ m/cell 2\,\text{m/cell} . Each cell is connected to its eight neighbors via cardinal and diagonal adjacency. Edge attributes include Euclidean distance, computed as the cell spacing for cardinal edges and 2 \sqrt{2} times the cell spacing for diagonal edges, and slope grade (%), derived from the elevation difference between adjacent cells.

Terrain elevation is generated procedurally via fractional Brownian motion (fBm) using Perlin noise [ 19 ] with six octaves, a persistence of 0.5 0.5 , and a lacunarity of 2.0 2.0 , following the terrain synthesis framework of Ebert et al. [ 20 ] . The resulting noise field is scaled to a configurable elevation range to produce terrain profiles representative of hilly or mountainous environments. Slope grade at each cell is computed from central finite differences of the elevation surface.

A second independent fBm noise layer [ 19 , 20 ] partitions cells into discrete land-cover classes modeled after the 19-class NALCMS taxonomy [ 18 ] . These classes are collapsed into categories distinguishable by the agent cost models described above. ## II-D Path Planning

Agent paths are generated using heap-based A* over the 8-connected grid. Two planning strategies are available, per loaded state and for each agent. The Fast strategy minimizes cumulative energy: metabolic cost via the Pandolf model [ 12 ] for the human and rolling resistance work (Eq. 2 ) for the UGV. The Safe strategy minimizes cumulative grade exposure by weighting each edge as | g % | × d |g_{\%}|\times d , producing conservative routes that favor gentle terrain at the expense of path length.

After A* returns a candidate path, a separate edge-by-edge simulation computes physically grounded traversal metrics. For the human, the full hybrid fatigue model (Section II-B1 ) is applied iteratively along the path waypoints; travel speed is an output of this simulation rather than a fixed input. For the UGV, a kinematic walk accumulates ∑ d i / v eff , i \sum d_{i}/v_{\text{eff},i} using the grade-penalized terrain speed (Eq. 3 ). Both agents report total energy (kJ), travel time (s), path length (m), cumulative grade exposure, and maximum single-edge grade.

## II-E Scenario Overview

The evaluation scenario (Fig. 1 ) defines a shared start position and a shared goal location for both agent types, and proceeds in two phases. In the approach phase , both agents depart from the shared start: the human team navigates to the goal location to retrieve the casualty, while the UGV travels to the first switch point , defined as a location where the casualty is handed off from one agent to the other.

In the return phase , the human team retrieves the 100 kg casualty at the goal and must deliver it to the start as quickly as possible. The casualty is exchanged between agents at three switch points along the return route, with the human and UGV alternately bearing the load before the UGV delivers the casualty to the start position.

This return phase is the focus of joint planning optimization. The human is slower but can traverse dense forest and steep terrain that the UGV cannot. The UGV travels faster but is restricted to roads, paths, and open terrain such as grassland. This asymmetry creates opportunities to hand off the casualty at intermediate locations whose placement determines the efficiency of the team. The three switch points are optimized to minimize casualty evacuation time, with the human and UGV moving concurrently between handoffs and the earlier-arriving agent waiting for the other.

For comparison, the human-only baseline assigns the entire casualty return to the human team, while the naive human–UGV strategy transfers the casualty at the UGV-reachable location nearest the goal without optimizing switch-point locations.

## II-F Switch Point Optimization

Joint planning requires determining the switch-point locations that minimize total mission time.
Jointly deciding the number of switch points and their locations leads to an optimization problem with design variables of varying cardinality, and classical optimization solvers struggle with problems involving varying cardinality design variables. To mitigate this issue, we fix the number of switch points to N = 3 N=3 in this work and optimize only their locations; jointly optimizing the number of switch points alongside their locations is left to future work.

For N = 3 N=3 switch points, we formulate the problem of computing the switch point locations as a nonlinear optimization problem with the design variable defined as 𝒫 = [ δ 1 , θ 1 , δ 2 , θ 2 , δ 3 , θ 3 ] \mathcal{P}=[\delta_{1},\theta_{1},\delta_{2},\theta_{2},\delta_{3},\theta_{3}] , where δ i \delta_{i} defines the distance (in meters) of switch point i i from switch point i − 1 i-1 , and θ i \theta_{i} defines the bearing (in degrees) of switch point i i from switch point i − 1 i-1 . The bearing angle θ i \theta_{i} is 0 ∘ 0^{\circ} if the switch point i i lies on the straight line connecting the switch point i − 1 i-1 to the start position. Any anti-clockwise deviation from this line leads to a positive bearing, and clockwise deviations result in negative bearings. The optimization is constrained such that none of the switch points lie in an area that is inaccessible by the UGV. For solving the optimization problem, we use the mixed discrete particle swarm optimization with diversity preservation, presented in [ 25 ] . The particle swarm optimization is run for 100 iterations with a population size of 100 particles. We use the default algorithm parameter value as presented in [ 25 ] .

2026-10-06.title: Odyssey: A Closed-Loop Benchmark for Long-Horizon Real-World Driving with Explicit Navigation Routes
2026-10-06.authors: Jungho Kim , Hongjae Shin , Seunghoon Yu , Heecheol Yoo , Myeongjun Kim , Jiyong Oh , Donghyuk Kwak , Seunghyeop Nam , Haesung Oh , Hyunju Kim , Hyungchan Cho , Jaehyun Park , Soo Won Seo , Jun Won Choi

2026-10-06.abstract:
Closed-loop evaluation of end-to-end driving requires continuous
rollouts that reveal how earlier decisions affect subsequent driving.
However, existing benchmarks evaluate
only short segments and fail to capture later consequences. Ambiguous directional commands also obscure
the intended navigation objective.
We introduce Odyssey, a closed-loop benchmark for long-horizon
driving comprising 100 scenarios, each reconstructed from a
100-second nuPlan driving log to preserve the context of navigation
maneuvers and traffic interactions.
To provide a consistent navigation objective, Odyssey replaces
directional commands with explicit standard-definition (SD) map
routes that specify which roads to follow, while sensor-based
planning determines local driving actions.
Throughout these rollouts, diffusion-based refinement of
3DGS-rendered images reduces rendering artifacts along the ego
trajectory.
To assess how effectively planners follow these routes and prepare
for upcoming maneuvers, we introduce SD Route Compliance and
Pre-Lane Change Score.
These assessments are complemented by RouteDS , which
extends the Driving Score with penalties for SD-route deviations
and failed lane preparation.
We adapt state-of-the-art planners, including
vision-language-action (VLA) models, and evaluate their
navigation performance using these metrics.
Odyssey highlights open questions in route representation and integration for E2E driving.
Benchmark code and adapted baselines will be released publicly.
2026-10-06.introduction:
A central challenge in autonomous driving is reliable navigation through complex traffic environments that ensure safety and comfort, as well as efficient progress toward an intended destination.
With the growing availability of large-scale driving data, planning-oriented end-to-end (E2E) paradigms have gained prominence ( Hu et al., 2023 ; Liao et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Kirby et al., 2026 ) , in which driving systems directly map onboard sensor observations to driving decisions. Such planners should be evaluated by their ability to sustain safe driving as the vehicle interacts with its environment over time. Since open-loop evaluation independently compares decisions at individual time steps against recorded driving logs, it cannot capture their downstream effects. Accounting for downstream effects via closed-loop evaluation is essential to assess driving performance under evolving traffic conditions.

For E2E planners, closed-loop evaluation requires sensor observations that reflect the consequences of the ego vehicle’s actions. Neural rendering provides this feedback by reconstructing 3D real-world scenes from driving logs and rendering new observations from the simulated ego pose. Early approaches relied on neural radiance fields (NeRFs) ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Tonderski et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) , whose volumetric rendering incurs substantial computational cost. To reduce this cost, recent methods adopt 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) ( Zhou et al., 2024b ; Hess et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024a ; Chen et al., 2025 ) for faster rendering while maintaining high visual fidelity. These developments have supported growing research on neural-rendering-based closed-loop benchmarks ( Ljungbergh et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) for E2E planners. However, existing benchmarks are limited in assessing a planner’s ability to handle long-term driving tasks (see Figure 1 (a)).

One limitation of existing closed-loop benchmarks ( Ljungbergh et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) is their short evaluation horizon, typically limited to approximately 20 seconds. Such short rollouts are insufficient to fully assess the navigation capabilities of E2E planners, particularly when navigation requires a sequence of coordinated maneuvers. For example, as shown in Figure 2 (a), completing an upcoming right turn may require changing lanes in advance. However, the evaluation may terminate before the turn occurs, making it hard to assess the planner’s ability to complete the maneuver sequence.
Furthermore, high-level meta-action commands used in many E2E benchmarks ( Caesar et al., 2020 ; Dauner et al., 2024 ; Cao et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) provide ambiguous guidance for navigation in real-world driving scenarios. As illustrated in Figure 1 (a), a directional command such as “turn right” may correspond to multiple possible maneuvers. For example, if two right exits occur in succession, the command alone does not indicate which exit the planner should take.
Annotating these commands in real-world driving datasets may not accurately reflect the driver’s intended maneuver ( OpenScene Contributors, 2023 ) , as shown in Figure 2 (b). Reliable long-horizon evaluation therefore requires more explicit navigation guidance than high-level meta-action commands alone can provide.

Another challenge is maintaining high rendering quality throughout long-horizon closed-loop simulations. When the ego vehicle deviates from the trajectory recorded during data collection, rendering quality may deteriorate because novel viewpoints lack sufficient observational support. The resulting artifacts can distort the visual input to E2E planners, influence their subsequent decisions, and undermine the reliability of both planning and evaluation. In addition, existing evaluation setups do not accurately model changes in traffic signals or pedestrian motion, further limiting their ability to represent realistic driving scenarios.

In this paper, we introduce Odyssey , a real-world closed-loop benchmark for evaluating E2E driving models over long-horizon rollouts. Odyssey uses neural rendering to reconstruct 3D scenes and support realistic closed-loop simulations. Each scenario includes an explicit navigation route represented on a standard-definition (SD) map. By combining long-horizon evaluation with explicit route guidance, Odyssey enables a comprehensive assessment of models’ ability to navigate complex road structures safely—a capability that existing benchmarks have not adequately evaluated.

For these extended rollouts, Odyssey builds on the explicit geometric representation of 3D Gaussian Splatting ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) , followed by diffusion-based refinement for improving visual fidelity. Using OmniRe ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , we reconstruct continuous 100-second driving environments with rigid vehicles and deformable pedestrians whose motion is controlled independently of the static background. We further apply its time-conditioned deformation field to traffic lights to model changes in their color states throughout the sequence.
To reduce blur and recover missing detail at novel ego poses, we apply single-step diffusion refinement ( Wu et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA, 2025b ) to the rendered camera images without modifying the underlying scene representation or simulated state.

Odyssey provides navigation routes as explicit guidance for E2E planners.
By specifying the intended sequence of road segments, they resolve the ambiguity inherent in directional commands and eliminate the need to determine when to issue individual high-level meta-action commands.
For each scenario, we construct an SD-map route from trip data of the data-collection fleet.
However, this road-level representation encodes only coarse road-level topology and does not specify lane-level structure or the precise goal location that a driving model should reach. E2E planners must therefore interpret the high-level route jointly with the scene perceived by onboard sensors and translate it into a concrete, scene-consistent navigation goal.
This requires the planner to reason about how an abstract road-level route is translated to appropriate lane-level maneuvers within the current road geometry.
Odyssey establishes a foundation for evaluating such reasoning capability of E2E planners.

We design the closed-loop benchmark to enable systematic comparison of different E2E planners. We curate 100 scenarios from the raw nuPlan data ( Karnchanachari et al., 2024 ) , covering sequences of complex navigation maneuvers and diverse road topologies.
We further introduce two evaluation metrics, termed Pre-Lane Change Score and RouteDS ,
which assess whether the vehicle is appropriately positioned
for upcoming navigation maneuvers, as well as driving safety
and progress along the intended route.
We evaluate a set of baseline planners adapted from recent state-of-the-art E2E and vision-language-action (VLA) models, incorporating navigation routes as additional input.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce Odyssey , a high-fidelity real-world closed-loop benchmark for evaluating whether E2E planners can sustain safe and goal-directed driving under explicit route guidance over long-horizon rollouts.

We evaluate planners over continuous rollouts based on
recorded 100-second sequences, with explicit SD-map routes
that resolve ambiguities in high-level driving commands
and enable consistent assessment of navigation performance
across complex road topologies.

We develop a closed-loop simulation framework that combines the structural consistency of 3DGS with diffusion-based refinement to improve rendering fidelity when ego-vehicle motion reveals poorly reconstructed or previously unobserved regions.

We will release the benchmark, evaluation code, and baseline results to enable reproducible comparison and facilitate further research on long-horizon closed-loop evaluation for autonomous driving.

2. We evaluate planners over continuous rollouts based on

2026-10-06.title: A Taxonomy on Collective Awareness
2026-10-06.authors: Guillermo GP-Lenza , Miguel Fernandez-Cortizas , Martín Molina , Ricardo Sanz , Pascual Campoy
2026-10-06.abstract: As robotic teams tackle increasingly complex tasks in dynamic and unstructured environments, effective coordination requires agents to maintain accurate, aligned representations of their environment, teammates, and mission state. We argue that Mutual Awareness, Shared Situational Awareness, and Team Situational Awareness — three concepts widely invoked in the multi-robot systems literature — are not interchangeable: they form a containment hierarchy in which each type subsumes the previous in scope, and span a distribution spectrum from fully individualized understanding (MA) to fully uniform understanding (SSA), with TSA occupying a mixed position. We establish this through a two-dimensional taxonomy organized along the object of awareness and awareness distribution axes. Treating these terms as synonyms obscures the precise coordination requirements each imposes on a robotic system. A Search and Rescue case study with heterogeneous aerial and ground robots grounds each taxonomy position in concrete coordination requirements. These findings provide a conceptual foundation for principled specification, design, and comparison of collective awareness in multi-robot systems.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Multi-agent systems in robotics represent an innovative approach to solving complex problems through the coordination and collaboration of multiple robotic units exhibiting emergent behaviors. These systems offer several advantages, including increased robustness, scalability, and flexibility in tackling diverse challenges across various domains, such as area mapping, collective construction, and target search and tracking. By leveraging collaboration and cooperation between its members, these robotic systems can achieve tasks that would be difficult or impossible for individual robots to accomplish alone, making them particularly useful in many applications ranging from automated construction to environmental monitoring Wooldridge (2009) .

More formally, a Multi-Agent System (MAS) is a collection of agents that concurrently sense and act upon an environment, transforming it through their combined activities, with emergent behavior arising from agent interactions rather than from any individual agent in isolation Weiss (2016) . A multi-robot system (MRS) constitutes a specific instantiation of this paradigm in which all agents are embodied robots interacting within a shared physical environment to accomplish tasks that exceed the capabilities of any individual unit Rizk et al. (2019) . MRS vary along several dimensions: they may be homogeneous or heterogeneous in robot composition, communicating or non-communicating in information exchange, and cooperative or competitive in their interaction objectives Verma and Ranga (2021) . Enabling robotic teams to pursue shared objectives without unnecessary overhead, such as resolving conflicts, redundantly synchronizing actions, or correcting misalignments, requires coordination Wooldridge (2009) Bond and Gasser (1989) . Awareness plays a central role in enabling this coordination, as agents must maintain accurate representations of their environment, their teammates, and the evolving mission state to anticipate and complement each other’s actions.

A key element of agent autonomy is the theoretical foundation laid by Endsley (1995) about Situation Awareness (SA) in the form of a model divided into three layers: perception of the environmental elements, comprehension of their meaning, and projection of their future status. In recent theoretical work, awareness has been proposed as the real-time understanding of sensory flows, where understanding is achieved when an agent successfully derives valid inferences about objects in its environment Sanz et al. (2024) . This framework enables individual agents to make informed decisions and act appropriately within their environment. Building on this foundation, concepts such as Mutual Awareness, Shared Situational Awareness, and Team Situational Awareness emerged to characterize how team members align their understanding to enable effective coordination in multi-agent contexts.

These concepts have been widely adopted by the multi-robot systems community, where researchers frequently invoke awareness as a fundamental notion in coordination capabilities Fernandez-Cortizas et al. (2024) . However, the three terms are often used interchangeably, without distinguishing the distinct requirements each imposes on a robotic system. We argue this conflation is consequential: MA, SSA, and TSA differ both in the scope of what agents must know and in whether that knowledge must be uniform across the team. Clarifying these distinctions raises two questions that remain underspecified in the literature:

What are the distinct requirements of the different awareness types, and how do they relate to each other?

What are the distinct requirements of the different awareness types, and how do they relate to each other?

What precise definitions can be established for each awareness type that characterize their distinct requirements and roles in multi-robot coordination?

Addressing these questions is essential for enabling principled system design and technical progress in multi-robot coordination. Drawing from cognitive science, multi-agent systems, and robotics, this article examines these three awareness types and develops a conceptual framework to clarify their distinct requirements and relationships. Section 2 reviews the three main forms of awareness identified in the literature, Mutual Awareness, Shared Situational Awareness, and Team Situational Awareness, analyzing their definitions and key distinctions. Section 3 presents a taxonomy that characterizes these awareness types along two axes, awareness distribution and object of awareness, and illustrates each classification using a Search and Rescue scenario involving a heterogeneous team of aerial and ground robots. Finally, Section 4 synthesizes the main findings and identifies directions for future research.

# 2 Awareness in Multi-Robot Systems

## 2.1 Mutual Awareness

Mutual Awareness (MA) is described as the mutual understanding of each other’s intentions, beliefs and activities She and Li (2017) . Schmidt Schmidt (1998) characterizes it more precisely as the perception and understanding that member A has of the activity, intention, status, possible results, and influence of member B. This definition highlights that MA is inherently directional and may be asymmetric: as noted by Villa et al. Villa et al. (2008) , if A can observe B but B cannot observe A, then A holds a watching awareness , whereas if A knows B is observing them but cannot reciprocate, A holds a watched awareness . Some theories propose that MA is essential for any cooperative activity Shu and Furuta (2005) , and several authors reduce MA to individual activity and mutual beliefs Grosz and Sidner (1990) ; Tuomela and Miller (1988) , which influence the thoughts and actions of team members. Similarly, Bratman Bratman (1992) states that mutual responsiveness, defined as responsiveness to the intentions and actions of others, which emerges when participants are committed to the same goal, is essential for achieving a shared cooperative activity. This matches the idea proposed in Grosz and Sidner (1990) regarding mutual beliefs about the intentions of other individuals being considered in the definition of a shared plan. Complementary to individual SA, mutual awareness is also mentioned in She and Li (2017) as a component of TSA, where authors describe MA as the understanding of each other’s activities, beliefs and intentions.

## 2.2 Shared Situational Awareness

Shared Situational Awareness (SSA) refers to the overlap between the SA requirements of different team members, or the degree to which team members possess the same SA across shared requirements Endsley Mica R. (2001) . Shared SA is also described as the overlap in situation awareness that is necessary among team members Endsley Mica R. (2001) . Complementing this view, Salas et al. Salas et al. (1995c) describe Shared SA as a continuously updated and integrated mental representation of a mission built from shared information among team members, emphasizing its dynamic and constructive character. Endsley also suggests that teams can develop internal mechanisms to facilitate the achievement of shared SA. Furthermore, Endsley and Jones state that the information to be shared across teams should be defined by examining the areas where SA requirements of each team overlap, to avoid excessive communication overload. This shared information is specifically characterized as critical Seppänen et al. (2013) .

## 2.3 Team Situational Awareness

Team Situational Awareness (TSA) has been the subject of varied interpretations, reflecting differing assumptions about how awareness is formed and maintained in teams. Some definitions of TSA describe it primarily as the combination or sharing of individual team members’ situational awareness (SA). From this perspective, TSA corresponds to the overlap of individual SA knowledge states McNeese et al. (2021) . A common definition captures TSA as the degree to which every team member possesses the SA necessary for fulfilling their responsibilities Endsley and M. Robertson (2000) including not only the environment but also each individual’s interaction with the cooperative task Shu and Furuta (2005) . Salas et al. Salas et al. (1995b) further identify two critical abstractions underlying TSA: individual SA and team processes, where the latter encompasses the teamwork behaviors and cognitive processes that facilitate team performance and that cannot be reduced to the sum of individual awareness states. In contrast, Salas et al. describe TSA as a shared understanding of the situation among team members at a given moment Salas et al. (1995a) . Similarly, another viewpoint characterizes it as a common perspective among two or more individuals regarding environmental events, their implications, and likely developments She and Li (2017) . Artman and Garbin Artman and Garbis (1998) expand on this, defining TSA as a collaboratively constructed model that is partly shared and partly distributed, enabling anticipation of future states. Finally, Stanton et al. describe TSA as knowledge of a dynamic organizational structure and environment, actively formed and sustained through interactions with both the external world and other team members Stanton et al. (2017) .

2026-10-06.title: Visual Swarm Navigation via Deep Reinforcement Learning and Evolutionary Hybrid Design
2026-10-06.authors: Álvaro Díez (Department of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, University of Alicante), Fidel Aznar (Department of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, University of Alicante)
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE)
