2026-10-06.abstract: Swarm robotics presents a robust and cost-effective paradigm for advanced automation in complex, dynamic environments, such as those encountered in search and rescue or environmental monitoring. A fundamental challenge for this field is the data-driven design of decentralized controllers capable of generating emergent collective behaviors. This paper proposes a novel, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven hybrid methodology for the automatic synthesis of swarm robotic controllers for autonomous visual navigation. This approach synergistically combines multi-agent reinforcement learning with neuro-evolutionary strategies, specifically leveraging implementations of the cross-entropy method and the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy to optimize a pre-trained individual navigation policy. The underlying deep architecture is engineered for low-cost, resource-constrained platforms, utilizing a compact neural network that relies exclusively on monocular camera imagery. This vision-based design emphasizes computational and energy efficiency, a critical requirement for practical swarm deployments. Experiments, performed in a high-fidelity physics simulator, demonstrate that the resulting controllers enable robust and scalable collective exploration of diverse indoor environments. The controller trained using our cross-entropy method achieves superior exploration coverage, visiting 36.20% more regions compared to the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy. Critically, our best vision-based policy achieves exploration performance statistically comparable to traditional methods relying on more expensive distance sensors, while delivering a significant 31.40% average reduction in energy consumption. These findings validate an effective and economically viable autonomous control system, establishing a path for deploying highly efficient collective intelligence in real-world engineering applications.
2026-10-06.introduction:
In recent decades, extensive research in robotics has focused on developing control methods for autonomous and intelligent agents. Roboticists have implemented strategies aimed at solving tasks traditionally performed by humans in complex environments ( Mukhlish et al., 2018 ) , characterized by high uncertainty and dynamism. Multi-agent systems, particularly swarm robotics, have emerged as a promising and cost-effective paradigm for addressing these challenges. Drawing inspiration from the collective behaviors observed in social animals, swarm robotics aims to develop decentralized control methods for multiple simple, autonomous agents that rely on local sensing and communication.

This approach offers a valuable alternative to traditional strategies that depend on a single, sophisticated, and expensive robot, which may be inefficient or prone to complete failure in high-risk operational environments ( Mukhlish et al., 2018 ) . For a swarm to function effectively, its members must self-organize through coordination and cooperation, enabling the emergence of robust, flexible, and scalable collective behaviors. This allows the system to maintain operational integrity despite agent loss ( Mukhlish et al., 2018 ) , adapt to changing environmental configurations ( Brambilla et al., 2013 ) , and perform diverse tasks effectively regardless of the swarm’s size ( Cheraghi et al., 2021 ) .

The design of controllers that facilitate such emergent behaviors is a significant challenge. While traditional behavior-based design methods have been employed, they are often labor-intensive and result in solutions tailored to specific problems in static environments ( Mukhlish et al., 2018 ) . This approach involves manually modeling, implementing, analyzing, and refining individual robot behaviors through iterative trial and error until satisfactory collective behavior emerges ( Brambilla et al., 2013 ) . Consequently, automatic design methods, primarily based on Reinforcement Learning (RL) ( Kaelbling et al., 1996 ) and Evolutionary Computation (EC) ( Bäck and Schwefel, 1996 ) , are strongly advocated for their ability to generate more adaptive solutions without explicit modeling of the problem or the desired collective behaviors ( Mukhlish et al., 2018 ) .

Recent advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have introduced powerful, large-scale generative models that are setting new benchmarks in robotics. Among the most prominent are transformers, such as Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT), which leverage attention mechanisms to process complex data sequences ( Feuerriegel et al., 2023 ) . However, this power comes at a significant cost. These models are exceptionally demanding, requiring massive datasets for training and consisting of an enormous number of parameters. Their complexity in terms of memory, processing, and energy consumption makes them unsuitable for the low-cost, resource-constrained platforms typically used in swarm robotics. These limitations underscore the need for more efficient and pragmatic architectures specifically designed for the constraints of swarm robotics.

This paper charts a different course, diverging from the trend of developing computationally expensive models. We propose a hybrid automatic design method for swarm robotics that uses Evolution Strategies (ES) to address Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) ( Ha and Tang, 2022 ) problems in autonomous navigation. Compared to traditional DRL algorithms, evolution strategies are highly parallelizable, scalable, and demonstrate greater robustness against the common challenges of temporal credit assignment and solution space exploration ( Salimans et al., 2017 ) , making them particularly suitable for training multi-agent systems.

Our approach is built on an efficient deep architecture, demonstrating that robust, flexible, and scalable collective navigation is achievable without massive computational overhead, an indispensable requirement for the deployment of swarm systems in the real world. This method is specifically engineered to learn collective visual navigation policies, enabling homogeneous swarm agents to perform collision-free exploration in uncertain and dynamic environments using only low-cost monocular cameras ( Kolar et al., 2020 ) .

While recent centralized visual-inertial Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) systems have achieved remarkable mapping richness and localization accuracy through cloud-based multi-robot feature fusion ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , such advanced paradigms inherently require substantial computational and communicational bandwidth. For swarm applications prioritizing hardware simplicity, our decentralized, map-less ( Güzel, 2013 ) strategy offers a complementary approach that significantly reduces implementation costs and energy requirements, making it highly viable for resource-constrained scenarios.

To validate our approach, this work addresses five fundamental research questions:

How effectively can a hybrid automatic design method combining deep reinforcement learning with evolution strategies generate functional swarm robotic controllers for autonomous visual navigation?

How effectively can a hybrid automatic design method combining deep reinforcement learning with evolution strategies generate functional swarm robotic controllers for autonomous visual navigation?

What level of stability do these automatically generated controllers maintain when subjected to sensory perturbations?

How do the controllers respond to unforeseen variations in environmental conditions not encountered during training?

What impact does varying the size of the robotic swarm have on the efficacy of the developed controllers?

Can vision-based swarm controllers achieve performance comparable to traditional methods that employ more expensive and heavier distance sensors?

The remainder of this article is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews the most relevant research directions in the automatic design of swarm robotic controllers. Section 3 presents the formal specification of our deep reinforcement learning problem. Section 4 details our training methodology for learning collective visual navigation behaviors, including two specific implementations of different evolution strategies. Section 5 compares and discusses the experimental results achieved by our two swarm controllers. Section 6 evaluates and analyzes the robustness, flexibility, and scalability of our controllers. Finally, Section 7 synthesizes our conclusions, addresses the limitations of this work, and outlines future research directions.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

Multi-Agent reinforcement learning extends traditional RL principles to systems comprising multiple interacting individuals ( Mukhlish et al., 2018 ) . Whereas a conventional reinforcement learning agent learns behavior through trial-and-error interactions with its environment ( Brambilla et al., 2013 ) , the multi-agent variant involves agents that interact with both the environment and each other ( Mukhlish et al., 2018 ) . In recent years, deep reinforcement learning has become a prominent technique for addressing collective autonomous navigation problems in swarm robotics.

Hüttenrauch et al. (2019) proposed a MARL approach based on the Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) training algorithm ( Schulman et al., 2015 ) . Their method was validated in two classic multi-robot scenarios: a rendezvous task requiring agents to gather at an arbitrary location, and a pursuit-evasion task where a group of agents must cooperatively capture one or more targets. Similar to our system, their swarm was homogeneous; however, their agents relied on local communication to exchange task-relevant information. This is a key distinction from our approach, which employs a communication-free framework to enhance system simplicity and robustness.

More recently, Batra et al. (2021) employed the popular Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) algorithm ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) to train decentralized control policies for drone swarms. Their MARL process, conducted in realistic simulated environments, successfully generated coordinated flocking behaviors that enabled the drones to maintain various formations while avoiding collisions with each other and with dynamic obstacles. Critically, the collective behaviors learned in simulation were successfully transferred to multiple small, real-world drones with limited computational resources, demonstrating the feasibility of deploying learned policies on hardware-constrained platforms, a central objective of our own research.

A study by Bloom et al. (2022) is also of particular relevance for its development of a MARL method for collective object transport, one of the three principal navigation behaviors in swarm robotics alongside coordinated movement and collective exploration ( Brambilla et al., 2013 ) . Consistent with our approach, their method utilized neural networks with few fully connected layers to learn collision-free navigation policies for a swarm of wheeled robots with differential drive ( Stefek et al., 2020 ) . A key difference, however, is that their agents perceived the environment through distance sensors, whereas our work addresses the more challenging task of navigation using only monocular camera imagery.

Recent literature continues to expand the capabilities of PPO-based algorithms for complex spatial coordination. For instance, Bezerra et al. (2025) proposed a decentralized framework that extends the Multi-Agent Proximal Policy Optimization (MAPPO) algorithm to address dynamic coalition formation in multi-robot task allocation. Although their primary focus lies in task assignment rather than explicitly in swarm robotic control, their framework intrinsically governs multi-robot spatial navigation, utilizing an end-to-end Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) ( LeCun et al., 2015 ) based on a U-Net architecture to process local grid observations and plan collision-free paths. While this MAPPO-based approach is highly effective in dynamic environments, it relies on explicit intention sharing among agents and uses sophisticated convolutional architectures to process spatial action maps.

In a similar vein, other recent advancements have sought to enhance the adaptability of learning-based models by integrating them with classical rule-based algorithms. For example, the adaptive cooperative path planning method proposed by Liu et al. (2025a) successfully utilized MARL to dynamically optimize rotational artificial potential fields, achieving efficient, collision-free navigation and effectively overcoming local minima in continuous action spaces.

Building upon these broad advances in multi-agent learning and hybrid optimization, our methodology explores an alternative paradigm: achieving robust collective navigation through a strictly communication-free approach, utilizing a lightweight, purely reactive perception and control architecture engineered specifically for severely resource-constrained platforms where heavy computational and communication overheads might be prohibitive.

The automatic design methods discussed in this subsection typically generate swarm behaviors through online reinforcement learning, which relies on numerous direct interactions between the agents and their environment. In contrast, deep architectures based on modern generative models, such as the generative pre-trained transformer, are often trained using offline reinforcement learning to mitigate the computational complexity of the online training phase. This offline paradigm utilizes data collected from a previously learned behavioral policy to find a new, optimal policy ( Boige et al., 2023 ) . Notable examples of such architectures include Decision Transformers (DTs) and Control Transformers (CTs).

A decision transformer solves RL problems through the generative modeling of trajectories, which consist of sequences of states, actions, and rewards ( Meng et al., 2023 ) , and can be adapted for multi-agent autonomous navigation applications. The control transformer, a variant of the former, seeks to improve generalization capabilities in tasks such as robotic navigation ( Lawson and Qureshi, 2023 ) . However, both decision and control transformers currently feature architectures that demand significantly greater computational resources compared to the models typically used in automatic swarm controller design, and particularly in comparison to the low-cost solution proposed in this study.

## 2.2 Neuro-Evolution

Neuro-evolution draws inspiration from Darwinian principles of natural selection and evolution, combining EC techniques with artificial neural networks to optimize network parameters ( Brambilla et al., 2013 ) . In robotics, this approach treats neural networks as black-box controllers and generally requires no heuristic domain-specific information about the problem to be solved ( Kuckling, 2023 ) . Neuro-evolution has proven highly effective for generating a wide array of swarm behaviors, including pattern formation, collective transport, task allocation, and foraging ( Mukhlish et al., 2018 ) .

Within the broader field of evolutionary computation, our research focuses on evolution strategies, a family of black-box optimization algorithms that function as heuristic search processes inspired by natural evolution ( Salimans et al., 2017 ) . For this study, we selected two prominent ES algorithms, the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) ( Rubinstein, 1999 ) and the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) ( Hansen and Ostermeier, 2001 ) , valued for their straightforward implementation and minimal hyperparameter tuning requirements.

The cross-entropy method is a stochastic, adaptive optimization algorithm that can be classified as an evolution strategy due to its operational similarities with such techniques ( Nguyen et al., 2021 ) . CEM has been applied to various single-agent ( Nguyen et al., 2021 ) and multi-agent robotic control systems. For instance, Fan et al. (2018) utilized this EC technique to evaluate a swarm of low-cost drones in two complex scenarios: a cooperative attack on a defended enemy base and a confrontation between two autonomous aerial teams. Similar to our methodology, they employed a neural network controller whose parameters were optimized using an ES-based method in a realistic simulation featuring agent interactions, varying initial conditions, and Gaussian noise ( Yogesh et al., 2017 ) . However, their network contained three hidden layers, whereas our work demonstrates the efficacy of an even more compact single-layer model.

CMA-ES, one of today’s most effective evolution strategies, is notable for its advanced capabilities in searching the solution space ( Hasselmann et al., 2021 ) . Its effectiveness in designing swarm robotic controllers was recently validated by Hasselmann et al. (2021) , whose work involved generating behaviors like aggregation and foraging and evaluating them in both simulation and on physical robots. Their comparative analysis confirmed the competitive performance of the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy against other neuro-evolutionary methods, including the Exponential Natural Evolution Strategy (xNES) ( Glasmachers et al., 2010 ) , the Neuro-Evolution of Augmenting Topologies (NEAT) algorithm ( Stanley and Miikkulainen, 2002 ) , and the basic EvoStick approach ( Francesca et al., 2014 ) , reinforcing its suitability as a powerful tool for the automatic design of collective behaviors.

Building upon the foundational principles of algorithms like NEAT, which seek to optimize both the structural architecture and the synaptic weights of neural networks, recent advancements have continued to explore this dual optimization paradigm for decentralized control. For example, a recent study by Hiraga (2026) proposed a topology and weight neuro-evolutionary method designed to foster social learning within robotic swarms. By utilizing a mutation-based evolving artificial neural network, their approach allows robots to dynamically alter their controller’s architecture through local interactions.

While evolving the topology offers theoretical flexibility and mitigates the need for manual network design, it inherently expands the search space and introduces significant computational overhead. In stark contrast, our methodology deliberately limits the evolutionary search space to the synaptic weights of an ultra-compact, fixed-topology controller. By coupling this static, highly efficient control policy with a deeply compressed representation of the visual input space, our approach bypasses the severe computational demands of topology mutation, guaranteeing rapid convergence and strict architectural efficiency for resource-constrained, vision-based navigation.

2026-10-06.title: DexForge: High-Fidelity Physics-Informed Dexterous Retargeting
2026-10-06.authors: Meizhong Wang , Kun Cao , Ruiqi Ni , Lihua Xie , Yiguang Hong
2026-10-06.abstract: Human demonstrations offer rich examples of precise dexterous manipulation and a promising source of robot training data. However, high-fidelity reproduction of demonstrated motions and hand–object interactions across robot embodiments remains challenging under physical constraints. We present DexForge, a differentiable physics-grounded framework for converting human video demonstrations into high-fidelity robot trajectories. We reconstruct spherical-Gaussian object models and hand–object motion from visual observations, then build a differentiable simulator combining efficient Gaussian collision detection with existing differentiable dynamics. Based on this simulator, DexForge combines contact-aware kinematic retargeting with force-aware dynamics retargeting: robot-adapted stable contacts guide kinematic reference construction and subsequent gradient-based control refinement for precise physical motion reproduction. Experiments on 130 DexYCB and HOT3D demonstrations across seven dexterous hands show success-rate gains of approximately 35–53 percentage points over the baseline, with object position and orientation tracking errors on successful trajectories reduced by approximately 34–67% and 71–78%, respectively. Further experiments demonstrate open-loop transfer to MuJoCo and real-robot execution. Our project page is available at https://wmz1226.github.io/DexForge/ .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Enabling robots with different embodiments to reproduce precise human manipulation is an important step toward transferring human expertise to robots ( Xu et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . High-fidelity reproduction requires more than task completion; the demonstrated motions and hand–object interactions must also be preserved. For example, establishing a stable grasp is only the starting point; precisely controlling the object’s subsequent movement and orientation captures finer aspects of manipulation. Human manipulation videos contain rich examples of these behaviors, yet translating them into high-fidelity trajectories executable by different dexterous hands remains challenging.

Recent advances in learning from human demonstrations and retargeting are narrowing this gap. Hand–object reconstruction recovers explicit 3D geometry and motion references from videos ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) , while kinematic retargeting adapts these references to robots, increasingly incorporating contact preservation ( Lakshmipathy et al., 2025 ) and collision constraints ( Tian et al., 2026 ) to improve geometric consistency. Building on these references, physics-based retargeting uses policy learning ( Li et al., 2025 ) or trajectory optimization ( Pan et al., 2026 ) to find controls that drive object motion in simulation, with contact guidance helping preserve demonstrated interactions ( Mandi et al., 2025 ) . Meanwhile, advances in differentiable collision detection ( Beker et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) and dynamics modeling ( Paulus et al., 2026 ) enable control optimization through simulation gradients, providing another route to precise trajectory refinement ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Together, these developments extend retargeting beyond geometric hand-motion matching toward physically grounded manipulation reproduction.

Despite these advances, high-fidelity reproduction across different robot hands remains difficult. Several problems need to be solved in sequence. First, the reconstructed object geometry must be accurate enough for collision and contact reasoning. Second, contacts from the human demonstration may not be reachable or stable for a robot with a different hand shape. Third, even a penetration-free robot trajectory with geometrically appropriate contacts may not be executable under contact dynamics and actuation constraints. Physics-based optimization also involves a trade-off. Sampling-based methods can handle complex contact changes, but obtaining very accurate trajectories may require many samples. Gradient-based optimization can refine trajectories more directly, but it is sensitive to initialization and local minima. This motivates us to use robot-adapted contacts to provide a good kinematic reference and continued guidance during gradient-based dynamics optimization.

We introduce DexForge, a differentiable physics-grounded framework for high-fidelity retargeting from human video demonstrations. Our key insight is that human contacts should not be copied directly to a robot with a different hand. Instead, we first adapt these contacts to the target robot, and then use the adapted contacts to guide both kinematic retargeting and dynamic control optimization. To support this process, we reconstruct spherical Gaussian object models that provide both visual appearance for pose estimation and geometry for collision checking. We then extract stable contacts from the human demonstration and refine them together with robot configurations so that they are reachable, collision-free, and stable for the target hand. These contacts are used to build a robot kinematic reference. Finally, we combine differentiable Gaussian collision with ComFree dynamics and optimize robot controls through simulation gradients to reproduce the demonstrated motion more accurately. We further use system identification to reduce the mismatch between simulation and the target system. Our contributions are:

We propose DexForge, a complete framework that combines visual reconstruction, contact-aware kinematic retargeting, and force-aware dynamics optimization to transform human video demonstrations into high-fidelity, executable demonstrations across robot embodiments.

We propose DexForge, a complete framework that combines visual reconstruction, contact-aware kinematic retargeting, and force-aware dynamics optimization to transform human video demonstrations into high-fidelity, executable demonstrations across robot embodiments.

We introduce robot-adapted stable-contact guidance through joint anchor and robot-configuration optimization, supporting both kinematic reference construction and dynamic refinement.

We jointly train spherical Gaussians for appearance and geometry and develop efficient differentiable collision detection for them, supporting integration with existing simulators.

We evaluate DexForge on 130 DexYCB and HOT3D demonstrations across seven hands, outperforming sampling-based baselines in retargeting success and object-tracking accuracy, and demonstrate open-loop MuJoCo transfer and real-robot execution.

1. We propose DexForge, a complete framework that combines visual reconstruction, contact-aware kinematic retargeting, and force-aware dynamics optimization to transform human video demonstrations into high-fidelity, executable demonstrations across robot embodiments.

2. We introduce robot-adapted stable-contact guidance through joint anchor and robot-configuration optimization, supporting both kinematic reference construction and dynamic refinement.

3. We jointly train spherical Gaussians for appearance and geometry and develop efficient differentiable collision detection for them, supporting integration with existing simulators.

4. We evaluate DexForge on 130 DexYCB and HOT3D demonstrations across seven hands, outperforming sampling-based baselines in retargeting success and object-tracking accuracy, and demonstrate open-loop MuJoCo transfer and real-robot execution.

# 2 Related Work

Dexterous Manipulation from Human Demonstrations. Human demonstrations can be collected through portable motion-capture systems ( Wang et al., 2024 ) and wearable interfaces ( Xu et al., 2025a ; Tao et al., 2025 ) . Egocentric human videos also provide scalable supervision for dexterous policy learning ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Explicit scene and motion references recovered from videos enable robot trajectory generation ( Mu et al., 2026 ; Paliwal et al., 2026 ) or guide policy learning in simulation ( Lum et al., 2025 ) . DexForge reconstructs object models from separate capture sequences and recovers hand–object motion from demonstration videos, then converts these references into high-fidelity robot trajectories through contact adaptation and physical optimization .

Dexterous Motion Retargeting. Kinematic retargeting maps human motion to robot configurations through geometric correspondence objectives ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Xin et al., 2026 ) . Interaction-aware methods further preserve contact regions or local hand–object geometry ( Lakshmipathy et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) , while constrained formulations incorporate collision avoidance ( Tian et al., 2026 ) . Such interaction structure can also be encoded through interaction meshes for whole-body retargeting ( Yang et al., 2026 ) and dexterous manipulation ( Feng et al., 2026 ) . The kinematic stage of C2Dex ( Ren et al., 2026 ) uses stable object-side contacts to guide reference construction. For grasp configurations, GenHand ( Qi et al., 2026 ) refines human-derived contact anchors through force-closure optimization, while GraspQP ( Zurbrügg et al., 2025 ) develops a differentiable force-closure energy for grasp synthesis. DexForge jointly optimizes robot keyframe configurations and anchors shared within stable-contact intervals, considering reachability and force closure .

Physics-based retargeting accounts for contact dynamics, with representative approaches using reference-guided reinforcement learning ( Li et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Mandi et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025b ; Ren et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) or sampling-based trajectory optimization ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Pan et al., 2026 ; Paliwal et al., 2026 ) . SPIDER ( Pan et al., 2026 ) progressively relaxes virtual contact guidance during optimization, while Do as I Do ( Paliwal et al., 2026 ) adapts sampling-based retargeting to noisy reconstructed references. Gradient-based transfer is also explored by QuasiSim ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , which progressively tightens physical constraints through a curriculum of parameterized quasi-physical simulators. DexForge uses robot-adapted stable contacts to construct collision-constrained kinematic references for initialization and retains the same refined anchors as interaction targets during gradient-based dynamics optimization.

Differentiable Simulation and Physical Scene Modeling. Differentiable collision detection provides geometric derivatives for optimization ( Tracy et al., 2023 ; Montaut et al., 2023 ; Beker et al., 2026 ) , while contact models and simulators advance differentiable dynamics ( Jin, 2024 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Paulus et al., 2026 ) . Gaussian representations ( Kerbl et al., 2023 ) also support physical modeling: ContactGaussian-WM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) unifies appearance and collision geometry with spherical Gaussians but optimizes geometry and appearance separately, whereas D-REX ( Lou et al., 2026 ) combines Gaussian rendering and mesh-based collisions with differentiable mass identification and grasping policy learning. DexForge jointly optimizes spherical Gaussians to better capture appearance and collision geometry, providing an efficient differentiable collision-query interface directly on these primitives. Integrating it with ComFree dynamics ( Borse, 2026 ) yields ComFree-GS, supporting contact-aware kinematic retargeting and gradient-based physical retargeting.

2026-10-06.title: Dual Variational Autoencoders for Efficient Sim-to-Real Transfer in Low-Cost Robotic Navigation
2026-10-06.authors: Álvaro Díez (Department of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, University of Alicante), Fidel Aznar (Department of Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence, University of Alicante)
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-06.comment: . Published in Image and Vision Computing under a CC BY 4.0 license
2026-10-06.abstract: Vision-based autonomous navigation for low-cost robots remains a fundamental challenge, primarily due to the significant gap between simulated training environments and real-world operational conditions. Direct policy transfer from simulation is often ineffective, while training exclusively on real data is impractical. We propose a hybrid transfer learning framework that effectively bridges the sim-to-real gap by combining domain randomization with feature-level domain adaptation. Our method employs a dual convolutional variational autoencoder architecture with a shared decoder, trained on an extensive set of 45225 simulated images and a minimal set of only 4556 real-world samples. This architecture learns a compact, common latent representation space that aligns the distributions of both domains. The adaptation process is further enhanced by two complementary data augmentation techniques designed to expand the limited real-world data. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that our method achieves an average success rate of almost 91% on image classification tasks for real-world indoor navigation, significantly outperforming both simulation-only and real-world-only training. We validate these findings through a direct, real-world deployment, where the proposed policy successfully guides a low-cost robot in a reactive exploration task. Furthermore, we validate the model’s efficiency through a rigorous computational estimation, confirming its suitability for resource-constrained embedded platforms such as the Raspberry Pi 4 and NVIDIA Jetson Nano. This work presents a practical solution for developing effective and efficient navigation policies for low-cost robotic systems.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Deep Learning (DL) [ 1 ] has achieved remarkable success in solving a diverse array of complex tasks, particularly within vision-based applications for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and robotics. These applications span from object detection and classification [ 2 , 3 , 4 ], fine-grained recognition [ 5 ], and human pose estimation [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] to embodied autonomous navigation [ 9 , 10 ]. Across many of these fields, it is common practice to learn policies within simulated environments and subsequently transfer them to real-world platforms.

As highlighted in [ 11 ], image-based learning in simulated environments offers a more straightforward training methodology compared to direct learning in reality. Physics simulators facilitate the rapid and cost-effective collection of large-scale, labeled data. In contrast, gathering extensive and properly annotated datasets in the real world can be a time-consuming, expensive, and logistically challenging endeavor.

However, the literature has also demonstrated that policies trained exclusively on simulation data often fail to generalize effectively to real-world scenarios [ 12 , 11 ]. These difficulties primarily arise from systematic discrepancies between real and simulated environments. In the broader context of visual perception, recent studies have emphasized the critical need for robustness against real-world disturbances, such as handling occlusions [ 13 ], suppressing background noise and information inequality [ 14 ], and defending against adversarial perturbations [ 15 ]. Similarly, in the scientific literature, the discrepancies specifically between simulation and reality are commonly referred to by the term Reality Gap (RG) [ 16 , 17 ].

To address these challenges, two principal sets of Transfer Learning (TL) methods have emerged: Domain Randomization (DR) [ 18 ] and Domain Adaptation (DA) [ 19 ], which can be effectively combined. Furthermore, as recently affirmed by researchers such as Azzam et al. [ 20 ], it is also possible to effectively transfer policies from simulation to reality without employing the aforementioned explicit TL approaches, instead utilizing so-called Zero-Shot Generalization (ZSG) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) [ 21 ].

Considering the DR and DA transfer learning approaches, which are the focus of the present work, we investigate three core hypotheses:

A DL model trained exclusively on real-world data will struggle to perform satisfactorily across novel scenarios in a real environment without an extensive, balanced training set of labeled real-world data.

A DL model trained exclusively on real-world data will struggle to perform satisfactorily across novel scenarios in a real environment without an extensive, balanced training set of labeled real-world data.

A DL model trained entirely on a large, balanced set of labeled simulation data will learn a policy with limited generalization capability to various scenarios in an equivalent real environment.

By generating a common representation space where distributions of both extensive simulation data and limited real-world data can converge, it will be possible to mitigate the discrepancies between simulated and real environments, thereby learning a policy with improved generalization accuracy in the real world.

This paper proposes a deep TL method for efficiently producing policies that can generalize and adapt to diverse situations in vision-based tasks within real environments. We focus particularly on real-time tasks requiring accurate and efficient image classification [ 22 ], such as visual navigation applications involving autonomous robots in the real world.

Specifically, our method constructs abstract low-dimensional representations from both simulation and real-world data using deep generative models. These models extract and learn meaningful features from synthetic and real images while simultaneously reducing their dimensionality. Our goal is to develop models capable of obtaining policies that can rapidly and efficiently solve various autonomous low-cost robot navigation tasks after training primarily in simulation and transferring to reality.

Our major contributions include:

The implementation of domain randomization by training our network with meaningful features extracted from extensive simulation data before policy transfer to reality. We collect synthetic training images using a single low-cost mobile robot in a realistic indoor environment modeled with a high-fidelity physics simulator.

The implementation of domain randomization by training our network with meaningful features extracted from extensive simulation data before policy transfer to reality. We collect synthetic training images using a single low-cost mobile robot in a realistic indoor environment modeled with a high-fidelity physics simulator.

The application of domain adaptation using two convolutional Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) [ 23 ] that share a common decoder. This decoder generates similar synthetic and pseudo-synthetic image data without requiring a direct, one-to-one correspondence between the simulated and real-world training samples, enabling successful policy generalization to novel real scenarios.

The creation of memory-efficient image representations, making our learned policies suitable for transfer to low-cost physical robots. This is particularly relevant for autonomous reactive navigation [ 24 , 25 ] applications that use a mobile robot equipped with a single cost-effective camera.

The validation of the developed method by transferring the proposed policy to a low-cost physical robot and executing a real-time, collision-free, map-less [ 26 , 27 ] visual exploration task in a real-world indoor corridor.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work on transfer learning and its main approaches, as well as specific studies on autonomous robot navigation applications in the real world. Section 3 details our proposed transfer learning method, including data acquisition, training methodology, and data augmentation techniques. Section 4 presents and analyzes our experimental results, including a proof-of-concept validation performed in the real world using a mobile robot with limited computational resources. Finally, Section 5 addresses our conclusions and directions for future research.

2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Domain Randomization

Domain randomization encompasses methods used to train more generalizable models in a source domain ( e.g. , a simulated environment) for effective prediction across systematically different target domains ( e.g. , distinct real-world environments) [ 28 ]. During training, various configurations are randomized in simulation, including object placement, illumination conditions, and surface textures.

Domain randomization has emerged as a pivotal strategy for mitigating the reality gap, functioning as a regularization technique that prevents a DL model from overfitting to individual simulation instances [ 18 ]. The underlying hypothesis is that if the variability in simulation is sufficiently extensive, the learned policy will become robust enough to be transferred directly to a physical robot without requiring any real-world data for fine-tuning [ 29 ].

Two seminal works were instrumental in establishing this TL approach in robotics. In 2017, Sadeghi and Levine [ 28 ] leveraged domain randomization for real-world navigation tasks. Their method generated a collision avoidance policy using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) [ 30 ] trained through deep reinforcement learning. Their model processed raw Red, Green, Blue (RGB) camera images to predict collision probability, enabling velocity command determination for collision-free indoor flight of a physical quadrotor.

Unlike our TL approach, which incorporates real-world data, their navigation policy relied entirely on synthetic training image data from a simulated environment. Their method did not require particularly high-fidelity simulation or extreme realism. Instead, Sadeghi and Levine extensively randomized rendering settings for their synthetic dataset, forcing the network to handle diverse obstacle appearances and lighting conditions. This approach made their learned high-dimensional representations invariant to surface appearance, enabling the model to learn geometric features for robust open space detection across different real indoor environments. The initial training phase of our proposed method is fundamentally rooted in this principle of procedural randomization.

Concurrently, Tobin et al. [ 29 ] popularized domain randomization for robotic manipulation tasks. One year later, in [ 31 ], they proposed a novel deep generative architecture for learning grasp sampling distributions across diverse objects. Their network was trained exclusively on unrealistic procedurally generated objects from physics simulation. The architecture developed by Tobin et al. employed an autoregressive model [ 23 ] that processed embedding representations mapped from target object observations through an image representation module. The model generated distributions over possible grasps using additional depth images captured by a simulated robot’s hand camera. The architecture aimed to select optimal grasps from the sampled possibilities. Their network achieved 92% success rate on unseen realistic objects during simulation testing and 80% success rate on real-world grasp attempts.

Like our DR method, the previous works are based on the so-called static domain randomization, which typically relies on uniform sampling from a fixed domain parameter distribution. This particular approach usually implements sim-to-real transfer using any real-world data. Although it represents a technique that can effectively, quickly, and relatively easily bridge the reality gap, learned policies tend to perform worse in the target domain than those produced adaptively. [ 18 ].

Adaptive domain randomization employs different strategies that refine the simulation distribution during the learning process, introducing efficiency and higher fidelity by closing the sim-to-real loop. On the one hand, curriculum-based approaches, such as automatic domain randomization, seeks to increase the sample efficiency by introducing a schedule of increasing difficulty [ 18 ]. On the other hand, active domain randomization aims to improve training efficiency by actively searching for the most informative or challenging simulation parameters for the current policy, thereby focusing computational effort on those hard cases that are most likely to improve robustness [ 32 ].

The most advanced methods belonging to adaptive domain randomization close the sim-to-real loop by using data from the real world to directly guide the simulation process. This represents a fundamental conceptual shift from generalization to adaptation. A notable example is the task-driven framework called AdaptSim, proposed by Ren et al. [ 33 ]. They meta-learned an adaptation policy through reinforcement learning using a simulator to adjust the simulation parameter distribution based on its performance on the target task. Subsequently, the policy was deployed in the real world, utilizing a few interactions to find the optimal simulation configuration for re-training.

Our proposed approach offers a compelling and practical alternative to online, simulator-centric adaptation schemes. Instead of adapting the simulator to match reality, our method adapts the model’s perception of reality by fine-tuning a pre-trained variational autoencoder using a small batch of real data. This model-centric adaptation strategy is offline and highly data-efficient, making it particularly suitable for low-cost platforms where continuous real-world interaction for iterative simulator tuning is impractical or unsafe.

## 2.2 Domain Adaptation

Whereas domain randomization operates exclusively on the source domain ( e.g. , a simulated environment) to foster generalization, domain adaptation is a transfer learning paradigm that actively leverages data from the target domain ( e.g. , a real-world environment) to align the distributions between the source and target environments [ 19 ].

Contemporary DA techniques for sim-to-real transfer can be broadly categorized into two main families: pixel-level adaptation, which modifies the visual appearance of source images, and feature-level adaptation, which aligns the underlying representations learned by the model [ 19 ]. Our proposed method employs generative feature-level domain adaptation to fine-tune a robust model initially pre-trained with domain randomization.

Pixel-level adaptation methods aim to bridge the reality gap by translating synthetic source images to appear as if they were drawn from the target domain’s distribution. This is predominantly achieved using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [ 23 ], particularly through unpaired image-to-image translation architectures like CycleGAN [ 34 ].

However, a critical challenge with this approach is the potential for semantic inconsistency. A GAN optimized solely for visual realism may produce photo-realistic images at the expense of altering or even removing task-critical content, such as obstacles or key objects, leading to catastrophic policy failure [ 35 ]. To mitigate this, task-aware extensions have been developed. A notable example is RL-CycleGAN, proposed by Rao et al. [ 35 ], which introduces an additional reinforcement learning-based consistency loss. Our proposed method circumvents the training instability and semantic consistency issues inherent in GANs by operating at the feature level, which offers a more stable and direct approach to aligning domain-invariant structural information.

Instead of altering input images, feature-level adaptation methods seek to learn a mapping that projects both source and target data into a common, domain-invariant representation space where their distributions are aligned. Within this shared feature space, a classifier trained on labeled source data can generalize effectively to unlabeled target data [ 19 ]. These methods are primarily divided into two families: statistical and adversarial.

Statistical methods directly minimize a distance metric between the feature distributions of the two domains. A prominent example is Deep Correlation Alignment (Deep CORAL), which introduces a CORAL loss to align the second-order statistics ( i.e. , covariances) of the source and target feature distributions within one or more layers of a deep network [ 36 ].

In contrast, adversarial methods employ a domain discriminator in a zero-sum game against the feature extractor. The discriminator is trained to distinguish the origin of the features ( i.e. , the source domain or the target domain), while the feature extractor is trained to produce features that fool the discriminator, thereby forcing the distributions to become indistinguishable [ 19 ]. A seminal work in this area is the Domain-Adversarial Neural Network (DANN), which uses a novel Gradient Reversal Layer (GRL) to enable end-to-end adversarial training [ 37 ]. These foundational methods, many of which are implemented in standard libraries like Awesome Domain Adaptation Python Toolbox 1 1 1 https://adapt-python.github.io/adapt/ (ADAPT), form the basis for modern feature-level adaptation.

Our work is situated within the domain of generative feature-level adaptation, which leverages deep generative models to learn a common latent space. The choice between a VAE and a GAN for this purpose involves a fundamental trade-off. While GANs can produce sharp, high-fidelity images, their adversarial training is notoriously unstable. VAEs, conversely, offer highly stable training and produce a continuous, structured latent space well-suited for control tasks, though their reconstructions tend to be blurry [ 23 ].

## 2.3 Zero-Shot Generalization

An alternative paradigm to explicit transfer learning is zero-shot generalization, which aims to train a policy entirely in simulation that can be deployed directly in the real world without any fine-tuning or adaptation on target domain data [ 21 ]. This zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is often pursued through hybrid approaches that combine reinforcement learning with domain randomization to create a robust policy [ 38 ]. However, a distinct line of research, and the focus of this subsection, investigates the feasibility of achieving ZSG by relying exclusively on RL, foregoing explicit DR or domain adaptation.

One prominent strategy for RL-only ZSG is to invest in creating a high-fidelity digital twin of the physical system. The underlying hypothesis is that if the simulator’s dynamics are sufficiently accurate, the reality gap becomes negligible, allowing a standard RL policy to transfer directly. A compelling demonstration of this approach is presented by Azzam et al. [ 20 ], who developed a navigation and collision avoidance policy for an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV). Their framework employs a hierarchical control structure where the RL agent learns high-level velocity commands, which are then executed by a low-level controller.

The key to their success in achieving direct sim-to-real transfer without any randomization was the meticulous system identification of the UAV’s dynamic model using a deep neural network-based method. By ensuring the simulated dynamics closely mirrored reality, the policy learned by Azzam et al. achieved a 90% success rate in real-world experiments. This result is remarkably comparable to the 90.88% classification accuracy achieved by our proposed method on our real-world test dataset.

Counter-intuitively, an alternative approach posits that lower, rather than higher, simulation fidelity can lead to superior sim-to-real transfer. This hypothesis, explored by Truong et al. [ 10 ], argues that high-fidelity physics simulations can be computationally slow and may cause the policy to overfit to simulator-specific inaccuracies that do not exist in the real world. Their solution is to strategically abstract away the complex dynamics. Truong et al. propose a hierarchical decomposition where a high-level navigation policy is trained with RL in a fast, low-fidelity kinematic simulation. This policy learns to output desired velocity commands, which are then passed to the robot’s native, potentially black-box, low-level controller for execution in the real world.

The approaches reviewed above highlight a fundamental trade-off in sim-to-real transfer. End-to-end RL systems for ZSG are predicated on minimizing the reality gap a priori , either by investing in robot-specific system identification [ 20 ] or by abstracting away complex dynamics [ 10 ]. Both strategies can be brittle. The former is sensitive to any unmodeled dynamics or changes in the physical robot over time, while the latter is limited by the expressive capacity of the abstracted action space [ 10 ].

In contrast, our proposed method acknowledges the inherent imperfections of any simulator. It adopts a hybrid, few-shot sim-to-real strategy that is more robust and flexible. By first leveraging domain randomization, it learns a generalized feature representation that is not overfitted to a single simulation instance. Subsequently, it performs a highly efficient, model-centric adaptation by fine-tuning a pre-trained variational autoencoder using a small batch of unlabeled real images.

A third and rapidly emerging pathway to generalization in robotics is through the use of large-scale, pre-trained foundation models. Models such as RT-2 [ 39 ] derive their remarkable generalization capabilities not from mastering simulation physics, but from being pre-trained on vast, internet-scale datasets of real-world images and text. This allows them to acquire a broad semantic understanding of objects, concepts, and actions, enabling impressive zero-shot and few-shot performance on a wide range of manipulation and navigation tasks. However, this approach introduces a critical trade-off. While foundation models excel at open-vocabulary reasoning, they are computationally massive, with memory and processing requirements that are prohibitive for the low-cost, resource-constrained robotic platforms [ 39 ] that are the focus of our research.

## 2.4 Real-World Autonomous Navigation Systems

Recent research in autonomous navigation has yielded a diverse array of specialized solutions, each tailored to specific application domains and operational constraints. In the automotive sector, studies range from the development of robust fuzzy logic controllers for enhancing electric vehicle stability and power quality [ 40 ] to the design of neural networks for the semantic segmentation of radar point clouds [ 41 ].

Biologically-inspired methods have also gained prominence in robotics research. Aljalbout et al. [ 42 ], for instance, developed a generalizable framework using spiking neural networks to instantiate central pattern generators for legged locomotion across different robot morphologies with minimal design effort. More aligned with our focus on mobile robots, Chen et al. [ 43 ] proposed the Cuckoo-Beetle Swarm Search (CBSS) algorithm for path planning [ 24 ] in heterogeneous robot teams. Their bio-inspired optimization method developed a navigation system for obstacle avoidance in indoor environments.

Consistent with the methodology of this study, Chen et al. first validated their system in simulation before deploying it on real Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs). However, a key distinction lies in the sensor modality; their method relied on a Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) sensor [ 44 ] for environmental perception. While LiDAR provides high-precision depth information, its associated cost and weight can be prohibitive for the low-cost platforms central to our research.

More closely aligned with our work’s emphasis on minimalist sensing, Othman and Rad [ 45 ] presented a visual system belonging to an end-to-end navigation strategy for behavior-based robots [ 46 ], focusing on doorway detection using only monocular RGB camera input. Their approach employed a convolutional neural network to classify scenes as containing an open door or not, guiding navigation through depth estimation and obstacle detection modules. The system was validated on a NAO humanoid robot, using a single camera to demonstrate the potential of minimal sensor configurations for executing complex navigation subtasks.

2026-10-06.title: Inspect Robots: Evaluating the Capabilities and Safety of Embodied AI
2026-10-06.authors: Christopher Leet , Achu Menon , Sravanthi Machcha , Sabrina Zou , Aayushya Patel , Aditya Kumar Singh , Anish Kr Singh , Galaba Vamsi , Javin Ahuja , Sai Asish Yamani , Tushar Anand , Vedang Alle , Zihan Jack Zhang , Tzu Kit Chan , Jay Chooi
2026-10-06.comment: Submitted to The Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS) Workshop at CoRL 2026
2026-10-06.abstract: General purpose language models are increasingly able to control robotic hardware. Understanding the capabilities and safety of these models when embodied is therefore increasingly important for understanding their societal impact and risks. To this end, we introduce Inspect Robots, a modular, open-source framework for developing and running evaluations of embodied agents. Inspect Robots pairs customizable, reusable abstractions for specifying physical evaluations and analyzing their results with infrastructure that automates evaluation setup, execution and termination. We demonstrate Inspect Robots by using it to evaluate the capabilities and safety of six policies based on frontier language models. Inspect Robots has seen significant early uptake, receiving nearly 100,000 downloads in the three months since its release.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Recent work has shown that embodied multimodal language models are increasingly able to carry out physical tasks without task specific training [ 6 , 13 ] . These models have successfully performed challenging manipulation tasks such as dice reorientation, throwing fruit, and towel folding [ 4 ] . As models increasingly interact directly with the physical world, understanding their capabilities and behavior on real robots will be crucial for understanding their potential impact and risks.

We argue that an evaluation framework for physical AI should have the following two properties. First, it should be explicitly designed to support both capabilities and safety evaluations. Prior work has shown that behavioral training can fail to generalize to different contexts [ 11 , 1 ] . Today, most safety training and testing takes place in virtual environments. There is therefore a need for frameworks that can help researchers study model behavior in real world settings. Second, as models generalize to new real world (and likely non-traditional) tasks, researchers will need to rapidly develop evaluations that measure their capabilities and associated risks in those settings. Evaluation frameworks should support this process by enabling code reuse across the evaluation stack.

Recent frameworks already provide a significant amount of reusable infrastructure for evaluating embodied agents. RoboDojo [ 2 ] , for example, provides a flexible platform for benchmarking general robot manipulation capabilities, while XPolicyLab [ 12 ] provides a standardized way to connect policies. In this paper, we introduce Inspect Robots, a framework which complements existing systems by emphasizing end-to-end code reuse and support for safety evaluation. Inspect Robots exposes standardized interfaces across the entire evaluation stack, from task specification to policy integration, to execution, recording and analysis, allowing researchers to reuse as many tested components as possible when prototyping new physical evaluations. These interfaces are structured around expressive, extensible abstractions designed to support a wide range of safety evaluations.

We demonstrate Inspect Robots by using it to evaluate policies built on top of frontier language models on two mini benchmarks: a 4 task capabilities mini-benchmark drawn from RoboDojo [ 2 ] , and a 4 task safety mini-benchmark drawn from RoboHarm, a safety benchmark for embodied AI [ 9 ] . Inspect Robots’ library of reusable components allowed each benchmark to be set up and run with an initial model in under two days. Once implemented, its automated evaluation infrastructure allowed each additional model to be evaluated in just 3–8 hours, depending on model latency. Inspect Robots has seen significant early uptake, receiving nearly 100,000 downloads in the three months since its release [ 8 ] .
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Evaluating General Purpose Agents. Many frameworks [ 7 ] have been proposed for evaluating general purpose, tool using agents in virtual environments. Among those emphasizing modularity and extensibility are Inspect AI [ 10 ] and the BrowserGym ecosystem [ 5 ] . Inspect AI provides reusable abstractions for specifying tasks, tools and scoring mechanisms together with logs for recording agent execution. BrowserGym defines common interfaces for a variety of web benchmarks and pairs them with a framework for running and analyzing evaluations. Inspect Robots extends this approach to physical robotics. It provides researchers with a modular, extensible framework for evaluating embodied general purpose agents in real world environments.

Evaluation Frameworks for Physical AI. There is a growing body of reusable infrastructure for evaluating physical AI. AutoEval [ 14 ] automates policy evaluation by combining policy execution with automatic success detection and scene resets, allowing physical trials to run with minimal human intervention. RoboDojo [ 2 ] provides a slate of standardized manipulation benchmarks along with infrastructure for simulated and physical evaluation. XPolicyLab [ 12 ] provides standardized interfaces for connecting policies to evaluation environments, allowing policy integrations to be reused across different benchmarks and embodiments. Inspect Robots complements these approaches by providing reusable interfaces across the entire evaluation workflow, allowing researchers to reuse tested code wherever possible. Its abstractions are explicitly designed to support safety as well as capability evaluation.

2026-10-06.title: GAMBIT: Learning to Plan Continuous Multi-Robot Trajectories
2026-10-06.authors: Rishabh Jain , Akmaral Moldagalieva , Lorenzo Magnino , Michael Amir , Keisuke Okumura , Ajay Shankar , Wolfgang Hönig , Amanda Prorok
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)
2026-10-06.abstract:
GAMBIT is an opening chess move in which a player sacrifices a piece, typically a pawn, to gain a positional advantage later in the game.
Analogously, in multi-robot coordination, individual robots may need to forgo locally reward-maximising behaviours to improve overall team performance.
Such self-sacrificial behaviours are difficult to capture with manually designed heuristics, particularly in dense, interaction-rich environments.
Focusing on double-integrator continuous dynamics, this work studies how to learn such coordinated heuristics over motion primitives for multi-robot trajectory execution.
Our framework, GAMBIT , first learns coordinated motion-primitive selection through imitation learning and subsequently fine-tunes the policy through reinforcement learning.
We further introduce a safeguarded rollout mechanism with backup trajectories that guarantees collision-free execution at all times.
Experiments demonstrate that GAMBIT substantially outperforms a range of baselines, including centralised motion planners and decentralised reactive planners, while exhibiting strong scalability.
In particular, it coordinates over a thousand robots with planning latency below a few hundred milliseconds in continuous domains.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Generating trajectory plans using motion primitives has been a successful paradigm for deriving potentially long-horizon, feasible motions to steer a robot—with applications ranging from autonomous driving to manoeuvres of aerial robots [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
While its multi-robot counterpart has also been studied [ 4 , 5 ] , a critical challenge in achieving fast and scalable planning remains the design of effective heuristics that evaluate how “good” each primitive is.
Designing such a heuristic is challenging even in the single-robot case, as accurate cost-to-go estimates become difficult to obtain for higher-order dynamics beyond simple point-mass models; the multi-robot case further requires reasoning about coordination among agents.
One could design a trivial heuristic based on an interaction-agnostic single-robot heuristic, but such approximations can get significantly distorted in interaction-rich multi-agent environments, where effective coordination may require non-greedy motions, such as temporarily moving away from the goal to accommodate other agents.

Using naïve or inaccurate heuristics for motion primitives can misguide the planning process, resulting in either considerable computational effort or highly suboptimal robot trajectories.
Manually capturing such coordination requires substantial engineering effort that scales poorly with the complexity of interactions.
This makes automatically learning these heuristics particularly attractive.
This study investigates how to realise this idea.

Learning agent-wise heuristics to synthesise coordination has proven effective in the discrete-state, grid-world multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) domain [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] , where the objective is to find conflict-free paths for multiple agents on a four-connected grid.
Recent work has developed high-performing heuristics using decentralised neural MAPF policies [ 9 ] , where each agent receives an observation and outputs an action distribution, trained using either reinforcement learning (RL) or imitation learning (IL) from expert data.
A natural question then arises: can we effectively transfer this knowledge to continuous state spaces?

With some adaptation, this transfer appears possible using action synthesis based on motion primitives;
however, the transition to continuous state spaces introduces fundamental challenges.
In the context of IL, acquiring a substantial amount of expert data for scenarios involving many agents is considerably more difficult than in MAPF,
where established and reliable planners are readily available [ 10 ] ,
a challenge we hereinafter refer to as data scarcity .
The multi-modality of solutions poses another challenge: trajectories belonging to different homotopy classes can have comparable costs, making it difficult to assign a unique target action to imitate.
The safeguarding gap in rollouts—i.e., the lack of mechanisms that clamp collision-causing actions and facilitate learning in strong neural MAPF policies [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] —weakens the reward signal, making training more difficult, particularly for RL.
Along with difficulties in scenario generation for providing informative training signals, these challenges collectively make it difficult to design advanced heuristics for multi-robot motion primitives.

We address these challenges with a framework we term GAMBIT : G raph- A ttentive M otion primitives with B ackup for I nteractive T rajectories .
Following the success of neural MAPF policies, our backbone architecture is based on a graph neural network (GNN) that outputs a categorical action distribution [ 14 , 8 ] , exploiting geometric locality to enable training on small-scale instances and deployment to larger teams.
The model is first pretrained via IL on instances with a small number of agents, using solutions generated by a centralised kinodynamic multi-robot motion planner [ 5 ] , as sufficient data are attainable at this scale to overcome data scarcity .
The model is then fine-tuned via RL to mitigate the multi-modality problem by biasing the policy towards consistent action choices.
RL training uses newly developed safety-preserving rollouts with backup trajectories that overcome the safeguarding gap and stabilise the learning process.
Effective learning is further facilitated by carefully designed scenario generation that ensures agent interactions in every training instance. Figure 1 illustrates this pipeline.

The resulting GAMBIT policy, combined with motion primitives and our specialised rollout, synthesises safe continuous actions for hundreds of robots at sub-hundred-millisecond latency, while producing substantially better-coordinated trajectories in densely populated environments than reactive planners [ 15 , 16 ] , computationally intensive centralised planners [ 17 , 5 ] , and existing learning-based approaches [ 18 ] .
We further validate GAMBIT through a physical deployment of eight multirotors [ 19 ] with closed-loop control.
Across both simulated and real-robot deployments, our backup mechanism guarantees safe and feasible execution at all times.

As a motion-primitive heuristic constitutes a lightweight and modular planning component, we view GAMBIT as a promising building block for designing capable planners beyond what we present here.
Furthermore, as policy rollout relies only on local interactions between robots, this scheme is also amenable to decentralised deployment.
In what follows, we present the problem formulation, training pipeline, safeguarding rollout, and experimental evaluation, in order.

Herein, we use ‘agent’ and ‘robot’ interchangeably.

## II-B Planning with Motion Primitives

A common approach to deriving such control sequences is via numerical optimisation, e.g., formulating trajectory optimisation as a non-linear program subject to dynamics and model constraints over a continuous control space, and solving it in a potentially decentralised manner [ 16 , 21 ] .
In contrast, this work follows a planning approach based on motion primitives, which restricts the infinitely many possible controls to a finite set, thus facilitating rapid discovery of coordinated actions.
Motion primitives have been explored for multi-robot navigation [ 22 , 23 , 5 ] , demonstrating their potential for computationally efficient coordination, but they typically rely on manually designed mechanisms for selecting the right primitive. Our primary objective is to automate this selection process through learning. Accordingly, we distinguish GAMBIT from learning-based multi-agent control approaches that directly output continuous controls (e.g., [ 24 , 25 ] ); instead, we formulate the learning problem as one of ranking the available primitives, making the learned heuristic naturally compatible with numerous global search-based planning methods.
Meanwhile, we also provide a safeguarded rollout scheme with motion primitives tailored to double integrator dynamics, demonstrating how the learned heuristic can be integrated into a practical deployment framework.

We define a motion primitive as a finite sequence of control inputs m = [ 𝒖 0 , 𝒖 1 , … , 𝒖 l − 1 ] m=[\bm{u}^{0},\bm{u}^{1},\ldots,\bm{u}^{l-1}] .
When applied to an initial robot state 𝒙 0 \bm{x}^{0} , a motion primitive induces a rollout state trajectory [ 𝒙 0 , 𝒙 1 , … , 𝒙 l ] [\bm{x}^{0},\bm{x}^{1},\ldots,\bm{x}^{l}] .
In this study, for simplicity, we set l = 1 l=1 ; i.e., each primitive represents a single acceleration command 𝒂 ∈ ℝ d \bm{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , although the proposed framework can be extended to larger values of l l .
We denote the set of available motion primitives by M M .
Our objective is then to learn a ranking function that ranks the primitives m ∈ M m\in M for robot i i given the current configuration Q Q ;
we interchangeably refer to this function as a heuristic , as it virtually assesses the quality of each motion primitive.

While learning for motion-primitive-based planning has been studied in single-robot settings [ 26 , 27 ] , our primary interest lies in multi-robot systems, which present challenges that stem from the interplay between agents.

## II-C Neural MAPF Policies

Learning heuristics for multi-agent action selection has been studied extensively in the context of grid-world MAPF [ 9 ] , under highly simplified discrete dynamics.
Typically, this line of work aims to design a policy that receives a local observation o i o_{i} for agent i i and outputs a distribution over five discrete actions: NORTH , WEST , SOUTH , EAST , and STAY .
To obtain effective policies, established learning pipelines use either imitation learning (IL) or reinforcement learning (RL) [ 28 , 14 ] .
We aim to leverage these insights beyond grid-world dynamics; however, several challenges hinder their direct adaptation to our setting, as highlighted in Sec. I ; that is, data scarcity , multi-modality , safeguarding gap , and scenario generation .
Below, we provide our GAMBIT approach to address these.

2026-10-06.title: Future Anchored Verification and Online Recovery for World Action Models
2026-10-06.authors: Zhibin Qin , Zhenxiong Tan , Xinchao Wang
2026-10-06.abstract:
World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic manipulation. They act by first predicting how a task should be performed and then decoding the actions from that future. However, the remaining actions are invalid once execution drifts from the prediction. Simply replanning from the already out of distribution state rarely restores what the task still requires; existing execution monitors decide when to stop, but not what to restore. We observe that the answer is already in hand: the future the WAM predicted before acting depicts exactly the states it intended to pass through. We introduce FAVOR ( F uture A nchored V erification and O nline R ecovery), a lightweight framework that keeps these predicted frames as anchors and uses them for verification and recovery. An Anchor Verifier compares each observation with its anchor, together with the executed actions, to flag deviations that break the task.
Anchor-Guided Recovery uses a vision-language model to turn the flagged anchor into a short corrective instruction. Under strengthened instruction guidance, the WAM executes this instruction to return to the intended future. It then resumes the task. FAVOR raises the task success of the base WAM from 97.85% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 72.60% to 72.98% on LIBERO-Plus without modifying the policy.
2026-10-06.introduction:
World action models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robotic
manipulation. They work in a forward and backward way: they first predict the visual future a task should pass through and then decode the actions that realize the future [ Du et al., 2023a ; Tian et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024b ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026b ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026a ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ] . Unlike policies that map current observations and task instruction directly to actions [ Chi et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ] , every action is thus grounded in an explicit future of where the scene should go.

That future is only a plan. Imprecise actions or external disturbances can push the scene off the predicted path, invalidating the remaining actions [ Li et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026b ] . Simply replanning from the deviated state, however, offers little help: WAMs are trained on successful demonstrations [ Ross et al., 2011 ; Laskey et al., 2017 ; Reichlin et al., 2022 ] , so neither the future predicted from such an unfamiliar state nor the actions decoded from it can be trusted. Execution monitors for WAMs help by flagging when the remaining actions should no longer be trusted [ Wang et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Agia et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ] , but say nothing about what to restore. Recovery methods address this gap, but obtain their target from outside the policy [ Dai et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2026 ] . This raises a natural question: can a WAM tell when execution has left its plan, and find its way back on its own?

Our observation is that the target of recovery is already in the policy’s hands. The future the WAM predicted depicts the states it intended to pass through, and the actions were generated under its guidance, so the actions remain valid exactly as long as the scene follows it. When a deviation occurs, this prediction still shows the condition that was lost, such as a mug held in the gripper, and that state lies in the region where the policy was trained. A deviation therefore invalidates the remaining actions, but not the states they were meant to establish. This suggests a simple principle: use the policy’s own predicted future as an anchor.

Following this principle, we propose FAVOR ( F uture A nchored V erification and O nline R ecovery), which keeps the predicted frames as anchors and uses them both to verify execution and to guide recovery. Two challenges stand in the way. (1) Not every mismatch is a deviation: the anchor is an image produced by a generative model and may contain visual artifacts, so pixel-level differences do not necessarily imply a semantic mismatch. (2) The challenge is to convey the anchor to the policy and elicit the intended correction: the anchor is an image, whereas a WAM accepts only an observation and an instruction. Moreover, it leans on visual context and largely ignores the instruction: with the observation fixed, the original and the empty instruction yield nearly identical attention maps (Figure 1 ). The anchor must therefore be conveyed through a corrective instruction, and the influence of that instruction must be strengthened to elicit the intended correction.

For challenge (1), we introduce the Anchor Verifier , which compares each observation with its anchor together with the executed actions and tracks the mismatch along the chunk. It thus responds to deviations that break the task rather than to any visual difference.

For challenge (2), we introduce Anchor-Guided Recovery to return the scene to a state the policy knows how to continue from. It hands the alarmed anchor, the current observation, and the task to a vision-language model, which issues one short instruction naming the condition to restore rather than the pixels to reproduce. The frozen WAM then executes it under strengthened instruction guidance to reach the intended future before deviation.

We evaluate FAVOR on LIBERO [ Liu et al., 2023a ] and LIBERO-Plus [ Fei et al., 2025 ] . FAVOR raises the task success of the base WAM from 97.85% to 98.10% on LIBERO and from 72.60% to 72.98% on LIBERO-Plus. The Anchor Verifier separates failed from successful episodes with an AUROC of 0.992, above distance-based and learned detectors [ Gu et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ] .

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

A future-anchored view of WAM execution: the future predicted before acting serves not only as a reference for verifying execution but also as the target that recovery should restore.

The Anchor Verifier, which grounds execution verification in the WAM’s own predicted future and executed actions, identifying when the scene no longer supports continuation.

The Anchor-Guided Recovery, which translates the alarmed anchor into a corrective instruction and strengthens instruction guidance, enabling a WAM to use its own predicted future as a recovery goal and return to a state from which the original task can continue.
