# II Related Work

## II-A Co-Speech Gesture Generation for Embodied Agents

Co-speech gesture generation has progressed from manually specified behavior rules to data-driven motion synthesis [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . Yoon et al. learned a mapping from speech transcripts to gesture sequences and demonstrated real-time execution on a NAO robot [ 6 ] . Gesticulator subsequently combined semantic and acoustic speech representations to generate joint rotations that capture both content-related and rhythmic gestures [ 2 ] . Other approaches incorporate speaker identity and multimodal speech context to model individual gesturing styles [ 22 ] , or represent motion using discrete gesture tokens to better capture the one-to-many relationship between speech and movement [ 23 ] . Context-aware systems have further conditioned robot gestures on nonverbal cues from an interaction partner [ 24 ] . Although these methods improve the appropriateness, diversity, and responsiveness of generated motion, they primarily focus on the articulated body and commonly treat facial behavior as a separate component.

## II-B Facial and Holistic Animation

Speech-driven facial animation has traditionally focused on accurate articulation and plausible full-face motion. MeshTalk separates audio-correlated articulation from weakly correlated behavior such as blinks and eyebrow movements [ 10 ] , while FaceFormer exploits long-range speech context through autoregressive attention [ 9 ] . CodeTalker instead maps speech to a learned discrete motion prior to alleviate the over-smoothing associated with direct motion regression [ 11 ] .
Recent work has further advanced speech-driven facial animation toward greater photorealism, expressiveness, and real-time performance. SyncTalk combines explicit synchronization control with neural radiance-field rendering to improve the alignment of speech, lip motion, facial expression, and head pose [ 25 ] . EMO adopts direct audio-to-video diffusion without relying on intermediate 3D models or facial landmarks [ 26 ] , while FLOAT performs flow matching in a learned motion latent space for expressive and temporally consistent portrait animation [ 27 ] . Teller supports real-time streaming generation through autoregressive motion modeling [ 28 ] . SoulX-FlashHead and LiveAvatar further enable long-duration facial animation from streaming audio [ 7 , 8 ] .
Although these methods produce high-quality facial motion, they do not address its coordination with actions executed by a separately embodied physical robot.

## II-C Multimodal Expressive Behavior for Social Robots

The coordination of verbal and nonverbal behavior has a long history in embodied-agent systems. BEAT transforms linguistic input into synchronized speech, gaze, facial displays, and gestures using explicit behavioral rules [ 1 ] . For hybrid physical-digital embodiments, Gomez et al. coordinate Haru’s mechanical motion and digital displays through animator-authored multimodal expressions [ 13 ] . More recent systems use language models to reduce manual behavior authoring. FurChat combines LLM-generated dialogue with facial expressions on the Furhat robot [ 12 ] , while Expressive Furhat generates context-dependent facial gestures and gaze behavior in real time [ 29 ] . On Haru, Wang et al. use conversational and affective cues to select expressive speech styles and pre-authored physical behaviors [ 4 ] .

LLMs have also been used to generate robot behavior more directly. GenEM translates natural-language descriptions of social behavior into parameterized control programs composed from available robot skills [ 30 ] . Galatolo and Winkle attach robot-specific behavior heads to a language model, enabling simultaneous generation of text and high-level communicative intentions that are mapped to facial expressions on Furhat or bodily gestures on Pepper [ 31 ] . Most closely related, Nichols et al. generate synchronized timelines for vocal, facial, and bodily expression on the Haru robot from a shared semantic analysis of dialogue [ 32 ] . Building on these complementary directions, our work considers a hybrid embodiment in which robot actions and digital facial animation are generated as composable outputs of a shared agent. Our focus is on preserving semantic and temporal coherence between the two channels while satisfying the distinct execution requirements of physical actuation and facial rendering.

2026-10-06.title: Robotizing Human Videos with Physically Consistent Interactions
2026-10-06.authors: Ching-Lam Cheng , Shengfeng He , Bin Zhu
2026-10-06.abstract:
Human videos offer scalable manipulation data, but the embodiment gap between human hands and robot manipulators limits their direct use. Existing video-editing methods replace hands with rendered robots, yet inaccurate interaction reconstruction and compositing can produce inconsistent grasps and implausible robot–object occlusions. We address these failures from two complementary physical aspects: interaction geometry and scene visibility. First, an interaction-aware contact reconstruction module combines hand–object segmentation with mesh-level contact prediction to recover dense 3D contacts, then converts them into temporally stabilized grasps for parallel-jaw grippers. Second, a depth-aware compositing module uses scene and robot depth to enforce physically consistent robot–object occlusions. The resulting videos preserve the interaction structure of human demonstrations in a robot-compatible form and are co-trained with robot demonstrations. Using identical human videos and robot data, we compare against robot-only training and the original Masquerade pipeline. Across four RoboTwin tasks and two Diffusion Policy visual encoders, our method achieves the highest average success rates, with especially strong gains under out-of-distribution scene variation.
Real-world deployment further shows that the proposed co-training approach improves robustness to visual distractors when the task geometry is observable, while performance on depth-sensitive grasps remains limited by the single-camera setup.
2026-10-06.introduction:
The advancement in robot learning has increasingly benefited from large and diverse demonstration datasets [ 2 , 3 ] . However, collecting robot demonstrations at scale remains fundamentally expensive because each trajectory requires physical hardware, environment interaction, and often human teleoperation or supervision [ 4 , 5 ] . Consequently, robot datasets remain far smaller and less diverse than the image, text, and video corpora that have driven progress in large language models [ 6 , 7 ] and video generation models [ 8 ] . This data bottleneck limits the diversity of interactions available during training and, in turn, the ability of manipulation policies to generalize across objects, tasks, and environments.

Human videos offer a compelling alternative source of manipulation experience. Large-scale egocentric video collections [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] capture everyday interactions across diverse objects, scenes, and behaviors at a scale that is difficult to reproduce with physical robots. In principle, these videos could provide robot policies with substantially broader manipulation experience. In practice, however, human demonstrations differ fundamentally from robot demonstrations [ 12 , 13 ] . Human hands differ from robot manipulators in appearance, kinematics, and contact mechanisms, while human videos typically lack robot-compatible action labels. This embodiment gap prevents conventional robot learning pipelines from directly treating human videos as robot demonstrations.

Recent work has begun to bridge this gap by converting human demonstrations into robot-compatible visual data [ 12 , 13 ] . In particular, Phantom [ 14 ] and Masquerade [ 1 ] introduce a video-editing paradigm that reconstructs human hand motion from egocentric video, removes the human hand through inpainting, and renders a robot manipulator along the recovered trajectory, as shown in the middle of Fig. . The resulting robotized videos reduce the visual embodiment discrepancy and can be incorporated into robot policy training. This offers a promising route for scaling robot learning with abundant human video.

However, successful human-to-robot conversion requires more than replacing the visual embodiment. A manipulation demonstration is informative because it encodes a physically coherent interaction between the agent, object, and scene. If the conversion process alters this interaction structure, the edited video may look robot-like while providing inconsistent supervision. This issue is particularly important because human-to-robot editing is a multi-stage process in which errors from hand reconstruction, grasp retargeting, and scene compositing can accumulate. For example, retargeting a robot gripper from hand pose or motion alone does not explicitly preserve where the human contacts the object, and can therefore produce a gripper pose that is kinematically plausible but inconsistent with the demonstrated grasp. Likewise, naively overlaying a rendered robot onto the edited scene ignores scene geometry and can place gripper pixels in front of object regions that should physically occlude them. Such artifacts create disagreement between robot motion, object interaction, and visual evidence, weakening the value of the converted video as policy supervision. We therefore argue that the key challenge is not only to reduce the appearance gap between humans and robots, but also to preserve the physical consistency of the demonstrated interaction.

To this end, we propose an interaction-faithful human-to-robot video-editing pipeline that addresses physical consistency from two complementary aspects: interaction geometry and scene visibility . First, we explicitly reconstruct hand–object contact rather than deriving the robot grasp from hand motion alone. Our interaction-aware contact reconstruction combines hand–object segmentation with mesh-level contact prediction to recover dense 3D contact regions on the human hand. We then reduce these contacts to a temporally stabilized thumb–opposing-finger contact pair that can be naturally mapped to a parallel-jaw gripper. Surface-normal constraints further favor contact pairs that correspond to geometrically plausible opposing grasp surfaces. This formulation grounds robot retargeting in the demonstrated hand–object interaction itself, rather than only in the reconstructed hand configuration. Second, we introduce depth-aware robot–scene compositing to preserve physically correct visibility. By comparing the predicted depth of the hand-inpainted scene with the rendered robot depth, we identify gripper regions that should lie behind the manipulated object and remove them from the final composite. Together, as shown in the right of Fig. , these components preserve both where the robot should interact with the object and how that interaction should appear in the scene.

We evaluate the resulting robotized demonstrations by co-training manipulation policies with real robot demonstrations. Using the same source human videos and robot training data, we compare our pipeline against robot-only training and the original Masquerade editing pipeline. Experiments span four RoboTwin manipulation tasks and two visual encoders within Diffusion Policy. Our edited demonstrations consistently improve policy performance, achieving the highest average success rates across settings. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution scene variation, suggesting that physically consistent human-video supervision provides useful interaction cues beyond the visual conditions observed in the robot training data.
We further validate the approach on a physical robot, where it improves robustness to visual distractors for tasks with sufficiently observable interaction geometry. Results on a depth-sensitive grasp also reveal the limitations imposed by ambiguous geometric cues in a single-camera setup.

Our main contributions are:

We identify interaction consistency as a key requirement for converting human videos into reliable robot-learning supervision.

We introduce interaction-aware contact reconstruction that recovers dense 3D hand–object contacts and retargets them into stable, geometrically plausible parallel-jaw grasps.

We propose depth-aware compositing that preserves physically consistent robot–object occlusions in edited videos.

We show across four RoboTwin tasks, two Diffusion Policy visual encoders, and real-robot experiments that our edited demonstrations improve average performance and robustness to out-of-distribution scene variation.

1. We identify interaction consistency as a key requirement for converting human videos into reliable robot-learning supervision.

2. We introduce interaction-aware contact reconstruction that recovers dense 3D hand–object contacts and retargets them into stable, geometrically plausible parallel-jaw grasps.

3. We propose depth-aware compositing that preserves physically consistent robot–object occlusions in edited videos.

4. We show across four RoboTwin tasks, two Diffusion Policy visual encoders, and real-robot experiments that our edited demonstrations improve average performance and robustness to out-of-distribution scene variation.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

Learning from egocentric human video. Egocentric video offers a scalable source of human manipulation experience from a viewpoint closely aligned with robot observations. Large-scale datasets such as EPIC-KITCHENS [ 9 ] , HD-EPIC [ 11 ] , and EgoVerse [ 10 ] capture diverse everyday interactions across objects, tasks, and environments. Despite this scale and diversity, directly using such videos for robot learning remains difficult because they depict human hands rather than robot manipulators and generally lack robot-compatible action labels, creating both embodiment and action-space gaps.
Several works address these gaps by incorporating human demonstrations directly into robot policy learning. EgoMimic [ 15 ] tracks human hand motion and aligns egocentric human demonstrations with robot data for joint imitation learning. EgoVLA [ 12 ] leverages egocentric human video as supervision for vision–language–action models, while EgoScale [ 13 ] studies how diverse egocentric data can scale dexterous manipulation learning. These approaches demonstrate that human videos can complement expensive robot-collected trajectories, but require learning mechanisms that explicitly accommodate the mismatch between human and robot embodiments.

Human-to-robot video editing. A complementary line of work addresses the embodiment gap at the data level by converting human videos into robotized demonstrations before policy training. Phantom [ 14 ] explores learning robot manipulation from human videos without requiring robot demonstrations. Masquerade [ 1 ] reconstructs human hand motion, removes the human hand through video inpainting, and renders a target robot along the recovered trajectory. The resulting videos visually resemble robot demonstrations and can be co-trained with conventional robot data, providing a direct way to reuse human manipulation experience within standard robot-learning pipelines.
Our work follows this data-editing and co-training paradigm, but focuses on a complementary problem: whether the converted video preserves the physical interaction encoded in the original demonstration. Existing editing pipelines primarily bridge the visual embodiment gap, while errors in grasp retargeting and scene compositing can still produce robotized demonstrations with inconsistent interaction geometry or visibility. We address these limitations from two complementary aspects. First, we incorporate explicit hand–object contact geometry when retargeting human grasps to robot grippers. Second, we use depth-based occlusion reasoning when compositing the rendered robot into the scene. Together, these components improve both the physical interaction and its visual consistency, producing more faithful robot-learning supervision from the same egocentric source videos.

2026-10-06.title: I-BFM: Reward-Conditioned Robust Humanoid Interaction via Unsupervised Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-06.authors: Ziqi Han , Yitang Li , Junhan Sun , Fanrong Dong , Yaojie Shen , Lei Ye , Zetong Jing , Yongqi Zhang , Yiming Zhang , Xue Wang , Hao Zhao
2026-10-06.comment: including appendix
2026-10-06.abstract: Behavioral foundation models (BFMs) have recently shown that a single humanoid policy can support diverse whole-body control, but extending such generality to physical interaction remains challenging. We introduce I-BFM , to our knowledge the first BFM for humanoid–object interaction. Rather than relying on task-specific policies or reference tracking, I-BFM learns a shared representation of the coupled dynamics among the humanoid, objects, and their contacts using forward-backward representations and unsupervised reinforcement learning. Given a downstream task reward, the same policy can be directly conditioned on a latent command to execute closed-loop interaction without task-specific policy optimization. To improve interaction control over different time scales, we further train the policy with both short-horizon interaction targets and longer-horizon goal targets. A single I-BFM policy performs carrying, pushing, and kicking, while also supporting goal reaching, motion tracking, stylistic control, and long-horizon task chaining. More importantly, it remains effective after large deviations from nominal execution: on Carry, I-BFM achieves 94.3% nominal success and retains 89.3% success after robot falls, compared with 1.3% for a planning-based baseline. Real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 further demonstrate diverse loco-manipulation behaviors, rapid recovery from interaction failures and external disturbances, and task chaining without task-specific retraining.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Humanoid robots are envisioned as general-purpose agents capable of performing diverse tasks across different environments. Beyond locomotion, physical interaction with objects is an indispensable capability for realizing this vision. A truly general-purpose humanoid should not only move robustly, but also perform diverse interaction behaviors and effectively recover from unexpected failures during long-horizon tasks.

Recent whole-body foundation models (BFMs) have demonstrated strong generality and robustness in humanoid motion [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . However, extending these capabilities to physical interaction remains challenging. Existing approaches often rely on open-loop teleoperation and behavior cloning, which are difficult to scale and provide limited failure recovery.

Another line of work focuses on humanoid-object co-tracking, where MoCap HOI trajectories are directly used as supervision. While these methods achieve high-quality interaction behaviors, they heavily rely on dense references and are inherently inflexible [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Some approaches introduce planners [ 7 ] to generate intermediate references for the tracker. However, planners introduce additional latency, especially after interaction failures, and constrain behavioral diversity to their predefined rules. More recently, style-learning-based approaches have shown some task-specific generalization, such as transporting boxes between arbitrary configurations, but remain insufficiently general and robust for long-horizon interaction.

These limitations raise a fundamental question: Can we endow a general-purpose humanoid controller with interaction capabilities while preserving its generality and robustness? Our key observation is that these desired properties—including generality, robustness and flexible behavior invocation—already emerge naturally in BFMs trained with forward-backward (FB) representations and unsupervised reinforcement learning (URL) [ 1 ] . FB learning enables a single learned representation to specify and retrieve
diverse behaviors through simple reward functions, making it well suited for
a range of interactive objectives. Meanwhile, URL optimizes for the FB objective rather than motion imitation, allowing the policy to prioritize task completion and recovery, and to deviate from reference motions when necessary. These properties motivate us to extend the same paradigm from general-purpose motion to physical interaction.

Based on this insight, we propose I-BFM , which learns a unified, Interactive Behavioral Foundation Model through unsupervised RL with an FB representation.
It jointly embeds the humanoid’s basic skills and interactive skills into a structured latent interaction space.
In interactive scenarios, the learned representation captures the coupled dynamics of the humanoid and objects, together with changes in their contact relationships.
By specifying simple high-level rewards, I-BFM can invoke and compose diverse interactive behaviors, allowing the humanoid to perform skills such as carrying, pushing, and kicking objects, while quickly recovering from disturbances and interaction failures.
Specifically, our Local–Goal Objective Geometry Operator (LOGO) uses metric-conditioned local and goal intents with residual actor regularization to improve controllability and robustness.

I-BFM consistently improves task success, object-placement accuracy, and disturbance recovery, while supporting skill chaining and controllable interaction styles. Real-world experiments further demonstrate diverse, robust interactions and rapid failure recovery (Fig. ). These results suggest that humanoid interaction can be learned as a reusable, object-centric, reward-addressable latent space rather than task-specific controllers or fixed motion plans. Our contributions are:

We introduce I-BFM , the first framework for building a promptable interactive BFM for general-purpose humanoid interaction. Using FB representations and URL, I-BFM enables zero-shot execution of diverse interactive behaviors through a simple reward interface.

We introduce I-BFM , the first framework for building a promptable interactive BFM for general-purpose humanoid interaction. Using FB representations and URL, I-BFM enables zero-shot execution of diverse interactive behaviors through a simple reward interface.

We incorporate object-contact information into the interaction state and LOGO as a local–goal metric-conditioned residual actor objective, improving controllability and robustness for humanoid-object interaction.

We demonstrate robust real-world humanoid behaviors with I-BFM , including carrying, pushing, kicking, long-horizon behavior chaining, and recovery from large disturbances, interaction failures, and falls.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Behavioral Foundation Models for Whole-body Control.

Learning-based whole-body controllers have shown that motion priors can provide reusable control skills for humanoids, supporting diverse motion tracking and command-conditioned behaviors. Recent systems have further transferred these capabilities to real humanoids for whole-body tracking, teleoperation, and data collection [ 8 , 3 , 9 ] . SONIC [ 2 ] further illustrates the potential of scaling motion tracking and synthesis to broad humanoid behaviors. Building on this foundation, behavioral foundation models (BFMs) [ 10 , 1 , 11 ] , seek a more scalable objective: learning a single general-purpose policy from large and diverse motion corpora that can be flexibly steered by latent behaviors, goals, or rewards. However, current BFMs remain largely body-centric, modeling humanoid motion without explicitly capturing objects and contact dynamics. In contrast, I-BFM incorporates object and contact states, extending whole-body priors to persistent physical interaction.

## II-B Humanoid–Object Interaction.

Existing humanoid–object interaction methods commonly rely on teleoperation [ 2 , 12 , 13 ] , behavior cloning [ 14 ] , task-specific reward design [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] , or dense motion-reference tracking [ 5 , 6 , 4 ] . For example, HDMI [ 4 ] learns interaction skills by co-tracking humanoid and object trajectories extracted from videos. Although these methods produce high-quality motions, their dependence on reference trajectories limits adaptation after contact loss or unexpected object displacement. Reference-free methods such as PhysHSI [ 18 ] and LessMimic [ 19 ] reduce reliance on motion tracking through task rewards or geometric interaction representations. OmniContact [ 7 ] improves flexibility by generating intermediate references online, but recovery requires additional planning and introduces latency. Rather than specializing inference for a particular interaction mode or replanning after failure, I-BFM uses one object-aware behavioral policy to compose diverse behaviors, while directly reacting to contact disruptions within closed-loop control.

## II-C Unsupervised RL and FB Representations.

Unsupervised reinforcement learning aims to acquire reusable behaviors without task-specific policy training. Forward-backward representations provide a particularly flexible framework by embedding states, rewards, and policies into a shared latent space, allowing new behaviors to be invoked through simple reward specifications [ 20 ] . Prior FB-based models have demonstrated promptable locomotion and whole-body control, but have not explicitly modeled coupled humanoid–object dynamics [ 10 , 1 ] . I-BFM extends FB representations from body-only behavior generation to contact-rich physical interaction: its latent representation jointly incorporates humanoid and object states, enabling reward-conditioned task composition and recovery without retraining a task-specific policy or invoking online replanning.

2026-10-06.title: Radar2Plan: Benchmarking 4D Radar for End-to-End Open-Loop Ego-Trajectory Planning
2026-10-06.authors: Ling Yao , Yichun Xiao , Jin Jin , Yihan Zhang , Fangqiang Ding
2026-10-06.abstract:
Adverse weather and poor illumination remain major challenges for robust ego-trajectory planning in mobile autonomy.
4D radar offers reliable sensing under adverse conditions and direct radial-velocity measurements.
However, sensing robustness does not necessarily translate into robust downstream planning, while existing 4D radar benchmarks focus primarily on perception rather than trajectory planning.
We present Radar2Plan , a modular benchmark for open-loop ego-trajectory planning using real-world 4D radar data. Radar2Plan connects sensor encoders, scene representations, and planning heads through common interfaces, enabling controlled comparisons between different sensor and planner configurations.
Using DSERT-RoLL and MAN TruckScenes, we evaluated seven combinations of camera, 4D radar, and LiDAR in four representative planning baselines and 12 weather and illumination conditions under a unified protocol.
To our knowledge, Radar2Plan is the first benchmark dedicated to evaluating real-world 4D radars for autonomous driving planning.
Experiments show that 4D radar alone supports competitive ego-trajectory planning and robust performance under adverse conditions.
Sensor-configuration comparisons further demonstrate its complementary value to other modalities, while revealing dependencies on sensor combination and planning architecture.
The modular design also supports additional datasets, sensing modalities, and planners, providing a flexible foundation for future research on radar-based autonomous driving planning.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Mobile autonomous systems, including autonomous cars and trucks, UAVs, and construction machines, operate in safety-critical environments and must plan reliable motion from sensor observations.
Cameras and LiDAR are widely used for environmental sensing, but cameras can be severely affected by poor illumination and adverse weather, while LiDAR measurements can also degrade in conditions such as rain, fog, and snow [ 11 , 5 ] , making robust motion planning challenging.
In comparison, the 4D radar is less sensitive to these conditions and directly measures range, azimuth, elevation, and radial velocity [ 5 , 7 ] , making it a promising sensing modality for robust planning of autonomous driving.
Fig. 1 illustrates the
robustness of 4D radar sensing under adverse conditions against camera and LiDARs and its benefits to downstream trajectory planning.

Despite these advantages, existing 4D radar studies have focused primarily on perception tasks such as object detection, tracking, and occupancy prediction [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] , leaving its value for downstream planning insufficiently evaluated.
This gap has become increasingly relevant as autonomous driving systems have shifted from modular perception-prediction-planning pipelines toward end-to-end models [ 13 , 14 ] that directly predict ego trajectories from sensor observations.
In such systems, the quality and robustness of the sensing modality can directly influence the resulting planning performance.
However, whether the sensing robustness of 4D radar translates into more robust ego-trajectory planning has not been systematically evaluated.

This motivates our central research question: Does the sensing robustness of 4D radar benefit downstream planning? We investigate this question from three complementary perspectives:
1) can a planner generate competitive ego trajectories using 4D radar as its only environmental sensing modality?
2) under adverse conditions, does radar-based planning achieve lower planning error than camera or LiDAR-based planning?
and 3) does adding 4D radar improve planning when combined with camera, LiDAR, or camera-LiDAR sensor inputs?
These questions examine the radar-only planning performance, the robustness of radar-based planning under adverse conditions, and its complementarity with other sensing modalities.

We therefore present Radar2Plan , to our knowledge, the first benchmark for open-loop ego-trajectory planning using real-world 4D radar data.
Supporting heterogeneous datasets, sensing modalities, and planning methods requires handling differences in data organization, sensor representations, and planner-specific interfaces.
If treated independently for each experimental configuration, these differences can introduce implementation-specific variations and hinder controlled comparisons.
To address this, Radar2Plan adopts a modular design that separates dataset adaptation, sensor input encoding, planning-specific scene representation, and the planning method through standardized interfaces.
This design allows individual components to be exchanged independently while maintaining a consistent evaluation protocol across sensor configurations and planning methods. Radar2Plan evaluates seven combinations of camera, 4D radar, and LiDAR in four representative planning baselines: GRU-based waypoint regression adapted from TransFuser [ 15 ] , sparse-query planning adapted from SparseDrive [ 12 ] , trajectory-vocabulary scoring adapted from VADv2 [ 16 ] and diffusion-based trajectory refinement adapted from DiffusionDrive [ 17 ] .

Across both DSERT-RoLL and MAN TruckScenes, planners using 4D radar as the sole sensing modality consistently outperform their camera and LiDAR-only counterparts.
Adding 4D radar also generally improves multi-modal sensing-based planning, with particularly pronounced benefits under adverse weather and illumination conditions.
These results demonstrate that the sensing robustness of 4D radar can translate into improved downstream ego-trajectory planning, and further highlight the importance of a dedicated benchmark for systematically evaluating this transfer across different sensor configurations, environmental conditions, and planning architectures.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate and systematically investigate whether the sensing robustness of real-world 4D radar translates into improved open-loop ego-trajectory planning.
To enable this study, we introduce Radar2Plan , which converts DSERT-RoLL and MAN TruckScenes into a unified planning benchmark with consistent task definitions, data splits and evaluation metrics.

We develop a modular design of the benchmark that enables controlled comparisons across datasets, sensing modalities, planner-specific scene representations, and planning methods, while allowing individual components to be changed or extended independently.

Through extensive evaluations across multiple sensor configurations and planning baselines, we show that 4D radar provides robust support for ego-trajectory planning, particularly under adverse sensing conditions.
The configuration-dependent results further highlight the importance of a dedicated benchmark for systematically assessing the planning value of 4D radar across different sensor combinations and planning architectures.

2. We develop a modular design of the benchmark that enables controlled comparisons across datasets, sensing modalities, planner-specific scene representations, and planning methods, while allowing individual components to be changed or extended independently.

# II Related Work

## II-A 4D Radar Perception and Datasets

Compared to conventional automotive radar, the 4D radar provides elevation-aware measurements and improved angular resolution while retaining robustness to poor illumination and adverse weather [ 11 , 5 ] .
These properties have motivated a growing number of 4D radar datasets and perception benchmarks.
K-Radar [ 5 ] , View-of-Delft [ 6 ] , TJ4DRadSet [ 7 ] , and DSERT-RoLL [ 8 ] , for example, primarily evaluate 4D radar through tasks such as 3D object detection and multimodal perception.
Radar-camera methods including CenterFusion [ 18 ] , CRN [ 19 ] , RCBEVDet [ 20 ] , RaCFormer [ 21 ] and ZFusion [ 22 ] further demonstrate that radar features can complement visual observations for better 3D scene understanding.
Collectively, these studies establish the sensing and perception value of 4D radar, but do not determine whether these advantages translate into improved downstream ego-trajectory planning.

Evaluating this question requires real-world datasets that provide synchronized 4D radar together with other commonly used sensing modalities and accurate ego-motion information.
Among existing datasets, DSERT-RoLL [ 8 ] and MAN TruckScenes [ 9 ] satisfy these requirements by providing synchronized and calibrated camera, 4D-radar, LiDAR, and ego-motion measurements.
They also cover complementary driving scenarios: DSERT-RoLL contains urban and suburban driving under diverse weather and illumination conditions, while MAN TruckScenes includes heavy-truck operation on motorways, feeder roads, and terminal roads.
These properties allow future ego trajectories to be constructed from real-world recordings and enable controlled comparisons among camera, radar, and LiDAR-based sensor configurations across different operating conditions.
We therefore use these two datasets to study whether the sensing robustness of 4D radar transfers to downstream planning.

## II-B End-to-End Ego-Trajectory Planning

End-to-end autonomous driving methods predict future ego trajectories directly from sensor observations [ 23 , 13 , 14 ] .
Existing approaches differ substantially in their scene representations and trajectory-generation mechanisms.
TransFuser, TCP, and ThinkTwice employ direct waypoint or trajectory regression [ 15 , 24 , 25 ] .
UniAD, VAD, and SparseDrive instead couple scene understanding and planning through learned queries, vectorized representations, or sparse scene representations [ 13 , 14 , 12 ] .
More recent methods explicitly model multiple possible ego trajectories:
VADv2 scores candidates from a predefined trajectory vocabulary [ 16 ] , GenAD learns a generative trajectory distribution [ 26 ] , and DiffusionDrive and GoalFlow generate multi-modal trajectories through truncated diffusion and flow matching, respectively [ 17 , 27 ] .

Despite this diversity in planning architectures, most existing methods rely primarily on cameras, LiDAR, or their combination for environment sensing [ 15 , 13 , 14 , 12 ] .
SpaRC-AD [ 28 ] is a closely related exception that incorporates conventional radar-camera fusion into a SparseDrive-based framework.
However, it evaluates normal radar within a single planning architecture and does not study 4D radar.
TruckDrive [ 10 ] provides real-world 4D radar data and a LiDAR-only UniAD ego-planning baseline.
However, its released planner does not use 4D radar as input.
Consequently, existing works cannot establish whether the planning benefit of 4D radar is consistent across fundamentally different end-to-end trajectory-generation mechanisms.

To distinguish modality-level effects to different planning methods, we evaluate 4D radar across four representative planning paradigms: direct waypoint regression, sparse-query planning, trajectory-vocabulary scoring, and diffusion-based trajectory refinement.
We adopt TransFuser [ 15 ] , SparseDrive [ 12 ] , VADv2 [ 16 ] , and DiffusionDrive [ 17 ] as representative methods for these four paradigms, respectively.
This selection enables us to examine whether the observed planning value of 4D radar persists across substantially different scene representations and trajectory-generation mechanisms.

As summarized in Table I , existing planning benchmarks and 4D radar datasets address complementary parts of the problem, motivating a unified benchmark to evaluate the planning value of 4D radar across sensor configurations, environmental conditions, and planning architectures.

2026-10-06.abstract: Multimodal imitation learning requires diverse executable futures under the same observation and consistent behavior across replanning cycles. We present Conditional Trajectory Peaks (CTP), a single-pass policy framework that jointly predicts complete action-chunk candidates, probability masses, and trajectory scales. Distribution-Aware Peak Specialization (DAPS) specializes trajectory peaks using trajectory-level posterior responsibilities and mass- and scale-modulated overlap constraints. Evidence-Gated Trajectory Belief Transport (ETBT) maintains cross-chunk consistency through geometric correspondence between exchangeable candidate sets, while allowing current policy evidence to override historical constraints. CTP achieves a coverage score of 91.40% on Push-T; success rates of 100.0%, 79.72%, and 84.44% on D3IL Avoiding, Aligning, and Sorting-2, respectively. On LIBERO, CTP achieves an average success rate of 97.25%. In real-world dual-arm experiments, CTP preserves both placement modes in a two-plate task, succeeding in all 50 trials. On bottle uprighting and pen placement into a holder, it maintains success rates comparable to π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} while reducing policy inference latency from 218.24 ms to 75.80 ms. These results demonstrate that single-pass trajectory modeling can combine multimodal behavior, closed-loop consistency, and efficient inference. Project Page: CTP
2026-10-06.introduction:
Robotic manipulation demonstrations are often multimodal: similar observations can admit different obstacle-avoidance paths, contact locations, pushing sequences, or subtask orders. Policies must represent these distinct executable futures rather than a single deterministic action. Squared-error behavioral cloning instead favors the conditional mean, which can enter low-probability or infeasible regions when trajectory modes are separated [ 1 ] . Diffusion Policy, BESO, and flow-matching policies model complex multimodal action distributions [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . However, diffusion denoising and numerical flow integration generally require multiple network evaluations per replanning cycle. This iterative generation increases latency and computation in high-frequency closed-loop control. This raises a central question: Can a policy generate trajectory-level multimodal actions with one network forward pass per replanning step?

A direct alternative is to predict multiple trajectories in parallel. Existing multi-hypothesis policies demonstrate single-pass batched candidate generation [ 6 , 7 ] , but parallel outputs do not guarantee effective multimodality. Permutation symmetry can drive candidates toward the same dominant high-density region early in training. This produces mode collapse : nominally distinct candidates represent identical or similar behaviors, leaving the model effectively unimodal. Additional output capacity therefore permits multiple modes without ensuring allocation to distinct data-supported regions. Fixed action anchors, offline clustering, or predefined mode quotas impose candidate roles through data processing or model design. Single-pass policies instead need data-driven specialization that assigns high-probability trajectories to distinct valid modes and reduces probability mass on unsupported redundant candidates.

Candidate diversity alone is insufficient for multimodal closed-loop control. Action-chunking policies execute only a chunk’s first few steps before replanning, so candidates must preserve behavioral continuity across decisions. Local probability changes can switch the policy between incompatible routes, stitching individually feasible chunks into discontinuous or unsuccessful behavior, a failure we call cross-chunk mode stitching . Unlike training-time mode collapse, stitching concerns behavioral identity across replanning cycles and can occur despite diverse candidates. Because finite mixture components are permutation-symmetric, their indices cannot identify corresponding behaviors across successive exchangeable candidate sets. We therefore formulate cross-chunk consistency as behavioral identity correspondence and sequential transfer : physical trajectory relationships identify continuations, while current policy evidence can revise or overturn earlier choices. Fig. 1 summarizes these challenges.

We therefore propose Conditional Trajectory Peaks (CTP) , a single-pass policy framework for multimodal closed-loop control. CTP models trajectory-level conditional peaks over complete action chunks. One shared network forward pass provides multimodal prediction with NFE = 1 \mathrm{NFE}=1 , jointly addressing peak specialization and behavioral consistency across replanning cycles.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We propose CTP, a single-pass framework for multimodal closed-loop control that jointly predicts multiple trajectory candidates, probabilities, and scales with N ​ F ​ E = 1 NFE=1 .

We introduce Distribution-Aware Peak Specialization (DAPS), which mitigates mode collapse through posterior responsibility assignment and probability- and scale-aware inter-peak regularization, without clustering or predefined mode assignments.

We introduce Evidence-Gated Trajectory Belief Transport (ETBT), which improves cross-chunk behavioral consistency by propagating beliefs across replanning cycles while adaptively revising them using current policy evidence.

2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Multimodal Policies for Robotic Imitation Learning

Squared-error behavioral cloning tends toward the conditional mean and struggles with multivalued action mappings. Mixture density networks (MDNs) predict mixture parameters, providing a classical probabilistic framework for continuous multimodal regression [ 1 ] . With vectorized action chunks, a trajectory-level MDN uses one discrete component to explain the entire trajectory and optimizes a normalized mixture likelihood in one forward pass.

IBC represents implicit conditional distributions through an energy function and approximates inference by sampling actions [ 8 ] . BeT clusters continuous actions into discrete categories and predicts cluster indices and continuous residuals [ 9 ] . ACT shortens the effective prediction horizon through action chunking [ 10 ] , while D3IL systematically evaluates how different policies learn diverse human demonstrations [ 11 ] . Energy Policy trains a noise-conditioned energy network to generate complete action sequences in parallel without iterative denoising [ 12 ] . Diffusion Policy and BESO demonstrate the effectiveness of iterative generation for multimodal robot control [ 2 , 3 ] . These approaches improve distributional expressiveness, temporal modeling, or generation quality, but trade-offs remain among multimodal representation, policy inference overhead, and closed-loop candidate selection.

## II-B Single-Pass Multi-Hypothesis Generation

IMLE Policy regresses the demonstration’s closest candidate among action sequences generated from random latent variables, and uses the previous chunk’s unexecuted suffix for consistency-based selection [ 6 ] . PRISM combines full-batch rejection-sampling IMLE, Performer, and learned action queries to generate multiple sequences in one batched forward pass [ 7 ] . Liquid Networks with Mixture Density Heads predicts a Gaussian mixture per time step [ 13 ] . Designs primarily trade off candidate sampling, learned action queries, and per-step mixtures. Direct parameterization of normalized complete action-chunk distributions in one shared forward pass, with one latent component spanning the entire horizon, remains insufficiently studied.

## II-C Consistency and Feedback across Action Chunks

BID samples multiple action chunks at inference, using backward coherence to preserve consistency with past decisions and forward contrast to guide candidate selection [ 14 ] . IntentVLA extracts short-horizon intent from recent visual history and conditions action-chunk generation on it, mitigating intent conflicts under observation aliasing [ 15 ] . IMLE Policy also uses the unexecuted suffix of the previous action chunk for consistency-based selection [ 6 ] . These studies highlight the importance of maintaining prior action intent. However, identifying the same physical route within candidate sets with permutable component indices, and actively releasing constraints when current evidence contradicts history, remain key challenges in receding-horizon execution.

## II-D Multimodal Trajectory Modeling in Motion Prediction

Motion prediction also represents multiple futures from limited history. AutoBots uses latent-variable set Transformers for single-pass scene-consistent trajectory prediction [ 16 ] ; MotionDiffuser models joint multi-agent trajectory distributions through diffusion [ 17 ] . Multi-hypothesis regression commonly uses winner-takes-all objectives; aWTA stabilizes optimization through annealing [ 18 ] , while ModeSeq explicitly models sequential relationships among modes [ 19 ] . Robotic closed-loop control shares trajectory-level multimodality with motion prediction but additionally handles receding-horizon replanning, contact feedback, and temporal permutations of finite mixture components. Single-step candidate diversity therefore cannot fully characterize closed-loop performance.

2026-10-06.title: Propagating Elevation-Map Uncertainty Through the Contact Maximum in Closed Form
2026-10-06.authors: Aleš Kučera , Karel Zimmermann
2026-10-06.comment: . Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Risk-aware planners score paths on uncertain elevation maps using the path
cost’s mean and standard deviation. Modeling rigid contact, however,
requires computing a maximum over several uncertain cells. First-order
propagation loses accuracy here by differentiating at only a single cell,
while Monte Carlo sampling requires a full path evaluation per draw. We
compute the moments of that contact maximum in closed form using Clark’s
pairwise recursion. By tracking each contact’s covariance against the
shared map cells, we propagate the smooth remainder using exact Gaussian
quadratic-form identities. A contest-depth calibration, fitted once on two
design traverses, closes the aggregate standard-deviation shortfall that
remains. On 317 317 held-out rover path segments, scored against a Monte
Carlo reference from the same belief, every pre-registered criterion was
met. The corrected Clark fold cuts the median error of the mean from
linearization’s 2.3 % 2.3\% to 0.19 % 0.19\% and attains the lowest CVaR 0.9 \mathrm{CVaR}_{0.9} error of every method tested. A benchmark plan costs
just 5.5 ​ μ 5.5~\mu s on a GPU. These accuracy gains concentrate at contested
contacts. While they seldom change which path is chosen on this terrain,
the fold still selects the reference-best path in 98 % 98\% of decisions
against linearization’s 93 93 to 96 % 96\% . On a second dataset the mean
transfers, though the risk number does not.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Robots navigating rough terrain rely on elevation maps subject to sensor
noise and estimation drift [ 1 ] . To
ensure safety, risk-aware planners evaluate paths using metrics such as the
conditional value at risk (CVaR) [ 2 ] .
Assuming a Gaussian path cost, these metrics are fully dictated by the
cost’s mean and standard deviation [ 2 ] .

The computational bottleneck in evaluating this cost is rigid contact.
Because a wheel rests on the terrain point that maximizes its elevation
(Fig. 1 a), a path’s cost is driven by the maximum of several
uncertain cells. Standard first-order propagation fails here because it
differentiates only at the cell that wins on the mean map. This single
choice ruins the estimation of both moments: it discards the statistical
inflation that Jensen’s inequality applies to the mean of a maximum, and it
reads the variance from one cell as though the others were not
competing for contact. Consequently, planners needing accurate moments must
fall back on expensive sampling, which demands one full rollout per draw.

A natural workaround is to soften the contact, replacing the maximum with a
temperature-weighted average as differentiable simulators do. However, no fixed
temperature can. A softmax weight is strictly a function of the gap
between two cells’ mean elevations. In reality, the probability that a cell carries
the load depends on that gap measured in units of the margin’s own spread. If the means are held constant while uncertainty grows,
the true probability approaches one half, yet the temperature-weighted
output remains unchanged (Section III-C ). Recovering the
contact maximum’s moments requires the belief’s second moment, not a
smoother maximum.

We compute those moments in closed form. Clark’s
identities [ 3 ] yield the exact first two moments of the
maximum of two Gaussians. Applied pairwise across a footprint, tracking each
folded contact’s covariance against the shared map cells, they return the
contact height’s mean and its covariance with every other contact. An exact
Gaussian quadratic form turns these into the path cost’s moments. While the
mean needs nothing further, the standard deviation requires a single
calibration fitted once on design data
(Section III-G ). We term this pipeline the corrected
Clark fold .

We evaluated the corrected fold on the BASEPROD semi-desert rover
dataset [ 4 ] , benchmarking against a 20,000 20{,}000 -sample
Monte Carlo reference drawn from the same map beliefs to isolate propagation
accuracy. Every pre-registered criterion was met. Across 317 317 held-out
segments, the corrected fold achieved a median mean error of 0.19 % 0.19\% (compared to 2.3 % 2.3\% for linearization) and the lowest median CVaR error, 2.7 2.7 times below linearization’s.
This accuracy advantage is earned primarily at contested folds
(Section III-H ); on this terrain, safety threshold verdicts do not
separate either fold from standard linearization
(Section IV -E).

Our main contributions are: (1) a characterization of rigid contact in
contest depth: why first-order propagation fails at it, why
no softened contact repairs that, and the depth at which the two
constructions coincide
(Sections III-B , III-C , III-H ); (2) a
GPU-accelerated closed form for the contact maximum, with the contest-depth
calibration that closes its aggregate standard-deviation deficit: the
corrected Clark fold (Section III-D onward);
and (3) a pre-registered evaluation on
held-out rover traverses alongside a zero-shot transfer check on a second
dataset (Section IV ).
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

We categorize prior work by how it resolves the maximum of uncertain heights
at a contact.

Ignoring the maximum. Methods like STEP [ 2 ] aggregate local risk from the map into a path-level CVaR. Because the robot
is modeled using surface normals and footprint plane fits rather than
discrete contact heights, the maximum is never actually formed.

Bounding the maximum. The ACE framework [ 5 ] and its
probabilistic successor, p-ACE [ 6 ] , evaluate
clearance using deterministic kinematic bounds. Because the maximum relies
on these bounds rather than the belief distribution, they cannot
analytically propagate the map’s mean or standard deviation through the
contact.

Replacing the maximum with a heuristic. For planetary landing,
Tomita et al. [ 7 ] compute exact lander slope moments
but approximate the worst-case point under the footprint by raising a
probability to an exponent fitted offline against sampled terrains.

Sampling. Monte Carlo approaches (e.g.,
ProTerrain [ 8 ] ) draw correlated terrains and simulate
them: exact per sample, but requiring one full physics simulation per draw.

Smoothing the maximum. Differentiable
simulators [ 9 ] expose terrain derivatives of a
rollout [ 10 , 11 ] ;
propagating the map’s variance through them is a first-order second-moment
(FOSM) linearization. To bypass pathological hard-contact
gradients [ 12 , 13 ] , remedies average them
over sampled perturbations [ 14 , 15 ] or use
a softmax.
However, softmax weights rely solely on mean elevations, ignoring
the probability that an uncertain point actually supports the contact
(Section III-C ).

Moments of the maximum. Clark [ 3 ] derived
exact formulas for the maximum of two correlated Gaussians, using a pairwise
recursion for larger sets. Block-based statistical static timing analysis (SSTA)
propagates circuit delay uncertainty through this
recursion [ 16 ] , and advanced variants buy back what
the Gaussian fit loses with a third moment and a skew-normal
maximum [ 17 ] . We instead locate the deficit we measure
(Section IV -C) in the aggregation rather than the fold,
and close it with a calibration in contest depth
(Section III-G ). To our
knowledge, no prior robotics work applies Clark’s recursion to a geometric
terrain contact maximum.

2026-10-06.title: Execution-Aligned Progressive Noise for Consistent Asynchronous Replanning in Generative Robot Policies
2026-10-06.authors: Di Wu , Ping Liu , Xuhua Chen , He Zheng , Lingfeng Zhang , Tao Zhang
2026-10-06.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract:
Continuous asynchronous replanning is essential for real-time generative robot policies, but independent stochastic initialization can cause mode switching and inconsistent continuation across action chunks. We propose Execution-Aligned Progressive Noise (EAPN), which introduces structured stochasticity at both inter-chunk and intra-chunk levels. Across replanning steps, EAPN propagates a shared noise trajectory and aligns it with the actual execution displacement, establishing execution-aligned inter-chunk correlation. Within each action chunk, it models temporal correlation along action time. The aligned stochastic history is further combined with committed
action context to condition subsequent generation, allowing new chunks to continue from execution-consistent generative states rather than restart from independent noise. We evaluate EAPN on D3IL, Kinetix, LIBERO, and real-world manipulation tasks. EAPN improves multimodal behavior consistency on D3IL and achieves an average success rate of 88.59% on Kinetix. On LIBERO, it remains robust and maintains strong task performance even under long inference delays. Real-robot experiments further achieve 90.0% success on Object Storage and 96.7% on bimanual Cloth Folding, demonstrating reliable continuous execution under asynchronous replanning. Project Page: EAPN
2026-10-06.introduction:
Generative models, including Flow Matching, support robot decision-making and action-sequence generation [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
Unlike deterministic regression policies, they can model multimodal conditional distributions over plausible future motions.
Their iterative generation, however, operates
at a lower frequency than closed-loop control.
To bridge this gap, generative robot policies commonly use Action Chunking: the policy predicts a future action sequence at each call [ 5 , 2 ] . High-latency Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models further use asynchronous execution, generating the next chunk while the current one is still being executed [ 6 , 7 ] . Because the robot continues moving during inference, the physical execution state has already advanced when the new prediction becomes available, causing prediction-execution misalignment, stale actions, and discontinuities between adjacent chunks.

Existing methods mainly address this issue through action-space constraints and execution-time alignment. RTC and
Training-Time RTC (ttRTC) condition generation on a committed action prefix [ 6 , 8 ] ; VLASH and FutureRTC estimate the execution-time context at which a new prediction will actually take effect [ 9 , 10 ] ; and Legato, SEAM, and Soft RTC improve continuation through learned dynamics, velocity guidance, or soft action priors [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . These approaches improve temporal consistency, but their constraints concentrate on the executed or imminently executed trajectory prefix. Beyond this explicitly constrained region, the remaining suffix is still largely determined by a newly sampled stochastic source. Stochastic-state dependency across consecutive generation processes therefore remains insufficiently modeled.

Most generative policies initialize every inference independently from Gaussian noise. For a multimodal conditional distribution, different stochastic initializations can drive temporally overlapping inferences toward different, yet individually high-probability, local modes. Thus, even when the committed prefix is continuous, the freely generated suffix may gradually deviate from the behavioral mode represented by the previous inference and switch to a trajectory with a different motion intent or manipulation strategy. Such cross-inference mode switching need not appear as a large single-step error and is therefore difficult to identify from local trajectory smoothness alone. In long-horizon manipulation, however, inconsistencies in motion direction, end-effector state, contact relation, or manipulation semantics can accumulate across successive Action Chunks and cause substantial execution deviations. This motivates modeling not only temporal alignment in action space, but also stochastic-state continuity across consecutive replanning steps.

Figure 1 provides empirical evidence for this view. Flow inversion of consecutive action windows reveals pronounced temporal locality in source latents within the same episode: correlations gradually decay as the temporal separation increases, whereas correlations across different episodes remain near zero. Although the base policy is trained with independent Gaussian sources, temporally continuous behaviors therefore exhibit stable cross-time latent dependency. This suggests that preserving execution-consistent stochastic relations across neighboring inferences may provide a useful prior for continuous replanning.

Motivated by this observation, we propose Execution-Aligned Progressive Noise (EAPN),
a stochastic-state dependency modeling method for
continuous generative replanning. Rather than directly
constraining deterministic action outputs, EAPN introduces structured stochasticity at two complementary levels.
First, execution-aligned inter-chunk correlation propagates stochastic states across consecutive policy
calls according to the actual execution displacement, so that temporally corresponding positions in neighboring Action Chunks share consistent stochastic context.
Second, intra-chunk temporal correlation models dependency along action
time within each chunk. Together, these components provide a temporally structured stochastic prior spanning both inference events and action time, reducing stochastic drift and unnecessary mode switching while remaining compatible with asynchronous execution. Our contributions are:

Execution-aligned latent correlation. Through Flow inversion, we show that neighboring Action Chunks exhibit correlated initial noise whose peak shifts with the actual execution displacement and decays as the window separation increases.

Execution-aligned latent correlation. Through Flow inversion, we show that neighboring Action Chunks exhibit correlated initial noise whose peak shifts with the actual execution displacement and decays as the window separation increases.

Joint inter- and intra-chunk stochastic modeling. EAPN recursively propagates noise
across consecutive inferences while introducing temporal correlation within each Action Chunk, reducing stochastic drift and unnecessary mode switching caused by independent reinitialization.

Evaluation across simulation and real robots. Experiments on D3IL, Kinetix, LIBERO, and two real-world tasks demonstrate improved task performance, multimodal consistency, cross-chunk continuity, and robustness to inference delays, achieving 90.0% on Object Storage and 96.7% on bimanual Cloth Folding.

# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Asynchronous Action-Chunk Execution and Temporal Alignment

Action Chunking reduces policy invocation frequency but introduces prediction–execution misalignment when inference overlaps continuous control [ 5 , 2 ] . RTC conditions generation on a committed action prefix, while Training-Time RTC learns this continuation during training [ 6 , 8 ] . REMAC handles discrepancies between planned and executed actions through masked chunks [ 14 ] ; VLASH and FutureRTC improve alignment using future-state rollout or execution-time state prediction [ 9 , 10 ] ; DiscreteRTC exploits discrete-diffusion inpainting [ 15 ] ; and Action ControlNet introduces a lightweight delay-aware residual adapter [ 16 ] . Related delay and chunk-overlap issues also arise in asynchronous World–Action Models [ 7 ] . These methods primarily align historical states/actions with newly generated trajectories.

## II-B Cross-Chunk Continuation and Multimodal Consistency

A complementary line of work targets continuation quality across chunks. BID selects candidates using backward coherence and forward contrast [ 17 ] , while Self-Guided Action Diffusion reuses the previous decision as sampling guidance [ 18 ] . Legato learns continuation dynamics for multimodal Flow Matching [ 11 ] ; SEAM uses velocity guidance derived from the previous chunk [ 12 ] ; and Soft RTC replaces a hard prefix with an editable action prior [ 13 ] . ChunkFlow, FocalPolicy, and POTR further improve chunk-boundary or long-horizon coherence through seam-aware objectives, frequency-aware modeling, or constrained sampling-time guidance [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] . These approaches encourage consistency through candidate selection, action/velocity guidance, overlap constraints, or learned continuation dynamics. EAPN instead asks whether the stochastic state from which each generation begins should itself remain temporally related across replanning events, providing a complementary mechanism to action-space continuation.

## II-C Source Priors and Correlated Stochastic Initialization

Beyond robot policies, PYoCo uses a correlated noise prior in video diffusion models to preserve temporal structure across frames [ 22 ] , showing that source correlation itself can support temporal consistency. Recent work has also revisited source distributions for generative robot policies. Streaming Flow Policy initializes near the previous action [ 23 ] ; Action-to-Action Flow Matching, WarmPrior, and Temporal Policy construct history-informed sources from recent actions or proprioception [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] ; and LeaP learns source mean and variance from the current proprioceptive state [ 27 ] . PAINT uses Flow inversion to select initial noise compatible with a historical prefix [ 28 ] . These studies establish the generative starting point as an important design dimension. Unlike PYoCo’s fixed correlation structure for video generation, EAPN models a persistent, execution-aligned dependency across consecutive robot replanning windows while simultaneously retaining structured temporal correlation within each chunk.

2026-10-06.title: Adaptive Mean Flow for Responsive Closed-Loop Robot Control
2026-10-06.authors: Aksel Vaaler , Marco Job , Christian Holden , Olav Egeland
2026-10-06.abstract: Diffusion- and flow-based robot policies have recently become widespread in robotic Imitation Learning (IL) due to their high performance and ability to model continuous and multimodal distributions. However, the iterative denoising procedure used by these models introduces significant prediction latency, hindering high-frequency closed-loop robot control and leading to jittery, unstable motion when frequent updates to the robot’s action predictions are used. Therefore, it is common practice to train models to predict chunks of actions that can be executed sequentially without feedback, even when this reduces responsiveness and may mean the most recent state information is not used. In this article, we present Adaptive Mean Flow (AMF), a flow-based IL method that enables smooth and responsive, fully closed-loop robot control. AMF uses Mean Flow, which is an accelerated form of Flow Matching (FM), to minimize prediction latency. To ensure smoothness and consistency across predictions, AMF uses a corrupted version of the trajectory from the previous step when predicting new robot actions, with the signal-to-noise ratio increasing over the time parameter of the trajectory. This discourages large changes in the prediction from one step to the next, while allowing freedom to adapt the predictions for future steps. We evaluate AMF across a wide range of simulated and real robot tasks and demonstrate significantly improved performance compared with baselines. Code: github.com/akselva/Adaptive-mean-flow-RoboticIL .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Diffusion and flow models rely on iterative refinement (denoising) to produce high-quality output samples, which means that multiple forward passes of the network are needed per model prediction. Considerable research has been conducted to accelerate the inference process while maintaining quality. For applications with real-time demands, such as robotics, the deterministic Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) sampler proposed in [ 11 ] has largely been preferred in favor of the stochastic Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) sampler originally proposed in [ 1 ] , as it generally requires fewer denoising steps to produce good samples. Consistency Policy [ 12 ] can produce high-quality robot actions with very few denoising steps by utilizing the diffusion distillation framework developed in [ 13 ] . Similarly, One-Step Diffusion Policy [ 14 ] proposes a distillation scheme that enables training a student model in a single denoising step to mimic the action predictions of a pre-trained Diffusion Policy [ 5 ] network. Streaming Diffusion Policy [ 9 ] and Diffusion Forcing [ 10 ] train the networks using varying noise levels across the action sequence. This allows inference using a “stair-case” noise structure, where action predictions for near-future time steps are initialized with less noise and thus require fewer denoising steps.

A flow model can itself be viewed as a faster alternative to diffusion, typically requiring far fewer integration steps compared with diffusion and DDPM sampling [ 3 ] . However, induced curvature in the probability flow field used to generate samples means that several ODE integration steps are still required [ 8 ] . Analogous to Consistency Policy [ 12 ] , Consistency Flow Policy [ 15 ] trains the network with additional consistency constraints on the flow ODE [ 16 ] to enable action generation with fewer integration steps. Streaming Flow Policy (SFP) [ 17 ] takes a different approach by formulating action trajectories as flows. Starting from the last robot action, SFP treats a step along the flow ODE as a step along the forward robot trajectory, meaning the next robot action is “ready” after a single integration step.

Our AMF method utilizes Mean Flow [ 8 ] , which was also used in [ 18 ] , and enables single-step action sequence prediction of high quality without the need for distillation, additional consistency losses, or complex inference algorithms.

The aforementioned works all address the problem of speeding up diffusion/flow inference, which offers immediate benefits in terms of smoother policy execution [ 17 , 9 ] . However, they still use action chunking to ensure consistent robot motion and thus do not fully utilize the responsiveness enabled by fast inference. Comparatively few works directly address the consistency-reactivity trade-off between action chunking and fully closed-loop, single-step action execution. However, there is a growing interest, particularly in developing test-time algorithms to improve the performance of pre-trained chunking-based policies during deployment. Bidirectional Decoding [ 7 ] and Past-Token Prediction [ 19 ] introduce algorithms that select the next action sequence from a set of candidates, with selection criteria that aim to balance consistency with the previous prediction and responsiveness to the most recent observation. Self-Guided Action Diffusion [ 20 ] and Real-Time Chunking [ 21 ] use weighted distances from the previous prediction to the current prediction to steer a diffusion/flow model during the denoising process, producing action sequences that more closely align with the trajectory prediction from the previous step. Temporal Action Selection [ 22 ] also employs a pre-trained IL policy, but uses online RL fine-tuning to train an action selector network to adaptively update the action trajectory based on current and previous predictions from the pre-trained policy.

In contrast, our AMF method uses no fine-tuning or additional test-time compute. By training the model on action sequences with dynamic per-step signal-to-noise ratio, flexibility is retained with respect to controlling the behavior of the policy. During deployment, AMF predicts actions rapidly in closed-loop, maintaining consistency simply by initializing the noisy samples around the previous action trajectory.

2026-10-06.title: Do VLAs Understand and Adapt to the Objects They Handle, or Simply Replay Learned Behaviors?
2026-10-06.authors: Xinnuo Xu
2026-10-06.abstract: This paper asks whether VLA generalization is grounded in a global understanding of objects’ physical properties that enables policies to adapt their motion to unseen setups, or if policies simply replay the motions they’ve learnt that happen to succeed in new setups. The former reflects genuine generalization; the latter reflects incidental robustness. We first examine awareness of physical properties in seven VLAs by applying linear probing and representational similarity analysis (RSA) to their activations. We find that physical properties, including mass , fragility , deformability , friction and size are less decodable than non-physical properties such as semantic category , material , sound and price in nearly every modality stream. Compared with their base VLMs, robot pre-training weakens the linear encoding of physical properties in the language stream. Neither pre-training nor downstream fine-tuning strengthens the alignment between physical-property differences and activation distances. We then ask whether the weak physical information present in these activations shapes the actions a VLA generates. In a controlled LIBERO case study, we increase the mass of an in-domain object and signal the change through language or vision. Most VLAs use similar lifting behaviour for the heavier and original- mass objects, leading to task success declines. The few exceptions change their behaviour in response to lexical or visual cues rather than to mass itself. These results suggest that VLAs encode physical properties weakly and do not reliably use them to adapt their motion.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision Language Action models (VLAs) trained on large robot corpora show some robustness to unseen objects and environments [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
A fundamental question, however, remains: is this generalization grounded in a global understanding of object physical properties, e.g. mass and deformability , that lets the policy adapt its motion to new setups, or does it just replay the motions they’ve learnt in training, and assume they are robust in unseen setups? We examine two dimensions.

Awareness : do VLAs represent the physical properties of the objects they manipulate in their latent representations? Following [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] , we quantify awareness with two metrics. Decodability fits a linear probe to the model’s activations and asks whether a property can be read out of them; representation geometry uses representational similarity analysis (RSA) to ask whether pairwise distances between object activations track differences in that property, such that objects with similar property values are represented similarly.
Across seven widely used VLAs on the OXE and DROID datasets, we find that all physical properties, including mass , fragility , deformability , friction and size , are less decodable than the other properties, such as category , material , sound and price , in almost every modality stream, and no stream’s pairwise activation distances align most strongly with differences in a physical property. Moreover, physical properties are less decodable from the language stream after robot-interaction pre-training and downstream fine-tuning than in the corresponding base VLMs, while neither stage strengthens the alignment between physical-property differences and activation distances (Sec. V ).

Behavioral adaptation : do VLAs adapt their actions to changes in objects’
physical properties? We answer this with a controlled case study of mass in
LIBERO (Sec. VI ). As shown in Fig. 1 , we select manipulable containers from LIBERO, preserve their geometry while adding the mass of realistic contents, and signal the change through language (top row in Fig. 1 ) or vision (bottom row in Fig. 1 ). Six VLAs execute 23 23 tasks with mass -amended and original objects under otherwise identical setups. Success falls for mass -amended objects, since for most VLAs the lifting-phase actions deviate no further from the original. Three policies are exceptions, but none tracks mass by exhibiting the human pattern of lifting heavier objects more slowly. Instead, the action divergence arises from either lexical rewording or pixel-level changes.

As a conclusion, the results suggest that VLAs encode physical properties weakly and do not reliably use them to adapt their motion.

# II Related Work

Probing VLA representations. Linear probes are widely used in LLMs, where
affine readouts recover high-level concepts encoded as activation
directions [ 12 , 13 ] . Applied to VLAs, they reveal symbolic object and action
states [ 7 ] , value-like success structure [ 8 ] , and
observable end-effector variables such as yaw and gripper
aperture [ 9 ] . Richer techniques expose complementary structure; for example,
sparse autoencoders recover motion primitives, task semantics and episode-specific
features [ 14 ] . We use linear probes for their simple, uniform readout across
architectures.
Prior work shows that robot training can degrade broad multimodal capabilities and
pretrained representations, with retention depending on the action representation and
training recipe [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . We study this degradation through
the lens of object representations, asking which physical properties are retained
or lost; our analysis is therefore complementary rather than a rediscovery of the
broader effect.

Representational similarity analysis. Introduced in systems
neuroscience [ 10 ] , RSA relates two systems through their dissimilarity structures
and is a standard tool for connecting neural and symbolic representations in language
models [ 11 ] . We apply it to VLAs to ask what a probe cannot: whether a property
organizes the representation. A property can be linearly decodable yet contribute
nothing to the distances between object embeddings.

Object physical properties. PhysObjects [ 18 ] annotates mass , fragility , deformability , material and other
properties in household-object images, and
uses them to ground a VLM that improves object selection by a high-level LLM planner.
Human-norm resources provide reference labels for some properties, including measured mass in YCB [ 19 ] and size in
THINGSplus [ 20 ] ; we use these to
validate our annotation (Sec. III ). That line of work targets task
planning , i.e. which object to pick for a goal, whereas we target motion
execution : whether a policy’s low-level actions reflect the properties of the object
it holds.
