2026-10-06.title: MagServo: Uncertainty-Resilient Hierarchical Magnetic Servoing via Learned Latent Representations
2026-10-06.authors: Yuhan Tan , Yameng Zhang , Pei Liu , Yao Zhong , Zhongliang Jiang
2026-10-06.abstract: Magnetic navigation provides contact-free and line-of-sight-independent feedback for robotic systems, yet existing approaches typically rely on explicit pose estimation or direct use of raw magnetic measurements, making accurate control susceptible to modeling errors, measurement noise, and disturbances. This work presents MagServo , a hierarchical learning-based framework for robust 6-DoF magnetic servoing directly using the learned latent magnetic feature. MagServo learns uncertainty-resilient magnetic representations through masked reconstruction and captures state-dependent interaction dynamics between robot motion and latent magnetic transitions without analytical magnetic models or explicit Jacobian supervision. Based on the learned dynamics, a hierarchical controller combines nonlinear model predictive control for coarse approach with local Jacobian inversion for precise fine regulation. Extensive physical experiments demonstrate submillimeter and subdegree accuracy, achieving mean terminal errors of 0.386 mm and 0.479 ∘ for 6-DoF pose reaching. MagServo further outperforms a localization-based control baseline in complex trajectory tracking and maintains robust performance under unseen magnetic-source configurations without retraining. A supplementary video of the real-robot experiments is available at https://youtu.be/rZt1NUP1Mr0 .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Magnetic localization and navigation technologies have attracted increasing attention due to their non-contact, real-time, and line-of-sight-independent nature, enabling reliable operation in visually occluded or confined environments [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Their radiation-free nature further makes them particularly well suited for medical applications, particularly robot-assisted endoscopic examinations and minimally invasive procedures [ 5 , 6 ] .
In these cases, visual feedback is often compromised due to poor lighting conditions or physical obstructions between the observer and the target, such as a robotic capsule for gastrointestinal examination [ 2 , 7 ] .

Magnetic navigation methods can be broadly divided into two categories: explicit localization-based navigation and direct raw magnetic data-based servoing. The former requires explicit estimation of the robot end-effector pose from real-time magnetometer measurements using an accurate magnetic model. Navigation is then achieved by minimizing the error between the estimated current pose and the desired pose. To establish the mapping between the magnetic flux density measured by the magnetometers and the robot pose, various magnetic models have been investigated, including the magnetic dipole model [ 8 ] , analytical model [ 9 ] , and complete elliptic integral model [ 10 ] . Considering the inherent nonlinearity and modeling uncertainties of this mapping, Son et al. adopted a quadratic measurement model for online calibration [ 11 ] . To further improve pose estimation accuracy, numerical optimization methods, such as particle swarm optimization [ 12 ] and the Levenberg-Marquardt algorithm [ 13 ] , are commonly employed to minimize the discrepancy between the measured and model-predicted magnetic fields. While these model-based approaches offer strong physical interpretability, they often require careful system calibration and computationally intensive iterative optimization, limiting their efficiency for real-time applications [ 14 ] .

Recently, to reduce the complexity associated with parameter identification and iterative optimization while improving localization accuracy, learning-based methods have emerged to directly estimate robot poses from magnetometer measurements. Su et al. proposed AMagPoseNet for 6-DoF pose estimation of an annular magnet, where PoseNet is pretrained using data generated from a mathematical model and CaliNet adapts the learned mapping to the real magnetic field using a small amount of experimental data [ 15 ] . This model-assisted learning strategy substantially reduces the need for large-scale real-world data collection. Similarly, Zhao et al. employed differential magnetic signals and a precisely calibrated magnetic model to generate large-scale simulated data for training a deep network, enabling accurate and real-time pose estimation [ 16 ] . Yang et al. proposed PRPosNet, which combines CNN-based local feature extraction, coordinate attention, and Transformer-based modeling to capture both local spatial characteristics and long-range dependencies among magnetic sensors [ 17 ] . Beyond direct pose regression, recent studies have increasingly incorporated physical priors into neural models to improve accuracy and generalizability. Shen et al. proposed a physics-informed residual network with a dual-branch architecture to explicitly correct discrepancies between the ideal magnetic dipole model and real magnetic measurements [ 18 ] . To account for measurement noise in practical magnetometers, Xie et al. augmented ideal magnetic data generated from a theoretical model with Gaussian noise and trained PoseNet on the synthetically corrupted measurements, achieving localization errors of approximately 1.54 mm in position and 2.24 ∘ 2.24^{\circ} in orientation [ 19 ] .

Instead of explicitly estimating the robot pose, direct raw magnetic data-based servoing uses magnetometer measurements as feature descriptors and directly actuates the robot end-effector to minimize the corresponding feature errors [ 20 ] . This eliminates the need to map magnetic flux density measurements into Cartesian poses. However, direct servoing requires a Jacobian matrix that relates robot motion to variations in magnetometer measurements, which is challenging to derive analytically. To address this issue, Su et al. pioneered an online Jacobian estimation approach, in which the Jacobian matrix is vectorized as a state variable within a state-space formulation and estimated online using a Kalman filter (KF) [ 21 ] . Building upon this formulation, Tan et al. and Edelmann et al. developed model-free control strategies for magnetically actuated endoscopes [ 22 , 23 ] . However, the performance of such methods strongly depends on appropriate characterization of the process and measurement noise statistics used by the KF. To relax the reliance on predefined static noise models, adaptive approaches have been introduced to dynamically update the process and measurement noise covariances during online control [ 24 , 25 ] . Nevertheless, these approaches primarily estimate the Jacobian from feature variations and robot motion at the current control step, making the estimation susceptible to instantaneous measurement noise and disturbances. To further improve servoing stability, Zhang et al. introduced a Jacobian consistency assumption and incorporated a moving window of historical feature-error and actuation data, which are linearly combined with current observations to achieve more robust Jacobian estimation [ 20 ] . However, this approach remains susceptible to environmental disturbances and transient measurement drift induced by sensor noise.

To address these challenges, we introduce MagServo , a hierarchical learning-based framework for robust and accurate magnetic servoing. MagServo learns uncertainty-resilient magnetic representations through masked reconstruction and captures their motion-conditioned dynamics without requiring analytical magnetic models or explicit Jacobian supervision. The representation and dynamics are further jointly refined through multi-step rollout learning, establishing a robust, control-aware latent space for magnetic servoing. Leveraging the learned dynamics, MagServo combines nonlinear model predictive control (MPC) for rapid coarse approach with local Jacobian inversion for precise fine regulation. By directly translating latent magnetic discrepancies into corrective robot motions, MagServo bypasses explicit magnetic-to-pose estimation and enables accurate closed-loop 6-DoF servoing. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We propose a direct magnetic servoing algorithm that uses learned latent magnetic representations as control features, eliminating explicit pose estimation and analytical magnetic modeling while remaining robust to measurement noise and disturbances.

We introduce MagServo, which jointly learns latent magnetic representations and state-dependent interaction dynamics and integrates them into a hierarchical coarse-to-fine controller, combining nonlinear MPC with local Jacobian inversion for accurate and reliable magnetic servoing.

1. We propose a direct magnetic servoing algorithm that uses learned latent magnetic representations as control features, eliminating explicit pose estimation and analytical magnetic modeling while remaining robust to measurement noise and disturbances.

2. We introduce MagServo, which jointly learns latent magnetic representations and state-dependent interaction dynamics and integrates them into a hierarchical coarse-to-fine controller, combining nonlinear MPC with local Jacobian inversion for accurate and reliable magnetic servoing.

# II System Overview and Problem Formulation

## II-A System Configuration

As shown in Fig. 1 , the system couples a robot manipulator carrying two permanent magnets with a stationary 4 × 4 4\times 4 array of three-axis magnetometers. The axially magnetized cylindrical magnets are rigidly attached to the end-effector, with their magnetization axes separated by 120 ∘ 120^{\circ} to reduce the rotational ambiguity of a single axisymmetric magnet. As the end-effector translates and rotates relative to the array, the resulting changes in the measured field provide feedback for regulating its motion.

The magnetic measurements are transmitted to a host computer, where the controller computes incremental Cartesian commands for the robot. After each increment is executed, a new observation is acquired to update the next command. This closed-loop interaction enables the robot to approach a desired magnetic observation through successive corrections. The relation between robot motion and magnetic feedback is learned from recorded data, without requiring an analytical magnetic field model.

## II-B Task Definition

Our objective is to achieve accurate 6-DoF end-effector positioning and path tracking using magnetic feedback. For single-pose reaching, the target is specified by a magnetic observation 𝐁 ⋆ \mathbf{B}^{\star} recorded at the desired position and orientation. The task is to reach this configuration from different initial poses. For path tracking, the target is an ordered sequence of magnetic observations { 𝐁 k ⋆ } k = 1 K \{\mathbf{B}_{k}^{\star}\}_{k=1}^{K} recorded along a reference path, and the task is to follow the corresponding configurations in sequence. In both tasks, the goal is to minimize physical position and orientation errors while maintaining stable motion within the robot’s operating constraints. Accurate reaching and tracking should be retained in the presence of magnetic measurement noise and disturbances. Performance is assessed using pose errors relative to the recorded reference configurations.

2026-10-06.title: Recon2Servo: Robotic Ultrasound Visual Servoing via Learned Image-to-Motion Inference
2026-10-06.authors: Yameng Zhang , Pei Liu , Dianye Huang , Yizhao Qian , Zhongyu Chen , Xiangyu Chu , K. W. Samuel Au , Zhongliang Jiang
2026-10-06.abstract: Ultrasound visual servoing is essential for autonomous robotic ultrasound, yet 6-DoF probe control from 2D B-mode images remains challenging due to limited and ambiguous out-of-plane motion cues. Existing methods typically rely on anatomical priors or handcrafted visual features, limiting their generalizability across imaging targets. Inspired by trackerless 3D ultrasound reconstruction, we propose Recon2Servo , a visual servoing framework that learns image-to-motion inference directly from B-mode images for 6-DoF probe control. A DINOv3 encoder with low-rank adaptation and a bidirectional relation module estimate the relative probe pose between current and target images to guide iterative closed-loop target-view alignment. The framework combines supervised relative-pose learning, reconstruction-guided closed-loop adaptation, and bounded residual pose correction to improve motion inference during servoing. Evaluations on a public dataset and an in-house dataset collected from 12 healthy volunteers using different ultrasound systems demonstrate its effectiveness in reconstructed-volume servoing. Additional real-robot demonstrations of target-view alignment and dynamic tracking on a human forearm are provided in the supplementary video: https://youtu.be/qwsOdI-GMYk .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Ultrasound visual servoing is a critical technology for robotic ultrasound, as it enables the robot to directly exploit real-time imaging feedback to regulate probe motion according to the observed anatomy, thereby supporting autonomous probe navigation, image stabilization, and target tracking [ 1 ] . However, conventional medical ultrasound typically provides cross-sectional 2D images. While in-plane motion can be relatively easily estimated from abundant visual features, out-of-plane probe motion is long-standing challenging to infer because it causes anatomical structures to disappear from or newly enter the imaging plane, providing limited and often ambiguous motion cues.

In a pioneering study, Abolmaesumi et al. proposed a shared-autonomy strategy combining human expertise with ultrasound visual servoing [ 2 ] . The in-plane 3-DoF probe motion was automatically controlled to center the carotid artery in cross-sectional ultrasound images, while the remaining three out-of-plane DoFs were teleoperated by a human expert. Recently, Qian et al. employed optical flow as a feature for high-frequency 3-DoF translational tracking [ 3 ] . Extending ultrasound visual servoing to fully control the 6-DoF probe motion, however, requires servoing features that encode both in-plane and out-of-plane motion. In 2006, Bachta et al. developed a servoing method to drive the probe from an arbitrary initial pose toward a desired ultrasound image [ 4 ] . The features were derived from object boundaries extracted from ultrasound images, with the target contour recovered using polynomial regression tailored to simplified egg-shaped objects.

To enable generic visual servoing without prior knowledge of object geometry, Krupa et al. exploited ultrasound speckle to estimate both in-plane and out-of-plane probe motion [ 5 , 6 ] . Speckle patterns exhibit spatial coherence across consecutive ultrasound images, providing intrinsic visual cues for estimating probe motion. However, speckle also degrades image quality and is therefore commonly suppressed by despeckling and image-enhancement techniques in modern ultrasound systems [ 7 ] , limiting its reliability and generalizability as a visual servoing feature. Beyond speckle-based approaches, alternative image representations have been explored to construct features for 6-DoF visual servoing. Mebarki et al. employed image moments to characterize the spatial distribution of image content [ 8 , 9 ] , while Nadeau et al. directly exploited image intensities as servoing features [ 10 ] . Moving toward less handcrafted feature representations, Duflot et al. first introduced subsampled shearlet coefficients as visual features for the control law [ 11 ] . By providing a redundant yet noise-robust representation of ultrasound image content in a selected frequency domain, the shearlet coefficients enabled accurate, repeatable, and robust visual servoing, as demonstrated in both simulation and phantom experiments.

With the rapid advances in deep learning, recent studies have increasingly explored reinforcement and imitation learning for standard-plane navigation. Li et al. formulated 6-DoF standard-plane navigation as a reinforcement learning problem with a handcrafted reward function [ 12 ] . To reduce the reliance on manually designed rewards, Jiang et al. employed inverse reinforcement learning to infer image-based rewards from a small number of expert demonstrations [ 13 ] . H. Jiang et al. further adopted imitation learning to directly learn probe navigation from demonstrations, demonstrating its effectiveness in standardized carotid ultrasound scanning workflows [ 14 ] . However, these approaches are typically trained for predefined target planes or scanning tasks and therefore cannot readily generalize to arbitrarily specified imaging planes, due to the lack of a reliable mapping between ultrasound image variations and the corresponding spatial probe motion.

To address this challenge, we draw inspiration from trackerless freehand 3D ultrasound reconstruction, which has attracted increasing attention in recent years. At its core, trackerless reconstruction aims to infer the spatial motion of the ultrasound probe directly from image sequences, as demonstrated by early inter-frame pose regression methods [ 15 ] . Recent studies have further improved motion estimation by modeling long-term sequence dependencies [ 16 ] , incorporating physics-guided speckle correlation [ 17 ] , learning fine-grained spatiotemporal representations with inertial alignment [ 18 ] , and separately encoding local motion and global anatomical context, as in DualTrack [ 19 ] . Collectively, these advances demonstrate that spatial probe motion can be inferred from ultrasound image sequences by jointly exploiting local image variations and broader anatomical context. Inspired by these advances, we explore whether the image-to-motion inference capability developed for trackerless reconstruction can be leveraged to establish a generalizable spatial representation for ultrasound visual servoing.

In this study, we propose Recon2Servo , a novel ultrasound visual servoing framework that directly learns 6-DoF probe motion from B-mode ultrasound images. To the best of our knowledge, Recon2Servo is the first approach to achieve 6-DoF ultrasound visual servoing through learned image-to-motion inference, without relying on sophisticated handcrafted visual features, whose design is particularly challenging in ultrasound due to substantial inter-operator variability and inherent imaging noise. Specifically, a DINOv3 encoder [ 20 ] , adapted using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) [ 21 ] , extracts multi-level visual features that are fed into a bidirectional relation module with dedicated translation and rotation motion tokens to infer the relative 6-DoF pose between the current and target images. The predicted relative pose is directly converted into probe motion through a fixed-gain controller. To improve robustness to states encountered during closed-loop servoing, we further introduce a dataset aggregation (DAgger)-style adaptation strategy [ 22 ] , which updates the pose estimator using labeled states visited during tracked reconstruction trajectories. Finally, a bounded residual head leverages frozen relational features and the mean pose estimate to further refine the motion prediction. To evaluate the proposed method, we assess relative-pose estimation accuracy and closed-loop target-view convergence using the public TUS-REC2024 dataset [ 23 ] and an in-house ultrasound dataset collected from 12 healthy volunteers. These evaluations examine the effectiveness of the learned image-to-motion representation and its adaptation across ultrasound acquisition domains.

2026-10-06.title: P3: Persistent Particle Planning for Constrained Diffusion Control
2026-10-06.authors: Hikmet Simsir , Mahyar Fardinfar , Ozgur S. Oguz
2026-10-06.comment: Under review at ICLR 2027
2026-10-06.abstract:
Diffusion models provide expressive priors over trajectories, but
adapting these priors to test-time constraints requires maintaining
feasibility and consistency across successive control decisions.
We introduce Persistent Particle Planning (P3), a sequential Monte Carlo
framework for diffusion control that maintains a weighted population
of candidate plans across replanning steps.
At each control step, P3 shifts and partially re-noises the candidate
trajectories, refines them under the latest observation, and uses
constraint-aware weighting and resampling to select among alternative
continuations without retraining the diffusion model.
We consider denoising and replanning as one Feynman–Kac particle system
and analyze it under an idealized repair.
We prove that the re-noising depth controls how reliably a kept plan
stays on its route, and that keeping a rare, well-separated route takes
far fewer plans than rediscovering it by sampling from scratch.
Experiments under multiple test-time constraint configurations show
that population reuse reduces route switching and improves success
without constraint violations.
Because P3 refines earlier plans instead of redrawing them, it also
needs fewer denoising iterations per replan.
On maze-navigation tasks, it plans faster than both regenerated
populations and methods that correct a single sampled plan by
constrained optimization.
Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/p3-username/p3-anon .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Diffusion models represent multiple ways of completing a task as a
distribution over trajectories ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) .
Requirements not included in the training data, such as an added obstacle,
must then be imposed at test time, typically by correcting each sample
during denoising, for instance by projecting it onto the feasible set ( Christopher et al., 2024 ; Römer et al., 2025 ) .
Such corrections act on the samples of a single planning call.

A controller, however, solves a sequence of planning problems.
In receding-horizon control, it executes the first action of a
finite-horizon plan and replans from the next observation ( Mayne et al., 2000 ) , so consecutive problems share almost their
entire horizon.
Regenerating the plan from noise at every step discards that shared
solution and lets the controller alternate between modes, for example passing an obstacle on one side at
one step and on the other at the next.
Diffusion controllers reduce changes between successive plans by
ensembling or inpainting overlapping action chunks ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2025 ) , selecting the sample most
coherent with the previous decision ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , or
warm-starting the next call from the previous plan by partial noising and
denoising, which Diffuser introduced to cut planning cost ( Janner et al., 2022 ) and which RDM ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) and
streaming diffusion policies ( Høeg et al., 2025 ) build into
replanning.
Warm-starting a single plan reuses the previous trajectory, but
constraint weighting cannot affect which plan is executed when there is
only one candidate.

We introduce persistent particle planning (P3), which retains a
weighted population of plans within and across replanning calls
(Figure 1 ).
Within each planning call, P3 runs sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) over the
denoising chain ( Gordon et al., 1993 ; Del Moral, 2004 ; Chopin and Papaspiliopoulos, 2020 ) , as
prior work does for conditional and reward-guided diffusion ( Trippe et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ) .
Particles follow the model’s own denoising steps, and the constraints act
only by reweighting and resampling them according to the violations of
their predicted plans.
Across calls, P3 applies the shift-and-re-noise warm start to every
particle and carries the weights forward. The population and its
selection history become part of the controller’s state.
To separate keeping plans from selecting among them, we run the two
population samplers, best-of- N N and SMC, both with and without carrying
the population.
Our contributions are:

Method. P3 carries a constraint-weighted population
of diffusion plans across control steps. It updates each plan by
shifting and partially re-noising it instead of redrawing it, and it
can rejuvenate the population with new plans. It needs no retraining,
and a warm call runs only t 0 + 1 t_{0}+1 of the K K denoising steps
(Section 3 ).

Theory. We consider denoising and replanning as a single
Feynman–Kac model and analyze it under an idealized repair. The
re-noising depth controls how reliably a kept plan stays on its
route. A rare but well-separated route can be kept with far fewer
plans than sampling from scratch needs to rediscover it. For independent
acceptable plans drawn from the model, one exact repair at a fixed
observation is at least as likely, on average, to leave an acceptable
plan as drawing a fresh population of the same size
(Section 3.4 ).

Evidence. We evaluate on obstacle-avoidance and
maze-navigation benchmarks whose constraints are added only at test
time. Persistence helps most where a feasible route is hard to find
from scratch. There, P3 reaches the goal without violations far more
often than a population of the same size regenerated at every step.
Elsewhere, it matches or exceeds regenerated populations. Controls
separate the two effects. Keeping plans reduces route switching, and
constraint weighting and resampling further raise success without
violations on several tasks. On maze navigation, P3 also plans faster than
regenerating the population or correcting a single plan by
optimization (Section 4 ).

2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

In decision making, diffusion models have been used as trajectory
generators whose samples are steered toward rewards or goals by guidance ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Ajay et al., 2023 ) , as visuomotor policies
that denoise action chunks and execute them in a receding-horizon loop ( Chi et al., 2023 ) , and as motion planners that combine the
learned prior with collision costs ( Carvalho et al., 2023 ) .
These models can represent multiple ways of completing a task ( Shafiullah et al., 2022 ; Jia et al., 2024 ) .
Model-based variants derive the score from a dynamics model rather
than from data ( Pan et al., 2024 ) .
P3 keeps the pretrained model and its transitions fixed and acts only on
which samples survive and which are reused.

Test-time constraints are usually imposed by modifying the sampling
path.
Gradient guidance adds the gradient of a constraint cost to the score ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Janner et al., 2022 ) , control-barrier
guidance enforces finite-time invariance of the denoising dynamics ( Xiao et al., 2025 ) , and projection methods map each iterate
or its clean prediction onto the feasible set ( Christopher et al., 2024 ; Römer et al., 2025 ) ; DiRecT argues
that projecting noisy iterates over-constrains the sampler and instead
enforces the constraint on the final sample through a receding-horizon
optimal-control formulation ( Giaretta et al., 2026 ) .
A separate line changes the model so that its state space is the
constrained domain ( Lou and Ermon, 2023 ; Fishman et al., 2023 ) .
These approaches modify the sampling dynamics or the samples themselves.
P3 leaves the proposal untouched and reweights its reference path law.
Unlike exact projection, reweighting does not place excluded mass on a
previously null constraint boundary; its accumulated path potentials
can still change the relative masses of feasible routes
(Appendices A.2 and A.6 ).

SMC approximations to Feynman–Kac models have been used for conditional
and reward-guided diffusion sampling.
SMC over the denoising chain conditions on partial observations ( Trippe et al., 2023 ) ; twisted proposals with telescoped
potentials give asymptotically exact conditional samplers ( Wu et al., 2023 ) ; and filtering formulations address linear
inverse problems ( Cardoso et al., 2024 ; Dou and Song, 2024 ) .
Related SMC methods are used for inference-time reward alignment ( Li et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Singhal et al., 2025 ; Skreta et al., 2025 ) ,
diverse batch sampling through joint potentials ( Corso et al., 2024 ) ,
and search over initial noises ( Ma et al., 2025 ) .
The choice of potential affects sampling efficiency, and twisting
functions can be learned ( Whiteley and Lee, 2014 ; Guarniero et al., 2017 ; Heng et al., 2020 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) .
These methods sample one target with a population created from noise
and discarded afterward.
P3 uses a plain plug-in potential, to which learned twisting could be
added, and keeps the population, its weights and its lineages across
replanning calls; for fixed observations this is one Feynman–Kac model
spanning denoising and replanning (Section 3 ).

Sampling-based model predictive control carries information across
control steps. MPPI and cross-entropy planners shift and perturb the
previous control sequence ( Williams et al., 2017 ; Chua et al., 2018 ) ,
SMC solves the open-loop problem at each step ( Kantas et al., 2009 ; Piché et al., 2019 ) , and Stein
variational MPC keeps control-sequence particles between steps to
preserve modes ( Lambert et al., 2020 ) ; particle filters recover from
a lost track by injecting fresh particles ( Thrun et al., 2005 ) and diversify by invariant moves ( Gilks and Berzuini, 2001 ) .
Diffuser warm-starts each plan by partially noising and denoising the
previous one ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Meng et al., 2022 ) , RDM reuses one
plan until the model’s likelihood triggers regeneration ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) , and Streaming Diffusion Policy rolls a
partially denoised trajectory forward ( Høeg et al., 2025 ) ; all
keep one trajectory.
Diffusion-ES mutates high-reward diffusion samples by partial noising
and denoising, and can warm-start its population with solutions from the
previous control step ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Guided flow-matching
samples have also been refined by MPPI with warm starts ( Mizuta and Leung, 2025 ) .
P3 weights and resamples particles during denoising, then carries the
plans and their weights across control steps. It repairs this population
by partial noising and denoising and can add fresh particles.

2026-10-06.title: Infant simulator with an embodied caregiver: Generating infant-perspective touch and vision during social interaction
2026-10-06.authors: Noemi Vaculinova , Matej Hoffmann
2026-10-06.abstract: Early development unfolds in caregiver–infant dyads, where infants’ sensorimotor streams are shaped by physical contact and face-to-face interaction. Yet developmental robotics simulators commonly model infants in isolation, limiting the study of caregiver-mediated experience. We present a caregiver-enabled extension of the Multi-Modal Infant Model (MIMo) in MuJoCo that turns MIMo into a controllable platform for replaying dyadic interaction and generating dense infant-perspective observations. The system provides (i) an articulated caregiver model compatible with MIMo morphologies, parameterized from anthropometrics and optionally resized to a recorded caregiver; (ii) a workflow to replay naturalistic caregiver–infant holding and soothing interactions; and (iii) logging and visualizing the infant’s first-person multimodal experience (we show touch and vision). We showcase the tool on touch by introducing origin-aware contact logging that disambiguates self-, caregiver-, and environment-generated contact and supports aggregation into touch-rate statistics comparable to manual coding. While we showcase tactile analysis, the platform is intended more broadly as a generator of multimodal dyadic datasets (touch and egocentric vision) for modeling the development of social interaction.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Early development unfolds in caregiver–infant dyads: caregivers shape infants’ sensorimotor statistics through physical handling, affective touch, and close-range face-to-face interaction.
Touch is among the earliest developing senses [ 32 ] and remains a primary channel for regulation and learning [ 15 ] . Caregiver touch plays a significant role in early regulation and clinical care ( e.g. , soothing touch and stroking) [ 37 , 25 ] . In clinical practice, tactile contact such as skin-to-skin (kangaroo care) is associated with improved outcomes, including for preterm infants [ 29 , 2 , 48 ] , and affectionate caregiver touch relates to neurodevelopment and dyadic synchrony [ 7 ] . Behavioral analyses have described major holding positions and their developmental progression [ 33 , 38 ] , motivating simulation scenarios in which caregiver posture and contact are central variables.
Similarly, although vision is quite poor at birth, it develops quickly and the details about how often, for how long, and from which angles the caregiver appears in the infant’s visual field may be important to understand the development of face processing [ 6 ] or the development of social cognition in general [ 27 , 44 ] .
Addressing these questions requires access to the infant’s first-person experience.

Looking at a single infant, manual video annotation can quantify spontaneous touches of the hand to the body [ 42 , 11 , 20 ] and touches to the floor [ 11 ] , but it is very laborious to code (cf. this dedicated tool https://github.com/ctu-vras/touch-coder ) and does not scale to whole-body contact, occluded body surfaces, or continuous force estimation.
Pressure mats can capture infant-surface contact only [ 22 ] .
Tactile stimuli are processed differently depending on the stimulus identity, namely on whether they are produced by oneself, by another person or by an inanimate object [ 41 ] . Thus, the source of contact has important developmental relevance.
Moreover, for affective touch, there are additional factors such as active generation of the touch or stroking speed.
A physics-based simulator with the infant and caregiver brings important advantages: whole-body contacts can be recorded and further differentiated into self-touch, caregiver touch, and contacts with the environment.

Seeing the world through the infant’s eyes is also critical for our understanding of development. Head-mounted cameras were employed by the groups of Linda Smith and Chen Yu to study what is in toddler’s view and the consequences on the development of perception and language [ 49 , 39 ] . There has been less work studying the presence of the caregiver in the infant’s view, with notable exceptions [ 3 , 12 , 40 ] .
However, head-mounted devices may still be intrusive and hard to apply on even younger infants.
Having both the infant and the caregiver simulated, incl. the visual streams from their eyes, brings several advantages. First, one can rely on infant and caregiver pose estimation from an external camera only and then retarget these motions into the simulator, without the need for wearable devices. The caregiver and infant in the simulator can also move autonomously and any scenario can be simulated. Second, the gaze is composed of the eye direction and head orientation and these can be studied independently in the simulator. In addition, one can also emulate the gradual maturation of infant vision in the simulator, manipulating the field of view, acuity, etc. [ 24 ] .

Physics simulation is widely used to generate repeatable, scalable experiments [ 8 ] .
Biomechanical simulators ( e.g. , OpenSim [ 9 ] ) provide detailed anatomy but can be computationally intensive.
MuJoCo [ 43 ] offers fast contact dynamics and is widely used in robot learning research.
Infant-focused simulators include a soft-body fetus-in-uterus model [ 21 ] and MIMo [ 26 ] , which provides multimodal sensing and a simplified rigid-body infant.
Recent work on MIMo added growth across infant ages and additional sensing features [ 24 ] .
Motion retargeting approaches can translate captured infant movements into simulations, enabling the estimation of contact streams [ 13 ] .
To our knowledge, existing infant simulators largely lack an embodied caregiver capable of physical interaction and contact generation.

Developmental robotics simulators commonly model infants in isolation, limiting the study of caregiver-mediated experience and its developmental consequences.
We address this gap by adding an embodied caregiver to MIMo [ 26 ] , a MuJoCo-based simulator designed to study early development with multimodal sensing and compatibility with learning pipelines ( e.g. , Gym/Gymnasium-style APIs [ 5 , 45 ] ).
Our goal is not to replace empirical studies but to provide a controllable platform that can generate dense tactile and visual observations from the infant’s perspective during caregiver interaction—including contacts that are difficult to observe in video ( e.g. , back-of-head and back-of-torso contact).
This work provides:

Caregiver model : an adult female caregiver compatible with the MIMo ecosystem, parameterized using anthropometric data [ 17 ] and optionally resized to a specific caregiver.

Interaction replay : a workflow to replay caregiver–infant interactions.

Logging and visualizing the infant’s first-person multimodal experience : We focus on touch and demonstrate also vision from the infant’s perspective. We extend MIMo touch processing to separate self- and caregiver-origin touches, log spatiotemporal contact with origin metadata, and generate touch-rate heatmaps over infant body regions.

Demonstrations and comparisons : evaluation of recorded holding/caressing scenarios inspired by behavioral descriptions of infant holding [ 33 , 38 ] , replayed with different infant ages [ 24 ] , and comparison to manually coded infant hand self-touch statistics [ 20 ] .

# II METHODS

## II-A System overview

In our expansion of the MIMo simulator, we
(i) model a caregiver compatible with MIMo, (ii) record caregiver–infant interaction motion with an actor holding a newborn-sized doll, (iii) retarget the motion to the simulated caregiver (and partially to the infant) using MuJoCo MoCap bodies, and (iv) log and analyze tactile contact on the infant’s body, distinguishing touch origin (caregiver vs. self vs. environment).
Fig. 1 summarizes the pipeline leading from the recorded motion to the touch and visual outputs.

## II-B MIMo infant model and sensing modalities

MIMo is a MuJoCo-based infant simulator with multimodal sensing, including proprioception, vestibular signals, binocular “eye” cameras, and tactile sensing [ 26 ] .
To support machine learning experiments, MIMo uses a rigid-body and a capsule-based morphology—trading anatomical detail for fast and robust collision handling.
Touch is represented by a set of surface sensors distributed over each body part.
In the newborn-sized model used here, the sensor count is on the order of a few thousand (about three thousand in the default configuration), with denser sampling on hands and feet than on the torso and limbs (mirroring differential tactile acuity).
Sensor density is independent of body size and can be adjusted per body part via modality parameters.

In this work, we focus on two modalities: (i) touch (for analyzing where and by whom the infant is contacted) and (ii) vision (for the infant’s egocentric view during interactions).
We also record a third-person render for qualitative inspection and debugging.

## II-C Caregiver model

The caregiver is implemented as a rigid-body, capsule-based articulated model, following MIMo’s design philosophy. We created a base model with proportions derived from the 50th percentile female measurements in a large anthropometric study [ 17 ] .
Segment masses were assigned using established body-segment mass distributions [ 35 ] with total body mass set to match the chosen anthropometric percentile.
To enable subject-specific replay, we provide a resizing procedure that scales the base model to measured limb lengths and circumferences of a recorded caregiver or actor (see Fig. 2 ). These measurements are then recalculated to parameters representing the capsules, spheres, boxes, and cylinders. This produces a body model matched to actual recorded caregiver.

Fig. 3 shows the infant and caregiver models used in this paper.
We use the “simple” MIMo hand/foot configuration (mitten-like hands) to match the caregiver’s simplified hands and because grasping dexterity is not included in the recorded replay scenarios.

## II-D Retargeting caregiver motions

In this work, we recorded an actor holding a realistic newborn-size stand-in-baby doll in positions inspired by the literature [ 33 , 38 ] . The actor was wearing a motion capture suit with markers. However, the pipeline could be modified to use, for example, 3d keypoints extracted from a video recording (see [ 30 ] ).

Using an infrared motion capture camera system, we recorded short mock caregiver–infant interactions (up to 40 s each) with an actor wearing a marker-based optical motion capture suit with 43 markers while holding and caressing a newborn-sized doll with markers on its head. Then, the recorded marker trajectories were labeled, cleaned, and exported as a time series.

In the simulator, we import the marker trajectories and drive the caregiver using MuJoCo MoCap bodies [ 28 ] . These are defined as massless and shapeless bodies, which are linked to the corresponding bodies of the models through standard MuJoCo equality constraints.
Because the recorded infant doll was not actuated, the simulated infant is treated as a passive physical body, whose pose emerges from physics and caregiver contact, rather than full-body kinematic retargeting.
This design choice trades pose accuracy for physically consistent collision and force generation, which is central to our target outputs (touch and vision). Also, having only three markers on the infant leads to fewer marker occlusions in the captured footage when the actor holds the doll.

A practical issue in close-contact scenarios is camera clipping in the eye views when the infant’s head is pressed against the caregiver body.
In these cases, we reduce the near clipping distance ( znear ) in the MuJoCo visual parameters to render near-surface geometry, enabling usable egocentric visual streams even in “hug” configurations.

## II-E Touch sensing, origin disambiguation, and time-series logging

MIMo implements touch using several thousand touch sensors distributed over the infant body.
At each simulation step, MuJoCo provides a list of contacts between bodies. From those, MIMo finds contact pairs with at least one participant equipped with sensors (meaning contacts to the infant). As the bodies used are rigid and simplified, the contact between them culminates in one contact point. To simulate human-like soft touches, the contacts are linearly spread around the contact point for further processing or visualization. The touch output is then a list of activated sensors and the forces acting on them.

We extend MIMo’s touch processing to
assign each contact a touch origin category as a context indicator about the participant who touches the infant sensors ( infant for self-touches, caregiver , or environment ).
For touch analysis purposes, we further map sensors to a coarser set of 50 body regions (front and back of the head, torso, upper/lower limbs, hands, feet, etc.), consistent with prior touch statistics heatmap visualizations [ 20 ] ; see Fig. 4 for a visualization of the areas on MIMo and the standardized infant illustration.

2026-10-06.title: How (and How Not) to Use Data Augmentation in VLA Post-Training
2026-10-06.authors: Bram Grooten , Joaquin Vanschoren
2026-10-06.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 workshop RoboPAD. Code and videos at this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models currently demonstrate strong performance in a wide range of real-world robotics tasks. However, they often still lack the generalization ability to handle large visual out-of-distribution shifts. Post-training of VLAs with reinforcement learning (RL) has been shown to benefit robustness, but significant room for improvement remains. In this work, we systematically study the effect of image augmentation on VLA post-training. We find that it is crucial to augment only the critic module during RL updates, while leaving the actor’s input clean during both rollouts and updates. For π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.5 this raises out-of-distribution success on LIBERO-Plus by 7.8 7.8 and 10.0 10.0 points respectively, while augmenting the actor collapses training entirely. We investigate a range of augmentation types and strengths, and provide practical recommendations for improving generalization in VLA post-training. 1 1 1 Code and videos are available at: https://bramgrooten.nl/vla-augm/
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as capable generalist robot policies, yet their performance degrades sharply under visual shifts that are common in the real world: new backgrounds, lighting, distractors, and camera poses ( Fei et al., 2025 ) . A promising route to closing this gap is post-training pretrained VLAs with reinforcement learning (RL), which has been shown to improve execution and semantic generalization by Liu et al. (2025b) . However, the authors also indicate that RL post-training alone does not consistently improve robustness to visual out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts, leaving a central limitation for real-world deployment unsolved.

Image augmentation is a natural, low-cost solution with a long history of improving visual robustness in deep RL, and the question of where to inject augmentation within an actor-critic network is well studied. Hansen et al. (2021) stabilized Q-learning by augmenting the value path while keeping the bootstrap target clean, and Almuzairee et al. (2024) later showed that, for standard convolutional policies, augmenting both actor and critic inputs (with a clean target network) is more effective. Yet this line of work studies small CNN encoders with Gaussian or categorical actors, a regime far from modern vision–language–action models. In VLAs the visual encoder is a large pretrained VLM whose features risk being corrupted, and the actor is a flow-matching head through which gradients must propagate. Whether existing augmentation recipes transfer to this setting remains unknown.

In this work, we provide the first systematic study of image augmentation for VLA post-training. We ablate where augmentation is applied (actor vs. critic), what type of augmentation is used, and how strongly it can be pushed before training collapses. Our central finding inverts prior wisdom: for VLAs post-trained with PPO, critic-only augmentation is most effective, and augmenting the actor is detrimental to training dynamics, which is the opposite of the conclusion drawn for convolutional policies ( Almuzairee et al., 2024 ) . Figure 1 shows both halves of that result: what the augmented observations look like, and what applying them in the wrong place does to post-training. Based on these results, we distill practical rules of thumb for robust VLA post-training.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Prior Work on Data Augmentation for VLAs

VLA models combine a pretrained vision-language backbone with an action head and are typically trained by imitation learning on large demonstration datasets ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) .
A growing line of work further fine-tunes VLAs with online reinforcement learning ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Zang et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2025 ) , including methods designed specifically for diffusion and flow-matching action experts ( Ren et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Lyu et al., 2026 ) .
These approaches mainly improve in-distribution task success. In a controlled study, Liu et al. (2025b) find that RL post-training improves execution and semantic generalization, but yields little to no gain on visual out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts such as background and texture changes.
How the backbone is adapted matters too: Hu et al. (2026) show that on-policy RL with low-rank adaptation preserves a VLA’s performance in continual learning over a sequence of tasks.

Image augmentation has a long history of improving sample efficiency and generalization in visual RL ( Laskin et al., 2020 ; Yarats et al., 2021 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) , and the question of how to apply augmentation within the update has been studied in detail. Hansen et al. (2021) stabilize Q-learning by augmenting the value path while keeping the bootstrap target clean, Raileanu et al. (2021) regularize policy and value toward invariance across augmentations, Grooten et al. (2024) mask distracting image regions, and Almuzairee et al. (2024) conclude that augmenting both actor and critic inputs, while keeping the target network clean, is most effective.
All of these works, however, consider small convolutional encoders with Gaussian or categorical actors, a regime far from modern VLAs with pretrained VLM backbones and flow-matching action experts.

Robustness benchmarks show that VLAs are brittle under visual perturbations; on LIBERO-Plus, for instance, success rates can collapse from 95% to below 30% under modest lighting or background changes ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Fei et al., 2025 ) .
Several recent methods target this gap. Grover et al. (2025) improve visual robustness by preserving pretrained VLM representations during fine-tuning.
On the RL side, Zhang et al. (2025a) add Jacobian and smoothness regularizers during post-training, Xie et al. (2026) decouple robustness learning from task alignment in a two-stage curriculum, and Peng et al. (2026) introduce paired auxiliary losses that enforce invariance to task-preserving visual changes and sensitivity to task-altering ones.
Other works move augmentation out of the RL update entirely: Gao et al. (2026) apply style augmentation inside a learned world model, Shi et al. (2026) rely on domain-randomized simulation for sim-real co-training, and Xue et al. (2025) augment the demonstration data itself via exploratory sampling.

Despite this activity, no prior work studies where image augmentation should be injected during RL post-training of VLAs—actor, critic, or both—even though this placement question is well understood for conventional visual RL ( Hansen et al., 2021 ; Raileanu et al., 2021 ) .
The closest works answer adjacent questions: Peng et al. (2026) achieve visual robustness in VLAs through auxiliary paired losses rather than augmentation, and Almuzairee et al. (2024) study augmentation placement only for small convolutional policies.
Our work fills this gap with a systematic study of where augmentation should be applied, what type works best, and how strong it can be during VLA post-training.

2026-10-06.title: A State Based Dispatch Controller for Hospital Delivery Robots with Shared Human and Infrastructure Resources
2026-10-06.authors: Krzysztof Siwek , Aleksandra Świetlicka
2026-10-06.abstract:
Hospital delivery robots share staff, elevators, charging stations, and cleaning facilities with clinical operations. We formulate adaptive resource aware dispatch (ARAD), a deterministic state feedback controller that maps each arriving request and the observable system state to human or robot assignment. Its admissibility conditions represent human availability, deadline slack, elevator pressure, human queue pressure, service station pressure, and a fleet reserve. We evaluate ARAD in a discrete event simulation based on 33,079 transport requests from the University Medical Center Freiburg and a synthetic task mix derived from MIMIC demo event counts. The model schedules robot loading, receiving, coordination, cleaning, and recovery on individual transporter shifts. It also enforces battery feasibility and shared elevator capacity. In the earlier experiment, a recalibrated human roster was compared with one, two, and four robot fleets in 30 paired replications. Two ARAD robots increased overall late or incomplete requests by 0.37 percentage points (95 percent Monte Carlo confidence interval, 0.26 to 0.49) and urgent lateness by 0.82 points (0.70 to 0.95). Human idle time in intervals of at least 10 minutes decreased by 11.5 minutes per 100 nominal beds per day, while robot support consumed 56.4 minutes on the same scale. A deadline feasible benchmark did not improve on the human roster. The formal controller and coupled resource model make the assignment logic reproducible, while the results show that an admissible robot mission need not improve system performance when human support and building congestion are included.
The updated operational study adds location aware travel and assignment, two full scenario grids totaling 2,160 runs, and 120 further deadline benchmark runs. In one high roster scenario, increasing assumed elevator capacity from two to four servers lowers human only lateness from 55.11 percent to 3.18 percent. The dispatch rules do not show a stable service gain across the updated grids. These conditional comparisons remain sensitive to unobserved staffing, deadlines, and building operations.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Hospital delivery robots share corridors and elevators with people, making their operation part of a broader human–robot interaction setting in which robotic systems must account for both human behavior and the shared environment [ 1 ] Mobile robots can perform some of these journeys, but service depends on more than travel speed. Robots also need elevators, charging stations, and cleaning facilities. A review and an observational study of robotics in nursing describe applications and implementation challenges [ 2 , 3 ] . For transport planning, another question is whether moving work to robots changes the timing of staff availability in a useful way.

Simulation, scheduling, and fleet control for hospital delivery robots are established research areas. Bhosekar and colleagues modeled hospital inventory and material handling [ 4 ] . Cheng and colleagues studied stochastic scheduling of autonomous mobile robots with time windows and hospital costs [ 5 ] . Guzmán Ortiz and colleagues described a fleet management architecture for healthcare environments [ 6 ] . Ge and colleagues used discrete event simulation to study automated guided vehicle systems in operating theaters [ 7 ] . Recent hospital pilots have also evaluated a modular logistics robot in clinical environments [ 8 ] . These studies show that the main research gap is not whether hospital robots can be simulated or scheduled. The unresolved question is how dispatch choices, shared building resources, and human support work jointly affect service and staff availability.

This study contributes a formal state and decision model for adaptive resource aware dispatch, a simulation architecture that couples robot missions to human support and shared infrastructure, and a reproducible evaluation against a deadline feasible controller and a feasible human roster. ARAD is a transparent rule based controller rather than a learned or globally optimized policy. Its purpose is to make every robot admission decision traceable to observable state and explicit constraints. The experiments report deadline performance, transporter idle interval structure, modeled energy, support burden, charging, cleaning, elevator traffic, and movement between assignments. The central question is conditional: when does a robot assignment remain beneficial after the resources required to complete that mission are represented explicitly?

This extended article retains the earlier experiments and adds the updated operational study reported in the current IEEE manuscript. The earlier primary model omits travel to pickups and uses a roster screened under that assumption. Its repositioning experiment is a separate stress case. The updated study instead includes worker and robot locations, travel to pickups and support handoffs, and nearest available assignment in every main scenario. The two studies have different operating models and rosters. Their absolute outcomes should not be treated as estimates from one unchanged experiment. Sections explicitly identify the earlier experiments and the updated operational analysis.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Hospital logistics robots and simulation

Hospital robotics includes material transport, disinfection, telepresence, rehabilitation, and direct clinical assistance. Reviews of this field show substantial technical diversity, but also limited evidence that robot deployment produces measurable improvements in routine clinical work [ 9 , 10 , 2 , 11 ] . This distinction is important for logistics applications. A robot may complete a transport mission successfully without reducing staff workload if people must still perform loading, receiving, access control, or recovery tasks.

Research on hospital material transport has examined both system design and operational performance. Özkil and colleagues analyzed existing hospital transport processes before defining requirements for a mobile service robot [ 12 ] . Fragapane and colleagues evaluated autonomous mobile robots for sterile instrument logistics and showed that the suitability of a transport system depends on its fit with the hospital layout and material flow [ 13 ] . Bhosekar and colleagues linked inventory decisions with hospital material handling through discrete event simulation [ 4 ] . Ge and colleagues used the same methodological approach to examine automated guided vehicle systems in operating theaters [ 7 ] . These studies establish simulation as an appropriate method for evaluating hospital transport systems, while also showing that demand structure, layout, routing, and operational rules must be represented explicitly.

Existing models often treat vehicle movement as the principal source of capacity. That abstraction is suitable for evaluating routing and fleet size, but it can overstate autonomy when mission completion depends on staff or shared facilities. Elevators, charging stations, cleaning facilities, and handoff activities can create queues that are not visible in a travel centered model. The present study therefore represents robot movement as one component of a coupled service process rather than as an independent replacement for human transport.

## II-B Task allocation and fleet control

Robot dispatch belongs to the broader class of task allocation problems. Gerkey and Matarić formalized this class in terms of robot capabilities, task characteristics, temporal structure, and allocation objectives [ 14 ] , while learning-based HRI research has also explored graph-based representations of human-generated information, including natural-language interactions [ 15 ] . Aziz and colleagues reviewed allocation methods for robot teams and emphasized the relation between decision structure, uncertainty, and performance criteria [ 16 ] . These frameworks indicate that a dispatch policy should identify its observable state, admissible actions, and objective rather than describe assignments only through simulation scenarios.

Several studies address allocation and scheduling in settings that are directly relevant to hospital logistics. Das and colleagues developed distributed auction and consensus mechanisms for heterogeneous robots in healthcare facilities [ 17 ] . Cheng and colleagues formulated stochastic scheduling of hospital mobile robots with time windows and operating costs [ 5 ] . Verma and colleagues considered dynamic allocation and task transfer in heterogeneous robot teams [ 18 ] . Guzmán Ortiz and colleagues proposed a fleet management architecture for healthcare environments, while López and colleagues linked simulation with control software for automated transport systems [ 6 , 19 ] . Meskar and Ahmadi-Javid incorporated explicit energy constraints into a location and routing model for autonomous delivery [ 20 ] .

The methods in this literature range from global optimization and distributed negotiation to online control rules. Optimization models can coordinate assignments over a planning horizon, but they require forecasts and a tractable representation of future system behavior. Distributed methods are appropriate when individual robots negotiate tasks, although they do not by themselves represent hospital staff or building resources. Transparent online rules require fewer assumptions and support direct interpretation, but their state variables and constraints must be stated precisely. The adaptive resource aware dispatch controller examined here belongs to the last category. It makes one resource class decision at each request arrival and does not claim horizon wide optimality.

## II-C Human work and deployment evidence

Evidence about staff capacity is less mature than research on routing and scheduling. Babalola and colleagues found that relatively few collaborative robot studies were designed around nursing workload [ 2 ] . Sommer and colleagues documented transport activities performed by nurses, but the observation of transport work does not establish that an automated trip creates a continuous interval that can be reassigned to clinical care [ 3 ] . Kim and colleagues similarly emphasized the importance of clinical context and workflow alignment when evaluating hospital robots [ 11 ] . These findings suggest that staff outcomes should be based on scheduled work and the temporal structure of released capacity, not on robot trip counts alone.

Deployment studies also show that technical performance is shaped by local workflow. A modular logistics robot has been evaluated in three European hospital pilots [ 8 ] . Li and colleagues reported a six month, single center comparison of manual and robot delivery for drugs and specimens [ 21 ] . Such studies provide useful evidence of operational feasibility, but their results depend on the selected tasks, hospital layout, handoff procedures, fleet configuration, and economic assumptions. Earlier organizational research likewise showed that robot performance depends on the social and physical environment in which a system is introduced [ 22 ] . Results from one deployment therefore cannot be transferred directly to another hospital without a comparable workflow and resource structure.

## II-D Research gap and study position

Prior work provides strong foundations for hospital robot design, fleet scheduling, and transport simulation. Three limitations remain relevant to claims about staff capacity. First, human loading, receiving, coordination, recovery, and cleaning support are rarely scheduled on the same workers whose capacity is expected to increase. Second, robot dispatch is not always expressed as a reproducible state dependent decision method with explicit admissibility conditions. Third, shared infrastructure and travel between consecutive assignments are often separated from the dispatch decision, even though they determine when a vehicle becomes available again.

This study addresses these limitations through a formal online controller embedded in a discrete event model of coupled human, robot, and infrastructure resources. The controller maps each arriving request and the observable system state to a human or robot assignment. The execution model then schedules the support work and shared resource use created by that decision. The contribution is therefore not a new navigation method or a globally optimal task allocator. It is a reproducible decision model for testing whether an admissible robot assignment remains beneficial after its human and infrastructure requirements are represented explicitly.

2026-10-06.title: From Social Reasoning to Embodied Interaction: An Agentic Framework for Social Robots
2026-10-06.authors: Ziyu Cheng , Yuewen Guo , Zhirui Liu , Dong Zhang , Haotao Lu , Jingyi Yu , Ye Shi , Jingya Wang
2026-10-06.abstract: Natural face-to-face human–robot interaction requires a robot to understand an evolving social situation, decide when to engage, and express its intent through coordinated physical behavior. Yet existing approaches rarely close this loop: foundation-model agents provide increasingly capable multimodal reasoning and memory but remain largely disembodied, while expressive virtual agents do not face the physical constraints of real robots, and physical social robots typically address social reasoning and embodied expression only partially. We present ARISE , a unified framework that bridges A gentic R easoning and I nteractive S ocial E mbodiment on the Sophia humanoid robot. ARISE integrates multimodal context understanding, long-term memory, and reactive and proactive interaction to determine when and what to communicate, and translates social intent into robot-native gestures coordinated with speech and mechanical facial expressions through streaming execution. Extensive evaluations on Sophia demonstrate strong perceived interaction quality, expressive and well-coordinated embodied behavior, and substantial latency reductions through streaming execution. These results highlight the importance of jointly reasoning about what to communicate, when to engage, and how to physically express social intent for natural interaction with humanoid robots. Project Page: https://robosocial.github.io/
2026-10-06.introduction:
Empowering embodied agents with social intelligence is central to realizing
general-purpose human–robot interaction. A capable social agent should not
only infer human intentions from multi-modal interactions and generate
appropriate responses, but also continuously perceive and reason about its
surroundings, maintain awareness over extended interactions, and proactively
engage with humans in real time [ 9 , 5 ] .
These capabilities become particularly compelling when embodied in humanoid
robots, where perception, reasoning, communication, and physical behavior are
tightly coupled in real-world interaction. Such physically grounded social
intelligence therefore represents a promising direction toward interactive
embodied agents that can naturally coexist and communicate with humans in
everyday environments.

Recent advances in foundation models have substantially expanded the
capabilities of digital social agents, enabling natural, context-aware
communication and long-horizon multimodal interaction [ 9 ] . Yet, such agents remain fundamentally disembodied,
lacking the nonverbal behaviors essential to social interaction. Video-based
avatars and 3D virtual humans have introduced expressive facial and full-body
behaviors, including human animation [ 10 , 11 ] ,
co-speech gesture generation [ 1 , 3 ] , and
real-time motion synthesis [ 12 , 2 , 13 ] ,
but remain confined to virtual spaces. Transferring these capabilities from
digital embodiments to physical robots remains challenging: virtual motion is
largely unconstrained, whereas physical execution must respect limited degrees
of freedom, joint limits, and hardware-specific actuation constraints.
Physical social robots have begun to integrate foundation-model reasoning with
expressive behavior, supporting affect-aware interaction [ 14 ] ,
proactive assistance [ 5 ] , interruption-aware
dialogue [ 15 ] , and expressive facial
behavior [ 16 , 6 ] . However, these capabilities
have largely been studied in isolation. A unified physical social agent that
can understand evolving social context, engage proactively, and coordinate verbal and nonverbal behavior remains largely unexplored.

To address this gap, we present a unified embodied social interaction system
deployed on the Sophia [ 17 ] humanoid robot. At its core, a
multimodal social agent directly reasons over conversational audio and visual
observations, augmented with long-term memory, online knowledge retrieval, and
proactive interaction to support both reactive and self-initiated engagement.
An embodiment-aware gesture planner further translates response intent into
verified symbolic gesture programs composed of executable upper-body motion
primitives. To realize these high-level decisions as coherent physical
behavior, we introduce a streaming multimodal orchestration scheme that
synchronizes speech with audio-driven facial animation and schedules gestures
online using the audio–facial stream as a shared temporal reference. Together,
these components couple multimodal social reasoning with coordinated verbal
and nonverbal behavior, enabling context-aware and proactive face-to-face
interaction on a physical humanoid robot.

We summarize our core contributions as follows:

We present ARISE , a unified framework for physical humanoid social interaction that combines multimodal social reasoning, long-term memory, and coordinated embodied expression, supporting both reactive and proactive engagement.

We bridge high-level agentic social reasoning and low-level
embodiment-aware gesture planning to translate social intent into executable robot behavior. Streaming Multimodal Orchestration further coordinates asynchronous speech, facial animation, and gesture streams for progressive embodied execution.

Extensive evaluations on Sophia demonstrate strong context-aware social interaction, effective proactive engagement, and expressive, coordinated embodied behavior.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II RELATED WORKS

## II-A Social Reasoning with Foundation Models

Large models have expanded social interaction from dialogue generation toward multimodal understanding, memory, and contextual planning [ 18 ] . Socratic Models [ 19 ] and embodied multimodal models such as PaLM-E [ 20 ] compose pretrained models through language to support multimodal reasoning and assistive dialogue. Generative Agents [ 21 ] integrate memory, reflection, and planning to produce sustained social behavior in simulated environments. M3-Agent [ 9 ] further extends memory-based reasoning to visual and auditory experience through episodic and semantic memory. Together, these approaches provide increasingly capable foundations for understanding social context and formulating appropriate responses. However, social reasoning alone does not deliver the physical presence and expressive behavior needed for immersive interaction. Our framework bridges this gap by translating multimodal, memory-augmented reasoning into coordinated speech, facial expressions, and upper-body gestures on a physical humanoid.

## II-B Co-speech Gesture Generation

Co-speech gesture generation has advanced toward expressive, holistic animation of 3D digital humans. EMAGE [ 1 ] integrates audio conditioning with masked gesture modeling to generate coordinated face, body, and hand motion. DiffSHEG [ 22 ] jointly models facial expressions and body gestures through diffusion, supporting synchronized motion generation for arbitrary-length speech. More recently, MIBURI [ 3 ] enables online, causal generation of expressive gestures and facial expressions alongside streaming dialogue. These methods advance motion quality and responsiveness primarily in virtual human representations. However, transferring such expressiveness to physical robots requires accommodating fewer degrees of freedom and hardware-specific joint limits. We address this challenge by composing and verifying robot-native gesture programs to support semantic expressiveness and speech coordination within the robot’s constrained motion repertoire.

## II-C Multimodal Interaction in Social Robotics

Social robotics has progressed from coordinated multimodal expression toward adaptive, reasoning-driven interaction. Early work by Aly and Tapus [ 4 ] combines emotional speech, facial expressions, and speech-accompanying head and arm gestures in narrative interaction. More recent systems advance social decision-making: Attentive Support [ 5 ] reasons about when and how to assist human groups, while Garello et al. [ 7 ] integrate LLM-based interaction management with knowledge-graph memory for adaptive tutoring. In parallel, speech-driven animatronic control and ExFace improve expressive facial actuation on physical robots [ 16 , 6 ] . ProAct [ 8 ] further connects memory-based proactive reasoning with streaming humanoid motion, bringing social planning and embodied behavior closer together.

However, these systems typically emphasize selected aspects of social reasoning or embodied expression, leaving their integration incomplete, as summarized in Table I . Our framework unifies memory-augmented reactive and proactive planning with coordinated speech, mechanical facial expressions, and verified upper-body gestures through a shared streaming pipeline, enabling context-aware, expressive, and responsive interaction on a physical humanoid.
