2026-10-06.title: Bayesian Data Augmentation for DNN Retraining with Binomial Outcomes in Vision-Based UAV Landing
2026-10-06.authors: Ashik E Rasul , Hyung-Jin Yoon
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.abstract: In GPS-denied or cluttered urban environments, vision-based landing is essential for reliable UAV missions. Real-world landing sites are often unstructured and highly variable, requiring strong generalization by the perception system. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) trained with synthetic data augmentation offer a scalable solution for learning landing-site features across diverse vehicle and environmental states. However, computationally expensive DNN retraining, along with challenging performance validation via test flights, limits exhaustive model fine-tuning and necessitates an optimized retraining pipeline. In this work, we deploy a Bayesian data augmentation framework integrated with a photorealistic simulator featuring high-fidelity vehicle dynamics to iteratively retrain the helipad detector DNN, maximizing landing performance as the objective function.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have gained significant popularity in recent times for a wide range of military and civilian applications. Traditional navigation methods for UAVs rely on GPS waypoint following, which can be unreliable in cluttered urban environments or provide insufficient accuracy when a high-precision landing is required. Vision-based landing can be a suitable alternative for such scenarios if the landing pad can be reliably detected and tracked throughout the landing maneuver. However, real-world landing sites are often unstructured with variable features, making consistent detection challenging. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) demonstrate superior performance in learning such complex features compared to traditional computer vision methods, and have been applied in a wide range of perception tasks [ 1 , 2 ] . However, training DNNs with random helipad images is not sufficient, as the same helipad may appear in different sizes, shapes, and appearances depending on the vehicle pose, environmental conditions, and camera parameter settings. For real-time object detection and control, general-purpose frameworks such as YOLO (You Only Look Once) [ 3 ] are therefore trained with domain-specific datasets [ 4 ] with data augmentation to improve the generalization of the model for different sizes, lighting, and aspect ratios of the object. This augmentation process can be validated and refined further based on the vision-based landing performance of the UAV.
However, collecting such landing performance data would involve using expensive aircraft for extended periods to cover varying scenarios, altitude ranges, times of day, and weather conditions.
Photorealistic simulators can substantially reduce this burden by providing controlled, repeatable environments for generating task-specific performance data at scale [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] Despite these advances, retraining and deployment of DNNs remains a challenging task.

For example, each iteration of refinement is computationally expensive, requiring substantial resources and time [ 8 ] . This high computational demand often becomes a bottleneck in the optimization process, necessitating improvements in the efficiency of the retraining process itself. The blackbox nature of the DNNs makes the task additionally challenging. Bayesian optimization can be a prominent method for such scenarios, as it systematically searches the decision variable space, balancing exploration and exploitation to identify optimal decision variables without knowing the objective function explicitly [ 9 ] . By leveraging feedback from simulation outcomes, such as the number of successful landings over a finite number of landing attempts, Bayesian optimization can iteratively refine the model, ensuring effective adaptation to varying vehicle and environmental states.
In this work, we address this challenge by introducing a retraining and deployment framework for perception DNNs, specifically for the autonomous landing operation of UAVs, as illustrated in Figure 1 . First, we introduce an iterative DNN retraining process leveraging Bayesian optimization, which optimizes the binomial outcome of the landing attempts (success/failure) by efficiently applying data augmentation to the DNN retraining pipeline.
This process consists of two phases. The first phase evaluates the binomial outcome (landing success/failure) as a performance measure of the vision-guided landing system, given the operation scenarios in a photorealistic simulation. In the second phase, the corresponding performance measure is used in a Bayesian optimization loop that applies the Gaussian Process (GP) prior and Laplace approximation of the posterior to generate the next set of hyperparameters for retraining the model. Finally, the updated model is evaluated in the first phase. These phases close the loop in the DNN refinement process.

To evaluate our approach, we use a simulation environment [ 10 ] built in Unreal Engine that models realistic aerial scenarios, including cluttered urban landscapes, varying altitudes, and dynamic lighting. This environment enables thorough testing of the proposed framework, allowing us to study the effect of uncertainty, limited observability, and control feedback in closed-loop settings.

Our key contributions are:

We present an iterative retraining pipeline for landing pad detection DNN, integrated to a photorealistic simulator, that optimizes the binomial landing outcomes within the simulator as an objective function leveraging Bayesian optimization with GP prior and Laplace approximation of the posterior distribution.

2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Literature Review

UAVs are being used for a wide range of applications, including terrain mapping [ 11 ] , road following [ 12 ] , shoreline investigation [ 13 ] , wildlife monitoring [ 14 ] , and autonomous package delivery [ 15 ] . Among different UAV configurations, multirotor planes with lift-and-cruise capability have gained popularity in the context of Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) [ 16 , 17 ] . These aircraft combine the cruise characteristics of fixed-wing aircraft with the vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) capability of multirotors. Unlike fixed-wing runway operations, vertical landing requires precise localization of the landing site directly beneath the aircraft. Vision-based perception has emerged as the dominant sensing modality for high-precision autonomous landing in GPS-denied or cluttered environments [ 18 , 19 ] . Despite significant progress, generalized DNN training for diverse landing environments, robustness under lighting and texture variations, and a generalized exploration policy for the landing pad from different UAV poses remain open research directions.

Early vision-based autonomous landing systems relied on cooperative visual markers of specific features, placed on the landing surface. One of the first implementations of such systems demonstrated helicopter landing using image processing-based tracking [ 20 ] . Later, vision-based quadrotor landing was achieved on a moving platform using an onboard camera and nonlinear control [ 21 , 22 ] . Vision-based autonomous landing was also demonstrated in GPS-denied environments using customized landing pad design, state estimation, and stabilization [ 23 ] . These works established the feasibility of marker-based autonomous landing even under motion and disturbances. However, these solutions face challenges in real-world adoption in unknown environments, as the landing markers may not follow a specific feature, shape, or orientation. A Faster Region-based Convolutional Neural Network (Faster R-CNN)-based landing sign identification was proposed to identify the position and direction of the landing sign [ 24 ] . Later, YOLO [ 25 ] has been widely integrated for safe landing area detection, pose correction, and navigation of UAVs [ 26 , 27 ] . However, training such perception models for autonomous landing requires large amounts of data collected covering diverse environments and vehicle states. For UAV perception, collecting data at scale can be expensive and unsafe, especially in the early stages of development. Moreover, comprehensive scenarios of varying environmental conditions and vehicle states can be challenging to recreate with real test flights. Photorealistic simulators equipped with high-fidelity vehicle dynamics can substantially reduce this gap by providing task-specific training data [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . CARLA [ 28 ] and AirSim [ 29 ] have been widely used for such synthetic data generation and control validation. However, the simulation-to-real gap still remains a major challenge for UAV perception model deployment, which can be further reduced by synthetically augmenting the training data itself through careful tuning of training parameters such as scale and brightness. Though such fine-tuning enables the DNNs to generalize well across varying altitude and lighting conditions, each iteration of retraining and validation is computationally expensive, which motivates the use of Bayesian optimization to efficiently search the hyperparameter space for optimal performance [ 9 ] . Bayesian optimization based on stochastic binary outcomes is successfully demonstrated for different robotics applications [ 30 , 31 ] . However, to the best of our knowledge, none of the prior works optimized perception DNNs for the autonomous landing task with a binomial simulation outcome.
In this work, we place a Gaussian prior over the true unknown function and adopt a binomial observation model. We deploy the Laplace approximation method to approximate the non-Gaussian posterior. Finally, we leverage upper confidence bound (UCB) as an acquisition function to explore the hyperparameter space [ 32 ] .

2026-10-06.title: Spacecraft Rendezvous Trajectory Generation with Modular Constraints via Diffusion Model Composition
2026-10-06.authors: Mariko A. Storey-Matsutani , Richard Linares
2026-10-06.abstract: Emerging mission classes such as on-orbit servicing, satellite inspection, and active debris removal require trajectory design methods that are adaptable to a variety of mission scenarios. We present a diffusion-based trajectory generation approach for rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) that enables flexible configuration of mission constraints. First, individual energy-based diffusion models are trained to satisfy distinct constraints such as approach cone and sensor line-of-sight from a set of optimized trajectories. Then, at inference time, the learned energy models can be composed with one another, or with an analytically defined energy field, to enforce specific constraint combinations. We validate this framework with the composition of a learned approach cone model and a learned sensor line-of-sight model, as well as a learned approach cone model and synthetic obstacle avoidance model, both of which yield constraint satisfaction rates that are within 1 percentage point of the single-constraint models or higher. These results indicate that our compositional diffusion framework can provide a modular approach to RPO trajectory design and enable reconfiguration for new constraint combinations without requiring model retraining.
2026-10-06.introduction:
In recent years, rapidly growing interest in space-based infrastructure has accelerated the need for advanced trajectory design methods. In particular, emerging mission classes such as on-orbit servicing, active debris removal, and in-space assembly have emphasized a focus on rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) maneuvers, which require spacecraft to operate in close proximity while satisfying dynamical and safety constraints [ 29 ] . The ongoing NASA Artemis program and commercial space station development efforts further motivate the need for robust autonomous RPO capabilities to expand human presence in space, as tasks like docking and resupply are prime examples of critical RPO maneuvers [ 26 ] .

The relative motion dynamics for RPO regimes are commonly modeled using linearized formulations such as the Clohessy–Wiltshire (CW) or Hill equations [ 29 , 5 ] . However, practical missions require further optimization methods to yield fuel-optimal trajectories that are typically prioritized in space missions [ 22 ] . Despite the benefit of these linearized models, trajectory design for RPO is fundamentally challenging because the close coordination of spacecraft introduces tightly coupled constraints that require full, six degree-of-freedom motion planning. The consideration of approach cone, sensor line-of-sight (LOS), plume impingement avoidance, and collision avoidance constraints can introduce nonconvex feasible regions in the state-control space [ 29 ] .

As shown in classical optimal control literature, one approach to solving such nonconvex trajectory optimization problems is sequential convex programming (SCP), which has been applied to RPO mission applications. [ 20 ] SCP works by iteratively approximating a convex subproblem of the original nonconvex problem formulation, which enables the application of traditional convex optimization methods [ 21 , 30 ] . While SCP has demonstrated strong performance in many path planning scenarios, its convergence can be sensitive to initialization and the addition or modification of constraint sets requires reformulation of the convexification strategy. [ 15 ] As missions increasingly rely on coordinated, multi-spacecraft operations in cislunar and Earth-orbit environments, there is a need for modular, flexible tools for trajectory design that can adapt to changing mission needs.

Given these limitations, recent work has explored learning-based alternatives for the generation of spacecraft trajectories. Reinforcement learning [ 4 ] , imitation learning [ 25 ] , and transformer-based architectures [ 2 , 10 , 31 , 13 ] have been used to approximate optimal policies or directly generate feasible trajectories, as well as to warm-start traditional solvers for nonconvex optimal spacecraft control. However, many existing approaches exhibit limited generalization across varying constraint configurations. As a result, changes in constraint geometry or combinations typically necessitate retraining, thus reducing flexibility and limiting deployment in adaptive mission contexts [ 3 , 17 ] .

To this end, existing research has begun to explore the application of diffusion models as an alternative approach to generative trajectory design [ 3 , 23 , 17 ] . Diffusion probabilistic models are a type of generative model capable of representing complex multimodal distributions through an iterative denoising process [ 12 , 28 ] . Originally developed for high-dimensional data such as images [ 12 ] , diffusion models learn probabilistic distributions over solution spaces and allow conditioning mechanisms that are well-suited for trajectory generation problems [ 14 ] . In particular, the formulation of diffusion models as energy-based models further supports model composition and posterior conditional sampling, enabling constraint-flexible trajectory generation without model retraining [ 7 ] .

Diffusion-based models have recently been applied to several spacecraft trajectory problems, including powered descent guidance, low-thrust transfers, and ballistic transfer generation [ 3 , 1 , 9 , 23 ] . These works show that diffusion models can learn complex solution manifolds, provide diverse and high-quality initial guesses, and accelerate warm-starting of indirect and direct optimal control solvers [ 3 , 17 , 9 ] . However, most existing applications focus on single-vehicle scenarios with relatively structured constraints, and do not directly address RPO-specific constraints like approach cones, collision avoidance, and sensor line of sight.

This gap motivates the compositional diffusion framework for RPO trajectory generation developed in this work. Instead of training a single complex model to satisfy all mission constraints simultaneously, we demonstrate the decomposition of the constraint space into modular components and train individual diffusion models on distinct constraint classes (e.g. approach cone, sensor line-of-sight). At inference time, these models are composed to generate trajectories that satisfy multiple constraints concurrently, enabling reconfiguration to new RPO mission constraint profiles while reducing retraining requirements.

2026-10-06.title: FOCUS: Fine-Grained Open-Vocabulary Change Detection for Uncertainty-Aware Semi-Static Scenes
2026-10-06.authors: Can Xu , Mingfeng Yuan , Mahan Mohammadi , Steven L. Waslander
2026-10-06.abstract:
Autonomous robots operating over long periods must keep their environmental memory up to date as the world changes between visits. In semi-static environments, an object may be replaced in place by a different but geometrically and semantically similar instance, making the identity change difficult to detect from geometry or coarse semantics alone.
We present FOCUS , an uncertainty-aware framework for object-level change detection and map maintenance. We formulate semi-static memory maintenance as probabilistic inference that fuses geometric likelihood with appearance likelihood rendered from a 3D Gaussian map. A recursive three-state estimator maintains whether each mapped object is persisted , replaced , or removed . To account for imperfect 3DGS rendering, we model the rendered appearance evidence probabilistically rather than using it as a direct change score, with the model parameters automatically calibrated from a change-free replay of the initial mapping session.
We evaluate our method on a new Isaac Sim warehouse benchmark with ambiguous in-place replacements and on the real-world TorWIC dataset. It improves object-level replacement F1 from 0.20 to 0.84 over a probabilistic baseline and transfers to real-world data without manual parameter retuning.
2026-10-06.introduction:
The rapid advance of foundation models in recent years has greatly expanded robots’ ability to recognize unseen objects and understand open-ended environments. This progress is pushing robotics beyond short-horizon perception and reactive behavior toward long-term autonomy, where robots must operate reliably over extended periods as the world evolves. A key step toward this goal is persistent embodied intelligence: the ability to maintain an up-to-date memory of the environment, understand how it changes, and use that knowledge to adapt future decisions. Such capability is essential for warehouse inventory auditing, long-term crop monitoring, construction-site inspection, and household service robots, where objects may be added, removed, moved, replaced, or undergo meaningful changes in appearance or state over time. These settings are naturally semi-static : most of the environment remains stable, while a small but important subset undergoes persistent change. Reliable operation in such environments therefore requires robots to distinguish genuine changes from viewpoint variation, sensing noise, transient observations, and subtle differences between visually similar objects.

Recent open-vocabulary scene representations and scene graphs have enabled robots to build increasingly rich object-centric memories of their environments [ 1 , 2 ] .

Existing semi-static mapping methods have begun to address this problem through geometric and probabilistic consistency estimation [ 3 , 4 ] . However, these methods are primarily designed to detect coarse scene changes rather than fine-grained changes in object identity or state. POV-SLAM [ 5 ] , for example, probabilistically estimates whether mapped objects remain consistent with current observations, but assumes prior semantic knowledge of mapped objects and models object state largely through geometric consistency. Khronos [ 4 ] similarly reasons about long-term scene evolution using geometric visibility and free-space evidence to verify whether previously observed structures remain present. These approaches are effective when changes produce a clear geometric signature, such as object addition, removal, or displacement. They become much more ambiguous under in-place replacement , where an object is replaced by another instance with nearly identical geometry and coarse semantics. For example, two cardboard boxes may occupy the same volume and share the same category while differing in a fragile label, plastic wrapping, or an open/closed state. Such differences may generate little geometric residual, yet can be operationally important for applications such as warehouse inventory reconciliation or long-term crop-condition monitoring.

Appearance can be used to augment geometric change detection, but appearance evidence is itself uncertain. Dense visual features can distinguish objects that share similar geometry and semantics, and recent methods exploit image descriptors such as DINO-based features for association across observations [ 6 ] . However, pairwise matching usually requires sufficiently overlapping views, which may not exist across long-term revisits. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides an attractive alternative by storing a view-conditioned appearance model that can render the expected appearance of a mapped object from the current camera pose [ 7 , 8 ] . This enables direct comparison between the current observation and the expected appearance without requiring a co-visible reference image. However, rendered appearance can be unreliable due to limited object visibility, incomplete reconstruction, floaters, pose errors, and illumination changes. A single-frame appearance residual is therefore insufficient for reliable change detection. Simply accumulating more observations is also problematic: along patrol-style trajectories, robots often observe an object from highly similar viewpoints over consecutive frames, causing correlated evidence to be repeatedly counted and resulting in overconfident decisions.

We therefore formulate semi-static memory maintenance as uncertainty-aware probabilistic inference over object state. For each mapped object, our system maintains a recursive three-state belief over persisted , replaced , and removed . Geometry and appearance provide complementary evidence: geometric cues are effective for detecting disappearance and newly occupied space, while rendered appearance provides the fine-grained signal needed to distinguish a persisted object from an in-place replacement. To make this appearance evidence reliable, we maintain an object-specific appearance baseline together with its uncertainty, compensate for frame-level appearance shifts, suppress unstable rendered evidence, and reduce the influence of temporally correlated observations. The resulting geometry and appearance likelihoods are fused in a recursive Bayesian estimator whose parameters are calibrated from a change-free replay of the reference session. In this way, our framework shifts semi-static memory maintenance from asking only “has the mapped geometry changed?” toward the finer question “is this still the same object?”

We summarize our contributions as follows:

We introduce an uncertainty-aware 3DGS appearance model for fine-grained object change detection, accounting for appearance variation and unreliable rendered evidence.

We formulate object-level memory maintenance as a three-state recursive Bayesian estimator over persisted , replaced , and removed , fusing complementary geometric and appearance evidence while accounting for unstable and correlated observations.

We introduce a multi-session warehouse benchmark for fine-grained semi-static changes, with challenging in-place replacements between geometrically and semantically similar objects and a complete set of object-level change annotations.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Long-Term Object-Level Map Maintenance

Long-term map maintenance has traditionally relied on geometric inconsistency across revisits. TSDF- and SDF-based methods detect persistent changes from reconstruction differences [ 9 , 10 ] , while Khronos [ 4 ] uses geometric and free-space evidence to infer long-term object persistence. Such methods are effective for additions, removals, and displacement, but can be ambiguous for in-place replacement between geometrically similar objects. To provide additional cues beyond geometry, recent object-centric maps incorporate semantic features and language descriptions [ 11 , 8 , 1 , 2 ] . However, coarse semantics may still be insufficient to distinguish visually similar instances. We instead target fine-grained object identity changes by combining geometry with uncertainty-aware, view-conditioned appearance evidence.

## II-B Appearance-Based Scene Change Detection

Appearance provides complementary evidence for cross-session change detection. Recent 3DGS-based methods exploit novel-view rendering to compare a reference scene with current observations. 3DGS-CD [ 12 ] detects 2D object-level changes from rendered references and fuses them across views to recover 3D change masks and object transformations, while Galappaththige et al. [ 13 ] extend this setting to online scene change detection with multi-view fusion and change-guided 3DGS updates. DynamicGSG [ 7 ] is particularly related to our setting: it renders visible mapped objects, compares them with current observations using SSIM, and removes objects whose similarity falls below a fixed threshold, treating them as moved or substituted. In contrast, we treat rendered appearance as an uncertain identity observation rather than a hard change decision, and recursively fuse it with geometric evidence to distinguish persisted , replaced , and removed objects.

## II-C Probabilistic Object-State Estimation

Change evidence from individual observations can be unreliable due to sensor noise, localization error, and imperfect segmentation. Persistence filtering therefore accumulates evidence over time rather than making single-frame decisions. Hashemifar and Dantu [ 14 ] incorporate feature-persistence reasoning into visual SLAM, while POCD [ 3 ] recursively estimates object stationarity from geometric and semantic evidence. Bogenberger et al. [ 15 ] , referred to as Perceive-Semantix, incorporate geometric and semantic similarity for persistent object-instance tracking. Building on this probabilistic formulation, we explicitly distinguish persisted , replaced , and removed states and recursively fuse geometry with uncertainty-aware appearance evidence.

## II-D Datasets for Semi-Static Change Detection

Several datasets support evaluation in changing indoor environments. TorWIC [ 3 ] provides multi-session warehouse sequences with object additions, removals, translations, and rotations for map-maintenance evaluation. 3RScan [ 16 ] contains repeated scans of indoor scenes with dense instance annotations, cross-session correspondences, and object transformations, primarily targeting object re-localization.

However, these datasets do not directly target fine-grained object-state estimation under ambiguous in-place replacement. Our benchmark therefore introduces geometrically and semantically similar replacements with per-object change states and globally consistent instance identities across sessions.

2026-10-06.title: Emergency Obstacle Avoidance Maneuvers in Differential-Drive Mobile Robots
2026-10-06.authors: Kautik Mandve , Nilay Kant
2026-10-06.abstract: Emergency obstacle avoidance requires a mobile robot to brake or change its heading within the available distance. This paper investigates the dependence of maneuver performance and odometric error on approach speed for a differential-drive robot. A footprint-clearance analysis and a normalized wheel-motion index provide a kinematic description of five braking and turning maneuvers. The principal experiment comprises 540 block-randomized trials on tile, of which 539 are retained, at commanded approach speeds of 45, 55, and 65 cm/s. An overhead camera provides an independent pose reference. When encoder, gyro, and camera heading changes are evaluated over complete motion records, the mean encoder discrepancy increases by 4.7–5.1 degrees for the two reverse-spin maneuvers between the lowest and highest speeds; the arc and brake-assisted pivot change by less than 0.4 degrees. Larger encoder discrepancy is associated with lower avoidance success after adjustment for distance, speed, maneuver, day, and turn direction. Gyro discrepancies remain approximately 3 degrees for the reverse spins. Estimated reaction distances for 90% success and their uncertainty quantify the maneuver trade-offs. The results support speed-specific empirical characterization of emergency maneuvers and distinguish encoder error from recovery motion and measurement-window mismatch.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Emergency obstacle avoidance requires a choice between reducing forward motion and redirecting it. The decision depends on the available reaction distance, the robot footprint, and the motion that the actuators can realize. Dynamic-window methods restrict candidate velocities using acceleration and stopping constraints [ 1 ] ; velocity obstacles describe velocities leading to future collisions [ 2 ] . Vehicle threat-assessment methods explicitly compare braking, steering, and acceleration maneuvers [ 3 ] . Reachability and control barrier functions provide complementary ways to characterize admissible motion under specified models and constraints [ 4 , 5 ] . Experimental characterization of execution error can inform these methods when nominal wheel motion differs from body motion.

Wheel odometry is particularly vulnerable to departures from the rolling assumption. Borenstein and Feng distinguish systematic calibration errors from nonsystematic errors caused by slip and surface irregularities [ 6 ] ; combining gyros and wheel encoders provides additional heading information [ 7 ] . Chong and Kleeman develop an odometry error model for mobile-robot motion estimation [ 8 ] . These contributions establish the importance of separating calibration and measurement uncertainty from departures of wheel motion from body motion.

Related work on tracked and wheeled skid-steer robots explicitly accounts for nonideal turning kinematics. Martínez et al. identify approximate tracked-vehicle models through effective instantaneous centers of rotation [ 9 ] , and Mandow et al. extend this experimental approach to wheeled skid-steer vehicles [ 10 ] . Dogru and Marques incorporate terrain and center-of-mass effects and evaluate different terrains and asymmetric loads [ 11 ] . Yi et al. combine skid-steer kinematics with low-cost inertial measurements for motion estimation [ 12 ] . These platforms have different contact constraints from the two-drive-wheel robot considered here; their identified parameters cannot be transferred directly. They nevertheless motivate measuring actual motion when evaluating nominal wheel profiles.

Slip estimation has also been studied using dynamic models [ 13 ] , motor current [ 14 ] , online odometry calibration [ 15 ] , and learned relationships between IMU and encoder signals in outdoor terrain [ 16 ] . Tire-dynamics treatments describe the force constraints underlying combined braking and steering [ 17 , 18 ] , while Kritayakirana and Gerdes study autonomous control at the limits of handling [ 19 ] . This literature supplies modeling and sensing approaches for nonideal motion. The present experiment instead characterizes the clearance and heading discrepancies of fixed emergency-maneuver profiles across approach speeds. It does not identify a tire-force model or evaluate a new online slip estimator.

High wheel-speed contrast can produce a rapid heading change, but does not by itself determine the distance needed to avoid an obstacle. The rotating footprint may advance toward the obstacle even if the robot reference point remains fixed. Incoming motion, transient braking, and subsequent recovery add further displacement. Moreover, a turn terminated at a prescribed encoder count need not produce the intended final body heading. These effects motivate joint measurement of clearance, net heading discrepancy, and approach speed.

This paper presents a geometric analysis of footprint clearance and a controlled comparison of five maneuvers. A normalized wheel-motion index describes the nominal profiles without interpreting them as measured tire forces. The principal dataset contains 539 usable trials from a balanced maneuver–speed experiment. Encoder and gyro heading changes are compared with the camera over complete motion records, and reaction-distance requirements are estimated with uncertainty. Two earlier campaigns, comprising 300 and 210 trials, respectively, motivated the controlled design; they are not pooled with the principal dataset. The resulting characterization relates maneuver selection to reaction distance and measured sensing error.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II formulates the clearance and heading-measurement problems. Section III develops the kinematic analysis. Section IV describes the apparatus and statistical methods. Section V presents the results. Sections VI and VII discuss their implications and conclude the paper.

2026-10-06.title: Building A Multi-Sensor Platform For Autonomous Driving Research: Challenges and Lessons Learned
2026-10-06.authors: Paulo Ricardo Marques de Araujo , Eslam Mounier , Qamar Bader , Emma Dawson , Aboelmagd Noureldin
2026-10-06.abstract: This paper reports on the challenges encountered and lessons learned during the development and deployment of a flexible multi-sensor platform for autonomous driving research. It aims to serve as a reference for researchers developing new multi-sensor systems. As the need for reliable, diverse datasets increases, novel environments and sensing configurations are essential to tackle real-world operational challenges. Consequently, many research groups create custom multi-sensory data collection platforms, where fundamental issues, such as mechanical design, sensor calibration, power management, and time synchronization, arise regardless of sensor types. We reflect on these challenges and share key insights to guide future platform designs, enhancing reproducibility and robustness in autonomous vehicle testing. We also summarize the mitigation strategies we adopted, for instance, system-wide time synchronization using GNSS timing and NTP protocols, custom calibration routines for different sensor configurations, and design practices to improve reliability and data integrity during field deployments.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Autonomous driving has attracted attention both in industry and academia in recent years. This research area involves a diverse set of disciplines, including scene classification, odometry, lane detection, object detection, semantic segmentation, and agent motion prediction [ 1 ] .

The development of autonomous driving algorithms is heavily reliant on high-quality datasets. There is a wide range of datasets available, each focusing on different aspects of autonomous driving. For instance, the KITTI dataset [ 2 ] is well known for facilitating research in object detection, tracking, optical flow, depth estimation, and visual odometry, while the Cityscapes dataset [ 3 ] has become a standard benchmark for semantic segmentation due to its high-quality labeled data. Other examples, such as the ApolloScape [ 4 ] and the nuScenes [ 5 ] datasets, offer extensive labeling and a large volume of images and multi-modal data, supporting tasks such as 3D map construction, object detection, tracking, and scene understanding. Other examples, such as the Boreas dataset [ 6 ] , the Hong Kong UrbanNav dataset [ 7 ] , offer multi-modal data collected in multi-season and dense urban environments, facilitating the research of autonomous driving-related tasks under adverse weather conditions and global navigation satellite system-denied environments.

Despite the numerous datasets available, little information has been published on the challenges and best practices involved in this process. For example, the Hong Kong UrbanNav dataset [ 7 ] provides a brief section with valuable information on the lessons they have learned during the creation of the dataset. In order to contribute to this research and address the technical gaps, this work explores and presents the challenges and lessons learned during the development years of the NavINST experimental setup. The NavINST dataset [ 8 ] has emerged as a new source of data for researchers interested in developing, for example, object detection, odometry, 3D map construction, and indoor positioning algorithms. It features multiple perception and inertial sensors, whose integration and time synchronization were sources of many challenges, as discussed in the following sections. Our objective with this paper is to share the insights gained in the development of the system in order to help practitioners interested in developing their own setup rigs to contribute to the autonomous driving research area.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Development Timeline

The Navigation and Instrumentation (NavINST) laboratory located at the Royal Military College of Canada is well known for its work on global navigation satellite system, inertial navigation, multi-sensor systems, and related areas.
To expand the research possibilities, a project of a multi-sensor experimental setup was defined.
The development of the experimental setup was driven by some initial pillars: (1) it must be portable and flexible, and (2) it must include perception sensors such as cameras, light detection and ranging, and radio detection and ranging. The first pillar was established, taking into account that the team would need to travel to different cities in Canada to collect data for different research purposes. The second pillar served as the backbone for the initial development of the system, which was mainly inspired by existing datasets in mid-2020. In addition, the number of datasets that offered radio detection and ranging data collected in urban environments at that time was limited, and this aspect became an additional motivation.

The experimental setup has evolved in recent years, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . The initial version, 2021, was inspired by previous experimental setups available in the laboratory for global navigation satellite system-based research. The reference system, composed of a high-end global navigation satellite system receiver and a high-end inertial measurement unit was located in the trunk close to the rear axle of the vehicle. Three stereo cameras, one mechanical light detection and ranging, and a global navigation satellite system antenna were installed on the roof.

In the second version, 2022, more stereo cameras along with radio detection and rangings and other inertial measurement units were installed. All sensors were moved to the roof to comply with the first development pillar, as detailed in the next section. In 2023, the third version was implemented with redesigned and optimized computing systems, updated stereo cameras, and the addition of a monocular camera and a modern solid-state light detection and ranging. The latest version of the experimental setup was deployed in 2024 and featured three solid-state light detection and rangings and new stereo cameras.

2026-10-06.title: TacGELLO: Tactile Contact Feedback for a 3D-Printed Teleoperation Leader
2026-10-06.authors: Younsoo Kim , Sangmin Song , Sarath Kodagoda , Marc Carmichael , Karthick Thiyagarajan
2026-10-06.abstract: Passive leader arms transmit an operator’s motion without returning remote contact or load cues. TacGELLO uses the existing servos of a 3D-printed leader for tactile contact feedback at the gripper trigger and current-based load cues at the arm joints. AnySkin contact detection activates a trigger position hold, while changes in follower joint current adjust leader-servo output limits to command resistance during lifting.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Leader-arm interfaces map an operator’s joint motion to a robot
manipulator for teleoperation and demonstration collection.
GELLO uses a low-cost, 3D-printed replica of the follower’s
kinematics [ 27 ] . ALOHA provides a related interface
for bimanual manipulation [ 31 ] .
In their passive configurations, both transmit motion without
returning remote contact forces. An operator grasping a fragile
object must infer contact visually while controlling closure.
UMI collects demonstrations with a handheld gripper that interacts
directly with the object [ 8 ] .

Force and tactile feedback have reduced applied forces and damaging
errors in surgical studies [ 25 , 16 ] .
Assembly studies show that the benefit depends on the task and
feedback quality [ 26 ] . In a door-opening
imitation-learning task, haptic feedback during demonstration
collection improved data quantity and downstream
performance [ 9 ] .
These findings support investigating inexpensive feedback for
leader arms. The effectiveness of a servo-based implementation
still needs to be evaluated in its intended task.

FACTR combines leader-arm feedback from follower joint-torque
estimates with gripper-current feedback at the
trigger [ 19 ] . Echo uses force-sensing resistors in
the follower fingers to provide grip feedback on a UR teleoperation
interface [ 4 ] . AnySkin measures spatially
distributed signals from fingertip deformation using magnetic
sensing [ 6 ] . We use these signals to detect
contact and activate a trigger position hold, without estimating
force in newtons. Our contribution concerns this contact signal
and rendering mechanism; FACTR has already demonstrated combined
arm and gripper feedback.

TacGELLO is a 3D-printed leader and tactile gripper for the Universal
Robots UR3 (Fig. 2 ). It uses existing leader servos for
two feedback channels: tactile contact feedback at the gripper
trigger and current-based load feedback at the arm joints.
Fingertip contact activates a capped hold on the trigger servo.
The load-feedback channel maps changes in UR3 joint current to
output limits on selected leader servos, commanding an arm-resistance
cue during lifting without a dedicated arm force/torque sensor.
This cue has not been calibrated as payload weight or rendered
joint torque. We contribute:

A UR3 leader and two-finger tactile gripper that render
fingertip contact through an existing trigger servo.

A current-based load-feedback channel that commands
resistance at selected leader-arm joints from UR3
joint-current changes.

A characterization of sent-command tracking, selected
software timings and exploratory fragile-object grasping
behavior, with arm-load pilots.

1. A UR3 leader and two-finger tactile gripper that render
fingertip contact through an existing trigger servo.

2. A current-based load-feedback channel that commands
resistance at selected leader-arm joints from UR3
joint-current changes.

3. A characterization of sent-command tracking, selected
software timings and exploratory fragile-object grasping
behavior, with arm-load pilots.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Low-cost teleoperation interfaces

GELLO uses kinematically matched leader replicas built from hobby
servos [ 27 ] . ALOHA and ALOHA 2 use backdrivable leader
arms for bimanual puppeteering [ 31 , 3 ] ,
and AirExo uses wearable exoskeletons [ 10 ] .
Passive remote leaders transmit the operator’s motion without
reflecting follower contact forces. UMI replaces the leader arm
with a handheld gripper [ 8 ] . Contact occurs locally
at the device during demonstration collection, so it does not
provide remote follower-force reflection.

## 2.2 Force feedback and bilateral control

Classical bilateral teleoperation established the tradeoff between
transparency and stability [ 18 , 12 ] .
Bilateral-control imitation learning uses observer-based force
estimation to exchange position and force information, recording
both for policy learning [ 1 , 7 , 17 , 29 ] .
FACTR provides compensated leader-arm feedback from follower
external joint torques and gripper feedback from follower gripper
current [ 19 ] .
FACTR 2 studies learned external-force estimation on commodity
arms [ 21 ] .
GELLO+F renders Franka external-torque estimates through
current-controlled leader motors [ 24 ] .
Input-gated bilateral teleoperation is another approach for
low-cost hardware [ 15 ] .

Echo uses a force-sensing resistor in each follower finger and
renders grip feedback at the leader trigger, with passive arm
joints [ 4 ] . Prometheus renders grip-force feedback
in a handheld motion-capture controller [ 23 ] .
TacGELLO uses magnetic fingertip contact sensing to activate a capped
trigger hold, alongside a separate arm-current cue. We have not
compared its effectiveness directly with these systems.

## 2.3 Tactile sensing and policy learning

2026-10-06.title: GR-LIO: A Local Ground-Aware LiDAR-Inertial Odometry System Using Body-to-Ground Height
2026-10-06.authors: Zhixin Zhang , Yang Song , Liang Zhao , Nathan Shankar , Barry Lennox , Pawel Ladosz
2026-10-06.comment: Journal
2026-10-06.abstract:
LiDAR–inertial odometry (LIO) is widely used for state estimation in ground-based autonomous mobile robots. However, the geometric constraints provided by the local ground surface remain largely underexploited in existing LIO systems.
This paper proposes a filter-based local ground-aware LIO framework that explicitly incorporates local ground plane geometry into the state estimation process to improve both localization accuracy and computational efficiency. Specifically, a local ground plane is parameterized by the robot orientation and the body-to-ground (B-G) height and continuously propagated within the state estimation process. Based on the proposed B-G geometry model, a propagated local ground plane enables efficient and reliable ground segmentation. The segmented ground points are then incorporated into the filter update through point-to-plane geometric constraints, improving both state estimation accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, a planar motion update is introduced to exploit the propagated local ground plane as an additional geometric constraint, effectively suppressing vertical drift and improving estimation robustness. To address the initially unknown B-G height, an efficient initialization strategy is developed, followed by an online calibration procedure for continuous refinement. The proposed system is evaluated on several public benchmark datasets and self-collected real-world datasets covering diverse operating scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms representative LIO methods in terms of both localization accuracy and computational efficiency.
2026-10-06.introduction:
LiDAR-based odometry has become a widely adopted solution due to its strong geometric perception capability and robustness in diverse operating environments [ 1 , 2 ] . By incorporating inertial measurement unit (IMU) data, LiDAR–Inertial odometry (LIO) systems [ 3 , 4 ] further improve motion observability and estimation robustness, especially in structure-less or LiDAR-degenerate scenarios.

For ground-based mobile robots, the ground surface provides one of the most stable and informative geometric structures in the environment. Accurate ground estimation not only facilitates reliable ground point extraction, but also provides valuable geometric priors for localization and state estimation. Despite the fact that some prior work has considered the ground plane in LiDAR point clouds to improve system performance, such approaches remain limited. For example, LeGO-LOAM [ 5 ] employs a ground segmentation algorithm to improve feature processing efficiency, while GND-LO [ 6 ] models a single plane using multiple ground patches to improve scan-to-scan matching accuracy. However, most existing LiDAR-based frameworks do not explicitly leverage the geometric relationship between the robot body and the ground plane, nor the planar motion characteristics inherent to ground-based platforms. In particular, the planar motion prior and the body–ground geometric coupling remain underutilized, leading to suboptimal estimation consistency and robustness. In this paper, we explicitly model the local ground plane by parameterizing the body-to-ground (B-G) height and the ground normal vector aligned with the robot vertical axis, and incorporate this geometric prior into the LIO state estimation framework to improve performance.

Specifically, a local ground plane representing the terrain in the vicinity of the robot is parameterized by the body-to-ground (B-G) height and the robot orientation. This representation introduces only a single additional parameter, reducing the state dimension and computational complexity compared with explicit ground plane estimation, and remains valid as long as the robot operates on locally planar surfaces, regardless of variations in the ground geometry, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . Ground points in the current scan are then efficiently segmented and incorporated into the state update through point-to-plane distance observations with respect to the estimated ground plane. Furthermore, a planar motion constraint is introduced based on the local ground plane to suppress drift in the vertical direction. To address an initially unknown or poorly calibrated B-G height, an efficient initialization strategy is proposed, followed by an online calibration procedure for continuous refinement. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A ground-aware LiDAR-Inertial odometry framework is proposed that explicitly models the local ground plane using the body-to-ground (B-G) height, requiring only one additional state variable.

An efficient local ground point segmentation method is developed, enabling the segmented ground points to be directly incorporated into the state estimation as point-to-plane constraints.

A planar motion update is introduced by exploiting local ground plane, effectively suppressing vertical drift and improving localization accuracy for ground robots.

A B-G height initialization and online calibration method is proposed to address unknown conditions and compensate for parameter uncertainty.

Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmark datasets and self-collected datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves localization accuracy and computational efficiency across different environments and LiDAR configurations.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the related work. Section III presents the proposed B-G geometry model, including ground plane propagation and the planar motion update. Section IV describes the proposed GR-LIO framework, together with the initialization and online calibration of the B-G height. Section V presents the experimental evaluation. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper.

1. A ground-aware LiDAR-Inertial odometry framework is proposed that explicitly models the local ground plane using the body-to-ground (B-G) height, requiring only one additional state variable.

2. An efficient local ground point segmentation method is developed, enabling the segmented ground points to be directly incorporated into the state estimation as point-to-plane constraints.

3. A planar motion update is introduced by exploiting local ground plane, effectively suppressing vertical drift and improving localization accuracy for ground robots.

4. A B-G height initialization and online calibration method is proposed to address unknown conditions and compensate for parameter uncertainty.

5. Extensive experiments on multiple public benchmark datasets and self-collected datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves localization accuracy and computational efficiency across different environments and LiDAR configurations.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Optimization-based LIO

Optimization-based methods have long been a dominant paradigm in LiDAR SLAM due to their robustness and estimation accuracy. In such approaches, IMU measurements are typically incorporated through preintegration factors [ 7 ] , while LiDAR observations are used to construct geometric constraints for state estimation, such as point-to-edge constraints [ 1 ] and point-to-plane constraints [ 8 ] . LIO-SAM [ 3 ] combines the LOAM-style feature extraction strategy proposed in [ 5 ] and IMU preintegration for tightly coupled state estimation, where ground and non-ground points are segmented to extract edge and planar features for efficient state estimation. Ye et al. [ 9 ] further proposed a tightly coupled LIO framework based on factor graph optimization that directly fuses raw IMU and LiDAR measurements. LIPS [ 10 ] represents planes using the closest-point (CP) formulation and incorporates point-to-plane constraints into a factor-graph-based LIO framework. Owing to the modular nature of factor-graph optimization, additional sensing modalities can be readily integrated into the framework. Representative examples include LVI-SAM [ 11 ] , which incorporates visual measurements, and GR-Fusion [ 12 ] , which further integrates GNSS and wheel encoder information.

## II-B Filter-based LIO

Compared with optimization-based methods, filter-based approaches are generally faster and require lower computational cost, although this efficiency may come at the expense of estimation accuracy. Early filter-based LIO methods, such as LINS [ 13 ] , adopt a feature extraction pipeline similar to LOAM [ 5 ] and employ an iterated error-state Kalman filter (IESKF) to reduce linearization errors. Building upon this framework, FAST-LIO [ 14 ] introduces an equivalent Kalman gain formulation that transforms the measurement dimension into the state dimension, significantly improving computational efficiency. FAST-LIO2 [ 4 ] further eliminates explicit feature extraction by directly constructing point-to-plane constraints from raw LiDAR points. Several subsequent works have focused on improving map management and nearest-neighbor search. For example, Faster-LIO [ 15 ] replaces the IKD-tree with iVox to further reduce search time while maintaining comparable localization accuracy.

Other LIO systems employ different Kalman filtering formulations. For example, the Multi-State Constraint Kalman Filter (MSCKF) is adopted in [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] to tightly couple IMU measurements with LiDAR features, whereas IMU, omnidirectional camera, wheel encoder, and LiDAR measurements are integrated within an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) framework in [ 19 ] . Compared with the conventional EKF and MSCKF, the IESKF performs iterative measurement updates, providing improved handling of nonlinear measurement models and reduced linearization errors. Among the existing filter-based frameworks, FAST-LIO2 provides an efficient and accurate direct LiDAR-Inertial odometry framework. Therefore, the proposed method is developed based on FAST-LIO2 by incorporating local ground plane observations and planar motion constraints into its IESKF framework.

## II-C Ground Plane in State Estimation

For ground robots, prior knowledge of the ground plane can often be exploited to improve the performance of LiDAR-based odometry systems. One common application is ground point segmentation, for which several algorithms have been proposed in [ 20 , 21 ] . After segmentation, some studies further utilize ground points to accelerate feature processing. For example, the methods presented in [ 3 , 5 ] distinguish ground points from non-ground points to improve computational efficiency. In addition, the approach proposed in [ 22 ] treats ground points as stable observations while considering the remaining points as potentially dynamic. GR-LOAM [ 23 ] further exploits the height between the LiDAR sensor and the ground plane for ground segmentation, assuming that the LiDAR sensor is approximately parallel to the ground, an assumption that may not hold in practical deployments. In contrast, the proposed method models the body-to-ground height instead of the LiDAR-to-ground height. Since the B-G height is defined in the robot body frame, it is independent of the LiDAR installation geometry and can be directly estimated as a calibration parameter within the state estimation framework.

Another prior commonly exploited for ground robots is the planar motion assumption, which has been widely adopted in vision-based state estimation systems, like in [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . For LiDAR-based systems, the methods proposed in [ 28 , 29 ] incorporate planar surface constraints into LO systems, while the approaches presented in [ 30 , 31 ] explicitly exploit ground plane information in LIO systems. However, these methods typically rely on fixed planar motion constraints or require frequent ground plane estimation, which may become unreliable in the presence of uneven terrain, sparse ground observations, or sensor noise. In contrast, the proposed framework explicitly models the local ground plane using the robot orientation and the B-G height. Rather than estimating the ground plane from scratch at every frame, the local ground plane is continuously propagated and refined through the state estimation process. To accommodate uneven or sloped terrain, an efficient local ground-consistency check is introduced to detect changes in the local ground geometry and trigger updates when necessary.

2026-10-06.title: Neural Barriers: An Online Certifiable Learning-enhanced Adaptive High Order Safety Critical Control
2026-10-06.authors: Lishuo Pan , Mattia Catellani , An Cao , Lorenzo Sabattini , Nora Ayanian
2026-10-06.abstract:
Control barrier functions are an effective model-based tool to formally certify the safety of a system. However, transferring their theoretical guarantees to real-world robotics systems requires high model fidelity. For example, payloads or wind disturbances can cause significant model perturbations to an aerial vehicle, leading to safety compromises.
In this work, we propose a certifiable online learning-enhanced robust adaptive control barrier function, which adapts to disturbances using a Neural ODE and quantifies its adaptation uncertainty with conformal prediction. Our approach guarantees safety at all time under unknown time-varying model disturbances. It adopts a conservative strategy when the adaptation uncertainty is high; and efficiently adapts to reduce controller conservativeness as it receives more data. Our approach provides a provable safety guarantee with a probability bound under suitable Lipschitz smoothness assumptions on the underlying model and trajectory.
These results demonstrate the potential of our method as a practical safety controller for robotics system operating under model perturbations.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Modern robotics planning and control problems face increasing challenges, including efficient scalable planning for large robot teams [ 1 , 2 ] , vision- and language-grounded control [ 3 ] , and high dimensionality and nonlinearity in complex mechanical systems [ 4 ] . As of today, data-driven approaches are broadly adopted in motion planning and control stacks; despite their advantages in efficiency, empirical solution quality, and multimodal reasoning, guaranteeing safety for these approaches remains a challenge. It is now a necessity to certify the safety of learning-based approaches.
Control barrier functions (CBFs) have become a powerful model-based tool for safety-critical control, owing to their guarantees on set invariance without compromising performance [ 5 , 6 ] . A real-world robotics model, however, can differ significantly from a nominal model, due to modeling errors or external disturbances, such as payloads, varying terrain, or wind. Model inaccuracies can compromise the safety guarantees of a CBF controller, highlighting the need to develop a CBF that extends its theoretical guarantees to tolerate certain model perturbations, while preserving certifiable safety in real-world applications.

A large body of work has addressed this problem through the lenses of adaptive control and residual learning. Yet, no existing work simultaneously satisfies the goals of flexible residual parameterization, provable safety guarantees with a probability bound, online adaptation, and real-time computational performance. In this work, we propose a method that achieves all these goals.

We propose a certifiable learning-enhanced high-order robust adaptive control barrier function (HO-RaCBF), namely Neural Barriers.
Our approach can be divided into three modules running concurrently, namely: ( i i ) a high-frequency HO-RaCBF optimization-based controller with learning-enhanced constraints; ( i ​ i ii ) hybrid online residual learning; and ( i ​ i ​ i iii ) online conformal prediction to evaluate the estimate uncertainty in residual learning.
Our approach learns a hybrid model, which consists of a known nominal model and a neural network residual model, from state-control data using Knowledge-based Neural ODEs (KNODE) [ 7 ] . Owing to the Neural ODEs formulation, our method can be trained on data sampled at irregular time intervals, making it well-suited for real-time systems. We combine weighted conformal prediction (WCP) with our Theorem 2 to derive an online confidence interval for the underlying true dynamics model. At each control step, the HO-RaCBF optimization queries the hybrid model and the WCP bound to augment its constraints, thereby solving for optimal control at 100 ​ Hz 100$\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z}$ , which guarantees safety with a specific confidence level. Our approach requires Lipschitz smoothness assumptions on the underlying dynamics model and trajectory. As a result, our online Neural Barriers provide a safety guarantee with probabilistic bounds and reduced conservativeness in the presence of complex unknown dynamics, without requiring any pre-training step.

The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:

an online certifiable learning-enhanced CBF that adapts to time-varying model uncertainty;

a provable safety guarantee with a probability bound under Lipschitz smoothness assumptions on model dynamics and states;

a control schema that decouples adaptation from control loop, allowing adaptation on long-horizon data and high frequency control.

Our controller demonstrates superior adaptation and safety under unknown time-varying simulated model perturbations compared to Robust HOCBFs, and HO-RaCBFs controllers. We further validate our controller through physical experiments on a 38 ​ g 38$\mathrm{g}$ nano quadrotor in the presence of a large-area wind disturbance, shown in Fig. 1 .

1. an online certifiable learning-enhanced CBF that adapts to time-varying model uncertainty;

2. a provable safety guarantee with a probability bound under Lipschitz smoothness assumptions on model dynamics and states;

3. a control schema that decouples adaptation from control loop, allowing adaptation on long-horizon data and high frequency control.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

Dynamics and residual learning have gained popularity due to their success in adaptive control [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Neural-Fly [ 10 ] learns an adaptation term in its control law directly and achieves online adaptation to severe wind disturbances, but it requires a significant offline training phase of approximately 12 12 -minute flight data under diverse wind conditions. In contrast, our method learns the model online and improves performance via a model-based controller, and it does not require offline training, while supporting it when desired. KNODE-MPC [ 9 ] improves MPC performance by learning a high-fidelity model, whereas our approach addresses adaptive control through the lens of the certifiable safety control problem. With a companion WCP module, we provide a provable safety guarantee with a probability bound under time-varying model perturbations.

Recent studies on adaptive CBFs (aCBFs) are effective in improving the safety of a CBF-certified controller [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . However, none of them provides a provable safety guarantee under model perturbations, arguably the most critical property of any safe controller. Among them, [ 12 , 13 ] require an offline pre-training step, leading to significant estimation error during deployment due to domain shift. Online adaptive CBFs [ 11 ] , while addressing the domain shift problem with an efficient learning-enhanced approach, lack a provable safety guarantee and result in safety violations due to training delays. Our certifiable learning-enhanced safety controller provides a safety guarantee with a probabilistic bound and adapts a time-varying residual model, i.e., the gap between the true and nominal models, online. In addition, we employ a physics-informed approach, namely Neural ODEs, to estimate the residual model directly from observable state-control data, without relying on numerical differentiation for residual dynamics supervision.

A large body of robust adaptive CBFs (RaCBFs) aims to provide safety guarantees under model perturbations. A typical safety certificate is obtained by adding a robustifying term to the CBF constraints. Robust CBFs were first studied in [ 14 ] , where the robustifying term is determined by
an assumed-known bound on the model uncertainty.
This approach, however, leads to an overly conservative controller. RaCBFs [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] mitigate over-conservativeness by estimating parametric uncertainty. In many practical dynamic systems, the relative degree of CBFs is larger than one; therefore, a high-order CBF (HOCBF) formulation is required. The authors in [ 18 ] extend the concurrent-learning RaCBFs in [ 19 ] to HO-RaCBFs. In these RaCBF works, a strong assumption is made that the residual is a linear model combining a known knowledge matrix and a learnable constant vector. Thus, this poses a challenge to feature engineering the knowledge matrix for deployment. The lack of a high-fidelity knowledge matrix breaks their safety guarantees. Careful tuning is also required for the concurrent-learning approach to work. Besides, concurrent-learning approaches compute the integral along samples in a history window in each control step, and quickly throttle the control frequency as the window grows. This prohibits them from capturing long-term patterns. In our approach, rather than assuming a specific form for the residual term, we use Neural ODEs as universal estimators of the underlying vector field, thereby capturing nonlinear residual dynamics. In addition, we decouple the adaptation and control loop, allowing long-horizon pattern recognition without throttling the control frequency.

Probabilistic CBF formulations also address uncertainty through stochastic models. Chance-constrained CBFs are formulated in [ 20 ] for autonomous vehicle merging by modeling motion uncertainty as Gaussian noise with known mean and covariance. SHIELD [ 21 ] learns a stochastic residual model from physical trajectories and integrates it into a stochastic discrete-time CBF for humanoid navigation.

2026-10-06.title: Robust 2D Traversability Mapping for Construction AMRs via Failure-Mode-Aware Fusion of LiDAR Geometry and Monocular Semantics
2026-10-06.authors: Manoj Karnekar , Om Mandhane , Gautham Ramkumar
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.comment: Extended version of a paper presented at the 5th Workshop on Future of Construction, IROS 2026
2026-10-06.abstract: Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) on active construction sites face severe navigational challenges: geometry-based traversability mapping (e.g., LiDAR) misses visually hazardous but geometrically flat surfaces like wet mud and ponding concrete, while abrupt geometry on drivable speed-breakers and inclines produces phantom obstacles. We propose a real-time, failure-mode-aware multimodal traversability pipeline on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, where LiDAR is the primary geometric safety estimate and monocular semantics act as a selective, class- and confidence-gated corrective signal. The representation retains distinct traversable classes, namely flat road, terrain, and rocky terrain, while flagging construction hazards. We also release a multimodal construction-site dataset from a custom AMR: four closed-loop ROS 2 sequences from two active sites (RGB, depth, LiDAR, IMU, GPS-RTK, odometry) plus 506 annotated frames across 28 semantic classes. By projecting LiDAR onto dense semantic masks, resolving sparsity via morphological in-painting, and applying failure-mode-aware fusion with Patchwork++, the system corrects complementary geometric failure modes for a local AMR costmap.
2026-10-06.introduction:
AMR deployment on active construction sites is hindered by unstructured terrain: amorphous hazards (deep mud, ponding concrete) and transient structures (scaffolding, rebar, temporary planks) violate structured-indoor-navigation assumptions. AMRs conventionally rely on 3D LiDAR for ground segmentation (e.g., Patchwork++ [ 1 ] ), which suffers two complementary failure modes here: (1) false negatives, where flat non-load-bearing hazards like wet mud or ponding concrete read as safe, traversable ground ( Z ≈ 0 Z\approx 0 ); and (2) false positives, where ground segmentation fails right after drivable elevation changes such as cresting a speed-breaker or climbing a steep earthen incline: the sharp negative gradient at the trailing edge is misread as a lethal obstacle (a “black line” in the costmap), causing navigational freezing. Purely semantic (camera-based) approaches address recognition but lack the metric reliability collision avoidance needs [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .

This motivates a fusion strategy in which the two sensors are not treated as interchangeable sources, but are assigned complementary roles according to their known failure modes. Prior fusion and learned approaches (Section II ) show the benefit of combining semantic appearance with geometric structure, but leave open the application-specific problem of assigning traversability to the resulting terrain representation.

We propose a failure-mode-aware semantic-geometric fusion architecture where LiDAR remains the primary safety estimate and a YOLOv26-m-seg model [ 8 ] provides class- and confidence-gated corrective evidence, overriding geometry only for identified failure modes. Rather than learn the final traversability decision end-to-end [ 6 , 9 ] , we use learning only for semantic recognition and keep sensor arbitration an explicit, auditable, deterministic policy. This suits our 506-image annotated set, which supervises recognition directly (a learned traversability predictor would need an additional target describing the desired traversability of robot-centric terrain regions, which existing learned approaches obtain from proprioceptive or self-supervised signals [ 6 , 9 ] ), and it gives the per-decision verifiability a safety-relevant system needs. The final costmap is derived deterministically from semantic evidence and measured LiDAR geometry, so the fusion logic can be designed explicitly around the construction-site failure modes considered in this work, and the result feeds our custom path-planning and navigation stack.

Contributions:

A deterministic, class- and confidence-gated sensor-arbitration strategy using semantic vision as a selective corrective signal for complementary LiDAR failure modes (flat hazards, phantom obstacles), with LiDAR as fallback. It addresses both geometric false negatives (flat wet mud, ponding concrete) and geometric false positives (speed-breakers, inclined terrain).

The public multimodal construction-site dataset detailed in Section III : four closed-loop ROS 2 sequences from two active sites (RGB, depth, LiDAR, IMU, GPS-RTK, odometry) plus 506 pixel-level annotated RGB frames spanning 28 construction-specific semantic classes. The taxonomy distinguishes traversable surfaces (flat road, terrain, rocky terrain) from construction-specific hazards, while the raw recordings preserve the temporal structure of robotic operation.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Geometric Ground Segmentation

Geometric approaches such as Patchwork++ [ 1 ] give robust, real-time ground-plane extraction from raw 3D LiDAR by adaptively fitting region-wise planes and rejecting partial under-segmentation; they are computationally efficient and metrically reliable, and our geometric branch is built directly on this approach. However, because they reason purely over spatial gradients and elevation, they cannot distinguish flat non-load-bearing hazards (e.g., wet mud) from safe ground, nor drivable elevation changes (e.g., ramps, speed-breakers) from lethal obstacles—the two central failure modes this paper addresses.

## II-B Off-Road and Urban Semantic Datasets

Large-scale urban datasets such as Cityscapes [ 10 ] established the benchmark methodology for pixel-level semantic segmentation, but their class taxonomy and structured-road assumptions do not transfer to unstructured terrain. Off-road semantic segmentation datasets such as RUGD [ 11 ] and RELLIS-3D [ 12 ] extend the Cityscapes paradigm to unstructured environments, introducing fine-grained terrain classes collected from mobile robots traversing natural environments; RELLIS-3D additionally provides multimodal LiDAR, camera, and inertial data in a ROS-based dataset. Neither, however, captures the transient, man-made hazard classes specific to active construction sites, such as rebar, scaffolding, ponding concrete, or loose pipe stacks.

TNS’s Complex Worksite Terrain (CWT) dataset [ 13 ] targets excavators with 669 RGB-only images and seven categories based on terrain and navigability. Our release instead focuses on live, active building construction sites: rather than primarily an annotated RGB corpus, it centers on a raw multimodal rosbag corpus (four closed-loop sequences: RGB, depth, LiDAR, IMU, GPS-RTK, odometry) plus a 28-class annotated subset, supporting fusion, mapping, loop-closure, and localization research along with segmentation. The taxonomy explicitly separates construction hazards and traversable surface types that are operationally important for a compact AMR.

## II-C Semantic-Geometric Fusion

Prior fusion work combines visual and geometric terrain cues [ 3 , 4 ] : Schilling et al. combine geometric and visual terrain information for autonomous mobile navigation, while Zhou et al. investigate terrain traversability mapping using LiDAR and camera fusion. These works establish the benefit of combining visual appearance with geometric terrain information. More recent learned approaches (BEVFusion [ 5 ] , RoadRunner [ 7 ] , METAVerse [ 9 ] ) learn multimodal or traversability representations end-to-end: BEVFusion provides a unified bird’s-eye-view representation, while RoadRunner and METAVerse demonstrate learned traversability estimation from multimodal observations or vehicle-terrain interaction. In contrast, our approach uses learning only for semantic recognition and keeps the final sensor arbitration a deterministic policy, so the fusion rules can be tied directly to the construction-specific LiDAR failure modes observed in our data.

## II-D Geometric-Semantic Fusion for Construction Machinery

TNS [ 13 ] is closest to our work, fusing elevation-grid slope/step-height features with RGB semantics to zero traversability for non-traversable categories on a 49-ton excavator. TNS takes a 3D LiDAR point cloud, an RGB camera stream, and the robot pose, constructs an elevation grid, estimates terrain features such as slope and step height, and incorporates semantic information into the resulting traversability representation. Its semantic-geometric fusion is explicit and deterministic: non-traversable semantic categories can be assigned zero traversability, while other regions retain or receive a geometric traversability score.

Deterministic semantic-geometric fusion itself is therefore not claimed as the novelty of our work, and the distinction from TNS is not that our method is deterministic while TNS is learned. The distinction lies in how semantic information is used in the final decision. TNS primarily produces a continuous traversability representation based on geometric terrain properties and semantic categories for excavator planning. Where TNS applies a uniform semantic override, our fusion logic is asymmetric, failure-mode-specific, and confidence-gated, treating semantic perception as a corrective signal for a local AMR costmap, tailored to the unstructured hazards of active building sites: high-confidence flat hazards override geometrically clear LiDAR cells, high-confidence traversable classes suppress geometric false positives from speed-breakers and ramps, and ambiguous classes (e.g., puddles) defer to LiDAR. For puddles, semantic perception confirms water presence but does not independently determine traversability; LiDAR geometry remains authoritative. We also preserve flat road, terrain, and rocky terrain as distinct states rather than a single traversable class, enabling surface-specific navigation costs and speed preferences.
