2026-10-06.title: VICON: Visual-Inertial-Contact based Hand-Object Tracking for Manipulation Datasets
2026-10-06.authors: Yubin Jeon , Uiseong Shin , Hwanchul La , Jaeseong Kang , Hyelim Choi , Yongseok Lee
2026-10-06.abstract:
Learning dexterous manipulation benefits from human demonstration datasets that capture diverse and natural hand-object interactions. In particular, contact points and forces provide supervision on where and how strongly to interact, which cannot be fully captured by motion trajectories alone. However, methods for jointly capturing hand and object motion, contact points, and forces remain limited. Moreover, severe occlusion from hand-object interaction challenges accurate tracking of both hands and objects. To address these limitations, we present a Visual-Inertial-CONtact based hand-object tracking (VICON) framework. It holistically captures both hand and object motion along with contact information during manipulation, even under severe occlusion. First, we adopt a visual-inertial glove [ 1 ] and an RGB-D camera for accurate hand tracking, and redesign the glove to incorporate contact sensing. Specifically, force-sensitive resistors (FSRs) are placed on the glove based on human grasp frequency to synchronously record contact states and calibrated normal forces.
Second, without requiring pre-existing CAD models, we estimate object poses using RGB-D images and a mesh reconstructed from a monocular video. We propose factor-graph-based object trajectory estimation that fuses object-pose estimates weighted by visibility under hand-object occlusion, FSR measurements, and a hand-motion prior. Across 40 motion-capture sessions with five objects, VICON achieves a 2.5% failed-frame rate compared with 50.9–64.6% for the baselines, with median errors of 3.9 mm and 3.0 ∘ under occlusion. Using VICON, we construct a dataset containing synchronized hand-object motion, contact points, and normal forces, and will publicly release an expanded dataset covering 10 object categories at https://github.com/VICON-dataset/dataset .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation is a fundamental capability for humanoid robots operating in human environments, where everyday tasks require coordinated hand motion and continuous physical interaction with objects. Learning such intricate behaviors heavily relies on rich demonstrations.
However, collecting demonstrations via teleoperation is challenging; differences in kinematics and workspace between human and robot hands make real-time control unintuitive, severely limiting data collection efficiency and degrading motion quality. In contrast, directly capturing human demonstrations bypasses these difficulties, naturally preserving human dexterity and task variability across diverse objects and environments [ 2 , 3 ] . Yet, to fully realize this potential, hand-object interactions must be measured reliably.
Rich demonstration data requires more than hand-object motion alone, since successful dexterous manipulation fundamentally depends on where contact occurs and how much force is applied. Such information is particularly important for learning contact-rich manipulation policies [ 4 ] and emerging force-aware vision-language-action models [ 5 ] . Demonstration data should therefore capture contact points and forces alongside hand and object motion. However, many existing datasets provide detailed hand-object geometry and contact annotations without directly measuring the applied forces [ 6 , 7 ] . Although recent tactile datasets and sensing systems provide richer contact information [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] , simultaneously capturing hand-object poses along with contact locations and forces remains challenging within a compact setup. In particular, achieving accurate ground truth often requires multi-view camera systems, restricting data collection to dedicated environments.

With a compact setup, occlusion presents another major challenge for reliable hand-object tracking. Under severe occlusion, even state-of-the-art vision-based pose estimators can become unreliable or fail entirely. Although existing works have attempted to mitigate occlusion in hand pose estimation [ 11 ] and hand-object tracking [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , these approaches still rely heavily on visual cues, which can become unreliable under severe or prolonged occlusion. Recent work has explored using hand motion as an additional constraint for object tracking [ 15 ] , but maintaining robust tracking when visual evidence is largely unavailable remains challenging.

Wearable hand tracking directly captures hand kinematics, providing reliable motion estimates where vision-only estimation fails. In particular, visual-inertial skeletal tracking (VIST) [ 1 ] combines inertial measurements with visual marker observations to robustly track hand motion under severe occlusions. Because hand and object trajectories are tightly coupled during manipulation, this robust hand motion can serve as a prior to guide object pose estimation when visual object cues become unreliable. However, this kinematic constraint is physically valid only when the hand and object are in direct contact. Contact sensing therefore serves as a crucial gate to determine when the hand-motion prior should be applied. To address this, we integrate force-sensitive resistors (FSRs) directly onto the glove, providing occlusion-invariant contact detection while simultaneously yielding calibrated normal force measurements.

Building on these components, we present VICON (Fig. 1 ), a multimodal tracking framework built on the VIST glove [ 1 ] integrated with eight FSRs, together with a single RGB-D camera. An offline factor graph fuses object-pose estimates from FoundationPose [ 16 ] , weighted by object visibility, with a contact-gated hand-motion prior to refine object trajectories under occlusion. Using the refined trajectories, contact points are located on the object surface, which are paired with calibrated FSR forces. The main contributions of our work are:

Visual-inertial hand tracking system with contact sensing.

Visual-inertial hand tracking system with contact sensing.

We integrate eight FSRs into the VIST glove [ 1 ] , positioned according to human grasp contact frequency [ 17 ] . Together with a single RGB-D camera, the resulting VICON-glove synchronously records hand motion, contact states, and calibrated normal contact forces.

Robust hand-object tracking algorithm under severe occlusion.

We fuse a contact-gated hand-motion prior with visibility-weighted object pose estimates to refine object trajectories and maintain robust tracking even under severe occlusion.

Scalable contact-rich dataset collection for custom objects.

We present a pipeline that reconstructs object geometry from monocular video and captures synchronized hand motion, object pose, object-frame contact points, and calibrated normal forces using only a VICON-glove and a single RGB-D camera. We will publicly release an expanded dataset covering 10 object categories.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Vision-Based Hand and Object Pose Estimation

Vision-based methods have been widely studied for recovering hand and object poses during manipulation from RGB or RGB-D observations.
For object pose estimation, MegaPose [ 18 ] estimates the 6-DoF pose of novel objects using rendered CAD views for coarse pose selection and iterative refinement.
FoundationPose [ 16 ] supports both estimation and tracking with CAD models or neural object representations learned from reference RGB-D images, although occlusion degrades the visual cues needed for reliable alignment.
A second line of work jointly estimates hand and object poses by aligning hand-object models with RGB-D observations using proximity-based contact and occlusion constraints [ 12 ] . HOLD [ 14 ] reconstructs both from monocular video using neural implicit surfaces and contact constraints without an object template.
More recently, ComPose [ 15 ] learns from monocular RGB video to weight hand joints and combine hand- and object-derived motion cues for object tracking.
Despite these advances, image-derived geometry and motion consistency may not reliably distinguish near-contact state from actual contact at an occluded surface, and none of these methods directly measures contact forces.

## II-B Hand-Tracking Gloves and Contact Sensing

Sensorized gloves have been developed to capture hand motion and tactile interactions during manipulation.
VIST [ 1 ] fuses glove-mounted IMUs with visual markers under hand kinematic constraints, using inertial propagation and visual corrections to maintain hand tracking through occlusion.
A markerless approach uses inertial pose priors to infer image keypoints and their uncertainty and combines the learned keypoint likelihoods with inertial observations in a factor graph [ 19 ] .
FSGlove [ 20 ] uses IMUs placed on the glove, whose alignment is calibrated from reference poses and fits a personalized hand shape using predefined finger contact constraints. However, an external dorsal tracker is additionally used to recover the hand’s global pose.
For contact sensing, STAG [ 8 ] records spatial patterns of normal force using 548 piezoresistive sensors distributed over the hand, and learns to identify objects and estimate their weights from these tactile signatures.
However, neither kinematic tracking nor tactile sensing is sufficient on its own; kinematic tracking cannot measure applied force, while tactile sensing requires hand-object kinematics to locate contacts on the object surface. Despite this clear complementarity, prior works rarely integrate both modalities in a single wearable system.

## II-C Hand-Object Interaction Datasets for Manipulation

Table I compares existing datasets in terms of pose annotations, contact and force signals, and recording setups.
EgoDex [ 2 ] pairs large-scale egocentric video with hand poses but has no object pose, contact, or force.
ContactPose [ 6 ] maps thermal imprints after static grasps onto object meshes alongside hand and object poses.
ARCTIC [ 7 ] derives contact from reconstructed hand-object geometry during bimanual manipulation of articulated objects, requiring a costly multi-camera motion-capture studio.

Tactile datasets pair measured pressure with hand motion.
OpenTouch [ 9 ] combines full-hand pressure, hand tracking, and egocentric video, but provides no object poses.
More recently, TactiDex [ 10 ] combines dense tactile gloves with hand-object motion capture, using pressure-gated proximity and tactile-constrained optimization, but requires a motion-capture workspace.

Force-aware robot datasets record external loads for contact-rich policy learning.
ForceVLA [ 5 ] synchronizes images, proprioception, and estimated six-axis tool-center-point (TCP) wrenches in ForceVLA-Data across five contact-rich tasks and fuses them in a vision-language-action policy. However, these wrenches describe net end-effector loads without resolving individual human hand-object contacts.

In contrast to these systems, VICON enables scalable collection of contact-rich demonstrations. Specifically, it is low-cost and wearable, since the VICON-glove builds on the VIST glove, whose material cost is about $100 and weight is 52–55 g [ 1 ] , and adds only eight FSRs. Moreover, it requires only one RGB-D camera and no motion-capture studio, so recording is not restricted to a dedicated capture space. In addition, it provides accurate data even under severe occlusion, as the glove tracks the hand robustly and the FSRs measure contact directly (Sec. V-C ). Finally, it pairs object-frame contact points with calibrated normal forces, a feature absent from prior datasets in Table I . As the volume of demonstration data becomes increasingly important for learning manipulation, this combination of low acquisition cost and high accuracy is a key advantage over costly studio-based systems such as ARCTIC [ 7 ] .

2026-10-06.title: Recursive Self-Improvement of Visuomotor Policies through Local Recovery Supervision
2026-10-06.authors: Yuzhi Zhang , Xinyu Liu , Yu Zhang
2026-10-06.abstract: Visuomotor policies can execute familiar tasks yet lack the corrective behavior needed after their own mistakes. We present a framework for recursive self-improvement through local recovery supervision. Each round audits the current policy, generates corrective demonstrations at supported failure states, and uses them to update the policy that drives the next round of collection. An offline auditor locates unresolved failures using coarse and dense temporal evidence and specifies observable repair goals. A fixed multimodal agent acts as a tool-using teacher, generating recovery actions through observation, computation, execution, and feedback. The frozen student tests whether each teacher endpoint supports further progress. If continuation fails, the system restores that endpoint and extends the demonstration. Action-level quality assessment then defines continuous training windows with aligned observations, quality weights, and validity masks. Only the student is deployed. In a preliminary LIBERO-Goal study, recovery-augmented post-training achieves 88 successful episodes out of 100 validation scenes, compared with 78 for original-data continuation from the same π 0 \pi_{0} checkpoint. An earlier BC-RNN study on robomimic Can improves success from 102/130 to 112/130 using 26 local recovery segments. Both comparisons match 2,000 additional optimization steps.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Visuomotor policies map visual observations and robot state to actions, optionally conditioned on a task instruction. Large demonstration datasets and generalist policies have expanded the range of tasks that can be learned with a shared model [ 46 , 38 , 11 , 22 , 4 , 41 ] . Action chunking and generative policies further improve the representation of manipulation behavior [ 51 , 7 ] . Yet knowing how to complete a task does not imply knowing how to recover when execution deviates from the demonstrations. Recent recovery benchmarks make this gap explicit by evaluating policies from intermediate failure states [ 27 , 31 ] . After missing a grasp, a policy may continue along a familiar transport motion with an empty gripper. The remaining task is recognizable, but the behavior needed to make its existing competence useful again is missing.

Failures expose this gap in a form that can guide further training. Interactive imitation learning queries expertise on states reached by the learner [ 44 , 25 ] ; human interventions provide corrections when autonomous execution needs help [ 20 , 34 , 12 , 30 ] . Recent work extends this principle through recovery learning, automated intervention generation, and policy post-training [ 15 , 13 , 40 , 39 ] . Our question is how an automatic teacher should turn the current visuomotor policy’s failures into useful action supervision. Completing the task is one possible response, but it does not determine when a demonstration should start, where it should end, or which of its actions deserve imitation.

This question becomes central when collection and learning repeat. Updating a policy changes the states it visits, the mistakes it makes, and the corrections it needs. A fixed recovery dataset may therefore cease to target its weaknesses. We formulate recursive self-improvement (RSI) as a policy-driven cycle: audit the current student, collect local recovery supervision, update its parameters, and audit the resulting policy again. The recursion lies in this feedback between policy behavior and subsequent training data. The multimodal teacher supplies additional competence while remaining fixed; the student determines both where correction is needed and whether a demonstration has gone far enough.

Consider a failed grasp. The final empty-gripper image reveals an unsuccessful outcome, but an earlier state may offer a better opportunity to correct it. Once the teacher secures the object, the immediate failure is resolved; the student may nevertheless release it before reaching the destination. The teacher then needs to demonstrate more than grasp acquisition. Conversely, requiring the teacher to finish every remaining step can spend collection effort on behavior the student already performs reliably. Even an accepted recovery may contain avoidable detours. A useful collection procedure must make these decisions separately.

We organize local recovery supervision around three boundaries: the entry supported by failure evidence, the endpoint supported by student execution, and the continuous intervals supported by action quality (Fig. 1 ). First, an offline auditor examines a coarse rollout and then dense evidence around an unresolved event. Focus prioritizes a critical intervention, whereas Coverage seeks complementary prevention, early-correction, and recovery opportunities. The selected state is paired with a prospective specification: the physical relation to establish, the observations needed to confirm it, and achieved progress to preserve.

A tool-using teacher generates a correction through observation, computation, bounded action, and inspection of the resulting scene. It can compute a new target or write a short program, but it must justify completion from observable physical evidence. The frozen student then executes from the teacher endpoint. If it cannot make and sustain useful progress, the system discards that diagnostic branch, restores the teacher endpoint, and appends a further correction. This makes demonstration length depend on the recipient’s behavior rather than on teacher confidence alone.

After a successful handoff, an offline evaluator grades each executed teacher action in the state from which it was actually taken. Maximal continuous intervals above a quality threshold become training windows. Their observations, targets, action context, and loss masks remain aligned; actions on student test branches never become imitation targets. Mixing these windows with the original data updates the student without retaining a teacher at deployment.

The contribution is a concrete procedure for recursive improvement of visuomotor policies: evidence-based entry selection and recipient-driven endpoint extension; a closed-loop tool teacher governed by local physical specifications; and continuous, quality-weighted recovery supervision for post-training. We describe the implementation and report a π 0 \pi_{0} study on a custom LIBERO-Goal split, together with an earlier BC-RNN experiment on robomimic Can. With 2,000 additional student updates in each comparison, recovery supervision raises success from 78/100 to 88/100 for π 0 \pi_{0} and from 102/130 to 112/130 for BC-RNN.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

DAgger makes the learner’s state distribution central to imitation learning [ 44 ] . DART exposes demonstrations to controlled perturbations, and HG-DAgger, intervention weighted regression, ThriftyDAgger, and SIRIUS organize when experts intervene and how their behavior enters training [ 25 , 20 , 34 , 12 , 30 ] . RaC scales recovery and correction data for long-horizon tasks [ 15 ] . RECAP combines experience and interventions through advantage-conditioned policy learning, while SOP provides an online system for collecting experience and updating generalist policies [ 40 , 39 ] . We construct local corrections for states poorly covered by the student’s demonstrations.

RoboCat uses trained policies to generate experience for subsequent training iterations [ 5 ] . EmbodiRSI combines agent-assisted corrections and adaptive data collection in task-specific simulations to improve policies before transfer to physical robots [ 24 ] . These works establish the broader feedback loop between policy capability and data acquisition. Our focus is how to construct local recovery supervision within that loop: failure evidence supports the entry, execution by the recipient policy supports the endpoint, and action quality determines the continuous intervals used for learning. The recursive setting motivates fresh audits, while these supervision decisions define the method studied here.

RACER augments demonstrations with recovery trajectories and rich language annotations, then uses a vision-language supervisor to guide a visuomotor actor [ 8 ] . FLARE teaches retries through perturbed demonstrations and learns reset skills for failures that disrupt the environment; an online monitor chooses between task execution and reset [ 50 ] . These methods connect recovery supervision with structured guidance during execution. Our teacher instead operates during data collection, and the resulting corrections are absorbed into a student that deploys alone. Fail2Progress addresses a related data problem by generating simulation environments resembling observed failures and adapting a skill effect model [ 17 ] . We target the actions needed to recover from a particular student’s execution state.

MimicGen and SkillMimicGen expand demonstrations through task structure and motion transfer [ 36 , 10 ] ; IntervenGen generates corrective interventions from a small human seed set [ 13 ] . WM-DAgger and Dream2Fix use predictive or counterfactual models to acquire corrective experience [ 48 , 26 ] . Kintsugi-VLA repeatedly restores failed-rollout states and probes a privileged expert to estimate recoverability, which guides recovery-start selection [ 45 ] . MAGMA-GEN validates proposed corrections by re-execution and downstream continuation, producing supervision over task-level tool calls [ 3 ] . Here, the frozen recipient policy tests the endpoint of an executed native-action demonstration. A failed check causes the teacher to extend its saved path, while the student branch supplies diagnostic evidence rather than training labels.

ProTracer uses proprioceptive changes and visual evidence to diagnose failures and localize their onset [ 9 ] . Sentinel combines monitoring of action consistency with reasoning about task progress, and ViFailBack uses visual symbols for diagnosis and correction [ 2 , 49 ] . We use temporal evidence to justify an actionable intervention state, which need not coincide with the first anomaly. For execution, SayCan, Code as Policies, and VoxPoser connect language reasoning to skills, programs, and spatial representations [ 18 , 28 , 16 ] . AERIS and AeroWeaver also connect language-agent decisions to closed-loop robotic execution [ 32 , 33 ] . Agent as Policy keeps a tool-using agent in the execution loop and provides the client underlying our control bridge [ 19 ] . We adapt this execution interface to local recovery collection with fixed specifications, completion evidence, saved endpoints, and student handoff checks.

SSDF scores imperfect trajectory segments using learned similarity, filters low-quality data, and applies weighted behavioral cloning [ 47 ] . We extend this perspective to supervision extracted from an extended recovery path. An action is assessed in the state actually reached; a necessary retreat after a poor approach can be useful even when the approach should be excluded. Retained transitions form continuous intervals with their true initial observations. For joint action-chunk prediction, validity also controls future action positions supplied as model input, in addition to the supervised loss. This preserves a distinction between accepting a handoff, archiving an executed path, and choosing its imitation targets.

OpenVLA-OFT studies how action decoding, chunking, and the training objective affect VLA adaptation [ 21 ] . SpatialVLA incorporates explicit spatial representations, while GeoPredict adds predictive kinematic and geometric supervision [ 43 , 42 ] . Cosmos Policy adapts a pretrained video model to generate actions, future observations, and values [ 23 ] . These approaches improve how policies represent and learn manipulation behavior. Local recovery collection addresses the complementary question of which corrective experience to provide. Applying that experience across architectures requires preserving each model’s action representation and objective, including its treatment of invalid action positions. This motivates comparisons within each student architecture under matched training conditions.

RoboRecover evaluates policies from execution-induced deviation states reconstructed by replay [ 27 ] . LIBERO-RECOVER organizes failures by the correction they require, from action retries to changes in object and environment state [ 31 ] . Both make recovery an explicit evaluation target beyond completion from nominal starts. This distinction is central to our setting: better task success after post-training and better recovery from a given failure are related but separate outcomes. The evaluation protocol therefore includes both nominal episodes and held-out failure states, with the original task unchanged.

2026-10-06.title: PB-STDG: A Prediction-Based Short-Term Decentralized Greedy Guidance Algorithm for a Drone Road System
2026-10-06.authors: Zhouyu Qu , Andreas Willig , Xiaobing Wu
2026-10-06.abstract: In recent years, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) or drones have been increasingly adopted in urban environments for applications such as parcel delivery, infrastructure inspection, emergency response, and drone light shows. A non-negligible issue is how to manage the increasing number of drones operated by different entities, to enable them to cooperatively avoid potential collisions and determine conflict-free short-term flight paths in urban airspace. This paper presents a Prediction-Based Short-Term Decentralized Greedy (PB-STDG) guidance algorithm for a structured Drone Road System (DRS). PB-STDG extends the original STDG algorithm by introducing a prediction mechanism that enables drones to anticipate the decisions of neighboring drones using additional information shared in beacon packets, aiming to address the over-conservative behavior observed in the STDG algorithm. Several simulation scenarios are used to evaluate and compare the proposed algorithm with STDG. The results show that PB-STDG improves traffic efficiency while maintaining a safety level comparable to that of STDG.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Continuous advances in drones, or unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), technology have significantly expanded the range of drone applications, attracting growing interest from both academia and industry. Although drones were initially developed for military operations [ 14 , 6 ] , their applications have gradually expanded into a wide range of civilian and commercial fields, such as aerial photography [ 12 , 25 , 32 ] , emergency response [ 26 ] , and infrastructure inspection [ 15 , 24 ] . More recently, drone applications have expanded into delivery and entertainment. Commercial drone delivery services are now being used for last-mile parcel distribution by companies such as Amazon Prime Air [ 3 ] and Google Wing [ 31 ] . Food delivery by drones has also entered commercial operation in cities including Shenzhen, China, where Meituan operates urban drone delivery routes [ 33 ] . Beyond delivery, large-scale drone light shows have become a popular feature of public celebrations, such as the drone show program at Darling Harbour in Sydney [ 17 ] , where coordinated drone swarms are deployed for regular night-time performances.

With the growth of these drone applications, the number of deployed drones is continuously increasing [ 8 ] . These drones generally share the same low-altitude airspace, particularly in urban environments. Unlike traditional ground traffic systems, most current drone operations are conducted in an unstructured and free-flight manner. Each drone independently plans its trajectory based on its own algorithms and available information. Although such an approach provides flexibility, it becomes increasingly difficult to maintain safety and manage large-scale drone operations involving different operators and service providers. Conflicts between competing flight paths may lead to traffic congestion or even collisions as the number of drones increases, which can degrade overall system efficiency and pose risks to public safety.

To address this challenge, several studies on structured airspace management have been proposed, aiming to organize low-altitude airspace into predefined aerial structures and constrain drone movements within them. A representative example is the NASA drone traffic management concept [ 11 ] . In this framework, the low-altitude airspace is organized into multiple layers based on altitude. High-speed fixed-wing UAVs are typically assigned to higher layers, while low-speed rotary-wing UAVs operate in lower layers. Within each layer, the airspace is further structured into different types of aerial structures, including sky-corridors, sky-tubes, and sky-lanes. Drones are allowed to fly freely within sky-corridors, whereas sky-tubes impose directional constraints on movement. Sky-lanes provide an additional level of restriction by regulating lateral motion, preventing drones from cruising in parallel within the same lane.

Several studies have explored layer-based approaches for drone traffic management, using different altitude layers to regulate drone movement and heading directions [ 7 , 27 , 19 ] . Other studies have proposed more structured drone road systems inspired by ground transportation networks, including corridor-based and lane-level structures [ 18 , 29 ] . Building on these concepts, [ 21 ] proposes a Drone Road System framework consisting of structured roads and ramps. All road segments are designed to be unidirectional, with a defined number of lanes and an allowed speed range, to support safe and predictable drone movement. The system can also be encoded in XML format, enabling flexible updates and efficient distribution across different platforms.

While drone traffic management systems such as drone road systems provide a structured framework for organizing low-altitude airspace, conflicts between drones can still occur within the constrained network, particularly under high-density traffic conditions. In such environments, drones may compete for optimal routes, and different types of conflicts may arise due to speed differences or directional changes during navigation. Therefore, effective drone guidance and collision avoidance mechanisms remain essential.

A large body of research has been devoted to UAV navigation and collision avoidance in free-flight environments. These include approaches such as [ 9 ] and [ 30 ] , which determine short-term collision-free paths for UAVs in environments containing obstacles and other dynamic constraints. The Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) approach [ 1 ] iteratively updates drone positions based on individual and global best solutions. Another widely studied approach is Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) [ 10 , 2 , 16 ] , which learns drone control policies through interaction with the environment. These methods typically use sensory inputs such as images, video streams, or onboard sensor data to generate control actions via deep neural networks. By optimizing a reward function, drones can learn collision-free navigation in dynamic and complex environments.

Specifically, several studies have investigated safe guidance and collision avoidance algorithms for drone delivery scenarios. In [ 20 ] , three collision avoidance strategies are proposed to manage large numbers of drones delivering goods to random destinations in urban environments. Similarly, [ 5 ] presents a centralized navigation approach for a fleet of drones to achieve safe point-to-point parcel delivery missions. In addition, [ 4 ] introduces two centralized algorithms to ensure safe delivery operations within a simplified two-layer airspace structure.

However, these approaches suffer from several limitations: (i) they often rely on global information of other agents, (ii) they require multiple types of onboard sensors, and (iii) they are primarily designed for free-flight environments and cannot be directly adapted to structured airspace systems. In the large-scale drone traffic system we focus on, where drones are owned by different operators and perform diverse tasks, these limitations become more critical. Specifically, global coordination is difficult to achieve in practice, as it is unrealistic for each drone to obtain or maintain global knowledge of all other drones in the city-scale airspace. Moreover, different navigation algorithms across different drones further increase system uncertainty, since individual drones are unable to accurately predict the behavior of others under inconsistent or unknown algorithms. They will also make different assumptions about the available sensors, and in this paper, we make very minimal assumptions, requiring only GPS and wireless communication.

Based on these challenges and assumptions, a research gap can be identified in the guidance of large-scale drone traffic under limited coordination. Existing approaches often rely on assumptions about the available sensing, communication, or coordination capabilities of drones. However, in a large-scale drone road system, drones may be operated by different manufacturers or service providers and may therefore have limited ability to coordinate with one another. There is therefore a need for a guidance approach that can manage interactions among a large number of independently operating drones without relying on extensive coordination or additional sensing capabilities.

To address this research gap, a baseline guidance algorithm for structured drone road systems is required that can be applied to different types of drones while relying on minimal information and limited sensing capabilities. In our previous studies [ 23 , 22 ] , STDG was proposed to address drone route navigation and collision avoidance challenges on the standardized Drone Road System introduced in [ 21 ] . The STDG algorithm relies only on position and velocity information exchanged between drones through beacon packets, and provides short-term, coordination-free, and decentralized guidance. Drones periodically execute STDG to make short-term lane and speed decisions based on the current traffic conditions and potential collision risks.

Previous simulation results for STDG revealed a key limitation: significant speed loss when avoiding potential collisions. Since the algorithm is coordination-free (i.e., drones only exchange beacon packets, with no other form of coordination) and only position and velocity information is shared, it is difficult for drones to accurately estimate or predict the decisions of others. As a result, lane switching may be suppressed when multiple neighboring drones simultaneously select the same lane to switch. In such cases, drones tend to remain in their current lanes and may further reduce their speed or even come to a complete stop until the surrounding traffic conditions change. This behavior significantly degrades traffic throughput and system efficiency. In our previous study, the algorithm settings that allow some potential risks to be disregarded result in an increase in average speed from around 7 m/s to 10 m/s, approaching the preferred speed of 12.5 m/s, with only a slight increase in the collision rate (i.e., from 1 to 5 collisions among 150,000 drones). The results show that STDG has room to improve its average speed, as a substantial speed increase can be achieved by slightly relaxing its treatment of potential collision risks with only a small increase in actual collisions.

This motivates the prediction of neighboring drones’ future actions to better distinguish potential risks from likely collisions, thus allowing drones to make more effective lane-switching and speed-selection decisions without unnecessary stops or slowdowns and avoiding additional collisions that may occur in such situations.

In this paper, we focus on designing a prediction-based extension to the previous STDG guidance algorithm. The proposed approach extends the beacon structure by including additional safety information, which allows drones to predict the movement decisions of their neighbors over the next short period. This capability helps reduce situations where drones tend to remain in their current lanes and encourages necessary lane changes, either to overtake slower predecessors or to move towards their target lanes without prolonged stopping.

Extensive simulations are conducted using the same simulation framework and largely the same experimental configuration as the original STDG study. The results show that, under the same traffic scenario, the proposed prediction-based algorithm substantially reduces the speed loss while maintaining a close-to-zero collision rate. Additional simulations are performed under different road-system configurations and algorithm parameter settings to comprehensively evaluate PB-STDG against the original STDG algorithm.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows.

We propose PB-STDG, a prediction-based extension of the original STDG algorithm that enables drones to predict the movement decisions of neighboring drones. The proposed approach reduces the tendency of multiple drones to remain in their current lanes during concurrent lane switching and, in the tested complex DRS, increases the average speed from 10.28 m/s to 12.18 m/s while maintaining a close-to-zero collision rate.

We design an extended beacon structure and an event-driven beacon transmission mechanism that provide the guidance algorithm with additional safety information for predicting the decisions of neighboring drones, with a modest increase in beacon packet size.

We conduct extensive simulations under different drone densities and algorithm configurations to evaluate the proposed algorithm and compare it with the STDG algorithm. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach across different traffic conditions and algorithm settings.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 briefly introduces the DRS adopted in this work and reviews the baseline STDG algorithm on which PB-STDG is built. Section 3 describes the system settings and assumptions, including the wireless communication and networking settings, beacon content, and beacon transmission mechanism. Section 4 presents PB-STDG in detail. Section 5 describes the simulation assumptions and configurations and evaluates PB-STDG against STDG through extensive simulation studies. Finally, Section 6 concludes the paper and discusses future research directions.

1. We propose PB-STDG, a prediction-based extension of the original STDG algorithm that enables drones to predict the movement decisions of neighboring drones. The proposed approach reduces the tendency of multiple drones to remain in their current lanes during concurrent lane switching and, in the tested complex DRS, increases the average speed from 10.28 m/s to 12.18 m/s while maintaining a close-to-zero collision rate.

2. We design an extended beacon structure and an event-driven beacon transmission mechanism that provide the guidance algorithm with additional safety information for predicting the decisions of neighboring drones, with a modest increase in beacon packet size.

3. We conduct extensive simulations under different drone densities and algorithm configurations to evaluate the proposed algorithm and compare it with the STDG algorithm. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach across different traffic conditions and algorithm settings.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Background

## 2.1 Drone Road System

For large-scale drone traffic management, the drone road system introduces a common framework to construct predefined routes. This framework simplifies traffic management and collision avoidance by making the movements of individual drones more predictable. The predefined road system can be represented in an XML file, which simplifies both road network updates and the transmission of updated information to drones currently cruising within the system.

Each drone road system consists of one or multiple roads and zero or multiple ramps. Both roads and ramps are unidirectional, meaning that drones within the same road or ramp follow the same travel direction. Road is the primary component of the system and consists of one central lane and multiple parallel lanes arranged in a hexagonal grid topology. Each lane is assigned a unique identifier ( i , j ) (i,j) and can have up to six neighboring lanes (shown in Figure 1 ), with the identifiers ( i + 1 , j ) (i+1,j) , ( i − 1 , j ) (i-1,j) , ( i , j + 1 ) (i,j+1) , ( i , j − 1 ) (i,j-1) , ( i + 1 , j − 1 ) (i+1,j-1) , and ( i − 1 , j + 1 ) (i-1,j+1) . Since roads may be curved, an arc-length parameter s s is introduced to represent the relative position of a drone along a lane. The value of s s represents the distance traveled by the drone from the beginning of the lane along the lane.

Ramp is a special type of road that consists of a single lane and is used either to connect two roads or to provide additional entry and exit access to the drone road system. When constructing a ramp, one or two connection points are defined on existing road lanes. If only one connection point is specified, the ramp is referred to as an on/off-ramp, where the other end serves as either an entry or exit of the system. Otherwise, the ramp connects two lanes and is referred to as a connecting ramp.

During its lifetime in the system, a drone first enters the network through either a road entry point or an on-ramp, and its end-to-end path planning is done in advance. In this study, we assume that the plan is never altered afterwards. It then navigates through the system by moving along lanes and may perform lane switching to overtake slower drones or to reach connected lanes leading to other roads or ramps. In this process, a drone can only directly switch to one of its neighboring lanes and then repeat the lane-switching maneuver until it reaches its target lane. Finally, the drone reaches its destination road or off-ramp and exits the system at the corresponding endpoint.

## 2.2 Short-Term Decentralized Greedy Algorithm

The Short-Term Decentralized Greedy (STDG) algorithm serves as a baseline guidance method for the drone road system introduced in Section 2.1 . STDG ensures that drones can successfully complete their trips within the road system while providing essential functionalities such as collision avoidance, lane-switching, and speed-selection. The algorithm generates short-term decisions based on the current local traffic situation over a limited time horizon. This enables drones to overtake slower neighbors and progress toward target connection points without missing them.

The inputs of STDG consist primarily of the position and velocity of the current drone and those of neighboring drones, obtained through periodic beacon transmissions. The algorithm is fully decentralized and does not require any explicit coordination beyond beacon exchange. At the start of the algorithm, a drone considers its current lane and all neighboring lanes as candidate lanes, and evaluates a weighted cost function for each candidate. The lane with the minimum cost is selected as the output lane. If the selected lane differs from the current lane, the drone performs a lane-switching action; otherwise, it remains in its current lane. After lane selection, the drone updates its speed based on either its preferred speed or the speed of its immediate predecessor in the selected lane, whichever is lower.

The total cost consists of three components: position cost, speed cost, and collision cost. The position cost is designed to guide drones toward their target connection points and support lane switching decisions toward subsequent roads or ramps. The basic position cost is defined based on the hop distance between the current lane and the target lane associated with the next connection point, and the distance to that connection point. For example, consider a drone located at lane ( 0 , 0 ) (0,0) with a target lane ( 1 , 0 ) (1,0) , assuming that all neighboring lanes are available and accessible. The basic position cost for each candidate lane is defined as (example shown in Figure 1 ):

0 , for lane ( 1 , 0 ) (1,0)

1 , for lanes ( 0 , 0 ) (0,0) , ( 0 , 1 ) (0,1) , and ( 1 , − 1 ) (1,-1)

2 , for lanes ( − 1 , 0 ) (-1,0) , ( 0 , − 1 ) (0,-1) , and ( − 1 , 1 ) (-1,1)

The speed cost imposes a penalty on drones when their deployable speed is lower than their preferred speed. The deployable speed for each candidate lane is determined by the drone’s preferred speed, the speed of its predecessor, and the distance-dependent constraints. Here, the predecessor refers to the nearest ahead drone in the same lane. If the distance to the predecessor is below a predefined threshold and the predecessor’s speed is lower than the drone’s preferred speed, the deployable speed is set to the predecessor’s speed. Otherwise, it is set to the drone’s preferred speed. The speed cost is then computed using an increasing function of the gap between the preferred speed and the deployable speed.

The collision cost is designed to prevent lane switching maneuvers that may lead to collisions. Its calculation consists of two steps. First, if any drone is detected in the candidate lane within a predefined distance of the current drone, the collision cost is set to the maximum value. This indicates that the candidate lane is infeasible for switching due to the high risk of an immediate collision. Second, if the cost is not set to the maximum value, the algorithm counts the number of drones in the lanes adjacent to the candidate lane that are within the same predefined distance of the current drone. The collision cost is then set equal to this count. This value represents the potential collision risk caused by multiple drones simultaneously attempting to switch into the same lane. A special rule is introduced for leading drones to break deadlocks that may occur when multiple drones are closely clustered and block one another. A leading drone is defined as the foremost drone that has no other drone ahead of it within a predefined safety distance. Such a drone is assigned the highest lane switching priority, and its cost in the second stage of the cost calculation is always set to zero. This allows the leading drone to switch lanes first, thereby creating opportunities for the following drones to resolve the blockage.

The final cost is calculated as the weighted sum of the three cost components. The corresponding weights are configurable algorithm parameters that can be adjusted for different traffic scenarios.

After selecting the output lane and speed, the drone determines whether it is sufficiently close to its target connection point or the road closing point. If so, and the selected output lane is the current lane, the drone enters a stop state. This decision aims to help the drone avoid missing its target connection point or entering the closed section of the road. In this case, the interval before the next algorithm execution is reduced to allow the drone to leave the stop state more quickly when an opportunity becomes available. Otherwise, the interval is set to its normal value. The drone then maintains the selected speed and stays at, or switches to, the selected output lane until the next execution of the algorithm.

2026-10-06.title: Now You Feel It, Now You See Me: Digital-Twin-based Teleoperation Interface for Dexterous Manipulation
2026-10-06.authors: Youngchan Shim , Kyutae Lee , JooYun Kim , Jaeseong Hwang , Harim Ji , Yongseok Lee
2026-10-06.abstract: Teleoperation is becoming increasingly important for collecting high-quality demonstrations to teach robots dexterous manipulation skills. For dexterous manipulation, bare-hand tracking provides a practical way to control robotic hands and demonstrate coordinated finger movements without gloves or exoskeletons. However, this type of teleoperation faces two key feedback limitations: a lack of force feedback and visual feedback of occluded region. The absence of force feedback hinders precise and safe manipulation, as operators must infer contact force visually rather than feel them directly. Occlusion by objects or other robot parts impairs the assessment of hand positions, approach distances, and pre-grasp configurations suited to the object’s shape. To address these limitations, we propose a digital-twin-based augmented reality (AR) teleoperation interface that integrates bare-hand tracking, bimanual robotic hands, and virtual representations of the robot and task objects. The interface renders tactile measurements on robot hand meshes as visuo-force feedback. Furthermore, it offers a user-controlled virtual view panel or occlusion-aware transparency rendering to provide occlusion-mitigating visual feedback. We evaluated the interface through user studies involving Task 1 and Task 2, examining how force visualization and visual assistance support demonstration collection in tasks requiring careful force regulation and manipulation under occlusion.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Teleoperation has become a primary means of collecting high-fidelity demonstration data for robot learning by recording robot actions and observations during human-guided manipulation. Specifically, for dexterous robot hand manipulation, human demonstrations provide high-dimensional joint trajectories during interactions with diverse objects for robot learning. Vision-based hand tracking and motion retargeting enable operators to control robotic hands through bare-hand movements across different robot configurations [ 1 , 2 ] . By eliminating the need for gloves or exoskeletons for motion input, bare-hand interfaces provide a practical means of demonstrating coordinated finger movements.

Despite these advantages, bare-hand teleoperation with typical visual feedback (i.e., bare-eyes or camera) provides limited information about hand–object interactions. In a headset-based setup, operators control the robot through tracked hand movements while observing the physical workspace through passthrough. Without force feedback, they must infer finger contact and contact forces from visual cues, hindering efforts to prevent slippage or excessive grasp forces. Moreover, occlusion by objects or other robot parts obscures finger placement and approach distances, hindering grasp formation. Collectively, these limitations impede the monitoring and correction of manipulation errors during demonstration collection.

Prior work has addressed the lack of force information through wearable haptic devices or visual feedback. Vibrotactile, cutaneous or exoskeleton haptic devices on Glove can convey contact forces, but require hand-worn hardware that can restrict finger motion and complicate deployment across operators [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . As a visual alternative, TactAR [ 6 ] renders a tactile sensor’s deformation field in AR and reports improved demonstration quality relative to teleoperation without this feedback. However, how to represent per-finger force information for dexterous hand teleoperation remains underexplored, particularly the relative benefits of force heatmap and force arrow representations.

To address occlusion, previous studies position or move physical cameras to obtain alternative views [ 7 ] or render the robot or selected links transparent to reveal hidden regions [ 8 , 9 ] . However, these studies neither directly compare the two approaches in dexterous hand teleoperation nor establish their interaction with force visualization.

We propose digital-twin-based AR interfaces combining visuo-force feedback with occlusion-mitigating visual feedback for bare-hand bimanual dexterous teleoperation. Digital-twins of the robot and task objects are updated according to robot states and tracked object poses to visualize contact forces and occluded spatial relationships. We design two force representations: (1) a force heatmap encoding tactile signal magnitude through pad-level color and (2) force arrows conveying direction and magnitude through fingertip-anchored arrows (Fig. 2 ). For occlusion handling, we introduce (1) a user-controlled virtual view panel, which displays an operator-controlled virtual camera view alongside passthrough, and (2) occlusion-aware transparency rendering, which reveals robot fingers through semi-transparent objects in the digital-twin layout (Fig. 4 ). These interfaces support force regulation and grasp formation without hand-worn feedback devices.

We evaluated the interfaces through a user study assessing task performance and perceived workload. The study compared force heatmap, force arrow, and no visuo-force feedback in Task 1, which requires careful force regulation with unobstructed contact regions. In Task 2, we combined the force visualization evaluated in the Task 1 user study with the user-controlled virtual view panel and occlusion-aware transparency rendering. We analyzed and evaluated its interaction with each occlusion-assistance technique during bimanual lifting with occluded grasp openings. In Task 1, both force visualizations significantly reduce perceived workload relative to no visuo-force feedback. The cup deformation rate is 13.3% with force arrow feedback, compared with 44.4% without visuo-force feedback. In Task 2, occlusion-aware transparency rendering achieves the highest observed success rate (82.1%) when combined with force arrow feedback.

The contributions of this work are as follows:

We propose digital-twin-based AR interfaces that combine per-finger visuo-force feedback with a user-controlled virtual view panel or occlusion-aware transparency rendering for bare-hand bimanual dexterous teleoperation.

We compare force heatmap feedback, force arrow feedback, and no visuo-force feedback during manipulation requiring precise grasp force regulation.

We evaluate the two occlusion-assistance techniques for supporting manipulation under occlusion and evaluate them with and without visuo-force feedback.

# II Related Works

## II-A Robot Hand Teleoperation

AnyTeleop [ 1 ] supports vision-based arm–hand teleoperation across different robot arm, hand, and camera configurations, emphasizing adaptability across hardware setups. Open Teach [ 2 ] combines HMD hand tracking with close-up visual feedback for multi-fingered and bimanual control. Open-TeleVision [ 10 ] couples arm and hand motion transfer with active stereoscopic feedback, integrating motion input with immersive workspace observation. Alongside these vision-based approaches, wearable gloves provide an alternative means of tracking hand motion for teleoperation [ 11 , 12 ] .

While these approaches support motion input and task observation, hand tracking alone does not convey robot contact forces, and scene views may leave hand–object interactions occluded. Our bare-hand AR interfaces therefore combine visuo-force feedback with occlusion-mitigating visual feedback to support perception of forces and hand–object spatial relationships during bimanual manipulation.

## II-B Tactile Feedback for Human Operators

Wearable haptic devices convey contact information through vibration [ 4 ] or combine hand tracking with force feedback for robotic manipulation [ 3 ] and virtual manipulation [ 5 ] . Visual feedback studies compare color-based force representations in robot-assisted surgery [ 13 ] and display forces as arrows at the end effector [ 14 ] . TactAR [ 6 ] presents tactile and force information as an AR deformation field registered to the robot end-effector.

Wearable approaches require hand-worn hardware, while the cited visual approaches examine surgical interaction, end-effector force display, or parallel-jaw grasping rather than a common dexterous hand setting. Their evaluations therefore do not directly establish how force heatmap and force arrow representations compare in bimanual dexterous teleoperation. We compare these representations with a baseline without force visualization on a task requiring precise grasp force regulation.

## II-C Occlusion-Mitigating Visual Feedback

Prior systems employ an assistant robot arm to adjust camera viewpoints [ 7 ] or a drone to provide task-relevant views [ 15 ] . VICARIOS [ 16 ] enables viewpoint changes within a virtual environment. Other approaches reveal occluded regions by rendering the robot transparent in diminished reality [ 8 ] or rendering selected digital-twin robot links semi-transparent during task demonstration [ 9 ] .

Although these studies explore viewpoint adjustment and transparency, they do not directly compare the two approaches within a common dexterous hand teleoperation setting. These studies also do not establish the collaboration effect between force feedback and occlusion-mitigating feedback. We therefore compare a user-controlled virtual view panel in a passthrough interface with occlusion-aware transparency rendering in a digital-twin interface, alongside a baseline without occlusion handling. Each interface condition is evaluated with and without visuo-force feedback during bimanual manipulation under occlusion.

2026-10-06.title: FreeLoc: Online Floorplan Localization via Diffusion-Aided Pose Refinement
2026-10-06.authors: Haocheng Peng , Boyang Zhou , Jiarui Hu , Xiyue Guo , Ziyang Zhang , Boming Zhao , Yifan Gao , Xiao Li , Hujun Bao , Zhaopeng Cui
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026
2026-10-06.abstract: Floorplans provide compact and widely available geometric maps for indoor localization, but existing high-performing floorplan-based methods still convert them into dense scene-specific offline databases, tying accuracy, storage, and runtime to the sampling resolution of the discretized pose space. We present FreeLoc, an online RGB-based floorplan localization framework that treats the floorplan as a directly queryable geometric map. FreeLoc introduces an efficient online geometric querying and diffusion-aided refinement scheme, which retrieves plausible pose anchors through on-the-fly floorplan ray querying and refines them into accurate continuous pose estimates. For sequential localization, FreeLoc develops an online likelihood construction strategy that bridges single-frame localization and probabilistic temporal fusion by constructing likelihoods from coarse-sampled candidates and refined pose hypotheses, enabling histogram-filter-based temporal fusion without offline databases. Experiments demonstrate real-time online inference and state-of-the-art performance in both single-frame and sequential localization, while real-world results validate practical deployability in indoor robotic localization scenarios.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Indoor camera localization is a core capability for robotic perception and embodied intelligence, providing the spatial grounding required for mobile robot navigation, human-robot interaction, and autonomous exploration. For robots operating in real indoor environments, a localization system should not only be accurate, but also be readily deployable in new scenes with minimal scene-specific preparation. Traditional indoor visual localization methods [ 20 , 2 , 27 , 35 ] typically rely on pre-built image databases or accurate 3D scene models. These representations are costly to construct, storage-intensive, and difficult to maintain, making them difficult to scale across many buildings and adapt to changing indoor environments.

Floorplans offer a lightweight and scalable map representation for indoor localization. Compared with image databases and 3D scene models, they are compact, widely available [ 13 , 32 ] , and relatively stable over time, making them attractive for localization systems deployed across many buildings. Ideally, a floorplan should serve as a directly queryable geometric map, allowing localization without constructing additional scene-specific databases. However, existing high-performing floorplan localization methods [ 5 , 12 , 45 ] still largely rely on a database-driven formulation: they discretize the SE ⁡ ( 2 ) \mathrm{SE}(2) pose space, precompute dense pose-indexed observations from the floorplan, and match query images against these entries for localization. In sequential settings, the same database-derived scores are further converted into observation likelihoods for histogram filtering, causing the database dependency to persist in temporal fusion. As a result, the limitation lies not merely in preprocessing cost, but in the discretized localization paradigm itself: once localization is tied to a finite pose-indexed database, localization precision, storage, and runtime all scale with the sampling resolution, creating an unfavorable trade-off among accuracy, efficiency, and scalability.

This motivates a more practical and challenging setting: given only a floorplan, can we directly query it online to achieve accurate RGB-based single-frame and sequential localization in new environments, without constructing a scene-specific offline database?

A useful clue comes from how humans localize themselves in unfamiliar indoor spaces. Rather than exhaustively comparing the current view with every possible location on the map, humans typically use the floorplan to narrow the search to a few plausible regions, and then refine their location by matching local geometric details with the current observation. However, realizing this coarse-to-fine intuition in an online localization system is non-trivial.
First, the system must rapidly search
the entire floorplan pose space online to identify plausible initial pose
hypotheses. Second, these retrieved poses are inherently approximate: finite
online sampling introduces discretization errors, while noisy and incomplete
RGB-derived geometric observations further limit matching accuracy, making it
challenging to recover accurate poses from such coarse hypotheses. Third, for
sequential localization with histogram filtering, observation likelihoods over
the discretized pose space are required to update the propagated motion prior,
yet these likelihoods can no longer be densely evaluated from a precomputed
scene-specific ray database.

To address these challenges, we propose FreeLoc, an online RGB-based floorplan localization framework that treats the floorplan as a directly queryable geometric map rather than a scene-specific offline retrieval database, as shown in Fig. 1 . FreeLoc first retrieves a compact set of plausible pose anchors by querying geometric rays from the floorplan on the fly using a GPU-accelerated rotation-aware ray kernel. To refine these approximate anchors, we introduce a diffusion-aided pose refinement network that estimates residual pose corrections from the discrepancy between image-side and floorplan-side ray observations. Instead of relying on one-shot deterministic regression, we formulate pose
refinement as an iterative denoising process, which better matches the nature
of residual pose optimization and progressively corrects imperfect coarse
anchors under ray-level geometric guidance. This allows FreeLoc to move beyond the resolution of coarse online samples and produce accurate pose hypotheses in continuous pose space without exhaustive dense sampling or precomputed scene-specific ray databases. To support sequential localization, we further integrate the online coarse-to-fine estimator into a probabilistic filtering pipeline. Rather than deriving dense observation likelihoods from an offline ray database, FreeLoc constructs observation likelihoods online from coarse-sampled candidates and refines their high-confidence regions using the refined pose hypotheses before Bayesian filtering [ 6 , 10 , 9 ] . This online likelihood construction bridges single-frame localization and temporal fusion without reintroducing a scene-specific database, enabling temporally consistent localization while preserving the immediate deployability of floorplans.

Our contributions are summarized as follows. First, we propose FreeLoc, an online coarse-to-fine framework for RGB-based floorplan localization that eliminates scene-specific offline database construction and enables immediate deployment in new environments. Second, we introduce an efficient online geometric querying and diffusion-aided refinement scheme, which retrieves plausible pose anchors directly from the floorplan and progressively refines them into accurate continuous pose estimates.
Third, we develop an online likelihood construction strategy that bridges single-frame localization and probabilistic temporal fusion, enabling histogram-filter-based sequential localization by constructing observation likelihoods from online sampled candidates and updating them with refined pose hypotheses.
Finally, experiments on various datasets demonstrate that FreeLoc achieves SOTA accuracy and efficiency across representative localization methods from different paradigms, while real-world experiments further validate its practicality for indoor robotic localization.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Visual Localization. Visual localization is a fundamental problem in robotic perception and has
been extensively studied for decades.
Early methods commonly
formulate it as
image retrieval [ 20 , 2 , 1 , 8 , 22 ] , where a query image is matched to a pre-built reference
database to infer its pose. With advances in 3D vision, correspondence-based
approaches [ 27 , 35 , 24 , 26 ] construct 3D scene models, typically via
structure-from-motion (SfM) [ 33 ] , and estimate the 6-DoF camera pose from 2D-3D
matches.
Beyond ground-level reference maps, cross-view localization
has also explored globally available satellite imagery as a spatial reference
for ground-level localization [ 14 ] .
More recently, neural scene representations such as NeRF [ 30 ] and 3DGS [ 23 ] have also been explored for pose estimation by
relating query images to scene-specific representations [ 50 , 48 , 18 ] . However, these approaches depend on pre-constructed databases or scene-specific representations, leading to high storage costs and limited generalization to unseen environments.

Floorplan Localization. Floorplan localization estimates camera pose with respect to a given floorplan, offering a lightweight alternative to image databases and full 3D reconstructions.
Early methods [ 4 , 42 , 11 , 46 ] rely on LiDAR scans matched against floorplan geometry, while later approaches [ 19 , 7 , 43 , 44 ] use depth cameras or visual odometry to obtain geometric observations.
Although effective, these methods require dedicated sensors or assumptions such as known room or camera height, limiting practical applicability.
To improve accessibility, recent works have explored RGB-only floorplan localization.
LaLaLoc [ 17 ] and LaLaLoc++ [ 16 ] embed panoramic observations and floorplan-derived layouts into a shared latent space for retrieval.
PF-Net [ 21 ] formulates localization as differentiable particle filtering, and LASER [ 31 ] aligns image features with rotation-aware circular map features rendered from rasterized floorplan geometry.
However, many of these methods assume upright camera poses, making them less suitable for handheld or head-mounted settings.
Another line of work [ 12 , 31 , 29 , 52 ] incorporates semantic cues, but semantic annotations are often unavailable in standard floorplans.
F 3 Loc [ 5 ] and UnLoc [ 45 ] take an important step toward practical RGB-based floorplan localization by using geometry-only floorplans and images captured under arbitrary camera poses.
They predict floorplan depth from gravity-aligned images and localize the camera by matching the resulting rays against a dense pre-sampled floorplan-ray database.
However, constructing such a database requires time-consuming scene-specific preprocessing and creates an inherent trade-off among localization accuracy, sampling density, and storage cost, limiting flexibility in new environments.
In contrast, our method performs online localization without scene-specific offline ray databases, enabling efficient and accurate deployment in new scenes using only the provided geometric floorplan.
