2026-10-06.title: Reward-DAgger: Robot-Gated Interactive Imitation Learning with General-Purpose Progress-Based Reward Models
2026-10-06.authors: Ryan Li , Yigit Korkmaz , Erdem Bıyık
2026-10-06.abstract:
Recent advances in robot learning have enabled generalist control policies capable of completing a wide range of tasks. However, their performance degrades when deployed in unseen environments, making it critical to detect failures and teach recovery behaviors.
Existing runtime monitoring methods often require task- and policy-specific training or hyperparameter tuning, limiting cross-task deployment and introducing additional overhead during iterative policy updates.
We present Reward-DAgger, a robot-gated interactive imitation learning framework that uses dense progress signals from a general-purpose reward model to determine when human intervention is needed. Our approach is agnostic to the underlying policy architecture, requires no access to policy internals, and can be applied across tasks without retuning the gating mechanism. Our results show that Reward-DAgger achieves a better failure-detection accuracy–latency tradeoff than existing runtime monitoring baselines. Across eight simulated and real-world tasks, Reward-DAgger consistently improves the downstream policy’s autonomous success rate throughout interactive learning and achieves strong return on human effort, outperforming the baselines in most settings. Importantly, the same gating configuration is used across tasks without task-specific hyperparameter tuning, demonstrating transfer across tasks, environments, and policy architectures. Code and videos are available at https://liralab.usc.edu/reward-dagger .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Modern learning-based robot policies, ranging from task-specific models [ 7 , 43 ] to generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models [ 16 , 4 , 34 ] , are increasingly capable of completing challenging manipulation tasks. Yet, these policies remain brittle during deployment: a missed grasp, a dropped object, or a misaligned insertion might cause an otherwise successful rollout to fail. Interactive imitation learning methods, such as DAgger [ 30 ] and its human-gated variants [ 24 , 18 , 14 , 26 , 28 ] , address this problem by collecting expert interventions from states where the policy struggles and using these corrections to iteratively improve the policy. However, continuously monitoring robot execution and deciding when to intervene places a substantial burden on the human expert, making such approaches difficult to scale to robot fleets.

Robot-gated interactive imitation learning instead seeks to automate this decision by requesting human assistance when the policy is likely to fail, thereby making more efficient use of costly human supervision. Existing robot-gating methods, however, commonly rely on either learned failure-prediction functions trained from explicit failure data [ 10 ] or policy-dependent uncertainty scores that require task- and policy-specific calibration [ 8 , 19 , 9 , 38 , 27 ] . The former requires collecting failures that are undesirable or infeasible during safety-critical deployment, while the latter couples the gating mechanism to a particular policy checkpoint. As the policy changes throughout interactive learning, the gate needs to be retrained or recalibrated, limiting its scalability.

Ideally, a scalable gating mechanism for interactive imitation learning should satisfy four properties: (1) detect failures early while avoiding unnecessary interruptions of successful behavior; (2) remain effective across iterations of interactive learning without repeated retraining or recalibration; (3) operate with different, potentially black-box, policy architectures; and (4) transfer across tasks without requiring a separate training or calibration procedure for each task.

Our key insight is that general-purpose progress-based reward models, which estimate task progress directly from visual observations and natural-language instructions [ 21 , 33 , 20 ] , provide a natural signal for such a gate. Unlike policy-dependent uncertainty measures, task progress describes what the robot has accomplished rather than how the policy generates its actions. Consequently, progress can be evaluated independently of the underlying policy architecture or checkpoint. This decoupling allows the gating mechanism to be fixed as the policy is updated and to be applied to different policies without access to their internal representations. Moreover, by leveraging reward models pretrained across diverse tasks, progress provides a common signal that can support gating across tasks without task-specific gate training.
Importantly, even under task distribution shift, the reward model only determines when to request assistance; the policy is still trained from human corrections, which provide valid task-specific supervision.

Based on this insight, we introduce Reward-DAgger , a robot-gated interactive imitation learning framework that uses a simple but effective two-timescale rule over progress estimates from a general-purpose progress-based reward model to trigger human takeover. A short-window gate detects rapid decreases in progress, capturing immediate failures such as dropping an object,
while a long-window gate detects progress plateaus corresponding to stalled behavior, such as repeatedly failed grasps. When either gate fires, control is transferred to a human expert, and the resulting corrections are used in the next policy update. Importantly, both the reward model and the gating configuration remain fixed throughout interactive learning, requiring no per-round retraining or recalibration.

We evaluate Reward-DAgger along three dimensions: failure-detection performance, cross-task transfer of the gating parameters, and downstream policy improvement. On four simulation tasks, Reward-DAgger achieves a strong accuracy–latency trade-off compared to existing robot-gating and runtime-monitoring baselines. We further find that a single gate configuration selected jointly on multiple source tasks transfers to held-out target tasks without reducing detection accuracy and with only a minor increase in detection latency. In simulation, Reward-DAgger consistently improves autonomous success rate across three rounds of interactive learning while achieving the highest return on human effort. Finally, we deploy the same simulation-selected gate configuration on four real-world manipulation tasks with large pretrained VLA policies. Without any task-specific hyperparameter tuning, Reward-DAgger achieves competitive performance across all tasks and outperforms the baselines in most settings in terms of autonomous success rate and return on human effort, demonstrating that the gating mechanism transfers across environments and policy architectures.

In summary, our main contributions are:

We propose a two-timescale, progress-based gating mechanism that detects both abrupt failures and stalled behavior during robot execution. The gate is independent of the underlying policy, remains fixed across policy updates, and supports cross-task configuration transfer.

We introduce Reward-DAgger, an interactive imitation learning framework that uses this gating mechanism to trigger human takeover and iteratively finetune the policy from the resulting expert corrections.

We extensively evaluate Reward-DAgger across four simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks with both task-specific diffusion policies and large pretrained VLAs, studying failure detection, cross-task transfer, downstream policy improvement, and human-effort efficiency.

1. We propose a two-timescale, progress-based gating mechanism that detects both abrupt failures and stalled behavior during robot execution. The gate is independent of the underlying policy, remains fixed across policy updates, and supports cross-task configuration transfer.

2. We introduce Reward-DAgger, an interactive imitation learning framework that uses this gating mechanism to trigger human takeover and iteratively finetune the policy from the resulting expert corrections.

3. We extensively evaluate Reward-DAgger across four simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks with both task-specific diffusion policies and large pretrained VLAs, studying failure detection, cross-task transfer, downstream policy improvement, and human-effort efficiency.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

Interactive Imitation Learning. Interactive imitation learning mitigates distribution shift in behavioral cloning by iteratively collecting expert actions on states visited by the learned policy [ 2 , 30 , 14 , 10 , 24 , 18 ] . In human-gated methods, a supervisor monitors execution and decides when to intervene [ 14 , 24 , 18 , 12 , 28 ] . This monitoring requirement becomes burdensome when supervision scales to many robots [ 25 , 11 , 40 ] . Robot-gated methods instead automate this decision using signals such as action disagreement, estimated risk, or policy uncertainty [ 10 , 19 , 9 , 23 , 27 , 5 ] . However, these gates commonly depend on task-specific learned criteria or policy-dependent signals that require additional training or calibration across tasks or policy updates. In contrast, Reward-DAgger uses an external task-progress signal that can be applied zero-shot across tasks and policy architectures.

Runtime Monitoring in Robot Manipulation. Runtime monitoring provides a closely related approach for identifying policy failures during deployment. These methods typically reduce observations, predicted actions, or internal policy representations to a scalar score, and then calibrate a conformal threshold for failure detection. Representative methods derive these scores from temporal inconsistencies among consecutive actions [ 1 ] , deviations from the nominal observation distribution [ 38 , 29 ] , action chunk entropy [ 29 ] , or learned failure predictors using internal VLA features [ 8 ] . However, these methods are primarily studied as deployment-time mechanisms without updating the monitored policy. Reward-DAgger closes this loop between monitoring and learning by using gate firings to collect expert corrections for subsequent policy updates without inducing expensive retraining or recalibration overheads.

General-Purpose Reward Models. Reward functions provide scalar feedback about the desirability of states or actions and are commonly used to guide policy optimization. Recently, significant effort has focused on developing general-purpose reward models that provide dense reward signals across diverse tasks [ 6 , 21 , 20 , 13 , 41 , 32 ] . A common approach is to estimate task progress from visual observations and language instructions and use this progress signal as a proxy for per-timestep reward [ 13 , 21 , 33 , 41 ] , with recent works demonstrating its use for reinforcement learning in real-world robotic manipulation. Despite these advances, directly optimizing policies with imperfect learned reward functions remains challenging, as they may exploit inaccuracies or spurious correlations in the learned reward, leading to reward hacking without completing the intended task [ 35 , 31 , 42 , 36 ] . Rather than directly optimizing the progress signal, our key insight is to use it as a runtime monitoring signal for interactive imitation learning. Since progress is evaluated independently of the underlying policy and represented on a shared scale across tasks, it provides a natural signal for determining when expert intervention is needed without additional task- or policy-specific training or calibration.

2026-10-06.title: A Biomimetic Gaze Control to Restore Head-Neck Movements
2026-10-06.authors: Colin Rubow , Haohan Zhang
2026-10-06.abstract:
Powered neck exoskeletons are developed to restore head-neck motions for those with neck muscle weakness. Current methods using hand-held input devices to control these robotic systems are unintuitive or non-viable for these populations. Alternatively, the eyes coordinate with the head to accomplish many daily tasks. Therefore, movements of the eyes can be a useful signal to control the neck exoskeletons without needing to use the hands. However, previous control models lack biobehavioral basis as well as means to personalize the control behavior, causing unnatural head-neck movements. This paper presents a novel eye-tracking controller design leveraging the vestibulo-ocular reflex to emulate natural eye-head coordination.
Personalization tools were also designed, consisting of sliders to allow users to adjust the parameters of this controller. Here, we present the technical design and validation of this system in human users. Compared to the previous eye-tracking model, the new controller provides natural head motions personalized to the user through more natural velocity profiles and a 24 percent average increase of accurate motion intent detection. This system provides a powerful platform for studying eye-tracking controllers in the context of personalization and preference, and ultimately restoring the lost head-neck mobility in patient populations.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Powered neck exoskeletons are developed to restore lost head-neck mobility for patients with dropped head syndrome [ 1 , 2 ] . Patients with this condition cannot maintain an upright head posture for an extended time due to fatigue, often resulting in a “chin-on-chest” posture [ 3 ] .
Everyday activities such as eating and conversing become extremely taxing for these patients [ 4 , 5 ] . The clinic standard method of using static neck collars to treat this condition is unsatisfactory [ 6 ] ; these collars only keep the head in an upright position and thus prohibit any voluntary head movements [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . As a result, these collars do not help with daily tasks for these patients, which is a critical unmet need.

In contrast, neck exoskeletons use external actuators to enable head-neck movements. Although the mechanical hardware of current neck exoskeletons provides sufficient support to the head [ 2 ] , controlling them effectively by the user remains challenging. For example, hand-held devices such as joysticks and keyboards were previously used [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , but such options are not viable for patients with concurrent poor hand functions, which is common in patients whose dropped head posture results from a neurodegenerative disease like amyotrophic lateral sclerosis [ 5 , 13 ] . Even when the hands are functional for using these hand-held input devices, mapping the hand motion to the head rotations is not an intuitive task; the consequences of making a wrong move could result in significant discomfort.

Surface electromyography has also been explored to assist neck muscles of healthy individuals [ 14 ] ; however, further study is necessary as benefits were only shown in a simulation. Additionally, neck muscles are used during activities like speaking and drinking [ 15 ] , which furthers challenges using these muscle signals to control neck exoskeletons. It is also unclear whether such control schemes would be effective for people with neck muscle weakness who may have reduced electromyographic signals.

As the head often coordinates with the eyes to gather visual information [ 16 ] , eye movements can potentially be a useful signal to control neck exoskeletons in a natural and intuitive manner. Two attempts to leverage eye-tracking for control have been implemented. The first utilized a gaze clicking method to control a two degrees of freedom (DoF) head support device attached to a wheelchair through a stationary eye-tracking device [ 17 ] . With this control method, the device can move the head in horizontal or vertical rotations but not at the same time. Because the eye-trackers were fixed to the chair, accuracy decreases as the head moves away from the stationary tracker. This strategy frees the hands, but is unnatural because the eyes must fixate on the screen during the control of the head motions.

Another attempt used a head-mounted eye tracker to control a wearable neck exoskeleton by moving the head when the gaze is in a predefined region [ 18 ] . The controller has four gaze regions (each occupies 90 ∘ range partitioned by 45 ∘ diagonal lines) acting like virtual buttons to command constant horizontal and vertical head rotation increments, and an elliptical central region which stops the head rotations. These rotations are performed in real-time while the gaze is outside the central region but, like the previous example, performs only constant-speed horizontal or vertical rotations separately. Diagonal trajectories are therefore performed in zigzag fashions because the gaze constantly moves between the borders of two adjacent regions.

Although utilizing concepts in head-eye coordination like the vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR), it is unlikely that this control strategy obeys the natural kinematics during coordination behaviors, due to its single directional rotations and fixed speeds. The fixed parameters (speed, shape and size of the central region) also disallow this controller to adapt to potential interpersonal variability. In the rest of this paper, we will refer to this controller as the “region-based controller”.

To address these limitations, we propose a novel eye-tracking control strategy for powered neck exoskeletons which is aimed to emulate essential head-eye coordination behavior and provides means for personalization. We will refer to this controller as the “vector controller”. Here, our contributions are: (i) design and validation of a simple control model, based on observed head-eye coordination data, to predict head rotations given gaze as the input; (ii) evaluation of this control model implemented on a powered neck exoskeleton with human users; and (iii) justification and preliminary evaluation of a method for personalizing the control model.
These contributions provide the technical foundation for future user experiments to determine optimal, personalized, and effective control strategy for powered neck exoskeletons to restore lost head-neck mobility.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: section II introduces the insights into developing the vector gaze control model, and section III describes the implementation of this control model with a powered neck exoskeleton. We then evaluated the exoskeleton control through a user study which is described in detail in section IV . This is then followed by sections V and VI which present and discuss the results from the human study. Finally, section VII summarizes the main contributions of the paper.

## II-A Eye-Head Coordination

In the literature, gaze is defined as the head angle plus the eye angle relative to the head, or, the direction of sight [ 19 ] . When a gaze shift is performed, the eyes quickly shift towards the target (saccade). The VOR then enables the counter rotations of the eyes and head so that the gaze remains fixed on the target while the eyes become centered in the head [ 20 , 21 ] .

Additionally, the peak velocity of the head during a gaze shift was found to be linearly proportional to the distance that the head would travel to recenter the eyes within the field of view [ 19 , 22 , 23 ] . We refer to this linear proportionality as the “velocity proportion” ( v p v_{p} ) in this paper. A smaller gaze deviation would therefore require a slower head movement, while a larger gaze deviation would need a faster head rotation during VOR. The specific trajectory of the head varies with each gaze shift; however, it has been shown that the head generally moves towards a gaze target in a straight path, even for targets that are not strictly vertical or horizontal [ 20 , 24 ] .

To enable visual exploration without head movements, there also must exist a region near the center of field of vision that induces no head movement should the gaze be inside it. In this paper, we refer to this region as the “deadzone”. Little is known, however, about the shape and size of this deadzone region. It was hypothesized in the region-based controller’s design that the deadzone should be elliptical in shape [ 18 ] ; however, justification for this was based on literature on detectable light increment thresholds [ 25 ] rather than the border of head moving induced gaze positions. As a result, the deadzone region in the previous model was a wide elliptical shape with fixed size parameters (24.72 ∘ horizontal diameter, and 12.96 ∘ vertical diameter). We also hypothesized that this region can be modeled using a simple elliptical model with the origin of the ellipse at the center of the field of vision. The rationale was based on that the shape of field of vision is conic [ 26 ] and that there exists variation of head contribution for gazing at vertical and horizontal visual stimuli [ 19 , 27 ] . Unlike previous work [ 18 ] , our elliptic model in this work will be verified with human participant data, and will be personalized to the user. 2026-10-06.title: Return-to-Home Feasible Micro-Aerial Vehicle Exploration for 3D Gaussian Splatting Reconstruction
2026-10-06.authors: Prajit Krisshnakumar , Fan Yang , Koichiro Niinuma
2026-10-06.comment: IEEE/RSJ International Conference on INTELLIGENT ROBOTS & SYSTEMS 2026
2026-10-06.abstract: Micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) enable rapid indoor 3D reconstruction for inspection and time-critical situational awareness, but must operate under strict flight-time budgets and safety constraints that require explicit return-to-home (RTH) feasibility with a conservative margin. We present a topology-first active reconstruction framework that decouples high-fidelity rendering from navigation. A dense 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) map is optimized as the reconstruction target, while a lightweight Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF)/occupancy scaffold supports conservative collision checking and online construction of a sparse 3D Voronoi skeleton roadmap. Since directly extracting roadmaps from TSDF geometry can be unstable under noisy and incomplete online fusion, we validate nodes and edges using carved free-space consistency and dense visibility checks, which suppress behind-wall phantom structure and stabilize planning. Viewpoints are selected on the roadmap using a flight-time-budget-aware objective and a lightweight receding-horizon lookahead to improve non-myopic exploration behavior. We evaluate on photorealistic indoor simulation benchmarks (ReplicaCAD, Gibson, and HM3D), reporting reconstruction coverage/error, RTH success, and computational cost. Results demonstrate improved or competitive performance relative to recent GS-based baselines under identical flight-time budgets.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) are increasingly attractive for indoor search-and-rescue (SAR) and first-responder missions because they can quickly enter confined or hazardous spaces and provide situational awareness before humans are deployed [ 1 ] .
In these environments, autonomy must handle cluttered, GPS-denied navigation through narrow doorways and corridors under strict flight-time limits.
If the MAV exhausts its battery deep inside a structure, safe recovery is not guaranteed and the mission may fail prematurely.
Consequently, a central operational requirement is return-to-home (RTH) feasibility. In multi-room indoor layouts, return cost is highly non-Euclidean, and straight-line distance can severely underestimate the true time required to navigate around walls and through doorways.
Therefore, viewpoint selection must trade off expected reconstruction gain against travel time while maintaining a conservative safety margin for possible interruptions during the return flight (Fig. 1 ).

Beyond geometric coverage, responders often require high-fidelity reconstructions that preserve appearance and
fine structure for inspection and decision making.
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [ 2 ] enables photorealistic reconstruction by representing scenes with explicit Gaussian primitives and fast differentiable rasterization, making online refinement feasible at interactive rates.
This has motivated active reconstruction systems that couple viewpoint planning with online map updates.
However, bringing 3DGS-based active reconstruction to MAVs is challenging because informative viewpoint selection must remain execution-aware under the above non-Euclidean travel and RTH constraints, and because a 3DGS map is rendering-centric and does not directly provide watertight surfaces or conservative free-space semantics for collision checking.
Practical autonomy therefore typically requires an auxiliary geometric scaffold for safe navigation and feasibility reasoning.

While recent work has begun coupling Gaussian splatting with active viewpoint planning, reliably integrating high-fidelity mapping with an execution-ready navigation abstraction under budget constraints in multi-room indoor scenes remains challenging.
ActiveGS [ 3 ] uses a voxel scaffold to represent unexplored space and guide exploration, which can become costly to maintain and query as the explored 3D volume grows. ActiveSplat [ 4 ] enables efficient planning using a planar topological abstraction, but this 2D workspace does not explicitly capture the 3D connectivity and occlusions that arise in indoor flight.

To bridge these gaps, we take a topology-first approach that decouples photorealistic reconstruction from conservative navigation reasoning.
The MAV incrementally optimizes a dense 3DGS map as the reconstruction output, while simultaneously fusing the same posed RGB-D observations into a lightweight TSDF and occupancy grid that provide explicit surfaces and conservative free-space evidence for planning.
From this evolving geometric scaffold, we construct a sparse 3D Voronoi skeleton roadmap whose vertices lie near the medial axis of free space and naturally provide high-clearance waypoint candidates, similar in spirit to classical Voronoi-graph roadmaps used for sensor-based exploration [ 5 ] .
Since online TSDF geometry is incomplete early in exploration and can contain holes and transient artifacts, directly extracting a roadmap can introduce behind-wall phantom nodes that waste flight time and jeopardize safe return. We therefore apply conservative validation using carved free-space consistency and dense visibility checks to keep the roadmap stable for MAV execution.
On the resulting roadmap, we formulate viewpoint actions as (node, yaw) pairs and select goals using a budget-aware objective that trades off information gain against shortest-path travel time while enforcing an explicit RTH safety margin.
Finally, to reduce myopic oscillations, we use a lightweight two-step receding-horizon
selection, motivated by receding-horizon next-best-view planning for aerial exploration [ 6 ] .

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce a drone-centric hybrid planning architecture that decouples photorealistic reconstruction from conservative navigation: a dense 3DGS map is optimized as the reconstruction target, while a lightweight TSDF occupancy scaffold enables collision checking and stable online extraction of a sparse 3D Voronoi skeleton roadmap via carved-free-space validation, behind-wall suppression, and free-space node injection.

We propose a budget-aware flight-time mechanism that couples structural awareness (information gain and frontier cues) with a travel-cost model. The resulting objective explicitly enforces a return-to-home safety margin and adaptively trades off information gain against travel time as remaining flight-time budget decreases.

We provide evaluation under continuous-time MAV execution in photorealistic simulation, including comparisons to recent GS-based active reconstruction baselines and ablations isolating the effect of roadmap construction and non-myopic selection.

# II Related Work

Informative Path Planning (IPP) selects sensing actions to maximize information gain or coverage under constraints such as time, range, or energy [ 7 ] . In unknown environments, IPP is commonly solved online using an evolving map so that viewpoint selection adapts to newly observed structure. For UAV exploration in large 3D spaces, scalable representations and clearance-aware planning are important; examples include low-memory mapping for exploration [ 8 ] and Voronoi-guided planning with adaptive layering [ 9 ] . Complementary work targets robust state estimation and globally consistent geometric mapping, such as GO-SLAM [ 10 ] , Voxgraph [ 11 ] , and Kimera [ 12 ] .

NeRF-based methods produce high-quality view synthesis but rely on expensive volume rendering, which limits real-time closed-loop use. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [ 2 ] provides an efficient alternative via explicit
Gaussian primitives and fast rasterization, enabling interactive rendering and online refinement and motivating NBV-style active reconstruction [ 6 , 13 ] . Recent systems estimate view utility from renderability or uncertainty cues [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] . Since 3DGS is rendering-centric and does not provide conservative free-space semantics, many approaches pair it with auxiliary geometric scaffolds or sparse navigation abstractions for safe planning, such as ActiveGS [ 3 ] , ActiveSplat [ 4 ] , and neural-map exploration methods [ 17 ] .

Indoor UAV reconstruction systems study exploration and mapping under practical sensing and execution constraints [ 18 , 19 ] . Recent 3DGS-focused planners also target quadrotor autonomy, including GS-Planner [ 20 ] and HGS-Planner [ 21 ] . Despite progress, robust autonomous reconstruction in cluttered multi-room indoor scenes remains challenging. Dense voxel scaffolds for unknown-space reasoning can become expensive as explored volume grows, while planar abstractions can miss 3D connectivity and occlusions important for indoor flight. Moreover, return-to-home feasibility is inherently non-Euclidean indoors because return cost must respect doors and walls, and sparse roadmaps extracted from online fusion can become unstable early in exploration without conservative validation. These limitations motivate hybrid architectures that optimize 3DGS as the reconstruction target while planning and safety reasoning are performed on a lightweight geometric scaffold under explicit budget and RTH feasibility constraints.

2026-10-06.title: SUAVE: Unified Video-Action Models via Masked Diffusion
2026-10-06.authors: Rhythm Syed , Jean Mercat , Sedrick Keh , Kushal Arora , Paarth Shah , Aykut Onol , Mengchao Zhang , Tony Dear
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

2026-10-06.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) inherit strong semantic grounding from pretrained vision-language backbones but are typically optimized for predicting actions rather than future observations. They can see and act, but they do not imagine the future before acting. World action models (WAMs) built on video diffusion backbones can imagine but treat language as frozen conditioning on a continuous latent space. Unified models bring these modalities into one architecture, but they either decode autoregressively, one token at a time, or keep video continuous with an auxiliary action head. In this work, we present SUAVE, a Single vocabulary Unified Action-Video modEl in which a masked diffusion transformer generates video and actions conditioned on language, with all three modalities represented as discrete tokens in a shared sequence. Choosing which tokens to mask at inference turns the same network into a world model, a robot policy, or a video-action model. For action-free co-training, the action positions of unlabeled video are filled with mask tokens and excluded from the loss. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate two findings. First, a single SUAVE model predicts long-horizon video and acts as a policy, competitive with dedicated world models and specialized action policies on static and dynamic manipulation tasks. On a real robot, our model generates subgoal images and an action chunk spanning one second of motion in 1,030 ms on an RTX 5090 GPU, sustaining closed-loop control at 2.5 actions per second. Second, pretraining on robot video and co-training on human video substantially improves policy performance and zero-shot robustness to distribution shift. Together, these results show that masked diffusion is a practical and versatile foundation for unified video-action modeling.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Robot learning has recently experienced a paradigm shift towards end-to-end policies trained on large datasets. This shift has been driven by two complementary model families. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] adapt pretrained vision-language backbones to output actions and inherit strong semantic grounding. World action models (WAMs) [ 4 ] adapt pretrained video diffusion backbones to output actions alongside predicted frames and inherit an understanding of physical dynamics. Both families have shown that a pretrained backbone plus robot actions is a viable recipe for general-purpose control. However, each family imposes architectural assumptions that limit its suitability for robotics.

A VLA sees and acts, but it is not trained to anticipate. It maps the current observation to an action chunk without explicitly predicting the visual consequences. Because the standard VLA objective is defined only over actions, it cannot learn from video that lack action labels, which represent a large portion of all video that exists. A WAM is trained to anticipate as a product of its future video prediction, but it does so in a continuous latent space. Although video prediction and control are often jointly trained, many architectures retain separate representations or prediction heads for the two outputs, making them inherently decoupled. Recent work on visual chain of thought [ 5 ] shows that predicting a subgoal image before acting improves VLA performance, which suggests that the two families are converging on the same idea: a policy should be able to imagine the future before acting. This motivates
a single generative model over language, video, and actions, rather than separate modules for each.

We model the three modalities in a shared sequence using masked diffusion, a method that is analogous to continuous diffusion but in the discrete space. If every video frame, action, and language token is drawn from one vocabulary, then a transformer trained to unmask tokens can learn to fill in video and actions across a few denoising steps. Which conditional the model samples at inference time is decided entirely by which positions are masked: mask the future frame and it becomes a world model, mask the actions and it becomes a robot policy, mask both and it becomes a video-action model that generates a visual subgoal and the actions needed to reach the subgoal. Excluding masked action positions from the loss allows video without action labels to enter the same batch as labeled demonstrations, enabling robot video with actions and human video without actions to share one training stage and one unified objective. Because all masked positions are predicted in parallel, decoding at inference only takes a handful of steps rather than one step per token. This is in contrast to fully autoregressive methods, which make generating a subgoal image alongside actions prohibitively slow for closed-loop control, as each image and action token needs to be predicted sequentially. The discrete formulation enables strong versatility, allowing the same model weights to control the robot, roll out long-horizon video, and learn from human video all in one objective.

We propose SUAVE, a S ingle-vocabulary U nified A ction- V ideo mod E l built on a masked diffusion transformer. SUAVE arranges a video context, a language instruction, a predicted goal frame, and an action chunk as one token sequence. Because every token is predicted by the same objective, the mask at inference selects whether the model acts as a world model, a robot policy, or a video-action model. Experiments in simulation and on a real robot support two findings:

One model is a competitive world model and robot policy. A single SUAVE checkpoint predicts long-horizon video at a quality comparable to dedicated world models. As a policy, it is competitive with specialized action policies on static manipulation tasks and exceeds every baseline on dynamic manipulation tasks. We show our results for real world tasks, LIBERO, LIBERO-PLUS, and the DOMINO benchmark.

One model is a competitive world model and robot policy. A single SUAVE checkpoint predicts long-horizon video at a quality comparable to dedicated world models. As a policy, it is competitive with specialized action policies on static manipulation tasks and exceeds every baseline on dynamic manipulation tasks. We show our results for real world tasks, LIBERO, LIBERO-PLUS, and the DOMINO benchmark.

Pretraining and co-training on video substantially improve performance and zero-shot robustness. Pretraining on robot video and co-training on action-free human video more than double the real robot task scores of models trained from scratch and roughly triple them under distribution shift, with the gap statistically significant in nearly every task and condition.

# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-language-action models

VLAs adapt a pretrained vision-language backbone to robot control by treating actions as an additional output modality. RT-2 [ 6 ] and OpenVLA [ 1 ] discretize actions into tokens and decode them autoregressively. OpenVLA-OFT [ 7 ] replaces sequential decoding with parallel regression over an action chunk. π 0 \pi_{0} [ 2 ] , π 0 \pi_{0} -FAST [ 8 ] , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 3 ] attach flow-matching heads or compressed action tokenizers to pretrained VLM backbones. All of these map the current observation and language instruction to action. CoT-VLA [ 5 ] extends this by predicting a single subgoal image before acting and shows that this visual chain of thought approach improves success through better grounding. However, because the subgoal is generated token by token, the authors report a 7 × \times slowdown in control. These models generate actions and at most one frame, however none model multi-step video. As their objectives are defined over actions, none can train on video that lacks action labels.

## II-B World models and world action models

A parallel line of work starts from video generation. iVideoGPT [ 9 ] , Interactive World Simulator [ 10 ] , and Cosmos [ 11 ] learn action- or latent action-conditioned video predictors. Recent world action models, such as DreamZero [ 4 ] , adapt pretrained video diffusion backbones to output actions alongside predicted frames. These models can imagine the future well, but they typically operate in a continuous latent space: when language is present, it enters only as conditioning from a frozen text encoder, and actions are produced by a separate head. Video, actions, and language are therefore handled by different components with different objectives. SUAVE takes the opposite approach: all three are represented as discrete tokens and processed by one network under a shared objective.

## II-C Unified video-action and unified multimodal models

Several recent works generate video and actions jointly. UWM [ 12 ] and UVA [ 13 ] are continuous diffusion models over frames and actions. UWM samples independent noise levels for the two modalities so that one network can act as a policy, a forward model, or an inverse dynamics model. It is the closest continuous analog to our approach, and our independent per-modality mask rates are the discrete counterpart of its independent time steps. UniVLA [ 14 ] unifies vision, language, and action as discrete tokens but decodes them autoregressively, one token at a time. On the language-model side, LLaDA [ 15 ] showed that masked diffusion scales to LLM-sized text models, and MMaDA [ 16 ] extends it to a shared text and image vocabulary with parallel decoding. SUAVE brings this backbone to robotics by adding video and actions. Existing designs fall into three families: models that decode autoregressively over discrete tokens, models with continuous diffusion over frames and actions, and hybrid models that combine a language model with diffusion heads. SUAVE presents a fourth design: one generative mechanism over one discrete vocabulary for every modality, so that all cross-modal interaction happens under a single objective, with subgoal frames and the action chunk decoded in parallel.

## II-D Pretraining and co-training on video for robot policies

Large scale video is a promising source of transferable supervision for robotics. Prior works have found several ways to use it in training. UniVLA [ 14 ] post-trains on video before learning a policy. UWM [ 12 ] sets the action diffusion timestep of action-free clips to maximum noise, allowing them to train alongside labeled demonstrations. SUAVE achieves this in the discrete setting by filling action positions with mask tokens and excluding them from the loss, so a human video clip and a robot demonstration share a batch. Our evaluation methodology follows LBM [ 17 ] , which shows controlled comparisons of data recipes on a fixed architecture with quantified uncertainty. We evaluate on LIBERO [ 18 ] , LIBERO-Plus [ 19 ] for robustness to perturbations, and DOMINO [ 20 ] for dynamic manipulation. Our contribution on this axis is a controlled evaluation of the effects of robot-video pretraining and action-free human video co-training, conducted under one protocol in simulation and on a real robot.

2026-10-06.title: REDIRECT: A 1% Fix for Bad Robot Habits
2026-10-06.authors: Yu Zhang , Jiazhuo Li , Yancong Wei , Kangkang Dong , Xiaojun Zhu , Houde Liu
2026-10-06.abstract: Robots can acquire bad habits from a few defective moments in otherwise useful teleoperation. In mixed-quality robot data, normal and problematic demonstrations share most task behavior and differ only at a local action continuation. Full retraining is costly, while fine-tuning on clean data alone offers limited recovery under a small update budget. We ask whether the local difference can instead be fixed with only 1% of the full-training sample-backward budget. Using only episode-level retained/problematic labels, Redirect localizes the branch, assigns a coherent retained continuation to the original observations around it, and anchors shared behavior, without frame-level annotations or additional interaction. Across three randomized ManiSkill tasks and three seeds, Redirect raises the mean success rate from 68.2% to 90.3%, recovering 88.8% of the clean-retraining gap versus 22.1% for matched-compute fine-tuning. On a PiPER arm, it recovers 86.7–92.9% of the clean-only gap across cup insertion and towel folding. Local robot habits can therefore be repaired by spending the update budget on the behavioral difference rather than relearning shared behavior.
2026-10-06.introduction:
A robot may insert a cup correctly yet repeatedly tip it over during release. Such failures can arise from brief teleoperation errors even when most of the demonstrated behavior remains useful. Full retraining incurs substantial computational cost, whereas fine-tuning on clean data alone may offer limited correction under a small update budget. This motivates concentrating repair compute on the local difference.

Can this difference be repaired with only 1% of the full-training sample-backward budget? We study ordinary and locally flawed demonstrations that execute the same task and share most behavior. A bad robot habit is a repeatable action-chunk deviation within an otherwise task-consistent trajectory. The auditor provides only episode-level labels; retained episodes supply normal continuations.

In this setting, the local difference naturally induces a behavioral branch : a problematic demonstration follows retained-compatible behavior until a local decision separates its action future and shifts later observations. Localizing this separation under unpaired trajectory variation isolates the repair from shared behavior.

Fine-tuning on retained data does not directly provide corrective action targets at observations from problematic demonstrations. Redirect localizes the branch, pairs observations around it with a coherent retained continuation, and anchors each update on retained demonstrations (Fig. 1 ).

The comparison is clean-conditioned but unpaired: motion, state, and RGB descriptors identify context-compatible retained futures, while action-future departure determines the branch. Synthetic branch timestamps are reserved for evaluation rather than supplied to the repair procedure.

At 1% of full-training sample-backward compute, Redirect raises the mean success rate in simulation from 68.2% to 90.3% and recovers 88.8% of the clean gap, versus 22.1% for matched-compute fine-tuning. Across ACT, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , cup insertion, and towel folding, it recovers 86.7–92.9% of the clean-only gap with branch-local changes.

This paper makes three contributions:

We formulate low-budget policy repair around behavioral branches in mixed-quality demonstrations.

We introduce Redirect : episode membership localizes the separation, one trajectory-consistent normal continuation reroutes it, and retained supervision anchors shared behavior without reward, rollout, or teacher.

Across ACT, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , simulation, and real robots, 1% of full-training sample-backward compute recovers 88.8% of the simulation gap with branch-local changes.

1. We formulate low-budget policy repair around behavioral branches in mixed-quality demonstrations.

2. We introduce Redirect : episode membership localizes the separation, one trajectory-consistent normal continuation reroutes it, and retained supervision anchors shared behavior without reward, rollout, or teacher.

3. Across ACT, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , simulation, and real robots, 1% of full-training sample-backward compute recovers 88.8% of the simulation gap with branch-local changes.

Behavior-cloning errors compound off distribution [ 1 ] . Interactive methods including DAgger and HG-DAgger [ 1 , 2 ] , intervention-weighted regression [ 3 ] , and ThriftyDAgger [ 4 ] improve policies with expert interventions; RaC scales recovery–correction segments [ 5 ] . Residual RL adds reward-driven refinement [ 6 ] , while set-supervised diffusion learns from paired corrections [ 7 ] . These approaches focus supervision on difficult states but require new rollouts, interventions, corrective labels, or rewards. ACT, Diffusion Policy, and the flow-matching-based π 0 / π 0.5 \pi_{0}/\pi_{0.5} [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] are policy backbones rather than repair procedures. Redirect instead performs offline post-training repair from episode-level retained/problematic labels and assigns a fixed budget to their local action-future branch.

Confidence-weighted imitation learning [ 13 ] and VILD [ 14 ] address imperfect or latent-quality demonstrations. Demo-SCORE curates demonstrations using online experience [ 15 ] , IntervenGen expands a small intervention set [ 16 ] , and S2I selects and refines demonstration segments through trajectory optimization and action relabeling [ 17 ] . Recent curation methods assess demonstration quality through state–action mutual information [ 18 ] or estimated influence on closed-loop return [ 19 ] . Redirect instead retains both episode sets and repairs an already-trained policy by localizing the dominant departure and assigning a retained continuation under a fixed update budget.

Behavior Retrieval queries unlabeled datasets for few-shot imitation [ 20 ] , while VINN predicts actions from nearby visual demonstrations [ 21 ] . CompILE discovers reusable variable-length temporal units in demonstrations [ 22 ] . Redirect uses retrieval neither as the deployed controller nor as generic skill discovery: it matches clean-conditioned futures to localize a branch onset and selects a single-source, time-consistent continuation as the local editing target.

LoRA reduces trainable parameters [ 23 ] , GradNorm balances gradient magnitudes [ 24 ] , PCGrad projects conflicting objectives [ 25 ] , and GEM/A-GEM constrain updates with memory gradients [ 26 , 27 ] . These tools address adaptation efficiency or interference, but do not determine where a robot policy should be edited or what executable behavior should replace a defect. Redirect couples branch localization, coherent continuation retrieval, retained replay, gradient balancing, and conflict projection to concentrate a fixed sample-backward budget while limiting drift on shared behavior.

2026-10-06.title: Sparse Calibration-Based Personalization of Kernel-Based Gait Phase and Speed Estimation Using Wearable IMUs
2026-10-06.authors: Myeongju Cha , Pilwon Hur
2026-10-06.comment: The 26th International Conference on Control, Automation, and Systems (ICCAS 2026)
2026-10-06.abstract: This paper presents sparse calibration-based personalization for kernel-based gait phase and walking speed co-estimation from wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs). A 28-speed reference library was constructed from bilateral thigh and shank trajectories in a 20-subject locomotion dataset. Rather than directly applying population-average kernels, the method combines a user-specific baseline estimated from three calibration speeds with a principal-component (PC) model of baseline-centered kinematic deviations. Offline validation showed that personalized kernels reduced phase error relative to the population kernel. In a single-participant online pilot evaluation, the personalized kernels produced numerically lower mean phase and speed errors and ran in real time on embedded hardware. However, the speed effect was not significant, and pairwise phase differences did not remain significant after multiple-comparison correction. The pilot evaluation establishes wearable implementation feasibility while indicating reference-to-online dataset mismatch and the need for larger-cohort validation.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Continuous gait phase and walking speed estimates support wearable robots, powered prostheses, and rehabilitation monitoring [ 1 ] . Phase describes within-stride timing, whereas speed represents the global locomotor condition. Portable inertial measurement units (IMUs) enable estimation outside motion-capture laboratories [ 2 ] , but their trajectories may differ from optical measurements because of sensor placement, segment definition, drift compensation, and calibration [ 2 , 3 ] . This mismatch matters when models learned from motion-capture-derived trajectories are applied to IMU-derived angles.

Continuous phase variables parameterize gait-cycle progression and provide joint-kinematic or impedance references for wearable-robot control. Robust phase estimation under changing locomotion conditions has therefore been studied using mechanical phase variables and phase portraits under perturbations, non-rhythmic tasks, and varying speeds and inclines [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Related approaches address phase-shifting compensation, slopes, stair descent, and speed-dependent walking [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Among these sources of variability, this study focuses on inter-user and speed-dependent differences during steady-state level-ground walking.

To estimate gait phase and locomotion condition efficiently, Posh et al. [ 11 ] proposed a sliding-kernel framework that selects the best-matching locomotion-mode kernel and its circular alignment. We adapt this principle to phase and speed co-estimation by treating each walking speed as a separate candidate kernel: the selected kernel determines speed, while its alignment determines phase. This approach is interpretable, computationally efficient, and suitable for embedded implementation.

However, matching accuracy depends directly on how well the candidate trajectories represent the current user and sensing modality. Population-average kernels may not capture inter-subject kinematic differences, and motion-capture-derived kernels may not match wearable-IMU measurements. Conversely, constructing a complete user-specific library would require calibration at every candidate speed, which is impractical. To address this limitation, we construct a 28-speed (0.50–1.85 m/s), four-channel reference model from 20 subjects and regenerate user-specific kernels from only three calibration speeds using baseline-centered principal component analysis (PCA) and quadratic PC1-speed regression. Thus, our contribution is not the recursive matching algorithm itself, but sparse personalization of its speed-indexed kernel library.

2026-10-06.title: MOSAIC-SV: Real-Time Adaptive Identification of Vessel Dynamics for the Control and Deployment of Aquatic Robots
2026-10-06.authors: Wensen Liu , Jerry Peng , Shravani Vedagiri , Aaron M. Johnson
2026-10-06.abstract: Model-based control of an aquatic robotic platform depends on a hydrodynamic model that is costly to identify and specific to the hull, payload, and conditions it was measured in. Here, we present MOSAIC-SV, a deployable real-time adaptive dynamics identification and control system that identifies a control-sufficient dynamics model from a spec-sheet engineering prior, without dedicated identification trials, and re-estimates it at every control step of a closed-loop mission while the controller plans on it. A physically admissible unscented Kalman filter re-estimates hydrodynamic, disturbance, and actuator parameters at every control step of the closed-loop mission; while a command-dependent consider projection withholds corrections the current command cannot attribute between actuator effectiveness and external force; and a model predictive path integral controller plans on the current estimate. In simulation on a CyberShip II plant, MOSAIC-SV recovers the transit performance of the calibrated model under static mismatch and transient changes, and stays within 20 % 20\% of its own transit time at the unscaled prior when its inertia or damping prior is wrong by an order of magnitude. In on-water field trials on the Blue Robotics BlueBoat, a twin-thruster catamaran, MOSAIC-SV transits at least 25 % 25\% faster and predicts its own motion with at least 56 % 56\% less error than its frozen engineering prior, including under an unmodeled payload. The same MOSAIC-SV system concept was also feasibly deployed on a 6.3-tonne dual outboard monohull.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Aquatic robotic platforms such as unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) have great potential to aid in marine conservation [ 1 ] , search and rescue [ 2 ] , and exploration [ 3 ] . Model-based control of a USV depends on a model of the hydrodynamic effects in its dynamics [ 4 ] . Current USV controllers typically use parametric physics-based maneuvering models (e.g. Fossen [ 5 ] , MMG [ 6 ] ) paired with predictive controllers [ 7 , 8 ] or learned policies [ 9 ] . However, these models are non-trivial to derive and calibrate [ 10 ] , particularly for unconventional hullforms and marine robots [ 11 ] . Several approaches address this.

One approach is to identify the model a priori from data, through parametric identification [ 12 ] or a learned dynamics model [ 13 ] , and give the controller the identified model. Abrougui et al. [ 14 ] identify a USV model from sea trials and design heading and speed controllers on it. Wang et al. [ 15 ] identify the maneuvering model with an extended Kalman filter on simulated excitation data before control, then run a disturbance observer alongside a nonlinear MPC in simulation. In each, the data collected and subsequent model are specific to that vessel and the conditions it was operated in; a change to the hull, payload, actuator, or sea state requires a new identification.

A second approach is to learn a correction on top of a known nominal model during operation. Zhang et al. [ 16 ] learn the mismatch between a nominal model and the measured yaw response online and add it to the prediction model of an MPC. Liu et al. [ 17 ] learn per-axis residual dynamics with a sparse Gaussian process that is refined recursively inside a nonlinear MPC. Outside the marine domain, Levy et al. [ 18 ] couple Kalman-filter adaptation of a dynamics model to MPPI on an off-road vehicle, but adapt along a basis meta-learned from previously collected vehicle-specific driving data. These methods, however, require a known nominal model of the test platform and require dedicated identification trials to train or calibrate the correction algorithms before deployment.

A third approach is to identify the physical model itself online, which previous work has explored as an estimation problem. Hydrodynamic coefficients are estimated as augmented states with an extended [ 19 ] or unscented Kalman filter [ 20 , 21 ] , with some estimators also identifying propeller and rudder force coefficients [ 21 ] . These studies primarily use recorded maneuvering-test data or simulation data and, when applicable, give a controller a fixed model [ 22 , 21 ] . Additionally, these identification methods use designed maneuvers such as zig-zag, turning-circle, and spiral tests [ 17 , 20 , 22 , 21 ] , as every coefficient must be excited by the test, a requirement Yue et al. [ 23 ] relax to interval excitation. Among the approaches, to our knowledge no published system starts a vessel from an engineering prior, identifies its physical model online during nominal operation, and plans on that model as it is re-estimated.

In this work we present MOSAIC-SV ( M aritime O nboard S ystem for A daptive I dentification and C ontrol of S urface V essels), a deployable real-time adaptive dynamics identification and control system. MOSAIC-SV identifies a control-sufficient dynamics model from a spec-sheet engineering prior, without dedicated identification trials, re-estimating it at every control step of a closed-loop mission while the controller plans on it. Additionally, the system is robust to poor engineering priors, remaining effective when the inertia or damping prior is wrong by an order of magnitude. MOSAIC-SV rests on two further contributions:

A physically admissible unscented Kalman filter over hydrodynamic, disturbance, and actuator parameters with a command-dependent consider projection that suppresses corrections along weak directions of the prior-scaled joint actuator and external-force map.

An evaluation in simulation under static mismatch, transient changes, and prior misspecification; paired field trials on a small twin-thruster catamaran against its frozen engineering prior; and a feasibility run on a 6.3-tonne dual outboard monohull.

1. A physically admissible unscented Kalman filter over hydrodynamic, disturbance, and actuator parameters with a command-dependent consider projection that suppresses corrections along weak directions of the prior-scaled joint actuator and external-force map.

2. An evaluation in simulation under static mismatch, transient changes, and prior misspecification; paired field trials on a small twin-thruster catamaran against its frozen engineering prior; and a feasibility run on a 6.3-tonne dual outboard monohull.

2026-10-06.title: GOTT: Object-centric Dexterous Manipulation with a Reusable Cross-Embodiment Primitive
2026-10-06.authors: Yulin Liu , Lai Wei , Yen-Jen Wang , Akash Sharma , Pieter Abbeel , Henrik I. Christensen , Haozhi Qi
2026-10-06.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-06.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: Foundation models and large-scale human data provide rich sources of manipulation intent, but translating this intent into multi-fingered robot behavior remains difficult. Dexterous hands still lack a reusable low-level primitive that reliably establishes contact across tasks and embodiments. We propose GOTT , a reach-acquire-move framework built around a single cross-embodiment contact-acquisition primitive. Given a robot-agnostic object trajectory and a reach specification, GOTT first brings the hand near a task-relevant contact region. The shared closed-loop primitive then establishes stable contact from this approximate initialization, and a pose-conditioned controller tracks the desired object motion. Reach specifications may come from future-aware planning, external models, or human demonstrations, while the primitive and tracking backend remain unchanged. Simulation and real-world experiments show that GOTT is able to establish robust contact across diverse objects, arm-hand platforms, and seen and unseen hand morphologies. It also consistently improves end-to-end task success over open-loop grasp execution.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Foundation models [ 16 , 40 ] and large-scale human data [ 60 , 3 ] provide rich sources of manipulation intent. For parallel-jaw grippers, such intent can be translated into robot actions through mature low-level primitives such as grasping, placing, and trajectory following [ 24 , 23 , 31 ] . However, the same approach does not directly extend to dexterous hands, which lack a comparable set of general-purpose low-level skills. These skills must establish complex contact configurations, coordinate high-dimensional actions, and adapt to different hand morphologies.

Existing dexterous manipulation methods usually address these challenges through task-specific sim-to-real learning [ 39 ] or hand-motion retargeting [ 30 ] . However, these approaches are not well suited to converting high-level intent into robot behavior. Task-specific policies [ 44 , 45 , 9 , 19 ] require retraining for each new behavior, making them difficult to scale. Retargeting recovers kinematic targets from demonstrations [ 37 ] , often without incorporating perceptual feedback [ 41 ] . This lack of feedback makes contact-rich tasks difficult to execute in the real world. This raises a key question: what is the right interface for translating high-level manipulation intent into low-level dexterous execution?

Object-centric motion representations provide a promising answer to this question. Prior work has shown that many rigid-object manipulation tasks can be described by the desired object motion [ 27 , 43 , 20 ] , abstracting away embodiment-specific robot motion. However, an object trajectory specifies how the object should move , but not where and how the hand should establish contact . This distinction is critical for functional manipulation: a geometrically stable grasp may still be unsuitable for pouring, sweeping, or tool use.
Prior methods address this gap by supplying a pre-grasp or hand reference [ 10 , 32 ] , or by learning contact acquisition jointly with trajectory execution [ 26 , 28 ] . While effective, these designs do not expose contact acquisition as a reusable skill across high-level sources and robot embodiments.

We propose General Object Trajectory Tracking ( GOTT ), a framework for executing diverse object motions across tasks and robot embodiments using a shared contact-acquisition primitive.
We represent high-level manipulation intent using a desired object trajectory and a reach specification , which specifies how to bring the hand near a task-relevant contact region. These components may come from different sources. For example, the object trajectory may be extracted from a video, while the reach specification may be generated through affordance-aware planning or obtained by retargeting a human trajectory.

GOTT implements this interface through a reach, acquire, and move decomposition. During reach , the robot follows the reach specification toward the selected contact region. During acquire , a learned closed-loop contact-acquisition primitive establishes stable contact from this approximate initialization. During move , an object-pose-conditioned controller tracks the desired object trajectory. The primitive uses only local hand-object geometry and proprioceptive history, while a canonical per-link representation allows the same policy to be shared across hands. Reach specifications can come from VLM-guided, future-aware planning, external models, or demonstrations, while the contact-acquisition primitive remains unchanged.

We evaluate GOTT in simulation and the real world. First, we test whether the contact-acquisition primitive can robustly grasp diverse objects across different hands and transfer zero-shot to unseen hand morphologies. We then evaluate the full pipeline on object-trajectory tracking tasks, including trash cleanup, pouring, whiteboard erasing, and tool use. We compare against end-to-end trajectory learning, showing that our decomposition enables robustness to workspace shifts and reuse across robot arms. We also show that the same primitive supports high-level specifications from generated videos, keyframes, human demonstrations, and hand-object interaction datasets. Finally, we conduct ablations on the primitive’s observation and reward design and the system’s planning modules.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

High-level task interfaces. Foundation models and human demonstrations can specify robot manipulation tasks through language, visual constraints [ 23 ] , code [ 31 ] , or generated videos [ 43 ] . ManipGen [ 12 ] combines reusable local policies with foundation models and motion planning. Another line of work learns from human videos by extracting intermediate motion representations, such as point trajectories, object flow, or object-centric motion plans [ 4 , 56 , 58 , 65 , 20 , 29 ] . SPOT [ 21 ] learns object-pose trajectory plans from human demonstrations and uses them to condition a robot policy. VLM-Scaffold [ 13 ] adapts a similar pipeline to dexterous hands but relies on task-specific residual RL, making it challenging to scale across tasks and embodiments. LUCID [ 18 ] learns embodiment-agnostic intent from unstructured human videos and connects it to embodiment-specific sensorimotor policies through object flow and a rough palm pose. In contrast, GOTT represents high-level intent using an object trajectory and a flexible reach specification, and connects these inputs to robot execution through a reusable dexterous contact-acquisition primitive.

Trajectory-based dexterous manipulation. D-Grasp [ 11 ] combines reference-conditioned grasp control with global motion synthesis to move objects to target poses. Methods that start from a reference trajectory typically follow one of two strategies. The first performs trajectory-specific transfer, converting a human or object trajectory into robot motion through kinematic optimization, sampling [ 41 ] , or reinforcement learning [ 30 , 37 ] . Human2Sim2Robot [ 33 ] uses a single object trajectory and a pre-grasp to learn a task-specific robot policy. ManipTrans [ 30 ] and REGRIND [ 15 ] transfer hand-object interaction trajectories through residual learning, while SPIDER [ 41 ] performs fast physics-informed retargeting. These transfer methods can reproduce a given demonstration but are often tied to a specific trajectory or embodiment.

The second strategy trains policies conditioned on multiple reference trajectories. ObjDex [ 10 ] and DexTrack [ 32 ] condition policies on object or hand trajectories. AdaDexTrack [ 1 ] adds online modulation to improve tracking of noisy references. OmniGrasp [ 36 ] learns to grasp diverse objects and follow object trajectories with a simulated humanoid. SimToolReal [ 26 ] and Dex4D [ 28 ] learn general object-centric policies conditioned on target object poses or point tracks, jointly handling contact acquisition and motion execution. Grasp to Act [ 17 ] combines human-guided grasp optimization with residual RL for online finger adaptation.
In contrast, GOTT factors execution into reach, acquire, and move : high-level inputs specify the desired object motion and a task-relevant reach, while a trajectory-agnostic primitive establishes contact before trajectory tracking begins. This decomposition enables the same contact-acquisition primitive to be reused across trajectories, objects, and robot embodiments.

Dexterous grasping. Existing learning-based methods develop generalizable tabletop grasping policies [ 59 , 50 , 35 , 64 ] . Grasp synthesis and evaluation methods instead generate or refine grasp targets [ 7 , 53 , 51 , 8 , 34 , 14 ] . GraspXL [ 62 ] and ConGraspXL [ 63 ] condition grasping motions on approach, contact-region, or pose constraints. Functional grasping methods use affordances, human grasp references, or language to select task-relevant grasps [ 2 , 22 , 52 ] . Cross-embodiment methods further share grasping policies or representations across hands: CrossDex [ 61 ] uses a unified observation space and retargeted eigengrasp actions, while OHRA [ 54 ] uses canonical hand representations and UniMorphGrasp [ 57 ] conditions grasp generation on morphology. GET-Zero [ 42 ] studies zero-shot transfer to unseen hand structures for in-hand rotation. These works advance grasping and cross-hand transfer, while primarily focusing on grasp acquisition itself. In contrast, GOTT treats contact acquisition as a reusable intermediate primitive that refines an approximate, task-relevant reach into stable contact before downstream object-trajectory tracking. This enables the same primitive to be reused across objects, tasks, trajectories, and hand embodiments.

2026-10-06.authors: Sungsan Park , Young-Sik Shin , Sanghyun Kim
2026-10-06.abstract:
Quadruped robots entering hospitals, care homes, and quiet offices must be
context-appropriate not only in where they move but in how loudly they move: a legged robot’s locomotion noise, dominated by foot–ground impacts,
is itself a social variable. Prior social navigation respects human space but
treats the robot as acoustically uniform, while quiet-locomotion methods reduce
noise to an operator-specified, context-blind level. We present TACET , a context-appropriate acoustic-social navigation method that
infers social context from the robot’s egocentric view and decides both where it walks and
how loudly, coupling a slow fine-tuned vision-language reasoner to a fast reactive
controller through a single compact behavior token, ⟨ \langle gait , speed , social_cost ⟩ \rangle . The same token conditions both a social costmap ( where to go) and
a quiet locomotion policy ( how loudly to move), while a structured
out-of-view memory keeps recently seen people in the reasoner’s context after they
leave the camera view. On a real quadruped, context-conditioned locomotion lowers
locomotion noise by up to 9.3 dBA at matched speed, and across our scenarios the full method
keeps personal-space compliance at 100% with low acoustic intrusion ( ≤ \leq 2.9 dBA),

2026-10-06.introduction:
Consider a quadruped crossing a shared building lobby
(Fig. 1 ). A geometry-only planner treats each person as an obstacle
and takes the shortest collision-free path, brushing past someone absorbed in
work at a table, then threading between people standing in conversation, its footfalls
fully audible. The path is safe, yet it is
socially inappropriate in two distinct ways: where the robot moves, as
it crowds personal space and cuts through a conversation, and how loudly it
moves, as its footfalls intrude on people who need quiet. Unlike wheeled
platforms, a legged robot is intrinsically loud because its locomotion noise is
dominated by foot–ground impacts [ 1 ] , so its acoustic footprint is a
social variable that must be managed online.

Prior work largely follows two threads, each addressing only half of this problem. Social navigation makes the robot respect human space, but treats it as acoustically uniform [ 2 , 3 ] ; quiet locomotion makes a quadruped quieter, but to an operator-specified degree that is blind to context [ 1 ] . Acoustic-aware planning relaxes this by predicting how loud the robot sounds to nearby listeners, yet it needs a prior visual scan of the environment and manages noise at the level of the path rather than the robot’s own gait [ 4 ] . To our knowledge, no prior method has demonstrated social-context reasoning coupled to a controllable acoustic footprint: the former knows where to go but not how quiet to be, while the latter can be quiet but not when to be.

To this end, we propose TACET ( T oken-aware A cousti C -social E tiquette T raversal), a context-appropriate acoustic-social navigation method for quadruped robots that closes this gap. A slow semantic reasoner, a fine-tuned vision-language model (VLM), reads the robot’s egocentric view together with a structured memory of nearby people, including those who have just left the camera’s field of view, and emits a compact behavior token with three fields: gait , speed , and social_cost . A fast reactive controller consumes this token to shape both a social costmap, which governs where to go, and a token-conditioned quiet locomotion policy, which governs how loudly to move, while a standard real-time planning stack preserves safety. The two processes are coupled only through this small token interface, allowing rich but slow social reasoning to steer real-time control without entering the safety loop. Because the same token scales spatial avoidance and acoustic effort together, the robot becomes context-appropriate rather than unconditionally quiet or fast.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce context-appropriate acoustic-social navigation : a robot infers social context and modulates not only where but also how loudly it moves, unifying spatial and acoustic compliance, previously treated in isolation, under one inferred signal.

We realize it as TACET: a fine-tuned VLM emits a compact behavior token that jointly drives a social costmap with out-of-view memory and a token-conditioned quiet locomotion policy, linking slow reasoning to a real-time controller through a small, interpretable interface.

We evaluate TACET on a Unitree Go2, where it reduces locomotion noise by up to
9.3 dBA at matched speed through context-conditioned locomotion, and it is the only method to keep full Personal Space Compliance in every
scenario, at a closest approach of 1.44–3.62 m against at most 1.35 m for any
baseline, showing that
acoustic and social compliance can be attained together rather than traded off.

# II Related Work

## II-A Social Robot Navigation

Classical social navigation builds on geometric planners such as the social-force
model [ 5 ] , which are efficient and well-validated but treat people as dynamic
obstacles, yielding socially blunt behavior. On the real-world SCAND dataset, geometric systems already match human demonstrations in
many situations, arguing for augmenting rather than discarding them [ 6 ] . Our
design inherits this view: we retain a validated real-time planning stack for
reactive safety and add VLM-based semantic reasoning above it.

Learning-based methods instead imitate human navigation or optimize social objectives with
reinforcement learning; Falcon, for example, predicts human trajectories and penalizes
actions that obstruct them [ 3 ] . These methods motivate the proxemics-grounded
metrics we adopt, but they operate kinematically in simulation and reason only about where to go, never the gait, foot–ground contact, or acoustics a physical quadruped
must manage.

More recently, VLMs have brought open-vocabulary social reasoning to navigation.
VLM-Social-Nav queries a VLM-based scoring module for a social cost term that corrects a
low-level planner, structuring the VLM output into linguistic heading and speed terms
mapped to linear and angular velocity [ 2 ] . Narrate2Nav instead embeds language reasoning implicitly in a visual encoder via a Barlow-Twins objective, enabling real-time RGB-only navigation that reasons in latent rather than token space [ 7 ] . In contrast to these spatial- and trajectory-level methods, which keep people’s space but assume an acoustically uniform robot and largely target wheeled platforms, TACET conditions both a social costmap and a quadruped’s quiet gait on VLM-inferred context, making the robot’s acoustic footprint itself a function of social context.

## II-B Quiet and Acoustic-Aware Locomotion for Legged Robots

The dominant source of quadruped locomotion noise is the foot–ground impact,
whose acoustic amplitude grows with foot velocity at contact [ 1 ] . MUTE reduces it through control alone, with a quiet factor that trades noise reduction
against agility and an evaluation protocol based on Mean and Peak Noise Levels (MNL, PNL)
at matched actual speed [ 1 ] . The desired quietness there is an
operator-specified parameter: the robot does not perceive who is nearby, and so cannot
determine when quietness is socially required.

On the acoustic-aware navigation side, ANAVI is closest to our motivation: it visually
estimates how loud the robot will sound at a listener’s location and uses this as a cost to
plan a quieter route [ 4 ] . It nonetheless depends on a prior visual scan of the environment and manages
noise at the level of the path rather than the gait, and the social weighting it proposes
is left unevaluated. In contrast, the token-conditioned policy in TACET is driven by VLM-inferred social context and decides online, without any prior scan of the environment, both when and how much to attenuate its own locomotion noise.

## II-C Lightweight VLM Reasoning for Navigation

Because large VLMs are computationally heavy and slow, a growing body of work
distills their social reasoning into deployable, lightweight models. Social-LLaVA fine-tunes a LLaVA-family VLM on a human-annotated social-reasoning VQA
dataset [ 8 ] ; OLiVia-Nav distills context captions into a lightweight model
whose embeddings select socially compliant trajectories [ 9 ] . These efforts build on egocentric and VQA resources
such as SCAND, MuSoHu, JRDB-Social, and SocialNav-SUB [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
Our reasoner shares the goal of making a large model’s social reasoning cheap enough to run
in the loop, but differs in its output interface: where these produce language, continuous
embeddings, or latent reasoning, we fine-tune a Qwen2.5-VL model to emit a discrete control-
and costmap-conditioning token, an explicit bridge from social reasoning to both low-level
locomotion and the costmap. That token conditions a social costmap and a controllable
acoustic footprint on the same quadruped, without any prior scan of the
environment.

2026-10-06.authors: Xuanyu Lu , Fengqing Jiang , Kaiyuan Zheng , Yichen Feng , Yaorui Ding , Yuetai Li , Zhen Xiang , Bhaskar Ramasubramanian , Basel Alomair , Luyao Niu , Radha Poovendran
