2026-10-06.abstract:
World models learn to predict how their environment will evolve, making them an important foundation for general-purpose robotic control. Yet World Action Models (WAMs) rely on camera inputs, and manipulating those inputs can corrupt the visual representations that underpin their tasks and action policies.
Existing attacks on these models optimize against actions or predicted futures and require access to victim outputs or generation modules. We propose TAPDreamer , a transferable fixed local patch whose pixel optimization uses only a public visual encoder and requires no target-policy queries. Its design addresses two requirements: a local modification should affect representations beyond its footprint, and the resulting disturbance should persist across observations. We optimize a fixed local patch on six frames from one source task by maximizing the mean L1 distance between clean and patched encoder outputs over all latent positions and channels. Mechanism analysis reveals that interactions between patch-induced changes in attention weights and value vectors broadcast a nearly identical representation shift beyond the patch footprint, while a shared perturbation response persists across task observations despite differences in clean latents. In closed-loop evaluation, one frozen patch per benchmark, covering about 6.5% of the input, reduces FastWAM’s success rate from 97.65% to 0.00% across 40 LIBERO tasks and from 90.86% to 0.00% across 50 RoboTwin tasks; matched random patches retain 81.45% and 79.20% success. The same patches reduce success to 1.45% and 1.00% on two DreamWAM configurations and to 10.60% on Motus. Behavioral analysis connects these representation shifts to grasping failures and separates rapid command recovery after patch removal from persistent physical consequences. These results show that protecting downstream action generation alone is insufficient: WAM defenses must also secure shared visual encoders against persistent local perturbations.
2026-10-06.introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) are emerging as a powerful foundation for general-purpose robotic control. Rather than predicting actions from the current observation alone, a WAM learns how the visual world evolves together with the robot’s actions. This world-modeling objective captures objects, spatial relationships, and motion, and can support action generation either through explicit future imagination ( Du et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) or through representations learned during video prediction ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) . By unifying visual prediction and control, WAMs promise policies that can reason about the consequences of their actions and replan as the environment changes ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) .

This coupling, however, also creates a security risk. Current WAM pipelines implicitly trust the visual representation on which world prediction and action generation are built. This assumption is fragile. Cameras expose a direct, externally accessible input channel. Moreover, visual encoders are often reused across tasks and models, making the exposed channel transferable among tasks. A perturbation that corrupts this shared interface can therefore bypass model-specific action heads. If the channel remains exposed, a perturbation can be injected consistently. In this paper, we investigate whether an attacker can exploit this vulnerability and launch attacks against WAMs that transfer to unseen tasks and models.

We propose TAPDreamer (illustrated in Figure 1 ), a transferable attack that applies a patch on visual inputs to WAMs. TAPDreamer maximizes the displacement of the final latent produced by visual encoder. The search uses a few demonstration frames from a single source task. Once the patch is found, the patch pixels, area, and position are frozen and the same artifact is deployed unchanged throughout each episode and across target tasks and models. Throughout the attack, TAPDreamer does not require action labels, task rewards, simulator, victim-model weights, or policy outputs, making TAPDreamer simple and inexpensive to initiate.

We evaluate TAPDreamer on 40 LIBERO tasks and all 50 RoboTwin tasks. TAPDreamer consistently outperforms attack baselines. On FastWAM, a single frozen patch covering approximately 6.5 % 6.5\% of the input reduces task success from 97.65 % 97.65\% to 0.00 % 0.00\% on LIBERO and from 90.86 % 90.86\% to 0.00 % 0.00\% on RoboTwin. Random patches retain 81.45 % 81.45\% and 79.20 % 79.20\% success, respectively. The same frozen patches also transfer across WAM architectures without retraining or target-model queries: success falls from 84.55 % 84.55\% and 86.10 % 86.10\% with matched random patches to 1.45 % 1.45\% and 1.00 % 1.00\% on DreamWAM-uncond and DreamWAM-joint, and from 82.40 % 82.40\% to 10.60 % 10.60\% on Motus.
We further trace how a fixed patch causes failure during closed-loop control.
Our results show that changing a small set of pixels distorts visual features across the scene, including those used to select actions, and thus leads to reduced task success rate.

2026-10-06.title: H-JEPA: End-to-End Learning of Hierarchical World Models for Visual Planning
2026-10-06.authors: Wancong Zhang , Basile Terver , Michael Rabbat , Yann LeCun , Randall Balestriero
2026-10-06.abstract:
Long-horizon planning with latent world models requires reasoning across
timescales and levels of abstraction. Existing task-agnostic JEPA world models
predict and plan in a single latent space, often at a single timescale.
We introduce H-JEPA , an end-to-end recipe for training a
hierarchy of action-conditioned JEPAs in which each level predicts farther ahead in its
own learned latent space. Planning proceeds top-down: the top level
optimizes progress toward the goal, and each level’s predictions become
subgoals for the planner below it. When factors in the data evolve at separated
timescales, higher levels discard fast, unpredictable detail and retain slower
task-relevant state. Across four simulated navigation and manipulation
environments, hierarchical planning improves over a flat JEPA;
on Visual AntMaze, a three-level hierarchy raises success from 18% to 73% using less planner compute. Ablations attribute these gains to both temporal decomposition
and higher-level goal representations. With inverse-dynamics supervision, the
approach extends to diverse real-robot videos from DROID, where hierarchy
improves offline planning fidelity at lower planner compute.
2026-10-06.introduction:
World models learn the dynamics of an environment from experience so that an agent
can predict, understand, and plan [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] .
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) learn such models by predicting
future latent states rather than
pixels [ 49 , 1 , 9 ] , avoiding both reward
and pixel
reconstruction [ 5 , 59 ] ,
and recent action-conditioned, task-agnostic JEPA world models plan zero-shot in
the learned latent
space [ 93 , 2 , 73 , 53 , 78 ] .
These models, however, predict and plan within a single latent space, often at a
single timescale.
This has two limitations. First, at a single timescale, long-horizon prediction
rolls out many fine-grained steps: prediction error compounds and the action search
space grows. Second, a
single shared latent space must support both low-level dynamics and goal
matching. A latent that carries every fast-varying detail may model low-level dynamics
well, but gives a poor goal-matching cost when the goal is more abstract
than the state (a location to reach rather than a pose to match;
§ 4.2 ).

A hierarchical world model divides this work. Each higher level predicts over a
longer horizon and keeps in its latent space what remains predictable. Higher levels
operate on slow features over long strides and serve long-range prediction and
high-level planning; lower levels operate on fast features over short strides and
serve short-range prediction and low-level control. The brain has such hierarchical structure: cortical areas
form a hierarchy of intrinsic timescales, with slower-varying representations
higher up [ 37 , 43 , 56 , 3 ] .
Hierarchical world models have been studied in video prediction and reward-driven
control (§ M , Table 13 ). Hierarchical latent
video models reconstruct pixels and are not used for
control [ 68 , 44 , 55 ] , while hierarchical
model-based reinforcement learning learns task-specific policies from
reward [ 32 , 36 , 27 ] .
Closest to our setting, HWM [ 92 ] is a task-agnostic JEPA
world model that plans hierarchically, but its predictors over different horizons
share one latent space. It decomposes the horizon but cannot match objectives in
more abstract spaces.

We introduce H-JEPA , a hierarchical JEPA architecture in which each level
predicts the future within its own latent space, at a coarser temporal stride and a
higher degree of abstraction than the level below, without reward or reconstruction
objectives. Fig. 1 shows the learned hierarchy and its
tradeoff between planner compute and success. We make four contributions:

We introduce an end-to-end training method for hierarchical JEPA world models (§ 2 ).

We introduce an end-to-end training method for hierarchical JEPA world models (§ 2 ).

We show that when factors in the data evolve at separated
timescales, higher levels discard fast detail they cannot predict
over their horizons and retain slower, predictable state
(§ 3 ).

We show that H-JEPA’s hierarchical planning outperforms
single-level planning at a fraction of the test-time compute
(§ 4.1 ). We identify two complementary mechanisms:
hierarchical latent spaces let higher-level planners score progress at
the goal’s own level of abstraction, while temporal decomposition breaks
long-horizon tasks into easier subproblems
(§ 4.2 ).

With an inverse-dynamics term, the method extends to DROID, a real-robot
manipulation corpus whose scene, lighting and objects change every
episode (§ 4.3 ).

2026-10-06.title: On Learning Optimal Corners in Orthogonal Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Galleries
2026-10-06.authors: Yassin Ben Mansour , Edwin Meriaux
2026-10-06.abstract:
The CADENCE algorithm solves the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art
Gallery Problem (POCGAGP) with formal coverage and connectivity guarantees,
but leaves unspecified which valid corner each agent should be deployed to,
a choice that strongly affects efficiency. We introduce two learned
corner-selection heuristics that preserve these guarantees: a CNN scoring
candidates on a grid encoding, and a GATv2 network trained with Deep
Q-Learning (DQN) on a visibility graph. Across 7,500 runs on random
orthogonal environments ( 50 2 50^{2} to 250 2 250^{2} ), our heuristics
outperform baseline CADENCE in both steps to full coverage and peak agent
count, with gains growing with scale, and improve on Incremental
Self-Deployment (ISDA) baselines in agent utilization while providing
guarantees ISDA lacks. Learned corner selection thus improves CADENCE
in speed and agent utilization at no cost to its formal properties.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Deploying mobile robot teams in unknown environments for disaster response and inspection requires balancing two coupled challenges: exploring the area and maintaining a mobile ad hoc network (MANET) for communication. Because new observations alter the topology and the map is unknown in advance, this dual requirement cannot be solved through offline planning.

The computational geometry community represents exactly this situation as
the Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Gallery Problem (POCGAGP).
POCGAGP is the partially observable variant of the Cooperative Guard Art
Gallery Problem (CGAGP), which in turn extends the classical Art Gallery
Problem (AGP) [ 1 ] . AGP asks for the smallest set of static guards whose
visibility polygons cover a given polygon, and computing that minimum set is
NP-hard [ 2 ] . CGAGP
adds the requirement that the guards form a connected visibility graph,
which is precisely the Mobile Ad Hoc Network (MANET) condition once mutual visibility is read as a
line-of-sight link. POCGAGP then removes the assumption that the polygon is
known in advance, leaving agents to extend coverage and connectivity from
whatever they have observed so far.

CADENCE solves POCGAGP by deploying agents one at a time to valid corners on the boundary of the observed region, this makes the number of deployed agents bounded by the number of valid corners: M valid := n + 2 ​ h − 4 2 M_{\text{valid}}:=\frac{n+2h-4}{2} , where n is the number of 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} or 270 ∘ 270^{\circ} interior angles, and h is the number of holes [ 3 ] . A valid corner [ 3 ] is a 270 ∘ 270^{\circ} reflex corner which is not at the top left of a hole (an obstacle not part of the outside wall) within the environment.

Reflex corners form the ideal candidate set as they mark the exact vertices where visibility is occluded, resolving line-of-sight barriers no interior placement can. This formulation is strictly two-dimensional and orthogonal: both the guard bounds and discrete corner extraction rely on orthogonality, surviving neither a move to general polygons nor to 3D. Since our aim is to improve CADENCE rather than propose a new solver, we operate directly within its defined setting.

While CADENCE identifies candidate corners, it lacks a criterion for selecting among them. These decisions compound over time because early placements dictate future candidate availability; a myopically attractive choice can easily preclude a shorter overall solution. However, evaluating candidates explicitly requires exhaustive visibility simulation and downstream lookahead—the exact computational burden the incremental formulation aims to avoid.

We replace this missing criterion with a learned scoring function that predicts candidate values and selects the optimal deployment. The central question is state representation: grid-based encodings allow convolutional networks to exploit spatial structure, whereas graph representations capture relational visibility between corners and cells. Comparing these distinct encodings forms the substance of this work. Our contributions are:

two learned valid-corner selection heuristics for CADENCE: a dense
CNN over a grid encoding, GATv2 networks over a
visibility-graph encoding;

# II Background

## II-A POCGAGP and CADENCE

Classical art gallery results assume the polygon is given in advance. The
robotics exploration literature relaxes that assumption using frontier-based
methods that drive robots toward the boundary between known and unknown
space [ 4 ] , but those methods are formulated over occupancy grids and carry
neither a geometric coverage guarantee nor an explicit connectivity
constraint. POCGAGP bridges the two, and CADENCE realizes it by maintaining
the observed region, extracting its valid 270 ∘ 270^{\circ} corners, deploying an
agent to one of them, and repeating until coverage is complete [ 3 ] . We modify
neither the POCGAGP formulation nor the connectivity machinery; we target
only the unspecified selection inside CADENCE’s loop.

## II-B Grid and Graph Representations

Convolutional networks exploit translation equivariance and local receptive
fields [ 5 ] , and an orthogonal environment discretizes onto a grid without
distortion. The quantities determining a corner’s value are local spatial
patterns: unseen area beyond it, surrounding wall orientation, and frontier
position. This makes a convolutional encoder a natural first hypothesis.
Its limitation is that visibility is not a spatially local relation: a corner
can reveal a cell far along a sightline while being blind to its immediate
neighbour behind a wall, so convolution must be deep enough to span
sightlines and must additionally learn occlusion logic the geometry already
provides.

Graph attention networks [ 6 ] operate directly on the visibility relation itself. When edges encode sightlines rather than spatial adjacency, a single message-passing step immediately propagates coverage information along line-of-sight paths. We use the GATv2 formulation, which resolves a key limitation of standard graph attention by allowing node rankings to depend on the target node. This distinction is critical here because visible cells vary in value: an already-observed cell adds nothing, whereas an unexplored frontier cell is highly valuable.

## II-C Learning to Score Candidates

Guiding a combinatorial search with a learned scoring function is an
established pattern in which the search retains its correctness conditions
and learning supplies only the ordering over candidates. A mis-scored
candidate therefore costs efficiency rather than correctness, since CADENCE
terminates with full coverage regardless of which valid corner is chosen.
Because a placement’s value depends on the placements that follow it,
selection is naturally sequential; we train the graph-based selectors by
deep Q-learning [ 7 ] against the CADENCE rollout, using newly discovered nodes as
the reward signal.

2026-10-06.abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate visual representations from video generation backbones to guide action prediction. Recent efficient WAMs adopt Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architectures and compute video representations once for reuse by the action expert. However, intra-expert iteration ( i.e. , multi-step action denoising) and inter-expert waiting ( i.e. , sequential execution of the video and action experts) still limit inference efficiency. To this end, we present RealtimeWAM, an extremely efficient WAM variant with one-step action generation and asynchronous inference, addressing these two bottlenecks. To reduce intra-expert iteration, we propose Teacher-Anchored Consistency Distillation (TACD) to address a local-global error gap: low local consistency error alone does not guarantee accurate final actions. TACD supplements local consistency with explicit supervision from the frozen teacher’s multi-step rollout endpoint, enabling accurate one-step action generation. Additionally, we propose Cross-Expert Wavefront Pipelining (CEWP) to eliminate unnecessary expert-level waiting. It overlaps the two experts through block-wise sharing of the video KV cache, synchronizing only immediately before the corresponding action attention consumes it. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks ( e.g. , LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus and RoboTwin) and model variants ( e.g. , Fast-WAM and Faster-WAM) demonstrate the superiority of RealtimeWAM. Notably, RealtimeWAM maintains near-lossless performance ( i.e. , < 1 % <1\% drop) across these benchmarks while delivering significant end-to-end speedup ( e.g. , ∼ 25 × \sim 25\times on H100).

2026-10-06.introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Bi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot manipulation by jointly modeling future visual observations and robot actions. Unlike conventional Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ( Shukor et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) that map visual observations and language instructions directly to actions, WAMs incorporate future visual prediction as an additional learning objective. This supervision encourages policies to capture the physical dynamics and temporal structure of robot–environment interactions.

Based on whether video and action modeling use the same network, WAM architectures can be broadly divided into two categories. Representative shared-backbone WAMs ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) jointly denoise video and action tokens within a single backbone. Consequently, iterative denoising of long token sequences through the heavy video backbone increases inference latency. In contrast, some efficient Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT)-based WAMs ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) offer a promising alternative: the video expert computes representations once , while a separate action expert reuses them for action generation.

Despite advancements in inference pipeline design, these MoT-based WAMs still incur substantial latency. Specifically, even on advanced GPUs ( e.g. , H100 in Fig. 1 ), these models ( e.g. , Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) ) require over 300 ms for a single inference call. We identify two inference bottlenecks that remain insufficiently addressed in existing MoT-based WAMs: ➀ Intra-expert iteration arises from multi-step action denoising. We observe that the action expert accounts for nearly 90% of end-to-end latency for action generation across diverse GPUs (see Fig. 1 ). ➁ Inter-expert waiting stems from sequential execution of the video and action experts. As shown in Fig. 4 (a), the action expert begins execution only after the video expert completes its forward pass, causing unnecessary waiting.

Motivated by the above analysis, we present RealtimeWAM , an extremely efficient post-trained variant based on any MoT-based WAM. To our knowledge, it is the first one-step WAM to achieve near-lossless performance compared with its multi-step counterparts.

To combat intra-expert iteration, we propose Teacher-Anchored Consistency Distillation (TACD) for one-step action generation. TACD addresses a local-global error gap in conventional consistency distillation, which only constrains local consistency while neglecting to explicitly penalize the global target action error. TACD adopts the frozen teacher’s multi-step rollout endpoint as a numerical proxy for the exact clean endpoint, explicitly aligning the student’s velocity prediction with the corresponding interval-averaged teacher velocity. From a theoretical perspective, we show that this teacher anchor directly constrains the total endpoint error, complementing local consistency supervision with an explicit action endpoint constraint.

To reduce inter-expert waiting, we introduce Cross-Expert Wavefront Pipelining (CEWP), which transforms coarse expert-wise execution into a fine-grained block-wise pipeline. Under conventional expert-wise execution, the Action Expert waits for the Video Expert to construct the complete block-wise KV cache. We first conduct an in-depth dependency analysis, observing that each action block requires the video KV cache only from its corresponding video block, rather than the complete output of the Video Expert. Motivated by this observation, CEWP overlaps the execution of the two experts through block-wise sharing of the video KV cache, synchronizing only immediately before the corresponding action attention consumes it, which significantly reduces unnecessary waiting.

RealtimeWAM achieves impressive results on representative MoT-based WAM architectures, including Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) and Faster-WAM ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , across diverse downstream benchmarks ( e.g. , LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) , and RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) ). On these benchmarks, it delivers approximately 14 ∼ 25 × 14\sim 25\times inference acceleration with an average < 1 % <1\% accuracy drop compared with the original multi-step models. Notably, RealtimeWAM’s per-call inference latency is significantly shorter than the corresponding execution time ( e.g. , 30 Hz control frequency), enabling real-time action generation. These results demonstrate that RealtimeWAM remains effective across diverse robot configurations, task horizons, and distribution conditions, and provide a practical path toward efficient WAM deployment.

To summarize, our contributions are as follows:

▶ \blacktriangleright We propose RealtimeWAM, a one-step asynchronous WAM that addresses both intra-expert iteration and inter-expert waiting in any MoT-based WAM for efficient robot manipulation. ▶ \blacktriangleright We propose Teacher-Anchored Consistency Distillation (TACD), which mitigates the local-global error gap by augmenting local consistency supervision with a teacher endpoint constraint for accurate one-step action generation. ▶ \blacktriangleright We introduce Cross-Expert Wavefront Pipelining (CEWP), which reduces unnecessary synchronization by overlapping block-wise execution of the Video and Action Experts according to their data dependencies. ▶ \blacktriangleright Extensive experiments demonstrate that RealtimeWAM achieves real-time action generation with < 1 % <1\% accuracy degradation ( i.e. , 12.2 ms inference latency with ∼ 25 × \sim 25\times speedup on an NVIDIA H100 GPU).

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 World Action Models

While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ( Shukor et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) rely on pretrained vision-language backbones to map visual observations and language instructions directly to actions, World Action Models (WAMs) ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Bi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ) incorporate future visual representations from video generation backbones to guide action prediction. Modern WAMs can be broadly classified into two categories. ➀ One line of work focuses on shared-backbone WAMs, which model future video and robot actions within a shared backbone, including DreamZero ( Ye et al., 2026 ) and Cosmos ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . ➁ In contrast, Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT)-based WAMs, such as Motus ( Bi et al., 2026 ) , employ separate video and action experts that interact through attention. Among these methods, Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) reduces inference overhead by computing video representations once for reuse by the action expert. Subsequent works, including Light-WAM ( Li et al., 2026c ) and Faster-WAM ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , further improve computational efficiency and out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness. Nevertheless, these methods may incur substantial performance degradation on challenging benchmarks or achieve limited speedups.

## 2.2 Few-Step Distillation

Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ) and flow models ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Albergo et al., 2023 ) have become cornerstones of modern high-quality image and video generation. However, their iterative sampling cost has motivated a series of few-step acceleration methods, including progressive distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ) , consistency models ( Song et al., 2023 ) , distribution matching distillation ( Yin et al., 2024 ) , MeanFlow ( Geng et al., 2025 ) , and adversarial distillation ( Sauer et al., 2024 ) . These distillation techniques have recently been introduced into World Action Models ( Akbari et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . The work most relevant to ours is Flash-WAM ( Akbari et al., 2026 ) , which identifies a modality-dependent noise-regime mismatch and introduces modality-specific consistency parameterizations. However, ➀ it focuses on few-step distillation for WAMs that retain future-video denoising during inference, such as LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026a ) ; and ➁ its ultra-few-step ( i.e. , one-step) distillation still exhibits noticeable performance degradation ( e.g. , RoboTwin and real-world tasks). These limitations motivate our investigation of one-step action distillation for MoT-based WAMs.

## 2.3 Asynchronous Inference for Robot Policies

Asynchronous inference has been widely studied for real-time robot control because it mitigates execution stalls, stale observations, and delayed responses caused by policy latency. Existing approaches can be broadly grouped into three categories: execution-level asynchrony, module-level asynchrony, and sampling-level asynchrony. Execution-level methods overlap prediction of the next action chunk with execution of the current one and maintain continuity through prefix conditioning, state correction, or chunk fusion ( Black et al., 2025a ; Black et al., 2025b ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Motubrain Team, 2026 ) . Module-level methods decouple a slow semantic or world module from a fast action module, allowing cached high-level representations to guide high-frequency action updates ( Hirose et al., 2026 ; Cai et al., 2026 ) . Sampling-level methods assign different action positions, chunks, modalities, or denoising streams distinct sampling schedules, enabling early action output or selective refinement without waiting for full decoding ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . In contrast, RealtimeWAM employs finer-grained asynchrony at the block level, distinguishing it from prior approaches.

2026-10-06.authors: Ziying Song , Yuchen Liu , Zhuoran Xu , Ziyang Liu , Jian Jin , Jiangtao Su , Haibao Yu , Lei Yang , Yuanpei Chen

2026-10-06.abstract:
Embodied world models predict the visual consequences of candidate actions before execution. However, existing action-conditioned world models often adopt uniformly weighted visual generation objectives that can be misaligned with embodied prediction needs. Even with explicit motion conditioning, these objectives can underemphasize spatially sparse changes that are critical to interaction.
We propose K i n e W o rld , a transport-aware world-modeling framework that extends robot kinematics from motion conditioning to the spatial allocation of generative supervision. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs renderer-derived, camera-aligned transport fields from commanded robot motion. Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates their motion support on the video-latent grid and reweights future-RGB flow matching through a normalized mixture of uniform and transport-focused distributions.
We train KineWorld using ALOHA–AgileX bimanual manipulation data from RoboTwin 2.0 . KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 in single-view evaluation and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in multi-view evaluation. These results support a shift from appearance fitting toward action-consequence modeling for embodied decision-making.
2026-10-06.introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) enable robots to anticipate how the visual world will evolve under candidate actions before executing them in the physical environment. By generating action-conditioned future observations, these models can serve as predictive simulators for policy learning, action evaluation, planning, and synthetic experience generation. Recent advances in large-scale video generation further provide strong appearance and dynamics priors, making it possible to construct visually realistic robot rollouts from limited embodied data Zhu et al. (2024) ; Guo et al. (2025) ; Liao et al. (2025) .

Existing world action models (WAMs) improve action responsiveness through numerical action tokens, learned latent codes, and spatially aligned conditions such as embodiment masks, action images, optical flow, and projected kinematic fields Zhu et al. (2024) ; Guo et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2026) ; Liao et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2026b) . Yet motion conditioning does not itself alter the spatial weighting of the primary RGB-generation objective. When action-responsive regions occupy only a small part of the frame, uniform token averaging can bias optimization toward static appearance. Motion-sensitive auxiliary objectives and flow-branch reweighting address related concerns Zhu et al. (2024) ; Chen et al. (2026b) . We further use robot kinematics to guide future-RGB supervision, aligning the model’s learning priorities with action consequences.
This raises a key question: how can robot kinematics guide the learning of action consequences?

Our key insight is that action conditioning and supervision allocation serve different purposes: the former specifies what motion to generate, whereas the latter determines which prediction errors receive greater weight during training. Robot kinematics provides a geometry-derived prior for this allocation by identifying where commanded robot motion is expected to appear in the camera view, without relying on generated future frames. This suggests using kinematic transport not only as a generation condition, but also as a spatial prior for the primary
video-generation objective.

Building on this insight, we introduce K i n e W o rld , a
transport-aware training framework for action-conditioned world modeling. Kinematic Transport Lifting (KTL) constructs camera-aligned transport, while Transport-Aware World Diffusion (TAWD) calibrates its motion support on the video latent grid and converts the resulting support into a normalized mixture distribution for the RGB flow-matching objective. The resulting objective redistributes supervision while preserving the aggregate token weight, without adding inference parameters or sampling steps. This extends kinematic priors from generation conditions to learning guidance for interaction- and decision-oriented world prediction.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Action-Consequence-Oriented Learning. We distinguish visual extent from interaction importance, motivating
kinematics-guided learning of interaction-critical local changes.

K i n e W o rld Framework. We propose K i n e W o rld , a transport-aware framework with KTL and TAWD. KTL constructs camera-aligned transport from the commanded rollout, while TAWD reweights RGB flow matching via a normalized mixture on the latent grid, preserving token weight and sampling.

Benchmark Evaluation. Trained on RoboTwin 2.0 ALOHA–AgileX bimanual manipulation data ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , KineWorld achieves an EWMScore-P of 68.95 and a TWB-Score of 54.82 in single-view and multi-view evaluation, respectively. Our framework and evaluations provide the community with a reference for action-consequence-oriented world modeling.

# 2 Related Work

World Action Models (WAMs) increasingly leverage pretrained video generators to connect visual prediction with robot control ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2025 ) . Existing approaches include action-conditioned video prediction ( Zhu et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) , joint video-action generation ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , and action decoding from visual latent representations ( Liao et al., 2025 ) . Recent systems further broaden this paradigm. RealWonder connects physical actions to video generation through simulated RGB and flow ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , while CLAP integrates heterogeneous action representations for cross-embodiment learning ( Liu & Shorinwa, 2026 ) . However, advances in generative architectures and action interfaces do not inherently prioritize interaction-critical changes in the primary RGB objective. When these changes occupy few visual tokens, uniform weighting can underemphasize their contribution. KineWorld addresses this complementary problem through kinematics-guided allocation of future-RGB supervision.

Existing WAMs encode robot actions as numerical tokens, learned latent codes, or spatially grounded visual cues ( Zhu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . Recent methods align actions with the visual domain through embodiment masks ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , multi-view action videos ( Zhen et al., 2026 ) , optical flow ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , and camera-aligned kinematic fields ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . Beyond conditioning, FlowWAM reweights its flow-branch loss using reference-relative latent deviations ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , while EA-WM uses frame-difference supervision to guide cross-stream fusion ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, KineWorld uses kinematic transport to directly reweight future-RGB flow matching without introducing auxiliary objectives.

2026-10-06.abstract: Diffusion transformers (DiTs) achieve state-of-the-art image generation, but their sampling cost limits deployment. Quantizing both weights and activations to 4 bits reduces this cost, yet existing methods fall short in one of two ways. Calibration-based methods are tied to a specific checkpoint and prompt distribution, whereas data-free Hadamard rotation, effective for LLMs, loses quality on DiTs. We show that this loss has a structural cause. Adaptive layer-norm conditioning adds a per-token mean to the activations, and at the widths of the evaluated DiTs, the Hadamard rotations used by data-free methods cannot spread this mean uniformly across coordinates. A single dominant direction therefore survives the rotation and sets the quantization range. We introduce CentriQ, a calibration-free quantizer that centers each token before rotation and restores the mean exactly through a rank-1 full-precision branch, so that per-token scales follow in closed form without data. Weights are fitted under a robust ℓ p \ell_{p} objective that tracks the dense mode of each group and discounts heavy tails. Across three DiTs, CentriQ matches the quality of calibrated SVDQuant at 4 bits, whereas calibration-free weight quantizers with plain per-token activation quantization collapse or degrade substantially. CentriQ outperforms the strongest calibration-free method reported to date at 2-bit weights. It is also the first calibration-free method to retain usable image quality at 2-bit activations.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Diffusion transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) underlie state-of-the-art text-to-image models, but sampling them is expensive. Each image requires many denoising steps, and each step is dominated by the linear layers of the transformer blocks. Unlike autoregressive LLM decoding, which at small batch sizes is limited by memory bandwidth, a DiT forward pass is compute-bound. Weight-only quantization (e.g. W4A16) therefore reduces memory but not latency, because the low-bit weights are upcast to 16 bits before the matrix multiply, so activations must be quantized as well.

The post-training methods that do reach W4A4 on diffusion models all rely on calibration. A prompt set is run through the model to fit smoothing factors, clipping ranges, rotations, or error-compensating weight updates to the activation statistics of that specific model. SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) , for instance, migrates activation outliers into the weights using smoothing factors computed from COCO caption prompts, absorbs the magnified weight outliers in a 16-bit low-rank branch, and in its final version also applies GPTQ to the residual.

Calibration has costs beyond its compute budget. It makes the quantized model depend on a dataset, it must be repeated for every model, fine-tune, and quantization configuration, and its quality depends on how well the calibration prompts and timesteps match the deployment distribution. Calibration-free methods that reach four-bit activations on image DiTs have appeared only recently (Sec. 2 ), and they evaluate on generation benchmarks that do not measure fidelity to the full-precision model.

Two properties of DiT activations make the calibration-free setting difficult. First, adaptive layer normalization shifts and rescales every token with conditioning-dependent parameters, so each activation vector carries a per-token mean. A normalized Hadamard rotation, the standard tool for spreading outliers, maps this component onto one or a few coordinates, and the resulting outlier sets the quantization range for the whole vector. Second, only regular Hadamard matrices, whose rows have equal sums, spread this component uniformly, and these exist only at orders n = 4 ​ u 2 n=4u^{2} . None of the hidden widths of PixArt- Σ \Sigma (1152), FLUX.1 (3072), and SANA-1.6B (2240) has this form, so rotation methods operate through block-structured or Kronecker constructions, which inherit the mean problem.

We present CentriQ, a calibration-free W4A4 post-training quantization method for DiTs that addresses both properties directly. It subtracts the per-token mean before rotation, quantizes only the residual, and restores the mean exactly as a rank-1 term in the layer output, so the quantization range no longer depends on the offset. The centered activation is rotated by a deterministic factorized Hadamard matrix, and weights are quantized to grouped INT4 under a robust ℓ p \ell_{p} ( p < 1 p<1 ) objective, so neither path uses calibration data.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We show that adaLN places a per-token mean in DiT activations, which a Hadamard rotation concentrates onto one or a few coordinates that set the quantization range (Figs. 1 and 2 ).

We show that after centering, the rotated operand, its per-token scale, and its quantization error contain no term that depends on the row sums of the rotation (Sec. 4.2 , App. C.5 ). The choice of rotation is thereby decoupled from the mean, so CentriQ mixes globally with factorized Hadamard matrices and restores the mean exactly as a rank-1 term in the GEMM epilogue.

CentriQ uses no calibration data and reaches FID and ImageReward that match calibration-based methods at W4A4 on three DiT families. Furthermore, it surpasses the strongest reported calibration-free method at W2A4 and is the first calibration-free method to hold image quality at W4A2 (Tab. 1 , Tab. 4 , Tab. 5 ).

# 2 Related work

Work on U-Net diffusion models showed that activation statistics drift with the timestep ( Li et al., 2023 ; Shang et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2023 ; So et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) . Methods for diffusion transformers inherit this diagnosis and absorb the drift with calibration: PTQ4DiT ( Wu et al., 2024 ) weights salient channels by timestep, Q-DiT ( Chen et al., 2025 ) and ViDiT-Q ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) use dynamic per-timestep or per-token activation scales, DiTAS ( Dong and Zhang, 2025 ) aggregates smoothing factors across timesteps, LRQ-DiT ( Yang et al., 2025 ) chooses rotations per layer from a calibrated metric, and AdaTSQ ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) allocates bit-widths along the trajectory with Fisher-weighted Hessian calibration. The fitted statistics belong to one checkpoint and sampler, so these methods must be refit when the model or guidance changes. Sampler-side corrections ( He et al., 2023 ; Ryu et al., 2026 ) act after quantization and are complementary to any quantizer, whereas training-based approaches ( He et al., 2024 ; Sui et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) fall outside the post-training setting.

LLM quantization spreads activation outliers across channels by rotating the residual stream, with random orthogonal matrices in QuIP ( Chee et al., 2023 ) , randomized Hadamard transforms in QuIP# ( Tseng et al., 2024 ) , and Hadamard rotations folded into the weights in QuaRot ( Ashkboos et al., 2024b ) . Learned rotations ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) recover accuracy that a fixed Hadamard loses, but they are fit on calibration data. All of these assume a Hadamard matrix of the model width, which the Sylvester construction gives only for powers of two, so other widths use a Kronecker product H 2 k ⊗ H m H_{2^{k}}\otimes H_{m} with a small hand-picked H m H_{m} .

SliceGPT ( Ashkboos et al., 2024a ) and QuaRot fold LayerNorm mean subtraction into the preceding weights, which is exact in LLMs. In a DiT, the adaLN modulation depends on the timestep and prompt and makes the mean vary per token, so this static fold does not apply. HadaNorm ( Federici et al., 2025 ) subtracts a per-channel mean computed over tokens at inference and applies SmoothQuant-style per-channel scales, fitted on a calibration set, before a Hadamard transform, and reports W4A4 on PixArt- Σ \Sigma . CentriQ removes the per-token mean instead and requires no calibration data. To our knowledge, no public implementation of HadaNorm is available, which precludes a direct comparison under our protocol. ConvRot ( Huang et al., 2025 ) spreads the mean with group-wise regular Hadamard transforms of order 4 k 4^{k} , which mix only within each group, whereas CentriQ removes the mean and mixes globally with factorized Hadamard matrices.

SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) was the first to reach reasonable 4-bit weights and activations on image DiTs, by keeping a low-rank branch in 16 bits after SmoothQuant-style migration ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) fit on captioned images, with fused kernels in Nunchaku. DiRotQ ( Sharify et al., 2026 ) preserves a calibration-derived PCA subspace of the activations at higher precision and quantizes weights with GPTQ ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) , improving over SVDQuant on PixArt- Σ \Sigma under the MJHQ-30K protocol, which is not directly comparable with the MJHQ-5k protocol used here. HQ-DiT ( Liu and Zhang, 2024 ) reaches 4-bit operands with a floating-point grid.

On the weight side, RTN, NF4 ( Dettmers et al., 2023 ) , HQQ ( Badri and Shaji, 2023 ) , and SINQ ( Müller et al., 2026 ) operate on the weight tensor alone. NF4 assumes near-Gaussian weights, HQQ fits the dense mode under an ℓ p \ell_{p} objective with p < 1 p<1 , and SINQ balances a second scale axis with Sinkhorn iterations. Calibration-free 4-bit activations on DiTs are recent. DVD-Quant ( Li et al., 2026 ) achieves W4A4 for video DiTs with grid refinement, rotated quantization, and adaptive bit switching. ConvRot achieves it on FLUX-family models with group-wise rotation, NVFP4 weights, and per-tensor FP8 activation scales. OrbitQuant ( Lee et al., 2026 ) quantizes weights and activations in a randomly permuted block-Hadamard basis with a Lloyd–Max codebook derived from the post-rotation marginal ( Zandieh et al., 2026 ) , and reports GenEval on FLUX.1 and Z-Image-Turbo down to W2A4. Neither image method removes the token mean, both mix within blocks whose order divides the width, and both evaluate on generation benchmarks that do not measure fidelity to the full-precision model.

CentriQ is calibration-free on both axes and produces integer W4A4 operands for every transformer-block projection. We evaluate it on PixArt- Σ \Sigma , FLUX.1-schnell, and SANA-1.6B with FID, ImageReward, LPIPS, and PSNR against the 16-bit reference on MJHQ, and compare against the published results of calibrated SVDQuant. To our knowledge it is the first calibration-free integer W4A4 method evaluated for fidelity across three image-DiT architecture families.

2026-10-06.title: EpicWorldModel: Exploration-driven Planning with Latent World Models
2026-10-06.authors: Bowen Feng , Julian Ost , May Mei , Anirudha Majumdar , Felix Heide
2026-10-06.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026.  (main text, appendix)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Latent world models based on Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) are deterministic by design.
While successful in fully observable scenarios, this paradigm breaks down when past observations and actions lead to multiple plausible future possibilities, e.g., due to occlusion.
We introduce EpicWorldModel , a framework to train stochastic JEPAs for environments and tasks with inherent uncertainty under partially observability.
We jointly train the EpicWorldModel predictor with its latent representation space to directly predict multiple potential future states using a flow-matching objective, when the goal-relevant scene content is absent from the conditioning history.
We show that flow predictive variance, motivated by its relation to an upper bound on predictive entropy, serves as a useful exploration guidance for planning.
By incorporating this uncertainty signal into Cross-Entropy Method (CEM)-based planning, our approach balances goal-reaching with exploration of uncertain regions where occluded goals are most likely to be located.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of EpicWorldModel through a series of latent planning experiments with the best or on-par performance across tasks, showing up to 22 % 22\% empirical improvement in success rate over LeWorldModel.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Learning world models for latent-space planning has seen increased applications in sequential decision-making, enabling agents to learn compact latent dynamics models and plan directly in the learned representation space ( Maes et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Bardes et al., 2023a ; Assran et al., 2025 ) .
Unlike model-free end-to-end visuomotor policy learning, latent-space planning with world models does not directly learn a policy that maps observations to actions.
Instead, it learns to compress high-dimensional sensory observations, such as visual inputs, into a structured latent representation and uses a learned dynamics model to perform model-based planning within this shared latent space.

Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) models have emerged as a promising family of models for this task. These methods learn predictive representations by mapping observations into an embedding space and predicting future or masked target embeddings from context embeddings, rather than reconstructing raw pixels ( LeCun and others, 2022 ) .
This principle has been instantiated in image representation learning through I-JEPA ( Assran et al., 2023 ) , video representation learning through V-JEPA ( Bardes et al., 2023a ; Assran et al., 2025 ) , and motion-aware predictive representation learning through MC-JEPA ( Bardes et al., 2023b ) .
Shown to be promising for representation learning, early world models suffered from collapse ( LeCun and others, 2022 ) when trained without complex training objectives, regularization through exponential moving averages and stop-gradients, the correct hyper-parameters ( Sobal et al., 2025 ) or pre-trained encoders ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) .
More recently, LeWorldModel ( Maes et al., 2026 ) stabilizes JEPA world model training with a simple yet effective regularization of the representation space to an isotropic Gaussian distribution.

However, a key limitation of existing JEPA-based world models is that their prediction objective is often a deterministic single-target regression in the latent space.
This formulation can be effective when the future state is largely determined by the historical observation context.
The contrary is the case when the conditioned observation history does not contain sufficient information to uniquely determine the future.
For example, consider the scenario where a robot is opening a drawer. From the robot’s perspective, any reasonable object could be inside the drawer. Further, the ground-truth future state could easily change over time, if the content of the drawer changed.
A world model predicting only a single future could lead to planning failure, if the predicted content of the drawer does not match the real world.
In such cases, multiple plausible futures may be consistent with the same observation history and the action chunk, but only a subset of them may lead toward the desired goal.
This raises a central question: How can we learn a world model to predict useful future representations when the future is inherently ambiguous? More broadly, we investigate latent-space planning that relies on predictive uncertainty to explore multiple plausible futures and select action sequences that effectively reach partially observed or occluded goals.

To this end, we propose EpicWorldModel: Exploration-based Planning with Latent World Model, a framework that trains a stochastic JEPA model to imagine multiple plausible futures in a jointly learned representation space, and plans under uncertainty, balancing goal-reaching and exploration.
At its core, EpicWorldModel learns to predict future observations through sampling from the conditional distribution of possible futures given a set of input actions.
In practice, we model this stochastic prediction as a conditional flow-matching process ( Pooladian et al., 2023 ) by predicting the average velocity ( Geng et al., 2025a ; Geng et al., 2025b ) between a random distribution and multiple future representations.
Past observations and actions serve as additional conditional signals. Encoder and predictor models are jointly learned ( LeCun and others, 2022 ; Maes et al., 2026 ) on pairs of past and future frames.

Our key insight is that when the model’s uncertainty on the future frames is high, the flow-matching predictor will exhibit high variance in generated future states. Conversely, for future frames that have been observed in recent history, the world model will produce near-deterministic predictions with low variance.
We motivate this intuition through an information-theoretic framework, relating flow predictive variance to an upper bound on predictive entropy and serves as an exploration guidance.
By incorporating this uncertainty signal into Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) planning, our approach balances goal-reaching with exploration of uncertain regions where occluded or unseen future states are most likely located.
We support our hypothesis and approach through both theoretical analysis connecting flow variance to information gain and empirical evaluation on planning tasks.
Experimental results show that EpicWorldModel achieves the best or on-par performance among all baselines, outperforming existing latent world models by up to 22 % 22\% across diverse partially observed tasks. Notably, EpicWorldModel also reaches state-of-the-art performance on visually restricted maze navigation tasks that were previously challenging for latent world models.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

World Models. Recent advances in world modeling has extended state-space dynamics learning to high-dimensional representations such as RGB images ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018b ; Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018a ) . Although action-conditioned video generation models have emerged as a popular paradigm for modeling photorealistic evolution of the world ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Quevedo et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) , their pixel reconstruction objective tend to be computationally costly, deeming them impractical for real-time inference and control. In contrast, latent world models aim to learn useful representations of the world as opposed to individual pixels, in particular with joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) ( LeCun and others, 2022 ) .
Video JEPA models ( Bardes et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) are trained on internet-scale video data to capture temporal structure for future prediction. D-JEPA ( Chen et al., 2024b ) incorporates diffusion and flow matching objectives into JEPA, extending applicability to image, video, and audio generation.
Conditioning on robot actions, models such as DINO-WM ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) and LeWorldModel ( Maes et al., 2026 ) leverage learned representations or enforce structure in the latent space, enabling direct application to robot planning and control.

Flow Matching. Early work on flow matching draws inspiration from Continuous normalizing flows (CNFs) ( Chen et al., 2018 ) originally introduced as a way to model ordinary differential equations (ODEs) from data pairs using black-box solvers.
CNFs modeled the underlying vector field v t v_{t} of the ODE.
As a descendant continuation conditional flow matching (CFM) ( Lipman et al., 2022 ) methods learned such CNFs for optimal transport between two distributions by only using linear solvers and samples from both distributions
This simplicity enabled brought use across data domains.
The image generation task has been most successfully solved by denoising diffusion probabilistic models ( Song et al., 2021 ) that stochastic differential equations (SDEs) before.
Flow matching offered an appealing alternative achieved by reformulating the denoising process as an ODE.
The continuous denoising path of CFMs in contrast to the inherent randomness in the path of SDEs resulted in less denoising steps, later further improved with the rectified flow objective ( Liu et al., 2022 ) .
Not only predominant in scaled image generation ( Esser et al., 2024 ) other data domains such as 3D shapes ( Xiang et al., 2025 ) , molecules ( Du et al., 2024 ) , or robotic planning ( Black et al., 2024 ) have seen successful implementations of generative models using flow matching.
Most relevant to out work are video generation models ( Wan et al., 2025 ; HaCohen et al., 2024 ) that have been continuously extended towards unbounded generation horizon ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024a ) and action conditioning ( Guo et al., 2025 ) rendering them useful for down-stream world modeling ( Team et al., 2026 ) .
Unlike video-generation world models that predict pixels, EpicWorldModel ’s stochastic predictor follows the JEPA paradigm by learning an expressive representation space and using a flow ODE to predict future representations.

Uncertainty-Aware Planning. Early work in uncertainty-aware planning grounded intrinsic motivation in prediction error within learned feature spaces ( Pathak et al., 2017 ) and modeled aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty through probabilistic ensemble dynamics for trajectory-sampled planning ( Chua et al., 2018 ) .
Plan2Explore ( Sekar et al., 2020 ) demonstrates that ensemble disagreement in latent dynamics models provides an effective intrinsic signal for directed exploration.
Subsequent work extends this paradigm to structured world models ( Sancaktar et al., 2022 ) , achieving zero-shot transfer to multi-object manipulation.
More recently, DreamerV3-XP ( Bierling et al., 2025 ) augmented the DreamerV3 model ( Hafner et al., 2023 ) with ensemble-based reward disagreement as an intrinsic exploration incentive.
EpicWorldModel draws insight from the exploration literature, and uses a stochastic JEPA world model for both goal-reaching and curiosity signals.

2026-10-06.title: Reachability-Aware Diffusion Policy Optimization
2026-10-06.authors: Hikmet Simsir , Kutay Demiray , Ozgur S. Oguz
2026-10-06.comment: Under review at ICLR 2027
2026-10-06.abstract:
Diffusion policies provide expressive action distributions for continuous-control reinforcement learning. However, safety-aware online diffusion policy optimization remains underexplored, particularly methods that use predictive reachability information without an explicit dynamics model.
We propose Reachability-Aware Diffusion Policy Optimization (RADPO), a model-free method that combines predictive first-hit safety estimation with cumulative-cost budget feedback.
RADPO learns a discounted first-hit reachability value that captures the discounted risk of a cost event, assigns larger weight to events that occur sooner, and uses this signal to shape the reward.
A separate dual-like multiplier adjusts the shaping strength according to realized episodic costs relative to a prescribed budget.
The diffusion actor improves through weighted denoising regression on candidate actions scored by the reward critic.
Our approach requires neither a learned dynamics model, action gradients through the critics, nor differentiation through the reverse diffusion sampler.
We establish theoretical properties of the reachability value and show that accumulated reachability penalty provides a conservative surrogate for future discounted cumulative cost.
Across ten continuous-control safety tasks, RADPO achieves competitive reward-cost trade-offs, with substantial reductions in constraint violations on several tasks relative to the compared baselines.
Our theoretical and empirical analysis supports that combining reachability with cumulative budget feedback is a viable approach to safety-aware diffusion policies.
2026-10-06.introduction:
A common formulation of safe reinforcement learning aims to maximize task performance while keeping expected cumulative safety cost below some budget ( Achiam et al., 2017 ; Stooke et al., 2020 ) . A central challenge is anticipating unsafe outcomes: an action may incur no immediate cost yet move the agent toward future violations. Cost critics address this by estimating accumulated future cost ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) , which captures violation magnitude and repeated exposure but does not explicitly isolate when the first cost encounter occurs. Reachability-based safety estimation provides a complementary
perspective by explicitly predicting future constraint
violations ( Yu et al., 2022 ; Ganai et al., 2023 ) instead. Discounted first-hit reachability captures whether a cost will be encountered while assigning greater weight to earlier encounters. We investigate whether this predictive signal can guide policy improvement while cumulative-cost feedback separately regulates the safety budget.

Diffusion policies provide expressive action distributions for continuous control ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2024 ) and can be optimized online through value-weighted denoising regression ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . However, most online diffusion-policy optimization methods focus on reward maximization ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Psenka et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) , while incorporating predictive safety information without an explicit dynamics model is relatively underexplored. We therefore propose Reachability-Aware Diffusion Policy Optimization (RADPO) , a model-free approach that combines discounted first-hit reachability with cumulative-cost budget feedback.

RADPO learns a discounted first-hit reachability value and uses the predicted reachability of successor states to shape the reward. An adaptive safety multiplier controls the shaping strength according to realized episodic costs relative to the prescribed budget, preserving information about cost magnitudes and repeated violations. The diffusion actor then improves through weighted denoising regression on candidate actions scored by the reward critic. This requires neither a learned dynamics model, action gradients through the critics, nor differentiation through the reverse diffusion sampler. This mechanism guides learning toward safer behavior. Figure 1 .A illustrates this behavior in a navigation scenario. SAC-Lag follows a greedier path close to the hazard boundaries and occasionally enters them, whereas RADPO takes a more conservative route with greater clearance.

Our main contributions are:

We introduce RADPO, a novel algorithm that combines discounted first-hit reachability with cumulative-cost budget feedback and integrates these signals into online diffusion policy optimization through value-weighted denoising regression.

We provide theoretical results for the discounted reachability value, including its first-hit interpretation and bounds relating accumulated reachability to discounted cumulative cost and repeated cost exposure. We further establish finite-candidate mirror-descent guarantees and analyze the safety-multiplier controller’s response to observed budget violations.

We evaluate RADPO on ten continuous-control safety tasks,
showing competitive reward–cost trade-offs and substantial
reductions in constraint violations on several tasks relative
to the compared baselines, complemented by design ablations.

2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Safe reinforcement learning is commonly formulated using constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), where expected return is maximized subject to cumulative-cost constraints. Some methods ( Achiam et al., 2017 ; Yang et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Milosevic et al., 2025 ) enforce these constraints through constrained or trust-region policy updates, while primal-dual approaches ( Tessler et al., 2018 ; Stooke et al., 2020 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) adapt Lagrange multipliers according to observed constraint violations. Beyond changing the policy update itself, other works modify the learned safety signal used by the optimizer; for example, USPC ( Demiray et al., 2026 ) replaces standard cost estimates with uncertainty-aware conservative safety surrogates. RADPO follows a similar approach, but instead introduces a distinct predictive reachability value alongside the cumulative-cost signal: episodic costs adapt the safety multiplier, while reachability shapes the reward used for policy improvement.

Reachability analysis attempts to determine whether target or unsafe sets can be reached under a dynamical system. Classical Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) methods compute backward reachable or viable sets from known dynamics ( Mitchell et al., 2005 ; Bansal et al., 2017 ) , with subsequent work connecting reachability analysis to learning-based control and reinforcement learning ( Fisac et al., 2018 ; Akametalu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . More recently, λ \lambda -Reachability ( Chen et al., 2026 ) introduces geometric-horizon Bellman targets that interpolate between discounted local updates and long-horizon max-over-trajectory safety values. In model-free safe RL, RCRL ( Yu et al., 2022 ) learns a reachability-based safety value to characterize feasible states, while RESPO ( Ganai et al., 2023 ) extends this idea to stochastic systems using a learned estimate of future constraint violation. RADPO instead targets a policy-conditional discounted first-hit cost value, assigning greater weight to violations occurring sooner. This predictive signal shapes the reward, while cumulative episodic cost is handled separately through budget feedback.

Several recent methods optimize diffusion policies using online reinforcement learning. DIPO ( Yang et al., 2023 ) and Q-Score
Matching ( Psenka et al., 2024 ) use critic gradients to improve
actions or policy scores, respectively. Other approaches optimize
a Q-weighted variational objective ( Ding et al., 2024 ) ,
backpropagate critic gradients through the diffusion sampling
process ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , or apply PPO-style policy-gradient
optimization to the denoising process ( Ren et al., 2024 ; Zou et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Most closely related to RADPO, DPMD ( Ma et al., 2025 ) derives diffusion-policy improvement from policy mirror descent using value-weighted denoising regression, avoiding both critic action gradients and differentiation through the reverse sampler. RADPO builds on this policy-improvement mechanism but evaluates candidate actions using a reward critic learned from rewards shaped by predictive reachability and an adaptive safety multiplier.

Safety and constraints have also been incorporated into diffusion-based decision making. Offline methods use cost-conditioned or feasibility-guided trajectory generation ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2024 ) , while barrier- and constraint-guided planners incorporate safety directly into diffusion sampling or denoising ( Xiao et al., 2025 ; Mizuta and Leung, 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . In the online setting, ALGD ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) uses an augmented-Lagrangian energy to guide diffusion-policy optimization under safety costs. Beyond environmental safety, diffusion policies have also been subject to behavior- or trust-region constraints that limit deviation during offline or online optimization ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Le et al., 2026 ; Simsir and Oguz, 2026 ) . RADPO instead combines fully online model-free diffusion-policy learning with a policy-conditional first-hit signal, separate episodic budget feedback, and value-weighted denoising without critic gradients or reverse-sampler differentiation.
