2026-10-06.title: Structural Foundations of Nonlinear Systems with Unknown Inputs: The UID-Induced Normal Form and Minimal-Sensing Structure-from-Motion
2026-10-06.authors: Agostino Martinelli
2026-10-06.subjects: Optimization and Control (math.OC) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.abstract:
This paper establishes the first general structural solution to the problem of state estimation for nonlinear systems driven by unknown inputs.
Building upon nonlinear unknown-input observability theory, we show that every such system admits a structurally equivalent representation, referred to as the UID-induced normal form .
The proposed representation decomposes the information carried by the unknown inputs into two complementary components: unknown-input directions that are structurally decoupled from the observable dynamics and observable quantities that completely represent the unknown-input information affecting the observable dynamics.
As a consequence, the UID-induced normal form provides a unified structural solution to unknown-input decoupling and unknown-input reconstruction, without requiring any model or stochastic assumption on the unknown inputs.
The practical significance of the proposed framework is demonstrated through a previously unexplored minimal Structure-from-Motion configuration.
The proposed representation enables recursive state estimation from only three point features and a single-axis gyroscope, allowing the recovery of the three-dimensional structure and camera motion up to an unknown global scale factor.
Experiments on real-world data validate the proposed framework and demonstrate the feasibility of this minimal sensing configuration.
2026-10-06.introduction:
State estimation for nonlinear systems driven by unknown inputs remains one of the fundamental open problems in robotics and control.
Unknown inputs may arise from unmodeled disturbances, environmental interactions, actuator effects, or motion components that are not directly measured.
Unlike unknown parameters or uncertain model coefficients, unknown inputs explicitly enter the system dynamics and continuously affect the state evolution.
Consequently, although the system equations are known, the actual dynamics followed by the state are not.
This lack of knowledge fundamentally limits state estimation.
All estimation methods for dynamical systems, whether based on recursive filtering, nonlinear observers, smoothing, or batch optimization, rely on the system dynamics to relate the state at different time instants.
In recursive estimation, this dependence appears explicitly in the prediction step, where the state is propagated according to the system dynamics before incorporating new measurements.
Since this propagation requires knowledge of the unknown inputs, the prediction model cannot, in general, be directly evaluated.
This difficulty lies at the heart of state estimation for nonlinear systems driven by unknown inputs.

To overcome this fundamental difficulty, the literature has traditionally followed three distinct research directions.

The first direction (modeling-based and state-augmentation methods) circumvents the problem by introducing additional models for the unknown quantities affecting the dynamics.
When these quantities have known dynamics, such as calibration parameters, sensor biases, or other constant system properties, they can be incorporated into an augmented state vector and estimated jointly with the system state.
This approach is widely used in robotics for sensor calibration and multi-modal state estimation, where observability analysis has been exploited to characterize the identifiability of calibration parameters and inertial quantities [ Mirzaei and Roumeliotis(2008) , Jones and Soatto(2011) ] .
More generally, visual–inertial estimation methods routinely augment the state with additional variables, such as inertial biases and calibration parameters, within filtering frameworks [ Mourikis and Roumeliotis(2007) , Hesch et al.(2014a) , Hesch et al.(2014b) ] .
For unknown inputs whose evolution is not available, however, state augmentation requires introducing an assumed dynamical model.
A representative example is MonoSLAM [ Davison et al.(2007) ] , where unknown camera accelerations are modeled as zero-mean Gaussian process noise in the prediction step of an EKF.
More generally, these approaches replace the original estimation problem with a different one by postulating an evolution model for the unknown inputs.
Their performance therefore ultimately depends on the validity of the adopted assumptions.

The second direction (unknown-input decoupling methods) seeks instead to solve the original problem without modeling the unknown inputs by eliminating their influence from the estimation dynamics.
This idea underlies the extensive literature on Unknown Input Observers (UIOs) and disturbance decoupling.
In the linear setting, the corresponding conditions are typically expressed through algebraic rank conditions and invariant subspace techniques (e.g., [ Hou and Müller(1992) ] ), whereas nonlinear extensions rely on differential-geometric constructions involving distributions, Lie derivatives, and coordinate transformations (e.g., [ Isidori(1990) ] ).
Despite decades of research, available nonlinear results remain limited to specific classes of systems and provide only partial structural conditions rather than a general characterization applicable to arbitrary nonlinear dynamics.

The third direction (unknown-input reconstruction methods) also aims at solving the original problem without introducing models for the unknown inputs.
Rather than eliminating their influence, these approaches attempt to recover the unknown-input information directly from output measurements and their time derivatives, typically through algebraic elimination or recursive differentiation techniques (e.g., [ Fliess et al.(2008) ] ).
In robotics, observability-based approaches have also been exploited to reconstruct unknown motion components directly from sensory measurements. For instance, Belo et al. [ Belo et al.(2010) ] showed that, in planar bearing-only SLAM, three known landmarks are sufficient to reconstruct the robot motion and the unknown inputs without assuming a motion model.
Although successful in several specific applications, the available methods remain problem dependent and no general structural framework is available for nonlinear systems.

These three research directions reflect fundamentally different strategies for overcoming the lack of knowledge of the system dynamics induced by unknown inputs.
The first circumvents the problem through modeling assumptions, whereas the second and the third seek to solve it directly by, respectively, eliminating or reconstructing the unknown-input information without assuming any model for its evolution.

In parallel with these developments, observability has progressively evolved from an analysis tool into a fundamental design principle for state estimation in robotics and computer vision.
Rather than merely characterizing which state components are observable, observability analysis has increasingly guided the design of filtering, smoothing, and optimization-based estimation algorithms by identifying the correct observable and unobservable directions of the system.

Early seminal works in SLAM and cooperative localization established that estimator inconsistency is directly linked to the incorrect handling of the system’s unobservable subspace, showing that preserving the correct observability properties is essential for consistent covariance propagation [ Huang et al.(2008) , Huang et al.(2010) , Mourikis and Roumeliotis(2007) , Hesch et al.(2014a) , Hesch et al.(2014b) ] .
Subsequent work further demonstrated that, in vision-aided inertial navigation, observability analysis must account for the geometry of indistinguishable trajectories, leading to refined notions of sensitivity and model reduction beyond the classical observable/unobservable dichotomy [ Soatto(2013) , Hernandez et al.(2015) ] .
Observability analysis has also enabled closed-form and algebraic solutions in sensor calibration [ Martinelli(2011) ] and visual–inertial sensor fusion [ Martinelli(2012) ] , and has subsequently guided the design of estimation algorithms for increasingly complex sensing systems, including visual–inertial and LiDAR–inertial navigation with heterogeneous geometric features [ Yang and Huang(2019) , Zhang and Huang(2020) ] .
More recently, observability has also been exploited in observability-aware trajectory planning [ Hausman et al.(2017) ] and to analyze the evolution of the unobservable subspace throughout practical visual–inertial estimation pipelines [ Tian et al.(2025) ] .

A common feature of all these developments is that they consider systems driven by known inputs, where the observability properties are entirely determined by the system geometry and the sensing configuration.
Whether observability can provide an equally general structural foundation for state estimation in the presence of unknown inputs has remained an open question.

This paper answers this question affirmatively.
We show that every nonlinear system with unknown inputs admits a structurally determined representation, referred to as the UID-induced normal form , that provides the first general structural solution to the two fundamental problems that have driven unknown-input estimation research for decades: unknown-input decoupling and unknown-input reconstruction.
The proposed result builds upon the first general solution of the nonlinear unknown-input observability problem established in [ Martinelli(2019) , Martinelli(2022) , Martinelli(2026) ] .
The key observation is that the corresponding observability analysis reveals a structural decomposition of the unknown-input information, rather than merely determining the observable component of the state.
In particular, the recursive algorithms developed in [ Martinelli(2022) , Martinelli(2026) ] generate a set of observable quantities, referred to as unknown input identifiers (UIDs).
We show that, once an admissible set of UIDs has been selected, every nonlinear system with unknown inputs admits a uniquely determined UID-induced representation, referred to as the UID-induced normal form .
Although the resulting representation depends on the selected set of UIDs, different admissible choices lead to equivalent UID-induced normal forms related by an invertible change of coordinates in the unknown-input space.
This representation holds for general nonlinear systems, including arbitrary nonlinear dependence on the state, known inputs, and unknown inputs (see Equation ( 2 )).
It is not an observer-dependent construction nor an ad hoc coordinate transformation, but an intrinsic structural property emerging from the observability analysis itself.

The UID-induced normal form decomposes the information carried by the unknown inputs into two complementary components.
The first consists of unknown-input directions that do not influence the evolution of any observable quantity and are therefore structurally decoupled from state estimation.
The second contains all unknown-input information that affects the observable dynamics.
Remarkably, this information is not represented through unknown variables but through observable quantities generated recursively by the observability analysis, and is therefore reconstructible from the system outputs and a finite number of their time derivatives.

This decomposition shows that unknown-input decoupling and unknown-input reconstruction are not independent problems, but two complementary manifestations of the same observability structure.
Unlike previous approaches, which provide decoupling conditions or reconstruction procedures only for restricted classes of nonlinear systems, the UID-induced normal form establishes a general framework in which both objectives emerge simultaneously from the same structural decomposition.
As a consequence, state estimation can be formulated without introducing dynamical models, stochastic assumptions, or independent estimators for the original unknown inputs.

We demonstrate the practical implications of the proposed framework through a Structure-from-Motion (SfM) problem, where the UID-induced normal form enables the design of a recursive estimator for a previously unexplored minimal sensing configuration.
Classical SfM seeks to recover, up to a global scale factor, both the three-dimensional structure of a scene and the motion of a moving monocular camera from image measurements.
Since the instantaneous camera motion has six degrees of freedom, corresponding to three linear and three angular velocity components, SfM naturally leads to estimation problems involving multiple unknown inputs.
In particular, when only a single gyroscope axis is available, five motion components remain unknown and can be treated as unknown inputs.

A fundamental result in multiple-view geometry is that three point features are sufficient for SfM only when the camera rotations are known, or equivalently when the relative orientations between camera poses are available.
In practice, this corresponds to having complete rotational information, for example from a three-axis gyroscope.
This setting is closely related to classical SfM formulations with known camera rotations, where structure reconstruction reduces to triangulation up to an unknown global scale factor [ Hartley and Zisserman(2004) ] .
In the absence of rotational information, classical SfM requires a larger number of visual features.
In particular, at least four point correspondences are typically required [ Hartley and Zisserman(2004) ] , while minimal two-view formulations require five point correspondences [ Nistér(2004) ] and classical epipolar geometry estimation relies on the well-known eight-point algorithm [ Longuet-Higgins(1981) ] .

The nonlinear unknown-input observability analysis developed in [ Martinelli(2019) , Martinelli(2022) , Martinelli(2026) ] reveals a minimal SfM configuration in which the three-dimensional structure and camera motion can be recovered, up to an unknown global scale factor, from only three point features and a single-axis gyroscope.
In this setting, the five remaining motion components are treated as unknown inputs.
To the best of our knowledge, this minimal sensing configuration has not been reported in the computer vision literature 1 1 1 The reason why this configuration does not arise in classical minimal SfM formulations is that nonlinear observability analysis is formulated in continuous time, whereas classical SfM problems are defined from a finite number of discrete images. In the latter setting, finite rotations about a single measured axis generally do not provide sufficient constraints because of the noncommutativity of three-dimensional rotations. By contrast, observability analysis relies on infinitesimal motions, whose first-order evolution is independent of Lie-bracket terms associated with rotational noncommutativity. The identified configuration should therefore be interpreted as the continuous-time counterpart of classical SfM, becoming practically relevant when visual and inertial measurements are acquired at sufficiently high rates relative to the system dynamics. .

In this minimal configuration, a standard recursive estimator cannot directly propagate the state because five components of the camera motion are unknown.
The UID-induced normal form resolves this difficulty by transforming the unknown-input dynamics into a representation where the observable subsystem evolves exclusively in terms of measurable quantities.
This enables the construction of an EKF-based recursive estimator without introducing any model for the unknown motion components.

Finally, we analyze more general sensing configurations involving multiple gyroscope axes as well as the purely vision-based case.
These correspond respectively to four, five, and six unknown motion components.
In particular, when four or more point features are available, the proposed framework can also be applied without gyroscope measurements, consistently with the observability properties predicted by classical SfM theory.
Experimental results on real-world data validate the proposed approach and demonstrate the practical feasibility of the identified minimal Structure-from-Motion configuration.

The contributions of this paper are as follows:

We provide the first general structural solution to the problem of state estimation for nonlinear systems driven by unknown inputs.
Specifically, we show that every nonlinear system with unknown inputs admits a uniquely determined representation, referred to as the UID-induced normal form , obtained from the unknown-input observability structure.
This representation provides a complete decomposition of the information carried by the unknown inputs into two complementary components: a component that is structurally decoupled from the observable dynamics and a component that is entirely represented through observable quantities generated by the observability analysis.
As a consequence, unknown-input decoupling and unknown-input reconstruction are no longer separate problems, but emerge as two aspects of the same decomposition revealed by the observability analysis.

This representation provides a complete decomposition of the information carried by the unknown inputs into two complementary components: a component that is structurally decoupled from the observable dynamics and a component that is entirely represented through observable quantities generated by the observability analysis.
As a consequence, unknown-input decoupling and unknown-input reconstruction are no longer separate problems, but emerge as two aspects of the same decomposition revealed by the observability analysis.

We demonstrate the practical relevance of the proposed framework through a Structure-from-Motion application.
Using the UID-induced normal form, we construct a recursive EKF estimator for a minimal sensing configuration consisting of three point features and a single-axis gyroscope, where the remaining motion components are treated as unknown inputs.
The proposed formulation reveals a previously unexplored minimal SfM configuration and provides a practical estimation framework validated through experiments on real-world data.
Moreover, we analyze additional sensing configurations, including cases with multiple gyroscope axes and the purely vision-based setting, showing the consistency of the proposed framework with classical SfM observability results.

For completeness and accessibility, we provide a concise description of the algebraic observability algorithm developed in [ Martinelli(2026) ] , together with a MATLAB implementation that facilitates the application of the proposed framework [ Unknown Input Observability Toolbox(2026) ] .

This setting corresponds to the estimation problems typically encountered in robotics, where the robot executes a prescribed task and the control actions are available to the estimator.

## 2.2 Active and Passive Unknown-Input Observability

The notion of observability considered throughout this paper is local with respect to the initial state, in accordance with the standard differential-geometric framework for nonlinear systems. Unless otherwise stated, all distinguishability properties are therefore understood with respect to sufficiently small neighborhoods of the initial condition.

For nonlinear systems driven by both known control inputs and unknown inputs, observability admits two complementary interpretations, which we refer to as active and passive observability. These two notions coincide in the absence of control inputs and differ only when the system is driven by inputs that can be assigned by the user.

We first consider the case in which both control inputs and unknown inputs are present. Let u ⁡ ( ⋅ ) u(\cdot) denote the known control inputs and w ⁡ ( ⋅ ) w(\cdot) the unknown inputs. In the active interpretation, two initial states are said to be distinguishable if there exists at least one admissible control input function u ⁡ ( ⋅ ) u(\cdot) such that, for any admissible unknown input trajectory w ⁡ ( ⋅ ) w(\cdot) , the corresponding output trajectories are different. A state is therefore said to be observable if it can be distinguished from all neighboring initial states in this sense.

In contrast, the passive interpretation fixes the control inputs a priori. Observability is then defined with respect to a given control input signal. In this setting, the system is regarded as driven by known time functions, and observability characterizes which components of the state can be reconstructed from the outputs and their time derivatives independently of w w . Consequently, observability in the passive sense depends explicitly on the chosen control input trajectory.

From a practical perspective, particularly in robotics, the passive interpretation is often the most relevant. In many applications, the control inputs are determined by a prescribed task, and the estimation problem is naturally formulated as: given these inputs, what part of the state can be inferred from available measurements?

In the special case where only unknown inputs are present, the two notions coincide. In this situation, there is no freedom of input selection, and observability reduces to an intrinsic property of the input-output map.

In earlier works such as [ Martinelli(2019) , Martinelli(2022) ] , observability was formulated in the active sense. In contrast, [ Martinelli(2026) ] and the present paper adopt the passive viewpoint. In fact, when control inputs are present but fixed, they can be equivalently regarded as known time-dependent terms within the system dynamics, effectively reducing the analysis to the passive setting.

2026-10-06.title: OGAM: Connecting Systematic Testing to Runtime Assurance through Object-Grounded Attention Monitoring for VLA Policies
2026-10-06.authors: Haki Darwish , Xiangyu Yin , Changwen Li , Rongjie Yan , Francisco Gomes de Oliveira Neto , Chih-Hong Cheng
2026-10-06.abstract:
Benchmarks expose vision-language-action (VLA) policies to few canonical
instructions, while exhaustive deployment testing is impossible. We introduce
Object-Grounded Attention Monitoring (OGAM), connecting systematic testing
to runtime assurance: testing reveals attention divergence between successful
and failed executions, and OGAM uses this signal to stop failures beyond
the finite suite. We generate scene-grounded instructions through pairwise
combinations of action templates and objects, and separately test
meaning-preserving paraphrases. All 87 out-of-benchmark cases
reveal problematic behavior across OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, UniVLA, and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} : none completes any of the 24 feasible instructions, while
infeasible or hazardous requests also trigger behavior substitution. At each
action query, we project gradient-weighted visual attention through object
masks and group it by instruction role for comparison across tasks and
policies. Dynamic time warping aligns this course with a successful reference
despite speed differences; conformal calibration on successful episodes sets
the early-stopping threshold for sustained deviations, with a nominal
false-stop target of α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 . Across four policies, OGAM stops
87–100% of failed episodes at median times of 5–12 s within a 20 s
budget, with observed false-stop rates of 3–5%, without failure-labeled
training. Finite testing thus identifies attention patterns that support
online intervention before failure fully unfolds.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] control robots through natural-language instructions, but assessing their
reliability beyond standard benchmarks remains difficult. Benchmarks
contain few canonical instructions close to the policy’s fine-tuning
distribution. Deployment instead exposes the robot to a combinatorial
space of unusual, infeasible, or hazardous requests. Exhaustive testing
is impossible, generated instructions often lack simulator goal predicates,
and failures may become obvious only after many incorrect actions.

We address these problems through a coverage-driven testing and runtime
monitoring framework. We extract action templates and interaction objects
from the scene specification, then use pairwise combinatorial
testing [ 5 ] to select a compact instruction suite.
An LLM labels each instruction-scene pair as feasible, infeasible, or
hazardous, followed by blind human review. Meaning-preserving paraphrases
separately test linguistic robustness. Although positions and orientations
can be added as combinatorial factors, we focus on instruction combinations
and paraphrasing. Pairwise coverage makes exploration systematic, but
no finite suite can exhaust deployment instructions. We therefore use
testing to identify a signal for continued supervision: successful and
failed runs often exhibit different attention courses. This divergence
motivates Object-Grounded Attention Monitoring (OGAM), which asks
whether a new execution still resembles a successful attention pattern.

To obtain a comparable signal, we construct an object-level attention
course at every action query. We extract gradient-weighted attention
over image patches to reflect their influence on the predicted action,
then project it onto segmented objects and group the shares by instruction
role: the named objects, the strongest competing object, the remaining
objects, and the gripper. Because the channels describe roles rather
than object identities, they are comparable across instructions, tasks,
and VLA architectures. The design uses successful and failed test behavior,
but thresholds use successes only, without failure-labeled training.

At deployment, an LLM maps a free-form request to a canonical action
schema and checks its safety and feasibility. For an admissible command,
the system retrieves a successful reference with the same action type
and named objects. Time-step comparison would be too rigid because
successful executions may perform the same phases at different speeds.
We therefore use dynamic time warping (DTW) [ 6 ] to align phases
while preserving their order. Two complementary readouts follow: on-track measures adherence to a successful path, while completion measures whether the complete attention program has appeared.
Conformal prediction [ 7 ] , using leave-one-out calibration,
sets the threshold height from successful episodes’ normalized sustained
deviations, accounting for both readouts and the sustain window with a
nominal 5% false-stop target. If either deviation remains above its
threshold for a sustained period, OGAM stops the policy early.

We evaluate OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, UniVLA, and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on
LIBERO-Goal [ 8 ] . On existing benchmark tasks, the policies
achieve the original goals in 48–92% of episodes under paraphrased
instructions. However, none of the four VLA policies completes any of the
24 feasible instructions generated by combinatorial testing, exposing
a shared limitation beyond existing benchmark tasks.
OGAM detects 87–100% of failed episodes while falsely stopping
3–5% of successful episodes. Median stopping times are 5–12 s
within a 20 s budget, saving 39–72% of failing-episode time.
Ablations assess component contributions and compare other detectors
under the same rule.

Contributions. (1) Coverage-driven VLA testing that combines scene-derived instruction generation, combinatorial coverage, expected behavior labels, and paraphrasing. (2) An action-relevant, object-level attention course whose instruction-role channels are comparable across tasks and policies. (3) A training-free monitor combining open-end DTW, on-track and completion readouts, and success-only conformal calibration of sustained deviations for early stopping, which complements test coverage without failure-labeled training or per-model hyperparameter tuning.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

Testing language-conditioned policies. LIBERO [ 8 ] benchmarks language-conditioned manipulation.
LIBERO-Para [ 9 ] shows that rewording instructions can sharply
reduce success, while [ 10 ] finds that policies may execute commands
contradicting the scene. Combinatorial software testing [ 5 ] covers parameter
interactions with small suites. We use action templates and scene objects as factors to isolate
linguistic variation. Each command receives an expected behavior label,
building on command feasibility, help seeking, and harmful
compliance [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] . Existing VLA testing platforms use language models to mutate scenes or
generate instructions [ 15 , 16 ] , primarily as black-box tests.
Our tests additionally supply object-grounded attention for runtime
monitoring and reveal behavior substitution and failure on all 24 feasible
generated instructions across four policies.

Failure detection for robot policies. Runtime detectors judge rollouts with separate
models [ 17 ] , monitor outputs through
action-chunk consistency [ 18 ] , entropy and observation
out-of-distribution scores [ 19 ] , learned action
probes [ 20 ] , or internal features [ 21 , 22 ] .
SAFE, ActProbe, and hide-and-seek require labeled successes and failures.
Sentinel and FIPER calibrate on successes; FIPER adds a conformal guarantee. Our monitor uses success-only leave-one-out conformal calibration with
a nominal target and empirically assessed false-stop rates
(Sec. III-D ). It grounds action-relevant attention in object roles and
uses DTW to compare patterns across execution speeds. Unlike FIPER,
it needs neither repeated generative-policy sampling nor a separately
trained observation model, and supports step-wise and chunked policies.
The closest attention-head monitor [ 23 ] does not combine
object-role grounding, time-warped alignment, and sustained early stopping.

Attention in VLA models. Attention supports policy modification through safety
filters [ 24 ] , training-free recalibration [ 10 ] , and visual
token pruning [ 25 ] . For post-hoc diagnosis,
VLA-Trace [ 26 ] uses techniques related to attention
rollout [ 27 ] and gradient-weighted relevance [ 28 , 29 ] .
We leave policies unchanged and, given debate over attention’s explanatory
meaning [ 30 ] , validate whether its DTW-aligned course detects
failures early enough to stop them.
Like [ 10 , 25 ] , we connect grounding failures with attention, but
make the signal object-level, temporal, and actionable through a runtime
stop rule.

2026-10-06.title: Controllable Road Marking Generation
2026-10-06.authors: Zhiyu (Joey)Cai, Yufan Zhang , Ruichen Tan , Zengxiang Lei , Satish Ukkusuri
2026-10-06.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.abstract: Lane and road markings provide critical guidance for vehicle navigation and multi-agent coordination, yet authoring them at scale remains a manual workflow that limits quantitative analysis and scenario testing. We introduce Controllable Road Marking Generation , which synthesizes a missing center-region marking layout from a drivable-area mask, optional outer-ring markings, and a textual description. Our benchmark uses deterministic, metadata-derived prompts and three output channels: lane dividers, road dividers, and pedestrian crossings. We develop a conditional bird’s-eye-view (BEV) pipeline that combines (i) a text-conditioned latent rectified-flow DiT trained with a topology-aware auxiliary loss, (ii) Gaussian-blurred training targets that stabilize learning of thin, sparse markings, and (iii) Structured Gaussian Render (SGR), a training-free post-process that recovers crisp divider geometry by extracting polylines, fitting cubic Bézier curves, and re-rendering them as anisotropic super-Gaussian primitives. On 4,597 Argoverse 2 test tiles, our system achieves Buffered F1 of 80.8 and clDice of 50.2, compared with 38.8 and 24.6 for an adapted state-of-the-art mask-refinement baseline. On Waymo dataset, it yields 88.0 Buffered F1 and 66.2 clDice. Component ablations show complementary connectivity gains from topology-aware supervision and SGR. Text-editing experiments reveal that stronger guidance improves edit success but also increases changes to non-target structures. We see this framework as a step toward simulation-ready road-marking variation, automated map completion, and early-stage infrastructure design exploration.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Lane and road markings are the visual syntax through which roads communicate traffic rules. They define lane boundaries, turning permissions, pedestrian priority, and other constraints that human drivers and automated vehicles use to interpret a scene [ 33 , 3 , 4 ] . Their quality affects measurable behavior and safety outcomes [ 5 , 12 ] . For autonomous-driving research, road markings are also a compact machine-readable map layer: they constrain planning, provide simulation context, and determine marking-level edge cases for perception and control.

Road-marking design remains a challenging workflow to scale. It requires civil-engineering expertise, regional guideline awareness, and substantial manual drafting or repair, which limits quantitative analysis and the exploration of design alternatives. Existing computational tools address adjacent parts of this workflow. Procedural generators and driving simulators instantiate road networks from hand-written templates [ 35 , 9 ] ; scenario-generation methods diversify agents and trajectories on fixed maps [ 43 , 37 ] ; and HD-map or lane-marking models reconstruct observed maps from sensor, aerial, or partial-map evidence [ 27 , 22 , 48 , 38 , 41 , 32 ] . This motivates a generative formulation of the road-marking layer itself: given a drivable-area geometry, optional surrounding markings, and a semantic request, what plausible marking layout could occupy the target region?

We formulate this problem as Controllable Road Marking Generation . Given a 100 ​ m × 100 ​ m 100\,\mathrm{m}\times 100\,\mathrm{m} bird’s-eye-view (BEV) tile,
the task is to generate the center-region road-marking mask conditioned
on a drivable-area mask, an optional outer-ring observation of existing
markings, and a textual description. The output contains three channels: lane dividers, road dividers, and pedestrian crossings. In our benchmark,
descriptions are generated deterministically from tile metadata. A useful generator should place markings within feasible road geometry, preserve thin divider topology, remain consistent with surrounding context, and respond measurably to semantic edits.

This setting poses a technical challenge because road markings are sparse, high-frequency, topology-constrained structures. A one- or two-pixel displacement can break a dashed divider or merge nearby parallel dividers, while aggregate pixel losses may still look acceptable because background dominates the raster. Direct training on hard binary targets therefore tends to produce softened, fragmented, or merged markings. We address this with a two-stage blur-then-render strategy: Gaussian-blurred targets provide a stable continuous-valued training field, and Structured Gaussian Render (SGR) recovers sharp lane- and road-divider geometry by extracting divider chains, fitting cubic Bézier curves, and re-rendering them with anisotropic super-Gaussian primitives.

This formulation could support offline map completion, simulation, and benchmark construction. Simulators and safety assessment pipelines gain map variation beyond fixed maps; urban design workflows gain rapid sketch-level alternatives; and controllable BEV map generation lets researchers test downstream systems under marking-level interventions [ 9 , 30 , 43 , 37 ] . We establish an Argoverse 2 benchmark, independently evaluate the same pipeline on Waymo, and report nuScenes results as an additional diagnostic. Our experiments assess structural completion fidelity, component contributions, and the trade-off between text-edit success and preservation of non-target structures.

Our contributions are as follows:

We introduce a conditional BEV synthesis task that generates rasterized road-marking layouts from drivable geometry, optional marking context, and natural language specifications. This offers controllable design of road markings beyond observation and then extraction.

We construct a three-channel Argoverse 2 benchmark and extend evaluation to Waymo open dataset and a diagnostic nuScenes split. Then evaluate both structural imputation and prompt-driven control with multiple metrics such as Buffered F1, clDice, prompt-edit success, false activation, and target channel change.
We develop a latent rectified-flow DiT with topology-aware supervision and a blur-and-render strategy, combining Gaussian-blurred training targets with deterministic curve-based rendering post-processing.

We evaluate against an adapted baseline and a learned CNN deblur ablation, showing strong structural gains and mask-parsed prompt-edit behavior across lane dividers, road dividers, and pedestrian crossings.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Road-Marking and HD-Map Reconstruction

The concept of using pavement markings to regulate traffic has developed over more than a century, originating from the first documented painted centerline applied in 1911 by Edward N. Hines in Wayne County, Michigan [ 31 ] . Since that major safety innovation, road markings have evolved into a highly standardized system that encodes lane boundaries, priority rules, and pedestrian crossing behavior, and their visibility and design affect driving and walking safety [ 33 , 3 , 12 ] . Most computational work, however, treats markings as structures to be recovered from observations [ 50 ] . Ego-view lane marking methods detect or parameterize visible dividers from camera images, including curve-based formulations such as BézierLaneNet [ 10 ] . RoadMark-cGAN [ 7 ] is closer to the road-marking domain, but it maps aerial orthophotos to visible road-marking masks through image-to-image translation, again making the input image the source of geometry. HD-map reconstruction follows the same observation-driven paradigm at map scale: aerial methods extract lane-level street maps [ 13 ] , while online vector-map systems such as VectorMapNet, MapTR, StreamMapNet, and BeMapNet reconstruct BEV map elements from onboard sensor features [ 27 , 22 , 48 , 38 ] . These works motivate our BEV representation and curve-aware decoding, but their objective is perception or map reconstruction under strong sensory evidence. In contrast, Controllable Road Marking Generation synthesizes the unobserved center-region marking layer from drivable geometry, optional surrounding markings, and a text request.

## 2.2 Generative Map and Mask Refinement

Recent generative models for road and map structure remain primarily reconstructive or uncertainty-oriented. General diffusion inpainting methods such as RePaint [ 28 ] show that denoising priors can fill masked regions, but do not encode road-map semantics or user controls. LSR-DM [ 41 ] , our closest baseline, uses diffusion to refine aerial lane-segmentation masks before lane-graph extraction; LOID [ 1 ] similarly uses generative inpainting to complete occluded lane segments from observations. MapDiffusion [ 32 ] samples vectorized HD maps from BEV features to estimate uncertainty, and LaneDiffusion [ 45 ] generates BEV centerline priors to improve centerline graph learning. SegRefiner [ 44 ] formulates coarse-to-fine mask cleanup as a discrete diffusion process. PolyDiffuse [ 6 ] diffuses structured polygonal or polyline parameters. These works apply generative modeling to structured maps and masks, but they either refine an existing prediction, condition on sensor-derived features, or presuppose a parametric output space. Our setting instead asks a raster diffusion model to produce semantically specified road-marking layouts from text and geometric conditions, then decodes thin divider geometry deterministically at inference.

## 2.3 Thin-Structure Priors and Structured Rendering

Road markings are sparse, elongated, and topology-sensitive, so our method is related to thin-structure segmentation and primitive rendering. Topology-aware delineation [ 34 ] , soft skeleton objectives such as clDice [ 42 ] , and recent skeleton-guided losses [ 24 ] address the weak supervision signal of pixel losses on curvilinear structures; we use this lineage to motivate topology-aware training, not as a complete generative solution. At inference, our SGR module follows the line of work that represents curves with differentiable or splatted primitives. Bézier Splatting [ 25 ] and Curve-Aware Gaussian Splatting [ 11 ] bind anisotropic Gaussian primitives to fitted curves, while differentiable vector and Gaussian image representations [ 20 , 29 , 47 , 18 , 49 , 51 ] cover the surrounding rendering context. Our contribution is to adapt this curve-bound Gaussian rendering idea as a deterministic post-process for controllable road-marking diffusion, where the primitive representation can preserve diverse road-line geometries such as dashed dividers, close parallel strokes, and double-yellow centerlines. This design targets the representation bottleneck of thin divider channels: it sharpens the diffusion output without retraining the generator, while keeping road-line instances separable when small raster displacements would otherwise blur, merge, or fragment them.

2026-10-06.abstract:
Post-training quantization has been shown to preserve VLA performance under standard evaluation conditions, but whether it preserves the full-precision model’s robustness and generalization remains underexplored.
In this study, we systematically study the robustness and generalization of post-quantized VLA policies under environmental disturbances.
Empirical results show that quantized policies can become fragile to subtle environmental variations despite retaining comparable in-distribution performance.
We further observe that action discrepancies are concentrated in a small subset of rollout states, while teacher guidance has opposite effects depending on discrepancy: it improves generalization at high-discrepancy states but can degrade it at low-discrepancy states.
These findings reveal that effective post-quantization recovery requires selectively intervening on vulnerable states rather than globally distilling the student.
We therefore propose Policy-Induced Vulnerability-Oriented Tuning ( PIVOT-Q ), a vulnerability-aware On-Policy Distillation (OPD) framework that selectively corrects vulnerable states encountered during quantized-student rollouts using the frozen full-precision policy as a teacher. PIVOT-Q identifies vulnerable states using discounted accumulated discrepancies over a short horizon, applies phase-balanced sparse supervision, and uses a Behavioral Anchor to prevent unnecessary changes.
Experiments under seven LIBERO-Plus environmental variations demonstrate consistent recovery across multiple VLA backbones and quantization methods.
Notably, PIVOT-Q consistently outperforms full-state distillation across all settings while using only 7.4% of its state-level distillation budget. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruanruan-andy/PIVOT-Q .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated strong capabilities in language-guided robotic manipulation, yet their substantial computational and memory footprints remain a major obstacle to efficient deployment ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . Post-training quantization (PTQ) provides a practical way to reduce these costs, and recent methods have shown that VLA policies can be substantially compressed while largely preserving their performance under in-distribution evaluation settings ( Frantar et al., 2023 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . However, preserving performance on the original evaluation does not guarantee comparable generalization under environmental variations. To the best of our knowledge, the effect of quantization on VLA generalization under such variations has not been systematically studied.

In this work, we begin from an empirical study of VLA generalization after post-training quantization. Across multiple VLA backbones and quantization methods, we identify a consistent post-quantization generalization gap: quantized policies degrade substantially more than their full-precision counterparts under subtle disturbances in the environment, such as slight change of lighting, initial object poses, etc.
For example, on LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2026 ) , QuantVLA reduces the success rate of GR00T-N1.5 from 82.1% to 67.0%, whereas it manages to preserve 97% success rate on its in-distribution LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) environments.
This finding raises a key question: what behavioral changes induced by quantization underlie this generalization gap?

To investigate this question, we analyze action discrepancies between quantized and full-precision policies during rollouts under environmental disturbances. Specifically, we roll out the quantized policy and, at each visited state, compare its predicted action with that of its full-precision counterpart.
Across the evaluated VLA models, these discrepancies consistently exhibit an approximately log-normal distribution: while most states incur only minor deviations, large discrepancies are concentrated in a sparse tail.
This highly non-uniform distribution suggests that a small subset of high-discrepancy states may play a disproportionate role in generalization degradation.
More importantly, selectively correcting high-discrepancy states substantially restores generalization, whereas correcting low-discrepancy states surprisingly leads to even worse performance.
Effective post-quantization recovery does not require correcting every state, it requires correcting the right states.

Motivated by these observations, we propose Policy-Induced Vulnerability-Oriented Tuning ( PIVOT-Q ), a vulnerability-aware On-Policy Distillation (OPD) framework that selectively corrects sensitive states encountered by the quantized student under the guidance of the frozen full-precision teacher. Rather than uniformly distilling the student, PIVOT-Q focuses supervision on states where quantization-induced deviations are most consequential, weighting their contribution according to their vulnerability. To prevent targeted recovery from disrupting behaviors already preserved after quantization, we further introduce a Behavioral Anchor that regularizes the student toward the original policy on reference states. Together, these components enable targeted correction where it matters most while preserving behaviors that are already robust to quantization.

We evaluate PIVOT-Q across four model–quantizer settings, including GR00T-N1.5 and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} with W4A8 QuantVLA, GR00T-N1.5 with W4A4 HoloQ-VLA, and OpenVLA-OFT with QVLA.
Entensive experiments are conducted on LIBERO-Plus under seven controlled distribution shifts. PIVOT-Q consistently improves the corresponding quantized policies.
It also outperforms full-state distillation in all four settings while using only 7.4 % 7.4\% of the state-level distillation budget.
These results demonstrate that vulnerability-oriented sparse supervision provides consistent post-quantization recovery across different VLA backbones, quantization schemes, and environmental shifts.

Our contributions include: ♠ \spadesuit We provide a systematic study of environmental generalization after VLA quantization, revealing a consistent generalization gap and a non-uniform distribution of action discrepancies. ♠ \spadesuit We propose PIVOT-Q , a vulnerability-aware post-quantization recovery framework that prioritizes a sparse set of student rollout states, while mitigating unintended policy drift with a Behavioral Anchor. ♠ \spadesuit We demonstrate the effectiveness of PIVOT-Q across multiple VLA backbones and quantization methods. PIVOT-Q consistently outperforms full-state distillation across all our evaluation settings while using only 7.4% of its state-level distillation budget.

# 2 Related Work

VLA Generalization and Quantization. VLA policies span discrete-action systems such as RT-2 ( Zitkovich and others, 2023 ) and OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , as well as continuous generative policies such as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black and others, 2025 ) and GR00T ( Bjorck and others, 2025 ) . Their environmental robustness has been evaluated under controlled variations in viewpoint, lighting, language, background, and other factors ( Fei et al., 2026 ) . In parallel, post-training quantization reduces inference cost through low-precision weights and activations ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Yuan et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) . Recent VLA-specific methods, including QuantVLA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , QVLA ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and HoloQ-VLA ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , further improve action preservation after quantization. However, their evaluations primarily focus on the original task distributions, leaving environmental generalization after VLA quantization largely unexplored.

Policy Distillation and On-Policy Adaptation. Knowledge distillation has been widely used for model compression and policy transfer ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Rusu et al., 2016 ; Fang, 2025 ) . Recent VLA methods extend this paradigm to action generation: VITA-VLA ( Dong et al., 2025 ) and ActDistill ( Ye et al., 2025 ) transfer action knowledge to lightweight policies, while VLA-OPD ( Zhong et al., 2026 ) performs distillation on student-visited states to better match the deployment-time state distribution. Quantization-aware approaches such as QAD ( Xin et al., 2026 ) and SQuaT ( Lee et al., 2026 ) further use high-precision teachers to recover low-precision models. However, existing recovery methods do not explicitly account for how the behavioral importance of quantization errors varies across rollout states, particularly under environmental shifts.

2026-10-06.title: StageVLN: Spatial and Trajectory Auxiliary Guidance for Efficient Vision-Language Navigation
2026-10-06.authors: Anh Dao , Quan-Dung Pham , Le Danh Vinh , The Anh Nguyen , Nguyen Viet Tri Pham , Yiyu Chen , Pham Tuyen Le , Van-Truong Nguyen , Quan Nguyen
2026-10-06.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) policies increasingly benefit from strong semantic priors provided by large vision-language models (VLMs). However, standard action supervision does not explicitly encourage intermediate representations to preserve scene geometry, relative orientation, or global episode progress. Incorporating depth estimators, explicit maps, point clouds, or geometry foundation models at inference can provide such structure but introduces additional computation, memory overhead, and architectural dependence during deployment. We introduce StageVLN, a training framework that shapes navigation representations through privileged spatial and trajectory guidance while preserving the original inference pathway. A frozen geometry foundation model provides multi-level spatial guidance to hierarchical navigator states, while relative-heading and expert-route progress objectives provide complementary trajectory-state supervision. All auxiliary components are used only during training and removed at deployment. On R2R-CE validation-unseen, StageVLN achieves 56.3% SR and 51.4% SPL with a 4B-parameter backbone, without an additional geometry encoder at inference. On RxR-CE, it achieves 54.3% SR without additional navigation training data or a geometry encoder at inference.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) tasks require an agent to process natural language instructions and egocentric visual observations to generate actions that reach a goal through diverse environments. The Room-to-Room (R2R) benchmark [ 1 ] established an instruction-grounded evaluation framework within real scanned scenes. Subsequently, Room-Across-Room (RxR) [ 2 ] extended this paradigm to support greater language and trajectory diversity, while Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) [ 3 ] further transitioned the task from discrete navigation graphs to continuous 3D spaces. In continuous settings, merely recognizing referenced objects is insufficient; navigation policies must also relate the visible structure of the environment to traversable motion, maintain spatial orientation across sequential observations, and continuously localize their position along the requested route.

Recent RGB-only systems [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] increasingly integrate VLMs into navigation policies, leveraging images, video context, memory, or world-action modeling objectives to learn more robust behaviors. However, their strong semantic priors do not guarantee that the hidden representations used for action prediction preserve the geometric and trajectory structure required for navigation in complex environments. A direct solution is to incorporate pretrained geometry models [ 9 , 10 ] into the inference pipeline, or to fuse depth, point clouds, maps, or latent 3D features directly into the navigation policy. While this paradigm has proven effective for spatial understanding in VLMs [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] and has recently been adapted for VLN [ 14 ] , it introduces extra runtime dependencies and increases deployment costs, particularly on real-world robots with constrained hardware. To address this limitation, our central question is: can geometric guidance and trajectory-state supervision improve the navigator while preserving its original deployment pathway? This perspective aligns with the broader principles of learning via auxiliary objectives and intermediate representation distillation [ 15 , 16 ] , while adapting them to the temporal structure of embodied navigation.

We propose StageVLN , a general framework for spatial and trajectory auxiliary guidance . The central idea is to introduce complementary supervision at three levels of navigation structure, progressing from local scene geometry to relational orientation and finally to global trajectory state . During training, a frozen geometry encoder provides multi-level spatial information by supervising intermediate visual states via representation distillation. Additionally, relative heading prediction encourages the learning of a relational orientation structure across observations, while progress prediction provides the agent with a global estimate of its position along the expert trajectory. Crucially, these objectives are applied strictly at training time, allowing the navigator to retain the benefits of geometric and trajectory supervision without requiring auxiliary components at inference. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , our contributions are threefold:

We introduce a training-only hierarchical geometry-teacher mechanism that transfers spatial representations into multiple navigator layers without requiring geometric feature fusion at inference time.

We propose a unified spatial-and-trajectory training formulation that combines multi-level spatial feature distillation with relative-heading and expert-route progress supervision.

We conduct extensive navigation evaluations and comprehensive component analyses , demonstrating improvements in success-related metrics while characterizing localization trade-offs and distinguishing auxiliary-free deployment from measured system efficiency.

1. We introduce a training-only hierarchical geometry-teacher mechanism that transfers spatial representations into multiple navigator layers without requiring geometric feature fusion at inference time.

2. We propose a unified spatial-and-trajectory training formulation that combines multi-level spatial feature distillation with relative-heading and expert-route progress supervision.

3. We conduct extensive navigation evaluations and comprehensive component analyses , demonstrating improvements in success-related metrics while characterizing localization trade-offs and distinguishing auxiliary-free deployment from measured system efficiency.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Vision-Language Models for Navigation

Recent VLN methods adapt pretrained vision-language models to
predict actions from egocentric observations and instructions.
NaVid [ 4 ] uses monocular video for end-to-end
navigation, while Uni-NaVid [ 5 ] extends video-based
action modeling to multiple embodied navigation tasks.
NaVILA [ 6 ] connects language-conditioned navigation
with legged locomotion through intermediate movement commands.
StreamVLN [ 7 ] addresses long observation streams
through slow–fast context modeling, memory compression, and KV-cache
reuse. StageVLN addresses the
complementary problem of supervising the spatial and trajectory
information encoded within an RGB–language policy. It introduces
additional training objectives while preserving the base policy’s
observation interface and action-generation architecture at deployment.

## II-B Geometry-Aware Representations and Spatial Distillation

Geometry foundation models provide representations learned from
geometric prediction tasks. VGGT [ 9 ] , for example,
jointly predicts camera parameters, depth, point maps, and point tracks
from images. JanusVLN [ 14 ] combines visual-semantic and spatial-geometric features with separate
implicit memories for navigation. In spatial question answering,
SpatialStack [ 12 ] integrates geometric features
at multiple language-model layers, demonstrating the value of
hierarchical geometry–language fusion. Both designs compute
geometric features as part of the inference pathway.

An alternative is to transfer teacher representations during training.
FitNets [ 17 ] established intermediate-feature
supervision as a mechanism for knowledge transfer. More directly
related, Spatial Forcing [ 18 ] aligns intermediate
visual embeddings of manipulation VLAs with pretrained geometric
representations while leaving their inference architecture unchanged.

## II-C Auxiliary Supervision for Navigation

Auxiliary objectives have long been used to improve navigation
representations beyond action imitation. The self-monitoring
agent [ 19 ] introduces progress estimation to
support instruction grounding. AuxRN [ 20 ] jointly
learns trajectory retelling, progress estimation, next-orientation
prediction, and cross-modal matching; its progress objective already
uses soft step-fraction targets with cross-entropy supervision. However, these auxiliary objectives do not explicitly transfer spatial representations from a pretrained geometry model into the navigation policy.

StageVLN combines hierarchical geometric feature transfer with two trajectory-state targets. Its heading objective supervises the accumulated relative rotation between historical and current views, rather than the orientation of the next expert action. Its progress target measures the fraction of expert forward actions already completed, excluding turns, and is predicted from a pre-action hidden state without access to the supervised action token. Together with current-view geometric alignment, they provide supervision for scene structure, inter-observation orientation, and route-level state. All auxiliary components, including the geometry teacher, are removed at inference, retaining the original RGB–language navigation pathway.

2026-10-06.title: Scenario-Based Compositional Statistical Model Checking for Safety Specifications
2026-10-06.authors: Abhinav Pomalapally , Arya Raeesi , Kevin Kai-Chun Chang , Beyazit Yalcinkaya , Sanjit A. Seshia
2026-10-06.subjects: Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO); Software Engineering (cs.SE); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-06.comment: . Extended version of paper accepted to The 26th International Conference on Runtime Verification (RV 2026)
2026-10-06.abstract:
In safety-critical domains such as autonomous driving, systems must be evaluated across a large number of environment conditions, often represented as composite scenarios built from primitive scenarios . Existing statistical model checking (SMC) approaches analyze each composite scenario independently, requiring many expensive simulations and resulting in substantial redundant computation when scenarios share common structure. This work introduces a scenario-based compositional SMC framework for safety and co-safety specifications, enabling efficient analysis of composite scenarios. Our approach decomposes scenarios into primitives and specifications into sub-specifications, verifies each primitive independently, and composes the resulting statistical estimates using importance sampling and kernel density estimation.
Our empirical evaluation shows that the proposed framework can accurately answer verification queries for previously unseen composite scenarios while reducing simulation cost through parallelization and trace reuse.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, including autonomous driving, robotics, healthcare, and cyber-physical systems in general.
As these systems become more pervasive, ensuring their safety and reliability remains a fundamental challenge. However, the complexity of modern AI-based systems renders traditional verification techniques largely inapplicable.
Classical formal verification methods typically require an explicit and tractable model of the system under analysis, an assumption that is often violated in contemporary AI systems due to their inherent opacity.

A practical alternative is to treat the system under analysis as a black box and reason about its behavior through simulation-based analysis [ 20 ] .
This approach is particularly prevalent in autonomous driving, where validating a system through exhaustive real-world testing is infeasible.
Instead, developers evaluate autonomous driving systems using a corpus of scenarios , either manually designed by domain experts or extracted from real-world driving data, and assess the system’s performance across these scenarios through repeated simulations.

Statistical model checking (SMC) provides a principled framework for such simulation-based verification [ 16 ] .
SMC is a formal verification technique that determines whether a stochastic system satisfies a given property within a particular scenario by analyzing a finite set of execution traces using statistical methods such as hypothesis testing or confidence interval estimation. By mitigating the state-space explosion associated with exhaustive model checking, SMC enables verification of systems whose complexity would otherwise make formal analysis intractable. Nevertheless, SMC continues to face significant scalability challenges. Obtaining meaningful and high-confidence verification results often requires executing a large number of computationally expensive, long-running simulations. Moreover, SMC must typically be repeated whenever the scenario defining the environment conditions changes, leading to redundant computation.

In this paper, we introduce a scenario-based compositional SMC framework for safety and co-safety specifications, i.e., specifications whose violation or satisfaction can be determined from finite executions. Our approach leverages both scenario and specification decomposition. Given a composite scenario , we first decompose it into a collection of primitive scenarios . Simultaneously, we decompose the target safety specification into a set of sub-specifications. The black-box system is then evaluated independently on each primitive scenario with respect to all relevant sub-specifications. These verification tasks can be executed in parallel and require shorter simulation runs than the original monolithic verification problem. Finally, we compose the resulting statistical estimates to obtain a verification result for the original composite scenario and specification.
Furthermore, our compositional framework enables the reuse of traces generated for primitive scenarios across multiple composite scenarios, thereby avoiding redundant simulation effort and significantly reducing overall verification cost.

We summarize our contributions as follows:
(i) we introduce a novel compositional statistical model checking framework for safety and co-safety specifications;
(ii) we implement the proposed framework and integrate it into VerifAI [ 9 ] , a toolkit for the formal design and analysis of AI-based systems; and
(iii) we conduct an empirical evaluation of the proposed approach and demonstrate its effectiveness in improving verification efficiency while maintaining accuracy.

To address the verification of AI-based systems, simulation-based formal analysis has been widely adopted [ 20 , 9 , 1 ] . Specifically, statistical model checking (SMC) [ 18 , 19 , 25 , 26 , 16 , 6 , 27 , 2 ] mitigates the state-space explosion of exact formal methods by evaluating a finite set of execution traces, providing probabilistic guarantees bounded by statistical confidence intervals. Seshia et al. [ 20 ] advocate for a compositional approach to scale up verification of AI systems. Classic compositional verification (e.g., [ 5 , 7 , 4 , 14 , 22 ] ) is not directly applicable to simulation-based verification of AI systems. Existing compositional approaches for AI systems vary in their axes of decomposition; while some frameworks decompose internal system architectures or neural network layers [ 21 , 10 ] , our work focuses on the spatial and temporal decomposition of environmental scenarios and specifications.

Dreossi et al. [ 8 ] has proposed a framework combining compositional analysis with simulation-based verification, but it focuses strictly on component-level decomposition and targets active falsification rather than SMC.
The closest prior work to the proposed framework introduces a compositional approach to SMC [ 24 ] .
However, it is strictly restricted to Markovian, i.e., memoryless, specifications. Our new framework extends compositional SMC to non-Markovian safety and co-safety specifications, overcoming a fundamental limitation.

Another related line of work explores scenario decomposition, where environments and specifications are divided into primitive segments either spatially [ 23 , 13 ] or temporally [ 3 ] . However, these differ significantly in their verification methods: they rely on explicit white-box access [ 13 ] , offline probabilistic abstractions [ 23 ] , or remain confined to falsification [ 3 ] . In contrast, our framework achieves black-box compositional SMC for safety and co-safety properties.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Motivating Example

Consider evaluating an autonomous vehicle across various driving scenarios ( Figure 1 ). A common approach to constructing such scenarios is to use a set of simpler primitive scenarios as building blocks for defining more complex composite scenarios. Suppose that our primitive scenarios consist of a straight road segment ( S ), an intersection ( X ), a roundabout ( O ), and a curved road segment ( C ). Scenario description languages such as Scenic [ 11 , 12 ] support this style of programmatic scenario construction through several composition operators. Sequential composition specifies the exact order in which scenarios are encountered (e.g., S → \rightarrow X ). Choice composition randomly selects one scenario from a set of alternatives (e.g., choose ​ ( S , X , O , C ) \texttt{choose}(\texttt{S},\texttt{X},\texttt{O},\texttt{C}) ). Finally, shuffle composition randomly permutes the order of a collection of scenarios (e.g., shuffle ​ ( S , X , O , C ) \texttt{shuffle}(\texttt{S},\texttt{X},\texttt{O},\texttt{C}) ).

Our goal is to efficiently test the autonomous vehicle in composite scenarios against safety and co-safety specifications, i.e., temporal specifications whose satisfaction or violation can be determined from a finite execution.
A monolithic application of SMC treats each composite scenario independently. For every new scenario and specification pair, SMC executes a large number of simulations and analyzes the resulting traces. As the complexity of composite scenarios grows, this process quickly becomes computationally expensive, requiring repeated execution of long-running simulations that often share substantial structure.

Our approach avoids this redundancy by shifting the computational effort to the primitive scenarios. Instead of directly evaluating every composite scenario, we execute the system independently within each primitive scenario and store the resulting traces. We then evaluate these traces against all sub-specifications induced by the target specification, corresponding to the sub-automata of its monitor automaton. Given a composite scenario, we compose the previously computed results to estimate the probability of satisfying the target specification.

A key challenge is that the distribution of behaviors observed in an isolated primitive scenario may differ from the distribution induced when that same primitive appears as part of a larger composite scenario. To account for this distributional mismatch, we employ importance sampling [ 15 ] together with kernel density estimation (KDE). Intuitively, traces generated from primitive scenarios are weighted according to their likelihood under the target composite scenario. This enables us to estimate results for previously unseen composite scenarios without actually running the system in those scenarios. Consequently, our approach generates computationally efficient and highly accurate estimates for SMC queries.

2026-10-06.title: Deep Prior Learning for Embodied Perception
2026-10-06.authors: Yimou Wu , Jiaxin Guo , Yun-hui Liu , Zheng Li
2026-10-06.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Embodied systems need geometric perception that exploits available
observations beyond images alone. Recent feed-forward 3D models
incorporate geometric priors, including camera poses, intrinsics, and
depth. However, handling noisy poses, preserving accurate priors, and
recovering physical scale require more than simply accepting these
inputs. We introduce Vision-Prior Geometry Grounded Transformer (VPGGT), a VGGT-based framework that extends OmniVGGT for prior-aware
embodied perception. We formulate sensor-motivated pose corruptions from ground-truth trajectories for training and introduce a parameter-free prior residual connection (PRC) to mitigate prior dilution , where predictions are less accurate than their supplied pose priors. Our noise formulation targets camera poses; supplied intrinsics and depth receive no additional corruption. We further introduce Metric Global Attention , which conditions a global
scale token on available pose and depth scales and predicts a shared
metric scaling factor for the geometric outputs. Experiments across four datasets show that PRC improves translation-direction accuracy and joint pose AUC over a matched training baseline when camera priors are provided for all views, under both exact and corrupted poses. These results support explicit prior access during refinement as a useful addition to feature-level conditioning.
2026-10-06.introduction:
We study feed-forward 3D perception from a set of images and optional
camera or depth priors (Fig. 1 ). DUSt3R ( Wang et al., 2024b ) and VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) have advanced image-based reconstruction by predicting multiple geometric attributes within a shared network. Their image-only inputs, however, do not exploit the camera estimates and depth observations often available to embodied systems. Pow3R ( Jang et al., 2025 ) , OmniVGGT ( Peng et al., 2026 ) , and MapAnything ( Keetha et al., 2025 ) extend feed-forward reconstruction to incorporate such geometric information alongside images, providing a common model for different input configurations.

Several challenges remain when these models are used with observations
from embodied platforms. First, camera priors are estimates rather than ground truth, and their errors can accumulate over a trajectory or vary independently between frames. Although previous work has examined incorrect camera inputs, training and evaluation under structured pose errors require further study. Second, a model may produce camera estimates that are less accurate than the supplied priors, even when those priors are exact. We refer to this shortfall as prior dilution (Sec. 3.2 ). Third, embodied systems require geometry in physical units, while normalizing geometric inputs removes their original scale. MapAnything ( Keetha et al., 2025 ) addresses metric reconstruction with a factored representation. Here, we study scale recovery while retaining the camera and dense-prediction heads of a pretrained VGGT-derived model.

In this paper, we introduce Vision-Prior Geometry Grounded
Transformer (VPGGT), a feed-forward model that combines images with
optional camera and depth priors. First, we formulate sensor-motivated pose corruptions from existing ground-truth trajectories for training
(Sec. 5 ). 1 1 1 We corrupt camera poses only. Supplied intrinsics and depth receive no additional corruption in this work. Second, we introduce a parameter-free Prior Residual Connection (PRC) that places scale-aligned priors in the camera head’s refinement state to mitigate prior dilution (Sec. 4.2 ). Third, Metric Global Attention conditions a global token on available pose and depth scales and predicts a shared metric factor (Sec. 4.3 ). The model retains the image-only setting when geometric priors are absent and a common interface for further platform-specific training.

Comprehensive experiments and systematic architecture ablations examine the effects of prior quality and availability on camera and
depth prediction. Under matched training configurations, PRC improves
translation-direction accuracy and joint pose AUC on all four datasets
when camera priors cover every view, for both exact and corrupted
poses. The improvements are largest on TUM RGB-D and C3VD, while results at partial coverage reveal remaining limitations. We study these effects separately from metric-scale recovery to distinguish better camera refinement from better estimation of physical scale.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Traditional reconstruction systems combine correspondence estimation,
camera recovery, and sparse or dense mapping through task-specific
modules ( Schonberger & Frahm, 2016 ; Furukawa et al., 2010 ; Campos et al., 2021 ) . Learned features, matchers, depth networks, and differentiable
optimization improve these components ( DeTone et al., 2018 ; Sarlin et al., 2020 ; Sun et al., 2021 ; Teed & Deng, 2021 ; Yao et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2024a ) . VGGSfM ( Wang et al., 2024a ) , for example, integrates learned
correspondences and camera estimation with differentiable bundle
adjustment. In contrast, DUSt3R ( Wang et al., 2024b ) predicts dense pointmaps from image pairs, while VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) jointly predicts camera parameters and dense geometry from multiple views. These models reduce the need for separately designed reconstruction
stages, but their image-only interfaces do not use external camera
or depth observations.

Embodied platforms may combine cameras with IMUs, wheel encoders,
LiDAR, and depth sensors ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Frey et al., 2026 ; Mao & Gu, 2025 ; Cullen, 2023 ) . Visual–inertial and multi-sensor SLAM fuse their measurements through state estimation and geometric optimization ( Qin et al., 2018 ; Campos et al., 2021 ) . Their observation models, uncertainty estimates, and calibration describe how individual sensors constrain the estimated motion. Prior-conditioned feed-forward models operate at a different level, taking geometric estimates rather than raw sensor measurements. Pow3R ( Jang et al., 2025 ) , OmniVGGT ( Peng et al., 2026 ) , and MapAnything ( Keetha et al., 2025 ) incorporate camera and depth information into dense reconstruction, with MapAnything also predicting metric scale. Pow3R examines responses to incorrect camera parameters, and MapAnything identifies noise and uncertainty in geometric inputs as a remaining limitation. Our work studies structured pose corruption, preservation of informative camera priors during refinement, and scale conditioning within a pretrained multi-view model.
