2026-10-06.abstract: Visual token pruning is an effective way to accelerate vision-language models and is especially useful for vision-language-action (VLA) inference, where many visual tokens must be processed before predicting robot actions. Existing pruning methods usually estimate which tokens can be pruned based on attention scores or feature diversity, retaining tokens that are either highly attended or visually different from others. However, most of them use fixed pruning schedules, such as pruning once at a preset layer or pruning at uniformly spaced layers. Such schedules can be risky for VLA models, because the model may not know which visual regions matter for the action in early layers. Tokens that look unimportant at first may become useful after the model combines visual observations with the language instruction. In this work, we propose SAPrune , a training-free visual token pruning framework for efficient VLA inference. Instead of pruning at fixed layers, SAPrune uses a small calibration set to observe how action-to-visual attention changes across layers, and chooses pruning layers only after the attention pattern becomes more reliable. At each selected layer, SAPrune applies a dual-path pruning rule: one path protects strongly attended visual tokens from pruning, while the other prevents useful surrounding context from being discarded. Experiments on LIBERO, SIMPLER, and real-world robotic tasks show that SAPrune prunes 87.5% of visual tokens and achieves up to 1.718 × \times inference speedup while maintaining competitive task success rates.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently shown strong potential for embodied decision making by mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Despite their effectiveness, VLA inference remains computationally expensive because a large number of visual tokens must be propagated through deep Transformer layers [ 5 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Visual token pruning is therefore a natural direction for reducing latency and computation, as shown in prior studies on efficient Vision Transformers and large vision-language models [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] .

Although recent studies have shown substantial redundancy in VLA inference, most pruning-oriented acceleration methods still decide token removal from local importance cues, visual saliency, feature-space diversity, or their fixed combinations [ 13 , 15 , 14 , 16 , 18 , 17 , 8 , 9 ] . This treats pruning mainly as a static token-selection problem. Such a formulation is insufficient for action generation, where visual evidence does not remain fixed across depth: it gradually emerges, redistributes, and stabilizes as the model forms an action decision. Moreover, visual distinctiveness alone does not imply decision usefulness, since tokens that are geometrically diverse may still be irrelevant to the current action. These limitations motivate us to reconsider VLA pruning from two questions: when pruning becomes reliable, and what action-relevant evidence should be preserved.

To understand when visual tokens can be safely pruned during VLA inference, we analyze the attention from action-related states to visual tokens across Transformer layers. Figure 1 shows that early layers attend to a broad set of visual tokens, while middle and deep layers gradually concentrate on tokens related to the target action. Figure 2(a) further quantifies this trend using the top- k k attention mass: the mass increases quickly from shallow to middle layers and then changes more slowly. This suggests that early layers have not yet clearly determined which visual tokens are useful for the action. Therefore, pruning too early may remove tokens that become important later, motivating us to delay pruning until the attention pattern becomes more stable. We further compare different pruning criteria in Fig. 2(b) . Attention-only selection tends to concentrate on dominant regions and may miss supportive context, whereas feature-space diversity-based selection may retain tokens that are visually distinctive but weakly related to the current action. These observations suggest that attention-only selection, feature-space diversity-based selection, and their fixed combination are all insufficient for aggressive VLA pruning.

Based on these principles, we propose SAPrune , a training-free visual token pruning framework for efficient VLA inference. SAPrune first selects pruning layers from rollout-level action-attention dynamics, and then applies a dual-path retention mechanism at each selected layer. The attention-core path preserves directly action-relevant tokens, while the functional-diversity path selects complementary tokens using query-conditioned functional signatures. Experiments on LIBERO [ 19 ] , SIMPLER [ 20 ] , and real-world robotic tasks show that SAPrune retains only 32 visual tokens, prunes 87.5% of the original visual tokens, and achieves up to 1.718 × \times speedup while maintaining competitive task success rates.

## 2.1 Related Works

Efficient inference for VLA models. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models extend large vision-language models by introducing an action modality, enabling robots to predict executable actions from visual observations and language instructions. Representative generalist robot policies include RT-1 [ 1 ] , RT-2 [ 2 ] , Open X-Embodiment / RT-X [ 3 ] , Octo [ 4 ] , OpenVLA [ 5 ] , π 0 \pi_{0} [ 6 ] . Although effective for general-purpose manipulation, these models repeatedly process dense visual tokens through deep Transformer layers, making inference costly for real-time robot deployment [ 7 , 8 , 21 , 22 , 9 ] .

Visual token pruning for VLMs. Visual token pruning reduces visual redundancy by retaining a compact subset of informative visual tokens. Early efficient Vision Transformer methods, such as DynamicViT [ 10 ] , EViT [ 11 ] , and ToMe [ 12 ] , reduce computation through token sparsification or merging. For large vision-language models, attention-based methods such as FastV [ 13 ] , SparseVLM [ 15 ] , FoPru [ 23 ] , HiPrune [ 24 ] , LVPruning [ 16 ] , IVTP [ 14 ] , and ZSPA-Prune [ 25 ] rank tokens by prefill attention, text-to-vision attention, or prompt-conditioned relevance. Other methods preserve diversity or global representativeness [ 17 , 18 , 26 , 27 ] , while calibration or layer-adaptive methods determine pruning layers, ratios, or progressive schedules from calibration statistics or cross-layer information flow [ 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 ] . However, these methods are mainly designed for VLM understanding and do not explicitly model action-dependent visual evidence in VLA inference.

Training-free acceleration for VLA models. Training-free VLA acceleration mainly follows temporal reuse, adaptive computation, and pruning-based acceleration. VLA-Cache [ 7 ] reuses visual features across adjacent timesteps, while VLA-ADP [ 22 ] dynamically reduces computation during manipulation. EfficientVLA [ 8 ] , SP-VLA [ 21 ] , SpecPrune-VLA [ 33 ] , and VLA-Pruner [ 9 ] reduce visual-token computation during VLA inference. These methods reveal substantial redundancy in VLA models, but often rely on fixed pruning locations, semantic relevance, temporal reuse, or additional acceleration modules. They leave underexplored how to choose pruning layers and preserve action-relevant evidence under aggressive token reduction.

2026-10-06.title: A Safe Action Is Not Enough: Feasible-Future Decoding for Vision-Language-Action Policies
2026-10-06.authors: Tu Nguyen , Matthieu Zimmer , Vu Anh Vu , Ziyi Wang , Jannik Hammel Nielsen , Xuebing Zhou , Haitham Bou Ammar
2026-10-06.abstract: A safe action is not necessarily a viable one. Under a frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policy, an action can be likely and locally admissible yet leave no policy-supported route to safe task completion. We call this the feasibility–likelihood gap: likelihood ranks the current action, whereas feasibility depends on the futures that remain after it.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-language-action ( VLA ) policies map visual observations and natural-language instructions into robot actions, drawing on broad semantic and motor priors learned from large-scale vision–language pretraining and robot demonstrations. Systems such as RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) , PaLM-E ( Driess et al., 2023 ) , OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , Octo ( Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ) , and π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) illustrate this breadth. Given an observation o t o_{t} , instruction x x , and interaction history h t h_{t} , the policy defines

An action can look safe in the moment and still steer the agent into a dead end. A candidate may be likely and pass every local safety check, yet leave no route to safe task completion under the frozen policy. We call this the feasibility–likelihood gap. Figure 1 makes the practical motivation concrete: reducing cost must be assessed alongside the ability to continue and complete the task. Deployment-time constrained decoding provides a natural way to address this gap by revising action selection as execution unfolds, without changing the underlying policy ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Kapoor et al., 2025 ; Hsu et al., 2023 ) .

Looking beyond the next action is especially difficult in robotics. In autoregressive language generation, a fixed prefix and candidate token determine the next symbolic prefix exactly, so future continuations branch from a fully determined prefix ( Ji et al., 2025 ) . Robot actions instead induce physical transitions,

We derive the target from the joint policy–environment trajectory law. Weighting trajectories by reward and cost, restricting them to safe task completion, and marginalizing over the future suffix yields an exact next-block marginal. This marginal combines the action prior and local reward–cost terms with the weighted mass of safe, successful continuations—the feasible-future mass .

This quantity is policy-relative by construction. A zero mass does not mean that safe completion is physically impossible; another controller may still succeed. Rather, it means that the frozen policy–environment process places no probability on safe completion after that action. The mass therefore captures two complementary aspects of the future: whether safe completion remains within the policy’s support and, when it does, how much weighted continuation mass is preserved. We formalize these as support and magnitude .

Computing this quantity exactly is generally impractical at decision time, so we turn to a selective finite-candidate approximation. Its score combines policy likelihood, local robustness, and a bounded continuation term, while a gate decides whether the sampled action is worth revisiting at all. Only then does the decoder rerank a small candidate set. This saves computation, but a dead end accepted by the gate never reaches the reranker. We therefore analyze intervention loss alongside errors in candidate availability, support handling, and approximate scoring. The resulting conditions show when the best retained viable candidate can still be recovered without reconstructing the exact mass.

We instantiate the rollout-free approximation as a training-free reranker driven by the current observation and interaction history. Across six Safety-CHORES settings ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , the generic VICS-G configuration consistently lowers observed safety cost while retaining near-policy task completion and episode length. This combination is the central practical benefit: a frozen VLA can act more safely while sustaining progress toward its task. Evaluating safety jointly with completion and episode length ( Fan et al., 2026 ) makes this benefit visible and distinguishes it from cost reductions that accompany early termination.

The same perspective extends naturally to imperfect execution and explicit lookahead. On safety-aligned Fetch, execution feedback yields a favorable observed safety–completion trade-off under perturbed actions, while a matched ablation supports preservation of task success within the preset tolerance. The theory invites us to test rollouts, letting sampled futures shape the next action. Even in simulation, however, those futures are costly to generate and only as reliable as the dynamics model behind them. We therefore study VICS-R , a modest rollout augmentation of VICS-G guided by safe-completion estimates under a limited simulation budget. On Fetch, it improves observed safe success and further reduces cost ( Section 4.4 ). These studies connect a rollout-free deployment-time decoder to richer sources of execution and continuation evidence.

Our contributions are threefold:

An exact next-block target for policy-relative safe completion. We derive the next-action marginal of a prior-preserving trajectory law restricted to safe completion. Feasible-future mass connects the current action to the safe continuations it leaves open: support captures whether such continuations remain, while magnitude captures their weighted mass.

A selective approximation theory with explicit failure interfaces. We separate intervention, coverage, support, and ranking errors, derive a recovery margin for the best retained viable action, and show when finite continuation rollouts preserve the ideal winner.

A practical route to safer execution with frozen policies. VICS-G combines selective, training-free intervention with consistent observed cost reductions and near-policy task completion across six Safety-CHORES settings. Ablations of execution feedback and rollout augmentation test the value of evidence from realized actions and sampled continuations.

2026-10-06.title: Direction-Conditioned Policies for Online Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-06.authors: S K Swaminathan , Damiya Gondha , Theyanesh Eswaramoorthy Rajahkrishnan , Aritra Hazra
2026-10-06.abstract: Contrastive Reinforcement Learning (CRL) learns representations that estimate goal reachability, yet its policy remains conditioned on raw goals and therefore does not directly exploit the geometry encoded by its critic. We introduce Direction-Conditioned Policies (DCP), a method built around a small modification to CRL: DCP selects previously visited states as waypoints during online training and conditions the policy on their direction and distance in representation space. At deployment, DCP applies the same interface directly to the final goal, requiring neither waypoint selection nor planning. Across nine navigation and manipulation tasks, DCP attains higher final success rates than CRL on seven tasks and spends more time near the goal on seven. Controlled maze experiments further show that DCP captures shortest-path geometry more accurately and that the supplied direction causally influences the actor’s behavior. We identify waypoint coverage and ranking as limits to exploration, and show that learned candidate generation improves goal reaching in two controlled mazes.
2026-10-06.introduction:
When learning to achieve goals through online interaction, an agent has to discover useful behavior before it has much successful experience to draw on. Contrastive reinforcement learning (CRL; Eysenbach et al., 2022 ) makes use of the states the agent reaches along the way. Its critic learns to distinguish achieved future goals from other goals, and the policy learns to choose actions that receive a higher critic score. This gives the agent a learning signal even when reaching the requested goal is rare. Recent work has made this approach increasingly effective through stabilization techniques, accelerated simulation, deeper networks, and action-sequence conditioning ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Bortkiewicz et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Korniak et al., 2026 ) .

However, the policy still receives the goal in raw coordinates. Consider a goal on the opposite side of a maze wall: the coordinate difference points through the wall, even though reaching the goal requires moving away from it first. The critic’s representation is learned from trajectories and can capture this route structure. This raises a simple question: can we use that representation to express the goal to the policy? Doing so would give the policy direct access to a geometric relation that the critic already learns. The difficulty is that the representation itself is being learned online. Early in training, a distant goal may lie outside the agent’s experience, making its learned direction unreliable. We therefore consider two parts of the problem together: how to express a target to the policy, and which targets to pursue while collecting experience. Previously visited states are natural candidate waypoints ( Eysenbach et al., 2019 ; Ecoffet et al., 2021 ) . Scoring these candidates against the final goal yields intermediate targets whose representations have been trained on collected experience.

We propose Direction-Conditioned Policies (DCP), a method built around a small change to the CRL actor. We encode the current achieved goal and the target using the critic’s goal encoder, then supply the normalized displacement and its magnitude to the actor, along with the full physical state. During collection, the target is a scored visited waypoint. During hindsight updates, it is a future achieved state. At deployment, it is the requested final goal. In this way, the same policy input supports all three stages, and the waypoint pool and scorer can be removed at deployment. Figure 1 illustrates these inputs.

Direction-conditioned policies and embedding differences have been used in skill learning and offline goal reaching ( Park et al., 2024b ; Park et al., 2024a ; Devin et al., 2019 ) . We investigate their use within online CRL, where the policy and representation develop together through the agent’s own experience. Our contributions are:

An online CRL method that uses the critic’s goal representation to condition the actor on direction and distance, with deployment requiring only the actor and goal encoder.

A five-seed comparison across nine tasks, with higher final mean success and time near goal than CRL on seven tasks each.

Controlled experiments that test route geometry, the actor’s use of direction, and waypoint selection, including improvements from learned generation in restrictive mazes.

Section 2 discusses related work, Section 3 describes DCP, Section 4 presents the experiments, and Section 5 concludes. The appendices provide implementation details and additional analyses.

1. An online CRL method that uses the critic’s goal representation to condition the actor on direction and distance, with deployment requiring only the actor and goal encoder.

2. A five-seed comparison across nine tasks, with higher final mean success and time near goal than CRL on seven tasks each.

3. Controlled experiments that test route geometry, the actor’s use of direction, and waypoint selection, including improvements from learned generation in restrictive mazes.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

CRL derives a goal-reaching objective from contrastive prediction of future states ( Eysenbach et al., 2022 ) . JaxGCRL makes large online comparisons practical through accelerated simulation ( Bortkiewicz et al., 2025 ) . Depth scaling ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and action-sequence conditioning ( Korniak et al., 2026 ) demonstrate that changes to architecture or critic inputs can substantially alter the capabilities learned with this objective. Single-goal CRL also demonstrates directed exploration before the first successful trial, without intermediate subgoals ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . We ask how much of the learned representation can be reused by the policy itself. DCP supplies relative goal-encoder features to the actor while retaining the baseline network depth and single-action policy.

HILP learns Hilbert representations and directional policies from offline data ( Park et al., 2024a ) ; METRA learns metric-aware representations and skills through online unsupervised exploration ( Park et al., 2024b ) . Plan arithmetic uses compositional differences and sums in learned plan representations ( Devin et al., 2019 ) . Dual Goal Representations encode goals through temporal distances from other states and improve offline goal reaching ( Park et al., 2026 ) . Relative targets also appear in FeUdal Networks, whose worker follows latent directions from a manager ( Vezhnevets et al., 2017 ) , HIRO’s state-offset subgoals ( Nachum et al., 2018 ) , LSD’s latent skill directions ( Park et al., 2022 ) , and HIQL’s latent subgoal actions ( Park et al., 2023 ) ; learned temporal distances ( Hartikainen et al., 2020 ; Myers et al., 2024 ) and quasimetrics ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Myers et al., 2025b ) supply the underlying geometry. We bring learned goal relations to an online contrastive actor–critic, retaining its actor objective and learning the representation from the experience the direction-conditioned policy collects.

Contrastive representations can support inference over intermediate states under specific modeling assumptions ( Eysenbach et al., 2024 ) . Planning invariance examines when an on-path waypoint and a final goal induce the same action ( Myers et al., 2025a ) . It arises for DCP, which trains on achieved targets but executes toward the final goal, and for flat policies bootstrapped from subgoal-conditioned ones ( Zhou and Kao, 2025 ) . We test whether on-path substitution preserves the action and how reliably the scorer selects such waypoints.

2026-10-06.title: Beyond LLM Serving: Characterizing Vision-Language-Action Workloads for Embodied AI System Design
2026-10-06.authors: Seonghun Jung , Sieun Moon , Jiyoung Jeong , Jimin Lee , Jaehyuk Huh
2026-10-06.comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 32nd ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS '27).
2026-10-06.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate multimodal observations into low-level robot
actions. During robot operation, each control period sets an inference deadline, and overruns
leave the robot acting on stale observations, reducing task success. Meeting this deadline
motivates on-device or nearby edge execution, where a single robot requires batch-1 inference
outside the design point of LLM serving systems. Although VLA architectures combine familiar
vision-language, autoregressive, and diffusion-style components, their runtime behavior in
this batch-1 control setting remains uncharacterized. We characterize four representative VLA
models on an edge GPU server and two onboard SoCs, using single-inference profiling and
43,200 closed-loop episodes. Action tensor dimensionality determines whether a stage is
memory- or compute-bound, platform balance can shift that bottleneck, and GPU frequency
scaling yields a platform-dependent energy–latency sweet spot. In closed-loop operation,
overlapping inference with action execution creates an accuracy–speed–energy tradeoff, and
no configuration is Pareto-dominant across deployment SLOs. These results guide joint design
of VLA model architectures, hardware, and runtime policies.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Embodied action generation models, often referred to as vision-language-action (VLA) models ( NVIDIA et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025b ; Shukor et al., 2025 ; Cheang et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Bu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Kim et al., 2026 ) , translate multimodal observations into low-level robot control signals for manipulation tasks. Real-world manipulation requires smooth and continuous motion, so models designed for real robots increasingly produce not a single next command but an action chunk , a fixed-length sequence of future commands that together form a short trajectory segment ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Jing et al., 2026 ) . To generate such chunks, these models typically combine a large perception backbone with a specialized action-generation head , a neural network that converts the backbone’s latent representation into the action chunk. Recent architectures generate action chunks through iterative denoising over compact action tensors ( NVIDIA et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025b ; Shukor et al., 2025 ; Cheang et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Bu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2025 ) , single-pass parallel decoding ( Kim et al., 2025a ; Song et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ) , or unified diffusion over spatiotemporal video latents ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . These action-generation choices produce different latency and resource profiles that shape deployment decisions.

During deployment, these models operate in a closed loop: the robot continuously senses the environment, invokes the
model, executes the resulting commands, and updates its next input based on the physical
outcome ( Sapkota et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . The control period, roughly 33 ms for
contact-rich manipulation, therefore acts as a recurring deadline rather than merely a per-request
latency target: inference that falls behind it leaves the robot acting on stale observations,
and task success degrades. Meeting this deadline favors on-device hardware or nearby
consumer-grade edge servers because remote serving adds round-trip delay to the same latency
budget. In the single-robot setting studied here, inference therefore runs at batch size one.

LLM serving research has produced a mature toolbox, including continuous batching, paged
KV caches, and prefill-decode disaggregation, designed around concurrent autoregressive
requests and token-level execution ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2026a ) . These
assumptions hold only partially in this setting: batch-1 serving provides no request concurrency, the
action-chunk models we evaluate produce their chunks non-autoregressively, and the dominant
stage varies with the architecture rather than with an autoregressive phase. Standard LLM
serving optimizations therefore apply selectively (Section 6 ). VLA model
families draw on familiar vision-language, autoregressive, and diffusion-style components, but
how these components interact under batch-1 closed-loop serving has not been characterized.

To fill this gap, we conduct a system-level workload characterization of VLA serving. We study four representative models, namely GR00T N1.6 ( NVIDIA et al., 2025b ) , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black et al., 2025a ) , OpenVLA-OFT ( Kim et al., 2025a ) , and Cosmos-Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , that span three action-generation paradigms: iterative denoising, parallel decoding, and video generation. We evaluate these models on three platforms that span over an order of magnitude in power budget: RTX 4090, Jetson Thor, and Jetson AGX Orin ( NVIDIA Corporation, 2026a ) . Our methodology combines four measurement techniques that target different levels of the system stack: stage-level latency decomposition, roofline-based bottleneck attribution, DVFS ( Pillai and Shin, 2001 ; Tian et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) sensitivity analysis, and closed-loop deployment on MuJoCo ( Todorov et al., 2012 ) with LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) benchmarks, totaling 43,200 closed-loop episodes.

Our single-inference analysis shows that action tensor dimensions separate memory-bound
stages from compute-bound ones. Memory-bound stages tolerate lower GPU clocks.
Reducing memory bandwidth, however, raises latency and energy on both SoCs.
The same bottleneck differences shape throughput per joule in deployment.
Overlapping inference with action execution ( Shukor et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2025c ) creates an accuracy–speed–energy tradeoff.
Accuracy degradation depends on model architecture, relative speedup is stable across
platforms, and energy scaling depends on platform characteristics.

To our knowledge, this is the first system-level workload characterization to connect
stage-level latency and roofline analysis with cross-platform DVFS sensitivity and closed-loop
deployment. Our contributions are as follows:

Cross-model characterization. We show that VLA serving has no uniform bottleneck profile: torch.compile speedups differ by over 5× between action-head-dominated and backbone-dominated models.
This implies that compiler and kernel-level optimizations must be applied selectively per architecture rather than uniformly.

Microarchitectural analysis. We show that the memory- versus compute-bound split is determined by action tensor dimensionality. Denoising-head GEMMs fall below the 163.9 FLOP/B ridge point, whereas large-sequence backbone and video-generation DiT GEMMs exceed it.
This provides a basis for accelerator bandwidth-to-compute provisioning in VLA-targeted hardware.

Platform and energy insights. We show that GPU frequency scaling yields an energy sweet spot whose benefit depends on platform balance, as the same sweep saves 24–32% energy on Orin but only 1–4% on Thor, while memory-bandwidth throttling provides no energy benefit on either SoC. We further show that, when evaluated in isolation, assigning each inference phase its own GPU frequency can reduce both latency and energy when the phases exhibit different frequency sensitivities. However, in end-to-end execution, the overhead of switching GPU frequencies between phases can offset these gains.

Closed-loop tradeoff analysis. We quantify a three-way tradeoff in which accuracy degrades by up to 56 percentage points, speed improves by up to 3.9 × \times , and energy scales by up to 5.1 × \times under increasing overlap, with no Pareto-dominant configuration across SLOs. This establishes that runtime systems must support SLO-aware operating-point selection rather than static configurations.

These observations motivate bottleneck-aware co-design across model architecture, hardware platform, and runtime policy for embodied AI system design.

# 2. Background & Motivation

## 2.1. Embodied Action Generation Models

Embodied action generation models produce low-level robot actions from visual observations and language instructions ( Sapkota et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) .
Recent architectures first encode the multimodal observation and the instruction into an internal representation, and then generate actions from it. They differ in the architecture that builds this representation and in the action-generation interface.

In the VLM-based models, the perception backbone typically combines a vision encoder (e.g., ViT ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) , SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) ) with a language model (e.g., Llama 2 ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) , PaliGemma ( Beyer et al., 2024 ) ) to produce contextual embeddings that capture both spatial and semantic information.
This stage performs a single forward pass through billions of parameters, inheriting the computational profile of large vision-language models.

The action-generation interface takes one of two forms: a sequence of discretized action tokens generated autoregressively, or an action chunk , a fixed-length
sequence of future robot commands produced jointly in one inference ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Jing et al., 2026 ) .

Autoregressive action-token interface. Token-based VLAs such as RT-2 ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ) and vanilla OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2025b ) represent a robot action as a sequence of discretized action tokens generated sequentially by
the backbone’s language-model decoder. In the OpenVLA formulation we profile, the target
robot’s action space has D D dimensions, and each dimension maps to one token. One action
therefore requires D D sequential token-generation steps: one prefill step followed by D − 1 D-1 cached-decode passes.

This sequential decode path is difficult to amortize under high-rate control. On the
RTX 4090, its six cached-decode passes take 140.90 ms in our 7-dimensional setting. This is
3.2 × \times the LLM prefill latency and accounts for 67% of the 209.56 ms inference
(Table 1 ). Cached decode therefore dominates the latency of autoregressive
action generation.

The same decode path exhibits the familiar LLM resource split. Prefill is mostly
compute-bound, whereas cached decode is entirely memory-bound
(Section 4.2 ). However, the fixed decode horizon leaves little opportunity
for KV-cache reuse. The cache grows by only D − 1 D-1 positions within an action and is discarded
when the action completes.

Because this interface emits one D D -token action per inference, producing K K future
actions repeats those D D sequential steps K K times. OpenVLA-OFT ( Kim et al., 2025a ) instead
emits an entire K K -action chunk in one pass. Its reported action throughput on LIBERO is
roughly 26 × \times that of autoregressive OpenVLA. This contrast motivates the action-chunk
interface, which amortizes one inference over K K future commands. Action-chunk models use
this interface but generate each chunk through one of three representative paradigms.

Iterative denoising heads. This paradigm generates the action chunk through a multi-step
denoising process that invokes the same neural network N N times
(typically 4–10) per action prediction.
Representative models refine a random initial tensor into the action trajectory,
using flow-matching objectives ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) (GR00T ( NVIDIA et al., 2025b ) , π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2025b ) , SmolVLA ( Shukor et al., 2025 ) ,
GR-3 ( Cheang et al., 2025 ) , GraspVLA ( Deng et al., 2025 ) ) or denoising
diffusion ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) (RoboDual ( Bu et al., 2024 ) ,
CogACT ( Li et al., 2024 ) , DiffusionVLA ( Wen et al., 2025 ) ).
Regardless of the training objective, the computational signature is
shared: the state being denoised is a compact action trajectory tensor
of shape [ B , action_horizon , action_dim ] [\text{B},\;\text{action\_horizon},\;\text{action\_dim}] (batch size 1 in single-robot deployment), so each denoising step runs
the network over this short, low-dimensional sequence.

Parallel decoding heads. This paradigm generates the entire action chunk in a single forward pass using parallel token prediction or regression.
Representative models include OpenVLA-OFT ( Kim et al., 2025a ) (L1 regression MLP), PD-VLA ( Song et al., 2025 ) , and CogVLA ( Li et al., 2025b ) .

Unified video generation. This paradigm embeds robot actions in the latent sequence of a pretrained video diffusion
model, treating action generation as a joint video–action prediction problem within a shared
latent space ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025a ) . Unlike the VLM-based models above,
Cosmos-Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) attaches no separate action head to a perception backbone:
it adapts Cosmos-Predict2 ( NVIDIA et al., 2025a ) into a unified policy in which one generative model predicts
actions together with future visual observations.

Cosmos-Policy reuses the spatiotemporal VAE tokenizer of its pretrained video backbone to
encode image sequences into compact latent frames. It then injects robot proprioception,
action chunks, and future observations into dedicated slots of this latent sequence. A DiT
(Diffusion Transformer, a Transformer operating on latent image
patches) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) denoises the target slots conditioned on the
current-observation frames ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . Actions are then read directly from the
denoised action slots rather than decoded from generated RGB frames. The resulting tensors are far larger than the compact action trajectories of the
action-only denoising heads above: 9 temporal frames at 28 × 28 28{\times}28 spatial resolution
yield 9 × 28 × 28 = 7,056 9{\times}28{\times}28=7{,}056 token positions of 16 channels each.

For cross-model profiling, we separate VAE encoding from DiT denoising and group the
latter under the action-head stage, because the action-generation computation occurs within
the DiT. This is an operational decomposition for stage-level comparison: the DiT remains
part of Cosmos-Policy’s unified video-diffusion architecture and also processes the other
latent slots.

Figure 1 illustrates the four action-chunk models
evaluated in closed loop: GR00T N1.6 (flow-matching DiT), π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black et al., 2025a ) (flow-matching Gemma Expert), OpenVLA-OFT (L1 regression MLP),
and Cosmos-Policy (video-generation DiT).
These four models span the three action-generation paradigms.

## 2.2. Closed-Loop Policy Serving

When these policies drive a robot in closed loop, each inference must complete within a fixed control period, typically 33 ms or less for the 30 Hz rates required by contact-rich manipulation tasks.
Current policy models are far from meeting this budget ( Kim et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026 ) : in our measurements, inference takes 117–396 ms on an edge-server GPU (RTX 4090) and 304–2603 ms on an edge SoC (Jetson AGX Orin), yielding effective control frequencies of only 2.5–8.5 Hz and 0.4–3.3 Hz, respectively.

In a synchronous execution scheme, the control loop captures a sensor observation, invokes the policy model, and dispatches the resulting action chunk to the actuator before the next cycle begins ( Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ; NVIDIA et al., 2025b ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ) .
This design maximizes observation freshness but, when inference overruns the control period, forces the pipeline to stall, repeating stale actions and introducing visible discontinuities in the robot’s motion trajectory.
Unlike offline evaluation, where a simulator simply pauses during inference, real-world deployment offers no mechanism to stop time, so every millisecond of excess latency directly degrades control quality ( Black et al., 2025c ) .

To bridge this gap, deployed systems employ asynchronous overlap ( Shukor et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2025c ) : the system issues the next inference request while the robot is still executing actions from the current chunk, hiding inference latency behind action execution (Figure 2 ).

However, asynchronous overlap introduces a tradeoff: because
inference is initiated before the current chunk completes, the
observation used for the next prediction ages while the robot
continues executing ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . We refer to this lag as observation staleness , the interval between observation
capture and the execution of actions derived from it:

## 2.3. Motivation

The workload described in Section 2.1 and Section 2.2 diverges from the assumptions that underlie LLM serving infrastructure in three ways. Each divergence motivates a distinct dimension of system-level characterization.

M1. Action-generation heterogeneity requires stage-level bottleneck analysis. LLM serving analyses decompose cost along the autoregressive phases of prefill and decode. That decomposition carries over to the action-token interface, which uses the same prefill–decode mechanism. The action-chunk models described in Section 2.1 , however, use heterogeneous iterative-denoising, parallel-decoding, and video-generation stages, which vary further within each paradigm through tensor shape and GEMM dimension choices. Characterizing them requires a stage-level decomposition organized around action-generation design.

M2. Latency and task accuracy are coupled, not orthogonal. In LLM serving, latency is a service-level property and response accuracy is a model property, and the two can be optimized independently. The accuracy–staleness tradeoff described in Section 2.2 removes this separation: per-inference latency affects the feasible overlap, which changes observation staleness and task success. Understanding this coupling requires measurement at the deployment level, not the per-inference level alone.

M3. Deployment frequently spans heterogeneous platforms. LLM serving has primarily targeted datacenter-class GPUs. Embodied action generation often runs on edge SoCs in addition to server GPUs, because autonomous operation may occur where network connectivity is unreliable or round-trip latency exceeds the control period. These platforms differ in compute, bandwidth, and power, so a characterization on a single tier does not readily transfer to others.

2026-10-06.title: GeoBridge-VLA: Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-06.authors: Hyun Song , Kangmin Kim , Loren Jinsoo Um , Minhui Han , Jaehyeok Park , Taewan Cho , Andrew Jaeyong Choi
2026-10-06.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models encode semantic information from
vision-language pretraining, but manipulation also requires precise spatial
reasoning. We present GeoBridge-VLA, a two-stage method for learning
geometric features from a pretrained VLA’s frozen visual encoder and using
them for action prediction. Stage I trains a feature bridge and geometry
decoder with depth supervision. Stage II freezes these modules and trains
a gated residual interface together with the action-side projections and
action expert. The residual augments the existing visual tokens without
adding a second image encoder or increasing the token count. Deployment
requires RGB, robot state, and language, but no depth observations.
Under matched evaluation conditions, GeoBridge-VLA achieves 70.9% success
on LIBERO, compared with 60.0% for SmolVLA. Disabling the residual in the
same trained checkpoint reduces success from 70.90% to 69.85%, with
mixed effects across suites. On a physical ROBOTIS OMY robot, GeoBridge-VLA
succeeds in 148 of 200 trials (74.0%) across four tasks, compared with
108 of 200 (54.0%) for SmolVLA.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models extend pretrained vision-language
representations to language-conditioned robotic manipulation [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Their pretrained representations provide
strong semantic priors for recognizing objects, interpreting instructions,
and generalizing across diverse scenes. Robotic manipulation, however, also
depends on geometric properties such as depth, relative position, object
extent, and local spatial relationships. Representations optimized primarily
for semantic alignment do not necessarily preserve this information with the
precision required for physical interaction.

Recent work has addressed this limitation through explicit depth or 3D
observations, external spatial representations, calibrated camera geometry,
and auxiliary geometric supervision. SpatialVLA introduces 3D-aware spatial
representations [ 5 ] , DepthVLA incorporates a pretrained depth
module [ 6 ] , FALCON injects features from a spatial foundation
model [ 7 ] , G 3 VLA introduces calibrated camera geometry into the
visual-token stream [ 8 ] , and GIFT shapes intermediate policy
representations through control-oriented structural supervision [ 9 ] . We investigate whether the frozen visual hierarchy of a VLA
can provide depth-supervised features for action prediction without a
separate image encoder, additional geometry tokens, or depth observations
at deployment.

We refer to this adaptation as geometry retrofit . GeoBridge-VLA
first learns a geometric readout from frozen intermediate visual features,
then transfers the resulting features to the action policy. Here, geometry
refers to the representation learned through depth supervision. In Stage I,
a feature bridge maps selected encoder features to a geometry decoder.
We train the bridge and decoder using simulator ground-truth depth for
LIBERO and teacher-generated pseudo-depth for OMY. In Stage II, we freeze
both modules and train a gated residual interface that adds decoder
features to the native visual tokens during action learning. The two
paths share the VLA’s visual encoder, preserving the token count and
existing conditioning pathway.

We evaluate GeoBridge-VLA across all four LIBERO manipulation suites and on a
physical ROBOTIS OMY platform. The complete adaptation pipeline improves
manipulation success over the SmolVLA baseline in simulation and physical
robot evaluation, while a same-checkpoint residual intervention tests the
trained policy’s sensitivity to the learned geometry-to-action pathway.
Detailed results are reported in Sec. V .

The main contributions of this work are:

We formulate geometry integration in pretrained VLAs as a geometry retrofit problem and introduce a shared-hierarchy pathway
that learns a depth-supervised geometric readout directly from frozen
intermediate VLA features without adding a separate image encoder to the
deployed policy.

We propose a two-stage geometry acquisition and geometry-to-action
transfer strategy in which depth supervision first adapts the feature
bridge and geometry decoder, after which they are frozen and a gated
residual interface transfers their representation into the native
visual-token space for action learning.

We evaluate the resulting policy across all four LIBERO suites and
on a physical ROBOTIS OMY robot under depth-free deployment, and further
analyze shared-encoder depth prediction and same-checkpoint residual
intervention to examine geometry acquisition and the trained policy’s
sensitivity to geometry-to-action transfer.

# II Related Work

## II-A Monocular Depth Estimation

Transformer-based monocular depth estimation has progressed from DPT and
ZoeDepth to large-scale foundation models such as Depth Anything V2 and
Depth Anything 3 [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . CLIP-based
approaches further demonstrate that depth-related information can be
recovered from frozen vision–language representations: DepthCLIP exploits
patch–text correlations, while SPACE-CLIP directly decodes semantic and
structural features from a frozen CLIP vision encoder [ 14 , 15 ] . These works primarily target depth prediction;
GeoBridge-VLA instead uses depth supervision to adapt geometric information
for closed-loop action generation.

## II-B Vision-Language-Action Models

VLA models extend pretrained vision–language representations to robotic
control. RT-2 and OpenVLA demonstrate large-scale vision–language-to-action
transfer [ 1 , 2 ] , while π 0 \pi_{0} uses flow matching for continuous
action generation [ 3 ] . Recent systems also emphasize efficient policy
design and deployment, including OpenVLA-OFT, TinyVLA, and SmolVLA [ 16 , 17 , 4 ] . We use SmolVLA as the policy backbone
throughout our action-policy experiments.

## II-C Geometry-Aware Vision-Language-Action Models

Recent VLA systems incorporate geometric or spatial structure through several
mechanisms. Explicit 3D approaches use depth, point clouds, or dedicated
spatial representations: 3D-VLA couples 3D perception and action generation [ 18 ] , FP3 and PointVLA operate on point-cloud features [ 19 , 20 ] , and 3D-CAVLA combines depth perception with
task-oriented spatial reasoning [ 21 ] . Other methods improve spatial
reasoning without requiring metric depth at deployment. IVRA reuses affinity
information from the native visual encoder at inference [ 22 ] , while
RetoVLA repurposes Register Tokens for spatial reasoning [ 23 ] .
FALCON injects features from an embodied spatial model [ 7 ] , and
GIFT imposes geometry-aware structural supervision on intermediate policy
representations [ 9 ] .

Other approaches incorporate geometric structure into VLA policies through
different mechanisms. SpatialVLA predicts depth and back-projects image
features into egocentric 3D structure [ 5 ] . G 3 VLA injects
calibrated camera geometry through geometric encodings and cross-view fusion [ 8 ] , while GP3 and AugVLA-3D introduce dedicated spatial encoders
or VGGT-derived 3D features before action prediction [ 24 , 25 ] .
QDepth-VLA and DepthVLA incorporate dedicated depth experts or pretrained
depth transformers [ 26 , 6 ] , whereas Evo-Depth extracts
implicit depth features from RGB and progressively aligns depth-aware
modulation with action learning [ 27 ] . Concurrent GaussVLA lifts
semantic and depth features into compact 3D Gaussian tokens for geometric
reasoning [ 28 ] .

GeoBridge-VLA instead learns a depth-supervised geometric readout directly
from intermediate features of the frozen native VLA visual encoder and
transfers the resulting representation through a gated residual interface.
This separates geometry acquisition from geometry-to-action transfer while
requiring neither a second image encoder nor additional visual tokens at
deployment.

2026-10-06.title: LightVLN: Efficient Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation with Compact Memory and History-Guided Local Aggregation
2026-10-06.authors: Yiming Zhao , Tianshun Li , Jingle He , Ruonan Chai , Xinhu Zheng
2026-10-06.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN) enables unmanned aerial
vehicles to execute long-horizon natural-language instructions from
visual observations in complex three-dimensional environments.
However, recent aerial VLN models often rely on large-scale
vision-language backbones and dense visual histories, imposing
substantial computation and memory costs that hinder onboard deployment.
We propose LightVLN, a lightweight history-aware aerial VLN framework
that combines a compact 0.5B language backbone with compact representations
of both historical and current observations.
LightVLN compresses each
historical frame into a single token using visual features already computed by the policy.
It further introduces history-
and instruction-conditioned local aggregation to reduce the current
observation from 256 to 32 visual tokens while preserving
navigation-relevant spatial information. With up to 16 historical frames,
the policy uses at most 48 observation-derived tokens.
On the public OpenFly dataset, LightVLN achieves 50.93% Test-Seen
and 36.14% Test-Unseen success rates (SR), outperforming the evaluated
7B language-backbone baselines on most reported metrics.
It also achieves 25.83% SR on AerialVLN-S Val-Seen.
In a reconstructed unseen campus, we deploy LightVLN on a DJI M350 RTK
with an external Jetson Orin NX 16 GB for closed-loop onboard-compute
real-to-sim hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) evaluation, achieving 14.61 Hz
model inference and 11.13 Hz end-to-end decision updates.
These results demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of LightVLN for aerial navigation.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Aerial vision-and-language navigation (VLN) enables unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) to follow long-horizon natural-language instructions from visual observations in complex three-dimensional environments [ 1 ] . It requires the UAV to connect instructions with visual observations and predict a sequence of actions toward the navigation goal. The AerialVLN benchmark established a foundation for this task through simulated aerial environments, annotated navigation trajectories, and a cross-modal alignment baseline [ 1 ] . Subsequent platforms expanded the realism and scale of aerial navigation data, supporting the development of more advanced navigation models [ 2 , 3 ] . Recent methods further improve spatial reasoning and long-horizon decision making through explicit spatial representations, semantic subgoals, grounded targets, and learned multimodal policies [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] .

Aerial navigation models have increasingly adopted larger language backbones and richer visual histories. Video-based navigation models [ 9 , 10 ] and aerial foundation-model policies [ 3 , 8 , 11 ] use large pretrained multimodal backbones for visual grounding and action prediction. Meanwhile, long-horizon aerial navigation has motivated retaining information across observation sequences through selected-frame histories [ 3 , 8 ] , structured spatiotemporal memory [ 12 , 13 ] , and relevance-aware or causal history integration [ 14 , 11 ] . These mechanisms provide access to historical visual information for subsequent navigation decisions. However, the use of larger language backbones and richer visual histories also brings substantial computation and memory demands at inference [ 9 , 15 ] .

Deploying aerial navigation models on resource-constrained UAV platforms remains challenging [ 15 ] . In particular, large backbones and extensive visual context increase computation and memory demands at inference. Recent deployment-oriented systems improve efficiency through optimized inference pipelines, lightweight action generation, shared perception, and fast–slow or asynchronous execution [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . Complementary to these deployment-oriented techniques, we target a compact language backbone and compact representations of both historical and current observations. Lightweight aerial VLN therefore also requires reducing the intrinsic resource demands of the navigation policy while preserving its navigation capability.

Designing such a policy poses two challenges: constructing low-cost historical memory that remains useful for action prediction, and compressing the current observation while preserving navigation-relevant spatial information.
First, for historical memory, existing aerial VLN methods typically control temporal redundancy and computation through keyframe selection or compact history representations [ 3 , 8 , 13 ] . These strategies reduce memory cost by limiting the number of retained observations or compressing their representations.
NativeMEM [ 18 ] addresses this trade-off by compressing each historical frame into a single action-supervised token, enabling substantially longer and denser visual histories. It constructs memory through a separately optimized visual-encoding path initialized from the policy’s vision encoder.
Second, for current-view compression, existing methods reduce visual redundancy through learned-query bottlenecks, regional aggregation, or language-conditioned token selection [ 19 , 20 , 9 , 21 ] . These methods effectively compress the current observation but do not exploit navigation history. DreamFly [ 11 ] incorporates historical context to enhance current-view representations through causal memory, but does not target lightweight visual token compression or low-cost memory construction.
These observations motivate an integrated lightweight design that combines low-cost historical memory with compact current-view representations.

To address these challenges, we propose LightVLN, a lightweight history-aware aerial VLN framework that combines a compact 0.5B language backbone with compact representations of both historical and current observations (Fig. ).
Each historical frame is compressed into a single token using visual features already extracted by the policy.
For the current observation, history- and instruction-conditioned local aggregation reduces 256 visual tokens to 32 while preserving navigation-relevant spatial information.
With up to 16 historical frames, the resulting visual context contains at most 48 observation-derived tokens.
We evaluate LightVLN on the public OpenFly splits [ 3 ] and AerialVLN-S [ 1 ] and conduct extensive same-backbone ablations on OpenFly. We further reconstruct a campus environment and construct a 500-episode unseen evaluation set, where LightVLN is deployed on a DJI M350 RTK with an external Jetson Orin NX 16 GB for closed-loop onboard-compute real-to-sim HIL evaluation.

The main contributions are:

We propose LightVLN, a lightweight history-aware aerial VLN
framework that combines a compact 0.5B language backbone with
low-cost historical memory and compact current-view representations.
With at most 48 observation-derived tokens, LightVLN provides a compact visual interface for aerial VLN with a substantially smaller language backbone.

We develop two complementary lightweight designs:
single-token historical compression that reuses visual features
already extracted by the policy, and history- and
instruction-conditioned local aggregation that reduces the current
observation from 256 to 32 visual tokens while preserving spatial
information relevant to navigation.

We evaluate LightVLN on OpenFly and AerialVLN-S and conduct
extensive same-backbone ablations on OpenFly. LightVLN achieves 50.93% Test-Seen and
36.14% Test-Unseen SR on public OpenFly, outperforming the
evaluated 7B baselines on most reported OpenFly metrics, and achieves 25.83% SR on
AerialVLN-S Val-Seen. We further conduct closed-loop onboard-compute
real-to-sim HIL evaluation in a reconstructed unseen campus, where LightVLN
reaches 14.61 Hz model inference and 11.13 Hz end-to-end decision
updates on Jetson Orin NX 16 GB.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation

Existing aerial VLN methods broadly include structured reasoning and
learned multimodal navigation approaches.
Structured methods introduce explicit spatial or semantic representations
to support navigation reasoning. STMR [ 4 ] constructs
spatial representations for language-guided reasoning, while
CityNavAgent [ 5 ] performs hierarchical semantic
planning with global memory. LookasideVLN [ 6 ] incorporates direction-aware reasoning, and Fly0 [ 7 ] uses persistent metric anchors for zero-shot navigation.
Learned multimodal approaches directly predict navigation decisions from
visual observations and language instructions.
AerialVLN [ 1 ] establishes an early cross-modal
navigation baseline, while OpenFly-Agent [ 3 ] scales
aerial VLN with pretrained multimodal models and historical observations.
AeroAct [ 8 ] further integrates spatial, temporal, and
embodied reasoning within a unified navigation model.

## II-B Efficient Aerial VLN and Onboard Deployment

Existing work improves the efficiency of aerial VLN through lightweight
inference, decoupled decision making, and computation reuse.
VLA-AN [ 15 ] combines lightweight action generation with
an optimized inference pipeline for onboard deployment.
FSD-VLN [ 16 ] adopts a fast–slow dual-system architecture,
separating high-level semantic reasoning from frequent navigation updates.
OnFly [ 17 ] shares perception features and reuses memory
across decision steps to reduce redundant computation and support
real-time onboard execution.

## II-C Compact Historical and Current Visual Representations

Existing work reduces visual redundancy from two complementary aspects:
historical representation and current-view compression.
For historical representation, OpenFly-Agent [ 3 ] and AeroAct [ 8 ] retain selected historical observations
to provide temporal context while controlling the number of stored views.
HETT [ 12 ] organizes historical information through
history-enhanced spatial representations, while LongFly [ 13 ] integrates compact spatiotemporal context for long-horizon navigation.
S2D [ 14 ] further emphasizes relevance-aware historical
information for decision making.
Beyond aerial VLN, NativeMEM [ 18 ] compresses each
historical frame into a single action-supervised token, enabling much
denser temporal memory. It constructs memory through a separately
optimized visual-encoding path initialized from the policy’s vision
encoder. Our memory directly reuses the policy’s existing patch features.

For current-view compression, BLIP-2 [ 19 ] uses a learned
query bottleneck to extract a compact set of visual features, while
TokenPacker [ 20 ] aggregates local visual tokens to
preserve spatial structure with fewer tokens.
NaVid [ 9 ] introduces language-conditioned visual
compression for navigation, and EvoComp [ 21 ] selects
task-relevant visual tokens through semantic guidance.
AeroAct [ 8 ] also employs regional visual aggregation in
aerial navigation.
These methods mainly focus on compressing the current observation itself,
whereas navigation history is usually handled as a separate source of
context.
DreamFly [ 11 ] instead uses causal memory to enhance
current-view representations with historical information.
We use compact historical memory to condition fixed-region aggregation
of the current view, while constructing that memory from visual
features already computed by the policy.

2026-10-06.title: Orchestrating Level-$K$ Policies Against Unknown Opponents in Partially-Observable Dynamic Games
2026-10-06.authors: Addison Kalanther , Sanika Bharvirkar , Daniel Bostwick , Chinmay Maheshwari , Shankar Sastry
2026-10-06.abstract: Level- K K reasoning generates a hierarchy of policies specialized to opponents with different reasoning levels. When an opponent’s level is unknown, a common deployment rule estimates that level and selects the corresponding response. In a dynamic, partially-observed game, this selection is repeated, with each choice shaping subsequent states and observations. The response associated with the most likely opponent level need not maximize expected return from the current history. We formulate this deployment problem as dynamic orchestration of a fixed, pretrained policy library in a partially observable Markov game. We compare classification-based orchestrators (CBOs) trained using offline data or on-policy data aggregation with a reinforcement-learning-based orchestrator (RLBO) trained to maximize expected discounted return. In pursuit–evasion experiments, on-policy training improves classification and return, yet RLBO achieves higher return than the on-policy and offline CBOs. Given a pretrained library, RLBO also reaches performance comparable to a policy trained directly over the pursuers’ action space with fewer training timesteps. These findings support treating a hierarchy of level- K K policies as a resource for orchestration, not a prescription for deployment.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Autonomous agents in adversarial settings need to reason about how their opponents make decisions. This raises a basic question: how should an agent model an opponent’s reasoning? One approach is bounded rationality, which recognizes that decision makers operate with limited information, computational resources, and time [ 1 , 2 ] . Level- k k reasoning represents strategic reasoning through a hierarchy of responses to less sophisticated opponents [ 3 , 4 ] . Together with the related cognitive hierarchy model [ 5 ] , it offers a structured alternative to assuming equilibrium play and can explain behavior observed in strategic decision experiments.

These models have attracted attention in control and robotics, including autonomous driving, pursuit-evasion, and vehicle coordination [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . In the standard level- k k construction, a level- 0 0 policy specifies baseline behavior, and a level- ( k + 1 ) (k+1) policy is computed as a best response to a level- k k opponent. For dynamic games, these responses specify behavior over an evolving interaction. Computing them offline produces a library of policies specialized to different opponent reasoning levels. This hierarchy specifies how responses are constructed; deciding how to use them during deployment is a separate problem.

This distinction becomes important when the opponent’s reasoning level is unknown. A policy optimized against one level may perform poorly against another. In a dynamic game, an agent must act while learning about its opponent, and its actions change the physical state and can affect subsequent observations. Deployment therefore involves repeated policy choices during a partially-observed interaction.

One approach maintains a belief over the opponent’s reasoning level using interaction history and plans future actions under that belief. Li et al. combine Bayesian inference with predictive control [ 7 ] , while Tian et al. use a partially-observable decision formulation and belief-space search to reason about latent human states [ 8 ] . Although precomputed opponent models and value functions can support such methods, online belief propagation and multi-step action optimization can remain computationally demanding as the state space and planning horizon grow. Selecting from a pretrained response library offers a complementary way to reuse offline computation during deployment.

Another approach estimates the opponent’s level online and deploys the corresponding response. Guan et al. use maximum likelihood estimation to adapt the agent’s reasoning level during pursuit-evasion [ 10 ] . Ho et al. study a related Bayesian rule that samples an opponent level from a belief distribution and responds one level higher [ 12 ] . The pairing of an opponent level with its response thus becomes a rule for deployment. Ho et al. also note that a best response to a distribution over opponent levels can fall outside the level- k k hierarchy.

Using this pairing during deployment raises two issues. First, when several opponent levels remain possible, the response paired with the most likely level need not yield the highest expected return. Classification accuracy also ignores how costly different estimation errors are. Second, switching policies mid-trajectory can produce states and histories unlike those encountered during an expert’s training. An approximately-learned best response may then be a poor choice, even when the opponent’s level is correctly identified.

We study this deployment problem as the orchestration of a fixed library of bounded-rational policies. Related ideas include reward-trained expert gating for opponent modeling [ 13 ] and Bayesian policy reuse [ 14 ] . Our focus is an orchestrator that can select and switch among separately trained level- k k responses at each time step of a partially observed encounter. We seek to use the hierarchy as a resource for decision making, allowing policy selection to be learned without enforcing the original level-to-response pairing. This leads to the following question:

How should an agent select and switch among pretrained level- k k responses as a partially-observable game evolves, to maximize its expected return against an opponent of unknown reasoning level?

We formulate this problem in a partially-observable Markov decision process and compare classification-based orchestration with reward-maximizing orchestration using the same fixed response library. The classification methods use either offline data or on-policy, DAgger-style data aggregation [ 15 ] ; the reward-based method learns policy selection through reinforcement learning.

In our pursuit-evasion experiments, reward-based orchestration achieves higher expected return than both classification-based methods. Training the classifier on histories generated by its own policy choices improves identification and return, but does not close the performance gap. Although the learned responses are specialized to different evaders, reward-based orchestration frequently selects a response other than the one paired with the evader’s true level. Given a pretrained response library, orchestration also reaches performance comparable to a policy trained directly over the pursuers’ action space, with fewer additional training timesteps. These results support treating the level- k k hierarchy as a resource for orchestration, not a prescription for deployment.

2026-10-06.title: Probabilistic Pedestrian Forecasts from a Handheld Phone: World-Frame Heat Maps, Visual-Inertial Height Drift, and Evaluation without Ground Truth
2026-10-06.authors: Danial Safaei
2026-10-06.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.abstract:
A pedestrian with a phone could be shown where nearby people will be in the
next few seconds, if the forecast stays on the ground while the phone moves,
is calibrated, and needs only a monocular camera and visual-inertial odometry
(VIO). We build and evaluate such a system. People are detected, lifted onto
the floor by ray–plane intersection, tracked in a gravity-aligned metric
frame, and forecast as per-step probability maps by a small U-Net trained with
a negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss on bird’s-eye (SDD) and first-person
(EgoTraj-Bench) trajectories. On handheld ADVIO recordings, vertical VIO drift
and the user’s own changes of level silently rescale monocular ground
positions (by 87 % within 90 s on one clip; on another, all
tracks are lost for the last 31 % of the clip); keeping the
camera’s height above the floor constant under a low-pass-filtered altitude
avoids this, though it lags on escalators. On the SDD and EgoTraj-Bench test
splits, the final forecaster lowers the NLL at 4.8 s by 1.51
and 1.37 nats relative to a fitted constant-velocity Gaussian.
Lacking ground truth for people in handheld video, we score forecasts against
the tracker’s own later raw measurements. In an internally pre-registered
evaluation on seven held-out clips, the final forecaster’s NLL is lower than
the benchmark-fitted baseline’s at 1.2, 2.4 and 4.8 s (by 0.17, 0.23 and
0.47 nats; 95 % intervals over people exclude zero), but by less
than half as much as on the development clips. Exploratory analyses cut both
ways: resampling clips instead of people widens the intervals to include zero
at 1.2 and 2.4 s, and once both forecasters are recalibrated on the
development clips the network is significantly better only at 1.2 s; but two
clips run with ADVIO’s reference poses favour the network much more when re-run
with the phone’s own poses. We discuss what such self-consistency scores can
and cannot show.
2026-10-06.introduction:
A pedestrian who walks with a phone in front of them, for instance a blind or
low-vision user of a navigation aid, or anyone following augmented-reality
directions, would benefit from knowing where the people around them will be
in the next few seconds. Three properties make such a forecast useful. It
must be metric and attached to the world , so that it stays on the
ground while the phone translates, pans and tilts. It must be probabilistic and calibrated : if the 90 % region is used to warn the
user or to plan a path, it should contain the person about 90 % of the
time. And it must come from what a phone has: a monocular camera and the
pose from its visual-inertial odometry (VIO), with no depth sensor on most
models and no fixed camera overlooking the scene.

Trajectory forecasting research mostly works with bird’s-eye trajectories from
fixed or drone cameras [ 43 ] and reports best-of- K K displacement errors [ 14 , 32 ] , which reward
spread-out forecasts [ 51 ] and say nothing about
calibration. First-person benchmarks record from robots or render from
simulators [ 52 , 29 , 50 ] ; assistive systems
that use a handheld phone track people but do not forecast them [ 26 ] ,
and head-mounted ones rely on stereo or offline SLAM [ 15 , 31 ] .
Finally, there is no public handheld-phone recording of pedestrians with
ground-truth trajectories, so it is unclear how to measure such a forecaster on
real video at all.

This paper builds and evaluates such a system end to end
( Figure 1 ). People are detected, lifted onto the floor by intersecting
pixel rays with a floor plane, tracked in a gravity-aligned metric world frame,
and forecast as per-step probability maps over the ground, either by a
training-free scene-and-physics prior or by a small U-Net trained with a
(slightly smoothed) negative log-likelihood loss on top-down (SDD) and real
first-person (EgoTraj-Bench) trajectories. The forecasts are re-projected into each new frame
with the current pose. We report four findings.

Vertical VIO drift breaks monocular lifting, and a simple rule
avoids it. On ADVIO’s handheld recordings [ 7 ] , the
phone’s reported height drifts by 1.2 m within 90 s while
ADVIO’s reference poses stay level, and on streets and escalators the phone’s
true height changes by metres. Holding the floor plane fixed in the world scales
every lifted distance by ( h + Δ ​ z ) / h (h+\Delta z)/h ; on one clip every track is lost for
the last 31 % of the clip. Keeping the camera’s height above the
floor constant under a low-pass-filtered altitude restores tracking on these
recordings and removes the rescaling in a synthetic test, although it lags
behind sustained climbs and descents such as escalator rides
( Sections 3.3 , 5.3 and 6 ).

Vertical VIO drift breaks monocular lifting, and a simple rule
avoids it. On ADVIO’s handheld recordings [ 7 ] , the
phone’s reported height drifts by 1.2 m within 90 s while
ADVIO’s reference poses stay level, and on streets and escalators the phone’s
true height changes by metres. Holding the floor plane fixed in the world scales
every lifted distance by ( h + Δ ​ z ) / h (h+\Delta z)/h ; on one clip every track is lost for
the last 31 % of the clip. Keeping the camera’s height above the
floor constant under a low-pass-filtered altitude restores tracking on these
recordings and removes the rescaling in a synthetic test, although it lags
behind sustained climbs and descents such as escalator rides
( Sections 3.3 , 5.3 and 6 ).

A heat-map network trained with negative log-likelihood beats a
physics prior. On the SDD TrajNet test split and the EgoTraj-Bench test split
the final forecaster, the network’s own heat map (chosen on validation data
over a mixture with the physics rollout) with a small constant-velocity
component, lowers the negative log-likelihood of the true position relative to
a constant-velocity Gaussian baseline by 1.51 and
1.37 nats at 4.8 s (Tier A: 0.59 and
0.18 nats), with 90 % regions smaller than those of the
CV baseline and of Tier A that contain the truth 0.93
and 0.93 of the time at 4.8 s, slightly more often
than nominal ( Section 5.1 ).

On real handheld video, part of the gain carries over in an
internally pre-registered test, but it is fragile. We score forecasts against
the tracker’s own later raw measurements, with forecast and baseline widened
by the same measurement noise. On seven ADVIO clips that were set aside until
the method and the analysis were frozen and committed, the final forecaster’s
NLL is lower than that of the constant-velocity baseline, whose widths come
from benchmark training data, by 0.17, 0.23 and
0.47 nats at 1.2, 2.4 and 4.8 s, with 95 % intervals over people
that exclude zero. That is less than half of the gain on the development
clips; the shortfall lies in the nearest distance band, which one escalator
clip with known geometric problems dominates ( Section 5.5 ). The
final forecaster’s 90 % regions contain the later measurement only
0.86, 0.79 and 0.76 of the time.
Exploratory analyses show how much the comparison depends on the clips, on the
baseline and on the poses: with clips as the unit of resampling only the
4.8 s difference excludes zero, and even it rests on four of seven clips; a
constant-velocity baseline refitted on the development clips as a mixture of
two Gaussians beats the final forecaster as configured, and when both are
recalibrated the network keeps a significant advantage (over people) only at
1.2 s; but two clips that the protocol evaluated with ADVIO’s offline
reference poses favour the network much more when re-converted with the
phone’s own poses ( Section 5.6 ).

Limits. Best-of-20 errors remain far from the state of the
art; self-consistency scores measure where the tracker will see a person, not
where the person is; and the pipeline processes 12.0 frames per
second on a workstation GPU, below the 30 of our converted clips
( Sections 5.7 and 6 ).

The code, the protocol and every result file needed to regenerate the tables
and figures are available from the author on request.
