# 2 Related work

Classical models treat walking as driven by goals and by repulsion from
obstacles and other people [ 16 ] . Learned forecasters model
interactions with recurrent networks and pooling [ 2 , 14 ] ,
attention over the scene and the neighbours [ 46 , 55 ] ,
graph-structured generative models [ 20 , 47 ] ,
endpoint- or goal-conditioned generation [ 33 , 32 , 6 ] and diffusion [ 13 , 34 ] . Our learned forecaster is
closest to Y-Net [ 32 ] , which predicts per-pixel goal and
trajectory heat maps with a U-Net [ 44 ] on a bird’s-eye
scene image. We keep the heat-map output but train it in metres, in a
heading-aligned crop, as a normalised distribution with a negative
log-likelihood loss, and on first-person noisy histories as well as top-down
ones. A constant-velocity model is a strong baseline that several learned
forecasters fail to beat [ 48 ] ; we use a
constant-velocity Gaussian with widths fitted to training data as the
reference throughout. Most of this work is
evaluated on fixed overhead or drone views such as the Stanford Drone
Dataset [ 43 ] in the TrajNet split [ 45 ] ,
or on interaction benchmarks such as TrajNet++ [ 24 ] .

Best-of- K K displacement errors [ 14 ] reward forecasts that
are spread out: the variety loss behind them converges to the square root of
the true density rather than the density [ 51 ] , which is why Thiede and Brahma [51] recommend reporting the likelihood of the ground truth
as well. Trajectron and Trajectron++ report a kernel-density negative
log-likelihood [ 20 , 47 ] . The
logarithmic score is strictly proper [ 12 ] , and good
probabilistic forecasts maximise sharpness subject to calibration [ 11 ] ;
we therefore report negative log-likelihood together with the coverage and
area of highest-density regions [ 19 ] . Recalibration [ 25 ] and conformal
prediction [ 28 , 9 ] can make the regions of
any forecaster calibrated, the latter with finite-sample coverage guarantees;
we measure coverage directly and use only simple parametric refits (one width
or a two-component mixture), in an exploratory analysis.

Forecasting from video rather than from coordinates alone can exploit the
appearance of people and scenes [ 27 ] . Forecasting from a
moving, first-person view has been studied in image
coordinates for chest-mounted cameras [ 53 ] and wearable
cameras with inertial cues [ 38 ] , and relative to a moving
vehicle [ 36 , 39 , 40 ] . Robot
datasets provide egocentric sensing with metric labels, such as
JRDB [ 35 ] and TBD [ 52 ] . T2FPV renders
first-person views of the ETH/UCY pedestrians to expose detection, tracking and
field-of-view errors [ 50 ] , and EgoTraj-Bench pairs real noisy
first-person histories, obtained with a detector and BoT-SORT [ 1 ] on the first-person video of the TBD platform, with clean metric
futures [ 29 ] .
RealTraj [ 10 ] makes forecasting robust to perception errors
by forecasting from past detections instead of tracks. Head-mounted systems
for blind users forecast pedestrians from a stereo camera with its visual-inertial
odometry [ 15 ] , or jointly localise and forecast from a
monocular camera with an offline SLAM ego-pose [ 31 ] . To our
knowledge, none of these evaluates density forecasts, or their calibration,
from a handheld phone.

LineChaser guides blind users in queues with a handheld iPhone, localising the
user with ARKit visual-inertial odometry and placing detected people in a map,
but does not forecast them [ 26 ] . A suitcase-shaped
guide with RGB-D cameras and LiDAR tracks pedestrians and extrapolates them with
constant velocity four seconds ahead to issue collision alerts [ 23 ] .
A chest-mounted phone LiDAR has been used to estimate time to impact [ 42 ] .
To our knowledge, no prior work forecasts other pedestrians as probability
distributions in a world frame from a handheld phone’s camera and
visual-inertial pose and measures their calibration on real handheld video.

Without depth, the ground position of a person follows from intersecting the
ray through their feet with the ground plane, which requires the camera’s height
and attitude. The known height of people constrains both [ 17 , 18 ] ;
we use this “people as the ruler” idea to estimate the camera height.
Tracking people on the ground plane rather than in the image makes the motion
model independent of camera motion [ 54 ] ; we track with
Kalman filters [ 22 ] in a gravity-aligned world frame and use
a Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoother [ 41 ] for evaluation. Image-space
multi-object trackers [ 56 , 1 ] are
complementary. The ADVIO benchmark [ 7 ] , which we use, compared
the visual-inertial odometry of ARKit, ARCore and Tango with ground truth and
found that ARKit “had severe problems with drifting in the outdoor
sequences” and that drift was worse in multi-floor cases. We show that the vertical component of such drift silently rescales every monocular
ground-plane position, and how to avoid it.

2026-10-06.title: Differentiable Ternary Temporal Logic Semantics with Polynomial Surrogate Networks
2026-10-06.authors: Ryan Matheu , Sai Sandeep Damera , John S. Baras , Calin Belta
2026-10-06.abstract: Temporal logic provides designers a formal reasoning tool for specifying complex spatio-temporal behaviors and tasks for autonomous systems. Many techniques exist for control synthesis according to temporal logic specifications, spanning a large variety of systems, including robotics. However, the vast majority of implementations are limited to Boolean temporal logics. Boolean temporal logic does not have an innate mechanism for quantifying abstention, rather verdicts are either definitively True or False . Recent work demonstrates that ternary logic is a capable formalism for reasoning about robotic behaviors, with the natural ability to classify uncertainty with the Unknown literal. Ternary temporal logic is still in its infancy, with work limited to synthesis for linear systems and monitoring. This work proposes a probabilistic relaxation of ternary temporal logic that allows for value and gradient computation through the same network while retaining exact verdicts on actual data. The relaxed network can be used as an objective in gradient-based control synthesis for both offline and online robotic control applications. We demonstrate the utility of our framework with two robotic manipulator tasks, one offline and one online, involving intermediate checking and sequencing of subtasks to demonstrate the benefit of our approach in terms of correct and timely execution.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Temporal logics like Signal Temporal Logic (STL) [ 13 ] have become prominent formalisms for specifying tasks for autonomous systems thanks to their rich expressivity, ability to specify time-dependent behaviors, and real-valued robustness semantics [ 6 ] . Temporal Behavior Trees (TBTs) [ 21 ] extend STL with the Sequence and Selector operators from behavior trees [ 4 ] , allowing designers to specify long-horizon tasks as a sequence of subtasks with fallbacks. However, the interpretation of STL and TBT formulas is binary, meaning the satisfaction of a formula is either True or False . This is limiting for robotic applications where a robot must reason about its task while it is still being executed. For example, in model predictive control (MPC), the satisfaction of a formula is evaluated over a partial trajectory ending at the prediction horizon. A task that has not been completed by the end of the horizon is neither satisfied nor violated, yet Boolean semantics force a verdict of False .

Ternary logic offers a natural remedy to this problem. Kleene’s strong logic K 3 K_{3} [ 11 ] introduces a third truth value Unknown to represent the case where there is not enough information to determine whether a proposition is True or False . In previous work [ 14 ] , we formulate the qualitative ternary semantics of STL and TBTs over partial trajectories, and demonstrate their utility as constraints in optimal control problems solved via mixed-integer programming. Mixed-integer formulations are exact, but suffer from high complexity as the horizon and number of subtasks grow, and are often restricted to linear or piecewise-linear dynamics [ 18 , 19 ] . Gradient-based methods using smooth approximations of the real-valued STL quantitative semantics scale to nonlinear systems [ 17 , 7 , 15 , 8 ] , but do not naturally quantify abstention and have not been implemented for the TBT operators. To the best of our knowledge, there is no smooth representation of the ternary semantics of temporal logic, so its suitability for gradient-based control synthesis remains open.

This work builds on the notion of using ternary logic gate networks as surrogates for temporal logic. In [ 5 ] , we showed that ternary logic functions admit unique polynomial surrogates that are exact on the trits { − 1 , 0 , + 1 } \{{-}1,\,0,\,{+}1\} , while being smooth by construction. In this paper, we demonstrate that the satisfaction of any ternary temporal logic formula over a partial trajectory can be unrolled into a Differentiable Ternary Logic Gate Network (DTLGN), providing a useful objective in gradient-based control synthesis.

Our primary contributions in this work are:

We show that the satisfaction of any ternary temporal logic formula can be represented exactly as a DTLGN.

We introduce a moment propagation scheme through DTLGNs that yields a smooth likelihood of satisfaction.

We demonstrate gradient-based control synthesis from ternary temporal logic specifications on a 7-DoF robotic manipulator for both open-loop and closed-loop (MPC) tasks.

This paper is organized as follows: Section II describes work related to smooth temporal logic semantics and ternary logic gate networks. In Section III , we provide the necessary preliminaries on ternary logic, temporal logic, and polynomial surrogates for logical functions. We formulate the main problem in Section IV and present our technical solution in Section V . Section VI demonstrates our framework with two control tasks using a simulated robotic manipulator.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Temporal Logic and Smooth Qualitative Semantics

Signal Temporal Logic (STL) [ 13 ] is a logical system for specifying spatio-temporal properties of real-valued signals, reasoning about the satisfaction of a formula with respect to a system trajectory. In addition to the qualitative (Boolean) semantics, STL has well-defined quantitative (robustness) semantics that measure how strongly a signal satisfies or violates a formula [ 6 ] . However, computation of the robustness of a formula consists of nested min \min and max \max functions, meaning the nominal robustness measure is not smooth. Temporal Behavior Trees (TBTs) [ 21 ] extend STL with the Sequence and Selector operators derived from behavior trees. These new temporal operators segment a trajectory into consecutive subtasks or fallbacks, and are equipped with a corresponding robustness measure. In previous work [ 14 ] , we formulate the ternary logic qualitative semantics for STL and TBTs and demonstrate their utility as constraints in optimal control problems solved via mixed-integer programming.

Closed-loop control synthesis with STL formulas as constraints on the system trajectory is traditionally posed as an online mixed-integer program. The Boolean satisfaction of a formula is encoded as a hard constraint, or the robustness is added to the cost as an objective to be maximized [ 18 , 19 ] . Such formulations are exact, but suffer from high complexity. To enable gradient-based optimization, the non-smooth robustness measure with is fitted with smooth approximations of min \min and max \max [ 17 ] , or alternative smooth under-approximations to preserve soundness [ 7 ] . Other approaches to smooth robustness semantics include a reformulation using the arithmetic-geometric mean [ 15 ] or a cumulative formulation [ 8 ] allowing for smooth semantics by construction. All of these approaches focus on a smooth quantitative measure of satisfaction. In contrast, we smoothen the qualitative ternary verdict itself. Our surrogate agrees exactly with the hard semantics on the trits, admits an Unknown verdict over partial trajectories, and covers STL as well as the TBT operators.

## II-B Ternary Logic Gate Networks and Reparameterization

In previous work [ 5 ] , we demonstrate that general k k -ary ternary logic functions can be constructed as logic gate networks with learnable parameters. Each neuron represents a two-input ternary logic gate with nine learnable coefficients, covering the full gate library consisting of 3 3 2 3^{3^{2}} unique functions. As an extension to that work, we demonstrate that Differentiable Ternary Logic Gate Networks (DTLGNs) are capable of learning to causally predict STL verdicts online, choosing to abstain from producing a verdict in the absence of sufficient information [ 20 ] . This work extends the notion of using ternary logic gate networks as surrogates for temporal logic monitoring, creating a representation for the satisfaction of a formula that is smooth by construction and provides exact verdicts on actual input traces.

The Gumbel-Softmax [ 9 ] and Concrete [ 12 ] distributions provide a continuous relaxation of categorical random variables, allowing discrete variables to be represented by a smooth, temperature-controlled distribution through which gradients can be propagated. In this work, our predicate relaxation follows from the same idea: logistic noise added to the predicate function turns each hard verdict into a random ternary variable, very much in the spirit of differentiable programming [ 2 ] , where differentiable relaxations such as smoothing programs have been interpreted in a probabilistic framework. Rather than sampling, we propagate the moments of these ternary variables analytically, which gives a deterministic objective and exact gradients.

2026-10-06.title: PermVLA: Factorization Order as a Regularizer for VLA Learning
2026-10-06.authors: Yanqiao Chen , Yuhan Rui , Dongsheng Hou , Zijie Nie , Yutong Wan , Qi Hao
2026-10-06.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly learn action chunks through a
fixed left-to-right (LTR) factorization, although the same expert trajectory
distribution admits many valid chain-rule factorizations. We identify
factorization order as an overlooked regularization choice and introduce
causally anchored permutation (CAP), which samples action reveal orders with
a tunable chronological prefix. Its auxiliary
objective trains one shared policy to predict actions from different known
subsets of the same expert chunk, while deployment retains deterministic LTR
control. We call this conditional-set augmentation : it creates multiple
conditional prediction problems from one expert chunk without adding
demonstrations. This discourages reliance on the single chronological prefix
used by ordinary teacher forcing. Controlled experiments show that CAP
consistently outperforms standard LTR training on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with
the same advantage appearing in cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation. A diagnostic
that measures the expected squared difference between a chunk’s joint log
likelihood under two reveal orders verifies that CAP training internalizes
agreement across reveal orders. These findings position sampled
subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives as a general recipe for constructing
VLA regularizers, illustrated by an extension to diffusion action generators.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) systems learn a conditional joint distribution
over a chunk of future actions. Recent work has explored robot pretraining,
action tokenization, diffusion and flow objectives, post-training, and
asynchronous execution ( Kim et al., 2025b ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ; Shukor et al., 2025 ) .
The chain rule introduces another modeling choice: the order in which action
variables are revealed and predicted. Autoregressive VLA training usually
fixes this order to chronological action time, conventionally modeled
left-to-right (LTR), leaving factorization order hidden inside the action
objective. We study it
as an independent modeling choice and ask whether alternative valid
factorizations can regularize VLA training.

Under LTR training, each action slot is always predicted from the same family
of preceding physical actions. Complete expert chunks make many other valid
conditioning subsets available. We hypothesize that exclusive training on
one teacher-forced chain encourages the policy to rely on
that single reveal order. Predicting the same physical action from different
known subsets should instead favor conditional dependencies among action steps
that remain predictive across conditioning patterns. This may improve
closed-loop control when visual, linguistic, or embodiment context shifts.

We instantiate this idea as PermVLA , a deliberately minimal VLA that
conditions a diagonal-Gaussian autoregressive action head on pretrained
vision-language model (VLM) embeddings. This design prioritizes controlled
analysis and attribution of causally anchored permutation (CAP)
regularization; closed-loop success measures its contribution within the
fixed architecture. CAP adds an auxiliary permutation likelihood to the
standard LTR objective. The tunable
prefix length K K fixes the first K K actions in physical-time order; K = 0 K=0 allows every reveal order. The shared policy minimizes ( 1 − λ ) ​ ℒ LTR + λ ​ ℒ CAP (1-\lambda)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LTR}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CAP}} ,
then deploys through deterministic LTR receding-horizon control.
Each expert chunk supplies prediction problems conditioned on different known
action subsets, with physical action identities and the deployment procedure
unchanged. We call this conditional-set augmentation .
Figure 1 illustrates these conditioning patterns and
summarizes their effect in matched LIBERO comparisons.

Permutation modeling has established foundations in orderless density
estimation, XLNet, and autoregressive diffusion ( Uria et al., 2014 ; Yang et al., 2019 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ) . Random autoregressive
factorization has also been applied to same-time multi-agent trajectories ( Rudolph and Brefeld, 2022 ) , while Uni[MASK], MaskDP, and Masked Trajectory
Models learn completion under variable masks ( Carroll et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) . We assign alternative
factorizations a distinct VLA role: a training-only regularizer over future
physical actions, with a tunable chronological prefix and paired with
the exact LTR deployment objective. This formulation makes factorization
order directly measurable under a fixed controller.

Sample-matched LTR-1pass and decoder-compute-matched LTR-2pass controls isolate
the training objective. LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) tests in-distribution
control, LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2026 ) tests zero-shot
out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness, and CALVIN ( Mees et al., 2022 ) tests
whether the gains extend to another benchmark.

In the matched reference experiments, CAP improves closed-loop success over
both LTR controls across these benchmarks. Likelihood diagnostics show
greater agreement across reveal orders while retaining the fit under LTR,
connecting the training objective to a measurable change in the learned policy.

This approach suggests a broader design principle: varying known action
subsets can construct auxiliary objectives for other action generators while
retaining their deployment procedures. We illustrate it with PermDiffusion , which conditions on clean action subsets and denoises
the remaining slots.

Our contributions are:

We identify action-chunk factorization order as a previously
overlooked VLA inductive-bias axis and formulate its regularization effect
as conditional-set augmentation.

We introduce CAP, an auxiliary factorization objective with tunable
prefix length that diversifies action conditioning during training and
preserves standard LTR deployment.

Matched controls, parameter studies, OOD evaluation, and CALVIN
demonstrate the empirical benefits. Likelihood diagnostics provide evidence
of agreement across reveal orders, and a diffusion extension illustrates
the broader design space.

1. We identify action-chunk factorization order as a previously
overlooked VLA inductive-bias axis and formulate its regularization effect
as conditional-set augmentation.

2. We introduce CAP, an auxiliary factorization objective with tunable
prefix length that diversifies action conditioning during training and
preserves standard LTR deployment.

3. Matched controls, parameter studies, OOD evaluation, and CALVIN
demonstrate the empirical benefits. Likelihood diagnostics provide evidence
of agreement across reveal orders, and a diffusion extension illustrates

2026-10-06.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

RT-1 and RT-2 established scalable vision-language robot policies with
tokenized control ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ) ; Octo and OpenVLA
extended open robot pretraining across datasets and embodiments ( Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025b ) . Recent action generators include the Action
Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , conditional denoising in Diffusion
Policy ( Chi et al., 2023 ) , flow matching in π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2025b ) , and compressed action tokens in FAST ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ) . OpenVLA-OFT, WorldVLA, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and SmolVLA
further study chunk decoding, auxiliary prediction, heterogeneous
pretraining, and asynchronous execution ( Kim et al., 2025a ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2025a ; Shukor et al., 2025 ) . CAP fixes the
backbone and continuous action generator to isolate factorization order as a
training intervention.

Orderless Neural Autoregressive Distribution Estimation (NADE) trains one
density estimator across autoregressive orders ( Uria et al., 2014 ) ; XLNet
combines permutation language modeling with two-stream attention ( Yang et al., 2019 ) ; and autoregressive diffusion models (ARDMs) connect
order-agnostic autoregression to absorbing diffusion ( Hoogeboom et al., 2022 ) . Rudolph and Brefeld (2022) carry the same
mechanism into trajectory modeling, pairing random autoregressive
factorizations with conditional two-stream attention for the same-time
movements of multiple agents. Uni[MASK], MaskDP, and Masked Trajectory Models
learn behavior from variable trajectory masks ( Carroll et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) . In each case, permutation
or masking constitutes the primary training objective itself, defined over
unordered variable sets or completion-style tasks.

Our contribution is to import the permutation idea of XLNet into VLA learning
in the form of a regularizer: the permuted likelihood enters as an auxiliary
term on top of the chronological density objective. Two properties of
physical-world action imitation make this transfer practical. The first is computational feasibility : expert action chunks are short
( H = 8 H=8 – 16 16 slots), so evaluating normalized likelihoods under M M sampled reveal orders adds modest decoder computation, while the parameter
count and deployment cost remain fixed. The second is temporal
adherence : the chronological LTR objective remains the dominant training
path and the only deployment path, so the policy keeps physical-time ordering
as its primary interface to control. The auxiliary CAP term then predicts
each target action from varied known subsets, discouraging over-reliance on
one generation path and on the visual correspondences specific to that path.
CAP assigns an ordered, normalized likelihood to each sampled order within one
future action chunk, whereas masked-completion objectives score unordered
variable sets with completion-style losses.
The tunable prefix length K K controls the order family, including fully
unrestricted orders at K = 0 K=0 . Our reference configuration draws only M = 1 M=1 sampled order per example, with a M = 4 M=4 ablation, so the
computational-efficiency argument above is validated only in the low- M M regime; scaling M M further and mapping the resulting
computation–regularization trade-off remains an open direction.

2026-10-06.title: Nonlinear Density-Driven Optimal Control (D2OC) for Multi-Agent Spatial Coverage via Sequential Convex Programming
2026-10-06.authors: Julian Martinez , Kooktae Lee
2026-10-06.subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
2026-10-06.abstract: This paper presents a nonlinear extension of Density-Driven Optimal Control (D 2 OC) for multi-agent spatial coverage with prescribed density distributions. Rather than assigning individual target locations, D 2 OC drives the collective spatial distribution of agents toward a desired density through a Wasserstein-based objective. We extend this framework to multi-step finite-horizon control for discrete-time control-affine nonlinear systems using sequential convex programming. At each control update, the nonlinear dynamics are locally linearized over the prediction horizon, yielding a strictly convex quadratic program that preserves the Wasserstein barycentric structure while directly incorporating input constraints. We further characterize the effect of constrained control deviations and nonlinear Taylor remainders on the accuracy of the local linear prediction, establishing an explicit finite-horizon error bound and a two-step specialization for receding-horizon implementation. The resulting method retains the decentralized, distribution-driven nature of D 2 OC while providing a computationally efficient optimization procedure for nonlinear multi-agent systems. Simulations with unicycle and quadrotor teams show coverage performance comparable to nonlinear model predictive control, while substantially reducing computation time. These results demonstrate a tractable and theoretically characterized framework for density-driven spatial coverage under nonlinear dynamics.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Multi-agent spatial coverage aims to distribute autonomous agents over a spatial domain according to sensing, monitoring, or mission-dependent requirements. Classical coverage control methods, such as the Voronoi-based framework, partition the workspace into agent-specific Voronoi cells and steer agents toward their cell centroids [ 1 ] . While effective for geometric coverage, such methods do not directly address non-uniform agent distributions. This motivates formulating non-uniform coverage as a spatial distribution-matching problem.

Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled framework for comparing and matching spatial distributions through Wasserstein distances [ 2 , 3 ] . This perspective has also been incorporated into multi-agent coverage control, where the objective is formulated directly in terms of the discrepancy between the empirical distribution of agents and a prescribed spatial density, rather than through individually assigned target locations [ 4 ] . Building on this distribution-based viewpoint, Density-Driven Optimal Control (D 2 OC) formulates non-uniform multi-agent coverage as a decentralized optimal-control problem that drives the empirical agent distribution toward a reference density through local sample selection, weight updates, and neighbor information exchange [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] .

The D 2 OC framework was initially developed for linear time-invariant (LTI) dynamics and later extended to linear time-varying (LTV) dynamics [ 6 , 7 ] . Its extension to nonlinear systems, however, has so far been limited to a one-step prediction horizon. A multi-step nonlinear formulation must account for nonlinear agent dynamics while preserving the Wasserstein-based coverage objective, decentralized structure, and input constraints.
NMPC provides a framework for nonlinear dynamics and constraints through repeated finite-horizon optimization [ 9 ] , while distributed receding-horizon methods address computational and communication requirements in multi-agent systems [ 10 ] .
Sequential convex programming (SCP), in contrast, locally approximates nonlinear dynamics and solves a sequence of convex subproblems, and has been applied to real-time nonlinear optimal control and successive convexification [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . This makes SCP a natural candidate for extending D 2 OC to multi-step nonlinear coverage although the resulting local approximation introduces a discrepancy between predicted and actual trajectories that must be characterized.

In this paper, we extend D 2 OC to discrete-time control-affine
nonlinear systems using sequentially linearized local models. Each
optimization step yields a strictly convex local Quadratic Program (QP) with input
constraints while retaining the Wasserstein-based coverage objective.
We further characterize constraint-induced control deviations and derive a finite-horizon bound on the resulting
linearization error.

Thus, the main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:
1) We extend the Wasserstein-based D 2 OC formulation to discrete-time control-affine nonlinear systems while preserving its decentralized coverage mechanism and distribution-matching objective;
2) We formulate each nonlinear D 2 OC update as a strictly convex local QP via sequential convex programming, retaining the Wasserstein barycenter structure and actuator constraints while enabling efficient computation;
3) We quantify input-saturation effects through the deviation between constrained and unconstrained QP solutions and incorporate this deviation into the linearization-error analysis;
4) We establish a finite-horizon error bound accounting for control deviations and second-order Taylor remainders, with a receding-horizon specialization for first-input application.

The resulting framework combines the distribution-level objective of D 2 OC with efficient local optimization and explicit prediction-error characterization for nonlinear multi-agent dynamics.

2026-10-06.title: RAGrasp: Geometry-Semantic Template Retrieval and Grasp Transfer
2026-10-06.authors: Shenzhe Zhu , Chengxiao He , Jan Harder
2026-10-06.abstract: We present RAGrasp, a retrieval-augmented pipeline for planar parallel-jaw grasping from a compact set of locally collected, grasp-annotated RGB-D (color and depth) templates. Unlike task-specific predictors trained primarily on large public or synthetic grasp datasets, RAGrasp requires no end-to-end retraining for a new deployment.Its template memory is constructed from observations collected with the deployment camera, robot, and gripper in the target workspace, thereby aligning stored examples with the local sensing and embodiment conditions. The system uses self-supervised DINOv2 visual features together with appearance and depth cues to prompt the Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), which isolates the query object. A two-stage geometry-semantic retrieval cascade then selects a template, and a confidence gate chooses one of two grasp-transfer estimators. The transferred grasp is refined using mask-support and silhouette-contact constraints before calibrated 2D-to-3D conversion. In real-world trials, RAGrasp achieves 20/20 successful grasps on seen objects and 19/20 on unseen objects. Within the evaluated setting, the results demonstrate deployment-specific grasp adaptation from limited local annotation and tolerance to the tested viewpoint and illumination changes.
2026-10-06.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Learning-Based Grasp Detection

Classical grasp analysis studies force closure, grasp quality, and simulation [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] ; comprehensive surveys trace the transition from analytic geometry to data-driven synthesis [ 5 , 6 ] . Early vision-based learning demonstrated grasp transfer to novel objects [ 7 ] . More recent methods include analytic-label learning in Dex-Net 2.0 [ 8 ] , pixel-wise planar prediction in GG-CNN [ 9 , 10 ] , descriptor-based category-level pose transfer in Neural Descriptor Fields (NDF) [ 11 ] , and six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) grasp generation from point clouds [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . Large benchmarks and simulated grasp corpora support this progress [ 15 , 16 ] .

Geometric proposal methods detect parallel-jaw grasps directly in point clouds [ 17 , 18 ] , while AnyGrasp extends dense grasp perception across spatial and temporal domains [ 19 ] . GraspSAM integrates promptable segmentation with grasp prediction [ 20 ] . RAGrasp instead stores successful grasps explicitly and focuses on retrieval, transfer, and geometric validation. Its compact memory is collected on the target setup, mitigating the sensor, embodiment, and scene mismatch between public training corpora and local deployment. This trades universal open-world coverage for deployment-specific precision and data-efficient adaptation. The approaches remain complementary: a learned detector may generate initial templates, while retrieval supplies inspectable instance-level memory.

## II-B Foundation Features and Promptable Segmentation

DINO (self-distillation with no labels) showed that a self-supervised Vision Transformer can organize image patches according to object and part structure without task-specific annotations [ 21 ] . DINOv2 extends this approach and provides two types of descriptors used in this work: a global image descriptor that summarizes the masked object and patch descriptors that retain local spatial information [ 22 ] . Objects with similar appearance or parts tend to have similar descriptors, making the representation useful for retrieval and correspondence.

The Segment Anything Model (SAM) is a promptable segmentation network: given an image and a small set of positive points or a bounding box, it returns a pixel-level object mask [ 23 ] . SAM2 extends this formulation while retaining the same prompt-to-mask interface [ 24 ] . RAGrasp uses DINOv2 features to help locate the object and to compare the query with stored templates; SAM2 converts the fused object proposal into the mask used by all later geometric operations. For local matching, classical methods use the scale-invariant feature transform (SIFT) [ 25 ] , whereas SuperGlue and LightGlue learn to match detected image features [ 26 , 27 ] . RAGrasp instead compares DINOv2 patch descriptors and retains pairs that are mutual nearest neighbors.

## II-C Geometric Registration and Grasp Transfer

Iterative closest point (ICP) aligns two geometric point sets by alternating between nearest-neighbor assignment and least-squares transform estimation [ 28 ] ; efficient variants improve correspondence selection and convergence behavior [ 29 ] . Local 3D descriptors such as fast point feature histograms (FPFH) can further support geometric matching [ 30 ] . Random sample consensus (RANSAC) estimates a model from repeatedly sampled correspondence subsets and rejects inconsistent matches as outliers [ 31 ] . Given an accepted correspondence set, Umeyama’s closed-form estimator recovers the least-squares rotation, translation, and uniform scale [ 32 ] . RAGrasp combines these tools rather than relying on a single estimator: contour ICP provides a conservative geometry-based transfer, while DINOv2 patch correspondences and RANSAC provide a semantics-aware alternative. Metric execution additionally relies on intrinsic camera calibration [ 33 ] and camera-to-robot hand-eye calibration [ 34 ] .

2026-10-06.title: Video2World: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Interactive World Modeling from Embodied Videos
2026-10-06.authors: Jinzhou Tang , Zijun Zhang , Jing Yang , Yuchen Yan , Kun Zhou , Lingjun Mao , Ruobing Han , Jinglin Cao , Wenpeng Xu , Lukun He , Minghao Fu , Fan Feng , Biwei Huang
2026-10-06.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract:
Building interactive simulators from real-world observations is a promising way to scale embodied data, but current pipelines still rely heavily on manual environment construction and calibration. We study whether frontier foundation models and coding agents can automate this process end to end. We formulate autonomous video-to-simulation as a software engineering task in which an agent observes an embodied video, constructs the corresponding simulated environment and robot behavior, and iteratively refines the result through execution feedback. To evaluate this capability, we introduce Video2World , a benchmark comprising 222 reconstruction instances derived from 189 robot and human demonstration videos. Video2World measures reconstructed worlds along geometric fidelity, dynamic fidelity, and functional correctness, capturing spatial perception, physical reasoning, and executable interaction. Evaluating 9 frontier coding-agent systems reveals a sharp improvement in Task success beginning with Claude Opus 5, rising from below 5% to over 15%, while substantial gaps to human-assisted reconstruction remain.
We further find that worlds that look better could work worse: better visual fidelity does not always lead to higher task success. This echoes the broader gap between perceptual realism and factual correctness observed in generative models.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Embodied AI aims to build intelligent systems that can perceive, reason, and act effectively in the physical world, enabling applications such as robotic manipulation, household assistance, and industrial automation ( Duan et al., 2022 ) .
Fully acquiring these capabilities requires large amounts of diverse embodied interaction data, which is expensive, time-consuming, and difficult to scale in the real world ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) .
To alleviate this bottleneck, many prior works have explored interactive simulation as a scalable data engine, where agents can act, observe state transitions, and automatically collect embodied experience ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2024b ) . Conventional Real-to-Sim pipelines, however, still require substantial engineering
effort to reconstruct and configure simulation environments, calibrate geometry and physical properties, align coordinate systems, and integrate perception and simulation components ( Torne et al., 2024 ; Han et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) .

In recent years, foundation models and agents have made rapid progress in spatial perception, visual understanding and planning, demonstrating increasingly strong capabilities in solving complex software and embodied tasks ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; You et al., 2026 ) . These advances make it increasingly promising to automate the full process of interactive world modeling in simulators through an agent itself ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . Such automation could substantially reduce the human effort, and enable the efficient conversion of real-world observations into scalable interactive environments for data generation, policy learning, and evaluation. However, existing benchmarks typically assess only one or a few isolated capabilities for interactive environment reconstruction, such as spatial understanding, physical rule following, scene reconstruction, or environment editing ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2026 ) . As shown in Table 1 , they provide only a fragmented view of performance and do not reveal how effectively current frontier models and agents can integrate these capabilities to autonomously build, execute, and refine interactive worlds.

To fill this gap and directly test whether foundation models and coding agents can autonomously construct interactive physical worlds, we formulate autonomous video-to-simulation as an end-to-end software engineering task ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) . Concretely, given an RGB video of an embodied interaction together with a target simulator, an agent must construct the environment, implement the robot behavior, and iteratively refine the simulation through execution feedback. To support systematic evaluation, we construct a dataset that pairs embodied videos with their corresponding simulator environments, including aligned scene configurations, object states, and interaction trajectories. This paired structure allows us to compare an agent-generated simulation directly against the underlying target environment and assess the full reconstruction quality. In this way, we measure not only whether an agent can understand the world, but also whether it can integrate embodied reasoning, physical understanding, spatial perception, and agentic coding abilities to recover an interactive environment that faithfully reproduces the demonstrated physical world.

We introduce Video2World , a benchmark for evaluating foundation models and coding agents on autonomous interactive world modeling from embodied videos. Video2World comprises 222 reconstruction instances across 39 task families, constructed from 189 video clips spanning robot executions, egocentric human recordings, and third-person human demonstrations. To evaluate reconstruction quality comprehensively, we design metrics from three complementary perspectives: geometric fidelity , which measures how accurately the reconstructed scene matches the spatial structure of the source environment; dynamic fidelity , which evaluates whether simulated object motions and state transitions reproduce the observed physical evolution; and functional correctness , which assesses whether the reconstructed environment supports successful task execution through physical interaction. Together, these metrics reflect an agent’s ability to integrate spatial perception, physical reasoning, and executable coding for end-to-end interactive world modeling.

We evaluate 9 frontier coding-agent systems under the same interface and uncover several key findings. First, current coding agents can construct executable simulated worlds, but reliably completing the demonstrated interactions remains challenging.
Second, reconstruction fidelity and functional correctness are related but not equivalent: models with stronger geometric accuracy do not necessarily achieve task success. Third, human-assisted reconstruction provides a substantially stronger reference, while still falls short of perfect task completion. Finally, different coding-agent systems exhibit distinct strengths across the evaluated dimensions, suggesting that overall video-to-simulation performance emerges from their combination rather than any single ability.

2026-10-06.title: Budget-Constrained Fault-Tolerant Mutual Visibility for Autonomous Robots under the Mobility Fault Model
2026-10-06.authors: Prakhar Shukla , Animesh Maiti , Shivam Kumar , Subhash Bhagat
2026-10-06.subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC) ; Computational Geometry (cs.CG); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.abstract: We investigate the mutual visibility problem for a swarm of n ≥ 3 n\geq 3 autonomous mobile robots under the budget-constrained mobility fault model. The robots are opaque, so if three robots are collinear, the middle robot obstructs the visibility between the other two. Each robot is assigned a finite movement budget, reflecting its limited energy, that bounds the total distance it may traverse during the execution. Moreover, an arbitrary number of robots may become permanently immobile due to mobility faults. The objective is to design a distributed algorithm that enables the non-faulty robots to coordinate their movements so that, within a finite time, every non-faulty robot attains unobstructed visibility of all robots in the system, including the faulty ones, while respecting the prescribed movement budget. We consider luminous robots operating under the 𝖲𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{SSYNC} model with non-rigid movements, without any agreement on their local coordinate systems, and equipped only with a common fixed reference point . We present a deterministic distributed algorithm that solves the problem despite an arbitrary number of mobility faults. The algorithm guarantees mutual visibility for the non-faulty robots, respects the movement budget of every robot, provides collision-free movements for the robots, and uses only 12 light colors.
2026-10-06.introduction:
We consider a finite set ℛ \mathcal{R} of n n anonymous, homogeneous, opaque, and luminous point robots deployed in the Euclidean plane. Robots have unlimited visibility, but their line of sight is obstructed by opaque robots. Each robot has its own local coordinate system, with no agreement on the coordinate axes or chirality, and executes the same deterministic algorithm. Communication is achieved only by observing the positions and light colors of visible robots. Robots are oblivious except for persistent lights operating under the FALL model. Each robot is equipped with a persistent light that can assume a color from a finite set shared by all robots. The selected color remains unchanged across subsequent activations until the robot explicitly changes it. Thus, the light serves both as persistent local memory and as a means of communication among the robots. The robots operate under the semi-synchronous ( 𝖲𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{SSYNC} ) model. Under the 𝖲𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{SSYNC} model, time is divided into discrete rounds. In each round, the scheduler activates an arbitrary nonempty subset of robots, while the remaining robots stay stationary. All robots activated in the same round simultaneously execute one complete Look–Compute–Move cycle. During the Look phase, each
activated robot takes a snapshot containing the positions and light colors
of all robots visible to it, together with its own current light color.
During the Compute phase, it uses the obtained snapshot to compute
a destination point according to the algorithm and may also update its
light color. Finally, during the Move phase, the robot moves toward
its computed destination. The scheduler is fair, meaning that every robot
is activated infinitely often. An epoch is the shortest sequence of
consecutive rounds during which every robot is activated at least once.
A robot may be activated multiple times within the same epoch. By the
fairness of the scheduler, every epoch is finite. Robot movements are non-rigid, i.e., a robot may be stopped before reaching its computed destination after moving at least an unknown positive distance δ \delta .
In addition, every robot can detect a common fixed external reference
beacon P ∗ P^{*} and obtain its relative position in its local coordinate
system during each Look phase.

Each robot is initially assigned the same finite movement budget B B , which bounds the total Euclidean distance it may traverse during the execution. A robot may suffer a mobility fault at any time, after which it becomes permanently immobile while retaining its sensing, computation, and light capabilities. Faulty robots cannot distinguish themselves from fault-free robots. Throughout the paper, we consider the budget-constrained mobility fault model, in which an arbitrary number of robots may become mobility faulty.

The mutual visibility problem for autonomous mobile robots was formally introduced by Di Luna et al. [ 9 ] in the classical oblivious robot model. Under obstructed visibility, robots are considered opaque, and hence a robot lying on the line segment joining two other robots prevents them from seeing each other. The objective is therefore to transform an arbitrary initial configuration into one in which no three robots are collinear, while avoiding collisions. Di Luna et al. studied the problem for oblivious robots under the 𝖲𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{SSYNC} scheduler and proposed a convex-hull-based solution. Closely related to mutual visibility is the problem of forming a general position . Bhagat et al. [ 3 ] studied this problem for asynchronous opaque robots under one-axis agreement and provided a collision-free algorithm that removes collinearities. Early investigations also focused on the efficiency of mutual-visibility algorithms. Sharma et al. [ 17 ] analyzed bounds on existing mutual-visibility algorithms, while subsequent work improved the running time for oblivious robots; in particular, Sharma et al. [ 20 ] obtained an 𝒪 ⁡ ( n ) \mathcal{O}(n) -time algorithm in the fully synchronous setting.

A major line of research considers the luminous robot model , in which each robot carries a persistent externally visible light whose color can be used both as a small amount of persistent memory and as a means of communication. Di Luna et al. [ 10 ] gave fundamental results for this model, showing that mutual visibility can be solved using two colors in the rigid 𝖲𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{SSYNC} setting and three colors in 𝖠𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{ASYNC} ; they also considered non-rigid movements and established solutions under additional assumptions such as one-axis agreement. Sharma et al. [ 18 ] subsequently studied the number of colors required and obtained color-efficient solutions. In parallel, Vaidyanathan et al. [ 24 ] investigated the time complexity of complete visibility and proposed a logarithmic-time algorithm for robots with lights. Sharma et al. [ 21 ] further reduced the running time to 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathcal{O}(1) rounds in synchronous settings. Bhagat and Mukhopadhyaya [ 5 ] considered an energy-oriented variant and proposed an algorithm that restricts the number of movements performed by each robot. For the asynchronous setting, constant-time complete visibility was subsequently obtained by Sharma et al. [ 22 ] . Thus, much of the luminous-robot literature has concentrated on reducing either the number of colors, the number of movements, or the overall running time.

Mutual visibility has also been investigated under alternative computational models and geometric domains. Bhagat and Mukhopadhyaya [ 6 ] considered the 𝖥𝖲𝖳𝖠𝖳𝖤 \mathsf{FSTATE} model, in which robots have a constant amount of persistent internal memory rather than externally visible lights, and showed that one bit of memory is sufficient in the semi-synchronous setting. This direction was further developed by Bhagat [ 7 ] , who studied optimum mutual visibility with finite-state robots. The problem has also been extended from point robots to robots having physical extent. Sharma et al. [ 16 ] studied complete visibility for fat luminous robots, whereas Sharma et al. [ 19 ] investigated the corresponding problem for non-transparent fat robots without lights. More recently, Bose et al. [ 8 ] considered a more realistic sensing model in which a fat robot is equipped with a slim omnidirectional camera and proposed a mutual-visibility algorithm under the 𝖲𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{SSYNC} scheduler. Another line of work restricts robot movements to discrete environments. Adhikary et al. [ 1 ] studied asynchronous luminous robots on an infinite grid, where movements are restricted to grid edges, and Kim et al. [ 11 ] subsequently investigated two-color complete-visibility algorithms on the grid under stronger coordinate-agreement assumptions. These results demonstrate that the difficulty of mutual visibility depends strongly on the robots’ geometric representation, movement domain, memory, and degree of coordinate agreement.

Fault-tolerant mutual visibility constitutes another important branch of the literature. Aljohani and Sharma [ 2 ] considered crash faults and gave a complete-visibility algorithm tolerating a faulty robot under coordinate-agreement assumptions. Poudel et al. [ 12 ] studied the more general mobility-fault model, in which a faulty robot loses its ability to move but can continue to execute the other phases of its Look–Compute–Move cycle. Their algorithm works under one-axis agreement and tolerates multiple mobility faults. A different fault model was considered by Sharma [ 23 ] , where faults affect the lights of the robots rather than their mobility. More recently, Pramanick et al. [ 13 ] investigated mutual visibility in the presence of angular inaccuracies in robot movements and also considered the simultaneous presence of mobility faults. Their algorithms work for luminous robots under one-axis agreement and show that mutual visibility can still be obtained despite bounded directional errors.

The assumption of a common axis was subsequently relaxed in fault-tolerant settings. Pramanick et al. [ 14 ] studied mobility failures for completely disoriented robots, i.e., robots having no agreement on their local coordinate systems. They established fault-tolerant algorithms for multiple faults in the 𝖥𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{FSYNC} setting and for a single fault in the 𝖲𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{SSYNC} and 𝖠𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{ASYNC} settings. More recently, Pramanick et al. [ 15 ] further investigated asynchronous fault-tolerant mutual visibility for disoriented robots. Along a different direction, Bhagat et al. [ 4 ] studied the min-move mutual visibility problem under the strong combination of disorientation, 𝖠𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{ASYNC} scheduling, and non-rigid movements. They showed that the problem is impossible without additional persistent information and proposed a luminous algorithm in which every robot moves at most once.

From the viewpoint of solution techniques, a large fraction of the above algorithms are convex-hull-based : robots progressively expand, contract, or otherwise manipulate the convex hull until all relevant robots occupy suitable hull vertices [ 9 , 10 , 24 , 21 , 18 , 22 , 16 , 19 , 14 ] . Although this approach is powerful, it generally requires robots to travel to geometrically prescribed hull positions and therefore provides limited control over the amount of movement performed by an individual robot. Non-convex-hull techniques instead remove collinearities by carefully selecting local destinations without requiring all robots to become vertices of a common convex hull. Such approaches have been used for general-position formation and movement-efficient mutual visibility [ 3 , 5 , 4 ] . However, existing non-convex-hull solutions either rely on additional coordinate agreement, do not tolerate mobility failures, or address substantially different fault assumptions.

To the best of our knowledge, no existing algorithm simultaneously provides a non-convex-hull-based solution for disoriented robots under mobility faults while also enforcing an explicit budget on robot movement. In this paper, we address this gap by studying the mutual visibility problem under a budget-constrained mobility fault model . Our algorithm follows a non-convex-hull strategy and is designed so that the motion of every non-faulty robot remains compatible with the prescribed movement budget. This additional constraint fundamentally distinguishes our setting from earlier mobility-fault algorithms [ 12 , 14 , 15 ] : directly moving robots toward convex-hull vertices may require an arbitrarily large displacement relative to the available budget, and hence the existing convex-hull-based techniques cannot be applied without substantial modification.

We study fault-tolerant mutual visibility under a finite movement budget, where
each robot can traverse a total Euclidean distance of at most B B . Existing
fault-tolerant solutions either rely on one-axis agreement or use convex-hull
based relocation strategies. In contrast, we assume no agreement on local
coordinate axes or chirality. Instead, every robot can identify a common fixed
reference point P ∗ P^{*} lying outside the convex hull of the initial configuration.
The point P ∗ P^{*} provides only a common geometric landmark; it does not induce a
common direction, orientation, or coordinate system.

We consider a strong fault-tolerant visibility requirement: every non-faulty
robot must eventually have unobstructed visibility of every robot in the
system, including mobility-faulty robots. We present a deterministic
non-convex-hull-based algorithm for luminous robots operating under 𝖲𝖲𝖸𝖭𝖢 \mathsf{SSYNC} with
non-rigid movements. The algorithm uses the relative distances of robots from P ∗ P^{*} to coordinate movements and resolve cyclic dependencies. Each movement
is chosen using local geometric clearances and the robot’s remaining movement
budget, so no robot is required to reach a prescribed distant target.

Our algorithm tolerates an arbitrary number of permanent mobility faults,
guarantees collision-free movements, respects the movement budget of every
robot, uses 12 12 light colors, and terminates in O ⁡ ( n ) O(n) epochs. Table 1 summarizes the main differences between the existing mutual visibility algorithms under mobility faults and our proposed approach.

2026-10-06.title: A Bird's-Eye View of Iterative Reward Design
2026-10-06.authors: Logan Mondal Bhamidipaty , Lauren Robson , Linda Petrini , Shengrui Lyu , Kamal Ndousse
2026-10-06.abstract: Designing effective reward functions in RL typically requires substantial expertise and trial and error. Recent work automates this process with LLM-based systems that generate and iteratively improve reward code using policy feedback. However, these methods are often hard to compare because they differ in implementation details, feedback assumptions, and evaluation environments. To address this, we introduce a B enchmark for I terative R eward D esign ( BIRD ) that expresses existing methods in a unified configuration and evaluation space. 1 1 1 https://github.com/safety-research/bird This lets us compare algorithms directly, ablate individual design choices, and prototype new components under matched feedback conditions and policy-training budgets. Across MuJoCo, Meta-World, Assistax, and HumanoidBench, we identify a small set of simple design choices that consistently improve performance. Combining these choices yields significantly better performance than the evaluated methods from prior work. Our results highlight the strength of simple baselines and motivate further study of when additional algorithmic complexity improves iterative reward design.
2026-10-06.introduction:
A central difficulty in reinforcement learning (RL) is designing reward functions that support efficient learning while remaining aligned with designer intent. At one extreme, a reward may be easy to optimize but poorly aligned: shaping terms and proxy rewards can improve sample efficiency but may bias the objective ( Ng et al., 1999 ; Pan et al., 2022 ) or induce reward hacking ( Amodei et al., 2016 ; Skalse et al., 2022 ) . At the other extreme, a reward may be well aligned but difficult to optimize: binary completion flags in robotics, for example, can be too sparse to support efficient policy learning without heuristics ( Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ) . Navigating this tradeoff often requires trial and error, which is unsurprisingly both laborious and error-prone even for expert designers ( Booth et al., 2023 ) .

This process, known as iterative reward design (IRD), follows a basic loop: propose a reward, train a policy, evaluate its behavior, revise the reward, and repeat as needed ( Figure 1 ). 2 2 2 Sometimes humorously referred to as “graduate student descent.” To reduce the burden on human designers, methods like Eureka ( Ma et al., 2024a ) and Text2Reward ( Xie et al., 2024 ) have proposed using LLMs to automate reward generation and revision. These rewards typically far surpass human-written ones and have thus inspired a large body of work on LLM-assisted IRD ( Hazra et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Jaswal et al., 2026 ) .

The growing literature offers a broad menu for generating, evaluating, and updating reward functions, but provides limited guidance about which design choices work reliably. Within papers, benchmarks and ablations typically test design choices within particular algorithms and environments, leaving unclear whether those choices also improve other algorithms, remain effective in other environments, or retain their benefits when combined. Across papers, differences in feedback assumptions, harness implementations, model backbones, and policy-training procedures make it difficult to compare methods fairly or isolate the effects of individual choices. Moreover, higher benchmark performance does not by itself establish better alignment with the intended objectives. These limitations leave four central questions unresolved: (1) Which IRD methods perform best across tasks? ; (2) Which design choices drive performance? ; (3) Can useful design choices be combined into better methods? ; and (4) Does better performance mean better alignment?

To address these questions, we develop a B enchmark for I terative R eward D esign ( BIRD ), built around a shared, configurable implementation of the IRD loop. BIRD represents each method as a configuration specifying how to generate candidate rewards, train and evaluate policies, and select and revise rewards. When methods share a design choice, they reuse its implementation. Researchers can therefore reproduce existing methods, modify individual choices, or combine choices from different methods within the same framework. BIRD pairs this implementation with a common evaluation protocol, enabling comparisons under matched feedback conditions and policy-training budgets.

Our contributions are fourfold.

We introduce BIRD ( Section 3 ), a unified framework for implementing, comparing, ablating, and developing IRD methods, with implementations for 14 published methods ( Appendix C ) and evaluation procedures for MuJoCo ( Todorov et al., 2012 ) , Meta-World ( Yu et al., 2019 ) , Assistax ( Hinckeldey et al., 2025 ) , and HumanoidBench ( Sferrazza et al., 2024 ) .

We compare 6 existing methods ( Section 4.1 ) and ablate 30 design choices ( Section 4.2 ) under matched experimental conditions. We find that many design choices, both from the literature and our own proposals, produce small or inconclusive effects when deployed across new tasks and algorithmic stacks, and that only a small set of simple design choices clearly helps. This suggests that intuition-driven design choices often fail to transfer across tasks and methods, and that systematic empirical benchmarking is a necessary complement.

Using BIRD, we develop two novel IRD algorithms ERA-U and ERA-S (unsupervised and supervised variants) that achieve significantly better performance over established baselines in their respective categories on the environment suites ( Section 4.3 ).

To preliminarily assess IRD alignment, we conduct a small human study ( n = 2 ) (n=2) . Consistent with prior work on specification gaming ( Krakovna et al., 2020 ) , we find that rewards designed by IRD methods can induce policies that score highly on benchmarks through unnatural or even harmful behavior ( Section 4.4 ).

# 2 Preliminaries

We assume most readers have a passing familiarity with RL and so omit the usual MDP and policy definition regurgitation; interested readers and those new to the field can consult Sutton and Barto (2018) . Instead, we focus on what iterative reward design is and how the process works. 3 3 3 We have written a “truly marvelous [prior work], which this margin is too narrow to contain” ( Appendix B ).

Iterative reward design (IRD) is the process of designing rewards by trial and error based on policy feedback, often using LLMs or VLMs.

Before walking through the stages, we strongly encourage readers to skim the terminology table in Appendix A , which clarifies frequently reused terms such as “design choice” and “reference reward.” As illustrated in Figure 1 , IRD algorithms can typically be decomposed into the following stages.

1. Reward generation. The process starts with an LLM or VLM proposing candidate rewards from a task description and information about the environment, often its source code. Any reward shipped with the environment (its reference reward ) is withheld, so the model designs rewards from scratch. Rewards are usually represented as Python functions (see Figure 2 ). On the first iteration, the model works only from what it is given about the task; on later iterations, it can also draw on feedback from earlier attempts.

2. Reward verification. Training a policy under every generated reward can get expensive, so some methods first screen candidates to decide which are worth training on. Checking for coding errors is particularly useful when using weaker models. Other checks try to estimate reward quality before training a policy. CARD, for example, retains a buffer of trajectories from earlier iterations and validates candidate rewards by checking whether they rank successful trajectories above failed ones ( Sun et al., 2025 ) .

3. Policy training. The surviving candidates then move on to policy training, which is essentially vanilla RL. One or more policies are trained under each reward function. The design choices at this stage are fairly standard: which RL algorithm to use (e.g., PPO or SAC), how many environment steps to train for, and whether to train from scratch or warm-start from an earlier policy.

4. Reward evaluation. In the next stage, methods determine how well each reward worked. Here methods split into two kinds. Supervised IRD methods use the benchmark score, which grades trained policies against the task ( Appendix A ); Eureka, for example, combines it with statistics about reward components over the course of training ( Ma et al., 2024a ) . Unsupervised methods never access the benchmark score: RDA, for example, replaces it with a VLM that rates task completion from image frames sampled uniformly across a policy rollout ( Lee et al., 2026 ) .

5. Reward selection. After curating information about each candidate, methods then select a winner or a set of elite candidates. A common design choice is to greedily keep the highest-scoring candidate, as in Eureka and RDA ( Ma et al., 2024a ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . Other methods use populations or search trees to keep more candidates in play ( Hazra et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) . The comparison itself can also be based on preferences: REvolve uses human preferences ( Hazra et al., 2025 ) , while Gran Turismo 4 4 4 Ma et al. (2025) do not name their method, so we refer to it by its environment: Gran Turismo. uses VLM preferences and then collects human feedback on the selected policy ( Ma et al., 2025 ) . These choices determine which rewards become the starting point for the next round of generation.

2026-10-06.title: SelectOccFlow: Selective Spatiotemporal Aggregation for 3D Occupancy and Scene Flow Prediction
2026-10-06.authors: Yuhang Wang , Kai Luo , Yuanfan Zheng , Kailun Yang
2026-10-06.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.abstract: Comprehensive 3D scene understanding for autonomous driving requires modeling geometry, semantics, and motion. However, camera-based occupancy and scene flow prediction are sensitive to unreliable spatial and temporal aggregation, caused by semantically incompatible image features, misaligned historical observations, and incomplete voxel structures. To address this issue, we propose SelectOccFlow, a selective spatiotemporal aggregation framework that progressively refines contextual evidence across image, temporal, and voxel domains. To obtain semantically compatible image evidence, we design Semantic-Guided Sampling (SGS) to regulate feature sampling with semantic priors. Since reliable image evidence alone cannot resolve temporal inconsistency, we then present State-Conditioned Temporal Aggregation (SCTA) to selectively retrieve historical evidence according to voxel states. To further enhance the structural completeness of voxel representations, we introduce Extent-Aware Spatial Aggregation (ESA), which exploits directional structural support to refine foreground geometry. Experiments on OpenOcc demonstrate that SelectOccFlow achieves a state-of-the-art OccScore of 44.9 44.9 , improving the previous best by + 4.2 % +4.2\% . It also maintains competitive occupancy performance on Occ3D-nus and improves the mean OccScore under nuScenes-C corruptions by + 11.1 % +11.1\% , demonstrating improved robustness to visual corruptions. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/muchen1021/SelectOccFlow .
2026-10-06.introduction:
Reliable autonomous driving requires a comprehensive understanding of the geometry, semantics, and motion of surrounding environments.
Camera-based 3D semantic occupancy prediction provides a dense voxel-level representation of scene geometry and semantic categories [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
However, occupancy primarily describes the instantaneous scene state and does not explicitly characterize motion at occupied voxels.
This limitation is particularly important in dynamic traffic, where geometrically similar scenes can evolve differently.
As illustrated in Fig. (a), similar occupancy states may correspond to different scene flows, implying distinct interactions with the ego path and potential risks.
Scene flow complements occupancy by estimating the voxel-wise direction and magnitude of motion [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
Together, 3D occupancy and scene flow provide a more complete representation for dynamic scene understanding.

Recovering this representation from multi-view images requires effective aggregation of complementary spatial and temporal evidence.
Existing camera-based approaches extract image features and lift them into BEV or 3D voxel space [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] , while temporal extensions incorporate historical observations [ 4 , 13 , 14 ] .
However, contextual evidence is not uniformly reliable.
Spatial evidence can be incompatible across object boundaries, whereas temporal evidence can become unreliable due to independent object motion, changing occlusions, or degraded observations.
Indiscriminate aggregation may therefore propagate errors throughout the prediction pipeline.
The key challenge is thus not only where and how to aggregate spatial and temporal evidence, but also which evidence to select at each stage.

Spatial incompatibility can arise both before and after image-to-3D transformation.
Before lifting, image features near object boundaries or crowded regions may mix foreground, background, and neighboring objects.
Adverse visual conditions can further degrade visual evidence [ 15 , 16 ] , thereby aggravating feature mixing near object boundaries.
After lifting, incomplete or noisy voxel features require spatial support, while indiscriminate aggregation may propagate errors across semantic boundaries.
Reliable spatial aggregation should therefore preserve semantically compatible image evidence before lifting and exploit structurally consistent voxel support afterward to recover foreground geometry.

Historical observations provide complementary cues for estimating scene dynamics, but their reliability depends on temporal alignment and observation quality.
Although ego-motion compensation aligns static structures, independently moving objects may remain misaligned across frames.
Changing occlusions and degraded visual observations can further produce incomplete or noisy histories [ 17 ] .
Moreover, temporal evidence varies across voxel states: stable voxels benefit from longer histories, motion-sensitive voxels require recent observations and adaptive spatial sampling, while free-dominant voxels need only limited temporal support.
A shared temporal range and sampling strategy may retrieve stale, misaligned, or noisy evidence.
Temporal aggregation should therefore adapt historical retrieval to voxel states through state-specific temporal ranges and spatial sampling.

Based on these observations, we propose SelectOccFlow , a selective spatiotemporal aggregation framework for 3D occupancy and scene flow prediction. It adaptively selects context according to spatial compatibility and temporal reliability.
Specifically, Semantic-Guided Sampling (SGS) uses semantic priors to regulate image-space sampling before lifting.
State-Conditioned Temporal Aggregation (SCTA) retrieves historical evidence with state-specific temporal ranges and spatial sampling.
Extent-Aware Spatial Aggregation (ESA) exploits structural voxel support to refine geometry.

Extensive experiments on OpenOcc [ 1 ] and Occ3D-nus [ 3 ] validate the effectiveness of SelectOccFlow for 3D occupancy and scene flow prediction.
As shown in Fig. (b), SelectOccFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance on OpenOcc across occupancy (RayIoU), scene flow (mAVE), and overall evaluation, with an OccScore of 44.9 44.9 .
It also maintains competitive occupancy performance on Occ3D-nus.
Under nuScenes-C corruptions [ 16 ] , SelectOccFlow further improves the mean OccScore across six corruption types on OpenOcc by 11.1 % 11.1\% , demonstrating improved robustness under degraded visual conditions.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose SelectOccFlow , a selective spatiotemporal aggregation framework that selects evidence based on spatial compatibility and temporal reliability.

We develop SGS , SCTA , and ESA for progressive image, temporal, and voxel aggregation, regulating sampling, historical retrieval, and voxel refinement.

Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on OpenOcc, competitive performance on Occ3D-nus, and improved robustness on nuScenes-C.

1. We propose SelectOccFlow , a selective spatiotemporal aggregation framework that selects evidence based on spatial compatibility and temporal reliability.

2. We develop SGS , SCTA , and ESA for progressive image, temporal, and voxel aggregation, regulating sampling, historical retrieval, and voxel refinement.

3. Extensive experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on OpenOcc, competitive performance on Occ3D-nus, and improved robustness on nuScenes-C.

# II Related Work

## II-A 3D Occupancy and Scene Flow Prediction

Camera-based 3D occupancy prediction methods lift features from monocular images [ 12 , 18 , 19 ] or surround-view observations [ 8 , 10 , 11 ] into 3D space to estimate voxel-wise occupancy states and semantic categories, providing dense representations of surrounding environments. Recent approaches further extend occupancy prediction through unified panoptic, compact, and sparse formulations [ 9 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . However, occupancy representations primarily describe scene geometry and semantics at a given time without explicitly encoding the motion of occupied voxels.

Scene flow complements occupancy prediction by estimating the motion of occupied voxels over time. Recent methods incorporate scene flow into occupancy frameworks to model semantic geometry and scene dynamics within a unified representation [ 23 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 13 ] .
Despite this progress, occupancy and scene flow remain closely coupled because inaccurate spatial structures can impair motion estimation, while unreliable temporal cues may hinder the recovery of both 3D occupancy and scene flow. Consequently, reliable dynamic scene understanding requires effective modeling of spatial observations and temporal evidence.

## II-B Spatiotemporal Modeling

Spatiotemporal modeling has been widely explored in camera-based 3D perception to enhance scene representation and dynamic understanding [ 4 , 13 , 24 , 25 ] .
Existing methods model spatial context through dense BEV or voxel representations [ 8 , 11 , 24 ] and sparse query-based aggregation [ 22 , 26 , 27 ] .
Dense representations aggregate context over structured grids, whereas sparse queries retrieve features around task-specific reference locations. However, spatial compatibility during feature aggregation before and after lifting remains less explored, and evidence from a single frame may be incomplete or ambiguous.

Temporal modeling mitigates this limitation by incorporating historical observations to complement current evidence and capture scene evolution.
Existing methods encode temporal context through recurrent BEV features [ 24 , 28 ] , aligned multi-frame perspective features [ 25 , 29 ] , or propagated object queries [ 30 , 31 ] . For occupancy prediction, recent approaches further employ multi-frame streaming temporal attention [ 13 ] , perform sparse voxel updates [ 4 ] , or introduce historical predictions as memory priors [ 32 , 33 ] .
Although effective, these methods determine how history is represented and fused, while variations in the relevance of historical evidence across voxel states remain insufficiently addressed.
Degraded visual observations caused by adverse weather, illumination changes, and sensor failures [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 34 , 35 ] can weaken spatial evidence and reduce the reliability of historical cues, while scene dynamics increase discrepancies between current and historical evidence.
