2026-10-06.title: Latent Safety Filters: When a Lossy Encoder Admits a Transferable Certificate
2026-10-06.authors: Johannes Mootz , Zahra Nili Ahmadabadi , Reza Akhavian
2026-10-06.subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.abstract:
Latent safety filters certify safety on a learned low-dimensional representation of the state, enabling constraints that resist analytic description.
Because the encoder is lossy, a filter can report safe while the physical state is unsafe, with no detectable model error.
Existing transfer conditions leave the effect of discarded safety information implicit.
We ask when a lossy encoder admits a safety certificate that transfers to the physical system, and show the answer is governed by the detectability of the discarded safety-relevant dynamics.
We construct a system whose latent model is exact and whose latent signals always report safe, while the physical state becomes arbitrarily unsafe.
For this system no certificate exists and no monitor downstream of the encoder can detect the failure.
When the discarded dynamics contract, a latent barrier certifies true safety up to two explicit margins, one for the latent-model error and one for the variation of safety across states the encoder cannot distinguish.
In the linear case and under boundedness and non-degeneracy conditions, every calibrated barrier transfers with a finite margin when the safety-relevant subspace is detectable, and none does otherwise.
On learned cartpole encoders, the model error does not indicate for which representations the estimated bound is non-vacuous, while the second margin does.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Latent safety filters replace the physical state with a learned representation and certify safety there.
This allows them to encode specifications that resist an analytical description, such as not spilling a container [ 1 , 2 ] , or not overheating its contents [ 2 ] , working directly from high-dimensional observations.
They have been realized as Hamilton-Jacobi reachability filters [ 1 ] , as smooth latent control barrier functions (CBFs) [ 3 ] , and as in-distribution barrier functions [ 4 ] .
Extensions add out-of-distribution awareness [ 5 ] , pre-trained vision backbones [ 6 ] , and runtime constraint adaptation [ 7 ] .
Often, encoder and latent dynamics are learned jointly as a world model, and the constraint is specified in its latent space [ 1 , 5 ] .

The guarantee must ultimately hold for the physical system and not for its representation.
Lutkus et al. give dynamics-aware conjugacy conditions and transfer a latent barrier or Lyapunov certificate back to the state, while charging a slack term for the latent-model error [ 8 ] .
Reduced-order models and simulation functions carry control barrier functions to a complex plant in the same way [ 9 , 10 ] .
In these works the measured quantity is the latent-model error, and the certificate holds with a conservative margin.
Reed et al. verify temporal-logic specifications on a finite abstraction of learned latent dynamics, with the encoder restricted to be convex so that the regions of interest are represented correctly [ 11 ] .

However, a margin on the model error controls only the part of safety that the representation can see, and restricting the encoder class does not help with an encoder that is already trained.
A learned encoder compresses information and is lossy, so distinct physical states can collapse to a single representation z z .
An encoder trained for reconstruction, or for the augmentation-invariance objectives common to DINOv2 backbones [ 12 ] , does not necessarily preserve safety-relevant information.
A barrier certified on the latent space can then read safe while the physical state is unsafe. If the motion of the representation is reproduced exactly, it can do so with no detectable model error.

Kim et al. demonstrate such failures on hardware [ 2 ] .
They identify two failure modes: estimation gaps, where the current observation does not reveal a safety-critical quantity, and prediction gaps, where a failure is visible once it occurs but cannot be anticipated.
A mutual-information measure of safety observability diagnoses the first and a rollout-based measure of predictability the second, and the countermeasures are privileged multimodal supervision and conformal calibration.
Both diagnostics are empirical, and their closing question, when a learned representation is sufficient for control, is the one we formalize for safety.
Our conditions add what an information measure does not account for, the dynamics of the missing feature.
A missing feature that contracts costs a finite margin, while one that is hidden, unstable and unbounded in the safety variable h h admits no certificate, and no calibration downstream of the encoder can mitigate it, since no causal function of z z and the input u u separates the safe from the unsafe trajectory.

Wu et al. evaluate a latent certificate in the worst case over the encoder image of a state-uncertainty set, and uncover point-based certificates that report safe when they should not [ 13 ] .
Their set is a bounded estimation error around a state estimate, while the fiber of a lossy encoder is fixed by the encoder, need not be bounded, and is not reduced by better sensing.

The prior literature leaves two questions open. The first is whether the representation retains enough of the safety variable h h for a latent certificate to stay valid [ 2 ] .
This is a weaker demand than reconstructing the full state.
The measurement-robust and output-feedback literature answers the related question of how a bound on estimation error becomes a safety margin [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] , but it assumes an explicit state estimate and not a learned representation.
The second question is which discarded directions are harmless to safety and which destroy it.
The geometric tools already exist: invariant foliations [ 18 ] and horizontal–vertical decompositions [ 19 ] .
For filters that certify an output of the physical state, this question is already answered.
Such a filter leaves the internal dynamics unconstrained, and [ 20 ] gives minimum-phase conditions under which the full state stays bounded.
There the filter’s own action drives a measured internal state unbounded, while the failure studied here occurs under zero input in a part of the state that the representation does not carry.

We show that detectability, in the sense of [ 21 , 22 ] , answers the second question and governs whether a certificate can exist at all.
The fiber defect, the variation of true safety across the states the encoder cannot distinguish, answers the first question and measures what an existing certificate guarantees.
Our contributions are the following.

We identify the discarded directions that defeat transfer.
A direction unobservable from the representation, unstable, and with true safety unbounded below along the fiber admits no certificate at all ( Proposition 1 ).
No causal monitor of ( z , u ) (z,u) can detect the failure ( Corollary 1 ).

We identify the discarded directions that defeat transfer.
A direction unobservable from the representation, unstable, and with true safety unbounded below along the fiber admits no certificate at all ( Proposition 1 ).
No causal monitor of ( z , u ) (z,u) can detect the failure ( Corollary 1 ).

We prove a transfer bound for the recoverable case ( Theorem 1 ). A latent control barrier function bounds true safety from below, up to two explicit margins, one for the latent-model error and one for the fiber defect.

We give conditions under which the bound applies.
Contracting discarded dynamics keep the defect finite ( Lemma 1 ), and in the linear case, under boundedness and non-degeneracy conditions, every calibrated barrier transfers with a finite margin when the safety-relevant subspace is detectable, and none does otherwise ( Proposition 2 ).

2026-10-06.title: CurveCodec 2: Skeleton-agnostic animation compression with a learned entropy model
2026-10-06.authors: Mingyi Shi , Huancheng Lin , Xuelin Chen , Taku Komura
2026-10-06.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract:
Skeletal motion is stored as every joint’s transform at every frame, yet most of it is implied by the body rather than by what the motion is about. Compression is one way to ask what a motion must still say once the body is known, and a production codec is where that question has to be answered for any skeleton, with a stated bound on the error. Our earlier codec, CurveCodec, reconstructed each joint curve from sparse anchors with a learned prior. It matched the mean error of ACL, the production library of modern game engines, but not its worst case, and it counted its payload as floating-point values rather than as bits.
Here we ask where the redundancy of skeletal motion lies, and which part of a codec a learned model should take over. A measured anatomy of ACL and a series of controlled experiments give three answers. At production precision the largest saving comes from predicting each quantized curve from its own past, and the second from choosing per joint, in closed loop through the hierarchy, which samples not to code. On the gaps such an encoder leaves, interpolation has little left to find: a nearest-neighbour oracle with millions of training samples as memory is no better than linear interpolation there, and none of the learned in-betweeners we tried paid for itself. What a network does learn is the distribution of the residuals the codec must send.
CurveCodec 2 puts these findings into one codec. Every sub-track becomes a curve, rotations in the log map and translations in centimetres, quantized in closed loop and thinned to rate–distortion-selected keys, and its prediction residuals are entropy-coded under a small learned model whose integer inference is bit-exact across platforms. Two contracts are verified on every decoded clip: ACL’s own worst case per joint, within a stated tolerance, or ACL’s mean error per clip.
On a held-out test side of 4,472 4{,}472 clips from 33 33 datasets, CurveCodec 2 needs 0.37 × 0.37\times ACL’s bytes at ACL’s default precision of 0.01 0.01 cm under the worst-case contract and 0.22 × 0.22\times at 0.1 0.1 cm under the mean contract. It decodes whole clips on one CPU core, typically in a fraction of a second, and transfers without retraining to a species absent from training.
2026-10-06.introduction:
A skeletal animation clip stores rotations and translations for tens to hundreds of joints at every sample, yet much of this is not what the motion is about. A performer decides what to do; the body, its morphology and its dynamics, determines most of how each joint gets from one place to the next. Compressing these data matters in production, where animation libraries face strict memory and streaming budgets, and in motion research, where corpora reach hundreds of hours and a model should spend its capacity on the decisions rather than on kinematics the body already implies. A codec is one way to probe this separation: what it must still send under a stated error bound is at least what the body did not predict. This is our motivation, not a claim the bit counts prove. If the body is only a prior, the representation should not be tied to one body: a production codec must serve arbitrary skeletons and motion without retraining, and it must bound its error, because a single visible pop on one joint is a defect regardless of how small the average error is.

ACL ( Frechette, 2023 ) is the industry standard. It folds the sub-tracks that do not move, reduces the range of the rest per clip and per segment, and quantizes each joint with one of a fixed set of bit widths under a per-joint error threshold. It decodes a pose in microseconds, but it models neither time nor the statistics of its own symbols. Learned motion encoders ( Ling et al., 2020 ; Yao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2024 ) take the opposite trade: their latent priors couple the representation to a training skeleton and domain, and they do not reach production precision.

Our previous work, CurveCodec ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , placed the learned prior on the smallest skeleton-independent unit of motion, the local joint curve, and reconstructed each curve from sparse anchors with a shared transformer. It reached three times ACL’s ratio at matched mean error, but its worst case exceeded ACL’s, its payload was counted in floating-point values rather than entropy-coded bits, and its decoder needed a GPU rather than a CPU core.

This paper asks a different question: where is the redundancy in skeletal motion, and which part of a codec should a learned model take over? We answer it by measurement, treating the codec as an instrument: under an explicit error contract and an exact bit count, every candidate structure of motion either pays or does not. We dissect ACL stage by stage and test every place where a learned component could enter. Three findings shape the result.
First, ACL’s ratio comes almost entirely from folding and from range reduction with variable bit widths. Its widths are nearly tight for independent samples, so an entropy coder on top of ACL’s own symbols would gain little; a substantially smaller stream needs its own quantizer, one whose integers remain predictable in time.
Second, at production precision the largest saving comes from predicting each curve from its own past, and the next from choosing, per joint and in closed loop through the hierarchy, which samples to omit. Leaving a sample out is by far the cheapest way to spend error, and its share of the stream grows as the precision loosens, until the two are comparable at the loosest precision we use.
Third, on the gaps such an encoder leaves, interpolation has little left to find. A nearest-neighbour oracle with millions of training samples as memory, which clearly beats cubic interpolation on random gaps, is no better than linear interpolation on the gaps the encoder actually leaves, and the learned in-betweeners we placed inside the codec did not pay. On our data, the in-betweener at the core of CurveCodec has little left to learn; what a network does learn is the distribution of the residuals that the codec still has to send.

These findings lead to CurveCodec 2. Every animated sub-track is coded as a curve: rotations in the log map, which removes the precision floor of ACL’s dropped quaternion component; a quantization step and a key set chosen in closed loop against the object-space error of the whole subtree; and prediction residuals coded with rANS under a small learned model of the curve’s own past, a causal transformer or, in the worst-case configuration, an MLP. The model sees no joint identity, so the codec is skeleton-agnostic, and its integer inference is bit-exact on ARM and x86. Two contracts are verified on every decoded clip: ACL’s own worst case per joint, within a stated tolerance, or ACL’s mean error per clip. A clip that fails is re-encoded with a margin or stored as ACL’s stream, and every number we report includes this fallback.

On a corpus of 906 906 hours from 33 33 datasets with a held-out test side, CurveCodec 2 needs 0.37 × 0.37\times ACL’s bytes at ACL’s default precision of 0.01 0.01 cm under the worst-case contract, and 0.22 × 0.22\times at 0.1 0.1 cm under either contract; against ACL with its default keyframe stripping the ratios are slightly larger and the picture is the same. It decodes on a CPU, typically a clip in a fraction of a second on one core, but only whole clips: it is a storage and distribution format decoded at load time, not a replacement for ACL’s constant-time sampling.

Our contributions are:

A quantitative anatomy of motion redundancy , measuring where a production codec’s bits go and which structure a codec exploited in our hands: temporal predictability and, increasingly as the precision loosens, per-joint sample sparsity did; interpolation from the decoded neighbourhood, cross-joint structure, and transforms under a worst-case criterion did not.

CurveCodec 2, a closed-loop, skeleton-agnostic rate–distortion codec under two explicit error contracts, with a stated fallback for the clips that fail.

A learned entropy model in the role where a network pays : small, causal, and bit-exact across platforms, it models the distribution of the residuals the codec must send, the one place where, in our measurements, a network consistently earns its cost.

A corpus-scale benchmark against ACL , with audits of ACL’s configuration and of our own contracts, and same-core speed.

# 2. Related Work

## 2.1. Hand-engineered Animation Compression

Before deep learning, animation compression removed temporal redundancy, inter-joint redundancy, and perceptually insignificant detail while keeping the motion faithful.
Mesh compression began with static connectivity and geometry ( Rossignac, 1999 ; Karni and Gotsman, 2000 ) ; animated meshes were then compressed through their vertex trajectories, by principal components ( Alexa and Müller, 2000 ) or space-time prediction ( Ibarria and Rossignac, 2003 ) . Arikan (2006) moved the problem to skeletal motion: joint angles were converted into virtual marker trajectories, fitted with cubic Bézier curves, and projected into clustered PCA subspaces.
Later work exploited low-dimensional structure with segment-level PCA and spline interpolation ( Liu and McMillan, 2006 ) , quadratic Bézier break-and-fit curves ( Khan, 2016 ) , wavelet coefficient selection ( Beaudoin et al., 2007 ; Lee and Lasenby, 2008 ) , and wavelets guided by perception ( Firouzmanesh et al., 2011 ) ; others indexed repeated motion patterns across a database ( Gu et al., 2009 ; Lin et al., 2011 ) .
ACL ( Frechette, 2023 ) is the production standard. It prioritizes per-track processing and constant-time random access over compression ratio, and Sec. 5.1 quantifies where its bits go.
Our keys relate to keyframe extraction ( Lim and Thalmann, 2001 ; Halit and Capin, 2011 ) and curve simplification ( Barkowsky et al., 2000 ) , which choose samples from a local error or saliency criterion. CurveCodec 2 instead chooses them by rate–distortion optimization against the object-space error of the whole subtree, and Sec. 5.2 shows that this closed loop, not the key representation itself, carries the gain. Unlike transform codecs, which we find lose to sparse keys under a worst-case criterion, CurveCodec 2 keeps the time domain and predicts each sample from its own past.

## 2.2. Learned Motion Representations and Codecs

Motion manifolds and deep motion representations show that valid character motion occupies a much smaller space than raw joint rotations ( Holden et al., 2015 ; Holden et al., 2016 ) . VAE-style priors support character control, action-conditioned synthesis, and pose estimation ( Ling et al., 2020 ; Petrovich et al., 2021 ; Rempe et al., 2021 ) ; tokenizers with vector or residual quantization compress motion into discrete codes ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2024 ) ; phase-based models organize motion by periodic timing ( Starke et al., 2022 ; Shi et al., 2023 ) ; and Learned Motion Matching ( Holden et al., 2020 ) amortizes an animation database into networks. Cross-skeleton methods learn representations for retargeting ( Villegas et al., 2018 ; Aberman et al., 2020 ; Lee et al., 2023 ) .
These representations target synthesis, control, or transfer at pose level, not a decodable bitstream at a stated precision; SAME ( Lee et al., 2023 ) in particular learns an embedding shared across skeletons, which is a different goal from ours rather than a competing codec. The learned encoders measured in CurveCodec ( Shi et al., 2026 ) under the shell metric reconstruct with errors two orders of magnitude above the 0.01 0.01 cm of a production codec, and the residual-VQ tokenizer we built has a precision floor of about 1.3 % 1.3\,\% of a track’s RMS (Sec. 5.4 ); we do not extend these bounds to methods we did not measure.
Implicit neural representations fit signals with coordinate networks ( Park et al., 2019 ; Tancik et al., 2020 ; Sitzmann et al., 2020 ; Dupont et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2021 ) , and NeMF ( He et al., 2022 ) applies the idea to kinematic motion. We find the same fidelity floor for per-window neural fields.
CurveCodec ( Shi et al., 2026 ) is our direct predecessor. It made the learned prior skeleton-agnostic by working on single sub-tracks, and reconstructed each from a first-frame state, a Fourier descriptor, and extrema anchors with a masked transformer, in the spirit of learned in-betweening ( Harvey et al., 2020 ) . CurveCodec 2 keeps the per-sub-track, skeleton-agnostic unit but moves the learned prior from the interpolator to the probability model, for reasons that Sec. 5.3 measures on our data.

## 2.3. Entropy Coding and Learned Probability Models

Lossless coding separates modelling from coding: an arithmetic coder ( Witten et al., 1987 ) or an asymmetric numeral system ( Duda, 2013 ) spends − log 2 ⁡ P -\log_{2}P bits per symbol, so the compression depends only on how well the model P P predicts the data. Predictive lossless coders such as LOCO-I / JPEG-LS ( Weinberger et al., 2000 ) and CALIC ( Wu and Memon, 1997 ) combine a fixed predictor with a context model of the residual, the structure CurveCodec 2 adopts per curve.
Learned image compression ( Ballé et al., 2017 ; Ballé et al., 2018 ; Minnen et al., 2018 ) showed that much of the gain of a learned codec comes from the learned probability model, and that decoding with a network requires deterministic, integer inference to keep encoder and decoder in sync across platforms ( Ballé et al., 2019 ) . General-purpose neural compressors use recurrent or transformer models as the probability model of a byte stream ( Goyal et al., 2019 ; Bellard, 2021 ; Delétang et al., 2024 ) .
Learned probability models have entered animation compression before: Chen et al. ( Chen et al., 2022 ) compress motion-capture sequences with a learned continuous-time latent model, and Qin et al. ( Qin et al., 2025 ) code mesh animations with a deep entropy model over vertex trajectories; neither holds an object-space worst-case bound through a skeleton. CurveCodec 2 combines per-curve learned residual probabilities with hierarchy-aware quantization and key selection under explicitly verified object-space error constraints, and our experiments indicate that for skeletal motion the probability model is the role where a network pays, while the learned interpolators, transforms, tokenizers, and neural fields we tried did not pay for themselves.

2026-10-06.title: Towards Safer Autonomous Driving in an Open World: A Dual-Process Approach
2026-10-06.authors: Simon Janssen , Michiel Braat , Chris van der Ploeg , Serge Thill , Jan-Pieter Paardekooper
2026-10-06.comment: Accepted for publication at the IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITSC), 2026
2026-10-06.abstract: Before autonomous driving systems can be deployed on public roads, it is vital that these systems comply with safety standards, traffic rules, and social norms. Although neural networks trained on large amounts of driving data perform well in routine driving tasks, these models often struggle in novel situations that are not well-represented in the data. In this work, we propose a novel framework that combines a neural network for intuitive, learning-based planning in routine driving tasks with model predictive control for reasoning-based planning in unfamiliar situations, inspired by Dual Process Theory. A meta-cognitive component is designed to switch between the two, using a knowledge graph to reason about contextual risk based on explicit perceptual information and relevant traffic rules and social norms. Contextual risk is represented through risk fields, guiding both the switching mechanism in the meta-cognitive component and compliance with safety standards, traffic rules, and social norms in the reasoning-based planner. The effectiveness of our framework is tested in CARLA for variations of a typical out-of-distribution situations involving (emergency) vehicles running a red light. We show that the novel architecture reduces the number of collisions in the scenarios by 89% and improves compliance with the special right-of-way rules, compared to the NN-only planner.
2026-10-06.introduction:
To fully automate driving, ADS need to be able to navigate complex and dynamic environments while also ensuring safe and collision-free behavior, obeying traffic rules, and taking into account driving requirements such as passenger comfort and route progression. Advances in machine learning have enabled significant progress in addressing these challenges. While NN have been used extensively in perception [ 17 ] , they are also increasingly being explored for planning [ 3 ] . NN -based planners can potentially learn more complex and human-like driving behaviors that are difficult to capture directly through hand-crafted rules or objective functions [ 24 ] . Moreover, NN enable end-to-end architectures, which unify perception, motion prediction, and planning [ 5 , 20 ] ,
making them less prone to error propagation and misalignment issues arising from inconsistencies between different modules.

Despite the large potential of NN for planning, important challenges remain. One of these challenges is how to improve generalization performance and robustness in out-of-distribution situations. ADS will inevitably encounter novel situations due to the complexity and unpredictability of the real world. To prevent serious accidents and fatalities in these situations, safe and predictable behavior is essential. Whereas NN excel at finding statistical patterns between input and output, they often struggle to learn the deeper semantic meaning behind this input-output mapping. Hence, when faced with novel inputs, these networks may generalize learned patterns based on semantically irrelevant factors, leading to over-confident or incorrect predictions as a result.

To facilitate adaptivity in the open world and improve safety, we propose a hybrid framework that combines the strengths of NN and traditional planners. Specifically, an end-to-end network is used to generate complex and human-like trajectories in familiar situations, while an MPC ( MPC )-based planner is used to explicitly take into account contextual information encoded in risk fields to comply with safety standards, legal constraints, and human values in out-of-distribution situations. The integration of the two systems is guided by principles from Dual Process Theory [ 12 ] , which similarly suggests that human intelligence arises from an intuitive system (System I) relying on prior experience, and a reasoning-based system (System II) engaging in more elaborate logical reasoning. To decide when to switch between System I and System II, a MCC ( MCC ) is designed that uses the same risk fields as the MPC -based planner to determine the safety and social desirability of the trajectory predicted by the end-to-end network. The main contributions of this work are as follows:

A hybrid architecture is proposed that combines neural networks and symbolic reasoning to improve generalization and robustness in out-of-distribution situations.

A hybrid architecture is proposed that combines neural networks and symbolic reasoning to improve generalization and robustness in out-of-distribution situations.

A meta-cognitive component capable of evaluating the safety and social desirability of an end-to-end neural network prediction and decide when to switch to a reasoning-based system.

The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through simulation experiments in the CARLA simulator.

# II Related Work

## II-A End-to-End Autonomous Driving

End-to-end autonomous driving methods have recently emerged as a promising alternative to traditional modular pipelines, which separate perception, planning, and control. The two most prominent end-to-end approaches are imitation learning [ 10 , 5 ] and reinforcement learning [ 2 , 20 ] . Several methods directly optimize the planning task, omitting intermediate perception and motion prediction steps [ 26 ] . For example, CIL [ 5 ] uses a conditional imitation learning architecture to directly map an input image, input measurements, and a high-level control command to a corresponding output action. Other methods improve interpretability and robustness by learning auxiliary tasks such as object detection, semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and future occupancy prediction [ 16 , 10 ] .

## II-B Safety in Autonomous Driving

A popular approach to improve the interpretability and safety of ADS is to design explicit rules or cost functions that penalize collisions, deviations from the lane center, and violations of basic traffic rules, as well as other factors related to comfort and progress. Rules or cost functions can be integrated into the model architecture itself, such as in modular end-to-end architectures [ 9 , 11 ] . They can also be applied externally as a separate safety system [ 8 ] . For example, SafetyNet employs a simple rule-based fallback layer that can modify the predicted trajectory of an end-to-end network when it is dynamically infeasible, violates traffic rules, or has a high likelihood of collision [ 24 ] . FusionAssurance determines the final safe trajectory using an MPC with a cost function that aims to follow the trajectory predicted by an end-to-end neural network, achieve the desired speed, improve comfort, and avoid obstacles modeled with risk functions [ 27 ] .

Recently, VLM have been explored to act as a safety layer [ mei_continuously_2024 ] . Unlike other methods, VLM can leverage their advanced world knowledge and reasoning capabilities to provide more context-aware interpretations of situations [ 7 ] , which can subsequently be used to refine the trajectories generated by an end-to-end or modular architecture [ 19 ] . In this work, we also employ a reasoning-based system to act as a safety layer. However, we do not rely on VLM , as these may be slow to respond and may suffer from hallucinations [ 7 ] . Instead, we follow the work in [ 21 ] and use an MPC -based planner and a knowledge graph to generate context-aware trajectories. Although this may result in less human-like behavior, this shortcoming is acceptable when used as a safety system, where the main objective is to ensure safe and socially desirable behavior.

## II-C Trajectory Evaluation

A vital aspect of the dual system architecture is the decision when to switch between the NN -based planner and MPC -based planner. This ties into the concept of meta-cognition, as it requires knowing when the NN -based planner cannot make a reliable decision [ 15 ] . Previous work has explored approaches that switch control when a trajectory scoring function exceeds a pre-defined threshold value [ 8 ] . A key advantage of using a trajectory scoring function is that individual predictions can be evaluated on actual measures of risk or reward, rather than approximate measures such as novelty or uncertainty [ 13 ] . Approximate measures often implicitly assume that end-to-end networks always perform reliably or poorly in certain situations, which may not hold in practice.

In this work, we design an MCC that uses risk fields in the trajectory scoring function to decide when to switch to the MPC -based planner. Unlike other trajectory scoring functions [ 11 , 9 , 8 ] , contextual information derived from a knowledge graph is used to shape these risk fields. This allows us to detect not only potential collisions, but also applications of more complex traffic rules and social norms. The proposed trajectory scoring function intentionally excludes comfort and route progression measures, as these factors are not directly relevant to determining the safety of a trajectory and in this work not important enough to switch system.

2026-10-06.introduction:
Discrete optimal transport (OT) is a standard tool in machine learning,
statistics, imaging, and robotics [ 12 , 13 ] . The scalable
default for large instances is entropic regularization [ 7 ] :
the smooth problem is solved by the Sinkhorn iteration [ 6 ] , and—for speed—by accelerated coordinate variants
such as Greenkhorn [ 8 , 9 ] . Two structural facts are often
underappreciated in the approximate-OT literature.

Balanced unit-mass discrete OT is the assignment
problem. With n n sources and n n targets of unit mass, a transport plan is
a doubly stochastic matrix and the optimum is attained at a permutation
matrix (Birkhoff–von Neumann; Proposition 1 ). The problem is
therefore a bipartite minimum-weight perfect matching—a special case of
the classical assignment problem [ 10 ] , solvable exactly by
shortest-augmenting-path methods [ 2 ] and, in its general
(non-bipartite) form, by Edmonds’ Blossom algorithm [ 3 ] as
implemented in Blossom V [ 4 ] and VI [ 5 ] . Exact
solvers return the optimal integer plan and its exact value. (Bipartite
matching is a strict special case of general matching, so Blossom applies
directly, but dedicated bipartite solvers such as Jonker–Volgenant or
shortest-augmenting-path are typically faster on dense bipartite inputs; we
use Blossom VI for the sparse k k NN-pool experiments and SciPy’s
Jonker–Volgenant routine for dense solves.)

2026-10-06.title: Barrier-Shaped Recurrent Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Landing on a Heaving Ship Deck
2026-10-06.authors: Ritwik Shankar , Chiranjeev Prachand , Abhishek , Soumya Ranjan Sahoo
2026-10-06.comment: . Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA). Video: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: This paper addresses autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) rotorcrafts on a heaving ship deck using a recurrent policy trained via asymmetric actor-critic reinforcement learning: the critic sees 6 ​ s 6\,\mathrm{s} of future deck height during training, while the actor sees only what the onboard sensors provide in flight, a 17-dimensional state made of the vehicle’s position, velocity and attitude relative to the deck and outputs world-frame velocity and yaw-rate commands. Training is performed across 4096 parallel simulated environments, followed by fine-tuning in 16 environments with an onboard vision pipeline in the loop. A control-barrier-function (CBF) stopping margin on the deck-relative vertical state is incorporated at two stages: as a reward term during training, where it halves the median simulated contact speed relative to a policy trained without it, and as a runtime safety filter at deployment, evaluated at every control step to abort and retry the descent when the margin is violated. Because the autopilot’s disarm logic cannot detect the vehicle resting on a moving deck, proximity-based thrust cutoff at touchdown is commanded directly in the landing pipeline. The proposed approach is validated using a parallel-manipulator-platform-based deck emulator that reproduces the heaving motion of the ship deck (scaled to 0.70 ​ m 0.70\,\mathrm{m} peak-to-peak, 7.5 ​ s 7.5\,\mathrm{s} mean period) and a quadcopter UAV with an onboard camera. Across 31 motion-capture and 20 vision-based trials, the UAV landed every time, with median times to contact of 6.5 6.5\,\mathrm{} and 7.3 ​ s 7.3\,\mathrm{s} ; 77% and 50% landed on the first attempt, with mean deck-relative speeds of 0.29 0.29\,\mathrm{} and 0.27 ​ m / s 0.27\,\mathrm{m/s} , respectively, at the instant of thrust cutoff, which is the last speed under the policy’s control. Supplementary video: https://youtu.be/S5hDkrSZJt4
2026-10-06.introduction:
Autonomous landing of a vertical take-off and landing (VTOL) capable unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) on a moving ship deck matters for maritime logistics and naval recovery. The vehicle must track a deck that translates and rotates, choose when to descend, and touch down within tight limits on relative velocity, attitude, and deck size. For ship-deck motions such as roll (about X X ), pitch (about Y Y ), sway (along Y Y ), and surge (along X X ), the vehicle can null the relative translation it currently observes, and it can decide to stop or continue the descent according to the tilt it observes at that moment. That observation is a sufficient statistic for landing. Early deck-landing systems accordingly focused on recovering the relative deck pose and controlling the vehicle’s angular and horizontal motion. Monocular and marker-based methods established this pipeline on laboratory motion platforms, simulated decks, and wave-perturbed small surface vessels [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
These systems established the perception and feedback required for landing under observable angular and lateral deck motion. With vertical deck travel absent, the current relative pose remained sufficient for deciding the control response.

Horizontal motion is a tracking problem; heave (along Z Z ), on the other hand, is a timing problem because a poorly timed descent can bring the vehicle into contact with a rising or upward-accelerating deck at a high relative velocity. The quantity that determines contact is now the relative velocity at an instant that has not yet arrived, so the current relative pose no longer determines the correct action. A constant descent makes the difficulty concrete. Taking every sample of a measured ship-heave record [ 5 ] as an instant at which the vehicle could arrive, and descending at a constant 0.5 ​ m / s 0.5\,\mathrm{m/s} , the rate an off-the-shelf autopilot uses to land, the relative speed at contact exceeds 0.5 ​ m / s 0.5\,\mathrm{m/s} at half of them, because the deck is rising as often as it is falling. A landing attempt must therefore be timed against motion that has not yet occurred, and a descent must be abandoned once safe contact can no longer be achieved. The landing must also end by itself. An autopilot disarms only after the airframe stops moving, and a heaving deck keeps it moving, so the vehicle would sit on the deck with its motors still running and never disarm. The policy therefore cuts the thrust itself, once it is within 7 ​ cm 7\,\mathrm{cm} of the deck. Cutting at contact instead is possible, since the camera gives the relative height, but a vehicle that is still producing thrust when the gear meets a moving deck can slide or tip before it settles. Dropping the last few centimeters lets it arrive with enough weight on the gear to settle in place. This operational insight motivated the adoption of a proximity-based disarm logic. The policy steers the descent up to that instant, and the vehicle falls unpowered after it, so the speed the policy achieves and the speed at contact are two different numbers.

Classical approaches decompose this task into estimation, motion prediction, descent planning, and safety logic. Precision landing on a vertically oscillating platform has been achieved by tracking its height [ 6 ] and by coupling a UKF estimate of known multi-sinusoidal motion to time-optimal trajectory generation [ 7 ] . Such pipelines rest on a forecast of the ship’s motion, from Kalman estimators [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] to learned time-series models [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] , coupled to a planned descent [ 14 ] . In maritime experiments, an FFT–Kalman observer and MPC reached the deck near zero roll and pitch with a forecast of about 1 ​ s 1\,\mathrm{s} , treating vertical motion as negligible and scoring success on tilt alone [ 15 ] ; a later system from the same group added onboard vision and landed on a rocking USV, reporting its hardware trials as roll and pitch [ 16 ] . Distributed MPC has selected a calm patch of water and a low-tilt touchdown time from a known wave model, in a two-dimensional simulation with a communicating vessel [ 17 ] . Prediction-driven implementations still require an explicit forecast, a hand-designed phase structure, and a tuned descent trigger.

Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a route to coordinating the coupled tracking and timing objectives within a policy. Landing policies have progressed from visual touchdown and inclined surfaces to continuous tracking of horizontally moving pads [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . End-to-end image-based landing with learned three-axis velocity commands has been demonstrated on a ground vehicle following a horizontal path at up to 1 ​ m / s 1\,\mathrm{m/s} ; the study identifies memory as a requirement for more complex platform motion [ 23 ] . Robust policies have also been trained for a sub-scale ship and wind disturbances [ 24 ] . That policy commands roll and pitch while a separate command executes the vertical landing, so heave stays outside the action space and the descent is not decided against deck motion.

The closest learned heave systems broaden the motion and validation envelope. A policy that infers platform motion from two successive sparse visual observations and commands attitude and thrust was evaluated in 411 onboard trials on a Stewart platform and a wave-excited pool float [ 25 ] . The success criterion of Angelis et al. [ 25 ] allows 1.5 ​ m / s 1.5\,\mathrm{m/s} of relative speed at contact. The two test platforms of Angelis et al. each exhibit one half of the problem: the Stewart platform moves 0.25 ​ m 0.25\,\mathrm{m} but follows a single sine wave, and the pool float moves irregularly but only 0.13 ​ m 0.13\,\mathrm{m} . The algorithm in our work does both at once, following recorded ship motion over 0.70 ​ m 0.70\,\mathrm{m} peak to peak, and a touchdown is scored against a 0.5 ​ m / s 0.5\,\mathrm{m/s} bound on the relative speed. WaveLander [ 26 ] starts from the same premise as our work, learning when to descend, hold position, and retreat through a recurrent policy that commands a scalar vertical-velocity reference. The WaveLander policy is trained without privileged information; the policy in our work gives the critic future deck height that the actor never observes, so the descent decision is learned against motion that the policy itself cannot see. The WaveLander training model constrains the vehicle to one vertical prismatic joint and drives the deck with synthetic multi-sinusoidal motion plus correlated noise; our work considers ship-heave motion [ 5 ] , which is not purely periodic in nature. In WaveLander, lateral tracking is a fixed controller; success is judged on attitude, and one deployment test is reported. In our work, the policy commands the lateral channels itself and is flown 51 times on a physically heaving deck emulator platform.

The literature leaves three gaps. First, heave timing is seldom learned from instantaneous measurements of ship motion. Second, policies are trained above a simulator-side controller that only approximates the autopilot that will fly them; putting the real autopilot in the loop fixes the mismatch, but runs one vehicle at a time [ 27 ] , which rules out the parallel training that these policies need. Third, learned maritime landing algorithms reach deployment without a runtime safety check on the descent they commit to [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] .

This paper closes all three gaps. The deck position a few seconds ahead decides the landing. A vehicle in flight cannot know it, but the simulator does, because it replays a recorded sea state. Only the critic is given that future deck height, and only during training. The actor is recurrent, so it reads the state of the deck from what it has just seen and decides when to descend. No forecast window or peak-selection rule is prescribed. A feed-forward actor sees a single observation and cannot do this, so the privileged critic has nothing to teach it; feed-forward runs did not learn to land, and the two are not compared here. For the second gap, the policy is trained above a Torch implementation of the PX4 cascade [ 28 ] , and it commands world-frame velocity and yaw rate. The deployed autopilot takes those same four channels, so the interface does not change between simulation and flight.

For the third gap, a control-barrier-function (CBF) [ 29 ] filter wraps the deployed policy in an outer loop and checks the vertical velocity it commands at every tick. The check reads the deck-relative vertical state and passes only while a feasible stopping margin remains. Once no margin remains, the filter overrides the command and aborts to hover, so a descent that has run out of stopping margin becomes a retry.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first learned ship-deck landing policy trained with privileged future deck motion and checked at run time by a control-barrier-function monitor on flight hardware.
The barrier is used in its standard role, and the work makes no claim of a new safe-learning theory. This work combines these elements and demonstrates their use for landing a vehicle on a physically heaving deck.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

a recurrent landing policy for a heaving deck, trained with an asymmetric actor–critic, where the critic sees the next 6 ​ s 6\,\mathrm{s} of deck motion and the actor only the deck-relative state available onboard, and which commands the autopilot through its own velocity interface;

a control-barrier-function filter around the deployed policy that aborts and retries when the stopping margin is exhausted, with the same margin used as a training reward, which halves the median simulated contact speed against the same policy trained without it;

51 hardware landings on a deck replaying measured ship heave at 0.70 ​ m 0.70\,\mathrm{m} peak to peak, 31 under motion capture and 20 under onboard vision, all successful, with 97 % and 95 % of disarms inside 0.5 ​ m / s 0.5\,\mathrm{m/s} ; the disarm speed the policy controls and the contact speed the airframe absorbs are reported separately, and the unpowered fall between them is measured.

2026-10-06.title: WAMJET: A Harness for World Action Model Acceleration
2026-10-06.authors: Le Chen , Lixin Liu , Jan Schneider , Zeju Qiu , Simon Guist , Bernhard Schölkopf , Dieter Büchler
2026-10-06.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-06.comment: project page: this https URL
2026-10-06.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video foundation models for robot manipulation, but their large backbones and video-action co-prediction are expensive. Although existing acceleration techniques offer many ways to reduce this cost, selecting and composing them requires substantial engineering for each model and hardware platform. To tackle this bottleneck, we present WAMJET, an agentic harness that accelerates WAM inference by equipping coding agents with reusable optimization guidance and measurement and validation tools. WAMJET follows a bottleneck-driven workflow where the agent profiles inference, modifies targeted code, validates effects, and iteratively refines the acceleration stack as bottlenecks shift, while preserving action quality. Experiments span six WAMs, three coding agents, and two GPU architectures. WAMJET achieves up to 9.95× lossless speedup over upstream implementations. Approximation and hardware-aware optimization yield additional latency reductions, with comparable success rates. The results show that WAMJET can produce effective acceleration stacks for WAM deployment.
2026-10-06.introduction:
Building generalist policies requires not only mapping visual observations to actions but also understanding and predicting the consequences of actions in diverse environments.
Video generation models learn representations of such dynamics from large-scale video datasets.
Many of these videos contain intentional behavior like object manipulation and scene changes because someone or something acted.
That makes video models attractive backbones for generalist manipulation.
Before seeing any robot actions, the backbone already encodes useful links between language, visual change, and plausible object interactions.
World Action Models (WAMs) build on these models and extend them with action-generation capabilities.
They inherit priors from video pretraining and couple action generation with video-based world modeling for more robust robot manipulation across diverse environments.
Compared with Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs), WAMs are appealing because predicting the future states of the environment may help capture better physical dynamics and temporal information.

Modern video generation models are often billion-scale parameter models and continue to scale toward higher generation quality and higher fidelity.
This scaling provides stronger priors about how visual scenes evolve but also increases inference cost.
The same backbones that make WAMs attractive also make them expensive to run. Inference may involve sampling a large video model, several denoising steps, and repeated vision-language processing. Beyond those computations, data movement, synchronization, and cache updates can also add substantial latency.
This computational burden poses a significant challenge for real-time control in robotics, where timely decision-making is crucial.

Many techniques can accelerate inference, including compilation, kernel fusion, caching, and quantization. The difficulty is deciding which techniques to apply and how to combine them. A model dominated by repeated conditioning needs different optimizations from one governed by attention or memory transfers. Hardware also affects which kernels or data types are efficient. Moreover, optimizations can interact, which means removing one bottleneck can expose another, and a change that initially gives little benefit may become useful later. Developing an effective acceleration strategy, therefore, requires repeated profiling, implementation, and measurement for each deployment.
Preserving the policy’s behavior adds another challenge. Reusing a prompt embedding while the instruction is unchanged can avoid redundant computation. Reusing visual features after the observation changes, however, approximates the policy’s input. Quantization can introduce further error, whose effect on manipulation may be difficult to predict from tensor differences alone. An optimization process must account for both inference speed and the effect of its changes on robot actions.

Accelerating WAM inference is not a one-time optimization but requires a recipe that composes techniques for a specific model, hardware stack, and task. The best recipe for a certain WAM may not directly transfer to other models. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , hand-crafting an acceleration strategy that works well on a specific model and hardware setup requires substantial engineering effort and may not generalize to other scenarios.
LLM coding agents offer a way to automate this process, but reliable optimization over many iterations requires clear constraints, appropriate tools, and feedback on both latency and correctness. Harness engineering provides this structure through agent-readable workflows, measurement tools, and explicit validation criteria [ 14 ] . This shifts human effort toward designing reusable guidance, while the agent conducts experiments, assesses their outcomes, and uses the evidence to guide subsequent optimizations.

In this work, we present WAMJET, an agentic harness for accelerating WAM inference. WAMJET equips coding agents with optimization guidance and tools for profiling, latency measurement, numerical comparison, and paired task analysis. Starting from a runnable policy, the agent identifies bottlenecks, implements lossless or approximate accelerations, and benchmarks and validates each candidate. It retains useful changes and repeats the process within a specified budget. Throughout the search, the agent adapts its optimization choices to the target hardware, records experiment outcomes, and stores reusable findings in external memory. This iterative process produces acceleration stacks tailored to the target policy and hardware.

Our contributions can be summarized in several aspects:

We introduce WAMJET, a harness that combines reusable optimization guidance with measurement and validation tools for accelerating WAM inference.

We develop a bottleneck-driven workflow that iteratively composes acceleration techniques and checks their effects on outputs, recurrent state, and task performance.

We evaluate WAMJET across different WAMs and GPU architectures, examining the optimizations found by different agent campaigns, the benefit of further search, and the gains and limitations of approximate inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our training-free framework can achieve significant acceleration.

1. We introduce WAMJET, a harness that combines reusable optimization guidance with measurement and validation tools for accelerating WAM inference.

2. We develop a bottleneck-driven workflow that iteratively composes acceleration techniques and checks their effects on outputs, recurrent state, and task performance.

3. We evaluate WAMJET across different WAMs and GPU architectures, examining the optimizations found by different agent campaigns, the benefit of further search, and the gains and limitations of approximate inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our training-free framework can achieve significant acceleration.

# II Related Work

## II-A Foundation Models for Robot Manipulation

Foundation models support robot manipulation through both direct action prediction and higher-level decision making.
RT-2 transfers vision-language pretraining into control by representing robot actions as tokens, while OpenVLA provides an open-source vision-language-action (VLA) model trained on diverse robot demonstrations [ 5 , 13 ] . π 0 \pi_{0} combines a pretrained vision-language backbone with flow-matching action generation, and Octo learns a generalist diffusion policy from heterogeneous robot data [ 3 , 26 ] .
Other approaches leverage language models: SayCan selects skills based on learned affordances [ 2 ] , while Code as Policies generates executable programs for robot control [ 21 ] .

A related line connects policy learning with future visual prediction.
UniPi formulates planning as text-conditioned video generation and extracts executable actions from the resulting visual plans [ 9 ] .
Unified models couple video and action learning: UVA learns a shared latent representation with decoupled diffusion heads, while UWM integrates video and action diffusion in a single transformer with independently controlled diffusion timesteps [ 17 , 38 ] .
DreamZero builds on a pretrained video diffusion backbone to jointly predict future observations and robot actions [ 33 ] .
WAMJET accelerates the inference code of a trained policy, with numerical and task evaluations used to assess the effect of each optimization.

## II-B Accelerating Video Generation and World Action Models

Diffusion acceleration operates at several levels of the inference computation.
DPM-Solver reduces the number of model evaluations through higher-order numerical integration, whereas progressive distillation trains a student to reproduce a longer sampling process with fewer steps [ 25 , 27 ] .
Training-free caching methods instead exploit redundancy along the denoising trajectory: TeaCache uses timestep-conditioned input changes to guide reuse, and TaylorSeer forecasts intermediate features rather than simply reusing them [ 23 , 24 ] .
Sparse VideoGen reduces attention computation through spatial-temporal sparsity, token merging reduces redundant token processing, and SVDQuant enables low-bit diffusion inference with a high-precision low-rank branch [ 29 , 4 , 16 ] .
These approximations differ from implementations such as FlashAttention, which accelerates exact dense attention through IO-aware tiling and reduced memory traffic [ 8 ] .

WAM-specific works explore both architectural efficiency and deployment-time optimization.
DreamZero combines caching, quantization, compilation, kernel optimization, and asynchronous execution in a model-specific control stack [ 33 ] .
Fast-WAM retains video co-training but removes test-time future-video generation [ 34 ] .
Light-WAM further adopts a compact video backbone and state-fusion action decoding, predicting action chunks without a generative action expert [ 20 ] .
These methods require retraining and thus are not drop-in optimizations for arbitrary checkpoints.
In contrast, C 3 ache is a training-free WAM accelerator that reuses action-expert residuals across consecutive inference chunks, exploiting cross-chunk redundancy [ 36 ] .

While these methods offer complementary acceleration mechanisms, they differ in the evaluation criteria: numerical equivalence, perceptual similarity, and task success are not interchangeable, e.g., video fidelity alone does not ensure manipulation performance.
WAMJET builds on these techniques, selecting and combining them according to the bottlenecks of each model and hardware platform.

## II-C Agentic Workflows and Harness Engineering

Agentic systems make iterative tool use and external feedback central to problem-solving. ReAct introduced the reasoning–action loop [ 32 ] , SWE-agent built an agent–computer interface for solving software engineering tasks [ 30 ] , and agent harnesses go further by designing the whole runtime system around the agent [ 37 ] .
In performance engineering, CUDA-LLM and CudaForge use executable correctness checks and hardware-level performance measurements to iteratively improve GPU kernels [ 6 , 35 ] .

Robotics harnesses apply these ideas to different stages of the robot-learning lifecycle.
HARBOR automates robot RL training by coordinating specialized agents from environment setup to reward tuning and to policy training [ 19 ] .
Nautilus standardizes policy-benchmark-robot integration through typed contracts and validated workflows [ 11 ] .
Show-Harness instead operates within the embodied control loop: it exposes compact semantic actions to a VLM and deterministically maps them into robot motion, with execution feedback from observations [ 7 ] .
WAMJET instead applies agentic optimization to the inference code of a trained WAM.

The most related framework is the Sol Video Inference Engine [ 18 ] , which optimizes video generation by assigning caching, sparse attention, token pruning, quantization, and kernel fusion to parallel agents, then integrating results using human quality feedback.
WAMJET addresses the additional requirements of action generation: optimizations must preserve the policy’s recurrent state, respond correctly to changing observations, and be evaluated for their effect on manipulation.
Our workflow combines bottleneck analysis with numerical and stateful checks and uses paired task evaluation to assess approximations.

2026-10-06.title: Tactile Perception through Fluid-Solid Interaction
2026-10-06.authors: Arman Goshtasbi , Minke Berghuis , Aida Parvaresh , Saravana Prashanth Murali Babu , Robert W. Style , Ahmad Rafsanjani
2026-10-06.abstract: Soft tactile sensors elevate robotic touch through enhanced flexibility and adaptability, yet most existing designs depend on embedded electronics that are susceptible to interference and environmental limitations. In this work, we leverage fluid-solid interactions to develop a class of soft tactile sensors that operate entirely without electronics at the sensing site. The sensor comprises a fluid-filled elastomeric channel connected to only two external pressure sensors. Touching different regions of the elastomeric surface displaces the viscous fluid, producing distinct pressure patterns that encode both touch position and force. These signals are decoded through a machine learning framework that integrates feature extraction, soft clustering, and adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference to achieve accurate localization and force estimation. We validate this concept through single-point touch localization and force estimation in a linear (1D) sensor and extend the same sensing principle to 2D tactile mapping by routing the channel across the surface using space-filling curves, while maintaining the same minimal hardware setup. This simple approach remains effective in environments where conventional electronic sensors often fail, such as underwater or in the presence of magnetic interference.

2026-10-07.title: QF3: Fast Flow RL with Filtered Q-Gradients
2026-10-07.authors: Chung Min Kim , Brent Yi , David McAllister , Hongsuk Choi , Himanshu Gaurav Singh , Jinkun Cao , Ken Goldberg , Pieter Abbeel , Carmelo Sferrazza , Angjoo Kanazawa
2026-10-07.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract: Flow policies have become a standard policy class for learning robot behaviors from demonstrations, but reinforcement learning is still critical for improving pre-trained flow policies or learning them from scratch through interaction. We introduce QF3 (Fast Flow RL with Filtered Q-Gradients), an online off-policy RL algorithm that trains a flow policy with flow matching plus the critic's action gradient, backpropagated through a one-step prediction of the flow's output. To keep updates where the critic and this prediction are reliable, QF3 applies the critic gradient only to action dimensions that stay near the replay action. To our knowledge, QF3 is the first off-policy flow RL method to train humanoid locomotion policies from scratch and transfer them zero-shot to hardware. Paired with a high-throughput off-policy training recipe, it trains humanoid locomotion and motion-tracking policies with a 10x wall-clock speedup over FPO++, a recent on-policy flow RL method. We further apply QF3 to fine-tune pretrained flow-based manipulation policies on both ABC-Sim and Robomimic tasks. These results suggest that QF3 can both learn robot policies from scratch and refine those acquired from demonstrations. Website: this https URL

2026-10-07.title: PEARS: Physical-Prior-Guided Efficient Adaptation via Failure Reasoning and Diffusion Steering for Tactile Manipulation
2026-10-07.authors: Kun Song , Yiming Wang , Yilin Chen , Tianyi Ding , Jiaxin Tian , Tianqi Gong , Daolin Ma , Jia Pan
2026-10-07.comment: . Project website: this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract:
Pretrained robotic policies can suffer substantial performance degradation
under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions encountered during deployment, motivating
post-training through real-world interaction. However, reinforcement-learning
(RL)-based post-training typically requires substantial environment interactions, a
burden that is especially significant in manipulation, where each trial
can be slow, costly, or destructive. Therefore, we present PEARS, a
physics-prior-guided hybrid RL framework for sample-efficient online adaptation
of pretrained policies with tactile feedback. After each episode, its
physics-guided force reasoning (PFR) module uses physical priors encoded in a
vision–language model (VLM) to diagnose failures from the visual outcome and
tactile interaction history and update task-appropriate contact-force
bounds. A high-frequency hybrid force–position controller then
enforces these bounds during contact. Complementarily,
tactile-conditioned diffusion steering reinforcement learning adjusts the
latent noise of the frozen flow-matching policy to correct errors in
free-space motion and contact timing without updating the base model.
In simulation, PEARS improves success rates by 12.4–37.4 percentage points over the strongest per-task baselines.
PEARS also reduces the number of interaction episodes required for a certain success threshold by up to 53.2% relative to the fastest baseline.
In real-world experiments, PEARS achieves success
rates of 95% on Whiteboard Erasing and 90% on Pipette Liquid Aspiration.
These
results show that combining the PFR module with policy
steering can accelerate adaptation while reducing costly interactions.
The project website is available at https://song-kun.github.io/pears .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Large-scale pretrained vision–language–action (VLA) models [ 1 ] , [ 2 ] have recently emerged as an important paradigm for robotic manipulation, achieving remarkable progress in task generalization across diverse real-world environments. For contact-rich tasks, such as surface wiping and grasping fragile objects, vision–tactile–language–action (VTLA) models [ 3 ] extend this paradigm by incorporating tactile feedback to sense and regulate physical interactions with the environment.
However, pretrained VLA and VTLA policies can perform poorly during deployment when scene configurations, object properties, or contact dynamics differ from those encountered during training. Such out-of-distribution (OOD) shifts can lead to positioning errors, mistimed contact, or inappropriate interaction forces [ 4 ] .

Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training with tactile feedback [ 5 , 6 ] provides a direct route for adapting pretrained policies to the target deployment environment through autonomous interaction.
However, traditional RL-based algorithms demand substantial interaction with the environment, which can be time-inefficient and high-cost.
For example, a failed online interaction in an industrial operation or chemical laboratory procedure may damage equipment or compromise the experimental setup.
This interaction cost is compounded by conventional online RL algorithms, which often rely on stochastic trial-and-error exploration and must visit a sufficiently diverse set of task-relevant states before effective behaviors can be learned.
Therefore, how to develop an efficient real-world RL fine-tuning method for contact-rich manipulation with tactile feedback is still an open-problem.

To this end, we introduce PEARS , a physics-prior-guided framework for interaction-efficient real-world adaptation in tactile manipulation. Its physics-guided force reasoning (PFR) module uses physical priors encoded in a vision–language model (VLM) to reason about episode-level failures and guide contact-force adaptation, rather than relying solely on random RL exploration.
After each episode, the PFR module jointly interprets the visual outcome and measured interaction forces to diagnose the failure cause and update task-specific contact-force bounds. During contact, a high-frequency hybrid force–position controller enforces these bounds along the force-control axes while maintaining position tracking in the remaining directions. Complementarily, tactile-conditioned DSRL [ 7 ] steers the frozen policy through latent-noise adaptation to correct positioning and contact-timing errors without updating the base model. By separating force adaptation through PFR from latent policy steering, PEARS reduces its reliance on costly real-world trial-and-error exploration.

We evaluated PEARS on three simulated tasks and two real-world manipulation tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that PEARS achieves superior performance, significantly outperforming representative policy adaptation baselines.
Our contributions are threefold:

We present PEARS , an interaction-efficient online fine-tuning framework that combines noise-space steering with VLM-based force reasoning using tactile sensing.

We develop the PFR module , which uses physical priors encoded in VLMs to diagnose failure causes and adapt task-specific contact-force bounds, reducing interaction numbers required for policy fine-tuning.

We conduct extensive experiments across simulated and real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of PEARS.

1. We present PEARS , an interaction-efficient online fine-tuning framework that combines noise-space steering with VLM-based force reasoning using tactile sensing.

2. We develop the PFR module , which uses physical priors encoded in VLMs to diagnose failure causes and adapt task-specific contact-force bounds, reducing interaction numbers required for policy fine-tuning.

3. We conduct extensive experiments across simulated and real-world contact-rich manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of PEARS.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Tactile-Aware Visuomotor Policies

Recent studies have increasingly incorporated tactile sensing into visuomotor policies.
These approaches employ tactile encoders [ 8 ] , [ 9 ] , [ 10 ] , [ 11 ] cross-modal alignment [ 12 ] , [ 13 ] , [ 14 ] or auxiliary tactile supervision [ 15 ] to leverage learned tactile representations to
guide action generation. [ 16 ] , [ 17 ] , [ 3 ] , [ 18 ] further pretrain vision–tactile–language–action (VTLA) models on tactile datasets collected across diverse tasks and heterogeneous tactile sensor configurations, enabling VTLA models to learn more unified and transferable tactile representations.

## II-B Reactive Tactile Policies for Contact-Rich Manipulation

Contact-rich manipulation requires high-frequency responses to tactile feedback. FOAR [ 19 ] uses predicted contact states to dynamically modulate vision-force fusion and trigger local action corrections.
RDP [ 20 ] introduces a slow-fast architecture that pairs slow action chunk generation with
a fast tactile-conditioned decoder, enabling within-chunk corrections. ForcePolicy [ 21 ] and ForceVLA2 [ 22 ] employ force feedback to perform high-frequency hybrid force-position
control. This reactive design has been extended to tactile-aware VLA models. VLA-Touch [ 23 ] uses tactile feedback to support both semantic replanning and action refinement. AT-VLA [ 24 ] separates slow vision-language reasoning from fast tactile control. FAVLA [ 25 ] adaptively adjusts
the action expert invocation frequency based on predicted force variations. UniTacVLA [ 26 ] combines predicted and measured tactile signals to apply high-frequency corrections to low-frequency action chunks.

## II-C Reinforcement Learning for Tactile Policy Adaptation

Beyond behavior cloning (BC), RL can further improve tactile policies through autonomous interaction with the environment. VLA-RL [ 27 ] optimizes autoregressive VLAs through trajectory-level RL. SimpleVLA-RL [ 28 ] presents an efficient and scalable RL framework tailored to VLAs. π 0.6 ∗ \pi^{*}_{0.6} proposes RECAP [ 29 ] , which trains a value function on demonstrations, autonomous rollouts, and expert interventions.
Rather than directly updating VLA parameters, DSRL [ 7 ] treats the initial noise of a diffusion or flow-matching policy as the RL latent action space and learns a noise policy, enabling effective autonomous policy improvement in the real world.
RL Token [ 30 ] compresses task-relevant internal VLA representations into a compact RL token and trains a lightweight actor-critic head on this representation to refine actions while anchoring behavior to the base VLA, enabling sample-efficient online adaptation on real robots.
Recent work extends RL-based VLA adaptation to contact-rich manipulation through tactile feedback. TacCoRL [ 5 ] improves tactile-conditioned VLA policies through simulation-based RL. OmniTacTune [ 6 ] learns a tactile residual policy through online RL to provide contact-aware action corrections. TORL-VLA [ 31 ] freezes a pretrained tactile-aware VLA during online RL and employs an intervention-censored critic for real-world adaptation.
However, most existing RL approaches require substantial environment interaction for stochastic exploration and lack explicit directional guidance, limiting their sample efficiency. To address these limitations, we propose the PEARS framework.
