2026-10-07.title: DepthWorld: 3D World Model for Robot Manipulation
2026-10-07.authors: Jai Bardhan , Josef Sivic , Vladimir Petrik
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-07.comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. Project page: this https URL . including supplementary material, 15 figures, 7 tables
2026-10-07.abstract: World models offer a data-driven alternative to traditional simulators for robotics, with applications spanning policy evaluation, improvement, and planning. All of these uses depend on faithful 3D geometry, yet current video-based world models are trained on RGB alone and produce rollouts that look correct frame-by-frame but do not compose into a consistent 3D world. Closing this gap requires progress on two fronts: large-scale 3D supervision for manipulation, and an architecture that can absorb it without disturbing strong pretrained video priors. We introduce a calibration pipeline that combines learned stereo depth with a joint factor graph, pooling all episodes collected from the same physical robot to recover its shared kinematic parameters alongside per-scene extrinsics. Applied to the DROID dataset, this yields DROID-3D, a calibrated 3D dataset providing dense metric depth and recalibrated multi-view extrinsics (achieving < 0.7 <0.7 px reprojection error on 90% of episodes for external cameras). We then train DepthWorld, a Stable Video Diffusion-based world model that jointly predicts multi-view RGB and depth via spatial latent tiling, leaving the pretrained Variational Autoencoder (VAE) unchanged. Depth supervision improves RGB prediction itself by +1.48 dB PSNR over an identical RGB-only baseline at equal training budget, while simultaneously yielding accurate metric depth for downstream geometric reasoning.
2026-10-07.introduction:
World models are a promising data-driven alternative to traditional simulators for robot learning, with the potential to simulate manipulation tasks that are difficult to capture with physics-based engines. Recent work has shown that finetuning pretrained video diffusion backbones with action conditioning on large-scale robotics datasets yields models that generate faithful action-consistent rollouts [ 12 , 2 ] . Such rollouts are increasingly used for policy evaluation [ 12 , 2 ] , policy improvement [ 12 , 8 ] , and planning [ 49 , 34 ] —uses in which the geometric fidelity of the rollout determines whether the signal is usable.

However, current video world models miss this geometric structure entirely. They are trained on RGB alone, and the training loss provides no signal to resolve the underlying 3D ambiguity of pixel sequences. The resulting models produce visually plausible rollouts whose geometry is internally incoherent:
predicted depth disagrees across views of the same scene, the model
struggles with geometric reasoning about occlusion and contact
(Figure 4 ), and object shape and identity degrade
over the course of a rollout (Figure 1 ).
For downstream uses that read off the rollout, this incoherence is the limiting factor.

The natural fix is to supervise geometry directly during training, the recipe behind recent geometric foundation models [ 40 , 19 , 39 , 41 , 21 , 17 ] . However, this approach does not directly apply to robot world models for two reasons.
First, geometric foundation models earn their generalization by training on datasets that already carry metric depth and calibrated poses [ 45 , 4 , 33 , 20 , 44 , 31 ] . Robot teleoperation datasets such as DROID [ 18 ] capture the appearance and dynamics of real manipulation at scale, but their geometric annotations are secondary outputs of the collection pipeline and not at the quality geometric pretraining demands. Lifting them into supervision-quality 3D is non-trivial: manipulation scenes are dominated by textureless and specular surfaces, and even a rig that is internally self-consistent under bundle adjustment can be kinematically decoupled from from the robot’s own coordinate frame, severing the critical link to the robot’s proprioception and end-effector actions.
Second, current video world models rely on delicate, pretrained image and video diffusion priors. Conventional architectural modifications for incorporating spatial modalities—such as expanding the input channels of the VAE or introducing parallel dual-branch U-Nets—require destructive weight re-initializations. These interventions risk corrupting the strong visual and motion priors that make these foundation backbones effective in the first place.

We address both through the following contributions:

We introduce a calibration pipeline for recovering metric depth and accurate multi-view extrinsics from any multi-view stereo teleoperation collection with a known URDF. The pipeline combines learned stereo depth with a joint factor graph optimization that pools all episodes of the same physical robot to recover its shared kinematic parameters (joint offsets, hand-eye calibration) alongside per-scene extrinsics. Applied to DROID [ 18 ] , this yields DROID-3D —a calibrated 3D corpus providing dense metric depth and recalibrated multi-view extrinsics for over 70,000 episodes.

We train DepthWorld , a Stable Video Diffusion-based world model that jointly predicts multi-view RGB and depth via spatial latent tiling that leaves the pretrained VAE unchanged.

We show that depth supervision improves RGB prediction : at equal training budget, DepthWorld gains + 1.48 +1.48 dB PSNR over an RGB-only baseline of identical architecture and data.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Robotic World Models. Action-conditioned video models have emerged as a learned substitute for physics-based simulators in manipulation, with applications spanning policy evaluation [ 12 , 2 ] , policy improvement [ 12 , 8 ] , and visual planning [ 49 , 34 ] . Recent works finetune pretrained video diffusion backbones with proprioceptive action conditioning: Ctrl-World [ 12 ] , an SVD-based controllable world model trained on DROID [ 18 ] forms our backbone; IRASim [ 51 ] along with other works [ 15 ] systematize the policy-evaluation use case. All these uses presuppose geometrically faithful rollouts.
Current video world models are trained on RGB alone, which does not generally serve as a strong geometric prior.
We close this gap by jointly predicting depth and supervising with point maps.

Geometric Foundation Models. A recent line of work regresses dense metric geometry directly from images: DUSt3R [ 40 ] and MASt3R [ 19 ] predict point maps from image pairs, VGGT [ 39 ] scales this to many-view inputs through
intermediate camera and DPT [ 32 ] heads, and MapAnything [ 17 ] unifies a broader class of supervision targets. These models inherit their generalization from large datasets [ 45 , 4 , 33 , 20 , 44 , 31 , 50 ] carrying dense metric depth and calibrated poses, drawn from structured light, LiDAR, and offline reconstruction.
None of these covers the visual distribution of real manipulation, with its indoor setting and extreme viewpoint differences between fixed external and wrist-mounted cameras. DROID-3D is our contribution at this distribution and scale.

Depth-Aware Video Diffusion. Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) [ 5 ] provides strong appearance and motion priors but is trained on RGB alone. Three approaches have been explored to add depth into this prior. Marigold [ 16 ] showed that an image diffusion VAE encodes depth maps essentially without loss,
repurposing the model as a depth predictor;
DepthCrafter [ 13 ] extends this to video. Joint RGB–depth prediction has been pursued through channel expansion [ 49 , 47 ] , which adds depth channels to the VAE’s input and output convolutions
and through dual-branch architectures [ 30 ] that run a parallel U-Net for depth with cross-connections to the RGB branch. Both modify the pretrained backbone substantially, preventing weight transfer. Our spatial latent tiling extends Marigold’s observation
from single-image depth prediction to multi-view RGB–depth video prediction.

Robot Datasets and Their Calibration. Large-scale teleoperation datasets have grown rapidly in size and diversity—BridgeData V2 [ 38 ] , RT-1 [ 6 ] and the Open X-Embodiment aggregation [ 29 ] , RH20T [ 10 ] , and DROID [ 18 ] —however; almost all carry geometry as a byproduct of the capture pipeline: monocular RGB in Open X, single RGB-D in Bridge, and ZED stereo in DROID. Simulation-based corpora such as RoboCasa [ 26 ] and ARNOLD [ 11 ] carry perfect geometry but inherit the sim-to-real gap that motivates training world models on real data in the first place. DROID is unique among real-world manipulation datasets at this scale in providing synchronized multi-view stereo with known baselines and a publicly released URDF, but its shipped geometric metadata is not at the quality level downstream geometric learning depends on. Post-hoc recalibration of DROID has been attempted: PointWorld [ 14 ] initializes per-scene extrinsics from VGGT and refines them against robot depth observations, and serves as our baseline in § 5 .

2026-10-07.title: LBA-CBF: Rapidly Adaptive Safety Filters via Parallel Dynamics Inference
2026-10-07.authors: Maitham F. AL-Sunni , Timeea-Andreea Radu , Hassan Almubarak , Henry Z. Liao , Michael Görner , Francesco Maurelli , John M. Dolan
2026-10-07.abstract:
Control barrier functions (CBFs) certify commands through an assumed dynamics model, so an abrupt, unmeasured regime change can undermine the certificate exactly when safety matters most. We present Look-Back Adaptive Control Barrier Functions ( LBA-CBF ) , which rank a finite bank of candidate dynamics by recent prediction error over a short look-back window and enforce the high-order CBF condition against every model within a tolerance of the best, spanning best-fit adaptation to full-bank robust filtering. The dynamics may depend nonlinearly on the unknown parameters, and no switching model or continuously parameterized estimator is required. We prove that any feasible filtered input satisfies the true CBF condition whenever a safety-representative candidate is retained. In quadrotor simulation with abrupt wind reversals and an unknown payload, LBA-CBF is safe and reaches the goal from all random initial conditions, matching an oracle, while adaptive and robust baselines achieve 0 0 – 88 % 88\% success. Banks of up to 250,000 250,000 models run inside the control loop, and Crazyflie 2.1 and F1TENTH experiments demonstrate adaptation to wind, payload release, and varying tire–road friction. Code, videos,
and project details are available at:
2026-10-07.introduction:
A control safety filter is only as trustworthy as the dynamics model used inside its barrier condition. Control barrier functions (CBF) [ 5 ] keep the state inside a safe set with minimal deviation from a nominal controller, but certify each input through the predicted evolution of the barrier under an assumed dynamics model. An abrupt, unmeasured change of dynamics regime , such as an unknown payload, a sudden wind gust, or a change in tire–road friction, therefore undermines the filter exactly when safety matters most.

Two main remedies exist. Robust CBFs certify the barrier against a fixed worst-case uncertainty set [ 10 ] , which can be conservative in a way that online data cannot reduce. Adaptive and learning-based CBFs reduce this conservatism by estimating unknown parameters or model errors online, but abrupt regime changes must be absorbed through an estimation transient. Robust adaptive CBFs combine adaptation with set-based uncertainty descriptions [ 14 ] , but under the standard constant-parameter formulation the admissible parameter set contracts as measurements accumulate and does not re-expand when the dynamics change. Safety certification thus remains tied either to a fixed uncertainty description or to the transient of a continuously updated estimate.

We propose Look-Back Adaptive Control Barrier Functions ( LBA-CBF ) , whose architecture is illustrated in Fig. 1 . Rather than committing the safety filter to a single continuously evolving estimate, LBA-CBF maintains a finite bank of candidate dynamics models and, at every control step, evaluates them in parallel by their prediction error over a look-back window of length W W . The best-fitting model can be used directly for rapid adaptation, while a prediction-plausible set retains models whose recent errors lie within a tolerance of the minimum and enforces the CBF condition for all retained models. After W W new transitions, pre-change observations no longer contribute to the residual, so the filter adapts to changes without a switching model.

CBFs have been extended to high-relative-degree and discrete-time safety constraints [ 22 , 23 ] . Under model uncertainty, robust CBFs certify safety against a prescribed uncertainty set [ 10 ] , while adaptive CBFs reduce conservatism through online parameter adaptation [ 19 ] . Robust adaptive CBFs (RaCBFs) combine adaptation with set-membership identification [ 14 ] , with extensions to high-relative-degree constraints [ 7 ] . Alternatively, safety can be embedded into an adaptive controller by augmenting the parametrically uncertain dynamics with barrier states [ 3 ] . More recent approaches accommodate time-varying uncertainty: robust CBFs in [ 18 ] admit time-varying parameters that enter the dynamics nonlinearly and use set-membership estimation to reduce conservatism, while [ 8 ] combines finite-time estimation of time-varying parameters with RaCBFs under a structured parameterization and bounded parameter variation. Disturbance-observer [ 21 ] and ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} [ 16 ] approaches instead estimate and compensate model mismatch through observer or adaptive dynamics. In contrast, LBA-CBF does not require a continuously parameterized estimator or an affine-in-parameter uncertainty model: it ranks a finite bank of candidate dynamics directly from recent prediction error and certifies the barrier against the dynamics hypotheses retained by the moving look-back window.

CBF methods for hybrid and switched systems construct mode-dependent safety conditions under a specified hybrid structure [ 24 ] , while learning-based approaches have estimated mode-specific barrier residuals for switching systems [ 1 ] . In contrast, LBA-CBF treats the active dynamics regime as latent and infers it from recent state–action transitions without requiring known guards or a transition model.

Adaptation through a finite bank of candidate dynamics is a classical multiple-model control idea [ 15 ] . More recently, multiple-model reasoning has appeared in safety-critical control: [ 11 ] combines CBF constraints with MPC for jump Markov linear systems under uncertain mode estimates, while [ 12 ] uses a supervisory multi-observer bank to estimate unknown parameters within an adaptive safety controller. Most closely related to our inference mechanism, the look-back bank of [ 4 , 13 ] ranks candidate vehicle models over a short window and selects the best-fitting model for adaptive racing model predictive control (MPC). LBA-CBF instead uses the windowed prediction residual for safety certification, retaining the best-fitting dynamics or a prediction-plausible subset and enforcing the high-order CBF (HOCBF) against them.

The main contributions of this work are:

Look-back adaptive safety filtering. LBA-CBF ranks a finite bank of candidate dynamics by recent prediction error and enforces the CBF condition against the best-fitting models. The parameters may enter the dynamics nonlinearly, including through the input gain, and no switching model or continuously parameterized estimator is required.

Safety guarantee and adaptive-to-robust filtering. Every feasible LBA-CBF input satisfies the CBF condition of the true dynamics whenever the retained set contains a safety-representative model. A finite tolerance that guarantees this exists whenever the bank contains such a model, and the same tolerance spans best-fit adaptation and full-bank robust filtering.

Real-time implementation and robotic validation. A parallel JAX implementation runs banks of up to 250,000 250,000 models inside the control loop. In quadrotor simulation, LBA-CBF is safe and reaches the goal from all random initial conditions, outperforming adaptive and robust baselines. Experiments on a Crazyflie 2.1 and an F1TENTH race car demonstrate adaptation to wind, a swinging payload with an abrupt release, and varying tire–road friction.

2026-10-07.title: PhoneBot: A Low-Cost Open Humanoid Robot Platform Reusing Smartphones
2026-10-07.authors: Ruochen Hou , Quanyou Wang , Daniel Koh , Dennis W. Hong
2026-10-07.abstract: The adoption of humanoid robots in education and research remains limited by high hardware costs, complex sensing systems, and substantial computational requirements. This paper presents PhoneBot, a low-cost, open-source humanoid robot platform that repurposes commodity smartphones as its primary sensing and computing unit. By using a smartphone’s integrated inertial measurement unit (IMU), camera, wireless connectivity, and onboard processing capabilities, PhoneBot reduces hardware costs and simplifies the system architecture. The robot combines a modular lower-body structure driven by 13 low-cost actuators with a torso-mounted smartphone that supports perception, control computation, and user interaction. We describe the mechanical design, software architecture, and real-time communication framework that support stable locomotion and capabilities including vision-based human following, conversational interaction, filming, and mobile telepresence. Experimental evaluations demonstrate reliable walking, perception-driven interaction, and straightforward deployment using off-the-shelf consumer smartphones. With fully open-source hardware and software designs, PhoneBot provides an affordable, reproducible platform for education, research, and rapid prototyping. More details are available at https://phonebot.dev .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Compact humanoid robots provide accessible platforms for studying locomotion, physical interaction, and embodied intelligence. Their reduced size supports experimentation in laboratories and classrooms with limited space and infrastructure. Recent platforms have improved accessibility through open-source hardware, accessible manufacturing methods, and commercially available components [ 1 , 2 ] . Nevertheless, hardware costs and system integration effort remain barriers to broader adoption in education and research. Beyond mechanical structure assembly, users must connect and configure components for motion control, perception, communication, and interaction. Further reducing these barriers requires simplifying the integration of sensing, computing, and communication capabilities.

As the widely available consumer devices, smartphones offer a practical basis for this approach, where they combine a camera, an IMU, wireless connectivity, onboard processing, and a user interface. Reusing these capabilities can reduce the need for separate sensing and computing hardware while providing an interface for robot operation and interaction. Applying this approach to a humanoid robot requires a system architecture that connects smartphone-based sensing and computation to actuator control and supports both locomotion and interactive behaviors.

We present PhoneBot (Fig. 1 ), a low-cost, open-source compact humanoid platform that combines a modular lower body with 13 actuators and a torso-mounted smartphone. By using the smartphone’s integrated functions, PhoneBot consolidates sensing, computation, communication, and user interaction in a single device, reducing the need for separate hardware components. We describe the mechanical design, software architecture, and communication framework that connect smartphone-based perception and control computation to the robot’s actuator control system. The platform supports walking, vision-based human following, fall recovery, and mobile telepresence.

Contributions. The contributions of this work are:
(i) a low-cost, modular, open-source humanoid that reuses smartphone sensing and computation to simplify hardware integration; (ii) a torque-aware locomotion pipeline in which sagittal mirroring produces left–right balanced walking and joint load, and also improves learning speed and consistency under actuator limits; and (iii) an integrated Android application for policy inference, vision, SLAM and human–robot interaction, validated on four old or low-cost smartphones.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Works

Compact humanoids support research in locomotion, control, and human-robot interaction. ROBOTIS OP3 is a miniature humanoid platform with integrated actuators, sensors, and an onboard computer [ 3 ] . BRUCE emphasizes dynamic motion through proprioceptive actuation and mechanisms that reduce leg inertia [ 4 ] , while Mini Pi provides a compact bipedal platform designed for robust locomotion [ 5 ] . Other platforms emphasize hardware accessibility and reproducibility. ToddlerBot combines a 3D-printed structure and commercially available actuators with tools for learning-based locomotion and manipulation [ 1 ] . Berkeley Humanoid Lite uses modular 3D-printed gearboxes and widely available components to reduce manufacturing costs [ 2 ] . These platforms demonstrate complementary approaches to balancing capability, cost, and reproducibility.

Smartphones integrate computation, sensing, wireless communication, and user interfaces in a single device. OpenBot uses these capabilities by pairing an Android smartphone with a low-cost wheeled body for onboard perception and autonomous navigation [ 6 ] . PhoneBot shares the objective of reusing smartphone capabilities to reduce dedicated hardware requirements, while integrating them into a compact humanoid platform for locomotion and interaction.

Humanoid locomotion has been studied through both model-based and learning-based approaches. Model-based methods use robot dynamics for motion planning, tracking, and balance control [ 4 , 7 , 8 ] . Reinforcement learning has enabled diverse bipedal locomotion behaviors, including walking, running, and jumping [ 9 ] . Successful simulation-to-real transfer depends on both policy design and the correspondence between simulated and physical robots [ 10 ] . Existing approaches include transformer policies trained in randomized simulation [ 11 ] , hardware designs that reduce simulation complexity [ 12 ] , and explicit modeling of parallel actuation mechanisms during policy training [ 13 ] .

GPU-accelerated simulation improves training efficiency by enabling large-scale parallel rollout collection [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] . Domain randomization and asymmetric actor–critic training have been used to support sim-to-real transfer [ 17 ] , while symmetry-based data augmentation can improve learning efficiency and gait symmetry [ 18 , 19 ] .

2026-10-07.title: Towards an Extensible Benchmark for Spoken Dialogue with Social Robots
2026-10-07.authors: Casey Kennington , Ross Mead , Saad Elbeleidy , Jesse Thomason
2026-10-07.comment: Accepted to and presented at the IROS 2026 Workshop on Human-Robot Dialogue
2026-10-07.abstract: Language models provide a plug-and-play interface between humans and robots, but important challenges remain when speech, dialogue, fast interaction, and collaboration are required. We propose a benchmark for the community to use as a way to explore common spoken dialogue artifacts between robots and humans, including requests for clarification, interruptions, embodied signals (e.g., head nods or facial cues), and time constraints. We also explain our vision to extend the benchmark for other aspects of human-robot interaction that are important to the larger research community. To facilitate the benchmark, we further propose using Retico , a real-time communication framework that fulfills important technical requirements to enable robots to have spoken dialogue capabilities.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Sketch of Potential Benchmark

## II-A Desiderata

Members of the SDS+HRI community identified several important desiderata for a proper benchmark for natural interaction with robots [ 3 ] :

multimodal : the data are composed of speech, vision, robotic, and other modalities;

co-located : the robot must have sensory access to the shared physical space;

high-stakes : the user and robot must work together to complete a task that neither could do alone, where common dialogue artifacts like building common ground, providing explanations, clarification requests, and interruptions are common;

bi-directional : interactions are not just commands from the user, and the robot also takes initiative when needed,

community-agnostic : the benchmark should work on multiple robotic platforms; and

low-cost : labs and research groups can easily and affordably acquire necessary items.

## II-B Benchmark Outline

Building on benchmarks that are meant for interactive dialogue with embodied agents [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] , our proposed sketch of a benchmark is a collaborative game. The task is simplistic, but complicated enough to require important desired dialogue artifacts. Other games, tasks, or settings might be better suited for a benchmark, and we encourage the community to critique this benchmark and continue the discussion.

The collaborative task will require a degree of asymmetrical knowledge and collaboration that neither the human nor the robot could do alone.

Figures 1 and 2 depict a possible setup using the Misty II robot. There are two roles: the instruction giver and the instruction follower (though we stress that these roles serve only to help explain the benchmark; the task is meant to be more collaborative). In our explanation, the robot is the instruction giver and the human is the follower , but those roles can easily be switched. The goal is for the human and robot to collaborate to put the puzzle together to match the final image that the robot “sees” (the setup might require an extra camera that is not part of the robot). The human has access to some of the puzzle pieces on a game board with two dividers: one divider on the left, and one on the right, each hiding a separate puzzle piece from the player (the dividers can be anywhere as long as the participant cannot see the pieces, but they are within reach). The robot is allowed to see everything including the final goal (top of the figure), a bird’s eye view of the two puzzle pieces that the human cannot see behind the dividers (left and right in the figure), and the game board area where the human is working to construct the puzzle (center area of the figure). The robot can explain to the human how to orient pieces (e.g., rotate left or right, flip, slide/shift left or right or up or down). The puzzle pieces themselves should have abstract shapes that require the human and the robot to initiate conversational grounding to determine how they describe or name the objects (e.g., pentomino puzzle pieces have shapes like letters L, T, or N). Furthermore, the puzzle pieces should have colors that might make some shapes less ambiguous, but not all puzzle pieces should have different colors.

Not all puzzle pieces on the table will be used—there will be at least two distractor pieces. The robot also determines when the human should take the pieces on the left or the right dividers (if at all), with the rule that the human can only take one of those pieces if they replace it with another piece and they can only take those pieces once (a mistake results in an inability to complete the puzzle and a failed game). Players can organize the space to mark which objects are no longer eligible for placement in the boxes. By the end of the interaction, the puzzle should be constructed and the two distractor pieces should be out of view behind the two dividers.

The robot minimally needs a camera that can move to look at the target, dividers, and game board with which the human is working. The robot can have any kind of face or use any kind of social capabilities, like eye gaze with the human, head nods, emotional displays, etc (e.g., [ 11 ] ). The robot can have hands for social interaction (e.g., deictic gestures [ 9 , 10 ] ), but the goal is not to require the robot to perform complex physical manipulations.

Some proposed metrics include: (1) number of puzzles started and completed, (2) time to task completion, (3) number of dialogue turns for both the human and the robot, (4) number of initiations from human, (5) number of initiations from the robot, and (6) number of clarification requests from the human and robot, among others (e.g., interruptions, barge-ins). We recognize that some of these metrics will require dialogue act classification and other automated tracking of the dialogue, which the benchmark platform should provide.

## II-C Extending the Base Task

The benchmark is meant to be simple, yet complex enough to enable different research fields and specific research labs to test different aspects of human-robot spoken dialogue interaction. The benchmark can be extended to include additional constraints or settings that make it more difficult or require more collaboration. Additional metrics should be included for each extension as seen fit by the research community. For example, some research labs might not be concerned with dialogue aspects per se and instead use a commercial language model as a placeholder, or they tune a local language model specifically for the task [ 12 , 2 ] , but they wish to focus on gestures. Others might be directly concerned with acoustics, or dialogue aspects such as clarification, social attitudes, or robot manipulation. Researchers are able to hold some aspects of the system constant and range over the aspects of the interaction that interest them. We list some examples below. The broader research field of human-robot dialogue will have made marked progress if evaluated systems can accomplish the base task and all of the extensions. We welcome others in the community to suggest additional extensions.

Despite advances in speech recognition, there are still many challenges that need to be overcome for humans and robots to be able to speak to each other in settings outside of the lab. One challenge with human-robot dialogue, or any setting where a robot needs to listen to its environment is acoustics: microphone quality and placement, room layout including placement of the robot, ambient noise, decibel level of human speech, and other phenomena. An extension of the benchmark can be an acoustics test suite that includes common acoustic challenges to the audio stream like adding the sound of white noise, robot actuators, alarms, a loud car driving by, decibel changes to the incoming speech, randomly changing words the speech recognizer outputs, etc. Researchers who would fit this benchmark extension include those working to address these challenges through improving speech recognition models, improving microphones and microphone arrays, experimenting with microphone placement, speaker diarization, robot voice filtering, etc.

To make the dialogue more challenging, one extension to the base task can be to introduce taboo words that the robot is not allowed to say—for example, puzzle piece colors, common shape names, or directions (e.g., “left”). This would require the robot to use other methods to explain itself. For example, if the robot wants to direct the human’s attention to a specific piece that is red in color, but “red” is a taboo word, then the robot must find another way to communicate about the piece, either by using its shape, spatial placement, or by saying something in comparison, e.g., the piece that is the color of your shirt . One of the metrics can be the number of taboo words the human is able to identify. The taboo words can be selected at the start of the session, or be dynamically introduced and revoked as the tasks progresses.

The base task is meant to be a social task only, prioritizing spoken dialogue where the human completes all of the manipulation; however, we envision an extension to the base task that gives robotics researchers the opportunity to add robot movement and manipulation to the task. The first and most simple is that, when needed, the robot moves the hidden pieces from behind the divider to the human and takes the replacement piece. Moreover, research labs interested in robot locomotion can place the hidden pieces various locations in the room so the robot has to retrieve them. We also envision an extension where the robot and human can swap roles; the human becomes the instruction giver who sees the target shape, the game board, and the hidden pieces and guides the robot (now the follower ), to construct the puzzle while the robot moves the pieces into place. A further extension might be that two robots take both roles and must communicate with each other to successfully put together the puzzle. A larger benchmark would require research lab teams to collaborate on pairing their robots and systems, with metrics extending to how the two robots work together.

“Pentomino objects” are a good starting point due to their simple shapes and solid colors, but an extension of this could be more complex and commonplace objects identified by the community. For the base task, these can be small tabletop objects, such as a mug, a pen, a book, a bottle, a phone, and other everyday objects. The objects and size of the game board could go beyond tabletop and be much larger, such as cinder blocks or chairs, spanning an entire room or even multiple rooms. We also envision a scenario where the objects are more difficult to carry so the human and robot need to work together. The number of hidden and distractor objects could also vary, adding complexity. Finally, one extension could be that distractor objects are in another room that needs to be described by the robot to a human or to another robot that retrieves and replaces the object (but it is only allowed to enter that room once in a single game).

The base task can be completed with dialogue alone, but humans often use methods other than complex descriptions to indicate objects that are in a shared space. An extension of the base task could therefore be to allow deictic and iconic gestures, with a potentially more complex game board starting state. Research labs who are interested in deictic gestures on robots would be able to test their theories using this extension, and labs interested in iconic gestures could use more complex puzzle pieces and configurations as needed.

The base task assumes that the robot and human are collaborating with each other, but we also envision an extension that would enable additional player attitudes that alter the social aspects of the interaction. For example, the human / instruction follower can be given instructions to be adversarial or reluctant to help (humans will very likely be commonly reluctant to interact with robots “in the wild” so it will be more ready to handle similar situations). If the robot / instruction giver detects reluctance or an adversarial attitude, it may need to switch to an alternative approach to social interaction—for example, to convince the human to help or to negotiate roles. Another attitude might include an adversarial instruction giver / robot that sometimes is reluctant to give information, or a robot that purposefully misguides or even lies about information (e.g., purposefully using the wrong word for a color feigning that it made a mistake) means the instruction follower has to ask clarification questions and adjust their strategy. Other attitudes include a human who is afraid of robots, different age categories, human disgust regarding certain robot morphologies, viewing robots as tools rather than social partners, over-trusting what the robot says even when it has made mistakes, feeling a sense of care over the robot (e.g., the robot mentions that it is depressed and needs help and doesn’t want to play the game anymore). Most of these attitudes are on the side of the human, but many of these attitudes could also be modeled on the robot.

The extensions described above are by no means exhaustive, but serve as a set of examples of how the benchmark can be extended to meet the needs of different communities. Taken together a robot that can complete all of the tasks would be a very capable robot, indeed.

2026-10-07.title: EgoLAP: Learning from Egocentric Human Data through Language-Action Reasoning
2026-10-07.authors: Lihan Zha , Shresth Grover , Tenny Yin , Samuel M. Bateman , Hengkai Pan , Mengchao Zhang , Aykut Onol , Allen Z. Ren , Dhruv Shah , Anirudha Majumdar
2026-10-07.comment: Project website: this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract:
Egocentric human data offer a path to scaling robot learning beyond costly robot demonstrations, yet the embodiment gap makes raw human trajectories a poor supervisory target for control.
Our key insight is that, although low-level actions are embodiment-specific, their underlying motion intent can capture task-relevant structure that transfers across humans and robots.
We introduce EgoLAP , a VLA pre-training framework that jointly learns from human and robot trajectories through a shared language-based action chain-of-thought.
EgoLAP expresses motion intent as structured, temporally abstracted language actions and pairs them with motion-level reasoning grounded in scene geometry, physics, and object affordances.
Across extensive real-world and simulated experiments, EgoLAP transfers human experience to robot control more effectively than alternative action representations and reaches 80.1 % 80.1\% mean real-world task progress, a 2.3 × 2.3\times performance gain over alternative action representations. Motion-level reasoning also outperforms a composite reasoning format that combines subtask, object-box, and visual-trace reasoning.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Robot foundation models have advanced rapidly by scaling robot demonstrations across tasks, environments, and embodiments [ 11 , 24 , 19 , 7 , 27 , 52 ] , yet such demonstrations remain costly to collect and narrow relative to the breadth of human activity. Egocentric human video offers the scale and behavioral diversity that robot data lacks, capturing long-horizon manipulation in everyday environments and growing independently of any robot platform.

To leverage human data for robot learning, prior work extracts intermediate representations through hand-engineered pipelines, such as interaction hotspots and affordances [ 37 , 45 ] , hand poses or image-space tracks [ 5 , 50 , 6 , 42 ] , latent plans [ 48 , 20 , 4 ] , or visually edited embodiments [ 2 , 30 , 29 ] .
These representations capture useful facets of human behavior, but inherit the inductive biases and failure modes of their extraction pipelines that restricts scalability.
Moreover, differences in morphology, kinematics, and control create an embodiment gap that limits the direct transfer of action-level knowledge from human data to robot policies [ 8 ] .

Our key insight is that humans and robots need not share low-level actions; instead, they need to share motion intent : what motion needs to be produced, and why it’s appropriate given the current physical state. We represent the what using language actions : structured, temporally abstract descriptions of changes in pose and gripper state, such as “move forward 3 cm, rotate clockwise 14 degrees, and close gripper.” Unlike embodiment-specific trajectories or non-linguistic action tokens [ 38 , 34 ] , language actions reuse the vocabulary and compositional structure of a vision–language model (VLM), thereby providing control-relevant supervision within its pretrained semantic space [ 55 , 17 , 16 ] . However, the same task may require different motions across embodiments, so specifying what motion to execute is insufficient. We therefore introduce motion-level reasoning to represent the why : local, physically grounded rationales that relate contact, geometry, and object affordances to the intended effect of the next motion. Unlike subtask plans or visual traces, which primarily specify what action to take or where to move [ 54 , 47 , 46 ] , motion-level reasoning captures the physical relationship between the current state and the motion required to achieve the intended effect, providing a form of supervision that can connect directly to low-level actions, yet transfer across embodiments. Together, motion-level reasoning and language actions define a physically grounded “action chain-of-thought”.

Statement of contributions. We introduce EgoLAP , a VLA pre-training framework that co-trains on egocentric human and robot trajectories through motion-level reasoning and language actions, achieving 44.9 44.9 points of real-world performance more than the strongest action representation. Unlike previous embodied reasoning methods [ 54 , 47 ] , EgoLAP only runs a lightweight action expert during inference time, where the textual targets provide auxiliary supervision and require no autoregressive generation.
Across extensive zero-shot real-world and simulation experiments on a bimanual robot, language actions transfer human experience better than non-linguistic action representations [ 38 , 34 ] , and motion-level reasoning contributes 44.7 44.7 points of real-world task progress more to EgoLAP than the baselines. Motion-level reasoning also strongly outperforms a strong composite of subtask, object-box, and visual-trace reasoning supervision. Finally, EgoLAP adapts effectively through reinforcement learning over language actions and motion-level reasoning.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 RELATED WORK

Learning Robot Policies from Egocentric Human Data. Human data provides scalable supervision for robot learning, but leveraging them requires bridging the embodiment gap. Prior methods rely on method-specific representations: interaction hotspots and affordances [ 37 , 45 ] , hand poses or image-space tracks [ 5 , 50 , 6 , 42 ] , latent plans [ 48 , 20 , 4 ] , or visually edited embodiments [ 2 , 30 , 29 ] . Although effective, these hand-designed interfaces require modular processing (e.g., hand-pose estimation, point tracking, or embodiment editing) and inherit its inductive biases and errors, limiting their scalability. The gap is evident in direct policy learning: despite the 3,000 hours of egocentric video available in Ego4D [ 15 ] , MimicPlay and Motion Tracks train on only about 10 minutes of task-specific human video, ATM evaluates transfer from 100 human videos, and Phantom trains on 250–350 demonstrations per task [ 48 , 42 , 50 , 30 ] .

Another line directly trains policies on large-scale egocentric human datasets [ 39 , 18 ] along with robot data [ 22 , 57 , 40 , 31 , 41 , 26 , 51 , 35 ] . These systems typically retain embodiment-specific pose targets or encode trajectories with non-linguistic action tokens as training targets [ 38 , 23 , 49 ] , which impede cross-embodiment transfer [ 55 ] . Language-Action Pre-training (LAP) [ 55 ] instead expresses motion as structured natural language, showing improved zero-shot transfer among robots. EgoLAP extends this representation to human–robot co-training and pairs it with motion-level reasoning, which provides both embodiments with shared language-based targets and improves human-to-robot transfer.

Action Representations for VLAs. VLAs commonly supervise a VLM with discretized action tokens [ 7 , 27 ] , sometimes alongside a separate continuous action expert [ 19 ] . The discrete target is especially consequential when gradients from the action expert do not reach the VLM backbone [ 13 ] . Learned tokenizers such as FAST, OAT, ActionCodec, and X-Tokenizer optimize action compression or token structure [ 38 , 34 , 12 , 21 ] ; LAP instead describes motion in natural language to remain compatible with the VLM’s pretrained semantic space [ 55 ] . EgoLAP applies this representation to bimanual human–robot co-training and shows that motion-level reasoning yields larger gains with language actions than with non-linguistic action tokens.

Reasoning for Visuomotor Control. Prior work augments visuomotor policies with textual reasoning over goals, subtask plans, and spatial cues, or with visual intermediates such as affordances and 2D point traces [ 54 , 47 , 56 , 28 , 53 , 9 , 46 ] . With human video, plans, reasoning labels, and dense annotations improve policy performance under distribution shift [ 36 , 14 , 25 , 10 ] . These results establish the value of reasoning supervision, but leave unresolved which reasoning content best supports cross-embodiment motion transfer. For example, DeMiAn finds that no single annotation type performs best across tasks [ 25 ] , while a large-scale study finds no benefit from conditioning actions on chain-of-thought traces [ 33 ] .

This gap motivates motion-level reasoning : supervision that captures the embodiment-invariant physical rationale underlying human and robot motions, thereby bridging the two data sources. Unlike prior approaches [ 54 , 9 ] , EgoLAP requires neither multi-stage distillation nor text generation at inference, simplifying training and ensuring fast inference.

2026-10-07.title: NMPP: Nonlinear Model Predictive Planning for Agile UAV Flight in Cluttered Environments
2026-10-07.authors: Ondřej Procházka , Juraj Pauko , Robert Pěnička , Martin Saska
2026-10-07.abstract:
Flying a quadrotor through a cluttered environment requires not only planning a collision-free reference trajectory based on perceived obstacles, but the reference also needs to be dynamically feasible and within the actuation limits of the vehicle, so that the controller can track it precisely.
Existing methods either optimize a smooth polynomial inside a convex corridor, which limits agility, or treat obstacles as soft costs traded against tracking performance.
We propose a nmpp ( nmpp ) that imposes perceived obstacles as hard geometric constraints and hands a full-state reference to an obstacle-blind S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) controller.
Our planner achieves a 58– 67 % 67\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} lower position RMSE than a linear Model Predictive Control trajectory planner and a 41– 70 % 70\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} lower RMSE than a polynomial trajectory planner.
It also completes all forest flights with up to 9.5 m s − 1 9.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} speed without collisions, and achieves 86 % 86\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} flight success rate under a more aggressive speed profile where a state-of-the-art planner has only 26 % 26\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} success rate.
The real-world deployment showed reliable execution flying up to 5.5 m s − 1 5.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} in an unknown cluttered environment.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Multirotor uav are increasingly deployed in missions that require flight through cluttered and initially unknown environments, including search and rescue [ 1 ] and infrastructure inspections [ 2 ] .
In such missions, the achievable flight speed determines how much of the environment can be covered within the vehicle’s limited endurance, which motivates operating the platform close to its dynamic limits.
Flying fast between obstacles requires a reference trajectory that is not only collision-free but also respects the uav ’s dynamics and actuation limits.
The obstacles are perceived by the onboard sensors only during the flight, so the trajectory has to be planned online.
The trajectory is often generated with simplified vehicle dynamics, causing a mismatch between the planned and flown trajectory [ 3 ] .
Moreover, collision avoidance and dynamic feasibility are commonly handled in separate stages, where a collision-free path is first found in a map and then converted into a trajectory for the controller.
Thus, the path ignores the dynamics and the trajectory ignores the obstacles.

This paper addresses the generation of such a trajectory in a single onboard optimization, which respects the uav dynamics and actuation limits while remaining collision-free with respect to the obstacles perceived by the onboard lidar ( lidar ) sensor.
The planner relies only on onboard sensing and has to return a solution within a few milliseconds of each planning period.
The result is continuously handed to an S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) geometric controller [ 4 ] as a full-state reference, so that the controller can follow it without deviating into the obstacles it was planned around.

Meeting these requirements in one optimization is difficult for three reasons.
First, the free space around obstacles is nonconvex, so imposing the obstacles as hard constraints makes the problem nonconvex and prone to local minima and infeasibility.
Second, the sensor returns a variable and unbounded number of obstacles, while the problem has to keep a fixed size for its computation time to stay predictable.
Third, a solution that is feasible at the discrete prediction nodes can still intersect an obstacle between two of them.
Existing work addresses these difficulties in two ways.
Corridor-based polynomial optimization restricts the trajectory to a convex subset of the free space, which removes the nonconvexity and allows online computation [ 5 , 6 ] .
However, the smooth polynomial representation keeps the vehicle from flying close to its dynamic limits.
Placing the avoidance inside the control loop instead preserves the reaction to what is currently perceived [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] , but the obstacles are then expressed as soft costs,
so that the avoidance is traded against tracking rather than guaranteed.

To this end, we propose nmpp ( nmpp ), which uses nmpc ( nmpc ) as a trajectory planner that generates a full-state reference for a separate controller rather than actuator commands.
Each optimization is initialized from the previously generated prediction rather than from the noisy state estimate, which allows imposing the obstacle constraint exactly.
The accumulated point cloud is converted into ellipsoids, of which a fixed number enters the problem, keeping its size constant regardless of the scene.
The hard constraint is complemented by a soft obstacle penalty and a softened acceleration-level hocbf ( hocbf ) condition [ 10 ] .
The full obstacle set validates the trajectory between prediction nodes.
To enforce actuation limits efficiently, the nmpc uses the thrust rate as its control input.
The thrust and angular-acceleration limits thus become linear constraints.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first planner that imposes lidar -perceived obstacles as hard constraints on the full quadrotor dynamics with thrust dynamics and runs onboard.

In simulation, nmpp is compared with two trajectory planners, one based on linear mpc ( mpc ) [ 11 ] and one based on polynomial trajectories [ 12 ] .
All three provide their reference to the same unmodified S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) controller [ 4 ] , so the reference is the only component that differs.
Across five constraint profiles with speed limits, nmpp achieves a 58– 67 % 67\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} lower position rmse ( rmse ) than the linear mpc trajectory planner and a 41– 70 % 70\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} lower rmse than the polynomial trajectory planner.
The obstacle avoidance is evaluated in a Poisson forest against SUPER [ 6 ] , with both planners flying in the same world towards the same goal. nmpp completed all flights without collision at speeds up to 9.5 m s − 1 9.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} ( super fast profile), whereas the success rate of SUPER dropped to 70 % 70\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} under that profile.
Under a more aggressive profile, the two planners reached the goal in 86 % 86\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} and 26 % 26\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of fifty flights, respectively.
Last but not least, we deployed the planner on a real quadrotor and validated it in a cluttered outdoor environment, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .
The uav successfully avoided obstacles while flying at speeds up to 5.5 m s − 1 5.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} .
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Methods for autonomous uav navigation in cluttered environments range from reactive collision avoidance to global, optimization-based, and learning-based trajectory planning.

Reactive methods compute avoidance commands directly from the current perception data. apf ( apf ) represent obstacles through repulsive potentials [ 13 ] , while Velocity Obstacles identify control velocities that may lead to a future collision [ 14 ] .
Extensions such as ORCA support reciprocal collision avoidance between multiple agents [ 15 ] .
Reciprocal velocity constraints have also been integrated into nmpc for mutual collision avoidance in agile uav flight [ 16 ] .
These approaches are computationally efficient, but their local decisions can lead to local minima and usually rely on simplified vehicle dynamics.

Global motion planners instead search for a collision-free path in a representation of the environment.
Graph-search and sampling-based algorithms, such as A*, RRT, and RRT*, can find paths through complex obstacle configurations [ 17 ] .
The resulting path is commonly used to further plan a smooth trajectory that can be tracked by the uav .
Minimum jerk/snap polynomial trajectories are widely used for this purpose because the differential flatness of a quadrotor allows smooth position trajectories to be mapped to reference attitude and thrust [ 18 , 19 ] .
Efficient polynomial representations further enable the generation of long trajectories with many segments [ 12 ] .
Minimum-time formulations based on a point-mass model exploit the maneuverability of the uav more effectively than polynomial trajectories, at the cost of a reference that is only partially feasible for the real vehicle [ 3 ] .
However, these methods generally require predefined waypoints or a collision-free corridor and do not themselves determine how to avoid newly perceived obstacles.

Optimization-based planners incorporate smoothness, dynamic feasibility, and collision avoidance into a single trajectory-planning problem.
Corridor-based methods such as GCOPTER [ 5 ] efficiently optimize polynomial trajectories while enforcing smoothness-based formulations.
Receding safe corridors can also be constructed incrementally along the flight, so that high-speed smooth trajectories are planned within them [ 20 ] .
The corridor, however, restricts the trajectory to a convex subset of the free space, so the motion that can be produced is limited by how the corridor was carved rather than by the capability of the vehicle.

mpc provides an alternative in which the future vehicle motion is optimized over a receding horizon.
It naturally supports state, input, and actuation constraints and has therefore been applied to uav trajectory tracking and collision avoidance [ 11 ] .
An nmpc controller that integrates the dynamics of the low-level flight controller was shown to reduce the tracking error on agile references [ 21 ] .
There, the optimization is placed at the controller level, where it produces the commands for the actuators, whereas the method proposed here places it at the planner level, where it produces a reference for a separate controller.
The CIAO and CIAO* methods, presented in [ 22 , 23 ] , respectively, formulate collision avoidance through convex inner approximations of free space, providing recursively feasible predictive motion planning in static and predictable dynamic environments.
The principal difficulty is that a nonlinear geometric constraint has to be introduced for every obstacle that the optimization accounts for, so the size of the problem grows with the number of obstacles that are taken into account.
When the environment is measured online, that number is neither known in advance nor bounded, which is what the following approaches, and nmpp have to address.

Several planners therefore reduce or avoid dense volumetric mapping.
NanoMap stores a local history of depth measurements and performs uncertainty-aware proximity queries without fusing all measurements into a global voxel-map [ 24 ] .
EGO-Planner removes the need for an esdf ( esdf ) by extracting obstacle information only when the optimized trajectory intersects an occupied region [ 25 ] .
SUPER generates polyhedral flight corridors directly from lidar point clouds and optimizes an exploratory and a backup minimum-snap polynomial trajectory within them, to distinguish high-speed progress from motion guaranteed to remain in observed free space [ 6 ] .
These methods substantially reduce mapping overhead, but collision avoidance is still performed through path search, corridor construction, and polynomial trajectory optimization.

A different line of work removes the modular pipeline altogether and learns a mapping from sensor data directly to control commands, which avoids the latency accumulated across mapping, planning and control [ 26 , 27 ] .
These methods embed little prior knowledge about the controlled vehicle, so a change of the platform or its parameters requires retraining on large amounts of data.

Another group of methods integrates perception directly into predictive control.
Local point clouds can be queried directly using KD-trees to construct obstacle costs inside a point-mass mpc formulation [ 28 ] .
Point-cloud constraints can be incorporated into cbf ( cbf )-based mpc by selecting risk points close to the predicted motion [ 7 ] .
For quadrotors, multiple obstacle constraints can be aggregated into a composite cbf and enforced by a high-rate safety filter operating on a third-order dynamic model [ 8 ] .
Alternatively, gmppi ( gmppi ) approach sampled uav rollouts directly into depth images [ 9 ] and evaluates collision without constructing an explicit geometric map.
These approaches demonstrate the benefits of connecting local perception with predictive control, but they either simplify the vehicle dynamics, apply collision avoidance as a separate safety filter, or represent obstacles only through soft collision costs.
In contrast, nmpp imposes the lidar -perceived obstacles as hard constraints on the full quadrotor dynamics with thrust dynamics, without restricting the trajectory to a convex corridor.
A fixed number of ellipsoids keeps the problem size constant regardless of the scene, and the planner runs onboard while providing a full-state reference.

2026-10-07.title: Magnet-Aware Control of Legged Robots
2026-10-07.authors: J. Playan Garai , S. B. Djuve , C. McGreavy , M. Khadiv
2026-10-07.abstract: Autonomous robots can increase uptime and reduce human exposure in Big Science facilities, but strong magnetic fields needed for their operation corrupt sensors and induce pose-dependent mechanical wrenches that destabilize robots and challenge conventional reactive controllers. This paper presents a control framework for modeling, estimating, and dynamically compensating for spatially varying magnetic wrenches acting on legged robots to improve robustness in these fields. We introduce a custom physics plugin for the MuJoCo simulator to model magnetic forces on rigid-body elements, alongside an inverse field-estimation framework to infer the latent magnetic field directly from quadruped dynamic responses and any number of sensor readings. Furthermore, we develop a Magnet-Aware Model Predictive Control (MPC) and Whole-Body Control (WBC) architecture that predicts and counteracts magnetic perturbations during locomotion to increase the range of magnetic fields in which the robot can operate. The effectiveness of the framework is validated through both simulation and physical hardware experiments. We show our method increases the the maximum rejectable disturbances from magnetic field in the force space by a factor of 2.5 and and between 1.6-2 times in torque space compared to a non-compensated system. Within the proposed magnetic field, this constitutes an increase in the area in which the robot can operate by 𝟐𝟗 , 𝟑𝟒 % \boldsymbol{29,34\%} of which 𝟏𝟎 , 𝟖𝟒 % \boldsymbol{10,84\%} would have previously caused an immediate collapse to non-compensated controllers.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Deploying autonomous robotic systems into Big Science facilities (such as high-energy physics and fusion energy experiments at CERN and ITER) is vital for automated inspection and maintenance. Operating within these sensitive environments requires high state estimation accuracy and robust disturbance rejection [ 1 ] . However, these facilities generate continuous, high-strength static magnetic fields reaching several Tesla ( T \text{\,}\mathrm{T} ) as a requirement for their operation, which jeopardises robotic operations. Robots unequipped to work in high magnetic fields are unable to withstand the magnetic fields in these facilities and can be pulled towards the magnetic field origin (Fig. 1 , red trace) causing the robot to fail and possibly damage the surrounding sensitive infrastructure. An adaptive, well-formulated compensation controller, however, could move through greater magnetic fields and reject higher induced disturbances using knowledge of the environment (Fig. 1 , blue trace), increasing the useful workspace of the robot.

All topologies are affected by these issues, from standard manipulators to more complex systems. However, Big Science facilities tend to be unstructured and multi-leveled, reducing the viability of wheeled mobile robots. Despite the added complexities of legged systems, these can overcome the presented challenges thanks to their enhanced mobility and adapting ground reaction forces to compensate existing perturbations.

Ferromagnetic components moving through a magnetic field experience significant forces and torques due to their interaction with the field. These induced perturbations impose continuous perturbations on the system that can threaten task completion. Additionally, electric brushless DC (BLDC) motors are most commonly equipped with Hall-effect encoders, which suffer from corrupted feedback and disrupted magnetic commutation [ 2 ] [ 3 ] , and will typically be the first point of failure in an electrically actuated system, forcing the motors to enter fault states and causing the collapse of the system. High-field environments also completely mask the Earth’s magnetic field, rendering IMU magnetometers ineffective for yaw drift correction in state estimation [ 4 ] [ 5 ] . Moving through steep magnetic flux gradients also induces parasitic currents in unshielded wiring (Faraday’s law [ 6 ] ), threatening logic circuits and sensor signals.

Hardware modifications, such as magnetic-immune capacitive encoders [ 7 ] , and software adaptations such as magnetic-field SLAM [ 8 ] [ 9 ] mitigate some sensing issues, a holistic, environment-aware approach is needed for the control problem. In some approaches, robots are constructed without magnetic components to remove the control complexity completely [ 10 ] , but non-magnetically susceptible components drastically degrade the capabilities of a system and are limited in their applications. Momentum observers [ 11 ] [ 12 ] [ 13 ] use the dynamic model of the robot and the momentum derivative to remove the need of noisy joint accelerations. A low pass filter is then added to create reactive strategies to compensate for, or measure, perturbations. However, this approach requires measurement or estimation of ground reaction forces (GRFs), and magnetic field induced disturbances are included in these GRF measurements and cannot be separated, leading to the disturbance force being masked within the GRF measurements. Projection approaches [ 14 ] [ 15 ] project rigid-body dynamics of the system into the null space of the contact Jacobian to remove contact forces and isolate unmodeled forces. In magnetic environments, however, the non-linear relationship between magnetic fields and induced wrenches amplifies minor modeling inaccuracies into large disturbance readings. Furthermore, physical realities such as foot slip or contact compliance violate null-space assumptions and cause large residual spikes [ 16 ] . Reactive or model-free disturbance rejection strategies with low-pass filtering aim for a high level of flexibility and adaptability, but, model-free approaches make decisions reactively based on sensor data within a moving window, leading to delays in compensating to magnetic field gradients, especially since such disturbances can not be detectable by these methods. Push recovery approaches to disturbance rejection [ 17 ] [ 18 ] assume external forces are transient, impulsive, or static, which is effective for short disturbances, but magnetic wrenches form continuous vector fields that vary dynamically with spatial gradients and the robot’s pose and joint configuration [ 19 ] .

Existing disturbance estimation and control frameworks are therefore not suitable for these environments since they fail to guarantee the robust dynamic balance needed for autonomous operations. An effective control framework for legged robotic operation in a magnetic field needs to account for the complex dynamics of induced magnetic wrenches and should incorporate models of magnetic fields and their effects on susceptible ferromagnetic components of robot structures.

To address these challenges, this paper focuses on modeling, estimating, and dynamically compensating for spatially varying magnetic wrenches on quadruped actuators. Critically, we will be assuming that the commutation in the motors is not done through Hall sensors but instead uses capacitive encoders as mentioned before. This will ensure our motors are reliable and robust even under magnetic fields.
Our main contributions can be summarised as follows:

A custom MuJoCo [ 20 ] physics plugin that simulates induced magnetic forces and wrenches on rigid body elements based on the ferromagnetic components in the system.

A custom MuJoCo [ 20 ] physics plugin that simulates induced magnetic forces and wrenches on rigid body elements based on the ferromagnetic components in the system.

An inverse magnetic field estimation framework that infers local field distributions from legged system dynamics and sensor readings.

A Magnet-Aware framework (Fig. 2 ) that actively predicts and compensates for magnetic perturbations during dynamic locomotion.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Sec. II details the background concepts and mathematical derivation of the magnetic wrench model. Sec. III describes the custom MuJoCo simulator implementation. Sec. IV outlines the Magnet-Aware MPC+WBC dynamic compensation framework. Sec. V presents the magnetic field estimation algorithm. Finally, Sec. VI details simulation and physical hardware experiments evaluating controller performance.

2026-10-07.title: Fast Non-Parametric Heteroscedastic Imitation Learning With Geometric Priors
2026-10-07.authors: Maximilian Mühlbauer , Arne Sachtler , Markus Knauer , Cem Küçükgenç , Yanlong Huang , Alin Albu-Schäffer , João Silvério
2026-10-07.abstract:
When learning probabilistic policies from human demonstrations, data-efficient learning and fast adaptations to new scenarios are key requirements.
One popular way to achieve intuitive and reliable adaptations is through non-parametric, typically kernel-based, methods.
However, existing solutions either fail to account for the geometry of manifolds common in robotics, limiting data efficiency, or, when geometry-aware, provide unreliable uncertainty estimates or require retraining to adapt.
We propose a non-parametric approach leveraging geometric priors in scenarios of data scarcity and heteroscedastic uncertainties for probabilistic modeling.
We utilize the method to formulate policies based on time or robot state, where non-separable diagonal kernels allow capturing uncertainty relations between degrees of freedom for same-sized in- and outputs.
Fast updates, requiring less than 3 ms 3\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} for a trajectory involving both position and orientation are possible through an optimized formulation.
Our approach supports both manifold-valued input and manifold-valued output with large orientation changes.
Using task parameterization, adaptation to different object poses is easily possible.
We evaluate the approach on a set of toy examples and on real robot manipulation tasks both in autonomous execution and in shared control scenarios.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Probabilistic representations of movement primitives are key in applications with requirements in robustness and safety guarantees, as for example in space robotics [ 1 ] , underwater robotics [ 2 ] or healthcare assistance [ 3 ] . Parametric approaches such as Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) [ 4 , 5 ] provide an aleatoric (inherent to the data) uncertainty estimate while non-parametric approaches like Gaussian Processes (GPs) [ 6 ] provide epistemic (lack of data) uncertainty [ 7 ] . Kernelized Movement Primitives (KMPs) [ 8 ] and their extensions [ 9 , 10 ] have shown remarkable qualities regarding modeling capability and adaptability, while in parallel providing both uncertainty estimates.
Both uncertainty types are required in applications – the epistemic uncertainty estimate can, e.g., be used to render the robot compliant when unsure about its actions [ 11 ] while the aleatoric uncertainty helps to compute control gains encoding task variability [ 12 ] .
Heteroscedasticity allows our method to model different uncertainties for different phases of a task, which is a key requirement in policy arbitration [ 13 , 12 ] . KMPs have already been applied to a range of learning problems, such as manufacturing tasks [ 11 ] , in space applications [ 1 ] or to guide reinforcement learning [ 14 ] .

Currently, these approaches are however only designed for Euclidean [ 8 , 10 ] or single tangent space (STS) [ 9 ] , linearizing curved manifolds at one point, thus inducing distortions [ 15 ] and not allowing to incorporate prior geometric knowledge.
In contrast, approaches for multiple tangent spaces as already developed for GMMs [ 4 ] induce much less distortion through the utilization of multiple linearization points.
A notable exception for KMPs is developed in [ 16 ] fusing multiple STS KMPs [ 9 ] on multiple tangent spaces on SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) , at the cost, however, of an intricate formulation and a lack of generalizability to other geometries.
Additionally, each of the STS KMPs still suffers from issues resulting from using a single linearization point.
Conversely, Lopez-Custodio et al. [17] developed a kernel-based, on-manifold approach which, however, uses different distributions per manifold which are hard to join in product manifolds and computationally slow.
This approach also only outputs aleatoric uncertainty, neglecting epistemic uncertainty which is fundamental in many imitation learning problems.
Our solution ( Fig. 1 ) combines the advantages of the aforementioned methods, namely fast predictions with aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty.
On selected manifolds such as SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) , we achieve global validity through the double-coverage by 𝒮 3 \mathcal{S}^{3} .
Using the Riemannian Gaussian distribution [ 4 , 5 ] , no discrete linearization points are required, removing the covariance distortions caused by STS methods ( Section III ).

Moreover, currently available kernel-based methods, using separable kernels, can only predict scalar-valued epistemic uncertainties as also seen in the decomposition in [ 11 ] .
Recently, matrix-valued kernels have become available [ 18 , 19 ] which allow for encoding correlations for same-sized inputs and outputs.
As a large step in the direction of such kernels, we leverage diagonal kernels to improve the learning of state-based Dynamical Systems (DSs) ( Section IV ).

Finally, as in any non-parametric method, runtime in KMPs is a function of the number of data points and in general slower than for parametric methods.
Especially adding or removing points is computationally expensive, requiring the inversion of a large matrix. Wang et al. [20] recently proposed a method for avoiding to recalculate the whole inverse.
Similar to GPs [ 6 ] , we leverage the Cholesky decomposition, significantly improving runtime over both vanilla KMP and [ 20 ] while keeping flexibility in adding and removing points ( Section V ).

In summary, the key contributions of our work are:

A Riemannian formulation of a non-parametric approach to imitation learning [ 8 ] providing both aleatoric and epistemic heteroscedastic uncertainties ( Section III-A );

The Riemannian derivation of two adaptation schemes for different requirements based on via points [ 8 ] as well as on a soft null space projector [ 10 ] ( Section III-B );

Task-parameterization of the method on different charts [ 21 ] on SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) ( Section III-C );

The integration of non-separable matrix-valued kernels in the approach to allow for the prediction of a matrix-valued epistemic uncertainty ( Section IV-B );

Computational improvements allowing for fast prediction and adaptation in several geometries commonly used in robotics problems ( Section V ).

At the end of Sections III , IV and V we provide toy examples evaluating the key contributions in simplified scenarios.
Furthermore, we have implemented both time-based policies and their modification as well as state-based DSs on a torque-controlled robot ( Section VI ). Section II covers background.
We discuss results in Section VII and conclude in Section VIII .

# II Background

## II-A Riemannian Manifolds, Optimization and Statistics

Many quantities in robotics, such as orientations in SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) , cannot be modeled using Euclidean geometry.
Riemannian manifolds allow for a principled treatment of such non-Euclidean geometries [ 5 ] .
