2026-10-07.title: HygieneRoboBench: Benchmarking Hygiene-Aware Planning for Household Robots
2026-10-07.authors: Yurun Chen , Josh Qixuan Sun , Jason Qin , Chengtai Li , Tianyi Wang , Mark Crowley , Wentao Zhu
2026-10-07.abstract:
Contact with contaminated objects can spread hazards through a household
robot’s grippers, tools, and shared surfaces, while new contacts can make
an existing plan unsafe. Existing benchmarks do not jointly assess how
planners identify hygiene risks from contact history and plan safe
continuations after new contact events. Planners must do so within time and resource
limits while respecting user priorities.
We introduce HygieneRoboBench, with 624 instances across 134 task families,
to evaluate safe resolution of household tasks from a given execution history.
Tasks capture contamination through two grippers and shared
objects, treatment costs, and user priorities. We combine controlled history,
profile, and event comparisons with independent plan evaluation. These assess
safe resolution, cost efficiency under user priorities, and responses to contact events.
Evaluation of LLM-based and symbolic planners shows that safely
completing a task does not guarantee the lowest execution costs under the
user’s priorities. To address this problem, we introduce
Hygiene-NSP. It combines LLM-based grounding, contact-history reconstruction,
and CP-SAT to jointly plan hygiene treatment and task execution under
user priorities. Hygiene-NSP achieves safe resolution and optimal safe
resolution rates of 94.4% and 90.4%, respectively.
Both rates are higher than those of the evaluated baseline planners on the full dataset.
Project page: https://euron-zc.github.io/HygieneRoboBench/ .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Hygiene is a basic requirement for household robots because their actions
directly affect the food, utensils, and personal items that people use.
Cross-contamination can spread harmful microorganisms to food and household
surfaces, creating risks of illness [ 2 , 3 ] .
As robots reuse grippers and tools across tasks, contamination acquired
during one activity can be carried into later interactions.
A robot may therefore complete the requested task while leaving the people
it serves exposed to hygiene hazards.

LLMs can interpret household requests and generate task
plans [ 4 , 5 ] . However, this ability does not
ensure that their plans address contact-dependent hygiene risks and satisfy
user requirements.
Planners must determine how
contamination spreads through contact, whether cleaning removes the relevant
hazards, and whether unexpected events invalidate an existing plan.
In Fig. , contamination passes from a tray through the
left gripper to a spoon. An unexpected handover then contaminates the right
gripper, making the original fruit-handling plan unsafe. In this example,
the grippers use washable, replaceable contact pads. The robot must
wash or replace the contaminated contact pad before handling the fruit.
Cleaning after every action consumes time and supplies and may prevent
the task from being completed within the available budget. The planner must
therefore determine when treatment is necessary and select an appropriate
option based on the remaining resources and user priorities.
Existing evaluations address execution safety, adaptive planning, and
personalization [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . However, they lack
a systematic joint assessment of these hygiene decisions. Such an assessment
must distinguish when contact history changes which continuation is optimal
and when the same continuation remains optimal.
Table I summarizes their coverage.

We introduce HygieneRoboBench to evaluate household service planning under
contact-dependent hygiene risks. It tests whether robots meet user needs despite
unexpected events and within time and resource limits. The benchmark contains
624 instances across 134 task families and spans seven household areas.
It covers five activity groups:
food preparation, dishware and dining, cleaning and laundry, bedroom and storage,
and pet and household care. Tasks capture contamination
propagation through two grippers and shared objects, resource trade-offs
between washing and replacement, and differences in user priorities over
time and consumables. We construct paired instances with the same current
physical configuration and task conditions but different contact histories.
These pairs test whether planners use history to make appropriate choices.
Event and profile comparisons further test plan adaptation and adherence to
user priorities. Human review and full-history replay checks validate
the constructed tasks. Evaluation covers three aspects: safe task resolution,
user priorities and execution costs, and responses to histories and events.

Following the language-to-symbolic planning paradigm exemplified by
LLM+P [ 15 ] , we develop Hygiene-NSP, a hygiene-aware neuro-symbolic
planner (NSP). It grounds household requests and reconstructs hygiene
conditions from contact history.
A trusted compiler builds the constraint problem, and
CP-SAT [ 16 ] jointly schedules treatment and service
actions according to user priorities. Optional state projection reduces
the planning representation while preserving the information needed for
the current continuation.

All seven evaluated planners show lower performance as the benchmark’s
structural task difficulty increases. On controlled history pairs, considering
cost optimality alongside safe completion changes the relative ranking of
planners. Hygiene-NSP achieves the highest overall rates of safe resolution
(94.4%) and optimal safe resolution (90.4%).

Our contributions are:

Problem and benchmark. We introduce HygieneRoboBench to evaluate
planning with contamination propagation through two grippers and shared
objects. It tests how robots use contact history and respond to unexpected
events while meeting hygiene and user requirements within time and resource limits.

Controlled construction and evaluation. We establish history,
profile, and event comparisons with metrics for safe resolution,
user-priority optimality, and decision responses. Human review, independent
plan evaluation, and certification by the Reference support task plausibility
and reliable evaluation.

Systematic evaluation and findings. We evaluate seven planners
across task difficulties and household activities. Controlled comparisons
reveal differences in optimal planning that safe completion alone does not
capture. Independent evaluation further identifies execution violations and
inefficiencies in resource use and scheduling.

Companion neuro-symbolic planner. We introduce Hygiene-NSP, which
combines language grounding, history-based state reconstruction, and
constraint solving to jointly optimize hygiene treatment and task execution
under user priorities.

1. Problem and benchmark. We introduce HygieneRoboBench to evaluate
planning with contamination propagation through two grippers and shared
objects. It tests how robots use contact history and respond to unexpected
events while meeting hygiene and user requirements within time and resource limits.

2. Controlled construction and evaluation. We establish history,
profile, and event comparisons with metrics for safe resolution,
user-priority optimality, and decision responses. Human review, independent
plan evaluation, and certification by the Reference support task plausibility
and reliable evaluation.

3. Systematic evaluation and findings. We evaluate seven planners
across task difficulties and household activities. Controlled comparisons
reveal differences in optimal planning that safe completion alone does not
capture. Independent evaluation further identifies execution violations and
inefficiencies in resource use and scheduling.

4. Companion neuro-symbolic planner. We introduce Hygiene-NSP, which
combines language grounding, history-based state reconstruction, and
constraint solving to jointly optimize hygiene treatment and task execution
under user priorities.

# II Related Work

Task and safety benchmarks. BEHAVIOR-1K and RoboCasa provide household activity definitions and
manipulation environments [ 1 , 17 ] .
EmbodiedBench, Embodied Agent Interface, and PlanBench assess agents’ ability
to interpret tasks, plan actions, and reason about their effects [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] .
SafeAgentBench evaluates safe task planning [ 9 ] .
IS-Bench evaluates interaction risks and their mitigation order [ 10 ] .
VestaBench studies long-horizon planning with multiple constraints and
adversarial settings [ 11 ] .
SafeManip checks temporal safety properties of manipulation traces [ 12 ] .
SIMMER models contamination and other latent failures in complete cooking plans [ 6 ] . HygieneRoboBench tests how past contact changes the safe
ways to complete a task under new conditions.

Adaptive and personalized planning. Inner Monologue uses environmental feedback to revise robot plans [ 21 ] .
AdaPlanBench tests plan revision as world and user constraints are revealed [ 7 ] .
PARTNR evaluates human–robot collaboration under temporal and capability constraints [ 13 ] .
PbP learns user preferences from demonstrations [ 8 ] .
MEMENTO uses past interactions to interpret personalized requests [ 14 ] .
HygieneRoboBench tests whether planners follow given user priorities when choosing
among plans that satisfy hygiene and service constraints.

Language and constraint-based planning. SayCan grounds action selection in robot affordances [ 4 ] .
ProgPrompt and Code as Policies generate programmatic plans and policies [ 5 , 22 ] .
LLM+P connects language interpretation to formal planning [ 15 ] .
VIRF verifies generated plans [ 23 ] , while ISR-LLM uses validator
feedback to refine them [ 24 ] .
SayCanPay guides cost-effective search with feasibility and payoff [ 25 ] .
JIT-Memory maintains safety-relevant information across embodied
interaction [ 26 ] .
Finite-trace temporal logic specifies execution properties [ 27 ] .
Scheduling research addresses shared-resource limits and revises schedules after
disruptions [ 28 , 29 ] .

2026-10-07.title: RIWANav: Recursive World-Action Models with Self-Improvement for Urban Navigation
2026-10-07.authors: Jing Xie , Shouwei Ruan , Yubin Wang , Yuxiang Zhang , Haitao Yang , Songchang Jin , Dianxi Shi
2026-10-07.abstract: Long-horizon urban navigation requires sequential local decisions whose errors can compound over time. Imitation learning (IL) rarely learns from failures, while physical trial-and-error reinforcement learning (RL) is costly. Action-conditioned world models can provide imagined feedback by predicting visual consequences for candidate actions. However, a frozen world model may become less reliable as the policy evolves. In this paper, we introduce RIWANav , a post-training framework that casts the coupled adaptation of a world model and an action model (policy) as task-specific recursive self-improvement (RSI). Each cycle alternates two updates. The world model evaluates policy actions through imagined outcomes, providing comparative feedback for group-relative policy optimization (GRPO). The improved policy then constructs a grounded self-curriculum, selecting expert-consistent action–video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error. The refined world model supplies feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive self-improvement loop. Experiments show that RIWANav outperforms training baselines and prior methods, validating the proposed recursive self-improvement loop between the policy and world model. Real-world trials further demonstrate its practical applicability.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Long-horizon urban navigation requires an agent to reach a language-specified destination from street-level observations and recent motion history. At each step, the agent must translate the global goal into a local decision, recover from mistakes, and determine when to stop. Existing methods commonly learn this behavior by imitating expert trajectories [ 1 , 2 ] . Although imitation learning (IL) provides strong initialization, it mainly supervises successful expert actions and cannot learn from policy-induced failures, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). This limitation is particularly consequential in urban navigation, where one inaccurate local motion changes the next observation and can compound over subsequent decisions [ 3 ] . Reinforcement learning (RL) can learn from such failures, but collecting long-horizon trial-and-error interaction is costly. Navigation post-training therefore needs outcome feedback without requiring every candidate action to be physically executed.

Action-conditioned world models serve as learned simulators for policy improvement. Navigation world models (NWM) [ 4 ] and recent world action models [ 3 , 5 , 6 ] predict future observations conditioned on candidate actions. Their imagined outcomes allow a policy to compare local decisions before execution. However, a world model used for policy optimization should not remain frozen, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (b). As the policy improves, the frozen world model does not adapt to the evolving distribution of urban navigation behaviors. Inaccurate predictions can then distort subsequent policy updates, making the frozen model a bottleneck of model-based post-training.

We therefore seek a training framework that adapts the world model alongside the policy. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) motivates a training process in which each improvement stage changes the conditions for the next [ 7 ] . We bring this principle to navigation post-training by coupling policy optimization with world-model adaptation. The improved policy determines which demonstrations the world model should learn next, while the refined world model provides updated feedback for subsequent policy learning. Self-improvement therefore emerges from a recursive training loop between the policy and world model.

We introduce RIWANav ( R ecursive Self- I mprovement of W orld– A ction Models for Nav igation), a post-training framework that recursively improves a world model and an action model (policy). Each cycle alternates two coupled updates, as shown in Fig. 1 (c). First, the action-conditioned world model predicts visual outcomes for multiple policy actions. Their relative quality provides imagined feedback for Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [ 8 ] . Second, the improved policy constructs candidate action–video pairs for adapting the world model to the policy’s evolving behavior distribution. To maintain valid supervision from the offline dataset, we retain candidates that remain locally consistent with recorded expert motion. A grounded self-curriculum then prioritizes these samples according to behavioral novelty and current prediction error. The refined world model supplies the imagined feedback for the next policy update, closing the recursive training loop.

Our contributions are concluded as follows:

We introduce RIWANav , a post-training framework that recursively improves a navigation policy and a visual world model.

We develop a self-curriculum that filters policy proposals by expert consistency and prioritizes accepted action–video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error.

Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across seen and unseen environments, with real-world deployment further validating practical effectiveness.

1. We introduce RIWANav , a post-training framework that recursively improves a navigation policy and a visual world model.

2. We develop a self-curriculum that filters policy proposals by expert consistency and prioritizes accepted action–video pairs by behavioral novelty and prediction error.

3. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements across seen and unseen environments, with real-world deployment further validating practical effectiveness.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Real-World Navigation

Real-world navigation policies are learned from diverse robot trajectories and goal-conditioned supervision [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] .
CityWalker [ 1 ] scales urban navigation learning with large collections of walking and driving videos. UrbanNav [ 2 ] aligns city-scale human trajectories with landmark-grounded language.
OmniVLA [ 12 ] learns a shared navigation policy across image, language, and mixed goal modalities.
Other works explore generative guidance: NoMaD [ 11 ] uses a goal-masked diffusion policy, whereas VENTURA [ 13 ] generates instruction-conditioned visual paths for downstream control.
These methods primarily improve navigation through data, supervision, and policy design. Our work instead focuses on post-training.

## II-B World Models for Policy Learning

World models support planning and policy learning through learned future dynamics [ 14 , 15 ] . PlaNet [ 16 ] and Dreamer [ 17 ] established latent imagination for policy learning, with later works scaling to broader domains [ 18 , 19 ] and high-dimensional visual observations [ 20 , 21 ] .
Recent world models extend to navigation and embodied control [ 22 , 23 ] , while increasingly connect visual prediction with policy optimization [ 3 , 24 ] . NWM [ 4 ] ranks navigation trajectories using controllable video prediction, whereas Fast-WAM [ 6 ] jointly models video and actions to improve policy learning without explicit future generation.
Rather than treating the world model as a fixed source of imagined feedback, we study how the world model and policy can continually adapt to one another as policy behavior evolves.

## II-C Recursive Self-Improvement

Recursive self-improvement traditionally studies systems that improve their own problem-solving process [ 7 ] . POET [ 25 ] co-evolves environment–agent pairs, generates new challenges, and transfers solutions across environments.
Model-based policy learning faces a related problem at the level of learned dynamics. Uncertainty-aware prediction and short rollouts reduce exploitation of model errors [ 14 , 15 ] , while conservative objectives penalize uncertain transitions [ 26 , 27 ] . PDML [ 28 ] adapts model learning toward the current policy distribution. Other approaches prioritize experience through learning progress, novelty, or curiosity [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] .
In this paper, we connect these directions: the world model improves the policy through imagined feedback, and the evolving policy guides the next world-model update. This closed loop enables the two components to improve one another recursively.

2026-10-07.title: Feeling Through the Load: Compliant Quadruped Locomotion under Payload Interactions
2026-10-07.authors: Shaunak A. Mehta , Mayank Mishra , Prajit KrisshnaKumar , Sebastian Scherer , Koichiro Niinuma
2026-10-07.abstract: Quadruped robots are increasingly expected to carry objects while moving through human environments. But what happens when a person interacts directly with the payload rather than with the robot? If the payload is unrestrained, the robot must distinguish intentional external interactions from ordinary payload motion, while still keeping the load balanced and maintaining stable locomotion. How can a quadruped infer and compliantly respond to such interactions using only onboard measurements? In this work, we develop a force-aware locomotion framework that treats payload interactions as commands that shape the motion of the combined robot-payload system. Our approach separates the learning of force-aware locomotion and force estimation on an unrestrained payload. We combine a compliant load-carrying policy with a causal force estimator, trained through estimator-in-the-loop data aggregation and finetuning, to predict interactions from onboard robot measurements. Our simulations and real-world experiments show that the resulting controller can maintain stable payload-carrying locomotion, yield compliantly to external interactions, and use the inferred force to support human-guided changes in the robot’s trajectory. Our project page is available at https://feelthroughload.github.io/
2026-10-07.introduction:
Imagine a quadruped robot operating on a factory floor, transporting a payload from one station to another along a given trajectory. The robot, however, is unaware of a potential hazard in its path, such as a liquid spill. A human operator notices that the robot is moving toward the hazard and intervenes by pushing on the payload to guide it away from the hazardous path (see Figure 1 ). In such a situation, the robot not only needs to recognize an external interaction acting on a payload that is not rigidly attached to its body, but also needs to react safely and compliantly by yielding to the interaction or changing its path. At the same time, the robot should also adjust its motion to account for payload slip or imbalance caused due to the human push or movement during transportation.

Recent research in quadruped control has begun moving beyond locomotion over challenging terrains toward robots that can interact compliantly with people and adapt to the payloads they carry. Some works focus on enabling robots to
respond to forces acting on their bodies, either by rejecting them as disturbances or yielding to them for safer physical interaction [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , while others adapt locomotion to the properties or motion of the carried payload [ 4 , 5 ] . More recent works on collaborative transportation use forces applied by a human or another robot to guide the robot’s motion, but generally assume a mechanically coupled payload [ 6 , 7 ] .

However, these assumptions may not hold in real-world transportation tasks. The payload may simply rest on the robot without being rigidly attached, its physical properties may be unknown, and adding sensors directly to the payload may not be practical. In such settings, the robot must rely on its own onboard measurements to infer the external interaction and determine how to respond. This leads us to the central question of this work: How can a quadruped infer and compliantly respond to external forces applied to an unrestrained payload?

In this paper, we address this question by treating the forces experienced on the payload as interactions that should influence the motion of the combined robot-payload system.
Inspired by recent extensions of impedance control from robotic manipulators to legged locomotion [ 3 , 8 , 7 ] , we use a virtual mass-spring-damper reference to describe how the robot should yield to these interactions.
We learn a force-aware load bearing locomotion policy that realizes this compliant response while keeping the payload balanced, together with a causal estimator that recovers the applied force from onboard robot measurements. The explicit force estimate can also guide higher-level behavior, allowing a human to redirect the robot’s trajectory by pushing directly on the payload.

Our work is most closely related to FACET [ 3 ] and prior work on collaborative load transportation [ 7 , 9 ] . FACET considers compliant locomotion under external forces acting on the robot, while collaborative transportation methods enable robots to respond to interactions through a shared payload assuming that the payload is mechanically connected to the robot. In contrast, we consider a robot carrying an unrestrained payload and investigate how it can respond compliantly to forces applied directly to the payload while keeping it balanced.

Overall, we make the following contributions:

Payload-Aware Compliant Locomotion. We formulate the problem of compliant locomotion under forces applied directly to an unrestrained payload. In this formulation, the payload interaction shapes the desired motion of the combined robot-payload system while the robot maintains stable locomotion and keeps the payload balanced.

Estimating and Responding to Payload Interactions. We introduce a three-stage learning pipeline for force-aware load bearing locomotion. We first learn a privileged policy with recurrent adaptation, followed by causal payload force estimation using onboard sensors, and estimator-aware policy finetuning. Together, these stages enable the robot to explicitly estimate and respond to interactions with an unrestrained payload using only onboard robot measurements, without instrumenting the payload.

Simulated and Real-World Experiments. We evaluate our approach under diverse payload, interaction-force, and impedance conditions in simulations and on a real quadruped. We further demonstrate that the explicit force estimate provides a useful signal for downstream behavior, allowing a human to guide the robot’s trajectory by interacting directly with the payload.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Compliant force adaptive locomotion. Impedance and admittance control have been widely used in robotic manipulation to prescribe compliant motion in response to external forces [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . These ideas have also influenced force-aware control for legged robots. Model-based methods incorporate compliant objectives and external disturbances into whole-body or optimization-based controllers [ 13 , 14 ] . Some other methods estimate external wrenches acting on the robot without dedicated force sensors using dynamics-based observers and state estimators [ 15 , 16 ] .

Learning-based methods have similarly been used either to reject external disturbances or interpret them as interaction commands [ 2 , 17 ] . The Seeing-Eye system jointly learns force-responsive locomotion and an onboard force estimator whose output guides navigation [ 1 ] . However, the interaction is transmitted directly to the robot through a leash or handle. Standard velocity-tracking policies do not prescribe a response to external forces and can therefore behave stiffly during interaction [ 18 ] . To tackle this, FACET learns to track the response of a virtual mass-spring-damper system [ 3 ] , HAC-Loco estimates external disturbances from proprioception to adapt locomotion commands [ 8 ] , and SAC-Loco combines adjustable compliance with a learned safety and recovery mechanism [ 19 ] . Force-conditioned policies have also been developed for legged loco-manipulation, where estimated or commanded forces regulate an end effector or modify its motion target [ 20 , 21 ] . In these settings, the interaction acts directly on the robot body or end effector. In contrast, we consider forces applied directly to a payload that is coupled to the robot only through frictional contact.

Payload-Aware Locomotion and Interaction. Prior work on payload-carrying quadrupeds has primarily considered how locomotion should adapt to the carried load. Model-based methods estimate payload properties such as mass and center-of-mass offsets online [ 22 ] , while learning-based approaches adapt locomotion to unknown or dynamically varying loads [ 4 ] . Beyond Robustness estimates the motion characteristics of an unrestrained payload from proprioceptive history and adapts locomotion to stabilize it [ 5 ] .
These methods address payload adaptation and stabilization, but do not consider an external agent intentionally interacting with an unrestrained payload to guide the robot.

Collaborative transportation instead uses interaction through a shared payload to infer partner intent. Passive impedance arms convert payload-induced deflections into guidance commands [ 6 ] , while suction-cup end effectors measure interaction wrenches for admittance-based transport [ 23 ] . External base wrenches have also been estimated for cooperative carrying through rigidly connected loads [ 9 ] . PAINT infers partner interaction wrenches from proprioceptive histories by exploiting the coupled dynamics of a shared payload [ 7 ] , and related human-humanoid work learns proprioception-only compliant coordination during shared-object carrying [ 24 ] .
However, these methods rely on a mechanically coupled object as the interaction interface.

Together, these works address force-aware interaction, payload stabilization, and collaborative transportation, but treat them as separate problems.
In contrast, we consider forces applied directly to an unrestrained payload that is coupled to the robot only through frictional contact. Our work addresses these jointly by estimating the payload interaction from onboard measurements and using it for compliant locomotion while maintaining payload stability.

2026-10-07.title: A Swarm-Coordinated Multi-Robot System for Early Stress Detection in Agricultural Rows Using Multimodal Leaf Sensing
2026-10-07.authors: Rishi Gupta , Astha Goyal , Vinay Vishwakarma
2026-10-07.abstract: Early stress detection in crops is a necessity today to improve efficiency and reduce waste of time, money, and effort. However, most modern techniques, such as hyperspectral imaging and AI-based systems, are too costly and complex for medium and small-scale farmers to implement. This paper showcases CropSentry, a low-cost, ground-based multi-robot system that uses multimodal leaf sensing to continuously monitor crop health by tracking stress levels. The system comprises two autonomous bots that continuously detect leaf color and environmental data row by row. The observations are spatially mapped and sent over to the master bot, which uses color-coded row segments to generate a real-time web-based dashboard displaying crop health. After 63 observations were collected during the experiments, the results showed an overall crop health classification accuracy of 84.12%, with 82.60% for healthy plants, 88% for nutrient-deficient plants, and 80% for diseased plants. Also, 100% wireless communication success rate across 10 slave observations was achieved. Close-range leaf inspection across multiple bots can detect early stress in crops while remaining affordable, accessible, and scalable. It provides farmers with timely information to improve resource utilization and crop management.

2026-10-07.title: One for All, All for One: Coordinated Multi-Agent Diffusion Steering via Stochastic Optimal Control
2026-10-07.authors: Riccardo Barbano , Vincent Pauline , Runchang Li , George Webber , Alexander Denker , Željko Kereta , Stefan Bauer , Francisco Vargas , Esmeralda S. Whitammer
2026-10-07.abstract:
Deep generative models often produce structured outputs composed of interacting components.
Modelling these outputs with a single model requires learning both the component distributions and their interactions.
We pursue a modular alternative: reuse independently trained component generators and learn only how to coordinate them to produce coherent structured outputs.
Our framework, C oordinated M ulti-Agent D iffusion S teering ( CMDS ), treats frozen pretrained diffusion models as reusable generative primitives and coordinates their reverse processes through a learned control .
We formulate coordination as a stochastic optimal control problem, balancing an assembly-level reward that specifies the desired properties of the combined output against deviations from the pretrained dynamics.
The learned control amortises this optimisation, allowing reuse across new task instances.
Experiments show that CMDS can recover a known target distribution, satisfy different spatial constraints with the same trained control, and recover individual sources from degraded mixtures.
Across multi-agent maze navigation, articulated robot planning, and text-conditioned human motion, CMDS turns frozen models into coordinated multi-agent generators.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Producing coherent structured outputs involves two distinct problems: modelling individual components and coordinating them when they are used together.
End-to-end generative models absorb both into a single generative distribution.
We instead build on a long-standing tradition of modular and compositional generative modelling ( Grenander, 1978 ; Bienenstock et al., 1996 ; Williams, 2025 ; Du and Kaelbling, 2024 ) .
Component generators, pretrained without joint-system supervision, capture component-level variability, while coordination is learned separately at the level of the structured output.
Diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ; Lai et al., 2025 ) are well suited to this decomposition, as each pretrained reverse process provides a reusable component generative prior whose dynamics can be steered via a learned control while the underlying model remains fixed.
Prior work on compositional diffusion generation typically resolves the required coordination at sampling time for each generated instance ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) .
This is sensible for one-off tasks, but becomes costly when related coordination problems recur across many instances.
In settings where related coordination problems recur across many instances–for example, across relational design specifications, source-separation observations, or multi-agent start-goal configurations–the associated computation can instead be amortised into a reusable control.
Building on recent work showing how controls or amortised samplers can steer pretrained diffusion processes towards task-specific target distributions ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2024 ; Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ; Venkatraman et al., 2024 ) , we thus ask:

The proposed framework begins with independently trained component generators, whose distributions form a reference product distribution over component configurations.
An assembly map combines their outputs into a candidate, while an assembly-level reward evaluates the candidate.
A learned control then coordinates the component generators towards high-reward joint outputs.
To make this concrete, consider planning the movements of several agents through a shared environment.
Each frozen copy of a single-agent trajectory model generates a path through the environment, using an agent-specific start and end as conditioning inputs.
Stacking these paths produces a candidate multi-agent plan.
Although each path may avoid walls in isolation, the assembled plan may still be invalid if agents collide.
This illustrates the role of the assembly-level reward.
It expresses requirements not captured by the independently trained component models and provides the signal used to coordinate their generation.
Generally, the framework requires no training examples of valid structured outputs , only (i) component-level data or pretrained component generators; (ii) an assembly map; and (iii) an assembly-level reward.

2026-10-07.title: Towards Efficient Robotic Manipulation Models with Self-Recursive Pruning
2026-10-07.authors: Zijia Chen , Yuenan Hou , Yu Li , Weijie Li , Li Liu
2026-10-07.abstract: Network pruning can reduce parameter redundancy in robotic policies. However, generic pruning criteria are tailored for image recognition tasks and commonly designed to preserve weight magnitude, local reconstruction, or language-model likelihood rather than closed-loop action behavior. Directly applying these pruning algorithms to robotic tasks yields unsatisfactory performance. In this paper, we propose Loss-Conditioned Activation-Moment (LCAM) pruning, a training-free method for unstructured pruning of pre-trained robotic manipulation policies. Specifically, we first rank connections using row-normalized weight contribution, activation moments measured on calibration demonstrations, and the sensitivity of output directions to the action-prediction loss. We further design a self-recursive coarse-to-fine procedure: importance is recalibrated after each nested coarse pruning stage, while held-out offline action distortion guides fine-grained budget allocation after a sparsity knee. Our algorithm is free from costly recovery training and simulator rollouts after pruning. Experiments on three LIBERO suites with competitive robotic policies, together with evaluations on OpenVLA, show that LCAM attains competitive performance across a broad range of pruning ratios. Notably, on LIBERO-Object with OpenVLA, our LCAM achieves 84.0 % 84.0\% success at 50 % 50\% unstructured pruning, retaining over 90 % 90\% of the dense policy’s success rate. Promising results on real-world robotic ping pong further demonstrate the effectiveness of our pruning algorithm.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Recent advances in robot learning have produced action policies that achieve strong manipulation performance across diverse manipulation tasks [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . However, modern robotic manipulation policies typically rely on high-capacity perception and cumbersome policy networks, leading to substantial storage and inference costs. This motivates the compression of robotic policies, with the objective of reducing parameter redundancy while maximally preserving the ultimate performance. We focus on unstructured pruning, which removes individual weights to induce sparsity in pretrained policies. Classical magnitude pruning and recent one-shot methods, such as SparseGPT and Wanda, have demonstrated effective unstructured sparsification for pretrained image recognition and language models [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . These pruning methods typically employ classification accuracy, perplexity, or reconstruction errors as pruning criteria. However, directly applying these criteria to robotic manipulation policies can be challenging.

The challenge stems from the closed-loop nature of robotic manipulation. Unlike language modeling, where pruning quality can often be assessed using token-level likelihood or layer-wise reconstruction errors, robotic policies are ultimately evaluated by the task success rate during closed-loop execution. Small action deviations introduced by pruning can accumulate during closed-loop execution and thus yield degraded manipulation performance [ 13 ] . Moreover, robotic demonstrations are typically scarce and task-specific, while modern policies combine heterogeneous perception, state, language, and action-generation modules that differ markedly in their sensitivity to parameter removal. To mitigate such degradation, recent robotic policy compression and post-pruning recovery methods often couple structural reduction with additional optimization or test-time correction [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . These procedures either introduce additional training cost or require intervention in test-time. Consequently, pruning objectives based on generic activation statistics or local reconstruction fidelity can not fully reflect the task-relevant behavior of robotic policies under closed-loop execution.

To address the aforementioned challenges, we propose Loss-Conditioned Activation-Moment (LCAM) pruning, a training-free framework for sparsifying pretrained robotic policies. At the connection level, LCAM ranks connections by combining row-normalized weight contribution, activation evidence on calibration demonstrations, and action-loss sensitivity. High-score connections are retained, whereas low-score connections are removed. At the allocation level, LCAM adopts a self-recursive coarse-to-fine pruning procedure. Starting from the dense policy, each subsequent stage begins with the previously pruned policy, recalibrates connection importance on the resulting sparse model, and removes only redundant connections. The procedure automatically transitions from coarse to fine-grained pruning when offline action distortion on validation demonstrations exhibits a sharp marginal increase, indicating a sparsity knee. It then refines the remaining pruning budget using smaller increments to preserve action behavior at high sparsity. Note that LCAM requires neither post-pruning retraining nor simulator rollouts during pruning.

We evaluate our LCAM against representative training-free unstructured pruning baselines on robotic manipulation policies in the LIBERO benchmark [ 18 ] , covering three LIBERO suites with MATE [ 19 ] policies and an evaluation on OpenVLA [ 7 ] . The results show that LCAM produces a competitive training-free pruning strategy across multiple sparsity levels. On the MATE policies, LCAM retains substantial task success rates in high-sparsity regimes where several weight-based, saliency-based, and reconstruction-based baselines undergo sharp performance drops or collapse. On LIBERO-Object where OpenVLA is adopted, LCAM achieves the highest success rate among competitive baselines at both 50 % 50\% and 60 % 60\% pruning, attaining 84.0 % 84.0\% success at 50 % 50\% pruning and retaining over 90 % 90\% of the dense policy’s success rate. Promising results on the real-world robotic ping pong task further underscore the effectiveness of our pruning algorithm.

# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Network Pruning

Network pruning aims to identify and remove redundant parameters while preserving the task performance of a pretrained model. Magnitude pruning is a classical and widely used baseline that removes parameters according to their absolute weight values [ 10 , 20 ] . Despite its simplicity, magnitude pruning ranks parameters solely by their absolute values, without accounting for input-dependent activation statistics or action-loss sensitivity.

More recent pruning methods incorporate additional information, such as loss sensitivity, activation statistics, or layer-wise reconstruction, to estimate parameter importance. Taylor-based pruning estimates the loss change induced by removing a parameter group using first- or second-order Taylor expansions [ 21 ] . Although originally developed for structured pruning, its loss-based saliency principle also motivates parameter-level importance criteria. For large pretrained Transformers, SparseGPT formulates pruning as a layer-wise reconstruction problem and uses approximate second-order information to enable accurate one-shot pruning [ 11 ] . Wanda provides a simpler training-free alternative by combining weight magnitude with input activation statistics, without updating the retained weights [ 12 ] . Pruner-Zero further uses genetic programming to search symbolic pruning metrics over weights, activations, gradients, and mathematical
operators [ 22 ] . AutoPrune takes a different approach by using an LLM-guided search procedure to automatically discover pruning metrics, together with a skew-aware dynamic sparsity allocation strategy for large language models [ 23 ] .

These methods were primarily developed and evaluated for image classification or language modeling, where pruning is commonly guided by proxy quantities such as loss sensitivity, activation statistics, or layer-wise reconstruction, and evaluated using task-level metrics such as classification accuracy or perplexity. Whether these criteria can reliably preserve task-relevant action behavior when transferred to robotic action policies remains an empirical question, since the optimization objectives and evaluation protocols differ substantially across these settings.

## II-B Model Compression and Pruning for Robotic Policies

Recent work has explored the compression of robotic policies. LightDP compresses diffusion policies through a unified pruning-and-retraining pipeline and combines network compression with consistency distillation to reduce the number of denoising steps [ 14 ] . RLRC applies structured pruning to vision-language-action models and recovers performance through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning [ 15 ] . Shallow- π \pi reduces the depth of flow-based VLA models and trains the compressed model through knowledge distillation [ 16 ] . These approaches couple structural compression with additional optimization or distillation to preserve policy performance.

Recent work has also investigated post-pruning recovery without additional training. GLUESTICK recovers a structurally pruned vision-language-action model by approximating the weight difference between the dense and pruned models with low-rank components, which are added as layer-wise corrections during inference [ 17 ] . Unlike these approaches, LCAM constructs pruning masks without recovery training, distillation, or inference-time correction.

2026-10-07.title: Micro Neural Policies for Safe Real-Time Robotic Control
2026-10-07.authors: Hongpeng Cao , Riccardo Curcio , Daniele Ottaviano , Marco Caccamo
2026-10-07.abstract: In this paper, we investigate the synthesis of Micro Neural Policies (MNP) to enable safe and robust real-time robotic control on computationally constrained embedded devices. We demonstrate that integrating Evolution Strategy (ES) and Statistical Model Checking (SMC) -based verification for policy search can drastically reduce neural network size without compromising safety and robustness. We conduct a large-scale training and evaluation of MNP on Cartpole and Quadrotor control tasks, varying control frequencies and network architectures. After validating these policies in simulation, we evaluate their deployability through zero-shot transfer to physical systems. Our experiments show that MNP can successfully achieve safe sim-to-real transfer without sacrificing control performance. We then show that the policies’ memory footprint, ranging from 0.5 0.5 to 7.5 ​ kB 7.5\,\mathrm{kB} , allows deployment on microcontrollers, where they achieve real-time inference latency with under 25 ​ ns 25\,\mathrm{ns} of jitter while leaving the chip idle for over 97% of the time for additional workloads. This makes them a highly practical solution for severely resource-constrained robotic systems.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Autonomous robotic platforms increasingly rely on neural network policies to tackle complex, highly dynamic tasks. While these approaches demonstrate remarkable capabilities, their deployment often relies on powerful embedded computing platforms. For example, state-of-the-art autonomous drone racing systems execute learned policies on embedded GPUs such as the NVIDIA Jetson TX2 [ 1 ] , a module with gigabytes of DRAM and a power envelope up to 15 ​ W 15\mathrm{W} .

In this paper, instead, we focus on bridging the gap between high-frequency neural control and severely resource-constrained hardware. We target microcontroller-class platforms with only kilobytes of memory, limited compute capability and milliwatt-level power budgets. Operating under such constraints is challenging for conventional learning approaches ( e.g. , Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) ), which often rely on highly parameterized policies (e.g., dense architectures with hidden layers of up to 512 × 512 512\times 512 units and hundreds of thousands of parameters) to facilitate optimization and maximize empirical performance in simulation [ 2 ] .

By jointly investigating policy compactness, safety and real-time execution, our findings demonstrate that statistically verified neural controllers can successfully operate under these extreme hardware limits, bringing learning-based control to severely resource-constrained robotic platforms.

Synthesizing Micro Neural Policies (MNP) can substantially reduce memory and computational overhead, enabling low-latency, energy-efficient and predictable inference directly on resource-constrained embedded hardware [ 3 ] . However, discovering such policies is challenging. Conventional learning approaches ( e.g. , DRL ) favor overparameterized policies to facilitate optimization and maximize empirical performance; therefore, aggressively reducing network size can compromise control quality, robustness and safety. This challenge is particularly critical for physical deployment, where compact policies must not only perform well but also satisfy safety requirements [ 4 ] .

In this paper, we explore the combination of Evolution Strategy (ES) [ 5 , 6 ] and Statistical Model Checking (SMC) [ 7 , 8 ] to search within extremely compact policy regimes. Here, ES provides a derivative-free mechanism for searching policy parameters, while SMC verifies whether the resulting policy satisfies prescribed safety and performance requirements. We conduct a large-scale investigation to assess whether these algorithms can synthesize MNP that remain safe and robust, while characterizing the resulting trade-offs among policy size, control performance, verifiability and real-world deployability.

We make the following contributions toward enabling safe and robust MNP for real-world deployment on severely resource-constrained robotic platforms:

We investigate the synthesis of progressively smaller MNP for Cartpole and Quadrotor benchmarks across different control frequencies ( 50 Hz 50\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} and 100 Hz 100\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} ). Using an integrated ES and SMC framework [ 7 ] , we extensively evaluate both fully Neural Network (NN) -parameterized policies and residual architectures in simulation under probabilistic safety and performance guarantees. We compare these results with safe DRL baselines, demonstrating that the latter generally fail to learn effectively under such strict constraints.

We investigate the synthesis of progressively smaller MNP for Cartpole and Quadrotor benchmarks across different control frequencies ( 50 Hz 50\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} and 100 Hz 100\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} ). Using an integrated ES and SMC framework [ 7 ] , we extensively evaluate both fully Neural Network (NN) -parameterized policies and residual architectures in simulation under probabilistic safety and performance guarantees. We compare these results with safe DRL baselines, demonstrating that the latter generally fail to learn effectively under such strict constraints.

We validate the policies on physical Cartpole and Quadrotor platforms to assess their zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. Our real-world experiments demonstrate that these MNP can be directly deployed, achieving highly effective and robust control in the real world.

We evaluate latency, memory footprint and energy consumption of our MNP on a modern Arm-based microcontroller (the Nordic nRF54L15-DK with a 128 MHz Cortex-M33 core), representative of current TinyML benchmark platforms [ 9 ] .
Results show that the policies achieve real-time onboard execution. Across forty deployed policies, cost scales with network size: 0.5 0.5 – 7.5 ​ kB 7.5\,\mathrm{kB} of memory, 10 10 – 259 ​ μ ​ s 259\,\mu\mathrm{s} per inference and 0.25 0.25 – 3.67 ​ μ ​ J 3.67\,\mu\mathrm{J} , each policy running with under 25 ​ ns 25\mathrm{ns} of jitter and consuming less than 2.6 % 2.6\% of its control period.

2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related work

Sim-to-Real Policy Transfer and Assessment. Simulation is widely used for policy synthesis [ 1 ] , yet sim-to-real discrepancies remain a major obstacle to physical deployment. Common approaches improve robustness through domain randomization, disturbance injection and adversarial perturbations [ 10 , 11 ] , typically within gradient-based DRL pipelines. While these techniques can substantially improve transfer, robustness is often assessed under a limited set of scenarios and does not by itself provide explicit evidence of deployment readiness. As an alternative optimization paradigm, ES offers derivative-free policy search [ 5 ] and has recently been combined with SMC -based verification to provide probabilistic safety and performance guarantees under prescribed disturbance and operating-condition distributions [ 8 , 7 ] .

Micro Policy for Robotic Control. Recent literature [ 12 , 6 ] , has shown that simple policies can successfully solve complex continuous control tasks, suggesting that minimal architectures can achieve competitive generalization with significantly lower computational overhead.
This perspective is further supported by theoretical and empirical analyses highlighting the efficiency and stability of policies inspired from classical control theory compared to learning-based approaches ( e.g. , DRL ) [ 13 ] .
A prominent example leveraging these insights is residual learning [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] , which grounds the policy on a fixed nominal policy and trains the NN to compute a residual correction.
Such compact architectural designs directly support the emerging paradigm of Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML), which focuses on executing neural inference directly on low power embedded devices [ 9 , 3 ] .

Post-Training Compression Methods. A common approach to deploy large NN -based policies onto embedded devices involves post-training model compression techniques, such as network pruning [ 17 ] and quantization [ 18 ] . While these methods successfully reduce the memory footprint and inference time of a NN , their direct application to Reinforcement learning (RL) presents unique pitfalls. Any post-hoc approximation of the network, including policy distillation [ 19 ] , can unpredictably shift the policy’s action distribution. This fragility is especially critical when a policy comes with statistical guarantees [ 8 ] , as post-hoc compression inherently invalidates the properties established for the uncompressed model.

2026-10-07.title: Pareto-Optimal Entropy-Regularized Trajectory Optimization
2026-10-07.authors: Dimitrios S. Georgiou , Augustinos D. Saravanos , Evangelos A. Theodorou
2026-10-07.abstract:
Trajectory optimization (TO) under nonlinear dynamics, actuation limits and collision avoidance constraints is a fundamental problem in robotics, albeit especially challenging due to its highly non-convex nature.
For this setting, Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) is an efficient second-order shooting method, yet its local structure renders it vulnerable to suboptimal basins.
Sampling-augmented variants mitigate this susceptibility through stochastic exploration, but often sample only around the few trajectories they retain for reoptimization, based solely on their cost which restricts exploration breadth.
We introduce P areto-Optimal E ntropy- R egularized DDP (PER-DDP), an entropy-regularized population framework derived from the free-energy/relative-entropy inequality.
Our method combines prior-guided sampling that shapes exploration around each retained trajectory, with expanded rollout evaluations that probe these sampling policies beyond the few retained candidates, and Pareto filtering for preserving task–constraint alternatives across iterations.
This decouples sampling effort from the optimization population size and broadens exploration without sacrificing the second-order structure that makes DDP effective.
Across multiple systems and hundreds of environments, PER-DDP achieves higher success rates than state-of-the-art sampling-augmented TO methods and finds reliable solutions in environments beyond the reach of all baselines. A supplemental video can be found here .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Autonomous robots must achieve task goals while respecting nonlinear dynamics, actuation limits, and safety constraints, a problem commonly cast as trajectory optimization (TO).
However, the induced optimization landscape is often highly non-convex: in cluttered environments, for example, distinct local basins correspond to qualitatively different motion strategies.
Consequently, local optimization methods commit to one such strategy early, e.g. , to one side of an obstacle, and cannot recover the alternatives no matter how well they converge.
Other popular approaches, such as sampling-based motion planning [ 1 ] and reinforcement learning [ 2 , 3 ] sidestep this issue through global search and offline training, respectively.
TO instead exploits available models and constraints directly, producing locally optimal, dynamically feasible trajectories, at the price of confronting the non-convex landscape within the optimization itself.

Derivative-based TO methods such as Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) [ 4 ] and Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) [ 5 ] exploit gradients and curvature to progress rapidly toward local solutions.
DDP is an especially appealing and scalable algorithm as it exploits the sequential structure of the dynamics through local second-order models, yielding control updates and feedback gains with linear complexity in the horizon.
These local models, however, are constructed around a single nominal trajectory, rendering DDP prone to suboptimal local minima [ 6 ] .
Escaping such suboptimal basins thus requires exploring alternative trajectories without sacrificing the local second-order structure that makes DDP effective.

Purely stochastic optimizers provide such exploration by sampling control trajectories broadly as in Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) [ 7 ] , Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control [ 8 ] , and STOMP [ 9 ] .
More recently, diffusion-inspired optimizers refine sampled trajectories through annealed noise schedules informed by the dynamics and cost [ 10 , 11 ] .
Related population-based optimizers maintain diverse trajectories through Stein variational updates [ 12 , 13 ] , explicit multimodal search [ 14 ] , evolution strategies [ 15 ] , or massively parallel multi-seed optimization [ 16 ] .

The idea of combining such exploration with DDP dates to guided policy search and its maximum-entropy iLQG variant [ 17 ] .
Sampling-augmented DDP methods later formalized and extended this construction. In particular, Maximum Entropy DDP (ME-DDP) [ 18 ] casts it as a trajectory optimizer, Generalized Maximum Entropy DDP (GME-DDP) [ 19 ] broadens the induced policy family, and Stein Variational DDP (SVDDP) [ 20 ] uses repulsive interactions to preserve trajectory diversity.
Despite their different mechanisms, these methods share an optimize–explore cycle in which a small set of refined trajectories defines the sampling modes, rollouts are generated around them, and selected ones are promoted for reoptimization.
However, as the same population drives both exploration and optimization, sampling concentrates around a few modes, breadth stays tied to the number of retained trajectories, and heuristics such as elite preservation and mode resampling become necessary.
This limitation sharpens in constrained TO, where ranking rollouts by a single aggregate cost discards trajectories that make meaningful progress in task performance or constraint satisfaction alone, exactly the alternatives that might later mature into high-quality solutions.

We address these limitations by introducing P areto-Optimal E ntropy- R egularized DDP (PER-DDP) ,
a prior-guided population framework that treats sampling modes, rollout evaluations, and retained candidates as independent budgets and selects candidates in the task-constraint objective space rather than through a scalarized cost (Fig. 1 ).
Its sampling policies follow from the free-energy/relative-entropy principle, generalizing maximum-entropy DDP to flexible priors, while Pareto-based selection guarantees a retained trajectory no worse in augmented cost than the DDP solutions.
The main contributions of this work are:

We derive a variational generalization of entropy-regularized DDP from the free-energy/relative-entropy principle, yielding prior-guided policies for bounded-uniform, Gaussian, and multimodal Gaussian priors.

We propose a Pareto-based selection principle for constrained TO that preserves task-constraint alternatives while guaranteeing no degradation in augmented cost relative to DDP at selection steps.

We then present the PER-DDP algorithm which explicitly decouples sampling modes, rollout budget, and retained trajectories, allowing sampling effort to scale independently of the optimization population.

We demonstrate consistent success-rate improvements on bicycle, quadrotor, and Franka Panda systems against state-of-the-art sampling-augmented TO methods, including environments that no baseline solves.

2026-10-07.title: WareFly-VLA: A Vision-Language-Action Framework for UAV Navigation and Human Tracking in Smart Warehouses
2026-10-07.authors: Thinh D. Le , Son T. Nguyen , Duong Q. Nguyen , Dung D. Le , Ngo Anh Vien , H. Nguyen-Xuan
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-07.abstract: Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models have achieved impressive results in robotic manipulation and ground-mobile navigation, yet language-conditioned control of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in smart warehouses remains largely unexplored. Progress is hindered by the lack of benchmarks that jointly provide continuous low-level flight actions, fine-grained natural-language target descriptions and realistic industrial environments. This paper introduces WareFly-VLA, a photorealistic UAV VLA framework and dataset for language-guided human search, localization and tracking in intra-logistics and warehouse environments. The dataset contains 507 human-teleoperated flight episodes and 8,504 non-terminal high-resolution RGB transitions collected in NVIDIA Isaac Sim; each transition is paired with a human-written appearance description of the target worker and a synchronized four-degree-of-freedom control command comprising translational and yaw changes. Two aerial embodied tasks are covered, target approach and person following, under realistic challenges including occlusion, long-range search, altitude variation and clutter. A unified benchmark of four representative open-source VLA architectures (SmolVLA, GR00T N1.7, π 0 \pi_{0} and OpenVLA) is established under a leakage-free episode-level protocol at two control rates. The results show that language-conditioned aerial control in warehouses remains far from solved: performance drops substantially under strict generalization settings, continuous action modeling consistently outperforms discrete action tokenization, only the forward channel is reliably learnable from a single frame, and current foundation-model interfaces transfer poorly from ground and humanoid embodiments to aerial platforms. The synchronized video, language, action, pose and difficulty annotations further support world-model research. The dataset, baselines and evaluation protocol are released to support language-grounded aerial autonomy in smart warehouses.
2026-10-07.introduction:
A long-standing objective of embodied artificial intelligence is to enable robots to interpret natural-language instructions, ground them in visual observations and execute appropriate low-level actions in dynamic environments. Recent Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models such as PaLM-E [ 13 ] , RT-1 [ 8 ] , RT-2 [ 7 ] , Octo [ 16 ] , OpenVLA [ 27 ] , RDT-1B [ 31 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 6 ] , SmolVLA [ 43 ] , TinyVLA [ 51 ] and Qwen-VLA [ 47 ] have demonstrated that large-scale multimodal training can produce policies that generalize across tasks, environments and robot embodiments. These advances suggest that a unified perception–language–control paradigm may provide a scalable foundation for future autonomous systems.

Despite rapid progress, contemporary VLA research remains heavily concentrated on robotic manipulation and ground-mobile platforms. Large-scale datasets and benchmarks predominantly focus on tabletop manipulation, mobile navigation or humanoid interaction, whereas aerial robots remain significantly underrepresented, even though vision-based control of multi-rotor aerial vehicles is a mature and active research area [ 35 ] . This gap is particularly notable because unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) present a distinct embodiment with substantially different sensing, motion and control characteristics. Being different from manipulators that operate within constrained workspaces or ground robots that navigate primarily in two dimensions, UAVs perform continuous motion in three-dimensional space while simultaneously regulating position, altitude and heading. Visual observations are highly dynamic due to rapid viewpoint changes, target scale variation and frequent occlusions. Consequently, transferring VLA paradigms developed for ground or manipulation settings to aerial systems is far from straightforward.

Among the many tasks relevant to aerial autonomy, language-guided human search and following represents a particularly compelling benchmark for embodied intelligence. Consider the instruction: “Track the worker wearing a yellow hard hat and a purple safety vest.” Successfully executing this command requires the integration of multiple capabilities. The UAV must first interpret fine-grained appearance descriptions, identify the correct individual among visually similar distractors, actively search when the target is not immediately visible, maintain target association over time and continuously generate flight-control commands that ensure safe and reliable tracking. In contrast to conventional UAV tracking benchmarks, where the target is initialized through a bounding box or visual template, language-guided following requires semantic target specification and persistent multimodal grounding throughout the entire trajectory. This setting naturally combines visual grounding, embodied language understanding, active perception and continuous control within a single task.

Existing datasets do not adequately support this problem formulation. Classical approaches such as Chen et al. [ 10 ] , aerial tracking benchmarks such as UAV123 [ 33 ] , and subsequent UAV tracking datasets [ 53 ] provide extensive flight recordings but rely exclusively on visual target initialization without language supervision. Vision-language navigation datasets such as AerialVLN [ 30 ] , AirNav [ 12 ] , EmbodiedCity [ 52 ] , UAV-VLN [ 48 ] and GeoText-1652 [ 32 ] introduced natural-language instructions but formulated navigation primarily as waypoint prediction or route planning rather than continuous low-level control. In a similar vein, large-scale drone footage datasets exist and are used to extract ground vehicle trajectories for driving research [ 50 ] ; however, the lack of ergo-centric controls makes them unsuitable for aerial embodied AI. Recent UAV-oriented VLA datasets and benchmarks remain limited in scope. CognitiveDrone [ 34 ] focused on simulation-based trajectory generation. UAV-VLA [ 41 ] targets mission-level reasoning from aerial imagery and RaceVLA [ 42 ] addressed drone-racing policies. Although these resources have advanced aerial embodied learning, none simultaneously provide appearance-grounded language descriptions, continuous flight-control supervision, human-demonstrated trajectories and warehouse-scale person-search-and-follow tasks.

To address this limitation, this paper introduces WareFly-VLA , a Vision–Language–Action dataset for language-guided human search and following in industrial warehouse environments. The dataset is collected from human-teleoperated UAV demonstrations performed in a photorealistic warehouse environment constructed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Each trajectory contains synchronized high-resolution RGB observations, fine-grained appearance-based language descriptions and continuous 4-DoF flight actions represented as body-frame motion commands. In contrast to scripted navigation policies or automatically generated expert trajectories, the dataset captures realistic human decision-making behaviors during target search, target acquisition and continuous following. The resulting trajectories naturally include recovery maneuvers, viewpoint adaptation, target re-identification and other behaviors that commonly arise during practical aerial operation.

WareFly-VLA is designed around two complementary embodied tasks: approach-and-locate and person-following . The dataset further incorporates diverse warehouse layouts, worker appearances, target distances, altitude changes, partial occlusions and cluttered industrial environments. Structured difficulty annotations enable systematic evaluation across multiple challenge dimensions and support future research on generalization, robustness and language grounding under realistic operating conditions.

Beyond dataset construction, a unified benchmark is established to evaluate representative open-source VLA architectures using a common leakage-free episode-level split. The benchmark spans multiple model families and action-representation paradigms, providing a standardized framework for studying aerial embodied intelligence. Experimental results indicate that language-conditioned UAV control remains a challenging open problem, highlighting substantial opportunities for future advances in multimodal representation learning, continuous action prediction and cross-embodiment transfer.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

WareFly-VLA , a human-teleoperated UAV Vision–Language–Action dataset for language-guided human search and following in warehouse environments, containing synchronized visual observations, appearance-grounded language descriptions and continuous 4-DoF flight actions.

WareFly-VLA , a human-teleoperated UAV Vision–Language–Action dataset for language-guided human search and following in warehouse environments, containing synchronized visual observations, appearance-grounded language descriptions and continuous 4-DoF flight actions.

A human-demonstration data collection pipeline built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim that captures realistic aerial search, target localization, target acquisition and continuously following behaviors from teleoperated quadrotor trajectories.

Aerial embodied benchmark tasks covering approach-and-locate and person-following scenarios under realistic challenges, including occlusion, altitude variation, long-range search, viewpoint changes and cluttered industrial environments.

A unified aerial VLA benchmark for evaluating representative open-source VLA architectures under a standardized leakage-free evaluation protocol.

An open-source research platform including dataset artifacts, benchmark configurations, training pipelines and evaluation tools to facilitate future research on aerial embodied intelligence, language-grounded UAV autonomy and Vision–Language–Action learning.

Open world-model research directions enabled by WareFly-VLA, including predictive representation learning, action-conditioned latent dynamics, language-conditioned planning and sim-to-real transfer for aerial embodied intelligence.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision–Language–Action models

VLA models have emerged as a unified paradigm for embodied intelligence by jointly learning perception, language understanding and control. Early efforts such as PaLM-E [ 13 ] demonstrated the feasibility of integrating visual observations into large language models for robotic decision making. Subsequent systems including RT-1 [ 8 ] , RT-2 [ 7 ] , Open X-Embodiment [ 39 ] , Octo [ 16 ] , OpenVLA [ 27 ] , RDT-1B [ 31 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 6 ] , SmolVLA [ 43 ] , TinyVLA [ 51 ] and Qwen-VLA [ 47 ] have demonstrated increasingly strong generalization across tasks, environments and robotic embodiments.

Recent research has further explored large-scale pretraining and cross-embodiment transfer. Open X-Embodiment [ 39 ] aggregated demonstrations from multiple robot platforms to investigate shared policy learning, while OpenVLA [ 27 ] , RDT-1B [ 31 ] and π 0 \pi_{0} [ 5 ] explored foundation-model approaches capable of adapting to diverse downstream tasks. Inference-time policy steering has further been proposed to deploy pre-trained VLAs on new tasks without fine-tuning [ 29 ] . Despite these advances, the overwhelming majority of VLA benchmarks remain centered on robotic manipulation, mobile navigation and humanoid control. The applicability of VLA models to aerial robots remains comparatively underexplored, largely due to the scarcity of UAV-specific datasets that combine language instructions with continuous flight-control supervision.

## 2.2 Language-grounded aerial navigation

Language-guided navigation has become an important benchmark for embodied intelligence, motivating a growing body of research on aerial vision-language systems. AerialVLN [ 30 ] introduced a large-scale simulation benchmark for instruction-following UAV navigation. Subsequent efforts expanded this direction through more realistic environments and richer navigation objectives, including UAV-VLN [ 48 ] , EmbodiedCity [ 52 ] , GeoText-1652 [ 32 ] , AirNav [ 12 ] and semantic-topometric aerial navigation frameworks [ 15 ] . Additional studies have investigated aerial dialogue navigation and interactive instruction following [ 14 ] , and vision-language policies for onboard drone navigation have been trained in radiance-field simulators [ 11 ] . In parallel, learning-based vision-driven following behaviors for UAVs, such as safe river following via reinforcement learning with a semantic dynamics model [ 49 ] , show that end-to-end visual control of aerial platforms is feasible, but they do not involve language-specified targets.

These datasets have significantly advanced aerial language grounding and instruction-conditioned navigation. However, most methods formulate navigation as waypoint prediction, route planning or localization rather than direct low-level control. As a result, they provide limited supervision for end-to-end VLA learning, where language instructions must be translated directly into continuous flight actions.

## 2.3 UAV VLA datasets and benchmarks

Recent studies have begun extending the Vision–Language–Action paradigm to aerial robotics. UAV-VLA [ 41 ] investigates mission-level planning and reasoning from aerial imagery, while RaceVLA [ 42 ] explores language-conditioned drone-racing policies derived from OpenVLA. CognitiveDrone [ 34 ] combines VLA policies with reasoning-oriented VLMs for simulation-based cognitive UAV navigation. Broader surveys have also highlighted the growing role of foundation models and LLMs in UAV autonomy [ 44 ] .

Although these efforts demonstrate the promise of foundation-model-based aerial autonomy, important limitations remain. Existing benchmarks are typically restricted to racing, navigation, mission planning or simulation-specific tasks. Many datasets rely on automatically generated trajectories or task-specific objectives that do not require semantic target grounding. Furthermore, appearance-based human search and following has received little attention within the UAV VLA literature.

Consequently, there remains no publicly available benchmark that simultaneously provides appearance-grounded natural-language target descriptions, continuous 4-DoF flight-control actions, human-teleoperated UAV demonstrations and language-guided human search-and-follow tasks in realistic warehouse environments. WareFly-VLA is designed to fill this gap and to provide a dedicated benchmark for aerial Vision–Language–Action learning.

2026-10-07.title: No Need to Stop the Fleet: Localized Anomaly Isolation via Dead Zones in AGV Fleets
2026-10-07.authors: Natalia Ogorelysheva , Falk Howar , Jian-Jia Chen
2026-10-07.abstract:
Automated Guided Vehicle (AGV) fleets in production and logistics environments rely on a system-wide emergency stop to handle local anomalies such as malfunctions, hazards, or contaminated areas. While safe, this approach halts the entire fleet even when only a small area is affected, causing unnecessary downtime. This paper proposes dead zones — a formally defined localized isolation approach that serves as an additional fail-operational mechanism for situations where a full system-wide halt is not strictly needed.
Rather than shutting down the entire fleet, a dead zone isolates the anomalous area, allowing unaffected robots to continue operating normally.
We introduce two operational strategies: basic dead zone handling, in which affected robots enter a dead zone and stop, and dead zone handling with escaping, in which robots that are sufficiently far from a dead zone reroute around it.
For escaping on counterclockwise trajectories we prove collision-freedom with a bounded arrival delay for all escaping robots, provided a minimum pairwise separation is kept between robots. Experimental evaluation confirms the theoretical guarantees and characterizes the throughput tradeoffs between all three approaches: full emergency stop, basic dead zone handling, and dead zone handling with escaping.
2026-10-07.introduction:
AGV fleets operating in production and logistics environments are subject to strict safety regulations. The European standard EN ISO 3691-4:2023 mandates emergency stop functionality on every driverless industrial truck: when triggered, all motion must cease immediately and a manual restart is required [ 9 ] . In practice, a local anomaly such as a malfunctioning robot, a fallen object, or a contaminated area triggers a system-wide halt, bringing the entire fleet to a standstill regardless of how many robots are actually affected. As fleets scale to hundreds of vehicles [ 13 ] , the cost of such system-wide halts grows proportionally [ 29 ] .

Looking ahead, emerging applications such as automated facilities in remote or resource-constrained environments, where robots are scarce, replacement is costly, and continuous operation is critical, make this problem even more acute. In such settings, losing even a single robot to a local anomaly may be unacceptable, and a system-wide emergency stop may not be a viable option at all [ 38 , 7 ] .

This motivates a more targeted approach: containing the anomaly within a designated area, a dead zone , and fencing it off from the remainder of the operational space, as an additional fail-operational mechanism for cases where a full system-wide halt is not strictly necessary. Robots outside the dead zone continue operating normally; only those inside or heading towards it need to respond. Since AGV fleets typically rely on centralized offline planning [ 6 , 21 ] , their ability to react dynamically is limited, making a pre-defined handling strategy essential. When a dead zone is announced, a robot has essentially three options depending on its position and remaining trajectory: enter the zone and stop, perform an escape maneuver, or continue if unaffected.

To the best of our knowledge, no existing work formally defines a localized isolation zone for offline-planned multi-robot systems, nor provides safety guarantees for the remaining fleet. Note, that dead zone and it’s handling are distinct from general collision avoidance. In our model we assume the system is already collision-free due to used planning method. Additionally, instead of proposing a dynamic collision avoidance due to a specific anomaly, we propose an efficient dynamic rerouting based on static rule with safety guarantees.
The contributions of this paper are as follows:

We introduce the dead zone (DZ), a formal model for localized anomaly isolation in offline-planned multi-robot systems, and provide a formalization of DZ handling based on multi-agent path finding (MAPF).

We introduce the dead zone (DZ), a formal model for localized anomaly isolation in offline-planned multi-robot systems, and provide a formalization of DZ handling based on multi-agent path finding (MAPF).

We define two DZ handling strategies: Basic DZ Handling, in which affected robots enter DZ and stop there, and DZ Handling with Escaping, in which robots sufficiently far from the zone reroute around it via a counterclockwise escape strategy.

We provide a formal proof of collision-freedom for the counterclockwise escape strategy, covering both cell and swap collisions, with a bounded arrival delay for all escaping robots.

We evaluate all strategies experimentally, confirming the theoretical guarantees and characterizing the throughput tradeoffs between safety and operational continuity.

Outline. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 introduces the dead zone concept through a motivational example. Section 3 presents the formal model, including the system model, dead zone definition, and basic dead zone handling. Section 4 introduces the escaping strategy. Section 5 describes the experimental setup and presents the results, before we discuss related works in Section 6 . Section 7 concludes the paper with a summary and an outlook on future work.
