# 2 Motivational Example

We demonstrate the idea of a dead zone with a small example.
Consider a multi-robot system operating on a discrete grid (with 4-connectivity as in [ 27 ] ), where robots continuously execute transport jobs. Fig. 1(a) shows five robots during normal operation at t = 4 t=4 : robots r 1 r_{1} , r 2 r_{2} , and r 3 r_{3} follow planned paths crossing the center of the grid, while robots r 4 r_{4} and r 5 r_{5} operate in separate corridors well away from the center.
All robots follow their pre-planned, collision-free trajectories without interference.

At t d ​ z = 5 t_{dz}=5 , a dead zone is announced at the center of the grid. The system must immediately decide how each robot should respond. Robots r 4 r_{4} and r 5 r_{5} are unaffected, their paths do not intersect the dead zone, and they continue operation without interruption. Robots r 1 r_{1} , r 2 r_{2} , and r 3 r_{3} , however, have remaining trajectories that are affected. Since all three are sufficiently far from the dead zone at t d ​ z t_{dz} , each executes an escape strategy. In this example we use one of the possible escape strategies, the counterclockwise bypassing strategy: a robot follows its original path up to the boundary of the DZ, traverses the safe perimeter counterclockwise, and rejoins its original trajectory on the other side. Fig. 1(b) shows the resulting escape paths immediately after the dead zone announcement.

An important requirement for any escape strategy is that it must guarantee collision-freedom — among the escaping robots themselves, which in this case share a common resource (the escape route along the perimeter of the dead zone) and between the escaping robots and the remainder of the unaffected fleet. For instance, in Fig. 1(b) , robot r 5 r_{5} continues on its original path while r 2 r_{2} executes an escape maneuver; both share a grid cell c = ( 10 , 16 ) c=(10,16) at different time points. The escape strategy must ensure that such interactions remain collision-free.
Fig. 1(c) shows the system at t = 30 t=30 : all five robots have completed their jobs and reached their goal positions. The escape detour introduces a small delay for each escaping robot, but no robot is lost and no collision occurs.

For contrast, Fig. 1(d) shows what happens when the dead zone is announced later, at t d ​ z = 9 t_{dz}=9 . Robot r 1 r_{1} happens to be inside the DZ at the moment of the announcement and is kept there until the anomaly is acted upon or resolved. By design the dead zone marks an area where the system can no longer guarantee safe operation. The nature of the anomaly may be entirely unknown and any robot inside it may itself be in an uncontrolled or unpredictable state. Allowing such a robot to leave the DZ and re-enter the operational area would risk introducing an uncontrolled agent into an otherwise collision-free operational area. The robot is therefore kept inside the dead zone and fenced off from the remainder of the system, ensuring that the anomaly remains localized and that the operating fleet can continue safely.

Note that the dead zone itself is independent of any particular robot response — it merely defines the fenced area. How robots react to it, whether by entering and stopping or by escaping around it, is determined separately by the chosen handling strategy.

2026-10-07.authors: Damini Rijhwani
2026-10-07.comment: Presented at the IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026) Workshop on Surgical Digital Twins (SurgTwin).
2026-10-07.abstract: Endovascular catheter navigation relies on continuous fluoroscopy, exposing patients and clinical staff to ionizing radiation throughout the procedure. We investigate whether a physics-based world model can sustain the navigation task between deliberately sparse X-ray acquisitions, and whether the model can signal when its internal state estimate is no longer reliable. We formulate sparse-fluoroscopy navigation as a partially observable Markov decision process where a Cosserat rod simulator supplies transition dynamics, sparse noisy projections provide observations, and a particle filter maintains a belief over the device state, reduced in this implementation to a tip state with a geometric contact proxy. We evaluate this formulation in a deliberately simplified setting: a synthetic planar vessel phantom with a quasi-static rod model and simulated projections, without clinical or animal data. In this setting, the belief-state model tracks the simulated tip with a root mean square error of 1.30 mm while acquiring observations at one fifteenth of the continuous rate (0.97 mm at every frame, 1.51 mm at one thirtieth), reported 90 percent credible intervals achieve 0.92 empirical coverage, and the belief-derived contact risk estimate discriminates unsafe contact events with an AUROC of 0.68. These results constitute a proof of concept on a simplified simulation rather than a demonstration of clinical readiness; their purpose is to establish that calibrated belief, rather than point-estimate accuracy alone, is the essential property a sparse-imaging world model must deliver.

The general formulation behind the transition model is Cosserat rod theory, which describes a slender instrument by a centerline 𝐫 ⁡ ( s , t ) \mathbf{r}(s,t) and cross-section orientation 𝐑 ⁡ ( s , t ) \mathbf{R}(s,t) over arc length s s , balancing linear and angular momentum under internal loads and distributed external forces [ 4 ] :

The planar implementation incorporates four specific simplifications of ( 2 ). Second, it is planar: the rod is inextensible and shear-free with pure bending, omitting torsion and out-of-plane motion. 2026-10-07.title: Behavioral Safety Assessment towards Large-scale Deployment of Autonomous Vehicles, Part II: Assessment Results
2026-10-07.authors: Henry X. Liu , Tinghan Wang , Xintao Yan , Haowei Sun , Zhijie Qiao , Kenneth Boyd , Shuo Feng , Greg Stevens , Greg McGuire
2026-10-07.abstract: Third-party evaluations of autonomous vehicle (AV) safety can play a vital role in improving public acceptance, building consumer confidence, and establishing effective safety standards. In Part I of this study [ 1 ] , we propose a dedicated third-party testing initiative for systematically evaluating AV behavioral safety. In this paper, we validate our proposed framework using Autoware.Universe, an open-source Level 4 Automated Driving System (ADS), tested both in simulated environments and on the physical test track at the University of Michigan’s Mcity Testing Facility 1 1 1 https://mcity.umich.edu/ . The results indicate that Autoware.Universe possesses 6 out of 14 behavioral competencies and exhibited a crash rate of 3.01 × 10 − 3 3.01\times 10^{-3} crashes per mile, approximately 1,000 times higher than the average human driver crash rate. During the tests, we also uncovered a number of unknown unsafe scenarios for Autoware.Universe. These findings underscore the necessity of behavioral safety evaluations for improving AV safety performance prior to widespread public deployment.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Third-party evaluations of autonomous vehicle (AV) safety are essential for improving public acceptance, gaining consumer confidence, and establishing effective safety standards.
The existing well-established testing programs for conventional vehicles, such as NCAP [ 2 ] and IIHS [ 3 ] , and notable standards, including ISO 26262 [ 4 ] , ISO 21448 [ 5 ] , ISO/PAS 8800 [ 6 ] , ISO 34502 [ 7 ] , and UL 4600 [ 8 ] , are inadequate for Level 4–5 AVs [ 9 ] for two key reasons: (1) they adopt a vehicle-centric perspective focused on passive and active safety features or system-level malfunctions, rather than evaluating an AV’s holistic driving behavior within complex traffic environments, and (2) they rely on deterministic assessment of predetermined scenarios, whereas modern AVs exhibit inherently non-deterministic behavior due to their reliance on deep learning models, necessitating probabilistic evaluation. These limitations underscore the necessity of shifting the AV evaluation paradigm from functional safety to behavioral safety, which evaluates whether a functionally sufficient AV can make safe decisions in reacting to and interacting with the traffic environment, without creating or exacerbating safety-critical situations.

While the need for behavioral safety evaluation is clear, conducting third-party evaluations presents significant challenges. First, modern AVs operate as black-box systems with limited interpretability, making failures unpredictable and necessitating holistic evaluation of basic behavioral competency rather than just extreme-case testing. Second, the naturalistic driving environment involves intricate spatial-temporal interactions among diverse road users, across varying road geometries, and under dynamic traffic conditions, making AV assessment highly complex. Third, safety-critical events occur with extreme rarity in real-world traffic, requiring billions of miles for meaningful evaluation [ 10 ] and rendering brute-force mileage-based testing impractical even in simulation.

To overcome these challenges, in Part I of this study [ 1 ] , we propose a dedicated third-party testing initiative for systematically evaluating AV behavioral safety.
The framework consists of two key components: the Behavioral Competency Test (BCT) and the Driving Intelligence Test (DIT).
The BCT evaluates AV performance in predefined scenarios of varying risk levels, akin to human driver’s license tests, to verify basic behavioral competency in both normal and safety-critical situations.
The DIT goes beyond known scenarios by constructing a Naturalistic and Adversarial Driving Environment (NADE) that leverages importance sampling to efficiently uncover unknown failure modes and statistically measure safety-critical event rates without bias. Together, the BCT ensures baseline competency in expected driving situations, while the DIT reveals long-tail risks that may only emerge at scale.

Part I establishes the evaluation pipeline and methodological foundation. In this paper (Part II), we first present a systematic evaluation of an open-source Level 4 Automated Driving System (ADS), demonstrating how the proposed framework is applied. We then report quantitative evaluation results, including pass/fail outcomes of the BCT across multiple behavioral competencies and unbiased statistical metric estimates from the DIT. Finally, we present a field test conducted on a real test track, validating the practical applicability of the framework beyond simulation.

More specifically, to demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we applied it to evaluate a Level 4 AV system running open-source automated driving software, Autoware.Universe [ 11 ] , in a simulated testing environment at the University of Michigan’s Mcity Test Facility.
We assessed the AV’s performance within an urban driving ODD, including intersections, roundabouts, and urban arterials, under normal weather conditions. High-fidelity testing scenarios and environments were constructed using large-scale real-world datasets that model human driving behavior.
For the BCT, we selected 14 representative behavioral competencies, comprising both single-agent and multi-agent scenarios, that span all major collision configurations (head-on, angle, rear-end, and sideswipe crashes, as well as crashes involving pedestrians), which together account for 63.3% of all reported crashes in the study area [ 12 ] .
The DIT was developed based on state-of-the-art intelligent testing methodologies [ 13 ] to obtain statistical performance of the AV accurately and efficiently.

Simulation results reveal that Autoware.Universe, the latest version of Autoware, possesses 6 out of 14 behavioral competencies in the BCT.
The DIT estimated a crash rate of 3.01 × 10 − 3 3.01\times 10^{-3} crashes per mile, about 1,000 times higher than that of an average human driver [ 14 ] ( 3.00 × 10 − 6 3.00\times 10^{-6} crash per mile).
These testing results successfully identified unknown unsafe events, exposing potential weaknesses and bugs in the AV’s software stack, such as its failure to navigate certain roundabouts, leading to unexpected stops.
This issue was reported to the developers, who were able to address and resolve it based on our feedback.
These findings highlight the framework’s effectiveness in detecting and diagnosing system vulnerabilities, particularly those unknown unsafe behaviors, which are essential for refining AV systems and supporting a closed-loop development process for large-scale deployment.

To further validate the applicability of our framework in real-world settings, we conducted physical tests using Mcity’s closed test tracks with a Tesla Model 3 (equipped with Full Self-Driving Version 12.5.5) and a prototyping vehicle equipped with Autoware.Universe on a Lincoln MKZ platform.
Due to the resource constraints, the goal was not comprehensive testing but to demonstrate feasibility.
For the BCT, we evaluated two behavioral competencies with the Tesla, one involving a vehicle and the other involving a vulnerable road user (VRU), both of which were successfully passed across multiple risk levels.
For the DIT, testing with the Autoware-equipped Lincoln MKZ revealed that the system could benefit from further improvements to proactively reduce risk and limit exposure to safety-critical situations.
These results highlight the framework’s versatility and effectiveness in evaluating AV systems across both simulated and physical environments, reinforcing its potential as a systematic, standardized, and third-party safety validation tool for AV deployment.

# II Experimental Setup of the Behavioral Safety Assessment

## II-A Development process of the Behavioral Competency Test

This section details the development process of the BCT. The initial step involves abstracting basic behavioral competencies and building a testing behavioral competency library grounded in real-world dynamic driving tasks.
Several existing studies, standards, and best practices contribute to the creation of the libraries [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] .
Based on this foundation, we compiled our testing competency set, considering the typical driving scenarios within the urban ODD.
Specifically, we leveraged the scenario library from Ref. [ 19 ] to guide our selection and curated 14 representative behavioral competencies, as shown in Fig. 1 , where the orange vehicle represents the AV under test, the blue vehicle represents the BV, and the blue human figure represents the VRU.
The selected competencies encompass both single-agent situations, such as detecting and responding to the traffic light, as well as multi-agent situations featuring various road user types.
Notably, these competencies cover every multi-vehicle collision configuration recorded in local crash statistics (head-on, angle or left-turn, rear-end, and sideswipe), as well as crashes involving pedestrians. Together, these crash types account for 63.3% of all crashes reported in Washtenaw County, Michigan, in 2021 [ 12 ] , offering reasonable coverage.
While the selected 14 competencies may not fully represent the entirety of the urban ODD, they were chosen to demonstrate our proposed methodology within the constraints of resources.
The methodology is designed to be flexible, allowing for the addition of more scenarios as needed.

Each behavioral competency follows a three-step development process: scenario modeling (parameterization in state space), parameter calibration (constructing the parameter’s NDE distribution), and case generation (building the NADE distribution for test case sampling).
As shown in Fig. 2 , we demonstrate the three-step process using behavioral competency (a), which is evaluated in cut-in scenario.
Since the AV is treated as a black box, the tester cannot control its speed during testing.
Therefore, for a cut-in scenario, the controllable variables are the relative speed and the relative longitudinal distance between the AV and the BV, and the BV will execute lane changes at a constant speed, following a sine-function trajectory.
As a result, it is modeled as a two-dimensional problem.
The constraints include the initial relative speed and the longitudinal distance between AV and BV equal to the given value, which means these two parameters uniquely determine the test case.

In the parameter calibration step, we aim to derive real-world distributions of constraint parameters.
Using the Argoverse 2 Motion Forecasting Dataset [ 20 ] , we extracted 11701 cut-in segments and developed the NDE distribution for this scenario, as shown in Fig. 2 (middle).
Rather than randomly sampling from the naturalistic distribution, we balance coverage and difficulty in the case generation process to account for different risk levels.
For each test case, the risk is calculated based on the minimum deceleration required by the AV to avoid a collision.
By referencing human drivers’ deceleration distributions in cut-in events from the NDD, we categorize the scenario state space into five risk levels (trivial, low, medium, high, and infeasible) based on the required deceleration.
These levels are color-coded in Fig. 2 (right): blue (trivial), green (low), yellow (medium), orange (high), and red (infeasible), corresponding to different percentiles of human deceleration: above 80%, 80%-10%, 10%-1%, below 1%, and beyond observed human capabilities.
For example, if the required deceleration falls between the 1st and 10th percentiles of the cut-in event data, the test case is categorized as medium-risk.
We will generate test cases from low-, medium-, and high-risk levels, with a higher sampling density in high-risk regions, and 95% confidence level.
Fig. 2 (right) illustrates the sampling results, where each black dot represents a test case.
The number of generated test cases for all scenarios is presented in the second column of Table I .
More development and implementation details of different scenarios can be found in the Supplementary Materials [ 21 ] .
Each test case is run 3 times to account for stochastic variability in the AV and testing systems.
A test case is considered a failure if a collision occurs in any run, and a success if no collisions occur.
By analyzing the results across different scenarios, we can assess the AV’s basic behavioral competency.
The AV is deemed to have failed the BCT if it encounters a failure in any of the testing scenarios.
An illustration video of the BCT is provided in Supplementary Movie 1.

## II-B Development process of the Driving Intelligence Test

This section details the development process of DIT.
Unlike the BCT, which models individual scenarios independently, the DIT begins by constructing a complete traffic environment through high-fidelity simulation of human driving behavior.
This simulated NDE encompasses all relevant components of the AV’s ODD, such as intersections and roundabouts, when evaluating performance in urban settings.
The DIT enables the evaluation of an AV’s capabilities over entire trips.
To achieve this, we have developed TeraSim [ 22 ] , an open-source, high-fidelity traffic simulation platform designed specifically for AV safety testing.
TeraSim employs a generative paradigm to construct traffic environments using two core models. The NDE [ 23 , 24 ] reconstructs realistic traffic conditions with statistical fidelity, ensuring that generated environments follow real-world distributions, particularly for those safety-critical events.
Building on NDE, the NADE [ 10 , 13 ] amplifies rare but critical events, systematically exposing AVs to safety-critical conditions to accelerate the evaluation of AV safety performance.

Our method enables high-fidelity simulation of the Mcity environment, which includes a 1,000-foot urban arterial, six signalized intersections (one with an unprotected left turn), three roundabouts, and various single and multi-lane roads, effectively replicating a realistic urban driving context.
A key requirement for AV testing in the NDE is the accurate reproduction of safety-critical events based on real-world data [ 23 , 10 ] .
To validate this, we compared the simulated crash rate in Mcity with ground-truth crash data from five years (2016–2021) in Michigan, US [ 14 ] .
The ground-truth crash rate is 3.00 × 10 − 6 3.00\times 10^{-6} crashes per mile, while our simulation yielded 2.93 × 10 − 6 2.93\times 10^{-6} crashes per mile, confirming the fidelity of the NDE.
Additionally, as shown in Fig. , the simulation successfully replicates the composition of crashes across various road geometries and crash types, closely mirroring real-world distributions from the city of Ann Arbor, Michigan [ 14 ] .
Moreover, our simulations capture a broad range of urban traffic conditions, including variations in traffic density, speed, and signalized travel delay, as illustrated in Fig. .
Traffic density represents the number of vehicles present within the simulation environment, vehicle speed reflects the instantaneous speed of each vehicle, and traffic light waiting time captures the duration vehicles spent at signalized intersections.
While we do not have real-world data for direct comparison, these results demonstrate the simulation’s ability to generate diverse urban traffic patterns, highlighting its potential for comprehensive traffic representation.

Testing AVs directly within the NDE can be time-consuming due to the rarity of safety-critical events [ 25 ] .
Studies suggest that hundreds of millions of miles of testing might be required to demonstrate AV safety performance at a human driver level [ 26 ] .
The NADE amplifies the likelihood of safety-critical events by training BVs to execute strategic adversarial maneuvers that challenge the AV under test.
This strategic approach significantly accelerates testing efficiency by orders of magnitude while ensuring that safety assessments remain unbiased [ 13 ] .
By deploying the AV in the NADE and conducting a large number of runs, the DIT provides a comprehensive statistical assessment of AV safety, including crash rates, crash types, and crash severity statistics.
Beyond efficiency, DIT offers a unique advantage in uncovering unknown unsafe behaviors.
Its interactive, large-scale, and dynamic testing environment continuously generates safety-critical situations tailored to the specific AV under test.
These emergent interactions naturally reveal failure modes that may remain hidden in static or scenario-based evaluations.
As a result, DIT not only provides rigorous statistical validation but also serves as a powerful tool for exposing latent vulnerabilities, delivering a comprehensive assessment of AV driving intelligence.

## II-C AV under test

In this study, we aim to validate the proposed methodology by assessing the behavioral safety of AVs in urban driving environments.
The AV’s ODD is typical urban conditions in U.S. cities, with a speed limit of 30 mph, during daytime hours, and in sunny or cloudy weather.
For our evaluation, we utilize an open-source Level 4 AV system: Autoware.Universe [ 11 ] , the latest version of the widely adopted Autoware platform.
Although its performance may not yet match that of commercial systems like Waymo, open-source platforms such as Autoware.Universe are among the most accessible and widely used Automated Driving System (ADS) available to the research community.

The evaluation was conducted at the Mcity testing facility at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor.
We began by assessing the performance of Autoware.Universe within the simulated Mcity environment.
To further demonstrate the real-world applicability of our framework, we extended the evaluation to two real vehicles: a Tesla Model 3 equipped with Full Self-Driving (version: v12.5.5) and a Lincoln MKZ equipped with Autoware.Universe.
Compared to simulations, real-vehicle testing provides higher fidelity by incorporating factors such as vehicle dynamics and other physical effects that are often challenging to replicate in simulation.

2026-10-07.title: Behavioral Safety Assessment towards Large-scale Deployment of Autonomous Vehicles, Part I: Methodology
2026-10-07.authors: Henry X. Liu , Tinghan Wang , Xintao Yan , Haowei Sun , Zhijie Qiao , Kenneth Boyd , Shuo Feng , Greg Stevens , Greg McGuire
2026-10-07.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) have significantly advanced in real-world deployment in recent years, yet safety continues to be a critical barrier to widespread adoption. Traditional functional safety approaches, which primarily verify the reliability, robustness, and adequacy of AV hardware and software systems from a vehicle-centric perspective, do not sufficiently address the AV’s broader interactions and behavioral impact on the surrounding traffic environment. To overcome this limitation, we propose a paradigm shift toward behavioral safety, a comprehensive approach focused on evaluating AV responses and interactions within the traffic environment. To systematically assess behavioral safety, we introduce a third-party AV safety assessment framework comprising two complementary evaluation components: the Behavioral Competency Test and the Driving Intelligence Test. The Behavioral Competency Test evaluates the AV’s reactive behaviors under controlled scenarios, ensuring basic behavioral competency. In contrast, the Driving Intelligence Test assesses the AV’s interactive behaviors within naturalistic traffic conditions, quantifying the frequency of safety-critical events to deliver statistically meaningful safety metrics before large-scale deployment. In Part II of this study [ 1 ] , an open-source Level 4 Automated Driving System (ADS) is tested to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Autonomous vehicle (AV) technology is transforming modern transportation, promising increased safety, efficiency, and accessibility. In recent years, AV deployments have expanded globally. Waymo, for example, opened its robotaxi services to the public in 10 U.S. cities as of early 2026, including Phoenix, the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Atlanta, Austin, and Miami, and plans to launch in further cities such as London later in 2026 [ 2 ] .
Similarly, Baidu’s Apollo Go has launched operations in Wuhan and other Chinese cities [ 3 ] .
However, these deployments have sparked widespread debate, particularly regarding AV safety [ 4 ] .
High-profile incidents, such as when a Cruise robotaxi in 2023 hit and dragged a pedestrian about 20 feet in San Francisco [ 5 ] , have intensified public scrutiny and eroded trust in AV technology.
A recent survey shows that only 13% of U.S. drivers trust riding in AVs [ 6 ] , highlighting the public’s skepticism and the pressing need to build confidence.
Public acceptance and consumer confidence depend heavily on perceived safety [ 7 ] , making unbiased, rigorous, transparent, and publicly accessible safety evaluation programs essential.
Furthermore, systematic AV safety assessment frameworks are crucial for regulators to establish effective safety standards and facilitate the seamless integration of AVs into existing transportation systems.

Despite the critical need, a systematic AV testing program, particularly one based on third-party evaluations, remains absent.
While well-established testing programs exist for conventional human-driven vehicles [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] , they are inadequate for Level 4–5 AVs [ 17 ] , as they adopt a vehicle-centric perspective focused on passive and active safety features or system-level malfunctions, rather than evaluating an AV’s holistic driving behavior in complex traffic environments.
While essential, a vehicle-centric approach is insufficient for evaluating AV safety in large-scale real-world deployments for two key reasons.
First, large-scale deployment requires evaluating AVs’ safety impact on the surrounding traffic environment, including not only their ability to mitigate or avoid hazards but also their capacity to avoid creating new safety hazards.
This necessitates an environment-based approach that evaluates how AVs react to and interact with dynamic agents in stochastic, diverse, and complex traffic situations, an aspect Functional Safety (FuSa) and Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF) do not address.
Second, AV testing must shift from deterministic assessment to probabilistic evaluation, as modern AVs rely heavily on deep learning models that exhibit inherently non-deterministic behavior.
In other words, safety evaluation based solely on predetermined scenarios is insufficient, and unbiased estimation of the overall crash rate is necessary to justify the net societal benefits of AVs and to prevent damage to consumer trust from singular and unreasonable risks.
It also helps answer the fundamental question, “How safe is safe enough?”

The above discussions underscore the necessity of shifting the AV evaluation paradigm from functional safety to behavioral safety, which evaluates whether a functionally sufficient AV can make safe decisions in reacting to and interacting with the traffic environment, without creating or exacerbating safety-critical situations.
Consequently, behavioral safety is fundamentally distinct from crashworthiness and functional safety, as shown in Fig. 1 a.
The CertiCAV Assurance Paper [ 18 ] by Connected Places Catapult of the United Kingdom also highlights the importance of behavioral safety, reinforcing our argument that functional safety alone is insufficient for AV evaluation.
However, it falls short of providing concrete definitions and practical methodologies for implementation, leaving a critical gap in the current AV testing approaches.
In recent years, while some AV companies have released information about their internal testing procedures [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] related to behavioral safety, these disclosures remain limited, and the specifics of their testing protocols are often inaccessible.
Therefore, developing a systematic, transparent, and robust third-party testing framework for the behavioral safety of AVs is an urgent priority.

Conducting third-party evaluations of AV behavioral safety presents significant challenges, as illustrated in Fig. 1 b. First, modern AVs, particularly end-to-end models, lack interpretability and operate as black-box systems, making failures unpredictable.
This means failures may occur not only in rare edge cases but also during routine driving.
Such unpredictability erodes public trust, especially when crashes happen under normal conditions.
A recent study shows that over 90% of AV crashes occur in situations with no unusual road conditions or dangerous pre-accident behaviors [ 22 ] , contradicting the common belief that AV testing should focus primarily on rare edge cases.
This highlights the need for a holistic evaluation of basic behavioral competency rather than just extreme-case testing.
Second, AV testing is inherently difficult due to the complexity of real-world traffic and the rarity of safety-critical events. The naturalistic driving environment (NDE) involves intricate spatial-temporal interactions among diverse road users, across varying road geometries, and under dynamic traffic conditions [ 23 ] .
Accurately replicating these factors in simulations requires high-fidelity modeling of both physical environments and human behaviors, making AV assessment highly complex.
Compounding this challenge is the curse of rarity [ 24 ] : safety-critical events occur infrequently, requiring billions of miles to collect sufficient data for meaningful evaluation [ 25 ] .
This renders brute-force mileage-based testing impractical, even in simulations, where the key challenge is generating safety-critical events both realistically and efficiently.

To address these challenges, we propose a dedicated third-party testing initiative for systematically evaluating AV behavioral safety.
The framework consists of two key components: the Behavioral Competency Test (BCT) and the Driving Intelligence Test (DIT), as illustrated in Fig. 1 c.
The BCT evaluates AV performance in predefined scenarios of varying risk levels, akin to human driver’s license tests, to verify basic behavioral competency in both normal and safety-critical situations.
The DIT, in contrast, goes beyond known scenarios by constructing a Naturalistic and Adversarial Driving Environment (NADE) that leverages importance sampling to efficiently uncover unknown failure modes and statistically measure safety-critical event rates without bias. Together, the BCT ensures baseline competency in expected driving situations, while the DIT reveals long-tail risks that may only emerge at scale.
Besides, both of them operate in a black-box manner, requiring no knowledge of the AV’s internal mechanisms, thus ensuring fairness and objectivity.

This study is presented in two parts.
This paper (Part I) establishes the overall framework and methodologies.
Section II reviews related work and identifies existing gaps.
Section III presents the proposed methodology: Section III-A defines behavioral safety and introduces the assessment framework, Section III-B formulates the problem, and Sections IV and V detail the BCT and DIT, respectively.
Section VI introduces the performance evaluation method.
Part II of this study [ 1 ] validates the proposed framework through both simulation and field test results.

# II Related Work

In this section, a brief overview of related work is provided from two areas: the well-established testing programs and standards, and existing work on behavioral safety evaluation.

There exist several well-established testing programs for conventional human-driven vehicles [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . For example, the New Car Assessment Program (NCAP) [ 8 ] is a safety rating program that primarily assesses vehicle crashworthiness and crash avoidance technologies such as Autonomous Emergency Braking (AEB). Similar programs have been adopted worldwide, including Euro NCAP [ 9 ] in Europe and C-NCAP [ 11 ] in China, while the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) [ 10 ] provides complementary vehicle safety evaluations in the United States. These programs all follow a similar paradigm focused on whether a specific passive or active safety feature performs correctly in predefined test scenarios rather than on evaluating a vehicle’s overall driving behavior, which is insufficient for Level 4–5 AVs.
For high-level AVs, notable standards include ISO 26262 [ 12 ] for FuSa, ISO 21448 [ 13 ] for SOTIF, and ISO/PAS 8800 [ 14 ] for Road Vehicles Safety and Artificial Intelligence, all of which address risks arising from hardware and software malfunctions or insufficiencies. In addition, ISO 34502 [ 15 ] introduces a scenario-based testing framework for SOTIF, while UL 4600 [ 16 ] provides methods for assessing AV’s overall safety case. However, these testing standards adopt a vehicle-centric perspective, assessing AV safety based on vehicle system function and capability, such as sensor failures (hardware) and perception errors (software).
These vehicle-centric approaches are insufficient for evaluating AV safety in large-scale real-world deployments, as we discussed in Section I .

Most of the existing AV safety assessment methods, including the scenario-based methods [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] and environment-based methods [ 30 , 25 , 23 ] , are not designed to evaluate behavioral safety.
Several researchers have also recognized the absence of rigorous AV behavioral safety evaluation.
In the CertiCAV Assurance Paper [ 18 ] by Connected Places Catapult of the United Kingdom, behavioral safety is defined as “the field of safety concerned with addressing the safety and sufficiency of the intended functionality of driving features.”
Its objectives include traffic rule compliance, active/tactical safety controls, and fallback behavior.
This definition, however, focuses on whether the intended functionality is safe and sufficient, and therefore remains oriented toward the specification and development process.
It falls short of providing practical testing methodologies for evaluating actual AV behavioral performance in traffic, leaving a critical gap in existing AV testing approaches.
In recent years, some AV companies have disclosed information about their internal testing procedures related to behavioral safety [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] .
Waymo published their approach for determining the absence of unreasonable risk, structured around architectural hazards, behavioral hazards, and in-service operational hazards [ 19 ] .
Although behavioral hazards bear some resemblance to behavioral safety, they are treated as one component of the AV development life cycle, decomposing the AV system and evaluating each subsystem individually.
This approach is inconsistent with our goal of treating the AV as a black box from a third-party evaluation perspective.
Cruise reported coverage of SOTIF, FuSa, physical safety/crashworthiness, passenger safety, and operational safety [ 20 ] , which is distinct from behavioral safety as defined in this work.
Similarly, Aurora grounded their behavioral safety processes in SOTIF and FuSa [ 21 ] .
Overall, these industry disclosures remain limited in scope, and the specifics of their testing protocols are largely inaccessible to the public.

2026-10-07.title: ActTune: Action-Aware Precision and GPU Operating-Point Adaptation for Energy-Efficient Vision-Language-Action Inference
2026-10-07.authors: Zou Qingyun , Bin Gao , Wenju Zhao , Weng-Fai Wong , Bingsheng He , Tulika Mitra
2026-10-07.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke inference to control robots, making graphics processing unit (GPU) energy a recurring cost of task execution. Reducing energy per inference call, however, may not reduce energy per successful task if numerical errors increase failures or slower inference prolongs execution. We therefore target GPU energy per successful task while preserving task success and keeping the inference-latency increase within 10%. Our approach builds on two observations: quantization sensitivity varies across action classes, model layers, and weights versus activations; and numerical precision changes the workload, shifting favorable GPU operating points. We introduce ActTune, an action-aware framework that connects layer-wise precision allocation with workload-dependent GPU operating-point selection over requested frequency–power-cap pairs. A lightweight decision tree learns its splits and leaf precision configurations directly from configuration action errors, then selects precision before each policy call. The controller forecasts the next workload and applies the selected GPU operating point asynchronously using a lookup table calibrated under a latency budget. A shared resident quantized weight bank enables configuration switching without weight reconstruction or additional policy evaluations. On LIBERO, a benchmark for lifelong robot learning, ActTune improves mean task success by up to 2.3% relative to state of the art. Relative to the original BF16 implementations, it delivers up to 2.02 × 2.02\times faster inference and, with GPU operating-point adaptation, reduces energy per successful task by up to 76.8%.
2026-10-07.introduction:
VLA models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions ( Kim et al., 2024 ) . For battery-powered robots, repeated onboard inference consumes limited battery energy and can shorten operation between charges. Reducing inference energy is therefore important for extending robot endurance. Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) offers a direct way to pursue this goal by lowering power consumption ( Tang et al., 2019 ) . However, lower frequencies prolong inference, which can offset energy savings and delay action updates. The need for timely responses therefore limits how aggressively frequency can be reduced.

Numerical precision and GPU operating-point control offer complementary ways to reduce this cost. Quantization lowers weight and activation precision, changing computation and memory traffic, but the resulting numerical errors can also perturb predicted actions. We define a GPU operating point as a requested frequency–power-cap pair. Adjusting these settings trades execution speed against power consumption. Lower frequencies may reduce power, yet longer inference can offset these savings and delay the robot’s response to new observations. Crucially, these two controls are coupled: precision determines the workload on which GPU operating-point control operates. An energy-efficient operating point for one precision configuration may therefore be less effective for another. Exploiting both controls requires connecting the precision needs of robot actions to the hardware characteristics of the resulting inference workload.

Existing work provides useful foundations for this connection. VLA quantization methods use action or task sensitivity to allocate precision ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Akbari et al., 2026 ; Ranjan and Savakis, 2026 ) , while temporal-dynamic-aware quantization for VLA models (DyQ-VLA) and motion-aware vector quantization (MotionVQ) adapt precision during execution using motion signals ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . However, compression objectives such as model size and bit-operation budgets do not directly capture GPU energy during task execution ( Ranjan and Savakis, 2026 ) . Other work studies energy efficiency through quantized robotic policies or device–edge execution placement ( Park et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) , and PiQi, a framework for partially quantized inference, combines partial quantization, processor placement, and DVFS for general deep neural network (DNN) inference ( Aghapour et al., 2024 ) . Building on these directions, we investigate how action-aware precision allocation and workload-dependent GPU operating-point selection can work together to reduce energy per successful robot task.

Our approach is motivated by two observations. First, quantization sensitivity depends on both the action being performed and where numerical error is introduced in the model. For example, coarse approach motion may tolerate small deviations, whereas final alignment may require greater accuracy (Figure 1 ). Using a fixed set of action classes learned from training actions, short quantized interventions reveal sensitivity differences across action classes, Transformer blocks, and weight versus activation precision (Figure 2 (b–c)). Second, hardware measurements show that different numerical precisions can favor different GPU operating points (Figure ). Together, these observations suggest a two-stage adaptation strategy: use action sensitivity to guide precision allocation, then use the resulting workload to guide GPU operating-point selection.

We introduce ActTune , an action-aware framework that implements this strategy. Before each action chunk is generated, a lightweight decision tree uses current proprioception and the preceding predicted action chunk to select a layer-wise weight and activation precision configuration. Offline calibration learns the tree splits and leaf configurations directly from action error against the BF16 reference policy under precision and storage budgets. A shared resident quantized weight bank supports configuration switching without reconstructing weights or storing a complete model copy for every leaf. This design enables action-aware precision selection with only one policy inference call per action chunk.

ActTune profiles frequency and power-cap settings on replayed training workloads with the precision selector fixed. It selects the candidate table with the lowest estimated energy while limiting the mean inference-latency increase to 10% relative to the same precision selector at the fixed reference GPU operating point, subject to action equality and memory checks. After each call, the controller forecasts the next workload and applies the selected GPU operating point asynchronously. Precision selection uses the current observation. Because matching actions on replayed inputs does not guarantee unchanged closed-loop behavior, the final assessment must consider complete episodes. We therefore evaluate closed-loop task success and energy per successful task, and check the 10% budget using the measured inference latency.
Our contributions are:

Empirical characterization. We firstly characterize how quantization sensitivity varies across action classes, Transformer blocks, and weight versus activation precision, and show that favorable GPU operating points depend on numerical precision.

Action-aware precision and GPU operating-point adaptation. We propose ActTune, which connects action-conditioned layer-wise precision allocation with workload-dependent GPU operating-point selection. A lightweight decision tree and a shared quantized weight bank enable online adaptation with one policy call per action chunk.

Quantitative evaluation. In the evaluated LIBERO comparisons, ActTune improves mean task success by up to 2.3% relative to QVLA, an action-centric VLA quantization framework, and action-guided quantization (ActQuant). It also reduces static model storage by up to 29.3% relative to the compared general-purpose quantization baselines at W4A8/W4A4 (Table ).
Compared with the original BF16 implementations, it achieves up to 2.02 × 2.02\times inference speedup and up to 76.8% lower energy per successful task with GPU operating-point adaptation.

2. Action-aware precision and GPU operating-point adaptation. We propose ActTune, which connects action-conditioned layer-wise precision allocation with workload-dependent GPU operating-point selection. A lightweight decision tree and a shared quantized weight bank enable online adaptation with one policy call per action chunk.

3. Quantitative evaluation. In the evaluated LIBERO comparisons, ActTune improves mean task success by up to 2.3% relative to QVLA, an action-centric VLA quantization framework, and action-guided quantization (ActQuant). # 2 Motivation

We examine two empirical questions that motivate ActTune:
(1) whether quantization sensitivity depends on the action and on where precision is reduced in the model, and
(2) whether different precision configurations favor different GPU operating points.
The first determines how precision should be allocated, while the second determines whether hardware settings should adapt to the resulting workload.

We first group training action blocks into three fixed classes, C0–C2, using principal component analysis (PCA) followed by K-means (Figure 2 (a)).
These classes describe patterns in the action data rather than prescribed physical task stages.
To measure quantization sensitivity, we insert an eight-action quantized intervention into matched BF16 trajectories and then return to BF16 control.
We measure final task success rate using equal-weight averages over Goal, Object, Spatial, and Long.
The matched BF16 reference achieves a mean task success rate of 95.0%. Figure 2 (b) shows that the same precision configuration can have substantially different effects across action classes.
At fixed A4, C1 achieves only 42.5–45.0% task success across the tested weight precisions, whereas C2 maintains 92.5–95.0%.
For C1, changing activation precision has a larger effect than changing weight precision, and increasing weight precision alone does not resolve the poor A4 outcomes. Sensitivity is also nonuniform across Transformer layers (Figure 2 (c)).
For C1, applying W4A4 to layer 0 yields 75.0% task success, compared with 97.5% when applying the same precision to the other tested layers.
Increasing layer-0 activation precision from A4 to A8 raises task success to 97.5%.
These results show that precision requirements depend jointly on the action class, model location, and quantized component, motivating action-conditioned, layer-wise allocation of weight and activation precision.

We next test whether numerical precision changes the preferred GPU operating point.
On an NVIDIA RTX A6000, we sweep requested GPU frequency at a fixed 300 W power cap and sweep power cap at a requested frequency of 1800 MHz (Figure ).
Measurements for each precision are normalized to its own 1800 MHz / 300 W reference, isolating the effect of hardware tuning from the energy differences introduced by quantization. At the kernel level, we benchmark resident INT4 × \times INT4, INT8 × \times INT8, and BF16 × \times BF16 GEMM workloads.
The measurements include the output epilogue but exclude input quantization, packing, and transfers. INT4 and INT8 reach their lowest measured GPU energy at different frequencies (Figure (a)), showing that the energy–latency tradeoff depends on numerical precision. An exploratory policy-level sweep shows the same tendency during VLA execution (Figure (b)).
In this exploratory sweep, among measured operating points that increase total benchmark time by at most 1%, the lowest-energy points reduce GPU energy by 20.4%, 22.7%, and 21.0% for BF16, W4A8, and W4A4, respectively, relative to their corresponding reference operating points.
These points use different frequency–power-cap combinations, motivating configuration-specific hardware profiling rather than a common operating point for all precision settings.

The clusters above serve as diagnostics; ActTune learns decision regions from each configuration’s action error (Section 3.2 ).
The hardware sweep uses four matched episodes and one measurement per setting, so it provides design evidence rather than a precise estimate of task-level savings.
These findings motivate action-aware precision allocation and workload-dependent GPU control.

2026-10-07.title: Safe Multi-Robot Collaborative Transport Using Density Functions
2026-10-07.authors: Jagannath Prasad Sahoo , Sriram S. K. S. Narayanan , Umesh Vaidya
2026-10-07.abstract:
This paper presents a hierarchical density-based model predictive control
framework for safe collaborative manipulation by multiple quadrupedal robots.
The framework enables a team of robots to push a shared object to a desired pose
using only the initial and goal poses, without requiring a precomputed reference
trajectory. A centralized box-level MPC optimizes contact forces while
enforcing a control-density constraint for goal convergence and obstacle
avoidance. Each robot then solves its own distributed robot-level
whole-body MPC, under a stated shared-information assumption, to track
its moving contact location while accounting for static obstacles and the
time-varying positions of neighboring robots. The
approach is evaluated in MuJoCo using whole-body contact dynamics for two and
three Unitree Go2 quadrupeds collaboratively pushing rigid objects through
narrow passages. Comparisons with matched Control Barrier Function and
RRT* based tracking baselines demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed
density-based formulation for push-only, force- and torque-coupled
manipulation tasks. Implementation videos are available at https://jaggu2606.github.io/go2-density-mpc-pushing/ .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Quadrupedal teams can support exploration, inspection, and search-and-rescue [ 1 , 2 ] , where coordinated,
collision-free motion is essential in cluttered environments [ 3 , 4 ] . Tasks such as debris removal
and material transport may also require teams to manipulate objects
beyond a single robot’s capacity. Collaborative
pushing requires the robots to coordinate their contact forces while
avoiding collisions with one another, the object, and surrounding
obstacles [ 5 ] . This is especially
challenging in push-only manipulation, where the contact forces couple
the object’s translation and rotation.

Collaborative pushing has been approached through planning, optimization-based
control, and learned coordination. Sampling-based planners such as RRT*
generate collision-free paths, but these plans must still be converted into
feasible object motions and robot actions [ 6 ] . For contact-rich loco-manipulation, a hierarchical
MPC for a single quadruped jointly optimizes contact forces and configuration
while coordinating with whole-body locomotion control, using a prescribed
object trajectory [ 7 ] . Related methods address uncertain
object mass and friction through adaptive force regulation [ 5 ] , and unmodeled payloads through
CLF-constrained MPC [ 8 ] . At the team level,
hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning has been used to coordinate
quadruped pushing through high-level subgoals and decentralized execution [ 9 ] , and collaborative pushing scenarios have been
included in multi-agent quadruped benchmarks [ 10 ] . These approaches demonstrate coordinated pushing, but do not provide
formal guarantees of collision safety for the robots and shared object
during execution.

Formal safety constraints have also been incorporated into robot control.
Control barrier functions provide conditions for forward invariance of safe
sets and have been used in MPC [ 11 ] ; distributed
barrier-based controllers further address safety and convergence in
multi-agent navigation [ 12 ] . These methods offer
formal guarantees under their stated assumptions, but do not address the
coupled problem of optimizing multiple push-only contact forces on a shared
object while coordinating robot-level motion around moving contact targets
and neighboring robots.

Density functions provide a complementary dual-space formulation
of safety and convergence, based on conditions on the evolution of
trajectory density [ 13 ] . Related ideas have been applied
to formation stabilization [ 14 ] , safe
navigation and data-driven planning [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] , and learned
transfer-operator models for off-road and legged locomotion [ 18 , 19 ] . Control density functions have been used to formulate convex and robust
safety constraints for quadratic-program controllers [ 20 , 21 ] , and have been applied to safe motion planning and control of robotic systems [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] .
These formulations are primarily developed for continuous-time systems.
More recently, control density functions have been incorporated into MPC
with tunable safety margins [ 25 ] . However, existing density-based safety methods have focused primarily on
single-agent systems and do not directly address predictive safety in multi-agent settings.

This paper presents a hierarchical density-constrained MPC framework for
collaborative manipulation by multiple quadrupedal robots, consisting of a
single centralized box-level MPC coupled with N N distributed robot-level
MPCs. A box-level MPC
selects the contact forces that drive the shared object toward a desired pose
while accounting for static obstacles. Each robot then solves its own
robot-level whole-body MPC locally to track
its moving contact location and enforce additional safety constraints with
respect to obstacles and neighboring robots, under the shared-information
assumption stated in Section II . The main contributions are:

A hierarchical multi-agent MPC framework for collaborative
pushing that couples a centralized object-level MPC for push-only
contact-force optimization with distributed robot-level MPCs for
tracking moving contact locations, enabling goal-directed transport
without a prescribed object trajectory.

A discrete-time safety constraint based on density functions,
established in Theorem 2 and
integrated into both MPC layers to enforce safe predictive control
for obstacle avoidance and inter-agent separation.

MuJoCo validation of collaborative transport with two and
three Unitree Go2 quadruped robots, including comparisons against matched
CBF-MPC [ 11 ] and
RRT* based tracking baselines [ 6 ] .

1. A hierarchical multi-agent MPC framework for collaborative
pushing that couples a centralized object-level MPC for push-only
contact-force optimization with distributed robot-level MPCs for
tracking moving contact locations, enabling goal-directed transport
without a prescribed object trajectory.

2. A discrete-time safety constraint based on density functions,
established in Theorem 2 and
integrated into both MPC layers to enforce safe predictive control
for obstacle avoidance and inter-agent separation.

3. MuJoCo validation of collaborative transport with two and
three Unitree Go2 quadruped robots, including comparisons against matched
CBF-MPC [ 11 ] and
RRT* based tracking baselines [ 6 ] .

2026-10-07.title: MIM-VLA: Learning Physical Interaction Representations from Gripper Motor Feedback
2026-10-07.authors: Jaeyoung Lee , Jiyeon Koo , Taehwa Kim , Yerin Cha , Andrew Jaeyong Choi
2026-10-07.comment: . Jaeyoung Lee and Jiyeon Koo contributed equally
2026-10-07.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies infer grasp actions primarily from
visual observations and robot state, but do not explicitly represent the
physical response observed after contact. We present MIM-VLA , a
motor-feedback-based architecture that encodes recent gripper current,
position, velocity, and signal validity as a 128-dimensional interaction
token 𝝉 \boldsymbol{\tau} . A motor-only Motor Interaction Module (MIM) is pretrained with
human-reviewed contact and interaction-phase labels and then conditions only
the gripper-action pathway of SmolVLA; arm actions and the position-control
interface remain unchanged. The same token supports the MEM selector VLM that
compares candidate interactions and produces evidence-conditioned selections
and explanations. We evaluate MIM-VLA in three real-world settings: comparing
the interaction resistance of visually different objects, disambiguating
visually similar real and replica objects through active probing, and gently
grasping fragile objects, including held-out instances. Across 13 object pairs,
MIM-VLA selects the higher-resistance object in 75.0% of trials, compared with
48.8% for the SmolVLA baseline. For the evaluated tasks, the approach uses
motor feedback already available from the gripper and does not require an
additional tactile array, force–torque sensor, calibrated force estimate, or
direct current control.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect images and natural-language
instructions to robot actions [ 1 , 2 ] . Their visual-language
priors support object recognition and task planning, yet appearance does not
fully specify how an object will respond after contact. Visually similar
objects may have different compliance, while fragile objects of different
sizes cannot be safely grasped by replaying one closing position. Joint
position alone also cannot distinguish free closing, contact, stable holding,
and continued compression.

Force- and tactile-aware policies address this limitation using dedicated
sensors or force-aware control [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . We instead
ask whether actuator telemetry already exposed by a smart gripper can provide
useful physical grounding. Motor current is not calibrated force and depends
on motion and actuator dynamics; consequently, we model its temporal relation
with measured position, velocity, and signal validity rather than applying an
instantaneous current threshold.

MIM-VLA, shown in Fig. 2 , uses a GRU-based Motor
Interaction Module (MIM) to encode recent gripper history as an interaction
token 𝝉 ∈ ℝ 128 \boldsymbol{\tau}\in\mathbb{R}^{128} . MIM is pretrained with
binary contact and five interaction-phase labels— idle , closing , squeeze , hold , and opening .
Video supports label generation but is excluded from the motor-only encoder
(Fig. 3 ). During policy learning, a lightweight
projector injects the token only into a dedicated gripper pathway. The
SmolVLM backbone and arm pathway are preserved, and the final outputs remain
position commands rather than current or force commands.

For these interaction states, position and velocity describe aperture and
closure progression, while current supplies the corresponding motor-load
response. MIM remains motor-only to avoid appearance shortcuts; vision stays
in the SmolVLM pathway and is not claimed to be replaced by telemetry.

The same representation supports interaction-level reasoning through the
Material Explain Module (MEM). Candidate-specific token histories are
summarized for a selector VLM, which compares measured interaction responses,
selects a candidate, and renders a short explanation; low-level execution
remains with the action policy. MEM demonstrates reuse of the same physical
token beyond low-level control. We evaluate three capabilities: (i) comparing
relative interaction resistance across visually different objects, (ii)
probing visually similar real and replica objects to identify the more
resistant candidate, as illustrated in
Fig. 1 , and (iii) minimally compressive grasping of
seen and held-out fragile objects. Comparisons include vanilla SmolVLA,
raw-motor conditioning, and a TA-VLA-inspired temporal-current baseline under
the same position-action interface.

Our contributions are:

a motor-only interaction representation pretrained from temporal
gripper telemetry and contact/phase supervision, without calibrated force
sensing;

a gripper-specific integration that preserves the pretrained
visual-language backbone, arm pathway, and position-control interface; and

a shared token interface for closed-loop gripper adaptation and
higher-level evidence-conditioned comparison and explanation through MEM,
evaluated in three complementary real-world settings.

1. a motor-only interaction representation pretrained from temporal
gripper telemetry and contact/phase supervision, without calibrated force
sensing;

2. a gripper-specific integration that preserves the pretrained
visual-language backbone, arm pathway, and position-control interface; and

3. a shared token interface for closed-loop gripper adaptation and
higher-level evidence-conditioned comparison and explanation through MEM,
evaluated in three complementary real-world settings.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Models

Vision-language-action models translate pretrained visual-language
representations into robot actions. OpenVLA presents an open-source generalist
policy pretrained on diverse robot demonstrations and supports efficient
adaptation to new settings [ 1 ] . More recent VLAs employ continuous
generative action models: π 0 \pi_{0} adopts flow matching for general robot
control [ 6 ] , while GR00T N1 couples a vision-language module with a
diffusion-transformer action module for generalist humanoid manipulation [ 7 ] . FLARE augments generative policy learning with future latent
representation alignment, encouraging the policy to model consequences in a
control-relevant feature space [ 8 ] . SmolVLA combines a compact
flow-matching architecture with asynchronous inference for efficient
deployment on affordable hardware [ 2 ] . These methods learn rich
representations for action prediction, but they do not explicitly preserve
object-associated evidence acquired through prior physical probing. Building
on SmolVLA, our approach summarizes gripper motor-response histories as
interaction tokens that can be associated with explored objects and used to
condition subsequent gripper control.

## II-B Physical Interaction for Robot Manipulation

Recent work incorporates physical feedback at different levels of the
perception–action hierarchy. Among the approaches most closely related to
ours, ForceVLA fuses real-time force–torque measurements with
vision-language features through a force-aware mixture-of-experts during
action decoding [ 3 ] . TA-VLA studies torque-aware adapters,
temporal torque history, and auxiliary torque prediction for integrating
physical feedback into existing VLA architectures [ 9 ] . ForceVLA2
introduces force prompts for task-level reasoning and combines them with
hybrid force–position control [ 10 ] . Tactile approaches align
touch with vision and language for contact-rich insertion, as in VTLA [ 11 ] , or use tactile feedback at both the planning and action-refinement
levels, as in VLA-Touch [ 12 ] . Bi-ACT instead learns position,
velocity, and force behavior from demonstrations collected with bilateral
control [ 5 ] .

These approaches primarily use explicit force or tactile signals to improve
ongoing planning and control, or require a force-aware demonstration and
execution interface. In contrast, MIM operates on the temporal current,
position, and velocity signals already exposed by the gripper. Wrist video is
used only to generate and review auxiliary pretraining labels; it is not an
input to the motor-only MIM. We do not interpret current as calibrated force.
Instead, MIM encodes the joint evolution of motor load and finger motion into
an interaction token, allowing the original position-action interface to be
retained.

## II-C Interaction Grounding with Vision-Language Models

Vision-language models connect visual observations with linguistic
descriptions. Qwen2.5-VL supports spatial object localization and temporal
event localization in long videos [ 13 ] , while SmolVLM provides a
compact architecture for image and video understanding [ 14 ] .
Visual evidence alone, however, may not reveal the physical response produced
during grasping. PaLM-E demonstrates that continuous robot-state estimates can
be interleaved with vision and language to support embodied reasoning [ 15 ] . Other work uses VLMs to reason over candidate robot behavior:
RoboMonkey samples actions from a VLA and applies a VLM-based verifier to
select among them [ 16 ] , whereas Uncertainty-Aware Policy Steering
chooses whether to execute, request clarification, or obtain a corrective
intervention according to calibrated semantic and action uncertainty [ 17 ] .

These systems do not retain candidate-specific motor evidence from the robot’s
preceding contact with an object for later comparison. Our Material Explain
Module (MEM) summarizes the MIM interaction histories of two probed candidates
and provides them to a selector VLM together with the task instruction. The VLM
predicts the selected candidate and relative position/current responses, and
generates a short explanation conditioned on the same summaries, while the
action policy remains responsible for low-level position commands. We evaluate
candidate selection in real-robot trials and analyze the effect of interaction-
summary capacity using structured response prediction, explanation
consistency, and candidate-swap consistency.

2026-10-07.title: Post-Grasp Kinematic Repair for Robotic Insertion via Object-in-Gripper Reorientation
2026-10-07.authors: Haegu Lee , Christoffer Sloth
2026-10-07.abstract: A stable grasp does not guarantee kinematically feasible robotic insertion because the object-in-gripper transform may force the robot towards singularities or joint limits along the prescribed insertion path. We study post-grasp kinematic feasibility repair through object-in-gripper reorientation. Given an achieved grasp and a fixed insertion path, we seek a small reorientation that restores kinematic feasibility. Sequential IK can miss such candidates by following an unfavorable joint-space path, while the nonsmooth feasibility landscape makes the search computationally expensive. We evaluate candidates using a branch-aware IK graph that maximizes the minimum feasibility margin over the discretized insertion path and use a learned task-conditioned prior to improve query ordering. The selected reorientation is executed through tactile-based extrinsic manipulation. In UR5e simulations, the planner without learned ranking reduces mean reorientation over successful trials by 51.5% compared with grid-based sequential IK. Adding learned ranking reduces this planner’s mean planning time by an additional 51.1%. Real-robot experiments validate the complete pipeline.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Robots can perform repetitive pick-and-place tasks with high precision in fixed environments. However, achieving the same task becomes more difficult when the environment or setup changes. Depending on the available robot dexterity, task feasibility can vary with the initial grasp pose, robot configuration, and task requirements. Many tasks begin by grasping an object, and the resulting object-in-gripper transform constrains the subsequent robot motion. Thus, grasp stability is necessary but not sufficient for downstream task feasibility [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .

Task-oriented grasp planning has been studied as a way to select grasps that improve downstream task feasibility [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
However, being able to grasp an object does not guarantee downstream task feasibility, and a task-feasible grasp may not exist among the grasp poses reachable from the initial robot configuration.
Once the object is grasped, the relative transform between the gripper and the object is effectively fixed, and the downstream task must be executed only through the motion of the robot. This can make the task infeasible.

To overcome the task infeasibility, extrinsic manipulation has been studied as a way to change the pose of a grasped object using contacts with the environment [ 7 , 8 ] . These methods enable object reorientation through in-hand or extrinsic interactions. Recent developments in tactile sensors [ 9 , 10 ] further make it possible to estimate the object motion relative to the gripper during such contact-rich reorientation [ 11 , 12 ] . However, these extrinsic-manipulation methods often assume that the desired object reorientation is already specified. This leaves a separate planning problem: which object-in-gripper reorientation should be chosen to make the downstream robot motion feasible?

In this work, we study post-grasp kinematic feasibility repair through object-in-gripper reorientation. Rather than assuming that a desired reorientation is given, we select it based on downstream kinematic feasibility. Each candidate transform induces a different robot motion for the same fixed object path. We evaluate each candidate with a branch-aware IK verifier that considers multiple IK solutions at each waypoint to assess kinematic feasibility along the prescribed insertion path. Because the resulting feasibility landscape is nonsmooth and costly to evaluate, we use an adaptive reorientation search with a learned task-conditioned prior for query ordering. Final acceptance remains determined by the branch-aware verifier.

The main contributions of this work are:

A post-grasp kinematic repair formulation that minimizes object-in-gripper reorientation while preserving the desired insertion path.

A branch-aware max–min verifier using multiple IK solutions per waypoint to identify feasible paths missed by sequential IK.

An adaptive reorientation search with learned candidate ranking that reduces IK-based feasibility evaluations.

1. A post-grasp kinematic repair formulation that minimizes object-in-gripper reorientation while preserving the desired insertion path.

2. A branch-aware max–min verifier using multiple IK solutions per waypoint to identify feasible paths missed by sequential IK.

3. An adaptive reorientation search with learned candidate ranking that reduces IK-based feasibility evaluations.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Task-oriented grasp planning

Robotic grasping requires accurate perception and control to identify stable and feasible grasp poses. Grasp quality is commonly evaluated using predefined metrics, including force-closure, wrench-space quality, or robustness under sensing and actuation uncertainty [ 13 , 14 ] . Recent methods have advanced general grasp synthesis by learning grasp quality functions or generative grasp distributions from large-scale synthetic and real datasets [ 15 , 16 ] . Task-oriented grasp planning extends this formulation by incorporating downstream task constraints into the selection of the initial grasp, for example through simulated self-supervision for tool manipulation [ 6 ] . Recent vision-language and vision-language-action models further enable task-conditioned grasp selection from semantic task descriptions [ 17 , 18 ] . However, these methods primarily focus on selecting task-compatible initial grasps, rather than recovering task feasibility through post-grasp adjustment.

## II-B In-hand manipulation and extrinsic dexterity

Robots with simple grippers can have dexterity using external forces, such as gravity or forces generated by contact [ 7 ] . Extrinsic dexterity was used to adjust the pose of objects that are difficult to grasp due to occlusions [ 19 ] . A recent study proposed primitive-based approaches to exploit environmental contacts to transform an initially ungraspable object into a graspable configuration before grasping [ 20 ] . Planar in-hand manipulation has been studied using motion cones, which characterize object motions admissible under frictional contact and support efficient sampling-based planning [ 21 ] and nonlinear trajectory optimization [ 22 ] . Robust extrinsic-contact manipulation was proposed for adjusting the in-gripper pose of a grasped object while maintaining stable environmental contact under model uncertainty [ 8 ] . With the development of tactile sensing, recent studies have explored tactile estimation for in-hand and extrinsic manipulation, enabling robots to localize grasped objects or estimate contact states during manipulation [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] . Other works have integrated tactile estimation with feedback control for extrinsic dexterity, allowing robots to track the pose of objects and regulate contact-rich reorientation using external contacts [ 11 , 12 ] .

## II-C Post-grasp task feasibility and IK verification

Post-grasp manipulation is strongly affected by uncertainty in the object-in-hand state. Prior work has modeled this uncertainty from sensor observations and combined it with task-specific success models to predict whether placing, dropping, or insertion actions are likely to succeed [ 2 ] . Related work in task and motion planning learns feasibility models to filter or guide high-level actions before invoking expensive geometric planners [ 26 , 27 ] . These approaches treat the achieved object-in-gripper transform as a fixed or uncertain state when estimating task success. In contrast, we optimize a post-grasp adjustment to this transform to make a fixed downstream task path kinematically feasible.

Kinematic feasibility is commonly evaluated by solving IK along a given path and checking pose accuracy, joint limits, and joint-space continuity. However, tasks involving force control are particularly sensitive to configurations near kinematic singularities. Since redundant manipulators can admit multiple IK solutions for the same end-effector pose [ 28 ] , sequential IK can remain on an unfavorable solution sequence and falsely reject a feasible path. RelaxedIK [ 29 ] generates motions from end-effector goals, whereas STAMPEDE [ 30 ] and IKLink [ 31 ] select among multiple IK branches for a fixed end-effector path.
In contrast, we optimize the object-in-gripper reorientation while keeping the desired object path fixed, thereby changing the induced end-effector path. For each induced path, our branch-aware verifier then selects IK solutions from multiple IK branches.
