2026-10-07.title: From Legs to Wheels: Embodiment-Aware Human Motion Retargeting for Mobile-Base Humanoids
2026-10-07.authors: Jiyeon Koo , Eunseom Pyo , Jeonghee Seo , Taehwa Kim , Andrew Jaeyong Choi
2026-10-07.abstract: Human video offers a scalable source of robot demonstrations, yet most human-to-humanoid retargeting methods assume a legged robot with human-like kinematics. This assumption does not hold for mobile-base humanoids equipped with a wheeled base, vertical lift, and two arms. Human walking must be expressed through base motion, while torso bending may require coordinated lift and arm motion. We address this mismatch with a task-conditioned framework that assigns reconstructed human motion to base, lift, and arm responsibilities before robot-specific realization. The allocator preserves the human-derived path, stabilizes heading, separates turn and translation when needed, retimes commands to satisfy base limits, and repairs lift and arm trajectories. A deployment adapter then converts the reference to 50 Hz commands using stationary-base detection, deadband and slew-rate filtering, time-consistent playback scaling, and separate linear and angular gains. We evaluate the resulting references with human-derived task-space comparisons, policy-free simulation replay, and a qualitative execution on a physical robot.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Humanoid motion imitation has advanced through the combination of human motion capture, retargeting, and reinforcement learning (RL). Recent systems retarget whole-body motion to legged humanoids and train policies to follow the resulting references in simulation or on hardware [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . These pipelines generally assume that the target is also a biped. Human walking, torso orientation, and limb motion can therefore be mapped to robot legs, trunk, and arms with fairly direct correspondence.

We consider a different embodiment: mobile-base humanoids . These robots retain a human-facing upper body and two arms, but replace the legs with a wheeled base and may use a vertical lift in place of a human-like spine. Simple joint correspondence is no longer sufficient. A person walking forward with still arms should induce base motion, whereas bending to reach a low object may require changes in base position, lift height, and arm configuration. Retargeting must therefore determine not only how to reproduce a motion, but also which robot subsystem should express each human cue.

Fig. 1 illustrates the embodiment mismatch, and Fig. 2 gives an overview of our approach. From a reconstructed motion sequence and a lightweight task condition, the framework extracts locomotion intent for the base, vertical reach and body-height intent for the lift, and manipulation intent for the arms. A robot-specific realization module converts these components into commands that preserve task-space behavior within kinematic and command limits.

The allocation formulation does not depend on a particular 3D human-motion reconstruction method. We use GMR for robot-specific upper-body realization and study retargeting quality, reference feasibility, simulation playback, and initial physical-robot execution. Learning-based tracking performance is outside the scope of this work.

The contributions are:

A task-conditioned motion allocator with explicit base, lift, and arm variables. Phase-gated human-motion cues replace one-to-one joint matching.

A subsystem-specific temporal repair method that preserves base-path progress, stabilizes heading, decouples turn and translation, retimes motion to platform limits, and coordinates lift and arm trajectories.

A 50 Hz deployment adapter for time-consistent command conversion, together with evaluation using human-derived task-space costs, component ablations, policy-free simulation replay, and qualitative physical-robot execution.

1. A task-conditioned motion allocator with explicit base, lift, and arm variables. Phase-gated human-motion cues replace one-to-one joint matching.

2. A subsystem-specific temporal repair method that preserves base-path progress, stabilizes heading, decouples turn and translation, retimes motion to platform limits, and coordinates lift and arm trajectories.

3. A 50 Hz deployment adapter for time-consistent command conversion, together with evaluation using human-derived task-space costs, component ablations, policy-free simulation replay, and qualitative physical-robot execution.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Monocular Human Motion Reconstruction

Human-video imitation typically begins by converting RGB observations into a body representation such as SMPL [ 4 ] . VIBE improves temporal consistency in pose and shape estimates [ 5 ] , while HuMoR uses a motion prior to handle noisy or missing observations [ 6 ] . More recent monocular methods recover world-grounded root motion in addition to local body pose. GLAMR estimates globally consistent motion under dynamic cameras and long occlusions [ 7 ] , and SLAHMR jointly models human and camera trajectories [ 8 ] . WHAM refines global motion using contact information [ 9 ] . TRAM combines camera trajectory recovery with in-the-wild body motion estimation [ 10 ] , whereas GVHMR uses gravity-view coordinates to reduce ambiguity and drift [ 11 ] . We use this line of work for RGB-to-3D reconstruction, then allocate the recovered motion to the actuation space of a mobile-base humanoid.

## II-B Human-to-Humanoid Motion Retargeting

Classical whole-body retargeting transfers human link poses to analogous robot links through geometric task objectives and inverse kinematics [ 12 ] . GMR and related tracking pipelines show that reference quality directly affects downstream policy learning and tracking robustness [ 13 ] . Infeasible poses and inconsistent contacts should therefore be corrected before control. Existing methods, however, mainly target legged humanoids and represent human locomotion through robot leg motion. Our setting instead has to express that locomotion with a mobile base.

RL-based imitation has evolved from reference tracking in DeepMimic [ 14 ] to reusable motion priors and skill embeddings learned from large motion collections [ 15 , 16 ] . PHC [ 17 ] , H2O [ 18 ] , ExBody [ 1 ] , HumanPlus [ 2 ] , OmniH2O [ 3 ] , and BeyondMimic [ 19 ] demonstrate whole-body tracking of retargeted references. Recent Humanoids work also learns poses from internet video [ 20 ] and generates editable motion through postural synergies [ 21 ] . Our focus is earlier in the pipeline: generating feasible references when the robot’s lower body is not human-like.

## II-C Mobile Manipulation from Human Demonstrations

Mobile ALOHA learns bimanual mobile manipulation from whole-body teleoperation data [ 22 ] . Related Humanoids studies cover compact mobile humanoid hardware [ 23 ] , non-holonomic whole-body impedance control [ 24 ] , and coupled versus decoupled embodiment in whole-body teleoperation [ 25 ] . Human demonstrations have also supported manipulation-speed adaptation [ 26 ] and assistive motion generation [ 27 ] . WARP retargets offline demonstrations to whole-body mobile manipulation while accounting for embodiment differences [ 28 ] . Our work asks a complementary question: how should reconstructed whole-body cues be divided among a mobile base, vertical lift, and two arms before GMR-based realization?

## II-D Optimization-Based Retargeting and IK

Retargeting is commonly formulated as constrained optimization over robot configurations. The objective minimizes task-space error subject to joint, velocity, collision, and smoothness constraints. Differential inverse kinematics tools such as Mink solve weighted velocity-level tasks in a constrained MuJoCo model [ 29 ] . Recent Humanoids work learns differentiable reachability constraints for motion generation [ 30 ] and uses continuous contact optimization for whole-body manipulation [ 31 ] . We add an allocation stage before GMR realization to decide whether each human cue should drive the base, lift, arms, or a combination of these subsystems.

2026-10-07.title: How Much Planning Is Enough? Reducing Search and Computation in World-Model Planning
2026-10-07.authors: Changbai Li , Sirui Li , Yichen Yang , Tongfei Chen , Zichao Feng , Shuwei Shao , Huobin Tan
2026-10-07.abstract:
Visual world models enable goal-directed control through decision-time
action search, but their deployment efficiency is often limited by
conservatively large planning budgets.
We show that competitive task performance can be achieved without
agreement with the Full-budget action, that sufficient budgets vary
across model–task pairs, and that iterative planners repeatedly encode
solve-invariant context.
To address these inefficiencies, we propose SufficientPlan, a
simple deployment framework that requires no modification to pretrained
world models or planner updates.
Its Paired Sequential Budget Certification (PSBC) component uses
paired closed-loop evidence to search for and certify a reduced model–task-specific
budget within a predefined Full-performance tolerance.
Its Static-Context Reuse (SCR) component caches observation and
goal representations across search iterations while preserving
candidate-dependent planning and selected actions.
Experiments across multiple world-model backbones and visual-control tasks
show that SufficientPlan substantially reduces search budgets and planning
latency while maintaining competitive control performance.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Latent visual world models, including those based on joint-embedding
predictive architectures (JEPAs), predict the effects of candidate actions
in a learned representation space and support goal-directed control
through model-based planning ( Zhou et al., 2025a ; Maes et al., 2026 ; Nam et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) .
In this paradigm, decision-time search is critical for translating learned
dynamics into effective control, but its computational cost directly
limits deployment efficiency ( de Boer et al., 2005 ; Williams et al., 2017 ; Pinneri et al., 2020 ) .
Existing world-model planners commonly use a large, globally fixed search
budget for different models and tasks ( Chua et al., 2018 ; Zhou et al., 2025a ; Maes et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) .
Such budgets determine how many candidate action sequences are evaluated
and how extensively they are refined before execution.
However, a fixed computational allowance does not account for whether
additional search meaningfully improves closed-loop task performance. However, we find that this practice introduces two complementary forms of redundancy. First, additional action refinement may continue even when a reduced
budget and Full planning achieve the same aggregate task performance. As shown in
Fig. 1 , the calibrated and Full planners follow distinct task- and action-space trajectories but achieve the same 96% success rate using 2,400 and 9,000 scored sequences, respectively. Moreover, the budget required to reach this outcome-sufficient regime varies considerably across model–task pairs (See Tab. 1 ). Second, iterative planners repeatedly encode the same observation history
and goal during candidate refinement, even though these inputs remain unchanged within a planning solve. As shown in Fig. 3 , the original planner places observation-history and goal encoding inside the CEM loop, causing the same solve-static inputs to be re-encoded in every iteration and resulting in 2 ​ K 2K static-encoder calls over K K refinement iterations.

To address these problems, we propose SufficientPlan, a simple, effective, and plug-and-play framework for improving the success-compute trade-off of world-model planning without retraining the underlying model or changing its control objective. SufficientPlan contains two complementary components.
First, Paired Sequential Budget Certification (PSBC) evaluates search budget proposals on paired development episodes and certifies a lower model–task-specific budget that remains within a predefined performance tolerance relative to Full planning. As shown in Fig. 2 , PSBC compares each current budget with the Full reference on the same episodes: uncertain cases receive additional paired evidence, insufficient proposals trigger a larger budget, and the first proposal satisfying the certification criterion is frozen for held-out deployment. Unlike action-matching criteria, PSBC directly evaluates task outcomes,
allowing a reduced budget to be certified even when its selected actions
do not agree with those of the Full-budget planner. Second, Static-Context Reuse (SCR) computes the solve-invariant observation and goal representations once and reuses them across all search iterations. As shown in Fig. 3 , SCR moves these solve-static encoding operations outside the CEM loop, reducing repeated solve-static encoding operations from 2 ​ K 2K to 2 2 over K K iterations. SCR preserves candidate-dependent action encoding, latent rollout, cost evaluation, and optimizer updates, thereby reducing repeated computation without changing the planner’s selected actions or closed-loop behavior.

Together, PSBC and SCR address two orthogonal sources of planning inefficiency: PSBC removes unnecessary search, while SCR removes redundant computation within the remaining search. Because both components operate entirely at deployment time, SufficientPlan can be applied to existing sampling-based world-model planners as a lightweight plug-in. Experiments across multiple world-model backbones and control benchmarks show that SufficientPlan substantially reduces candidate evaluation and planning latency while preserving competitive closed-loop task performance. Our main contributions are summarized below:

We identify a mismatch between closed-loop task success and
Full-budget action agreement: comparable task performance can be achieved
with different actions, and the sufficient search budget varies
substantially across models and tasks.

We identify a mismatch between closed-loop task success and
Full-budget action agreement: comparable task performance can be achieved
with different actions, and the sufficient search budget varies
substantially across models and tasks.

We introduce SufficientPlan, a simple and plug-and-play planning-efficiency framework combining PSBC, which sequentially searches for and certifies a reduced outcome-sufficient search budget, and SCR, which exactly reuses solve-invariant representations during iterative planning.

We evaluate SufficientPlan across multiple world-model backbones and control benchmarks, demonstrating substantial reductions in search computation and planning latency while preserving closed-loop performance.

with different actions, and the sufficient search budget varies
substantially across models and tasks.

2. We introduce SufficientPlan, a simple and plug-and-play planning-efficiency framework combining PSBC, which sequentially searches for and certifies a reduced outcome-sufficient search budget, and SCR, which exactly reuses solve-invariant representations during iterative planning.

3. We evaluate SufficientPlan across multiple world-model backbones and control benchmarks, demonstrating substantial reductions in search computation and planning latency while preserving closed-loop performance.

# 2 Related Work

Latent World Models for Visual Planning. World models learn predictive representations of environment dynamics
for decision making ( Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018 ) .
PlaNet and the Dreamer family perform planning or policy optimization in
compact latent spaces ( Hafner et al., 2019 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ; Hafner et al., 2021 ; Hafner et al., 2023 ) , while
MuZero, EfficientZero, and TD-MPC show that task-relevant latent dynamics
can support control without pixel-perfect future reconstruction ( Schrittwieser et al., 2020 ; Ye et al., 2021 ; Hansen et al., 2024 ) .
Joint-embedding predictive architectures, including I-JEPA, V-JEPA, and
V-JEPA2, further learn predictive representations without reconstructing
raw pixels ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) .
DINO-WM uses pretrained visual features for goal-conditioned planning ( Zhou et al., 2025a ) ; LeWM learns a lightweight world model end-to-end from
pixels, and Fast-LeWM accelerates candidate evaluation through
action-prefix prediction ( Maes et al., 2026 ; Gao & Xu, 2026 ) .
INTACT learns an intent-to-action mapping for direct control and optional
local search ( Sun et al., 2026 ) .
Object-centric methods instead represent scenes as entities and model
their dynamics and interactions ( Locatello et al., 2020 ; Kipf et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Mosbach et al., 2025 ; Nam et al., 2026 ) .
Unlike these methods, which primarily improve representations, dynamics,
or action priors, SufficientPlan keeps the pretrained model and planner
fixed and reduces decision-time computation.

Efficient Decision-Time Planning. Sampling-based optimizers such as CEM and MPPI optimize action sequences
under learned dynamics without requiring differentiable models ( de Boer et al., 2005 ; Williams et al., 2017 ) .
Methods such as PETS and PDDM apply this principle in receding-horizon
control ( Chua et al., 2018 ; Nagabandi et al., 2019 ) , but their cost grows with the candidate
population and search depth.
Prior work improves efficiency using learned policies or behavior priors ( Wang & Ba, 2020 ; Argenson & Dulac-Arnold, 2020 ) or
sample-efficient CEM refinements such as elite reuse and distribution
warm-starting ( Pinneri et al., 2020 ) .
Adaptive replanning instead reduces how frequently the planner is invoked
across environment steps ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) .
SufficientPlan targets two complementary sources of deployment
overcomputation. Paired Sequential Budget Certification (PSBC) uses paired
closed-loop evidence to select a model–task-specific search budget,
which is calibrated on a development set and frozen for held-out
deployment.
Unlike adaptive replanning or per-state early stopping, PSBC changes the
budget assigned to each model–task pair without modifying the world
model or planner update rule. Static-Context Reuse (SCR) encodes the solve-invariant
observation history and goal once and reuses them across refinement
iterations, while preserving candidate evaluation, planner updates, and
the selected action.
Thus, PSBC reduces the amount of deployed search, whereas SCR removes
repeated computation within the retained search.

2026-10-07.title: Event-Driven Proactive Robot Assistance through Vision-Language Reasoning
2026-10-07.authors: Fengkai Liu , Hao Su , Haozhuang Chi , Rui Geng , Congzhi Ren , Xuqing Liu , Chenfei Xu , Yuichi Ohsita , Liyun Zhang
2026-10-07.abstract:
Assistance in collaborative manipulation is often initiated by user instructions, making high-level reasoning request-driven.
In fluent human teamwork, however, partners often infer the next helpful step from the observed outcome of an action rather than waiting for instructions.
Motivated by this, we investigate an event-driven formulation of proactive assistance, where human–object interaction outcomes initiate assistive reasoning without user-provided task specifications at inference time.
To this end, we propose an event-driven framework that monitors workspace state changes with an event monitor and, upon event completion, extracts stabilized pre/post snapshots that characterize the resulting state transition.
A frozen pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM) then uses its semantic priors to infer the task context, decide whether assistance is appropriate, and, when needed, generate a sequence of assistive actions from the observed transition.
To make outputs executable and verifiable, we restrict actions to a set of action primitives and reference objects via integer IDs.
We evaluate the same framework across three distinct real world tabletop collaboration tasks without task-specific training or fine-tuning.
The event-driven framework achieves performance comparable to variants given user instructions.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Recent advances in embodied intelligence have enhanced robots’ ability to interpret task instructions, ground them in perception, and generate executable actions in diverse manipulation settings [ 1 , 2 ] .
However, instruction following mainly addresses what to do once a specification is provided.
To move toward fluent teamwork, a robot should be able to decide when to intervene and what assistance to provide by inferring human intention, the unobserved internal states or goal-oriented constructs that underlie observable human behavior [ 3 ] .
Recent reviews further suggest that proactive interaction can be facilitated by anticipation from observations and contextual information, often without explicit input from a human [ 4 ] .

Translating this vision into practice reveals a bottleneck: many assistive systems remain request-driven, meaning that robot actions are initiated only after the human issues a request to the robot.
Requests can be explicit, for instance a natural language command that specifies what to do [ 7 , 8 ] , or implicit, conveyed through underspecified verbal instructions [ 6 ] or instructive nonverbal cues [ 9 ] .
Even with large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), whose contextual reasoning can support goal inference [ 10 ] , high-level reasoning in many recent embodied systems is still initiated from a preceding instruction or user cue [ 6 ] .
Consequently, interaction often remains in a request–response loop, which limits proactive assistance when step-by-step guidance is absent.

Motivated by this gap, we move from request-driven assistance to an event-driven proactive assistance setting.
In human-human teamwork, partners often do not wait for explicit instructions after every step.
Instead, they use the observed outcome of an action to infer the likely next sub-goal and decide whether to assist.
Motivated by this interaction pattern, we define an event as the human–object interaction interval initiated by the human that induces a sustained workspace state change.
While prior work has used workspace changes for adaptive planning under a shared task description [ 11 ] , we further use event completion itself to initiate assistance without such a specification.
Under this framework, the robot monitors the workspace for human–object interaction events and forms stabilized pre/post observations representing each resulting workspace state transition.
At event completion, it queries a VLM with the stabilized pre/post evidence to infer a task-level goal and plan an appropriate assistive response, without requiring an additional user request specifying the next step.
This event interface allows a frozen pretrained VLM to perform the required semantic reasoning without additional task-specific training.
To improve reliability and mitigate errors from generative planning, we incorporate multi-layer safeguards in the control loop, including schema-constrained outputs, ID-grounded references, and local verification.
We validate the framework on a real tabletop manipulation platform and compare event-driven assistance with request-driven variants under a shared evaluation protocol.
Our contributions are threefold:

A paradigm shift from request-driven assistance to event-driven proactive assistance. We cast proactive assistance in our setting as an event-driven process in which robot actions are initiated by workspace state transitions caused by human–object interactions, rather than user-provided requests or task specifications.

An embodied framework for event-driven assistive reasoning and execution. We implement this formulation with runtime event detection, compact pre/post context selection, pretrained VLM reasoning, and an ID-grounded action interface with local verification.

A multi-task evaluation of effectiveness and adaptability. We validate our framework on multiple real-world collaborative tasks, demonstrating effectiveness across different task settings and performance comparable to variants provided with user instructions.

2. An embodied framework for event-driven assistive reasoning and execution. We implement this formulation with runtime event detection, compact pre/post context selection, pretrained VLM reasoning, and an ID-grounded action interface with local verification.

2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Request-Driven Assistance

Many collaborative robot systems remain request-driven: even as foundation models improve the perception of human behavior and contextual reasoning, robot actions are still typically initiated from explicit or inferred user requests.

Systems based on explicit requests initiate robot actions from user-provided commands or task specifications.
Language-to-plan pipelines condition action generation on the given instruction and ground candidate steps for execution [ 5 ] , while other systems translate instructions into executable code or task structures combine visual perception [ 12 , 13 ] with reusable robot skills [ 14 , 7 , 15 ] .
Interactive feedback and execution-time refinement can further adapt robot behavior when uncertainty or failures arise [ 8 , 15 ] .

Recent embodied foundation models substantially expand instruction-conditioned manipulation through multimodal reasoning and grounded execution [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] .
Recent VLA systems further extend instruction modalities and generalist manipulation capabilities [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] .
Despite differences in architecture and execution interface, these systems still typically initiate high-level reasoning from an instruction or stated goal.

Other systems operate from a user request, control cue, or task framing that indicates an intended goal without fully specifying the robot action.
The robot must therefore combine this information with observed context to infer appropriate assistance.
Prior work resolves ambiguous language using physical context, preceding human actions, or situational reasoning [ 22 , 23 ] , while recent work using foundation models infers latent human goals or task structure from under-specified instructions to guide planning [ 24 , 25 , 6 ] .
Nonverbal or partial control signals can serve a similar role: gaze is combined with scene context to infer manipulation intent [ 9 ] , while shared-autonomy systems combine partial user control with environmental observations to infer or refine user goals [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] .
Related VLM work further demonstrates contextual inference of latent goals, human states, or manipulation intent from visual or multimodal observations [ 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 ] .
Complementary work captures individual differences in human judgments through annotator-specific modeling [ 33 ] and learning from incomplete annotations [ 34 ] .
Collaborative systems can likewise combine shared task framing with changing workspace observations to infer human intent and update robot actions [ 11 ] .
Across these settings, contextual observations complement an already supplied but incomplete request, cue, or task framing, rather than determining when assistance reasoning is initiated.

Despite increasingly capable intent inference, request-driven systems still depend on a user request, control cue, or task framing to initiate assistance.
This leaves the initiative primarily on the human side, even when the robot can infer substantial task context on its own.
To support proactive collaboration closer to human–human teamwork, robots should also be able to initiate assistance from the observed outcomes of human interaction without waiting for an additional request.
This motivates the event-driven assistance setting considered here.

## II-B Event-Driven Assistance

Prior work has taken steps toward proactive collaboration by using observed human activity and context to derive cues for assistance without relying on a user request [ 35 ] .
Such systems typically model semantic aspects of the ongoing interaction, including anticipated human–object interactions [ 36 ] , action completion [ 37 ] , human intent or latent goals [ 38 , 39 ] , or broader mental states [ 40 ] .
These estimates are then used to determine or adapt robot assistance.

Across these approaches, proactive assistance is mediated by semantic representations of human behavior, such as human–object interactions, action progress, intent, goals, or mental states.
Many methods use dedicated predictors or structured inference models to obtain these representations.
We explore a complementary route in which physical interaction outcomes provide a common event interface that a frozen pretrained VLM can interpret without additional task-specific training.
Related work has used pre/post observations to recognize manipulation outcomes or responded to workspace changes by adapting existing plans [ 41 , 42 ] .
In our setting, a completed human–object transition serves both as the event that initiates assistance and as the paired evidence from which the VLM infers the next assistive action.

2026-10-07.title: SC3BF: Shifted Collision Cone Control Barrier Function for Dynamic Obstacle Avoidance
2026-10-07.authors: Amin Kashiri , Yasin Yazıcıoğlu
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-07.comment: Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC)
2026-10-07.abstract: The collision cone used by velocity-space control barrier functions is conservative: it rejects every relative velocity aimed into an obstacle, however slow. We propose the shifted collision-cone CBF (SC3BF), which adds a state-dependent allowance to the cone condition, so the robot may approach the obstacle at a rate that grows with distance and with its own speed. SC3BF is enforced by an ordinary quadratic program, and its safe set is forward invariant under bounded inputs without a minimum forward speed or a clearance margin. We prove that a nonzero allowance preserving safety always exists, and derive one in closed form. Against three velocity-space baselines on a kinematic bicycle among up to 100 100 moving obstacles, SC3BF reaches the goal more often and modifies the nominal input less than half as much.
2026-10-07.introduction:
A vehicle navigating among moving obstacles must avoid collisions while progressing toward its goal, subject to kinematic constraints and input limits. A common approach combines a nominal controller with a safety filter that modifies its input as little as possible. Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) [ 1 ] represent the safe set as the region where a scalar function of the state is nonnegative, and constrain how fast that function can decrease. For dynamics that are affine in the input, this is a linear inequality on the input, which can be enforced with a small quadratic program (QP).

The QP is cheap to solve, but finding a suitable barrier function is difficult. For an acceleration-controlled vehicle, the distance derivative does not contain acceleration, so a distance-based barrier cannot impose braking. Braking-distance barriers [ 2 ] bring the acceleration into the inequality, but certify only the brake maneuver, and therefore reject states from which the vehicle could in fact pass safely using steering. High-order CBFs [ 3 ] instead differentiate the distance a second time, so that the acceleration appears, but certify a subset of the original safe set and introduce auxiliary class- 𝒦 \mathcal{K} functions that are difficult to tune.

A second line of work builds the barrier in the space of relative velocities, where the input appears after one differentiation of the barrier function. Following the classical velocity obstacle [ 4 ] , the Collision-Cone CBF (C3BF) [ 5 ] keeps the relative velocity outside the cone of velocities aimed into the obstacle. The result is a valid barrier for the unicycle and the bicycle dynamics, and [ 6 ] applies the velocity-obstacle principle with CBFs to unicycle-type vehicles that must keep a positive forward speed. The cone is conservative, however, since it rejects every velocity aimed into the obstacle, however slow. The Dynamic Parabolic CBF (DPCBF) [ 7 ] reduces that conservatism by replacing the cone with a parabolic region whose boundary depends on the relative velocity, so a slow approach is allowed where a fast one is not. However, as Sec. II sets out, the parabolic region rests on minimum-speed and clearance assumptions that their controller does not enforce, and neither construction covers the singularity of the barrier at contact.

The safe set need not be described by a single barrier function. Boolean compositions of several barriers are treated in [ 8 ] , combinatorial compositions in [ 9 ] , and the feasibility of compositions under input constraints in [ 10 ] . The velocity-obstacle-based CBF (VOCBF) [ 11 ] has this structure. It writes the outside of the cone as the union of the two half-spaces its edges define, and enforces a disjunction of the two edge-wise barrier inequalities, with binary variables selecting which holds. Its mixed-integer formulation scales poorly in the number of obstacles.

We introduce a velocity-space barrier for the kinematic bicycle, the shifted collision-cone CBF (SC3BF), which adds a state-dependent allowance to the cone condition, so the robot may approach the obstacle at a rate that grows with distance and with its own speed. The resulting filter needs neither a minimum forward speed nor a clearance margin. Our contributions are as follows:

We construct the barrier and the quadratic program that enforces it, and prove that the safe set is forward invariant under bounded inputs, including at contact.

We prove, for the kinematic bicycle, that for every choice of the bicycle’s and the obstacle’s parameters some nonzero allowance preserves safety, and derive one in closed form. We also introduce a certification procedure that yields substantially larger allowances for a given system.

We compare SC3BF to C3BF, DPCBF and VOCBF in simulation, among up to 100 100 moving obstacles. SC3BF reaches the goal more often at every obstacle count and modifies the nominal input less than half as much as any of them.

2026-10-07.title: Communication-Free Obstacle Localization from Aggregate Wrench Measurements in Leader--Follower Cooperative Transport
2026-10-07.authors: Amin Kashiri , Aditya Mohan , Yasin Yazıcıoğlu
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-07.comment: Submitted to the 2027 American Control Conference (ACC)
2026-10-07.abstract: We consider obstacle localization for a team of robots cooperatively transporting a rigid payload without explicit inter-robot communication. A leader robot directs the payload’s motion, while follower robots assist and react to locally detected obstacles. The leader measures the followers’ aggregate wrench, i.e., the combined force and torque they exert on the payload, but cannot directly distinguish their individual reactions. We design a follower control law that allows the leader to recover obstacle locations from these measurements. Each follower resists motion toward nearby obstacles, resulting in a piecewise-linear relationship between the payload’s translational and angular velocity and the aggregate wrench. Changes between adjacent linear regions reveal an obstacle’s bearing and distance and identify the responding follower. We give sufficient conditions for exact recovery at a fixed payload configuration and develop an adaptive probing procedure in which the leader applies translational and rotational inputs to the payload to obtain the required measurements. We demonstrate the performance of the proposed method in simulations.
2026-10-07.introduction:
When a team of robots carries a shared payload without communicating, the payload is their only coordination channel. In leader–follower schemes, a leader that knows the destination steers the payload while each follower reinforces the motion measured at its own grip, so the team transports a rigid body with no communication at all [ 1 , 2 ] ; the principle has been implemented on robots [ 3 ] and extended to flexible payloads [ 4 ] . Where communication or a shared model is available, transport is instead posed as decentralized optimization [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] or adaptive control over a broadcast common state [ 9 ] . In these works, obstacle information is either absent or supplied directly to the robot that plans around it.

A follower, however, may sense an obstacle that the leader cannot, and without communication it can convey this only through how it pushes on the payload. Such interaction has been used for inference: followers infer the motion intended by a leader that knows the obstacles [ 10 ] , a leader recovers obstacles from the input of the single follower in a two-robot team [ 11 ] , and inverse safety filtering infers constraints from the safety-filtered actions of other agents [ 12 ] . Each attributes the observed response to one robot. With several followers, the leader instead senses one aggregate wrench, three numbers regardless of team size, in which all reactions are summed, so no single measurement reveals which follower responded or to what.

In this paper, we show that the leader can separate these reactions by actively probing the payload. We design a follower law under which each follower resists only motion carrying it toward a nearby obstacle. The map from payload twist to aggregate wrench then becomes piecewise linear, and the change between adjacent linear regions encodes one obstacle’s bearing and distance together with the follower that detected it. Recovering piecewise-linear maps from queries is well studied for hybrid systems [ 13 ] and ReLU networks [ 14 ] ; here, the structure is designed into the team so that every region boundary has a physical meaning. Our contributions are: (i) a communication-free follower law that makes individual obstacle reactions separable in the aggregate wrench; (ii) sufficient conditions under which measurements at a fixed payload configuration uniquely determine every detected obstacle and its responding follower; and (iii) an adaptive probing procedure that selects the leader’s test motions to obtain these measurements, evaluated in simulation.

# II Problem Formulation

## II-A Setup

We consider N N robots transporting a rigid payload in the plane. Each robot maintains a rigid grip on the payload and can apply
both force and torque. Robot 1 1 is the leader and alone
knows the destination, while robots 2 , … , N 2,\dots,N are the followers . The followers
do not know their world positions or the destination, and they do not observe
other robots’ states or inputs. The robots do not explicitly communicate with each other.

We express vectors in a world frame for the analysis,
while each follower evaluates the control laws in its own grip frame, fixed to
the payload. Let 𝒓 i \bm{r}_{i} denote robot i i ’s grip offset from the payload’s
center of mass, expressed in the world frame, and let 𝒑 i ∈ ℝ 2 \bm{p}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} denote the
grip’s world position. Following the balanced-grip assumption in [ 15 ] ,
we assume ∑ i = 2 N 𝒓 i = 𝟎 \sum_{i=2}^{N}\bm{r}_{i}=\bm{0} .
This arrangement ensures that equal forces at the follower grips produce no

2026-10-07.title: Humanoid Horizon: Extending Task Horizon in Whole-Body Loco-Manipulation via Parallel Training, Dynamic Starting, and Reward Gating
2026-10-07.authors: Haozhuo Zhang , Qiang Zhang , Jian Tang , Mingzhe Ni , Michele Caprio , Angelo Cangelosi , Wei Pan
2026-10-07.comment: Videos and results are available at this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract: Cluttered indoor environments, where large and heavy objects are scattered across diverse surfaces, require humanoid robots to sequentially navigate, grasp, transport, and accurately place each item at its target location within a single uninterrupted episode. This long-horizon, whole-body loco-manipulation task remains a significant challenge for current methods. Previous approaches often suffer from two main issues: easy-reward bias, where training overemphasizes early transport stages at the expense of later ones, and catastrophic forgetting, where focusing on later stages leads to a decline in earlier-stage performance. In this work, we introduce Humanoid Horizon, a unified policy framework designed to overcome these limitations through three interrelated mechanisms. The Parallel Training Strategy organizes N N scenes into S S concurrent stage streams governed by a shared policy, ensuring all transport stages receive continuous gradient updates and removing the bottleneck of sequential optimization. The Dynamic Starting Mechanism updates each environment’s initial state with terminal states from upstream rollouts, gradually broadening transition coverage and enhancing robustness at stage boundaries. Reward Gating sets the reward to zero for the rest of the episode in later-stage streams when the immediately preceding object is displaced beyond a set threshold, so the shared policy learns not to disturb a just-placed object and earlier placements are preserved throughout the episode. Collectively, these strategies achieve per-stage success rates exceeding 80% on the two-object LHM-Humanoid benchmark (350 training scenes, 66 held-out scenes). As the number of sequentially transported objects grows beyond two, success declines with the horizon, but the degradation is graceful relative to the sharp drop seen in all baselines. Additionally, we demonstrate that the RL teacher policy can be distilled into a Vision-Language-Action student via DAgger. When provided only with egocentric RGB or depth observations and natural language instructions, the student successfully replicates the teacher’s long-horizon, multi-object behaviors, highlighting the potential for perception-driven deployment on real humanoid robots. Videos and results are available at https://haozhuo-zhang.github.io/Humanoid-Horizon-project-page/ .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Humanoid agents that imitate human motion, perceive cluttered scenes, and manipulate objects are a central yet difficult research target. Prior work has advanced locomotion and control Peng et al. (2021) ; Tessler et al. (2023) ; Luo et al. (2023) ; Zhu et al. (2023) , scene interaction Starke et al. (2019) ; Hassan et al. (2023) ; Xiao et al. (2023) ; Pan et al. (2024) , and manipulation Xu et al. (2024) ; Wang et al. (2023b) ; Xie et al. (2023) ; Lin et al. (2025) . A key gap remains: long-horizon whole-body loco-manipulation, i.e., continuously transporting multiple large objects over long task chains without environment resets.

This gap is fundamental. Compared with arms or quadrupeds, humanoids are less dynamically stable and must coordinate balance, locomotion, and manipulation throughout long episodes. As a result, long-horizon pipelines developed for more stable platforms are hard to transfer directly. Despite progress in interface and perception conditioning Xu et al. (2024) ; Ding et al. (2025) , most current methods still focus on short-horizon single-object skills Wang et al. (2024) ; Xu et al. (2025) ; Pan et al. (2025) , often relying on fixed starts, and thus struggle with continuous multi-object loco-manipulation. When these methods are extended to longer task chains, two failure modes become prominent: easy-reward bias (over-optimizing early-stage transport while under-exploring later-stage behaviors) and catastrophic forgetting. In our context, catastrophic forgetting specifically means that a policy already capable of single-object transport is further trained from post-first-object terminal states to transport the next object, yet after this shift it loses the ability to re-execute first-object transport-and-release, even under substantial robot-initial-state randomization. LHM-Humanoid Zhang et al. (2026) provides a concrete instance of this behavior (e.g., teacher model 2), which then motivates dual-teacher distillation into a student and, in turn, constrains scalability to longer multi-object horizons.

We present Humanoid Horizon, a framework for long-horizon whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation that uses one policy to perform continuous long-horizon loco-manipulation across multiple objects, without resets, auxiliary models, or handcrafted task-specific modules; it has three coupled components: Parallel Training Strategy, which jointly optimizes all transport stages in one policy to avoid easy-reward bias in sequential curricula and forgetting risks in decoupled stage-wise training (including distillation-heavy pipelines such as LHM-Humanoid) Zhang et al. (2026) , enabling scalable learning as object count grows; Dynamic Starting Mechanism, which writes each stage terminal state to the corresponding downstream environment buffer and initializes the next stage from that buffer in the next epoch, so coverage of transition states expands through temporal accumulation across epochs; and Reward Gating, which zeros the remaining reward in a later stage once the immediately preceding object is displaced beyond a tolerance, so the policy learns not to disturb a just-placed object and earlier placements are preserved over the episode.

We evaluate on the LHM-Humanoid benchmark Zhang et al. (2026) : 350 training/evaluation scenes and 66 unseen scenes for generalization, and we follow LHM-Humanoid to test longer-horizon settings with more than two sequentially transported objects. Combining these mechanisms yields per-stage success above 80% in two-object sequential transport. As more objects are carried in one episode, success declines with the horizon, but the degradation is graceful relative to the sharp drop seen in prior baselines, and a single policy still completes multi-object rearrangement across diverse scenes. As an exploratory deployment study, we distill the teacher policy into a vision-language-action (VLA) student using DAgger Ross et al. (2011) , and with egocentric RGB or depth inputs plus language instructions, the student preserves long-horizon multi-object behaviors learned by the teacher.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We present Humanoid Horizon , a single-policy framework for long-horizon whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation that supports continuous multi-object rearrangement without resets, auxiliary models, or handcrafted task modules.

We introduce a Parallel Training Strategy that jointly optimizes all transport stages, reducing easy-reward bias and catastrophic forgetting, and improving scalability to longer task horizons.

We propose a Dynamic Starting Mechanism and Reward Gating that together improve inter-stage transition robustness and preserve previously completed placements throughout long-horizon execution.

We demonstrate strong long-horizon performance on 350 benchmark scenes plus 66 unseen scenes, and show that DAgger-based VLA distillation transfers the learned behavior to egocentric RGB/depth inputs.

1. We present Humanoid Horizon , a single-policy framework for long-horizon whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation that supports continuous multi-object rearrangement without resets, auxiliary models, or handcrafted task modules.

2. We introduce a Parallel Training Strategy that jointly optimizes all transport stages, reducing easy-reward bias and catastrophic forgetting, and improving scalability to longer task horizons.

3. We propose a Dynamic Starting Mechanism and Reward Gating that together improve inter-stage transition robustness and preserve previously completed placements throughout long-horizon execution.

4. We demonstrate strong long-horizon performance on 350 benchmark scenes plus 66 unseen scenes, and show that DAgger-based VLA distillation transfers the learned behavior to egocentric RGB/depth inputs.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 RELATED WORK

## 2.1 Physically-Based Motion Synthesis and Human-Scene Interaction

Motion synthesis spans computer graphics, vision, and robotics, and is commonly divided into kinematics-based methods Jiang et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2023) and physics-based methods Tessler et al. (2023) ; Zhu et al. (2023) ; Peng et al. (2021) ; Peng et al. (2018) . Kinematic approaches emphasize semantic coherence, while physics-based approaches learn dynamically feasible control policies in simulation. Foundational systems such as AMP Peng et al. (2021) and DeepMimic Peng et al. (2018) have enabled later extensions with adversarial priors, latent skill representations, and language conditioning. In human-scene interaction, InterScene Pan et al. (2024) and InterPhys Hassan et al. (2023) move beyond earlier inverse-kinematics or hand-designed controllers toward dynamic object interaction, and RL-based methods show strong manipulation skills Xu et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2024) . In parallel, embodied AI studies integrated navigation and manipulation Yenamandra et al. (2023) ; Weihs et al. (2021) , including commonsense-guided policies Wu et al. (2023) . However, most systems still use simplified embodiments (e.g., mobile bases with parallel grippers) and remain short-horizon and single-object. HumanVLA Xu et al. (2024) advances humanoid manipulation of heavier objects but remains limited to single-object tasks with fixed initial states. LHM-Humanoid Zhang et al. (2026) is an important step toward continuous multi-object vision-language loco-manipulation, yet its sequential training and task-specific designs limit scalability: as horizons grow, catastrophic forgetting and easy-reward bias become pronounced. Our method addresses these issues with a unified policy using Parallel Training Strategy, Dynamic Starting Mechanism, and Reward Gating, enabling robust, scalable long-horizon multi-object loco-manipulation without environment resets.

## 2.2 Long-Horizon Loco-Manipulation

Long-horizon execution has been studied in fixed-base arms Wang et al. (2023a) ; Lin et al. (2024) ; Zhao et al. (2024) , mobile manipulation Jiao et al. (2021) ; Zhi et al. (2025b) ; Zhi et al. (2025a) , and aerial manipulation, but remains difficult because long action chains accumulate physical constraints Bu et al. (2025) ; Fan et al. (2025) ; Feng et al. (2025) ; Zhang et al. (2024) . Typical strategies decompose tasks via subgoals Shridhar et al. (2023) ; Borja-Diaz et al. (2022) , world-state prediction Feng et al. (2025) , trajectory prediction Fan et al. (2025) , or historical observations Wang et al. (2025) , yet often depend on task-specific priors and generalize poorly. Progress is more limited in humanoids: most teleoperation systems remain short-horizon and open-loop He et al. (2024) ; Cheng et al. (2024) ; Ji et al. (2024) because reliable real-time bipedal state estimation is hard, and although legged odometry has advanced Wisth et al. (2022) ; Ou et al. (2024) ; Allshire et al. (2025) , transfer to humanoids is still limited (CLONE Li et al. (2025) only partially mitigates drift with LiDAR odometry). Autonomous long-horizon whole-body humanoid loco-manipulation is therefore still nascent, with representative attempts including LessMimic Lin et al. (2026) and LHM-Humanoid Zhang et al. (2026) . As horizons grow, these methods still face the same two bottlenecks discussed above: catastrophic forgetting and easy-reward bias. Motivated by this gap, Humanoid Horizon targets horizon scalability by maintaining stage-wise competence while preserving previously completed placements as task length increases. Learning those stage transitions also depends on where each stage begins. Reverse-curriculum learning Florensa et al. (2017) grows the set of start states backward from the goal, and so needs the agent to be reset into hand-specified near-goal configurations. Reset-free autonomous RL Eysenbach et al. (2017) avoids manual resets by training a separate reset or backward policy, with its own reward. Curricula taken from expert demonstrations Dai et al. (2021) start the agent from demonstrated states. Dynamic Starting (Sec. 3.3 ) is aimed at the handoff between stages instead: the next stage begins from the terminal state the preceding stage has just produced, with no reset policy, demonstration source, or extra reward.

2026-10-07.title: Sensor-Layout-Agnostic Navigation via Geometric Observation Canonicalization
2026-10-07.authors: Welf Rehberg , Kostas Alexis
2026-10-07.abstract: Existing visual navigation policies are inherently bound to fixed camera configurations, creating a fundamental barrier to zero-shot deployment across heterogeneous robot sensor layouts. To overcome this limitation, we present an embodiment-informed navigation policy capable of generalizing across diverse depth sensor configurations on a specific aerial platform. Instead of implicitly learning spatial alignments, our approach explicitly unprojects depth measurements from arbitrary depth sensor payloads, varying in sensor count, mounting extrinsics, and intrinsics, into a shared robot-centric frame, stitching them into a unified spherical range image and a binary validity mask. This mask allows the downstream policy to explicitly distinguish covered space from unobserved blind spots. Trained via reinforcement learning with aggressive camera randomization, our policy generalizes zero-shot to unseen layouts featuring up to seven cameras, scaling success rates from 78 % 78\mathrm{\%} to 95 % 95\mathrm{\%} as total spatial sensing coverage increases. Finally, real-world flight trials on a physical quadrotor, conducted in an obstacle-filled corridor and an outdoor forest, validate the policy’s zero-shot transfer across camera configurations and its resilience to sudden online sensor dropouts.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Deploying diverse autonomous robots across unstructured environments often requires custom tuning or re-training policies whenever sensor hardware changes. Consequently, zero-shot generalist policies are essential to eliminate per-platform engineering and enable seamless deployment across diverse, evolving robot fleets. To navigate reliably, a generalist policy must ingest raw sensor information observations and map them directly to control commands across highly diverse embodiments. A major barrier to this generalization is that navigation policies are historically bound to specific camera configurations and vehicle frames [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . This tight coupling means even minor adjustments to the sensor payload, such as varying mounting heights, altering pitch angles, or integrating auxiliary cameras, render the policy unusable, traditionally demanding expensive network retraining.

Recent research has progressed significantly on generalizing policies to robots with different dynamic responses [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] and kinematic chains [ 7 , 8 ] . However, existing visual generalists either suffer from high computational latency or rely on simplified geometric assumptions, thereby preventing lightweight, real-time 3D navigation across heterogeneous camera layouts.
In this work, we address the problem of reactive local collision avoidance for a broad family of multi-sensor depth camera setups on a fixed dynamical system. Rather than forcing the neural network to implicitly associate visual coordinates with motion primitives, we inject a strong geometric prior into the network’s perception pipeline. We unproject exteroceptive depth measurements from a variable number of arbitrary sensors and map them into a shared, unified egocentric spherical coordinate system, yielding a range image and an associated binary validity mask expressed in the robot’s base coordinate frame. Canonicalization projects all sensor measurements into a common coordinate system, removing the need for the policy to implicitly learn sensor-to-body frame alignments. An overview of the method is shown in Fig. 1 .
Through extensive simulated evaluations and real-world quadrotor deployments, we demonstrate that our embodiment-informed policy achieves robust, zero-shot transfer across highly heterogeneous exteroceptive configurations and environments and is robust to sensor dropouts on systems with redundant sensor configurations. Specifically, the contributions of this paper are four-fold:

We introduce an exteroceptive canonicalization pipeline that maps arbitrary depth feeds to a unified, egocentric spherical range tensor and a binary validity mask, enabling generalization to sensor count, mounting extrinsics, and sensor intrinsics.

We present a reactive navigation policy trained via reinforcement learning under aggressive sensor extrinsics and intrinsics randomization, eliminating the need to implicitly learn sensor-body-coordinate alignments.

We demonstrate zero-shot generalization in simulation to ood ( ood ) layouts featuring up to seven cameras, achieving navigation performance comparable to specialized, layout-specific policies.

We validate our approach on a physical quadrotor across different sensor configurations navigating cluttered indoor corridors and dense forests, demonstrating robust real-world zero-shot transfer and resilience to sudden online sensor dropouts.

1. We introduce an exteroceptive canonicalization pipeline that maps arbitrary depth feeds to a unified, egocentric spherical range tensor and a binary validity mask, enabling generalization to sensor count, mounting extrinsics, and sensor intrinsics.

2. We present a reactive navigation policy trained via reinforcement learning under aggressive sensor extrinsics and intrinsics randomization, eliminating the need to implicitly learn sensor-body-coordinate alignments.

3. We demonstrate zero-shot generalization in simulation to ood ( ood ) layouts featuring up to seven cameras, achieving navigation performance comparable to specialized, layout-specific policies.

4. We validate our approach on a physical quadrotor across different sensor configurations navigating cluttered indoor corridors and dense forests, demonstrating robust real-world zero-shot transfer and resilience to sudden online sensor dropouts.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Within the domain of cross-embodiment control, existing research predominantly focuses on adapting low-level motor or joint commands to variations in physical dynamics, such as mass, inertia, and joint kinematics [ 5 , 4 , 7 , 6 , 8 ] . However, this body of work leaves the challenge of exteroceptive perception geometry largely unaddressed, assuming static or platform-specific sensor arrangements.
Recently, extending generalization capabilities to visual navigation has gained significant momentum. Frameworks such as GNM [ 9 ] , ViNT [ 10 ] , and X-Nav [ 11 ] enable generalized navigation across diverse physical embodiments, spanning mobile robots, quadrupeds, and aerial vehicles. Despite their success, these architectures operate under a restrictive assumption: they assume a fixed nominal sensor payload per platform, most commonly a single forward-facing camera. While these models implicitly absorb minor camera height or pitch variations that are present across large training datasets, they lack explicit mechanisms to handle multi-camera setups, arbitrary 3 3 D mounting extrinsics, or variable sensor counts.
While X-Nav [ 11 ] targets hardware-agnosticism by deterministically projecting depth images into a 1 1 D laser scan format, their training pipeline and evaluation are restricted to a single nominal camera configuration with a 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} fov ( fov ). Consequently, the policy is never exposed during training to vastly different camera poses, different camera intrinsics, multi-camera setups, or unobserved spatial gaps. Furthermore, reducing depth observations to a 1 1 D horizontal representation fundamentally restricts the system to a 2 2 D plane, precluding its application to 3 3 D aerial flight where elevation-aware obstacle avoidance is essential.

Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) navigators [ 12 , 13 ] incorporate multi-view visual feeds by scaling up high-capacity visual transformers to associate RGB tokens with high-level semantic subgoals. However, these models target low-frequency planning rather than local collision avoidance and suffer from high computational latency ( [ 13 ] requiring off-board GPU infrastructure), making them incapable of the high-frequency control loops needed for real-time onboard flight in cluttered environments. Additionally, the work in [ 12 ] severely limits the number of sensors (max 2 2 ) and assumes that one sensor faces strictly forward, while [ 13 ] accommodates up to 8 8 cameras but randomizes only mounting height and horizontal fov continuously, selecting the underlying sensor layout from 6 6 predefined discrete configurations.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce a single generalist policy for real-time, onboard 3 3 D reactive collision avoidance across heterogeneous sensor layouts. Rather than relying on heavy transformer backbones or predefined sensor configurations, our lightweight model runs onboard embedded hardware, operating zero-shot across arbitrary sensor counts, extrinsics, and intrinsics. By unprojecting arbitrary depth feeds into an egocentric spherical range tensor paired with a binary validity mask, we decouple policy execution from viewpoint alignment. Trained across wide continuous variations in camera counts, 3 3 D mounting extrinsics and sensor intrinsics, our policy architecture learns to reason over visibility and obstacle proximity, achieving robust zero-shot ood transfer and online fault tolerance on physical hardware.

2026-10-07.title: Mitigating Concept Drift in QoS Prediction for Teleoperation of Autonomous Vehicles Using Historic Data
2026-10-07.authors: Xiyan Su , Jianning Gao , Mahmoud Ashri , Frank Diermeyer
2026-10-07.comment: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics (SMC)
2026-10-07.abstract: Teleoperation serves as the fallback solution to autonomous driving but reliable functions of the teleoperation require a certain amount of mobile network resources, which cannot be guaranteed at all times. Therefore, predictive quality of service (pQoS) is introduced as a concept to increase the resilience of the teleoperation. In this paper, based on a data measurement campaign, we propose a prediction framework to prediction two important network KPIs of teleoperation: uplink data-rate and round-trip latency. Furthermore, we introduce a method to alleviate the performance degradation of machine-learning-based prediction models on previously unseen data due to concept drift by incorporating historic data into the prediction pipeline. Additionally, we introduce the metric of critical scenario detection to evaluate the prediction performance specifically for teleoperation.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Teleoperation serves as the fallback solution in the level-4 ad ( ad ) defined by SAE [ 1 ] . In teleoperation, the vehicle sends sensor data to the operator and the operator sends control commands to the vehicle over mobile network. The mobile network is proven to be sufficient for teleoperation in general [ 2 ] . However, reliable functions require a certain amount of network resources, which the mobile network is not able to provide at all times currently. For example, 5gaa ( 5gaa ) defines in its technical report that it requires 32 Mbps ul ( ul ) data-rate and 99% reliability for a safe teleoperation scenario [ 3 ] . However, the current measured commercial mobile network cannot provide such resources at all times.

In the latest version of [ 4 ] , some efforts have gone into reducing the data-rate usage of teleoperation, such as using the state-of-the-art video codec to reduce the data-rate of the video streams while maintaining the same video quality, and using multiple links to increase the available bandwidth. However, these efforts still cannot guarantee a safe operation through the network at all times. It is worth noticing that, in most critical scenarios, the vehicle can still be teleoperated with degraded quality, e.g., with lower video quality due to limited ul data-rate, or with velocity restrictions due to high speed latency [ 5 ] .

In this context, the concept of pqos ( pqos ) is put forward by 5gaa [ 6 ] . pqos allows ad vehicles to predict the upcoming network quality and adapt to it proactively. This particularly increases the resilience of the teleoperation against the fluctuating mobile network quality.

As described in [ 6 ] , pqos can be deployed either at the mno ( mno ), or be provided as an ott ( ott ) solution by a third party. The 3rd Generation Partnership Project also introduced the Network Data Analytics Function that defines the data exchange between different parties to enable the functionality of pqos [ 7 ] . However, the functionality of pqos is still not supported ubiquitously by the mno . Therefore, we focus on the ott deployment in this paper, i.e., the pqos is provided as a service on the vehicle by a third-party service provider, e.g., vehicle manufacturer.

Predicting the qos ( qos ) of mobile network per se is a complex problem, as it is affected by different aspects of the network, e.g., ran ( ran ), core network, and routing. Some works have gone into analyzing the qos data. The results in [ 8 ] show the temporal and spatial variance of the lte ( lte ) dl ( dl ) data-rate as well as the influence of signal quality and main transport protocol on it. In [ 9 ] , it discusses the cause of the asymmetry of modern lte technology in detail and shows that the dl channel indicators, such as rsrp ( rsrp ), sinr ( sinr ), and rsrq ( rsrq ) are suitable indicators for ul performance. Therefore, the similar phy ( phy ) kpi are considered for the prediction in this paper.

Some works try to tackle this problem as a spatial-agnostic problem, usually with classic ml ( ml ) or dnn ( dnn ) algorithms. In [ 10 ] , the authors train a lstm ( lstm ) model to predict throughput. To compensate for the lack of position information, low-level mobile network parameters and abstracted location information, e.g., surrounding building size and street type, are used. In [ 11 ] , an architecture using bi-directional lstm is proposed to predict dl data-rate for multiple prediction horizons. In [ 12 ] , the authors investigate the performance as well as the interpretability and explainability of ml models systematically and conclude that they can capture the underlying principles of the qos without being explicitly programmed, which defends the usage of ml and dnn models for pqos . Furthermore, they show that gradient-boosted decision tree models can even outperform dnn . More importantly, the authors discuss the problem of data splitting and data distribution in depth and reveal the fundamental problem of ml usage in pqos : the models only try to generalize the data distribution based on the training data. This implies that the prediction performance of such trained models can degrade when deployed without explicit retraining in another area due to the difference in data distribution. The phenomenon is often referred to as concept drift . To deal with it, the ml and dnn models need to be retrained with new data, which can be time and resource-consuming. The results in [ 13 ] confirm the same problem, but disagree upon the generalization capability of the ml methods.

The ml and dnn models excel in capturing the temporal and inter-feature dependency of the data, while downplaying the static spatial features. The spatial dependency is often depicted as a rem ( rem ) [ 14 , 13 ] . Other works, such as [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] also use the name connectivity map . The rem stores the historic data about the mobile network, including phy kpi , such as rsrp , rsrq , sinr , as well as application layer kpi , such as throughput, data-rate, round-trip latency, etc. In [ 18 ] , the authors use the historic data recorded by another vehicle, which was previously driven by the adjacent location, to predict the qos for the current vehicle, proving the feasibility of pqos using historic data.

In this paper, we intend to incorporate the two different methods. To achieve that, we first launch a data measurement campaign to generate a dataset. Then, we propose a framework that predicts two important kpi of the mobile network for teleoperation: the ul data-rate and the round-trip latency. We introduce a method that incorporates the historic data in the form of a rem into the prediction framework by training the ml model to learn the difference between the target value and the reference values from the historic data, which alleviates the prediction performance degradation due to concept drift without explicit retraining.

This paper is structured as follows: Chapter II describes the data measurement campaign and the static analysis of the data. Chapter III introduces the prediction framework. Chapter IV shows the performance of the proposed framework and method based on our dataset. Chapter V concludes the paper and discusses future research directions.

## II-A Measurement Setup

To investigate the qos of mobile network for teleoperation, we first launch a data measurement campaign to collect data for network condition of teleoperation in real-world, which is made publicly available online [ 19 , 20 ] . We use the research vehicle EDGAR for the data measurement campaign [ 21 ] .

For data measurement, we designed two routes that consist of different odd for teleoperation, as shown in Fig 1 . For the training data, we have also taken the temporal factor into consideration. The data are measured at different times on a day and on different days in a week, with a focus on Thursday morning and Sunday afternoon, representing weekdays and weekends. The ml model is only trained with data from the first route. The second route represents data outside the area where the training data are collected. The ml model is not trained with any data from the second route at all.

The data measurement includes two types of kpi of the mobile network of teleoperation, i.e., the phy kpi and the application layer kpi . The phy kpi are recorded using the Milesight UR75 Industrial 5G Router on board. The application layer kpi are recorded between the teleoperated vehicle and the remote operator PC located on campus. The round-trip latency is measured using ping by sending an icmp packet. During the latency measurement, a set of constant video streams with 4500 Kbps is sent from the teleoperated vehicle to the remote operator PC to simulate realistic teleoperation. The ul data-rate is measured using iperf3 by sending UDP packets from the teleoperated vehicle to the remote operator PC [ 22 ] . The latency and ul data-rate are measured in different runs, since the ul data-rate measurement will use practically all ul bandwidth and therefore render the latency unrealistically high.

The measured data are synchronized into data frames between different data sources using the timestamps. The data recorded on the first route are also split by runs for the model performance evaluation. The data recorded on the second route are split as historic data to generate a rem .

2026-10-07.title: HexaGripper: A Single-Actuator, Winch-Deployed Gripper for Autonomous Aerial Parcel Collection
2026-10-07.authors: Nimantha Adikaram , Mahen Abeyratne , Lakmina Chandrajith , A. H. T. E. De Silva , Isira Naotunna , Asanka Perera
2026-10-07.abstract: Autonomous aerial parcel collection remains constrained by package-transfer operations that require manual loading, landing, or dedicated ground infrastructure. This letter presents HexaGripper, a single-actuator, winch-deployed six-plate gripper for autonomous collection of cuboid parcels. The proposed mechanism provides synchronized grasping with a wide capture region and tolerance to positional misalignment during pickup. The system integrates vision-based alignment, range sensing, winch deployment, and state-based control to enable autonomous collection while maintaining UAV separation from the pickup surface. Experimental evaluation covered static grasping, capture-workspace assessment, and end-to-end outdoor aerial collection. Static experiments achieved 100% pickup success (15/15 trials) across three parcel geometries, while workspace experiments achieved successful pickup at all 28 tested positions up to a 150 mm radial offset. End-to-end outdoor aerial collection achieved an 80% success rate (4/5 trials). These results demonstrate the feasibility of mechanically synchronized, winch-deployed grasping for landing-free autonomous aerial parcel collection.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Parcel-delivery networks increasingly require rapid transportation in dense urban areas, remote communities, and locations with limited road access. Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) can reduce dependence on ground infrastructure; however, parcel pickup and transfer often still require human intervention or dedicated infrastructure [ 1 ] . Existing delivery
approaches primarily rely on packages attached before takeoff [ 2 ] , landing-based
transfer [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] , tethered lowering [ 6 ] , or dedicated docking infrastructure [ 2 , 4 , 6 ] . Collecting or dispatching a package
requires a suitable surface and brings the aircraft close to obstacles and it
makes the UAV more vulnerable to collisions, whereas hover and tethered delivery maintains separation from
the parcel but generally does not address autonomous collection and dispatching.
A self-loading and unloading UAV must therefore establish and verify a secure mechanical
connection with a parcel despite positioning error.

Aerial manipulation has been investigated using several mechanism classes.
Multi-finger robotic hands [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] provide broad object compatibility but introduce additional actuators, sensing, and contact-control requirements. Passive bio-inspired grippers [ 10 ] can reduce active control and achieve rapid mechanically triggered closure, while foldable aerial manipulators [ 11 ] provide compact stowage and extended reach at the cost of additional articulated degrees of freedom and endpoint positioning requirements. Compliant and tentacle-based grippers [ 12 , 5 ] can accommodate irregular object geometries, although pneumatic or multi-arm implementations introduce additional hardware and packaging
requirements. In [ 13 ] , rapid aerial pickup was demonstrated using a specialized capture mechanism, and linkage-based aerial grippers [ 3 ] have demonstrated the use of mechanical synchronization and sensing to simplify aerial grasping. For tethered manipulation, in [ 6 ] , the locomotion of the end-effector is used to correct the positioning error after the deployment. Overall, these approaches involve tradeoffs among object adaptability, actuation complexity, positioning tolerance, and payload capacity. However, autonomous parcel collection and dispatch introduces several additional requirements. The gripper must tolerate UAV positioning errors, vibration, securely enclose parcels, and maintain low actuation complexity. Tethered deployment enables parcel collection and dispatch while maintaining separation
between the UAV and the pickup surface. These requirements motivated the authors to design mechanically mechanically synchronized gripping elements with a wide capture region. Given the UAV’s 6.5 kg payload capacity, a maximum mass of 1.5 kg was allocated to the tethered-winch subsystem. The mechanism was also required to fit within the landing-gear envelope when stowed and retain the parcel without continuous winch actuation.

This letter presents HexaGripper (Fig. 1 ), a
winch-deployed mechanism for autonomous collection of approximately cuboid
parcels. A single rotary cam synchronizes six gripping plates, while a
pin-in-slot mechanism as shown in Fig. 2 (e)-(f), couples radial translation with 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} rotation
to provide a wide capture aperture and progressive grasp. A
worm-geared winch provides vertical deployment and recovery while resisting
back driving under load. ArUco-based visual alignment, range sensing, and
state-based control coordinate the alignment-deploy-grasp-recover sequence,
while the mechanically enlarged capture region facilitates tolerating position error positioning error without independent actuation of the six plates.

The main contributions of this work are:

Single-actuator radial grasping mechanism: A six-plate mechanism coupling synchronized radial translation with 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} plate rotation to provide a wide capture aperture and
progressive parcel grasp.

Winch-deployed autonomous collection: Integration of the gripper with a worm-geared winch, vision and range
sensing, and state-based control for autonomous
alignment-deploy-grasp-recover operation.

Mechanical and experimental validation: Characterization of the proposed mechanism through analytical modeling,
Finite-Element Analysis (FEA), and experimental evaluation of static grasping,
capture workspace, winch performance, and end-to-end outdoor aerial
parcel collection.

The remainder of this letter is organized as follows.
Section II presents the mechanical design of the
HexaGripper, followed by the perception and autonomous collection framework
in Section III . Section IV evaluates the
proposed system through structural analysis and experimental testing.
The resulting findings are discussed in Section V , while
Section VI presents the limitations and directions for
future work. Finally, Section VII concludes the letter.
