# II Mechanical Design

## II-A Design Architecture and Operating Principle

The HexaGripper comprises six identical plate assemblies arranged
symmetrically around a central rotary cam, as shown in
Fig. 2 . The six extenders are
mechanically synchronized by a single rotary actuator, thereby avoiding
independent actuation of the gripping surfaces. Each extender undergoes 30 mm of radial travel. During the initial 15 mm,
the plates translate radially while approximately maintaining their
orientation. Over the remaining 15 mm, a pin-in-slot mechanism converts the
radial displacement into plate rotation, producing approximately 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} rotation at maximum extension. The fully open configuration
therefore forms a wide, approximately planar capture region, whereas
reversing the cam motion rotates and translates the plates inward to enclose
the parcel. This coupled radial-angular motion reduces the tendency of a
vertically oriented plate to displace an off-center parcel and increases
tolerance to lateral positioning error during pickup. Each gripping plate is 150 mm high and incorporates a 20 mm lead-in region
inclined at 33 ∘ 33^{\circ} . This geometry guides a slightly misaligned parcel
toward the enclosure during collection while avoiding a sharp 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} contact edge. Curved plates were selected such that the six surfaces
approximate a cylindrical profile when closed, providing a compact external
geometry during flight. The aerodynamic benefit of this geometry was not
quantified in the present study.

## II-B Mechanism Evolution and Selection

The grasping mechanism was decomposed into three functional requirements:
opening/closing actuation, vertical deployment, and secure parcel retention.
A morphological analysis was then used to systematically generate candidate
configurations from alternative solutions to these functions. Seven grasping
concepts were considered: bird-leg cable actuation [ 14 ] ,
independently actuated fingers [ 7 ] , a circular-cam
extender [ 15 ] , converging struts [ 3 ] , a
funnel-and-pin interface [ 16 ] , a linkage
collector [ 17 ] , and a geared three-finger
mechanism [ 9 ] . Each concept was combined with direct and
winch-based deployment [ 6 , 18 ] , resulting in 14 candidate
configurations. The configurations were evaluated using the six weighted criteria in
Table I . The weighted score was calculated as S j = ∑ i = 1 6 w i ​ s i ​ j S_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{6}w_{i}s_{ij} , where w i w_{i} is the criterion weight and s i ​ j s_{ij} is the corresponding score from 1 (poor) to 5 (excellent). The circular-cam mechanism with winch deployment achieved the highest weighted score of 4.05/5 and was selected for further development. The selected mechanism was subsequently refined to improve the capture of
laterally misaligned parcels. The design incorporates 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} plate rotation
(Fig. 2 (f)), allowing the plates to approach a
near-horizontal orientation when open and progressively enclose the parcel
during closure. The coupled radial and rotational motion provides a wide
capture region for accommodating lateral parcel-positioning errors.

## II-C Archimedean-Spiral Cam Design

The six radial extenders are synchronously driven by slots incorporated into
a central rotary cam. An Archimedean-spiral profile [ 19 ] , defined by r ⁡ ( θ ) = a + b ​ θ r(\theta)=a+b\theta , was selected to provide constant radial displacement
per unit cam rotation, where r ⁡ ( θ ) r(\theta) is the follower radius, θ \theta is
the cam rotation angle measured from the initial position, a a is the initial
follower radius, and b b is the radial growth per radian. For a required

and β = 150 ∘ = 2.618 \beta=150^{\circ}=2.618 rad, b = 11.46 b=11.46 mm/rad. For an ideal radial follower, the instantaneous pressure angle is α ⁡ ( θ ) = tan − 1 ⁡ [ b / r ⁡ ( θ ) ] \alpha(\theta)=\tan^{-1}[b/r(\theta)] and is therefore maximum at the minimum cam radius. With a = 26 a=26 mm, the maximum pressure angle is α max = tan − 1 ⁡ ( 11.46 / 26 ) ≈ 23.8 ∘ \alpha_{\max}=\tan^{-1}(11.46/26)\approx 23.8^{\circ} , which remains below the adopted 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} design limit and decreases as the follower moves outward. For parametric CAD implementation, the spiral centerline was defined as x ⁡ ( θ ) = ( a + b ​ θ ) ​ cos ⁡ ( θ + θ 0 ) x(\theta)=(a+b\theta)\cos(\theta+\theta_{0}) and y ⁡ ( θ ) = ( a + b ​ θ ) ​ sin ⁡ ( θ + θ 0 ) y(\theta)=(a+b\theta)\sin(\theta+\theta_{0}) , where θ 0 \theta_{0} is the
angular offset used to align the six equally spaced slots with their
followers. The resulting
cam converts a single rotary input into equal 30 mm radial displacements of
all six plate assemblies.

## II-D Coupled Translational-Rotational Plate Mechanism

Each plate connector was designed to convert the final 15 mm of extender
displacement into angular plate motion, thereby enlarging the capture
aperture without increasing the radial travel of the cam. As shown in
Fig. 2 (d), the connector acts simultaneously as a hinge and a
motion-conversion link. The initial slot geometry consists of a straight
segment followed by a curved section, such that the plate initially
translates radially and subsequently rotates during the final stage of
extension. For a 15 mm arc length producing a nominal 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} rotation, the
corresponding slot radius is R slot = s / θ = 15 / ( π / 2 ) = 9.55 R_{\mathrm{slot}}=s/\theta=15/(\pi/2)=9.55 mm. In the implemented mechanism, the follower pin is
offset from the plate hinge, and the plate rotation therefore depends on
their relative motion. This relationship is approximated by R l sin θ p = R slot sin ϕ s R_{l}\sin\theta_{p}=R_{\mathrm{slot}}\sin\phi_{s} , where R l R_{l} is the distance
between the plate hinge and follower pin, θ p \theta_{p} is the plate rotation,
and ϕ s \phi_{s} is the angular displacement of the pin along the curved slot. The offset geometry amplifies the angular response of the plate, producing
approximately twice the plate rotation relative to the angular displacement
traversed along the slot. Consequently, the required 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} plate
rotation is achieved within the available 15 mm radial displacement while
maintaining a compact connector geometry. As illustrated in
Fig. 2 (c) to Fig. 2 (a), this motion transforms the plate from its
closed orientation to the fully open configuration without requiring an
additional actuator.

## II-E Actuator and Torsion-Spring Design

The actuator was sized for simultaneous loading of the six cam followers.
The required cam torque [ 20 ] was approximated as T c = N ​ F ​ r ​ tan ⁡ ( α + ϕ ) T_{c}=NFr\tan(\alpha+\phi) , where N = 6 N=6 is the number of simultaneously
loaded cam followers, F F is the radial force per
follower, r r is the instantaneous cam radius, α \alpha is the pressure
angle, and ϕ = tan − 1 ⁡ μ \phi=\tan^{-1}\mu is the friction angle. Using an assumed realistic friction coefficient of μ = 0.45 \mu=0.45 during operation, the corresponding
friction angle is ϕ = tan − 1 ⁡ ( μ ) ≈ 24.2 ∘ \phi=\tan^{-1}(\mu)\approx 24.2^{\circ} . This relation was
used for actuator sizing because friction, spring preload, and assembly
effects are difficult to model accurately. An LX-5560MG-class servo with a rated torque of
6.37 N ⋅ \cdot m at 7.4 V was selected. Each plate uses a
torsion spring to resist opening under the parcel load. For a 1 kg design
parcel, assuming equal load distribution among the six plates, the load
supported by each plate is approximately 0.167 kg. Including the 0.050 kg
moving plate assembly, the resulting moment was estimated as M g = ( 0.167 + 0.050 ) ​ ( 9.81 ) ​ ( 0.065 ) = 0.138 M_{g}=(0.167+0.050)(9.81)(0.065)=0.138 N ⋅ \cdot m. Applying a safety factor
of 1.5 gives a required spring torque of 0.207 N ⋅ \cdot m. With a 10 ∘ 10^{\circ} preload and 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} plate rotation, the required
torsional spring stiffness was calculated as k s = k_{s}= 0.119 0.119 N ⋅ \cdot m/rad. This value was used as the spring-design target.

## II-F Winch Deployment Mechanism

The HexaGripper is vertically deployed using a winch to maintain separation
between the UAV and the pickup surface while allowing limited passive
realignment of the suspended gripper. A JGY-370 worm-geared motor was
selected because the transmission resists backdriving and can maintain the
suspended load without continuous motor torque. For a suspended mass m tot = 1.2 m_{\mathrm{tot}}=1.2 kg, effective spool radius R eff = 15 R_{\mathrm{eff}}=15 mm, and drivetrain efficiency η = 0.65 \eta=0.65 , the
required output torque was estimated as T w = m tot ​ g ​ R eff / η = 0.271 T_{w}=m_{\mathrm{tot}}gR_{\mathrm{eff}}/\eta=0.271 N ⋅ \cdot m.
A 100 rpm motor was selected to balance output torque and deployment
speed. The winch uses an 8 mm carbon-steel shaft, 8 × 22 × 7 8\times 22\times 7 mm bearings, and an 8 × 8 8\times 8 mm shaft coupler,
and demonstrated a suspended-load capacity of 1.2 kg.

## II-G Prototype Fabrication and Integration

The fabrication and assembly process of the HexaGripper is shown in
Fig. 4 . The gripping plates, holders, radial extenders,
connectors, bearing holders, and winch spool were 3-D printed in PLA+ with
40% infill, while the gripper base and winch plates were laser-cut from
acrylic. Steel torsion springs, shafts, fasteners, heat-set inserts, and
bearings were used at load-bearing and rotating interfaces. Since the
printed components exhibit orientation-dependent properties, the homogeneous
material approximation used in Sec. IV-A is
considered when interpreting the structural results. The integrated gripper
and winch (Fig. 2 (d)) weigh 0.80 kg and 0.52 kg,
respectively, giving a combined mechanical mass of 1.32 kg and leaving
approximately 0.18 kg of the 1.5 kg subsystem allocation for wiring and
interface hardware.

2026-10-07.title: UWB Meets Crazyflow: Simulating Degraded Feedback at Scale for Aerial Robotics
2026-10-07.authors: Martin Schuck , Marcel P. Rath , Yufei Hua , Abhishek Goudar , SiQi Zhou , Angela P. Schoellig
2026-10-07.comment: Accepted to 1st Workshop on Robot Meets GNSS and Ranging for Seamless Autonomy @ ICRA 2026
2026-10-07.abstract: In this work, we introduce Crazyflow , an accurate, differentiable simulator built on JAX. By leveraging just-in-time compilation via XLA, Crazyflow unifies physics and control into a single differentiable computation graph, enabling massive parallelization on accelerated hardware without sacrificing modeling accuracy. This architecture achieves order-of-magnitude speedups over existing baselines, capable of training deployable reinforcement learning agents in seconds. To highlight its highly modular design, we demonstrate how easily Crazyflow can be extended by integrating a complete, high-fidelity Ultra-Wideband (UWB) and Inertial Measurement Unit (IMU) simulation pipeline coupled with a full-state Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). This capability allows for massive parallel controller evaluation under realistic, degraded state feedback with minimal impact on GPU throughput. By combining speed, accuracy, and extensibility, Crazyflow serves as a foundational tool for the next generation of aerial robotics research.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Owing to their high agility, mechanical simplicity, and cost-effective design, quadrotors have emerged as a canonical platform across a broad spectrum of robotics applications, from infrastructure inspection and safety-critical tasks [ 1 , 2 ] to recreational domains such as racing and shows [ 3 , 4 ] . Advancing capabilities in either pushing individual robots toward their physical limits or scaling up multi-agent systems necessitates high-performance, efficient simulation tools that enable rapid algorithmic iteration and task optimization.

Widely used simulators such as RotorS [ 5 ] , CrazyS [ 6 ] , and swarm-oriented frameworks like Crazyswarm [ 7 ] and CrazySim [ 8 ] are built on top of modular frameworks and provide accurate models suitable for controller development. However, evaluating controllers under imperfect, noisy state feedback—such as realistic UWB or vision pipelines—across thousands of parallel rollouts remains a significant scaling bottleneck, as these tools are generally not designed for massively parallel GPU execution.

To address the computational demands of large-scale learning, frameworks like PRL4AirSim [ 9 ] , gym-pybullet-drones [ 10 ] , and Aerial Gym [ 11 ] leverage distributed or tensorized physics to achieve high throughput. While highly scalable, they typically do not expose analytical gradients of the underlying dynamics, which are required by a range of advanced learning- and optimization-oriented methods. Emerging differentiable frameworks attempt to bridge this gap [ 12 , 13 ] , but often compromise on model fidelity or lack demonstrated sim-to-real capabilities outside of simplified settings.

In this work, we introduce Crazyflow (Fig. 1 ), a high-fidelity, highly extensible, differentiable simulator built on JAX. Crazyflow unifies physics, modular sensor pipelines, and controllers into a single computation graph. To demonstrate this robust capability, we seamlessly integrate a UWB and IMU sensing pipeline with an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF). This allows for realistic controller evaluation under imperfect state estimation at massive scale without sacrificing the core tenets of the simulator: high-speed, direct sim-to-real transfer, and full differentiability.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II The Crazyflow Design

## II-A Core Dynamics and Sim-to-Real

Modeled natively after the Crazyflie quadrotor family, Crazyflow provides two highly accurate dynamics models: a detailed first-principles model [ 14 , 15 ] capturing non-linear motor dynamics, and an abstracted attitude dynamics model designed for standard mid-level control interfaces. Beyond direct compatibility with Crazyflies, Crazyflow incorporates a streamlined system identification pipeline. This allows users to effortlessly adapt the simulation framework to extract and match the physical parameters of entirely new drone platforms, guaranteeing reliable sim-to-real transfer regardless of the hardware.

## II-B Extensibility: Sensing and Estimation

Because Crazyflow is built on a foundation of stateless, pure functions, the architecture permits extensive customization. To highlight this modularity, we integrated a complete sensing and state-estimation pipeline directly into the simulator step execution ahead of the controller.

The sensor models feature an IMU and a UWB network. The IMU simulates body-frame specific force and angular velocity, corrupted by additive white noise and slowly varying bias random walks [ 16 ] .
The UWB model simulates one tag on the drone interacting with eight fixed anchors located at x , y ∈ { − 2.5 , 2.5 } ​ m x,y\in\{-2.5,2.5\}\,$\mathrm{m}$ and z ∈ { 0 , 3 } ​ m z\in\{0,3\}\,$\mathrm{m}$ .
It outputs the true Euclidean distance corrupted by Gaussian noise with a fixed standard deviation σ \sigma and a mean μ i \mu_{i} . Assuming line-of-sight (LoS) conditions throughout the flight, this mean is uniformly sampled at initialization per anchor i i and held constant per episode to reflect realistic hardware offsets [ 17 ] .

These measurements are fused via a full-state EKF that tracks 19 states: position, quaternion attitude, linear velocity, angular velocity, and the respective accelerometer and gyroscope biases. The prediction step propagates the mean through a nonlinear IMU-driven dynamics model and propagates covariance using first-order linearization via Jacobians. The correction step uses the UWB range measurement model and its linearization with respect to position. This allows users to seamlessly switch the controller input source between perfect ground-truth state and realistic estimated feedback.

2026-10-07.title: VOMMI: Collecting and Leveraging Portable Demonstrations for Mobile Manipulation
2026-10-07.authors: Yutian Zhang , Xingrui Xiong , Siyuan Ma , Yang Li , Jiawen Wen , Jiaqi Zhai , Liwen Yang , Ce Hao , Haozhen Chi , Yangkun Zhu , Yifan Zhu , Xiaowen Chu , Dong Wei , Qiaojun Yu , Dibo Hou
2026-10-07.abstract:
Portable mobile-manipulation demonstrations can help alleviate data scarcity for embodied intelligence, but obtaining reliable, low-cost, and robot-free motion supervision from RGB observations remains challenging.
Existing approaches often rely on teleoperation or specialized devices equipped with additional sensing hardware, while directly using estimated visual odometry (VO) trajectories can introduce inconsistencies due to accumulated drift and imperfect motion supervision.
We present the Visual-Odometry-Conditioned Mobile Manipulation Interface (VOMMI), a portable demonstration collection and learning framework that connects portable RGB demonstrations to vision-language-action (VLA) post-training through offline trajectory reconstruction and online visual-motion conditioning.
VOMMI synchronizes body and hand views to capture navigation context and local object interactions without requiring human–robot kinematic correspondence calibration.
R2-VO refines offline demonstration trajectories using sparse geometric anchors and produces causal local-motion tokens over multiple prediction horizons for online policy conditioning.
An action-group residual adapter incorporates these tokens only into the base branch.
Experiments use a 500-trajectory portable for each task, with 75 trajectories held out for RGB-VO evaluation, and 200 robot demonstrations as references.
Our policy, post-trained only on portable demonstrations, achieves 18.2% lower base-velocity error than a policy trained with robot-collected demonstrations, while maintaining comparable end-effector translation accuracy.
Offline reconstruction reduces absolute trajectory errors for the body and hand streams by 24.6% on average relative to the best evaluated baseline for each stream.
The complete system improves the mean success rate by 8.3 percentage points over OpenPI 0.5 across three real-robot tasks.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Mobile manipulation is a foundational capability for embodied intelligence, enabling robots to interact with the physical world in applications ranging from domestic assistance and infrastructure inspection to industrial automation.
Mobile manipulation data collection typically involves long-horizon tasks, composed of multiple sequential stages,
requiring a generalizable policy that can coordinate precise whole-body motion with fine-grained end-effector (EE) manipulation.
Recent whole-body vision-language-action models (VLAs) [ 1 , 2 ] and world action models (WAMs) [ 3 , 4 ] advocate learning mobile manipulation as an integrated whole-body behavior rather than as separate navigation and arm-manipulation skills, but scaling such learning remains challenging due to the limited availability of demonstration data.
Existing demonstration-collection paradigms often rely on teleoperation, which is expensive, slow, and difficult to scale for scene generalization.
Cross-embodiment collection methods, such as UMI [ 5 ] and its variants [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] , use handheld grippers with mounted cameras to collect manipulation demonstrations,
while egocentric approaches use head-mounted cameras to capture broader scene context [ 10 ] .
For mobile manipulation tasks, existing methods have shown that portable demonstration collection is feasible [ 11 , 9 , 8 ] .

However, these approaches commonly depend on special devices, such as high-quality IMU sensors, GoPro cameras, iPhones, and VR headsets,
which raise the hardware barrier for more accessible data collection and limit the number of demonstrators who can participate.
Using visual odometry (VO) can reduce the complexity of the data-collection hardware, but it remains vulnerable to drift over long trajectories and large rotations, which can degrade data quality or even make the data unusable.
Existing portable collection pipelines typically require accurate device calibration to recover reliable trajectories, placing strict demands on data post-processing, especially for mobile manipulation tasks.

As shown in Figure 1 , we propose a VO-conditioned mobile-manipulation interface (VOMMI) to establish the data pipeline for
training whole-body VLA policies from portable demonstrations.
VOMMI records RGB videos from body and hand views and uses VO to recover local motion cues, enabling low-cost demonstration collection.
Collection-time pose references are used only for offline metric supervision and evaluation, while deployment relies solely on RGB observations, camera intrinsics, timestamps, and robot proprioception.
To improve trajectory quality during offline data processing, VOMMI can leverage pretrained visual geometry for base movement.
These tokens are fed into the VLA post-training interface and connected only to the base-action residual adapter, while the manipulation
residual remains blind to body motion. This design provides the missing local visual proprioception for navigation-conditioned mobile manipulation without
claiming global localization or a new general-purpose VO algorithm. VOMMI is designed to test whether portable RGB demonstrations can improve long-horizon
mobile-manipulation competence in a VLA policy, while making the answer auditable by separating portable-data supervision from robot-data supervision.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a portable data-collection protocol for mobile manipulation with separate body and hand
views, requiring no access to the target robot or human–robot kinematic correspondence calibration.

We present R2-VO, a real-time and refined RGB motion reconstruction module that produces low-latency
local motion tokens for online VLA inference and anchor-refined trajectories for offline dataset processing.

# II Related Work

## II-A Portable Demonstration Interfaces

Portable data collection is fast, cheap, and easy to deploy for mobile manipulators in diverse environments.
UMI [ 5 ] records in-the-wild manipulation with a portable
handheld interface and transfers relative EE actions to a robot.
To enhance mobility, UMI-on-Legs combines this interface with a manipulation-centric whole-body controller [ 11 ] , while
Mobile UMI [ 9 ] introduces multiple views and decoupled planar-base and EE representations for mobile manipulation. HoMMI [ 8 ] and EgoHumanoid [ 10 ] further use egocentric human demonstrations to capture whole-body task context.
These systems demonstrate the value of extending portable whole-body data from fixed-base to mobile manipulation tasks, but they require customized, dedicated hardware.
In contrast, VOMMI addresses a complementary sensing question: how to recover the demonstrator’s motion from RGB observations without requiring metric pose or IMU measurements as policy inputs.

## II-B Robot Learning for Mobile Manipulation

Mobile manipulation requires coordinated locomotion and manipulation over extended workspaces.
HomeRobot integrates perception, navigation, and manipulation in realistic environments [ 12 ] .
Recent whole-body learning methods address complementary control challenges, from force-aware compensation for contact-rich loco-manipulation to latent policies for unified loco-manipulation [ 1 , 13 ] .
In addition, bimanual manipulation learning uses egocentric demonstrations to learn active perception behaviors [ 14 ] .
DECOWAM [ 15 ] trains adapters by separating base and arm latents and conditioning on base velocity to improve both future-video and action prediction.
Despite these advances, existing portable-demonstration-based mobile manipulation policies often lack an explicit representation of recent ego-motion when learning from portable RGB demonstrations.
VOMMI addresses this gap by incorporating visual-odometry (VO) observations directly into the VLA and introducing separate residual pathways for body and manipulation actions.
This design enables motion-aware whole-body correction without requiring metric pose or IMU measurements as policy inputs at deployment.

## II-C Visual Body Motion for Policy State

Learning-based VO systems such as DROID-SLAM and DPVO improve sequential motion estimation, while VGGT and VGGT-SLAM 2.0 extend feed-forward geometry
toward camera and real-time scene reconstruction [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] .
Beyond geometric reconstruction, recent robot learning studies also explore
recovering actionable trajectories from human or egocentric demonstrations,
such as observation-only imitation and scalable egocentric data collection [ 20 , 21 ] . However, these approaches either
optimize geometric consistency or focus on embodiment alignment, rather than
extracting policy-oriented motion for mobile manipulation.

VOMMI considers visual motion from a policy-oriented perspective.
This causal local representation reduces sensitivity to constant world-frame offsets while
preserving short-term ego-motion cues relevant for whole-body control. The
resulting token provides a compact visual proprioceptive state for policy
conditioning rather than a globally consistent trajectory or localization
memory.

2026-10-07.title: Compact Robot Policies Need Fine-Grained Visual Representations
2026-10-07.authors: Nanhe Chen , Runqiu Yang , Jiawei Tang , Sichao Liu , Yuquan Wang
2026-10-07.abstract:
Multi-task manipulation policies differ in architecture, scale, and pretrained priors all at once, so published comparisons cannot attribute performance to any single component. We argue that most of it comes from the visual representation, and that parameter scale and generative priors are largely incidental .
To test this, we build CoRP (Compressed Representation Policy), a deliberately compact policy ( 48.9M parameters, no vision-language model and no video-generative prior ) that factorizes into a representation extractor and a flow-matching action generator.
It reaches 97.0% on LIBERO and 75.78%/73.36% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Randomized , matching systems 40.9–163.6× larger.
Holding the action generator fixed, we then vary one extractor property at a time. Pretrained initialization is decisive : a random ViT-S/14 drops to 78.1% and an ImageNet ResNet-34 to 74.5% on LIBERO. Pretraining alone is not enough, as freezing the encoder costs 19.8 points. Compression matters as much : resampling each view to 48 tokens beats passing all patch tokens ( 97.0% vs 83.2% ), and a variational information bottleneck over those tokens is worse than a hard token budget, cutting LIBERO-Goal from 95.8% to 33.0% by suppressing the instruction-dependent token selection the policy relies on. Language conditioning contributes only where the observation leaves the goal ambiguous (LIBERO-Goal: 9.2% to 95.8%), while on RoboTwin 2.0, where observations are unambiguous, removing it slightly improves success.
Therefore, we argue that a compact policy works when its representation is pretrained, task-adapted, and compressed. Project page: https://corp-policy.github.io/
2026-10-07.introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have become the dominant paradigm for multi-task robotic manipulation, mapping images and language instructions directly to robot actions ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025b ) .
These systems typically couple a pretrained vision–language model (VLM) with a generative action head, carrying billions of parameters to generalize across tasks ( Kim et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025b ) .
More recently, world-action models (WAMs) go further, adding video-generative priors that jointly predict future observations and robot actions ( Ye and others, 2026 ) . Because these systems differ in architecture, scale, pretraining, data, and training recipes, we cannot attribute their success to any single component.

We factor a manipulation policy into representation extraction and conditional action generation:

We instantiate the factorization as the Co mpressed R epresentation P olicy ( CoRP ), a deliberately compact and modular policy.
CoRP has only 48.9M parameters and four standard components: a DINOv2-initialized ViT-S/14 visual encoder ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) , a T5-Efficient-Tiny language encoder with a lightweight adapter ( Raffel et al., 2020 ; Tay et al., 2022 ) , a learned-query cross-attention resampler that compresses each camera view into 48 tokens, and a single-block DiT action generator trained with flow matching. With few interacting parts, each intervention changes exactly one factor, so we can directly attribute its effect. Despite having neither a VLM nor a video-generative prior, CoRP reaches 97.0% average success on LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , matching VLA and WAM systems 40–160× larger, and 75.8%/73.4% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean/Randomized ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , surpassing π 0 \pi_{0} , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and X-VLA while remaining below video-pretrained WAMs (Tables 1 and 2 ). This result is our starting point, not our contribution: our controlled interventions locate its source.

Our interventions identify the representation extractor as the main source of this performance and show what makes it fine-grained enough for control: the representation must be pretrained, task-adapted, and compressed . Our study is restricted to closed-set benchmarks; we do not evaluate the open-world semantic and physical generalization that VLAs and WAMs target ( Black et al., 2025a ; Ye and others, 2026 ) .

We summarize our contributions as follows:

Compressed Representation Policy (CoRP) , a 48.9M-parameter policy without any VLM or video-generative prior that is competitive with systems up to 163× larger on LIBERO and RoboTwin 2.0, and serves as a controlled testbed for isolating the role of representation.

A controlled ablation study shows that effective compact policies require visual representations that are pretrained, task-adapted, and compressed, and that language helps only when the goal is visually ambiguous.

Real-robot validation on three bimanual tasks (closed-loop adaptation to object displacement, coordinated two-arm placement, and precision plug insertion), providing qualitative evidence that CoRP, pretrained on our large-scale real-world corpus, transfers to physical hardware.

2. A controlled ablation study shows that effective compact policies require visual representations that are pretrained, task-adapted, and compressed, and that language helps only when the goal is visually ambiguous.

3. Real-robot validation on three bimanual tasks (closed-loop adaptation to object displacement, coordinated two-arm placement, and precision plug insertion), providing qualitative evidence that CoRP, pretrained on our large-scale real-world corpus, transfers to physical hardware.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Generative and Pretrained Policies. Diffusion Policy ( Chi et al., 2023 ) and ACT ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) established generative action heads as strong baselines for visuomotor control, but each model trains on a single task.
Octo ( Ghosh et al., 2024 ) scaled such policies across tasks and embodiments by pretraining on large multi-robot datasets, but learns its visual tokenizer from robot data rather than initializing it from a large-scale pretrained vision model, a choice our encoder ablation examines directly (Section 4.3 ). VLAs instead build the policy on a pretrained vision–language model to inherit its richer visual and semantic representations ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ) . World-action models add video-generative priors to target temporal and physical generalization, either alongside a vision–language understanding module ( Bi et al., 2026 ) or in place of it ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Across both lines, however, the visual pathway changes alongside the language model, the generative prior, and the parameter count, so no single factor can be credited with the gains. In contrast, we hold a small flow-matching action generator fixed and vary only the representation extractor, testing how far a compact policy can go without either prior.

Visual Representation Learning. Supervised pretraining on large labeled datasets established convolutional ( He et al., 2016 ) and patch-based Transformer ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2021 ) backbones as sources of transferable visual features, and our ImageNet ResNet-34 ablation follows this recipe.
Self-supervised methods remove the need for labels: the DINO series ( Caron et al., 2021 ; Oquab et al., 2024 ; Siméoni et al., 2026 ) yields the fine-grained patch features our resampler consumes. Recent work pushes further toward dense geometric structure, for example through masked boundary modeling ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . Another line pretrains representations specifically for manipulation from human video, masked image modeling, or sensorimotor prediction ( Nair et al., 2023 ; Radosavovic et al., 2023 ; Majumdar et al., 2023 ) , and finds that the benefit of pretrained features varies substantially across tasks and evaluation settings ( Burns et al., 2025 ; Hansen et al., 2023 ) . However, these studies mostly evaluate frozen features with single-task or lightweight policy heads, leaving open how initialization, fine-tuning, and token compression jointly shape a multi-task, language-conditioned generative policy. We address this gap by comparing a DINOv2-initialized ViT-S/14 against random and ImageNet-supervised alternatives, frozen and fine-tuned, under an identical action generator (Sections 4.3 and 4.4 ).

2026-10-07.title: Nested Power Models for Multirotor Propulsion: From Aerodynamic Drag to Electrical Losses
2026-10-07.authors: Antonio Franchi , Aaron Saini , Ahmed Ali , Chiara Gabellieri
2026-10-07.abstract: Speed-only aerodynamic power models for multirotor propulsion cannot represent acceleration-dependent effects. This work develops a nested sequence of propulsion-power models that starts from aerodynamic power dissipation and progressively introduces a reversible kinetic-energy rate, torque-dependent electromechanical dissipation, and lumped speed-proportional dissipation. The models are identified using one subset of experiments and validated using the other on a motor-drive–propeller unit. Independent estimates of rotational inertia and aerodynamic drag complement predictive validation by assessing whether the models correctly attribute the measured power to reversible kinetic-energy exchange and irreversible dissipation and, within the latter, to aerodynamic and electromechanical losses. The results show that the reversible kinetic-energy rate is necessary but insufficient for accurate dynamic power prediction. Dissipation proportional to the squared motor torque provides the main additional improvement, while speed-proportional dissipation further prevents irreversible losses from being attributed to reversible kinetic-energy exchange. The resulting methodology provides a reusable and experimentally verifiable basis for developing and selecting dynamic propulsion-power models for multirotor systems.
2026-10-07.introduction:
The limited onboard energy of multirotor aerial vehicles makes propulsion-power modeling important for endurance estimation, vehicle and propulsion-system design, mission planning, trajectory generation, and control allocation. Flight-level models relate power consumption to vehicle velocity, thrust, climb rate, and flight direction to estimate consumption, range, endurance, and optimal flight speed [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Experimental and data-driven approaches have similarly identified the power or energy consumption associated with complete flight trajectories [ 4 ] , while design-oriented methods support propulsion-system selection, sizing, and efficiency optimization [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Together, these approaches demonstrate that compact and physically grounded power models can influence both vehicle design and the way aerial tasks are planned and executed. However, their primary objective is generally to predict total power, energy consumption, or propulsion performance.

At a finer level, propulsion models represent the battery, electronic speed controller, electric motor, and propeller as interconnected electrical, mechanical, and aerodynamic subsystems [ 8 , 9 ] . Such descriptions can predict thrust, rotor speed, current, or total electrical power and support component selection, diagnosis, simulation, and model-based control. They do not generally assess how the predicted power is attributed among reversible kinetic-energy exchange, aerodynamic dissipation, and electromechanical dissipation.

Dynamic power prediction is especially relevant when rotor speeds vary rapidly. Trajectory shape and acceleration can have a substantial effect on quadrotor energy consumption [ 10 ] , while multirotor control and experimental platforms increasingly support precise and agile motion [ 11 , 12 ] . In these conditions, the power required to accelerate the motor–propeller assembly is not described by a steady-state speed-only relation. Rotor acceleration changes the rotational kinetic energy, but it also changes motor torque and current and may therefore affect irreversible electromechanical dissipation.

Furthermore, rapid rotor-speed modulation is not limited to fast translational flight. It also arises in aerial physical interaction, where the vehicle may remain nearly stationary with respect to the surrounding air while producing rapidly varying forces and torques against the environment. Aerial manipulators and multidirectional-thrust platforms have been developed for contact inspection, manipulation, and other interaction tasks [ 13 , 14 ] . Fully actuated and redundantly actuated multirotors can regulate interaction wrenches and vehicle attitude with limited or no translational motion, but doing so relies directly on coordinated and potentially rapid variations of individual rotor speeds [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . Related systems employ reconfigurable propulsion or contact mechanisms to improve interaction accuracy [ 18 ] , while recent omnidirectional aerial-interaction experiments further demonstrate the relevance of rotor-level actuation models during contact-rich operation [ 19 ] . More generally, the growing range of multirotor physical-interaction tasks makes actuator dynamics, limits, and energetic behavior increasingly important [ 20 ] .

Despite these developments, accurate total-power prediction does not establish correct attribution among the underlying physical contributions. During accelerated rotor motion, reversible kinetic-energy exchange, aerodynamic dissipation, and torque-dependent electromechanical losses may have correlated effects over a finite operating domain. A model may therefore reproduce the measured electrical power while assigning irreversible loss to the reversible kinetic-energy rate or compensating an inaccurate aerodynamic contribution through an electromechanical-loss term. Such confounding becomes problematic when the model must determine not only the energy required by a trajectory, but also how much is temporarily stored, how much is irreversibly lost, and which propulsion component should be improved.

This work addresses this gap by developing and experimentally assessing propulsion-power models with progressively richer energetic decompositions. The models are identified on one group of complete dynamic experiments and evaluated on separate experiments excluded from identification. Held-out predictive validation is complemented by independent estimates of rotational inertia and aerodynamic drag to assess whether the measured power is attributed consistently among reversible kinetic-energy exchange, aerodynamic dissipation, and electromechanical dissipation.

The main contribution of this work is a physically motivated sequence of multirotor propulsion-power models that starts from aerodynamic power dissipation and progressively introduces the reversible kinetic-energy rate, torque-dependent electromechanical dissipation, and lumped speed-proportional dissipation. Experiments show that the kinetic-energy rate is necessary but insufficient during accelerated rotor motion, that torque-dependent dissipation provides the principal additional predictive improvement, and that speed-proportional dissipation further improves power attribution and the joint recovery of inertia and aerodynamic drag.

This contribution is supported by:

a dynamic identification methodology based on realizable speed–acceleration trajectories and validation on complete experiments conducted at nominal acceleration rates excluded from identification; and

a validation framework combining held-out predictive accuracy with independent inertia and aerodynamic-drag estimates to assess the attribution of measured power among reversible kinetic-energy exchange, aerodynamic dissipation, and electromechanical dissipation.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows.
Section II reviews power and energy models across aerial-vehicle configurations and modeling scales, and positions the contribution of this work. Section III develops the nested propulsion-power models. Section IV defines the criteria and methodology used to identify and assess them, while Section V presents the experimental realization and independent aeromechanical estimates. Section VI evaluates predictive accuracy and power attribution along the model sequence, and Section VII discusses the scope, implications, and conclusions.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Rotor aerodynamics and speed-only power models

The cubic dependence of rotor power on angular speed originates from standard rotor and propeller aerodynamics. For fixed geometry and operating conditions, thrust and resisting torque are commonly approximated as quadratic functions of rotor speed, so mechanical power scales cubically. Low-Reynolds-number propeller measurements and blade-element–momentum models show, however, that thrust and power coefficients depend on propeller geometry, inflow, Reynolds number, and scale effects [ 21 , 22 ] . Multirotor models consequently range from constant-coefficient quadratic thrust and drag-torque laws used in dynamics and control [ 23 ] to rotor-power-coefficient models embedded in flight simulation [ 24 ] .

When the aerodynamic coefficients are treated as constant, these actuator laws induce the speed-only cubic power model. This representation has supported aerodynamic-power control at the propulsion-unit level [ 25 ] , system-level power-consumption models [ 1 ] , and efficiency analysis of morphing multirotors [ 26 ] . Such models compactly represent aerodynamic dissipation, but speed alone cannot express the reversible kinetic-energy exchange and the additional losses associated with rotor acceleration that are central to the present work.

## II-B Electric propulsion-chain modeling and design

A second line of work models the propulsion chain by interconnecting the power source, electronic speed controller, motor, shaft, and propeller. Analytical design methods combine propeller theory, motor constants, current and speed limits, battery capacity, and vehicle requirements to select components and estimate performance [ 27 , 28 ] . Broader sizing correlations extend this reasoning across electric and fuel-powered UAV categories [ 29 ] , while multicopter-specific optimization selects motor, propeller, and battery combinations for efficiency [ 5 ] . Experimental characterization and sizing studies further address large or heavy-lift multirotors whose propulsion components operate far from the small-quadrotor regime [ 6 ] .

Component-resolved dynamic models have been developed for both fixed-wing and multirotor propulsion. Fixed-wing formulations separately represent the electrical source, controller, motor, and propeller to predict thrust, rotor speed, and current [ 8 ] ; related dynamic models describe the coupled electric motor and propeller over transient operation [ 9 ] . More recent physics-informed approaches combine dimensional analysis, propeller data, test-rig measurements, and torque-based current prediction to improve cross-configuration endurance estimation [ 30 ] . These approaches increase propulsion-model fidelity, whereas the present study asks which compact acceleration-dependent terms are identifiable from source-side power and whether the resulting decomposition is physically consistent.

## II-C Battery, range, endurance, and vehicle-level power

Battery-aware aircraft models connect propulsion demand to stored electrical energy, voltage variation, discharge rate, and degradation. Classical electric-aircraft analyses derive range and endurance while accounting for battery-discharge behavior [ 31 ] ; subsequent work examines how battery degradation changes optimal endurance and range over the aircraft life cycle [ 32 ] . For multirotors, practical endurance estimators combine hover and forward-flight requirements with battery and payload information [ 33 ] , while integrated aerodynamic, motor, and gray-box battery models estimate range, endurance, and optimal speed across multicopter designs [ 2 ] . Alternative architectures seek endurance gains through hybrid power systems [ 7 ] or solar augmentation at MAV scale [ 34 ] .

At vehicle level, empirical models fit power or energy directly from flight measurements and operating conditions. Examples include comprehensive battery-based energy models for UAV maneuvers [ 35 ] , quadrotor energy models identified from experimental voltage data [ 4 ] , and comparisons of drone and ground-vehicle delivery energy [ 36 ] . Analytical multirotor models instead express power as a function of thrust, forward velocity, climb rate, flight direction, and aerodynamic contributions [ 3 ] . Reviews of drone-energy factors and models show that the appropriate abstraction depends strongly on whether the objective is component design, flight-time estimation, mission planning, or energy management [ 37 ] . Across these approaches, accurate total-energy prediction does not by itself establish whether transient power is attributed correctly among stored energy and individual loss mechanisms.

## II-D Energy-aware trajectory, allocation, and mission planning

Power models become decision criteria when trajectories, actuator commands, or missions are optimized. Polynomial-trajectory studies show that kinematic choices can substantially change quadrotor energy consumption [ 10 ] . Integrated physical models can be embedded directly in trajectory optimization and feedback control, yielding experimentally verified reductions in consumed energy [ 38 ] . Coverage-planning methods use experimentally derived energy models together with sensing-resolution and return-safety constraints [ 39 ] , while multi-UAV planners jointly optimize coverage assignment and flight speed under battery constraints [ 40 ] . Recent logistics planners further combine multirotor dynamics, obstacle avoidance, mission duration, payload, and energy-efficiency objectives [ 41 ] .

Communication and deployment studies use rotary-wing propulsion models to optimize trajectory and service time jointly with communication energy [ 42 ] . Comparative mission simulators extend this perspective to both rotary-wing and fixed-wing vehicles [ 43 ] . Within redundant actuation, energy-optimal allocation selects among multiple actuator combinations that realize the same body wrench [ 17 ] . These applications make model attribution consequential: if a transient reversible term is treated as dissipation, or an irreversible loss is hidden in an inertial coefficient, the optimization may select a different trajectory, speed, or actuator evolution than a physically resolved model would.

## II-E Fixed-wing, flapping-wing, and convertible MAVs

Fixed-wing and flapping-wing MAVs emphasize energetic mechanisms that differ from hovering multirotors. Long-endurance fixed-wing MAV design couples aerodynamic efficiency, lightweight construction, propulsion selection, speed, and stored energy [ 44 ] . The program in [ 45 ] integrates aerodynamic, mechanical, sensing, and autonomy constraints in flapping-wing systems, while subsequent robotic-flapper experiments reveal unsteady aerodynamic coupling during rapid maneuvers [ 46 ] . These platforms reinforce the broader need to separate actuator-energy storage, aerodynamic force production, and irreversible conversion losses even though their actuation principles differ from those considered here.

Convertible aircraft combine multirotor-like vertical flight with wing-borne cruise. Tailsitter control spans hover, transition, and forward flight despite strongly changing and imperfectly known aerodynamics [ 47 ] ; tilt-rotor VTOL systems add configuration redundancy and dynamic allocation under actuator failures [ 48 ] . Reconfigurable and morphing multirotors likewise use additional actuation to change the relation between rotor thrust and body wrench [ 18 ] . At the vehicle-design level, a fully actuated tilting-propeller quadrotor demonstrates the modeling and control implications of redundant actuation [ 49 ] . These systems motivate energetic models that remain meaningful when rotor states change rapidly even if the vehicle motion changes comparatively little.

## II-F Aerodynamic interaction and physically interactive flight

The surrounding flow can change rotor thrust, resisting torque, and efficiency. Ground-effect experiments characterize both complete and partial ground interaction in multirotors [ 50 ] , while obstacle-proximity studies map aerodynamic effects near surfaces and infrastructure [ 51 ] . Rotor–rotor interference, vehicle-body interaction, payload aerodynamics, and wake recirculation create further deviations from isolated-rotor models. Such effects are especially relevant in aerial manipulation and inspection, where the vehicle operates close to the environment and may sustain interaction forces with limited translational motion.

The aerial-manipulation literature ranges from early system [ 13 ] to broad assessments of the field’s development and open challenges [ 14 , 20 ] . Fully actuated and redundantly actuated platforms support six-dimensional interaction and contact-force regulation [ 15 , 16 ] , while recent reconfigurable and omnidirectional systems extend these capabilities [ 19 ] . Control surveys and shared experimental infrastructures have helped standardize multirotor modeling, control, and reproducible deployment [ 11 , 12 ] . In these interaction regimes, rotor acceleration and source power can vary substantially even when vehicle velocity is small, making rotor-level transient-power models particularly relevant.

## II-G Position of the present work

The reviewed literature provides models for propeller aerodynamics, electric propulsion, battery discharge, vehicle-level consumption, endurance, trajectory optimization, convertible flight, redundant allocation, and physical interaction. These models have enabled increasingly accurate prediction and optimization across diverse aerial platforms. Their principal outputs are typically thrust, current, total power, range, endurance, or mission energy. Comparatively less attention has been given to experimentally determining which acceleration-dependent terms are required to attribute source-side electrical power consistently among reversible kinetic-energy exchange, aerodynamic dissipation, and electromechanical dissipation. The present work addresses this attribution problem through a nested model sequence, held-out dynamic experiments, and independent aeromechanical reference estimates.

2026-10-07.title: ViDAL: A Visual Dynamics-Grounded Action Latent Space for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-07.authors: Yuan Xu , Yixiang Chen , Qisen Ma , Jiabing Yang , Peiyan Li , Kai Wang , Jianhua Yang , Jianlou Si , Jun Huang , Jing Liu , Nianfeng Liu , Yan Huang , Liang Wang
2026-10-07.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a central paradigm for robot policy learning, which predict actions in three forms: raw action chunks, discrete action tokens, or continuous action latents. However, existing action representations primarily model action trajectories, with limited consideration of the visual dynamics induced by these actions. We introduce ViDAL, a Visual Dynamics-grounded Action Latent Space that anchors continuous action latents in the future visual dynamics of the scene. Specifically, ViDAL learns action latent space by training an Action Variational Autoencoder (Action VAE) to reconstruct action chunks while aligning its latent with future scene dynamics. When integrated into downstream robot policies, the proposed Action VAE serves as a plug-in action interface compatible with multiple VLA architectures and enables optional future-video prediction as an additional capability. Empirically, ViDAL outperforms competitive baselines on LIBERO with 98.1% average success, improves a multi-task π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy on RoboTwin 2.0 from 54.3% to 65.5% (Clean) and from 33.2% to 43.1% (Random) success rates over 50 dual-arm tasks, and yields 20.0% and 23.4% absolute success-rate gains on real-world single-arm Franka and dual-arm ARX robot platforms.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] have emerged as a popular paradigm for generalist robot manipulation, directly predicting actions from visual observations and language instructions. Since actions define the interface between the VLA policy and robot control, their representation determines both the learning target and the executable control output. In recent VLA systems, action representations usually take three predominant forms: raw action chunks regressed by a continuous head [ 4 , 5 , 7 ] , discrete action tokens produced by a tokenizer [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] , or continuous action latents produced by a learned autoencoder [ 12 ] . These representations primarily model action trajectories, but manipulation actions are meaningful through their effects on the scene, such as object motion, contact changes, and task-state transitions. Accordingly, as VLA gradually scales to long-horizon, multi-task and multi-scenario manipulation [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] , an effective action representation should account for not only the action trajectory but also the visual dynamics induced by the action.

Recent works have pursued two complementary directions: learning compact action representations and incorporating visual dynamics into VLA policies. As shown in Figure 1 (a), early action tokenizers or autoencoders compress action chunks into compact tokens or latents [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] , yielding representations primarily optimized for action reconstruction, without modeling visual dynamics. As shown in Figure 1 (b), VLAs with visual prediction use future video or world-model signals to guide policy learning [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . Together, these directions suggest that visual dynamics benefit action learning, but leave open how they should shape the action representation. Since actions are visually contextual, the challenge is learning an executable, visual dynamics-grounded action latent space.

We propose ViDAL (Visual Dynamics-grounded Action Latent Space, Figure 1 (c)) to inject visual dynamics directly into the action latent during representation learning. In ViDAL, a frozen video VAE extracts the initial and future visual latents from each robot trajectory, and an Action VAE encodes the corresponding action chunk into a continuous action latent. A lightweight visual-dynamics predictor then maps the initial visual latent and the action latent to the future visual latent, training the action latent to preserve executable actions while explaining future scene dynamics conditioned on the current observation. For downstream policy learning, only the frozen Action VAE is required: its encoder produces action latent targets for VLA training, and its decoder maps VLA-predicted latents to executable robot actions. Thus, the decoupled design lets ViDAL plug into both regression (e.g., OpenVLA-OFT [ 23 ] ) and flow-matching (e.g., π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 5 ] ) action experts without modifying the VLM backbone. The video VAE also enables future-video prediction for visualizing the learned dynamics.

We evaluate ViDAL on two simulation benchmarks (LIBERO [ 24 ] , RoboTwin 2.0 [ 25 ] ) and two real-world platforms (single-arm Franka, dual-arm ARX), using both regression (OpenVLA-OFT [ 23 ] , StarVLA-OFT [ 26 ] ) and flow-matching ( π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 5 ] ) action experts as the downstream policy. # 2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language backbones to predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 27 , 28 , 16 , 6 ] . Recent VLAs differ mainly in how their action experts generate actions: flow-matching experts in π 0 \pi_{0} [ 4 ] and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 5 ] support high-frequency continuous control, while one-step regression experts in OpenVLA-OFT [ 23 ] and StarVLA-OFT [ 26 ] target faster inference. ViDAL is orthogonal to these backbones and experts: it changes the action target to a dynamics-grounded latent and decodes the predicted latent back to executable actions, without modifying the underlying VLA architecture.

Action Representations for VLA Models. VLA action representations take three predominant forms, each shaped by a different supervision signal. Raw action chunks are regressed under behavior-cloning [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 29 ] ; discrete action tokens compress trajectories via quantization [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] ; and continuous action latents use an autoencoder bottleneck without quantization [ 12 ] . All three are shaped only by reconstruction, token efficiency, or imitation losses, and rarely consider how the scene visually evolves under each action. ViDAL explicitly introduces visual dynamics as a direct supervision signal for the action latent, anchoring the representation to the visual effect of each action chunk.

Visual Dynamics for VLA Policies. There is also a complementary line that uses visual dynamics to guide VLA policies. JEPA-style methods pretrain on video to provide dynamics-aware features that condition the policy [ 17 , 30 ] . Future-prediction approaches inject future-frame or video-diffusion signals into the VLM backbone or the policy as auxiliary supervision [ 18 , 31 , 32 ] . Other methods use dynamics or world-model signals for action reasoning [ 19 , 21 , 20 , 22 ] . These designs entangle dynamics learning with policy training and tie the visual signal to a VLA architecture, so the dynamics machinery must be retrained for every new backbone. ViDAL confines visual dynamics to the action latent during representation learning and freezes it before policy training, so the same dynamics-grounded Action VAE can be plugged into different VLM backbones and action experts.

2026-10-07.title: VLA-ACL: Action-Consistent Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-07.authors: Owen Du , Yang Yue , Jie Zhang , Jiaqi Pi , Chi Bene Chen , Gao Huang
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-07.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models achieve strong robotic manipulation performance but incur high computational costs from processing long token sequences at every control step, limiting real-time deployment.
Visual token pruning offers a direct solution, as visual patches dominate the input sequence and contain considerable redundancy. Existing approaches, however, either rely on indirect training-free heuristics, such as attention scores and motion thresholds, or require costly fine-tuning of the base VLA model.
We introduce VLA-ACL ( Action Consistency Learning ), which learns a lightweight visual token pruning policy through action-level supervision while keeping the base VLA model entirely frozen.
The training objective encourages actions produced from pruned visual contexts to remain consistent with the full-context teacher, with ground-truth actions as auxiliary supervision. This directly ties token selection to its effect on the downstream control output.
Experiments on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks show that VLA-ACL prunes up to 87.5% of visual tokens while retaining competitive performance, reduces computation by up to 75%, and achieves a 1.5 × \times inference speedup. These results establish a stronger performance–efficiency trade-off than existing frozen-VLA pruning methods and demonstrate the value of action-level supervision for visual token selection. Code available .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine pretrained vision-language representations with action prediction to achieve strong performance in robotic manipulation [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . However, their computational cost limits real-time deployment. At every control step, these models process long multimodal sequences dominated by visual tokens from camera observations. Processing these tokens through a large language backbone incurs substantial computation and latency, constraining the frequency at which the policy can respond to changes in the environment.

One promising direction for closing this gap is to exploit visual redundancy through token pruning or caching. Pruning reduces the number of visual tokens processed, while caching reuses visual representations across control steps.
Prior work [ 5 ] shows that VLA policies can tolerate even random token removal at moderate pruning rates, suggesting substantial redundancy in the visual input. The challenge is to exploit this redundancy more aggressively while preserving the visual information needed for effective control.

Existing approaches largely fall into two categories. Training-free methods [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 5 , 12 ] freeze the base VLA and select tokens using heuristics such as attention scores, temporal changes, and motion thresholds. However, these signals only indirectly estimate token importance and do not capture the actual impact of token removal on model performance. Moreover, such methods often require carefully tuned layer- or timestep-specific hyperparameters or access to internal states and attention maps, limiting compatibility with existing acceleration techniques. Training-based approaches [ 13 , 14 ] instead learn token selection jointly with the base VLA, incurring substantial backbone fine-tuning costs [ 2 ] . This also couples the resulting VLA checkpoint to the specific pruning mechanism, limiting its deployment flexibility. These limitations motivate a central question: Can we learn effective visual token selection from its impact on downstream actions while keeping the base VLA frozen?

To this end, we introduce VLA- ACL ( A ction C onsistency L earning), a visual pruning framework for VLAs that trains a lightweight token selection policy based on its effect on the predicted action: actions produced from pruned visual contexts should remain consistent with those produced by the same VLA using the full visual context (Fig. 2 ). Combined with auxiliary ground-truth action supervision, this teacher-consistency objective directly links visual token selection to downstream control behavior. VLA-ACL trains a patch scoring network to assign an importance score to each visual token and retains the K K highest-scoring tokens per camera view before passing them to the language backbone at inference.
During training, to enable gradient flow to the patch scorer, we use a soft Top- K K relaxation [ 15 ] to gate visual embeddings and gradually sharpen the selection weights, reducing the mismatch with hard pruning at inference. Our framework neither accesses nor modifies the internal states of the base model, making it broadly compatible with existing VLA architectures.

Empirically, VLA-ACL requires just a few hours of training on a single GPU, using only a lightweight Transformer [ 16 ] as the patch scorer, and avoids costly multi-GPU fine-tuning of the full policy. We evaluate VLA-ACL on LIBERO and real-world manipulation tasks. Our framework supports aggressive pruning rates up to 87.5% of visual tokens and reduces FLOPs by up to 75%, while maintaining success rates comparable to full-context inference.
These results demonstrate a strong performance–efficiency trade-off against frozen-VLA pruning baselines, as shown in Fig. 1 and Table I . VLA-ACL thus establishes action consistency as an effective learning signal for visual token selection, enabling aggressive pruning while preserving the information needed for control.

# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Models

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models build on pre-trained vision-language representations [ 17 , 18 ] to predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions [ 19 , 20 ] . Representative models include OpenVLA [ 1 ] and the π \pi -series [ 3 , 4 ] . OpenVLA processes visual patch tokens and language instructions through a large language backbone [ 21 ] , while OpenVLA-OFT [ 2 ] improves action-generation efficiency through parallel decoding of action chunks. Despite these advances, processing long visual token sequences remains computationally expensive, hindering their practicality for real-world tasks.

## II-B Efficient VLA Inference

VLA inference acceleration has been explored through compact architectures [ 22 , 23 ] , dynamic depth control [ 24 ] , and visual token pruning. Among pruning approaches, training-free methods operate on a frozen VLA stack and offer plug-and-play inference acceleration. Building on token pruning for vision-language models [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] , these methods commonly score visual tokens using text-to-vision attention magnitudes.
Recent approaches further incorporate feature diversity, edge saliency, temporal feature changes, and moving averages of action-to-vision attention to guide token selection in sequential robotic observations [ 10 , 11 , 5 , 9 ] .

Besides selection criteria, methods further differ in layer-aware treatment, as attention patterns shift across the language backbone’s layers. Attention scores from deeper layers, which more directly reflect action-relevance, are used to guide token selection [ 9 , 8 ] . However, since these scores are only available from the previous forward pass, relying on them degrades performance at low retention rates [ 28 ] . Other methods instead vary the pruning rate itself across layers, guided by heuristics such as attention entropy [ 6 , 5 , 10 ] .

Pruning is further regulated along the temporal dimension: full-context forward passes are executed at the beginning of the control sequence to fill up caches [ 6 , 9 ] or the pruning rate is adjusted according to signals such as end-effector velocity [ 7 , 11 , 5 ] . In both cases, these strategies rely on carefully tuned thresholds.

These layer and time-varying mechanisms come with an additional cost: accessing and modifying internal attention mechanisms are incompatible with fused-attention kernels such as FlashAttention [ 29 ] or graph-compiled inference, offsetting the very speedups they aim to provide. Taken together, training-free methods still struggle at high pruning rates, as they rely on a growing stack of heuristic-driven strategies that each require carefully tuned hyperparameters, rather than a signal tied directly to task performance.

Training-based methods instead learn the pruning decision jointly with the VLA. To handle the non-differentiable hard pruning objective, LightVLA [ 13 ] trains the entire VLA stack using a Gumbel-softmax [ 30 ] token selector. Grid-S [ 14 ] replaces discrete token selection with a differentiable grid-sampling module fine-tuned end-to-end. Both report strong performance at aggressive pruning ratios, but the pruner and the backbone have to be re-trained, which can take multiple days even on 8 frontier GPUs [ 2 ] using parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA [ 31 ] .

VLA-ACL sits in the gap between these two regimes: like the training-free methods, it keeps the VLA frozen, and it trains only a small patch scorer in just a few GPU hours; like the training-based methods, the pruning decisions are learned. A single hyperparameter K K controls how many visual tokens are kept per view, applied before tokens ever enter the language backbone. This mechanism remains constant at every control step, eliminating the need for temporal controllers and keeping VLA-ACL compatible with existing inference-acceleration techniques. Crucially, rather than scoring tokens through intermediate proxies, VLA-ACL learns this scoring function by optimizing action consistency between pruned and full-context forwards of the same frozen VLA, directly tying token selection to its effect on the predicted action.

2026-10-07.title: Beyond Waypoint Regression: Query-Based Cost Learning over Reachable Ego Futures for End-to-End Driving
2026-10-07.authors: Ahmed Abouelazm , Rupert Polley , Qingyuan Zhang , Yin Wu , Philip Schörner , Carl Esselborn , J. Marius Zöllner
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-07.comment: Accepted in the 18th Asian Conference on Computer Vision (ACCV 2026)
2026-10-07.abstract:
End-to-end planners based on waypoint regression achieve strong open-loop accuracy, but they primarily learn to mimic expert geometry and remain difficult to adapt to deployment-time safety constraints.
We propose a query-based cost-learning framework that estimates bounded costs for dynamically reachable ego trajectory queries, rather than dense BEV cells or a small regressed trajectory set.
Compact joint scene tokens capture coherent multimodal agent futures, while contingency-aware cost aggregation and cost-guided intra-cluster MPPI mixing convert the learned cost topology into feasible ego plans.
On nuScenes, our method improves over prior cost-estimation planners such as ST-P3 and NMP, outperforms most regression baselines in collision rate, while remaining competitive in L2, and retaining an interpretable cost interface.
On real-world driving logs, the proposed planner reduces collision rates compared with SparseDrive and Alpamayo without fine-tuning, while maintaining a diverse set of candidate trajectories.
2026-10-07.introduction:
End-to-End (E2E) driving has progressed from direct sensor-to-control learning [ 11 , 2 ] to unified systems that jointly learn perception, prediction, and planning [ 5 , 10 ] .
Recent sparse representations make these systems more scalable by allocating capacity to compact task- or instance-level tokens instead of dense raster features [ 13 , 24 , 12 ] .
However, the final planning interface remains a bottleneck: decisions should remain risk-aware, interpretable, physically feasible, and adaptable to deployment-time safety constraints.

Waypoint regression approaches are effective because they directly predict a short horizon of future ego motions. However, imitation objectives primarily reward spatial similarity to expert demonstrations and do not explicitly distinguish safe behavior from collision-causing hard negatives [ 26 ] .
Consequently, regression planners are difficult to inspect or repair, may produce infeasible behavior under distribution shift, and weakly incorporate safety through post-hoc rescoring of a limited top- k k set.
Cost maps offer a more abstract alternative by exposing a risk landscape that can be optimized, repaired, and combined with external costs at runtime.

Existing E2E cost-map planners such as Neural Motion Planner (NMP) [ 31 ] and ST-P3 [ 9 ] , however, estimate dense rasterized costs over many unreachable cells, spreading supervision away from feasible trajectories.
Their flexibility has therefore often come at the cost of lower open-loop planning accuracy than direct regression.
Moreover, many planners rely on marginal motion modes, which can ignore cross-agent correlations and miss scene-consistent interaction outcomes [ 23 ] .
This motivates a cost representation that preserves the optimization benefits of cost maps while avoiding dense supervision over irrelevant space.

We propose a vectorized, query-based E2E cost planner that narrows this gap by learning a cost estimation over the reachable ego trajectories rather than over a dense spatial grid.
The model estimates mode-conditioned costs for sampled ego trajectory queries from compact joint scene tokens built from vectorized map and agent representations.
It then aggregates costs over coherent future scene modes with a contingency strategy and refines trajectories through cluster-based MPPI-style mixing guided by the learned cost topology.
This design retains the flexibility of cost optimization while approaching regression-style accuracy and improving transfer to real-world driving. The key contributions of this work are:

Query-based cost estimation over sampled reachable ego trajectories instead of dense raster grids.

Compact joint scene tokens that condition ego costs on coherent multimodal futures for contingency planning.

Cost-guided intra-cluster mixing for continuous reachable-space coverage beyond top- k k selection.

Ranking-based cost learning objective driven by expert trajectories, collision risk, and off-road violations.

1. Query-based cost estimation over sampled reachable ego trajectories instead of dense raster grids.

2. Compact joint scene tokens that condition ego costs on coherent multimodal futures for contingency planning.

3. Cost-guided intra-cluster mixing for continuous reachable-space coverage beyond top- k k selection.

4. Ranking-based cost learning objective driven by expert trajectories, collision risk, and off-road violations.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Sparse and vectorized end-to-end planning.

E2E driving has moved from intermediate-representation and sensor-fusion models, such as DSDNet [ 32 ] and TransFuser [ 5 ] , toward planning-oriented architectures such as UniAD [ 10 ] and DriveTransformer [ 12 ] . In parallel, vectorized and sparse representations have reduced the computation cost of dense BEV representations. MapTR introduced structured queries for online map reconstruction [ 19 ] ; VAD, SparseDrive, and SparseAD extend this idea to end-to-end driving with compact map and agent queries [ 13 , 24 , 33 ] .
While these methods improve scene encoding and planning efficiency, the final decision is commonly obtained through trajectory regression. They also often reason over marginal agent modes, which can fail to capture coherent scene understanding and complex interactive futures [ 23 ] . In contrast, our planner learns a cost landscape over reachable ego trajectories conditioned on joint scene tokens, so each action is scored against coherent multimodal scene hypotheses rather than independently selected futures.

## 2.2 Cost-based and safety-aware planning.

Cost-based planners provide an interpretable interface between perception and action by exposing a cost landscape that can be optimized or repaired. Neural Motion Planner [ 31 ] , QUAD [ 1 ] , and MP3 [ 4 ] estimate costs from BEV or map-conditioned features and score sampled ego trajectories, while ST-P3 learns a spatial-temporal BEV cost volume for multi-camera planning [ 9 ] . These works demonstrate the value of learned costs, but dense BEV cost supervision disperses learning over large regions that are irrelevant to the ego vehicle’s reachable motion. This can make optimization less stable, blur the distinction between reachable and unreachable costs, and has often led to weaker planning performance than direct regression.

In addition, cost learning is connected to Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL), which treats expert demonstrations as evidence of an underlying reward or cost function. Maximum-entropy IRL formalizes this idea by recovering costs whose induced trajectory distribution matches expert behavior [ 30 ] , with later extensions to spatial-temporal costmaps [ 16 , 15 , 25 ] .
However, these methods usually supervise costs indirectly through expert likelihood or policy matching, often requiring an inner planning or policy-inference loop.
On the other hand, purely supervised trajectory regression has safety limitations: Wang et al. [ 26 ] show that distance-to-expert losses fail to separate safe and collision-prone alternatives. We instead learn a query-based cost landscape in which expert behavior, collision risk, and off-road violations supervise the ordering of reachable ego queries.
