2026-10-07.title: iGPC: Generative Motion Priors for Object-Aware Humanoid Interaction
2026-10-07.authors: Anujith Muraleedharan , Abdul Ahad Butt , Nolan Fey , Yash Prabhu , Anamika J H , Sandor Felber , Maurice Rahme , Ivan Laptev
2026-10-07.abstract:
Humanoid robots operating in unstructured environments must combine robust whole-body control with the ability to perceive and physically interact with surrounding objects. While large-scale human motion data provides powerful priors for natural and versatile humanoid control, effectively transferring such priors to perception-driven object interaction remains challenging. To address this bottleneck, we propose a framework that extends the recently proposed Generative Pretrained Controller (GPC) from general human motion to full-body humanoid–environment interaction. First, we adapt GPC into interaction experts conditioned on scene affordance cues and privileged state information. These experts leverage the pretrained human motion prior while learning task-specific contact behaviors, including reaching toward objects, grasping environmental supports for stabilization, and pushing movable objects. Second, we introduce a perception-driven student that retains the pretrained GPC policy and distills interaction skills from the experts using onboard sensory observations.
To bridge the gap between privileged expert observations and sensory inputs, we propose two complementary training objectives that enable effective adaptation of the pretrained motion prior during distillation.
Notably, our experiments across multiple whole-body interaction tasks demonstrate that large-scale generative human motion priors provide an effective foundation for learning deployable policies for humanoid interactions in contact-rich real-world environments.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Recent advances in humanoid control have demonstrated that
large-scale human motion data can provide powerful priors
for learning natural and versatile whole-body behaviors.
Motion-tracking approaches such as ASAP and BeyondMimic
transfer agile human motions to humanoid
robots [ 1 , 2 ] , while generalist
controllers such as GMT and SONIC scale this paradigm to
increasingly diverse motion repertoires and command
modalities [ 3 , 4 ] .
More recently, generative approaches have gone beyond motion
replay by learning reusable distributions over motor behaviors.
In particular, GPC [ 5 ] learns an autoregressive
generative motor prior from large-scale motion data and
adapts this prior to downstream control tasks.
These results suggest an appealing alternative to learning
individual humanoid skills from scratch: pretrain a general
motor prior once and adapt it to increasingly complex
downstream behaviors.

A key challenge, however, is extending such motion priors from free-space whole-body control to physical interaction with the environment. Reaching for an object, grasping a support to maintain balance, or pushing a heavy object requires the robot to coordinate locomotion, posture, and contact according to its surroundings. Human motion priors provide useful knowledge about coordinated whole-body movement, but do not by themselves tell the robot where and how to interact with a particular scene .

Recent approaches address perceptive humanoid control through terrain-conditioned motion tracking [ 6 , 7 ] , reference-conditioned object interaction [ 8 , 9 ] , or perception-based loco-manipulation [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Nevertheless, it remains unclear how a generative motor prior learned from large-scale human motion can be systematically adapted to object-aware interaction and subsequently retained when the controller must operate from onboard sensing rather than privileged state information.

We address this problem with iGPC , a framework that extends GPC from generative motion control to object-aware, perception-driven humanoid interaction . First, we develop an improved interaction expert that conditions the GPC motion prior on scene affordances describing object geometry, contact, and robot stability. We initialize adaptation using human interaction motions aligned with scene geometry and subsequently optimize task-specific behaviors with reinforcement learning. The resulting experts exploit large-scale human motion priors while learning task-specific interactions, including reaching, grasping environmental supports for stabilization, and pushing movable objects, without requiring reference motions at execution time.

To enable real-world deployment, we propose a perceptive student that retains the same GPC motion prior rather than replacing it with a separately learned action policy. The student uses onboard depth, LiDAR, and proprioception to estimate the interaction and body-state context required by GPC. We introduce distillation objectives that supervise both autoregressive motor-token decisions and resulting joint targets, together with prior-input calibration

and task-adapter refinement. Consequently, the large-scale human motion prior benefits both the experts and perceptive controllers.

Experiments demonstrate strong improvements at both the expert and student levels. For object-aware reaching, iGPC achieves 99.32% contact success, compared with 31.30% for GPC, while the sensor-based student retains 95.95% success and substantially reduces body collisions. The approach also improves hand-supported recovery from strong disturbances and sustained box pushing, where both the expert and student substantially outperform VisualMimic [ 13 ] . Together, these results show that generative human motion priors provide an effective foundation for both privileged interaction learning and perception-driven humanoid control.

In summary, our main contributions are threefold:

Object-aware interaction experts. We extend GPC with scene affordance, contact, and stability conditioning, enabling motion-prior-based reaching, support-assisted stabilization, and object manipulation without reference motions at execution time.

Object-aware interaction experts. We extend GPC with scene affordance, contact, and stability conditioning, enabling motion-prior-based reaching, support-assisted stabilization, and object manipulation without reference motions at execution time.

Motion-prior-based perceptive control. We introduce a multimodal distillation framework that transfers privileged experts to onboard depth, LiDAR, and proprioception while retaining the pretrained GPC motor prior and decoder.

Extensive experimental validation. We demonstrate strong performance of iGPC across reaching, stabilization, and box pushing, with ablations validating our expert and student designs and comparisons showing substantial improvements over the baselines.

1. Object-aware interaction experts. We extend GPC with scene affordance, contact, and stability conditioning, enabling motion-prior-based reaching, support-assisted stabilization, and object manipulation without reference motions at execution time.

2. Motion-prior-based perceptive control. We introduce a multimodal distillation framework that transfers privileged experts to onboard depth, LiDAR, and proprioception while retaining the pretrained GPC motor prior and decoder.

3. Extensive experimental validation. We demonstrate strong performance of iGPC across reaching, stabilization, and box pushing, with ablations validating our expert and student designs and comparisons showing substantial improvements over the baselines.

2026-10-07.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos 3 jointly generate future video and robot actions from an observation and instruction. Adapting one such model, with a lightweight LoRA fine-tune, to a robot absent from pre-training, a Unitree G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands, exposes a video–action asymmetry: the video already renders plausible task executions, while the co-generated action is systematically mis-targeted. We score closed-loop real-robot trials at three cumulative stages: pre-grasp (hand reaching a graspable pose), grasp, and pick-and-place, where the native action, on pilot objects, succeeds only ≈ 17 % \approx\!17\% / 10 % 10\% / 7 % 7\% of the time, worse still on held-out objects. We propose AutodidactWAM : a hand-pose estimator trained without teleoperation, followed by inverse kinematics, run on the model’s own generated video to recover an action estimate a ^ \hat{a} through those same three stages. Paired with the native prediction a − a^{-} , the resulting preferred target a + a^{+} fine-tunes only the action-related layers, with the training loss evaluated on action outputs while the generated video is teacher-forced. We compare two ways to use this pair: plain supervised relabeling and a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO, rather than committing to either. After one-time embodiment adaptation, self-distillation requires no additional task-specific teleoperation. The recovered-action a ^ \hat{a} gate reaches ≈ 75 % \approx\!75\% / 47 % 47\% / 42 % 42\% pre-grasp/grasp/pick-and-place success, against the native 17 % 17\% / 10 % 10\% / 7 % 7\% . A hybrid self-distillation objective combining preference supervision, supervised target fitting, and Cartesian trajectory anchoring (DPO+SFT+DTW) produces the strongest policy among the configurations tested: on Oreo, our training object, it reaches 90 % 90\% pre-grasp and 20 % 20\% full-task success; on the held-out object, it reaches 80 % 80\% and 30 % 30\% . Plain Flow-DPO, trained without any additional losses, reaches 0 % 0\% success everywhere despite 1.000 1.000 validation preference accuracy—evidence that it is the combination of terms, not the contrastive objective alone, that drives the gains above.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Progress on generalist robot manipulation is gated by action-labeled data: teleoperation is slow, robot-specific, and must be repeated for every new embodiment [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , hardest for dexterous multi-fingered hands. World-action models (WAMs) address this via large-scale pre-training that predicts both future video and actions from vision and language [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Cosmos 3 [ 5 ] is one such model: video and action tokens are noised and denoised jointly within one rectified-flow sampling trajectory [ 9 , 10 ] (Sec. III-A ).

We adapt Cosmos 3 to a Unitree G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands, an embodiment absent from pre-training, via a lightweight LoRA fine-tune on a mixed in-house G1 corpus. The two output modalities transfer very unequally: the generated video is usually visually plausible and temporally coherent, although occasional hallucinations remain and are characterized separately (Sec. IV ); the co-generated action output looks plausible on its own but is systematically mis-targeted in space, completing the task in only ≈ 7 % \approx\!7\% of closed-loop pick-and-place trials and reaching pre-grasp in just ≈ 17 % \approx\!17\% (Table I ).

This suggests task-consistent information is represented more effectively in the generated video than in the co-generated action tokens, and more fine-tuning does not fix it: SFT loss decreases and DPO validation preference accuracy saturates at 1.000 1.000 within the first round, while the on-policy task metric that tracks real behavior — headline wrist DTW/path — does not follow (Fig. 3 , Sec. VII ). This points to a residual cross-modal consistency problem between the video and action outputs of one generation, related to a forward–inverse asymmetry [ 11 ] , an executability gap [ 12 ] , or a mismatch between plausible video and control-relevant dynamics [ 13 ] in concurrent work. We recover that correspondence with a frozen perception stack — hand detection [ 14 ] , a hand-pose model [ 15 ] adapted once to the robot hand, and inverse kinematics — run on each generated rollout to give a full action trajectory a ^ \hat{a} , paired with the native prediction a − a^{-} to fine-tune the action-related layers toward the resulting target a + a^{+} (Sec. III-G ).

We compare two ways to use this pair (Sec. III-D ): plain supervised relabeling onto a + a^{+} , and a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO [ 16 ] that prefers a + a^{+} over a − a^{-} , since token-level DPO [ 17 ] needs a tractable likelihood actions do not have. The generated video is teacher-forced as clean conditioning in both cases, so gradients update only the action-related layers and cannot degrade video quality; using the model’s own prediction as the rejected sample mirrors self-play preference optimization [ 18 ] . Every training example needs only a composited anchor frame; seeds and LLM-generated prompt variations [ 19 ] turn it into an effectively unbounded stream of ( video , a ^ , a − ) (\text{video},\hat{a},a^{-}) tuples with no manual annotation, in the lineage of self-training and self-distillation [ 20 , 21 , 18 ] applied here across the outputs of one model. The perception stack itself carries only a one-time training cost from synthetic renders (Sec. III-C ), so the method adds no further teleoperation as it scales; relative to recent work on the same gap, we repair the action output offline rather than with reinforcement learning [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 22 ] (Sec. II ).

Contributions.

We identify and quantify a video–action generalization asymmetry in a jointly-trained WAM adapted to an unseen dexterous humanoid embodiment: the generated video renders the task on most seeds, while the co-generated action output produces plausible-looking but mis-targeted motion, reaching the pre-grasp pose only ≈ 17 % \approx\!17\% of the time and completing the full pick-and-place task in ≈ 7 % \approx\!7\% of closed-loop trials on the real robot (Table I ).

We propose AutodidactWAM , which recovers executable action targets from the model’s own generated video and uses them to align the action prediction for the adapted embodiment, without collecting additional task-specific teleoperation (Sec. III-D , IV ).

We introduce a scalable synthetic data engine that generates self-distillation pairs from a small set of static observations through seed, prompt, and object-placement diversification.

# II RELATED WORK

VLA policies and video-as-control. Action policies trained on heterogeneous robot corpora [ 3 , 23 , 24 , 6 ] , often with a diffusion action head [ 25 ] , still generally need demonstrations on a robot outside the training mixture; our starting point — Cosmos 3 with a lightweight LoRA on the new embodiment — sits in this family, and our contribution begins where it usually ends, when the adapted action branch still does not produce competent behavior. Separately, world models have served as planners or manipulation pretraining, with a separate policy or inverse-dynamics model turning predicted frames into actions [ 8 , 26 , 7 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ] . We differ in that video and action are two outputs of one model and the generated video repairs that same model’s action branch rather than driving a downstream controller; the recovered target a + a^{+} is used contrastively against the model’s own a − a^{-} , not as a plain regression target.

The video–action gap, and preference optimization. Several recent methods target the same mismatch: WAV [ 11 ] frames it as a forward–inverse asymmetry with a subgoal generator and a sparse inverse model; EVA [ 12 ] names it the executability gap and RL-tunes the video branch against an inverse-dynamics reward trained on real robot data; VAMPO [ 13 ] and WMPO [ 22 ] apply policy optimization to sharpen visual dynamics or run in-world-model RL for a VLA policy. We differ on four points: we correct the action branch and leave video untouched; the optimization is offline and preference-based, with no reward model, no training-time rollouts, and no real-robot inverse-dynamics data; the extractor is a hand-pose reconstructor with IK, for the dexterous contact-rich regime where low-dimensional inverse models are weakest; and every signal is a contrastive pair against the model’s own a − a^{-} for the same generation. That contrastive step builds on DPO [ 17 ] and its diffusion extension [ 16 ] (Sec. III-D adapts the latter to rectified flow) and on self-improvement from a model’s own outputs [ 21 , 20 , 18 ] ; AutodidactWAM applies this across modalities of one model, the stronger (video) supervising the weaker (actions).

2026-10-07.title: Energy-Aware Path Following: Comparative Analysis of Reinforcement Learning and NMPC for Electric Vehicles
2026-10-07.authors: Mohamed Sabaa , Mostafa Emam
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-07.comment: currently submitted for review at the journal (Robotics and Autonomous Systems) this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract: Path-following control strategies typically follow the bi-objective optimization dilemma: minimizing deviations from a reference path while maintaining smooth speed profiles. The latter objective is especially relevant for Electric Vehicles (EVs), since their limited driving range can be extended by recovering energy through regenerative braking, a feature that has not yet been sufficiently studied in the literature. In this work, we perform a comparative analysis of four controllers under one common Frenet frame-based kinematic vehicle model, utilizing a validated energy model (VT-CPEM) with explicit regenerative braking. Herein, we implement the following controllers: Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC), Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), gain-scheduled Ackermann state-feedback baseline (PID-SF), and a Stanley geometric baseline. To satisfy real-time requirements, we implement the NMPC using JIT-compiled CasADi. Moreover, we train the PPO using traditional straight and S-curve tracks, after which we successfully transfer the unmodified policy to unseen tracks, including: an ISO 3888-1 lane-change, a chicane, randomly-generated parameterized-splines, and a ± 3 ∘ \pm 3^{\circ} graded road. In addition, the policy transfers to a dynamic single-track vehicle model with linear tires, zero-shot with an acceptable initial performance, which was optimized after brief fine-tuning. Thereby, we demonstrate that our PPO is readily transferable to more comprehensive vehicle models. We conclude with a performance analysis of developed controllers and discuss ideas for future work.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Among its advantages, Autonomous Driving (AD) is pursued because an estimated 94% of crashes are attributable to driver (i.e., human ) error, and as it promises to extend personal mobility to individuals unable to drive themselves Paden et al. (2016) . Electric vehicles (EVs) are increasingly becoming the platform of choice for this transition, yet they remain constrained by limited driving range, which makes accurate, real-time estimation and management of energy consumption during travel a first-order design requirement rather than an afterthought Ding et al. (2024) .

The decision-making pipeline of a self-driving vehicle is commonly decomposed into route planning , behavioral decision-making , motion planning , and local feedback control Paden et al. (2016) ; Wu et al. (2024) ; Zhao et al. (2024) . This paper addresses the last layer. Herein, a reference path and a path-parameterized reference speed trajectory are assumed to be provided by an upstream planner, where the developed controllers are tasked with computing steering-rate and longitudinal-acceleration/deceleration commands in real-time, with the objective of minimizing tracking errors while adhering to actuator bounds. To meet strict real-time requirements, path-following controllers typically decouple these dynamics, addressing longitudinal and lateral tracking independently or sequentially. However, due to the nonholonomic nature of EVs, the resulting control commands are suboptimal Paden et al. (2016) ; Liu et al. (2021) . Moreover, the performance evaluation benchmarks predominately focus on tracking errors without reporting energy metrics, excluding a fundamental criterion for the deployment of EVs Liu et al. (2021) ; Lee and Yim (2023) . This work intends to address this research gap by: (i) accommodating the path-following problem with coupled dynamics, (ii) satisfying strict real-time requirements, and (iii) providing a comprehensive analysis covering both tracking errors and energy-consumption metrics. Thereby, we establish a theoretical foundation and provide practical benchmarking results for future studies investigating real-time, energy-aware path-following controllers with coupled dynamical models.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Literature Review

Nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) has emerged as a central framework for path-following in AD applications, owing to its explicit handling of multi-variable vehicle dynamics, constraints, and performance objectives within a receding-horizon optimization setting Rawlings et al. (2017) . Recent works highlight the continued relevance of MPC-based controllers, in particular due to its ability to integrate trajectory tracking, constraint satisfaction, and robustness considerations into a unified formulation Stano et al. (2023) ; Zhao et al. (2024) . For example, Belkebir et al. (2026) addressed real-time path tracking by integrating path-following and curvature-aware velocity tracking objectives into a unified NMPC cost function, solving the resulting optimization problem with CasADi/IPOPT for real-time feasibility. Beyond nominal tracking, other studies focused on operation near the limit of handling, where accurate prediction of tire and vehicle dynamics is critical. For instance, Fu et al. proposed an NMPC strategy with stable limit handling, while Domina and Tihanyi developed an LTV-MPC formulation for path-following at the handling limits Fu et al. (2022) ; Domina and Tihanyi (2022) . Reiter et al. demonstrated the importance of coordinate and model representations, showing that Frenet-Cartesian formulations can improve NMPC-based obstacle avoidance and tracking performance in AD contexts Reiter et al. (2023) . Consequently, these contributions emphasize that NMPC is particularly well-suited for safe path-following when both geometric accuracy and dynamic feasibility are required Rawlings et al. (2017) ; Stano et al. (2023) .

Contrary to traditional methods, Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a data-driven alternative for vehicle control, offering a flexible approach to situations where hand-crafted control laws are costly to tune across varying driving conditions. Early works demonstrated that RL and deep learning can be effectively utilized for lateral control in AD applications, motivating further research into learning-based path-following controllers Li et al. (2019) , with subsequent studies focusing on policy learning, employing deep deterministic approaches and reward-shaping strategies tailored to autonomous racing and trajectory tracking Hess and Ljungbergh (2021) ; Evans et al. (2021) . More recently, RL has been combined with model-based control, for instance through MPC demonstrations or stochastic MPC structures to enhance stability and sample efficiency Wu et al. (2025) ; Zarrouki et al. (2024) . In addition, Frenet-frame formulations have been adopted to simplify trajectory learning and improve geometric interpretability in autonomous driving tasks Yoon et al. (2024) . Survey studies further highlight the increasing relevance of RL-based methods for AD behavior planning; however, these methods remain heavily reliant on careful design of reward functions, adequate choice of training data, and effective integration with safety-oriented fallback conventional controllers Wu et al. (2024) .

Curriculum Learning (CL) naturally complements RL by structuring the training process from simpler to more complex driving tasks, thereby improving convergence and policy robustness Bengio et al. (2009) . In AD applications, CL has been implemented in staged training regimes for learning lane-keeping and maneuvering under increasingly challenging conditions Anzalone et al. (2021) . Furthermore, Bécsi proposed RRT-guided experience generation to bias exploration toward informative trajectories for autonomous lane keeping, interpreting this as a curriculum-like mechanism for accelerating RL training Bécsi (2024) . These works indicate that curriculum design is particularly valuable in RL-based vehicle control, where direct end-to-end learning from scratch is often inefficient and unstable.

With the increasing adoption of EVs, researchers began to investigate energy-aware vehicle control strategies, since electrified powertrains inherently integrate energy efficiency as an essential component of motion planning and control. Fiori et al. developed and validated a power-based energy consumption model, establishing a foundation for incorporating energy terms into control and planning objectives Fiori et al. (2016) . More recent studies have utilized this approach to refine control actions, such as optimal regenerative braking strategies that consider braking intention and enhance energy recuperation Tang and Zhang (2024) . Furthermore, NMPC-based approaches have been extended to accommodate safety and stability requirements while adhering to the dynamics of EVs Liu et al. (2024) . At the planning level, energy-efficient hybrid MPC and trajectory optimization, incorporating energy-model-aware design, indicate that trajectory generation algorithms can achieve balanced behavior between travel efficiency, drivability, and energy consumption Ding et al. (2024) ; Tian et al. (2025) . Collectively, these developments highlight that energy awareness is becoming an essential design criterion in AD control, particularly for EVs.

As previously mentioned, path-following controllers typically do not explicitly include an energy model, limiting the driving range and negatively impacting the adoptability of EVs. Moreover, energy-aware controllers generally prioritize longitudinal or velocity control, thereby limiting an accurate representation of the consumed energy due to suboptimal lateral behavior. A notable exception is the work of Tian et al. (2025) , which addresses energy-aware trajectory optimization by generating feasible quintic candidate trajectories within the Frenet frame and, subsequently, refining them through an online nonlinear programming (NLP) step to enhance fuel efficiency. However, since the approach relies on candidate generation, it offers no guarantees regarding optimality nor robustness. Furthermore, the study does not report solution times, raising questions regarding its real-time applicability.

The remainder of this work is structured as follows:

We start with presenting our fundamental vehicle model; a coupled kinematic vehicle model in the Frenet frame, providing a compact yet adequate basis for longitudinal–lateral path-following control.

Using this model, we develop and compare four control strategies: (i) an NMPC controller implemented with JIT acceleration via CasADi and tuned using Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS), (ii) an RL-PPO controller with preview information and an energy-aware reward designed through five-phase CL, (iii) a PID-SF controller based on Ackermann state feedback and tuned with pole placement, and (iv) a Stanley-geometric baseline with a proportional inner loop and a longitudinal PI law shared with PID-SF.

Afterwards, we perform a dedicated comparative study of the RL-PPO reward design, including the five CL phases, to quantify its influence on learning and closed-loop behavior. Similarly, we discuss the policy transferability and undertaken measures to enhance robustness against noise and unmodelled disturbances.

We conduct an energy analysis for our developed controllers, reporting the overall energy consumption and the amount of successfully recovered energy through regenerative braking.

For a more comprehensive evaluation, we simulate our controllers on a dynamic single-track plant and across standardized tracks, including an additional LQR baseline for reference.

Finally, we summarize our findings and present our ideas for future work.

2026-10-07.title: Reactive Exploration of Unknown Environments for Redundant Robots using Virtual Model Control
2026-10-07.authors: Alessio Canzolino , Omar Faris , Alessandro De Blasi , Fulvio Forni
2026-10-07.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
2026-10-07.abstract: The exploration of confined, occluded, and partially known spaces poses significant challenges in robotic manipulation. The overall pose of the robotic arm must be carefully controlled to respect tight geometric constraints while avoiding newly discovered obstacles. We address this problem by proposing an active exploration approach for redundant robotic arms with an eye-in-hand camera configuration. Our approach navigates and acquires information in real-time based on a novel scoring method that directly selects a target voxel from the unexplored space using the robot’s current state and expected information gain. To move the robot safely toward the target voxel, we utilize Virtual Model Control, which guarantees compliance and enables whole-body reactive obstacle avoidance without the need for path replanning. Simulated and real-robot experiments in both confined and open environments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving over 90 % 90\% mapping coverage across all tested environments in under 120 120 seconds without colliding with obstacles.
2026-10-07.introduction:
The ability to explore unknown environments while acquiring information is a crucial goal of modern robotics and a fundamental enabler for deploying robots in everyday societal settings. These include search and rescue in unstructured environments [ 1 ] , inspection of hazardous settings [ 2 ] , and mapping of complex agricultural orchards [ 3 ] . This classical problem has been extensively investigated for mobile robots [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] but remains less explored in robotic manipulation. The use of robotic arms for active exploration presents unique challenges and risks, such as tight tolerances in confined spaces, occlusions, the non-trivial volume occupied by the arm’s posture, and the complexity of physical interactions with multiple objects. These critical factors are particularly pronounced in robotic manipulation compared to mobile robotics, and lie at the core of nearly all manipulation tasks in industrial and domestic settings (such as reaching and grasping within shelves, boxes, drawers, etc.).

Active exploration with robotic arms requires movements that respect the robot’s configuration and kinematics. Researchers typically address this by incorporating information about the arm posture and surrounding obstacles into motion planners that aim to reach a desired view [ 5 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . However, such methods are not optimized for confined, heavily occluded environments because planning latency prevents real-time, reactive motion around newly discovered obstacles. Furthermore, the choice between planned and reactive motion directly impacts sensing performance. To capture fine details in cluttered spaces, short-range depth sensors are preferred. These yield a small, local field of view that is ideal for reactive feedback control, but less effective for global trajectory optimization.

Our approach to active confined environment exploration with whole-body obstacle avoidance relies on
two main components, both designed to take advantage of redundant robotic arms equipped with eye-in-hand camera configuration. First, we propose a novel scoring method that utilizes the arm posture to select the next target voxel within the unknown space. Existing methods [ 7 , 8 , 10 ] typically select views that maximize information gain over the unexplored region from a feasible set defined by the known space or its frontiers. In contrast, our scoring criterion evaluates voxels of the unknown space by ranking them using three metrics, relevance, frontality, and distance, which jointly account for the robot’s kinematics and the expected information gain of each candidate voxel.

The second component is a control strategy based on Virtual Model Control [ 11 , 12 ] . The control action emulates a virtual mechanism attached to the robot, pulling it toward the target voxel in a reactive manner. This virtual mechanism serves as an interface between the robot and the environment, generating predictable, physics-driven motion without requiring path planning or explicit inverse kinematics computations. This enables whole-body obstacle avoidance and allows the robot to traverse narrow spaces by dynamically adjusting its posture.

We evaluate our approach across various unknown environments. The main test environment involves a three-tier shelving unit containing obstacles, shown in Fig. 1 , and a simulated benchmark of free-standing cubes with varying levels of clutter. These scenarios demonstrate active navigation through confined, partially known spaces while progressively acquiring environmental data. To highlight real-world applicability, we evaluate the system on additional two practical use cases: scanning three boxes containing internal objects and inspecting an artificial strawberry plantation with occluded fruits, which are tasks that require the robot to maneuver close to objects to capture fine structural details. The main contributions of this work are:

A novel criterion for selecting the next target voxel in the unexplored space.

A new feedback controller, based on Virtual Model Control, that drives the robot towards the target with whole-body avoidance of newly discovered obstacles.

Experimental validation on simulation and real robot across various confined and open environments.

2. A new feedback controller, based on Virtual Model Control, that drives the robot towards the target with whole-body avoidance of newly discovered obstacles.

3. Experimental validation on simulation and real robot across various confined and open environments.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Background & Related Works

## II-A Eye-in-hand Environment Exploration

Autonomous exploration algorithms can generally be classified as frontier-based [ 13 ] or sampling-based [ 14 ] . Frontier-based methods drive the robot towards the best unexplored region adjacent to the explored workspace (i.e., the “frontier”). Sampling-based methods adapt conventional probabilistic path planners, such as RRT [ 15 ] , to exploration tasks, using them to sample views from the known free space. Modern exploration algorithms use these views to select a “next best view”, defined as the view that maximizes the information gain about the unexplored regions [ 16 ] .

For robot arms with eye-in-hand camera configuration, researchers usually augment the next-best-view concept with the kinematic constraints of robotic arms to ensure feasible paths towards the chosen view. The algorithm proposed in [ 17 ] generates a collision-free path in the configuration space towards the next-best-view sensor pose. The algorithm was later improved in [ 18 ] by conditioning the selection of the next-best-view to the feasible joint configurations adjacent to the current robot pose, resulting in faster exploration. In [ 7 ] , the sensor pose was directly sampled in the Cartesian space rather than the configuration space, demonstrating efficient exploration in occluded and densely cluttered environments. The approach of [ 19 ] selects the next view based on learnt motion direction and information gain quantification, and [ 5 ] relies on potential fields to generate candidate views to map the entire environment around the robot.

Other works focused on combining generation of next-best-views and motion planning. [ 8 ] derives the next-best-configuration from high manipulability metrics rather than solely maximizing the information gain. Similarly, [ 10 ] plans the next-best-view in confined environments by balancing information gain, manipulability, and motion cost. [ 9 ] derives the next-best-trajectory considering information gain metrics about the full trajectory rather than just the target view. [ 3 , 20 , 2 ] rely on deep reinforcement learning to train next-best-view generation policies.

All these works focus on the efficient computation of next-best-views for poses reachable by the robotic arm along the frontier or within the known free space. While these approaches are well-suited for open environments, they appear less effective in confined spaces where the arm must traverse tight, cluttered areas. Our approach specifically targets this challenge. Instead of evaluating candidate poses that maximize information gain based on the existing map, we select the next target voxel using an aggregate score across all unknown voxels in the workspace. The robot is then driven directly toward this target voxel, relying on real-time reactive obstacle avoidance to navigate safely as new obstacles appear along the path.

## II-B Virtual Model Control

In Virtual Model Control [ 11 , 12 ] , the controller emulates virtual mechanisms attached to the robot that constrain and shape its motion. Virtual components, such as masses, springs, dampers, etc. generate forces on the robot body according to physics. The concept was originally introduced for bipedal locomotion [ 11 ] and utilized later for quadrupedal locomotion [ 21 ] . Virtual Model Control preserves the compliance of the robot motion and natively handles kinematic redundancy as it directly produces torque commands for the motors. These characteristics have made Virtual Model Control a successful methodology in collaborative and interactive tasks in unstructured environments, such as compliant reaching [ 22 ] , object handovers [ 23 ] , vegetable cutting [ 24 ] , and collaborative drilling [ 25 ] .

In this work, we rely on Virtual Model Control for active environment exploration by designing virtual mechanisms that drive the robot towards the target voxel, eliminating the need for computationally demanding inverse kinematics. The robot is pulled toward the target voxel by virtual forces generated by contracting nonlinear springs and dampers attached between the camera and the target voxel. Concurrently, repulsive non-linear springs between newly discovered occupied voxels and the robot body govern whole-body collision avoidance during exploration, bypassing the need for motion planning algorithms. Motion planning and motion control are integrated. Interaction forces exerted by these virtual components render the target voxel an attractor and obstacles as repellers, guiding safe, reactive robot navigation.

2026-10-07.title: Navigation with RF Cues: Embodied Perception Action under Multipath Uncertainty
2026-10-07.authors: Wenlihan Lu , Tianshun Li , Liuqing Yang , Shijian Gao
2026-10-07.abstract: Smart-factory inspection requires robots to reach connected equipment without a prior map or known target coordinates. Radio-frequency (RF) signals from the target can provide directional cues to complement visual observations when occlusion or poor lighting limits target detection. However, multipath propagation can distort these cues, making it difficult to infer the target’s true direction from instantaneous RF measurements. To enable navigation research under these conditions, we first construct a Habitat–Sionna RT benchmark that uses detailed scene geometry and assigned material properties to generate aligned visual and RF observations in response to robot actions. Building on this benchmark, we propose an uncertainty-aware multimodal navigation framework that jointly estimates target direction and its uncertainty from a history of RF, visual, and pose observations. These estimates inform action selection alongside visual context. Experiments in unseen scenes show relative improvements of 18.2% in success rate (SR) and 11.5% in success weighted by path length (SPL) over the strongest evaluated baseline.
2026-10-07.introduction:
In smart factories, mobile robots may need to approach connected equipment for inspection despite lacking indoor localization information. This poses an embodied navigation task in which the robot must use onboard observations to find and reach a target whose coordinates are unknown. Visual observations support exploration and obstacle avoidance, but machinery and storage racks may obscure the target and limit visual guidance. For equipment with Wi-Fi or Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) connectivity, radio-frequency (RF) measurements of received signal strength [ 1 , 2 ] and direction of arrival [ 3 ] can provide additional location cues. These measurements exploit signals emitted during normal communication [ 4 , 5 ] to complement visual observations, without requiring dedicated navigation beacons.

The reliability of these location cues is affected by multipath propagation in indoor environments. Reflections create multiple signal paths between the target and the robot, and a strong reflected component can cause the estimated direction of arrival to deviate from the true target bearing. Interference among paths also causes received signal strength to fluctuate, so stronger reception does not necessarily indicate that the robot is approaching the target. As the robot moves, changes in the relative lengths and strengths of these paths further vary the observed RF cues, making it difficult to navigate consistently toward the target using instantaneous measurements alone.

To mitigate misleading RF cues, mmWave-LSC [ 6 ] combines path estimation and link-state classification to select between RF directional guidance and visual exploration. PIRL [ 7 ] incorporates propagation characteristics into reward design, while PiPRL [ 8 ] uses symbolic programs and estimated link states to guide navigation. These methods require detailed channel measurements from mmWave hardware, limiting their direct applicability to Wi-Fi- or BLE-only targets. Moreover, compact receive arrays have limited spatial resolution, making multipath components difficult to distinguish and goal direction uncertain. We therefore jointly estimate goal direction and its uncertainty from multimodal observation history and integrate both with visual context for action selection.

Evaluating navigation under multipath requires an interactive benchmark that supports the perception–action loop of embodied navigation: the robot executes an action and receives visual and RF observations at the resulting pose for the next decision. Existing datasets such as P2SLAM [ 9 ] and WAIS [ 10 ] provide real-world Wi-Fi measurements alongside visual and motion data. However, their fixed trajectories cannot supply observations for arbitrary actions selected by a navigation policy, limiting their use for closed-loop evaluation. The simulation benchmark in mmWave-LSC [ 6 ] supports such interaction, but its RF simulation relies on simplified floor-plan-based geometry that omits finer scene details. These limitations motivate an interactive RF navigation benchmark that preserves detailed scene geometry and generates aligned visual and RF observations in response to the robot’s actions.

To address unreliable RF cues and the lack of interactive benchmarks with detailed scene modeling, we develop a navigation framework and a simulation benchmark. Our framework combines an uncertainty-aware goal predictor with an adapted scene memory transformer [ 11 ] . The predictor estimates a target-bearing distribution from a multimodal observation history comprising RF observations (RSSI and the MUSIC spatial spectrum), RGB images, depth images, and pose information, while scene memory integrates it with visual and pose features for action selection. Our Habitat–Sionna RT benchmark uses MP3D scenes [ 12 ] to couple embodied navigation [ 13 ] with RF simulation [ 14 ] , preserving detailed geometry and material-dependent propagation effects while generating observations in response to robot actions. Across 1,350 episodes in 27 unseen scenes, our method achieves an SR of 0.546 and an SPL of 0.456, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 18.2% and 11.5%, respectively.

2026-10-07.title: Vector Map Quality Metrics for Contextual Autonomous Driving Systems
2026-10-07.authors: Marie-Ngoïe Badibanga Kalenda (1,2), Philippe Bonnifait (1), Marie-Anne Mittet (2) ((1) Université de Technologie de Compiègne, CNRS, Heudiasyc, France, (2) Ampere Software Technology, Guyancourt, France)
2026-10-07.abstract:
Ensuring safety in autonomous driving requires continuous map maintenance supported by reliable quality indicators. In this context, it is crucial to identify when and where map updates should be triggered, for instance through crowdsourced data, and under which conditions a new map compilation should be deployed. This paper focuses on effective metrics for assessing the quality of vector maps and guiding such decisions.
We present a new metric called GOSPA M \text{GOSPA}_{M} designed to measure map discrepancies in terms of location errors, existence, and completeness. Through detailed simulations on both point and polyline feature maps, we analyze its sensitivity to common map degradation such as bias, false positives, false negatives, and coordinate errors. The results demonstrate that GOSPA M \text{GOSPA}_{M} offers a unified and interpretable measure that effectively captures various forms of map deviation, making it a strong candidate for map quality assessment in automotive applications.
2026-10-07.introduction:
The reliability and accuracy of vector maps (Fig. 1 ) are central for the development and deployment of autonomous driving systems. These systems rely on detailed digital representations of the road environment to take decisions in real time. However, the presence of errors, omissions or obsolete data in maps can compromise the safety, efficiency and robustness of autonomous vehicles.

In the rapidly evolving automotive industry, the maintenance of digital maps has undergone a significant transformation, largely influenced by the widespread adoption of Mobile Mapping Systems (MMS) [ 7 ] . This shift has given rise to a new era of challenges marked by uncertainties and complexities, driven by the integration of crowdsourcing initiatives. The complexities arising from the variability in sensor performances, diverse vehicle fleets and varied environmental conditions [ 1 ] emphasize the need for a sophisticated approach to ensure accurary and effective mitigation strategies.

Recent surveys [ 15 , 3 ] have highlighted that the lifecycle of HD maps—especially for autonomous driving systems—relies heavily on continuous updates to reflect real-world changes in road infrastructure and traffic signage data. Traditional map update approaches, which depend on high-precision MMS, are increasingly replaced by crowdsourced strategies that leverage fleets of connected vehicles [ 10 , 4 ] . These vehicles, though equipped with lower-cost sensors, can collectively generate high-density data, enabling scalable and cost-effective maintenance [ 13 ] .
Crowdsourcing use the vehicle sensors data of cars already on the roads. Their sensors have lower performances, but the idea of crowdsourcing is that the high number of vehicles at different locations give the possibility to maintain the map at a good level.
However, challenges such as sensor variability, uncertain localization estimates, and partial feature visibility remain major obstacles to ensuring consistency, accuracy, and timeliness of map updates [ 16 ] .

To address these challenges, multiple strategies have been proposed in recent literature. For example, feature-level patching of maps using graph-based SLAM and road model inference has been explored to correct outdated or missing structures [ 13 ] . Advanced filtering and matching algorithms, such as DBSCAN and KD-Tree [ 11 ] , have been employed to detect outliers and efficiently compare incoming observations with existing map data. More recently, mathematical models for systematic map updating have emerged, seeking to formalize when and where to apply updates [ 8 ] . Despite these efforts, a unified metric capable of capturing geometric errors, missing detections, and semantic inconsistencies in a single framework remains largely absent. This motivates our exploration of new metrics, which aim to bridge this gap by offering a unified and interpretable tool to HD map evaluation and maintenance.

This research paper delves into the critical importance of employing a diverse range of metrics, both traditional and innovative, to monitor and address uncertainties in automotive map maintenance effectively.
We focus on identifying metrics that can be used to assess the quality of a given map. In particular, we present a new metric that is called GOSPA M \text{GOSPA}_{M} .

Punctual objects: e.g. traffic signs,

Linear objects (links or polylines,): e.g. lane markings,

Each feature can be a:

False Positive (FP): the feature does not exist in the real world (Red cross in Fig. 2 )

False Negative (FN): a feature that exists in the real world that is not represented in the map (Blue disc in Fig. 2 )

Since the free space is not explicitly represented in a vector map, True Negatives (TN) cannot be evaluated.

When analyzing a map, three main aspects need to be evaluated : feature existence, feature location and feature semantic.

Technically, a good navigation map should have :

A high semantic exactness

A high metric exactitude

A low number of FNs

A low number of FPs

All these elements need to be measured and evaluated through metrics.

2026-10-07.title: Reactive Task-Oriented Robot-Human Handovers via Generative Hypothesis Selection
2026-10-07.authors: Carmen Scheidemann , Andreea Tulbure , Pascal Burkhardt , Marco Hutter
2026-10-07.comment: Accepted to the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026
2026-10-07.abstract: When humans hand each other objects, they incorporate both geometric and semantic information into this process. For example, passing a knife with the handle towards the recipient, rather than the blade, is both more ergonomic and safer. Recent state-of-the-art methods for task-oriented robot-human handovers have progressed from modeling object geometry to incorporating object affordances. However, they often forgo predicting the explicit, task-specific hand poses a human selects to utilize an object. Since many objects support multiple interaction modalities, e.g., a claw hammer used to strike or pull nails, this variability must be modeled to achieve robust task-oriented handovers. To tackle this, we propose a novel approach, GENESIS-Handover (GENErative HypotheSIS), which leverages VLM image generation to produce a variety of task-specific hand-object interaction hypotheses. These hypotheses are matched in real time to the observed human hand pose, enabling inference of the most suitable handover configuration. By leveraging VLMs as priors of plausible hand-object interactions, the method produces task-conditioned handover strategies for previously unseen object-task pairs. We evaluate the standalone interaction proposal module before deploying the full system on a mobile manipulator. In a user study with 12 participants across five task-object pairs, 83.3% perceived our method to have better task understanding than the previous state of the art.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Methods enabling robots to pass objects to humans have evolved from simple object transfer toward interactions that account for safety, coordination, and task requirements. In particular, during task-oriented handovers, objects are presented in configurations that facilitate their intended use.
Imagine, for example, someone passing you a screwdriver: if you aim to use it immediately, you would probably prefer the handle to be pointing towards you as you receive it.
Previous strategies to enable this relied on deriving how to present an object from predicted graspable regions or affordances [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , e.g. the screwdriver handle, or from geometric and ergonomic criteria [ 4 , 5 ] . While these strategies enable comfortable grasping, they do not explicitly model post-handover object use. This may result in configurations that are feasible but suboptimal for the intended task, causing the human to reorient the object in their hand, which requires time and attention.

Recent learning-based methods move beyond heuristic strategies by predicting grasp configurations from object properties [ 6 ] or synthesizing task-consistent handover configurations with generative models [ 7 ] . While these approaches capture aspects of human tool-use behavior and enable more precise presentation, they typically predict only a single handover configuration. In contrast, humans often use multiple valid grasp strategies for the same object and task, and collapsing this variability to a single prediction can limit interaction flexibility and result in suboptimal handovers.

In this work, we address these limitations by explicitly modeling intended object use through VLM image generation.
Rather than relying on heuristic presentation rules or predicting a single grasp configuration, we generate multiple diverse plausible hand-object interaction hypotheses, each representing a different hand-object configuration in which the object could be used after the handover. This enables the system to represent multiple plausible task-conditioned grasp configurations instead of collapsing interaction variability into a single estimate.
As depicted in Fig. 1 , at handover onset, the system observes the human hand and selects the interaction hypothesis that best matches the user’s hand configuration. During execution, the robot continuously tracks the human hand and adapts to its motion in real time. In this way, the method combines generative modeling of task-conditioned hand-object interactions with continuous alignment to the user’s hand pose.

We evaluate the proposed approach through targeted data analysis and a user study with a legged manipulator, demonstrating that generative interaction hypotheses improve immediate usability, particularly for tool-oriented tasks, and better align with the user’s observed grasp configuration than heuristic presentation strategies [ 2 ] . The main contributions of this work are:

GENESIS-Handover: a framework that formulates task-oriented handovers as a multimodal hand-object interaction hypothesis selection problem, leveraging generative models.

Full system integration on a legged manipulator relying only on on-board sensing.

A user study revealing improved subjective and objective handovers over a heuristic baseline for a variety of task-oriented handovers. We show a 2.67x increase in handovers requiring no human adjustment and an 83.3% improvement in perceived task understanding.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Object Presentation for Task-Oriented Handovers

A common approach to object presentation in task-oriented robot-human handovers is to derive grasp configurations from predicted affordances or likely human grasp regions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , orienting the object to make these regions accessible. While such strategies improve accessibility and grasp comfort, they do not explicitly model post-handover object use.

Other approaches optimize geometric and ergonomic criteria: Chan et al. [ 10 ] combine affordance reasoning with distance minimization, while Meng et al. [ 4 ] adapt handover poses based on reachability, safety, and comfort. Similarly, Lagomarsino et al. [ 5 ] use reinforcement learning to optimize object orientation, distance, and motion from human-centric signals such as comfort and attention. Although these methods improve interaction quality, object presentation remains driven primarily by geometric or ergonomic considerations rather than intended object use.

Methods that explicitly account for intended use include affordance-aware optimization combining task context, object affordances, and human mobility constraints [ 11 ] , collaborative tool-use handovers based on functional object regions [ 12 ] , and learning-based grasp prediction from object properties [ 6 ] . However, these approaches typically predict a single hand-object configuration, limiting their ability to capture the variability of human grasping.

## 2.2 Generative Modeling of Human-Object Interaction

Generative modeling has emerged as a promising paradigm for capturing the diversity of human-object interactions. In computer vision and graphics, diffusion-based methods such as Text2HOI [ 13 ] and DiffH2O [ 14 ] generate plausible interactions conditioned on object geometry or textual descriptions, while generative grasp synthesis methods model distributions over feasible grasps [ 15 ] .
These ideas have also been applied to robotic manipulation and handovers. GRIM-TOG [ 16 ] , for example, models human grasp behavior to guide robot grasp synthesis, while [ 7 ] generates task-consistent handover configurations by predicting human hand poses and object placements. Although such methods capture aspects of grasp diversity, they ultimately collapse this variability into a single predicted configuration.

Overall, task-oriented robot-to-human handovers commonly determine object presentation through (I) heuristic or affordance-based rules, (II) geometric and ergonomic optimization, or (III) learned or generative prediction of a single grasp configuration. While these approaches improve accessibility and comfort, they typically approximate task-oriented handovers with a single grasp configuration, limiting their ability to model the multimodal structure of human grasp behavior. In contrast, we model object presentation through synthetic hand-object interaction hypotheses capturing different ways an object may be used, enabling handovers that better align with the user’s intended grasp.

2026-10-07.title: IronMan: Information-Constrained Video-Action Learning for Robot Manipulation
2026-10-07.authors: Yuanshuo Zhang , Wenzhe Zhao , Zixing Lei , Bin Chen , Siheng Chen
2026-10-07.abstract: Video Action Models (VAMs) couple visual dynamics modeling with action generation for robot manipulation. However, video representations are not naturally suited to action generation, as exposing the action policy to excessive visual detail can impair its generalization ability. Therefore, we introduce IronMan ( I nformation-const R ained vide O -actio N learning for robot MAN ipulation), a robust video-action learning framework built on information bottleneck principle. The core principle of this framework is to impose information constraints that suppress irrelevant visual information while preserving action-relevant dynamics cues. IronMan employs a dynamics-aware bottleneck that distills noisy, entangled one-step video features into compact world representations. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate strong in-distribution (ID) performance and out-of-distribution (OOD) robustness while maintaining efficient inference. IronMan achieves success rates of 99.0% on LIBERO and 79.4% on RoboTwin clean2clean, outperforming all the evaluated baselines. Under OOD shifts, IronMan achieves a success rate of 79.1% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding the strongest baseline by 10.4 percentage points. Project Page: https://youngsoul0731.github.io/ironman-project-page/
2026-10-07.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a prominent class of foundation models for robot manipulation ( Kim and others, 2024 ; Black and others, 2024 ; Physical Intelligence and others, 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . However, most VLAs inherit priors from Vision-Language Models (VLMs) pretrained primarily on static image–text data, and therefore lack dynamics modeling.
This limitation has motivated a video-action learning paradigm that couples visual dynamics with action generation, enabling these Video-Action Models (VAMs) to learn inverse dynamics within predictive representations ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2026 ; Ye and others, 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . These advances reveal the great
potential of jointly modeling video dynamics and actions.

However, video and action generation inherently impose different information requirements. A video backbone needs to preserve rich visual details to reconstruct future frames. But an action policy should primarily leverages action-relevant cues. Therefore, the rich information from video backbones is not naturally aligned with the needs of action generation. Existing approaches typically connect video features to the action policy through learned projections or attention mechanisms ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2026 ) . Such interfaces do not explicitly suppress features irrelevant to action generation.

This can undermine the robustness of action policy. When excessive visual cues are exposed to the policy, the model may exploit incidental correlations, which are unreliable under visual distribution shifts. For example, camera noise, light conditions, and background may become shortcuts, leading to degraded generalization in unseen scenes. Therefore, a key challenge is how to transform rich video features into compact representations that capture the dynamics essential for manipulation while avoiding spurious visual correlations.

The information bottleneck (IB) theory offers a principled way to regulate the video-action interface by constraining how much information can pass from input features, while encouraging the latent representation to retain sufficient information for prediction target ( Tishby et al., 1999 ; Alemi et al., 2017 ) . Prior work applies IB-style objectives to regularize visuomotor representations for robot manipulation ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Du et al., 2022 ) . However, these methods do not address the more challenging video-action interface, where features from a generative video backbone entangle predictive dynamics with visual details.

Motivated by this, we introduce IronMan ( I nformation-const R ained vide O -actio N learning for robot MAN ipulation), a robust video-action learning framework. As illustrated in Figure 1 , unlike inverse dynamics model (IDM)-based VAMs, IronMan extracts one-step video features from the video backbone, substantially reducing inference overhead. Although these features already encode physical dynamics, they remain highly noisy and entangled with redundant visual cues. Applying an information constraint on these features alone does not specify how spatial and temporal cues should be used for action generation. Therefore, we introduce a dynamics-aware bottleneck in Figure 2 which first aggregates the video features with a Qformer-style module ( Li et al., 2023 ) , and then maps the aggregated features to a parameterized latent distribution through a Gaussian head. These latents constitute world tokens, forming an efficient and compact video-action interface. To instantiate the information bottleneck in our video-action learning framework, we adopt a variational formulation ( Alemi et al., 2017 ) that penalizes the KL divergence between the latent distribution and a standard Gaussian prior, and combine this regularization with video and action supervision to form our joint learning objective.

To evaluate the effectiveness of IronMan, we conduct simulation experiments across two datasets and four benchmarks covering both in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings: LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin clean2clean, and RoboTwin clean2random. We further evaluate three real-world manipulation tasks under ID and OOD settings with background and layout shifts. Across these evaluations, IronMan achieves strong ID performance and OOD robustness while maintaining efficient inference.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision Language Action Models

Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models, such as RT-2 ( Brohan and others, 2023 ) , OpenVLA ( Kim and others, 2024 ) , π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black and others, 2024 ) , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence and others, 2025 ) , and GR00T ( NVIDIA et al., 2025b ) , have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robot manipulation by transferring the rich visual and semantic knowledge of pretrained vision–language models (VLMs) to embodied control. Leveraging large-scale pretraining on diverse image–text data, VLAs enable robots to better understand instructions, recognize a wide range of objects and scenes, and generalize across tasks and environments beyond the limited coverage of robotic datasets. This has substantially improved the versatility and generalization of robotic policies, establishing VLAs as a prominent direction toward general-purpose robot manipulation. Despite these achievements, modeling physical dynamics remains a fundamental limitation of current VLAs. Because their VLM backbones are pretrained predominantly on static image–text pairs, they receive little direct supervision about temporal evolution. Recent approaches seek to mitigate this limitation during post-training by aligning VLM representations with features of future observations extracted by vision foundation models, thereby injecting dynamics into a VLM backbone ( Zheng et al., 2025b ; Su et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Cen et al., 2025b ; Cen et al., 2025a ) . In contrast, our work directly uses a pretrained video generative model as the source of physical dynamics priors.

## 2.2 Video Action Models

Recent Video-Action Models (VAMs) increasingly leverage generative video models to provide rich physical dynamics priors ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2026 ; Ye and others, 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . A paradigm is explicit future prediction, where future frames are generated to guide action generation ( Li et al., 2026a ; Ye and others, 2026 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2025 ; Liang et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . However, these methods require full video denoising, introducing substantial inference overhead. This has motivated a more efficient line of work based on implicit future prediction, which bypasses full video denoising and directly extracts one-step features from video backbones ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Pai et al., 2026 ) . One-step video features are obtained at the start of denoising process and thus retain redundant visual cues for reconstruction, making them noisy and highly entangled. Existing video-action interfaces allow the action policy to attend to these redundant visual details without explicit information constraints: Ma et al. (2026) ; Pai et al. (2026) directly connect one-step features to action tokens through cross-attention. Hu et al. (2025) ; Yan et al. (2026) transform them with learned projection modules. To address this limitation, we introduce an information-constrained interface that explicitly limits the information transferred from video to action.

## 2.3 Information Bottleneck

The Information Bottleneck (IB) principle provides a framework for learning compact representations that preserve task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant variations ( Tishby et al., 1999 ) . Its extensions to deep learning, particularly the Variational Information Bottleneck (VIB) ( Alemi et al., 2017 ) , make such information constraints tractable and have been widely adopted to improve representation compactness, invariance, and generalization. In robot manipulation, recent works further apply IB-style objectives to suppress redundant information in visuomotor representations and retain features relevant to action prediction ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Du et al., 2022 ) . Building upon this theoretical foundation, we address a more challenging and specialized problem: learning compact and manipulation-relevant representations from highly noisy, redundant, and entangled video features. Such representations jointly encode rich visual details and dynamics, making it difficult to isolate information useful for control. This problem has remained largely unexplored in prior IB-based methods for robot manipulation.

2026-10-07.title: Commit While Futures Agree: Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking for Robot Manipulation
2026-10-07.authors: Yuyan Li , Yujia Wang , Yusong Huang , Junjie Yang , Yanggang Sheng , Ziyi Shi , Wenpeng Xu , Xiaoyang Zhou , Haoang Li , Hongliang Lu , Xinhu Zheng
2026-10-07.comment: including appendix
2026-10-07.abstract: Action-chunking policies predict multi-step control sequences, but a fundamental question remains: how much of a predicted action chunk should be committed before replanning? Existing systems typically execute a fixed-length prefix, implicitly assuming that the same execution horizon remains trustworthy across states. Some adaptive methods estimate this horizon from the similarity or stability of predicted actions. However, different actions may lead to the same successful outcome, whereas similar actions can produce different futures, suggesting that commitment should be determined by agreement among imagined futures rather than by similarity in action space. To this end, we propose Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking (CA 3 C), an inference-time framework built on a simple principle: commit while imagined futures agree, and replan when they diverge . Without modifying or retraining the base policy, CA 3 C uses an action-conditioned world model to imagine the future consequences of multiple candidate action chunks under the same sampling noise. Using these imagined consequences, we formulate execution-horizon estimation as a Bayesian change-point inference problem and select the execution candidate through future consensus. Across multiple simulation benchmarks and real-world robot manipulation tasks, CA 3 C consistently improves diverse action-chunking policies, achieving up to a 71.8% relative reduction in failure rate over the corresponding base policies.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Modern robot manipulation policies increasingly predict actions in chunks rather than one step at a time [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
This way captures richer temporal structure, reduces myopic switching, and amortizes expensive inference [ 4 , 5 ] .
However, one fundamental question remains: after predicting an action chunk, how much of it should the robot execute?

Most existing systems answer this question with a fixed execution prefix, implicitly assuming that predictions remain reliable for as long as they can be generated.
Prediction capability, however, does not imply execution reliability.
In free space, a policy may safely support long open-loop execution, whereas near grasping, contact, or precise placement, only a short execution prefix may remain reliable.
This discrepancy becomes even more pronounced under distribution shift, where an unfamiliar object pose or scene layout may invalidate an otherwise reliable open-loop plan much earlier than expected.
Conversely, frequent replanning can interrupt reliable execution, increase inference cost, and reduce motion consistency across independently generated action chunks.
Taken together, these limitations suggest that execution should be adaptive rather than governed by a fixed horizon.

Recent work makes execution adaptive using action entropy [ 6 ] , agreement across prediction horizons [ 7 ] , or stability along a flow policy’s denoising trajectory [ 8 ] .
These methods recognize the importance of state-dependent commitment, but their confidence estimates are derived solely from the policy’s action generation process.
Action ambiguity, however, does not necessarily imply execution risk.
Different action trajectories may produce the same successful outcome, while nearly identical actions near contact can instead lead to entirely different task outcomes.
Consequently, confidence measured in action space cannot directly determine whether the resulting future remains consistent and task-safe.
Taken together, the key question is not whether actions appear reliable, but whether the futures they induce remain consistent.

In this study, we propose Consequence-Aware Adaptive Action Chunking (CA 3 C), an inference-time framework for consequence-aware commitment.
Rather than asking whether sampled actions look alike, we ask whether their predicted effects remain mutually consistent.
Specifically, we introduce world models as an imagined-future consequence comparator.
At each replanning point, CA 3 C samples candidate action chunks and predicts their future latent trajectories while holding world-model sampling noise fixed.
It then measures candidate-induced disagreement relative to the total predicted scene change.
A Bayesian change-point test determines whether, and where, this disagreement begins to rise faster; no task-specific uncertainty threshold is introduced.
Finally, CA 3 C executes the candidate closest to the future consensus up to the selected boundary.
The resulting principle is concise: commit while imagined futures agree, and replan when they diverge.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We use an action-conditioned world model to select the execution length of each action chunk by locating where candidate-conditioned imagined futures begin to diverge.

We use the same imagined futures to select the candidate closest to cross-candidate consensus, yielding a representative action sequence for execution.

Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa, and real-world AgiBot G2 tasks, CA 3 C consistently outperforms the corresponding base policies and strong baselines.

1. We use an action-conditioned world model to select the execution length of each action chunk by locating where candidate-conditioned imagined futures begin to diverge.

2. We use the same imagined futures to select the candidate closest to cross-candidate consensus, yielding a representative action sequence for execution.

3. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa, and real-world AgiBot G2 tasks, CA 3 C consistently outperforms the corresponding base policies and strong baselines.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Adaptive Action Chunking

Most action-chunking policies use a fixed execution horizon: they predict a multi-step sequence and execute the same preset number of actions before each replanning step [ 4 , 5 , 2 , 3 ] .
Fixed-horizon execution is widely combined with temporal ensembling, guided candidate decoding, and asynchronous chunk stitching to improve temporal consistency or tolerate inference latency [ 4 , 9 , 10 ] .
Recent research instead makes commitment state-dependent, using signals derived from policy outputs or the generation process [ 11 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] , learned horizon selectors optimized through task feedback [ 12 ] , or verification between predicted and subsequently observed futures [ 13 ] .
CA 3 C likewise adapts commitment online, but determines the execution boundary before acting from agreement among the action-conditioned consequences of multiple candidate chunks, rather than from action-space confidence or post-execution prediction–observation discrepancies.

## 2.2 World Models for Robot Manipulation

World models predict how observations or latent states evolve under actions, enabling imagined-future reasoning in robot manipulation [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] .
Existing work uses such predictions primarily for visual planning and goal-conditioned control [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] , policy or representation learning in imagination [ 15 , 23 , 17 , 24 , 25 ] , and action-conditioned simulation for policy evaluation, improvement, or data generation [ 16 , 26 ] .
Thus, imagined futures generally serve as plans, learning signals, or surrogate environments.
CA 3 C instead uses the world model as an execution-time consequence comparator for policy-proposed chunks: disagreement among candidate-conditioned futures determines how long to commit, while consensus identifies which candidate to execute.
To our knowledge, this use of a world model to jointly guide action-chunk truncation and candidate selection has not been studied previously.
