2026-10-07.title: Adapting Vision-Language-Action Models to Unknown Visual Disruptions During Execution
2026-10-07.authors: Ahin Lee , Jinwoo Seo , Youngsoo Jang , Taesik Gong
2026-10-07.abstract:
Visual disruptions can arise while a robot is executing a task, leaving a
vision–language–action (VLA) policy to respond without knowing the
disruption type or timing.
We introduce Self-supervised Adaptation from Leftover Trajectories (SALT) , which uses the leftover trajectory, the unexecuted part of the previous
action chunk, as self-supervision for test-time adaptation.
Because consecutive chunks overlap in time, the leftover provides a temporally
aligned target for the current prediction over the same future control interval.
At the onset of a visual shift, the leftover can retain a plan formed before the
corruption, so updating the policy toward it anchors the adaptation across the shift (Transition Anchoring).
SALT keeps the adapted policy and regenerates the current chunk, whose leftover
becomes the target at the next replan, carrying the correction forward along the
execution trajectory (Sequential Correction Propagation).
Supervision comes entirely from the policy’s own predictions, requiring no disruption annotations, expert actions, or target-domain demonstrations, and a lightweight adaptation gate calibrated only on nominal trajectories decides when updates begin.
On LIBERO-10, SALT increases average success across five persistent visual
corruptions from 43.9% to 53.2% with SmolVLA and from 58.7% to 66.0% with GR00T N1.7, while largely preserving nominal performance.
On a real robot, it raises task progress averaged over digital and physical
disruptions from 0.49 to 0.61 .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions, enabling a single policy to perform diverse manipulation tasks ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) . Despite these capabilities, reliable deployment remains challenging when unexpected changes in visual conditions occur during task execution ( Fei et al., 2026 ; Morgan et al., 2026 ) .
Changes in lighting, image quality, or camera visibility can perturb the observation stream on which the policy relies and abruptly change its action predictions (Figure 1 , right), which can substantially degrade task performance.
We refer to such execution-time events as visual disruptions , which induce a visual shift from the nominal observation condition while the task is already underway.

Test-time adaptation (TTA) provides a framework for adapting pretrained models to distribution shifts using signals available at deployment, such as predictive entropy ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Gong et al., 2023 ) or teacher predictions ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Döbler et al., 2023 ) .
Existing VLA adaptation methods rely on signals prepared outside the current episode, such as delayed feedback, learned progress estimates, or target-domain demonstrations ( Zang et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Bai et al., 2025 ) .
When a disruption arises during execution with unknown type and timing (Figure 1 , left), such resources are not available, and the policy must respond within the ongoing rollout using only what execution has already produced.
We ask: How can a VLA adapt online to an unknown visual disruption using only information already produced during execution?

Our key observation is that action-chunked execution already exposes a useful learning signal within the rollout.
At each replan, a VLA predicts an action chunk ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) but executes only a prefix ( Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . We refer to the remaining, unexecuted action sequence from the previous chunk as a leftover trajectory .
Because the leftover and the prefix predicted at the next replan cover the same future control interval, the policy obtains temporally aligned supervision without any new expert label. At the shift boundary, this leftover was planned from a nominal observation, so it retains the intended plan that the corrupted prediction has lost.

Building on this observation, we introduce S elf-supervised A daptation from L eftover T rajectories ( SALT ), a leftover-supervised mechanism for test-time adaptation of VLAs within the ongoing episode. Once adaptation is activated, SALT uses the previous chunk’s leftover as self-supervision under the current policy input, updates the policy, and regenerates the action chunk before execution. The same supervision plays two complementary roles. Across the visual shift, the nominal-side leftover can provide Transition Anchoring . Thereafter, SALT retains the adapted policy state and refreshes the leftover target at successive replans, yielding Sequential Correction Propagation along the execution trajectory. To deploy SALT when disruption timing is unknown, we use a lightweight adaptation gate calibrated only on nominal trajectories. The gate determines when these leftover-supervised updates begin without requiring annotations of the disruption type or timing.

We evaluate SALT on LIBERO-10 tasks ( Liu et al., 2023 ) under five persistent visual corruptions from LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2026 ) . With SmolVLA ( Shukor et al., 2025 ) , SALT raises average success across corrupted conditions from 43.9% to 53.2% , and with GR00T N1.7 ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , it raises success from 58.7% to 66.0% , while largely preserving nominal performance.
The leftover target approaches an oracle target that is unavailable at
deployment. On SmolVLA, SALT reaches 53.2%, within 3.7 points of
supervising with the policy’s clean-input prediction (56.9%), whereas other
nominal targets, such as another episode’s plan, remain at or below the frozen
level (43.9%). On a real robot, SALT raises task progress from 0.46 to 0.61 under digital disruptions and from 0.51 to 0.62 under physical disruptions such as switching off the lights or covering a camera.
Because SALT relies only on the temporal overlap between consecutive action chunks for supervision, its core mechanism is compatible with action-chunked backbones without requiring architectural modifications.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

VLA policies have shown strong performance across diverse manipulation
tasks ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) ,
but visual shifts such as sensor noise and lighting changes can sharply
degrade execution ( Fei et al., 2026 ; Morgan et al., 2026 ) . Prior work
improves visual robustness through training on perturbed images ( Xie et al., 2026 ) or learned visual adapters ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , intervenes on or restores
observations at inference time while keeping the policy fixed ( Hancock et al., 2025 ; Orjuela et al., 2026 ) , or adapts from target-domain demonstrations ( Kang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Unlike these approaches, SALT updates the policy when a visual
shift of unknown type and timing arises mid-episode, using only observations
and action predictions from the ongoing rollout without target-domain
demonstrations or corruption-specific training.

Test-time adaptation methods for visual perception update models from
unlabeled test data through entropy-based objectives ( Wang et al., 2021 ; Gong et al., 2023 ) , teacher predictions ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Döbler et al., 2023 ) ,
or activation-statistics matching ( Mirza et al., 2023 ) . These objectives
do not directly provide targets for temporally aligned continuous action
chunks. VLA-specific approaches instead use delayed episode feedback ( Zang et al., 2026 ) ,
learned progress estimates ( Bai et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) , predicted and
observed future images in visual-foresight policies ( Park et al., 2026 ) ,
a proxy task trained before deployment ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , or additional
exploratory rollouts ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .
Several of these assume discrete action tokens or a future-image head and do
not transfer directly to recent flow-based action experts. Unlike methods that
depend on such feedback, auxiliary components, or extra rollouts, SALT uses
temporally aligned leftover actions already generated during the same
episode as targets for online updates, and applies to any action-chunked
backbone.

Prior work uses overlapping action chunks to improve execution: ACT
temporally ensembles predictions ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , SEAM smooths chunk
transitions ( Zhan et al., 2026 ) , BID selects chunks consistent with previous
actions ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , and RTC freezes actions committed during
inference latency ( Black et al., 2026 ) . AAC adjusts the execution
horizon from action uncertainty ( Liang et al., 2026 ) .
These methods reuse overlapping predictions to improve inference-time continuity, chunk selection, or execution while keeping the policy parameters fixed. In contrast, SALT uses temporally aligned leftover actions as self-supervision for online policy updates under within-episode visual shifts, which to our knowledge has not been explored before.

2026-10-07.title: OpenWAM: An Open Framework for Composable World-Action Models
2026-10-07.authors: Heng Yu , David D. Yuan , Juze Zhang , Changan Chen , Yao Feng , Michelle Baldonado , Steve Cousins , Li Fei-Fei , Jiajun Wu , Ehsan Adeli
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-07.comment: . Project page: this https URL ; Code: this https URL ; Code and project page released June 4, 2026. Equal contribution: Heng Yu, David D. Yuan, Juze Zhang
2026-10-07.abstract:
World–action models (WAMs) couple future prediction with robot control, yet
existing systems often vary the video backbone, interaction structure,
supervision, and inference procedure simultaneously, making their design
choices difficult to compare. We introduce OpenWAM , an open
world–action modeling framework built around a common causal robot-video
foundation and configurable video–action interaction.
Starting from Wan2.2-5B, we perform causal robot-video pretraining on over 10,000 hours of video, then integrate an action expert through a shared Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that supports joint, video-then-action, action-then-video, and decoupled generation. OpenWAM achieves high success rates on four LIBERO suites and real-world bimanual tasks; robot-video training with causal adaptation improves VTA success on LIBERO-Long from 68.4% to 97.8%.
The same configurable architecture naturally extends to inverse and forward
dynamics, allowing us to study how counterfactual transitions improve
independently trained dynamics models beyond demonstrations alone.
When only the video predictor is adapted to a new task, a frozen local-context
inverse dynamics model trained on counterfactual data and demonstrations achieves 84.0% mean success across four held-out
LIBERO-90 tasks, compared with 47.0% for a full-context inverse model and
21.5% for a local-context model trained only on demonstrations.
For forward dynamics, counterfactual supervision reduces RGB prediction error by
34.5% and raises outcome identification from 21.1% to 71.3% among 16
same-state outcomes. OpenWAM provides a common testbed for comparing WAM interaction designs and for studying dynamics learning from video data beyond successful demonstrations.
2026-10-07.introduction:
World-action models (WAMs) integrate future-observation prediction with robot control. Recent systems such as DreamZero [ 90 ] , DVA [ 71 ] and LingBot-VA [ 43 , 97 ] use pretrained video models to couple future-observation prediction with robot action generation. However, differences in their backbones, training data, objectives, and inference procedures make it difficult to isolate the effect of video–action interaction.

Two challenges arise when studying these systems systematically. First, video–action interaction spans multiple choices: video and actions can be generated jointly, sequentially, or through restricted cross-modal connections. A shared architecture and evaluation protocol would allow these interaction patterns and generation orders to be compared under controlled conditions.
Second, successful demonstrations cover only a limited subset of possible action–outcome relationships. Other interactions, including failures, exploratory behavior, and counterfactual rollouts, can provide additional supervision about local dynamics. However, it remains unclear whether such data can improve the reuse of an action-grounding component when the visual predictor is adapted to a new task. We study this question by independently training local-context dynamics models and evaluating their transfer across adapted video predictors.

To this end, we introduce OpenWAM , an open framework and model series for controlled world–action modeling, summarized in Figure 1 . Starting from a pretrained general-purpose video model, we adapt its visual prior through causal robot-video training without action labels, then introduce an action branch through a Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) architecture [ 49 ] . The resulting model supports joint, sequential, and restricted video–action interaction. These configurations share the video initialization, representations, and evaluation pipeline, allowing us to compare how their interaction patterns affect the control performance.

Furthermore, OpenWAM trains local-context inverse and forward models independently. The inverse model predicts actions from the current observation and a future visual trajectory, while the forward model predicts that trajectory from supplied actions.
In simulation, we broaden their training data by executing alternative action sequences from the same initial state.
This local-transition formulation is also compatible with failed and exploratory interactions, because it does not require a successful task outcome or a success label.
Each recorded transition supplies dynamics supervision regardless of whether it completes the task. At inference, a video predictor can propose a visual trajectory and a separately trained inverse model can translate it into executable actions.

We evaluate robot-video pretraining, closed-loop policy success across
video–action interaction modes and dynamics-component reuse. In transfer experiments, task-adapted video predictors are paired with frozen inverse models to compare demonstration-only with counterfactual-augmented supervision and local-context with full-context conditioning. We additionally evaluate forward prediction under alternative actions from the same initial state.

This work makes three contributions:

A controlled WAM framework. OpenWAM combines a causal video backbone with configurable video–action models under shared training and evaluation protocols.

Local-context dynamics interfaces. We independently train inverse- and forward-dynamics models from demonstrations and broader local transitions and evaluate their composition with separately trained predictors.

Controlled empirical analysis. We measure the effects of robot-video pretraining, interaction design, transition coverage, and conditioning context on policy performance and component reuse.

1. A controlled WAM framework. OpenWAM combines a causal video backbone with configurable video–action models under shared training and evaluation protocols.

2. Local-context dynamics interfaces. We independently train inverse- and forward-dynamics models from demonstrations and broader local transitions and evaluate their composition with separately trained predictors.

3. Controlled empirical analysis. We measure the effects of robot-video pretraining, interaction design, transition coverage, and conditioning context on policy performance and component reuse.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Visuomotor Policies and Predictive Control

Behavior cloning provides the standard supervised formulation for visuomotor
policy learning, mapping observations and task context directly to demonstrated
actions. Action chunking and generative action prediction have become effective
control primitives [ 101 , 12 ] , while large-scale
vision–language–action models extend this paradigm through language
conditioning, pretraining, and cross-task or cross-embodiment learning [ 8 , 7 , 38 , 6 , 33 , 58 , 70 ] .

Predictive control introduces an additional interface by explicitly modeling
future observations or latent states. Early visual-foresight methods combined
action-conditioned video prediction with model-predictive control for robotic
manipulation [ 17 , 16 ] . Subsequent work learns latent
or visual dynamics to support policy learning, planning, and imagined rollouts [ 24 , 25 , 82 , 80 , 11 , 107 ] . Predictive rollouts have also been used to evaluate policy behavior [ 47 , 22 ] .

Action-conditioned world models provide a complementary perspective by
predicting how an environment evolves under supplied or candidate actions.
Recent methods use such predictions for simulation, candidate evaluation,
proposal refinement, and self-verifying planning [ 31 , 106 , 61 , 95 ] . Together, these lines show that predictive models can
support action generation, simulation, planning, and evaluation. However,
action-conditioned prediction and video–action policy generation are often
developed as separate components, leaving open how explicit
prediction–action interfaces affect component reuse across tasks.

## 2.2 Video Foundations and World–Action Architectures

Recent world–action models connect predictive video representations with
robot control through several forms of video–action coupling. Joint
generation models predict future visual content and actions together [ 90 , 1 , 66 , 21 ] , while
causal video-first formulations generate or represent visual futures before
action prediction [ 43 , 71 ] . Other architectures use
specialized video and action pathways with explicit cross-modal exchange [ 87 , 96 ] , or leverage egocentric and large-scale
video priors for robot grounding and generalization [ 41 , 105 , 85 , 62 ] .

A closely related line studies the interface between predictive visual
information and executable actions. Predicted visual states or representations
can condition inverse dynamics [ 72 , 26 , 46 ] , while
other approaches translate generated futures through dense correspondence,
pseudo-action labeling, intermediate denoising features, or latent
representation alignment [ 39 , 34 , 55 , 74 ] . These methods differ in where and how predictive visual
information enters the action-generation pathway.

Unified formulations instead expose multiple predictive and control modes
within a shared system. UWM and UVA [ 108 , 45 ] support combinations of policy, inverse-dynamics, forward-dynamics, and video
prediction objectives, while related systems combine action generation with
world prediction, simulation, planning, or evaluation [ 10 , 37 , 68 , 4 , 20 ] .

Recent work further isolates particular choices in the WAM design space.
Predictive computation can be reduced, sparsified, reordered, or scheduled
asynchronously [ 94 , 69 , 77 , 89 , 48 , 29 , 28 , 59 ] . Alternative work studies the
representation through which world prediction interacts with control [ 53 , 76 , 63 , 99 , 67 , 92 , 35 ] , or augments
world–action learning with structural, geometric, and tactile supervision [ 104 , 18 , 56 ] . Temporal
abstraction, data and model scaling, humanoid control, and long-horizon memory
provide additional design axes [ 44 , 52 , 103 , 100 ] ;
recent surveys summarize the rapidly expanding landscape [ 78 , 54 ] .

Concurrent work, also named OpenWAM [ 79 ] , develops a modular
framework for systematic WAM pretraining and design studies. Our focus is
complementary: OpenWAM fixes a common causal robot-video foundation and training
interface while explicitly varying generation order and future cross-modal
visibility, enabling joint, video-then-action, action-then-video, and decoupled
interaction to be compared under a shared evaluation protocol. We further study
the reuse of independently trained inverse- and forward-dynamics components
through explicit trajectory interfaces.

## 2.3 Dynamics Learning Beyond Successful Demonstrations

Successful demonstrations provide valid transitions, but they cover only the
action–outcome relationships selected by the demonstrating policy. A
complementary analysis shows that observational demonstrations alone may not
identify the consequences of unsupported actions [ 93 ] .
Classical imitation-learning methods address the resulting distribution shift
by collecting supervision on learner-visited states, perturbing expert
trajectories, or soliciting corrective interventions [ 65 , 40 , 57 , 27 , 32 ] . These approaches broaden state coverage beyond clean
expert rollouts and improve robustness to execution errors.

More recent work expands supervision through synthetic failures,
counterfactual augmentation, autonomous experience, and other non-successful
interactions [ 2 , 15 , 42 , 98 , 91 , 60 , 4 , 88 ] .
Such data have been used for recovery, policy improvement, failure
understanding, and predictive modeling. Particularly related to our setting,
Fail2Progress [ 30 ] targets data collection toward
observed failures to improve skill-effect models, while
UniPi [ 14 ] decouples video planning from inverse dynamics and
allows the inverse model to learn from a separate, potentially suboptimal
dataset.

OpenWAM focuses on a different question: how transition coverage and conditioning
scope affect the reuse of independently trained dynamics components after
visual task adaptation. We branch alternative action continuations from
task-relevant simulator states and use the resulting state–action–outcome
transitions as local dynamics supervision.

2026-10-07.title: PACE: Stage-Consistent Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation via Progress-Aligned Context for Execution
2026-10-07.authors: Yenan Chen , Junjie Shi , Lu Chen , Zhongxiang Zhou , Rong Xiong
2026-10-07.abstract: Demonstration-conditioned policies provide a natural interface for specifying robot behavior, yet long-horizon manipulation remains difficult when visually similar states recur across different stages or when demonstrations and executions proceed at different speeds. We identify the resulting failure mode as stage confusion and introduce Progress-Aligned Context for Execution (PACE), a stateful method that continually reinterprets a complete demonstration according to realized execution progress. PACE compresses the demonstration into ordered multimodal prompt tokens and uses training-only dual-edge attention supervision to expose its latent stage structure. During execution, an episode-local fast-weight memory causally encodes realized action–observation transitions and modulates prompt cross-attention, producing a progress-aligned context for a unified diffusion action expert without test-time stage labels or stage-specific policies. PACE improves success from 88.9% to 94.0% on LIBERO-Gen Goal Chain, from 79.1% to 83.3% on Spatial Combination, and from 33.3% to 73.3% on the two-step Block Routing tasks. Failure analysis further indicates that structured demonstration alignment and causal execution memory jointly mitigate stage confusion.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Enabling robots to adapt to new tasks from minimal user input without retraining is a central objective of general-purpose robotic manipulation. Recent visuomotor policies have increasingly supported task conditioning through language, goal images, and multimodal demonstrations [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Among these, a perception–action demonstration conveys the global task objective, the sequence of operations, and fine-grained motion details, enabling policies to adapt to new execution objectives without updating model parameters [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 2 , 8 , 9 , 4 ] .

However, long-horizon multi-stage manipulation requires a policy to continually track task progress and interpret the demonstration relative to the current execution state. This is particularly challenging when different stages contain similar or recurring observations: similar states may require different actions depending on what has already been completed. Retrieving a demonstration segment inconsistent with the current progress may cause the policy to regress to an earlier stage, skip or repeat a stage, or terminate prematurely. We refer to this class of failures as stage confusion , illustrated in Fig. 1 . Stage confusion primarily arises from two related factors: cross-stage observation aliasing , whereby distinct latent stages exhibit similar observations, and demonstration–execution temporal-scale mismatch , whereby the robot and the demonstrator complete the same behavioral stage at different speeds.

Existing approaches address this problem only partially. Explicit stage or subgoal models often require predefined task decompositions, semantic subgoals, or manual stage annotations [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] , while frame- or window-level localization is vulnerable to recurring observations and execution-speed variation [ 14 , 15 ] . Long-context and memory-augmented policies retain longer execution histories [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] , but typically use history as additional input to action prediction rather than to continually revise which part of the demonstration is relevant. These limitations motivate a mechanism that recovers stage structure from demonstrations without manual annotations and uses causal execution history to dynamically determine which part of the demonstration should guide the current behavior.

Event cognition research suggests that humans parse continuous activity into structured events and update an active event model at perceptual boundaries [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . Inspired by this view, we adopt a functional abstraction in which an event model is realized not necessarily through parametrically independent modules, but through context dynamically constructed during execution. Specifically, the policy combines current perception with within-episode execution history to locate and aggregate demonstration segments consistent with the current progress, forming an evolving event context that enables a shared policy to produce stage-appropriate behavior.

Building on this insight, we introduce Progress-Aligned Context for Execution (PACE) , a stateful progress-alignment method for long-horizon demonstration-conditioned manipulation. During training, PACE automatically extracts and monotonically aligns action-stage boundaries, imposing dual-edge attention supervision and effective-support regularization. During execution, an episode-local fast-weight memory causally encodes realized action–observation transitions and modulates observation queries before cross-attention with the full demonstration. The resulting progress-aligned demonstration context conditions a unified diffusion action expert. Stage boundaries are used only for training supervision; at inference time, PACE requires neither explicit event segmentation, discrete stage prediction, nor stage-specific policies.

We evaluate PACE on compositional long-horizon manipulation benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks. On the LIBERO-Gen Spatial Combination and Goal Chain, PACE improves the success rate from 79.1% to 83.3% and from 88.9% to 94.0%. On the two-step Block Routing tasks, which exhibit pronounced cross-stage observation aliasing, PACE raises the mean success rate from 33.3% to 73.3%. Stage-level analyses further show that structured demonstration alignment and causal execution memory work synergistically to suppress stage confusion.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We systematically study stage confusion in long-horizon demonstration-conditioned manipulation, attributing it to cross-stage observation aliasing and demonstration–execution temporal-scale mismatch.

We introduce PACE , centered on a causally updated, episode-local fast-weight state that encodes realized action–observation transitions and modulates observation queries before prompt cross-attention, allowing visually similar current observations to attend to different demonstration stages under different execution histories. PACE further combines automatic stage-structure discovery with dual-edge attention supervision and effective-support regularization, without requiring manual stage annotations or stage-specific policies.

We validate PACE on compositional simulation tasks and real-world robotic tasks with held-out demonstrations, and use stage-level analyses to elucidate how it mitigates stage confusion.

1. We systematically study stage confusion in long-horizon demonstration-conditioned manipulation, attributing it to cross-stage observation aliasing and demonstration–execution temporal-scale mismatch.

2. We introduce PACE , centered on a causally updated, episode-local fast-weight state that encodes realized action–observation transitions and modulates observation queries before prompt cross-attention, allowing visually similar current observations to attend to different demonstration stages under different execution histories. PACE further combines automatic stage-structure discovery with dual-edge attention supervision and effective-support regularization, without requiring manual stage annotations or stage-specific policies.

3. We validate PACE on compositional simulation tasks and real-world robotic tasks with held-out demonstrations, and use stage-level analyses to elucidate how it mitigates stage confusion.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Demonstration-Conditioned Robot Policies

Complete perception–action demonstrations provide a natural
inference-time interface for specifying task objectives, operation
sequences, and motion details without updating policy parameters.
Existing methods relate human demonstrations to robot observations
through cross-attention or learned cross-embodiment representations [ 2 , 8 ] , retrieve or align relevant
demonstration segments [ 23 , 24 ] ,
encode task identity from one or a few demonstrations [ 5 , 6 ] , or jointly model
demonstration and execution trajectories as prompted, in-context
sequences [ 3 , 9 , 4 ] .
In particular,
Behavior Prompting Policy (BPP) treats a complete perception–action
demonstration as a behavioral prompt for closed-loop action generation [ 4 ] . However, these approaches generally use the
demonstration as a static conditioning sequence and do not continually
reinterpret it according to realized execution progress, leaving them
susceptible to cross-stage observation aliasing.

## II-B Temporal Alignment and Stage-Structured Manipulation

Temporal correspondence methods, including frame-level metric learning,
temporal cycle consistency, dynamic time warping, and optimal transport,
align sequences with different appearances or execution speeds [ 14 , 15 , 25 , 26 ] .
Local correspondences become ambiguous when visually similar states
recur, while sequence-level alignments are typically computed offline
or remain fixed during execution. Related hierarchical approaches
represent progress using skills, options, subgoals, or keyframes [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] , but often require predefined
decompositions, semantic labels, or separate skill policies. Although
unsupervised skill discovery reduces annotation requirements [ 27 ] , it does not directly establish an
execution-conditioned correspondence with a new demonstration.
Latent-plan methods learn reusable long-horizon structure from play or
human video [ 28 , 29 ] , but likewise
do not continually realign a provided demonstration using the realized
execution history.
PACE instead learns ordered demonstration structure without manual
stage labels and dynamically interprets that structure during execution.

## II-C History and Memory for Long-Horizon Manipulation

Long-horizon manipulation is partially observable because similar
current observations may require different actions depending on prior
interactions. Recurrent policies, history-aware Transformers, and
memory-augmented models address this problem by retaining execution
history [ 16 , 17 ] . Test-time
training further represents history as recurrently updated fast weights [ 18 ] , and RoboTTT applies this mechanism to long-horizon
visuomotor control [ 19 ] . These approaches primarily
use history to improve action prediction. In contrast, PACE uses an
episode-local fast-weight state to modulate observation queries before
prompt cross-attention, allowing execution history to determine which
part of the demonstration guides the current action.

2026-10-07.title: From Model to Prototype: Design and Motor-Flap Propulsion Control of a Twin-Wing Metamorphic UAV
2026-10-07.authors: Anja Bosak , Dorian Erić , Ana Milas , Stjepan Bogdan
2026-10-07.abstract:
This paper presents the design and control strategy for MetaMorpher , a metamorphic Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), capable of both spinning-wing hover and fixed flying-wing cruise flight.
Since control of the cruise configuration is comparatively well established in the literature, this paper focuses on control of the MetaMorpher in hover mode, building on the flight dynamics model and conceptual design validated in previous work. The control algorithm is implemented using one of two phase-synchronized strategies: motor propulsion, which pulses motor thrust in synchrony with the vehicle’s rotation, or flap propulsion, a novel strategy that pulses the deflection of the wing-mounted elevons. We evaluate both strategies in simulation through different flight experiments. Simulation results confirm the mathematical model and show stable reference tracking, demonstrating flap propulsion as a lightweight, decoupled alternative for hover control. Experimental testing validated the vertical-dynamics propulsion model against the physical prototype, demonstrating very good steady-state agreement across different configurations.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) capable of both vertical
takeoff and hovering, as well as efficient long-range cruising, are needed for tasks such as power-line monitoring [ 1 ] and bridge inspection [ 2 ] , which require confined launch sites and extended range. Conventional rotorcraft and fixed-wing aircraft each satisfy only one of these requirements. Metamorphic UAVs meet both, reconfiguring their airframe between hover- and cruise-optimized shapes. However, turning from this concept into a flying, controllable vehicle requires an actuator layout and suitable control strategy.

We address this challenge with MetaMorpher , which builds on previously developed spincopter [ 3 , 4 ] , an inherently stable UAV whose twin-wing rotating structure generates lift by spinning two wings with a pair of propellers. MetaMorpher extends this platform into a metamorphic design that folds between the spinning-wing hover configuration and a fixed flying-wing cruise configuration. Its conceptual design and a nonlinear, segmented-aerodynamics flight dynamics model have previously been presented and validated through simulation in [ 5 ] .

Implementing position control in the hover configuration, however, poses a challenge that conventional Vertical Take-Off and Landing (VTOL) controllers do not face. In this case, the aerodynamic surfaces and propulsion units rotate with the airframe, a fixed-axis control input cannot produce a constant horizontal force. Instead, the control action should be synchronized with the vehicle’s rotational phase and applied only within selected angular sectors of each revolution. The spincopter implemented this principle by pulsing the imbalance between its two motor thrusts [ 3 , 4 ] , an approach that couples horizontal and vertical control since both motors also determine the vehicle’s overall lift [ 3 ] .
Since MetaMorpher’s cruise mode already requires a pair of wing-mounted elevons for attitude control, a well-established problem ( [ 6 ] ), that we do not address in detail here, motivated us to use it as an alternative channel for the novel control principle.

Therefore, this paper presents the design and control algorithm for the MetaMorpher. The resulting vehicle has a 0.7 m wingspan and an estimated ready-to-fly mass of approximately 454 g, with two independently driven wing-mounted propellers and two independently actuated trailing-edge elevons. For position control in hover mode, we implement and compare two phase-synchronized strategies: motor propulsion, which pulses the motor thrust imbalance following the spincopter approach in [ 3 ] , and flap propulsion, a novel strategy that instead pulses the elevon deflection in synchrony with the vehicle’s rotation while motor speed is held constant. We evaluate both strategies using a nonlinear Simulink model, demonstrating stable waypoint tracking in simulation.

The main contributions of this work are:

Physical design of a MetaMorpher prototype that implements the airframe and actuator layout derived from the mathematical model in [ 5 ] .

Implementation and comparison of two phase-synchronized control strategies for position control in hover mode: motor propulsion and flap propulsion, a novel scheme that repurposes MetaMorpher’s cruise-mode elevons for hover-mode actuation validated through simulation tests.

Parameter identification of the throttle-to-spin-rate response in simulation and on the physical prototype.

An open-source Simulink code of the control strategy to support reproducibility.

This paper is divided into six sections. Section II reviews related work on different designs and control algorithms of MetaMorpher-like vehicles. Section III describes the MetaMorpher prototype. Section IV presents the motor- and flap-propulsion control strategies. Sections V and VI report the simulation and experimental setup and flight-test results, respectively, to validate the design of the vehicle. Finally, Section VII presents conclusions and directions for future work.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related work

Conventional UAV airframes typically use a single configuration, trading hover capability for cruise efficiency. Metamorphic designs avoid this trade-off through approaches ranging from bio-inspired wing folding [ 7 ] to dedicated tilt-rotor [ 8 ] and tail-sitter [ 9 ] layouts. However, most of this work stops at mechanical concepts and theoretical analysis. Accurate simulation models and physical prototypes with control strategies validated through flight tests remain rare.

Few review papers address the design of morphing aircraft alongside their flight control. For instance, Chu et al. [ 10 ] reviewed the broader field of morphing aircraft, covering configuration design methods, the nonlinear dynamics and aerodynamic interference introduced by wing morphing, and the flight control strategies used to address them. Authors in [ 11 ] focused more specifically on control, surveying shape, flight-dynamics, and aeroelastic control strategies for a wide range of fixed-wing morphing concepts. Harvey et al. [ 12 ] took a different angle, reviewing avian-inspired morphing in which wing sweep, dihedral, twist, and camber replace conventional control surfaces to provide pitch, roll, and yaw control, including on tailless airframes; camber-morphing trailing edges, similar to elevons, provide pitch control when actuated symmetrically and roll control when actuated asymmetrically. Across these reviews, the scope remains fixed-wing or gliding flight, while none address vehicles like MetaMorpher that transition between rotary-wing hover and fixed-wing cruise.

Several hardware platforms have demonstrated metamorphic hover-to-cruise flight. Low et al. [ 13 , 14 ] developed the Transformable HOvering Rotorcraft (THOR), which inspired MetaMorpher’s wing sizing and models the vehicle as a rigid body in each flight mode. Sufiyan et al. [ 9 , 15 ] introduced a multimodal vehicle, jointly optimizing design and control parameters through a collaborative co-evolutionary approach. State-of-the-art control papers have also focused on specific aspects of the transition problem. Yuksek et al. [ 16 ] developed a six-degree-of-freedom nonlinear model for transition control of a tilt-rotor UAV and validated it through both simulation and a physical flight demonstration on their TURAC prototype. Zhao et al. [ 17 ] proposed Kriging-based control allocation for a flying-wing UAV with a morphing trailing edge, validated in simulation, addressing control-surface actuation without full airframe metamorphosis or a hover mode.

Both of MetaMorpher’s control strategies, detailed in Section IV , rely on synchronizing the control input with the vehicle’s rotational phase rather than producing a fixed control force in the body frame. This principle is closely related to cyclic pitch control on a conventional helicopter rotor, where blade pitch is varied once per revolution to redirect the rotor’s thrust in a commanded inertial direction [ 18 ] .
On the spincopter, this principle was implemented entirely through differential motor thrust [ 3 , 4 ] . Phase-synchronized flap deflection has also been investigated on single-wing, samara-inspired monocopters, where a trailing-edge flap is deflected within selected angular sectors of each revolution to produce horizontal control forces [ 19 ] .
To the best of our knowledge, no existing metamorphic UAV has achieved horizontal control through elevon deflection on a twin-wing spinning platform, nor directly compared it against motor pulsation on the same model.

This work bridges these gaps by implementing MetaMorpher’s previously validated model as a flight-ready prototype and evaluating two phase-synchronized control strategies for its hover mode. Finally, this work lays the foundation for combining motor and flap propulsion into a single control architecture and for extending phase-synchronized control across the transition between hover and cruise flight.

2026-10-07.title: Beyond Retargeting: Low-Latency and Robust Humanoid Whole-Body Teleoperation with Learned Atomic Motion Primitives
2026-10-07.authors: Xiayan Xu , Jiyu Yu , Xingzhou Chen , Siyi Qian , Zongyu Ma , Lilu Liu , Ling Shi , Haodong Zhang
2026-10-07.abstract:
Humanoid whole-body teleoperation translates human motion into stable robot behavior in real time.
Existing systems typically rely on online motion retargeting to bridge human–robot morphological differences, but this process adds latency and can produce physically infeasible targets.
Meanwhile, diverse, noisy, and partial human-motion observations often fall outside the training distribution, potentially causing unstable robot behavior.
We propose a retargeting-free policy that maps raw human motion directly to robot joint commands in a single forward pass, eliminating online kinematic adaptation.
To improve robustness, we learn a codebook of full-body motion primitives that projects out-of-distribution observations onto plausible motion prototypes and recovers full-body motion from partial inputs.
Experiments on a Unitree G1 in simulation and on hardware, using virtual reality, optical mocap, text-to-motion generation, and monocular video inputs, show that our method outperforms baselines in latency and robustness.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Humanoid robots provide a general-purpose embodiment for environments designed around humans.
Whole-body teleoperation maps an operator’s full-body motion to a humanoid in real time through virtual reality (VR), motion capture, or other interfaces, enabling intuitive whole-body control and demonstration collection for downstream learning.
However, direct human-to-humanoid control is challenging because the two bodies differ in link proportions, joint topology, and actuation limits, while teleoperation requires low latency, accurate tracking, and stable behavior.

Most existing systems use online retargeting: human motion observations are first converted into robot-joint reference trajectories, which are then executed by a tracking policy [ 7 , 37 , 38 , 23 ] . Although this decomposition decouples morphology adaptation from control, retargeting lies on the command path and typically requires per-step kinematic optimization or iterative inverse kinematics (IK). Its delay compounds sensing, communication, and actuation latency, reducing responsiveness in dynamic teleoperation. Retargeting-free alternatives [ 9 , 15 ] often use only head and hand signals, but provide limited lower-body control.

Robustness is an equally important challenge. Deployment observations often differ from the clean mocap references used for training because human motion varies across body proportions, movement styles, and motion patterns, while real sensing pipelines introduce noise, calibration errors, and partial observations.
Such inputs are therefore frequently out of distribution (OOD) in teleoperation, and may drive a tracking policy toward unstable or dynamically infeasible behavior [ 28 ] .
This challenge is amplified in retargeting-free whole-body control.
Without online retargeting, a single policy must bridge morphology and sensing gaps, maintain balance-aware dynamics, and infer plausible full-body motion from unreliable observations.

We address this problem with a learned full-body motion prior. Instead of predicting actions directly from each raw observation, our policy maps the input to a compact set of learned motion prototypes and predicts actions from the recovered descriptor. This discrete prior pulls noisy or partial observations toward the training support and selects a plausible full-body completion rather than averaging incompatible motions.

Our framework uses two training stages. First, a privileged Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) [ 26 ] teacher is trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) [ 24 ] to track a large library of retargeted mocap clips. Second, the teacher is distilled into a codebook student whose input is only a raw human-motion descriptor and proprioceptive history. At deployment, the student outputs robot joint commands in one forward pass, without online retargeting or kinematic adaptation—to our knowledge the first whole-body teleoperation policy that directly maps raw human motion to robot commands without online retargeting or future-reference conditioning. The factorized categorical codebook is learned from clean motion references and allows the student to recover feasible motion prototypes from noisy, partial, or OOD observations.

Our contributions are:

Low-latency retargeting-free whole-body teleoperation. We directly map raw human full-body motion to robot joint commands in one forward pass, removing online retargeting and kinematic adaptation from deployment.

A discrete motion prior for distribution shift and partial observation. We introduce a factorized categorical codebook of full-body motion primitives that maps partial or OOD observations to feasible prototypes before action prediction.

Simulation and real-robot evaluation. On a Unitree G1, our method outperforms prior human-to-humanoid and whole-body trackers in tracking accuracy, OOD robustness, and latency. The same checkpoint transfers to real-robot control driven by virtual reality, motion capture, text-to-motion, and monocular video without task-specific fine-tuning.

1. Low-latency retargeting-free whole-body teleoperation. We directly map raw human full-body motion to robot joint commands in one forward pass, removing online retargeting and kinematic adaptation from deployment.

2. A discrete motion prior for distribution shift and partial observation. We introduce a factorized categorical codebook of full-body motion primitives that maps partial or OOD observations to feasible prototypes before action prediction.

3. Simulation and real-robot evaluation. On a Unitree G1, our method outperforms prior human-to-humanoid and whole-body trackers in tracking accuracy, OOD robustness, and latency. The same checkpoint transfers to real-robot control driven by virtual reality, motion capture, text-to-motion, and monocular video without task-specific fine-tuning.

# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Humanoid teleoperation and online retargeting

Early systems mainly used inverse kinematics, task-space retargeting, model predictive control, and whole-body control to convert human motion into feasible robot commands online [ 12 , 20 , 5 , 25 ] .
Recent learning-based methods have expanded teleoperation input interfaces—from RGB and VR to human shadowing, scalable data collection, and isomorphic cockpits—and have made real-time whole-body teleoperation practical [ 10 , 9 , 7 , 38 , 2 ] .
Despite this progress, most still rely on an online retargeting or target-generation stage before control, which improves feasibility but adds latency and may fail when targets are delayed, discontinuous, or dynamically infeasible.

## II-B Direct human-to-robot control

A more direct alternative maps human observations to robot actions without an explicit retargeting module [ 9 , 15 ] .
For instance, ExtremControl [ 36 ] constructs robot-space link targets through an online, morphology-dependent Cartesian mapping based on human–robot body scales, shoulder locations, limb lengths, and fixed foot offsets.
However, such hand-designed or directly regressed mappings remain vulnerable to the distribution shift between clean training references and real deployment observations [ 28 ] : because robot actions must satisfy balance, contact, and morphology constraints, they can behave unreliably once inputs depart from their training or calibration support.
In contrast, our policy learns the human–robot morphology mapping jointly with control directly from human-frame full-body observations, retaining the low-latency benefit of direct control while using a learned primitive prior to constrain action prediction toward plausible whole-body behavior.

## II-C Whole-body humanoid motion tracking

Adversarial motion priors, latent skill spaces, and large-scale tracking policies have enabled diverse whole-body motion tracking for simulated characters and humanoids [ 22 , 21 , 33 , 16 , 17 , 4 , 39 , 14 , 11 ] .
General systems such as GMT further improve reference tracking through adaptive sampling and MoE policies [ 3 ] .
These methods typically require dense robot-frame references at runtime, often supplied by an external retargeter in teleoperation.
In contrast, our method uses robot references only during teacher policy training; the deployed student directly maps human observations to robot commands.

## II-D Motion priors and discrete primitives

Motion priors are widely used to regularize high-dimensional motion generation and control.
Continuous latent models, including conditional Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), learn compact spaces for physically valid character motions [ 35 , 8 ] , while phase-based and local-motion representations organize motion to improve prediction and control [ 31 , 29 ] .
For teleoperation, continuous regression can transmit corrupted observations or average multiple plausible full-body completions into infeasible motion.
Discrete representation learning, including vector-quantized autoencoders [ 34 ] , instead maps inputs to a finite learned code set and favors motion patterns supported by training data.
We use this property within the deployed policy: the codebook is supervised by clean full-body motion and acts as a denoising and completion prior before robot-action prediction.

2026-10-07.title: CUSP: CUSUM-Governed Survival Hazard Alarms at the Perception Onset for Off-Road Navigation
2026-10-07.authors: Inuk Kang , Seung-Woo Seo
2026-10-07.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract:
Off-road navigation exposes a robot to potentially hazardous terrain en route.
Although learning-based navigation uses safety
supervision to choose which path to drive, it provides no runtime
alarm when the robot following that path is heading into danger.
Such an alarm must be learned from field logs, where human
intervention preempts the failure and the failure itself is therefore
never observed. The human judges driving unsafe early but typically
intervenes only once failure is clearly near, so the intervention
marks that judgment late. That earlier judgment is what a runtime alarm
must detect, yet no prior intervention-supervised method has targeted
it. To address this problem, we introduce CUSP ( CU SUM-governed S urvival model of the P erception onset), a model-agnostic runtime hazard alarm
that learns this moment from intervention-terminated logs. “Cusp” is a word for the point at which one state is about to
turn into another, and the moment we target is exactly such a cusp:
the point at which safe driving turns unsafe in a human’s judgment.
We call this point the perception onset and annotate it separately
from the intervention. A visual hazard head is trained on the annotated
onset with a discrete-time survival objective so that driving with and
without an onset both supervise the head, and a CUSUM accumulates the
predicted onset risk into alarms. We evaluate CUSP at five unseen sites, two
autonomous and three teleoperated, with 142 events and every method
tuned to the same rate of ten false alarms per hour. CUSP detected 85
events compared to 26 for the best of nine adapted baselines, and the
margin comes from hazards to which every signal in the navigation
model is blind.
2026-10-07.introduction:
The safety issue in learning-based off-road navigation is handled
within the navigation policy. Visual methods [ 1 , 2 ] predict how the terrain will affect the robot from the camera image ahead. Experience-based methods [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] learn
that outcome from the robot’s own driving. Uncertainty-aware
models [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] raise the cost of terrain they
have not seen. Risk-aware planners [ 9 ] optimize the tail of
the cost distribution, and learned policies score sampled
trajectories with a critic [ 10 ] or push them away from
estimated obstacles [ 11 ] . In every case, the safety issue is
addressed before a path is committed to by choosing among
candidates. Once the robot is driving the chosen path, however, no
component judges whether continuing it is still safe, and even when every
candidate is hazardous, the navigation model still selects the least
hazardous one and continues to generate paths without any signal that the
situation has changed (Fig. 1 ). The navigation
model therefore leaves a gap at runtime that only an alarm can fill,
and none of these methods raises one.

Runtime failure detection has recently been studied for manipulation
and vision–language–action policies [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] , but under bounded episodes with observable outcomes and
repeatable resets. Continuous off-road driving offers neither. A run
has no natural endpoint, and failures cannot be reproduced at will.
Simulation has advanced considerably, yet it still does not capture
the full range of robot–terrain interaction, and a real rollover or
immobilization can end a field campaign. What the logs contain
instead is the human’s intervention, which preserves the approach to
a hazard while censoring the failure it prevents, so interventions
are far more plentiful than failures.

Prior work has used these interventions as supervision. LaND [ 17 ] predicts the upcoming intervention from the current observation, and
PAAD [ 18 ] predicts failure states along a planned path, but both
targets are late: the intervention arrives only after the human has
recognized the hazard and reacted, and the failure state comes later
still.

We instead target the moment at which the human’s judgment shifts
from safe to unsafe to continue, and we call this moment the perception onset . The intervention does not mark this moment,
because by the time the human takes over, the robot has already been
in a state severe enough to require intervention for some time. The
human may watch the situation develop before deciding that
intervention is necessary, so a label anchored at the intervention
describes driving that has been unsafe for a while rather than
driving that is turning unsafe. The onset is a human-dependent label
rather than an objective safety boundary, but a runtime alarm
should reproduce this judgment, and the onset precedes the
intervention-based targets discussed above.

Two properties of field logs shape the alarm. Most of the recording
captures uneventful driving, and the few onsets it contains
are sparse. Discrete-time survival analysis [ 19 , 20 ] uses both kinds of record. It models the probability that the onset
falls in each upcoming interval given that it has not occurred yet.
So a segment that reaches an onset supervises when it happened and a
segment that ends without one supervises that it had not happened
yet. A CUSUM [ 21 ] then converts the predicted risk into an
alarm. It accumulates the excess over the nominal level frame by
frame, so isolated spikes decay and only a sustained rise reaches the
threshold.

CUSP ( CU SUM-governed S urvival model of the P erception onset) implements this in two parts. A lightweight
hazard head over frozen vision-foundation features estimates an
onset-risk score at every frame. A one-sided CUSUM then accumulates
that score into an alarm, with the threshold set from the site’s own
normal driving to meet a chosen false-alarm rate. Unlike prior intervention-supervised
alarms [ 17 , 18 , 22 ] , CUSP is supervised by the human’s
unsafe-to-continue judgment itself and treats the onset as a
time-to-event target rather than a binary label. To our knowledge, it
is the first runtime alarm to annotate this onset separately from
the intervention and learn it as a time-to-event target.

We make three contributions.

We define the perception onset , the moment at which the
human judges continued autonomy unsafe, and annotate it separately
from the intervention, which no intervention-supervised alarm has
done before.

We propose CUSP, which supervises a visual hazard head on the
onset with a discrete-time survival objective and turns the predicted
onset risk into alarms with a one-sided CUSUM at a false-alarm rate
set from the site’s normal driving.

We show at five unseen sites under a common target false-alarm budget
that CUSP detects 85 of 142 events against 26 for the best of nine
adapted baselines.

2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Safety in Off-Road Navigation

The traversability and policy methods surveyed in
Sec. I decide which path to take, and none of
them judges whether the path already committed to remains safe to
continue. Vehicle-centric monitors based on zero-moment-point
criteria [ 23 ] and terramechanic assurance [ 24 ] rest on modeled criteria and each targets one hazard mechanism, and
anomaly-based traversability estimation [ 25 ] flags terrain that differs from previously traversed terrain, but
novelty and hazard do not coincide, since unfamiliar terrain may be
safe and familiar terrain may become unsafe through robot–terrain
interaction. None of these approaches uses the human’s judgment as
supervision.

## II-B Supervision for Learned Runtime Alarms

Runtime alarms for learned manipulation and vision–language–action
policies detect task-contextual anomalies [ 12 ] or flag failure
from task progress, calibration on successful rollouts, action
distributions, or internal representations [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] – all on finite-horizon rollouts with an explicit end and a
success or failure label, which continuous off-road driving lacks.

What off-road driving does have is the human’s intervention.
LaND [ 17 ] predicts the upcoming intervention from the current
observation and candidate actions; PAAD [ 18 ] defines binary
failure states and predicts future failure states from perception and a
planned path. GAFT [ 22 ] adapts a vision foundation model on
frames from intervention-verified approach runs, labeled by outcome as
binary hazard. All three anchor the label to the intervention or its outcome that occurs after the human
has already recognized the hazard. So the label is late by at least
the time the human takes to decide that intervention is necessary,
and no intervention-supervised method annotates the earlier moment at
which the human first judged continued autonomy unsafe.

## II-C Survival Analysis and Sequential Change Detection

Survival analysis models time to an event while retaining observations
that end without the event as right-censored information, and in
discrete time the hazard is the probability that the event occurs in an
interval given that it has not occurred earlier [ 19 , 20 ] . OSCAR [ 26 ] recently applied it to robot navigation
with an obstacle clearing as the event, whereas CUSP takes the
human-annotated perception onset as its event rather than the physical
outcome that intervention makes unavailable.

CUSUM [ 21 ] detects sustained change by accumulating evidence for
a post-change distribution and resetting when nominal evidence
dominates, with classical optimality results under specified change
models [ 27 , 28 ] . CUSP neither treats its learned score
as a likelihood ratio nor invokes these guarantees, but standardizes the score against the site’s normal driving, accumulates sustained elevations, and selects the threshold empirically from that driving.

2026-10-07.title: Multi-Robot Multi-Goal Motion Planning with Stochastic Skills
2026-10-07.authors: William Schnyder , Valentin N. Hartmann , Stelian Coros
2026-10-07.abstract:
As robots are increasingly deployed in groups and share workspaces to execute real-world tasks, planning their concurrent motions around complex manipulation skills becomes essential.
These skills involve continuous physical execution and may exhibit stochastic behavior, resulting in variable execution times and uncertain continuous trajectories.
Existing planners either limit execution to single-robot scenarios, rely on open-loop paths, or use post-hoc scheduling that prevents dynamic coordination.
In this paper, we address this gap by integrating stochastic skills into sampling-based multi-robot planning by formulating the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) over a multi-modal composite roadmap.
For stochastic skills, solving the MDP yields a reactive policy that allows controllable robots to dynamically adapt their motions in response to other robots’ execution of manipulation skills.
By resolving skill uncertainty directly at planning time, this approach avoids the pessimism of conservative baselines and unlocks robust, dynamic multi-robot coordination.
Code for the planners is available at www.vhartmann.com/stochastic-skills .
2026-10-07.introduction:
In modern industrial and automated environments, maximizing throughput is a central objective. This naturally drives the adoption of multi-robot systems, where several robots share a single workspace to execute tasks in parallel rather than in sequence.
Realizing this gain requires reasoning jointly about the motion of all robots and the tasks they must complete, since robots operating in the same space can block, delay, or collide with one another.
Relying on decoupled approaches, such as prioritized planning, avoids the complexity of the composite state space but often recovers only a fraction of the achievable throughput.

While motion planners excel at collision-free navigation, real-world tasks like grasping involve complex physical contact dynamics.
To abstract this, robots typically execute tasks as skills driven by feedback controllers or learned policies, rather than following purely geometric paths.
Integrating these skills into a multi-robot planner presents two major challenges.
First, a skill involves a continuous physical execution governed by an autonomous low-level controller that the motion planner cannot steer.
Consequently, while the skill-executing robot acts as an uncontrollable dynamic agent during skill execution, the planner actively coordinates the remaining controllable robots to operate safely in the shared workspace.
Second, physical skills are inherently stochastic .
In real-world assembly tasks, uncertainty requires the controller to adjust, leading to variable execution times (e.g., a fast grasp vs. a slower one) or spatial trajectory variations.
Rather than ignoring this uncertainty until execution, our planner models skills as stochastic distributions.
As a result, a single deterministic path is no longer sufficient.
Coordinating concurrent motion around these variable outcomes requires computing a closed-loop policy specifying how surrounding robots should dynamically react.

The multi-modal multi-robot multi-goal (MRMG) formulation of Hartmann et al. [ 1 ] provides composite-space planners for multi-robot problems.
However, it assumes purely geometric planning and cannot handle the uncertain execution of real-world skills.
To address this gap, we extend MRMG planning to integrate skills natively at planning time.

Within this framework, we treat deterministic skill planning as a noise-free special case.
As skill uncertainty increases, open-loop deterministic plans fail.
To solve planning problems in stochastic environments, we formulate the problem as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) over a multi-modal composite-space roadmap, and compute a reactive policy that minimizes expected cost and allows controllable robots to adapt their motions in real time as skills execute.

We evaluate our framework across three experimental settings.
First, we validate the native integration of skills into multi-robot planning under nominal, deterministic execution, comparing how different underlying planner architectures handle continuous skills.
Second, in environments with stochastic skills, we compare our closed-loop reactive policy against a conservative open-loop baseline to highlight the advantages of real-time adaptation over worst-case scheduling.
Finally, we evaluate our reactive planner on multi-arm manipulation tasks to demonstrate scalability to higher-dimensional composite state spaces.

# II Related Work

## II-A Planning with Manipulation Skills

A skill is a temporally extended, closed-loop behavior whose execution the planner does not steer.
Such behaviors are commonly modeled as options, which assume that the planner only needs to make a decision at the temporal boundaries of the skill [ 2 ] .
In a multi-robot shared workspace, however, this abstraction fails: the planner must continuously coordinate controllable robots to avoid collisions with the autonomously executing skill.

Existing planners compose skills sequentially for a single robot.
Task and Skill Planning (TASP) wraps skill policies in head and tail motion plans [ 3 ] and chains them with a Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) solver, allowing force-controlled skills to be sequenced with kinematic motion [ 4 , 5 ] .
MOSAIC instead lets the skills guide the search via physics simulation, handling stochastic skills by summarizing a batch of rollouts into a success fraction that penalizes graph edge costs to yield a single nominal skill sequence [ 6 ] .

For multiple robots, skills are typically coordinated only after planning.
Multi-Robot Asynchronous Planning and Execution (APEX-MR) produces a turn-based sequential plan in which only one robot moves or executes a skill at a time, with each task solved as a single-robot motion planning problem, and skills entering only through a nominal reference path used for collision checking [ 7 ] .
APEX-MR then recovers parallelism and absorbs timing variations online by post-processing its sequential plan into a temporal plan graph (TPG) [ 8 ] .

## II-B Planning under Uncertainty

Planning under uncertainty is commonly formulated as computing a policy over a discretization of the state space.
The Stochastic Motion Roadmap (SMR) tackles this by randomly sampling configurations and simulating the robot’s motion model to estimate transition probabilities.
This transforms the roadmap into an MDP that can be solved with Dynamic Programming (DP) to maximize the probability of reaching the goal [ 9 , 10 ] .
Incremental algorithms, such as incremental Markov Decision Process (iMDP) and incremental Policy (iPolicy), refine this construction over time by expanding the state space and updating the policy iteratively, yielding anytime solutions that converge to the optimal one [ 11 , 12 ] .

Other approaches make a single open-loop trajectory robust [ 13 ] , or plan in belief space under imperfect state observation [ 14 ] .
While their observability assumptions vary, these methods primarily address environmental uncertainty such as dynamic obstacles, sensing noise, or the motion disturbances of a single controlled robot.

The Anytime Task and Motion Markov Decision Process (ATM-MDP) computes branching task and motion policies for a single robot by coupling a stochastic shortest-path solver with a motion planner [ 15 ] .
To handle uncertainty, ATM-MDP branches on the discrete success or failure of high-level tasks, such as a grasp failing.
In contrast, uncertainty in multi-robot settings has largely been handled by abstracting away continuous motion entirely, relying instead on discrete graphs to solve task allocation or robust scheduling against timing delays and task failures [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] .

Prior work either addresses continuous uncertainty for a single robot or coordinates multi-robot skills through open-loop and post-hoc methods.
Bridging these domains, our framework computes feedback policies for concurrent multi-robot motion, focusing specifically on the execution uncertainty of autonomous skills in a shared workspace rather than general environmental uncertainty.

2026-10-07.title: Model-Based Geometry-Aware Generative Optimization for Constrained Locomotion Planning
2026-10-07.authors: Zhilin He , Xinyuan Wang , Changliu Liu
2026-10-07.abstract:
Constrained Locomotion Planning (CLP) for quadrupeds and humanoids, where robots must satisfy collision avoidance, contact consistency, kinematic feasibility, and support constraints, is challenging under high-dimensional dynamics and highly non-convex environments. Recent Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) approaches recast trajectory optimization as posterior sampling over trajectories, using known dynamics and Monte Carlo rollouts to analytically estimate the denoising score function without demonstration learning. While constrained variants further incorporate feasibility into model-based score rollouts and show promising performance, they are still limited by (1) lacking a task-modulated active constraint geometry that shapes the score direction and reverse stochasticity, and (2) using deterministic DDPM-style reverse transport without adaptive scheduling across different generative transports. Therefore, we introduce Model-Based Geometry-Aware Generative Optimization (2GO) for constrained locomotion, which turns active constraint geometry into executable denoising operators through normal- induced metric shaping, tangent-space stochastic filtering, and CFS-based retraction. 2GO further decouples generative transport from reverse stochasticity through an adaptive diffusion and flow-like schedule. Experiments on constrained quadruped and humanoid locomotion demonstrate strong performance in discrete foothold selection and continuous posture planning, with higher success rates, fewer violations, and improved execution compatibility.

2026-10-07.introduction:
Consider a quadruped crossing sparse stepping stones or a humanoid traversing a narrow obstacle field: the planner must decide a sequence of body motions, foothold or contact choices, and posture references while satisfying collision, kinematic, support, and actuation constraints [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . The challenge is not merely to find a collision-free path, but to produce a dynamically executable reference that remains consistent with contact transitions, hybrid dynamics, and the tracking limitations of the low-level controller [ 4 , 5 ] .

Recent approaches recast locomotion planning as probabilistic inference, using score-based generative models to sample and denoise trajectory posteriors into clean, multimodal behavior trajectories [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Compared with conventional trajectory optimization and Model Predictive Control (MPC) methods, some of which rely on local linearization, prescribed contact schedules, or good initialization and may struggle with multimodal contact choices and non-smooth feasibility boundaries in high-dimensional locomotion [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] , generative approaches can flexibly synthesize trajectories, condition on goals or rewards, and represent high-dimensional multimodal action distributions. However, learned generative policies often rely heavily on demonstrations, and their learned priors alone do not ensure consistency with robot dynamics, environment geometry, or imposed safety constraints.

Model-based approaches address this limitation by leveraging Monte Carlo rollouts under known dynamics to estimate the denoising score function, thereby eliminating the need for demonstration data [ 12 , 13 ] . Recent constrained variants and related diffusion planners further incorporate feasibility into the denoising process through Emerging Barrier (EB) or inexact Augmented Lagrangian Method (iALM) priors, Control Barrier Function (CBF)-constrained projections, and adaptive scheduling of feasibility enforcement [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . Although these methods move beyond post-hoc projection, existing methods remain limited in ( 1 ) explicitly using task-modulated active constraint geometry to shape both denoising refinement and reverse stochasticity, and ( 2 ) coordinating deterministic reverse transport with separately controlled stochastic exploration under a unified adaptive schedule. Here, reverse stochasticity refers to perturbations added to the reverse update, distinct from randomness in candidate sampling. Consequently, task-specific feasible geometry remains underused in directing multimodal exploration and balancing it with deterministic refinement as the local constraint geometry becomes better resolved.

We propose a Model-Based G eometry-aware G enerative O ptimization ( 2GO ) framework (Fig. 2 ) for Constrained Locomotion Planning (CLP), which builds an active constraint geometry from violation proxies and task context to shape model-based denoising refinement through a metric and stochastic exploration through a regularized tangent filter, complemented by optional Convex Feasible Set (CFS)-based correction [ 18 ] . 2GO further extends the deterministic Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) [ 19 ] -style reverse transport used in MBD with separately controlled reverse stochasticity, where task-modulated scheduling balances stochastic exploration and deterministic refinement towards a clean trajectory. Our C ontributions are two-fold:

C1: We develop a geometry-aware reverse process with active-set selection, normal-induced metric shaping, and regularized tangent filtering, explicitly shaping both denoising refinement and stochastic exploration, with CFS-based correction for residual constraint violations.

C2: We formulate a model-based generative reverse update that decouples the transport family from reverse stochasticity, accommodating DDPM, Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) [ 20 ] , and flow-like transports under adaptive task-geometry scheduling.

# II Related Work

## II-A Score-Based Generative Models for Robot Motion Planning

Existing approaches on score-based generative models for robot motion planning aim to obtain a feasible trajectory by learning the score function from demonstration data and then sampling from a posterior over trajectory distributions [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] . Current works further adapt to constrained environments through weighted penalty, or augmented Lagrangian methods [ 24 , 25 ] , and projection to safe sets within the generative reverse process [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] , and real-time control for deployment [ 29 , 7 , 6 ] . While such methods improve safety, they still rely on large-scale demonstrations and do not rigorously enforce dynamics.

Model-Based Diffusion [ 12 ] recovers trajectories through model rollouts to enforce dynamics, driving the reversing trajectories toward low-cost solutions without demonstrations. More recent works ensure safety through Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based or CFS-based projections within the model-based rollouts [ 14 , 15 , 30 , 16 ] . However, those methods use projection to satisfy constraints, but do not expose active constraint geometry to the score direction and reverse stochasticity.

## II-B Optimization-Based and Geometry-Aware Planning

Optimization-based locomotion methods formulate locomotion as optimal control problems and solve them with contact-implicit MPC, whole-body models, or sampling-based MPC for high-dimensional quadrupeds and humanoids [ 10 , 11 , 13 , 31 ] . In parallel, geometry-aware motion generation methods such as covariant trajectory optimization [ 32 ] , Riemannian Motion Policies [ 33 ] , and geometric fabrics use task-space metrics, natural-gradient-like updates, or manifold structures to shape robot trajectories and motion policies based on obstacles, tasks, and environments [ 34 , 35 , 36 ] .

While these methods exploit models and geometric structure for trajectory optimization and motion-policy generation, we apply geometry-aware shaping to denoising refinement and reverse stochasticity within a model-based generative planner.
