2026-10-07.title: StairVLA: Stage-Aware Hierarchical Action Generation for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-07.authors: Shangyuan Yuan , Xinda Qi , Yujiang Pu , Wenliang Guo , Xiaobo Tan
2026-10-07.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly rely on diffusion- or flow-matching-based action heads to generate continuous robot actions. These action heads typically process the denoising trajectory in a largely uniform manner. However, we observe that the conditioning focus naturally shifts across denoising stages: early stages combine language instructions and visual observations to establish a coarse action trajectory, whereas later stages place greater emphasis on current visual observations for action alignment. Based on this insight, we introduce StairVLA, a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework that uses partially denoised actions as a natural interface between coarse long-horizon action generation and local refinement. A high-level VLA performs early denoising to produce a reusable long-horizon partially denoised action trajectory, while a lightweight refiner operates at a higher frequency to refine local action chunks using the latest observations. This design amortizes expensive high-level VLA computation while preserving frequent closed-loop correction. On LIBERO, our GR00T-style instantiation improves average success from 96.5% to 97.8% while reducing amortized inference latency from 115.0 ms to 44.2 ms per action chunk. More broadly, across two VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot tasks, StairVLA consistently reduces inference cost while maintaining strong task performance. Project page: https://dicomsky.github.io/projects/stairvla
2026-10-07.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of robot manipulation tasks ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , combining vision-language understanding with generative action heads to translate multimodal context into continuous robot actions ( Black et al., 2024 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) . Specifically, these diffusion- or flow-matching-based action heads are conditioned on language instructions, visual observations, and robot states to progressively transform noise into executable action trajectories ( Chi et al., 2025 ) . Despite this progressive generation process, multimodal conditioning is typically applied throughout the entire denoising trajectory, leaving open whether different types of conditioning information should always be processed together during action generation.

Intuitively, language instructions typically specify task intent that remains stable over many control steps, whereas visual observations and robot states continuously change during execution. Task-level information therefore need not be processed as frequently as the feedback required for precise closed-loop control. Existing hierarchical VLAs exploit this temporal asymmetry by processing high-level information at a lower frequency and communicating it to higher-frequency controllers through subgoals, waypoints, macro-actions, or learned representations ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026 ) . Such hierarchies are typically introduced through externally designed representations or model components. This leads to our central question: can such a hierarchy arise directly from the generative action process itself?

In practice, we observe that the denoising trajectory itself already exhibits such a structure. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , substantial action structure emerges well before denoising is complete, while the interaction between evolving action and multimodal conditioning continues to change throughout denoising stages. Intermediate actions are therefore not merely noisy versions of the final prediction: they already encode meaningful structure, even as subsequent denoising continues to reshape them toward execution. This reveals a natural stage dependence in generative VLA action formation, with different denoising stages serving distinct functional roles.
This behavior is also consistent with the coarse-to-fine progression commonly observed in generative denoising ( Balaji et al., 2022 ; Falck et al., 2025 ) .

This observation suggests a direct way to exploit the hierarchy already present in denoising: expensive task conditioning can be concentrated in less frequent early-stage generation, while later stages perform frequent local refinement using up-to-date observations. However, this separation raises a key challenge: how can the refiner preserve task information without repeatedly processing the full instruction?
Our key insight is that partially denoised actions themselves can bridge the two stages. By the end of early denoising, they already encode task-relevant action structure while remaining open to further refinement. The low-level refiner can therefore operate directly on these intermediate actions together with the latest observation, preserving high-level task information without repeatedly processing the full instruction.

Based on this insight, we introduce StairVLA , a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework. A high-level VLA performs the early denoising stages over a long-horizon action trajectory and outputs partially denoised actions that are cached across multiple control steps. For each local chunk, a lightweight refiner takes the corresponding local action segment together with the latest observation and cached high-level context, and completes the remaining refinement before execution. This allows expensive task-conditioned generation to be reused across multiple control steps while keeping local actions responsive to the evolving environment. Importantly, the two stages communicate directly through intermediate states of the generative action trajectory, rather than through an externally designed action abstraction.

We evaluate our approach across two VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot manipulation tasks. On LIBERO, our GR00T-style instantiation improves average success from 96.5% to 97.8% while reducing amortized inference latency from 115.0 ms to 44.2 ms per action chunk, with consistent performance-efficiency gains on a π \pi -style VLA backbone. Although performance gradually degrades as the reuse horizon increases, further analysis shows that StairVLA maintains strong performance over longer high-level reuse horizons than prior hierarchical VLA methods.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We reveal stage dependence in generative VLA action formation, showing that task-relevant action structure emerges progressively while the role of multimodal conditioning evolves throughout denoising.

We introduce StairVLA, a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework that uses partially denoised actions as a natural interface between coarse long-horizon action generation and local observation-conditioned refinement.

We validate the proposed design across two generative VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot tasks, demonstrating substantially reduced inference cost while maintaining strong task performance.

1. We reveal stage dependence in generative VLA action formation, showing that task-relevant action structure emerges progressively while the role of multimodal conditioning evolves throughout denoising.

2. We introduce StairVLA, a stage-aware hierarchical action generation framework that uses partially denoised actions as a natural interface between coarse long-horizon action generation and local observation-conditioned refinement.

3. We validate the proposed design across two generative VLA backbones, simulation benchmarks, and real-robot tasks, demonstrating substantially reduced inference cost while maintaining strong task performance.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Unified VLA models typically map language instructions, visual observations, and robot states into action sequences within a single policy. Recent VLA models further adopt generative action heads based on diffusion or flow matching to produce continuous actions ( Black et al., 2024 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) . These methods commonly use action chunking, predicting a sequence of future actions rather than a single-step action to improve temporal consistency and reduce policy invocation frequency ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) . However, action chunking introduces an inherent horizon trade-off: short chunks require frequent invocation of computationally expensive VLMs, while long chunks weaken closed-loop feedback and real-time correction during execution ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Therefore, processing different information and generating actions at a single temporal scale may be unnecessarily restrictive.

Recent works increasingly adopt hierarchical structures to bridge high-level task understanding and low-level robot control. Earlier methods use explicit intermediate goals to guide low-level policies, such as subgoals, waypoints, keypoints, or language sub-instructions ( Hu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) . More recent works further integrate this hierarchy into the model architecture and explore different high-to-low-level interfaces, including VLM tokens, learned features, discrete macro-actions, and coarse action representations ( Cui et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) . Other dual-system approaches focus more explicitly on temporal organization, using event-driven high-level updates or allowing different levels to operate at different frequencies ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . Despite their different forms, these methods highlight a common design question in hierarchical VLA: how should high-level task intent be transferred to low-level action generation? Rather than using manually designed or learned interfaces, we directly leverage intermediate states formed during action generation as a natural high-to-low-level interface.

Diffusion- and flow-based generation progressively transforms noise into executable actions. In both generative modeling and robot policies, prior works assign different denoising experts to different sampling stages to better accommodate stage-specific generation requirements ( Balaji et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Reuss et al., 2025 ; Du et al., 2026 ; Niu et al., 2026 ) . Another line of work reuses partially denoised trajectories or constructs better warm starts to reduce redundant sampling and control latency ( Høeg et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . Our method further uses partially denoised actions to transfer task intent across stages, enabling high-level coarse action generation and local refinement to use different conditioning and operate at different frequencies.

2026-10-07.title: CoRE: Learning Collaboration-Role Experts for Decentralized Collaborative Manipulation with One Policy
2026-10-07.authors: Yanan Zhou , Zhaoyan Qian , Zihao Li , Mingyuan Ba , Ranpeng Qiu , Weiming Zhi
2026-10-07.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract: Collaborative manipulation requires robots to perform complementary actions as interactions unfold. We study single-policy decentralized collaboration: every robot runs the same policy from its visual observations and proprioception, without task prompts, identity labels, or inter-robot messages. The challenge is to learn complementary team behaviors within shared parameters and select appropriate actions from each robot’s local observations. We introduce CoRE, which learns Co llaboration- R ole E xperts from pooled multi-task, multi-robot demonstrations. Fused appearance and geometry provide local interaction evidence. Query-conditioned cross-attention experts provide adaptable prediction paths, which a local router combines at each action-chunk position. During training, an action–expert alignment loss supervises expert selection using relative forced-route prediction errors against demonstrations under fixed inputs, without role labels. Across simulation benchmarks, CoRE achieves the highest average performance among evaluated decentralized methods. Physical experiments demonstrate effective collaboration across diverse manipulation tasks and robustness to partner delays and slowdowns. Project page: https://aus.bot/research/core/ .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Imitation learning of visuomotor policies is enabling individual robots to acquire increasingly diverse manipulation skills. Yet many real-world tasks require multiple robots, such as moving large furniture or performing collaborative assembly. A common approach is centralized control, which aggregates observations from all robots in a single controller and generates actions for the entire team. Everyday human collaboration suggests another possibility. People often coordinate without discussing each action, using visible changes in the object and their partners’ behavior to adjust their movements and timing. This motivates learning decentralized collaboration from demonstrations.

In Fig. 1 , panel (a) centralizes team observations and action prediction, whereas panel (b) assigns a separate policy to each robot. Sequential Asymmetric Imitation (SAI) [ 1 ] learns coupled policies that collaborate from local observations without communication. Panels (c) and (d) instead share one policy across robots. As tasks or team composition change, parameter sharing provides a single model to update and deploy throughout the team. Panel (c) additionally uses explicit coordination inputs, such as exchanged capability descriptors [ 2 ] . We study single-policy decentralized collaboration in panel (d): each robot predicts its own actions from visual observations and proprioception, without task prompts, robot identities, role labels, or inter-robot messages.

This setting requires a shared policy to produce complementary behaviors as the interaction unfolds. During an object handover, the same robot may first maintain its grasp, then offer the object to a partner, and finally release it. The appropriate action depends on the progress of the interaction rather than robot identity alone. We refer to this interaction-dependent action responsibility as a collaboration role . Learning from pooled multi-task, multi-robot demonstrations requires both preserving the behaviors needed for different responsibilities and selecting appropriate actions from local observations. Demonstrations specify actions, but not how to organize and select these behavioral capabilities.

To address this challenge, we introduce Collaboration-Role Experts (CoRE). Cross-attention experts provide separately adaptable paths for complementary behaviors within a shared action-chunking policy, while a local router selects their contributions from appearance–geometry evidence and action queries. During training, action–expert alignment compares forced-route predictions from the full decoder against demonstrations under fixed inputs. Their relative errors guide expert selection alongside imitation, without role labels.

CoRE achieves the highest average performance among evaluated decentralized methods across three simulation benchmarks, including 84.2% success on RoboFactory [ 3 ] . Real-world experiments achieve 91.3% success across five tasks spanning coupled motion, asymmetric cooperation, and sequential placement. Sharing comparisons and ablations examine team-demonstration sharing and expert selection. Routing visualizations show expert reuse across robots and changes across stages; partner perturbations test robustness to delays and slowdowns.

Our contributions are as follows.

We formulate single-policy decentralized collaboration as a visuomotor imitation learning problem. Multi-task, multi-robot demonstrations teach complementary team behaviors to one policy, which each robot runs independently to predict collaborative actions from local observations.

We formulate single-policy decentralized collaboration as a visuomotor imitation learning problem. Multi-task, multi-robot demonstrations teach complementary team behaviors to one policy, which each robot runs independently to predict collaborative actions from local observations.

We introduce CoRE, which organizes complementary behaviors through cross-attention experts and uses action–expert alignment to supervise local routing. Demonstrations thereby guide both action learning and expert selection for the current collaboration requirements.

We validate the performance advantages of one shared policy through simulation benchmarks and physical experiments, and demonstrate robustness to partner pauses and slowdowns across coupled, asymmetric, and sequential collaboration.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Visuomotor policy learning. Regression-based visuomotor policies predict action chunks for bimanual manipulation [ 4 ] ; Diffusion Policy models multimodal action sequences [ 5 ] ; and π 0 \pi_{0} combines pretrained vision–language representations with continuous action generation across robot embodiments [ 6 ] . StereoPatch strengthens spatial perception through appearance–geometry fusion [ 7 ] . At deployment, PATCH monitors action-conditioned local visual changes to trigger intervention and policy resumption [ 8 ] . These advances provide foundations for action prediction, spatial perception, and execution monitoring. CoRE studies how to learn complementary team behaviors within one policy and select actions from each robot’s local observations.

Collaborative manipulation. Cooperative impedance control regulates object motion and internal forces [ 9 ] , while local force feedback can support collaboration without explicit communication [ 10 ] . TriManPolicy retimes demonstrations to train a centralized visuomotor policy that jointly controls three arms [ 11 ] . Learned collaboration also uses Gaussian scene representations in GauDP [ 12 ] , partner-behavior embeddings in LatentToM [ 13 ] , and collaborative latents conditioned on local images and task instructions in CLS-DP [ 14 ] . MIMIC-D jointly trains distinct diffusion policies for decentralized coordination [ 15 ] ; SAI trains separate coupled policies through a sequential partner-training curriculum [ 1 ] . CHORUS executes copies of one vision–language–action policy without inter-robot communication, using robot-identifying prompts [ 16 ] . CoRE learns complementary team behaviors through shared collaboration-role experts, supervising their selection with demonstrated-action errors. Each robot selects expert contributions based on its local observations.

Mixture-of-experts learning. Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models allocate capacity through input-dependent expert combinations [ 17 ] . Sparse gating [ 18 , 19 ] and expert-choice routing [ 20 ] scale conditional computation by selecting which inputs and experts interact. Sparse Diffusion Policy applies expert modularity to robotic action prediction [ 21 ] . The central issue for CoRE is how to select experts for the current collaborative action. Existing routing guidance includes pretrained observation–action latents in LAR-MoE [ 22 ] , semantic concept priors in CoRDE [ 23 ] , and vision-teacher targets in TGR-MoE [ 24 ] . Expert–router coupling uses proxy-token activations to align routing with expert capabilities [ 25 ] ; alternative routes have also been evaluated through next-token predictions [ 26 ] . CoRE compares the shared decoder’s forced-route predictions against demonstrations under fixed inputs. Their relative errors supervise each action query’s routing during imitation learning, linking expert selection to complementary action requirements without a separate teacher or role labels.

2026-10-07.title: Seeing Through the Displaced Frame: Privileged Noise Distillation for Vision-Force Precision Assembly
2026-10-07.authors: Ching-Hsiang Chang , Tzu-Yu Chuang , Yi-Hsiu Lee , Yi-Ting Chen , Yuan-Fu Yang , Min Sun
2026-10-07.abstract: Pose error in precision assembly can corrupt not only what a robot observes but also the coordinate frame in which it acts. On the FORGE benchmark, the official state-based policy succeeds in 97 % 97\% to 99 % 99\% of episodes with the true pose but only 32 % 32\% to 60 % 60\% at the benchmark’s σ = 5 \sigma=5 mm pose-noise setting. The same estimated pose enters the observation and anchors the action frame , making the offset unidentifiable from proprioceptive state alone before contact. We supply this missing information during training in two ways. A privileged teacher observes the offset in simulation, while clean demonstrations can instead be relabelled into the displaced frame in closed form. The deployed student is trained with behaviour cloning followed by one DAgger round and receives only noisy state, a raw wrench window, and two RGB cameras at test time. On the unmodified FORGE tasks, the teacher-route student maintains 92 % 92\% to 99 % 99\% success across σ = 0 \sigma=0 to 5 5 mm, while six non-privileged baselines fall to 2 % 2\% to 80 % 80\% . A matched behaviour-cloning experiment isolates the source of this robustness. With the same student architecture, data budget, and training procedure, demonstrations generated without offset access yield only 31.5 % 31.5\% success at σ = 5 \sigma=5 mm, whereas privileged and relabelled demonstrations reach 88.7 % 88.7\% and 95.8 % 95.8\% . Deployed zero-shot on a Franka, the student reaches 83.3 % 83.3\% pooled success at σ = 5 \sigma=5 mm against 34.4 % 34.4\% for the strongest state-based policy. Deployable sensing alone is insufficient. Robustness requires supervision that encodes compensation for the latent frame offset.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Precision assembly policies can approach saturation in simulation when the fixture pose is accurately known. On the three FORGE tasks [ 4 ] , peg insertion with a radial clearance of 0.114 0.114 mm, gear meshing, and M16 nut threading, the official policy reaches 97 % 97\% to 99 % 99\% success. Yet at σ = 5 \sigma=5 mm of fixture-pose noise, the same policy falls to 31.8 % 31.8\% , 49.9 % 49.9\% , and 60.4 % 60.4\% .

This degradation is not simply a perception failure. Section III identifies a more specific mechanism. In FORGE, as in standard task-frame formulations [ 19 ] , the same estimated pose that enters the observation also anchors the action frame . The policy commands displacement relative to the frame defined by that estimate. A single draw of pose noise shifts the observation and command frame together, making the underlying offset unidentifiable from proprioceptive state alone before contact. This coupling turns pose-estimation error into a control-frame offset that is latent to proprioception before contact.

We expose this offset during training and use it to supervise a policy that must compensate from deployable sensory cues at test time (Fig. 1 ). We instantiate this supervision in two ways. A privileged teacher receives clean privileged state together with the offset and generates compensating demonstrations. When the displacement is a known translation, clean demonstrations from the official policy can instead be relabelled into the displaced frame in closed form, removing the need for a privileged teacher. The deployed student uses only noisy state, a raw six-axis wrench history, and two RGB cameras, and is trained with behaviour cloning (BC) followed by one DAgger round. The target may be visible, yet visibility alone does not determine how the policy should compensate for the displaced action frame. A supervised frame corrector provides an additional control by estimating the offset from vision and correcting the frame for the untouched official policy.

Our experiments isolate this distinction. The paired study of Sec. VI-B fixes the student architecture, data volume, training procedure, and evaluation protocol while changing only the source of the demonstrations. In this BC-only comparison on peg, the identical student reaches 31.5 % 31.5\% success at σ = 5 \sigma=5 mm when trained from demonstrations generated without offset access, but 88.7 % 88.7\% and 95.8 % 95.8\% when trained from privileged and relabelled demonstrations. The non-privileged student closely reproduces its teacher’s collapse despite receiving the same deployable sensing. Failure analysis supports the same mechanism. Between 87 % 87\% and 100 % 100\% of its failures involve contact without insertion, and although the target remains visible, the commanded motion stays referenced to the displaced frame. Deployable sensing alone is insufficient. Robust behaviour requires supervision that encodes compensation for the latent frame offset. We make three contributions.

A mechanistic analysis of pose-error failure under a displaced action frame. We show that when the same estimated fixture pose enters the observation and anchors the action frame, the resulting offset is unidentifiable from proprioception before contact. A controlled teacher-swap experiment isolates offset-aware supervision, rather than deployable sensing alone, as the source of robustness.

A mechanistic analysis of pose-error failure under a displaced action frame. We show that when the same estimated fixture pose enters the observation and anchors the action frame, the resulting offset is unidentifiable from proprioception before contact. A controlled teacher-swap experiment isolates offset-aware supervision, rather than deployable sensing alone, as the source of robustness.

Two forms of offset-aware supervision for robust precision assembly. Fixture-offset compensation is encoded either by a state-based reinforcement learning (RL) teacher with access to the true offset or by closed-form relabelling of clean demonstrations from the official policy. BC and DAgger distil this supervision into a student restricted to deployable sensing. Under the primary randomisation-on protocol, the student maintains at least 96.5 % 96.5\% success through σ = 5 \sigma=5 mm, where the official policy falls to 31.8 % 31.8\% to 60.4 % 60.4\% . Relabelled demonstrations recover the benefit across all three tasks, while a learned frame corrector provides an additional control on peg.

Robustness that survives transfer. Under one frozen protocol, the student outperforms six non-privileged baselines, including matched-law noise augmentation and an asymmetric critic with offset access. Deployed zero-shot on a Franka across all three tasks, it reaches 83.3 % 83.3\% pooled success at σ = 5 \sigma=5 mm versus 34.4 % 34.4\% for the strongest state-based policy.

# II Related Work

Simulated contact-rich assembly. Factory [ 1 ] , IndustReal [ 2 ] , and AutoMate [ 3 ] made large-scale simulated assembly practical, increasingly robust to pose error and diverse in geometry. FORGE [ 4 ] adds force-threshold conditioning and trains with pose noise hidden from the policy, exposing the coupling between observation and action frame studied here. We use its three Isaac Lab [ 5 ] tasks without modification. Recent FORGE-family results are not directly matched to this setting. CoRMA [ 6 ] uses a Marvin arm, SI-Diff [ 28 ] retrains on custom assets, FORGE-plus [ 29 ] removes pose noise, while MATCH [ 27 ] and a tactile study [ 30 ] use Factory tasks. We therefore reproduce the unmodified FORGE gyms for comparison, preserving their task assets, action frame, reward, and success criteria.

Privileged distillation and relabelling. Privileged simulator state is commonly distilled into deployable sensing in locomotion [ 10 , 32 ] and driving [ 11 ] . DAgger [ 14 ] addresses covariate shift, while rapid motor adaptation (RMA) [ 17 ] distils a teacher that observes extrinsics. The work of Fuchioka et al. [ 31 ] , whose teacher observes the true peg pose, is the closest precedent. Our privileged variable is instead the error between clean and observed pose, supplied to the actor rather than only the critic [ 18 ] . Our closed-form relabelling shares SPARTN’s [ 24 ] algebra but perturbs the pose estimate , leaving recorded images and forces valid without re-rendering, replayed interventions [ 25 ] , retargeting [ 33 ] , or noise injection [ 22 , 23 ] . SIDO’s pose-channel displacement [ 26 ] is the closest concurrent operation.

Online adaptation and vision-force policies. RMA-style adapters [ 17 ] and CoRMA [ 6 ] infer context from recent history, while residual RL [ 34 ] and InsertionNet [ 35 ] correct nominal insertion poses from vision and force. Section VI-C reimplements both strategies and tests the limitation of history-based offset inference in our setting. Vision-force fusion for insertion is established [ 20 , 15 , 16 , 9 ] . Our student uses ManipForce’s cross-attention primitive [ 9 ] without claiming architectural novelty or attributing the robustness gain to fusion (Sec. VI-E ).

2026-10-07.title: ESP: Energy-Score Policy for One-Step Multimodal Action Generation
2026-10-07.authors: Lilika Makabe , Heecheol Kim , Yasuyuki Matsushita
2026-10-07.abstract: Generative action models based on diffusion and flow matching have been increasingly adopted in vision-language-action (VLA) policies for their ability to capture diverse behaviors, including multiple valid action sequences under the same observation and instruction. Their iterative sampling procedures, however, require repeated network evaluations to generate each action chunk, increasing inference latency in closed-loop control. We propose ESP (Energy-Score Policy), a teacher-free approach that maps policy context and noise directly to an action chunk in a single network evaluation. ESP trains the action head with the energy score rather than mean squared error. Whereas squared-error regression targets the conditional mean, the energy score is strictly proper: its expected value is uniquely minimized by the target distribution. This provides a principled objective for learning multimodal action distributions without iterative sampling, with exact recovery at the population optimum when the model can represent the target distribution. Experiments on both simulation and real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate competitive task success with substantially lower action-generation latency than the flow matching baseline. These results support direct distributional learning as an efficient alternative to iterative generative robot policies. Project page
2026-10-07.introduction:
Diffusion and flow matching models are increasingly used in robot policies, including vision-language-action (VLA) models, to represent diverse behaviors conditioned on observations and instructions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . These models can capture multiple valid action sequences for the same context rather than restrict the policy to a single deterministic prediction. Their standard sampling procedures, however, require repeated network evaluations to transform noise into an action chunk. Therefore, their action generation is inherently time-consuming, motivating faster one-step action generation with a single network evaluation.

We propose ESP (Energy-Score Policy), where we cast conditional action generation as strictly proper distributional regression and generate an action chunk in a single network evaluation (Fig. 1 ).
The proposed ESP predicts the entire multimodal distribution of actions that are valid for a given context. We use the energy-score objective [ 4 , 5 ] ; in expectation over the data, it becomes smallest exactly when the generated actions match the distribution of the training data (demonstrations), and larger for every other distribution. Unlike previous one-step and few-step approaches, such as distillation and consistency-based methods [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] , ESP directly trains on the training data alone in a single stage, with no pretrained teacher, no trajectory or velocity targets, and no auxiliary critic. Different from recent teacher-free generators [ 10 , 11 ] , whose objectives can also be minimized by distributions other than the training one, ESP retains this uniqueness while keeping single-evaluation inference.

To apply ESP to an existing VLA model, we retain its pretrained vision-language backbone and policy conditioning unchanged and replace its action head with our ESP for one-step action generation. The VLM backbone can remain frozen while the ESP action-head parameters are trained without teacher distillation. For each training context, we generate several action chunks from different noise inputs, and the energy score evaluates the generated chunks against the demonstrated chunk and against one another. At inference, one single noise draw produces one action chunk in one network evaluation, without multi-step numerical integration or candidate ranking.

Experiments on synthetic regression and the LIBERO manipulation benchmark as well as real-robot experiments demonstrate that ESP can generate multimodal actions in a single network evaluation and achieves task success comparable to the flow matching baseline with substantially lower action-generation latency. These results establish energy-score training as an effective approach to fast, one-step generative action policies.

Contributions. Our chief contributions are:

We cast conditional action generation as strictly proper distributional regression and propose an energy-score policy (ESP) for action generation.

Unlike diffusion/flow matching policy that requires multi-step integration, our ESP can learn the conditional noise-to-action generation in a single network evaluation, leading to faster action inference, while retaining the competitive task success rate.

With the same action-head architecture, in one-step, ESP achieves a competitive task success rate on LIBERO compared with the multi-step flow matching policy. Increasing the number of action-head parameters further improves the mean success rate given the same inference time budget to the flow matching policy.

1. We cast conditional action generation as strictly proper distributional regression and propose an energy-score policy (ESP) for action generation.

2. Unlike diffusion/flow matching policy that requires multi-step integration, our ESP can learn the conditional noise-to-action generation in a single network evaluation, leading to faster action inference, while retaining the competitive task success rate.

3. With the same action-head architecture, in one-step, ESP achieves a competitive task success rate on LIBERO compared with the multi-step flow matching policy. Increasing the number of action-head parameters further improves the mean success rate given the same inference time budget to the flow matching policy.

# II Related Work

Learning robot actions from demonstrations is a conditional distribution modeling problem: the same observation and instruction can correspond to several valid behaviors. We review multimodal prediction and generative policies, followed by objectives for efficient one-step generation.

Multimodal prediction and generative action policies. Early approaches modeled multimodal conditional distributions with mixture density networks [ 12 ] , conditional latent-variable models [ 13 ] , and conditional adversarial generators [ 14 ] . Generative moment matching networks [ 15 ] train feedforward generators using Gaussian-kernel MMD (Maximum Mean Discrepancy) [ 16 ] . These Gaussian-kernel MMD objectives require selecting a kernel bandwidth, whereas our energy-score objective does not require the kernel-bandwidth hyperparameter. Diffusion and flow matching subsequently emerged as expressive high-dimensional samplers that transport noise to data through a learned denoising process or vector field [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] .

Representing such multimodal, high-dimensional distributions is particularly relevant to robot action prediction, where the same visual observation and language instruction can correspond to several successful behaviors. Diffusion Policy [ 1 ] models action sequences with conditional denoising, while more recent VLAs such as π 0 \pi_{0} [ 2 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 3 ] , GR00T N1 [ 20 ] , and FLOWER [ 21 ] use flow matching to generate action chunks. These methods can represent multimodal action distributions, but require multiple network evaluations. Our work preserves the stochastic & multimodal action representation while achieving action generation only with a single network evaluation.

One-step generation and distributional objectives. Reducing the cost of iterative generation has motivated distillation, consistency training, and objectives designed for few-step or one-step sampling. Distillation methods compress a multi-step model into a shorter sampler [ 6 ] , while consistency models can learn outputs that agree along a diffusion trajectory [ 7 ] . In robot learning, FlowPolicy imposes self-consistency on a flow field [ 8 ] , MeanFlow-VLA learns an average velocity [ 9 ] , and Let It Be Simple retains flow matching while emphasizing the high-noise regime used by one-step inference [ 22 ] .
Drifting methods construct a training target by moving the generator’s own samples toward the data with a data-adaptive drift, then train the generator to match this detached (stop-gradient) target [ 10 , 23 ] .
However, without additional assumptions, even globally minimizing the ideal population drifting loss does not guarantee that the generated distribution matches the data distribution [ 10 ] .

Efficiency alone, however, leaves open how a direct one-step generator should learn a multimodal distribution.
Multiple-choice learning, multiple-hypothesis prediction, and IMLE emphasize the best-matching candidates through hard or relaxed assignments [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . Forward XM follows this candidate-selection principle: for each training example, it evaluates the loss under several sampled noise inputs and updates the generator using the lowest-loss candidate [ 11 ] . While effective, with a fixed finite candidate budget, the hard-min endpoint-distance objective is not, in general, strictly proper: its minimum does not necessarily correspond to the data distribution.

Energy-score training instead follows the statistical lineage of proper scoring rules. The multivariate energy score combines distances to the observation with pairwise distances between generated samples. Under finite first moments, its expected value is uniquely minimized by the data distribution [ 4 ] . DISCO Nets train conditional generators using an energy-score objective and apply them to 3D hand pose estimation from depth images [ 5 ] . We also use this established objective for one-step action generation, scoring the conditional action samples produced by the deployed action head. Minimizing its expected value recovers the target conditional distribution when the model can represent it.

2026-10-07.title: ExoBridge: Learning a Bare Hand to Hand-Worn Exoskeleton Mapping through Human Limb Coupling
2026-10-07.authors: Ruitong Tian , Xianyao Li , Noah B. Wilson , Fang Xu , Eric Jing Du
2026-10-07.abstract: Human video offers a scalable source of experience for dexterous robot learning, but obtaining motion and tactile supervision while preserving bare hand interaction remains challenging. We present ExoBridge, a framework that leverages human limb coupling to learn a bridging function from bare hand video to the motion and tactile state of a sensorized exoskeleton. Our central idea is to use coordinated bimanual behavior to connect an uninstrumented visual source with a measured manipulation interface. During collection, one hand remains bare and provides visual observations, while the opposite hand wears the exoskeleton and supplies synchronized motion and tactile measurements. These paired demonstrations train a temporal visual model to predict fingertip contact, continuous tactile intensity, and relative encoder motion from bare hand video alone. The exoskeleton defines an intermediate state space whose motion coordinates are linked to a dexterous robot hand through existing calibration. Evaluation on 1,215 demonstrations across four manipulation tasks uses held out collection sessions and yields a pooled any contact AUROC of 0.916 and a Pearson correlation of 0.790 for tactile intensity. The learned bridge also predicts relative changes in exoskeleton configuration from bare hand video. These results demonstrate that human limb coupling can turn exoskeleton measurements into supervision for bare hand video, establishing a learned bridge between human visual demonstrations and a robot oriented manipulation interface.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Human manipulation is a useful source of experience for dexterous robot learning, and video can capture it without requiring a robot during every demonstration. Recent methods use human observations together with motion supervision to learn representations and policies that transfer across embodiments [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Bare hand video is particularly attractive because the observed hand can interact with objects without wearing a sensing interface [ 6 ] . However, the resulting images do not directly provide the encoder state and tactile measurements recorded by an interface designed for a robot hand. Connecting these visual observations to a measured manipulation state remains an important step between collecting human video and using it for robot learning.

Motion and tactile supervision address different parts of this problem. Hand tracking and retargeting connect visible motion to a robot configuration, while visual tactile learning associates images with measured contact or pressure [ 1 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . A sensorized exoskeleton brings both signals into one collection interface. DexUMI records encoder motion and fingertip tactile measurements during direct interaction, with an existing mapping between exoskeleton configuration and a target robot hand [ 12 ] . The exoskeleton therefore provides a useful target space. The question is how to learn this state from a visual stream in which the observed hand remains bare.

Our central idea is to use human limb coupling to construct supervision between the two hands. Studies of intermanual coordination describe dependencies between the timing and organization of coordinated actions [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . We use this principle to pair two roles during data collection. One hand supplies the visual observation, while the opposite hand supplies motion and tactile measurements. Rather than prescribing an identical joint trajectory for both hands, we learn the predictive relationship produced by their coordinated execution of the same manipulation objective [ 17 ] . This leads to the central question of this work: How can human limb coupling be used to learn a bridging function from bare hand video to exoskeleton motion and tactile state?

We introduce ExoBridge, shown in Fig. 1 , to learn this mapping from coordinated bimanual demonstrations. The bare left hand interacts with one object copy within the camera view. The right hand wears a sensorized exoskeleton from the DexUMI family and performs a coordinated instance of the same task on a separate copy [ 12 ] . Synchronized recordings pair the bare hand video with the exoskeleton measurements. A temporal visual model learns a tactile mapping that predicts fingertip contact and continuous tactile intensity, together with a motion mapping that predicts changes in encoder configuration relative to the first sampled state. At inference, the model uses only the bare hand RGB stream. The measured target space gives the bridge a concrete output definition, while the existing configuration calibration connects its motion component to a chosen robot hand.

We evaluate the proposed bridge across egg carton opening, lid twisting, soldering tool orientation, and USB insertion. Recordings from each collection session remain together during training and evaluation, so the reported predictions are obtained on held out sessions. Contact discrimination, continuous intensity prediction, and relative motion estimation test complementary outputs of the same mapping framework. The results show predictive contact and intensity information across all four tasks, together with relative motion correspondence that is strongest in active channels. An aligned sequence then illustrates how these outputs describe the same manipulation episode.

Our contributions are threefold.

A cross-hand supervision framework that leverages human limb coupling to learn a mapping from bare hand RGB video to the tactile and relative motion state of a contralateral sensorized exoskeleton.

An empirical characterization of predictively transferable interaction information across coordinated hands, demonstrating contact discrimination, continuous tactile intensity prediction, and relative encoder motion prediction on held out sessions across four manipulation tasks.

A paired dataset of 1,215 coordinated bimanual demonstrations with synchronized RGB, tactile, and encoder measurements, together with session-level splits and evaluation code for reproducible study of cross-hand state prediction.

1. A cross-hand supervision framework that leverages human limb coupling to learn a mapping from bare hand RGB video to the tactile and relative motion state of a contralateral sensorized exoskeleton.

2. An empirical characterization of predictively transferable interaction information across coordinated hands, demonstrating contact discrimination, continuous tactile intensity prediction, and relative encoder motion prediction on held out sessions across four manipulation tasks.

3. A paired dataset of 1,215 coordinated bimanual demonstrations with synchronized RGB, tactile, and encoder measurements, together with session-level splits and evaluation code for reproducible study of cross-hand state prediction.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Human Demonstrations for Dexterous Robot Learning

Human demonstration interfaces provide motion information that can connect human experience to robot control. UMI records manipulation through a portable gripper interface, while DexCap captures wrist and finger motion alongside visual observations and retargets the motion to a robot hand [ 18 , 1 ] . EgoMimic learns from egocentric human and robot demonstrations, and EgoScale uses motion supervision and aligned human and robot data to support transfer from human video [ 2 , 3 ] . These approaches make the representation connecting human observations and robot actions an explicit part of the learning problem [ 19 ] . ExoBridge studies a related mapping at the state estimation level. Its output includes measured fingertip interaction as well as relative motion, and the supervision is supplied by an exoskeleton worn on the opposite hand.

## II-B Wearable Interfaces and Exoskeleton State

Wearable interfaces allow an operator to demonstrate manipulation through direct interaction while recording motion for a target robot [ 20 , 21 ] . DexUMI uses a hand exoskeleton to reduce kinematic mismatch and record encoder and tactile signals [ 12 ] . ExoStart uses sensorized exoskeleton demonstrations to initialize robot learning, while DexEXO studies wearability and hardware alignment for demonstration collection [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] . These systems place the wearable interface in the demonstration process to obtain measurements related to robot manipulation. In ExoBridge, the exoskeleton instead provides the supervised target for a separate bare hand visual stream. Its encoder coordinates define the motion output, and its fingertip sensors define the tactile output. This separates the hand that is observed from the hand that provides the measurements while retaining a target space associated with a robot interface.

## II-C Visual Tactile Estimation and Bilateral Supervision

Visual tactile estimation connects hand appearance and motion to measured interaction [ 27 , 28 ] . PressureVision++ estimates fingertip pressure from RGB images, and EgoPressure studies pressure and hand pose from egocentric observations [ 7 , 8 ] . EgoTac predicts tactile signals from egocentric video, while TouchAnything studies bimanual tactile estimation using visual observations and synchronized sensing [ 29 , 30 ] . These methods motivate learning contact and continuous sensor responses from visual input, with the target representation determined by the available measurements [ 31 , 32 ] .

Obtaining supervision while retaining bare hand appearance is a separate collection problem [ 33 ] . Glove2Hand synthesizes bare hand imagery from sensing glove recordings while retaining the associated physical measurements [ 34 ] . EgoTactile provides a bilateral alternative by pairing a visible bare hand with a synchronized gloved hand outside the camera view [ 35 ] . ExoBridge uses coordinated bimanual supervision to learn a different target: the relative encoder motion and fingertip tactile state of a sensorized exoskeleton during manipulation. The proposed bridging function is therefore defined by both the supervision relationship and the exoskeleton state space to which the video is mapped.

2026-10-07.title: EigenDEXplore: Structured Exploration for Dexterous Manipulation with Human Priors
2026-10-07.authors: Harsh Gupta , Tyler Ga Wei Lum , Changhao Wang , Chuer Pan , C. Karen Liu , Jeannette Bohg , Shuran Song
2026-10-07.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract: Dexterous manipulation poses a challenging high-dimensional optimization problem, as useful behaviors require coordinated motion across many hand joints. In reinforcement learning (RL) and sampling-based trajectory optimization, exploration commonly relies on independent robot joint perturbations, making coordinated behaviors difficult to discover. Prior work reduces this search space for grasp learning using low-dimensional spaces of coordinated joint motions learned from human hand data, but this restricts the expressivity required for general manipulation. Some combine learned and joint-space actions to restore expressivity, but this increases dimensionality and introduces redundancy. We study these effects across diverse manipulation settings, varying action dimensionality, exploration strategy, and the source of human data. Our experiments suggest that human-motion priors are most effective when used to structure exploration rather than change the action representation. Motivated by this finding, we propose EigenDEXplore, which induces correlated exploration by adding perturbations along human-derived eigenvectors to independent joint-space noise, leaving the action space unchanged. Across multiple dexterous hands, EigenDEXplore consistently outperforms joint-space and learned action-space baselines in grasping, in-hand reorientation, and contact-rich manipulation. These gains span unstructured and reference-guided RL, trajectory optimization, and sim-to-real deployment, and are largest in settings with less reward shaping and curriculum design. Project page: eigendexplore.github.io .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Dexterous hands enable versatile grasping, in-hand manipulation, and precise interaction with tools and articulated objects. Discovering these contact-rich behaviors, however, is challenging because effective manipulation relies on highly coordinated finger motions that occupy only a small fraction of the hand’s high-dimensional action space. Reinforcement learning (RL) and sampling-based trajectory optimization commonly explore this space using independent Gaussian perturbations across joints, making it difficult to discover such coordinated behaviors efficiently. As a result, these methods often require substantial computation and carefully engineered rewards, costs, or curricula.

Learning from human hand motion offers a way to capture useful coordination patterns, providing guidance that would otherwise need to be designed for each task. Prior work captures these patterns in low-dimensional action spaces, including linear eigen-spaces learned using PCA ( Ciocarlie et al., 2007 ; Agarwal et al., 2023 ) and nonlinear latent spaces learned using VAEs ( Dimou et al., 2021 ; Dimou et al., 2024 ) . These spaces let the policy directly command coordinated movements such as grasping and twisting (see Fig. 2 ). Sampling actions corresponding to these modes during RL exploration can also provide more informative feedback per sample for policy updates and accelerate learning ( Agarwal et al., 2023 ; Lum et al., 2024 ) . However, these reduced action spaces cannot express the independent joint control required for general manipulation ( Gupta et al., 2026a ) . Another approach combines these learned and independent joint-space actions to restore expressivity ( Gupta et al., 2026b ) , but increases the action dimensionality and introduces redundancy. It remains unclear whether the benefits come from directly controlling coordinated motions, the noise-induced exploration, or changes to action-space dimensionality and expressivity.

To disentangle these effects, we systematically compare action representations and exploration distributions across diverse manipulation tasks and robot hands. These comparisons suggest that the primary benefit of human-motion priors comes from correlated exploration, while action constraints or redundancy can hinder performance. Joint-space actions already allow the policy to express both coordinated and independent joint movements. The difficulty is discovering useful joint combinations, which correlated noise makes easier to sample. Motivated by this finding, we introduce EigenDEXplore , a simple method that incorporates this human-motion prior into the sampling distribution while retaining the original joint-space actions. It combines two noise components: perturbations along the learned PCA directions encourage coordinated motion, while independent joint-space noise maintains exploration coverage. The prior is derived from hand motion recovered from large-scale human video data ( Lightwheel, 2026 ) , without requiring task-specific trajectories. After RL training, the eigenbasis can be discarded and the policy deployed deterministically.

We compare EigenDEXplore with joint-space and learned eigen-space baselines across unstructured RL with SimToolReal ( Kedia et al., 2026 ) and DeXtreme ( Handa et al., 2023 ) , reference-guided bimanual RL with DexMachina ( Mandi et al., 2026 ) , and trajectory optimization with SPIDER ( Pan et al., 2025 ) , spanning six dexterous hands. EigenDEXplore consistently outperforms them, with 34% more consecutive successes in early SimToolReal training, larger gains in extended runs, and 40% more in DeXtreme. These gains transfer to hardware, raising SimToolReal average progress across 4 tasks from 33% to 82% and DeXtreme consecutive successes by 41%. In DexMachina, it improves average object-tracking accuracy by 28% without contact reward shaping or curricula, with larger gains on higher-DoF hands, enabling learning where joint-space sampling struggles or fails. In SPIDER, it reduces retargeting cost by 16% on average across six hands, again most on higher-DoF hands. We also find that large-scale egocentric video ( Lightwheel, 2026 ) yields stronger human-motion priors than smaller, task-focused motion-capture datasets ( Taheri et al., 2020 ; Fan et al., 2023 ) , and validate our choice of retained PCA dimensionality through exploration-distribution experiments.

In summary, our main contribution is EigenDEXplore, a method that guides exploration with human-derived coordination patterns while preserving joint-space actions. We identify correlated exploration as the primary source of improvement and demonstrate the method’s effectiveness across reinforcement learning, trajectory optimization, and sim-to-real deployment. We release benchmarking code, a plug-and-play implementation, and pretrained PCA models for six dexterous hands.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Human priors for manipulation. Human data can guide dexterous manipulation by providing examples of useful behavior and desired outcomes. Demonstrations and pose priors support learning through policy supervision ( Rajeswaran et al., 2018 ; Qin et al., 2022 ; Guzey et al., 2025 ) , initialization ( Bauza et al., 2025 ; Dasari et al., 2023 ) , and reward design ( Mandikal and Grauman, 2021 ) . Hand and object trajectories provide task objectives for RL ( Lum et al., 2025 ; Gupta et al., 2026a ; Mandi et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) and trajectory optimization ( Pan et al., 2025 ; Paliwal et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , allowing robot motions to adapt to embodiment differences and contact dynamics. Procedurally trained controllers can also execute human-derived goals at deployment ( Yin et al., 2025 ; Kedia et al., 2026 ; Gupta et al., 2026b ; Kuang et al., 2026 ) . The success of task guidance from even a single video or demonstration motivates examining how larger human datasets can support learning across tasks.

Action representations for dexterous manipulation. Early studies showed that a few coordinated patterns capture much of the variation in human grasp postures ( Santello et al., 1998 ) , motivating eigen-space grasp planning ( Ciocarlie et al., 2007 ; Ciocarlie and Allen, 2009 ) . Encoding joint coordination in control representations supports RL and transfer in dexterous manipulation ( Agarwal et al., 2023 ; Lum et al., 2024 ; Dimou et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ; Puang et al., 2025 ; Berg et al., 2024 ) and lowers trajectory-optimization cost for a fixed number of sampled trajectories ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . However, low-dimensional eigen-space control can restrict dexterity ( Lum et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , including the fine adjustments needed to establish sufficient contact during tool manipulation ( Gupta et al., 2026a ) . Adding eigen-space residuals to joint-space actions preserves full expressivity and can improve learning over joint-only control despite introducing redundant action coordinates ( Gupta et al., 2026b ) . Reduced dimensionality therefore cannot explain all reported gains, raising the question of how these interfaces shape exploration.

Structure in exploration. These interfaces can turn independent action noise into correlated joint perturbations, confounding the benefits of coordinated commands and coordinated sampling. Temporal correlations ( Raffin et al., 2021 ; Eberhard et al., 2023 ; Hollenstein et al., 2024 ) and policy-derived correlations across actuators ( Chiappa et al., 2023 ) show how structuring exploration noise can improve learning efficiency. Human motion offers such structure, with the source data and learned representation determining which movements are encouraged. Existing priors often use grasp-focused recordings or small task-specific demonstration sets, with learned representations that vary in implementation and dimensionality ( Lum et al., 2024 ; Dimou et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Our study separates the effects of human-motion priors on exploration from their use in the action representation, and examines how source data and prior dimensionality influence manipulation performance.

2026-10-07.title: SMART: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Articulated Object Manipulation via Large-Scale Synthetic Pretraining
2026-10-07.authors: Jicong Ao , Shuhan Jiang , Yuling Zhong , Yanwen Liu , Yuhan Gao , Jiangyuan Zhao , Yang Zhang , Shiqiang Zhu , Chenjia Bai , Xuelong Li
2026-10-07.comment: Technical Report
2026-10-07.abstract:
The ability to interact with articulated objects is essential for embodied intelligent systems, but collecting large-scale real-world demonstrations for these interactions remains challenging due to the precise contact and constraint-following motions involved.
Although simulation provides a promising alternative, existing synthetic data efforts cover limited articulated-object categories, while general-purpose synthesis pipelines lack explicit designs for part-level semantics and articulation constraints, hindering agentic task generation and scalable synthesis of high-quality articulated-manipulation demonstrations.
To bridge this gap, we introduce SMART , a scalable system leveraging
large-scale S ynthesized M anipulation demonstrations for ART iculated-object manipulation.
At its core, we develop SMART-Sim , a simulation platform with articulation-aware design that enables effective task generation and efficient demonstration collection.
Building on SMART-Sim , we apply agentic task generation and design a scalable distributed synthesis system, using them to synthesize SMART-Data , comprising over 1M demonstrations across 44 atomic task types, 5 robot setups, and 2,507 articulated objects.
The vision-language-action (VLA) model pretrained on SMART-Data shows competitive performance on simulation benchmarks
and achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and scalable performance in real-world articulated-object manipulation tasks.
This highlights the potential of synthetic demonstrations in providing effective and scalable supervision for improving VLA model performance in contact-rich articulated-object manipulation.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Articulated objects are ubiquitous in human environments and central to many everyday activities.
Their movable parts enable rich functionality while imposing structured geometric and physical constraints on interactions.
Compared with rigid-object manipulation, articulated-object manipulation requires reasoning about functional parts and joint-constrained motions while maintaining precise and sustained contact throughout the interaction ( Ma et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2025c ; Wang et al., 2025 ) .
Enabling robots to engage in such interactions can facilitate the emergence of intelligent behaviors, making it an important step toward embodied intelligence.

Traditional approaches to articulated-object manipulation often rely on explicit object models, online kinematic estimation, and affordance prediction ( Ma et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Ling et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) , which require task-specific assumptions and limit scalability across diverse objects and long-horizon interactions.
Recently, vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose manipulation ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2025 ) , with their capability largely shaped by the scale, diversity, and quality of training demonstrations ( Black et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025a ; Wu et al., 2026 ) .
Yet such data is still predominantly collected through human teleoperation ( Wu et al., 2025b ; AgiBot-World-Contributors et al., 2025 ) , which is costly and hard to scale.
To alleviate the burden of robot-based data collection, Universal Manipulation Interface ( Chi et al., 2024 ; Zhaxizhuoma et al., 2025 ) and egocentric approaches ( Hoque et al., 2026 ; Kareer et al., 2025 ) have been proposed to collect demonstrations through handheld devices or human-centric embodiments.
However, transferring these demonstrations to robot platforms introduces embodiment mismatches and physical infeasibilities ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) , which can degrade demonstration quality.
These challenges are particularly pronounced in articulated-object manipulation, where effective demonstrations require precise and sustained contact with functional parts while satisfying articulation constraints.
As a result, high-quality real-world demonstrations for articulated-object manipulation remain difficult to collect at scale.

Simulation offers a natural alternative to real-world demonstration collection.
Prior works ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ; Nasiriany et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2023 ) show that simulation can scale demonstration collection at low cost.
Recent systems such as InternData-A1 ( Tian et al., 2025 ) and MolmoBot ( Deshpande et al., 2026 ) further highlight this potential by generating large-scale synthetic datasets for general manipulation and evaluating sim-to-real transfer using only simulated data.
Despite this progress, existing simulation-based datasets for articulated-object manipulation often cover only a narrow range of object categories or remain limited in scale ( Cui et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) .
Although works such as InternData-A1 ( Tian et al., 2025 ) and MolmoBot ( Deshpande et al., 2026 ) demonstrate sim-to-real transfer across several manipulation tasks, their synthetic data covers only a limited range of articulated-object categories.
In addition, their general-purpose demonstration synthesis pipelines do not explicitly account for part-level semantics and articulation constraints, leading to limited adoption of agentic task generation and challenges in synthesizing high-quality demonstrations for articulated-object manipulation.
Consequently, large-scale synthetic data for VLA learning and sim-to-real transfer across diverse articulated-object manipulation remains underexplored.

To fill this gap, we propose SMART ,
a scalable system leveraging S ynthetic M anipulation data for ART iculated object manipulation.
We first introduce SMART-Sim ,
a simulation platform with specialized articulation-aware designs for rapid task specification and effective motion generation.
We further employ agentic task generation to create articulated-object manipulation tasks with varying complexity and temporal horizons. Combined with our distributed data synthesis system, this enables efficient and scalable generation of articulated manipulation tasks and trajectories, resulting in SMART-Data , a large-scale synthetic dataset covering diverse articulated objects and manipulation skills.
We conduct behavior cloning pretraining exclusively on SMART-Data , with the pretraining effect first evaluated on simulation benchmarks.
To further explore SMART-Sim ’s potential in data synthesis, we conduct zero-shot sim-to-real experiments and performance scaling experiments on representative articulated-object manipulation tasks.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose SMART-Sim , a scalable simulation platform with specialized articulation-aware designs for asset annotation, motion generation, skill design, and domain randomization, enabling efficient and effective task and motion generation for articulated-object manipulation.

We propose SMART-Sim , a scalable simulation platform with specialized articulation-aware designs for asset annotation, motion generation, skill design, and domain randomization, enabling efficient and effective task and motion generation for articulated-object manipulation.

We develop an agentic task generation approach and a distributed synthesis system , and use them to construct SMART-Data , a large-scale synthetic articulated-object manipulation dataset with over 1M trajectories across 5 robot setups and 23 object categories, providing diverse supervision for articulated-object manipulation learning.

Extensive simulation and real-world experiments show that pretraining on SMART-Data can improve VLA performance on downstream tasks.
Furthermore, data synthesized by SMART-Sim enables zero-shot sim-to-real policy transfer with positive scaling trends, highlighting the potential of synthetic data as a scalable supervision source for contact-rich articulated-object manipulation.

2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Articulated object manipulation. Compared to rigid-object manipulation, articulated-object manipulation requires additional reasoning about functional parts, joint constraints, and sustained contact during interaction.
Early works address these challenges by leveraging pretrained encoders to extract auxiliary information such as the articulation axis ( Wang et al., 2024b ) and affordance ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Ling et al., 2024 ) for manipulation.
Recognizing the value of simulation in providing accurate articulation models and supervision, GAPartManip ( Cui et al., 2025 ) and Infinigen-Articulated ( Joshi et al., 2025 ) develop curated articulated-object datasets and automated pipelines for generating simulation-ready assets with articulation annotations.
Building on such simulated articulated-object models, subsequent works either construct explicit models for manipulation ( Ma et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) or train more capable affordance prediction models ( Chen et al., 2026b ) .
Despite their effectiveness, these approaches often rely on simplified object models and accurate perception of object geometry and articulation, limiting their scalability to diverse objects and real-world settings.

VLA models and Real-world data. Vision-language-action models have recently become a prominent approach to general-purpose robot control, and their performance depends on high-quality, diverse, and large-scale demonstration datasets.
Works like the π \pi series ( Black et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) , LingBot-VLA ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , and PRTS ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) heavily rely on teleoperated robot demonstrations, using more than 10,000 hours of multi-robot data, approximately 20,000 hours of real bimanual data, and 167 billion tokens of manipulation and embodied-reasoning data, respectively.
However, teleoperation remains hard to scale because of its high cost and low data collection efficiency.
To reduce this burden, studies on UMI ( Chi et al., 2024 ; Zhaxizhuoma et al., 2025 ) enable portable robot-free demonstration collection through handheld interfaces, with Hy-Embodied-0.5-VLA ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) further performing effective pretraining with more than 10,000 hours of UMI data.
Additionally, egocentric demonstration collection offers another robot-free alternative by capturing human wrist and hand motion, with Ego4D ( Grauman et al., 2022 ) and EgoDex ( Hoque et al., 2026 ) providing egocentric human interaction data and EgoMimic ( Kareer et al., 2025 ) , EgoVLA ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and EgoScale ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) demonstrating its value for VLA pretraining.
Despite improved collection efficiency and lower cost, these methods either face a trade-off between tracking precision and portability or require pose estimation, retargeting, and robot alignment to recover executable actions.
These limitations are particularly problematic for articulated-object manipulation, where small action errors can break sustained contact or violate joint constraints.
Overall, current real-world demonstration collection methods struggle to simultaneously provide high-quality data, broad diversity, and high collection efficiency for articulated-object manipulation tasks.

Simulation and synthesized data for robot manipulation. Simulation offers a controllable and repeatable setting for generating executable robot trajectories.
Frameworks such as Isaac Lab ( NVIDIA et al., 2025b ) and robosuite ( Zhu et al., 2020 ) provide reusable assets and frameworks for robot-learning experiments.
Building on these infrastructures, SceneFoundry ( Chen et al., 2026a ) and SceneSmith ( Pfaff et al., 2026 ) provide methods to construct interactive, simulation-ready scenes for simulation tasks, while RoboCasa ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) , RoboCasa365 ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) , and BEHAVIOR-1K ( Li et al., 2023 ) provide household environments and task suites with broad scene and task coverage.
MimicGen ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) , RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , and HumanoidGen ( Jing et al., 2025 ) then scale trajectory generation through demonstration recombination, automatic task programming, and constraints generated by a large language model (LLM) with trajectory optimization, respectively.
At the dataset level, InternData-A1 ( Tian et al., 2025 ) and MolmoBot ( Deshpande et al., 2026 ) use 7,433 and 5,704 hours of synthetic data for VLA pretraining,
showing that large synthetic datasets can support policy pretraining and real-world transfer.
However, large-scale synthetic data for VLA learning remains underexplored for diverse articulated-object manipulation, especially for contact-intensive tasks that demand precise contact and constrained motion.
