2026-10-07.title: Silicon Language: A Robot-Native Knowledge Exchange Framework for Heterogeneous Robots
2026-10-07.authors: Yi Liu (1 and 2), Xianglin Meng (2), Chang Chen (3), Jingjing Fan (3) ((1) School of Mechanical Engineering, Beijing Institute of Technology, Beijing, China, (2) Yulin Saiyi Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd., Yulin, China, (3) Yulin Intelligent Unmanned Equipment Innovation Center Co., Ltd., Yulin, China)
2026-10-07.abstract: Reusing a capability across heterogeneous robots still requires substantial human adaptation and verification: transferring a skill often means re-engineering interfaces, retuning parameters, and re-validating safety. We introduce Silicon Language, a robot-native knowledge exchange framework that treats the robot as the active subject of its own capability evolution. In this framework, a robot that wants a capability encodes its own experience into knowledge packets, publishes them, retrieves peer packets, translates them for its own sensors and actuators, and reviews them through independent local trial. A receiver-side usability evaluation procedure lets each robot decide for itself whether an external packet is useful, and progressive blending with automatic rollback is designed to reduce the risk of negative transfer when adopting it. The system combines a three-layer infrastructure—edge agent, Silicon Transfer Protocol (STP), and knowledge hub—with a capability stack inspired by the human scholarly system. We report a 30-day proof-of-concept deployment at an above-ground simulated-mine laboratory in Yulin, with following trials on an outdoor sand road and an indoor factory floor. Two heterogeneous robots encoded and translated three capabilities across embodiments through operator-assisted file copies mediated by the Silicon Language translation layer; source-side trials of the dust-locked following behavior were recorded on Taurus. Project records indicate that per-capability adaptation time dropped from days to hours; we present these figures as descriptive deployment records rather than controlled measurements. The deployment provides initial evidence for cross-embodiment knowledge exchange; fleet-level autonomous evolution and controlled with/without-packet comparisons remain future work.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Reusing a capability across heterogeneous robots still requires substantial human adaptation. Engineers label data, write code, design training pipelines, evaluate outcomes, and deploy updates. When robot A learns a useful skill in one environment, robot B—with different sensors, actuators, and constraints—cannot inherit it directly; humans must repeat much of the adaptation and verification cycle for B. In this prevailing workflow the robot is a knowledge object : humans decide what to transfer, how to adapt it, and whether it is safe. The robot itself is not the agent of its own capability growth.

This human-centric bottleneck caps the scalability of robot fleets: as the number of robots, environments, and required capabilities grows, the human effort required grows with it. Human researchers, by contrast, operate inside a scholarly ecosystem: they write papers, publish them, cite prior work, translate ideas across fields, subject claims to peer review, revise versions, and debate at conferences. What is needed is not merely a faster human-driven pipeline, but a robot-native scholarly system in which the robot itself is the active subject—a robot that wants a capability encodes its own experience, publishes it, retrieves peer knowledge, translates it for its own embodiment, reviews it through independent trial, and revises it through versioned iteration.

Prior work has addressed pieces of the problem, but usually keeps agency on the human side. RoboEarth and KnowRob let robots share semantic maps and action recipes [ 1 , 2 ] ; RoboEarth in particular demonstrated cross-robot upload, retrieval, and reuse across heterogeneous platforms. However, the shared representations and action recipes were largely human-predesigned, and the receiving robot did not independently judge whether an incoming artifact was useful or safe for its own embodiment through a local trial protocol. RoboBrain builds large knowledge graphs for cross-modal reasoning [ 3 ] , yet it does not support receiver-side adaptation, publication, retrieval, review, or iteration across robots. Federated learning and Open X-Embodiment aggregate gradients or data [ 4 , 5 ] , but what is shared cannot leave the training process, and robots do not decide what is worth sharing. ROS/DDS and FABRIC provide communication and coordination [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] , while IEEE 2751 standardizes 3-D map-data exchange [ 9 ] . Recent agentic systems narrow the gap from another direction: Voyager lets an LLM-driven agent autonomously write, execute, and store skills as code in Minecraft [ 10 ] ; Code as Policies shows that language-model programs can express robot control logic on real robots [ 11 ] ; and embodied foundation models such as PaLM-E [ 12 ] , RT-2 [ 13 ] , RoboCat [ 14 ] , and Octo [ 15 ] further scale generalizable skill generation and reuse [ 16 ] . These systems demonstrate that machines can produce and reuse executable knowledge; they do not address the cross-embodiment, cross-robot exchange problem, in which the receiving machine has different sensors, actuators, and constraints and must independently judge whether externally produced knowledge is useful and safe for itself .

We introduce Silicon Language , a robot-native knowledge exchange framework whose central design principle is that the robot is the subject of its own capability evolution. The framework provides the lifecycle primitives a robot needs to act as a knowledge subject : writing its experience into packets, publishing them, retrieving peer packets, translating them to its own morphology, reviewing them through local trial, and revising them through versioned iteration. Our contributions are:

A robot-native, robot-centric knowledge exchange framework. A three-layer infrastructure (edge agent, Silicon Transfer Protocol, knowledge hub) plus a knowledge-packet abstraction and a receiver-side review protocol, organized as a capability stack inspired by the human scholarly system. The receiving robot—not a human engineer and not the publisher—decides what to adopt and how to validate it for its own embodiment ( section III ).

Encoding-independent usability evaluation with negative-transfer risk mitigation. Receiving robots independently judge whether a published packet is useful, partially useful, or unusable for them through local trial. Progressive blending and automatic rollback are designed so that the fallback outcome of a failed adoption is a return to the prior software state ( sections III-D and IV ).

A robot-centric proof-of-concept deployment. A 30-day deployment with two heterogeneous robots at an above-ground laboratory configured to simulate an underground coal mine in Yulin. The reported Taurus following trials took place separately on an outdoor sand road and an indoor factory floor, not inside the simulated mine. The robots encoded, published, and translated capabilities across embodiments on their own edge agents. The cross-robot file copy was operator-assisted only because the production STP exchange is not yet running. Per-capability adaptation time dropped from days to hours in our engineering records ( section V ). We report these figures as descriptive deployment records, not controlled measurements.

We deliberately scope this paper as a proof of concept for the exchange framework. The empirical study is small (two robots, one simulated mine environment, one deployment cycle), the efficiency baselines rely partly on engineering estimates, and the fitness-driven evolutionary mechanisms described in section III-E are part of the framework design but not yet validated at fleet scale; their implementation status will be confirmed in the code audit. We state these limits explicitly in section V-G .
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Early systems such as RoboEarth and KnowRob provided Web-accessible knowledge bases in which robots could share semantic maps, object models, and action recipes [ 1 , 2 ] . RoboEarth in particular showed that robots could upload experience, retrieve peer knowledge, and reuse it across heterogeneous platforms through a shared representation and a robot-specific skill-abstraction layer. These systems established that cross-robot knowledge reuse is possible, but the knowledge formats and task recipes were largely human-predesigned, and the receiving robot did not independently judge whether an incoming artifact was useful or safe for its own embodiment through a local trial protocol. RoboBrain later scaled cross-modal knowledge graphs for single-robot reasoning [ 3 ] , yet it did not address receiver-side adaptation, publication, retrieval, review, or iterative evolution across a fleet.

Federated learning lets multiple agents train models while keeping data local [ 4 ] . However, federated learning shares gradients or weights, not reusable knowledge artifacts; aggregation rules are human-designed; and knowledge cannot leave the training run. Open X-Embodiment demonstrated the power of pooling diverse robot data for centralized training [ 5 ] , but the data are human-collected and curated, and robots remain objects of data collection rather than subjects of knowledge production.

Voyager showed that an LLM-driven agent can autonomously write, execute, verify, and store skills as code, building a growing skill library in Minecraft [ 10 ] . Code as Policies demonstrated that language-model programs can express reactive robot control logic, with deployments on several real robot platforms [ 11 ] . More recently, vision-language-action models and embodied multimodal language models have transferred web-scale semantics directly into robot control [ 13 , 12 ] ; RoboCat and Octo train generalist manipulation policies across multiple embodiments [ 14 , 15 ] ; and diffusion policies provide a flexible generative model for visuomotor skills [ 17 ] . These works establish that machines can produce and reuse executable knowledge. The distinguishing problem we target is cross-embodiment exchange between independent robots : the receiving machine has different sensors, actuators, and constraints from the producer, and must independently adapt the incoming knowledge and judge—through its own trial protocol—whether it is useful and safe to adopt. Neither a shared skill library nor human-prompted code generation addresses this receiver-side adaptation and acceptance problem.

ROS topics and DDS provide real-time message passing [ 6 , 7 ] ; FABRIC adds decentralized coordination with identity verification and encrypted data sharing [ 8 ] . IEEE 2751 standardizes 3-D map-data exchange [ 9 ] . These systems enable the dialogue layer of robot interaction, but they do not provide the higher layers of the exchange lifecycle: writing, publishing, retrieving, translating, reviewing, and versioning knowledge.

Learngene and related work study how neural-network knowledge can be decomposed, compressed, and transferred across tasks [ 18 ] . Progressive neural networks and related methods accumulate task-specific columns [ 19 ] . Recent benchmarks such as LIBERO formalize forward transfer and negative backward transfer in lifelong robot learning [ 20 ] , and Reset & Distill directly targets negative transfer in continual reinforcement learning [ 21 ] . Cross-embodiment methods align latent state-action spaces [ 22 ] , discover shared skills from human and robot videos [ 23 ] , encode embodiment descriptors via transformers [ 24 ] , or train one policy across diverse locomotion morphologies [ 25 ] . These approaches address the technical question of how to transfer knowledge, but not the ecological question of who decides what to publish, who validates it, and how it evolves over time.

Silicon Language is distinguished by two properties. First, it treats knowledge as a first-class, versioned, reviewable artifact (a knowledge packet) rather than a by-product of training. Second, the receiving robot—not the publisher, not a human—decides through a defined trial protocol whether a packet is useful for its own embodiment, which is the property that makes cross-embodiment exchange viable without human re-engineering.

2026-10-07.title: OntoPlan: An Ontology-Grounded Scene Representation and Agentic Framework for Scalable Robot Task Planning
2026-10-07.authors: Hyeongwoo Nam , Woongje Cho , Juwon Kim , Jongeun Choi
2026-10-07.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026.
2026-10-07.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based robot task planning is promising for open-ended instruction following, but degrades on long-horizon tasks in large environments. When spatial information is conveyed to the LLM through text, the model can fail to capture spatial context, and token cost grows with environment size. Generating action sequences directly with an LLM also makes it difficult to satisfy the current world state and action preconditions. We address this with an ontology-grounded scene representation that aligns objects, spaces, relations, and states in a shared symbolic vocabulary for spatial reasoning and task planning, and with OntoPlan , an agentic framework that interprets instructions, selectively retrieves task-relevant information, formalizes goals and constraints, and produces executable plans. Across 150 general tasks spanning five indoor environments and three scene scales, OntoPlan achieves 0.89 average task success, compared with 0.27 for the strongest baseline, while using 18.1k total tokens per task on average, about 5.6 × \times fewer than the most efficient baseline. These advantages persist as scene scale increases, whereas prior methods degrade more sharply in success and remain far more costly in tokens. OntoPlan also responds appropriately to ambiguous or infeasible instructions by asking follow-up questions or reporting insufficient information rather than committing to invalid plans. Code available at https://github.com/namhyeongwoo/OntoPlan .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as flexible interfaces for open-ended problem solving [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Rather than requiring rigid formal specifications, they let users express intent in natural language and use commonsense knowledge to organize underspecified requests into subgoals or solution steps [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . This makes them well suited to robot task planning, where instructions are open-ended and key details are often implicit. Robots must infer the intended task together with the relevant objects, spaces, and constraints.

Robot task planning, however, requires more than language understanding. A valid solution must ground task-relevant objects, spaces, and relations in large scenes and generate long-horizon action sequences that remain executable under the current world state. This exposes two limitations of LLM-only planning. First, flattening structured spatial representations such as 3D scene graphs into text prompts can cause spatial reasoning errors, including hallucinated or omitted relations, while prompt cost grows with scene size [ 8 , 9 ] . Second, directly generated action sequences are unreliable under grounded execution, often violating action preconditions, safety or feasibility constraints, or the intended goal [ 10 , 11 ] . Alternatively, LLMs can formulate planner-facing PDDL problems for symbolic planners, but this step remains vulnerable to errors such as missing initial facts, misused predicates, and incomplete goals or constraints [ 12 , 13 ] . The central challenge is to maintain consistency across instruction interpretation, scene grounding, and executable planning.

We address this challenge with OntoPlan , which separates the roles of LLMs and structured tools. LLM agents handle high-level instruction interpretation, clarification, and goal and constraint formalization, while structured tools handle selective scene access and executable long-horizon planning. To make this separation reliable, OntoPlan maintains a shared symbolic state in an ontology-grounded world model aligned directly with a PDDL domain [ 14 ] . The Scene query tool retrieves task-relevant objects, spaces, and relations from this shared state, while the PDDL plan tool generates executable plans from the same world state and explicit constraints. Fig. 1 illustrates how the shared world model connects scene grounding, task formalization, planning, and world-state updates.

This paper makes two contributions. First, we propose a PDDL-aligned ontology-grounded scene representation that supports shared scene grounding, direct world-state extraction, and consistent symbolic updates. Second, we develop a tool-using planning framework that combines the Scene query tool for selective scene access with the PDDL plan tool for executable long-horizon planning. We evaluate OntoPlan across five indoor environments and three scene scales, and further analyze its behavior on ambiguous and infeasible instructions. OntoPlan improves task success and token efficiency over LLM-based baselines and remains more robust as scenes grow or when instructions are ambiguous or infeasible.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Structured Scene Grounding. Structured scene representations encode objects, spaces, and relations, providing a more reliable substrate for spatial reasoning than free-form scene descriptions [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . SayPlan retrieves task-relevant context from hierarchical 3D scene graphs, passes it to an LLM as text, and replans using feedback from a scene-graph simulator [ 21 ] . While such methods demonstrate the value of structured grounding, they still route graph structure through natural-language context. Flattening graph-structured information into text can obscure relational dependencies [ 8 , 22 ] and increases prompt length as scenes grow, which often leads to a critical failure in context utilization [ 23 , 24 ] . This motivates keeping scene knowledge queryable in symbolic form and retrieving only task-relevant evidence [ 25 , 26 ] .

LLM-Assisted Symbolic Planning. Direct LLM planning remains unreliable on formal planning tasks, especially for long-horizon validity and reasoning about state change [ 10 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] . Hybrid approaches instead use LLMs to interpret instructions or construct planner-facing specifications, then delegate planning to external symbolic planners [ 30 , 31 ] . Prior work has shown that LLMs can translate natural-language goals into formal planning goals [ 4 ] , construct or correct PDDL models [ 32 , 33 , 34 ] , and convert natural-language problems into PDDL [ 12 , 35 , 36 ] . DELTA combines scene-graph pruning with autoregressive subgoal decomposition for embodied long-horizon planning [ 13 ] . These approaches reduce reliance on direct plan generation, but remain vulnerable to the formalization errors noted in Section 1 . NL-PDDL extends PDDL into a natural-language representation for lifted regression planning with commonsense entailment in partially observed environments [ 37 ] , whereas OntoPlan assumes full observability with a typed vocabulary shared by the world model and PDDL domain.

Interactive Planning under Ambiguity. Interactive planning work studies how systems should respond to underspecified instructions or when execution feedback reveals failures [ 38 , 39 ] . Inner Monologue incorporates scene descriptions, success signals, and human feedback into closed-loop planning [ 40 ] . DEPS revises plans using execution descriptions and self-explanations while selecting among subgoals [ 41 ] . Introspective Planning explicitly reasons about uncertainty under ambiguous instructions and asks follow-up questions when needed [ 42 , 43 ] . These studies motivate planning loops that support clarification and feedback-driven revision rather than single-pass plan generation.

Positioning. Taken together, prior work spans perceptually grounded construction and querying of spatial and spatio-temporal memories [ 17 , 44 , 20 ] as well as planning over structured scene representations, but does not fully integrate selective access to large structured scenes with executable planning over the same symbolic state. Such memories could serve as upstream inputs after mapping their contents to the ontology–PDDL vocabulary, while OntoPlan uses the resulting symbolic state for scene grounding, task formalization, planner-state extraction, primitive-action synthesis, and symbolic state update.
This architecture instantiates the LLM-modulo framework [ 30 ] and follows the broader tool-use paradigm for language models [ 45 ] , supporting consistency across high-level reasoning and grounded execution.

2026-10-07.title: Beyond Task Reward: A Controller-Restriction Protocol for Evaluating Embodiment-Dependent Competence
2026-10-07.authors: Siyuan Zhang
2026-10-07.abstract:
Co-design methods optimize a robot’s body and controller jointly and judge the result by one
number, the task reward of the fully optimized pair. That number cannot separate morphologies
whose competence depends on the controller to very different degrees. We evaluate a morphology by
restricting its controller instead, recording the task competence it retains under an explicitly
declared, low-complexity controller family, environment, task and search budget. On three EvoGym
locomotion tasks, task reward explains only 39 % 39\% , 33 % 33\% and 10 % 10\% of the variance in this
quantity, and geometric descriptors do not predict it under run-grouped cross-validation. The
measurement is reliable across optimizer restarts (ICC ( 2 , k ) = 0.956 (2,k)=0.956 – 0.986 0.986 ) but depends on the
declared family: phasing the drive by actuator index instead of position ranks the same
morphologies at Spearman 0.50 0.50 – 0.63 0.63 and reverses reward-matched pairs. As a second search
objective the axis improved competence at matched task reward in 3 3 of 5 5 paired runs, short of
a pre-registered bar of 4 4 . Used after an ordinary reward-only search instead, to choose within
its top task-reward band, it selected a different body in all 8 8 runs offering a choice, at a
cost of at most 0.10 0.10 reward units, and in 6 6 of 8 8 that body also scored higher under a
held-out family. Restricted-control competence is therefore a reportable property of a co-designed
morphology, interpretable only with the controller family that defines it.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Co-design methods jointly optimize a robot’s body and its controller, and are almost universally
judged by a single number: the task reward achieved by the co-optimized pair. That number says
whether the pair works, but not how much of the working depends on the controller.

Two morphologies can be indistinguishable by that number yet behave very differently once the
controller is taken away. Fig. 1 shows a pair from our runs whose fully optimized
task rewards differ by 0.2 % 0.2\% , a gap no co-design report would treat as meaningful. Replacing the
trained policy with a low-complexity feedback-free drive separates them by 2.8 × 2.8\times . The
distinction matters to anyone who has to build the robot, yet it is invisible in the quantity the
field publishes.

We make it measurable by restricting the controller rather than by inspecting the body: given a
morphology, we optimize within a declared family of low-complexity controllers under a declared
budget and record the task competence that remains. The declaration is the substance of the
proposal, because the score depends on the family, the task, the environment and the search
budget, and we report all four with every number. Our own data forced that emphasis. We began with
a family that phases a periodic drive by actuator index, so renumbering a fixed body’s actuators
changed its score; a family phased by actuator position removes that defect exactly. Yet
the two families rank the same 874 874 morphologies at Spearman 0.50 0.50 , 0.53 0.53 and 0.63 0.63 and
reverse individual reward-matched pairs, including the pair in Fig. 1 . Both are
defensible, so a restricted-control result is reproducible only with its family attached, and the
useful object is a profile across families rather than a single score.

Our contributions are (i) an evaluation protocol that quantifies the task competence a morphology
retains under a declared, permutation-invariant, low-complexity controller family, task,
environment and budget, shown to be invariant, reliable, converged and discriminative; (ii) the
finding that task reward leaves most of this competence unexplained and geometry does not predict
it, together with the family sensitivity above; and (iii) two uses of the measurement in design, a
pre-registered multi-objective search that falls short of its bar at a fixed generation budget for
a reason the search trajectories identify, and an exploratory screening step that changes the
chosen body at negligible task-reward cost.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

Co-design of morphology and control. Jointly optimizing body and controller goes back to
Sims’s evolved virtual creatures [ 1 ] and the first physically instantiated
evolved machines [ 2 ] . Evolutionary methods optimize morphology in an outer
loop and train a controller per candidate, over voxel grids [ 3 ] , graph
grammars [ 4 ] , learned latent spaces [ 5 ] or populations of
graph-structured agents [ 6 ] ; reinforcement-learning formulations fold the design
decision into the policy [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] , and a
recent line replaces the search with a generative model [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . These methods differ in how they search but agree on what
they report: the task reward of the co-optimized pair, a joint property of a body and a controller
fitted to each other. It cannot distinguish a morphology whose competence persists under a much
simpler controller from one whose competence exists only alongside its trained policy, and nothing
in the reported quantity makes that distinction recoverable afterwards.

Quantifying morphological computation. That a body can perform work otherwise delegated
to a controller is a long-standing idea in embodied intelligence [ 13 ] ,
formalized mainly through information theory as measures on the dependencies between sensors,
actions and world states [ 14 , 15 ] , with a parallel
line modeling compliant bodies as physical reservoirs [ 16 ] . A body can take
part in that information flow while contributing nothing to the task, and the converse also holds;
our measure is behavioral instead. Closest in spirit is Haeufle et
al. [ 17 ] , who disable a central pattern generator in a
neuromusculoskeletal model and attribute the residual oscillation to passive dynamics. The
intervention matches ours, but their read-out is an information-theoretic measure on one
biological model, not task competence across evolved morphologies.

Restricting a controller versus measuring it. The family we declare is a positional
traveling wave, close to the low-dimensional oscillators of central pattern generator
models [ 18 ] , and serves here as an instrument: few parameters, a count
independent of body size, exact invariance to actuator relabeling, and a reimplementable
specification. Closest to this paper is Xie et al. [ 19 ] , a concurrent
preprint relating morphology complexity to the computational cost of the controller driving it on
the same platform. The distinction is between measuring a controller and intervening on it: cost in floating-point operations varies across bodies only through
the observation and action dimensionality the morphology induces, so two bodies with equal voxel
and actuator counts score the same even if an open-loop oscillator drives one and the other
collapses without feedback. Controller restriction poses that counterfactual directly. The
methodological concern is familiar from reinforcement learning, where reported performance was
shown to depend heavily on the evaluation protocol [ 20 , 21 ] .

2026-10-07.title: TacZero: Training-Free Peg Insertion Using a General-Purpose Vision-Language Model with Tactile Feedback
2026-10-07.authors: Kazutoshi Tanaka
2026-10-07.abstract:
Robots that autonomously determine their actions from language instructions and sensory observations could perform new contact-rich manipulation tasks without task-specific training or hand-designed rules.
To perform these tasks, robots must infer how objects contact one another and move as a result, then select actions.
For contact inference and action selection, prior approaches involve designing estimation models and tactile feedback control laws, or learning models for object-motion estimation, action-outcome prediction, and action selection from tactile data.
Instead, we propose TacZero, which uses a pretrained general-purpose vision-language model (VLM) to interpret visual and tactile observations and select robot actions without additional tactile or manipulation training or task-specific rules for contact interpretation or action selection.
TacZero provides the VLM with camera images, robot state, and three-axis tactile responses represented as numerical values or vectors overlaid on the images.
From these observations and interaction history, the VLM generates commands specifying target end-effector positions and gripper opening or closing, which a low-level controller executes.
In real-world cylindrical-peg insertion experiments, TacZero succeeded in 15 of 20 trials with numerical tactile input, compared with 10 of 20 without tactile input.
This study provides a concrete starting point for further research on contact-rich manipulation using general-purpose VLMs and highlights challenges in pursuing this direction.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Robots that autonomously determine their actions from language instructions and sensory observations could perform new contact-rich manipulation tasks [ 1 , 2 ] , such as peg insertion [ 3 ] , without task-specific training or hand-designed rules.
Contact-state estimation and reasoning about how contact constrains object motion can guide action selection in these tasks [ 4 , 5 ] .
Tactile sensing supports contact-state estimation by providing information about contact that is difficult to obtain from vision alone [ 6 ] .

Prior work has developed model-based and learning-based approaches to contact-state estimation and action selection.
Model-based approaches combine tactile measurements with geometric and contact constraints to estimate contact states [ 3 ] and determine robot motions through designed tactile feedback control laws [ 7 ] .
Learning-based approaches train models to estimate object motion [ 3 ] or predict action outcomes from tactile data [ 8 ] , or learn policies to select actions [ 9 ] .
Other studies learn tactile representations that can be reused across perception tasks [ 10 ] or incorporate tactile feedback into pretrained robot policies through fine-tuning on demonstrations from multiple manipulation tasks [ 11 ] .
These approaches enable tactile-based manipulation through the design of models and control laws for contact-state estimation or action selection, or through learning from tactile data.

Vision-language models (VLMs) have enabled robotic manipulation without task-specific training [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
These models use visual observations and language instructions to generate task plans [ 15 ] , robot programs [ 16 ] , and spatial targets or constraints for motion execution [ 13 , 14 ] .
These advances suggest that a pretrained general-purpose VLM could also interpret visual and tactile observations and select robot actions without additional tactile or manipulation training or hand-designed task-specific rules for contact interpretation or action selection.

To explore this possibility, we propose TacZero (Fig. 1 ), which uses a pretrained general-purpose VLM to interpret contact from visual and tactile observations and select robot actions, without additional tactile or manipulation training or hand-designed task-specific rules for contact interpretation or action selection.
At each step, TacZero provides the VLM with the task instruction, visual and tactile observations, robot state, and the within-trial interaction history.
The VLM outputs commands specifying target end-effector positions and gripper opening or closing, which a low-level controller executes.
In real-world cylindrical-peg insertion experiments, TacZero succeeded in 15 of 20 trials with numerical tactile input, compared with 10 of 20 without tactile input.

Our contributions are:

We present a research direction in which a pretrained general-purpose VLM interprets visual and tactile observations and selects robot actions without additional tactile or manipulation training or hand-designed task-specific rules for contact interpretation or action selection. We provide a concrete starting point for future research and highlight challenges in pursuing this direction.

We introduce TacZero, which provides a general-purpose VLM with a task instruction, visual and tactile observations, robot state, and interaction history, and executes the VLM’s output commands specifying target end-effector positions and gripper opening or closing.

2026-10-07.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Robotic Manipulation with Pretrained Language Models and Vision-Language Models

Researchers have proposed robotic manipulation methods in which pretrained language models (LMs) and VLMs generate policy code or action sequences before execution.
Liang et al. proposed Code as Policies (CaP), which employs an LM to generate programs that process perception outputs, compute positions and trajectories, and invoke control application programming interfaces (APIs) [ 17 ] .
Fang et al. proposed MOKA, in which a VLM selects grasping and interaction keypoints, pre-contact and post-contact waypoint regions, and motion attributes, which are then converted into robot motions using depth information and geometric processing [ 13 ] .
Huang et al. proposed CoPa, in which a solver computes a target pose from VLM-generated spatial constraints between object parts, and the VLM also specifies subsequent numerical displacements and gripper opening [ 14 ] .
Whereas these methods execute the generated programs or action sequences without calling the LM or VLM again for action selection during execution, TacZero calls the VLM after each action to determine the next action from fresh observations.

Other researchers have proposed methods that call LMs or VLMs again based on execution feedback to update plans or actions.
Zhi et al. proposed COME-robot, which generates code that calls exploration, navigation, grasping, and placement functions and revises its plans using images and execution feedback [ 16 ] .
Kwon et al. proposed a method that generates code to compute end-effector pose sequences and gripper commands from object geometry, then supplies observed object motion after trajectory execution to the LM for failure detection and replanning [ 18 ] .
Wang et al. proposed Wonderful Team, in which VLM agents identify and refine target locations in images, specify action sequences, compute waypoints using generated functions for trajectory-based tasks, and support replanning based on execution results [ 15 ] .
Nasiriany et al. proposed PIVOT, which presents candidate relative end-effector translations on the current image at each action selection and iteratively updates the candidate distribution based on VLM selections [ 12 ] .
Whereas these methods specify motions through operation-level functions, trajectory-generating code, image-space target coordinates, or motion-candidate selection, TacZero uses the VLM to specify the next end-effector target position numerically.
Singh et al. proposed MALMM, which distributes planning, code generation, and coordination across multiple LM agents and replans using environmental observations obtained after intermediate execution steps [ 19 ] .
In MALMM, the LM specifies numerical end-effector target positions within generated code; similarly, the VLM in TacZero determines numerical end-effector target positions.

None of the methods discussed in this subsection provide tactile observations to the LM or VLM.
In contrast, TacZero provides a general-purpose VLM with tactile observations in addition to vision, robot state, and interaction history.

## II-B Tactile and Force Feedback for Robot Action Selection and Control

Researchers have proposed methods that integrate tactile feedback into robot action selection and refinement through additional training.
Hao et al. proposed TLA, which uses sequential tactile images and learns corrective insertion actions from tactile-action-instruction data [ 20 ] .
Zhang et al. proposed VTLA, a vision-language-action (VLA) model that uses supervised fine-tuning and preference learning to select corrective actions from visual and temporal tactile observations [ 21 ] .
Bi et al. proposed VLA-Touch, which uses object-property descriptions from a pretrained tactile-language model for VLM-based planning and a trained tactile-conditioned controller to refine action sequences generated by a VLA.
Although they also evaluated planning with tactile images supplied directly to a VLM, their main architecture assigns tactile-to-language interpretation and action refinement to dedicated models [ 22 ] .
Van der Merwe et al. proposed TAP-VLA, which overlays tactile shear vectors onto camera images and fine-tunes a VLA on these images [ 23 ] .
TacZero adopts a tactile overlay representation inspired by TAP-VLA. Unlike TAP-VLA, which fine-tunes a VLA on the overlaid images, TacZero supplies these images to a general-purpose VLM without additional training.
Whereas these approaches use models trained for tactile-based action selection or refinement, TacZero uses a single general-purpose VLM to interpret visual and tactile observations and select robot actions without additional tactile or manipulation training.

Other researchers have proposed methods that combine a VLM with force-based control and search procedures without additional training.
Yajima et al. proposed a method that employs a VLM to identify the mating hole and determine the relative orientation, and executes insertion using predefined force-based control and search procedures [ 24 ] .
Whereas the VLM in their method identifies the mating hole and determines the relative orientation, leaving insertion motions to predefined control and search procedures, the VLM in TacZero determines the next end-effector target position from observations at each step.

2026-10-07.title: Nine Trials to Recover: A Reproducible Benchmark for Repertoire-Free Soft-Robot Damage Adaptation
2026-10-07.authors: Siyuan Zhang
2026-10-07.abstract:
We present a repertoire-free benchmark for soft-robot damage recovery under nine online trials.
The protocol pairs damage masks within each morphology, retains a measured nominal fallback,
and separates method development from evaluation on new bodies. A Gaussian-process
expected-improvement (GP-EI) reference controller adapts actuator phases using three initialization
probes and six feedback-selected rollouts. Across two disjoint 75-body cohorts, it outperforms
random search, Sobol, CEM, and CMA-ES under equal budgets. GP-EI improves the worst-mask gain on
69/75 confirmation bodies and exceeds these four baselines by 0.235 0.235 – 0.310 0.310 mean worst-mask reward.
A TuRBO-style local GP is the closest comparator; the paired confidence interval includes zero.
Post-confirmation fixed-controller replay finds 5.06 voxel widths of mean recovery together with
a 0.0031 increase in worst-mask p99 geometric edge strain; a strict no-added-demand deployment
gate retains 48.7% of mean gain. In a frozen development stress test that physically removes
10% of occupied voxels, GP-EI improves 71/75 bodies and exceeds official BoTorch TuRBO by 0.356 0.356 mean worst-mask gain. Together, the replayable controllers,
body-level inference, and frozen-cohort
evaluation provide a reference for measuring the added value of learned damage priors and
future adaptation methods.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Robots operating outside a laboratory must cope with physical changes that were not represented
at design time [ 1 , 2 ] . A convincing recovery result requires more than a high average reward: it
must reveal the physical-query cost, retain failed trials, prevent favorable damage masks from
inflating the sample size, and separate development from confirmation. We target this evaluation
gap in a low-data setting—new morphology, new actuator failure, no retraining, no
offline repertoire, and only nine complete trials—while retaining the damaged nominal gait as
a deployment fallback.

Prior work has shown that robots can adapt after damage by consulting an offline behavior map and
using Bayesian optimization (BO) to select compensatory behaviors [ 2 ] . Such
repertoires are powerful but require extensive precomputation for a particular platform. Other
approaches exploit differentiable regeneration or learned adaptation [ 3 ] .
We ask: how far can direct numerical feedback go when the
body is previously unseen, no damage-conditioned repertoire is available, and only nine complete
rollouts can be purchased?

We answer this question with the loop in Fig. 1 , implemented in EvoGym [ 4 ] . Each controller consists only of the
phases of open-loop sinusoidal actuators. A Gaussian-process (GP) surrogate includes the damaged
nominal controller as a shared observation; three paid probes span fixed local radii, and expected
improvement (EI) selects the remaining six trials from a mixed global/local pool. This construction
provides a compact, replayable reference implementation. It establishes a performance bar for
testing whether a prior, safety layer, or optimizer improves low-budget recovery.

Three design choices support the comparison. First, every method receives the same nine-rollout
budget and nominal fallback, with every exploratory outcome retained. Second, the primary score
is the worse of two damage masks within each body, making morphology the unit of inference.
Third, the main claim is evaluated twice. The second 75-body cohort was generated with
new morphology and damage seeds, had zero overlap with all earlier cohorts, and was sealed before
any damage or optimizer outcome was evaluated.

The benchmark combines an actionable controller baseline with a protocol for testing improvements
on new morphologies. Our contributions are:

a repertoire-free cross-morphology benchmark and evaluation protocol with equal
nine-rollout budgets, two masks per body, body-level worst-mask inference, unstable-rollout
retention, and a prospectively sealed confirmation cohort;

a replayable GP-EI reference implementation with a shared nominal incumbent and an
anytime deployable best-so-far controller;

replicated GP-EI gains over random and CEM in a prospective confirmation, followed by
an equal-budget Sobol, CMA-ES, and TuRBO-style comparison under a locked extension protocol; and

matched component and execution-noise tests, topology-removal and non-flat-terrain
stress tests, and a fixed-controller audit that reports recovery beside deformation demand.

1. a repertoire-free cross-morphology benchmark and evaluation protocol with equal
nine-rollout budgets, two masks per body, body-level worst-mask inference, unstable-rollout
retention, and a prospectively sealed confirmation cohort;

2. a replayable GP-EI reference implementation with a shared nominal incumbent and an
anytime deployable best-so-far controller;

3. replicated GP-EI gains over random and CEM in a prospective confirmation, followed by
an equal-budget Sobol, CMA-ES, and TuRBO-style comparison under a locked extension protocol; and

4. matched component and execution-noise tests, topology-removal and non-flat-terrain
stress tests, and a fixed-controller audit that reports recovery beside deformation demand.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Damage recovery. Self-modeling robots infer changes in their embodiment and synthesize
compensatory behavior [ 1 ] . T-Resilience combines simulation with
transferability estimates for post-damage search [ 5 ] . Intelligent
Trial-and-Error uses a precomputed behavior map and BO [ 2 ] , drawing on the
repertoire perspective formalized by MAP-Elites [ 6 ] . Reset-free Trial-and-Error
extends adaptation to task execution without repeated resets [ 7 ] .
Our benchmark isolates the online recovery stage across unseen morphologies: each optimizer
receives the same nominal gait and nine independently reset trials, with zero repertoire cost.

Controller adaptation. BO allocates expensive observations through a
probabilistic surrogate and acquisition function [ 8 , 9 ] , including
gait learning on physical robots [ 10 ] . Automatic prior selection incorporates
information from simulation or related tasks [ 11 ] ; local BO scales search
through trust regions [ 12 ] . We compare these online search ingredients with
uniform random search, Sobol designs [ 13 ] , CEM [ 14 ] ,
and covariance adaptation [ 15 ] under one shared physical-query budget.
Safety-constrained BO [ 16 , 17 ] addresses feasible exploration;
our incumbent rule addresses which measured controller to deploy.

Morphology and priors. Multi-material voxel bodies support rich
shape/control co-design [ 18 , 4 ] ; SoftZoo broadens the
environment and locomotion tasks [ 19 ] . Differentiable simulation supports
gradient-based optimization [ 20 ] , including morphological regeneration after
damage [ 3 ] . Here the damaged structure is held fixed while actuator phases
adapt. Learned and language-derived skills or value maps provide additional structured
priors [ 21 , 22 ] ; the benchmark supplies a common endpoint for
testing their incremental recovery value.

Reproducible evaluation. Variability across runs and tasks can obscure algorithmic
progress [ 23 , 24 ] . We combine paired body-level intervals,
explicit rollout accounting, and a prospective cohort split with reproducibility practices
for releasing code and complete experimental records [ 25 ] .

2026-10-07.title: Learning Grasp Targeting from Point Clouds for Log Pile Clearing on a Hydraulic Crane
2026-10-07.authors: George Sideris , Lucas Bessai , Heshan Fernando , Elie Ayoub , Nicolas Lemieux , Inna Sharf
2026-10-07.comment: . Supplementary video: this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract: In mill yards, log loaders clear dense piles by a sequence of bundle grasps: hundreds of logs rest in contact, and each removal changes the pile available to the next grasp. A learned policy chooses where to place and orient the grapple from unsegmented point clouds and runs on a trailer-mounted hydraulic forestry crane. The policy classifies at which observed point to grasp and predicts depth and grapple orientation there. The same network outputs support behavior cloning (BC), reinforcement learning (RL), and deployment. BC learns from successful top-of-pile demonstrations; RL explores for improvements by fine-tuning the cloned policy (BC → \to RL) or by training from scratch. In simulation, BC clears 98 of 100 piles of 200 logs, while BC → \to RL improves load stability. Twelve field trials compare a geometric heuristic, RL from scratch, BC, and BC → \to RL through complete grasp-transport-deposit cycles. BC and BC → \to RL deposit 93.8% and 88.9% of pooled inventory, against 80.4% for the heuristic. BC → \to RL deposits logs on 83.6% of its cycles, against 79.6% for the heuristic and 65.7% for BC, while its simulated stability gain does not carry over to the crane testbed. Trained entirely in simulation and run unchanged on the crane, the learned policies clear more than the hand-filtered heuristic while observing unfiltered clouds that still contain the storage rack’s rails and poles.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Log handling is repetitive work in forestry and mill yards, where automation could ease operator shortages and reduce exposure to unstable loads [ 1 , 2 ] . A grapple-equipped crane repeatedly grasps and lifts bundles from a dense pile, in which hundreds of logs rest against one another, then carries them to the mill’s infeed deck. Each such grasp, carry, and deposit forms a cycle , and every cycle changes the scene for the next decision: closing the grapple moves the captured bundle and the surrounding material, and as the pile depletes, broad mounds give way to isolated logs beside rails and poles.

The decision studied here is where to place and orient the grapple, given a partial, noisy point cloud of the pile. The learned policy runs on a trailer-mounted hydraulic forestry crane with a passively suspended grapple (Fig. 1 ). A common controller executes the resulting grasp, transport, and deposition; learning concerns only the grasp decision.

A top-of-pile rule is the natural start, but a camera cloud requires distinguishing logs from rack structure and stray returns; geometric filters depend on scene geometry and calibration, and a segmentation network needs its own labels. Learning the cloud-to-grasp mapping trains material selection and grasp prediction together, without segmentation.

Behavior cloning (BC) learns from successful grasps of a simulated expert that knows the log poses and targets the highest log. Reinforcement learning (RL) explores for improvements: fine-tuning seeks better bundle handling, while RL from scratch explores for more effective grasp sequences beyond the expert’s top-of-pile strategy.

The contributions of this paper are:

A learned grasp policy for sequential clearing of packed log piles from unsegmented point clouds. It classifies at which observed point to grasp and predicts the depth and the yaw, the grapple’s rotation about the vertical axis, at that point; one network serves BC, RL fine-tuning, and deployment (Fig. 2 ). The point selection matters: a regression head trained on the same demonstrations fails to clear the piles (Sec. V-B ).

Twelve field trials on the crane testbed in which BC and BC → \to RL, trained entirely in simulation and run with unchanged weights on unfiltered clouds, deposit more inventory than the deployed geometric heuristic on two of three pile shapes and overall.

A comparison of the geometric heuristic, RL from scratch, BC, and BC → \to RL in simulation and on the crane testbed showing that the learned policies’ clearing advantage carries over while fine-tuning’s handling gain does not, with field failures classified by cause and trial phase.

It classifies at which observed point to grasp and predicts the depth and the yaw, the grapple’s rotation about the vertical axis, at that point; one network serves BC, RL fine-tuning, and deployment (Fig. 2 ). The point selection matters: a regression head trained on the same demonstrations fails to clear the piles (Sec. V-B ).

2. Twelve field trials on the crane testbed in which BC and BC → \to RL, trained entirely in simulation and run with unchanged weights on unfiltered clouds, deposit more inventory than the deployed geometric heuristic on two of three pile shapes and overall.

2026-10-07.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

Forestry automation includes crane motion planning [ 3 , 4 ] , learned control [ 5 ] , vision-guided single-log grasping [ 6 ] , and loading by an unmanned forwarder [ 7 ] . Learned grasp planning has also been evaluated for small log clusters on a real loader [ 8 ] , for groups of two to five logs [ 9 ] , and for clusters of up to seven [ 10 ] . These works automate motion for a given target or plan one grasp on a static scene; none addresses sequential clearing of a pile whose state evolves under its own actions or reports pile-scale hardware trials.

Learned grasping addresses isolated objects and clutter [ 11 , 12 ] . Sequential bin picking [ 13 ] and push-grasp policies [ 14 ] explicitly account for changes induced by earlier actions. That literature assumes loose, separable clutter and pinch grasps that singulate one object; mill-yard logs are packed in layers, nothing can be singulated, and the grapple takes bunches in one power grasp that reshapes the pile.

PointNet [ 15 ] provides per-point and global cloud features; point-cloud policies support imitation [ 16 ] and simulation-to-real RL [ 17 ] , and HACMan [ 18 ] selects point-cloud contact locations with continuous motion parameters for non-prehensile manipulation. Demonstration-initialized RL [ 19 ] , proximal policy optimization (PPO) [ 20 ] , and critics with privileged observations [ 21 ] are the learning tools.

2026-10-07.title: Modeling Latent Disturbances for Robust Decision-Making in World Models
2026-10-07.authors: Junwon Seo , Andrea Bajcsy
2026-10-07.abstract: In this paper, we study robust decision-making in the latent space of world models (WMs). Robust optimization is a mathematical framework where, given explicitly specified dynamics and physically meaningful disturbances, a robot can select actions that remain effective even under worst-case disturbances. However, applying this principle to the learned latent space of WMs introduces a fundamental challenge: because WMs have fully learned state spaces and dynamics inferred from high-dimensional observations, it is unclear how to define latent-space disturbances that faithfully represent uncertainty in the underlying physical system. Our key idea is to model a latent-space disturbance as a perturbation to the learned latent dynamics that induces pessimistic but plausible transitions. Specifically, we construct a set of plausible latent dynamics by combining a dynamics-aware similarity metric that captures physically plausible transitions with out-of-distribution detection that excludes implausible latent states. We calibrate this uncertainty set over latent dynamics using conformal prediction, ensuring that WM imaginations induced by the latent disturbance remain plausible without becoming overly pessimistic. We then jointly optimize robust robot actions and the worst-case latent disturbances within the calibrated uncertainty set through efficient game-theoretic optimization. We leverage this latent-space robust optimization framework to robustify policy steering under uncertainty, considering two paradigms: latent safety filtering and sample-and-verify style steering of a generative control policy. Our controlled simulation experiments show that our latent disturbance enables robust decision-making directly in WM latent spaces, and hardware experiments with a Franka manipulator show that modeling latent disturbances enables robust policy steering, reducing failures by 70 % 70\% in safety filtering and 54 % 54\% in sampling-based policy steering.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Consider a robot manipulator serving a sunny-side-up egg by sliding it from a spatula onto a plate (Fig. Modeling Latent Disturbances for Robust Decision-Making in World Models ). This task is deceptively challenging: it not only requires precise motor control from visual observations, such as carefully tilting the spatula, but the outcome of each robot action is uncertain: the same serving motion may successfully slide the egg onto the plate or accidentally flip it sunny-side-down depending on unobserved factors such as the egg’s mass or the amount of oil on the spatula. How can the robot choose actions that are robust to these uncertainties?

A formal way to model such robust decision-making under uncertainty is via robust optimization , which selects a robot action that remains effective under any possible realization of a disturbance, which represents system uncertainty [ 1 ] :

Robust optimization typically requires a structured dynamical system model, where the state and disturbance are represented, often by an expert, to have clear physical meaning (e.g., position and velocity as states and external forces as disturbances [ 7 , 2 ] ). However, latent world models (WMs) [ 8 , 9 ] have recently shown promise for representing hard-to-model systems directly from high-dimensional sensor observations. By jointly learning compact latent representations and their associated dynamics from datasets of robot observations and actions, WMs enable complex systems to be modeled directly in a learned latent space, such as interactions with deformable objects [ 10 ] and complex rigid bodies [ 11 ] .

However, extending robust optimization in ( 1 ) to the learned latent space of WMs raises a fundamental challenge: how to define a latent-space disturbance that faithfully represents uncertainty in the underlying physical system? Unlike disturbances in physically interpretable state spaces [ 12 ] , arbitrary perturbations in the learned latent space need not correspond to physically plausible system evolutions. For example, in Fig. Modeling Latent Disturbances for Robust Decision-Making in World Models , factors such as friction or the amount of oil on the spatula are not directly observed or explicitly represented by the world model. This motivates the central question of our work:

Our key idea is to model a latent-space disturbance as a perturbation to the learned latent dynamics that induces pessimistic world-model imaginations, based on the observation that predictive uncertainty in the latent dynamics reflects disturbances in the underlying system. The main challenge is to construct an uncertainty set [ 6 ] of latent disturbances, a set of plausible latent dynamics that is broad enough to cover possible transitions while excluding implausible ones that would lead to overly conservative decisions [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . This is particularly important in high-dimensional latent spaces, where nearby or high-likelihood states may still correspond to physically infeasible or hallucinated out-of-distribution (OOD) transitions [ 11 , 16 ] . If such OOD transitions are not properly excluded from the uncertainty set, the disturbance can exploit these regions, producing implausibly pessimistic imaginations and leading to overly conservative decisions.

To address this, we propose Latent-space Uncertainty-Calibrated In-distribution Disturbance (LUCID) , a model of latent-space disturbance, which combines a dynamics-aware similarity metric with out-of-distribution detection to construct an uncertainty set of plausible latent dynamics. We calibrate this uncertainty set using conformal prediction [ 17 , 18 ] , ensuring that world-model imaginations induced by the latent disturbance remain plausible without becoming overly pessimistic. We then jointly optimize the worst-case disturbance and robust action through game-theoretic optimization, using an efficient parameterization of the latent disturbance for tractable optimization. We instantiate LUCID for robust policy steering, including latent safety filtering [ 10 , 11 , 19 ] and sampling-based policy steering [ 20 , 21 ] , which can anticipate potential failures without overestimating safety and steer the policy with actions that remain safe under adverse uncertainty.

Through experiments, we show that: (i) in controlled settings with access to the true system dynamics, LUCID approximates the optimal solution to robust optimization in the world-model latent space; (ii) in high-fidelity simulated vision-based manipulation, where we can control system disturbances such as friction and mass, LUCID robustly prevents task failures despite unobservable disturbances; and (iii) in hardware experiments with a Franka robot, LUCID synthesizes a robust safety filter that proactively detects potential failures without becoming overly pessimistic, reducing the failure rate ( 44 % → 13 % 44\%\rightarrow 13\% ), and enables robust policy steering through pessimistic yet plausible WM imaginations, improving the success rate of visuomotor policies ( 35 % → 70 % 35\%\rightarrow 70\% ).
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Robust Decision Making Under Uncertainty. Robust optimization formalizes robust decisions that remain effective across a set of plausible system evolutions, including worst-case realizations [ 22 , 6 ] , by optimizing worst-case performance over an uncertainty set. The uncertainty set characterizes plausible variations in the system [ 1 ] , often in physically interpretable terms such as external force [ 3 ] , model errors [ 23 , 24 ] , or uncertainty estimated from data [ 25 , 13 ] . Similarly, distributionally robust optimization defines the uncertainty set over probability distributions to account for distribution shifts in environments or model dynamics [ 26 , 27 ] . The problem is commonly formulated as a game between the controller and an adversary that selects worst-case disturbances [ 26 , 28 , 27 ] with game-theoretic methods [ 12 , 3 ] or Lagrangian approximations [ 29 , 27 ] . A related perspective is risk-sensitive control [ 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 ] , which accounts for adverse outcomes using risk measures such as conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) [ 34 ] . Certain risk measures can also be expressed as worst-case expectations over corresponding sets of probability distributions, providing a connection between risk-sensitive and robust optimization [ 35 ] . In robust reinforcement learning, policies are optimized against adverse perturbations to observations [ 36 , 37 , 27 ] , dynamics variations [ 5 , 38 ] , distributional shifts encountered at deployment, and out-of-distribution state-action regions [ 39 , 40 , 41 , 42 ] .

A key design choice in robust optimization is the disturbance and its uncertainty set, often defined using physically meaningful bounds specified by experts [ 12 , 3 , 43 ] or estimated from data [ 13 , 44 , 45 , 46 ] , where an overly broad set may admit implausible system evolutions, leading to overly conservative decisions [ 47 ] . This issue is more pronounced in the learned latent space of world models, where latent-space similarity does not necessarily reflect the underlying physical dynamics [ 48 ] and may include implausible out-of-distribution states [ 11 , 49 , 16 ] . Our work addresses this challenge by constructing a conformalized uncertainty set over plausible latent dynamics, optimizing for worst-case within this set to produce pessimistic but plausible world-model imaginations.

World Models in Robotics. World models predict the outcomes of robot actions directly from high-dimensional observations such as RGB images, enabling vision-based policy learning [ 8 ] , planning [ 50 ] , policy evaluation [ 51 , 52 ] , and policy improvement [ 53 , 54 ] through imaginations [ 55 , 56 , 57 ] . Compared to video world models that predict future observations directly in pixel space [ 58 , 15 ] , latent world models jointly learn compact latent representations and their associated dynamics [ 59 , 9 ] , enabling efficient decision-making directly in the learned latent space [ 10 , 11 , 60 ] . Because world models operate under partial observability, latent dynamics models are often probabilistic models such as recurrent state-space models [ 61 ] and diffusion models [ 62 ] . However, defining disturbances that meaningfully represent uncertainties for robust optimization is challenging [ 27 , 63 ] , while model errors and unseen inputs can further produce hallucinated states during imagination [ 11 , 16 ] . Consequently, world models typically use finite samples from learned dynamics [ 64 , 65 , 66 ] , which can miss rare but high-impact outcomes in high-dimensional spaces [ 15 ] . Our work introduces a latent-space disturbance that directly searches for worst-case latent dynamics with gradient-based optimization.

Latent Safety Filters. Safety filtering is a control-theoretic approach that safeguards dynamical systems from failures given known safety constraints and a system dynamics model [ 67 ] . Safety filters can be implemented through minimally restrictive switching with a safety fallback policy synthesized via Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis [ 7 ] , control barrier functions (CBFs) [ 28 ] , or predictive rollout-based methods such as model predictive safety filtering [ 68 , 69 ] . While such filters can be synthesized using dynamic programming [ 70 ] , self-supervised learning [ 71 ] and reinforcement learning (RL) [ 23 ] have enabled scalable approximations for high-dimensional systems [ 72 ] . Latent safety filters extend this idea to the latent space of learned world models, enabling safety filtering for hard-to-model tasks and safety constraints from high-dimensional observations [ 10 , 11 , 19 ] . By anticipating future failures within world-model imaginations, these methods can proactively steer robots away from failures such as spilling the contents of deformable bags [ 73 ] or toppling complex rigid-body structures [ 11 ] . However, existing latent safety filters evaluate safety under nominal latent dynamics and may therefore overestimate safety under optimistic imaginations. Our method enables the synthesis of robust safety filters using game-theoretic adversarial RL [ 12 , 3 , 43 ] in the learned latent space of world models.

2026-10-07.title: The Robot Is Not Its Description: GaugeBench for Representation Robustness in Morphology-Aware Policies
2026-10-07.authors: Rahath Malladi , Arshia Sangwan , Rajesh K. Gupta , Tauhidur Rahman
2026-10-07.abstract: A robot description does more than specify a physical mechanism: it also encodes arbitrary conventions, such as joint-axis direction, joint-angle zero, and the order and names of links and joints. Morphology-aware policies consume interfaces built from these descriptions, yet cross-embodiment evaluation typically changes the robot while keeping those conventions fixed. This leaves a simple question unanswered: does behavior survive when the robot stays fixed but its description changes? GaugeBench isolates this case by rewriting a fixed mechanism under physically equivalent conventions, verifying that its physics and policy interface are preserved, and then evaluating the same policy weights. The result is stark: three MetaMorph policies score 4030.6 on 80 familiar robots, but only 51.6 when those same robots are equivalently re-described, while 98 genuinely held-out robots score 1489.6. A new description can therefore be more damaging than a new robot. Tracing the failure reveals that axis reversal alone reproduces the collapse, joint-angle zero changes are nearly harmless, and reordering lies between them; moreover, changing joint-state and torque coordinates alone is sufficient to cause the failure, while changing description-derived features alone is not. The same phenomenon appears in ModuMorph and an unrelated PyBullet framework. Yet it is not irreversible: exact two-description transport restores the original controller, and training across equivalent axis conventions raises retained return under axis reversal from 3.6% to 80.6%. Together, these results separate mechanism robustness from representation robustness and show that cross-embodiment evaluation should test both.
2026-10-07.introduction:
One physical mechanism admits many numerical descriptions. Two files can agree on every link, mass, inertia, and joint placement and still disagree on the direction an engineer called positive for a hinge, on the pose that hinge calls zero, and on the order and names of parts. Classical rigid-body equations transform covariantly under a consistent change of generalized coordinates, so a textbook routine returns the same world-frame motion from either file [ 1 , 2 ] . A robot is a mechanism. A description is one way of writing it down.

Cross-embodiment robot learning increasingly conditions a single policy on a structured robot description, and tests it by changing the robot. Robustness here has two distinct axes, and that practice measures only one of them. Mechanism robustness asks whether a policy transfers from the machines it trained on to a new one, M train → M new M_{\mathrm{train}}\rightarrow M_{\mathrm{new}} . Representation robustness asks whether it preserves behavior when one fixed mechanism M M is expressed by two physically equivalent descriptions D ⁡ ( M ) D(M) and D ′ ​ ( M ) D^{\prime}(M) , with the machine itself untouched. Existing cross-robot benchmarks probe the first while keeping one description convention per robot [ 3 ] . GaugeBench isolates the second (Fig. 1 ).

Nothing here assumes that an unconstrained neural policy should be invariant to a coordinate convention it never saw. In general, it has no reason to be. The question is what that costs an evaluation. Cross-embodiment results are read as evidence that a policy has learned something about robots, and we ask how much of that evidence rests on a convention the benchmark never varies. Answering it requires a mechanism that stays fixed while its description changes.

The answer is not graceful degradation. Across three MetaMorph policies, mean return falls from 4030.6 on 80 familiar robots to 51.6 on those same robots under certified equivalent descriptions, while 98 physically held-out robots from the same procedural generator return 1489.6. Across the three baseline policy families we evaluate, every policy loses more from re-describing a robot it was trained on than from meeting the held-out population. A new robot can be easier than a new description of the same robot. We call this comparison the Same-Robot Paradox .

Changing the conventions one at a time shows that a single one is enough. Reversing joint-axis directions retains 3.6 percent of the original return against 97.7 for joint-angle zeros and 35.8 for reordering, and driving axis reversal’s two channels separately, joint-state and torque coordinates alone retain 2.5 percent while description-derived features alone retain 37.6 percent. The effect is not specific to one implementation, reproducing on ModuMorph and, under axis reversal alone, on released policies from an unrelated line of work on modular robot control running in PyBullet. Exact interface transport then recovers the original controller with unchanged weights, and training over randomly drawn equivalent axis conventions raises retained return under axis reversal from 3.6 to 80.6 percent.

Contributions: First, an evaluation axis. GaugeBench separates mechanism robustness from representation robustness, scoring fixed morphology-aware policies on descriptions whose physics and policy interface are certified equivalent before any episode is run. Second, a same-robot representation failure, and which channel reproduces it. An equivalent description of a familiar robot costs these policies more than a physically held-out robot, and controlled interventions show that changing joint-state and action coordinates alone reproduces the collapse while changing description-derived features alone does not. Third, generality and response. The failure reproduces on ModuMorph and on an independent PyBullet system. Exact transport recovers the original controller with unchanged weights, and axis-convention randomization raises retained return under axis reversal from 3.6 to 80.6 percent for the one convention family it samples.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Morphology-aware policy learning

MetaMorph [ 4 ] tokenizes a kinematic graph for a Transformer, ModuMorph [ 5 ] modulates a shared backbone with per-robot context, and Body Transformer [ 6 ] masks attention by embodiment graph, each treating the description as a stand-in for the robot under one convention per machine. Current work extends the interface to morphology tokens [ 7 ] and morphology-conditioned world models [ 8 ] , while cross-embodiment benchmarks evaluate transfer to novel embodiments [ 3 ] . Policies conditioned on images and language [ 9 , 10 ] fix proprioception and action ordering in a comparable way, though we do not transform those interfaces and make no claim about them. We evaluate released systems whose interfaces can be reproduced and transformed exactly, which is what makes a causal test possible.

## II-B Symmetry, equivariance, and canonicalization

In classical rigid-body mechanics, these conventions are bookkeeping, and physical predictions do not depend on which one is chosen [ 1 , 2 ] . Whether learned policies that consume descriptions inherit that independence is an empirical question. Four changes are easy to conflate. Cross-robot benchmarks vary the mechanism. Geometric deep learning handles a rigid motion of a whole scene under global S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) symmetry [ 11 ] , with gauge-equivariant networks addressing tangent-frame choice on manifolds [ 12 ] . Morphological symmetry exploits a symmetry a mechanism genuinely has, such as left–right limb pairs [ 13 ] . Ours is the fourth: a rewrite of one fixed mechanism’s numbers, which leaves the mechanism and its asymmetries where they were and so exists for every robot, symmetric or not.

Repairing such a rewrite is standard machinery, and we claim no novelty for it. Conjugating a fixed policy by an exact interface transport is the lifted policy of an MDP isomorphism [ 14 ] . Canonicalization maps an input to a canonical representative, applies a base model, and transports the output back, whether by frame averaging [ 15 ] , a learned canonicalizer [ 16 ] , or an S ​ E ​ ( 2 ) SE(2) wrapper around a trained manipulation policy [ 17 ] . Proposition 1 only specializes that construction to the full policy-visible input. What is new here is the evaluation axis: certifying physically equivalent descriptions before scoring, measuring what re-description costs against what a new mechanism costs, decomposing that cost by convention, and replicating it across independent systems.

## II-C Closest recent work

Tai [ 18 ] shows that one vision–language–action checkpoint becomes a different controller when its action-scaling metadata changes, so fixed weights can depend on non-physical metadata. That change also alters the physical action produced, so the controller itself is not preserved. We instead certify physical equivalence before evaluation and put the loss in context against held-out robots. Yang and Hatton [ 19 ] make inverse-dynamics identification independent of the generalized-coordinate chart. Their object is a model-fitting objective scored by prediction accuracy, whereas ours is a closed-loop policy scored by task behavior.
