2026-10-07.title: BiGym 2.0: Benchmarking Learned and Agent-Developed Policies for Humanoid Household Manipulation
2026-10-07.authors: Zexi Zhang , Zecheng Zhu , Zidong Chen , Zulkhuu Tuya , Stephen James
2026-10-07.abstract: Humanoid household manipulation requires the arms to act while the body balances, steps and changes posture. We present BiGym 2.0, an adaptation of BiGym for the Unitree G1 across 20 household tasks using a unified whole-body controller for demonstration and evaluation. The suite provides 60 native human virtual-reality demonstrations per task with synchronised multi-camera views and full-body execution records. We benchmark vision-language-action fine-tuning, imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning, and cold-start coding agents given the interaction budget of online reinforcement learning. With the same onboard views, proprioception and whole-body controller for every method, vision-language-action fine-tuning has the highest nine-task mean, and agent-developed programs outperform every demo-driven reinforcement learning baseline on this mean and lead on bimanual reaching. Cross-workspace stacking remains open, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} stays low on pick-box, and multi-object transport is hard for imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning and coding agents. All environments, human demonstrations, and evaluation traces are open-sourced at https://github.com/swirl-uk/BiGym2 .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Humanoid robots are expected to perform household tasks that combine walking with manipulation. Carrying an object, reaching into a dishwasher and changing working height require the arms to act while the legs support and move the body. Today, robot capabilities are produced along two distinct routes: data-driven policy learning (VLAs, imitation learning and demo-driven RL) and agentic policy development (coding agents synthesising executable programs from environment APIs). Recent simulation platforms support G1 loco-manipulation through learned controllers [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] , but no current benchmark combines household tasks, native human demonstrations collected through active whole-body control, deterministic restoration of controller state, and common evaluation of learned and agent-developed policies. This combination matters because both routes must confront the same physical execution stack: unlike a wheeled base that executes velocity commands directly, a walking controller realises them through dynamic gaits that lag, oscillate and perturb the torso [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . We ask what each route can reliably complete under this execution condition, where their capabilities diverge and where they fail together.

BiGym [ 8 ] provides the closest foundation: 40 H1 household tasks with human virtual reality (VR) demonstrations. It offers a 23-dimensional full-joint whole-body mode and a mobile-bimanual mode, but its released demonstrations use the latter. Its floating base directly commands body translation, height and yaw, with planar motion equivalent to an omnidirectional autonomous mobile robot (AMR) base (Fig. 2 ). This separation isolates mobile-bimanual learning from locomotion control. We instead study legged execution, where gait and balance dynamics couple directly into manipulation. We modify BiGym for the G1 by adapting task geometry, collecting demonstrations through active whole-body control, restoring controller state at evaluation, and supporting learned and agent-developed policies.

Coding agents synthesise robot policies by composing perception, kinematics and control APIs into executable programs [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . We formulate a cold-start capability audit: given environment APIs and three synchronised camera views of a single human demonstration, can a coding agent develop reliable household programs within a bounded interaction budget? To match the learned policies, the agent takes three onboard 84 × 84 84\times 84 views and proprioception as input and outputs the same arm, gripper and body commands, with no camera calibration or inverse-kinematics tools. This cold-start setting measures how reliably an agent develops a program without a pre-built skill library, and gives a baseline against which later work can measure skill accumulation.

We present BiGym 2.0, a G1 household loco-manipulation benchmark based on BiGym. Our contributions are: (i) adapting 20 tasks to the G1 workspace, integrating frozen GR00T-WBC walking and balance policies [ 1 ] , and collecting 60 native human VR demonstrations per task through the same controller used for evaluation (Fig. , Section III ); (ii) comparing VLA fine-tuning, imitation learning, online and offline demo-driven RL on nine representative tasks with deterministic evaluation that restores controller states (Table II , Section IV ); (iii) auditing coding agents (GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5) under matched observation and action interfaces ( 84 × 84 84\times 84 views, direct joint control, no IK tools), showing that their programs lead on bimanual reaching, where a program can control each arm separately, and evaluating a tool-augmented cold-start reference to quantify the benefit of classical robotics tooling (Section V ); and (iv) showing that vision-language-action fine-tuning leads plate and cup transport but not box transport, that multi-object transport remains difficult for imitation learning, demo-driven reinforcement learning and code synthesis, and that cross-workspace stacking remains an open frontier (Sections IV and V ).
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Manipulation benchmarks. RLBench [ 13 ] , LIBERO [ 14 ] and robomimic [ 15 ] support studies of task variation, learning from demonstrations and transfer, while RoboCasa [ 16 ] , BEHAVIOR-1K [ 17 ] and ManiSkill3 [ 18 ] scale household scenes, activities and simulation throughput. MimicGen [ 19 ] and DexMimicGen [ 20 ] generate additional demonstrations from a small human set. BiGym [ 8 ] provides 40 household tasks with human demonstrations on the H1. BiGym 2.0 modifies its task layouts and control interface for legged execution on the G1, with demonstrations collected on the adapted system.

Whole-body control and teleoperation. ExBody [ 21 ] , HOMIE [ 22 ] , AMO [ 23 ] , TWIST [ 24 ] and GR00T [ 1 ] provide interfaces for humanoid whole-body motion. HumanPlus [ 25 ] , OmniH2O [ 26 ] and Open-TeleVision [ 27 ] support human teleoperation. We use a frozen GR00T-WBC controller during both VR collection and policy evaluation.

Humanoid learning environments. HumanoidBench [ 28 ] studies locomotion and manipulation with RL, while EgoVLA [ 29 ] provides a humanoid manipulation benchmark with teleoperated data. HumanoidMimicGen [ 3 ] studies data generation for a nine-task G1 loco-manipulation benchmark. SIMPLE [ 2 ] combines collection and rendering with evaluations of imitation, VLA and world-action model (WAM) policies, and HumanoidArena [ 4 ] evaluates hierarchical policies under visual, semantic and execution changes. FetchMan [ 30 ] studies visual reach-and-pick learning from synthetic demonstrations followed by RL. Humanoid Everyday [ 31 ] collects real-robot humanoid manipulation data across everyday activities. Our focus is a suite of household contact and transport tasks with native human demonstrations, supporting comparisons of VLA fine-tuning, imitation learning, demo-driven RL and agent-developed programs. Table I summarises the related settings.

Policy learning and program development. Pretrained VLAs such as OpenVLA [ 32 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 33 ] and GR00T N1 [ 34 ] can be fine-tuned on demonstrations, while ACT [ 35 ] and DP [ 36 ] learn action sequences by imitation learning. CQN-AS [ 37 ] , which extends coarse-to-fine RL [ 38 ] to action sequences, and DrQ-v2+ [ 39 , 38 ] combine demonstrations with online interaction. DEAS [ 40 ] learns from a fixed offline dataset.

Language models generating robot policy code have an established research basis [ 9 ] . CaP-X studies how interface abstraction, interaction and perception affect code-policy performance [ 10 ] . RHO uses reflection and search to optimise policy repositories during development, deploying frozen code in its CaP-Bench experiments [ 11 ] . ASPIRE uses fine-grained execution traces to diagnose failures, validate repairs and accumulate reusable skills [ 12 ] . We follow this code-policy route to benchmark programs developed by GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 within a charged interaction budget on G1 household loco-manipulation. We isolate cold-start policy synthesis per task to measure development reliability, while using the suite to define the progression toward cumulative skill reuse. Section III-E specifies the agent protocol and Section V the tool interfaces.

2026-10-07.title: OpenSplatGraph: From Dense Semantic Maps to Structured Scene Graphs for Open-Vocabulary Robot Perception
2026-10-07.authors: Binh Long Nguyen , Kien Nguyen , Clinton Fookes , Peyman Moghadam
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-07.comment: Accepted to ACCV 2026
2026-10-07.abstract:
Dense 3D mapping with semantic understanding is essential for robotic perception in complex environments. Recent 3D Gaussian Splatting-based mapping approaches enable high-fidelity geometry and efficient open-vocabulary perception, but typically represent semantics as unstructured feature fields that limit object-centric reasoning. In contrast, 3D scene graphs explicitly model objects and their relationships for structured reasoning, but are commonly constructed from sparse geometric representations that do not fully exploit dense semantic maps.
In this work, we present OpenSplatGraph , a unified framework that constructs persistent 3D scene graphs directly from an online Gaussian-based open-vocabulary semantic map. The proposed framework augments the dense semantic map with a reliability-aware semantic field that maintains lightweight observation statistics for confidence-aware, query-conditioned object extraction. Extracted object instances are associated with persistent graph nodes, allowing object attributes and relationships to be incrementally updated across observations and queries. By tightly coupling dense semantic mapping with persistent object-centric representations, our framework supports both language-guided object grounding and structured relational reasoning while preserving the geometric fidelity of Gaussian-based mapping.
Comprehensive evaluations on standard 3D scene understanding benchmarks and real-world robotic experiments demonstrate that OpenSplatGraph achieves competitive performance for online open-vocabulary perception and downstream robotic tasks.
Project page: https://csiro-robotics.github.io/OpenSplatGraph .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Dense 3D mapping with semantic understanding is fundamental to robotic perception, supporting navigation, manipulation, and interaction in complex environments [ 9 , 11 , 38 ] . Recent advances in vision-language foundation models [ 24 , 18 ] have further enabled open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding that responds to natural language queries and generalizes to previously unseen objects.

Meanwhile, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3D-GS) [ 13 ] has established an efficient representation for high-fidelity 3D reconstruction with real-time rendering. Online GS-based mapping systems [ 12 , 21 , 8 ] integrate Gaussian primitives with Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) for geometrically consistent mapping. Building on this representation, open-vocabulary approaches [ 23 , 33 , 34 , 22 ] incorporate vision-language features into dense Gaussian maps, enabling language-guided retrieval of scene regions. However, semantics are often represented as unstructured per-voxel or per-Gaussian feature fields rather than explicit object-level entities. Consequently, they provide limited support for object-centric reasoning and modeling inter-object relationships.

In parallel, 3D Scene Graphs (3DSGs) address this limitation by representing environments as graphs whose nodes correspond to objects and whose edges encode semantic or spatial relationships [ 1 ] . Recent advances have extended scene graphs to online incremental systems [ 32 , 10 ] , open-vocabulary reasoning [ 7 , 16 , 20 ] , and large-scale robotic applications [ 5 , 35 ] . Most open-vocabulary scene graph methods construct graphs from RGB-D observations by projecting 2D detections into point clouds or meshes. While these approaches provide compact and interpretable scene abstractions for reasoning, they typically rely on sparse geometric representations that cannot fully exploit the dense geometric and semantic information available in Gaussian-based maps.

As illustrated in Fig. 1 , robotic systems benefit from these two complementary scene representations.
Dense geometric-semantic maps provide high-fidelity 3D reconstruction for language-grounded perception and localization, whereas object-centric scene graphs explicitly model objects and their relationships for structured reasoning and task planning. However, existing approaches typically emphasize one representation over the other, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve both high-fidelity mapping and structured scene understanding.

In this paper, we propose OpenSplatGraph , a framework that bridges these two paradigms by grounding 3D scene graphs directly in an online open-vocabulary 3D-GS semantic map. Rather than treating the dense semantic field and the scene graph as alternative representations, we maintain both throughout operation, allowing each to serve a complementary role.
The dense semantic map preserves fine-grained geometric and semantic information for open-vocabulary perception, while the scene graph incrementally accumulates persistent object-centric knowledge for structured reasoning.
To support object construction, we introduce a reliability-aware semantic field that augments the dense semantic map with lightweight observation statistics, enabling confidence-aware ranking of query-conditioned object instances.
Extracted object instances are assigned persistent identities and incrementally incorporated into a 3D scene graph, allowing object attributes and relationships to be consistently accumulated across multiple queries.
By jointly maintaining these two representations, OpenSplatGraph preserves the geometric fidelity of dense mapping while progressively constructing an interpretable object-centric representation for language grounding, relational reasoning, and downstream robotic tasks.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce OpenSplatGraph , a unified framework that constructs persistent 3D scene graphs directly from online open-vocabulary Gaussian semantic maps, enabling high-fidelity dense mapping and structured scene understanding within a single system.

We propose a reliability-aware semantic field that leverages lightweight per-voxel observation statistics for robust query-conditioned object extraction under partial observations and semantic ambiguity.

We design a scene graph construction strategy that associates extracted object instances with persistent identities and incrementally accumulates object-centric knowledge across queries for structured relational reasoning.

We validate the framework on standard 3D scene understanding benchmarks and real-world robotic experiments, demonstrating competitive performance for online open-vocabulary perception and downstream robotic tasks.

1. We introduce OpenSplatGraph , a unified framework that constructs persistent 3D scene graphs directly from online open-vocabulary Gaussian semantic maps, enabling high-fidelity dense mapping and structured scene understanding within a single system.

2. We propose a reliability-aware semantic field that leverages lightweight per-voxel observation statistics for robust query-conditioned object extraction under partial observations and semantic ambiguity.

3. We design a scene graph construction strategy that associates extracted object instances with persistent identities and incrementally accumulates object-centric knowledge across queries for structured relational reasoning.

4. We validate the framework on standard 3D scene understanding benchmarks and real-world robotic experiments, demonstrating competitive performance for online open-vocabulary perception and downstream robotic tasks.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Understanding

Vision-language foundation models [ 24 , 18 ] have enabled open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding by aligning visual representations with natural language. Early methods, such as PointCLIP [ 37 ] and ConceptFusion [ 11 ] , leverage language features for point cloud understanding, while LERF [ 14 ] extends language-guided retrieval to Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) representations.
More recently, 3D-GS [ 13 ] has emerged as an efficient representation for open-vocabulary 3D perception and robotic applications [ 22 , 40 ] . Representative methods, including LangSplat [ 23 ] , LEGaussian [ 26 ] , OpenGaussian [ 33 ] , and InstanceGaussian [ 17 ] , associate language features with Gaussian primitives for open-vocabulary querying. However, these methods primarily represent semantics as unstructured feature fields, limiting their support for object-centric and relational reasoning.

## 2.2 3D Gaussian-Based Scene Mapping

3D-GS has been integrated into SLAM systems for efficient online dense mapping and high-fidelity rendering. Methods such as SplaTAM [ 12 ] , MonoGS [ 21 ] , and GS-ICP SLAM [ 8 ] jointly optimize Gaussian representations and camera poses for real-time reconstruction. Subsequent works incorporate semantic information through supervised labels [ 19 , 39 ] or open-vocabulary features, as demonstrated by OpenGS-Fusion [ 34 ] .
These approaches provide geometrically accurate and semantically rich maps for robotic perception.
However, they primarily focus on online reconstruction and semantic fusion, without explicitly maintaining persistent object-centric representations for structured reasoning and task planning.

## 2.3 3D Scene Graphs

3DSGs [ 1 ] represent objects as nodes and their relationships as edges, providing interpretable scene abstractions for planning and human-robot interaction [ 25 , 31 ] .
Recent advances [ 3 ] highlight rapid progress from online incremental graph construction [ 10 , 32 ] to open-vocabulary scene understanding through ConceptGraphs [ 7 ] , Open3DSG [ 16 ] , and Clio [ 20 ] , and large-scale robotic applications [ 5 , 35 ] .
These methods typically construct graphs from point clouds or meshes, providing compact object-centric representations for downstream reasoning. Despite these advances, many open-vocabulary approaches infer object relationships from 2D observations using Vision-Language Models (VLM) , resulting in graph representations that are weakly grounded in dense 3D geometry.

Recent studies [ 6 , 30 ] have explored grounding scene graphs directly in Gaussian representations. Our work follows this emerging direction but adopts a different architectural perspective. Rather than treating the dense maps and the scene graph as alternative world models, we explicitly maintain both throughout operation. The dense semantic field serves as the geometric and semantic foundation for reliable object extraction, while the scene graph incrementally accumulates object-centric knowledge for structured and relational reasoning.

2026-10-07.title: Seeing the Invisible: Physics-Guided Visual Prompting for Temperature- and Radiation-Aware VLA Navigation
2026-10-07.authors: Hojoon Son , Fan Zhang
2026-10-07.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a major paradigm for Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN). However, in safety-critical facilities, invisible risks such as radiation or temperature spikes cannot be detected by an RGB camera, and handling each risk is expensive, requiring a new encoder, new data, and model retraining. We propose Physics-Guided Visual Prompting ( PG-VP ), a plug-and-play multimodal perception module that instead reuses what a frozen VLA model already does well: avoiding visible obstacles. Given a proximal radiation or thermal source, PG-VP performs a physics-guided risk assessment to determine the avoidance direction and overlays a corresponding virtual obstacle that moves across consecutive frames ( Dynamic Visual Prompting ). The navigation policy then naturally detours around this invisible hazard. The identical virtual obstacle is used regardless of hazard type, so the visual prompting pattern remains fixed as sensors are added. When no hazard is detected, nothing is rendered, and the policy behaves exactly as it would without PG-VP. We evaluate PG-VP on OmniNav using the val-unseen splits of R2R-CE and RxR-CE, where it guides the policy toward intended low-risk actions in 84.9% and 83.2% of cases, at a cost of 6.8 and 7.9 percentage points in navigation success rate. We further test it with distinct scenarios on a real robot in the presence of actual thermal and radiation sources, all without any retraining. The real test shows that PG-VP effectively avoids these invisible hazards, improving worst-10% average trajectory safety by 63.45% and 32.59% against thermal and radiation sources, respectively.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) is a core problem in achieving generalist navigation capabilities guided by natural language instructions. In particular, implementing VLN in safety-critical facilities, such as nuclear power plants (NPPs), is beneficial for their operations and maintenance (O&M). Son et al. [ 1 ] proposed a systematic catalog of potential robotic applications in NPP O&M by analyzing historical nuclear incidents using domain-specific large language models (LLMs). Based on their insights, NPP O&M requires multi-task robots rather than task-specific ones. Therefore, VLN systems with generalist robots can be valuable not only in everyday environments but also in safety-critical domains.

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged, leveraging the foundational
capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to unify the perception-to-action pipeline into a jointly trained policy that maps multimodal inputs directly to action tokens, and now represent the latest paradigm of VLN [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Still, a key challenge remains for VLA-based navigation in safety-critical environments: visual perception alone is insufficient. Invisible hazards, such as radiation or temperature spikes, can arise during navigation [ 1 ] , but they leave no signature in the visible spectrum, and thus cannot be detected by a standard RGB camera. A straightforward solution would be to extend a VLA model’s input modalities, but this is expensive: it requires a new encoder, new paired multimodal-language data, and retraining for every new modality [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . More critically, the model offers no guarantee that it preserves its original navigation performance in scenarios without such invisible hazards.

We propose the physics-guided visual prompting (PG-VP) module, which guides the navigation trajectory to naturally detour around invisible proximal hazards by leveraging the frozen VLA model’s foundational capability to avoid visible obstacles. It assesses the risk posed by proximal radiation or thermal sources, identifies the avoidance direction, and overlays the corresponding virtual obstacle onto the VLA model’s input images. Instead of overlaying a static obstacle onto the scene, PG-VP shifts the virtual obstacle across frames to smoothly guide the trajectory, which we call dynamic visual prompting. As a result, the VLA model treats the injected context as a real obstacle and implicitly avoids the invisible hazards. The main benefits of PG-VP are as follows:

PG-VP is a plug-and-play visual prompting module that injects non-geometric multimodal physical context into a VLA-based navigation framework in a zero-shot manner, without touching the model weights. When no hazard is detected, it renders no virtual obstacles, fully preserving the native navigation performance.

PG-VP requires only a risk assessment model per modality. Building this model is far cheaper than adding an encoder, collecting new data, and retraining.

PG-VP renders the same virtual obstacle regardless of modality type. Because the model interprets a single visual prompting pattern rather than a different one for each modality, the alignment with the training distribution remains consistent across sensing modalities.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A VLA-based Robot Navigation

NaVid [ 14 ] was an early attempt to leverage video-based VLMs, directly mapping natural language instructions to low-level navigation actions from an RGB stream; Uni-NaVid [ 15 ] and NaVILA [ 2 ] established this formulation as a VLA paradigm for navigation. Since then, this has advanced along several directions: broadening generalization across embodiments, tasks, and goal modalities through large-scale training [ 16 , 17 , 5 ] ; compressing accumulated video context and improving systemic efficiency for real-time deployment [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] ; injecting geometric priors to recover 3D spatial understanding from RGB input alone [ 21 , 22 ] ; decoupling high-level semantic reasoning from low-level control in dual-system architectures [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] ; and post-training the policy with self-correction data flywheels [ 26 ] . At the intersection of these directions, OmniNav [ 3 ] adopts a fast-slow design: a fast system generates short-horizon continuous-space waypoints via a flow-matching policy, while a slow system plans long-horizon sub-goals from frontiers and visual memory. We adopt OmniNav’s fast system as our underlying vision-only navigation policy.

## II-B Extending Perception Beyond RGB

In VLA-based manipulation, depth can be reconstructed from RGB alone, but contact force, sound, and temperature leave no signature in the visible spectrum. To include these physical quantities in the VLA policy input, researchers must add an additional sensor, and several studies have pursued this approach [ 6 , 8 , 7 , 27 ] . Yet, adding a new sensor is costly. A new modality requires collecting additional robot data [ 9 ] and retraining the model to recover the pretrained alignment [ 28 , 29 ] . Furthermore, for deployment, platforms without the additional sensor require a separate policy [ 30 ] .

In VLA-based navigation, geometric quantities, such as goal coordinates and poses, are directly incorporated into the policy [ 4 , 31 , 17 , 3 ] , or 3D structure is reconstructed from RGB images [ 21 , 22 ] . In some cases, additional geometric sensors fall outside the VLA policy. For example, NaVILA [ 2 ] leverages LiDAR readings for its locomotion controller, while the VLA policy itself relies only on visual input. However, to the best of our knowledge, no prior research has used non-geometric physical quantities as input to VLA navigation.

## II-C Visual Prompting

Overlaying marks on input images has proven effective for guiding a model’s interpretation. BYOVLA inpaints a task-irrelevant region to recover the nominal behavior under visual distraction [ 32 ] , and Visual Attentive Prompting (VAP) applies a tint to the personalized target object [ 33 ] . For navigation, waypoint prediction can be enhanced by placing markers on a navigable region [ 34 ] , grounding goal pixels [ 35 ] , or, in concurrent work, segmenting traversable (green) and non-traversable (red) regions [ 36 ] . These visual prompts emphasize, remove, or label information already present in input images. In contrast, we inject visual context entirely absent from the scene: a moving virtual obstacle.

2026-10-07.title: Task-Space Imitation Guidance for Efficient Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-07.authors: Salar Asayesh , Hossein Darani , Todd Cao , Evgeny Andriash , Mani Ranjbar
2026-10-07.comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026
2026-10-07.abstract:
We introduce Task-Space Imitation Guidance for Efficient Reinforcement Learning (TIGER), a reward-construction and pretraining framework for sparse-reward tabletop robotic manipulation.
TIGER treats an action-chunked imitation policy not as an executable controller or action prior, but as a local task-space progress estimator:
predicted action chunks are converted, using controller-aware action-to-motion mapping, into short-horizon end-effector references,
and the RL agent receives dense progress rewards toward these references while the sparse environment reward remains the dominant objective. During pretraining,
TIGER uses imitation-guided look-ahead signals to relax conservative value penalties for actions predicted to make task-space progress,
reducing off-manifold exploration during early online RL. Across simulation and real-robot experiments,
TIGER improves early sample efficiency and reduces measured safety violations while matching or improving final success rates relative to prior RL and IL–RL baselines on the evaluated tasks.
Videos and an overview of this work are available at https://sanctuary.ai/news/tiger/ .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Robotic imitation learning (IL) has become a central paradigm for learning
manipulation skills from demonstrations, with action chunking, diffusion
policies, and generalist robot policies showing strong results on diverse
tasks [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
By learning directly from demonstrations, these methods avoid manually
engineered dense rewards and accurate task dynamics models.
However, deployment-oriented manipulation exposes limitations that are less
visible in benchmark settings: policies must maintain high success under
variation while also satisfying reliability and cycle-time constraints.
Achieving this with pure IL typically requires broad, high-quality
demonstration coverage, making physical data collection costly through
teleoperation or careful curation.
More fundamentally, imitation objectives optimize agreement with demonstrated
actions rather than task success, robustness, or execution time.
Thus, IL provides a strong behavioral prior, but not a mechanism for autonomous
task optimization or systematic improvement beyond demonstrations [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .

Reinforcement Learning (RL) can improve beyond imitation by directly optimizing
task success through interaction.
Unlike IL, RL can collect new experience and discover behaviors that are more
reliable or efficient than the demonstrations.
Discounted objectives also favor receiving task rewards earlier, making RL
appealing when cycle time matters.
However, direct robot RL remains difficult: sparse or binary rewards provide
little feedback during early exploration, while unstructured exploration can
cause unsafe motions, workspace violations, object drops, or frequent manual
resets.
Thus, RL provides a principled mechanism for task optimization, but requires
structured guidance to become sample-efficient and practical for real-world
manipulation.

Prior IL–RL methods improve sample efficiency by using demonstrations for
initialization, replay-buffer augmentation, auxiliary losses, or action
proposals [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] .
However, in sparse-reward settings these approaches can still rely on unreliable
early critics to balance imitation and exploration.
Dense trajectory-alignment rewards offer another source of feedback [ 10 , 11 ] , but typically require ground-truth state trajectories,
image-level alignment, or task-specific supervision.
This motivates extracting dense guidance from imitation itself: demonstrations
naturally specify task-relevant motion, while hand-engineered rewards require
detailed state, models, or task-specific design.
Rather than using imitation only as an action prior, such guidance can provide
task-aligned feedback before sparse rewards or accurate value estimates are
available.

We propose Task-Space Imitation Guidance for Efficient Reinforcement
Learning (TIGER) , which turns imitation policies into dense task-space rewards
and imitation-guided critic pretraining for sparse-reward robotic manipulation.
TIGER treats an imitation policy not as an executable controller or action
prior, but as a local task-space progress estimator: given the current
observation, the policy predicts an action chunk that is mapped to a short-horizon
end-effector reference trajectory.
The RL agent receives dense reward for making progress toward this reference,
while the sparse environment reward remains the dominant task objective.
TIGER also uses imitation-guided look-ahead signals to modulate conservative
critic pretraining, reducing early off-manifold exploration.
Because guidance enters through rewards and pretraining, TIGER can
combine with different off-policy RL algorithms.
TIGER targets tasks where short-horizon end-effector motion is informative for
progress, assuming reliable end-effector pose estimates and an approximate
action-to-end-effector mapping.

We evaluate TIGER in simulation and on real robots across sparse-reward
manipulation tasks with randomized initial conditions, including grasping,
opening, and insertion.
Across settings, TIGER improves early sample efficiency, reduces measured safety
violations, and achieves competitive or higher final success rates than prior RL
and IL–RL baselines.

Our contributions are:
(i) an imitation-guided reward construction method that maps predicted action
chunks into short-horizon task-space reference motion and dense progress rewards
for sparse-reward manipulation;
(ii) an offline pretraining objective that uses imitation-guided
look-ahead signals to stabilize value learning before online interaction; and
(iii) simulated and real-robot evidence that TIGER improves early sample
efficiency and reduces measured safety violations while maintaining competitive
final success rates.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

A related line of research studies learning from fixed datasets—offline reinforcement learning—as formalized by Levine et al. [12] , where off-policy methods must mitigate value overestimation from out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Kumar et al. [13] introduce pessimistic regularization that lowers the value of unsupported actions, Kostrikov et al. [14] restrict policy learning to the dataset support, and Nakamoto et al. [15] add a calibration mechanism that stabilizes online fine-tuning. Building on these advances, several approaches combine offline pre-training with online fine-tuning ( Nair et al. [16] , Nakamoto et al. [15] , Haldar et al. [17] ), achieving substantial gains in sample efficiency, though most rely on dense reward signals.

Kostrikov et al. [14] constrain policy learning to the dataset support, and Nakamoto et al. [15] calibrate value estimates to stabilize online fine-tuning. Building on these advances, several approaches combine offline pretraining with online fine-tuning [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] , achieving substantial gains in sample efficiency, though most assume access to dense rewards.

A complementary line of work uses demonstrations to address sparse or binary rewards in contact-rich manipulation.
Replay mixing with demonstrations [ 8 , 18 ] can accelerate
learning, but becomes less effective as task horizons grow. Other methods regularize the policy toward the
demonstrated action distribution [ 19 , 20 ] .
GAIL [ 21 ] and AIRL [ 22 ] instead learn imitation objectives through adversarial
discriminator or reward optimization. Li et al. [23] learns a state-only goal-proximity reward from constrained demonstrations
and extends it to online states
through confidence-guided interpolation. TIGER uses a fixed imitation policy to provide task-space
guidance without online discriminator or reward learning.

Recent advances show that end-to-end reinforcement learning on physical robots is feasible within practical time budgets. For instance, Luo et al. [7] , building on Ball et al. [8] , introduce a unified framework where careful system design enables scalable real-world training from scratch, though many approaches restrict operational space and focus on short-horizon tasks. In contrast, Hu et al. [9] train an imitation policy from few demonstrations to guide exploration and bootstrap value estimation, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency but lacking a principled early-stage balance between imitation and exploration, which can slow or destabilize convergence.

More recently, dense surrogate rewards from learned perceptual or task-space representations have guided exploration in sparse-reward settings. For example, Zhao et al. [11] employ a pretrained DINOv2 encoder to construct an embedding space for forward prediction, encouraging exploration near demonstration trajectories and enabling efficient real-robot learning, albeit under constrained randomization and increased computational cost.
ReWiND [ 24 ] , Robometer [ 25 ] , and RoboReward [ 26 ] instead estimate task progress in learned visual or vision-language spaces.
TIGER converts imitation-predicted action chunks into short-horizon task-space progress signals.

2026-10-07.title: ReDex: Repairing Sim-to-Real Dexterous Policies by Finger-Level Compliant Interaction
2026-10-07.authors: Jinzhou Li , Hadi Tabatabaee , Kelin Yu , Yuyin Sun , Cheng-Hao Kuo , Roberto Martín-Martín , Nima Fazeli , X. Alice Wu , Xianyi Cheng
2026-10-07.abstract:
Dexterous manipulation policies trained in simulation often fail to transfer to the real world because of errors in contact timing and force regulation. Yet these policies can retain useful multi-finger coordination for task progression. We propose ReDex, a framework for adapting a simulation-trained base policy to the real world by correcting
local contact failures and incorporating tactile feedback.
Starting from a proprioception-only base policy, ReDex allows a human operator to physically correct contact failures at selected fingers under compliant control during real-world rollouts, while the frozen base policy continues to control the remaining fingers. These rollouts combine base policy execution, human-corrected finger motion, and fingertip force observations. We reconstruct force-informed targets from these rollouts to train a standalone force-conditioned policy via behavior cloning.
This design reduces human correction effort, enables learning of contact regulation from real-world interaction, and introduces force feedback into a proprioception-only policy without tactile simulation or complex full-hand teleoperation.
We evaluate ReDex on two challenging, contact-rich dexterous manipulation tasks on real hardware. Compared with sim-to-real transferred base policies, ReDex increases Object Flipping success rate from 14% to 86% across two objects and average Screwdriver Rotation progress from 26.0% to 95.3% across three objects.
2026-10-07.introduction:
For multi-finger hands, large-scale simulation training provides an efficient way to learn the coordination required for dexterous manipulation [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . However, sim-to-real transfer proves difficult for several reasons such as errors in contact placement, timing, or contact force regulation. Fingers may touch the wrong surfaces, release contact prematurely, or apply excessive or insufficient force [ 6 , 3 ] . Addressing these errors through further simulation training is challenging because real-world contact dynamics are difficult to model accurately. Repeatedly retuning rewards or ranges of domain randomization and retraining policies in simulation can be costly without necessarily resolving the specific contact failures observed in real-world experiments.

Learning from human corrections on a real robot offers a direct way to address failures due to real-world physics. Existing correction approaches typically rely on teleoperation or kinesthetic teaching to modify the robot’s end-effector or arm-level motion [ 7 , 8 ] . Extending human corrections to multi-finger hands remains difficult due to three challenges: 1) kinesthetic teaching for multi-finger hands is difficult to execute as finger motions must be simultaneously controlled to ensure stable contact during manipulation, 2) teleoperation does not accurately reflect the optimal contact force profile for completing the target task and 3) collecting successful full-hand demonstrations may require substantial effort.

Existing methods address some of these but not all. A skill-assisted interface reduces this burden by combining human wrist control with learned finger motions [ 9 ] , but does not allow adjustment of individual finger contacts. Hand-motion retargeting enables finger pose corrections [ 10 , 11 ] but does not ensure appropriate contact forces: a corrected finger pose may still produce insufficient force to prevent slipping or excessive force that impedes motion. Furthermore, identifying and correcting these force errors remains difficult because human operators typically lack direct perception of the contact forces experienced by the robot [ 12 , 13 ] .
Therefore, a key gap remains in multi-finger dexterous manipulation on enabling human operators to easily correct finger motion and contact forces from simulation-trained policies to enable better task performance and real-world success rate.

To this end, we introduce ReDex, a framework that adapts a simulation-trained dexterous policy to the real world through finger-level physical correction under compliance control, together with real-world fingertip force feedback (Fig. 1 ). Our key insight is that these sim-to-real failures are usually local : the frozen base policy still produces the multi-finger coordination the task needs, and only a few finger contacts are misplaced or apply the wrong force. ReDex therefore preserves this coordination and lets a human physically repair only the failing fingers, while fingertip tactile sensing captures the contact force each correction applies. Confining correction to where the real world breaks the policy preserves the simulation-learned behavior and keeps the required human effort small.

Specifically, ReDex proceeds in three stages. First, we train the proprioceptive base policy in simulation. Second, we roll out the frozen base policy on the real hand and let the operator physically correct only the fingers that deviate, selectively increasing their compliance so the operator can guide them while the base policy continues to control the remaining fingers in closed loop; each rollout records the full-hand motion and fingertip forces throughout execution, capturing both base-policy-controlled behavior and human physical corrections. Third, we reconstruct force-informed joint-position targets and distill the recorded human corrections and successful base-policy execution into a standalone force-conditioned policy via behavior cloning.

We evaluate ReDex on two challenging dexterous manipulation tasks, Object Flipping and Screwdriver Rotation, across five objects with varying sizes and geometries. Our real-world experiments show that ReDex substantially improves autonomous task performance with a small amount of finger-level correction per object. Ablation studies further highlight the value of tactile feedback both in constructing force-informed supervision and in enabling the learned policy to respond to contact changes during execution.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We introduce a human correction framework based on selective finger compliance, enabling direct physical correction of individual finger behavior while the base policy continues to control the remaining fingers, reducing the operator’s coordination burden;

We develop efficient learning of finger contact regulation via a relabeling pipeline that turns corrected motion, real-world tactile feedback, and base policy continuation into dense supervision;

We demonstrate that a few minutes of physical correction per object can turn a simulation-trained policy into an improved force-conditioned real-world policy.

1. We introduce a human correction framework based on selective finger compliance, enabling direct physical correction of individual finger behavior while the base policy continues to control the remaining fingers, reducing the operator’s coordination burden;

2. We develop efficient learning of finger contact regulation via a relabeling pipeline that turns corrected motion, real-world tactile feedback, and base policy continuation into dense supervision;

3. We demonstrate that a few minutes of physical correction per object can turn a simulation-trained policy into an improved force-conditioned real-world policy.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Learning Dexterous Manipulation via RL

Training dexterous policies directly on hardware is difficult because collecting demonstrations and running real-world reinforcement learning are costly [ 14 ] . Simulation instead enables large-scale parallel training, privileged state information, and domain randomization for dexterous manipulation, including in-hand reorientation [ 2 , 1 , 4 ] and tool use [ 5 , 9 ] . However, sim-to-real transfer remains challenging due to differences in object properties, contact mechanics, and robot actuation, even with domain randomization and system identification [ 6 , 3 , 9 ] . Our method preserves simulation-learned multi-finger coordination while correcting selected fingers on real hardware.

## II-B Learning from Human Correction

Human corrections provide a direct way to improve robot policies from deployment failures. Interactive imitation learning methods including DAgger [ 15 ] and its variants [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] collect corrective actions on learner-visited states, while human feedback has also been incorporated into real-world reinforcement learning [ 19 ] . More recently, human corrections have been used to adapt simulation-trained policies during real-world deployment. TRANSIC [ 7 ] learns a gated residual policy from teleoperated corrections, while CR-DAgger [ 8 ] uses compliant physical interaction to collect corrections and learn residual actions over a base policy. These methods primarily consider arm motion, whereas correction for dexterous hands requires controlling multiple fingers through changing contacts. DexScrew [ 9 ] reduces this burden by combining human wrist control with a learned full-hand manipulation primitive, preserving learned finger coordination but not allowing direct correction of individual finger contacts. DexHiL [ 10 ] and HandITL [ 11 ] instead retarget human hand motion for full-hand or hand–arm intervention, enabling direct finger control but requiring the operator to coordinate the hand during correction. ReDex instead intervenes only on the failed fingers while the base policy continues controlling the remaining fingers, preserving learned coordination during correction.

## II-C Learning with Contact Feedback

Learning contact-rich manipulation requires both motion coordination and contact regulation. Force feedback provides contact information that is difficult to infer from motion alone. One line of work incorporates real contact information through demonstrations or physical guidance [ 12 , 20 , 21 ] . In particular, DexForce [ 12 ] uses contact forces measured during kinesthetic demonstrations to construct force-informed actions for policy learning. Compliance has also been used to support physical guidance, allowing an operator to directly modify contact through physical interaction [ 20 , 22 , 23 ] . While these approaches provide real contact information, collecting force-rich demonstrations or physical guidance for dexterous manipulation can still require substantial human effort.
Another line of work models tactile sensing in simulation to support contact-aware policy learning and sim-to-real transfer [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] . These approaches require sensor-specific modeling and calibration, while accurately simulating contact-rich interactions remains challenging. More recent work introduces force or tactile feedback after learning an initial policy [ 9 , 27 , 8 ] . We follow this post-training setting and use finger-level compliance to correct only selected fingers while the base policy continues to control the remaining fingers. The measured forces are then used both to reconstruct force-informed supervision and as policy observations, enabling learning from real contact without full-hand force-rich demonstrations.

2026-10-07.title: ProCut: Probabilistic Cutting Topology for Autonomous Electrosurgical Tissue Dissection
2026-10-07.authors: Xiao Liang , Fei Liu , Florian Richter , Genie Rubaiyat , Michael Yip
2026-10-07.abstract: Accurately modeling and tracking the deformation of soft tissue is critical for a wide range of interventional and surgical procedures. However, current methods struggle in scenarios involving topological changes—such as cutting and dissection—due to the inherent non-linearity and discontinuity introduced by explicit changes in connectivity. In this work, we present a novel, fully differentiable framework that enables robust estimation and modeling of topological changes during deformable tracking. Our method introduces a continuous, sigmoid-based formulation to smooth the otherwise discrete event of tissue cutting, making it amenable to gradient-based optimization within a differentiable Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) simulation. To account for uncertainty and improve robustness in the presence of noisy visual data, we incorporate Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD) for particle-based probabilistic inference, generating multiple hypotheses for topological state estimation. Building on this foundation, we develop an autonomous dissection algorithm for thin-shell tissues that leverages topological updates to guide closed-loop cutting trajectory control. We evaluate our approach in both simulated and real-world electrosurgical environments, demonstrating significant improvements in topological estimation accuracy and dissection precision over existing methods. Our results highlight the potential of this framework to advance automation in soft-tissue surgical procedures by enabling reliable perception and control in the presence of complex structural changes.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Modeling and tracking of deformable objects, such as soft tissue and human organs, play a crucial role in various interventional and surgical procedures [ 36 ] . The process includes capturing soft bodies deformation [ 7 ] and enabling understanding and prediction of physical behaviors of the deformable objects over time [ 19 ] .
In interventional procedures with CT and MRI data, deformable tracking methods elevate the reliability of procedures such as radiation therapy [ 39 ] and image-guided biopsy [ 27 ] .
In image-guided surgery, this technology assists surgeons by providing additional visual guidance [ 3 ] , reducing their cognitive load. Recent efforts in surgical autonomy such as tissue manipulation [ 11 ] , blood suction [ 31 ] , and suturing [ 12 ] , have also relied on deformable tracking algorithms applied to endoscopic image data, serving as crucial cues for the autonomous agents.
Despite being broadly used, a significant limitation remains: existing deformable modeling and tracking methods struggle to handle tissue connectivity changes that is ubiquitous in surgery.
This limitation poses a challenge for further advancement in bringing autonomy to surgery including accurate tissue visualization after dissections or even autonomy of tissue dissection itself.

Most prior methods in deformable tracking and modeling rely on visual inputs,
whether optimization-based [ 23 , 33 ] or learning-based [ 17 , 7 ] , commonly incorporate spatial smoothness objectives to encourage physically plausible deformation estimation.
However, these computer vision techniques do not explicitly consider topological changes leading to over-regularizing and inaccuracies in regions with topological changes.
Other works integrates visual observations with physics-based modeling, including physics-based deformable registration [ 42 ] and real-to-sim state estimation [ 38 ] .
These approaches are also limited by their underlying physics models, which are not designed to accommodate topological changes.
Explicit estimation of topological changes has been explored through direct deletion of mesh edges based on a heuristic-strategy [ 30 , 41 ] and learning approaches [ 5 ] .
However, these approaches are limited in robustness due to their sensitivity to observation noise, reliance on handcrafted rules or training data, and reduced generalization ability to unseen topological variations.

To overcome these limitations, we propose ProCut , a differentiable formulation for tracking, modeling, and applying topological changes during tissue cutting tasks.
Tissue cutting introduces a highly non-linear transformation, as it involves explicit removal of mesh connectivity.
Our approach makes this non-linearity amenable to gradient-based optimization by smoothing the connectivity change using a sigmoid function.
formulation is integrated into a differentiable physics simulator, Position-Based Dynamics (PBD), for deformable tracking and modeling [ 19 ] .
Additionally, we incorporate the estimation of topological changes into a particle-based probabilistic estimation algorithm, Stein Variational Gradient Descent (SVGD), enabling multiple hypotheses to initialize the optimization process and providing uncertainty of the estimated topological change.
Leveraging this fully differentiable framework, an autonomous dissection algorithm is devised that is tailored to thin-shell tissue, using topological updates as cues for closed-loop dissection trajectory control. In summary, the main contributions of this work are:

A differentiable cutting topology model that represents tissue
connectivity through a smooth, gradient-compatible formulation, enabling
end-to-end optimization of dissection trajectories within a differentiable simulator.

A probabilistic topology estimator based on SVGD that maintains a distribution over cutting curves
from visual observations, providing calibrated uncertainty estimates to
guide closed-loop dissection under deformation and observation noise.

An autonomous electrosurgical dissection pipeline integrating the above components into a real-time perception-planning-control
loop, validated in both simulation and on ex-vivo tissue, and demonstrating
recovery from topology estimation errors without replanning from scratch.

connectivity through a smooth, gradient-compatible formulation, enabling
end-to-end optimization of dissection trajectories within a differentiable simulator.

2. A probabilistic topology estimator based on SVGD that maintains a distribution over cutting curves
from visual observations, providing calibrated uncertainty estimates to
guide closed-loop dissection under deformation and observation noise.

3. An autonomous electrosurgical dissection pipeline integrating the above components into a real-time perception-planning-control

# II RELATED WORK

Deformable Cutting Simulation. The simulation of soft body cutting has been extensively studied using methods such as rope-grid [ 8 ] , PBD [ 45 , 2 ] , Finite Element Methods (FEM) [ 43 ] [ 35 , 34 ] , and the Material Point Method (MPM) [ 44 ] . These works provide valuable testbeds, but they
are designed as forward simulators, but lacks the ability to incorporate real-world feedback.
A second line of work has introduced differentiability into cutting
simulation to enable gradient-based optimization.
SliceIt! [ 1 ] proposes a differentiable simulator for
training cutting agents, but similarly does not address topology estimation
from real observations.
DiSECt [ 10 ] is the most closely related effort: it
formulates cutting as the gradual weakening of virtual springs connecting
nodes across a predefined cutting plane , which restricts the geometry
of admissible cuts. In contrast, our method introduces a differentiable cutting-curve representation that directly parameterizes the cut path
on the tissue surface, allowing the topology itself to be an optimization
variable inferred from visual feedback, which is essential for closed-loop dissection. [ 30 ] combined visual feature tracking with an FEM-based tissue simulation to update the model topology.
Nevertheless, this approach relies on hand-crafted heuristics to detect topological changes, making it susceptible to noise in observational data.

Autonomous Cutting and Dissection. [ 9 ] proposed a vision-based closed-loop controller to ensure accurate knife cutting depth along a predefined trajectory. [ 28 , 37 ] developed reinforcement learning algorithms to simultaneously perform tensioning and cutting on surgical gauze pads.
Electrosurgical dissection is more often used in tissue dissection in robotic surgeries.
For instance, [ 32 ] experimented with a near-infrared marking method for electrosurgery on porcine tongue samples. [ 6 ] introduced a suction gripper to retract tissue, facilitating electrocautery procedures.
Similarly, [ 20 ] focused on dissection assistance that helps reveal the surgical site during electrocautery procedures. [ 29 ] proposed a framework that leverages semantic segmentation and key-point detection for electrocautery along tissue boundaries.
Furthermore, [ 14 ] designed a reinforcement learning-based approach to control a cautery tool to remove tissue attachments.
While these methods demonstrate progress in automating Electrosurgical dissection tasks, they are largely constrained to controlled environments and do not account for real-world challenges such as noise, disturbances, and changing tissue topology.

2026-10-07.title: MobileVISTA: Generative Data Augmentation for Pose Generalization in Mobile Manipulation
2026-10-07.authors: Suzannah Wistreich , Stephen Tian , Isabella Huang , Vitor Campagnolo Guizilini , Sergey Zakharov , Katherine Liu , Jiajun Wu
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-07.abstract:
Mobile manipulators such as humanoid robots are increasingly deployed in dynamic, unstructured environments to perform dexterous manipulation tasks.
However, end-to-end manipulation policies trained to imitate demonstration data collected from a single robot pose are brittle: even centimeter-scale deviations in robot pose at deployment can drive egocentric observations and end-effector trajectories out of the training distribution, leading to sharp drops in performance.
We introduce MobileVISTA , a data generation framework that transforms demonstrations captured at canonical poses into diverse, pose-perturbed training data by jointly (1) augmenting egocentric visual observations and (2) retargeting actions to compensate for base pose changes. Unlike prior methods, which assume a camera rigidly mounted off the actuated chain or non-trivial articulated robot geometry largely out of frame, MobileVISTA targets compatibility with egocentric platforms (e.g., humanoids) where the camera is both influenced by and must observe the robot’s kinematic chain as it moves. We study MobileVISTA in simulated tasks spanning humanoid and bimanual embodiments, and on a real Galaxea R1 Pro. We find policies trained on MobileVISTA -augmented data demonstrate improved robustness to previously out-of-distribution poses encountered at test time, without additional demonstration collection or a trained generative model. Additionally, we find MobileVISTA ’s benefit is largest on tested humanoids, where the camera rides the actuated chain and the robot fills much of the frame. Additional videos and appendix can be found on our website: https://sdwistreich.github.io/mobilevista
2026-10-07.introduction:
Mobile manipulators increasingly execute complex skills in settings where navigation and manipulation are tightly sequenced, transitioning directly from locomotion to dexterous interaction from whatever configuration state navigation leaves them in. However, visuomotor policies trained to imitate a small set of task-specific demonstrations overfit to the narrow distribution of robot configurations seen during training. Large-scale pretrained policies aim to broaden this distribution [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , but deploying on a new task often still relies on task-specific demonstrations, with the fine-tuned policy inheriting their restricted pose distribution.
These policies therefore fail to generalize beyond the narrow set of base poses and camera viewpoints seen during training. Even centimeter-scale base pose perturbations [ 4 ] —such as those arising from reasonable navigation error—can push the robot into out-of-distribution states.

Re-collecting demonstrations from many base poses is often impractical and scales poorly with the diversity of poses met at deployment, so a desirable property is solving tasks from whichever configuration the robot occupies without new demonstrations. Several methods synthesize novel visual observations [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] to emulate camera viewpoint changes with the robot base fixed, leaving action labels unchanged. In mobile settings, however, a base shift alters both onboard camera observations, whose viewpoints depend on the full kinematic chain from base to camera, and the actions needed to complete the task. Recent work generates the two jointly [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] , but assumes either a camera fixed rigidly to the base or a view containing little robot geometry beyond a gripper. Humanoids satisfy neither: the camera rides an actuated torso, so the target viewpoint is settled by the same inverse-kinematics solve that produces the retargeted action, and the arms and torso fill much of that view.

Toward addressing these limitations, we present MobileVISTA , a data generation framework that transforms manipulation demonstrations collected from a single canonical base pose into diverse, pose-perturbed training data for mobile manipulation. Our key contributions are:

MobileVISTA , a data generation framework for pose-robust mobile manipulation that produces physically consistent training data for arbitrary
base configurations entirely offline, without additional data collection.

An explicit geometry-based observation synthesis procedure that removes the robot from the observation, reprojects the scene with the perturbed base pose, and composites a re-rendering of the robot with retargeted joint configurations. One solve yields both the extrinsics of the synthesized view and the robot link poses within it, separating our setting from prior work (Table I).

A controlled comparison against learned novel view synthesis [ 11 ] : explicit geometry-based reprojection with robot segmentation and re-compositing better preserves scene geometry and yields stronger downstream policy performance, and benefit scales with how much of the egocentric frame the robot occupies.

We evaluate MobileVISTA in simulation and on a real Galaxea R1 Pro humanoid, improving over baselines that leverage 3D representations and large-scale pretrained policies under unseen base perturbations. MobileVISTA offers a practical data generation approach for robust mobile manipulation under deployment conditions where robot pose cannot be precisely controlled.

1. MobileVISTA , a data generation framework for pose-robust mobile manipulation that produces physically consistent training data for arbitrary
base configurations entirely offline, without additional data collection.

2. An explicit geometry-based observation synthesis procedure that removes the robot from the observation, reprojects the scene with the perturbed base pose, and composites a re-rendering of the robot with retargeted joint configurations. One solve yields both the extrinsics of the synthesized view and the robot link poses within it, separating our setting from prior work (Table I).

3. A controlled comparison against learned novel view synthesis [ 11 ] : explicit geometry-based reprojection with robot segmentation and re-compositing better preserves scene geometry and yields stronger downstream policy performance, and benefit scales with how much of the egocentric frame the robot occupies.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Learning robust mobile manipulation. Learned policies for navigation and manipulation have been widely studied for mobile manipulators. End-to-end approaches train whole-body controllers that jointly produce base and arm actions [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . In contrast, modular approaches treat navigation and manipulation as sequential, decoupled components [ 15 , 16 ] . Although this “park-and-manipulate” paradigm is less expressive than end-to-end control, it requires less training data and is more interpretable. A key challenge in modular systems is ensuring reliable manipulation after navigation, as the post-navigation state may fall outside the manipulation policy’s training distribution. ASC [ 17 ] addresses this by learning a corrective policy that adapts existing manipulation skills to such states. In contrast, Mobi- π \pi [ 4 ] , MoTo [ 18 ] , and N2M [ 19 ] optimize the robot’s base pose to remain within the manipulation policy’s training distribution. We instead pursue a complementary direction by designing manipulation policies that are inherently robust to a wide range of base poses.

Synthetic data generation in robot learning. Synthetic data generation is a promising approach to augmenting scarce human demonstration data. Some methods generate synthetic images to improve generalization to novel object and scene configurations [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Another application is generating cross-embodiment data, e.g. from human to robot [ 25 ] or robot to robot [ 7 ] . Synthetic observations can also improve robustness to eye-in-hand observations [ 26 ] .

Viewpoint-robust demonstration generation. Several recent methods generate paired observation–action data for viewpoint robustness. RoboSplat [ 27 ] edits a Gaussian Splatting reconstruction to vary object pose and type, appearance, lighting, and camera pose, while 1001 Demos [ 10 ] couples Gaussian-Splatting rendering of an eye-in-hand fisheye camera with trajectory optimization, compositing gripper geometry into rendered views. However, both assume a fixed base and a per-scene reconstruction captured in advance. VISTA [ 5 ] and ROPA [ 6 ] fine-tune image diffusion models to render the scene and robot from novel third-person poses, while R2RGen [ 9 ] avoids image synthesis entirely, requiring that “the RGB-D sensor be fixed during task execution.”

Two distinguishing properties characterize our target setting: (1) the camera rides the actuated chain, so its pose is known only once inverse kinematics resolves a configuration for the retargeted action; and (2) the robot kinematic chain is visible in frame, so synthesis must re-render articulated geometry rather than composite a rigid end-effector.
Prior methods satisfy at most one (Table I ). Closest to our setting is EgoDemoGen [ 8 ] , generating paired egocentric observations and actions under planar base perturbations, but whose “egocentric camera is rigidly mounted on the robot head, which is fixed to the base.” MobileVISTA instead targets cameras on the actuated chain, and synthesizes via explicit geometry rather than a per-domain fine-tuned video generator.

We do not run the methods of Table I as baselines. Five methods assume a fixed base and therefore define no action at a perturbed pose. Of the two that consider a mobile base, R2RGen synthesizes no images, and EgoDemoGen, which synthesizes with a learned video generator, has no public implementation as of submission. We instead compare against learned NVS directly, using GEN3C (Section IV-C ), and isolate the contribution of robot re-rendering through a Fixed Robot Geom. ablation (Section IV-B ).
