2026-10-07.title: Risk-Sensitive Crowd Navigation with Adaptive Ellipsoidal Conformal Prediction
2026-10-07.authors: Ruihan A. Li , Ziyao Guo , Yingying Li
2026-10-07.abstract: Safe crowd navigation under distribution shift requires uncertainty representations that capture structured human-motion prediction errors and safety objectives that account for rare but consequential failures. Existing uncertainty-aware methods typically represent prediction errors using isotropic regions, which can be either overly conservative or poorly aligned with directional motion uncertainty. We introduce a risk-aware navigation framework that uses anisotropic conformal ellipsoids to translate structured prediction uncertainty into an episode-level conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) signal that regulates the Lagrangian safety penalty. In particular, adaptive ellipsoidal conformal prediction (AECP) captures directional prediction errors and adaptively calibrates uncertainty regions under distribution shift, while the resulting CVaR-regulated navigation policy is optimized using Lagrangian proximal policy optimization. We evaluate our proposed method under both in-distribution settings and out-of-distribution (OOD) settings involving shifts in pedestrian motion patterns. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, our method maintains competitive in-distribution performance while improving success rates by 5.68–7.44 percentage points and reducing collision rates by 5.44–6.64 percentage points across OOD settings. We further deploy the trained policy without fine-tuning on a physical robot with onboard perception and CPU-only inference, showing that the full pipeline is feasible in physical crowd navigation.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Safe robot navigation in crowded environments requires reliable decision making despite the variability and uncertainty of human motion [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Learning-based crowd-navigation methods have made substantial progress by modeling human–robot interactions and predicting future trajectories of pedestrians [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . However, strong performance under familiar crowd conditions does not necessarily translate to reliable behavior when human-motion patterns change. For example, differences in crowd flow, pedestrian dynamics, and interaction patterns can induce distribution shifts that affect both trajectory prediction and downstream policy decisions. Therefore, achieving safety under distribution shifts remains an important challenge for learning-based crowd navigation [ 7 , 8 ] .

Human-trajectory prediction provides useful information about how pedestrians may move, but prediction errors can change substantially when crowd dynamics differ from those encountered during training [ 6 , 7 ] . Recent uncertainty-aware navigation methods use Conformal Prediction (CP) to quantify such errors and adapt prediction uncertainty online [ 7 , 9 , 8 , 10 , 11 ] . For example, Dynamically-tuned Adaptive Conformal Inference (DtACI) has been incorporated into crowd-navigation policies to improve robustness under distribution shift [ 7 ] . However, existing DtACI-based crowd navigation constructs uncertainty from Euclidean prediction errors, resulting in circular prediction regions around future human positions. Although adaptive CP methods can update the sizes of circular prediction regions, the isotropic geometry of circular regions cannot represent directional variation in prediction errors. As illustrated in Figure 1 , prediction errors under distribution shift can exhibit anisotropic structures. To accommodate large errors along a dominant direction, a circular region must expand uniformly in all directions, which can introduce unnecessary conservatism and significantly reduce the free space available for navigation. In contrast, prior work on multivariate conformal prediction has shown that ellipsoidal regions can capture dependence and directional structure in prediction errors [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] , motivating an uncertainty representation for crowd navigation that can adapt both its geometry and scale online for anisotropic human-trajectory prediction errors.

In this work, we introduce Adaptive Ellipsoidal Conformal Prediction (AECP) for crowd navigation under distribution shift. For each human and prediction horizon, AECP causally estimates the directional structure of trajectory-prediction residuals and uses it to construct an ellipsoidal uncertainty geometry. The resulting shape determines the orientation and relative axis lengths of the prediction region, and DtACI is employed to independently adapt the conformal scale online. This separation allows the uncertainty representation to respond to directional prediction errors without conflating geometric shape with conformal calibration. We incorporate the resulting ellipsoidal uncertainty regions into a constrained reinforcement-learning framework. To improve sensitivity to rare high-cost interactions, we incorporate episode-level CVaR to regulate tail risks [ 16 , 17 ] . In summary,
our main contributions are listed below.

We introduce Adaptive Ellipsoidal Conformal Prediction (AECP) for crowd navigation, combining causally updated residual-adaptive ellipsoidal geometry with DtACI-based online scale calibration to represent anisotropic human-trajectory-prediction errors under distribution shift.

We incorporate AECP into a risk-sensitive PPO-Lagrangian framework that uses episode-level CVaR to regulate the Lagrangian safety penalty under high-cost interactions.

We evaluate the proposed framework under in-distribution settings and out-of-distribution shifts involving crossing flows, merging flows, and changes in pedestrian velocity. Our proposed framework improves success rate by 5.68–7.44 percentage points and reduces collision rate by 5.44–6.64 percentage points relative to state-of-the-art baselines across the three OOD settings as shown in Table I . Further, we numerically compare the coverage and area of AECP with adaptive circular conformal prediction, which shows a 2.62–6.07 percentage points mean empirical coverage improvement while reducing the uncertainty area by 60%.

1. We introduce Adaptive Ellipsoidal Conformal Prediction (AECP) for crowd navigation, combining causally updated residual-adaptive ellipsoidal geometry with DtACI-based online scale calibration to represent anisotropic human-trajectory-prediction errors under distribution shift.

2. We incorporate AECP into a risk-sensitive PPO-Lagrangian framework that uses episode-level CVaR to regulate the Lagrangian safety penalty under high-cost interactions.

3. We evaluate the proposed framework under in-distribution settings and out-of-distribution shifts involving crossing flows, merging flows, and changes in pedestrian velocity. Our proposed framework improves success rate by 5.68–7.44 percentage points and reduces collision rate by 5.44–6.64 percentage points relative to state-of-the-art baselines across the three OOD settings as shown in Table I . Further, we numerically compare the coverage and area of AECP with adaptive circular conformal prediction, which shows a 2.62–6.07 percentage points mean empirical coverage improvement while reducing the uncertainty area by 60%.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Conformal Prediction. Conformal prediction (CP) constructs prediction sets around a predictive model using held-out calibration scores, providing distribution-free coverage under standard exchangeability assumptions. First introduced by [ 18 ] , it becomes a useful tool for quantifying uncertainty behaviors. Adaptive conformal inference (ACI) extends this framework to online settings with distribution shift by dynamically adjusting the calibration level [ 19 ] . [ 20 ] studied PID-based online conformal calibration. [ 21 ] subsequently proposed dynamically-tuned adaptive conformal inference (DtACI), which adaptively tunes the ACI update rate to improve robustness across unknown forms and rates of distribution shift. In crowd navigation, [ 7 ] apply DtACI to quantify human trajectory uncertainty and use these uncertainty estimates to guide robot behavior through Constrained Reinforcement Learning (CRL) with Lagrangian PPO under a safety constraint.

Beyond constrained RL, interaction-aware CP in which human-motion uncertainty depends on the robot’s motion plan, has also been explored in crowd navigation environment developed under Model Predictive Control (MPC), alternating the algorithm between robot behavior planning and conformal uncertainty calibration. [ 22 ] . CP can also be used to train conformal predictive safety filters for pre-trained RL controller instead of updating the policy itself [ 9 ] . More broadly, CP has also been applied in dynamic environments, showing that calibrated uncertainty sets can support probabilistic safety guarantees in dynamic agents environments [ 23 , 8 , 10 , 11 , 24 ] and extended to sequential and multi-horizon prediction [ 25 , 26 ] .

Beyond circular conformal prediction, ellipsoidal conformal prediction has been studied for multivariate outputs by exploiting dependence across prediction errors. [ 12 ] introduced Mahalanobis-based conformal ellipsoidal uncertainty sets, while [ 13 ] constructed covariance-aware ellipsoidal conformal regions for multi-target regression using locally estimated residual covariance. [ 14 ] extend ellipsoidal conformal prediction to non-exchangeable multivariate time series through sequential calibration. More recently, [ 15 ] propose Sample-Cloud Predictive Adaptive Conformal
Ellipsoids, which derives time-local ellipsoidal geometry from the current predictive sample cloud and adaptively selects a same-regime calibration window under distribution shift. Beyond ellipsoidal sets, [ 27 ] construct multimodal conformal prediction by optimizing convex shape templates.

In contrast, our setting uses a point trajectory predictor and causally updates horizon-specific ellipsoidal geometry from available prediction residuals, while retaining DtACI for online scale calibration and integrating the resulting uncertainty sets into closed-loop risk-sensitive crowd navigation.

Tail Risk in Navigation and Planning. CVaR is a measure of tail risk proposed by [ 16 ] [ 17 ] , and has then been widely applied in many areas. Recent work applied CVaR to risk-aware navigation, MPC, motion planning, and safety filtering [ 28 , 1 , 2 ] . Moreover, in motion planning, CVaR can be treated as a constraint to limit safety risk in a proposed two stage framework [ 29 ] or as a safety filter to reduce collision risk in an uncertain environment [ 30 ] . On the algorithmic side, CVaR-constrained safe RL has been studied through percentile-risk Lagrangian methods [ 31 ] and CVaR-constrained policy optimization [ 32 , 33 ] . These methods typically incorporate CVaR into the policy update itself. Moreover, [ 34 ] couple human-motion forecasting with CVaR-aware PPO-Lagrangian and a separate shielding layer. In contrast, we use CVaR over cumulative episode costs directly as the violation signal for updating the Lagrange multiplier.

Learning-Based Crowd Navigation Learning-based crowd navigation methods have been widely explored. For instance, deep-RL crowd-navigation methods learned efficient and socially compliant behavior through reward design and interaction modeling [ 4 ] [ 5 ] , with later incorporate recurrent and graph-based modeling [ 35 , 36 , 37 ] . CrowdNav++ further incorporated multi-step pedestrian trajectory predictions into a graph-based RL policy [ 6 ] . GenSafeNav then introduced DtACI-based predictive uncertainty into a PPO-Lagrangian constrained-RL formulation [ 7 ] . PPO-Lagrangian has also been widely used as a standard constrained-RL baseline [ 38 ] .
PID-Lagrangian methods dynamically adjust the Lagrange multiplier using proportional, integral, and derivative feedback to improve constrained-RL training [ 39 ] . Taken together, these studies suggest that adaptive/dual Lagrangian updates are practical for diverse decision-making problems. We then build on learning-based crowd navigation and Lagrangian safe RL, but define the constrained objective over episode-level CVaR.

2026-10-07.title: SURGE: Sonar-fUsed Reconstruction and localization via image-gated Graph Estimation
2026-10-07.authors: Mohammed Ibrahim M , Vallabh Deogaonkar , Trung Dong , Jane Shin , Abhilash Somayajula , Xiaomin Lin
2026-10-07.abstract: Remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) are widely used to explore and inspect underwater environments such as caves, shipwrecks, and submerged infrastructure. These missions require accurate 3D understanding of the surrounding environment, which depends on both reliable vehicle localization and metric scene reconstruction. However, external positioning is often unavailable underwater, requiring small ROVs to rely primarily on onboard perception. Optic vision provides rich visual and geometric information but suffers from scale ambiguity and trajectory drift, whereas 2D imaging sonar provides metric range but incomplete 3D geometry. Existing underwater reconstruction approaches typically address these limitations separately or assume known sensor poses, leaving localization and reconstruction disconnected. We present SURGE , a camera sonar framework that jointly estimates the ROV trajectory and target location by integrating visual and acoustic observations within a factor graph, then uses the recovered metric poses for sonar Gaussian splatting. Experiments on real underwater RGB sonar observations show that SURGE substantially improves localization consistency over conventional vision based pose estimation and produces a more compact, natively metric reconstruction than RGB Gaussian splatting baselines.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Remotely operated vehicles are increasingly used for underwater exploration and inspection of environments such as caves, shipwrecks, and submerged infrastructure [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . These missions require accurate three dimensional understanding of the environment for navigation, inspection, and spatial mapping. Building such representations, however, depends on both reliable vehicle localization and metric scene geometry.

Underwater localization is particularly challenging because external positioning is often unavailable, forcing small ROVs to rely on onboard perception [ 24 ] . Monocular cameras provide rich visual and geometric information but suffer from scale ambiguity and trajectory drift, especially when visibility and feature quality degrade underwater [ 25 ] . Forward looking imaging sonar provides complementary metric range measurements and remains effective under poor visibility, but conventional two dimensional sonar observes range and azimuth while leaving elevation ambiguous [ 30 , 31 ] . Neither modality alone therefore provides both reliable metric localization and complete scene geometry, as shown in Fig. 1 .

Recent acoustic optical methods such as AONeuS and Z Splat demonstrate the benefit of combining camera and sonar measurements for underwater reconstruction [ 8 , 9 ] . However, these approaches largely assume known sensor poses, while other methods address pose estimation and reconstruction primarily within a single sensing modality [ 10 , 13 , 14 ] . This leaves a gap between multimodal reconstruction and the localization needed to support it in real underwater operation.

This separation is limiting in practice because reconstruction quality depends directly on the accuracy and metric consistency of the estimated sensor trajectory. We present SURGE , a camera sonar framework for joint underwater localization and metric reconstruction. Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce a multimodal factor graph that jointly estimates the ROV trajectory and the location of a compact underwater target from monocular RGB and two dimensional forward looking imaging sonar observations.

We introduce a multimodal factor graph that jointly estimates the ROV trajectory and the location of a compact underwater target from monocular RGB and two dimensional forward looking imaging sonar observations.

We develop a multi view sonar aggregation strategy and a target extent aware acoustic residual that provide stable metric constraints for joint pose and target estimation.

We use the recovered metric poses for target-scoped sonar
Gaussian splatting and demonstrate improved localization consistency
and more compact metric reconstruction than RGB Gaussian-splatting
baselines on real underwater data.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Multi-modal Reconstruction with Known Poses

Camera and sonar provide complementary information for underwater reconstruction, motivating methods that combine optical appearance with acoustic geometry. AONeuS [ 8 ] and Z-Splat [ 9 ] demonstrate that acoustic measurements can improve three dimensional reconstruction when optical observations are degraded by underwater visibility. Collado-Gonzalez et al. similarly combine image regions with sonar range measurements for reconstruction in turbid environments [ 26 ] . These methods establish the value of acoustic optical fusion, but primarily assume externally provided sensor poses. As a result, they address reconstruction once the trajectory is known rather than recovering localization and reconstruction from the same measurements.

## II-B Single-Modality Reconstruction with Estimated Poses

A parallel line of work relaxes the requirement for known poses, but generally within a single sensing modality. SonarSplat [ 10 ] extends Gaussian splatting to forward-looking sonar while jointly optimizing the acoustic scene representation and sensor poses. Differentiable space carving reconstructs occupancy from imaging-sonar observations when poses are available [ 37 ] , while other approaches address reconstruction under pose drift [ 11 ] or recover sonar geometry without supplied poses using priors from vision foundation models [ 12 ] . Together, these methods show that acoustic observations can support both pose reasoning and reconstruction despite the geometric ambiguity of imaging sonar.

For optical sensing, SeaSplat [ 13 ] and WaterSplatting [ 14 ] reconstruct real underwater scenes from RGB imagery using COLMAP poses, while AquaSplat [ 17 ] introduces a dual-branch representation for underwater RGB reconstruction. These methods improve the representation of underwater appearance and geometry, but their reconstruction remains tied to trajectories recovered from visual Structure-from-Motion. Thus, pose-aware reconstruction has been explored for both optical and acoustic sensing, but primarily without using their complementary measurements jointly to recover a metric trajectory.

## II-C Underwater Factor-Graph SLAM

Underwater SLAM provides the complementary perspective of estimating vehicle motion from multiple sensor constraints. Existing systems combine acoustic range, inertial sensing, and optical observations to estimate trajectories and map features [ 15 , 16 , 35 , 36 ] . Imaging-sonar multi-robot systems further recover trajectories and object-level maps from multibeam measurements [ 27 , 28 ] . These approaches demonstrate the value of acoustic constraints for underwater localization, but are not designed to connect monocular RGB and 2D FLIS localization directly to downstream target reconstruction.

The observation model is also different for compact extended targets. Conventional landmark formulations typically associate acoustic observations with discrete features, whereas the dominant return from an extended object can move across its visible surface as the viewpoint changes. SURGE therefore models the sonar observation relative to the spatial extent of the target rather than forcing every acoustic return to coincide with a single geometric center.

## II-D Position of the Present Work

Prior work therefore establishes three complementary capabilities: acoustic optical fusion can improve underwater reconstruction when poses are known, single-modality methods can reconstruct scenes while estimating or tolerating pose uncertainty, and underwater SLAM can recover vehicle trajectories from acoustic and visual constraints. What remains less explored is their combination: jointly estimating metric vehicle motion and target location from monocular RGB and 2D forward-looking sonar, then using the recovered trajectory for reconstruction in real underwater environments without external positioning.

SURGE addresses this gap by coupling visual and acoustic observations within a factor graph and using the resulting metric poses for target-scoped sonar Gaussian splatting. The framework therefore connects localization and reconstruction through the same complementary camera-sonar measurements rather than treating accurate poses as an independent prerequisite.

2026-10-07.title: Dynamics Modeling of a Multi-UAV Slung Load System Using a Discrete-Link Cable Approach
2026-10-07.authors: Harvey Merton , Ian W. Hunter
2026-10-07.comment: Presented at ICRA 2026 as an accepted paper
2026-10-07.abstract: A common assumption to simplify the problem of controlling a multi-UAV slung load system (MUSLS) is that the flexible cables can be modeled as massless rigid rods. In this work, we propose an alternative Euler-Newton derived dynamical model which uses a series of rigid links to model the flexible cables. The model is specifically designed to allow efficient simulation using Featherstone’s articulated body algorithm. We perform real-world validation of this model on gentle, aggressive, and tension-engagement maneuvers and run a parameter sweep to determine the number of links, joint damping, and joint friction to achieve the greatest model fidelity. The model closely matches real-world flight data with mean load translation errors below 132 mm (5.5% of the cable length) and orientation errors below 11.4 degrees. We make the real-world flight data publicly available for the development of future cable models.
2026-10-07.introduction:
A common strategy for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) payload transport is to suspend the payload from a flexible cable, yielding a slung-load configuration [ 1 ] . When multiple UAVs cooperate to carry a single load (Fig. 1 ), they can transport heavier payloads and, in principle, regulate the load’s full six-degree-of-freedom pose [ 2 ] .

As applications mature, there is a growing need to simulate multi-UAV slung-load systems (MUSLS) within off-the-shelf toolchains. In these settings, the dynamics model must be plug-and-play with standard rigid-body simulators, operate near real time, and remain stable across regimes that include loss and re-engagement of cable tension.

Accurately modeling general flexible cables is difficult because they exhibit nonlinear, high-dimensional dynamics and undergo abrupt transitions when tension is lost or re-established. Approaches to cable modeling can be categorized as discrete or continuous [ 3 ] . Discrete approaches include mass–spring systems [ 4 ] , multibody chains of rigid links [ 5 ] , and finite-element methods [ 6 ] ; continuous formulations include elastic-rod and spline-based dynamics [ 7 , 8 ] .

Within the MUSLS literature specifically, prior work can be grouped into three subsets of the discrete approach. Massless rigid links. The most common approach assumes each cable is a massless, always-taut rod forming a straight line between attachment points [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . This simplifies analysis and controller design but reduces simulation fidelity, particularly when cables go slack. Hybrid tension models. To handle slack-cable transitions, some works augment rigid-link models with hybrid dynamics that explicitly switch between taut and slack regimes [ 9 , 14 ] . While more physically accurate during tension re-engagement, these models still rely on custom numerical simulators and are not easily integrated with general-purpose robotics toolchains. Discrete rigid links. Discrete-link formulations have been applied to MUSLS primarily for differential-flatness-based planning and LQR control [ 15 , 16 ] and for stabilizing geometric control [ 17 ] . These works emphasize control-theoretic insights rather than validating cable-model fidelity against real-world MUSLS data, and they offer no insight into how joint properties affect predictive performance. Moreover, all prior discrete-link MUSLS works concentrate link masses at joint connections rather than distributing inertia along each link. While this simplifies the state representation, it increases the number of elements required for convergence relative to rod-inertia models [ 18 ] and prevents treating links as standard rigid bodies. This is a key obstacle to integration with general-purpose simulators, most of which target tree-structured rigid bodies solved with Featherstone’s articulated-body algorithm (ABA) [ 19 ] .

This paper focuses on the construction and performance quantification of a multi-discrete-link cable dynamics model in a MUSLS context. The model is specifically designed to be easily integrated with a range of rigid-body robotics simulators. The key contributions are:

a dynamical model of a MUSLS with a discrete-link cable model which includes the effect of link inertias and tunable joint properties,

a dynamical model of a MUSLS with a discrete-link cable model which includes the effect of link inertias and tunable joint properties,

a systematic selection of key parameters to balance computational efficiency and predictive performance of a multi-link cable model,

a quantification of the performance of a multi-link cable model over a variety of trajectories (including tension engagement), and

real-world flight data made publicly available [ 20 ] to allow the development of future cable models.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the MUSLS dynamical model, with emphasis on the multi-link cable formulation and how it differs from existing approaches. Section III describes the approach to testing the model with a position control based scheme. Section IV discusses model tuning and the performance of a multi-rigid-link cable model for MUSLS simulation. Section V provides concluding remarks.

1. a dynamical model of a MUSLS with a discrete-link cable model which includes the effect of link inertias and tunable joint properties,

2. a systematic selection of key parameters to balance computational efficiency and predictive performance of a multi-link cable model,

3. a quantification of the performance of a multi-link cable model over a variety of trajectories (including tension engagement), and

4. real-world flight data made publicly available [ 20 ] to allow the development of future cable models.

2026-10-07.title: Entropy-Gated Belief Coordination for Decentralized Multi-Agent Search Under Intermittent Communication
2026-10-07.authors: Mohamed Abdelnaby , Kevin Leahy
2026-10-07.abstract:
We study decentralized multi-agent target search where homogeneous agents communicate intermittently at Poisson-distributed times. Standard unconditional belief fusion wastes communication opportunities by synchronizing agents during high-entropy exploration, when diverse independent beliefs provide better coverage than a premature consensus.
We introduce entropy-gated belief coordination , in which agents skip fusion while their collective entropy ratio exceeds a threshold θ \theta and merge only during exploitation, consistent with the bifurcation structure of nonlinear opinion dynamics and the submodular structure of the per-step information gain objective.
We further derive I step ​ ( α , β ) I_{\mathrm{step}}(\alpha,\beta) , the expected mutual information per observation step between two agents’ binary sensors, as an interpretable, communication-free measure of sensor informativeness that motivates the gating design and guides system-level analysis.
Experiments across 103,680 trials (nine grid sizes up to 100 × 100 100{\times}100 , Poisson communication timing, four target movement patterns) show that the Entropy-Gated Trust-Decay Planner ( EG-TDP ), which adds a detection-probability planner switch in exploitation mode, achieves mean belief quality Q ¯ = 0.300 \bar{Q}=0.300 (mean belief mass at the true target cell, averaged across all trials and steps), a 58.9 % 58.9\% gain over arithmetic mean and a 37.4 % 37.4\% gain over visit-weighted fusion. On representative configurations, EG-TDP also outperforms a joint-Bayesian reference that uses all agents’ observations at every step, despite operating under random intermittent contact only.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Coordinated multi-agent search arises in search-and-rescue, environmental monitoring, and inspection, where a team must locate a target of interest with noisy sensors and intermittent communication. Each agent maintains a probabilistic belief map updated via Bayesian recursion from local observations. At communication events, agents fuse beliefs to pool independently gathered evidence.

The Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence provides a principled framework to decide how to combine their beliefs into a single consensus map when agents meet. The minimizer of a weighted forward KL objective is the arithmetic mean and the minimizer of the reverse KL is the geometric mean [ 5 , 6 ] . Our prior work [ 1 ] applied these classical results to multi-agent tracking and introduced visit-weighted fusion to suppress ghost targets, with an implementation linear in the number of agents and the size of the environment. The present paper asks instead when agents should fuse, and how the planner should respond to the team’s information state.

Two problems motivate this work. First, fusing beliefs during high-entropy exploration synchronizes agents who should be maintaining diverse, complementary views of the search space. Premature consensus forces all agents to plan from the same belief, causing them to select correlated positions and undermining their search efforts. Second, a natural response to stale beliefs from long communication blackouts is temporal trust decay , in which the merged belief is weighted toward a prior or uniform distribution in proportion to elapsed blackout time on the grounds that older evidence is less reliable. However, the decay factor cannot distinguish between a correct peak and a ghost peak, because both produce the same entropy. Therefore, this method cannot be applied directly to the belief map.

In this work, we

derive I step ​ ( α , β ) I_{\mathrm{step}}(\alpha,\beta) , a communication-free constant
computable from the sensor false-positive rate α \alpha and false-negative rate β \beta alone, that quantifies how quickly two homogenous agents’ beliefs diverge during a communication blackout and informs the design of the coordination policy;

introduce entropy-gated merging ( EG-KL ), in which agents fuse beliefs only when team entropy falls below threshold θ \theta , preserving exploration diversity and decoupling performance from communication frequency;

propose EG-TDP , which adds a planner switch from
entropy-reduction to detection-probability scoring upon entering
exploitation mode, enabling convergence at large scales where
entropy-reduction Model Predictive Control (MPC) alone cannot commit
to pursuit within the step budget, while reducing inter-agent belief transmission by over 97% at 100 × 100 100{\times}100 scale; and

propose EG-Istep , a variant of EG-TDP that replaces
the binary planner switch with a continuous blend weighted by γ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \gamma\in(0,1] , a trust-decay factor derived from I step I_{\mathrm{step}} that
decays with blackout length to discount detection-probability scoring
as beliefs grow stale, providing a sensor-dependent criterion for
choosing between continuous and hard-threshold planner switching.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Our work sits at the intersection of distributed belief fusion, multi-robot search under communication constraints, and coordination under intermittent connectivity. We describe each area and the specific gap that motivates our approach.

A substantial body of work addresses how agents should combine probability distributions when they meet. Classical opinion pooling theory establishes that logarithmic pooling (geometric mean) is externally Bayesian when agents share a likelihood model, while linear pooling (arithmetic mean) is preferred under potential bias [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Covariance intersection [ 8 ] provides conservative Gaussian fusion guarantees under unknown correlations, and event-triggered schemes [ 9 , 11 ] reduce communication overhead while maintaining stability. None of these works poses the conditional question of whether agents should adopt a shared belief at all on a given event, or how that belief should alter path planning. Our prior work [ 1 ] derived KL-optimal pooling rules and visit-weighted variants for binary-sensor tracking but applied fusion unconditionally, leaving open the question of when fusion is beneficial and how the planner should respond.

Several approaches address multi-robot active information gathering under limited communication. Lauri et al. [ 12 ] formulate the problem as a Dec-POMDP but require complete knowledge of target dynamics and treat communication as absent rather than Poisson-distributed. Deep reinforcement learning approaches such as [ 13 ] learn cooperative strategies end-to-end but are sensitive to the training environment and do not address when to share beliefs. Krause et al. [ 3 ] and Corah and Michael [ 10 ] establish near-optimal greedy strategies under submodular information objectives. Earlier treatments of decentralized probabilistic search established the problem structure underlying this literature [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . Across this literature, agents share information freely and the shared representation is immediately used for planning.

The work most directly related to ours is Ristic and Skvortsov [ 14 ] , who study decentralized area-restricted search with intermittent information and consensus coordination. When agents communicate they always fuse. Hollinger et al. [ 18 ] address how to fuse during multirobot search by weighting observations by communication channel quality, but the fusion decision is treated as fixed whenever agents meet. Roth et al. [ 19 ] adopt a multi-agent POMDP framework with stronger optimality guarantees, but joint policy computation becomes intractable at the grid scales we consider. The question of whether to fuse is never raised, and the planner objective does not change with collective confidence. Event-triggered control [ 9 , 11 ] determines when to communicate but treats the fusion rule and its planning consequence as fixed. Our work separates these decisions. Given that a Poisson event has fired, should the team merge beliefs, and how should that change the way agents plan?

Deciding when to merge beliefs and how to plan with the result is a form of the exploration-exploitation tradeoff. Bizyaeva et al. [ 2 ] formalize this as a bifurcation between a disagreement regime, where agents maintain diverse independent views, and an agreement regime, where they commit to a shared estimate, controlled by a sensitivity parameter. This motivates using the team’s collective entropy as a coordination signal, formalised in Section IV-C . The opinion dynamics model operates on continuous scalar opinions with no planning component. Translating the bifurcation insight into an operational policy for discrete belief maps, coupled with a planning objective that adapts when the regime switches, is the contribution of this paper.

2026-10-07.title: RACER: Residual-Adaptive Closed-Loop Estimation for Sampling-Based Planning in Wheeled-Quadruped Racing
2026-10-07.authors: Yuxiang Liu , Marla Eisman , Lizhi Yang , Aaron Ames , Francesco Borrelli
2026-10-07.abstract: We present RACER, a hierarchical control framework for wheel-based quadruped racing that combines an MPPI planner with a learned residual dynamics model and a low-level RL velocity tracker. The planner augments a nominal unicycle kinematic model with a neural residual term to capture the closed-loop tracking behavior of the RL policy. To train this residual model under limited real-world data, we propose Low-Rank Residual Adaptation (LoRRA), a two-stage approach that pre-trains on large-scale simulation data for broad coverage and then fine-tunes on a small real-world dataset with a low-rank constraint. In simulation, we empirically validate our engineering choices by showing (A) Residual dynamics improve the overall performance of our pipeline by capturing the tracking error of RL velocity tracker at high-speed cornering. (B) Residual dynamics trained with both source-domain and target-domain data gives racing performance significantly better than the residual dynamics trained with only target-domain data. (C) Low-rank constraint at target-domain adaptation gives higher success rates and higher performance than full-tune and from-scratch when domain gap in ground coefficient or joint gain increases.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Racing a wheeled quadruped is challenging. First, wheeled quadruped inherits the high-dimensional dynamics of a quadruped with the nonlinear tire dynamics of a racing car [ 3 , 21 ] . This complexity challenges many classical model-predictive control (MPC) approaches: optimizing long-horizon trajectories over such a high-dimensional and non-linear system is challenging [ 14 , 2 ] . At the same time, long-horizon is a must in the context of racing [ 26 ] . This long-horizon requirement makes naive end-to-end reinforcement learning (RL) approaches equally impractical [ 17 ] . A long planning horizon creates an extremely sparse reward landscape that destabilizes RL training, and even if clever curriculum or reward-shaping techniques succeed in training an agent, the resulting policy rarely generalizes beyond its training distribution.

To handle the system complexity and long-horizon nature of the racing task, we adapt hierarchical control. An RL policy can handle the nonlinear, high-dimensional dynamics of the wheeled quadruped over a short horizon. It is trained to track velocity commands. It abstracts the full joint-space dynamics into a compact, low-dimensional interface of linear and angular velocity [ 13 , 28 , 21 ] . A sampling-based planner [ 33 , 34 ] , can then operate over this interface to plan trajectories across a long horizon.

While this hierarchical architecture is conceptually sound, a naive implementation will fail at high-velocity(Sec. IV-A ). We find that if the planner uses simple reduced-order models to propose trajectories [ 3 , 2 ] , the resulting commands will systematically diverge from the robot’s true behavior, because velocity tracking is always imperfect: hardware latency, actuator saturation, and tire slip all introduce tracking errors that a kinematic model cannot predict. To bridge this gap, we augment the reduced-order model (namely the unicycle model) with a learned residual dynamics network that compensates for the difference between the analytic kinematic prediction and the actual closed-loop next state of the RL tracker [ 27 , 16 ] . Training such a residual model, however, is highly nontrivial since it requires both broad data coverage across the state-action space and high data quality that reflects real-world dynamics. Simulation can provide coverage but suffers from the sim-to-real gap [ 31 , 19 ] ; real-world data provides fidelity but is scarce and expensive to collect on a fragile racing platform.

To this end, we propose Low-Rank Residual Adaptation (LoRRA), a two-stage training pipeline that first pre-trains the residual network on a large simulated dataset for coverage( 10,000,000 10,000,000 state transitions). By coverage we mean that these transitions span the range of velocities, yaw rates, and commands the planner queries during high-speed rollouts, so the residual is accurate across the states DIAL-MPC actually visits rather than only near a handful of collected trajectories. # II Related Work

Bjelonic et al. [3] introduce online trajectory optimization for hybrid walking–driving locomotion on ANYmal-on-wheels, and extend it to whole-body MPC with single-rigid-body dynamics. [ 2 ] . Lee et al. [21] take a complementary learning-heavy direction, integrating RL locomotion, learned high-level navigation, and large-scale path planning for kilometer-scale urban autonomy. These works mainly focus on hybrid locomotion and urban traveling while high-speed racing with wheeled quadruped is still an engineering setting largely underexplored. The only work to directly address wheeled-quadruped racing [ 8 ] approaches it from a vehicle-dynamics standpoint. In contrast, we focus on functionalities of residual dynamics. [ 8 ] and our approach serve as complementary roles.

Sampling-based MPC, and MPPI in particular [ 33 ] , is a natural consumer of learned dynamics because it only requires forward simulation. Roth et al. [27] learn a perceptive forward dynamics model on ANYmal and roll it out inside MPPI for safe navigation, reporting a 41 % improvement in position prediction; Kim et al. [16] pair a learned quadruped forward model with an informed trajectory sampler for safe local planning.
On the ground-vehicle side, Kato et al. [15] fuse a physical model with a neural residual and use MPPI to optimize PID gains for a mini-forklift, and Song et al. [30] learn a continuous-time residual via input-concomitant Neural ODEs. Pezzato et al. [25] sidestep model learning by treating IsaacGym itself as the rollout simulator, while Xue et al. [34] push sampling MPC to torque-level quadruped control using full-order dynamics and a diffusion-style annealing schedule that we adopt for our planner.
Relative to this body of work, our residual is distinctive in two ways. First, it is parameterized at the planner’s command interface (rather than at the full robot state); second, its training pipeline is dual-phased, consuming both simulation data and hardware data.

Heiden et al. [11] augment a differentiable rigid-body simulator with neural networks that absorb unmodeled contact effects; Cheng et al. [6] tune controller parameters through auto-differentiation, and Krishna et al. [18] co-tune controller and simulator parameters from a few deployment rollouts. He et al. [10] learn a delta-action residual on a humanoid to realign IsaacGym with the deployed robot; Levy et al. [22] learn semi-structured dynamics from three minutes of real Go1 data to bootstrap model-based RL from scratch. These works exclusively focus on the sim-to-real of policy, and to the best of our knowledge, we are the first work that studies the sim-to-real transfer of residual dynamics. [ 20 ] is the closest work. [ 20 ] freezes a symbolic-regression base learned in low-fidelity simulation and fits a fresh neural residual per target domain, at the level of open-loop plant dynamics queried directly by MPC. In contrast, RACER (i) parameterizes its residual at the planner’s command interface to model the closed-loop tracking error of a learned RL velocity tracker, and (ii) transfers the pretrained residual itself across the domain gap under a low-rank constraint, rather than re-fitting a residual from scratch.

Low-Rank Adaptation [ 12 ] freezes pre-trained weights and trains low-rank updates that can be merged with no runtime cost; in robot learning, Daneshmand et al. [7] combine LoRA with a recovery-policy safety mechanism to fine-tune a Unitree Go2 locomotion policy , reporting 46.5 % lower fine-tuning time and rank-1 adapters sufficing to recover pre-trained real-world performance. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first work that investigates the impacts of low rank constraint on the training of residual dynamics rather than policy adaptation.

2026-10-07.title: An Autonomous, 3D Printed, Waterjet-Powered, Open-Source Robotic Trimaran for Environmental Inspection and Monitoring
2026-10-07.authors: Reuben O'Brien , Martin Lambrechtse-Reid , Minas Liarokapis
2026-10-07.comment: . Accepted version. Published in the 2024 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). Finalist for the IROS 2024 Best Application Paper Award
2026-10-07.abstract:
Versatile, autonomous robotic boats can offer excellent environmental inspection and monitoring solutions for remote, dangerous, hard to reach, or access protected water bodies.
This paper introduces such a platform in the form of an autonomous, cost-effective, waterjet-powered robotic trimaran. Motivated by the need for an efficient aquatic monitoring, particularly in Aotearoa - New Zealand’s diverse environments, the trimaran provides an efficient, low-cost, and easy to replicate alternative to resource-intensive research vessels. The proposed platform, costs $600-1,500 USD to develop (depending on the sensing system configuration), weighs under 5 kg, and excels in bathymetry and water quality testing. The trimaran can reach speeds of up to 2 m/s offering obstacle avoidance of natural features, such as rocks. Utilizing off-the-shelf components and 3D printing technology, the proposed platform offers excellent reproducibility and robustness while operating in shallow waters with its jet propulsion system. The paper presents in detail the design characteristics, the sensing system employed, testing results focusing on bathymetry, and highlights the ability of vessel and the potential for future research and data collection.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) have witnessed a surge in popularity in recent years, driven by advancements in autonomous technologies and their diverse applications in aquatic environments. These vehicles offer a promising avenue for scientific exploration, environmental monitoring, and resource management. The flexibility and adaptability of USVs make them particularly attractive for tasks ranging from data collection to environmental surveillance.

In the case of Aotearoa - New Zealand, the rivers and water streams constitute a significant 425,000 kilometres of length [ 1 ] , accompanied by a coastline length of 15,000 kilometers [ 2 ] . This diverse aquatic landscape encompasses a myriad of ecosystems, each demanding monitoring to ensure longevity and health. In the Aotearoa - New Zealand Biodiversity Strategy [ 3 ] , it details the key themes, with one being ecosystem protection, necessitating the application of seafloor and freshwater photogrammetry. This approach facilitates habitat mapping, characterization, and the study of aquatic species distributions. Presently, research in this field relies on manned research vessels, which are resource-intensive and incapable of accessing numerous freshwater rivers, streams, and wetlands.

To address the inefficiency of conventional systems, alternate solutions, notably USVs, have been proposed. The inaugural USV, developed in 1993 by MIT Sea Grant College Program [ 4 ] , marked the initiation of a field that has since witnessed the design of over 60 prototypes [ 5 ] . They each boast varying levels of autonomy and aquatic monitoring capabilities [ 6 ] . This count surpasses 60 when including vessels developed for USV competitions like RoboBoat [ 7 ] and Robot X [ 8 ] , platforms where students actively contribute to advancing research and development in the field.

Among the systems focusing on research, a significant number are open-sourced, with the majority featuring a fiberglass or plastic mouldered catamaran hull design [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] . These vessels are designed to be operated by 1-2 individuals and incorporate waypoint tracking capabilities. The overall cost of these USVs varies, starting from $3,000 USD and increasing depending on the selected sensors [ 15 ] . Notably, the most cost-effective and straightforward design utilizes an off-the-shelf plastic container as the hull, costing $1,557 [ 16 ] . Commercial alternatives, such as the Blue boat USV [ 17 ] , are available but surpass $4,200 USD, excluding training and ongoing maintenance costs.

For all USVs, effective trajectory mapping is crucial [ 18 ] , as is the integration of sensors to prevent collisions [ 19 ] . Several papers have investigated strategies for interpreting data and determining optimal avoidance maneuvers when encountering other ships or objects [ 20 , 21 ] . Probabilistic approaches have been explored, relying on a framework to assess the mission capability of USV systems [ 22 ] . Common strategies encompass real-time analysis using LiDAR [ 15 ] and cameras [ 23 ] , employing algorithms such as YOLO [ 24 ] . Moreover, the integration of swarm robotics [ 25 ] , [ 26 ] further amplifies the capabilities of USVs, allowing for collaborative and coordinated efforts in data gathering and monitoring. This collective approach enhances the efficiency and coverage of surveillance operations in large water bodies, contributing to a more comprehensive assessment and understanding of complex aquatic ecosystems.

In response to the need for an affordable, easy to replicate, and robust platform, this paper proposes a USV powered by a waterjet system that has a development cost of $600-1500 USD and that leverages off-the-shelf components and 3D printing for its manufacturing. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section II sections delves into the design of the platform, Section III discusses the experimental validation and presents the results, while Section IV concludes the paper, discussing the proposed solution’s potential.

# II Design

## II-A Trimaran Design

Considering the aforementioned specifications, opting for a mono-hull design would introduce inherent instability in the roll axis, hindering the effective operation of sensing electronics. While catamaran hulls offer better roll stability, they often require dual propulsion systems, contributing unnecessary weight and power consumption for the imposed specifications. Consequently, a trimaran configuration (see Fig. 2 ) was chosen for its roll stability akin to a catamaran but with the advantage of requiring a single propulsion system. The proposed trimaran has been optimized to dimensions of 850 mm in length and 500 mm in width, tailored for a weight of 5 kg and speeds of 2 m/s. The detachable side hulls are affixed using bolts and enable convenient transport, resulting in a compact package size of 850 mm x 250 mm x 200 mm.

Figure 3 a illustrates the gradual reduction in cross-sectional area at the stern, while Figure 3 b depicts the tapering from the underside. This design is crucial for a displacement hull that remains submerged throughout all operational speeds. The tapered hull enhances efficiency by ensuring a smooth flow of water, minimizing the creation of vortices at the ends. The inverted bow in figure 3 a, is similar to that of combatant naval hull forms [ 27 ] , such as the US Navy destroyer Zumwalt 1000, along with the Mayflower, a autonomous research vessel [ 28 ] . This design choice aims to reduce the wake around the boat and prevent pitching by piercing the waves rather than riding up and over them [ 29 ] . While alternative designs, such as a axe bow are shown to be effective, they were not selected due to the anticipated pitch of the hull caused by the propulsion system. This alternative nose design would lead to increased water riding up the sides of the boat. However, being unmanned, this area is completely sealed off with a constant curve to facilitate water runoff rather than accumulation.

To minimize the submerged hull height, a flat bottom is used, tapering up from the edges of the jet inlet. This design increases buoyancy at shallower depths while providing a smooth surface to prevent snagging and local damage, which could be prevalent with the use of a keel or a sharp V bottom.

Simulation analysis of the trimaran hull was done in the MAXSURF software that allowed for mesh creation, followed by hydro-static and resistance analysis. In Figure 3 a side on view of the hull can be seen which outlines the waterline of the hull at 46 mm which is achieved at an overall weight of 5 kg. If the weight of the hull is reduced the waterline lowers along with the center of buoyancy, therefore the hull will ideally always operate at this weight. To ensure the center of mass is lower than the center of buoyancy the electronics are layed out along the length of the hull, along the base. They are positioned according to the longitudinally center of buoyancy (LCB) which is located at 310 mm from the stern. The LCB is the point at which buoyancy acts upwards against the hull. The transverse center of buoyancy is located along the center-line due to the symmetry of the hull. When electronics are mounted inside the hull of the platform, it is crucial that the center of gravity lines up with this in both directions so as to ensure a stable design.

The righting level 4 calculation was performed with the hull at a weight of 5 kg at a height of 30 mm from the base which can be achieved by mounting the batteries to the base. If the weight is reduced the peak lever will decrease from the current peak at 38.2 deg. According to [ 30 ] a righting lever shall be more than 30 degrees but no less than 25 degrees. The point of vanishing stability is at 120 degrees of inclination, which will allow this hull to perform well in all weather conditions.
Reducing the wake of a hull, reduces the resistance acting on the hull allowing for greater speeds and increased efficiency. Analysing the predicted wake, 5 the greatest disturbance occurs directly behind the hull in three separate forms from each hull.

As the disturbance moves back the waves build upon one another creating peaks and troughs to the edges. More than a meter from the stern the wake disperses from the center and leaves it relatively undisturbed.

Safety is the major concern here, with the proposed robotic vessel being unmanned and the goal of conducting unsupervised inspection and monitoring operations of unstructured environments. Since the size of the proposed platform is relatively small, people may try to interact with it and the use of a regular propeller driven system could lead to injuries. This is not the case with a jet impeller that is completely housed. Since it is housed stronger materials can be used such as stainless steel for the impeller which allows for improved durability and efficiency compared to plastic alternatives. Jet drive systems also allow for no additional clearance under the submerged hull, allowing operation in depths of 60 mm onwards.

Turn radius compared to alternate systems is greatly improved from similar sized systems from 2.5 m [ 14 ] and 5 m [ 12 ] to 1 .5 m. When the jet is under power the thrust is all directed in the way of the single vectoring nozzle. This is a significant improvement over prop wash gained from fixed propeller using rudders, and results in similar performance to skid steering from the use of multiple propulsion systems. Skid steering was not selected due to the requirement of two independent motors and ESCs. One of the downfalls with jet drives is their inability to turn when no thrust is applied. Another is reversing which can only be achieved by using an actuated bucket over the nozzle [ 31 ] that redirects the jet stream back under the boat. This allows for speeds up to 0.5 m/s but it is an inefficient and unstable system.

A brushless DC motor was chosen with the key considerations being the expected power output and speed with a jet pump where available torque is more important than the maximum rotational speed. Therefore a lower KV motor is preferred in the range of 1000-4000 kv. To reduce current draw to the motor and ESC while still having the required power ouptut, a 6s battery was selected. Cooling of the motor and ESC is achieved through water cooling that is connected to the inlet of the jet and exits besides the jet stream.

The trimaran design is optimized for 3D printing on consumer-grade printers with a minimum print bed size of 250 mm x 210 mm x 210 mm. Consequently, all individual parts, are tailored to fit within these dimensions. While this choice constrains the overall hull size of the proposed trimaran platform, a multi-part design ensures the required payload size is still achievable.

Material selection for 3D printing includes PLA, ABS, PETG, and TPU. PLA, while easy to use, lacks UV resistance and is prone to degradation and warping in outdoor conditions, particularly in direct sunlight, making it unsuitable for this application. ABS addresses these issues but introduces complexity and the need for add-ons like an enclosure during printing. Therefore, PETG emerges as the preferred material, overcoming PLA’s drawbacks without the added challenges of printing ABS.

Although TPU is not suitable for the main hull due to a thin wall thickness of 1.5 mm, it is ideal for the nose piece, being capable of deforming and absorbing energy upon impact. Sections are securely attached using epoxy applied to overlapping flanges detailed into each part. Additional components, including covers, electronic brackets, and side hulls, utilize heated inserts for easy removal using M3 bolts.

Alternative methods of manufacture include 3D printing negatives of the hull to be able to create fiberglass bodies that are significantly more robust and result in a lower weight. This can lead to an increased ability to carry more sensing or measuring electronics. The caveat is that the skills, materials, and equipment required to create a fiberglass hull are specialized, therefore, this method was excluded. Hulls such as [ 10 ] vacuum formed around a mould creating a single piece for the submerged region of the hull. This requires access to a vacuum former of over 1 m 2 .

## II-B Control and Sensing Hardware

To power the trimaran there are two independent power sources which allow the flight controller and the GPS to have redundant power as seen in figure 6 . Therefore if the auxiliary (LIPO 3S) battery dies the system can still return in either the auto mode through GPS navigation or on manual through the controller. If the power supply for propulsion (6s) runs out, it is still capable of locating itself and sending these commands to a the remote data collection laptop.

The flight controller running Ardupilot is the central unit and all the commands are going through it to the propulsion system. Key inputs are the wireless controller that is capable of switching the mode of the system from auto to manual so as to allow for recovery in case of autonomous control failure. While in auto mode the GPS and built-in IMU in the flight controller allow it to locate and orientate itself within 2 m of accuracy in outdoor environments. Raw data from the LiDAR is processed within the flight controller and is filtered into 4 segments that provide a 180° field of view to prevent obstacle collisions.

The Raspberry Pi acts as the data logger for the camera and any other sensors on-board such as an sonar echo-sounder.
To control the trimaran a proportional and integral (PI) controller is used to control the steer rate and thrust response relative to the desired location and speed set point. The flight controller is capable of doing this, but to use more complex controllers such as model predictive controllers [ 15 ] the Rasberry Pi is needed.

2026-10-07.title: What the Elevation Map Cannot See: Semantic-Aware Locomotion and Execution-Aware Navigation for Humanoid Robot
2026-10-07.authors: Shunyu Yao , Songyang Liu , Dinghao Chen , Yuanyuan Lei , Shuai Li
2026-10-07.abstract: Navigation for humanoid robots is critical, yet large-scale evaluation on physical hardware is often impractical due to cost and safety concerns, making simulation benchmarks essential. Existing VLN benchmarks achieve physically executable navigation, but still assume (1) all hazards are observable from elevation maps; (2) realized motions closely match desired motions. In real environments, however, fallen bottles may be ambiguous in elevation maps, while phones and water spills may be difficult to differentiate; hazard avoidance by the locomotion policy can cause the robot’s actual trajectory to deviate from the path intended by the VLN policy. Such command-execution mismatch can accumulate and lead the robot toward unintended locations. To expose these failure modes, we introduce a benchmark that models both elevation-subtle hazards and execution deviations, together with a closed-loop VLN + locomotion control framework that continuously realigns high-level navigation with the robot’s actual state. We evaluate navigation in simulation and further validate the locomotion policy on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid robot. Results show that semantic input reduces contact with hazards poorly represented in elevation maps, while anti-deviation improves navigation success. These findings highlight the need to evaluate humanoid navigation jointly in terms of route completion and hazard avoidance.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Humanoid robots are increasingly expected to assist people in everyday household environments, where navigation requires moving through rooms and corridors while avoiding furniture and floor-level hazards. Small objects and water spills in these environments may be poorly represented in depth-derived elevation maps, posing challenges beyond geometric obstacle avoidance. Although humanoids offer mobility advantages over wheeled platforms, large-scale real-world evaluation is costly, time-consuming, and potentially unsafe. Simulation benchmarks therefore enable repeatable, scalable evaluation before physical deployment.

Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) allows robots to navigate according to natural-language instructions rather than predefined metric goals. Early VLN benchmarks moved agents between predefined viewpoints, abstracting away locomotion and obstacle interaction [ 1 ] . Continuous-environment VLN replaced this graph-based formulation with local actions in continuous 3D environments [ 10 ] . More recently, physics-based benchmarks such as VLN-PE [ 19 ] , VLNVerse [ 12 ] , and VLN-CE-Isaac [ 3 ] further introduce robot kinematics, collision dynamics, and continuous motion, advancing VLN toward physically executable navigation.

Nevertheless, physics-based VLN evaluation retains two implicit assumptions. First, obstacle observability assumes that locomotion hazards are detectable from depth or elevation maps. Yet wet floors and small objects such as phones or cables may have weak or absent geometric signatures, so geometric traversability does not imply safety. Second, command-execution consistency assumes that realized motion matches high-level commands. Safe humanoid locomotion may instead require sidesteps, shorter steps, or turns. Repeated avoidance can accumulate pose and heading errors, shift observations away from those expected by the VLN policy, and undermine navigation.

These limitations are coupled: avoiding a semantically detected hazard can alter the trajectory assumed by the VLN policy. Existing benchmarks emphasize geometric traversability and collisions rather than this perception-execution feedback loop. Strong simulation performance may therefore conceal missed non-geometric hazards or lost task progress when subsequent decisions ignore avoidance-induced deviations.

We introduce a humanoid VLN benchmark that exposes these failure modes through hazards with different levels of geometric observability, including those weakly represented or absent in elevation maps. It distinguishes commanded from realized motion, enabling controlled evaluation of execution deviations caused by safety-aware low-level behavior. This formulation measures whether an agent reaches its language-specified destination while remaining safe and recovering its navigation state after local deviations.

We develop a hierarchical framework coupling a high-level VLN module with a semantic-aware whole-body locomotion policy. The VLN module generates relative target poses from language instructions and visual observations, while the locomotion policy tracks the derived velocity commands with local terrain and hazard awareness. Closed-loop feedback of the robot’s realized state corrects avoidance-induced deviations. We evaluate navigation in simulation and validate locomotion on a physical Unitree G1 with hazards poorly represented by geometry alone.

Our contributions are two-fold:

Semantic-aware locomotion + anti-deviation VLN: The semantic branch provides a ”steppability” prior to fill the blind spots of the elevation map, while anti-deviation correction compensates local
deviations before they accumulate into navigation drift or
render subsequent commands unsafe.

Hazard taxonomy and benchmark: Incorporate ”geometrically invisible hazards” and ”physical disturbances” into the VLN evaluation benchmark, complemented by new metrics such as the Hazard Contact Rate. Evaluation: Navigation is evaluated in simulation, while locomotion is evaluated in both simulated and real-world environments.

# 2 Related Works

## 2.1 Humanoid Navigation Benchmark

VLN datasets such as RxR [ 11 ] and REVERIE [ 17 ] extend language and object grounding without modeling humanoid execution. HumanoidBench [ 18 ] evaluates physical control but not language-guided navigation. Recent physics-based VLN benchmarks incorporate robot embodiment and locomotion [ 19 , 3 , 12 , 16 ] , complementing these language- and control-focused evaluations.

These benchmarks advance physical evaluation but cover a more limited range of perturbations and obstacles. We introduce richer perturbation and obstacle settings to jointly diagnose semantic hazards and safety-induced execution deviations. We target hazards poorly represented in elevation maps, such as wet surfaces and small objects, and evaluate safety and navigation recovery when low-level avoidance alters commanded motion.

## 2.2 Humanoid Locomotion and Whole-Body Control

Perpetual Humanoid Control (PHC) [ 13 ] provides motion imitation and fall recovery for simulated avatars. ExBody [ 4 ] combines upper-body imitation with velocity-tracking locomotion on hardware, while OmniH2O [ 6 ] learns deployable whole-body control from retargeted human motion and privileged teachers. HOVER [ 7 ] unifies velocity, pose, and upper-body control interfaces; ExBody2 [ 8 ] and TWIST [ 23 ] emphasize motion tracking and coordinated locomotion–manipulation. Their primary focus is reference tracking rather than semantic navigation hazards. Terrain-aware methods incorporate environmental geometry. Humanoid Parkour [ 26 ] uses vision-based reinforcement learning for obstacle traversal. Attention-Based Map Encoding (AME) [ 5 ] attends to elevation maps for foothold selection, and AME-2 [ 24 ] adds uncertainty-aware mapping. Hiking in the Wild [ 25 ] instead maps depth and proprioception directly to humanoid joint actions. Geometry alone, however, cannot distinguish similarly shaped surfaces with different semantic risks.

Related quadruped systems address complementary aspects: ViNL [ 9 ] couples visual navigation with locomotion that steps over household clutter, while Yang et al. [ 22 ] learn terrain-semantic speed and gait selection from human demonstrations. Our focus is humanoid foot-level hazard avoidance using aligned geometric and semantic maps, coupled with realized-motion feedback for correcting deviations during language-guided navigation.

2026-10-07.title: AeroBuoy: A Drone Deployable, 3D Printed, Autonomous Robotic Buoy for Environmental Inspection in Remote and Hazardous River Systems
2026-10-07.authors: Reuben O'Brien , Angus Lynch , Minas Liarokapis
2026-10-07.comment: . Accepted version. Published in the 2025 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS). Winner of the IROS 2025 Best Paper Award on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics in memory of Motohiro Kisoi. Reuben O'Brien and Angus Lynch contributed equally
2026-10-07.abstract: Monitoring of waterways such as remote and hazardous rivers and streams is important so as to assess the impact of external factors including construction runoff or climate change. Versatile, autonomous robotic boats can offer excellent environmental inspection and monitoring solutions for remote, dangerous, or access protected water bodies but they have several shortcomings in terms of maneuverability. This paper proposes an environmental inspection system consisting of an autonomous data collection buoy which is designed to be deployed to inaccessible river systems using a drone. The system can perform a drop off and pickup of the buoy depending on the requirements of a particular location and monitoring task. Utilising the natural flow of the river the buoy autonomously steers down, using GPS and magnetometers so as to maintain the desired trajectory. The buoy is capable of measuring water temperature but it can also be equipped with a range of sensors such as water oxygen meter, sonar for river bed inspection, or turbidity for water clarity. This paper describes the system design, presents an analysis of the self-righting capabilities of the buoy, and shows a full system demonstration at the Ōrewa River in Auckland, New Zealand.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Environmental monitoring in remote and dangerous rivers and other aquatic environments is a critical task for which robotic systems can provide a reliable, low-cost solution. Traditional methods, such as deploying boats or canoes for data collection or water sampling, present numerous challenges. These conventional platforms are often oversized relative to the narrow and winding nature of rivers, making them difficult to maneuver, particularly in confined spaces and turbulent waters. Additionally, their directional design can limit their ability to navigate sharp turns or reverse course, and they are highly susceptible to becoming entangled with floating debris and aquatic plants.

To mitigate some of these issues, jetboats have become a common choice for river navigation. Jetboats, with their impeller-based propulsion systems, are capable of operating in shallow waters and executing tighter turns. However, even these specialized vessels are not without their drawbacks. Their size and operational characteristics can still be suboptimal for the complex and dynamic environments often encountered in rivers, where factors such as shallow areas, debris, and rapid currents can pose significant risks.
The need for more efficient, adaptable, and resilient platforms for environmental inspections is evident, especially in locations where traditional methods are impractical or unsafe. The development of such systems can offer new possibilities for routine monitoring and rapid deployment in response to emerging environmental concerns. Furthermore, as rivers are often difficult to access, particularly in remote or hazardous regions, the ability to deploy and retrieve monitoring systems remotely would be highly advantageous. This capability would not only enhance the safety and efficiency of environmental monitoring efforts but also provide a consistent stream of valuable data over time.

This paper presents a novel 3D-printed, autonomous robotic buoy (Fig. 1 ) for environmental monitoring in inaccessible rivers. Its key novelty lies in the combined functionality of drone-based deployment/retrieval on both water and land along with a robust, self-righting design, enabling operation in debris-ridden waters. The buoy autonomously traverses downstream, driven by the river’s flow, collecting temperature, imagery, and flow data. In this paper the design and experimental validation of the system is detailed.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Environmental monitoring using autonomous systems has gained traction, particularly in remote and hazardous locations. Unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) and autonomous drones have emerged as viable platforms for gathering data in inaccessible environments. According to [ 1 ] , applications for these technologies span seven categories: rescue, military, patrolling, disaster relief, environmental monitoring, inspection, and water sports rescue. Their primary benefits include reduced human involvement, faster response times, increased flexibility, and the ability to cover vast areas.
Several fixed autonomous systems have been developed to monitor environmental conditions. For example, [ 2 ] describes a stationary, moored buoy designed for continuous water quality monitoring. This system includes sensors to ensure safe drinking water standards are maintained in rivers. Despite its effectiveness, stationary solutions like this are constrained by their inability to move, making them less suitable for large or dynamic environments like rivers. Larger mobile systems have also been explored for monitoring aquatic environments, in [ 3 ] , a USV raft capable of traversing oceanic environments while measuring various parameters at different speeds was presented. These larger systems, although effective in open waters, are less suited for narrower or obstacle-laden rivers due to their size and limited manoeuvrability. The propulsion systems, like wave gliders [ 4 ] , which rely on ocean waves for long-distance travel, also fall short in river environments where wave energy is minimal. Smaller, motorized buoy systems have shown promise in autonomous monitoring. For example, in [ 5 ] a motorized buoy with dual thrusters was developed that optimizes path planning and manoeuvrability. However, even with improved efficiency, systems designed for calm lakes may struggle in dynamic and debris-filled river environments. This is where leveraging natural river currents could significantly reduce energy consumption. MIT designed and built the ‘BoB’ system offering a significant innovation in the buoy movement. Designed for omnidirectional travel, this 7.4 kg system uses three points of propulsion to achieve high stability in calm waters [ 6 ] . It was later upgraded to be a 3.3 kg system [ 7 ] . Although it shows promise in lake environments, its application to river systems remains limited by its inability to navigate turbulent waters.

Research on autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) specifically designed for rivers is ongoing. Systems such as [ 8 ] provide a low cost, monitoring system, but it is limited by its size and weight. In [ 9 ] , the authors proposed a method for using ultrasonic sensors to help ASVs monitor oil spills while avoiding obstacles like rocks and branches. This sensor-based navigation is critical for buoys and drones in river environments, where river currents [ 10 ] and debris create unpredictable challenges, within the river boundaries [ 11 ] . Drone integration with buoys has gained attention as an effective deployment strategy in remote or hazardous areas. In [ 12 ] a stationary monitoring buoy that is deployable and retrievable by a drone was demonstrated. It featured floats for safe water landings, showcasing the potential for drone-based buoy deployment in dynamic environments. However, other drone systems, like [ 13 ] , which deployed lifebuoys using a servo mechanism, lacked retrieval capabilities and required manual loading. Simulated dynamic models for a tethered buoy and drone are presented in, [ 14 ] , [ 15 ] , showing potential in both calm and wave conditions. Real-world testing of a similar system has been done in ‘The Bathy Drone’ [ 16 ] , which demonstrates a tethered drone system capable of bathymetry. The sonar is attached to a multi-hull boat that is towed over open water.

Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV’s) or ‘drones’ have been developed to have many different ways of implementing aerial grasping and manipulation. In [ 17 ] , the authors review many of these methods, involving all kinds of mechanisms and actuation methods. In [ 18 ] , a grasping mechanism on a drone is implemented using a dynamixel motor, where the drone uses it’s grasper to perch onto a power line. In [ 19 ] a system where multiple drones support a net using tethers mounted to the underside of the drone is shown. [ 20 ] presents a drone which is able to lower a net based mechanism, suspended from a cable below the drone to pickup packages for delivery. The mechanism is actuated by motors mounted onto the net itself, so would be unsuitable to pickup or drop off into water. [ 21 ] presents the design of a three-fingered claw mechanism installed on a drone for picking up objects, particularly debris from power lines. A similar approach could be adapted for aquatic buoy retrieval by integrating a larger tether, ensuring the drone remains at a safe distance from the water.

This paper proposes a novel approach to addressing the challenges of river-based environmental monitoring. Section III delves into the design of the proposed system, focusing on its novel aspects. Section IV discusses the experimental validation of the platform in the Ōrewa River and presents the results. Finally, Section V concludes the paper, discussing the potential impact of this solution on future environmental monitoring efforts.
