2026-10-07.title: Expressiveness, Equivalence, and Uncertainty in Velocity Obstacles and Closest Point of Approach Metrics
2026-10-07.authors: Elizabeth Dietrich , Liam M. Imagawa , Hanna Krasowski , Aurora Haraldsen , Murat Arcak , Kristin Y. Pettersen
2026-10-07.abstract:
Time to Closest Point of Approach (TCPA), Distance to Closest Point of Approach (DCPA), and Velocity Obstacles (VOs), are widely used to assess and mitigate collision risk in autonomous navigation, yet their relationship and behavior under uncertainty remain largely unexplored.
Assuming perfect state information, we establish a relationship between these representations over finite and infinite prediction horizons and derive conditions under which they provide equivalent characterizations of collision risk.
Under bounded uncertainty, we extend the Closest Point of Approach (CPA) metrics and VO to convex relative-state sets.
We show that in this setting, independently computed TCPA and DCPA bounds lose the joint relationship required for VO membership, while uncertainty-aware VOs preserve this relationship through a set-valued representation of collision-inducing velocities.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Collision risk metrics are essential for monitoring and control of autonomous navigation, where potential collisions must be identified and mitigated in a timely manner [ 1 , 2 ] .
In unstructured environments, including maritime [ 3 , 4 ] , aviation [ 5 ] , and space [ 6 ] domains, risk assessment for navigation cannot rely on predefined lanes or other environmental structures. Instead, collision risk must be determined from observations of the relative kinematics and embodiment of nearby agents. We focus on criticality metrics that capture the spatial and temporal proximity of potential collisions across domains, in particular the CPA ( CPA ) metrics [ 7 , 8 ] and the VO ( VO ) [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] .

CPA metrics assess collision risk by considering the minimum separation between agents over a prediction horizon.
Specifically, the DCPA ( DCPA ) and the TCPA ( TCPA ) provide scalar measures of collision risk for a given relative velocity and position, yielding a compact trajectory risk measure [ 11 , 14 , 12 , 15 , 10 ] . To support their use in practical evasive maneuvering, CPA metrics have been extended to incorporate domain-specific information, including traffic rules, agent dimensions, and other movement information [ 4 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] .

However, from a control perspective, collision avoidance requires evaluating collision risk over all feasible velocities across the prediction horizon. The VO provides a set-valued
representation that partitions the velocity space into collision-inducing and collision-free velocities, enabling direct identification of evasive control actions.
The VO has been applied in a variety of motion planning and control contexts, both as a collision-avoidance mechanism and as a component of broader control frameworks, including integration with control barrier functions [ 19 , 20 ] , model predictive control [ 21 , 22 ] , and reinforcement learning [ 23 ] .

Despite their common objective of characterizing collision risk, the relationship between CPA metrics and VO representations remains largely unexplored.
Existing work relates VO membership to the DCPA condition [ 3 ] , but does not account for the TCPA condition. When the TCPA is negative, the point of closest approach occurs in the past; therefore, the DCPA condition alone does not indicate a future collision. We show that the DCPA condition is necessary but not sufficient for VO membership, and formally establish the additional TCPA condition required for equivalence.
Furthermore, the geometric equivalence between the VO boundary and the DCPA condition for non-negative TCPA , established in [ 14 , Prop. 2.1] , is recovered as a special case of our results.
Our main contributions include:

We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for VO membership in terms of TCPA and DCPA over finite and infinite prediction horizons.

We formulate an uncertainty-aware VO for general convex uncertainty sets, preserving its exact geometry.

We demonstrate that under bounded uncertainty, independently computed TCPA and DCPA bounds lose the joint relationship required for VO membership.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
Sec. II introduces the considered metrics. Sec. III derives necessary and sufficient conditions for VO membership using CPA metrics. Sec. IV formulates an uncertainty-aware VO . Finally, Sec. V evaluates the metrics under bounded uncertainty.

1. We derive necessary and sufficient conditions for VO membership in terms of TCPA and DCPA over finite and infinite prediction horizons.

2. We formulate an uncertainty-aware VO for general convex uncertainty sets, preserving its exact geometry.

3. We demonstrate that under bounded uncertainty, independently computed TCPA and DCPA bounds lose the joint relationship required for VO membership.

2026-10-07.title: ScanSTL: Parallel Robustness Evaluation for Signal Temporal Logic
2026-10-07.authors: Gokhan Alcan
2026-10-07.abstract:
Repeated evaluation and differentiation of Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness can become a computational bottleneck in robot planning and control.
Sequential temporal recurrences limit parallelism, while dense masking increases memory requirements.
We propose ScanSTL, which combines associative temporal aggregation with parallel scans and ordered block reductions.
Eventually and Always use range extrema, while inclusive strong Until composes compact segment representations.
A common range engine handles bounded and shifted intervals, including the guards required before delayed Until witnesses.
Each exact temporal operator computes complete robustness traces with linear work and storage and logarithmic parallel depth on uniformly sampled finite signals.
An open source JAX implementation supports automatic differentiation, batching, and compilation.
We compare ScanSTL with STLCG and STLCG++ using CPU and GPU operator benchmarks and nine composed specifications.
Across these nine specifications at 512 samples, ScanSTL achieves geometric mean speedups of 243 × 243\times for forward evaluation and 104 × 104\times for gradient computation over STLCG++ in JAX on the CPU.
On an RTX 5090 GPU, ScanSTL evaluates unbounded Until over more than two million samples with median times below 0.1 0.1 ms for forward evaluation and 0.25 0.25 ms for gradient computation.
Simulated escort and patrol experiments with a robot dog further demonstrate faster repair of violating plans and greater solver capacity in model predictive control.
Supplementary materials, videos and codes can be found at project website: https://alcanlab.github.io/ScanSTL/
2026-10-07.introduction:
In many robotic applications, successful task execution requires satisfying conditions on both motion and the times at which events occur.
A robot may need to always avoid obstacles, eventually visit regions within deadlines and remain near a person until the person reaches safety.
Signal Temporal Logic (STL) expresses such requirements over real-valued signals [ 1 ] .
Its quantitative semantics assign a robustness value whose sign indicates satisfaction or violation and whose magnitude provides a margin [ 2 , 3 ] .
This makes a specification useful for verifying and optimizing trajectories.

STL has consequently been incorporated into model predictive control (MPC) [ 4 ] and optimization using smooth robustness objectives [ 5 , 6 ] .
Automatic differentiation propagates robustness through robot dynamics to control inputs [ 7 ] .
Each optimizer iteration evaluates the specification and its gradient, while nested temporal operators also require sub-formula values at multiple starting times.
Complete robustness traces are therefore central to this computation, whose cost grows with horizon and sampling resolution.

Existing differentiable evaluators expose a tradeoff between temporal dependencies and storage (Fig. 1 ).
STLCG [ 7 ] uses recurrences with sequential dependencies along the trace.
STLCG++ [ 8 ] exposes parallelism through dense temporal masks.
When the window grows with the trace, its storage is quadratic for Eventually and Always and cubic for strong Until.
Until is particularly demanding because each witness is combined with a condition that must hold up to that witness.
These costs limit repeated evaluation within a planning or control budget.

To address this problem, we propose ScanSTL, a unified parallel evaluator for exact STL robustness.
ScanSTL combines associative temporal aggregation [ 9 ] with parallel scans [ 10 ] and ordered block reductions [ 22 , 23 ] to evaluate complete robustness traces without dense temporal masks or sequential recurrences along the full horizon.
Eventually and Always use range extrema, while inclusive strong Until composes compact segment representations.
A common range engine handles bounded and shifted intervals, including the conditions that must hold before an Until witness becomes eligible.
Each exact temporal operator requires linear work and storage and logarithmic parallel depth under explicit finite trace semantics.
For differentiable predicates, JAX supports automatic differentiation through the resulting piecewise differentiable computation without requiring smoothing.
Smooth Eventually and Always also retain this scan structure.

The main contributions of this work are:

A unified parallel evaluation algorithm for exact Eventually, Always, and inclusive strong Until, combining associative temporal aggregation with scans and range reductions. Each temporal operator computes complete robustness traces with linear work and storage and logarithmic parallel depth under finite-horizon semantics.

A common parallel range engine for bounded unary operators and Until pairs that preserves operand order and avoids duplicate contributions. It incorporates the guards required by shifted Until and also supports smooth unary reductions that are not idempotent.

An open-source JAX implementation of ScanSTL
supporting automatic differentiation, batching, and just-in-time compilation for use in optimization and control.

An evaluation across CPU and GPU operator benchmarks, nine composed STL specifications, and simulated robot planning and MPC tasks, quantifying computational gains in robustness evaluation, verified plan repair, and closed-loop solver capacity.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Control Using STL Robustness

STL robustness guides control synthesis [ 2 , 3 ] .
Raman et al. [ 4 ] encoded STL constraints in mixed-integer MPC, while subsequent work reduced the number of binary variables [ 11 ] .
Direct robustness optimization supports nonlinear dynamics through smooth approximations [ 5 , 6 ] .
Arithmetic-geometric mean robustness accounts for satisfaction beyond the most critical sample [ 12 ] , robustness-to-go prevents past bottlenecks from obscuring differences between future plans [ 13 ] , and GradSTL [ 14 ] provides smooth STL semantics and derivatives for neurosymbolic reasoning and learning.
These approaches develop control formulations or robustness objectives for optimization and learning.
ScanSTL addresses the complementary cost of repeatedly evaluating robustness and its gradients within optimization.

## II-B Exact Monitoring and Associative Algorithms

Early approaches to efficient STL monitoring reused computations across overlapping temporal windows.
Donzé et al. [ 15 ] combined temporal decompositions with sliding extrema algorithms [ 16 ] .
Deshmukh et al. [ 17 ] developed robustness intervals for incomplete traces, and RTAMT [ 18 ] translates bounded future formulas into past formulas for incremental monitoring in discrete and dense time.
TLTk [ 19 ] parallelizes monitoring on CPUs and GPUs with linear trace storage for a fixed formula, but its reported time bound retains a temporal window factor.
Rodionova et al. [ 20 ] interpreted Boolean MTL as filtering, with separate quantitative kernel scores that differ from spatial robustness.
Jakšić et al. [ 21 ] compute semantic distances invariant to formula rewrites through weighted automata, whose size can be exponential in the formula.
Mamouras et al. [ 9 ] established associative Since/Until pairs and ordered window aggregation with constant amortized work per sample. Their online monitor already achieves linear total work for a fixed formula, but does not develop input derivatives or logarithmic parallel depth across time.
ScanSTL adapts the local pairs to inclusive Until and combines Blelloch’s scan and recurrence construction [ 10 ] with block prefix and suffix reductions [ 22 , 23 ] .

## II-C Differentiable and Parallel STL Evaluation

Leung et al. [ 7 ] introduced STLCG to express STL robustness as a computation graph, enabling backpropagation for trajectory optimization, parameter fitting, and learning with logical constraints.
Its temporal operators reuse intermediate results through recurrent updates, but the resulting dependencies limit parallel evaluation along the trace.
Kapoor et al. [ 8 ] developed STLCG++ to expose this temporal parallelism by applying masks to expanded signal tensors.
The framework supports automatic differentiation in JAX and PyTorch.
This construction improves parallel utilization at the cost of larger intermediate arrays.
When temporal windows grow with the trace, storage is quadratic for Eventually and Always and cubic for Until, whose witnesses each require a prefix condition.
These two designs therefore highlight a tradeoff between sequential dependencies and memory use in differentiable robustness evaluation.
ScanSTL combines associative scans and ordered range reductions to compute each exact temporal operator with linear work and storage and logarithmic parallel depth, while retaining automatic differentiation in JAX [ 24 ] .
We use STLCG and STLCG++ as baselines to evaluate how this formulation addresses the temporal dependencies of recurrence and the storage cost of dense masking.

2026-10-07.title: SharedKV-BT: Node-Local Typed Decisions for Behavior-Tree Agents
2026-10-07.authors: Naoki Wake , Justin Wagle
2026-10-07.comment: . Last updated on October 5th, 2026
2026-10-07.abstract: Agent tasks require sequences of interdependent decisions. Autoregressive models support more flexible decision interfaces than conventional classifiers but incur the latency of token-by-token generation. Recent shared-prefix methods reduce this cost by reusing encoded context and scoring multiple decisions in parallel, but do not model decision dependencies or verify execution. We propose SharedKV-BT, where each active node of a behavior tree (BT) exposes stage-local fields and candidates, and Shared-KV scores the candidates in parallel and passes the selected decision to a separate execution system. We tested SharedKV-BT on robot manipulation, mobile navigation, and computer-use tasks. Across three tasks, SharedKV-BT made typed decisions 2.36 2.36 – 4.15 × 4.15\times faster than prompt-matched autoregressive decoding. On the manipulation task, node-local Shared-KV improved joint decision accuracy from 75% to 94% and closed-loop success from 0% to 60%. Fixed-score policy replay showed that stage gating prevented out-of-order actions and external postconditions prevented premature completion.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Agents must make sequences of interdependent decisions to achieve a goal. A robot cannot place an object before grasping it, and a computer-use agent cannot paste a file before selecting its source and opening the destination. An appropriate action and its arguments, such as the target object or destination, need to be selected based on the current execution stage and environment state.

Conventional classifiers select from a predefined set of classes [ 1 ] . Open-set recognition extends this setting by rejecting inputs from classes not seen during training [ 2 , 3 ] , but it still does not provide application-defined, stage-specific decision interfaces.
Autoregressive models support flexible interfaces specified through text [ 4 ] , but sequential token decoding incurs inference latency that increases with output length [ 5 , 6 ] . More recently, typed-decision systems such as Jev ask a model to fill named fields by choosing among application-defined candidates, avoiding token-by-token generation [ 7 ] .

Typed-decision interfaces, however, focus only on choosing the value of each field and do not manage execution itself [ 7 ] . They do not define when a decision should be made, which candidates are valid at that point, or whether the chosen action succeeded. As a result, they can act out of order, repeat a completed action, or stop because the model claimed success. Behavior trees (BTs), on the other hand, are commonly used to structure agent execution through conditional branching and failure recovery [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .

In this paper, we propose SharedKV-BT, which combines a Jev-style typed-decision interface with BT control (Fig. 1 ). Each BT node defines the current execution stage and exposes only the fields and candidates that are valid at that stage. For example, in the schematic pick-and-place example, Acquire , Transport , and Deposit nodes expose different skills and arguments. This node-local design focuses the model on the decisions relevant to the current stage. The model encodes the instruction and observed state once as a task-state prefix and reuses the resulting key-value (KV) cache to score complete candidates in parallel. A separate execution system executes the selected action, while the BT’s external postcondition checks the system state after execution and controls progression and retry. Section III-C specifies the experiment-specific interfaces.

Our findings answer three questions:

Efficiency. How much does shared-prefix reuse reduce decision cost? On model inputs saved at decision points, Shared-KV was 2.36 2.36 – 4.15 × 4.15\times faster than prompt-matched constrained autoregressive decoding; a controlled comparison using identical candidate batches isolated a 1.29 1.29 – 2.09 × 2.09\times benefit from cache reuse alone (Section IV-A ).

Focus. Does exposing only the current node’s choices improve decisions and execution? Yes. Relative to an interface that exposed all fields and candidates at every decision (the global interface), node-local Shared-KV improved correct joint typed decisions from 75% (90/120) to 94% (113/120) and closed-loop completion from 0% to 60% (Section IV-B ).

Authority. Which errors do stage gating and external postconditions prevent? Stage gating prevented out-of-order actions, while external postconditions prevented model-reported completion from advancing an unsatisfied task (Section IV-C ).

The contributions of this paper are:

An architecture in which each active BT node provides a typed-decision interface with predefined candidates, while a shared task-state prefix supports parallel candidate scoring.

An architecture in which each active BT node provides a typed-decision interface with predefined candidates, while a shared task-state prefix supports parallel candidate scoring.

Controlled evidence for the three corresponding mechanisms: prefix reuse for efficiency, node-local interface routing for focus, and stage gating with external postconditions for execution authority.

End-to-end evaluations across robot manipulation, mobile navigation, and computer-use tasks, with decision errors separated from downstream execution failures.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Robot Execution Architectures

Robot architectures separate fast action-level skills from higher-level decision making. Subsumption uses priority-ordered layers [ 11 ] , whereas Gat’s three-layer architecture [ 12 ] and 3T [ 13 ] place an executive between planning and real-time control. BTs formalize periodic updates (ticks) and success or failure returns [ 14 ] and have been studied for sequential composition [ 9 ] , robustness and safety [ 10 ] , and robotic applications [ 8 ] . BT learning includes branch and tree design [ 15 ] and continuous action-node parameters [ 16 ] .

In a separate line of work, task and motion planning (TAMP) methods jointly search over discrete action sequences and continuous robot motions, propagating geometric failures back to task-level search [ 17 , 18 ] . SharedKV-BT instead operates at a different layer, selecting among candidates exposed by a predefined BT rather than planning action sequences or trajectories.

## II-B Language-Model Planning and Skill Selection

Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have generated or revised task procedures from prompts, demonstrations, fine-tuning, or heuristic planning [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] , including runtime-generated visual-condition nodes [ 23 ] , language-model action sequences [ 24 ] , and multimodal plans from demonstrations [ 25 ] .

Reusable skill libraries separate task descriptions from hardware execution [ 26 ] , and Plan-and-Act studies when to invoke an LLM [ 27 ] . Other systems span free-form code or plan generation [ 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ] and predefined skill selection: SayCan combines language-model scores with scores of whether an action is feasible [ 32 ] , ProgPrompt specifies available actions in program-like prompt context [ 33 ] , and Inner Monologue conditions later reasoning on feedback [ 34 ] . Unlike these methods, SharedKV-BT combines fast candidate scoring through Shared-KV with stage-constrained decision making through the BT.

## II-C Complete-Candidate Scoring and Shared-Prefix Inference

Complete-candidate likelihood scoring is not novel [ 4 ] ; prior work has also examined alternative label wordings and prompt-dependent calibration [ 35 , 36 ] . Related structured-generation methods constrain outputs through token masking or schemas, including XGrammar, Outlines, and Structured Outputs [ 37 , 38 , 39 ] , while Toolformer learns when to insert tool calls during generation [ 40 ] . Jev frames structured inference as typed decisions over application-defined candidates [ 7 ] , and concurrent work scores candidate identifiers in parallel [ 41 ] .

Shared-prefix inference has also been studied at the systems level. PagedAttention manages KV caches [ 42 ] , SGLang reuses prefixes through RadixAttention [ 43 ] , Hydragen separates shared-prefix from candidate-specific computation [ 44 ] , and ArborKV manages caches for branching search [ 45 ] . SharedKV-BT applies shared-prefix reuse to multi-step agent execution, with each BT node exposing multiple typed fields and candidates that share a task-state prefix.

2026-10-07.title: Towards Decentralized Formation of Minimum-Length Communication Networks Using Robot Swarms
2026-10-07.authors: Genki Miyauchi , Mohamed S. Talamali , Julian Rau , Roderich Groß
2026-10-07.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
2026-10-07.abstract: Multi-robot missions in infrastructure-denied environments frequently rely on reliable communication links between spatially separated locations. We propose a fully decentralized framework for constructing and dynamically maintaining communication networks without centralized topology planning or global positioning infrastructure. Driven strictly by local interactions, robots reconfigure local network topologies and adjust their physical positions to minimize overall network length while adhering to communication constraints. Formal analysis shows that our local reconfiguration operations guarantee continuous network connectivity, strictly decrease network length with every branch transfer, and bound worst-case performance to the shortest starlike tree. Embodied simulations and physical multi-robot experiments confirm that our approach forms networks near the length of centrally computed Euclidean Steiner trees. Additionally, the system dynamically adapts to moving targets and optimizes deployment by utilizing only necessary connectors, preserving excess robots for auxiliary tasks. This work enables autonomous swarms to self-organize adaptive ad hoc communication infrastructure in communication-denied environments, which could support applications varying from subterranean exploration to planetary missions.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Multi-robot communication networks can support the exchange of task-relevant information and coordination among spatially separated robots, particularly in remote environments where communication infrastructure and positioning systems may be unavailable or unreliable. To maintain such networks over large distances, some robots can act as relay nodes, hereafter called connectors, by positioning themselves between distant robots and maintaining communication links with neighboring robots (see Fig. 1 ).
The remaining robots can then be used to perform other tasks.

Because robots have limited communication range, networks of excessive lengths generally require more connectors, which can consume a substantial fraction of the robot team.
They can also increase the distance traveled by robots navigating or transporting goods along the network, as well as the number of relay hops required for communication.
Thus, beyond maintaining connectivity, reducing the total length of the communication network can improve how efficiently it supports the robot team.

When only two locations of interest must be connected, the minimal-length communication network is a path graph. For three or more locations, minimal-length networks take the form of tree structures known as the Euclidean Steiner trees [ 1 ] . However, directly computing and deploying a Steiner tree is not realistic for the settings considered here: the robots do not have access to a shared global coordinate frame, knowledge of all robot positions, or a central authority that assigns network positions and connections. Moreover, the robots have limited communication range, and connectivity must be maintained as the robots move.

Existing approaches to multi-robot connectivity maintenance have demonstrated robot teams that preserve communication links [ 2 ] , form chains or trees [ 3 , 4 ] , and adapt to changing task locations [ 5 , 6 ] . Nevertheless, many decentralized approaches primarily focus on maintaining connectivity rather than reducing the total length of the resulting network. Therefore, the placement of connectors may be inefficient, causing the network to use more robots than necessary. Centralized approaches can optimize relay placement or network structure directly [ 7 ] , but they typically require global position information and centralized assignment of robot behaviors.

This paper proposes a decentralized controller that enables a group of mobile robots to form and maintain short, Steiner-tree-like communication networks.
The robots do not rely on global positioning, global communication, or a central planner. Instead, they use local sensing and communication to decide when to add connectors to maintain connectivity, when redundant connectors can be removed, and when network connections should be reassigned to nearby connectors to reduce total edge length. In addition, each connector locally adjusts its position relative to its network neighbors to make the communication network approach Steiner-tree-like structures.
We show that the network remains connected at all times, stabilizes to a shortest starlike tree without merging redundant edges, and can be further shortened by merging redundant edges.
Through embodied simulations, we show that the proposed approach forms networks that are shorter than the shortest starlike trees and qualitatively closer to Steiner trees.
We further demonstrate its practical applicability through experiments with physical robots.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews prior work on Steiner tree problems and multi-robot connectivity maintenance, followed by the problem formulation in Section III . Section IV then introduces the proposed decentralized network formation method, while Section V analyzes its network-length properties and connectivity preservation. The approach is evaluated in simulation and on physical robots in Sections VI and VII , respectively. Finally, Section VIII concludes the paper.

# II Related Work

## II-A Steiner Trees and Relay Placement

A Euclidean Steiner tree connects a set of terminals with minimum total network length by allowing additional points, called Steiner points, beyond the terminals themselves [ 1 ] . Computing such a tree is NP-hard [ 8 ] .
Classical Steiner trees impose no upper bound on edge length, whereas communication links between robots are typically limited by their communication range. The Steiner tree problem with a minimum number of Steiner points and bounded edge length therefore seeks the fewest additional relays required to connect a set of terminals while respecting a maximum edge length [ 9 ] . Algorithms for the bounded-edge Steiner problem [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] and relay-node placement in wireless sensor networks [ 12 , 13 ] centrally determine relay positions from a set of terminal locations; see [ 14 ] for a broader survey of node-placement strategies.

Related robotic approaches have also used relay placement and Steiner-tree formulations. Yanmaz et al. [ 15 ] jointly planned the trajectories of search UAVs and dedicated relay UAVs while maintaining connectivity to a ground station. Nguyen et al. [ 16 ] considered target coverage and connectivity using a weighted Steiner-tree formulation, while Lee et al. [ 7 ] used a central controller to add, remove, and relocate branches in a robot network for resource transport. Kent et al. [ 17 ] proposed an architecture in which a base station computes a Semi-Steiner tree from global task locations and propagates the resulting topology through the swarm.

These methods can directly optimize relay placement or network geometry, but require globally available information and centralized computation, even when robot-level deployment is distributed. In contrast, we address the decentralized formation of a bounded-edge network, without any robot or external entity computing its complete structure.

## II-B Connectivity-Preserving Control

Distributed connectivity-maintenance methods regulate robot motion so that the communication graph remains connected while the robots perform other tasks. Krupke et al. [ 2 ] proposed a cohesive swarm controller that maintains a redundant connected structure under external leader forces. Imran et al. [ 18 ] used local virtual forces to improve connected coverage, while Luo et al. [ 5 ] combined task behaviors with global and subgroup connectivity maintenance. Connectivity constraints have also been enforced using control barrier functions [ 19 ] .

These approaches primarily treat connectivity as a constraint on robot motion or swarm cohesion. Although some methods select particular communication links or spanning structures to enforce connectivity, they do not generally optimize the geometric structure of a relay network, its total length, or the number of robots assigned as relays.

## II-C Distributed Relay-Network Formation

Other distributed approaches explicitly construct or modify relay-network topology while preserving connectivity. Majcherczyk et al. [ 3 ] deployed robots into starlike networks connecting multiple locations.
Varadharajan et al. [ 4 ] formed and repaired relay chains between a base and a moving leader. Miyauchi et al. [ 6 ] formed a dynamic chain connecting two moving operators, enabling communication and robot exchange between them. Yi et al. [ 20 ] inserted relay robots into the communication topology to enable task robots to reach their destinations. Soma et al. [ 21 ] characterized connectivity-preserving local topology-manipulation operations for robot swarms.

Although these works address different aspects of relay-network formation and reconfiguration, they do not jointly address the decentralized construction of a general multi-terminal tree, reduction of its total edge length, and removal of unnecessary relays. Our approach addresses this combination while maintaining connectivity and without centrally computing the final network topology.

2026-10-07.title: Lego-Like Stiffness Configuration of Planar Compliant Modules for Task-Specific Flexible Interfaces
2026-10-07.authors: Siyue Yao , Xiaochi Xie , Shixuan Zhao , Yutong Li , Hao Li , Mark R. Cutkosky , Genliang Chen
2026-10-07.abstract:
Compliant mechanisms provide compact and intrinsic structural compliance for regulating physical interactions between mechanisms and environments.
However, different tasks demand distinct stiffness characteristics, often requiring task-specific optimization and redesign due to limited geometric design space and inherent coupling among multiple stiffness components.
This paper presents a Lego-like stiffness configuration approach using stackable planar compliant modules.
Three complementary module geometries are introduced, with their stiffness characteristics further regulated through beam width, plate thickness, and module orientation.
A unified stiffness model is established for quantitative analysis of individual and composed modules.
Further, a two-stage optimization method is presented to achieve desired stiffness profiles, combining a genetic algorithm for configuration and sequential quadratic programming for parameter refinement.
Experimental verification shows deviations below 6.5 % 6.5\% for simulated stiffness.
A flexible wrist is further developed as a representative implementation, exhibiting distinct compliant and dynamic responses under different stiffness characteristics.
An optimized modular composition realizes prescribed stiffness values and maintains compliant obstacle interaction during high-speed motion at 1 ​ m / s 1m/s , with a maximum tested angular compliance of approximately 15 ∘ 15^{\circ} .
The proposed framework provides a systematic approach for constructing flexible interfaces with task-specific stiffness characteristics.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Contact-rich manufacturing and industrial tasks, including assembly, surface finishing, and manipulation, require flexible interfaces to accommodate geometric uncertainties while maintaining desired contact conditions [ 1 , 2 ] . However, different interaction configurations impose distinct stiffness requirements.
As illustrated in Fig. 1 A, peg-in-hole and gluing impose different directional interaction requirements and consequently favor different stiffness configurations, with greater rigidity along motion or load transmission directions and increased compliance along accommodation directions [ 3 ] .
Moreover, the task-dependent stiffness is often demanded within a prescribed range, making task-specific and quantitatively defined stiffness configuration an important design requirement for flexible interfaces [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .

Kinematics-based approaches are commonly employed for the synthesis of compliant mechanisms.
The pseudo-rigid-body model (PRBM) [ 7 ] facilitates design through equivalent rigid-link representations, while constraint-based design and Freedom and Constraint Topology (FACT) systematically construct flexure topologies according to desired degrees of freedom (DoFs) and constraints [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
However, quantitative stiffness configuration requires further parametric optimization beyond the initial mechanism design.

Topology optimization provides another solution by directly optimizing material distribution within a prescribed design domain [ 11 , 12 ] .
Prescribed stiffness characteristics are incorporated into topology optimization by defining stiffness-based objectives and constraints.
Zhang et al. [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] developed a series of topology optimization formulations based on stiffness and Jacobian characteristics, enabling multi-DoFs synthesis, motion decoupling, and prescribed compliance while incorporating structural constraints.
Further, Seltmann et al. [ 16 ] incorporated stiffness and adaptive volume constraints to synthesize compliant mechanisms with distributed compliance and prescribed structural stiffness.
However, the attainable design region is restricted by geometry constraints.
Moreover, changes in stiffness requirements generally require redesign, which is often time-consuming.

Beyond mechanism optimization as a whole, building-block approaches provide a higher-level design paradigm by composing predefined compliant elements [ 17 ] .
Kim et al. [ 18 ] characterized compliant building blocks using stiffness and compliance ellipsoids and synthesized mechanisms through their combinations.
DiBiasio et al. [ 19 ] employed serial and parallel flexural blocks for rapid concept design.
Li et al. [ 20 ] developed the Compliant Building Elements (CBE) method, in which a library of basic compliant elements is assembled in serial or parallel.
These composition-based methods enable rapid mechanism design by assembling predefined and characterized elements, which can be designed through intuition, kinematics, or topology optimization [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] .
However, the design space remains constrained by the geometric restrictions within the mechanism.

To this end, this paper proposes a Lego-like stiffness configuration approach using stackable planar compliant modules, as illustrated in Fig. 1 B.
By distributing stiffness contributions across multiple modules stacked along the thickness direction, the proposed framework introduces an additional design dimension that alleviates the geometric constraints of a single planar domain and enlarges the attainable stiffness range.
With predefined module geometries, task-specific stiffness is configured through module selection, geometric parameters, orientation, and parallel composition.
Three complementary planar modules, a unified stiffness model, and an optimization framework are developed and experimentally validated.
A flexible wrist is further developed in Fig. 1 C as a representative implementation of flexible interfaces, showcasing the effectiveness of the proposed method in achieving desired stiffness characteristics.

The main contributions include:

(1) Proposed a Lego-like stacking strategy using planar compliant modules for task-specific stiffness regulation.

(2) Established a unified stiffness model for parameterized modules and their parallel compositions, enabling quantitative characterization and analysis.

(3) Developed a two-stage inverse design method for optimizing module configurations and parameters to achieve prescribed stiffness requirements.

This paper is organized as follows.
Planar compliant module designs, stiffness modeling, and optimization method are presented in Sec. II .
Section III experimentally characterizes the module stiffness to validate the simulated results.
Implementation of a flexible wrist with an optimized modular composition for desired compliance and dynamic performance is shown in Sec. IV .
Section V discusses the capabilities, limitations, and potential future extensions.
Finally, conclusions are drawn in Sec. VI .

# II Design and Modeling

## II-A Lego-Like Planar Compliant Module Design

Decoupled stiffness characteristics between translation and rotation, and along different axes, are desired for manipulation and assembly interfaces, which reduce parasitic motion and provide a clear correspondence between task-level loading directions and the resulting structural deformation.
Accordingly, each compliant module is constructed as a parallel mechanism with symmetrically distributed compliant chains, such that the off-diagonal terms of the stiffness matrix ideally vanish.
One advantage of the proposed parallel composition is to allow a symmetric compliant mechanism with potential in-plane interference to be decomposed into two mirrored half-modules and stacked in separate planes, thereby preserving symmetry while expanding the design space.
Further, the modules are designed as planar compliant mechanisms, with the plate thickness t t comparable to or larger than the in-plane chain width w w .
On this basis, the out-of-plane translational stiffness is treated as the load-support component rather than a principal configuration objective, which is required to remain within a task-dependent range.

Three planar modules with distinct geometries are introduced, as illustrated in Fig. 2 A.
Their geometries are intuitively devised based on the stiffness characteristics of curved beams.
For a moderately curved beam, the in-plane translational stiffness along the axial direction u , defined by the line connecting the two endpoints, is higher than that along the tangential direction v , because deformation along u involves a greater contribution from axial stretching or compression, whereas deformation along v is dominated by bending.
In contrast, the in-plane rotational stiffness exhibits the opposite trend.
The difference between the two directional stiffnesses gradually diminishes as the beam curvature increases.
Accordingly, the first module, Type-I , is constructed using beams with relatively small curvature.
As the curved beam extends into a spiral geometry, its stiffness characteristics, particularly the rotational components, change substantially.
Specifically, the rotational stiffness associated with the u direction becomes higher than that associated with v .
This observation motivates the second module, Type-II , in which a curvature reversal is introduced.
In addition, a higher-order wavy geometry is adopted for the compliant chains of Type-III , which reduces the relative out-of-plane rotational stiffness compared with the in-plane ones.
The illustrative stiffness characteristics of the three modules are depicted by the radar plots in Fig. 2 B using a common scale.
These comparisons show that the three devised modules provide complementary combinations of the five principal stiffness components.

Besides the choices of module geometry, w w and t t serve as design parameters for tuning the stiffness characteristics.
Since w w and t t influence the axial and bending stiffness at different rates, varying these parameters changes the relative ratios among the stiffness components.
An illustration of tuning w w and t t for Type-I is depicted in Fig. 2 B, where the different growth rates between each component are revealed, demonstrating the potential of achieving distinct stiffness characteristics through composition.
The in-plane orientation of each module provides a further configuration variable, with a 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} rotation used to swap the directional stiffness between the two in-plane axes.
Accordingly, the three geometries, design variables { t , w } \{t,w\} , and orientations jointly determine the stiffness properties.
Task-specific stiffness profiles can then be regulated through module design and parallel composition, allowing the overall stiffness characteristics to be tailored toward the desired task requirements.

The advantage of the proposed Lego-like planar compliant module composition strategy lies in separating topology design from stiffness configuration.
With the module geometries predetermined, the time-consuming topology optimization is replaced by lower-dimensional parameter optimization for task-specific stiffness regulation.

The x x -axis is defined along the normal direction of the module plane, while the y y -axis is oriented vertically.
The z z -axis is then determined according to the right-hand rule.
Each curved compliant chain is discretized into n n segments with equal arc length.
Each segment is further represented by a kinematically equivalent six-DoFs serial mechanism consisting of rigid links and elastic joints.
Based on the local curvature, a local frame is established for the j j -th segment of the i i -th chain.
Specifically, the x i , j x_{i,j} -axis remains parallel to the global x x -axis, while the z i , j z_{i,j} -axis is aligned with the local tangential direction of the curve.

2026-10-07.title: Embedded Bare-Metal Radar-Inertial Odometry
2026-10-07.authors: Nicolai Adil Øyen Aatif , Morten Nissov , Kostas Alexis
2026-10-07.abstract: Compact extraplanetary rovers and micro aerial vehicles require robust state estimation frameworks designed to operate under strict computational constraints in unforgiving environments. Typical solutions involving vision- or LiDAR-based sensing are computationally expensive and vulnerable to environments with perceptual degradation, making them poorly suited for resource-constrained platforms and austere conditions. Alternatively, Frequency Modulated Continuous Wave (FMCW) radar offers both robustness and computational efficiency by directly providing velocity measurements coupled with inherent resilience to perceptual degradation. These factors enable robust estimation, thereby reducing reliance on human operators for supervision to ensure platform safety in challenging environments. In this manuscript, we propose an embedded radar-inertial estimator tailored for low-compute platforms. All sensor drivers, data processing, and aided inertial navigation are performed on a single-core microcontroller, demonstrating its computational efficiency. Flight experiments show translational APE of $0.51-0.82\,\mathrm{m}$ and RPE of $<$3\,\% against motion capture, alongside closed-loop flight through an unmodified PX4 stack. The firmware and printed circuit board design are openly available on GitHub at \href{ this https URL }{ntnu-arl/embedded\_rio} and \href{ this https URL }{ntnu-arl/embedded\_rio-pcb} respectively.

2026-10-07.title: Distribution-Transfer Safe-Horizon MPC under Mode Uncertainty
2026-10-07.authors: Stephen Crawford , Nora Ayanian
2026-10-07.abstract: Scenario-based MPC is an attractive strategy for chance-constrained motion planning that approximates uncertainty via a finite set of sampled scenarios. As a sampling-based method, scenario-based MPC is sensitive to distribution mismatch. We address this problem in the context of Safe-Horizon Model Predictive Control (SH-MPC) with obstacles governed by switching dynamic modes. From finite mode observations, we construct a confidence set for the unknown categorical mode law and derive a multiplicative domination bound that transfers a Safe-Horizon collision-risk certificate from a selected scenario-sampling distribution to every law in the confidence set. Wasserstein geometry is used to regularize probability reallocation among modes according to the similarity of their induced trajectory predictions, while a collision-risk surrogate biases sampling toward dangerous modes. The resulting certificate explicitly quantifies the additional tightening required under distribution mismatch and exposes the multiplicative conservatism that arises when several obstacle-wise transfer factors are combined.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Scenario-based optimization provides a tractable surrogate for chance-constrained control by enforcing constraints on finitely many sampled realizations of uncertainty [ 1 , 2 ] . In MPC, this approach has been used to reduce conservatism relative to analytic convex approximations while preserving real-time feasibility [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Scenario-based optimization is used as the basis of Safe-Horizon Model Predictive Control (SH-MPC), which probabilistically bounds the joint probability of collision over a trajectory [ 4 ] .

Despite the promising potential of SH-MPC, it shares the limitations of any sampling-based approach. As a bound derived from traditional scenario theory [ 1 ] , the Safe-Horizon joint collision-risk bound only applies with respect to the distribution of chance constraints that were sampled. Consequently, when distribution mismatch exists, we lack guarantees with respect to the true distribution. This problem exists across scenario-based MPC, but is particularly easy to see in the context of obstacles with switching dynamics. In cases where we must sample across multiple discrete dynamic modes, scenario generation requires a probability distribution over the horizon-level behavior mode used to generate each obstacle trajectory. The same transfer argument can be applied more broadly to scenario-optimization-based MPC formulations when certification is defined with respect to a known sampling law. Other relevant works include per-step chance-constraint formulations [ 3 ] , candidate-path scenario representations [ 5 ] , and reinforcement-learning-augmented scenario-based MPC [ 6 ] .

Our approach first constructs a finite-sample confidence set for the unknown categorical mode law. From this set we derive coordinate-wise probability envelopes that yield a multiplicative change-of-measure bound. We then select a scenario-sampling distribution 𝐪 ⋆ \mathbf{q}^{\star} using a Wasserstein-constrained risk-aware optimization that prevents modes classified as dangerous from being downweighted relative to nominal sampling. A Safe-Horizon certificate computed under 𝐪 ⋆ \mathbf{q}^{\star} can then be transferred, after an explicit tightening by the domination factor, to every mode law in the finite-sample confidence set.

Our construction differs from conventional Wasserstein distributionally robust MPC, where ambiguity is typically embedded directly into the control problem through worst-case expectations, risk measures, or robust chance constraints [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] . We do not optimize a worst-case expected cost or chance constraint over a Wasserstein ball. Instead, Wasserstein geometry regularizes the redistribution of probability among discrete trajectory modes while robustness to categorical mode-probability mismatch is provided by the distribution-transfer certificate developed below.

Schuurmans and Patrinos’ work [ 15 ] is particularly relevant because it explicitly models uncertain transition probabilities in a Markov jump system and embeds the resulting ambiguity-induced risk measures into a multistage control problem. Our formulation instead makes the narrower assumption of independent horizon-level categorical mode observations over the calibration interval. This permits a finite-sample categorical confidence construction while leaving the downstream SH-MPC problem unchanged; extension to state-conditioned or Markov mode laws is left for future work.

We make three main contributions. First, we construct a finite-sample confidence set for the unknown categorical mode law. Second, we derive a multiplicative domination certificate that transfers Safe-Horizon violation guarantees from a selected sampling law to every mode law in this confidence set. Third, we introduce a Wasserstein-constrained risk-aware rule for choosing the scenario-sampling distribution while explicitly controlling its domination factor. We also empirically quantify certificate tightness, closed-loop performance, and computational overhead.

2026-10-07.title: Fluorescence-enhanced Whisker Array with Vision-based Deformation Analysis for Underwater Source Localization
2026-10-07.authors: Xiaochi Xie , Hao Li , Shixuan Zhao , Siyue Yao , Shuran Song , Mark R. Cutkosky
2026-10-07.abstract:
Deep-water biological observation is essential for understanding marine organisms and their interactions with the environment.
However, conventional optical and acoustic approaches can introduce stimuli that alter animal behavior and bias biological observations.
This paper proposes a fluorescence-enhanced whisker array sensing system that pinpoints underwater hydrodynamic sources through local optical readout rather than direct source imaging.
Five spatially oriented whiskers, fabricated with nitinol cores and fluorescent urethane shells, are integrated with ultraviolet excitation and a monocular camera.
Image enhancement and segmentation are applied to track the whisker deformation.
A lightweight convolutional neural network captures temporal and cross-whisker features from 2 ​ s 2\,s sequences to estimate source localization.
Pool experiments achieve a mean spatial localization error of 88 ​ m ​ m 88\,mm , with 73.5 ​ m ​ m 73.5\,mm in radius and 2.5 ∘ 2.5^{\circ} in angle, across a test region of 600 ​ m ​ m 600\,mm with ± 30 ∘ \pm 30^{\circ} .
Real-time localization of a moving thruster demonstrates the capability of the proposed method in dynamic scenarios, highlighting its potential for integration into underwater robots for hydrodynamic source detection, localization, and tracking in low-light environments.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Deep-water biological and environmental observation is essential for understanding marine organisms and their interactions with the surrounding environment [ 1 ] .
However, conventional underwater observation,
commonly relies on vision-based sensing with artificial illumination [ 2 ] or active acoustic sensing such as sonar and scientific echosounders [ 3 ] , may alter creature behavior and consequently bias biological observations [ 4 , 5 ] .
Such disturbances become increasingly problematic in deep water [ 6 ] .
These findings motivate sensing approaches that acquire sufficient information under low ambient illumination while minimizing observation-induced disturbance.

Hydrodynamic sensing provides cues by exploiting object-generated disturbances without requiring direct visual observation [ 7 , 8 ] .
Inspired by the fish lateral line, distributed flow sensors have demonstrated wake detection and source
localization [ 9 ] .
Pressure and flow-velocity sensor fusion has enabled dipole-source localization [ 10 ] .
Pressure histories have been further used to estimate a moving propeller’s lateral state at fixed longitudinal separations [ 11 ] , while distributed
optical flow sensors have reconstructed moving-source
positions [ 12 ] .
However, these distributed methods obtain spatial information using multiple sensors with individual data, which introduces substantial complexity in sensor placement, calibration, synchronization, and system integration, particularly when scaling to larger sensing arrays.

Inspired by the trail-following capability of harbor seals using their whiskers, researchers have developed compliant sensing mechanisms to perceive hydrodynamic cues and estimate the location of the source [ 13 ] .
Several mechanisms are applied to acquire this information based on artificial whiskers.
Strain-gauge arrays have been utilized to predict dipole-source positions [ 14 ] .
Dai et al. [ 15 ] integrated a three-axis Hall sensor into a magnetic film coupled with a whisker array to estimate flow and wake characteristics, further deducing source direction.
Glick et al. [ 16 ] developed Fiber Bragg Grating (FBG) sensors to estimate disturbance arrival direction and propagation speed.
A compliant whisker with root-mounted FBGs has been presented to support wake-guided robotic branch selection [ 17 ] .
However, these approaches typically deploy one dedicated sensor to measure one mechanical response, leading to a bulky system when scaling to larger arrays in order to capture additional features of the source.

A shared imaging interface offers a solution to retain a collection of responses while reducing the need for multiple sensors [ 18 , 19 ] .
Zhang et al. [ 20 ] proposed FlowSight, utilizing an internal camera to observe the deformation and motion of a tentacle for sensing the speed and direction of flow.
Wang et al. [ 21 ] developed fluorescent silicone cilia with a fisheye camera to estimate local flow velocity and direction.
These systems infer local flow parameters rather than the coordinates of the source that generates the flow [ 20 , 21 ] .
Elshalakani et al. [ 22 ] further map the mechanical response of optically tracked whisker tips to the position of an upstream cylinder in a planar setting.
While static source localization has been demonstrated, real-time localization of dynamically moving sources requires further exploration.

To this end, we present a fluorescence-enhanced whisker-array sensing system that uses a monocular camera to capture flow-induced whisker deformations and a CNN-based regression model to estimate the position of an underwater source, as illustrated in Fig. 1 A.
A moving-source scenario is presented, achieving real-time localization of a dynamically moving source position, as demonstrated in Fig. 1 B.

The main contributions include:

(1) a proposed a fluorescence-integrated whisker fabrication process, enabling optical observation under low illumination;

(2) a monocular vision-based platform that tracks the deformation of five spatially oriented whiskers through image enhancement and segmentation;

(3) a lightweight CNN regression framework for static source localization and further demonstration on real-time position sensing of a moving source.

This paper is organized as follows.
Section II presents the sensing system design and whisker fabrication.
Section III presents the vision-based deformation analysis and learning-based source localization pipeline.
Section IV presents the results of experiments and demonstrates dynamic source localization potential.
A discussion and conclusions are provided in
Sections V and VI .
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Design and Fabrication

## II-A System Overview

As illustrated in Fig. 2 A, the key sensing element is a compliant whisker, featuring a wavy geometry, a longitudinally tapered profile, and an elliptical cross-section, which is bio-inspired by seal whiskers.
This undulating and tapered geometry has been shown to substantially reduce self-excited oscillations as the whisker is dragged through water [ 23 , 13 ] .
The whisker gradually decreases in thickness from the base to the tip.
These features introduce geometric anisotropy along the whisker body and are utilized to transduce flow-induced hydrodynamic loading into observable deformation.

Figure 2 B demonstrates the overall configuration of the proposed fluorescence-enhanced whisker array for underwater source localization.
The sensing system includes a monocular camera, two fixed low-power ultraviolet (UV) light sources, and an array with five whiskers.
The camera captures the flow-induced deformation of the whiskers at a resolution of 1920 × 1080 1920\times 1080 pixels at 60 frames/second.
The UV light sources have a nominal 365 ​ n ​ m 365\,nm excitation and provide a relatively low optical power of approximately 100 ​ m ​ W 100\,mW .
This power is sufficient to produce clearly distinguishable fluorescence from the whiskers for reliable camera-based detection, while limiting illumination and disturbance to the surrounding environment.
Since the illumination area of a single UV light is small, two sources are arranged on opposite sides of the camera, directed toward the whisker array from different lateral directions to obtain a high-quality view.
Excluding the soft protruding whiskers, the sensing platform is compact, with overall dimensions of approximately 150 × 100 × 250 ​ m ​ m 150\times 100\times 250\,mm .

The sensing head contains five whiskers, denoted as # ​ L \#L , # ​ M ​ L \#ML , # ​ M \#M , # ​ M ​ R \#MR , and # ​ R \#R , respectively, which are arranged with different pitch and yaw angles, as shown in the top and side views in Fig. 2 B.
Rather than lying within a common plane, the whiskers span distinct spatial orientations, thereby introducing angular diversity into the array.
As a consequence, individual whiskers interact differently with the incident flow field according to their orientations relative to the local hydrodynamic loading.
Different source positions therefore generate distinct combinations of deformation magnitude and direction across the five whiskers.
Although the monocular camera observes the whisker array from only a single view, and therefore does not directly preserve the complete three-dimensional deformation of each individual whisker, the angular diversity of the whisker array provides complementary deformation information within the image plane.
Specifically, for a given condition, a deformation component that is weakly observable for one whisker may be pronounced for other whiskers with different pitch and yaw orientations.
The array responses therefore reduce the directional ambiguity associated with single-view observation and preserve source-dependent deformation patterns that may not be evident from any individual whisker alone.
This complementary sensing mechanism provides sufficient visual information for subsequent deformation analysis and source localization using a single camera.

## II-B Fabrication

The fabrication process of the fluorescence-enhanced compliant whisker is depicted in Fig. 3 A, which is adapted from the two-stage molding procedures presented in [ 17 ] .
First, a rigid positive mold with designed whisker geometry is 3D-printed and enclosed in a mold box. 20 ​ g 20\,g silicone rubber ( M ​ o ​ l ​ d Mold S ​ t ​ a ​ r T ​ M Star^{TM} 16 16 F ​ A ​ S ​ T FAST ) is prepared, stirred thoroughly for 3 ​ m ​ i ​ n 3\,min and vacuum-degassed, before being poured around the positive mold.
The silicone is then cured at room temperature for 6 6 hours.
After curing, the positive mold is withdrawn to obtain a single-use compliant negative mold.
Subsequently, a superelastic nitinol (NiTi) rod with 0.4 ​ m ​ m 0.4\,mm in diameter is inserted into the mold cavity.
For each whisker, fluorescent pigment is incorporated during the preparation of the urethane overmold.
A total of 5 − 8 ​ g 5-8\,g casting mixture is prepared, mixed by two parts of urethane rubber ( V ​ y ​ t ​ a ​ F ​ l ​ e ​ x T ​ M VytaFlex^{TM} 60 60 ) and green fluorescence ( S ​ i ​ l ​ c Silc P ​ i ​ g T ​ M Pig^{TM} E ​ l ​ e ​ c ​ t ​ r ​ i ​ c Electric ).
The fluorescent pigment constitutes 5 % 5\% by weight of the uncured mixture.
The pigment is first thoroughly dispersed in Part A , then Part B is added.
The mixture is stirred thoroughly for 3 ​ m ​ i ​ n 3\,min and vacuum degassed.
After the mixture is injected into the silicone mold around the nitinol wire and cured at room temperature for 16 16 hours, the silicone mold is peeled apart to release the finished whisker.
The NiTi rod remains within the fluorescent urethane shell to provide the desired elasticity and toughness.

The effect of incorporating fluorescent pigment is illustrated in Fig. 3 B by comparing whiskers with and without fluorescent additives under different illumination conditions.
Without UV excitation, the visual appearance of the fluorescent whisker remains comparable to that of the non-fluorescent counterpart.
However, the whisker containing fluorescent pigment exhibits substantially higher visual contrast under UV illumination, making its contour readily distinguishable from the dark background.
Consequently, a low illumination intensity can be applied to achieve sufficient image contrast for subsequent deformation analysis.
This fluorescence-enhanced contrast enables reliable visual tracking while reducing unnecessary light exposure to the surrounding underwater environment.

2026-10-07.title: Robust Nonprehensile Object Transport with Quadruped Robots
2026-10-07.authors: Ainoor Teimoorzadeh , Riccardo Pretto , Mario Selvaggio , Gokhan Alcan , Sami Haddadin
2026-10-07.abstract:
In this paper, we present a robust nonprehensile object transportation framework for quadruped robots. An uncertainty-aware trajectory optimization method generates object motions with minimal closed-loop sensitivity to uncertain parameters.
The resulting reference trajectory is tracked using a coupled convex model predictive controller that jointly predicts the CoM dynamics of the quadruped and the payload followed by a whole-body QP that enforces ground reaction constraints.
The approach is evaluated through extensive simulations and real-world experiments under variations in the object’s inertial parameters.
Its performance is compared with fixed-orientation and straight-line trajectories as baseline.
The results show that the optimized object motion reduces the sliding by
approximately 50 % \displaystyle 50\% compared with the fixed-orientation baseline and 30 % \displaystyle 30\% compared with the straight-line baseline, while also achieving
lower robot CoM tracking errors.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Manipulation is a core capability that robots need to acquire to become helpful human assistants across various domains [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Nevertheless, most existing manipulation approaches still rely on form- or force-closure [ 4 ] , often requiring sophisticated and fragile grasping operations.
Dynamic nonprehensile manipulation [ 5 ] has broadened the range of robotic manipulation applications by offering advantages such as controlling more degrees of freedom than the manipulator itself possesses [ 6 ] , or widening its workspace through human-like manipulation actions such as tossing and catching [ 7 ] .
Dynamic nonprehensile object transportation, also known as friction-based manipulation or dynamic grasp, keeps a non-grasped object in contact with a tray-like end-effector throughout the robot motion [ 8 ] .
Some existing approaches, which realize this manipulation primitive by enforcing non-sliding conditions, include shared control with haptic feedback [ 9 ] , Quadratic Programming (QP) based trajectory optimization methods [ 10 ] , and Model Predictive Control (MPC) frameworks [ 11 , 12 ] .

However, most of the existing approaches are designed for dexterous robotic arms, which are well-established platforms for such tasks [ 13 ] .
Although robotic arms can execute fast and precise motions while keeping the object in nonsliding conditions [ 14 , 15 ] , their workspace is limited by their reach.
Mobile manipulators overcome this limitation by combining the extended workspace of a mobile base with the manipulation capabilities of an arm [ 11 , 16 ] .
Legged robots further extend this mobility to complex environments, such as stairs and uneven terrain, that may be inaccessible to wheeled platforms.
Yet, keeping non-grasped objects fixed to an actuated legged platform comes with additional challenges: dynamic phenomena, such as high-frequency chassis vibrations, intermittent impacts from the trotting gait, cause unpredictable friction variations at the object’s interface.
Moreover, the presence of an object alters the robotic system’s center of mass and causes unexpected inertial shifts, making precise trajectory tracking a major control challenge motivating the adoption of robust control techniques [ 17 ] .

In contrast to the well-established robust control methods, such as adaptive control [ 18 ] , passivity based control [ 19 ] , H ∞ \displaystyle H_{\infty} or μ \displaystyle\mu -synthesis [ 20 ] ,
closed-loop sensitivity approach allows a dynamical system to fulfill the control objective by designing control-aware trajectories whose execution is minimally sensitive to physical parameter uncertainties [ 21 ] .
Despite its promising results in domains such as aerial manipulation [ 22 , 23 ] , the approach remains largely unexplored in nonprehensile manipulation settings, with only limited work reported to date [ 24 ] .

To address this gap, we present an integrated planning and control
framework for robust nonprehensile object transportation using a
quadrupedal robot.
We consider a cylindrical object which is transported on a back-mounted plate of a quadruped robot.
The object is constrained only by friction on one of its circular faces, making it free to slide relative to the support surface.
While this configuration bypasses the mechanical and control complexities of integrating a dedicated robotic arm [ 25 ] , it introduces significant transport challenges, as the sliding object can only be indirectly prevented through the regulation of the robot motion itself.

The proposed framework, therefore employs closed-loop sensitivity-based trajectory optimization to generate object-centric
motions which are tracked using a coupled robot-object MPC and a whole-body controller.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are:

Formulation of a closed-loop sensitivity optimization to generate object-centric motions for an unsecured payload carried directly on a quadruped.

A tailored coupled quadruped-object convex MPC
with whole-body control for nonprehensile transportation on a back-mounted platform, extending previous arm-based quadruped approaches.

Validation of the proposed approach through simulation in MuJoCo environment and hardware experiments, showing reduced object sliding compared with baseline trajectories.

Nonprehensile object transportation has been extensively studied for fixed-base and mobile manipulators. Early approaches formulate the waiter’s problem as a trajectory-planning problem and generate motions that satisfy contact-stability constraints or optimize execution time [ 8 , 26 , 14 , 27 , 15 ] .
These methods, however, generally assume accurate knowledge of the object and contact properties and evaluate feasibility using nominal models.
Consequently, trajectories that are feasible for the assumed parameters may become fragile when the actual mass distribution, inertia, or friction differs from its nominal value.
Feedback-based methods partially alleviate this limitation by adapting the robot motion during execution.
The MPC formulation in [ 12 ] explicitly accounts for object dynamics, frictional contact, and robot constraints, but relies on a known object model.

In [ 28 ] , MPC is augmented with value functions learned from demonstrations, enabling empirical generalization to previously unseen objects, learning robustness from data.
More recently, the work in [ 16 ] introduced robust sticking constraints for uncertain CoM and inertial parameters. That approach plans motions that remain feasible
over a prescribed uncertainty primarily addressing robustness at the planning level.

Sensitivity-aware planning and control constitutes an alternative approach. Minimum-sensitivity trajectory generation was introduced in [ 21 ] and experimentally validated on aerial robots in [ 22 ] , while [ 23 ] incorporated state sensitivity into MPC for robotic systems with parametric uncertainty. These works demonstrate that nominal performance alone is insufficient to characterize robustness: trajectories with comparable nominal behavior can produce substantially different deviations under parameter errors. The closed-loop sensitivity framework was applied to nonprehensile manipulation in [ 24 ] to reduce the effect of inertial-parameter errors on the object motion. However, its validation is likewise limited to manipulation platforms whose supporting surface can be commanded independently of locomotion. Nevertheless, the use of this principle to jointly plan and control the motion of an unsecured payload carried by a legged robot remains largely unexplored.

To transport an object using a quadruped robot, the work in [ 25 ] equipped it with an arm and combined a momentum-based observer with a QP-based whole-body controller to compensate for external disturbances.
Although this architecture compensates for external disturbances, it requires an additional manipulator, increasing the system’s mass, mechanical complexity, and energy consumption.
LocoTouch [ 29 ] , instead, uses the robot’s back directly as a carrying surface and employs distributed tactile sensing and a learned locomotion policy to transport unsecured cylindrical objects. Its focus is on tactile-reactive locomotion—particularly for cylinders whose rolling dynamics can be directly detected through the back-mounted sensor—rather than model-based robustness to uncertain object and contact parameters.

Using the quadruped’s dorsum as a carrying surface introduces a coupling that is absent from conventional waiter-type manipulation. The platform motion is not generated by a rigidly controlled manipulator alone but results from the interaction between locomotion, intermittent ground contacts, body stabilization, and payload dynamics [ 25 ] . Gait-induced body oscillations and foot-impact disturbances can excite sliding or tipping of the unsecured object, while errors in its mass distribution, inertia, or contact properties alter both the predicted payload motion and its interaction with the robot. Thus, robustness cannot be obtained solely by enforcing nominal contact constraints or by rejecting disturbances at the whole-body-control level [ 16 ] .

In contrast to the existing literature, this work combines sensitivity-aware trajectory planning with MPC-based execution for an unsecured object placed directly on a quadruped’s dorsal carrying surface. The planned motion is selected not only for nominal task feasibility but also to reduce the propagation of object-parameter uncertainty into the closed-loop state. The MPC subsequently tracks this sensitivity-aware reference while accounting online for payload dynamics and contact constraints. This combination addresses a previously unexplored problem: exploiting the quadruped body as a lightweight, manipulator-free carrying platform while explicitly shaping the robustness of nonprehensile transport against parametric uncertainty and gait-induced disturbances.

We consider the case of a cylindrical object resting with its circular base in contact with flat surface rigidly mounted on the back of a quadruped robot.
Our aim is to compute rest-to-rest trajectories that, when executed via closed-loop control, transport the object between two prescribed points (as shown in Fig. 1 ) and exhibit minimal sensitivity to variations in the object’s dynamic parameters, including friction with the robot surface.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows.
Preliminaries and system modeling are explained in Sec. II in a nutshell.
Robust trajectory optimization and controller are presented in Sec. III .
Finally, the simulation results of the closed-loop manipulation task and preliminary experimental results are shown in Sec. IV Conclusions are presented in V .
