2026-10-07.title: Monocular Navigation Relative to Unknown Spacecraft Using a Transformer-Aided Kalman Filter
2026-10-07.authors: Pol Francesch Huc , Simone D'Amico
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-07.abstract:
As space becomes increasingly congested and contested, robust autonomous navigation is essential for servicing, debris removal, and situational awareness with respect to unknown resident space objects.
This work presents a novel learning-based pipeline for pose estimation of uncooperative and unknown spacecraft using only monocular images from a single servicer.
The approach combines a transformer-based neural network with a Multi-State Constraint Kalman Filter (MSCKF) to estimate the pose (i.e., position and orientation of the target spacecraft relative to the camera) throughout rendezvous and proximity operations.
Unlike existing vision-based methods that require prior knowledge of the target shape or inertia properties, rely on additional sensing modalities such as depth, lidar, or stereo, or only recover translation up to scale, the proposed pipeline generalizes to previously unseen spacecraft using a single monocular camera.
The transformer network estimates the odometry, the change in pose between images up to scale, from SuperPoint features matched by LightGlue.
These odometry estimates serve as MSCKF pseudo-measurements.
2026-10-07.introduction:
The space industry is experiencing a resurgence in interest, especially in the realm of autonomous rendezvous, proximity operations, and docking (RPOD).
These missions generally require satellites, denoted as servicers, to be close to their target with separations on the order of meters to contact.
However, the target may not always be cooperative (because it is defunct, not designed for RPOD, or adversarial) and so the satellite is required to independently perform pose estimation of the target to successfully complete its mission.
Unknown or damaged targets may also require autonomous shape reconstruction.
Cameras are an attractive choice for this kind of mission since they are generally cheap, lightweight, power-efficient, and already ubiquitous on satellites as they are used in attitude estimation.

The approach taken in this work is to first estimate the pose of the target with respect to the servicer, without having access to the 3D model.
Pose estimates support safe operation during image collection and provide inputs for concurrent shape estimation.
The pose of the target is estimated from an incoming stream of images taken by the servicer during close range operations after being initialized by an earlier phase of the mission such as an approach using Angles-Only Navigation (AON) [ 1 ] .

Although pose estimation of known targets through monocular images is a mature technology [ 2 ] , the same cannot be said of unknown targets.
This work combines a novel odometry network with a Multi-State Constraint Kalman Filter (MSCKF) [ 3 ] for monocular pose estimation of unknown targets.
A notional pipeline is shown in Figure 1 .

Because monocular measurements are scale-free, the range must be made observable when no prior on the target’s size or range is available.
To achieve this, the filter requires a known metric displacement of the camera center, in the direction transverse to the line of sight.
Several options from the AON literature exist which can supply this displacement, and the particular choice and derivation are provided in Section V .
As images are collected they are immediately added to the sliding window 𝒲 t \mathcal{W}^{t} which stores the most recent images in a cache.
Images which provide large pose diversity are stored in a cache of selected keyframes 𝒦 t \mathcal{K}^{t} , and are replaced only by images that increase that diversity.

From these images, features are extracted by SuperPoint [ 4 ] .
Since the target 3D model is unknown, regressing the pose of the target from a single set of features or image is difficult, as is seen by the poor pose estimates in the work by Park et al. [ 5 ] .
Instead, this work estimates features in sets of images, and uses the state-of-the-art feature matcher LightGlue [ 6 ] to match the features between the images.
LightGlue is fine-tuned on the novel dataset SPE3R+ to adapt it to spacecraft imagery.

SPE3R+ builds upon the original SPE3R [ 5 ] dataset, which included 1,000 images and masks per model for 64 satellite models, with 7 of those models reserved for a test set (so they were never seen during training).
SPE3R+ includes these 64 original models, but adds 39 new models (103 total, 11 in test set) with 5,000 higher resolution images per model, masks, and metric depth.

These feature matches on their own are not sufficient to estimate the pose, and typical computer vision pipelines will use the 8-point algorithm along with RANdom SAmple Consensus (RANSAC), or similar, to estimate the fundamental matrix and the odometry between pairs of images [ 7 ] .
As will be shown, the estimation accuracy from this method is poor, and so the Spacecraft Odometry Network (SON) is introduced to estimate the odometry from noisy feature matches.

Because SON only provides an odometry measurement, subsequent filters are prone to divergence since this is a form of dead reckoning.
Two additional measurements are used to prevent this divergence: feature tracks and loop closure.
Feature tracks are features observed across multiple images in the sliding window and provide multi-frame relative constraints that limit local drift.
Loop closure provides a longer-baseline relative attitude constraint between the current image and a retained keyframe.

An MSCKF is then introduced to estimate the pose of the target over a trajectory.
The MSCKF is used to leverage the feature tracks directly, as these provide the geometric constraint needed for this kind of filter without needing to incorporate the feature locations on the target in the filter state.
Outlier rejection and covariance inflation are also leveraged to remove potentially noisy feature track and loop closure measurements as well as reduce the overconfidence in the relative orbit estimate.

This work contributes:

An expanded and re-rendered dataset of 103 satellite models with grayscale images, masks, and depths, SPE3R+ 1 1 1 Dataset to be released before conference start.

A fine-tuning strategy for LightGlue which improves performance on spacecraft imagery by raising the RANSAC pose AUC@ 20 ∘ 20^{\circ} on test spacecraft from 4.0 4.0 to 17.0 17.0 and match recall from 15.7 % 15.7\% to 49.1 % 49.1\%

A novel network for odometry estimation from noisy feature matches, SON, providing median rotation errors of 2.6 ∘ 2.6^{\circ} and translation direction errors of 4.4 ∘ 4.4^{\circ} on previously unseen spacecraft under large illumination changes, compared with 9.9 ∘ 9.9^{\circ} and 45.2 ∘ 45.2^{\circ} for the classical baseline

An evaluation of the front-end on synthetic and hardware-in-the-loop images from the SHIRT dataset [ 8 ] , where SON maintains a 4 4 – 6 6 times lower median translation unit direction error than the baseline

A novel implementation of the MSCKF for pose estimation of targets in space with ROE and attitude state tracking, learned odometry pseudo-measurements, and keyframe loop closure. The MSCKF achieves median ROE error of 2.2 % 2.2\% of the range and attitude error of 3.7 ∘ 3.7^{\circ}

A Monte Carlo evaluation on 11 unseen spacecraft (550 trials) with ablations quantifying the value-added of each component of the pipeline

This paper begins by discussing the state of the art in this field in Section II .
Next, the proposed architecture is discussed in Sections III – VI .
The implementation details are discussed in Section VII covering key assumptions, datasets used, and hyperparameter selection. Section VIII evaluates the components individually where possible, and the complete pipeline.

# II State of the art

The state of the art in monocular pose estimation begins with known targets.
DARPA’s Orbital Express demonstrated cooperative vision-based rendezvous in 2007 using a camera and target-mounted retro-reflectors [ 9 ] .
D’Amico et al. [ 2 ] instead used classical computer vision techniques to detect edge features on the target and then use the known 3D model to regress the 6D pose, demonstrating uncooperative pose estimation.
Improvements on the pose estimate have been made through the use of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) [ 10 ] , which have more recently been traded for Vision Transformers (ViT) [ 11 ] for reduced computational cost and increased robustness to the domain gap.
The process has been shown to be robust to out of distribution images through the implementation of an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) [ 8 ] and by refining the network on the target domain [ 12 ] .
Recent surveys [ 13 , 14 ] identify deployability on space-grade hardware, further closing of the domain gap, and reliable uncertainty under domain shift as the open problems in this line of work, all of which still assume a known target.

These methods, and others, are trained on a large amount of images and their popularity has led to the release of image datasets of different satellites.
The dataset by Dung et al. [ 15 ] compiles real spacecraft imagery with bounding-box, segmentation, and component level annotations, but does not provide metric poses.
URSO [ 16 ] in contrast uses photorealistic rendering to generate synthetic spacecraft images with pose labels for known target geometries.
SPEED+ [ 17 ] , SHIRT [ 8 ] , and MAN-DATA [ 18 ] include synthetic and real images in a space-surrogate environment and provide reference truth poses, but only of one target each.
Finally SPE3R [ 5 ] is a dataset of synthetic images only, but it includes 64 real satellites in its dataset along with the pose labels.
Due to the number of targets and the availability of poses SPE3R is most useful for this work, however the images are provided at a very low resolution and so it is improved here.

Literature on unknown target pose estimation in space is much more limited.
Park et al. [ 5 ] introduce a CNN to estimate the pose and shape from a single image, however the pose estimates have errors in the tens of degrees for the test set, and the network does not estimate the scale.
Bates et al. [ 19 ] improve pose estimation by addressing canonical pose ambiguities, but still do not recover the metric scale.
DreamSat [ 20 ] and DreamSat-Pose [ 21 ] predict shape and, in the latter case, pose, but still do not estimate the scale and provide similar errors as Park et al. [ 5 ] .
CRISP [ 22 ] has better pose estimates than Park et al. [ 5 ] , but requires RGB-D images.
Barad et al. [ 23 ] also simultaneously estimate the shape and pose, but they do so using a sequence of RGB-D images which provides the scale, and tracking tends to drift over long duration trajectories.
Dor et al. [ 24 ] apply Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM) using ORB-SLAM [ 25 ] to space-like imagery, but validation is limited to 3-DOF motion and tracking is inconsistent.
Augenstein [ 26 ] implements a landmark-based SLAM using monocular images only, and recovers both the pose and shape but again does not estimate the scale.
Capuano et al. [ 27 ] and Tweddle et al. [ 28 ] both estimate the pose of unknown targets, but they are aided by a laser range finder and stereovision, respectively.

Two works do provide monocular vision-based pose estimation, but they also include significant drawbacks.
Ticozzi et al. [ 29 ] implement a factor-graph based active SLAM method which generates an attitude guidance strategy to minimize the target shape model uncertainty.
Their strategy relies on perfect initialization (the first two poses are assumed to be known) and feature matching is assumed to be perfect as well.
The method is only validated over a short horizon, at most 23 poses.
Legrand et al. [ 30 ] follow a two-stage approach, where a NeRF model [ 31 ] is used to generate imagery for training a conventional known target pose estimation network [ 12 ] .
However, the first stage requires pose estimates which limits the online applicability.

Terrestrial vision-based pose estimation on the other hand is a much larger field. Algorithms like COLMAP [ 32 , 33 ] estimate the pose and structure from a set of images, but are typically run offline.
These have been recently complemented by learning-based reconstruction from image pairs, such as DUSt3R [ 34 ] and MASt3R [ 35 ] , which regress dense pointmaps with large transformers on terrestrial scenes.
Feature-based methods use feature matches between two images in order to estimate the odometry between the images, mostly by estimating the fundamental matrix [ 7 ] .
Early feature detectors and matchers include SIFT [ 36 ] , SURF [ 37 ] , and ORB [ 38 ] , but they are increasingly being replaced by learning based methods in current literature.
SuperPoint [ 4 ] supplies learned features for attention-based matchers SuperGlue [ 39 ] and LightGlue [ 6 ] , with the latter reducing inference time through early stopping.
Other learned approaches include DISK [ 40 ] , dense matchers such as RoMa [ 41 ] , and simultaneous extraction and matching methods such as
LoFTR [ 42 ] .

Some terrestrial methods focus then on improving the odometry estimation (sometimes with scale) that must occur from these feature matches.
Rockwell et al. [ 43 ] introduce a transformer which regresses the odometry directly from an image pair, and FAR [ 44 ] extends this by combining such a learned prediction with a match-based solver.
Although FAR supports multiple feature and correspondence front ends, its learned metric-scale prior is trained on terrestrial scenes and does not directly address unknown spacecraft with arbitrary physical scale.
Arnold et al. [ 45 ] introduce map-free visual relocalization where odometry estimation is done directly from images, but this requires a large training dataset not available for space applications.

Existing work does not yet resolve the problem of accurate monocular pose estimation of unknown targets.
Solutions which target space-like imagery generally make simplifying assumptions, such as the availability of additional sensors, or do not estimate the range to the target.
Terrestrial methods on the other hand are not purpose built for space-like imagery, and so do not function out of the box with the same performance as they do on the domain they are designed for.
This work seeks to resolve this by leveraging some terrestrial state-of-the-art methods and adapting them to the space problem, along with a novel learning-based solution to odometry estimation.

2026-10-07.title: RoboCap: A New Platform for Egocentric Robot Learning
2026-10-07.authors: Grounded Superintelligence , BitRobot
2026-10-07.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)
2026-10-07.abstract: Despite its promise for scaling robot learning, egocentric manipulation data is still scarce today. Collection at scale requires vertically integrating ergonomic hardware with centimeter-precise 3D algorithms, at a precision that has not been publicly demonstrated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboCap, a 250 g six-camera dual-IMU hat designed for in-the-wild egocentric data capture, and the Grounded API, a suite of device-agnostic 3D algorithms tuned for RoboCap. In this report, we demonstrate how hardware, calibration, and 3D algorithms interact to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the public benchmarks: our SLAM across diverse settings and rigs, our depth estimation on egocentric settings, and our hand tracking when adapted to third-party devices.
2026-10-07.introduction:
In the history of large-scale end-to-end robot learning, the field has witnessed the emergence of several data classes, each with known tradeoffs. Simulation scales with compute, but demands human engineering effort that grows with the diversity it aims to produce. Teleoperation captures the exact states and actions a robot requires at inference, at the cost of unnatural and unscalable demonstration through cumbersome robot hardware. UMI deploys only the end-effector for better scalability, but does not scale beyond low-DoF manipulators and requires retargeting. Egocentric data maximizes scalability by equipping humans with an unintrusive headworn device, but recovers states and actions only by estimation and also requires retargeting.

The quality of egocentric data is bounded by the accuracy of its 3D labels, namely the human hand and head poses. Retargeting maps an estimated human pose onto a robot embodiment [ 34 , 27 , 43 , 25 ] , so estimation error enters the policy’s training distribution directly as label noise: egocentric capture is a metrology problem before it is a video collection problem, and a large-scale 3D computer vision problem in practice. Centimeter-level accuracy must hold under occlusion, motion blur, varied lighting, and operator diversity, on footage collected outside any lab. The field has not converged on a device the way it has on teleoperation and UMI rigs, and the reason is that the two halves of the problem (form factor and 3D algorithms) have never been available together. Meta’s Project Aria glasses [ 15 ] are the best form factor candidate, but are gated by application programs, hardware costs, and offline APIs that are difficult to scale. Mixed-reality headsets are heavy, socially intrusive, and expose only opaque on-device tracking whose error characteristics cannot be inspected or improved offline. A team that wants to collect its own egocentric data at the precision policy learning requires cannot currently assemble the stack to do so.

We argue that the estimation problem in egocentric data is an artifact of hardware that was never designed for it. Because consumer smart glasses and mixed-reality headsets optimize for display, audio, and human-facing UX, their sensing suites are byproducts. When the device is instead designed backward from the requirements of the 3D estimation stack–stereo baselines, FoV overlap, hardware-synchronization, global-shutter sensors–the gap between estimated and measured state collapses to a level sufficient for policy learning. As we explain in Section 4 , RoboCap’s layout is what makes this concrete. Two calibrated stereo pairs supply metric scale that monocular systems can only infer, while wide-angle lateral coverage keeps the hands in frustum through natural motion and keeps the trajectory solver constrained during close-range manipulation.

We also design our 3D algorithms to be device-agnostic. The same binaries run on handheld fisheye rigs, aerial stereo platforms, consumer VR headsets, and research glasses whose divergent cameras share almost no field of view, with no per-dataset tuning. This is not incidental to the argument above but rather evidence for it: portability establishes that our results reflect general 3D estimation rather than models overfit to a single device. Our SLAM, for instance, borrows from both monocular-inertial and stereo-inertial designs, which let it fuse whatever cues a rig provides–six cameras with two calibrated baselines on RoboCap, or two divergent cameras with no stereo overlap on Aria–into a single estimation pipeline.

Our contributions are twofold:

RoboCap, a purpose-built 250 g six-camera dual-IMU egocentric capture device whose sensing suite is designed minimally and sufficiently for metric 3D estimation, available for purchase.

Grounded API, which serves SLAM, depth estimation, and hand tracking algorithms that achieve state-of-the-art accuracy across diverse visual settings and hardware rigs.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related work

## 2.1 Egocentric wearables

Egocentric capture hardware spans repurposed consumer devices to purpose-built research platforms. Early large-scale egocentric datasets were collected with head-mounted action cameras [ 11 , 20 ] , which provide only monocular RGB with rolling shutter and no inertial or calibration guarantees, precluding metric 3D annotation. Mixed-reality headsets such as Apple’s Vision Pro and Meta’s Quest 3 offer richer sensing and supply head and hand pose estimation [ 25 , 3 ] , but these devices are heavy, socially intrusive, and expose their sensing only through on-device tracking APIs.

The closest platform in spirit to ours is Meta’s Project Aria [ 15 ] : lightweight research glasses with calibrated RGB, monochrome SLAM cameras, and IMUs, that have powered a family of egocentric datasets [ 36 , 37 , 39 , 3 ] . Aria validates the thesis that calibrated multi-camera visual-inertial wearables enable high-quality 3D annotation, and prior works in robotics have demonstrated its use in learning robot manipulation policies from human data [ 34 , 27 ] . Aria remains, however, a general-purpose research device rather than a scalable manipulation capture platform: its cameras are laid out for scene understanding rather than for the near field, and its complexity has kept it relatively inaccessible for robot learning at scale.

There is also a lineage of research prototypes aimed at estimating human poses. For example, [ 44 , 59 , 1 ] propose head- or cap-mounted downward-facing fisheye rigs, but for target body pose rather than manipulation. More recent works combine mocap gloves with an egocentric device to estimate hand pose, but are too clunky and brittle to occlusions [ 53 , 50 ] . These prototypes introduce intrusive hardware in an attempt to measure hand pose accurately, but thereby sacrifice the naturalness and scalability. Inevitably, a single egocentric device must natively compute accurate hand poses directly from vision in order to maximize the scalability of egocentric data capture.

## 2.2 3D estimation

Multi-sensor rigs are typically calibrated offline by continuous-time batch optimization over a fiducial target [ 16 ] , jointly recovering intrinsics, camera–IMU extrinsics, and time offsets. Factory calibration degrades in the field through mechanical and thermal stress, motivating online self-calibration from natural correspondences during operation [ 12 , 35 ] . As we demonstrate in Section 4.1 , this drift becomes important when needing to achieve sub-centimeter 3D estimation errors.

Classical sparse visual-inertial systems establish the standard factor-graph formulation fusing feature reprojection with IMU preintegration [ 7 , 42 , 31 , 52 , 48 , 19 ] , with global consistency recovered through appearance-based place recognition [ 17 ] and pose-graph optimization [ 21 ] . GPU-accelerated implementations extend this to multi-camera rigs at real-time rates [ 28 ] . A learned line trades classical sparse optimization for dense correspondence and feed-forward geometry [ 51 , 38 , 54 ] , while rendering-based backends push offline reconstruction quality at significant compute cost [ 69 , 8 ] .

These systems are evaluated on a small set of standard benchmarks with external ground truth, spanning aerial stereo-inertial, handheld fisheye, multi-sensor rigs [ 6 , 49 , 18 ] , and most recently consumer VR headsets [ 14 ] , the closest existing benchmark to the egocentric regime. Egocentric head motion is a distinctly adversarial setting for all of them: rapid rotation, close-range parallax, dynamic scene content from the wearer’s own hands, and irregular motion during initialization. This motivates both our multi-camera wide-FoV configuration and our offline post-processing of the estimated trajectory.

Deep stereo matching progressed from cost-volume CNNs to iterative recurrent refinement [ 9 , 33 , 32 , 58 , 55 ] , but these models require per-domain fine-tuning and degrade sharply out of distribution. A more recent class trains on large-scale high-fidelity synthetic corpora, bootstrapping monocular foundation priors to achieve strong zero-shot generalization for the first time [ 56 , 57 ] . Monocular metric alternatives [ 4 , 65 , 5 , 62 , 63 ] remove the calibrated-baseline requirement, but their metric scale is inferred from learned priors rather than measured from geometry, which is exactly the failure mode our hardware exists to eliminate.

Parametric hand recovery is dominated by the MANO model [ 46 ] . Monocular mesh recovery has scaled steadily from early regression and real-time keypoint systems [ 47 , 67 ] to transformer-based reconstructors trained at scale [ 40 , 41 ] . Critically, all monocular methods regress pose under a weak-perspective camera, which infers shape and depth from apparent hand size against a learned prior. Not only are monocular outputs metrically ambiguous, they are also not consistent enough across views for accurate triangulation, which inevitably must be learned with neural network design [ 61 , 26 ] . World-space extensions recover trajectories from moving egocentric video, but are still susceptible to scale ambiguity as well as SLAM inaccuracies [ 68 , 66 ] .

Multi-view systems resolve the metric ambiguity of monocular prediction, but at the cost of added hardware dependency. Production-grade egocentric trackers fuse several head-mounted fisheye views into a single metric prediction [ 23 , 24 ] , and the multi-view egocentric benchmarks built on their data [ 3 , 45 ] evaluate this setting directly. These systems derive their training labels from motion-capture installations or closed on-device trackers, so annotation cost scales with instrumentation rather than with compute. Furthermore, motion capture confines collection to instrumented spaces, which recent work [ 45 ] addresses by building a large exoskeleton cage. Yet the difficulty of hand tracking is in-the-wild, where metric accuracy must persist through occlusion, motion blur, and operator diversity. Our method solves this by enforcing geometric consistency from monocular priors, allowing us to generate a large corpus of in-the-wild pre-training data without any motion capture. Section 4.4 evaluates models trained on this corpus against baselines trained on motion-capture-derived data [ 24 , 3 , 45 ] .

2026-10-07.title: AIM: Adaptive Interaction Modeling Networks for Real-to-Sim Soft-Body Simulation
2026-10-07.authors: Tiancheng Yang , Dingshuo Chen , Tianle Chen , Zhaocheng Liu , Qiang Liu
2026-10-07.abstract: Deformable-object manipulation is essential for robotic tasks such as folding laundry and handling food, where robots must control shape changes as well as object motion. Predictive soft-body simulation supports these tasks by anticipating deformation under external interactions. However, spatial neighborhoods can misrepresent deformation dependencies, introducing local errors that accumulate over successive predictions. Models fitted to individual scenes must also accommodate changes in object geometry and manipulation conditions. In this work, we propose AIM , an Adaptive Interaction Modeling framework that treats real-to-sim soft-body simulation as a local-global interaction modeling problem. AIM uses motion history and geometry to adapt particle relations over current spatial neighbors and retained connections, while geometry-conditioned global communication coordinates object-wide responses. A unified kinematic control-point interface represents different manipulation configurations, and multi-step autoregressive supervision trains the model on its own predicted trajectories. Experiments on PhysTwin and PGND demonstrate improved motion accuracy and visual fidelity, with a 20.0% reduction in future-prediction tracking error relative to PhysTwin and a 22.8% reduction in mean long-horizon particle error across six object categories relative to PGND. The framework further supports transfer across actions, object instances, and scenes, including zero-shot transfer from robot interactions to human manipulation without target-domain dynamics fitting.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Everyday tasks such as folding laundry, preparing food, and assisting with dressing require robots to control how objects deform under contact, making deformable-object manipulation an important capability for embodied intelligence ( Sanchez et al., 2018 ; Lin et al., 2021 ) . Unlike rigid-object manipulation, these tasks involve spatially distributed responses to local actions. Predictive soft-body simulation enables robots to anticipate these responses and evaluate manipulation strategies before physical execution ( Lin et al., 2022 ; Lin et al., 2021 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) . While visual reconstruction captures observed deformation in increasing detail ( Pumarola et al., 2021 ; Park et al., 2021 ; Luiten et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) , simulation must predict its evolution under external interactions. Particle- and mesh-based simulators provide a relational foundation through graph message passing ( Battaglia et al., 2016 ; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020 ; Pfaff et al., 2020 ) , and recent methods such as PhysTwin, PGND, and SoMA connect dynamics modeling with real observations and manipulation settings ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . Despite this progress, predicting object deformation remains challenging over long rollouts and under new interaction conditions, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .

Local deformation depends on structural coupling that spatial proximity alone cannot describe: folding brings structurally distant regions together, while stretching separates regions whose responses remain coupled ( Lin et al., 2022 ) . Misrepresenting these dependencies or their effects across the object introduces local motion errors ( Fortunato et al., 2022 ) , which can accumulate into long-horizon drift as autoregressive simulation repeatedly advances from its own predictions ( Um et al., 2020 ) . Addressing these modeling and prediction errors within a single scene is only part of the challenge, as practical manipulation also requires the simulator to generalize across objects and interactions. Changes in object geometry and manipulator contacts alter how actions induce deformation, challenging the generalization of learned interaction patterns beyond the training setting ( Zhang et al., 2024a ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . Generalization therefore involves both accommodating the new configuration and preserving deformation accuracy throughout the resulting rollout.

In this work, we propose AIM , an A daptive I nteraction M odeling framework for real-to-sim soft-body simulation. AIM combines history-conditioned adaptive particle relations with geometry-conditioned global context to model local deformation and coordinate object-wide responses. A unified kinematic control-point interface represents external interactions without action-category or manipulator-specific labels. The framework is trained through multi-step autoregressive prediction to learn dynamics from recursively generated states.

We evaluate AIM on PhysTwin and PGND through resimulation, future prediction, and cross-condition transfer. Our method improves geometric and visual accuracy, reducing mean long-horizon MDE by 22.8% relative to PGND across six object categories and future-prediction tracking error by 20.0% relative to PhysTwin. We further demonstrate generalization across objects, actions, and scenes, including zero-shot transfer from robot interactions to human manipulation.

The main contributions of this work are three-fold:

❶ We formulate real-to-sim soft-body simulation as an adaptive local-global interaction modeling problem, emphasizing how deformation-dependent particle relations and shared object-level context jointly support coherent dynamics under changing manipulation conditions.

❷ We introduce AIM , a particle-based framework that combines history-conditioned adaptive relations with geometry-conditioned global communication to coordinate local and object-wide responses under a unified kinematic control interface.

❸ Experiments on PhysTwin and PGND demonstrate improved geometric and visual accuracy, with a 22.8% reduction in mean long-horizon MDE over PGND across six object categories and a 20.0% reduction in future-prediction tracking error over PhysTwin, alongside transfer across objects, actions, and manipulation domains.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Real-to-Sim Deformable Dynamics. Recent real-to-sim methods connect visual observations with interactive simulation. PhysGaussian, Spring-Gaus, and PhysTwin couple visual representations with explicit physical models ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Zhong et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) . Alternatively, GS-Dynamics, PGND, and SoMA learn action-conditioned state transitions from observed interactions ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . These approaches differ in their physical representations and transfer assumptions, ranging from new interactions with an identified object to unseen object instances. Our work follows the learned-dynamics direction, studying how interaction representations support both within-domain prediction and transfer across objects and manipulation conditions.

Graph-Based Interaction Modeling. Interaction Networks, GNS, and MeshGraphNets model physical evolution through local relational computations ( Battaglia et al., 2016 ; Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020 ; Pfaff et al., 2020 ) . Latent relation inference ( Kipf et al., 2018 ; Graber and Schwing, 2020 ) and multiscale propagation ( Fortunato et al., 2022 ; Grigorev et al., 2023 ) address complementary questions of which elements should communicate and how information travels across an object. Building on the node–edge–global formulation ( Battaglia et al., 2018 ) , our framework couples history-conditioned relation learning with shared object context and geometry-conditioned particle updates. Appendix A discusses the broader physical, structural, and temporal modeling literature.

2026-10-07.title: TeleHairing: A Teleoperation Baseline for Robotic Haircutting
2026-10-07.authors: Zhendai Huang , Aleksi Vilkki , Jianan Huang , Bolin Liao , Chunbo Luo , Leopoldo Angrisani , Shuai Li
2026-10-07.abstract: Robotic haircutting requires controlled tool motion near the head while simultaneously accounting for communication, visual feedback, tool actuation, and interruption handling. Existing studies still lack an operator-in-the-loop reference for analyzing these coupled behaviors before human trials or stronger autonomy. This paper presents TeleHairing, a closed-loop teleoperation architecture for mannequin-based robotic haircutting evaluation under local, relay, and remote deployment conditions. Logged timing shows that the main remote latency increase occurs before the robot-side control endpoint: overall timing reached 190.5 ms in remote mode, while robot-side command queue, control processing, and control-to-robot timing remained similar across modes. Trajectory analysis shows that the larger remote command-following error was dominated by the terminal withdrawal segment rather than accumulated uniformly over the path; excluding this segment reduced remote root-mean-square error (RMSE) from 45.1 mm to 9.6 mm. Detection-loss trials further show that rebase events resumed motion without a large target jump under the tested condition. These results clarify how deployment, execution, and interruption affect the robotic haircutting teleoperation loop, providing a quantitative reference for future autonomy, safety, and user-facing studies.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Haircutting is a personal-care task that requires close physical interaction and skilled manual control. It also requires continuous adaptation to an individual’s head shape, hair condition, and styling intent. Interest in alternatives to conventional in-person haircutting has increased when access to human barbers is limited, such as during the COVID-19 pandemic and in assistive personal-care settings [ 1 ] . Related robotic studies on head-proximate grooming, including combing and compliant hair manipulation, suggest that near-head hair interaction is feasible. They also show that the task remains contact-rich, comfort-sensitive, and operationally constrained [ 2 , 3 ] . Robotic haircutting is distinct from generic manipulation because tool motion must be coordinated near the head while hair geometry, visual occlusion, tool actuation, and user-comfort constraints remain part of the operating context. These observations motivate robotic investigation of haircutting.

At the same time, autonomous robotic haircutting remains a challenging and not yet well-defined problem. The robot must move cutting tools near sensitive regions while maintaining continuous spatial control under limited safety margins [ 4 ] . The task is also affected by variation in head geometry, hair density, hair texture, hair length, and user preference [ 5 ] . Recent reviews identify real-time decision-making, hair variability, user customization, safety assurance, and precision path-planning as persistent challenges in robotic haircutting [ 6 ] . In practice, the problem is difficult not only because of motion accuracy, but also because tool use, constrained visual feedback, communication delay, and fault handling all become part of the control loop. Before autonomous haircutting can be evaluated responsibly, teleoperation studies are needed to characterize how sensing, communication, execution, tool actuation, and interruption handling interact during robotic haircutting.

For this reason, teleoperation provides a practical starting point for robotic haircutting research. It keeps the human operator in the loop and exposes system behavior for quantitative analysis. It also allows communication, execution, and operational safeguard behavior to be studied under controlled conditions before stronger autonomy is considered. Prior work provides useful pieces of this problem, but not yet the full system picture considered here. Related teleoperation studies have already shown the importance of communication-aware system behavior under deployed conditions [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Related robotic studies near the head have focused more on grooming, hair interaction, perception, and task-level constraints than on dedicated haircutting systems. Recent work has also begun to frame haircutting robots from a mobile-robotics and deployment perspective [ 10 ] , but accessible teleoperation studies have tended to emphasize navigation or general manipulation rather than near-head tool use. As a result, deployable teleoperation systems for robotic haircutting remain rarely reported, especially those combining monocular input, clipper actuation, remote deployment, and system-level analysis.

This paper presents TeleHairing, a prototype teleoperation system for robotic haircutting. The purpose is not to demonstrate autonomous haircutting or to assess haircut quality, but to study how a robotic haircutting system behaves under deployment, sensing, execution, tool-actuation, and interruption constraints. The paper makes three contributions. First, it introduces a task-specific teleoperation architecture for robotic haircutting that treats operator-side sensing, message transport, robot-side execution, clipper actuation, video feedback, and safeguards as separable but coordinated parts of one teleoperation loop. This modular design enables deployment-dependent communication effects, robot-side execution timing, and tool-state handling to be independently examined without changing the underlying haircutting task interface. Second, it establishes a repeatable mannequin-based evaluation framework for studying system-level robotic haircutting teleoperation under local, relay, and remote deployment conditions. Third, it quantitatively characterizes communication timing, command-following behavior, and interruption handling, thereby showing how the main components of the closed-loop teleoperation system can be decomposed and interpreted. Together, these contributions position TeleHairing as a quantitative reference for future research on robotic haircutting teleoperation.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on teleoperation, head-proximate grooming and haircutting systems, accessible deployable interfaces, and fault-handling mechanisms for human-centered robot operation. Section 3 presents the TeleHairing architecture, including the communication layer, relative-pose control pipeline, tool actuation, and operational safeguards. Section 4 describes the experimental setup and evaluation, focusing on deployment-dependent timing, proxy-task trajectory following, operator and network-path variation, and runtime fault handling. Section 5 discusses the system-design implications, and Section 6 concludes the paper.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Background and Related Work

Robotic haircutting is not only a motion-generation problem. It also requires an operator or autonomy stack to coordinate visual observation, communication, robot execution, tool actuation, and operational constraints around the head. The related work most relevant to TeleHairing therefore spans teleoperation, near-head hair manipulation, deployable service-robot interfaces, and fault-aware human-robot interaction. Each area provides part of the required capability, but none directly replaces a robotic haircutting teleoperation system that combines near-head tool motion, clipper actuation, deployment-dependent communication, and interruption handling within the same evaluated loop.

Teleoperation provides the first building block because it treats robotic manipulation as a closed loop among operator input, communication, remote execution, and sensory feedback [ 11 ] . For remote robot operation over nonideal links, predictive teleoperation and networked-control studies have treated communication delay, quality-of-service variation, and controller-side timing as part of the control problem rather than as external implementation details [ 12 ] . Recent vision-based systems extend this closed-loop view to dexterous manipulation, demonstration collection, and immersive bimanual operation [ 13 , 14 ] . Prior networked teleoperation studies, already discussed in the Introduction, further show that communication structure can affect remote manipulation. For systems intended to be operated across local and remote settings, performance-evaluation frameworks therefore motivate reporting latency, usability, and task behavior as system properties [ 15 ] . However, this literature typically evaluates general remote manipulation, navigation, or dexterous tasks; it does not specify how the teleoperation loop changes when the robot must operate an actuated haircutting tool near the head.

The task-side constraints come from robotic hair interaction and near-head personal care. Existing haircutting reviews and the grooming systems cited in the Introduction identify perception, hair variability, contact-rich interaction, user preference, precision planning, and safety as persistent difficulties. Additional physical-platform studies reinforce this point from adjacent tasks: feedback-driven brushing shows how hair interaction can require online correction, while root-centric front-hair styling shows how robot motion can be planned around local hair geometry [ 16 , 17 ] . These studies show that robotic interaction with hair near the head is feasible. Their focus, however, is mainly autonomous or semi-autonomous grooming, offline planning, or task-specific manipulation policies rather than deployable teleoperation for haircutting. They therefore do not characterize the combined behavior of human operation, communication, robot-side execution, and cutting-tool actuation during robotic haircutting teleoperation.

This connection raises a deployability question. A robotic haircutting teleoperation system should not rely only on a tightly integrated laboratory interface if the goal is to study local, relay, and remote operation. Accessible teleoperation studies of assistive mobile manipulators highlight the hardware, interface, and deployment constraints that arise when remote operators interact with robots in less controlled environments [ 18 ] . Visual fiducials such as AprilTags are widely used for robot pose estimation and calibration [ 19 ] , and they offer a practical route to low-barrier operator-side visual input. These methods support deployable interfaces and remote operation, but they are commonly validated on navigation, fetch-and-deliver, or generic manipulation tasks. As a result, they do not establish how such lightweight operator-input methods, cloud-mediated control, robot-side execution, and video feedback perform when applied to clipper-based robotic haircutting near the head.

Near-head tool use also makes safety and fault handling part of robotic haircutting system behavior rather than an external concern. Prior work on virtual fixtures, steady-hand teleoperation, adaptive assistance, and fail-safe contact behavior shows how protective constraints can shape human-supervised robot motion near the body [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] . Haircutting-specific safety discussions further clarify that risks arise from tool motion near the scalp and from degraded sensing or control conditions [ 24 ] . These studies provide important mechanisms and safety concepts, but they do not integrate tracking interruption, communication behavior, tool actuation, and robot recovery into one robotic haircutting teleoperation loop.

In summary, the missing element is not a single component such as a fiducial tracker, a teleoperation link, or a protective mechanism. The gap is a specifically designed and experimentally characterized robotic haircutting teleoperation system that brings these elements together. TeleHairing addresses this integration gap by studying a tool-actuated, locally and remotely deployable platform with logged timing, trajectory, and runtime fault-handling behavior.

2026-10-07.title: Demo: Vision-Language Model-Guided Online Calibration of an Electromagnetic Digital Twin
2026-10-07.authors: Zerui Kang , Yishen Lim , Zhouyou Gu , Seungnyun Kim , Seung-Woo Ko , Tony Q.S. Quek , Jihong Park
2026-10-07.abstract: An electromagnetic (EM) digital twin gives mobile robots wireless situational awareness but depends on material conductivities that change with the environment. Online calibration faces initialization sensitivity and measurement travel costs. We demonstrate a vision-language model (VLM)-guided framework using a Unitree G1 robot and NVIDIA Sionna, with two VLM calls: material classification maps visible materials through ITU-R P.2040 to conductivity priors for Sionna’s gradient descent on accumulated received signal strength (RSS) measurements; waypoint planning selects the next measurement location online using residual RSS calibration error and image coverage. In a real indoor scenario, the framework achieves a normalized mean absolute conductivity error of 1.74 × 10 − 4 1.74\times 10^{-4} within 20 m of travel; random initialization never converges, while random waypoints require over twice the travel.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Electromagnetic (EM) digital twins model the radio propagation characteristics of a physical environment to provide mobile robots with situational awareness of the wireless environment. Their fidelity relies on estimates of environmental EM properties, which must be recalibrated from radio measurements as the environment changes. While existing methods estimate EM properties via differentiable ray tracing, e.g., NVIDIA Sionna ( Hoydis and others, 2023 ) , they typically operate offline on pre-collected measurements. For example, Hoydis et al. ( Hoydis and others, 2024 ) learn material and antenna parameters from recorded indoor data, while Ai et al. ( Ai and others, 2026 ) densify sparse measurements through a Bayesian channel map. To reduce the human effort of repeated measurement campaigns, mobile robots with onboard sensing offer a promising approach for online calibration , where measurements are acquired progressively and travel-efficient selection becomes important. Our prior work ( Kang and others, 2026 ) uses a VLM to initialize material parameters and select measurement positions from a scene view, but these positions are fixed in advance and cannot adapt to evolving RSS calibration errors. Measurement positions should instead be selected from preceding observations to target poorly calibrated regions.

An aim of this paper is to propose a VLM-based online calibration framwork for an EM digital twin. The key idea is to couple two VLM calls in a perception-calibration-movement loop. Unlike ( Kang and others, 2026 ) , where the VLM initializes all parameters once from a complete view and fixes the measurement positions before calibration starts, both calls are made online in every round. First, since one viewpoint reveals only a few objects, the material parameters cannot be initialized once for the whole scene. A material-classification call therefore initializes the objects newly observed at each waypoint from the camera images and their segmentation masks, which lets the VLM assign a material to each object rather than to the whole image. Priors close to the true values place the parameters where the RSS gradient points toward the true values, so every RSS measurement moves the parameters closer to the true values and the calibration converges within a few rounds. Second, since one measurement calibrates only the materials along its propagation paths, measuring where the nearby materials are already calibrated wastes travel. A waypoint-planning call therefore selects the next waypoint from the RSS calibration error and the image coverage, so that each measurement reaches the materials still uncertain and each camera view covers the objects not yet observed, and the calibration converges with the least travel. Together, these two calls close the loop: visual observations initialize newly observed materials, RSS-based calibration errors guide the next waypoint, and newly collected images and RSS measurements feed into the next round.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2. System Design

We demonstrate the framework in the indoor scenario of Fig. 1 (a) with a fixed 5G NR base station and a Unitree G1 humanoid robot carrying a 5G dongle and an RGB camera. A desktop with an NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 GPU hosts the EM digital twin in Sionna and GPT-5.4 as the VLM. The dongle records RSS measurements from the fixed transmitter, while the Sionna configuration uses the same carrier frequency and antenna locations as the physical setup. The following three stages run once per round at each waypoint. For simplicity, we calibrate only the material conductivities.

Perception: sThe scene images in the four directions around the robot and the segmentation masks are provided to the *material-classification* call, which labels the material of each segmented object, and each label is mapped through the ITU-R P.2040 database to a conductivity value ( ITU-R, 2023 ) , as shown in Fig. 1 (b). The VLM outputs are conductivity priors for the visible objects and an image-coverage record of the objects observed so far, while objects outside all camera views retain their estimates from the previous round.

Calibration: Sionna in Fig. 1 (c) refines the conductivities by gradient descent on the error between measured and simulated RSS, and reports a convergence indicator, namely the steadiness of the loss and the parameters over the last 50 50 iterations. Since the VLM initializes the parameters close to the true values, gradient descent can quickly converge before the next measurement arrives, leaving small RSS-based calibration errors to the next round.

Movement: The RSS at a waypoint depends predominantly on the materials along the propagation paths from the base station to the robot, so a measurement can calibrate only those materials.
The waypoint-planning call therefore takes the room layout, the RSS-based calibration error, and the image coverage, and picks the next waypoint whose propagation paths interact with the materials of still-uncertain conductivity and whose camera view covers objects not yet observed. Fig. 1 (d) shows the waypoints selected online.

2026-10-07.title: Behavioral Cloning Mystery
2026-10-07.authors: Seohong Park , Sergey Levine
2026-10-07.abstract:
Behavioral cloning (BC), despite its simplicity, exhibits many counterintuitive phenomena in the real world.
For example, the performance of BC often keeps increasing as the model overfits more to the dataset,
and fully closed-loop policies often completely fail without action chunking.
Unfortunately, properly studying these anecdotal phenomena (“behavioral cloning mysteries”) is challenging:
in the real world, datasets and experiments are costly and not fully controllable;
in simulation with synthetic data, these phenomena are often not easily observed
partly due to the discrepancy between scripted policies and human demonstrations.
In this work, we propose OCBench,
a robotic manipulation benchmark with controllable scripted policies that have similar properties to human demonstrations.
We show that, by mimicking key properties of human demonstrations,
OCBench reproduces many anecdotal BC-related phenomena in controlled settings.
With its GPU-accelerated environments and scripted policies,
we demonstrate how OCBench enables scientific studies of previously reported BC-related phenomena
by analyzing and refuting various hypotheses.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Behavioral cloning (BC) is a foundational technique for large-scale robotic control ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ) .
Despite its simplicity,
behavioral cloning exhibits many counterintuitive phenomena (“mysteries”),
especially when trained on complex, large-scale, human-collected data.
For example, researchers have anecdotally found that
BC performance often increases as it overfits more ( Mandlekar et al., 2021 ; Allshire et al., 2026 ) ,
fully closed-loop policies often fail completely whereas partially open-loop control with action chunking works well ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Lazzati et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) ,
and history conditioning can hurt performance despite providing strictly more information ( de Haan et al., 2019 ; Wen et al., 2020 ; Sobol Mark et al., 2026 ) .

Unfortunately, properly studying these empirical phenomena is challenging.
In the real world, robotic experiments are not perfectly reproducible,
human-collected data are expensive and less controllable,
and different factors cannot be easily isolated.
Simulated benchmarks with scripted policies provide more control over data,
but they often do not reproduce all these real-world phenomena (see Section 3 ),
likely because previous scripted policies do not have the same properties as actual human demonstrations.

The main goal of this work is to provide a suite of simulated tasks and datasets,
which we call OCBench , that has similar structural properties to human demonstrations,
to enable scientific, controlled studies of realistic behavioral cloning and robotic control.
We show that by mimicking the key properties of human demonstrations
( e.g. , trajectories being very narrow, non-Markovian, and smoothly random),
we can reproduce many anecdotal BC-related phenomena in controlled settings,
including those that are not clearly observed in previous synthetic benchmarks.

We implement the OCBench tasks and scripted policies in MJWarp, a GPU-accelerated MuJoCo based on NVIDIA Warp ( Macklin, 2022 ) .
On a single H100 GPU,
OCBench can collect synthetic trajectories highly efficiently, at up to 200 200 K environment steps per second.
This makes streaming-data training practically feasible,
meaning that we can train an agent using a continuous stream of freshly generated data.
This allows us to study the “limit” of different algorithms and design choices under effectively unlimited data.

In this paper, based on our controlled reproduction in OCBench,
we discuss four non-intuitive phenomena that happen with real-world behavioral cloning.
We provide (and refute) possible hypotheses and discuss implications of each mystery,
demonstrating how OCBench’s controlled datasets and streaming-data training enable scientific studies
of anecdotal phenomena reported in the literature.

Contributions. The main contributions of this work are twofold.
First, we introduce OCBench,
a new GPU-accelerated benchmark suite accompanied by scripted policies that mimic the structural properties of human demonstrations.
This enables controlled studies of diverse phenomena observed in real-world behavioral cloning.
Second, we reproduce four previously reported, non-intuitive phenomena in OCBench,
making them scientifically studyable.
We also provide analyses and hypotheses for these phenomena with concrete evidence in controlled settings.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Behavioral cloning. Modern large-scale robotic control is mainly based on behavioral cloning and imitation learning ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ) .
Among diverse behavioral cloning techniques, including those based on multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) ( Fu et al., 2020 ; Mandlekar et al., 2021 ) ,
tokenized actions ( Shafiullah et al., 2022 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ) ,
and energy-based models ( Florence et al., 2021 ) ,
the most popular approaches to date are diffusion ( Chi et al., 2025 ) and flow matching ( Black et al., 2025b ) .
Researchers have scaled up flow behavioral cloning with large transformers,
demonstrating its effectiveness across a wide array of robotic tasks ( NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ) .
Accordingly, we mainly focus on flow behavioral cloning in this work,
although many of the phenomena studied in this work may apply to other behavioral cloning techniques as well.

Analyses of behavioral cloning. Several works have analyzed diverse phenomena and failure modes in behavioral cloning.
One line of work has focused on test-time distribution shift and DAgger
from both theoretical and empirical perspectives ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Spencer et al., 2021 ; Park et al., 2024 ; Simchowitz et al., 2025 ) .
Another body of work has analyzed the effect of modern techniques,
such as action chunking and open-loop control ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lazzati et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) ,
as well as history conditioning ( de Haan et al., 2019 ; Wen et al., 2020 ; Sobol Mark et al., 2026 ) .
Many of the aforementioned works rely primarily on relatively small, fixed, human-collected datasets
( e.g. , 50 50 – 300 300 demonstrations per task).
In contrast, recent large-scale robotic systems train on orders of magnitude more robot data ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ) .
The difference in data scale often serves as a confounder,
making it unclear whether these issues will eventually go away with more data or are fundamental to behavioral cloning.
In this work, rather than relying on limited human-collected data,
we mimic the structural properties of human demonstrations with GPU-accelerated scripted policies,
enabling effectively unlimited data generation at up to 200 200 K steps per second,
while reproducing many phenomena observed in real-world behavioral cloning.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to systematically reproduce multiple real-world BC phenomena
using GPU-accelerated,
fully controllable scripted policies.

Behavioral cloning and reinforcement learning benchmarks. A variety of simulated benchmarks have been proposed for behavioral cloning and data-driven reinforcement learning (RL).
Previous behavioral cloning benchmarks typically provide
simulated tasks with tens to a few hundred human-collected demonstrations per task ( Mandlekar et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2023a ) .
Unlike them, we instead design scripted policies that mimic human data’s properties to enable unlimited generation of controlled trajectories.
Among existing BC benchmarks, MimicGen ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) is particularly relevant,
which supports systematic human-like data generation.
Unlike MimicGen,
which generates trajectories by first recording about 10 10 human trajectories per task and “replaying” their segments in new randomized configurations,
OCBench generates data using fully scripted policies having human-like properties
and provides a host of controllable knobs ( e.g. , motion speed, mistake probability, coverage degree, etc.),
enabling both diverse data generation and scientific analyses.
Another line of simulated benchmarks ( Fu et al., 2020 ; James et al., 2020 ; Yarats et al., 2022 ; Lu et al., 2023 ; Tao et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2025a ) provides scripted or RL-trained policies to generate data.
Compared to these previous benchmarks, OCBench provides more human-like scripted policies,
enabling us to reproduce diverse phenomena that happen in real-world behavioral cloning
but are not easily observed in previous scripted benchmarks ( Section 3 ).
We also provide GPU-accelerated environments and scripted policies based on MJWarp.
OCBench’s closest predecessor is OGBench ( Park et al., 2025a ) , and we compare them in detail in Appendix B .

2026-10-07.title: BRACE: Adapting Whole-Body References for Force and Terrain Aware Humanoid Motion Tracking
2026-10-07.authors: Sudarshan Harithas , Chen Yu , Juan Borbon , Shubhankar Mondal , Winston Zha , Srinath Sridhar , Dingqi Zhang , Jiuguang Wang
2026-10-07.abstract:
Whole-body tracking has become the interface through which operators drive humanoid robots, yet the references it consumes are recorded on level ground and carrying nothing, so the tracker is aware of neither the forces the robot must exchange with objects nor the terrain it must stand on.
Existing controllers address one side of this gap: force-capable policies command an end-effector force but prescribe no whole-body pose, while terrain-adaptive trackers treat loads as disturbances to reject rather than wrenches to command.
We present BRACE, a whole-body tracker that exerts and compensates commanded hand forces from diverse poses while following a flat-ground reference on sloped terrain. Rather than leaving the tracker to absorb the load and the slope, BRACE folds both into the reference it follows: terrain conformance lifts footholds and root onto the local surface, and a wrench transformation resolves the hand displacement that produces a force jointly with the center-of-mass and center-of-pressure shifts it induces, bounded by teacher-specific arm-effort limits.
Separate exertion and compensation teachers are distilled by DAgger into one flow-matching student that runs on proprioception alone, without a height map or measured wrench, so a teleoperator (even in remote locations) can supply a flat-ground trajectory and the robot resolves slope and load onboard.
We extensive experiments on the Unitree-G1 to demonstrate the ability of BRACE to exert, compensate force and handle diverse terrain in simulation and real robot experiments.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Whole-body tracking has become the standard route from human motion to humanoid
motion: a trajectory retargeted from a demonstrator is followed by a controller that keeps the
robot upright while it reproduces the
reference [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . The
approach has scaled because its data has. Motion capture [ 8 ] and in-the-wild
video [ 9 ] supply reference trajectories in quantity, and recent systems use the
resulting trackers as a teleoperation interface, collecting demonstrations for downstream
policies [ 1 , 2 , 6 ] .

What those corpora do not contain is force. A demonstrator is recorded on level ground,
carrying nothing, and the record preserves the path the body took but not the loads it bore or
the reactions it absorbed. For locomotion and gesture little is lost. For the work humanoids
are meant to do, what is lost is the specification: moving a payload, pulling a
door against its closer, or steadying a workpiece while turning a tool is defined by the wrench 𝐰 = [ F , τ ] \mathbf{w}=[\,F,\,\tau\,] the robot exchanges with its environment at least as much as by
the trajectory it follows. Terrain is missing for the same reason, and under teleoperation the
two omissions compound: the operator stands unloaded in a capture volume on level ground while
the robot walks a ramp with a box in its hands. Pushing a cart up a grade is the simple case,
where the slope changes both the force the robot must supply and the lean it must adopt to
supply it, and the retargeted motion shows neither.

Existing controllers address one or the other. Force-capable legged systems accept an
end-effector force alongside a base velocity [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] , or accept
impedance parameters in place of a force [ 14 ] ; since none prescribes a dense whole-body
pose, the question of producing a force while holding a posture does not arise.
Terrain-adaptive controllers infer ground geometry from
proprioception [ 15 , 16 , 3 ] , but treat loads and pushes as
disturbances to reject rather than wrenches to command.

Combining the two inside a whole-body reference is difficult because each signal contradicts
that reference. A commanded wrench is conventionally realized by displacing the end
effector [ 10 , 17 ] ; displace it without adjusting the rest of the body and the robot
loses balance once the reaction arrives, while the pose the tracker is asked to hold diverges
from the pose that would produce the force. The operator’s support surface is likewise not the
robot’s, leaving reference footholds and root height systematically wrong, and no dataset pairs
retargeted humanoid motion with the terrain it was executed on, so the correction cannot be
learned directly.

BRACE (Body Reference Adaptation for Contact and Elevation) resolves this conflict at its source by correcting the reference rather than the controller. A flat-ground reference is adapted analytically to the terrain the robot stands on and to the wrench it is asked to exert, so that tracking the adapted reference already yields the footholds, hand displacement, and bracing the task requires. Two privileged teachers learn on these references, one that exerts a commanded wrench and one that holds the reference against an external one, and both are distilled into a single flow-based student that runs from proprioception and operator commands alone, inferring terrain and load on the fly. BRACE focuses on proprioception centric WBC and deals with non-flat terrains that can be handled with proprioception [ 15 ] , which include slopes, rough surface inconsistencies, and small platforms.
To our knowledge, BRACE is the first whole-body tracker that exerts or rejects a wrench and adapts to terrain at the same time, enabling tasks such as inserting a syringe, turning a winch, lifting a barbell, and pushing a cart up a slope (Fig. 1 ).
Our results (Sec. IV ) indicate that BRACE reduces global drift at an average of 40 40 percentage points and results in an overall average improvement in success rate by 18.25 18.25 percentage points.
We further deploy the BRACE policy on the Unitree-G1 to demonstrate its operation in the real world.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Whole-Body Tracking on Terrain and Under Load

Reinforcement learning has been highly successful for training motion imitation models in character animation [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] and humanoid control [ 1 , 21 , 2 , 4 , 6 , 7 ] . Recent work has pushed whole-body tracking (WBT) toward real-world robustness [ 3 , 22 , 21 ] .
Any2Track [ 3 ] separates tracking from dynamics adaptation to handle sim-to-real mismatch and diverse terrain, while HEFT [ 22 ] focuses on tracking under hand-carried payloads.
These advances improve motion tracking under environmental disturbances, but leave open the joint problem of tracking whole-body motion and exerting commanded wrenches across varied terrain.

In particular, HEFT handles payloads as quasi-static gravitational loads, and Any2Track treats external pushes as unmodeled perturbations; neither exposes a commanded interaction wrench to the operator.
Other terrain-aware approaches generate motion references online from perception [ 23 , 24 ] , coupling the reference to the robot’s local terrain.
BRACE instead accepts a flat-ground reference and internally adapts tracking to the terrain and interaction task.
This allows the operator to specify the intended motion and wrench while the controller reconciles them with the robot’s support surface and loading conditions.
Such a separation supports applications including remote teleoperation, where the operator and robot need not share the same terrain or physical load (Sec. IV-E ).

## II-B Force Control in Locomotion

Force exertion and compensation are two key paradigms in force control that in focus of BRACE.
For force exertion, UNIFP [ 10 ] commands an end-effector force alongside a base velocity, while FACET [ 14 ] commands impedance rather than force, imitating a virtual spring–damper at the CoM.
For force compensation, which asks the robot to hold a pose against external forces, decoupled frameworks such as FALCON [ 11 ] , HAFO [ 12 ] , and KinAware [ 13 ] pair a lower-body agent for standing with an upper-body agent for end-effector tracking under force curricula.

What these interfaces share is the absence of a dense whole-body pose target: the operator supplies a root velocity or an end-effector goal, and the remaining degrees of freedom are resolved by the controller rather than prescribed. BRACE instead holds a full whole-body reference against a commanded wrench, so the wrench must be reconciled with the reference rather than absorbed by unconstrained degrees of freedom. Moreover, each of these methods addresses a single paradigm, whereas BRACE must distinguish producing a commanded wrench from holding a motion against an external load, and switch between them on command.

## II-C Behavior Models and Multi-Teacher Distillation

Generalist controllers consolidate diverse skills and command interfaces into a shared policy. In character animation, PULSE [ 18 ] learns a variational motion prior that can be reused for downstream tasks, while MaskedMimic [ 19 ] supports diverse control inputs through masked motion conditioning. Related approaches extend generalist control to humanoid robots: HOVER [ 25 ] distills multiple control modes into one controller, and BFM-Zero [ 26 ] learns a shared latent representation of motions, goals, and rewards. BeyondMimic [ 4 ] uses guided latent diffusion to compose motions and specify tasks, while OmniXtreme [ 27 ] distills motion-specific experts into a flow-matching policy through DAgger.

Building on these approaches, BRACE addresses the joint demands of whole-body motion tracking, wrench interaction, and terrain adaptation. The controller must distinguish producing a commanded wrench from preserving a motion against an external load, even in similar body configurations. We distill separate privileged exertion and compensation teachers into one student through DAgger [ 28 ] . A motion goal, wrench command, and explicit interaction mode specify the desired response. This formulation extends multi-teacher distillation to complementary interaction behaviors while retaining whole-body motion tracking across terrain and loading conditions.

2026-10-07.title: LEAP: Making Privileged Geometry Supervision Effective for Visuomotor Learning
2026-10-07.authors: Han Fang , Yunpeng Jiang , Jianshu Hu , Zhiyuan Guan , Ruiguo Sun , Shujia Li , Paul Weng , Xiao Li , Yutong Ban
2026-10-07.abstract:
Privileged 3D supervision uses additional geometric information during training to guide RGB-based visuomotor policy learning, without requiring geometric inputs at deployment.
However, low reconstruction error does not ensure that visual representations capture geometry useful for control. We identify three limitations that weaken this supervision: proprioceptive shortcuts, dominant-view reliance, and reconstruction objectives dominated by task-irrelevant geometry. To address these limitations, we propose Latent Encoding with Aligned Privileged Geometry (LEAP).
Our framework uses an auxiliary decoder to reconstruct point clouds within the manipulation workspace from visual features alone, while retaining proprioception for action prediction.
Alongside full reconstruction, we introduce wrist-view dropout and partial reconstruction targets matched to the retained wrist, encouraging the encoder to capture complementary local geometry.
The auxiliary decoder is removed at inference, leaving only RGB observations and robot state as policy inputs.
Extensive experiments on RoboTwin, ManiSkill, and real-world tasks demonstrate consistent and substantial improvements over Diffusion Policy and ACT, with only a small increase in parameter count and no reduction in inference speed.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Reliable robotic manipulation depends on the 3D relationships among objects and the robot. RGB-based imitation learning methods, such as Diffusion Policy ( Chi et al., 2023 ) and ACT ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , learn complex skills from demonstrations, but their training objectives do not explicitly require visual features to encode these relationships.
Point-cloud policies such as DP3 ( Ze et al., 2024 ) provide explicit geometric inputs, but require depth sensing and point-cloud processing at deployment, adding sensing requirements and computational cost.
Privileged geometry supervision instead uses 3D information during training, through auxiliary geometric prediction ( Li et al., 2025c ; He et al., 2026a ; Kim et al., 2026 ) or representation alignment ( Li et al., 2025b ) , while retaining an RGB policy at deployment.

While RGB-based policies are easier to deploy, this line of work suffers from the following potential issue.
Without explicit 3D observations at deployment, an RGB policy must infer task-relevant geometry from its images.
A low geometric training loss does not establish that it has done so.
In this paper, considering policies that take multi-view RGB images and robot state as input, we investigate the following two questions:
(1) when does privileged supervision with depth-derived geometric information fail to make the visual representation capture task-relevant 3D structure?
(2) how can privileged 3D supervision be formulated to circumvent this failure?
To answer the first question, we identify three limitations of privileged geometry supervision: proprioceptive shortcuts , view dominance , and task-irrelevant global prediction .
To address the second, we propose a novel training framework.
We expand on those points next.

A proprioceptive shortcut occurs when an auxiliary geometry decoder uses robot state to reduce reconstruction error without extracting the corresponding geometry from images.
Such shortcuts have been studied in action prediction ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) , but their effect on privileged geometry supervision remains underexplored. View dominance occurs when the broad-coverage camera explains much of a fused reconstruction target, leaving the contribution of other views unclear.
Finally, task-irrelevant global prediction can devote much of the auxiliary reconstruction objective to background and robot geometry while giving little weight to the local contact and occlusion geometry needed for control. Together, these limitations allow low geometric loss without ensuring that the visual features preserve the geometry relevant to manipulation.

To overcome these limitations, we propose L atent E ncoding with A ligned P rivileged Geometry (LEAP), a training framework that directs privileged geometry supervision toward task-relevant visual learning.
Its geometry decoder receives only visual features, limiting proprioceptive shortcuts.
During training, we randomly mask views and matches a partial geometry target to the remaining views, making wrist contributions easier to identify.
At deployment, the policy uses only multi-view RGB images and robot state.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We identify proprioceptive shortcuts, view dominance, and task-irrelevant global prediction as limitations of privileged geometry supervision for multi-view visuomotor learning.

We introduce LEAP, combining visual-only geometric reconstruction, view dropout with visibility-aligned partial reconstruction, and workspace-constrained supervision.

We evaluate these limitations and the corresponding designs through abundant controlled experiments and policy evaluations across simulation and real-robot settings with different RGB-based policy architectures.
