2026-10-07.title: RMRRT: Riemannian Barrier Metric RRT for Inequality-Aware Steering on Equality Manifolds
2026-10-07.authors: Minhyeong Kang , Sanghyun Kim
2026-10-07.abstract: This paper presents a motion planning framework that unifies equality and inequality constraints within a single geometric formulation for sampling-based planning in high-dimensional robotic systems. In conventional sampling-based planners, equality constraints are typically enforced through projection, whereas inequality constraints are handled separately through binary validity checks such as collision testing, often leading to inefficient exploration. To address this limitation, we propose Riemannian Barrier Metric RRT (RMRRT), which constructs a unified local geometry for planning on equality-constrained manifolds. RMRRT first builds an ambient barrier metric from inequality-sensitive barrier terms and then induces a tangent-space metric via a G G -orthogonal projection associated with the equality constraints. The resulting tangent-space metric is used consistently in both steering and nearest-neighbor selection, biasing exploration away from nearby inequality boundaries while preserving first-order equality consistency. In this work, the metric is instantiated from signed-distance-based geometric proxy inequalities to provide collision-informative tangent-space directions; hard feasibility is enforced separately through standard validity checks. Experimental results show that RMRRT achieves a 100% success rate across diverse constrained manipulation tasks in both simulation and real-world settings, while reducing planning time relative to representative constrained planning baselines. Ablation studies further demonstrate that the proposed metric improves exploration quality by reducing rejected samples and shortening path length. Experiment videos and source code are available at: https://rcilab.github.io/rmrrt
2026-10-07.introduction:
Sampling-based motion planning becomes particularly challenging when robotic systems are subject to simultaneous equality and inequality constraints [ mu2025efficient , stilman2007task , xian2017closed ] . Equality constraints commonly arise from closed-chain kinematics [ bordalba2020randomized , jang2022motion , park2024constrained ] , grasp maintenance [ liu2025planning , dogar2019multi , zimmermann2020multi ] , and cooperative multi-arm manipulation [ shi2025distributed , alonso2015local ] , restricting feasible configurations to an implicit manifold embedded in the ambient configuration space [ suh2011tangent , jaillet2012path , kim2016tangent ] . Inequality constraints, such as obstacle avoidance [ quiroz2019whole , guo2012new ] , self-collision [ grassmann2018smooth , Hu_2021_CVPR , cai2025just ] , and joint limits [ stilman2007task , li2024quadratic ] , further restrict admissible regions through state-dependent boundaries. Under such conditions, feasible configurations typically occupy only a small fraction of the ambient space, making exploration efficiency and steering quality central to planning performance. Fig. 1 illustrates a representative coupled-constraint task in which three manipulators cooperatively transport a chair while maintaining closed-chain grasp constraints and avoiding collisions.

In conventional sampling-based planners, equality constraints are typically enforced through projection onto the constraint manifold, whereas inequality constraints are handled separately through binary validity checks such as collision testing [ suh2011tangent , jaillet2012path , kim2016tangent , berenson2009manipulation ] . This decoupled treatment often leads to inefficient sample rejection and unstable steering, particularly in highly constrained environments where admissible regions are narrow or fragmented. Consequently, integrating equality and inequality constraints into a unified exploration framework remains a fundamental challenge in sampling-based motion planning. In this work, we address this challenge by proposing a unified geometric formulation that directly incorporates inequality-induced boundary geometry into exploration on equality-constrained manifolds.

Sampling-based robot motion planning under constraints has been studied from multiple perspectives, largely distinguished by how equality and inequality constraints are represented and incorporated into planning. Prior work can be broadly organized into four categories:
(i) manifold-based approaches that plan directly on equality-constrained manifolds,
(ii) metric-based approaches that encode inequality-induced geometry into costs, distances, or local metrics,
(iii) data-driven approaches that accelerate exploration using learned or precomputed priors, and
(iv) trajectory-optimization approaches that treat equality and inequality constraints jointly over an entire trajectory.

Manifold-based motion planners operate directly on implicitly defined equality-constrained manifolds and aim to preserve equality feasibility throughout planning [ jang2022motion , suh2011tangent , jaillet2012path , kim2016tangent ] . Atlas-based planners approximate the manifold using collections of local charts and transition between neighboring charts during exploration, improving robustness in highly curved regions [ jaillet2012path , jaillet2016path ] . Tangent-space methods instead generate local motions in the Jacobian-defined tangent space and apply manifold-consistent correction, such as local projection, to obtain equality-feasible extensions [ suh2011tangent , kim2016tangent ] . In most such approaches, however, tangent-space information is used primarily to maintain equality feasibility, whereas nearest-neighbor selection and steering are not consistently informed by nearby inequality boundaries. Consequently, inequality constraints often influence exploration only through post-hoc rejection by external validity checks, such as collision testing [ kingston2018sampling ] . This separation can lead to repeated unproductive extension attempts in narrow or cluttered environments [ hsu2003bridge , pan2016fast ] .

Metric-based approaches incorporate inequality constraints into costs, distance measures, or state-dependent metrics to discourage motion toward constraint boundaries and bias exploration toward admissible regions. Classical examples include artificial potential fields and continuous obstacle-based trajectory costs [ khatib1986real , ratliff2009chomp ] .
More recent Riemannian approaches construct non-Euclidean metrics from curvature, Hessian, or other differential information associated with inequality constraints [ manjunath2021safe , yang2019sampling ] . Related reactive frameworks such as RMPflow use task-space Riemannian structures to combine multiple local motion objectives [ cheng2021rmpflow ] ,
building on the Riemannian Motion Policies of Ratliff et al. [ ratliff2018riemannian ] , which formalize a metric-as-geometry viewpoint for task-space motion generation. Although these approaches effectively encode inequality-aware local geometry, they are generally formulated in the ambient configuration space and do not directly generate equality-consistent motion on an implicitly defined constraint manifold. Additional projection or correction mechanisms are therefore required when they are applied to equality-constrained steering or tree expansion.

Data-driven approaches accelerate constrained planning by exploiting learned or precomputed structure in the feasible space. Representative directions include learning low-dimensional latent representations of equality-constrained manifolds [ park2024constrained , zhang2025local ] , learning samplers or policies that bias expansion toward promising regions, and constructing offline roadmaps that reduce online search through precomputed feasible-state connectivity [ jang2022motion , csucan2012motion ] . These methods can substantially improve planning efficiency when the learned prior or precomputed structure matches the target problem. Their performance, however, may depend on training coverage, prior quality, and the suitability of the offline representation under changes in environments, robot models, or constraints.

A complementary line of work addresses equality and inequality constraints jointly through trajectory optimization on constraint manifolds. Representative approaches include embedded sequential convex programming [ bonalli2019trajectory ] , direct collocation for constrained robotic systems [ bordalba2022direct ] , and analytic-IK-based bimanual planning [ cohn2024constrained ] . These methods consider both classes of constraints at the trajectory level and typically refine an initialized trajectory toward a locally optimal solution. This setting differs from the satisficing, exploration-based problem considered here. Trajectory optimization generally improves a prescribed trajectory initialization according to an objective and a set of constraints, whereas sampling-based planning focuses on discovering a feasible connection through nonlocal exploration. The two paradigms therefore play complementary roles: trajectory optimization provides strong local refinement, while sampling-based planning can explore alternative connections and is less dependent on a favorable initialization.

Despite their respective strengths, the approaches reviewed above do not generally construct a single explicit local geometry that is simultaneously equality-consistent and inequality-aware throughout sampling-based exploration. In manifold-based planners, equality constraints define admissible first-order motion through tangent spaces and projection operators, but the geometry used for nearest-neighbor selection and steering remains largely insensitive to nearby inequality boundaries. In metric-based planners, inequality constraints reshape local distances or energies, but the resulting geometry is typically defined in the ambient space and does not directly yield equality-consistent motion. Data-driven methods can bias exploration toward favorable regions, but they generally do so through learned or precomputed priors rather than through an explicit geometric object coupling the two constraint classes. Trajectory optimization can treat both classes of constraints over an entire trajectory, but it typically operates by locally refining an initialization rather than by defining an exploration geometry for sampling-based search.

This separation reflects a geometric mismatch rather than merely a modeling choice.
A natural way to encode inequality constraints as a continuous local geometry is through a barrier-induced metric that grows near active constraint boundaries.
Such a metric is naturally defined in the ambient configuration space, whereas admissible first-order motions under equality constraints are restricted to a Jacobian-defined tangent space.
Simply combining an ambient barrier metric with a standard Euclidean null-space projector does not preserve compatibility between these two geometric structures.
The projection itself must be defined with respect to the metric that shapes local motion. This observation leads to the central construction of RMRRT: a metric-compatible tangent projection and its induced tangent-space metric, used consistently in nearest-neighbor selection, local steering, and manifold correction.
Together, these components provide a common geometric structure through which equality feasibility and inequality-aware exploration are coupled throughout the planner.

The work of Bohigas et al. [ bohigas2013planning ] is particularly relevant because it also introduces a unified geometric construction for constrained sampling-based planning. Their method constructs a global, higher-dimensional geometric representation to obtain singularity-free paths in closed-chain systems. RMRRT instead constructs a local barrier-induced tangent-space metric that biases exploration away from obstacles and other active inequality boundaries. The two methods therefore address different geometric objectives and operate at different scales: Bohigas et al. use a global construction for singularity avoidance, whereas RMRRT uses a local metric for inequality-aware exploration on an equality-constrained manifold.

As discussed above, existing sampling-based planners do not provide a single local geometry that is simultaneously equality-consistent and inequality-aware. This geometric mismatch requires a projection that is compatible with the metric defining the local geometry, which leads to the G G -orthogonal projector and the induced tangent-space metric used in this work. Motivated by this observation, we propose Riemannian Barrier Metric RRT (RMRRT), a sampling-based planner that redefines local planning geometry on equality-constrained manifolds. The key idea is to endow equality-consistent motions with a barrier-informed Riemannian structure that captures the local influence of nearby geometric inequality boundaries.

Concretely, we first construct a state-dependent ambient barrier metric from inequality-sensitive barrier terms, and then induce a metric on the tangent space through a barrier-compatible projection associated with the equality-constraint Jacobian. The resulting geometry not only preserves equality consistency, but also reshapes local exploration according to nearby inequality boundaries. In the evaluated instantiation, this boundary geometry is constructed from signed-distance-based geometric proxy inequalities, which capture the dominant robot–obstacle boundary geometry in cluttered constrained settings. Inequalities without tractable differential structure are handled separately through standard validity checks. Thus, the metric acts as an exploration bias, while hard feasibility is enforced independently by validity checking.

Based on this induced geometry, RMRRT performs local steering by selecting tangent directions that make first-order progress toward the target while penalizing motions toward nearby inequality boundaries. The same induced tangent-space metric is also used in nearest-neighbor selection, yielding a notion of local connectability that is consistent with equality-constrained expansion. As a result, inequality information affects the exploration mechanism itself rather than entering only through post-hoc validity checks.

We introduce an ambient barrier metric and a G G -orthogonal projection that together induce a tangent-space metric for sampling-based planning on equality-constrained manifolds. This construction captures both manifold structure and inequality-boundary sensitivity within a single local geometry.

Building on this construction, we develop a bidirectional RRT-based planner for inequality-aware exploration on equality-constrained manifolds. The proposed planner incorporates the induced tangent-space metric into the expansion process so as to bias tree growth away from nearby inequality boundaries while preserving equality consistency.

We use the same induced tangent-space metric consistently in both steering and nearest-neighbor selection, establishing planner-wide geometric consistency during exploration. This aligns node selection with the local directions favored during expansion, in contrast to planners that rely on Euclidean proximity for selection and enforce equality consistency only during steering.

The results show improved planning efficiency and reliability over representative constrained planning baselines in challenging environments with coupled equality and inequality constraints [ berenson2009manipulation , jaillet2012path , kim2016tangent , csucan2012motion , park2024constrained ] .

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the necessary preliminaries, including equality-constrained manifolds and barrier-based metrics. Section III presents the proposed RMRRT methodology in detail. Section IV reports experimental results on a variety of constrained manipulation scenarios. Finally, Section V concludes the paper and discusses directions for future work.

2026-10-07.title: Generalizable Robustness Testing of DNN-Based Robotic Navigation Systems via XAI-Guided Search
2026-10-07.authors: Khizra Sohail , Miren Illarramendi , Aitor Arrieta
2026-10-07.abstract: Context: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are increasingly used to control Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs), but small input perturbations may propagate into unsafe system-level behavior. Existing perturbation-generation approaches commonly optimize for individual images, potentially producing input-specific tests, and are often evaluated only in simulation without examining whether the identified failures transfer to physical systems.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Cyber-Physical Systems (CPSs) integrate computational components with physical processes through sensing, computation, communication, and control. They are increasingly deployed in domains such as autonomous driving, mobile robotics, industrial automation, and other safety-critical applications. In these systems, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are progressively replacing or complementing conventional perception and control components because of their ability to learn complex mappings directly from high-dimensional sensory data [ 24 , 9 ] . For example, an autonomous navigation system may use a DNN to map camera images directly to steering commands. However, the behavior learned by these models is difficult to characterize exhaustively, and relatively small changes in their inputs may lead to unexpected variations in their outputs [ 35 ] . When the output of the DNN directly influences a physical process, such variations may propagate to the system level and result in unsafe behaviors, such as lane departures or collisions. Consequently, systematically testing the robustness of DNN-based CPSs under perturbed operating conditions is essential before their deployment.

Several approaches have been proposed to generate perturbations that expose weaknesses in DNNs. These include gradient-based and black-box adversarial techniques [ 21 , 15 , 3 ] and search-based techniques that explore the input space to identify failure-inducing conditions [ 23 , 37 ] . Nevertheless, existing approaches commonly optimize a perturbation with respect to a single input image [ 33 , 16 , 41 , 36 ] . Although such a perturbation may effectively alter the output produced for that particular image, it may exploit image-specific characteristics and fail to generalize to other observations of the same operational scenario. This problem is particularly relevant for autonomous systems, where the controller receives a continuous sequence of images rather than a single isolated input.

Optimizing perturbations over multiple images can reduce this form of overfitting by requiring the generated perturbations to remain effective across different observations. However, directly evaluating every candidate perturbation over a large collection of images substantially increases the computational cost of the search. This limits the number of images that can be considered and, consequently, the diversity of operational situations represented during optimization. Moreover, mutation operators employed by evolutionary and black-box approaches are commonly unaware of which image regions influence the controller most strongly [ 3 , 16 , 41 ] . As a result, a considerable part of the search effort may be spent modifying regions with little effect on the controller’s behavior.

A further limitation concerns how the generated perturbations are evaluated. Most existing studies assess perturbations either using image-classification benchmarks or exclusively within a simulated environment [ 33 , 16 , 36 ] . Simulation provides a controllable and repeatable environment in which many test executions can be conducted at relatively low cost. Nevertheless, failures observed in simulation do not necessarily transfer directly to a physical system. Conversely, conducting the complete search on a physical robot would be costly, slow, difficult to reproduce, and potentially unsafe. Therefore, an important open problem is to determine whether perturbations generated and assessed in simulation preserve their effectiveness when transferred to the corresponding physical system.

To address these challenges, this paper presents an explainability-guided, multi-objective evolutionary framework for testing the robustness of DNN-based autonomous navigation systems. Instead of optimizing one perturbation independently for each image, the framework searches for a common perturbation structure that is evaluated over a representative set of images. The perturbation is composed of sparse circular regions and is optimized to simultaneously maximize its effect on the steering decisions of the controller and minimize its modification cost. Considering multiple images during the search encourages the resulting perturbations to capture weaknesses that are shared across different observations rather than characteristics that are specific to a single image. To improve the efficiency of this multi-image search, the framework incorporates information obtained through Integrated Gradients [ 34 ] . Attribution maps are computed for the images considered during optimization and aggregated into a global map representing the image regions that most strongly influence the steering behavior of the controller. This information is then converted into a probabilistic mutation mechanism that prioritizes influential regions while preserving sufficient randomness to explore other parts of the input space. In this manner, explainability is not used only to interpret the decisions of an already trained model, but as operational information for directing the generation of robustness tests.

We evaluate the framework using a DNN-controlled LeoRover mobile robot and its corresponding Gazebo simulation environment. Through an ablation study, we separately investigate the effects of optimizing over multiple images and of guiding the evolutionary operators with attribution information. We then execute the generated perturbations repeatedly in simulation and validate a representative subset on the physical robot. This enables us to assess not only their capacity to induce system-level failures, but also the extent to which simulation-based observations transfer to the real system.

The main contributions of this paper are:

A formulation of robustness testing that optimizes perturbations across representative operational scenarios rather than individual observations, reducing the image-specific overfitting of existing perturbation-generation approaches.

A formulation of robustness testing that optimizes perturbations across representative operational scenarios rather than individual observations, reducing the image-specific overfitting of existing perturbation-generation approaches.

An explainability-guided search strategy that aggregates attribution information from multiple observations and exploits it to bias evolutionary search toward image regions that consistently influence the controller.

A search-based robustness testing framework that jointly optimizes perturbation effectiveness and perturbation cost, producing a diverse set of candidate robustness tests.

A comprehensive empirical evaluation, including an ablation study that isolates the contribution of multi-image optimization and XAI guidance, together with a sim-to-real validation on a physical robotic platform.

1. A formulation of robustness testing that optimizes perturbations across representative operational scenarios rather than individual observations, reducing the image-specific overfitting of existing perturbation-generation approaches.

2. An explainability-guided search strategy that aggregates attribution information from multiple observations and exploits it to bias evolutionary search toward image regions that consistently influence the controller.

3. A search-based robustness testing framework that jointly optimizes perturbation effectiveness and perturbation cost, producing a diverse set of candidate robustness tests.

4. A comprehensive empirical evaluation, including an ablation study that isolates the contribution of multi-image optimization and XAI guidance, together with a sim-to-real validation on a physical robotic platform.

# 2 Background

## 2.1 DNN-Based Robotic Navigation Systems

Robotic navigation systems operate as closed-loop CPSs in which sensory observations are continuously processed to determine control actions. In vision-based navigation, a camera captures an image x t x_{t} of the environment at time t t , and a controller f f maps this observation into a control command u t = f ​ ( x t ) u_{t}=f(x_{t}) , such as the linear and angular velocity of the robot. The execution of u t u_{t} changes the physical state of the robot and, consequently, the image received during the next control cycle. Therefore, errors in individual predictions may, or may not, propagate over time and ultimately lead to system-level failures.

At the model level, robustness can be assessed by measuring how input
variations affect the output of the DNN. However, a large change in the controller output does not necessarily imply that the robotic system will fail, while a sequence of comparatively small deviations may accumulate and cause unsafe behavior. Consequently, robustness testing of robotic navigation systems should complement model-level measurements with system-level execution outcomes.

## 2.2 Search-based Software Testing

Search-based software testing aims at recasting a software testing problem (e.g., test generation) into an optimization problem [ 29 , 22 ] . For instance, in the context of test generation, instead of enumerating the complete input
space, a search algorithm iteratively generates and evaluates candidate test inputs according to one or more fitness functions. Each candidate represents a potential test case, while variation operators such as mutation are used to explore neighboring regions of the search space. The fitness functions guide the search toward inputs that are more likely to expose failures or exercise relevant system behavior.

Robustness-test generation commonly involves conflicting objectives. For example, a perturbation should have a substantial effect on the system while remaining small or localized. Multi-objective search addresses this by identifying a set of non-dominated solutions rather than aggregating all criteria into a single value. A solution dominates another when it is no worse in every objective and better in at least one, commonly known as Pareto-optimality. The resulting Pareto front represents alternative trade-offs from which testers can select according to their needs.

In DNN-based systems, search-based techniques have been used to explore high-dimensional input spaces and generate failure-inducing images [ 37 , 3 ] . Candidate inputs can be modified through transformations or localized perturbations, while fitness functions quantify changes in model predictions, coverage, uncertainty, or system-level behavior. Nevertheless, the effectiveness of these approaches depends strongly on the representation, fitness functions, and information used to guide the search.

2026-10-07.title: Mission-Aware Attestation Envelopes for Time-Critical Autonomous Action: A Hardware-in-the-Loop V2I Study
2026-10-07.authors: Dimitrios Nikou , Nikolaos Kekatos , Sophia Petridou , Stylianos Basagiannis
2026-10-07.subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-07.comment: . Accepted at Modelling and Simulation for Autonomous Systems (MESAS 2026), to appear in Springer LNCS
2026-10-07.abstract:
An autonomous system that asks for a privileged physical action is usually
gated on integrity evidence: a platform proves what it is running, and the
request is granted or refused on that basis. Such a gate is normally treated as a
predicate, yet the evidence behind it has an age, the decision that consumes it
has a latency, and the physical system that waits for it has a deadline. In this
paper, we formulate mission-aware attestation as a runtime assurance contract
that holds only when integrity is valid, the evidence is fresh enough, and the
decision completes inside a budget derived from the current physical state. The
contract yields four operational outcomes where a binary gate yields two, and it
separates a refusal caused by tampering from one caused by evidence that had
already aged and from one caused by a decision that arrived too late. We evaluate
it on a hardware-in-the-loop vehicle-to-infrastructure platform in which a
driving simulator supplies the physical state and the authorisation deadline,
while a microcontroller on-board unit and a TPM-backed roadside unit running
Linux integrity measurement supply the assurance evidence. Combining
simulator-derived mission state with measured assurance behaviour lets us
construct the attestation envelope in which a security verdict is still
actionable, and compare the region a security-blind model admits against the
region a hardware-informed one admits. The first admits the whole space and the
second three quarters of it, and every point it refuses fails the freshness
margin rather than the response margin. Moving the attestation
interval across the range the verifier itself permits costs about as much as a
fivefold scaling of the latency distribution, and the interval is directly configurable
rather than a property of the hardware, which makes it the immediately actionable
deployment parameter. We also show that the two margins interact: if the freshness bound
does not exceed the authorisation budget, every late decision is also stale and
lateness becomes unobservable, which makes the attestation interval and the
freshness bound design parameters that cannot be chosen from security
requirements alone.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Intelligent transportation systems now place a substantial amount of
decision-making in vehicles and in the roadside infrastructure they talk to, and
vehicle-to-infrastructure (V2I) exchange is the channel through which that
coordination happens [ 8 ] . Such exchanges let a vehicle request a change to infrastructure it does not own,
of which emergency-vehicle signal preemption is the canonical
example [ 11 , 21 ] , and the security services protecting those
messages are standardised [ 15 ] . Automating them enlarges an attack surface
already well catalogued for automated vehicles [ 24 ] , and
communication delay is an established input to preemption
performance [ 21 ] . The privileged action, in other words, is granted
to a remote party over a shared channel, on evidence that party supplies.

The mechanism that makes such a grant defensible is remote attestation: a
platform produces evidence about what it is running, and a verifier decides
whether to believe it [ 5 ] . On general-purpose hosts that evidence is
rooted in a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) [ 30 , 23 ] and produced
by the Linux Integrity Measurement Architecture (IMA) [ 25 ] , with
continuous verification against a policy provided by frameworks such as
Keylime [ 27 , 12 ] . On constrained embedded devices, where a discrete
root of trust is often absent, software and hybrid alternatives range from
scalable collective attestation [ 2 ] to control-flow attestation of
the running program [ 1 ] . In each case a verdict is produced, and
systems built on top consume it as a predicate.

Treating it as a predicate is where the difficulty begins, and the attestation
literature has already identified the pieces without assembling them. Freshness
has been foundational to remote attestation since the area was set out
systematically [ 7 ] , and the architecture standardised for it treats
the freshness of evidence and of attestation results as a matter of policy,
discussing expiry explicitly [ 5 ] , so age is a recognised dimension. Work on real-time
mission execution integrity argues that autonomous cyber-physical systems need
attestation that is timely as well as correct [ 33 ] , so timeliness is
recognised too. The conflict between security mechanisms and timing guarantees
is a mature line in real-time systems [ 13 ] . What is missing is the
coupling: none of this asks whether a verdict is still decision-valid for
a physical action whose admissible response time is set, at run time, by where
the requester is and how fast it is moving.

Three distinct requirements therefore have to be satisfied before a privileged
action is authorised. The evidence must be valid , meaning integrity measurement
reports no violation; fresh , meaning it describes the platform recently
enough to be informative about it now; and the decision must be timely ,
landing while the physical system can still act on it. A cryptographically valid
quote can be stale; a fresh quote can arrive too late; a timely result can report
a violation. Only the conjunction permits the action, and a binary gate collapses
three distinct reasons for refusal into one, or reports trusted on evidence aged
past usefulness.

We treat the gate as a runtime assurance contract with two margins. The physical
state at a request supplies an authorisation budget through a mission-specific
deadline function, giving a response margin, and the timestamp of the attested
evidence gives a freshness margin against a configured bound. An authorisation is
assurance-valid only when integrity passes and both margins are non-negative, so
the contract has four outcomes rather than two and the outcome names the reason.
Runtime verification supplies the framing for monitoring such obligations over an
execution [ 4 , 10 ] and its extension into
cyber-physical settings is an active concern [ 26 ] ; what we add is
that one bound of the obligation is fixed by physical state at the moment the
obligation is created.

The deadline is a function of physical state, so something has to supply that
state across the operating space. A driving simulator does, at speeds and
geometries impractical to instrument on a road [ 9 ] . The assurance behaviour cannot be obtained the same way,
because its distribution depends on a real TPM, a real integrity-measurement
stack and a real network. Combining the two in a hardware-in-the-loop (HIL)
arrangement, the established way of exercising real components against a
simulated plant [ 16 ] , is what lets us ask where in the simulated
operating space the real security mechanism can meet its contract, and the answer
is a region rather than a number. We describe the simulator as a simulator: it is not synchronised with
or calibrated against a physical intersection, so it is not a digital
twin [ 32 ] .

We formulate mission-aware attestation as a runtime assurance contract
requiring integrity validity, evidence freshness and completion before a
state-dependent physical deadline, with four operational outcomes in place of a
binary verdict, and we show the two margins interact: below a threshold on the
freshness bound, lateness is unobservable (Sect. 3 ).

We formulate mission-aware attestation as a runtime assurance contract
requiring integrity validity, evidence freshness and completion before a
state-dependent physical deadline, with four operational outcomes in place of a
binary verdict, and we show the two margins interact: below a threshold on the
freshness bound, lateness is unobservable (Sect. 3 ).

We give a simulation and HIL methodology that combines simulator-derived
mission state with measured TPM, IMA and verifier behaviour to construct an
attestation envelope, and that compares the envelope admitted by a
security-blind model against that admitted by a hardware-informed one
(Sects. 4 and 5.2 ).

We characterise the envelope empirically and show that the attestation
interval is a design parameter of comparable weight to decision latency, and one
that a deployment can change without touching the hardware
(Sect. 5 ).

The evaluation asks four.

How much of the authorisation budget does the assurance loop consume,
and does channel contention change it?

Over what region of trigger distance, approach speed and evidence age
is the integrity verdict still actionable?

How much does a security-blind model of the physical process
overestimate that region?

How sensitive is the envelope to the attestation interval, against
latency?

Latency is reported as a measured distribution and never as a worst-case bound,
and the deadline enforced is an authorisation-decision budget within the
experimental scenario rather than the full preemption budget a fielded controller
would need [ 11 ] . Sect. 6.1 sets out the remaining
limits.

the requester’s credential, and compromise of the plant are outside the model.

The third capability defeats neither identity checking nor platform integrity,
and could nonetheless deny the privileged action by increasing decision latency
and exhausting the response margin M R M_{R} . The budget D ⁡ ( x r ) D(x_{r}) is fixed by
physical state and is not itself attackable. It is the capability whose reach
this paper measures without exercising it.

## 2.4 Limitations of a Binary Gate

Written as a predicate over a verdict, the gate has two answers, while the scenario
contains four relevant failure cases spanning three distinct causes of refusal.

A rogue or unenrolled requester presents an identity absent from the
admitted table, which is what identity checking is for and the gate reports it.
An enrolled requester whose firmware has been replaced is a different matter;
Sect. 4 explains why this pillar does not address it. A compromised decision point is subtler, because the deciding platform is
itself a target: an attacker able to modify files on V V can change what it
grants.
Binding V V ’s execution to a hardware root of trust is what integrity measurement
adds, and the gate reports that too.

The third failure is a decision that is correct and arrives after the plant has
passed the point at which actuation is usable. The gate returns a verdict and the
verdict is right, and under a fail-secure policy the privileged action is refused
anyway, so the infrastructure stays safe and the requester loses the service.

The fourth is invisible to a binary gate. Platform integrity is periodic, so at
an arbitrary moment the most recent evidence is up to T T old, and up to T max T_{\max} in the worst case the verifier permits. A gate that reads the current
status reports trusted, and what it means is that V V was trusted at some point
within that window. Whether that is adequate is a question about W W rather than about the
cryptography.

2026-10-07.introduction:
Verification is central to self-improvement: it supplies feedback for policy optimization and determines which training examples are worth learning from ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Kumar et al., 2026 ) . However, policy improvement also changes the judge demands, and the rapid progress of foundation models has increasingly outpaced the ability to evaluate them reliably ( Gu et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Most existing approaches rely on a static verification judge, whose capability can quickly become a bottleneck as the policy improves ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . Once the policy approaches or exceeds the judge’s effective verification boundary, the resulting feedback can become increasingly inaccurate, leading to reward hacking, distribution shift, and even performance degradation ( Khalaf et al., 2026 ) . Meanwhile, static training data also become progressively less informative ( Koh et al., 2026 ) for further improvement with verification: as previous scenarios are solved, the training distribution becomes dominated by well-solved samples, leaving limited learning signal. This raises a central question for verification: How can verification be scaled so that the judge, training curriculum, and policy co-evolve to continuously push the performance frontier?

Recent advances in agentic systems and autoresearch ( Anthropic, 2025 ; OpenAI, 2025 ) offer a natural framework to realize this co-evolution task by coordinating specialized skills and analyzing failures during iterative optimization. In this work, we study scaling verification within an agentic framework for embodied reasoning, using driving and robot navigation as representative tasks. Unlike conventional language tasks, embodied agents require reasoning in the physical world and handle spatial grounding, temporal understanding, causal reasoning, and safety-aware decision-making ( Zhang et al., 2025c ) , making reliable verification challenging.

Prior work on verification for embodied reasoning focuses on action quality or task completion ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) , while evaluating free-form embodied reasoning remains underexplored. Existing reasoning evaluators often rely on constrained question-answering formats and costly human-annotated references ( Sima et al., 2024 ) ; even LingoJudge ( Marcu et al., 2024 ) only compares against human reasoning without using visual information. Such reference-based evaluation is difficult to scale and sensitive to annotation noise. In contrast, a reference-free judge can assess reasoning directly from physical context, enabling scalable verification and adaptive data selection that filters well-solved scenarios and prioritizes emerging policy failures.

To this end, we study scaling verification as expanding the ability to recognize emerging policy errors and convert them into reusable supervision, and introduce 0.06275 0.47843 0.73725V0.12157 0.52157 0.63529e0.18039 0.56471 0.53333r0.23922 0.60784 0.43137i0.29804 0.65098 0.32549F0.35686 0.69412 0.22353i0.41569 0.73725 0.12157n0.47451 0.78039 0.01961e \__color_backend_reset: \__color_backend_reset: \__color_backend_reset: \__color_backend_reset: \__color_backend_reset: \__color_backend_reset: \__color_backend_reset: \__color_backend_reset: , an agent harness framework for continuous self-improvement through scaling verification. # 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Scaling Verification.

Verification assesses the quality or correctness of candidate outputs and provides feedback for selection, monitoring, and policy optimization ( Kwok et al., 2026a ) . At inference time, verification can directly enable test-time scaling with a verifier by allocating additional compute to candidate generation, search, and ranking ( Snell et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025d ) , while the fine-grained critics with the verifier can diagnose errors and guide iterative revision or recovery ( Gou et al., 2024 ; Xie et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2026 ) . During training, verification within judges can provide objectives for policy optimization ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) , while also filtering noisy samples and prioritizing high-value data to concentrate learning on unresolved failures ( Zang et al., 2025 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) . Existing work has begun to construct judge benchmarks ( Tan et al., 2025b ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) and explore judge improvement ( Saha et al., 2025 ; Whitehouse et al., 2026 ) . However, existing work focuses on the improvement of the individual roles of verification ( Singh et al., 2026 ) , but does not scale verification to close feedback loops among adaptive data selection, policy optimization, judge evolution, and selective human calibration, thereby continuously pushing the performance frontier.

## 2.2 Self-improvement and Autoresearch.

Agent-driven self-improvement through hypothesis formation, experimentation, and iterative refinement has emerged as a prominent paradigm, particularly in goal-oriented autoresearch ( Schmidgall et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . As self-improvement continuously strengthens the policy model, its verifier must adapt to the resulting capability and distribution
shifts ( Ding et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026b ) . Recent work has begun to consider the policy and judge improvement together ( Zhou et al., 2026a ; Zha et al., 2026 ) or dynamically adapt the judge to policy behavior ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Xu et al., 2026a ) . Rubric-based judges have also gained increasing attention because structured criteria provide fine-grained and more accurate judgment beyond a single final score ( Gunjal et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Nevertheless, autonomous self-improvement eventually encounters bottlenecks when the verifier approaches its effective limit or self-generated feedback becomes unreliable ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . At this stage, a small amount of selectively acquired human guidance can become necessary to recalibrate the judge ( Dwaracherla et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) . We connect this adaptation to curriculum construction: emerging policy failures guide selective human–agent calibration, and the resulting judge refinements shape subsequent data selection and policy optimization.

## 2.3 Embodied Reasoning.

Embodied reasoning requires spatial grounding, temporal understanding, causal reasoning, and safety-aware decision-making ( Xiong et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Lee et al., 2026 ) , making reliable verification challenging. Recent work on driving reasoning has introduced structured reasoning datasets ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026b ) and demonstrated the benefits of reasoning for scene understanding ( Nie et al., 2024 ; Coscoy et al., 2026 ) , generalization ( Peng et al., 2026 ; Gerstenecker et al., 2026 ) , and planning ( Zhou et al., 2026b ; Zhou et al., 2026c ) . However, existing evaluators largely use constrained question-answering formats with costly human references ( Marcu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) , while driving-specific judges mainly assess trajectory quality ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . In robotics, recent judge models focus on evaluating task progress or completion from video ( Ma et al., 2025 ; Tan et al., 2025a ; Huang et al., 2026a ; Liang et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) and action-instruction alignment ( Kwok et al., 2026b ) rather than on high-level free-form reasoning itself. Direct video-grounded verification of free-form embodied reasoning without costly human-annotation references remains underexplored.

2026-10-07.title: Demo: Closed-Loop Sionna-Isaac Sim Co-Simulation Framework for Wireless-Aware Robot Navigation over ROS 2
2026-10-07.authors: Yi Shen Lim , Seungeun Oh , Jihong Park
2026-10-07.comment: . Accepted as a Demo paper at ACM MobiHoc 2026. Demo video: this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract: A robot that offloads its control loop to the network carries the receiver with it, so link quality is decided by where it goes. Simulating this requires both a physics engine and a site-specific propagation model at once; to our knowledge no simulator natively unifies both, with existing couplings of the two limited to offline analyses. We demonstrate a real-time co-simulation framework coupling NVIDIA Isaac Sim and NVIDIA Sionna over ROS 2 that closes the perception–action–communication (PAC) loop between them. Sionna ray-traces the base-station-to-robot channel over the exact geometry Isaac Sim simulates on—rather than modeling it stochastically—and feeds channel states back into the control loop in real time. Ray-traced on GPU, the coverage map is refreshed in ∼ 16 {\sim}16 ms ( ∼ 60 {\sim}60 Hz), fast enough for real-time control. To showcase the framework’s utility, we implement a wireless-aware navigation application in an OpenStreetMap(OSM)-derived SUTD campus twin with two Nova Carter robots: the closed-loop planner eliminates communication outage at only + 7.4 % +7.4\% traversal time over the shortest-path baseline (which spends 7.9 7.9 s of its 81.2 81.2 s run disconnected).
2026-10-07.introduction:
Cloud robotics, teleoperation, and autonomous logistics offload perception and decision-making to edge servers, so a robot’s control loop depends on a low-latency wireless link.
Link quality varies with the robot’s own position, as structures reflect, diffract, and block the signal. Where the robot goes will decide the connectivity it gets, coupling planning and communication into one PAC loop ( Calvo-Fullana and others, 2021 ) .
Safe deployment requires a platform where motion and site-specific propagation can be studied, before a robot meets a dead zone.

No single simulator offers this. Robotic simulators lack channel models, and wireless ones (Sionna ( Hoydis and others, 2023 ) , ns-3) lack physics.
Communication-aware planning ( Muralidharan and Mostofi, 2021 ) feeds the planner a statistical channel map; DT-RaDaR ( Amatare and others, 2024 ) ray-traces an OSM/Blender twin with Sionna, as we do, but once and offline, with no physics engine.
Robot–network co-simulators ( Calvo-Fullana and others, 2021 ) close the PAC loop, but over stochastic propagation.
Ray-tracing twins such as CAVIAR ( Borges and others, 2024 ) , AODT ( NVIDIA, 2025a ) , and SimART ( Yan and others, 2026 ) are site-specific but close the loop only on communication-side decisions (e.g., beam selection), with mobility given, not planned.
None, to our knowledge, combines site-specific ray tracing, a physics engine, and a channel that reaches the motion planner online, at control-loop rates.

We demonstrate a framework that does, coupling NVIDIA Isaac Sim ( NVIDIA, 2025b ) (a GPU-accelerated robotics simulator for physics and sensors) and NVIDIA Sionna ( Hoydis and others, 2023 ) (a differentiable wireless ray tracing library) over ROS 2 (Robot Operating System 2, the standard robotics publish–subscribe middleware), inheriting planning (Nav2, ROS 2’s navigation stack), robot interfacing, and visualization (RViz2) from the ROS 2 ecosystem.
Isaac Sim, Sionna, and the planner exchange states over ROS 2 as asynchronous nodes. The ray-traced coverage map is published as a standard costmap layer that any ROS 2 planner can consume, and a campus-scale demo quantifies the resulting connectivity–travel-time trade-off.

The difficulty is not running the two simulators in parallel but unifying them: both must share one scene geometry—so the ray-traced map registers cell-for-cell with the navigation grid and a moved obstacle casts physical and RF shadows simultaneously—while loops at milliseconds (ray tracing), tens of milliseconds (physics), and seconds (planning) must interlock without stalling.
We resolve the first with a single OSM-derived twin. Its Blender-extruded building footprints serve as Isaac Sim’s physics geometry, Sionna’s ray-tracing scene, and the 0.5 0.5 m navigation grid, so ray-traced cells register with navigation cells and moved obstacles updates all three at once. We resolve the second in real-time, running asynchronous, message-triggered ROS 2 nodes (Sec. 2 ).

2026-10-07.abstract: Learned surgical simulators and world models can roll out plausible procedural futures, but they carry no grounded estimate of how often interventional devices actually harm patients. We propose treating population-scale adverse-event surveillance as a distinct belief layer of the surgical digital twin, and we evaluate a federated Bayesian protocol for learning it under formal privacy guarantees. Each site holds per-class Gamma-Poisson posteriors over adverse-event rates and exchanges only Rényi-differentially-private natural-parameter updates. We benchmark on the complete FDA MAUDE cohort for thrombus-retrieval catheters (product code NRY): 8,617 reports, of which 6,491 are classified by transparent keyword rules into five thrombectomy complication classes and partitioned across K = 8 K{=}8 manufacturer sites. At a matched privacy budget of ( ε ≈ 2.09 , δ = 10 − 5 ) (\varepsilon{\approx}2.09,\delta{=}10^{-5}) , the conjugate protocol attains a held-out Poisson score of − 5.78 -5.78 per test event versus − 26.58 -26.58 for FedAvg with differential privacy. The non-private federated model also outperforms centralized pooling ( + 3.19 +3.19 vs + 2.93 +2.93 ), evidence that manufacturer-specific complication profiles are real and that federation preserves them. Because MAUDE lacks procedure denominators, outputs are relative rate orderings rather than absolute risks, and we report all privacy-utility operating points.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Surgical robotics is increasingly adopting world models, using learned simulators to predict action outcomes before execution. World foundation models now evaluate surgical robot policies in silico [ 1 ] , digital twins are proposed to ground foundation models in operating rooms [ 2 , 3 ] , and surgical digital twin research is developing rapidly [ 4 ] . Endovascular intervention, especially mechanical thrombectomy, is a primary target of this effort.

These systems share a clear blind spot. A learned simulator can predict that a retriever will deform a vessel, but cannot estimate how often retrievers of that class perforate vessels in clinical practice, since that information resides in fragmented, sensitive post-market records rather than surgical video. Real-world failure statistics for thrombectomy devices exist in scattered form: registry studies of the FDA Manufacturer and User Facility Device Experience (MAUDE) database document device-specific complication patterns in peripheral and pulmonary procedures [ 5 , 6 ] , with reproducibility remaining an active concern [ 7 ] . Individual hospitals rarely see enough events to estimate rates reliably, and procedural records cannot be centralized.

We propose that surgical digital twins require a distinct population risk layer : calibrated beliefs over adverse-event rates by device class and complication type, learned across institutions without transferring raw records, to condition per-procedure simulations. This paper introduces this layer and evaluates it on real public data:

A federated Bayesian surveillance protocol. Sites maintain per-class Gamma-Poisson posteriors and exchange only Rényi-differentially-private (RDP) natural-parameter updates of dimension 2 ​ Z 2Z per round. Conjugacy reduces each update to a two-scalar sufficient statistic per class instead of a gradient.

Sites maintain per-class Gamma-Poisson posteriors and exchange only Rényi-differentially-private (RDP) natural-parameter updates of dimension 2 ​ Z 2Z per round. Conjugacy reduces each update to a two-scalar sufficient statistic per class instead of a gradient.

A thrombectomy benchmark from complete public data. We provide the recipe for a manufacturer-federated partition of the complete MAUDE cohort for thrombus-retrieval catheters: 8,617 reports, with 6,491 classified into five complication classes across major thrombectomy manufacturers.

Evidence that federation preserves manufacturer heterogeneity. The federated per-site model outperforms centralized pooling even in the absence of privacy noise, indicating that complication profiles differ across device makers, a structure that pooled models erase.

Scope. This paper evaluates population-level rate estimation on public surveillance data. It does not evaluate per-procedure simulation, device control, or clinical decision-making, and its outputs are not evidence of comparative device safety.

2026-10-07.title: Context-Conditioned Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability for Adaptive Safety Filtering
2026-10-07.authors: Ali Fuat Sahin , Yunus Yazoglu , John Talbot , Zeyuan Feng , James Dallas , Somil Bansal
2026-10-07.abstract: Hamilton–Jacobi reachability constructs safety certificates for specified dynamics and safety constraints, tying each certificate to the deployment context for which it is synthesized. We ask whether a single certificate can instead represent a family of context-dependent safety problems and be queried across deployment conditions without re-synthesis. We learn a backward reachable tube for an eight-state vehicle model conditioned on local boundary geometry, friction coefficient, and adversarial disturbance scale. Geometry enters through an ego-frame boundary observation that defines the local containment constraint, while friction and disturbance scale enter as explicit operating-condition variables. This allows the same value function to be queried across friction coefficients from 0.4 to 2.0 and on geometries absent from synthesis. On 11 held-out evaluation geometries, the certificate maintains containment across the full tested friction range, including simultaneous geometry and grip shifts, while remaining within 1.2 percentage points in intervention rate and 0.09 m/s in speed of certificates re-synthesized with knowledge of the test geometry. We then deploy the certificate as a sampled discrete-time control barrier function filter on a full-scale vehicle near the handling limit. Lateral containment holds in every hardware session under both adversarial driving and autonomous racing, with 99th-percentile acceleration magnitude reaching 0.99 g. Across three certificates evaluated under a fixed autonomous racing controller, lap time varies by only 3.1%, demonstrating that a context-conditioned reachability certificate can transfer to deployment geometries absent from synthesis with modest performance cost.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Safety-critical control depends on knowing not only which states are safe, but under which conditions they are safe. For a vehicle operating near the limit of tire adhesion, those conditions can change substantially across deployments: track geometry determines the admissible region, while tire–road friction determines which states can still be recovered within that region. A safety certificate synthesized for one deployment is therefore tied to the context in which it was constructed.

Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability makes this dependence explicit. Given a dynamics model, safety constraint, and disturbance model, HJ reachability computes a value function whose zero level set separates states from which the constraint can be maintained from those from which it cannot [ 1 , 2 ] . Changing the deployment context can consequently change the reachable set itself. For a vehicle, this occurs not only when the track changes, but also when the available grip differs from the value assumed during synthesis. In particular, a certificate synthesized under optimistic friction can overestimate the set of recoverable states when deployed on lower-grip pavement. This raises a broader question: can a single value function represent a family of context-dependent reachability problems, rather than requiring a new synthesis for every deployment condition?

We learn a backward reachable tube for an eight-state vehicle model conditioned on local boundary geometry, friction coefficient μ \mu , and adversarial disturbance scale s d s_{d} . Geometry is provided as an ego-frame boundary observation, allowing the same value function to be queried at runtime on geometries absent from synthesis. This formulation makes it possible to distinguish the context assumed by the certificate from the conditions encountered by the vehicle, providing a direct way to study transfer under geometry and grip mismatch.

We test the learned certificate in simulation on held-out track geometries and across a range of friction levels, including simultaneous changes in geometry and grip. We compare against certificates re-synthesized for the target geometry or grip condition, quantifying the safety and performance cost of avoiding context-specific synthesis.
The central finding is that context conditioning makes reachability transferable without making it overly conservative: one certificate maintains containment across the tested contexts while staying close in intervention rate and speed to certificates specialized to the test condition.
We then deploy the resulting certificate as a sampled discrete-time control barrier function filter on a full-scale vehicle at a skidpad (Fig. 1 ). The filter is exercised both by a professional driver instructed to approach the boundary and by an autonomous racing controller. Rather than treating absence of violations as the sole measure of success, we characterize both containment and the cost of transfer, including the intervention required to maintain containment and the resulting performance cost.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of context-conditioned HJ reachability for transferable safety certificates across deployment conditions, validated on a full-scale vehicle at the handling limit.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

Vehicle safety at the handling limit. At the limit of grip, vehicle safety is commonly enforced by restricting the vehicle to a set of states considered recoverable, either as constraints in predictive control or as triggers for shared control [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . On full-scale vehicles, Dallas et al. [ 8 ] filter steering and drive commands during drifting using a closed-form safe set with a fixed friction coefficient, identifying adaptation to model uncertainty as an open problem. Closest to our setting, concurrent work learns a control barrier value function by boundary sampling along Pontryagin characteristics and deploys it as a filter for full-scale shared-control drifting [ 9 ] . These works demonstrate safety filtering near the handling limit, but their certificates are synthesized for a specific deployment condition.

Learned reachability and its guarantees. Neural reachability methods have made high-dimensional reachable sets tractable [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , including gradient-free formulations that propagate discrete-time Bellman–Isaacs values without requiring spatial value gradients [ 13 ] . Because a learned value function is an approximation, its zero level set is not a certified safe set; scenario optimization and conformal prediction supply probabilistic correction bounds for learned tubes [ 14 , 15 ] . Such guarantees are typically formulated for specified dynamics and constraints, so extending them across a continuous context space requires additional treatment. We therefore treat our learned tube as an uncertified certificate, report containment empirically, and regard formal verification as complementary.

Conditioning and transfer of safety certificates. Parameter-conditioned reachability represents families of reachable sets by lifting scalar problem parameters, such as disturbance magnitude or obstacle size, into the state [ 16 , 17 ] . Learned safe sets have also been conditioned on perceptual observations of unknown surroundings, for quadrupedal navigation [ 18 ] and for simulated racing from ego-vision [ 19 ] . In these works, the conditioning captures aspects of the surrounding environment while the underlying dynamics remain fixed. Our setting couples two distinct forms of conditioning: local boundary geometry determines the safety constraint, while friction and disturbance scale determine the recoverable envelope under the vehicle dynamics. This combination couples changes in the safety constraint with changes in the recoverable envelope within a single learned representation.

On full-scale vehicles, prior reachability-based filtering has used grid-computed sets over low-dimensional state spaces and has been demonstrated in ordinary driving rather than at the handling limit [ 20 ] . Model mismatch has instead typically been addressed by adapting the dynamics, for example through friction estimation [ 21 , 22 ] or learned corrections to a nominal model [ 23 ] , or by robustifying the barrier condition against parametric uncertainty [ 24 , 25 ] . These approaches modify the model or margin used by the controller; they do not characterize how a learned reachability certificate transfers when deployment conditions differ from those assumed during synthesis. In contrast, our formulation retains a single learned certificate and exposes the relevant deployment conditions as queryable context, allowing transfer to be evaluated directly against certificates re-synthesized for the target condition. This gap is particularly consequential near the handling limit, where modest changes in grip or vehicle dynamics can change the recoverable set. We therefore evaluate transfer both in simulation, across geometry and grip shifts, and on a full-scale vehicle operating near the friction limit.

2026-10-07.title: EmbodiedSmith: Scaling Embodied Data through Recursive Self-Improvement Flywheel in Simulation
2026-10-07.authors: Yikai Qin , Yifei Deng , Mingjian Liang , Wenxuan Song , Zepeng Lin , Zhiyi Jiang , Jiajun Fu , Qiao Sun , Huashuo Lei , Xicheng Gong , Jiayi Chen , Han Zhao , Shuanghao Bai , Pengxiang Ding , Pengwei Wang , Haoang Li
2026-10-07.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-07.abstract: Scaling robotic foundation models requires diverse training data and reliable evaluation environments. Simulation offers a scalable solution, yet existing generation pipelines remain constrained by predefined assets and skills, a disconnect between scene generation and task generation, and limited support for complex embodiments and physics. We introduce EmbodiedSmith, a framework for scalable embodied data generation through recursive self-improvement (RSI). EmbodiedSmith unifies asset, scene, and task generation in a pipeline that supports autonomous creation and language-driven customization. Its core is an agentic refinement loop: scene generation anticipates downstream task requirements, while task generation guides targeted scene edits, allowing scenes and tasks to iteratively improve one another. This joint refinement improves task generation success, including for long-horizon tasks. The framework further supports mobile manipulators, humanoids, and dexterous hands, as well as interactions involving deformable objects and fluids, broadening the range of behaviors and physical phenomena represented in generated data. Together, these capabilities provide a flexible simulation engine for both robot pretraining and evaluation. Extensive experiments validate the quality, diversity, and generation efficiency of the resulting data, while downstream policy experiments demonstrate that increased data diversity improves generalization.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Large-scale pretrained models have been validated as an effective path towards robot generalists that can perform everyday tasks across diverse environments ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026b ) .
A growing body of work has focused on collecting large-scale robot datasets and training high-capacity robotic foundation models.
These models have demonstrated meaningful generalization to novel objects, environments, and tasks, showing great promise towards developing broadly capable policies.

Simulation plays an important role in advancing large-scale pretrained models.
First, as shown in Figure 1 (a), real-world robot data closely matches the target hardware but offers limited diversity and scalability, whereas egocentric and UMI data exhibit the opposite trade-off ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . Simulation data combines scalability and diversity with close alignment to the target hardware, making it an important data source for robot pretraining ( Tian et al., 2026 ; Nasiriany et al., 2026 ; Authors, 2024 ) .
Second, simulation environments enable low-cost, fast, and reproducible large-scale evaluation ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) and provide an ideal evolving environment for robotic agents.
Thus, as recursive self-improvement (RSI) techniques advance ( Weng, 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) , simulation environments are becoming an essential component of robotics infrastructure ( Liu et al., 2026b ; Authors, 2024 ) .

However, existing simulation generation methods still face several limitations:
(1) limited diversity and customizability of scenes, assets, and skills, where the scenes and assets are already available in the dataset and skills are typically predefined or rule-based ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) ;
(2) limited physical realism ( Wang et al., 2026a ) due to inadequate support for deformable objects and fluids, both of which are essential components of the physical world; (3) low task execution success rates, as scene generation is decoupled from robot task generation, leaving the feasibility of planned actions unverified. This issue becomes more pronounced as tasks grow more complex or longer-horizon;
(4) limited support for complex embodiments, including mobile manipulators, dexterous hands, and humanoids. Task generation for these embodiments is challenging ( Li et al., 2026a ) , while missing these embodiments limits robots’ ability to acquire human-like dexterous behaviors.

We introduce EmbodiedSmith, a framework for scalable embodied data generation through RSI. It is structured around four features:

High Data Diversity: We design strong 3D generation methods to generate any novel object, layout, and scene.
Besides, we construct effective agents that autonomously create and compose new skills to accomplish diverse task generation. These generation capabilities, spanning multiple levels of abstraction, are integrated into a unified pipeline that supports autonomous generation and language-driven customization.

Rich Physics Simulation: We support assets and tasks involving more complex physics, including deformable objects and fluids, addressing gaps in existing data diversity and narrowing the gap between simulation and the real physical world.

RSI Data Generation: Scene generation anticipates downstream task requirements, while task generation can revise the scene through targeted editing. This agentic loop enables scene and task generation to recursively refine one another. This process substantially improves task generation success rates, allowing our simulation engine to maintain high success rates even for long-horizon tasks.

Human-level Dexterity : We extend robot task generation to mobile manipulators, humanoids, and dexterous hands, enabling EmbodiedSmith to generate data involving human-like dexterity.

By integrating these components, our EmbodiedSmith provides an effective, flexible, and comprehensive simulation data engine for robotic foundation models. It serves as an efficient source of pre-training data and enables systematic analysis of how task, environment, and embodiment diversity affect pre-trained models. It can also function as an effective evaluator, providing metrics and feedback that facilitate the iterative advancement of foundation models. Through extensive experiments, we validate the quality, diversity, and generation efficiency of the produced environments and demonstrations. Furthermore, experiments integrating the data with downstream policies demonstrate that greater data diversity improves model generalization.

1. High Data Diversity: We design strong 3D generation methods to generate any novel object, layout, and scene.
Besides, we construct effective agents that autonomously create and compose new skills to accomplish diverse task generation. These generation capabilities, spanning multiple levels of abstraction, are integrated into a unified pipeline that supports autonomous generation and language-driven customization.

2. Rich Physics Simulation: We support assets and tasks involving more complex physics, including deformable objects and fluids, addressing gaps in existing data diversity and narrowing the gap between simulation and the real physical world.

3. RSI Data Generation: Scene generation anticipates downstream task requirements, while task generation can revise the scene through targeted editing. This agentic loop enables scene and task generation to recursively refine one another. This process substantially improves task generation success rates, allowing our simulation engine to maintain high success rates even for long-horizon tasks.

4. Human-level Dexterity : We extend robot task generation to mobile manipulators, humanoids, and dexterous hands, enabling EmbodiedSmith to generate data involving human-like dexterity.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

3D Scene Generation. 3D scene generation has been studied through learned generative models, procedural and foundation-model-guided pipelines, and agentic systems. Data-driven methods learn object distributions and spatial relations from 3D scene datasets: DiffuScene and Mixed Diffusion model indoor layouts using diffusion processes ( Tang et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) , while PhyScene introduces collision, accessibility, and interaction constraints to improve physical plausibility ( Yang et al., 2024a ) . Procedural methods instead assemble environments using predefined grammars and geometric rules, as demonstrated by ProcTHOR and Infinigen Indoors ( Deitke et al., 2022 ; Raistrick et al., 2024 ) . To enable open-vocabulary control, foundation-model-guided methods translate user instructions into structured scene layouts through direct coordinate prediction ( Feng et al., 2023 ) , language-guided asset retrieval ( Yang et al., 2024b ) , vision-language-based layout optimization ( Sun et al., 2025a ) , hierarchical scene composition ( Pun et al., 2025 ) , or explicit constraint planning ( Sun et al., 2025b ) . Agentic methods introduce iterative reasoning and refinement, including self-reflective tool use ( Yang et al., 2025 ) and coordinated semantic and physical correction ( Gao et al., 2025 ) . SAGE, SceneSmith, and EmbodiedGen V2 extend this paradigm toward embodied simulation by coupling multi-agent generation with task-aware composition, physical validation, interactive assets, and simulator-ready deployment ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Pfaff et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) .

Sim-ready 3D Assets Generation. 3D asset generation is increasingly moving beyond visual fidelity toward interactive and physically grounded representations required by simulation. To make static assets interactive, articulated generation models part structure and kinematics from visual or geometric inputs, as explored in PAct ( Liu et al., 2026a ) and SIMART ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Agentic approaches further make this process iterative and verifiable, with articulation refined through closed-loop visual feedback in Articulate-Anything ( Le et al., 2024 ) and constructed through program synthesis with executable validation in Articraft ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . Beyond kinematics, physical generation seeks to model how assets behave during interaction. Joint reasoning over geometry, articulation, and physical properties is introduced in PhysX-Anything ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , while functional and kinematic constraints guide asset synthesis in PhysForge ( Yang et al., 2026b ) . Recent work moves toward broader physical grounding through intrinsic property modeling in UniPhysGen ( Li et al., 2026b ) , unified rigid, articulated, and deformable generation in PhysX-Omni ( Cao et al., 2026 ) , and simulation-diagnosed deformable refinement in DiagGen ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . At the system level, automated validation and simulator deployment are integrated with asset generation in EmbodiedGen V2 ( Wang et al., 2025 ) .

Simulated Robot Demonstration Generation. Humanoid simulation benchmarks increasingly cover locomotion and object interaction within the same embodiment. HumanoidBench ( Sferrazza et al., 2024 ) provides a standardized suite of whole-body locomotion and dexterous manipulation tasks, while SIMPLE ( Wei et al., 2026 ) combines contact-rich simulation and photorealistic rendering with motion-planning and teleoperation pipelines for demonstration collection. More directly, HumanoidGen ( Jing et al., 2025 ) generates language-conditioned bimanual tasks and demonstrations through spatial constraints, and HumanoidMimicGen ( Lin et al., 2026 ) adapts segmented source demonstrations to new configurations using whole-body planning. These works establish important benchmark and synthesis capabilities, but their reported settings center on curated task suites, annotated manipulation primitives, or source-demonstration-dependent skill sequences. Mapping newly instantiated scene–task combinations to executable, feasibility-checked whole-body demonstrations through a reusable skill interface remains less systematically examined.
