2026-10-07.title: Revisiting Temporal Regularization for Smooth Control in Deep Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-07.authors: SungJae Ahn , Jeong Woon Lee , Kyoleen Kwak , Hyoseok Hwang
2026-10-07.comment: Submitted to ICRA 2027
2026-10-07.abstract:
Deep Reinforcement Learning policies can produce nonsmooth action oscillations
that hinder deployment on physical robots. Existing architectural and
penalty-based approaches seek spatial smoothness by directly reducing sensitivity to
changes in state inputs, but their broad constraints can degrade task performance
as stronger smoothing is pursued. Temporal regularization instead constrains
action differences along observed transitions, but has been considered unable
to provide the spatial smoothness needed under observation noise. We revisit
this assumption by proving that the temporal penalty bounds the expected action differences
between current states sharing a next state, revealing a spatial effect that
empirically extends to spatial smoothness. Building on this finding, we propose
Conditioning for Action using only Temporal Smoothness (CATS), which
combines a temporal penalty with linear ramp-up. We highlight
temporal regularization’s ability to provide spatial smoothness while better
preserving task performance than explicit spatial regularization.
Through linear ramp-up, CATS allows the policy
to learn rewarding behavior before progressively smoothing its actions,
improving return preservation and both temporal and spatial smoothness.
Experiments in both simulation and the real world show that
CATS substantially reduces action oscillation without degrading task
performance, with little computational overhead.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Deep Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful
framework for continuous control [ 1 ] ,
enabling robots to acquire complex motor skills through interaction
with their environment [ 2 ] .
However, due to optimization instability in deep RL [ 3 ] and observation noise [ 4 , 5 ] , policies for robotic control can produce nonsmooth action oscillations that hinder their deployment on physical systems [ 6 , 7 ] .
Such oscillations not only compromise control reliability [ 8 ] , but also accelerate mechanical wear, jeopardize hardware safety, and increase energy consumption [ 4 , 9 ] .

Reducing action oscillations in real-world deployment
calls for two policy properties, temporal smoothness and spatial smoothness [ 4 ] .
Temporal smoothness refers to low policy sensitivity
to state inputs received over time and directly relates to action
oscillation in simulation. Spatial smoothness refers to low policy sensitivity to small changes
in state inputs, thus reducing sensitivity to real-world noise.
To promote either or both, prior work has
employed corresponding regularization methods.

Although action oscillation is fundamentally a change
in policy outputs over time, many existing methods view action smoothness as a property
of the policy function without considering the temporal ordering of its inputs.
Accordingly, these spatial regularization methods seek spatial smoothness
directly by encouraging actions to vary less across any local state changes.
While these approaches can reduce action oscillation
and noise sensitivity, they act across all state-space directions and may
therefore restrict action changes needed for high return.

Temporal regularization, in contrast, exploits the temporal ordering
of policy inputs to reduce action variation over time. Because it constrains the policy only along
transition directions that are actually observed, it can pursue stronger
smoothness with less degradation in task performance.
This same focus, however, appears to leave other directions
unconstrained, so even a policy that is smooth along its trajectories may remain
sensitive to observation noise in those directions. Temporal
regularization has thus been regarded as unrelated to spatial smoothness and
has commonly been paired with a spatial
penalty [ 4 , 10 , 11 , 3 ] ,
reintroducing broad state-space constraints and leaving the relative
weighting of the two penalties unclear.

The complexity introduced by existing smoothness
methods is another, often underappreciated challenge. While these methods aim
to facilitate real-world deployment by
reducing action oscillation, this complexity can hinder the very deployment
they target. Robotic RL
already involves many interacting hyperparameters and demanding training
pipelines, while evaluations are expensive and performance is sensitive to
configuration choices [ 12 , 13 ] .
Expanding the hyperparameter space or increasing training time
therefore makes smoothness methods harder to apply in practice.

In this work, we aim to develop a practical approach
that achieves both temporal and spatial smoothness while preserving task
performance. To this end, we
revisit the assumption that temporal regularization cannot
provide the spatial smoothness needed under observation noise.
During training, the temporal penalty acts on next
states drawn from a distribution rather than a single fixed next state. When two current states share a next state,
their actions are encouraged to approach the same next-state action,
indirectly becoming similar.
We establish this spatial effect by proving that the temporal penalty bounds
the expected action difference between these states. We further hypothesize that this effect
extends to spatial smoothness when nearby states share
more possible next states (Fig. 1 ). Our experiments confirm this effect and the
resulting spatial smoothness, showing that a temporal penalty alone is
sufficient for both forms of smoothness in the evaluated tasks.

Building on this finding, we propose Conditioning for
Action using only Temporal Smoothness ( CATS ), a lightweight
regularizer that applies a temporal penalty with a
linearly increasing coefficient (linear ramp-up). We highlight
temporal regularization’s ability to provide spatial smoothness while preserving
performance, unlike explicit spatial regularization methods.
Linear ramp-up also strengthens these benefits by allowing the policy
to learn rewarding behavior before smoothing its actions, rather than seeking
rewarding behavior under smoothness constraints.
CATS uses no spatial penalty and adds only one
hyperparameter, with little computational overhead and minimal implementation
changes.

Extensive experiments show that CATS substantially reduces action
oscillation without decreasing return, particularly on higher-dimensional tasks,
and continues to do so under observation noise. We
also directly examine the spatial smoothness induced by CATS, compare it with
that produced by explicit spatial regularization, and introduce a simple
extension that broadens the induced spatial effect. Finally, sim-to-real
experiments show that CATS effectively reduces action oscillation
on a physical robot despite its simple design.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Spatial Regularization

Architectural approaches formulate smoothness solely as a property of
the policy’s input-to-output mapping. These methods
often promote spatial smoothness by reducing the policy’s Lipschitz constant [ 14 ] without assumptions about the input states.
LipsNet [ 15 ] enforces this constraint in its forward pass,
requiring Jacobian computation at inference. LCP [ 9 ] and LipsNet++ [ 5 ] instead constrain
the policy’s Lipschitz constant through computationally expensive gradient-based
penalties during training.

Penalty-based spatial regularization methods seek
spatial smoothness by explicitly penalizing action differences between nearby
states. CAPS [ 4 ] draws
Gaussian-perturbed states around the current state.
L2C2 [ 16 ] narrows the neighborhood using the
displacement between consecutive states. ASAP [ 11 ] aligns the current action with an expected action prediction using
transitions from the previous state. SR 2 L [ 17 ] instead searches for perturbations
through iterative gradient ascent during each policy
update.

## II-B Temporal Regularization

Temporal regularization promotes temporal
smoothness by penalizing policy-output differences along sampled next-state
directions, as in CAPS [ 4 ] .
Grad-CAPS [ 18 ] instead penalizes changes in action differences,
allowing actions to vary while changing smoothly.
However, it requires two consecutive transitions, adding computation and
requiring buffer modifications to retain the additional state.
Because temporal regularization has been regarded as unrelated to spatial
smoothness, prior methods have combined it with a separate spatial
penalty [ 4 , 10 , 11 , 3 ] .
These additional penalties introduce hyperparameters and computational overhead, with no clear
criterion for balancing the two penalties.

Reward penalties are a widely used form of temporal
regularization that penalizes action changes over time, but prior work has
reported that they can instead increase action
oscillation under sparse rewards [ 19 , 15 , 5 ] .
Other approaches exploit temporal information
through policy architectures [ 20 , 21 ] or action-selection mechanisms [ 19 , 22 ] .
Compared with loss-based regularization, these
approaches can increase implementation complexity, hyperparameters, and computational cost.

2026-10-07.title: Belief-Informed Hybrid Control with Almost-Sure Target-Set Convergence
2026-10-07.authors: Clinton Enwerem , Saleh Kemal , John S. Baras , Calin Belta
2026-10-07.subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
2026-10-07.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-07.abstract:
Controlling a hybrid system to a target set under parameter uncertainty can require informative actions that temporarily drive the system state away from the specified set. We propose a belief-informed dual-control algorithm that combines belief-space receding-horizon selection with an expected-decrease constraint on a nonnegative target-set progress function. To accommodate exploratory deviations, a scalar controller state bounds the constraint’s cumulative slack. Our algorithm’s two-step lookahead selection uses predicted observations to update the parameter belief before evaluating the subsequent action’s admissibility. Under distance-comparison bounds, correct conditional prediction, and recursive feasibility, we prove almost-sure target-set convergence at decision times and bound both the sum of expected progress-function values and the expected neighborhood-entry time. Upper confidence bounds extend these convergence guarantees to bounded model samples with summable error probabilities. In planar regulation with an unknown control direction, we verify recursive feasibility: the proposed two-step selection reduces the Euclidean state norm below 0.01 within 11 decisions for either sign, whereas a myopic one-step selection loses admissibility immediately after zero input. In a simulated bimanual assembly task, our algorithm’s one-step implementation uses clearance feedback to complete the assembly under nominal friction, yielding a 96.4% lower infinity-norm relative-position error than the reference-tracking baseline at the method’s completion time. At lower friction, its posterior conditioning successfully detects an empty admissible set, whereas a fixed-prior alternative admits an action that violates the conditional decrease constraint.
Project page: https://clintonenwerem.com/belief-hybrid-control/ .
2026-10-07.introduction:
Consider the bimanual assembly task in Fig. 1 , where a robot with anthropomorphic end-effectors must acquire two free-body parts, align and insert one into the other, and withdraw its end-effectors without perturbing the assembly. Continuous robot and object motion combines with contact- and pose-triggered mode transitions, giving a hybrid control system [ 1 , 2 ] . Unknown friction affects the response to control inputs, while object motion and contact forces inform its estimation [ 3 ] . A probing motion can reveal slip but also displace a part from its desired pose. Requiring immediate progress can therefore exclude actions that improve subsequent decisions. We seek a feedback-action selector that anticipates these physical and informational effects while ensuring convergence to a target set satisfying task requirements. This coupling of regulation and identification also arises in autonomous driving with uncertain surrounding-vehicle models [ 4 ] and industrial process control [ 5 ] .

In stochastic systems, control inputs exert a dual effect: they drive the system toward a target while reducing uncertainty that affects future decisions [ 6 ] . Dual and adaptive predictive control methods address this coupling by anticipating future observations and parameter-estimation error [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] , but at substantial computational cost. Tractable belief-space methods therefore introduce approximations such as nominal observations [ 10 ] , Gaussian beliefs [ 11 ] , or localized sequential action optimization [ 12 ] in place of full belief-state dynamic programming [ 13 , 14 ] .

Uncertainty alone, however, does not capture systems that also undergo discrete mode transitions. Hybrid stability theory provides the corresponding framework for continuous flows, discrete jumps, and target sets [ 1 ] , encompassing switched systems [ 15 ] , rigid-body impacts [ 16 ] , and stochastic recurrence [ 17 , 18 ] . Control Lyapunov functions and receding-horizon methods [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] then provide tools for enforcing progress across such dynamics. Recent work extends these ideas to belief evolution in POMDPs [ 22 ] , bringing hybrid stability and stochastic estimation into a common setting.

Belief-space control functions regulate both task progress and estimation uncertainty, coupling information gathering with goal reaching and safety [ 23 , 24 ] . We build on this perspective by defining a progress function over the observed hybrid state and using the parameter posterior to predict the endpoints of feedback actions through both flows and jumps. A conditional expected-decrease constraint allows temporary increases through bounded cumulative slack while preserving the convergence argument for recursively feasible selectors. Posterior-conditioned lookahead then ranks actions by possible next-observation outcomes, while hybrid barrier conditions [ 2 ] restrict the candidate actions to those satisfying safety requirements.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate hybrid action selection with bounded cumulative slack and posterior-dependent two-step lookahead ( Secs. II , III and IV , Alg. 1 ). Second, under distance comparison, correct prediction, and recursive feasibility, we prove almost-sure target-set convergence and bound the sum of expected progress-function values and expected neighborhood-entry time ( Thm. 1 ), with a sampled extension ( Prop. 1 ). Third, we verify the convergence hypotheses and informative lookahead in planar regulation ( Sec. 2026-10-07.title: Preserving Unstable Modes Through Inverse Dynamics in JEPA World Models
2026-10-07.authors: Leonardo F. Toso , Yann LeCun , James Anderson , Oumayma Bounou
2026-10-07.subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
2026-10-07.abstract: Robotic systems often exhibit unstable modes, along which small perturbations and disturbances can cause unbounded growth unless corrected through feedback. Controlling such systems from high-dimensional visual observations requires representations that preserve these modes. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) provide a natural framework for learning such representations and their dynamics from visual data. However, we demonstrate that next step prediction combined with anti-collapse regularization does not guarantee that controllable unstable modes are preserved: the training loss can be minimized while these modes are collapsed, making stabilization from the learned representation impossible. To address this, we augment world-model training with an action reconstruction objective (i.e., an inverse dynamics loss) that encourages control-aware representations, namely, visual representations that preserve crucial features for control. We prove that exact action reconstruction makes the encoder injective on the finite-horizon reachable subspace. Thus, the encoder cannot discard any state direction reachable by an action sequence within H H steps. Moreover, we show that, as H H grows, the dominant eigenspace of the finite-horizon controllability Gramian converges to the controllable unstable subspace. We establish our theoretical results for linear systems and demonstrate empirically that our findings extend to nonlinear visual control tasks (CartPole, Walker2D, and PointMaze), highlighting the benefits of control-aware representation learning.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Quadrotors and legged robots operate around unstable equilibria where small perturbations can grow catastrophically without corrective feedback ( Mellinger and Kumar, 2011 ; Ames et al., 2014 ) . Controlling such systems requires actions that not only minimize a cost (e.g., goal reaching), but also stabilize the physical dynamics; otherwise, incorrect feedback can rapidly drive the system from its intended operating regime and compromise safe deployment ( Ames et al., 2016 ; Marco et al., 2021 ) .

Latent world models have found their way into robotics as a computationally efficient solution for learning dynamics and designing control actions from high-dimensional sensory observations. They compress pixel observations into a lower-dimensional representation, learn action-conditioned latent dynamics, and optimize actions by rolling out these dynamics, with limited interaction with the physical system ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2019 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ; Hafner et al., 2021 ; Hafner et al., 2023 ) . Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) follow this recipe without pixel-level reconstruction ( LeCun, 2022 ; Sobal et al., 2025 ; Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ) : an encoder extracts a latent representation, a predictor forecasts its evolution, and anti-collapse mechanisms (e.g., SIGReg ( Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ) , EMA ( Assran et al., 2023 ) , and others ( Bardes et al., 2021 ) ) prevent representation collapse. Planning can then be performed efficiently directly in this learned latent space ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Toso et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) . However, deploying JEPAs on unstable systems remains largely unexplored.

When actions are designed using the learned latent representation and dynamics, the representation must preserve the physical information required for feedback control.
For open-loop unstable systems, this requires preserving the unstable modes that feedback must observe and correct
(Lemma 1 ) ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Werner and Peherstorfer, 2024 ; Toso et al., 2025 ; Lutkus et al., 2025 ) . That is, if a controller cannot “see” an unstable mode, it cannot stabilize it.

However, learning to accurately predict latent dynamics while preventing representation collapse does not guarantee that this control-theoretic information is preserved.
In fact, the objective combining next-step prediction and anti-collapse regularization, the standard recipe for JEPAs, can be minimized while the encoder discards every unstable mode (Lemma 2 ).
To preserve these modes, we augment the JEPA predictive learning objective with an “endpoint inverse-dynamics” (EP-IDM) loss, which reconstructs the underlying action sequence from the initial and final latent states (see Figure 1 ), so that the encoder cannot discard directions the actions can reach ( Mhammedi et al., 2020 ; Ivashkov et al., 2026 ) .
Our contributions are summarized below.

Prediction does not guarantee stabilization. We show that a controller acting on the latent states can stabilize the system if and only if the encoder keeps every unstable mode (Lemma 1 ). We then show, with SIGReg as the anti-collapse regularizer, that the training objective can reach its minimum while the encoder discards all unstable modes (Lemma 2 ).

Prediction does not guarantee stabilization. We show that a controller acting on the latent states can stabilize the system if and only if the encoder keeps every unstable mode (Lemma 1 ). We then show, with SIGReg as the anti-collapse regularizer, that the training objective can reach its minimum while the encoder discards all unstable modes (Lemma 2 ).

Inverse dynamics preserves unstable modes. We introduce EP-IDM, which reconstructs the action sequence from the initial and final latent states. We prove that, with sufficient action excitation, exact reconstruction keeps every direction reachable within H H steps, and hence every unstable mode reachable within H H steps (Theorem 1 ).

Unstable subspace recovery. We prove that, as H H grows, the dominant eigenspace of the finite-horizon controllability Gramian converges to the unstable subspace (Theorem 2 ).

Numerical validation. We show on synthetic linear systems and a linearized CartPole that EP-IDM preserves the unstable direction and enables latent stabilization, while SIGReg does not. We further validate the benefits of EP-IDM on nonlinear visual control tasks (CartPole, Walker2D, and PointMaze), where representations and dynamics are learned from images and proprioceptive measurements.

# 2 Related Work

Our work lies at the intersection of joint-embedding predictive world models and latent feedback stabilization.

Joint embedding predictive world models. JEPAs learn representations by predicting future latent states rather than reconstructing pixels ( LeCun, 2022 ; Assran et al., 2023 ) . Recent work applies this recipe to action-conditioned prediction and planning using pre-trained visual encoders ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Toso et al., 2026 ) , end-to-end anti-collapse mechanisms ( Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ; Maes et al., 2026 ; Kuang et al., 2026 ) , or objectives that shape latent dynamics and geometry ( Sobal et al., 2025 ; Parthasarathy et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Nath et al., 2026 ) . While this body of work primarily addresses total representation collapse and planning, we demonstrate that standard JEPA objectives can selectively collapse directions required for feedback stabilization.

Most closely related, Ivashkov et al. (2026) use one-step inverse dynamics to prevent collapse. We share the principle that actions provide a control-relevant learning signal but we study feedback stabilization of open-loop unstable systems. Our EP-IDM loss reconstructs the entire action sequence from the endpoint latent states. We prove that exact reconstruction preserves the finite-horizon reachable subspace and characterize its convergence to the controllable unstable subspace, connecting action reconstruction to detectability and latent stabilizability.

Latent feedback stabilization. Control from visual observations requires retaining the state information needed for stabilization. Prior work studies stabilization of linear systems under unknown nonlinear observation maps ( Mhammedi et al., 2020 ) , characterizes the sample complexity of learning to stabilize ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Werner and Peherstorfer, 2024 ) , and learns low-dimensional unstable subspace representations ( Toso et al., 2025 ; Lutkus et al., 2025 ) . In particular, preserving only the unstable subspace can suffice, since stable modes already decay without correction ( Toso et al., 2025 ) . More than just constructing those sufficient representations, we also ask whether standard JEPA training can learn them in the first place. In particular, we connect latent world model training objectives to the control-theoretic information that their representations must preserve.

2026-10-07.title: MRPilot: Supervising and Intervening LLM-Based Multi-Robot Teams through Mixed Reality
2026-10-07.authors: Xiaoran Yang , Xun Qian , Yang Zhan , Nathan Tran , Ziyi Liu , Qiao Jin
2026-10-07.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) let users direct heterogeneous multi-robot systems (MRS) through natural language, but make task interpretation, robot assignment, and coordination difficult to inspect and change. Based on a formative study with 12 non-expert users, we developed MRPilot, a mixed reality system organized around four stages of supervision and intervention. MRPilot represents robot-team plans and execution states as structured commitments shared across synchronized situated and overview views. Across four stages, it helps users resolve ambiguous references (Forming), review plans before execution (Reviewing), monitor distributed execution (Following), and make robot-level or team-level changes when problems arise (Repairing). In a within-subjects study with 20 participants in a virtual reality-simulated home, MRPilot reduced workload, increased situational awareness, transparency, trust, and perceived control compared with a conventional LLM-based conversational interface using the same LLM planner and robot capabilities. We provide design implications for multi-scale intervention, adaptive supervision, and calibrated reliance in LLM-based MRS.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Multi-robot systems (MRS) consist of multiple robots that coordinate to complete shared or related tasks ( Rizk et al., 2019 ; Parker, 2008 ) .
Traditional MRS interfaces often require users to specify tasks, assign robots, define routes or waypoints, and manage execution through system-specific controls ( Chen et al., 2010 ; Chen and Barnes, 2014 ) . Large language models (LLMs) allow users to instead describe high-level goals in natural language. The system can then interpret the instruction, decompose it into subtasks, assign robots based on their capabilities, and produce a coordinated execution plan ( Kannan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Mandi et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) .
However, transferring this coordination work to an LLM can make task interpretation, robot allocation, and planning decisions less visible to users ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Ren et al., 2023 ) .
Because LLMs may misinterpret underspecified instructions or generate actions that do not fit the current context ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) , human supervision remains necessary for supplying context, evaluating plans, and correcting execution ( Chen and Barnes, 2014 ; Parasuraman et al., 2000 ) .

Effective human supervision and intervention in LLM-based MRS remain challenging. First, LLM-generated plans may appear plausible while containing errors, such as assigning tasks to robots without the required capabilities or omitting necessary preconditions ( Huang et al., 2022 ; Kannan et al., 2024 ) . Users therefore need to inspect and revise task interpretations, robot assignments, action dependencies, and planning rationales before and during execution. Second, multi-robot execution is spatially distributed and interdependent. Robots may operate outside the user’s field of view ( Chen et al., 2007 ; Roldán et al., 2017 ; Walker et al., 2023 ) , and understanding one robot’s behavior often requires relating it to the broader execution structure ( Korsah et al., 2013 ; Nunes et al., 2017 ) . In heterogeneous MRS, this also requires users to relate each robot’s capabilities to its assigned role ( Rizk et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) . Such plans combine spatial information about robots, objects, and locations; temporal relationships among actions; and contextual constraints ( Korsah et al., 2013 ; Gombolay et al., 2018 ) . These relationships can be difficult to inspect and modify through chronological text-based interfaces ( Ge et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) .

Mixed Reality (MR) may support the supervision of spatially distributed MRS by embedding task states, planned actions, and robot-specific information in the physical environment, directly linking them to the entities and locations they describe ( Suzuki et al., 2022 ; Walker et al., 2023 ; Walker et al., 2018 ) . Such situated representations can reduce the need to mentally map abstract interface information onto the environment ( Hedayati et al., 2018 ; Szafir and Szafir, 2021 ) . However, spatial embedding can also increase visual search and perceptual costs, whereas 2D overview representations can better support comparison and global decision-making ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Existing interfaces provide limited support for connecting the LLM’s interpretation and planning decisions with the spatial and temporal structure of multi-robot execution. It remains unclear how an interface can support users in inspecting instruction interpretation, evaluating coordination plans, maintaining awareness during execution, and making targeted corrections.

To identify the specific breakdowns and user needs that such an interface should address, we first conducted a formative study with 12 participants interacting with an LLM-based MRS. Based on the findings, together with prior work on situated visualization and overview visualization, we developed MRPilot, an MR system for spatially situated supervision and intervention of LLM-based MRS . MRPilot represents planning decisions as structured commitments that connect each robot action to its referents, location, dependencies, and rationale across the LLM planner, interface, and robot execution. Its workflow supports users in resolving ambiguous references during Forming, inspecting and modifying plans during Reviewing, monitoring spatially distributed execution during Following, and making robot- or team-level corrections during Repairing.
We compared MRPilot with a conventional text-and-voice LLM-based interface in a within-subjects study with 20 participants in a Virtual Reality (VR)-simulated home. The results showed that MRPilot reduced task completion time compared with the conventional interface. It also showed improvements in transparency, trust, situation awareness, and workload. The qualitative results further showed that intuitive interaction, spatial visualization, and visualization of the execution process were three key factors through which MRPilot improved users’ situation awareness and trust, while also introducing corresponding challenges. At the same time, these mechanisms introduced some interaction costs, field-of-view limitations, and issues with explainability.

This work makes three contributions:

Empirical findings from a formative study characterizing how non-expert users supervise LLM-based heterogeneous MRS and the difficulties they encounter during this process.

MRPilot, an MR system that supports spatially situated supervision and intervention in LLM-based MRS through coordinated situated and overview representations.

Findings from a controlled within-subjects study comparing MRPilot with a conversational interface for supervising and intervening in an LLM-based heterogeneous MRS.

1. Empirical findings from a formative study characterizing how non-expert users supervise LLM-based heterogeneous MRS and the difficulties they encounter during this process.

2. MRPilot, an MR system that supports spatially situated supervision and intervention in LLM-based MRS through coordinated situated and overview representations.

3. Findings from a controlled within-subjects study comparing MRPilot with a conversational interface for supervising and intervening in an LLM-based heterogeneous MRS.

# 2. Related Work

## 2.1. LLM-based Heterogeneous Multi-Robot System

Heterogeneous multi-robot systems (MRS) combine complementary morphologies and capabilities and are suited to complex real-world tasks ( Tranzatto et al., 2022 ) .
However, heterogeneity complicates interaction. Allocation must account for each robot’s capabilities rather than workload alone ( Wang and Lewis, 2008 ) , and plans must be coordinated across robots with different action spaces ( Wang and Lewis, 2007 ) . Users must therefore integrate information from multiple robots, increasing workload and reducing situation awareness ( Roldán et al., 2017 ; Dahiya et al., 2023 ) . Controllers and task specifications also typically require expert programming for each task, which is slow and hard to adapt during deployment ( Strobel et al., 2024 ) .
LLMs reduce this burden but introduce new problems. First, users act only as one-time instruction providers at the start of a task ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and the capability-matching process is invisible to them ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Second, LLM errors are hard to correct in time ( Feng et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) : models may produce hallucinated or inconsistent plans, refer to nonexistent objects, or propose infeasible actions ( Rivera et al., 2025 ; Yao et al., 2026 ) that look plausible until inspected ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . Heterogeneity adds cross-robot state errors, such as one robot pursuing a subgoal another has already completed ( Yu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) ; once execution begins, such errors accumulate with few chances to intervene. Third, whereas traditional interfaces expose robot states through camera feeds and maps ( Dahiya et al., 2023 ) , LLM-based systems drive behavior through model decisions whose reasoning is hidden ( Das et al., 2021 ) , limiting failure anticipation and diagnosis and reducing trust ( Yıldız et al., 2026 ) .
Existing feedback mechanisms allow robots to report failures to the LLM, which can reassign tasks or request operator help ( Li et al., 2025b ; Borate et al., 2026 ; Hasegawa et al., 2026 ) . These mechanisms primarily support system-initiated recovery, involving users only after the system detects a failure ( Hasegawa et al., 2026 ) . To support continuous human-in-the-loop monitoring and intervention in LLM-based heterogeneous MRS, we begin with user needs and focus on small-scale robot teams of 2–5 robots with 2–5 morphologies, typical of current systems ( Kannan et al., 2024 ; Mandi et al., 2024 ) .

## 2.2. Human Supervision and Intervention in Multi-Robot Systems

Human oversight of MRS involves two related activities: supervision and intervention ( Sheridan, 1992 ) . Supervision requires operators to acquire and interpret current system states and anticipate future ones ( Parasuraman et al., 2000 ) . Traditional MRS interfaces support this process by presenting each robot’s video and status ( Wang and Lewis, 2007 ) , while exposing team plans and decision rationales can improve supervisory performance and support calibrated trust without increasing workload ( Mercado et al., 2016 ; Chen and Barnes, 2014 ) . LLM-based MRS add another layer because plans are generated from natural-language instructions during interaction rather than specified in advance ( Kannan et al., 2024 ; Mandi et al., 2024 ) . Operators must therefore understand how the model interprets instructions, assigns robots, and coordinates their actions. Some systems expose parts of this process through inter-robot dialogue ( Mandi et al., 2024 ) , but these logs grow with team size ( Chen et al., 2024b ) and lack structured views ( Epperson et al., 2025 ) .
Intervention refers to corrective actions humans take to modify or redirect autonomous behavior ( Steinfeld et al., 2006 ) . It includes teleoperating a robot ( Sheridan, 1992 ) , taking over a subtask ( Sellner et al., 2006 ; Scerri et al., 2002 ) , reallocating tasks, or invoking predefined plays ( Miller and Parasuraman, 2007 ; Parasuraman et al., 2005 ) , and may be initiated by the operator or system ( Sellner et al., 2006 ; Li et al., 2025b ) . LLM-based systems support task-level intervention by allowing users to confirm or modify assignments ( Li et al., 2025b ) and provide corrective natural-language feedback ( Ji et al., 2026 ) . However, intervention remains concentrated before execution or after failure ( Li et al., 2025b ; Ji et al., 2026 ) , with limited support for targeted corrections during execution.
MRPilot addresses this gap by presenting team plans and execution states through linked situated MR and overview views while supporting robot- and team-level intervention through spatial selection, direct controls, and natural-language commands.

## 2.3. Mixed Reality in Multi-Robot System

Mixed reality (MR) registers virtual content with the physical world ( Azuma, 1997 ; Cao et al., 2019 ) , allowing robot states and planned actions to be presented at their referenced locations ( Walker et al., 2018 ; Yanco et al., 2004 ) . Spatial cues such as trajectories, goal markers, and anchored labels can communicate robot intent and support situation awareness ( Suzuki et al., 2022 ; Walker et al., 2018 ; Hedayati et al., 2018 ; Debernardis et al., 2013 ) . MR also supports situated intervention by allowing operators to refer to robots, objects, and locations through pointing or gaze and to create or edit waypoints in place ( Williams et al., 2019 ; Suzuki et al., 2022 ) .
However, MR provides an egocentric and partial view, whereas MRS supervision requires a persistent overview of the robot team ( Rule and Forlizzi, 2012 ) . Spatial overlays can also become cluttered as robot numbers increase ( Rule and Forlizzi, 2012 ) , head-mounted displays are poorly suited to dense text ( Rzayev et al., 2018 ) , and map views can better communicate global task structure ( Liu et al., 2026 ) .
This combination is particularly relevant to LLM-based MRS. Their textual plans are repeatedly revised ( Mandi et al., 2024 ) and accumulate during execution ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , allowing the current plan to become buried in a linear text stream ( Jiang et al., 2023 ) . Because these plans encode spatial information ( Kannan et al., 2024 ; Mandi et al., 2024 ) , MR can connect plan steps to their objects and locations, helping users identify inconsistencies between the plan and environment ( Chandan et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . MR can also ground open-ended instructions through speech and spatial reference ( Williams et al., 2019 ) and bind dialogue-based corrections ( Kim et al., 2024 ) to selected robots or plan elements ( Krupke et al., 2018 ) . Yet prior MR robotics work focuses mainly on individual robots ( Suzuki et al., 2022 ; Walker et al., 2018 ; Hedayati et al., 2018 ) or MRS with predefined behaviors ( Adekoya et al., 2026b ) . LLM-based MRS instead remain largely text-based ( Li et al., 2026 ) , requiring users to infer team states and robot identities from dialogue ( Mandi et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025b ) without direct spatial links to the robots or environment ( Yang et al., 2026b ) .
Building on these complementary strengths, we investigate how linked overview and situated MR representations can support plan inspection, execution monitoring, and targeted intervention in LLM-based MRS.

2026-10-07.title: Sim-to-Real Transfer of Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments Using an Ackermann-Steered Mobile Robot
2026-10-07.authors: Chalindu Abeywansa , Sahan Gunasekara , Devindi De Silva , Seniru Dissanayake , Ranga Rodrigo , Peshala Jayasekara
2026-10-07.abstract:
Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) enables robots to navigate through environments using natural language instructions, making human-robot interaction intuitive.
Traditional VLN models often rely on navigation graphs, 360-degree views, and perfect localization which pose significant challenges when adapting these models to real-world settings. This work addresses these limitations by performing a simulation-to-real domain shift of a VLN approach that operates in continuous environments without requiring navigation graphs or panoramic views. The proposed system integrates vision-language models that align visual inputs and linguistic instructions within a shared embedding space, facilitating natural language-driven navigation.
We employ a Cross-Modal Attention (CMA) based architecture trained on an existing dataset in a simulated environment and fine-tune it using real-world data collected from a custom-built Ackermann-steered robot equipped with a camera and a LiDAR sensor.
By utilising linear photometric adjustments and fine-tuning on a limited number of episodes, our model successfully adapts to real-world environments, achieving effective navigation while running offline on dedicated hardware. Experimental results, evaluated using Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) and Normalized Dynamic Time Warping (nDTW) metrics, demonstrate the robustness and adaptability of our approach.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Vision-Language Navigation (VLN), where robots navigate through an environment by following natural language instructions, has garnered significant attention due to its intuitive approach to robotic control. This emerging field leverages the ability of vision-language models to map visual data (from images captured by the robot) and language instructions into a shared embedding space, enabling the prediction of actions within a specified action space.

Most early VLN studies use simulated environments, which were often discrete [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . These implementations frequently rely on: (i) oracle navigation, which is capable of accurately traversing multiple meters in the presence of obstacles; (ii) known topology, where agents operate on a fixed network of traversable nodes (graph); (iii) ideal 360-degree panoramic RGB imagery and depth information; and (iv) perfect localization, where agents are given their precise location and heading at all times. These assumptions present a major challenge when transferring VLN models trained in simulated environments to real-world continuous environments.

Transferring a VLN agent from a simulated environment to the real world (sim-to-real) introduces additional complexities [ 6 ] .
Visual domain gaps can exist between the simulated training environment and the real world due to differences in the camera quality, dynamic range, and lighting conditions.
Viewpoint variations, even slight ones, can degrade the agent’s performance.
In simulations, the VLN agent is trained with a high-level discrete action space, yet real robots operate in a continuous low-level motor control space.
While the sim-to-real work by Anderson et al. [ 6 ] is notable for being one of the first such implementations, it relies on SLAM [ 7 ] for navigation in physical world.

To bring VLN significantly closer to real-world scenarios, Krantz et al. [ 8 ] introduced VLN-CE, which removes the need for discrete graph assumptions while adopting a more generalized approach for navigation in continuous environments. It uses a 3D continuous environment simulator (Habitat) [ 9 ] for the VLN task. Nevertheless, as a simulation-based work, it cannot be directly applied to an embodied real-world implementation due to the aforementioned sim-to-real challenges.

In this work, we present a real-world VLN framework leveraging VLN-CE while addressing sim-to-real complications. Our model encodes the image and depth information using two ResNet50 networks and encodes natural language instructions using a Bi-LSTM encoder. Then, through cross-modal attention, we predict an action among a discrete action space. We train our model using the VLN-CE [ 3 ] dataset in simulated environment.
Then, through linear photometric adjustments and fine-tuning, we enhance the model performance in real-world settings.
We used a custom Ackermann-steered mobile robot to implement the sim-to-real VLN system utilizing Robot Operating System (ROS) [ 10 ] framework.
We validate the efficacy of our approach through experiments demonstrating the robot’s ability to interpret and follow language instructions across diverse real-world settings.

The contributions of this work are as follows:

We introduce a VLN sim-to-real architecture without navigation graphs and 360-degree views.

We demonstrate successful navigation in real-world indoor environments using an Ackermann-steered mobile robot with minimal fine-tuning in sim-to-real transfer.
To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to attempt VLN using an Ackermann-steered robot.

We provide a ROS implementation for offline VLN system deployment, enabling practical applications.

1. We introduce a VLN sim-to-real architecture without navigation graphs and 360-degree views.

2. We demonstrate successful navigation in real-world indoor environments using an Ackermann-steered mobile robot with minimal fine-tuning in sim-to-real transfer.
To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first to attempt VLN using an Ackermann-steered robot.

3. We provide a ROS implementation for offline VLN system deployment, enabling practical applications.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Vision-Language Navigation

The concept of VLN was first introduced by Anderson et al. [ 3 ] , and their work laid the foundation for the VLN task, where the agent perceives its surroundings through RGB images and navigates based on high-level language commands.
This pioneering effort utilized the Room-to-Room (R2R) [ 3 ] dataset, a benchmark for training and evaluating VLN models in simulated environments.
Subsequent research in VLN [ 1 , 2 , 11 ] has largely focused on enhancing the model’s ability to interpret language and visual inputs more effectively. Early models, such as those based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and attention mechanisms, demonstrated the feasibility of combining visual and linguistic modalities for navigation tasks [ 8 , 12 ] . However, these models were often constrained to discrete environments and action spaces, limiting their application to pre-defined environments with fixed viewpoints and requiring navigation graphs for path planning.

## II-B Navigation Graphs

Models operating in discrete action spaces rely on predefined navigation graphs that map out possible routes within the environment [ 13 , 14 ] . These navigation graphs consist of nodes (representing specific locations) and edges (representing navigable paths between nodes), facilitating structured movement from one point to another. This approach faces significant limitations when applied to real-world scenarios.
Moreover, the reliance on 360-degree views and exact localization is often unachievable in real-world applications, where visual input may be obstructed or incomplete due to environmental factors.

## II-C Sim-to-Real Transfer

Sim-to-real transfer has been a crucial focus in VLN to bridge the gap between performance in simulated environments and real-world applications.
Early works in VLN achieved notable success by training agents in high-fidelity simulated environments with controlled settings, predefined maps, and panoramic images [ 2 , 1 , 3 , 15 ] .
These simulated environments allowed researchers to evaluate navigation tasks using structured visual data and idealized conditions, but transitioning these systems to the real world introduced substantial challenges. Visual domain gaps can exist between the simulated environment and the real world due to differences in the camera quality, dynamic range, and lighting conditions.
One of the main difficulties is the sim-to-real gap, which encompasses discrepancies in visual quality, and the sensor fidelity of real-world environments.
Anderson et al. [ 6 ] addressed these challenges by employing domain randomization to handle visual differences and using a subgoal prediction model to translate high-level actions from simulation into the continuous, real-world action space required by physical robots. Their work demonstrated that sim-to-real transfer is feasible with the support of pre-mapped environments and annotated navigation graphs, but performance degraded significantly when these aids were removed, underscoring the limitations of sim-to-real strategies in previously unseen settings.
LM-Nav [ 16 ] leverages pre-exploration and large pretrained models to enhance navigation in complex environments, relying heavily on external processing and prior knowledge.
In contrast, our implementation does not depend on precomputed maps, allowing the robot to operate autonomously in unknown environments with limited processing power.

## II-D Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments

The transition from discrete, graph-based navigation to continuous environments has been a significant step forward in the development of VLN systems. VLN in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) by Krantz et al. [ 8 , 12 ] , comes first in that transition.
VLN-CE [ 8 ] focuses on enabling agents to operate in more realistic, unbounded settings where actions are not restricted to a set of predefined paths. The action space of VLN-CE results in significantly longer-horizon tasks, with an average of 55.88 steps compared to the 4-6 steps typical in discrete environments (R2R). While recent research enhances VLN in continuous environments, it still relies on the use of pre-computed navigation graphs [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] and 360-degree panoramic visuals [ 12 ] , and remains limited to simulation-only implementations.

2026-10-07.title: R2RI: A Multi-View Event and RGB Dataset for Robot-to-Robot Interaction
2026-10-07.authors: Gabriele Magrini , Riccardo Catalini , Federico Becattini , Guido Borghi , Pietro Pala , Roberto Vezzani , Lorenzo Seidenari
2026-10-07.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-07.abstract:
Understanding and modeling interactions between autonomous agents is a fundamental challenge in robotics, with broad implications for collaborative systems, social robotics, and human-robot coexistence. Although the study of robot interactions has emerged as a compelling research direction, progress has been severely hampered by the absence of large-scale benchmarks. In this paper, we introduce Robot-to-Robot Interaction (R2RI), the first dataset specifically designed to address the Robot-Robot Interaction (RRI) task. R2RI consists of different humanoid robots and realistic interactions modeled on real human social behaviors. Complementary viewpoints are available, i.e. , an egocentric perspective from each robot’s onboard sensors, and an exocentric perspective from external fixed cameras, thus enabling rich spatial and contextual understanding of the interaction dynamics.
The dataset comprises more than 6.5 6.5 M frames and ≈ 5000 \approx 5000 videos at 120 120 fps, including Event and RGB domains. We investigate pros and cons of each domain, comparing state-of-the-art approaches for a number of key sensing and interaction based tasks.
We publicly release the dataset and its annotations for all tasks and modalities at https://github.com/MagriniGabriele/R2RI .
2026-10-07.introduction:
As autonomous robotic systems are increasingly deployed in shared environments - factories, hospitals, public spaces, and homes - endowing them with analogous interaction-aware capabilities becomes not merely desirable, but essential [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . However, while substantial research has been devoted to Human-Robot Interaction (HRI) [ 4 ] and, more broadly, to the perception of human actions and intentions, the specific problem of Robot-Robot Interaction (RRI) has received comparatively little systematic attention. Yet this is a setting with profound practical relevance: multi-robot systems must coordinate, negotiate space, communicate intent, and avoid conflict in real time, often without explicit communication channels and under strict latency constraints [ 5 , 6 ] .

Despite the rapid evolution of robotic hardware and learning-based control systems [ 7 , 8 ] , progress in data-driven interaction modeling remains constrained by the scarcity of large-scale, diverse, and publicly available interaction datasets. Existing data collections, as detailed in the following, often suffer from limited viewpoint diversity, limited robot types, narrow task definitions, or reliance on a single sensing modality. As a result, current models are bounded by scarce data availability [ 5 ] , and as such, complex and complete analysis on their performances are limited.
At the same time, acquiring real-world data is expensive, time-consuming, and difficult to scale due to strict safety constraints. Furthermore, the annotation process of real sensor streams is prone to noise and human error. To circumvent these limitations, synthetic data is a viable alternative as it provides a highly controllable, safe, and scalable environment to automatically generate massive amounts of perfectly annotated, multi-modal data.
Following these motivations, we present Robot-to-Robot Interaction (R2RI) , the first large-scale synthetic dataset specifically designed for the Robot-Robot Interaction (RRI) task. Several key properties distinguish R2RI: first, it consists of multiple models of recent commercial humanoid robots; second, it adopts a multiview capture strategy, providing both egocentric streams from each robot’s onboard sensors and exocentric streams from static external cameras. Egocentric data reflects the information actually available to a robot during deployment, while exocentric data provides the global spatial context necessary for a complete understanding of the interaction. Third, the dataset is multimodal, offering synchronized RGB images and event camera data.
Event cameras, with their microsecond temporal resolution and high dynamic range, are particularly well-suited to the fast, precise motions characteristic of robotic systems, yet remain underexplored in robot interaction datasets. Together, these modalities offer complementary representations that can support a diverse range of computer vision-based architectures.

Given that humanoid (or anthropomorphic) robots are increasingly resembling humans in both appearance and behavior [ 9 ] , the dataset is specifically constructed starting from a dataset containing human interactions ( ie , the recent INTER-X Dataset [ 10 ] ). We propose a novel human-to-robot mapping algorithm, applicable to different robot models starting from their Unified Robot Description Format (URDF) model [ 11 ] .
The dataset is created by rendering multiple controlled robots to simulate the same human interactions as the original dataset: this allowed for the automatic generation of a large number of frames with different robots, interaction type, background, and illumination conditions, with automatic annotation of each frame. The high frame rate (120 fps) enabled by the simulated environment allowed for the simultaneous rendering of RGB frames and event streams from different points of view.
In addition to dataset construction, we conduct a comprehensive comparative analysis of RGB and event-based approaches using state-of-the-art models for each task. This evaluation provides practical insights into modality-specific strengths and trade-offs, particularly regarding the modalities’ complementary qualities.
The dataset and annotations are publicly released: we believe this resource will serve as a foundational benchmark for the emerging RRI task, and hope it will stimulate the development of robust, generalizable methods for autonomous agents operating in shared social environments.

In summary: (i) We introduce R2RI, the first large-scale multimodal dataset for robot-robot interaction, with heterogeneous humanoid platforms in egocentric and exocentric views. (ii) We propose a principled data collection and annotation methodology grounded in human interaction modeling. (iii) We provide comprehensive baseline evaluations across eight perception tasks using RGB and event modalities.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Robot-Robot Interaction Datasets. From a general perspective, to the best of our knowledge, there are no datasets in the literature explicitly designed to study the task of Robot-Robot Interaction. A summary of literature datasets is reported in Table 1 .
Most of the existing datasets concerning the use of robots have been developed for the study of the Robotic Manipulation (RM) task [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , and, despite their large size, they primarily focus on the use of non-humanoid robotic arms and end-effectors, manipulating static objects on a workspace surface.

Another major family of robotic datasets is devoted to Robot Pose Estimation (RPE), i.e. the task of predicting the position of robot joints using only images [ 15 , 16 ] . In these datasets, typically only a single robot is present, with annotations related to its pose, and no interactions are included. Finally, some datasets contain an extremely limited number of annotated frames or robot models [ 20 , 19 ] , which prevents the training and, more generally, the effective use of the most recent deep learning techniques available in the literature.
Other datasets in the literature have been specifically created for the Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) task. However, these datasets generally involve primarily verbal interaction, where one or more participants communicate with each other and, only at certain times, with the robot (Human-Human-Robot-Interaction, HHRI) [ 22 ] . Consequently, the datasets of this category do not provide annotations related to robot localization and pose [ 24 ] .

Robot Detection and Pose Estimation. Detecting the presence of robots in visual data has been approached from several directions [ 26 ] .
Early methods relied on engineered visual cues such as fiducial markers [ 8 , 27 ] , specific sensors [ 28 ] , or access to the robot’s proprietary software [ 7 ] – not always feasible –, achieving reliable detection only under controlled conditions and for known robot models. With the rise of deep Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), detection approaches shifted toward learned representations, adapting general-purpose architectures such as Faster R-CNN [ 29 ] and YOLO [ 30 ] to the robot detection task through fine-tuning on domain-specific data.

While robot pose estimation has recently gained significant research attention, most existing studies focus primarily on RGB images.
From a general point of view, these solutions can be divided into two categories: i) hand–eye calibration methods and ii) rendering strategies. Hand–eye calibration methods typically rely on fiducial markers, such as ArUco patterns [ 27 ] , usually attached to the robot’s end effector and observed by one or more cameras. However, these methods have an intrusive nature, due to the presence of markers on the robot, which may not always be feasible.
In contrast, rendering-based solutions [ 31 , 32 ] adopt a render-and-compare framework, in which the estimated pose is progressively optimized by repeatedly projecting a rendered model into the image and minimizing the discrepancy with the observed camera data.

Simba dataset [ 18 ] was one of the first datasets for 3D robot pose estimation [ 33 ] , including both RGB and depth information. DREAM [ 16 ] introduced an encoder-decoder network to detect 2D keypoints of the robots and use PnP to recover extrinsics and then 3D pose; their authors also created a dataset which comprises both real and synthetic images of widely robot manipulators ( eg. , Panda, Kuka, or Baxter robots), that is now one of the most affirmed baselines in the task. Despite the success of these methods, they solely focus on robot manipulators leaving out humanoid robots.

Event-based Vision. Event cameras [ 34 , 35 ] , also known as neuromorphic cameras, have recently defined a new paradigm in vision sensing. Instead of synchronous frames, event cameras generate asynchronous streams of pixel-level activations (events), corresponding to brightness changes [ 36 ] .
Neuromorphic sensors are effective because they generate sparse, motion-driven data, respond to logarithmic brightness changes with high dynamic range, perform well in low-light conditions, and capture events at microsecond-level temporal resolution, greatly reducing motion blur [ 37 , 38 , 39 ] .
Recently, event cameras have been used for a variety of applications (including tracking [ 40 , 41 , 42 ] , object detection [ 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 ] , face analysis [ 47 , 48 ] ), with a particular focus on robotics [ 49 , 50 ] , due to their low power consumption requirements.
Although prior research has explored human detection and pose estimation, to the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first application of event cameras to the tasks of robot to robot interaction.

2026-10-07.title: Educating future engineers about LLMs: A scalable workshop
2026-10-07.authors: R. Zhang , J. C. F. de Winter , T. Dicke , D. Dodou , Y. B. Eisma
2026-10-07.subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC) ; Computers and Society (cs.CY); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-07.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into engineering workflows, students require hands-on experience to learn how to collaborate with them critically. This paper presents a scalable gamified workshop designed for engineering Master's students to practice human-AI collaboration in navigation planning. Using a mobile web interface across 10 workshop sessions, a total of 226 students wrote prompts for a non-reasoning and a reasoning LLM to solve grid-based navigation tasks of increasing complexity. The system returned robot-executable plans, trajectory visualizations, and automated scoring, culminating in a live demonstration on a Boston Dynamics Spot robot. In a post-workshop questionnaire, 81.5% reported substantial learning and 91.0% reported high engagement. Analysis of the submitted prompts revealed that students changed their strategies from step-by-step instructions for the non-reasoning LLM toward providing higher-level guidance for complex problem-solving tasks. We conclude that such interactive simulation-to-reality environments are viable for teaching the verification and collaboration skills necessary for responsible LLM use in engineering. 2026-10-07.title: Hierarchy-GBP: Accelerating Factor Graph Inference via Abstraction and Recovery
2026-10-07.authors: Yuzhou Cheng , Tom Yates , Ignacio Alzugaray , Danyal Akarca , Pedro A. M. Mediano , Andrew J. Davison
2026-10-07.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-07.comment: including appendices
2026-10-07.abstract:
Gaussian Belief Propagation (GBP) is a distributed inference algorithm that passes messages in graphical models, making it attractive for scalable spatial intelligence.
However, we find GBP most effective locally: it rapidly smooths message errors that vary sharply between neighbor variables, but corrects global errors across distant graph regions incrementally through long-range message propagations.
We propose Hierarchy-GBP (H-GBP) , an iterative, two-stage framework that accelerates GBP by first solving these global errors with a coarse graph approximation (abstraction) and projecting the results back to the original graph (recovery), then refining the remaining local errors with GBP. We prove H-GBP convergence to the optimum by deriving the combined matrix operator of our abstraction and recovery steps and analyzing its spectral radius.
Experiments on linear sparse graphs show that H-GBP converges fundamentally faster than standard GBP. Moreover, we validate H-GBP on two important spatial problems: Pose Graph Optimization (PGO) and Bundle Adjustment (BA). H-GBP markedly accelerates large-scale PGO and achieves state-of-the-art runtime across all tested BA scales.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Gaussian Belief Propagation (GBP) is an efficient distributed graphical inference algorithm ( Pearl, 2022 ; Yates et al., 2026 ) that has been successfully applied in error-correcting decoding ( Frey and MacKay, 1997 ) , multiuser detection ( Bickson et al., 2008 ) , and solving large-scale linear systems ( Shental et al., 2008 ) .
Inference proceeds by passing Gaussian distributions between nodes in a probabilistic graphical model, iteratively updating each variable’s marginal belief.
This local, decoupled, and scalable computational model makes GBP a highly promising inference and reasoning framework for future spatial intelligence systems ( Davison and Ortiz, 2019 ) .

GBP has the desirable property that, if it converges on a Gaussian graph, it converges to the global optimal mean ( Weiss and Freeman, 1999 ) .
However, its convergence rate is compromised by graph structures like local loops or long graph diameters ( Malioutov et al., 2005 ; Malioutov et al., 2006 ; Du et al., 2018 ) , and GBP can often require many iterations ( El-Kurdi et al., 2012 ; Liu et al., 2012 ) .
Algebraically, GBP behaves as a smoother: it quickly damps local (high-frequency) errors that vary sharply between neighboring nodes, while global (low-frequency) errors across distant graph regions require many iterations to reduce.
We observe the local-versus-global error separation in many spatial inference problems, including SLAM, 3D computer vision, and sensor networks.

This motivates a two-level view of GBP (see Fig. 1 ). The fine space is the original variable space where GBP performs local message passing, while the coarse space is a low-dimensional graph approximation suitable for removing low-frequency errors. We solidify this idea with a localized low-rank abstraction . Variables are grouped locally and abstracted via their most prominent eigenvalues, forming a coarse problem that captures low-frequency errors ( Briggs et al., 2000 ; Nataf et al., 2011 ; Spillane et al., 2014 ) .

Our algorithm Hierarchy-GBP (H-GBP) alternates coarse residual correction with fine-level synchronous GBP.
For linear Gaussian factor graphs, we derive an operator describing a ‘V-cycle’ of alternating coarse and fine steps, which lets us compute the spectral radius and predict a large improvement in convergence rate compared to standard GBP on the fine graph. Experiments on sparse spatial factor graphs ( Dellaert and Kaess, 2017 ; Davison, 2018 ; Papadimitriou, 2025 ; Jiao et al., 2026 ) verify this predicted acceleration in linear problems. We also show that the abstraction-and-recovery principle extends to practically important, non-linear Pose Graph Optimization (PGO) (see Fig. 2 ) and Bundle Adjustment (BA) (see Fig. 3 ).

Specifically, our main contributions are:

H-GBP framework We introduce a multilevel GBP framework for general sparse factor graphs. H-GBP builds a low-rank coarse space from low-eigenvalue modes, and alternates coarse corrections with GBP updates on the original fine graph.

Empirical validation H-GBP converges faster than standard GBP on sparse linear factor graphs empirically. Extensive experiments on PGO and BA benchmarks show H-GBP’s speed and accuracy benefits, and demonstrate the potential for broader spatial intelligence applications.

Convergence theory For linear factor graphs, we establish a global precision convergence rate and derive a reduced cycle operator whose spectral radius is a geometric global convergence criterion. We prove the local convergence of H-GBP on manifolds.

1. H-GBP framework We introduce a multilevel GBP framework for general sparse factor graphs. H-GBP builds a low-rank coarse space from low-eigenvalue modes, and alternates coarse corrections with GBP updates on the original fine graph.

2. Empirical validation H-GBP converges faster than standard GBP on sparse linear factor graphs empirically. Extensive experiments on PGO and BA benchmarks show H-GBP’s speed and accuracy benefits, and demonstrate the potential for broader spatial intelligence applications.

3. Convergence theory For linear factor graphs, we establish a global precision convergence rate and derive a reduced cycle operator whose spectral radius is a geometric global convergence criterion. We prove the local convergence of H-GBP on manifolds.
2026-10-07.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

GBP on linear-Gaussian graphs has a strong theoretical foundation. Weiss and Freeman (1999) shows that when loopy GBP converges on a Gaussian
graphical model, it recovers the correct posterior means, though the variances can be
overconfident. Subsequent work connected GBP to walk-sum expansions and
linear/quadratic solvers, clarifying that its behavior is governed by global coupling
structure rather than by any single local loop in isolation ( Malioutov et al., 2006 ; Shental et al., 2008 ; Moallemi and Van Roy, 2009 ) . More recent analyses extended
these perspectives to vector-valued Gaussian models, which arise in estimation problems ( Du et al., 2018 ; Yates et al., 2026 ) .
Our H-GBP analysis takes a matrix-operator view of the underlying dynamics.

A second line of work improves GBP efficiency while remaining on a flat graph. Representative
ideas include residual scheduling ( Elidan et al., 2006 ) , relaxation or damping ( El-Kurdi et al., 2012 ) , and structural
modifications such as feedback message passing ( Liu et al., 2012 ) . These methods can
reduce oscillation or avoid unnecessary updates, but they do so by
reordering or partially restructuring message passing on the original graph.
They do not build a coarse representation to divide and counter
long-range, low-frequency error components.

H-GBP is inspired by domain-decomposition methods, where local smoothers remove high-frequency errors and coarse spaces correct slowly varying components ( Briggs et al., 2000 ) . The closest prior work combines GBP with multigrid for PDE/FEM systems ( El-Kurdi et al., 2014 ; El-Kurdi et al., 2015 ) . In contrast, H-GBP constructs the hierarchy directly on sparse factor graphs and derives the coupled coarse/fine message dynamics. To our knowledge, it is the first multilevel GBP framework formulated and analyzed for general sparse factor graphs beyond PDE/FEM discretizations.

Our work is also related to the factor-graph optimization literature in robotics ( Tazaki, 2022 ) . Factor graphs
have become a standard abstraction for large-scale estimation and SLAM, while sparse nonlinear
solvers such as g2o and Ceres remain the dominant practical baselines ( Dellaert and Kaess, 2017 ; Kümmerle et al., 2011 ; Agarwal et al., 2023 ) . Recently, there has
been renewed interest in GBP as a distributed inference engine for spatial estimation, including multi-robot localization, continuous-time SLAM, and bundle adjustment on graph processors ( Murai et al., 2024 ; Hug et al., 2024 ; Ortiz et al., 2020 ) . H-GBP
sits between these threads: it preserves the locality and parallelism of GBP with an abstract-then-recover acceleration mechanism.
