2026-10-07.title: Statistical Turbulence and High-Fidelity Disturbance Fields for Quadrotor Flight Control
2026-10-07.authors: Xun Huang
2026-10-07.abstract: Reinforcement-learning quadrotor controllers are usually trained under simplified wind models, yet the impact of wind-field fidelity—as opposed to magnitude—on policy robustness remains unquantified. This paper compares five disturbance-fidelity levels, from wind-free flight and discrete 1-cosine gusts through statistical turbulence and synthetic coherent structures to large-eddy-simulation fields of the atmospheric boundary layer, in a full cross-fidelity train–test evaluation of proximal policy optimization (PPO) agents, with cascaded PID and geometric SE(3) controllers as training-free references, over a 0–12 m/s wind sweep. Before any controller comparison is made, all disturbance data are validated: every synthetic generator is checked quantitatively against its analytical or certification-standard reference, and the large-eddy-simulation fields against the imposed log law. On a racing-class quadrotor in hover, the train × \times test matrix is remarkably flat, and the cheapest structured training wind—discrete-gust domain randomization—ranks first in every test column, a ranking replicated on a wind-sensitive 27 g platform; a once-tuned geometric controller brackets the learned PPO policies at zero crash rate. Mechanism diagnostics show that control authority, not wind realism, bounds robustness, so wind-fidelity investment should scale with platform wind sensitivity.
2026-10-07.introduction:
Low-altitude aviation is undergoing rapid expansion [ 1 ] . Atmospheric turbulence remains the dominant environmental disturbance for such operations, imposing unsteady loads that challenge both classical and learning-based control architectures. Winds are neither stationary nor Gaussian in practice: coherent structures, shear-driven streaks, and intermittent gusts populate the atmospheric boundary layer, yet the vast majority of flight control simulations—and hence the training environments for learned policies—represent turbulence as a stationary, spectrally shaped random process, or worse, as independent white noise. The gap between the simplified wind models used for flight control training of drones and the physical complexity of real atmospheric flows is rarely treated as an independent variable, which motivates the current study.

For quadrotors, reinforcement-learning-based controllers have demonstrated agile and robust performance in both simulation and hardware deployments. At the larger end of the scale, online adaptive reinforcement learning flight control laws have been successfully flight-tested on CS-25-class transport aircraft [ 2 ] . Beyond standard architectures, hybrid evolutionary–reinforcement learning schemes have been developed for safety-informed fault-tolerant control, with training deliberately conducted on high-fidelity models to ensure reliability [ 3 ] . For high-speed applications, reinforcement learning controllers for hypersonic vehicles have undergone structured performance comparisons against classical designs [ 4 ] . At a methodological level, experience-replay mechanisms from deep reinforcement learning have been shown to strengthen the excitation conditions of neural-network adaptive control, thereby tightening the connection between learning-based and classical adaptive flight control [ 5 ] .

As learned controllers move toward flight-test and certification contexts, the fidelity of the simulation environments in which they are trained becomes a prerequisite question rather than an implementation detail. Evaluation methodology is evolving in response: deep reinforcement learning itself has been used to search out worst-case failure scenarios of complex nonlinear flight-control designs, complementing classical verification and validation [ 6 ] , and learning-based adaptive-dynamic-programming control has reached wind-tunnel validation, alleviating gust-load peaks by morphing camber [ 7 ] . Yet a recurring observation across the literature is that learned policies are exquisitely sensitive to the disturbances under which they are trained: a policy that is robust to the particular random process used during domain randomization may fail abruptly when the disturbance realization at test time differs in flow structure , not merely in magnitude. Wind is the dominant external disturbance for low-altitude quadrotor operations, and it is almost universally modeled in the learning-control literature as a stationary, Gaussian, spectrally shaped random process—or, worse, as independent white noise on the force and torque residuals.

This sensitivity is not surprising when the environment under control is the atmosphere. In autonomous cross-country soaring, hierarchical reinforcement-learning policies succeed or fail according to how wind fields and thermal updrafts are represented to the agent [ 8 ] ; for rotorcraft—the certified-aircraft category closest to the multirotor disturbance regime—gust reconstruction from vehicle response has been shown to hinge on closed-loop shaping of the vehicle–wind interaction [ 9 ] . In both lines of work the wind field itself is taken as given; its physical fidelity is not treated as an experimental variable.

Recent careful-comparison studies have established that conclusions about learned versus classical controllers depend strongly on simualtion and experimental protocols. Kunapuli et al. [ 10 ] showed that, under matched conditions, classical and learned quadrotor trajectory-tracking controllers occupy a much narrower performance gap than commonly claimed, and that protocol details—task definition, tuning budget, disturbance injection—dominate the comparison. Chen et al. [ 11 ] systematically ablated the ingredients of a zero-shot sim-to-real reinforcement learning quadrotor policy, identifying observation design and dynamics randomization as decisive factors. Neither study treats the physical fidelity of the wind field itself as an independent variable: turbulence models of very different structure (discrete gusts, stationary stochastic spectra, coherent vortical structures, and turbulence-resolving simulation output) are usually conflated.

Wind-disturbance modeling practice in the wider aerospace literature confirms the abovementioned gap from two directions. On the measurement side, the classical statistical gust models are now being calibrated directly against atmospheric data—the parameters of a three-dimensional gust model have been estimated from airborne wind-lidar measurements [ 12 ] , and the disturbances actually encountered by a large commercial aircraft have been reconstructed from flight data [ 13 ] —and both studies quantify, case by case, how far realized atmospheric turbulence departs from the stationary Gaussian models used in simulation and training. On the estimation side, wind information is beginning to enter the control loop explicitly, adaptively and with uncertainty quantification in an empirical-Bayesian framework [ 14 ] , and with flight-test validation in model-based H ∞ H_{\infty} filtering [ 15 ] ; yet both lines of work still presuppose a modeled wind-field structure against which the estimate is computed.

Wind-aware learning controllers have recently begun to emerge. Tasim and Sun [ 16 ] trained a wind-aware reinforcement learning policy with a learned onboard wind estimator in von Kármán turbulence; Wang et al. [ 17 ] proposed a physics-informed wind-adaptive network for quadrotor dynamics prediction under wind; Hsieh et al. [ 18 ] addressed online adaptation for quadrotors flying in tight formations, where aerodynamic interaction dominates. Each of these works commits to a single disturbance model class, so the marginal value of flow fidelity—statistical turbulence versus coherent-structure-laden versus large eddy simulation (LES) derived fields—remains unquantified. The same gap exists in the guidance-and-control literature at large: recent work on learning-enhanced control [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] demonstrates the maturity of learning-based methods across platforms, but evaluation disturbances are invariably simplified relative to the turbulence that the underlying aircraft actually traverse.

A parallel development on the fluids side makes the fidelity question timely: flow fields of CFD quality are now routinely coupled to aerospace vehicle applications. Full-scale wind databases based upon reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes equations over real urban geometry, compressed online by gappy proper orthogonal decomposition, already drive minimum-energy quadrotor trajectory planning [ 23 ] . At the gust-physics end, iterative maneuver optimization against high-fidelity simulation and experiment has clarified how a wing should respond to a transverse discrete-gust encounter [ 24 ] , and wind-tunnel measurements of wings submerged in turbulent bluff-body wakes show that the ratio of coherent wake-eddy scale to wing span governs the unsteady loads [ 25 ] —precisely the organized structure that stationary statistical turbulence does not contain by construction. Real-time data-driven adaptive lift regulation in developing long-duration gusts, demonstrated without any prior gust model [ 26 ] , completes the picture: controllers are now expected to cope with gusts whose structure is neither Gaussian nor stationary. What none of these works does is vary the fidelity of the disturbance field itself as an experimental variable; each commits to a single field generator, so the marginal value of physical fidelity remains unmeasured across the entire spectrum from discrete gusts to turbulence-resolving simulation output.

To address the gap, this paper asks a deliberately narrow question with broad practical consequences: does the physical fidelity of the training wind field matter for the robustness and transferability of learned quadrotor controllers? We should admit that the present study is deliberately simulator-based; its aim is to establish a protocol and to identify which fidelity level suffices, before flight-test resources are committed.
Precisely because the study is simulator-based, the rigor of the data used to develop and assess this question is treated as a first-class requirement: each disturbance generator is validated quantitatively against the analytical or certification-standard model it implements, the vehicle model is a peer-reviewed benchmark with documented system identification, cross-level data are matched on dimensionless grounds, and the assessment statistics are fixed a priori.

The remaining structure of the present paper and the corresponding contributions are:

A hierarchy of five wind-disturbance fidelity levels (L0–L4), from wind-free flight to LES-derived flow fields, with complete mathematical definitions and dimensionless matching criteria (turbulence intensity, integral-scale-to-airframe ratio, spectral shape) that allow fair cross-model comparison (Secs. II – III ).

A full train-fidelity × \times test-fidelity cross-evaluation protocol applied to proximal policy optimization (PPO) controllers with a training-free proportional-integral-derivative (PID) reference under matched fairness conditions, with mechanism-level diagnostics (control-input spectra, saturation duty) in addition to performance metrics (Secs. IV – V ).

2026-10-08.title: RoboPrompt: Intuitive Robot Policy Steering with Sparse Human Input
2026-10-08.authors: Yanwen Zou , Chenyang Shi , Guoxuan Xu , Wenye Yu , Wendi Chen , Ye Pan , Cewu Lu , Chuan Wen
2026-10-08.abstract: End-to-end robot policies trained through imitation learning remain constrained by limited data diversity, making reliable zero-shot deployment in real-world settings challenging. Shared-autonomy methods enable human correction through teleoperation, but specialized hardware and operator training hinder deployment at scale. Other approaches incorporate human guidance as additional policy inputs, often requiring architectural changes and dedicated training for steerability, which limits their applicability across policies. We present RoboPrompt, a general-purpose, lightweight robot policy steering system that enables users to guide policy behavior through intuitive, sparse inputs, including drawn traces, target points, and coarse directional instructions. RoboPrompt decouples human-intention translation from the underlying policy: a reusable module converts human guidance into action drafts, which are refined through the diffusion or flow-matching dynamics of the base policy. By controlling action generation in noise space, RoboPrompt balances human intent with the policy prior without modifying the base policy architecture or fine-tuning it for steerability. Experiments demonstrate effective steering across Diffusion Policy, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and FastWAM. We further use steered rollouts for online policy improvement through DAgger. After 2-3 rounds of iteration, average success rates increase by 15.5% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} across three tasks and by 21.3% across three policies(Diffusion Policy, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , FastWAM) on the Insert Bread task, while average human intervention counts decrease by 44.0% (2.86 to 1.60) and 81.9% (2.60 to 0.47), respectively.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] and world-action-models(WAM) [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] have significantly improved the generalization capability of robotic manipulation.

Scaling beyond laboratory settings remains constrained by scarce real-world interaction data [ 9 ] , unlike the web-scale corpora available to language and vision models [ 10 , 11 ] . This creates a chicken-and-egg dilemma: limited data diversity causes deployment failures, which in turn restrict deployment and further data collection.

Human-in-the-loop deployment addresses this dilemma by letting robots act autonomously while humans monitor and correct execution. However, end-to-end policies [ 12 , 3 , 13 , 14 , 5 ] offer limited intervention interfaces. Language specifies task objectives but often provides weak fine-grained control [ 15 , 16 ] , especially when the intended behavior is semantically ambiguous [ 17 , 18 ] .

Shared-autonomy approaches allow humans to correct failures through teleoperation [ 13 , 19 , 20 ] , but require additional hardware and operator training, hindering adoption by everyday users after large scale deployment.

We argue that scalable human-in-the-loop deployment requires an intuitive steering interface with minimal physical and cognitive burden. Drawing 2D sketches on camera observations or providing coarse directional instructions could enable task completion while collecting corrective data for policy improvement.

Realizing such an interface presents several challenges. First, unlike teleoperation, natural human instructions only provide partial information rather than full 6D actions with temporal dynamics. Second, long-horizon prompt following is non-trivial under action-chunked policies. Effective correction may require actions outside the base policy’s learned action manifold, which the policy cannot reliably produce on its own, so steering should initially prioritize human intention and gradually transition toward the policy prior across subsequent action chunks. Finally, existing prompt-conditioned approaches often rely on whole policy fine-tuning or architectural modifications [ 21 , 17 , 22 ] , which ties steerability to a particular policy design and makes it difficult to reuse the same steering interface across pretrained policies with different architectures or weights.

We propose RoboPrompt , a two-stage system that translates sparse human input into executable actions, integrates them with pretrained policies, and uses steered rollouts for policy improvement. Our main contributions are:

From intention to action draft. We introduce a lightweight human-intention translator based on a 0.77B VLA model [ 23 ] , together with a data processing pipeline for its training. The translator converts 2D traces, points, and coarse directional instructions into spatially and temporally complete action chunks, serving as a task-agnostic yet physically plausible action generator.

From intention to action draft. We introduce a lightweight human-intention translator based on a 0.77B VLA model [ 23 ] , together with a data processing pipeline for its training. The translator converts 2D traces, points, and coarse directional instructions into spatially and temporally complete action chunks, serving as a task-agnostic yet physically plausible action generator.

From action draft to fine-grained movement. We propose Progressive Biased Denoising (PBD) , which refines action drafts by exploiting the properties of diffusion- and flow-matching-based policies. Increasing the denoising level across action chunks extends a prompt’s influence over long-horizon behavior while smoothly shifting control toward the policy prior.

Steering and improving real-world policies. RoboPrompt achieves ≥ 95 % \geq 95\% prompt alignment on Diffusion Policy [ 14 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 13 ] , and FastWAM [ 5 ] without fine-tuning for steerability. We introduce Time-weighted Optimal Transport (TOT) to filter steered rollouts for DAgger training, improving task progress across real-world tasks while reducing human intervention.

2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

Robot learning for manipulation tasks. Learning-based visuomotor policies, ranging from task-specific robot policies [ 14 ] to large-scale robot foundation models including VLAs [ 13 , 12 ] and WAMs [ 7 , 5 ] , have achieved increasingly strong capabilities in robotic manipulation through imitation learning. These policies are typically trained end to end to map visual observations and task instructions directly to robot actions, allowing them to benefit from large-scale robot datasets. However, this end-to-end formulation provides few interfaces for humans to intervene during policy execution.

Policy steering. To improve manipulation performance, recent works have explored steering a base policy with additional conditioning signals during execution. Steerable Policies [ 21 ] enable users to provide diverse prompts for refining policy behavior by translating them into language inputs to condition the policy. π 0.7 \pi_{0.7} [ 12 ] takes a step further toward more grounded conditioning by prompting a world model to convert subtask-level language prompts into goal images. While language is effective for specifying high-level tasks and semantic intent, language alone often cannot express the full set of fine-grained spatial and motion-level information required for effective steering [ 17 , 24 ] . Inference-Time Policy Steering [ 25 ] enables training-free intervention by using visual guidance objectives to bias the sampling process of diffusion policy [ 14 ] . However, reweighting remains constrained by the base policy’s own action distribution, limiting its ability to realize corrective actions outside the policy’s learned action manifold that may be necessary for effective failure recovery. Instead, RoboPrompt uses an independent module to convert human input into an action draft and refines it using Progressive Biased Denoising (PBD) and Noise-Augmented Flow Reversal Steering (NA-FRS) with a tunable initial denoising step, preserving human intent while adjusting its influence relative to the base policy prior.

Interactive robot learning. Interactive robot learning enables a learned policy to receive human guidance or intervention during execution. Such interactions improve task completion when autonomous execution is unreliable, and the resulting trajectories can further serve as online data for policy improvement methods such as HG-DAgger [ 26 ] . Existing collaborative-control systems [ 27 , 28 , 20 ] commonly realize this interaction through teleoperation, where users directly provide low-level motion commands. Shared-autonomy methods such as HAJL [ 29 ] reduce the control burden by employing a diffusion-based assistive policy that refines teleoperation commands during the diffusion process, continuously interpolating between manual and autonomous control. Nevertheless, these approaches still depend on teleoperation devices and expert operators to produce precise low-level commands. To reduce this dependence on skilled teleoperation, RoboPrompt uses sparse, intuitive human guidance and relies on the base policy as an action prior to infer executable low-level behavior.

2026-10-08.title: Long-WAM: Scaling the Context of World-Action Models
2026-10-08.authors: Wei Huang , Bohan Zhang , Chenzhi Liu , Isabella Liu , Shuai Yang , Weian Mao , Luozhou Wang , Yicheng Xiao , Weifeng Lin , Qixin Hu , Bryan Chu , Sifei Liu , Linxi Fan , Xiaojuan Qi , Song Han , Yukang Chen
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-08.abstract:
Abstract: Real-time robot control demands enough visual history to infer motion and
task progress, but processing that history can delay action.
We present Long-WAM , a model–system framework for scaling the context
of causal world-action models under real-time control constraints.
Our central finding is that access to history is not the same as using it:
longer histories pay off far more when the video foundation is pretrained
autoregressively (AR).
We first learn causal prediction from robot and egocentric videos without
action labels, then preserve this history-to-future structure during
world-action adaptation.
On RoboCasa GR-1, increasing context from 0.0 to 19.2 seconds raises success
from 63.3% to 78.7%, whereas a bidirectionally pretrained initialization shows
no net gain; robot-domain AR pretraining further raises peak success on GR-1
and LIBERO-Long. Long-WAM also achieves the best results among compared methods
on LIBERO-Long, RoboTwin 2.0, and DOMINO. Streaming observation encoding,
asynchronous execution, and hardware-specific acceleration enable deployment
on RTX 5090, DGX Spark, and Jetson AGX Thor without dropping future prediction;
on RTX 5090, each action chunk, including future-video latent prediction, takes
107.4 ms. Real-time deployment on Unitree G1 and YAM supports dynamic and
long-horizon manipulation, including 95% success on dynamic cup stacking,
where π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and Fast-WAM succeed in none of 20 trials.
As a memory-informed executor, Long-WAM also complements higher-level planning
in composite tasks.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Fast robot control requires understanding how the scene is changing.
A single image can reveal an object’s position but leave its motion and
interaction progress ambiguous. World-action models (WAMs) bring video
prediction to closed-loop control [ 3 , 52 , 26 ] ,
making visual history a natural resource for action. Yet processing more
history can delay the response it is meant to improve. We therefore ask: how does WAM control scale with visual context, and how can those
gains be retained under real-time constraints?

Recent WAMs retain history through causal caches and persistent or selected memories [ 50 , 44 , 47 , 42 ] .
Yet access to history is distinct from learning to predict from it .
DreamZero [ 52 ] and LingBot-VA [ 26 ] adapt
bidirectionally pretrained video generators to causal video–action prediction,
whereas LingBot-VA 2.0 [ 55 ] jointly pretrains causal
video and learned latent actions. We investigate a complementary route:
first learn autoregressive (AR) video prediction,
then adapt to actions while preserving its history-to-future structure. Appendix 2 discusses related work.

We introduce Long-WAM (Figure 1 ), a model–system
framework for context scaling in real-time robot control. Our central finding
is that the value of longer context depends on how the video foundation
is pretrained (Figure 6 ). On GR-1, both AR-pretrained
foundations gain from extending context from 0.0 to 19.2 seconds, whereas a
bidirectional initialization does not; the robot-domain AR model’s lead
over it grows from 3.3 points without history to 17.1 points at 19.2 seconds.
AR pretraining already learns the causal temporal factorization that WAM
adaptation retains, giving the model a basis for using history rather than
merely accessing it. Our LongLive2.0-Robot foundation learns from roughly
10,000 window-equivalent hours of robot and egocentric video; we preserve its
causal structure during action adaptation, and robot-domain pretraining further
raises peak success on both LIBERO-Long and GR-1.

Longer context helps only if the controller still responds in time, so we
co-design asynchronous execution and edge acceleration while retaining future
prediction. Predictive conditioning from the AR video foundation supports
smooth action handoffs without blending or prefix guidance; streaming VAE
encodes incoming observations while the robot executes, reducing post-trigger
computation; and NVFP4 quantization with device-specific kernel tuning
accelerates the video–action pipeline on RTX 5090, DGX Spark, and Jetson AGX
Thor. With four denoising steps per expert, the optimized pipeline takes
107.4 ms per action chunk on RTX 5090, including the full observation VAE
computation, a 3.3 × 3.3\times speedup over BF16 eager execution
(Section 4 , Table 6.2 ).

On RoboCasa [ 33 ] GR-1 Tabletop [ 36 ] , increasing the history window from 0.0 to
19.2 seconds raises success from 63.3% to 78.7% (+15.4 points).
On LIBERO-Long [ 30 ] , 2.4 seconds of history improves
success from 94.5% to 99.5%. Long-WAM also achieves 94.4% average success
on RoboTwin 2.0 [ 9 ] and 34.9% success on DOMINO [ 15 ] , the highest among compared methods.
On a Unitree G1, Long-WAM grasps cups from a conveyor moving at 7.5 cm/s in
90% of trials and stacks moving cups in 95%, settings in which neither π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 38 ] nor Fast-WAM [ 54 ] succeeds once. On YAM, it completes tasks lasting over
40 seconds on average with 81.7% success, extending the evaluation from rapid
interception to sustained execution. Long-WAM also serves as the executor of a
hierarchical system on RoboCasa365 [ 34 ] : pairing
its unchanged checkpoint with GPT-6 Astra raises overall success from 31.4%
to 54.4%, versus 25.2% for the planner alone. Planner augmentation yields a
larger gain for Long-WAM (+23.0 points) than for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} (+13.6;
Section 6 ), suggesting that stronger execution
lets planning pay off more. Together, these results suggest that context is a
resource for generative control whose value depends on both predictive
pretraining and timely execution.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

WAMs connect visual dynamics to executable actions. Motus [ 3 ] combines pretrained video, vision–language, and action experts; DreamZero [ 52 ] and LingBot-VA [ 26 ] adapt
bidirectional video backbones to causal control. Their video pretraining
supplies visual priors, while causal prediction and action coupling are learned
downstream. LingBot-VA 2.0 [ 55 ] instead jointly pretrains
causal video and learned latent actions in a shared representation.
EVA [ 48 ] aligns video generation with executable actions through
inverse-dynamics rewards, and ω \omega -EVA [ 45 ] evaluates
latent action consequences. Long-WAM develops a staged route: action-free
robot-video AR pretraining followed by action adaptation under the same causal
ordering. The action model thus inherits a visual dynamics prior explicitly
trained for history-to-future prediction, separating predictive pretraining
from learning an embodiment’s action representation.

Cache capacity, physical history duration, and the cost of rebuilding visual
context are distinct quantities. Causal caches, compressed histories, and
event retrieval provide complementary memory interfaces [ 52 , 26 , 50 , 44 , 47 , 42 ] . Echo-Memory [ 25 ] studies memory for
camera-conditioned video generation; RoboTTT [ 20 ] studies
context scaling in robot policies; WAM-TTT [ 16 ] adapts memory
from human video to steer a frozen WAM. Long-WAM studies the robot’s own
observed interaction history: we vary its temporal extent across trained
causal WAM variants and examine closed-loop success and online computation.
Our focus is how predictive pretraining shapes the benefit of longer context,
complementing work on memory compression, retrieval, and adaptation.

Large video backbones make online WAM control expensive. Prior systems reduce
this cost through caching, few-step generation, pipelined execution, action-only
decoding, or hierarchical update rates [ 52 , 26 , 54 , 7 ] .
LongLive-2.0 further develops parallel AR training, compressed KV caches,
low-precision execution, and asynchronous VAE decoding [ 11 ] . Complementary work on compilation, kernel
orchestration, and video-DiT quantization reduces inference cost [ 2 , 19 , 57 ] .
Asynchronous deployment additionally requires consistency between consecutive
action chunks. Existing methods constrain these transitions
through inference-time guidance, prefix-conditioned training, or denoising-time
blending [ 5 , 6 , 29 ] .
An empirical WAM study highlights the importance of temporal alignment and the
precision–smoothness trade-offs of transition strategies [ 32 ] . Long-WAM exhibits robust
continuity under direct asynchronous switching while retaining explicit future
visual conditioning. We preserve this imagine-then-act path and address its
sequential cost through streaming observation encoding and device-specific
acceleration, targeting continuity and speed together.

2026-10-08.title: Rephrase Before You Act: Characterizing and Mitigating Language Sensitivity in Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-08.authors: Mikey Watts (Independent Researcher), Yuchen Cui (University of California, Los Angeles)
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-08.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) are strikingly sensitive to
instruction phrasing and do not inherit the language robustness of the
vision-language models they are built on. A one-word edit can move success by tens of points: π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} turns on a LIBERO stove 100% of the time for “switch on the stove” and 2% for “switch on the hot plate”, and a π 0 \pi_{0} checkpoint finetuned with rephrase augmentation still shows swings of up to 61 points. We characterize this sensitivity
with statistically tested single-edit swings and an oracle phrase search,
which shows that phrasing alone nearly closes the 21-point gap between
in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks. We then reduce it without
modifying the policy. Because the sensitivity is systematic, it can be expressed as explicit rules: we score many phrasings of a few training tasks, have a large language model distill the evidence into ten to twenty rephrasing rules, and at deployment rewrite each incoming instruction once under these rules. The rules improve the frozen π 0 \pi_{0} by 16 to 27% relative
on twelve held-out tasks across adversarial, VLM-generated, and
human-generated phrasings, with gains concentrated on out-of-distribution tasks. The pipeline replicates on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and LIBERO, lifting
in-finetune success from 93.6% to 97.8%. The method requires no
retraining and no per-step verification, and applies zero-shot to unseen
tasks and instructions.
Project website: https://sttawm.github.io/rephrase-before-you-act
2026-10-08.introduction:
General-purpose robots that average end users can direct in their own words remain a long-standing goal of the field, and such users cannot be expected to phrase a request the way the robot was trained. Generalist vision-language models (VLMs) have progressed rapidly, and vision-language-action models (VLAs) extend them to robot control in the hope of inheriting their capabilities, including robustness to how an instruction is phrased. This hope is often not met. Telling π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} to “switch on the stove” succeeds 100% of the time, whereas “switch on the hot plate” succeeds 2% of the time, and telling π 0 \pi_{0} that the “purple eggplant goes on the sponge” succeeds 69% of the time on a SIMPLER task, whereas dropping the color adjective lowers the success rate to 8%.

A robot that executes a task only under particular wording is not a robot that non-experts can instruct. The standard remedy is training-time augmentation, which relabels demonstrations with additional phrasings [ 1 , 2 ] . The π 0 \pi_{0} checkpoint we study was finetuned with rephrase augmentation [ 3 ] , which is worth a 20% relative improvement on naturally phrased requests in our measurement, yet it still exhibits the swings above. This residual sensitivity is the problem we address, and existing deployment-side methods do not close it. Test-time verification [ 4 , 1 ] selects among many phrase-action candidates at every step, which multiplies inference cost without improving over the unmodified policy in our setting. Instruction optimization [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] needs online interaction with each task, so nothing transfers to an unseen one. No existing method leaves the policy’s weights untouched, acts once per episode, and transfers zero-shot to tasks it has never seen.

Our key observation is that a VLA’s language sensitivity is systematic rather than idiosyncratic to each task, and can therefore be captured by a small set of explicit rules. We generate many phrasings of eight training tasks, roll each out in simulation, and have a large language model distill the scored phrasings into ten to twenty natural-language rules, for example “‘coke’ stays ‘coke’, never ‘cola’, ‘soda’, or bare ‘can’ ” and “never swap a common noun for its sibling (keep ’plate’, not ’dish’)” . At deployment, a rephraser conditioned on the rules and the scene image rewrites each incoming instruction once, before the episode begins, and passes the rewrite to the frozen VLA (Fig. 1 ). Only the instruction changes, so the VLA’s weights are never modified, and because the rules describe how the policy parses language in general, they transfer to tasks that contributed no evidence.

We first characterize the sensitivity for π 0 \pi_{0} on SIMPLER’s Bridge tasks and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on LIBERO, through statistically tested single-edit swings and an oracle phrase search that estimates the headroom phrasing alone leaves a frozen policy. Two findings shape the paper. First, oracle phrasing nearly closes the 21-point gap between in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks, so much of the apparent generalization gap is a phrasing gap. Second, on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} adversarial phrasing costs 50 points on tasks inside the finetuning set and nothing measurable outside it, which suggests that the policy attends to language only where training has taught it to [ 8 , 9 ] .

We evaluate on the rephrase-augmented π 0 \pi_{0} across twelve sealed SIMPLER tasks that contributed no evidence, under adversarial, VLM-generated, human-generated, and canonical phrasings. Rules distilled from eight tasks improve success by 16 to 27% relative over the no-rephraser baseline on the adversarial and natural sets, with gains concentrated on out-of-distribution tasks. The effect is stable across three applier models and three independent distillations.

In summary, this paper contributes:

a statistically grounded characterization of language sensitivity in π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} showing that much of the apparent gap between in- and out-of-distribution tasks is attributable to phrasing alone;

a weight-free, once-per-episode method that distills rollout evidence into explicit rephrasing rules which transfer zero-shot to unseen tasks;

an evaluation on held-out tasks across three phrasing styles and three applier models, with a comparison to test-time verification and a replication on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and LIBERO.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

Measuring language sensitivity. Embodied red teaming uses a VLM to search for instructions that break language-conditioned robot policies [ 10 ] . LIBERO-PRO perturbs LIBERO along objects, initial states, instructions, and environments. On the language axis it finds that paraphrased instructions leave accuracy intact, but so do nonsensical ones, because the policy executes the same memorized trajectory regardless [ 8 ] . LIBERO-Plus charts the same sensitivity across ten VLAs, where instruction perturbations cost between 14 and 50 points, and reaches the same conclusion that much of the apparent robustness stems from models ignoring the instruction [ 9 ] . Our single-edit swings are the complementary, finer-grained observation that when the policy does attend to language, a single word can move success by tens of points, and our oracle search quantifies how much of the apparent generalization gap is in fact attributable to phrasing rather than to genuine task novelty.

Model-side remedies. The standard remedy is augmentation, which relabels demonstrations with additional phrasings so that the policy sees many surface forms of each
instruction [ 1 ] , or, as in DIAL and SPRINT, with instructions generated by a VLM or LLM that extend the training vocabulary [ 2 , 11 ] . A recent multilingual study reports that training on seven phrasings per task roughly halves phrasing sensitivity [ 12 ] .
Steerable Policies trains the VLA on synthetic commands at several levels of abstraction so that language can steer low-level behavior [ 13 ] . Stable Language Guidance instead marginalizes decoding over LLM-expanded paraphrases [ 14 ] . All of these change the policy’s weights or its decoding, whereas the π 0 \pi_{0} checkpoint we study was already trained with rephrase augmentation [ 3 ] , and our method targets what remains after such training, without any further training of the policy.

Deployment-time remedies. Two families leave the weights untouched. Test-time verification samples several candidates at every inference step and selects among them with a verifier. RoboMonkey scores candidate actions with a VLM-based verifier [ 4 ] , Do What You Say selects the action sequence whose simulated outcome best matches the VLA’s own textual plan [ 15 ] , and CoVer selects the best phrase-action pair among several rephrasings and actions with a contrastively trained verifier [ 1 ] . CoVer is our closest comparison, evaluated in § VI-E , and differs in that we act on phrasing only, never on actions, and rephrase once per episode rather than at every step, so per-step inference cost is unchanged. Instruction optimization searches the language input of a frozen policy. SARL learns by online reinforcement
which prompts steer a generalist policy to a given
task [ 5 ] , VLA Grounder trains an instruction-to-command
translator against rollout reward for a black-box
VLA [ 6 ] , and PALO optimizes language subtask
decompositions for few-shot adaptation [ 7 ] . Each optimizes per task through interaction with that task, so what it learns does not transfer. Closest to our method, Jeong et al. search for language that improves a frozen VLA and distill the result into a learned language feedback policy that intervenes per state [ 16 ] . Our rules are instead explicit and human-readable, distilled once offline from eight tasks, applied once per episode, and applied zero-shot to tasks that contributed no evidence.

Language as the interface between VLMs and VLAs. RT-2 and PaLM-E showed that web-scale vision-language pretraining
transfers to robot control [ 17 , 18 ] , and
Hi Robot places a VLM above a VLA to turn open-ended prompts into instructions the low-level policy can follow [ 19 ] , and embodied chain-of-thought trains the VLA itself to reason in language before acting [ 20 ] . SayCan
grounds an LLM planner in learned value functions so that proposed plans
respect the robot’s skills [ 21 ] , and Inner Monologue
closes the loop with execution feedback [ 22 ] . These systems decide which instruction to issue, whereas ours learns which surface forms of an instruction this executor parses reliably and rewrites each incoming instruction into one of those forms. Written guidance as a reusable artifact has precedent in PromptBook, which curates prompting guidance for LLM-written robot code [ 23 ] , and DROC, which distills human corrections into a knowledge base retrieved for later tasks [ 24 ] . Our rulebook is instead distilled automatically from rollout evidence and targets the phrasing the executor parses.

2026-10-08.title: Factorized Tactile Representation and Control for Sim-to-Real Manipulation
2026-10-08.authors: Siqi Shang , Bianca Aumann , Tye Brady , Joshua Migdal , Taskin Padir
2026-10-08.abstract:
Tactile sim-to-real learning must bridge simulated contact and
device-specific sensor responses while preserving information needed
for control. We propose a factorized tactile representation and
control framework that maps normal force and contact patch to an
effective contact response recoverable from sensor readings. The
response is separated into contact geometry, force distribution, and
temporal contact change, with representation-specific encoding and
randomization. A Tactile Gated Policy preserves these representations
separately through control and operates over all mask configurations
without retraining. We evaluate the approach through response
reconstruction, spatial alignment, force regulation, and contact-rich
adversarial peg insertion in simulation and the real world, enabling
the utility and transfer reliability of different tactile
representations to be assessed independently. The approach achieves < < 1 mm 1\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} contact localization, 1.69 N 1.69\text{\,}\mathrm{N} force-tracking error on unseen geometries, and a
35% improvement in real-world adversarial peg insertion over the
unfactorized response, with different tactile representations
benefiting different interactions.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Learning reliable contact-rich manipulation remains a central challenge
in robotics. Large-scale demonstration datasets have enabled substantial
progress, but acquiring diverse physical interactions requires
considerable hardware resources and human
effort [ 1 ] . Sim-to-real reinforcement learning
offers a scalable alternative through autonomous interaction in
simulation. For tactile manipulation, however, transferring a policy
requires transferring the contact feedback on which its behavior
depends. Physical tactile measurements reflect contact mechanics and
sensor-specific responses that are difficult to reproduce in
simulation. Enabling simulation-trained policies to use this feedback
reliably is therefore an important step toward scalable contact-rich
manipulation.

Recent advances such as TacSL and HydroShear demonstrate the potential
of tactile simulation for learning transferable contact-rich
behaviors [ 2 , 3 ] . An important remaining challenge is making the information available from compact capacitive arrays equally useful for sim-to-real control. These arrays provide
sparse measurements, yet their distributed responses can carry
fine-grained information about contact geometry, force distribution, and temporal
evolution. Simplifying touch into binary contact or compact
force-and-location summaries can facilitate transfer, but reduces the
information exposed to the
controller [ 4 , 5 ] . We instead seek
to retain distributed contact information in a common representation
across simulation and hardware, and to use that information in a
factorized manner throughout sensing and control. This distinction
matters because the information needed for a behavior and the
uncertainty it should tolerate are not the same for every component of
touch: geometric inference should tolerate variation in response
magnitude, force regulation requires loading magnitude to remain
informative, and relative temporal changes can remain useful despite
uncertainty in absolute sensor gain. Our objective is therefore not only to transfer a richer tactile response, but also to keep different forms of tactile information separately accessible to the policy rather than commit to one representation for every interaction.

We introduce factorized tactile representation and control for
capacitive tactile arrays (Fig. Factorized Tactile Representation and Control for Sim-to-Real Manipulation ). Normal force and
contact patch define an effective contact response r, while
per-taxel calibration recovers the same response from sensor readings.
From this common response, we construct three tactile representations:
contact geometry (G), force distribution (F), and temporal
contact change (C). To preserve this factorization through control,
we introduce the Tactile Gated Policy. It encodes the three
representations separately and supports representation-specific
randomization. A tactile mask keeps their latent features independently
selectable before they enter the policy. For each task, one policy is
trained across all eight mask configurations, allowing us to evaluate
each representation and change the active representations at deployment
without retraining. Using a parallel gripper
equipped with two 28-taxel capacitive pads, we validate the approach
from held-out response reconstruction to real manipulation. The
representation supports sub-millimeter contact localization with 6.25 × 5.71 ​ mm 6.25\times 5.71\,\mathrm{mm} taxel spacing, while the best force-aware mask achieves 1.69 N 1.69\text{\,}\mathrm{N} real-world force-tracking MAE on unseen geometries. Tactile alignment,
grasp-force regulation, and adversarial peg insertion further
demonstrate how this common response supports precise and
contact-rich control through separately and jointly usable tactile
information.

Our contributions are:

An effective contact response defined from normal force and
contact patch and recoverable from capacitive sensor readings,
providing a shared sim-to-real tactile interface while retaining
distributed spatial and loading information.

Factorized tactile representation and control that preserve
contact geometry, force distribution, and temporal contact change
through representation-specific encoding and randomization, while the
Tactile Gated Policy keeps them independently selectable within one unified
policy.

A real-world evaluation on a parallel gripper with two sparse
capacitive pads, demonstrating response reconstruction on unseen contact
geometries, sub-mm contact localization, grasp-force regulation, and
challenging adversarial peg insertion.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Tactile Simulation and Sim-to-Real Transfer

Tactile simulation has advanced rapidly for vision-based sensors,
where the measurement is an image that can be rendered directly.
TACTO [ 6 ] and Taxim [ 7 ] model
GelSight-style sensors, while TacSL [ 2 ] and
Tac2Real [ 8 ] bring visuotactile simulation to
GPU-parallel policy learning.

Taxel arrays require a different mapping from simulated contact to
distributed sensor responses. Kasolowsky and Bäuml [ 9 ] model a soft tactile skin by reconstructing local penetration from
contact geometry and force, allowing contact to spread across multiple
taxels in a rigid-body simulator. A recent digital twin of the TSF-85
instead simulates a deformable sensing field and learns a mapping to
physical tactile counts [ 10 ] . Our approach avoids
reconstructing a deformation field. We define an effective contact
response from normal force and contact patch that is recoverable from
sensor readings and retains distributed information for policy
learning.

## II-B Tactile Representations for Sim-to-Real Manipulation

Tactile representation is itself an important design choice for
sim-to-real manipulation. TactileRL shows that abstractions of
simulated tactile observations can transfer better than full tactile
images [ 4 ] . Beyond Binary introduces a
physics-grounded center-of-pressure representation that retains force
and contact-location information while supporting zero-shot
transfer [ 5 ] . These works show that successful
transfer need not require reproducing the full sensor observation.

A parallel line learns transferable tactile embeddings across sensors
and modalities, including AnyTouch [ 11 ] and
TacX [ 12 ] . Our objective is different. Rather than
compressing touch into one transferable representation, we preserve
contact geometry, force distribution, and temporal contact change
separately through encoding and control. This allows their utility
and sim-to-real behavior to be evaluated independently and their
availability to the policy to be changed without retraining.

2026-10-08.title: HuMBLE: Human Motion-Driven Behavior Learning for Embodied Locomotion
2026-10-08.authors: Mike Zhang , Dongho Kang , Kevin Bergamin , Nicola Burger , Robin Deits , Jonathan Foster , Bilal Hammoud , Katie Hughes , Francesco Iacobelli , Twan Koolen , M. Eva Mungai , Zach Nobles , Shane Rozen-Levy , Jean Pierre Sleiman , Fangzhou Yu , Yunbo Zhang , Alfred Rizzi , Jessica Hodgins , Scott Kuindersma , Yeuhi Abe , Sylvain Bertrand , Farbod Farshidian
2026-10-08.abstract:
Despite recent advances in humanoid locomotion, controllers optimized for command tracking and robustness tend to produce mechanical gaits, whereas controllers tied to human motion data often fail to generalize to commands outside the data distribution. This work introduces a learning framework that balances these competing objectives to synthesize real-time steerable, robust, and biomimetic locomotion policies from human data. Using an in-house curated locomotion dataset covering diverse speeds and directions, we first learn a natural locomotion prior policy through a teacher–student distillation process. Specifically, we train a full-body reference-conditioned policy with Reinforcement Learning (RL), then distill it into a lightweight prior policy conditioned solely on proprioception and a planar torso-velocity steering command. Next, we fine-tune the prior policy with multi-task RL to expand command coverage and robustness beyond the data distribution, pairing a goal-conditioned task that tracks arbitrary commands with a reference-guided task that tracks the human data as an explicit style regularizer. We validate our framework on three humanoid robots: the Boston Dynamics Atlas R1, Atlas D1, and Unitree G1.
Experimental results demonstrate robust performance across real-world scenarios, including direct user-controlled locomotion in indoor and outdoor environments, and integration as the locomotion layer within hierarchical control stacks. Benchmarks against Tabula Rasa RL policies trained without human data and ablation studies confirm that our framework yields a lightweight, deployable policy that reconstructs coordinated whole-body behavior from a steering command, retaining the human gait characteristics while remaining robust and fully steerable.

2026-10-08.title: Agentic RSR: Real-to-Sim-to-Real through Scene Reconstruction and Execution-Grounded Robot Policies
2026-10-08.authors: Yihan Li , Yating Feng , Shengjiu Sun , Jianing Chen , Hao Ren , Bowen Yang , Weisheng Xu , Qiwei Wu , Hui Cheng , Renjing Xu
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-08.comment: including appendices, 5 figures
2026-10-08.abstract: A simulation of a real robot workspace must preserve task-relevant interactions, while policies developed in it must operate on observations available to the real robot. Yet scene reconstruction and policy development are often treated separately. We present Agentic Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Agentic RSR) , a framework that links scene reconstruction, policy development, and real-robot execution through the same manipulation task. Given a workspace video, a task description, and a known robot model, an agent recovers metric scale, iteratively refines the scene using visual feedback, and checks task-relevant interactions in MuJoCo. A coding agent then develops an executable policy, progressing from privileged object poses to visual observations and randomized simulation. The policy can interleave multiple observations and actions within one invocation, while the agent uses execution feedback to continue, retry, or revise its approach. A shared task-level interface carries the policy and accumulated experience to the real robot, where fresh observations and safety checks guide execution. Across 18 reconstructed scenes involving two robots, the mean four-view Depth MAE against reference depth estimates is 0.1057 m, the mean Lab Δ ​ E 76 \Delta E_{76} is 11.04, and the mean grayscale SSIM is 0.6990. In real-robot experiments, the aggregate task success rate reaches 80% of the simulation task success rate, indicating substantial retention of simulated performance on hardware. Code and reconstructed scene data will be made publicly available.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

RL-GSBridge and GSWorld combine high-fidelity scene representations with robot simulation, while Re 3 Sim and RoboSimGS couple rendering with interaction geometry for manipulation and sim-to-real learning ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . RoboSnap builds simulation-ready scenes from a single RGB image ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Scalable Real2Sim recovers physics-aware assets through robot interaction, whereas TwinAligner addresses visual and dynamic alignment for policy transfer ( Pfaff et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2025 ) .

ACDC generates digital cousins that preserve task-relevant affordances, while SIMPLER studies how simulated evaluation relates to real-robot performance ( Dai et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Holodeck generates prompt-conditioned environments; Gen2Sim produces 3D assets, tasks, and rewards for robot learning ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Katara et al., 2024 ) . SceneSmith, PhyScensis, SimWorld Studio, and Articraft respectively explore vision-language scene generation, physics-guided arrangement, coding-agent environments, and programmatic articulated assets ( Pfaff et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . Closer to video-based real-to-sim, Agentic Real2Sim uses agents and simulator-in-the-loop refinement to turn recorded robot–object interactions into simulatable episodic twins, while SimFoundry generates interactive scenes and digital cousins for policy evaluation and sim-to-real training ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Ranawaka et al., 2026 ) .

Code as Policies and Instruct2Act compose perception and actions into executable programs ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2023a ) . SayCan pairs language planning with feasible pretrained skills, while VoxPoser uses 3D value maps for closed-loop trajectory planning ( ichter et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2023b ) . Inner Monologue incorporates environmental feedback into planning; CaP-X studies multi-turn coding agents and code-policy transfer across simulation and hardware ( Huang et al., 2023c ; Fu et al., 2026 ) . ASPIRE and ENPIRE explore feedback-driven skill development; Show-Harness offers a semantic action interface, and RoboClaw orchestrates learned primitives for long-horizon tasks ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026 ) .

Visual and dynamics randomization support sim-to-real transfer ( Tobin et al., 2017 ; Peng et al., 2018 ) , while RT-2, OpenVLA, Octo, and π 0 \pi_{0} develop data-driven visuomotor rather than executable robot policies ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ) . Our focus is to connect reconstruction of a particular captured workspace with a programmatic policy for the same task, evaluated in simulation and on real robots.

2026-10-08.title: Robotic Boomerang Throwing via Model-Based Release Design
2026-10-08.authors: Yang Liu , Colin Jones , Aude Billard
2026-10-08.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract: Throwing objects that generate aerodynamic lift can greatly extend robot throwing beyond ballistic flight. A returning boomerang is a challenging example because its flight depends strongly on the release velocity, attitude, and spin, while robotic manipulators cannot readily reproduce the rapid motions used in human throwing. We present a model-based framework for robotic boomerang throwing centered on the release state. We identify the boomerang flight dynamics in stages to predict how flight changes across design variations. To systematically design the robot throwing motion, we screen candidate parameters according to how strongly and consistently they control release spin under uncertain contact conditions. These models are then used to design the throwing motion and boomerang for a 6-DoF manipulator with limited joint speeds. To our knowledge, this is the first robotic manipulator to generate a returning boomerang flight. In the demonstrated returning trial, the boomerang is released at 51 ​ rad / s 51~\mathrm{rad/s} ( 8.1 ​ rev / s 8.1~\mathrm{rev/s} ), reaches 2.03 ​ m 2.03~\mathrm{m} from the robot base, and returns to touch down 0.31 ​ m 0.31~\mathrm{m} from the base. The successful release differs significantly from the measured human throws, showing that a robot need not imitate human throwing motion to achieve a returning flight. The project page is available at https://robot-boomerang.github.io .
2026-10-08.introduction:
A returning boomerang converts the kinetic energy of a throw into sustained aerodynamic flight. Released with sufficient forward speed and spin, its rotating blades generate lift, while aerodynamic moments acting on the spinning body cause gyroscopic precession. These effects bend the trajectory into a loop and bring the boomerang back toward the thrower [ 1 , 2 ] . Unlike an ideal ballistic projectile, however, the flight depends not only on translational velocity, but also strongly on the attitude and spin at release.

Beyond recreation, this return capability has been proposed for aerial sensing without onboard propulsion. For example, a boomerang could be launched from a surface platform or balloon on Venus or Titan, collect measurements during flight, and return toward the launcher [ 3 ] . Such applications require a dedicated mechanism that can produce the release conditions needed for returning flight.

In this work, we ask whether a robotic manipulator can generate such a returning flight despite having very different motion capabilities from a human thrower. We show that it can. To our knowledge, this is the first robotic manipulator to produce a returning boomerang flight (Fig. 1 ).

There are two main challenges in designing a returning throw for a robot.

Challenge 1: Release and flight dynamics. The boomerang does not simply leave the gripper with the motion of the robot fingertips. During the approximately 100 ​ ms 100~\mathrm{ms} gripper-opening interval, the normal force decreases and the boomerang can pivot and slide between the fingers. Friction during this transient changes its motion, so the velocity and spin at detachment can differ substantially from those of the fingertip [ 4 ] . After detachment, the problem changes from contact dynamics to aerodynamic flight. The boomerang undergoes six-degree-of-freedom rigid-body motion, while its rapidly rotating blades operate at low Reynolds number and periodically experience reversed flow. Aerodynamic moments also change the attitude through gyroscopic precession, coupling the attitude evolution to the flight path [ 1 ] . Predicting a throw from robot motion therefore requires models for both the transient release and the subsequent flight.

Challenge 2: Robot speed limits. Returning boomerangs require fast throwing motion and high release spin. Measurements of rapid human overhand throwing report joint angular velocities above 70 ​ rad / s 70~\mathrm{rad/s} and angular accelerations on the order of 10 3 ​ rad / s 2 10^{3}~\mathrm{rad/s^{2}} [ 5 , 6 ] . Robotic manipulators operate under different actuator limits. Gear reduction increases output torque at the expense of joint speed, while motor back electromotive force further limits speed during rapid motion. Directly reproducing human throwing motions is therefore generally infeasible. Instead, the release must be generated using the motion that the robot can achieve.

Facing these challenges, we propose a model-based design procedure centered on the release state. A transient release model maps the robot throwing motion to the boomerang state at detachment, while a flight model maps the release state and boomerang design to the subsequent flight. To guide boomerang design, we identify the flight dynamics in stages to predict how the flight changes with the boomerang design. To achieve the high release spin required for return, we systematically screen motion parameters according to their effect on release spin using the release model.

Together, these models guide the design of the throwing motion and boomerang for a 6-DoF manipulator with limited joint speeds. The resulting robot throw operates in a substantially different aerodynamic regime from the measured human throws, showing that a returning throw can be designed for the robot rather than imitating human motion.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

Robot throwing of complex objects. Over the past four decades, robot throwing research has progressively expanded both the variety of objects that can be thrown and the outcomes that can be controlled. Early systems considered nonprehensile throwing of specially shaped objects released from an open palm [ 7 ] , as well as in-hand throwing and catching with high-speed multifingered hands [ 8 ] . Prehensile throwing later extended the object set to arbitrary and deformable items, using either large-scale real-world throwing data [ 9 ] or zero-shot robust throwing with model-based motion synthesis [ 10 ] . More recently, robot throwing has also considered control of object rotation and landing pose [ 11 , 12 ] . Across these works, the main modeling challenge lies in the robot–object interaction before detachment, while the subsequent flight is typically described by projectile dynamics under gravity, sometimes with simple air drag.

Throwing aerodynamic objects extends robot throwing beyond ballistic flight because lift can continue to shape the trajectory after release. Aslam et al. [ 13 ] throw darts using learned corrections for a given set of dart designs, while Obayashi et al. [ 14 ] use hundreds of throws with a fixed robot motion to optimize the shape of paper airplanes. Boomerang throwing couples release and flight more strongly: the release velocity, attitude, and spin determine the subsequent aerodynamic flight, while the high release spin needed for a returning flight is difficult to generate under the joint-speed limits of robotic manipulators. We therefore consider the boomerang design together with the throwing motion that launches it.

Boomerang flight dynamics. Though primarily used for recreational sport, the boomerang’s unusual flight dynamics have attracted a substantial body of aerodynamic research. Hess [ 1 ] combined wind-tunnel force and torque measurements of rotating boomerangs with numerical integration of spin-averaged rigid-body dynamics. Azuma et al. [ 15 ] developed an analytical blade-element model of the aerodynamic coefficients, while Vassberg [ 2 ] derived a closed-form approximation of the circular flight radius under steady-flight assumptions. Gudem and colleagues further refined the aerodynamic modeling of reversed flow over the retreating blade [ 16 ] , with wind-tunnel validation of the predicted lift [ 17 ] .

Smart boomerangs have also been proposed as passive returning probes for planetary exploration [ 3 ] . In hardware tests, hand throws of the prototype reached speeds below 18 ​ m / s 18~\mathrm{m/s} and spins of about 2 ​ rev / s 2~\mathrm{rev/s} , but did not produce a returning flight. A purpose-built crossbow launcher could not independently control release timing, speed, and spin, leaving the generation of suitable launch conditions as a key challenge.

Overall, the boomerang literature has focused primarily on how aerodynamics and geometry determine flight, while treating the launch condition as given. Human throwing techniques, e.g. [ 18 ] , are difficult to reproduce on robotic manipulators because of their different kinematics and dynamic limits. Robotic boomerang throwing therefore requires linking the flight dynamics to release conditions that the robot can actually generate.

2026-10-08.title: CMP-IRRT*: A Perception-Assisted Height-Adaptive Planner for Quadruped Robots
2026-10-08.authors: Mingfan Zhao , Wendong Mao , Zhongfeng Wang
2026-10-08.comment: Accepted at the 18th Asian Conference on Machine Learning (ACML 2026)
2026-10-08.abstract: Quadruped robots can traverse low obstacles, but many 2D planning pipelines still model obstacles as binary occupied regions and rely on sampling-based search that can be inefficient under a limited budget. We propose a perception-assisted height-adaptive planning framework based on CMP-IRRT*, a Channel Mamba PointNet-guided Informed RRT* planner. Given a calibrated top-view RGB observation, the perception module estimates obstacle regions and converts depth predictions into a ground-relative height map. The planner then performs height-conditioned collision checking, treating high obstacles as blocked while allowing low obstacles to be traversed, and uses the CMP guide to bias sampling toward promising regions while retaining standard free-space and informed sampling fallbacks. Experiments on 2D planning benchmarks show that CMP-IRRT* reduces explored nodes and iterations compared with classical and neural-guided baselines, and a controlled ablation supports the contribution of the Mamba-based guide. In constructed traversability-aware scenarios, the proposed planner reduces path length by up to 16.3% when low obstacles are traversable, and a Unitree Go2 demonstration further shows executable bypassing and traversal behaviors. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/MingfanZhao/height-adaptive-planner .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Quadruped robots can move in environments that are difficult for wheeled platforms, partly because their legs allow them to step over or traverse low obstacles. However, many 2D path planning pipelines still model the environment as a binary occupancy map: an obstacle is either free or blocked. This representation is simple and widely used, but it can lead to unnecessary detours when an obstacle is low enough for a legged robot to cross safely. For quadruped navigation, the planner should therefore consider not only obstacle position, but also obstacle height and the robot’s traversal capability.

Sampling-based planners such as RRT* and Informed RRT* are attractive for robot path planning because they can handle complex environments and improve path quality over time. Learning-guided planners further improve finite-budget search by predicting promising regions of the state space. Nevertheless, these methods usually focus on where to sample and how to avoid collision, while treating all detected obstacles as non-traversable. In this work, we study a complementary question: how can visual perception and robot-specific traversability constraints be incorporated into a planning pipeline so that low obstacles can be crossed instead of always bypassed?

We propose a visual perception-assisted traversability-aware path planning pipeline for quadruped robots. The system uses a calibrated top-view RGB observation to estimate obstacle shape, location, and height. These obstacle attributes are combined with a robot-specific height threshold to decide whether an obstacle should be treated as blocked or traversable during planning. The resulting height-conditioned collision check is integrated with a Channel Mamba PointNet-guided Informed RRT* planner (CMP-IRRT*) to improve search efficiency under a limited planning budget. The output path is decoded into velocity commands and motion modes for execution on a quadruped robot.

This paper does not claim a new optimality theory for RRT-based planning. Instead, it contributes a practical formulation and implementation of perception-conditioned traversability-aware planning. The main contributions are:

We formulate a traversability-aware planning problem for quadruped robots, where obstacle handling depends on both perceived obstacle height and robot crossing capability.

We design a modular perception-assisted planning pipeline that estimates obstacle geometry from a top-view RGB image and uses height-conditioned collision checking to decide whether to bypass or traverse obstacles.

We introduce a Channel Mamba PointNet-guided IRRT* planner to improve finite-budget sampling efficiency by predicting promising search regions.

We validate the framework on 2D planning benchmarks, constructed traversability-aware scenarios, and a Unitree Go2 demonstration, showing reduced explored nodes and iterations for CMP-IRRT* and up to a 16.3% path-length reduction when low obstacles are traversable.

1. We formulate a traversability-aware planning problem for quadruped robots, where obstacle handling depends on both perceived obstacle height and robot crossing capability.

2. We design a modular perception-assisted planning pipeline that estimates obstacle geometry from a top-view RGB image and uses height-conditioned collision checking to decide whether to bypass or traverse obstacles.

3. We introduce a Channel Mamba PointNet-guided IRRT* planner to improve finite-budget sampling efficiency by predicting promising search regions.

4. We validate the framework on 2D planning benchmarks, constructed traversability-aware scenarios, and a Unitree Go2 demonstration, showing reduced explored nodes and iterations for CMP-IRRT* and up to a 16.3% path-length reduction when low obstacles are traversable.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Sampling-Based and Learning-Guided Planning

Classical path planning methods include graph-search algorithms such as A* ( Hart et al., 1968 ) , sampling-based planners such as RRT* ( Karaman and Frazzoli, 2011 ) , and potential-field methods ( Khatib, 1985 ) . Informed RRT* improves the efficiency of RRT* by restricting sampling to an ellipsoidal subset once an initial solution is found ( Gammell et al., 2014 ) . Learning-guided planners further use neural networks to predict useful search regions or guidance maps. Neural A* encodes planning instances into a differentiable search guidance map ( Yonetani et al., 2021 ) , while NIRRT* uses point-cloud constraints to guide Informed RRT* ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . These approaches improve search efficiency, but they usually treat obstacles as binary collision regions. Our work is complementary: it introduces a traversability-aware collision model for quadruped robots and combines it with a learned sampling guide.

## 2.2 Traversability-Aware Planning for Legged Robots

Legged robots differ from wheeled robots because they can step over low obstacles and exploit multiple locomotion modes. Reviews of legged robot motion and design emphasize that locomotion capability depends on the robot’s morphology and control constraints ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . In many planning pipelines, however, this capability is not explicitly reflected in the 2D map representation. We focus on a practical setting in which obstacle height is estimated from visual perception and compared with a robot-specific crossing threshold. This allows the planner to treat some obstacles as traversable while still avoiding obstacles that exceed the robot’s capability.

Representative terrain-referenced elevation-mapping methods maintain 2.5D per-cell terrain geometry from range sensing and state estimation for legged locomotion and navigation ( Fankhauser et al., 2014 ; Miki et al., 2022 ) . Our method addresses a complementary operating regime. It converts a calibrated top-view RGB observation into an image-aligned ground-relative height map and directly supplies object-level height information to CMP-IRRT*, without maintaining an online terrain-map fusion pipeline. Elevation maps retain dense terrain detail, but they depend on range measurements, pose estimates, and map fusion. Our formulation instead emphasizes direct perception-to-planning integration for the approximately planar-topped obstacles in the static scenes evaluated here. It remains sensitive to monocular depth errors, calibration, occlusion, and non-planar objects. A rigorous cross-paradigm comparison would require common sensing inputs and mapping conditions. We therefore do not directly compare performance with elevation-map planners in the present study. Our evaluation instead focuses on finite-budget sampling and height-conditioned traversability within the calibrated top-view setting studied here.

## 2.3 Vision-Based Obstacle Perception

Vision-based perception provides the geometric information required by traversability-aware planning. Object detection models such as YOLO ( Redmon et al., 2016 ; Khanam and Hussain, 2024 ) can identify obstacle regions, while monocular depth models such as Depth Anything V2 ( Yang et al., 2024 ) provide depth estimates from RGB images. In this paper, we do not propose a new depth estimation model. Instead, we use existing perception modules to provide obstacle position and height estimates for the planner. This design keeps the planning contribution separate from the perception backbone and makes the assumptions of the pipeline explicit.

2026-10-08.title: LLA-MPPI: Rapidly Adaptive Whole-body Control of Legged Robots with GPU-Accelerated Parallel Simulations
2026-10-08.authors: Sebin Jung , Maitham F. AL-Sunni , Juan Alvarez-Padilla , Zachary Manchester , Changliu Liu , John M. Dolan
2026-10-08.comment: The first two authors are co-first authors (contributed equally to the work)
2026-10-08.abstract: Real-time whole-body controllers for legged robots typically plan through a fixed nominal model and degrade when the deployed dynamics change. Adaptive methods typically require model structure that contact dynamics do not provide, or they need offline training for each anticipated condition. We present Look-back and Look-ahead Adaptive Model Predictive Path Integral control (LLA-MPPI) . The method converts whole-body adaptation into selection over a bank of GPU-batched contact simulators with different physical or structural parameters. Windowed prediction errors select the simulator that best explains recent motion. A whole-body MPPI planner optimizes controls through the selected model. The framework requires no offline training, and its selected hypotheses are physically interpretable. Across four simulated tasks, it achieves 97.5 % 97.5\% success while the strongest baseline reaches 74 % 74\% and an oracle with the true model reaches 98.5 % 98.5\% . Hardware validation on a Unitree Go2 shows the robot walking under a payload added mid-run, walking after one leg is disabled, and pushing a box to its goal while increasing its mass on the fly.
