2026-10-08.introduction:
Legged robots encounter dynamics that change during operation:
payloads shift, ground friction varies, terrain tilts, and actuators
degrade. Real-time whole-body control has become practical [ 3 , 27 , 29 , 23 ] ,
but such controllers typically plan through a fixed nominal model and
degrade under model mismatch. Existing remedies either reduce the
model until a classical estimator applies, losing contact-mediated and
structural uncertainty, or train policies offline whose adaptation is
implicit and bounded by the training distribution.

In adaptive control of legged systems, the identification model is
typically coarser than the control model. Estimators recover a small
number of inertial parameters on floating-base, single-rigid-body, or
centroidal models [ 7 , 21 ] ;
lump mismatch into an external wrench [ 14 ] ; or absorb it
into a black-box error model [ 28 , 30 ] . Within sampling-based
control, adaptation has instead targeted controller gains [ 26 ] or pre-designed gait modes [ 10 ] , rather
than the dynamics model.

This reduction reflects the structure required by classical
estimators. Model-reference and ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} adaptive control,
recursive least squares, disturbance observers, and recursive Bayesian
filters respectively require matched uncertainty [ 17 , 8 ] , an affine regressor [ 16 ] , a discrepancy representable as a generalized
force [ 4 ] , or a fixed parameterization with
sufficient excitation [ 6 ] . Whole-body contact
dynamics generally do not provide these structures, leaving
contact-mediated uncertainty such as foot–ground friction and
structural uncertainty such as actuator failure outside the
identification model.

Multiple-model adaptive control (MMAC) removes the regressor
requirement by scoring a finite set of candidate models against
observed data [ 18 ] . Recent work recasts this
principle as massively parallel model selection for ground and aerial
vehicles. A large bank of models is scored using one-step prediction
error over a look-back window, and the selected model is passed to a
look-ahead predictive controller or safety filter. This approach was
introduced for autonomous racing in simulation [ 1 ] , subsequently deployed on an F1TENTH vehicle [ 15 ] , and extended to safety-critical
control of an F1TENTH vehicle and a Crazyflie quadrotor [ 2 ] . Unlike classical MMAC, these methods maintain
thousands of candidate models, score only recent transitions, and use
the selected model directly in the look-ahead stage rather than
choosing among pre-designed controllers.

However, extending this principle to whole-body legged control is not
straightforward. Prior formulations rely on low-dimensional models of
known functional form and on motion that sufficiently excites the
uncertain dynamics. Neither assumption holds generally for
contact-rich locomotion. The whole-body transition map changes across
contact modes and admits no single smooth closed-form description, while
candidate models may become indistinguishable whenever
motion does not excite the corresponding uncertainty.

A parallel line of work uses reinforcement learning instead of
explicit model-based adaptation. Domain randomization trains policies
across distributions of dynamics [ 13 , 20 ] , teacher–student methods infer
latent environment representations [ 12 ] , and mixtures
of specialized policies cover discrete failure modes [ 24 ] . These methods can perform well within their
training distributions, but additional anticipated modes generally
require retraining, the inferred latent is not a physical quantity,
and out-of-distribution degradation may occur without an explicit
indication of model mismatch.

To remove the model-structure assumptions above, we perform adaptation
directly over simulation-fidelity contact dynamics using GPU-batched
model selection. Candidate hypotheses need only be steppable by the
physics engine; no differentiable, affine, or closed-form
parameterization is required. GPU-parallel physics makes this practical
by advancing thousands of independently parameterized worlds
concurrently. We introduce Look-back and Look-ahead Adaptive MPPI
(LLA-MPPI) , which maintains a bank of full-contact simulators in
MuJoCo Warp [ 5 ] spanning physical and structural hypotheses. A windowed
prediction residual selects the model that best explains recent motion,
while a switching margin retains the incumbent when intermittent
excitation makes hypotheses difficult to distinguish. A whole-body
MPPI controller [ 25 ] then plans directly through
the selected model. Relative to prior multiple-model formulations,
LLA-MPPI removes the requirement for a low-dimensional model of known
functional form and regularizes online selection under intermittent
contact excitation. The method requires no offline policy training,
and its selected hypotheses retain direct physical meaning.

Our contributions are threefold:

A whole-body adaptive control framework that performs online
identification over a bank of full-contact simulators under
intermittent contact excitation, covering parametric and structural
uncertainty in a common hypothesis space without requiring
differentiable, affine, or closed-form dynamics.

A decoupled heterogeneous architecture that runs GPU-batched
identification concurrently with CPU whole-body planning, so
increasing model-set resolution primarily consumes GPU throughput
rather than increasing the planner’s critical-path latency.

An evaluation across four contact-rich locomotion and
loco-manipulation tasks against model-based adaptive-control
baselines, together with a comparison to domain-randomized RL.

2026-10-08.title: FoldBack: Self-Correcting Masked Generative Policy for Long-Horizon Garment Folding
2026-10-08.authors: Lipeng Zhuang , Shiyu Fan , Yingdong Ru , Zhuo He , Florent P. Audonnet , Paul Henderson , Gerardo Aragon Camarasa
2026-10-08.abstract:
We present FoldBack, a self-correcting masked generative policy for long-horizon garment folding. Existing long-trajectory policies may continue after a missed or slipped grasp even when the garment has not reached the intended configuration. We structure FoldBack’s recovery mechanisms around three inference-time decisions: when to refine and verify , how to roll back , and where and how to retry . FoldBack aligns refinement and grasp verification with pick-and-place events, returns the robot to a retryable pre-grasp configuration while preserving successful grasps, and selectively regenerates the failed segment and selected future actions while avoiding previous failed grasp locations.
To our knowledge, FoldBack is the first editable full-trajectory policy to unify these decisions, enabling failed interactions to be detected, undone, and repaired before execution continues, without recovery demonstrations or base-policy retraining.
Across 33 real garments from six categories, FoldBack achieves 75.2 % 75.2\% final folding success and 0.837 0.837 final-mask IoU, versus 45.7 % 45.7\% and 0.689 0.689 for the strongest prior baseline.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Garment folding is a long-horizon manipulation task that requires executing a sequence of precise single-arm or bimanual pick-and-place actions. Each action changes the garment configuration, which in turn determines the conditions for subsequent folding actions. A missed or slipped grasp therefore invalidates subsequent folding actions [ 1 ] .
For example, a robot may close its gripper and lift without successfully moving the garment, leaving it in a configuration incompatible with the next folding action.
Reliable folding not only requires long-horizon action generation but also a mechanism for detecting grasp failures and recovering from them before execution advances.

Visuomotor imitation learning enables robots to learn complex behaviors from demonstrations [ 2 , 1 , 3 ] . Short-horizon policies generate action chunks myopically given recent observations, enabling reactive execution [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . However, grasp failures can produce out-of-distribution observations that cause subsequent predictions to stall, drift, or lose coherence with the overall folding strategy. Long-horizon generative policies generate complete, coherent action sequences and can refine future action tokens as observations arrive [ 8 , 9 ] ; yet executed action tokens remain fixed in the trajectory history without verifying the intended manipulation outcome. Thus, execution may advance to the next folding stage without revisiting the failed interaction. Runtime monitors can detect such failures but do not themselves revise the policy trajectory [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , while recovery-aware methods often rely on additional recovery data, policy adaptation, or large-model reasoning [ 1 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] .

Motivated by these limitations, we introduce FoldBack, an outcome-gated masked generative policy for long-horizon garment folding that supports recovery from grasp failures. FoldBack represents the full action trajectory as discrete tokens and maintains a grasp-verified history, a tentative grasp-critical window, and an editable future. Executing a grasp-critical window does not immediately add it to history. The window is added only after all required grasps are verified; otherwise, the history remains unchanged and the failed window stays editable (Fig. 1 ).

FoldBack is then organized around three inference-time decisions which constitute the contributions of this paper:

when to refine and verify (Sec. III-A ),

how to roll back after a failure (Sec. III-B ), and

where and how to retry (Sec. III-C ).
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

Learning-based garment manipulation. Garment-folding policies typically compose prescribed primitives or generate local action segments [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . SpeedFolding [ 20 ] and UniFolding [ 2 ] execute parameterized primitives, while BiFold [ 21 ] predicts a language-conditioned pick-and-place action at each step. Model-based methods learn cloth dynamics for planning [ 22 , 23 ] , while UniClothDiff [ 24 ] uses diffusion models for generative state estimation and dynamics prediction within model-predictive control. Other generative policies model distributions over action primitives (DeformPAM [ 25 ] ), closed-loop or local manipulation trajectories (FoldNet [ 1 ] and HALO [ 26 ] ), or stage-wise point-cloud trajectories (MetaFold [ 27 ] ).
These methods are effective for local or stage-wise manipulation, but long-horizon folding requires consistent execution across multiple strategies with both single- and bimanual actions. FoldBack addresses this with full-trajectory masked generation for an editable plan (Sec. III ), Key-Action-Aligned Inference for event-aligned refinement and grasp verification (Sec. III-A ), Verified Rollback to keep failed windows revisable (Sec. III-B ), and Structured Plan Repair to selectively revise the affected trajectory (Sec. III-C ).

Imitation learning. Imitation learning learns visuomotor policies from demonstrations. Short-horizon policies generate local action sequences and replan from observations, including ACT [ 5 ] , Diffusion Policy [ 6 ] , DP3 [ 7 ] , 3D Diffuser Actor [ 28 ] , BeT [ 29 ] , and VQ-BeT [ 30 ] .
Recent methods improve temporal consistency or inference efficiency through sequence-level generation and action-chunk refinement [ 8 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 ] , but do not maintain an editable task plan.
MGP-Long [ 9 ] instead generates a complete trajectory, fixes executed tokens as history, and refines uncertain future tokens. Thus, it cannot revisit failed grasps. FoldBack addresses this by adding grasp-critical windows to the grasp-verified history only after verification (Sec. III-B ) and regenerating failed windows during plan repair (Sec. III-C ).

Failure monitoring and recovery. Runtime monitoring methods detect anomalous behavior or insufficient progress but do not generate recovery actions [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Some recovery-aware methods instead learn corrective behavior from additional data. For instance, FoldNet uses KG-DAgger recovery trajectories [ 1 ] , while RACER [ 13 ] trains a VLM-supervised, language-conditioned policy on generated recovery trajectories and fine-grained annotations. More general correction frameworks include CycleVLA [ 15 ] , which combines VLA-based progress prediction with VLM-guided backtracking, while FAR [ 16 ] adapts a diffusion policy from test-time failures and perturbs retry actions. Bellman-Guided Retrials [ 35 ] performs progress-guided retrials, while Rewind-IL [ 36 ] rewinds policies to verified checkpoints.
As described in Sec. III-B and Sec. III-C , FoldBack instead reopens failed windows within an editable full trajectory and selectively repairs the affected trajectory while preserving grasp-verified history.
It requires neither failure-recovery demonstrations, base-policy adaptation, nor auxiliary LLM/VLM reasoning.

2026-10-08.title: RFPO: Rectified Flow Policy Optimization for Embodied Control
2026-10-08.authors: Ting Huang , Lisiyu Pan , Haoyu Wang , Zeyu Zhang , Siyuan Qian , Yanjun Li , Yandong Guo , Boxin Shi , Hao Tang
2026-10-08.abstract:
Flow-based policies provide an expressive framework for continuous robot control, but their iterative ODE integration incurs substantial inference cost.
Naively reducing the integration budget can severely degrade control, since policies optimized under full-step execution are not explicitly constrained to remain reliable under coarse numerical integration.
We refer to this mismatch as the few-step discretization gap .
To address this problem, we introduce RFPO, a flow-policy optimization framework for reliable few-step execution.
Reward-aware online Reflow rectifies student-induced transport paths during on-policy learning, making the resulting policy more robust to coarse integration.
A frozen Gaussian PPO controller supplies complementary action-space supervision at full and intermediate integration budgets, while the deployed policy remains a single flow student executed with one Euler step.
Across Unitree Go2, Boston Dynamics Spot, Unitree H1, and Unitree G1, RFPO consistently preserves full-step control performance under one-step execution, with one-step returns remaining within 2.4 % 2.4\% of their corresponding 64-step values across both zero and random initialization.
On Unitree Go2, one-step execution retains 98.5% of the 64-step reward while reducing onboard mean inference latency from 4.39 4.39 ms to 0.08 0.08 ms, yielding a 54.9 × \times speedup .
Real-robot experiments further validate stable one-step locomotion.
Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/RFPO .
Website: https://aigeeksgroup.github.io/RFPO
2026-10-08.introduction:
Learning expressive and efficient continuous-control policies is a central problem in robotics.
Conventional reinforcement learning typically parameterizes actions with simple distributions such as diagonal Gaussians, which are easy to optimize but can be restrictive when multiple control strategies are valid under the same observation.
Generative policies provide a more expressive alternative and have shown strong performance in visuomotor and geometry-aware robot control [ 3 , 33 ] .
In particular, flow matching [ 12 ] and rectified flow [ 13 ] model action generation as an ODE that transports simple noise distributions into continuous actions.
Flow-based policies have since been adopted for efficient robot manipulation [ 34 ] and large-scale vision-language-action models such as π 0 \pi_{0} [ 1 ] , highlighting their potential as an expressive policy class for robot control.

Beyond demonstration-supervised learning, recent work has increasingly optimized generative policies directly from environment rewards.
Diffusion-based approaches such as DPPO [ 21 ] , DIME [ 2 ] , and GenPO [ 4 ] extend reinforcement learning to iterative generative action distributions.
For flow-based policies, ReinFlow [ 35 ] enables online fine-tuning through stochastic flow dynamics, while Flow Q-Learning [ 18 ] and SAC Flow [ 36 ] explore offline and off-policy optimization.
FPO [ 16 ] constructs an on-policy surrogate directly from conditional flow-matching losses, and FPO++ [ 32 ] further improves this formulation with per-sample flow ratios and asymmetric trust-region updates.
These advances make reward-driven optimization of expressive flow policies increasingly practical.

However, high-reward flow policies are not necessarily reliable when the numerical integration budget is aggressively reduced.
Existing flow-policy RL objectives optimize control return under the training integration budget but do not explicitly constrain the resulting vector field to remain numerically reliable under coarse integration.
Consequently, reducing the number of Euler steps can substantially change the generated action and lead to severe control degradation, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .
We refer to this mismatch between full-step optimization and low-budget execution as the few-step discretization gap .
Although Reflow [ 13 ] , consistency learning [ 26 ] , fast ODE solvers, and policy distillation [ 19 , 34 ] have enabled efficient few-step generation, these techniques are primarily developed for generative modeling, imitation learning, or post-hoc policy acceleration rather than jointly with on-policy reward optimization.
This motivates directly shaping reward-optimized flow policies for reliable few-step execution.

To address this problem, we introduce RFPO, a flow-policy optimization framework for reliable few-step control.
The key mechanism is reward-aware online Reflow, which repeatedly constructs student-induced full-step endpoints and rectifies their transport paths during on-policy learning, making the learned vector field more amenable to coarse numerical integration.
A frozen Gaussian PPO controller supplies complementary action-space supervision at full and intermediate integration budgets, anchoring the quality of the learned actions without directly supervising one-step execution.
The original on-policy objective is retained throughout training, and all training-only components are removed at deployment, leaving a single flow student executed with one Euler step.
We evaluate RFPO across two quadruped and two humanoid embodiments: Unitree Go2, Boston Dynamics Spot, Unitree H1, and Unitree G1.
Across all four embodiments and both zero and random initialization, one-step execution remains within 2.4 % 2.4\% of the corresponding 64-step return, whereas FPO++ and distillation-only baselines exhibit substantial degradation under aggressive step reduction.
On Unitree Go2, RFPO retains 98.5% of its 64-step reward while reducing onboard mean inference latency from 4.39 4.39 ms to 0.08 0.08 ms, yielding a 54.9 × \times speedup .
Real-robot experiments further demonstrate stable one-step locomotion across forward, lateral, and yaw commands.

Our contributions are threefold:

We identify the few-step discretization gap in reward-optimized flow policies, where aggressive reduction of the numerical integration budget can severely degrade control despite strong full-step performance.

We introduce RFPO, which uses reward-aware student-induced online Reflow to regularize transport geometry during on-policy learning, together with complementary multi-budget action-space supervision from a frozen Gaussian PPO controller.

Extensive evaluations across two quadruped and two humanoid embodiments demonstrate robust one-step execution.
On Unitree Go2, RFPO retains 98.5% of 64-step reward with a 54.9 × \times onboard inference speedup and transfers to real-robot locomotion.

1. We identify the few-step discretization gap in reward-optimized flow policies, where aggressive reduction of the numerical integration budget can severely degrade control despite strong full-step performance.

2. We introduce RFPO, which uses reward-aware student-induced online Reflow to regularize transport geometry during on-policy learning, together with complementary multi-budget action-space supervision from a frozen Gaussian PPO controller.

3. Extensive evaluations across two quadruped and two humanoid embodiments demonstrate robust one-step execution.
On Unitree Go2, RFPO retains 98.5% of 64-step reward with a 54.9 × \times onboard inference speedup and transfers to real-robot locomotion.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

Generative and flow policies for robot control. Generative policies provide an expressive alternative to Gaussian actors for modeling multimodal robot behaviors.
Diffusion Policy [ 3 ] and 3D Diffusion Policy [ 33 ] demonstrate strong visuomotor and geometry-aware manipulation performance using iterative generative action models.
Flow matching [ 12 ] and rectified flow [ 13 ] provide an ODE-based alternative and have been adopted by robot policies such as RF-Policy [ 6 ] , FlowPolicy [ 34 ] , and ManiFlow [ 31 ] , as well as large-scale vision-language-action models such as π 0 \pi_{0} [ 1 ] .
Recent work has further accelerated iterative robot policies through consistency learning and policy distillation [ 19 , 30 ] .
These methods are predominantly trained from demonstrations or supervised robot data, whereas our work studies few-step execution of flow policies optimized directly from environment rewards.

Reinforcement learning with generative policies. Generative models have increasingly been incorporated into planning and reinforcement learning.
Diffusion-based methods have been used for trajectory planning and expressive offline policies [ 8 , 29 , 9 ] , while Q-score matching connects diffusion-policy scores with reward-derived action gradients [ 20 ] .
DPPO [ 21 ] , DIME [ 2 ] , and GenPO [ 4 ] further optimize iterative generative policies with reinforcement learning.
For flow-based policies, ReinFlow [ 35 ] studies online fine-tuning, while Flow Q-Learning [ 18 ] and SAC Flow [ 36 ] consider offline or off-policy optimization.
FPO [ 16 ] and FPO++ [ 32 ] instead develop on-policy objectives directly from conditional flow-matching losses.
These methods primarily optimize control return, while our work addresses the complementary problem of preserving policy behavior when the numerical integration budget is aggressively reduced.

Few-step generative policy acceleration. Reducing the inference cost of iterative generative models has motivated both solver-based and learning-based acceleration.
Training-free approaches such as DDIM [ 25 ] and DPM-Solver [ 15 ] reduce the number of numerical integration steps, while learning-based approaches include progressive distillation [ 23 ] , consistency models [ 26 ] , consistency trajectory models [ 10 ] , improved consistency training [ 27 ] , and Shortcut Models [ 5 ] .
For flow-based models, Reflow [ 13 ] and InstaFlow [ 14 ] reshape transport trajectories to support coarse or one-step generation.
Related ideas have been transferred to robot policies through Consistency Policy [ 19 ] , One-Step Diffusion Policy [ 30 ] , FlowPolicy [ 34 ] , and ManiFlow [ 31 ] .
These approaches largely target generative modeling, imitation learning, or post-hoc policy acceleration.
In contrast, RFPO performs student-induced Reflow during on-policy reward optimization, directly regularizing the transport geometry encountered by the evolving policy.
A frozen deployable controller provides complementary action-space supervision at full and intermediate integration budgets rather than direct one-step supervision.

Learning-based legged locomotion and sim-to-real. Deep reinforcement learning has enabled agile legged locomotion through simulation-based training, robust policy learning, and massively parallel simulation [ 7 , 28 , 22 ] .
Subsequent work has improved real-world robustness through rapid adaptation and perceptive locomotion [ 11 , 17 ] .
These studies primarily address dynamics mismatch, terrain variation, and online adaptation, whereas our work focuses on a complementary deployment bottleneck: preserving the behavior of reward-optimized flow policies under aggressive reductions of the numerical integration budget.

2026-10-08.title: AirGroundVLN: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Goal-Oriented Air-Ground Collaborative Vision-and-Language Navigation
2026-10-08.authors: Zhenxuan Zeng , Qingle Wu , Wei Suo , Maojia Wu , Bairong Zhang , Hangzheng Yu , Peng Wang
2026-10-08.abstract: Goal-oriented Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to locate and reach targets described in natural language without prescribed routes. Air–ground collaboration is valuable for tasks requiring both wide-area search and fine-grained localization. However, systematic study of goal-oriented air–ground collaborative VLN remains limited by the lack of large-scale, diverse benchmarks and two core challenges: 1) substantial differences between aerial and ground views, together with useful observations becoming unavailable as navigation proceeds, make it difficult to maintain spatially consistent context across platforms and over time; and 2) asymmetric spatial observability makes ground perception locally detailed but spatially limited and aerial perception broad but locally coarse, limiting the reliability of single-platform planning. To address these limitations, we introduce AirGroundVLN , a benchmark containing 10,281 navigation episodes and 955 target instances across 19 Unreal Engine environments, with seen/unseen splits and an aerial-visibility protocol for systematic evaluation. Alongside the benchmark, we propose AG-CoNAV, a trainable reference framework comprising two key components: Spatiotemporally Anchored Collaborative Memory (SACM) and Aerial-Guided Regional-to-Local Planning (AGRLP). SACM maintains and retrieves spatially consistent historical context across aerial and ground observations. Meanwhile, AGRLP combines regional aerial guidance with fine-grained ground navigation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of AG-CoNAV and establish AirGroundVLN as a comprehensive benchmark for future exploration.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Goal-oriented vision-and-language navigation (VLN) is a core problem in embodied intelligence ( Qi et al., 2020 ; Zhu et al., 2021 ) , requiring an agent to interpret a language-specified target, search for it, identify the correct instance, and reach it without prescribed intermediate routes. Existing goal-oriented VLN studies predominantly consider two types of embodied platforms: (1) Ground Platforms , such as wheeled Unmanned Ground Vehicles (UGVs), quadruped robots, and humanoid robots ( Krantz et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . (2) Aerial Platforms , typically Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) . In large-scale outdoor environments, ground platforms provide fine-grained observations of local scene structure and target appearance and can physically approach ground-level targets. In contrast, aerial platforms provide broader spatial coverage and global scene context, enabling efficient wide-area search and route-level reasoning. As two popular embodied platforms, substantial research has focused on separately expanding their perception ( Huang et al., 2023 ) , reasoning and planning ( Ahn et al., 2022 ; Song et al., 2023 ) , and execution capabilities ( Zhou et al., 2020 ; Kumar et al., 2021 ) .

But consider such a real mission in a large industrial complex, where robots are instructed to rescue a worker in a red jacket near a damaged warehouse . In this mission, an aerial platform can rapidly survey the area and search for the worker from a global viewpoint, but its observations may be obstructed by trees, roofs, or collapsed structures, and it cannot provide physical rescue. Meanwhile, a ground platform can closely approach the worker, inspect regions hidden from the aerial viewpoint, and provide assistance, but damaged roads, debris, and collapsed buildings may render routes infeasible. Such a mission calls for aerial and ground platforms to work together, combining wide-area search with fine-grained target localization and physical access. This complementary division of capabilities motivates heterogeneous air–ground collaboration for goal-oriented navigation.

However, systematic study of goal-oriented air–ground collaborative VLN remains limited by three key issues: (1) Although recent efforts have explored air–ground VLN ( Li et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) , they remain limited in scale and diversity, with AirGroundBench and AGC-VLN evaluated on only 115 and 100 episodes, respectively. To our knowledge, a large-scale benchmark for goal-oriented air–ground collaborative VLN is still lacking, limiting systematic evaluation. (2) Beyond benchmark limitation, aerial and ground observations differ in viewpoint, while useful observations from either platform may become unavailable during navigation. Therefore, effective collaboration requires spatially consistent context across views and time. (3) Aerial and ground platforms exhibit asymmetric spatial observability: ground perception is locally detailed but spatially limited, whereas aerial perception covers broader regions but provides less fine-grained obstacle information, making either platform alone insufficient for reliable navigation.

To address this gap, we first introduce AirGroundVLN , a large-scale benchmark for goal-oriented air–ground collaborative VLN. AirGroundVLN contains 10,281 navigation episodes, 955 target instances, and 19 Unreal Engine environments, covering urban areas, towns, industrial areas, and other complex outdoor environments. Each episode includes aerial and ground observations together with a goal-oriented instruction describing the target appearance and its surrounding environmental context, rather than prescribing intermediate navigation actions. We provide seen and unseen environment splits to evaluate cross-environment generalization. An aerial-visibility protocol is further defined to distinguish targets visible from above and those occluded by overhead structures, enabling evaluation under different target-visibility conditions.

Alongside the benchmark, we develop AG-CoNAV , a trainable reference framework addressing the above two key challenges of air–ground collaborative VLN. First, to maintain spatially consistent spatiotemporal context across heterogeneous aerial and ground observations, we introduce the Spatiotemporally Anchored Collaborative Memory (SACM), which stores and retrieves historical evidence by associating observations of physically related regions over time. Second, to overcome limitations of single-platform planning under asymmetric spatial observability, we introduce the Aerial-Guided Regional-to-Local Planning module (AGRLP), which combines regional aerial guidance with locally executable ground planning. In addition, to establish reference baselines for AirGroundVLN, we construct training-free and trainable methods for air–ground collaborative VLN and evaluate them alongside AG-CoNAV across seen/unseen environments and aerial-visible/aerial-occluded conditions. These evaluations establish reference performance for AirGroundVLN and demonstrate the effectiveness of AG-CoNAV. Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce AirGroundVLN , a large-scale benchmark for goal-oriented air–ground collaborative Vision-and-Language Navigation. It contains 10,281 navigation episodes and 955 target instances across 19 Unreal Engine environments, together with goal-oriented instructions, seen/unseen splits, and an aerial-visibility protocol for systematic evaluation.

We develop AG-CoNAV , a trainable reference framework for heterogeneous air–ground collaborative VLN. It incorporates a Spatiotemporally Anchored Collaborative Memory (SACM) for spatiotemporally consistent context association and historical retrieval, together with an Aerial-Guided Regional-to-Local Planning module (AGRLP) that coordinates regional aerial guidance with fine-grained ground execution.

We provide a diverse suite of training-free and trainable baselines for AirGroundVLN, establishing a comprehensive evaluation suite for this new setting. Systematic evaluations across environment generalization and aerial-visibility conditions provide reference performance for the benchmark and validate the effectiveness of AG-CoNAV.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision-and-Language Navigation Benchmarks

Early VLN benchmarks such as R2R and R4R focus on route following in indoor environments ( Anderson et al., 2018b ; Jain et al., 2019 ) , while Touchdown and Talk2Nav extend language-guided navigation to outdoor scenes ( Chen et al., 2019 ; Vasudevan et al., 2021 ) . VLN-CE moves navigation from discrete panoramic graphs to continuous environments ( Krantz et al., 2020 ) , and AerialVLN further extends route-oriented VLN to UAV navigation in large-scale outdoor environments ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . Beyond route following, REVERIE and SOON study goal-oriented navigation toward language-described targets ( Qi et al., 2020 ; Zhu et al., 2021 ) , while TravelUAV, UAV-ON, and CityNav extend goal-oriented language guidance to aerial platforms ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advances, most benchmarks still focus on a single embodied platform. AirGroundBench begins to study heterogeneous UAV–UGV perception through 62K diagnostic VQA instances and 115 closed-loop VLN episodes ( Li et al., 2026 ) , but large-scale goal-oriented air–ground collaborative VLN remains underexplored.

## 2.2 Multi-Agent Collaborative Navigation

Multi-agent navigation studies focus on homogeneous teams of ground robots ( Burgard et al., 2000 ; Gao et al., 2022 ; Tan et al., 2022 ) or aerial agents ( Westheider et al., 2023 ) . Vision-language research extends collaboration to language-conditioned navigation, with CoNavBench studying VLN among ground robots ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , and AeroDuo and CoNav-UAV exploring complementary viewpoints within multi-UAV teams ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2026 ) . Moving toward heterogeneous collaboration, AGOS-Bench studies closed-loop UAV–UGV cooperative object search with visual-reference goals ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , while AGC-VLN introduces language-conditioned air–ground navigation through a shared bird’s-eye map linking aerial context with ground planning ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . However, dedicated trainable air–ground collaborative VLN remains underexplored.

2026-10-08.title: RobotWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Robot Use Across Diverse Tasks and Embodiments
2026-10-08.authors: Zhiqin Yang , Chenxin Li , Xiaomeng Hu , Yibin Liu , Weidong Huang , Jiankai Sun , Haitao Li , Zijian Wu , Yuzhi Huang , Fanding Huang , Hanwen Sun , Jiashun Liu , Jingqi Tong , Mingxin Huang , Shaoli Hu , Shijue Huang , Tianyi Bai , Xinyuan Wang , Yunlong Lin , Zhengyang Tang , Zhexin Zhang , Zhuo Chen , Xierui Song , Juntao Dai , Boyuan Chen , Jiaming Ji , Fangneng Zhan , Mengkang Hu , Wei Xue , Yonggang Zhang , Han Hu , Tsung-Yi Ho , Yike Guo
2026-10-08.abstract: General-purpose agents increasingly write code, use tools, and complete complex digital tasks, raising the question of how far these capabilities carry into the physical world. To investigate this, we introduce RobotWorld , a challenging simulation testbed for robot use : turning instructions and observations into physical task execution through robot interfaces. Its 84 tasks span manipulation, mobile manipulation, locomotion, driving, and aerial control, with explicit interaction budgets and executable success checks. By analysing task outcomes alongside execution traces, we identify both the capabilities that transfer and the gaps that prevent reliable completion. Furthermore, we find that current agents can construct sophisticated perception and control workflows, including image segmentation, camera calibration, spatial estimation, and dynamics-based computation. These capabilities, however, do not consistently compose into successful behaviour: agents lose task-relevant object states despite reaching commanded poses, fail to correct ineffective actions, recover too late, or mistake unfinished tasks for completion. This uneven transfer also differs across models: Astra succeeds more often on spatial and constrained-contact goals, whereas Opus 5.5 succeeds more often on continuous-balance and timed-interaction goals. By linking these outcomes to execution behaviour, RobotWorld provides both a rigorous proving ground and an empirical account of the remaining capability gaps, thereby establishing concrete targets for training and designing more reliable physical-world agents.
2026-10-08.introduction:
General-purpose agents are becoming useful actors in the digital world. They develop software, operate browsers, and carry out multi-step knowledge-work tasks through frontier harnesses and systems such as Operator and Claude Cowork ( OpenAI, 2025 ; Anthropic, 2026b ) . Their capabilities extend beyond producing answers: they inspect an environment, use tools, observe the consequences, and revise their actions. Robotics presents a natural next question: how far can these capabilities take agents into the physical world? Recent studies of frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have made robot control an increasingly concrete possibility ( Anthropic, 2026a ; Galbot Team et al., 2026 ) . Community experiments now include robot-arm control and simulated dexterous apple grasping, while real-time robot rollouts also expose the gap between an impressive demonstration and practical execution speed ( Chooi, 2026 ; Huang, 2026 ; Duan, 2026 ) . The challenge is to establish which capabilities already transfer, which remain missing, and what should improve next.

These experiments have also prompted debate about what progress in robot use should mean. Malik questions whether pick-and-place demonstrations establish competence in dexterity and dynamics; Isola and Fu emphasise the potential of agents that use controllers and robotics tools ( Malik, 2026 ; Isola, 2026 ; Fu, 2026 ) . This motivates a broader empirical question: across which physical demands can a general-purpose agent act reliably, with what control support, and where does its feedback loop fail? Physical interaction tests how perception, reasoning, and program construction work together. An agent may estimate a grasp from images, write a segmentation program, fit camera geometry, or calculate a controller from approximate dynamics. Each is useful only insofar as it supports successful action. Describing a grasp does not secure the object; reaching a target pose does not establish insertion; recovering balance for an instant does not satisfy sustained stability. Across different robot bodies, the agent must interpret its observations, anticipate action consequences, correct errors, and judge completion. We use robot use to describe this ability to turn instructions and feedback into task execution through robot interfaces.

Recent work is turning general-purpose models into agents that execute robot tasks through programs, tools, and feedback. EmbodiedSWE studies coding agents that construct executable solutions for long-horizon dexterous tasks ( Shen et al., 2026 ) . PyRUA-Lean investigates how programmatic action composition and selective observation improve execution efficiency ( Si et al., 2026 ) , while RPG uses simulation practice and failure diagnosis to refine reusable robot skills ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . These advances make systematic evaluation increasingly important: across which robot bodies and physical demands do current agents act reliably, and where does execution break down? We study this question across manipulation, locomotion, driving, and flight, connecting task outcomes to how agents combine perception, computation, and feedback. Our aim is to turn promising demonstrations into measurable capability gaps and concrete targets for future training and agent design.

We introduce RobotWorld, a simulation benchmark of robot use across diverse tasks and embodiments. It brings together 84 task specifications with documented robot interfaces, task budgets, and executable success checks (see Figure 2 ). Multimodal agents interact through a shared execution harness, with each task’s observations and controller assistance specified. Recorded actions, tool interactions, and outcomes support analysis beyond aggregate scores. Sections 3 – 5 describe the environments, benchmark construction, and evaluation protocol; our central empirical question is what these executions reveal about agents’ physical capabilities.

Our trajectory analysis reveals both substantial capabilities and persistent gaps. Agents construct perception and control workflows involving colour segmentation, camera-geometry fitting, spatial estimation, and numerical dynamics calculations. They also use feedback to revise motions and recover from execution errors. Yet these local capabilities do not consistently compose into task completion: a robot may reach the requested pose while losing the object, remain in navigation without reaching the next subgoal, regain stability too late, or stop correcting an unfinished task because it believes the goal is already met. These failures locate weaknesses in state interpretation, action revision, temporal coordination, and completion assessment.

The models also exhibit different task and interaction profiles. Across the task groups analysed in Section 6.6 , Astra succeeds more often on spatial and constrained-contact goals, whereas Opus 5.5 succeeds more often on continuous-balance and timed-interaction goals. Among eight tasks solved by both, Astra uses fewer tool calls in seven but fewer control steps in only six, showing that interaction cost and physical execution cost need not agree. Together with the observed workflows, these patterns suggest different ways of composing visual-spatial reasoning, explicit computation, and feedback control. We treat this as an exploratory explanation of the model profiles. By connecting outcomes to execution mechanisms, RobotWorld aims to make evaluation useful for directing progress towards more capable physical-world agents.

Our contributions are twofold:

A challenging, rigorous proving ground for robot use. RobotWorld gives the community a systematic way to test whether general-purpose agents can turn digital capabilities into successful physical action. Its 84 tasks from 20 source projects span diverse embodiments and control demands, with explicit interfaces, budgets, and executable success checks. Substantial remaining headroom makes it a testbed for developing and measuring the next generation of physical-world agents.

An empirical capability profile and directions for improvement. Through execution traces and cross-model comparisons, we reveal how current agents combine perception, computation, and control, where reliable task completion breaks down, and how strengths and weaknesses differ across models. These findings identify concrete priorities for future training and agent design, including grounding perception and computation in action, recovering from execution errors, coordinating actions over time, and recognising task completion.

# 2 Related Work

Vision–language–action (VLA) models such as RT-2, OpenVLA and π 0 \pi_{0} generate actions from visual observations and language instructions ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) ; π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} further studies open-world generalisation through heterogeneous co-training ( Black et al., 2025 ) . World–action models (WAMs) connect action generation with future-observation prediction. Recent work examines complementary aspects of this coupling: SelfWAM models action-conditioned visual consequences ( Pan et al., 2026 ) , OpenWAM systematically studies world–action pretraining and information flow ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , and Rolling-WAM distributes joint video–action denoising across replanning cycles to improve responsiveness ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . These directions study closely related capabilities: selecting actions from sensory inputs and modelling how actions change the world. Robot-use agents can express both through reasoning, programs and feedback. Our trajectories include direct visual estimates used to choose motions, as well as geometric and dynamics calculations used to anticipate motion and derive control commands. RobotWorld examines how these capabilities are combined during execution and whether they produce reliable task completion across diverse physical demands.

Agents use reasoning, programs, and tools to connect instructions to physical action. Code as Policies and VoxPoser generate executable control logic and spatial representations for robot motion ( Liang et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2023 ) , while Show-Harness exposes semantic robot actions to VLMs ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . EmbodiedSWE studies coding agents that construct executable solutions for dexterous and mobile manipulation ( Shen et al., 2026 ) . Recent work develops how such agents use execution feedback: PyRUA-Lean composes robot primitives into Python cells with conditional checks, local retries, and selective observation ( Si et al., 2026 ) ; ASPIRE accumulates validated program repairs into reusable skills ( Lu et al., 2026 ) ; and RPG uses simulation practice and failure diagnosis to revise a shared skill library and system prompt ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . These approaches develop complementary ways to organise robot execution, from decisions within an episode to skills retained across tasks. RLE-Bench examines the broader use of coding agents for robotics research and engineering, including policy learning, perception, mechanical design, and interactive control ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . Our focus is the breadth and reliability of robot use: how agents combine available capabilities during execution, and which mechanisms support or obstruct task completion.

CaP-X evaluates coding agents for manipulation under different primitive abstractions and feedback settings, with extensions to mobile manipulation ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . EmbodiedBench evaluates visual agents across high-level planning and lower-level navigation and manipulation, with capability-oriented task subsets ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . VLABench examines language-conditioned manipulation and long-horizon reasoning, evaluating both action policies and VLM-based workflows ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) ; EmbodiedEval spans navigation, object and social interaction, and embodied question answering ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) . At the decision-module level, Embodied Agent Interface separately evaluates goal interpretation, subgoal decomposition, action sequencing, and transition modelling ( Li et al., 2024b ) . These agent evaluations build on a wider ecosystem of robot-learning task suites, including RLBench, CALVIN, LIBERO, BEHAVIOR-1K, and RoboCasa365 ( James et al., 2020 ; Mees et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024a ; Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) . RobotWorld brings together diverse embodiments and physical demands, including spatial manipulation, sustained stabilisation, and interaction with moving targets. Alongside task outcomes, we analyse feedback use, recovery, completion assessment, and interaction cost to characterise model strengths and failure mechanisms. Table 1 compares control interfaces and coverage beyond manipulation. Direct commands and generated programs are distinct entry points: RobotWorld can interleave both within one episode, while retaining the declared native controllers.

2026-10-08.title: RoboQuest: Generalist Physical Agents that Search, Inspect and Test
2026-10-08.authors: Liu Renhang , Navonil Majumder , Tej Deep Pala , Soujanya Poria
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-08.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have made them capable generalist physical agents for a range of manipulation tasks. However, successful operation in an unfamiliar environment may require an agent to seek task-relevant information through interaction when it is absent from the observations: it may need to determine where a relevant object is, inspect an unobserved property, or discover the effect of an unfamiliar tool. We thus introduce RoboQuest, a benchmark for goal-directed embodied exploration, where agents must actively acquire task-relevant information through physical interaction, use the resulting evidence to adapt subsequent actions, and autonomously decide when to commit to task completion. RoboQuest comprises ten mobile manipulation tasks centered on three forms of uncertainty: search, manipulation-based inspection, and interactive testing. We evaluate five frontier multimodal agents through a common visuomotor interface, as well as a π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy fine-tuned on the full-episode demonstrations we release. The best agent succeeds in only 23% of the episodes, and the fine-tuned policy almost never succeeds. Isolated tests of the execution skills the tasks are built from, with the hidden information supplied, show that the agents can carry out most of the required actions, and our failure analysis attributes only a minority of the failures to execution. Our failure analysis further finds that the agents often stop exploring too early as they make decisions before observing the required evidence for task completion. We also find that agents rarely prevent or repair the disturbances caused by their exploration. Moreover, learning by trial and error remains difficult for most models.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Recent advances in generalist robotic agents have enabled increasingly complex manipulation, yet such strong execution may not necessarily translate into successful task completion without ready access to key task-relevant information in the observation. In such settings, the robot must actively determine what it needs to know, how to obtain that information, and how each new observation should shape what it does next. This may require searching an environment, inspecting objects from informative configurations, or deliberately interacting with the world to reveal its behavior. Current robotic manipulation benchmarks Nasiriany et al. (2026) ; Chen et al. (2026a) ; Tao et al. (2024) ; Li et al. (2026b) do not demand such open-ended information-seeking physical interactions from the agents and policies. With the increasing preponderance of generalist robotic agents, such exploratory benchmarking becomes pivotal to truly evaluate the zero-shot capabilities of such agents that may encounter unseen challenges in new environments.

Consider a situation where a robot is searching an unfamiliar room in darkness with only a portable light source. The robot can observe only what the light is aimed at. The challenge here comes from the dual use of the same gripper to carry the light and retrieve objects as well. Exploration is also consequential; for example, a searched compartment may contain the target, nothing, or a key that can be used to access other regions. In other words, each observation can change both its beliefs and next possible actions. The robot must therefore decide where to look, how each discovery should redirect its behavior, and when it has learned enough to act. Similar challenges arise beyond search when a robot must determine whether an object has been sufficiently inspected or choose a physical test to probe certain hidden property of an object.

The underlying principle is longstanding. Active and interactive perception study acquiring task-relevant information through decisive actions rather than passively consuming fixed observations Bajcsy (1988) ; Bohg et al. (2017) . However, evaluating this capability requires more than simply hiding information from the initial observation. If every uncertainty has an obvious one-step resolution, successful completion primarily tests if the agent performs that prescribed interaction. Thus, the challenge is beyond simply unveiling missing information, that is autonomously conducting an effective investigation in service of a physical goal, where different actions may expose different evidence. Furthermore, information may need to be accumulated across interactions and acquiring them may affect the state of the task. This question is becoming increasingly palpable as frontier multimodal agents such as GPT-6 Astra can now act directly as robot policies across diverse and previously unseen manipulation tasks without task-specific fine-tuning. Improved execution shifts the bottleneck toward deciding what to investigate, how to investigate it, and when enough has been learned.

Thus, we introduce RoboQuest , a benchmark for assessing goal-directed embodied exploration , in which a robot must autonomously gather task-relevant evidence through physical interaction, use that evidence to guide subsequent actions, and decide when it knows enough to commit to a solution. RoboQuest contains ten tasks organized into three families: Search & Explore , Object Inspect , and Testing . These are mobile manipulation tasks set in full kitchens with a mobile manipulator: exploring often means traversing the kitchen as well as precisely manipulating objects. The tasks involve uncertainty about the location and properties of the relevant objects, and making inferences from the outcomes of physical interactions. Rather than instructing the robot with the investigation approach, each task just specifies an externally verifiable physical goal and leaves the investigation strategy to the agent—from evidence gathering steps to conditions of evidence sufficiency and commitment.

Our evaluations reveal a substantial gap between general manipulation competence and the ability to explore effectively under uncertainty. The best frontier agent succeeds in only 23% of the episodes, and the fine-tuned π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} seldom succeeds. Yet the strongest agents execute most of the required physical actions in isolation when the hidden information is supplied ( Section 4.3 ), and our failure analysis ( Section 5 ) attributes only a minority of the failures to execution. The majority involve exploration and decision making. The agents often stop exploring too early, or prematurely make decisions before observing their ramifications. Their exploration also disturbs the scenes that they rarely prevent or repair. Learning by trial and error remains difficult for most models. These results highlight a persistent gap between stronger robotic execution and the ability to autonomously explore, resolve uncertainty, and achieve a given physical goal.

Our main contributions are:

RoboQuest , a benchmark for goal-directed embodied exploration with ten carefully designed tasks in which exploration shapes subsequent decisions and final task success.

A demonstration dataset that explores , with 5,000 episodes (500 per task, 366 hours at 20 Hz) from scripts that can easily generate more. The demonstrations show how a robot explores and then acts, with a subtask caption on every frame.

A systematic evaluation of general-purpose and trained robotic agents , including five frontier multimodal agents and a RoboQuest-finetuned π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , with isolated tests of the execution skills the tasks require and a detailed failure analysis, which together characterize where exploration under uncertainty breaks down.

2. A demonstration dataset that explores , with 5,000 episodes (500 per task, 366 hours at 20 Hz) from scripts that can easily generate more. The demonstrations show how a robot explores and then acts, with a subtask caption on every frame.

3. A systematic evaluation of general-purpose and trained robotic agents , including five frontier multimodal agents and a RoboQuest-finetuned π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , with isolated tests of the execution skills the tasks require and a detailed failure analysis, which together characterize where exploration under uncertainty breaks down.

# 2 Related Work

Standard manipulation benchmarks such as RLBench ( James et al., 2020 ) , CALVIN ( Mees et al., 2022 ) , LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , ManiSkill3 ( Tao et al., 2024 ) , RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , BEHAVIOR-1K ( Li et al., 2023 ) , and RoboCasa ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ; Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) evaluate multi-task learning and long-horizon motor control. However, these benchmarks operate under complete or immediately accessible task observability, making the objective primarily execution-centric ( Table 1 ). In contrast, RoboQuest focuses on goal-directed embodied exploration: task-critical information is fundamentally absent from initial observations and cannot be resolved by passive viewing, requiring physical interaction to gather evidence before goal completion.

In most manipulation benchmarks, relevant information for task progression and completion is always present in the current observation/state, as compared in Table 1 . In RLBench, LIBERO, and CALVIN, the agent must exercise the correct motor skills, but need not explore to uncover some necessary information. In contrast, every RoboQuest task requires information acquisition. Moreover, success still depends on perception and motor execution as well. Aggregate success rates therefore cannot isolate and probe a single capability. Hence, we analyze every episode in full to examine what evidence the agent gathered, retained, and used before it committed to some action ( Section 5 ).

When task relevant information is not immediately observable, robots must rely on active perception to acquire missing information ( Bohg et al., 2017 ) . While recent benchmarks investigate camera repositioning ( Liu et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026a ) , visual occluders ( Li et al., 2026b ) , container retrieval ( He et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ) , or history retention ( Chen et al., 2026a ) , they restrict active sensing to viewpoint adjustment or single-step un-occlusion. RoboQuest expands physical exploration into three dimensions: directed search, active inspection, and interactive testing. These exploratory interactions can alter the environment in irreversible ways, forcing agents to reason about the consequences of their actions.

Robotic foundation models either employ frontier multimodal models as zero-shot high-level planners ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) or train Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models for direct low-level control ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Existing evaluations test both paradigms in fully observed scenes. When information must be actively gathered, reasoning agents often prematurely commit or hallucinate unobserved states, while Markovian VLAs struggle with multi-step hypothesis testing. RoboQuest provides an architecture-neutral benchmark to evaluate both paradigms under physical uncertainty.

2026-10-08.title: NeRFifyMesh: Optimizing Neural Radiance Fields from Textured Meshes for Robotics Scene Building
2026-10-08.authors: Nillan Nimal , Mahboubeh Asadi , Sajad Saeedi
2026-10-08.comment: Accepted to IROS2026
2026-10-08.abstract:
In robotics, scene representation plays a pivotal role
in understanding and interacting with the environment. The
advent of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and its variants, as
a novel representation, has opened a new frontier of research.
In applications such as semantic mapping and simulation, roboticists aim to build scenes using multiple NeRF models, each representing an object. While extensive datasets of 3D mesh models already exist, there is an urgent need to develop tools to convert these assets to NeRF models for rapid algorithm development and testing. This paper presents a new pipeline for converting existing mesh models to NeRF representations by artificially generating a ground truth point-based radiance field through sampling mesh geometry and texture. This approach alleviates the need for camera-based sampling or rendering multi-view images of the original mesh to train the NeRF model. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates that our method yields comparable rendering quality to the baselines. Additionally, the application of this representation is shown by constructing unified NeRF scenes and performing collision simulations with extracted geometry.
2026-10-08.introduction:
In 3D digital graphics and computer vision, the accurate and efficient representation of objects and scenes is paramount. Popular methods for representing 3D structures vary based on their characteristics and applications. Point clouds capture geometric detail sparsely through individual data points. Meshes define surface geometry by using interconnected points, or vertices, which together form polygonal units like triangles [ 14 ] . Voxels offer a distinct approach by discretizing space into uniform, grid-like structures [ 5 ] . Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) represent the distance of a point from the surface of a 3D shape where the sign is negative inside the surface and positive outside [ 30 ] . Recently, Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) have emerged as a novel representation [ 23 ] . Optimized for visual consistency, NeRFs can achieve state-of-the-art results for novel view synthesis and image-based rendering tasks.

The ability to transition between diverse model representations can be immensely valuable. Different fields and applications often require or benefit from specific 3D representations. For instance, while robotics might leverage SDFs for object interaction, computer graphics might prefer mesh models for detailed visual rendering. As such, the interoperability between these representations can bridge the gap between fields and facilitate a wider range of applications. Converting between mesh and NeRF format is particularly interesting given the prevalence of mesh models in computer graphics and robotics. Textured mesh models are widely available in databases such as Amazon Berkeley Objects [ 9 ] , Google Scanned Objects [ 13 ] , ShapeNet [ 6 ] , and Objaverse [ 12 ] .

Developing an efficient and automated representation conversion tool has many applications in robotic systems, such as composing large-scale scenes out of many NeRF models, where the NeRF models are built from existing mesh models. However, traditional pipelines to convert representations entail rendering images of the mesh model from known camera poses that encompass the entire model to serve as the ground truth for optimizing a NeRF. This approach has significant drawbacks. Rendering high-quality images from mesh models is computationally expensive and training images that omit areas of the model can lead to poor results. Additionally, the rendered images require storage, which can be problematic when working with large-scale datasets such as Objaverse [ 12 ] .

In this paper, we propose NeRFifyMesh, a pipeline that removes the rendering optimization step from the training process and alleviates the need for high-quality ground-truth images and camera poses of the mesh model (see Fig. 1 ). We achieve this by sampling the mesh to generate a discrete point-based radiance field with the properties of color ( c gt \textbf{c}_{\text{gt}} ), binary opacity ( α gt \alpha_{\text{gt}} ), point normals ( n → gt \vec{n}_{\text{gt}} ), and their significance, w c w_{c} , w α w_{\alpha} , and w n → w_{\vec{n}} respectively. We then proceed to train our neural representation directly on this discrete field. By including point normals in our representation, we can relight our rendered scene post-training, recover accurate geometry through surface reconstruction, and facilitate applications that rely on geometric information, such as robotics simulation. The contributions of this work are:
1) A mesh-derived Neural Radiance Field representation is proposed, where neural supervision is performed on a discrete radiance field generated from mesh geometry and texture. This method alleviates the need for multi-view image supervision or camera-pose information during training.
2) Surface normals are learned by the representation, enabling normal-based shading during rendering and supporting geometry-dependent applications.
3) The effectiveness of the representation is demonstrated through model compression, relighting, surface extraction and collision simulation experiments in constructed scenes.
The project page and videos can be found at: https://sites.google.com/view/nerfifymesh

The rest of the paper is organized as follows.
Sec. II presents the related works.
Sec. III describes the proposed method.
Sec. IV presents the results.
Sec. V concludes the paper.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Neural Implicit Representations

Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) [ 23 ] are a novel representation, mapping a 2D ray viewing direction ( OPEN ϕ , θ ) \phi,\theta) and Cartesian coordinates for a 3D location ( x , y , z x,y,z ) to volume density ( σ \sigma ) and emitted view-dependent radiance ( r , g , b r,g,b ). Other neural implicit representations can also parameterize the geometry and/or appearance of meshes in a continuous and compact manner. Neural SDFs [ 25 , 27 ] model surfaces implicitly as the zero-level set of signed distance functions. For example, Neural Geometric Level of Detail (NGLoD) [ 31 ] represents a neural SDF as a collection of feature vectors in a sparse voxel octree (SVO) where the levels of the SVO define levels of detail.
Occupancy Networks [ 22 ] employs a neural network-based binary classifier to implicitly define surfaces as a set of 3D points. Instant-NGP [ 24 ] addresses the computational costs of utilizing fully connected neural networks by introducing a multi-resolution hash encoding that allows for accelerated training and rendering of neural graphics primitives such as NeRF and Neural SDFs.

In addition, mesh autoencoders [ 40 , 16 ] apply convolutional operations to meshes directly to create latent representations for mesh reconstruction. Although these works either directly utilize mesh data or derive point clouds from sampled meshes, their focus is limited to mesh geometry encoding and reconstruction.

Volume rendering-based methods [ 34 , 38 , 21 ] and Scene Representation Networks (SRNs) [ 28 ] take a different approach. They represent 3D scene geometry and appearance derived from multi-view images. NeuS presents a volume rendering method for surface reconstruction from multi-view images that addresses the limitations of NeRF which lacks surface optimization [ 34 ] . NeuMesh [ 37 ] , which is supervised with NeuS, utilizes a mesh-based scaffold with learnable disentangled geometry and texture features to encode a neural implicit field. These approaches require the synthetic generation of images from the mesh model. This leads to reconstruction inaccuracies for regions of the mesh that are rarely visible or occluded in the generated images.

## II-B Mesh-based NeRF Pipelines

The extraction of accurate underlying 3D geometry from NeRFs presents a challenging problem given that they are not explicitly optimized for geometry. Consequently, current works [ 26 , 32 ] , have developed methods for extracting meshes from volumetric NeRF representations, enabling integration with common computer graphics pipelines and real-time rendering. NeRFMeshing [ 26 ] utilizes a signed surface approximation network (SSAN) to represent a triangle mesh of the scene and an appearance network to capture view-dependent colours. NeRF2Mesh [ 32 ] extracts meshes with view-independent diffuse textures and view-dependent specular textures.
Additional approaches incorporate a mesh representation of the target scene to edit NeRFs [ 39 , 36 , 18 ] or improve rendering efficiency [ 8 ] . For example, DE-NeRF [ 36 ] attaches learnable disentangled features to an extracted triangle mesh of the scene to allow for editing the model.

Mesh2NeRF [ 7 ] showed that training directly on meshes significantly
improves rendering quality. However, their method samples from virtual cameras
rather than mesh geometry, does not learn surface normals, bakes in
lighting, and relies on off-the-shelf NeRF backbones. Our representation
instead uses a custom architecture that leverages mesh geometry directly,
enabling relighting and accurate geometry extraction through learned
surface normals.

## II-C NeRFs in Robotics Applications

There is an increasing prevalence of NeRFs in robotics due to their continuous scene representation and photorealistic rendering capabilities. For robotics applications, NeRFs have been leveraged for data generation, perception, mapping, simulation, and multi-robot agents [ 2 ] .

Neural Sim [ 15 ] , presents a pipeline to generate synthetic data with NeRFs to train vision models, enabling applications such as object detection and scene understanding. Similarly, Wang et al. [ 35 ] investigates the performance of a NeRF model that uses only semantic data for tasks such as segmentation and detection.

Additionally, NeRFs have demonstrated potential in robot navigation and mapping. Adamkiewicz et al. [ 1 ] demonstrated vision-only navigation of robots in a learned radiance field, with trajectory algorithms to avoid high-density regions corresponding to obstacles.

In terms of physics-based simulations, Cleac’h et al. [ 20 ] produce a differentiable neural object pipeline which includes NeRFs for simulating the motion of objects. This allows for the estimation of dynamics properties such as friction and mass from visual data. NeRF2Real [ 4 ] synthesized scenes composed from static NeRF environments and dynamic objects and utilized a physics-engine to compute contact dynamics for sim2real policy transfer.

Together these works demonstrate the advancing interest of NeRFs in robotics. Consequently, a pipeline to convert meshes to NeRFs will be useful by allowing existing mesh assets to be integrated into NeRF-based simulation and perception frameworks.

2026-10-08.title: OpenViTac: Learning and Benchmarking Visuo-Tactile Policies in a Unified Sim-and-Real Framework
2026-10-08.authors: Yifan Wu , Qin Li , Nan Min , Guojin Zhong , Haoyu Zhao , Zhiyuan Li , Houze Xu , Shengqi Xu , Xingyao Lin , Zijie Diao , Zhaoxiang Liu , Shiguo Lian , Shunlin Lu , Shihao Zhao , Ziyi Ye , Zuxuan Wu , Yu-Gang Jiang
2026-10-08.comment: Project website: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract:
Tactile feedback provides embodied agents with physical information beyond visual observations, enabling more reliable interaction with the real world.
However, despite the rapid progress of vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policies, there remains a lack of unified benchmarks for evaluating tactile-enabled robot manipulation across simulation and the real world.
To address this gap, we introduce OpenViTac , a visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark for evaluating robot policies across simulation and the real world.
OpenViTac organizes contact-rich manipulation into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions and provides paired simulation–real-world settings for consistent evaluation of VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies.
Building upon this benchmark, we investigate how different tactile representations and integration strategies affect the performance of pretrained VLA models.
Correspondingly, we introduce OpenVTLA , a tactile augmentation framework that combines the best-performing representation and integration strategy.
Furthermore, we leverage the paired benchmark setting to study sim–real co-training and analyze factors affecting cross-domain policy learning.
Together, OpenViTac provides a unified platform for evaluating and advancing visuo-tactile robot manipulation.
2026-10-08.introduction:
“The ideas of sight and touch make two species entirely distinct and heterogeneous.” — George Berkeley

Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [ 2 , 16 ] have enabled robots to leverage large-scale visual and linguistic knowledge for increasingly generalizable manipulation [ 12 ] .
These foundation policies have demonstrated strong performance across diverse manipulation scenarios [ 20 , 15 ] , yet remain primarily grounded in visual observations.
However, many real-world interactions require understanding physical states that are not directly observable from vision alone, such as object properties, contact dynamics, and interaction forces [ 9 ] .
By providing direct feedback from physical interaction, tactile sensing [ 8 , 31 ] augments visual perception with complementary physical information, enabling embodied agents to better understand and interact with the physical world, such as contact geometry, force cues, and material-dependent responses.
This has motivated a shift from purely vision-based policies toward Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) models [ 11 , 43 , 28 ] , which combine global scene understanding from vision with local interaction feedback from touch.

Driven by the promise of tactile feedback, recent VTLA studies have rapidly expanded the design space of tactile-enabled robot policies, exploring different tactile representations [ 46 , 10 , 9 ] , fusion strategies [ 26 , 39 ] , and policy architectures [ 43 , 28 ] .
Nevertheless, these approaches are typically evaluated under different sensors, tasks, robot embodiments, and experimental protocols, making systematic comparison challenging and leaving the contribution of tactile sensing insufficiently understood.
Existing manipulation benchmarks, such as LIBERO [ 20 ] , RoboTwin [ 5 ] , and RoboDojo [ 4 ] , primarily focus on vision-based policies and do not support tactile sensing.
Recent visuo-tactile benchmarks, such as Tabero [ 37 ] and UniVTAC [ 3 ] , have started to introduce tactile observations and contact-rich tasks for evaluation.
However, as shown in Tab. 1 , existing benchmarks still lack comprehensive coverage of tactile-relevant capabilities, diverse hardware configurations, and sim–real correspondence.

To address this, we introduce OpenViTac , a unified benchmark for evaluating visuo-tactile robot manipulation across simulation and the real world.
As shown in Fig. , OpenViTac organizes tactile-enabled manipulation into four capability dimensions: physical property perception, fragility-aware manipulation, contact-rich manipulation, and precision manipulation, covering diverse scenarios that require understanding object properties, contact states, and fine-grained interaction dynamics.
We evaluate representative VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies [ 12 , 7 , 47 , 38 , 23 , 34 , 1 , 44 , 18 , 32 , 43 , 33 ] on OpenViTac, providing a comprehensive comparison of their tactile-enabled manipulation capabilities.

Building upon OpenViTac, we further investigate how tactile observations can be incorporated into vision-based policies through two design choices: tactile representation and tactile integration.
Our study reveals that stronger tactile representations and effective integration strategies consistently improve performance on contact-sensitive manipulation tasks.
Based on this analysis, we introduce OpenVTLA , a tactile augmentation framework for pretrained VLA models.
Quantitatively, the strongest VLA, WAM, and VTLA baselines achieve 51.5%, 53.3%, and 61.2% average success rates in simulation, respectively, while OpenVTLA reaches 68.7%.
The same trend holds in real-world evaluation, where OpenVTLA achieves 54.6%, compared with 43.1%, 48.5%, and 51.9% from the strongest VLA, WAM, and VTLA baselines.
Finally, leveraging the paired sim–real setting of OpenViTac, we investigate sim–real co-training as a strategy for improving real-world policy learning through additional simulation data.

Overall, our contributions are threefold:

A unified visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark. We introduce OpenViTac , a tactile-centric benchmark with four capability dimensions and paired simulation–real-world settings for evaluating VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies.

A unified visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark. We introduce OpenViTac , a tactile-centric benchmark with four capability dimensions and paired simulation–real-world settings for evaluating VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies.

An investigation of tactile adaptation for pretrained VLAs. We investigate tactile representation and integration strategies for adapting vision-based policies to touch, leading to OpenVTLA , a tactile augmentation framework achieving strong performance across simulation and real-world evaluations.

A sim–real co-training study. We leverage OpenViTac’s paired sim–real setting to investigate sim–real co-training and analyze the factors affecting cross-domain policy learning.

2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Visuo-Tactile Robot Learning

Recent robot foundation policies have largely developed around vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) [ 16 , 12 ] .
Tactile feedback provides complementary contact and physical-property information that can improve contact-sensitive manipulation, motivating tactile-augmented policies such as VTLA models [ 43 , 33 , 28 , 36 ] and tactile-aware world-action models [ 21 , 32 ] .
Existing approaches, however, differ substantially in how touch is incorporated, including feature modulation [ 26 ] , action-level conditioning [ 33 ] , dedicated tactile experts [ 43 ] , and late-stage action refinement [ 28 , 36 ] .
Given the lack of consensus on how tactile information should be incorporated into pretrained VLAs, in this paper we systematically study representative tactile integration strategies under a shared π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} backbone.

## 2.2 Visuo-Tactile Datasets and Benchmarks

General manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO [ 20 ] , RoboTwin [ 5 ] , and RoboDojo [ 4 ] provide standardized evaluation across diverse simulated tasks, but primarily focus on vision-based manipulation.
A broad range of tactile datasets has been developed for representation learning [ 42 , 14 , 10 , 9 ] , while tactile-enabled real-robot manipulation data have only recently begun to scale across tasks, sensors, and embodiments [ 43 , 31 , 21 ] .
For policy-level evaluation, ManiFeel [ 22 ] and TacO [ 48 ] study tactile sensing in downstream manipulation, while UniVTAC [ 3 ] and NeoSim [ 31 ] further provide systematic evaluation in simulation.
However, existing simulation benchmarks still exhibit substantial discrepancies from real-world settings.
OpenViTac provides a unified tactile-centric benchmark with aligned sim–real tasks and additional real-world data across multiple tactile sensors.
