2026-10-08.title: Semantic-Aware Predictive Mapping for Exploration and Navigation
2026-10-08.authors: Kenneth J.K. Ong , William W.J. Teo
2026-10-08.comment: Accepted at IEEE TENCON 2026
2026-10-08.abstract: Predictive mapping can support robotic exploration and navigation by estimating unseen geometric layouts from partial occupancy observations. However, occupancy-only representations may fail to distinguish semantically different structures with similar geometry. This is particularly relevant for indoor doors, which may appear as occupied cells like walls but indicate possible connected rooms or corridors beyond the observed region. This work investigates whether semantic door cues improve predictive geometric occupancy mapping around such ambiguous regions. We modify a subset of the CogniPlan dataset by inserting door-induced ambiguities into partial occupancy maps while keeping the ground-truth layouts unchanged. We compare a geometry-only control model with a semantic-cued model trained on the same modified dataset, where the semantic-cued model receives an additional door channel. Evaluation uses L1 error, F1 score, and Intersection over Union (IoU) over both the full map and a 10-pixel door-region mask. Full-map performance remains broadly similar between models, but localized door-region results show a clear qualitative improvement: L1 decreases from 0.004342 to 0.000025, while F1 and IoU improve from 0.031311 and 0.015905 to 1.000000 and 1.000000, respectively. These results suggest that semantic cues can improve predictive occupancy completion in regions where geometric observations alone are ambiguous.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Autonomous exploration and navigation in unknown environments remain fundamental challenges in robotics. Mobile robots operating in partially observed environments commonly rely on geometric representations such as occupancy maps constructed from onboard sensors, including LiDAR and RGB-D cameras. Exploration and navigation are then typically performed using geometric planning strategies, including frontier-based exploration [ 1 ] , next-best-view methods [ 2 , 3 ] , learning-based methods [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] , sampling-based planning [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] , and classical path planning [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Despite differences in planning strategy, these methods primarily reason over geometric occupancy structure and traversability.

Predictive mapping approaches [ 7 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] extend this setting by inferring unseen geometric layouts from partial observations. For example, CogniPlan [ 21 ] predicts and combines multiple possible map layouts to support uncertainty-aware waypoint planning in partially observed environments. In parallel, semantic prediction and semantic mapping methods have been explored for reasoning about unobserved spaces and supporting navigation, including semantic annotations over BEV maps [ 22 , 23 ] , occupancy maps [ 24 ] , and point clouds [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] . For instance, Zhang et al. [ 28 ] predict the semantic composition of unseen regions, including likely object locations.

However, geometric predictive mapping and semantic prediction are often treated as separate problems. Predictive mapping methods mainly focus on occupancy completion and traversability estimation, while semantic prediction methods focus on object or scene semantics in unseen regions. As a result, semantic information is rarely used to directly improve predictive geometric layout modeling and spatial connectivity inference.

This limitation is particularly relevant in indoor environments containing doors. From a purely geometric occupancy perspective, closed doors may be represented as occupied obstacles, making them difficult to distinguish from walls. Semantically, however, doors indicate possible room connectivity and the existence of traversable space beyond the current observation boundary. Inferring such hidden connectivity requires reasoning beyond local occupancy geometry alone. Fig. 1 illustrates the motivation for distinguishing geometric occupancy information from semantic door cues in predictive mapping.

In this work, we investigate semantic-aware predictive mapping for indoor exploration and navigation. Specifically, we study whether semantic cues related to doors and room connectivity can improve the prediction of unseen geometric structures behind geometrically occluded regions. While doors are used as the case study, this work highlights the broader role of semantic information in predictive geometric mapping for robotic exploration and navigation.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

Using doors as a case study, we demonstrate that incorporating semantic information into predictive occupancy mapping can improve the completeness of inferred unseen structures beyond geometrically occluded regions.

We motivate the broader integration of semantic understanding into future predictive world models for robotic exploration and navigation.

# II Methodology

## II-A Overview

This work adopts and extends the predictive mapping framework introduced in CogniPlan. CogniPlan learns to predict unseen geometric layouts from partially observed occupancy maps, enabling improved waypoint planning for exploration and navigation in unknown environments. The original framework primarily relies on geometric occupancy information without explicitly incorporating semantic understanding of the environment.

Our work investigates whether semantic cues can improve predictive geometric reasoning in indoor environments containing semantically meaningful structures such as doors. This work focuses on incorporating semantic information into the predictive mapping pipeline and evaluating its effect on layout prediction quality.

## II-B Dataset Modification

To evaluate whether semantic cues can improve predictive geometric mapping around door-induced ambiguity, we modify a subset of the original CogniPlan occupancy-map dataset. The modification is applied only to the partial observation inputs, while the corresponding ground-truth occupancy layouts are kept unchanged. This ensures that all models are evaluated against the same underlying map structure.

In the original occupancy representation, occupied cells do not distinguish between different types of barriers. A wall, closed door, or other occupied structure is represented using the same occupied-space encoding. Consequently, a model that receives only geometric occupancy information cannot determine whether an occupied segment corresponds to a permanent wall or a door that may imply connected traversable space beyond it.

To introduce this ambiguity, we insert artificial door segments at selected room entrances and corridor entrances in the partial occupancy maps as illustrated in Fig. 2 . In the geometry-only modified input, each inserted door segment is encoded as occupied space, identical to surrounding walls. This produces a door-induced ambiguity. The input suggests that the entrance is blocked, while the unchanged ground-truth map still contains the connected room or corridor beyond that location.

For training, we use maps from 500 rooms in the original CogniPlan dataset, of which 50 rooms are modified to include artificial door segments. Each room comprises multiple layouts, with each individual layout containing one to two doors. Evaluation is conducted on a separate, dedicated validation set of 5 modified rooms containing door-induced ambiguity, specifically spanning 7 distinct layouts and 8 total doors.

The key property of the modified dataset is that the ground-truth occupancy map remains unchanged across the geometry-only and semantic-aware variants. Only the partial observation input is modified. This allows the experiment to test whether semantic information about door locations helps the model predict connected unseen regions that are geometrically occluded in the partial observation.

## II-C Experimental Setup and Evaluation

Two predictive mapping configurations are evaluated in this work:

Geometry-Only Control Model – A CogniPlan-based model trained on the door-modified dataset without the semantic door channel. In this setting, door regions are encoded only as occupied cells, identical to walls. This model serves as the control condition and evaluates whether a model trained on the modified dataset can infer hidden connectivity using geometric occupancy information alone.

Geometry-Only Control Model – A CogniPlan-based model trained on the door-modified dataset without the semantic door channel. In this setting, door regions are encoded only as occupied cells, identical to walls. This model serves as the control condition and evaluates whether a model trained on the modified dataset can infer hidden connectivity using geometric occupancy information alone.

Semantic-Cued Predictive Model – A CogniPlan-based predictive mapping model trained on the same door-modified dataset, but with an additional semantic door channel. The original occupancy input is preserved, while door regions are provided as explicit semantic cues as illustrated in Fig. 3 . This model receives semantic information distinguishing doors from structural walls.

Both models are trained and evaluated on the same modified dataset. The only difference between the two configurations is the presence or absence of the semantic door channel. This provides a controlled comparison for evaluating whether explicit semantic door cues improve predictive occupancy mapping around door-induced ambiguous regions.

Both models are trained for 500,000 iterations with a batch size of 32, following the training configuration used in the CogniPlan framework.

For evaluation, we report L1 error, Intersection over Union (IoU), and F1 score, following the predictive mapping metrics used in CogniPlan. These metrics are computed at two levels. All metrics are derived from a single prediction using solely a room-type conditioning vector [ 21 ] . To assess overall performance, we gather all pixels from all 5 evaluation rooms into a single combined set and compute the metrics globally once.

First, we report metrics over the full predicted occupancy map to provide an overall measure of predictive mapping performance. Second, since the main focus of this work is whether semantic door cues improve the prediction of connected traversable space beyond doors, we additionally compute localized metrics over the unknown-region cells within a 10-pixel radius of annotated door locations. We estimate 10 pixels to be the typical door-adjacent room boundaries for this dataset. For threshold-dependent metrics (IoU and F1), the outputs—which range from -1 to 1—are binarized using a threshold value of 0.

The localized 10-pixel evaluation region is illustrated in Fig. 4 . This localized evaluation directly targets the regions where door-induced geometric ambiguity occurs, and therefore provides a more focused quantitative measure of how well each model predicts occupancy structure around potential connectivity points.

2026-10-08.title: MultiFly: A Real-World Multimodal Aerial Dataset with Annotation-Efficient Label Transfer and Cross-Modal Semantic Consistency
2026-10-08.authors: Markus Gross , Andreas Greiner , Taehyoung Kim , Sivasubiramaniam Subbiah , Tomaž Cotič , Sai Bharadwaj Matha , Conrad Christoph , Oussema Dhaouadi , Simon Zieher , Surya Vijaya Kumar , Gordon Elger , Henri Meeß , Olaf Wysocki , Paul Spannaus , Daniel Cremers
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-08.abstract:
We introduce MultiFly, a real-world, low-altitude UAV dataset for semantic perception across RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar modalities.
MultiFly provides 17,272 synchronized samples from four suburban scenes with frame-wise annotations for 15 semantic classes, together with calibration and GNSS-RTK/IMU measurements.
To avoid costly and inconsistent modality-specific annotation, we propagate labels from only 115 manually annotated RGB images through shared geometric representations to all four modalities.
This approach generates semantic labels for 17,157 additional RGB images, 17,272 thermal images, 840M LiDAR points, and 3.4M radar points.
Transferred annotations achieve 89.93% average agreement with held-out manual annotations, and 90.94% average semantic consistency across all six modality pairs.
We further establish semantic segmentation benchmarks for all four modalities, revealing distinct architectural behavior for dense LiDAR and sparse radar data.
Taken together, MultiFly provides a scalable foundation for multimodal aerial perception and, to the best of our knowledge, the first public real-world low-altitude aerial benchmark that combines consistent frame-wise semantic annotations for RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar.
Data at https://github.com/markus-42/multifly .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Semantic scene understanding is fundamental to aerial perception [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . However, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) data remains substantially underrepresented in large-scale multimodal datasets, which increasingly drive modern foundation models. Notably, this is not simply a data-volume problem: UAV perception introduces distinct scene statistics, object scales, and viewing geometries, ranging from nadir to oblique perspectives, that are poorly represented in conventional ground-based datasets. Autonomous driving illustrates the contrast, where large-scale multimodal datasets have enabled systematic alignment across sensors, while similarly comprehensive resources for UAV perception remain limited.

This gap is particularly evident for semantic segmentation. Existing aerial datasets generally provide a single modality or limited modality combinations [ 10 , 5 , 6 ] , while no public real-world UAV dataset, to the best of our knowledge, provides synchronized frame-wise semantic annotations across RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar. Moreover, these modalities differ substantially in geometry and sampling, making consistent annotation difficult and costly.

To address these challenges, we introduce MultiFly, a calibrated and time-synchronized four-modal aerial sensing platform and semantic dataset.

# II Related Work

## II-A Multimodal Semantic Aerial Datasets

Semantic perception has evolved from single-sensor benchmarks [ 11 , 12 ] toward multimodal datasets that enable learning across complementary sensors. In autonomous driving, early resources established core camera-LiDAR perception tasks, while second-generation datasets such as nuScenes [ 13 ] expanded to large-scale, synchronized multimodal sensing. This shift enabled not only sensor fusion, but also temporal and multi-task perception, prediction, and planning, and increasingly multimodal foundation models that unify these capabilities.

UAV perception has yet to undergo a comparable transition. Existing aerial datasets remain fragmented across sensing modalities and annotation formats: most are unimodal [ 14 , 15 , 10 ] , while others combine only two modalities [ 3 , 16 , 6 ] , rely on synthetic data [ 17 , 18 ] , or provide map-wise rather than frame-wise annotations [ 19 , 20 ] . Consequently, the data required to develop and systematically evaluate unified multimodal UAV perception models remains largely unavailable. In particular, no public real-world low-altitude UAV dataset, to the best of our knowledge, provides synchronized frame-wise semantics across RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar.
MultiFly provides this missing substrate (Table I ), combining synchronized and registered RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar data with inertial measurements from Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs) and global positioning from a Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) with real-time kinematic (RTK) corrections.

## II-B Cross-Modal Semantic Consistency

Beyond sensor coverage, multimodal learning requires semantic supervision that is consistent across modalities. Independent annotation can introduce conflicting boundaries and labels, motivating geometry-based approaches that propagate semantics through a shared representation. KITTI-360 [ 21 ] transfers labels between images and 3D geometry, while WildScenes [ 22 ] projects multi-view image annotations into LiDAR.
UAVScenes [ 6 ] similarly annotates reconstructed 3D maps and renders them into camera frames before projecting labels onto LiDAR, while SegFly [ 5 ] adopts a 2D-3D-2D pipeline to lift sparse RGB annotations into a reconstructed point cloud and renders them into RGB and thermal images. These approaches demonstrate the feasibility of geometry-driven annotation, but remain limited in modality coverage, and require manual verification and correction.

MultiFly extends this paradigm to four modalities through a unified geometry-driven pipeline, propagating sparse RGB annotations to RGB, thermal, LiDAR, and radar, while ensuring high semantic consistency without the necessity of manual correction. It therefore offers not only broader sensor coverage, but a shared frame-wise semantic reference for multimodal UAV perception and cross-modal evaluation.

2026-10-08.title: Hall Effect-Based Tactile Force Detection Sensor for Robot-Assisted Minimally Invasive Surgery
2026-10-08.authors: Charles DeLorey , Michael Brockdorff , Adam Metcalf , Benjamin Calmé , Pietro Valdastri , Dominic Jones
2026-10-08.abstract: Robotic minimally invasive surgery has revolutionized surgical practice. However, as the surgeons are mechanically separated from the surgical tools, loss of tactile feedback occurs. We present a compact force sensor with three, millimeter scale sensing elements (taxels) that can be affixed to the grasping face of a robotic surgical tool. The sensor features a miniaturized design using Hall effect sensors and magnets embedded in a deformable elastomer contact layer. Sensor calibration is achieved with a 6 degree of freedom (DoF) parallel robot. Each taxel can detect applied normal and shear forces with average RMSE of 2.133 kPa. The calibrated sensor was validated on phantom and ex vivo porcine tissue, demonstrating tactile sensing during  retraction as well as  slip. This work introduces a small-scale Hall effect based tactile sensor, enabling sensing for force-sensitive robotic surgical applications.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Robot-Assisted Minimally Invasive Surgery (RAMIS) offers the gold-standard in surgical treatment for a range of procedures and provides improved visualization and dexterity with teleoperated instruments.
In traditional open surgery and manual laparoscopy, surgeons heavily rely on tactile sensations through their fingertips to assist in safe manipulation, feeling the tissue contact either directly or through the tool linkage [ 19 ] .
Modern RAMIS systems, such as Intuitive Surgical’s da Vinci platform, physically decouple the surgeon from instrument–tissue interaction via remote teleoperation.
This improves precision but removes natural tactile perception at the end-effector, leaving surgeons to infer the forces visually [ 15 ] .
Trauma from incorrect force application comes through two routes: excessive grasping can crush tissue leading to ischemia,  while insufficient force risks slip and abrasion.
Additionally, grip force in RAMIS has been shown to vary significantly between instrument as well as platform versions [ 12 ] , with different tissue types requiring different target levels of force.

Recently, the da Vinci 5 (Intuitive Surgical) integrated on-instrument force sensing and visuohaptic feedback [ 7 ] . However, these capabilities only offer a bulk kinesthetic  force feedback, with no information as to the contact forces the tissue experiences. Despite extensive research in surgical force sensing [ 17 ] , reliable local force measurement directly at the grasper–tissue interface remains unresolved. Existing approaches either estimate forces indirectly, or provide bulk interaction forces but are unable to sense compressive force on the tissue.

Force sensing can be introduced at several points along the RAMIS instrument chain: 1. motor-torque estimation at proximal actuators (indirect, model-dependent), 2. bulk sensing in the shaft (global reactions; e.g., da Vinci 5) [ 18 ] , 3. sensors at  the trocar (extra-corporeal, decoupled from local contact), 4. wrist-mounted sensors (requiring kinematic back-projection), and 5. the contact face of the jaws.
Of these, on-jaw sensing  provides the most direct access to  local contact mechanics.
Such on-jaw sensing is especially critical for observing contact pressures, distributed shear, and tissue-dependent friction behavior in highly variable surgical conditions.

Prior work has explored several transduction mechanisms for instrumented surgical graspers.
Piezoresistive MEMS offer high bandwidth at the cost of drift and the need for careful compensation and encapsulation [ 6 ] .
Capacitive tactile films provide thin, conformable coverage with normal and shear sensing and low power, but are susceptible to fluids and humidity that shift the dielectric and demand shielding and packaging attention [ 20 , 28 ] .
Optical waveguide or imaging-based tactile devices sized for MIS tips achieve high spatial resolution and multi-axis estimation with remote optoelectronics, though maintaining optical paths and routing within tight curved jaws raises integration complexity [ 11 ] . Fiber Bragg grating sensing enables electromagnetic interference-immune, multiplexed measurements for flexible endoscopic tools, yet requires extremely expensive interrogators and bonding strategies that can place sensing away from the true contact interface [ 21 ] .
Finally, magnetic Hall-effect tactile approaches have demonstrated grasp-aware control with compact packages, electrical simplicity, and high sampling rates, but require compensation to mitigate stray-field and orientation biases [ 25 , 27 , 4 ] . A comparison of these related works is shown in Table I .

Contact interface sensors open the potential for a new approach in surgical grip control: sensing and predicting slip events.
Incipient slip is the earliest stage of sliding when only part of the contact patch begins to move while the rest still adheres [ 24 ] .
Detecting slip in these regions allows the grasping force to be adjusted to prevent a full slip from occurring.
An initial approach presented a thermal-based sensor within the surgical jaw to detect movement of the tissue as slip began to occur [ 2 ] , but only offers a binary state of either slip or no slip. On-grasper optics have been used to detect slip in a surgical grasper [ 10 ] , however this approach also only measures displacement.
Others have utilized distributed force sensing to monitor the progression of slip across a full grasping surface [ 24 , 27 ] . The approach was successful for rudimentary grip control to prevent the slip [ 25 ] ; however, it utilized a large-scale model an order of magnitude too large for a real surgical instrument.
To  our knowledge, localized tactile slip sensing directly on the jaw contact surface has not yet been demonstrated at this scale for RAMIS graspers.

In this letter, we present a replaceable on-jaw Hall-effect magnetic tactile sensor  for RAMIS graspers, capable of 3-DoF force and slip observability at the tissue contact interface.  Multiple taxels were needed to provide sufficient coverage of the grasping area to detect slip and force across the grasping surface. Given tool-tip dimensions, PCB manufacturing constraints, Hall effect sensor size, low-cost materials, and  the need to maintain a safe radius for magnets, a design of three taxels was achieved, resolving a mean pressure of 74.49 kPa. We validate the sensor on silicone phantoms and ex vivo tissue, showing local contact pressures and taxel-wise shear progression during incipient slip under clinically relevant loading, and further demonstrate live force profiles during human manipulation with da Vinci teleoperation.

# II Methods

## II-A Sensor design requirements

To address problems of in-hand multi-axis force sensing on a miniaturized scale, we present a miniaturized force sensing array with three 3-DoF taxels, small enough to be affixed to the grasping jaw of a robotic surgical instrument. This device is small, lightweight, inexpensive, and enables sensing of grasp forces on the instrument jaws. The multiple taxels also enable directional slip sensing on the grasping face. By comparison, commercial sensors are bulky, costly, and lack the sensing density achieved in this work.

To achieve force sensing on a surgical instrument, we target certain performance metrics: Detecting normal and shear forces within 0-2 N [ 1 ] , small sensor footprint, resolution of 0.1 N [ 13 ] ,  a tunable design to fit the force range of the application [ 22 ] , and a low-cost scalable manufacturing process [ 23 ] . As tissue rarely spans the full jaw, sensing elements must cover the entire grasping surface, necessitating multiple taxels. More taxels enable local pressure measurement as well as cascading pressure changes over the interface, detecting slip. We maximize this to fit three taxels arranged along the principal axis of the jaw.

## II-B Sensing principle

The sensor operates using magnetic displacement sensing, where embedded magnets move relative to Hall sensors under applied force, producing measurable changes in magnetic flux density [ 22 ] . The magnet islands are magnetized along their thickness and produce a field B x , y , z B_{x,y,z} . When the magnet is displaced by pressure and/or shear stress F x , y , z F_{x,y,z} , the magnetic islands will shift relative to their respective Hall sensors d x , y , z d_{x,y,z} (Fig. 2 ). The displaced position of the magnetic island results in a change in the detected magnetic flux density of the Hall effect sensors beneath, which causes a voltage change in the Hall effect sensor. This voltage change is converted into magnetic field values onboard the sensor.

Each taxel uses a pair of Hall sensors to provide a richer magnetic field measurement for force reconstruction. The proximal sensor pair are reserved for background stray field compensation, leaving three taxels in the current sensor design.

The force reference system of the sensor is shown in Fig. 1 a, where the z-axis is normal to the sensor face, the y-axis is along the long axis of the sensor face (axis connecting the three taxels), and the x-axis is perpendicular to the y-axis on the sensor face.

## II-C Sensor development

In order to detect force and detect slip, we propose a Hall effect-based force sensor using magnetic displacement to measure applied normal and shear forces.

The assembled sensor has overall dimensions of 9.3 × \times 6.5 × \times 19.5 mm (Fig. 4 ) and a mass of 2.06 g, with three individual taxels, each 2.50 × \times 1.20 × \times 2.50 mm. We use rigid NdFeB magnets for their high remanence, giving a measurable magnetic field signal at small scale.

To transduce the field, we use a custom PCB (2.5 mm × \times 12 mm × \times 0.5 mm) with eight 3-axis Hall effect sensors (AK09973D, Asahi Kasei Microdevices, Japan).
The elastomeric sensing skin layer was fabricated using a 3D printed mold (HTL Resin, MicroArch 240, Boston Micro Fabrication, USA). For each taxel, two permanent magnets (0.5 × \times 0.5 × \times 0.2 mm; SuperMagnetMan, USA) are placed within the mold, held in position by a single larger permanent magnet on the exterior of the mold (Fig. 3 a). Ecoflex 00-30 elastomer (Smooth-On Inc., USA) is mixed (ARE-250 Thinkymixer, Thinky Corp., Japan), and vacuum degassed (5/01 Vacuum Caster, Renishaw, UK), before pouring into the mold and leveled (Fig. 3 b) then cured at 40°C.
The cured elastomer is removed from the mold (Fig. 3 c), with a 0.5 mm elastomer thickness on one side and the magnets encased in the other (Fig. 3 d). The sensor skin is then affixed to a 3D-printed mounting housing the custom PCB (Fig. 4 ai-iv). This assembly is mounted to the grasper jaw using a second 3D printed mount.

With the thickness of the elastomer layer underneath the magnets, the distance between the magnet and its respective sensor pair is 0.7 mm, a value determined by experimental evaluation of sensor sensitivity and desired responsiveness of the final tactile sensor. The maximum elastomer thickness of 1 mm was chosen to allow for adequate magnet displacement during contact ( ≤ \leq 50%), while maintaining a small form factor. Furthermore, as the magnetic field decays cubically as a function of distance, the small magnets must be sufficiently close to the sensor [ 22 , 16 ] . Additionally, the contact surface has a 10° offset face from the grasper face (Fig. 4 a-b), to account for the thickness of the sensor, but reducing the maximum open jaw angle of 90° [ 8 ] . As the sensor covers the existing teeth and fenestration of the tool jaw, the contact area is now the sensor face (107 mm 2 ). The sensor is connected to a microcontroller (Teensy 3.6, PJRC LLC., USA), which is connected to a PC for data recording over serial connection. The sensors are sampled at 500 Hz.

## II-D Sensor calibration

A high-precision parallel robot platform (Solano, Symétrie, France) is used to apply precise deformations to the sensor elastomer surface. A 5 mm diameter 3D-printed circle indenter on a 6-axis load cell (Nano 17, ATI, USA) is affixed to the end of the parallel robot to record the applied forces and torques to the sensor (Fig. 7 ). Data acquisition is accomplished with a LabVIEW script (LabVIEW, National Instruments Corp., USA). Data is collated and synchronized with a MATLAB script (MATLAB, MathWorks Inc., USA).

Calibration forces were applied along vectors spanning a cone centered on the surface normal. Indentation angles ranged from 0 − 45 ​ ° 0-45\degree{} , producing combined normal and shear loads. Indentations reached a maximum depth of d = 0.5 d=0.5 mm from the taxel surface (Fig. 8 a). All indentation vectors originated from the taxel normal axis and were distributed radially with a maximum incident angle θ = 45 ​ ° \theta=45\degree (radius 0.5 mm). Four concentric rings were defined around the normal axis, with linearly increasing radius and evenly spaced points, giving 21 total indentation locations (Fig. 8 d).
The sensor was indented at a rate of 0.01 mm/s and sampled at 490 Hz. The calibration was downsampled and synchronized, yielding a rate of 150 Hz, totaling ~400,000 datapoints per taxel for calibration. The indenter translated to each coordinate without rotational adjustment.

Before calibration, the load cell forces are filtered with a 3rd order Butterworth filter, a sampling frequency of 1 kHz, and a cutoff frequency of 10 Hz, to remove high frequency noise. Each taxel provides two sets of XYZ magnetic field measurements, denoted as 𝐁 n \mathbf{B}_{n} and 𝐁 n + 1 \mathbf{B}_{n+1} (Fig. 5 ).

To account for stray magnetic fields as the sensor changes orientation, the average measurement from the first pair of sensors ( s 1 s_{1} and s 2 s_{2} , most proximal along the sensor, Fig. 5 "Reference") is subtracted from the respective 𝐁 \mathbf{B} measurement on each taxel. 𝐁 \mathbf{B} values from the corresponding sensor pair of each taxel, along with the ground truth forces acquired during calibration indentations, are used to train a Feed-Forward Neural Network (NN) [ 26 ] using PyTorch [ 14 ] , denoted as f \mathit{f} in ( 1 ). A neural network regression model was used to capture the nonlinear relationship between magnetic field measurements and applied forces resulting from elastomer deformation and magnetic field coupling. The resulting calibration for taxel i i is 𝐅 𝐢 \mathbf{F_{i}} = ( 𝐅𝐱 𝐢 \mathbf{Fx_{i}} , 𝐅𝐲 𝐢 \mathbf{Fy_{i}} , OPEN 𝐅𝐳 𝐢 ) \mathbf{Fz_{i}}) , where i = [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] i=[1,2,3] . 𝐅 𝐢 \mathbf{F_{i}} are vectors containing timeseries force data resulting from the NN calibration, synced with the corresponding raw magnetic sensor values. The network consisted of a single hidden layer with 25 neurons using ReLU activation. Bayesian regularization was applied during training to reduce overfitting.

The network is trained to fit the tactile sensor magnetic data to the forces. These forces are converted to pressure using the area of the calibration indenter (5 mm ⌀ \diameter , A=19.635 mm 2 ), as the calibrations are performed with an area indenter rather than point forces. Calibration results are shown in Table II , with the lowest and highest RMSE in z being Taxel 3 and Taxel 2, respectively. The calibrations are restricted by the resolution of the load cell (1.4 mN, 0.198 kPa in fx, fy, and fz).

To show the stray field compensation prevents sensor orientation from affecting the magnetic sensing, angular evaluation was performed. Starting in the zero home position (robot arm pointed downwards), the robot was driven from -40° to 40° on the first and second joints of the robot, equating to X and Y rotation of the sensor. The results show at most a 0.765 kPa deviation in force signal when no contact is applied (Table IV ), within the range of angles.

## II-E Characterization

To assess the performance characteristics of the proposed sensor, a series of characterization tests were performed. Hysteresis tests in the sensor’s Fz axis to a depth of 0.3 mm at 0.01 mm/s, n=10 tests were achieved (Fig. 6 top), as well as creep tests indenting 0.3 mm and holding for 20 s were performed (Fig. 6 bottom). The results of these are shown in Table III .

Given the tight tolerances required to fit in the small grasper jaw, submillimeter magnets were selected. To validate the magnetic behavior of the taxel magnets, a FEM simulation (COMSOL Multiphysics, COMSOL Inc., Burlington, MA, USA) was developed.  The dimensional and magnetic parameters of the magnets (0.5 × \times 0.5 × \times (2x 0.2 mm), neodymium, N50) were input to the simulation, which showed minimal interaction between their fields even when displaced (as Taxel 2 was displaced 0.5 mm Z-, Taxel 1 had maximum magnetic field changes in Bx, By, Bz of 14%, 7%, 13% while Taxel 3: 26%, 9%, 10%, respectively). In only Y-axis displacement, Δ ​ B y \Delta B_{y} of the adjacent taxels was still at most 26%.

While increasing the magnet size (1x, 1.5x, 2x) shows increased sensitivity in the Y and Z-axes (1x: 4.15 mT, 1.5x: 13.42 mT, 2x: 15.55 mT), respective crosstalk generally increases (1x: y-15.4%, z-18.3%; 1.5x: y-13.9% z-12.8%; 2x: y-15.3% z-17.3%).

This indicates that the selected magnet is a suitable size to achieve required sensitivity, and well within these upper bounds of magnetic crosstalk. The  taxel magnets are arranged in a North-South-North orientation, which encourages the magnetic fields to "flatten" or be pulled closer to the magnet surface plane, restricting the flux from reaching adjacent sensors or magnets.

Magnetic crosstalk is observed with each taxel indented in a 5-point trajectory (X ± \pm 0.5 mm, Y ± \pm 0.5 mm, Z+0.5 mm). For the other two taxels, the maximum deviation from the magnetic field value at rest was computed, shown in Table V . Taxel 1 experiences the largest crosstalk, at 8.1% and 9.9% from Taxel 2 and 3, respectively.

To understand the effect of different size indenters on taxel calibration and validation, five different indenters (2, 3, 4, 5, 20 mm) were used to calibrate and test the taxel. Tests of indenter calibrations on the same sizes yielded low RMSE (under 1.5 kPa), however mismatched tests found large errors. Smaller indenter calibration models under-predict on larger test data, and vice versa (around ± \pm 18 kPa at the extremes). Direction of mismatch flips the sign of the bias, meaning negative for models calibrated on larger indenter than the test, positive for models calibrated on smaller indenter than the test.

2026-10-08.title: Energy-Efficient Gait Adaptation via Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Quadrupedal Locomotion Across Diverse Terrains
2026-10-08.authors: Ammar Issa , Anubhav Singh , Anton Tsaritsin , Sergey Kolyubin
2026-10-08.comment: . Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027. Ammar Issa, Anubhav Singh, and Anton Tsaritsin contributed equally
2026-10-08.abstract: While energy efficiency is a critical objective for legged-robot locomotion control, achieving low energy consumption while maintaining robust performance across different velocity ranges and terrain conditions remains a key challenge. This is particularly true for end-to-end RL policies, where gait generation, motion execution, and energy optimization are tightly coupled, leading to high sensitivity to reward design. In this work, we propose a hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) framework that separates a high-frequency policy for stable and robust joint-level motion execution from low-frequency gait adaptation that explicitly minimizes the cost of transport (CoT). The three-stage Isaac-based training procedure enables zero-shot sim-to-real transfer with improved tracking accuracy, robustness, and energy efficiency. The learned hierarchy exhibits automatic speed-dependent gait adaptation, transitioning from pacing at low speeds to trotting at higher speeds. We validate the proposed approach in simulation against representative single-policy and hierarchical locomotion baselines, demonstrating reduced CoT over a broad range of commanded velocities, while maintaining robust locomotion across flat, uneven rough, and inclined terrains. We further demonstrate its practical feasibility through zero-shot deployment on a physical Unitree AlienGo quadruped.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Energy efficiency is essential for quadruped robots operating in
long-duration and energy-constrained tasks. Their nonlinear
dynamics, intermittent contacts, and speed-dependent gait
energetics make it difficult to achieve both stable locomotion and
low energy consumption. Biological studies show that different
gaits become energetically favorable at different speeds [ 1 ] , motivating controllers that adapt gait rather
than rely on a single locomotion pattern.

Model-based methods use model predictive control (MPC), trajectory optimization, and quadratic programming (QP)-based control to generate dynamically feasible and energy-conscious
motions [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Bio-inspired approaches exploit
passive dynamics or central pattern generators (CPGs) to obtain interpretable gait structures [ 6 , 7 ] , with recent methods
using reinforcement learning (RL) to adapt oscillator parameters and
generate multiple gaits and transitions [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . However, these
approaches often depend on accurate models, predefined motion
structures, or hand-designed oscillator representations.

RL has enabled robust quadrupedal locomotion
without explicit dynamics models [ 11 , 12 ] . Such policies are
typically trained using algorithms such as proximal policy optimization (PPO) [ 13 ] , with tracking, stability, imitation,
and energy objectives combined through reward design [ 14 , 15 ] . Energy-aware methods
penalize power or CoT and can produce efficient, speed-dependent
gait transitions [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . Nevertheless, end-to-end
policies jointly optimize gait generation, stabilization, tracking,
and energy efficiency, making them sensitive to reward weighting
and reducing interpretability.

Hierarchical methods address this coupling by separating
gait-level decisions from low-level motor control [ 20 ] . Existing approaches generate
CPG-based gait commands [ 21 ] , combine
learned gait parameters with MPC [ 22 ] , or switch
between pretrained energy-efficient gait policies [ 23 ] . While effective, many still rely on
discrete switching, predefined gait libraries, or model-based
low-level controllers.

In this work, we propose a fully learning-based hierarchical
reinforcement learning framework for energy-efficient quadruped
locomotion across different speeds and terrains. A high-frequency
low-level policy performs velocity tracking and stabilization,
while a slower high-level policy continuously modulates
interpretable gait parameters. Energy efficiency is incorporated
directly into the high-level objective through CoT-related
optimization, enabling adaptive gait modulation without predefined
gait libraries or manually designed transition rules.
Representative locomotion behaviors, including flat-ground
walking, slope traversal, and speed-dependent gait modulation,
are shown in Fig. 1 .

The main contributions of this work are:

A hierarchical RL framework that separates low-frequency gait adaptation
from high-frequency velocity tracking and stabilization, followed
by post-training finetuning.

A high-level objective that explicitly incorporates
CoT-related energy optimization for continuous gait-parameter
modulation.

Evaluation of tracking and CoT across different speeds and
terrains, together with zero-shot deployment on a physical Unitree AlienGo.

2026-10-08.title: Temporal Visuo-Tactile Learning for Dexterous Grasp Stability
2026-10-08.authors: Ken Nakahara , Aleksei Buvailik , Prokhor Kotov , Roberto Calandra
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-08.comment: . Website: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract:
Humans can grasp everyday objects with almost perfect success rates using fingertip tactile feedback, yet much of the robotic grasping literature emphasizes vision-based grasp selection with parallel grippers.
In this work, we systematically investigate how high-resolution, dynamic tactile sensing contributes to grasp stability prediction and model-guided grasping in dexterous robotic hands.
To this end, we collected a dataset of 10,000 grasp trials across 200 objects using a multi-fingered robotic hand equipped with four Digit 360 tactile sensors, recording external vision, proprioception, and tactile streams throughout each grasp.
With this dataset, we trained end-to-end temporal multimodal models to predict post-lift stability from pre-lift grasp observations and compared sensing modalities and encoding backbones.
Experimental results and controlled input ablations show that incorporating touch, and particularly high-resolution, dynamic touch, improves grasp stability prediction.
Finally, we deployed the learned predictor as an online stability gate on the real robot, where visuo-tactile model-guided regrasping improved the success rate among executed lifts by 10.5 percentage points over a non-tactile gate.
These results show how rich fingertip sensing and expressive temporal models that capture the dynamics of touch can support learned grasping with multi-fingered hands without explicit contact or force modeling, providing a scalable data-driven path from tactile experience toward stable dexterous manipulation.
The dataset is publicly available at https://lasr-lab.github.io/dexterous-grasp-stability/ .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Stable grasping with multi-fingered hands cannot be reduced to selecting a grasp pose from visual observations alone.
It is an inherently interactive problem, where stability depends on how contacts form and contact forces evolve as the hand closes around an object, shares load across multiple fingertips, and begins to lift.
Humans handle these changing contact conditions by combining vision with tactile feedback about fingertip contacts that are difficult to observe externally [ 1 , 2 ] .
However, much research on robotic grasping has focused on vision-based grasp selection, often for simple parallel grippers [ 3 , 4 ] .
Recent visuo-tactile learning approaches have shown that tactile input improves grasp outcome prediction compared to vision-only baselines [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
At the same time, modern vision-based tactile sensors are becoming more capable and accessible, enabling richer contact measurements during manipulation [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
For multi-fingered grasping, however, it remains unclear which sensing modalities are most informative for stability prediction, how tactile spatial detail and temporal dynamics contribute, and how to model these signals effectively.

In this paper, we study how temporal multimodal sensing supports post-lift stability prediction from pre-lift grasp observations and model-guided grasping with multi-fingered hands, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .
We center our study on grasp stability prediction and practical real-robot deployment: what to sense, which spatial and temporal cues matter, and how to model them to enable stable grasping across diverse objects.
Our contributions are threefold:

We collect a large-scale multimodal dataset of 10,000 dexterous grasp trials across 200 objects, with continuous recordings of external vision, high-resolution tactile signals from four Digit 360 sensors, and proprioception throughout the full grasping process.

We systematically evaluate dexterous grasp stability prediction across sensing modality combinations and static and temporal encoders under object-disjoint cross-validation. We further use controlled input ablations to isolate the roles of tactile spatial detail and temporal cues in prediction.

We deploy the learned visuo-tactile stability predictor as an online lift-or-regrasp gate on a multi-fingered robotic platform and achieve higher success among executed lifts on unseen objects than a non-tactile gate.

1. We collect a large-scale multimodal dataset of 10,000 dexterous grasp trials across 200 objects, with continuous recordings of external vision, high-resolution tactile signals from four Digit 360 sensors, and proprioception throughout the full grasping process.

2. We systematically evaluate dexterous grasp stability prediction across sensing modality combinations and static and temporal encoders under object-disjoint cross-validation. We further use controlled input ablations to isolate the roles of tactile spatial detail and temporal cues in prediction.

3. We deploy the learned visuo-tactile stability predictor as an online lift-or-regrasp gate on a multi-fingered robotic platform and achieve higher success among executed lifts on unseen objects than a non-tactile gate.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Grasp Stability Prediction

Grasp stability prediction aims to determine whether a grasp will remain secure after lifting.
Analytical grasp quality measures often assume known contact geometry and force models [ 11 ] , which are difficult to obtain reliably on real hardware.
Tactile grasp controllers provide useful principles, but often rely on hand-tuned tactile-event thresholds and grip adjustment rules [ 12 , 13 ] , motivating learned stability assessment from tactile and robot-state observations [ 2 , 14 ] .
End-to-end models using vision-based tactile sensors have demonstrated the benefits of touch over vision alone for stability prediction and enabled model-guided regrasping [ 5 , 6 ] .
Subsequent work has explored attention-based visuo-tactile fusion [ 15 ] , Transformer-based grasping of deformable objects [ 7 ] , and the addition of sound for stability and gentleness prediction [ 16 ] .
Tactile stability prediction for multi-fingered hands remains comparatively underexplored, with prior work including Bayesian haptic exploration with fingertip force sensing [ 17 ] .
Our work systematically examines how sensing modalities and tactile spatial and temporal cues contribute to multi-fingered stability prediction, and deploys the learned predictor as an online stability gate.

## II-B Learning and Control for Tactile Dexterous Grasping

Multi-fingered hands support diverse contact configurations and enveloping grasps, providing structural advantages for robust grasping.
Despite recent progress in learning-based dexterous grasping, robust real-world execution remains challenging due to high-dimensional hand control and uncertain hand-object contacts [ 18 ] .
Existing approaches include physics-aware grasp synthesis [ 19 ] and hand-centric object representations for robust policy learning [ 20 ] .
Tactile sensing complements these approaches by providing local contact feedback during multi-fingered grasping.
Such feedback has enabled adaptive visual-tactile grasp refinement [ 21 ] , paper picking using diffusion policies [ 22 ] , gentle grasping with anthropomorphic hands [ 23 ] , and grasp adaptation using full-hand tactile sensing [ 24 ] .
Building on this line of dexterous tactile grasping research, we use rich tactile sensing alongside vision and proprioception to predict post-lift stability from temporal pre-lift observations.

## II-C Vision-Based Tactile Sensors

Vision-based tactile sensors typically capture deformation of a compliant contact surface as images [ 25 ] , enabling the use of standard image-processing methods and deep visual encoders.
Representative examples include GelSight [ 8 ] for high-resolution contact geometry and TacTip [ 9 ] for biomimetic soft optical fingertip sensing.
Compact and low-cost sensors such as DIGIT [ 10 ] have been used to learn visuo-tactile prehensile manipulation with multi-fingered hands (e.g., [ 16 , 26 ] ).
Digit 360 [ 27 ] extends this line to a multimodal fingertip, combining an internal fisheye camera for high-resolution tactile imaging across a hemispherical contact surface with additional sensing modalities such as audio and pressure.
Recent work has used Digit 360 to learn multisensory touch representations from roughly one million contact-rich interactions [ 28 ] and visuo-tactile world models for contact-aware prediction and planning [ 29 ] .
We use four Digit 360 fingertips to investigate how rich, dynamic tactile sensing supports learned dexterous grasping.

2026-10-08.title: Making Task Abstractions Executable: Control-Aware Layout Repair for a Fixed Controller
2026-10-08.authors: Chiyoung Kim , Seungyeon Back , Sumin Shim , Doyoung Heo , Rita Singh
2026-10-08.abstract:
A task abstraction can specify the intended events while its spatial layout prevents a fixed agent and controller from completing them.
Starting from a supplied structured task record, we compile whole-task tracking, clearance, and actuation requirements into auditable affine layout constraints.
We repair only declared continuous coordinates, preserving event order, timing, topology, and the controller.
A most-violated-row update admits conditional finite-certification and net-displacement bounds; a same-compiler quadratic projection separates the representation from the optimizer.
On three researcher-authored task abstractions, both backends certify all three layouts and complete all 300 fresh paired rollouts per backend.
A risk-target sweep also exposes fixed event tests that the chosen certificate cannot satisfy through layout edits alone.
2026-10-08.introduction:
A task abstraction fixes what a robot should accomplish without determining whether a proposed scene supports that behavior.
Systems that generate tasks or environments from language descriptions make this gap practically relevant [ 1 , 2 ] .
For example, the event sequence switch → \rightarrow door → \rightarrow goal specifies an order, but a door that accommodates the body may still be too narrow for closed-loop tracking error.
Likewise, correctly ordered targets may require more acceleration than the fixed actuator permits.
The missing condition is not another event in the task: it is a compatible continuous layout.

We study this interface after a structured task specification has been supplied.
The task record fixes event identities and order, predicate types and tolerances, timing, and topology; the agent and controller are also fixed.
Our compiler maps tracking, clearance, and actuator requirements to affine conditions on editable scene coordinates.
These conditions provide an auditable, sufficient test of whether a layout supports the supplied task under the stated control model.
Repair changes the spatial realization, not the declared task.
The task records in our evaluation are researcher-authored; producing them from language or demonstrations is outside our scope.

Our contributions are a control-derived constraint representation, a simple row-update backend with conditional finite-certification and displacement guarantees, and a comparison with quadratic projection under the same compiler.
Three structured tasks isolate door clearance, checkpoint clearance, and fixed-time travel.
We evaluate 1,200 fresh paired method–rollouts and a risk-target sweep, while reporting earlier calibration-selected stress runs separately.

# 2 Related Work

WrightHere connects user descriptions to explorable environments [ 2 ] , GenSim generates robot tasks and demonstrations [ 1 ] , and ReShoot augments recorded demonstrations through generative visual domain randomization [ 3 ] .
Our method instead takes a structured task and initial layout as inputs and repairs their continuous realization for a fixed controller.
Generate–repair also appears in level design [ 4 ] ; our tests additionally include feedback tracking, actuator limits, and ordered events.
Funnel and stochastic-safety methods certify closed-loop behavior [ 5 , 6 ] ; we use a certificate to constrain editable geometry.
The update is related to Motzkin relaxation [ 7 ] ; the contribution is the control-derived compiler and its task–execution interface, not a new projection algorithm.

2026-10-08.title: Benchmarking Behavioral Steerability in Behavior Foundation Models
2026-10-08.authors: Minghe Gao , Zhanxi Yan , Jiahui Liu , Wendong Bu , Xiaoting Chen , Qizhou Wang , Yi Su , Siliang Tang , Jun Xiao , Yueting Zhuang , Tat-Seng Chua , Juncheng Li
2026-10-08.abstract: Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) are emerging as a paradigm for translating human intentions into executable humanoid behaviors. As these models evolve beyond behavior generation toward general-purpose behavioral systems, a fundamental question arises: can they be reliably steered according to user intentions? In this paper, we introduce the concept of behavioral steerability , defined as the ability of BFMs to faithfully generate behaviors that satisfy user-specified intentions. To study this capability, we present RoboSteer , the first benchmark for behavioral steerability in BFMs. RoboSteer organizes behavioral steerability into a three-level hierarchy—Conditional Steering, Constraint Steering, and Compositional Steering—and establishes a unified evaluation framework supported by a large-scale multimodal motion corpus. Using RoboSteer , we conduct the first large-scale empirical study of behavioral steerability across 9 existing BFMs. We view behavioral steerability as more than a capability for controlling motion: it concerns how embodied systems translate human intentions into purposeful actions. We hope RoboSteer will advance research on intention realization as a foundation for general-purpose embodied intelligence.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) represent an emerging family of humanoid foundation models that directly translate diverse human intentions into executable whole-body behaviors through a single general-purpose model [ 27 , 34 , 32 , 17 , 7 , 35 ] . Unlike task-specific robot policies or vision-language-action models that predict low-level control actions, BFMs operate in a unified behavior space, enabling motion generation, imitation, completion, and editing under diverse multimodal conditions [ 29 , 5 , 13 ] . These capabilities have enabled increasingly sophisticated humanoid behaviors. However, generating complex behaviors does not mean that a model can reliably satisfy specific user requirements. As BFMs become a more general interface for human–robot interaction, an important question is how to adapt their behavior generation to diverse and evolving human intentions.

The evolution of large language models offers a precedent. As shown in Figure 1 (a) , as language foundation models became increasingly general, the emergence of ChatGPT [ 22 ] transformed them from powerful text generators into steerable interactive systems [ 1 , 31 , 19 ] . This transition redefined the role of foundation models: beyond generating high-quality outputs, they are now expected to be reliably steered according to human intentions. BFMs are now entering a similar stage: as they become the primary interface through which humans communicate behavioral intentions to robots, their role extends beyond synthesizing realistic behaviors to reliably translating diverse human intentions into the intended behaviors. This raises a fundamental question:

Can a behavior foundation model be steerable?

In this paper, we define behavioral steerability as the ability of BFMs to generate behaviors that faithfully satisfy user intentions. Moving from behavior generators to general behavioral systems requires more than generating physically plausible behaviors; BFMs must also reliably adapt behavior generation to diverse user requirements, including desired conditions, execution constraints, or compositional instructions. In real-world human–robot interaction, users rarely request unconstrained behavior [ 14 , 30 , 33 ] ; instead, they specify how a behavior should be performed. For example, a user may ask a robot to follow a reference motion while moving faster, avoiding one arm, and passing through a target location. Such requests remain challenging for existing BFMs, which are primarily optimized to generate behaviors rather than adapting them to evolving user intentions [ 26 , 37 , 9 ] . We therefore argue that behavioral steerability is a defining capability to evolve from behavior generators into general behavioral systems. Figure 1 (b) illustrates the distinction.

To study behavioral steerability, we introduce RoboSteer , the first benchmark for defining and evaluating this capability in BFMs. As shown in Figure 3 , RoboSteer organizes behavioral steerability into three increasingly levels: Conditional Steering , which evaluates behavior generation under a specified behavioral condition (e.g., following a reference motion or a textual behavior description); Constraint Steering , which measures compliance with explicit behavioral requirements (e.g., movement speed, body-part restrictions, or target locations); and Compositional Steering , which evaluates whether models can simultaneously satisfy multiple interleaved behavioral requirements from different sources (e.g., imitating a reference video and then following a textual instruction with a speed constraint). RoboSteer further offers an open-source framework for evaluating behavioral steerability in simulation and real-world settings.

To support this benchmark, we leverage pre-processed web-scale human motion data and retarget and track the motions to form a multimodal corpus for humanoid behavioral steerability evaluation. The data are represented as joint-level motion trajectories, together with associated videos, text, audio, and keyframes. The resulting corpus comprises 38,522 source motions, 77,044 human and rendered sequences, totaling 91.58 hours and 773,716 tasks.

Using RoboSteer , we conduct a large-scale empirical study of behavioral steerability across 9 BFMs with diverse paradigms and multimodal inputs. Our results reveal a clear gap between behavior generation and behavioral steerability, which widens as steering complexity increases. Current BFMs also exhibit weaker fine-grained spatial and body-part control, while struggling to satisfy multiple behavioral requirements simultaneously. These findings highlight behavioral steerability as a distinct capability beyond behavior generation and suggest the need for more fine-grained and multimodal behavioral control.

Our findings invite a broader question: what does it mean for embodied intelligence to move beyond generating behaviors toward realizing human intentions? The ability to fulfill intentions gives behaviors their purpose in human–robot interaction, enabling robots to adapt what they do and how they do it to human needs. By formalizing behavioral steerability, RoboSteer provides a starting point for investigating this capability as a potential foundation for more general embodied intelligence. Its implications may extend from intention-guided low-level control to higher-level perception, decision-making, and action in VLA and VLN systems. Understanding how intention realization can shape these capabilities may open new directions toward embodied intelligence that is not only capable of acting, but also responsive to human goals, advancing toward the broader vision of AGI.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Existing Related Works

## 2.1 Behavior Generation as Dominant Paradigm

Existing research on BFMs has largely been organized around behavior generation. Recent advances span motion generation, imitation learning, motion completion, motion editing, multimodal behavior modeling, and embodied interaction, all aiming to improve the ability of BFMs to generate realistic and executable behaviors [ 32 , 34 , 23 , 11 , 36 ] . Correspondingly, numerous datasets and benchmarks have been developed to evaluate behavior generation capability through measures such as motion quality, generation fidelity, and task completion [ 10 , 24 , 18 ] . Together, these efforts implicitly assume that successful behavior generation provides a sufficient characterization of BFM capability. As BFMs continue to evolve toward more general behavioral systems, however, generating high-quality behaviors alone is no longer sufficient; models must also be evaluated by how faithfully they transform human intentions into executable behaviors.

## 2.2 Toward Steerable Behavior Systems

Recent research has increasingly explored controllable behavior generation as BFMs become more general and interactive. Representative efforts include motion editing, instruction-conditioned behavior generation, constraint-aware motion synthesis, and vision-language-action models that condition behaviors on language or multimodal observations [ 25 , 30 , 2 ] . Collectively, these studies signal an important shift in humanoid behavior modeling—from generating behaviors to controlling how behaviors are generated. However, these approaches primarily propose new control mechanisms rather than defining behavior control as a measurable capability that can be systematically compared across BFMs. Consequently, the field still lacks a unified formulation and evaluation framework for behavioral steerability.

2026-10-08.title: Design of a Fully Actuated 4-DOF Robotic Finger With Joint-Specific Hybrid Remote Actuation
2026-10-08.authors: Hyojae Kang , Hyun-mok Jung , Joonho Lee , Dongil Park , Hyunmin Do , Jongwoo Park , Jeongdo Ahn
2026-10-08.comment: . This manuscript has been submitted for possible publication
2026-10-08.abstract: This paper presents a fully actuated 4-DOF robotic finger using a joint-specific hybrid remote-actuation architecture. The metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint is driven by two coordinated rigid-link transmission sets, whereas the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints are independently actuated by closed-loop wire transmissions incorporating circular rolling-contact joints (RCJs). A larger transmission radius is used at the PIP joint than at the DIP joint. The RCJ wire geometry maintains the total wire-loop length during joint rotation, and the DIP wire routing is designed so that PIP motion does not affect its differential actuation for a fixed MCP configuration. The distal wire transmission, MCP linkage, and fingertip kinematics are analytically modeled. In experiments, the transmission behavior was quantitatively evaluated from the ball-screw displacements measured using ArUco-marker tracking. MCP actuation produced measurable displacements of the PIP and DIP transmission units, whereas isolated PIP and DIP actuation with the MCP fixed supported the intended mechanical decoupling between the distal transmissions. The mean peak fingertip forces under isolated MCP, PIP, and DIP actuation were 21.28 N, 9.22 N, and 5.75 N, respectively. The resulting finger postures were also examined using objects of different geometries and sizes.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Robotic hands require multiple controllable degrees of freedom (DoFs) to generate diverse finger postures for grasping and manipulation [ 1 ] . Fully or highly actuated hands preserve joint-level controllability by assigning independent actuation to multiple finger DoFs [ 2 , 3 ] . However, increasing the number of actuated joints also increases the number of actuators and transmission components. Packaging these components within the hand is especially restrictive in multi-DoF fingers because the available installation volume decreases toward the distal phalanges, while distal actuator placement increases the mass and structural volume carried by the finger.

Remote actuation separates actuator placement from joint location. Rigid-linkage transmission provides deterministic kinematics and direct force transmission, whereas tendon- or wire-driven transmission provides greater routing flexibility through confined structures [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Their complementary characteristics have motivated hybrid linkage–tendon architectures [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . However, the appropriate transmission type can differ according to joint location and mechanical function. For a proximal multi-DoF joint such as the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint, a rigid-link transmission can transmit the motion of multiple proximal actuators to a multi-DoF joint while avoiding additional tendon-routing elements around the finger base. In contrast, flexible transmission is advantageous for serial distal joints because it allows actuation to be remotely located without placing actuators within the phalanges.

Extending wire transmission to multiple serial joints introduces additional requirements. Bidirectional actuation requires either passive restoration or opposing agonist–antagonist transmission paths because a wire transmits tensile force only while tensioned [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . In addition, a wire driving a distal joint must traverse moving proximal joints, and configuration-dependent changes in routing length can generate unintended interjoint coupling. Recent studies have addressed these issues using antagonistic remote transmission and joint-centered routing [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] . A fully actuated multi-DoF finger therefore requires both independent actuation inputs and a transmission arrangement that accommodates the different mechanical requirements of the proximal and distal joints while avoiding unintended coupling between the distal joints.

This paper presents a fully actuated 4-DOF robotic finger based on a joint-specific hybrid remote-actuation architecture, combining rigid-link transmission for the 2-DOF MCP joint with independent closed-loop wire transmissions for the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joints using circular rolling-contact joints (RCJs). This architecture retains independent actuation of all four DoFs without placing actuators in the distal finger links, while the distal wire routing prevents differential coupling between the PIP and DIP transmissions for a fixed MCP configuration. Experiments quantify the MCP-induced displacement of the distal transmission units and evaluate the mechanical decoupling between the PIP and DIP transmissions for a fixed MCP configuration, together with the fingertip force and object-interaction behavior of the fabricated finger.

The main contributions are:

A joint-specific hybrid remote-actuation architecture for a fully actuated 4-DOF finger, combining two coordinated rigid-link transmission sets at the 2-DOF MCP joint with remote wire transmissions at the serial PIP and DIP joints.

A closed-loop RCJ wire transmission that maintains bidirectional actuation and provides mechanical decoupling between the PIP and DIP transmissions for a fixed MCP configuration.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews robotic finger actuation architectures relevant to the proposed mechanism. Section III presents the mechanical design, and Section IV provides the kinematic and transmission analyses. Section V experimentally evaluates joint motion, fingertip force, and representative object interaction. Section VI concludes the paper.

1. A joint-specific hybrid remote-actuation architecture for a fully actuated 4-DOF finger, combining two coordinated rigid-link transmission sets at the 2-DOF MCP joint with remote wire transmissions at the serial PIP and DIP joints.

2. A closed-loop RCJ wire transmission that maintains bidirectional actuation and provides mechanical decoupling between the PIP and DIP transmissions for a fixed MCP configuration.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Robotic fingers and hands can be broadly categorized as underactuated or fully actuated according to the relationship between their DoFs and degrees of actuation (DoAs). Underactuated mechanisms use fewer actuators than controllable joint DoFs, typically relying on mechanical coupling, passive adaptation, or compliant elements to coordinate multiple joint motions [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] . In contrast, fully actuated systems including DLR-Hand II [ 2 ] , KITECH-Hand [ 27 ] , LEAP Hand [ 28 ] , RAPID Hand [ 29 ] , and EyeSight Hand [ 30 ] assign independent actuation to each controlled DoF, enabling direct control of multiple finger coordinates. This increased controllability, however, requires a corresponding number of actuators and transmission components, making actuator packaging a major design consideration, particularly in multi-DoF fingers. Remote transmission addresses this issue by separating actuator placement from joint location. The ILDA Hand [ 6 ] employs a rigid-linkage-based proximal transmission, while hybrid systems such as MCR-Hand II [ 8 ] and REL Hand [ 11 ] distribute linkage and tendon transmission among different finger functions.

Tendon- and wire-driven fingers enable actuators to be located away from distal joints, but their performance depends on tension management and routing geometry [ 4 , 14 , 7 , 20 ] . Passive elastic restoration has been used in underactuated mechanisms such as the LUTA Hand [ 17 ] , whereas antagonistic architectures actively drive both directions using opposing tensile paths [ 12 , 13 , 15 , 16 , 19 ] . For serially arranged joints, the wire path to a distal joint can also change as a proximal joint moves, producing unwanted coupling. Choi et al. [ 18 ] addressed this problem by routing wires through revolute-joint centers so that proximal rotation does not alter the effective routing length of distal transmissions.

RCJs provide an alternative to conventional pin joints by constraining adjacent surfaces to roll relative to each other, allowing the joint trajectory and transmission geometry to be designed simultaneously [ 31 ] . RCJs have been applied to underactuated prosthetic fingers [ 32 ] , tendon-driven compliant manipulators for cable-slack suppression [ 33 ] , adaptive hands with passive elastic restoration [ 17 ] , and mechanisms with optimized noncircular rolling surfaces and transmission geometries [ 34 ] .

In the proposed finger, the proximal 2-DOF MCP joint is driven by two rigid-link transmission sets, whereas the serial PIP and DIP joints are driven by closed-loop wire transmissions. This joint-specific allocation avoids additional tendon-routing elements around the MCP while keeping the distal actuators outside the phalanges. At the PIP and DIP joints, circular RCJs are incorporated into closed agonist–antagonist wire loops for bidirectional actuation. The DIP wire is routed through the PIP structure so that PIP motion does not produce differential DIP actuation, providing mechanical decoupling between the two distal transmissions for a fixed MCP configuration. Thus, the architecture combines full joint-level actuation with remote distal actuation without requiring a single transmission type to satisfy the different mechanical requirements of the proximal and distal joints.
