2026-10-08.title: Do Vision-Language-Action Models Understand Instructions? A Mechanistic Interpretability Study on Language Grounding
2026-10-08.authors: Theodor Wulff , Angelo Cangelosi
2026-10-08.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action models are designed to generalise across environments and task descriptions, raising the question of whether their action generation actually depends on the language instruction, or whether they largely rely on visual cues and superficial correlations.
Robustness to variance in the visual and linguistic observation space is critical for real-world deployment, yet VLAs lack explicit grounding modules and instead rely on the intrinsic language grounding capabilities of their Vision-Language model backbones.
For this reason, we conduct a controlled mechanistic interpretability study on the language grounding capabilities of two state-of-the-art Vision-Language-Action models, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.7, by applying activation and attribution patching to the residual stream of the action generation modules.
We systematically corrupt the task instruction of input samples of the LIBERO benchmark following five strategies: synonym replacement, semantic scaling, directional corruption, random object substitution, and empty string.
Our experiments find that both models are comparatively insensitive to abstract rephrasing and to referencing non-existent objects, but react strongly to empty task descriptions and, especially, to directional language.
During action generation, this sensitivity is concentrated in different loci for each model: mainly in the early, periodic cross-attention layers for GR00T N1.7, versus distributed across the earliest and selected later layers for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . For GR00T N1.7, directional perturbations drive some of the largest causal effects while leaving the internal representational geometry comparatively unchanged, a dissociation we do not observe clearly for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Finally, the reliability of attribution patching is model-dependent: it closely tracks activation patching for GR00T N1.7 but not for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Robotic systems deployed in real-world environments must be robust, as unpredictable behaviour may lead to severe and potentially catastrophic consequences.
Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) achieve impressive generalisation across different environments and task formulations, and yet the internal mechanisms underlying this behaviour remain largely a black box.
This creates a gap between empirical performance and scientific understanding.
Mechanistic interpretability has yielded insights in Large Language Wang et al. (2022) and Vision models Goh et al. (2021) , but only a handful of works exist that investigate Vision-Language-Action models from a model-internal perspective Grant et al. (2026) ; Miao et al. (2026) , particularly with respect to their action decoding strategies.
While findings in NLP and Computer Vision might transfer to the shared underlying Language and Vision-Language model backbones, VLA action generation strategies regularly introduce specific action expert modules with varying decoding strategies that particularly require the generation of language-conditioned outputs.

To this end, we address the gap between generalisability and understanding of the model’s internal computations by analysing the action expert modules of two state-of-the-art VLAs: π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} Black et al. (2025) and GR00T N1.7 NVIDIA et al. (2025b) .
Like many VLAs, both models employ a modular architecture in which an action expert incorporates visuolinguistic information from a Vision-Language model (VLM) backbone into a conditional flow-matching process for action generation.
However, they differ in how this conditioning is implemented: π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} integrates language via shared attention between action expert and backbone layers, while GR00T uses dedicated masked cross-attention layers.
This contrast lets us ask whether such differences in conditioning have measurable consequences for how language is causally used inside the action expert.

We apply the mechanistic interpretability techniques attribution patching and activation patching to the residual stream of the transformer layers in each model’s action expert, and complement these causal measures with Centred Kernel Alignment (CKA) between clean and perturbed activations.
Pairing a causal measure with a representational-similarity measure lets us distinguish two failure modes that are otherwise easy to conflate: (i) where a model’s representations are simply insensitive to a perturbation, and (ii) where representations shift but the action expert routes only a subset of that shift into behaviourally relevant computation.
By following a systematic language perturbation scheme, we construct the required corrupted instructions from the clean instructions for the corresponding patching methods.
Our perturbation scheme operates on five categories of increasing severity: synonym replacements, semantic scaling, directional perturbations, random object substitution, and empty string.
While the first two address sensitivity toward less specific inputs and alternate formulations on a verb and noun level, the directional perturbations directly investigate the effect of processing directional attributes within the action expert.
We test whether the model can fall back on purely visual information by rendering the task impossible due to referencing objects not visible in the current scene or dropping the instruction altogether.
Since all perturbed predictions are evaluated against the original demonstration, our experiments establish whether and where language causally influences the action, not whether it is interpreted correctly.

Specifically, our contributions can be summarised as follows:

A combined causal/representational analysis framework for diffusion/flow-matching VLA action experts. We integrate attribution patching, activation-patching verification, and CKA into a single evaluation framework applicable to transformer-based diffusion action heads, and use activation patching to directly quantify where attribution patching’s linear approximation deviates from the true causal effect of language conditioning, and for which model this approximation is reliable.

Language-perturbation sensitivity is model-specific. GR00T N1.7 exhibits a periodic layer-wise pattern that coincides with the placement of its cross-attention conditioning blocks, whereas π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} shows stronger effects concentrated in early and selected later layers.
Because the two models differ in more than their conditioning mechanism, we regard the link to architecture as a hypothesis. π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} is comparatively more sensitive to verb perturbations, while GR00T N1.7 is more sensitive to noun perturbations.
GR00T N1.7 also exhibits larger CKA shifts across several perturbation conditions, whereas π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s global representational geometry remains relatively stable.

Causal attribution and representational geometry dissociate for directional language in GR00T N1.7. In GR00T N1.7, directional perturbations elicit some of the largest attribution-patching effects of any perturbation type, yet leave the residual stream’s representational geometry, as measured by CKA, comparatively unchanged.
We do not observe this dissociation clearly for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} .
For synonym, hypernym, and empty-string perturbations, causal and representational effects track one another more closely and follow our proposed perturbation-severity ranking.
We hypothesise that this dissociation arises because directional phrases occupy a narrow, tightly clustered region of the embedding space, so the model’s action output is highly sensitive to the perturbation despite the underlying representation shifting comparatively little.

2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision-Language-Action Models

Inspired by the successes and generalisable capabilities of foundation models in domains such as NLP and image generation OpenAI et al. (2023) ; Dubey et al. (2024) ; Betker et al. (2023) ; Rombach et al. (2022) , Vision-Language-Action models aim to create robot policies that generalise across tasks, environments and embodiments Liu et al. (2024) ; Gemini Robotics Team et al. (2025) ; Qu et al. (2025) ; Belkhale et al. (2024) ; NVIDIA et al. (2025b) ; Kim et al. (2025) .
VLAs are usually built on top of pretrained VLM backbones to inherit their vision-language understanding.
They either add a dedicated action decoder module Black et al. (2025) ; NVIDIA et al. (2025b) to generate embodiment-specific trajectories or utilize the VLM vocabulary to assign discrete actions to tokens Kim et al. (2025) .
The action decoding strategies employed by VLAs range from simple linear mappings to sophisticated diffusion-based action decoders.
The latter employ flow matching or traditional diffusion denoising strategies as used by Chi et al. ( Chi et al., 2024 ) .
As input, they take at least a task instruction in natural language alongside a visual observation.
While VLAs show promising directions to generalising to differently formulated instructions as seen by their task success rates, it remains unclear how strong their language grounding actually is.

## 2.2 Mechanistic Interpretability for Multimodal Foundation Models

Early mechanistic interpretability work at the intersection of vision and language focused on foundation models, uncovering multimodal neurons that respond to shared visual-linguistic concepts Goh et al. (2021) and interpreting CLIP’s image representations directly Gandelsman et al. (2023) ; Radford et al. (2021) . Sparse autoencoders have since been widely applied to further disentangle CLIP’s internal representations Rao et al. (2024) ; Ro et al. (2026) ; Joseph et al. (2025) , while causal tracing tools originally developed for LLMs have been extended to vision-language models Palit et al. (2023) ; Basu et al. (2024) ; Neo et al. (2024) and, more recently, video models Shi et al. (2026) , typically to localize task-relevant subgraphs Rajaram et al. (2024) or via probing-based analysis Salin et al. (2022) .
Extending this line of work to embodied settings, recent studies have begun steering vision-language-action models (VLAs) Häon et al. (2025) , with a concurrent mechanistic study across five VLAs finding that these models process heterogeneous token sequences interleaving vision, language, and proprioception, and that mean-pooling activations across token positions destroys action-critical information despite high reconstruction quality Grant et al. (2026) .
To the best of our knowledge, no prior study has systematically examined, at the level of internal model computation, how VLAs respond to different types of perturbations in the language space, or where this processing occurs within their action-decoding components.
We address this gap by analysing the token-generation process in the action expert of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and the action decoder of GR00T N1.7 using attribution and activation patching alongside representational analyses.

## 2.3 Circuit Discovery

Mechanistic interpretability treats neural networks as computational graphs, with nodes corresponding to attention heads, MLPs, or individual neurons and features, and edges representing activation flow between them Heimersheim and Nanda (2024) , a framing established by foundational work on transformer circuits Elhage et al. (2021) , circuit-level case studies such as the IOI circuit Wang et al. (2022) and the greater-than arithmetic circuit Hanna et al. (2023) , and formalized theoretically through causal abstraction Geiger et al. (2025) .
Early circuit discovery relied on manual activation patching, that was later refined into path patching and automated via ACDC, which systematically searches a model’s computational graph for task-relevant subgraphs Conmy et al. (2023) , alongside related causal techniques such as causal mediation analysis, interchange interventions, and causal tracing Basu et al. (2024) .
Because these intervention-based methods scale poorly, attribution patching emerged as a more efficient alternative:
Attribution Patching approximates activation-patching effects via gradients Nanda (2023) ; Kramár et al. (2024) , and subsequent work has shown attribution patching can outperform automated circuit discovery empirically Syed et al. (2024) .
More recently, sparse autoencoders have enabled higher-resolution circuit analysis by exposing individual features as causally implicated nodes Marks et al. (2025) , though at the cost of vastly larger node counts that make direct intervention prohibitive; this has motivated frontier approaches combining cross-layer transcoders with backward Jacobian tracing to construct partial feature-level circuit maps Lindsey et al. (2025) , including per-prompt attribution graphs over transcoder features in production-scale models.

2026-10-08.title: Lifelong small-object navigation in changing object layouts: a benchmark and method
2026-10-08.authors: Jiagan Huang , Zikun Zhou , Zijian Ni , Hongpeng Wang , Guangming Lu , Jun Yu , Wenjie Pei
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-08.abstract:
Household robots need to continually navigate to different objects in the same environment, many of which are small and portable, such as tools and toys. Their small visual footprint and frequent occlusion make reliable observation difficult, and they may be moved by people without the robot observing the changes. We formulate this challenging task as Lifelong Small-object Navigation in Changing Object Layouts ( LiSoNav-COL ). Agents must seek suitable viewpoints for reliable observation, accumulate and reuse scene knowledge to efficiently locate subsequent targets, and update outdated memory after object relocation. To eliminate the need for prior scene scanning, we also require agents to start navigation with empty scene memory. Although practical, this task still lacks benchmarks designed around its defining assumptions. To bridge this gap, we introduce LiSoNav-Eval , a dedicated benchmark spanning 28 indoor scenes with 45 small-object categories. Its lifelong navigation sequences include both unchanged and relocated targets to evaluate memory reuse and adaptation to object relocation. To address this challenging task, we propose a navigation method based on multi-view Inspection with Viewpoint-Anchored Memory, dubbed IVAM-Nav . IVAM-Nav actively observes supporting surfaces from complementary viewpoints for reliable small-object perception and anchors the resulting memory to their observation viewpoints, supporting relational memory reuse and revalidation under similar viewing conditions.
Extensive experiments on LiSoNav-Eval demonstrate favorable performance of IVAM-Nav against representative methods. Benchmark analyses also show that smaller objects, larger environments, and longer relocation distances pose greater challenges. The dataset and code are available here .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Object-goal navigation requires embodied agents to search for and navigate to target objects specified by images or language ( Krantz et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2021 ) . In household environments, robots may repeatedly perform such tasks in the same scene, motivating lifelong navigation that retains and reuses experience across successive tasks ( Khanna et al., 2024b ) . Scene memory supports this process by preserving previously acquired object information to reduce redundant exploration.

In everyday household activities, many objects that robots need to locate and manipulate are small, portable items, such as tools and toys. People may move objects unnoticed by the robot, leaving its scene memory outdated and requiring verification and updates. These objects also occupy only a small portion of the visual field and are often occluded, making them difficult to observe clearly ( Wang and Soh, 2023 ) .
These real-world challenges motivate us to study Li felong S mall- o bject Nav igation in C hanging O bject L ayouts ( LiSoNav-COL ). In this task, an agent starts with no prior scene memory and navigates to successive small-object goals within the same environment, incrementally acquiring scene knowledge throughout the navigation. Given that unobserved object relocations may render its memory outdated, the agent must learn to reuse accumulated scene knowledge while adapting to these changes for accurate and efficient navigation. Starting with an empty memory eliminates the need for a separate scene-scanning phase in real-world applications.

Existing navigation benchmarks adopt task assumptions that differ from those of LiSoNav-COL. The mainstream lifelong navigation benchmarks ( Wani et al., 2020 ; Khanna et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2026 ) mainly evaluate experience reuse in static scenes, where target locations remain unchanged across subtasks. OpenIN ( Tang et al., 2025 ) evaluates sequential navigation after object relocation, but starts with a preconstructed scene graph and relocates objects before the task sequence begins. This setting assesses the use of prior scene knowledge after relocation, rather than its online acquisition and maintenance through repeated changes. Meanwhile, the small-object navigation benchmark ( Wang and Soh, 2023 ) focuses on perception and target search in static scenes under a single-goal setting. These evaluation settings do not jointly capture the requirements of LiSoNav-COL: acquiring scene knowledge from an initially empty memory, reusing it across small-object navigation tasks, and adapting to repeated object relocation.

To support systematic evaluation of LiSoNav-COL, we introduce LiSoNav-Eval , a new benchmark comprising navigation sequences and an evaluation protocol for this task.
Figure 1 presents an illustrative example of our benchmark, where the agent completes
a sequence of small-object navigation subtasks (each corresponding to a specific goal) in the same environment, starting with no prior scene memory and retaining the knowledge acquired during task execution. Specifically, each navigation sequence comprises multiple episodes, each containing several navigation subtasks. Object locations remain unchanged within each episode, while randomly selected objects are relocated between episodes without the agent observing the changes.
By including both unchanged and relocated targets, LiSoNav-Eval preserves opportunities to benefit from previously acquired knowledge while testing adaptation when remembered locations become outdated. Together, these settings support the evaluation of small-object navigation as agents accumulate scene knowledge, reuse it across tasks, and respond to changes in object layouts.

In LiSoNav-COL, incomplete or unreliable small-object observations can limit the effectiveness of existing scene-memory methods ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) . Object relocation compounds these observation difficulties, making memory reuse and revalidation more challenging.
In this paper, we propose IVAM-Nav , a lifelong small-object navigation
method based on multi-view I nspection and V iewpoint- A nchored M emory, to address these challenges. Our key idea is to actively inspect the supporting surfaces where the target may be located from multiple viewpoints and anchor the memory to these viewpoints.
Specifically, the agent acquires reliable and complementary observations around potential supporting surfaces and stores them with their camera poses and semantic associations. These records enable reobservation under similar viewing conditions to effectively verify and update the memory.
Extensive experiments on LiSoNav-Eval demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm. Our contributions can be summarized as:

We formulate LiSoNav-COL, a new task for lifelong small-object navigation from empty scene memory under changing object layouts. We also introduce LiSoNav-Eval, a dedicated benchmark for evaluating agent performance on this task.

We formulate LiSoNav-COL, a new task for lifelong small-object navigation from empty scene memory under changing object layouts. We also introduce LiSoNav-Eval, a dedicated benchmark for evaluating agent performance on this task.

We propose IVAM-Nav, which constructs a viewpoint-anchored graph memory through active multi-view inspection. This design supports relational memory reuse and memory revalidation under similar viewing conditions, enabling robust navigation.

Extensive experiments on LiSoNav-Eval demonstrate favorable performance of IVAM-Nav against representative methods, and benchmark analyses identify smaller objects, larger environments, and longer relocation distances as persistent challenges.

1. We formulate LiSoNav-COL, a new task for lifelong small-object navigation from empty scene memory under changing object layouts. We also introduce LiSoNav-Eval, a dedicated benchmark for evaluating agent performance on this task.

2. We propose IVAM-Nav, which constructs a viewpoint-anchored graph memory through active multi-view inspection. This design supports relational memory reuse and memory revalidation under similar viewing conditions, enabling robust navigation.

3. Extensive experiments on LiSoNav-Eval demonstrate favorable performance of IVAM-Nav against representative methods, and benchmark analyses identify smaller objects, larger environments, and longer relocation distances as persistent challenges.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Lifelong navigation in changing environments. Existing navigation tasks and benchmarks span single-goal, sequential, and lifelong settings in largely static scenes ( Chaplot et al., 2020 ; Krantz et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2021 ; Wani et al., 2020 ; Khanna et al., 2024b ; Miao et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2025 ; WANG et al., 2026 ) , while dynamic settings consider moving objects and spatiotemporal retrieval ( Kurenkov et al., 2023 ; Dorbala et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Bogenberger et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . Most closely related to our setting, OpenIN studies changing object layouts but requires a preconstructed scene representation before navigation, with its evaluation data and implementation currently unavailable ( Tang et al., 2025 ) . LiSoNav-Eval instead evaluates lifelong small-object navigation from empty memory under changing object layouts.

Memory construction, reuse, and revalidation. Existing navigation methods construct and query scene memory through object- or scene-centric graphs, visual observations, and spatial representations ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Werby et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2024 ; Wang and Soh, 2023 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Ge et al., 2026 ) , while dynamic-memory methods further update or reassess stored information based on new observations ( Tang et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Ko et al., 2025 ) . APRR and MSGNav actively adjust viewpoints after target detection or localization for manipulation or final-view selection ( Qin et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, IVAM-Nav builds reliable small-object memory via complementary multi-view inspection and uses acquisition viewpoints as persistent anchors for relational retrieval and revalidation.

2026-10-08.title: RealtimeWAM: How Fast Can I Run My World Action Model?
2026-10-08.authors: Huanan Liu , Ye Li , Kangye Ji , Xiaoyu Chen , Hanyun Cui , Yutian Shen , Yuan Meng , Chenglei Wu , Jingyan Jiang , Bo Li , Zhi Wang
2026-10-08.comment: including appendix. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) combine visual dynamics modeling with action
generation, but their high inference latency limits responsive robot control.
Recent efforts accelerate inference by removing explicit future-video
generation at test time, as in FastWAM, an approach that requires a
specially tailored architectural design. More general caching
strategies exploit feature redundancy, but redundancy alone does not capture
the changing computational demands of closed-loop control. To address these
challenges, we present RealtimeWAM, a general, training-free framework that
coordinates parallel execution with adaptive computation for low-latency
inference across diverse WAM architectures. We exploit layerwise dependencies
to overlap observation processing with prediction. However, concurrent
branches still compete for GPU resources, limiting the benefit of parallel
execution. We therefore adapt computation throughout the pipeline through
selective reuse, caching observation features in visually stable regions and
reusing Transformer residuals while reserving additional refinement for
small predicted adjustments. We evaluate RealtimeWAM on FastWAM and OpenWAM across RoboTwin, LIBERO,
and LIBERO-Plus. On an RTX 4090, measured mean inference latencies
are 24.09 and 63.09 ms, corresponding to average speedups of 8.90 × \times and 10.67 × \times . Average success rates are 82.75% and 87.41%, respectively,
within 0.02 and 0.53 percentage points of native inference.
Across five real-world tasks, RealtimeWAM improves average success rates over
native inference by 17.2 and 37.2 percentage points on FastWAM and OpenWAM,
respectively.
Project page: https://anonymous.4open.science/w/realtimewam/ .
2026-10-08.introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) integrate visual dynamics modeling with action
generation, providing predictive representations for robotic control ( Cen et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) .
However, their substantial inference cost limits how quickly a robot can
respond to changes in its environment. This limitation is particularly
problematic in dynamic manipulation, where the scene continues to evolve
while the model generates an action ( Black et al., 2025b ) . For example, a moving object on a
conveyor may shift away from its observed position before the predicted
action is executed. Reducing latency from observation to action is therefore essential
for using WAMs to control robots in real time.

Recent work has reduced inference cost through architectural simplification
and computational reuse. For example, FastWAM removes future-video generation at inference while retaining
joint training with video ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , and diffusion caching methods such as TeaCache
avoid repeated Transformer computation by reusing residual features ( Liu et al., 2025a ) . These advances leave two further questions for
WAM execution in real time. First, reducing computation alone does not
resolve how observation processing and prediction should be scheduled
under their data dependencies and shared hardware constraints. Second,
caching decisions based on denoising similarity are not explicitly tied
to the responsiveness and precision required by the current action.
Fixed evaluation schedules likewise apply the same computational budget
throughout a rollout, despite changing execution requirements. Further
acceleration therefore calls for coordinating parallel execution with
computation that adapts to the current observation and predicted motion.

To address these challenges, we present RealtimeWAM, a framework that coordinates parallel
execution with adaptive computation for existing WAM architectures
without additional training. We first exploit the layerwise dependencies
between processing the current observation (Prefill) and prediction. As each
layer produces the required observation features, the corresponding
prediction computation can begin while Prefill continues (Figure 2 ). This allows
Prefill to overlap with action prediction and, when present, future-video generation. However, concurrent branches compete for shared GPU compute
resources, limiting the speedup achievable through overlap alone.

To ease this contention, we exploit temporal redundancy across observations
to reduce the Prefill workload. Changes in the current observation guide
which tokens receive fresh computation, while cached features supply
the remaining positions. However, reducing
the number of refreshed tokens does not always reduce latency, as different
token counts can fall within the same latency plateau
(Table 3 , right). We use this
available capacity to refresh additional tokens with larger feature changes
in the first layer, limiting reuse error at little extra latency. This reuse
policy accounts for hardware latency and reduces the workload competing
with prediction while keeping observation features current.

Token reuse reduces the cost of the first stage, but
subsequent denoising still requires repeated network evaluations. To further
accelerate inference, we adapt the refresh schedule of cached Transformer
residuals according to predicted motion. A coarse action prediction provides a
displacement signal for deciding whether further refinement is needed.
Motion amplitude and the effect of additional computation vary within an
episode (Figure 3 ), motivating a budget adapted to motion.
We allocate fewer evaluations to large predicted movements to favor rapid
replanning, while retaining additional evaluations for small adjustments.
We evaluate this allocation through closed-loop ablations in
Section 4.4 and paired prediction comparisons in
Appendix E .
Refinement continues from the same initial denoising trajectory, preserving
the computation already performed.

We evaluate FastWAM and OpenWAM on RoboTwin, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus.
Combining execution optimizations with adaptive computation gives measured
average speedups of 8.90 × \times and 10.67 × \times , respectively, relative
to native inference. Average success rates decrease by 0.02 and 0.53 percentage
points (Table 1 ). Controlled experiments examine
which scheduling and computation allocation choices account for these gains.

Our main contributions are:

We design a parallel schedule guided by layer dependencies that overlaps
observation processing with action prediction and, where applicable,
future-video generation.

We develop a token reuse policy that reduces the Prefill workload
and exploits hardware latency plateaus to refresh additional
informative tokens.

2026-10-08.title: Distributed Motion Planning for Multi-Robot Systems under Topological Constraints
2026-10-08.authors: Gianpietro Battocletti , Dimitris Boskos , Dimos V. Dimarogonas , Bart De Schutter
2026-10-08.abstract:
Efficient and distributed coordination of mobile robots is one of the main challenges in multi-robot systems. Topological constraints, often expressed as topological braids, are a popular tool to encode complex coordination patterns between multiple mobile robots, as they offer a compact and abstract representation of the desired qualitative relation between the space-time trajectories of the robots.
However, execution of joint motion plans encoded as braid-based topological constraints via distributed controllers is challenging, with existing approaches, generally based on the execution of one braid generator at a time, producing slow and suboptimal trajectories.
We propose a distributed controller based on Model Predictive Control (MPC) to efficiently execute braid-based topological specifications.
Rather than directly tracking the braid specification, we propose to use winding numbers, which are topological invariants for braids, as a proxy. This has the twofold benefit of converting braids into a continuous function, which can be easily tracked by an MPC controller through an appropriate term in the cost function, and of decoupling the global braid specification into a set of pairwise specifications, which can be tracked distributedly through the solution of only local MPC problems.
To maintain global coordination, we propose a consensus-based progress estimation approach, which allows the robots to synchronize their motion toward the desired specification.
We validate the proposed approach in simulation and in real-world experiments, where we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach and the improvement over existing approaches in terms of execution speed and control effort.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Autonomous multi-robot systems are becoming increasingly widespread, with applications ranging through many different domains. Modern hardware allows for a high degree of autonomy of mobile robots, enabling them to perform on board all the necessary tasks required for autonomous operation, such as mapping, localization, planning, and control. This also allows for multi-robot systems to operate with distributed or decentralized control architectures, increasing their scalability and removing the need for a central coordinator. Under those control architectures, robots sharing the same environment must coordinate with each other in order to avoid collisions, to optimize their motion trajectories, and to perform shared tasks.
To this end, topological constraints represent an increasingly popular coordination tool ( Bhattacharya et al., 2021 ) , thanks to their ability to compactly represent the qualitative relation between the trajectories of different robots.

In the last decade, the success of topology-based motion planning approaches for single-robot systems has lead to a growing interest in the development of novel methods to extend their use to multi-robot systems.
However, while several algorithms have been proposed to solve multi-robot coordination tasks by computing some type of topological specification, the same does not hold for methods designed for the execution of such specifications. In fact, only a limited number of algorithms exist to execute multi-robot motion plans encoded as topological constraints, and they present several limitations.
The most widely used approach to execute joint motion plans encoded as braid-based specifications and grid-based specifications is that of discretizing the set of positions the robots can take in the environment, and sequentially swapping the relative positions of pairs of robots, which results in practice in the execution of one element of the specification at a time ( Diaz-Mercado et al., 2015 ; Diaz-Mercado and Egerstedt, 2017 ; Cao et al., 2023 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) .
While this approach is effective, it is slow and scales poorly with the number of robots, as robots only move one pair at a time, and need to wait for others to complete their swap before being able to move.
Another popular approach is that of selecting a set of trajectories compatible with the desired specification and tracking them ( Imran et al., 2026 ; Mavrogiannis et al., 2023 ; Mavrogiannis and Knepper, 2020 ) .
However, this method is sensitive to the sampling strategy, and usually produces suboptimal motion trajectories.
A third possible approach is that of using winding numbers to encode pairwise swaps between agents. The sign of winding numbers indicates if the swap must happen in clockwise or counterclockwise fashion; the robots are then tasked with computing trajectories that maximize the increase of the winding numbers corresponding to the traveled paths, while matching the desired sign ( Mavrogiannis et al., 2022 ; Nakao et al., 2025 ; Mavrogiannis and Knepper, 2018 ; Mavrogiannis and Knepper, 2021 ) . However, algorithms based on this approach are only suitable for the execution of a limited class of topological specifications, composed by those with at most one swap for each pair of robots. Moreover, those approaches provide no guarantees that the desired specification will be executed due to the absence of a temporal ordering of the swaps being encoded in the pairwise winding numbers.

In this work, we aim at bridging this gap by proposing a distributed motion planning algorithm for a multi-robot system capable of executing general topological specifications, i.e., of making so that the trajectories traveled by the robots lie in the topological equivalence class encoded by the specification.
Without loss of generality, we focus on a specific type of topological constraint, namely, topological braids, as it is the most widely used one in works on multi-robot systems ( Cao et al., 2023 ; Diaz-Mercado and Egerstedt, 2017 ; Mavrogiannis and Knepper, 2020 ) .
Moreover, other types of constraints, such as sequences of permutation grids and winding numbers, can be translated into topological braids ( Cao et al., 2025 ; Berger, 2001 ) , allowing to apply the proposed algorithm with little modifications.

To achieve our goal, we propose the use of winding numbers as a way to translate the braid specification, which is a discrete object by nature, into a continuous one.
This conversion retains the topological properties of the braid, since winding numbers are topological invariants for braids ( Berger, 2001 ) .
We then attain the execution of the specification via a distributed MPC-based braid controller that takes as input the winding numbers obtained from the braids, and computes feasible collision-free trajectories to track them thanks to the inclusion of a winding tracking term in the MPC cost function.
Through this approach, we are able to track general braids, differently from existing works considering a winding tracking controller, which are limited to braids that include at most one swap for each pair robots such as in ( Mavrogiannis et al., 2022 ; Mavrogiannis and Knepper, 2021 ) , and where winding numbers are often used solely as a mean to expedite the swap of position between pairs of robots.
One challenge in this approach arises from the fact that braids do not provide a timing specification for the execution of the specification, which can make it challenging to synchronize the robots during their execution, in particular when considering a distributed control architecture. For this purpose, we propose to estimate the progress along the specification through the comparison of the winding numbers associated to the trajectories of the robots with those computed from the braid specification.
This progress estimate can be computed locally and agreed upon through distributed consensus, and avoids the need for a pre-specified timing law for the tracking of the braid, which in general will be suboptimal if it requires executing the specification too slowly, or unattainable if it requires the execution to be too fast.

The contributions of this work with respect to the state of the art are summarized as follows:

We introduce a novel approach to translate discrete braid-based topological specifications into continuous functions by means of winding numbers, which yield invariants for topological braids.
The use of winding numbers results in splitting the global interaction pattern encoded by the braid in pairwise interaction patterns, which can be tracked distributedly.

We propose a distributed MPC-based control approach to execute braid-based multi-robot topological specifications, based on the tracking of winding numbers.
Winding numbers can be directly computed from the trajectories of the robots, allowing to search for motion trajectories that minimize the mismatch of the trajectories’ winding numbers from the target winding numbers (i.e., those computed from the braid specification). This approach is scalable and efficient, since it requires the solution of only local MPC problems.
We prove that the distributed MPC controller is recursively feasible, ensuring the existence of collision-free trajectories that satisfy state and input constraints.

We introduce a consensus-based progress variable to track the progress of the robots along the topological specification, that also serves as a coordination tool to synchronize the robots toward the desired interaction pattern.

The contributions are validated by means of numerical simulations, in which we show the benefits of the proposed controller with respect to existing approaches, and via real-world experiments, where we assess the robustness and effectiveness of the proposed approach in the presence of disturbances.

# 2 Related work

In this section, we expand on the overview we have provided in Section 1 of approaches that compute motion plans for mobile robots and encode them as topological constraints.

In single-robot systems, topological tools allow to qualitatively categorize the possible trajectories of a robot depending on the homotopy class to which they belong. This corresponds to grouping together trajectories that can be continuously deformed into one another, establishing a qualitative equivalence between them ( Lee, 2010 ) .
In practice, the most common approach to determine the homotopy class where a trajectory lies in, is that of computing a topological invariant of the trajectory, with the most widely used being the so-called homotopy signature ( Bhattacharya and Ghrist, 2018 ) .
Homotopy signatures can be used to identify the homotopy class where a trajectory lies, and can also be used as a topological specification to impose a homotopy class constraint in the motion planning problem for mobile robots ( Grigoriev and Slissenko, 1998 ; Kim et al., 2014 ; Yang et al., 2022 ; Pokorny et al., 2016 ) .
Topological invariants other than signatures have also been considered for this purpose, such as the number of times a trajectory loops around each obstacle in the environment ( Yershov et al., 2013 ; Narayanan et al., 2013 ) , and the integral of the trajectory of a robot in the complex plane ( He et al., 2022 ; Bhattacharya et al., 2012 ; Bhattacharya, 2010 ) .
Alternatively, homotopy-class constraints can be cast as mixed-integer constraints ( Park et al., 2015 ) , which can be more easily included in optimization-based planners.
In the context of optimization-based motion planning approaches, homotopy-based methods can be used to generate topologically-distinct initial solutions for the trajectory optimization problem. The parallelized optimization of trajectories in different homotopy classes has been shown to lead to motion plans closer to the global optimum ( De Groot et al., 2024 ; Wong et al., 2025 ; Sahin and Bhattacharya, 2024 ) .
Another notable application case of homotopy-based topological specifications is that of tethered robots, where the presence of a tethered connection between the robot and a fixed anchor point introduces topological constraints in the motion planning problem.
Several approaches have been proposed to tackle this problem, with the majority of them leveraging topological invariants such as homotopy signatures to search feasible paths in distinct homotopy classes, and to find one where the trajectory of the robot is compatible with the maximum tether length ( Kim et al., 2014 ; Tanner et al., 2013 ; Teshnizi and Shell, 2021 ) .

Topological constraints in multi-robot systems require more complex topological tools.
In fact, topological constraints in multi-robot systems must capture, in addition to the relations between the trajectories of the robots and the obstacles present in the environment, also the relations between the trajectories themselves.
For this reason, the main challenge these tools need to address is that the classification of multi-robot trajectories in topological equivalence classes jointly depends on the topological relations between the trajectories.
Several types of topological tools have been considered to represent the topological equivalence classes of the trajectories of multiple robots, such as topological braids ( Mavrogiannis et al., 2017 ; Diaz-Mercado and Egerstedt, 2017 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , sequences of permutation grids ( Cao et al., 2025 ) , winding numbers ( Mavrogiannis et al., 2022 ; Nakao et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2025 ) , and representative sets of topologically distinct paths ( Wu et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; McBeth et al., 2023 ) .
Topological specifications based on these topological objects have been shown to be a powerful tool for the coordination of multiple robots, both in centralized ( Imran et al., 2026 ) , distributed ( Mavrogiannis and Knepper, 2019 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) and decentralized settings ( Mavrogiannis et al., 2023 ; Mavrogiannis et al., 2024 ) .
Those topology-based methods have been successfully employed in several applications for the coordination of multi-robot systems ( Mavrogiannis et al., 2023 ) , including crowd navigation ( Mavrogiannis and Knepper, 2019 ; Martinez-Baselga et al., 2026 ) and traffic control ( Mavrogiannis et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) .
Similarly to the single-robot case, also multi-robot systems composed of multiple tethered robots represent a prime application case for topological specifications, since the tethers of the robots naturally give raise to multiple topological equivalence classes where each tether can lie with respect to the others. In this context, braid-based planning approaches have been proposed for the entanglement-free navigation of tethered mobile robots ( Cao et al., 2025 ; Zhang and Pham, 2019 ) .
Moreover, in ( D’Antonio et al., 2026 ) topological specifications have been used to compute trajectories leading to the formation of knots between the tethers of multiple drones, which can be used to grab and lift a payload for transportation purposes.

Multiple methods have been proposed in the literature for the execution of motion plans encoded through topological constraints, but with several limitations.
The most popular approaches have been reviewed in Section 1 , where their limitation have also been highlighted, such as their suboptimality and slow speed in executing the topological specification.
In this work, we propose a distributed control method to overcome the limitations of existing approaches, producing efficient trajectories that satisfy the target topological specification.

2026-10-08.title: Video-to-Model: Automatic Modeling of Deformable Linear Objects
2026-10-08.authors: Akshun Sharma , Kimia Forghani , Yancy Diaz-Mercado
2026-10-08.abstract: This paper presents a video-to-model framework for automatically modeling the motion of a deformable suture thread from an input video. We utilize a recently developed CBF–CLF–QP numerical model that simplifies the characterization of deformable string motion through the selection of a small number of parameters. A perception module first localizes and tracks the thread in video, producing an ordered sequence of thread nodes. The observed thread motion is then processed by a spatio-temporal CNN network that estimates the effective parameters of a structured CBF–CLF–QP model. These parameters are used to simulate the thread under a user-defined needle velocity input. Experiments using unseen thread configurations and motion demonstrate that the framework can reliably reconstruct the thread behavior from video, automatically configure the structured model, and reproduce the expected thread motion with low tracking error. The proposed approach reduces the need for manual parameter tuning and provides a step toward automatic video-based modeling of deformable linear objects.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Deformable linear objects (DLOs) are encountered in applications such as robotic suturing [ 1 ] , cable routing [ 2 ] ,
and wire-harness assembly [ 3 ] , where predicting their behavior can support reliable robotic perception, planning, and control. However, their flexibility gives them many degrees of freedom, making them difficult to model. Unlike a rigid object, whose motion can be described
using a small number of state variables, DLOs can be represented in different ways depending on the modeling approach [ 4 ] . For example, a common discrete representation approximates a DLO as a
sequence of connected nodes whose state is defined by their positions and velocities [ 5 ] .

In this work, we focus specifically on surgical suture threads, which are highly flexible DLOs whose
motion is governed by their geometry, material properties, and interaction with the surrounding environment. Furthermore, variations in bending, stretching, and stiffness can produce different thread responses to the same input. [ 4 ] .
Consequently, accurately modeling thread behavior remains challenging.

Accurately modeling the thread is particularly important in robot-assisted suturing, where a
robot must anticipate the thread’s response to needle motion. Conventional physics-based approaches describe a thread using masses, elastic forces, damping forces, and contact models [ 6 , 7 ] . However, more modeled elements increase computational cost, while uncertain material properties and unmodeled dynamics can reduce prediction accuracy.

Another formulation introduced in [ 8 ] represents the thread using a collection of ordered nodes governed by a
control-barrier-function and control-Lyapunov-function quadratic program
(CBF–CLF–QP). Instead of explicitly calculating all mechanical forces on the thread, the
model computes node velocities that satisfy structural constraints. Connectivity CBFs prevent neighboring nodes from
separating beyond a safe threshold, while a CLF drives the thread
to its rest state to model stiffness. The QP objective ensures that the resulting motion is limited to what is
necessary to satisfy the CBF and CLF constraints, each corresponding to specific aspects of thread behavior.

Although this framework provides a structured way of modeling thread dynamics, its parameters must be selected so that the simulated thread matches the observed response to the same needle motion. This motivates an approach that identifies model parameters directly from thread observations rather than through manual tuning.
This work addresses this gap by developing a video-to-model framework that automatically configures the CBF–CLF–QP model from observed thread motion. Given a video of a moving thread, the proposed method observes its motion and estimates the parameters of the framework
introduced in [ 8 ] , producing a thread-specific model whose simulated behavior reproduces the observed motion.

The main contributions of this work are: (i) a U-Net [ 9 ] based perception module that localizes the
thread in video frames and converts it into a
temporally consistent trajectory of ordered nodes; (ii) a spatio-temporal Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) module that uses the tracked response of the thread to needle motion to estimate model parameters and automatically configure the CBF–CLF–QP framework.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 introduces the CBF–CLF–QP formulation. Section 3 defines the problem statement.
Section 4 presents the proposed localization, tracking, model-configuration, and simulation pipeline.
Section 5 presents the experimental results, and
Section 6 concludes the paper and discusses future work.

2026-10-08.title: Tactile Reconstruction of Contact Task Frames and Forces for Hybrid Force/Motion Control
2026-10-08.authors: Antonio Rapuano , Simone Orelli , Barbara Bazzana , Antonio Franchi , Alessandro De Luca
2026-10-08.comment: . Video: this https URL . Dataset: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract: Hybrid force/motion control requires knowledge of the interaction force and of a task frame defining the force- and motion-controlled directions. These quantities are usually obtained from force/torque sensing or model-based residuals, often assuming also a nominal environment model. This work addresses the online estimation of the contact force and a possibly time-varying task frame using only soft optical tactile sensing, under the assumption of locally planar contact with a negligible contact moment. The proposed method maps a single image of the deformed elastomer of a soft optical tactile sensor to observable contact variables: indentation depth, two surface-to-sensor tilt angles, and 3D contact force, each with a per-sample uncertainty estimate. The mapping is learned through a self-labeling acquisition procedure, in which a manipulator imposes controlled contacts while an auxiliary Force/Torque sensor is used offline to provide ground-truth labels. The tactile measurement is then fused with robot proprioceptive data in an Extended Kalman Filter, producing a continuously updated estimate of the contact task frame and of the interaction force. Control experiments with a DigiTac sensor mounted on a UR10 manipulator demonstrate closed-loop contact force regulation against a flat rigid board in linear and angular motion by a human operator, with touch as the only exteroceptive feedback.

2026-10-08.title: Decoding Neural Population Dynamics through Robotic Analog
2026-10-08.authors: Wenhui Chen , Jiyue Tao , Yitao Cheng , Yutong Shi , Feitian Zhang , Xitong Liang , Ke Liu
2026-10-08.abstract: Animal evidence shows that precise voluntary movements arise from rotational neural population dynamics in motor cortex, but their physical effects remain unknown. We developed a robotic analog of biological motor systems with artificial muscles, multimodal sensors, and a neural network controller trained via reinforcement learning. The robotic analog exhibited accurate movements, robustness to damage, and neural population dynamics akin to animals. This task-driven, embodied model illuminates the causal link between neural population dynamics and motor outcomes. We discovered that neural rotations generate oscillatory maneuvers orthogonal to the reaching direction, optimizing trajectory adjustments, which is confirmed by primate neural data. The model also revealed counterintuitive neural energy principles under sensor and motor redundancies, and striking Eureka moments during motor learning, bridging biological and artificial systems. These findings provide new perspectives on how neural dynamics contribute to accurate and flexible movement, inspiring future intelligent robots with animal-like mobility.

2026-10-08.title: Borrowed Eyes: Markerless Nano-UAV Flight with an Active Quadruped Observer
2026-10-08.authors: Alejandro Lorite Mora , Dimitrios Arapis , Andrés Faíña
2026-10-08.comment: . Submitted to ICRA 2027
2026-10-08.abstract: Nano unmanned aerial vehicles (nano-UAVs) can navigate confined spaces that larger robots cannot, but their payload capacity severely limits the sensors and compute available for self-localization in global navigation satellite system (GNSS)-denied environments. We present a vision-based system that localizes a nano-UAV from a quadruped robot with an arm-mounted camera. The quadruped tracks the drone, estimates its position in its own coordinate system using segmentation masks and depth, and transmits that position over a real-time radio link. To ensure continuous tracking, we developed a perception-aware nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) that dynamically adjusts the quadruped’s body and arm to maximize the drone’s visibility, treating observation reliability as a primary control objective. Relying solely on this external estimate, the nano-UAV executed predefined trajectories from takeoff to landing with a median 3D localization error of 59 mm. The system demonstrates robustness against short visual occlusions by smoothly transitioning to onboard inertial flight when line-of-sight is temporarily lost. Ultimately, this framework allows a quadruped to offload the localization burden of a nano-UAV, enabling inspection of complex spaces that neither robot could navigate alone.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Industrial assets such as storage tanks, pressure vessels, pipes, and tunnels require regular inspection for corrosion, cracks, and other structural damage. Manual inspection is time-consuming, costly, and hazardous, especially in narrow or elevated spaces. Nano unmanned aerial vehicles (nano-UAVs), weighing only tens of grams, are well suited to reaching and inspecting areas inaccessible to larger robots.

However, autonomous nano-UAV deployment is severely constrained by onboard localization. Larger UAVs can carry stereo cameras or LiDAR to run visual-inertial odometry (VIO) or simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), but these sensors exceed the payload and power capacity of nano-scale platforms [ 1 ] . Confined industrial settings also feature repetitive, textureless steel surfaces and uneven illumination, which degrade feature-based localization even when sufficient computation is available.

In laboratory settings, nano-UAVs rely on external localization infrastructure like motion capture or ultra-wideband (UWB) beacons. However, installing fixed infrastructure across industrial facilities is costly, inflexible, and often impractical. Operating in real environments requires localization that preserves the nano-UAV’s payload margin without permanent infrastructure.

Rather than increasing the sensing burden on the drone or instrumenting the environment, we offload localization to a mobile ground robot with greater sensing and computational capacity (Fig. 1 ). The quadruped localizes itself and estimates the 3D position of the nano-UAV using an arm-mounted camera, while the drone flies using this externally supplied estimate. Crucially, the estimate is expressed directly in the quadruped’s global coordinate map rather than in an onboard frame. This provides a shared spatial representation for heterogeneous collaboration, allowing the nano-UAV to scout confined spaces and report points of interest in a frame the ground robot can directly use.

Our prior work [ 2 ] demonstrated this cooperative division of labor using fiducial markers on a nano-UAV [ 3 ] . However, physical markers add considerable payload mass, increase aerodynamic drag, and enlarge the vehicle’s footprint. In addition, reactive camera tracking often loses visual contact during fast maneuvers or temporary occlusions.

To overcome these limitations, we introduce a markerless localization and active observation framework for nano-UAVs. Our main contributions are: (i) Markerless external localization: A position-only perception pipeline that estimates the 3D position of a bare nano-UAV in the quadruped’s map frame, using depth-integrity gates to discard corrupted measurements and convert sensor failures into safe dropouts. (ii) Perception-aware active observation: A nonlinear Model Predictive Controller (NMPC) that coordinates the quadruped’s body and arm motion to preserve line-of-sight and optimize viewing geometry. (iii) Closed-loop flight under intermittent perception: Closed-loop flight validation from takeoff to landing on the external vision feed alone, demonstrating autonomous recovery from visual occlusions through onboard inertial coasting.

# II Related Work

Ground-Aerial Collaborative Localization. Leveraging ground robots to assist UAV localization is an established strategy for global navigation satellite system (GNSS)-denied environments. Existing approaches utilize ultra-wideband radios on both platforms to achieve decimeter-level localization [ 4 ] , employ ground vehicles as external references to refine onboard state estimates [ 5 ] , or use legged robots as mobile magnetic beacons, achieving tracking errors of 8 to 11 cm [ 6 ] . These methods either require dedicated onboard payload hardware [ 5 ] or provide lower accuracy than close-range visual localization [ 4 , 6 ] .

Markerless inter-robot observation has been explored in multi-robot SLAM, where mutually observing robots use visual detections to refine their state estimates [ 7 ] . However, such observations have not been demonstrated as the primary external position source for closed-loop flight of a nano-UAV. Removing fiducial markers eliminates added mass and aerodynamic penalties, but requires localizing a small, dark, weakly textured, and symmetric airframe directly from appearance and depth. While render-and-compare 6D pose estimators [ 8 , 9 ] address similar challenges, we exploit the flight controller’s internal attitude estimation and compute only 3D position, reducing the vision pipeline to the essential external state (Section III-B ).

Vision-Based Localization of Small Aerial Targets. Prior work on aerial target detection predominantly targets larger platforms. Vrba et al. [ 10 ] detected a 0.55 m quadrotor using stereo vision up to 50 m, with subsequent work reporting ranges up to 20 m [ 11 ] . Carrio et al. [ 12 ] localized drones using onboard depth maps at 16 Hz up to 8 m, but evaluated a 517 mm platform and attributed range limits to sensor constraints rather than target dimensions. In LiDAR-based studies [ 13 ] , classification degrades when a target returns fewer than 40 points. A bare nano-UAV challenges these limits at much closer range, where its small surface area returns very few depth points. We explicitly quantify this relationship up to 3.1 m in Section IV-A .

Aerial Navigation Through Narrow Apertures. Navigating confined spaces has been addressed through collision-tolerant platforms operating through manhole-sized openings [ 14 , 15 ] , or commercial caged inspection drones with full onboard SLAM. 1 1 1 Flyability Elios 3, https://www.flyability.com/elios-3/ Both strategies require structural protection and compute payloads well beyond the capacity of nano-UAVs. This leaves an important capability gap for nano-UAVs, which can access tighter spaces but cannot carry the heavy sensor packages assumed by existing platforms.

2026-10-08.title: Many Ways to Succeed: Diversity-Driven RL Fine-Tuning for VLA Generalization
2026-10-08.authors: Haoru Li , Jinmei Liu , Zhiyong Wang , Xiaoming Li , Zhenhong Sun , Daoyi Dong , Chunlin Chen , Zhi Wang
2026-10-08.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning improves vision-language-action (VLA) policies through closed-loop experience, yet generalization beyond the fine-tuning distribution remains limited. Our analysis reveals a selective reshaping of exploration: RL contracts behavior globally, yet diversifies successful trajectories, elicits success with fewer rollouts, and covers more of the latent task-valid solution space than supervised fine-tuning. Broader successful-mode coverage may provide alternative strategies under distribution shifts. Inspired by this, we introduce DRIVE ( D iversity-driven R L f I ne-tuning for V LA g E neralization), which turns successful-behavior diversity into an explicit RL objective. DRIVE groups rollouts under matched task conditions, compares their trajectories with temporal alignment, and derives a success-conditioned intrinsic reward from relative behavioral diversity. This design encourages broader coverage of feasible solutions without rewarding diverse failures or superficial timing differences. Across LIBERO-Plus, ManiSkill3, and RoboTwin 2.0, DRIVE improves the average out-of-domain (OOD) performance over vanilla RL fine-tuning by 5.3 points on π 0 \pi_{0} and 2.0 points on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . On a dual-arm AgileX PiPER-X platform, DRIVE further increases average OOD success from 64.1% to 73.3% (+9.2 points), demonstrating gains that persist under physical deployment.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) models have substantially expanded the range of manipulation tasks that robots can perform from visual observations and language instructions ( Kim et al., 2024 ) .
VLA models are trained primarily through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on robot demonstrations, acquiring broad manipulation skills by imitating a fixed behavior distribution ( Intelligence et al., 2025b ) .
Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) complements this paradigm with self-generated experience, using outcome feedback to explore beyond demonstrations and optimize closed-loop task performance ( Intelligence et al., 2025a ) .
Recent studies have shown that RL fine-tuning, particularly with PPO, can improve VLA generalization in semantic understanding and execution robustness ( Liu et al., 2025a ) .
However, such gains do not transfer uniformly across distribution shifts, and VLA policies remain sensitive to changes in visual appearance, scene configuration, and execution conditions ( Fei et al., 2025 ) .
Robust VLA generalization is essential for real-world deployment, yet remains challenging beyond the fine-tuning distribution.
To understand how RFT reshapes the range of behaviors available to VLA policies, we analyze both how rollout distributions evolve and how readily their successful modes can be elicited (see Sec. 3 ).
As training progresses, similarity increases across all rollouts but decreases among successful ones, revealing global behavioral contraction alongside successful-mode diversification.
Pass@k measures how readily any successful behavior can be elicited, showing that RFT requires far fewer rollouts than SFT to obtain a success.
Coverage@k instead measures the breadth of these successes, showing that, under the same rollout budget, RFT covers a substantially broader portion of the latent task-valid solution space than SFT.
Together, these results suggest that RFT makes task-valid solutions more accessible even as the overall behavior distribution contracts. Broader coverage of this space may provide alternative strategies under distribution shifts, revealing an underexplored opportunity to improve generalization through successful-behavior diversity .

Turning this opportunity into a useful training objective is nontrivial. Standard binary task rewards distinguish success from failure but not among different successful solutions, providing no explicit incentive to maintain broad successful-mode coverage.

Although diversity has been studied in unsupervised skill discovery ( Eysenbach et al., 2019 ) , policy diversification ( Masood and Doshi-Velez, 2019 ) , and embodied exploration ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , directly applying these approaches to VLA fine-tuning can reward superficial differences caused by execution speed, temporal misalignment, or irrelevant motion, as well as noisy and unsuccessful behaviors.
A suitable diversity objective must therefore compare trajectories under matched task conditions, account for temporal variation, and reward behavioral differences only when the trajectories remain task-valid.

Motivated by these observations, we propose DRIVE ( D iversity-driven R L f I ne-tuning for V LA g E neralization), a framework that turns successful-mode diversity into an explicit optimization target for promoting generalization.
DRIVE groups rollouts collected under matched task conditions, quantifies their behavioral novelty using temporally aligned GAK (global alignment kernel) similarity, and assigns a relative novelty bonus only to successful trajectories.
This design focuses the diversity incentive on distinct task-valid solutions rather than arbitrary variation across tasks, timing, or failures.
Then, we formulate the intra-group diversity as an intrinsic reward and design a potential-based reward shaping scheme to preserve optimal policy invariance.
By encouraging broader coverage of successful behaviors during fine-tuning, DRIVE provides alternative task-solving strategies that may transfer under distribution shifts.
Across LIBERO-Plus, ManiSkill3, and RoboTwin 2.0, DRIVE improves 11 of 12 benchmark-split results on each backbone, raising the OOD macro-average from 48.1% to 53.4% for π 0 \pi_{0} and from 71.1% to 73.1% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . On a dual-arm AgileX PiPER-X platform, DRIVE further increases average OOD success across two tasks and three distribution shifts from 64.1% to 73.3% (+9.2 points).
Together, these results validate successful-mode diversity as a practical objective across simulated distribution shifts and physical deployment.

In summary, our main contributions are threefold:

We show that global behavioral contraction coexists with successful-mode diversification, revealing successful-behavior diversity as an underexplored route to VLA generalization.

We introduce DRIVE, which converts temporally aligned comparisons of grouped trajectories into a success-conditioned intrinsic reward for diverse task-valid exploration.

We demonstrate consistent generalization gains across LIBERO-Plus, ManiSkill, and RoboTwin, and confirm that DRIVE’s improvements persist under physical deployment.

1. We show that global behavioral contraction coexists with successful-mode diversification, revealing successful-behavior diversity as an underexplored route to VLA generalization.

2. We introduce DRIVE, which converts temporally aligned comparisons of grouped trajectories into a success-conditioned intrinsic reward for diverse task-valid exploration.

3. We demonstrate consistent generalization gains across LIBERO-Plus, ManiSkill, and RoboTwin, and confirm that DRIVE’s improvements persist under physical deployment.

# 2 Related Work

VLA Models and Generalization. VLA models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, typically combining pretrained vision-language representations with supervised learning from robot demonstrations ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) . However, systematic evaluations reveal sensitivity to changes in visual appearance, scene configurations, robot initial states, and execution conditions ( Fei et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ) . To improve generalization, prior work has explored data augmentation and domain randomization ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Xue et al., 2025 ) , large-scale pretraining and heterogeneous co-training ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Intelligence et al., 2025b ) , and model designs that strengthen spatial representations and embodied reasoning ( Qu et al., 2025 ; Zawalski et al., 2024 ) . These efforts primarily focus on training data and model capabilities, with less attention to how behavior distributions shaped during RFT affect generalization.

Reinforcement Fine-Tuning for VLA. RFT complements demonstration-based SFT with self-generated experience and task-level feedback from closed-loop interaction, with successful deployments in LLMs ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Yan et al., 2025 ; Zhan et al., 2026 ) , VLMs ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Hu et al., 2026a ) , and VLAs ( Intelligence et al., 2025a ; Liu et al., 2025a ) .
Recent PPO-based ( Lu et al., 2025 ; Tan et al., 2025 ) and GRPO-based methods ( Li et al., 2026 ) use this feedback to optimize task-completion or progress rewards. Empirical studies report that such fine-tuning improves task success over SFT and can enhance OOD generalization, particularly in semantic understanding and execution robustness ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Chen et al., 2025a ) .
However, this line of work primarily examines the performance benefits of task-reward optimization, with less attention to how successful-behavior distributions evolve during RFT or how broader coverage of the successful behavior space can be explicitly promoted. Behavioral Diversity and Exploration. Unsupervised skill discovery promotes diverse behaviors without task rewards ( Eysenbach et al., 2019 ; Sharma et al., 2020 ) , while intrinsic-motivation methods encourage exploration through prediction-based novelty rewards ( Pathak et al., 2017 ; Burda et al., 2019 ) .

Task-aware methods instead combine return maximization with differences between policy-induced trajectory distributions ( Masood and Doshi-Velez, 2019 ) or encourage diversity among near-optimal behaviors ( Kumar et al., 2020 ; Hu et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) .
In VLA learning, diversity has been used to guide exploration through trajectory expansion and behavior conditioning ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Kong et al., 2026 ) , and to enrich pretraining data with diverse successful trajectories ( Yang et al., 2025 ) .
In contrast, DRIVE applies a success-conditioned diversity reward across rollouts under matched task conditions, targeting broader task-valid solution coverage rather than global behavioral variation.

2026-10-08.title: Juno: Taming Predictive Latents for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-08.authors: Yuchen Zhu , Chenyi Xu , Yulin Zhang , Gang Xu , Wentao Zhu
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
