2026-10-08.abstract:
Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict masked or future
observations in representation space, offering a natural source of predictive
latents for vision–language–action (VLA) models. Yet making these latents
useful across pretraining, policy learning, and deployment requires addressing
three failures: mismatch with embodiment-specific control, interference with
action learning, and teacher miscalibration under distribution shifts. We
introduce Juno , a unified framework built around one
action-conditioned JEPA that serves as a control-aligned representation
backbone, a predictive teacher, and an adaptable dynamics model. During pretraining , we train it on embodiment-matched trajectories and use a dynamic
CLS loss to transfer motion-weighted patch dynamics to a compact global state.
During policy learning , we fuse current-frame JEPA patches into VLA perception
and use a decoupled reasoning branch with separate transformation parameters
to distill future latent states for action generation. During deployment , we
adapt the world model on all observed transitions, including failed rollouts,
freeze the adapted teacher, and re-align the policy on verified executions
using LoRA adapters and a trainable action head, without expert corrections or
task rewards. On SimplerEnv, Juno raises average success from 60.9 % 60.9\% to 68.5 % 68.5\% over Qwen3GR00T, the strongest baseline, and test-time
adaptation further reaches 72.7 % 72.7\% ; on a real robot, it retains 70 % 70\% – 75 % 75\% success under background, height, and object shifts where the
base policy collapses to 0 % 0\% .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) predict masked or future
observations in representation space rather than in
pixels ( LeCun and others, 2022 ; Baevski et al., 2022 ; Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) .
This principle has progressed from image and video level self-supervision
to action-conditioned prediction for embodied
agents ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Maes et al., 2026 ) . A growing number of
vision–language–action (VLA) systems further show that such predictive
latents benefit policy learning, whether through latent world models ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) ,
future-representation alignment ( Zheng et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Xia et al., 2026 ) , foresight tokens ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Qian et al., 2025b ) , or latent
subgoals ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . The question is therefore no longer whether prediction helps, but how to make it useful across
the VLA lifecycle.

Making a predictive latent useful meets three obstacles, one per stage.
At pretraining , representations learned from broad internet video
are visually strong but poorly matched to embodiment-specific controllable
motion ( Assran et al., 2025 ) . At policy learning , predictive
objectives are typically grafted onto the shared vision–language
pathway ( Zheng et al., 2025b ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , where
prediction gradients interfere with control and future-aligned states need
not be action-decodable. At deployment , adaptation methods assume
a reliable frozen
teacher ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Park et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) , yet
severe shifts miscalibrate the teacher itself, and the failed rollouts
dominating deployment data cannot serve as policy targets. We show that a single action-conditioned JEPA addresses all three, serving as a
control-aligned representation backbone, a predictive teacher, and an
adaptable dynamics model. Juno realizes these roles through Control-Aligned Pretraining , Decoupled Predictive Reasoning , and Dynamics-First Test-Time Adaptation .

For representation learning, we choose a lightweight action-conditioned
JEPA ( Maes et al., 2026 ) and train it from pixels on the same
embodiment-matched trajectories used for policy learning. This choice is
motivated by the qualitative evidence in
Fig. 2 : its patch features respond locally
to robot–object interaction, while features from a large internet-video
teacher spread across the scene. Its compact global token, however,
dilutes exactly these local changes, so we introduce a dynamic CLS loss
that transfers motion-weighted patch dynamics onto the global token,
applied in a second stage with a frozen patch supervisor.

For policy learning, we fuse current-frame JEPA patch features into the
VLA’s visual tokens ( Miao et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2023 ) and append learnable reasoning
queries processed by a decoupled branch with separate transformation
parameters under shared causal
attention ( Liang et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Qian et al., 2025a ) . The branch is distilled
against the frozen teacher’s future latent states, one reasoning query
per future step, and its hidden states condition the flow-matching action
decoder. Future observations provide targets only during training; at
deployment the branch acts on the current observation and instruction.
Since the branch receives both alignment and action gradients, the aligned
state is trained to be decodable into actions rather than merely
predictive.

For deployment, even a control-aligned teacher miscalibrates under severe
shifts, and updating a policy against a miscalibrated teacher confounds
world-model error with policy error. Our key observation is an asymmetry:
failed actions are poor policy targets, but their consequences remain
valid dynamics supervision. Juno-TTT therefore adapts the world model on
all observed transitions, freezes the adapted teacher, and re-aligns the
policy on verified executions with LoRA adapters and a trainable action head, without expert corrections or task rewards.

Our contributions follow the three stages:

Control-Aligned Pretraining. We propose a dynamic CLS
loss that aligns the global state token with motion-weighted patch
dynamics, and show that matching the predictive teacher to the
embodiment and control distribution can matter more than pretraining
scale alone.

Decoupled Predictive Reasoning. We integrate JEPA
features into a VLA through patch-level fusion and a decoupled
reasoning branch distilled from future latent states, so that
predictive computation supports action generation without
restructuring the VLA backbone.

Dynamics-First Test-Time Adaptation. We propose a
failure-aware adaptation procedure that exploits all deployment
transitions, successful or not, for world-model adaptation, followed
by conservative policy re-alignment on verified data with the adapted
teacher held fixed.

1. Control-Aligned Pretraining. We propose a dynamic CLS
loss that aligns the global state token with motion-weighted patch
dynamics, and show that matching the predictive teacher to the
embodiment and control distribution can matter more than pretraining
scale alone.

2. Decoupled Predictive Reasoning. We integrate JEPA
features into a VLA through patch-level fusion and a decoupled
reasoning branch distilled from future latent states, so that
predictive computation supports action generation without
restructuring the VLA backbone.

3. Dynamics-First Test-Time Adaptation. We propose a
failure-aware adaptation procedure that exploits all deployment
transitions, successful or not, for world-model adaptation, followed
by conservative policy re-alignment on verified data with the adapted
teacher held fixed.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Latent Predictive World Models. Generative world models often expend capacity on task-irrelevant visual
details ( Hafner et al., 2025 ; Hansen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ) , whereas
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) predict future
representations directly, without pixel reconstruction ( LeCun and others, 2022 ; Baevski et al., 2022 ; Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ) . This principle now extends to
action-conditioned prediction and embodied planning ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Terver et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Maes et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , and to
latent-action abstractions from unlabeled videos ( Bruce et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2025 ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Tharwat et al., 2025 ) . Yet none of
these works determines which predictive state best matches a particular
robot controller.

World Action Models. VLA policies increasingly incorporate world-model signals for temporal
reasoning ( Zheng et al., 2025b ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Cen et al., 2025 ) :
representation-centric methods align policy states with future-observation
embeddings from visual teachers ( Miao et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Xia et al., 2026 ) , while
others expose predicted dynamics to action generation through foresight
tokens, latent subgoals, or aligned visual–action tokens ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Su et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Luo et al., 2026 ) .
Across these granularities, however, future
alignment alone does not show that the aligned policy state can be decoded into the corresponding action.

Test-Time Training in Robotics. Test-time training (TTT) adapts models to deployment inputs via
self-supervised inner-loop optimization, without revisiting the training
set ( Sun et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2020 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Hansen et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2021 ) .
In robotics, test-time updates either adapt latent prompts, adapters, or
policy components via state-grounding, future-consistency,
prediction-error, or progress signals ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Park et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Ji et al., 2026 ) ,
or serve as adaptive memory over interaction histories and unlabeled videos ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) .
These methods, however, all assume a reliable frozen teacher: under a
severe shift, the world model that provides the adaptation target may
itself be miscalibrated.

2026-10-08.title: Towards Accurate End-Effector Localization for UMI-Style Robotic Manipulation Teaching
2026-10-08.authors: Junjie Zhang , Deteng Zhang , Zhisong Xu , Bo Sun , Liuyang Li , Yihong Tian , Jie Yin
2026-10-08.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract: Recovering end-effector trajectories for robot demonstration learning requires localization to remain accurate and temporally complete as a gripper approaches objects, occludes the camera, and interacts with the workspace. Existing SLAM benchmarks emphasize navigation motions, whereas manipulation datasets prioritize policy learning over localization evaluation. We introduce MILD, a Manipulation-Interface Localization Dataset with real-world and simulation sequences. The real-world subset provides 86 sensor sequences from Insta360 X5 and Insight9 across 15 repeated tabletop tasks, calibration assets, and a per-execution robot end-effector reference trajectory. The simulation subset, MILD-Sim, extends task coverage in Isaac Sim for controlled manipulation-replay studies. Benchmarking visual–inertial and fiducial-aided systems on instrumented real-world recordings reveals large differences in both TCP-relative trajectory error and temporal coverage, even under the same nominal task. To support marker-augmented teaching workspaces without a pre-surveyed fiducial map, we present AprilVINS, which combines fisheye visual–inertial estimation with sequence-local AprilTag geometry and separates prior admission from guarded export of the jointly optimized state. On Insta360 AprilTag4 recordings, AprilVINS(full) under a unified protocol with sequence-specific profiles reaches millimeter-level SE(3)-aligned TCP-relative APE RMSE with high time completion and lower reported error than the tested routes under their respective protocols, whereas fisheye VIO without tag factors remains at centimeter scale. Ablations separate accuracy from exportability, and a MILD-Sim replay study provides task-specific tolerance references for interpreting those error magnitudes. Together, MILD and AprilVINS provide a diagnostic benchmarking framework for UMI-style demonstration collection. Code, datasets, and evaluation manifests will be released upon acceptance.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Demonstration collection for robot manipulation requires recovering the demonstrated end-effector trajectory from a portable manipulation interface. UMI systems have made in-the-wild data acquisition practical through a map-then-localize pipeline [ 1 ] , but close-range manipulation stresses localization: hands and objects occlude the camera, useful features leave the field of view near contact, and slow motions can break visual–inertial initialization. These conditions resemble the degradation cases studied in ground-robot SLAM [ 2 , 3 ] , but at tabletop scale with tighter coverage requirements. A low-error fragment is not enough when the rest of a demonstration is untracked, so manipulation-interface localization should report both trajectory accuracy and temporal coverage.

Existing localization benchmarks target aerial, hand-held, and mobile-robot motion [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] , whereas manipulation datasets focus on policy learning [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . MILD complements the latter by benchmarking the sensing layer that determines whether a collected demonstration is replayable, rather than evaluating downstream policy quality directly.

This gap matters because localization error enters a demonstration twice: it changes the recovered path used for learning and, during replay, changes the spatial relation between the gripper and the object. The relevant tolerance is task dependent. Free-space transport may absorb centimeter-scale offsets, whereas insertion, stacking, and sustained contact can fail after only a few millimeters. A useful benchmark should therefore connect estimator-level metrics to task-level consequences instead of treating aggregate trajectory error as the final criterion.

We introduce MILD with real-world and simulation subsets. An AGIbot G2 humanoid executes 15 tasks under uninstrumented, textured, and fiducial-marker workspace variants while Insta360 X5 fisheye and Insight9 stereo/RGB-D sensors record the motion. Each execution has its own TCP reference, so error is measured against the motion actually executed. MILD-Sim adds Isaac Sim tasks for controlled replay studies (Sec. V-E ). Benchmarking on MILD motivates AprilVINS (Sec. IV ), which estimates sequence-local AprilTag geometry without a pre-surveyed map, inserts admitted tag priors into a fisheye VIO window, and guards export of the optimized trajectory.

We summarize the core contributions of this work as follows:

We introduce a manipulation-interface localization benchmark named MILD for demonstration collection, featuring repeated tabletop tasks, multi-sensor recordings, scene variants, calibration assets, per-execution end-effector reference trajectories, and a paired simulation subset MILD-Sim.

We develop AprilVINS, an AprilTag-assisted fisheye VIO system that estimates sequence-local tag geometry without an externally surveyed map, inserts admitted tag priors into a sliding window, and guards export of the joint state; ablations show that tag factors drive most accuracy gains while the output gate restores export continuity.

We establish a multi-metric evaluation protocol—APE RMSE, time completion, and continuity—for vision-only, fiducial-aided, visual–inertial, and commercial demonstration-tracking routes, and use MILD-Sim replay curves as task-specific tolerance references for the reported error magnitudes.

# II Related Work

## II-A Visual–Inertial Localization

Modern VIO and visual SLAM systems combine feature tracking, inertial preintegration, and sliding-window optimization [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . Handheld interfaces already carry cameras and IMUs, and fisheye models are common on manipulation-mounted cameras [ 17 ] . Close-range demonstrations nonetheless break navigation assumptions: short trajectories, fast rotation near the workspace, repeated occlusion, and the need to convert camera poses into replayable end-effector trajectories.

## II-B Localization Benchmarks and Multi-Sensor SLAM

EuRoC and TUM-VI standardize visual–inertial evaluation [ 4 , 5 ] , while ground-robot datasets such as M2DGR, Ground-Challenge, MARS-LVIG, and FusionPortable broaden sensor coverage and degradation cases [ 6 , 2 , 18 , 19 ] . Recent fusion systems target visual degradation, LiDAR degeneracy, and GNSS denial [ 3 , 7 , 20 , 21 ] . MILD complements these lines by benchmarking close-range manipulation-interface localization with repeated workspace variants and end-effector references. Manipulation introduces a different failure regime: the workspace is compact, but occlusion is frequent and trajectory completeness directly determines whether a demonstration can be replayed.

## II-C Manipulation and UMI-Style Datasets

Large-scale manipulation datasets such as DROID, BridgeData V2, RH20T, and Open X-Embodiment target policy learning [ 8 , 22 , 9 , 23 ] . UMI-style interfaces reduce collection overhead [ 1 , 10 , 11 , 24 ] but rarely evaluate localization directly. MILD is intended as a complementary diagnostic benchmark for that collection stack.

## II-D Fiducial-Aided Localization

Fiducial markers provide six-degree-of-freedom pose observations from images [ 25 ] . TagSLAM and UcoSLAM combine fiducials with factor-graph or feature-based pipelines [ 26 , 27 ] . Marker visibility alone does not guarantee a replayable trajectory, because fisheye projection, map consistency, synchronization, and temporal coverage all matter under close-range manipulation. This motivates estimating tag geometry online and guarding the exported trajectory rather than treating every detected tag pose as ground truth.

2026-10-08.title: Enhancing Robotic Perception and Adaptability through Sensor Fusion and Origami-Inspired Designs
2026-10-08.authors: Namai Chandra , Jaison Jose , Kavi Arya , Shivaram Kalyanakrishnan
2026-10-08.abstract:
Compact mobile robots must recover scene geometry under changing lighting and surface
texture while working within tight payload and cost limits.
We present a compact mobile robot that uses origami-inspired wheels for locomotion and
active control of its sensing geometry. As the wheels move between terrain-adaptive
configurations, the changing chassis pitch sweeps a 2D LiDAR through intermediate
elevations; held wheel
positions provide a chosen viewing angle. An IMU accounts for chassis attitude, and a
fusion node projects LiDAR returns into the RGB-D depth stream supplied to RTAB-Map.
The arrangement uses the wheel actuation already present on a sub-$300, sub-2 kg
prototype to extend the scanner’s viewing geometry. We assess depth fusion in a
textureless indoor corridor and an outdoor sunlit area, with three runs per sensor
configuration in each setting. Mean full-frame invalid-depth fractions fell from
21% to 11% indoors and from 48% to 18% outdoors. The prototype combines improved
depth coverage with a continuously adjustable LiDAR viewpoint using the same actuation
that reconfigures its wheels.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Compact mobile robots are of growing interest for constrained search-and-rescue (SAR)
scenarios such as collapsed buildings, rubble-strewn corridors, and partially obstructed
indoor spaces [ 1 , 2 ] . Initiatives like DARPA SubT have highlighted
the appeal of small, reconfigurable platforms in such settings. A persistent challenge,
however, is achieving usable 3D environmental perception on a robot that is also small,
lightweight, and inexpensive enough to be considered semi-expendable. Our system
addresses these constraints with an origami-inspired chassis whose wheel poses also
steer a 2D LiDAR’s scan plane. We study the resulting fusion and active scanning on a
compact prototype in indoor and outdoor sunlit tests.

No single low-cost sensor provides both accurate range and visual detail in every
setting.

Stereo vision estimates depth by triangulating the disparity between two
viewpoints. While intuitive, its accuracy degrades rapidly with distance (depth error grows
quadratically with range), and it fails entirely on textureless surfaces such as blank
walls, uniform rubble, or featureless corridors, where no visual features exist to match.

Active-stereo depth cameras , such as the Intel RealSense D435i, use two IR
imagers and an optional projected texture to improve stereo matching [ 3 ] .
Projected texture helps on low-texture surfaces nearby, while range and direct sunlight
can reduce depth completeness. The D435i provides both color images and a per-pixel depth
map for appearance-based visual SLAM and geometric verification.

LiDAR sensors measure distance by timing laser pulse returns, providing
millimeter-to-centimeter accuracy invariant to lighting conditions and surface texture.
A 3D LiDAR (e.g., Velodyne VLP-16, Ouster OS1) produces dense omnidirectional point
clouds, but these units cost $1,000–$10,000+ and weigh 500 g–1 kg, impractical
for small, expendable disaster-response robots. A 2D LiDAR such as the RPLiDAR A2M12 is
lightweight ( ∼ \sim 190 g), affordable ( ∼ \sim $100), and accurate up to 12 m [ 4 ] ,
but captures depth in only a single horizontal plane with no associated visual
information, insufficient for full 3D mapping or appearance-based loop closure.

We combine the camera’s dense image with LiDAR range where their fields of view
overlap. Wheel reconfiguration then changes the LiDAR scan plane as the robot moves
through its operating geometry.

Our design couples RGB-D and 2D LiDAR fusion with the robot’s origami-inspired chassis.
Wheel reconfiguration changes the robot’s geometry for traversal and simultaneously
steers the LiDAR scan plane:

Fusion mitigates the RGB-D camera’s intrinsic weaknesses. Invalid or low-confidence stereo depth pixels are augmented by a confidence-weighted
blend with 2D LiDAR returns within the camera–LiDAR overlap. In our test runs this
reduced per-frame depth-void
fractions in both the indoor textureless and outdoor sunlit scenarios
(Section VI ); we report this as a descriptive statistic of the depth
stream, not as an accuracy benchmark.

Fusion mitigates the RGB-D camera’s intrinsic weaknesses. Invalid or low-confidence stereo depth pixels are augmented by a confidence-weighted
blend with 2D LiDAR returns within the camera–LiDAR overlap. In our test runs this
reduced per-frame depth-void
fractions in both the indoor textureless and outdoor sunlit scenarios
(Section VI ); we report this as a descriptive statistic of the depth
stream, not as an accuracy benchmark.

The morphing wheels are re-used to drive a tilted LiDAR sweep. A 2D LiDAR on a flat, fixed-wheel chassis is confined to a single scan plane;
dedicated “nodding” servo mechanisms have long been used to pitch a 2D scanner [ 5 , 6 ] . Rather than add a dedicated nodding servo, we re-use
the locomotive degree of freedom provided by the morphing wheels to tilt the chassis,
for active perception [ 7 ] . During a wheel transition, the LiDAR
samples intermediate elevations without a separate scanner servo
(Section VI-B ).

IMU-based attitude estimation prevents the tilt from corrupting the map. A Madgwick gradient-descent filter estimates chassis attitude from the onboard IMU,
so that each tilted LiDAR scan is projected into a gravity-aligned global frame.
Without this step the morphing-induced tilt would inject systematic error into the
map rather than add vertical coverage.

The full sensor stack is under $300 and under 2 kg on a custom prototype platform.
The perception unit can be detached and tripod-mounted for handheld mapping, which is
how parts of the dataset reported here were collected.

Prior work establishes RGB-D and LiDAR depth fusion [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] , mechanical sweeping of a
2D scanner [ 5 , 6 , 13 ] , and morphing wheel structures [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . We connect these capabilities on one compact robot: wheel movement changes the
LiDAR viewpoint, the IMU aligns scans during reconfiguration, and the fusion node
supplies depth to a standard SLAM backend. We measure depth completeness under two
sensor stressors and document the scan motion produced by the wheels. Table I locates the design choices relative to the relevant prior work.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A RGB-D and LiDAR Fusion

Geometric alignment of camera and LiDAR measurements is well established. Dieterle
et al. [ 8 ] combine RGB-D and LiDAR for object tracking, and Song et al. [ 9 ] use both sensors for relative localization. Zheng et al. [ 12 ] study indoor 3D mapping with a 2D LiDAR and RGB-D camera; Feng and Kuang [ 10 ] and Liu et al. [ 11 ] also combine these sensing modes
for mapping or navigation. Wu et al. [ 18 ] review learned LiDAR fusion methods.
We use a lightweight geometric fusion node because our immediate goal is to supply a
more complete depth image to RTAB-Map on the Jetson Orin Nano.

## II-B Active Scanning and Mapping

Surmann et al. [ 5 ] and Wulf et al. [ 6 ] sweep a 2D LiDAR
with a dedicated actuator to build 3D measurements. Our wheel mechanism also changes
the scan-plane elevation, but its actuator serves locomotion and cannot position the
scanner independently of the chassis. Morales et al. [ 13 ] examine 2D
LiDAR and RGB-D integration on a mobile robot. Our design joins that sensor pairing
to chassis-driven scanning.

We use RTAB-Map’s existing graph-based backend and visual loop closure [ 4 ] . Other visual or visual-inertial systems include ORB-SLAM3 [ 19 ] and VINS-Fusion [ 20 ] ; LiDAR-centred alternatives include
Cartographer [ 21 ] , LOAM [ 22 ] , LIO-SAM [ 23 ] , and
FAST-LIO2 [ 24 ] . We leave RTAB-Map unchanged and improve the depth stream
it receives where camera and LiDAR observations overlap.

## II-C Origami-Inspired Wheels

Origami mechanisms provide compact structures that can change shape with few inputs [ 25 , 14 , 15 , 17 , 26 ] . The flasher pattern [ 16 ] motivates our folding wheel geometry. We use wheel reconfiguration for
terrain adaptation and to change the LiDAR viewpoint as the chassis tilts. The
connection between movement and sensing follows the active-perception principle of
choosing sensor viewpoints through action [ 7 , 27 ] . Mechanical
scanning itself is established [ 5 , 6 ] ; here the wheel motion
supplies that scan motion on the same prototype.

2026-10-08.title: End-to-End Autonomous Generation of Human Assembly Plans
2026-10-08.authors: Faustin Arion von Arx , Millicent Schlafly , Mark D. Fuge
2026-10-08.abstract: Turning a CAD design into an assembly plan is still largely done by hand, requiring engineers to reason about geometric feasibility, tool access, stability, and the ergonomics of human assembly. In this work, we encode long-established design for assembly (DfA) principles into a contained, end-to-end approach for generating assembly plans. Our approach takes only a mesh assembly and produces either a step-by-step assembly manual or a structured failure report, requiring no joint metadata, fastener annotations, or additional information. Four major components of a manufacturing plan are addressed autonomously: an assembly tool list, the assembly sequence and subassemblies, an assembly manual, and design feedback for improving assemblability. For determining the sequence plan, we systematically disassemble the object in a physics simulator and apply a cost function that encodes DfA principles. Manual generation, tool labelling, and assembly feedback rely primarily on multimodal large language models. Compared with a baseline that always removes the outermost part first from Tian et al., DfA-aware sequence planning reduces simulated assembly time, measured with a robot-arm assembly-time proxy, by 35% on 136 assemblies of 5 to 30 parts. The correct tool is selected for 88.6% of assembly steps. A vision-language model judge compares the generated manuals against ablated variants, identifying which page elements carry the information a reader needs. The presented approach and open-source code are available for use by engineers or AI agents looking to rapidly accelerate the creation of manufacturing plans for a given product design.

2026-10-08.title: On-Demand Robotic Assembly via Differentiable Geometric Part Repair
2026-10-08.authors: Millicent Schlafly , Fabio Schaub , Diogo Costa Pais , Luca Lelli , Janne Dvorak , Claire Colmont , Sven Marti , Mark D. Fuge
2026-10-08.comment: and 2 tables
2026-10-08.abstract: Transitioning from a digital design to a robotic assembly process currently requires months of expert manual tuning to reconcile part geometries with robotic constraints. This paper presents an end-to-end, autonomous pipeline for the design and physical construction of bespoke wooden assemblies. A generative AI agent translates user prompts into initial 3D geometries, balancing the visual fidelity of the design with select physical constraints. The assemblability of the design is further improved by a gradient-based repair stage that backpropagates through a graph attention network surrogate to adjust component geometries. In addition to correcting for disjointed and overlapping components, we demonstrate hardware-specific corrections, differentiably optimizing the geometry of components to enable robot screwdriving for 86.7 % 86.7\% of 60 60 novel natural language inputs, significantly outperforming prior work by a factor of ten. For ten of the structures, we physically demonstrate assemblability with two UR5e robots. This work marks a meaningful step toward on-demand robotic manufacturing, enabling the rapid production of customized, low-volume goods.
2026-10-08.introduction:
The economic promise of on-demand robotic manufacturing hinges on its ability to produce highly customized, bespoke goods at speeds comparable to traditional mass production. However, a critical industry-wide bottleneck persists in the transition from an initial digital design to a final assembled product. Currently, reconciling complex part geometries with the rigid physical constraints of robotic cells—such as reachability, collision-avoidance, and end-effector clearances—is a labor-intensive process governed by manual design for assembly principles [ 1 ] . This disconnect necessitates months of expert manual tuning and specialized knowledge to refine a design into a buildable structure [ 2 ] , rendering the production of low-volume, customized goods prohibitively slow and expensive. Furthermore, the challenge of on demand robot manufacturing is compounded by the heterogeneity of industrial environments; each manufacturing facility utilizes different robotic hardware and software architectures, which impose unique, site-specific constraints on design feasibility.

Despite the challenge, the advent of generative AI—and its ability to translate human inputs into 3D structures—has reinvigorated interest in on demand manufacturing and subsequently research in Design for Robotic Assembly [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] . In this work, we demonstrate how the geometry of a part can be differentiably optimized to enable robotic assembly. Our approach builds upon prior methodologies that primarily rely on stochastic perturbations [ 3 ] or post-hoc filtering [ 5 , 6 ] to alter part arrangements. The necessity for geometric adaptation arises from the stringent constraints associated with complex robotic fastening mechanisms—for example, screwing—and the use of non-uniform components. Beyond generalizable feasibility criteria such as physical overlaps and structural stability, many designs remain unfeasible due to mechanical bottlenecks like insufficient clearance for the robot gripper and screwdriver or part thicknesses that exceed available screw lengths. Addressing these issues nearly always require fundamental changes to the part geometries themselves rather than only adjustments to their poses.

Learning-based methods offer a robust framework for adjusting part geometries for assemblability, providing a unified representation to account for diverse assembly failure modes. While computational design optimization is well-established in other domains, its application to the specific constraints of robotic assembly has been limited. Our methodology involves training a surrogate model to map part geometries to assembly success probabilities, subsequently leveraging the model’s gradients to locally optimize designs for enhanced assemblability. Provided a high-fidelity simulation of the manufacturing cell is available for generating labeled training data (e.g., via Gazebo, MuJoCo, Isaac Sim, etc.), our framework is extensible to varied robotic setups.

To investigate the benefits of geometry optimization for improving robot assembly outcomes, we develop an end-to-end autonomous pipeline for the on-demand robotic assembly of novel wooden objects. In contrast to prior work that assembles objects using pick-and-place operations, our robot manufacturing setup includes a robotic screwdriver and an additional robot arm, significantly complicating robot assembly and consequently imposing additional constraints on the feasible design space. Nevertheless, we show that we can learn critical aspects of assemblability, optimizing over the geometry of the parts to enable robot assembly. We validate our end-to-end autonomous pipeline for generating, editing, and assembling novel objects on ten unseen natural language prompts. Our novel approach to differentiably optimizing part geometries results in the successful modification of 52 / 60 52/60 unseen inputs (and 22 / 60 22/60 satisfying all cell constraints end-to-end), significantly outperforming Blox-Net [ 3 ] , which was only able to produce 5 / 60 5/60 designs that passed the target assembly checks (and 4 / 60 4/60 for end-to-end assembly). By leveraging a differentiable surrogate model to suggest geometric changes to part designs, this work makes significant strides toward the automated production of customized goods.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

Recent research has made notable strides in building systems that bridge the gap between natural language prompts and robotic assembly. Projects like Blox-Net [ 3 ] and the work of Kyaw et al. [ 4 ] have introduced frameworks where Vision-Language Models generate assembly sequences and instructions for physical construction. Similarly, BrickGPT [ 5 ] and Prompt-to-Product [ 6 ] utilize generative AI to create physically stable structures from text. While we achieve a similar goal—turning imaginative ideas into physical products—our approach involves modifying part geometries, which we find to be essential to enabling constuction with more complex assembly mechanisms.

Concurrently, progress is being made in automating multi-step robot assembly planning. AutoMate [ 11 ] presents a learning framework that uses simulation to train specialist and generalist assembly policies over a diverse dataset of 100 geometries, and Fabrica [ 12 ] tackles the dual-arm assembly of general multi-part objects, expanding to multistep assemblies through the simultaneous optimization of sequences and grasp location. While AutoMate and Fabrica rely on simulation to acquire zero-shot policies for each assembly, BrickCraft [ 13 ] learns visuomotor skills from 692 demonstrations that are then applied to unseen structures. Additionally, complementary approaches address the inference of sequence steps by modeling it as a graph, shape-matching, or sequence-to-sequence problem, allowing systems to autonomously deduce feasible assembly instructions directly from digital blueprints or visual observations [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] . Our work stands adjacent to the prior papers, improving robot assembly performance primarily through hardware-specific design changes.

The design of a product affects the success rates and speed of a manufacturing process [ 1 ] . Until recently [ 3 ] , methods for improving assembly outcomes required a human designer with extensive knowledge of the manufacturing process to manually apply documented principles [ 17 , 18 ] , meaningfully delaying manufacturing [ 2 ] . Without an efficient and automated mechanism for changing designs to be assemblable, researchers working in automating robot assembly must limit the scope of which mechanisms are tested according to the specific hardware available [ 12 ] .

Existing autonomous design for robot assembly methods rely on stochastic perturbation and post-hoc filtering to ensure buildability. The IDfRA framework [ 7 ] and Blox-Net [ 3 ] evaluate design stability through iterative trial-and-error rather than proactive geometric modification. Furthermore, most current research restricts designs to modular, discrete units—such as lattices [ 8 ] or standard blocks [ 9 ] . These systems often require specialized, hard-coded simulators like BRICKSIM [ 10 ] to handle complex interlocking mechanics, which limits their application to bespoke, non-modular geometries. Our approach differs from prior methods by considering the component geometry as a continuous, optimizable variable.

GNNs have proven effective as surrogates for physical and combinatorial systems, learning forward dynamics on particle graphs [ 19 ] and unstructured meshes [ 20 ] 1–2 orders of
magnitude faster than the underlying solver, transferring to engineering design [ 21 ] , and approximating constraint
satisfaction problems [ 22 ] . We adopt a GNN with attention [ 23 ] as
our surrogate for part-geometry assemblability.

2026-10-08.title: AeroEval: Staged Program and Execution Validation for AI-Generated Drone Missions
2026-10-08.authors: Kautuk Astu , Naina Rabha , Yogesh Simmhan
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
2026-10-08.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate drone programs from natural-language mission descriptions, but syntactically valid programs may still violate user intent, environmental constraints, and mission-level behavior. This problem is pronounced in cyber-physical applications, where correctness depends on the interaction among generated code, mobile sensing, environmental geometry, event-driven analytics, and physical execution. Existing drone code-generation systems primarily use prompt guardrails or simulator outcomes and provide limited failure localization. We present AeroEval , an agent-assisted middleware for staged validation of AI-generated drone missions. AeroEval combines deterministic program analysis with context-grounded LLM agents. It first validates program syntax, platform API usage, and mission intent, and then evaluates the realized behavior using execution trajectories, mission requirements, and environmental context. Each stage returns structured failure information for iterative regeneration. In our evaluation using 20 navigation tasks and five analytical mission types over AirSim and Gazebo simulators, AeroEval improves navigation success from 55 % 55\% to 95 % 95\% . In a stagewise ablation study, our Code and Trajectory Validators by themselves achieve mean run-level success rates of 44 % 44\% and 56 % 56\% , respectively, while the full AeroEval pipeline achieves 88 % 88\% ; the stages detect complementary failures in program structure, API usage, mission intent, obstacle avoidance, altitude, coverage, and event-driven transitions and the guided regeneration corrects for them. Across the main analytics missions, AeroEval increases aggregate run-level success from 34 % 34\% for one-shot AeroGen to 88 % 88\% within the regeneration budget. These results demonstrate the benefit of combining program-level and execution-grounded agentic validation for AI-generated drone applications in the evaluated environment.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Large Language Models (LLMs) allow users to construct drone applications by specifying missions such as delivery, survey, inspection, and target tracking in natural language [ 14 , 31 , 33 , 4 ] . The generated programs coordinate navigation, mobile sensing, analytics, and control across drone, edge, and cloud resources. Their correctness therefore depends on more than syntactic validity. A program must use the available platform interfaces, preserve user intent, respond to sensed events, and satisfy spatio-temporal constraints imposed by the physical environment. AI-generated drone missions are consequently pervasive cyber-physical applications whose software behavior must be interpreted relative to their execution context [ 5 , 35 , 1 , 9 ] .

However, existing code generation workflows provide limited evidence that a plausible program actually realizes its requested mission. A syntactically valid program may fly directly through an obstacle, survey a region along the wrong orientation, leave part of a search region uncovered, or fail to transition from search to tracking after detecting a target. These errors depend on environmental geometry, sensing events, and realized trajectories, and may remain undetected by code-level checks. Conversely, a simulator failure alone does not identify whether the cause is an invalid API call, an intent mismatch, or incorrect physical behavior. Hence, validating generated drone applications requires both program-level and execution-grounded evidence .

Existing cyber-physical code-generation systems provide only part of this lifecycle. Structured prompting improves generated drone code but discovers failures primarily through subsequent execution [ 31 ] . Simulation-guided generation has also been applied to autonomous-driving software, where rule-based assessments of critical traffic scenarios are returned to an LLM for code repair [ 19 ] . CLG similarly uses simulator feedback to iteratively refine drone navigation programs [ 33 ] , while AeroGen combines planning, code generation, sensing, and analytics for more complex missions [ 4 ] .
However, these systems do not systematically separate failures caused by program structure, platform API usage, mission interpretation, and realized physical behavior. Validation frameworks for autonomous systems combine formal specifications, simulation, digital twins, and domain-specific tests [ 2 , 25 ] , but typically assume that the application logic and testable properties have already been authored. In contrast, an AI-generated mission is an untrusted program synthesized from an informal user specification [ 34 , 24 ] .

We present AeroEval , an agent-assisted middleware that performs staged validation between AI-based mission generation and drone execution. Its Code Validator combines deterministic syntax and API checks with context-grounded validation of mission intent. Programs that pass this stage execute in a physics-based simulator . The Trajectory Validator then evaluates the realized behavior using the mission specification, robot and world descriptions, execution trajectory, and observed events. For navigation tasks with a reference path, AeroEval uses numerical trajectory comparison. For analytical missions without a unique reference path, a bounded validation agent evaluates properties such as obstacle avoidance, altitude, coverage, orientation, and event-driven transitions. A failed stage returns a structured diagnosis to the generator for refinement .

The key novelty of our work is the composition of program-level and execution-grounded validation within a common mission lifecycle. Figure 1 summarizes both its impact and the reason for staged validation. Under a common budget of at most three regeneration cycles, the Code and Trajectory Validators alone achieve mean run-level success rates of 44 % 44\% and 56 % 56\% , respectively, while their composition in the complete AeroEval workflow achieves 88 % 88\% . Relative to the underlying generators, AeroEval improves navigation success over the closed-loop CLG baseline from 11 / 20 11/20 to 19 / 20 19/20 tasks, and analytical run-level success over one-shot AeroGen from 17 / 50 17/50 to 44 / 50 44/50 runs. This is because program validation detects structural, API, and intent errors, while execution-grounded validation detects violations that arise from the interaction between the generated program and its physical environment.

In this paper, we make the following key contributions:

We propose a staged validation lifecycle that separates program validity, mission-intent alignment, and realized physical behavior, and returns stage-specific feedback for iterative regeneration (Sec. 3 ).

We develop context-grounded behavioral validation for analytical missions without a unique reference trajectory. The validation agents combine mission requirements, program artifacts, robot and world descriptions, and execution observations to evaluate spatio-temporal and event-driven properties (Sec. 3.4 ).

We evaluate AeroEval across 20 navigation tasks and five analytical mission types using two generators, two simulators and two reasoning models. The evaluation includes stagewise ablations, failure localization, limited physical-drone execution, and validation overheads (Sec. 4 ).
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

AeroEval lies at the intersection of AI-based drone program synthesis, validation of autonomous systems, and middleware for pervasive cyber-physical applications. Prior work has studied these concerns largely independently. We instead examine how program analysis, mission context, and execution observations can be combined to validate and repair AI-generated drone applications.

LLMs can translate natural-language specifications into executable programs for embodied control [ 14 ] . In the drone domain, GSCE uses structured prompts, API constraints, and examples, but detects failures primarily through subsequent execution [ 31 ] . CLG incorporates simulator observations into a refinement loop for navigation tasks, regenerating programs that violate waypoint, altitude, yaw, or geometric requirements [ 32 , 33 ] . AeroGen extends single-shot generation to analytical missions that compose navigation, sensing, analytics, and deployment over heterogeneous resources [ 4 ] .

Simulation-guided generation has also been applied to autonomous-driving software, where generated control code is evaluated over predefined critical scenarios and rule-based assessments are returned for repair [ 19 ] . Corrective robot-code generation similarly uses physics-based execution or static text-based simulation to predict navigation failures and refine generated operations [ 33 ] . These approaches demonstrate the value of execution feedback, but organize validation around scenario outcomes or deviations from specified navigation behavior.

AeroEval instead proposes a validation lifecycle that separates deterministic syntax and API checks, context-grounded intent validation, and post-execution behavioral validation. This distinction is necessary because invalid API usage may not be observable from a trajectory, while collision, coverage, orientation, and event-transition violations may not be inferred reliably from program text. Further, AeroEval supports analytical missions with multiple valid trajectories by evaluating mission-specific spatio-temporal and event-driven properties using the mission specification, generated program, environment descriptions, and execution trace.

Validation and Verification of autonomous systems commonly use formal specifications, simulation, digital twins, scenario-based testing, and runtime monitoring [ 2 , 25 , 29 , 16 , 3 ] . PolyVerif treats validation of AI-enabled Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) as an infrastructure problem requiring reusable simulators, test environments, and analysis tools [ 25 ] . Co-zyBench similarly uses co-simulation middleware and Digital Twins to evaluate context-dependent behavior before physical deployment [ 15 ] .
These techniques typically assume that application logic has been authored and that the evaluated properties can be formally or procedurally specified. In contrast, an AI-generated mission is an untrusted program synthesized from an informal user specification and may misinterpret the task before controller-level properties can be examined.
AeroEval instead validates program structure, platform interfaces, mission intent, and realized spatio-temporal behavior before physical execution; formal verification and runtime assurance remain complementary.

LLM-guided validation has also been used to translate natural-language driving policies into checkable specifications, analyze their consistency with autonomous-driving software, and generate simulation tests [ 37 ] .
This approach validates software against explicit safety policies,
whereas AeroEval localizes failures across generated program structure,
mission intent, and realized behavior for navigation and analytical
drone missions.

Middleware and runtime systems support mobile applications across robots, sensors, edge devices, and cloud resources. Service-oriented Drones-as-a-Service (DaaS) systems provide abstractions for navigation, sensing, analytics, scheduling, and data management [ 23 ] , while microservice-based platforms coordinate mission planning and resource allocation across multiple drones [ 6 , 21 ] . Context-adaptive middleware such as Furcifer selects among local, edge, split, and cloud execution according to network and system conditions [ 17 ] , while OctopInf performs workload-aware scheduling for edge video-analytics pipelines [ 18 ] . Aerial-edge systems similarly combine UAV mobility with communication and computation placement [ 13 ] . These systems optimize the execution of supplied applications, whereas AeroEval examines whether AI-generated mission logic satisfies its program-level and physical-context requirements before execution.

Drones also operate as mobile sensing and analytics platforms in
context-dependent environments. Prior systems perform on-board
crowd-motion analysis under changing viewpoints [ 1 ] and use drones to collect data from
batteryless sensors under environment-dependent communication
conditions [ 9 ] . These applications illustrate that
drone behavior depends jointly on mobility, sensing, communication,
computing resources, and physical context, but assume that application
logic is authored and suitable for execution.

Prior work has developed AI-based drone generators, validation techniques for autonomous systems, and middleware for context-aware mobile applications. However, generators provide limited failure localization, validation techniques typically assume authored application logic, and execution middleware assumes that supplied programs are suitable for execution. AeroEval connects these areas through a staged lifecycle that separates program validity, mission-intent alignment, and realized physical behavior. Its technical distinction is context-grounded validation of analytical missions without a unique reference trajectory, together with stage-specific feedback for iterative repair.

2026-10-08.title: ΔWAM: Distilling Action Tangent Fields into World Action Models
2026-10-08.authors: Ke Wu , Hanwen Huang , Bo Gu , Kaizhao Zhang , Xiangting Meng , Yupeng Zheng , Zijun Xu , Jieru Zhao , Wenchao Ding
2026-10-08.abstract: World Action Models (WAM) improve robot policies by augmenting sparse action supervision with dense future prediction. However, much of the predictable future is dominated by appearance and scene persistence rather than action-dependent dynamics. We observe that several recent WAM designs, including optical flow, motion-centric representations, and latent actions, can be understood from a common perspective in which world supervision becomes more efficient as it contains a higher proportion of action-relevant variation. Based on this insight, we introduce Action Tangent Fields, which reformulate world supervision through a local Taylor expansion of how actions induce changes in future dynamics. We represent future dynamics in Residual-VAE space, where the future latent remains recoverable from the current latent and its residual, and use a strong action-conditioned world model (ACWM) to probe the local correspondence between action variations and residual-world variations. This local first-order structure is distilled into the WAM to guide its denoising supervision toward dynamics that are more tightly coupled to action, rather than merely predictable from appearance. Across LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin, and RoboTwin2.0-Plus, our method consistently improves robustness to lighting, background, camera, layout, and other environmental perturbations. Despite using no large-scale embodied pretraining, it achieves stronger robustness under several distribution shifts than pretrained policies. We further distill multi-step VideoDiT denoising into a single step for efficient inference. Our results suggest that effective WAM supervision should remain information-rich while concentrating its predictive capacity on the directions along which actions change the future.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Behavior cloning labels each demonstrated observation with an action. World Action Models (WAMs) also predict the future video, giving dense supervision for object motion, contact, and state changes that a single action label cannot describe. A video target, however, rewards predictability rather than control relevance. Backgrounds, camera views, and untouched objects are already determined by the current frame and persist as the robot acts, so a model that reproduces them reduces its loss substantially while learning little about the consequences of its own actions. The value of world supervision therefore depends less on how much of the future it covers than on how much of that future is action-dependent.

Recent WAM designs change the target itself. Optical-flow and motion-centric targets keep only what moves, and latent-action targets compress the future into a compact code. Both reduce the supervision spent on static appearance, which is why they help, but both rely on motion as a proxy for action-dependence: a lighting change or a moving distractor alters the future with no contribution from the robot, and dropping appearance removes cues that contact-rich manipulation needs. A change of target also cannot reveal which directions of the future respond to the action, because each demonstration records one action and the single future that followed it. It is an isolated point of the action–dynamics relation, and its local neighborhood is never observed.

Our first step therefore keeps the target information-rich and changes its coordinate instead. Given the current frame, we subtract a broadcast reference derived from it, so the residual describes how the scene departs from the observed frame rather than restating it. Reference and residual recover the future VAE latent exactly, so no information is lost, and because the reference depends only on the current frame, subtracting it leaves the response to an action perturbation unchanged.

The second step supplies the missing neighborhood through a probe. For a fixed scene, an embodiment-specific action-conditioned world model (ACWM) is queried at small, temporally smooth perturbations of the expert action. The resulting residual futures differ mainly along directions the ACWM treats as action-sensitive, and their normalized differences span an Action Tangent Field (ATF), a low-dimensional estimate of those directions. Post-training keeps every element of the demonstrated residual in the loss and adds weight along the ATF, which makes the world loss anisotropic, ordinary world post-training is the isotropic special case. The probe sets the weighting, never the targets.

We first mid-train the Wan VideoDiT on a modest amount of robot manipulation video to adapt its prediction space to the residual latent space, then post-train a Fast-WAM-style policy with cached ATFs. Caching keeps the ACWM out of policy training and inference. Extensive experiments show that supervising dynamics-relevant world representations enables our method to generalize to visual perturbations substantially better than competing methods.

Our contributions are as follows.

We introduce an information-preserving Residual-VAE target that shifts world prediction toward scene dynamics while retaining exact recovery of the future video.

Motivated by a first-order Taylor expansion of the action-to-future dynamics map, we introduce Action Tangent Fields to estimate locally action-responsive directions and emphasize them during denoising supervision of the real demonstrated future.

We obtain efficient world features with one VideoDiT evaluation at inference. Aggregate success improves from 51.5% to 87.8% over Fast-WAM on LIBERO-Plus and from 72.7% to 79.3% on RoboTwin 2.0-Plus.

1. We introduce an information-preserving Residual-VAE target that shifts world prediction toward scene dynamics while retaining exact recovery of the future video.

2. Motivated by a first-order Taylor expansion of the action-to-future dynamics map, we introduce Action Tangent Fields to estimate locally action-responsive directions and emphasize them during denoising supervision of the real demonstrated future.

3. We obtain efficient world features with one VideoDiT evaluation at inference. Aggregate success improves from 51.5% to 87.8% over Fast-WAM on LIBERO-Plus and from 72.7% to 79.3% on RoboTwin 2.0-Plus.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 World Action Models

World Action Models (WAMs) complement sparse action labels with future prediction, encouraging policies to retain object states, interactions, and temporal dynamics. Predict-then-act methods such as GE-Act generate compact visual futures and recover controls through inverse dynamics, while GE-Act 2.0 scales this design with heterogeneous interaction data ( Liao et al., 2025 ) . Joint models instead couple world and action generation: LingBot-VA autoregressively interleaves both outputs, whereas Cosmos Policy represents future observations, actions, and values as latent frames of a video diffusion model ( Li et al., 2026c ; Kim et al., 2026 ) .

A complementary line treats prediction primarily as representation supervision. Fast-WAM and Light-WAM retain video co-training but omit explicit generation at deployment ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026d ) , whereas Efficient-WAM and Faster-WAM preserve future latents while reducing generation or video–action interaction costs ( Li et al., 2026b ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . The prediction target nevertheless determines how model capacity is allocated: full video latents preserve rich details but are dominated by static appearance and other variations weakly related to control, whereas flow, residual, and motion-centric targets emphasize change but may discard useful cues. In contrast, Action Tangent Fields retain an information-rich residual future space and selectively emphasize locally action-responsive directions.

## 2.2 Action-Conditioned World Models

Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs) predict visual consequences under specified controls. Recent systems broaden the control interface: Cosmos 3 jointly models language, images, video, audio, and actions ( NVIDIA Cosmos Team, 2026 ) , Hydra-0 represents actions as pixel-space flow for cross-embodiment transfer ( Li et al., 2026a ) , and Pelican-Sim combines a unified numerical action space with rendered action videos ( Zou et al., 2026 ) . These methods condition generation through native action tokens, visual motion, and action-rendered observations, respectively.

Another line improves simulation reliability. ABot-PhysWorld uses physics-aware data and preference optimization to suppress implausible interactions ( Chen et al., 2026b ) . Ctrl-World combines multi-view prediction, frame-level action conditioning, and pose-aware memory for policy-in-the-loop rollouts ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , while WALL-SS uses coarse-to-fine autoregression and compressed memory for long streaming generation ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) . WorldSync addresses failures on off-expert commands through broader action coverage, dynamics grounding, and intervention-effect alignment ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . Unlike these approaches, we neither plan with generated rollouts nor use synthetic futures as supervision targets. Instead, we perturb demonstrated actions and use the ACWM as a local differential probe in Residual-VAE space, transferring the resulting first-order action–world geometry while retaining real demonstrations as prediction targets.

2026-10-08.title: YUBI-STAG: Contact and Semantic-Rich Alignment for VLAs via Automated Video-Language Grounding

2026-10-08.introduction:
A robot demonstration shows how the task was executed, but its label records
only what the task was.
A session of sorting industrial parts into bins shows which gripper acts, which
part it contacts, and how that part is grasped, handed between grippers, and
released.
However, all of it is annotated as “pick a part and place it in a box”, which omits interaction details.
This matters because vision-language-action (VLA) models acquire broad
manipulation capability from large-scale
pretraining [ Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ] ,
and language is the only channel through which that capability is elicited.
A language label therefore does more than document an episode, while current
datasets include one task-level label per episode and repeat it across every
demonstration of the same task class.
For instance, recent robot-free handheld interfaces such as
UMI [ Chi et al., 2024 ] and YUBI [ Ohkawa et al., 2026 ] offer large-scale data
(e.g., 8434 hours of bimanual interaction by YUBI) at higher throughput than
teleoperation systems [ Zhao et al., 2023 ; Fu et al., 2024 ] .
Yet fine granularity and diversity of that language remain the bottleneck.

Existing VLA post-training pipelines rely on coarse episode-level language
instructions and unsegmented action sequences [ Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2024 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ] .
This coarse supervision fails to convey spatio-temporal dynamics, such as
gripper-object contact transitions, grip affordances, and bimanual coordination,
required for contact-rich, high-precision manipulation.
Inspired by the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis in LLMs [ Zhou et al., 2023 ] ,
which posits that pre-trained models already possess extensive world knowledge
and post-training primarily elicits proper output formats, we argue that a
similar paradigm holds for VLAs.
Pre-trained VLAs already encode rich geometric and physical representations;
their limitation is not innate capability but the lack of precise alignment
signals during post-training [ Chen et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ] .
Existing instruction augmentation and intermediate representations
either describe execution in language [ Xiao et al., 2023 ; Blank et al., 2024 ; Belkhale et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026 ] or ground actions and spatial plans in image coordinates [ Zawalski et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ] .
None jointly recovers which gripper contacts which object, at which pixels, over
which interval, and how the two grippers coordinate from moving wrist views,
then uses this structure to align pretrained VLAs.

We present YUBI-STAG , a framework that resolves this mismatch by
annotating demonstrations with the interaction structure they already contain,
and then post-training a VLA on those annotations.
Spatio-Temporal Annotation and Grounding (STAG) pairs a trained contact-object
segmentation module with a staged annotator built on an off-the-shelf multimodal
LLM [ Qwen Team, 2026 ] .
The segmentation module localizes contact intervals and contacted-object masks
from both wrist views.
The resulting contact tracks identify when each gripper interacts with
which object, allowing YUBI-STAG to chain localized visual evidence across
interactions to recover object identities, per-gripper actions, bimanual
coordination, and state changes.
Because YUBI-STAG requires a temporally localized action sequence
and many model calls, we distill its structured annotation capabilities into YUBI-VLM , aligning a pretrained VLM with the fine-grained interaction
semantics of YUBI data. YUBI-VLM directly annotates raw, unsegmented video
without predefined action boundaries and from wrist views alone, enabling
portable data collection. We evaluate its annotation capabilities on our new
benchmark, YUBI-STAG-Bench .

Finally, we evaluate contact- and semantic-rich alignment of VLAs using
the STAG annotations.
We pre-train a π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -based policy [ Black et al., 2025a ] on
8434 hours of YUBI data, then post-train it with PA
instructions enriched by task-relevant STAG annotations, including object
identities, attributes, target locations, and spatial relations. We also
provide explicit handedness and contact-phase labels (approach, grasp, hold,
release) and use contact-prioritized sampling.
Experiments on a bimanual Franka robot show that alignment with these rich
annotations improves fine-grained language following, contact-robust
manipulation, and compositional generalization to complex tasks.

The contributions of this paper are:

YUBI-STAG and YUBI-VLM ( Sec. 3 ). A contact-anchored annotation
pipeline that turns coarsely labeled bimanual demonstrations into grounded
spatio-temporal annotations, and a distilled model that produces them directly
from raw, unsegmented, wrist-view-only video without action-boundary
supervision.

YUBI-STAG-Bench ( Sec. 4 ). A benchmark of structured annotation quality on unseen bimanual tasks, covering contact intervals and object masks, PA segmentation and descriptions, object identities and attributes, coordination, spatial relations, and state transitions.

Contact- and semantic-rich VLA post-training ( Sec. 5 ). A contact and semantic-rich post-training recipe supplying handedness, contact phases, and
contact-aware sampling to a π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -based policy, extending data-centric
alignment from instruction text to physical interaction.

2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2. Related Work

## 2.1. Scalable Collection of Unconstrained Manipulation Data

Recent advances in low-cost bimanual systems [ Zhao et al., 2023 ; Fu et al., 2024 ] ,
teleoperation [ Qin et al., 2023 ] , and portable handheld
grippers [ Chi et al., 2024 ; Ohkawa et al., 2026 ] have enabled large-scale
collection of diverse robot demonstrations [ Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2024 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; Walke et al., 2023 ] .
As collection scales toward in-the-wild settings, however, demonstrations
increasingly contain background clutter, camera motion, operator variation,
and lack explicit action boundaries [ Mandlekar et al., 2021 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2023 ] .
Converting such noisy, unsegmented data into fine-grained supervision therefore
requires substantial curation and annotation, creating a new bottleneck for
scalable robot learning.

## 2.2. Video-Language Grounding and Automated Data Annotation

Foundation models have enabled scalable annotation of robot
data [ Chen et al., 2024 ; Qwen Team, 2026 ; Lin et al., 2024b ] .
One line relabels demonstrations with finer-grained language, including
execution details such as the active arm and contact
region [ Xiao et al., 2023 ; Blank et al., 2024 ; Belkhale et al., 2024 ; Smith et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2026 ] ,
but does not jointly localize gripper–object contact in pixels and time.
Another grounds intermediate representations such as boxes, traces, and
contact points in images [ Zawalski et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ] .
SPARC [ Blank et al., 2026 ] and Robo2VLM [ Chen et al., 2025b ] derive grasp
or manipulation phases from gripper state and other proprioceptive cues, which
can miss non-grasping contacts.
In contrast, YUBI-STAG detects gripper–object contact visually, akin to
hand–object contact [ Shan et al., 2020 ] and its
fine-grained dynamics [ Tateno et al., 2026 ] , and recovers
per-gripper contact intervals, contacted-object masks, and bimanual
coordination from moving wrist views. YUBI-VLM uses the resulting contact
tracks to annotate raw, wrist-only video.

## 2.3. Data-Centric Post-Training Alignment in VLA Policies

In NLP, the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis [ Zhou et al., 2023 ] posits that
vast knowledge and reasoning capability are acquired during pre-training, whereas post-training alignment primarily elicits output formats and behavioral styles using
high-quality supervision signals.
Its strong form is contested: stylistic alignment is recoverable from the base
model [ Lin et al., 2024a ] , while task competence continues to scale with
post-training data [ Raghavendra et al., 2024 ] .
While this data-centric alignment paradigm is well-known in LLM/VLMs, its
extension to Vision-Language-Action (VLA)
models [ Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025a ] has only
recently begun to be explored.
Existing VLA alignment efforts optimize preferences [ Zhang et al., 2026 ] ,
curate which demonstrations to train on [ Chen et al., 2025a ] , or pair fixed
trajectories with fine-grained instructions [ Hu et al., 2026 ] .
However, these efforts, like standard behavior cloning, provide no explicit
supervision at contact transitions (approach, grasp onset, hold, release) or
bimanual coordination moments.

2026-10-08.title: RoboPace: Contact-Aware Time-Optimal Retiming for Action-Chunk Policies
2026-10-08.authors: Mimo Shirasaka , Takehiko Ohkawa , Takuya Okubo , Nicola Scianca , Tatsuya Matsushima , Kei Ota
2026-10-08.comment: Project: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-08.introduction:
Robot manipulation is increasingly benefiting from demonstrations collected
across embodiments. Teleoperated demonstrations on low-cost bimanual platforms Zhao et al. [2023] have been complemented by handheld interfaces that
allow people to record demonstrations without a robot in the loop Chi et al. [2024] ; Ohkawa et al. [2026] , making data collection more
scalable. These interfaces record end-effector trajectories, from which policies
can learn to predict sequences of actions (action chunks) Black et al. [2025a] that are realized on a target robot. This flexibility introduces an embodiment gap spanning morphology,
kinematics, and dynamics Ohkawa et al. [2026] . Successful deployment depends not only on whether the robot can reproduce a
demonstrated motion, but also on how quickly and reliably it can execute it.

The timing encoded in a demonstration is inherited from the demonstrator but does not necessarily transfer to the target robot. Near contact, the same motion may be too fast for a robot with different compliance, actuator limits, and tracking dynamics, leading to overshoot or unintended impact. In free space, the mismatch runs the other way: the demonstrator’s pace is no bound on the robot, which could move faster. A single global speed factor cannot resolve this trade-off. Slowing the whole trajectory makes contact more reliable but gives
up the speed available elsewhere, while speeding it up increases the risk of failure near contact.

Resolving this trade-off requires execution speed to vary along the predicted motion according to predicted contact, while respecting the target robot’s kinematic and dynamic constraints. Prior work adapts execution timing at training time or
inference time. Training-time methods modify demonstration timing through acceleration or downsampling based on entropy or semantic criteria Guo et al. [2025] ; Kim et al. [2026a] , or explicitly represent execution tempo in the policy Ijspeert et al. [2013] ; Nam et al. [2025] . Such approaches can improve execution efficiency, but adapting to a target robot with different dynamic limits may require modifying the training data or retraining the policy. Inference-time methods instead adapt execution while leaving the policy unchanged. Time-optimal path parameterization (TOPP) Pham and Pham [2018] has been applied to chunked policies Kim et al. [2026b] to retime predicted paths under the robot’s kinematic and dynamic constraints, but has no notion of contact. Criticality-based speed adaptation Arachchige et al. [2025] instead switches between preset global rates based on motion complexity or gripper events. Neither line of work jointly derives a contact-dependent speed constraint along the predicted motion and incorporates it into retiming under the target robot’s kinematic and dynamic constraints.

We address this gap with RoboPace, an inference-time retiming method that imposes a position-dependent velocity ceiling that limits speed near predicted contact and incorporates it with the robot’s kinematic and dynamic constraints in a single time-optimal path parameterization. RoboPace predicts contact using two complementary cues: geometric proximity and wrist-camera prediction. Forward kinematics places the robot’s hand meshes
along the predicted path and measures proximity to the other hand and the
table, limiting speed when either is approached. The wrist-camera model
predicts the remaining steps until hand-to-object contact. Either cue can
tighten the velocity ceiling, with smooth transitions back to full speed away
from contact. RoboPace retimes newly predicted action chunks online during execution, requires no policy
retraining, and sits between trajectory generation and low-level tracking
without modifying either the policy or the tracking controller.

We evaluate RoboPace in real-world experiments on a dual-arm robot across five
commands spanning three contact-rich tasks, Cup , Socks , and Pyramid . We compare against the 30 30 Hz rollout rate used in training
(the demo speed hereafter), uniform speed scaling, and physical-limit-only
retiming Kim et al. [2026b] .
RoboPace achieves a 64 % 64\% overall success rate, compared with 44 % 44\% for slow
uniform execution, while completing four of five commands in about half its
time.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2. Related Work

## 2.1. Training-time speed adaptation

One line of work changes the temporal structure of demonstrations before
training. DemoSpeedup down-samples segments according to an entropy-based proxy
for required precision Guo et al. [2025] , whereas ESPADA uses
semantic judgments to choose the down-sampling schedule Kim et al. [2026a] . A complementary line makes timing part of the learned
policy: dynamical movement primitives include an explicit temporal constant Ijspeert et al. [2013] ; SpeedAug and TempoVLA condition policy execution on
tempo through reinforcement fine-tuning and retimed data, respectively Nam et al. [2025] ; Jing et al. [2026] ; and AutoSpeed learns stage-adaptive
motion speeds Hu et al. [2026] . B-spline Policy instead changes the
action representation to a continuous curve that can be temporally scaled at
execution Han et al. [2026] . These methods alter data, training objectives,
or policy representations; adapting learned timing to a new embodiment
generally modifies one of them.

## 2.2. Inference-time speed adaptation

Time-optimal path parameterization (TOPP) computes the fastest timing of a
fixed geometric path subject to robot constraints. These solvers handle joint velocity,
acceleration, and torque limits via convex
optimization Verscheure et al. [2009] , numerical integration Pham [2014] , or reachability analysis (TOPP-RA) Pham and Pham [2018] . Cartesian constraints, including
end-effector velocity bounds, can likewise be imposed along the path.
TOPP-RA, Cartesian velocity constraints, and proximity-based speed reduction
are established components Marvel and Norcross [2017] ; Haddadin et al. [2009] .

RACE Kim et al. [2026b] converts predicted action chunks into geometric paths
and applies TOPP-RA under the robot’s
kinematic and dynamic constraints; it also uses a test-time search over candidate chunks to
address asynchronous-inference misalignment. While its retiming formulation
uses the robot’s kinematic and dynamic constraints, it does not introduce a path-dependent velocity
constraint from predicted contact. SAIL Arachchige et al. [2025] adapts speed using criticality cues by switching among preset rates.
SAIL exemplifies adaptive speed modulation, but its rate-selection rule does
not formulate it as a path-parameterization problem subject to
the robot’s kinematic and dynamic constraints.
Other inference-time methods address different aspects of action-chunk
execution. Real-time chunking Black et al. [2025c] and
masked action chunking Wang et al. [2026] maintain consistency across
asynchronous chunk transitions; PACE Nie et al. [2026] selects an execution
horizon; and TRACT Liu et al. [2026] routes chunks across procedural phases.

Prior work has separately addressed two complementary aspects of execution-speed
adaptation: robot-limit-aware time-optimal retiming and criticality-based speed
modulation. To our knowledge,
these elements have not been integrated for online retiming of policy-predicted
action chunks by using predicted contact to define a path-varying velocity
constraint that is jointly enforced with the target robot’s kinematic and dynamic constraints.
RoboPace provides this inference-time integration while leaving the policy and
its predicted geometry unchanged, without policy retraining.
