2026-10-08.title: Do Better Visual Representations Always Lead to Better End-to-End Autonomous Driving?
2026-10-08.authors: Zihao Zhang , Haochen Tian , Tianyu Li , Changhui Jing , Jingliang He , Naisheng Ye , Ziyuan Pu , Zhenjie Yang
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-08.abstract:
Visual foundation models (VFMs) are increasingly integrated into end-to-end autonomous driving for their powerful representations, yet it remains unclear when these representations improve driving performance.
To investigate this question, we introduce ViRA, a planner-agnostic visual representation alignment framework that keeps the planner architecture and inference cost unchanged.
Our study reveals three findings:
(1) VFM-guided visual representations consistently improve driving performance across diverse end-to-end planners, with gains extending to zero-shot closed-loop evaluation.
(2) The choice of VFM target matters for planning performance, and alignment to a different VFM can further benefit planners with pre-trained VFM encoders.
(3) Auxiliary perception supervision reduces sensitivity to VFM target selection, narrowing the EPDMS spread across five targets from 2.7 to 0.5 points and potentially compensating for less effective VFM targets.
Guided by these findings, we develop ViRA-Diffusion, a diffusion-based planner trained without auxiliary perception supervision, which achieves 92.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest, outperforming recent methods in our comparison by at least 1.9 points.
The results motivate jointly considering target selection and planner supervision when integrating VFMs into end-to-end autonomous driving.
The results and demo are available at https://github.com/OpenDriveLab/ViRA .
2026-10-08.introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving is considered a promising route to scalable real-world deployment ( Chen et al., 2024a ; Guan et al., 2026 ) .
Within this pipeline, visual representations provide the planner with information about the environment, making the learning of high-quality visual representations an important research problem ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ) .
As visual foundation models (VFMs) advance in semantic understanding and 3D geometry ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Carion et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2025 ) , an increasing number of studies either use VFMs directly ( Sima et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Naeinian et al., 2026 ) or incorporate their pre-trained representations through distillation and representation alignment ( Strong et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Xie et al., 2026 ) .
However, most studies focus on a single planner–VFM pairing ( Zuo et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , and systematic comparisons of planning gains across different pairings remain limited.
It remains unclear whether the advantages of VFMs on visual tasks consistently translate into improved driving performance.

To answer this question, we introduce ViRA, a VFM-guided representation alignment framework illustrated in Figure 1 (a).
ViRA aligns the planner’s intermediate features with those of a frozen VFM target while keeping the planner architecture and inference cost unchanged ( Yu et al., 2025b ; Singh et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ) .
Using this framework, we compare different combinations of end-to-end planners and VFM targets on NAVSIM v2 ( Cao et al., 2025 ) and HUGSIM ( Zhou et al., 2025a ) .
We find that VFM-guided visual representations consistently improve driving performance across the diverse planners, but the gains depend on both the VFM target and planner design.
We further examine these findings below, focusing on overall driving gains, the effects of VFM target selection, and the role of auxiliary perception supervision.

VFM-guided visual representations improve end-to-end driving performance. As shown in Figure 1 (c-i), ViRA improves driving performance across regression-based ( Chitta et al., 2023 ) , diffusion-based ( Liao et al., 2025 ) , and scoring-based ( Feng et al., 2026 ) planners, yielding average gains of 7.9 and 8.6 EPDMS points over their respective baselines on NAVSIM v2 navtest and navhard, respectively.
These benefits extend to zero-shot closed-loop evaluation on HUGSIM, where overall HD-Score improves by an average of 4.0 points.
Figure 1 (b) shows that driving gains are accompanied by improved perception performance.
To test whether the gains come from pre-training rather than loss regularization alone, we compare pre-trained and randomly initialized targets under the same alignment objectives.
Randomly initialized targets fail to reproduce these perception and planning gains, supporting the importance of pre-trained VFM representations.
This raises the question of whether VFMs with different pre-training objectives yield different planning benefits.

The choice of VFM target matters. As shown in Figure 1 (c-ii), gains for the same Rap ∗ ( Feng et al., 2026 ) architecture range from 6.6 to 12.1 EPDMS points across VFM targets (a 5.5-point spread), with DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) yielding the largest gain.

This dependence on the VFM target also appears in TransFuser ( Chitta et al., 2023 ) when trained without auxiliary perception supervision, with DINOv3 again performing best.
With auxiliary perception supervision, however, TransFuser and DiffusionDrive ( Liao et al., 2025 ) achieve similar planning performance across these targets.
We hypothesize that auxiliary perception supervision affects how planners learn from VFM targets.

Auxiliary perception supervision reduces sensitivity to VFM target selection. To examine this factor, we compare TransFuser with and without auxiliary perception supervision.
Across the same five VFM targets, planning gains over the respective baselines without representation alignment range from 5.2 to 5.7 EPDMS points with auxiliary supervision and from 3.8 to 6.5 points without it.

More specifically, the highest score stays nearly unchanged, while the lowest drops from 88.8 to 86.4, indicating that auxiliary supervision mainly compensates for the less effective targets.
These results show that, in this setting, auxiliary perception supervision narrows the differences in gains across alignment targets, making planning performance less sensitive to VFM target selection.

These findings make a concrete prediction: a planner can achieve strong planning performance when its auxiliary perception supervision is removed, and a suitable VFM target is supplied in its place.
We verify this with ViRA-Diffusion , a diffusion-based ( Liao et al., 2025 ) planner trained with ViRA using DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) as the target and no auxiliary perception supervision.
It reaches 92.3 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 ( Cao et al., 2025 ) navtest, outperforming the recent state-of-the-art method by 1.9 points. We highlight the main contributions of this paper below:

We systematically study the driving benefits of pre-trained VFM representations across planners and targets using ViRA, a planner-agnostic experimental framework that preserves the deployed planner architecture and inference cost.

2026-10-08.title: NAViLoss: An Underwater Navigation-Aware Dual-Residual Objective for Physics-Consistent Learning
2026-10-08.authors: Arup Kumar Sahoo , Itzik Klein
2026-10-08.abstract:
Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) commonly rely on inertial navigation systems (INS) aided by Doppler velocity logs (DVLs) for reliable underwater navigation. Accurate DVL velocity estimation is therefore essential for successful operation. Recent learning-based methods have demonstrated improved DVL velocity estimation, particularly under degraded measurement conditions. However, their training objectives typically rely on conventional regression losses that are highly sensitive to large residuals and corrupted observations. Additionally, they do not explicitly account for the physical consistency and measurement uncertainty associated with the underlying sensing process. To address these limitations, this paper introduces navigation-aware loss (NAViLoss), a robust and uncertainty-aware objective function for learning-based AUV velocity estimation. NAViLoss jointly penalizes the velocity-estimation residual in the navigation-state domain and the
beam-consistency residual in the DVL measurement domain. Its bounded
formulation limits the influence of large residuals, while an adaptive
mechanism regulates the uncertainty in beam geometry.
Furthermore, NAViLoss is integrated with a DeepONet architecture to form a novel NAVi-DeepONet model for seamless estimation of an underwater vehicle’s velocity.
Lastly, our model is evaluated
using approximately 10,000m of semi-synthetic
AUV experimental data collected during multiple
real-world sea trials.
Experimental results demonstrate a 44% improvement in velocity-estimation accuracy compared with conventional and learning-based baselines. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of navigation-aware and uncertainty-adaptive loss design for robust learning-based underwater velocity estimation.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) have been increasingly deployed for maritime research, seafloor mapping, offshore resource exploration, environmental monitoring, and subsea infrastructure inspection [ 23 , 40 , 31 , 32 ] . Reliable estimation of their position, velocity, and orientation is fundamental to the successful execution of these operations.
AUVs predominantly operate in underwater environments and have no access to global navigation satellite system (GNSS) signals and external aids. Therefore, they typically rely on inertial navigation systems and Doppler velocity logs (DVL) [ 33 , 38 , 10 ] for accurate navigation. An INS continuously propagates the navigation solution from accelerometer and gyroscope measurements, but measurement noise and
sensor biases lead to accumulated errors and increase drift over time [ 15 , 30 , 14 ] . DVLs are therefore commonly employed to constrain this drift by providing independent velocity information.
In bottom-lock mode, four acoustic beams are directed toward
the seabed, and their Doppler frequency shifts are used to determine the
vehicle velocity [ 37 , 11 ] .
The resulting beam measurements are related to the vehicle
velocity through a known DVL observation geometry.

Despite the importance of DVL measurements in underwater navigation, they are susceptible to degradation. Acoustic interference, environmental conditions, vehicle motion, limited bottom visibility, and partial beam availability can introduce corrupted measurements or result in the loss of one or more DVL beams. Such degradation directly affects the quality of the velocity information available for navigation. In particular, missing beams alter the measurement geometry and reduce the information available for estimating the three-dimensional vehicle velocity. Over the years, various model-based approaches have been investigated to improve DVL-based velocity estimation, including least-squares (LS) estimation, loosely and tightly coupled integration, factor-graph optimization, and information-aided estimation methods [ 34 , 13 , 7 ] . Nevertheless, robust velocity estimation under noisy and incomplete DVL measurements remains an important challenge for reliable AUV navigation.

Recent advances in deep learning, computational power, and open-source libraries have substantially improved the adoption of learning-based (LR-based) technologies to address these limitations.
LR-based methods have been increasingly investigated for underwater velocity estimation, sensor fusion, DVL beam reconstruction, and navigation under degraded measurement conditions [ 8 , 24 , 18 , 20 ] .
In a pioneer research, DCNet [ 36 ] employed convolutional neural networks (CNN) to improve DVL calibration, whereas UDON [ 39 ] applied a data-driven framework for DVL-based underwater odometry. In recent research, a physics-guided PiDR [ 25 ] model was introduced for AUV navigation using inertial measurements. Building on the same concept, A-LUKF [ 19 ] , a physics-guided filtering model, was proposed for AUV navigation in degraded underwater environments.
In the domain of multi-sensor fusion, DMIAN [ 3 ] offered a
LR-based inertial/DVL fusion through navigation error-state
estimation. ResAlignNet [ 11 ] further addressed inertial/DVL sensor alignment by estimating the transformation matrix
between the two sensing modalities. These approaches can learn complex relationships between inertial/DVL measurements and have demonstrated improved estimation capability compared with conventional model-based approaches under nominal operating conditions.

While considerable attention has been devoted to developing advanced LR-based architectures, comparatively less attention has been given to the objective functions used to train them. The choice of the loss function influences the optimization behavior, robustness, and generalization capability of the learned model. Existing LR-based approaches are typically optimized
using conventional regression objectives such as mean squared error (MSE), mean absolute error (MAE), Huber loss,
or weighted variants.
Among these, the MSE remains particularly popular owing to its minimal complexity and computational efficiency. However, its quadratic penalization makes it highly sensitive to
large residuals and corrupted observations. The MAE reduces the influence of large errors through linear penalization, whereas
Huber loss, Smooth- L 1 L_{1} , log-cosh, and Charbonnier losses provide intermediate
behavior between quadratic and linear penalties [ 35 , 29 ] . More robust
objectives, including the Cauchy, Welsch [ 16 ] , Geman–McClure [ 6 ] , Tukey biweight [ 21 ] ,
Barron’s adaptive robust loss [ 2 ] , and RoBoSS loss [ 1 ] , further reduce the influence
of large residuals through bounded or slowly increasing penalties.
Despite their robustness characteristics, these objectives primarily operate in the prediction
space. They do not explicitly exploit the physical observation model that
relates the predicted state to the measured state.

Physics-informed learning provides a natural means of bridging this gap by incorporating prior physical knowledge into neural-network optimization [ 22 , 5 , 26 ] . For DVL-based navigation, the known geometric relationship between the three-dimensional vehicle velocity and the measured beam velocities provides an additional source of physical information during learning. A physics-informed learning objective can therefore consider not only the error between the predicted and reference velocities but also the consistency of the prediction with the observed DVL beams. However, simply combining these residuals using conventional quadratic penalties [ 24 ] does not account for changes in measurement uncertainty.
Additionally, these objectives generally assume complete observations or well-defined physical constraints.
This limitation becomes particularly important under partial beam availability, where the information provided by the DVL measurements depends on the available beam measurement geometry. Hence, a navigation-oriented learning objective should simultaneously account for prediction accuracy, measurement consistency, robustness to large residuals, and variations in measurement uncertainty.

To address these limitations, this paper introduces NAViLoss , a
navigation-aware robust loss function for LR-based AUV velocity estimation. NAViLoss jointly penalizes residuals in the navigation-state space and the DVL beam-measurement
space. Its bounded formulation limits the influence of large residuals, while an uncertainty-aware mechanism adapts the contribution of the beam-domain information according to the available DVL measurement geometry.
The proposed objective therefore integrates prediction accuracy, DVL
measurement consistency, robustness, and uncertainty awareness within a
unified optimization framework. In addition to the proposed formulation, we establish the fundamental analytical
properties of NAViLoss and characterize its behavior under both small
and large residual regimes. The proposed loss is further integrated with a DeepONet backbone to form NAVi–DeepONet , enabling robust AUV velocity estimation.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A novel navigation-aware objective function, the NAViLoss has been introduced.

A novel navigation-aware objective function, the NAViLoss has been introduced.

The theoretical aspects of NAViLoss are proven to hold crucial properties such as:
vanishing influence for large residuals, quadratic behaviour for small residuals, uncertainty-aware attenuation, and
dual-domain consistency.

Fusion of NAViLoss into the uniquely designed DeepONet algorithms to introduce a novel physics-guided NAVi-DeepONet model with two variants.

To support the reproduction of results and encourage future research and benchmarking, our codebase has been made publicly available on https://github.com/ansfl/NAViLoss .

The proposed NAVi-DeepONet framework is evaluated on semi-synthetic AUV data derived
from real-world sea trials conducted in the Mediterranean Sea, Israel,
covering approximately 10,000m of traveled distance. Comprehensive
experiments are performed under noisy sensing, DVL beam outages, and
reduced measurement availability. The experimental results demonstrate
that the proposed framework maintains accurate and robust velocity
estimation across these challenging operating conditions, achieving an
average improvement of 44% over the considered baseline methods.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section 2 presents the problem formulation.
Section 3 introduces the proposed NAViLoss function and
NAVi–DeepONet framework.
Section 4 discusses the experimental evaluation.
Finally, Section 5 summarizes the main findings,
discusses the limitations of the proposed approach, and concludes the paper.

2026-10-08.title: Design optimization of tendon-driven robots considering tendon wrapping and shortcut
2026-10-08.authors: Yuta Sahara , Kento Kawaharazuka , Kei Okada
2026-10-08.comment: Accepted to Advanced Robotics, website: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract: This study proposes a multi-objective optimization method for tendon-driven arm design, addressing the inherent trade-off between joint torque and arm thickness through tendon wrapping and shortcut effects. We formulate the problem to simultaneously maximize torque and minimize thickness, solved using NSGA-II. The algorithm optimizes tendon routing, pulley configurations, and attachment points. Results reveal Pareto-optimal designs with effective moment arm expansion via strategic shortcuts, providing practical guidelines for compact high-torque arms. The optimized configurations demonstrate non-trivial patterns beyond conventional design intuition, offering new insights for engineering efficient robotic systems.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Thus far, various tendon-driven robots have been developed.
Among these, musculoskeletal humanoid robots such as ECCE1 [ 1 ] , Anthrob [ 2 ] , Kengoro [ 3 ] , and Musashi [ 4 ] represent bio-inspired designs,
while non-biomimetic wire-driven systems like Super Dragon [ 5 ] , SAQIEL [ 6 ] , and Twist Snake [ 7 ] have also been investigated through research and development efforts.
Among these diverse forms, this study focuses on serial-link tendon-driven arms with pulleys, where high joint torque is required under space-limited conditions.
This class includes both musculoskeletal and non-biomimetic wire-driven systems, and in such systems the tendon-routing geometry strongly influences torque capability and arm thickness.
Therefore, our scope is defined by routing geometry rather than by a specific actuation source.

Tendon-driven systems offer several advantages.
First, increasing the moment arm enables torque amplification.
Additionally, separating actuation units from joints enhances design flexibility in robotic configurations.
Furthermore, control benefits include variable stiffness control [ 8 ] and redundancy against tendon failure [ 9 ] .
However, maximizing these advantages requires careful consideration of tendon placement.
Designing robots that fully exploit tendon-driven mechanisms is therefore non-trivial.
Specifically, elements such as tendon pathways and pulley design significantly influence overall robotic performance.
Consequently, designers must meticulously evaluate these factors to achieve optimal system configurations.

Based on these considerations, studies have explored methodologies for optimizing tendon configurations.
Tsai et al. [ 10 ] proposed an isotropic design method for tendon-driven manipulators
to ensure uniform force transmission characteristics, providing fundamental design guidelines for tendon routing.
In [ 11 ] , for the leg section of a musculoskeletal robot, the muscle pathways per pulley were analyzed and optimized;
however, this study fixed the moment arm and did not account for changes in moment arms due to joint angle variations. [ 12 ] further optimized tendon configurations by determining optimal positions for start points, endpoints, and intermediate via-points of tendons during operation, explicitly considering dynamic changes in moment arms caused by joint movements.
However, among methods to amplify moment arms more effectively, designs that leverage tendon wrapping around pulleys and tendon shortcuts are notable.
In such designs, moment arms are maintained through tendon-wrapping on pulleys. Additionally, tendon shortcuts—caused by angular changes in joints—further expand the effective moment arm beyond the pulley’s radius, thereby enhancing joint torque.
Despite their potential, optimization studies incorporating these phenomena remain limited in prior research.
This is likely due to the computational complexity involved:
calculating tendon pathways for each joint angle while accounting for wrapping and shortcut transitions requires intricate modeling.
Furthermore, practical challenges arise in robotic arm applications.
Tendon shortcuts can increase arm thickness, restricting achievable poses and operational workspace.
For robots like [ 5 ] , which operate in extremely confined spaces, minimizing arm diameter is critical to ensure maneuverability.
Thus, designs exploiting tendon wrapping/shortcuts face a trade-off between increasing joint torque and reducing arm thickness.
Engineers must navigate this dilemma: maximizing torque through dynamic moment arms inherently conflicts with the need for slender arms in narrow operational environments.
This necessitates innovative solutions to simultaneously optimize torque enhancement and compact design—a central challenge in tendon-driven robotic systems.

Based on these considerations, this study proposes a design optimization method incorporating tendon shortcuts for serial-link tendon-driven arms with pulleys.
Specifically, we address two objectives:

Enhancing joint torque by leveraging moment arm enlargement caused by tendon shortcuts in the tendon pathways, and

Minimizing arm thickness by preventing excessive tendon shortcuts.

The following sections outline the structure of this study.
Section 2 describes the design parameters of the tendon-driven arm to be optimized,
explains computational methods for tendon pathways and muscle length Jacobian,
details evaluation methodologies for joint torque and arm thickness, and outlines the multi-objective optimization framework employed.
In Section 3 , we conduct multi-objective optimizations by varying the number of joints and tendons in the system, presenting the results of these optimizations.
Section 4 critically examines the optimization outcomes to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method through systematic analysis.
Finally, concluding remarks summarizing the study’s contributions are provided in Section 5 .

# 2 METHOD

## 2.1 Overview of Optimization

The problem formulation of this study is described as follows.
In this research, we address an optimization problem concerning tendon configurations in a two-dimensional serial-link arm driven by multiple tendons.
Specifically, maximizing the distance between each tendon and joints—the moment arm—enables enhanced capability to generate joint torque.
Achieving this objective necessitates careful design of tendon configurations.
For instance, increasing the moment arm can be achieved not by wrapping all tendons around every pulley but rather through strategically shortcutting certain pulleys.
However, this short-cutting of tendons also results in an increase in the overall thickness of the arm.
This creates a trade-off between improving joint torque and minimizing arm thickness.
This study formulates an optimization problem for tendon configurations while explicitly considering this trade-off relationship.

2026-10-08.title: Fast and Robust Teach-and-Repeat Navigation Using MixVPR Visual Place Recognition*
2026-10-08.authors: Václav Truhlařík , Tomáš Pivoňka , Libor Přeučil
2026-10-08.comment: European Conference on Mobile Robots (ECMR)
2026-10-08.abstract: Teach-and-repeat navigation systems employing advanced visual place recognition techniques for localization exhibit key attributes for long-term mobile robot navigation, such as the ability to operate in unstructured and dynamic environments. However, existing solutions based on deep-learning techniques have high computational requirements, limiting their applicability. This work introduces a novel and efficient teach-and-repeat system built on the modern visual place recognition method MixVPR. Real-world testing demonstrated its ability to operate both indoors and outdoors, achieving robustness and navigation precision comparable to other state-of-the-art systems. In addition, its lower hardware requirements make it suitable for a wide range of robotic platforms and practical applications.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Reliable navigation of mobile robots in unstructured and changing environments is the key area of research for long-term robot autonomy. Modern robots can be equipped with various specialized sensors; however, they are usually expensive and unsuitable for some types of applications. In addition, processing all the data requires a lot of computational power. Therefore, efficient systems working with a single forward-looking monocular camera, such as the Teach-and-Repeat (T&R) navigation system introduced in this article, are valuable, especially for real applications.

T&R systems are capable of following previously traversed trajectories. They operate in two stages. At first, the desired trajectory is taught during a traversal when a human operator or an outside algorithm controls the robot. Subsequently, in the second stage, the robot autonomously repeats the trajectory using current sensor data and information captured in the teaching phase.

There are two main approaches to T&R navigation: position-based and appearance-based. The position-based system localizes the robot in space and guides it based on the difference to the corresponding position from a database. By contrast, appearance-based systems need only 1D localization or tracking along the taught trajectory. When localized, the shift between the current and corresponding database image is used to control the robot heading reactively.

The article focuses on the appearance-based approach with the use of advanced visual place recognition systems for localization. The work is motivated by previous systems of this type [ 1 , 2 ] , which proved the ability to operate under challenging lighting conditions and in low-structured environments. However, their main limitation is long computational time, which is caused by the high demands of the used visual place recognition systems.

The presented system solves this limitation by using a more efficient one-stage Visual Place Recognition (VPR) system - MixVPR [ 3 ] , reaching performance close to state-of-the-art systems [ 4 ] . The introduced T&R system builds on the previously mentioned system SSM-Nav2 [ 2 ] . Besides the direct replacement of the original VPR method by MixVPR, a new approach to horizontal shift computation is introduced. It takes advantage of MixVPR architecture and extracts local visual features from its convolutional neural network backbone. Capabilities of the new T&R system were tested against other state-of-the-art appearance-based T&R systems in outdoor and indoor spaces as well as on the new dataset for appearance-based methods testing presented in [ 2 ] .

This type of T&R system has many practical applications. Robustness in monotonous environments without an additional infrastructure of visual markers makes them ideal for industrial settings (e.g., autonomous warehouses). Additionally, the option to share the visual information collected in the teaching phase implies simple use in multi-robot systems following the same path.

The rest of the article is structured as follows. Sect. II introduces the related T&R systems. The new T&R system and its individual components are described in Sect. III . The results of an experimental evaluation on the dataset and real robot are presented in Sect. IV . Finally, the achieved results are summarized in Sect. V .
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Teach-and-Repeat Systems Overview

As described in the previous section, T&R systems are classified into position-based and appearance-based. This subsection summarizes the fundamental works from both categories.

A position-based system using SURF [ 5 ] local visual features capable of following multi-kilometer-long trajectories was presented in 2010 [ 6 ] . In following years, various modifications and extensions of this system were published as the system with multi-experience teaching of the trajectory [ 7 ] or the system using deep-learned local visual features [ 8 ] . Contrarily to the appearance-based solutions, all these systems require a stereo camera for creating local 3D maps.

The first appearance-based systems combining robot position tracking along the taught trajectory and reactive control based on stored images emerged in the 1990s [ 9 ] . This approach was further improved with the arrival of robust local visual feature detectors. Such a system for polygonal trajectories using SURF features [ 5 ] was introduced in [ 10 ] . Later, it was followed by the BearNav system [ 11 ] , which is capable of navigating along general trajectories. It mostly relies on odometry, using the SURF feature matching only to correct drifts and accumulated errors.

An alternative robust shift computation technique not using local visual features is presented in [ 12 ] . This deep-learning approach employs a Siamese network to encode the information from the compared images into 3D vectors. The best horizontal shift is computed by the cross-correlation of these vectors. This technique serves in new systems, following on BearNav, to directly compute horizontal shifts [ 13 ] or to support local feature matching [ 14 ] .

## II-B Teach-and-Repeat Using Visual Place Recognition

The main disadvantage of T&R systems using tracking to localize a robot along the trajectory is that they require starting from the initial position. In contrast, systems performing basic localization can start in the middle of the trajectory and recover from various failures. That motivated the development of T&R systems using robust VPR methods for basic localization along the trajectory. VPR systems using deep-learning techniques are able to work in changing environments, including day-night or seasonal changes, which is a crucial property for long-term autonomy.

SSM-Nav [ 1 ] was the first T&R system based on an advanced VPR. It uses the Semantic and Spatial Matching Visual Place Recognition (SSM-VPR) [ 15 ] . This system performs recognition in two stages, using local visual features extracted from the inner layers of a convolutional neural network. The actual position is estimated by a particle filter that fuses VPR-based localization with wheel odometry. Horizontal shift for steering corrections is computed using shifts between matched local visual features from the second stage of VPR. The system proved the ability to work outdoors and indoors, including challenging lighting conditions or environments with many monolithic surfaces.

A similar experimental system was also developed to navigate a small Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) [ 16 ] . As the UAV does not provide reliable odometry information, this system is purely vision-based. Despite that, it proved the ability to navigate in challenging indoor environments.

In 2025, the new version of the SSM-Nav system was introduced [ 2 ] . The main improvements are the multi-platform design, supporting both ground and aerial vehicles, and the employment of new re-ranking techniques (second stage of VPR) introduced in [ 4 ] . The re-ranking is based on D2-Net local visual features [ 17 ] , also used for the horizontal shift computation. The method computes a 2D histogram of shifts from matched features, in which each match votes for its position by a Gaussian function. The main disadvantage of all these systems based on advanced two-stage VPR is the high computational requirement for real-time performance.

## II-C MixVPR

MixVPR [ 3 ] is a modern and efficient system for VPR based on deep learning, achieving performance close to the current state-of-the-art systems [ 4 ] . Contrarily to most of these systems, it performs recognition in one stage instead of two standard steps - filtering and re-ranking. Its main advantages are efficient image representation suitable for large databases and fast recognition.

The system is built on a new neural network architecture combining a standard convolutional backbone with a new function block called Feature Mixer. The entire network computes a global image descriptor, which is then used to search for the most similar images based on the distances of descriptors. At the beginning of the network, the image is transformed by cropped ResNet network [ 18 ] into a 3D tensor. This tensor is sliced into multiple 2D feature maps that are subsequently flattened into 1D vectors. Then, the Feature Mixer transforms these vectors separately by a cascade of multi-layer perceptron blocks, preserving their dimension. Output vectors are connected into one feature map, whose size is reduced by two fully connected 1D layers applied in horizontal and vertical directions. Finally, the 2D map is flattened and normalized to obtain the image descriptor.

2026-10-08.title: Adaptive Code Generation for Controlling Robots
2026-10-08.authors: Justus Flerlage , Thorsten Wittkopp , Alexander Acker , Odej Kao
2026-10-08.comment: International Symposium on Leveraging Applications of Formal Methods, Verification, and Validation 2026
2026-10-08.abstract:
Deploying robots as Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS) in unknown and dynamic environments necessitates a transition from rigid command libraries toward intention-based autonomy, as natural language represents the only medium capable of articulating complex goals beyond the capacity of finite instruction sets.
While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer a path toward natural language goal description, their integration introduces significant challenges: the formalization gap between imprecise intentions and executable actions, the taxonomy gap induced by unpredictable environments, and the challenge of maintaining temporal state and progress awareness.
This work introduces an architectural framework that enables robotic control by leveraging generative AI.
The system follows a dual-AI design: an LLM translates high-level intentions into executable program code restricted to a formal robotic library and constrained by verifiable syntax, while a Vision-Language Model (VLM) provides semantic grounding via a distillation process.
To ensure robustness, the framework incorporates environment-driven replanning triggers based on geometric and semantic thresholds, complemented by continuous runtime monitoring and an adaptive planning loop.
Benchmarked across frontier models, our framework architecture demonstrates that grounding generative AI in a reactive, constrained loop enables robust fulfillment of complex intentions in dynamic and unknown environments.
2026-10-08.introduction:
CAS are designed to operate under uncertainty, partial knowledge, and continuous environmental change.
Rather than relying on a single centralized controller with a complete model of the world, CAS coordinates heterogeneous components whose collective behavior emerges through feedback, adaptation, and interaction with a dynamic environment [ 24 , 1 ] .
Robotic systems operating outside static industrial settings constitute a particularly challenging instance of this paradigm.
They must interpret high-level goals, perceive incomplete and changing environments, select appropriate actions, and revise their behavior when assumptions about the world become invalid.

However, conventional robotic systems are typically designed for static and well-defined environments and tasks.
The prevailing paradigms of conventional robotics have historically centered on low-level control, symbolic planning, and rule-based systems [ 13 , 20 ] .
Within industrial environments, such as automotive assembly lines, robots execute predetermined operations based on a closed-world assumption, utilizing deterministic algorithms, fixed rule sets, and task models that are entirely specified in advance.
Even in domains where Artificial Intelligence (AI) appears to provide greater flexibility, such as autonomous driving or industrial manipulation, system behavior remains constrained by predefined environmental assumptions [ 11 , 16 ] .
A notable illustration of this is autonomous driving, wherein AI models are trained to recognize a specific set of object classes, such as pedestrians, traffic signs, and lane markings [ 11 ] .
While such approaches are demonstrably effective within their intended domains, they remain inherently limited in scope due to their reliance on predefined taxonomies and fixed execution models.
To provide an example, an autonomous car may navigate safely through a city, but it may fail to respond appropriately when a traffic officer overrides traffic signs or signals in a manner not represented in the vehicle’s training data.
Consequently, they are unable to generalize to dynamic and open-ended environments in which robots encounter novel objects, conditions, and unknown tasks [ 7 ] .

This leads to the first challenge in the field of adaptive robotics, where robots are expected to operate in environments and task settings that cannot be fully specified at design time.
Addressing this challenge requires a shift toward natural language as a versatile medium for task specification, enabling robots to interpret and execute a virtually limitless range of complex instructions that cannot be captured by rigid, predefined taxonomies.
The inherent flexibility of natural language introduces a significant secondary challenge: such high-level intentions are frequently underspecified, leaving a wide semantic gap between a human’s intent and the granular actions a robot must perform.
To illustrate this point, one may consider a scenario in which a robot is assigned the intention of requesting a coffee.
It is conceivable that such tasks could encompass the instruction of a robot to explore an unknown environment, inspect a room, search for relevant objects, operate a machine, and retrieve a requested coffee.
However, this instruction does not include several key elements.
Firstly, the text provides no indication as to which objects the robot is to encounter and how to react to them.
Secondly, the text fails to specify which areas the robot should visit first.
Thirdly, the text does not provide a definitive timeframe within which the exploration should be deemed complete.
In conclusion, translating a simple human intention into a concrete operational plan remains a major hurdle, as the robot must autonomously infer the missing procedural details and environmental constraints.

Recent advances in generative AI offer a promising foundation for this type of intention-driven adaptation.
LLMs have the capacity to interpret natural language instructions, infer task goals, generate action plans, and reason about task progress [ 6 , 2 , 17 , 18 ] .
Nevertheless, intention-driven robotic control also necessitates the grounding of these plans in the physical environment.
To achieve this, VLMs provide a mechanism for deriving semantic descriptions from visual observations, enabling robots to reason about objects and spatial relations that extend beyond predefined categories [ 19 ] .
The integration of generative AI into robotic control systems introduces a fundamental tension, as the properties that render generative models attractive for open-ended adaptation also render them difficult to integrate into reliable control loops.
It is evident that both LLMs and VLMs possess a degree of flexibility that enables them to function on instructions that are underspecified and on incomplete scene information.
However, it is important to acknowledge that the outputs of these systems are non-deterministic and not guaranteed to be correct.
Furthermore, these outputs are based on continuously evolving representations of the environment.
For CAS, this necessitates a framework where generative AI is embedded into an adaptive feedback architecture without compromising reliability.
This challenge motivates the following research question:

How can generative AI be integrated into a Collective Adaptive System for robotic control such that user intentions can be translated into reliable robot behavior under uncertainty, incomplete knowledge, and continuous environmental change?

The question is addressed by means of an architectural framework for intention-driven robotic task execution in dynamic and unstructured environments.
The architectural framework implements the MAPE-K feedback loop, meticulously decomposing the process of robotic adaptation into five distinct phases: monitoring, analysis, planning, execution, and knowledge management [ 4 ] .
A VLM-based perception component is responsible for monitoring the environment and producing open-ended semantic descriptions of the robot’s surroundings.
A planning component, based on an LLM, is capable of interpreting user intentions and generating executable robot behavior.
A library of robotic control functions constrains the LLM’s output to valid actions, thereby enabling syntactic verification before execution.
A workflow-monitoring and knowledge component maintains information about execution progress, previous actions, and observed scene changes, thereby supporting adaptation over long-running tasks.

Our architectural framework addresses three fundamental challenges in the domain of intention-driven adaptive robotics.
Firstly, it mitigates the formalization gap between imprecise natural language intentions and the precise control structures required for robotic execution.
Our framework employs an advanced LLM that translates user intentions into workflows.
Secondly, it addresses the taxonomy gap that arises when robots encounter objects and situations that cannot be fully anticipated at design time.
Rather than relying exclusively on a fixed object taxonomy, the VLM provides open-ended semantic grounding, which is stabilized over time through repeated observations.
Thirdly, it addresses the temporal state problem of generative controllers by maintaining explicit execution state, thus allowing the system to distinguish between completed subtasks, failed actions, and pending objectives.

In order to investigate the aforementioned research question, a proof-of-concept implementation of the proposed architecture for a quadruped robot performing exploration tasks is presented.
The robot receives high-level user intentions rather than explicit programs and must autonomously generate, execute, and adapt task behavior in response to its environment.
The system is evaluated across a range of object-identification and exploration tasks and scenarios, utilizing both finite and open-ended tasks.
Furthermore, a range of LLMs are being benchmarked to ascertain how variations in generative models impact task success, robustness, replanning behavior, and termination control.

The following contributions are made by the paper:

The present paper proposes a MAPE-K-inspired architectural framework for intention-driven robotic control in dynamic and unstructured environments.

The present paper proposes a MAPE-K-inspired architectural framework for intention-driven robotic control in dynamic and unstructured environments.

The integration of LLMs and VLMs into a constrained adaptive feedback loop that combines semantic grounding, executable code generation, monitoring, and persistent task knowledge is demonstrated.

The performance of three state-of-the-art LLMs is evaluated as a fundamental component for intention-driven robotic control in dynamic and unstructured environments, utilizing exploration tasks that necessitate spatial and temporal reasoning, executable code generation, programming capabilities, and mathematical problem-solving.

In Section 2 the framework architecture is presented.
While Section 3 describes the methods and implementation, Section 4 shows an evaluation.
After Section 5 addresses the related work, Section 6 concludes our work.

# 2 Framework Architecture

The proposed framework architecture is founded on the principles of MAPE-K, a standard architectural pattern in CAS [ 4 ] .
This loop, comprising Monitoring, Analysis, Planning, and Execution, operates over a shared knowledge base that functions as a stigmergic medium.
As illustrated in Figure 1 , the framework architecture is divided into a perception component, a cognition component, and a centralized world state.
Rather than serving as a passive repository, this world state provides the environmental cues and geometric grounding necessary to drive adaptation through the environment itself.
The framework architecture is specifically engineered to address the inherent complexities of autonomous robotic adaptation by targeting three critical challenges: the taxonomy gap, formalization gap, and the temporal state problem.

The perception component mitigates the taxonomy gap, the discrepancy between a robot’s fixed internal categories and the infinite variety of the physical world, by decoupling geometric grounding from semantic identification.
Instead of relying on closed-set classifiers, the system utilizes a VLM to perform open-ended semantic enrichment of raw sensor data.
This information is synchronized with the world state, which functions not as a passive repository but as a stigmergic medium that provides the environmental cues necessary for cognitive reasoning.
By grounding abstract semantic labels in precise geometric coordinates, the system ensures that the robot can interact with and reason about previously unidentified objects without requiring a predefined taxonomic library.

Bridging the formalization gap between high-level user intentions and low-level robotic control requires a rigorous approach.
Within the cognition component of this framework architecture, processes are organized around workflows modeled as Turing-complete imperative programs.
This structure allows the system to map ambiguous natural language intentions onto a formal sequence of actions restricted to a predefined library of high-level robotic primitives for movement control, ensuring both safety and controllability.
The LLM acts as the central decision-making entity within this planning phase, analyzing the current world state and the active workflow to generate updated logic in response to environmental triggers.
This transformation of intent into executable code provides a formal bridge between the non-deterministic nature of human language and the deterministic requirements of robotic execution.

To maintain operational continuity during these adaptations, the framework architecture explicitly addresses the temporal state problem, which occurs when a system loses track of its execution progress upon receiving a new plan. The executor facilitates this by utilizing a virtual machine capable of capturing snapshots of the internal execution state, including instruction pointers and variable bindings. When a change in the environment triggers a re-planning event, the current state is preserved and provided to the LLM, enabling the synthesis of an adapted workflow that can be hot-reloaded mid-execution. This approach ensures that the robot does not reset its task upon every environmental shift, but rather adapts its behavior while maintaining full state awareness. Consequently, the entire MAPE-K loop operates as an event-driven paradigm where the system continuously perceives its surroundings, reasons about semantic and geometric changes, and executes formal, state-aware adaptations in real-time.

different ropes. This is challenging because rope dynamics are hard to model, no demonstrations exist, distinct

Deformable linear objects (DLOs), such as ropes, cables, wires, and hoses,

manipulation , where a robot swings or casts the object so that it reaches a
commanded goal [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 2 ] . The goals
considered so far mainly describe the object’s position, typically a 2D or
3D point for the rope tip to reach. We extend rope-tip targeting to a 4D goal that specifies both the tip’s 3D position and its arrival direction. Many tasks depend on how the tip arrives. For example, striking a spinning top in the direction of rotation helps maintain its spin, while striking against it can slow it down. Similarly, knocking an obstruction aside requires a strike that pushes it out of the way.

We consider a robot arm that holds one end of a rope. The robot receives a goal g = ( p ∗ , d ∗ ) ∈ ℝ 3 × S 1 g=(p^{*},d^{*})\in\mathbb{R}^{3}\times S^{1} and must execute a single swing whose tip passes through p ∗ p^{*} while moving along d ∗ d^{*} . The task covers any point in the reachable
workspace, any arrival direction, and any rope. Even for a person, hitting a point with the tip of a rope requires deliberate practice, and reaching it from a specified direction is harder still. Complex dynamics and object properties: a swung rope is a
stiff, nonlinear, aerodynamically damped continuum whose tip amplifies every
command error, and its response depends on properties that vary between
ropes.

# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Goal-conditioned dynamic rope manipulation

Robots have learned to swing ropes and cables toward commanded goals.
IRP [ 3 ] hits 2D targets with a robot-held rope by correcting the action
over repeated real-world attempts. Whip primitives [ 5 ] reach 3D points
with low-dimensional open-loop motions, and Lost Arc [ 4 ] vaults,
knocks, and weaves a cable around obstacles. Wiggle&Go [ 6 ] strikes 3D points on new ropes. It predicts the rope’s simulation parameters
from a short wiggle with a network trained in simulation, then optimizes the
motion for each goal in the simulator. DeformX [ 2 ] reaches 2D
targets in a fixed plane with per-step reinforcement learning. These goals mainly describe where the tip
should be and leave how it arrives unconstrained. Several of these systems are
also restricted to a plane or need repeated real attempts for each goal. We
specify the goal by both the 3D position of the tip and its arrival
direction, and reach any such goal in the workspace with a single zero-shot strike.

## II-B Planner-generated training data

When demonstrations are scarce, planners can generate training data instead.
Zhu et al. [ 13 ] show that sampling-based planners produce
inconsistent demonstrations on which even expressive diffusion policies
degrade. PhysicsGen [ 14 ] obtains consistent data by re-solving
trajectory optimization warm-started from a few demonstrations under perturbed
conditions. Dynamic rope striking adds two difficulties. There is no
demonstration set to warm-start from, and swings that reach the same goal
differ in how reliably they transfer to hardware. TRACE starts from a single swing verified on hardware and warm-starts each new target from the stored swing whose tip path passes closest to it, which keeps the solutions for nearby goals consistent. Its cost favors an extended rope and smooth tip motion to keep swings repeatable, and each verified swing is labeled with its achieved outcome as in hindsight relabeling [ 15 , 16 ] .

## II-C Generative policies for multimodal action distributions

Diffusion Policy [ 17 ] and flow matching [ 10 , 18 ] model
distributions over actions instead of a single prediction.
DA-MMP [ 19 ] builds on motion manifold primitives [ 20 ] and
applies conditional flow matching to goal-conditioned throwing. In rope
striking, distinct motion patterns reach the same goal, making the action distribution inherently multimodal.
A regressor tends to average across these patterns, often producing an invalid swing. A generative model avoids this average, but its samples still spread between patterns when the goal enters only at the network input.
Our flow-matching policy injects the goal into every residual block through zero-initialized modulation [ 11 , 12 ] , which keeps its samples within a pattern and raises one-shot accuracy.

## II-D Sim-to-real calibration

One line of work identifies physical parameters and uses them downstream.
Wiggle&Go [ 6 ] predicts rope parameters with a learned network and
optimizes each goal in simulation with them, and
GenDOM [ 21 ] conditions a policy on parameters estimated from one real
demonstration. Another line corrects actions from observed outcomes.
TossingBot [ 22 ] learns a residual on a ballistic release
velocity, and IRP [ 3 ] refines the swing action over repeated real
attempts at each target. Our proposed RECAP fits rope and rig parameters to a few calibration swings for each rope, and a delta policy trained in simulation and conditioned on these parameters corrects the base action for the error the fit still misses.

2026-10-08.title: Targeted Modality Dropout for Real-Robot Manipulation Robust to Intermittent Vision Loss
2026-10-08.authors: Genki Shikada , Kazuki Osamura , Masaru Ide , Tetsuya Ogata , Kanata Suzuki
2026-10-08.comment: . Submitted to the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration (SII 2027)
2026-10-08.abstract: Imitation learning policies that integrate multiple sensory modalities are prone to overreliance on a dominant modality, such as vision, during training, which can disrupt policy execution when that modality is lost at inference time. In this paper, we introduce Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), in which the dependence on each modality is estimated using attention and the most dominant modality is selectively dropped. This is combined with entropy regularization over the dependence distribution. Through real-robot evaluation using a bimanual manipulator, we show that under vision loss the success rate of the baseline policy drops substantially, whereas TMD sustains task execution. In contrast, a conventional dropout that selects the dropped modality at random, without the entropy regularization, fails on many tasks even without vision loss.
2026-10-08.introduction:
In imitation learning, a manipulation policy is developed directly from demonstrations, without a tailored reward function or controller. A human operator teleoperates the robot to perform a task while the camera images, the robot’s own state and the commanded actions are recorded. The policy is then trained via supervised learning to predict the actions from the observations. At run time the task is executed in a closed loop; thus, each step is driven by the sensor inputs available at that moment. Recent studies have increasingly adopted vision-language-action models, which encode images and language instructions using pretrained foundation models and generate actions from the resulting representation [ 1 , 2 ] . In contact-rich manipulation, vision alone does not reveal how much force is applied or whether contact has been established; thus, integrating several modalities such as vision, language, and force is intuitive [ 3 ] .

However, when a policy is trained by integrating multiple modalities, potential overreliance on a particular modality may lead to underuse of the others [ 4 ] . Vision, in particular, tends to become dominant because it is information-rich; consequently, vision loss at inference time can severely impair policy execution. Camera failures and occlusions do occur in real-world deployment, making overreliance on a particular modality a practical robustness concern, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .

Modality dropout can intervene in this bias by stochastically removing modalities during training [ 5 , 6 ] . Randomly removing modalities, however, does not account for which modality is dominant and thus does not correct the bias itself. In this study we propose Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), which estimates each modality’s dependence from attention and drops the modality with the largest dependence as a target. We further introduce entropy regularization over the dependence distribution to alleviate concentration on any single modality.

To date, robustness to missing modalities has been assessed mainly using multimodal classification benchmarks or simulated manipulation. Situations where vision is lost while a real robot executes a task, i.e., robustness in a closed loop, have rarely been examined. In this study we apply TMD to a real bimanual manipulator and evaluate whether task execution is sustained when vision is stochastically lost at inference time. We also examine the effect of dependence-based targeted selection by comparing TMD with a conventional dropout in which the dropped modality is selected at random, referred to as Random Modality Dropout (RMD).

The contributions of this study are as follows:

We propose Targeted Modality Dropout (TMD), which drops the dominant modality as a target based on the dependence estimated from attention, together with entropy regularization.

Through real-robot closed-loop evaluation using a bimanual manipulator, we demonstrate that TMD sustains task execution under vision loss and that its action commands are disturbed less.

We show that RMD, which replaces the targeted selection with a random one and omits the entropy regularization, fails on many tasks even without vision loss.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Multimodal Imitation Learning for Manipulation

In manipulation, the modalities received by a policy carry different types of information. Images provide the position and orientation of the objects, and a language instruction specifies the task to be performed. Force or tactile signals report the contact that images cannot capture [ 3 ] . Transformer-based policies treat these inputs as a single token sequence to generate an action chunk [ 7 ] . In vision-language-action models, pretrained encoders provide the visual and language tokens [ 1 , 2 ] . These inputs substitute for one another only partially. Thus, losing one of them at inference time does not uniformly degrade the performance of the policy; only what that input alone was supplying is lost. Nevertheless, the extent to which a policy relies on each input is determined implicitly through training, and such policies are typically developed under the assumption that all inputs are available.

## II-B Controlling Modality Reliance

When a policy is trained on multiple modalities, it may over-rely on a dominant one and fail to use the others [ 4 ] . Several lines of research have addressed this issue. Fusion-mechanism design suppresses the dominance of a particular modality through architectural choices [ 3 ] ; however, this approach is closely tied to the specific policy architecture. Phase-dependent weighting dynamically adjusts the contribution of each modality according to the task phase [ 8 , 9 ] , but presupposes that all modalities remain available. Visual degradation during training reduces the policy’s reliance on vision [ 10 ] but does not examine which modality is dominant. Gradient rebalancing modulates the gradient of each modality based on its contribution at each iteration [ 11 , 12 ] but does not train the policy to handle the absence of a modality. Modality dropout stochastically drops modalities during training [ 5 , 6 ] , but randomly selecting the dropped modality does not account for modality dominance. In a setting closer to ours, modality dropout has been used to keep a network from ignoring the weaker of two modalities in audiovisual facial animation [ 13 ] , with the probability of dropping each modality tuned in advance based on prior knowledge of the dominant modality rather than on a quantity estimated during training. Because this study targets robustness to the loss of the dominant modality, we identify the dominant modality using attention and selectively drop it during training (Section III ).

## II-C Evaluation under Missing Modalities

Most of the methods described above are evaluated under normal operating conditions that do not involve complete modality loss. Research on visuotactile fusion addresses vision-constrained conditions, but remains limited to situations where vision is only partially restricted [ 14 ] . Robustness to missing modalities has been studied mainly outside real-robot closed-loop settings: on multimodal classification benchmarks [ 15 ] or simulated manipulation [ 16 ] . The scenario in which vision is stochastically lost while a real robot executes a task in closed loop has rarely been examined. Unlike existing studies, this study focuses on evaluating real-robot task execution under inference-time vision loss.

2026-10-08.title: MagCilia: A Compact Magnetociliary Tactile Sensor with 3D Force Sensing for Robotic Contact Perception and Grasping Feedback
2026-10-08.authors: Yu Feng , Hao Wu , Haotian Guo , Haoming Liu , William Su , Jingxiang Guo , Jiankun Li , Masayoshi Tomizuka , Wen Jung Li , Jianshu Zhou
2026-10-08.abstract: Robotic grasping and surface exploration benefit from simultaneous measurement of normal and tangential forces and from surface information obtained through contact. Here, we present a compact magnetociliary tactile sensor (MagCilia) that combines a flexible magnetic-cilia structure with a Hall sensor for 3D force sensing. Quasi-static finite element analysis is used to investigate structural deformation and magnetic responses under multidirectional loading. To reconstruct forces from the coupled magnetic channels, we propose causal history fusion regression (CHFR), which combines current magnetic-field measurements with their recent changes. Five-fold cross-validation grouped by calibration record yields root-mean-square errors of 0.40, 0.57, and 0.69 N for F x F_{x} , F y F_{y} , and F z F_{z} , respectively, with corresponding coefficients of determination of 0.93, 0.90, and 0.92. Robotic experiments demonstrate tangential-force-guided gripper adjustment and multi-axis load monitoring under external perturbations. Frequency-domain features of the reconstructed forces distinguish six surface categories with 99.39% accuracy in three-fold cross-validation grouped by acquisition session. An online robotic demonstration additionally identifies all six tested surfaces. These results demonstrate 3D force reconstruction, grasping feedback, and surface recognition using a single compact tactile unit.
2026-10-08.introduction:
As robots increasingly move from structured environments to complex physical interaction scenarios, grasping and manipulation place greater demands on tactile sensing [ 1 ] . Contact forces characterize the mechanical interaction between the end effector and the object [ 2 ] . The normal force indicates the degree of gripping and compression, whereas object weight, external perturbations, and relative motion at the contact interface can generate tangential loads in different directions. Simultaneous measurement of normal and tangential loads therefore provides a more complete description of the contact interaction and supports stable grasping and precise manipulation [ 3 ] .

In recent years, tactile sensors capable of measuring 3D contact forces have provided richer tactile information for dexterous robotic manipulation by sensing both the direction and magnitude of contact loads [ 4 ] . Various approaches have been developed for multi-axis contact force measurement, including piezoresistive [ 5 ] , capacitive [ 6 , 7 ] , non-vision-based optical [ 8 , 9 ] , visuotactile [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , and magnetic tactile sensing [ 13 , 14 ] . Magnetic tactile sensors measure changes in the local magnetic field caused by deformation of flexible magnetic structures under contact loads. Their multi-axis sensing characteristics are closely related to the coupling among the magnetization configuration, structural deformation, and magnetic-field readout [ 15 , 16 ] .

The design of flexible magnetic structures is a key aspect of multidimensional sensing in magnetic tactile sensors. Existing studies have explored various configurations, including sinusoidally magnetized films [ 17 ] , stacked orthogonally magnetized films [ 18 ] , combinations of magnetic films and flexible pillars [ 19 ] , and magnetic cilia [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Magnetic cilia convert contact loads into changes in the position and orientation of magnetic material through compression and bending, providing a direct mechanical response for sensing contact states and surface features. For magnetic-cilia sensors, quantitative 3D force reconstruction is complicated by coupling between the mechanical deformation and the three magnetic-field channels. In a tactile structure comprising a magnetic-cilia skin and a flexible supporting layer, external loads induce not only compression and bending of the cilia but also displacement of the base membrane and shear deformation of the supporting layer. These deformations jointly alter the local magnetic field, so a force applied along one axis can affect multiple magnetic channels. This coupling limits the use of a direct, channel-by-channel mapping for 3D force reconstruction [ 25 , 26 ] .

Here, we present MagCilia, a compact single-unit magnetociliary tactile sensor for 3D force sensing (key parameters in Supplementary Table ). The sensor integrates a magnetic-cilia skin, a PDMS buffer layer, and a Hall sensor. CHFR combines the current three-axis magnetic readout with causal history features to jointly reconstruct the normal force and two tangential force components from the coupled responses. Calibration experiments yield root-mean-square errors of 0.40, 0.57, and 0.69 N for F x F_{x} , F y F_{y} , and F z F_{z} , respectively. Signals are acquired at 246 Hz, and the reconstructed forces are used for robotic grasping feedback and active surface recognition. Robotic experiments demonstrate multi-axis force responses during grasping, stepwise loading, and multidirectional perturbations, with the reconstructed forces used to adjust the gripper opening under external loading. Frequency-domain force features distinguish six surface categories with 99.39% accuracy in three-fold offline evaluation grouped by acquisition session, and scan-level recognition is demonstrated online. These experiments examine force reconstruction and two robotic applications using the same tactile unit.

The study combines the sensing mechanism, force reconstruction, and robotic use of the reconstructed signals. The grasping experiments examine load magnitude and direction at the contact interface, whereas surface scanning uses the temporal structure of those same force signals to distinguish surface categories.

# II MagCilia Structure and Sensing Mechanism

## II-A Sensor Structure and Fabrication

The overall structure of MagCilia is shown in Fig. 1 . It consists of a magnetic-cilia skin, a PDMS buffer layer, a Hall sensor, and a housing. The upper magnetic-cilia skin contacts the object, and the underlying PDMS buffer layer supports the skin and deforms with it under load. The Hall sensor on the readout circuit board measures the resulting magnetic-field changes. The housing supports and aligns the assembled layers.

The magnetic-cilia skin has in-plane dimensions of 7.8 × 10 7.8\times 10 mm, a base-membrane thickness of 1 mm, and a cilia height of 2.5 mm. The skin is magnetized along its surface normal. The underlying PDMS (Sylgard 184) buffer layer has dimensions of 26.15 × 22.4 × 3.3 26.15\times 22.4\times 3.3 mm. The magnetic-cilia skin and buffer layer are bonded through PDMS curing, and the Hall sensor is aligned in-plane with the center of the magnetic-cilia skin. Material preparation and fabrication conditions are provided in Supplementary Note .

## II-B Magnetic Vector Response

Fig. 2 illustrates the typical deformation of MagCilia under normal, tangential, and oblique loading. Normal loading primarily compresses the magnetic cilia and supporting layer, changing the relative position between the magnetic material and the Hall sensing point. Tangential loading bends the cilia and is accompanied by displacement of the magnetic base membrane and shear deformation of the supporting layer, thereby changing both the position and local orientation of the magnetic material. Oblique loading combines normal and tangential components, producing compression, bending, and shear that jointly affect the magnetic-field output.

The magnetization model assumes a relative permeability of μ r = 1 \mu_{r}=1 , an initial magnetization normal to the skin, and conservation of magnetic moment per reference volume. The magnetic moment rotates with the material according to the local rotation from the polar decomposition of the deformation gradient. The detailed magnetic dipole field integral is provided in Supplementary Note . This formulation accounts for changes in the position and orientation of the magnetic material caused by cilia bending, base-membrane displacement, and buffer-layer deformation. Here, 𝐁 h \mathbf{B}_{h} denotes the three-axis magnetic-field vector at the Hall sensing point. Structural deformation simultaneously changes the position and local orientation of the magnetic material relative to the Hall sensing point, resulting in coupling among the three magnetic-field components, with the corresponding sensitivities also varying with the loading state [ 25 ] . This state-dependent coupling motivates a joint mapping from the three magnetic channels to the three force components. The reconstruction model described below additionally incorporates recent magnetic changes to represent temporal dependence. The state-dependent cross-channel sensitivities indicate that directional information is distributed across the three magnetic components, motivating joint rather than channel-wise force reconstruction.

Quasi-static finite element analysis is performed in COMSOL to investigate structural deformation and magnetic-field responses under normal, orthogonal tangential, and oblique loading. The model dimensions are consistent with the actual magnetic skin and buffer layer. Both layers are modeled as nearly incompressible neo-Hookean materials, with a fixed bottom surface and loading through a rigid top plate. Under shear along the positive and negative orthogonal directions, the dominant transverse magnetic-field response reverses sign with the loading direction, whereas oblique shear produces changes in both transverse components. Different loading directions therefore produce distinct, coupled magnetic responses. 2026-10-08.title: Contact-Aware Imitation Learning Through Contact Factorization
2026-10-08.authors: Jiho Hong , Daeun Song , Sanghyun Kim , Mingyo Seo
2026-10-08.abstract:
Generalizable contact-rich manipulation requires robots to preserve intended task behavior while adapting its physical realization to changing contact conditions.
However, interaction forces can vary substantially with small changes in surface geometry, orientation, and friction, making policies trained directly on raw force measurements difficult to transfer beyond demonstrated conditions.
We introduce FACE , a contact-factorized imitation learning framework that separates intended task behavior from environment-dependent contact factors.
Our representation expresses interaction forces in normalized, contact-relative coordinates, while a learned contact-normal estimator and an online friction estimator infer the local contact normal and effective friction scale.
Together, these estimators enable force observations to be encoded and policy outputs to be decoded into physical motion and force commands during execution.
In this way, FACE adapts execution to current contact conditions while preserving the intended task behavior, without updating the policy parameters.
We evaluate FACE on real-robot contact-rich manipulation under unseen variations in surface properties and geometry, demonstrating robust generalization across contact conditions through controlled comparisons with variants that adapt prior approaches to our setting.
Videos and additional materials can be found on the project page: https://rcilab.khu.ac.kr/face .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Recent advances in robot learning have enabled robots to acquire complex manipulation behaviors from scalable human demonstrations [ 19 , 36 , 3 , 33 ] . This progress has been strong for tasks in which visual observations provide much of the information needed to choose an action. However, contact-rich manipulation also depends on physical properties of the environment that may not be known before interaction. The same intended behavior can require different forces across surfaces or objects, and those forces may need to be applied along different directions as the contact geometry changes. Consequently, directly imitating raw force measurements can tie a learned policy to the conditions seen during demonstration rather than the interaction required by the task.

Force/torque and tactile feedback have enabled force-aware imitation learning, tactile-guided control, adaptive compliance, and multimodal policy learning for contact-rich manipulation [ 32 , 18 , 5 , 17 , 13 , 31 , 14 ] . These methods substantially improve contact awareness and robustness, but they generally represent forces in physical quantities whose scale and orientation depend on the environment. During sliding, the required tangential force varies with friction and normal loading, while force directions vary with surface orientation. Consequently, generalization across contact conditions can depend heavily on demonstration coverage or adaptation learned implicitly by the policy.

Our key idea is to separate what is task-specific from what changes with the contact environment. The intended task behavior should be preserved, while its physical motion and force commands adapt to the current contact conditions. We realize this idea with normalized force coordinates defined in the local contact frame: normal loading is expressed relative to prescribed operating bounds, while tangential loading is expressed relative to friction-scaled normal loading. The same contact factorization is used for observations and actions, while friction scale and contact orientation are estimated separately and used both to encode force observations and to map the learned output back to physical commands.

To capture the intended task behavior, we collect demonstrations with a handheld gripper equipped with force/torque sensing and visual-inertial tracking. The handheld form allows the demonstrator to physically perform contact-rich interactions while synchronized end-effector motion and interaction wrench are recorded. At deployment, the friction scale and local contact normal are estimated online and used to map normalized policy outputs back to physical motion and force commands. The policy itself remains fixed, allowing the demonstrated behavior to be preserved across surfaces with different frictional properties and curvatures.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

A contact-factorized representation of force observations and actions, using bounded normal loading and friction-relative tangential loading in the local contact frame.

An online reparameterization framework that converts outputs of a fixed policy into motion and force commands using the estimated friction scale and contact normal.

A force-sensing handheld demonstration interface and real-robot evaluation under variations in friction, surface geometry, and their combination.
