# II Related Work

## II-A Force-Aware Demonstration and Imitation Learning

Recent work has increasingly incorporated physical interaction signals into imitation learning. One common approach acquires force-aware demonstrations through teleoperation and enables policies to attend explicitly to interaction feedback [ 17 ] . While effective, such systems require an instrumented human-robot interface and closed-loop robot execution during demonstration, and the recorded force signals remain tied to the physical conditions under which they are collected.

Complementary to teleoperation-based collection, robot-free and human-centered interfaces enable demonstration collection through handheld tools and direct human interaction [ 25 , 30 , 4 , 23 , 24 , 32 ] . More recent systems extend this paradigm to capture interaction forces during demonstration and learn force-aware manipulation policies [ 18 , 5 ] . These approaches facilitate natural acquisition of coupled motion and force information and improve contact regulation. Their learned force and compliance targets can nevertheless remain dependent on the contact conditions represented in the demonstrations.

Beyond data collection, recent visuomotor policies incorporate force or tactile sensing through reactive architectures, multimodal fusion, and slow-fast policy structures [ 9 , 29 , 2 ] . Concurrent work also analyzes characteristic failure modes of force-aware vision-language-action policies in contact-rich tasks [ 21 ] . Together, these works establish the importance of physical interaction feedback. Our focus is on how that interaction is represented across changing contact conditions.

## II-B Contact-Aware Action Representation

Beyond force-aware observation and demonstration, another key question is how contact-rich actions should be represented and executed.
Classical force-control methods structure contact-rich actions by separating force- and motion-controlled directions in task-related coordinates [ 22 , 1 ] , while later learning-based approaches infer changing constraint frames from demonstrations [ 6 ] .
Learning-based work has also explored action representations that expose physically meaningful control variables, such as end-effector motion together with variable impedance, to improve learning in contact-rich tasks [ 20 ] .
More recent policies learn task-dependent compliance or force regulation [ 11 , 28 ] , and combine learned visuomotor policies with interaction-frame estimation or hybrid force-position execution [ 7 , 15 ] . These approaches improve contact stability and force regulation through learned compliance and contact-aware execution. We focus on normalizing tangential loading by friction-scaled normal loading to represent interaction across changing contact conditions.

Other methods use physical feedback at inference time to calibrate predicted states or steer generated actions toward safer or more feasible interactions [ 26 , 34 , 27 ] . Concurrent work further explores fast force reflexes, asynchronous vision-force policy composition, and object-centric contact-wrench guidance [ 12 , 10 , 35 ] . Our approach uses the estimated contact normal and friction scale to encode force observations in contact-factorized coordinates and decode the outputs of a fixed policy into physical motion and force commands.

2026-10-08.title: Not All Uncertainty Matters: Simulation-in-the-Loop Fast-Slow Reasoning for Decision-Critical Autonomous Driving System
2026-10-08.authors: Jiayi Chen , Shuai Wang , Guangxu Zhu , Derrick Wing Kwan Ng , Chengzhong Xu , Kaibin Huang
2026-10-08.abstract: Large vision-language models (VLMs) offer powerful open-world perception and reasoning capabilities for autonomous driving. However, their high computational overhead and non-negligible inference latency make continuous cloud-side invocation impractical for real-time operations. This limitation motivates a fast–slow collaborative architecture, where efficient onboard modules perform real-time perception and control tasks while cloud-based models provide selectively high-level reasoning when necessary. The central challenge in such systems is accurately determining when slow cloud reasoning should be involved and allowed to influence time-critical driving decisions. Existing approaches typically rely on perception uncertainty, heuristic triggers, or resource-driven policies, which fail to explicitly evaluate whether resolving a particular uncertainty will actually improve the downstream planning outcome. To address this issue, we propose SIGMA , a simulation-in-the-loop planning-gain modeling and assessment framework for effective task-oriented fast–slow collaboration. The key insight is that not all perception uncertainty equally affect decisions: perception ambiguity when it substantially alters the feasible trajectory set or significantly affects the associated planning cost. Rather than measuring uncertainty solely at the perception level, SIGMA embeds the planner directly into the uncertainty assessment loop to systematically evaluate how plausible scene realizations affect motion-planning outcomes. Specifically, SIGMA constructs candidate scene realizations under semantic and geometric uncertainty, evaluates them through a simulation-in-the-loop planning framework, and estimates the expected reduction in planning cost if the uncertainty is resolved. Building on this formulation, we introduce expected planning gain (EPG), a decision-level metric that quantitatively captures the expected trajectory-level improvement obtainable from cloud reasoning. EPG serves as a unified criterion for managing cloud invocation, cloud-guidance integration, and prioritizing cloud requests under deadline and resource constraints. Extensive experiments in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that SIGMA significantly reduces unnecessary cloud interactions while significantly improving planning performance, driving efficiency, and navigation success in both static and dynamic obstacle scenarios. Compared with fixed-period collaboration, SIGMA reduces unnecessary cloud interactions by 50%, improves navigation success rate by more than 6%, and achieves up to 26.2% reduction in finish time in dynamic scenarios. The implementation of our prediction-time 3D bounding-box-level uncertainty estimator is publicly available at https://github.com/cjychenjiayi/3D_Bbox_uncertainty .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Recent advances in large vision, language, and vision–language models have enhanced open-world perception, semantic understanding, and reasoning for autonomous driving [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . However, their high computational cost and inference latency make continuous invocation impractical for real-time driving systems, especially in resource-constrained edge–cloud settings. This limitation motivates a fast–slow architecture, where efficient onboard modules provide real-time perception, planning and control tasks, while cloud-based models offer slower but more powerful reasoning when necessary [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . The central challenge is not merely how to leverage large models, but when slow reasoning should be invoked and allowed to influence real-time driving decisions under incomplete knowledge of the surrounding world.

Existing autonomous driving systems often determine cloud usage or decision refinement based on perception uncertainty, fixed offloading intervals, communication constraints, or heuristic triggers. Meanwhile, uncertainty-aware perception and planning methods have studied object detection uncertainty, unknown objects, conformal prediction, and robust decision-making under perception ambiguity [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Although these methods improve safety and robustness to a certain extent, they do not directly answer a more decision-centric question: whether resolving the current uncertainty would change or improve the final driving decision . This limitation reflects a fundamental mismatch between perception-space uncertainty and planning-space decision making. For instance, a perception module may exhibit high uncertainty about distant or irrelevant objects without affecting the planned trajectory, while seemingly confident predictions near critical regions may still result in unsafe or suboptimal driving decisions. Thus, not all uncertainty matters ; what truly matters is whether alternative plausible scene realizations would induce different downstream planning outcomes.

We argue that the root limitation is not simply inaccurate uncertainty estimation, but the absence of an explicit decision-evaluation mechanism that systematically considers multiple plausible realizations of the world . In real-world driving, the environment is only partially observed, and a single perception output may admit multiple valid semantic and geometric interpretations. Therefore, uncertainty should not be treated only as an intrinsic property of perception, but as a decision-induced quantity defined by its effect on planning outcomes. This view is related to forward-simulation-based planning and the emerging “simulate before execute” paradigm [ 10 , 11 ] . It is also aligned with the agentic-harness perspective for physical AI systems, where model outputs are mediated by runtime verification, safety, and execution-control modules before being deployed in the physical world. However, our goal is not to learn a comprehensive generative world model or perform simulation for its own sake. Instead, we leverage forward simulation as a lightweight decision evaluation tool: before allowing slow cloud reasoning to affect the onboard controller, the system estimates whether plausible scene variations would result in meaningful changes in planning outcomes. In this sense, the proposed simulation-in-the-loop EPG module can be viewed as a planning-grounded verification layer for fast–slow autonomous driving.

To this end, we introduce SIGMA , a Simulation-In-the-loop planning-Gain Modeling and Assessment framework for decision-aware fast–slow collaboration. Rather than relying on a single estimated world, we construct multiple plausible scene realizations by decomposing ambiguity into semantic “ what ” and geometric “ where ” components. These realizations are then propagated into a simulation-in-the-loop forward simulation, where their downstream effects are evaluated according to the resulting planning costs. By comparing decision outcomes across scene hypotheses, the system can determine whether the ambiguity is decision-relevant and quantifies the potential planning benefit of resolving it. In this formulation, uncertainty is evaluated relying sidely on its decision impact , rather than through perception-level proxy metrics.

This perspective naturally leads to a planning-gain-guided view of fast–slow collaboration. The onboard system retains real-time control authority and continuously generates safe and dynamically feasible trajectories, while the cloud provides slower but more reliable semantic reasoning and high-level guidance only when its expected benefit justifies the additional latency and cost. Instead of heuristically switching between onboard and cloud decisions, we introduce a decision-level metric, termed expected planning gain (EPG), which estimates the expected improvement in planning quality if additional information or reasoning is incorporated. EPG can be interpreted as a task-specific approximation of the value of information, and it governs both when to invoke cloud intelligence and whether its output should be integrated into local planning . Under limited computation and communication resources, cloud collaboration is further handled through a planning-gain-aware request prioritization rule that favors requests according to their expected impact on decision outcomes [ 6 , 12 ] .

Overall, the framework integrates uncertainty modeling, simulation-in-the-loop forward simulation, and planning-gain-guided invocation and integration of cloud guidance into onboard planning . As illustrated in Fig. 1 , it shifts the objective of fast–slow collaboration from optimizing proxy metrics such as uncertainty, latency, or invocation frequency to optimizing decision outcomes under scene variability .

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

Decision-coupled uncertainty modeling. We formulate perception uncertainty as planning-relevant ambiguity rather than standalone confidence, and decompose it into semantic uncertainty for unknown-object screening and geometric uncertainty for obstacle-level risk modeling. This yields an explicit semantic–geometric interface from open-world perception to MPC constraints, including a data-driven optimize for semantic screening and probabilistic obstacle inflation for geometric uncertainty.

Simulation-in-the-loop planning value estimation. We introduce EPG as a decision-level metric that quantifies the value of resolving current ambiguity. EPG is derived as the expected normalized MPC-cost reduction over plausible scene realizations and estimated via budget-aware Monte Carlo rollouts. By propagating multiple plausible scene realizations through MPC, EPG identifies uncertainty that truly changes planning outcomes, rather than merely appearing uncertain in perception space.

Planning-gain-guided fast–slow collaboration. We design a planning-gain-aware mechanism that adopts EPG to regulate cloud invocation, cloud-guided MPC reference switching, and deadline-aware prioritization. The cloud acts as selective guidance, while real-time feasibility and safety remain by onboard MPC.

End-to-end validation in open-world driving scenarios. We implement SIGMA in CARLA and evaluate it under static and dynamic unknown-obstacle scenarios. Compared with fixed-period collaboration, SIGMA reduces unnecessary cloud interactions by 50%, improves navigation success rate by more than 6%, and achieves up to 26.2% reduction in finish time in dynamic scenarios.

# II Related Work

## II-A Uncertainty Estimation in Autonomous Driving Perception

Reliable uncertainty estimation is crucial for autonomous driving, as perception errors can propagate to downstream planning and compromise safety. Existing works primarily focus on uncertainty at the perception level, including robust detection under adverse conditions [ 24 ] , probabilistic object detection with localization uncertainty [ 25 ] , unknown-object discovery [ 26 , 27 ] , and uncertainty calibration with statistical guarantees [ 9 , 28 , 29 ] . These approaches improve the detection reliability and provide more accurate characterization of uncertainty in open-world perception.

However, such methods treat uncertainty mainly as an intrinsic property of perception outputs, focusing on robustness, calibration, or unknown-instance awareness. They do not explicitly address whether a given uncertainty is decision-relevant , i.e., whether resolving it would change the downstream planning outcome. In contrast, our work adopts a task-oriented perspective, where uncertainty is evaluated based on its impact on planning rather than its magnitude alone.

## II-B Motion Planning Under Perception Uncertainty

Another line of work incorporates uncertainty into motion planning and decision making. Classical approaches include formal verification and robust control [ 30 , 31 ] , as well as planning frameworks that explicitly account for uncertainty through chance-constrained optimization, MPC variants, or integrated perception–planning pipelines [ 32 , 7 , 33 , 11 , 34 , 8 ] . Related studies have investigated distributed or collaborative planning under uncertainty [ 35 , 36 ] . More broadly, some prior work on informative planning and forward-simulation-based exploration explicitly accounts for uncertainty when evaluating and selecting candidate actions [ 10 , 37 , 38 ] .

These works primarily aim to improve safety and robustness under uncertainty, typically treating uncertainty as a factor to be handled conservatively once it appears. What remains underexplored is whether all uncertainty should be treated equally, and more importantly, whether resolving a particular uncertainty would improve the optimal decision . Our work addresses this gap by explicitly quantifying the planning gain of uncertainty resolution through simulation-in-the-loop evaluation, enabling the system to distinguish between decision-critical and decision-irrelevant uncertainty.

## II-C Fast–Slow Collaborative Driving

Recent autonomous driving systems increasingly adopt a fast–slow collaborative paradigm. On one hand, cloud- and edge-assisted frameworks enable vehicles to offload computation tasks and collaborate with external resources [ 39 , 40 , 4 , 5 , 41 , 6 ] . On the other hand, large models have been introduced to substantially enhance semantic understanding and high-level decision making in autonomous driving, including language-guided planning and driving agents [ 1 , 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 , 47 , 2 , 3 ] . These studies demonstrate the potential of coupling lightweight onboard modules for real-time perception, planning, and control with more capable cloud-side reasoning in complex scenarios. However, existing collaborative systems typically rely on heuristic triggers, predefined pipelines, or capability-driven designs to decide when cloud or large-model reasoning should be invoked. Likewise, large-model-based driving methods mainly focus on improving reasoning capability, but often assume that the generated guidance, once available, should directly affect downstream decision making. As a result, slow reasoning may be unnecessarily triggered even when it brings little planning benefit, and its outputs may be incorporated without explicitly assessing their impact on the final driving decision.

In contrast, our framework introduces a decision-centric perspective for fast–slow collaboration: both the invocation of cloud reasoning and its integration into local planning are governed by a unified planning-gain criterion. By evaluating whether uncertainty resolution leads to measurable improvements to planning performance, the system allocates both computational resources and decision authority.

## II-D Positioning of Our Work

Existing studies on perception uncertainty, uncertainty-aware planning, and collaborative driving are largely developed along separate directions: perception works estimate uncertainty, planning works handle uncertainty, and collaborative or large-model systems enhance reasoning capability. What remains underexplored is a unified decision-oriented perspective, where both uncertainty resolution and external reasoning are governed by their expected impact on downstream planning. Our work adopts this view by evaluating uncertainty and fast–slow collaboration through EPG, a planning-level criterion.

Table I further positions SIGMA against representative studies in perception uncertainty, uncertainty-aware planning, collaborative perception, and edge–cloud service scheduling. Existing collaborative and resource-aware systems provide strong mechanisms for computation offloading, communication scheduling, perception enhancement, or service-cost optimization, including under uncertain network or workload conditions. However, these systems generally optimize proxy objectives such as perception quality, resource usage, latency, or service cost, rather than the downstream planning gain obtained by resolving uncertainty. SIGMA differs by using simulation-in-the-loop planning cost to decide both when uncertainty deserves slow reasoning and when the resulting guidance should affect real-time control.

2026-10-08.title: Sparse Feature Policy Unlearning Mitigates State Hallucination in Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-08.authors: Jiho Lee , Jeongeun Park , Heayoun Choi , Taekyung Kim , Eunwoo Kim
2026-10-08.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models.
However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors.
In this work, we study state hallucination , a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved.
Our analyses find that state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions, and a mechanistic interpretation via sparse autoencoders reveals that hallucination-associated sparse features are activated when these failures occur.
Based on this analysis, we propose SOUL (Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination behaviors, where sparse features identified from hallucination failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively.
Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show that our method substantially reduces hallucinated failures and improves task success without substantially compromising the existing manipulation capabilities.
These results suggest that interpretable feature analysis provides a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising approach for bringing foundation models into robot manipulation [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
By integrating visual and language understanding with action generation, VLAs can translate high-level instructions into continuous robot control.
Large-scale pretraining on heterogeneous robot and vision-language data has further enabled generalization across tasks, objects, environments, and robot embodiments [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
Despite this progress, VLAs still exhibit unreliable behaviors, including unstable or premature actions, long-horizon drift, failures to recover from execution errors, and infeasible actions [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
This is particularly concerning in physical robot execution, where erroneous actions directly affect the robot and its environment.

Within this broader set of failures, we focus on a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues a manipulation sequence based on a robot-object state that has not actually been achieved.
We refer to this behavioral pattern as state hallucination , because the policy acts as if an unrealized physical state were true.
For example, a VLA may close its gripper before reaching an object and subsequently execute transport and place motions as though the object has been successfully grasped, as shown in Fig. 1 1(a) .
Such a mismatch can persist across subsequent actions, allowing a local execution error to propagate over multiple stages.
This recurring and persistent behavior motivates us to investigate whether policy knowledge associated with state hallucination can be selectively removed while preserving successful manipulation capabilities.

We first examine how the policy’s internal representations differ between hallucinated and successful behaviors.
Such hallucinated rollouts exhibit weakened attention to task-relevant regions, such as the gripper and target object, together with more spatially dispersed attention.
Through a mechanistic analysis with sparse autoencoders, we also observe that sparse features exhibit distinct activation patterns during hallucinated and normal executions.
To characterize these sparse feature activation patterns, we define a feature association score that contrasts activations across execution outcomes, such as failures with hallucination, failures without hallucination, and successful executions.
Based on this score, we categorize sparse features according to whether they are more strongly associated with hallucinated failures or successful executions.

Building on these observations, we propose S parse feature p O licy U n L earning ( SOUL ), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination, where sparse features identified from hallucinated failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively.
This feature-level policy unlearning objective suppresses activations of the forgetting targets while enhancing activations of the retention targets, thereby mitigating recurring hallucination behavior while minimizing interference with useful manipulation capabilities.
We validate our approach with OpenVLA [ 2 ] and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 3 ] on LIBERO-Plus [ 9 ] , RoboCasa [ 14 ] , and a real-world Franka robot, achieving an average 21.7%p reduction in hallucination rate and a 22.1%p improvement in task success while preserving 89% of behaviors that were successful before unlearning.
These results demonstrate that interpretable feature analysis can reveal internal representations associated with recurring policy failures, providing a practical basis for selectively unlearning such behaviors in embodied foundation models.
Our contributions are as follows:

We characterize state hallucination as a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as though an unrealized robot-object state has been achieved.

We analyze state hallucination through visual attention and sparse features, revealing weakened attention to task-relevant regions and distinct feature patterns associated with state hallucination.

We introduce a sparse feature policy unlearning method that selectively unlearns recurring state hallucination behavior by suppressing hallucination features while enhancing features that support successful manipulation.

1. We characterize state hallucination as a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as though an unrealized robot-object state has been achieved.

2. We analyze state hallucination through visual attention and sparse features, revealing weakened attention to task-relevant regions and distinct feature patterns associated with state hallucination.

3. We introduce a sparse feature policy unlearning method that selectively unlearns recurring state hallucination behavior by suppressing hallucination features while enhancing features that support successful manipulation.

# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Models

Vision-language-action models have become a major direction for generalist robot manipulation.
Prior work has improved generalization through larger pretrained vision-language representations, heterogeneous robotic data, and stronger action generation architectures [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] .
Deployment reliability has also been improved through intermediate reasoning [ 19 , 20 ] , failure detection and recovery [ 12 , 21 ] , and test-time sampling or verification [ 22 , 23 ] .
These approaches primarily focus on improving policy outputs during deployment, rather than directly modifying policy knowledge associated with recurring failures.
Recent concurrent mechanistic interpretability studies have begun to analyze and steer VLA behavior at inference time by intervening on representations, such as feed-forward activation directions [ 24 ] and sparse features [ 25 ] .

In contrast, we formulate the selective modification of undesirable policy behavior as a policy unlearning problem, where knowledge associated with recurring hallucinated behavior is removed while representations supporting successful execution are preserved.
Encoding this modification in the pretrained policy parameters enables persistent behavior correction without repeated intervention at inference time.

## II-B Machine Unlearning

Machine unlearning aims to make a trained model forget knowledge associated with selected data without retraining the model from scratch [ 26 , 27 ] .
Prior work has studied unlearning mainly in classification tasks, where the influence of selected training data is removed from trained models [ 28 , 29 ] , and in language tasks, where factual knowledge or undesired responses are suppressed [ 30 , 31 ] .
A central challenge is balancing the removal of targeted knowledge with the preservation of useful model capabilities.
This trade-off is particularly consequential for robot policies, where modifying one behavior can inadvertently disrupt multiple tightly coupled skills.
Motivated by this, we introduce feature-level selective policy unlearning by explicitly identifying features for forgetting and retention to suppress undesirable behavior while preserving useful manipulation capabilities.

## II-C Sparse Autoencoders

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense model activations into sparse latent representations, enabling individual features to be associated with more localized and interpretable patterns in model behavior [ 32 , 33 , 34 ] .
They are trained to reconstruct the original activations under a sparsity constraint, such that only a small subset of latent features is active for each input.
A commonly used variant is the Top- k k SAE, which imposes this sparsity constraint explicitly by retaining only the k k largest latent activations.
In VLAs, SAE features have recently been used to interpret and repeatedly steer policy at test time [ 25 ] .
In contrast, the proposed method identifies recurring internal patterns associated with unreliable behaviors using sparse features and translates these patterns into forgetting targets to guide targeted policy unlearning.

2026-10-08.title: SiGNgapore - An Interactive Dataset for Sign-based Visual Navigation
2026-10-08.authors: Nicky Zimmerman , Joel Loo , Zishuo Wang , David Hsu
2026-10-08.abstract: The future of autonomous robots in human-oriented environments depends on their ability to navigate in the absence of prebuilt maps; exploiting navigational aids, such as navigational signs, designed by humans for humans is critical for enabling autonomy. This manuscript introduces a unique dataset collected using a handheld device, at various public spaces across Singapore, representing environments that humans frequent daily, and focusing on sign-centric decision making for mapless navigation. The dataset includes RGB, sparse depth, odometry and IMU measurements of scenarios centered around navigational signs and the complex environments where they are placed. Additionally, we provide 56 long-horizon navigation missions and over 450 sign-centric scenarios. All data is provided in a human-readable format, as well as utility scripts for conversion to ROS 2. Lastly, we provide venue maps and GPS aligned scene graphs of the test environments. We discuss the potential use cases for this dataset.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Human-built spaces are often densely annotated with navigational signage to guide humans through unfamiliar environments without maps. However, robots at present make little use of these highly informative semantic cues, instead relying heavily on prior maps or other learned priors to guide them in navigation and search. To advance robots’ capabilities in this respect, we introduce a dataset to benchmark decision-making in navigation based on signage. Our dataset collates a wide variety of “missions” across diverse public spaces in Singapore (Fig. 1 ). Each “mission” is a multi-step navigation task, requiring an agent to accurately perceive and interpret information from signage, then select appropriate navigational decisions based on the interpreted information (Fig. ). We posit that a benchmark for this task can drive progress in mapless navigation using powerful semantic cues already embedded in everyday environments, empowering robots to navigate open-world, human-centric environments.

Mapless navigation is a crucial ability for autonomous agents and has attracted significant interest in recent years ( [ 2 , 9 , 16 ] ). As navigational signs enable humans to navigate unfamiliar environments without maps, robots can similarly exploit signs for mapless navigation in the open world. The first step for sign-based navigation is grounding the navigational signs - associating a location with a navigational instruction and then mapping it to a physical region in the agent’s local environment, based on visual input. Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) offer the semantic common-sense and reasoning capabilities required for this task, with a few emerging works building on foundation models to tackle this problem of sign-based navigation. [ 1 ] formalized the problem of Navigational Sign Understanding , where navigational signs were decomposed into pairs including a location and its associated direction. [ 18 ] utilized navigational sign understanding to globally localize in a large-scale topological map, matching the extracted spatio-semantic information to nodes in the graph. Both [ 10 ] and [ 6 ] proposed to use navigational signs for navigation in human-built environments, but targeted only simplified signs that do not represent the complexity of real-world signage. Due to perception limitations, signs were assumed to have straightforward design where arrows can be associated with locations in a rule-based fashion, only a few canonical directions were considered ( ← , ↑ , → ) (\leftarrow,\uparrow,\rightarrow) and instructions that are conveyed through symbols (i.e. up-the-stairs) were ignored. [ 5 ] also proposed a sign-based navigation approach, although they assumed that the semantic content of the signs is already extracted. [ 7 ] presented a signage-aware exploration where shop names were used as landmarks in order to optimize the coverage, given a list of goal landmarks. Recently, [ 19 ] extended the formulation of Navigational Sign Understanding beyond cardinal directions, to include navigational instructions such as “up-escalator”. Additionally they formulated the problem of Visual Sign Grounding , which maps a location and its associated navigational instruction into a region in the sign’s local environment. Overall, although prior work has explored navigation by following sequences of signs and making decisions at each one, the problem remains challenging: most approaches rely on unrealistic assumptions about sign formats or perceptual capabilities that do not hold in real-world settings.

While the problem is drawing interest from the research community, only a small sign-related dataset was provided by [ 1 ] , exclusively targeting navigation sign understanding. This dataset includes 160 images of signs and addresses sign parsing - the task of associating a location with a navigational instruction. In contrast to our dataset, it does not tackle the problem of grounding the instruction in the physical world and does not include information about the environment around each sign. [ 14 ] provide a Habitat-based ( Savva et al., 2019 ) simulation with real-world scans from public spaces. The simulation is intended for testing behavioral controllers and highlights signs as an important source of information for decision making. However, the environments conform to a Manhattan world structure and the behavior primitives are limited to ( ← , ↑ , → ) (\leftarrow,\uparrow,\rightarrow) , reflecting the simplistic, visually uniform and auto-generated signage that only includes these 3 directions and no goal locations or symbols. In essence, the arrows were used as a visual stimuli for behaviors, without associating a goal with the desired navigational instruction. Lin et al. (2025) provides more realistic embodied simulation with Isaac Sim ( NVIDIA Corporation, 2026 ) . Both simulation benchmarks are limited to static, generic and limited environments that do not reflect the difficulty of navigating in crowded, visually and topologically distinct human-oriented spaces and does not include realistic signage.
While real-world navigation experiments can capture the complexity of operating in human-oriented environments, they are expensive, platform dependent and unreproducible. VQA datasets attempt to fill the gap by collecting real-world data from complex environments while remaining platform agnostic. NaviTrace ( Windecker et al., 2025 ) is a recent VQA-style benchmark for evaluating whether VLMs understand embodied navigation: given an image, a natural-language instruction, and an embodiment type such as human, legged robot, wheeled robot, or bicycle, the model must output a 2D navigation trace, with results showing that current VLMs still lag behind humans due to poor spatial grounding and goal localization. Nevertheless, NaviTrace evaluates each scenario in isolation, and it does not include a long-range navigation mission that requires sequential decision-making.

This dataset maintains the VQA format, but requires reasoning on a sequence of observations collected around the navigational sign, capturing dynamics and 3D scene information. The dataset includes synchronized and timestamped range, visual, inertial and odometric measurements, collected in multiple public spaces in Singapore, such as malls, hospitals, campus buildings, transportation hubs and outdoor areas. As shown in Figure 1 , these public spaces cover many of the environments that humans navigate daily, and enabling mapless navigation in such environments will greatly improve the autonomy of mobile agents.
In addition to data from the hand-held device, multiple venue maps of the test site are included. The dataset goes beyond single-step visual sign grounding, by introducing long-horizon missions with multi-step decision making.

Our dataset distinguishes itself from other datasets
described in the literature in several ways. Specifically, it
provides:

Real-world sign-centric scenarios for visual sign grounding

Complex, topologically and visually distinct environments capturing the difficulty of reasoning about navigational actions in human-built spaces

Multi-step structure for mapless, sign-centric long-range navigation missions

Apart from simply benchmarking decision-making, we hope that this dataset can be further useful to researchers seeking to answer critical questions around using signage for mapless navigation in novel environments, including:

How can navigational signage be perceived and interpreted, and how can its instructions be grounded to concrete actions?

How can common-sense priors be useful for interpreting navigational signage and grounding their instructions?

How can navigational systems effectively identify and recover from failures in decision-making?

How can complex, hierarchical human goal specifications be related to the observed navigational cues?

# 2 Benchmark Tasks and Intended Use

## 2.1 Navigational Sign Understanding

Following the definition of Navigational Sign Understanding from Agrawal et al. (2026) , we define a navigational sign as a navigational aid that contains information about places and their associated navigational instruction. This spatio-symbolic information can be extracted as a collection of tuples, where each tuple associates a location L j L_{j} with a navigational instruction I j I_{j} . For the benchmark evaluation, we compare the location-instruction associations of selected locations with manually labeled ground truth labels.

## 2.2 Visual Sign Grounding

We borrow the formulation for visual sign grounding from Zimmerman et al. (2026b) and define it as a mapping of a location and its associated navigational instruction to a region in the sign’s local coordinate system. For the benchmark evaluation, we frame the visual sign grounding problem as a multiple-choice question where path options are provided (Fig. 4 ) for a queried location.
The format of the VQA and how it can be processed is detailed in Sec. 4 .

## 2.3 Multi-Step Decision Making for Navigation

While Zimmerman et al. (2026b) viewed the visual sign grounding problem for each scenario in isolation, this dataset introduces a multi-step VQA challenge, chaining decision making and action prediction into a long-range visual navigation task. The action prediction in each scenario will dictate which scenario will be encountered next, with the purpose of completing multi-step sign-based navigation to a destination.

Each environment in the dataset is represented as a sign-centric topological graph (Fig. ), where edges represent navigational behaviors, such as turning right, going up the stairs, etc. Nodes in the graph belong to one of two types; scenario nodes that contain a sequence recorded around a sign, and terminal nodes representing a destination point. Each scenario node includes raw data and a multiple-choice VQA-style annotations indicating the potential actions. Once an action is chosen, the next scenario is rolled out based on the sign-centric topological graph.
The benchmark is primarily evaluated on missions - multi-step VQAs driven by a destination. For each mission with a starting node and destination, there exists an optimal path on the graph to the goal node, based on the navigational instructions encoded in the signs. Upon reaching a terminal node that corresponds to the destination, the mission is completed.
Both the sign-centric topological graph and the VQA are manually annotated.

For each environment we attempt to collect as many signs as possible and achieve high coverage. From the places indicated in the signs, we sample our destinations. We create a subgraph with all nodes in the topological graph that contain a reference to a specific destination. We then select the furthest node as the starting node and compute the sign-optimal path (Fig. 3 ) on the subgraph as our ground truth for the multi-task VQA.
Our missions can be categorized into three different levels in terms of reasoning effort. The easiest missions include a simple goal description such as ”COM1”, which appears explicitly in all nodes on the optimal path. The medium-effort missions include a simple goal description such as ”COM2”, which may appear implicitly in signs under descriptions such as ”COM1-COM3”. The hardest missions include a complex language instruction such as ”go to programming lab 4 in the COM1 building”. This requires decomposition to subgoals prior to the visual sign grounding.

2026-10-08.title: Precise SE(3) End-Effector Tracking in Whole-Body Humanoid Control
2026-10-08.authors: Joohwan Seo , Xiaofeng Guo , Jinkun Cao , Roberto Horowitz , Rocky Duan , Guanya Shi , Koushil Sreenath
2026-10-08.abstract:
Precise end-effector tracking during humanoid whole-body motion is challenging due to floating-base oscillations, gravity, dynamic coupling, and locomotion-induced disturbances. We propose ResGAC , a whole-body humanoid controller for precise end-effector pose tracking that combines geometric admittance control (GAC) with residual reinforcement learning. GAC provides structured S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) task-space feedback and generates nominal arm joint-position targets, while residual RL compensates for unmodeled dynamics and coordinates locomotion and balance in the shared joint-position action space. The left-invariant geometric formulation allows the same GAC law to be used across manipulation reference frames. This enables the use of a ground-attached heading frame that preserves planar locomotion while removing pelvis roll, pitch, and heave from the manipulation reference, thereby reducing reference-induced end-effector motion during locomotion.
ResGAC is validated on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across four standing end-effector tracking benchmarks, ResGAC consistently outperforms representative baselines, including SONIC, achieving lower translational and rotational errors. Real-world experiments further demonstrate reduced propagation of pelvis motion to the desired end-effector pose using the proposed ground-attached heading frame. ResGAC achieves 90 % 90\% success in a standing peg-in-hole task compared with 50 % 50\% for SONIC, and accurate world-frame S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) end-effector pose tracking during lower-body motion. Experimental videos are included in the supplementary material and are also available on the project website: https://resgac.github.io/ResGAC-website/ .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Recent advances in learning-based humanoid control have enabled increasingly versatile whole-body behaviors through large-scale motion tracking [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . However, manipulation via humanoid robots requires more than motion naturalness: the robot needs to accurately track commanded end-effector poses while performing locomotion and maintaining balance. This is challenging because manipulation is coupled with base oscillations, gravity, whole-body dynamics, and foot-impact disturbances, particularly for end-effector tracking in S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) where both translational and rotational precision are required.

Most humanoid controllers are built around dense motion-tracking objectives [ 4 , 5 ] , whereas manipulation tasks are often more naturally specified through sparse workspace commands. Recent works, such as [ 6 , 7 , 3 ] , therefore move toward task-space end-effector interfaces, allowing the controller to resolve the remaining whole-body motion. Related works further investigate direct end-effector regulation [ 8 ] , including S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) pose tracking for mobile manipulation in quadrupeds [ 9 ] and end-effector stabilization against locomotion-induced disturbances in humanoids [ 10 , 11 ] . Recent approaches extend this task-space perspective to physical interaction through controllable compliance and force-adaptive control [ 12 , 13 ] . Nevertheless, high-precision tracking of the end-effector pose in S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) , jointly accounting for translational and rotational accuracy during humanoid whole-body motion, remains comparatively under-emphasized.

Residual learning provides a practical mechanism for combining structured priors with the robustness of learned whole-body control. Existing approaches employ different forms of such priors: A pretrained general motion-tracking policy is refined through residual RL in [ 14 ] , while joint-space residual corrections around an inverse kinematics (IK)-derived kinematic prior are learned in [ 7 ] . An IK-derived joint-position reference is similarly corrected in joint space, while model-based feedforward and gravity-compensation torques are separately incorporated into the final control command [ 15 ] in quadruped loco-manipulation.
In [ 11 ] , operational-space compensation and task-control torques are analytically derived but used only to guide the training of a policy whose deployed action is represented in joint space.

The choice of manipulation reference frame is another important consideration for whole-body end-effector control. A natural choice is the pelvis frame. However, command representation on the pelvis frame transmits periodic pelvis roll, pitch, and vertical motion during locomotion to the desired end-effector pose. Recent humanoid-control implementations [ 16 , 3 ] address part of this issue using a heading frame, which retains the floating base position and yaw while removing its roll and pitch.

Motivated by these observations, we propose ResGAC, a framework for precise S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) end-effector tracking
in whole-body humanoid control. An explicit geometric admittance controller (GAC) [ 17 , 18 ] is formulated on the floating base to generate nominal joint-position targets from S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) task-space feedback, and residual RL is applied in the same joint-position action space, allowing the learned correction to be directly composed with the structured feedback command while compensating for unmodeled dynamics and coordinating locomotion and balance. In addition, the left-invariant geometric formulation [ 18 ] allows the same GAC law to be utilized across manipulation reference frames. We introduce a ground-attached heading frame that additionally prevents vertical pelvis motion from propagating to the desired end-effector pose through the manipulation reference while retaining the planar motion of the humanoid.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We propose ResGAC , integrating floating-base geometric admittance control (GAC) with residual RL in a shared joint-position action space, combining geometric S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) task-space feedback with learned corrections for whole-body control.

The left-invariant GAC formulation is extended across manipulation reference frames, and a ground-attached heading frame is introduced to
prevent pelvis roll, pitch, and heave from propagating to the desired end-effector pose while preserving planar locomotion.

ResGAC is validated on the real-world Unitree G1 through end-effector position-and-orientation tracking, static arm-holding during walking, peg-in-hole manipulation, and world-frame tracking, consistently outperforming representative baselines, including SONIC [ 3 ] .

1. We propose ResGAC , integrating floating-base geometric admittance control (GAC) with residual RL in a shared joint-position action space, combining geometric S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) task-space feedback with learned corrections for whole-body control.

2. The left-invariant GAC formulation is extended across manipulation reference frames, and a ground-attached heading frame is introduced to
prevent pelvis roll, pitch, and heave from propagating to the desired end-effector pose while preserving planar locomotion.

3. ResGAC is validated on the real-world Unitree G1 through end-effector position-and-orientation tracking, static arm-holding during walking, peg-in-hole manipulation, and world-frame tracking, consistently outperforming representative baselines, including SONIC [ 3 ] .

2026-10-08.title: TMT: Runtime Backdoor Detection for Vision-Language-Action Policies on Unseen Tasks
2026-10-08.authors: Zirun Zhou , Jingfeng Zhang , HaoChuan Xu , Xizhe Zhang , Elliott Wen , Jing Sun , Hong Jia
2026-10-08.abstract: Backdoored vision-language-action (VLA) policies can preserve benign task performance while producing malicious actions when a trigger appears. Detecting such activation is difficult because malicious behavior can comprise individually plausible actions, while unfamiliar tasks introduce legitimate changes in observations and behavior. We introduce TMT, a runtime backdoor detector based on T oken M anifold and latent T ransition modeling. Trained on benign rollouts, its two branches assess input-token structure and prediction errors in adjacent-layer latent dynamics. A suspicious rollout identified by the token manifold branch, once confirmed through latent deviations, guides transition selection for subsequent monitoring. We further explore policy purification through self-distillation: a frozen copy of the backdoored policy provides benign-input actions to supervise a student on paired benign and triggered observations, without requiring a separate clean reference policy. For evaluation, we adapt traditional backdoor detectors and repurpose anomaly and failure detection methods as VLA backdoor detectors. In a post-hoc comparison with ten baselines, TMT achieves state-of-the-art backdoor detection performance on unseen tasks across three VLA backdoor attacks. Our project page is available at https://zzr42.github.io/tmt/ .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies translate visual observations and language instructions into robot
actions ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . A compromised policy can retain its performance on benign inputs while changing its behavior when a trigger appears. Recent attacks demonstrate that backdoor activation can disrupt task execution, redirect the robot toward an attacker-specified goal, or induce an undesired low-level action ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025b ) . For example, backdoor activation could cause a robot to suddenly drop a knife it is holding, posing a physical safety risk. This coupling between backdoor activation and physical execution motivates runtime backdoor detection in VLA policies.

Existing inference-time backdoor detectors for classifiers assess suspicious inputs by examining how class predictions respond to input perturbations ( Gao et al., 2019 ; Liu et al., 2023b ) . VLA policies, however, generate task-conditioned control actions, and backdoor activation need not produce a fixed target output across states and timesteps. We consider four requirements for runtime backdoor detection in this setting. ① The detector must learn from benign rollouts without prior knowledge of the trigger pattern or access to the VLA policy’s original training process. ② The detector must distinguish backdoor-induced behavior from benign execution even when both involve the same actions. This distinction depends on which goal the resulting sequence serves. ③ The detector must generalize to unseen tasks without mistaking legitimate changes in observations and behavior for backdoor activation. ④ The detector must identify backdoor activation with minimal delay after trigger onset.

To address these challenges, we introduce TMT , an inference-time backdoor detector that combines T oken M anifold and latent T ransition modeling using internal representations of the deployed VLA policy (Figure 1 ). TMT examines both the structure of input-token representations and how these representations evolve across backbone layers. Our t-SNE visualizations show that the input-token representations of triggered queries are shifted relative to those of benign queries in the projected space, while the two groups still overlap (Figure 2 ). This motivates examining layer-wise transitions alongside token structure. Trained on benign rollouts, the token manifold branch assesses token structure conditioned on the preceding policy query, while the latent transition branch scores prediction errors in adjacent-layer latent dynamics. Both branches evaluate each policy query, and TMT raises an alarm when either score exceeds its calibrated threshold.

In this paper, we focus on detecting backdoor activation on unseen manipulation tasks, with TMT fitted using benign rollouts from seen tasks. For comparison, we adapt traditional backdoor detectors ( Gao et al., 2019 ; Liu et al., 2023b ; Hou et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) and repurpose anomaly and failure detection methods ( Ruff et al., 2018 ; Burda et al., 2018 ; He et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025a ; Römer et al., 2026 ) for detecting backdoor activation (see Appendix A ). Detectors are fitted using benign rollouts from three LIBERO-10 tasks ( Liu et al., 2023a ) and evaluated on the remaining tasks under BadVLA ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) , GoBA ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and DropVLA ( Xu et al., 2025b ) . In the post-hoc comparison, TMT achieves the highest or joint-highest trigger detection rates (TDRs) of 100 % 100\% , 83.43 % 83.43\% , and 73.6 % 73.6\% , respectively, with observed false-rejection rates (FRRs) of 0.57 % 0.57\% , 8.57 % 8.57\% , and 0 % 0\% . Branch ablations show that, for GoBA and DropVLA, the token manifold branch provides broader detection coverage on tasks represented during fitting, whereas the latent transition branch provides broader coverage on unseen tasks. We further examine detection in real-world robot execution, and observe that TMT achieves a TDR of 100 % 100\% with an observed FRR of 0 % 0\% .

Beyond detection, we explore policy purification through self-distillation without a separate clean reference policy. A frozen copy of the backdoored policy serves as the teacher, and the student is initialized from the same checkpoint. We execute the teacher’s benign-input actions in both benign and triggered environments, collecting paired observations under a shared action history. The student is trained to reproduce each benign-input action from both observations. Results show that original-task success rates under triggered inputs increase to 92.2 92.2 – 95.5 % 95.5\% , while benign-input success rates change by at most 2.2 % 2.2\% . Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce TMT, an inference-time VLA backdoor detector that combines input-token structure and latent dynamics learned from benign rollouts.

We propose policy purification through self-distillation without a separate clean reference policy, using the victim’s benign-input actions to supervise paired benign and triggered observations.

We adapt existing detection methods to VLA backdoor detection and evaluate them under three kinds of VLA backdoor attacks. Our post-hoc results show strong backdoor detection performance on unseen tasks.

1. We introduce TMT, an inference-time VLA backdoor detector that combines input-token structure and latent dynamics learned from benign rollouts.

2. We propose policy purification through self-distillation without a separate clean reference policy, using the victim’s benign-input actions to supervise paired benign and triggered observations.

3. We adapt existing detection methods to VLA backdoor detection and evaluate them under three kinds of VLA backdoor attacks. Our post-hoc results show strong backdoor detection performance on unseen tasks.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Backdoor attacks on VLA policies implant trigger-dependent control behaviors while preserving benign performance. BadVLA ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) uses objective-decoupled optimization to separate triggered and benign visual representations and induce control deviations. GoBA ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) poisons demonstrations with physical-object triggers to redirect high-level goals, whereas DropVLA ( Xu et al., 2025b ) relabels selected action targets to induce low-level failures such as premature gripper opening. Attack demonstrations appear in Appendix E . These attacks expose the need for runtime detection across different malicious behaviors. TMT addresses this need by monitoring token manifolds and latent transitions without assuming a specific target action.

Existing detectors screen inputs through prediction responses or representation statistics. STRIP ( Gao et al., 2019 ) measures prediction entropy under perturbations, while TeCo ( Liu et al., 2023b ) compares the corruption severity needed to change predicted labels across corruption types. DeDe ( Hou et al., 2025 ) uses decoder reconstruction errors to screen inputs to self-supervised encoders; DUP-MS ( Hu et al., 2026 ) combines class-agnostic Mahalanobis distances with spectral statistics of inter-layer feature differences. Concurrent work, TrustVLA ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , uses token- and layer-wise epistemic uncertainty for VLA detection. STRIP, TeCo, DeDe, and DUP-MS were originally developed for image or language models. We adapt them to VLA backdoor detection, but our post-hoc comparison shows limited detection on unseen tasks, whereas TMT achieves higher TDRs.

Learning a reference distribution from normal data provides a basis for detecting previously unseen deviations. Deep SVDD ( Ruff et al., 2018 ) scores learned representations by distance from a hypersphere center, while RND ( Burda et al., 2018 ) measures prediction error against fixed random features. ReDiffuser ( He et al., 2024 ) uses RND confidence to guide diffusion-based planning. LogPZO ( Xu et al., 2025a ) models successful-rollout observations with a flow and scores their inferred latent noise. FIPER ( Römer et al., 2026 ) requires both embedding-space RND and action-chunk entropy to exceed calibrated thresholds over short windows. These methods struggle to distinguish benign execution on unseen tasks from trigger-induced execution. Our post-hoc results show that TMT distinguishes these cases more effectively.

2026-10-08.title: RobotAPO: Adversarial Physics Preference Optimization for Robotic Manipulation Video Generation
2026-10-08.authors: Kerui Li , Zhe Jing , Chenyi Huang , Xiaofeng Wang , Zheng Zhu , Haoming Cui , Huaibo Huang
2026-10-08.abstract:
Robotic manipulation videos are increasingly used as visual plans for embodied agents, but optimizing purely for visual plausibility often fails to capture the fragile physical manifold of real-world interactions.
Even minor physics-violating errors at the interaction boundary, such as interpenetration or premature object motion, can completely invalidate the inferred timing and pose needed for downstream execution.
Because standard supervised fine-tuning lacks the direct pressure to penalize these localized failures, we introduce \texorpdfstring AgiBot-PhysPref AgiBot-PhysPref.
This rigorously curated 10,000 10{,}000 -sample preference dataset isolates condition-matched physics-violations, turning the generator’s own failure distribution into a foundational signal for physical consistency.
Building upon this, we propose \texorpdfstring RobotAPO RobotAPO, an adversarial physics preference optimization framework operating in the continuous flow-matching denoising space.
To prevent the policy from merely memorizing static curated failures, \texorpdfstring RobotAPO RobotAPO employs a lightweight adversarial counterfactual proposer that learns a condition-dependent, physical-failure-biased direction in denoising space.
This encourages the model to explore and better respect the physical interaction boundary, all while maintaining a pure prompt-and-reference inference interface without requiring external structural conditioning.
Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that explicitly correcting these localized physics-violations improves downstream robot execution from generated videos.
On held-out AgiBot conditions, \texorpdfstring RobotAPO RobotAPO outperforms the strongest controlled internal baseline in physical consistency by 6.8 % 6.8\% hard score and 10.0 % 10.0\% soft score.
Crucially, in real-robot replay, it translates these physical-consistency gains into a 37.4 % 37.4\% relative improvement in task success over the strongest controlled internal baseline.

2026-10-08.title: TempoBridge: Language-Guided Tempo Control for Vision-Language-Action Policies
2026-10-08.authors: Yeonseo Lee , Hyosup Shin , Guebin Hwang , Sungho Jo
2026-10-08.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are effective at understanding what task to perform, but provide limited control over how it should be executed, such as moving quickly or slowly.
We introduce TempoBridge, a lightweight framework that uses frozen VLA representations to modulate actions according to tempo cues in the instruction at each task phase,
without additional tempo-conditioned robot demonstrations or tempo-specific base-policy fine-tuning.
TempoBridge extracts tempo cues from contextual VLM representations,
aligns them with task progress through a causal phase router, and modulates nominal motion commands during execution.
Across LIBERO tasks, TempoBridge improves Tempo Success Rate from 52.6% to 89.7% under canonical tempo instructions while retaining high task success.
It also preserves near-baseline performance when no tempo cue is present and generalizes to unseen tempo expressions without additional training.
Experiments on a physical robot further demonstrate language-conditioned tempo modulation in real-world manipulation.
Project page: https://lysees.github.io/tempobridge-page/
2026-10-08.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a promising
paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, enabling a single policy to
execute diverse tasks from natural-language instructions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Existing VLAs increasingly understand what to do, but provide limited control over how to execute it [ 4 , 5 ] .
In many practical settings, however, execution manner is an important part of
the user’s intent [ 6 , 7 ] .
For example, a robot may be asked to move quickly for efficiency or slowly for deliberate execution.
These preferences may also vary as a task progresses, as in “ quickly pick up the object, then slowly place it on the target .”
In this work, we study this capability as language-conditioned tempo control .

A straightforward approach is to train a policy on trajectories associating tempo instructions with execution speeds.
However, collecting demonstrations at different speeds is costly and difficult to scale across tasks, objects, and environments [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
Temporal augmentation can reduce the cost of collecting additional demonstrations [ 4 ] , but incorporating the augmented trajectories into the policy still requires computationally expensive fine-tuning [ 11 ] .

Pretrained VLA representations may already encode semantic distinctions associated with manner expressions such as quickly and slowly, and prior work has shown that internal features related to such concepts can be identified and manipulated to influence VLA behavior [ 5 ] .
This raises the possibility of using semantic tempo information available in the frozen representation as an interface for execution control, rather than learning tempo interpretation entirely from newly collected robot trajectories.
The key challenge is to connect these semantic tempo cues to an explicit execution-time control mechanism while accounting for task progress.
We therefore ask: Can semantic tempo cues from a frozen VLA be connected to execution-time motion modulation, enabling language-conditioned tempo control without tempo-specific robot demonstrations or policy fine-tuning?

To address this question, we introduce TempoBridge , a lightweight framework that reads semantic tempo information from a frozen VLA’s internal language representations and connects it to phase-aware motion modulation.
TempoBridge takes a frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy [ 12 ] as its base policy and uses a prototype-based tempo readout to extract a compact tempo sequence from the instruction.
When the requested tempo varies within a task, a causal phase router aligns this sequence with task progress using visual features reused from the policy and robot-state history.
The selected tempo then modulates the nominal motion commands during closed-loop execution.
The base VLA continues to generate the nominal task actions,
while TempoBridge modulates their execution according to the requested tempo and estimated task phase.

This design keeps the pretrained policy fixed while separating tempo interpretation and phase estimation from nominal action generation. The tempo readout is constructed from text examples, whereas the phase router is trained on existing task demonstrations annotated with phase-transition intervals, without tempo labels.
Consequently, TempoBridge requires neither tempo-conditioned robot demonstrations nor tempo-specific fine-tuning of the base policy.
When no tempo cue is detected, the readout returns NORMAL and the nominal actions remain unchanged.
Because the readout operates on contextual VLM representations, the same fixed readout can also be applied to previously unseen tempo expressions without retraining.

We evaluate TempoBridge on 40 manipulation tasks across the Spatial, Object, Goal, and Long suites of LIBERO [ 13 ] .
TempoBridge raises Tempo Success Rate from 52.6% to 89.7% under canonical quickly/slowly instructions,
while preserving near-baseline performance without tempo cues and improving tempo compliance for unseen expressions.
Real-robot experiments further validate language-conditioned tempo modulation.

Our main contributions are:

We formulate language-conditioned tempo control for frozen VLAs and investigate whether semantic tempo cues in their internal representations can serve as an interface for execution-time motion modulation, without additional tempo-conditioned robot demonstrations or tempo-specific base-policy fine-tuning.

We introduce TempoBridge , a lightweight framework that combines prototype-based tempo readout, causal phase routing, and execution-time action modulation while keeping the entire base policy frozen.

We evaluate physical tempo compliance, task competence under original instructions, and transfer to unseen tempo expressions across 40 LIBERO tasks, and further validate TempoBridge in real-world manipulation experiments with a physical robot.

# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Models

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models transfer semantic and world knowledge from pretrained vision-language models into robotic control. RT-2 [ 1 ] established this paradigm by co-finetuning web-scale VLMs with robot trajectories in a shared token space, and subsequent generalist policies scaled language-conditioned manipulation across heterogeneous embodiments [ 14 , 2 ] or coupled pretrained representations with continuous action experts for dexterous, long-horizon execution [ 3 , 12 ] . Across these paradigms, however, language specifies what should be achieved, while how an action is executed remains implicit in the demonstration distribution. Temporal characteristics such as speed or caution, therefore, do not surface as explicit control variables, even though the corresponding linguistic concepts are plausibly already represented in the pretrained backbone.

## II-B Controlling Execution in Pretrained VLAs

Approaches to controlling how a policy executes differ mainly in what part of the system they modify, and therefore in what supervision they require.

One line modifies data and weights. Language motions as an intermediate action representation, counterfactual relabeling, and semantically aligned action tokenizers [ 7 , 15 , 16 ] all learn how a linguistic modifier maps to physical execution from robot trajectories. TempoVLA [ 4 ] conditions on an explicit speed scalar and re-times demonstrations by temporal augmentation, with a VLM scheduler dispatching per-chunk speeds at deployment. This still requires retraining the policy, and tempo arrives as a numeric input from an external module.

A second line intervenes on a frozen policy’s internal activations, differing in how the directions are identified [ 5 , 17 , 18 ] and how the intervention is regulated once found [ 19 , 20 ] . Häon et al. [ 5 ] show that linguistic concepts such as slow survive VLA training in the backbone and remain causally linked to end-effector motion, though they identify features heuristically by token similarity and steer by overriding their activations with a selected coefficient rather than a physically interpretable execution variable. Buurmeijer et al. [ 17 ] make such intervention systematic by training linear observers for robot states and actions and computing the minimal representation-space edit that places an observed feature inside a desired interval. In both cases, the target is an externally specified number rather than read from language, and identifying the directions requires either manual inspection or labeled robot data.
CTRL-STEER [ 19 ] instead regulates the magnitude of the intervention online with a feedback controller, although the target concept is still supplied externally and the controller is fitted per task.

In contrast, TempoBridge reads tempo cues from the language instruction through frozen VLA representations and connects them to phase-aware motion modulation, without tempo-conditioned demonstrations or tempo-specific VLA fine-tuning.

2026-10-08.title: IVG-UAV: An Intelligent Voice-Guided UAV System for Autonomous Ripe Fruit Harvesting with Vision-Based Classification and Adaptive Path Planning
2026-10-08.authors: Dinh Trung Duong
2026-10-08.abstract: In tropical regions, their agricultural sectors remain highly dependent on manual labor for fruit harvesting. On large-scale farms, this dependency often results in significant labor cost and logistic complexities. This project presents the development and simulation of a voice-controlled Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) system designed to automate harvesting tasks in extensive plantations. The proposed system integrates speech recognition using Whisper [ 1 ] and LLM, computer vision–based ripeness classification, and adaptive path planning within a unified framework. The entire system is modeled and validated in a Gazebo simulation environment, allowing performance evaluation under controlled agricultural scenarios.
2026-10-08.introduction:
In tropical nations, their agricultural sectors remain highly dependent on manual labor for fruit harvesting. On large-scale farms, this dependency often results in significant labor cost and logistic complexities. With recent developments, robots have been introduced to reduce this burden as well as improve the productivity. A diversity of harvesting robots have been significantly investigated ranging from ground-based mobile manipulators to aerial platforms such as unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). These systems are mostly equipped with vision-assisted technologies, enabling fruit detection, ripeness classification, and localization through advanced computer vision and deep learning algorithms. However, the majority of existing robots depends on fully automated programming paradigms, where robots autonomously navigate and search for ripe fruits based solely on pre-defined algorithms and perception models. This leads to the lack of real-time human interaction and adaptability, particularly during the fruit-searching and decision-making stages. This functionality allows the robot to adapt its flight trajectory according to user instructions. Additionally, it enables the UAV to handle edge cases through human intervention. This project proposes the integration of voice-guided interaction into the robotic system. This human-in-the-loop approach allows adaptive decision-making during the harvesting process, which enhances operational flexibility. To address the existing challenges, this work introduces IVG-UAV, a unified voice-guided UAV harvesting pipeline that integrates speech recognition, LLM-based command interpretation, vision-based fruit detection using YOLOv8 and RGB-D sensing, and adaptive path planning for autonomous navigation in orchard environments.

Figure 1 illustrates the overall functionality of the proposed voice-guided interactive harvesting system. The framework integrates aerial perception, obstacle-aware navigation, adaptive task planning, and human-in-the-loop voice interaction into a unified architecture for intelligent fruit harvesting. Initially, the UAV performs journey exploration of the orchard and scans fixed trees using vision system. Robot performs a thorough scan by applying row-following strategy, that ensures all the trees in the farm are scanned. Unlike fully autonomous harvesting systems, the proposed framework enables real-time human guidance through voice commands. The operator can issue high-level instructions such as “Harvest all the ripe fruits” or “Take ripe fruits from three trees.” These commands are processed by a speech recognition module and translated into structured task constraints that influence the target selection and planning modules. During visiting a tree, a drone system can use vision perception to classify the ripe fruits and can actually detach them from the tree. In a flight journey, UAV system can avoid obstacles to find a target tree and using RRT* [ 2 ] algorithm to find the shortest path that leads to the next target tree.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related works

## II-A Vision-assisted Avocado Harvesting UAV

In order to harvest avocados, this paper developed a vision-assisted robotic harvesting system which utilizes an aerial robot with a bimanual manipulation mechanism. The device integrates a dual-arm UAV manipulator with a gripper arm and a fixer arm with computer vision for avocado detection and posture estimation. A motion planner uses the location and orientation of the avocados determined by the visual perception module to direct the robotic arms. The gripper arm rotates to effectively separate the avocado while the fixer arm holds the fruit stem in place during harvesting. The system can recognize and pick avocados on its own in outdoor settings, according to experimental data, demonstrating the promise of aerial robotic manipulation for agricultural automation. [ 3 ]

## II-B Deep learning–based computer vision with robotic manipulation

This work suggested an intelligent robotic harvesting system that combines robotic manipulation and deep learning-based computer vision for automated fruit picking. In order to increase harvesting efficiency, the system focuses on forecasting the best fruit gripping locations. In order to accomplish this, the authors created an image processing pipeline based on deep learning that recognizes apples in pictures and determines the proper gripping area for robotic picking. For fruit recognition, a lightweight one-step object detection network is used, allowing the system to instantly recognize fruits from visual input. The robotic manipulator is then guided by the detected fruit attributes to identify appropriate grabbing places and carry out the harvesting process. [ 4 ]

Both studies focus on automating fruit harvesting using computer vision–based perception and robotic manipulation techniques. In particular, they utilize visual sensing to detect fruits, estimate their position, and guide robotic systems to perform harvesting tasks. Although both strategies significantly rely on computer vision technology, their system architectures are different: the latter focuses on vision-based grasp prediction utilizing lightweight deep learning models for robotic manipulators, whereas the former incorporates aerial robotics with bi-manual manipulation. Despite these differences, both works share similar limitations. The systems lack natural human–robot interaction mechanisms, such as voice-guided instructions, which could allow users to intuitively guide or supervise the harvesting process. This limitation reduces system usability in practical agricultural environments where human workers may need to interact with robotic systems dynamically.
