2026-10-08.title: Immiscible Diffusion Policy: Preserving Multimodal Robot Actions through Label-Free Noise Assignment
2026-10-08.authors: Xiao Zhang , Yuxin Chen , Zhixuan Liang , Guojian Zhan , Chenran Li , Chenfeng Xu , Masayoshi Tomizuka , Yiheng Li
2026-10-08.abstract: When diffusion policies were first introduced, they were expected to recover multi-modal action distributions. However, we find this expectation does not always hold as diffusion policies often collapse to a single modality even when we guarantee the balance of dataset modalities and exact within-batch symmetry. Our analysis indicates that independent action-noise pairing contributes to this failure by increasing mixing and crossing among diffusion paths (the “miscibility” in [ 1 ] ), which can produce averaged denoising responses and suppress modality-specific behavior. It is especially severe in robot planning, as action spaces are dense and low-dimensional, significantly increasing such mixing and crossing. To alleviate this problem, we propose Immiscible Diffusion Policy , a label-free training-time add-on to diffusion policy that uses action-noise assignment to preserve relative distinct noise-to-action routes without modifying policy architecture or inference. Across five simulated and two real-world humanoid manipulation tasks spanning state, RGB, and point-cloud observations, our method significantly improves the policy’s modality preservation while maintaining strong task performance. It increases the non-dominant-modality proportion by 6.0 × 6.0\times - 14.6 × 14.6\times across three two-modality tasks and recovers demonstrated modalities entirely absent from vanilla policy roll-outs on both four-modality tasks. These results demonstrate that Immiscible Diffusion Policy provides a simple yet robust approach to preserving action multi-modality in general robot learning tasks.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Diffusion-based policies have achieved strong performance in robotic manipulation by modeling complex action distributions through iterative denoising [ 2 ] . Because different initial-noise samples can generate different action trajectories, diffusion policies are heuristically expected to preserve multiple valid action modalities. In practice, however, we find that this expectation does not always hold. For example, in Push-T, the T-shaped object is initialized 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} from its target orientation, creating two symmetric action modalities: clockwise and counterclockwise pushing. As shown in the lower rollout comparison of Fig. , a vanilla Diffusion Policy is sampled ten times from this fixed observation, yet all ten generated trajectories follow a single modality. We further repeat this experiment across 10 independent training seeds, enforcing exact symmetry in every batch by pairing each demonstration with its mirrored counterpart. Nevertheless, all 10 vanilla diffusion policies collapse to a single action mode, with the selected mode varying across seeds, as shown in Tab. I (a). This collapse does more than reduce behavioral diversity; it can eliminate alternative actions that become essential when the initially preferred mode is infeasible at deployment.

Preserving action multimodality is therefore important for robust and safe execution under distribution shifts. Because robotic training data cannot cover every deployment condition, changes in obstacles, workspace boundaries, object configurations, or execution constraints may invalidate one demonstrated action mode while leaving another viable. A policy that has collapsed to the invalid mode may consequently fail despite having observed a feasible alternative during training [ 3 ] . This issue also arises in data-rich domains such as autonomous driving, where rare but consequential situations motivate predicting multiple plausible futures for downstream planning [ 4 ] .
Existing approaches often rely on mode-specific supervision, predefined mode structures, or modifications to the policy architecture or inference procedure, making them difficult to apply when action modes are continuous, numerous, or unknown in advance. We therefore seek a label-free method that preserves action modality in existing diffusion policies without requiring the number or semantics of the underlying modes to be specified.

To address this problem, we propose Immiscible Diffusion Policy , a label-free training-time add-on for preserving action multimodality in diffusion policies. Inspired by [ 1 ] , we achieve this by explicit data-noise coupling that helps reduce the mixing and crossing of diffusion paths, thereby keeping each action modality reachable from distinct regions of the Gaussian noise space. We use Hungarian matching to couple action chunks with noise samples during training while leaving the policy architecture and inference procedure unchanged. As illustrated in Fig. , the assignment organizes noise into modality-correlated regions that preserve distinct denoising paths. Across all seven evaluated tasks, Immiscible Diffusion Policy consistently improves action-modality preservation while maintaining strong task performance. Our policy increases the non-dominant-modality proportion in the three simulated two-modality tasks by 6.0 × 6.0\times - 14.6 × 14.6\times . It further recovers demonstrated modalities entirely absent from vanilla policy rollouts on both four-modality tasks and produces a balanced 1 : 1 1{:}1 distribution on two real-world humanoid tasks. Our analyses and ablations further verify that action-modality collapse is strongly connected to diffusion-path mixing in low-dimensional, clustered action spaces and show that action-noise assignment preserves the modality-specific denoising responses needed to keep demonstrated action modalities reachable.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We identify and systematically characterize action-modality collapse in diffusion policies, showing that it occurs even with balanced demonstrations and exact within-batch symmetry. Theoretical and empirical analyses connect this failure to denoising averaging induced by diffusion-path mixing and crossing in low-dimensional, clustered action spaces.

We introduce Immiscible Diffusion Policy, a label-free, training-time-only add-on to diffusion policy that preserves action multimodality without requiring additional modality annotations or modifying the policy architecture and inference procedure.

We demonstrate the effectiveness of Immiscible Diffusion Policy across diverse robotic tasks in simulation and the real world, different policy architectures including Diffusion Policy and 3D Diffusion Policy, and different observation representations. Further ablations show it preserves or restores non-dominant modalities that collapse under the vanilla policy, while keeping the dominant modalities’ success rates almost intact.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Action Multimodality in Robot Learning

Multiple task-equivalent action sequences often exist for the same observation in robot learning [ 5 , 6 ] . Preserving action’s multimodality maintains the behavioral diversity present in demonstrations and can improve robustness by providing alternative strategies under environmental changes or perturbations [ 7 , 3 ] .

To keep this multimodality, prior methods often represent diverse behaviors through different policy formulations. Latent-variable approaches, including Play-LMP and ACT, condition actions on learned latent plans but require a dedicated latent representation [ 7 , 8 ] . Implicit Behavioral Cloning represents alternative actions as distinct low-energy regions at the cost of iterative inference-time optimization [ 5 ] . Behavior Transformer and VQ-BeT instead capture behavioral modes through explicit action discretizations [ 6 , 9 ] .

Diffusion Policy models multimodal action distributions by denoising sampled Gaussian noise into action sequences and has demonstrated both short- and long-horizon multimodality [ 2 ] . This formulation has been extended to point-cloud and goal-conditioned policies [ 10 , 11 ] . Efficiency-oriented alternatives include Hybrid Consistency Policy and Consistency Policy, with the latter reporting reduced Push-T multimodality after distillation [ 12 , 13 ] . IMLE Policy [ 14 ] studies multimodal action generation under limited demonstrations using a single-step alternative, while Deep Diffusion Policy Gradient [ 3 ] explicitly discovers behavior modes for mode-aware online training. Our work identifies a different failure in the standard Diffusion Policy: demonstrated modalities can be suppressed or lost during training despite balanced multimodal data without explicit modality introduction in the model. Our Immiscible Diffusion Policy addresses this collapse through training-only, label-free action-noise assignment, without modifying the policy architecture or inference procedure, requiring pre-specified modalities, or limiting the number of covered modalities.

## II-B Data-Noise Assignment in Diffusion Models

Prior work has explored data-noise assignment to simplify the generative transport learned by diffusion and flow-based models. In flow matching, mini-batch optimal-transport coupling assigns source noise to target data to obtain straighter paths and improve training or sampling efficiency [ 15 , 16 ] . Immiscible Diffusion similarly introduces structured image-noise assignment to reduce diffusion-path mixing [ 1 ] . Improved Immiscible Diffusion further shows that reducing such miscibility simplifies denoising and accelerates diffusion training, primarily in high-dimensional, sparsely distributed image spaces [ 17 ] .

Robot planning operates in a substantially lower-dimensional and denser space than image generation. Consequently, action clusters corresponding to distinct strategies can lie close together and overlap across a broad range of noise levels, making diffusion-path mixing and the resulting modality collapse substantially more pronounced. Motivated by this image-noise coupling principle, our method introduces batch-level action-noise assignment to preserve demonstrated action modalities in conditional diffusion policies. Unlike prior coupling methods that primarily target generative efficiency, our objective is action multimodality preservation, while the policy architecture, noise schedule, and test-time sampler remain unchanged.

2026-10-08.title: COOL: Curiosity-Driven Object Ownership Learning for Personalized Robotic Assistance
2026-10-08.authors: Samira Huber , Ruben Hammele , Sören Pirk
2026-10-08.comment: Accepted to CoRL 2026
2026-10-08.abstract: Robots are increasingly expected to provide personalized services in everyday environments. To do so, they must ground natural-language commands such as Where is my backpack? or Find my bottle and execute them by reasoning about object instances, people, locations, and ownership. This is challenging because ownership is rarely labeled explicitly and must be inferred from long-term, behavioral evidence of human–object interactions. To address this, we present COOL , a novel robotic framework for autonomously learning object ownership from everyday observations and maintaining a long-term spatial memory of its environment. To keep its memory current, COOL uses an agent-based curiosity-driven data collection strategy that guides the robot toward the most promising locations to gain information and refresh stale observations. Offline experiments, ablation studies, and real-world evaluations show that COOL can infer ownership relations from real-world interactions and use this knowledge for ownership-conditioned navigation and task execution. Code, prompts, and evaluation data are available at: https://samirahuber.github.io/cool .
2026-10-08.introduction:
In everyday human environments, robots are increasingly tasked with providing personalized services through natural-language commands. In such settings, users may issue instructions such as Where is Simba’s backpack? or Find my bottle . Executing such commands requires more than object detection and navigation: the robot must identify the intended object instance, determine who it is associated with, and know where it is likely to be located.
This is particularly challenging in shared environments such as offices or homes, where ownership is often ambiguous because objects may be visually similar, shared, borrowed, or moved over time.
Ownership is rarely directly observable: people do not continuously label their belongings, and ownership can become ambiguous when objects are shared, borrowed, or moved. Object ownership must therefore be inferred indirectly from repeated observations, spatial context, and human–object interactions. A service robot must collect and maintain long-term evidence about people, objects, places, and interactions.

Existing work addresses parts of this problem, but not the full ownership-learning pipeline.
Memory-based navigation systems store spatial, semantic, or temporal observations for object search and embodied question answering, but do not model persistent ownership relations [ 41 , 2 , 20 , 15 , 46 , 65 , 40 ] . Conversely, personalized object-search systems often require explicit user input, demonstrations, or visual references [ 56 , 18 , 7 , 38 , 4 , 25 , 26 , 43 ] . What remains missing is a robotic system that autonomously learns ownership from long-term observations and uses it for task execution.

In this paper, we address this gap by treating ownership as a latent relation inferred from long-term robot observations rather than as an explicit label. Our framework associates repeated detections of people and objects, records human–object interactions, and converts accumulated evidence into ownership-conditioned actions for personalized object search.
Specifically, we present COOL ( C uriosity-Driven O bject O wnership L earning for Personalized Robotic Assistance ), an integrated framework for ownership-aware object search in shared human environments. COOL maintains a long-term spatial memory that links people, object instances, locations, and interaction histories over time. It continuously clusters repeated observations using re-identification, detects human–object interactions as ownership evidence, and records where people and objects have been observed. A curiosity-driven agent guides the robot toward under-observed areas to refresh stale or incomplete memory. At query time, a user-facing agent resolves commands such as Find Simba’s backpack by retrieving relevant observations, inferring likely person–object relations, and selecting the corresponding object instance (see Fig. 1 ).

We evaluate COOL through offline experiments, ablations, and real-world tests in an office environment. These experiments assess the framework’s ability to associate repeated observations of the same people and objects and infer ownership relations from human–object interaction evidence. It updates object locations over time and uses this knowledge for object search and navigation. Combining long-term spatial memory, re-identification, interaction detection, and active data collection enables robots to autonomously acquire ownership knowledge and apply it to personalized tasks.

In summary, the main contributions of this paper are:
(1) Ownership inference : a dynamic framework for inferring person–object ownership from long-term robot observations, without explicit labels, demonstrations, or dialogue.
(2) Persistent spatial memory : a structured memory linking people, object instances, locations, and human–object interaction histories.
(3) Ownership-conditioned task execution : a tool-using agent that answers ownership-conditioned questions and executes navigation commands from memory.
(4) Memory refresh : an autonomous data-collection agent that seeks informative locations and refreshes stale observations.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Memory-based Navigation. Recent work gives embodied agents long-term memory for object search, exploration, and embodied question answering.
These methods store prior observations as maps, graphs, vector memories, or scene graphs, and often combine them with large language models (LLMs) or vision-language models (VLMs) for retrieval and reasoning [ 41 , 2 , 20 , 15 , 46 , 65 ] .
Retrieval-augmented navigation and multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reuse prior episodes or perceptual streams for navigation and temporal reasoning, while general LLM memory systems focus on textual recall and memory consolidation [ 40 , 33 , 42 , 11 , 57 , 6 ] . Unlike prior work, COOL links persistent people, objects, locations, and interaction histories to infer person–object ownership relations for personalized robot assistance. Re-Identification. Visual re-identification links observations of the same entity across time using image embeddings. Many general-purpose backbones provide strong visual features [ 31 , 10 , 48 , 47 ] , while
Person ReID models such as OSNet are optimized for identity matching [ 70 , 71 , 72 ] .
Tracking-by-detection methods link detections across nearby frames using motion, appearance, and confidence cues [ 68 , 12 , 23 ] .
Recent work improves robustness under deployment shift, heterogeneous sensors, and multimodal object appearance [ 63 , 61 , 17 , 62 , 58 , 53 , 14 , 52 , 54 ] . COOL differs by using tracking and re-identification as components of long-term robot memory, linking repeated observations of people and object instances to spatial observations and interaction histories for ownership-conditioned navigation. Object Ownership. Recent work has studied social relations and personalization cues for robotic assistance.
Early systems model owner–object relations with probabilistic inference, visual cues, or demonstrations [ 56 , 18 ] .
Recent personalized search and navigation methods use dialogue, user feedback, open-vocabulary grounding, or image/language-specified object instances [ 7 , 38 , 4 , 25 ] .
Other methods localize personal objects from limited examples or on-device visual matching [ 26 , 43 ] . COOL infers owner–object associations from long-term robot observations and uses them to decide where to search for or navigate to objects associated with a specific person. Human–Object Interaction (HOI). HOI recognition identifies how people interact with objects.
Recent work extends HOI beyond closed-set triplets toward open-vocabulary and open-world recognition with vision-language or multimodal language models [ 28 , 27 , 59 , 49 ] .
Related embodied work uses interaction reasoning for long-horizon hand-object manipulation from language [ 69 ] . In contrast, COOL stores detected interactions with person, object, place, and time information, and uses these histories as evidence for ownership-conditioned navigation.

2026-10-08.title: Learning Unknown Constraints without Unsafe Data via Optimality and Counterfactual Regularization
2026-10-08.authors: Zhouyu Zhang , Chih-Yuan Chiu , Glen Chou
2026-10-08.abstract:
Learning from demonstrations (LfD) provides a framework for inferring unknown constraints from locally optimal, constraint-satisfying expert behavior.
Existing approaches largely fall into two paradigms, constrained inverse optimal control (CIOC) and inverse constrained reinforcement learning (ICRL).
CIOC exploits optimality conditions such as the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions but typically assumes known dynamics and structured constraint representations.
Meanwhile, ICRL accommodates complex unknown constraints and unknown transition dynamics but often requires extensive online exploration, during which unsafe constraint violations may occur.
In this work, we introduce Counterfactual KKT (CF-KKT), a constraint learning framework that leverages learned dynamics and locally optimal demonstrations to recover unknown constraints without requiring known dynamics or additional risky exploration, thereby combining the data efficiency and safety advantages of CIOC with the flexibility of ICRL. First, we use a locally learned differentiable dynamics model to impose KKT-inspired optimality conditions directly on the demonstrations. Second, we use the learned dynamics to generate reward-improving counterfactual behaviors near the demonstrations, revealing behaviors that would be preferable in the absence of the unknown constraint and thus providing synthetic infeasible data. When the constraint parameterization is known, the same learned-dynamics framework enables direct CIOC-based parameter recovery, and we characterize its sensitivity to dynamics misspecification. Across high-dimensional robotic control tasks, our approach learns neural constraint representations with improved safety and data efficiency relative to state-of-the-art offline ICRL baselines.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Autonomous systems deployed in safety-critical
applications, such as autonomous driving and warehouse operations,
must adhere to constraints that encode safety and task specifications ( Altman, 1999 ; Achiam et al., 2017 ; Borkar, 2005 ; Mayne et al., 2000 ; Berberich et al., 2021 ; Magni and Scattolini, 2004 ) .
Given the difficulty of manually engineering such constraints and the advent of data-driven methods,
learning from demonstration (LfD) has attracted increasing attention as a promising framework for recovering constraints from locally optimal and constraint-abiding expert trajectories ( Chou et al., 2020a ; Chou et al., 2022 ; Quan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) .
LfD-based constraint learning paradigms are often either based on inverse optimal control (IOC) ( Englert et al., 2017 ; Keshavarz et al., 2011 ; Johnson et al., 2013 ; Rickenbach et al., 2024 ; Wulfmeier et al., 2017 ; Chou et al., 2020a ; Chou et al., 2020b ; Chou et al., 2018 ) or inverse constrained reinforcement learning (ICRL) ( Scobee and Sastry, 2019 ; McPherson et al., 2021 ; Malik et al., 2021 ; Papadimitriou et al., 2022 ; Liu and Zhu, 2022 ; Liu and Zhu, 2024 ; Park et al., 2020 ; Jang et al., 2023 ) .
IOC-based methods recover constraints by enforcing consistency with the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions that characterize the local optimality of a given set of demonstrations ( Rickenbach et al., 2024 ; Menner et al., 2019 ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chiu et al., 2026 ) under the dynamics models ( Rickenbach et al., 2024 ; Menner et al., 2019 ) and control methodology ( Nguyen et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chiu et al., 2026 ) from which the demonstrations were obtained.
However, such methods assume access to known, smooth system dynamics, which precludes their applicability to high-dimensional, black-box systems.
In contrast, ICRL-based constraint recovery ( Scobee and Sastry, 2019 ; McPherson et al., 2021 ; Malik et al., 2021 ; Papadimitriou et al., 2022 ; Liu and Zhu, 2022 ; Liu and Zhu, 2024 ; Park et al., 2020 ; Jang et al., 2023 ) accommodates unknown dynamics and flexible neural constraint representations.
However, such methods usually require computation- ( McPherson et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) and data-heavy ( Scobee and Sastry, 2019 ; Liu and Zhu, 2022 ; Quan et al., 2024 ) online exploration, may induce unsafe constraint violations during training ( Malik et al., 2021 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Quan et al., 2024 ) , and have few theoretical guarantees of constraint recovery accuracy ( Malik et al., 2021 ; Park et al., 2020 ; Quan et al., 2024 ) .
While recent offline variants ( Quan et al., 2024 ) avoid online exploration during training, they still rely on offline data generated by potentially constraint-violating policies to identify unsafe regions, which can be difficult or unsafe to collect in real-world systems.

In this work, we bridge CIOC and ICRL to enable constraint learning under unknown dynamics and constraint representations without requiring constraint-violating data. Our approach, Counterfactual KKT (CF-KKT) , learns local dynamics from constraint-satisfying expert demonstrations and uses them to combine KKT-inspired optimality conditions with synthetic reward-improving counterfactual trajectories. These counterfactuals provide information about constraint-violating states without requiring constraint-violating trajectories to be executed in the environment. We further show that locally learned dynamics can support CIOC-based parameter recovery when the constraint parameterization is known.
Concretely, our contributions are:

For settings with closed-form a priori known constraint parameterizations, we present a two-stage framework which first learns system dynamics without additional demonstration data, then leverages the learned system dynamics to infer the unknown constraint via CIOC;

For settings with neural network (NN)-represented constraints, we introduce Counterfactual KKT (CF-KKT), which combines KKT-inspired optimality conditions with model-generated counterfactual trajectories to learn unknown constraints without observed constraint-violating data;

We present a theoretical analysis of the sensitivity of the recovered constraints to system dynamics misspecification;

We evaluate CF-KKT in simulation across low- and high-dimensional systems with black-box dynamics, demonstrating improved constraint recovery and downstream safety over existing offline ICRL methods while structurally using
less data, all of which are safe.

# 2 Related Work

Our work relates most closely to constrained inverse optimal control (CIOC), which infers constraints from expert demonstrations using Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) optimality conditions ( Englert et al., 2017 ; Keshavarz et al., 2011 ; Johnson et al., 2013 ; Rickenbach et al., 2024 ; Chou et al., 2020a ; Chou et al., 2018 ; Menner et al., 2019 ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Chou et al., 2019 ; Pérez-D’Arpino and Shah, 2017 ; Chiu et al., 2026 ) .
Existing CIOC-based constraint learning methods are typically highly data-efficient because they exploit the local optimality of demonstrations directly ( Chou et al., 2020a ) .
However, many such approaches assume known differentiable dynamics and structured constraint parameterizations ( Chou et al., 2020a ; Chou et al., 2020b ) , which hampers their applicability to high-dimensional and neural network-represented systems.
While GP-based approaches relax parameterization assumptions ( Chou et al., 2022 ) , they scale poorly with dataset size and still require known dynamics.
In contrast, our work considers high-dimensional unknown dynamics and unknown constraint representations while preserving data efficiency, and enables further data-efficiency gains when the constraint parameterization is provided.

Partly in parallel with CIOC, ICRL-based methods ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) were developed for inferring constraints from expert trajectories generated via constrained MDPs (CMDPs) ( Malik et al., 2021 ) .
ICRL usually assumes access to a simulator rather than closed-form dynamics (in contrast to CIOC), and can be adapted to settings with unknown system dynamics or rewards ( Liu and Zhu, 2022 ; Liu and Zhu, 2024 ; Park et al., 2020 ; Jang et al., 2023 ) .
However, ICRL-based constraint recovery typically relies on iterative online environment exploration and constrained RL subroutines, leading to high computational cost, high sample complexity, and potentially unsafe exploration during training, which are unacceptable in time-sensitive and safety-critical settings.
Uncertainty-aware ICRL methods aim to reduce constraint violation risk ( Xu and Liu, 2024 ; Subramanian et al., 2024 ) but nonetheless still require online data. Offline ICRL ( Liu et al., 2025 ) avoids online exploration.
The primary prior offline method, ICSDICE ( Quan et al., 2024 ) , constructs higher-reward constraint-violating distributions to identify unsafe regions (echoing earlier CIOC work by Chou et al. (2018) ); however, doing so still requires a fixed dataset containing behaviors that are not guaranteed to satisfy the unknown constraint.

In contrast to the literature surveyed above, our work combines the safety and data efficiency advantage of CIOC with the representational flexibility of ICRL. Our approach leverages learned local dynamics to enable KKT-inspired inference under unknown dynamics, while synthetic reward-improving counterfactual data provide off-demonstration evidence of infeasibility without requiring observed constraint violations. In contrast, Chou et al. (2019) uses hit-and-run sampling to generate counterfactuals but still relies heavily on known parametric constraints and explicit dynamics.

2026-10-08.title: MCFR: A Mask-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Regression Framework for Robust Multi-Variant Board-to-Board Connector Assembly
2026-10-08.authors: Guanghui Shen , Song Wang , Dan Wu
2026-10-08.comment: . Accepted for presentation at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026). Finalist for the IROS Best Paper Award for Industrial Robotics Research for Applications
2026-10-08.abstract: Automated insertion of board-to-board (BTB) connectors in 3C manufacturing requires both high visual accuracy and strong deployment robustness. This problem remains challenging because multi-variant connectors exhibit significant morphological and appearance variations, making stable cross-variant generalization difficult, while the mismatch between training and deployment under fixed-view inspection settings induces background spurious correlation and degrades real-world performance. To address these issues, this paper proposes MCFR, a Mask-Guided Coarse-to-Fine Regression framework for multi-variant BTB connector assembly. By introducing an object-aware mask prior and explicit photometric refinement, the proposed method suppresses background interference and improves alignment accuracy and robustness in practical deployment. Experiments on a self-constructed multi-variant dataset, a BTB batch insertion testbed, and a real smartphone assembly task show that MCFR consistently outperforms representative baselines and achieves an average real-world insertion success rate of 99.25%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness and practical potential of MCFR for automated assembly of multi-variant BTB connectors.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Within the 3C manufacturing sector (computers, communications, and consumer electronics), automated insertion of board-to-board (BTB) connectors is a critical process for realizing flexible assembly of intelligent terminals [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . BTB connectors are characterized by substantial category diversity, miniature dimensions, pronounced appearance variations, and weak discriminative localization features [ 4 , 5 ] . In addition, their assembly process imposes extremely stringent tolerance requirements, typically within ±0.2 mm and ±1.5 ° [ 6 ] . Consequently, the accuracy and robustness of relative pose detection directly determine the feasibility of automated insertion for multi-variant BTB connectors, thereby constituting the principal bottleneck that hinders the stable deployment of such automation systems [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] .

To address this bottleneck, existing studies typically adopt YOLO-based object detection methods [ 10 ] , [ 11 ] or directly employ end-to-end deep networks for relative pose regression [ 12 ] , [ 13 ] , [ 14 ] . Although these methods have demonstrated a certain degree of effectiveness in controlled scenarios, they still face two critical challenges in real flexible production-line deployment. First, purely data-driven implicit regression models are often highly sensitive to the geometric morphology and appearance distribution of connectors, making it difficult to achieve stable generalization across multiple BTB connector variants with substantial morphological differences. Second, in practical visual inspection settings with a fixed viewpoint, training samples are commonly generated by moving the connector through random displacements using a robotic arm, causing the target and the background to exhibit coupled rigid-body transformations in the image. However, in actual assembly, the initial pose mismatch is mainly induced by grasping errors [ 7 ] , whereas the background usually remains completely static. In this paper, we refer to the phenomenon arising from this mismatch between training and deployment distributions—where the model tends to rely on background displacement cues rather than object-intrinsic features—as background spurious correlation. This issue substantially degrades the generalization performance of end-to-end methods in real-world open scenarios, and can be viewed as a task-specific manifestation of shortcut learning under distribution shift [ 15 ] .

To mitigate this issue, this paper proposes MCFR, a mask-guided coarse-to-fine robust pose regression framework for multi-variant connectors in real-world open scenarios. Rather than relying on direct end-to-end black-box regression, MCFR introduces the visual foundation model Segment Anything Model (SAM) [ 16 ] to generate an object-aware probability mask. As a visual prior, this mask can explicitly indicate the spatial distribution of the BTB connector and its effective localization features, thereby suppressing background interference at the source. The original image and the mask prior are then jointly fed into a Vision Transformer (ViT)-based pose regression network [ 17 ] to produce an initial coarse pose estimate. Finally, to ensure robustness under open scenarios and to resist performance degradation caused by real environmental factors, we design an explicit photometric refinement module that performs pixel-level precise alignment of the coarsely regressed pose through robust optimization.

We conduct systematic evaluations of the proposed method on a self-constructed multi-variant BTB connector dataset, a batch insertion test platform, and a real smartphone assembly scenario. Experimental results show that MCFR outperforms existing baseline methods in both relative pose estimation error and real insertion success rate.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows.

We propose MCFR, a robust pose detection framework that overcomes the morphological generalization challenges of multi-variant BTB connectors, providing a reliable visual solution for high-precision physical assembly.

We propose MCFR, a robust pose detection framework that overcomes the morphological generalization challenges of multi-variant BTB connectors, providing a reliable visual solution for high-precision physical assembly.

We reveal the issue of background spurious correlation in fixed-viewpoint relative pose detection and design a mask-guided architecture with explicit photometric refinement to mitigate background reliance and enhance robustness in open scenarios.

Extensive experiments on datasets and real-world assembly platforms demonstrate that MCFR achieves superior error metrics and a near-perfect (99.25%) insertion success rate, significantly outperforming existing baselines.

2. We reveal the issue of background spurious correlation in fixed-viewpoint relative pose detection and design a mask-guided architecture with explicit photometric refinement to mitigate background reliance and enhance robustness in open scenarios.

# II Related Work

## II-A Analytical Pose Estimation Based on Feature Engineering

Such methods typically begin by extracting local localization features from images, such as edges, keypoints, or specific color patches. These features are then combined with geometric or statistical analysis algorithms (e.g., Principal Component Analysis (PCA) [ 18 ] , Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) [ 19 ] , or specific geometric solvers) to calculate the relative pose. Early feature extraction primarily relied on traditional image processing operators like Canny edge detection [ 20 ] and the Hough transform [ 21 ] . However, because traditional operators heavily depend on manually set empirical thresholds, their generalization capability and robustness to interference are relatively limited when faced with complex backgrounds or multiple part categories. To overcome this bottleneck, recent studies have increasingly introduced deep learning object detection models, such as YOLO [ 22 ] , leveraging their powerful high-dimensional feature representation capabilities to extract more robust localization features. This has significantly improved the stability of front-end feature acquisition; nevertheless, their representations are generally biased towards object-level detection, resulting in a relatively limited capacity to describe fine geometric details.

For instance, Wang et al. [ 23 , 24 ] proposed 6-D pose estimation methods that extract the upper and lower surface edges of components, combined with Dual-Space Reprojection Closed-Loop Optimization (DSRCEO). While this method achieved high alignment precision in the assembly of commonly shaped thin-plate components, it imposes strict requirements on edge extraction quality and is more suitable for structured scenarios with minimal background interference. Mou et al. [ 11 ] presented a framework integrating a YOLO network with manifold learning. By detecting the internal pins of flexible connectors and utilizing their specific geometric layout features to regress the relative pose, they verified the method’s effectiveness in insertion tasks for specific connectors.

Overall, feature engineering-based methods are constrained by the design cost and extraction quality of handcrafted features. Particularly when dealing with BTB connectors characterized by a wide variety, significant appearance variations, and a lack of unified, salient geometric features, it is extremely difficult to design a feature engineering pipeline that balances both high precision and strong generalization capabilities.

## II-B End-to-End Pose Regression and Perception Enhancement

To reduce reliance on manual feature design, end-to-end methods exploit the feature representation and data fitting capabilities of deep networks to map sensory inputs directly to pose deviations or control commands. These approaches circumvent tedious explicit feature design and demonstrate stronger representational capacity in modeling the complex appearances of objects.

Yu et al. [ 12 ] were among the earliest to propose a relative pose regression method based on Siamese Convolutional Neural Networks (Siamese CNN), directly predicting pose deviations from images, thereby validating the feasibility of end-to-end visual regression in low-tolerance connector insertion tasks. Addressing occlusion issues in micro-assembly, Yang et al. [ 25 ] introduced a Digital Twin (DT) mechanism to compensate for physical visual blind spots via virtual multi-viewpoints, enhancing measurement capabilities in occluded scenarios. Furthermore, Yang et al. [ 6 ] modeled Flexible Printed Circuit (FPC) position recognition as a tactile image alignment problem and utilized a Deep Siamese Network (DSN) to achieve relative position regression. Building upon this, Li et al. [ 14 ] proposed a visuo-tactile fusion framework, V-HCP, which handles missing modalities through a compensation branch, further enhancing perceptual robustness under complex working conditions.

In summary, end-to-end methods possess distinct advantages in reducing manual design and enhancing representation capabilities for complex scenes. However, most of these methods are constructed for specific object categories and sensor configurations, lacking explicit constraints on spatial geometric relationships. In real production scenarios, when test samples fall out-of-distribution (OOD), or when the system simultaneously faces background variations and transitions between multi-variant objects, these models are still prone to performance degradation. Consequently, they struggle to meet the requirements of flexible production lines for stable deployment and cross-category generalization.

To mitigate the aforementioned shortcomings, this paper focuses on the robust, high-precision pose detection of multi-variant BTB connectors under a fixed viewpoint. Distinct from direct end-to-end pose regression methods, we propose a three-stage framework combining object-aware mask priors, coarse regression, and explicit optimization. This approach aims to simultaneously enhance cross-category generalization, open-scenario robustness, and high-precision alignment capabilities [ 26 ] .

2026-10-08.title: ClimbLab: MATLAB Simulation Platform for Legged Climbing Robotics
2026-10-08.authors: Kentaro Uno , Warley F. R. Ribeiro , Yusuke Koizumi , Keigo Haji , Koki Kurihara , William Jones , Kazuya Yoshida
2026-10-08.comment: Author's version of a manuscript in the proceedings of CLAWAR 2021. The final published version is available at: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract: This paper presents an open-sourced MATLAB simulation and analysis platform dedicated to legged climbing robots. This simulator enables the design of any limbed robotic system as an articulated multi-body with a floating base and simulates it walking and climbing in an arbitrary environment. The main variable environmental parameters are inclination, gravity, and ground stiffness, and any point cloud can be installed as the terrain map. Furthermore, the simulator employs a rigid body dynamics engine. This paper first describes the simulator structure, and the computational flow and next presents the representative simulation examples where quadrupedal robots assumed gripping on the wall or climbing on the steep slope.
2026-10-08.introduction:
To date, legged robots have been showing more usefulness in many deployment cases due to their high locomotive ability in harsh environments such as steep natural terrain with unevenness and obstacles or complex artificial terrain with steps and other movable hazards. The installation of a gripping mechanism at the feet enables the legged robots to climb on steeply inclined slopes, overhanging walls, and even ceilings. Examples of such robots are the Ninja series which can move on glass walls and ceilings [ 1 ] ; the Lemur robot series which can traverse rocky cliff faces [ 2 ] ; and Magneto, which uses magnets to move along metal structures [ 3 ] .

It is generally not simple to perform experiments with climbing robots because of difficulties accessing harsh natural terrain. In addition, testing often requires large-scale equipment to ensure the safety of the robot and operators. Simulation-based study plays an essential role in developing such a robot that must work reliably in a harsh environment. In the design phase, simulation analysis gives us the fundamental mechanical requirements to decide link geometries, mass distribution, and actuator selection. Also, in the validation phase, simulation in severe or high-risk situations is vital to assess the climbing performance without any physical risks before real-world deployment.

There have been many physics simulators that have been developed for robot modeling in customizable environments, for example, Gazebo [ 4 ] , V-Rep [ 5 ] , and RaiSim [ 6 ] . The operation and execution of physics calculations of these simulators require relatively little memory due to them being written and supported using mainly C/C++ and Python programs. However, for beginners and middle-level students and researchers, MATLAB has the advantage of the immediate expression of ideas thanks to its intuitive coding style [ 7 ] .

The Robotics Toolbox for MATLAB [ 8 ] is one of the most valuable and popular platforms to design and simulate any type of robot, in addition to MathWorks’s own Robotic Systems Toolbox. However, these versatile toolboxes support all types of robots and a large variety of libraries. As a result, they are huge, and it can be challenging to understand and familiarize with the whole system.

To the authors’ best knowledge, simulation platforms focusing purely on legged climbing robots have not yet been established. Therefore, targeting those who want to begin research and development of legged robots with ease and simplicity, we open-sourced the standalone simulation platform: ClimbLab 1 1 1 Made available at https://github.com/Space-Robotics-Laboratory/ClimbLab . ClimbLab is dedicated to legged robots walking and climbing. So far, this simulator depends on only one single toolbox: SpaceDyn [ 9 ] for rigid-body dynamics computation, which was also developed and is maintained by the same authors. SpaceDyn is installed automatically with ClimbLab.

This proceedings paper is the initial report to detail the simulation flow of ClimbLab, and also presents some application examples. First, the simulator structure and the computation flow are summarized. Then, representative samples are displayed to show the inspiration of usage.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 ClimbLab

ClimbLab is a standalone simulator integrating all essential aspects necessary for climbing robotics, such as designing robots, simulating various gait strategies under different environmental constraints, and analyzing static and dynamic equilibrium, etc. Almost all functions are usable independent from any MATLAB toolboxes. Instead, dedicated scripts were developed and integrated into a single framework to compute all necessary variables for further analysis of those aspects. The simulator structure and the computational flow are summarized in this section.

ClimbLab has one main script file and several function files, divided according to their role inside the simulation. Fig. 2 shows a simple diagram for the simulation flow, and further detailed information is described below.

Initialization : at the beginning of the simulation, various parameters are defined according to some preset files set by the simulator developers or by arbitrary parameters set by the user.

Initialization : at the beginning of the simulation, various parameters are defined according to some preset files set by the simulator developers or by arbitrary parameters set by the user.

The robot model is defined according to the SpaceDyn configuration. Currently, insect-type and mammalian-type quadruped robots have been implemented.

The ground surface is loaded from a file that contains Cartesian position information. Currently implemented map options are a flat plane, rough terrain generated from fractal structures, and rough terrain extracted from sensed data of a test field made of the sport climbing holds. Other environment parameters can be defined, such as gravitational acceleration, surface inclination, step-time, and simulation time.

For periodic gaits, gait parameters can also be initialized, such as step length and height.

Files are created to save variables for future analysis.

Environment Sensing : at the beginning of the main simulation loop, information from the surface is obtained, as it would be on an actual robot collecting point cloud data from a camera. ClimbLab also implements functions to consider a camera field of view to gather only observable data and algorithms to detect graspable point candidates according to the geometry of the surface and the gripping device.

Locomotion planning : at this section of the simulator, gait planning and local step motion planning are computed.

Different gait types are already implemented in ClimbLab, such as the periodic crawl gait and non-periodic diagonal gaits. The main structure for these gaits is based on the following sequence: checking available grasping points inside the reachable area of each limb, select the next moving limb, select the next point to be grasped, select the next position for the base center of mass (COM), and check kinematic feasibility of next stance. Other gait strategies could also be easily implemented by using this structure.

In motion planning, we define how to move each limb or the robot’s base by planning the motion trajectory in Cartesian space. Currently, spline trajectories are implemented as an option to connect the initial and final positions. From the desired trajectory and current step time, the current step positions are calculated. Finally, the necessary joint angular positions are computed using analytical inverse kinematics.

Equilibrium Evaluation : dynamic and static equilibrium of the robot is computed considering the robot’s pose, gravity and acceleration effects, and gripping force. Visual plotting of center of gravity and support polygon made by contact points can be used for the classical equilibrium evaluation approach [ 10 ] . Additionally, it is possible to compute the tumble stability margin (TSM) [ 11 ] and the gravito-inertial acceleration (GIA) margin [ 12 ] . These two methods are recommended for cases of robots with grippers since they also include the effect of the maximum holding force into the tumbling moment.

Control : the input signal of the actuator of the simulated robot is calculated to achieve the desired joint position. Currently, a proportional and derivative torque control law is performed.

Physics Engine : the judgment of contact and its resultant ground reaction force is calculated.

The current model for the ground reaction forces is a compliant contact model for all three Cartesian directions, as described in Eq. ( 1 ). In the equation, 𝐅 r j \mathbf{F}_{r}^{j} is the ground reaction force acting at the j j -th limb end-effector, 𝐱 j \mathbf{x}^{j} is the position of the j j -th limb end-effector and 𝐱 c j \mathbf{x}_{c}^{j} is its contact point on the surface. The stiffness and damping coefficient matrices for the contact between limb end-effector and surface are 𝐊 s \mathbf{K}_{s} and 𝐃 s \mathbf{D}_{s} respectively. In the case of a robot with grippers, the unilateral condition for contact is not required, so the ground reaction force keeps acting even when the end position is above the surface, as long as the grasping conditions are satisfied. In ClimbLab, we can set the condition for the gripper to detach based on the equilibrium evaluation criteria or on the computed force value and the maximum holding force of the gripper.

The equation of motion of a multiple rigid body system with a floating base is solved using the SpaceDyn Toolbox [ 9 ] , which is also used to compute forward kinematics. SpaceDyn Toolbox numerically solves the Equation of Motion (EoM) described in Eq. ( 2 ) using the Runge-Kutta method for integration. In the equation, 𝐇 \mathbf{H} is the inertia matrix of the robot, 𝐪 \mathbf{q} is the vector of independent coordinates, including base position and orientation and joints position, 𝐜 b ​ m \mathbf{c}_{bm} is the term of Coriolis and centrifugal effects. 𝐠 b ​ m \mathbf{g}_{bm} is the term for gravity effects, 𝐮 \mathbf{u} is the input forces or torques for the joints, 𝐉 \mathbf{J} includes the Jacobian matrices for the base and end-effectors, and 𝐅 r \mathbf{F}_{r} is the term of ground reaction forces.

Visualization : simple real-time plots of the robot and surface using MATLAB built-in functions do not require extra toolboxes and do not need a significant computational time for realistic rendering. Additional information can be displayed in the animation, such as support polygons, graspable points, reachable areas, force/acceleration vectors, sensed region, etc. After this section, the simulation iteratively loops back to Sensing until the final step time.

Simulation End : After the end of the main simulation loop, a file with selectable variables is saved, and time history graphs can be plotted for data analysis.

2026-10-08.title: Predicted Futures Are Not Enough: Learning Executable Goals for Robot Manipulation
2026-10-08.authors: Tzu-Yu Chuang , Ching-Hsiang Chang , Yi-Hsiu Lee , Yi-Ting Chen , Min Sun , YuanFu Yang

2026-10-08.abstract:
Generative world models provide rich predictions of how manipulation scenes may evolve toward task objectives, yet those futures do not directly expose the compact task variables required by control. When training supervises future prediction alone, terminal goal accuracy is not an explicit learning objective, even when geometric recovery is available. We present Entity-Level Goal Readout , a learned prediction-to-execution interface that makes the executable terminal goal an explicit output of a 3D trace world model. It combines object-centric pose prediction with translation grounded in observed depth to produce a compact goal in S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) . A shared Pose-Native Executor consumes this fixed goal with online object-pose feedback for closed-loop control without rerunning the world model. Across five manipulation tasks, the pipeline achieves a mean success rate of 79.69 % 79.69\% . Goal diagnostics directly measure terminal goal accuracy, while controlled translation perturbations characterize how execution degrades under goal error. Zero-shot deployment on a Franka arm achieves 73.33 % 73.33\% success on nominal StackCube, 66.67 % 66.67\% with distractors, and 75.00 % 75.00\% on PickPlate with a target unseen during policy training. These results support treating the prediction-to-execution interface as an explicit learned component of world-model planning rather than incidental post-processing in the control pipeline itself.
Project page: https://claire0730.github.io/executable-goals/
2026-10-08.introduction:
Generative world models support robot manipulation by predicting how scenes can evolve toward task objectives. Yet rich future predictions do not by themselves expose the compact task variables required by control. Video, point trajectories, and scene geometry require a prediction-to-execution interface. Figure 1 frames this gap between prediction and execution. Geometric fitting can convert predicted motion into a terminal goal, but future prediction training does not optimize recovered goal accuracy. Prediction errors can still produce inaccurate control targets. Figure 2 illustrates inconsistencies in generated futures. Our comparisons show that terminal goal errors remain after predictor training losses converge. Converged prediction objectives do not guarantee accurate goals for control.

The design question is not whether a conversion procedure exists, but whether the task variables consumed by control are explicitly learned and exposed. We make terminal goal prediction part of the learning objective through object-centric prediction and observed geometry. The prediction-to-execution interface is learned as part of the model rather than left to incidental post-processing. We present Entity-Level Goal Readout , a learned interface between a 3D trace world model and a Pose-Native Executor. Figure 3 traces this interface from the world-model representation to closed-loop execution. An entity branch predicts terminal object pose, while a map branch grounds translation in observed depth to construct a compact executable goal in S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) . A shared executor combines this goal with pose feedback to correct execution error without rerunning the world model. This separates episodic planning from continuous control while preserving the task variables required by control.

We evaluate the interface through goal accuracy, manipulation success, and sensitivity to goal error. Across five tasks, our pipeline achieves higher mean success than both rigid readout pipelines under shared executor weights, with the largest gains on PickCube and StackCube. Goal error distributions characterize the targets delivered by the planner, while controlled translation perturbations measure the fixed executor’s response to imposed goal error. Real robot trials extend evaluation to distractors and a target unseen during policy training. Our contributions are threefold:

A Learned Goal Interface. Entity-Level Goal Readout makes control-relevant terminal variables explicit learning targets by combining object-centric pose prediction with depth-grounded spatial readout to expose executable goals from the world-model representation.

Execution Trained for Imperfect Goals. A shared Pose-Native Executor is trained under measured planner goal errors using privileged teachers and online pose feedback, without rerunning the planner or receiving privileged guidance during execution.

An Empirical Account of Goal Usability. Goal diagnostics across prediction representations, shared-executor evaluations, controlled perturbations, and real robot trials provide an empirical account of how goal quality translates into closed-loop execution.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

Generative World Models. World model planners represent future motion as generated observations, point trajectories, or scene geometry. Dream2Flow [ 4 ] and TesserAct [ 3 ] recover motion or object goals from generated observations. ATM [ 5 ] and Track2Act [ 6 ] predict 2D point trajectories, with Track2Act recovering geometric poses for control. TraceGen [ 7 ] and μ 0 \mu_{0} [ 8 ] predict 3D traces, PointWorld [ 9 ] predicts action-conditioned 3D motion, and Structured-4D [ 10 ] forecasts scene geometry. Across these representations, our focus is how predicted futures become task goals consumed by control.

From Predicted Futures to Executable Goals. Geometric readouts recover control targets through pose estimation or rigid registration, including Kabsch fitting with random sample consensus (RANSAC) [ 11 ] , [ 12 ] . Dream2Flow [ 4 ] connects video generation to control through 3D object flow. Such interfaces determine how predicted futures are exposed to control, but future prediction supervision alone does not directly optimize terminal goal accuracy. Our readout makes the terminal goal an explicit learning target and evaluates the resulting goal quality in Table I .

Goal-Conditioned Control. Diffusion Policy [ 13 ] , DP3 [ 14 ] , and vision language action models map rich observations to actions. Our Pose-Native Executor instead receives one fixed pose goal in S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) per episode. Dataset aggregation and privileged teacher methods motivate its distillation strategy [ 15 ] , [ 16 ] , [ 17 ] . 2026-10-08.title: Adaptive Risk-Certified Event-Triggered Replanning for Dynamic Navigation
2026-10-08.authors: Richie R. Suganda , Bin Hu
2026-10-08.comment: for associated mpeg file, see this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract: Safe navigation in dynamic environments requires robots to plan under obstacle predictions whose errors are uncertain, non-stationary, and can induce rare but safety-critical failures. Existing control-barrier-function safety filters can reject immediately unsafe controls, but they provide little guidance on when the current finite-horizon planning mode itself is becoming unsafe as prediction uncertainty evolves. We propose Conformal Event-Triggered Risk-Certified Replanning ( CERT-Replan ), a framework that uses calibrated barrier risk as an early-warning signal for replanning. CERT-Replan calibrates horizon-indexed obstacle-prediction residuals online and uses the resulting uncertainty radii to evaluate dynamic-obstacle safety margins. A one-step safety filter protects the next applied control, while a horizon-level risk monitor evaluates the upper-tail CVaR of predicted barrier-violation losses along the current MPC rollout. When this risk exceeds an allocated budget, CERT-Replan rejects the current planning mode and selects a lower-risk alternative, such as a different speed profile, corridor, or homotopy class, rather than repeatedly correcting the same nominal plan. In a non-stationary benchmark, CERT-Replan achieves an 83.3 % 83.3\% collision reduction relative to the safety-filter-only baseline and a 77.8 % 77.8\% reduction relative to simple replanning triggers , while reducing average safety-filter intervention by 32.4 % 32.4\% . With Trajectron++, CERT-Replan achieves 96 % 96\% collision-free operation. Hardware experiments and onboard runtime profiling demonstrate computational feasibility.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Autonomous robots operating in crowds, warehouses, sidewalks, and mixed-traffic environments must make local planning decisions from imperfect predictions of nearby agents. A typical navigation stack estimates obstacle states from onboard sensing, predicts short-horizon obstacle motion, computes a local plan, and applies a safety filter before execution. Certifying this pipeline is challenging because obstacle-prediction errors are rarely stationary or uniform: they can grow under occlusion, close interaction, dense traffic, abrupt intent changes, and changes in sensing geometry. Modern multi-agent predictors capture rich interaction patterns, but their uncertainty can be multi-modal and can shift as the robot enters new sensing or interaction regimes [ 3 , 16 , 33 , 28 , 37 , 52 , 7 , 45 ] . As a result, a nominal forecast may be accurate in benign scenes but unreliable in rare, safety-critical tail events.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a principled optimization-based mechanism for rejecting immediately unsafe controls [ 4 ] . For dynamic-obstacle navigation, however, the safety margin depends not only on the robot state but also on uncertain future obstacle states. Dynamic parabolic CBFs (DPCBFs) improve dynamic-obstacle avoidance by incorporating relative velocity in a line-of-sight frame, thereby reducing the conservatism of purely distance-based or collision-cone-like constraints in dense scenes [ 29 ] . Robust, distributionally robust, and perception-aware CBFs further address model, sensing, and obstacle-state uncertainty [ 9 , 26 , 51 , 42 ] . Yet these filters are fundamentally local in time: they protect the next executed input, but a nominal or one-step filtered control does not by itself indicate whether the current finite-horizon planning mode is becoming unsafe as prediction uncertainty evolves.

Risk-aware safety filters partially address this issue by replacing pointwise safety constraints with constraints on the distribution of safety margins. Conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) barrier functions protect against low-probability, high-severity events by constraining the adverse tail of the safety-margin distribution [ 1 , 2 ] , and risk-adaptive CVaR methods tune the risk level online to balance conservativeness and feasibility [ 47 ] . These methods, however, still require uncertainty samples or error models that remain representative under distribution shift. Adaptive conformal inference (ACI) provides a complementary mechanism by recalibrating uncertainty online from recent prediction residuals without assuming a fixed parametric error model [ 15 , 11 ] . Conformal planning has been used to construct calibrated prediction regions for dynamic environments [ 25 ] , and recent work has extended conformal ideas to adaptive POMDP planning, recursively feasible MPC, and time-aware planning in dynamic scenes [ 36 , 39 ] . In this paper, we use online conformal calibration as the data-driven adaptation mechanism that supplies horizon-indexed uncertainty radii to both immediate safety filtering and horizon-level plan evaluation.

The key gap we address is temporal. A one-step safety filter can repeatedly modify unsafe controls, but repeated correction of the same nominal plan may still push the robot toward regions where future feasible controls are scarce or unavailable. Similarly, resolving the same MPC problem at every step does not answer the higher-level question of when the robot should change the local reference, speed profile, corridor, homotopy class, or risk allocation. Event-triggered replanning provides the appropriate abstraction: update the plan only when a task-relevant condition indicates that the current mode should no longer be trusted [ 43 , 12 , 17 ] . Our central idea is to use calibrated barrier risk as this condition. Rather than treating risk only as a constraint on the next input, CERT-Replan uses it as an early-warning signal for replacing the current local planning mode.

This paper makes four contributions:

We introduce a horizon-indexed adaptive conformal calibration mechanism for dynamic-obstacle prediction errors, producing online position and velocity uncertainty radii that are shared by immediate safety filtering and horizon-level mode evaluation.

We formulate an ACI+Adaptive-CVaR-DPCBF safety filter that uses calibrated geometric tightening and lower-tail CVaR constraints to protect the next applied control under non-stationary prediction uncertainty, while adapting the CVaR tail mass to preserve feasibility.

We propose a finite-horizon CERT risk monitor that evaluates the current local planning mode through upper-tail CVaR of predicted barrier-violation losses, yielding a conditional risk certificate for the evaluated mode.

We integrate this certificate into an event-triggered MPC replanning layer that replaces the current mode when its allocated horizon-risk budget is exceeded, and validate the resulting framework in randomized simulations and hardware-in-the-loop experiments.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Classical reactive and local-planning methods include dynamic-window approaches, graph replanning, sampling-based motion planning, and trajectory optimization [ 13 , 40 , 22 , 32 , 30 , 21 ] . These methods can react to dynamic scenes, but they typically require additional uncertainty handling to provide probabilistic safety under prediction errors. Risk-aware planning methods incorporate chance constraints, distributional robustness, coherent risk measures, or sampling-based risk estimates to account for uncertain obstacle motion [ 31 , 10 , 44 ] . Event-triggered and self-triggered control methods update communication or control actions only when needed to preserve system-level properties under resource or uncertainty constraints [ 43 , 18 , 19 ] . Event-triggered MPC and learned replanning policies reduce unnecessary replans and can improve navigation efficiency, but existing triggers are often based on tracking error, feasibility, map updates, or learned heuristics rather than calibrated tail risk [ 12 , 17 ] . In contrast, our trigger is tied to a calibrated finite-horizon risk certificate for the current local planning mode.

Multi-agent trajectory prediction is often multi-modal due to latent goals and interactions [ 3 , 16 , 33 , 28 , 37 , 52 , 7 ] . Conformal prediction gives distribution-free finite-sample coverage under exchangeability [ 35 , 5 ] , while adaptive conformal inference updates the miscoverage level online to handle distribution shift [ 15 ] . In robot motion planning, conformal prediction has been used to construct prediction regions for dynamic obstacles [ 25 ] , adaptive conformal prediction has been used for online planning among dynamic agents [ 11 , 41 ] , and recent work has extended conformal ideas to time-aware dynamic-environment planning and CBF safety certification [ 24 , 50 ] . Our method differs by using calibrated residuals inside a risk-sensitive barrier filter and by using horizon-level tail risk as a replanning trigger.

CBFs have become a standard tool for safety-critical control because they can be embedded in optimization-based controllers [ 4 , 14 ] . CVaR-CBFs extend this idea to stochastic safety and protect against poor-tail outcomes [ 1 ] . Risk-adaptive CVaR barrier functions adjust the CVaR level online to avoid unnecessary conservativeness while preserving feasibility [ 47 ] . Recent safety-filter and predictive-control methods combine CBFs with differentiable optimization, sampling-based MPC, learned neural barriers, and conformal prediction for uncertainty-aware safety certification [ 8 , 48 , 38 , 50 ] . DPCBFs improve dynamic-obstacle avoidance by shaping the safe set with both relative position and relative velocity [ 29 ] . Closely related MPC-CBF and predictive-CBF methods encode barrier conditions over a prediction horizon and provide feasibility or safety analyses under modeled dynamics and constraints [ 49 , 46 , 6 ] . Our framework is complementary: rather than proposing a new nominal DPCBF or MPC-CBF formulation, we use adaptive conformal calibration and CVaR barrier risk to decide when the current local planning mode should be replaced under non-stationary obstacle-prediction uncertainty.

2026-10-08.title: Co${}^{2}$Skill: Whole-Body Control via Skill Composition for Long-Horizon Human-Environment Interaction
2026-10-08.authors: Jeonghwan Kim , Hyeonwoo Kim , Hanbyul Joo
2026-10-08.abstract:
Achieving human-level dexterity in complex, unstructured environments requires the seamless integration of whole-body scene interaction and dexterous object manipulation skills.
While existing physics-based controllers generate physically plausible behaviors in each domain, they largely address these two capabilities independently.
In this paper, we present Co 2 Skill that integrates scene interaction and dexterous manipulation through a unified policy formulation.
Built on a pretrained motion prior, the policy uses task and phase dependent observation masks to select information relevant to the current interaction goals.
We introduce a goal-conditioned loco-manipulation curriculum that combines partial reference guidance for precision with exploration from varied initial states while allowing goal-directed execution beyond the demonstrated trajectories.
We further introduce a cross-task curriculum that jointly trains individual skills and selected task sequences, preserving physical states across task boundaries and maintaining grasps during subsequent scene interactions.
Together, these support sequential task execution and simultaneous scene interaction with object manipulation.
We evaluate sitting, standing, climbing, stair traversal, and goal-directed manipulation, together with sequential execution and with random different conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate skill compositions in indoor environments, illustrating their integration within the same control formulation.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Everyday activities at home rarely consist of a single skill. A person may walk to a shelf, pick up a phone, and then sit down on a chair while still holding it. For a simulated humanoid, this means coordinating locomotion, whole-body interaction with the surrounding scene, and finger-level grasping across a room-scale space rather than on an empty floor or a tabletop. Each skill must also remain physically stable when it starts from whatever state the previous skill leaves behind.

Physics-based character control with deep reinforcement learning has made steady progress toward such behavior. Tracking policies trained on large motion capture collections now imitate a wide range of human movement ( Peng et al., 2018 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Tessler et al., 2024 ) , and motion priors distilled from these policies can be reused for new downstream tasks ( Luo et al., 2024 ) . Building on such learned motor skills, two lines of work have developed largely in isolation. Human-scene interaction (HSI) controllers move the whole body relative to furniture and terrain, for example to sit on a chair or climb a staircase ( Xiao et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2025 ) , while the hands (with no fingers attached) play little role. Human-object interaction (HOI) controllers achieve precise finger contact and object control ( Luo et al., 2025 ; Tessler et al., 2025 ) , but they typically operate close to the object and often depend on dense reference trajectories from datasets such as GRAB ( Taheri et al., 2020 ) .
Ideally, a single controller should both interact with the surrounding scene and manipulate the objects within it.

Combining these capabilities is harder than simply putting the two kinds of skills together. First, scene interaction and manipulation depend on different inputs. Scene interaction needs scene geometry and spatial targets, while manipulation needs object motion, hand poses, and contact. Second, each skill usually learns from a fixed set of starting states, which differ from the states it meets in a longer task. A sitting policy that learns from a normal standing pose never starts with an object in its hands, and a grasping policy mostly starts from the pose in its reference clip. Switching between separate specialist policies does not solve this problem, and it cannot handle cases where a scene task and a grasp must be performed at the same time. Third, reference motions give the detailed guidance needed for precise contact or large body adjustment, but they cover only the situations present in the motion capture data. A controller that relies on them therefore struggles to approach a chair or an object from new positions.

We address these challenges with our Co 2 Skill, a physics-based controller that performs scene interaction and dexterous manipulation with a single policy. We build the policy on top of a pretrained motion prior and decoder ( Luo et al., 2024 ) . To handle the different inputs of each task, we design a transformer that reads task tokens for the character, scene, object, and hands, enabling only those relevant to the current task and phase. To handle the gap between training and initial states and the limited coverage of reference motions, we introduce two curricula. The goal-conditioned loco-manipulation curriculum uses reference motions to guide close-range interactions such as sitting down or forming a grasp, while exploration from varied starting states teaches the policy to reach the same goals beyond the reference. The cross-task curriculum trains individual tasks together with task sequences, such as lifting an object and then sitting while holding it, so that the policy learns from the states that sequential execution actually produces.
Our shared policy outperforms MaskedMimic across five scene-interaction tasks and achieves success rates matching or exceeding per-task specialists on four of five tasks. We also evaluate pick-move-place task and qualitatively demonstrate manipulation-to-scene transitions while maintaining object grasps.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

A Unified Framework for Scene Interaction and Dexterous Manipulation. We introduce a unified control framework that combines whole-body scene interaction and dexterous object manipulation within a single goal-conditioned policy.

A Goal-Conditioned Loco-Manipulation Curriculum. We combine reference-guided interaction learning with exploration from varied initial states, using partial motion guidance to learn precise interactions while allowing goal-directed execution beyond the reference trajectory.

A Cross-Task Curriculum for Sequential and Simultaneous Interactions. We jointly train individual tasks and selected task sequences, preserving physical states across transitions and maintaining grasp conditions during subsequent scene interactions.

1. A Unified Framework for Scene Interaction and Dexterous Manipulation. We introduce a unified control framework that combines whole-body scene interaction and dexterous object manipulation within a single goal-conditioned policy.

2. A Goal-Conditioned Loco-Manipulation Curriculum. We combine reference-guided interaction learning with exploration from varied initial states, using partial motion guidance to learn precise interactions while allowing goal-directed execution beyond the reference trajectory.

3. A Cross-Task Curriculum for Sequential and Simultaneous Interactions. We jointly train individual tasks and selected task sequences, preserving physical states across transitions and maintaining grasp conditions during subsequent scene interactions.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Human-Scene Interactions

Understanding human-scene interactions requires datasets that faithfully capture spatial relations between human motion and environmental context. Early mocap datasets of humans interacting with static environments ( Starke et al., 2019 ; Hassan et al., 2021 ) enabled training models to predict behavior given goal targets. Interaction Replica ( Guzov et al., 2022 ) extended this by tracking interactions with partially dynamic scenes. Locomotion-Action-Manipulation ( Lee and Joo, 2023 ) synthesizes human-scene interactions in 3D environments by coordinating locomotion with manipulation actions. More recent work augments datasets by capturing human behavior and applying VR rendering to diversify indoor environments ( Jiang et al., 2024b ; Jiang et al., 2024a ) . These datasets establish foundations for learning human behavior in environments.

## 2.2 Human-Object Interactions

Human behavior naturally incorporates manipulation of objects in the surrounding environment. BEHAVE ( Bhatnagar et al., 2022 ) and Object Motion Guided Human Motion Synthesis ( Li et al., 2023 ) capture human body motion with dynamic objects (e.g.,, suitcases) without hand grasping. Hand-only datasets ( Chao et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) focus on finger grasping sequences without body motions. GRAB ( Taheri et al., 2020 ) and ARCTIC ( Fan et al., 2023 ) capture whole-body manipulation with hand articulation but limited action diversity. ParaHome ( Kim et al., 2025 ) captures indoor sequences with both locomotion and finger-level manipulations. For kinematic synthesis, IMoS ( Ghosh et al., 2023 ) generates intent-driven full-body motions for object interactions, and FORCE ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) introduces physics-aware synthesis with force modeling.

## 2.3 Physics-Based Character Control

DeepMimic ( Peng et al., 2018 ) demonstrated that deep RL can successfully track reference motion in physics simulation. Adversarial reward settings ( Peng et al., 2021 ; Xu and Karamouzas, 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) introduced stylized control without explicit reference tracking, while latent-based methods ( Peng et al., 2022 ; Dou et al., 2023 ; Tessler et al., 2023 ) learn reusable skill-embeddings for compositional task execution. Recent work scaled motion tracking with large-scale datasets ( Mahmood et al., 2019 ) to learn single policies for real-time tracking ( Luo et al., 2023 ) , with adaptations for language control ( Juravsky et al., 2022 ; Juravsky et al., 2024 ) and multi-task composition via masked observations ( Tessler et al., 2024 ) . For physics-based manipulation, D-Grasp ( Christen et al., 2022 ) synthesizes dynamic grasps for hand-object interactions, and PhysHOI ( Wang et al., 2023 ) tackles physics-based imitation of dynamic human-object interaction. For scene-level interactions, InterPhys ( Hassan et al., 2023 ) synthesizes physical character-scene interactions with contact handling, UniHSI ( Xiao et al., 2024 ) performs HSI using chain-of-contacts with LLM planning, and TokenHSI ( Pan et al., 2025 ) demonstrates multi-task composition with task tokenization.

## 2.4 Behavior Foundation Models

A behavior foundation model ( Tirinzoni et al., 2025 ) refers to a universal policy that generalizes across diverse motion styles trained with large-scale datasets.
MoConVQ ( Yao et al., 2023 ) uses discrete representations as compact motion priors that interface with language models. PULSE ( Luo et al., 2024 ) trains a universal policy with CVAE aimed for adaptation to diverse downstream tasks. More recent work utilizes task-specific tokens as flexible representations to adapt general tracking policies ( Tessler et al., 2024 ; Vainshtein et al., 2025 ) . Composite motion learning ( Xu et al., 2023 ) enables task-aware skill composition for complex behaviors. Based on these advances, we aim to integrate locomotion datasets ( Mahmood et al., 2019 ) and whole-body manipulation datasets ( Taheri et al., 2020 ) through a staged training strategy that learns a general motion prior and then steer the trained model to perform various tasks.
