2026-10-08.title: A Unified Kinematic Representation Enables Reusable Biological Joint Moment Estimation
2026-10-08.authors: Jinwoo Hwang , Ilseung Park , Changseob Song , Vu Phan , Eni Halilaj , Inseung Kang
2026-10-08.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
2026-10-08.abstract: Objective: Data-driven models that estimate physiological states, particularly biological joint moments, are widely used in exoskeleton control. However, these estimators are often coupled to device-specific sensor configurations, limiting controller transfer and the use of open-source biomechanics datasets. Methods: We proposed joint kinematics as an intermediate representation that decouples hardware-specific sensing from downstream biological joint moment estimation. A joint-moment estimator using joint angles and angular velocities was trained exclusively on open-source biomechanics data and evaluated using kinematics from a hip exoskeleton, knee exoskeleton, and inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensor suite during level-ground, ramp-ascent, and ramp-descent walking. Results: The estimator achieved an root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.17 Nm/kg and coefficient of determination ( R 2 R^{2} ) of 0.79 using hip exoskeleton kinematics, 0.19 Nm/kg and 0.62 using knee exoskeleton kinematics, and 0.15 Nm/kg and 0.85 using kinematics derived from IMUs across bilateral hip, knee, and ankle joints. Conclusion: Joint kinematics enabled an estimator trained only on open-source data to operate across distinct wearable platforms. Significance: This framework may reduce target-device data collection and support transferable biological joint moment estimation for exoskeleton control and wearable biomechanics.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Lower-limb exoskeletons and other wearable robotic systems can augment movements [ 1 , 2 ] , restore mobility [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] , and support independence for individuals with impaired locomotion [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Because movement patterns and mechanical demands vary across users, speeds, terrains, and tasks, effective assistance generally requires adaptive control rather than a single fixed strategy [ 4 , 9 , 10 , 2 ] . Such controllers adjust assistance based on estimates of the user’s biomechanical state, including joint kinematics, contacts, gait phase, and joint moments.

Many exoskeleton controllers represent this state using discrete variables such as gait phase or terrain class [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Although useful for dividing locomotion into phases or tasks, these representations do not fully capture continuous changes in mechanical demand. Biological joint moments instead quantify the net mechanical contribution generated by the user’s musculoskeletal system at each joint, providing a continuous and mechanically interpretable measure of locomotor demand. Data-driven joint-moment estimates have consequently been used for subject-independent and task-agnostic exoskeleton control across diverse activities [ 14 , 15 , 9 ] .

Inverse dynamics has been the standard to obtain biological joint moments, but this method requires motion capture and force plate systems, only available in high-end gait laboratories, motivating the use of wearables and machine learning as an alternative combination for estimation of these quantities. Existing data-driven estimators commonly operate directly on device-specific signals, including inertial measurement units (IMUs), motor encoders, and pressure sensors [ 9 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . These approaches can achieve accurate estimates when deployment and training use the same sensing configuration [ 14 , 15 , 9 ] . However, they are generally overfitted to specific systems because the learned models also capture differences in sensor modality, placement, orientation, calibration, attachment, and preprocessing. This can alter the input distribution, limiting transfer to devices that do not reproduce the original inputs.

Prior work has addressed this transfer challenge through online model adaptation and sensor-signal transformation. Kang et al. [ 4 ] adapted a gait-phase estimator to new users and locomotion conditions across exoskeleton platforms by transforming sensor signals between devices. Deep domain adaptation has similarly addressed sensor-domain mismatch by aligning representations between source and target wearable configurations [ 17 ] . Although these approaches can reduce or eliminate the need for labeled target-domain biomechanics, they still require recordings from the target user or sensing configuration. Changes in hardware, sensor placement, or preprocessing may therefore require new target-domain data and another adaptation procedure. This motivates a complementary strategy in which the downstream estimator operates on a common physical representation rather than hardware-specific signals.

Hardware-specific inputs also limit the use of open-source biomechanics data, which provide extensive lower-limb kinematics, ground-reaction forces, and inverse-dynamics moments across participants and locomotor conditions [ 21 , 16 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] . These resources can support generalizable estimators and biomechanical foundation models without requiring each group to reproduce the original laboratory data collection [ 30 ] . However, their wearable signals rely on the original sensing configurations and cannot represent every custom exoskeleton or future device. The key limitation is the absence of a generalized input representation to reuse existing labeled data across wearable systems.

Joint kinematics, such as joint angles and angular velocities, provide a potential intermediate representation as they can conveniently and accurately be obtained from motor encoders, segment-mounted IMUs, and inertial motion-capture systems [ 31 , 32 , 33 ] . In the proposed framework, each platform converts its available signals into a unified kinematic representation, which a downstream model maps to biological joint moments (Fig. 1 ). Because these inputs have consistent biomechanical meaning across platforms, the joint-moment estimator can be reusable across any device on which joint angles and angular velocities are available.

In this study, we investigated whether wearable-derived joint kinematics can serve as a common intermediate representation for biological joint moment estimation across heterogeneous sensing platforms. We trained causal temporal convolutional models exclusively on open-source kinematics and inverse-dynamics moments and then applied them, without fine-tuning on the target device, to a bilateral hip exoskeleton, a unilateral knee exoskeleton, and an IMU sensor suite. We evaluated single-joint and multi-joint estimation and examined the benefit of adjacent-joint context.

To the best of our knowledge, this study provides the first demonstration of a biological joint-moment estimator trained exclusively on open-source biomechanics data and deployed across previously unseen wearable platforms without target-device training, adaptation, or fine-tuning. We further validate this approach on physical hip and knee exoskeletons, demonstrating that a common kinematic representation can support joint moment estimation across distinct hardware configurations. Despite using no data from the target devices during training, hip-moment estimation performance was comparable to prior device-specific approaches trained directly on the hardware on which they were evaluated.

# II Methods

## II-A Open-Source Data for Model Training

All biological joint-moment estimators were trained using publicly available biomechanics data (Fig. 1 (a)). The curated database combined level-ground, ramp-ascent, and ramp-descent walking trials from the datasets used in Camargo et al. [ 21 ] , Scherpereel et al. [ 16 ] , and Molinaro et al. [ 9 , 15 ] . Acyclic activities, such as squatting, and stair-negotiation trials were excluded because they were outside the scope of the present evaluation. Under the participant-level split used for the hip-, knee-, and ankle-moment models, 51 participants were assigned to training, 2 to validation, and 3 to testing. The training partition contained approximately 15.2 h of retained walking data: 12.06 h of level-ground walking, 1.91 h of ramp ascent, and 1.23 h of ramp descent, corresponding to 79.3%, 12.6%, and 8.1% of the training duration, respectively. The full 56-participant pool contained approximately 20.6 h of retained walking data.

The datasets were aggregated to increase variability across participants, walking speeds, and walking conditions. Level-ground walking provided the largest amount of data and the broadest speed coverage, including both treadmill and overground walking, whereas the smaller ramp-ascent and ramp-descent subsets supplied kinematic and joint-moment patterns for inclined walking. Before training, all retained trials were mapped to consistent joint definitions, coordinate conventions, and moment signs. Left- and right-limb data were also transformed to a common limb convention where applicable.

Training windows were formed only over intervals in which all required input and target samples were finite. Consequently, the distribution of valid windows differed from the distribution of retained recording duration. Before condition balancing, level-ground, ramp-ascent, and ramp-descent walking contributed 7,362,539, 931,791, and 440,661 valid windows, respectively, corresponding to 84.3%, 10.7%, and 5.0% of the available training windows. To prevent the substantially larger level-ground subset from dominating model optimization, the resulting windows were oversampled by locomotor condition so that level-ground walking, ramp ascent, and ramp descent contributed equally to training exposure. Thus, ramp windows were sampled more frequently relative to their raw prevalence in the aggregated dataset. No dataset-level ablation was performed, so the relative contribution of the individual source datasets was not evaluated independently.

Sagittal-plane joint angles and net joint moments were extracted from the processed motion-capture and ground-reaction-force data. Joint angular velocities were then computed from the filtered joint-angle trajectories: for planar kinematic chains such as the knee and ankle, each angle time series was fit with a cubic spline and differentiated analytically; for spatial kinematic chains such as the hip, Euler angles were converted to rotation matrices, finite-differenced in time, and converted to angular velocity. Joint moments were normalized by participant body mass (Nm/kg). Lower-body kinematics sampled at 200 Hz in the open-source data were downsampled to 100 Hz to match the control frequency of the evaluated exoskeletons. Models received kinematic inputs in physical units and directly predicted mass-normalized joint moments, without input or output normalization.

## II-B Biological Joint-Moment Estimator

We used a causal temporal convolutional network (TCN) [ 34 ] to estimate biological joint moments from joint kinematics. The network contained five temporal convolutional blocks with 80 hidden channels, a kernel size of five, and dilation factors of 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16. Each block included causal convolution, batch normalization, rectified linear unit activation, and dropout ( p = 0.1 p=0.1 ). The input was a causal window of the preceding 100 samples, corresponding to 1.0 s at 100 Hz.

Models were implemented in PyTorch [ 35 ] and trained on a workstation equipped with an Intel Core i9-14900KF CPU (24 cores, 32 threads), an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 GPU (24GB VRAM), and 64GB of system memory, running Ubuntu 22.04. Training used Huber loss with a transition parameter of 0.5 Nm/kg. We used AdamW with a weight decay of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} , a batch size of 512, and gradient clipping at a norm of 1.0. A cosine-annealing scheduler reduced the learning rate from 2 × 10 − 5 2\times 10^{-5} to 1 × 10 − 6 1\times 10^{-6} . Training continued for up to five epochs, with early stopping based on validation mean squared error and a patience of two epochs. Separate models were trained using either single-joint kinematics or combined hip, knee, and ankle kinematics. The trained models were converted to TensorRT engines [ 36 ] for GPU-accelerated edge inference.

## II-C Wearable Sensing and Exoskeleton Platforms

Hip-exoskeleton experiments used a bilateral device (4.3 kg) developed for sagittal-plane assistance [ 37 ] , featuring brushless actuators (AK80-9, CubeMars, China) with integrated motor encoders and an onboard computing system (Jetson Orin Nano, NVIDIA, USA) (Supplementary Table S2, Supplementary Figure S1(a)). Hip angle and angular velocity, derived from the encoders and relative movement of pelvis- and thigh-mounted IMUs, were provided to the shared single-joint hip-moment estimator (Fig. 1 (b)). Output torque for each leg was commanded as:

Knee-exoskeleton experiments used a unilateral quasi-direct-drive device worn on the right leg. The actuated knee module (1.3 kg) and a waist-mounted electronics module (0.9 kg) communicated at 100 Hz. Knee angle was obtained from the motor encoder, while angular velocity was estimated from thigh- and shank-mounted IMUs (Fig. 1 (c), Supplementary Figure S1(b)). The knee controller mirrored the structure of 1 , but used a scaling factor of α k ​ n ​ e ​ e = 0.09 \alpha_{knee}=0.09 with no additional command delay. Because commanded motor torque varied with participant mass, the scaling factor was selected to keep peak torque below approximately one-half of the motor’s peak instantaneous torque capacity. This range also limited torque-induced motor displacement, while behavior at higher torque levels was beyond the scope of this study. The onboard control architecture for both exoskeletons is outlined in Supplementary Fig. S1(c).

A wireless inertial sensing system [ 38 ] (MTw Awinda, Movella, Netherlands) provided bilateral multi-joint kinematics (Fig. 1 (d)). Sensors were affixed to the posterior pelvis, lateral thighs, lateral shanks, and dorsal feet (Supplementary Figure S1(d)). Unconstrained joint kinematics were obtained following the IMoveLab workflow [ 39 ] . Specifically, 3-axis accelerometer, 3-axis gyroscope, and 3-axis magnetometer measurements were fused to estimate sensor orientations using the versatile quaternion-based filter (VQF) [ 40 ] . Sensor-to-body calibration for the IMUs was applied to convert these orientations of the sensors to those of the body segments, all expressed in the inertial frame. This calibration process was performed priori using data from a static standing trial to identify the proximal-distal axis (Y) of all body segments; and then a static toe-touch trial to identify the medio-lateral axis (Z) and anterior-posterior axis (X) of the pelvis; and a treadmill walking trial to identify the other axes of the remaining body segments. Each joint kinematics was calculated as the relative orientations between the two consecutive body segments.

## II-D Participants

Eight healthy adults (six males, two females; age: 26.3 ± 2.3 26.3\pm 2.3 years; height: 1.74 ± 0.06 1.74\pm 0.06 m; body mass: 72.3 ± 13.3 72.3\pm 13.3 kg) participated in this study (Supplementary Table S1). Participants were excluded if they presented with a current musculoskeletal injury, neurological disorder, cardiovascular condition, or any other impairment that could affect walking or safe completion of the experimental protocol. All participants provided written informed consent prior to participation, and the study protocol (Protocol #STUDY2026_00000119) was approved by the Carnegie Mellon University Institutional Review Board. Each participant completed the experimental protocols using the hip exoskeleton, knee exoskeleton, and IMU sensor suite in one experimental day.

## II-E Experimental Protocol

Experiments were conducted on a force-instrumented split-belt treadmill (FIT5, Bertec, OH). Participants performed level-ground walking (LG) at 0.8, 1.2, and 1.6 m/s, ramp ascent (RA, + 10 ∘ +10^{\circ} ) at 0.8 m/s, and ramp descent (RD, − 10 ∘ -10^{\circ} ) at 0.8 m/s. The hip exoskeleton was evaluated during LG and RA, the knee exoskeleton during RA and RD, and the IMU sensor suite across all conditions. These exoskeleton-specific task subsets reflected joint-specific locomotor demands: uphill walking increases positive mechanical work at the hip, whereas downhill walking shifts a greater proportion of lower-limb work toward negative work at the knee [ 41 , 42 ] . Accordingly, RD was omitted from the hip-exoskeleton protocol, while LG was omitted from the knee-exoskeleton protocol because powered knee assistance has shown greater metabolic benefit during inclined than unloaded level-ground walking [ 43 ] . Each trial lasted approximately 80 s, with the first and last 10 s trimmed to isolate steady-state gait. We analyzed 31 hip exoskeleton trials, 16 knee exoskeleton trials, and 39 IMU sensor suite trials, excluding specific 0.8 m/s and 1.6 m/s LG trials due to poor marker data.

## II-F Reference Biomechanics and Moment Estimation

Reference kinematics were collected at 100 Hz using a 24-marker optical motion-capture system (Vero, Vicon, UK) with 10 cameras. Participant-specific musculoskeletal models based on the OpenSim Gait 2392 model [ 44 , 45 , 46 ] were scaled for each session using OpenSim 4.5 [ 47 ] , directly incorporating the added mass and inertia of the hip (2.0 kg pelvis, 0.5 kg per femur, 1.3 kg torso) or knee (0.9 kg pelvis, 0.91 kg right femur, 0.39 kg right tibia) exoskeletons. Marker trajectories were used to estimate joint kinematics through OpenSim’s constrained inverse kinematics, and the resulting coordinates were low-pass filtered at 6 Hz before calculating net sagittal-plane joint moments via inverse dynamics. For assisted trials, biological joint moments were estimated by aligning and subtracting the measured exoskeleton motor torque from the OpenSim-derived net joint moment prior to normalization by the participant’s body mass.

## II-G Model Evaluation

Model performance was evaluated using mass-normalized root mean square error (RMSE) and the coefficient of determination ( R 2 R^{2} ) between predicted and reference moments.

Unless specified, results are reported as mean ± \pm standard deviation. The hip-exoskeleton analysis included 31 trials, with one level-ground trial at 1.6 m/s excluded due to failed inverse dynamics stemming from poor marker data. The knee-exoskeleton analysis included all 16 collected trials. The IMU sensor suite analysis included 39 trials, with one level-ground trial at 0.8 m/s excluded for the same reason. Detailed joint-moment prediction metrics across all joints, conditions, and platforms are summarized in Table I .

For the IMU sensor suite trials, multi-joint and single-joint models were compared using matched trial–channel pairs for six joint-level outcomes (RMSE and R 2 R^{2} for the hip, knee, and ankle). One-sided paired t t -tests were used to test whether the single-joint model had higher RMSE and lower R 2 R^{2} than the multi-joint model. Left and right channels were pooled within each joint, yielding 78 paired observations per joint after exclusion of the invalid trial. The six joint-level tests were corrected together using the Holm–Bonferroni procedure ( α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 ).

2026-10-08.title: World Models Dream of Success: Diagnosing and Repairing Failure Insensitivity in Robot World Models
2026-10-08.authors: Jiuyi Xu , Xiao Hu , Meida Chen , Peng Gao , Yang Ye , Yangming Shi
2026-10-08.abstract:
Robot world models support policy evaluation, planning, and synthetic data generation, but these applications require predictions that distinguish successful actions from failures.
Across four released checkpoints from two architecture families, we observe weak sensitivity to action changes and success-like predictions on verified failures.
Although recent work incorporates failures into model training, which data can repair released checkpoints without changing their architecture or training objective still remains underexplored.
To this end, we introduce CureWM , which constructs alternative actions from successful demonstrations across a severity grid, verifies their outcomes through execution in simulation or on hardware, and fine-tunes released models on the resulting failures and surviving successes alongside nominal demonstrations.
This construction provides controlled action contrasts from shared starting contexts.
On 484 held-out LIBERO failure counterfactuals, optimism falls from 80% after fine-tuning on the official data to 30–43% across four independently fine-tuned CureWM models (38% mean).
In two separate evaluations on a physical robot arm, failure predictions scored as success-like by a latent-distance diagnostic decrease from 90% after fine-tuning on successful demonstrations alone to 33% with CureWM.
With failure counts per task, successful replay data, and training budget matched, counterfactual failures yield a success–failure value gap of 0.124, compared with 0.014 for freshly collected on-policy failures.
These findings support execution-verified counterfactual replay for post-hoc repair and show why reduced optimism must be evaluated alongside success–failure discrimination.
Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/CureWM .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Robot world models learn to predict how environments evolve in response to actions, from latent dynamics models to generative video simulators ( Hafner et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA, 2025a ) .
In the robotic domain, their predictions support policy evaluation in imagination ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , action selection and planning ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , and synthetic experience generation for policy learning ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) .
These applications require more than visually plausible futures: a model must distinguish actions that accomplish the task from those that fail.
If failing actions receive high success values or generate success-like futures, decisions based on these predictions can favor actions that do not achieve the intended outcome.

However, how to repair failure prediction in released robot world models still remains underexplored.
MiraBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) found optimism bias in action-conditioned predictions, but diagnosing such failure insensitivity does not tell us which training data could correct it.
In particular, failed trajectories need not teach a model how alternative actions from the same context change the outcome.
This distinction matters for released checkpoints: simply adding failures may lower predicted success across both successful and failing actions, reducing the optimism without improving discrimination.
Therefore, the question is which kind of data enable post-hoc repair of action-conditioned predictions, and how to distinguish that repair from a general shift toward pessimism. Concurrent work, such as FACT ( Peng et al., 2026 ) , combines failed policy rollouts with action conditioning and failure-aware masking in a world-action model.
However, it does not directly address how to repair released checkpoints while retaining their architecture and training objective, or which failure data are most effective under these constraints.

To fill these knowledge gaps, we introduce CureWM , motivated by the
observation that correctly predicting the outcome of an observed
action does not imply knowing how a different
action in the same context would change the outcome.
CureWM perturbs successful demonstrations across
a severity grid while preserving actions before
intervention, verifies outcomes through execution,
and retains failed and successful replays for
post-training.
The architecture and training objective remain unchanged.
We evaluate four released checkpoints from two architecture families, which are Cosmos Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) and Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , and test CureWM in simulation and on a physical robot arm.
The ALOHA checkpoint is evaluated for diagnosis only (Appendix C ).
Experiments on LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) and a physical
robot show improved success–failure discrimination.
Matched comparisons favor counterfactual failures
over fresh policy failures, while ablations examine
successful replays and verified outcome labels.
These results also show why reduced optimism alone
does not establish repair.
Our contributions are as follows:

We introduce CureWM, which repairs released world models using execution-verified counterfactual replays without changing their architecture or training objective.

We demonstrate repair in simulation and on
a physical robot, including improved
success–failure discrimination and failure detection.
Matched LIBERO comparisons show stronger discrimination
than training on fresh policy failures.

We show that reduced optimism alone can overstate repair, and evaluate success–failure discrimination together with false alarms on successful actions.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

World models and action-conditioned reliability. Cosmos Policy ( Kim et al., 2026 ) predicts actions, future observations, and values for control and planning, while Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2026 ) supports policy evaluation and synthetic trajectory generation through action-conditioned video prediction.
MiraBench ( Yang et al., 2026 ) evaluates physics adherence, action following, and optimism bias, and provides the perturbation families used in our experiments.
WorldArena ( Shang et al., 2026 ) likewise distinguishes perceptual quality from functional utility.
We study post-hoc repair.
Our support argument relates to causal confusion
in imitation learning ( de Haan et al., 2019 ) ,
but does not identify a causal mechanism inside
the model.

Failure and counterfactual supervision. Learning from unsuccessful behavior and constructed examples has been widely studied: Dex-Net ( Mahler et al., 2017 ) learns grasp robustness from synthetic examples with analytic labels,
HER ( Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ) reuses unsuccessful attempts through goal relabeling,
and CoDA ( Pitis et al., 2020 ) constructs counterfactual transitions using locally factored dynamics.
AHA ( Duan et al., 2025 ) synthesizes manipulation failures to train a vision-language model for failure detection and natural-language reasoning.
Concurrent FACT ( Peng et al., 2026 ) incorporates failed rollouts into world-action model training.
We do not claim novelty in adding failure examples.
CureWM combines controlled perturbations, execution-verified outcomes, and successful replay partners to repair released checkpoints with their original architecture and objective.
Furthermore, matched comparisons test which data choices improve repair.

Conservative values, failure detection, and predictive repair. Offline RL addresses unreliable extrapolation through data-constrained action selection ( Fujimoto et al., 2019 ) , conservative value learning ( Kumar et al., 2020 ) , and uncertainty-aware penalties or pessimistic dynamics ( Yu et al., 2020 ; Kidambi et al., 2020 ) .
These methods motivate caution about unsupported actions, but conservative decision-making and accurate outcome discrimination are distinct objectives.
Our label ablation illustrates that reduced optimism
can accompany underestimated success predictions.
It does not evaluate those offline RL algorithms.
Foresight ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) instead learns failure detection from action-conditioned world-model representations.
CureWM updates the world model’s own predictions.
We assess whether it better distinguishes successful
from failing actions, rather than simply assigning
lower success values to both.

2026-10-08.title: FlashNeRD: Performance-First Contact-Rich Neural Robot Dynamics
2026-10-08.authors: Mohammadmehdi Ataei , Mohammad Amin Nabian , Jie Xu , Miles Macklin , Yashraj Narang , Eric Heiden , Octi Zhang , Yunrong Guo , Ruben D'Sa , Oliver Hennigh , Gavriel State , Sanjay Choudhry
2026-10-08.abstract: Compared with analytical physics, learned dynamics models promise robot simulation that is faster, inherently differentiable, and easily adaptable to real data. Neural Robot Dynamics (NeRD) pursues this by keeping collision detection analytical and replacing a simulator’s numerical dynamics for the robot with a learned model. Three limitations remain. NeRD offers little speedup over the simulator it learned from, accepts contact only at predefined points, and has no two-way coupling with objects it manipulates. FlashNeRD removes all three with a parallel streaming architecture that makes each prediction faster and more accurate, an encoder that accepts contacts wherever they occur, and two-way coupling with objects simulated by analytical solvers. Experiments across five robots show faster and more accurate dynamics, faster policy learning, and faster inference-time planning. Across three robots, FlashNeRD’s dynamics model is up to 55 × 55\times faster than an optimized NeRD and more accurate over long rollouts. This speedup extends to policy learning, where PPO trains an ANYmal locomotion policy in 34 seconds, 3.8 × 3.8\times faster than the analytical simulator and 2.7 × 2.7\times faster than an optimized NeRD. With DIAL-MPC, a sampling-based MPC method, the robot climbs all six test platforms where fixed-contact NeRD manages one, at approximately half the analytical simulator’s planning time. Cube-reorientation policies trained with FlashNeRD complete within 2% of the simulator-trained policy’s target count.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Robot learning and planning require many dynamics predictions, making simulation cost a practical bottleneck. Analytical simulators such as MuJoCo [ 1 ] and GPU-parallel platforms such as Isaac Lab [ 2 ] and Newton [ 3 ] , whose MuJoCo Warp (MJWarp) backend we use unless otherwise stated, meet this demand by stepping thousands of environments. Three limits persist. Calls to an iterative contact solver bound throughput per GPU, many simulators are not differentiable, and fitting a simulator to real-robot data means tuning a few physical parameters that cannot express unmodeled effects such as actuator dynamics.

Neural robot dynamics learns the robot’s transition function from data, addressing all three limits in principle. Batched network evaluation has fixed cost and can outpace iterative contact solves. The model is differentiable by construction. The model can also be fine-tuned on real trajectories without selecting physical parameters to adjust. Neural Robot Dynamics (NeRD) [ 4 ] is the state of the art, using one transformer per robot, trained on randomized states and actuator commands such as position targets or motor torques, with collision detection left analytical. Because the data are task- and controller-independent, the model learns generic robot dynamics rather than task-specific dynamics and serves any controller on the robot. NeRD also showed zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on reach tasks.

Three limitations remain. (i) NeRD re-encodes the full history window at every step, so inference cost is similar to the analytical simulator’s and the throughput advantage goes unrealized. (ii) Contact enters through predefined probe points, which are insufficient for more complex tasks where contacts happen at edges or surfaces, such as climbing. (iii) NeRD assumes the environment surrounding the robot is fully static, ruling out manipulation. FlashNeRD removes each limitation, and each fix unlocks a capability.

A parallel architecture with streaming inference that processes only the newest frame per step. This gives up to 55 × 55\times the model-only throughput of an inference-optimized NeRD baseline ( Optimized NeRD ) with lower rollout error, and is fast enough that end-to-end policy training also runs faster than in the analytical simulator.

A set-based contact encoder that accepts contacts wherever collisions are detected, so contact-rich tasks such as platform climbing need no hand-placed probes.

Two-way coupling via hybrid simulation , in which FlashNeRD predicts the robot’s free motion while MJWarp analytically simulates the objects and resolves their contacts with the robot, so forces flow in both directions and learned dynamics extend to manipulation.

This gives up to 55 × 55\times the model-only throughput of an inference-optimized NeRD baseline ( Optimized NeRD ) with lower rollout error, and is fast enough that end-to-end policy training also runs faster than in the analytical simulator.

2. A set-based contact encoder that accepts contacts wherever collisions are detected, so contact-rich tasks such as platform climbing need no hand-placed probes.

3. Two-way coupling via hybrid simulation , in which FlashNeRD predicts the robot’s free motion while MJWarp analytically simulates the objects and resolves their contacts with the robot, so forces flow in both directions and learned dynamics extend to manipulation.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

Neural simulation has been explored for fluids [ 5 ] , deformable bodies [ 6 , 7 ] , and rigid bodies [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Among neural simulators for articulated rigid bodies, NeRD [ 4 ] learns robot-specific physics from robot-centric states, controls, and contact features independent of downstream tasks. FlashNeRD builds on it with higher inference speed, variable contacts, and two-way coupling. Three bodies of work inform the design. Efficient transformer inference, including parallel attention and feedforward branches [ 14 ] , multi-query attention [ 15 ] , sliding-window attention [ 16 ] , IO-aware kernels [ 17 ] , and object-level attention in RigidFormer [ 11 ] , motivates the architecture of Secs. III-B and III-C . In place of contact representations such as implicit signed distance functions [ 18 ] , mesh-face graphs [ 19 ] , and predicted binary contacts [ 20 ] , FlashNeRD pools the analytical detector’s unordered contact set. Coupling schemes between solvers [ 21 , 22 ] or learned models [ 23 ] motivate the shared contact solve of Sec. III-E .

2026-10-08.title: Workhorse: Learning Robust Whole-Body Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from Human Data
2026-10-08.authors: Songbo Hu , Qiayuan Liao , Yufeng Chi , Kevin Zakka , Yakun Sophia Shao , Pieter Abbeel , Koushil Sreenath
2026-10-08.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract:
Humanoid robots still struggle to plan contact-rich whole-body manipulation from egocentric RGB and proprioception.
Workhorse learns such manipulation from robot-free human demonstrations.
A visual planner predicts five-link targets: the poses of the torso, both wrists, and both feet.
A reinforcement-learning whole-body tracker follows them on the robot.
Both policies train separately on the same recorded human poses, without retargeting.
We augment the training data of each policy to imitate the errors that the other makes at deployment.
On a real Unitree G1, Workhorse sorts boxes with its hands and a kick, catches a thrown box, and topples and climbs a suitcase.
During box sorting, we show recoveries after a person pushes the robot or takes the box away.
In a simulated copy of the demonstration room, the system completes box sorting in 77 % 77\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of episodes, and in 64 % 64\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} under 40 N ⋅ s 40\text{\,}\mathrm{N}\text{$\cdot$}\mathrm{s} pushes.
With both policies retrained from the same demonstrations, a simulated second humanoid completes box sorting in 83 % 83\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of episodes without pushes.
2026-10-08.introduction:
We want humanoid robots to interact with the world using whole-body motions, much like humans do.
Humans can squat to lift a box, brace a leg against an object to push or topple it, and climb onto objects to reach higher places.
Although humanoid robots can execute such whole-body motions using learned motion trackers [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , these methods require a whole-body reference trajectory to be specified.
For manipulation tasks, however, no such reference is available, so the robot must plan its own whole-body motion to perform the task.
Doing so from only egocentric RGB observations and proprioception is challenging, and becomes even more difficult when the robot must move dynamically, respond to changes in the scene, and recover from unexpected perturbations.

The robot can learn to plan whole-body motions for manipulation tasks from demonstrations.
Teleoperation captures demonstrations directly on the robot, but each demonstration requires both a robot and a skilled operator [ 4 , 5 ] .
Robot-free rigs instead record human motion without a robot in the loop [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] .
For example, HuMI [ 6 ] uses wearable trackers on the pelvis and feet to capture whole-body motion.
However, in most tasks studied with either approach, the feet are primarily used for locomotion rather than as active tools for manipulation.
Moreover, these tasks largely remain quasi-static, with little emphasis on dynamic motion or recovery from perturbations.

We present Workhorse (Fig. Workhorse: Learning Robust Whole-Body Humanoid Loco-Manipulation from Human Data ), which learns whole-body loco-manipulation from robot-free human demonstrations.
A visual planner and a whole-body tracker (Fig. 2 ) communicate through a shared interface consisting of the poses of the torso, both wrists, and both feet.
Because the interface specifies task-space poses rather than robot-specific joint angles, it is naturally embodiment-agnostic.
During training, the poses come directly from human demonstrations, without requiring retargeting to a robot.

We demonstrate Workhorse on a real Unitree G1 across three whole-body loco-manipulation tasks: box sorting with a kick, box catching, and suitcase pushing, toppling, and climbing.
Each task has its own planner and whole-body tracker.
For box sorting, we demonstrate recovery from perturbations such as a person pushing the robot or removing the box.
In simulation, we use the same human demonstrations to train both the planner and tracker for a second humanoid, demonstrating transfer across embodiments.

Our contributions are:

Robot-free human data collection. We develop a system with five wearable trackers and a chest-mounted camera for recording whole-body demonstrations without a robot.

Visual planner and whole-body tracker. We train the visual planner and whole-body tracker separately from the same five link poses extracted from the human demonstrations, without robot-specific retargeting.
Data augmentation prepares each policy to handle errors from the other, with the tracker’s reward designed for accurate wrist tracking and robust foot placement.

Closed-loop evaluation in simulation. We reconstruct the demonstration environment as a Gaussian splat and test the complete system in closed loop.

# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Humanoid Whole-Body Controllers

Motion trackers reproduce a whole-body reference motion [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Some tolerate external disturbances [ 9 ] or noisy reference motions [ 10 ] .
Other controllers accept a sparse or latent command [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
The command of all these controllers is usually a retargeted motion or a teleoperator’s input, which most of them treat as ground truth.
A planner’s command drifts until the planner sends a new plan, and then it jumps.
We train the whole-body tracker on such commands (§ IV-C2 ).

## II-B Human Data Collection Devices

Marker-based optical capture [ 15 ] is precise but expensive.
The pose estimate of inertial sensors worn on the body drifts [ 16 ] .
UMI [ 17 ] and DexUMI [ 18 ] put a device with a camera in the demonstrator’s hands, and each device recovers its own pose by odometry.
A whole-body version needs five such devices, including one on each foot.
Each device has its own drift and its own clock, and odometry from a camera on a foot is poorly conditioned.
An arm exoskeleton with a back-mounted LiDAR measures the arms and the torso [ 19 ] , but it constrains the demonstrator.
Our rig is lightweight and quick to set up.
It reports the poses of the torso, the wrists, and the feet together, in one gravity-aligned frame.

## II-C Humanoid Policies from Human Demonstrations

Teleoperation [ 5 , 4 ] records the demonstration on the robot itself, so the data needs no conversion.
Its interface can limit how reactive and how dynamic the demonstration is.
Robot-free rigs record the poses of a few key body parts and RGB video [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 20 , 21 ] .
To our knowledge, the feet only walk in the tasks reported with these rigs.
Some of these systems turn the human motion into joint references for a whole-body controller by inverse kinematics or retargeting [ 6 , 7 ] .
Other systems retarget human motion capture or video and train a whole-body controller on it [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] .
Some of them use the feet on objects, for example to kick a box or a door [ 23 , 24 ] .
Retargeting is specific to one robot, and it changes the demonstrated motion.
In Workhorse, the five recorded link poses are the training target of both policies, with no retargeting (§ IV-A ).
A new humanoid needs five measurements on its body, its simulation model, and retraining of both policies from the same demonstrations (§ V-C ).

2026-10-08.title: MimicX: Policy-in-the-Loop Supervision Refinement for Video-Driven Humanoid Motion Tracking
2026-10-08.authors: Shuaijun Liu , Chenglong Zhang , Xuhao Liu , Feiyang You , Yifan Liao , Shuyang Hao , Chaozhe Zhang , Chengyu Wu , Zhen Sun , Ningxin Su
2026-10-08.comment: including references and appendices. Project website: this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract:
Human videos provide rich motion targets for humanoid learning, yet visually
plausible references can still produce persistent failures under physics-based
execution. These failures reveal where training supervision should change.
We present MimicX, a policy-in-the-loop framework that uses execution
feedback to refine video-driven humanoid motion tracking. Starting from
reconstructed and retargeted motion, MimicX localizes difficult transitions
and affected body regions, then jointly adapts tracking objectives and the
reset curriculum for policy continuation. Repeated rollout verification
selects execution-priority improvements subject to tracking guards.
Across four core video tasks, MimicX consistently improves tracking
accuracy and Robust Execution Horizon relative to the Fixed Reference
baseline. Task-averaged results show a 25.7% reduction in body-tracking error
and a 255.6% increase in execution horizon. Additional video, motion-reference,
and collision-scene studies evaluate the method beyond the core tasks, while
MimicX-HLoop accelerates feedback through heterogeneous execution.
Overall, MimicX turns policy failure into actionable supervision for
deciding what to refine and which refinement to retain.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Human video provides a scalable specification of whole-body behavior.
World-grounded reconstruction, retargeting, and physics-based tracking turn
that specification into humanoid skills ( Shen et al., 2024 ; Araujo et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . Yet a robot must realize
the motion with different geometry and dynamics: plausible contact timing,
root motion, or limb coordination can repeatedly fail at the same transition.
Policy execution should therefore inform the supervision used to learn it.

Our central insight is that rollout failures reveal when execution
becomes unreliable, which body regions deviate, and how local,
global, and dynamic errors develop together. MimicX uses this structure
in a diagnosis–refinement–verification loop
(Figure 2 ). Reconstruction and retargeting supply a
reference; diagnosis conditions objective and curriculum updates, followed
by policy continuation. A lower-body failure can jointly strengthen foot
position, height, and velocity supervision around the difficult transition,
while a root failure emphasizes anchor and torso consistency.

Reliable selection matters because a higher reward need not imply more
reliable execution: a candidate can improve reward yet shorten the worst-case
execution horizon. MimicX
prioritizes completion, horizon, and tracking fidelity across repeated
rollouts, retaining the current policy when a proposal fails verification.
MimicX-HLoop accelerates feedback through heterogeneous execution.

Across four core video skills, MimicX improves both tracking error and
worst-case execution horizon relative to Fixed Reference.
Tennis achieves full-horizon success in nine of nine evaluations versus one
of nine for the baseline. Additional video, supplied-motion, direct-policy, and efficiency studies
evaluate broader motion coverage and execution behavior.
Figure 22 presents recorded motions in task scenes.
Our contributions are (1) a policy-in-the-loop refinement framework
that converts localized, body-specific execution errors into coordinated
objective and curriculum updates; (2) repeated execution verification
that selects reliable improvements while protecting stronger current policies;
and (3) a heterogeneous backend that accelerates feedback while preserving selection outcomes.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

SMPL-X, GVHMR and GMR provide human geometry, world-grounded motion and robot
references ( Pavlakos et al., 2019 ; Shen et al., 2024 ; Araujo et al., 2025 ) . Physics-based imitation and
motion priors support tracking, recovery and partial-motion control ( Peng et al., 2018 ; Peng et al., 2021 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Tessler et al., 2024 ) . BeyondMimic emphasizes
difficult segments and guided diffusion; SONIC scales generalist tracking ( Liao et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . MeshMimic couples reconstructed scene geometry with contact-aware motion
retargeting ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . MimicX instead makes measured execution
failure an explicit input to supervision revision and validates the resulting
policy through repeated rollouts.

Contact-aware tracking, timing adaptation and dynamics alignment motivate
coordinated local, global and dynamic supervision ( Xie et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2025 ) . Recent methods separate motor
learning from physical refinement, combine references with task goals, and
compose long-horizon or end-effector skills ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Wu et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2026 ) .
MimicX uses a diagnosis–proposal–verification loop to select supervision
updates through execution. Appendix H provides the detailed method-by-method comparison.

2026-10-08.title: PhysEvo: Astra Can Act, Let It
2026-10-08.authors: Wenqing Tian , Zeyu Zhang , Zhaocheng Liu , Fengwei Liu , Qiang Liu , Liang Wang
2026-10-08.abstract: Astra can act, yet reliable manipulation depends on the system through which it observes and controls the world. We introduce PhysEvo, a framework for physical recursive self-improvement (RSI) around a single frozen model. A task agent executes robot tasks; a meta-agent uses the resulting trajectories to diagnose failures, revise tools and skills, and test corrections. The meta-agent can also improve its own diagnostic tools, so retained revisions support both later action and later self-improvement. This process develops joint-level control, evidence-seeking observation, and reusable manipulation skills without model-weight updates or a separately trained action policy. Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, held-out-layout evaluation of retained task-specific deployment versions yields a five-dimension average score of 68.14/100 and 62.00% success, compared with 47.17% for RoboDawn’s one-shot Astra agent, the strongest published reference in our comparison. On eight manipulation tasks challenging direct Astra, PhysEvo achieves 55.00% success, compared with 1.25% for the direct-Astra reference. Deploying the simulation-evolved harness on AgileX PiPER and continuing skill revision yields 90.60/100 average score and 84.00% success across 25 trials on five real-world tasks. PhysEvo turns the consequences of action into persistent, testable changes to how a frozen model acts and improves.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Astra can already control a robot, but demonstrated competence does not guarantee reliable execution. In a ten-task RoboDojo evaluation, direct Astra reaches 100% success on object classification yet succeeds on only 26% of attempts overall. Pairing it with the specialized vision–language–action (VLA) policy π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} raises success to 48% ( Su et al., 2026 ) . These results pose a question: what prevents capabilities that are already present from being used reliably?

Our executions expose bottlenecks in the harness : the tools, skills, and execution logic between the model and the robot. During pouring, the held bottle obscures the wrist view needed to monitor liquid delivery. With a tool-center-point (TCP) interface, local inverse kinematics (IK) can fold the arm into an obstructive posture, while leaving Astra no explicit way to choose the joint configuration ( figures 3 and 4 ). These failures call for more than a new action through an unchanged interface: the agent needs a useful view or direct authority over posture.

Why should the same model be able to fix a failure it did not prevent? Retrospective diagnosis has access to evidence that was unavailable during action selection. A trajectory reveals the consequences of a command; aligned images, robot states, and code help trace those consequences to a cause. Astra can then propose a concrete intervention, such as maintaining a free-arm side view or exposing joint reconfiguration, and test it through further execution. In our pouring case, revised skill guidance changes the observation strategy, and the subsequent episode succeeds. Physical interaction thus provides both evidence for a correction and a test of whether it works.

A correction need not end with the episode. Retained tools and skills change later execution; retained diagnostic tools change how later failures can be investigated. In our packing case, Astra reuses a review tool it built earlier to trace box displacement to preceding contact and revise clearance guidance ( figure 5 ). We call this loop physical recursive self-improvement (RSI): experience revises the system used for action and diagnosis, and the revised system is inherited by subsequent rounds.

We introduce PhysEvo , which implements this loop with one frozen Astra in two roles. The task agent observes and controls the robot. The meta-agent inspects execution, edits tools and skills, tests revisions, and retains useful changes, including changes to its own diagnostic resources. The resulting framework combines joint-level control, active and historical observation, geometry tools, and manipulation skills.

Across 42 RoboDojo tasks, held-out-layout evaluation of retained task-specific deployment versions achieves 68.14/100 score and 62.00% success under equal five-dimension weighting. This exceeds the 47.17% reported by RoboDawn’s one-shot Astra agent, the strongest reference in our comparison ( table 1 ) ( Guo et al., 2026a ) . On the ten-task comparison with direct and hybrid policies, PhysEvo reaches 68.00% success versus 26.00% and 48.00%, respectively. On eight manipulation tasks challenging direct Astra, it reaches 55.00% versus 1.25% , a 53.75-point gain ; Simate-beta, the strongest robot-policy reference on this subset, reports 50.83% ( figures 1 and 3 ) ( RoboDojo Team, 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026d ) .

On AgileX PiPER, the simulation-evolved harness serves as a starting point for continued adaptation. Across five trials on each of five real-world tasks, PhysEvo achieves a mean score of 90.60/100 and 84.00% success. Revisions compensate for liquid-flow effects and replace geometry-first localization with a visually guided approach followed by close-range geometric refinement ( section 5.6 ). The same loop can therefore revise both how the robot moves and when it seeks geometric evidence.

Our contributions are (i) a physical RSI framework in which one frozen model acts, revises, and inherits task and meta resources; (ii) an evolved interaction architecture combining joint control, evidence-seeking observation, and reusable skills; and (iii) a 42-task evaluation with mechanism-focused cases and a five-task evaluation of continued adaptation on real hardware.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision–language–action models such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} learn control from robot data ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Code as Policies instead composes perception and control APIs, while Inner Monologue incorporates environmental feedback ( Liang et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2022 ) . CaP-X and Guava study tool, action, and observation design ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ) ; Show-Harness and obstacle-aware harnesses address embodiment and geometric constraints ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . RoboDawn couples discrete commands with feedback and demonstrations ( Guo et al., 2026a ) . Thea and PhyAgentOS structure persistent state and outcome verification ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026b ) , while Harness VLA and RoboHarness use execution memory to guide primitives or route heterogeneous policies ( Zhang et al., 2026e ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . These systems establish the importance of the interface around a model.

Reflexion retains verbal feedback, and GEPA evolves prompts from execution traces ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Agrawal et al., 2025 ) . ADAS searches code-defined agents; SICA and DGM modify agent implementations ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Robeyns et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . AutoHarness, Meta-Harness, and Self-Harness synthesize or revise executable harnesses from feedback ( Lou et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Recursive Harness Self-Improvement evolves a prompt-level harness with a fixed optimizer ( Lee et al., 2026a ) , whereas STOP and Hyperagents also modify the improvement procedure ( Zelikman et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . RRSI regularizes harness edits, and Dream-RSI uses discovery histories to improve exploration ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Hyperagents’ robotics experiment evolves rewards for PPO controllers ( Zhang et al., 2026b , App. C.3) ; PhysEvo instead uses the same frozen model for robot decisions and software revision.

REFLECT diagnoses failures from execution summaries ( Liu et al., 2023 ) ; Voyager and RATs accumulate executable skills through interaction and autonomous play ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) . EmbodiSkill distinguishes faulty skills from failures to follow valid guidance ( Ju et al., 2026 ) ; ASPIRE retains manipulation and debugging knowledge from multimodal traces ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . RoboRSI organizes skills hierarchically ( Noematrix Team, 2026 ) , and Zetta evolves critics, recovery, and tools around a frozen action policy ( Ding et al., 2026 ) . SHAPER evolves skills and context-construction code with one frozen model serving as planner and optimizer, while fixing the action interface and executor ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . ENPIRE automates real-world policy development ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) . RHO evolves multi-file robot repositories, including prompts, tools, and control code for LLM-in-the-loop execution ( Elmaaroufi et al., 2026 ) . HarnessPAI revises programs and repair skills across rollouts, keeping the selected high-level program fixed within each rollout ( Wang et al., 2026c ) . PhysEvo focuses on the joint evolution of skills, robot-facing action and observation interfaces, and diagnostic resources: the same frozen model acts through revised interfaces and reuses self-built tools to diagnose later failures.

2026-10-08.title: HULK: Learning Whole-Body Forceful Loco-Manipulation for Humanoids
2026-10-08.authors: An Dang , Arturo Flores Alvarez , Yu-Ming Chen , Conor Mc Gartoll , Helen Sun , Aaron Ames , Nima Fazeli , Manikantan Nambi
2026-10-08.comment: IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation 2027
2026-10-08.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation of large, heavy objects demands forceful interaction across the entire body. However, such payloads shift a humanoid’s center of mass and impose sustained loads across the upper body, challenging balance and tracking. We present HULK, a whole-body control framework for forceful loco-manipulation. Using model predictive control (MPC) to guide reinforcement learning with predictions of the loaded dynamics, we train two teachers: one tracks arm motions under wrist forces, and the other locomotes while holding large objects against the body. A capture-point control barrier function augments the wrist-force teacher during training to improve balance under load. We distill both teachers into a single policy. We evaluate our method on a Unitree G1 in both simulation and the real-world. In simulation, the teacher with the barrier function achieves the lowest forward and lateral velocity tracking errors at 10 10 kg per arm among evaluated controllers and reduces aggregate balance metric by 35.7 % 35.7\% relative to MPC-guided reinforcement learning alone. Our wrist-force teacher withstands torso push disturbances of up to 130 130 N.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Humanoid robots are a compelling form factor for a world
built around the human body. The promise is a single platform that can
perform the same physical labor as people, in the same unmodified
spaces. Realizing this promise, however, requires forceful
whole-body work: lifting a loaded tote, leaning into a cart, or
carrying a heavy object against the chest while walking. These tasks recur throughout logistics, manufacturing, and assistive
applications. What these tasks share is a load the robot must
sustain rather than reject: it persists for the task’s duration, shifts where the robot’s weight sits, and competes for
actuation that keeps it balanced.

Current approaches to humanoid loco-manipulation have converged on
a layered control strategy. At the bottom sits a learned whole-body
controller (WBC): a policy that turns a compact set of task-space
commands, such as base velocity, torso pose, and arm targets, into
joint actions that keep the robot balanced. Above it, planners,
teleoperation interfaces, and agentic pipelines issue those
commands without reasoning about balance themselves, treating the
WBC as a low-level “System 0” [ 1 , 2 ] .
Massively parallel reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation has
made this bottom layer reliable enough to serve as that
substrate [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] , and progress above it has been rapid
along two fronts: agility , pushing the dynamism of
whole-body skills [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] , and perception , closing the loop on terrain and
obstacles [ 12 , 13 ] .

Forceful interaction, however, remains comparatively underexplored. Unlike agility and perception, it requires the WBC to adapt its balance strategy to large and sustained external wrenches. A heavy payload changes the forces and moments that must be supported by the robot, with their effect varying continuously with the arm configuration and the object’s pose relative to the body. Existing approaches address parts of this problem. Compliance-based methods lower the effective stiffness of the robot so that it yields under unexpected contact [ 14 ] ; while effective for incidental interaction, this behavior is poorly suited to supporting a heavy payload against gravity. The strongest forceful controllers instead learn to resist applied forces, but only at the wrists [ 15 ] , or only for horizontal push–pull moments [ 16 , 17 ] . Carrying a load further requires this adaptation to persist: the disturbance is not a transient to be rejected, but a condition that remains throughout the task. The robot must therefore maintain balance under a continuously applied wrench while simultaneously producing the forces required for manipulation.

We address the displaced center of mass and sustained balance under
load in a single learned policy. Model predictive
control (MPC) supplies reward guidance during RL [ 18 ] ,
giving the policy a model-based signal for how a load moves the
centroidal state rather than requiring it to discover that
relationship from reward alone. We then augment the wrist-force teacher
with a capture-point control barrier function (CBF) [ 19 , 20 ] .
Following CBF-RL [ 21 ] , the barrier acts during training to improve
learned balance recovery under load while retaining network-only inference. Our contributions are:

We extend learned whole-body control to forceful interactions
between external objects and contacts across the humanoid upper body.

We extend learned whole-body control to forceful interactions
between external objects and contacts across the humanoid upper body.

We use MPC reward guidance to train robust locomotion and
loco-manipulation under sustained payloads.

We augment the wrist-force teacher with training-time
capture-point constraints, improving loaded tracking and balance
recovery while retaining network-only inference.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Works

Whole-body Control. Whole-body controllers have lately been trained using reinforcement learning to follow high-level commands while actively stabilizing the humanoid. Several works [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 8 ] demonstrate the capabilities of sim-to-real reinforcement learning for motion tracking or teleoperation of the humanoid for human-like behavior on hardware. Large-scale models now expose whole-body control as a general-purpose interface: SONIC [ 7 ] supersizes motion tracking toward natural whole-body control using a large human motion tracking dataset. These methods address kinematic tracking rather than forces and persistent loading.

Forceful Whole-body Control. Two efforts define the forceful direction. FALCON [ 15 ] rejects force perturbations at the wrists with a wrist-force curriculum and a dual-network architecture, but struggles to hold commands while doing so. Thor [ 16 ] leans the torso to recruit the robot’s own weight, using ZMP analysis of sagittal-plane wrist forces, and so addresses horizontal push–pull rather than downward payload forces. Neither models whole-body object interaction during training, so the payload-augmented center of mass degrades locomotion under heavy load. HAFO [ 17 ] and load-aware adaptation [ 22 ] target force-adaptive control, but heavy payloads remain open, while Hold My Beer [ 23 ] and FACET [ 24 ] stabilize a payload under gentle motion rather than sustaining large loads.

Outside the learned-WBC setting, payload carrying has been addressed by hierarchical optimization [ 25 ] and by distilling trajectory optimization into skills [ 26 ] , both indicating that a model of the loaded dynamics is valuable; Dao et al. [ 27 ] show sim-to-real box loco-manipulation without a whole-body command interface. AMO [ 28 ] provides such an interface but assumes both feet remain in contact.

Closest to our approach, Li et al. [ 18 ] use model predictive control for reward guidance and demonstrates cart-pushing and payload carrying. However, this method treats interactions as forces applied at the wrists rather than incorporating a payload wrench into reference generation, and it does not address contact against the torso. We extend it to a whole-body controller accepting height, torso-tilt and arm commands, with payloads entering the model through force perturbations and whole-body grasp force profiles.

Balance Constraints in Learned Control. Control barrier functions are ordinarily enforced by a runtime quadratic program that minimally corrects a nominal controller [ 19 , 20 , 29 ] , which for a learned policy means shipping a reduced-order model, gradient and solver alongside the network. CBF-RL [ 21 ] instead applies the correction during training and penalizes the residual in the reward, so the requirement is internalized and deployment carries no extra machinery. We adopt that formulation. Because a sustained external wrench displaces the center of mass for a whole episode, the quantity to constrain is a balance state under load, for which the capture point model [ 30 ] , is the natural choice.

2026-10-08.title: Toward Evidence-Driven Human-Agent-Robot Teaming for Earth-Independent Anomaly Triage
2026-10-08.authors: Ignacio G Lopez-Francos , Alexis Gallagher , Samira Shalal
2026-10-08.comment: Accepted to the Space Robotics Workshop at 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
2026-10-08.abstract: Deep-space crews cannot rely on real-time ground support for urgent off-nominal events. Initial alerts may underdetermine cause, while discriminating evidence may reside in crew observations or at locations that are unsafe, costly, or unavailable for crew inspection. We present an evidence-driven architecture for human-agent-robot teaming in Earth-independent anomaly triage. Agentic AI is treated as a coordinator over explicit state and bounded, inspectable services rather than as a fully autonomous vehicle controller. A triage state manager maintains hypotheses, evidence provenance, uncertainty, operational context, and tool status; a crew-facing embodied agent elicits observations and explains assessment changes; and a mobile robot acquires targeted, localized evidence. Typed interfaces separate dialogue and orchestration from monitoring, robot command, context retrieval, and safety-critical control. Two scenarios illustrate the architecture: a crewed deep-space mission based on an actual ISS ammonia false alarm, where suspected contamination restricts crew access, and a power-interface anomaly at a crewed lunar base, where robotic inspection distinguishes a local connector fault from other causes ambiguous in remote telemetry. Our contribution is an authority-bounded closed evidence-loop architecture, exercised in a hardware-in-the-loop integration prototype using Reachy Mini and an Innate MARS mobile robot.
2026-10-08.introduction:
As human missions extend beyond low-Earth orbit, crews will increasingly conduct time-critical operations without real-time Mission Control support. Mars missions can experience one-way communication delays of up to 22 minutes and extended disruptions, precluding synchronous troubleshooting [ 1 , 2 ] . Earth-independent operations therefore require onboard support for time-critical anomaly response, not merely onboard copies of ground displays [ 3 ] .

An initial alert may indicate a serious condition without resolving its cause or safest response. The next step may therefore be a targeted observation from vehicle telemetry, the crew, a deployable sensor, or a mobile robot rather than an immediate repair attempt. Treating the robot as a relocatable sensing resource follows active perception, in which sensing actions are selected to reduce uncertainty [ 4 ] , and extends targeted off-world fault investigation [ 7 ] by closing the loop from an unresolved distinction to robot tasking, structured evidence return, hypothesis revision, and crew review.

Tool-using language agents can interleave reasoning and external action [ 5 ] and ground instructions in finite robot skill sets [ 6 ] , but safety-critical operations require explicit state, provenance, tool preconditions, and authority boundaries. We ask: How can an onboard agent coordinate crew and robot sensing to reduce diagnostic uncertainty while keeping evidence traceable and the crew in control? We contribute (1) an architecture linking anomaly events, crew interaction, robot inspection, hypothesis refinement, and crew-authorized action; (2) a bounded tool-use pattern separating information gathering from operational action; and (3) two scenarios showing the same evidence loop in a Mars-transit spacecraft and a lunar surface habitat. Here, triage denotes decision support under unresolved uncertainty, not autonomous anomaly detection or emergency management.

# II Evidence-Driven Agentic Architecture

## II-A Operational Scope and Explicit State

The architecture continuously receives structured events from caution-and-warning systems, conventional fault detection, isolation, and recovery (FDIR), anomaly detectors, and crew reports. An off-nominal event initiates triage; independently designed automated safing may act in parallel when delay is unacceptable. The architecture then supports situation assessment and early response, when additional evidence can distinguish plausible causes and guide the next safe action. Here, agentic denotes high-level coordination among finite, evidence-acquisition, context-retrieval, and communication capabilities exposed through typed interfaces and governed by explicit authority constraints, rather than unconstrained direct control of vehicle behavior.

The triage state manager owns a time-indexed record containing the initiating event, ranked hypotheses and uncertainty, evidence, operational context, robot and task status, applicable procedure context, and an append-only decision trace. Each evidence item records its source, modality, time, location, quality, provenance, and underlying artifact. Missing evidence, failed acquisition, and a measured-negative result remain distinct; dialogue history is not authoritative vehicle state.

## II-B Fixed Roles and Typed Interfaces

The architecture follows a hub-and-spoke workflow. A central agentic orchestrator receives structured anomaly notifications, manages dialogue through the crew-facing embodied agent, queries triage state, and routes typed requests and results among bounded services. It may sequence candidate evidence-acquisition actions and explanations, but it does not own authoritative state, assign diagnostic confidence, validate its own authority, execute critical actions, or issue low-level robot commands. Event and monitoring services emit structured anomaly events and immutable observations. The triage state manager owns the authoritative state, admits validated evidence, checks freshness and conflict, and enforces state transitions. The crew-facing embodied agent renders alerts and questions, confirms crew reports by readback, and explains assessment changes. Diagnostic, evidence, context/procedure, perception, and robot-tasking services expose bounded functions through typed interfaces.

A mobile inspection robot receives a typed task contract specifying the target, sensing objective, permitted modalities, completion and stop conditions, and timeout, then returns status, localized observations, and quality flags. An authority and safety layer validates schemas, permissions, operational constraints, and confirmation requirements for every request. During crewed operations, consequential actions require crew authorization; during uncrewed periods, only pre-authorized, reversible actions within verified constraints may execute automatically. Delayed ground may review the trace and provide advisory analysis when communications permit.

## II-C Closed Evidence Loop and Authority Boundaries

When an event arrives, the orchestrator asks the state manager to instantiate or retrieve the corresponding state and requests an initial diagnostic update. From the unresolved distinctions, it proposes a bounded evidence action: a crew question, data or context request, or robot inspection. The authority layer validates the request and obtains any required confirmation. The selected service executes it, the evidence service checks the result for schema, provenance, freshness, and quality, and the state manager admits it to the authoritative record. A diagnostic service revises the hypothesis ranking, and the crew-facing interface explains the supporting evidence, remaining uncertainty, and response options. The crew may accept, modify, decline, or defer; the trace remains available to delayed ground.

The architecture distinguishes epistemic actions , which gather information, from operational actions , which alter vehicle configuration or commit the crew to a consequential response. The orchestrator selects epistemic actions only from a bounded catalog with typed preconditions and outputs. Operational actions use a deterministic execution path and require crew authorization except for pre-approved safing. Capability access therefore does not confer operational authority, and the orchestrator cannot declare resolution without an appropriate validated measurement and operational approval.
