2026-10-08.title: From Wearable Interfaces to Dexterous Policies: Contact Shifts and Tactile Representations
2026-10-08.authors: Ruitong Tian , Fang Xu , Noah B. Wilson , Xianyao Li , Eric Jing Du
2026-10-08.comment: . Submitted to ICRA 2027
2026-10-08.abstract:
Unlike conventional teleoperation, wearable interfaces allow operators to
collect dexterous demonstrations through their own hand motions while directly
interacting with task objects. This direct interaction reduces dependence on
the target robot during collection, but it also makes the collection hardware
part of the physical process that generates each demonstration. Interface
geometry can influence both how a task is performed and what tactile
observations are recorded for learning. We study two versions of a
DexUMI-family exoskeleton that share the same robot command definition, mapping
procedure, and tactile module type but differ in hand-side geometry. The
revised interface reduces reported physical demand, improves selected device
ratings, enables tactile access in a precision grasp that is mechanically
blocked by the baseline, and produces task-dependent changes in recorded
contact. Lid twisting primarily exhibits a change in contact location, whereas
egg carton opening primarily exhibits a change in contact occurrence. We then
train matched policies using either a binary aggregate input or a
spatial-plus-force input. On lid twisting and egg carton opening, policies trained on
revised-interface demonstrations achieve higher success than those trained on
baseline demonstrations, with a significant pooled interface effect. Across these and two additional tasks,
USB insertion and soldering tool pick and place, the spatial-plus-force input
likewise outperforms binary aggregation. These results show that wearable collection
hardware is part of the data-generation process for robot learning. Such interfaces should therefore be evaluated not only through operator
experience, but also through the tactile interactions they make recordable and
the policy performance their demonstrations support.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Learning dexterous manipulation policies requires demonstrations that preserve
both high-dimensional hand motion and contact-rich interaction. Human-hand
videos and motion-capture systems can collect data without a robot, but
recovering precise contact and robot-feasible joint commands remains
difficult [ 1 ] . Robot-side teleoperation and
hand-over-hand interfaces provide actions closer to the deployment embodiment,
yet they require the physical robot hand during collection and can be
cumbersome for contact-rich tasks [ 2 ] . Wearable
interfaces offer a complementary solution: the operator manipulates objects
directly, receives natural contact feedback, and records demonstrations without
bringing the complete robot system into the collection
environment [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] .

To make these demonstrations transferable, a robot-specific exoskeleton
constrains human motion and measures joint states corresponding to the target
hand. This correspondence is a central strength of systems such as
DexUMI [ 3 ] , but it also creates a human–robot design
tension. In our system, the wearable interface maps the operator’s fingers to
the joint-command space of a fully actuated 12-DoF XHand. Preserving this
correspondence can impose robot-derived finger spacing, joint clearances, and
linkage geometry on the human hand. Such constraints are particularly
consequential for the thumb, whose natural opposition and circumduction do not
necessarily align with the target robot’s kinematic structure. The resulting
mismatch can increase physical burden, restrict motion, and create localized
discomfort during repeated data collection [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .

Unlike a passive sensing system, a wearable collection interface participates
directly in the physical interaction that generates each demonstration. A
restrictive linkage can change a grasp trajectory, while material surrounding
a fingertip sensor can prevent the tactile surface from reaching the object.
The resulting difference may appear as a change in whether contact is
accessible, where contact occurs on the pad, or how often contact is detected.
Tactile representation further determines which of these differences a learned
policy can receive: a binary aggregate input preserves per-finger contact
occurrence while discarding within-pad contact location and force, whereas a
spatial-plus-force input retains contact location on the pad and aggregate
fingertip force [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] .

This motivates our central question: when a revision of wearable collection
hardware changes physical contact during demonstration collection, how do the
collection interface and the tactile representation each affect downstream
robot policy performance? We study this question through a controlled hand-side revision
within a robot-aligned wearable interface. The baseline and revised interfaces
retain the same 12-DoF XHand command definition, encoder assignment,
calibration procedure, tactile module type, and robot platform, while differing
in hand-side geometry. We first test whether the revision changes operator
experience and tactile-pad accessibility. We then measure whether it changes
where or how often contact is recorded in matched demonstrations. Finally, we train policies that cross the two collection interfaces with a
binary aggregate or a spatial-plus-force input and evaluate them on the same
XHand, which measures the contribution of each factor to policy success.

Our contributions are:

We show that wearable interface geometry can alter the tactile data generated during demonstration collection while the robot
command, mapping, calibration, and sensing pipeline remain fixed.

We characterize these effects through task-dependent changes in
tactile-pad accessibility, within-pad contact location, and contact
occurrence across matched demonstrations.

Through matched real-robot rollouts that cross collection interface with
tactile representation, we show that revised-interface demonstrations and a
spatial-plus-force input each increase dexterous policy success in the pooled
comparisons.

1. We show that wearable interface geometry can alter the tactile data generated during demonstration collection while the robot
command, mapping, calibration, and sensing pipeline remain fixed.

2. We characterize these effects through task-dependent changes in
tactile-pad accessibility, within-pad contact location, and contact
occurrence across matched demonstrations.

3. Through matched real-robot rollouts that cross collection interface with
tactile representation, we show that revised-interface demonstrations and a
spatial-plus-force input each increase dexterous policy success in the pooled
comparisons.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Demonstration Collection Interfaces

Dexterous demonstrations can be collected from human observations, motion
capture, and robot-mediated interfaces. Human video scales to diverse behavior,
and motion-capture systems such as DexCap improve wrist and finger tracking
without the target robot, but both still require human motion and contact to be
converted into robot-feasible actions [ 1 ] .
Robot-mediated teleoperation and hand-over-hand collection provide commands
closer to the deployment platform but retain dependence on robot hardware
during collection [ 2 ] . Portable handheld and
visuotactile systems reduce that dependence and support direct object
interaction through gripper-like or task-specific collection
embodiments [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] .

Wearable interfaces maintain direct correspondence with a target hand while
allowing the operator to manipulate objects through their own fingers.
Representative systems use robot-specific kinematics, shared mechanisms, or
wearable sensing and feedback to acquire transferable multifinger
demonstrations [ 3 , 5 , 4 , 6 , 22 , 7 ] . This correspondence also places the collection hardware
inside the physical interaction. Wearability-oriented systems such as DexEXO and WHED introduce new exoskeleton
designs for comfortable, natural collection and evaluate each design as a
complete system [ 5 , 8 ] . We instead hold the robot command, calibration, and
sensing fixed and compare the tactile data and policies produced before and
after a controlled hand-side revision.

## II-B Mechanical Correspondence and Human Interaction

Mechanical correspondence makes wearable demonstrations transferable, but it
also allows robot-hand geometry to constrain the operator. Finger spacing,
joint axes, clearances, and thumb geometry designed around a robot’s
configuration can restrict natural finger trajectories or create localized
pressure. Prior exoskeleton systems therefore emphasize passive accommodation,
wearability, calibration, or returned haptic and fingertip
cues [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .

For demonstration learning, these constraints can also change the data itself.
A restricted finger trajectory can alter a grasp, while material surrounding a
fingertip sensor can prevent a physically possible contact from being measured.
We therefore treat operator experience and recorded contact as two consequences
of the same hand-side interface revision.

## II-C Tactile Representation and Downstream Learning

Prior tactile policies use binary contact signals, per-finger force summaries,
dense taxel arrays, spatial features, and multiresolution tactile
representations [ 11 , 12 , 26 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 27 ] . These inputs preserve different properties of
physical interaction. A binary aggregate signal can retain whether a finger is
in contact while discarding within-pad location and force distribution,
whereas a spatial tactile representation can retain those distinctions. A
contact difference can therefore be present in the recorded tactile array yet
disappear before reaching the policy. We compare two complete policy inputs—binary aggregate and spatial plus
force—derived from the same tactile measurements and evaluated on the same
robot.

2026-10-08.title: Trajectory Planning without Trajectory Data: A Manifold-Guided Approach
2026-10-08.authors: Silong Yong , Anji Liu , Cunxi Dai , Carl Busart , Guanya Shi , Yilun Du , Katia Sycara , Yaqi Xie
2026-10-08.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Code can be found in this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract:
A common way for trajectory planning is to leverage generative models trained on large collections of expert trajectories. At inference time, the model generates executable trajectories by conditioning on task goal constraints.
However, trajectory-based methods rely on costly supervision, scale poorly with sequence length, and often generalize poorly to unseen constraints such as novel start-goal pairs. We propose an alternative to learn the underlying state-space manifold and use the geometry of the manifold for trajectory planning. This approach requires only state observations and enables generalization to unseen constraints by constructing trajectories on the learned manifold of the state space.
Experiments on Maze2D and robotic motion-planning benchmarks show that Ariadne constructs feasible paths from state-only supervision and generalizes to unseen
start-goal combinations. On high-dimensional dual-arm planning, it remains
competitive with trajectory-supervised and classical planners, while requiring no
trajectory data for training. Code can be found in https://github.com/SilongYong/Ariadne/ .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Trajectory planning aims to find a time-parameterized sequence of states that satisfies environment dynamics, task objectives, and constraints. Classical approaches typically rely on search or optimization over explicit dynamics models Tassa et al. (2012) ; Posa et al. (2014) ; Kavraki et al. (2002) ; Kuffner and LaValle (2000) , which can become computationally expensive in high-dimensional spaces.

Recent learning-based methods instead leverage generative models, such as diffusion models Ho et al. (2020) , to learn trajectory distributions from offline data, enabling flexible plan synthesis via conditional sampling Janner et al. (2022) ; Chi et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2024a) ; Luo et al. (2025) . By bridging sampling and planning, these methods model distributions over trajectory sequences. However, the trajectory space is exponentially large and highly structured, making it impractical to achieve sufficient coverage with finite data. As the sequence length increases, the number of feasible trajectories grows combinatorially, requiring prohibitively large datasets to learn a reliable model (Fig. 1 , top-left). Empirically, this leads to poor generalization when conditioning on unseen start–goal pairs: the generated trajectories often fail to reach the goal or violate environment constraints, even when the constituent states have been observed during training (Fig. 1 , top-right).

We aim to improve the generalizability of generative-model-based trajectory planning while reducing the need for extensive trajectory supervision. Instead of learning from expert trajectories, we consider a setting where only state observations are available, i.e., a generative model is trained to capture the distribution of valid states (Fig. 1 , bottom row). Under the manifold hypothesis Tenenbaum et al. (2000) ; Hinton and Salakhutdinov (2006) ; He et al. (2023) ; Chung et al. (2022) , these states are assumed to lie on a low-dimensional manifold embedded in the ambient space, i.e., a space that can be curved or complex overall, but looks locally like a flat Euclidean space. While learning such state distributions is well understood, a key challenge remains: how can we leverage this learned representation to construct feasible trajectories? We address this by interpreting trajectory planning as searching for valid paths on the learned state manifold, and propose a method that constructs trajectories by explicitly exploiting its geometry.

We view trajectory construction as following a vector field defined over the state space, where a trajectory corresponds to an integral curve of this field. Intuitively, at each state, the vector field specifies a local direction of motion, and integrating these directions produces a path connecting the start and goal states. This vector field is constrained to lie on the underlying state manifold, ensuring that the resulting trajectory remains in feasible regions of the state space. This perspective raises three key challenges: identifying the local geometry of the manifold, defining a vector field that respects this geometry, and ensuring meaningful notions of distance for projection.

Our key insight is that generative models provide rich geometric information about the data manifold. In particular, the score function captures local first-order structure, while higher-order information reveals the full normal space. Leveraging this, we construct a geometry-aware vector field that remains on the manifold and connects given endpoints. To enable stable projection, we further derive a Riemannian metric from the score function Béthune et al. (2025) ; Du et al. (2023) .

We first verify the idea in the classical planning domain where a 2D maze is considered. We demonstrate that with only state information provided during training a generative model, our method is able to extract the geometry and perform sequence modeling by providing feasible planned path towards the goal. Our method therefore overcomes a key limitation of learning-based sequence modeling, where models only perform well on start-goal pairs whose trajectories were seen during training.
We further demonstrate that our method can also be adopted to higher-dimensional space where a 6 DoF robot arm is tasked to avoid obstacles in a table top settings. Our method is also extended to two 7 DoF robot arms control problem where the two arms need not only to avoid obstacles but also avoid each other and achieves comparable results to the State-of-the-Art trajectory-learning-based planning method.
Overall, our contributions are as follows:

We extend the manifold hypothesis on score-accessible generative models to not only confirm the existence but also extract general geometry without strong assumptions from it.

We extend the manifold hypothesis on score-accessible generative models to not only confirm the existence but also extract general geometry without strong assumptions from it.

We propose a novel trajectory planning framework which requires only state-space training data by utilizing the geometry and introducing an endpoint constraint by connecting the non-linear interpolation formulation with iterative projection method.

We evaluate Ariadne against classical search, trajectory-supervised diffusion
planners, and geometry-based trajectory optimization, and show competitive planning
performance from state-only supervision across Maze2D and robotic motion-planning tasks.

1. We extend the manifold hypothesis on score-accessible generative models to not only confirm the existence but also extract general geometry without strong assumptions from it.

2. We propose a novel trajectory planning framework which requires only state-space training data by utilizing the geometry and introducing an endpoint constraint by connecting the non-linear interpolation formulation with iterative projection method.

3. We evaluate Ariadne against classical search, trajectory-supervised diffusion
planners, and geometry-based trajectory optimization, and show competitive planning
performance from state-only supervision across Maze2D and robotic motion-planning tasks.

# 2 Background and Motivation

Learning-based trajectory planning is typically formulated as learning from trajectory datasets. Let a state be denoted by x ∈ 𝒳 x\in\mathcal{X} , where 𝒳 \mathcal{X} is the state space. A trajectory is a time-indexed sequence τ = ( x 0 , x 1 , … , x T ) \tau=(x_{0},x_{1},\dots,x_{T}) describing a feasible transition between a start state x 0 x_{0} and a goal state x T x_{T} . A task specifies trajectory-level conditions, such as initial states, goal states, or intermediate constraints. A dataset 𝒟 traj = { τ i } i = 1 N \mathcal{D}_{\text{traj}}=\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} consists of sampled trajectories collected from demonstrations or rollouts. During training, a model learns to approximate the distribution over trajectories p ⁡ ( τ ) p(\tau) from 𝒟 traj \mathcal{D}_{\text{traj}} . At inference time, the model is conditioned on task specifications and generates a trajectory that is evaluated by task completion and feasibility. The most prominent requirements Janner et al. (2022) for task specifications are that the trajectory terminates at a specified goal state. This start-goal formulation is fundamental in robotics and motion planning and our work specifically focus on this setting.

As illustrated in Fig. 1 (top-left), trajectory datasets inevitably provide incomplete coverage of the space of feasible trajectories. Certain valid trajectories, although physically realizable, may be absent from the dataset (shown as dashed curves), due to limited data collection or biased sampling.

This incomplete coverage leads to a well-recognized generalization issue in generative planning models Janner et al. (2022) ; Chen et al. (2024b) ; Liang et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2025) . Because the model learns a trajectory-level distribution, it becomes biased toward motion patterns observed during training, i.e., biased patterns in the training set. At inference time, when tasked with generating trajectories that were not explicitly present in 𝒟 traj \mathcal{D}_{\text{traj}} , the model often fails to produce valid solutions (Fig. 1 , top-right). This failure arises from trajectory-level distribution mismatch: the required trajectory lies outside the support of the learned trajectory distribution, even though it may be perfectly feasible in the underlying environment.

We propose a new paradigm to address this limitation. We argue that many trajectory-level out-of-distribution (OOD) failures originate from bias in trajectory data rather than from insufficient state coverage. While trajectory samples may be sparse or incomplete, the underlying state distribution often exhibits significantly broader coverage (Fig. 1 , bottom-left). That is, even if certain trajectories are missing, their constituent states may still lie within the observed state space. This observation motivates a fundamental question: can we learn planning from state data alone, without relying on trajectory supervision?

Eliminating trajectory supervision immediately raises a key challenge: without access to explicit path information, how can trajectories be reconstructed at inference time? We observe that, for most planning problems, valid trajectories correspond to smooth curves in the state space that remain within dynamically feasible, low-energy regions. If a model can learn the geometric and energetic structure of the state space from state-only data, then trajectory construction can be framed as a curve generation problem under task constraints (e.g., specified endpoints). Moreover, collecting state data is often substantially easier and less restrictive than collecting full trajectory demonstrations, making this paradigm more scalable in practice.

Formally, given a learned state-space model and task-level conditions such as start and goal states, our objective becomes: how can we construct a feasible curve at inference time that obeys these conditions while remaining in valid regions of the state space? We present Ariadne 1 1 1 Ariadne refers to Ariadne’s thread in Greek mythology, which guides Theseus through the labyrinth. We use it to reflect our goal of constructing a path through complex state spaces. below, which exploits the geometry of the learned data manifold and formulates trajectory construction as integrating an ordinary differential equation (ODE) that evolves along it.

2026-10-08.title: CIRRA: Dual-Level Continual Instruction Reconciliation with Ongoing Execution for Embodied Robot Agents in Interactive Household Tasks
2026-10-08.authors: Ci Zhang , Enfu Nan , Arman Akbari , Lin Zhao , Li Wang , Chen Wang , Weiwei Chen , Yanzhi Wang , Geng Yuan
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-08.abstract: As the demand for assistance with household chores continues to grow, household robots have become a major focus of embodied intelligence. Real-world household deployment, however, inherently requires continuously replanning on human–robot interaction, as users may issue new instructions while previous requests are still under execution. Existing robot agents commonly accommodate such instructions by regenerating or extensively revising the remaining task sequence, which can introduce plan ambiguity, logical inconsistency, and redundant execution. To address these limitations, we formulate continual instruction reconciliation and propose CIRRA (Continual Instruction Reconciliation for Robot Agents), a dual-level framework combining LLM-based semantic reasoning with rule-constrained structural integration. CIRRA first uses semantic reasoning to determine whether an incoming instruction can be grounded to a unique executable skill and whether its required execution location is specified, resolving underspecified action and location information when necessary. It then preserves the ongoing subtask sequence as an execution backbone and generates fine-grained integration candidates by inserting the incoming subtasks into location-matched segments of the current task chain. Finally, the semantic reasoner evaluates only the modified segments to identify task dependencies and potential conflicts and select the most logically coherent local integration. By coupling structure-preserving local integration with semantic grounding and logical selection, CIRRA maintains alignment with the robot’s current execution, mitigates plan ambiguity and logical inconsistency, and reuses shared subtasks to reduce redundant execution. We further introduce CHIRP (Continual Household Instruction Reconciliation and Planning), a text-based benchmark of 120 episodes spanning eight household environments and six categories of everyday activities. On CHIRP, CIRRA reaches 74.2% decision agreement, 30 points above the strongest replanning baseline, and every correct fusion decision it makes yields a correctly placed, conflict-free schedule. On a Unitree G1 humanoid, CIRRA interrupts ongoing skills at the correct moment in every trial and significantly outperforms all baselines on every metric.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Recently, household robots have emerged as a major focus in embodied intelligence, driven by the growing demand for everyday assistance amid the accelerating pace of modern life, population aging, and persistent labor shortages in care and domestic services. Recent advances in robotic foundation models, particularly vision-language-action models Brohan et al. (2022) ; Zitkovich et al. (2023) ; Kim et al. (2024b) ; Physical Intelligence et al. (2025) ; Bjorck et al. (2025) , have made general-purpose household assistance increasingly feasible, enabling robots to understand natural-language instructions, perceive complex environments, and execute a diverse range of navigation and manipulation skills.

However, even capable action models alone remain insufficient for autonomous household operation Shi et al. (2025) ; Yang et al. (2025) ; Koo et al. (2025) . To bridge this gap, embodied robot agents have extensively studied high-level task decomposition and long-horizon skill coordination Dalal et al. (2024) ; Yuan et al. (2025) , task-state tracking and memory Wang et al. (2025) ; Koo et al. (2025) , and adaptive replanning in response to execution failures or environmental changes Huang et al. (2022) ; Skreta et al. (2024) . These advances enable an agent to translate a high-level user goal into a coherent sequence of executable skills, monitor task progress, and revise its plan when execution deviates from expectation.

Despite this progress, a critical challenge for household deployment remains comparatively underexplored: how to integrate a newly arriving task instruction with one that is already under execution. Although existing interactive agents can engage in dialogue and respond to user corrections, feedback, or task changes Wei et al. (2022) ; Kambhampati et al. (2024) ; Shinn et al. (2023) ; Li et al. (2023) ; Joublin et al. (2024) ; Borate et al. (2025) ; Lu et al. (2025) , a common strategy for accommodating such input is to re-invoke a high-level model with the updated instruction and current execution context to regenerate or revise the remaining task sequence. Without explicit constraints on preserving unaffected portions of the ongoing plan, this generative replanning can introduce three key issues. First, it may create plan ambiguity , as a minor instruction update can cause substantial plan churn, unnecessarily reorder pending subtasks, and obscure how the revised plan aligns with the current execution state. Second, it may produce logical inconsistency by violating task dependencies or introducing conflicting action orderings. Third, it may lead to execution redundancy by failing to identify and reuse subtasks shared between the ongoing and incoming instructions. These limitations highlight the need for fine-grained, execution-aligned instruction integration rather than unconstrained plan regeneration.

To address these limitations, we propose CIRRA, a dual-level framework that combines LLM-based semantic reasoning with rule-constrained structural integration. Upon receiving a new instruction, the semantic reasoning level first determines whether its action description can be grounded to a unique executable skill and whether the location required for execution is explicitly specified (shown in Ambiguity Detection in Fig. 1 ). It resolves underspecified action and location information to obtain a complete, location-aware representation of the incoming instruction. For a non-emergency instruction, the structural integration level then treats the robot’s ongoing subtask sequence as an immutable execution backbone(shown in Task fusion in Fig. 1 ): it retains every existing subtask and their relative ordering, and generates fine-grained integration candidates by inserting the incoming subtasks into segments of the sequence associated with the same execution location. The semantic reasoning level is subsequently invoked again, but only over the modified segments, to evaluate their task dependencies, identify potential conflicts, and select the most logically coherent local integration. In this way, CIRRA prevents the LLM from globally regenerating or reordering the ongoing plan, while still leveraging its semantic reasoning to accurately ground the incoming instruction and determine its logically appropriate placement. The two levels therefore provide complementary guarantees: rule-constrained integration preserves the robot’s current execution strategy, whereas LLM-based reasoning ensures instruction completeness, placement accuracy, and the logical coherence of each modified segment. Together, they enable fine-grained instruction reconciliation without disrupting ongoing execution or introducing redundant actions.

Existing household benchmarks primarily focus on instruction following, dialogue, and task execution under predefined user goals, but are not designed to evaluate replanning when new task requests arrive during ongoing execution Shridhar et al. (2020) ; Padmakumar et al. (2022) ; Gao et al. (2022) . Conversely, existing replanning benchmarks and evaluation settings largely study plan revision in response to execution failures or environmental changes, rather than continual user-driven task updates in interactive household settings. Consequently, there remains no dedicated benchmark at the intersection of household interaction and instruction-triggered replanning. To fill this gap, we introduce CHIRP (Continual Household Instruction Reconciliation and Planning), a text-based benchmark specifically designed to evaluate how embodied robot agents revise an ongoing household task plan in response to newly arriving user instructions. The benchmark spans eight representative household environments: bedroom, study room, kitchen, bathroom, living room, basement, garage, and yard. And covers six major categories of household activities: object fetching, cleaning, tidying, cooking, appliance operation, and waste disposal. Across all evaluated environments and task categories, CIRRA consistently outperforms existing replanning baselines, producing more accurate instruction integrations, more logically coherent task sequences, and less redundant execution.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Robotic Action Foundation Models

Vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models Zitkovich et al. (2023) ; Team et al. (2024) ; Kim et al. (2024b) ; Li et al. (2024) ; Physical Intelligence et al. (2025) ; Qu et al. (2025) ; Bjorck et al. (2025) ; Bu et al. (2025) ; Shukor et al. (2025) have shifted robot control from separately trained, task-specific policies toward reusable, language-conditioned action models that transfer across tasks, environments, and embodiments. By grounding the semantic knowledge of pretrained vision-language models in continuous action generation, these models increasingly serve as general-purpose skill interfaces that higher-level robotic systems can invoke. As a result, the bottleneck of household autonomy moves to the higher level: deciding which skills to execute and in what order, especially when new instructions arrive during execution.

## 2.2 Embodied Agents for Task Planning and Replanning

At this higher level, LLM-based embodied agents translate user goals into executable robot behaviors. SayCan grounds LLM-proposed actions in the affordances of pretrained skills Ahn et al. (2022) , ProgPrompt and Code as Policies generate program-like plans over available actions and control APIs Singh et al. (2022) ; Liang et al. (2023) , and Inner Monologue feeds success detection, scene descriptions, and human feedback back into planning Huang et al. (2022) .

Subsequent agents add hierarchical skill orchestration Dalal et al. (2024) ; Yuan et al. (2025) , persistent task memory Wang et al. (2025) , and online user feedback Shi et al. (2025) , and increasingly rely on replanning for robust long-horizon execution: CAPE corrects violated skill preconditions Raman et al. (2024) , AdaPlanner refines plans from environmental feedback Sun et al. (2023) , RePLan revises behavior after plan failures or unforeseen obstacles Skreta et al. (2024) , and PRED pre-emptively revises upcoming actions when the environment changes Kim et al. (2024a) . However, these methods predominantly treat replanning as recovery under a fixed user goal: the task itself stays unchanged, and the agent only adapts its behavior to execution-state mismatches.

This leaves an important case underexplored: in interactive households, users may issue additional task instructions while an earlier task chain is still being executed. Interactive agents incorporate corrections, feedback, or clarifications about the ongoing task Huang et al. (2022) ; Shi et al. (2025) , but do not address how a new task should be reconciled with it. Simply prompting an LLM with the new instruction and the execution context gives no guarantee that unaffected subtasks and their order are preserved. A small update may thus cause plan ambiguity , where excessive plan churn obscures how the revised plan relates to the current execution state; logical inconsistency , where task dependencies are violated or actions are ordered in conflict; and execution redundancy , where navigation or manipulation subtasks shared by the ongoing and incoming instructions are not reused. To our knowledge, CIRRA is the first embodied-agent framework for continual, instruction-triggered replanning over an ongoing task chain. It combines execution-aligned structural integration with LLM-based semantic reasoning to preserve the unaffected part of the current plan while resolving all three issues.

2026-10-08.title: Autonomous Droplet Navigation via Model-Based Reinforcement Learning: Zero-Shot Transfer and Emergent Dynamics
2026-10-08.authors: Rajneesh Anand , Mayuresh V. Kothare
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-08.comment: Accepted for presentation at the Robotics & Automation in Self-Driving Laboratories 2026 Workshop, IROS 2026. this https URL
2026-10-08.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are transforming chemical and materials discovery through closed-loop automation, yet automated infrastructure for physical manipulation of soft, deformable matter remains beyond current robotic platforms. A critical instance is autonomous droplet transport on an open surface, where interfacial physics produce partially observable dynamics that pose significant challenges for classical model-based controllers. We introduce the first robotic platform for closed-loop autonomous liquid droplet navigation on an open, unconfined surface using model-based reinforcement learning. A two-axis tilting board coated with a thin silicone oil film drives the droplet, while an overhead camera provides real-time feedback. A learned policy was trained on just 50 to 150 physical episodes depending on geometric complexity, without simulation or analytical models. Beyond performance alone, the platform demonstrates three capabilities of interest to the SDL community: it robustly transfers zero-shot to unseen geometries; it autonomously discovers an oscillatory depinning strategy to free the droplet when it sticks; and it completes its full training pipeline in under 90 minutes. These results extend reinforcement-learning manipulation from rigid microrobots to deformable soft-matter systems for next-generation SDLs.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are transforming chemical and materials discovery by integrating robotic platforms, automated instrumentation, and machine learning into experiments [ 1 ] .
While SDLs have automated reaction design and synthesis, automated infrastructure for physical manipulation of soft, deformable matter, where the agent has no rigid structure and the dynamics resist analytical modeling, remains beyond current robotic platforms.
A critical instance is autonomous droplet transport on an open surface. Droplet-based operations underpin lab-on-a-chip diagnostics, combinatorial chemical synthesis, and high-throughput biological assays, yet existing droplet transport platforms rely on either preprogrammed actuation sequences or manual control. The governing physics, including contact-angle hysteresis, pinning, and surface heterogeneity from lubricant depletion, introduce partially observable dynamics that pose significant challenges for classical model-based controllers.

A liquid droplet transported on an open surface is precisely such a system. Unlike rigid microrobots [ 2 ] , a droplet is deformable, prone to pinning, and governed by interfacial forces [ 3 , 4 ] that render its response to actuation nonlinear and history-dependent. Its dynamics couple contact-line motion, lubricant-film depletion, and meniscus deformation, which are computationally expensive to resolve and impractical to simulate, making the design of a classical model-predictive controller (MPC) challenging.

Contributions. This paper demonstrates first autonomous droplet navigation on a tilt-actuated platform through open channel across five different geometries with increasing complexities. We show a zero-shot transfer learning framework in which a policy trained on the simpler (I-) shape navigates the droplet on the L-in-, Arc-in-, and a new Staircase-shape that introduces greater complexity. This study shows the first demonstration of a latent world-model agent (DreamerV3) [ 5 ] trained fully offline on experimental data, without any simulator or analytical model.

# II Methods

## II-A Camera

We install an overhead See3CAM _ \_ 24CUG camera that was mounted on T-slotted aluminum extrusion profiles with a 3D-printed mounting plate to hold the camera at a fixed height. The camera provides a 1920 × \times 1200 RGB image of the board and droplet at 60 fps (frames per second).

## II-B Motors

In order to control the inclination of the Labyrinth, both manual control knobs were removed by prying them and two Dynamixel motors were coupled to the exposed tilt shafts. Pilot holes were drilled into the Labyrinth frame, and 3D-printed motor housings were slid over the motors and bolted to the frame to fix the motors in place. Both motors were daisy-chained using a ROBOT X3P cable extended by splicing additional wire between the corresponding pins. The motor chain was connected to a U2D2 USB-to-Dynamixel adapter mounted on a U2D2 Power Hub Board, which was powered by a 5V3A USB supply. The U2D2 and camera were connected to the host laptop via USB. A complete closed-loop hardware chain is shown in Fig. 1 .

## II-C Control Unit

The control unit uses two computers: a CPU-only laptop that runs the ROS2 control loop and motor communication via the U2D2 adapter, and a separate GPU platform used for offline world-model training. Collected episodes are transferred to the GPU for training, and the resulting policy is sent back for evaluation. This decoupled setup prevents training latency from interfering with real-time control.

2026-10-08.title: Taming an End-to-End Autonomous Driving Policy for Urban Navigation of Quadruped Robots
2026-10-08.authors: Joochan Kim , Chanuk Yang , Tackgeun You , Ziran Wang , Hwasup Lim
2026-10-08.comment: Accepted to IROS 2026 Workshop on AI Meets Autonomy
2026-10-08.abstract:
We present Go2-DrivoR, a goal-conditioned adaptation of the end-to-end autonomous driving trajectory planning framework DrivoR for urban navigation with quadrupedal robots.
By conditioning trajectory generation on a local-frame subgoal through a goal token and adapting the vehicle-centric scoring formulation, the method extends DrivoR to short-horizon goal-conditioned local planning without redesigning its core decoders.
Specifically, we redefine drivable-area compliance for sidewalk-oriented navigation and reformulate the original ego progress term as goal-conditioned ego progress.
Trained exclusively on TartanGround simulation data, Go2-DrivoR improves waypoint-conditioned planning performance on unseen simulation environments and transfers zero-shot to open-loop real-world trajectory prediction.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Urban navigation with quadrupedal robots requires short-horizon goal-conditioned local planning under legged motion constraints.
In contrast to autonomous vehicles, quadrupedal robots operate in roadways, walkways, and mixed urban environments where lane centerlines and fixed route geometries are not generally available.
A navigation policy must therefore generate local trajectories from visual observations and proprioceptive states while accounting for obstacles, pedestrians, surface variation, and the tracking limitations of a downstream locomotion system.
These characteristics make the direct application of vehicle-centric planning methods nontrivial [ 1 , 2 ] .

Recent end-to-end autonomous driving methods integrate learned scene representations with trajectory planning [ 3 , 4 ] .
DrivoR is particularly relevant to this setting because it combines register-token-based visual encoding with a disentangled trajectory-scoring architecture for multi-camera planning [ 5 ] .
However, DrivoR is designed for vehicle-centric environments, where candidate trajectories are evaluated using road-aligned notions of drivable-area compliance and progress [ 6 , 7 ] .
Although its safety-related terms can be retained with robot-footprint-aware evaluation, the original drivable-area compliance criterion does not encode the relative desirability of sidewalks, roads, and out-of-bounds regions for quadrupedal navigation.
Moreover, the original formulation lacks explicit goal conditioning; it neither conditions trajectory proposals on a local lookahead waypoint nor measures progress toward that target.

To address this problem, we adapt DrivoR to short-horizon goal-conditioned quadrupedal navigation while retaining its core decoder architectures.
We condition trajectory proposals on a local-frame lookahead waypoint through a goal token.
For trajectory scoring, we retain the existing safety criteria with robot-footprint-aware evaluation and redefine drivable-area compliance (DAC) using sidewalk, road, and out-of-bounds regions.
We also augment the original ego-progress (EP) term with goal-directed progress to obtain goal-conditioned ego progress (GEP), aligning trajectory evaluation with the supplied local goal.

To assess sim-to-real transfer, we train the model exclusively on simulation data from TartanGround [ 8 ] .
Real-world logs collected with the Unitree Go2 are withheld from training and used solely for zero-shot open-loop trajectory evaluation.
We evaluate the model on seen and unseen simulation environments and real-world Unitree Go2 logs.
This protocol evaluates the transferability of the proposed goal-conditioned adaptation without real-world fine-tuning [ 9 ] .

# II METHODS

## II-A Go2-DrivoR

We formulate urban quadrupedal navigation as goal-conditioned local trajectory planning.
Given four surrounding fisheye images, the robot’s proprioceptive state, a high-level directional command, and a two-dimensional goal in the current ego frame,
Go2-DrivoR generates K K candidate trajectories and selects the one with the highest predicted score.
The output consists of eight ( x , y , θ ) (x,y,\theta) waypoints over a four-second horizon, expressed in the current ego frame.

Our model builds on DrivoR [ 5 ] , retaining its visual feature extractor, trajectory decoder, scoring decoder, and winner-takes-all trajectory objective.
We introduce goal-token conditioning for trajectory generation and adapt the scoring criteria through sidewalk-oriented drivable-area compliance and goal-conditioned ego progress (GEP).

This state is projected by a linear layer to obtain the ego status token 𝐞 ego ∈ ℝ D \mathbf{e}_{\text{ego}}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} .

Compared with the original six-component scoring formulation of DrivoR, our adapted scorer uses five supervised components: no-fault collision (NOC), drivable-area compliance (DAC), time-to-collision (TTC), goal-conditioned ego progress (GEP), and comfort.
The driving-direction compliance (DDC) component is omitted because quadrupedal robots are not constrained to follow a prescribed road or lane direction during destination-based navigation.
The following paragraphs describe the robot-footprint-aware safety evaluation and the adapted DAC and GEP formulations.

We retain DrivoR’s NOC and TTC formulations but replace the vehicle footprint with the quadrupedal robot footprint for collision and time-to-collision evaluation.
To reflect sidewalk-oriented navigation, we redefine DAC using semantic regions along each candidate trajectory.
A candidate receives a DAC score of 1 1 if all sampled waypoints lie on the sidewalk, 0.5 0.5 if at least one waypoint lies on the road while no waypoint lies outside the allowable region, and 0 0 otherwise.
These semantic-region labels are used to construct the DAC oracle targets for scoring supervision.

ego frame, this component measures the candidate trajectory’s

The GEP target is defined by combining the original ego-progress target with the goal-directed progress value:

At inference, the predicted sub-scores are combined using the log-domain formulation of the original DrivoR scorer. Let ℓ k , c \ell_{k,c} denote the predicted logit for candidate trajectory τ k \tau_{k} and score component c c , and let

For evaluation, we compute an adapted PDMS-style aggregate
score from oracle-evaluated sub-scores:

The scoring decoder is trained using component-wise

We jointly optimize the trajectory and scoring losses with equal weights. Both update the shared perception encoder, but scoring gradients do not pass through predicted trajectories to the trajectory decoder.

## II-B Simulation and Real-World Data Collection

We train the planner on high-fidelity simulation data and evaluate its zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on real-world Unitree Go2 logs.
Both domains undergo a standardized preprocessing and serialization pipeline to unify sensor modalities, coordinate systems, and high-level routing interfaces into the planner’s input format.

TartanGround [ 8 ] serves as our simulation dataset, providing photorealistic multi-camera renderings, IMU telemetry, and dense semantic point clouds across diverse synthetic environments.
We process the data through a three-stage pipeline.
First, the original multi-camera pinhole images provided by TartanGround are reprojected into four fisheye views—front, left, right, and rear—using a calibrated double-sphere camera model.
Second, the resulting images are paired with expert kinematics, and pose, velocity, and body acceleration are transformed from the simulation coordinate system to ENU (East–North–Up) and FLU (Front–Left–Up) frames.
To follow the NAVSIM convention, we convert the long continuous TartanGround trajectories into local planning samples using a sliding-window procedure.
For a sample at time t, the local-frame goal is defined as the expert pose four seconds after t and is expressed in the current ego frame.
This four-second lookahead waypoint is used as the conditioning goal for the corresponding local planning sample, rather than as a global destination.
High-level four-way commands are then synthesized from the lateral displacement of the same four-second lookahead waypoint in the ego frame.
Finally, semantic point clouds are projected onto a 2D grid to construct boundary, roadway, and walkway vector layers for scoring.

For real-world data collection, the Unitree Go2 is equipped with four GMSL Owl cameras mounted at 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} azimuthal intervals around the robot, providing front, left, rear, and right views.
A human operator teleoperated the robot during data collection, and the recorded robot motion serves as the expert trajectory for open-loop evaluation.
The collected logs consist of multi-camera video streams and synchronized state records indexed by frame markers.
We align the visual streams with the proprioceptive logs via temporal cross-referencing, and the raw fisheye images are used directly as input without rectification.
The kinematic states are converted from the robot’s native FRD (Front-Right-Down) frame to FLU, and goal-oriented commands are inferred from lookahead targets using a lateral threshold before serialization.

2026-10-08.title: Context-Aware Adaptive Pesticide Spraying for Agricultural Robots under Changing Weather and Terrain Using Vision-Language Models
2026-10-08.authors: Cong-Thanh Vu , Yen-Chen Liu
2026-10-08.comment: Accepted for publication in Computers and Electronics in Agriculture
2026-10-08.abstract: Precision pesticide spraying is essential for optimizing application efficiency and ensuring uniform chemical distribution. Spraying performance is influenced by multiple factors, including environmental conditions such as temperature and wind speed, pesticide type, and the robot’s capability to accurately perceive crops and target spray locations. Existing approaches predominantly emphasize crop detection and rely on predefined spraying parameters, whereas human operators dynamically adjust their spraying strategies by considering environmental conditions, region-specific crop characteristics, and the type of pesticide being applied. In this study, we propose a context-aware adaptive spraying framework based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs), which enables robots to leverage spatial reasoning and integrate information from multiple sources, including crop type, pesticide type, and weather data, to make adaptive and optimized spraying decisions. Subsequently, a trajectory-tracking controller based on Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control is employed to ensure precise navigation and accurate spraying at crop locations. The comparative results demonstrate that the proposed method improves accuracy by at least 30% in detecting crop rows. In addition, the experimental evaluations conducted in two environments further demonstrate the robot’s ability to flexibly adjust spraying volume and travel speed, while reducing pesticide drift.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Pesticide application has long been an essential component of agricultural production, helping protect crops from pests and diseases and reducing yield losses. However, current spraying practices, ranging from manual backpack spraying to autonomous systems, still present several limitations. During manual spraying, human operators can directly observe crop conditions and adjust spray volume, modify their movement direction based on wind or weather conditions, vary walking speed, or alter spraying patterns when encountering dense canopies, severely infected plants, or hard-to-reach areas. Although this flexibility is valuable, it depends heavily on operator experience, is physically demanding, and often results in inconsistent performance, which can negatively affect human health ( Dasgupta et al., 2007 ; Shekhar et al., 2024 ) . In contrast, mechanized and semi-automated sprayers lack such human-like adaptability; they typically apply pesticides continuously at fixed rates without accounting for spatial variability in canopy structure, leaf density, or disease severity ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Rahimi Azghadi et al., 2025 ; Berenstein and Edan, 2018 ) . As a result, excessive pesticide deposition frequently occurs, increasing production costs, generating unnecessary chemical waste, and posing risks to both the environment and human health ( Owen-Smith et al., 2019 ) . These limitations underscore the need for more intelligent and adaptive spraying solutions that combine automated operation with decision-making capabilities resembling those of skilled human operators ( Liu et al., 2021 ; Raja, 2024 ) .

Over the past two decades, numerous studies have focused on developing automated systems to minimize pesticide waste and improve precision spraying. These systems aim to detect crops accurately and apply pesticides only where needed, rather than uniformly across the field. For example, Nguyen et al. (2023) proposed a camera-based system that estimates tomato leaf density and selectively activates nozzles, overcoming the limitations of fixed spray trajectories, though the number of independently controllable spray positions remains limited. To improve coverage, Fu et al. (2022) introduced adjustable nozzle heights for consistent deposition across varying plant structures. Fu et al. (2026) further enhanced detection by compensating for camera tilt caused by uneven terrain. Despite these advances, vision-based systems struggle under low-light conditions; to address this, Jiang and Ahamed (2025) integrated thermal imaging with LiDAR for robust crop detection in visually degraded environments.

Beyond crop detection for targeted spraying, weed detection and treatment have also attracted significant attention. Ahmadi et al. (2024) developed a weeding platform that identifies weeds and generates spray plans to avoid damaging nearby crops. Jin et al. (2025) combined ultra-fine needle injectors with deep learning to treat individual weeds with high precision. Instead of detecting weeds directly, Hu et al. (2022) represented weed-infested areas as line segments and optimized nozzle allocation using binary linear programming to maximize coverage efficiency. Research on accurate target identification has also expanded to aerial platforms. Luo et al. (2024) used LiDAR point clouds to analyze canopy structures for drone spraying decisions, while Wei et al. (2024) employed YOLO-based fruit detection to enable tree-specific, highly localized pesticide applications.

Although crop detection and spraying decision-making systems have proven effective in reducing pesticide usage, several challenges remain. Variability in crop size and canopy structure makes maintaining a consistent spray rate difficult ( Hussain et al., 2025 ; Taseer and Han, 2024 ) . To address this, Berenstein and Edan (2018) developed a device that adjusts flow rate and droplet size based on crop dimensions, but its reliance on color-based target detection and neglect of environmental factors limited its adaptability. Building on this, Hu et al. (2025) proposed a multi-dimensional prescription map using 3D point clouds, incorporating leaf–wood separation via LSTM, nozzle position optimization, and spraying-unit division. RGB-D imagery has also been leveraged for real-time canopy segmentation and dynamic flow-rate adjustment ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , while Zhang et al. (2025) fused camera and laser data to estimate canopy volumes for adjusting spray flow. Beyond flow control, regulating spray direction is crucial; Shi et al. (2024) introduced an active nozzle-orientation mechanism that aligns sprays with the canopy, minimizing off-target deposition and environmental impact.

Research on crop recognition and spray-rate adjustment has contributed significantly to reducing pesticide loss and mitigating environmental impact. However, these approaches still face many challenges, particularly in adapting spraying strategies flexibly to varying conditions, as a human operator would. In agricultural environments, farmers rely on contextual information, adjusting pesticide amounts based on variations in plant density, canopy structure, and disease status. They also consider weather conditions and the characteristics of each pesticide to determine appropriate movement directions and speeds, ensuring effective application according to temperature and wind. These factors, which are critical for spray coverage and droplet adhesion, have been largely overlooked in previous studies that primarily assume fixed movement trajectories. Therefore, developing an autonomous spraying system capable of making movement and spraying decisions in a human-like manner holds significant potential for advancing smart agriculture.

Recently, foundation models, such as Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), have achieved significant breakthroughs in human-like decision making and reasoning by leveraging large-scale Internet data. These models have been successfully applied in various robotics domains, including autonomous driving ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , natural-language-guided navigation using hand-drawn maps ( Tan et al., 2025 ) , and map-free outdoor navigation ( Song et al., 2025 ) . They also show strong potential in agriculture, helping overcome the limitations of previous methods that were often tailored to specific problems and difficult to generalize ( Sapkota et al., 2025 ; Kuska et al., 2024 ) . Several studies have explored these reasoning capabilities to enhance agricultural applications, such as multi-level tea bud detection with generative AI support during training, agriculture-specific model designs ( Yang et al., 2025 ) , and LLM-based analysis of data collected from agricultural environments ( Fang et al., 2025 ) .

In this study, we propose a novel approach for autonomous pesticide application using VLMs. The method enables the robot to execute a context-aware adaptive spraying strategy based on weather conditions and the operational environment. The main contributions of this study are as follows:

We introduce a framework that integrates VLMs into autonomous pesticide spraying, enabling the robot to generate adaptive pesticide application strategies that take into account crop types, the operational environment, and external environmental factors such as wind direction and temperature.

We propose a crop-row detection method based on VLMs for global planning and compare it with other crop-row detection methods using unsupervised algorithms such as KMeans ( Jiang and Ahamed, 2023 ) , DBSCAN ( Vu et al., 2024 ) , or manual adjustments ( Schönegg et al., 2024 ) . The proposed approach significantly improves crop-row detection accuracy by at least 30%.

We develop a path-tracking controller based on the Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) framework for pesticide spraying tasks, enabling the robot to follow the spraying trajectory while simultaneously avoiding obstacles during navigation.

The proposed method is evaluated in two different field environments. The results show that our approach generates context-aware adaptive spraying strategies under varying environmental conditions and also helps reduce pesticide loss caused by environmental factors.

1. We introduce a framework that integrates VLMs into autonomous pesticide spraying, enabling the robot to generate adaptive pesticide application strategies that take into account crop types, the operational environment, and external environmental factors such as wind direction and temperature.

2. We propose a crop-row detection method based on VLMs for global planning and compare it with other crop-row detection methods using unsupervised algorithms such as KMeans ( Jiang and Ahamed, 2023 ) , DBSCAN ( Vu et al., 2024 ) , or manual adjustments ( Schönegg et al., 2024 ) . The proposed approach significantly improves crop-row detection accuracy by at least 30%.

3. We develop a path-tracking controller based on the Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) framework for pesticide spraying tasks, enabling the robot to follow the spraying trajectory while simultaneously avoiding obstacles during navigation.

4. The proposed method is evaluated in two different field environments. The results show that our approach generates context-aware adaptive spraying strategies under varying environmental conditions and also helps reduce pesticide loss caused by environmental factors.

# 2 System Design

This section presents the autonomous pesticide-spraying robot used in the experiments. The robot is developed based on the Bunker Mini platform manufactured by Agilex. This compact chassis employs a tracked mobility system, enabling stable operation on uneven and complex terrains commonly found in agricultural fields, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .

At the front of the robot, we integrate a ZED X camera connected to the Jetson Orin onboard computer via a GMSL2 interface, along with a Livox Mid-360 3D LiDAR connected through Ethernet to support crop detection and spatial mapping. All sensor data processing and execution of the proposed algorithms are performed on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin edge computing device, which provides real-time performance through CUDA-accelerated parallel computation. The control framework is developed based on ROS2 Humble. The robot communicates with the Jetson Orin via a CAN bus to receive velocity commands and transmit status information.

For the spraying system, we design two independent modules mounted on the left and right sides of the robot, enabling side-specific spraying decisions instead of relying on a single central pump. This design helps optimize chemical usage and reduce waste. To control the two pump modules, an Arduino Uno is used as an intermediary controller, communicating with the Jetson Orin through Serial to receive pump commands. The Arduino then converts these commands into PWM signals to drive the ESCs and regulate the pump speed. The selected pump is the Eagle Power Wa3510, a compact BLDC motor capable of generating high pressure. Each side is equipped with two adjustable nozzles, allowing the spray diameter to be tuned for optimal chemical usage and coverage under varying field conditions. These pumps are connected to a 20-liter pesticide tank mounted on the robot chassis.

2026-10-08.title: SAFE: Unified Slip and Fracture Detection with Low-Cost Acoustic Sensing in Robotic Grasping
2026-10-08.authors: Zerun Wang , Vivek Kamat , Shekhar Bhansali
2026-10-08.abstract: Manipulating fragile objects remains challenging as robots must understand the state of what they grasp, such as slip or fracture, to respond appropriately, especially when material properties are unknown. In this paper, we present SAFE: a low-cost, general-purpose sensing approach that detects both slip and fracture in real time using two passive polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) acoustic sensors and motor proprioception, without relying on vision or prior material knowledge. The sensors are mounted on a compliant Fin Ray gripper, and a unified HistGradientBoosting classifier reports the state (normal, slip, or fracture) from a 79-dimensional feature vector. Under leave-one-grasp-out cross-validation, SAFE achieves an Alert-F1 of 0.884 with near-zero slip-fracture confusion, and ablations confirm that acoustic sensing is indispensable. An adaptive grasp controller built on this detection layer runs at 104 Hz on a Jetson Orin Nano, achieving 91.3% success across 46 closed-loop robot trials spanning diverse object categories, while each fixed-force strategy drops to 0% on object conditions that mismatch its preset. It further reaches 82.4% success on novel objects unseen during training, demonstrating robust, failure-aware grasp control without object-specific calibration.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Tactile Sensing for Contact-Rich Manipulation

Tactile sensing allows robots to feel forces, textures, and object shapes, providing contact information that is unavailable from vision alone, and has become a key enabling technology for contact-rich manipulation. Visual-tactile sensors reconstruct contact force and geometry from deformable membranes inside grippers at high spatial resolution [ 30 , 9 ] , and have been integrated into Fin Ray structures through embedded cameras that capture the contact surface directly [ 13 , 12 ] , as well as through mechanical transmission of structural deformation [ 15 ] . Most notably, GelSight FlexiRay achieves full-coverage multimodal perception, including proprioception, contact force, texture, and slippage, on Fin Ray grippers using a multi-mirror visual-tactile design [ 24 ] . However, such vision-based tactile approaches face optical and imaging trade-offs: temporal responsiveness is bounded by the frame rate of the imaging sensor, while structural form factor is constrained by the camera’s field of view and focal length [ 24 , 11 ] . Barometric sensing offers an alternative: integrated into Fin Ray grippers, it enables force and slip estimation with low latency, but pneumatic channels remain vulnerable to temperature-induced pressure drift, limiting deployment in thermally variable scenarios [ 22 ] .

While comprehensive tactile reconstruction benefits general-purpose manipulation, many grasp-control tasks do not require full contact-state estimation. Instead, reliably recognizing a small number of task-critical interaction events can be sufficient for closed-loop grasp control. For fragile object manipulation with unknown material properties, two such events define the safe grasping window from opposite directions: fracture, when grasp force exceeds what the object can withstand, and slip, when grasp force falls short of what is needed to hold it.

## II-B Fracture Detection

Excessive grasp force can cause irreversible damage, making timely fracture detection critical for safe grasp-force regulation. Early approaches monitor contact pressure using compliant fluid fingertips to identify pressure changes and regulate grasp force to avoid damage [ 17 ] . More recent learning-based methods exploit tactile observations to anticipate impending fracture during robotic food manipulation [ 7 ] , with follow-up work improving object generalization by learning fracture-related representations from reusable surrogate objects rather than task-specific fragile items [ 28 ] . These studies demonstrate the value of tactile sensing for reducing grasp-induced damage, but they also expose two limitations. First, existing approaches rely primarily on pressure or deformation sensing, whereas acoustic-emission studies have shown that crack initiation and propagation generate high-frequency elastic waves, with AE activity emerging before yielding and characteristic burst signals accompanying fracture initiation and crack growth [ 3 , 14 ] . Such signals provide sensitive indicators of damage evolution before macroscopic failure becomes apparent. Second, many tactile sensing approaches rely on relatively rigid taxel arrays, which can complicate integration with highly compliant end-effectors such as Fin Ray grippers.

More fundamentally, all of the above methods address only one half of the grasp-force problem: they provide an upper bound that prevents excessive force, but say nothing about whether the applied force is sufficient to hold the object. Successful grasping of unfamiliar fragile objects requires both avoiding fracture and avoiding slip, and fracture-only perception cannot by itself determine an appropriate grasp force.

## II-C Slip Detection

Symmetric to the fracture case, insufficient grasp force leads to object slip and grasp failure, making slip perception the complementary lower bound for adaptive grasp control. Early work demonstrates that grasp force can be regulated according to incipient slip, mimicking human grasp stabilization [ 20 ] . Subsequent studies develop tactile slip detection coupled with reactive grasp controllers based on incipient-slip estimation [ 4 , 8 ] , and more recent learning-based methods further improve robustness and object generalization across diverse manipulation scenarios [ 32 ] . Most relevant to our approach, A-SLIP extends passive acoustic sensing from binary slip detection to continuous estimation of slip direction and magnitude using multi-channel piezoelectric microphones and learning-based fusion, demonstrating in closed-loop tasks that continuous slip vectors enable more reliable motion tracking and stopping behavior than binary detection alone [ 29 ] . While slip direction may not be significantly useful for parallel-type grippers because they have only one closing direction, magnitude information, in principle, could support force controllers to scale grip-force increments based on the severity of observed slip for faster adjustments. However, without fracture detection limiting the upper bound, there is a risk that the increment is too large and directly exceeds the fracture limit.

## II-D Acoustic Sensing

The two sections above demonstrate that acoustic signals carry valuable information for grasping state sensing. Acoustic emission literature identifies high-frequency vibration as the earliest indicator of fracture, while A-SLIP and other works show that acoustic signals also encode fine-grained slip dynamics. This suggests that a single acoustic sensing layer may be capable of resolving both failure modes, a possibility that, to our knowledge, has not been tested.

Acoustic sensing captures mechanical vibrations generated during physical interaction and has been explored for a variety of robotic manipulation tasks. Passive contact microphones capture high-frequency vibrations from the contact interface, enabling continuous slip vector estimation [ 29 ] , material classification [ 18 ] , and contact-rich manipulation tasks [ 10 , 27 ] . In contrast, active acoustic methods emit a probing signal and infer contact state from the received acoustic response [ 31 ] . Among acoustic transducers, polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) film has been widely adopted for contact acoustic acquisition in grasping, owing to its flexibility, broad frequency response, low acoustic impedance, and high sensitivity to dynamic mechanical stimuli [ 26 , 19 , 33 ] . Unlike resistive or capacitive tactile sensors, PVDF responds to transient deformation and vibration rather than static contact force, making it well suited to dynamic tactile events such as contact transitions, impacts, and slip [ 26 , 19 ] . Existing studies have integrated PVDF sensors into cable-driven robotic hands for slip-triggered grasp-force regulation [ 16 ] and into compliant robotic grippers for vibration-based slip estimation [ 21 ] .

However, every acoustic-sensing study above targets a single failure mode with a single sensing channel: slip detection via one microphone and a hand-tuned threshold, or fracture-relevant acoustic emission studied only outside robotic manipulation. None uses acoustic sensing to resolve both slip and fracture from a shared, low-cost sensing layer, and none demonstrates that a single learned classifier can distinguish the two failure signatures reliably enough for real-time closed-loop control. This is the gap SAFE addresses: two passive PVDF channels on a single compliant Fin Ray finger, combined with motor proprioception, feeding a unified classifier that resolves both the upper (fracture) and lower (slip) bounds of the safe grasping window from one sensing modality.

2026-10-08.title: A Review Of Robotic World Models For Dynamic Environments Based On Factor And Scene Graphs
2026-10-08.authors: Marco Giberna , Miguel Fernandez-Cortizas , Jose Luis Sanchez Lopez , Holger Voos
2026-10-08.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-08.comment: 8 figures
2026-10-08.abstract: Models based on graphs have emerged in robotics as a powerful foundation for internal world representations, where factor and scene graphs are among the most prominent model types found in the related literature and in successful robotic solutions. Initially, many of these models were assuming static environments as a simplification. Herein, factor graphs mainly provide uncertainty-aware geometric estimations while scene graphs enable a structured semantic abstraction. However, real-world robotic environments are often dynamic, posing severe challenges for purely static world representations. Therefore, this review presents a comprehensive view on how dynamic aspects of real-world environments can be addressed in such graph-based world models. We organize our assessments around three main aspects: (I) suitable representations, (II) pipelines to construct and update the representations, and (III) their exploitation for downstream tasks. We review approaches that are either based on factor or scene graphs, but put special emphasis on novel approaches that combine both types to form hybrid models. We mainly analyze how different types of dynamics can be modeled herein, and categorize common architectural patterns. Finally, emerging trends and open challenges are identified, including uncertainty propagation from learned perception through the representation layers, the observability of dynamic-entity motion and scale under minimal sensing, scalable lifelong maintenance, and the lack of datasets and evaluation protocols that ground world-model quality in downstream task performance under dynamics.

2026-10-08.title: Never Look Back: Understanding Persistence in 3D Object Memory from Egocentric Videos
2026-10-08.authors: Shravan Chaudhari , William Paul , Suchi Saria , Rama Chellappa , Homanga Bharadhwaj
