2026-10-08.title: LeCuration: A Tiny World Model as a Data Curation Multi-Tool
2026-10-08.authors: Mayank Sengupta , Nirmit Desai , Eric Song , Kunal Sawarkar
2026-10-08.subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-08.abstract: Many applications of physical AI run within finite or closed physical worlds with a limited set of physical laws governing object behavior. Examples include robots working in a warehouse and agents moving around in a video game. In order to better organize, filter, and curate data for physical AI applications, we propose a new approach centered on the unique settings and physical laws of individual datasets. We train LeCuration, a small world model intended to serve as a data curation tool for a separate, larger downstream model . To build this model, we choose LeWorldModel (LeWM) ( Maes et al., 2026 ) as our latent encoder and predictor, adding a diffusion transformer (DiT) decoder to add visuals to autoregressive gameplay rollout. We find that the embeddings of this model can be used as an anomaly detection signal and as a content-based clustering heuristic, and that auto-regressively predicting the game state with this model allows us to qualitatively check for action-state consistency. This paper presents a qualitative, proof-of-concept case study on CS:GO gameplay data; we do not yet report quantitative curation metrics or downstream training results, which we identify as the key next step.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Intelligently curating data prior to training is key to ensuring a high quality model, especially for use cases in physical AI. The straightforward alternative, feeding a model everything, teaches it the full distribution of the source data, including its degenerate corners. Filtering by hand does not scale. Rule-based filters require access to the physics engine state, which is hidden in most cases or impossible to access if your physics engine is the real world. Most importantly, it is impossible to understand the effect of a curated dataset without training a model on it. Therefore, we need a small, quickly trainable curation that has learned enough about a dataset to characterize it, identifying what is typical, what is rare, and what is surprising.

We train such a model on Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO) gameplay recordings. LeCuration is a deliberately small model: the encoder has roughly 2M parameters, the predictor roughly 13M. By training it on this dataset in a matter of hours, we allow the model to produce representations and predictions that are semantically meaningful enough to drive curation decisions at scale. On top of this, we built a diffusion decoder as a visualization tool, letting us decode embeddings back to pixels to inspect what the model has learned.

Concretely, this paper’s contributions are: (1) an adaptation of LeWM into a compact, quickly-trained curation tool operating on a TAESD latent space (Sec. 2 ); (2) a qualitative demonstration that its embeddings organize gameplay footage into semantically coherent clusters usable for rebalancing and degenerate-content filtering (Sec. 3 ); and (3) an unsupervised anomaly signal, derived from autoregressive embedding divergence, that flags frames where the predictor’s expectation and the observed frame disagree (Sec. 4 ). We emphasize that this is a proof-of-concept study: we validate these primitives qualitatively on a single CS:GO map, and we have not yet trained a downstream model on LeCuration-curated data or established quantitative metrics for any of the three primitives above; we discuss this scope explicitly in Sec. 5 .

The JEPA model training paradigm has been applied almost exclusively to two settings.

The first is visual control and robot planning : V-JEPA 2 ( Assran et al., 2025 ) trains on over one million hours of internet video to enable zero-shot robot manipulation by planning in latent space; Causal-JEPA ( Nam et al., 2026 ) introduces object-level latent interventions to learn causal world structure; JEPA-based LiDAR models ( Zhu and Choromanska, 2026 ) apply the same framework to spatiotemporal occupancy forecasting for autonomous driving.

The second is representation learning for downstream classification and video understanding : I-JEPA, V-JEPA, and VL-JEPA all frame prediction as a pretext task for learning transferable visual features.

The inspiration of LeCuration is LeWorldModel (LeWM) ( Maes et al., 2026 ) . LeWM’s central contribution is a stable end-to-end JEPA that trains directly from raw pixels using only two loss terms: a next-embedding prediction loss and a Sketch Isotropic Gaussian Regularizer (SIGReg) that prevents representation collapse without stop-gradients, frozen encoders, or exponential moving averages. Much like the rest of the works in the space, LeWM is presented entirely as a planning and control model. Given a goal frame, the predictor optimizes a sequence of actions whose predicted latent trajectory minimizes distance to the goal embedding.

We decided to build on this architecture for three main reasons:

At roughly 15M parameters, it is among the most compact world models that have demonstrated competitive performance on continuous control benchmarks. The smaller the model, the faster it trains, and the more practical it is to adapt it to new datasets if it is deployed in production.

At roughly 15M parameters, it is among the most compact world models that have demonstrated competitive performance on continuous control benchmarks. The smaller the model, the faster it trains, and the more practical it is to adapt it to new datasets if it is deployed in production.

The authors establish the model’s rich latent-space properties in their ablations. Physical quantity probing shows that agent position, object location, and object orientation are linearly recoverable from the CLS embedding (which is trained to be the overall per-frame world state). Surprise evaluation shows that the model assigns higher prediction error to physically implausible events (teleporting objects) than to matched visual perturbations that do not violate physics. Additionally, temporal path straightening shows that latent trajectories become increasingly linear during training, a property the authors argue reflects the emergence of a smooth, locally Euclidean world model.

LeWM is not just a single-frame encoder model. While each frame is indeed individually encoded to the latent space, the predictor module of LeWM actually uses a history of 6 6 previous vectors before predicting the next latent world state. This allows the model to understand the kinematics of domain-specific data, predicting world state not just from position, but also from velocity.

We modify LeWM for a fundamentally different use: as a data curation tool for a separate, larger downstream model , rather than as a planner. LeCuration does not plan actions and is not evaluated on any control benchmark. Instead, its embeddings and predictor outputs are used to analyze the training corpora.

Through this adaptation, we uncover several interesting properties. By clustering the embeddings, we find that we can qualitatively separate training data into visually and semantically distinct groups, such as frames from different map locations and camera framings (Sec. 3 ); we have not measured this against ground-truth location or orientation labels. We can also run the predictor module autoregressively and compare the predictions with the encoded ground truth to find any possible anomalies or unexpected shifts in data. In addition, we build a diffusion transformer (DiT) decoder to recover gameplay frames conditioned on autoregressive CLS tokens output by the predictor module. By feeding a starting frame and a sequence of actions (key pushes) into the model, we are able to reconstruct near-photorealistic gameplay video from only a sequence of 196-dimensional world-state vectors, showing that despite its small size and very quick training time, LeCuration can indeed model the laws of a physics engine.

1. The first is visual control and robot planning : V-JEPA 2 ( Assran et al., 2025 ) trains on over one million hours of internet video to enable zero-shot robot manipulation by planning in latent space; Causal-JEPA ( Nam et al., 2026 ) introduces object-level latent interventions to learn causal world structure; JEPA-based LiDAR models ( Zhu and Choromanska, 2026 ) apply the same framework to spatiotemporal occupancy forecasting for autonomous driving.

2. The second is representation learning for downstream classification and video understanding : I-JEPA, V-JEPA, and VL-JEPA all frame prediction as a pretext task for learning transferable visual features.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Architecture and Training

## 2.1 Stable Diffusion/TAESD Latent Space

LeWM encodes directly from pixels. We decide to instead map our entire dataset to a much smaller intermediate latent representation before any training. We choose to use the same autoencoder as Stable Diffusion ( Rombach et al., 2021 ) , as it has been standard practice, and is able to do 48 × 48\times compression while losing relatively few important details. However, the autoencoder used by Stable Diffusion has 74 74 M parameters, and a much more efficient alternative, called Tiny AutoEncoder for Stable Diffusion (TAESD) ( Bohan, 2023 ) , accomplishes the exact same task at a fraction of the cost. Distilled from the standard Stable Diffusion autoencoder, TAESD only has 2.4 2.4 M parameters and a single forward pass is roughly 20 × 20\times faster than that of the original autoencoder on the same device ( Bohan, 2023 ) .

Our dataset is thus compressed from 224 × 224 × 3 224\times 224\times 3 frames to 4 × 28 × 28 4{\times}28{\times}28 TAESD latents. Each frame has a corresponding action vector, which is a 51 51 -dimensional one-hot encoded vector representing the keys pressed at that frame (key presses, mouse movements, and so on).

## 2.2 Latent Encoder and Predictor

The latent encoder and predictor were inspired by LeWM but adapted to the TAESD latent space. The Latent Encoder is a patch-ViT operating on TAESD latents (patch size 4 4 , 49 49 spatial patches plus a CLS token [the world state], projected to 196 196 dimensions via 4 4 transformer layers). For each gameplay frame, it produces a single 196 196 -dimensional world state e t + 1 e_{t+1} (the CLS token) that summarizes the frame’s content. The patch tokens are discarded after each forward pass.

The latent predictor is a causal transformer ( 512 512 hidden dimension, 8 8 layers, 16 16 heads) that takes a sliding window history of 6 6 frame embeddings plus action embeddings and predicts the next frame’s embedding. Actions are projected to 196 196 dimensions by a small action embedder before being fed to the predictor. The action embedder is a 1d-convolution (kernel_size=10, stride=1) followed by a 2-layer MLP (hidden_dim=768) which transforms the 51-dimensional one-hot encoded action vector into a 196-dim embedding.

At each autoregressive step the predictor outputs world state e ^ t + 1 \hat{e}_{t+1} : its expectation of what the next frame should look like in embedding space, given the recent context and the action taken. The quality of this prediction—and in particular the gap between e ^ t + 1 \hat{e}_{t+1} and the observed e t + 1 e_{t+1} —is the primary curation signal.

## 2.3 Diffusion Transformer Decoder

A Diffusion Transformer (DiT) Decoder ( 512 512 hidden dimension, 8 8 layers, CFG dropout 0.1 0.1 ) is trained to denoise TAESD latents conditioned on the frozen CLS
embedding. This lets us decode any embedding back to pixels to visually
inspect what the encoder has captured. All figures showing rendered frames
use this decoder. It is trained after JEPA pre-training and plays no role in
the curation pipeline.

## 2.4 Training Recipe

We pre-encode and shard all frames in the dataset as TAESD latents. Performing this forward pass exactly once per frame not only saves redundant compute, but slashes I/O cost, as (1) 48 × 48\times less data is fetched per training step and (2) compressing the dataset allows us to fit all of the frames and corresponding actions on disk, so that we don’t have to repeatedly fetch batches from our cloud bucket.

Like all JEPA architectures, LeCuration training is self-supervised: the predictor’s output is compared against a stop-gradient target produced by a slow EMA copy of the encoder (EMA decay 0.9999 0.9999 ). For a frame at arbitrary time step t t in a gameplay sequence, the loss is calculated as:

There are two stages of training for the latent encoder and predictor.

First, we pre-train the encoder on randomly sampled frame-action pair sequences, asking the encoder to find the world state of 6 6 history frames and the predictor to predict only the next immediate world state. This allows the encoder to form initial representations for the training data.

Next, we do supervised auto-regressive post-training, where, starting from a window of 6 6 frames, we ask the predictor to auto-regressively roll out word states for the next 50 50 frames, comparing them with the world states encoded directly from the ground truth frames. We use a discount factor of 1.03 1.03 to emphasize frames further away. This significantly improves the quality of longer rollouts from the predictor, and also allows the encoder to refine its world state embeddings.

No part of the model is frozen in either of these two stages. Pre-training takes 120 minutes for 300 300 epochs, and post-training takes 60 minutes for 20 20 epochs. We define an epoch to be 1600 batches, rather than a full pass through the entire dataset. Pre-training batch size is 32 32 and post-training is 16 16 . A batch denotes 7 7 frame-action pairs in pre-training ( 6 6 history frames + 1 1 current frame) and 56 56 frame-action pairs in post-training.

For the DiT decoder, we embedded TAESD latents from the dataset as world states with the trained latent encoder, and trained the decoder to generate the TAESD latents conditioned on each world state. This way, the DiT decoder performance is unable to affect the world model quality. This step was also very fast (30 mins for 600 epochs).

## 2.5 Dataset and Compute

The dataset in our experiments in this paper is composed of CS:GO gameplay recordings of various skill levels restricted exclusively to the de_dust2 map. The data was provided anonymously by our data partner. Both frames and key presses are sampled at 16 16 Hz. No curation or episode filtering is applied at training time; the model can be used for curation applications after being trained on the full, uncurated set. The idea is to train LeCuration on any training corpus and then apply it to curate sample-efficient training sets.

All experiments were conducted on a runtime with a 40GB Nvidia A100 GPU accessed through Google Cloud Platform (GCP). Our data was also stored in GCP buckets.

2026-10-08.title: An Informational Curse of Horizon in Goal-Conditioned Policy Learning
2026-10-08.authors: John L. Zhou , Yuxuan Dong , Jonathan C. Kao
2026-10-08.abstract: The difficulty of learning goal-reaching policies is often attributed to a “curse of horizon” that manifests as bias accumulation in temporal-difference backups and noisy advantage estimates. In this work, we identify an additional informational curse of horizon in goal-conditioned policy learning, where increasing the goal relabeling horizon can significantly reduce policy generalization and performance. Through a series of controlled experiments with oracle planners, we decouple the goal horizons sampled during training from those that the policy is asked to reach at test time. Even when evaluated only on a sequence of nearby subgoals, goal-conditioned behavioral cloning (BC) policies suffer from severe, training horizon-dependent performance degradation that is mitigated by reinforcement learning (RL) objectives. We explain this phenomenon as a horizon-dependent decrease in the conditional mutual information between actions and hindsight-relabeled goals, and find empirically that both BC and RL policies trained on longer-horizon goals exhibit a shift in sensitivity from goal to state information, as measured by the policy’s input Jacobians. Motivated by this observation, we find that distilling the input Jacobians of short-horizon policies into long-horizon policies yields significant performance gains, especially in combinatorial manipulation tasks. Taken together, our results highlight goal relabeling horizon as an important consideration when learning generalist policies from offline data.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Learning to reach any state from any other state is an elegantly simple problem that allows an agent to acquire diverse behaviors from data, without supervision ( Kaelbling, 1993 ) . A core component of standard goal-conditioned policy learning involves hindsight goal relabeling ( Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ) , which allows an agent to learn from arbitrary experiences regardless of the actor’s original intentions. However, simply providing a policy with auxiliary input in the form of goal observations or natural language instructions does not necessarily produce a policy that is capable of following such instructions. A goal-reaching policy must learn to meaningfully utilize information about the desired goal to generate actions, and we argue that this dependence can only emerge when knowing the goal provides meaningful additional information about the policy learning objective.

We formalize this additional goal-related information as the conditional mutual information (MI) ℐ ⁡ ( A ; G ∣ S ) \mathcal{I}(A;G\mid S) between the goal G G and action A A conditioned on the current state S S , which we refer to as the action-goal mutual information . Under standard hindsight relabeling, action-goal MI is non-increasing with the relabeling horizon [ Proposition 3.2 ]. This points to a distinct informational curse of horizon in goal-conditioned policy learning: increasing the horizon of relabeled training goals not only introduces well-characterized learning challenges ( Park et al., 2025 ) , but may also alter how the policy is learned. Specifically, as distant goals provide progressively less information about which action should be taken, the policy may converge to a solution that is globally less sensitive to goal information—even when conditioned on nearby goals.

However, disentangling these two effects is surprisingly difficult in standard goal-reaching benchmarks ( Park et al., 2024 ) . Long-horizon evaluation goals are typically more challenging and require longer sequences of correct actions, while policies must also be trained on distant goals to simply keep them in-distribution at evaluation time. This makes it virtually impossible to distinguish failures due to increased task difficulty from failures due to weaker goal conditioning.

To isolate the effect of training horizon H train H_{\mathrm{train}} on performance, we construct a series of controlled experiments using an oracle hierarchical planner that “prompts” a learned, goal-conditioned policy with optimal, fixed-distance (sub)goals at test time. We find that behavioral cloning (BC) policies degrade severely as H train H_{\mathrm{train}} increases, even when the distance of goals presented at test time H plan H_{\mathrm{plan}} remains fixed. On the other hand, reinforcement learning (RL) policies are substantially more robust to increased training goal horizons, although this robustness is closely tied to the RL objective (weighted BC or reparameterized policy gradient) and policy class (Gaussian or conditional flow matching) [ Section 3.1 ]. These results suggest that poor policy performance is not only due to higher task difficulty, but also a degradation in the learned policy’s ability to achieve simpler goals.

Our theoretical analysis predicts that longer-horizon goals provide less action-relevant information, but how might this be reflected in a policy parameterized by a neural network? In our empirical studies, we use the Jacobian norm of the action with respect to the state or goal as a local measure of policy sensitivity. For certain parameterizations, e.g., fixed-variance Gaussians, the Jacobian norm can be directly related to Fisher information [Box 3.3 ]. Across BC and RL objectives, as well as Gaussian and flow-matching policy classes, we find that increasing the training goal horizon systematically shifts sensitivity away from goal conditioning towards the current state. Furthermore, explicitly reducing the action-goal MI by training on some proportion of arbitrary, unrelated goal states produces a similar reduction in goal sensitivity.

To determine if there is a causal relationship between goal sensitivity and performance, we then ask if preserving the sensitivity structure of policies trained exclusively on short-horizon goals can improve the performance of policies trained on longer-horizon goals. We propose Sobolev bootstrapping , a simple modification of existing policy bootstrapping methods that additionally distills the input Jacobians of a short-horizon teacher policy into a long-horizon student policy. This simple intervention significantly boosts performance in a suite of 16 diverse locomotion and manipulation environments, with especially large gains in combinatorial manipulation tasks.

2026-10-08.title: StableGrasp: Reconstructing Physically Stable Human Hand Grasps from Single Images
2026-10-08.authors: Han Jiang , Etienne Vouga , Qixing Huang , Georgios Pavlakos
2026-10-08.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Graphics (cs.GR); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-08.abstract:
Reconstructing a physically stable human grasp from a single RGB image is challenging because physically modeling grasps is itself difficult, and the problem requires estimating not only a visually constrained hand pose but also a control target that stabilizes the grasp.
Existing methods either model only visual hand geometry without considering physics, or rely on less plausible physical modeling, which limits the physical validity of the resulting grasps.
In this paper, we present StableGrasp, a differentiable simulation-based optimization framework that explicitly separates the visual hand pose from the control target that determines the grasping forces.
Our method jointly optimizes hand geometry and control by minimizing the kinetic energy of the grasp in a differentiable simulator, while regularizing the hand geometry to preserve visual consistency and geometric plausibility.
The reconstructed grasps are substantially more stable under rigorous physical simulation, while remaining visually consistent with the input images and geometrically plausible.
Experiments show that our approach produces far more stable grasps than alternative hand-control strategies, benefiting visual-only grasp reconstruction pipelines by turning their outputs into physically stable grasps.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Recovering the 3D pose of a human hand and the grasped object from image observations has been extensively studied in computer vision.
Methods for hand-only reconstruction estimate the pose and shape of the 3D hand ( Boukhayma et al., 2019 ; Ge et al., 2019 ; Lin et al., 2021a ; Lin et al., 2021b ; Pavlakos et al., 2024 ; Potamias et al., 2025 ) . Methods for hand-object reconstruction also estimate the geometry of the object and the spatial relationship between hand and object. Methods attacking this problem have proposed using interaction constraints ( Tekin et al., 2019 ; Hasson et al., 2019 ) , contact-aware refinement ( Grady et al., 2021 ) , implicit hand-object representations ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2023b ; Qi et al., 2024 ) , unified hand-object estimation ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , or hand-guided reconstruction of held object geometry ( Ye et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023b ; Fu et al., 2024 ; Aytekin et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) . Many of these methods represent the hand using MANO ( Romero et al., 2017 ) , a parametric model that maps the pose and shape of the hand to a skinned mesh.

However, these methods only aim to recover visually-plausible hand and object poses that are consistent with the input observations, while StableGrasp’s reconstruction is physically stable, verified by forward simulation of the coupled hand-object system.

The stricter problem of recovering a grasp that is stable under gravity has also received significant attention. “Physical stability” has been modeled in several different ways. One simplified approach is to consider only one-way hand→ object coupling, and to analyze stability of the object in terms of contact forces exerted at a set of contact points where the object touches a static hand.

Classical grasping theory in robotics studies this problem through force closure and grasp wrench space analysis ( Ferrari and Canny, 1992 ; Bicchi and Kumar, 2001 ) , which evaluates whether contact forces can resist external object wrenches. This and similar quasi-static criteria have been widely used for dexterous grasp synthesis and evaluation ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Zurbrügg et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ; Chen et al., 2023a ; Li et al., 2023a ) . Along similar lines, works like Grasp’D ( Turpin et al., 2022 ) and Fast-Grasp’D ( Turpin et al., 2023 ) optimize hand configurations with simulation-based stability objectives, while DeepSimHO ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and UGG ( Lu et al., 2024 ) use learned simulation surrogates to refine reconstructed interactions. Other methods introduce explicit contact forces at fingertips as optimization variables ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) or enforce physics-inspired priors on sliding and penetration at the contact points ( Zhang et al., 2024b ) .

With a static hand, object stability does not establish whether an actuated hand can generate the required contact forces or maintain the grasp over time.
In contrast, our approach models the full two-way coupling between an actuated hand and the object. We reconstruct not only a contact-consistent hand pose but also a control target whose induced joint torques realize those contacts and keep the grasp stable under forward simulation.

A visually or geometrically plausible hand pose is not a stable grasp unless it is paired with an appropriate control strategy that holds the hand and object in place over time. As seen in a line of works in robotics ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ; Lum et al., 2024 ) , stable grasping is more fundamentally a control problem, not only a geometric optimization or pose estimation problem.

Several works incorporate hand control yet do not rigorously model the two-way coupling. Zhao et al. (2022) optimize a monocular reconstruction under a simulated stability criterion, holding the hand at the reconstructed pose with heuristic control that is never optimized, limiting the stability of the result. HOIC ( Hu et al., 2024 ) imitates hand-object interaction in simulation, but it allows extra compensation force and torque applied directly to the object, so the object is not driven by two-way coupling physics alone. In contrast, D-Grasp ( Christen et al., 2022 ) and Grasp-and-Lift ( Choi et al., 2026 ) model strict two-way coupling: D-Grasp learns a policy that controls a hand through PD targets, and Grasp-and-Lift refines vision-aligned hand-object trajectories with physics-in-the-loop optimization.
However, both focus on dynamic settings in which control can vary throughout time to maintain the grasp. Our method operates in a static setting: the unobserved control is represented by one fixed PD target . This imposes a distinct constraint on grasp reconstruction, since stability must be explained without freely changing the visible grasp or adapting the control target over a dynamic trajectory.

2026-10-08.title: On the complexity of the single-move labeled token routing problem
2026-10-08.authors: Nicolas Bousquet , Remy El Sabeh , Amer E. Mouawad , Naomi Nishimura
2026-10-08.subjects: Computational Complexity (cs.CC) ; Discrete Mathematics (cs.DM); Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Robotics (cs.RO); Combinatorics (math.CO)
2026-10-08.abstract:
In neutral-atom quantum simulators and computers, loaded atoms must be moved
to desired target positions along paths of positions that are empty at the
time of each move, and a target position may be reserved for one species of atom. Motivated by this task, we introduce Single-Move
Labeled Token Routing : every source and every target vertex of a graph is
assigned a set of labels, and tokens occupy the sources. A solution consists
of a matching that assigns each source to a compatible target (one whose label
set intersects its own), a route for each matched pair, and a movement
order in which, when a token is moved, its route contains no other token.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Neutral-atom quantum simulators and computers use optical traps to hold
individual atoms. The
goal is to place atoms in the target traps , a chosen subset of the
optical traps; the interactions that define the quantum system occur only
between nearby atoms, so the resulting arrangement of atoms, the target
configuration , determines the structure of the system being simulated
or used for computation [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Loading atoms directly
into the target traps may not succeed, as the loading process does not guarantee
that every target trap receives an atom. To increase the chances of obtaining
the target configuration, one may instead load atoms into a larger set of traps
and then rearrange the atoms that were successfully loaded. Some atoms may
already occupy target traps and need not move, while other atoms are moved from
occupied traps to empty target traps, each along a path of traps that are
empty when the atom is moved. Computing the rearrangement, a task known as Atom Reconfiguration , requires choosing which atoms should move to
which target traps, choosing routes for the moving atoms, and choosing a
movement order so that no atom blocks a route when that route is
used [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Each additional move takes time and creates another
opportunity for errors or atom loss, which motivates keeping the number of
moves of each atom small.

Atom Reconfiguration admits a graph-theoretic formulation. Vertices
represent optical traps, source vertices are initially occupied by tokens
representing atoms, and target vertices correspond to positions in the target
configuration. A solution assigns sources to targets, chooses a route for each
assigned pair, and orders the corresponding moves. Every move takes a token from
its current vertex to an unoccupied vertex along a path no other vertex of which
is occupied, the target included [ 1 ] . In
general, a token may be moved several times. We study the restriction in which
each token moves at most once.

Atoms that are not interchangeable. In Atom Reconfiguration , atoms are interchangeable: any
loaded atom may be moved into any empty target trap. This is no longer the case
as soon as atoms of two species , that is, of two chemical elements or of
two isotopes of one element, are loaded together, as in dual-species
settings, also called
mixed-species settings [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
Mixtures of two species are loaded deliberately, for instance to form a
rubidium-caesium molecule from one atom of each species at every designated
site [ 15 , 16 ] . In these
settings, a target trap may be designated for one species, so an atom of the
wrong species is not an acceptable occupant [ 13 , 14 ] .
Thus, exchanging two atoms may turn a valid target configuration into an
invalid one.

Restricting, for each target trap, which atoms may occupy it gives rise
to the problem studied in this paper, Single-Move Labeled Token Routing , in which each source and
each target is assigned a set of labels, and a source may be matched to a target
if and only if their label sets intersect; in this case the source and the
target are said to be compatible . Assigning the same label to every
source and every target yields Atom Reconfiguration restricted to at
most one move per atom, which
we call the all-matching case ; whether a rearrangement exists can
then be decided in polynomial
time [ 1 , 8 , 17 ] .
At the opposite extreme, which we call the unique-matching case ,
every source is compatible with exactly one target and every target with
exactly one source. Between these two extremes, the set of compatible source-target pairs can be
arbitrary.

Our goal is to understand how the labels assigned to sources and targets,
together with the structure of the underlying graph, affect the complexity of Single-Move Labeled Token Routing . We study several graph classes and
parameterizations, proving both negative and positive results that focus on one question: how much information must an algorithm carry across a cut of
the graph? Bounding the treewidth, or even the pathwidth, of the graph does not make
the problem tractable, since the problem is hard even on graphs of pathwidth
three [ 2 ] . As we prove in this paper, bounding how many routes of a solution may
share an edge does not either, since the problem is hard on grids even when
the routes of a solution can be chosen pairwise edge-disjoint.
Our main algorithmic result concerns trees, where every edge is a cut:
bounding, for every edge, the number of compatible source-target pairs whose
path uses that edge still does not make the problem tractable, but adding a
bound on the maximum degree does, as does bounding, for every vertex, the
number of compatible pairs whose paths contain that vertex.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 discusses related
work and Section 3 presents an overview of our
results. Section 4 introduces the necessary notation.
Section 5 proves the hardness results,
Section 6 the algorithmic ones, and
Section 7 concludes with open problems.
2026-10-08.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Atom Reconfiguration , the problem motivating our work, is the setting
in which every atom may move to every empty target trap, and in which one
typically seeks to fill every target trap while minimizing some measure of
the rearrangement. Atom reconfiguration has been carried out
experimentally for one-, two-, and three-dimensional target
configurations [ 4 , 5 , 18 , 6 , 7 ] .
On the algorithmic side, the assignment of atoms to target traps was first
formulated as a minimum-cost matching problem [ 19 ] . Later
algorithms treat the routes and the movement order as parts of the problem
in their own right: after the targets and the routes are chosen, an order in
which to execute the moves must still be
found [ 9 , 8 , 10 ] . All
of these algorithms assume interchangeable atoms and allow each atom to
move more than once. The measures being minimized increase with the number of
moves. Whenever the target traps can be filled at all, they can be filled
by moving every atom at most
once [ 1 ] , a fact we reprove in our
terminology. The all-matching case of our problem is exactly Atom Reconfiguration with as many atoms as target traps, restricted to at most
one move per atom. Deciding whether
every target trap can then be filled takes polynomial time
(Theorem 1 ). Reconfiguration algorithms for two species
of atoms have also been
proposed [ 20 , 21 ] . The
parameterized complexity of atom reconfiguration is known for
interchangeable atoms and for the case in which each atom has its own
target: most tractability results for the former become hardness results
for the latter [ 17 ] . In this paper, we study
what lies between these two cases: each atom may be compatible with an
arbitrary set of targets.

Other models of token movement differ from ours in what a single move is
and in which targets a token may be assigned to. We use the word token as a generic term for a moving object; the works below call
their objects pebbles, agents, robots, or coins. Our move, along a path no
vertex of which other than its first is occupied, was studied by Călinescu, Dumitrescu, and
Pach [ 1 ] for interchangeable tokens, with
the objective of minimizing the number of moves. They prove that at most k k moves suffice, where k k is the number of
tokens, and that such a sequence can be chosen with no token moving twice.
They also prove that minimizing the number of moves is NP -hard even on
grids. A sequence of moves in which no token moves twice is a solution of our
all-matching case, so their setting and ours differ only in the objective: they
minimize the number of moves, whereas we decide feasibility. In Pebble Motion , a move takes a token along
a single edge instead, and feasibility is decidable in linear
time [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] . In other models, several
tokens move along edges at the same
time [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ] , or two tokens are
swapped along the edge joining
them [ 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 ] . The assignment of
tokens to targets takes one of three forms: it is fixed, each token having
its own target; it is given by colors , each token and each target
carrying one color and a token being assignable to every target of its
color [ 25 , 36 , 37 , 3 ] ; or each token carries a set of targets to which it may be
assigned [ 37 , 38 ] .
Label sets express exactly the third form, which contains the other two.
To our knowledge, arbitrary compatibility relations have not been studied
before for moves along paths of unoccupied vertices.

In our problem, every token moves at most once; in the robotics
literature, a sequence of moves with this property is called monotone [ 39 ] . Three results on monotone sequences of
moves relate directly to ours. First, when both the
matching and the routes are given as part of the input, feasibility is
decided in polynomial time by an acyclicity test on a precedence
digraph [ 40 , 38 ] ; we state this as
Observation 10 and use it in
Section 6 . Second, when the matching is given but the
routes are not, the problem is hard. Geft, Halperin, and
Nakar [ 2 ] study Monotone Sliding
Reconfiguration , whose discrete form is exactly our unique-matching case,
in which every source is compatible with exactly one target and every
target with exactly one source. They prove it NP -complete on 3 × w 3\times w grid graphs, and NP -hard even when every token but one
has a specified route. Section 5.2 shows that the hardness
persists on instances that, when solvable, admit a solution with pairwise
edge-disjoint routes. Third, in
work independent of and concurrent with ours, Geft [ 3 ] proves that it is NP -hard to decide whether a Pebble
Motion instance with two colors on a tree of maximum degree three can be
solved with as many moves as the sum of the distances from the sources to
the targets. In our terms, a color is a label set of size one, so such an
instance uses two distinct labels. Geft further proves that a solution
attaining this bound can be reordered so that each token traverses the
path from its source to its target in consecutive moves, during which no
other token occupies that path; such a
traversal is exactly one move of our model. Hence, Single-Move Labeled Token Routing is NP -complete on trees
of maximum degree three even when only two distinct labels are used.

2026-10-08.title: GUARD: Geometric Uncertainty-Aware Point Cloud Denoising and Segmentation for Robotic Hard Disk Drive Disassembly
2026-10-08.authors: Zuoxu Wang , Xiao Liang
2026-10-08.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-08.abstract:
Reliable robotic disassembly requires part-level representations that distinguish genuine component geometry from scanning and reconstruction artifacts. In point clouds of hard disk drives (HDDs), structured ghost artifacts can resemble valid components locally while remaining inconsistent with the overall geometry, allowing erroneous measurements to receive plausible semantic labels. This creates an engineering information problem: semantic prediction confidence alone does not establish whether the underlying geometry is reliable.
We propose GUARD , a geometric uncertainty-aware framework that performs point filtering and segmentation within a single forward pass by modeling the reliability of learned geometric representations. GUARD combines a multi-scale geometric transformer with a multi-bandwidth random Fourier feature Gaussian Process to estimate per-point geometric uncertainty, complemented by predictive entropy to suppress unreliable measurements while preserving informative structures.
Evaluation on 2,745 real HDD point clouds shows that GUARD improves PointNet++ segmentation mean intersection over union from 0.7739 to 0.8318. Additional experiments on ShapeNetPart and ScanNet examine robustness across corruption types, point-cloud domains, and segmentation backbones. On manually annotated ScanNet samples, geometric uncertainty achieves a corrupted-point detection F1 score of 0.7931, compared with 0.2212 for predictive entropy. The results demonstrate the value of distinguishing geometric reliability from semantic confidence and reveal a tradeoff between artifact suppression and preservation of informative structures. GUARD contributes a reliability-aware approach to interpreting imperfect 3D measurements for component identification and subsequent robotic handling. 2026-10-08.introduction:
The rapid replacement and upgrading of electronic devices has led to a continuously increasing volume of electronic waste (e-waste), creating growing demands for efficient material recovery, component handling, and recycling. Hard disk drives (HDDs), for example, contain multiple reusable or valuable components and materials that require accurate identification, handling, sorting, and disassembly during automated processing [ 1 , 2 ] . However, these operations still rely heavily on manual labor, which is time-consuming, repetitive, and difficult to scale. With recent advances in industrial robotics, robotic systems have shown increasing potential for automating component handling and disassembly, thereby improving the efficiency, consistency, and scalability of e-waste processing [ 3 , 4 ] .

Reliable perception is a critical prerequisite for robotic disassembly [ 5 ] . Before a robot can grasp, remove, or manipulate an individual component, it must accurately identify the corresponding part and understand its three-dimensional geometry. This requirement is particularly important for electronic devices such as HDDs, where multiple small components are densely arranged within a limited workspace [ 6 ] . Point clouds provide a suitable representation for this purpose because they preserve explicit 3D geometric information and allow the robot to reason about fine-grained part structures and spatial relationships. Consequently, accurate part-level point cloud segmentation is an important perception capability for automated disassembly and manipulation [ 7 ] .

In real-world deployment, however, point clouds obtained from depth sensors or multi-view reconstruction are rarely free from corruption. Sensor noise, partial observations, occlusion, reflective surfaces, and reconstruction errors can introduce inaccurate or redundant measurements [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . More importantly, multi-frame scanning and 3D reconstruction can produce structured ghost artifacts, where duplicated, shifted, or partially reconstructed surfaces appear around the true object geometry [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Unlike isolated floating outliers, these ghost structures may preserve locally coherent shapes that closely resemble portions of real components. As a result, they can be particularly difficult to distinguish from valid points and may cause segmentation networks to assign plausible but incorrect semantic labels.

Although point cloud denoising has been extensively studied, most existing methods primarily focus on random perturbations, sparse outliers, or general surface noise. For example, supervised denoising methods such as PointCleanNet [ 14 ] learn to remove corrupted points from paired clean and noisy data, while more recent robustness-oriented approaches attempt to suppress high-risk or unreliable samples. However, structured ghost artifacts receive considerably less attention. This type of corruption is fundamentally more challenging because the erroneous points are not necessarily isolated or geometrically irregular; instead, they may form locally realistic structures similar to genuine object parts. Moreover, obtaining point-level annotations of such artifacts from real scans is expensive and impractical. Therefore, reliably identifying geometrically unreliable regions while preserving valid fine-grained structures remains an important challenge for robust point cloud segmentation in real robotic perception.

Motivated by these limitations, this study investigates how geometric consistency and uncertainty can be represented and used to improve part-level interpretation of artifact-corrupted engineering scans. In particular, local geometric plausibility and confident semantic prediction do not necessarily imply that a measured structure is valid. A useful perception method must therefore evaluate the reliability of geometric evidence while preserving the fine structures needed for component recognition.

We address this question through GUARD, a framework that combines multi-scale geometric representations, geometry-conditioned uncertainty estimation, and semantic prediction entropy. Rather than relying solely on classification confidence, GUARD evaluates how well a point’s geometric representation is supported by the learned feature distribution and uses this information to guide filtering. The resulting single-pass framework couples part segmentation with an explicit assessment of measurement reliability.

We first evaluate GUARD on a real-world HDD point cloud dataset collected from practical scanning and reconstruction pipelines, where sensor noise and reconstruction-induced ghost artifacts directly affect part-level perception for automated component handling and disassembly. This dataset serves as our primary engineering evaluation and reflects the types of geometric corruption encountered in realistic robotic deployment. To further assess robustness beyond the HDD setting, we conduct controlled experiments on ShapeNetPart [ 15 ] with synthetic sensor noise and ghost-cluster corruption, and extend the evaluation to ScanNet [ 16 ] to examine the behavior of the proposed uncertainty modeling in large-scale indoor scenes. Across these settings, GUARD consistently improves robustness to corrupted geometry while maintaining competitive segmentation accuracy on cleaner inputs, demonstrating its potential as a practical perception component for robotic systems operating under imperfect 3D sensing.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

Reliability-aware interpretation of engineering point clouds. We introduce a framework that couples part segmentation with unreliable-point filtering, addressing the distinction between recognizing a component and determining whether its observed geometry is trustworthy. The framework targets structured scanning and reconstruction artifacts encountered in real HDD point clouds.

Geometry-conditioned uncertainty modeling. We develop a multi-scale geometric representation and a multi-bandwidth random Fourier feature Gaussian Process that estimates uncertainty in geometric feature space. Fusion with predictive entropy combines evidence about geometric reliability and semantic ambiguity within a single-pass architecture that can be integrated with different segmentation backbones.

Empirical analysis of the denoising–segmentation tradeoff. Through evaluation on real HDD scans and complementary benchmarks, we show that geometric uncertainty and semantic confidence provide different information about corrupted measurements. Backbone comparisons and filtering analyses characterize when artifact removal improves segmentation and when removal of informative points can limit those gains, providing evidence for selecting reliability-aware filtering strategies.

# II Related Work

Engineering information for robotic disassembly Recent research in engineering informatics has investigated robotic disassembly from the perspectives of human–robot collaboration, sequence planning, and manufacturing-system optimization.
For example, Guo et al. [ 4 ] studied human–robot collaborative disassembly sequence planning, Liang et al. [ 2 ] addressed disassembly line balancing, and Zhang et al. [ 3 ] investigated responsive collaborative disassembly optimization.
These studies primarily focus on planning and coordination within remanufacturing and disassembly systems.
Complementary to these efforts, the present study focuses on the reliability of the geometric information used to interpret components during robotic disassembly.

Point Cloud Segmentation. Deep learning on point clouds has evolved rapidly since the introduction of PointNet++ [ 17 ] and DGCNN [ 18 ] , which establish hierarchical and graph-based paradigms for local feature aggregation.
Most subsequent advances, including attention-based frameworks and robustness-oriented methods, build upon these backbones.
For example, PointNeXt [ 19 ] revisits PointNet++ with improved training and scaling strategies, while attention-based variants such as UPA [ 20 ] , SOE-Net [ 21 ] , and PointCloud-At [ 22 ] introduce self-attention to enhance local feature modeling.
Recent models such as Point Transformer [ 23 ] , although attention-driven, still follow the hierarchical neighborhood aggregation paradigm introduced by PointNet++ and DGCNN, and can be viewed as an attention-based extension of these backbones.
As a result, PointNet++ and DGCNN remain representative foundations for modern point cloud segmentation networks and plug-in robust segmentation methods.
We therefore adopt them as benchmarks for fair comparison, and further evaluate our method on the most advanced Point Transformer backbone to verify its generalization.

Robust and Noise-Aware Learning. Several approaches have been proposed to improve robustness under noisy or corrupted point clouds.
PointCleanNet [ 14 ] learns to restore clean shapes through supervised noise–clean correspondences, while PointCVaR [ 24 ] leverages conditional value-at-risk optimization to emphasize hard or corrupted samples.
REAL3D-AD [ 25 ] and PO3AD [ 26 ] further explore uncertainty-guided 3D anomaly detection by reconstructing clean geometry and identifying abnormal regions through residual-based discrepancies.
Although conceptually related, their reconstruction-driven formulation targets anomaly localization rather than general noise suppression, and struggles to handle fine-grained geometric perturbations or ghost-cluster misalignment.
Overall, these methods either require explicit noise annotations or involve multiple forward passes and resampling, making them computationally expensive and less suitable for real-time applications.

Uncertainty Estimation. Uncertainty modeling provides a principled way to handle distributional shifts and ambiguous inputs.
Bayesian deep learning [ 27 , 28 ] and ensemble methods [ 29 ] offer reliable uncertainty estimates but are computationally expensive.
Spectral-normalized neural Gaussian processes (SNGP) [ 30 ] introduce scalable uncertainty estimation by combining random Fourier features with spectral normalization, enabling efficient, single-pass predictive variance computation.
Recent works integrate similar uncertainty modules into 2D vision tasks [ 31 ] , but their application to large-scale 3D segmentation remains underexplored.

Summary. Prior research has established complementary advances in engineering informatics for robotic disassembly, point-cloud segmentation and denoising, and scalable uncertainty estimation.
The remaining challenge addressed in this work is how to integrate these capabilities when corrupted measurements form locally plausible structures that may still receive confident semantic predictions.
GUARD addresses this issue by modeling uncertainty in learned geometric representations and combining it with semantic entropy to guide reliability-aware filtering during segmentation.
This formulation provides a reliability-aware representation of imperfect geometric information, supporting more robust part-level interpretation of engineering point clouds affected by structured reconstruction artifacts.

2026-10-08.title: Shared-Roadmap Generation and Evaluator for Multi-Agent Path Planning Using Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network
2026-10-08.authors: Brandon Ho , Nikola Rogers , Seung-Kyum Choi
2026-10-08.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-08.abstract:
Multi-agent path planning (MAPP) in continuous environments often relies on roadmaps to balance safety and search efficiency.
However, traditional roadmap generation methods, such as lattice grids or standard sampling-based approaches, frequently face a trade-off between graph density and the likelihood of finding feasible, high-quality solutions.
In this paper, we propose a scalable heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for the automated generation and evaluation of shared multi-agent roadmaps.
Our model covers the representation of waypoints, agent locations, and task locations as distinct nodes in a heterogeneous graph, allowing it to reason over global connectivity and inter-agent interactions.
By training on occupation density maps aggregated and collected from expert solver trajectories, the GNN learns to identify critical points of interest and prune redundant nodes and edges.
This process produces a compact, coordination-aware roadmap that is invariant to task permutations and is reusable for multi-agent pick and delivery tasks.
Experimental results demonstrate that our framework can reduce planning effort and can potentially find better solutions, reaching at least 40 % 40\% reduction in runtime and in graph size for dense roadmaps.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Multi-agent path planning (MAPP) has been a central challenge in domains such as autonomous driving [ 1 , 2 ] , aerial swarms [ 3 ] , and warehouse automation [ 4 , 5 ] , where overall system performance depends critically on both safety and efficiency.
In real-world deployments, safety requirements typically take precedence over efficiency, often constraining agents to move along predefined edges and vertices within a structured environment, commonly referred to as a shared roadmap.
A simple solution is a lattice grid, where autonomous agents or automated guided vehicles (AGVs) are restricted to moving between cardinal neighboring cells.
However, unlike lattice grids, roadmaps that approximate continuous state spaces allow agents to move more flexibly and can yield more practical and higher-quality solutions.
Such non-lattice roadmaps better capture the underlying geometry of real environments and reduce discretization artifacts. Nevertheless, roadmap generation itself is a non-trivial problem.
Poorly constructed roadmaps can significantly degrade the performance of MAPP, underscoring the importance of principled methods for a shared multi-agent roadmap generation.

The main challenge of roadmap generation lies in balancing graph density with the likelihood of finding a feasible solution [ 6 ] .
A dense roadmap may better capture high-quality or even the optimal solution, but it enlarges the search space.
Conversely, a sparse roadmap might expedite the search process but risk of finding a valid solution.

A common approach for constructing effective roadmaps is a two-step iterative process: (1) use sampling-based motion planning (SBMP) [ 7 ] to generate multiple roadmaps and then (2) evaluate these roadmaps using a MAPP algorithm.
Although this paradigm has been widely adopted for single-agent navigation [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] , extending it to multi-agent settings is non-trivial due to the inter-agent interactions.
While prior work has explored roadmap generation for multi-agent scenarios [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , existing approaches impose certain constraints, such as generating non-shared roadmaps for each agent, limiting connectivity (e.g., non-bidirectional edges).

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown promising results in scalable recommendation systems where information can be represented in a relational graph [ 15 ] .
By coding individual entities as nodes and their interactions as edges, GNNs are able to learn structured representations that generalize to environments with a variable number of elements.
Given an existing roadmap, we encode waypoints, agent locations, and task locations as nodes in a heterogeneous graph, while encoding spatial relationships and task-relevant information as edge features.
On this structured representation, our heterogeneous GNN model evaluates roadmap quality and reasons over global connectivity and agent interactions.
Additionally, the GNN learns to identify critical points of interest and prune less informative nodes or edges, thereby producing a refined roadmap that is both compact and better suited for efficient multi-agent coordination.
Figure 1 showcases our proposed framework.

Our contributions are as follows:

We propose a dynamic and scalable heterogeneous Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for roadmap generation and evaluation. Our model identifies critical points of interest within an existing roadmap and prunes less informative nodes and edges, producing a more compact and coordination-aware graph.

We design our model to be task-agnostic for multi-agent path planning (MAPP) and readily extensible to multi-agent pickup and delivery (MAPD). By representing agent locations and task locations under the same node type as landmarks, the constructed roadmap becomes invariant to task configuration permutations, enabling flexible deployment across varying task assignments

We demonstrate the potential of our approach by training on MAPP instances up to four agents and testing up to 16 agents. Experimental results show that our GNN-based framework reduces planning effort, achieving at least a 40 % 40\% reduction in runtime and graph size for dense roadmaps, and can potentially find better solutions.

# II Related Works

## II-A Multi-Agent Pathfinding (MAPF)

Multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF), a problem of multi-agent path planning (MAPP) in discrete space, has been applied in various AI and robotics applications where the objective is to find a set of collision-free paths on a graph.
Popular approaches include, but are not limited to, conflict-based search (CBS) algorithms [ 16 ] , increasing cost tree search [ 17 ] , and prioritized planning (e.g., HCA* [ 18 ] , SIPP [ 19 ] , etc.
More recently, research demonstrates the potential in using machine-learning techniques for solving MAPF.
These methods learns from either demonstrations collected offline for imitation learning, a sequence of observations for reinforcement learning, or using graph neural networks, leading to finding solutions in multi-agent path planning (MAPP).
Despite such progress, many algorithms simplify the scope of their problem instances, typically in a grid map, where the spatial graph structure has uniform travel cost, and collisions only occur when point-particle agents occupy the same vertices or edges [ 18 ] .
These assumptions restrict the algorithms’ capabilities to only discrete time and space, making their real-world applications limited.

## II-B Roadmap Generation

Roadmap generation has been a research topic of interest mainly for single-agent cases, as it allows the agents to move in continuous space, leading to more practical and better solutions.
A roadmap refers to an undirected connected graph that is either shared across agents or tailored for each agent.
An ideal roadmap entails that any two points on the graph can be connected by at least one path, and the graph should be sparse as possible.
Popular methods in generating a roadmap include, but not are not limited to, probabilistic roadmaps (PRMs) [ 20 ] , constrained Delaunay Triangulation (CDT) [ 21 ] , visibility graph [ 22 ] , and rapidly exploring random graphs (RRGs).
CDT and visibility graph construct a roadmap by utilizing the obstacle boundary as either constraints or points of interest, while PRM and RRG iteratively sample points in free space.
Research on single-agent roadmaps studies how to densify the representation of the environment to balance optimality and density [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] .

For multi-agent roadmaps, most continuous MAPP methods [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] rely on some roadmap to operate.
Their primary challenge lies in scaling to large numbers of agents in real time, as the search space grows significantly and collision checking must be performed at high frequency.
In contrast, we investigate a complementary research direction: instead of improving the planner itself, we explore what types of roadmap representations are most effective for solving MAPP in continuous space.

There have been relatively few studies on multi-agent roadmap generation and refinement. [ 14 ] constructs a shared roadmap with bias-based sampling, focusing on narrow passages, but is less suited for sparsely distributed obstacles. [ 13 ] employs a generative model to construct separate but not shared roadmaps per agent that incorporate inter-agent interactions.
The most relevant work is [ 12 ] , where they optimized already constructed roadmaps through online learning.
However, their optimization is limited to directed edges and does not remove redundant or unnecessary vertices, thereby restricting the extent to which the roadmap can be structurally refined.

In contrast, our method identifies critical points of interest within an existing roadmap and reconstructs a shared, refined graph.
A shared roadmap provides constraints where safety can be better tracked as the agents follow on set guided paths.
By labeling agents’ initial and task locations as landmarks, the model ensures connectivity among essential nodes, improving coverage, reusability, and generalization across varying multi-agent tasks, including pickup and delivery scenarios.

2026-10-08.title: LASER: Latent Space Adjoint Matching for Support-Constrained Entropy-Regularized Offline RL
2026-10-08.authors: Songyuan Zhang , Oswin So , Eric Yang Yu , Matthew Cleaveland , Peter Crowley-Dolen , Chuchu Fan
2026-10-08.subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO); Optimization and Control (math.OC); Machine Learning (stat.ML)
2026-10-08.comment: . Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
2026-10-08.abstract:
While offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy optimization from static datasets without costly online interaction, it remains bottlenecked by the risk of executing out-of-distribution (OOD) actions.
Recent approaches mitigate this by learning a behavior-cloning policy through flow matching and then performing RL within its constrained latent space.
However, naïvely optimizing the latent policy can easily cause the policy to collapse into a brittle mode or exploit sharp artifacts of the learned critic.
In this work, we find that entropy regularization is essential in latent-space RL for addressing these challenges.
We introduce LASER , a novel offline RL algorithm that applies latent-space adjoint matching to achieve entropy-regularized latent-space RL with expressive flow policies while avoiding backpropagation through time.
Through comprehensive experiments on 40 challenging OGBench tasks with varying dataset qualities, we show that LASER achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, LASER uses
fixed method-specific hyperparameters across all tasks and outperforms the evaluated baselines, including those with task- and dataset-specific tuning, which highlights the robust applicability of LASER .
Project website: https://mit-realm.github.io/laser/ .
2026-10-08.introduction:
Offline reinforcement learning (RL) aims to learn policies that improve upon the behavior policy using only a static dataset generated by that behavior policy, without further environment interaction [ 1 ] .
This creates a central tension: improvement requires deviating from the behavior policy while choosing actions where the dataset provides reliable supervision.
For a fixed state, actions outside the dataset support may receive spuriously high predicted values, which can be exploited by policy optimization to yield out-of-distribution (OOD) actions that perform poorly when deployed [ 1 ] .

A major line of work regularizes a statistical distance between the learned and behavior policies to mitigate OOD actions [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
However, depending on the distance used, these methods can be either too restrictive and produce an overly conservative policy (e.g., KL divergence), or not restrictive enough and still produce OOD actions (e.g., Wasserstein distance, MMD distance) [ 7 ] .

This has motivated a more direct alternative: enforce support constraints on the policy extraction process to guarantee that the actions produced lie within the support of the action distribution of the behavior policy [ 8 , 7 ] .
In particular, these methods learn a flow-based generative model using flow matching [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] to imitate the behavior policy, resulting in a compact latent space that maps to the behavior policy.
Assuming the decoder maps the latent prior’s support into the behavior policy’s support, any latent policy restricted to that support produces in-support actions, while allowing their probabilities to differ from those of the behavior policy.
Policy optimization performed on this latent space, either via gradient descent (as in [ 7 ] ) or SAC [ 12 ] (as in [ 8 ] ), yields a policy that satisfies support constraints by construction.

In this work, we argue that support constraints are only part of the story.
Once policy optimization is restricted to the support, the central difficulty becomes policy extraction: how should one reliably select high-value actions from the support without collapsing to brittle modes or exploiting sharp artifacts of the learned critic?
Even when actions remain in support, the critic may be sharp, irregular, or locally overestimated, and a low-entropy extraction procedure can collapse onto brittle modes.

We study entropy regularization as an explicit objective for support-constrained flow policy optimization.
While entropy regularization is well studied in online RL for its role in improving exploration [ 13 , 12 ] and robustness [ 13 , 14 ] , its role in offline RL, and in particular in support-constrained policy extraction, has not been isolated and made explicit.
We argue that entropy regularization is also crucial in offline RL, not only in discouraging premature collapse of the policy to local minima, but also in smoothing the policy optimization landscape by regularizing the critic [ 15 ] .

To this end, we propose L atent Space A djoint Matching for S upport-Constrained E ntropy- R egularized Offline RL ( LASER ),
a framework for entropy-regularized support-constrained policy extraction with latent-space flow policies. LASER builds on the latent support parameterization used in recent flow-based offline RL methods [ 7 , 8 ] ,
but replaces implicit or architecture-dependent regularization with an explicit entropy-regularized policy improvement objective.
The main technical challenge is that computing and optimizing the entropy of a flow policy in latent space is nontrivial.
We address this using adjoint matching [ 16 ] ,
which enables entropy-regularized optimization of expressive flow policies in latent space while preserving the support constraints induced by the learned latent space.

We make the following contributions:

We identify entropy regularization as a central ingredient for stable support-constrained policy extraction with flow-matching policies in offline RL.

We reinterpret recent support-constrained flow policy methods, including DSRL and ReFORM, through the lens of entropy regularization.

We introduce LASER , an algorithm for entropy-regularized offline policy improvement with latent-space flow policies that preserves dataset-support constraints while enabling smoother and more reliable policy extraction.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that LASER , using a fixed set of method-specific hyperparameters , achieves the strongest performance profiles among the evaluated flow-policy baselines.

2026-10-08.title: FlightMagNav: An Open Dataset and Probabilistic Map Learning and Validation Framework for Outdoor Magnetic Field-Based Positioning
2026-10-08.authors: Isaac Skog , Miguel Ramos Galrinho , Martin Gelin
2026-10-08.abstract: Magnetic field-based positioning is a resilient positioning technology that requires no external infrastructure and is hard to jam at scale. To facilitate research on magnetic field-based positioning for aerial platforms operating close to the Earth’s surface, an open dataset is presented with measurements collected using an unmanned aerial vehicle carrying two optically pumped magnetometers, a type of quantum magnetometer, and a global navigation satellite system-aided inertial navigation system. The dataset includes measurements for both magnetic-field map learning and validation. Along with the dataset, a probabilistic framework for magnetic-field map learning and validation is presented and used to illustrate how the dataset may be used. Finally, we outline research directions that may be explored using the dataset.
2026-10-08.introduction:
Recent geopolitical developments have highlighted the need for resilient positioning technologies that can complement global navigation satellite systems (GNSS). One potential source of positioning information is the spatial anomalies in the Earth’s magnetic field caused by ferromagnetic material in the Earth’s crust. These magnetic anomalies are omnipresent and can be exploited for map-matching-based positioning in a way similar to using terrain height profiles in terrain navigation [ 1 ] .

Recent advances in compact optically pumped magnetometers, a type of quantum magnetometer, have made it possible to equip small aerial platforms with highly sensitive and power-efficient magnetometers. Moreover, unlike classical flux-gate magnetometers, these magnetometers can measure magnetic-field magnitude directly, avoiding the need to reconstruct it from vector measurements. This reduces sensitivity to orientation and axis-misalignment errors, making it easier to reliably measure small magnetic-field anomalies [ 2 ] .

Currently, the development and evaluation of magnetic-field-based
positioning techniques for small aerial platforms is limited by the
availability of open datasets representative of small and slow-moving
platforms operating at low heights. Existing datasets for magnetic-field-based
positioning research, such as the DAF-MIT AIA airborne magnetic
navigation dataset [ 3 ] , have mainly been collected using
larger fast-moving platforms operating at greater heights. Low-height
magnetic-field datasets collected using unmanned aerial vehicles also
exist, see, e.g., [ 4 , 5 ] . However, these
datasets have primarily been collected for geophysical surveying and for
studying platform disturbances, sensor noise, and magnetic compensation,
rather than for positioning research. Likewise, conventional magnetic-field
survey data, e.g., [ 6 ] , are typically collected
with relatively coarse horizontal sampling and do not include data from
other navigation sensors, such as inertial sensors. Hence, available
survey data are typically not suitable for developing and evaluating
magnetic field-based positioning theories and methods. To that end, there
is a need for datasets of densely sampled magnetic-field and inertial
measurements collected on small, slow-moving platforms operating at low
heights.

This paper presents FlightMagNav , an open dataset for outdoor magnetic field-based positioning and map learning. The dataset contains high-rate measurements from two optically pumped magnetometers and a GNSS-aided inertial navigation system collected during multiple unmanned aerial vehicle flights over an area of approximately 1 km 2 {\mathrm{km}}^{2} . The dataset includes measurements from flights with lawnmower-pattern trajectories designed to learn magnetic anomaly maps, as well as flights with trajectories to validate the learned maps and study how the maps generalize to different operating heights.

In addition to the dataset, the paper presents a probabilistic framework for learning magnetic anomaly maps and for validating how well a learned map describes measurements from independent flights. The validation is performed by estimating the effective noise level using the marginal likelihood, i.e., the model evidence conditioned on the learned map. This provides a compact measure of how well the learned map generalizes to measurements from new flights and how the map’s predictive accuracy changes with flight height.

Reproducible research: The code and data can be downloaded at https://doi.org/10.71775/kth.ggkzd-jtk39

# II FlightMagNav Dataset

## II-A Sensor Platform

A drawing of the sensor platform used during the data collection is shown in Fig. 1 , along with the placement of the sensors. The platform carries two QuSpin MAGPIE sensor modules and one Xsens MTi-680 sensor module. Each QuSpin MAGPIE sensor module contains an optically pumped total-field magnetometer, a GNSS receiver, a low-cost inertial measurement unit, and an add-on coil for measuring the vector components of the magnetic field. The Xsens MTi-680 provides a GNSS-aided inertial navigation system (INS) solution. Tab. I summarizes the sensors and the measurements they produce.

## II-B Data Collection

The data were collected outside Skövde, Sweden, over two days using a
quadcopter to carry the sensor platform shown in
Fig. 1 . The sensor platform was suspended below
the quadcopter using two approximately 8 m 8\text{\,}\mathrm{m} long ropes, allowing it to hang
freely during flight. Videos of the complete setup are included with
the published dataset. Temporal variations in the magnetic field were
monitored using a stationary QuSpin magnetometer located on the ground in the
vicinity of the flight area.

A total of eight flights were conducted. Flight 1 was a test flight used
to verify the functionality of the equipment. Flights 2–5 were designed for map learning and followed
lawnmower patterns covering different quadrants of an approximately 1 km 2 1\text{\,}{\mathrm{km}}^{2} area. The separation between adjacent flight legs was
approximately 50 m 50\text{\,}\mathrm{m} . The corresponding flight trajectories are shown in
Fig. 2(a) . During these flights, the sensor platform
was operated at a height of approximately 55 m 55\text{\,}\mathrm{m} relative to the takeoff
point. The terrain over the flight area was approximately level, and the
height relative to the takeoff point closely corresponds to the
height above ground; see Fig. 2(c) .

Flights 6–8 were designed for validation of the learned map and for
investigating how well the map generalizes to flight heights different
from those used during map learning. The validation trajectories were all
well within the area covered by the map-learning flights, such that the
validation primarily tests generalization with respect to flight height
rather than horizontal extrapolation. The corresponding flight trajectories
and height profiles are shown in Fig. 2(b) and
Fig. 2(d) , respectively. During all flights, the speed
was approximately 10 m s − 1 10\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} .

The local on-ground reference magnetometer did not provide usable data during
Flight 1, and the measurements from Flights 2 and 7 contain disturbances
caused by sensor movement and a passing vehicle. Therefore, magnetic-field
measurements from the Uppsala geomagnetic reference station, approximately 270 km 270\text{\,}\mathrm{km} from Skövde, are also included in the dataset as an additional source of information about the
temporal variations in the magnetic field.
Despite this distance, during flights when the local reference sensor measurements were undisturbed, significant correlations can be observed between the temporal variations measured by the Uppsala reference station and those measured by the local sensor.

## II-C Dataset Organization

The published dataset contains both the raw data as acquired by the sensors
and a MATLAB data file, FlightMagNav.mat , containing parsed and
synchronized data. The raw data are included to enable independent
processing of the measurements, while the parsed data provide a convenient
starting point for map learning and localization experiments. The structure
and organization of the two data representations are briefly described
next.

The raw data are organized by acquisition rather than by individual
flight. Each acquisition folder contains the recordings from the airborne
sensors and, when available, the local on-ground reference magnetometer. Consequently,
an acquisition folder may contain measurements corresponding to more than
one flight. Data from the Uppsala geomagnetic reference station are stored
separately and shared between all flights collected on the same day. The
correspondence between flights, acquisition folders, and start and stop
times is given in the accompanying metadata file. The raw data files are
summarized in Tab. II .

The parsed dataset is organized by flight, where each element of the
MATLAB structure contains the measurements and metadata corresponding to
one flight. The organization of the parsed data is summarized in
Tab. III .

The GNSS-aided INS defines the common time reference for the parsed data and has a sample rate of 100 Hz 100\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} . Unfortunately, the GNSS timestamps associated with the MAGPIE measurements were insufficiently accurate for direct synchronization because of an incorrect configuration during data collection. Therefore, the MAGPIE measurements were synchronized to the GNSS-aided INS by correlating angular-rate measurements from the inertial sensors in the different sensor modules. A synchronization accuracy of about 50 ms 50\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} was achieved.

The scalar total-field measurements from the front and rear MAGPIE sensors
were synchronized and resampled to the 100 Hz 100\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} time grid of the GNSS-aided INS. Before resampling, the total-field measurements were low-pass filtered
with a cutoff frequency of 45 Hz 45\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} to avoid aliasing of the 50 Hz 50\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} power-line disturbance.

The vector magnetic-field measurements were also synchronized to the
GNSS-aided INS time reference. However, they were not upsampled to 100 Hz 100\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} , and their original sampling rate of 125 / 3 125/3 Hz \mathrm{Hz} was retained. Hence, the vector measurements are time-aligned with the GNSS-aided INS while retaining their original sampling rate. Further, the measurements from both the local reference magnetometer and the Uppsala
geomagnetic reference station were resampled and aligned with the
time grid of the GNSS-aided INS.

The vector magnetic-field measurements and the inertial measurements from
the different sensor modules are provided in their respective sensor
coordinate frames. No rotation into a common coordinate frame has been
applied in the parsed dataset.
