# 2 Related Work

Generalist policies learn to perform many tasks from images and language instructions by training on diverse robot demonstrations. RT-2 and OpenVLA adapt pretrained vision-language models to predict actions for robot manipulation ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) . π 0 \pi_{0} combines a vision-language backbone with flow matching to produce continuous actions across single-arm, dual-arm, and mobile manipulators ( Black et al., 2025b ) ; π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} extends this approach to generalization across environments through training on robot data and semantic supervision ( Black et al., 2025a ) . World-action models (WAMs) add future-video prediction: DreamZero jointly predicts video and actions, while DiT4DiT uses video-model features to condition action prediction ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) .

This generalist approach also extends to humanoids. GR00T and Ψ 0 \Psi_{0} train on diverse robot demonstrations and use task-specific teleoperation to adapt to target tasks ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) . Ψ 0 \Psi_{0} also pretrains its vision-language model to predict human wrist and hand actions, while its robot joint-command predictions are trained on robot demonstrations. Humanoid policies differ in how they pass their predictions to low-level control. Helix 02 predicts whole-body joint targets that a controller tracks ( Figure AI, 2026 ) . Concurrent MotionWAM instead predicts SONIC body latents alongside direct hand or gripper commands ( Zheng et al., 2026a ) . Human videos train MotionWAM’s video-prediction branch, while robot demonstrations supervise its actions.

VioLA builds on VLA and WAM backbones, with learned motion latents as the policy outputs for both the body and hands. A pretrained body controller and hand decoder turn these predictions into joint commands. Their paired motion encoders provide targets for the same outputs from both human and robot demonstrations.

Motion imitation provides a way to learn joint coordination before learning a task. DeepMimic trains controllers to track reference movements ( Peng et al., 2018 ) ; ASE, latent-space priors, and MoConVQ learn motion representations that higher-level policies can use to control characters ( Peng et al., 2022 ; Gehring et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2024 ) . OmniH2O, HOVER, and SONIC bring motion tracking to humanoid hardware ( He et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2025b ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . In particular, SONIC pairs motion encoders with a body controller that executes their latents. LeVERB connects vision and language to motion control by first learning a latent space from rendered kinematic demonstrations, then training a controller to execute those latents ( Xue et al., 2025 ) . Its hardware experiments replay latent sequences generated in simulation.

VioLA starts with SONIC’s pretrained body encoders and controller, together with separately pretrained hand encoders and their paired robot decoders. These modules remain frozen during generalist-policy training. The generalist policy learns to predict their body and hand motion latents from images and instructions, and uses the robot’s current camera observations to update its predictions during deployment.

Human demonstrations can supply robot training data through physical shadowing, as in HumanPlus ( Fu et al., 2025 ) , or through reconstruction and simulation: VideoMimic reconstructs human motion and scene geometry from videos, then trains humanoid controllers to reproduce the movements ( Allshire et al., 2025 ) . Other methods use recorded human motion to supervise policies directly. EgoMimic shares pose supervision between humans and robots while retaining a robot joint-action head ( Kareer et al., 2025 ) . HAT and EgoVLA predict human-centric wrist and hand motion, which is converted to robot commands at deployment ( Qiu et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . EgoScale pretrains on human wrist and retargeted finger motion before adapting with human–robot and task-specific robot data ( Zheng et al., 2026b ) .

Another line of work learns action labels for policy pretraining. Being-H0 pretrains a vision-language policy to predict tokenized human wrist and finger motion, then adds a robot action head during post-training ( Luo et al., 2025 ) . LAPA and WholeBodyVLA infer latent actions from video and use robot demonstrations to learn robot-command prediction ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . UniT learns shared human–humanoid tokens through visual and action reconstruction ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Predicting these tokens aligns policy features, while a separate prediction head produces robot-specific commands; the shared tokens themselves are not passed to a robot controller for execution.

VioLA uses annotated human body and hand motion to label the original human images with the same latent commands that its frozen robot decoders execute. Human demonstrations therefore supervise the generalist policy’s deployed action outputs without a corresponding physical robot demonstration. Because the motion encoders and robot decoders are pretrained together, generalist-policy training does not need to learn a new mapping from human motion labels to robot joint commands.

2026-10-09.title: FAITH: Feasibility-Aware Safety-Filtered RL for High-Dimensional Systems
2026-10-09.authors: Songyuan Zhang , Baljeet Singh , Sarthak Ranjeet Kaingade , Chuchu Fan , Bryan Trinh
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-09.abstract: Safe reinforcement learning commonly places safety and task performance in the same policy objective, where they can introduce competing updates. Safety filters separate them at action execution, but classical designs require an analytic safety function and dynamics model, and standard minimal-intervention filters are myopic to long-horizon task return because they minimize only instantaneous action deviation. Hard projections are also undefined when no safe action exists. We present FAITH , a feasibility-aware, model-free framework that approximates the optimal state-action safety value and amortizes minimal-intervention filtering with a feedforward network. The task policy optimizes the task return through the filtered dynamics, which recovers the feasible constrained problem without a competing safety term in the task-policy update. When no action satisfies the learned safety condition, the same filter approaches the action with minimum predicted peak harm. On a double integrator example and a Safety Gym environment, FAITH achieves the highest return among methods with no feasible-start violations and matches the lowest harm from infeasible starts. On a 29 29 -DoF humanoid, it reaches a 99.95 % 99.95\% safety rate while retaining 97 % 97\% of the unfiltered return in Walking-Avoid, and obtains the highest measured safety rate in Push-Avoid by learning to sacrifice balancing and fall away from the protected region. The same policies are also demonstrated on a real-world Unitree G1 humanoid.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has enabled agile behaviors for high-dimensional legged and humanoid robots [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Deploying these behaviors around people or equipment, however, requires keeping every robot link outside protected regions.
This requirement is difficult for contact-rich, underactuated systems because safety depends not only on the current geometry, but also on whether future actions can prevent a violation eventually.
A strong disturbance can also make violation unavoidable, and therefore, a controller should maximize task return safely when safety is feasible and only minimize harm otherwise.

Feasibility-aware RL uses reachability-based safety values to estimate whether a safe future trajectory exists [ 4 , 5 ] , and guides policy optimization toward harm reduction when safety is infeasible, and return maximization otherwise [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] .
Safety requirements are often enforced within policy optimization through a penalty, a multiplier, or a constraint-reduction update [ 9 , 10 ] .
However, task and safety signals act on the policy itself in all cases.
When return improvement and harm reduction favor different actions, their policy updates can oppose one another.
For weighted penalty methods, a small safety weight can permit violations, whereas a large weight can make the policy conservative.
Primal-dual methods adapt the weight, but replace manual tuning with an unstable saddle-point problem [ 10 ] .
Thus, even when the formulation distinguishes the feasibility of states, safety competes with performance inside policy optimization.

Safety filters offer a natural separation by correcting a nominal action generated by a task policy before it reaches the system [ 11 , 12 ] .
Classical filters typically require an analytic safety function and a dynamics model, then solve an optimization problem at every control step.
Learning-based methods can remove the explicit model, but they usually retain online action sampling or optimization [ 13 , 14 ] , which becomes difficult as the action dimension grows.
In addition, a fixed task policy cannot adapt to the effect of safety interventions on long-horizon return.
Some methods address this limitation by training the task policy through the filter, allowing it to adapt to safety interventions [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] .
A separate difficulty arises when no admissible action exists: hard projection is then undefined and does not by itself specify how to minimize harm.

Considering these challenges, we propose F easibility- A ware safety-f I l T ered RL for H igh-dimensional systems ( FAITH ), a model-free framework that combines learned safety value functions, feedforward action filtering, and task-policy training through the filter. FAITH approximates the optimal state-action safety value using a safety critic and a backup actor, which guides a feedforward filter to approximate the minimal action correction.
The task policy is trained through the filter using the unmodified task reward.
Safety therefore changes the dynamics experienced by the policy but does not appear as a competing term in its objective .
When no action satisfies the learned acceptance condition, the same filter prioritizes the action with minimum peak harm, without a feasibility classifier, a mode switch, or a separate recovery controller.
At deployment, control requires only forward passes through the task policy and safety filter.
To summarize our contributions,

We introduce FAITH , which approximates the optimal safety critic and trains the task policy through a learned feedforward safety filter.
Under a perfect filter and global policy optimization, FAITH recovers the constrained optimum on feasible states, without a competing safety term in the task-policy objective.

In infeasible states, the same controller approaches the action with minimum predicted peak harm, without a mode switch or fallback policy.

Experiments on a double integrator, Safety Gym, and a 29 29 -DoF humanoid demonstrate high task performance and safety in feasible settings, and reduced harm in infeasible settings.
Qualitative demonstrations also show the learned controller operating on a physical humanoid.

1. We introduce FAITH , which approximates the optimal safety critic and trains the task policy through a learned feedforward safety filter.
Under a perfect filter and global policy optimization, FAITH recovers the constrained optimum on feasible states, without a competing safety term in the task-policy objective.

2. In infeasible states, the same controller approaches the action with minimum predicted peak harm, without a mode switch or fallback policy.

3. Experiments on a double integrator, Safety Gym, and a 29 29 -DoF humanoid demonstrate high task performance and safety in feasible settings, and reduced harm in infeasible settings.
Qualitative demonstrations also show the learned controller operating on a physical humanoid.

2026-10-09.title: Control-Ready Uncertainty for Trajectory Diffusion
2026-10-09.authors: Zhiwei Xue , Jia Yue Kam , Jinhang Qiu , Yifeng Cheng , Ege Gursoy , Jiaming Wang , Vincent Bonnet , Harold Soh
2026-10-09.comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026 as a Spotlight presentation.
2026-10-09.abstract: Diffusion models can represent complex, multimodal trajectory distributions, but extracting uncertainty from them typically requires costly Monte Carlo sampling. This limits their use in real-time control, where robots must rapidly assess risk and maintain safety margins. We introduce Score-Curvature for Online Precision Estimation (SCOPE), a lightweight module that augments diffusion trajectory models with control-ready uncertainty. SCOPE learns a structured precision matrix around each nominal trajectory by distilling score-curvature information and producing calibrated Gaussian tubes with low overhead and without repeated Monte Carlo sampling. These tubes provide per-timestep covariance estimates that can be used both as predicted occupancy for moving agents and as adaptive exploration guides for robot control. We evaluate SCOPE with mode-conditioned multimodal diffusion backbones in pedestrian forecasting, crowd navigation, Maze2D control, and real-world Franka Panda manipulation. Across these settings, SCOPE provides fast uncertainty estimation, which leads to better closed-loop performance. Project page .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Diffusion models have recently gained wide adoption for their ability to represent complex and high-dimensional distributions. In robotics, they serve two complementary roles. As policies , diffusion models generate robot motion plans or action sequences, enabling expressive behavior synthesis that captures the multimodality inherent in many manipulation and locomotion tasks [ 17 , 8 ] .
As world models , diffusion models can represent stochastic future evolutions of the environment, including scene dynamics, object motion, and interactions among agents. One important instance of this broader use case is trajectory prediction, where diffusion-based models [ 12 , 19 , 24 , 3 , 46 ] forecast the future motion of surrounding agents such as pedestrians, vehicles, or human collaborators; these predictions can then be used by controllers such as MPPI [ 25 , 39 ] to anticipate and avoid collisions.

However, in interactive robotics, accurate prediction is often insufficient. The robot should also be aware of the aleatoric uncertainty in those predictions: the uncertainty arising from inherently stochastic future behavior. For example, a robot approaching a pedestrian must reason about both the pedestrian’s likely future trajectory and the “spread” around each plausible future before deciding whether to pass, yield, or maintain a safe distance. This control-relevant uncertainty allows the robot to assess collision risk and preserve safety margins.

The challenge is to extract this uncertainty fast enough for control. Diffusion models represent uncertainty implicitly through their generative distribution, and making it explicit usually requires post hoc Monte Carlo sampling [ 31 , 44 ] . Since each sample requires a reverse diffusion chain, reliable estimates can be too slow for closed-loop control even with GPU batching. This delay can leave the robot acting on an outdated motion forecast, increasing collision risk. Reducing the sample count can recover speed but degrades estimation fidelity. Hence, this raises a natural question: can we obtain control-ready uncertainty rapidly, without Monte Carlo sampling?

In response, we propose Score Curvature for Online Precision Estimation (SCOPE), a lightweight module that efficiently distills control-ready aleatoric trajectory uncertainty from a diffusion model.
Our key observation is that a trained score model encodes the local geometry of the learned trajectory density (Fig. 1 , top).
Around a predicted trajectory, uncertainty depends on how quickly likelihood falls away in nearby directions: sharp decay yields a narrow, high-precision tube, while flat decay yields a wider region of plausible futures.
Through Laplace’s method, this local geometry corresponds to the curvature of the log-density, whose negative Hessian defines a precision matrix. But forming and querying this full (often large) curvature matrix at control time is impractical. Instead, SCOPE learns a structured precision head from score-curvature information using efficient Hessian-vector products (HVPs) during training. At inference, one diffusion pass followed by one lightweight head evaluation efficiently produces per-timestep marginal covariances, yielding a mixture of tubes : multiple trajectory hypotheses, each equipped with analytic confidence regions that plug directly into controllers.

We evaluate SCOPE along three axes: uncertainty quality, inference speed, and downstream control performance. On pedestrian trajectory forecasting, SCOPE matches the uncertainty quality of diffusion ensembles while avoiding their costly repeated sampling; this makes uncertainty estimation fast enough for closed-loop control. We then demonstrate two control use-cases. As a policy-side guide, it uses trajectory tubes to adapt MPPI exploration in concave mazes, improving both sample efficiency and success rate. As a world model, SCOPE provides pedestrian motion tubes that allow MPPI to anticipate collision risk in crowded navigation. Finally, we validate practical viability on a real Franka Panda arm in a cluttered tabletop pick-and-place task (Fig. 1 , bottom), which demonstrates closed-loop collision avoidance under tight control-rate constraints.

To summarize, we make the following contributions:
(i) We introduce SCOPE, a lightweight module that extracts control-ready, per-timestep trajectory uncertainty from a diffusion model with low overhead, avoiding repeated Monte Carlo sampling;
(ii) We improve inference efficiency by parameterizing uncertainty as a block-banded plus low-rank precision matrix, which enables efficient HVP-based training and marginal covariance queries at test time;
(iii) We validate SCOPE in forecasting, pedestrian navigation, Maze2D control, and real-robot manipulation, where it improves closed-loop performance over strong baselines.

2026-10-09.title: RoboRSI: Stable, efficient, and reusable robot self-evolution in complex real-world environments
2026-10-09.authors: Zimo Wen , Yijin Chen , Yuxuan Cao , Wendi Chen , Yanwen Zou , Wenye Yu , Fuhang Kuang , Han Xue , Jun Lv , Chuan Wen , Cewu Lu
2026-10-09.abstract:
A generalist robot in complex real-world environments should not only
perform diverse tasks but also improve through experience, turning what it
learns during execution into capabilities that later tasks can reuse. Robot agents that act through code
can already repair programs from execution feedback, yet it remains a
central challenge to organize this experience around the task structure
that gives it meaning, so that each repair is attributed to the responsible
capability, supported by execution evidence, and validated before it is
reused. We introduce RoboRSI, a robot self-improvement system built on
Top-Down Skill Refinement (TSR). TSR decomposes tasks into compound, atomic,
and base skills with scoped responsibilities and explicit input–output
contracts, attributes each execution outcome to the responsible branch, and
confines revision to that branch. Building upon this structure, a Manager,
Planner, Engineer, and Reviewer coordinate planning, execution, diagnosis,
and the validated release of new skills, while people steer the process
through objectives and corrections; stable skill sequences are further
consolidated into reusable compound skills. On a mobile manipulator, RoboRSI
develops multi-object household cleanup over 104 rounds. In simulation, it
achieves the highest success rate on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-Plus, and
RoboTwin, exceeding the strongest baseline by 2.7 to 11.0 percentage points. Project page: https://lab.noematrix.ai/blog/2-roborsi-research-preview/ Code: https://github.com/nssmd/RoboRSI
2026-10-09.introduction:
The vision of generalist robotics is to develop robots that perform a broad range of tasks reliably in complex real-world environments, where objects, layouts, and instructions keep changing, while improving through experience. This shifts the goal of robot agents from episode-level task completion toward sustained capability accumulation: failed grasps, stale object locations, and recovery situations are valuable only if the robot can identify the capability involved, refine it using execution evidence, and make the resulting behavior available to later tasks.

A promising route lets foundation models act through code. Code as Policies ( Liang et al., 2023 ) composes perception and control primitives into executable robot programs, and CaP-X ( Fu et al., 2026 ) studies how abstraction, grounding, and interaction shape such programs. Subsequent work closes the loop with execution feedback: ETA/OpenETA ( Chen et al., 2026b ) interleaves planning and tool execution with fresh observations, ASPIRE ( Lu et al., 2026 ) adds repaired programs to a growing skill library, and ENPIRE ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) carries this loop into physical experimentation. Execution feedback thus shifts from a signal for correcting a single attempt to a resource for building capabilities that persist across tasks.

Execution experience, however, becomes a reusable capability only when it is organized around the task structure that gives it meaning. A repair must remain connected to the objective that motivated it, belong to the capability responsible for the observed behavior, and be validated before it is reused. Without such structure, repeated attempts fill the context with complete trajectories, local fixes drift from the overall objective, and people are drawn back into resetting environments, reading logs, and deciding where each fix belongs.

Our observation is that this structure must serve both the people directing the robot and the agents implementing its behavior, which calls for two complementary abstractions. Human-friendly steering lets people express objectives, domain knowledge, constraints, and safety judgments at the level of the service they need. Agent-friendly structure gives agents task-relevant context, explicit interfaces, and bounded responsibilities for execution and revision.

Based on this observation, we introduce RoboRSI , a multi-agent system for robot self-improvement organized by Top-Down Skill Refinement (TSR) . TSR decomposes each task into compound, atomic, and base skills with scoped responsibilities and explicit input–output contracts, attributes each execution outcome to the responsible branch, and confines the revision to that branch: an inadequate decomposition revises the task structure, an unreliable composition the corresponding compound skill, and a failed operation the responsible atomic or base skill. A Manager, Planner, Engineer, and Reviewer carry out planning, execution, diagnosis, and validated release, and stable skill sequences are consolidated into compound skills that later executions select and monitor instead of reconstructing every tool decision.

We evaluate RoboRSI on a mobile manipulator that performs multi-object household cleanup across a scene change while its skills are developed over 104 rounds, and in simulation against robot-agent baselines on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO, and RoboTwin, with frozen capability transfer to LIBERO-Plus. RoboRSI achieves the highest success rate on all four benchmarks, exceeding the strongest baseline by 5.3 points on LIBERO, 11.0 on LIBERO-PRO, 5.7 on LIBERO-Plus, and 2.7 on RoboTwin.

Our contributions are threefold:

Complementary abstractions for robot self-improvement: we
identify that execution experience becomes reusable only when it is tied to
the task structure that gives it meaning, and that this structure must
serve both human-friendly steering and agent-friendly structure.

RoboRSI Framework: a system that realizes these abstractions through
Top-Down Skill Refinement, which verifies each atomic task’s postcondition
before completion and revises each failure at its earliest failing node, and a multi-agent
execution–refinement loop that validates and releases skills across tasks.

Real-world and simulated evaluation: skill development on a
mobile manipulator over 104 rounds, the highest success
on four simulation benchmarks, and ablations of role separation, skill
refinement, and compound skills.

# 2 Related Work

Code as Policies ( Liang et al., 2023 ) showed that language models can write
robot programs that compose perception and control APIs, turning high-level
instructions into executable behavior. Follow-up work examines what these
programs should be built from: CaP-X ( Fu et al., 2026 ) studies the
abstraction level of primitives, perceptual grounding, and interaction, and
GRACE ( Sun et al., 2025 ) encodes affordances and geometry as executable
concepts. ASPIRE ( Lu et al., 2026 ) goes further by repairing failed
programs and keeping the repaired skills in a growing library. Once programs
are kept and reused, however, a repair to one skill can affect every task
that calls it, and deciding where a repair belongs becomes as important as
writing it. RoboRSI addresses this through TSR, which gives each capability
an interface and a declared responsibility, so that a repair is made at the
responsible branch and composes with the skills around it.

RSI studies how an agent’s experience improves its later behavior. Language
agents first did so through verbal feedback: Reflexion stores reflections on
failed attempts, and Self-Refine iteratively critiques and revises its own
outputs ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Madaan et al., 2023 ) . Voyager moved from
text to executable skills, accumulating a code library through open-ended
interaction ( Wang et al., 2024 ) . Multimodal agents extend this idea with
skills acquired from external resources, execution feedback, and reusable
procedures, as in RESOURCE2SKILL, EvoSkill-GUI, and
OmniHarness ( Fan et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Xu et al., 2026 ) .
Robot-specific work detects and explains failures during execution:
ProgPrompt adds assertions to generated programs ( Singh et al., 2023 ) ,
REFLECT summarizes robot experience to explain and correct
failures ( Liu et al., 2023b ) , DoReMi and Code-as-Monitor monitor
language- or code-specified constraints to trigger
recovery ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and AHA trains a
vision-language model to detect and reason about manipulation
failures ( Duan et al., 2025 ) . These methods detect a failure within an
episode; RoboRSI additionally decides which skill should change and
validates the change before later tasks reuse it.
In embodied settings, EmbodiSkill diagnoses errors at the level of
individual skills ( Ju et al., 2026 ) , and ENPIRE couples physical
evaluation with coding-agent refinement of policies ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) .
Physical execution adds a difficulty that software environments largely
avoid: a failure may originate several steps before it is observed, and a
change to a shared skill affects tasks that were not part of the failed run.
RoboRSI therefore attributes each failure to its earliest failing node,
validates revisions against the recent history of the affected tasks, and
reuses capabilities through explicit skill interfaces.

Large language models first entered robotics as planners. Early work
grounded generated plans in admissible actions ( Huang et al., 2022a ) ,
and Inner Monologue fed environment feedback back into
planning ( Huang et al., 2022b ) . Advances in multimodal
understanding ( Alayrac et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023a ; Gemini Team and others, 2024 ) ,
embodied grounding ( Driess et al., 2023 ) , and interleaved reasoning and
acting ( Yao et al., 2023 ) then allowed models to reason directly over
observations, and VoxPoser ( Huang et al., 2023 ) and
ReKep ( Huang et al., 2024 ) used generated code to compose 3D value maps and
relational keypoint constraints for motion planning. A parallel line trains
robot foundation models end to end. Vision–language–action models such as
RT-2, OpenVLA, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} learn visuomotor control from large
robot datasets ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) ;
world-action models such as Zero-WAM add predictive visual
dynamics ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) ; and Gemini Robotics and Gemini
Robotics-ER 1.5 combine control with embodied
reasoning ( Gemini Robotics Team and others, 2025 ) . As general-purpose models have
become more capable, recent systems use them directly for robot decisions
and actions. Maestro orchestrates perception and control
modules ( Shi et al., 2025 ) , ETA/OpenETA closes the loop between planning,
execution, and feedback ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , GPT-Policy performs in-context
control ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) , two RoboHarness systems adapt through
memory ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , and UniDomain and
UniPlan connect symbolic planning with visual
grounding ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . RoboRSI complements these
directions at the system level: TSR and multi-agent execution maintain
reusable skills, and the trajectories collected during execution can train
policies that return as tools in the same hierarchy.

2026-10-09.title: GLIO2: A GPU-Parallelized Tightly-Coupled LiDAR-Inertial-GNSS System for Robust and Real-Time Global Localization and Mapping
2026-10-09.authors: Qi Zhang , Xikun Liu , Qijun Qin , Xiangru Wang , Junzhe Wang , Naigui Xiao , Jianhao Jiao , Weisong Wen
2026-10-09.abstract: Globally consistent, real-time state estimation in large-scale, perceptually degraded environments is essential for autonomous vehicles and aerial robots, and requires fusing LiDAR, inertial, and GNSS measurements. Existing fusion methods, however, share a scan-to-map front-end with two failure modes. First, each scan is aligned to an incrementally built map that drifts under degeneracy, and once the estimate diverges the error is irrecoverable. Second, even without divergence, a registration biased by dynamic objects or wrong correspondences is propagated as a single pose constraint with an over-confident covariance, leaving its correspondences unavailable for GNSS to re-weight or relinearize. We propose GLIO2, a tightly-coupled LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS system whose GPU-parallel front-end jointly optimizes scan-to-multiscan LiDAR, IMU pre-integration, and raw GNSS measurements in a single sliding-window factor graph, sustaining real-time operation on edge hardware. A complementary offline back-end reuses the same cached factors to refine the entire trajectory in batch, completing the 30 30 -min, 4.51 4.51 -km UrbanNav Whampoa sequence in about 24 24 s. Across three public benchmarks (UrbanNav, MARS-LVIG, M3DGR) and self-collected UAV and vehicle data, GLIO2 attains the best overall accuracy among evaluated systems. On a 5.66 5.66 -km bridge traversed at up to 96 96 km/h, where every competing baseline diverges under LiDAR degeneracy, it maintains 1.6 1.6 m horizontal accuracy. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, the full pipeline runs at about 25 25 Hz ( 39.60 39.60 ms per scan). The source code and datasets will be released.
2026-10-09.introduction:
An autonomous vehicle in a dense urban canyon and a micro-aerial vehicle surveying open farmland face the same estimation problem: the state must be globally consistent over the whole mission, locally smooth at control rate, robust to sensor degradation, and computed in real time on the limited compute carried onboard. LiDAR, inertial measurement units (IMUs), and global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) each meet part of these demands and fail another.

LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] exploits the rich structural information in point clouds to produce high-frequency, locally smooth, and locally accurate motion estimates together with dense 3D geometric maps. The IMU predicts inter-scan motion to deskew each scan and bridge the gaps between LiDAR frames, though it drifts rapidly when integrated alone. Relying primarily on local geometric constraints, however, LIO accumulates drift over long trajectories and degrades severely under geometric degeneracy (weak, repetitive, or insufficient structure such as open fields, long tunnels, and flat or sparsely featured scenes), where the registration loses observability along its under-constrained directions [ 4 ] .

GNSS, in contrast, provides drift-free absolute positioning in a globally referenced Earth-fixed frame, bounding the global error that LIO cannot [ 5 ] . Yet its measurements arrive at only 1 1 – 10 10 Hz and are corrupted by multipath, non-line-of-sight (NLOS) reception, and outright outages in the urban canyons, tunnels, and indoor spaces a robot must traverse, where a single contaminated observation can inject errors of tens of meters.

The two modalities are thus complementary: GNSS anchors the estimate to an Earth-fixed frame and bounds the global drift that LIO accumulates, while LIO carries the estimate through GNSS outages and down-weights GNSS outliers with its more precise local geometry. Fusing LiDAR, IMU, and GNSS in a single tightly-coupled factor graph [ 6 ] exploits this complementarity, jointly relinearizing the raw heterogeneous measurements as new information arrives [ 7 , 8 , 5 ] . Building such an estimator that is at once globally and locally consistent, robust under sensor degradation, and real-time on edge platforms, however, raises three central challenges.

a) Front-end fragility : LiDAR–GNSS systems such as LIO-SAM [ 3 ] , LIGO [ 8 ] , GIL [ 9 ] , and GLIO [ 7 ] all build their LiDAR estimate on a scan-to-map (S2M) front-end, which fuses past scans into a single deterministic map and aligns each new scan to it. In scenes such as a sea-crossing bridge, a flat open plain, or a UAV flying close to a repetitive high-rise facade, severe geometric degeneracy rapidly destabilizes this scan-to-map LiDAR localization, so the front-end can no longer produce a correct estimate; once it diverges, the back-end GNSS estimate cannot be recovered either. Even GLIO’s offline scan-to-multiscan (S2MS) batch is insufficient, as it still requires a non-divergent front-end as its initial guess. The first challenge, then, is the inherent limitation of the front-end design adopted by these mainstream methods.

b) Frozen, over-confident LiDAR : Mainstream S2M methods first reduce each scan to a fixed LiDAR constraint (a 6 6 -DoF pose-with-covariance prior in LIGO [ 8 ] , a relative-pose factor in LIO-SAM [ 3 ] ) and fuse it with GNSS. In urban scenes, however, dynamic objects, passing traffic, and changing structure create wrong correspondences that bias this constraint. It then enters the fusion under an over-confident covariance that outweighs the GNSS correction, and because the past point clouds are never re-associated or relinearized, the bias is frozen into the trajectory rather than corrected. The second challenge is thus to admit LiDAR into the GNSS fusion as raw relative constraints, so that LiDAR information constrains the local geometry without being imposed as a potentially overconfident prior on the global frame. Active correspondences can then be re-associated and their residuals relinearized as the joint estimate updates.

c) Real-time cost : Addressing the first two challenges motivates replacing S2M with S2MS registration and keeping the raw point residuals in one joint optimization, so that LiDAR and GNSS relinearize together. The price is computational. Each scan forms dense voxel correspondences against several keyframes, and every nonlinear iteration must recompute all correspondences, fused covariances, and Jacobians as the keyframe poses move. Even on a high-performance CPU (e.g., the Intel Core Ultra 7 265KF), each per-scan sliding-window update must relinearize hundreds of thousands of point residuals across the active keyframes; on denser scans, our CPU implementation already consumes the full 100 100 ms budget of a 10 10 Hz LiDAR and peaks at 200 200 – 300 300 ms (Sec. 5-5.3 ). GLIO [ 7 ] , for example, performs its dense S2MS and raw-GNSS joint optimization in the offline back-end, while its online stage retains the S2M front-end described above. The third challenge is thus to sustain this dense, raw-domain joint optimization online, within a per-scan budget that our CPU implementation cannot consistently meet.

Motivated by these observations, we present GLIO2, a unified tightly-coupled LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS system. A GPU-parallel front-end fuses dense LiDAR, IMU, and raw GNSS in one real-time sliding-window graph, and an offline batch back-end refines the trajectory by reusing the same factors. The first two contributions respond to the three challenges; the third validates and releases the system.

The contributions of this work are as follows.

A unified online LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS front-end. GLIO2 fuses scan-to-multiscan LiDAR, raw double-differenced pseudorange and Doppler, and IMU pre-integration in a single real-time sliding-window graph (Sec. 3 ). Each scan contributes relative scan-to-keyframe constraints without being reduced to a fixed-map LiDAR pose prior. The raw correspondences are re-associated and relinearized at every iteration, allowing registration errors to be revised as the joint estimate updates. Tightly coupling both modalities on the raw measurements keeps the estimate robust to LiDAR degeneracy and to GNSS dropouts (Sec. 5-5.3 ).

Real-time onboard operation with a fast offline back-end. GPU-parallel per-point linearization enables the joint LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS optimization to run at the LiDAR rate on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. The offline back-end reuses compact relative-pose LiDAR factors generated online to refine the full trajectory without re-registering the point clouds. It improves trajectory accuracy and runs approximately 12 12 – 20 × 20\times faster than the GLIO back-end on the three tested sequences (Sec. 4-4.9 , Fig. 14 ).

Validation and open-source release. On three public benchmarks (UrbanNav [ 10 ] , MARS-LVIG [ 11 ] , M3DGR [ 12 ] ) and self-collected UAV and vehicle data, under both GNSS NLOS/multipath and LiDAR degeneracy, GLIO2 achieves the lowest 3D ATE RMSE among the evaluated LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS systems after batch refinement (Sec. 5 ). A single-receiver variant runs without a base station (Appendix 9 ). The source code and self-collected datasets will be released.

To our knowledge, GLIO2 is the first system to jointly optimize dense scan-to-multiscan LiDAR factors, IMU pre-integration, and raw GNSS observations fully online at the LiDAR rate on an embedded GPU. We evaluate it on eleven sequences drawn from three public benchmarks (UrbanNav [ 10 ] , MARS-LVIG [ 11 ] , M3DGR [ 12 ] ) and four self-collected UAV and vehicle runs, spanning dense urban canyons, indoor–outdoor transitions, a 5.66 5.66 km sea-crossing bridge, and feature-poor farmland. The online front-end completes all eleven sequences, with 3 3 D ATE RMSEs of 3.54 3.54 m on UrbanNav- Tst , 7.76 7.76 m on Whampoa , 1.98 1.98 m on our dense-canyon Urban route, and 3.59 3.59 m on the LiDAR-degenerate Bridge , where every evaluated LiDAR-based baseline diverges. With offline batch refinement, these errors decrease to 2.58 2.58 , 2.99 2.99 , 1.33 1.33 , and 2.55 2.55 m, respectively. Across all eleven sequences, the batch solution achieves the lowest 3 3 D ATE RMSE among the evaluated LiDAR–inertial–GNSS systems. The front-end averages 39.6 39.6 – 55.5 55.5 ms per scan across the tested LiDARs on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, below the 100 100 ms scan period, while the offline back-end re-optimizes the full 30 30 -min Whampoa trajectory in 24.2 24.2 s.

Each scan contributes relative scan-to-keyframe constraints without being reduced to a fixed-map LiDAR pose prior. The raw correspondences are re-associated and relinearized at every iteration, allowing registration errors to be revised as the joint estimate updates. Tightly coupling both modalities on the raw measurements keeps the estimate robust to LiDAR degeneracy and to GNSS dropouts (Sec. 5-5.3 ).

2. Real-time onboard operation with a fast offline back-end. GPU-parallel per-point linearization enables the joint LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS optimization to run at the LiDAR rate on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX. The offline back-end reuses compact relative-pose LiDAR factors generated online to refine the full trajectory without re-registering the point clouds. It improves trajectory accuracy and runs approximately 12 12 – 20 × 20\times faster than the GLIO back-end on the three tested sequences (Sec. 4-4.9 , Fig. 14 ).

3. Validation and open-source release. On three public benchmarks (UrbanNav [ 10 ] , MARS-LVIG [ 11 ] , M3DGR [ 12 ] ) and self-collected UAV and vehicle data, under both GNSS NLOS/multipath and LiDAR degeneracy, GLIO2 achieves the lowest 3D ATE RMSE among the evaluated LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS systems after batch refinement (Sec. 5 ). A single-receiver variant runs without a base station (Appendix 9 ). The source code and self-collected datasets will be released.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 LiDAR Registration Paradigms

Scan matching provides the geometric constraints in LiDAR odometry, and the way a scan is matched determines the form of constraint it produces and thus what LiDAR contributes to the joint estimator.

Scan-to-map (S2M) registration is adopted by most real-time LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) systems, which registers each new scan against an incrementally built reference map (e.g., a surfel or implicit-surface map [ 13 , 14 ] ) and produces a single absolute pose [ 1 , 15 , 3 ] . Building on classical pairwise scan registration [ 16 , 17 ] , S2M is efficient and locally accurate. However, it treats the fused map as a fixed reference, so potentially erroneous earlier map points are never corrected by later scans, and each scan is summarized by one absolute pose rather than by its raw correspondences.

Scan-to-multiscan (S2MS) registration instead keeps several keyframe poses as optimization variables and jointly refines them through relative constraints. The estimated poses update the world-frame geometry, while each keyframe’s point cloud remains in its local frame. S2MS builds on the joint multi-scan alignment of Lu and Milios [ 18 ] and nScan-matching [ 19 ] , and modern formulations bring a distribution-to-distribution registration metric (GICP [ 20 ] , NDT [ 21 ] , and its voxelized form VGICP [ 22 ] ) into a multi-scan factor graph. The main cost is computational: as the keyframe poses move, the correspondences, residuals, and Jacobians must be re-associated and relinearized for many scan pairs at every iteration, so dense S2MS has traditionally run at low rate or offline, as in the global LiDAR bundle adjustment of BALM [ 23 ] and the GNSS-coupled global batch optimization of GLIO [ 7 ] . Lightweight and GPU-accelerated formulations reduce this cost: FF-LINS [ 24 ] uses a frame-to-frame association on a solid-state LiDAR, while Koide et al. apply GPU acceleration to dense factors for real-time LiDAR-inertial odometry [ 25 ] and faster global mapping [ 26 ] , an approach consolidated in GLIM [ 2 ] .

## 2.2 GNSS Observables

A GNSS receiver outputs three raw observables, the pseudorange (PSR), the Doppler (DOP), and the carrier phase (CP). Prior work fuses these observables in different ways.

The simplest is Single Point Positioning (SPP), which estimates an absolute position from a single receiver’s pseudoranges, modeling the ionospheric and tropospheric delays and the satellite and receiver clock errors [ 27 ] . GVINS [ 28 ] , the raw-GNSS visual-inertial estimator of Liu et al. [ 29 ] and gnssFGO [ 30 ] tightly couple raw pseudorange and Doppler, the Doppler providing a global velocity observation. Precise Point Positioning (PPP) applies precise orbit and clock products and estimates the receiver clock and tropospheric delay, removing the first-order ionosphere either by the ionosphere-free combination (GIL [ 9 ] ) or with external ionosphere maps (P3-LINS [ 31 ] ). Differential methods instead suppress most of these errors directly: double-differencing (DD) the pseudorange against a reference station [ 32 ] cancels the satellite and receiver clock errors and largely removes the spatially correlated atmospheric delays over a short baseline, leaving meter-level constraints, as in GLIO [ 7 ] . The carrier phase is far more precise but carries an integer ambiguity; the dominant strategy resolves the double-differenced ambiguity [ 33 ] in a between-station/between-satellite formulation ( Real-Time Kinematic , RTK), as in GLINS [ 34 ] , GIVL-SLAM [ 35 ] , and FGO-GIL [ 36 ] , reaching centimeter accuracy. An alternative differences the carrier phase across epochs ( Time-Differenced Carrier Phase , TD-CP); since the integer ambiguity is time-invariant, this differencing cancels it when no cycle slip occurs, leaving a smooth epoch-to-epoch motion constraint, as in LIGO [ 8 ] .

## 2.3 LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS Integration Systems

A LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS system couples LiDAR, IMU, and GNSS measurements, which supplies the globally referenced, drift-free positioning that LiDAR and inertial sensing alone cannot. We group existing systems by how GNSS is coupled to the estimator: loosely-coupled, tightly-coupled filter-based, and tightly-coupled factor-graph methods (Tab. 1 ).

Loosely-coupled methods combine LiDAR and GNSS at the state-estimation level: a position solved from GNSS enters as a constraint in the LiDAR-inertial estimator. LIO-SAM [ 3 ] and LIO-Fusion [ 37 ] add the GPS/RTK solution as a position factor in the graph, with LiDAR entering as the relative pose of a LIO front-end, and He et al. [ 38 ] add GNSS-derived poses to a mapping graph as pose factors. Others apply quality management to the RTK output and fuse only the validated fixed solutions [ 39 , 40 ] , or extend this state-level fusion to GNSS together with multi-sensors [ 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 ] . This bounds the long-term LiDAR drift, but reduces GNSS to a single pose: one epoch corrupted by multipath or NLOS can drag the whole solution off, or be rejected outright even when many of its satellites remain usable.

Tightly-coupled filter-based methods fuse the raw GNSS observables in a recursive filter. GIL [ 9 ] , P3-LINS [ 31 ] , and the GNSS/IMU/LiDAR estimator of Li et al. [ 45 ] couple raw PPP measurements with IMU and LiDAR and reach precise positioning without a reference station. GIL and P3-LINS adopt an error-state EKF, Li et al. use a very short window MSCKF. All three share the same drawback: a recursive filter absorbs each measurement once and marginalizes past states rather than re-optimizing them. This is especially damaging for GNSS, whose measurements are noisy and often corrupted by NLOS and multipath. A single committed outlier biases the current state, and from there it propagates into every estimate that follows.

Tightly-coupled factor-graph methods fuse the raw observables in a sliding-window factor graph, keeping a window of states available for relinearization, so GNSS outliers can be re-weighted as later measurements arrive. FGO-GIL [ 36 ] and GIVL-SLAM [ 35 ] both register each LiDAR keyframe against a fixed submap and directly fuse with GNSS RTK in a factor graph optimization. Because the submap is held fixed during optimization, scan-to-submap matching returns an absolute pose in the map frame, which enters the factor graph as an absolute constraint on the state. GNSS RTK provides an absolute constraint as well. The two anchor the state to different references and differ in accuracy, so their fusion comes down to weighting one absolute constraint against the other, with their contributions depending on relative weighting and consistent frame alignment.

gnssFGO [ 30 ] , Beuchert et al. [ 46 ] , and LIGO [ 8 ] all adopt a hierarchical tightly-coupled design, optimizing a relative pose from a LiDAR-odometry front-end together with raw GNSS in a sliding-window graph, which avoids the absolute-constraint competition. gnssFGO uses a scan-to-scan front-end in a continuous-time formulation, Beuchert et al. use ICP scan-to-submap, and LIGO runs a Point-LIO [ 15 ] EKF front-end. In all of them the LiDAR registration is solved once and frozen into the resulting pose factor, and the back-end never relinearizes the raw point cloud. So when the scans are geometrically degenerate, or a moving object causes a wrong registration, the pose carries an error, yet it is passed to the back-end with an over-confident covariance; the GNSS observations that remain informative can no longer correct it, and the estimate either diverges or keeps an error it cannot recover from.

GLINS [ 34 ] uses a landmark-based tightly coupled formulation. Instead of registering against a fixed map, GLINS promotes stable planes from the LiDAR voxel map to explicit landmark states and jointly optimizes them with the poses, IMU biases, and raw GNSS RTK observations in a single sliding-window graph. Each scan therefore contributes a relative constraint, and the map co-evolves with the global GNSS correction. This joint refinement also creates a possible path for error propagation: if a GNSS bias that survives outlier rejection distorts the estimated landmark geometry, subsequent scan-to-landmark constraints can carry that distortion into later pose estimates.

GLIO [ 7 ] comes closest to our goal: a real-time (RT) S2M front-end feeds an offline back-end that fuses S2MS LiDAR with raw double-differenced PSR and DOP in a global batch optimization, yielding strong global consistency. But that consistency is obtained only offline. The S2MS batch still requires a non-divergent S2M front-end as its initial guess, so once the front-end diverges under sustained degeneracy the batch has nothing valid to refine; and because the back-end re-registers the point clouds, it is slow.

GLIO2 addresses these problems within a single tightly-coupled factor graph that fuses raw double-differenced pseudorange and Doppler with dense scan-to-multiscan LiDAR over one large sliding window. First, on the LiDAR side, GLIO2 retains voxel maps in individual keyframe frames without maintaining a fused, fixed world-frame reference map. It forms direct dense correspondences between the scans in the window and exposes them as relative constraints without introducing a fixed-map LiDAR pose prior. Second, because these correspondences and their residuals are re-associated and relinearized at every iteration, a registration error from geometric degeneracy or a moving object can be revised as the joint estimate updates while the associated scans remain active in the window. Third, GLIO2 builds on the GPU-accelerated scan-matching factors of GLIM [ 2 ] and extends dense LiDAR–inertial smoothing with raw GNSS factors and jointly estimated global-frame states, allowing the combined optimization to run online at the LiDAR rate.

2026-10-09.title: LeWAM: A JEPA World Action Model with Diffusion-Steering-Based MPC
2026-10-09.authors: Shashank Hegde , Alexander Popov , Elie Aljalbout , Nikolai Smolyanskiy
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-09.abstract:
World action models (WAMs) predict actions and future observations, typically from a reconstruction-based representation that carries noisy, redundant information which can complicate downstream predictions.
We introduce LeWAM, a bidirectional transformer for forward, backward, inverse dynamics and policy prediction, on a decoder-free JEPA latent trained end-to-end through all four modes.
We see the following benefits:
1) Alignment: linear probes read robot and object state from LeWAM’s latent better than from a regular Le World Model (a forward-only JEPA world model), while the latent ignores visual distractors as well as LeWM does and far better than a reconstruction-based WAM.
2) Acting: Closed-loop evaluations of LeWAM match a regular flow-matching policy trained on the same encoder at matched size, while also providing a world model.
3) Planning: Sampling raw actions when planning with WAMs lets MPC exploit dynamics-model inaccuracies; planning in the noise space of the policy head instead improves the closed-loop performance of these WAMs.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Robotic control increasingly relies on predictive models to anticipate environmental dynamics. Traditional world models learn a latent space through image reconstruction, subsequently training policies conditioned on these representations [ 12 , 13 ] .
A recent evolution of this paradigm, termed world action models (WAM), explicitly couples future-state prediction with action generation to ground control directly in learned dynamics [ 42 , 19 , 37 ] . While these generative approaches successfully integrate vision and action, they predominantly rely on pixel-level reconstruction to shape their underlying representations [ 42 ] . Consequently, their latent spaces are forced to encode every visual detail a decoder might render, regardless of its relevance to the task [ 42 ] . In visually complex environments, this architectural choice inherently wastes model capacity on noisy, task-irrelevant information, complicating downstream predictive tasks [ 39 , 33 ] .

To circumvent the limitations of reconstruction, alternative frameworks such as the joint-embedding predictive architecture model dynamics exclusively in latent space [ 20 , 3 , 5 ] . By discarding the pixel decoder entirely, these architectures inherently resist task-irrelevant appearance details [ 9 , 38 ] . Recent instantiations demonstrate stable, end-to-end training from pixels using regularization techniques that prevent representational collapse without relying on heuristics [ 24 , 4 ] . Despite these representational advantages, existing frameworks in this category typically separate the dynamics model from the policy, lacking the unified multi-modal structure found in modern WAMs [ 24 ] .

Bridging this gap, we propose LeWAM, a unified, reconstruction-free world action model. Building upon foundational decoder-free predictors, LeWAM introduces a bidirectional transformer capable of simultaneous forward dynamics, backward dynamics, inverse dynamics, and policy prediction [ 24 ] . The predictor is conditioned on actions, while the encoder is trained end-to-end directly from task pixels under a strict regularizer. Because the architecture eschews pixel decoders, tokenizers, and pixel-space losses, its representations are shaped entirely by the dual objectives of accurate dynamics prediction and robust action generation [ 22 , 23 ] .

Integrating a generative policy within a world model naturally invites test-time intervention through planning [ 18 , 36 ] . However, executing sampling-based model predictive control over raw actions often fails in practice [ 8 ] . When optimizing over action space, the planner tends to exploit inevitable inaccuracies within the learned dynamics model, leading to plans that optimize for hallucinated futures and subsequently fail during deployment [ 1 ] . To resolve this, we shift the decision variable of the sampling-based planner from the action space to the deterministic noise space of the flow-matching policy [ 34 , 32 , 29 ] . This diffusion steering approach searches strictly within the world model’s imagination, evaluating candidates decoded at imagined states [ 15 ] . By projecting proposals onto the sampler’s typical set, the search remains constrained to actions the policy head was explicitly trained to produce.

We evaluate our approach on human-generated demonstration datasets augmented with visual distractors [ 7 , 26 ] . Our investigation yields the following primary contributions:

Alignment: We demonstrate representational alignment; the latent space captures dynamic robot and object states as effectively as reconstruction-based baselines, while successfully ignoring visual distractors.

Acting: We validate robust acting capabilities; the integrated flow-matching policy matches the performance of standard behavioral cloning policies while simultaneously providing a world model for dynamics prediction.

Planning: We establish a stable planning paradigm; steering the generative process by sampling within the policy’s noise space prevents the exploitation of dynamics errors and significantly improves closed-loop performance during inference [ 31 , 35 , 17 ] .

1. Alignment: We demonstrate representational alignment; the latent space captures dynamic robot and object states as effectively as reconstruction-based baselines, while successfully ignoring visual distractors.

2. Acting: We validate robust acting capabilities; the integrated flow-matching policy matches the performance of standard behavioral cloning policies while simultaneously providing a world model for dynamics prediction.

3. Planning: We establish a stable planning paradigm; steering the generative process by sampling within the policy’s noise space prevents the exploitation of dynamics errors and significantly improves closed-loop performance during inference [ 31 , 35 , 17 ] .

# 2 Related work

World Models such as Dreamer [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] learn a recurrent latent space primarily via reconstruction and then train policies conditioned on latents in this space.
The main shortcoming of reconstruction-based world modeling is in the capacity wasted on noisy and task-irrelevant information.
Many approaches have been proposed to address this problem.
For instance, DreamerPro and bisimulation methods [ 9 , 38 ] drop the decoder to resist task-irrelevant appearance [ 39 , 33 ] .
TD-MPC2 [ 16 , 15 ] plans by MPPI over a decoder-free latent and value.
JEPA world models [ 40 , 5 , 2 ] plan by CEM-MPC on a goal-latent distance, and LeWM [ 24 ] trains its encoder end-to-end under SIGReg [ 4 ] . LeWAM adds the action head and multi-mode skeleton to LeWM’s latent. We present a clear comparison to these methods in Table 1 . Note that the head on LeWM’s frozen latent we present in our experiments is our control, not an intrinsic part of LeWM.

One recent trend in robotics is to couple future-state prediction with action generation, grounding robot control in learned dynamics in an architecture referred to as world action models.
Dreamitate adapts a video generator to task-specific human demonstrations and tracks tools in its predictions to obtain executable trajectories [ 21 ] .
Unified World Models (UWM) makes this connection explicit through independently controlled video and action diffusion, allowing one model to serve as a policy, forward model, or inverse model [ 42 ] .
Other methods such as DreamZero exploit pretrained video priors to generalize to unseen tasks and motions [ 37 ] .
How such priors guide action varies, for instance, Cosmos Policy incorporates actions, future states, and values into the video model’s native diffusion process, enabling both control and planning [ 19 ] .

Frozen diffusion and flow-matching policies [ 7 , 22 , 23 , 6 ] offer several points of intervention for test-time control.
Guidance steers the sampling process itself [ 18 ] , whereas candidate ranking selects among policy samples using a learned value [ 27 , 19 ] or world-model rollouts [ 41 , 30 ] .
Rather than merely selecting a proposal, MPC can refine it through MPPI in action space, potentially leaving the policy’s support [ 1 , 14 ] , while Diffusion-ES alternates simulator-based scoring with re-noising and denoising [ 36 ] .
A different route is to optimize the noise that generates the action.
DSRL learns a policy over this noise through environment interaction, without a world model or planning [ 34 , 32 ] .
Golden Ticket instead searches offline with CEM, using real task-reward rollouts to find one task-specific noise vector that is reused at every step [ 29 ] . DS builds on this formulation rather than introducing a new optimizer: both its decision variable and DS-CEM’s update match Golden Ticket’s.
The distinction lies in when and where search happens, and how candidates are evaluated.
At every decision, DS searches within world-model imagination, decoding action chunks at imagined states and scoring them by goal-latent distance, without search-time environment interaction or a learned value function.
This formulation accommodates different sampling-based updates such as CEM [ 31 , 8 ] , MPPI [ 35 ] , and CMA-ES [ 17 ] .

2026-10-09.title: A Physics-Informed Collision Learning Framework for Collaborative Robot Motion Generation
2026-10-09.authors: Chen Cai , Steven Liu
2026-10-09.abstract:
Close-proximity multi-arm manipulation requires collision models that are both geometrically accurate and differentiable enough for real-time optimization. Classical geometry checkers provide reliable distances but are difficult to use inside gradient-based model predictive control, while conservative proxy models can restrict tightly coupled motion. We present PI-UDF, a physics-informed unified differentiable framework for body-to-body collision distance prediction between articulated robots. PI-UDF combines analytical forward kinematics with learnable link-geometry embeddings and a shared residual network to predict pairwise inter-arm distances directly from robot configurations. To improve safety-critical fidelity, we combine
quota-driven boundary mining with an asymmetric
boundary-crossing penalty that emphasizes false-safe sign
errors near the collision boundary. The learned distance field is integrated into nonlinear MPC as a differentiable inter-arm clearance term. We validate the framework on a real dual-Franka platform through high-speed close-proximity 14-DoF dual-arm swapping, sustained single-arm dynamic evasion, and dynamic-evasion planning configurations with frozen, predicted, and target-switching treatments of the moving arm. Hardware experiments and offline Drake/FCL replay show that PI-UDF provides a differentiable inter-arm clearance estimate suitable for closed-loop collision-aware collaborative robot motion generation.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Close-proximity multi-arm manipulation requires multiple robots to move through tight shared workspaces while maintaining continuous inter-arm clearance. Classical
mesh-based checkers such as FCL [ 1 ] provide
reliable geometry queries for offline validation, but their
discrete and non-smooth computations are difficult to embed in gradient-based model predictive control. Real-time
controllers often replace full geometry with
simplified convex proxies; for example, distributed MPC can
approximate robot links by line segments and ellipsoids [ 2 ] . These proxies reduce computation,
but their inflated clearances can restrict tightly coupled
motion and cause deadlock-like behavior in dense
workspaces [ 3 ] .

Signed distance fields provide a continuous clearance signal
and gradients that are useful for optimization-based collision
avoidance. Neural SDF variants extend this idea to robot
configuration spaces; for example, Neural-JSDF uses MLPs
for joint-space distance fields [ 4 ] , while
Bernstein-polynomial representations improve storage
efficiency [ 5 ] . However, most such
formulations remain centered on point-to-robot queries rather
than direct body-to-body clearance between two moving
articulated arms.

For multi-arm planning, treating one moving arm as a set of
query points for the other arm requires dense online point
sampling or proxy-shape approximations. Both choices scale
poorly with link complexity and weaken the geometry signal
available to a closed-loop optimizer. What is needed is a
compact, differentiable body-to-body distance model that
reasons directly over robot configurations.

PairwiseNet [ 6 ] is an important step
toward direct link-pair distance learning. It decomposes the
global collision problem into pairwise subproblems and
conditions a shared regressor on pairwise relative transforms
and point-cloud-derived shape descriptors, thereby avoiding
dense online point sampling during planning. Our framework builds
on this established pairwise relative-pose factorization and
focuses its contribution on the co-design of geometry
representation, boundary-focused supervision, and
differentiable integration into downstream motion generation.

Boundary-focused data acquisition has also been studied for
high-DoF collision-distance learning. Kim and
Park [ 7 ] iteratively update a fixed-size
configuration dataset with samples near the current model’s
global collision boundary and use a redundant link- S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) n SE(3)^{n} representation to improve distance learning.
Their approach is model-in-the-loop: the learned collision
boundary guides subsequent data generation. In contrast,
our retained-set construction is driven by ground-truth
coverage deficits over link-pair classes and distance zones,
rather than by the boundary of an intermediate model.

Against this background, we propose the Physics-Informed
Unified Differentiable Framework (PI-UDF), a compact
framework for body-to-body collision distance learning
between articulated robots. PI-UDF provides a differentiable
collision-distance representation that can be queried by
downstream motion-generation modules; in this work, we
instantiate this interface within nonlinear MPC. The model
conditions a shared residual regressor on FK-derived relative
poses and task-optimized link embeddings learned end-to-end
from signed-distance supervision. PI-UDF further combines
pair-level boundary mining with an asymmetric
Boundary-Crossing Penalty that emphasizes false-safe
prediction errors.

2026-10-09.title: ARC: A Reasoning Recipe for Robot Foundation Models
2026-10-09.authors: Gokul Puthumanaillam , Tao Sun , Elie Aljalbout , Moritz Reuss , Zhaoshuo Li , Fabio Ramos , Ankit Goyal , Jenai Xuning Yang
2026-10-09.abstract:
The prevailing approach to improving robot foundation models (RFMs) relies on larger models, more robot demonstrations, and costly training at scale. We show that there exists an effective and efficient complementary approach: the right reasoning recipe can substantially improve the zero-shot task performance of existing state-of-the-art RFMs. We refer to this recipe as Arc . It consists of three key ingredients: a reasoning trace, a scalable automatic labeling pipeline, and a strategy for adapting pretrained RFMs to use these traces for control. First, we find that effective reasoning traces should be grounded in the robot’s next action and explain its causal structure: why the action is appropriate and what effect it should produce. Second, we show that these traces can be generated automatically from existing demonstrations, enabling us to construct Arc -Trace-DROID from DROID without collecting new robot data. Third, we show how state-of-the-art VLAs such as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and WAMs such as Cosmos3-Nano-Policy can learn to use these traces for control, with fine-tuning and inference tailored to each model’s architecture and capabilities.
Using Arc , we obtain gains in zero-shot RFM performance that, to our knowledge, are unprecedented without additional robot demonstrations or foundation-scale training. The adapted models establish a new state of the art on RoboLab-120 and MolmoSpaces, with gains of up to 50 percentage points on RoboLab-Reasoning-50. On real robots, Arc improves π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s task success by 82.2 percentage points. Project website: https://arc-robot-reasoning.github.io/
2026-10-09.introduction:
Robot foundation models (RFMs), trained by imitation on large demonstration datasets, have become broadly capable at manipulation ( Kim et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA, 2026 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ) . Yet the dominant recipe for making them better remains brute-force scaling, with more robot data, larger models, and another round of foundation-scale training. This makes every gain in task success expensive to obtain. How can we improve the performance of existing RFMs without modifying their architectures, adding new robot data, or training at the scale of foundation models?

In this work, we study this problem. Specifically, we find that adding or refining the reasoning capabilities of RFMs is an effective and efficient strategy for improving them. With the right recipe, reasoning can substantially improve the performance of existing state-of-the-art models such as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black et al., 2025a ) and Cosmos3-Nano-Policy ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) (Fig. 1 ). To our knowledge, this is the first work to achieve such substantial gains in zero-shot RFM performance through any strategy that does not require additional robot demonstrations or foundation-scale training. We call this reasoning recipe Arc .

In Arc , we bring together three pieces: the right reasoning content, a scalable source of supervision, and a training procedure that adapts the model to use that reasoning for control.
First, what should the reasoning contain? We find that reasoning for control should be causal, explaining why an action is appropriate in the current situation and what effect it should produce, as well as grounded in action, specifying the concrete step the robot should take to bring about that effect. We introduce action-grounded causal traces that connect what is true now to what the robot should do next and what should become true as a result.
Second, how do we obtain this supervision at scale? Robot demonstrations record observations and actions but typically omit the reasoning behind individual decisions. We present an approach for automatically labeling demonstrations with causal traces aligned to action chunks. We use it to construct Arc -Trace-DROID by relabeling DROID ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) .
And third, how do we adapt models to use this reasoning for control? We show that an RFM can be fine-tuned to condition its behavior on reasoning traces while retaining its existing control capabilities. We use the same reasoning traces and training data across models and show how to tailor the fine-tuning and inference procedures to each model’s architecture and capabilities.

We evaluate this recipe on two representative state-of-the-art RFMs: Cosmos3-Nano-Policy ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) , a world action model (WAM), and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black et al., 2025a ) , a vision-language-action model (VLA). We find that Arc improves both RFMs across all three settings on RoboLab-120, with the adapted models ranking first and second in each setting. On MolmoSpaces, task success improves by 27.2 and 18.6 percentage points (p.p.) for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and Cosmos3-Nano-Policy. These results establish a new state of the art on RoboLab-120 ( Yang et al., 2026 ) and MolmoSpaces ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . On the reasoning-focused RoboLab-Reasoning-50, Arc improves task success by 46.8 p.p. for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 50.0 p.p. for Cosmos3-Nano-Policy. Further, these improvements carry over to real world execution, where the Arc gains 82.2 p.p. on reasoning and long-horizon tasks. Across these evaluations, Arc -trained models more reliably follow underspecified instructions, infer missing steps, complete long-horizon tasks, adapt to changes, and recover from mistakes.

We further quantify how different components of the recipe contribute to performance. Our results show that adding intermediate language without the right structure provides limited improvement; larger gains arise from combining causal reasoning content with a training procedure that grounds it in action. As a side effect, the recipe also improves training and inference efficiency. Cosmos3-Nano-Policy reaches baseline success with 4.3 × 4.3\times fewer training updates, while π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and Cosmos3-Nano-Policy match their base policies at inference with 10 × 10\times and 2 × 2\times fewer denoising steps.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Robot foundation models. General-purpose robot policies have been developed by learning across tasks and embodiments ( Reed et al., 2022 ; Jang et al., 2022 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ; Bousmalis et al., 2023 ; O’Neill et al., 2024 ) and transferring pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge to action prediction ( Driess et al., 2023 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ) . Video-pretrained and world-action models additionally learn how the environment evolves during execution ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Cheang et al., 2024 ; Cen et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA, 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . Our work builds on these pretrained controllers and investigates how reasoning supervision can improve their performance using robot demonstrations already available.

Reasoning in foundation models. Reasoning allows pretrained models to work through intermediate decisions before producing a final answer ( Wei et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Prior work improves this process by considering alternative solutions ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Yao et al., 2023a ) , incorporating tools and feedback ( Yao et al., 2023b ) , and learning from intermediate supervision ( Zelikman et al., 2024 ; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025 ) . In robotics, these ideas have been used in two particularly relevant ways: to determine the steps a robot should execute, and to train a policy to reason about the actions it predicts. The first includes selecting available skills to accomplish an instruction ( Ahn et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2023b ) , generating programs that combine perception and control ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2022 ) , and revising plans using observations and execution feedback ( Huang et al., 2022 ; Zeng et al., 2022a ) . The second uses reasoning annotations to teach a policy which information matters for action prediction ( Zawalski et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . Both approaches allow robots to benefit from knowledge beyond their demonstrated motions, but require the controller to understand the guidance it receives. Recent work addresses this requirement through richer steering commands and visually grounded hierarchical control ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .

Reasoning modalities. There are several ways to express the intermediate decisions needed for robotic control. Spatial representations specify where an interaction should occur through image features, action maps, or voxel representations ( Zeng et al., 2022b ; Shridhar et al., 2021 ; Shridhar et al., 2023 ) , while keypoints and geometric constraints describe relationships that the robot should establish between objects ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2023a ; Huang et al., 2024 ) . Motion-based representations provide guidance through trajectory sketches and visual traces ( Gu et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ) . Predictive representations specify how the scene should evolve, using future predictions ( Du et al., 2023 ; Ko et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zhen et al., 2024 ) . These approaches give the controller an explicit spatial or temporal target. Their connection to control depends on the representation. Geometric constraints can be solved through motion optimization ( Huang et al., 2023a ; Huang et al., 2024 ) , depth and trajectory predictions can be encoded as intermediate tokens ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , and visual traces can be presented through the existing image input ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . While these methods demonstrate the value of structured guidance, our interest is in reasoning supervision that can be shared across RFMs without additional architecture changes.

Natural language offers this opportunity because it can describe task conditions, spatial relationships, and intended outcomes without committing to a particular set of robot coordinates. It is already supported by the pretrained tokenizers and language components of many robot foundation models ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025a ) , and its annotations can be generated from existing demonstrations ( Zawalski et al., 2024 ) .
Prior work uses natural language to describe fine-grained motions ( Belkhale et al., 2024 ) , convey the current semantic subtask ( Black et al., 2025a ) , and reason about plans, objects, and robot state before predicting actions ( Mu et al., 2023 ) . These methods show that language can provide useful intermediate supervision.
