2026-10-09.title: Embodied Turing Machines: Stateful Code for Robot Recursive Self-Improvement
2026-10-09.authors: Kairui Hu , Siyuan Hu , Fangzhou Hong , Zhaoxi Chen , Ziwei Liu
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-09.abstract:
Most robot policies keep a model in the control loop: a VLA maps
observations to actions, and an Agent Harness, such as Agent-as-Policy or Harness VLA queries a VLM for decision making
at run time. We propose a different view: the embodied world is an Embodied Turing Machine , whose tape is the robot and environment state and rules are the policy. If this state can be represented
accurately, the decision making can be written entirely in code. We therefore propose Code-Only-as-Policy (COAP) : code measures and tracks the robot,
environment, and task state from camera images and proprioception, and makes
every decision from it. The same code applies across episodes, and different tasks
share one library without a VLM or VLA in the loop. Compared with VLAs
and Agent Harnesses, we analyze three advantages of COAP: (i) Explicit State : the
state can be stored in code; (ii) Execution : code makes decision
making controllable, recovers from failures flexibly, and runs fast and cheaply
online; (iii) Extensibility : new tasks reuse, inherit, or extend the
shared library, so capabilities can accumulate over tasks. These advantages make COAP a suitable
medium for recursive self-improvement (RSI) : coding agents develop the
library in a closed loop, and each change is explicit and controllable. On
RoboDojo’s 42 bimanual tasks, the resulting library reaches a success
rate of 70.24% without a model at test time. The upper bound of COAP lies in how accurately the state
is represented for decision making and how robust the code logic is. We thus
propose COAP as a new paradigm for embodied tasks; since it applies across
episodes, it can also serve as an efficient data engine for VLAs and Agent
Harnesses.
2026-10-09.introduction:
“It is possible to invent a single machine which can be
used to compute any computable sequence.”

A Turing machine comprises a tape that stores symbols and a set of fixed rules
that read from and write to the tape [ 60 ] . With the
rules fixed and only the tape varying, the same rules can process arbitrary
inputs. The same abstraction applies to the physical world, where the world
state is analogous to the tape. A robot reads this tape through perception and
writes to it through action, and its policy plays the role of the rules. We
therefore model a robot and its environment as an Embodied Turing
Machine , whose tape holds two kinds of state: the environment state (e.g.,
object poses and their spatial relations) and the robot state (e.g., arm pose
and reachable poses).

Both kinds of state are accurately observable. The robot state is available
directly through proprioception, and object poses can be recovered from RGB
images using measured object geometry. A policy that acts
on this state gains two advantages. First, more accurate state enables more
precise action. Second, when objects are rearranged (like different episodes in a task), only the tape changes, and
the same rules (policy) still apply.

A policy can map state to action in three ways, which differ in how explicit
this mapping is. (i) Vision-language-action models (VLAs). A VLA
takes observations, such as camera images, as input and
learns the mapping to action, which remains implicit in its
weights [ 4 , 19 ] .
(ii) Agent harnesses. The vision-language model
(VLM) either controls the robot
directly, as in Agent-as-Policy, or directs a VLA, as in
Harness VLA [ 9 , 55 ] . The
harness makes part of the process explicit, such as textual memory, but the
VLM and VLA remain black boxes, so we may still neither fully inspect nor control how an action is derived.
(iii) Code-Only-as-Policy (ours). In contrast, code is a white box that implements the Embodied Turing Machine
directly: the state, such as object poses, is stored in code variables, where
it remains accurate, persistent, and explicit; the rules are written as code
logic that computes each action from this state. With both the state and the
rules explicit, no model is required at runtime: the code is frozen and serves as
the sole policy during execution. Code thus becomes a universal interface to the
physical world : a single code program takes over the roles of the VLAs, the prompts and skills of Agent-as-Policy, and the memory of Harness VLA.

Existing code-based policies either (i) ask a model to write new code-as-policy online
in each episode of a task [ 21 , 59 , 62 ] ,
or (ii) take the state from a model or the simulator’s
oracle [ 11 , 39 ] (Figure 2 ). COAP instead measures the state with its own
code and builds a shared code library for perception and execution. Different
tasks run the same library code, and only a small part of the logic is
task-specific: 83% of the code that a new task runs comes from the library.
Nor is the code written for a particular episode: one program runs on every
episode of a task. Because the task is fixed, code that is robust enough needs
no VLM or VLA in the loop; if it still needs one, the code is not yet robust
enough to run reliably across episodes.

Code-Only-as-Policy has three advantages (§ 4.3 ).
(i) Explicit State : the state is stored in code variables, and every
decision is made from them (§ 4.3.1 ). (ii) Execution :
the code gives fine-grained control over the state and actions, recovers from
failures flexibly by backtracking and re-attempting, and runs fast and cheaply
online (§ 4.3.2 ). (iii) Extensibility : a new task reuses,
inherits, or extends the shared library, so the code evolves quickly and
capabilities accumulate (§ 4.3.3 ). Hence, COAP is a suitable medium for stable recursive
self-improvement (RSI) (§ 4.4 ). Since the code is not specific to any
episode, one policy runs on different episodes and can generate successful
trajectories efficiently for VLAs and Agent Harnesses
(§ 5.5 ).

We evaluate COAP on RoboDojo’s 42 bimanual tasks [ 7 ] . A coding agent (Opus 5.5 Max) develop the code
library in a closed RSI loop that we design: under fixed rules, such as no hack
for single episodes and no oracle state at test time, the coding agent summarizes, writes,
and debugs the code without human in the loop. The development does not involve test set of a benchmark. The resulting COAP policy reaches 70.24% success rate, 38.9% above the state-of-the-art method. The upper bound of COAP can be pushed further if the state representation gets more accurate and code logic grows more robust.

The weakness of COAP mainly lies in its generalization capabilities since it
needs a small amount of task-specific code logic. However, Agent-as-Policy and Harness VLA also involve
task-level memories, and some even rely on episode-level logic.
In this work, our aim is to explore the upper bound of Code-Only-as-Policy for the community.
Moreover, COAP also generates successful trajectories stably and efficiently, which can
benefit the development of VLAs and Agent Harnesses (§ 5.5 ). Our contributions are:

Code-Only-as-Policy. We view the embodied world as a Turing
machine in which the robot and environment state can be
represented explicitly.
The same code applies to different episodes, and different tasks use a shared library developed offline by coding agent.

Advantages of Code-Only-as-Policy. We analyze three
advantages of code over VLAs and Agent Harnesses: Explicit State , Execution , and Extensibility . We explore code-only as a new paradigm for embodied task: when the code is robust enough and applies across episodes, no VLM or VLA
is required during runtime.

Code as the medium of RSI. Code iterates efficiently,
and each change is controllable. Code-Only-as-Policy can also serve as an efficient data engine to
produce beneficial trajectories as new training data for VLAs, Agent-as-Policy, etc.

The same code applies to different episodes, and different tasks use a shared library developed offline by coding agent.

2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Existing robot policies built with foundation models differ in where they keep the
state and how they choose each action from it (Table 1 ): a VLA
encodes the state implicitly in its weights, and an Agent Harness
(Agent-as-Policy or Harness VLA) stores it as text in a model’s context.

RT-2, OpenVLA, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} learn language-conditioned visuomotor
policies end to end [ 5 , 19 , 4 , 36 ] ,
and recent foundation models scale data and training further [ 48 , 18 ] . A VLA cannot be inspected
or edited directly, so each improvement requires new data and a new training
run, and LIBERO-PRO shows that benchmark success can reflect memorized
training configurations [ 58 ] . In comparison, we keep the state in code
variables, so we can backtrack from a failure to the
variable that caused it and fix the code logic that derived it. Each accepted fix
is merged into the code without breaking existing logic, so improvements accumulate , while training a
VLA on a new task can degrade its performance on earlier tasks [ 61 ] .

ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions [ 53 ] , and Toolformer
teaches a model to call tools [ 38 ] . In robotics,
SayCan grounds language-model plans in learned affordances [ 1 ] , and Inner Monologue feeds environment feedback back to
the planner [ 16 ] . Recent harnesses let a VLM agent call
analytic or learned primitives [ 9 , 55 ] ,
and GPT-6 Astra [ 34 ] has been evaluated directly as an
embodied policy [ 43 , 56 ] . In these systems, the model is queried repeatedly during execution to output actions, so there is randomness at each call, even if the prompt is the same. Moreover, every episode is of high cost due to extensive
model calls [ 35 ] . In our approach, models are used only
offline: coding agents write the code, and the robot runs it without a
model during online execution. The code computes each action from the state
through explicit rules, so the robot’s behaviour is reproducible ,
and each decision is cheap because model calls are not required.

Code-based policies differ in when the program is written and in the source
of the state used (Figure 2 ). Code-as-Policies and
ProgPrompt prompt a language model to write code that calls perception and
control APIs [ 21 , 41 ] , and VoxPoser writes code that
composes spatial value maps [ 17 ] . Later works add
execution feedback, repeated generation, and skill discovery [ 12 , 30 , 26 ] . PyRUA-Lean has a model
write code cell by cell as each episode runs [ 59 ] , and
Skill2Real has a model compose a new program from frozen skill memories at
each decision stage [ 62 ] . In these systems, a model writes
the program at runtime, and the state is provided by learned perception
models:
object detectors in Code as Policies, and SAM in PyRUA-Lean and Skill2Real. In RHO and
EmbodiedSWE, coding agents write one program offline, but its state still
comes from outside the code: RHO likewise obtains it from SAM and Molmo [ 11 , 6 ] , and the solvers of EmbodiedSWE read
the simulator’s oracle values [ 39 ] . These perception
models are black boxes, and their uncertainty are not controlled by the code. In contrast, our code tracks the state
itself, so the state is programmable : when a measurement is wrong,
coding agents fix the measurement code, and the state becomes more
accurate over time .

Outside robotics, code has become the medium through which agents act and
improve. CodeAct uses executable code as the action space of an agent [ 46 ] , and exposing tools as a code API lets a model compose
them with fewer tokens [ 2 , 44 ] . Voyager grows
a library of code skills through interaction [ 45 ] , and
software agents solve long-horizon repository tasks through tests and diffs [ 50 , 33 ] . In these settings, the environment
provides the state explicitly, as files, test results, or game API values. A
robot, in contrast, must measure its state from sensors, and our code performs
this measurement itself. In robotics, RoboRSI runs RSI as a loop of manager,
planner, engineer, and reviewer agents with a no-regression gate, but a VLM
still makes the decisions during execution [ 32 ] . A
change that passes the gate only steers this black box, whose uncertainty and
errors cannot be fully controlled, so the tested behaviour may not be the
behaviour at runtime. Our policy is code with explicit state, so the tested
behaviour is the behaviour at runtime, and coding agents can improve it the way
software engineers improve a program: every change is tested offline ,
and only changes that improve results without regressions on other
tasks are merged .

LIBERO measures knowledge transfer in lifelong robot learning [ 24 ] , RoboTwin 2.0 generates domain-randomized bimanual tasks [ 8 ] , and RoboCasa365 scales household simulation [ 31 ] . RoboDojo spans memory, precision, open
instructions, generalization, and long-horizon manipulation in one protocol [ 7 ] . Its memory and precision tasks directly test how
well a policy retains and measures state, and the shared protocol lets us compare
VLAs, world models, agents, and code on the same 42 tasks.

2026-10-09.title: LiteNWM: Efficient Latent World Models for Onboard Visual Navigation in the Wild
2026-10-09.authors: Linkai Liu , Yuntian Zhang , Zhenshan Bing , Chen Chen , Lingjuan Lyu , Shangguang Wang , Mengwei Xu , Dongqi Cai
2026-10-09.abstract:
Direct visual navigation policies generate trajectories efficiently but do not explicitly evaluate their future consequences.
Generative navigation world models provide this foresight through visual rollouts, which are costly when evaluating multiple candidates.
We present LiteNWM, a latent navigation world model that shares visual encoding across candidates and jointly predicts their action-conditioned future representations at multiple horizons and a learned scorer uses these predictions to select trajectories.
In offline evaluations on RECON, SCAND, and SACSoN, LiteNWM reduces macro-averaged trajectory error by 17.56% relative to NoMaD+NWM-XL and achieves a 128.00 × \times end-to-end speedup on an RTX 5090.
The same evaluator transfers from NoMaD to MBRA without proposer-specific retraining, reducing MBRA’s macro-averaged trajectory error by 16.2%.
In real-robot experiments in unseen indoor and outdoor environments, LiteNWM improves navigation success from 43.3% to 83.3% relative to NoMaD.
These results demonstrate that LiteNWM can be deployed for future-aware planning and closed-loop navigation on a physical robot.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Goal-conditioned visual navigation enables a robot to reach a visually specified target using egocentric observations [ 1 ] .
Recent generalist navigation policies, such as GNM, ViNT, and NoMaD, learn navigation from large and diverse robot datasets [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
Diffusion-based policies can further generate multiple plausible trajectories for each observation.
However, these policies select trajectories without explicitly evaluating their future consequences, which can lead to suboptimal decisions in challenging environments.

As illustrated in Fig. , Navigation World Models (NWM) address this limitation through future-aware trajectory selection [ 5 ] .
Given multiple trajectories proposed by a navigation policy, NWM predicts future visual observations conditioned on each candidate and selects the trajectory based on its predicted outcome.

In our component profile with prediction horizon H = 4 H=4 and K = 16 K=16 candidate trajectories, candidate-conditioned RGB rollout accounts for 97.6% of the captured NoMaD+NWM-XL computation (Fig. 3 ). Its end-to-end wall time is 221.97 s per decision state (Sec. IV-E ), motivating a less expensive evaluation path.

We present LiteNWM, a navigation trajectory evaluator designed around the rollout bottleneck identified above.
Action-conditioned latent prediction already supports navigation without RGB reconstruction.
LiteNWM targets candidate-wise rollout cost through shared visual encoding and joint H1–H4 prediction across candidates. A learned incumbent-relative scorer uses the predicted consequences and proposal-set context to guide trajectory selection. This design combines an efficient prediction path with relative outcome evaluation while keeping the navigation policies frozen.

We evaluate LiteNWM on development cohorts from three navigation datasets and examine its deployment on a physical robot.
LiteNWM improves trajectory accuracy while achieving 128.00 × \times and 16.86 × \times end-to-end speedups over NoMaD+NWM-XL and NoMaD+NWM-S, respectively, on an RTX 5090 (Fig. (d)).
The frozen evaluator also transfers to MBRA without proposer-specific retraining.
Ablations attribute the accuracy gain to dynamic multi-horizon latent prediction.
LiteNWM supports closed-loop navigation on a Unitree Go2 EDU in unseen environments.
Our main contributions are:

We identify candidate-wise RGB rollout as the dominant evaluation cost and restructure the evaluation path around shared encoding and joint candidate-future prediction.

We combine pose-conditioned prediction with incumbent-relative scoring to compare candidate consequences using proposal-set context.

We validate accuracy and end-to-end efficiency on matched initial proposal pools, achieving a 128.00 × \times speedup over NoMaD+NWM-XL on an RTX 5090, and demonstrate cross-proposer transfer and real-robot deployment.

1. We identify candidate-wise RGB rollout as the dominant evaluation cost and restructure the evaluation path around shared encoding and joint candidate-future prediction.

2. We combine pose-conditioned prediction with incumbent-relative scoring to compare candidate consequences using proposal-set context.

3. We validate accuracy and end-to-end efficiency on matched initial proposal pools, achieving a 128.00 × \times speedup over NoMaD+NWM-XL on an RTX 5090, and demonstrate cross-proposer transfer and real-robot deployment.

# II Related Work

## II-A Generalist Navigation Policies and Trajectory Selection

Learning-based visual navigation has increasingly shifted toward policies trained on heterogeneous robot experience.
GNM introduced a shared goal-conditioned formulation across robot
platforms [ 2 ] , while ViNT scaled this direction with a Transformer trained on diverse navigation data [ 3 ] .
NoMaD further combines goal masking with a diffusion decoder to represent multimodal navigation behaviors [ 4 , 18 ] .
Proposal generation and trajectory selection become distinct operations when multiple stochastic trajectories are exposed at inference.
NavDP couples diffusion-based trajectory generation with a learned critic for selection [ 6 ] , while ViLiNT ranks generated trajectories using an embodiment-conditioned path-clearance predictor [ 7 ] .
LiteNWM keeps trajectory generation fixed and focuses on evaluating the resulting proposals using predicted future evidence.

## II-B Generative World Models for Navigation

Visual world models provide such evidence by predicting observations along candidate action sequences.
Pathdreamer generates unobserved panoramic views for look-ahead planning in indoor navigation [ 8 ] .
Moreover, NWM predicts future RGB observations conditioned on candidate actions and uses the synthesized futures both for standalone planning and for ranking trajectories sampled from an external policy [ 5 ] .
NWM therefore establishes that future-conditioned trajectory reranking and a modular proposer–evaluator interface are prior art.
The question narrows to whether short-horizon trajectory candidates can instead be compared directly from action-conditioned future latent features rather than reconstructing an RGB future for every candidate.

## II-C Latent Predictive and World–Action Models

Latent world models provide an alternative by supporting decision making directly through learned predictive representations.
Such explicit visual generation also introduces computation that is not directly required by the downstream ranking objective, which is well established by previous work: PlaNet performs online planning in learned latent dynamics [ 9 ] , while TD-MPC2 optimizes trajectories using a decoder-free implicit world model [ 10 ] .

More recently, DINO-WM predicts action-conditioned DINOv2 patch features for test-time action optimization [ 12 ] , V-JEPA 2-AC enables model-predictive control through action-conditioned latent prediction [ 19 , 11 ] , and DINO-world extends feature-space prediction to a generalist video model that can be adapted to observation–action trajectories [ 13 ] .
DF 3 further demonstrates decoder-free feature forecasting, though its current formulation is observation-only and cannot model the consequences of alternative actions [ 14 ] .
ReL-NWM avoids RGB reconstruction through latent-space planning [ 15 ] , but retains sequential autoregressive rollouts.
LiteNWM targets rollout latency through shared visual encoding and joint multi-horizon prediction, eliminating autoregressive feedback across prediction horizons.

In contrast, WAM-Nav and NavWAM take a different direction by coupling visual foresight with action generation inside unified world–action policies [ 16 , 17 ] .
LiteNWM addresses a narrower question: whether action-conditioned latent prediction provides sufficient predictive evidence to distinguish among trajectory proposals from a frozen navigation policy.

2026-10-09.title: PLaW-VLA: Predictive Latent World Modeling for Vision-Language-Action Policies
2026-10-09.authors: Yu Liu , Hetian Guo , Tianlv Huang , Ziyi Cai , Wudi Chen , Hantang Wang , Qiutong Liu , Yingzhi Peng , Wei Han , Peijun Tang , Jianan Wang , Zipei Fan , Zhiyuan Zha , Xuan Song
2026-10-09.comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
2026-10-09.abstract: Learning to predict how the world evolves can provide vision-language-action (VLA) policies with predictive context for long-horizon control, but its effectiveness depends on what future representation is modeled and how it conditions action generation. We introduce PLaW-VLA, which models task-relevant future states in a pretrained prediction-oriented representation space, reducing the need to predict control-irrelevant visual details. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, PLaW-VLA conditions action generation on observation history, current task semantics, and predicted future states through structured causal attention. Experiments show a + 11.8 +11.8 percentage-point (pp) gain over reactive policies on RoboTwin Hard Horizon III and a + 1.77 +1.77 pp gain over reconstruction-oriented latent prediction on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, supporting improved long-horizon control and generalization under distribution shift, respectively. By avoiding low-level visual reconstruction, PLaW-VLA lowers the burden of future prediction, enabling a lightweight latent world model with parallel future prediction and about 1 / 19 1/19 the inference latency of generative world–action modeling at comparable policy performance.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision-language representations to language-conditioned robot manipulation [ 33 , 4 , 17 , 52 , 29 , 16 ] . Long-horizon manipulation requires not only interpreting the current scene but also tracking how the task evolves across successive interactions. Under partial observability and execution perturbations, the current observation alone may be insufficient to infer the underlying task state. Effective long-horizon control therefore benefits from both modeling temporal context from observation history and anticipating future state evolution for action generation.

Recent studies incorporate predictive representations and future modeling into VLA through future-representation alignment [ 49 , 39 ] , visual feature fusion [ 27 ] , future-conditioned action generation [ 7 , 26 , 31 ] , and joint world–action modeling [ 51 , 36 , 44 , 3 , 8 , 9 ] . This raises two key questions for control: what future representation should be predicted, and how should it condition action generation? Existing predictive targets derived from visual reconstruction or generation require modeling both task dynamics and appearance variations, even when the latter are irrelevant to control. This increases the prediction burden, while errors in these irrelevant components may propagate to action generation when the predicted future directly conditions the policy.

We propose PLaW-VLA (Fig. 1 ), a VLA framework that integrates predictive latent world modeling with action generation. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, PLaW-VLA combines observation history, current task semantics, and predicted future latent states to generate continuous robot actions. The framework is designed around two key choices in future modeling for control. First, PLaW-VLA predicts task-relevant future latent states in a pretrained prediction-oriented representation space, emphasizing state transitions and interaction dynamics rather than low-level visual reconstruction. Second, these predicted future states directly condition the action model through structured causal attention, providing explicit predictive context for action generation.

PLaW-VLA follows a three-stage video-to-robot training pipeline. Stage I pretrains the latent world model on human and robot videos without action supervision, learning to predict visual dynamics in the representation space defined by the frozen encoder. Stage II transfers these representations to robot control by introducing action-annotated robot trajectories and jointly optimizing future-state prediction and action generation, thereby aligning predictive dynamics with action-relevant behavior. Stage III further adapts the resulting policy to the target task and robot embodiment. This training paradigm enables predictive knowledge acquired from large-scale videos to be reused for robot policy learning, providing a scalable path from generic visual dynamics to task-specific control.

We evaluate PLaW-VLA on three simulation benchmarks and diverse real-world manipulation tasks. It outperforms π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} by 11.8 percentage points on RoboTwin Hard Horizon III and achieves 72.7% task-weighted success on zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, supporting long-horizon control and generalization under distribution shift. By modeling future dynamics in latent space rather than reconstructing low-level visual content, PLaW-VLA reduces the complexity of future prediction and enables a compact latent world model with parallel prediction, providing an effective trade-off between policy performance and inference efficiency.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

VLA models transfer pretrained visual and language representations to robot policies [ 52 , 30 , 17 , 4 , 33 , 29 ] . Continuous action prediction [ 16 , 22 ] , flow-based decoding [ 4 , 33 ] , and action tokenization [ 32 ] provide different interfaces between multimodal representations and robot actions. Complementary approaches augment policy context with memory [ 37 ] , spatial representations [ 34 ] , and hierarchical task reasoning [ 46 , 14 ] . PLaW-VLA complements these directions by augmenting the policy with predicted future visual representations as additional context for action generation.

World models have been increasingly incorporated into robot control by predicting future observations, latent states, or joint video-action trajectories. Visual-imagination approaches generate future images or videos and recover actions through inverse dynamics [ 11 , 18 , 41 , 50 ] . More recent methods jointly model future observations and actions through autoregressive formulations [ 9 , 8 , 21 ] or video-action generative architectures [ 51 , 36 , 7 , 26 , 44 ] . Motus [ 3 ] unifies understanding, video generation, and action prediction within a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, while mimic-video [ 31 ] conditions action generation on partially denoised video latents. These methods demonstrate the utility of future prediction for control, but most predictive targets are derived from observation reconstruction or generation objectives. In contrast, PLaW-VLA predicts future features in the space defined by a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder [ 1 ] , using a prediction-trained representation space rather than a reconstruction-oriented target space.

Predictive representation learning provides an alternative to explicit observation generation by learning latent features that capture temporal structure. FLARE [ 49 ] aligns diffusion-policy features with embeddings of future observations, while VLA-JEPA [ 39 ] learns latent action representations through future V-JEPA 2 feature prediction. JEPA-VLA [ 27 ] incorporates V-JEPA 2 visual representations into existing VLAs through feature fusion. These methods differ primarily in how predictive representations interact with policy learning: as auxiliary supervision, latent action representations, or visual features. PLaW-VLA instead predicts future representations from observation history and uses the predicted future state directly to condition action generation. It therefore combines a prediction-trained target space with explicit future-state conditioning for policy learning.

2026-10-09.title: Toward Lunar Legged Robots: Field Deployment Lessons at LUNA
2026-10-09.authors: Adrian Fuhrer , Joseph Church , Oliver Fischer , William Talbot , Nicolas Faesch , Yannic Hofmann , Hendrik Kolvenbach , Yusuke Tanaka , Marco Hutter
2026-10-09.comment: Proceeding to the IEEE iSparo Conference 2026
2026-10-09.abstract: Legged robots are promising candidates for future lunar surface missions because they can traverse steep, loose, and obstacle-rich terrain that challenges conventional wheeled rovers. However, readiness for lunar deployment is limited by uncertainties in foot-regolith interaction, dust generation, illumination-driven perception degradation, and operational constraints. This paper reports lessons from the 2025 LUNA analogue campaign, where ANYmal-D and Magnecko traversed loose regolith simulant and crater-like terrain and collected long-horizon navigation and visual-inertial data under challenging lighting. We show that quadrupedal robots can traverse regolith simulant, but performance is affected by sinkage and slip, dust-generating contacts, and perception failures caused by overexposure, shadows, and low-texture regions. These results motivate tighter integration of regolith-aware locomotion policies, illumination-robust perception, repeatable analogue testing, and mission-level operational validation for future lunar legged robots.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Planetary exploration is entering a renewed phase of activity [ 1 ] , with increasing interest in sustained surface operations [ 2 ] , infrastructure construction [ 3 , 4 ] , and scientific access to challenging terrain [ 5 ] . While wheeled rovers remain central to planetary mobility, their traversability is limited in steep, loose, or obstacle-rich terrain [ 6 ] . This limitation is particularly relevant on the Moon, where loose regolith and difficult-to-access regions motivate alternative mobility systems [ 6 , 5 ] .

Legged robots are increasingly being considered for future lunar surface operations [ 7 ] because they can actively adapt contacts, step over obstacles, and traverse terrain that may be inaccessible to wheeled platforms [ 8 , 5 , 9 ] . However, despite recent progress in agile locomotion, perception, and navigation for terrestrial quadrupeds, a gap remains in understanding which improvements are critical for deployment on the Moon. In particular, open questions remain in how learning-based locomotion policies should account for regolith interaction, how foot designs could affect traction, sinkage, and dust generation, and how perception and navigation stacks should handle low-texture terrain, strong shadows, and changing illumination.

Analogue testing provides an important intermediate step toward addressing these questions. Lunar analogue testing campaigns allow robotic systems to be evaluated under more realistic terrain, operational, and integration constraints than typical laboratory settings [ 3 , 10 ] . Such campaigns are especially valuable for identifying not only locomotion limitations, but also system-level bottlenecks involving terrain interaction, perception, navigation, and deployment logistics.

This paper reports system-level deployment lessons from operating two quadrupedal robots, ANYmal-D 1 1 1 https://www.anybotics.com/robotics/anymal/ and Magnecko [ 11 ] , in the ESA/DLR LUNA lunar analogue facility [ 12 ] . The testing campaign was conducted in 2025 and identifies practical gaps that emerge when legged robotic systems are operated on lunar-regolith simulant under facility-scale terrain, lighting, sensing, and operational constraints. These observations provide insight into how regolith interaction, dust generation, illumination-dependent perception, and field logistics affect the readiness of legged robots for future lunar surface missions.

The main contributions of this paper are:

field deployment observations from two quadrupedal robots operating in the LUNA lunar analogue facility.

analysis of key system-level challenges in regolith locomotion, perception, dust exposure, and field operations.

lessons and design implications for future lunar legged robots and repeatable analogue testing.

1. field deployment observations from two quadrupedal robots operating in the LUNA lunar analogue facility.

2. analysis of key system-level challenges in regolith locomotion, perception, dust exposure, and field operations.

3. lessons and design implications for future lunar legged robots and repeatable analogue testing.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Background and Campaign Context

Legged robots have been investigated for space and planetary exploration because they have the potential to traverse steep [ 8 , 9 ] , irregular, and discontinuous terrain [ 13 ] that is difficult for conventional wheeled rovers. Legged and limbed systems have demonstrated walking, hopping [ 14 , 15 ] , climbing [ 13 , 16 ] , and contact-rich mobility [ 17 , 3 ] for planetary scenarios.

Recent progress in agile and learning-based legged locomotion has further improved the robustness of quadrupedal robots in complex terrestrial environments [ 18 ] . However, for lunar applications, these controllers must also address reduced gravity [ 19 ] , limited power and thermal budgets, and interaction with loose regolith. Learning-based locomotion policies are still trained with simplified contact models [ 20 ] , leaving gaps in understanding their behavior on granular terrain and dust generation.

Lunar analogue campaigns bridge simulation, lab testing, and mission deployment [ 10 ] , revealing system-level issues in locomotion, perception, navigation, communication, and operations [ 21 , 22 ] . Key questions remain on regolith interaction for RL policies, foot design trade-offs, and perception in low-texture, high-contrast, changing illumination. The LUNA testing campaign addressed these gaps using ANYmal-D and Magnecko in a controlled lunar analogue facility.

2026-10-09.title: Walking on Roofs: Exploring the Potential of Walking Robots for Construction Work on Roofs
2026-10-09.authors: Bjoern-Felix Dettmar , Arne Roennau
2026-10-09.comment: Preprint of paper which appeared in the Proceedings of CLAWAR 2026, 29th International Conference on Climbing and Walking Robots and the Support Technologies for Mobile Machines, Cranfield University, Cranfield, Beford, United Kingdome, 2026
2026-10-09.abstract: This paper investigates the feasibility of deploying quadruped walking robots for the automation of work in roof environments. While quadrupeds have demonstrated versatility across various domains, their large-scale deployment remains limited, partly due to lack of application-specific designs. Roof environments represent a novel and unexplored use case, combining high safety risks for human workers with repetitive, strenuous tasks that could benefit from robotic assistance. A dedicated test rig of a roof’s surface was designed to evaluate the baseline performance of a commercial quadruped, the Unitree Go2 , in this new environment. Experiments revealed that standard ball feet are inherently inadequate for locomotion on sloped roofs: slippage increased quadratically with incline angle, get-up and lie-down sequences were only possible on small inclines, and critical failures already occurred regularly on moderate inclines of 25 ° 25\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} . This work provides the first systematic assessment of quadruped locomotion in roof environments, highlighting both the potential and the current limitations of this application and establishes a baseline for future research. Effective solutions will require a combination of task-oriented foot designs, advanced contact mechanics and environment-specific control strategies, such as reinforcement learning for roof-adapted gaits.
2026-10-09.introduction:
The construction industry is among the least automated sectors with respect to robotics, despite its substantial economic relevance Haghsheno et al. (2024) . Within this domain, work on roofs represents a particularly hazardous area. Tasks such as construction, maintenance, installation, and inspection expose workers to significant risks, with slipping and falling accidents constituting a major cause of fatalities Health and Safety Executive (2020) . At the same time, many tasks on roofs are physically demanding and repetitive, providing a strong motivation to explore robotic assistance. In Germany alone, the roofing industry employed over 99,000 workers across more than 13,500 companies in 2023, generating a sales volume of nearly 12.9 billion euros Zentralverband des Deutschen Dachdeckerhandwerks (2023) . This highlights both the scale of the sector and the potential impact of automation.

Quadruped robots have become an increasingly active research field over the past decade and have consequently attracted growing interest from the industrial sector Majithia et al. (2024) . For commercial applications, both academia and industry have predominantly proposed sectors such as Inspection & Maintenance , Search & Rescue , and Military & Surveillance Li et al. (2025) . Although these tasks have been proposed for a long time and quadruped capabilities have rapidly advanced, commercialization and deployment in these applications remain limited. This is exemplified by Boston Dynamics , one of the earliest and best-known developers of quadrupedal robots, which reported deploying only about 2,100 units of their flagship model Spot in industrial settings by 2023 Boston Dynamics () . This is in strong contrast to the rapid development of quadrupedal capabilities. Today, quadrupeds exhibit high mobility, adaptability in complex environments, and increasing energy efficiency Li et al. (2025) ; Taheri and Mozayani (2023) . Furthermore, with the emergence of deep learning, quadrupeds are becoming progressively more autonomous: their gaits are increasingly adaptable, and they can perform intelligent real-time monitoring and decision-making based on sensor data Wang et al. (2024) . Thus, to enable quadruped deployment at scale, novel fields of applications with well defined tasks and challenges should be investigated.

A potential new environment for quadruped robots to operate in is presented by roofs, offering a unique set of challenges and tasks. Quadrupeds could be deployed in roof environments for a multitude of applications, which are presented in Table 1 . Residential buildings often feature moderate to steep inclines ( 25 ° to 60 ° 25\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}60\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} ), smooth roof tile surfaces, and regularly repeating structural elements such as convex and flat areas or tile row steps, making locomotion inherently difficult Blaß () . Conversely, the repetitive nature of standardized roof tiles provides an opportunity to tailor quadrupeds feet specifically for this environment.

This work provides:

The first systematic experimental evaluation of quadruped locomotion in tiled roof environments.

Quantitative failure thresholds for balanced standing, get-up/lie-down motions, and incline walking establishing a baseline for future research.

A motion-capture-based methodology for objectively observing foot slippage during inclined locomotion.

1. The first systematic experimental evaluation of quadruped locomotion in tiled roof environments.

2. Quantitative failure thresholds for balanced standing, get-up/lie-down motions, and incline walking establishing a baseline for future research.

3. A motion-capture-based methodology for objectively observing foot slippage during inclined locomotion.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Evaluating Quadruped Locomotion in Roof Environments

In roof environments, quadruped locomotion performance is primarily determined by two factors: friction and stability. To objectively evaluate and compare quadruped locomotion, an accurate measurement methodology is required. In this work the main focus is placed on friction as the primary performance indicator, while loss of stability, referred to as critical failure, marks the upper performance limit when the robot falls. Friction can be estimated by measuring slippage on a defined incline angle. This necessitates an external measurement system. For this purpose, the OptiTrack system – a motion capture system based on infrared light and reflective markers – is employed. The system can be calibrated to achieve a measurement accuracy of below 1.0 mm 1.0\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} OptiTrack () .

The feet of a quadruped robot are the primary, and often only, components that directly interact with the environment Li et al. (2023) . While other end-effectors in robotics, such as hands and grippers, have received considerable attention, the development of non-humanoid feet has received less focus Catalano et al. (2022) ; Eckert and Ijspeert (2016) . Currently, most major manufacturers and research institutes employ a simple round foot geometry Ranjan et al. (2024) ; Kalogroulis et al. (2024) . This design is widely adopted due to its simplicity, robustness, and reliable performance across diverse environments Kalogroulis et al. (2024) . Further, the ball-shaped design allows for a simplified contact modeling approach, reducing the simulated contact to a point or line Eckert and Ijspeert (2016) . However, such feet provide a limited contact area, resulting in high stress concentrations and an increased risk of slippage, particularly on inclined surfaces, as rubber friction is area dependent Ranjan et al. (2024) ; Kalogroulis et al. (2024) ; Richhariya et al. (2023) . Moreover, ball feet lack adaptability to varying terrains, restricting their effectiveness in complex environments Ranjan et al. (2024) . Due to these drawbacks and the highly difficult roof environment, the development of customized and environment adapted feet is worth investigating in future work.

2026-10-09.title: Real-Time Motion Planning with Dynamic Hazards: Classical vs. Learning-Based Methods
2026-10-09.authors: Eran Iceland , Alexander Tuisov , Oren Gal , Ariel Barel , Alfred M. Bruckstein
2026-10-09.comment: This paper is scheduled to be presented at the 2027 International Symposium on Artificial Life and Robotics (AROB 2027)
2026-10-09.abstract:
We study real-time motion planning in dynamic hazard fields through a controlled comparison between classical planning and learning-based methods. Rather than introducing a new planner, we construct a unified benchmark in which representative classical and learning-based methods face the same environments, motion constraints, information assumptions, and evaluation metrics. The test environment consists of planar domains populated with rotating sprinkler-like hazards that generate time-varying forbidden regions via sweeping angular sectors.
Our results show a clear regime shift. In deterministic environments, classical planners achieve near-perfect success and higher-quality paths, though sometimes at the cost of substantial planning or replanning time. Under stochastic obstacle dynamics, however, online search becomes strongly budget-sensitive: low budgets lead to frequent failure, while high budgets improve success at the cost of latency and longer trajectories. PPO-based policies, trained under the same scenario distribution, consistently outperform in latency, success rate, and path quality in these stochastic regimes. Overall, the results indicate that uncertainty in obstacle evolution, more than partial observability, is the dominant factor determining which planning paradigm is practically effective for the problem at hand.
2026-10-09.introduction:
We consider motion planning in planar environments with dynamic hazards, a setting that has been extensively studied through both classical and learning-based approaches. Classical methods provide precise geometric or safety-driven guarantees under explicit modeling assumptions, while recent Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based planners offer adaptability and scalability in partially known or stochastic environments. Despite substantial progress on each side, relatively few works provide a controlled, side-by-side comparison between classical and RL-based methods under consistent modeling assumptions and evaluation criteria. In contrast to prior work that introduces new algorithms, our goal is to enable a controlled comparison under a shared problem formulation, isolating regime-dependent performance differences rather than architectural novelty, while providing practical guidance on when each paradigm should be preferred. To achieve that, we construct a unified testbed that is simple enough to admit principled classical treatment, yet rich enough to expose the limitations of each paradigm. We begin with the simplest regime, in which the full evolution of the environment is known in advance, and progressively introduce complexity along two axes: visibility (full vs. limited) and obstacle dynamics (deterministic vs. stochastic). This yields four regimes, ranging from globally known, deterministic settings to partially observable and randomly evolving environments, enabling a systematic comparison under controlled conditions. This design choice intentionally prioritizes comparability over novelty in algorithm design, allowing us to attribute observed performance differences to problem structure rather than to formulation mismatches. We formalize the problem setting as follows. Under full visibility, we consider a deterministic formulation via an X ​ Y ​ T XYT lifting [ AdinBruckstein1991 , KimmelKiryatiBruckstein1998 , fujimura2002time ] .
The robot is modeled as a holonomic point moving at fixed speed and bounded turn rate in the plane while time advances monotonically, i.e. the agent must advance monotonically along T T at unit rate. Dynamic obstacles make feasibility time-dependent, creating a tight coupling between spatial motion and temporal progression.

In 2D with static obstacles, classical path planning commonly relies on geometric constructs such as visibility graphs, Voronoi-based roadmaps, or search-based methods such as A* over discretized grids [ LozanoPerezWesley1979 , Latombe1991 , Mitchell2000ShortestPaths , Choset2005 ] . The setting is simpler because the environment is fixed; the main difficulty is a continuous-space combinatorial search. When obstacles are dynamic in 2D, the search naturally lifts to the spacetime domain X ​ Y ​ T XYT : feasibility must hold simultaneously in space and time, increasing dimensionality and introducing temporal constraints. Early work on real-time navigation in dynamic environments addressed these temporal constraints through analytic, safety-driven online planners.
In particular, velocity-obstacle-based approaches explicitly avoid states of inevitable collision by selecting admissible motions over a carefully chosen time horizon [ GalShillerRimonICRA2009 ] .
Subsequent work introduced adaptive time-horizon selection, reducing conservatism while preserving online safety guarantees in crowded and time-varying scenes [ ShillerGalRazIROS2011 ] . Classical tools in such settings include time-expanded graphs originating from dynamic-flow formulations [ FordFulkerson1958 ] , reachability-based methods grounded in Hamilton-Jacobi optimal control analysis [ MitchellBayenTomlin2005 ] , and reactive models such as velocity obstacles or the dynamic window approach [ FioriniShiller1998 , Fox1997 ] .

In 3D with static obstacles, geometric complexity rises: obstacle representations, distance queries, and feasibility checks become more expensive. Sampling-based planners such as PRM and RRT/RRT* are widely used for high-dimensional, non-convex environments [ Kavraki1996 , LaValleKuffner2001 , KaramanFrazzoli2011 , LaValle2006 ] . With dynamic obstacles in 3D, the problem extends to X ​ Y ​ Z ​ T XYZT , introducing non-convex and often non-linear planning challenges that require predictive obstacle-motion models and uncertainty-aware reasoning [ Thrun2005 ] .

Recent surveys of deep RL for navigation in dynamic and crowded environments highlight strong empirical promise, while emphasizing persistent challenges in generalization and real-world deployment [ Zhu2025DRLDynamicReview , Le2024CrowdedDRLReview ] .
They also note that results are often difficult to compare across papers due to heterogeneous assumptions about sensing, obstacle dynamics, and safety constraints [ AbuJabal2024DynamicPathPlanningSurvey ] .

These observations motivate our controlled evaluation: we compare classical and RL-based planners under consistent assumptions and metrics to isolate regime-dependent performance differences.

We focus on the 2D dynamic-obstacle setting because it allows a consistent treatment across all regimes of interest while remaining computationally tractable. Under full visibility, the problem admits principled solutions that leverage the known evolution of the environment, including spacetime formulations and asymptotically optimal planning methods [ KaramanFrazzoli2011 ] . Under limited visibility, the same formulation naturally leads to incremental and online replanning strategies as information is revealed during execution [ Stentz1995 , KoenigLikhachev2002 ] . This duality makes the setting particularly well-suited for systematic evaluation of both classical and RL-based planners within a unified problem formulation.

Our contributions are primarily empirical and methodological. We introduce a unified testbed for motion planning in dynamic environments, enabling a controlled comparison between classical and RL-based methods under consistent modeling assumptions. The testbed spans four world models defined by two axes: visibility, either full or limited, and obstacle dynamics, either deterministic or stochastic. For these regimes, we implement classical baselines tailored to the available information and dynamics assumptions, together with a consistent RL formulation using a geometrically interpretable action space and compatible observation models. We then provide an empirical evaluation comparing the resulting planners in terms of success rate, path quality, computational cost, and robustness to uncertainty.

Our objective is not to model a specific robotic platform or deployment scenario, but rather to isolate the effect of information availability and obstacle uncertainty on planning performance within a controlled experimental framework.

2026-10-09.title: Fixed-Reference Pose Residuals for Measuring Cross-Dataset Cue Transfer in Human-Robot Interaction Anticipation
2026-10-09.authors: Bowen Yang , Xinliang Xiao , Wenjing Zhang , Li Yang , Wei Zhou
2026-10-09.comment: . Supplementary material available as an ancillary file
2026-10-09.abstract: Social and service robots in public spaces need to anticipate which nearby person is about to approach and touch them, so that a response can be prepared before contact. It is largely unknown which cues support this anticipation when a model trained with one robot is used on another robot at a different site. We study this question with a fixed-reference pose residual (FRPR) model: a geometry predictor built from the person’s bounding box and mask is trained and frozen, and a temporal network then learns from body pose an additive correction to its logit, so that every prediction splits exactly into a geometry term and a pose term. Between two public egocentric datasets recorded by different robots, HUI360 and SSUP-A, with every choice made on source data, the pose correction raised average precision (AP) from 0.277 to 0.321 from SSUP-A to HUI360 and gave no measurable gain in the opposite direction; the same asymmetry held over a stronger, source-selected geometry reference. Freezing gave no AP advantage over joint training, and simple geometric baselines and tree ensembles remained competitive or better, so the construction serves measurement rather than prediction accuracy. A head-orientation residual added small gains in both directions. Post hoc, whether a person faces the camera kept its discriminative direction across datasets, whereas head pitch reversed. With thresholds chosen on source data, the neural models that use geometry detected at most 17% of target interactions. Code and processed data are available at https://github.com/WeiZhou96/FRPR-interaction-anticipation .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Service and delivery robots that share sidewalks, lobbies and shops with the public are approached, touched, stopped and handed objects by people they have never met ( Bu and Ju, 2025 ; Lorenzo-Louis et al., 2026 ; Arreghini et al., 2024b ) . Approach, greeting and engagement behaviours designed for such robots, and socially aware navigation among people, depend on an early estimate of who is going to interact ( Satake et al., 2009 ; Kato et al., 2015 ; Avelino et al., 2025 ; Mavrogiannis et al., 2023 ; Francis et al., 2025 ) . About one second of warning allows a robot to slow down, turn its interface towards the person or keep moving when nobody needs it. The two kinds of anticipation error have different costs. A missed interaction leaves the robot unprepared when a person reaches it; a false alarm makes it stop, turn or address someone who is only passing, which interrupts its task and may be perceived as intrusive ( Rios-Martinez et al., 2015 ; Mead and Matarić, 2017 ) . The lead time with which a correct warning arrives determines which of these behaviours can still be executed. Both kinds of error are borne by the people around the robot, which makes the estimate a concern of human-centred system design ( Ozmen Garibay et al., 2023 ) and not only of recognition accuracy.

The perception problem has recently been cast as interaction anticipation : given a short observation of a tracked person in the robot’s egocentric video, predict whether a physical interaction with the robot follows ( Abbate et al., 2024 ; Lorenzo-Louis et al., 2026 ) . The label is an observable event, contact with the robot body, rather than a mental state, which makes the task well defined and lets it be annotated at scale. Three families of cue are available for each track. Approach geometry describes where the person appears in the image, how large the box and mask are, and how these quantities change. Body pose is the sequence of two-dimensional keypoints, which carries body orientation, arm movement and gait. Head orientation indicates whether a person faces the robot, a signal that engagement models for social robots have long used as evidence of attention ( Michalowski et al., 2006 ; Sidner et al., 2005 ; Anzalone et al., 2015 ; Belardinelli, 2024 ) . Existing anticipation models feed such cues to a single classifier ( Abbate et al., 2024 ; Arreghini et al., 2024c ; Lorenzo-Louis et al., 2026 ) .

A social robot is rarely deployed where its training data were recorded. Robots differ in camera height and placement, and sites differ in layout, crowd density and the reasons people have to approach. Cross-dataset results show that anticipation performance drops when the platform changes ( Lorenzo-Louis et al., 2026 ) , and performance in intent prediction depends on the robot’s environment ( Thompson et al., 2024 ) . For a designer, the useful question is which cues keep their meaning under such a change. Geometry is low-dimensional and tied to the task by construction, since nobody touches a robot from afar; pose and head orientation depend on the estimator, the camera and the viewpoint, and pose estimates from robot-mounted cameras suffer from occlusion and scale variation in crowds ( Vendrow et al., 2023 ) . Once all cues enter one fused network, the contribution of each can no longer be read from the model, and, as Section 5.4 shows, the same holds for an additive two-branch model trained jointly.

We therefore treat the geometry predictor as a reference and ask each further cue for a correction . A small geometry network is trained on the source domain and frozen; a causal temporal convolutional network then learns from the pose sequence a scalar that is added to the reference logit, starting from a zero-initialised head. We call this the fixed-reference pose residual (FRPR) model. The reference remains a deployable predictor with unchanged weights, every prediction splits exactly into a reference logit and a pose correction, and the difference between FRPR and its own reference is a paired measurement of what pose adds under that reference. A further cue is attached in the same way as one more frozen stage; with head orientation we obtain FRPR-H. The construction is intended as a measurement instrument, not as a stronger predictor, and we evaluate it as such.

We study both transfer directions between HUI360 ( Lorenzo-Louis et al., 2026 ) and SSUP-A, the annotation of the SSUP-HRI street recordings ( Bu and Ju, 2025 ) released with HUI360. All preprocessing statistics, hyperparameters, checkpoints and thresholds are chosen on source data. From SSUP-A to HUI360 the pose correction raises average precision (AP) over its reference by + + 0.044 (95% interval [ + + 0.024, + + 0.082]), and controls with permuted or coordinate-free pose input show no such gain; from HUI360 to SSUP-A no gain is observed. The asymmetry persists over a stronger reference selected on source data, so the pose gain is not only a compensation for a weak reference. Freezing brings no AP advantage over joint training, and simple geometric baselines and tree ensembles are competitive or better. Geometry and pose keep their ranking quality in opposite transfer directions; among head-orientation cues, whether a person faces the camera keeps its discriminative direction across the two robots and sites, whereas head pitch reverses. At thresholds chosen on source data, the neural models that use geometry detect at most 17% of target interactions.

The contributions are as follows.

A reference–correction formulation of interaction anticipation, with a frozen geometry reference and zero-initialised residuals, under which the contribution of each cue is an exact, paired quantity and freezing can be examined as a single experimental factor.

A bidirectional cross-dataset measurement, with source-only model selection, date-level uncertainty and strong simple baselines, of how geometry, body pose and head orientation transfer between two robots and sites, including a check against a stronger, source-selected geometry reference.

An analysis of which cues can be expected to carry over to a new platform, which reverse, and how far rankings and thresholds transfer.

2. A bidirectional cross-dataset measurement, with source-only model selection, date-level uncertainty and strong simple baselines, of how geometry, body pose and head orientation transfer between two robots and sites, including a check against a stronger, source-selected geometry reference.

3. An analysis of which cues can be expected to carry over to a new platform, which reverse, and how far rankings and thresholds transfer.

# 2 Related work

## 2.1 Anticipating interaction with a robot

Engagement, the process by which interaction partners establish and maintain a connection ( Sidner et al., 2005 ; Oertel et al., 2020 ) , has been estimated from position and orientation relative to the robot ( Michalowski et al., 2006 ) , from directed and mutual gaze ( Rich et al., 2010 ) , from proxemic, body and face features ( Vaufreydaz et al., 2016 ) , with classifiers for a multi-party bartender robot ( Foster et al., 2017 ) , and with metrics built from head and body posture ( Anzalone et al., 2015 ) . Field studies in shopping malls turned trajectory-based estimates of who is willing to interact into approach behaviours ( Satake et al., 2009 ; Kato et al., 2015 ) , proxemics has been modelled for socially aware navigation ( Rios-Martinez et al., 2015 ; Mead and Matarić, 2017 ) , and greeting strategies for first encounters with mobile robots have been compared in the wild ( Avelino et al., 2025 ) . These works design or evaluate the robot’s response; the present study concerns the perception estimate that such behaviours consume.

Recent anticipation models are data-driven. Abbate et al. (2024) let a service robot label its own encounters by whether an interaction eventually happened and trained classifiers on pose and motion features; adding gaze features to such a self-supervised classifier improved its ranking and the distance at which it was accurate ( Arreghini et al., 2024c ) , and a deployment in two crowded public locations compared proactive behaviours triggered by distance and by behavioural cues ( Arreghini et al., 2024b ) . PAR-D ( Thompson et al., 2024 ) collects approach data around a public robot for intent prediction; Bian et al. (2024) forecast intent to interact jointly with attitude and social action from whole-body skeletons; and MINT-RVAE ( Mohsen and Safa, 2025 ) predicts frame-level interaction intent from pose and emotion cues. HUI360 ( Lorenzo-Louis et al., 2026 ) provides 360° egocentric recordings from a mobile robot with tracked persons, poses and masks, defines interaction as physical contact, reports baselines and feature ablations, and evaluates across datasets against SSUP-A. Forecasting human motion for robot behaviour generation uses the same ingredients, body pose and position over time ( Valls Mascaro and Lee, 2025 ) ; trajectory prediction benefits from box and pose cues and can be made robust to missing ones ( Saadatnejad et al., 2024 ) , and datasets recorded from a social robot annotate the actions, groups and poses of the surrounding people ( Ehsanpour et al., 2022 ; Vendrow et al., 2023 ) . We adopt the task, data and bidirectional evaluation of Lorenzo-Louis et al. (2026) . Our model differs from these predictors in retaining a separately trained geometry prediction as an unchanged term of the final score, and our question differs in asking which cue carries over, not which model scores highest.

## 2.2 Head orientation as an attention cue

Face and head orientation are standard evidence of attention in engagement models ( Michalowski et al., 2006 ; Sidner et al., 2005 ; Rich et al., 2010 ; Anzalone et al., 2015 ) , and gaze is reviewed as an early cue of intention in HRI ( Belardinelli, 2024 ) ; mutual gaze has been detected at distances of up to 5 m for this purpose ( Arreghini et al., 2024a ) . Most of these systems observe a person who is already near the robot or in conversation with it, often with a frontal camera. In the anticipation setting the person is further away, seen by a panoramic camera mounted on a moving platform, and must be judged before any exchange starts. We measure head orientation relative to the camera from dense face keypoints ( Khirodkar et al., 2024 ) ; we do not estimate gaze direction, and a person facing the camera is not necessarily looking at the robot.

## 2.3 Combining cues on a fixed base

In jointly trained multi-branch classifiers, branches overfit and generalise at different rates ( Wang et al., 2020 ) , and a dominant modality suppresses the optimisation of the others ( Peng et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . In work on dataset bias, He et al. (2019) fit a biased classifier, freeze it, and train an additional classifier through the loss of the summed scores, which is, in its training mechanics, the nearest neighbour of FRPR. Their goal is to discard the biased branch at test time, whereas our reference is a legitimate cue that stays in the deployed model. Learning a correction to a fixed predictor is also the principle of gradient boosting ( Friedman, 2001 ) , which has been used to train modalities in alternation ( Hua et al., 2024 ) . None of these components is new; we use their combination to measure what a cue adds to a geometry-based prediction and whether that addition survives a change of robot and site. Our setting is that of domain generalisation, in which no target data are available during training ( Zhou et al., 2023 ) ; because cross-domain claims are sensitive to model selection ( Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2020 ) , all selection uses source data only. Skeleton-based recognisers are known to lose accuracy across datasets ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , which motivates measuring the transfer of the pose cue separately.

2026-10-09.title: From Language to Motion: Task-Conditioned Focal-Stack Trajectory Integration for Microscopic Robots
2026-10-09.authors: Junjie Xie , Chuxuan He , Junkai Huang , Heng Zhang , Angen Ye , Yujia Song , Yuqing Li , Pengsong Zhang , Dapeng Zhang
2026-10-09.abstract: Microscopic robots require accurate task geometry despite changes in language, parts, and focus. We present a semantic-to-physical framework that maps instructions to constrained geometric operators, reuses frozen open-vocabulary perception, and integrates locally reliable focal-plane trajectories by confidence weighting and dynamic programming. Calibrated multi-view geometry connects 2-D paths to physical execution. Prompt, unseen-part, and geometry reconfiguration tests yield 6.30–6.59-pixel RMSE. Relative to part-specific U-Net training with 20–100 labels, the proposed zero-new-label configuration takes 15 rather than 72–165 min. Across nine part–illumination conditions, trajectory-space integration reduces RMSE from 14.41 to 6.28 pixels (56.4%) and P95 error from 20.07 to 8.13 pixels (59.5%) compared with image-first multi-focus fusion. An ablation isolates the roles of confidence and path-wise selection. In representative robot experiments, target-region coverage improves from 83.5% to 92.9%. Dispensing provides a measurable physical trace, not a task-specific limitation of the method.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Microscopic robot tasks such as probing, contour following, and local material deposition require an ordered geometric path, not only an object category. The relevant edge, centreline, or offset contour must be localized under shallow depth of field and ultimately transformed into the robot frame. A practical microscopic vision system should therefore address two distinct bottlenecks: task reconfiguration when the part or requested geometry changes, and geometric accuracy when different path segments are in focus in different images. Figure 1 outlines our language-to-physical-trace pipeline.

Part-specific systems can achieve high accuracy by collecting images, annotating masks, and training specialized networks such as U-Net and nnU-Net [ 1 , 2 ] . In high-mix, low-volume manipulation, however, that development loop incurs repeated annotation and training cost [ 3 ] . Open-vocabulary detection and promptable segmentation [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] offer reusable visual components. Rather than treating these backbones as novel, we connect them to a constrained task specification: language specifies which object, region, and geometric primitive to measure, while visual measurements and geometric operators specify its image coordinates. This separation allows reconfiguration by editing the instruction and operator settings instead of retraining a dedicated detector. We test the resulting accuracy and adaptation-time trade-off against supervised baselines.

Shallow depth of field creates a different limitation. Focus varies along a three-dimensional contour, so no single plane necessarily reveals the complete path. Shape-from-focus exploits focal variation [ 7 , 8 ] ; multi-focus image fusion (MFIF) combines focal evidence into an all-in-focus image [ 9 , 10 ] . Yet a visually acceptable composite can shift or obscure the very edge that defines the robotic trajectory. We therefore invert the processing order: extract local trajectories from the individual focal planes, associate geometrically consistent hypotheses, and integrate them directly in ordered path space. Confidence weighting exploits locally reliable evidence, while dynamic programming promotes continuity and discourages arbitrary focal-source switching, with an explicit null option when evidence is inadequate.

For execution, we associate the separately recovered 2-D paths across calibrated views and reconstruct a 3-D task trajectory using standard multi-view geometry. Approximately orthogonal views are a platform-specific configuration, not a requirement of the algorithm. A trace-preserving dispensing experiment provides a physical measurement of the outcome after geometry recovery, calibration, and robot motion; dispensing is a validation instrument rather than the target application.

Our contributions are threefold:

Language-to-geometry reconfiguration. A constrained specification and reusable perception front end support new wordings, unseen parts, and different trajectory operators; accuracy and adaptation time are compared with part-specific supervised training.

Confidence-weighted focal-stack trajectory integration. Local path hypotheses are combined without requiring all-in-focus synthesis. Nine matched conditions quantify trajectory error, and component ablations measure the effects of confidence and dynamic programming.

Perception-to-physical evaluation. We separately quantify 2-D geometry and downstream physical-trace outcomes, using calibrated multi-view reconstruction and robot execution as the bridge rather than claiming a new 3-D reconstruction algorithm.

The framework targets geometric requests expressible by the available operators and supported by sufficient image evidence. It does not assume arbitrary language instructions can be executed without task configuration.

2. Confidence-weighted focal-stack trajectory integration. Local path hypotheses are combined without requiring all-in-focus synthesis. Nine matched conditions quantify trajectory error, and component ablations measure the effects of confidence and dynamic programming.

3. Perception-to-physical evaluation. We separately quantify 2-D geometry and downstream physical-trace outcomes, using calibrated multi-view reconstruction and robot execution as the bridge rather than claiming a new 3-D reconstruction algorithm.

# II Related Work

## II-A Language-Grounded Geometry Extraction

U-Net and nnU-Net are supervised segmentation baselines [ 1 , 2 ] . Reusable segmentation has also been demonstrated by Cellpose [ 11 ] and microscopy-adapted foundation models [ 12 , 13 ] . Language–image pretraining [ 14 ] enables text-driven perception: Grounding DINO detects described objects [ 4 ] , SAM estimates masks [ 5 ] , and Grounded SAM composes them [ 6 ] . Robot systems have also used natural language to structure downstream planning [ 15 , 16 ] . Here language specifies what geometry to measure, not motor actions or metric locations; calibrated visual processing is still responsible for where it lies. We do not propose a new visual foundation model.

## II-B Focus Variation and Task-Space Fusion

Shape-from-focus recovers depth cues from focal variation [ 7 , 8 ] . Multi-focus image fusion (MFIF) instead synthesizes a composite image [ 10 ] . Focus transitions and image blending may displace edges used for downstream measurements [ 17 , 18 ] . Recent semantic or task-driven image fusion includes SAMFF [ 19 ] and TDFusion [ 20 ] , but a fused image remains the output variable. We target an ordered geometric path directly: each focal plane contributes local hypotheses, and a path-level optimizer selects a consistent solution. The ability to leave an interval unspecified rather than force an unreliable prediction is related to selective prediction [ 21 ] .

## II-C Perception-to-Execution Bridge

Multi-view reconstruction and vision-based robot control provide the established mathematical bridge from image measurements to robot motion [ 22 , 23 ] . Tracking quality is sensitive to upstream measurement uncertainty [ 24 ] , particularly in high-precision micromanipulation [ 25 ] . Physical traces can be measured against a registered desired path, as in deposition metrology [ 26 ] . Our methodological focus is the upstream 2-D geometry passed to these established components. We report image-space trajectory errors and, separately, downstream target-relative physical-trace outcomes to evaluate both perception and execution.
