2026-10-09.title: Residual Modeling Closes the Regression and Generative Policy Gap in Robot Learning
2026-10-09.authors: Yuchen Zhou , Jiacheng You , Weikang Wan , Weijun Dong , Yang Gao , Jiayuan Mao
2026-10-09.abstract:
Learning from demonstration has enabled impressive robot behaviors.
A common choice for policy learning is to use diffusion or flow matching (Flow-Policies), which often outperforms direct action regression trained with mean squared error (MSE-Policies). This gap is commonly attributed to multimodal demonstrations.
We revisit this gap from the perspective of statistical modeling: how action-prediction residuals shape policy optimization.
Our analysis of real-world robot demonstration data reveals substantial state-dependent variation in residual scales and heavier-than-Gaussian tails.
While both MSE-Policies and Flow-Policies exhibit heavy-tailed action residuals, their training gradients behave differently: MSE allocates more gradient magnitude to observations with large action residuals, which hurts optimization. Motivated by these findings, we introduce heteroscedastic Student- t t action regression (HT-Policies), which learns input-dependent residual scales and reduces the influence of heavy tails.
HT-Policies predict action chunks with a single feed-forward pass and can reuse pretrained flow-matching-based policy networks as the backbone.
Across four simulation benchmarks and real-robot evaluations, HT-Policies achieves success rates competitive with generative policy baselines, both when trained from scratch and from pretrained vision-language-action and world-action models, despite being faster in training and inference.
Together, these findings shed light on the practical advantages of generative objectives in robot learning from demonstrations and offer an efficient direct-regression alternative for a range of architectures and tasks. Project Page: https://the-labone.github.io/regression-policy-project/
2026-10-09.introduction:
Learning robot policies from demonstrations is typically formulated as a supervised learning problem, in which an action chunk — a short sequence of consecutive actions — is predicted from observations and goal specifications ( Mandlekar et al., 2021 ) . A common approach for policy learning is to use generative models, such as diffusion and flow-matching models ( Chi et al., 2023 ; Pan et al., 2026 ) . In practice, these models often outperform direct action regression trained with mean squared error (MSE-Policies). This performance gap is commonly attributed to multimodality: generative policies can model multiple action modes, whereas MSE-Policies tend to average across modes, potentially producing actions that do not correspond to any demonstrated behavior.

Recent results suggest that explicitly modeling multimodal action distributions is not necessary for competitive performance. Minimal Iterative Policy (MIP), introduced by Pan et al. (2026) , uses a deterministic network in two successive passes for action prediction. The first pass predicts an action chunk conditioned only on the policy inputs; the second pass additionally conditions on the first prediction to refine it. During training, the network is supervised with a denoising objective. MIP closes the performance gap with Flow-Policies and attributes its success to iterative refinement, which helps keep predicted actions on the manifold of demonstrated actions. However, this explanation remains largely empirical, with limited formal characterization and real-data verification.

In this paper, we revisit this problem from a statistical modeling perspective. Specifically, we examine the residual models implicit in different training objectives and how they affect policy optimization. This perspective offers a way to understand the benefits of denoising supervision and motivates a direct action regression objective that can resemble those benefits without iterative inference.

We begin by examining the action residuals of trained policies. From a likelihood perspective, MSE regression corresponds to a fixed-scale Gaussian residual model. Empirically, however, both MSE-Policies and Flow-Policies exhibit heavy-tailed action residuals. One source of these tails is variation in residual scale across observations: for example, reaching toward a hole and making fine adjustments during insertion may involve different prediction-error scales. Yet scale variation alone does not fully account for the observed tails, which remain heavier than Gaussian after per-observation scale normalization, as illustrated in Figure 1 b.
This structure matters for optimization because the gradient of MSE with respect to the predicted action is proportional to the residual. We show that high-residual samples account for a dominating share of gradient magnitude under MSE. Flow matching exhibits a similar concentration at high noise levels, but distributes gradient magnitude more evenly, especially at low noise levels due to its denoising training objective.

Motivated by these findings, we introduce heteroscedastic Student- t t action regression (HT-Policies) ( Lange et al., 1989 ) . HT-Policies incorporate the observed residual structure directly into the regression objective, predict action chunks with a single feed-forward pass, and can reuse pretrained flow-matching policy networks as backbones.
In four simulation benchmarks and real-robot evaluations, HT-Policies achieve success rates competitive with generative policy baselines. They perform well both when trained from scratch and when fine-tuned from pretrained vision-language-action and world-action models, while improving training and inference efficiency. Our gradient analysis shows reduced concentration of gradient magnitude on high-residual observations, supporting our hypothesis about the role of residual modeling in policy optimization. Together, these findings shed light on the practical advantages of generative objectives in robot learning and offer practitioners an efficient direct-regression alternative across a range of architectures and tasks. To summarize, our contributions are as follows:

We characterize robot-policy residuals, revealing input-dependent scales and heavy tails that expose a mismatch with the fixed-scale Gaussian assumption of MSE.

We further show that this mismatch causes MSE to overemphasize large-action-residual samples, whereas flow matching distributes gradients more evenly, especially in low-noise regimes. We explain the mechanism of this by studying the denoising objectives.

We introduce HT-Policies, which explicitly model input-dependent scales and heavy tails. Across simulation and real-robot tasks, they match generative baseline performances while enabling more efficient training and inference.

1. We characterize robot-policy residuals, revealing input-dependent scales and heavy tails that expose a mismatch with the fixed-scale Gaussian assumption of MSE.

2. We further show that this mismatch causes MSE to overemphasize large-action-residual samples, whereas flow matching distributes gradients more evenly, especially in low-noise regimes. We explain the mechanism of this by studying the denoising objectives.

3. We introduce HT-Policies, which explicitly model input-dependent scales and heavy tails. Across simulation and real-robot tasks, they match generative baseline performances while enabling more efficient training and inference.

# 2 Related Work

Variations in robot demonstration data. Human demonstrations exhibit variation arising from multiple sources, including differences in task strategies ( Shafiullah et al., 2022 ; Gandhi et al., 2023 ; Jia et al., 2024 ) , action rates ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , and execution errors or inaccuracies ( Chen et al., 2025 ) .
Prior work has addressed such variation from two main perspectives.
One line of work treats it as distributional multimodality and models it with Gaussian mixtures ( Mandlekar et al., 2021 ) , diffusion models ( Chi et al., 2023 ) , or conditional VAEs ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) .
Others treat variation as undesirable noise and seek to suppress it ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) .
While these approaches can accommodate diverse demonstrations, they largely study how variation should be modeled or filtered empirically, rather than understanding its statistical structure and how it affects learning.

MIP ( Pan et al., 2026 ) shows that averaging flow-policy outputs leaves performance largely unchanged, a finding we extend to VLA and WAM policies (Appendix A.2 ). Instead of avoiding mode averaging, it argues that flow’s iterative refinement moves predictions toward the data manifold, but provides limited formal characterization. Moreover, its study of off-manifold error on out-of-distribution states does not distinguish manifold adherence from generalization. We revisit the gap by studying the statistical residual modeling in MSE-Policies and its effects on policy learning.

Robust and heteroscedastic regression. Huber losses ( Huber, 1964 ) and Student- t t likelihoods ( Lange et al., 1989 ) improve regression robustness to large residuals; adaptive robust losses can learn the appropriate degree of robustness from data ( Barron, 2019 ) .
Complementarily, heteroscedastic regression models input-dependent residual scales ( Nix and Weigend, 1994 ) , although variance-based reweighting under Gaussian likelihoods can adversely affect mean estimation ( Seitzer et al., 2022a ) .
These objectives have been widely explored in computer vision, including bounding-box regression ( Girshick, 2015 ) and depth prediction ( Kendall and Gal, 2017 ) .
In imitation learning, OpenVLA-OFT shows strong LIBERO performance with L 1 L_{1} regression ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , although L 1 L_{1} still underperforms MSE on
three of four LIBERO suites when fine-tuning π 0 \pi_{0} ( Pan et al., 2026 ) .
Robust classification objectives have also been studied ( Tangkaratt et al., 2021 ) .
We combine robust regression with input-dependent scale learning for action learning.

2026-10-09.title: Sim-to-Real RL for ASVs using SysID
2026-10-09.authors: Cody Sheltraw , Tsimafei Lazouski , Maani Ghaffari , Alan Papalia
2026-10-09.comment: . Submitted to ICRA 2027. Code available at: this https URL
2026-10-09.abstract:
Autonomous Surface Vehicles (ASVs) operating in dynamic marine environments require robust control policies for tasks such as path following and station keeping, making reinforcement learning (RL) a promising alternative to classical controllers.
However, existing ASV simulators rarely support parallel environments for RL training.
Such existing simulators require accurate hydrodynamic modeling from computational fluid dynamics solvers or towing tank tests for setting hydrodynamic parameters to address the sim-to-real gap.
To address these challenges, we present an ASV simulator and accompanying pipeline that enables training policies starting from unknown vehicle dynamics.
Our framework uses only a CAD model and brief set of open-water field trajectories for approximating and refining both hydrodynamic and thruster parameters.
Real-world deployments on a BlueBoat ASV demonstrate successful zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in path following and station-keeping tasks without prior hydrodynamic and propeller information.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) operating in marine environments require robust control despite non-linear hydrodynamic interactions, uncertain propulsion characteristics, and environmental disturbances, such as wind, waves, and currents [ 1 , 2 ] .
Since these hydrodynamic forces depend directly on the vehicle’s operating state and surrounding sea conditions,
accurate modeling and controller tuning are challenging for tasks such as path following and station keeping.
Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an attractive alternative for such tasks by learning control policies directly from interactions, without explicit modeling of each relevant dynamic interaction, necessitating the availability of RL-capable simulators. In other robotic domains, RL policies have demonstrated the ability to control complex non-linear systems in challenging operating conditions [ 3 , 4 ] .
However, transferring policies trained in simulation to real-world deployment remains challenging for ASVs due to the sim-to-real gap between simulated and real marine dynamics [ 5 , 6 ] .

To reduce this sim-to-real gap, an adequate representation of the vessel dynamics is needed.
Such high-fidelity models traditionally rely on towing tank experiments or computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solvers for accurate hydrodynamic system identification (SysID), creating a high barrier to entry. Furthermore, using real-world SysID parameters in a simulator does not guarantee improved sim-to-real performance [ 7 ] . The mismatch between real-world and simplified simulator dynamics means parameters identified from the real vessel may not align with the simulator parameters that best reproduce its observed behavior.
To compensate for this, other works in the marine domain rely on heavy domain randomization (DR), which can lead to conservative policies [ 8 ] and decreased real-world performance [ 9 ] .

To address these limitations, this work presents a simulator and an accompanying real-to-sim-to-real pipeline that facilitates the deployment of simulation-trained policies on a physical ASV using little real-world data.
Our approach reduces the sim-to-real gap by grounding the simulated dynamics in observed real-world ASV behavior using the covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) over a set of trajectories.
Starting with unknown vessel dynamics, our method reduced station-keeping position error by 63.9 % 63.9\% (1.074 m to 0.388 m RMSE) and heading error by 40.1 % 40.1\% (17.30 ∘ to 10.37 ∘ MAE) over an analytical SysID approach under varying currents on a physical BlueBoat [ 10 ] .

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

ASV Simulator : An RL-focused ASV simulator based on NVIDIA Isaac Sim with hydrodynamics, wind-wave disturbance, and propeller-thrust modeling.

Accessible real-to-sim pipeline : A CAD model and a single set of open-water trajectories are used to ground simulated vessel behavior, eliminating the costly need for towing tanks or CFD solvers.

Field sim-to-real evaluation : Station-keeping and path following policies trained using our simulator and methodology are deployed and evaluated on a real ASV in a river environment.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Marine Simulation

Several marine simulators with RL capabilities are available today, including one that was built specifically for the ASV application, and whose policies have been deployed in the field [ 5 , 6 , 11 ] . However, it is strictly limited to planar dynamics, not accounting for roll or pitching motions, and constant force and torque are used to simulate water currents. Other notable RL marine simulators focus on the underwater domain [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , and adaptations of these simulators for surface vehicles are still in development.
Our simulator, exclusively built for surface vehicles, is developed using real-world field data, separating it from existing purely analytical solutions. To our knowledge, this is also the first ASV simulator that supports parallel environments for RL with geometric wave displacement updating the submerged volume of an ASV.

## II-B Sim-to-Real

Domain randomization (DR) and grounded simulation learning (GSL) [ 15 ] are two proven methods used to reduce the sim-to-real gap.

Domain randomization (DR) adds
variations to the space of simulated environments to prevent trained policies
from overfitting [ 16 ] . DR has been used extensively in the field of robotics for the
zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of
drones [ 17 , 18 ] ,
legged robotics [ 19 ] , and
ASVs [ 20 , 5 ] . While heavy DR
improves generalization, even for unmodeled
disturbances [ 18 ] , the resulting policies tend to be
conservative [ 8 ] .
Therefore, heavy DR should primarily be used for unmodeled dynamics and unknown disturbances, such as wind and water in the marine domain, instead of parameters with measured real-world values.

GSL is an iterative process of using real-world data to ground a simulator, deploying the policy in the real world, and then refining simulation parameters based on expected dynamics versus real telemetry. While multiple iterations provide slight improvements over time for legged robots [ 15 ] , they assume zero environmental disturbance over the same task, which makes multiple iterations unrealistic for the marine domain. Grounded Action Transformation (GAT) [ 21 ] is another framework extending GSL, but instead treats the simulator as a black box. A task-specific transformation mapping is learned to match the system’s actions in the source domain to actions in a target domain. Since we can modify the hydrodynamics of our simulator, we can perform task-agnostic grounding without GAT.

2026-10-09.title: MAP2: Model- and Acceleration-Based Pursuit with MPC and Gaussian Process Residual Learning for Autonomous Racing
2026-10-09.authors: Weizhan Huang , Cheng Hu , Edoardo Ghignone , Nicolas Baumann , Yiqin Wang , Hongye Su , Lei Xie , Michele Magno
2026-10-09.abstract: Autonomous racing requires accurate trajectory tracking near the handling limits of a vehicle while maintaining low computational latency. Geometric controllers are computationally efficient, but the Ackermann steering geometry becomes invalid under limit-handling conditions. Model- and Acceleration-based Pursuit (MAP) preserves the simplicity of geometric approaches while leveraging tire dynamics. Yet MAP remains fundamentally a geometric controller that relies on Ackermann steering geometry, and its tire model may not fully capture the vehicle’s actual dynamic response. This paper presents MAP2, a model-based pursuit controller that combines a curvature-based kinematic MPC and a Sparse Gaussian Process (SGP) residual correction. The proposed algorithm uses MPC to optimize kinematic control inputs over a prediction horizon and maps them to steering commands through a tire dynamics model augmented with SGP residual correction. Real-world vehicle experiments demonstrate substantial reductions in lateral tracking error and lap time. Compared with MAP and Pure Pursuit (PP) , MAP2 reduces the average lateral tracking error by 37.99% and 44.65%, respectively, while reducing average lap time by at least 1.5%.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Autonomous racing challenges autonomous driving systems to achieve accurate, low-latency trajectory tracking near the vehicle’s handling limits. These challenges, prevalent in racing scenarios, also offer valuable insights for standard driving situations [ 1 ] . Academic competitions, from full-scale events such as Formula Student Driverless (FSD) [ 2 ] and Indy Autonomous Challenge (IAC) [ 1 ] to F1TENTH-scale racing [ 3 , 4 ] , provide testbeds for studying these challenges. Though these competitions vary, their common goal is to complete laps in the shortest time [ 2 , 1 , 4 ] .

This goal introduces a complex control challenge, pushing Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS) to operate at their physical limits. The highly nonlinear behavior of racecars, dominated by vehicle and tire dynamics at the limits of friction [ 5 , 6 , 4 ] , makes precise trajectory tracking at these limits the paramount control task in autonomous racing [ 6 ] .

Traditionally, Model Predictive Control (MPC) is widely used for high-performance autonomous racing [ 5 , 7 ] , offering predictive control but depending on accurate vehicle models and incurring increasing computational cost as model complexity grows. Consequently, while MPC theoretically delivers an optimal control solution for autonomous racing, practical limitations such as state estimation inaccuracies and model mismatches often curtail its effectiveness [ 6 ] , complicating its deployment in a dynamic racing environment. Hence, an alternative to MPC controllers, MAP [ 6 ] , has been introduced, which integrates a geometric controller with the complex tire dynamics, through a Lookup Table (LUT) -based approach. However, the geometric nature of its underlying PP [ 8 ] and the mismatch between the offline LUT and the real vehicle dynamics still leave a large margin for tracking performance.

Therefore, in this paper, we propose MAP2, a computationally lightweight controller architecture that builds upon the proven capabilities of the MAP controller [ 6 , 4 ] . MAP2 significantly enhances tracking performance by integrating a highly efficient MPC that adopts the model-based approach of the original MAP , and a residual SGP on top of the LUT baseline. This integration allows MAP2 to achieve constraint satisfaction and execute accurate steering commands over a receding horizon while preserving the simplicity and parameter robustness of MAP . We have experimentally validated the MAP2 controller on the computationally constrained 1:10-scale F1TENTH platform, comparing it against State-of-the-Art (SotA) autonomous racing controllers such as MAP [ 6 ] and the traditional PP controller. The main contributions of this work are as follows:

MPC-Based Predictive Lateral-Acceleration Generation: A Frenet-frame kinematic MPC is introduced to replace the geometric look-ahead based lateral acceleration calculation in MAP . Instead of deriving the lateral acceleration command a c a_{c} from the look-ahead distance L d L_{d} , the proposed MPC optimizes virtual inputs over a prediction horizon then convert them into a c a_{c} . This formulation enables predictive lateral acceleration planning for operation near the vehicle’s handling limits.

SGP-Based Compensation for Model Mismatch: An SGP residual model is learned from real-vehicle data to compensate for this mismatch by correcting the LUT -based steering commands. The sparse formulation reduces the computational cost of SGP inference to 2.0 ms, enabling real-time residual correction.

Real-world Experimental Validation and Open Source: MAP2 is validated on a computationally constrained 1:10-scale F1TENTH platform through comparisons with MAP and PP , as well as an ablation study without SGP residual correction. The experiments demonstrate reduced lateral tracking errors and lap times, together with robustness to tire-parameter modeling errors. To support reproducibility and further research, we release our implementation at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/MAP2-1F88/ .
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

MPC has become one of the dominant approaches for high-performance autonomous racing. By repeatedly solving a finite-horizon optimization problem, MPC predicts the future vehicle motion and computes control inputs. Dynamic MPC and Model Predictive Contouring Controller (MPCC) have demonstrated strong performance on autonomous race cars because they can jointly optimize trajectory tracking and vehicle speed [ 5 , 7 , 2 ] . However, this performance depends on accurate vehicle and tire models. Near the handling limits, tire forces are highly nonlinear. Modeling these effects accurately is difficult, and discrepancies between the identified model and the real vehicle can directly degrade the control performance [ 9 ] . GP-based residual learning provides one way to address this limitation. Hewing et al. augment a nominal dynamics model with a GP that learns model errors from data and accounts for the remaining uncertainty within MPC [ 10 ] . Sparse GP formulations have likewise been used to compensate for model mismatch online in safety-critical vehicle control [ 11 , 12 ] . Nevertheless, online optimization and GP prediction introduce computational demands that must be considered on embedded racing platforms [ 4 , 13 , 6 ] .

Geometric controllers provide a computationally efficient alternative. These methods derive the steering command from the geometric relationship between the vehicle and a reference trajectory, and therefore do not require a detailed dynamic model. PP is a representative example: it selects a reference point ahead of the vehicle at a look-ahead distance L d L_{d} and computes the steering angle using an Ackermann kinematic relationship [ 8 ] . Because of its low computational cost and simple implementation, such a controller can achieve good tracking performance at low or moderate speeds after proper parameter tuning. However, its geometric assumptions become less accurate as the vehicle approaches the handling limits. At high speed, the lateral dynamics become more nonlinear, tire slip becomes significant, and the curvature of the track may require steering inputs close to the available tire-force and steering limits. The look-ahead distance also introduces an inherent trade-off: a short L d L_{d} can cause oscillatory steering, whereas a long L d L_{d} can increase the tracking error and cause corner cutting. Speed-dependent or otherwise adaptive look-ahead strategies can alleviate this trade-off, but they still do not explicitly describe the nonlinear relationship between tire slip, lateral acceleration, and steering angle.

MAP introduces vehicle dynamics into this lightweight control structure by using a tire model to construct a LUT that maps the desired lateral acceleration and vehicle velocity to the steering angle [ 6 ] . Compared with a purely geometric PP controller, this mapping allows the controller to account for tire slip and the velocity-dependent relationship between lateral acceleration and steering. As a result, MAP retains the low online computational cost of a pursuit controller while providing more accurate lateral control in high-speed and nonlinear operating conditions. Nevertheless, MAP still calculates the desired lateral acceleration from target-point geometry and L d L_{d} , without optimizing vehicle motion over a prediction horizon. Its steering commands also remain sensitive to model approximations and parameter identification errors in the LUT .

These limitations motivate a hybrid design that keeps the online pipeline of a geometric controller while adding short-horizon prediction and data-driven compensation. Unlike [ 10 ] , which augments a dynamic model with a GP inside an MPC , this work applies an SGP residual learning to the LUT -based steering mapping, so that the nominal controller remains lightweight. The SGP uses a small set of inducing points to summarize information from the training data, reducing the inference costs to support real-time compensation (see Table I ).

2026-10-09.title: MiniWAM: Learning Compact Future Targets for Efficient World-Action Modeling
2026-10-09.authors: Jie Chen , Ruofei Bai , Yuxin Cai , Yifeng Zhang , Chengyang He , Jun Li , Wei-Yun Yau , Guillaume Sartoretti
2026-10-09.abstract:
World modeling has emerged as an effective co-training objective for robot policies, giving rise to World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly predict actions and future states.
However, most WAMs predict future states in the native representation space of pretrained visual backbones, resulting in high-dimensional targets with substantial training cost.
We introduce MiniWAM, which instead predicts compact future representations learned from privileged current–future transitions.
To construct these targets, we propose Predictive Representations via Inverse Spatiotemporal Modeling (PRISM), which combines inverse-dynamics supervision with feature reconstruction to emphasize control-relevant transition information while preserving useful future-state information. With the learned PRISM encoder frozen, MiniWAM is trained to jointly predict the resulting targets and robot actions from current observations.
With 65 × 65\times fewer native future feature tokens, MiniWAM consistently outperforms native future-feature prediction with both DINOv3 and WAN2.1 VAE features, while achieving up to an 8 × 8\times speedup in world–action training.
At 0.25B parameters, MiniWAM is already competitive with substantially larger WAMs on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 simulation benchmarks. Representation analyses further show that PRISM contributes behavioral structure beyond feature reconstruction alone. These results demonstrate that effective world–action modeling does not require predicting native visual futures, and that compact predictive representations provide a strong and substantially more efficient target for policy learning. The project page is available at: https://j1dan.github.io/MiniWAM .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Learning to predict future observations alongside robot actions provides a powerful training signal for robot control.
Recent World Action Models (WAMs) exploit this idea by jointly learning robot actions and future visual states, encouraging policy representations to capture environment dynamics relevant to control ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026b ; Yuan et al., 2026a ; Cen et al., 2025 ) .
This paradigm has led to strong results across simulated and real-world manipulation.
However, it also introduces a substantial computational burden. Most WAMs model the future through high-dimensional visual representations, typically dense video-VAE latents inherited from video-generation models ( Wan et al., 2025 ) .
Predicting these representations requires processing large spatiotemporal token sequences, making world modeling considerably more expensive. Yet preserving every detail in the native feature space may not be necessary for action learning.

Prior work has increasingly sought to improve the efficiency of WAMs by reducing the cost of future generation ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) , sparsifying world–action interaction ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , or shrinking the model and token budget devoted to visual prediction ( Li et al., 2026 ) .
A complementary line of work replaces dense visual prediction with compact latent future supervision, using representations of future observations to shape policy-internal latent states ( Zheng et al., 2025 ; Su et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) .
Together, these approaches suggest that the benefits of future modeling need not rely on explicit high-dimensional visual rollouts.
However, existing efficiency-oriented WAMs still retain rich visual representations as their world-modeling targets, while latent approaches primarily incorporate future information through internal policy states or auxiliary conditioning spaces.
This leaves a distinct question: can we directly learn a compact yet control-relevant future representation that replaces dense visual prediction as the world-modeling target of a WAM for efficient training?

To learn such a representation, we propose Predictive Representations via Inverse Spatiotemporal Modeling (PRISM).
We aim to learn a compact representation that preserves information about both the actions underlying an observed transition and the resulting visual state.
During representation learning, a bottleneck encoder compresses current and future visual features into a compact set of latent tokens.
Inverse-dynamics supervision encourages these tokens to retain transition information informative of the underlying actions, while feature reconstruction encourages them to preserve future-state content, without requiring the full detail of the native visual representation.

We then introduce MiniWAM , which separates learning what to represent about the future from learning how to predict it.
First, PRISM learns to encode current–future visual transitions into compact targets through inverse-dynamics supervision and feature reconstruction.
The representation encoder is then frozen, and MiniWAM is trained to jointly predict the resulting PRISM target and robot actions given the current observation.
In this way, MiniWAM changes what the world model branch is trained to predict, rather than merely reducing the cost of predicting an otherwise unchanged visual future.

PRISM is not tied to a particular visual feature space, because the bottleneck is learned downstream of the visual representation. We instantiate the framework with both generative WAN2.1 VAE features ( Wan et al., 2025 ) and discriminative DINOv3 features ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) .
By replacing dense future representations with a compact set of latent tokens, PRISM reduces the number of future tokens by 65 × 65\times .
Despite this substantial compression, MiniWAM consistently outperforms matched variants that directly predict the corresponding native future representations, while requiring substantially less training computation.
These controlled comparisons show that the benefit does not arise simply from choosing a stronger visual encoder: replacing its dense future representation with the compact PRISM target improves the performance–efficiency trade-off.
This performance–efficiency advantage is illustrated in Figure 1 .

Empirically, MiniWAM reduces WAM training cost by up to 8 × \times while outperforming native future-feature prediction across simulation benchmarks.
A 0.25B MiniWAM is already competitive with WAMs built upon substantially larger pretrained video-generation backbones. Ablations show that adding inverse-dynamics supervision to reconstruction-only bottlenecks consistently improves performance across bottleneck capacities.
These results suggest that strong world–action modeling does not require predicting the native visual future: compact learned representations can provide a stronger and substantially more efficient target for predictive co-training.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

World models learn predictive representations of environment dynamics to support planning and policy learning, often in latent or pretrained feature spaces rather than pixel space ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) .
Building on this principle, recent methods increasingly integrate future prediction directly into policy training, giving rise to World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly model future states and robot actions ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026b ) .
Using future prediction as a co-training objective, WAMs encourage the policy to capture structured environment dynamics while sharing information between world and action streams. This formulation has achieved strong manipulation performance, but typically requires predicting dense spatiotemporal visual representations, such as video-VAE latents, substantially increasing the cost of policy training.

Recent work improves WAM efficiency through architectural simplification and reduced future-modeling computation ( Yuan et al., 2026b ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) .
A complementary line replaces dense future prediction with compact latent supervision, aligning or supervising policy-internal representations with features derived from future observations ( Zheng et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Su et al., 2026 ) .
These approaches show that predictive information can be represented more compactly than the original visual future, but typically retain native visual features as world-modeling targets or use compact representations primarily as internal policy states or conditioning signals.
Concurrent work ( Wang et al., 2026 ) shows that channel-wise compression of semantic prediction targets can yield strong world–action co-training performance.
PRISM instead learns a control-relevant transition representation as the world-prediction target, jointly compressing its spatial and temporal dimensions to substantially reduce the number of predicted tokens and the cost of world–action co-training.

2026-10-09.title: RESETTLE: Robotic Recovery through Disagreement-Triggered Retrieval and Efficient Corrective Control
2026-10-09.authors: Yuxin Chen , Senqiao Yang , Zixuan Wang , Jinhui Ye , Changsheng Lu , Pengguang Chen , Shu Liu , Zhuotao Tian , Jiaya Jia
2026-10-09.abstract:
Reliable robotic manipulation requires timely intervention to correct emerging deviations and restore progress after execution errors. However, recovery methods based on repeated vision-language reasoning or iterative online optimization can incur substantial latency, delaying intervention.
To address these challenges, we introduce RESETTLE ( R obotic r E covery through di S agr E ement- T riggered re T rieva L and E fficient Corrective Control), a model-agnostic framework that provides computationally efficient recovery at the action-execution interface of frozen robot policies.
RESETTLE triggers recovery when two action proposals independently sampled under identical conditioning persistently disagree. It retrieves a same-task demonstration reference using an adapted V-JEPA encoder and combines a state-servo prior with a guarded visual residual to execute one corrective action without online trajectory optimization or additional vision-language reasoning, then returns control to the base policy.
Across six base policies in simulation, RESETTLE achieves up to 8.70%, 6.28%, and 6.83% absolute success-rate gains on LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World, and RoboCasa Tabletop, respectively, with further improvements on four real-world tasks using two policies. In QwenPI-based comparisons, its monitoring-and-recovery computation latency is 74.04%–93.57% lower than VoLoAgent’s monitoring-and-planning latency for grasp and place tool calls. It also raises Harness VLA’s LIBERO-Pro Swap success from 42% to 50%, demonstrating compatibility with high-level agentic planning. Code available at: https://github.com/JIA-Lab-research/RESETTLE
2026-10-09.introduction:
Timely recovery is essential for reliable robotic manipulation, helping robots correct potentially harmful motions before an error occurs and restore task progress after errors. For example, adjusting the gripper orientation while approaching a moka pot can help avoid an ineffective grasp, whereas repositioning the gripper after a bowl is dropped can enable regrasping and subsequent placement.
These interventions support continued execution by addressing both emerging problems and the consequences of earlier mistakes. Despite substantial progress in vision–language–action (VLA) policies and world–action models (WAMs) ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026b ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) , environmental changes and imperfect actions can still drive execution into unfamiliar states where the policy struggles to make progress, highlighting the need for timely corrective intervention.

To equip robots with such corrective capabilities,
existing approaches broadly follow three strategies. First , corrective policy training incorporates
recovery behavior through additional supervision:
DAgger collects expert labels on learner-visited
states ( Ross et al., 2011 ) , while IntervenGen
generates recovery trajectories from human
interventions ( Hoque et al., 2024 ) .
Both expand the policy’s corrective experience but require
additional data and policy updates. Second , VLM-supervised recovery coordinates
corrective behaviors through semantic assessment.
Agentic Robot uses visual verification to trigger
corrections and retries ( Yang et al., 2025 ) ,
while VoLoAgent switches between policy execution and
recovery tools ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .
This supports flexible task-level recovery, but repeated
verification and recovery computation introduce latency. Third , inference-time action correction preserves
base-policy weights while adjusting action generation. LPB uses expert-feature distance to trigger dynamics-guided denoising on diffusion policies ( Sun and Song, 2026 ) . When extended to generalized VLA/WAMs, however, we observe greater overlap between feature-distance distributions of successful and failed executions, reducing its effectiveness for error detection; VLA-Corrector detects visual prediction discrepancies and applies gradient-guided replanning ( Pan et al., 2026 ) , while the online gradient computation adds recovery overhead. To push forward this line of research direction, we ask: Can we efficiently identify when a frozen policy
needs assistance and directly generate corrections
before deviations escalate into task failure?

To answer this question, we introduce RESETTLE , a framework for efficient action-level
recovery with frozen robot policies.
Many generative robot policies sample actions from noise
conditioned on observations and task
instructions ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ) .
This sampling process allows us to probe the stability
of action choices under identical conditioning.
For QwenPI, Figure 1 shows that
training-data inference and successful executions align
in the dominant low-disagreement region, whereas failed
executions exhibit heavier tails.
Motivated by this observation, RESETTLE monitors two
independently sampled proposals and triggers intervention
when their disagreement persists.
To guide recovery, we use successful demonstrations as
empirical anchors without requiring them to cover the
policy’s entire feasible operating range.
We initialize the recovery representation from
V-JEPA 2-AC ( Assran et al., 2025 ) and adapt it through
dynamics prediction and corrective-action supervision,
encouraging features useful for reference matching
and control.
The adapted encoder retrieves the nearest same-task
demonstration reference in its representation space,
together with the associated robot state.
A state-servo prior provides motion toward this reference
state, while a guarded visual residual uses current and
reference observations to adjust the motion to the scene.
Each intervention executes one corrective action before
returning control to the base policy with a fresh observation.
This design directly constructs recovery actions without
online trajectory optimization or additional
vision-language reasoning.

Our experiments assess both the effectiveness and
computational cost of local recovery.
Across six base policies on LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World,
and RoboCasa Tabletop ( Fei et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2020 ; Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) ,
RESETTLE improves aggregate task success while keeping
the base policies frozen.
Further improvements across four real-world tasks with
two policies support its applicability beyond simulation.
In QwenPI-based comparisons, measured monitoring-and-recovery computation latency is 74.04%–93.57% lower than VoLoAgent’s combined monitoring-and-planning latency for grasp and place tool calls, supporting the efficiency of direct correction.
Integration with Harness VLA on LIBERO-Pro
Swap ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) further
demonstrates that action-level recovery complements
high-level agentic planning.

Our contributions are twofold: i) We introduce RESETTLE , an efficient
action-level recovery framework that combines persistent
disagreement monitoring, demonstration retrieval, and direct
corrective control for frozen VLA policies and WAMs,
without base-policy fine-tuning, additional vision-language
reasoning calls for recovery, or online trajectory optimization; ii) We validate its effectiveness in simulation
and real-world manipulation, quantify reductions in
monitoring-and-recovery computation latency, and demonstrate
that local recovery complements high-level agentic planning
through integration with Harness VLA.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Generative VLA and World-Action Models. Generative policies such as Diffusion Policy, π 0 \pi_{0} ,
and SmolVLA produce actions through diffusion or
flow matching ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Shukor et al., 2025 ) .
Video-action architectures such as DiT4DiT and FastWAM
incorporate visual dynamics into policy learning,
with FastWAM omitting explicit future-video generation
at inference ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) .
Together, these approaches advance policy representations
and action generation.
RESETTLE complements these capabilities through
execution recovery at the action interface, leaving
base-policy weights and action-generation mechanisms
unchanged.

Latent World Models and JEPA-Based Control. DINO-WM and V-JEPA 2-AC predict visual latents under candidate actions and use online optimization for goal-directed control ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) . INTACT learns an intent-to-action interface with latent dynamics supervision, enabling control without online search ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . RESETTLE uses dynamics supervision during training, initializing its encoder and predictor from V-JEPA-2-AC. Its deployment role is selective recovery: demonstration states anchor a servo prior, refined by a guarded visual residual, before control returns to a frozen policy. The dynamics predictor is inactive at deployment.

Failure Recovery in Visuomotor Policies. DAgger incorporates expert labels on learner-visited states
into policy training, while RACER uses language-annotated
recovery trajectories ( Ross et al., 2011 ; Dai et al., 2025 ) .
Further, Agia et al. (2024) combine temporal action consistency with VLM for progress monitoring. The existing works show that semantic supervision supports failure diagnosis ( Duan et al., 2024 ) , constraint-based replanning ( Guo et al., 2024 ) , and recovery coordination ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) .
LPB and VLA-Corrector preserve policy weights, but they rely on gradient-guided action
refinement which adds computational burden ( Sun and Song, 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026 ) . Instead, our RESETTLE monitors persistent disagreement under identical
conditioning and directly constructs reference-based corrections, avoiding online dynamics prediction,
gradient guidance, and additional VLM reasoning while
complementing high-level supervision.

2026-10-09.title: Unifying Policy Learning and State Prediction through Spatial Language Modeling
2026-10-09.authors: Minye Wu , Zehao Wang , Tinne Tuytelaars
2026-10-09.abstract: Learning how actions change scene geometry can provide complementary supervision for goal-directed manipulation. We introduce Spatial Language Modeling, which represents scene contours, goals, action targets, and future states with a shared vocabulary of discrete coordinates and semantic tokens. A task-specific grammar organizes these elements into spatial sequences, allowing one autoregressive Transformer to learn action generation and action-conditioned state prediction through a common next-token objective. We train the model from scratch using random-play transition pretraining followed by joint action and state training on expert demonstrations. During pretraining, recorded action coordinates condition subsequent state predictions and are excluded from the prediction loss. During control, the model decodes only executable action targets and updates its history with newly observed states. We evaluate the approach on Push-T in simulation and on a real robot. The model achieves competitive simulation performance and higher task success and target coverage than the evaluated real-robot policy baselines. Training ablations show improved control with joint action and state sequences, with further gains from random-play pretraining. Given supplied action trajectories, the same model also predicts successive scene states, capturing the geometric effects of pushing.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Robot manipulation requires selecting actions that transform a scene toward a goal. In the Push-T task [ 6 ] , a planar pusher moves a T-shaped block to a target pose. The resulting motion depends on both object geometry and contact: the same pusher displacement can induce different combinations of translation and rotation depending on the contact location and the block’s orientation. Demonstrations of these interactions provide two complementary training signals: expert actions indicate how to act, while subsequent observations reveal the geometric changes that follow.

Policies such as Action Chunking Transformers, Diffusion Policy, and vision-language-action models learn actions from demonstrations [ 44 , 6 , 27 , 1 ] . World models use future predictions for rollout generation and planning [ 16 , 23 ] , while recent work also jointly models actions and future observations [ 18 ] . Predicting the geometric consequences of actions can provide complementary supervision for policy learning and enable the use of non-expert interaction data. A shared prediction interface allows this transition supervision to update the same model parameters used for action generation. We therefore seek a spatial representation that makes both targets accessible to the same autoregressive model.

Discrete workspace coordinates provide such an interface at the level of explicit geometry. We divide a bounded planar workspace into grid cells and assign each cell a coordinate token. Object contours, target regions, pusher positions, and action trajectories can then be represented in the same spatial vocabulary. A coordinate retains the same physical reference whether it appears in an observed contour, an executable action target, or a predicted future state. Semantic tokens identify whether coordinates belong to the pusher, the manipulated object, the goal, or a movement command. Geometry and actions thus retain their distinct roles within a shared spatial reference frame.

We develop this representation as Spatial Language Modeling . A task-specific grammar organizes scene observations, goals, action targets, and optional subsequent states into a Spatial Language Sentence (SLS). The grammar specifies how these elements are ordered and identified, while the model learns their coordinate content. A serializer converts observed geometry and recorded actions into spatial sentences, and a parser maps generated action blocks back to pusher targets. This formulation turns action generation and action-conditioned state prediction into sequence-completion tasks that share an output vocabulary and a next-token training objective.

We train an autoregressive Transformer from scratch using two sources of interaction data. Random-play pretraining first trains the model to predict scene transitions conditioned on recorded pusher motions. The action coordinates remain in the input sequence, but their prediction losses are masked; subsequent states supply targets describing the resulting geometry. Expert-demonstration training then supervises both action targets and selected subsequent states. These losses update the same parameters, making the geometric effects of interaction an explicit learning target alongside goal-directed action generation. This training scheme connects transition information from random interactions with action supervision from expert demonstrations.

During closed-loop control, an observed-history SLS prefix describes recent scene states and pusher actions. The model completes this prefix with consecutive action blocks, which are parsed into target coordinates and executed by the robot. Future-state blocks are excluded from control decoding, and new observations refresh the history for the next completion. The policy can therefore use a model trained with transition supervision while generating only actions at execution time. The same model also supports a separate prediction setting: given an initial scene and a supplied action trajectory, it generates successive scene states, using its previous state predictions as context.

We evaluate the formulation on Push-T in simulation and on a real robot. The model achieves competitive simulation performance and higher task success and target coverage than the evaluated real-robot policy baselines. Comparisons of training variants show improved control with interleaved action and state sequences, with further gains from random-play pretraining. In the state-prediction setting, predicted object states retain substantial geometric overlap with simulator reference states across the evaluated rollout horizon.

Our contributions are as follows:

We introduce a grammar-structured spatial representation that expresses observed geometry, goals, action targets, and future states in a shared coordinate vocabulary, enabling action and state prediction through autoregressive sequence completion.

We develop a training scheme that combines action-conditioned transition pretraining on random interactions with joint action and state supervision on expert demonstrations, and supports closed-loop execution through action-only decoding.

We demonstrate closed-loop Push-T control in simulation and on a real robot, and report results and comparisons that support the proposed formulation.

1. We introduce a grammar-structured spatial representation that expresses observed geometry, goals, action targets, and future states in a shared coordinate vocabulary, enabling action and state prediction through autoregressive sequence completion.

2. We develop a training scheme that combines action-conditioned transition pretraining on random interactions with joint action and state supervision on expert demonstrations, and supports closed-loop execution through action-only decoding.

3. We demonstrate closed-loop Push-T control in simulation and on a real robot, and report results and comparisons that support the proposed formulation.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Policy Learning and World Modeling. Imitation-learning policies use demonstrations to supervise action distributions. Action Chunking Transformers predict temporally extended action sequences, while Diffusion Policy generates actions through trajectory denoising [ 44 , 6 ] . Vision-language-action models connect action learning to vision-language pretraining, heterogeneous robot data, and fine-tuning [ 27 , 17 , 1 ] . Sequence modeling also provides a direct route to control: Decision Transformer predicts actions conditioned on returns and trajectory history, and Behavior Transformers combine action discretization with continuous corrections to model multimodal demonstrations [ 3 , 32 ] .

World models learn scene transitions and connect future predictions to control through several interfaces. DreamGen generates visual trajectories and obtains action labels through inverse dynamics or latent-action models for policy training [ 16 ] . LingBot-VA interleaves video prediction and action decoding in a causal sequence [ 18 ] . RoboDreamer synthesizes compositional video plans [ 46 ] , Dreamitate tracks generated tool trajectories for robot execution [ 20 ] , and LeWorldModel predicts future latent embeddings for planning [ 23 ] . Our formulation uses coordinate-level scene transitions and action targets within one next-token objective, combining random-play transition pretraining with joint action/state training on demonstrations.

Language Models in Spatial Computation. Language models have been applied to spatial intelligence through several representations of 3D scenes. PointLLM and 3D-LLM connect point-cloud or scene features to language models for object and scene understanding [ 38 , 14 ] . SegPoint extends this connection to instruction-conditioned segmentation [ 13 ] . LSceneLLM adaptively selects task-relevant scene details, while Scene-LLM combines scene-level and egocentric features for 3D visual reasoning [ 45 , 10 ] . Other approaches expose spatial structure through prompting: SayPlan uses hierarchical 3D scene graphs for robot task planning [ 31 ] , and 3DAxisPrompt supplies visual coordinate axes and masks for 3D grounding and reasoning [ 22 ] .

Geometric sequence models provide another route to spatial representation. PolyGen autoregressively generates mesh vertices and faces, and MeshGPT generates discrete codes from a learned geometric vocabulary [ 25 , 33 ] . Geometry-aware patch tokenization also supports mesh classification and segmentation [ 8 ] . LLaMA-Mesh and MeshLLM connect mesh generation to language models through textual representations of geometry [ 35 , 7 ] . In 2D vision, Pix2Seq represents bounding boxes and class labels as discrete output tokens, formulating detection as sequence prediction [ 5 ] .

Scene Understanding and Generation. 3D scene understanding develops geometric representations for identifying objects and their relationships. PointNet, PointNet++, PointConv, and Point Transformer learn features directly from point sets [ 29 , 30 , 37 , 43 ] . VoxFormer predicts volumetric geometry and semantics from images [ 19 ] , while ScanRefer and context-aware grounding models connect language to objects in reconstructed scenes [ 2 , 41 ] . Semantic scene graphs explicitly represent object relations [ 34 ] , and PointCLIP models extend recognition using vision-language priors [ 42 , 48 ] . Complementary generative methods synthesize voxel shapes [ 36 ] , surfaces and textured meshes [ 12 , 11 ] , or point clouds [ 40 ] . DreamFusion, Magic3D, and Fantasia3D use text-to-image diffusion priors for text-conditioned 3D content creation [ 28 , 21 , 4 ] . GALA3D organizes scene generation through layout-guided Gaussian representations [ 47 ] , while SmartSpatial uses depth and attention control to improve spatial arrangements in generated images [ 15 ] .

Across these directions, spatial representations provide the interface between scene geometry and task-dependent predictions. Our work organizes object contours, goals, action targets, and future-state targets into coordinate and semantic token sequences, with their roles and temporal order specified by a task grammar. In Push-T, this interface supports joint action/state training and direct closed-loop execution through one autoregressive language model.

2026-10-09.title: Instance-anchored interaction evidence: Grounding robot plans in human pointing and handling
2026-10-09.authors: Xinliang Xiao , Bowen Yang , Wenjing Zhang , Li Yang , Wei Zhou
2026-10-09.abstract: A robot that assists people must often act on what a person has shown rather than said: which of several identical cartons was pointed at, or which box was handled. The plan is executed from the final scene, whereas the evidence occurs earlier, possibly on objects that have since moved. We propose instance-anchored interaction evidence (IAE), which registers every object of the final scene to its public identifier, keeps each identity through the video by backward mask propagation, and describes every frame by the geometry between hands, forearms and these instances. An evidence network trained only from task outcomes scores the instances. For pointing tasks, a grammar-constrained dynamic program trained with a structured loss decodes object–destination programs; symbolic programs handle reference disambiguation and, without learning, episodic tasks. On 1,255 WatchAct benchmark requests, scored by symbolic execution, IAE reaches 64.2% plan success on implicit-intent tasks against 27.5% for a 32B vision-language model (strict success 49.7% against 15.4%), and 46.4% against 27.0% on restoration, reversal and imitation without task-specific training. Controls with the same perception overlays, the same 32 frames, forward tracking, or a relation model trained on the same labels do not explain the gain. Given IAE’s evidence as text with its meaning explained, the same language model reaches 57.4%: most of the gain comes from the instance-anchored evidence, and the explicit programs add 6.8 points at a fraction of the cost. Pointing remains the hardest case, with 16.9% strict success. The code is available at https://github.com/WeiZhou96/iae-watchact .
2026-10-09.introduction:
People frequently instruct others by acting instead of speaking. They point at the carton that should go into the tray, pick up one of two butter boxes and put it back, or rearrange a few objects and expect them to be restored later. For a robot that joins such a task, the video of the person carries information that the language instruction leaves out. The WatchAct benchmark [ 1 ] formalizes this setting: each instance pairs a real human-action video and an instruction with a simulated scene, and the robot plan is scored after execution. Its evaluation of current vision-language models (VLMs) shows that the video-to-plan step remains the main bottleneck.

A common approach is to give the video frames and the instruction to a VLM and let it produce the plan directly [ 2 , 3 ] . This works when the plan follows from what the scene looks like, but it breaks down when the plan depends on which instance a person interacted with. Scenes in these tasks contain several visually identical objects, the plan must refer to them by identifiers defined in the final scene, and the relevant gesture happens seconds earlier, sometimes on an object that has since been moved. Recent studies report that multimodal models ground pointing gestures poorly and are drawn to salient or nearby objects [ 4 ] , and that they perform close to chance when identical objects must be told apart by tracking them through time [ 5 ] . In our experiments, a 32B VLM reaches 27.5% plan success on the implicit-intent tasks of WatchAct and solves only 16.5% of restoration tasks, which require remembering where each object started.

The difficulty lies in the link between an observed interaction and a specific physical instance at execution time. Gesture-aware robot policies add hand skeletons or fingertip rays to the robot’s current observation [ 6 , 7 ] , and egocentric grounding methods resolve a single pointing act to a box [ 8 , 9 ] . In a third-person demonstration, however, the person may issue several deictic cues whose order defines which object goes where, and the identities that the plan needs are only defined at the end of the video. Mapping a whole video to a plan with a VLM leaves both the temporal composition and the identity bookkeeping implicit.

We propose to make this link explicit. Instance-anchored interaction evidence (IAE) registers every object of the final scene to its public identifier by fitting the public layout to the detections, propagates instance masks backwards through the video so that each identity is kept while objects are handled and moved, and describes each frame by the geometric relation between the detected hands, forearms and these instances. On top of this representation, simple programs produce the plan: which instances were indicated and in which order for pointing tasks, which instances were selected for reference disambiguation, and which instances moved and where they came from for episodic tasks.

Pointing is the case in which the raw geometry is least reliable. A downward point at a tray from behind the table can land on the basket in the image, and a retracting hand sweeps across other objects. Instead of annotating gesture episodes, we train a small evidence network from task outcomes only. The objects and destinations that appear in the goal of a training activity serve as video-level labels for a multiple-instance loss, and a dynamic program that enforces the deictic grammar of object and destination cues turns the frame-level evidence into a complete program. A structured loss on whole programs, computed with the same decoder, trains the evidence to make the decoded program correct rather than only to rank candidates.

Our contributions are:

An instance-anchored representation of human interaction in demonstration videos that combines public-layout registration, identity-preserving backward tracking and hand–forearm geometry, and that serves pointing, selection and manipulation tasks alike.

A weakly supervised learning scheme for deictic evidence that uses only task outcomes, combining a multiple-instance loss, grammar-constrained program decoding and a program-level structured loss.

An evaluation on 1,255 WatchAct requests with official and strict success metrics, activity-grouped and recording-order-blocked cross-validation, forward-tracking, same-supervision and matched-sampling controls, and baselines from two VLM families, including 8B and 32B models that receive the same perception overlays, the evidence of IAE itself, or are asked to verify ambiguous decisions.

1. An instance-anchored representation of human interaction in demonstration videos that combines public-layout registration, identity-preserving backward tracking and hand–forearm geometry, and that serves pointing, selection and manipulation tasks alike.

2. A weakly supervised learning scheme for deictic evidence that uses only task outcomes, combining a multiple-instance loss, grammar-constrained program decoding and a program-level structured loss.

3. An evaluation on 1,255 WatchAct requests with official and strict success metrics, activity-grouped and recording-order-blocked cross-validation, forward-tracking, same-supervision and matched-sampling controls, and baselines from two VLM families, including 8B and 32B models that receive the same perception overlays, the evidence of IAE itself, or are asked to verify ambiguous decisions.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Robot planning from human videos. Several systems derive robot plans or skills from human demonstration videos. GPT-4V has been prompted to convert task videos into executable robot programs [ 2 ] , SeeDo combines keyframe selection, perception and VLM reasoning for long-horizon pick-and-place plans [ 3 ] , and VLMimic grounds object-centric movements for fine-grained skills [ 10 ] . Video-conditioned policies such as Vid2Robot [ 11 ] , XSkill [ 12 ] and Track2Act [ 13 ] learn to act from demonstrations or predicted point tracks. Benchmarks now evaluate these abilities separately from low-level control: WatchAct [ 1 ] measures video-to-plan reasoning over 14 tasks, EgoPlan-Bench [ 14 ] evaluates egocentric planning, and RoboReel [ 15 ] evaluates learning from observation. These systems mostly rely on the VLM to resolve which object was involved. We instead compute this binding explicitly and keep the VLM only as a baseline and a verifier.

Understanding pointing and deictic gestures. DeePoint recognizes pointing and estimates its direction from body joints [ 16 ] . YouRefIt [ 17 ] shows that gestures matter as much as language for embodied reference, and the Touch-Line Transformer [ 18 ] constrains the referent to lie on the eye–fingertip line. GIRAF combines gesture detectors with language-model reasoning for table-top assistance [ 19 ] , and a gesture pseudo-language combines several types of gestures into sentences that state an action and its parameters, such as the object and its destination, parsed in real time against the object poses that the robot perceives [ 20 ] . Recent work adds hand skeletons and fingertip rays to vision-language-action policies [ 6 , 7 ] , feeds hand-keypoint tokens to multimodal models [ 9 ] , or benchmarks egocentric pointing resolution [ 8 , 4 , 21 ] . Most of these methods resolve one pointing act in the current view. Gesture sentences do compose several cues, but they are addressed to the robot as commands and interpreted in the scene it currently observes. Our setting differs in three respects that are evaluated together: the cues are observed in a third-person video, objects may move after they were indicated, so the operations must be bound to the instances of the scene at the end of the video, and the evidence model is learned from task outcomes without frame-level labels.

Weak supervision and structured decoding over time. Multiple-instance learning from video-level labels is standard for weakly supervised temporal action localization [ 22 ] . Transcript-supervised segmentation trains frame scores through differentiable alignment, for example with discriminative dynamic time warping [ 23 ] or outlier-robust alignment [ 24 ] . Our decoder is a dynamic program over deictic events, and our supervision is weaker than a transcript: only the final object–destination relations are known, while the order and the timing of the cues are latent.

Tracking, identity and program-based reasoning. Keeping track of objects that are handled, occluded or contained is a known weakness of video models [ 5 , 25 ] . Fine-tuning a VLM to generate object trajectories as explicit intermediate reasoning largely removes this weakness on a shell-game benchmark [ 5 ] ; such reasoning keeps the identities for the model’s own answer, whereas we bind them to the instances of the execution scene and do not fine-tune a VLM. Dedicated methods maintain object identity across long egocentric videos [ 26 ] . Promptable video segmentation [ 27 ] makes such tracking practical for arbitrary objects. Program-based visual reasoning composes perception modules with generated code [ 28 , 29 ] , and visual prompting overlays marks on images to improve grounding [ 30 ] . IAE follows the modular view but fixes the program structure by task and learns only the evidence that the programs consume. Uncertainty-aware planners ask for help when a plan is ambiguous [ 31 , 32 ] ; we use the decoding margin of our programs to report selective prediction.
