2026-10-09.title: Leveraging Human-In-The-Loop Demonstrations in Reinforcement Learning for Digital Twin-Driven Robot Flexibility
2026-10-09.authors: Yuzhu Sun , Mien Van , Nguyen Minh Nhat , Stephen McIlvanna , Sean McLoone
2026-10-09.abstract: Growing automation makes collaborative robots work in more variable environments, increasing the need for adaptation. We propose a human-in-the-loop online training framework combining a digital twin (DT), reinforcement learning (RL), and human demonstrations. Unlike DTs used mainly to generate synthetic data before task execution, our DT is synchronized with the physical system in real time through camera feeds, allowing the virtual robot to update its observations and policy from real-world feedback. A dual actor framework integrates imitation learning (IL) without adding a direct imitation loss to the RL actor, so demonstrations can guide adaptation instead of manual reprogramming. The proposed framework is demonstrated on the Ufactory Xarm5 collaborative robot, where the robot’s end-effector aims to reach the target position while avoiding obstacles. The experiments show that the framework can resume training after a change in the physical workspace and that, with a fixed set of non-optimal demonstrations, the dual actor framework achieves a much higher final success rate than two methods that add an imitation loss to the actor. The same pattern holds with real human demonstrations collected in virtual reality (VR): with demonstrations that never reach the goal, the dual actor framework reached 83–100% mean deterministic evaluation success, against 0–17% for the two imitation-loss methods.
2026-10-09.introduction:
With growing automation in Industry 5.0, sensor-equipped collaborative robots increasingly work alongside people rather than behind safety cages. More complex and unpredictable workspaces therefore require greater adaptability and flexibility [ 1 ] .
Artificial intelligence (AI), particularly reinforcement learning (RL), can improve robot autonomy by learning through trial and error from environmental feedback [ 2 ] .
Training RL agents directly on physical robots is costly, potentially hazardous, and often impractical.
A digital twin (DT) represents the physical workspace in simulation, allowing an RL agent to train and receive feedback without repeated physical trials.
Digital twins have often been used to generate synthetic data or provide simulated environments for training perception and control models before deployment [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Sim-to-real transfer methods seek to bridge the remaining differences between these virtual environments and the physical robot [ 7 , 8 ] . This separation between training and operation becomes a problem when the workspace changes: the twin may no longer reflect the physical scene, and the model or policy may need to be updated [ 9 ] . Such updates can interrupt task execution.

We address this gap with a PyBullet digital twin of the Ufactory Xarm5 [ 10 ] , linked to the physical robot through the Robot Operating System (ROS). Camera feeds keep the twin synchronized with the workspace in real time. If the twin detects that the current policy fails an obstacle-avoidance task after a workspace change, the RL agent resumes training in simulation.

During this resumed training, an operator can demonstrate the desired behaviour to guide the robot’s adaptation. This lets the operator contribute task knowledge without manually reprogramming the robot or needing specialist AI expertise.
Previous work has used demonstrations in offline reinforcement learning [ 11 , 12 ] and in methods combining imitation learning (IL) with RL [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Many studies use datasets generated by pre-trained experts, which help evaluate algorithms but differ from demonstrations collected from operators during deployment. For value learning, demonstrated transitions also need reward labels [ 12 ] ; raw human motion data do not provide these automatically. This makes it harder to use operator demonstrations during the resumed training described above.
To address this, we capture the operator’s movements in virtual reality (VR) and transfer them to the DT, where they guide the virtual robot. The DT evaluates each demonstrated step using the task reward and labels the resulting transitions automatically. The same environment therefore supports both resumed RL training and the preparation of human demonstrations.

The DT provides reward labels for human demonstrations, but it cannot make the demonstrated behaviour optimal. In our experiments, methods that combine IL and RL through an imitation loss on the RL actor [ 16 , 15 , 17 , 14 ] performed poorly with noisy, non-optimal demonstrations. The imitation loss encourages the actor to repeat those actions, potentially limiting its exploration of better solutions.
To address this limitation, we use two actors with distinct roles: an RL actor learns from interactions with the DT, while an IL actor learns from human demonstrations. Both paths contribute to the critic target, which favours the one with higher estimated value. With non-optimal demonstrations, the proposed framework reached over 80% mean final training success, while two imitation-loss baselines rarely completed the task. Fig. 1 shows the framework. Our main contributions are:

A hardware-in-the-loop DT that stays synchronized with the physical workspace and resumes RL training when a change causes the current policy to fail. Unlike DTs used mainly for synthetic data or training before deployment [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 3 ] , it updates the learned policy during operation until the task can again be completed.

A hardware-in-the-loop DT that stays synchronized with the physical workspace and resumes RL training when a change causes the current policy to fail. Unlike DTs used mainly for synthetic data or training before deployment [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 3 ] , it updates the learned policy during operation until the task can again be completed.

A dual actor framework in which demonstrations train a separate behaviour-cloning actor and guide the RL actor only through the critic target. Without a direct imitation loss, the RL actor can explore beyond poor demonstrations.

An evaluation with real human VR demonstrations that the DT labels with task rewards automatically. We report collection effort and workload; with complete demonstrations, the dual actor framework converged in all six seeds, compared with at most one for the imitation-loss baseline methods. We also test retraining in three additional modified scenes.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III describes the DT, and Section IV details the dual actor framework. Section V presents the experiments and discussion; Section VI concludes the paper.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Reinforcement Learning for Robotic Manipulation

RL has been used to learn robot behaviour from reward feedback [ 18 ] , with applications in path and motion planning [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] , task allocation [ 23 ] , human-robot collaboration [ 24 , 25 ] , and learning from demonstrations [ 26 ] . For collaborative robots, adapting a learned policy as people and workspaces change is particularly important. In [ 27 ] , RL balances human avoidance with task efficiency using an avatar animated from camera-based skeleton data. In [ 2 ] , goal-conditioned RL combines collision avoidance and contact-rich tasks while the co-worker’s hand follows random trajectories. Both [ 27 ] and [ 2 ] , however, train the policy before deployment and do not include a mechanism that detects a change in the environment during operation and resumes training in response. In contrast, this paper investigates hardware-in-the-loop retraining combined with DT technology, in which training is resumed during task execution whenever the DT detects that the environment has changed. This shifts the human effort from re-programming the robot to simply providing a few demonstrations.

## II-B Digital Twin

DTs provide virtual representations of physical systems [ 28 ] . Since Grieves first formulated the DT concept in the context of product lifecycle management [ 29 ] , the term has broadened from a static virtual replica into a decision-support layer that is expected to monitor, predict and optimize its physical counterpart [ 30 ] . A twin that is calibrated once at design time and not updated during operation can, however, become inaccurate when the environment changes, which limits its value precisely in the situations where an autonomous robot needs it most. Their connection to physical systems makes simulation useful for developing and testing robotics methods without repeated physical trials. Applications include grasping [ 31 , 32 ] , navigation [ 33 ] , obstacle avoidance [ 34 ] , and task allocation [ 35 , 36 ] .

For machine learning, DTs often provide synthetic data or simulated training environments before a robot begins its task. Some of these twins are synchronized with the physical system in real time [ 4 , 5 ] , others only in part [ 3 , 6 ] , and the grasp-detection model in [ 4 ] is updated by continual learning when new objects are introduced; these updates, however, are offline training sessions on collected data rather than training resumed during task execution. After training, workspace changes can leave the DT out of sync with the physical robot and require remodelling or reprogramming. In [ 37 ] , video feeds update a bridge-inspection robot’s DT so its path can be replanned online. The DT in [ 37 ] , however, drives an online planner rather than a learning agent, and the accuracy of the twin itself can drift over time after deployment. Building on this idea, this paper couples a continuously synchronized DT directly to the RL training loop, so that policy learning itself, and not only planning, reacts to real-time changes in the environment.

## II-C Integrating demonstrations into RL

Demonstrations can guide the RL updates made possible by a synchronized DT. Initializing or guiding RL with supervised learning from demonstrations is an established idea [ 38 ] . Prior studies have used them to improve exploration and sample efficiency [ 39 , 38 , 40 , 41 , 16 , 42 , 43 , 44 ] , but differ in how the data enter the learner.

Methods include (i) retaining demonstrations in a prioritized replay buffer [ 40 ] , (ii) pre-training with IL or offline RL before fine-tuning with RL [ 11 , 38 , 13 ] , and (iii) adding an IL loss to the RL actor objective [ 16 , 15 , 17 , 14 , 38 ] . A fourth approach selects between human teleoperation and autonomous controllers for each episode based on predicted success, with one controller learned online from demonstrations and RL [ 43 ] . In [ 40 ] , a simulated arm tracks a guided physical arm, and the demonstrations remain in a replay buffer alongside the agent’s experience; the effect of non-optimal demonstrations was not evaluated. In [ 38 ] , behaviour-cloning pre-training is followed by policy-gradient fine-tuning with a demonstration term whose weight decays. These training arrangements differ from ours, in which RL training resumes when the synchronized DT detects a change during operation.

Another line of work learns from demonstrations without manually assigned task rewards. Adversarial imitation learning [ 45 ] and inverse soft-Q learning [ 46 ] learn from raw trajectories, while SQIL [ 47 ] assigns a fixed reward to demonstrated transitions. These methods use demonstrations as examples of the desired behaviour. AWAC [ 11 ] , by contrast, uses reward-labelled offline data, including suboptimal transitions, and improves the policy through online interaction. In our framework, raw VR motion is replayed in the synchronized DT, which assigns the task reward to every transition. This allows an actor-critic learner to use human demonstrations without manual reward annotation. Demonstrations recorded in simulation are labelled automatically in [ 40 , 16 ] as well; here, the same synchronized DT also supports training resumed during operation.

Methods such as [ 16 , 15 , 17 ] add an auxiliary imitation loss directly to the RL actor. The Q-Filter in [ 16 ] addresses suboptimal demonstrations by disabling imitation of actions the critic values below the actor’s own actions. We therefore compare our dual actor framework with imitation-loss baselines with and without this filter. Table I summarizes their differences in online adaptation, DT synchronization, and treatment of non-optimal demonstrations.

2026-10-09.title: SuperNav: An Agentic Navigation System for Any Task in Any Scene
2026-10-09.authors: Jinkai Zhang , Jingyi Xu , Yuanhong Yu , Jiarui Guo , Ruizhen Hu , Hujun Bao , Xiaowei Zhou , Sida Peng
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-09.abstract:
General-purpose service robots need navigation systems that can handle diverse human requests in unfamiliar environments, combining task generality with scene generality.
Some existing methods fine-tune multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to predict navigation actions, making their behavior dependent on the coverage of navigation training data and potentially limiting generalization to new requests and environments.
Our key insight is to let the MLLM focus on interpreting requests, understanding scenes, and making decisions while preserving its general-purpose capabilities and delegating motion execution to navigation tools.
To realize this idea, we introduce SuperNav , which equips a pretrained MLLM with a specialized agent harness without navigation-specific fine-tuning of the MLLM.
Our harness supports these decisions with Navigation Skills, agent-oriented Tools for physical interaction, and task-progress and context management.
A unified visual-point interface connects decision-making to motion by allowing the model to specify destinations directly in images and revise its decisions from execution feedback.
Together, these components support sustained navigation across different task requirements and environments.
SuperNav outperforms four evaluated baselines on instance-level, multi-object, and demand-driven tasks.
Category-level evaluation on HM3D and deployment on a real quadruped robot further demonstrate its applicability across environments.
Project Page: https://zju3dv.github.io/SuperNav/
2026-10-09.introduction:
General-purpose service robots need navigation capabilities that can fulfill diverse human requests in unfamiliar environments.
These requests range from finding a specific object and visiting multiple targets to satisfying high-level needs and gathering evidence for embodied questions ( Batra et al., 2020 ; Khanna et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) .
For example, finding a specified object requires identifying the intended target, whereas “finding a place to rest” requires interpreting the need and deciding which objects in the scene can satisfy it.
Such differences change not only what the robot seeks, but also how it explores, tracks progress, and determines completion.
General navigation therefore requires both task generality , adapting to different requests, and scene generality , operating effectively in environments unseen during training and system development.

Task generality remains constrained by predefined workflows in modular zero-shot navigation systems.
These methods typically use pretrained vision-language models to assess the semantic relevance of observations to a goal and incorporate these assessments into goal-directed exploration scores ( Yokoyama et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) .
Although these scores adapt search to new observations, task-specific logic still determines when the model participates, how exploration transitions to goal confirmation, and when execution ends.
When a request changes from finding an object category to identifying a particular instance, visiting multiple targets, or satisfying an abstract need, its goal interpretation, progress tracking, and completion conditions also change, often requiring corresponding changes to this workflow.

End-to-end navigation methods seek to support diverse tasks within a single model, but their generalization across both tasks and scenes remains constrained by the coverage of navigation training data.
These approaches typically fine-tune pretrained vision-language models on paired navigation instructions and trajectories to predict actions from visual observations and language ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ) .
The resulting models encode associations between observations, instructions, and navigation behavior; transfer depends on whether those associations remain useful under new visual appearances, spatial layouts, and interaction conditions.
Consequently, learning to navigate in the training environments does not establish reliable navigation beyond them, and our cross-environment evaluations reveal substantial task-completion gaps for the evaluated methods (Section 4.1 ).

To address these constraints, we introduce SuperNav , a navigation framework that equips a pretrained multimodal large language model (MLLM) with a specialized agent harness for task and scene generality (Figure 1 ).
Our design is motivated by the success of general-purpose agents across diverse computer-use tasks, where harnesses support sustained tool use and context management ( Lopopolo, 2026 ; Young, 2025 ) .
Specifically, we use the MLLM’s existing capabilities to interpret requests, understand visual observations, and reason about subsequent actions.
To turn these decisions into sustained physical interaction, our harness provides optional Navigation Skills for procedural guidance and agent-oriented Tools for observation, motion, and task management.
It also maintains task-progress records and manages the interaction context, enabling the model to continue reasoning across successive actions.
This division of responsibilities lets the MLLM adapt its use of navigation capabilities to the current request and scene without navigation-specific fine-tuning.

Connecting these decisions to physical motion requires an interface that grounds the MLLM’s text outputs in the observed scene.
We therefore design a unified visual-point interface : the MLLM specifies a destination directly in an observation image, and the navigation tool executes the movement and returns feedback for the next decision.
Compared with predicting low-level actions directly ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Zhang et al., 2024a ) , this interface lets the model focus on selecting destinations while supporting different motion backends through the same interaction pattern.
SuperNav achieves higher success rates than these two action-prediction baselines on our single-object and demand-driven task sets (Table 1 ).

We construct an instance-navigation benchmark in Habitat-GS using InteriorGS scenes to evaluate single-object and ordered multi-object navigation.
We also evaluate demand-driven navigation using tasks from Demand-Bench ( Anonymous, 2026 ) under an adapted protocol, and category-level navigation on HM3Dv2 and HM3D-OVON, complemented by real-quadruped deployment.
SuperNav achieves 78.00% success on single-object navigation and 59.50% on demand-driven navigation, compared with 34.00% and 37.50% for the respective strongest baselines, UniNaVid and OmniNav’s Action Former (Table 1 ).
For category-level navigation, SuperNav achieves 73.33% success rate (SR) and 0.4105 success weighted by path length (SPL) on a 120-episode HM3D-OVON val-unseen subset at a 1 m threshold, without OVON-specific training or adaptation.
At the stricter 0.25 m threshold, it achieves 68.33% SR and 0.3837 SPL (Table 2 ).
These results examine the complete system across task requirements and scene settings, with motion-backend effects and evaluation-protocol differences analyzed in Section 4 .

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce SuperNav, a specialized agent harness that enables a pretrained MLLM to direct navigation across different requests through tool execution, task-progress tracking, and context management.

We design agent-oriented Tools with a unified visual-point motion interface and optional Navigation Skills, connecting model decisions to physical execution and providing reusable guidance for search, verification, and recovery.

We evaluate the system across category-level, instance-level, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation, together with real-robot deployment, examining its applicability across task and scene settings.

1. We introduce SuperNav, a specialized agent harness that enables a pretrained MLLM to direct navigation across different requests through tool execution, task-progress tracking, and context management.

2. We design agent-oriented Tools with a unified visual-point motion interface and optional Navigation Skills, connecting model decisions to physical execution and providing reusable guidance for search, verification, and recovery.

3. We evaluate the system across category-level, instance-level, multi-object, and demand-driven navigation, together with real-robot deployment, examining its applicability across task and scene settings.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Modular systems integrate semantic reasoning into dedicated mapping, exploration, and verification components.
SemExp ( Chaplot et al., 2020 ) , L3MVN ( Yu et al., 2023 ) , and VLFM ( Yokoyama et al., 2024a ) guide object search through learned exploration, language priors, or image–text relevance.
VoroNav ( Wu et al., 2024 ) and SG-Nav ( Yin et al., 2024 ) add topological or scene-graph context, while ApexNav ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) combines adaptive exploration with multi-frame target identification.
These systems assign models specific roles within task-oriented pipelines; SuperNav instead lets the MLLM select and coordinate available capabilities at runtime.

Hierarchical systems couple high-level model reasoning with dedicated navigation modules.
InstructNav ( Long et al., 2024 ) translates predicted actions and landmarks into trajectories through value maps; OmniNav ( Xue et al., 2026 ) combines prospective exploration and subgoal planning with a fast waypoint policy; SysNav ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) delegates within-room exploration and motion to classical algorithms under room-level VLM reasoning.
These systems already support online adaptation, demonstrating cooperation between model reasoning and learned or geometric execution.
SuperNav focuses on the interfaces and runtime through which the model chooses and combines capabilities across a task.

Agentic systems organize execution through callable capabilities and feedback.
Inner Monologue ( Huang et al., 2022 ) incorporates environmental feedback into planning, Code as Policies ( Liang et al., 2023 ) composes robotics APIs into executable policies, and SWE-agent ( Yang et al., 2024 ) studies how action and observation interfaces affect software-task performance.
Embodied harnesses extend this perspective: Show-Harness ( Chen et al., 2026b ) translates semantic actions into robot motion, AgenticNav ( Li et al., 2026 ) combines pixel-goal motion with depth queries and historical-image retrieval, and HarnessVLN ( Chen et al., 2026a ) maintains event memory and a spatiotemporal graph while validating action and termination proposals.
Concurrent DemandAgent ( Anonymous, 2026 ) addresses dependency-aware human demands through an Adaptive Demand Ledger, spatial memory, and embodied Skills, and introduces Demand-Bench. SuperNav studies task and scene generality through a unified visual-point interface with interchangeable motion backends, supported by context pruning and Navigation Skills.
Task-level action selection and semantic completion judgments remain with the MLLM.

2026-10-09.title: PIER: An Evidence-Gated Execution Interface for Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-09.authors: Zoe Li , Anze Wang , Zhongyu Chen , Jingran Hu
2026-10-09.comment: . Ancillary files include reproducibility code and retained experimental records
2026-10-09.abstract: Generating a plausible robot action does not establish that current observations justify its execution. Motivated by exploratory observations of high-confidence visual outputs under severe occlusion, we present PIER, an execution-authorization interface that separates evidence checks, decision provenance, and stage-scoped re-observation from hardware control. The deterministic gate evaluates declared visual and tactile inputs, while its caller maintains a budget of at most one re-observation per stage. We evaluate the implementation using 1,600 threshold-grid cases and 1,200 paired synthetic traces spanning score noise, missing tactile inputs, stale observations, and falsely reassuring scores. The finite grid yields zero declared invariant violations, and a matched Boolean baseline reproduces all non-recovery decisions. Under synthetic score noise, re-observation reduces valid-state denials from 57/120 to 18/120 while increasing invalid-state proceeds from 5/120 to 7/120. Stale and falsely reassuring inputs expose limitations that threshold checks alone cannot resolve. Exploratory visual, tactile, and robot setup records provide context but do not establish physical task performance. These results characterize an inspectable authorization interface and its input-contract limitations, without claiming superiority over equivalent rule logic, calibrated tactile accuracy, or certified physical safety.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Action generation and execution authorization are distinct problems. This distinction motivated an exploratory integration of video perception with SAM3 [ 12 ] , a model for prompted detection, segmentation, and tracking. A retained D405/SAM3 observation report describes severe-occlusion cases with maximum confidence 0.926–0.938 in which a downstream visual authorization rule nevertheless continued. The model produces perceptual outputs; the rule, not SAM3 itself, makes the continuation decision. Complete inference configurations and raw outputs were not recovered, so this observation motivates our question rather than serving as verified evidence of method effectiveness.

The question is whether a candidate action is supported by the observations required at its execution boundary. High model confidence is not itself a task-specific sufficiency certificate. Additional modalities may help, but missing, stale, or falsely reassuring tactile evidence creates its own failure modes. Re-observation can restore availability while also giving a noisy false positive another opportunity to pass. These trade-offs require explicit testing rather than an assumption that more modalities or retries always improve safety.

PIER emits proceed , re-observe , or safe stop , retaining evidence identifiers and decision reasons. A separate adapter and operator control physical execution. We position this work as an authorization-interface and software-verification study. Its contributions are: (1) an implemented scalar-evidence interface, trace session with caller-maintained per-stage retry state, and separate offline evidence-bundle validator; (2) reproducible finite checks and a matched synthetic stress suite that expose decision equivalence, noisy retry trade-offs, and input-contract gaps; and (3) an explicit separation of verified software behavior from exploratory sensing and setup observations. The threshold predicate is not a new control algorithm, and physical Touch/Insert performance remains unevaluated.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Runtime assurance and authorization

Simplex separates advanced control from a backup controller and manages control authority to maintain safety. Black-Box Simplex uses runtime checks without requiring controller internals and establishes safety under its stated assumptions [ 11 ] . PIER addresses a narrower interface: declared perceptual checks, evidence IDs, decision reasons, and per-stage re-observation accounting. It neither implements a verified backup controller nor proves invariant preservation for robot dynamics. Its finite checks and traces should therefore not be equated with runtime-assurance guarantees. Ordinary Boolean logic can reproduce its predicate; the evaluation characterizes this implementation and its limitations.

## II-B Cable manipulation and visuomotor policies

Cable spatial representations [ 1 ] , hierarchical imitation learning [ 2 ] , and tactile-driven primitives [ 3 ] motivate retaining route progress and local contact state. Diffusion policies model action distributions for visuomotor control [ 5 ] . PIER does not replace these policies; it defines an inspectable decision boundary around proposed actions. The present experiments do not compare policy learning or physical manipulation performance against these methods.

## II-C Tactile sensing and multimodal data

Optical tactile sensing, including DIGIT [ 4 ] , makes contact observations available at the end effector. WireFishing-M provides multimodal cable-insertion data [ 6 ] , and reactive visual–tactile policies exploit complementary feedback rates [ 7 ] . Our focus is how evidence availability affects authorization, rather than learning tactile features. In particular, the observed Xense image-difference signal is not equated with calibrated force or contact probability. Public datasets support interface checks only to the extent actually audited.

2026-10-09.title: UNITAS: A 3D-Native World Action Model for Embodied Manipulation
2026-10-09.authors: Ruixiang Wang , Yongyi Su , Wenlve Zhou , Bo Yue , Hengyan Liu , Dekun Lu , Yuxin Tian , Yihan Fang , Zerui Wu , Xing Hu , Jietao Chen , Yong Guo , Ziyan He , Junbin Yuan , Guiliang Liu , Xiaofen Xing , Kui Jia
2026-10-09.abstract:
World action models (WAMs) aim to answer a coupled physical question: given a task instruction, what motion should the robot execute, and how will that motion change the surrounding world? Most existing WAMs build on pretrained video generators and represent world evolution through images or visual latents. Robotic interaction, however, takes place in metric three-dimensional space, while images are view-dependent projections whose pixel distances do not directly encode physical distances.
We introduce Unitas , to our knowledge the first 3D-native world action model that unifies observations, actions, and scene dynamics in a shared metric 3D frame within each interaction, using a common representation across robot embodiments and human hands. Action flow represents human hands and robot grippers as 3D point trajectories, while scene flow describes scene-point displacements conditioned on these trajectories. World-aligned 3D positional embeddings ground visual tokens with or without depth input, and a physical-time trajectory tokenizer encodes each point trajectory as one token anchored at its current 3D position. This interface supports both direct action execution and
action-conditioned scene prediction.
With 1.7B parameters, Unitas achieves the best action-conditioned
scene prediction on RoboTwin among the compared methods,
with up to 49% lower displacement errors than PointWorld,
and state-of-the-art manipulation success, including 99.8%
on LIBERO and an average of 85%
across real-world tasks. The code is available at https://github.com/DexForce/UNITAS .
2026-10-09.introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) aim to answer a coupled physical question: given a task instruction, what motion should the robot execute,
and how will that motion change the surrounding world? Most existing WAMs couple action learning with prediction of future
images or visual latents, increasingly building on pretrained video models ( Yang et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026b ; Zhou et al., 2026b ) .
Robotic interaction, however, takes place in metric three-dimensional
space, and an image is only a view-dependent projection of that space.

The same robot motion, object displacement, or contact event can produce
different pixel changes across views, and equal pixel displacements
need not correspond to equal physical distances ( Ze et al., 2024 ; Qu et al., 2025 ) .
Differences in camera intrinsics and camera-to-robot poses further
make this mapping vary across embodiments.
Evaluations of video-based WAMs report sensitivity to viewpoint and
robot-state changes ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and a
photorealistic prediction may still misrepresent object displacement,
deform rigid geometry, or allow static regions to drift ( Huang et al., 2026 ) .
Such visual representations leave metric motion and contact relationships
implicit for spatial reasoning, prediction, and control.

Recent methods incorporate depth, optical flow, scene flow, or
reconstructed 4D geometry into prediction ( Zhen et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) or ground action generation in explicit 3D structure ( Shridhar et al., 2023 ; Ze et al., 2024 ; Zhen et al., 2024 ; Qu et al., 2025 ) .
Yet geometry often serves as an input cue or auxiliary prediction target,
rather than a shared interface for action generation and scene dynamics.
PointWorld ( Huang et al., 2026 ) directly predicts metric point
flows conditioned on externally supplied robot motion, rather than
generating that motion from a task instruction.
A 3D-native WAM should place observations, actions, and resulting scene
changes in a shared metric frame, enabling task-conditioned behavior,
consequence prediction, and executable control.

We introduce Unitas , UNI fied T rajectories for A ction and S cene flow.
To our knowledge, it is the first 3D-native world action model that
aligns observations, actions, and scene dynamics in a shared metric
frame within each prediction window, using a common representation
across robot embodiments and human hands, as illustrated in
Fig. 1 .

Realizing this 3D-native world action model presents three challenges.
First, visual observations must be grounded in metric space even
when depth is unavailable. We propose world-aligned 3D position embeddings derived from observed depth or learned weights over
candidate positions along calibrated camera rays. Second, human hands and robot grippers have different morphologies
and control interfaces. We propose action flow , which represents their motion as trajectories of corresponding 3D points in the shared frame. Third, trajectories differ in frame rate and duration across data sources. Representing each timestep as a token allocates backbone capacity
across unequal physical-time intervals. We propose a physical-time trajectory tokenizer , which aligns each trajectory to elapsed time and encodes the whole trajectory as one token before the backbone. Scene flow describes scene-point displacements decoded from trajectory
tokens conditioned on action flow.

In the backbone, observation tokens
are grounded in world coordinates, while action-flow tokens across
embodiments and scene-flow tokens are anchored at each point’s current
3D position, allowing the network to model motion through features
associated with fixed spatial anchors.
Given the instruction and current observations, a layer-coupled
Mixture-of-Transformers jointly models point trajectories and executable
commands. This supports two modes: policy mode directly generates
executable actions, while simulator mode predicts scene changes
conditioned on externally supplied action flow.
A causal attention mask enables key–value caching of shared context
across denoising steps, reducing repeated computation and accelerating
inference.

We evaluate Unitas on action-conditioned scene prediction and
robotic manipulation.
In simulator mode, it leads the compared methods across all four
RoboTwin scene-prediction metrics, reducing Moving ADE, Moving FDE,
and Static ADE by 35%, 21%, and 49%, respectively, relative to
PointWorld ( Huang et al., 2026 ) .
In policy mode, it achieves 99.8% success on LIBERO and outperforms
larger video-based WAMs on RoboTwin.
It leads the compared methods in VLABench success rate and progress
score, and reaches 89.1% success on LIBERO-Plus with strong robustness
to camera and robot-state changes.
Real-robot success reaches 90% on Organize Books and 65% on Pack the Ball , exceeding both baselines.
Ablations show that world-aligned visual grounding, action- and scene-flow
supervision, and motion history improve policy performance and robustness.

Our contributions are:

To our knowledge, Unitas is the first 3D-native world action
model that aligns observations, actions, and scene dynamics in a
shared metric frame, using a common representation across robot
embodiments and human hands.

Action flow represents human hands and robot grippers through
point trajectories, while scene flow represents the environmental
response conditioned on that motion. Both policy and simulator modes
use this interface.

World-aligned positional embeddings ground visual observations
with or without depth, and a physical-time trajectory tokenizer
encodes each point trajectory as one token spatially anchored at its
current 3D position.

With 1.7B parameters, Unitas achieves leading action-conditioned
scene prediction and strong manipulation performance in simulation
and on real hardware.

1. To our knowledge, Unitas is the first 3D-native world action
model that aligns observations, actions, and scene dynamics in a
shared metric frame, using a common representation across robot
embodiments and human hands.

2. Action flow represents human hands and robot grippers through
point trajectories, while scene flow represents the environmental
response conditioned on that motion. Both policy and simulator modes
use this interface.

3. World-aligned positional embeddings ground visual observations
with or without depth, and a physical-time trajectory tokenizer
encodes each point trajectory as one token spatially anchored at its
current 3D position.

4. With 1.7B parameters, Unitas achieves leading action-conditioned

and on real hardware.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Video world–action modeling. Video-based policies use future prediction for control ( Hu et al., 2024 ) ,
with early WAMs coupling prediction and action learning through shared
representations and generative objectives ( Li et al., 2025b ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025a ) .
Video-generation priors subsequently support joint video–action learning
and future-conditioned policies ( Liao et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) ,
while heterogeneous robot and video-only data support cross-task and
cross-embodiment transfer ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) .
Efficient variants omit future generation at deployment or replace it
with latent subgoals ( Yuan et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) .
These models primarily represent world evolution in images or visual
latents. Reported sensitivity to viewpoint and robot initial-state changes ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Hong et al., 2026 ) highlights the importance
of grounding perception, world evolution, and executable actions in a
shared physical space.

Policy learning in 3D space. Explicit 3D representations improve spatial understanding for manipulation ( Shridhar et al., 2023 ; Ze et al., 2024 ; Zhen et al., 2024 ; Qu et al., 2025 ) .
Geometry-aware world models augment visual prediction with image-aligned
geometric signals ( Zhen et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) .
In policy learning, LaMP ( Wang et al., 2026b ) and
GeomVLA ( Xiong et al., 2026 ) use intermediate motion features from
trajectory denoising to condition action generation. PointWorld ( Huang et al., 2026 ) follows the complementary direction, predicting scene flow conditioned
on robot motion for planning. Unitas jointly models agent motion and
its conditional scene response through point flows, while supporting
direct command execution without generating scene flows.

Unified action representations for manipulation. Cross-embodiment learning must reconcile different morphologies and
control interfaces ( Chi et al., 2024 ) . Generalist policies use
embodiment-specific prompts, canonical state–action formats, and aligned
end-effector conventions ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026a ; Xiaomi Robotics Team et al., 2026 ) .
Point flows provide transferable motion targets across embodiments ( Yuan et al., 2024 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025b ) ,
connecting object-motion prediction to control ( Zhi et al., 2025 ; Dharmarajan et al., 2025 ) and representing
robot and object trajectories ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . Unitas unifies human-hand, robot-gripper, and scene trajectories with
a shared physical-time tokenizer.

2026-10-09.title: ManiUnit: A Manipulation Skill Dataset and Benchmark for Long-Horizon Tasks
2026-10-09.authors: Guoting Wei , Dawei Yan , Xia Yuan , Gengming Zhang , Yelin He , Guodong Du , Jiaquan Ye , Heng Zhang , Xinming Wei , Xianbiao Qi , Chunxia Zhao , Haokui Zhang , Rong Xiao
2026-10-09.abstract:
Long-horizon mobile manipulation requires a robot to navigate multi-room environments and execute a sequence of manipulation skills under a single natural language instruction.
Learning and evaluating these skills present three challenges: similar observations under a fixed task instruction may make skill selection ambiguous; even when a preceding skill succeeds, the robot state inherited by the next skill may deviate from its demonstrated starting states and affect execution; and task-level metrics hinder skill-specific diagnosis, while early failures leave later skills untested.
We therefore introduce ManiUnit, a manipulation skill dataset and benchmark built from 50 BEHAVIOR-1K activities.
Its dataset contains 137,899 segments across 21 skill types and 417 subtasks, and its benchmark contains 1,260 test instances.
Correspondingly, ManiUnit pairs each segment with an explicit subtask instruction; measures sensitivity to perturbations of the robot’s starting base position or joint configuration; and restores intermediate simulator states and defines local success conditions so that each skill can be evaluated without executing preceding stages.
Evaluations of representative vision-language-action (VLA) policies show that similar aggregate scores can hide substantial per-skill differences.
The tested starting-state perturbations also degrade execution: on the full benchmark, joint perturbations reduce success rates by approximately 56% relative to those from demonstrated starting states.
On two long-horizon activities, a skill policy trained on ManiUnit segments achieves 78.7% local manipulation success, compared with 49.3% for a task policy trained on complete demonstrations.
The trained skills further support complete-task execution on these activities, as coordinating the task and skill policies through a planner raises full-task success from 4.0% to 18.0%.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Enabling robots to complete long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks in everyday environments is a central challenge for embodied AI.
Unlike tabletop manipulation, which operates in a fixed workspace, this setting requires robots to navigate across multi-room environments and execute a sequence of interdependent manipulation skills guided by a single natural language instruction.
Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025 ) have achieved strong results on tabletop benchmarks: StarVLA- π \pi ( StarVLA Community, 2026 ) , for example, reaches 95.7% success on LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) and 88.8% under the randomized setting of RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .
Despite this progress, reliable execution of long-horizon tasks remains
challenging: the winning entry in the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge achieved
a full-task success rate of only 12.4% on the held-out test set ( Larchenko et al., 2025 ) , leaving substantial room for improvement.

Consider one such task, “make microwave popcorn,” which requires navigation interleaved with opening the microwave door, picking up the popcorn bag, placing it inside, closing the door, and turning on the microwave. Such sequences pose three challenges for skill learning and evaluation.
(1) Skill ambiguity : when a policy follows the same task instruction throughout execution, it needs to infer the current stage from its observations and act accordingly.
This inference can break down when different stages share similar visual context: before loading food, the robot faces a closed microwave door and must open it, but after placing the food inside and closing the door, it again faces the same closed door yet must now turn on the microwave instead of opening the door.
(2) Starting-state mismatch : during sequential execution, even a successfully completed skill may leave the robot in a base position or joint configuration that differs from the starting states in the next skill’s training demonstrations, and this mismatch can cause a policy that succeeds from demonstrated starting states to fail when following a preceding skill.
(3) Evaluation opacity : overall task success reflects both navigation and manipulation, making it difficult to identify which skills limit performance; moreover, an early failure can prevent later skills from being attempted.

These challenges motivate treating individual manipulation operations as units of training and evaluation.
We therefore introduce ManiUnit, a manipulation skill dataset and benchmark built by segmenting long-horizon BEHAVIOR-1K demonstrations ( Li et al., 2023 ) into such operations.
Figure 1 maps each challenge to the corresponding design choice. For skill ambiguity , ManiUnit attaches an explicit subtask instruction to each segment, naming the operation, the objects it acts on, and the spatial context, keeping the intended operation explicit during skill learning and evaluation. For starting-state mismatch , ManiUnit evaluates each skill
under three conditions: the demonstrated state, a base-position
perturbation, and a joint-configuration perturbation.
These controlled tests measure how variations in the robot’s
starting state affect skill execution. For evaluation opacity , ManiUnit constructs test instances by restoring intermediate simulator states and defining local success conditions for each subtask, so every skill can be evaluated independently without first executing the stages that precede it.
The dataset covers 50 activities with 21 skill types, 417 subtasks, and 137,899 segments with a mean duration of 17.9 seconds, each paired with head and wrist RGB streams, robot states, and actions.
The benchmark contains 1,260 test instances, drawn from 20 operation starts per skill type under the three starting-state conditions.

Evaluating representative VLA policies on ManiUnit shows that similar aggregate scores can hide substantial differences in per-skill performance.
The evaluations also reveal pronounced sensitivity to the tested starting-state perturbations: on the full benchmark, joint perturbations reduce success rates by approximately 56% relative to those from demonstrated starting states.
On Turning On Radio and Picking Up Trash, we compare task and skill policies initialized from the same pretrained weights.
The skill policy trained on ManiUnit segments achieves 78.7% local manipulation success, compared with 49.3% for the task policy trained on complete demonstrations.
To deploy these skills in complete tasks, a planner coordinates the task and skill policies and supplies the appropriate subtask instructions (Figure 1 , bottom).
On the same activities, the combined system achieves 18.0% full-task success, compared with 4.0% for the task policy alone.

Our contributions are threefold.
(1) We introduce the ManiUnit dataset: 137,899 segments from 50 BEHAVIOR-1K activities with explicit subtask instructions, organized by skill type and subtask to support mixed-skill training and targeted data selection.
(2) We construct the ManiUnit benchmark: 1,260 test instances from restored intermediate states with local success conditions and separate base and joint perturbations, enabling independent per-skill evaluation and measurement of starting-state sensitivity.
(3) We evaluate representative VLA policies to characterize skill performance and starting-state sensitivity, and show on two long-horizon activities that ManiUnit-trained skills improve local manipulation success and support complete-task execution through policy composition.

# 2 ManiUnit Dataset and Benchmark

## 2.1 Overview

To study manipulation skills independently within long-horizon tasks, we construct ManiUnit from the 2025 Challenge demonstrations of 50 BEHAVIOR-1K activities ( Li et al., 2023 ) .
ManiUnit comprises a dataset of manipulation segments paired with explicit subtask instructions and a benchmark for evaluating selected operations from restored starting states.
Figure 2 summarizes how the source demonstrations are processed into these training and evaluation resources.

The dataset distinguishes three levels of organization.
A skill type identifies an operation category, such as Pour.
A subtask is defined by an instruction specifying the operation, objects, and spatial context, such as “pour the grated cheese from the tupperware onto the pizza dough.”
A segment records one demonstrated execution of that subtask.
Grouping segments by skill type and subtask allows researchers to pool demonstrations across source activities or select data for particular operations. ManiUnit-Full contains 21 skill types, 417 subtasks, and 137,899 segments.
We also curate ManiUnit-Lite , a subset of 10,588 segments across 7 skill types, to reduce the computational cost of repeated experiments.
Table 4 in Appendix B.1 reports the per-skill inventory of ManiUnit-Full.

For evaluation, we select operation starts from the source demonstrations and restore the corresponding robot and scene states.
For each selected subtask, we manually define a local BDDL goal that specifies the object states and relations required to complete the manipulation operation.
The restored state, subtask instruction, and local goal together form a test instance, allowing the operation to be evaluated without executing preceding task stages.
To measure sensitivity to starting-state variations, we construct three conditions for each selected start: Original, Base Perturbation, and Joint Perturbation.
The Full and Lite evaluation suites contain 1,260 and 186 test instances, respectively.
Sections 2.2 and 2.3 describe the dataset and benchmark construction procedures.

## 2.2 Dataset Construction

As shown in Figure 2 , the source demonstrations contain RGB observations, robot states, and actions, together with temporal annotations of navigation and manipulation.
Each annotation records an action label, the participating objects, and the action’s start and end frames.
However, these intervals do not always correspond to the manipulation segments needed for training.
For example, pushing an object into reach and picking it up may be annotated separately despite contributing to the same Pick Up operation, while a recorded pickup interval may also include navigation before grasping or inactivity afterward.
To preserve complete manipulation operations while reducing surrounding navigation and inactivity, we extract and merge the relevant action intervals and refine their boundaries.
We then curate an explicit subtask instruction for each resulting segment.

We first extract manipulation intervals based on the annotated actions.
For each source activity, we manually specify which annotations to retain and apply this selection across its episodes.
For example, in the Picking Up Trash activity, we retain all annotated pickup and placement actions, each yielding an initial segment.
The recorded start and end frames of each retained annotation provide the initial segment boundaries.

Since supporting motions may be annotated separately from the operation they serve, we define merging rules to combine them into complete manipulation segments.
In the board-game example in Figure 2 , pushing the game toward the bed edge prepares it for grasping.
We therefore combine the push and subsequent pickup into one Pick Up segment.
The merged segment spans the start of the first contributing action through the end of the last, retaining all intervening frames.
Appendix B.2 details the extraction and merging rules.

We refine the boundaries of the extracted and merged segments to reduce navigation and inactivity around the target operation.
Reaching for and handling objects often require raising or extending the arms, so we use deviations from a fixed lowered-arm reference posture as a heuristic cue for manipulation.
We measure this deviation as

The extracted segments retain their action labels and participating objects from the source annotations.
We group segments by their action and object combination.
For each group, we convert the simulator object identifiers to readable names and define an instruction template that specifies the action and the objects’ roles.
For example, Pour segments with grated cheese, tupperware, and pizza dough yield “pour the grated cheese from the tupperware onto the pizza dough,” explicitly naming what is transferred, its source, and its destination.
We then manually review every episode across all source activities, checking each segment’s instruction against its video.
This review refines the description of the operation, objects, and spatial relations, and corrects errors inherited from the source annotations.

The curated segments are grouped by skill type and subtask instruction, supporting pooled training across activities and targeted selection of particular operations.
Each segment contains its skill-type label, subtask instruction, three RGB streams from the head and both wrist cameras, and temporally aligned robot states and actions.
We retain each segment’s source activity and episode, frame boundaries, and object identifiers.
These records enable benchmark construction to locate the operation’s starting state and identify the corresponding simulator objects (Section 2.3 ).
Appendix E presents recorded examples with their subtask instructions.

## 2.3 Benchmark Construction

The curated segments provide recorded demonstrations for training, but evaluating a policy on these operations requires running the policy in simulation.
For each selected operation, we therefore restore a reference starting state from its source demonstration so that the policy can begin without executing preceding task stages.
We also define a local goal that specifies when the operation is complete.
Together with the segment’s curated subtask instruction, the restored state and local goal form a test instance:

The reference starting state must preserve the effects of earlier task stages on the robot and scene.
For example, a Place operation may begin with the target object already in the robot’s gripper.
We locate this starting point using the segment’s source episode and start frame.
A single recorded frame may not describe the complete scene: the states of sleeping objects are not always recorded, and object additions and removals are stored separately.
We therefore start from the episode’s saved scene configuration and replay the recorded states and transitions up to the selected frame.
Because the saved state may lack the simulator’s assisted-grasp constraint, we recover it where needed so that held objects remain attached when physics resumes.
We also stabilize the restored state to reduce drift caused by residual velocities from the preceding motion.
Appendix C.1 details the restoration procedure.

Restoring the starting state allows an operation to be executed independently, but evaluating its outcome also requires a success condition for that operation.
The original task goal describes completion of the entire activity and does not directly specify when each intermediate operation has succeeded.
We therefore manually define a local goal g g for each evaluated subtask using the original task definition, the curated instruction ℓ \ell , and the source action annotations.
We express the required object states and relations as BDDL predicates ( Srivastava et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ) .
The segment’s recorded object identifiers bind these predicates to the same simulator objects named in the instruction.

For example, placing a soda can o o in a trash can c c requires the can to be inside c c and no longer touching the robot r r :

During sequential execution, each skill begins from the robot configuration left by preceding operations.
Even when those operations succeed, the resulting configuration may differ from those represented in training and affect the next skill’s execution ( Gu et al., 2023 ) .
To measure sensitivity to this starting-state mismatch, we treat each selected operation start as an evaluation anchor and construct three starting-state conditions for it.
Original uses the reference state restored from the source demonstration.
Base Perturbation translates the robot’s base while preserving its orientation and the arm, torso, and gripper configurations.
Joint Perturbation changes selected arm or torso joint positions while preserving the base pose and gripper configuration.
The subtask instruction ℓ \ell , target identities, and local goal g g remain fixed across conditions.

Each perturbed state must preserve the preconditions for beginning the operation; a Place operation, for example, must still begin with the intended object in hand.
We therefore verify the intended configuration changes and reject variants that introduce unintended collisions or disrupt the required object relations.
Appendix C.3 describes these checks and the realized perturbation magnitudes.

Before accepting a test instance, we load it through the evaluation pipeline to verify the restored state, object bindings, and manipulation preconditions.
We also check that the local goal is initially unsatisfied, g ⁡ ( s 0 ) = 0 g(s_{0})=0 , and manually inspect the rendered starting scene.
Invalid instances are corrected or replaced and validated again.
Appendix C.5 details these checks.

Beyond robot-state variations, the same construction procedure supports targeted tests of how scene factors affect a chosen skill.
We demonstrate this with Pick Up by varying target position, target color, and the presence of a nearby distractor, one factor at a time.
The robot’s starting configuration, target identity, subtask instruction, and local goal remain fixed across these variants.
For position changes, associated objects or contents are moved with the target as needed to preserve their spatial relations.
Appendix C.4 describes the construction of these variants.

To extend these tests to another skill, researchers can select source demonstrations and a factor of interest, specify the object bindings and local goal, and reuse the restoration and validation procedures above.
The shared subtask definitions link each test instance to corresponding training segments, supporting targeted data selection and fine-tuning where evaluation reveals weaknesses.

2026-10-09.title: A Minimal Optical-Flow Representation for Vision-Based Tactile Rotation Classification in Robotic Manipulation Across Gravity Domains
2026-10-09.authors: Oscar Martinez-Bernal , Mario Cavero-Vidal , Francesco Grella , Carol Martinez
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-09.abstract:
Vision-based tactile sensors provide rich contact information, but processing high-resolution images can be costly for resource-constrained platforms such as space robots.
This work investigates whether a compact representation of tactile motion can classify object rotation across different gravity conditions. Dense optical flow from a simulated GelSight Mini is aggregated over a 7 × 9 7\times 9 grid into 126 features and used to classify the direction of load-induced rotation under Earth, Mars, Moon, and orbital gravity. Gravity causes a small but significant shift in these features, accounting for 1.6% of their variance ( R 2 = 0.016 R^{2}=0.016 ). Despite its small magnitude, this shift affects models trained only on Earth data: XGBoost accuracy decreases from 94.4% on Earth to 75.9% in orbit. In contrast, a single model trained across all four gravity domains achieves 96.3% overall accuracy and 95.1–97.0% across individual domains, without using gravity as an input. The representation can also be reduced to 40 features while retaining 95.7% accuracy, with XGBoost requiring only 0.14 ms per inference. These findings show that Earth-gravity performance alone is insufficient to establish the transferability of tactile perception for space robotic manipulation, highlighting the need to account for gravity-induced domain shifts during training and validation.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Contact-rich manipulation is essential for space robotic operations such as on-orbit servicing [ 1 ] , in-space assembly, maintenance, inspection, and planetary sample collection [ 2 ] . These operations require robots to interpret local contact under limited sensing, uncertain object properties, and gravity conditions that differ from those on Earth. Reliable contact perception is therefore important for safe robotic manipulation [ 3 ] . Vision-based tactile sensors offer a promising solution by converting local contact interactions into high-resolution images [ 4 ] .

While these images provide rich contact information, processing them directly can be computationally expensive for resource-constrained platforms such as space robots. Compact representations can reduce this computational burden. In particular, optical flow captures tactile motion using a reduced set of features and has been used to estimate displacement, deformation, geometry, and force, as well as for lightweight classification tasks [ 5 ] .

However, tactile perception methods are typically developed and validated under Earth gravity. Changes in gravity affect object dynamics and may therefore alter the tactile signals observed during manipulation. Consequently, a representation or classifier that performs well on Earth may not transfer directly to reduced-gravity environments. This is particularly relevant for space robotics, where tactile perception systems must operate under conditions that are difficult to reproduce and validate experimentally on Earth.

Therefore, this work investigates two questions: (1) whether a compact representation of tactile motion is sufficient to classify a manipulation event, and (2) whether its performance transfers across gravity conditions. These questions are studied in simulation using the load-induced rotation of a grasped object as a controlled interaction event. The direction of rotation describes how the object moves relative to the grasp and can provide information for corrective manipulation before grasp stability is compromised. Unlike a wrist-mounted force/torque sensor, tactile sensing observes this motion directly at the contact interface and preserves its local spatial structure.

The tactile response is represented by dense optical flow between consecutive frames of a simulated GelSight Mini. The flow field is spatially aggregated over a fixed grid and used as input to lightweight classifiers, without providing gravity as an input. The same interaction task and representation are evaluated under Earth, Mars, Moon, and orbital gravity. This controlled setup allows us to measure how gravity affects the tactile representation and whether this domain shift affects classification performance (Fig. 1 ).

The analysis first quantifies the effect of gravity on the optical-flow representation. Classifiers trained only under Earth gravity are then evaluated on unseen gravity domains to assess cross-gravity generalization. Finally, a single model is trained using data from all four gravity conditions, followed by an ablation study to determine how far the tactile representation can be reduced while preserving classification performance.

The main contributions are:

A quantitative analysis of the gravity-induced domain shift in a compact tactile optical-flow representation, showing that classifiers trained only under Earth gravity lose accuracy under unseen reduced-gravity conditions.

A cross-gravity classification approach based on a single model trained across Earth, Mars, Moon, and orbital gravity, achieving consistent performance across all four domains without requiring gravity as an input.

A reduced optical-flow representation of 40 features that retains 95.7% accuracy, less than one percentage point below the full 126-feature representation.

Together, these contributions provide a basis for developing computationally efficient tactile perception methods that account for gravity-domain shifts in space robotic manipulation.

1. A quantitative analysis of the gravity-induced domain shift in a compact tactile optical-flow representation, showing that classifiers trained only under Earth gravity lose accuracy under unseen reduced-gravity conditions.

2. A cross-gravity classification approach based on a single model trained across Earth, Mars, Moon, and orbital gravity, achieving consistent performance across all four domains without requiring gravity as an input.

3. A reduced optical-flow representation of 40 features that retains 95.7% accuracy, less than one percentage point below the full 126-feature representation.

# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Based Tactile Sensing

Vision-based tactile sensors convert contact into images, either marker-based or intensity-based [ 6 ] , and have become a primary route to high-resolution touch for manipulation [ 7 ] . Sensors of this type measure the deformation of a soft elastomer with a camera and infer geometry, force, and slip from it [ 4 ] . Force-oriented reviews show that marker tracking, optical flow, physical modelling, and learning-based methods are all used to estimate contact forces [ 8 ] , and recent learned estimators regress force distributions or 3D forces directly from vision-based tactile images [ 9 ] . Optical flow in particular has been used to estimate contact shape and force in DelTact [ 10 ] , force, geometry, and depth in GelFlow [ 5 ] , and 3D contact point clouds [ 11 ] . In contrast, this work evaluates a compact optical-flow representation of consecutive markerless tactile images for classifying the direction of load-induced rotation and analyses its transferability across gravity conditions.

## II-B Tactile Simulation

Tactile simulation enables controlled, reproducible datasets without real hardware. TACTO [ 12 ] , Taxim [ 13 ] , and TacSL [ 14 ] render vision-based tactile images from simulated contact, and SimTacLS extends the idea to large-scale tactile skin [ 15 ] . Models trained on simulated tactile images do not transfer to real sensors by default, and the gap is addressed with physically accurate simulation [ 16 ] or domain adaptation [ 17 ] . The present study uses TacEx, which combines contact simulation with tactile rendering in Isaac Sim for GelSight Mini [ 18 ] , and it treats gravity as the domain variable of interest rather than the sim-to-real gap. Only the grayscale version of the simulated images is used, in the PhysX rigid-body configuration.

## II-C Tactile Sensing in Space Robotics

Space robotic manipulation involves contact-rich tasks such as capture, servicing, assembly, and sample collection, where contact dynamics and ground verification remain major challenges under microgravity and reduced gravity [ 2 ] . Tactile sensing has entered this domain primarily through hardware designed to survive the environment. Jahanshahi and Zhu review resistive, capacitive, piezoelectric, and optical technologies for orbital and planetary platforms [ 3 ] , and the same authors review learning-based grasp control for space [ 19 ] . Fibre-optic tactile pads have been demonstrated on a gripper designed for the Astrobee free-flying robots [ 20 ] , a sensor based on optical-fibre knots measures pressure, hardness, and texture for on-orbit servicing [ 21 ] , and force-sensing grippers have been proposed for on-orbit capture [ 22 ] . Contact experiments have also flown, with gecko-inspired adhesive grippers tested aboard the International Space Station [ 23 ] . That gravity changes the control of a grasp is documented in human studies, where the coordination of grip and load forces adapts differently under Mars, Moon, and microgravity during parabolic flight [ 24 ] . The effect of gravity on the tactile signal itself, on the features that a classifier consumes, has not been measured in any of these works. This study addresses that gap with one representation and one controlled task, so that the observed change can be attributed to gravity, and asks whether rotation-direction classification generalises across gravities without richer tactile images, marker displacement, reconstructed geometry, learned force maps, robot state, or a gravity input.

2026-10-09.title: SkillWeave: Weaving Heterogeneous Demonstrations into Long-Horizon Manipulation Skills
2026-10-09.authors: Ryosei Tamura , Xiaoxiang Dong , Uksang Yoo , Yuemin Mao , Romina Mir , Jonathan Francis , Jeffrey Ichnowski
2026-10-09.comment: IROS 2026 Workshop on Haptics and Dexterous Manipulation
2026-10-09.abstract:
Dexterous manipulation requires both large-scale task progression and precise contact-rich interaction, making it challenging to collect demonstrations that effectively support both regimes.
We present SkillWeave, a heterogeneous demonstration framework for long-horizon dexterous manipulation that combines teleoperation for coarse reaching and transport with kinesthetic teaching for precise, contact-rich skills.
To address the visual mismatch introduced by the demonstrator’s presence during kinesthetic data collection, we propose an object-mask-conditioned diffusion policy that uses offline object segmentation for training supervision and a lightweight learned mask predictor at deployment, avoiding online segmentation and image inpainting.
To mitigate distribution shift between independently trained sub-task policies, we introduce successor-aware terminal steering, which selects among actions sampled from the predecessor policy to guide the system toward states supported by the successor’s demonstrated initial-state distribution.
Across three real-world long-horizon tasks, SkillWeave achieves 27% average end-to-end success. Mask-conditioned kinesthetic policies improve dexterous sub-task success to an average of 65%, while successor-aware handoffs achieve an average composition efficiency of 87%.
These results show that matching demonstration modality to interaction regime, explicitly addressing kinesthetic visual mismatch, and steering policy handoffs toward successor-supported states substantially improves long-horizon dexterous manipulation. Videos and code are available at skillweave-authors.github.io .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation combines high-dimensional control with repeated and often discontinuous changes in contact. Such behaviors have been studied through model-based control, reinforcement learning, and sim-to-real transfer [ 1 , 2 ] .
Demonstrations offer a complementary route by placing the learner directly on task-relevant state–action trajectories. They have been used both to accelerate reinforcement learning and to train expressive visuomotor policies through behavior cloning [ 3 , 4 ] .
Demonstration data can also be obtained or expanded through human videos and automated trajectory generation [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
Regardless of its source, however, the resulting policy can learn only from the states and interactions represented in the data; demonstration collection therefore directly shapes the capabilities and failure modes of the learned behavior [ 8 ] , and the specific type of demonstration collection strategy used thus has a strong effect on the properties of the downstream policy [ 9 ] . Teleoperation captures task progression and spatial coverage, but retargeting and indirect contact feedback can limit precision during dexterous interaction [ 10 , 11 ] .
On the other hand, kinesthetic teaching provides direct guidance through robot-feasible contact configurations, but introduces demonstrator occlusion into the recorded images [ 12 , 11 ] . These complementary limitations motivate our central hypothesis: under long-horizon dexterous manipulation, which alternates between free-space motion and contact-rich interaction, each phase should be demonstrated through the modality best suited to its interaction regime. We combine teleoperation demonstrations for task-level coverage with kinesthetic demonstrations at contact-rich phases.
Collecting each subtask separately also makes the data cheaper to gather, since a failed attempt costs one subtask rather than the whole episode.

However, data matched to the modulus of subtasks alone do not guaranty a successful composition. Each boundary introduced by the decomposition must be reached through two different processes: the demonstrator reaches it during data collection, whereas at deployment it must be reached by the preceding policy. Small prediction errors accumulate throughout that subtask, causing the predecessor’s terminal state to drift away from the states represented in the demonstrations. The successor policy therefore begins from an out-of-distribution state and may fail despite succeeding in isolation; this mismatch can compound over a sequence of subtasks.
This terminal-to-initial distribution mismatch is a known limitation of naive skill composition [ 13 , 14 ] .
Illustrated by , we address this issue by inserting a short bridging motion between consecutive policies. The bridge guides the robot from the predecessor’s realized terminal state toward the region of states represented by the successor’s demonstrated initial state distribution.

Kinesthetic data also creates an observation mismatch: the demonstrator occludes the object during training but is absent during autonomous execution. Prior approaches remove visible embodiments through inpainting [ 15 , 16 , 11 ] , which requires reconstructing unobserved content near the interaction region.
We instead use SAM 3 to generate object masks offline for the training demonstrations [ 17 ] .
These masks supervise a learned mask predictor whose output conditions the diffusion policy during deployment.
This removes SAM 3 and image inpainting from the online control loop.

Our experiments test three claims: matching demonstration modality to interaction regime improves long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation; bridging into the successor’s demonstrated initial states is necessary when independently learned behaviors are composed; and object-mask conditioning makes kinesthetic policy learning more robust to changes in background and scene.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

We introduce a multi-modal demonstration framework that uses teleoperation for long-horizon coverage and free-space reaching, and kinesthetic
teaching for precise contact-rich interaction.

We develop successor-aware terminal steering to guide predecessor policies toward the successor’s start-state distribution, reducing distribution shift at policy boundaries for reliable long-horizon composition.

We develop an object-mask-conditioned diffusion policy for kinesthetic demonstrations . SAM 3 provides offline training masks, while a learned predictor supplies masks during deployment, improving robustness across backgrounds
and scenes without online SAM 3 or image inpainting in the control loop.
