# II Related Work

## II-A Human Tactile Demonstration Acquisition

STAG and Flex-Glove enable distributed human tactile capture through inexpensive sensing and personalized fabrication [ 5 , 13 ] . OSMO uses the same glove on humans and robots, while DexViTac combines multimodal acquisition and kinematics-grounded representation learning with matched tactile hardware [ 14 , 15 ] . ForceMimic records interaction wrenches and motion for force-centric imitation learning. TACROSS connects a piezoresistive human glove to a capacitive robot hand, addressing sensor heterogeneity with measurement validity and causal synchronization.

## II-B Cross-Sensor Tactile Alignment

Domain-adversarial training uses gradient reversal to learn task-discriminative, domain-invariant features [ 16 ] . UniTacHand aligns heterogeneous touch through masked MANO-UV maps and paired interactions with contrastive, reconstruction, and adversarial objectives [ 17 ] . TactAlign learns a rectified-flow mapping from interaction-derived pseudo pairs, supporting unpaired demonstrations and dynamic contact [ 18 ] . TACROSS represents regional contact state, relative intensity, duration, spatial descriptors, and phase. Sensor-specific adapters feed shared causal temporal and inter-finger encoders. Positive windows match task/object metadata and contact semantics without cross-domain frame synchronization. Field-level validity masks distinguish missing measurements from valid no-contact observations.

## II-C Learning from Human and Robot Demonstrations

EgoMimic jointly trains policies on human and robot demonstrations [ 11 ] . FreeTacMan combines temporal tactile pretraining with ACT and evaluates optical cross-sensor generalization [ 8 ] . MimicTouch learns from multimodal human demonstrations and bridges the embodiment gap through online residual reinforcement learning [ 19 ] . TACROSS uses human touch for representation learning and robot actions for ground-truth supervision. HaMeR [ 20 ] and calibrated retargeting provide human hand pseudo-targets for confidence-weighted, validity-masked auxiliary supervision. Arm targets require separate supervision. ACT [ 21 ] takes the robot tactile latent, RGB, and proprioception, using robot observations at deployment.

2026-10-09.title: STAG: A Sparse Traversability-Aware Graph Representation from Grid-Based Costmaps for Robotic Navigation
2026-10-09.authors: Gabriel Manuel Garcia , Stéphanie Aravecchia , Miguel Angel Olivares-Mendez
2026-10-09.abstract: Autonomous rovers navigating large unstructured environments need efficient global planning that accounts for terrain traversability. However, searching dense grid-based costmaps becomes computationally expensive as the mapped area grows. We introduce STAG, a Sparse Traversability-Aware Graph that converts costmaps into compact graphs. STAG combines a medial-axis topological backbone, representative nodes for homogeneous traversability regions, and transition nodes near strong traversability gradients. Edges encode geometry and traversability to account for path length and terrain difficulty. We compare A* on STAG and dense grids using synthetic cave maps, mine maps and the DARPA CERBERUS dataset. Across five benchmark categories comprising 203 map instances and 101,200 queries, STAG reduces median planning time by 3.4 × 3.4\times to 9.9 × 9.9\times and peak query memory by 2.1 × 2.1\times to 15.4 × 15.4\times , with median relative path-length differences of − 2.9 % -2.9\% and + 7.6 % +7.6\% . STAG offers a compact representation for global planning, trading dense-grid traversability optimality for faster, less memory-intensive search.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Autonomous robots operating in large unstructured environments require internal terrain representations that support safe and efficient path planning. This requirement is particularly important for terrestrial and planetary caves, lava tubes, mines, and subterranean environments, where robots must navigate over long distances with limited onboard computation and limited communication with human operators. In such environments, the representation must capture not only which areas are free or occupied, but also how difficult the terrain is to traverse.

Grid-based traversability costmaps are widely used for this purpose because they provide a simple and spatially detailed representation of obstacles and terrain difficulty. However, planning directly on a dense grid becomes increasingly expensive as the explored area grows. Each traversable cell becomes a potential planning state, and repeated path queries over large maps can lead to high computation times and memory requirements [ 9 , 24 ] . This creates a practical limitation for long-range autonomous missions, where global planning must be performed repeatedly on resource-constrained platforms.

In this paper, we address the problem of reducing the computational cost of path planning over grid-based traversability costmaps while preserving the terrain information needed for risk-aware global navigation. Instead of planning directly over all traversable cells, we convert the costmap into a sparse graph that preserves the main free-space connectivity and selected traversability structure.

Existing graph-based representations provide useful tools for reducing planning complexity. Topological and skeleton-based methods, such as generalized Voronoi graphs and distance-field skeletons, compactly represent the connectivity of free space [ 1 ] , [ 3 ] . Such abstractions have been used successfully in large-scale exploration systems, including subterranean navigation frameworks [ 6 ] , [ 14 ] . However, purely topological graphs mainly encode geometry and do not explicitly preserve terrain-cost variations. Traversability-aware graph methods reduce the search space while encoding terrain risk, but their representations are often coupled to particular sensing modalities, connection strategies, or dedicated planners [ 10 , 21 , 23 ] .

To address these limitations, we introduce STAG, a Sparse Traversability-Aware Graph representation. STAG converts a grid-based traversability costmap into a compact multi-source graph composed of three complementary elements: a medial-axis topological backbone, region nodes that summarize homogeneous traversability areas, and transition nodes placed near strong traversability gradients. The resulting graph stores geometric and terrain-related attributes on its edges, allowing standard graph-search algorithms to evaluate both path length and terrain difficulty without searching over the full grid.

The contribution of this paper is a sparse traversability-aware representation for global path planning over costmaps. More specifically, we make the following claims:

STAG reduces the number of planning states compared with the original grid-based traversability costmap.

STAG reduces the number of planning states compared with the original grid-based traversability costmap.

Using the same A* search formulation and matched start-goal queries, STAG reduces query time and memory relative to dense-grid search.

STAG preserves global path geometry closely, while exposing a measurable trade-off between sparse search efficiency and dense-grid traversability optimality.

These claims are evaluated on 200 generated cave and mine maps, one long synthetic mine, and two DARPA-derived traversability maps by comparing grid-based A* planning with STAG-based A* planning. The evaluation focuses on representation size, planning time, peak query memory, path length, and accumulated traversability cost. The results show that STAG provides a lightweight global planning representation for repeated path queries over traversability maps, while highlighting the expected loss of fine terrain-cost optimality caused by sparse abstraction.

1. STAG reduces the number of planning states compared with the original grid-based traversability costmap.

2. Using the same A* search formulation and matched start-goal queries, STAG reduces query time and memory relative to dense-grid search.

3. STAG preserves global path geometry closely, while exposing a measurable trade-off between sparse search efficiency and dense-grid traversability optimality.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Grid-Based and Multi-Resolution Representations

Grid costmaps represent free space, obstacles, and navigation costs on a regular lattice and are commonly searched using Dijkstra’s algorithm or A* [ 8 , 7 ] . Their principal advantage is that the planner can directly exploit the complete spatial and terrain-cost resolution of the map. However, the number of search states increases with map extent and resolution, which can make repeated global queries expensive [ 9 ] . Multi-resolution methods reduce this burden by coarsening portions of the search space while retaining finer resolution where necessary [ 24 ] . Such approaches nevertheless remain coupled to a grid hierarchy and its refinement policy. STAG instead constructs an explicit reusable graph whose vertices are selected from the geometry and traversability structure of the input costmap.

## II-B Skeleton and Topological Graphs

Topological representations reduce planning complexity by preserving the principal connectivity of free space with fewer states. Generalized Voronoi graphs provide obstacle-clear routes through an environment [ 1 ] , while skeleton-based approaches derive sparse roadmaps from distance fields or medial-axis structures [ 2 , 3 , 12 , 13 ] . Incremental Euclidean signed-distance-field systems such as Voxblox provide geometric and clearance information that can support these abstractions [ 4 ] . Sparse topological graphs have also been used for large-scale and subterranean exploration, including multi-robot systems operating under limited communication [ 5 , 6 , 14 , 15 ] .

These methods demonstrate that free-space topology can substantially reduce representation size while retaining long-range connectivity. Their graph construction is nevertheless driven primarily by geometry, clearance, or exploration structure. Areas with similar geometry but different traversal difficulty may therefore remain indistinguishable. STAG adopts a medial-axis backbone for geometric connectivity, but augments it with nodes selected directly from the traversability field and stores terrain-related statistics on graph edges.

## II-C Traversability-Aware and Region-Based Graphs

Traversability-aware planners associate terrain risk or cost with graph nodes and edges. TRG-Planner constructs a traversal-risk graph and jointly uses it with a risk-aware planning strategy for navigation in unstructured terrain [ 10 ] . Other approaches construct topological graphs through generalized-Voronoi sampling [ 11 ] , derive weighted traversability graphs from three-dimensional terrain data [ 21 ] , or associate traversability with connections between visually defined places for long-range off-road navigation [ 23 ] . Hierarchical terrain-aware systems further combine multiple graph or map resolutions to support exploration and navigation decisions [ 17 ] . These works demonstrate the value of incorporating terrain information into sparse planning structures, but their representations are commonly coupled to a particular sensing modality, sampling procedure, or specialized planner.

Region-based abstractions provide another means of reducing representation size. Topological maps can represent convex or spatially coherent free-space regions as graph elements [ 16 , 20 ] , while graph-based segmentation methods estimate traversable terrain from LiDAR or other sensor data [ 18 , 19 ] . The latter primarily address perception and terrain estimation rather than compression of an already available planning costmap, and are therefore complementary to STAG.

STAG specifically targets an existing two-dimensional traversability costmap. It combines three deterministic node sources: a medial-axis backbone, representatives of connected homogeneous traversability regions, and nodes near strong traversability transitions. The resulting graph retains explicit edge geometry, clearance, and traversability attributes and can be searched using a standard graph-search algorithm. This separates the contribution of the environment representation from that of a dedicated perception or planning pipeline.

2026-10-09.title: WAND: Learning Robust Navigation under Complex Wind Disturbances and Dense Obstacles for Quadrotors
2026-10-09.authors: Zhonghan Tang , Chenhui Li , Shuai Liang , Zhongrui You , Jianan Li , Bin Zhao , Zhigang Wang , Xuelong Li
2026-10-09.abstract: Robust navigation in cluttered environments remains a fundamental challenge for quadrotors, particularly when strong wind disturbances arise, which perturb vehicle dynamics, limit control authority, and substantially increase collision risk. Existing learning-based navigation policies typically rely on obstacle perception and proprioceptive observations, requiring the policy to infer time-varying disturbance effects implicitly and thereby limiting robustness under partial observability. This paper proposes WAND (Wind-Aware Navigation with Disturbance Estimation), a reinforcement learning framework for navigation under time-varying wind disturbances in dense obstacle fields. Specifically, WAND estimates wind-induced disturbance acceleration from historical proprioceptive states using a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN). This estimation is integrated into the policy via a zero-initialized residual module, WindAdapter , while simultaneously providing feedforward compensation for low-level control. The dual use of the estimate couples disturbance-conditioned navigation with feedforward disturbance rejection. Across 12 wind-disturbed simulation settings, WAND improved the observed success rate by 8.3 percentage points on average relative to feedforward compensation alone. Controlled opposite-crosswind experiments further showed wind-direction-dependent trajectory adaptation. In indoor fan-induced flight tests, WAND succeeded in 18 of 20 trials, demonstrating the feasibility of real-time onboard navigation.
2026-10-09.introduction:
In recent years, micro quadrotors have seen rapid adoption in exploration [ 1 ] , emergency rescue [ 2 ] , and urban delivery [ 3 ] . Driven by breakthroughs in low-power computing and micro-sensing [ 4 , 5 ] , these vehicles can now operate under extreme Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) constraints, granting them access to dense and confined environments. In such settings, the wind disturbance experienced by the vehicle can vary over time as the airflow interacts with surrounding structures, for example, through flow acceleration near gaps or recirculation around obstacles [ 6 , 7 ] . Due to their limited actuation authority, micro quadrotors are highly susceptible to unsteady airflow, increasing the risk of collision in cluttered environments.

Traditional navigation stacks separate geometric planning from low-level control. Geometry-oriented planners [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] focus on trajectory feasibility, whereas robust planners [ 11 , 12 ] and predictive controllers [ 13 ] account for disturbances or tracking uncertainty but depend on assumed models and sufficient control authority. Strong, rapidly varying wind can therefore leave residual tracking errors that erode trajectory clearance in confined environments.

In contrast, learning-based methods integrate perception and control through learned navigation policies. NavRL [ 14 ] learns safe navigation in dynamic clutter, while end-to-end approaches map LiDAR [ 15 , 16 ] or visual features [ 17 ] to low-level commands and support sim-to-real transfer [ 18 ] . However, these policies primarily condition on obstacle perception and proprioception rather than explicit wind estimates. They therefore infer time-varying aerodynamic effects implicitly, although the same observation can require different actions under different winds. This partial observability complicates robust wind-aware navigation.

To address this issue, we propose WAND, a wind-aware RL framework for safe navigation in windy, cluttered environments. A Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) estimates wind-induced disturbance acceleration from proprioceptive histories, and the proposed WindAdapter encodes this estimate into wind-conditioned features. The policy combines these features with obstacle perception and the current proprioceptive state, while the same estimate is reused for feedforward compensation. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , WAND is deployed onboard for real-time navigation in a cluttered indoor environment under fan-induced airflow.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We propose WAND, a wind-aware RL framework for quadrotor navigation in cluttered environments under wind disturbances. WAND explicitly estimates wind-induced disturbance acceleration from proprioceptive histories and integrates it into the policy through a zero-initialized residual WindAdapter , while also reusing it for feedforward compensation during execution.

We validate WAND through simulation and real-world flight experiments under diverse wind conditions, demonstrating improved robustness and disturbance-adaptive behaviors compared with baseline methods.

1. We propose WAND, a wind-aware RL framework for quadrotor navigation in cluttered environments under wind disturbances. WAND explicitly estimates wind-induced disturbance acceleration from proprioceptive histories and integrates it into the policy through a zero-initialized residual WindAdapter , while also reusing it for feedforward compensation during execution.

2. We validate WAND through simulation and real-world flight experiments under diverse wind conditions, demonstrating improved robustness and disturbance-adaptive behaviors compared with baseline methods.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Hierarchical Navigation in Cluttered Environments

Autonomous navigation in cluttered environments has been widely studied within hierarchical planning frameworks. Representative methods such as Fast-Planner [ 8 ] and EGO-Planner [ 9 ] achieve real-time collision-free trajectory generation by exploiting geometric constraints derived from occupancy maps. More recent works [ 19 , 10 ] further improve computational efficiency and trajectory quality in dense obstacle fields, demonstrating strong performance in structured navigation tasks. However, these planners are primarily designed for geometric feasibility and typically rely on the low-level controller to track the reference trajectory with sufficient accuracy. To improve tracking robustness against external disturbances, prior works have explored disturbance-compensation strategies [ 13 ] . Nevertheless, in most hierarchical pipelines, disturbance rejection is primarily handled by the tracking controller. As a result, the planned trajectory may not explicitly account for time-varying aerodynamic effects, and severe wind gusts can drive the quadrotor beyond the intended safety margins, increasing the risk of collision.

## II-B Learning-Based Navigation

Learning-based navigation directly learns obstacle-avoidance and goal-reaching behaviors from data. Early learning-based approaches demonstrated sim-to-real navigation in clutter with CAD2RL [ 20 ] and privileged learning for high-speed flight in unstructured environments [ 21 ] . Building on this, Song et al. [ 17 ] combine imitation and reinforcement learning through a privileged learning-by-cheating framework that tightly couples perception and control. Xu et al. [ 15 ] and Fan et al. [ 16 ] design task-relevant LiDAR representations for safe and reactive navigation, while NavRL [ 14 ] addresses dynamic environments with moving obstacles through tailored state representations and adaptive architectures. Yu et al. [ 22 ] leverage memory-augmented latent representations with varying-speed strategies to enhance navigation performance.

History-conditioned latent adaptation has been applied to quadrotor control by inferring a latent representation of vehicle and environment parameters from recent state–action histories and conditioning the controller on that representation [ 23 ] . In WAND, temporal conditioning is grounded in a supervised estimate of wind-induced disturbance acceleration, thereby making the conditioning signal physically interpretable. Complementary onboard estimators recover wind or external forces from proprioceptive or visual–inertial measurements [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] , while adaptive learning and control methods improve dynamics prediction or trajectory tracking under wind disturbances [ 27 , 28 ] . WAND integrates these directions by using the explicit disturbance estimate both to adapt obstacle-aware navigation actions and to provide low-level feedforward compensation.

2026-10-09.authors: Qing Huang , Yifei Yang , Ziqing Zou , Anzhe Chen , Zhenjie Zhu , Yufei Wei , Rong Xiong , Yue Wang
2026-10-09.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies typically predict actions at fixed time
intervals, coupling the route a robot follows with its execution pace. This
coupling complicates adaptation from teleoperation: useful geometric guidance
comes with timing shaped by interface delays and operator behavior. Our key
insight is to bring the path-time parameterization of classical motion
planning into the learned action representation of a VLA. We introduce
PathTime-VLA, which represents motion as a progress-indexed interaction path X ⁡ ( s ) X(s) and a positive interval-time profile. The latter defines a monotone
time law t ⁡ ( s ) t(s) , yielding controller commands X ⁡ ( s ⁡ ( t ) ) X(s(t)) . For a given path,
alternative executions are expressed through the time profile, allowing
chunk-wise speed choices without changing the geometric prediction target.
This representation supports a staged post-training procedure: demonstrations
and DAgger interventions establish a target-domain prior, Speed-DQN learns
execution multipliers from robot interaction, and Path-AWR uses rollout
outcomes to refine the diffusion path generator. A path-conditioned action
expert realizes the resulting motions while maintaining distinct learning
interfaces for path generation and execution timing.
Across three tasks, the complete method achieves 58 / 60 58/60 successes versus 57 / 60 57/60 for PathTime-VLA under BC + DAgger at fixed 1 × 1\times , with approximately 39 39 – 52 % 52\% shorter mean completion times over successful trials.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising foundation for household
and service robots that must translate everyday instructions into useful physical actions [ 1 , 2 ] .
However, handling objects, opening appliances, and putting items away require both semantic
understanding and reliable manipulation. Adapting pretrained visuomotor priors
to a target domain still requires robot interaction data.

Teleoperated demonstrations are a practical source of adaptation data,
while DAgger supplies corrective paths around failure-prone states
visited by the learned policy [ 3 , 4 ] . Although these
data provide useful spatial guidance, their recorded timing may also
reflect network latency, limitations of the teleoperation interface,
and operator behavior, and therefore need not define an efficient
autonomous execution schedule. We consequently use them to establish
a target-domain path prior and an initial timing model, and subsequently
optimize execution timing from real-robot outcomes.

Many action-chunking VLA policies predict future actions at fixed
control intervals [ 2 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Under this representation,
changing the pace along the same geometric path also changes the full action sequence used as supervision.
Improving execution timing therefore becomes entangled with learning where the robot should move.
Our central insight is to bring classical path-time
parameterization into the learned VLA action space , thereby exposing
distinct post-training interfaces for geometry and timing.

Classical trajectory generation separates a geometric path from the time law used to traverse
it [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . We make this established distinction explicit in the learned
action representation: the policy predicts a progress-indexed interaction path, sampled at fixed increments of
spatial motion, together with a separate interval-time profile. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , composing the path with its
timing recovers controller-rate actions.

For a given path, different execution schedules can be expressed through the time profile while leaving
the geometric target unchanged. This allows geometry and timing to exploit different sources
of post-training supervision: demonstrations and DAgger provide dense target-domain supervision for the path,
while robot interaction supplies task outcomes for evaluating execution schedules and the paths realized under
them. Timing can therefore be optimized from execution feedback without requiring a new geometric
target for each execution speed.

Building on this idea, we introduce PathTime-VLA, whose post-training pipeline is illustrated
in Fig. 3 . Human demonstrations and DAgger first establish and expand a
supervised prior for target-domain manipulation. Speed-DQN then uses execution feedback to learn
adaptive chunk-level pacing while keeping the path generator fixed. Finally, Path-AWR refines path
generation from rollout outcomes while retaining the learned timing policy. In this way, geometry
and timing are post-trained through learning signals suited to their respective roles, while their
composed behavior is still evaluated under the same task-level outcomes.

Our contributions are fourfold:

We introduce a path-time decoupled action representation for VLAs that separates a progress-indexed interaction path from its
interval-time profile, providing distinct post-training interfaces for
geometry and timing.

We develop Speed-DQN to optimize chunk-wise execution multipliers
through low-dimensional online reinforcement learning with a fixed
action expert.

We develop Path-AWR to refine the diffusion path prediction head through
advantage-weighted learning from executed rollout paths, anchored by
supervised demonstrations and interventions.

We conduct a substantial real-world data collection and evaluation
effort across three manipulation tasks, spanning teleoperated
demonstrations, DAgger interventions, online DQN rollouts, and 600 real-robot evaluation trials.

1. We introduce a path-time decoupled action representation for VLAs that separates a progress-indexed interaction path from its
interval-time profile, providing distinct post-training interfaces for
geometry and timing.

2. We develop Speed-DQN to optimize chunk-wise execution multipliers
through low-dimensional online reinforcement learning with a fixed
action expert.

3. We develop Path-AWR to refine the diffusion path prediction head through
advantage-weighted learning from executed rollout paths, anchored by
supervised demonstrations and interventions.

4. We conduct a substantial real-world data collection and evaluation

# II Related Work

## II-A Large-Scale VLA Pretraining and Action Generation

Large-scale VLA pretraining transfers semantic and visuomotor priors through
web knowledge [ 12 ] and heterogeneous robot data [ 13 ] . Action
generators include token prediction in OpenVLA [ 1 ] , Transformer
policies in Octo [ 2 ] , and flow or diffusion models in π 0 \pi_{0} and
RDT [ 5 , 6 ] . Related policies use conditional latents [ 14 ] ,
iterative denoising [ 15 ] , or compact sequence
tokenization [ 16 ] .
Despite these differences, future actions are commonly indexed by control
steps, leaving path geometry and execution timing within the same prediction
target.

## II-B Path-Time Parameterization and Speed Control

Classical motion planning separates a geometric path from its time law. Early
work studied minimum-time traversal of a prescribed manipulator path subject
to robot dynamics and actuator limits [ 9 , 10 ] . TOPP and
TOPP-RA subsequently provided efficient numerical and reachability-based
solutions [ 11 , 17 ] . These methods address model-based retiming of
prescribed geometric paths.

Learned policies address speed at two related but distinct levels: system-level
action generation and execution cadence, and physical traversal speed.
OpenVLA-OFT supports high-frequency execution [ 7 ] , RTC executes
chunks asynchronously under inference delay [ 18 ] , and SAIL accelerates
imitation policies through adaptive speed modulation and controller-aware
execution [ 19 ] . TempoVLA conditions time-indexed outputs on desired
physical speed [ 20 ] ; we instead pair a progress-indexed path X ⁡ ( s ) X(s) with interval traversal times, so retiming leaves the geometric target
unchanged.

## II-C Interactive Imitation and Reinforcement Post-Training

DAgger collects expert labels at learner-visited states [ 3 ] , while
HG-DAgger lets a human decide when to intervene [ 4 ] . They expand
coverage around failures, but timestamped imitation also inherits operator-
and interface-dependent timing. HIL-SERL combines demonstrations and
interventions with real-world RL [ 21 ] , using outcomes in addition to
intervention labels.

Recent VLA post-training increasingly uses interaction outcomes to refine
pretrained policies through consistency regularization, scalable RL, or
value-derived experience conditioning [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] .
Our factorization combines
DQN-style value learning for discrete timing choices [ 27 ] with AWR-style
path refinement [ 28 ] . Unlike direct diffusion-policy updates or general
offline-to-online actor updates [ 29 , 30 ] , it isolates rollout-based
refinement to path generation.

2026-10-09.title: UltraLight Luma: A Novel Edge-Deployable Perception Network for Crop-Row Segmentation in Agricultural Robotics
2026-10-09.authors: Dhanushka Balasingham , Shamod Ginigaddarage , Hanojhan Rajahrajasingh , Nuwan Kodagoda , Rajitha de Silva
2026-10-09.comment: This work has been accepted for publication in IECON 2026. The final published version will be available via IEEE Xplore
2026-10-09.abstract: Reliable crop-row perception is essential for autonomous agricultural robots, but low-cost deployment is constrained by computation, memory, power, and inference time. This paper addresses crop-row detection and navigation-line extraction using UltraLight Luma, a compact encoder–decoder segmentation network with a progressive learning strategy and only 13.1k trainable parameters. The predicted crop-row masks are processed using a post-processing algorithm to estimate row alignment for downstream visual servoing. UltraLight Luma improves parameter efficiency over U-Net, YOLOv8, and YOLOv26 while maintaining reliable crop-row detection performance. The model required only 25.23 mJ per inference, demonstrating its suitability for resource-constrained agricultural robots.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Autonomous agricultural robots can reduce labor demand and improve field productivity, but reliable crop-row detection remains essential for navigation, localization, weeding, spraying, and inspection. Deployment on low-cost mobile platforms is constrained by computation, battery capacity, and hardware cost, while high-computation models often require expensive processors and consume more power [ 1 ] . Therefore, crop-row detection must be accurate, efficient, cost effective, and fast enough for real-time operation.

In this work, crop-row detection is formulated as an image segmentation task using forward-facing red-green-blue (RGB) images from mobile agricultural robots. The goal is to identify visible crop-row regions for row following and navigation under practical field challenges such as shadows, weeds, missing plants, uneven soil, and perspective distortion. The target platform is a low-cost, compute-constrained embedded device with limited memory, power, and inference time.

The proposed approach uses an ultra-lightweight segmentation model to predict crop-row regions from RGB images in real time on constrained hardware. Unlike classical thresholding or line-fitting methods, it is designed to be more robust to changes in illumination, plant density, and row structure, while avoiding the high memory, power, and processor requirements of heavier deep networks [ 1 , 2 ] . Thus, the method balances accuracy, speed, and deployability for low-cost agricultural robots.

The key contributions of this paper are: (1) A novel ultra-lightweight encoder-decoder segmentation network, UltraLight Luma, is proposed with a progressive learning strategy for crop-row segmentation on low-cost agricultural robotic platforms using only 13.1k trainable parameters. (2) A navigation-line extraction module based on the Triangle Scan Method (TSM) is applied to the segmented mask to estimate the crop-row navigation line. (3) A comparative analysis against state-of-the-art models is conducted through experimental assessment.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

Vision-based crop-row detection has used traditional image-processing methods [ 3 ] , which are efficient but sensitive to illumination and field variability. Deep learning improves robustness, including YOLO-based bounding box methods [ 4 , 5 ] , but these require centroid extraction and line fitting, which can introduce errors under canopy overlap and weed interference [ 6 ] . In contrast, semantic segmentation provides pixel-wise crop-row localization for more accurate row-geometry estimation [ 7 , 8 ] .

Multiple semantic segmentation models have been explored for crop-row detection in agricultural environments. Among them, U-Net–based approaches have demonstrated effective pixel-wise segmentation performance for identifying crop-rows under varying field conditions [ 8 , 7 ] . For example, Doha et al. reported competitive mean Intersection over Union (IoU) scores using U-Net architectures for crop-row segmentation tasks. However, conventional U-Net architectures consist of deep encoder–decoder networks with numerous convolutional layers, resulting in increased computational complexity and inference time. Consequently, more computationally efficient architectures such as LinkNet have been investigated to enable real-time agricultural navigation applications [ 8 ] .

Although LinkNet is more computationally efficient than U-Net, it still contains approximately 11.5 million parameters [ 9 ] . To further reduce computational cost, efficient architectures such as Efficient Neural Network (ENet) [ 2 ] , YOLO-based models [ 10 ] , and MobileNet-based backbones [ 11 ] have been investigated for agricultural vision tasks, including crop-row identification. These models have demonstrated promising performance. However, their parameter counts remain relatively high for extremely constrained embedded deployment. To the best of current knowledge, existing lightweight approaches for crop-row detection have not achieved a parameter count below 0.1 million. In contrast, the proposed model uses only 13.1k parameters for crop-row segmentation, providing a substantially more compact alternative for low-cost robotic platforms.

2026-10-09.title: 2DGS-Planner: Rasterization-based Path Planning in 2D Gaussian Splatting Map
2026-10-09.authors: Jiwon Park , Dong-Uk Seo , Hyun Myung
2026-10-09.abstract:
Gaussian splatting provides an explicit and efficiently rasterizable scene representation for robot navigation.
However, individual Gaussian primitives may not reliably represent obstacles as they are jointly optimized through alpha-composited rendering from a finite set of reconstruction views.
We propose 2DGS-Planner, a path planner for ground robots that reads planning-relevant geometry from a 2D Gaussian splatting (2DGS) map through rasterization, rather than treating individual Gaussian primitives as obstacles.
During offline roadmap construction, multi-view attribution converts rendered normal dispersion into structural scores for non-ground disks supported by the reconstruction views.
These scores guide adaptive node sampling on the ground.
Path-aligned orthographic queries validate candidate edges, while cylindrical queries estimate local clearance fields that are cached on the edges.
During online planning, graph search initializes a route, and path refinement reuses the cached fields while accounting for the robot’s dimensions and ground constraints.
Experiments demonstrate improved roadmap connectivity, more accurate clearance estimation, and higher planning success compared with the tested baselines.
These results support rasterization as an effective geometric query interface for planning directly on Gaussian maps.
Code and data are available at https://2dgs-planner.github.io/ .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Autonomous navigation requires spatial reasoning about the environment to find safe and efficient paths.
This reasoning is closely tied to how the environment is represented, since planners interact with a map through the spatial queries it can support efficiently.
Occupancy grids enable graph-based search through discrete occupancy lookups [ 1 ] , while signed distance fields provide differentiable distance queries for gradient-based trajectory optimization [ 2 , 3 ] .
Point-based geometric maps can be queried directly for collision checking in sampling-based planning [ 4 ] .

Recently, learned scene representations have been explored as environment maps for navigation [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
Neural Radiance Field-based approaches obtain collision evidence directly from the learned density [ 5 ] .
Other methods rely on rendered outputs for localization, image-goal navigation, and traversability-aware planning [ 6 , 7 ] .
Both approaches rely on evaluating an implicit field, which can be computationally expensive for real-time planning.

Gaussian splatting [ 11 ] provides an explicit alternative, encoding scenes with Gaussian primitives and rendering images from arbitrary viewpoints through differentiable rasterization.
Existing Gaussian splatting-based planners generally treat the primitives directly as obstacles or convert the map into an intermediate geometric representation [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
However, visually plausible renderings do not guarantee that the underlying primitives align with the composited surface (Fig. 2 ).
Individual primitives may therefore fail to reliably represent scene geometry.

Two properties of GS training motivate rasterization-based geometric queries.
First, the primitives are jointly optimized through their contributions to alpha-composited renderings, so the training objective constrains the composited geometry rather than any individual primitive.
This motivates querying the composited geometry instead of treating primitives as independent obstacles.
Second, this supervision comes from only a finite set of posed training views.
Geometry outside their observation support is therefore less constrained by the training data.
A planner should consider not only the rendered surface geometry but also how well that surface was observed during training.

We therefore propose 2DGS-Planner (Fig. 1 ), a ground-robot path planner that treats rasterization as the geometric query interface to a Gaussian splatting map.
We build on 2D Gaussian splatting [ 12 ] , whose training aligns each disk with the local surface through a normal consistency term, so that surface normals become a rendered channel alongside depth and alpha.
The framework constructs a roadmap directly from rasterized geometric queries without converting the scene into an intermediate geometric representation.
During offline roadmap construction, multi-view attribution derives structural scores from rendered normal dispersion.
Scores from non-ground disks supported by the reconstruction views guide adaptive node sampling on the ground, placing more nodes near corners and cluttered areas and fewer in open regions.
Path-aligned orthographic queries validate candidate connections, while cylindrical queries estimate local clearance fields that are cached on retained edges.
During online planning, graph search finds an initial path, which is then refined using the cached fields while accounting for the robot’s dimensions and ground constraints.

The main contributions are as follows:

We propose 2DGS-Planner, a ground-robot path planner that queries 2DGS maps through rasterization without an intermediate geometric representation.

We introduce multi-view attribution that converts rendered normal dispersion into structural scores for adaptive roadmap sampling.

We formulate path-aligned orthographic and cylindrical queries for edge validation and local clearance estimation, with the clearance fields cached for path refinement.

We evaluate the proposed framework from geometric reasoning to complete planning, including structural attribution, clearance estimation, end-to-end path planning, and real-world robot experiments.

1. We propose 2DGS-Planner, a ground-robot path planner that queries 2DGS maps through rasterization without an intermediate geometric representation.

2. We introduce multi-view attribution that converts rendered normal dispersion into structural scores for adaptive roadmap sampling.

3. We formulate path-aligned orthographic and cylindrical queries for edge validation and local clearance estimation, with the clearance fields cached for path refinement.

4. We evaluate the proposed framework from geometric reasoning to complete planning, including structural attribution, clearance estimation, end-to-end path planning, and real-world robot experiments.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II.A Rasterization-based Geometry in Gaussian Splatting

3D Gaussian splatting [ 11 ] represents a scene with volumetric Gaussian
primitives, while 2D Gaussian splatting [ 12 ] replaces them with planar
Gaussian disks to impose a surface-oriented geometric representation.
During rasterization, the 2D Gaussian splatting renderer computes ray–disk
intersections and alpha-composites the intersected disks along each ray, yielding geometric quantities such as depth and surface normals in 3D.
Recent methods have increasingly exploited such rasterized quantities
as geometric signals.
PGSR [ 13 ] renders plane distances and normals for surface
reconstruction, while RaDe-GS [ 14 ] derives depth and surface
normals directly from rasterized 3D Gaussians.
3DGUT [ 15 ] further extends Gaussian rasterization
beyond standard pinhole projection to support secondary rays.
These methods use rasterization primarily for rendering or reconstruction, while we use it as a geometric query interface for path planning on a fixed 2D Gaussian splatting map.

## II.B Planning on Gaussian Splatting

GS-based motion planning and control differ in how they obtain collision information.
Splat-Nav [ 8 ] constructs safe corridors from Gaussian ellipsoids, while SAFER-Splat [ 16 ] formulates control barrier functions over the primitives.
SPLANNING [ 17 ] derives collision-probability bounds from a normalized Gaussian field, and
FOCI [ 18 ] optimizes trajectories using overlap between Gaussian representations of the robot and the scene, including trajectories for a legged ground robot.

Other approaches use auxiliary geometric representations.
Splatblox [ 9 ] supports wheeled and legged outdoor navigation through a traversability-aware Euclidean signed distance field, while LiftNav [ 19 ] uses a joint TSDF–GS map for semantic navigation and trajectory
optimization.
SplatlessDF [ 20 ] couples 2D Gaussian splatting with a separately parameterized continuous distance field
that supplies distance and gradient queries for planning.

Rendering has also been used directly for collision avoidance.
ReMoSPLAT [ 21 ] renders depth from virtual cameras attached to a mobile manipulator and uses the resulting distances for reactive control.
Whereas ReMoSPLAT targets reactive collision avoidance, we use rasterization for ground-robot path planning on a fixed 2D Gaussian splatting map, with queries organized around candidate ground motions to evaluate and retain clearance for subsequent refinement.

2026-10-09.title: From Solo to Ensemble: A Hierarchical Framework for Composable Multi-Agent Human-Object Interaction
2026-10-09.authors: Zekai Deng , Kangyi Chen , Ye Shi , Jingya Wang
2026-10-09.abstract: Physics-based human-object interaction has achieved robust single-agent manipulation skills, yet extending them to multi-agent cooperative tasks remains challenging. Existing approaches typically adapt interaction policies through task-specific fine-tuning, which entangles low-level contact-rich execution with high-level coordination and limits reuse across object geometries, interaction types, and team sizes. We propose a hierarchical framework that converts a single-agent HOI policy into a reusable Object-oriented Motion Skill . Specifically, we reinterpret teacher rollouts as object-oriented action supervision by extracting short-horizon object-proxy motions from executed trajectories, and distill task-specific teachers into a low-level skill operating in an Object-oriented Action Space . For downstream tasks, the distilled skill is frozen as a reusable executor, while a high-level policy coordinates multiple agents by generating region-wise object-oriented actions conditioned on the shared object, task goal, agent states, and local manipulation regions. This formulation shifts multi-agent HOI learning from direct contact-rich full-body control to compact object-level proxy-motion coordination. Experiments on diverse HOI tasks show that the distilled Object-oriented Motion Skill supports robust proxy-motion execution and enables composable policy learning across different interaction types, object geometries, and team sizes.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Physics-based character control has made substantial progress in learning robust full-body skills from motion imitation, adversarial motion priors, latent skill learning, and unified humanoid controllers [ 43 , 45 , 44 , 58 , 57 ] . Recent human-object interaction (HOI) methods further extend these advances to contact-rich object manipulation and human-scene interaction [ 62 , 63 , 59 , 40 , 70 ] . However, multi-human HOI introduces a distinct coordination challenge: multiple humanoids must coordinate contact locations, motion directions, and force application around the same manipulated object.

Existing methods have explored transferring interaction skills to multi-human tasks.
For example, CooHOI [ 5 ] adapts learned interaction policies to cooperative manipulation through object-level coupling. Such transfer is typically realized through policy initialization or task-specific fine-tuning. Although the adapted policy can solve a specific cooperative task, it still entangles low-level motor skill and high-level coordination within a single task policy. As a result, the learned behavior is difficult to reuse, compose, or transfer to new object geometries and cooperative configurations.

Our key insight is that a single-human HOI policy should not be directly fine-tuned into a task-specific multi-human policy. Instead, it should be preserved and converted into a reusable Object-oriented Motion Skill that can realize local proxy motions across downstream HOI tasks. With this skill, downstream learning only needs to reason in the Object-oriented Action Space . This leads to a hierarchical and decoupled control framework, where the low-level Object-oriented Motion Skill handles contact-rich execution and the high-level policy performs compositional object-level coordination through proxy-motion planning.

To make the skill reusable, the control interface should neither be tied to a specific task goal nor over-constrain the humanoid motion. We therefore define the Object-oriented Action Space as short-horizon motions of an object proxy, allowing the low-level policy to learn how to realize desired proxy motion through contact selection, balance control, and full-body coordination.

Specifically, we reinterpret rollouts from single-human HOI teacher policies as object-oriented action supervision by extracting future object-proxy motions from their executed trajectories. This converts task-specific teachers into an Object-oriented Motion Skill that can be frozen and reused as a low-level executor. In downstream tasks, a high-level policy observes the shared object, task goal, agent states, and local manipulation regions, and generates region-wise object-oriented actions. In this way, downstream RL no longer optimizes contact-rich full-body control directly, but instead learns cooperative decision making within the compact Object-oriented Action Space.

Our contributions are threefold:

We establish a transferable formulation for physics-based multi-human HOI, shifting the focus from task-specific cooperative policy learning to transferable object-oriented motion coordination.

We develop a distillation-based hierarchical learning framework that converts single-human HOI knowledge into a reusable Object-oriented Motion Skill, enabling high-level policies to coordinate multiple humans through short-horizon object-proxy motions.

We validate the framework on cooperative HOI tasks, showing that an Object-oriented Motion Skill distilled from a single-human skill supports robust proxy-motion execution and enables high-level policy learning across different interaction types, object geometries, and team sizes.

1. We establish a transferable formulation for physics-based multi-human HOI, shifting the focus from task-specific cooperative policy learning to transferable object-oriented motion coordination.

2. We develop a distillation-based hierarchical learning framework that converts single-human HOI knowledge into a reusable Object-oriented Motion Skill, enabling high-level policies to coordinate multiple humans through short-horizon object-proxy motions.

3. We validate the framework on cooperative HOI tasks, showing that an Object-oriented Motion Skill distilled from a single-human skill supports robust proxy-motion execution and enables high-level policy learning across different interaction types, object geometries, and team sizes.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Character animation and motion synthesis have extensively studied human motion in 3D scenes and human-object interaction, including kinematic human-scene and dynamic-object interaction methods [ 27 , 76 , 71 , 82 , 23 , 65 , 64 , 52 , 83 , 53 , 16 , 77 , 73 ] .
Recent diffusion-based approaches further improve motion diversity and controllability by conditioning on scene constraints, text, action labels, or object trajectories [ 10 , 11 , 56 , 72 , 81 , 26 , 25 , 46 , 42 , 78 , 17 , 15 ] .
However, such kinematic generation methods often lack physical validity, especially for long-horizon contact-rich interactions that require sustained contacts, force exchange, and object dynamics.

Physics-based character control addresses this issue by learning closed-loop policies for physically plausible full-body behaviors from motion imitation, adversarial motion priors, latent skills, and large-scale motion datasets [ 43 , 45 , 44 , 58 , 34 , 18 , 57 ] .
These techniques have been extended to physics-based HOI and human-scene interaction, enabling contact-rich behaviors such as object catching and manipulation, scene-level interactions, dynamic HOI imitation, reusable sports skills, task-tokenized scene interaction, and whole-body HOI control across diverse objects [ 38 , 1 , 68 , 8 , 62 , 63 , 74 , 29 , 30 , 67 , 40 , 70 ] .
While these methods substantially improve physical realism and task coverage, their control abstractions are usually tied to reference motions, task labels, or single-human interaction settings.

Compared with single-human HOI, cooperative interaction introduces a stronger coordination challenge: a shared object-level task must be decomposed into per-human contacts, motions, and force application.
Existing multi-person datasets and kinematic animation methods have enabled visually plausible human-human interactions and choreographic motions [ 21 , 49 , 4 , 69 , 31 , 75 , 20 , 22 , 50 , 66 , 28 , 55 , 48 , 6 , 54 , 80 , 84 , 2 , 7 , 13 ] .
However, these methods mainly target motion synthesis and do not guarantee physically valid contacts, forces, or shared object dynamics.
Recent physics-based multi-character methods improve physical plausibility by combining generated motions with controllers or converting multi-human motions into executable policies [ 12 , 59 , 19 , 79 , 33 , 32 , 14 , 24 ] , but they mostly focus on human-human interaction, sports, reaction, or collision avoidance rather than contact-rich cooperative object manipulation [ 9 , 47 , 35 ] .

Cooperative object manipulation has also been explored in legged robotics, including multi-robot payload transport, pushing, and collaborative carrying [ 39 , 61 , 51 , 60 , 3 , 41 ] .
These systems demonstrate object-level coordination, but they typically rely on quadrupedal morphology, engineered manipulation interfaces, or task-specific control designs, and do not address full-body humanoid HOI with motion priors. Most closely related to our setting, CooHOI [ 5 ] learns cooperative human-object interaction through shared object dynamics, but its adaptation still couples low-level motor execution with task-specific multi-human coordination. In contrast, our method preserves single-human HOI skills as a reusable low-level skill operating over object-oriented proxy motions, enabling high-level policies to compose local object motions across object geometries, interaction types, and team sizes.

2026-10-09.title: YOCO: You Only Calibrate Once! Fast Mocap Calibration for Dexterous Teleoperation
2026-10-09.authors: Yu Zhang , Yunqi Li , Yushi Du , Yi Ma , Yanchao Yang
2026-10-09.abstract: Dexterous teleoperation requires reliable human-hand state estimations. However, common low-cost motion-capture gloves and markerless trackers often exhibit biases that vary across users, glove fit, and recording sessions, degrading retargeting and demonstration quality. We present YOCO , a fast few-shot, fine-tuning-free calibration framework that corrects biased hand-pose streams from a small set of paired raw and target poses. Instead of optimizing a separate model for every operator or session, YOCO conditions a calibration HyperNet on the paired examples and predicts LoRA-style updates for a frozen MANO hand-estimation module, turning per-user calibration into a lightweight feed-forward adaptation step while preserving the geometric prior of MANO and the efficiency of a compact estimator. We train YOCO with synthetic drift augmentations on InterHand2.6M and evaluate on augmented InterHand sequences, offline real glove data, and dexterous teleoperation tasks. Across these settings, YOCO improves calibration efficiency, hand-state estimation quality and teleoperation performance compared with uncalibrated input and standard calibration baselines.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Teleoperation is a key tool for collecting dexterous hand demonstrations, but its effectiveness depends on the fidelity of the operator’s hand-state estimates. High-end motion-capture systems can provide accurate kinematics, yet they are expensive and often difficult to deploy at scale. Lower-cost gloves and markerless trackers are more accessible, but their outputs are affected by user hand morphology gap, device fit, sensor drift, and session-dependent bias. Such errors are particularly detrimental in dexterous manipulation, where even small fingertip or joint offsets can alter contact patterns, pinch geometry, and retargeted robot motion.

Prior hand-mocap calibration typically operates within a particular sensing pipeline, learning glove-signal-to-pose mappings, correcting IMU alignment and drift, or personalizing sensor-to-pose models [ 34 , 16 , 41 , 6 ] . We instead formulate few-shot calibration at the derived 3D hand-keypoint interface, after a tracker has produced its pose estimate. Given K K paired raw and target poses from a user and session, YOCO conditions a HyperNet on those examples and generates LoRA updates for a frozen MANO-based estimator in one pass, without per-session gradient optimization. This couples a sensor-independent pose interface with amortized, session-conditioned weight generation: unlike a LoRA initialization shared across sessions, the generated updates depend on the current calibration set (Appendix B ). The formulation requires no access to device-specific raw signals; our real-device evaluation remains limited to one tensile glove.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate calibration of derived 3D hand keypoints from a few pose pairs, separating the correction from device-specific sensor-to-pose calibration. Second, we generate session-conditioned LoRA weights for a frozen MANO estimator in one pass; learned-prior and set-conditioned residual controls test whether the gains stem from pair-conditioned weight generation beyond a shared prior or set conditioning alone. Third, we evaluate accuracy and adaptation cost on augmented InterHand2.6M and paired real-glove/AVP data, then test the resulting hand poses in physical teleoperation.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Mocap Devices: High-fidelity dexterous teleoperation depends on reliable capture of the operator hand, yet existing mocap interfaces exhibit a strong accuracy-accessibility trade-off. Glove- and exoskeleton-based systems provide stable kinematics but are costly, cumbersome, and sensitive to user-specific geometry and donning conditions [ 4 , 34 , 37 , 16 ] . The resulting joint biases or fingertip drift propagate directly into the collected demonstrations. Markerless and RGB-based pipelines, including FreiHAND, MediaPipe Hands, and HaMeR, have improved accessibility [ 26 , 39 , 40 , 8 , 36 , 19 , 21 ] , but still struggle with occlusion, hand-object interaction, cross-user morphology, and temporal stability. YOCO is complementary: rather than introducing a new tracker, it calibrates existing glove-based streams so that inexpensive devices become more consistent for downstream use.

Prior Hand-Mocap Calibration: Wang and Neff [ 34 ] learn a mapping from glove measurements to hand motion. Gosala et al. [ 6 ] use optical reference data to personalize a wearable sensor-to-pose model through side-tuning. FSGlove [ 16 ] jointly optimizes IMU alignment, hand shape, and kinematics, while the Transformer IMU Calibrator [ 41 ] estimates time-varying IMU drift and offsets. These approaches address calibration within particular sensing pipelines. YOCO instead takes their downstream 3D-keypoint representation as its input and learns to generate a session-specific correction of a frozen MANO estimator from a few paired poses. This interface makes the formulation independent of raw sensor modality; generalization beyond the evaluated tensile glove remains to be tested.

Dexterous Hand Retargeting and Teleoperation: Recent teleoperation systems have made dexterous data collection cheaper, more immersive, and more hardware-agnostic. Vision-based systems such as DexPilot and AnyTeleop reduce dependence on instrumented gloves [ 9 , 23 , 17 ] , while VR-based platforms such as Open-TeleVision and OPEN TEACH improve operator immersion [ 1 , 11 ] . In parallel, learning-based retargeting methods close the embodiment gap beyond purely kinematic alignment [ 28 , 20 , 15 , 35 ] , and new master-side or robot-side designs improve transferability and contact richness [ 33 , 5 , 12 ] .
These efforts largely assume that the upstream hand observation is already accurate; YOCO targets that bottleneck and is compatible with the downstream stacks above.

HyperNetworks and Parameter-Efficient Adaptation: HyperNetworks generate the weights of one network with another [ 7 ] , and task-conditioned variants support efficient cross-task adaptation [ 32 , 14 , 38 , 24 , 31 ] . In parallel, parameter-efficient methods such as Compacter and LoRA specialize a frozen backbone with compact low-rank updates [ 13 , 10 ] , and hypernetworks have been shown to predict such updates from limited conditioning input [ 27 ] . YOCO brings these ideas to dexterous teleoperation: h ψ h_{\psi} predicts LoRA-style updates Δ ​ W \Delta W for the hand estimator from a handful of paired calibration poses, yielding fast and robust adaptation.

2026-10-09.title: Scalable LEO Conjunction Screening using Adaptive Synthetic-Covariance Thresholds
2026-10-09.authors: Vedant Srinivas , Grace Ra Kim , Duncan Eddy , Mykel J. Kochenderfer
2026-10-09.abstract: As orbital populations grow, conjunction screening must search an increasing number of object pairs to identify those that may pass close enough to pose a collision risk. Existing pipelines rely on inexpensive early-stage filters, such as an apsis filter, to eliminate pairs whose orbital altitude ranges cannot plausibly result in a close approach. However, these filters typically apply the same fixed threshold to every object, making the screening unnecessarily conservative for well-constrained objects while potentially insufficient for objects with greater orbit-prediction uncertainty. In this work, we present an uncertainty-aware conjunction screening method that replaces a single fixed apsis threshold with object-specific thresholds derived from propagated radial uncertainty. The resulting thresholds vary across both objects and prediction time, becoming narrower when propagated uncertainty is small and wider when uncertainty grows. We pair this adaptive screening rule with a binary-search altitude sweep that makes the resulting heterogeneous intervals efficient to evaluate at catalog scale with log-linear search complexity. We evaluate the method on 33,791 objects from the Space-Track General Perturbations (GP) catalog using the preceding eight public ephemeris snapshots and a seven-day prediction horizon. The adaptive sieve retains 162.8 million candidate pairs, reducing the candidate set by 28.78% relative to a fixed 50 km apsis threshold and by 71.48% relative to brute-force all-pairs screening. It retains all close approaches identified in two independently propagated reference sets. At the largest tested catalog size, the binary-search sweep is 27 times faster than exhaustive interval evaluation while returning the same candidate set. These results demonstrate that uncertainty-aware screening can substantially reduce the candidate burden passed to downstream conjunction analysis, providing a scalable path toward managing increasingly large and heterogeneous orbital populations.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Over 40,000 Earth-orbiting objects are currently tracked by space surveillance networks, and this number is projected to grow substantially to over 100,000 satellites in 2030 [ 6 ] . As the orbital population grows, so does the number of potential close approaches, or conjunctions, that could occur between space objects that must be assessed for collision risk. The scale of this problem is already substantial; Spencer et al. report more than 130,000 conjunctions with separation distances below 5 km in a single week and note that this number is likely to increase with the growing population of operational satellites [ 18 ] . NASA has observed the same trend operationally. The number of conjunction events processed by NASA’s Conjunction Assessment Risk Analysis (CARA) program remained relatively stable from 2016 through 2020, before increasing sharply as additional payloads entered the orbital regimes of NASA assets [ 14 ] . Motheram et al. simulated LEO populations increasing from 10,885 to 94,581 satellites and found that the number of conjunctions over a three-month period increased from 8,377 to 511,177 as the population size grew, even without additional debris generation [ 13 ] . As orbital populations and conjunction events continue to grow, conjunction-assessment systems must efficiently identify object pairs that warrant further analysis.

Conjunction screening identifies potential close approaches between space objects over a future time window. Given a catalog of objects with their associated orbital elements, screening systems propagate object trajectories and test pairs of objects for separations below a predefined, static miss-distance threshold. In the United States, the U.S. Space Force maintains the Satellite Catalog and distributes orbital data for tracked objects through Space-Track [ 20 ] . These catalog data support conjunction-screening systems such as SOCRATES, which uses publicly available orbital elements and SGP4 propagation to identify potential close approaches [ 11 , 21 ] . Conjunction screening enables satellite operators to identify encounters that require further collision-risk assessment, allowing operators to determine when collision-avoidance maneuvers are necessary. The primary challenge in catalog-scale conjunction screening is computational scalability. For a catalog containing N N objects, an all-vs-all search contains N ⁡ ( N − 1 ) / 2 N(N-1)/2 unique pairs, so the number of pairwise comparisons grows as O ⁡ ( N 2 ) O(N^{2}) . The projected growth of spacecraft populations means that even basic conjunction screening may become computationally impractical, threatening the scalability of downstream collision-risk assessment.

A common way to reduce the cost of all-vs-all screening is to apply a sequence of conservative filters, or sieves, that remove object pairs from consideration before performing more computationally expensive analysis. Hoots et al. showed that analytic prefilters could accelerate close-approach detection by eliminating geometrically incompatible satellite pairs [ 9 ] . Later work organized these tests into increasingly selective filter sequences that progressively reduce the candidate set [ 22 , 3 ] . The apsis, or altitude, filter is typically applied first and removes pairs whose orbital altitude ranges cannot overlap. Path filters then test whether the two orbital trajectories can approach closely enough, while time or phase filters determine whether the objects can occupy the relevant region of their orbits at approximately the same time, as illustrated in Figure 1 .

These filters are intentionally conservative: they may retain pairs that do not ultimately conjunct, but they aim to avoid discarding pairs that could produce a conjunction. The surviving candidates then proceed to more computationally expensive processing, including higher-fidelity propagation, time-of-closest-approach refinement, and collision-risk analysis. Because the apsis filter is applied first, every pair it removes avoids computation in all subsequent stages, making its filtering efficiency especially impactful at reducing computational cost at catalog scale.

Beyond sieve-based filtering, prior work has addressed conjunction-analysis scalability through improved search algorithms, data structures, machine learning, and parallel computation. Mercurio et al. use a hierarchical k k -d tree to reduce the number of object interactions that must be evaluated, while Budianto-Ho et al. use spatiotemporal indexing to restrict conjunction searches to relevant regions of space and time [ 12 , 2 ] . Hellwig et al. develop spatial data structures designed for parallel CPU and GPU execution [ 8 ] . Stevenson et al. formulate all-vs-all conjunction screening as a classification problem and evaluate learning-based methods on large sets of candidate pairs [ 19 ] . Motheram et al. use GPU-parallel propagation and conjunction analysis in the VESTA framework to study simulated LEO populations approaching 100,000 satellites [ 13 ] . At a broader scale, MIT’s MOCAT framework models the long-term evolution and carrying capacity of the LEO environment, but does not perform object-pair conjunction screening or assess the risk of specific conjunction events [ 10 ] . These approaches complement conservative geometric filtering at the beginning of the conjunction-analysis pipeline, where reducing the candidate set lowers the computation required by every downstream stage.

The effectiveness of the apsis filter depends on the threshold used to expand each object’s radial bounds. Larger thresholds make the filter more conservative but allow more candidate pairs to survive for downstream processing; smaller thresholds improve pair reduction at the cost of greater sensitivity to orbit-prediction and filtering errors [ 1 ] . Fixed, hand-tuned thresholds are commonly used in practice, with prior works applying a fixed 50 km apsis threshold as the first-stage filter in a catalog-scale all-vs-all conjunction-screening study [ 19 ] . A fixed threshold applies the same padding regardless of the uncertainty of the underlying orbit estimate. For a well-characterized object, the threshold may be unnecessarily large and retain pairs that cannot realistically conjunct. For an object with larger prediction uncertainty, the same threshold may be too small to remain conservative. This mismatch motivates object-specific apsis thresholds that adapt to orbit-prediction uncertainty.

To address this limitation, we introduce an uncertainty-aware apsis filter that replaces the fixed catalog-wide threshold with an object-specific, time-dependent threshold derived from each object’s propagated synthetic covariance. We estimate the synthetic covariance by propagating several recent GP element sets for the same object to common epochs, comparing the resulting predicted states with the state predicted from the most recent element set, and using the dispersion of these differences to construct an object-specific covariance estimate. We then propagate this synthetic covariance estimate over the screening horizon to capture how that uncertainty evolves with time. The resulting radial uncertainty determines the apsis threshold for each object. Well-characterized objects receive tighter thresholds, allowing more infeasible pairs to be removed before downstream analysis, while objects with larger prediction uncertainty receive wider thresholds to preserve conservative screening. These thresholds are not capped at 50 km and can widen beyond the fixed baseline when the predicted uncertainty warrants it. The filter therefore allocates screening conservatism according to object-specific uncertainty rather than uniformly across the catalog.

At catalog scale, evaluating apsis overlap by comparing every pair of altitude intervals becomes increasingly expensive. To make these comparisons tractable, we use a binary-search-based altitude sweep that applies to both fixed and adaptive apsis thresholds. By sorting the intervals and using binary search to identify possible overlaps, the sweep replaces O ⁡ ( N 2 ) O(N^{2}) pairwise interval testing with an O ⁡ ( N ​ log ⁡ N ) O(N\log N) search while preserving the same apsis-screening condition.

We evaluate the proposed approach on a snapshot of the Space-Track catalog containing 33,791 valid objects, using the preceding eight public ephemeris snapshots to estimate synthetic covariances where sufficient data are available. At a seven-day look-ahead horizon, the adaptive sieve reduces the 570.9 million possible catalog pairs to 162.8 million candidates, compared with 228.6 million under a fixed 50 km threshold. The adaptive sieve therefore retains 28.78% fewer candidates than fixed screening and 71.48% fewer than brute force. Additional experiments evaluate close-approach recall and the computational scaling of the altitude sweep.

2026-10-09.title: Neural Networks for Temporal Pattern Recognition and Dynamic Arm Gesture Speed Estimation for Robot Control
2026-10-09.authors: Milán Zsolt Bagladi , László Gulyás
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-09.comment: . Published in Proceedings of the Intelligent Robotics FAIR 2026 (IntRob '26), June 18-19, 2026, Budapest, Hungary, ACM
2026-10-09.abstract: Deploying intelligent robotic systems that interact with humans through gestures requires neural networks capable of recognizing diverse temporal patterns. We present a systematic benchmark of ten abstract sequential tasks—five permutation-invariant (set) and five order-dependent (sequence) problems—evaluated across eighteen neural network architectures spanning recurrent, convolutional, attention-based, and set-function families. Beyond the core architecture–task grid, we explore numerous preprocessing and target-variable transformations, yielding more than 250 distinct experimental configurations. All variants are trained and tested under strictly identical conditions (fixed random seeds, shared hyperparameters, shared data splits) to ensure fair and reproducible comparison. Ranking across all ten tasks reveals four consistently top-performing architectures—BiGRU, TCN, Conv1D, and GRUReLU—all compact enough for real-time deployment (under 2 000 parameters in the benchmark setting). Based on this ranking, we apply three architecturally diverse top models (BiGRU, TCN, and GRUReLU) to a practical robotics problem: estimating the execution speed of dynamic arm gestures from skeletal keypoint sequences. Three speed interpretations (peak count, period time, and mean spike spacing) are evaluated on a custom dataset of eight traffic-related gesture classes comprising 256 710 frames recorded via OpenPose. The best configuration achieves a mean absolute error of 0.198 on the peak-count interpretation, corresponding to roughly 5% relative error, while the period-time interpretation reaches approximately 4% relative error, and the mean spike spacing interpretation approximately 8% relative error. These results demonstrate that neural networks can reliably estimate gesture speed from skeletal data, opening a path toward speed-aware gesture-controlled robotic systems.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Human arm gestures are used to convey precise, safety-critical commands in a wide range of real-world scenarios: traffic officers regulate vehicle flow at intersections, railway signalers authorize train movements, and airport ground crew guide aircraft during taxiing and parking. In all these cases, automating the recognition of such gestures can improve safety and operational efficiency. In our prior work ( Bagladi et al., 2025 ) , we developed a real-time pipeline for recognizing the type of dynamic arm gestures using OpenPose keypoint extraction, a 1 × 1 1\times 1 normalization scheme, and a GRU-based classifier. That system achieved high accuracy across varying camera angles and gesture speeds, and was successfully demonstrated controlling a TurtleBot 3 mobile robot.

However, recognizing what gesture is performed is only part of the problem. In many practical scenarios, the speed at which a gesture is executed carries additional meaning. For example, a rapid circular arm motion may signal urgency, while a slow one indicates a routine command. Our prior pipeline was shown to be largely insensitive to speed variations during classification —an advantage for type recognition, but a limitation when speed itself must be measured.

The speed measurement problem can be formulated as follows: given a sliding window of skeletal keypoint frames depicting a cyclic gesture, estimate a scalar value that characterizes its execution speed. As shown in ( Bagladi et al., 2025 ) , this can be approached algorithmically by selecting a characteristic starting position (null position) for each gesture, computing the per-frame distance from this position, and measuring the number of frames between consecutive local minima of the resulting distance curve. This yields a discrete speed value (in frames per cycle) that can be directly linked to wall-clock time given the camera’s frame rate.

A natural question arises: can neural networks learn to perform such speed estimation directly from the raw distance curves, without manually written rules to detect local minima? More broadly, which neural network architectures are best suited for recognizing abstract temporal patterns in sequential data?

To answer this question rigorously, we designed a benchmark of ten abstract tasks that isolate specific pattern-recognition capabilities required for speed estimation and related problems. Five tasks are set-type (permutation-invariant), where the order of elements does not affect the target value, and five are sequence-type , where temporal order is essential. We evaluate eighteen diverse neural network architectures on all ten tasks under strictly controlled, identical experimental conditions, rank the architectures by aggregated per-task performance, and apply the three top-ranked models to a real-world gesture speed estimation problem using three distinct speed interpretations on a custom dataset of eight traffic-related arm gestures. Our experiments show that neural networks can estimate gesture speed from skeletal data with relative errors ranging from 4% to 8% across three speed interpretations, validating the approach for practical robotics deployment.

The main contributions of this paper are:

A systematic benchmark of 18 neural network architectures across 10 abstract sequential tasks (5 permutation-invariant, 5 order-dependent), with over 250 experimental configurations evaluated under strictly controlled, identical conditions.

A rank-based aggregation methodology that enables fair cross-task architecture comparison despite heterogeneous output scales, yielding a reproducible global architecture ranking.

Validation of the benchmark findings on a practical robotics problem: neural speed estimation of dynamic arm gestures from skeletal keypoint data, achieving relative errors at or below 5% on two of three speed interpretations.

The paper begins with a review of related work on gesture recognition and neural sequence modeling (Section 2 ), then introduces the benchmark task suite that captures the key pattern-recognition capabilities needed for speed estimation (Section 3 ). Section 4 presents the eighteen evaluated architectures, spanning recurrent, convolutional, attention-based, and set-function families. The experimental protocol and ranking methodology are detailed in Section 5 , followed by the benchmark results and global architecture ranking in Section 6 . Building on these findings, Section 7 applies the top-ranked models to real gesture speed estimation, and Section 8 concludes with a discussion of future directions.

1. A systematic benchmark of 18 neural network architectures across 10 abstract sequential tasks (5 permutation-invariant, 5 order-dependent), with over 250 experimental configurations evaluated under strictly controlled, identical conditions.

2. A rank-based aggregation methodology that enables fair cross-task architecture comparison despite heterogeneous output scales, yielding a reproducible global architecture ranking.

3. Validation of the benchmark findings on a practical robotics problem: neural speed estimation of dynamic arm gestures from skeletal keypoint data, achieving relative errors at or below 5% on two of three speed interpretations.
