2026-10-09.title: SafeInferCom: Safe Inference-Time Compute via Verifier-Guided Mid-Generation Intervention for Robotic Task Planning
2026-10-09.authors: Weizhe Xu , Jialiang Fan , Mengyu Liu , Fanxin Kong
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)
2026-10-09.abstract:
Large Reasoning Language Models (LRLMs) enable multi-step reasoning for robotic task planning, but continued reasoning can overwrite valid intermediate plans or leave constraint violations unresolved, reducing planning reliability and wasting inference-time computation.
We develop an inference-time monitor that exposes and verifies intermediate plans without disrupting the original decoding trajectory.
Building on this monitor, we propose SafeInferCom, a formal verifier-guided framework that preserves valid intermediate plans and directs error correction during generation.
Experiments across multiple LRLMs and planning domains reveal reasoning–response inconsistency and limited self-correction under one-shot inference.
SafeInferCom improves planning success and accelerates error correction relative to one-shot inference.
When combined with iterative refinement, it further improves success while reducing token usage compared with refinement alone.
We additionally evaluate SafeInferCom in VirtualHome and provide a real-world robotic-arm demonstration.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Robotic task planning converts high-level goals into executable action sequences while ensuring that safety constraints are satisfied throughout execution.
Classical planners provide a principled and auditable solution when an accurate symbolic model is available: planners such as Fast Downward search over explicit action models, while validators such as VAL verify candidate plans against the given specification [ 1 , 2 ] .
However, this formalism has two practical limitations.
First, it requires rigid symbolic task representations and carefully engineered domain models.
Second, symbolic search can become computationally expensive as the number of objects, applicable actions, and planning horizon increase [ 3 ] .
Learning-based planners enable fast inference through learned policies, but depend on training data and generally lack explicit safety guarantees [ 4 , 5 ] .

Large Language Models (LLMs) have been explored for robotic task planning, leveraging their ability to interpret high-level instructions and contextual descriptions to generate candidate action sequences [ 6 , 7 ] .
While conventional LLM planners typically generate a final plan directly from the input, Large Reasoning Language Models (LRLMs) first perform explicit multi-step reasoning before producing the final output [ 8 , 9 ] .
By allocating additional computation at inference time to this intermediate reasoning process, LRLMs can deliberate over candidate actions and constraints before committing to a plan.

However, additional reasoning does not always lead to a better plan.
Through fine-grained analysis, we observe reasoning–response inconsistency across models and planning domains.
In some cases, a model develops a safe and goal-satisfying intermediate plan but later overwrites it through continued reasoning, ultimately producing an incorrect final output.
Conversely, constraint-violating intermediate plans may persist across successive reasoning steps without effective correction.
Such instability reduces planning reliability and wastes inference-time computation on trajectories that could have been terminated or corrected earlier.

Existing approaches improve LLM-based planning reliability by using external formal verifiers to validate completed plans, followed by iterative refinement or verification-based candidate selection [ 10 , 7 , 11 , 12 ] .
While these methods can improve final-plan validity, the verifier typically provides feedback only after a candidate has been fully generated.
For LRLMs, a valid intermediate plan may therefore be overwritten, or a constraint violation may persist, before external verification occurs.
This motivates integrating formal verification into the reasoning process to preserve valid intermediate plans and guide correction before generation is complete.

To systematically analyze reasoning-level safety issues, we first develop an inference-time reasoning monitor that instruments LRLM generation without altering its primary decoding trajectory.
The monitor extracts structured action sequences at selected reasoning transitions and evaluates them with an external formal verifier, while allowing the model to resume reasoning from the original state.
This enables fine-grained analysis of reasoning–response consistency under standard one-shot inference.

Building on this monitoring infrastructure, we introduce SafeInferCom , a verifier-guided mid-generation controller with four actions: continue a safe but incomplete trajectory, inject diagnostic feedback after a detected violation, terminate generation once a valid plan is identified, or trigger replanning after persistent violations.
Unlike post-hoc refinement, SafeInferCom intervenes before a complete failed trajectory is generated, allowing violations to be corrected during reasoning and earlier valid candidates to be preserved without restarting the entire inference process.
In this way, SafeInferCom shifts formal verification from post-hoc plan checking toward mid-generation guidance, improving planning reliability while avoiding unnecessary continued reasoning once a valid intermediate plan is identified.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:
(1) An inference-time reasoning monitor that extracts and formally verifies intermediate plans from LRLM reasoning prefixes while preserving the original decoding trajectory, enabling fine-grained analysis of reasoning–response inconsistency.
(2) SafeInferCom , a verifier-guided mid-generation controller with four actions: continuation, targeted correction, early termination, and replanning after persistent violations.
(3) A comprehensive evaluation across multiple LRLMs and robotic planning domains, characterizing intermediate-plan fidelity, self-correction behavior, and the success–compute trade-off against one-shot inference and post-hoc refinement. Additional VirtualHome and real-robot manipulation studies demonstrate the method in more realistic settings.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Classical, Learned, and Language-Based Task Planning

Classical planners search over explicit symbolic transition models, providing formal plan validation [ 1 , 2 ] .
However, they require carefully constructed symbolic representations and can incur explosive search cost as the number of objects, applicable actions, or planning horizon grows [ 3 ] .
Reinforcement and imitation learning instead learn policies or search guidance from demonstrations or environment interaction [ 4 , 5 ] .
These methods amortize planning computation through learned policies, but their performance remains tied to the training distribution and formal guarantees require an external verifier.
Language-based planners offer greater input flexibility by generating action sequences from natural-language instructions and contextual descriptions [ 13 , 14 ] , motivating recent efforts to combine language-model planning with symbolic reasoning and verification.

## II-B Language Models with Symbolic Planning and Verification

Language models can play different roles in symbolically grounded planning systems.
Some works translate tasks into formal representations and delegate planning to symbolic solvers [ 6 , 15 ] .
ISR-LLM instead uses an LLM to generate plans from symbolic domain and problem descriptions and refines them using formal validator feedback [ 11 ] .
Following a similar problem setting, other approaches also use external formal verification or temporal-constraint-based checking to validate LLM-generated plans against explicit task specifications [ 16 , 10 , 7 , 17 ] .

These methods typically invoke formal verification after a complete candidate plan has been generated, or between successive generation rounds.
Consequently, they do not directly regulate the intermediate reasoning trajectory within a single inference pass.
For CoT and LRLM-based planners, continued reasoning may therefore overwrite an already valid intermediate plan or allow an invalid candidate to persist before verification occurs.
SafeInferCom instead applies formal verification to candidate plans induced from intermediate reasoning prefixes and uses the resulting feedback for mid-generation control.

Following this line of work [ 11 , 16 , 10 , 7 , 17 ] , we study language-model-based planning under the same general setting, where candidate plans can be checked against an explicit task specification using an external formal verifier.

## II-C Evaluation of Language-Model Reasoning

Beyond outcome-level metrics such as accuracy and Pass@k, prior work has examined the quality of intermediate reasoning in language models.
Some evaluation frameworks [ 18 , 19 ] assess properties including consistency, correctness, and informativeness within reasoning traces.
Step-aware verifiers further evaluate intermediate reasoning steps to support final-answer selection [ 20 , 21 ] , while other studies investigate critique, error detection, reflection, and self-correction capabilities across linguistic, mathematical, and symbolic reasoning tasks [ 22 , 23 ] .

These efforts primarily evaluate reasoning quality at the language or logical level rather than the validity of the action sequences implied by intermediate reasoning under an explicit robotic task specification.
A reasoning trace may therefore appear coherent while inducing a candidate plan that violates action preconditions, safety constraints, or task goals.
Moreover, intermediate-reasoning evaluation alone does not provide an online mechanism for correcting an ongoing trajectory or preserving an already valid candidate during generation.

## II-D Inference-Time Compute Scaling and Regulation

Recent work has shown that additional inference-time computation can improve the performance of reasoning models [ 24 ] .
Inference-time scaling methods allocate more reasoning steps or sample additional trajectories to improve solution quality on challenging tasks.
Adaptive approaches further regulate computation during generation through restarting, pruning, or early termination [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] .

These methods primarily regulate inference based on predicted response quality, confidence, or the expected utility of additional computation.
In contrast, SafeInferCom uses external formal verification of intermediate candidate plans as the control signal.
This enables both corrective intervention and verified early termination, directly linking inference-time compute regulation to planning validity under an explicit task specification, while reusing the prefix decoding state to reduce monitoring overhead.

2026-10-09.title: How Firm Should a Grasp Be?
2026-10-09.authors: Matthew Beveridge , Shree K. Nayar
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-09.abstract: An ideal robot grasp is firm enough to securely handle an object, yet gentle enough to avoid damaging it. Achieving this balance requires knowledge of the object’s material properties, such as its mass, elasticity, and surface friction. These properties, however, are seldom precisely known a priori . In this work, we propose a visuotactile approach to estimating material properties in real time, during the process of grasping. Our method uses these estimated properties to determine the minimum grasp force required to handle the object. We contribute a new dataset of real-world objects (fruits and vegetables) with measured physical properties (shape, mass, elasticity, and friction), which we use to construct our force estimation model via simulations. We experimentally validate our approach to grasp force control using a robot with a parallel-jaw gripper. We demonstrate our system’s ability to gently grasp a wide variety of objects, in each case adapting to their unique physical properties.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Given an object and a desired interaction with it, the ideal grasp should exert no more force on the object than necessary to complete the task. While the notion of damage is often considered in catastrophic terms ( e.g . , a glass shattering), it can also be more subtle. For example, with excessive force, a fruit may bruise, a cardboard box might dent, or a plastic toy could crack or get scratched. In addition, there is a temporal element to damage: repeated interactions without care for an object’s fragility can cause cumulative wear over time. In this work, we are interested in the gentle grasping of objects, where the goal is to minimize the potential for damage during a grasp.

Since the material properties of an object are seldom precisely known a priori , how do we, humans, determine how firm its grasp should be? Dynamic grasp adaptation is intuitive to us [ 1 , 2 ] – we use our vision to obtain priors on the object’s material composition [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] , and rely on tactile feedback to refine these priors while grasping the object [ 6 , 7 ] . Since some of the material cues we need to understand an object’s physics cannot be known from vision alone, we estimate them via touch during the nascent stage of a grasp. We use these estimates to continuously adjust the forces we apply to the object and are thus able to gracefully handle it without conscious effort.

For a robot to gently grasp an object, it must either know the object’s material properties beforehand or be able to infer them during the grasp. Unless the object is precisely engineered or measured in detail, the best the robot has to work with is a rough approximation of its properties. One method to refine this approximation is for the robot to interact with the object before attempting a grasp. That is, the robot “probes” the object with a sequence of exploratory actions to estimate, for instance, its hardness [ 8 , 9 ] . Such an approach is time-consuming and hence not suitable for applications where speed is critical. Instead, we propose to leverage the dynamic, ephemeral tactile signals that are sensed during a grasp to estimate the object’s properties in real time. The robot is therefore able to adjust the force it applies to the object on-the-fly, in situ .

In a typical robotic grasping task, there are four initial phases as illustrated in Fig. 1 . The first is observe , where, from a distance, the robot can visually identify the class of the object, its shape, and its location. During the approach phase, the robot positions itself at a suitable grasp location determined by the object’s geometry and pose. Next, we have grip , where the gripper squeezes the object to take hold. Finally, the robot lifts the object before executing a goal task, such as moving it to a new location or mating it with another object. In our work, we focus on the observe , grip , and lift phases. The observe phase reveals the class of the object (“pepper” in Fig. 1 ), giving us a prior on its properties (mass, elasticity, friction, etc . ). During the grip and lift phases, we use haptic feedback to continuously refine these priors and control the force applied to the object. For approach , we assume a reasonable grasp pose is provided by an existing planner [ 10 , 11 ] .

While haptic signals during a grasp encode an object’s material properties, different combinations of material parameters could lead to the same haptic signals. Therefore, material estimation can be viewed as a challenging inverse problem. To develop our solution, we have chosen the domain of fruits and vegetables. This is an interesting domain as two samples, even when of the same class, can be expected to differ in their properties ( e.g . , a raw and a ripe avocado). We first collected a dataset, called Squash , that includes material measurements and 3D scans of 270 samples across 52 different classes of fruits and vegetables. 1 1 1 The dataset is available through the project webpage . From Squash , we derived class-level property distributions, which reduce the search space for instance-level properties.

Using Squash , we simulated numerous object grasps, with augmentations of material properties to span real-world variability. We trained a sequence model on the evolution of the simulated haptic data ( i.e . , tactile images and load cell measurements) to distill instance-level material properties from class distributions. We have integrated our visuotactile model for force control into a robot’s operating system, where it runs at 250 Hz \mathrm{Hz} . We used a 6 DoF arm and a parallel-jaw gripper with GelSight tactile sensors to validate our approach. Our system achieved more than a 2 × \times reduction in excess applied force for a successful grasp compared to non-adaptive baselines.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

For grasping, it is beneficial to recognize an object’s material class ( e.g . , peach) passively during the observation stage. However, precise class-level visual recognition ( i.e . , peaches vs. nectarines) requires elaborate optical measurements, such as the reflectance distribution function (BRDF) [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , which is hard in dynamic, cluttered robotics settings. Hence, class recognition is most often done from appearance alone [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] , using filter banks, statistical analysis, and deep learning. These approaches do not directly relate appearance to material properties, which has been the goal of more recent work [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . In our work, we rely on appearance to identify class-level material properties during observation , while recognizing that additional sensing modalities are needed to resolve instance-level variation within a class.

During the grip and lift stages, haptic feedback provides material-related signals for the specific object of interest ( e.g . , this peach has this hardness). In the general context of measuring physical properties, exciting objects with ultrasound and physical impact have been shown to reveal useful material cues [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] . In the realm of robotics, vision-based tactile sensors have been used to provide detailed insights related to contact mechanics. For example, GelSight [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] and DIGIT [ 29 ] have been used for hardness estimation [ 30 ] and shear/slip detection [ 31 ] . Beyond optical sensors, piezoresistive [ 32 , 33 ] and magnetic tactile skins [ 34 ] , which measure pressure distributions, have been integrated into grippers for fine-grained visuotactile manipulation [ 35 , 36 ] . Cross-modal methods have also been developed to relate visual appearance to tactile properties [ 37 , 38 , 21 , 39 , 40 ] . In our work, we use GelSight to image contact geometry, shear, and slip during a grasp. However, our approach can apply to various tactile sensors.

A classical approach to avoiding object damage is to regulate contact force via impedance control [ 41 ] , or to adjust grasp force reactively using tactile feedback [ 42 , 43 , 44 ] , e.g . , upon detecting incipient slip [ 45 , 46 ] . For this purpose, tactile sensors have also been integrated into soft robotic hands due to their passive compliance [ 47 , 48 ] . Purely vision-based methods [ 49 , 50 , 51 , 52 , 53 , 54 , 55 ] have also demonstrated successful deformation-aware grasping, but are shown to be more effective when fused with tactile sensing [ 56 , 57 ] . More recently, human and robot demonstrations have enabled end-to-end gentle grasping of objects [ 58 , 8 , 9 , 36 , 59 ] , and diffusion-based policies conditioned on tactile signals have been used for force-aware manipulation of fragile objects [ 60 ] . Nevertheless, these methods are not real-time, do not expose inferences about the object’s material, and only yield predictions of an “acceptable” grasp force based on heuristics.

Several large-scale 3D object datasets have been developed for robotic manipulation [ 61 , 62 , 63 , 64 , 65 ] and broader 3D vision tasks [ 66 , 67 , 68 ] . These datasets provide geometry and appearance but do not include measured material properties. The recent work by Cao and Kalogerakis [69] uses annotated simulated objects with material parameters, where the parameter values are assigned using material-category labels rather than measurements made on individual instances. For deformable objects, smaller datasets exist that include detailed annotations of the deformation process through finite element analysis [ 49 , 70 ] . One of our contributions is Squash , a dataset that pairs 3D scans of fruits and vegetables with per-instance measurements of material properties (elasticity, mass, and surface friction parameters). It is the first 3D object dataset specifically designed for deformable object simulation with measured properties. Beyond its utility in robotics, we expect Squash to be a valuable resource for simulation and rendering in computer graphics and animation.

2026-10-09.title: Demonstrating Arena 5.0: A Photorealistic ROS2 Simulation Framework for Developing and Benchmarking Social Navigation
2026-10-09.authors: Volodymyr Shcherbyna , Linh Kästner , Duc Anh Do , Hoang Tung , Huu Giang Nguyen , Maximilian Ho-Kyoung Schreff , Tim Seeger , Eva Wiese , Ahmed Martban , Huajian Zeng , An Tran , Nguyen Quoc Hung , Jonas Kreutz , Vu Thanh Lam , Ton Manh Kien , Harold Soh
2026-10-09.comment: . Published at Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) 2025
2026-10-09.abstract: Building upon the foundations laid by our previous work, this paper introduces Arena 5.0 , the fifth iteration of our framework for robotics social navigation development and benchmarking. Arena 5.0 provides three main contributions: 1) The complete integration of NVIDIA Isaac Gym, enabling photorealistic simulations and more efficient training. It seamlessly incorporates Isaac Gym into the Arena platform, allowing the use of existing modules such as randomized environment generation, evaluation tools, ROS2 support, and the integration of planners, robot models, and APIs within Isaac Gym. 2) A comprehensive benchmark of state-of-the-art social navigation strategies, evaluated on a diverse set of generated and customized worlds and scenarios of varying difficulty levels. These benchmarks provide a detailed assessment of navigation planners using a wide range of social navigation metrics. 3) Extensive scenario generation and task planning modules for improved and customizable generation of social navigation scenarios, such as emergency and rescue situations. The platform’s performance was evaluated by generating the aforementioned benchmark and through a comprehensive user study, demonstrating significant improvements in usability and efficiency compared to previous versions. Arena 5.0 is open source and available at https://github.com/Arena-Rosnav .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Social navigation has gained increasing importance across various sectors such as healthcare, logistics, and assistive robotics. Despite its growing adoption, navigating human-centric environments remains a significant challenge. A major concern is bridging the gap between simulation-based research and industry-grade applications (sim2real) [ 1 ] . Consequently, there is a growing demand for realistic and comprehensive simulation platforms, as emerging approaches must be thoroughly tested and benchmarked prior to real-world deployment. Common issues include non-reproducible research findings and highly specialized outcomes that are difficult to generalize for practical applications. Moreover, many existing platforms continue to rely on legacy software (e.g., ROS1), complicating the transition from simulation to reality and further widening the sim2real gap. This reliance impedes progress and underscores the necessity for updated simulation frameworks that better facilitate technology transfer to industry-grade systems [ 2 ] .

Most open-source benchmarking platforms concentrate on specific navigation aspects without addressing broader concerns such as real-robot integration, deployment, and practical applicability. Owing to varied setups—ranging from in-house simulators to proof-of-concept demonstrations—numerous approaches are overly simplified and challenging to replicate in real-world scenarios. Additionally, many available simulation environments either cater to specialized tasks (e.g., learning-based methods) or offer limited functionality. In contrast, sophisticated state-of-the-art simulators such as Isaac Sim present substantial usability challenges, are not fully open source, and consequently have a restricted user base [ 2 , 1 , 3 ] . To address these issues, we introduced world generation capabilities and social interaction modules in Arena 3, followed by a platform-wide migration to ROS2 and extended world-generation functionalities in Arena 4.0. Building on these foundations, Arena 5.0 integrates Isaac Gym to offer photorealistic simulations, thereby aligning with both research and industry requirements. By providing an enhanced world and scenario generation process, as well as a direct link to Isaac Gym, Arena 5.0 enables more realistic and comprehensive evaluations, bridging a critical gap in social navigation research and deployment. The main contributions of this work are as follows:

Full Integration of Isaac Gym into the Arena Framework: This includes a comprehensive ROS integration of Isaac Gym, facilitating seamless inter-operation with ROS-based systems. This integration aims to leverage Isaac Gym’s advanced simulation capabilities within the Arena framework to enhance the development and testing of autonomous robots in realistic environments.

Benchmarking: Establishment of rigorous benchmarks for evaluating the performance of social navigation algorithms. This includes metrics for assessing accuracy, efficiency, and real-time performance of robots within simulated human-centric environments.

Automated and Customizable Scenario Generation Pipelines: Development of flexible scenario generation pipelines that allow researchers to automatically create diverse and complex environments. This feature supports customization to address specific research needs and scenarios, thus accelerating the testing and refinement of navigation algorithms.

2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Works

Social navigation is increasingly critical for daily tasks, and a variety of research works have been conducted for the development, training, and testing of navigation approaches in social environments [ 4 ] , [ 5 ] , [ 6 ] , [ 7 ] . However, although many social navigation approaches continue to emerge, their reproducibility, applicability, and validity are often hard to assess due to highly specific settings, simulators, labs, and installation setups. In a recent studies, by Francis et al. and Singamaneni et al. [ 8 ] , [ 2 ] the lack of a unified benchmark for social navigation approaches is highlighted as one of the main bottlenecks in social navigation robotics research.
Navigation benchmarks such as Bench-MR by Heiden et al. [ 9 ] , Robobench by Weisz et al. [ 10 ] , CommonRoad by Althoff et al. [ 11 ] , and the Benchmarking Suite by Moll et al. [ 12 ] focus solely on 2D simulation and only consider static environments.
Other benchmarks such as SocNavBench [ 13 ] by Biswas et al., DynaBARN by Nair et al. [ 14 ] , or SocialGym by Holtz et al. [ 15 ] employ dynamic environments but contain simplistic and limited navigation approaches for proof of concepts. Other social navigation benchmarking platforms include SEAN and SEAN2.0 by Tsoi et al. [ 16 , 17 ] , HuNavSim by Perez-Higueras et al. [ 18 ] , MRPB 1.0 by Wen et al. [ 19 ] , SRPB by Karwowski et al. [ 20 ] , or the Social Evaluation Platform by Gao et al. [ 21 ] . However, they often face limitations in scenario diversity or robot variety. Furthermore, these environments are frequently constrained by their simulation capabilities or the scenarios they offer. Additionally, they do not cover recent approaches utilizing other sensor modalities such as rgbd, sonar, imu sensors, and often utilize legacy software frameworks. Other social navigation benchmarks focus on incorporating multi-agent reinforcement learning, such as SAMARL by Wang et al. [ 22 ] or Socialgym2.0 [ 23 ] . However, they are limited to 2D simplistic simulations and showcase proof-of-concepts approaches. As industry is shifting towards ROS2 usage, and with the advent of increased computational power, photorealistic simulators and more sensor modalities are often required to employ sophisticated approaches. Notably, Isaac Gym [ 24 ] by Makoviychuk et al. has been making strides in generating diverse, complex, dynamic environments and has also been adopted by numerous laboratories. However, due to its recent release, the documentation and usability remain challenging and are primarily accessible to experts in the field. Additionally, it is not open source, limiting its availability to a wider audience. To address aforementioned issues, we propose Arena 5.0, which offers a variety of different simulation environments, sensor modalities, a comprehensive suite of robots and planners, as well as modules for complex world and scenario generation in social settings making it a useful platform for social navigation robotics research.

2026-10-09.title: OmniDex: Scaling Dexterous Hand Grasping to Diverse Cluttered Scenes
2026-10-09.authors: Naiyu Fang , Zhongjin Luo , Yuxin Mo , Siyuan Huang , Jianbo Liu , Yufei Liu , Zheyuan Zhou , Chenkai Jin , Xiaogang Wang , Hongsheng Li
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-09.abstract: Dexterous grasping is the foundational primitive in embodied AI, demanding massive data to train robust models. As real-world data collection is expensive, simulation has become the mainstream paradigm. Yet, while cluttered scenes best reflect real-world applications, learning to grasp within them is bottlenecked by a critical scarcity of large-scale data. To resolve this, we curate high-quality 3D objects and supporting bases, proposing a scalable seed-and-filter strategy that bypasses sluggish scene-level optimization. This yields an unprecedented benchmark comprising over 2.6 million scenes and 0.4B scene-specific grasp ground truths, featuring diverse realistic layouts paired with rich semantic and geometric observations. Furthermore, we introduce the OmniDex model to overcome the grasp multimodality and last-millimeter precision errors plaguing current generative models. By coupling Soft Winner-Takes-All learning with human-inspired physical constraints during training, and utilizing physics-driven ranking, our approach achieves robust dexterous grasping without the latency of post-optimization. Experimental results show that OmniDex model achieves state-of-the-art performance and strong generalization across diverse scenes, views, and unseen objects.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Dexterous hands mark a critical milestone in embodied artificial intelligence (AI) [ 8 ] . Unlike parallel-jaw grippers [ 10 , 9 ] , they offer the kinematic flexibility and fine-grained manipulation essential for complex, human-centric tasks. At the core of this capability lies grasping—the foundational primitive upon which all advanced interactions are built. For an intelligent agent, predicting a valid grasp pose acts as the "key frame" that dictates the success of all subsequent tasks. However, training grasp pose generation models is severely bottlenecked by a profound scarcity of high-quality data. Since collecting high degree-of-freedom (DoF) grasp poses in the real world is expensive and unscalable [ 14 ] , simulation-based data synthesis [ 31 , 3 ] has emerged as the mainstream paradigm. To drive dexterous grasping task toward greater robustness and real-world applicability, this paper introduces a large-scale simulation benchmark targeting cluttered scenes, coupled with a novel learning framework.

Real-world dexterous grasping is inherently messy and cluttered. Yet, the standard setting in prior dexterous grasping literature oversimplifies the problem by isolating a single object in floating space or on a clear tabletop [ 24 , 30 ] . Recent efforts tackle cluttered scenes [ 32 , 33 ] ; however, robust performance in complex real-world settings remains an open problem due to three underlying challenges. First, current approaches rely on depth-based pseudo point clouds as their primary perceptual input. This forces models to focus on geometric shapes at the expense of semantic awareness. Consequently, agents struggle with target object localization in cluttered scenes (e.g., distinguishing geometrically identical Coke and Sprite cans), since their geometries are nearly identical. Second, existing benchmark scales are critically constrained by computationally expensive data generation pipelines. Scene-level optimization for grasp ground truths [ 32 ] incurs prohibitive time costs, limiting existing cluttered-scene benchmarks to only 0.4K–8K scenes (e.g., DexGraspNet 2.0: 8K; Tab. 1 ). Yet, massive scale is indispensable. Unlike single-object floating setups, cluttered scenes feature complex spatial dynamics among object. Thus, models require a large-scale dataset to effectively learn these spatial relationships and master scene-specific grasping, such as avoiding adjacent items or table penetration. Finally, prior works neglect diverse supporting bases and spatial layouts, compromising robustness and real-world generalization.

Beyond the data bottleneck, existing dexterous grasping generation models face critical algorithmic hurdles when mapping perceptual inputs to high-DoF kinematic space. Dexterous grasping is a multimodal problem, as an object affords numerous viable grasp poses. To capture this complex distribution, data-driven approaches rely heavily on intermediate representations, such as affordance maps [ 32 , 12 ] , rendering the generation pipeline inherently non-end-to-end. However, pure data-driven methods struggle with critical last-millimeter precision errors. A mere millimeter of deviation translates directly to catastrophic contact failures in simulation. To compensate for this inherent inaccuracy, current methods resort to costly post-optimization or test-time fine-tuning [ 27 , 33 ] , severely compromising inference efficiency.

To address these data and algorithmic bottlenecks, we introduce a holistic paradigm comprising a large-scale cluttered scene benchmark and a novel end-to-end generation framework. To bypass the prohibitive computational cost of scene-level optimization, our OmniDex benchmark employs a scalable seed-and-filter strategy. We first establish a reusable library of free-space seed grasps for single objects, then filter them through collision constraints in cluttered scenes within gravity-stabilized simulations. Leveraging high-quality 3D object assets and high-fidelity rendering, this pipeline yields multi-modal RGB-D observations from multiple fixed camera views, aligned with scene-aware grasp ground truths. Ultimately, our OmniDex benchmark delivers unprecedented scale: over 2.6 million scenes and 0.4B scene-specific grasp pose labels, covering diverse objects, supporting bases, and realistic cluttered layouts. We hope this benchmark will spur a new wave of research in cluttered scenes dexterous grasping. Empowered by this benchmark, OmniDex model fundamentally avoids the pitfalls of non-end-to-end intermediate representations and sluggish test-time fine-tuning. Instead, we internalize physical dynamics directly into training. By coupling a Soft Winner-Takes-All learning to capture grasp multimodality with a human-inspired physics-constrained loss—which enforces direct hand-object interaction—we effectively bridge the critical last-millimeter precision gap to ensure close and stable grasping. During inference, the optimal grasp pose is rapidly identified via a physical ranking mechanism, achieving both exceptional fidelity and real-time efficiency.

• We introduce a massive cluttered-scene OmniDex benchmark via a scalable seed-and-filter paradigm, yielding an unprecedented dataset of over 2.6 million realistic scenes and 0.4B scene-specific validated grasp ground truths, featuring diverse supporting bases and rich multi-modal observations.

• We propose OmniDex model, a novel end-to-end grasp generation framework that couples Soft Winner-Takes-All learning with human-inspired physical constraints to capture grasp multimodality and bridge the last-millimeter precision gap, with physics-driven ranking for robust inference.

• Experimental results show that OmniDex achieves state-of-the-art performance on the OmniDex benchmark. It generalizes well across scene subsets, supporting bases, input views, and unseen objects, demonstrating robustness in realistic cluttered scenes.

# Related Works

## Dexterous Grasping Datasets and Benchmarks

Real-world dexterous grasping datasets largely rely on human teleoperation [ 14 , 25 , 29 , 11 ] . While capturing human-like priors, this labor-intensive paradigm limits dataset scale and object diversity. Consequently, the community shifted to simulation-based synthesis for isolated objects. Pioneering works [ 24 , 35 , 3 , 23 ] leveraged optimization and physical priors to generate massive single-object grasps, culminating in billion-scale datasets like Dex1B [ 31 ] . Despite this impressive scale, these single-object benchmarks fail to model the spatial dynamics of real-world clutter. While recent efforts have introduced cluttered-scene benchmarks [ 32 , 5 ] to bridge this reality gap, they remain bottlenecked by costly per-scene optimization. In stark contrast, our efficient seed-and-filter strategy entirely bypasses this sluggish optimization, yielding an unprecedented 2.6 million complex scenes and 0.4B physically validated ground truth, thereby establishing a new benchmark for diversity and scale in cluttered grasping.

## Dexterous Grasp Generation Methods

Learning-based generative models promise real-time dexterous grasp generation, yet mapping visual inputs to high-DoF kinematics is fundamentally plagued by grasp multimodality. To capture this one-to-many manifold, data-driven methods typically rely on heuristic proxies—such as contact maps [ 30 , 33 ] or affordance fields [ 32 , 19 ] , making the pipeline non-end-to-end. Furthermore, these models struggle with the last-millimeter precision, where minute deviations cause catastrophic contact failures. To mitigate this, recent frameworks [ 27 , 12 ] use computationally heavy test-time optimization [ 4 ] , compromising real-time efficiency. While some attempts internalize physical priors during training to bypass this latency [ 35 ] , their geometric penalties remain insufficient for dense clutters. In stark contrast, our framework resolves these bottlenecks: we capture the multimodal distribution via a Soft Winner-Takes-All objective, and directly bridge the precision gap using a human-inspired physical constraint during training, coupled with a physical ranking during inference.

2026-10-09.title: Higher-Order Action Supervision Makes A Strong Policy Class
2026-10-09.authors: Peng Cheng , Yunxian Hou , Zhi Zhou , Qian Zhang , Chang Huang , Xianyuan Zhan
2026-10-09.abstract: Modern data-driven decision-making methods, such as imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL), have achieved great success in solving many complex tasks. However, these methods often suffer from serious control instability and robustness issues when applied in real-world applications such as robotics and autonomous driving, posing notable challenges for their practical deployment. We argue that this instability issue stems largely from their limitations on solely supervising and optimizing zeroth-order actions (i.e., the action labels), failing to account for higher-order action dynamics and temporal consistency. In this paper, we show that simultaneously supervising both zeroth- and first-order actions can dramatically enhance policies’ performance and control robustness. To achieve this, we introduce a novel and elegant loss scheme supported by formal theoretical guarantees that can equip any off-the-shelf policy model (e.g., deterministic, stochastic, or flow policies) with the capability for higher-order action supervision, without requiring any structural modifications. Moreover, our proposed method can serve as a lightweight plug-and-play module that seamlessly integrates with a broad spectrum of existing offline RL frameworks. Extensive evaluations on OGBench and D4RL demonstrate that our approach yields substantial performance and robustness improvements across a wide range of continuous control environments. Notably, our method can also enhance policies’ out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization capability in the challenging low-data regime, making it an ideal tool in tackling many real-world control problems.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Learning-based decision-making methods, such as imitation learning (IL) and reinforcement learning (RL), have achieved notable success in many complex tasks, such as games ( Mnih et al., 2015 ; Silver et al., 2017 ) , robotics ( Kalashnikov et al., 2018 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) , and autonomous driving ( Kendall et al., 2019 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ) . However, when these learning-based approaches are deployed in real-world control problems, they are frequently criticized for their control instability and poor robustness. Examples of such issues include lack of smoothness in action outputs, severe jittering across consecutive steps, and poor generalization in offline learning under data sparsity ( Dulac-Arnold et al., 2021 ; Song et al., 2023 ; Cheng et al., 2023 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) .

In contrast to conventional control theories ( Kirk, 2004 ) that place heavy emphasis on control stability and higher-order behavior modeling, contemporary learning-based decision-making methods in the AI community predominantly only focus on supervising and optimizing zeroth-order actions (i.e., the actual action labels).
In realistic control scenarios, the neglect of higher-order temporal consistency in actions frequently leads to control instability and non-smooth action execution, which constitutes a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment ( Dulac-Arnold et al., 2021 ) . Under physical hardware constraints, such high-frequency action fluctuations can cause excessive mechanical wear and energy consumption, drastically shortening the lifespan of both the system and its constituent parts ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Mysore et al., 2021 ; de La Presilla et al., 2023 ; Zhan et al., 2022 ; Zhan et al., 2025 ) . These vulnerabilities pose severe safety risks and degrade operational reliability across various domains, including drone control ( Mysore et al., 2021 ; Shi et al., 2019 ) , robotic manipulation ( Yu et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and autonomous driving ( Cai et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2021 ; Wasala et al., 2020 ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . Fundamentally, this issue arises because the policy becomes excessively sensitive to minor state-action perturbations, yielding disproportionately large action variations ( Song et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2021 ) . We empirically illustrate this vulnerability using a maze navigation task in Figure 1 . As shown in Figure 1 (a), the policy learned via standard behavior cloning (BC), which lacks higher-order action supervision, produces large and highly oscillatory first-order actions, eventually producing a suboptimal trajectory. By contrast, jointly supervising both zeroth- and first-order actions enforces much stronger behavioral regularization, resulting in significantly smoother and optimal execution (Figure 1 (b)).

However, incorporating higher-order action information in policy modeling is not an easy task. As the 0 th 0^{\text{th}} -order action a a and the 1 st 1^{\text{st}} -order action a ˙ \dot{a} live in two completely different action spaces, naïvely predicting these two sets of actions not only doubles the action space, causing learning difficulties, but also faces potential conflicting gradient issues that are commonly encountered in multi-task learning ( Yu et al., 2020 ) . Therefore, existing works on action smoothness improvement primarily focus on introducing action fluctuation penalty regularizations ( Mysore et al., 2021 ; Kobayashi, 2022 ; Shen et al., 2020 ; Zhao et al., 2022 ) , or designing special neural network architectures to constrain the network’s Lipschitz constant, e.g., via spectral normalization or specialized modules like LipsNet ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2025 ) . However, both streams of work suffer from a number of limitations. Adding smoothness penalties relies on task-specific ad-hoc design and cumbersome tuning efforts, whereas using specialized, heavily regularized neural network architectures loses generality and restricts the model’s expressivity to capture complex data distributions.

In this work, we introduce a novel and elegant learning scheme that can achieve simultaneous 0 th 0^{\text{th}} - and 1 st 1^{\text{st}} -order action supervision. The best part is, we can easily transform any given policy model into a more powerful policy class without making any structural modification. The secret recipe is to leverage the intrinsic property of the policy model’s time derivative for supervision, i.e., π ˙ ​ ( s ) = ∇ s π ​ ( s ) ⋅ s ˙ \dot{\pi}(s)=\nabla_{s}\pi(s)\cdot\dot{s} . We provide practical instantiations of loss schemes for deterministic, stochastic, and generative flow matching policy classes, supported by formal theoretical guarantees for the IL setting. Moreover, we show that our enhanced policy class is naturally compatible with the continuous-time RL paradigm, like the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) framework. This leads to a plug-and-play enhancement module that can be seamlessly integrated with a wide spectrum of existing offline RL algorithms with minimal code modifications. We evaluate our method through extensive experiments on diverse tasks from the large-scale OGBench ( Park et al., 2025a ) and widely used D4RL ( Fu et al., 2020 ) benchmarks. Despite its simplicity, our approach achieves consistent and significant performance improvements when added to different offline policy optimization paradigms. Notably, in challenging small-dataset settings, our proposed modification excels by providing robust OOD generalization support, enabling the agent to maintain stable and high performance even on tasks where the base algorithms fail or severely degrade. This makes our method an ideal tool for tackling many real-world control problems.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Smoothness and robustness enhancement for policy learning. Mitigating action fluctuation and trajectory drift remains a critical challenge for deploying policies in physical systems ( Dulac-Arnold et al., 2021 ; Song et al., 2023 ) . To enforce action smoothness and robustness, prior studies in continuous control have primarily explored two directions: penalty-based regularizations ( Mysore et al., 2021 ; Kobayashi, 2022 ; Shen et al., 2020 ; Zhao et al., 2022 ) and architectural enhancements ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2025 ) . Penalty-based regularization approaches, such as CAPS ( Mysore et al., 2021 ) , L2C2 ( Kobayashi, 2022 ) , and SR 2 L ( Shen et al., 2020 ; Zhao et al., 2022 ) , introduce action fluctuation penalty regularizations to their policy optimization objectives. However, they inherently rely on querying or sampling synthetic states to enforce local action consistency. In the offline setting, where interaction with the environment is not permitted, such state-dependent sampling may
introduce significant OOD extrapolation errors, and often suffer from significant performance
variability across environments ( Christmann et al., 2024 ) . In contrast, architectural enhancement methods explicitly constrain the network’s Lipschitz constant, e.g., via spectral normalization or specialized modules like LipsNet ( Song et al., 2023 ; Song et al., 2025 ) . However, imposing extra structural priors can also restrict the model’s expressivity. This introduces a fundamental trade-off: while the policy becomes smoother, the restricted capacity commonly leads to underfitting, degraded control performance, and additional computational overhead during inference.
Concurrently, there are also a few attempts to incorporate higher-order action derivatives to enhance control smoothness, such as TaSIL ( Pfrommer et al., 2022 ) , which minimizes the gap between the Taylor series expansion of the learned and expert policies. Although promising, it remains more theoretical rather than practical, due to the complex evaluation procedure involved.

Offline RL and continuous-time RL. In this study, we primarily focus on offline policy learning, such as offline IL (e.g., behavior cloning, BC) and offline RL, which directly imitate or optimize over a fixed offline dataset without environment interaction. Compared with IL, offline RL is more complex, which optimizes the cumulative return while being regularized towards the behavior data to avoid extrapolation error accumulation ( Levine et al., 2020 ; Kumar et al., 2019 ) . Depending on how the learned policy is parameterized, existing offline RL algorithms can be classified into three categories. The first category employs deterministic policies and explicitly constrains the learned actions toward the dataset using distance-based behavior cloning penalties ( Fujimoto and Gu, 2021 ; Li et al., 2023b ; Cheng et al., 2023 ) . The second and also the more popular category adopts stochastic policies (e.g., Gaussian policies) ( Wu et al., 2019 ; Kumar et al., 2019 ; Kumar et al., 2020 ; Kostrikov et al., 2022 ; Lyu et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2022a ; Xu et al., 2022b ; Niu et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023a ; Mao et al., 2024b ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , which maximizes the likelihood of high-return actions under some distribution-based data regularizations. Recently, the third category of offline RL methods has emerged, which leverages expressive generative models, such as diffusion or flow matching policies, to capture the complex, multimodal action distributions in the datasets ( Wang et al., 2022 ; Janner et al., 2022 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Mao et al., 2024a ; Zheng et al., 2024 ; Park et al., 2025b ; Zheng et al., 2025a ; Liang et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . However, all of the above methods are restricted to learning policies in the 0 th 0^{\text{th}} -order action spaces, which suffer from notable control stability and robustness issues. Incorporating higher-order action supervision in offline RL remains entirely unexplored.

Another research avenue closely related to our work is continuous-time RL, which transcends the structural limitations of discrete-time Markov decision processes (MDPs) by modeling state and action evolution continuously over time ( Doya, 2000 ; Wang et al., 2020 ; Munos, 2006 ) . The Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation serves as the core theoretical foundation for this domain ( Lee and Sutton, 2021 ; Vamvoudakis and Lewis, 2010 ; Bhasin et al., 2013 ; Vamvoudakis et al., 2014 ) . Recent advancements have successfully utilized HJB-based frameworks to demonstrate how continuous-time structural priors can directly guide stable policy evaluation and control ( Kim et al., 2021 ; Jia and Zhou, 2022 ; Lien et al., 2024 ) . Although the HJB-based framework naturally requires 1 st 1^{\text{st}} -order action a ˙ \dot{a} information to capture Q Q -value’s variation in continuous time, due to the lack of a proper strategy to evaluate a ˙ \dot{a} from policy π \pi , existing methods often resort to a crude approximation or replace it with a fixed bounding value. This drastically degrades the value estimation quality under the HJB framework and leads to suboptimal performance.

2026-10-09.title: PMTRM: Pseudo-Memory Temporal Re-encoding Module for Embodied Policy Learning
2026-10-09.authors: Changchuan Yang , Haoxuan Xu , Wenbo Chen , Shuai Ren , Jianlong Zheng , Huarui Zhang , Tianfu Li , Guanzhong Tian
2026-10-09.abstract:
Robotic manipulation often contains repeated motions whose local observations look similar at different phases.
When these phases require different actions, a policy that relies mainly on the current observation may repeat completed motions or switch phases at the wrong time. To address this phase ambiguity, we present the Pseudo-Memory Temporal Re-encoding Module (PMTRM), a lightweight plug-in module with only 7.61M parameters that encodes a bounded history of executed states and actions into a latent sequence for existing policies. To help distinguish phases, a temporal heterogeneity objective penalizes positive similarity between distant positions in this sequence, while anchor and reconstruction losses preserve information needed for action prediction. The reconstruction decoder is used only during training, leaving the temporal re-encoder to supply history to the policy at inference. We train the module progressively on synthetic sequences and robot data, then jointly with the policy, using temporal masking to accommodate partial histories. This integration retains the original action head and action space and adds auxiliary losses to the original policy loss. Experiments with multiple policy backbones in simulation and on a real robot show improved task success on tasks with phase ambiguity, with little additional computation.
2026-10-09.introduction:
In robotic manipulation, the same or similar observation may occur at different execution phases that require different actions.
For example, a button may look unchanged after a press [ 1 ] , and a robot moving along the same path in opposite directions may need history to identify the current phase [ 2 ] .
We use phase ambiguity to describe this situation: observations from different execution phases are locally similar, but the appropriate next action depends on the preceding execution history.
A policy without sufficient history may therefore repeat a completed motion or switch phases at the wrong time.
Recent work on cyclic manipulation further shows the need to track progress when an action must be repeated a specified number of times [ 3 ] .
Reliable action selection in these settings therefore requires a representation of execution history that distinguishes phases with similar observations.

Recent imitation learning and embodied policy frameworks have substantially improved robotic action prediction, with representative examples including ACT [ 4 ] , Diffusion Policy [ 5 ] , and vision-language-action models such as OpenVLA [ 6 ] . Nevertheless, resolving phase ambiguity requires temporal representations that preserve relevant execution history and distinguish phases with similar observations. Existing memory mechanisms commonly provide this context through recurrent states [ 7 ] , learned history tokens [ 2 ] , or retrieval from a memory bank [ 1 ] , as conceptually shown in Fig. 1 (a). These mechanisms support decisions that depend on past interactions, but maintaining and accessing memory can require dedicated update rules, retrieval components, or policy-specific fusion layers. Such requirements increase integration effort across policy backbones, even when the relevant phase information is contained in a bounded recent history. The challenge is therefore to preserve action information and distinguish execution phases through a lightweight history representation that requires minimal changes to the policy. In practical robotic deployment, such a module should introduce limited computational overhead and remain scalable across different policy backbones rather than relying on additional memory banks or large architectural modifications.

To learn such a representation, we introduce PMTRM, which combines a temporal re-encoder, representation learning objectives, and a progressive training procedure.
The re-encoder maps a bounded history of executed states and actions to a latent sequence for the policy, as shown in Fig. 1 (b).
To discourage similar representations at distant time steps, we apply a temporal heterogeneity objective directly to this sequence.
Anchor and reconstruction losses preserve information needed for action prediction, balancing temporal discrimination with reconstruction of the input history.
These objectives use temporal distance rather than phase labels during training.
We first pretrain PMTRM on synthetic sequences, adapt it to robot data, and apply mirror augmentation and temporal masking before joint policy training.
Joint training adds the auxiliary objectives to the original policy loss.
At inference, only the re-encoder is retained, providing recent history through the policy input adapter while preserving the original action head and action space.
The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We propose PMTRM, a lightweight bounded-history temporal representation module with 7.61M parameters, whose policy-facing latent is explicitly regularized for distant-phase discriminability while remaining reconstructable.

We combine temporal heterogeneity with anchor and reconstruction losses to encourage temporal discrimination while preserving action information, without phase labels.

We evaluate PMTRM across action-policy backbones and phase-ambiguous tasks in simulation and on a real robot, and analyze the effects of the proposed objectives and mirror-mask training.

1. We propose PMTRM, a lightweight bounded-history temporal representation module with 7.61M parameters, whose policy-facing latent is explicitly regularized for distant-phase discriminability while remaining reconstructable.

2. We combine temporal heterogeneity with anchor and reconstruction losses to encourage temporal discrimination while preserving action information, without phase labels.

3. We evaluate PMTRM across action-policy backbones and phase-ambiguous tasks in simulation and on a real robot, and analyze the effects of the proposed objectives and mirror-mask training.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Temporal Memory and Pseudo-Memory

History-aware policies encode past interactions through recurrent states [ 7 ] , working-memory tokens [ 2 ] , or retrieved perceptual and cognitive features [ 1 ] . These mechanisms provide historical context, while cyclic manipulation also requires tracking execution progress [ 3 ] . PMTRM focuses on a bounded state-action history and directly regularizes its latent sequence to distinguish distant temporal positions.

## II-B Policy-Side Temporal Conditioning

ACT predicts action chunks with a Transformer [ 4 ] , while Diffusion Policy generates multimodal actions by denoising [ 5 ] . PMTRM neither replaces these policy mechanisms nor compresses history into a single summary: its two-stage design exposes the full bounded latent sequence to the unchanged action head and uses a separate decoder only during training. It is preferable when recent phase aliasing matters and a low-latency, backbone-agnostic adapter is needed; explicit memory remains preferable for semantic retrieval or context beyond the queue.

## II-C Temporal Discriminability

Prior work learns temporally structured representations through temporal correspondence, sequence alignment, or future prediction [ 8 ] , while robot-learning methods further exploit temporal organization for hierarchical actions and progress modeling [ 9 , 10 ] . PMTRM instead directly regularizes the bounded history representation consumed by the policy, suppressing similarity between temporally distant positions while preserving action-relevant information through anchor and reconstruction objectives. This design motivates the temporal heterogeneity objective introduced next.

2026-10-09.title: Distributed Relative Localization Based on Ultra-WideBand and LiDAR for Multi-robot with Limited Communication
2026-10-09.authors: Zhiqiang Cao , Ran Liu , Billy Pik Lik Lau , Chau Yuen , U-Xuan Tan
2026-10-09.comment: This paper has been published in IEEE Transactions on Instrumentation and Measurement
2026-10-09.abstract:
Relative localization is crucial for a multi-robot system to collaboratively perform tasks, such as exploration and formation.
However, this is highly challenging for homogeneous robots with similar appearance in GPS-denied and communication-limited environments.
In this paper, we propose a fully distributed relative position estimation approach for a team of robots based on onboard UWB and LiDAR sensors, in which LiDAR is utilized to obtain the position of anonymous objects in Line-of-Sight (LOS), and UWB is used for ranging between robots.
We construct two graphs, namely UWB connection graph and LiDAR connection graph, to represent the spatial relationship among objects (robots and obstacles) based on UWB and LiDAR measurements.
Identification and relative position estimation are formulated as a common subgraph matching problem.
A falsely-matched robot identification approach is designed to recognize the falsely-matched results caused by obstacle blockage in LiDAR field of view.
These robots are then localized by leveraging the well-matched robots and the UWB ranging measurements in the UWB connection graph.
We conducted experiments to evaluate the performance of our approach.
The results show that the proposed approach is capable of achieving satisfactory positioning accuracy for a team of robots in a distributed manner with only exchanging limited information.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Multiple robot systems have received a lot of attention from the robotics community in the last decades [ 1 ] .
There is evidence that multi-robot systems play a vital role in rescue and high-risk scenarios due to their collaborative capabilities, enhancing efficiency, coverage, and adaptability compared to single-robot systems.
NASA released a Cooperative Autonomous Distributed Robotic Exploration (CADRE) project [ 2 ] that aims to develop a network of small mobile robots that improve autonomous robot swarm exploration on the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

The relative position between robots is an essential component for multi-robot system to execute decision-making [ 3 ] and collaborative operations [ 4 ] .
In general, the system framework can be divided into two main categories, namely centralized and distributed [ 5 ] .
The centralized approach is deployed on a server, requiring intensive communication and vulnerability to any server failure [ 6 ] .
In the distributed approach, each robot performs pose estimation based on local measurements and a small amount of data shared by neighboring robots.
Compared to the centralized system, the distributed system is well-suited for situations with limited communication bandwidth [ 7 ] .

At present, most of the relative localization solutions focus on Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) or visual cameras.
Both solutions have proven feasible in achieving accurate relative position estimation for objects in Line-of-Sight (LOS) scenarios [ 8 ] .
However, the robots’ similar appearance poses challenges to correctly identifying teammates in a multi-robot system [ 9 ] .
Compared to LiDAR and visual cameras, Ultra-WideBand (UWB) can provide unique identification information for each node.
Meanwhile, it provides centimeter-level peer-to-peer ranging accuracy in ideal conditions and can also transmit a small amount of data to surrounding UWB nodes [ 10 ] [ 11 ] .
These features are vital for a multi-robot system with similar appearance working in communication-constrained scenes.
However, the need for bearing information among nodes affects UWB’s practicality in localization.
Some researchers utilized the Angle of Arrival (AoA) technique to estimate the bearing [ 12 ] [ 13 ] for UWB localization.
Nevertheless, AoA solutions usually require rigorous clock synchronization.

This paper presents a distributed relative localization approach for a team of robots with similar appearance, employing UWB and LiDAR sensors without any external communication and positioning infrastructures, as shown in Fig. 1 .
The UWB sensor is utilized to measure the range between robots and broadcast a few ranging data to nearby robots, while the LiDAR detects and localizes the surrounding objects in LOS.
We first construct UWB and LiDAR connection graphs, using the distance information between objects, to represent the spatial relationship among objects (Section III-A ).
Second, we adopt an advanced common subgraph matching method inspired by [ 15 ] to retrieve all potential common subgraphs between two connection graphs and obtain the optimal vertex correspondences from these common subgraphs (Section III-B ).
In order to guarantee the precision, a normalized Euclidean distance dissimilarity-based approach [ 16 ] is proposed to recognize the falsely-matched robots (Section III-C ).
Finally, those robots, which are not estimated but within UWB communication range, are localized based on the well-matched robots and the relevant UWB ranging measurements (Section III-D ).
The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We propose a distributed relative position estimation method for a group of homogeneous robots, leveraging UWB ranging and LiDAR measurements. The identification and relative position estimation are formulated as a common subgraph matching problem.

We propose a distributed relative position estimation method for a group of homogeneous robots, leveraging UWB ranging and LiDAR measurements. The identification and relative position estimation are formulated as a common subgraph matching problem.

We present an approach to recognize the falsely-matched robots due to obstacle occlusion, then re-localize these robots using the well-matched robots and the relevant UWB ranging measurements.

We conducted extensive experiments to validate the performance of the proposed approach. The results show that our approach can effectively localize the robots in both LOS and NLOS scenes with the assistance of UWB.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: the related works are introduced in Section II .
Section III describes the proposed approach in detail.
The experiments and results are demonstrated in Section IV .
Finally, the conclusion and future works are summarized in Section V .

1. We propose a distributed relative position estimation method for a group of homogeneous robots, leveraging UWB ranging and LiDAR measurements. The identification and relative position estimation are formulated as a common subgraph matching problem.

2. We present an approach to recognize the falsely-matched robots due to obstacle occlusion, then re-localize these robots using the well-matched robots and the relevant UWB ranging measurements.

3. We conducted extensive experiments to validate the performance of the proposed approach. The results show that our approach can effectively localize the robots in both LOS and NLOS scenes with the assistance of UWB.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related work

In the past decades, multi-robot systems have been widely adopted in various robotic applications, such as multi-robot exploration, formation, etc [ 17 ] [ 18 ] .
Among these applications, the relative localization between robots is a fundamental component, allowing coordinated operations for multi-robot systems.
Visual, LiDAR, and UWB-based solutions are becoming popular, particularly in situations where GPS and communication are restricted [ 19 ] .

For visual-based relative localization solutions, the classical methods require significant visual overlap between images from different robots [ 20 ] [ 21 ] .
Moreover, receiving the image or feature information from another robot depends on favorable communication conditions.
To reduce the reliance on communication, Pavliv et al. [ 22 ] estimated the relative position of each robot based on a headset with a camera and IMU, employing the YOLOv3 algorithm [ 23 ] and agent tracker. This method assigns ID information to each robot automatically, but the IDs will be reassigned randomly after being re-tracked.
To guarantee the data association, Xun et al. [ 24 ] utilized active infrared LEDs to encode drone ID for easily identifying each drone. They then employed the Double Sphere (DS)
projection model of the fisheye camera [ 25 ] and UWB ranging measurements to estimate relative position.
However, this method requires pre-designed passive LEDs with fixed flashing rates for ID detection.
It is not conducive to scalability for a multi-robot system.

In addition to visual-based solutions, LiDAR is also widely used in relative localization for multi-robot systems.
LiDAR-based clustering algorithms [ 14 ] [ 26 ] are capable of clustering objects (including robots and obstacles) and estimating their positions in LiDAR’s frame.
However, all clusters’ IDs are designated randomly, resulting in challenges in data association and relative position estimation.
To address this issue, Zhu et al. [ 27 ] used a temporary tracker based on Kalman Filter (KF) to track robots and recognize the robot’s ID by matching the trajectories of tracked objects and odometry from other robots.
However, this method requires that the robots move along non-parallel paths in favorable communication conditions.
Shalihan et al. [ 28 ] proposed an approach to identify robots from LiDAR clusters, using adaptive clustering [ 14 ] , by comparing the UWB ranging with the cluster’s distance. Nevertheless, this method lacks robustness and cannot localize the occluded robots.

While visual and LiDAR-based methods can provide excellent positioning accuracy, they are limited to LOS scenes.
Radio-based relative localization methods, such as UWB sensors [ 29 ] [ 30 ] , can work well in NLOS scenarios and provide unique identification for each robot.
Cao et al. [ 31 ] presented a relative localization method based on the least-square algorithm for a multi-robot system, which only relies on multiple UWB ranging nodes placed at different positions on the robot.
Despite its fully distributed nature, this method shows limited accuracy and is unsuitable for small robots.
To enhance the performance of UWB-based solutions, Liu et al. [ 32 ] and Nguyen et al. [ 33 ] accomplished robot-to-robot relative pose estimation based on optimization method, using a sequence of odometry and UWB ranging measurements collected continuously over the network.
Table I presents a comprehensive survey of existing studies on relative localization.
