2026-10-09.title: FOCUS: From Privileged States to RGB-D with Controlled Modality Switching and Representation Alignment
2026-10-09.authors: Filip Grigorov , Kourosh Darvish , Nandita Vijaykumar
2026-10-09.abstract:
Vision-based reinforcement learning for robotic manipulation is
sample-inefficient because RGB-D observations are high-dimensional and noisy.
Privileged state information available in simulation can accelerate training,
but its absence at test time creates a train–test modality gap. We propose
FOCUS, a single-stage PPO framework that trains the critic on privileged state
while automatically regulating whether the actor collects rollouts from RGB-D
or privileged-state latents. Regulation is driven by the KL divergence between
the action distributions induced by the two modalities, while representation
alignment encourages consistent action selection across them. Together, these
mechanisms limit RGB-D rollouts when the actor’s action distributions from
RGB-D and privileged-state latents disagree. As they align, RGB-D exposure
increases, shifting on-policy training toward the RGB-D inputs used at test
time. Across five manipulation tasks, FOCUS raises average test success from
0.71 to 0.93 relative to the strongest RGB-D-at-test baseline on each task.
When accounting for each method’s complete training pipeline,
budget-normalized training-success AUC increases from 0.47 to 0.65. On
Pick-and-Place, test success rises from 0.47 to 0.86, while AUC increases from
0.12 to 0.61, a 5.0 × \times improvement in learning efficiency over the fixed
interaction budget.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Reinforcement learning enables robots to learn closed-loop manipulation policies through trial-and-error interaction and optimize them directly for task success. However, reinforcement learning for robotics remains limited by poor sample efficiency, sensitivity to reward design, and the cost and safety risks of real-world trial-and-error data collection [ 3 ] . Simulation-based RL mitigates some of these issues through resettable environments, parallel rollouts, controlled task variation, and access to training-only privileged information.

Learning manipulation policies directly from RGB-D observations is difficult because visual inputs are high-dimensional and noisy [ 35 , 34 , 15 ] . In some settings, visual observations may also provide an incomplete view of task-relevant state [ 11 , 35 ] . In simulation, however, training can access compact privileged state information, such as object and gripper poses, contact signals, and task-goal variables, that helps determine which action should be taken [ 2 ] . This creates an opportunity to use privileged state during RL training to improve sample efficiency while still producing an RGB-D policy that does not require privileged state at test time.

The difficulty is addressing the modality gap between privileged-state training and RGB-D-based action selection at test time. While privileged states can accelerate policy learning, reliance on them during training can produce representations and action decisions that are poorly matched to the RGB-D observations available at test time. Conversely, training only from RGB-D avoids this mismatch but can be sample-inefficient. The problem we address is therefore how to adapt the actor from privileged-state rollouts toward RGB-D control during RL training while avoiding premature RGB-D exposure.

Prior work improves sample efficiency with privileged information during training in several ways. Asymmetric actor–critic methods give privileged state to the critic while training the actor from visual inputs [ 18 ] . This can improve value estimation and the resulting policy updates, but the actor still generates rollouts from high-dimensional visual observations throughout training. More broadly, asymmetric learning methods use full-state information during training to improve policies that operate from partial observations [ 30 ] . However, these methods do not explicitly regulate visual rollout exposure according to whether privileged-state and visual inputs induce compatible action distributions. Teacher–student and distillation methods transfer knowledge from a trained teacher to a student model or policy [ 5 , 19 , 16 ] . In robotics, privileged simulator state is often used to train a teacher policy or world model that is then transferred to a vision-based student [ 33 , 13 , 22 , 24 ] . Such pipelines typically separate privileged teacher training from visual student transfer. In contrast, FOCUS performs this transition online within a single PPO run by using cross-modal policy disagreement to regulate whether rollouts are generated from privileged-state or RGB-D latents. Other privileged-learning methods use training-only information to guide visual attention, provide auxiliary learning signals, or regularize reliance on privileged inputs [ 20 , 6 , 7 ] . Separately, visual RL methods improve learning from pixels through representation learning and data augmentation [ 23 , 9 , 34 ] . These directions are complementary, but they do not use cross-modal action agreement to regulate which modality generates on-policy rollouts. We ask whether privileged information can be used online for this purpose.

In this work, our goal is to improve the sample efficiency and training reliability of RGB-D policies in simulated PPO-based manipulation without requiring RGB-D-based rollout collection from the start or separating privileged training and RGB-D transfer into distinct stages. We propose FOCUS , a single-stage RL framework applied to PPO [ 21 ] for privileged-to-vision transfer in robotic manipulation. FOCUS is based on two complementary ideas. First, we use cross-modal representation alignment to reduce mismatch between training-time and test-time inputs. Second, we introduce an online KL-guided switching mechanism that regulates when the actor uses RGB-D rather than privileged-state latents. An upper-quantile KL budget reduces RGB-D exposure when rare
high-disagreement states remain. This progressively shifts on-policy
training toward the RGB-D inputs available at test time while retaining
privileged-state value estimation.

Contributions.

(1) We formulate FOCUS as a single-stage PPO-based method that makes privileged-state and RGB-D actor representations compatible while adaptively regulating whether on-policy rollouts are generated from privileged-state or RGB-D latents.

(2) We introduce KL-guided modality switching, which uses disagreement between the action distributions produced by the same policy from privileged-state- and RGB-D-derived actor inputs to regulate RGB-D-based rollout collection. An upper-quantile KL budget reduces the probability of RGB-D rollouts when rare high-disagreement states remain.

(3) Across five IsaacLab manipulation tasks, FOCUS raises average test success
from 0.71 to 0.93 relative to the strongest RGB-D-at-test baseline on each task,
while end-to-end budget-normalized training-success AUC increases from 0.47 to
0.65. On Pick-and-Place, test success increases from 0.47 to 0.86 and AUC from
0.12 to 0.61 (5.0 × \times ). Replacing adaptive KL-controlled exposure with a
fixed ramp reduces Pick-and-Place AUC to 0.36, while the lightweight
switch-plus-policy-KL variant (FOCUS-simple) matches or exceeds FOCUS on
two of three discriminative tasks for each metric, suggesting simplified future
variants.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

We review prior work related to privileged-to-vision transfer, focusing on teacher–student distillation, asymmetric actor–critic methods, and privileged-information-guided learning.

Knowledge distillation transfers behavior or representations from a teacher to a student [ 5 , 19 , 16 ] .
In robotic learning with privileged information, a policy or world model is often first trained using privileged state, and its knowledge is then transferred to an RGB- or depth-based student [ 33 , 13 , 22 , 24 ] .
Such pipelines typically separate privileged training from visual transfer. Related asymmetric imitation methods use a privileged expert to guide a policy that operates from limited observations [ 30 ] . Recent methods reduce this separation through joint teacher-student training or adaptive data sharing [ 32 , 28 , 14 ] ,
but still organize learning around distinct teacher and student policies and do not directly use their current behavioral agreement to determine which observation pathway collects on-policy experience. FOCUS instead uses privileged-state and RGB-D paths within a single actor and regulates their rollout use according to policy disagreement, limiting premature RGB-D rollout collection while allowing the RGB-D path to learn directly from task rewards. By reducing low-quality RGB-D rollouts early in training, this design aims to improve sample efficiency while preserving or improving RGB-D test-time success.

Asymmetric actor–critic methods provide privileged information to the critic while training the actor from observations available at test time [ 18 , 36 , 8 ] .
The privileged critic can improve sample efficiency by providing more informative value estimates without making the actor depend on privileged information at test time.
Related dual-critic methods combine privileged-state and observation-based critics to improve learning under partial observability [ 12 ] .
However, the actor must still learn perception and control jointly from RGB-D from the start of training, so an immature visual pathway can generate low-quality on-policy experience and slow learning.
FOCUS retains a privileged-state critic, but additionally provides privileged-state and RGB-D actor paths and regulates which path generates rollouts according to their policy disagreement. This aims to reduce inefficient early RGB-D experience while improving RGB-D-only success at test time.

Privileged information has been used during training to guide visual attention, strengthen auxiliary learning components, or regularize reliance on privileged inputs [ 20 , 6 , 7 ] .
These methods can improve sample efficiency and final visual-policy performance, but they do not explicitly align privileged-state and RGB-D actor paths at the level of action selection or use their agreement to control rollout generation.

Separately, visual RL methods improve learning from pixels through reconstruction, latent dynamics models, contrastive representation learning, and data augmentation [ 35 , 10 , 23 , 9 , 34 ] .
These methods directly optimize the test-time visual policy and can improve both learning speed and final success, but still rely on RGB-D-generated experience from the start of training.
FOCUS combines privileged-state and RGB-D actor paths, using action-level alignment and policy disagreement to limit inefficient early RGB-D rollouts while continuing to optimize RGB-D-only test-time performance.

Gated fusion, Transformer-based attention, multimodal transformers, FiLM conditioning, and representation switching provide useful mechanisms for combining or selecting representations [ 1 , 27 , 25 , 17 , 26 ] .
However, they do not address replacing training-only privileged state with RGB-D-based action selection at test time.

2026-10-09.title: Towards Path-Creative Navigation: Robot Navigation through Embodied Interaction
2026-10-09.authors: Haoyu Xi , Siwei Cheng , Xiangyuan Liu , Brenda Li , Wei Zhang
2026-10-09.abstract:
Autonomous navigation in cluttered and constrained environments typically assumes a fixed environment and searches only for paths within existing free space. However, a route can be blocked by an articulated structure, a movable object, or a pedestrian, and reaching the goal may therefore require appropriate embodied interaction with the environment.
This paper formulates Path-Creative Navigation (PCN), a navigation paradigm in which the robot recovers free space by coordinating locomotion and embodied interaction, and addresses one class of PCN tasks with a mapless framework.
The vision-LiDAR-odometry framework integrates local observations, obstacle geometry, and robot-state estimates through a unified navigation system, providing stable semantic and geometric information for navigation and interaction.
The traversability-aware decision method utilizes visual and LiDAR distance information to determine whether a blockage is actionable and whether it can be safely bypassed, enabling the robot to interact only when necessary while supporting articulated structure pushing, movable object pushing, obstacle avoidance, and pedestrian requests.
We design simulation scenarios and evaluate different methods in both simulation and two real-world tasks that cannot be completed by conventional navigation alone without embodied interaction.
These results demonstrate that our framework achieves higher task completion than the baseline methods by coordinating navigation and interaction in cluttered and constrained environments. Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/path-creative-navigation/ .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Autonomous navigation enables robots to plan routes and avoid obstacles in cluttered and constrained environments. However, most navigation systems assume a fixed environment and search only for paths within existing free space. In homes, offices, or warehouses, a route may instead be blocked by an articulated structure, a movable object, or a pedestrian in a narrow passage. In such cases, reaching the goal may require changing the environment rather than searching for another collision-free path. The key challenge is therefore not only how to interact with the environment, but when interaction is actually necessary for navigation.

This challenge presents three requirements, particularly in cluttered and constrained environments where free space is limited. First, the robot must determine whether an object truly blocks the route or can be safely bypassed. Interacting with every detected object is inefficient and unsafe, whereas treating all obstacles as immutable may leave a recoverable route blocked.
Second, potential blockers impose different constraints: fixed obstacles require avoidance, movable objects may be pushed, articulated doors must be operated according to their constrained motion, and pedestrians may require a non-contact request.
Third, interaction must remain tightly coupled with the navigation objective as the scene changes. After interacting with a blocker, the robot must reassess whether the passage is traversable and resume navigation when possible.
Consequently, the task requires geometric reasoning about route blockage and bypass feasibility, semantic reasoning about potentially actionable objects, and closed-loop interaction as the scene changes.

Existing approaches address individual aspects of this challenge but may not fully satisfy the three requirements.
Conventional navigation cannot recover a route that requires an environmental change. Navigation among movable obstacles (NAMO) [ 1 ] allows a robot to move obstacles and clear free space, while interactive navigation [ 2 ] permits physical interaction to support goal reaching. These methods focus on movable-object interaction or predefined manipulation tasks.
Map-based methods [ 3 , 4 ] rely on pre-built maps for global planning, but maps provide incomplete path information when traversable regions are not explicitly represented or are only partially observable. LLM-based methods [ 5 , 6 ] use semantic reasoning to determine whether and how to interact with objects and plan feasible routes, but LLM-based reasoning adds communication latency and computational overhead.
Task-and-Motion Planning (TAMP) [ 7 ] integrates navigation and manipulation through explicit action sequences, typically involving higher-level task planning. In parallel, humanoid loco-manipulation methods [ 8 , 9 ] provide the physical skills required for door opening and object pushing. This paper focuses on the complementary navigation-level problem of determining when interaction is required to recover free space and continue toward the goal.

To address this problem, we formulate Path-Creative Navigation (PCN), which explicitly treats the restoration of traversability as part of the navigation problem itself, and jointly reasons about whether the robot should navigate within the current free space or change the environment to make a route traversable.
PCN covers a broad range of tasks, and this paper addresses one class of them, in which the blockage comes from a movable object, an articulated structure, or a pedestrian. For this class, we present a mapless humanoid navigation framework that integrates vision, LiDAR, and odometry. Visual perception provides object semantics and distance estimates, while LiDAR and odometry provide local geometry and robot-pose information.
A traversability-aware decision method jointly reasons about object semantics, route blockage, and bypass feasibility.
The decision uses only local observations, without a pre-built map or a language model in
the loop.

In summary, the main contributions of this paper are as follows:

We formulate Path-Creative Navigation (PCN), a navigation paradigm that reasons over locomotion and actionable embodied interaction to recover free space across different types of route blockages.

We formulate Path-Creative Navigation (PCN), a navigation paradigm that reasons over locomotion and actionable embodied interaction to recover free space across different types of route blockages.

We propose a traversability-aware decision method that considers local observations to determine whether a blockage is actionable and whether it can be safely bypassed, triggering interaction only when necessary to restore route traversability.

We design a vision-LiDAR-odometry fusion framework that combines object semantics, local obstacle geometry, and robot-state estimates within a unified navigation system, supporting articulated structure pushing, movable object pushing, pedestrian request, and navigation toward the goal.

We evaluate our framework in both simulation and real-world experiments, demonstrating higher task completion and more reliable interaction selection while coordinating navigation and interaction.

1. We formulate Path-Creative Navigation (PCN), a navigation paradigm that reasons over locomotion and actionable embodied interaction to recover free space across different types of route blockages.

2. We propose a traversability-aware decision method that considers local observations to determine whether a blockage is actionable and whether it can be safely bypassed, triggering interaction only when necessary to restore route traversability.

3. We design a vision-LiDAR-odometry fusion framework that combines object semantics, local obstacle geometry, and robot-state estimates within a unified navigation system, supporting articulated structure pushing, movable object pushing, pedestrian request, and navigation toward the goal.

4. We evaluate our framework in both simulation and real-world experiments, demonstrating higher task completion and more reliable interaction selection while coordinating navigation and interaction.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Robot Mobile Manipulation

Navigation Among Movable Obstacles (NAMO) relaxes the assumption that the environment remains fixed during navigation. Affordance-based NAMO [ 10 ] estimates whether an unknown obstacle can be moved and uses contact-aware planning to complete an otherwise infeasible navigation task. Social concerns also apply when a robot changes the environment. Socially aware NAMO [ 11 ] adds a placement cost so that a displaced object is less likely to block a corridor, doorway, or other space needed by people. These methods mainly reason about which objects should be moved and where they should be placed. In contrast, our framework does not perform global planning or optimize final object placements; it uses local semantic and geometric observations around the robot-to-goal corridor to assess local traversability and coordinate predefined responses to doors, movable objects, fixed obstacles, and pedestrians within a unified humanoid navigation system.

Interactive navigation permits physical interaction to support goal reaching. Recent methods mainly improve the decision and control required for path clearing. Yang et al. [ 12 ] use hierarchical policy learning to estimate obstacle properties and generate pushing actions for a mobile manipulator. Dai et al. [ 3 ] combine adaptive object-dynamics learning with non-prehensile mobile manipulation. For legged manipulators, Bi et al. [ 4 ] learn an arm-pushing controller that moves large obstacles in narrow spaces. Manipulate-to-Navigate [ 13 ] combines visual affordances and manipulability priors to learn feasible end-effector poses for Reach and Door tasks. These methods show that interaction can make a blocked route feasible. However, most of these learning-based approaches train policies or object models for specific interaction tasks and settings. Our framework applies to new visual instances within supported categories, such as doors and boxes with different colors and appearances, without fine-tuning or retraining.

Task-and-Motion Planning (TAMP) connects discrete action choices with continuous geometric and kinematic feasibility.
A major challenge is the large search space of long-horizon tasks. VLM-TAMP [ 14 ] addresses this problem by using a vision-language model to generate intermediate subgoals, which divide a long manipulation task into shorter TAMP problems. When a subgoal cannot be refined into a feasible motion, the system queries the model again and replans. Sung et al. [ 15 ] improve long-horizon TAMP through learned backjumping heuristics. Unlike general TAMP, our framework does not search for or revise a long-horizon sequence of task and motion actions; it makes local traversability decisions.

## II-B Robot Loco-manipulation

Loco-manipulation provides the physical skills needed to execute
such interactions. Recent work improves whole-body safety for mobile manipulators in cluttered environments [ 16 ] .
DemoHLM [ 8 ] generates diverse synthetic trajectories from one simulation demonstration for each task and uses them to train high-level manipulation policies on top of a universal whole-body controller. ULTRA [ 9 ] combines physics-driven motion retargeting with a unified controller that accepts either dense motion references or sparse task goals.
Our framework performs local observations reasoning from semantic and geometric information around the robot-to-goal corridor, coordinating predefined responses to different blocker types.

Door opening is a related mobility skill, but a door is an articulated structure
rather than a freely movable rigid object. Its motion is constrained by a
hinge, and the robot must coordinate the arm, body, and door state. Jang et al. [ 17 ] formulate approaching, opening, traversing, and closing as a coupled planning
problem for a mobile manipulator. Zhang et al. [ 18 ] learn a
policy that opens and traverses both push and pull doors with a legged
manipulator. These works demonstrate that changing the
state of an articulated structure may be necessary for mobility.
In our work, however, opening the door is not the task goal itself.
The action is selected only when the current door state blocks goal
reaching and opening it can create sufficient free space.

2026-10-09.title: A Reconfigurable Fabric Based Pneumatic Actuator with Button Fastened Constraint Modules for Multi Mode Actuation
2026-10-09.authors: Kentaro Kimura , Hiroki Ishizuka , Yusuke Sakaue , Sei Ikeda , Osamu Oshiro
2026-10-09.abstract: Soft pneumatic actuators are widely used in soft robotics; however, their actuation modes are typically fixed by internal chamber designs or reinforcements, making post-fabrication reconfiguration difficult. This paper presents a reconfigurable fabric-based pneumatic actuator that enables rapid, tool-free, and reusable switching among multiple actuation modes by attaching constraint fabric modules to a buttoned textile sleeve. By rearranging low-stretch constraint parts on a single actuator body, the proposed system realizes four actuation modes—isotropic expansion, contraction, bending, and twisting—without redesigning or disassembling the actuator. We further introduce an attachable capacitive fabric-based tactile sensor module that can be mounted at arbitrary locations on the actuator surface for task-dependent contact sensing. Experiments demonstrated an elongation ratio of 1.2, a maximum bending angle of approximately 60 degrees, and a twisting angle of approximately 90 degrees at 24 kPa, while achieving blocking forces exceeding 10 N across all modes. The tactile sensor exhibited a monotonic, force-dependent increase in capacitance with low hysteresis (approximately 12%) and stable cyclic responses under preload. Finally, we constructed soft robotic arms composed of multiple actuators and demonstrated in-situ motion reconfiguration for grasping by changing the attached constraint patterns. These results indicate that the proposed modular constraint-and-sensing framework improves the functional adaptability of fabric-based soft robots while preserving a simple, robust actuator structure.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Soft robots have gained attention for their compliance and safety in physical interactions.
Made from flexible elastomers, soft robots can adapt to objects and environments via large deformations.
Unlike rigid robots, they conform to objects and interact safely without excess force.
Owing to these features, soft robotic systems have been actively investigated for applications in medical robotics, disaster response, and physical assistance [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .

Despite their versatility, the actuation and target tasks of many robots, including soft robots, are largely constrained by mechanisms and structures designed at the outset.
Thus, robots often need to be designed specifically for the intended task, and they may not be able to adapt their behavior to changing requirements or situations [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
A promising approach to address this demand is to enable robots to reconfigure their shape or structure in response to the environment and use case, thereby achieving greater adaptability to tasks and surroundings [ 8 ] .

Modular robotic systems have long been studied as a practical way to realize such reconfigurability [ 9 , 10 ] .
By rearranging constituent elements, a robot can be transformed into a different robot with distinct capabilities.
For example, modular systems have been demonstrated that can change their morphology from a quadruped to a snake-like robot [ 11 ] .
In soft robotics, reconfigurable robots have also been explored.
Kwok et al. demonstrated that multiple configurations, such as a common gripper and a quadruped robot, can be constructed by reconnecting components via magnetic coupling embedded in silicone rubber [ 12 ] .
Kang et al. showed a flexible electronics system capable of shape reconfiguration using self-healing polymers and liquid-metal wiring [ 13 ] .
Legrand et al. demonstrated that simulated reconfigurable robots can be implemented as physical systems by leveraging self-healing polymers [ 14 ] .
While these studies successfully alter robot functions through reconfiguration, they often involve rearranging the overall robot structure rather than reconfiguring the actuator itself.

Soft actuators are key mechanical elements that determine soft robot behaviors; however, attempts to reconfigure the actuators themselves remain limited [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Soft pneumatic actuators typically provide limited deformation modes, set during fabrication by their geometry and reinforcements.
To make soft actuators reconfigurable, it is essential to devise structural or material strategies, and several approaches have been proposed.
Yoshida et al. proposed a method to change actuation by locally melting a low-melting-point metal, but the demonstrated reconfiguration was limited to modifying a bending motion [ 15 ] .
Bhat et al. proposed an approach in which detachable tapes provide surface constraint patterns to modulate actuator deformation [ 16 ] .
Koasaka et al. proposed a reversible method to change actuation by attaching a less-stretchable self-healing polymer layer on the surface of a soft pneumatic actuator [ 17 ] .
However, these methods may require specialized materials and/or rework constrained regions when switching actuation modes, increasing the effort and time required for reconfiguration.
Several studies have explored reconfigurability by replacing the entire actuator or exchanging an outer skin [ 16 , 18 , 19 ] .
While effective in controlled settings, these approaches still require disassembly or replacement of the actuator.
Therefore, a tool-free, reusable reconfiguration mechanism that is independent of the actuator body — i.e., enabling switching without disassembly, redesign, or replacement of the actuator — remains needed.

In this study, we propose a fabric-based pneumatic actuator with easily attachable and detachable constraints inspired by fabric patches used for clothing reinforcement.
Although elastomers offer high flexibility, their low stiffness often leads to rupture under high internal pressure; therefore, fiber-reinforced or fabric-based constraints are frequently used to improve durability and constrain deformation [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] .
Viewing the actuator surface as a “wearable-like” substrate enables us to mount functional fabrics in a modular manner [ 25 , 26 ] .
In this work, we exploit fabrics with different stretchability as constraint elements to impose desired deformation patterns on demand.
By leveraging a button-like fastening structure commonly used in clothing, constraint fabrics can be attached and detached in a simple, tool-free manner, enabling rapid, reversible actuation switching.
Unlike conventional approaches that rely on internal chamber redesign or embedded reinforcements [ 27 , 23 ] , the proposed method preserves the simplicity and robustness of a single actuator body while enabling repeated reconfiguration through reusable constraint modules.

Furthermore, the same attachment concept allows sensors to be mounted at arbitrary locations on the actuator surface, which is crucial for acquiring environmental and self-state information [ 28 , 29 , 30 ] .
Such flexibility is particularly important because the informative contact region can vary across tasks (e.g., grasping vs. supporting), configurations, and interaction conditions, and because sensors may need to be repositioned or replaced in response to damage or changing requirements.
Accordingly, we also integrate a soft, attachable tactile sensor as a functional module on the actuator.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We propose a reconfigurable, fabric-based pneumatic actuator and experimentally demonstrate that reusable, attachable constraint modules enable switching among desired deformation modes without redesigning or disassembling the entire actuator body.

We develop a soft tactile sensor module that can be attached to arbitrary locations on the actuator surface, enabling flexible placement for task-dependent sensing.

We construct soft robotic arms composed of multiple soft pneumatic actuators and demonstrate that their motion can be reconfigured by changing the attached constraints.

1. We propose a reconfigurable, fabric-based pneumatic actuator and experimentally demonstrate that reusable, attachable constraint modules enable switching among desired deformation modes without redesigning or disassembling the entire actuator body.

2. We develop a soft tactile sensor module that can be attached to arbitrary locations on the actuator surface, enabling flexible placement for task-dependent sensing.

3. We construct soft robotic arms composed of multiple soft pneumatic actuators and demonstrate that their motion can be reconfigured by changing the attached constraints.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Method

## II-A Principle of Actuator

Figure 1 illustrates the concept of the proposed fabric-based pneumatic actuator. By changing the placement of externally attachable constraint parts on the actuator surface, the deformation mode of a single actuator can be reconfigured after fabrication.

The proposed actuator has a hybrid structure comprising an elastic elastomeric bladder (an internal expansion chamber) and a stretchable fabric sleeve. Buttons are integrated on the fabric sleeve, and the constraint parts are mechanically fixed to the actuator surface via these buttons, enabling rapid attachment, detachment, and rearrangement.

The base design of the fabric-based pneumatic actuator is an isotropic cylindrical body that exhibits nearly uniform radial expansion when the internal pressure increases, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). By selectively attaching non-stretchable constraint parts to the sleeve, local non-uniformity in stiffness is introduced. The key mechanism of the proposed actuator is the induced strain anisotropy caused by local constraints, which converts the original uniform expansion into task-oriented deformations. Therefore, the specific deformation mode is determined by the spatial arrangement of the constraint parts.

For example, Contraction is achieved by attaching less-stretchable constraint parts around the entire circumference of the actuator, as shown in Fig. 1 (b). These constraint parts locally fix the lateral surface length, creating an alternating pattern of constrained and unconstrained regions along the body. Under internal pressure, each constrained segment maintains its longitudinal length, while each unconstrained segment expands predominantly in the radial direction, forming a bulged (approximately spherical) shape. The accumulation of these local radial expansions results in a net reduction in the overall axial length, thereby inducing contraction of the actuator.

When constraint parts are placed on one side of the actuator and perpendicular to the elongation direction, axial elongation on the constrained side is inhibited relative to the unconstrained side. This strain gradient produces a bending motion toward the constrained surface, as shown in Fig. 1 (c).

Twisting is achieved by arranging the constraint parts in a helical pattern along the lateral surface, as shown in Fig. 1 (d). This configuration suppresses length changes along the helical path while allowing the unconstrained regions to expand. The resulting surface deformation generates rotational displacement around the actuator axis. The twisting angle depends on the input pneumatic pressure and the constraint density, which is determined by the number of helical turns per unit length.

## II-B Fabrication Process of Actuator

The fabrication of the proposed fabric-based pneumatic actuator integrates silicone casting with textile assembly, as shown in Fig. 2 . The process is categorized into the fabrication of the internal silicone rubber body for pneumatic actuation (Fig. 2 (Upper)) and the fabric skin (Fig. 2 (Bottom)).
The internal silicone rubber body was constructed by assembling multiple silicone rubber components. The cylindrical section and the air inlet section were fabricated using soft silicone rubber (Ecoflex 00-30, Smooth-On). The base liquid and curing agents were mixed at a 1:1 mass ratio, thoroughly degassed in a vacuum chamber, and cast into resin molds printed by a 3D printer (Form 3, Formlabs).
After the silicone rubber was fully cured, the cylindrical body and inlet component were removed from the resin molds and bonded together with uncured silicone rubber to ensure an airtight pneumatic seal. Then, a polyurethane tube for pneumatic pressure was inserted into the inlet component. The photograph of the fabricated cylindrical body is shown in Figure 3 (a).

The external skin was designed using a stretchable textile. A high-stretch knit fabric (wt-10-1099150, Takisada Nagoya Co., Ltd.) was used for the actuator’s side surfaces. This fabric exhibits mechanical anisotropy; thus, it was oriented so that its high-elasticity axis aligned with the actuator’s longitudinal axis. To facilitate the attachment of constraint parts, a grid of buttons was sewn onto the skin using an electronic sewing machine (S71-SL, Brother Industries, Ltd.). To prevent unexpected deformation at the proximal and distal ends where constraint parts cannot be attached, these extremities were reinforced with a less-stretch woven fabric lining. The top portion of the actuator was capped with a similar low-stretch fabric. The constraint parts were fabricated from a less-stretchable satin fabric (Plain Satin Fabric, Marushin Co., Ltd.). The fabric was cut from a template into rectangular strips measuring 160 ​ mm × 15 ​ mm 160\,\text{mm}\times 15\,\text{mm} . Buttonholes, each 12 mm in length, were precisely opened at 24 mm intervals to ensure a secure and repeatable interface with the actuator’s button grid, shown in Figure 3 (b).
For the twisting actuation, patch samples with buttonholes spaced at 33 mm intervals were additionally prepared.

Figure 3 (c) shows the fabricated soft pneumatic actuator. The fabricated soft pneumatic actuator is cylindrical, with a total length of 160 mm and an outer diameter of 40 mm. The internal silicone bladder has a wall thickness of 5 mm. The arrangement of the constraint parts can be freely adjusted, as shown in Fig. 3 (d)-(f). These pictures show arrangements for bending, contraction, and twisting, respectively. The reconfiguration requires only a few tens of seconds without special tools.

## II-C Design Principle of Capacitive fabric-based tactile sensor

The proposed capacitive fabric force sensor detects external loads by measuring changes in capacitance caused by the deformation of a dielectric layer [ 33 , 34 ] . The tactile sensor is composed of conductive fabric electrodes sewn onto a fabric, with soft silicone rubber acting as the dielectric layer.

The principle of the fabric-based tactile sensor is shown in Fig. 4 (a). This tactile sensor can also be fixed onto the soft actuator via buttons, in the same manner as the constraint parts. The capacitive fabric-based tactile sensor was fabricated by layering conductive fabrics and a soft silicone rubber to ensure both structural flexibility and ease of assembly. The detailed structure of the sensor is depicted in Fig. 4 (a). 2026-10-09.title: ActiveReg: Information-Driven Active Regional Probing for Partial-to-Full Bone Registration
2026-10-09.authors: Tiancheng Li , Yingyu Wang , Peter Walker , Liang Zhao , Shoudong Huang
2026-10-09.abstract: Accurate bone registration is essential for orthopedic surgical navigation and robotic assistance. In a common workflow, the surgeon needs to identify and probe a number of prescribed locations on the exposed bone surface to obtain data points for registration, which can be difficult and time-consuming under limited surgical exposure. Reducing the number of required points while providing clear probing guidance would ease the surgeon’s acquisition task intra-operatively. We present ActiveReg, a closed-loop framework that recommends probing regions rather than individual points, allowing flexibility in the exact contact location. A D-optimal planner that takes into account the already acquired points and the uncertainty of current registration information helps achieve accurate registration with fewer points. An online assessment combines pre-update innovation consistency with uncertainty at predefined surgical task locations improves the reliability of completion decision, without requiring ground truth. Simulations across four anatomical scenarios demonstrated that ActiveReg can achieve competitive accuracy compared with baseline registration methods while using substantially fewer acquired points. Real phantom experiments with optical and electromagnetic tracking demonstrated comparable mean target registration error to the Gradient-SDF framework, using only 24-28 acquired points instead of 771-1263.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Surgical navigation and robotic-assisted technologies in orthopedic surgery require pre-operative plans to be accurately mapped to the patient’s anatomy [ 1 ] . In total hip and knee arthroplasty, this mapping supports bone preparation and implant placement [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Bone registration achieves this mapping by establishing the spatial relationship between the pre-operative model and intra-operative patient coordinate frame. In a common workflow, intra-operative points are acquired from the exposed bone surface using a tracked probe and registered to a pre-operative model derived from computed tomography (CT) [ 5 ] . Reducing the number of probe contacts can ease the surgeon’s acquisition effort, provided that the collected points retain sufficient geometric constraints for accurate registration. The acquisition strategy must therefore address both the informativeness of the points to be acquired how surgeons are guided during probing.

One approach is to guide intra-operative probing using prescribe surface points. For example, the current state-of-the-art orthopedic robotic system, MAKO Robotic Arm Interactive Orthopedic System (Stryker), specifies three initial anatomical landmarks followed by 32 prescribed points for each of the acetabulum and femur in the enhanced workflow [ 6 ] . These instructions requires the surgeon to identify and accurately contact the prescribe locations under limited exposure (Fig. 1 (a)), which becomes even more difficult when the bone surface is obscured by blood and surrounding tissue [ 7 ] . Correspondence-free surface registration methods offer greater flexibility in contact placement since acquired points do not need to be paired with prescribed model points. For example, the Gradient-SDF framework [ 8 ] supports bone registration from sparse points freely acquired with a surgical probe moving on the exposed bone surface, without requiring predefined point correspondences. However, this freedom leaves the surgeon to decide where to probe and requires many contacts to acquire.

This motivates an acquisition strategy that provides explicit guidance on where to place the probe while allowing flexibility in the exact contact location. A straightforward way is to recommend a surface region within which the surgeon can choose where to probe, without having to identify and contact a single prescribed point precisely (Fig. 1 (b)). To reduce the number of contacts, the recommended region should guide the acquisition toward geometric information that complements the constraints provided by previously acquired contacts [ 9 ] . Since the surgeon can choose the contact location within each region, subsequent recommendations should be updated using the actual acquired points to address the remaining registration uncertainty. Alongside guidance on where to probe, an online completion assessment determines whether the acquired measurements support the required registration accuracy or further probing is needed.

Therefore, we present ActiveReg, a closed-loop framework for achieving accurate bone registration with few probe contacts through
information-driven active regional probing and online completion assessment. ActiveReg uses the current registration estimate and information matrix to plan an informative surface region for the next probe contact. The surgeon probes a location within this region, and the actual acquired point is incorporated into correspondence-free signed distance field (SDF) registration to update the pose estimate and information matrix. Online completion assessment then determines whether to end acquisition or use the updated registration state to plan the next region.

The main contributions are:

A closed-loop active regional probing framework that uses the current registration estimate to guide acquisition and uses actual probe measurements to update registration, reducing point requirements while maintaining registration accuracy.

A D-optimal region construction combining information gain with connectivity and minimum-area requirements, providing explicit guidance while allowing flexible contact placement within the recommended region.

An online completion assessment that combines pre-update innovation consistency with task-space uncertainty to determine whether further probing is needed.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Registration for Orthopedic Surgery

Registration is a fundamental task to estimate a rigid transformation that align the geometric datasets. The Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm [ 10 ] is considered a milestone in point cloud registration, which alternates between closest-point correspondence estimation and transformation updates. Coherent point drift (CPD) [ 11 ] formulates alignment as a Gaussian mixture model estimation problem. Go-ICP [ 12 ] combines branch-and-bound search with local ICP refinement to globally optimize the point-to-point registration objective. TEASER [ 13 ] reformulates the registration problem using a Truncated Least Squares cost.

These methods provide general tools for geometric alignment, while sparse measurements and partial overlapping lead to additional challenges in intra-operative bone registration in orthopedic surgery [ 14 ] . Srivatsan et al. [ 15 ] proposed deterministic and probabilistic SPNR methods requiring intra-operative point positions and surface normals for bone registration. Min et al. [ 7 ] combined tangents estimated from intra-operative points with pre-operative surface normals. These approaches improve registration by extracting additional geometric constraints from acquired measurements. ActiveReg instead guides probing using the current registration estimate and updates it with each new measurement, coupling registration and acquisition in a closed loop.

## II-B Active Acquisition and Registration Assessment

Information-driven action planning has been widely studied in active simultaneous localization and mapping [ 16 ] . In registration, Gelfand et al. [ 9 ] selected points from existing surface data to constrain unstable transformation directions in ICP. For online acquisition, Murali et al. [ 17 ] selected touch actions based on predicted information gain and sequentially updated the object pose using acquired measurements. However, those methods were not designed for bone registration. ActiveReg uses the current registration estimate to plan informative region for next probing and use the actual probe measurements to update bone registration. Fitzpatrick et al. [ 18 ] showed that, in point-based registration, a small fiducial registration error can coexist with a large target registration error under an unfavorable fiducial configuration. It motivates evaluating uncertainty at task-relevant locations. ActiveReg combines this assessment with pre-update innovation consistency to guide acquisition completion.

2026-10-09.title: iAm.md: Robot Skill Self-Assessment through Agentic Introspection for Unknown Open-Vocabulary Domains
2026-10-09.authors: Vincenzo Guarino , Emanuele Musumeci , Vincenzo Suriani , Daniele Nardi
2026-10-09.comment: . Accepted at the 13th Italian Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Robotics (AIRO 2026). Project page: this https URL
2026-10-09.abstract: Agentic AI based on Large Language Model generalization capabilities offers a wide range of potential applications, including planning for embodied tasks. For example, embodied agents based on Foundation models can generate plausible plans in autonomous robotics scenarios. Due to limited context windows or hallucinatory phenomena in the next-token prediction formulation, behaviors may be generated without establishing whether the deployed robot and the observed environment actually support the requested operation, in what we call a ”grounding failure”. Thanks to the recent improvements in reasoning capabilities of foundation models, autonomous robot behavior generation problem can be formulated as a code generation problem. We present iAm.md , a Markdown standard and generation framework, that allows anchoring this process in complementary forms of deployment evidence. Through open-vocabulary semantic mapping, we combine local vision-language detections and object segmentation and refer them to persistent object records in this intermediate standardized representation, allowing agentic introspection. We then study this new technique on a simulated TIAGo, on navigation-and-manipulation tasks, showing how this standardized representation jointly supports skill self-assessment and executable task generalization.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Translating a Natural Language (NL) task request into physical robot behavior typically requires a closed representation of the task and operating environment: neuro-symbolic planning makes plan validity conditional on the quality of a provided abstraction of the world state and actions Fikes and Nilsson (1971) ; McDermott et al. (1998) ; Garrett et al. (2021) . As robots move toward open environments, prompt engineering is an increasingly important step of plan and executable code generation Brown and others (2020) ; Chen and others (2021) , but this capacity creates a grounding problem: a language model may complete an underspecified request with synthetic knowledge even when the necessary evidence has not been observed Ji and others (2023) , and generated action sequences can violate the preconditions of the actions they invoke Valmeekam et al. (2023) . Once connected to robot tools, an unsupported assumption becomes a physical action, which can lead to obvious safety and ethical issues.

In this way, a generated program may refer to an unobserved object, or it may call for an operation that the deployed platform does not support. Scene grounding alone does not resolve the second problem, since a plan reasonable for one robot may fail on another. Robot self-assessment frames the missing judgment as the ability to ”predict, estimate, or measure how well it can perform a task in a given context and environment” Norton and others (2022) . We investigate to what extent an embodied foundation model agent operating in an unknown open-vocabulary domain can use persistent scene memory and a structured robot self-description to perform skill self-assessment and produce executable plans. Here agentic introspection means the agent is capable of inspecting the representations available inside its own planning process before committing to generated code. Our contributions are: (i) an open-vocabulary semantic memory that uses local vision-language inference and segmentation to provide persistent object identities and locations; (ii) iAm.md 1 1 1 Project page: https://yurimachine.github.io/iAm.md/ . , a structured Markdown standard and generation framework representing specific robot information, resolved interfaces, and explicit unknowns; and (iii) an introspective embodied agent that combines semantic-map queries, introspection, task code generation, and robot execution for NL requests.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Hierarchical 3D scene graphs (Kimera Rosinol et al. (2021) , Hydra Hughes et al. (2022) ) and dense vision-language feature maps (VLMaps Huang et al. (2023) , ConceptFusion Jatavallabhula and others (2023) ) accumulate persistent spatial structure but do not maintain robot-specific execution evidence. Language-conditioned code-generation methods (SayCan Ahn and others (2022) , Code as Policies Liang et al. (2023) , ProgPrompt Singh et al. (2023) ) compose developer-provided APIs but assume feasible instructions and pre-authored platform documentation; feasibility-assessment methods (PlanBench Valmeekam et al. (2023) , CodeBotler Hu et al. (2024) , KnowNo Ren and others (2023) ) require a complete action model rarely available for a configured robot. Robot knowledge frameworks Tenorth and Beetz (2017) ; Beßler et al. (2021) ; Silva et al. (2025) relate tasks to capabilities through data entered before an episode. Closest to our work, EMPOWER-ADF Suriani et al. (2026) grounds task entities against a NL robot description but selects from a fixed action vocabulary without physical execution. We instead derive the robot description from the deployment itself and use it, with live interface evidence, to write task-specific code.

2026-10-09.title: Higher-Order Morphology Priors for Quadruped Reinforcement Learning Under Actuator Degradation
2026-10-09.authors: Derek You , Zafir Shamsi , Keqin Wang , Christine Allen-Blanchette
2026-10-09.abstract: Actuator degradation turns quadruped locomotion into a coordination problem requiring joints to compensate for lost actuation. Prior work suggests that morphology-aware graph policies improve learning and generalization under body perturbations. We ask whether these benefits can be strengthened by explicitly modeling higher-order mechanical structure. We represent the Unitree Go1 as a cell complex with limb- and body-level rank-2 cells and apply Hodge-based message passing. Under degradation training, the node-edge-face Hodge actor achieves the highest return on unseen actuator degradations, with higher survival and lower velocity-tracking error. These results support higher-order morphology as a useful inductive bias for whole-body compensation under actuator degradation.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Learning-based controllers have made quadruped locomotion increasingly robust to terrain variation, uncertain dynamics, and changes in external loading [ 1 , 2 ] . Actuator degradation instead directly reduces the control authority available at specific joints, requiring the remaining body to compensate. Existing fault-tolerant approaches address this challenge through explicit mechanisms for adapting to the fault [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . This motivates the question: rather than adding dedicated fault-handling mechanisms, can robustness emerge simply from how the quadruped is represented in the policy?

Morphology-aware policies show that representations of robot morphology shape locomotion and transfer [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Most such work encodes morphology as a classical graph, with joints as nodes and links as edges. At a higher level, joints form mechanical units such as limbs and body-level structures. Such a graph can represent the edges bounding these structures, but not the structures themselves as higher-order objects. We therefore ask whether enriching the graph with mechanically meaningful higher-order structure provides a useful inductive bias for coordinated compensation under actuator degradation.

To investigate this question, we represent the Unitree Go1 as a cell complex whose rank-2 cells encode four limb-level structures and one body-level structure, and apply Hodge-based message passing over nodes, edges, and faces. The resulting faces make these multi-joint units explicit rather than leaving them implicit in their bounding edges.

The main contributions of this work are twofold. (1) We introduce a higher-order morphology representation for the Unitree Go1 with mechanically motivated rank-2 limb and body cells, and a node-edge-face Hodge actor over it. (2) Through a capacity-matched healthy/degradation training-evaluation study, we show that our approach outperforms competitive baselines on held-out compound actuator degradation data.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

Learned quadruped locomotion. Reinforcement learning now yields quadruped controllers that traverse demanding terrain [ 12 , 13 ] , transfer to hardware [ 14 , 1 ] , adapt online [ 2 ] , and train in minutes [ 15 , 16 ] . These are typically centralized networks over a flat
observation vector, leaving the body’s mechanical organization implicit.

Fault-tolerant locomotion. Robot damage adaptation has been studied through both online search and learning-based control. Cully et al. [ 3 ] rapidly adapt to physical damage by searching a repertoire of precomputed behaviors. Recent quadruped methods instead incorporate faults into policy learning, including hierarchical fault-tolerant control [ 4 ] , fault-conditioned locomotion [ 5 ] , teacher-student distillation across compensatory gaits [ 6 ] , and gait adaptation under actuator power loss [ 7 ] . Rather than introducing a new adaptation mechanism, we ask whether the policy’s morphology representation itself facilitates coordinated compensation under a fixed learning protocol.

Morphology-aware locomotion. Morphology-aware policies organize computation according to an agent’s articulated body, typically using graph-based architectures [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . NerveNet [ 8 ] and Shared Modular Policies [ 9 ] showed that morphology-structured communication improves transfer across embodiments and disabilities, and DMAP [ 10 ] found these benefits become more pronounced under larger body perturbations. Body Transformer [ 11 ] , however, showed that purely local morphological communication can bottleneck information propagation on harder tasks. These works establish morphology as a useful prior, but model it through pairwise relations. We instead enrich it with mechanically meaningful higher-order relations.

Higher-order graph learning. Higher-order neural architectures extend graph learning beyond pairwise edges by placing signals on edges, faces, and higher-dimensional cells and coupling adjacent ranks through incidence and Hodge operators [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] . Simplicial neural networks and message-passing simplicial networks generalize graph propagation to simplicial complexes, while cellular and Hodge-based constructions further support communication among cells of different ranks [ 24 , 25 ] ; the underlying signal processing rests on Hodge Laplacians [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] . We use this machinery in a different role: rank-2 cells represent persistent mechanical structures of a quadruped, and higher-order message passing serves as a policy-level morphology prior whose effect is evaluated under actuator degradation.

2026-10-09.title: When Listening Becomes Easier: Scrubbing Visual Cues for Shortcut-Free VLAs
2026-10-09.authors: Jasper Gerigk , Kenzo Aspuru-Takata , Chin-Hsuan Wu , Mohammad Mohammadi , Shuhong Zheng , Igor Gilitschenski
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-09.abstract:
Shortcut learning is a prevalent issue in robot learning.
The limited diversity of robot demonstration datasets can mislead policies into exploiting spurious correlations between tasks and irrelevant features, such as viewpoint or background.
Collecting sufficiently diverse robot demonstrations is costly and inefficient, motivating algorithmic alternatives.
We focus on vision-language-action (VLA) models and discover that different vision-language model backbones exhibit substantially different levels of susceptibility to visual shortcut learning.
We find that model behavior correlates with our proposed representation-level metric, action margin , which requires no policy rollouts.
Visual shortcuts consistently enter action representations in early layers, with models differing in the extent to which later layers correct them by incorporating language information.
To boost models’ attention to language, we introduce task scrubbing, a new domain-adversarial training method that decreases models’ likelihood of using visual shortcuts and improves VLAs’ generalization.
Experiments in both simulation and the real world across multiple VLAs and visual cues show that task scrubbing improves out-of-distribution robustness and often eliminates visual shortcut learning.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are general-purpose robot policies built on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) [ 1 , 23 ] for their visual and linguistic abilities [ 6 , 21 ] .
Although a large variety of different VLA models [ 5 , 27 , 36 , 29 ] have been proposed, they share a common design:
a VLM encodes and processes visual and language information and produces representations which are then used to predict actions.
Actions are predicted either by the same backbone [ 21 , 3 ] or by a separate transformer, commonly called an action expert, that attends to the VLM representations.
This design has produced policies that transfer pretrained vision-language knowledge to diverse manipulation tasks and generalize beyond individual training environments [ 6 , 5 , 4 ] .
Its appeal rests on an implicit premise: the policy should inherit sufficiently strong visual-language understanding from the VLM to condition its actions on the language instruction.

However, in practice, this premise is less reliable than benchmark performance suggests [ 19 , 10 , 32 ] .
VLAs remain brittle to visual perturbations and initial-state changes [ 10 ] , may fail to generalize across linguistic paraphrases [ 20 ] , and can lose useful pretrained structure while adapting their representations to precise spatial and action demands [ 9 , 16 , 8 ] .
More generally, robot policies tend to rely on irrelevant features captured in their training distribution [ 31 ] .
For example, proxies such as viewpoint, background, object color, distractors, or proprioceptive state may provide a strong signal for task identity in the limited diversity of the training data [ 28 , 15 ] .
This behavior is an instance of shortcut learning [ 13 , 31 ] .
Models affected by shortcut learning achieve high in-distribution (ID) success but follow inconsequential cues when determining the task under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions and thus fail.

We focus on visual shortcuts ( Figure 1 ): task identity-correlated visual features that the policy uses as substitutes for the language instruction.
These shortcuts are especially common as small visual variations between tasks can easily enter training demonstrations through shifts in camera position, background changes, or task setup.
When this unwanted association is broken, a shortcut policy executes the visual cue-consistent behavior instead of the instructed behavior.
Existing work largely describes this failure as a data-diversity problem [ 31 ] , without studying why different VLA architectures trained on the same data can have different shortcut propensities.
It also remains unclear how shortcuts enter action computation or how the visual shortcut pathway can be suppressed without discarding useful visual information.

To understand how model architectures influences shortcut susceptibility, we evaluate multiple existing VLAs and our own variants to better understand the effect of VLM choice.
We find that shortcut susceptibility varies substantially across VLM backbones on the same dataset.
Further, we introduce the action margin metric, which tracks whether a model is likely to shortcut by the alignment of the action-token hidden states with task- and cue-consistent reference states.
Using this metric, we can directly track the development of shortcut actions during inference and find a mechanistic explanation.
Attention knockout [ 14 ] shows that task-correlated visual features shift action representations toward the shortcut in early layers with models differing in whether later computation restores alignment with the instruction.
Based on these findings, we introduce task scrubbing to encourage models to attend to language information.
Task scrubbing is an adversarial auxiliary loss that causes visual representations that predict task identity to shift during training, making them less reliable for action prediction.
The intervention increases the relative influence of language when the model learns to predict actions, without removing information from the visual input.

Our contributions are:

we show that shortcut susceptibility is strongly architecture dependent: VLA variants trained on the same data behave substantially differently, while VLM backbone size and general performance do not predict robustness;

we introduce a systematic framework for analyzing shortcut behavior: action margin tracks behavioral shortcut reliance without rollouts, while attention knockout identifies how visual and language information shape action representations; and

we introduce task scrubbing, a gradient-reversal method that makes task prediction from the visual pathway harder during training and causes policies to rely more strongly on language, thereby reducing shortcut learning.

2. we introduce a systematic framework for analyzing shortcut behavior: action margin tracks behavioral shortcut reliance without rollouts, while attention knockout identifies how visual and language information shape action representations; and

3. we introduce task scrubbing, a gradient-reversal method that makes task prediction from the visual pathway harder during training and causes policies to rely more strongly on language, thereby reducing shortcut learning.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Background and Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Models

VLAs map visual observations, language instructions, and, in many systems, proprioceptive state to robot actions [ 6 , 21 ] .
They vary in how they connect pretrained visual-language representations to control.
Some models predict tokenized actions autoregressively with the VLM backbone itself [ 21 , 3 ] , whereas others pass image and text representations to a separate action expert that generates continuous action chunks [ 5 , 27 ] .
Multi-pathway systems such as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} make this separation more explicit by assigning goal semantics and motor generation to different components [ 4 ] .
Across these designs, the expected benefit is that the VLM supplies broad semantic and visual abstractions while the action component adapts them to motor execution.

Despite their successes, VLAs face general robustness and representation-learning challenges.
LIBERO-Plus [ 10 ] documents brittleness under distractors, initial-state changes, and other visual variations, while LIBERO-Para shows that robustness to linguistic rephrasing cannot be assumed from VLM pretraining [ 20 ] .
VLM features may omit fine spatial or action-relevant details, motivating adaptation during policy training [ 9 ] .
However, broad fine-tuning can degrade pretrained visual-language structure and hurt generalization [ 16 , 8 ] .
Freezing the pretrained VLM to prevent information loss does not generally help and can reduce task performance without improving language generalization [ 20 ] .
VLAs therefore face a tension between adapting representations to predict actions accurately and preserving the general structure to enable generalization.
Various approaches have been proposed to improve representations, such as using stronger VLMs [ 30 ] , utilizing more informative visual embeddings [ 24 ] , or adding representation-preserving objectives [ 9 , 16 ] .
Larger systems such as π 0.7 \pi_{0.7} combine broader data, model, and training changes to improve generalization [ 26 ] .
These results suggest that architecture and training affect representation quality and robustness.

## II-B Shortcut Learning in Robot Policy Training

Shortcut learning occurs when a policy exploits a predictive correlation that is easier to learn than the intended task rule and consequently fails under distribution shift [ 13 ] .
In generalist robot policies, insufficient dataset diversity and fragmentation allow task identity to become entangled with particular scenes, embodiments, camera configurations, or
trajectories [ 31 ] .
More data reduces this problem only when it introduces the relevant variation.

Mechanistic studies find weak prompt control when visual appearance already determines the behavior and identify internal features associated with memorized trajectories [ 15 , 28 ] .
These findings challenge the assumption that a successful VLA necessarily learns a compositional mapping from instruction and scene to action.
The model may instead interpolate among visually indexed motor programs.

Existing mitigations attempt to break shortcut correlations through broader data collection [ 31 ] .
Such interventions can be costly, benchmark-specific, and difficult to transfer.
Removing shortcut-prone observation channels can also improve generalization [ 34 ] , but permanently discarding an input removes information that other tasks may require.
AC-VLA addresses visual shortcut reliance by selectively removing wrist-camera observations when the gripper is closed [ 25 ] .
DeLock takes an alternative approach of recovering the pretrained knowledge after fine-tuning using a contrastive prompt and steering [ 18 ] .
We expand on prior analysis and investigate how the model’s vision-language backbone impacts a policy’s propensity to follow visual shortcuts.
Rather than permanently removing information or requiring additional data, we develop a training modification which causes VLAs to avoid relying on visual shortcuts.

## II-C Adversarial Representation Learning

Domain-adversarial representation learning [ 12 ] is a general approach to make representations from different data sources indistinguishable to prevent models from improperly relying on them when making decisions.
It relies on an auxiliary classifier to predict a selected attribute from a representation and reverses its gradient into the encoder [ 12 ] .
The classifier learns to recover the attribute, while the encoder is trained to make that prediction difficult.
This mechanism is commonly used to promote invariance to domains or nuisance variables, particularly in computer vision [ 33 , 11 ] , but has not yet been applied in related robotics settings.
While making two sources of data completely indistinguishable can be very difficult, we find that continually shifting task-predictive visual representations during training can be sufficient to make the policy rely on the instruction rather than the visual shortcut.
