2026-10-09.title: Informationally Decoupled Trajectory Design for Sim-to-Real System Identification
2026-10-09.authors: Sangwoo Shin , Ashvin Anilkumar , Ryan Gao , Josiah P. Hanna
2026-10-09.abstract:
Sampling-based system identification estimates physically meaningful parameters by tuning a simulator to reproduce the target system dynamics, providing an interpretable approach to improving sim-to-real transfer.
Yet when the collected trajectories do not distinguish the effects of different parameters, multiple parameter combinations can reproduce those trajectories, leading to unreliable parameter estimates.
To address this challenge, we introduce an Informationally Decoupled Trajectory Design framework ( IDTD ),
which formulates the objective for the exploration policy built on the Schur complement score derived from the Fisher information matrix.
To faithfully reflect parameter separability in the exploration objective, IDTD normalizes the score against the per-parameter information,
selects the most favorable trajectory segment for each parameter, and aggregates the resulting scores logarithmically.
The optimized trajectory is therefore composed of complementary intervals, each exposing a distinct subset of parameters whose contribution to the motion over that interval can be attributed unambiguously.
Across diverse simulation environments, ranging from a linear-dynamics system to the Go2 quadruped, G1 humanoid, and Crazyflie quadrotor, IDTD reduces the parameter identification error by 39.6 % 39.6\% on average relative to the strongest prior active-exploration baseline and attains improved downstream policy transfer.
Furthermore, we validate the proposed trajectory design on a real K1 humanoid, demonstrating that the resulting identified parameters accurately capture the real-system dynamics.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) in massively parallel simulation has become
a widely adopted approach
for learning-based robot control, yet policies trained in simulation degrade on hardware whenever the simulated dynamics deviate from the target physical system [ 1 , 2 ] .
A common remedy is domain randomization, which trains a policy over a distribution of physical parameters, such as inertial properties, actuator gains, and friction, so that the real system falls within its support [ 3 , 4 ] .
This approach, however, requires covering a wide range of parameters, which tends to produce conservative policies that sacrifice performance for robustness.

System identification (SysID) offers an alternative approach.
Rather than training against a broad range of possible dynamics, SysID explicitly estimates the physical parameters that make the simulator reproduce the target system dynamics.
Within SysID, sampling-based methods have recently gained traction [ 5 , 6 ] , as massively parallel GPU simulation makes black-box search over physical parameters practical.
These methods evaluate candidate parameter vectors through forward dynamics simulation and search for the parameters under which the simulated trajectories best match the recorded real-world trajectories.
By avoiding differentiation through the simulator, sampling-based SysID can directly leverage modern physics simulators with contact and actuator dynamics [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] while retaining physically interpretable parameters.

While sampling-based approaches make the parameter search practical, their success depends critically on solving the complementary problem of determining which trajectories should be collected from the target system for reliable identification. Prior work addresses this question by seeking informative trajectories, where informativeness is quantified through the Fisher Information Matrix (FIM), whose inverse lower-bounds the covariance of the parameter estimate [ 11 ] .
Based on this bound, active exploration methods search for a policy that collects trajectories minimizing the trace of the inverse FIM, aggregating the estimation uncertainty across all parameters into a single objective [ 6 , 5 ] .
However, this criterion does not treat the amount of information and the separability of the parameters as distinct quantities, so increased excitation can improve the aggregate criterion even when some parameter effects become less distinguishable.
Consequently, errors in different parameters can compensate for one another, allowing simulations using the identified parameters to closely match the real-world trajectories even when the individual parameters differ substantially from their true values.
For instance, consider identifying the mass m m and the damping c c of a one-dimensional system, where a force is applied to a point mass.
A trace-based excitation makes the mass move faster and more abruptly, since larger, more energetic motion carries more total information about the parameters.
Under such motion, however, the sensitivities to m m and c c stay nearly collinear, so increasing the mass while reducing the damping produces nearly the same trajectory under the same control input.
The criterion therefore keeps improving even though the two parameters remain difficult to tell apart.
In this simple example, the excitation can be manually designed to alternate between acceleration-dominant ( c ​ x ˙ ≈ 0 c\dot{x}\approx 0 ) and velocity-dominant ( m ​ x ¨ ≈ 0 m\ddot{x}\approx 0 ) phases to distinguish the mass from the damping.
Extending such parameter-specific excitation to the dozens of coupled parameters in modern robot models, however, is highly challenging, as each parameter may require a different excitation regime.

To address this challenge, we present I nformationally D ecoupled T rajectory D esign ( IDTD ), which searches for motions under which every parameter leaves a unique effect on the trajectory that no other parameter can reproduce.
Specifically, IDTD builds on a per-parameter score derived from the Schur complement of the Fisher information, which measures how much of a parameter’s effect on the motion remains after the effects of all other parameters are accounted for.
A parameter whose effect can be reproduced by the others scores near zero, while a parameter with a distinct effect scores high; a high score thus means the parameter is cleanly distinguishable, or decoupled, from the rest.
Furthermore, to prevent the objective from being improved through excitation alone, for instance by moving a few responsive joints more aggressively without better separating their parameter effects, IDTD normalizes each score by the information carried by the corresponding parameter.
It then evaluates the normalized scores across multiple trajectory segments to encourage complementary excitation of different parameters throughout the trajectory.
As a result, IDTD designs trajectories that expose every parameter somewhere along the motion rather than accumulating information for only a small subset.

We evaluate IDTD in simulation on a linear-dynamics system, Unitree Go2, Unitree G1, and Crazyflie, demonstrating improved parameter identification, target-system prediction, and downstream policy transfer.
We further validate IDTD on a real Booster K1 humanoid, where the identified parameters more accurately capture the target-system dynamics.

The main contributions of our work are as follows. (i) We address the challenging yet practical problem of designing exploration trajectories that distinguish the effects of physical parameters, enabling reliable sampling-based system identification. (ii) We propose IDTD , a trajectory design framework that explicitly balances information quantity with parameter distinguishability through a normalized Schur-complement score and parameter-wise trajectory coverage. (iii) We demonstrate that IDTD improves parameter identification accuracy and downstream policy transfer across simulated Unitree Go2, Unitree G1, and Crazyflie platforms, and better captures real-world dynamics on a Booster K1 humanoid.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Sim-to-Real Transfer and System Identification

Reducing the sim-to-real gap has been approached from two complementary directions.
Domain randomization exposes the policy to a wide distribution of dynamics so that the real system falls within the training support [ 3 , 4 ] ; the resulting robustness, however, comes at the cost of conservative behavior, and the randomization ranges themselves require tuning.

System identification instead estimates the physical parameters of the specific robot and its environment from real-world data.
Classical approaches exploit the linearity of rigid-body dynamics in the inertial parameters and estimate them by least squares over hand-designed excitation [ 12 , 13 ] , but they require an explicit structured dynamics model and do not scale to the contact-rich, hard-to-model effects of real robots.

As massively parallel simulation has become fast and reliable, system identification is increasingly performed by tuning simulator parameters until simulated trajectories match real trajectories.
One line of work makes the forward dynamics differentiable with respect to the parameters, so the identification objective can be minimized by backpropagating gradients directly through the simulation [ 14 , 15 ] . Its reliance on smoothed contact models, however, limits its scalability to contact-rich tasks.
Recent work therefore favors sampling-based identification, which pairs the simulator with a black-box search algorithm and sidesteps differentiation while keeping the estimated parameters physically interpretable [ 5 , 6 ] .

Our work follows the sampling-based paradigm but addresses the complementary question of how exploration should be designed so that every parameter leaves a distinct effect on the resulting trajectory, enabling reliable system identification.

## II-B Active Exploration and Optimal Experimental Design

The choice of excitation has long been recognized as central to identification quality.
In the classical context, exciting trajectories are optimized offline against criteria defined on the regressor matrix, which linearly relates the unknown dynamic parameters to the measured forces for a given trajectory.
A common objective is to minimize the condition number of the regressor, producing excitations that yield parameter estimates more robust to measurement noise [ 16 , 13 ] .
The objective is inherently coupling-aware, since an ill-conditioned regressor indicates that different parameters influence the measurements along nearly identical directions.

For policy-driven system identification, where the excitation is produced by a closed-loop policy, SPI-Active and ASID [ 5 , 6 ] optimize the A-optimal Fisher-information criterion tr ⁡ ( F − 1 ) \operatorname{tr}(F^{-1}) to encourage informative trajectories.
Contact-implicit trajectory optimization likewise maximizes tr ⁡ ( F ) \operatorname{tr}({F}) over excited contact modes [ 15 ] .
Optimal experimental design offers related criteria, including D-optimality ( log det ( F ) \log\det(F) ) for reducing the overall uncertainty of the parameter estimate and E-optimality ( λ min ​ ( F ) \lambda_{\min}(F) , the smallest eigenvalue of F F ) for improving the least informative direction [ 17 , 18 ] .
In the transition from regressor-based trajectory design to sampling-based identification, the Fisher information has been carried over as the measure of a trajectory,
whereas parameter separation is addressed only implicitly through aggregate objectives.
The Schur complement provides an explicit characterization of parameter separation by quantifying the information that remains for a parameter subset after accounting for correlations with the remaining parameters [ 19 ] .
QOED [ 20 ] leverages this quantity to improve the distinguishability of a subset of task-relevant parameters, leading to improved sim-to-real policy transfer.
However, system identification requires all physical parameters to be identifiable, rather than only a selected subset.

To the best of our knowledge, IDTD is the first exploration objective for sampling-based system identification that uses per-parameter separability to enforce coverage of all physical parameters.

2026-10-09.title: OmniHOI: Dexterous Hand-Object Interaction from Monocular Human Video
2026-10-09.authors: Ting Mao , Yanming Shao , Ziheng Wang , Haoyu Liu , Yiqun Wang , Xuanye Wu , Yao Mu
2026-10-09.comment: The project page is available at this https URL
2026-10-09.abstract:
Monocular videos of human manipulation provide abundant dexterous demonstrations, yet reconstructing hand-object interaction from a single view and transferring it to robot hands remain difficult, limiting their direct use for robot execution.
Prior methods either require task-specific RL training, limiting scalability, or assume clean motion-capture trajectories and thus cannot operate directly on video.
We present OmniHOI , a pipeline that turns an RGB video of hand-object interaction into an interaction-faithful trajectory on dexterous hands.
The key idea is to enforce physical consistency using the evidence available at each stage: image evidence during reconstruction, contact geometry during retargeting, and dynamics during physics-in-the-loop refinement. Each stage optimizes the corresponding representation directly, correcting errors before they propagate downstream or must be absorbed by a learned policy.
Across 150 motion-capture trajectories transferred to each of five dexterous hands with 6 to 22 DoF, we achieve 39–89% success, compared with at most 31% for prior transfer methods. On 60 monocular video clips, we achieve 53% success, compared with 28% for the best prior video-to-robot pipeline.
Its trajectories also execute on a real bimanual robot across diverse tasks.
The project page is available at https://hydrofoooil.github.io/OmniHOI/ .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation demonstrations must capture both hand motion and object interaction.
Such data are typically collected through teleoperation or wearable captures ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Hoque et al., 2026 ) , while human manipulation videos are far more abundant.
Recent monocular reconstruction models such as MoGe-3 ( Kong et al., 2026 ) , SAM 3D ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , and WiLoR ( Potamias et al., 2025 ) can recover scene geometry, object meshes, and hand poses from a single view,
making these videos a promising source of robot demonstrations.
Turning such video into dexterous robot action requires more than recovering visually plausible motion.
Monocular depth ambiguity can confuse occlusion with contact, small geometric errors can turn contact into penetration or separation,
and a motion feasible for a human hand may become infeasible on a robot hand with different morphology and dynamics.
These errors must be resolved both when reconstructing the interaction and when transferring it to the robot.

Existing methods make different assumptions about the input and where errors are handled.
VideoManip ( Chen et al., 2026a ) and related methods ( Lum et al., 2025 ; Hsieh et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Mu et al., 2026 ) reconstruct hand-object motion from video and then train a task-specific policy,
leaving the policy to compensate for reconstruction errors.
ManipTrans ( Li et al., 2025 ) and SPIDER ( Pan et al., 2025 ) start from clean motion-capture trajectories and do not address noisy video reconstruction;
SPIDER also degrades when the reference motion is noisy.
Do as I Do ( Paliwal et al., 2026 ) starts from video without training, but relates the hand and object mainly through centroid alignment and handles contact explicitly only in simulation.
Across these pipelines, geometric errors introduced early can survive retargeting and become harder to correct later.
A slight finger-object penetration in reconstruction, for example, can turn into a robot link passing through the object after retargeting, leaving the final optimizer with an invalid contact state.

We present OmniHOI , a pipeline that reconstructs hand-object interaction from video and transfers it to dexterous robot hands. During reconstruction, dense hand-scene correspondences recover the hand-object geometry,
followed by refinement for occlusion, contact, penetration, and finger crossing.
During retargeting, the robot hand is optimized to preserve demonstrated contact while removing morphology-induced penetration and crossings.
The resulting keyframes are then refined in simulation with CMA-ES optimizer ( Hansen and Ostermeier, 2001 ) to improve object tracking, contact, and grasp stability.
Each stage corrects the errors exposed by its own evidence before they propagate to the next stage.

We evaluate OmniHOI on reconstruction, motion transfer, and end-to-end video-to-robot execution.
It achieves lower hand pose error than prior reconstruction methods while maintaining low hand-object intersection.
Across 150 motion-capture trajectories transferred to five dexterous hands with 6 to 22 DoF, we achieve 39–89% success, compared with at most 31% for prior transfer methods.
On 60 video clips, we achieve 53% success, compared with 28% for VideoManip and 25% for Do as I Do, and execute the resulting trajectories on a real bimanual robot.
Our contributions are:

A monocular video-to-dexterous-robot pipeline that maintains physical consistency across reconstruction, retargeting, and execution.

A hand-object reconstruction method that resolves occlusion, contact, penetration, and finger-crossing errors.

A contact- and dynamics-aware transfer method that produces task-effective motion across diverse dexterous hands.

1. A monocular video-to-dexterous-robot pipeline that maintains physical consistency across reconstruction, retargeting, and execution.

2. A hand-object reconstruction method that resolves occlusion, contact, penetration, and finger-crossing errors.

3. A contact- and dynamics-aware transfer method that produces task-effective motion across diverse dexterous hands.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Human videos have supplied manipulation
priors ( Nair et al., 2022 ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Shaw et al., 2022 ; Singh et al., 2025 ; Bahl et al., 2023 ; Agarwal et al., 2023 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) ,
but these require robot data or target grippers, and precise dexterous
demonstrations still rely on gloves, AR glasses or
headsets ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Guzey et al., 2025 ) .
Closest to ours are pipelines that reconstruct the interaction from video and train
a policy on
it ( Qin et al., 2022 ) , like the systems discussed in Section 1 .

Hands are recovered robustly in the
wild ( Pavlakos et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) ; the held object is
predicted by learned
models ( Hasson et al., 2019 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) such as iHOI ( Ye et al., 2022 ) , lifted with large
pretrained models as in EasyHOI ( Liu et al., 2025c ) and FollowMyHold ( Aytekin et al., 2026 ) , or fit per
sequence ( Fan et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2024 ) . Fitting-based methods optimize
the two together under contact, collision and occlusion
constraints ( Hasson et al., 2021 ; Cao et al., 2021 ; Grady et al., 2021 ; Jiang et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ) ,
whereas robot-learning pipelines such as VideoManip and Do as I Do relate them only
through keypoint depth or centroids and leave the
contact–occlusion ambiguity open, which OmniHOI resolves with pixel-aligned
registration and per-finger occlusion-order, contact and crossing corrections.

Kinematic retargeting, such as WujiHand Retargeting ( He and Zhang, 2026 ) , maps human keypoints to robot
joints ( Handa et al., 2020 ; Qin et al., 2023 ; Yin et al., 2025 ) ,
and interaction-preserving variants such as OmniRetarget ( Yang et al., 2025 ) keep spatial or contact relations to the
object ( Ho et al., 2010 ; Lakshmipathy et al., 2025 ) , but both
preserve how the hand looks, not whether it holds the object.
Dynamics-aware methods track the reference in simulation through RL or
optimization ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Mandi et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Liu et al., 2024a ) or training-free
sampling ( Williams et al., 2016 ; Howell et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2010 ; Ye and Liu, 2012 ) ,
but, apart from Do as I Do, assume clean motion-capture references. OmniHOI resolves contact geometrically before simulation, then refines keyframe
offsets with CMA-ES in rolling horizons.

2026-10-09.title: Cross-Embodiment Robot Foundation World Models with Latent Actions
2026-10-09.authors: Huang Huang , Sriram Yenamandra , Arjun Majumdar , Elie Aljalbout , Tushar Nagarajan , Tsung-Yen Yang , Akshara Rai , Michael Rabbat , Li Fei-Fei , Jiajun Wu , Tingfan Wu , Franziska Meier
2026-10-09.abstract:
The diversity of robot embodiments and action spaces makes it challenging to build robot world models that generalize across different embodiments. We introduce the Latent Action-Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM), which operates within a learned unified latent action space shared across diverse embodiments. This unified action space improves the world model’s performance when adapted to previously unseen robot embodiments. We compare LAC-WM with an Explicit Action-Conditioned World Model (EAC-WM), which conditions on explicit motion labels. Our results shows that explicit action conditioning leads to disjoint action representations across embodiments, limiting downstream performance when adapting to new robots.
We evaluate both models on dexterous manipulation tasks and a modified LIBERO benchmark. LAC-WM improves downstream performance over EAC-WM by up to 46.7% on dexterous manipulation and 11.7% on LIBERO. Crucially, the unified latent action space allows LAC-WM’s downstream performance to scale positively with the number of embodiments used during pretraining.
In contrast, the disjoint action space in EAC-WM leads to decreased performance as the number of pretraining embodiments increases. These results highlights the importance of a unified action space for efficient cross-embodiment learning, addressing a key challenge in robotics. Project website: https://lacwm.github.io/
2026-10-09.introduction:
Robot action-conditioned video generation models, or robot world models , offer a complementary approach to robot policies based on imitation learning, allowing robots to predict future states and evaluate planned actions before execution, improving planning and decision-making.
However, a fundamental and persistent challenge in robotics is the vast and evolving diversity of robot embodiments. Robots differ widely in their physical structure, sensors and actuators, and control strategies, and new embodiments are constantly emerging. This creates a critical need for robot world models that can efficiently learn from cross-embodiment data ( Zheng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Doshi et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025b ) and adapt quickly to previously unseen robot forms.

We propose learning a unified latent action space that aligns action representations across different embodiments, including both human and different robot agents. This latent space abstracts away embodiment-specific details while preserving task-relevant information, enabling the model to integrate heterogeneous data during pretraining. We show that such a unified latent space will empower the world model to learn more efficiently across embodiments during pretraining and adapt quickly to unseen embodiments through finetuning, laying the groundwork for a truly generalizable foundational world model for robotics.
Latent action spaces have primarily been explored for extracting action representations from unlabeled video data ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) . However, most robotic datasets come with action annotations, and advances in human pose estimation provide scalable motion information, including detailed hand poses and camera movements. This enables learning action spaces directly from motion data. Despite this, there is a lack of comparative analysis for action embedding alignment across different embodiments between representations derived directly from motion data and those learned through latent action models.
We hypothesize that training action encoders solely on motion data leads to disjoint latent spaces for different embodiments ( Figure 2 ), which limits cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and degrades generalization performance on unseen embodiments.

We focus on learning a foundational robot world model that learns efficiently from cross-embodiment data during pretraining and adapts quickly to unseen embodiments through finetuning. Specifically, we investigate two key research questions: (1) Do latent action models better unify cross-embodiment action representations compared to explicit action labels? and (2) Does a unified action space enhance cross-embodiment robot world model learning compared to a disjoint latent space? We propose the Latent Action Conditioned Robot World Model (LAC-WM), which predicts future observations conditioned on a unified latent action space. LAC-WM consists of four components: an inverse dynamics model (IDM), an forward dynamics model (FDM), a motion decoder and an action projector, as in Figure 1 . The IDM encodes pairs of consecutive image observations into latent actions, which condition the FDM to predict the next frame. The motion decoder, following Nikulin et al. (2025) , decodes latent actions back into explicit motion labels. The IDM and FDM are trained jointly on datasets combining human manipulation videos and robot data. Since future observations, required by the IDM, are unavailable at inference time, we train an action projector that maps explicit actions into the latent action space ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , enabling the world model to directly consume action inputs.

We evaluate LAC-WM in a cross-embodiment transfer setting, where the model is pretrained on multiple embodiments and fine-tuned on a previously unseen robot using an action projector. We compare against an explicit action-conditioned world model (EAC-WM), which directly encodes motion information into action latents. Our results show that LAC-WM produces higher-quality future predictions than EAC-WM and improves task success rate by up to 46.7% on dexterous manipulation. We further validate LAC-WM on a modified LIBERO benchmark with unseen object and location variants, where it improves the average success rate from 82.4% to 92.0% over EAC-WM. Moreover, LAC-WM exhibits positive scaling in downstream planning performance as the number of pretraining embodiments increases, whereas EAC-WM shows the opposite trend, likely due to its disjoint latent space, which hinders effective cross-embodiment learning.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

World Models in Robotics. World models (WMs) have emerged as a way to achieve controllable video generation ( Bruce et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Po et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Valevski et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) .
Robotic world models serve as scalable and explainable compliments to imitation learning based policies. Prior work has explored training navigation world models ( Hu et al., 2023 ; Bar et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2024 ; Hassan et al., 2025 ) with well-defined action spaces (e.g., velocity). Robot manipulation world models involve diverse action spaces due to differences in robot morphologies, and as a result, they typically rely on action-free video prediction during pretraining ( Gupta et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) , or use text or video conditioning ( Agarwal et al., 2025 ) , adding action conditioning only during fine-tuning ( Gupta et al., 2022 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2025 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) . Zhu et al. (2025) incorporate action conditioning for a single robot embodiment but do not evaluate cross-embodiment transfer.
In contrast, LAC-WM  directly tackles the challenge of heterogeneous action spaces with a unified latent action space, enabling efficient cross-embodiment learning and better generalization.

Latent Action Modeling. Latent Action Models (LAM) have emerged as a promising approach to
learn action representations from large-scale unlabeled data.
Prior work has explored LAMs for training latent action policies for game environments ( Schmidt and Jiang, 2024 ) , and fine-tuning expert-level policies from these, with limited labels.
Other works have explored LAMs for robot manipulation, by extracting latent actions from large-scale unlabeled human videos as labels to fine-tune vision-language models, and subsequently vision-language-action (VLA) models ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Bu et al., 2025b ; Jang et al., 2025 ; Cui et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) . Liang et al. (2025) ; Nikulin et al. (2025) introduced an auxiliary motion decoding loss which aligns latent actions with explicit control actions, to encourage the latent space to capture actionable content. Zhang et al. (2026) explores various best practices for training LAMs. LAC-WM also uses a motion decoding loss and learns a continuous latent action space. Instead of focusing on policy learning as in prior work, we learn a unified latent action space from cross embodiment labeled datasets, for building robot world foundation models.

Latent Action World Models. Bruce et al. (2024) ; Ren et al. (2025) introduce a latent action model (LAM) paired with a world model, trained on datasets that include robot data. However, their approach does not involve cross-embodiment pretraining across diverse embodiments, nor does the world model support conditioning on raw robot actions at inference time. Chen et al. (2024) train LAMs with data augmentation to regularize latent actions that feed into a foundation policy and world models for robotic manipulation.
However, they focus on action-free video pretraining and do not demonstrate adaptation to unseen robot embodiments. Gao et al. (2025) demonstrate that a pretrained latent action-conditioned world model can be adapted for robot manipulation by projecting raw action signals into the latent action space. But they also focus on action-free video pretraining and lack comparisons with robot world models trained using explicit action labels.
In contrast, we leverages labeled cross-embodiment data for robot world model training and investigate the comparison between a learned latent action space and directly encoding the motion labels. We show a unified latent action space benefits cross-embodiment learning with better downstream robot planning performance, particularly when adapting to unseen embodiments.

2026-10-09.title: Skill-SLM: Agent Skill-driven Small Language Models for Reliable Robot Operation
2026-10-09.authors: Wenhao Wang , Yanyan Li , Jiawei Yuan
2026-10-09.abstract: Small language models (SLMs) have been increasingly adopted for onboard robot operation because they enable intelligent decision-making. However, existing approaches are mainly distillation-oriented and rely on enumerating representative task-solution pairs. This makes dataset construction difficult and limits generalization to diverse robot tasks whose possible forms grow rapidly. This paper proposes Skill-SLM, a framework that reformulates SLM-driven robot operation as a task-decomposition and skill-composition problem. Given a natural language task instruction, Skill-SLM decomposes the task into subtasks, selects appropriate skills from the skill library, and orchestrates the selected skills into executable robot operations. First, to support the skill-driven workflow, we propose a novel robot operational skill aware context-free grammar (CFG) to extract the skills required to accomplish tasks and build the skill library accordingly. Then, we configure LLM teachers to induce and synthesize training datasets for the SLMs, enabling SLMs to decompose tasks and orchestrate skills reliably. Additionally, we employ a progressive skill orchestration strategy to improve the reliability of skill implementation and overall robot operation. Experiments on UAV operation tasks indicate that Skill-SLM substantially outperforms distillation-oriented baselines, especially on unseen tasks that require generalization of capabilities. Additional experiments on ground vehicle tasks further demonstrate that Skill-SLM can be applied to different robot platforms 1 1 1 https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SKILL-SLM .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) have enabled robots to interpret human natural language instructions and generate executable actions for navigation [ 1 ] , planning [ 2 ] , and manipulation [ 3 ] . However, deploying LLMs on resource-constrained robot platforms (e.g., UAVs) is often impractical due to their substantial computational and memory requirements. As a result, increasing efforts have been focused on enabling onboard deployable language models (i.e., SLMs) to perform reasoning and decision-making reliably through task-specific training and knowledge distillation from LLMs [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] .

Despite recent advances, a key challenge remains in enabling SLMs to generalize reliably to diverse robot tasks and novel instructions. Recent studies have enhanced SLMs’ generalization ability by extensively enumerating and synthesizing representative task-solution examples [ 4 , 5 ] . However, these data-driven approaches rely on the SLMs to memorize training examples, which limits their generalization when tasks require unseen combinations of learned capabilities or tasks were insufficiently represented during training. Covering these unseen cases by continually enumerating new task-solution examples is expensive, and SLMs’ limited memorization capacity becomes unreliable when learned knowledge becomes large [ 9 ] . Moreover, it is difficult to anticipate all possible task variations in advance.

Given the compositional nature of robotic operations, recent studies have investigated agent skills [ 10 ] to enable LLMs to generalize to unseen tasks by decomposing them into subtasks and tackling them by composition of skills [ 11 , 12 ] . However, SLMs’ intrinsically smaller model scale hinders their ability to achieve reliable compositional reasoning like LLMs [ 13 ] . Specifically, SLMs can be distracted by irrelevant or ambiguous information in the context [ 14 ] and struggle to effectively interpret task-relevant context for a given task instruction, resulting in incorrect task decomposition and incorrect skill usage. In addition, SLMs can overlook skill dependencies and fail to coordinate skills into a coherent execution [ 15 ] . Earlier skills selected by SLMs can define targets, variables, or robot states that later skills must preserve, and incompatible preconditions can make a plausible operational code fail. These limitations highlight the urgent need for methods capable of bridging the broad generalization of compositional reasoning with reliable SLM-driven robot operation.

To address these limitations, we propose Skill-SLM, a framework in which SLM agents solve robotic tasks by task decomposition and skill composition, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . Skill-SLM consists of two agents: a decomposition SLM agent decomposes a task instruction into subtasks and selects appropriate skills from the skill library; an orchestration SLM agent then orchestrates the selected skills into executable robot operations. Unlike prior methods that map task instructions to complete robot operations end-to-end, the proposed Skill-SLM captures the compositional nature of robotic tasks; it not only improves the seen task performance through compositional reasoning, but also facilitates generalization to diverse robotic tasks.

Specifically, we first construct a skill library to support the skill-driven workflow. We configure an operational skill aware LLM CFG constructor to induce a CFG that captures the skills that can effectively complete the tasks. Based on the captured skills, we construct a skill library with expert knowledge, in which each skill is documented in terms of its functionality, usage, and dependencies. The SLM can refer to these skill documents when orchestrating skills into executable robot operational code. On top of that, we distill LLMs’ reasoning to enable the SLM to effectively perform compositional reasoning, we leverage LLMs to synthesize two distillation datasets that capture different stages of the reasoning process. The decomposition dataset consists of task instructions, subtask descriptions, and selected skills, which trains the decomposition SLM agent to learn how to decompose tasks into subtasks and select the appropriate skills for each subtask. The orchestration dataset contains subtask descriptions, skill specifications, and their corresponding robot operation code, and is used to train the orchestration SLM agent to accomplish each subtask by orchestrating the selected skills into executable robot operation code. Additionally, to improve the reliability of the orchestration agent, we introduce a progressive orchestration strategy that generates executable robot operation code progressively while preserving the task context, intermediate variables, robot states, and cross-skill dependencies.

We conduct extensive experiments on UAV and ground vehicle operations to evaluate the effectiveness and generalizability of Skill-SLM. Qwen3-8B [ 16 ] achieves 100 % 100\% task success rate on Seen-Pattern tasks, 100 % 100\% on New-Combination tasks, and 94 % 94\% on New-Capability tasks. Skill-SLM also generalizes to ground vehicle operations, achieving 100 % 100\% , 95 % 95\% , and 100 % 100\% task success rates on the three task sets, respectively. Compared with the baselines [ 4 , 5 ] , our method consistently achieves higher task success rates, particularly on unseen tasks that require knowledge recombination. These results demonstrate that Skill-SLM is promising for reliable onboard SLM-driven robot operation across different robot platforms.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Agent Skills

Several prior studies have explored skill-like representations. SkiROS2 [ 17 ] represents robot skills as parameterized procedures with explicit execution conditions. LRLL [ 18 ] proposed to learn skills via exploring and summarizing. These methods show that reusable skills can improve generalization, but they mainly focus on model-learned skills and are restricted to a constrained environment. The recent agent-skills paradigm [ 10 ] provides a modular, file-based knowledge package that can be discovered and loaded by an agent when relevant [ 19 ] . Therefore, the agent can dynamically acquire and utilize skills as needed in solving different task scenarios, especially for tasks that are unseen in prior training or require knowledge recombination. Inspired by this principle, this studies investigated how a given task can be reformulated as an agent skill-driven problem.

## II-B Skill Discovery and Characterization

Prior work has investigated identifying skills. Ref. [ 20 ] derives a taxonomy of manipulation benchmark tasks from existing evaluation protocols, while [ 21 ] systematically analyzes robot skill frameworks to identify recurring task–skill–primitive structures and common robot capabilities. More recently, the BEHAVIOR Robot Suite [ 22 ] analyzes the 1,000 household activities in BEHAVIOR-1K to identify a set of core whole-body capabilities required for everyday manipulation. These approaches provide useful abstractions for characterizing task corpora, but largely rely on manually specified taxonomies, classification criteria, or capability categories. NavNuances [ 23 ] instead introduces a CFG-based decomposition of navigation instructions, enabling fine-grained analysis of model performance over task units. Its CFG is constructed by starting from a manually designed grammar and iteratively refining it with LLM assistance. In contrast, we leverage the semantic knowledge of LLMs to infer robot operations from the task corpus and automatically construct the CFG, eliminating the need for handcrafted production rules.

## II-C SLM-enabled Robotics

LLMs have been widely used to connect natural language instructions with robot planning, control, and tool use [ 24 , 2 , 25 , 26 ] . However, relying on large cloud-hosted models can be impractical for robots operating with unreliable networks (e.g., disaster response) or privacy-sensitive scenarios. This has motivated recent work on SLM-enabled robotics, where smaller models that can be deployed on the robot’s computing unit are configured for robotic tasks [ 5 , 6 , 4 ] . For example, PRISM distills an LLM-enabled planner into an SLM for high-level robot planning [ 5 ] and conducts parameter-efficient training with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 27 ] to reduce GPU memory usage. Ro-SLM [ 4 ] leverages LLMs to synthesize a dataset and train SLMs for mapping instructions to robot operational code. For a low-level robotic controller, Baumann et al. [ 6 ] train SLMs to generate parameters for model predictive control in an autonomous driving system. These approaches demonstrate the feasibility of transferring LLM capabilities to smaller models, but they still largely depend on enumerating representative task-solution mappings for SLMs to memorize. However, such enumeration becomes increasingly difficult as robot tasks become more diverse. Additionally, the small scale of SLMs makes memorization unreliable when the learned facts become large [ 9 ] . In contrast, Skill-SLM solves tasks by recombining reusable capabilities rather than memorizing all the task solutions.

2026-10-09.title: Diagnosing and Recovering from Observation-Space Shift at Long-Horizon Skill Seams
2026-10-09.authors: Pranav Wagh , Yu Fang , Yue Yang , Mingyu Ding
2026-10-09.abstract:
Long-horizon robotic manipulation is often built by chaining skills that are trained independently.
Although individual skills can be reliable in isolation, long-horizon task performance can degrade sharply when these skills are chained: each downstream skill must start from the state produced by its predecessor rather than from its training distribution.
We study this failure mode, known as Observation-Space Shift (OSS), and investigate what aspects are responsible for such skill-seam failures.
Through privileged simulator resets, we identify that the dominant shift arises from displaced scene state (e.g., an open drawer or secondary objects left behind by preceding skills), rather than from the robot joint configuration or the object manipulated by the downstream skill.
To test this diagnosis, we build a fully learned detect–restore–resume system that restores the components the analysis identifies: a task-progress monitor detects the stall, a learned policy restores those components, and seam-robust fine-tuning lets the skill resume .
It recovers the seam where every tested alternative fails, which is evidence for the diagnosis rather than a general purpose method.
On the BOSS-44 benchmark, our system improves full-chain success from 7.6% to 26.5%, a 3.5 × 3.5\times improvement over the base policy and 51% of a privileged restoration oracle.
In contrast, best-of- K K resampling, a Diffusion Policy, and world-model-based baselines fail to recover from the evaluated OSS seam states.
During real-robot experiments on a real Franka arm running π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy, the same progress monitor is limited by external camera observability, yet closing the loop still recovers some otherwise-terminal failures. This motivates wrist and gripper sensing.
These results suggest that some long-horizon composition failures are better addressed by restoring the scene before resuming the policy, rather than retrying from an off-support state.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Long-horizon robotic manipulation often requires composing multiple skills into a single task [ 1 , 2 ] .
For example, a robot may first open a drawer, then move an object, and finally place it at a target location.
A common strategy is to train individual manipulation skills independently and execute them sequentially in a chain at deployment.
Although these skills can be reliable when evaluated from their own training distributions, long-horizon task performance can degrade drastically once they are chained together.

The challenge arises at the skill seams , where one skill terminates and the next begins:
A downstream skill does not start from the canonical initial states on which it was trained;
instead, it inherits whatever scene state its predecessor leaves behind.
For example, an “open drawer” skill may leave the drawer open before a “place bowl” skill, trained with the drawer closed, begins execution.
The downstream skill is therefore asked to act from an unfamiliar state and may stall even though it succeeds reliably in isolation.
This mismatch between the downstream skill’s training distribution and the state encountered during skill composition is known as Observation-Space Shift (OSS) [ 2 ] .
On the three-skill chains studied in BOSS-44 [ 2 ] , success through the chain drops from 88.5 % 88.5\% after executing the first skill, to 34.3 % 34.3\% after two skills (one seam), and to 7.6 % 7.6\% after all three skills (two seams), despite the component skills achieving 79.0 % 79.0\% average success when evaluated independently from their canonical initial states.

What changes at a skill seam that causes the downstream skill to fail?
We consider three potential sources of shift: the preceding skill may
(1) leave the robot arm in an unfamiliar state;
(2) displace the object manipulated by the downstream skill;
or (3) alter other elements of the scene.
To identify which components are responsible, we diagnose OSS through privileged simulator interventions.
Using a teleportation oracle and component-wise resets, we selectively restore different state components to their canonical values.
We find that
(1) resetting the robot arm provides little improvement;
(2) the object manipulated by the downstream skill is typically already close to its canonical position;
and (3) the dominant recovery comes from restoring articulated scene state (e.g., an open drawer) and secondary objects (i.e., other objects displaced by preceding skills but not manipulated by the downstream skill).
Moreover, these effects are complementary: restoring articulation or secondary objects individually yields only partial gains, whereas restoring them jointly recovers substantially more of the oracle performance.

This diagnosis suggests that recovery should modify the state responsible for the failure rather than repeatedly invoke the policy from off-support states.
As shown in Fig. 1 , we introduce a detect–restore–resume framework: a fully learned, non-privileged system that recovers much of the oracle from cameras and proprioception alone.
A task-progress monitor detects when execution has stalled.
A learned restoration policy modifies the displaced scene state, after which the downstream skill resumes execution.
Since learned restoration only approximately returns the scene to its canonical state, we additionally apply seam-robust prevention fine-tuning on post-restoration hand-off states to improve robustness during re-entry.
On BOSS-44, our system improves three-skill full-chain success from 7.6 % 7.6\% to 26.5 % 26.5\% , compared with 51.8 % 51.8\% under a privileged oracle that exactly restores the scene to its canonical state.
A matched re-home-and-retry baseline reaches only 12.9 % 12.9\% , showing that the improvement cannot be explained simply by additional execution attempts.
Best-of- K K resampling and a Diffusion Policy trained on the same canonical demonstrations also fail from the evaluated OSS seam states, indicating that retrying or changing the policy architecture alone does not resolve these failures.
On a real Franka arm with a π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy, the same monitor runs unchanged but transfers only weakly from an exterior camera. Closing the loop also recovers some otherwise-terminal failures, a proof of concept that isolates the observability (wrist and gripper sensing) as an important requirement for deployment.

Our contributions are three-fold.

We provide a diagnosis of OSS at long-horizon skill seams. Through privileged simulator interventions, we show that skill-seam failures are driven primarily by displaced articulation and secondary scene objects.

We propose a learned detect–restore–resume framework for long-horizon skill composition. The system detects stalled execution, restores the displaced scene toward the downstream support, and resumes execution using only deployable observations at test time.

Experiments on both BOSS-44 demonstrate that our framework achieves a 3.5 × 3.5\times improvement in full-chain success, outperforming other baselines. We provide empirical analysis of when restoration is a better intervention than retry. On a real Franka, the same monitor runs unchanged but it limited by exterior-camera observability. Closing the loop recovers a fraction of otherwise-terminal failures, a proof of concept that motivates wrist and gripper sensing.

1. We provide a diagnosis of OSS at long-horizon skill seams. Through privileged simulator interventions, we show that skill-seam failures are driven primarily by displaced articulation and secondary scene objects.

2. We propose a learned detect–restore–resume framework for long-horizon skill composition. The system detects stalled execution, restores the displaced scene toward the downstream support, and resumes execution using only deployable observations at test time.

3. Experiments on both BOSS-44 demonstrate that our framework achieves a 3.5 × 3.5\times improvement in full-chain success, outperforming other baselines. We provide empirical analysis of when restoration is a better intervention than retry. On a real Franka, the same monitor runs unchanged but it limited by exterior-camera observability. Closing the loop recovers a fraction of otherwise-terminal failures, a proof of concept that motivates wrist and gripper sensing.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

Skill chaining, observation-space shift, and recovery. Composing pretrained skills into long-horizon behavior is central to hierarchical and library-based control [ 3 , 4 , 2 , 1 ] , where a transition succeeds only when one skill’s termination region meets the next’s initiation set [ 5 , 6 ] . A seam is a violation of that condition. The mechanism is the behavior-cloning covariate shift at composition, where a downstream skill inherits a state its predecessor produced but never trained on [ 7 , 8 ] . This is not specific to small policies: generalist vision-language-action models [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] and modern imitation learners [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] clone actions and inherit the same off-support behavior when chained. Unlike work that reports chaining loss as an aggregate drop, we localize the shift causally to specific state components. Prior fixes act at training time, regularizing a skill’s terminal distribution toward the next initiation set [ 17 ] or appending recovery and correction data [ 18 ] . Test-time recovery instead retrieves and replays demonstration sub-trajectories [ 19 ] , backtracks to a prior skill, takes object-centric keypoint steps back onto the manifold [ 20 ] , or learns local RL recovery policies [ 21 ] . We test faithful instances of retrieval, backtracking, and library-inverse correction and find none re-manipulates the displaced scene. Our restoration skill supplies that behavior as a learned reset controller, the objective of reset-free RL and learned resets [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] , but invoked at a detected seam rather than every episode. It is trained with SAC [ 25 ] and RLPD [ 26 ] from real failure states and distilled to a camera-only student. We compare it against a training-time prevention condition built with data generation [ 27 ] rather than only asserting the distinction.

Detection and test-time alternatives. Detecting task failure without labels has converged on task-progress and value estimation from pixels: Generative Value Learning [ 28 ] elicits per-frame completion from a VLM, and process-reward models such as Robometer [ 29 ] train per-frame progress on robot data. Our monitor keeps the progress-as-normalized-time target but trains a ∼ 1 \sim\!1 M-parameter head over a frozen encoder with an added success/stall contrast loss, and fires a calibrated stagnation trigger in the spirit of distribution-free failure detection [ 30 , 31 ] . Unlike runtime monitors that add temporal-consistency terms [ 32 ] or world-model prediction surprise, we find progress alone is the correctly signed signal at stalls. The alternative to restoration is planning or search: imagine-score-execute pipelines plan with learned dynamics [ 33 , 34 , 35 , 36 ] and sampling-based shooting (e.g., MPPI [ 37 ] ) selects actions by simulated return, while a separate line scales test-time compute by sampling K K rollouts and keeping the best [ 38 ] . Evaluated from OSS seams, a world model as generator, monitor, or planner gives no benefit or is falsified, and best-of- K K cannot select what the policy cannot produce. These both point to restoration over planning or sampling.

2026-10-09.title: Same Action, Different Outcome: Variability in Dynamic Cloth Manipulation
2026-10-09.authors: Mahed Dadgostar , Guillem Alenyà , Júlia Borràs
2026-10-09.abstract:
Although cloth is known to exhibit different outcomes under repeated fast dynamic motions, even when the same trajectory is applied, this variability has not yet been systematically characterized. Quantifying it is essential to assess the reliability of learned manipulation policies and the extent to which simulation can reproduce real-world behavior.
To study this, we execute the same trajectory ten times across four dynamic tasks, two of which are novel, each tested with three cloths of very different properties and at up to three execution speeds, with a total of 269 recorded rollouts. For all of them, we record small marker positions on the cloth and synchronized stereo camera. We then formalize different metrics to quantify variability,
and our results show how it is significant in every test condition,
in most cases one to three orders of magnitude above the repeatability inherent to the robot and sensing noise.
Our results also show variability is driven mainly by the cloth physical properties but also grows with speed.
By replaying all the rollouts in four calibrated modern cloth simulators, we show that none of them can reproduce the variability magnitude we observed in real cloth, nor its ordering.
Together with our analysis, we publish the dataset with synchronized OptiTrack, vision and robot logs and their corresponding simulator twins.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Most available deformable object manipulation datasets contain slow folding tasks or unfolding pick-and-place,
in which inertial effects can be ignored, and the motion is referred to as quasi-static manipulation [ 1 , 2 ] . In contrast, dynamic manipulation consists of motions in which the inertia effects and accelerations of the target objects are significant during execution: a bimanual setup can fold a cloth slowly by grasping its two corners, but a single robotic arm can perform the same task by leveraging inertia to handle it faster [ 3 , 4 ] .

With advances in foundational models for natural language processing and computer vision, researchers have extended this paradigm to robotics through vision-language-action (VLA) models [ 5 , 6 ] . However, the cloth manipulation tasks they perform are typically quasi-static, such as folding laundry [ 5 ] , and their perception and inference run at a few hertz [ 6 ] . In the dynamic manipulation regime, aerodynamic, frictional and other environmental effects affect the reliability and success of the task. The works that do manipulate cloth dynamically [ 7 , 8 , 4 ] report only policy success rates, which do not characterize the variability in cloth behavior that arises even across nominally identical trials.

Another challenge, often overlooked in sim-to-real transfer, is the inconsistent cloth behavior between the real environment and the simulator, especially in dynamic tasks. For example, if one executes a swinging trajectory in a deterministic physics simulator for N N samples, the cloth states across all samples remain the same if the cloth’s initial state and grasp have not changed. However, if the same experiment is performed in the real world, the cloth-state trajectories diverge across rollouts (Fig. 1 ). This is because the available simulators account for aerodynamics only coarsely [ 9 ] and not at all for air turbulence or micro-level changes in the cloth state, such as the grasp posture or the cloth history of wrinkles and fold lines. This means that this issue cannot be addressed even with domain randomization [ 10 , 11 ] , since these effects are not parameters of the simulator. Modeling these aerodynamic effects can be extremely complex; in this sense, one could say that dynamic manipulation of cloths is nondeterministic. However, like aleatoric uncertainty [ 12 ] , it can be characterized by quantifying how much variability remains after accounting for everything the robot can observe and control. This work aims to quantify precisely this residual variability.

To do so, we replay the same commanded trajectory ten times with the same trial conditions. We evaluate across four different tasks, each performed with three cloths, and up to three execution speeds to show that this variability exists and to characterize its magnitude, controllable factors, and modes. We believe that improving the modeling parameters of cloth dynamics can only go so far, and that identifying the controllable factors of this interaction inconsistency tells us how to mitigate it. For instance by acting more slowly on a cloth sensitive to aerodynamic effects, or estimating how much data a policy needs and when gathering more data cannot improve task success.

The main contributions of this work are:

A formalism to show that the same dynamic manipulation of cloths yields different outcomes depending on the nature of the manipulation and the cloth’s features, together with the analysis of the results on four dynamic tasks.

An evaluation of four cloth simulators, calibrated per cloth and replaying the measured inputs, showing that this variability is poorly modeled: no engine reproduces its magnitude or its ordering reliably.

A dataset of 269 motion-captured rollouts, with synchronized stereo video, robot logs, and corresponding simulator twins in 4 different simulators, for 4 dynamic cloth manipulation tasks.

The dataset, available on the paper’s website 1 1 1 https://cloth-var.github.io , contains two of the most commonly studied dynamic tasks: swing-to-place flat, also known as fling [ 7 , 8 ] , and dynamic folding on the table, using a single hand [ 13 , 4 , 14 ] . It also includes two novel dynamic tasks that, to the best of our knowledge, have not been studied: moving the grippers inward toward each other, with and without a swing (Fig. 1 - right). Humans perform this motion to fold in the air.

1. A formalism to show that the same dynamic manipulation of cloths yields different outcomes depending on the nature of the manipulation and the cloth’s features, together with the analysis of the results on four dynamic tasks.

2. An evaluation of four cloth simulators, calibrated per cloth and replaying the measured inputs, showing that this variability is poorly modeled: no engine reproduces its magnitude or its ordering reliably.

3. A dataset of 269 motion-captured rollouts, with synchronized stereo video, robot logs, and corresponding simulator twins in 4 different simulators, for 4 dynamic cloth manipulation tasks.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II State of the Art

Several examples exist in the literature that prove the advantage of dynamic manipulation. For instance, quasi-static pipelines smooth garments by sequences of pick-and-place actions [ 15 , 16 ] . A fling unfolds a cloth in a fraction of those interactions [ 7 ] , and other dynamic actions followed: flings that align garments [ 8 ] , single-arm folding [ 3 , 4 , 14 ] and placing [ 17 ] .

That nominally identical dynamic executions leave the cloth in different states has been observed but not characterized. Coltraro et al. [ 18 ] repeat one dynamic laying motion fourteen times on their lightest fabric and find a considerable spread of the final corner positions. Hietala et al. [ 4 ] record ten open-loop dynamic folds per fabric, but do not discuss their spread. Neither work, nor any other we know of, has analyzed the spread in relation to the fabric, the speed or the grasp, or separated it from the repeatability of the robot.
However, in the context of flexible sheets, similar studies have proven useful showing how in a flow these sheets flap above a critical speed and become chaotic at higher speeds [ 19 ] , so micro-differences between trials are amplified in flight.

In works where the variability is handled, it is assumed rather than measured; robust MPC certifies constraint satisfaction against a bounded disturbance set [ 20 ] , and iterative learning control assumes the disturbance repeats from trial to trial [ 21 ] , as does the trial-to-trial refinement of deformable-object actions [ 22 , 23 ] . Which of these assumptions dynamic cloth manipulation satisfies is unknown, because the distribution of its outcome has not been reported; measuring it requires the cloth state in flight, where self-occlusion and motion blur defeat vision [ 24 ] . To overcome this challenge, we use motion capture as in [ 18 ] , manually linking markers that go occluded for short periods and in addition, we add a registered stereo camera. In [ 18 ] , they prove that these small markers are light enough not to affect the dynamics of the cloth. Therefore, our dataset improves on [ 18 ] by adding novel dynamic tasks, including synchronized image perception.

2026-10-09.title: NavGPT-3: Harnessing Context in a Hierarchical Navigation Runtime
2026-10-09.authors: Gengze Zhou , Yicong Hong , Jiazhao Zhang , Xunyi Zhao , Jian Zhou , Zixing Lei , Zun Wang , Chongyang Zhao , Xionghui Chen , Stephen Gould , Anton van den Hengel , Qi Wu
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-09.abstract: Language models trained with long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning can generalize knowledge through reasoning, express precise actions, and pursue goals over many steps, raising the ceiling on what an embodied agent can understand and decide. Physical interaction, however, remains the domain of action policies, which provide dense, low-latency control. We present NavGPT-3 , a harness that connects the two models, with an OS-like runtime built above it: reasoning, acting, and monitoring run as threads with their own context, tools, and permissions, while the runtime schedules them and decides which thread controls the robot’s motion, so that the robot can react to sudden real-world events through interruption and thread switching. Beneath it, our action policy NavGPT VLA, trained on 19.28M examples, allocates visual tokens using codec allocation, in proportion to scene change; its 8B model alone reaches 74.51 SR on R2R-CE and leads RxR-CE with 78.19 SR. With the complete harness, NavGPT-3 sets the state of the art on R2R-CE (81.51 SR) and, for the first time, brings an autonomous agent to human level: on RxR-CE it matches human followers in success (90.43 vs. 90.4 SR) and path fidelity (78.47 vs. 77.7 nDTW) at 1 min 22 s per episode, versus roughly 3 min for a human. We comprehensively ablate the harness design and the interaction between the two models, showing how tools and the action policy shape the path from language-model reasoning to physical control: when NavGPT VLA executes the route, the reasoning loop shortens and the system’s minimum reaction time falls from 3–19 s per language-model decision to 0.5–1 s per action-policy step (1–2 Hz). These results show that designing this embodied interface is central to connecting frontier language-model intelligence with low-level physical control. We will release all models, code, and evaluation records.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Language models trained with long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning generalize knowledge through reasoning, express actions as tool calls and code, and pursue goals over many steps ( OpenAI, 2026 ; Anthropic, 2026b ; Anthropic, 2026a ; Qwen Team, 2026b ) . In Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), successive generations of language models absorb more of what navigation systems once built as separate modules: commonsense grounding, spatial description, progress estimation, and long-horizon tool use. Execution is the exception. It runs on the world’s clock rather than the model’s, and control must proceed at a rate that step-by-step reasoning cannot sustain. The world also does not pause while a model thinks: observations arrive during inference, motion continues past the decision that began it, and a hazard may demand a stop before any reasoning finishes. An action policy is also far smaller and weaker at following instructions than the model that plans, so it drifts over a long rollout and must report back evidence the reasoner can check. Existing systems address part of this by combining reasoning and execution hierarchically, with a planner issuing subgoals to a learned controller ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Chiang et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026b ) , and recent agents add graph memory and backtracking ( Liu et al., 2026 ) or verification and recovery skills ( Wang et al., 2026b ) .

Connecting these abilities to physical control therefore requires a complete interaction loop: grounded context for deciding, spatial tools for acting, persistent state for remembering, and execution evidence for revising a route. A harness shapes model behavior through this loop, defining the context models receive, the tools they can call, and the state and feedback retained across calls ( Zhong and Zhu, 2026 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) . Real robots add a coordination requirement: reasoning, execution, and monitoring must be able to progress asynchronously. A runtime above the harness manages these activities as threads and controls which thread may move the robot.

We present NavGPT-3 , which combines a complete navigation harness with an OS-like runtime. The harness brings context management, spatial tools, persistent route state, and model execution into one embodied interface. The Planner can act through those tools or delegate execution of a navigation instruction to NavGPT VLA. Returned route images, execution feedback, an observed map, and numbered visited places make the resulting rollout inspectable and revisable: the Planner can return to a visited place, repair the route locally, delegate again, and explicitly decide when the task is complete. We developed these harness interfaces through recursive self-improvement (RSI), using automated research iterations over tool definitions and visual prompts ( Section 4.1 ). The runtime builds on these interfaces to schedule threads and control motion authority : review can overlap execution, and monitoring can interrupt motion without waiting for reasoning ( Figure 2 ). Tool-capability and visual-context studies examine the harness design alongside Planner–VLA interaction ( Sections 4.2 and 4.3 ).
Beneath the harness, NavGPT VLA predicts eight waypoints from the instruction and visual history. Because the visual context is bounded, we use codec allocation from video coding: the first observation of each view is a full reference (I-frame), and later observations (P-frames), receive visual tokens in proportion to how much they change ( Tang et al., 2026 ; An et al., 2026 ) .

Across benchmarks, the 8B NavGPT VLA alone leads published methods on RxR-CE (78.19 SR); under the runtime, NavGPT-3 sets the state of the art on R2R-CE (81.51 SR) and, on RxR-CE, matches human followers in both success (90.43 vs. 90.4 SR) and path fidelity (78.47 vs. 77.7 nDTW). The same runtime transfers to object-goal navigation and embodied question answering ( Tables 6 , 8 and 8 ). Ablating the harness tools and the VLA interaction shows how this interface governs the path from reasoning to control: given good tools, a strong language model navigates well by itself but decides only once every 3–19 s, whereas letting the VLA execute the route lowers the system’s minimum reaction time to 0.5–1 s per step (1–2 Hz; Table 3 ).

# 2 Related Work

Agentic Vision-and-Language Navigation with LLMs. VLN requires an agent to follow natural-language instructions in unseen environments, first on discrete navigation graphs ( Anderson et al., 2018 ; Ku et al., 2020 ) and then in continuous environments ( Krantz et al., 2020 ) . NavGPT initiated the line of work asking how much of navigation a LLM can carry on its own ( Zhou et al., 2024b ) : given observations in text, the language model reasons about instruction progress and decides each move zero-shot, without any training on action data. Later navigators extend this recipe with maps, discussion, and open-vocabulary grounding ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2023 ; Long et al., 2023 ; Qiao et al., 2025 ) , and recent agents let the model act on the embodiment directly through code ( Zhou et al., 2026b ) . A parallel line of work targets physical execution, tuning Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into VLA policies that provide dense, low-latency control while retaining the generalization of the VLM ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Cheng et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2025b ; Wei et al., 2025a ; InternVLA-N1 Team, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; AMAP CV Lab, 2026 ; Qwen Team, 2026a ; Mistral AI, 2026 ) . NavGPT-2 pursues both at once, emphasizing the role of reasoning in language models while training a policy that acts faster and more accurately, with the language and action heads decoupled over one shared representation ( Zhou et al., 2024a ) . However, such training cannot perfectly align the reasoning and the actions. NavGPT-3 combines the two at the system level, connecting a reasoning model and a trained VLA policy through a harness with an OS-like runtime built above it.

Language models over learned policies. Hierarchical systems pair a planning model with a learned controller in navigation ( Chiang et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026 ) and manipulation ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , and harness engineering treats context, tools, and state as the unit of design ( Zhong and Zhu, 2026 ; DeepSeek-AI, 2026 ) . These systems already cover graph memory, backtracking, verification, and recovery. The closest system, NavMCP, retains trajectory evidence across calls to a navigation foundation model in order to answer questions ( Lei et al., 2026 ) . NavGPT-3 instead uses returned evidence to revise an instruction-following route: after a delegated VLA rollout, the Planner can inspect the route, return to any visited place, repair locally, and decide completion.

Visual context in navigation policies. Navigation policies must fit long, multi-view observation histories into a bounded visual budget. Existing policies compress history by merging or pruning visual tokens ( Zhang et al., 2025b ; Wei et al., 2025b ) or distribute a fixed budget across time and views ( Qwen Team, 2026a ) . NavGPT VLA allocates tokens in proportion to scene change, as codec-aligned video encoders do ( Tang et al., 2026 ; An et al., 2026 ) .

2026-10-09.title: TAPNAV: Humanoid Navigation through Tactile Active Perception
2026-10-09.authors: Huaze Liu , Zhenyu Wu , Jaehwi Jang , Junjie Sheng , Andrew Collins , Aaron Xie , Zhaoyuan Gu , Kaijie Zhu , Ding Jiang , Kevin Cai , Ye Zhao
2026-10-09.abstract: Navigation in vision-denied environments is challenging for humanoid robots because proprioceptive odometry drifts and localization uncertainty accumulates rapidly. We present TapNav , a tactile active-perception framework that enables humanoid navigation toward a goal by actively probing surrounding structures without relying on vision. TapNav maintains a pose belief from odometry, IMU, and tactile contact observations, and couples uncertainty-aware global route planning with information-gain-driven local probing. The global planner searches for routes that keep predicted localization uncertainty bounded by exploiting opportunities for tactile correction, while the local planner selects probe actions that maximize expected information gain. A whole-body controller coordinates the humanoid’s locomotion and end-effector contact to execute the planned navigation and probe motions. We evaluate TapNav in simulation and on a Unitree G1 across different floor plans and obstacle geometries. TapNav achieves lower state estimation error and a higher task completion rate than baselines. These results demonstrate that actively planning physical interactions with the environment can provide localization cues for reliable humanoid navigation without vision. More results are available at TapNav project page .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Humanoid robots hold great promise for bringing intelligent physical assistance to human-centered environments [ 1 ] . To succeed in indoor environments, humanoid robots require not only robust locomotion but also reliable localization and navigation under safety-critical and perceptually degraded conditions. This capability is particularly important in hazardous or inaccessible scenarios such as fire emergency response, industrial gas-leak inspection, and engine-room operation with degraded lighting.

Recent progress in humanoid perception and navigation has largely relied on RGB-D cameras and LiDAR for environment sensing and state estimation [ 2 , 3 ] . These sensing modalities, however, can become unreliable in visually degraded environments, compromising both localization and navigation capabilities. In contrast, humans can compensate for limited vision through haptic interactions, which offer an alternative source of geometric information when visual observations are unreliable.

Motivated by how people navigate with haptic feedback, this study equips a humanoid robot with tactile sensors for contact-based navigation. Traditionally, robotic tactile sensing has been widely researched in fine-grained tasks such as identifying grasped objects, estimating in-hand pose, or reconstructing local shape [ 4 , 5 ] . Extending tactile sensing to humanoid navigation requires selecting informative contacts while maintaining whole-body balance. Sparse tactile observations must then be integrated with motion estimates to support localization throughout navigation.

We introduce TapNav : Humanoid Nav igation through T actile A ctive P erception, as shown in Fig. . TapNav is an integrated framework that guides a humanoid to a goal using tactile sensing without relying on cameras or LiDAR. To the best of our knowledge, TapNav is the first system to use actively planned tactile probing, rather than reactive or incidental contact, to navigate a humanoid through an office-scale indoor environment without vision.

We evaluate TapNav in simulation and on a Unitree G1 humanoid, covering indoor layouts with long hallways, corners, pillars, and free-standing islands.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

A belief-space tactile navigation planner that balances route progress with localization uncertainty by exploiting opportunities for tactile correction.

An active tactile probing framework that selects contact actions based on their expected information gain, accounting for both contact and contact-free outcomes to actively reduce robot pose uncertainty.

An integrated vision-denied humanoid navigation system that couples belief-space planning and active tactile perception with reinforcement learning-based whole-body locomotion control, validated in both simulation and real-world hardware experiments in office-scale environments.

1. A belief-space tactile navigation planner that balances route progress with localization uncertainty by exploiting opportunities for tactile correction.

2. An active tactile probing framework that selects contact actions based on their expected information gain, accounting for both contact and contact-free outcomes to actively reduce robot pose uncertainty.

3. An integrated vision-denied humanoid navigation system that couples belief-space planning and active tactile perception with reinforcement learning-based whole-body locomotion control, validated in both simulation and real-world hardware experiments in office-scale environments.

# II Related Work

## II-A Tactile Localization and Active Sensing

Tactile sensing has been widely applied to object-centric state estimation. Learned tactile representations and probabilistic estimation account for ambiguous contact observations, while additional contacts and sequential measurements constrain the set of plausible poses [ 6 , 7 ] . Joint pose and shape estimation has also been studied through visuo-tactile neural reconstruction and tactile-only geometric modeling, allowing object geometry to be estimated alongside its
motion [ 8 ] .
Active sensing couples these estimation problems with the selection of subsequent interactions. Learned exploration policies use tactile feedback to select motions that improve surface coverage or object recognition [ 9 , 10 ] . Information-based approaches evaluate candidate interactions through expected information gain or contact-aware information, selecting informative motions for estimating object pose, geometry, or physical parameters [ 8 , 11 ] . On the other hand, contact sensing has also been used for robot localization, where geometric and terrain information from gait-induced contacts is incorporated without active action selection [ 12 ] .

## II-B Belief-Space Planning and Active Localization

Belief-space planning explicitly reasons about state uncertainty when selecting navigation actions, accounting for how motion and future observations affect the robot’s belief [ 13 ] .
Active localization further couples navigation with sensing decisions, selecting informative viewpoints or deciding when to acquire observations to improve pose estimation [ 14 , 15 ] .
These approaches, however, primarily assume that localization information can be obtained through remote perceptual observations. In contrast, TapNav enables active localization in vision-denied settings by planning motions that leverage contact observations to maintain an accurate robot-state belief.

## II-C Contact-Rich Humanoid Loco-Manipulation

Recent advances in humanoid loco-manipulation have enabled whole-body coordination of locomotion and manipulation for tasks such as object transport and door opening [ 16 , 17 ] , dynamic catching [ 18 ] , payload transport [ 19 , 20 ] , and force-regulated interaction [ 21 ] . These methods demonstrate increasingly capable coordination between lower-body locomotion and upper-body manipulation, including maintaining stability under interaction forces. Unlike conventional loco-manipulation, where contact typically serves the manipulation objective, TapNav uses contact as a sensing action: the planner dynamically selects when and where the robot should probe to reduce localization uncertainty.
