2026-10-09.title: Masked Generative Motion Planning with Geometry-Guided Token Search
2026-10-09.authors: Lipeng Zhuang , Yingdong Ru , Shiyu Fan , Edmond S. L. Ho , Gerardo Aragon Camarasa , Paul Henderson
2026-10-09.abstract:
Generative motion planners typically use learned trajectory priors for initial generation, while leaving test-time repair to local continuous refinement.
We introduce Masked Generative Motion Planning (MGMP), which extends the learned prior from efficient parallel generation to structural repair.
A masked generative transformer generates discrete trajectory candidates in parallel, and Geometry-Guided Token Search (GGTS) uses scene geometry to target where to edit and which prior-supported alternatives to evaluate.
This turns refinement into an efficient search over discrete motion alternatives, enabling route-level restructuring beyond local trajectory deformation.
MGMP achieves 96% success on Ring Maze and 82% repair success on Controlled Route Invalidation on Kuka , exceeding the strongest external baselines by 23 and 25 percentage points, respectively.
It further generalizes to unseen layouts, additional obstacles, unseen geometries, single- and dual-arm planning, and real-world Baxter tasks.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Motion planning in robotics aims to find a feasible trajectory between a start and goal configuration while satisfying geometric constraints ( LaValle, 2006 ) . Trajectory-optimization methods directly refine trajectories against task-specific objectives ( Ratliff et al., 2009 ; Schulman et al., 2014 ) , but their performance is typically sensitive to initialization in cluttered and non-convex environments ( Pan et al., 2014 ) . Generative planners mitigate this sensitivity by learning multimodal trajectory priors and producing diverse candidate motions that can subsequently be refined to satisfy collision constraints.
Generative motion planning therefore involves two coupled inference problems: efficient initial trajectory generation and effective test-time geometric refinement .

Existing planners make trade-offs on both fronts. For initial generation , diffusion-based methods rely on iterative denoising in a high-dimensional continuous space ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Carvalho et al., 2023 ) , leading to high inference cost; fewer denoising steps improve efficiency but can reduce sample quality.
For test-time refinement , generated trajectories are typically refined through continuous guidance or trajectory optimization ( Carvalho et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . Weak guidance may leave collisions unresolved, while stronger guidance can move trajectories away from the learned prior ( Yang et al., 2025 ) .
Such continuous refinement is effective when feasibility can be recovered through local adjustments; however, in harder cases such as near-enclosing obstacles, reaching a feasible alternative may require many iterations, remain sensitive to initialization and guidance strength, and still fail to escape unfavorable local basins. ( Pan et al., 2014 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) .

We therefore ask: How can a learned trajectory prior directly expose qualitatively different routes as candidates for structural repair, rather than expecting continuous refinement to reach them?

We introduce Masked Generative Motion Planning (MGMP), which addresses this question by formulating motion planning as masked generation over discrete trajectory tokens, reusing the same token space for test-time structural repair.
A trajectory tokenizer learns compact motion tokens from feasible trajectories. For initial generation, a Masked Generative Transformer (MGT) ( Chang et al., 2022 ; Chang et al., 2023 ) predicts token sequences in parallel, producing high-quality trajectory candidates in a single forward pass and reducing the need for costly resampling and post-hoc repair during online planning. Importantly, the same representation allows us to cast repair as a guided search over prior-supported motion alternatives, instead of continuously deforming the current trajectory.

To make this search effective, we introduce Geometry-Guided Token Search (GGTS) , which uses scene geometry to guide two decisions: where to edit and what to fill .
Geometric attribution determines where to edit by selecting the token positions most responsible for the current violation while preserving unaffected parts of the trajectory. To decide what to fill , the MGT proposes alternative motion tokens within the selected repair region, which are first screened by a geometric score and then verified through exact trajectory evaluation before an improving edit is finalised.
This targeted, coarse-to-exact search avoids unguided perturbations and exhaustive codebook scans; instead, a small number of targeted discrete replacements induce large, coordinated changes in motion structure, enabling exploration of alternative routes beyond the current planning basin.

We validate MGMP on diverse tasks and environments, showing that it generalizes across unseen layouts, additional obstacles and unseen geometries, scales to 14-DoF dual-arm planning, and transfers to real-world Baxter tasks.
We also introduce two diagnostic benchmarks: Ring Maze , which requires substantial route changes to escape local planning basins, and Controlled Route Invalidation , which fixes the same invalidated trajectory across methods to isolate repair from initial-generation quality.
MGMP achieves 96% success on Ring Maze and 82% repair success on Controlled Route Invalidation, exceeding the strongest external baselines by 23 and 25 percentage points, respectively.

In summary, this paper makes the following three contributions:

We introduce MGMP, which reframes generative motion planning by extending the learned trajectory prior beyond efficient parallel generation to test-time structural repair.

We propose Geometry-Guided Token Search (GGTS) , which turns test-time refinement into an efficient, targeted search over discrete motion alternatives, using scene geometry to determine where to edit and which candidates to evaluate, enabling structural repair when local continuous refinement is insufficient.

We introduce Ring Maze and Controlled Route Invalidation to evaluate basin escape and isolate structural repair from initial-generation quality, and validate MGMP across unseen obstacle layouts, additional obstacles, unseen geometries, and real-world Baxter tasks.

1. We introduce MGMP, which reframes generative motion planning by extending the learned trajectory prior beyond efficient parallel generation to test-time structural repair.

2. We propose Geometry-Guided Token Search (GGTS) , which turns test-time refinement into an efficient, targeted search over discrete motion alternatives, using scene geometry to determine where to edit and which candidates to evaluate, enabling structural repair when local continuous refinement is insufficient.

3. We introduce Ring Maze and Controlled Route Invalidation to evaluate basin escape and isolate structural repair from initial-generation quality, and validate MGMP across unseen obstacle layouts, additional obstacles, unseen geometries, and real-world Baxter tasks.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Classical planners either explore configuration space or locally refine a
trajectory. Sampling-based methods ( Kavraki et al., 1996 ; LaValle, 1998 ; Karaman and Frazzoli, 2011 ; Gammell et al., 2015 ) can discover alternative routes but often
require extensive sampling and collision checking in cluttered or
high-dimensional spaces ( Orthey et al., 2024 ; Kavraki et al., 1996 ; Hauser, 2015 ) .
Trajectory optimizers ( Ratliff et al., 2009 ; Zucker et al., 2013 ; Kalakrishnan et al., 2011 ; Schulman et al., 2013 ; Mukadam et al., 2016 ) efficiently refine collision and
smoothness objectives, but remain sensitive to initialization and local planning
basins ( Pan et al., 2014 ; Schulman et al., 2014 ) .
This motivates learning reusable structure across planning problems ( Qureshi et al., 2021 ; Fishman et al., 2023 ; Das et al., 2024 ) . Learning-based planners reduce online planning cost by learning sampling
distributions, predictors, policies, or latent representations ( Qureshi et al., 2021 ; Qureshi and Yip, 2018 ; Yu and Gao, 2021 ; Fishman et al., 2023 ; Yamada et al., 2023 ) .
Generative planners further model multimodal trajectory distributions, with
diffusion-based methods producing diverse candidates through iterative denoising ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Carvalho et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) .
Because generated trajectories may violate scene constraints, they commonly
require guidance, correction, or trajectory optimization ( Carvalho et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Seo et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) .
Such continuous refinement is effective for local correction but typically cannot move from an infeasible region of configuration space to a feasible region when this requires a substantial route change to escape a local optimum.

Discrete latent representations have been used to compress actions and
trajectories for planning and learned sampling ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Johnson et al., 2023 ) .
Masked generative models instead predict multiple discrete tokens in parallel
and iteratively revisit selected tokens over only a few refinement steps ( Chang et al., 2022 ; Chang et al., 2023 ) .
This paradigm has been applied to trajectory modeling, model-predictive control,
human motion generation, and robotic imitation learning ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Wen et al., 2025 ; Pinyoanuntapong et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2024 ; Zhuang et al., 2025 ) .
We extend masked generation to collision-constrained robot motion planning,
using learned motion tokens for efficient parallel trajectory generation.

Generated trajectories are commonly adapted to scene-specific constraints through
gradient-based guidance or trajectory optimization ( Ratliff et al., 2009 ; Kalakrishnan et al., 2011 ; Schulman et al., 2014 ; Carvalho et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) .
These methods are effective for local geometric correction, but remain sensitive to initialization when feasibility requires a global route change ( Pan et al., 2014 ; Schulman et al., 2014 ) .
Recent masked generative methods revisit selected tokens during inference, but their update decisions are designed for generic generative quality rather than scene-specific geometric constraint violations ( Peng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) .
Beyer and Karaman Beyer and Karaman (2026) instead search compressed trajectory tokens under test-time objectives, but use fixed coarse-to-fine traversal and candidate evaluation rather than a learned conditional prior to focus token proposals or geometric failure signals to target repair.
MGMP instead turns the learned trajectory prior itself into a geometry-guided, targeted search space for efficient structural repair over prior-supported route alternatives.

2026-10-09.title: TacHair: Tactile Contact-Distribution Guided Online Correction for Robotic Hair Stroking and Perception
2026-10-09.authors: Ruiyi Hu , Yongqiang Zhao , Daniel Bak , Yupeng Wang , Xuyang Zhang , Shan Luo
2026-10-09.abstract: Hair stroking is common in daily grooming and personal care, and is also widely used in hair-product evaluation, motivating robots with similar physical interaction capabilities. Existing robotic hair-care and surface-following methods mainly rely on trajectory planning, compliance, force regulation, or tactile-conditioned policies, but deformable hair can remain in contact while gradually drifting across the end-effector, making local interaction difficult to regulate. We propose TacHair, a tactile contact-distribution guided online correction framework that represents high-resolution tactile observations as a spatial hair-contact distribution. A visuotactile imitation policy generates the nominal stroking motion, while a separately trained residual module corrects local contact deviations, separating task progression from contact recovery. We evaluate TacHair in 525 real-robot trials across five head geometries and three hair conditions. A successful stroke requires both sufficient task progression and contact maintenance; our method improves success from 42.9% to 62.3% and contact maintenance from 59.4% to 88.0% over the same visuotactile policy without correction. These results demonstrate spatial tactile contact distributions as an effective feedback representation for contact-preserving interaction with deformable and visually occluded surfaces. Demos, code, and datasets are available at https://tachair.github.io .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Hair stroking is a common physical interaction in daily grooming, personal care, and interpersonal assistance. Similar stroking and combing motions are also widely used in hair-product evaluation and hair-condition assessment, where the interaction between an applicator and hair provides information about properties such as smoothness, friction, and combability [ 1 , 2 ] . As robots increasingly enter domestic, assistive, and product-development environments, it is therefore desirable for them to acquire comparable capabilities for sustained and adaptive physical interaction [ 3 , 4 ] . Unlike conventional pick-and-place manipulation, hair stroking requires the robot to continuously progress along a curved surface while maintaining an appropriate local interaction with highly deformable fibers. The difficulty lies not only in reaching the desired region, but also in regulating contact throughout the entire motion as the interaction interface evolves.

Existing robotic hair-care systems address related problems mainly through visual trajectory planning, compliant mechanisms, and force feedback. Prior work has demonstrated autonomous hair combing using hair segmentation and path planning [ 5 ] , adaptive brushing based on interaction forces [ 6 ] , compliant head-care systems for washing and massage [ 7 ] , and soft end-effectors for contact-rich tasks such as head patting and finger combing [ 8 ] . In parallel, tactile surface-following methods estimate contact pose, shear, or contour features and use them for closed-loop servoing over rigid or geometrically structured surfaces [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . These methods provide important mechanisms for maintaining physical contact, but hair stroking introduces a different interaction regime. As hair fibers deform, slide, and redistribute beneath the end-effector, contact may remain present while its spatial location gradually shifts across the tactile surface. This drift is particularly difficult to observe using an external camera because the relevant interaction occurs directly underneath the end-effector. Consequently, successful trajectory progression, force regulation, or binary contact detection alone does not necessarily indicate that the robot is maintaining a spatially well-aligned stroking interaction.

To explicitly capture this local interaction, we represent sensor–hair contact as a spatial tactile contact distribution. High-resolution tactile observations are mapped to a compact representation describing the location and extent of hair-contact evidence over the sensing surface. To the best of our knowledge, prior robotic hair-care systems have not explicitly represented this spatial contact distribution as a feedback variable for learned online correction during continuous hair stroking.
The desired interaction is defined directly in tactile image space as a central contact region, avoiding the need to reconstruct the instantaneous 3D contact geometry of deformable hair. Building on this representation, we separate the control problem into nominal stroking and contact recovery . The nominal visuotactile policy is learned from complete expert demonstrations and generates the overall crown-to-back motion under near-nominal interaction. Because substantial contact deviations and recovery behaviors are sparse in such demonstrations, we additionally collect dedicated recentering data from laterally biased contacts and train a residual module to modify the nominal action only when the observed contact distribution leaves the desired region. This decomposition allows the nominal policy to focus on task progression while the correction module specializes in local contact recovery.

We evaluate the proposed framework in 525 real-robot trials across five head geometries and three hair conditions. Task success requires both sufficient stroke progression and contact maintenance. Compared with the same visuotactile policy without online correction, our method improves task success from 42.9% to 62.3% and contact maintenance from 59.4% to 88.0%, while maintaining a comparable stroke-completion rate. Continuous contact metrics further improve in 14 of the 15 tested headform–hair combinations. These results indicate that explicit contact recovery complements tactile conditioning within the nominal policy and that spatial tactile contact distributions provide a useful intermediate representation between high-dimensional tactile sensing and reactive control for deformable, visually occluded interactions.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are:

We formulate robotic hair stroking as a deformable surface-following problem in which physical contact can persist while spatially drifting, and introduce a compact tactile contact distribution to explicitly represent the location and extent of local hair–sensor interaction.

We propose a contact-distribution guided online residual correction framework that separates nominal task progression from local contact recovery, using complete stroking demonstrations for nominal behavior and dedicated recentering demonstrations for corrective behavior.

We demonstrate through 525 real-robot trials that the proposed correction substantially improves contact-preserving task success over vision-only and visuotactile imitation-learning baselines across diverse head geometries and hair conditions.

1. We formulate robotic hair stroking as a deformable surface-following problem in which physical contact can persist while spatially drifting, and introduce a compact tactile contact distribution to explicitly represent the location and extent of local hair–sensor interaction.

2. We propose a contact-distribution guided online residual correction framework that separates nominal task progression from local contact recovery, using complete stroking demonstrations for nominal behavior and dedicated recentering demonstrations for corrective behavior.

3. We demonstrate through 525 real-robot trials that the proposed correction substantially improves contact-preserving task success over vision-only and visuotactile imitation-learning baselines across diverse head geometries and hair conditions.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Robotic Hair Interaction and Tactile Surface Following

Robotic hair interaction has been studied for personal-care tasks including
brushing, combing, detangling, and head care. Early head-care systems used
compliant mechanisms and force regulation for scalp washing and
massage [ 12 ] . Dennler et al. [ 5 ] combined visual hair segmentation with trajectory planning for autonomous
hair combing, while Hughes et al. [ 6 ] used
brushing-force feedback to adapt stroke strategies during hair detangling.
More recently, MOE-Hair [ 8 ] introduced a soft compliant
end-effector for contact-rich hair-care tasks such as head patting and finger
combing, with interaction forces estimated from visual deformation and tendon
measurements. These studies primarily address hair configuration change,
compliant physical interaction, or force-aware manipulation. In contrast,
we focus on maintaining spatially well-aligned contact throughout a continuous
stroking motion as the hair–sensor interaction evolves.

Hair stroking is also closely related to tactile surface following. Prior
work has estimated local contact pose from tactile observations for closed-loop
servoing on unknown surfaces [ 9 ] , while pose-and-shear
tactile servoing further accounts for tangential interaction and sensor
deformation [ 10 ] . More recently, VBT-MPC [ 11 ] directly regulates tactile contour features using model predictive control.
These methods demonstrate the effectiveness of tactile feedback for contact
regulation, but typically operate on rigid or geometrically structured
interfaces. Hair introduces a deformable and continuously changing interaction
layer in which contact can remain present while its spatial distribution
gradually shifts across the sensor. Our work therefore uses the spatial
distribution of tactile hair-contact evidence as an explicit feedback
representation for detecting and correcting such contact deviations online.

## II-B Visuotactile Policy Learning and Online Tactile Correction

Visuotactile policy learning has shown that tactile sensing can complement
vision in contact-rich manipulation by providing local physical information
that is difficult to infer visually. Recent approaches integrate tactile
observations into imitation or diffusion policies through multimodal feature
fusion [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , while generalist manipulation
models further incorporate tactile sensing into language-conditioned
policies [ 16 , 17 ] . These methods primarily use
tactile information as part of the observation space for action generation.

A complementary line of work uses tactile feedback for reactive action
adaptation. Reactive Diffusion Policy [ 18 ] combines a
temporally coherent diffusion policy with a high-frequency tactile-reactive
module, while VLA-Touch [ 19 ] uses a tactile-conditioned
controller to refine actions produced by a pretrained VLA (Vision-Language-Action) policy.
MimicTouch [ 20 ] similarly combines imitation learning with
residual policy adaptation. Our work follows the general principle of
separating nominal behavior generation from local reactive correction, but
focuses on a task-specific feedback representation for deformable hair
interaction. Rather than relying only on implicit tactile features, we
explicitly represent hair–sensor interaction as a spatial contact distribution
and use its deviation from a desired region to activate and condition learned

2026-10-09.title: Teaching a Robot Dog New Tricks: Diverse Quadruped Skills via Combined Reinforcement and Imitation Learning with Adversarial Task Selection
2026-10-09.authors: Lemon Foxmere , Anthony Furman , Yizheng Du , Oliver Chang , Leilani Gilpin , Steve McGuire
2026-10-09.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has enabled legged robots to perform a range of skills in single-task settings. However, applications such as farm robotics or space exploration require diverse skills such as locomotion, digging, or close-range surveying. Training an end-to-end policy to address this problem remains difficult due to challenges such as sample inefficiency and gradient conflict between tasks in multi-task learning. We propose a three-stage method that trains a single policy to perform distinct tasks such as walking, digging, and hopping, and compose them into novel behaviors such as crawling. First, multiple teacher policies are trained using RL on narrowly defined tasks. Then, two additional stages train a student policy with a multi-teacher distillation setup that uses a combined RL and Imitation Learning (IL) objective under an adversarial task selection process that focuses training on the worst-performing task. With this method, we train a student policy that performs 22 tasks using 8 teachers. Evaluations show our method preserves motion quality and tracks commands more accurately than PPO and distill-then-finetune baselines, and in some cases generalizes to new tasks without explicit training. Finally, we demonstrate real-world robustness by deploying the resulting policy on a Unitree B1 quadruped.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Reinforcement Learning (RL) has gained much popularity in the domain of legged robotics in recent years, enabling robots to perform a diverse range of challenging tasks in single-task, real-world settings [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Despite this, the use of such robots remains limited in practice; applications like farm robotics and space exploration require many diverse skills such as locomotion, digging, and close-range surveying. One approach to this problem, known as Multi-task Reinforcement Learning (MTRL), is to train a single end-to-end policy that can perform many distinct tasks on command. However, doing so remains an open challenge. RL’s sample inefficiency means that many techniques are often limited to learning only one task per policy, or tasks that have substantial shared structure [ 4 , 5 ] . Reward gaming makes training difficult and tedious, and can yield policies that do not produce desirable behaviors [ 6 ] . Finally, challenges such as gradient conflict and catastrophic forgetting hinder effective policy convergence [ 7 , 8 ] .

Imitation learning (IL) offers an alternative approach, circumventing several of RL’s core difficulties [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Reference motions from motion capture data have been successfully applied to create realistic legged locomotion [ 12 ] , and many works use synthetic demonstrations produced by “teacher” policies trained with RL to distill a student model [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] .

Given the strengths and limitations of each method, combining the two paradigms has been studied extensively [ 16 , 11 , 15 ] , with IL providing training stability and behavioral fidelity and RL enabling robust generalization to out-of-distribution (OOD) states [ 16 , 15 ] . Notably, Rudin et al. [ 15 ] adopt a Distill-then-Finetune (DtF) structure, first pre-training a strong student policy through multi-teacher distillation, then finetuning it with RL to learn new tasks and improve on existing ones. The resulting policy demonstrates robust performance in rough terrain locomotion.

Building on this DtF structure, we propose a three-stage training method for effectively learning multiple distinct tasks, performing them on command, and composing multiple tasks to form novel behaviors. Under our method, we first train multiple teacher policies to perform narrowly defined tasks using RL. These teachers are used as the imitation target in our optimization objective, and are trained to prioritize natural movements over perfect task performance. Then, in two additional stages of training, we optimize a student policy over a combined IL and RL objective. Finally, to allocate training effort across tasks of uneven difficulty, we introduce an adversarial task selection strategy that preferentially samples commands on which the student currently performs worst.

The resulting policy is capable of learning multiple distinct tasks from its teachers and composing several tasks together to create new behaviors. For example, a policy trained for body height tracking and omni-directional walking can learn to compose the two to create a crawling motion (i.e., walking at a low height). We demonstrate this capability by training a student model to perform 22 total tasks: 8 taught by the teacher policies and 14 learned by composing two teacher tasks at once. Evaluations show that policies trained under this method preserve motion quality and track commands more accurately than PPO and DtF baselines, and exhibit minimal effects of reward gaming. The policies also generalize well to tasks beyond what is trained, meaningfully composing three or more tasks despite never encountering such compositions during training. Finally, we show that these policies exhibit robustness in real-world deployment while maintaining high motion quality and command responsiveness.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

Model distillation, first introduced to compress model sizes, was later used to distill domain-specific knowledge from expert models to a single model [ 17 , 18 ] . Following Rusu et al. [ 13 ] , model distillation was popularized in the context of RL, where one or more expert models trained using RL can distill their knowledge into a single student model. However, the student often suffers from degraded performance compared to any given teacher [ 13 ] . Using multi-teacher distillation, Caluwaerts et al. [ 1 ] distilled several specialist quadruped locomotion policies into a single generalist policy and demonstrated success on their Barkour benchmark.

A parallel line of work addresses this performance gap by combining IL and RL into a joint objective. Rajeswaran et al. [ 11 ] introduced DAPG, which augments a standard RL policy gradient objective with a behavioral cloning (BC) auxiliary loss, allowing demonstrations to guide early exploration while RL drives final performance as the demonstration term decays. Lu et al. [ 16 ] extend this formulation to autonomous driving at scale by using a combined BC and soft actor-critic objective (BC-SAC), demonstrating that the BC auxiliary loss preserves naturalistic behavior while the RL objective provides robustness in OOD scenarios. Similarly, Schmitt et al. [ 19 ] add a multi-teacher distillation loss to the RL objective but reduce its weight over training. In contrast, our method retains a nonzero imitation weight throughout training so that the BC term continues to anchor motion quality. Another approach to address motion quality is Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP), which replaces style-rewards with a discriminator trained on reference motion [ 20 ] . AMP has since been successfully demonstrated in quadruped locomotion, producing natural and energy-efficient motion [ 12 ] . DAgger-style online data collection [ 21 ] , where teachers are queried under the student’s own state distribution rather than a fixed offline dataset, further addresses distributional shift during online learning by keeping demonstration data on-policy.

In the context of MTRL, problems such as gradient conflicts [ 7 ] , sample inefficiency, and catastrophic forgetting all remain obstacles that hinder effective policy optimization [ 8 ] . Methods such as PCGrad address gradient conflicts in MTRL by minimizing contradictory gradient signals through gradient projections, and have seen success in MTRL training on humanoid robots [ 7 , 14 ] . Techniques combining multi-teacher distillation with RL have since been demonstrated on quadrupedal platforms as an effective solution for tasks such as rough terrain locomotion [ 15 , 22 ] . Notably, in Rudin et al. [ 15 ] , task switching is context-driven and occurs automatically rather than through explicit command inputs, and task composition performance is highly dependent on training setups due to the student’s tendency to overwrite previously acquired behaviors. Huang et al. [ 22 ] have demonstrated that a Mixture of Experts structure (MoELoco) can be used to realize multiple behaviors under one system, as well as compose novel behaviors from multiple experts. However, this method relies on a specialized gating network with multiple expert models, and is not an end-to-end solution.

2026-10-09.title: Does Dynamic-Point Filtering Help When Texture Is Scarce? A Controlled Study of ORB-SLAM2 Front-Ends in Synthetic Indoor Scenes
2026-10-09.authors: Zekui Xue
2026-10-09.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-09.comment: submitted to IROS 2026. Open-source code and dataset available
2026-10-09.abstract: Dynamic-point filters are routinely added to feature-based visual SLAM, and several recent systems argue that removing dynamic features can leave too few static features in low-texture regions. So far, these systems have been evaluated only on texture-rich benchmark sequences. We present a controlled study that isolates this interaction. We render synthetic indoor sequences in which surface texture (four levels, quantified by FAST-corner density and image-gradient entropy) and scene dynamics (three levels) are varied factorially along identical camera trajectories, with stereo, RGB-D, ground-truth poses and dynamic masks. On this grid we compare ORB-SLAM2 without filtering, with an optical-flow and epipolar-residual filter (FLOW), and with a multi-view depth-consistency filter (GEOM), and report trajectory error, tracking completeness and surviving static features over five runs. Because the masks give per-keypoint ground truth, we also measure each filter’s dynamic-point precision and recall and its static-feature false-removal rate, so that mechanistic explanations can be tested directly. We do not propose a new filter. On 720 runs over 24 sequences, filtering helped mainly in the most dynamic cells; the benefit did not decline monotonically with texture, but at the lowest level filtering reduced tracking completeness, and ORB-SLAM2 never initialised in static L3 scenes. Contrary to our hypothesis, GEOM discarded more static keypoints than FLOW (median FRR 6.8% vs. 1.5% for RGB-D, 19.6% vs. 1.5% for stereo); its RGB-D advantage tracked dynamic-point recall and vanished in stereo mode. Data and code are available at https://github.com/felixxxue/texture-dynamics-slam .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Feature-based visual SLAM systems such as ORB-SLAM and ORB-SLAM2 [ 1 , 2 ] estimate the camera pose from keypoints that are assumed to lie on static structure. Moving people and objects violate this assumption, and a large family of dynamic-SLAM front-ends therefore removes keypoints that are judged to be dynamic before, or during, tracking. Two classical cues for this decision are optical flow with an epipolar consistency test , as in the moving-consistency check of DS-SLAM [ 3 ] , and multi-view geometry , as in the depth and parallax test of DynaSLAM [ 4 ] ; both were built on ORB-SLAM2.

Filtering has a cost that is easy to overlook in texture-rich scenes: every removed keypoint, whether truly dynamic or a false positive, is one fewer constraint for pose estimation. When the scene offers few keypoints in the first place, for example white walls, uniform floors and plain furniture, the same filter may push the tracker below the number of static features it needs. Evaluation studies have shown that sparse feature-based systems such as ORB-SLAM2 and ORB-SLAM3 are severely affected in textureless environments [ 5 ] . Three recent systems state the interaction explicitly: IL-SLAM notes that dynamic removal creates the new problem of insufficient remaining point features and adds line features when needed [ 6 ] ; SR-SLAM scores frame reliability partly by feature richness [ 7 ] ; and SFSE-SLAM observes that “removing dynamic feature points often leaves insufficient static features in low-texture regions” and compensates with a density-driven adaptive threshold [ 8 ] . However, these systems are evaluated on TUM RGB-D [ 9 ] and Bonn [ 10 ] sequences (and, for SR-SLAM, on real robot runs), none of which varies texture in a controlled way. Whether, and by how much, the benefit of dynamic-point filtering shrinks as texture becomes scarce has, to our knowledge, not been measured.

This paper measures it. We hold scene geometry, camera trajectory and the motion of dynamic agents fixed, vary surface texture and the number of moving agents factorially in simulation, and run ORB-SLAM2 with no filter, a flow-based filter and a geometry-based filter in both stereo and RGB-D modes. We do not propose a new filter ; our aim is to quantify, under controlled texture, when existing filtering principles help or hurt, and why.

Contributions.

Data. We release 24 synthetic indoor sequences in which surface texture (four levels, quantified by a reproducible texture metric) and scene dynamics (three levels) are varied factorially along identical camera trajectories, with stereo images, RGB-D, ground-truth poses and per-pixel dynamic masks (Sec. III-C ).

Interaction. Using these data, we quantify how the effect of flow-based and geometry-based dynamic-point filtering on ORB-SLAM2 changes with texture, reporting ATE, RPE, tracking completeness and surviving static features over N r = 5 N_{r}=5 runs per configuration (Sec. IV-A ).

Mechanism. Using the ground-truth masks, we measure each filter’s per-keypoint dynamic-point precision and recall and its static-feature false-removal rate, and test whether these explain the accuracy differences between filters (Sec. IV-B ); in our data they do, but not in the way we hypothesised. As an additional analysis, we compare stereo and RGB-D input, whose depth sources depend differently on texture (Sec. IV-C ).
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

Dynamic visual SLAM. DynaSLAM [ 4 ] extends ORB-SLAM2 (monocular, stereo and RGB-D) with Mask R-CNN segmentation and, for RGB-D, a multi-view geometry test that projects points from overlapping keyframes and flags them by depth discrepancy and parallax angle; it also inpaints the occluded background. DS-SLAM [ 3 ] combines ORB-SLAM2 with SegNet and a moving-consistency check that tracks features with Lucas–Kanade optical flow [ 11 ] and tests them against the epipolar constraint. Detect-SLAM [ 12 ] runs an SSD detector on keyframes and propagates moving probabilities to map points. FlowFusion [ 13 ] segments dynamic regions from PWC-Net optical flow in dense RGB-D SLAM, and ReFusion [ 10 ] detects dynamics from TSDF residuals and released the Bonn RGB-D Dynamic dataset. DynaPix SLAM [ 14 ] estimates per-pixel motion probabilities without semantics and feeds them into ORB-SLAM2’s map-point selection and bundle adjustment, evaluating on the synthetic GRADE data and on TUM RGB-D. Our Flow and Geom filters (Sec. III-B ) are generic, semantics-free instances of the DS-SLAM and DynaSLAM geometric principles; we study them as isolated factors rather than as complete systems.

Low-texture SLAM. Feature scarcity is addressed by point-and-line systems [ 15 , 16 ] , by structural and planar constraints [ 17 , 18 ] , by dedicated weak-texture pipelines such as RWT-SLAM [ 19 ] , by direct and semi-direct methods [ 20 , 21 ] , and by learned dense methods such as DROID-SLAM [ 22 ] . SID-SLAM [ 21 ] also released the DLR Minimal Texture dataset of real RGB-D sequences with motion-capture ground truth. In these works texture is typically a categorical condition (e.g., the TUM structure/texture sequences [ 9 ] , OpenLORIS corridors [ 23 ] or dedicated minimal-texture recordings) rather than a continuous, controlled variable. Evaluation studies [ 5 , 24 ] compare systems across challenge categories; Bujanca et al. [ 5 ] report texture and dynamics as separate categories, not crossed.

Feature-scarcity-aware dynamic SLAM. IL-SLAM [ 6 ] triggers line features when a feature-awareness criterion indicates that too few points remain after dynamic removal; it is evaluated on TUM sequences. SR-SLAM [ 7 ] computes a frame reliability score from detection confidence, spatial distribution, feature richness on a 3 × 3 3\times 3 grid and depth quality, and falls back to direct photometric and depth refinement when features are scarce; it is evaluated on TUM, Bonn and real robot runs. SFSE-SLAM [ 8 ] adds texture-aware compensation through a threshold driven by global feature density, evaluated on TUM and Bonn. These papers motivate our question; our study is complementary, since it does not add a mechanism but measures the underlying effect under controlled texture.

Synthetic data and benchmarks. ICL-NUIM [ 25 ] provides static synthetic indoor scenes with largely low-texture walls. TartanAir [ 26 ] provides photo-realistic sequences with stereo, depth, segmentation, optical flow and moving objects. VIODE [ 27 ] renders each of three environments at four dynamic levels that progressively add moving objects, with instance masks. GRADE [ 28 ] generates indoor dynamic scenes with animated humans in Isaac Sim, and a companion study [ 29 ] found that DynaSLAM achieved good ATE on such data while losing track for at least about 27 s, i.e. ATE alone can hide failures. The CSE dataset [ 30 ] provides static and dynamic versions of service environments with identical trajectories. Robust-SLAM [ 31 ] perturbs Replica scenes with image, depth and trajectory corruptions under an explicitly static-world assumption, and VSLAM-LAB [ 32 ] offers a unified pipeline for re-running baselines. Table I summarises which of these control texture and dynamics; in the sources we consulted we found none that varies both factorially along the same trajectory.

2026-10-09.title: VersaCamVLA: Camera-Configurable VLA Policies for Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-09.authors: Boyao Han , Chen Shi , Jingjing Qian , ZhuoTan Tian , Li Jiang
2026-10-09.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-09.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-09.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful foundations for robotic manipulation, but their reliance on fixed camera configurations during training makes them brittle to changes in camera count or pose during deployment.
To overcome these limitations, we propose VersaCamVLA , a camera-configurable framework that decouples camera-set representation from action learning.
VersaCamVLA learns a unified scene-token interface that maps an arbitrary, variable set of posed RGB views into fixed-size latent scene tokens. This is achieved via multi-signal target-view prediction and Wrist-Augmented Pose Sampling (WAPS), which leverages natural wrist-camera motion for free pose diversity. At deployment, a lightweight spatial encoder injects these compact scene tokens into a pretrained base VLA as a supplementary visual condition, requiring no explicit 3D sensing or novel-view rendering.
Experiments on RoboTwin, LIBERO, and a real-robot platform demonstrate that VersaCamVLA consistently outperforms prior VLA methods and direct multi-view baselines, maintaining robust performance across varying camera counts and unseen camera poses.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have become a powerful foundation for robotic manipulation, adapting pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to map visual observations, language instructions, and proprioception to robot actions [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] , and their semantic priors and few-shot adaptability make them attractive as general policies across diverse tasks and environments.
However, fine-grained tasks such as precise insertion, and bimanual assembly demand reliable spatial perception, which is tightly coupled to the cameras used during training: changing the number of cameras or shifting a camera’s pose alters the visual token distribution and degrades the policy.
This poses a obstacle for deployment, where camera placement is often constrained by the robot, workspace, or task, and a useful view on one platform may be unavailable or suboptimal on another, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .

Prior work has addressed camera sensitivity through several complementary directions.
One line of work improves viewpoint robustness by collecting demonstrations from multiple camera poses [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] or synthesizing novel views for training-time augmentation [ 13 ] and training-free test-time adaptation [ 14 ] .
However, multi-pose collection is costly on real robots, and synthesis-based methods depend on the fidelity of generated views.
Another line introduces geometric priors through depth, point clouds, or rendered views [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] , as well as geometric features extracted from RGB images by pretrained 3D foundation models [ 19 , 20 ] .
Finally, multi-camera policies often append visual tokens from additional cameras to the policy input [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] .
This direct multi-view formulation improves coverage, but it still binds the policy to the camera count and view layout used during action learning, and its token length grows with the number of input views.

We argue that a VLA should instead support a camera-configurable visual pathway that accepts a variable number of posed RGB views, makes no assumption on camera poses, and presents the action policy with a unified fixed-size scene representation.
To this end, we present VersaCamVLA , a camera-configurable VLA framework that decouples camera-set representation learning from action learning.
Rather than redesigning the VLA backbone or requiring explicit 3D reconstruction, VersaCamVLA learns a unified scene-token interface between raw camera observations and the policy.
This interface maps any non-empty set of posed RGB views into fixed-size scene tokens, allowing different camera configurations to be represented through the same policy-facing visual format.

VersaCamVLA is trained in two stages: unified scene-token interface learning and scene-token-conditioned VLA policy learning.
In Stage I, a scene encoder aggregates a source set of posed RGB views into latent scene tokens, and a training-only scene decoder queries these tokens with target-camera rays predict RGB, semantic, and edge signals at target views.
This multi-signal target-view objective encourages the scene tokens to preserve view-consistent spatial information while providing object-level and boundary-aware supervision beyond raw pixel reconstruction.
To expose the encoder to diverse camera configurations without collecting additional multi-pose demonstrations, we introduce Wrist-Augmented Pose Sampling (WAPS), which turns the natural motion of wrist cameras into a free source of pose diversity.
At each training frame, WAPS varies the source camera subset while asking the decoder to reconstruct all available views, producing both self-reconstruction and cross-view prediction signals for the same scene tokens.

In Stage II, VersaCamVLA discards the decoder and prediction heads, freezes the scene encoder, and integrates the learned scene tokens into a pretrained VLA policy. The base VLA keeps its native fixed-view RGB input and action-learning objective, while a lightweight spatial encoder compresses the learned scene tokens into a compact supplementary visual condition. Camera flexibility therefore enters through the auxiliary scene-token pathway: any available posed camera subset can be encoded into the same fixed-size representation, while the action expert receives a stable conditioning interface. At deployment, VersaCamVLA supports versatile camera setups and requires only RGB images with camera intrinsics and extrinsics. No novel-view rendering, depth estimation, point-cloud processing, or explicit 3D reconstruction is needed.

We evaluate VersaCamVLA on RoboTwin [ 24 ] , LIBERO [ 25 ] , and a real-robot platform with varying camera counts and poses.
Across these scenarios, VersaCamVLA consistently outperforms prior works and direct multi-view baselines.
These findings show that learning a unified scene-token interface effectively makes pretrained VLA policies more robust to practical
camera-configuration changes.
In summary, our main contributions are threefold:

We formulate camera-configurable VLA policy learning, where a policy must operate with a variable number of posed RGB views without assuming fixed camera poses, while maintaining a fixed-size visual interface for action prediction.

We propose VersaCamVLA, a two-stage framework that learns a unified scene-token interface through target-view prediction,
then injects the resulting scene tokens into a pretrained VLA as supplementary visual conditioning. Wrist-Augmented Pose Sampling is introduced to exploit wrist-camera motion as free pose diversity for scene-token learning.

We validate VersaCamVLA on simulation and real-robot manipulation benchmarks, showing consistent improvements over prior VLA methods and direct multi-view baselines under changing camera counts and unseen camera poses.

1. We formulate camera-configurable VLA policy learning, where a policy must operate with a variable number of posed RGB views without assuming fixed camera poses, while maintaining a fixed-size visual interface for action prediction.

2. We propose VersaCamVLA, a two-stage framework that learns a unified scene-token interface through target-view prediction,
then injects the resulting scene tokens into a pretrained VLA as supplementary visual conditioning. Wrist-Augmented Pose Sampling is introduced to exploit wrist-camera motion as free pose diversity for scene-token learning.

3. We validate VersaCamVLA on simulation and real-robot manipulation benchmarks, showing consistent improvements over prior VLA methods and direct multi-view baselines under changing camera counts and unseen camera poses.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision-Language-Action Models

Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 22 , 6 , 4 , 5 , 26 ] adapt pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to robot control by training on large-scale teleoperation and egocentric data, generalizing across novel scenes, objects, and instructions.
However, recent evaluations show that VLAs are sensitive to camera-configuration shifts, especially viewpoint variations [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] , mainly because their 2D RGB inputs lack explicit camera-pose awareness.
Most VLA policies further fix the number of input cameras during post-training, limiting adaptation to camera additions, removals, or pose changes.
Our work targets this underexplored camera-configuration flexibility for pretrained VLAs.

## 2.2 Viewpoint Generalization for Vision-Language-Action Policies

Recent work addresses viewpoint brittleness in visuomotor and Vision-Language-Action policies through data augmentation, test-time view synthesis, and geometry-aware representation learning.
Data augmentation broadens viewpoint coverage through multi-pose demonstrations [ 9 , 10 , 12 ] or novel-view synthesis [ 30 , 31 ] , but is limited by collection cost and synthesis fidelity.
Geometry-aware methods inject priors such as depth [ 17 , 32 ] , point clouds [ 33 , 15 , 34 ] , or view-aligned 3D features [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 35 , 36 , 37 , 16 ] , as well as geometric features extracted from RGB images by pretrained 3D foundation models [ 19 , 20 ] .
In contrast, our method learns compact scene tokens from posed RGB views, improving unseen-pose robustness without explicit 3D reconstruction at deployment or extra multi-pose demonstrations, while requiring calibrated camera intrinsics and extrinsics.

## 2.3 Multi-Camera Perception for Vision-Language-Action Policies

Multi-camera perception is a common strategy in imitation learning and robot manipulation.
Prior policies [ 21 , 22 ] concatenate image features or tokens from multiple cameras and feed them into a transformer-based action predictor.
Recent VLA-style approaches [ 38 , 22 , 23 , 39 , 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 ] adopt a similar design by appending external-view tokens to the policy input.
This direct multi-view formulation is simple and effective, and has been widely used to improve scene coverage, reduce occlusion, and enhance policy performance on fine-grained manipulation tasks.

2026-10-09.title: Learning Which Correspondences to Trust: Confidence-Weighted Event-Camera Localization in LiDAR Maps
2026-10-09.authors: Panagiotis Kiousis , Kuangyi Chen , Jun Zhang , Friedrich Fraundorfer
2026-10-09.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-09.comment: /tables. Submitted to IEEE ICRA 2027 (under review). Code: this https URL
2026-10-09.abstract:
Localizing an event camera against a pre-built LiDAR map can be cast as dense optical-flow estimation
between a rendered depth view and an event image, followed by a Perspective- n n -Point (PnP) solver over
the induced 3D–2D correspondences. Existing pipelines rely on geometric consensus during pose estimation, but do not explicitly model the reliability or pose informativeness, i.e., how strongly a correspondence constrains the camera pose, of individual correspondences. We show that the natural way to learn it—using the per-correspondence error to constrain the learning of confidence—suffers from a depth-dependent bias: small pixel errors reside predominantly at large depths and do not lead to high pose informativeness. Instead, in our method (CELL), we learn
a per-correspondence confidence end-to-end through the pose , using a differentiable
probabilistic PnP whose log-partition term encourages weight configurations that yield a better-constrained pose distribution. The
learned confidence is used in three ways: (i) it reweights the flow supervision in a decoupled training scheme that keeps pose gradients out of the flow/edge backbone; (ii) it drives a probabilistic
correspondence selection at test time; and (iii) together with the network’s edge-probability it weights
a final edge-matching refinement. We further design a partial-completion depth representation that
adds signal without hallucinating across large gaps. On M3ED and DSEC our full system improves over the LEAR baseline on the majority of the evaluated sequences: it reduces the median translation error by up to 26.9 % 26.9\% and the median rotation error
by up to 15.8 % 15.8\% .
2026-10-09.introduction:
Event cameras report asynchronous per-pixel brightness changes with microsecond latency and very high
dynamic range, making them attractive for visual perception in fast-motion and challenging-lighting
regimes where frame cameras struggle. A practical form of the problem is map-relative localization: given a pre-built LiDAR point-cloud map, recover the six-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) pose of an event camera in that
map. Recent methods [ 1 , 2 ] formulate the problem as cross-modal optical-flow
estimation between a rendered depth view and an event image: a sparse depth image is rendered from the
map at a guessed pose, dense flow is estimated between that depth view and an event image with a
RAFT-style recurrent network [ 3 ] , the flow is lifted to 3D–2D correspondences, and a pose
is solved with PnP [ 4 ] .

A key limitation is that, beyond rejecting geometrically inconsistent correspondences during pose estimation, the baseline does not explicitly model correspondence reliability or how strongly each correspondence constrains the pose. Structured errors can remain mutually consistent and may survive RANSAC [ 5 ] -based consensus filtering, while geometrically consistent correspondences can still differ substantially in their usefulness for pose estimation.

A natural strategy is to supervise the correspondence confidence using per-correspondence error [ 6 ] and retain only high-confidence correspondences at inference. However, image-space error is not necessarily well aligned with pose estimation in our setting. Because pixel-space residuals are depth-dependent, distant correspondences can exhibit small flow errors while providing weak constraints on camera translation. As a result, flow-error-supervised confidence can favor correspondences that appear accurate in image space but are not necessarily the most informative for pose estimation, as we show in Sec. V-C . We therefore learn the confidence directly through the pose using differentiable probabilistic PnP [ 7 ] . Instead of matching confidence to an image-space error target, the probabilistic pose objective optimizes the correspondence weights according to how well they constrain the pose distribution. The resulting confidence is therefore learned with respect to the pose-estimation objective rather than using flow error as a proxy for correspondence quality.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a pose-supervised correspondence confidence learned through differentiable
probabilistic PnP, together with a decoupled training strategy that uses the learned confidence
to reweight flow supervision without propagating pose gradients into the backbone.

We use the learned confidence for probabilistic correspondence selection and
confidence-weighted edge-matching refinement, and introduce partial depth completion to increase useful
correspondences while preserving geometric boundaries.

Experiments on M3ED and DSEC demonstrate improvements over the LEAR baseline on the
majority of the evaluated sequences, with gains in translation, rotation, and localization
accuracy.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

Event-based localization. Existing event-based localization methods can be broadly grouped into place recognition, direct pose regression, and map-based localization. Place-recognition approaches retrieve the closest entry from a reference database using event representations such as reconstructed images [ 8 ] , edge maps [ 9 ] , sparse informative pixels [ 10 ] , or learned descriptors [ 11 ] . These methods provide coarse localization but do not directly recover a metric 6-DoF pose. Pose-regression methods instead predict the camera pose directly from event data [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] , but typically encode scene-specific information in the learned model, which can limit generalization to unseen environments. Map-based approaches estimate the pose with respect to an explicit 3D representation, either geometrically by aligning events with semi-dense maps [ 16 , 17 ] , or photometrically by matching events against appearance predicted from photometric maps [ 18 , 19 ] or Gaussian-splatting representations [ 20 ] . LiDAR maps, in contrast, provide dense metric geometry unaffected by illumination, motivating event-camera localization directly against LiDAR maps.

Event-to-LiDAR localization. Cross-modal event–LiDAR matching is comparatively underexplored. Early efforts target
extrinsic calibration—marker-based [ 21 ] or target-free from edge
correspondences [ 22 ] —but under controlled conditions that limit scalability, while
E2PNet [ 23 ] learns an image-like event representation for point-cloud registration but
reports only coarse accuracy. Closest to this work, EVLoc [ 1 ] casts localization as
dense event–depth flow estimation with a RAFT-style network [ 3 ] and lifts the flow to
3D–2D correspondences for a PnP solver; LEAR [ 2 ] augments this with a jointly-trained
depth-edge detector and cross-task fusion, making the rendered depth more “event-like” and improving robustness. We build directly on LEAR. Its final pose estimation already uses PnP with RANSAC to reject geometrically inconsistent correspondences, but correspondence quality is not explicitly learned before the geometric estimation. In particular, RANSAC inlier rejection does not distinguish between correspondences that are geometrically consistent yet differ substantially in how strongly they constrain the camera pose. Our work therefore complements, rather than replaces, geometric consensus by learning a pose-supervised correspondence confidence.

Confidence-based correspondence learning. Down-weighting unreliable correspondences before a geometric solve is well studied outside the event
domain. NG-RANSAC learns sampling weights for RANSAC [ 24 ] ; DROID-SLAM predicts
per-pixel confidence weights consumed by a differentiable bundle adjustment [ 25 ] ; and
EPro-PnP makes PnP itself differentiable through a probabilistic formulation, learning 2D–3D
correspondence weights end-to-end via a pose loss [ 7 ] . A related strategy uses reprojection error as a supervision or guidance signal; for example, EGFS [ 6 ] uses low-error regions to guide scene-coordinate regression. We observe a limitation of using image-space correspondence error as the supervision signal for confidence learning: pixel-space error is inherently depth-dependent, so low-error correspondences can be biased toward distant, low-parallax points whose small image-space residuals do not necessarily imply strong pose constraints, particularly for translation. We therefore learn confidence directly through a probabilistic pose objective rather than using correspondence error alone as the confidence supervision target.

2026-10-09.title: Digital Twin for Pre-Deployment Validation of AI-Driven Safety-Critical Industrial Edge Control Loops
2026-10-09.authors: Sara Cavallero , Federico Tonini , Tony Chahoud , Giampaolo Cuozzo , Davide Borsatti , Walter Cerroni , Maurizio Fodrini , Riccardo Marini
2026-10-09.abstract: Industrial environments are increasingly characterized by the tight interaction among physical processes, communication infrastructures, and intelligent applications. In this context, Digital Twins (DTs) have emerged as a key technology for system analysis and optimization. However, existing DT solutions typically focus either on industrial processes or communication networks, while lacking an integrated and application-aware perspective. To fill this gap, this paper proposes a modular DT framework for industrial environments that jointly models physical processes, wireless communications, and application logic within a unified architecture. The feasibility of the proposed framework is experimentally validated through a real-world Proof-of-Concept (PoC) implemented in the BI-REX pilot line, involving a 5G-connected Autonomous Mobile Robot (AMR) transporting hazardous liquids and remotely controlled by an AI-driven application. The proposed DT is used to reproduce the behaviour of the real deployment and to investigate the impact of different placements of the AI application, including on-premise, edge, and remote cloud execution scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate a close agreement between DT predictions and PoC measurements in terms of both network-level metrics, such as Reference Signal Received Power (RSRP) and latency, and end-to-end application metrics, including application-level Round-Trip-Time (RTT). Moreover, the analysis shows how inaccuracies of network modeling can critically affect the feasibility of latency-sensitive industrial control loops, highlighting the potential of integrated DTs as tools for the pre-deployment design and validation of next-generation industrial systems.
2026-10-09.introduction:
Modern industrial scenarios are evolving toward highly interconnected cyber-physical environments characterized by a continuous exchange of heterogeneous data streams [ 1 ] . This phenomenon is enhancing efficiency at the expense of an increased complexity. Indeed, industrial plants typically comprise a large number of heterogeneous devices, including sensors, actuators, programmable logic controllers, industrial robots, autonomous guided vehicles, edge computing nodes, and cloud-based services [ 2 ] . These elements generate data with different temporal granularities, reliability levels, semantic meanings and application requirements. Additionally, industrial processes are intrinsically related, meaning that disturbances occurring in one subsystem can propagate and affect production performance, operational safety, and communication efficiency across the entire facility. Relying on wireless networks for such interconnections is becoming a reality due to their flexibility and scalability, but this further requires careful design, as their performance is influenced by dynamic factors such as interference, mobility, environmental changes, and traffic fluctuations [ 3 ] .

This trend poses significant challenges for system design, optimization, and validation. Experimental evaluations conducted directly on operational industrial infrastructures are often costly, time-consuming, and potentially disruptive to production activities. Furthermore, the large number of interacting parameters makes exhaustive testing under all possible operating conditions practically infeasible.

In this context, Digital Twins (DTs) have emerged as a key enabling technology for the analysis and management of next-generation industrial systems [ 4 , 5 ] . A DT provides a virtual representation of the physical environment capable of observing, monitoring, and optimizing complex industrial processes while reducing the need for extensive experimentation on the actual plant [ 6 ] .

However, most existing DT solutions either focus on the process/asset side (e.g., monitoring, predictive maintenance, plant simulation) or on the network/infrastructure side (e.g., performance analysis and optimization, also known as Network Digital Twin (NDT) [ 7 , 8 ] ), and rarely provide an integrated, application-aware mechanism to jointly model application dynamics (data acquisition, processing, decision, actuation) together with network behavior in a unified, modular architecture. Such an integrated perspective is particularly important for industrial applications relying on closed-loop control mechanisms, whose performance simultaneously depends on physical processes, communication latency, data quality, and application decisions.

To address this gap, this paper proposes and experimentally validates a modular DT framework for industrial environments that jointly models industrial processes, wireless communications, and application-level intelligence. The proposed framework combines a Process DT , responsible for reproducing the industrial environment and the kinematic behaviour of mobile assets, a Network DT , which captures radio propagation and network-level performance, and a Decision Module capable of reproducing the logic and decision-making processes executed by industrial applications.

The proposed framework is validated through a real-world industrial Proof-of-Concept (PoC) implemented within the BI-REX pilot line, one of the eight Italian Competence Center for Industry 4.0 1 1 1 For more information, visit https://bi-rex.it/en/. . The considered use case involves an Autonomous Mobile Robot (AMR) connected through an OpenAirInterface (OAI) -based 5th generation (5G) Non-Public Network (NPN) and transporting hazardous liquids. A remote Artificial Intelligence (AI) -based application logic continuously analyzes telemetry information and predicts future robot movements that may lead to liquid spilling due to abrupt accelerations or braking manoeuvres. Upon detecting a potentially dangerous condition, the application proactively sends a command to the robot to close an onboard clamp and prevent the liquid from being spilled. This use case represents a representative example of an industrial closed-loop control system in which the performance of the overall application critically depends on the interplay between physical processes, communication networks, and application-level intelligence [ 9 ] .

The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

We propose a modular industrial DT architecture for industrial environments that jointly models industrial processes, wireless network behaviour, and application logic within a unified framework;

We propose a modular industrial DT architecture for industrial environments that jointly models industrial processes, wireless network behaviour, and application logic within a unified framework;

We implement the proposed architecture for a real-world industrial use case involving a 5G -connected AMR , remote AI -based decision making, and proactive safety actions aimed at preventing hazardous liquid spills;

We experimentally validate the proposed framework by comparing synthetic predictions generated by the proposed DT with measurements collected in the real industrial deployment, considering both end-to-end application metrics, such as Round Trip Time (RTT) , and network-level metrics, including Reference Signal Received Power (RSRP) and communication latency.

We leverage the proposed DT to perform a deployment study of the AI-driven application logic of the PoC , providing quantitative guidelines for the placement of latency-sensitive industrial applications as a function of the accuracy of the network and application modeling.

To the best of our knowledge, this is one of the first works providing an experimentally validated industrial DT framework capable of jointly modeling physical processes, communication networks, and application intelligence while demonstrating its effectiveness through a real-world industrial deployment.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the related literature on industrial DTs . Section III presents the proposed DT framework for industrial environments. Section IV introduces the considered industrial case-study relative to the industrial PoC developed within the BI-REX pilot line. Section V describes the implementation of the proposed DT for the considered industrial case-study. Section VI defines the performance metrics adopted for the DT validation. Section VII discusses the experimental results obtained by comparing synthetic and real-world measurements. Finally, Section VIII concludes the paper and outlines future research directions.

1. We propose a modular industrial DT architecture for industrial environments that jointly models industrial processes, wireless network behaviour, and application logic within a unified framework;

2. We implement the proposed architecture for a real-world industrial use case involving a 5G -connected AMR , remote AI -based decision making, and proactive safety actions aimed at preventing hazardous liquid spills;

3. We experimentally validate the proposed framework by comparing synthetic predictions generated by the proposed DT with measurements collected in the real industrial deployment, considering both end-to-end application metrics, such as Round Trip Time (RTT) , and network-level metrics, including Reference Signal Received Power (RSRP) and communication latency.

4. We leverage the proposed DT to perform a deployment study of the AI-driven application logic of the PoC , providing quantitative guidelines for the placement of latency-sensitive industrial applications as a function of the accuracy of the network and application modeling.
2026-10-09.related_work:
# II Related Work

Recent literature highlights how DTs are revolutionizing industry, enabling the digital representation of assets, processes, and networks to optimize operations, predictive maintenance, and resource management [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Process DTs are widely adopted for asset monitoring and predictive maintenance, using real-time data from industrial sensors and data-driven models, to simulate, analyze, and optimize the behavior of industrial assets and plants in domains such as industry and manufacturing [ 14 , 10 , 15 , 16 ] . In parallel, NDTs and DT -centric architectures for critical infrastructures and logistics replicate sensors, actuators, and communication technologies to support real-time monitoring, diagnosis, and optimization of networked systems, but often remain focused on maintenance and operations rather than application-layer control [ 17 , 12 ] . Standardization and reference architectures for industrial DTs are actively discussed, with surveys and domain reviews highlighting the need for interoperable service‐oriented DT stacks and robust communication, computing and security support in industrial domains [ 11 , 12 ] . However, a significant gap remains in the integration between process DTs and NDTs for the closed-loop optimization of complex industrial systems. Most existing works either focus on process-related aspects (e.g., predictive maintenance and asset optimization) or on the communication infrastructure, and typically adopt relatively monolithic DT architectures. In contrast, this paper proposes a modular DT framework that tightly integrates process, network, and application-level models within a unified closed-loop architecture. The proposed framework is built upon a fully modular Microservice-Based Architecture (MBA) , where each component of the process and network twins is explicitly decoupled, yet synchronized to jointly support application-level decision making and robotic control. This modular design allows individual components to be independently developed, deployed, updated, scaled, and reused across different industrial applications without redesigning the entire DT . Furthermore, unlike most existing studies, the proposed framework is not only presented from an architectural perspective but is also experimentally validated through a real-world industrial PoC , demonstrating its capability to accurately reproduce both network- and application-level behaviors under realistic operating conditions.

2026-10-09.title: Autonomous thermodynamic cycles via robotic mobility and sensing
2026-10-09.authors: Sofia Kuperman , Ezra Ben-Abu , Yaron Veksler , Anna Zigelman , Sefi Givli , Amir D. Gat
2026-10-09.subjects: Soft Condensed Matter (cond-mat.soft) ; Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Applied Physics (physics.app-ph)
2026-10-09.abstract: Thermodynamic cycles are the foundation of energy conversion across natural and engineered systems, transforming heat into useful work. However, these cycles traditionally operate between fixed thermal reservoirs, restricting them to specific locations and temperature differences. Here, we introduce autonomous thermodynamic cycles enabled by robotic mobility and sensing, allowing robots to perform thermodynamic cycles by accessing spatially varying temperature fields. We experimentally realize this concept using multistable gas-filled capsules that circulate within the system across a thermal gradient. Our model reveals that rapid transitions in the capsules’ energy states allow the system to operate as a mobile heat engine that harvests and stores energy. By linking the capsule-scale internal energy dynamics to the robot’s large-scale navigation strategy, we optimize locomotion paths that balance motion cost and energy harvesting. These findings demonstrate that thermodynamic cycles can emerge when autonomous systems navigate their environments, offering an artificial analog of organisms that forage for energy across spatial resources.
