2026-10-12.title: Noise Space Learning for VLA Adaptation
2026-10-12.authors: Junjie Lu , Chuheng Zhang , Yucen Wang , Yuhua Jiang , Xinyao Qin , Min Xu , Li Zhao
2026-10-12.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-12.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly combine pretrained visual-language representations with continuous action generation. Early VLAs such as RT-2 [ 3 ] predict discretized actions as tokens. Octo [ 20 ] subsequently combines a generalist robot transformer with a diffusion action head to model continuous, multimodal behavior. More recent VLAs, including π 0 \pi_{0} [ 2 ] and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 23 ] , use flow matching to transform standard Gaussian noise into action chunks, with the flow generator conditioned on visual observations and language. This progression has made flow matching an increasingly prominent approach to continuous action generation. The broad manipulation priors of flow-matching-based VLAs provide a starting point for deployment, but precise alignment, contact handling, and dynamic manipulation still require adaptation to the target task.

The central challenge in VLA adaptation is to acquire task-specific behavior efficiently while preserving useful pretrained priors. Full-parameter updates to a large VLA are costly and can disturb these priors when training is limited to narrow task experience. For example, low-data supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can leave a policy fixated on training objects or spatial targets, even when a new instruction specifies a different target [ 12 ] . A parameter-efficient alternative is low-rank adaptation (LoRA), which keeps the VLA backbone fixed and trains low-rank adapters. This approach can better preserve VLM-derived visual-semantic recognition than full-parameter fine-tuning [ 35 ] , and retain earlier skills with substantially less forgetting in continual VLA adaptation [ 11 ] . These observations motivate efficient adaptation that freezes the VLA backbone and learns a small task-specific module.

Keeping the VLA backbone fixed can help preserve pretrained priors and improve adaptation efficiency, but does not by itself ensure effectiveness. Different ways of adapting a fixed backbone face different limitations. Adapting only the action head can underfit task execution despite better preservation of visual-semantic knowledge [ 35 ] . Inference-time candidate selection can improve task success, but seeking better actions through a broader search requires generating and scoring more candidates, increasing inference cost [ 34 ] . Residual adaptation learns action corrections, but keeping these corrections close to the base policy for stable learning can limit the behavioral changes it can achieve [ 1 ] . These trade-offs motivate a central question:

How can we adapt a VLA effectively and efficiently while preserving its priors?

To address this question, we study noise space learning (NSL) for flow-matching-based VLAs. NSL trains a lightweight noise actor to produce a context-conditioned distribution over the noise that initializes action generation while keeping the VLA backbone fixed. This formulation builds on learning a conditional noise actor in DSRL [ 33 ] and noise supervision obtained by inverting corrective actions in UniSteer [ 18 ] and FlowDAgger [ 19 ] . NSL targets effective adaptation by favoring useful behaviors already represented by the generator, supports efficient learning through lightweight actor updates, and preserves the pretrained noise-to-action mapping. The practical challenge is how to optimize the noise actor to realize these benefits. We develop NSL variants based on three reinforcement learning paradigms: on-policy policy optimization with PPO [ 27 ] , off-policy actor–critic learning with SAC [ 9 ] , and advantage-weighted regression (AWR) [ 22 ] that uses supervised learning as subroutines.
We study how these variants are impacted by different implementation techniques such as noise limit, task balancing, and success/failure balancing.
Based on these results, we conclude which algorithms are effective and which implementation choices yield strong performance, aiming to establish best practices for NSL under different resource and deployment constraints.

We evaluate NSL on two simulation benchmarks, LIBERO [ 17 ] and RoboTwin [ 5 ] , and four real-robot manipulation tasks, cup stacking, toy fishing, sequential insertion, and bead placement, under the following constraints: The interaction constraint refers to the sample budget for adaptation, which differs between simulation and real-robot experiments and influences algorithm choice. The computation constraint refers to the computational effort allowed in adaptation and may limit the performance. The execution constraint concerns the safety of learned behavior on physical robots. We observe that noise distributions far from standard Gaussian can be tolerated in simulation but are associated with unsafe motions and safety interventions, such as emergency stops, on real robots.

Our contributions are threefold.
First, we formulate NSL as a VLA adaptation interface that maximizes success rate through a context-conditioned noise actor that steers action generation while keeping the VLA backbone fixed. Second, we analyze NSL’s adaptation efficiency through an information-theoretic comparison with generator adaptation and residual adaptation. Third, we develop NSL variants based on PPO, SAC, and AWR through implementation refinements, and evaluate them on simulation and real robots.
Our experiments show that NSL-SAC performs well in simulation with ample interaction budgets and requires more computation. However, its noise distribution can deviate from standard Gaussian, with associated unsafe motions and emergency-stop interventions on real robots.
In contrast, NSL-AWR is better suited to interaction-limited real-robot adaptation, combining lower computational cost with safer execution.
NSL-PPO also achieves competitive performance in simulation, benefiting from more rollouts while showing limited average gains from additional updates.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Supervised and parameter-efficient methods update the effective action generator through either full-model fine-tuning or parameter-efficient updates to a limited set of weights [ 14 , 15 , 10 , 13 ] . Reinforcement-learning methods instead optimize generative policies using denoising or flow-transition likelihoods, critic-derived targets, or policy gradients [ 24 , 36 , 4 , 28 ] . These approaches can expand or reshape the behaviors produced by the VLA, with retention and computational cost depending on the update recipe. In continual VLA adaptation, full-parameter RL can cause substantial forgetting of earlier skills, while LoRA-based updates can improve retention [ 11 ] . Residual methods such as ResFiT [ 1 ] leave the base policy intact and correct its output, whereas hybrid methods such as EXPO-FT [ 7 ] combine generator fitting with action editing and selection. Inference-time methods instead alter integration or select among generated candidates [ 26 , 34 , 8 ] .
While prior designs aim to balance effectiveness, prior preservation, adaptation and inference efficiency, we argue that NSL provides a better option for this balance.

DSRL [ 33 ] uses a conditional noise actor for frozen diffusion policies and adopts an actor-critic variant.
UniSteer [ 18 ] , FlowDAgger [ 19 ] , and Flow Reversal Steering [ 31 ] use approximate inversion to convert action-level corrections into noise supervision. These methods share a noise-space interface and differ in feedback requirements and critic construction. Golden Ticket [ 21 ] improves generative robot policies by searching for a single, context-independent noise vector. LP-DS [ 30 ] learns constrained noise perturbations for continuous control and robotic manipulation. LeaP [ 6 ] jointly learns a noise prior and generator for robotic imitation learning. Together, these studies establish noise-distribution design as a promising direction for improving generative robot policies.
We build NSL upon these precedents and formulate it into a unified interface for adapting flow-matching-based VLAs.

2026-10-12.title: Chronos Policy: Learning Robot Policies on Physical Time
2026-10-12.authors: Changhao Wang , Jaden Clark , Shuran Song
2026-10-12.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-12.abstract: Robot policies often convert sensing and control into fixed-rate observation--action sequences, leaving physical time implicit in sequence position. This assumption breaks when observation rates or delays vary, or when inference latency changes. We introduce Chronos Policy 1 1 1 “Chronos” is the Greek word for time, reflecting that the policy reasons directly over physical time. , which makes physical time explicit by conditioning on observation capture times and desired action execution times. We study two ways to incorporate time into a diffusion transformer: adding timestamp embeddings to token features, or encoding physical time in positional encoding through time-aware rotary positional encodings (time-aware RoPE). We find that time-aware RoPE is more robust, allowing attention to depend directly on physical time while keeping token content unchanged. During training, we temporally randomize which observations are sampled and when the action chunk begins, exposing the policy to a wider range of sensing and execution schedules that may occur during deployments. This also enables learning from asynchronous, multi-rate data without forcing all measurements onto a fixed temporal grid. Across simulation and real-world experiments, Chronos Policy improves performance on dynamic tasks, where observation-to-action timing is critical, and on multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters. On standard quasi-static tasks, it preserves nominal performance while improving robustness to changes in sensing and inference timing. Project website: https://changhaowang.github.io/chronospolicy/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Real robot systems rarely run on a fixed clock. Consider a robot grasping a moving object from a conveyor belt: the same displacement between two images can correspond to very different object velocities depending on whether the images were captured 20 ms or 200 ms apart. Likewise, the appropriate grasp depends on when the predicted action will actually be executed. Successful control therefore depends not only on what the robot observes, but also on when observations are captured and when actions execute .

More generally, robot learning systems are exposed to timing variation at every stage of sensing and control. Sensors operate at different rates and latencies, inference takes time, controllers may execute at different frequencies. Yet many imitation learning methods convert demonstrations into fixed-rate observation–action sequences, using sequence position as a proxy for physical time. This assumes a consistent relationship between sequence position and elapsed time; when that relationship changes, the policy cannot tell how much time has passed between observations or how far in the future an action will execute. Prior work has addressed specific deployment-time effects, such as latency matching ( Chi et al., 2024 ) and asynchronous action-chunk execution ( Black et al., 2026 ) . We take a different approach: instead of treating timing variation as an external mismatch to correct, we represent it explicitly as part of the policy input.

Concretely, we formulate the policy as:

A key design choice is how this timing information should enter the policy. One option is to encode timestamps and add them directly to the token embeddings, mixing what a token represents with when it occurs. We instead find it more effective to keep the token content unchanged and use physical time only as positional encoding in attention. Chronos Policy therefore replaces index-based positional encoding with time-aware rotary positional encodings (time-aware RoPE): observation tokens use their capture times t o t_{o} , while noisy action tokens use their queried execution times t a t_{a} as rotary coordinates. Attention then depends on elapsed time t i − t j t_{i}-t_{j} , directly representing observation-to-observation, observation-to-action, and action-to-action timing while remaining invariant to the choice of clock origin.

Timestamps also allow us to vary the timing of training examples. We randomly change which observations are selected and when the action chunk starts. Because the policy sees these timestamps, it can correctly interpret each sampled sequence even when its timing differs from the nominal training setup. This exposes the policy to timing variations that may occur at deployment and lets it use measurements that fixed-rate downsampling would otherwise discard.

We evaluate Chronos Policy across three types of tasks: dynamic tasks, where observation-to-action timing affects the correct control; multisensory tasks, where the relative timing between observations matters; and standard quasi-static tasks, where precise timing is less critical. Across simulation and real-robot experiments, Chronos Policy improves robustness to sensing and inference variation while preserving performance on quasi-static tasks where timing matters less.

Our contributions are threefold:

We formulate robot policy learning in physical time by conditioning on observation capture times and queried action execution times.

We introduce Chronos Policy, a diffusion transformer with time-aware RoPE that learns directly from asynchronous, multi-rate observations, without aligning them to a fixed temporal grid.

We develop benchmarks that implement realistic timing variation and show that Chronos Policy improves dynamic manipulation through better observation–action timing and multisensory manipulation through better observation–observation timing, while preserving nominal performance on standard tasks and improving robustness to deployment-time mismatch.

1. We formulate robot policy learning in physical time by conditioning on observation capture times and queried action execution times.

2. We introduce Chronos Policy, a diffusion transformer with time-aware RoPE that learns directly from asynchronous, multi-rate observations, without aligning them to a fixed temporal grid.

3. We develop benchmarks that implement realistic timing variation and show that Chronos Policy improves dynamic manipulation through better observation–action timing and multisensory manipulation through better observation–observation timing, while preserving nominal performance on standard tasks and improving robustness to deployment-time mismatch.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Multisensory observations provide feedback that enables imitation learning policies to succeed on contact-rich tasks where vision alone is insufficient ( Li et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Hou et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2026 ; Choi et al., 2026 ; Clark et al., 2026 ) .
However, heterogeneous sensors often operate at different sampling rates, motivating methods that explicitly account for these differing temporal resolutions. Reactive Diffusion Policy combines slow visual planning with fast tactile feedback using separate modules ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , while ImplicitRDP integrates both streams within a single network ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . ManipForce uses frequency-aware embeddings and cross-attention to fuse asynchronous RGB and force/torque streams ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . LAG-Fusion composes modality-specific diffusion policies at their native inference rates, rebasing delayed guidance before fusion ( He et al., 2026 ) , and FA-RDP adapts inference frequency to the manipulation phase ( Zhuo et al., 2026 ) . These approaches establish the importance of preserving high frequency feedback.

Inference delay creates a mismatch between when observations are captured, when a policy predicts an action, and when that action is executed ( Xiao et al., 2020 ; Chi et al., 2024 ) . For action-chunk policies, this also raises a consistency problem between newly predicted actions and commands already committed for execution. Prior work addresses this through consistency-based decoding ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , overlapping inference and execution with prefix inpainting ( Black et al., 2026 ) , training-time conditioning on committed actions ( Black et al., 2025 ) , masked action generation ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026a ) , or predicting the future execution-time state ( Tang et al., 2025 ) . Most closely related, Delay-Aware Diffusion Policy conditions on measured inference delay and constructs delay-compensated targets ( Liao et al., 2025 ) . Another line of work reduces inference latency by changing the diffusion process itself. Diffusion Forcing introduces independent noise levels for individual sequence positions, enabling flexible partial denoising schedules ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , while Streaming Diffusion Policy applies variable noise levels across the action horizon to generate near-term actions with fewer denoising steps and lower latency ( Høeg et al., 2024 ) . These approaches reduce the timing mismatch by making policy inference faster, while Chronos Policy makes the remaining sensing and execution timing explicit to the policy; the two directions are complementary.

In addition to observation and inference delay, prior work has also made time
an explicit variable in robot control. Locomotion policies have conditioned on
the time available to reach a target, allowing behavior to adapt to temporal
requirements ( Rudin et al., 2022 ) . More recently, manipulation policies
have been conditioned on remaining task time and a time-ratio signal, enabling
a single policy to vary its execution strategy across different temporal
regimes ( Jia and Chen, 2025 ) . Other work makes control timing itself adaptive:
CTCO selects continuous options with variable durations ( Karimi et al., 2023 ) , while TARC jointly predicts actions and their
application durations to vary control frequency online ( Sukhija et al., 2025 ) . These works use time to control the speed or duration of behavior. Chronos Policy instead represents when observations are captured and when actions are executed. This gives a more general and natural formulation that covers observation rate, sensor delay, cross-modal timing, and action execution delay within a single policy.

Explicit time representations are well established for irregular time series. mTAN learns continuous-time embeddings for attention over irregular observations ( Shukla and Marlin, 2021 ) , and ContiFormer combines continuous dynamics with transformer attention ( Chen et al., 2023 ) . RoPE introduces relative positional dependence through rotations of attention queries and keys ( Su et al., 2024 ) . Recent video models have similarly moved beyond fixed sequence indices: variable-frame-rate video models adapt positional representations to changing temporal spacing ( Zhong et al., 2026 ) , while VideoRoPE introduces adjustable temporal spacing within rotary embeddings for video ( Wei et al., 2025 ) . Most closely related, BulletTime conditions video generation on continuous world-time coordinates through time-aware rotary embeddings ( Wang et al., 2026c ) . Chronos Policy brings this continuous-time view to robot imitation learning, jointly representing the timestamps of heterogeneous observations and the requested execution times of actions.

2026-10-12.title: BT-Agent: Deploying Onboard Robot Agents with Behavior Trees and Multi-Fidelity Evaluation
2026-10-12.authors: Fabio Hübel , Adam Lilja , Yue Yin , Siming He , Claire Tomlin , Shankar Sastry , Jonas Frey , Marco Pavone
2026-10-12.abstract: Deploying language-model agents onboard mobile robots requires task reasoning and responsive execution within limited compute and memory. We propose BT-Agent, an onboard architecture combining LLM-driven task decisions with predefined behavior-tree (BT) skills. These skills enforce execution conditions and return structured failure feedback. We demonstrate fully onboard operation with a 9B model on a quadruped across five task categories. Intervention tests show that local checks stop ongoing navigation without waiting for another model decision, while the agent remains active to retry or report constraints. To compare agent designs efficiently, we introduce a 161-task multi-fidelity benchmark, evaluated in text on all tasks and in Habitat on 39. Text supports 10.9× higher evaluation throughput, while simulation reveals how perception and motion failures change task outcomes. BT-Agent’s largest success gains over the strongest Act/ReAct baseline occur at 4B and 9B: approximately 10 and 5 percentage points. Ablations identify structured tool calls and informative failure feedback as the most useful components.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Mobile robots increasingly receive high-level goals that require sequences of physical actions.
During search, inspection, and manipulation, they need to track partial
information and adapt when an action fails [ 1 ] . For
operation independent of remote compute, this reasoning must run onboard,
sharing finite memory and compute with perception and control. Deploying an
agent on an embedded platform therefore involves both task-level decision
making and responsive physical execution.

Language-model robot agents interleave task-level reasoning with action through
skill selection, execution feedback, and programs over robot APIs [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . These
methods primarily address what the agent should do next. There is, however, no
shared interface across these approaches for how selected robot skills expose
execution state, enforce conditions, and support interruption. Behavior trees
(BTs) provide a modular, robotics-native basis for such an
interface [ 6 ] .

To this end, we propose BT-Agent, a deployment-oriented architecture that
separates task-level model reasoning from reactive robot execution through
predefined BT skills (Fig. ). An onboard Actor selects
skills and arguments using the task, state, and previous observations. A
supervisor BT starts each skill and returns structured feedback, forming a
reasoning-and-acting (ReAct) loop [ 7 ] . Within each skill, guards
recheck conditions on every tick and can interrupt a running action without
another model decision. The Actor cannot modify skill implementations or
guards, so their logic can be reviewed and tested independently of the
task-level policy. This combines established BT execution mechanisms with
flexible, feedback-driven task reasoning: the model adapts its decisions,
while the BT enforces the conditions under which each skill can run.

Evaluating this architecture means checking both the agent’s decisions and
how its skills perform. We need controlled comparisons across models and
harnesses, alongside trials where perception and motion can fail. We therefore
construct a multi-fidelity benchmark with 161 text tasks derived from Habitat
and Isaac scenes, sharing task goals and skill interfaces with simulator
execution. Text trials support inexpensive
comparisons of task performance, inference cost, and responses to injected
faults such as navigation timeouts and observation failures. Paired trials on
39 primary Habitat tasks examine where perception and motion change the outcome. Robosuite
experiments [ 8 ] additionally examine task-level orchestration
in manipulation. Finally, real-robot trials demonstrate fully onboard task
completion with a 9B model, while intervention tests validate the architecture’s
reactive skill execution.

In summary, our contributions are:

An agentic robot architecture, BT-Agent, for onboard deployment, combining
model-driven task decisions with predefined BT skills, reactive execution
checks, and structured feedback.

A multi-fidelity evaluation methodology connecting a 161-task
text benchmark, simulation-informed fault injection, and physical execution
through shared task goals and skill contracts.

An empirical evaluation across model sizes and execution
backends, characterizing task success and inference cost, demonstrating
fully onboard deployment with a 9B model, and achieving
10.9 × \times higher evaluation throughput in text than in Habitat at eight
concurrent workers.

We will release the BT-Agent implementation and benchmark code under the
Apache-2.0 license.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

Behavior trees for robot execution. Behavior trees (BTs) organize robot behavior into modular, reactive control
structures [ 6 ] . PA-BT combines
planning and acting by expanding trees during execution [ 9 ] . VLM-BT generates trees with visual condition
nodes [ 10 ] , while BTGenBot-2 uses a small model to generate
and repair executable trees [ 11 ] . Ahmad et al. combine
VLM failure analysis with reactive BT planning [ 12 ] .
Contract-grounded synthesis validates generated trees against robot-reported
skills and permitted operators before execution [ 13 ] . Our onboard agent selects fixed BT skills with local checks and
interruption support (Table I ).

Agentic systems and onboard deployment. Language-model robot systems select skills or compose programs using task and
execution feedback [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] .
Thea combines callable robot tools with scene context and action evaluation [ 14 ] ; RoboHarness uses execution memory to coordinate
heterogeneous policies [ 15 ] . ROSClaw provides
model-independent ROS integration with pre-execution action validation [ 16 ] . These agent-planning studies do not report evaluation of their
task-level decision model under robot-borne compute limits; Thea identifies onboard inference
as future work [ 14 ] . Explicit onboard deployments are still
limited among the systems reviewed here. PRISM runs distilled planners onboard
ground and aerial robots [ 17 ] , while Kwon et al.
demonstrate on-device VLM interaction on a quadruped [ 18 ] .

Multi-fidelity robot evaluation. BEHAVIOR-1K supports realistic physical evaluation of everyday activities [ 19 ] , while Embodied Agent Interface uses symbolic
representations of BEHAVIOR and VirtualHome tasks to study embodied decision
making [ 20 ] . ALFWorld connects text interaction with visually
grounded execution [ 21 ] . Building on these precedents, we align task goals and skill interfaces
across text and simulation while retaining backend-specific perception,
dynamics, and control.

2026-10-12.title: HorizonNav: Geometry-Guided Video Diffusion for Anticipatory 3D Robot Navigation
2026-10-12.authors: Hajira Amjad , Valerii Serpiva , Viacheslav Liubimov , Didar Seyidov , Dzmitry Tsetserukou
2026-10-12.abstract:
We present HorizonNav, a video diffusion-based framework for anticipatory robot navigation that transforms a single RGB image and a text prompt into a geometrically aligned representation of plausible surrounding 3D space. Given the initial observation and a textual description of the reconstruction objective, a vision-language model, guided by designed instructions, interprets the scene and constructs structured prompts for a video diffusion model. The resulting video sequence provides plausible future observations of the environment, which are subsequently processed using monocular ORB-SLAM3 for camera pose estimation and Video Depth Anything for dense depth prediction. Our central contribution is a geometry-guided depth alignment stage that combines the estimated camera poses with triangulated visual landmarks to constrain dense depth predictions across multiple views. This alignment improves the geometric consistency of the reconstructed 3D environment, addressing inconsistencies that temporal coherence of the generated video alone cannot resolve. The experimental evaluation of navigation in imagined 3D environment shows that across a 19-scene horizon study, planning-feasible scenes increase from 13/19 at P20 to 15/19 at P81, while successful RRT trials increase from 62/90 to 75/90. In a separate corridor study, 6 of 25 evaluable generated-camera trajectories violate the reconstructed collision constraints; RRT planner recovers feasible alternatives in 5 of those 6 cases. A larger archive contains 58 usable reconstructions from 67 attempted cases, of which 36 support a downstream plan and 22 do not, exposing reconstruction and free-space failure modes rather than hiding them without lidar
Across 15 corridor reconstructions, the mean reconstruction error is approximately 0.30 m at matched structural landmarks.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Autonomous navigation in unfamiliar environments requires robots to act before their surroundings are fully explored. Visual simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) reconstructs observed scene structure, while regions outside the current field of view remain unknown. A robot that can form plausible spatial hypotheses before motion may be able to evaluate candidate routes earlier, but such hypotheses are useful only if their geometry is treated cautiously rather than as ground truth.

Recent generative world models use predicted observations for navigation and action reasoning. Navigation World Models [ 1 ] predict action-conditioned observations, while ImagiNav [ 2 ] combines language-guided video generation with trajectory extraction. WonderWorld [ 3 ] , WorldExplorer [ 4 ] , and GEN3C [ 5 ] further demonstrate that generative models can expose spatial structure beyond a single image. However, a generated trajectory need not be safe to execute, and generated views may contain deformations or inconsistent occlusions that alter free-space connectivity.

Dense depth estimation provides per-pixel depth information for generated observations, but it does not by itself enforce a geometrically aligned 3D reconstruction across views. Video Depth Anything [6] produces temporally coherent depth maps and explicitly achieves this without introducing geometric priors or video generation priors. However, temporal consistency alone does not necessarily guarantee accurate multi-view geometry. In contrast, methods such as VGGT [7] and Depth Anything 3 [8] explicitly target multi-view geometric estimation, while World Reconstruction From Inconsistent Views [9] addresses contradictions between generated observations through non-rigid alignment. These developments motivate combining exploratory video generation with explicit geometric constraints to transform temporally consistent depth predictions into spatial representations that are more geometrically coherent and useful for robot planning.

We present HorizonNav a framework that transforms a single RGB image and a language prompt into a geometrically aligned representation of plausible surrounding space. Starting from one RGB observation and a language task, a vision-language model produces structured exploration instructions and Wan 2.2 generates complementary virtual camera motion. ORB-SLAM3 [ 6 ] estimates the corresponding virtual camera poses and sparse 3D landmarks, whereas Video Depth Anything predicts dense relative depth maps for the generated frames. We align the dense depth estimates with the sparse geometric structure recovered by ORB-SLAM3, jointly resolving scale and geometric consistency across views. A measured scene reference resolves monocular scale, after which RRT [ 7 ] searches the resulting obstacle representation independently of the generated camera motion. HorizonNav combines exploration-oriented VLM prompting, sparse-landmark-guided depth alignment, and multivideo map fusion to connect generative visual exploration with explicit spatial reasoning for navigation.

This design deliberately separates three questions that are often conflated: whether generated frames contain enough repeatable visual structure for multi-view reconstruction, whether the resulting spatial hypothesis preserves free-space connectivity well enough for planning, and whether a map-feasible plan transfers to the physical robot.

# II Related Work

## II-A Generated Futures for Robot Planning

Generated video is increasingly used to reason about robot motion before execution. Navigation World Models [ 1 ] , ImagiNav [ 2 ] , and NavDreamer [ 8 ] use predicted observations to evaluate candidate behavior or derive actions and waypoints. Schrödinger’s Navigator [ 9 ] , Aerial Navigation World Model [ 10 ] , Uncertainty-Aware Navigation World Model [ 11 ] , and GVP-WM [ 12 ] extend this idea by reasoning over multiple futures, uncertainty, or learned feasibility constraints.

These methods show that generated futures can be useful for navigation; in many cases, the final decision remains tied to the generated sequence or to a learned world representation. HorizonNav studies a different use of generated video. The generated video serves as a form of visual imagination, enabling the reconstruction of a plausible 3D representation of the surrounding environment, which is subsequently used for robot navigation and path planning.

## II-B Geometric Reconstruction from Generated Observations

Several recent systems connect generative models with explicit 3D structure. Dream-SLAM [ 13 ] introduces dreamed observations into an active SLAM loop, while WorldMAP [ 14 ] converts generated futures into persistent spatial representations. WonderWorld [ 3 ] and WorldExplorer [ 4 ] build explorable 3D environments from generated content. Voyager [ 15 ] , Sora3R [ 16 ] , Geometry Forcing [ 17 ] , and GEN3C [ 5 ] improve geometric or camera consistency by changing the generation process itself.

Direct multi-view geometry methods provide another relevant comparison. DUSt3R [ 18 ] , MASt3R [ 19 ] , VGGT [ 20 ] , Depth Anything 3 [ 21 ] , and MASt3R-Nav [ 22 ] estimate geometry directly from visual observations. World Reconstruction From Inconsistent Views [ 23 ] specifically addresses contradictions in generated sequences through non-rigid alignment. HorizonNav instead asks whether generated views can provide enough trackable multi-view evidence for a planning-oriented spatial hypothesis without modifying the generator.

## II-C 3D Reconstruction and Navigation Planning

Single-image depth methods such as MiDaS [ 24 ] , Depth Anything V2 [ 25 ] , Depth Pro [ 26 ] , and MoGe [ 27 ] provide dense geometric cues from individual images. Video Depth Anything [ 28 ] improves temporal consistency across video frames. In HorizonNav, dense depth is not assumed to be geometrically correct merely because it is temporally smooth; we evaluate VDA separately as a densification diagnostic.

ORB-SLAM3 [ 6 ] provides the primary sparse multi-view geometry used in the reported planning experiments. RRT [ 7 ] is the downstream planner. Neither ORB-SLAM3 nor RRT is presented as an algorithmic contribution. The research question is whether generated virtual observations can supply enough geometric evidence to construct a useful pre-motion spatial hypothesis, while keeping the executed plan independent of the generator’s camera trajectory.

2026-10-12.title: Mapless, Stabilizing, and Anti-Stuck Flipper Control for Articulated Tracked Robots
2026-10-12.authors: Valentýn Číhala , Pavel Sarga , Martin Pecka , Tomáš Svoboda , Karel Zimmermann
2026-10-12.abstract:
Nearly every autonomous or semi-autonomous flipper controller assumes access
to an elevation map of the terrain under and in front of the robot. The terrain beneath the chassis is occluded in the sensors, so the map is remembered through odometry integration, whose drift corrupts it. We present Stabilizing Anti-Stuck (SAS),
a mapless controller that combines a stabilization term for body roll
and pitch with an anti-stuck term that frees the robot when it gets stuck. As input, SAS uses the IMU, the flipper joint angles, and a motion cue that only
tells whether the robot is moving. The cue is computed over a short window and never
accumulated, so SAS does not inherit the odometry-integration drift that corrupts the
map. We deploy SAS on a tracked robot with four flippers and evaluate it against manual
teleoperation and prior flipper controllers in a large comparison, both in
simulation and on a real obstacle. In simulation and on the real robot, SAS achieves traversal quality comparable to state-of-the-art
map-based controllers. On a log hidden in tall grass, invisible to the LiDAR, the best map-based controller gets stuck
while SAS traverses the hidden obstacle without a problem.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Tracked and wheeled robots cannot ascend an obstacle taller than their leading wheel. Articulated tracked robots address higher obstacles with flippers,
independently actuated sub-tracks that reshape the robot’s morphology on the fly: they
can be used to reach beyond the leading wheel to ascend what tracked and wheeled robots cannot, and to
free the robot when it gets stuck [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .

Prior flipper controllers assume an elevation map. Across the literature, semi-autonomous and autonomous flipper controllers share a
precondition: they consume an elevation map of the terrain under and in front of the
robot as their dominant
input [ 2 , 4 , 1 , 3 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] .
Fully manual teleoperation needs no map because the operator sees the terrain from a
third-person view but must drive all four flippers by hand.

On a real robot, the map is a dead-reckoning artifact. Where the estimate of that terrain drifts due to body occlusion, the commanded flipper
angles are computed for incorrect terrain. Onboard sensors
observe what is ahead, but the body occludes their view of the terrain beneath it.
Dedicated underbody sensors could measure it, but they are rarely fitted and have very
low resolution. That terrain can therefore mainly be remembered : observed earlier, accumulated into an elevation
map, and carried beneath the robot as it advances by integrating wheel or LiDAR odometry [ 9 ] . Every stage of this
pipeline is a dead-reckoning process: point-cloud deskewing warps each scan by the estimated
sensor trajectory, and elevation mapping registers successive scans through the
estimated motion [ 10 ] . On the loose, deformable,
step-like terrain where flippers are needed, odometry is least reliable: tracks slip, and
the chassis pitches and drops abruptly, saturating the IMU; therefore, inertial integration cannot
recover the estimate either [ 11 ] . Reflected, invalid LiDAR returns add obstacles that do
not exist, such as the spike behind the robot in Fig. 1 .

The hardest case is a hidden obstacle. When a rigid obstacle is hidden (Fig. 3 ), optical sensors, such as LiDAR or cameras, return the
compliant canopy above it, while the load-bearing obstacle beneath remains invisible until the
chassis stalls on it. Neither a dedicated underbody sensor, which is blinded by the same vegetation, nor foliage-penetrating radar, which is bulky and low-resolution, resolves this in practice.

Our contribution: control of the flippers without a map and without an accumulated
pose. We present Stabilizing Anti-Stuck (SAS), a reactive controller that requires no
elevation map. It has two terms: a
stabilization term that stabilizes the robot body regardless of the terrain, whether
climbing or descending an obstacle, and an anti-stuck term that frees the robot when it
gets stuck by driving the flippers down. To tell a stuck robot from a moving one, the
anti-stuck term needs a motion cue: a thresholded answer to whether the robot is
moving, which requires neither an accurate nor a metric estimate of the motion. Because the
cue is computed over a short window and is never accumulated, SAS never inherits the drift that corrupts the map.

Contributions:

We propose SAS, a mapless flipper controller that needs only a
thresholded motion cue, combining continuous roll and pitch stabilization with a reactive
anti-stuck term under a safe directional-priority blend.

We measure the degradation of the elevation map caused by body occlusion and
odometry drift by evaluating map-based baselines under both a ground-truth map and
the onboard map, in a large comparison in simulation of SAS against twelve map-based baselines and two manual baselines on a twelve-obstacle course; every controller
drives the full course ten times, with the perception stack reset at each obstacle.

We perform the large comparison in a real obstacle arena with AprilTag ground
truth: on a four-track robot, each controller drives ten times over a pallet obstacle.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Manual control

In direct teleoperation, the operator drives the flippers by hand [ 12 ] , or
switches between preset flipper modes [ 13 , 8 ] . Manual control
needs no map: the operator observes the terrain from a third-person view, closes the control
loop by hand, and also stabilizes the robot.

## II-B Reactive and geometry-based control

These controllers are the most dependent on an explicit terrain model because they compute the flipper commands either
reactively [ 12 ] or by planning. Chen et al. combine dynamic programming with a
fast geometry-based pose predictor over the elevation
point cloud [ 2 ] ; Yuan et al. plan in the flipper configuration space
from known stair geometry with motion-capture ground truth [ 1 ] ; Oehler
and von Stryk predict pose on a signed-distance field built from
LiDAR [ 4 ] ; Xu et al. solve a receding-horizon hybrid trajectory
optimization over a simplified terrain sampled from a prebuilt 3D occupancy map with
FAST-LIO2 odometry [ 3 ] ; and most recently, Zhang et al. plan the path and flipper
maneuvers with RRT* over a contact-model pose predictor, using learned semantic
segmentation of the elevation map only as a perception front-end [ 14 ] .

## II-C Imitation learning

These controllers learn from demonstrations which low-level behavior to apply. The
adaptive-traversability line [ 15 ] classifies
terrain into discrete flipper modes from an elevation map.
A learned state machine [ 8 ] switches among seven hand-crafted flipper morphologies selected from an elevation map. In addition, each
state overlays a roll -stabilization term and a stagnation-triggered anti-stuck term that lowers all four flippers to free the robot [ 8 ] .

## II-D Reinforcement learning

Pecka et al. learn a
safety-constrained policy (Constrained REPS) whose state is the body pitch and the terrain
height 20 cm 20\text{\,}\mathrm{cm} ahead of the robot, observed from an occupancy map built online from the LiDAR scans [ 16 ] . Discrete-action variants dominate the
flipper-specific literature: Pan et al. learn a dueling double-DQN over discrete
front/rear flipper increments [ 6 ] and extend it with an
intrinsic-curiosity module [ 5 ] ; both take the chassis pitch and the average
terrain heights of a few segments ahead of, below, and behind the robot. Their reward favors smooth pitch only, and getting stuck is a terminal
penalty. Mitriakov et al.
learn staircase negotiation with a policy-gradient method from step-edge geometry [ 17 ] , injecting stability through center-of-gravity and
pitch-rate reward shaping. Most recently, C-TRAC learns a contact-aware latent representation from noisy LiDAR and
drives an asymmetric-SAC policy that stabilizes both roll and pitch via a
normalized-energy-stability-margin reward [ 7 ] . We train our RL baselines in
FTR-Bench [ 18 ] , an Isaac Lab framework that benchmarks standard RL
algorithms on a flipper robot.

## II-E Attitude stabilization and mapless posture control

Flipper-based attitude stabilization has been studied before, but nearly always on top of
an elevation map: a roll-only stabilization term inside a map-based state
machine [ 8 ] , and C-TRAC stabilizing both roll and pitch from a reward computed
on the map-based simulator state [ 7 ] . Rocha et al. [ 19 ] regulate
roll, pitch, and ground clearance of an articulated tracked vehicle from the IMU and the
flipper joints.

## II-F Evaluating traversal quality

To evaluate traversal quality, multiple metrics were proposed: IMU-based smoothness
measured on the robot’s body, such as pitch swing and vertical
shock [ 2 ] , body attitude, and chassis-to-ground clearance read from the
ground-truth map [ 12 , 15 ] .

2026-10-12.title: MC-EvoBench: Auditing Experience-Driven Self-Improvement in Minecraft Agents
2026-10-12.authors: Jingwei Song , Zhisheng Chen , Bingfan Zeng , Jing Tang , Yubo Hou , Jinhao Jing , Zhengwei Xie , Linfeng Zhang
2026-10-12.abstract: A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source–target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source .
2026-10-12.introduction:
One of the central ambitions of autonomous intelligence is recursive self-improvement (RSI) ( Chen et al., 2026 ) : an agent should use experience from its own actions to become more capable over time. The goal is larger than learning one policy or storing one successful trajectory. An RSI system should turn experience into a capability, retain it, and apply it when the task, world, or required action changes. This loop is central to long-horizon autonomy: as tasks become harder, the agent must build on what it has already learned.

This view differs from evaluation settings in which training is separated from testing and improvement is summarized by a single score ( Ren et al., 2026 ) . For RSI, the important question is whether a gain remains useful after the original interaction has ended. A capability should survive a change in local conditions, help with a related goal, and combine with actions that were not part of the source task. RSI is therefore a systems problem: learning, memory, planning, and physical interaction must work together, while the resulting gain remains visible and attributable.

Embodied agents make this problem concrete and difficult. Their behavior depends on both internal state and physical state. A later success may reflect a tool left in the inventory, a changed world, a favorable location, or more source interaction rather than a reusable capability. A useful benchmark must therefore show that improvement survives a reset and appears in observable behavior.

We study this question through later behavior. A memory, skill file, or model update shows that an agent changed internally. It does not show that the agent gained a useful capability ( Li et al., 2025b ; Park et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . The evidence must link internal change to later action. It must also distinguish capability from favorable execution. To test that claim, we compare target behavior after a world reset and check both task outcomes and stage-level records.

Existing benchmarks address parts of this problem. MCU ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) evaluates diverse and combined Minecraft tasks with automatic verification. LifelongAgentBench ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , EvoAgentBench ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and PAST-Bench ( Xue et al., 2026 ) study learning across tasks, transfer, and persistent state in other settings. Embodied evaluation also needs to separate world resources from agent state, match source budgets, and record where a task chain fails ( Ni et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . Otherwise, a score difference may reflect an easier world, more source interaction, or an early failure that hides later behavior.

Minecraft makes these controls practical. Collecting resources, crafting tools, and using them create visible task dependencies. A task-state graph represents these relations, and environment evidence verifies each stage. Resetting the world and inventory removes physical carryover, while stage records show progress before a chain stops ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) .

We introduce MC-EvoBench to evaluate embodied RSI in Minecraft. Figure 1 shows its mechanism: measure progress, transfer only a declared agent artifact, and use matched controls to assess experience gains. Table 1 compares this design with representative Minecraft benchmarks ( Guss et al., 2019 ; Fan et al., 2022 ; Hill et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . MC-EvoBench provides a task catalog, verifiers, and three short probe families for wood-species crafting, wooden-tool transfer, and stone-tool transfer. The framework can study capability formation, transfer, retention, and composition. This paper focuses on forward transfer between graph-related tasks.

Our main contributions are as follows:

Embodied RSI as attributable capability change. We formalize an agent as a policy, a persistent state, and an update rule, and separate this persistent state from the world state. A gain counts as experience-driven only when it appears after the target world is reset, only a declared artifact crosses the source–target boundary, and matched unrelated and shuffled sources rule out alternative explanations.

Embodied RSI as attributable capability change. We formalize an agent as a policy, a persistent state, and an update rule, and separate this persistent state from the world state. A gain counts as experience-driven only when it appears after the target world is reset, only a declared artifact crosses the source–target boundary, and matched unrelated and shuffled sources rule out alternative explanations.

MC-EvoBench, an executable audit of experience-driven improvement. It instantiates this definition in Minecraft with a task-state graph of 80 tasks, 111 states, and 369 typed edges organized into 19 chains; stage-level verifiers with three complementary metrics, Task Success Rate (TSR), Weighted Graph Progress (WGP), and Verified Milestone Progress (VMP); and a four-condition paired protocol with matched environment-step budgets and provenance records.

Controlled evidence on embodied transfer. Controller-based agents clearly outperform planner-backed variants in direct capability. Under matched controls, the reference method shows no stable transfer gain, even though its related sources earn more verified progress and, on the longer probes, more computation, and early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks leave later capabilities unobserved. Future RSI methods must therefore first clear these execution bottlenecks, and their gains should be claimed only after a controlled audit.

Section 2 reviews related benchmarks and agents. Section 3 defines the framework and benchmark. Section 4 reports the reference results. Appendices A – G give the task, environment, protocol, and reproduction details.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Minecraft combines visual control, persistent resources, and tasks with many prerequisites. MineDojo provides a large open-world task collection and a knowledge base that supports broad embodied-agent research ( Fan et al., 2022 ) . BEDD extends MineRL ( Guss et al., 2019 ) with demonstrations and evaluation for tasks whose success can be difficult to describe with a single exact goal. MinePlanner focuses on long-horizon planning in large Minecraft worlds, while OpenHA studies open-source hierarchical agents and their execution in the same environment ( Hill et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Voyager uses a curriculum, a skill library, and environment feedback for continued exploration and skill reuse, including in a new world ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . MCU evaluates a broad set of tasks, their combinations, and automatic assessment ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . Together, these benchmarks cover open-world interaction, planning, task diversity, and automatic verification. They do not, however, isolate whether a controlled source interaction causes a later improvement after the target world is reset.

Several recent benchmarks study improvement across tasks and the use of stored experience. LifelongAgentBench tests skill gain, retention, and transfer across databases, operating systems, and knowledge graphs ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . EvoAgentBench uses agent traces to identify abilities and groups tasks by shared procedures, making transfer between related tasks explicit ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . PAST-Bench compares runs with and without persistent state and tracks how experience is saved and reused in personal-agent settings ( Xue et al., 2026 ) . These studies establish useful ideas for measuring persistence and transfer, but their tasks do not expose the same physical-state confounds as embodied environments. In Minecraft, an apparent gain can instead come from a carried tool, a modified world, or a different starting location. MC-EvoBench addresses this boundary by resetting inventory and world changes while allowing only a declared agent artifact to transfer. Its task-state graph makes prerequisites and progress visible.

Memory systems provide a practical mechanism for experience-driven improvement. Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) stores language feedback from failed attempts and uses it to guide later decisions. Agent Workflow Memory extracts reusable procedures from interaction traces for later tasks ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Skill libraries and model updates offer related ways to preserve information beyond a single episode. These methods show how an agent can store and retrieve experience, but reuse alone does not establish that a capability transferred. MC-EvoBench treats experience-driven improvement as an attribution problem. It separates source and target episodes, resets the physical state, and transfers only a declared artifact. Matched source conditions, verifier predicates, and stage records distinguish capability transfer from carried-over resources and partial execution.

2026-10-12.title: Dream to Remember: Continual Steering of Generalist Robot Policies with World Models
2026-10-12.authors: Bahey Tharwat , Iman Nematollahi , Marvin Alles , Xingyuan Zhang , Akshay L Chandra , Abhinav Valada
2026-10-12.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-12.abstract: Generalist robot policies are trained with imitation learning and are bounded by the quality and coverage of their demonstrations. Reinforcement learning can improve and extend them, either by fine-tuning the policy weights or by training a small module to steer the input noise of a frozen generative policy. When tasks arrive sequentially, both approaches suffer from catastrophic forgetting. Fine-tuning on a task degrades prior tasks, and steering only shifts forgetting to the shared steering module. We propose Dream to Remember (D2R), which continually steers a frozen generalist policy toward new tasks, while retaining its earlier skills. As the steering module learns a new task, a frozen pretrained world model rehearses prior tasks through imagined rollouts, anchoring the module to its earlier behavior without a replay buffer or new data. When the world model is faithful enough, D2R learns the new task entirely in imagination. Otherwise, it learns the task in the environment while using the world model only to rehearse prior tasks. On CALVIN, D2R improves eight tasks in sequence entirely in imagination, raising average success from 63.7% to 74.8%, while LoRA fine-tuning on the same sequence drops it to 11.7%. With a frozen off-the-shelf generalist policy and world model, $\pi_0$ and A2World, D2R learns unseen LIBERO-90 tasks in the environment while keeping $\pi_0$'s performance on the LIBERO suites it was fine-tuned on, even though the world model is not accurate enough for policy optimization. Finally, on a real Franka robot, D2R improves three tasks in sequence entirely in imagination while retaining the earlier improvements.

2026-10-12.title: When LiDAR Fades, Radar Takes Over: LiDAR Reliability-Aware Adaptive Localization Under Airborne Obscurants
2026-10-12.authors: Moumita Mukherjee , Avijit Banerjee , Anton Koval , George Nikolakopoulo
2026-10-12.abstract: LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) is widely used for real-time localization and mapping, but its reliability can degrade substantially in subterranean environments affected by smoke, dust, and other airborne obscurants, whereas radar remains comparatively robust. This article presents a one-class temporal learning framework for LiDAR degradation detection and reliability-aware localization under such conditions. A broad set of degradation-sensitive cues, including spatial, cross-modal, geometric/motion, intensity, and measurement-recency features, is evaluated to characterize changes in LiDAR sensing quality. Their temporal evolution is modelled over sliding windows using an LSTM autoencoder trained exclusively on nominal operation, enabling deviations from healthy sensor behaviour to be detected without requiring labelled degradation data. The resulting LiDAR reliability estimate governs adaptive selection between LIO and radar inertial odometry (RIO), retaining LIO during reliable sensing and transferring localization authority to RIO when degradation is detected. The framework is evaluated using real-world ground robot data collected in GNSS-denied subterranean tunnels under nominal and dense-smoke conditions. Experimental results demonstrate degradation detection, adaptive modality switching, and continued localization output under severe LiDAR degradation. A feature family ablation study further shows that a reduced feature representation can improve degradation-aware localization performance in the evaluated dense-smoke scenarios, highlighting the importance of feature parsimony in one-class sensor degradation detection. The code will be released as open source to support reproducibility and further research.
2026-10-12.introduction:
The rapid advancement of LiDAR technology has significantly improved localization, mapping, and three-dimensional perception in challenging environments. However, in GNSS-denied subterranean environments such as tunnels and underground facilities, dense smoke, rain, and other airborne particulates can substantially degrade LiDAR measurements [ 1 , 2 ] .

Such degradation may reduce the number of valid returns, alter their spatial distribution, and change pointcloud density, thereby reducing the reliability of LiDAR-based perception in real-world deployments [ 3 , 4 ] . Although radar is comparatively robust under degraded visibility, LiDAR remains valuable for its high-resolution geometric information. Reliable localization therefore
requires both complementary sensing modalities and the ability to identify when LiDAR measurements become unreliable, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .

This motivates degradation-sensitive LiDAR feature extraction that captures changes in spatial occupancy, density, temporal consistency, and related sensing characteristics. LiDAR
degradation may be observed as abrupt changes, missing observations, or persistent deviations from nominal behaviour. Existing anomaly detection methods include distribution, clustering, distance, and density based approaches [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
However, these methods typically operate on individual observations and do not explicitly model the temporal evolution of sensor degradation. This limitation motivates the sequence based formulation adopted in this article.

LiDAR pointclouds are unordered and variable in size, making direct temporal modelling computationally demanding. Representations based on subsampling, projection, or learned point-wise features can reduce this complexity, but may suppress local variations in point concentration and spatial occupancy that are informative for sensor degradation [ 8 , 9 ] . Voxel-based representations provide a structured alternative by preserving three-dimensional spatial organization while enabling compact characterization of return density and occupancy [ 10 , 11 ] . These statistics provide interpretable reliability cues through changes in the number, concentration, and spatial distribution of valid LiDAR returns. Accordingly, the proposed framework combines voxel-based spatial statistics with complementary temporal, geometric, cross-modal, inertial, and intensity related features for sequence based degradation detection.

Conventional anomaly detection methods, including clustering, Isolation Forest, and support vector machines, can identify observations that deviate from nominal feature distributions [ 12 ] . However, such approaches typically assess individual feature vectors and do not explicitly model the temporal evolution of sensor degradation. This is important for LiDAR reliability monitoring, where degradation may develop progressively over consecutive observations rather than as an isolated outlier. Autoencoder based methods provide a suitable one-class [ 13 ] learning framework by modelling nominal sensor behaviour without requiring labelled failure data. Deviations from the learned nominal representation are reflected by increased reconstruction error. # II Problem Formulation

This article considers a non-holonomic ground robot operating in a GNSS-denied subterranean environment and equipped with radars, a 3D LiDAR, and an IMU. Under nominal conditions, LiDAR provides reliable geometric information for LiDAR inertial odometry (LIO) [ 15 ] . Under airborne obscurants such as smoke and dust, however, LiDAR measurements may progressively degrade through reduced or corrupted returns, altered spatial density and intensity, and measurement staleness. Since these changes may also arise from scene geometry, surface properties, or robot motion, LiDAR degradation cannot be robustly characterized by a single measurement cue [ 2 ] . The objective is therefore to estimate LiDAR reliability from complementary sensor and odometry cues, detect departures from nominal LiDAR behaviour, and determine when LiDAR-based localization becomes unreliable. The resulting degradation estimate is used to adaptively select between LIO during reliable LiDAR operation and radar inertial odometry (RIO) when LiDAR is degraded or unavailable, thereby maintaining localization in GNSS-denied obscurant conditions.

2026-10-12.title: SmolWAM: A Latent World-Action Model for Robotic Manipulation on Edge Devices
2026-10-12.authors: Timi Owolabi , Hikmah Olawore , Frances Adelakun , Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
2026-10-12.comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Robot Learning with World Models Workshop. Code: this https URL Project: this https URL
2026-10-12.abstract:
World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot’s actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices.
We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk’s attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step.
Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11 × \times faster than its teacher with 18.5 × \times fewer FLOPs and 3.2 × \times less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
Code: github.com/iitimii/SmolWAM ; project page: smolwam.vercel.app .
2026-10-12.introduction:
World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot’s next actions together with the observations they should produce [ 15 , 41 , 23 ] .
Cosmos Policy [ 15 ] builds one from the Cosmos-Predict2 video model [ 28 ] by treating actions, future observations, and values as latent frames of a single denoising sequence, and reaches 98.5% success on LIBERO [ 19 ] .
Its inference stack, however, was built for video generation: a 4.8B-parameter T5-XXL text encoder [ 32 ] , a VAE that encodes a 33-frame clip per query, and five denoising steps of a 2B-parameter transformer over 1,764 tokens, which cost 624 ms, 42.6 TFLOP, and 7.55 GiB per 16-action chunk on an A100 even with cached text features.

Efficient policies usually give up the world model or the video prior: compact vision-language-action (VLA) models such as SmolVLA [ 33 ] and TurboVLA [ 39 ] predict only actions, and Fast-WAM [ 42 ] skips future prediction at test time.
We ask whether a strong pretrained WAM can itself be made small while still predicting the future.

We present SmolWAM (Fig. 1 ).
Our premise is that much of the teacher’s cost comes from an interface designed for video generation, not from what control requires.
SmolWAM reuses the trunk’s weights, token positions, and rectified-flow readout; it encodes single frames through a small adapter, replaces T5-XXL with cached BERT features [ 8 ] padded to preserve the trunk’s attention sinks, keeps 12 of 28 blocks, and reads actions from 28 state-conditioned queries.
Most changes break the trunk zero-shot, so a distillation curriculum recovers from pruning before compaction.

We contribute (i) SmolWAM, which retains 97% of its teacher’s success at 11 × \times lower latency; (ii) a method, with a diagnostic behind each step, for deriving compact WAMs from pretrained video WAMs (Sec. 3 ), including three pitfalls (attention-sink padding, jointly fatal blocks, and chunks that cannot be cut short); and (iii) findings that the compressed world head preserves motion forecasting, whereas latent-action cascades or visual-reward fine-tuning degrade control (Sec. 4 ).

# 2 Related Work

Generalist VLAs bring pretraining to control [ 4 , 16 , 29 , 10 , 2 , 31 ] , often with diffusion [ 7 ] or chunked [ 44 ] action heads; OpenVLA-OFT [ 14 ] , TinyVLA [ 36 ] , SmolVLA [ 33 ] , and TurboVLA [ 39 ] speed them up; SmolWAM borrows TurboVLA’s principles but retains a world model.
Latent world models learn dynamics in feature space [ 46 , 1 , 45 , 24 , 9 ] , and GR-1 [ 37 ] , PAD [ 11 ] , and WorldVLA [ 5 ] generate future images and actions jointly.
Recent WAMs build on video models [ 15 , 41 ] and add action evaluation [ 47 ] , modalities [ 27 ] , object state [ 21 ] , geometry [ 22 ] , or latent actions [ 6 ] ; Fast-WAM [ 42 ] drops future prediction at test time and Light-WAM [ 17 ] decodes actions from a smaller video backbone, whereas SmolWAM reads future latents from its action pass.

2026-10-12.title: Towards a Unified Taxonomy of Agricultural Harvesting Technologies: Linking Physical Interaction, Automation, and Selectivity
2026-10-12.authors: Renato Cristiano Torres , Fabiano Mariath D Oliveira , Claudio Gottschalg Duque
2026-10-12.abstract: Harvesting technologies have evolved from conventional mechanized systems based on bulk mechanical interaction toward increasingly automated and robotic systems capable of perception, decision-making, and localized actuation. However, this technological evolution has also created a classification problem. Harvesting systems are commonly described according to crop type, mechanical removal principle, sensing technology, robotic architecture, or degree of automation, making direct comparison between mechanized, automated, and robotic approaches difficult.
2026-10-12.introduction:
The adoption of agricultural mechanization technologies must be understood within a broader historical, economic, and social context. In a comparative analysis of the history of agricultural mechanization, Binswanger [ 5 ] demonstrates that the introduction of machinery in agricultural systems does not occur in a linear manner, nor is it driven exclusively by technological availability. Factors such as relative labor costs, land tenure structure, capital availability, public policies, and agronomic characteristics of crops play a decisive role in the adoption or rejection of mechanized and automated technologies. These factors shape not only the feasibility of technological implementation but also its economic and operational sustainability across different production systems.

Mechanization is defined as the use of mechanical energy and machinery to replace or reduce human or animal labor [ 12 ] , whereas automation refers to systems capable of monitoring, decision-making, and actuation through sensors, controllers, and actuators [ 14 ] . Although conceptually distinct, these two paradigms increasingly coexist in modern agricultural systems.

Harvesting is among the most labor-intensive and costly operations in agriculture, particularly in high-value horticultural and fruit production systems. Previous studies indicate that harvesting may account for approximately 30–50% of total production costs [ 3 , 4 ] . Labor shortages and rising wages have intensified the adoption of agricultural automation technologies, a trend further reinforced by changes in consumer behavior, which increasingly demand consistent and high-quality products [ 17 ] .

Unlike operations such as seeding and spraying, harvesting involves direct interaction with fragile biological materials, requiring simultaneous perception, decision-making, and precise mechanical manipulation [ 25 ] . The heterogeneity of harvested products in terms of size, shape, rigidity, and maturity stage significantly increases the complexity of harvesting operations. Despite advances in robotics, computer vision, and artificial intelligence, economic, operational, and crop-adaptation challenges continue to limit the widespread diffusion of automated harvesting technologies.

Modern agricultural machines increasingly incorporate GPS-based navigation, electronic controllers, onboard sensors, and yield monitoring systems. However, the incorporation of these technologies does not automatically change the physical principle used to harvest the crop. A machine may become more automated while still applying the same cutting, pulling, vibration, impact, or combined harvesting mechanism. In this sense, mechanization and automation are not mutually exclusive categories but different dimensions of a harvesting system.

This distinction creates a conceptual problem for comparison. Conventional harvesting machinery is usually described primarily by the physical mechanism used to detach, collect, or transport the product, whereas robotic harvesting systems are more frequently discussed in terms of perception, manipulation, motion planning, and autonomy. As a consequence, technologies belonging to different stages of harvesting automation are often described using classification criteria that are not directly comparable.

The problem becomes even more evident because increasing automation does not necessarily imply increasing selectivity. Automated navigation or automatic adjustment of process parameters may improve operational efficiency while preserving bulk harvesting. A qualitative transition occurs only when perception and decision-making begin to influence product-level actuation, allowing the system to discriminate between harvestable and non-harvestable targets.

Accordingly, this study argues that agricultural harvesting technologies require a unified classification framework capable of describing both their physical interaction mechanisms and their level of automation while explicitly evaluating selectivity. Two primary classification axes are adopted: (i) the physical principle governing plant–machine interaction during product removal and (ii) the degree of automation associated with perception, decision-making, and actuation. Selectivity is treated as an emergent functional attribute that expresses the biological and spatial scale at which the harvesting action is targeted.

The objective of this paper is therefore not only to review existing harvesting technologies, but to demonstrate the conceptual need for a unified taxonomy capable of positioning mechanized, automated, and robotic harvesting systems within a common analytical framework. The main contributions are:

to separate the physical mechanism of product removal from the automation level of the harvesting system;

to identify selectivity as a central linking attribute between physical interaction and automation;

to organize conventional mechanized, semi-automated, collaborative, and autonomous robotic harvesting within a common framework; and

to clarify the technological transition from distributed or bulk harvesting toward localized and selective product-level interaction.

# 2 The Classification Problem in Agricultural Harvesting

Agricultural harvesting technologies span a wide range of mechanical and computational complexity. At one end are conventional machines designed to remove, separate, or collect products through mechanical forces applied to the crop as a whole or to large portions of the plant. At the other end are robotic systems that identify individual products, estimate harvest readiness and pose, plan motions, and execute localized cutting, grasping, or suction actions [ 19 , 21 , 24 , 27 , 35 , 43 ] .

These two technological domains are often discussed using different vocabularies. Agricultural machinery literature typically emphasizes mechanical principles, field efficiency, crop architecture, machine stability, and compatibility with production geometry [ 9 , 22 , 23 , 39 ] . Robotic harvesting literature, in contrast, emphasizes sensing, visual perception, target recognition, manipulation, planning, control, and autonomy [ 19 , 21 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 35 , 43 ] . Both descriptions are valid, but neither dimension alone is sufficient to position the full range of contemporary harvesting technologies.

A physical classification alone cannot distinguish a manually controlled vibrating harvester from a sensor-regulated vibration system. Conversely, an automation-based classification alone does not reveal whether the product is detached by cutting, pulling, vibration, impact, grasping, or suction. Moreover, systems with similar automation levels may differ significantly in selectivity. This produces overlapping categories and makes direct comparison difficult.

The need for a unified taxonomy therefore arises from three observations. First, the physical harvesting principle and the level of automation are conceptually distinct. Second, mechanization can incorporate automation without becoming selective. Third, selectivity depends on whether perception and decision-making affect the location and target of physical actuation. A useful taxonomy must therefore preserve these distinctions rather than collapse them into a single linear scale.

Table 1 illustrates the fragmentation of emphasis across representative reviews cited in this manuscript. The comparison is not intended as a ranking of previous studies, but as a conceptual synthesis of the principal dimensions emphasized in their reported scopes. Mechanization-oriented reviews tend to foreground harvesting mechanisms and crop–machine compatibility, whereas robotic-harvesting reviews tend to foreground perception, manipulation, planning, and autonomy. Selectivity is explicit in some robotic reviews, but is not generally integrated with physical harvesting principles and automation level within a single classification structure.
