2026-10-12.title: Cooperative Aerial Transportation of a Payload with a Sliding Cable Attachment
2026-10-12.authors: Sebastian Tilaguy Lezama , Diego S D'Antonio
2026-10-12.abstract: This paper presents a dual-quadrotor hook-suspended transport system for cooperative aerial manipulation of a payload that is not rigidly attached to a fixed point along the cable. Two quadrotors are connected by a single inextensible cable that passes through a frictionless hook mounted on the payload, allowing the cable to slide between its two segments. This introduces a cable-distribution variable that couples the quadrotor motion, cable geometry, and payload dynamics. A feasible reference-generation framework is formulated using the desired payload pose, cable distribution, and system shape while satisfying the cable-length constraint and elliptical workspace. The quadrotors track the geometrically generated trajectories while maintaining positive cable tension and respecting actuator limits. The payload pose is estimated from the system geometry, and its measured position is used only to validate the desired trajectory. The approach is evaluated through experimental demonstrations.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Cooperative aerial systems have expanded the capabilities of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) beyond surveillance and conventional logistics. Through distributed actuation and coordinated motion, multiple UAVs can perform tasks that exceed the physical limitations of a single platform, including heavy-payload transportation, infrastructure interaction, and emergency response [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Aerial logistics has therefore received increasing attention for rapid operation in remote or hard-to-reach environments, motivating scalable and autonomous multi-robot transportation strategies [ 4 ] .

Cable-suspended transportation provides several advantages for aerial manipulation. By separating the payload from the aerial platform, the cable reduces the direct transmission of disturbances and allows the UAVs to maintain a safer distance from the transported object. It can also facilitate payload attachment and release while the aerial vehicles remain in flight [ 5 , 6 ] .
Early studies primarily considered payloads suspended from a single UAV, which inherently limits the available lifting capacity and controllability of the payload. Cooperative multi-UAV systems address these limitations by distributing the payload weight among multiple aerial vehicles and coordinating the cable forces applied to the load [ 7 ] .

Several approaches have addressed cooperative cable-suspended transportation through differential flatness, coordinated rotorcraft motion, inertial sensing, autonomous hook-based grasping, and nonlinear model predictive control [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . These methods enable trajectory generation, cooperative transport, payload grasping, and constrained full-pose manipulation. However, they generally assume fixed cable attachment points and do not consider cable-length redistribution through a sliding payload-mounted hook.

Cable-suspended aerial lifting is commonly divided into setup , pull , and raise stages [ 13 , 14 ] . While the pull and raise stages have received significant attention, setup often requires manual cable attachment, reducing autonomy and limiting operation in hazardous or inaccessible environments. A catenary robot , formed by two aerial vehicles connected by a flexible cable, can manipulate the cable to interact with objects [ 15 ] . However, engaging a payload-mounted hook allows the cable to slide, coupling UAV motion, cable geometry, payload dynamics, and cable-length distribution.
Motivated by this gap, this work introduces the Dual-Quadrotor Hook-Suspended Transport System (DQ-HSTS), shown in Fig. 1 . Two quadrotors are connected by a single cable passing through a frictionless hook rigidly attached to the payload. Unlike conventional systems, the cable slides through the hook, redistributing its total length between the two cable segments.

This paper addresses quadrotor coordination for payload-pose and cable-distribution control without fixed cable attachments. The contributions are threefold: i) the DQ-HSTS, in which a cable slides through a payload-mounted hook; ii) trajectory generation parameterized by payload pose, cable distribution λ \lambda , and system shape γ \gamma ; and iii) coordinated trajectory tracking under tension, geometric, and actuator constraints, validated in experiments.

2026-10-12.title: AutoBio+: Benchmarking Dexterous Manipulation with Dynamic Experimental Phenomena in Realistic Laboratories
2026-10-12.authors: Xuanye Wu , Yue Shi , Yongcan Yang , Yiqun Wang , Zhaoqi Wan , Dayu Xia , Jiezhang Cao , Xiangfei Li , Yao Mu , Guangtao Zhai
2026-10-12.abstract:
Automating biological laboratories requires robots to perform dexterous tool interactions
under realistic visual conditions while handling dynamic experimental phenomena,
presenting significant challenges for robotic manipulation. To enable systematic
evaluation under these conditions, we introduce AutoBio+, a simulation benchmark and
framework for dexterous manipulation in realistic biological laboratory environments.
AutoBio+ comprises 14 tasks across 4 robot embodiments, spanning functional tool use,
precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation.
We introduce controllable dynamic experimental phenomena, including flames, vapor, and
bubbles, to capture the evolving visual conditions of laboratory procedures. To further
enhance environmental realism, we develop a hybrid rendering pipeline that integrates
interactive simulated foreground objects with Gaussian-splatting backgrounds reconstructed
from 6 real laboratory scenes. For efficient large-scale data generation and evaluation,
we further build a parallel simulation framework on top of mjlab, proposing Parallel
Finite-State Machine (PFSM) and integrating batched rendering with decoupled trajectory replay
for demonstration generation and model-independent closed-loop policy evaluation. Our
evaluation reveals substantial variation in policy performance across tasks, exposing
distinct strengths and weaknesses of current manipulation policies. Real-world experiments
further demonstrate a reduced sim-to-real gap, supporting the validity of AutoBio+ for
realistic manipulation evaluation. Supplementary materials are available at https://autobio-plus.github.io/AutoBioPlus.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Automated laboratories, often referred to as AutoLabs, are transforming scientific experimentation by shifting routine
procedures from manual operation toward autonomous execution [ 9 , 10 ] . Conventional laboratory automation,
however, typically relies on task-specific instruments and tightly coupled workflows. Although such
systems are efficient in structured settings, adapting them to new experimental protocols, tools,
or operating conditions often requires substantial hardware modification and system reintegration.
General-purpose robotic manipulators equipped with dexterous hands or grippers provide a more flexible alternative, allowing
laboratory procedures to be adapted through demonstrations and learned policies rather than
hardware-specific re-engineering. This flexibility is particularly important in biological
laboratories, where robots must perform fine-grained operations such as manipulating pipettes and
tweezers, inserting tubes, actuating instruments, and coordinating multiple objects over
long-horizon procedures.

Recent robot-learning methods, particularly vision-language-action (VLA) policies,
have demonstrated strong manipulation capabilities in household
and industrial environments [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
To evaluate these learned policies,
recent benchmarks have explored manipulation from several complementary perspectives.
General-purpose manipulation benchmarks such as RoboTwin 2.0 [ 14 ] and LIBERO [ 15 ] provide diverse household and industrial tasks with
controlled object interactions. Scientific robotics
benchmarks [ 5 , 8 , 6 ] introduce
laboratory-specific objects and procedures, while dexterous manipulation benchmarks such as
DexJoCo [ 4 ] , DexVerse [ 3 ] , and
Bi-DexHands [ 2 ] focus on complex hand–object coordination.
Recently, Labimus [ 7 ] extends dexterous manipulation evaluation
to chemical laboratory scenarios. However, laboratory procedures often introduce temporally
varying visual conditions, such as flames, vapor, and bubbles, which are underrepresented in
existing manipulation benchmarks.

To address this gap, we introduce AutoBio+ ,
a simulation benchmark for dexterous manipulation in realistic biological laboratory environments.
AutoBio+ comprises 14 tasks across four robot embodiments, covering functional tool use,
precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation.
It incorporates controllable dynamic experimental phenomena, including flames, vapor,
and bubbles, to capture visually evolving conditions during laboratory procedures.
To improve visual realism while preserving physical interaction, AutoBio+ proposes a hybrid
rendering strategy that combines interactive simulated foreground objects with
Gaussian-splatting backgrounds reconstructed from six real laboratory scenes.
Leveraging mjlab as the simulation foundation, we design a parallel simulation
framework centered around the Parallel Finite-State Machine (PFSM) policy,
together with batched rendering and decoupled trajectory replay,

# II Related Work

Visuomotor Policies. Visuomotor policies for robot manipulation have evolved from directly regressing actions
from visual observations toward increasingly structured generative policies. Early
Transformer-based approaches predict temporally coherent action chunks from visual observations,
improving the consistency of long-horizon execution [ 11 ] . Diffusion-based
imitation policies then model the action distribution through iterative denoising, providing a
flexible way to represent multimodal behaviors and contact-rich motions [ 12 , 16 ] .
Building on these low-level visual policies, VLA models incorporate
large vision-language representations and language-conditioned action generation, enabling a single
policy to connect scene understanding, task instructions, and continuous control [ 13 ] .
As VLA research has advanced, it has become increasingly clear that predicting how the world will
evolve under candidate actions can provide useful temporal and physical information for manipulation.
This insight has led to World Action Models (WAMs), which augment the VLA formulation by jointly
learning action generation and future visual-state prediction [ 17 , 18 ] .
Despite these advances, existing visuomotor policies have been developed and evaluated predominantly
on general-purpose manipulation tasks. Their capabilities in scientific laboratory settings,
particularly for the fine-grained, contact-rich, and dexterous operations required in biological
experiments, remain insufficiently explored.
Our benchmark is designed to address the lack of evaluation for dexterous manipulation in
photorealistic biological laboratory settings, featuring a diverse set of tasks that capture
fine-grained operations.

Manipulation Benchmarks. Existing manipulation benchmarks commonly evaluate general robotic capabilities in household or
industrial environments.
Benchmarks such as RoboTwin 2.0 [ 14 ] , RLBench [ 19 ] , and
BEHAVIOR-1K [ 20 ] cover a wide variety of tasks, and select parallel-jaw grippers as their robot embodiments.
The low-dimensional control space of these grippers supports efficient trajectory collection and
large-scale evaluation, yet it can hardly fully represent the fine-grained coordination required for
human-like manipulation.
In contrast, dexterous manipulation benchmarks such as Bi-DexHands [ 2 ] ,
DexVerse [ 3 ] , and DexJoCo [ 4 ] emphasize multi-fingered hand
control and complex, contact-rich interactions.
They provide valuable testbeds for studying coordinated finger motion, bimanual control, and
generalization across objects, tasks, or robot embodiments.
These benchmarks provide valuable foundations for studying dexterous manipulation, but laboratory-specific procedures involving diverse tools, instruments, and dynamic experimental phenomena remain less explored. Meanwhile, recent simulation frameworks have investigated the integration of neural rendering with interactive physics simulators to improve visual realism while preserving physical interaction [ 21 ] . However, such simulation advances have not yet been integrated into benchmarks for evaluating dexterous laboratory manipulation under realistic and evolving experimental conditions.

Scientific Robotics Benchmarks. Recent scientific robotics benchmarks have begun to investigate robotic manipulation in laboratory
environments. Chemistry3D [ 5 ] and LabUtopia [ 6 ] provide
scientific manipulation scenarios, but primarily focus on gripper-based interactions.
AutoBio [ 8 ] extends this line of work to dexterous manipulation with a limited
set of laboratory tasks, while simplifying hand control to binary open–close actions.
In a related direction, Labimus [ 7 ] studies dexterous manipulation by humanoid
robots in chemical laboratories.
Against this backdrop, AutoBio+ broadens the scope of scientific robotics benchmarking with a
larger and more diverse task suite, multiple robot embodiments, and richer dynamic visual effects,
enabling a more comprehensive evaluation of robot-learning models.

2026-10-12.title: JitterVLA: A Replay Benchmark for Motion Quality in VLA-Driven Human-Robot Manipulation
2026-10-12.authors: Faith Ogunwoye , Didar Seyidov , Konstantin Gubernatorov , Dzmitry Tsetserukou
2026-10-12.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller’s effect. We apply it to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a physical UR3. Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk for every source, by 83% (615 to 106 m/s 3 ) on human motion with 200 ms delay, at a 2.0 cm tracking cost , and the effect replicated on 598 new episodes; jerk-limited generation lowered jerk further at a larger cost. Entropy–discontinuity associations had opposite, replicated signs in two pipelines , and entropy gating helped in one but not the other. On the UR3, interpolation lowered accelerometer-derived jerk by 3.0–14.0% in all six exploratory pairs , while a position-derived metric did not resolve the contrast. JitterVLA supports screening before human-centred studies; code and data will be released.
2026-10-12.introduction:
A person hands a manipulator an object, guides its target, or works beside it. The high-level policy produces a sensible action, but its targets arrive sparsely and at irregular times, so the low-level controller receives discontinuous goals. What the person experiences is not the predicted action but the motion the robot executes. VLA policies such as OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2025b ) run at a few hertz, one to two orders of magnitude below the robot’s control loop ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , and remote or shared inference adds network delay. Human-robot interaction (HRI) research links onset latency to teleoperation performance ( Rakita et al., 2020 ; Khalil and Kwon, 2026 ) and robot motion to observers’ responses and perceived safety ( Kulić and Croft, 2007 ; Rubagotti et al., 2022 ) .

Timing is not only latency. A constant delay shifts every command, whereas timing jitter (variation in delay and arrival spacing, including bunching) changes which targets the controller sees and when. Remedies exist at several layers: action chunking and asynchronous execution ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Guo and Guo, 2026 ; Kim et al., 2025a ) , interpolation and jerk-limited trajectory generation such as Ruckig ( Berscheid and Kröger, 2021 ) , geometry-guided jerk reduction in VLA execution ( Yun et al., 2026 ) , and stiffness adaptation ( Ferraguti et al., 2013 ) . Each paper evaluates its remedy with its own inputs, delays, plant and metrics, so the remedies cannot be compared fairly. JitterVLA addresses that comparison problem. It evaluates the middle of the chain (command stream, timing, controller, executed motion) before candidate behaviours are shown to people. It does not replace human studies.

We ask four research questions (RQ1–RQ4). RQ1 (timing): how do timing irregularities change motion-quality proxies for identical command streams? RQ2 (control): how do stepped, interpolated, entropy-gated, constant-gain and jerk-limited strategies move the jerk–tracking trade-off? RQ3 (cross-source): do these relationships hold across synthetic, human and three VLA action representations, and on new episode draws? RQ4 (physical): are the contrasts observable on a real UR3 under a bounded protocol?

Contributions. (1) A paired replay benchmark and protocol that holds the command source and delay realization fixed while varying the controller. (2) An evaluation that progresses from controlled synthetic reaches to 20-person human motion, three VLA pipelines with a planned replication on 598 new episodes, and measured network traces (Table 1 ). (3) Findings: a consistent jerk–tracking trade-off for interpolation, representation-dependent uncertainty associations, and a failure of entropy gating on some inputs. (4) A bounded UR3 check, including a null result for the planned position-derived metric. Code, the transformed VLA streams, the human windows and the traces will be released.

Terms. Latency is delay; jitter is its variation. Command discontinuity is the spatial jump between successive targets or chunks. Jerk is the benchmark plant’s jerk proxy, or a sensor-derived estimate on the UR3. Tracking error is the root-mean-square error (RMSE) against the undelayed reference. Jerk, tracking error, log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) and spectral arc length (SPARC) ( Balasubramanian et al., 2015 ) are motion-quality proxies ; comfort, preference and safety were not measured.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2. Benchmark design

Paired replay. Within a comparison, every controller receives the same source (episode, person or synthetic reach) and the same delay realization (seed or trace offset). Differences are therefore attributable to the controller rather than to different stochastic inputs. Statistics are paired over the source unit: episodes, people or seeds. Intervals are 95% unit bootstraps (5000 resamples), not time-sample intervals.

Timing pipeline. For VLAs, measured inference service times from one RTX 5090 feed a single-worker first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue. A network delay is then added: zero, Gamma-distributed with mean 0–400 ms (shape 2), or sequential samples from 12 h of measured lab-path traces: local area network (LAN), internet round trip, and a cold HTTPS request. Delivery is in order, and the newest delivered target wins. Separating the mean delay from its spread lets RQ1 test jitter as well as latency.

Plant and controllers. Delivered targets drive a generic three-axis point mass (3 kg, critically damped impedance, 20 ms force lag, 3000 N/s force-rate cap, 1 ms steps). It is not a UR3 model; absolute jerk values are not hardware predictions. Controllers:

B0 holds each delivered target (stepped).

B2 interpolates linearly over one command period.

A2 adds entropy-gated stiffness to interpolation.

B3 (Ruckig, jerk limit 25 m/s 3 ) is an explicit jerk-limited trajectory generator.

Evidence hierarchy. Protocols were frozen before data were seen: frozen analyses (v1.1, v1.3), a planned replication on new draws (v1.4), post-outcome robustness checks (v1.5: traces, LDLJ/SPARC, Ruckig, pi0.5 ( Black et al., 2025a ) ), and an exploratory hardware follow-up (v1.2a). We label results accordingly and never pool across these labels.

2026-10-12.title: RARA: Robust Policy Fine-Tuning through Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment for Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-12.authors: Xuhui Kang , Sung-Wook Lee , Yan Zhuang , Tianle Zhong , Yen-Ling Kuo
2026-10-12.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-12.abstract:
Pre-trained robot policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models , provide a strong foundation for generalist robotic manipulation, but adapting them to new tasks with only a few demonstrations remains challenging. Directly fine-tuning a pre-trained policy often achieves strong in-distribution performance, yet it can distort the representations learned during pre-training and weaken the model’s generalization ability under out-of-distribution shifts.
We propose Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment (RARA), a two-stage adaptation method, to address this issue. First, RARA retrieves pre-training demonstrations with similar task intent and motion, and aligns the policy’s representations of the target demonstrations with the pre-trained representations of the retrieved demonstrations.
Second, RARA fine-tunes the policy on the target demonstrations while limiting how much its representations of the retrieved demonstrations change during fine-tuning.
By reducing the representation mismatch before action learning and preserving pre-trained knowledge during adaptation, RARA limits unnecessary representation drift during fine-tuning. Experiments with Diffusion Policy and GR00T on 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot show that RARA improves the average success of fine-tuning by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, and outperforms all compared baselines. Project page: https://shua-kang.github.io/RARA_robot/
2026-10-12.introduction:
Pre-training on large-scale robot demonstrations followed by fine-tuning on a small target dataset has become a standard practice in learning robot manipulation policies ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) .
By leveraging supervision from large and diverse robot demonstration datasets, pre-training provides useful initial representations that help adaptation to a new task.
However, fine-tuning on limited target data can still overfit the policy to the narrow distribution seen during adaptation:
A policy may succeed on the target task under the in-distribution conditions, but fail when the camera viewpoint, background, or object properties change ( Fei et al., 2026 ) .
This vulnerability arises because standard fine-tuning on limited data can severely distort the representations learned during pre-training ( Kumar et al., 2022 ; Kachaev et al., 2026 ; Yadav et al., 2026 ) .
Therefore, robust policy fine-tuning , which requires learning a target task while maintaining generalization to out-of-distribution shifts, remains a critical challenge when adapting pre-trained robotic policies to new tasks.

Existing methods have explored several ways to preserve generalizable representations when adapting policies to new tasks.
One line of work constrains the adapted policy toward its pre-trained initialization, for example by regularizing fine-tuned weights toward the pre-trained weights ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , merging pre-trained and fine-tuned weights ( Yadav et al., 2026 ) , or aligning policy representations with those of a frozen pre-trained visual encoder ( Kachaev et al., 2026 ) .
Another line of work distills knowledge from multiple pre-trained models into a shared representation for downstream robot learning ( Shang et al., 2024 ) .
While these approaches preserve broad pre-trained knowledge, they do not provide a principled way to focus alignment to pre-training demonstrations that are most relevant to the target task.

We propose R etrieval- A nchored R epresentation A lignment ( RARA ), which uses task-relevant pre-training demonstrations as anchors for fine-tuning (Fig. 1 ).
RARA retrieves relevant demonstrations from the pre-training data by matching both task instructions and robot motions to the target demonstrations. For example, demonstrations of removing a pot lid may be retrieved for target tasks like opening a blender and remove a bottle cap.
The retrieved demonstrations support adaptation in two complementary ways.
Before fine-tuning, RARA aligns every target frame with the retrieved frames whose upcoming actions are most similar, so each frame is matched to the same stage of the motion in the retrieved demonstrations (e.g., a frame in which the gripper closes around the blender lid is matched to frames in which it closes around a pot lid).
The pre-trained policy has seen these stages under many visual conditions, so alignment lets the target frames reuse this robust representation instead of fitting the target demonstrations from scratch.
During fine-tuning, an anchor loss keeps the representations of the retrieved demonstrations close to their pre-trained values, so the small target dataset does not overwrite this robust structure.
Unlike a standard drift regularizer, the anchor acts only on the retrieved demonstrations. It therefore does not pull the target representation back, and it preserves only the pre-trained structure that is related to the target task.

We fine-tune a pre-trained Diffusion Policy on four RoboTwin tasks, and a DROID-pre-trained GR00T policy on five RoboCasa tasks and four real-robot tasks. We evaluate each policy in the conditions covered by its demonstrations (in-distribution, ID) and under new camera poses, backgrounds, distractors, objects or object positions (out-of-distribution, OOD). Across these 13 tasks, RARA improves the average success rates of fine-tuned policies by 9.5 9.5 % points in ID and 13.6 13.6 % points in OOD settings, consistently outperforming the baseline methods.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) we introduce RARA, a framework for robust policy fine-tuning that uses task-relevant pre-training experience to guide representation learning; (2) we evaluate RARA across different policies, simulated environments, and real-world manipulation tasks, measuring performance of target tasks and robustness to unseen conditions; and (3) we conduct extensive studies that separate initial alignment from representation constraints during fine-tuning, and examine how the choice of source data and network layer affects adaptation.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Robust fine-tuning. The goal of robust policy fine-tuning is to learn a downstream task without erasing the generalization acquired during pre-training ( Yadav et al., 2026 ; Grover et al., 2025 ; Hancock et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Driess et al., 2025 ) . In transfer learning, Kumar et al. (2022) show that full fine-tuning can distort pre-trained features and hurt OOD robustness, motivating staged or constrained updates. Other methods keep the fine-tuned features close to those of the pre-trained model ( Mukhoti et al., 2024 ) , or use auxiliary data with rich semantics as anchors that preserve OOD generalization ( Han et al., 2024 ) . In robot learning, one line of work freezes parts of the model and adds lightweight trainable modules, such as adapters or task-specific heads, to preserve existing capabilities while specializing to new tasks ( Liang et al., 2022 ; Sharma et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) .
Another line preserves the capabilities of the pre-trained policy more directly. Weight-space methods merge the pre-trained and fine-tuned weights ( Yadav et al., 2026 ; Dey et al., 2025 ) or constrain how far the weights move ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . Other methods keep a frozen copy of the pre-trained model next to the adapted one, as a frozen encoder with a trainable branch ( Grover et al., 2025 ) , a frozen prior in an ensemble ( Bagatella et al., 2025 ) , or a frozen expert that guides an adaptation expert ( Guo et al., 2026 ) . Representation-space methods align the features of the adapted policy with those of a frozen copy or teacher on the target data ( Dalal et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) .
These methods preserve the pre-trained policy through its architecture, its weights, or the representation of the target data. RARA instead anchors the representation of retrieved pre-training demonstrations:
it aligns the target representation with the pre-trained representation of these demonstrations, and then limits how much it changes during fine-tuning,
without restricting the architecture or which weights are updated.

Domain adaptation. Robot policies often face domain gaps between simulation and the real world, different embodiments, or pre-training and downstream deployment environments. Domain adaptation methods therefore seek task-relevant representations or data that transfer across such shifts. For VLA models, Kachaev et al. (2026) identify degradation of visual representations after action fine-tuning and preserve visual grounding through alignment with a frozen vision teacher, while Luo et al. (2026) show that action generation can become insufficiently sensitive to relevant visual tokens in deeper layers, and Kim et al. (2026) regularize VLA representations with a contrastive loss whose positives are defined by robot states. In sim-and-real co-training, Maddukuri et al. (2025) show that mixing simulated and real data improves real-world success, Cheng et al. (2025) align joint observation-action distributions with optimal-transport-inspired objectives,
while Lei et al. (2026) combine adversarial alignment with explicit domain conditioning, which keeps the sim and real domains distinguishable in the learned representation space.
Data selection offers a complementary route: Behavior Retrieval and FlowRetrieval retrieve prior data that are similar to the target demonstrations in state-action or motion space ( Du et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) , and Dass et al. (2026) select useful data from a pre-training dataset for a target imitation-learning task, improving the adapted policy with task-relevant source examples.
Similarly, RARA selects task-relevant data from the pre-training dataset, but it uses the selected demonstrations as anchors for representation alignment rather than as additional training data: it aligns the target representation with that of the selected demonstrations and limits how much their representation changes during fine-tuning.

2026-10-12.title: ATHLETE: Learning Reactive Humanoid Tennis via Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching
2026-10-12.authors: Zhihao Tian , Zifan Wang , Enzheng Zhu , Xun Yang , Jialong Qin , Mengbo Wang , Junwei Liang
2026-10-12.abstract: Humanoid tennis requires reactive whole-body coordination under rapidly changing ball dynamics, yet collecting task-specific motion-capture demonstrations that cover diverse approach states, contact locations, and timing conditions is costly. Inspired by how humans acquire new skills by combining reusable motor experience with task-specific demonstrations, we present ATHLETE, a framework for learning reactive humanoid tennis from generic locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos. ATHLETE combines LAFAN1 locomotion with video-derived striking motions and uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to construct diverse task-conditioned whole-body references. These references are transformed into a reactive policy through physics-based teacher–student learning with online DAgger distillation, followed by PPO fine-tuning for the tennis task. The resulting policy responds directly to robot and ball observations without requiring reference-motion inputs at deployment. On a real humanoid robot, ATHLETE achieves forehand and backhand hit rates of 90.00 % 90.00\% and 86.67 % 86.67\% , respectively, and enables multi-shot rallies with human players. These results demonstrate that ATHLETE can learn dynamic humanoid tennis skills from reusable locomotion data and video demonstrations. Result videos and code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ATHLETE2027/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Humanoid tennis requires rapid locomotion, precisely timed whole-body strikes, and continuous adaptation to incoming balls.
A central challenge is data coverage: a successful policy must handle diverse approach states, contact locations, and arrival times, while collecting task-specific motion-capture demonstrations for all such variations is costly.

Existing works such as LATENT [ 1 ] and AdaPT [ 2 ] demonstrate that human motion data can provide strong priors for humanoid tennis.
However, collecting or reconstructing task-specific tennis motions that sufficiently cover the combinations of locomotion, contact position, and timing remains difficult.
At the same time, public motion datasets such as LAFAN1 [ 3 ] and AMASS [ 4 ] already contain abundant reusable human locomotion, while ordinary tennis videos provide task-specific striking motions.
This raises a natural question: can dynamic humanoid tennis be learned by composing reusable locomotion experience with only sparse task-specific striking demonstrations?

We present ATHLETE to answer this question.
Our key idea is to treat locomotion and striking as complementary motion sources rather than requiring complete tennis demonstrations.
ATHLETE uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to compose generic locomotion with video-derived strikes under task, contact, and transition constraints, producing diverse whole-body approach-and-strike references.
These references are then converted through physics-based teacher–student learning into a reactive policy that no longer requires reference-motion input, online motion retrieval, or explicit motion planning at deployment.
The resulting controller directly responds to the robot state, ball observations, and task target.

Our contributions are threefold:

Task-conditioned motion composition from heterogeneous motion sources. We introduce TGMM to combine abundant generic locomotion with sparse video-derived striking motions.
By explicitly enforcing approach, contact, and transition constraints, the method generates diverse whole-body tennis references without collecting dedicated tennis motion-capture demonstrations.

From composed references to reference-free reactive control. We develop a deadline-adaptive teacher–student learning framework that transfers reference-motion and contact-timing supervision into a deployable reactive policy.
The final controller operates without reference motions, online motion matching, or an explicit motion planner.

Real-world humanoid tennis from low-cost motion sources. We validate ATHLETE on a humanoid robot, achieving reactive forehand and backhand returns and multi-shot human–robot rallies, demonstrating that reusable locomotion data and sparse visual demonstrations are sufficient to support dynamic whole-body tennis skills (Fig. ).

By explicitly enforcing approach, contact, and transition constraints, the method generates diverse whole-body tennis references without collecting dedicated tennis motion-capture demonstrations.

2026-10-12.related_work:
# II RELATED WORKS

## II-A Data Generation for Humanoid Robots

Motion matching retrieves and blends database motions using pose and trajectory features [ 5 ] , while Learned Motion Matching approximates this pipeline with neural networks to reduce memory usage [ 6 ] .
Perceptive Humanoid Parkour [ 7 ] combines sparse atomic skill demonstrations with locomotion to generate long-horizon references with diverse approach states.

Generative models synthesize motion from history, text, or kinematic constraints [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] ; humanoid extensions also condition references on velocity commands, terrain, or multimodal inputs [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] .
ATHLETE uses optimized approach trajectories to compose locomotion and strikes under contact and transition constraints, followed by physics simulated tracking.

## II-B Humanoid Whole-Body Control

Reference-tracking methods learn whole-body skills from human motions through reference adaptation, dynamics alignment, and large-scale training [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] .
Perception-conditioned controllers adapt these skills to terrain and obstacles [ 7 , 20 ] .
Interaction-aware retargeting and imitation incorporate object and scene constraints to support whole-body interaction [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] .

For tennis, LATENT [ 1 ] learns a correctable latent action space from imperfect motion primitives and composes skills through a high-level policy.
AdaPT [ 2 ] combines video-derived motions with hierarchical planning and speed-adaptive tracking.
TaskNPoint [ 24 ] organizes demonstration-guided learning around critical interaction windows and randomized task targets.
ATHLETE adopts its motion-tracking and goal-conditioned striking rewards, adds deadline-conditioned phase adaptation, and distills the resulting skills into a single reactive policy.

2026-10-12.title: Beyond Successful Robot Demonstrations: Learning from Human Interactions and Modeling Failure Dynamics
2026-10-12.authors: Peiyan Tu , Cong Wang , Hanxin Zhu , Xin Jin , Zhibo Chen
2026-10-12.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-12.abstract:
Action-conditioned world models offer a promising foundation for generalist robotic intelligence by predicting the consequences of actions.
However, existing robotic datasets provide limited coverage of the diverse interaction dynamics required for generalizable world modeling. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer complementary interaction experience, yet the embodiment gap between human hands and robotic manipulators hinders effective cross-embodiment learning. Meanwhile, the predominance of successful demonstrations leaves failure dynamics substantially underrepresented, limiting the ability of world models to anticipate unsuccessful executions.
To address these limitations, we introduce HF-WM , an action-conditioned world model that combines H uman interaction learning with F ailure-aware post-training. To bridge the embodiment gap, we develop a dual-branch framework that couples video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction, using stabilized pointflow as a unified motion representation across human and robot interactions while suppressing egocentric camera motion. To improve failure modeling, we further perform Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training on perturbed actions derived from successful demonstrations, guided by action alignment and physical plausibility rewards, enabling the model to learn plausible failure dynamics without paired ground-truth videos.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that HF-WM achieves state-of-the-art performance in action-conditioned video generation and exhibits strong utility for policy evaluation in downstream robotic tasks.
2026-10-12.introduction:
With the rapid advancement of video generation models ( Wan et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2026 ) , world models have witnessed significant breakthroughs and are increasingly regarded as a promising pathway toward generalist robotics ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . In particular, action-conditioned world models take robot action sequences as input and model the resulting state transitions to predict future states ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . This predictive capability supports scalable data generation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning in generated environments ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Tseng et al., 2026 ) , thereby closing the loop between imagination, evaluation, and policy improvement. This paradigm has emerged as a key foundation for learning and improving robot action planning systems.

Despite these advances, action-conditioned world models still struggle to accurately capture interaction dynamics and execution outcomes, largely due to the limited scale and coverage of high-quality embodied data ( Mei et al., 2026 ) .
To alleviate this limitation, recent studies have turned to large scale egocentric human object interaction datasets ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Wu and Gao, 2026 ) , leveraging human demonstrations to enhance model performance. 1) However, a substantial domain gap persists between human and robotic manipulation, and egocentric recordings are often affected by camera jitter and unstable viewpoints, which can obscure interaction-relevant regions and hinder the learning of physically meaningful representations. Consequently, effectively exploiting human egocentric data for embodied world model learning remains an open challenge ( Mei et al., 2026 ) . 2) In addition, existing embodied datasets are heavily biased toward successful demonstrations, with limited coverage of failure cases and off-target interactions ( Yang et al., 2026a ) . Yet world models for embodied scenarios require not only modeling successful trajectories, but also capturing failure dynamics and counterfactual outcomes induced by erroneous or suboptimal actions ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . In the absence of failure demonstrations, how to effectively synthesize failure scenarios to improve physical reasoning remains an important open problem.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

To this end, as shown in Fig. 1 , we propose a set of key insights to address the aforementioned challenges. 1) Firstly, we introduce a skeleton grounded action representation that bridges human and robotic action spaces through a shared spatial formulation ( Wu and Gao, 2026 ) , mitigating the cross embodiment gap. To better exploit egocentric human interaction data, we introduce pointflow supervision as a motion constraint that tracks point trajectories, capturing interaction driven dynamics ( Huang et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . We further apply a stabilization procedure on pointflows to suppress camera induced motion, ensuring that point trajectories primarily reflect interaction driven dynamics rather than viewpoint variations. This allows the model to better focus on physically meaningful motion signals and improves the effective utilization of egocentric human interaction data. The primary challenge in introducing failure cases is the lack of real failure video supervision, which limits direct learning under failure scenarios. 2) To address this, we propose a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) based reinforcement learning framework ( Liu et al., 2026 ) for post-training, enabling better modeling of failure dynamics using reward signals without requiring ground-truth failure video supervision.
Specifically, we construct pseudo failure actions by perturbing successful action trajectories, thereby inducing counterfactual action conditions. These perturbed actions are then used as conditions for video generation, where the model is optimized via reward-based feedback under GRPO.
The reward function consists of two complementary terms: a skeleton-based action following score that measures the consistency between the generated motion and the given action condition ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , and a physical plausibility score that evaluates whether the predicted dynamics remain physically consistent. Both rewards are computable without paired ground-truth videos, enabling GRPO post-training on perturbed actions to strengthen failure-aware dynamics modeling without direct supervision of the corresponding outcomes.

In summary, our main contributions are:

We present HF-WM, an action-conditioned world model that learns from egocentric human interactions and counterfactual action perturbations for embodied dynamics modeling.

We introduce a dual-branch framework with auxiliary pointflow supervision, establishing a shared motion representation across human and robot interactions that enables embodied world models to learn more effectively from egocentric human data.

We present a GRPO based post-training framework that enables failure aware optimization without paired failure video supervision.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that HF-WM achieves state-of-the-art performance in action-conditioned video generation, and further validate its effectiveness as a policy evaluator for downstream robotic tasks.

Controllable video generation. Controllable video generation as an important extension of video foundation models, aims to introduce diverse external control signals beyond text conditioning to enable fine-grained control over generated content. Recent work on controllable generation incorporates a variety of conditioning signals into existing video foundation models, including spatial structural information (e.g., human poses ( Hao et al., 2026 ) , depth maps ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , and skeletons ( Wu and Gao, 2026 ) ), temporal dynamics (e.g., optical flow ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , motion trajectories ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and camera parameters ( Tu et al., 2026 ) ), as well as multimodal inputs such as reference images or audio. These methods typically inject external control signals into pretrained video diffusion models through dedicated condition encoders ( Zhen et al., 2025 ) , cross-attention mechanisms ( YU et al., 2025 ) , or ControlNet architectures ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , thereby constraining and guiding the generation process.

Action-conditioned world models. Recent advances have positioned action-conditioned world models as a key interface between generative video modeling, action-conditioned dynamics prediction, and policy evaluation in embodied intelligence ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . IRASim ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) incorporates robotic trajectories into the video generation process, demonstrating the feasibility of synthesizing future visual states under explicit action conditions. Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2025 ) extends this paradigm to multi-view embodied generation, where three-view synthesis improves the spatial coverage of generated environments and yields practical gains in real-robot deployment. SC3-Eval ( Tseng et al., 2026 ) further closes the loop by leveraging world models as offline policy evaluators, enabling policies to be assessed without costly physical rollouts.
Despite recent progress, existing action-conditioned world models remain constrained by limited embodied data and failure coverage ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Wu and Gao, 2026 ) , motivating us to study how human object interaction data and counterfactual failure samples can improve the modeling of action consequences and physical dynamics.

2026-10-12.title: RESCUE: Is This Alarm Worth Acting On? Counterfactual Evaluation of VLA Runtime Monitors
2026-10-12.authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal , Abdelwahed Khamis , Mohammad Ali Armin , Lars Petersson
2026-10-12.abstract:
Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions.
Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed.
We introduce RESCUE, a counterfactual framework for evaluating whether a monitor’s alarms enable useful interventions.
By restoring simulator and policy states at execution checkpoints, RESCUE compares alternative actions, identifies the latest checkpoint satisfying a specified recovery criterion, and evaluates whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost.
We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} over LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus using 128,340 counterfactual branches.
Recoverability depends on the state–intervention pair rather than on robot state alone: at τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 , 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, compared with 34 of 66 under continuation or scripted recovery, while recovery reduces recoverability in other conditions.
On the primary strong-policy conditions, favourable detection scores do not establish lower intervention cost.
Under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0–3.3% false-alarm rate before unnecessary resets outweigh the savings from stopping failures early.
These results show that monitor value depends jointly on the intervention available and the workload in which it is deployed.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly capable of executing diverse robotic manipulation tasks from visual observations and language instructions [ 1 , 2 ] .
Despite this progress, long-horizon execution remains vulnerable to compounding errors, environmental perturbations, and out-of-distribution conditions.
Runtime monitors therefore aim to detect impending or ongoing failures from policy representations, observations, or predictive world models so that execution can be stopped, recovered, replanned, or escalated [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
These monitors are commonly selected using discrimination, calibration, or timing-aware detection metrics.

However, predicting failure and deciding whether to intervene are different problems.
A monitor may accurately distinguish failed from successful executions while still providing a poor intervention rule: an alarm may arrive after useful recovery has disappeared, or a false alarm may interrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed.
Conversely, an imperfect predictor may still be useful if it alarms while an effective and inexpensive intervention remains available.
Related agent studies similarly show that better failure prediction or calibration need not improve outcomes under intervention [ 7 , 8 ] .
In robotics, this distinction is particularly important because interventions alter physical state and may incur reset, delay, or damage costs.

Timing-aware evaluation addresses part of this problem, but elapsed time alone is insufficient. VLA-FAIL [ 4 ] incorporates detection time into monitor evaluation, PREFAIL [ 9 ] identifies an actionable intervention window for lift-and-place failures, and CheckVLA [ 5 ] defines an intervention-relative irreversibility time by testing whether a fixed set of repairs can still restore success.
CheckVLA establishes that actionability depends on available repairs, but leaves open how intervention value changes across the trajectory and whether acting remains preferable once false alarms and intervention costs are included [ 5 ] .
The same robot-policy state can therefore have different value under continuation, recovery, or stop-and-reset.

We introduce RESCUE ( R ecoverability E valuation of S topping C riteria U nder E xecution), a counterfactual framework for evaluating existing runtime monitors as intervention rules.
As illustrated in Fig. RESCUE: Is This Alarm Worth Acting On? Counterfactual Evaluation of VLA Runtime Monitors , RESCUE restores simulator and policy states at action-chunk boundaries and evaluates alternative interventions, estimating action-conditioned task success under a declared intervention repertoire 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , execution model ξ \xi , and remaining task budget B B .
Evaluating these outcomes across the trajectory yields a recoverability horizon : the latest checkpoint at which the declared repertoire satisfies a specified recovery criterion.
The horizon therefore depends explicitly on the available interventions, execution model, and task budget.

Recoverability establishes what can still succeed, but not whether intervention is worthwhile. Stopping a failed execution can save time, whereas an unnecessary stop incurs a reset and another attempt.
RESCUE therefore evaluates interventions in a common cost-to-completion space incorporating failure prevalence, alarm timing, false alarms, and intervention cost.
For stop-and-reset, this yields a closed-form break-even false-alarm rate computable from ordinary execution logs, allowing a monitor’s realised operating point to be compared directly with never intervening.

We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus [ 10 , 11 ] , comprising 1,562 trunk episodes and 128,340 counterfactual branches.
At τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 , only 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, while 34 of 66 clear under continuation or scripted recovery.
Under stop-and-reset, even an idealised detector that identifies every failure immediately can afford only a 2.78–3.32% false-alarm rate under the evaluated cost model.
A steps-since-progress monitor tuned to a nominal 5% operating point instead costs + 0.0835 +0.0835 reset-equivalents per completed task relative to never intervening.
Across matched evaluation sets, conventional detection and timing metrics admit the real monitors in 61 of 75 verdicts, whereas decision value admits none of 15 against never intervening.
These results show that failure-prediction quality alone does not establish intervention value.
Our contributions are:

We formulate runtime-monitor evaluation over state–intervention pairs and introduce a counterfactual branching protocol that estimates intervention success along robot-policy trajectories, yielding a recoverability horizon conditional on the intervention repertoire, execution model, and remaining task budget.

We complement recoverability with a decision-value formulation accounting for failure prevalence, alarm timing, false alarms, and intervention cost, and derive a closed-form break-even false-alarm criterion for stop-and-reset from standard execution logs.

We evaluate the framework at scale across two VLA policies and show that recoverability changes substantially with the available intervention, while monitors favoured by conventional detection and timing metrics can remain decision-negative when evaluated against the intervention they trigger.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

Runtime Failure Monitoring for Robot Policies. Runtime monitors detect execution failures using policy representations, action consistency, and predictive world models.
Sentinel [ 12 ] pairs temporal action consistency with VLM-based task-progress reasoning.
FIPER [ 13 ] combines embedding-space out-of-distribution detection with action-chunk uncertainty, conformally calibrating both scores on successful rollouts.
For VLA policies, SAFE [ 3 ] predicts failures from policy representations, VLA-FAIL [ 4 ] introduces AUCPDT to assess detection accuracy and timing, and Foresight [ 6 ] uses action-conditioned world-model latents to detect long-horizon manipulation failures.
These works primarily evaluate how reliably and how early failures are identified.
CheckVLA [ 5 ] couples detection to repair by evaluating suffix rewrites from restored simulator states.
It defines an irreversibility time beyond which none of its tested repairs restores success, and reports rescue, harm, and task success.
RESCUE instead compares alternative interventions throughout execution and evaluates whether acting on alarms lowers expected task-completion cost under the workload’s failure prevalence and intervention costs.

Failure Recovery and Intervention Timing. Recovery methods address how a robot should respond when execution goes wrong.
AEGIS [ 14 ] selectively escalates to a stronger policy,
B2FF [ 15 ] selects a pre-imagined familiar future as a recovery goal, and
Rewind-IL [ 16 ] returns the robot toward a previously verified safe state.
PREFAIL [ 9 ] identifies the latest actionable intervention time for lift-and-place failures, assessing whether predictions arrive early enough to prevent failure.
These works focus on designing recovery behaviour or assessing whether intervention occurs within an actionable window.
RESCUE instead evaluates declared branchable interventions from every saved action-chunk boundary, allowing recovery opportunities to be measured throughout execution rather than only at a single trigger point.
The recoverability estimate is conditional on the intervention repertoire, execution model, and remaining task budget.
RESCUE therefore defines the recoverability horizon as the latest checkpoint satisfying the recovery criterion, without assuming that recoverability decreases monotonically with execution time.

From Prediction Quality to Decision Value. Predictive accuracy does not guarantee beneficial decisions, a distinction reflected in cost-sensitive learning [ 17 ] and critiques of aggregate evaluation measures [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] .
ThriftyDAgger [ 21 ] studies intervention budgets in interactive imitation learning.
For LLM agents, Vasudev et al. [ 7 ] show that interventions can both rescue failed executions and disrupt successful ones.
Zhang et al. [ 8 ] measure intervention advantage by branching alternative actions from the same execution prefix, showing that better risk calibration need not reduce control regret.
RESCUE brings this decision-oriented view to robot manipulation, where interventions alter physical state and resets require another attempt.
It evaluates existing monitors by comparing counterfactual interventions from restored robot-policy states and measuring expected cost per completed task under a reset-and-retry model.
Rather than computing a model-based reachable set [ 22 ] , RESCUE estimates action-conditioned recoverability empirically from restored execution states.
For stop-and-reset, this yields a break-even false-alarm rate computable from ordinary execution logs.

2026-10-12.title: Reflect-VLA: Internalizing Reflective Guidance via Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation for Autonomous Driving
2026-10-12.authors: Yuechen Luo , He Chong , Fang Li , Shaoqing Xu , Hexin Zhang , Ruiqi Zhang , Ziying Song , Lei Yang , Zhi-Xin Yang , Fuxi Wen
2026-10-12.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) substantially improves planning performance in autonomous-driving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar trajectory rewards that measure overall quality but fail to identify specific planning errors or provide actionable correction signals. In long-tail scenarios, errors in scene understanding, behavior selection, and trajectory execution are compressed into a single score. We observe that Reflective Guidance turns trajectory evaluation into explicit diagnoses and corrective instructions, substantially improving planning accuracy. Yet such guidance requires an initial prediction and its evaluation results, making it unavailable for direct single-pass inference. We propose Reflect-VLA , which treats Reflective Guidance as training-time privileged information and internalizes its planning benefits through Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation (Dual-OPSD) . Unlike scalar-reward optimization, Dual-OPSD uses the driving score only to route student-generated trajectories. It distills dense token-level corrective distributions from the teacher for risky trajectories while applying self-imitation to preserve reliable ones. To provide reliable corrective distributions on student rollouts, the teacher is progressively constructed through Driving-Knowledge Pretraining, Planning-and-Refinement SFT, and Self-Refinement Rejection Sampling. At inference time, Reflect-VLA generates trajectories in a single pass without explicit guidance or iterative refinement. Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 and Bench2Drive demonstrate competitive planning performance while reducing training time by over 90% compared with RL.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Autonomous driving is shifting from conventional modular pipelines toward end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems ( Jiang et al. 2025b ) . Unlike modular systems ( Hu et al. 2023 ; Jiang et al. 2023 ; Chen et al. 2024 ) that coordinate perception, prediction, and planning through handcrafted interfaces, VLA models integrate visual observations, language instructions and action generation within a unified architecture. Recent driving VLA methods commonly adopt a multi-stage training paradigm ( Li et al. 2025c ; Zhou et al. 2025b ; Luo et al. 2025a ; Luo et al. 2026b ; Lu et al. 2026 ) . They first acquire domain knowledge from large-scale driving question-answering data, then learn trajectory generation through supervised fine-tuning, and finally improve the policy using reinforcement learning or planning-oriented objectives.

Despite progress, VLA models struggle to learn from planning failures, especially in complex and long-tail scenarios. A scalar planning score can identify a poor trajectory but cannot reveal whether the error arises from scene understanding, behavior selection, or trajectory execution, nor indicate how to correct it. Trajectory-level rewards collapse these heterogeneous failure modes into a single value, leaving the model without a direction for improvement. ELF-VLA ( Luo et al. 2026a ) alleviates this problem by introducing structured failure information, showing that detailed feedback can guide the correction of failed trajectories. However, how to convert feedback-assisted correction into an intrinsic single-pass planning capability remains underexplored.

We begin with a key observation: Reflective Guidance provides substantial planning gains . As illustrated in Fig. 1 , a VLA model may produce an incorrect trajectory during direct inference, yet generate a markedly better trajectory when provided with evaluation-derived diagnoses and corrective suggestions ( Yang et al. 2026 ; He et al. 2026 ; Chen et al. 2026b ) . Constructing the guidance requires both an initial trajectory and its evaluation results, whereas an autonomous driving system must produce an executable plan before acting. The central challenge is therefore not to perform iterative refinement at inference time, but to transfer the planning preferences induced by Reflective Guidance into the model’s direct trajectory-generation policy.

To this end, we propose Reflect-VLA , a training framework that treats Reflective Guidance as privileged information and internalizes its planning benefits through Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation (Dual-OPSD) . Starting from the same VLA checkpoint, the model supplied with Reflective Guidance acts as the frozen teacher, while the model receiving standard inputs acts as the student. The student first generates trajectories from the input available at deployment. A planning score then routes each trajectory to one of two learning paths. For risky or suboptimal trajectories, the teacher provides dense token-level distributions that encode corrective planning preferences. For reliable trajectories, a self-imitation objective preserves the student’s existing decisions. The scalar score is therefore used only for trajectory-quality-aware routing, while the teacher distribution supplies the fine-grained supervision required for correction.

Effective self-distillation requires a teacher that can refine trajectories drawn from the student’s rollout distribution. We construct this teacher using a progressive strategy comprising Driving-Knowledge Pretraining, Planning-and-Refinement SFT, and Self-Refinement Rejection Sampling. The first two stages establish driving knowledge, direct trajectory generation, and guidance-assisted refinement. The final stage exposes the teacher to student-generated failures and retains verified refinements, reducing the distribution gap between offline refinement data and on-policy trajectories. After Dual-OPSD, Reflect-VLA performs single-pass trajectory generation without Reflective Guidance, an online planning evaluator, or an iterative correction procedure.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We construct Reflective Guidance that converts trajectory evaluation results into structured, trajectory-specific diagnoses and corrective suggestions, and use it as privileged information available only during training.

We propose Dual-OPSD, a trajectory-quality-aware self-distillation method that transfers corrective distributions for risky trajectories while preserving reliable planning.

We develop a progressive teacher-construction strategy that combines driving-knowledge pretraining, planning-and-refinement supervision, and self-refinement rejection sampling to support stable guidance internalization and efficient single-pass planning.

1. We construct Reflective Guidance that converts trajectory evaluation results into structured, trajectory-specific diagnoses and corrective suggestions, and use it as privileged information available only during training.

2. We propose Dual-OPSD, a trajectory-quality-aware self-distillation method that transfers corrective distributions for risky trajectories while preserving reliable planning.

3. We develop a progressive teacher-construction strategy that combines driving-knowledge pretraining, planning-and-refinement supervision, and self-refinement rejection sampling to support stable guidance internalization and efficient single-pass planning.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 VLA models for autonomous driving

VLMs and VLA models have been increasingly studied for autonomous driving, with applications ranging from scene understanding ( Jiang et al. 2024 ; Jiang et al. 2025a ; Marcu et al. 2024 ) to direct trajectory prediction ( Xing et al. 2025 ; Zhao et al. 2025 ; Liu et al. 2025 ; Fu et al. 2025 ) . To improve interpretability and planning accuracy, several methods introduce explicit intermediate reasoning, such as Chain-of-Thought reasoning ( Liu et al. 2025 ; Zhao et al. 2025 ; Luo et al. 2025b ) . Their training pipelines typically begin with supervised fine-tuning on driving data and subsequently apply reinforcement learning, including Group Relative Policy Optimization, to improve planning performance ( Luo et al. 2025a ; Zhou et al. 2025b ) . Although scalar planning rewards provide a direct measure of trajectory quality, they offer limited supervision when diverse failure causes receive similarly low scores ( Chen et al. 2026a ) . This issue is especially pronounced in long-tail scenarios, where repeated low-reward rollouts can make policy optimization inefficient. ELF-VLA ( Luo et al. 2026a ) addresses this limitation by using teacher-generated feedback to diagnose planning failures and construct improved training samples. Our work instead focuses on internalizing the benefit of such structured guidance so that it is no longer required during inference.

## 2.2 On-Policy Distillation and On-Policy Self-Distillation

On-policy distillation (OPD) and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) are post-training approaches that supervise a student on trajectories sampled from its own policy ( Agarwal et al. 2024 ; Zhao et al. 2026 ) . Unlike off-policy distillation, this formulation queries a teacher with student-generated prefixes, thereby providing token-level supervision over the distribution encountered during training. OPD commonly relies on a separately trained teacher, whereas OPSD can derive the teacher from the same model by conditioning it on privileged information ( Ye et al. 2026 ; Sang et al. 2026 ) , such as ground-truth answers, additional instructions, or preference information. Recent work has combined dense token-level signals from OPD with reinforcement learning for VLA post-training ( Zhong et al. 2026 ) , but its application to autonomous-driving planning remains limited. We formulate Reflective Guidance as privileged information and use it to obtain corrective teacher distributions on student-generated trajectories. Dual-OPSD further accounts for trajectory quality by distilling corrections only when needed and preserving decisions that are already reliable.

2026-10-12.title: ManeuverFlow: Maneuver Hypothesis Generation with Future Evidence for Trajectory Evaluation and Refinement in End-to-End Autonomous Driving
2026-10-12.authors: Yuhao Wei , Yong Chen , Chen Yang , Yingchen Wang , Delin Ouyang , Lingfeng Qi , Qi Lan , Zhanhua Zhang , Jie Li , Guofa Li
2026-10-12.abstract:
End-to-end planning in complex scenes must model diverse driving intentions and select the most appropriate trajectory using scene context and future risks.
However, multi-query regression may collapse to one mode, while anchor-based and generative planners share a scaling bottleneck: small candidate sets limit maneuver coverage or discovery of high-quality trajectories, whereas large sets increase generation and scoring costs.
We propose ManeuverFlow to generate trajectories for distinct intentions in one step and evaluate and refine them using current and future evidence.
The model selects relevant maneuver modes, draws corresponding noise from the Gaussian mixture prior, and maps it to intention-specific trajectories through a maneuver-routed mixture-of-experts MeanFlow field.
Current features and future features predicted by the world model are aggregated along each candidate path into trajectory-specific evidence for PDM-factor prediction.
Using the same evidence, the refiner predicts local Frenet residuals for selected candidates; refined and retained candidates are then jointly re-scored for selection.
With a lightweight TransFuser-style ResNet-34 backbone, ManeuverFlow achieves 90.6 PDMS and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v1/v2 navtest , respectively.
On WorldEngine’s recent 3DGS closed-loop benchmark, it attains the highest listed PDMS ∗ scores of 75.19 and 74.58 under logged and IDM-controlled traffic, respectively.

2026-10-12.introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving maps sensor observations, ego states, and navigation cues directly to future ego motion, unifying perception and planning under a single objective ( Chitta et al. 2023 ; Hu et al. 2022b ; Hu et al. 2023 ; Jiang et al. 2023 ; Jia et al. 2023 ; Sun et al. 2025 ) . Complex traffic scenes often admit multiple plausible driving hypotheses, so a single trajectory cannot capture the underlying decision space. Multimodal motion forecasting represents this ambiguity with fixed anchor vocabularies or mode-specific queries ( Chai et al. 2020 ; Shi et al. 2022 ) ; recent planners further use learned queries, trajectory anchors, and diffusion- or flow-based generators to produce candidates, then select a final plan through candidate–scene interactions ( Jiang et al. 2026 ; Li et al. 2024b ; Liao et al. 2025 ; Xing et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2026 ) . As shown in Fig. 1 (a), learned queries without explicit mode-level structure may concentrate in similar regions of trajectory space, producing redundant candidates and risking mode collapse.

Standard diffusion and ODE-based flow sampling is iterative ( Lipman et al. 2023 ; Liu, Gong, and Liu 2023 ) , although recent driving planners reduce the process to two steps in DiffusionDrive ( Liao et al. 2025 ) or one step in GoalFlow and MeanFuser ( Xing et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2026 ) . MeanFuser generates multiple proposals in one MeanFlow step, but its Adaptive Reconstruction Module (ARM) attends to and fuses them into a single output trajectory; the initial hypotheses thus do not remain explicit candidates for downstream evaluation, refinement, and selection ( Wang et al. 2026 ) . Fixed anchors encode predefined modes but may allocate part of the candidate budget to modes weakly relevant to the current scene. For a frozen generator, Fig. 2 retrospectively shows that larger pools expose stronger candidates. This motivates improving candidate quality under a compact proposal budget through scene-adaptive hypothesis generation and evidence-conditioned local trajectory refinement.

Candidate generation also requires reliable selection. Candidate-tree and generation–evaluation planners pair ego hypotheses with conditional predictions or learned evaluators ( Huang et al. 2024 ; Huang et al. 2025 ) , whereas current-only scorers do not explicitly query predicted future scene states along candidate paths. WoTE provides such evidence through one future rollout per candidate (Fig. 1 (b)), repeating future BEV prediction across candidate trajectories and multiple future time steps ( Li et al. 2025b ) .

Together, these limitations define a fixed-budget hypothesis-lifecycle problem. We therefore ask: How can a planner generate scene-relevant, mode-distinct hypotheses under a fixed budget and use current/future evidence to evaluate, refine, and select them?

To this end, we propose ManeuverFlow , a unified Hypothesize–Verify–Improve framework that preserves explicit maneuver-indexed hypotheses, as shown in Figs. 1 (c) and 3 . The Maneuver Gaussian Mixture Prior (M-GMP) predicts scene-conditioned weights over motion-defined components, and M 3 F generates base hypotheses by maneuver-routed one-step transport. Once per planning step, the world model predicts one candidate-independent future BEV field; a learned trajectory-guided probe projects each hypothesis into the current and predicted fields to form path-specific Trajectory Evidence Memory. Metric Prism pre-scores candidates through learned PDM factors. The Evidence-Coupled Frenet Refiner (ECFR) uses the same evidence to predict local Frenet residuals for selected hypotheses. Refined hypotheses replace selected bases, re-query the shared field, and compete with retained hypotheses under the same Metric Prism scoring function.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Scene-adaptive maneuver generation. We introduce a maneuver-structured generator that combines M-GMP with the maneuver-routed M 3 F to model motion-defined maneuver components and generate scene-adaptive, intent-conditioned trajectory hypotheses as explicit alternatives in one step.

Future-evidence verification and refinement. A learned probe projects each candidate onto a shared future BEV field to extract trajectory-specific evidence for PDM-aligned scoring and ECFR’s local Frenet refinement. Metric Prism jointly re-scores refined and retained hypotheses for final selection.

With a lightweight ResNet-34 TransFuser (TF) perception backbone, ManeuverFlow-TF achieves 90.58 PDMS and 90.14 EPDMS on NAVSIM v1/v2 navtest , respectively. Its camera-only Latent TransFuser (LTF) variant further obtains 75.19 and 74.58 PDMS ∗ under replayed and reactive traffic on WorldEngine, delivering the highest listed composite planning scores across all reported benchmark and traffic settings.

2. Future-evidence verification and refinement. A learned probe projects each candidate onto a shared future BEV field to extract trajectory-specific evidence for PDM-aligned scoring and ECFR’s local Frenet refinement. Metric Prism jointly re-scores refined and retained hypotheses for final selection.

2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 End-to-End and Generative Planning

End-to-end planners predict ego motion from sensor observations, ego states, and navigation commands. TransFuser fuses camera and LiDAR features, while later systems introduce planning-oriented queries and sparse scene representations ( Chitta et al. 2023 ; Hu et al. 2023 ; Jiang et al. 2023 ; Sun et al. 2025 ) . Generative planners model multiple feasible decisions through structured latent spaces, diffusion, or flow matching: GenAD learns a trajectory latent space, Diffusion Planner and DiffusionDrive denoise trajectory distributions, and GoalFlow applies goal-conditioned flow matching ( Zheng et al. 2024 ; Zheng et al. 2025a ; Liao et al. 2025 ; Xing et al. 2025 ) . MeanFuser combines a Gaussian-mixture source with one-step MeanFlow and aggregates sampled proposals into a single ARM output ( Geng et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2026 ) . MM-FM jointly designs a Gaussian-mixture source and mode-dependent coupling for general multimodal generation ( Luo et al. 2026 ) . A challenge is to organize driving-specific motion modes and retain diverse hypotheses as an explicit interface for evaluation and refinement.

## 2.2 World Models for Planning

Driving world models predict visual observations, occupancy, or latent states to support planning. MILE jointly learns latent dynamics and a driving policy, Think2Drive trains a planner through interaction with a compact latent world model, and LAW learns self-supervised latent dynamics ( Hu et al. 2022a ; Li et al. 2024a ; Li et al. 2025a ) . Drive-WM, Drive-OccWorld, World4Drive, and WorldRFT use predicted visual, occupancy, or latent futures for planning evaluation and optimization ( Wang et al. 2024 ; Yang et al. 2025 ; Zheng et al. 2025b ; Yang et al. 2026 ) . For online evaluation, WoTE runs a recurrent BEV world model for each anchor-refined candidate and selects the highest-scoring trajectory ( Li et al. 2025b ) . Candidate-conditioned rollouts provide trajectory-specific futures but require separate computation for every candidate. Shared predictions, such as the future occupancy used by ST-P3, amortize forecasting across candidates ( Hu et al. 2022b ) but do not directly provide path-specific evidence. Extracting discriminative, trajectory-specific evidence from a shared forecast without repeated candidate-wise rollouts therefore remains a key challenge.

## 2.3 Trajectory Refinement and Selection

Candidate-based planning requires both reliable discrimination and local geometric improvement. VADv2 models a distribution over a discrete planning vocabulary, while Hydra-MDP distills human and rule-based teachers into metric-specific trajectory heads ( Jiang et al. 2026 ; Li et al. 2024b ) . DTPP learns context-dependent costs, Gen-Drive learns a candidate evaluator, and DriveSuprim improves hard-negative discrimination through coarse-to-fine filtering and self-distillation ( Huang et al. 2024 ; Huang et al. 2025 ; Yao et al. 2026 ) . For trajectory refinement, ThinkTwice and ResWorld use predicted future information to update an initial plan ( Jia et al. 2023 ; Zhang et al. 2026 ) . These lines of work separately strengthen candidate evaluation and trajectory refinement, but their coordination within a common hypothesis pool remains less explored. Retaining unrefined alternatives and directly comparing retained and refined trajectories under the same future-conditioned evaluator thus remains an open design problem.
