2026-10-12.title: Robot-WATCHDOG : failure detection through object-centric graph representation
2026-10-12.authors: Quentin Rolland , Fabrice Mayran de Chamisso , Jean-Baptiste Mouret
2026-10-12.abstract: Reliable real-time failure detection is critical for deploying learned robotic policies, yet defining failures explicitly is infeasible in open-world settings. This motivates failure detection from nominal demonstrations alone. Existing methods, however, struggle to balance robustness to benign variations with the ability to capture semantic and interaction-level errors. We introduce Robot-WATCHDOG , a self-supervised framework that models manipulation scenes as object-centric spatio-temporal graphs. Building on this representation, we investigate two complementary failure scores: Trajectory Projection and Correlation (TPC) , a non-parametric measure of geometric deviation and relational consistency, and GnnT , a Graph Attention Network with a Transformer that predicts future object states. We evaluate both on a public benchmark and on a new dataset of semantically complex manipulation tasks, across six tasks and ten random seeds. Both scores outperform image-based failure detectors, particularly on semantic and interaction-level failures. TPC provides the strongest performance in AUPR and MCC on both dataset averages, with low variance across seeds. Qualitative results are made available at https://cea-list.github.io/Robot-WATCHDOG/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Learned robotic policies provide no guarantees beyond the distribution induced by training demonstrations [ 2 ] . Detecting deviations from expected behavior is therefore essential for accountable deployment, and increasingly emphasized in regulation for high-risk AI systems such as the EU AI Act [ 18 , 37 ] . As imitation learning and vision-language-conditioned policies increasingly enable long-horizon, closed-loop manipulation [ 9 , 42 , 6 , 24 , 21 , 30 ] , policies are executed autonomously in real time and without step-by-step human intervention, motivating dedicated monitoring systems that operate online, require no failure examples, and can identify anomalous behavior before errors propagate.

Explicitly enumerating all possible failures, however, is infeasible in open-world robotic settings. The standard framing therefore casts failure detection as a one-class problem [ 41 , 32 , 33 ] : a monitor trained exclusively on nominal demonstrations must identify, at runtime, deviations from expected behavior. Existing approaches divide broadly into two families. Visual failure detectors [ 35 , 15 , 43 , 32 ] flag deviations in raw image space or learned visual representations. They are sensitive to benign background changes, lighting shifts, and visual clutter, producing frequent false positives that erode operational efficiency. Kinematic and action-based monitors [ 27 , 14 , 38 ] instead operate on trajectory or joint-space signals; they are robust to visual noise but structurally blind to the environment. They only verify whether the movement itself is familiar, failing to detect if the robot is interacting with the wrong object or operating in an environment that mismatches training.

This division points to a broader limitation. A substantial class of failures in robotic manipulation does not arise from abnormal motion or corrupted observations, but from incorrect interactions between otherwise familiar objects: grasping the wrong item, violating task-order constraints, or placing an object in an incorrect spatial relation to others [ 23 , 8 ] . These failures emerge naturally in manipulation tasks whose success depends on object identity, relative placement, and sequential consistency, yet they remain difficult to capture when monitoring is restricted to either image appearance or motion trajectories alone.

The central idea of this work is to recast robotic failure detection as monitoring the evolution of object interactions over time. Rather than treating visual and kinematic signals as separate modalities, we represent the scene as a spatio-temporal graph of interacting objects, where nodes encode object states and edges encode their pairwise spatial relationships throughout execution. This object-centric formulation generalizes prior monitoring approaches: visual detectors can be interpreted as operating on node appearance, while kinematic monitors correspond to tracking motion along trajectories. By jointly modeling objects, their relations, and their temporal evolution in a unified representation, the proposed framework captures both the signals targeted by prior work and the relational structure required to detect task-relevant interaction failures.

Failure detection then becomes a well-posed problem: deviations from reference relational dynamics constitute anomalies. We instantiate this principle in Robot-WATCHDOG, a self-supervised framework that abstracts a manipulation episode into an object-centric spatio-temporal graph and scores each timestep against expert demonstrations. Within this representation we study two scoring functions. TPC (Trajectory Projection and Correlation) is non-parametric: it measures orthogonal projection distances to expert trajectories together with deviations in the pairwise correlation structure between objects. GnnT couples a Graph Attention Network with a Transformer encoder to predict future object dynamics from a sliding observation window, and flags prediction errors. Both are converted into binary decisions by conformal prediction calibrated on held-out expert demonstrations, which sets the decision threshold from a user-specified level without tuning the threshold on failure examples.

We evaluate Robot-WATCHDOG on four tasks of the public BotFails benchmark [ 32 ] and on a newly introduced dataset featuring two relationally challenging manipulation tasks: structured table setting and waste sorting on a moving conveyor belt. All results are averaged over ten seeds, each redrawing the expert partition and the network initialisation. Both object-centric scores outperform image-based detectors, and TPC is consistently the stronger of the two: averaged per dataset it reaches AUPR 0.81 and maximum MCC 0.75 (BotFails) and 0.81 / 0.72 (Watchdog), against 0.62 / 0.49 and 0.65 / 0.63 for GnnT, while the best baseline reaches only 0.44 / 0.32 and 0.35 / 0.34. After conformal calibration, TPC attains MCC 0.68 and 0.64 where the strongest baseline reaches 0.22 and 0.33. The learned score only leads in the continuously dynamic conveyor scene. Methods that perform well on simple kinematic deviations struggle with relational failures involving object identity and spatial arrangement, the very setting Robot-WATCHDOG addresses.

Our main contributions are: (i) identifying relational anomalies as a key yet underexplored failure mode in robotic manipulation, arising from dependencies on object identity, spatial arrangement, and temporal consistency; (ii) introducing two scoring functions: TPC (Trajectory Projection and Correlation) a non-parametric, geometric method and GnnT, a spatio-temporal graph formulation ; and (iii) releasing a benchmark of relationally challenging manipulation tasks with annotated relational failures.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 RELATED WORK

## 2.1 Graph oriented object representation

A growing line of work in robotics and visuomotor learning has explored object-centric graph representations, where nodes encode task-relevant entities and edges capture spatial, label-conditioned, or action-conditioned relations [ 44 , 25 , 4 ] . Such representations improve invariance to irrelevant visual variations and provide a structured way to model interactions between objects. Building on this paradigm, several approaches construct dynamic or action-conditioned scene graphs to model evolving environments, improving robustness and generalization in manipulation tasks [ 22 , 19 ] . In parallel, graph neural networks have been leveraged for relational policy learning, planning, and dynamics prediction, demonstrating improved scalability in multi-object settings [ 20 , 36 ] . More recently, Vosylius et al. [ 39 ] show that graph-structured representations can support in-context policy adaptation by modeling demonstrations over relational structures. Recent progress in vision-language models and object tracking has also made these representations increasingly practical in robotics, enabling automatic extraction of task-relevant objects and trajectories directly from RGB observations. To our knowledge, while object-centric graph representations have shown strong promise for policy learning and planning, they have received limited attention for online failure detection, motivating their investigation in this work.

## 2.2 Failure detection in autonomous robotics

Existing real-time monitors struggle to balance environmental awareness, robustness to benign variations, and sensitivity to task-relevant object interactions. Furthermore, many traditional failure classifiers [ 13 , 28 , 29 ] require collecting explicit failure data a priori , a time-consuming process that scales poorly to open-world robotic deployment. Consequently, recent efforts focus on one-class methods trained exclusively on nominal demonstrations. However, vision-based detectors like FIDeL [ 32 ] remain highly sensitive to visual clutter. Sentinel [ 1 ] attempts to bridge the modality gap by combining STAC : a statistical measure of kinematic action consistency, with a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for visual verification. Yet, STAC remains blind to environment-only failures, and the VLM fallback introduces severe inference latency unsuited for reactive continuous control. Similarly, FAIL-Detect [ 41 ] merges modalities through latent concatenation, while FIPER [ 33 ] relies on brittle logical conjunctions.

Crucially, these approaches often struggle to capture failures involving object identity, spatial arrangement, or task progression, such as grasping the wrong object, executing sub-actions out of order, or misplacing items. Such errors often produce nominal kinematic profiles and only subtle pixel-level changes, making them difficult to detect with action-consistency metrics or standard visual anomaly detectors.

Our framework, Robot-WATCHDOG, addresses these limitations through an object-centric representation of scene dynamics. By abstracting tracked entities into a spatio-temporal graph, the framework reduces sensitivity to irrelevant visual variation while preserving explicit environmental context unavailable to kinematic-only monitors. Representing the scene in a relational geometric space also enables anomaly detection based on changes in object interactions over time, either directly, by comparing object trajectories and their pairwise correlations to expert demonstrations (TPC), or through a predictive GNN-Transformer that jointly models object identities, spatial configurations, and temporal dependencies (GnnT). Both enable real-time detection of relational failure modes that remain challenging for existing multimodal baselines, without requiring failure demonstrations during training.

2026-10-12.title: EndoRSI: Physical-Evidence-Driven Recursive Improvement of Endoscopic Robot Policies
2026-10-12.authors: Chi Kit Ng , Yidong Zhang , Tianchun Wu , Siu Hing Lui , Hanlin Zhao , Huxin Gao , Hongliang Ren
2026-10-12.abstract: Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate scientific discovery, yet physical robot-policy research still relies on scientists and engineers to interpret experimental failures and decide how controllers should be revised. We present EndoRSI (Endoscopic Recursive Self-Improvement), a human-governed, self-improving robotic research system in which the embedded EndoForge coding agent iteratively develops and refines endoscopic robot policies using evidence from physical experiments. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best-performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot-policy research.

2026-10-12.title: PartiGen: Part-Aware Representations for Language-Conditioned Humanoid Motion Generation
2026-10-12.authors: Chuxuan Huang , Zhanxiang Cao , Tianyue Zhan , Haoyang Li , Yang Zhang , Liyun Yan , Chenlin Ming , Keqi Zhu , Yizhi Chen , Shengcheng Fu , Zihao Zhou , Xinyi Peng , Kaixuan Zhang , Boyang Xing , Jiawei Bao , Yang Yang , Yue Gao
2026-10-12.abstract: Translating language into humanoid motion requires coordinating body parts, determining motion duration, and producing references suitable for robot execution. We introduce PartiGen , a part-aware latent diffusion framework that incorporates anatomical structure into a shared whole-body motion representation. Part-specific attention processes anatomically masked frame features, and its outputs are fused to combine local limb information with whole-body context. Conditioned on text and motion history, the model generates motion primitives autoregressively. Forward-kinematics supervision encourages kinematic consistency, while a learned end-of-sequence predictor selects a frame-level endpoint after generation. On HumanML3D retargeted to the Unitree G1, PartiGen achieves a segment-level FID of 3.165, a 16.8% reduction over TextOp, and improves R@1 by 1.4 percentage points. In the duration study with 16-frame primitives, endpoint prediction reduces mean absolute duration error from 12.471 to 3.080 frames compared with a fixed-length cutoff. We further evaluate robot execution using a pretrained, frozen GRIT tracker: 409 of 500 generated references (81.8%) pass the posture-based stability screen in MuJoCo. Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 attempted motions are judged successful on the real G1.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Natural language offers an intuitive interface for specifying whole-body humanoid behaviors. Text-to-motion generation ( Guo et al., 2022a ; Tevet et al., 2022 ; Guo et al., 2024 ) supports their synthesis, but visually plausible motion may violate robot joint limits, dynamics, actuator capabilities, or contact constraints. We study a system in which a language-conditioned generator specifies a whole-body reference and its temporal extent, while a tracking controller uses robot-state feedback to produce joint-level control targets. The challenge is to generate references that express the requested behavior while accounting for the robot’s motion constraints and the task’s temporal organization.

An instruction such as “walk while waving” illustrates the challenge: the arm gesture and locomotion must coexist within a single robot trajectory, with consistent root motion, joint configurations, and timing. A reference generator therefore needs to preserve the distinct roles of body parts while representing their relationships within a shared whole-body context. Part-aware modeling ( Zhong et al., 2023 ) and physics-guided generation ( Yuan et al., 2023 ) provide relevant foundations for addressing these requirements. We investigate how an anatomical prior can guide local feature processing within a shared robot-motion representation, together with kinematic supervision of the resulting trajectory. Its temporal extent must also reflect the instruction, with an endpoint that need not coincide with the boundary of a fixed-length motion primitive. These considerations connect body-part structure, kinematic consistency, and endpoint selection within the same robot reference-generation problem.

We propose PartiGen , integrating language-conditioned humanoid motion generation and execution. Part-aware attention builds a shared whole-body representation from anatomically masked inputs. Text- and history-conditioned latent diffusion generates motion primitives under forward-kinematics supervision, followed by frame-level endpoint selection on the complete candidate trajectory. A pretrained, frozen GRIT controller ( mrzuang, 2026 ) tracks the references using robot-state feedback in MuJoCo and on the Unitree G1.

Our contributions are:

An anatomical input-grouping mechanism for robot motion representation learning. Fixed masks select joint-angle channels before independent Q/K/V projections, while shared motion features and a single whole-body latent retain access to global context.

A language-conditioned motion generation framework with frame-level endpoint prediction. Conditioned on text and motion history, the framework autoregressively generates motion primitives in the shared latent space under forward-kinematics supervision. A learned end-of-sequence predictor then selects an endpoint within the complete candidate trajectory.

Simulation and real-world validation. Integrated with a frozen GRIT controller, PartiGen achieves an 81.8% posture-screen pass rate over 500 simulated references. Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 motions attempted on a physical Unitree G1 are judged successful by the authors.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Large-scale motion datasets ( Guo et al., 2022a ; Mahmood et al., 2019 ; Punnakkal et al., 2021 ) provide a foundation for data-driven generation. Common modeling paradigms include variational motion models ( Guo et al., 2020 ; Petrovich et al., 2021 ; Petrovich et al., 2022 ) , diffusion-based generation ( Tevet et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) , and discrete motion tokenization ( Guo et al., 2022b ; Jiang et al., 2023 ) . Motion representation learning ( Zhu et al., 2023 ) and controllable diffusion priors ( Karunratanakul et al., 2023 ; Shafir et al., 2023 ) offer complementary approaches to encoding and manipulating motion. DART and TextOp ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) further address autoregressive generation and interactive control. Building on autoregressive primitive generation, PartiGen incorporates anatomical input masks and EOS-based endpoint prediction.

Part-aware attention ( Zhong et al., 2023 ) and skeleton-aware latent diffusion ( Hong et al., 2025 ) incorporate anatomical structure into motion representations. Hierarchical models address fine-grained semantic control ( Jin et al., 2023 ) and human-object interaction ( Pi et al., 2023 ) , while cross-skeleton models accommodate varying skeletal structures ( Khani et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Gat et al., 2025 ) . Skeleton conditioning has also been explored for human image generation ( Ju et al., 2023 ) . PartiGen places its anatomical prior at the attention input through fixed masks on raw frame features before part-specific Q/K/V projections. Each head receives its selected joint angles together with shared root/contact features and all joint-angle increments. Head outputs are fused into a shared stream, retaining a single motion latent rather than independent part latents.

PhysDiff and InterDiff incorporate physical constraints into motion or interaction generation ( Yuan et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2023 ) . Language-conditioned humanoid generation and control ( Jiang et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , motion retargeting ( Araujo et al., 2025 ) , and whole-body teleoperation ( Ze et al., 2025 ) connect motion modeling to robot behavior. A2CF supports humanoid policy learning through state-dependent assistive forces that gradually diminish as proficiency improves ( Cao et al., 2025 ) . HiWET uses hierarchical reinforcement learning for world-frame end-effector tracking in long-horizon humanoid loco-manipulation ( Cao et al., 2026 ) . PartiGen combines FK-supervised motion generation with an execution component based on the pretrained, frozen GRIT controller ( mrzuang, 2026 ) . Kinematic supervision regularizes references during generator training; execution evaluation measures their tracking under this adopted controller.

Sequence continuation and termination are distinct design choices. Related temporal generation frameworks include latent audio diffusion ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , neural-codec speech modeling ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , and autoregressive video diffusion ( Henschel et al., 2025 ) . For motion, PartiGen selects an endpoint at frame resolution. It generates a complete candidate sequence before applying an EOS probability threshold to select its endpoint; this selection does not stop generation online.

2026-10-12.title: Evo-RL: Iterative Robot Reinforcement Learning from Selective Experience
2026-10-12.authors: Kai Ye , Yifan Jin , Qianhang Luo , Hongru Zhang , Jiedong Zhang , Shuyuan Hu , Song-Yuan Wu , Jihai Xu , Jie Zhao , Bo Zhao
2026-10-12.abstract: Existing real-world reinforcement learning methods improve robot policies by combining human corrections with autonomous rollouts. However, accumulated experience varies in its value for policy improvement, and even successful trajectories can contain inefficient or redundant behavior, motivating more selective experience reuse. To this end, we propose Evo-RL, an iterative reinforcement learning method that combines human interventions with advantage-guided experience selection. Evo-RL uses human corrections and experience with positive estimated advantages from successful trajectories to iteratively refine the policy. To support learning from these different experience sources, we introduce RW-RL-Dataset, which spans over 1,000 hours across four robot embodiments. On a real-world high-precision manipulation task, Evo-RL improves attempt success rate over RECAP by 30.46%. Our code, model checkpoints, and dataset are publicly available.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models generate robot actions by conditioning on visual observations and language instructions [ 1 ] . Recent advances have extended their applicability to a wider range of tasks and robot embodiments [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] and improved deployment efficiency [ 5 ] . Yet policies trained on demonstrations can still encounter unfamiliar states during deployment, where errors can accumulate and recovery may be difficult [ 6 ] . These limitations motivate continued policy improvement using experience collected during execution.

Existing approaches support this improvement through human corrections and reinforcement learning. Human interventions supply corrective behavior at states visited by the deployed policy [ 7 , 8 ] , while autonomous rollouts provide feedback beyond the initial demonstrations. RECAP [ 9 ] combines demonstrations, autonomous rollouts, and human interventions, using value-estimated advantages to condition policy training and iteratively update the policy with deployment data.

The value of accumulated experience for policy improvement varies across and within trajectories. Even successful trajectories may contain hesitation, repeated attempts, or other inefficient behavior, so the contribution of experience to policy improvement must be assessed at a finer level. Human corrections target deployment difficulties, but policy actions in the same trajectories may include behavior that prompted the intervention. These observations motivate Evo-RL’s selective update procedure: estimated advantages guide the selection of experience for policy updates, while only human-controlled portions of successful intervention trajectories are retained for corrective fine-tuning.

We propose Evo-RL, an iterative real-world reinforcement learning method that combines human corrections with advantage-guided experience selection. Starting from a demonstration-trained policy, Evo-RL collects human interventions and autonomous rollouts during deployment. It trains a value model on demonstrations, intervention data, and autonomous experience, using rewards that account for execution time and human takeovers, and then estimates advantages to guide experience selection. For policy fine-tuning, Evo-RL retains only the human-controlled portions of successful intervention trajectories, keeps the original demonstrations, and adds selected positive-advantage experience from demonstrations and successful autonomous rollouts. RECAP trains the policy on accumulated experience with a binary advantage label as an additional input. Evo-RL instead uses estimated advantages to select experience for policy updates and increase the sampling weight of selected experience. The updated policy is then redeployed for the next iteration.

To advance the real-world RL research, we further introduce RW-RL-Dataset which organizes demonstrations, human interventions, and autonomous experience with action-source metadata and semantic annotations. It spans over 1,000 hours across four diverse robot embodiments and includes the task-specific training experience used in our experiments.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We propose Evo-RL, an iterative method that combines corrective supervision with selective reuse of experience guided by positive estimated advantages. Under our evaluation protocol, first-round Evo-RL achieves an attempt success rate (ASR) 30.46% higher than RECAP on a real-world manipulation task requiring high-precision alignment.

We present RW-RL-Dataset, a collection of over 1,000 hours of real-world data from four robot embodiments, pairing synchronized camera observations with robot states and actions. Its annotations specify task instructions and scene context, execution quality and error counts, subtask intervals, and whether each frame records human or policy control.

2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Model and Robot Datasets

Large-scale robot datasets collectively cover diverse household, office, and industrial manipulation tasks across single-arm, dual-arm, and humanoid platforms [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] . This diversity provides a foundation for VLA pretraining, enabling policies to learn reusable manipulation skills across tasks and robots [ 14 ] . Building on these skills, models such as OpenVLA can adapt to new tasks and robot setups through fine-tuning on additional demonstrations [ 2 ] . However, even after fine-tuning, policies may still fail in situations poorly covered by datasets. Human interventions provide targeted corrections in these situations, yet the resulting corrective experience is less systematically captured and organized.

## II-B Human Interventions and Data Aggregation

Out-of-distribution (OOD) situations refer to scenarios that differ from those encountered during training and may therefore challenge the policy’s ability to generalize. During deployment, human interventions can be introduced in such OOD situations, not necessarily only after an execution error occurs. These interventions provide corrective demonstrations that can be incorporated into the training data, helping the policy improve its responses when similar situations arise in the future. Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) formalizes this process by querying expert actions for states visited by the current policy and aggregating the resulting state–action pairs into the training set [ 6 ] .

Building on this paradigm, subsequent research focuses on two related questions: when human interventions should be triggered and how the resulting correction data should be incorporated into policy learning. Some methods let human operators decide when to intervene [ 7 ] , whereas others use state novelty or failure risk to determine when to request human assistance [ 15 ] . Because intervention samples often constitute only a small fraction of the collected data, their influence on policy updates can be limited. IWR addresses this imbalance by increasing the relative weight of intervention samples, while using non-intervention samples to regularize policy updates and help retain previously learned skills [ 8 ] . However, corrective action labels alone do not explicitly indicate which states are likely to lead to failure or which trajectories are of higher quality. Incorporating such evaluations can provide additional supervisory signals for further policy improvement.

## II-C Real-World RL and Iterative Policy Improvement

Reinforcement learning enables robots to improve their policies through interaction with the environment. Early work on RL for VLA models focused on offline preference alignment [ 16 , 17 ] , such as GRAPE [ 17 ] , which employs Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) [ 18 ] to align robot trajectories with human intent. More recent approaches incorporate experience collected during deployment into VLA post-training. RECAP trains a value function on demonstrations, human interventions and autonomous rollouts then uses advantage-based indicators to condition policy training and guide iterative improvement [ 9 ] . To reduce the cost of online adaptation, RLT compresses latent representations into an RL token and trains a lightweight actor–critic to refine action chunks while keeping the VLA frozen [ 19 ] . Beyond action-level optimization, LaST-R1 extends reinforcement learning to the latent space, jointly optimizing reasoning and execution [ 20 ] . Our Evo-RL is motivated by RECAP, as both methods combine human corrections with autonomous rollouts to realize value-guided iterative policy improvement.

2026-10-12.abstract: Memory-dependent manipulation requires a policy to track execution state and recover visual evidence that is no longer observable. We propose dual-stream memory for vision-language-action policies, assigning these requirements to complementary representations. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet compresses history into one temporal token, supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. A task-conditioned retriever retains frames above a fixed relevance threshold; linear multi-scale fusion encodes each frame into sixteen spatial tokens. We then freeze the temporal compressor and jointly optimize retrieval and policy learning. Across sixteen RoboMME tasks, the complete model achieves 49.22% mean success versus 44.51% for the published FrameSamp+Modul reference, improving fourteen tasks and all four suite means. On four real-robot tasks, mean success reaches 62.5% versus 37.5%, with the largest gains on repeated actions requiring execution-stage discrimination. These results support combining execution context with selective visual access, while failures under cup swaps expose persistent identity tracking as an unresolved requirement.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation can produce perceptually similar observations that require different actions, depending on prior execution or earlier visual evidence. Repeated actions require execution-stage information, whereas occlusion and target reidentification require distinguishing visual detail that may no longer be observable. These requirements motivate separate representations for evolving execution context and accessible historical evidence (Fig. Dual-Stream Memory for Vision-Language-Action Policies ).

Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and instructions to robot actions [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Large-scale robot data, action chunking, and generative action models broaden their capabilities [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . However, they do not determine which episodic information a policy should retain. Recent memory-augmented policies preserve perceptual observations, cognitive summaries, or representations at several temporal scales [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Which historical information should be compressed, and which should remain directly accessible?

Recurrent compression summarizes execution history, but a compact state need not preserve detail for later target identification. Storing historical features preserves access, but uniform sampling may miss brief evidence, and spatial pooling may discard distinguishing detail. We therefore distinguish execution context, frame relevance, and within-frame detail.

Our design combines recurrent temporal memory with selected spatial evidence (Fig. 2 ). We make three contributions:

We introduce a task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet (GDN) compressor supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. These objectives encourage execution context and reconstructable visual history in one temporal token.

We formulate task-conditioned evidence access as threshold retrieval with shared temporal and spatial supervision. The retained-frame count adapts to the available evidence.

We introduce linear multi-scale fusion to combine coarse context and fine spatial detail within sixteen tokens per retained frame.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Memory for robot policies

Robot memory research distinguishes sequencing skills from retaining information within an episode. CALVIN and LIBERO study sequential manipulation and knowledge transfer [ 13 , 14 ] ; RoboMME targets Counting, Permanence, Reference, and Imitation [ 15 ] . Its FrameSamp+Modul baseline exposes sampled historical features to a VLA policy.

Beyond sampled observations, memory interfaces compress and organize history. Latent bottlenecks and cross-attention provide mechanisms for reading visual context [ 16 , 17 ] . MemoryVLA combines perceptual and cognitive memory, MEM organizes video and text at multiple temporal scales, and NativeMEM learns policy-aligned memory tokens [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Our design separates recurrent state from retrieved evidence, with distinct operations for execution context, frame selection, and spatial detail.

## II-B Recurrent compression and selective access

Content-based attention reads stored representations [ 18 ] ; Transformer-XL, Compressive Transformer, and Recurrent Memory Transformer extend historical access through recurrence or compression [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] . Linear attention and state-space models instead maintain recurrent states [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] . DeltaNet introduces delta-rule updates, while GDN adds data-dependent forgetting [ 25 , 26 ] . Test-Time Training and RoboTTT further explore expressive recurrent states and robot-policy context [ 27 , 28 ] . We build on GDN by supervising execution progress and reconstructable visual history, with a separate spatial memory bank for direct evidence access.

## II-C Spatial representations for memory

Patch encoders provide spatial features [ 29 ] : DINO learns self-supervised visual structure [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] , whereas CLIP and SigLIP learn image–text correspondence [ 33 , 34 ] . Feature pyramids, hierarchical Transformers, and mixed-resolution tokenization preserve information across spatial scales [ 35 , 36 , 37 ] ; PerAct emphasizes spatial structure for manipulation [ 38 ] . We use DINOv3 for temporal compression and frozen SigLIP for retrieval and spatial memory. Our fusion aligns coarse, base, and fine features within sixteen slots, enriching retained frames without enlarging their token budget.

2026-10-12.title: Beyond Actions: Learning Future Operation Targets for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-12.authors: Min Lin , Bokai Zhou , Jianqi Lin , Kaiyuan Yang , Yicheng Chang , Junjie Yu , Xiaofan Liu , Jianhua Han , Rui Li , Shen Zhao , Xiaodan Liang
2026-10-12.abstract: Actions specify what a robot should execute, but do not describe what those commands will achieve. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies nevertheless learn primarily by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state. We introduce Action–Future Coupled Effect Learning (AFCE), which makes a future-grounded physical Effect the policy’s primary prediction target. An offline tokenizer constructs temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Reconstruction objectives encourage the representation to retain executable detail and observed physical change. A flow-matching VLA predicts Effects from current images, instruction, and robot state, while a state-conditioned decoder converts them into action chunks. Embodiment-specific interfaces allow single- and dual-arm tasks to share the Effect model. On DexJoCo, AFCE achieves 50.97 % 50.97\% overall success, improving over π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and UVT by 11.82 and 15.21 percentage points, respectively. It leads on all five bimanual tasks, highlighting the value of Effect supervision for coordinated dexterous manipulation. The project page is available at https://afceproject.github.io/AFCE-Web/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made substantial progress toward generalist robot control by mapping images, language, and robot state to continuous actions ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ) . Yet the target used to train this mapping usually describes what the robot commanded , not what the command changed . An action sequence specifies motor behavior, but leaves its effects on the robot and environment implicit. In dexterous manipulation, this gap matters: contact, hand configuration, and object pose can turn similar commands into different outcomes, while different motions can achieve the same task-relevant change. The challenge is to make physical progress part of the policy’s prediction target without sacrificing the detail needed to execute an action.

Predicting the future offers one way to expose such progress. World and world-action models use future observations or latent dynamics to support control ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . However, a complete visual future contains changes due to appearance, occlusion, and camera motion that need not determine the next control command. Conversely, a scene change alone may leave out the contact timing, finger coordination, and robot motion required to produce it. Latent-action and future-informed visuomotor methods provide more compact targets ( Ye et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026b ) , but compactness alone does not resolve whether a target is both predictable from the current observation and sufficient for precise action decoding.

We therefore seek a target that connects three requirements: it must be predictable before acting, retain task-relevant information about the resulting physical transition, and support recovery of executable continuous actions. We introduce AFCE (Action–Future Coupled Effect Learning) , which learns a temporal Effect from synchronized demonstrations of executed actions, realized robot-state changes, and sparse world changes. Rather than specifying the Effect through hand-designed semantic labels, we let these sources interact and constrain a shared representation through joint reconstruction. The action objective retains control detail, while the robot-response and world-change objectives ground that detail in observed consequences.

Figure 1 illustrates the resulting training interface. An offline tokenizer constructs Effect targets from recorded trajectories, where future evidence is available. The VLA then learns to predict these targets using only the current images, language instruction, and robot state. At deployment, a decoder maps the predicted Effect and current state to an action chunk. Thus, future observations shape the supervision without becoming inputs to the deployed policy.

The central test of this interface is whether the Effect remains useful after prediction . Accurate reconstruction from a ground-truth Effect does not ensure that the VLA can predict that Effect, nor that decoded actions succeed under closed-loop control. We evaluate these questions separately: reconstruction tests what the representation retains; ground-truth-Effect replay tests whether it supports execution; and predicted-Effect rollout tests the complete policy against direct action supervision under the same evaluation protocol. In mixed single- and dual-arm training, AFCE improves aggregate task success, particularly on dual-arm tasks, while some fine-control tasks remain challenging.

Our contributions are:

We formulate VLA target learning around three coupled requirements: predictability from current observations, information about task-relevant future changes, and continuous-action executability.

We introduce AFCE, a temporal Effect learned by jointly reconstructing executed actions, realized robot response, and sparse world change from a shared representation.

We evaluate the representation and the complete policy through reconstruction, ground-truth-Effect replay, and predicted-Effect closed-loop control, showing aggregate gains under mixed single- and dual-arm training while identifying remaining fine-control limitations.

1. We formulate VLA target learning around three coupled requirements: predictability from current observations, information about task-relevant future changes, and continuous-action executability.

2. We introduce AFCE, a temporal Effect learned by jointly reconstructing executed actions, realized robot response, and sparse world change from a shared representation.

3. We evaluate the representation and the complete policy through reconstruction, ground-truth-Effect replay, and predicted-Effect closed-loop control, showing aggregate gains under mixed single- and dual-arm training while identifying remaining fine-control limitations.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 VLA Policies and Action Supervision

Vision-language-action (VLA) models have established a powerful interface between semantic understanding and robot control. RT-2 casts discretized actions as language-like tokens, while Octo and OpenVLA learn generalist policies from heterogeneous robot data ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) . π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} further combine pretrained visual-language representations with a flow-matching action expert for continuous control ( Black et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ) . Complementary advances such as ACT, Diffusion Policy, and FAST improve action prediction through chunking, expressive generative modeling, and efficient tokenization ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Pertsch et al., 2025 ) . Together, these methods provide increasingly capable ways to generate robot commands. They also motivate a closer examination of what the policy is asked to predict: an action records the commanded motion, whereas the resulting robot and scene changes carry additional information about the intended manipulation. Building on these advances, AFCE preserves the VLA observation interface and continuous action execution while introducing a physical Effect as the policy’s intermediate supervision target.

## 2.2 World Models and Future-Informed Control

Future-aware learning offers a complementary route to stronger visuomotor policies. GR-1 and VidMan use video dynamics to inform manipulation, while WorldVLA and DreamZero connect predictions about the evolving world to action generation ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . FutureVLA and Being-H0.7 further show how future-informed representations can guide policies that act from current observations ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026b ) . Collectively, these studies establish future information as a valuable training signal for control. AFCE asks how that signal can be organized into a target that is both informative about physical change and directly useful for producing actions. Demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions jointly specify the Effect during training; at deployment, the policy predicts it from the current context and a state-conditioned decoder converts it into robot commands. This formulation explicitly links future-grounded supervision to the action interface used for closed-loop execution.

## 2.3 Latent Actions and Transferable Policy Targets

Latent-action learning provides intermediate targets that capture structure beyond individual action coordinates. LAPA derives latent actions from visual transitions, while UniVLA and villa-X develop representations for learning from robot and video data ( Ye et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . JALA and LARA connect transition-derived features to actions and policy learning ( Luo et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . UVT combines demonstrated action chunks with discrete visual dynamics codes into a decodable policy target ( Feng and Jain, 2026 ) . AFCE develops this direction by constructing a temporal Effect from demonstrated commands, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Its action and response branches relate observed scene changes to both the issued commands and the motion actually realized. Realized responses are particularly informative in dexterous manipulation, where contact and hand configuration can make similar commands produce different outcomes. Temporal Effect tokens preserve the progression from initial contact to subsequent object interaction. A state-conditioned decoder maps the Effect to native actions, making the learned target useful for continuous control. Embodiment-specific adapters accommodate different native state and action dimensions while retaining a common Effect shape.

2026-10-12.title: PATACON: GPU-Parallel Tangent-Bundle RRT-Connect for Constrained Motion Planning
2026-10-12.authors: Gahyun Oh , Junho An , Suhyun Jeon , Suhan Park
2026-10-12.abstract: Fast whole-body motion planning enables continuous replanning for humanoid robots in dynamic environments while satisfying collision avoidance and kinematic constraints. However, constrained motion planning incurs substantial computational cost due to repeated constraint projection in addition to collision checking and nearest-neighbor search. Recently, GPU-based massively parallel planners have been proposed to reduce computational cost. Nevertheless, these planners still steer in the ambient configuration space, so projecting candidates that deviate from the manifold remains a significant source of overhead, particularly in highly constrained, high-dimensional problems. In this work, we introduce PATACON, a GPU-parallel bidirectional planner that explores tangent space to exploit the local manifold geometry induced by known constraint functions. Experiments on dual-arm closed-chain and humanoid whole-body constrained planning tasks show that PATACON outperforms the prior work as configuration-space dimension and constraint codimension grow, achieving up to an 11.25 times speedup. These results suggest that GPU-parallel tangent-space exploration brings constrained whole-body motion planning closer to real-time performance.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Dual-arm closed-chain and humanoid whole-body motion require maintaining task-dependent kinematic relationships while satisfying joint limits and avoiding collisions. These kinematic requirements can be formulated as nonlinear equality constraints, which define a lower-dimensional constraint manifold embedded in a high-dimensional configuration space [ 1 ] . In sampling-based motion planning, collision checking and nearest-neighbor queries are generally major sources of computational cost [ 2 , 3 ] . Planning on a constraint manifold introduces additional overhead because constraint projection is performed repeatedly throughout tree expansion. Reducing this computational burden is particularly important in scenarios that require repeated replanning as the target, obstacles, or task conditions change, where low planning latency is essential for responsive execution.

A widely used approach generates candidate motions in the ambient configuration space and projects them onto the manifold as the tree grows [ 1 ] . cpRRTC [ 4 ] brought this approach to the GPU by assigning each thread block to steer from the nearest node toward a random sample, project the waypoints of the resulting straight-line segment in parallel, and perform collision checks with early termination. This reduces constrained planning to milliseconds, but the exploration scheme is unchanged; each extension still steers in the ambient space and relies on projection to satisfy the constraints.

Ambient-space steering, however, ignores the shape of the manifold. Kim et al. [ 5 ] showed that a target sampled in the ambient space can contribute little progress along the manifold once projected, and that the resulting large number of projections degrades both computational efficiency and the Voronoi bias of RRT. Because the constraint Jacobian provides the tangent space at any configuration, displacements can instead be restricted to it: Stilman [ 6 ] observed that tangent displacements are more likely to remain within the constraint tolerance, and TB-RRT [ 5 ] grows trees on tangent spaces bounded by the local curvature, outperforming projection-based planners with larger gains on more complex problems. However, TB-RRT expands one node at a time, incurs additional preprocessing and bookkeeping for its tangent spaces, and relies on lazy projection. Therefore, the feasibility checked on tangent spaces must be re-evaluated after projection.

We propose PATACON ( PA rallel TA ngent-bundle RRT- CON nect), a GPU-parallel bi-directional planner that brings tangent-space-guided exploration to massively parallel tree expansion, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .
Unlike TB-RRT, PATACON projects and validates every candidate before tree insertion, so every node is feasible. Its efficiency has two sources: tangent-space candidates are more likely to remain within the constraint tolerance [ 6 ] and avoid ambient targets whose projections make little progress along the manifold [ 5 ] , and a single sample and nearest-neighbor query yield multiple candidate edges that are validated concurrently on the GPU, which amortizes the preprocessing and bookkeeping of tangent spaces over multiple edges.

Our main contributions are as follows:

Tangent-space-guided GPU-parallel extension. PATACON replaces the ambient-space steering of existing GPU-parallel planners with extension along local tangent spaces, so that candidates follow the manifold geometry before projection.

Tangent-space-guided GPU-parallel extension. PATACON replaces the ambient-space steering of existing GPU-parallel planners with extension along local tangent spaces, so that candidates follow the manifold geometry before projection.

Shared tangent-space banks. Tangent spaces are maintained
in tree-specific banks shared across thread blocks, together with the
correspondence between projected manifold states and their tangent-space
coordinates, so that multiple blocks can explore different regions of the
manifold concurrently.

Speculative multi-edge expansion. From one sample and one nearest-neighbor query, PATACON generates consecutive candidate edges along a tangent direction, validates them concurrently, and inserts the longest valid prefix, unlike the step-by-step CONNECT heuristic of RRT-Connect [ 7 ] .

We evaluate PATACON on eight benchmarks ranging from 7-DoF manipulation to 35-DoF humanoid whole-body planning. Although cpRRTC is faster on low-dimensional problems, PATACON shows increasing advantages with configuration-space dimension and constraint restrictiveness, reaching a 11.25 × 11.25\times speedup with a 100% success rate.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

Sampling-based constrained motion planners enforce nonlinear equality constraints through numerical projection or local approximations of the constraint manifold [ 1 ] .
Projection-based methods range
from randomized gradient descent for closed chains [ 8 ] to Jacobian-based tangent-space sampling and first-order
retraction [ 6 ] and CBiRRT [ 9 ] with Task
Space Regions [ 10 ] , whereas AtlasRRT [ 11 ] and TB-RRT [ 5 ] grow trees on local charts or tangent spaces, and
Kingston et al. [ 12 ] unify these mechanisms. These methods,
however, are primarily sequential.

Learning-based planners reduce online search through learned latent
spaces [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] or constraint-aware
samplers [ 16 ] , but require offline data generation and
training; we instead accelerate planning directly from the given
constraint functions.

Parallelization reduces the wall-clock cost of planning through GPU
collision checking [ 17 , 18 ] , multiple
or shared trees on CPUs [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] ,
SIMD vectorization [ 22 , 23 ] , and GPU trajectory
optimization [ 24 ] . pRRTC [ 25 ] and BatchRRT [ 26 ] run RRT-style tree growth on the GPU, and cpRRTC [ 4 ] extends
pRRTC to constrained planning by projecting motion-segment waypoints in
parallel. However, the steering methods remain in the ambient space, so
parallelism lowers the cost of each projection but not the off-manifold
motion to be projected.

Simply adding tangent-space steering to such planners is insufficient,
because tangent-space management and local nearest-neighbor search add
per-extension overhead. PATACON instead exploits the fact that
tangent-space candidates stay close to the manifold: one sample and
nearest-neighbor query yield several consecutive candidate edges, which
are validated in parallel on the GPU to amortize this overhead.

2026-10-12.title: Prediction-Informed Landing Window Planning for UAV Landing on USV in High Sea States
2026-10-12.authors: Kaizhen Li , Xi Zhou , Dan Zhang , Xiaowei Li
2026-10-12.abstract: Autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) on unmanned surface vehicle (USV) is difficult in high sea states. Existing hierarchical landing methods often infer future USV motion only implicitly from short observation histories, which limits their ability to adapt to severe and rapidly changing sea conditions. This paper presents a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework. A pretrained model is developed to explicitly predict the USV attitude during high-level landing decisions. The prediction helps identify suitable landing windows and choose the right touchdown time, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains UAV stability and tracks motion commands. To evaluate the framework under realistic disturbances, a real-sim validation setup is constructed in which USV-motion data collected in real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo USV. The experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using explicit attitude prediction to improve landing-window selection and support timing-aware UAV landing planning in rapidly varying marine environments.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and unmanned surface vehicle (USV) are increasingly used as a complementary robotic team in search and rescue, offshore inspection, environmental monitoring, and maritime surveillance. UAV provide rapid aerial observation and wide-area coverage, whereas USV provide endurance and direct access to the water surface. Reliable autonomous landing is therefore essential for sustained UAV-USV operation because it enables UAV recovery, recharging, and redeployment without continuous human intervention.

Landing a UAV on a moving USV is particularly challenging in high sea states [ 1 ] . Wave-induced heave, roll, and pitch continuously change the relative pose and velocity between the vehicle and the deck. During the final descent, USV attitude can vary substantially within the time required for the UAV to reach the deck, so a touchdown condition that is safe at the current instant may become unfavorable before contact. Wind, sensing uncertainty, and control delay further reduce the available touchdown margin. The landing problem therefore involves not only stabilizing the vehicle and tracking the USV, but also choosing a touchdown time that is consistent with the future motion of the deck.

This temporal decision becomes more difficult as sea conditions become more dynamic. A controller that reacts only to the current USV attitude may begin to descend when the platform is temporarily favorable but fail to anticipate the rapid closure of the corresponding landing window. Conversely, an overly conservative controller may miss short favorable intervals and increase the recovery time. These observations motivate a landing architecture that preserves reliable low-level flight control while providing the high-level decision layer with explicit information about future platform attitude.

In this paper, we develop a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework for UAV landing on USV in high sea states. A pretrained temporal model forecasts the short-term evolution of USV attitude, and the predicted attitude is used to evaluate feasible touchdown windows and guide the high-level landing decision. A conventional low-level flight controller remains responsible for vehicle stabilization and motion tracking. The framework is evaluated in a real-to-simulation setting, where USV-motion data collected under real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo landing platform.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

A prediction-informed hierarchical landing framework is developed by coupling explicit platform-attitude forecasting with high-level landing-window planning and conventional low-level flight control.

A pretrained temporal prediction model is introduced to provide future attitude information for touchdown-window assessment under rapidly varying sea states.

A real-to-simulation validation setup is established by replaying platform-motion data collected in real sea conditions on a MuJoCo platform, enabling evaluation under realistic disturbance patterns.

1. A prediction-informed hierarchical landing framework is developed by coupling explicit platform-attitude forecasting with high-level landing-window planning and conventional low-level flight control.

2. A pretrained temporal prediction model is introduced to provide future attitude information for touchdown-window assessment under rapidly varying sea states.

3. A real-to-simulation validation setup is established by replaying platform-motion data collected in real sea conditions on a MuJoCo platform, enabling evaluation under realistic disturbance patterns.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

Learning-based methods have been investigated to improve the adaptability of UAV landing under uncertain platform motion. Compared with controllers that depend on an accurate analytical model, such as NMPC-based cooperative UAV-USV tracking and landing [ 3 ] and synchronized-motion-based cooperative landing [ 2 ] , reinforcement learning (RL) can learn a feedback policy from repeated interaction with a simulator or physical system. Polvara et al. explored end-to-end UAV landing through deep reinforcement learning, mapping visual observations to landing actions [ 4 ] . Rodriguez-Ramos et al. extended deep RL to landing on moving platforms, demonstrating that a learned policy can adapt its control behavior to platform motion [ 5 ] . Subsequent work considered autonomous multi-rotor landing and vision-based ship landing under disturbance, further showing the potential of learning-based policies in dynamic landing scenarios [ 6 ] , [ 7 ] .

Despite this adaptability, fully end-to-end learning is difficult to deploy in safety-critical flight systems. High-dimensional visual inputs, the simultaneous learning of stabilization and landing decisions, and the absence of an explicit temporal representation can increase training complexity and reduce interpretability. These limitations have motivated hierarchical formulations, in which a learned policy makes high-level landing decisions while a conventional flight controller maintains attitude stability and tracks motion commands. WaveLander is representative of this direction: its recurrent RL policy uses a compact platform-relative observation and outputs a scalar vertical-velocity reference, while the low-level controller handles stabilization and tracking [ 8 ] .

The main limitation of current hierarchical learning-based landing methods is their limited awareness of future landing windows. In WaveLander, timing-aware behavior is learned from short observation histories, recurrent hidden states, and attitude-aware reward shaping. The policy can therefore slow down, hold, or retreat when the current platform condition is unfavorable, but its prediction of future platform motion remains implicit. Under rapidly changing high-sea-state conditions, this reactive mechanism may identify an unfavorable touchdown condition only after a safe landing interval has started to close. The policy is consequently required to infer both the platform trend and the appropriate touchdown timing from limited short-term evidence.

Explicit platform-motion prediction provides a complementary solution to this limitation. Li et al. used recurrent prediction to estimate USV attitude and exploit favorable motion phases during cooperative landing [ 2 ] . Such methods demonstrate that future attitude information can support temporal coordination, but the prediction module is commonly coupled to a specific synchronization or tracking controller. The predicted motion is not necessarily exposed as a general landing-window interface for a hierarchical planner. In contrast, the present work treats attitude prediction as an independent high-level information source: the predicted attitude evolution is used to assess candidate touchdown windows and guide the descent decision, while the conventional low-level flight-control stack is retained. This formulation separates prediction, landing-window planning, and stabilization, and is intended to improve temporal awareness without requiring the learned component to directly control UAV actuators.

2026-10-12.title: Grounded-Dreamer: Robot Learning from World Model Synthetic Data with Physical Grounding
2026-10-12.authors: Feng Jiang , Shu Chen , Yuanfei Wang , Yuan Li , Zhenhao Shen , Jiaqi Liang , Yang Chen , Lei Wei , Chen Xie , Ruihai Wu
2026-10-12.abstract:
Scaling robot manipulation policies requires large amounts of diverse, action-labeled data, yet collecting such data in the real world remains expensive and difficult to scale.
Existing methods either depend on human teleoperation, rely on simulation with limited visual realism, or use human videos that lack embodiment-specific annotations.
In this paper, we introduce Grounded-Dreamer, a framework for synthesizing physically grounded robot manipulation data with video world models while avoiding human teleoperation demonstrations.
Grounded-Dreamer combines the visual realism of generative video models with simulator physics engines.
Starting from a small set of real images depicting robot task initial states, our method automatically reconstructs task-relevant objects and camera geometry, aligns them in simulation, and collects physically valid trajectories.
These trajectories are used to post-train both a video world model and an inverse dynamics model, enabling the generation of visually realistic robot manipulation videos and corresponding robot actions from real images.
To filter physically implausible rollouts, Grounded-Dreamer replays generated trajectories in the reconstructed simulation and retains only those that successfully complete the tasks.
The real-world robot policies are trained solely on the grounded synthetic trajectories without any human demonstrations.
Empirical results in real-world tasks demonstrate that Grounded-Dreamer can synthesize physically grounded data and substantially facilitate policy learning without requiring human teleoperation effort.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Building general-purpose robot policies capable of performing diverse manipulation tasks across varied environments requires large-scale, high-quality data. However, robot data is difficult to scale, and existing sources present a challenging trade-off between quality and quantity. Real-world teleoperation provides high-fidelity demonstrations but is limited by intensive human labor. While UMI data collection ( Chi et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) improves efficiency, there remains a need for manual operations. Conversely, simulation data offers inexpensive, action-labeled trajectories but is hindered by the sim-to-real visual gap. Human-centric videos are abundant and diverse, yet they lack the robot action annotations essential for direct policy training. Consequently, the field remains trapped between costly manual collection and the limitations of imperfect proxy data.

This dilemma motivates the pursuit of scalable robot data synthesis. Prior efforts such as DemoGen ( Xue et al., 2025 ) and MimicGen ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) have attempted to augment existing datasets by diversifying robot demonstrations; however, these methods still rely on human-collected trajectories as initial seeds. Other approaches, including RoboGen ( Wang et al., 2024b ) and GenSim ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Hua et al., 2025 ) , leverage Large Language Models (LLMs) and simulators to automate task generation and trajectory collection. While these frameworks significantly reduce human intervention, the resulting data remains confined to simulation, leaving the visual sim-to-real discrepancy unresolved.

Generative video world models offer a potential alternative. Trained on internet-scale data, these models capture rich visual and world dynamics priors, enabling the generation of manipulation rollouts. When paired with an Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM), such videos can be converted into action-labeled trajectories. However, pretrained models like Cosmos ( NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) are primarily trained on human-centric videos. Directly applying them to robotic tasks often results in "hallucinated" physics, such as inconsistent object motions or non-physical contacts.

In this work, we introduce Grounded-Dreamer , a framework that synthesizes high-fidelity robot manipulation data without a single human teleoperation demonstration. Our core insight is to link the visual realism of generative world models with the grounding of physics simulators. We first build an automatic real-to-sim pipeline that calibrates camera poses, reconstructs task-relevant objects, and aligns them with the scene. Within this reconstructed simulator, we automatically collect diverse trajectories by leveraging the simulator’s ground-truth states. These grounded trajectories serve as the foundation for post-training both the video world model and the IDM.

During data synthesis, the post-trained world model generates visually realistic manipulation videos from real-world initial images, while the IDM extracts the corresponding robot actions. To guarantee physical validity, we implement a closed-loop verification step: replaying the inferred trajectories within the reconstructed simulation. This process filters out physically inconsistent generations, ensuring that only successful, grounded trajectories are used for further policy training.

We evaluate Grounded-Dreamer across seven diverse real-world manipulation tasks, spanning short-to-long horizon sequences and sophisticated tool use. Our empirical results demonstrate that policies trained exclusively on grounded synthetic data achieve performance competitive with those trained on real-world human demonstrations. Furthermore, owing to the inherent visual diversity and our targeted augmentation strategies, Grounded-Dreamer significantly outperforms real-data policies in out-of-distribution scenarios, showcasing robust zero-shot generalization across novel scenarios.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose Grounded-Dreamer , a data synthesis framework that eliminates the need for human demonstrations by linking video world models with simulator physics engines.

We introduce an automated real-to-sim reconstruction and collection pipeline, enabling data synthesis that maintains both high visual fidelity and strict physical grounding.

We demonstrate through extensive real-world experiments that our grounded synthetic data effectively facilitates policy learning, achieving robust performance across diverse scenarios through purely autonomous data generation.

1. We propose Grounded-Dreamer , a data synthesis framework that eliminates the need for human demonstrations by linking video world models with simulator physics engines.

2. We introduce an automated real-to-sim reconstruction and collection pipeline, enabling data synthesis that maintains both high visual fidelity and strict physical grounding.

3. We demonstrate through extensive real-world experiments that our grounded synthetic data effectively facilitates policy learning, achieving robust performance across diverse scenarios through purely autonomous data generation.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Robot Data Synthesis

Simulation has been widely used to generate diverse conditions for robot data. Early sim-to-real work relied on visual or dynamics randomization ( Tobin et al., 2017 ; Peng et al., 2018 ) . Later environments extended this idea to broader robot-learning settings: RLBench standardizes manipulation tasks ( James et al., 2020 ) , robosuite and SAPIEN provide modular robot-object simulation platforms ( Zhu et al., 2020 ; Xiang et al., 2020 ) , and Isaac Gym and RoboCasa emphasize scalable physics or household manipulation ( Makoviychuk et al., 2021 ; Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) .

Recent generative frameworks, such as
GenSim, GenSim2, and RoboGen, use language or foundation models to generate tasks, scenes, demonstrations, or supervision ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Hua et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024b ) . Their data quality, however, still depends on generated task programs, planners, solvers, or simulator assumptions. For manipulation, local grounding outweighs global visual realism. Incorrect object pose, axis, or camera frame can make a plausible trajectory physically misleading. 6D pose estimation and reconstruction recover task-relevant structure from real observations ( Hodan et al., 2018 ; Wen et al., 2024 ) , while structure-from-motion, NeRF, and 3D Gaussian Splatting facilitate view-consistent geometry or appearance ( Schönberger & Frahm, 2016 ; Mildenhall et al., 2020 ; Kerbl et al., 2023 ) .

Another route reuses collected trajectories. A series of studies adapt human demonstrations to new object configurations ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) , corrective interventions ( Hoque et al., 2024 ) , long-horizon skills ( Garrett et al., 2025 ) , and bimanual dexterous manipulation ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) . DemoGen further adapts one demonstration and edits the 3D scene to synthesize new observations ( Xue et al., 2025 ) . DROID and Open X-Embodiment instead scale real robot data directly, but require substantial collection effort ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; O’Neill et al., 2024 ) . Grounded-Dreamer lies between these directions: it grounds synthetic data in real scene-object inputs, preserves physical structure through simulation, and expands the distribution with world-model rollouts.

## 2.2 World Models for Robot Learning

World models were originally developed as learned dynamics models for predicting future states before acting ( Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ; Hafner et al., 2025 ) . In robotics, visual foresight leveraged video prediction for model-based control by selecting actions whose predicted futures match a goal ( Finn & Levine, 2017 ) . More recently, diffusion-based video models have enabled realistic rollout generation from images or text ( Ho et al., 2022 ) , while systems such as UniSim and Genie move toward controllable visual worlds ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Bruce et al., 2024 ) .

However, visually plausible videos are not directly usable robot training trajectories, as they often lack actions, embodiment constraints, and physically reliable interactions. DreamGen adapts video world models to robot learning by recovering pseudo actions through latent action or inverse dynamics models ( Jang et al., 2025 ) , while GigaBrain-0 further scales world-model-generated data for VLA training ( GigaBrain Team, 2025 ) . Prior works have also explored inverse dynamics models to bridge observations and actions ( Agrawal et al., 2016 ; Pathak et al., 2018 ) . Once converted into action-conditioned trajectories, such generated data can train policies including Diffusion Policy, RT-2, and π 0 \pi_{0} ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ) . Grounded-Dreamer builds on this line of work by coupling world-model rollouts with reconstructed scene inputs and simulation-based grounding to ensure both visual realism and physical consistency before policy learning.

2026-10-12.title: Low-Latency Mapless ESDF Queries for MAV Reactive Collision Avoidance
2026-10-12.authors: Leonard Freißmuth , Cedric Le Gentil , Helen Oleynikova , Stefan Leutenegger
2026-10-12.abstract:
Reactive collision avoidance in unknown, cluttered environments must perceive obstacles and correct motion within milliseconds.
Existing methods rely on maps for high-rate collision queries , but their acceleration structures require pre-processing.
That cost is amortized in long-horizon planning, where a map serves millions of queries; reactive planning, however, is a near-field, short-horizon problem with potentially only hundreds of queries per measurement, where building a map may not pay off.
We propose a mapless, Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) -accelerated Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) query with negligible pre-processing that operates directly on posed depth images, with resolution set by pooling the image rather than by a voxel size.
On an embedded GPU it is simultaneously more accurate and lower in total latency than every voxel-grid configuration we measured between 2 cm and 20 cm 2\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}20\text{\,}\mathrm{cm} , at one to two orders of magnitude less memory at matched resolution.
With our query integrated into a Model Predictive Controller (MPC) , simulated runs in laser-scanned forests at up to 9 m / s 9\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} collide in 0.4 % 0.4\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} through dense branches, against 5.9 % 5.9\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} with the best voxel grid and 5.5 % 5.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} with the best mapless baseline at our resolution, whose failures we attribute to voxel resolution and total latency respectively.
We deploy the system onboard at two forest sites and fly at commanded speeds of up to 4 m / s 4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} .
2026-10-12.introduction:
For fast Micro Air Vehicle (MAV) flight in cluttered environments, reactive collision avoidance may require obstacle perception and motion correction within milliseconds.
The local planner must therefore rely on the latest sensor data for fine, near-field obstacles such as branches emerging from the occlusion of nearer geometry.
Standard approaches integrate sensor measurements into a map—such as occupancy grids [ 1 , 2 ] or distance fields [ 3 , 4 ] —and query that map for collision.
For a reactive safety layer, the relevant quantity is the total latency from a new depth measurement to a collision answer.
It comprises two terms: the pre-processing required to build or update the map, including any acceleration structure over it, and the query time itself, which grows with the number of queries.
A map trades constant pre-processing cost for lower per-query cost, which pays off in long-horizon planning where a measurement may be reused for millions of queries.
Reactive planning, however, is a near-field, short-horizon problem: the controller queries only its immediate neighborhood, on the order of 10 2 10^{2} times per sensor update.
In this regime the pre-processing term, rather than the per-query term, dominates total latency, which raises the question whether a map pays off at all.

Voxel maps are a common choice for such local planning, but their fixed voxel size has to be traded off twice.
A depth camera resolves finely nearby and coarsely far away, so a fixed voxel size under-represents the near field or over-represents the far field, and finer voxels cost more compute and memory.
Prior mapless methods avoid these tradeoffs by retaining posed depth images, querying each frame through a per-frame KD-tree [ 5 , 6 ] or an occlusion-aware pyramid [ 7 ] .
We instead evaluate depth pixels directly in parallel on the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) , with local depth minima and maxima for pruning as the only pre-processing.
The resulting sensor-space Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) (Fig. 1 ) keeps the sensor’s range-dependent resolution, controlled by pooling, returns distances and gradients, handles unknown space optimistically or conservatively, and carries a covariance-based pose-uncertainty margin.
On a Jetson Orin NX it answers the 400 400 queries of our reactive planner in 6.2 ms 6.2\text{\,}\mathrm{ms} at full resolution, one to two orders of magnitude below KD-tree and mesh baselines, and at that setting both more accurate and lower in total latency than every voxel grid we measured, at the least memory at matched resolution (Sec. IV-B ).
In closed-loop simulation through laser-scanned forests at up to 9 m / s 9\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} , runs of a Model Predictive Controller (MPC) are safer with our query than with voxel grids, which fail through resolution, or with KD-trees or meshes, which fail through total latency (Sec. IV-C ).
We deploy the system in ten forest flights at commanded speeds of up to 4 m / s 4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} .

Our contributions are:

A parallel sensor-space distance query algorithm that fuses posed depth views, with pooling-controlled resolution and conservative or optimistic handling of unknown space, benchmarked on an embedded GPU for total latency, accuracy, and memory.

A covariance-based uncertainty margin that inflates obstacles by the odometry uncertainty.

A closed-loop evaluation comparing voxel-grid, KD-tree, mesh, and our representation in laser-scanned forests behind one MPC on the embedded platform, separating the effects of total latency and resolution, and a demonstration of the running system in ten real-world forest flights at commanded speeds of up to 4 m / s 4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} .

1. A parallel sensor-space distance query algorithm that fuses posed depth views, with pooling-controlled resolution and conservative or optimistic handling of unknown space, benchmarked on an embedded GPU for total latency, accuracy, and memory.

2. A covariance-based uncertainty margin that inflates obstacles by the odometry uncertainty.

3. A closed-loop evaluation comparing voxel-grid, KD-tree, mesh, and our representation in laser-scanned forests behind one MPC on the embedded platform, separating the effects of total latency and resolution, and a demonstration of the running system in ten real-world forest flights at commanded speeds of up to 4 m / s 4\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} .
