# II Related Work

## II-A Reactive Collision Avoidance

We categorize reactive methods as corridor-based, predictive, or learned.
We assume static geometry over the buffered horizon, as prior mapless methods do [ 5 , 6 ] ; moving obstacles require motion prediction [ 8 ] and are out of scope.

These optimize a trajectory [ 9 ] within overlapping convex sub-volumes of free space, polyhedra [ 10 , 11 ] or spheres [ 12 , 6 ] , tracked by lower-level controllers, and reach 20 m / s 20\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} in sparse forests with LiDAR [ 10 ] .
Without a prior map they can be trapped in local minima [ 13 ] .
Our query targets the reactive layer beneath a global planner and can alternatively serve these optimizers, which query the neighborhood sparingly.

Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) scores perturbed rollouts on the GPU [ 14 , 15 ] but needs large sample counts, making collision queries the bottleneck; MPCs [ 16 ] exploit gradients to converge with fewer queries.
Their collision constraints use a local map [ 17 ] , a learned latent representation [ 18 , 19 ] , or (neural) control barrier functions [ 20 , 21 ] .
EGO-Planner [ 22 ] reports millisecond optimization times, yet on a separately maintained map whose update bounds its total latency, as it does for Fast-Planner [ 23 ] and chance-constrained planning over voxel grids [ 24 ] .
All of them could consume our query, and we adopt an MPC to demonstrate it.

Learned policies map depth to commands, distilled from a privileged planner [ 25 ] , learned from demonstrations [ 26 ] , or trained through differentiable physics [ 27 ] .
They avoid the map at fixed inference latency, at the price of training data, sim-to-real transfer, and a policy tied to its domain and vehicle that cannot be constrained geometrically, whereas our query is training-free and returns distances and gradients usable as hard constraints, as a safety filter beneath a policy, or as supervision.

## II-B Local Map Representations

Point clouds dominate for LiDAR sensors and are queried through KD-trees [ 28 , 29 ] , made incremental [ 30 ] or rebalancing-free [ 31 ] , or interpolated into continuous fields [ 32 ] .
Maintaining the structure is a constant overhead that dominates total latency at low query counts, and unknown space must be recovered separately [ 33 , 34 , 35 ] , whereas our query represents it natively.

Voxel grids integrate measurements into occupancy or distance fields and model occlusion explicitly [ 36 ] .
Octrees [ 1 , 37 , 2 ] curb the cubic memory growth at the cost of traversal overhead.
Voxel hashing and incremental ESDF updates make fixed-resolution integration efficient on the CPU [ 38 , 3 , 39 ] and, with NVBlox [ 4 ] , on the GPU .
Yet cells remain fixed-size, which is memory-inefficient at high resolution, and the per-frame integration can dominate total latency at low query counts.

Mapless methods query in sensor space.
RAPPIDS [ 7 ] partitions the free space of the most recent image into pyramids for a binary collision test that provides neither distance nor gradient, and a single image gives a limited field of view [ 40 ] .
A history of posed images, queried per frame through KD-trees [ 5 , 6 ] , covers more.
We keep this buffer but replace the per-frame structures with a direct pixel-space query at negligible pre-processing cost that, unlike prior mapless methods, returns a signed distance with gradients under either handling of unknown space.

2026-10-12.title: Human2Dex: Dexterous Robot Learning from Wrist-Centric Human Demonstrations
2026-10-12.authors: Jiachen Zhang , Yuanyuan Li , Shaqi Luo
2026-10-12.abstract: Collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations for each robot hand requires repeated task-specific data acquisition. We ask whether one shared corpus of natural human demonstrations can instead serve as a reusable data interface for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot. We present Human2Dex, a wrist-centric human demonstration interface that separates shared human observation and motion semantics from embodiment-specific execution. It aligns observations through local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation with consistent structural semantics across human and robot observations. It constructs executable supervision by retargeting fused human hand motion to each target hand, and introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation ( GPIR ) to express tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket. The corpus is converted into separate training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, while action labels, normalization, training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain hand-specific. Across six real-world tasks, Human2Dex achieves 109/120 (90.8%) successes on Linker O6 and 97/120 (80.8%) on Wuji. Across both hands, Human-Raw achieves 63/240 (26.3%) successes, whereas the complete Human2Dex configuration achieves 206/240 (85.8%). These results support the use of wrist-centric human demonstrations as a reusable interface across calibrated dexterous hands while retaining embodiment-specific policy learning. The project website is publicly available at https://human2dex.pages.dev/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation policies require demonstrations that jointly capture arm motion, high-DoF hand configuration, and contact-rich task progress. Acquiring such demonstrations separately for each target hand is costly and difficult to scale. Many existing systems make data collection more compatible with robot deployment through instrumented motion capture, robot-like interfaces, or wearable hardware [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . These interfaces can reduce the correspondence burden during transfer, but they often establish robot compatibility partly through the acquisition setup, control interface, or embodiment-aware mapping. When the target embodiment changes, the corresponding conversion or embodiment-specific setup must still be established for the new hand. This motivates a higher-level question: how can a reusable human demonstration interface convert the same human manipulation episodes into executable training data for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot?

We study this question from a wrist-centric perspective. Head-mounted egocentric video provides scalable human data and broad scene context [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] , whereas a wrist-mounted camera provides local hand–object observations that more closely correspond to the eye-in-hand views used for close-range dexterous control. This similarity in observation arrangement makes wrist-centric acquisition a natural starting point for demonstration reuse. However, matching the observation arrangement does not by itself establish correspondence between human and robot data. The two settings can still differ in hand appearance, articulated structure, kinematics, command spaces, and grasp-related geometry.

Even under wrist-to-eye-in-hand alignment, three linked mismatches remain. First, human and robot hands differ in appearance and articulated structure, so the same visual content does not automatically provide the same structural semantics. Prior work has addressed this issue through appearance adaptation, robot-hand rendering, and structured hand representations [ 12 , 4 , 13 , 14 ] . Second, human motion is not itself an executable command for a target hand: Linker O6 and Wuji have different kinematic structures, degrees of freedom, joint limits, and native action spaces. Human-to-robot retargeting and embodiment-aware motion mapping therefore remain necessary for constructing target-specific supervision [ 1 , 13 , 15 , 16 ] . Third, even after observation semantics are aligned and executable supervision is constructed, a policy must infer how the task object is positioned relative to the hand’s current grasp configuration. Image-centered object coordinates indicate where an object appears, but do not directly express its relation to the closing hand. Existing work has explored hand–object and functional grasp representations for grasp synthesis, contact modeling, and perception [ 17 , 18 , 9 , 19 , 20 ] . Thus, structural correspondence supports observation interpretation, executable supervision supports target-hand policy learning, and an explicit object–hand relation can provide a more direct interaction cue, particularly when grasp alignment matters.

We present Human2Dex, a reusable wrist-centric human demonstration interface that shares human demonstrations and their observation and motion semantics across embodiments while retaining target-hand-specific executable supervision and policy learning. To align observations, Human2Dex combines mask-guided local hand-appearance adaptation with a shared 21-point hand representation, establishing consistent structural semantics for human and robot observations. To construct executable supervision, fused human hand motion is retargeted separately to each calibrated target hand, producing native action labels for Linker O6 and Wuji. To represent interaction geometry, Human2Dex introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation ( GPIR ), which expresses tracked task objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket defined by the thumb–index grasp center. The same human demonstration corpus is therefore converted into separate training sets for the two target hands, while action labels, normalization statistics, policy training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain specific to each hand–task pair. No task demonstrations are collected with the target robot hands.

We evaluate whether this interface supports human-data reuse across embodiments under real-world dexterous manipulation. A matched Linker O6–Croissant study examines wrist- versus head-centric observation, while the main evaluation covers Linker O6 and Wuji across six real-world tasks. Additional reference-frame and task-wise analyses examine selected design choices and the task dependence of interaction grounding.

Our contributions are:

A reusable human demonstration interface for multiple dexterous embodiments. Human2Dex converts one wrist-centric human demonstration corpus into separate hand-specific training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, allowing each hand to learn an independent policy without collecting task demonstrations on the target robots.

A grasp-centered interaction representation for policy conditioning. The Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation expresses tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket, complementing structural observation alignment and target-specific action supervision with an explicit object–hand relation.

A two-hand, six-task physical evaluation with targeted design analyses. We evaluate the complete interface on two calibrated dexterous hands and six real-world tasks, complemented by controlled comparisons of observation viewpoint and object-reference coordinates and task-wise analysis of interaction-grounding behavior.

1. A reusable human demonstration interface for multiple dexterous embodiments. Human2Dex converts one wrist-centric human demonstration corpus into separate hand-specific training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, allowing each hand to learn an independent policy without collecting task demonstrations on the target robots.

2. A grasp-centered interaction representation for policy conditioning. The Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation expresses tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket, complementing structural observation alignment and target-specific action supervision with an explicit object–hand relation.

3. A two-hand, six-task physical evaluation with targeted design analyses. We evaluate the complete interface on two calibrated dexterous hands and six real-world tasks, complemented by controlled comparisons of observation viewpoint and object-reference coordinates and task-wise analysis of interaction-grounding behavior.

# II Related Work

## II-A Learning Robot Policies from Human Demonstrations

Human-data interfaces differ in where compatibility between human demonstrations and robot execution is established. Portable robot-like tools, motion-capture systems, teleoperation platforms, and wearable interfaces introduce deployment-relevant visual, kinematic, or contact signals during collection [ 21 , 2 , 3 , 1 , 22 , 14 , 23 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 24 ] . Recent UMI-style systems extend demonstration interfaces toward richer physical sensing and broader motion coordination. OmniUMI [ 25 ] integrates visual, tactile, and force-related sensing within a handheld interface for contact-rich manipulation. BifrostUMI [ 26 ] combines lightweight VR tracking with UMI-inspired grippers to collect robot-free demonstrations, from which a policy predicts human keypoint trajectories that are retargeted for humanoid whole-body execution.

Other approaches preserve more natural human behavior through egocentric video, human play, or human–robot co-training, while some convert human data through simulation or limited robot data [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 27 , 10 , 11 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ] . Among the closest interface-based approaches, UMI establishes
deployment-compatible observations and actions through a portable
robot-like gripper, while DexUMI [ 4 ] further reduces the human–robot
kinematic gap using a wearable hand exoskeleton together with robot-hand
visual adaptation. RealDexUMI [ 5 ] instead shares the dexterous end-effector
and sensing modules between demonstration collection and deployment,
thereby minimizing end-effector mismatch. HumanEgo [ 9 ] follows a different
route by lifting egocentric human video into an explicit entity-level
hand–object interaction representation. Human2Dex studies a complementary
setting: the source remains wrist-centric bare-hand manipulation, and
embodiment adaptation is performed after collection to construct native
action supervision and separate policies for dexterous hands with different
kinematics and action spaces.

## II-B Visual and Kinematic Cross-Embodiment Alignment

Cross-embodiment alignment involves both visual identity and articulated motion. Visual adaptation methods reduce differences between source and target hands through cross-painting, robot-hand rendering, or fine-grained hand–object segmentation [ 12 , 4 , 32 ] . Hand estimators and teleoperation systems provide structured landmarks or mappings for transferring human motion under different morphologies and kinematic constraints [ 33 , 34 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 35 ] . Human2Dex uses a 21-point hand representation as an intermediate interface for shared observation semantics and motion fusion, while retaining embodiment-specific retargeting, action labels, and policy checkpoints for each target hand. Thus, the shared representation defines data semantics rather than a common robot action space.

## II-C Object-Centric and Functional Grasp Representations

Object-centric representations provide relational information beyond isolated hand or object states. FunctionalGrasp and D(R,O) Grasp use semantic hand–object structure or robot–object descriptions for grasp generation, while ContactPose and HOT3D support contact modeling and egocentric hand–object tracking [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . Human2Dex uses the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation ( GPIR ) for a narrower purpose: sequential wrist-view policy control. GPIR expresses tracked task objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket and retains object scale and tracking reliability. It is therefore a low-dimensional grasp-relative interaction cue, rather than a general object reconstruction, universal grasp representation, or complete contact model.

2026-10-12.title: The value of information and the emergence of communication in evolved e-puck robots
2026-10-12.authors: Fernando Montes-Gonzalez
2026-10-12.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Neural and Evolutionary Computing (cs.NE)
2026-10-12.comment: . Code and data: this https URL (archived at this https URL )
2026-10-12.abstract: We study when communication emerges between autonomous agents and what role an innate action selection architecture plays. Two e-puck robots, reconstructed in PyBullet from their Webots model and validated against it, must find a feeding zone that can only be detected when a robot passes over it. Each robot can emit a one-bit signal whose direction is detected by the receiver. Control is provided by a GRU recurrent network with a residual path, either operating alone or as a channel within an Embedded Action Selection Architecture (EASA). Fitness measures only the time the robots spend over the food. When the robots receive a compass pointing to the food, use of the signal disappears completely. Without a compass, in a small arena, three independent runs achieved similar performance using different strategies: a referential signal, a permanent beacon, or no use of the signal. As the arena expands, the strategy based on a referential signal generalizes best. In contrast, evolving directly in the large arena does not increase the frequency of communication, but it does separate the strategies, and the referential signal clearly outperforms solitary searching. Within EASA, innate reflexes constrain the network and reduce performance. As its priorities evolve, evolution consistently weakens those reflexes. The results suggest that communication emerges in proportion to the value of the information it transmits, and that an innate scaffolding designed for isolated agents can be an impediment in a social task.

2026-10-12.title: Forward Dynamics Models
2026-10-12.authors: Zipei Ma , Junzhe Jiang , Jiahui Zhang , Juntong Zhang , Chun Gu , Bozhou Zhang , Jiankang Deng , Xiatian Zhu , Li Zhang
2026-10-12.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively.
Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions.
We present Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world-state prediction through an action-to-future paradigm.
Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end-to-end training lets ground-truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions.
At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost.
The paradigm is backbone-agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones.
Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Frontier vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs) offer two complementary foundations for robotic action learning.
Vision-language-action (VLA) models adapt VLMs to map current observations and task instructions directly to actions ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2026b ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) , following the action-imitation paradigm ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ) ( Figure 1 (a) ).
While effective, this paradigm learns what to do without explicit supervision on what happens next , leaving the rich signal in future world states unused.
World action models (WAMs) instead build on video backbones to model visual dynamics alongside actions ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Pai et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2026a ) .
A prevalent design first predicts future world states and then infers actions from them in an inverse-dynamics manner ( Li et al., 2026b ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026c ; Ma et al., 2026b ; AgiBot Research Team et al., 2026 ; Tian et al., 2024 ) ( Figure 1 (b) ).
However, future prediction is inherently error-prone, since every visual detail matters across both space and time.
Placing it before action prediction means its errors accumulate and amplify into the actions, and future generation also adds substantial inference overhead.
Other works predict future frames and actions jointly or in parallel ( Ye et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2026b ) , align policy features with future embeddings ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , or train an action model and an action-conditioned world model side by side ( Cen et al., 2025b ) .
These designs motivate studying the specific contribution of future supervision through action features, beyond supervision through shared context.

We investigate whether a policy can benefit from future supervision without ever depending on predicted futures.
To this end, we introduce Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models built on an action-to-future learning paradigm.
Borrowing the classical notion of forward dynamics ( Jordan & Rumelhart, 1992 ; Agrawal et al., 2016 ) , the mapping from state and action to the next state, FDM connects action learning with future world state prediction:
given the current world state and task instruction, FDM jointly predicts actions and future world states with asymmetric conditioning.
Future prediction reads action features, while action prediction cannot access future information.
The model is trained end to end, so the future-prediction loss backpropagates through these action features into the policy.
Action-to-future specifies this one-way information dependency within joint prediction.

This reverses the conditioning direction of future-conditioned WAMs and brings several advantages:
(1) Robustness : action prediction does not depend on predicted future world states, so errors in those predictions cannot propagate into actions;
(2) Action-grounded supervision : ground-truth future states supervise the action features used to generate actions, complementing action imitation with supervision from observed consequences;
(3) Efficiency : action-only inference skips future generation while retaining the context processing required for action prediction;
(4) Flexibility : either a VLM or a VGM can serve as the backbone.
As shown in Figure 2 , FDM w/ VLM improves real-world success at comparable latency to π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , while FDM w/ VGM improves success with 1.8 × 1.8\times faster inference than FastWAM-Joint. Table 1 contrasts the formulations of the three paradigms.
Our analysis further confirms that, unlike FastWAM-Joint, whose action error grows with the quality degradation of predicted futures, FDM’s action error is insensitive to future-prediction quality ( Section 4.4 ).

Our contributions are threefold: (i) We introduce FDM, a novel family of robotic action models that learns in an action-to-future manner during training, with future supervision flowing into the policy through its action features, and requires no future prediction at inference; (ii) We build VLM- and VGM-based instantiations of FDM, demonstrating its backbone flexibility; (iii) Experiments in simulation and on real robots show that FDM achieves strong or competitive performance across VLM- and VGM-based settings, and analysis shows that it avoids the error propagation of future-conditioned designs.

# 2 Related work

Vision-language-action models. VLA models adapt pretrained vision-language models to predict robot actions ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026a ; Ye et al., 2026b ; Black et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Contributors, 2025 ; Cai et al., 2026b ; Shukor et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) .
Recent approaches also predict future observations or their latent representations ( Cen et al., 2025b ; Ma et al., 2026b ; Cheang et al., 2024 ; Cen et al., 2025a ; Lv et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , using future prediction as a learning objective or an input to action generation, as in visual chain-of-thought policies ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) .
Our FDM w/ VLM builds on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and conditions future prediction on action features and the current context, establishing an action-to-future dependency.

World action models. Video models provide visual dynamics representations for robot control ( HaCohen et al., 2024 ; Ali et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2025 ) .
WAMs use these representations to condition action decoding ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Pai et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026c ) or jointly predict video and actions ( Bi et al., 2026a ; Ye et al., 2026c ; Li et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026c ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Tian et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) .
Extensions combine predicted outcomes with value estimates for planning ( Bi et al., 2026b ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , while asynchronous designs improve efficiency through different denoising budgets or prediction horizons ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Cai et al., 2026a ) .
Our FDM w/ VGM places future prediction downstream of action features, keeping the action path independent of predicted video.
Deployment therefore omits future-video computation while retaining current-observation processing.

Joint predictive models use visual supervision for action learning ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Ye et al., 2026a ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Won et al., 2025 ) .
UVA and Fast-WAM also enable action-only deployment via separate video–action decoders and structured attention, respectively ( Li et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026b ) .
FDM conditions future prediction on action features and backpropagates prediction errors into them.
Our context-only and stop-gradient controls isolate action conditioning and backward supervision, respectively.

2026-10-12.title: ReAT: Residual Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Robot Policies
2026-10-12.authors: Dijia Zhan , Zhuo Li , Xuemiao Xu , Sun Zheng , Jinyi Li , Wenjun Wang , Jie Tang
2026-10-12.abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Autoregressive robot policies generate future actions by predicting discrete tokens one at a time ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . To connect this prediction process to continuous motion, action tokenizers encode future action chunks into token sequences and decode the predicted tokens back into executable actions ( Mete et al., 2024 ; Pertsch et al., 2025 ) . The encoded sequences provide the policy’s training targets, so the tokenizer determines how action information is distributed across tokens and how each token depends on its predecessors ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ) . The question is then how to structure these targets so that each token has a clear role in reconstructing the action chunk.

Learned action tokenizers use reconstruction objectives to compress action chunks into discrete sequences for policy learning ( Lee et al., 2024 ; Mete et al., 2024 ) . Recent work further shows that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient to characterize these representations, as token organization also affects downstream policy learning ( Dong et al., 2026 ) . Ordering constraints and prefix supervision provide additional structure by encouraging earlier tokens to preserve essential action information and later tokens to add detail ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . However, these objectives do not by themselves explicitly define each token’s contribution relative to the actions already reconstructed. That contribution can remain implicit in the learned encoder–decoder mapping, leaving an opportunity to ground successive tokens in the action information still missing from the current reconstruction.

The residual between a target action chunk and its current reconstruction provides a concrete description of this missing information. Because it is measured in the reconstructed actions, it reflects what preceding tokens have actually recovered, including the effects of quantization and decoding. Encoding this residual gives the next token an explicit target tied to the reconstruction produced so far. This motivates Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which structures action sequences as successive corrections to an evolving action draft.

ReAT implements this formulation through explicit reconstruction feedback. During tokenizer training, the encoder maps the remaining reconstruction error to a discrete token, and the decoder uses that token together with the current action draft to produce a learned correction (Figure 1 ). The updated draft then provides the basis for constructing the next token. Each additional token thus represents a correction to the existing action draft, with Figure 2 illustrating how reconstruction improves as tokens are added. The resulting residual tokens provide structured prediction targets for observation-conditioned autoregressive policies.

We evaluate ReAT on 19 manipulation tasks spanning LIBERO, MetaWorld, RoboCasa, and real-world bucket stacking. With 8 tokens, ReAT outperforms the evaluated action-tokenization and diffusion-policy baselines in task success on all three simulation benchmarks and the real-world task. On LIBERO, it surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines using only 4 tokens. LIBERO ablations further support the contribution of explicit reconstruction feedback to policy performance and show that prefix supervision enables effective control with shorter token sequences.

In summary, our contributions are:

We introduce ReAT, an action tokenizer that constructs each successive token from the residual left by the decoded prefix, explicitly incorporating quantization and decoding effects into token construction.

We combine a draft-conditioned recurrent decoder with prefix reconstruction supervision to turn residual tokens into successive action corrections. Each nonempty prefix reconstructs a complete action chunk, allowing a single autoregressive policy to use different token budgets without retraining.

Experiments across three simulation benchmarks and real-world bucket stacking show that 8-token ReAT outperforms the evaluated action-tokenization and diffusion-policy baselines in task success. On LIBERO, 4-token ReAT also surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines, while mechanism ablations support the contributions of reconstruction feedback and prefix supervision.

1. We introduce ReAT, an action tokenizer that constructs each successive token from the residual left by the decoded prefix, explicitly incorporating quantization and decoding effects into token construction.

2. We combine a draft-conditioned recurrent decoder with prefix reconstruction supervision to turn residual tokens into successive action corrections. Each nonempty prefix reconstructs a complete action chunk, allowing a single autoregressive policy to use different token budgets without retraining.

3. Experiments across three simulation benchmarks and real-world bucket stacking show that 8-token ReAT outperforms the evaluated action-tokenization and diffusion-policy baselines in task success. On LIBERO, 4-token ReAT also surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines, while mechanism ablations support the contributions of reconstruction feedback and prefix supervision.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Robot policies generate actions through continuous representations or discrete token sequences. Continuous approaches include variational action-chunk prediction ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , diffusion-based generation ( Chi et al., 2023 ) , and flow-matching action experts ( Black et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) . Discrete autoregressive policies predict action symbols sequentially ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , while recent extensions explore parallel continuous-chunk decoding ( Kim et al., 2025 ) and discrete-action pretraining followed by flow-matching post-training ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . HiFlow further combines scale-wise autoregressive generation with flow matching in continuous action space ( Yashima et al., 2026 ) . These approaches primarily advance the mechanisms for generating actions, while leaving open how discrete action targets should be structured to support progressive correction. ReAT addresses this representation question by making residual correction the organizing principle of action tokenization, providing autoregressive policies with corrective prediction targets.

Learned action tokenizers compress action chunks into quantized representations for policy learning ( Lee et al., 2024 ; Mete et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , while FAST exploits temporal regularity through frequency-domain coding and byte-pair encoding ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ) . Beyond compression, CARP organizes action representations into scales for next-scale prediction ( Gong et al., 2025 ) , and ActionCodec examines how token structure affects downstream policy optimization ( Dong et al., 2026 ) . Ordered tokenizers use nested dropout to prioritize information in early prefixes ( Rippel et al., 2014 ) , enabling flexible-length reconstruction in image and action domains ( Bachmann et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Compact representations and ordered prefixes improve the usability of action tokens, but do not by themselves make the remaining action reconstruction error an explicit basis for subsequent token construction. ReAT introduces this connection, giving successive tokens a correction target defined by what earlier tokens have actually reconstructed.

Residual quantization successively approximates latent features, with applications in image generation ( Lee et al., 2022 ) , neural audio compression ( Zeghidour et al., 2021 ; Défossez et al., 2022 ) , and action tokenization ( Lee et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Gong et al., 2025 ) . However, latent approximation error does not directly characterize the error remaining in decoded actions. Recurrent image codecs address the analogous distinction by feeding decoded-output errors back into progressive compression ( Toderici et al., 2016a ; Toderici et al., 2016b ) . ReAT brings this reconstruction-feedback perspective to action tokenization, constructing corrective representations for autoregressive policy learning.

2026-10-12.title: Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion: Object-Centric Flow Replanning for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
2026-10-12.authors: Chen Yu , Sudarshan S Harithas , Juan Borbon , Dingqi Zhang , Jiuguang Wang
2026-10-12.abstract:
People often learn how an unfamiliar object moves through a small exploratory
push, using its response to guide their next motion. Inspired by this behavior, we study humanoids
pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are initially unknown. Our object-centric
framework closes online estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control into a loop,
creating a tension: replacing the plan whenever the belief shifts disrupts the maneuver under way,
while keeping it strands the robot on a path its evidence has ruled out. Belief-Overlap Partial
Inversion (BOPI) scales revision to agreement, inverting the flow under the old belief only as far
as the beliefs disagree before reconstructing under the new one. Across 18 simulated goals it lowers
pooled final position and yaw error by roughly 33% and 47% against fixed-depth replanning, and on
hardware it translates and turns a non-holonomic cart.
2026-10-12.introduction:
People rarely commit to a way of moving an unfamiliar object before testing it; a short push reveals
whether it rolls freely, resists, or veers off line, and the plan is adjusted before the motion has
finished. We pursue this ability in humanoids pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are
unknown at the outset [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . What is at stake is the path and not merely the
effort: an omnidirectional cart can be driven laterally to its goal, whereas a constrained rear axle
admits only a curved approach, so the geometry of the maneuver is settled by a property the robot
cannot observe until it is already pushing.

Our framework treats the cart, rather than the robot, as the thing being planned for. A recurrent
estimator maintains a belief over the cart’s physical properties, a conditional flow planner
generates a timed object trajectory conditioned on that belief, and a whole-body controller tracks
that trajectory while preserving grasp and balance. Because motion is what produces evidence, the
three components close a loop in which every correction arrives mid-maneuver, and that timing is the
difficulty: regenerating the plan from each new belief, on top of noisy pose estimates, perturbs the
very trajectory the controller is following, while refusing to regenerate leaves the robot committed
to a path its own measurements no longer support. Building on plan-reuse
methods [ 1 , 6 , 7 ] , we ask: how much should a new estimate change the robot’s plan?

Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) answers with the beliefs themselves. As the
replanning component of our framework, it partially reverses plan generation
under the old belief and reconstructs under the updated one, with the depth of reversal set by how
far the two beliefs overlap: when successive beliefs agree the plan is barely disturbed, and as they
diverge more of it is rewritten. The rule requires no per-situation tuning, and the change it
induces in the encoded plan vanishes as the overlap approaches one.

Experiments span a controlled nonlinear benchmark, where BOPI attains higher task success with
smaller cumulative plan changes, and 18 goals in G1–Dex3 simulation. Figure shows
object-centric control across cart types ( A–D ), real-robot translation and
turning ( E–J ), and simulation replay of recorded plans and updates ( K–P ).

Our contributions are: (i) an object-centric estimation–planning–control framework that
adapts cart trajectories while tracking continues; (ii) BOPI, its belief-adaptive
replanning method, with an exact-integration bound under which the encoded
plan change vanishes as belief overlap approaches one; and (iii) simulation and hardware
evaluations showing lower goal error in simulation and lower final position and tracking error on
hardware.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related work

## II-A Object-centric loco-manipulation

Loco-manipulation couples locomotion with manipulation through whole-body
control [ 8 , 9 , 5 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . A
recurring move is to state the task on the object rather than on the robot. Mittal et
al. [ 13 ] plan interactions with articulated objects in unknown scenes;
Omnigrasp [ 14 ] and MaskedManipulator [ 15 ] drive
simulated humanoids from desired object motion; ResMimic [ 16 ] adds an
object-conditioned residual to a general motion tracker; and OmniContact [ 17 ] chains contact-level skills for generalizable loco-manipulation. We share the object-level
specification with this line of work and differ in what happens afterwards: the object trajectory is
not fixed once issued but revised as the object’s properties are inferred.

## II-B Cart pushing under unknown dynamics

Cart pushing is the classical instance of that coupling. Harada et al. [ 18 ] derive walking motion for pushing manipulation, Scholz et al. [ 19 ] treat the
cart as a movable obstacle during mobile-manipulator navigation, and Hawley and
Suleiman [ 20 , 3 ] control a humanoid pushing a loaded cart and later
navigate with it under SLAM. Because the cart’s response turns on parameters the robot cannot see,
several works estimate them while pushing: Sun et al. [ 21 ] identify cart
parameters online, Foster et al. [ 4 ] keep inertial estimates physically consistent for
humanoid loco-manipulation, Zhang et al. [ 22 ] optimize the push pose and
reject disturbances without an accurate dynamic model, and Sriganesh et
al. [ 23 ] couple estimation with planning for quadrupedal pedipulation.
Our question is orthogonal to how the estimate is formed: we ask what the planner should do with it
once it moves.

## II-C Cross-embodiment control

Differences in physical properties or morphology change a system’s dynamics and constraints, the
concern of cross-embodiment
control [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ] .
Rather than adapting control of the robot itself, we study how the object’s path within the
robot–object system should change as its properties are inferred.

## II-D Adaptive planning

Once properties are inferred [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] , the plan has to follow. Diffusion
and flow models [ 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 , 36 ] generate trajectories that can be regenerated under a new condition, and several methods reuse the
previous solution instead of discarding it. SDEdit [ 37 ] noises an input and denoises it under
the new condition; Replanning with Diffusion Models (RDM) [ 1 ] applies this to replanning by
adding a fixed proportion of noise to the current plan before reconstruction.
FlowEdit [ 2 ] avoids inversion altogether, editing a trajectory by integrating the difference
between the flow fields the old and new conditions induce, while DDIM [ 38 ] supplies
the deterministic inversion such methods rely on. A parallel line decides when to re-solve
rather than how much of the old solution to keep, through real-time
chunking [ 6 , 7 , 39 ] and noise-space
steering [ 40 ] . What none of these supplies is a principled setting for the amount
of revision: RDM’s noise level is a fixed hyperparameter, and FlowEdit’s edit follows from the field
difference alone. BOPI ties that amount to the overlap between the beliefs that produced the two
plans, so the plan changes as much as the evidence has.

2026-10-12.title: VICAR: Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting for Humanoid Interactive Skills
2026-10-12.authors: Dvij Kalaria , Bike Zhang , S. Shankar Sastry
2026-10-12.abstract: Third-person human videos offer a scalable alternative to task-specific reward engineering, teleoperation, and manually scripted demonstrations for humanoid loco-manipulation. Recent video-to-humanoid systems have shown that noisy human motion, object trajectories, and contacts can be extracted from unstructured videos and refined into deployable skills. However, a key gap remains for contact-rich imitation: the task is often defined by world-frame contacts whose poses, timing, and speed must survive embodiment mismatch and runtime scene changes. Towards this, we present VICAR (Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting), a pipeline for learning humanoid interactive skills from third-person human videos. The system first recovers human motion, reconstructs task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, and then retargets the motion to a humanoid while preserving global contact poses, motion speed, and collision clearance. Unlike retargeting methods that only remove penetration or preserve local interaction geometry, our formulation represents user-specified contact poses and collision clearance as high-priority Lagrangian penalty terms and optimizes the full motion to remain smooth through contact-rich transitions. The resulting motions are used to train a contact-conditioned motion generator whose inputs include movable contact points enabling runtime adaptation to new contact positions. We demonstrate the framework on ten diverse third-person video skills, including six table-tennis serves, three object-pickup tasks, and ladder climbing, and deploy the learned skills on hardware. These results suggest that contact-preserving retargeting is a practical step toward humanoids that learn useful interactive behavior by watching humans.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Humans routinely learn interaction skills by watching other humans. A child does not need an adult to physically guide their body through every action, in the way teleoperation is often used to train robots; they can learn by observing that a cup should be reached on the table, that the table edge can support the body while crouching, or that a tossed ball must be met at a precise point in space. For humanoid robots, however, this mode of learning remains difficult: third-person videos provide abundant motion cues, but the robot must execute them with a different morphology, different joint limits, and different contact geometry. These tasks are organized around sparse contact events: a hand must arrive at an object, a foot must land on a rung, or a racket must meet a ball at the right pose and time. A trajectory can therefore resemble the source motion yet remain unusable if those events drift in the world frame.

The embodiment gap becomes especially severe for contact-rich tasks. Consider a standing adult picking up an object from a table. For the adult, the table may be near waist height; for a shorter humanoid such as Unitree G1, the same table may be near the chest, as shown in Figure 2 . A retargeted motion that only matches human joint or keypoint motion will miss the object. The same issue appears when a robot crouches to pick up an object under a table while using the other hand for support: success depends on preserving the support contact, avoiding the table, and keeping the motion dynamically trackable. Collision avoidance alone does not resolve this ambiguity: several collision-free poses may exist, but only a small subset preserves the demonstrated contact and approach speed.

Many video-imitation pipelines rely on egocentric or robot-view demonstrations, but the web and everyday recordings contain a plethora of third-person human videos that can provide strong priors for humanoid whole-body motion learning. Recent systems show that monocular videos can provide scalable skill data for humanoids. VideoMimic [ 1 ] reconstructs human-scene geometry from casual videos and uses the resulting meshes and retargeted motions for contextual control. HDMI [ 2 ] learns humanoid-object interaction policies from monocular RGB videos by co-tracking robot and object states. OmniRetarget [ 3 ] improves interaction-preserving retargeting by preserving human-object-terrain relations through an interaction mesh and hard kinematic constraints. These works make major progress, but our target setting places a different emphasis: we want the robot to preserve specific global contact poses that may move at runtime, such as the ball-hit point in a table-tennis serve or the object position in a pickup task. The challenge is thus not only to reconstruct what the human did, but also to identify which interaction quantities must remain invariant after embodiment transfer.

We introduce VICAR, a video-to-humanoid learning pipeline centered on contact-aware retargeting. Given a third-person video, VICAR extracts human motion using GENMO/GEM [ 4 ] , reconstructs task-relevant obstacle geometry using monocular depth and semantic segmentation. The selected regions are unprojected into a point cloud, voxelized into collision geometry, and scaled following the human-scene alignment ideas of VideoMimic [ 1 ] . We then retarget the motion in two stages: an initial OmniRetarget-style [ 3 ] pass gives a feasible robot reference, and a second optimization uses high-priority collision and global contact-pose penalties while preserving motion speed.

Our retargeted motions are not merely static references. They seed a motion generator conditioned on movable contact points that can be adjusted online during inference: for example, the ball-hit point in a table-tennis serve can move with the perceived ball position, and object-pick motions can be adapted to different object placements. A downstream policy then tracks the generated reference using proprioception and gravity observations, allowing deployment on hardware.

This paper makes the following contributions:

We formulate contact- and speed-preserving retargeting for third-person video imitation, using high-priority global contact-pose and collision penalties derived from monocularly reconstructed obstacles.

We connect this retargeting stage to a contact-conditioned motion generator that supports dynamic contact locations and contact-point augmentation.

We evaluate the pipeline on ten diverse skills, including six table-tennis serves, object pickups above and below a table, bimanual box pickup and placement, and ladder climbing. All skills are deployed on hardware except ladder climbing.

1. We formulate contact- and speed-preserving retargeting for third-person video imitation, using high-priority global contact-pose and collision penalties derived from monocularly reconstructed obstacles.

2. We connect this retargeting stage to a contact-conditioned motion generator that supports dynamic contact locations and contact-point augmentation.

3. We evaluate the pipeline on ten diverse skills, including six table-tennis serves, object pickups above and below a table, bimanual box pickup and placement, and ladder climbing. All skills are deployed on hardware except ladder climbing.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

Human video is an attractive supervision source because it is easier to collect than teleoperation, motion capture, or robot demonstrations. Recent systems learn pose or locomotion from large video collections [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 1 , 9 ] , adapt robot-free videos to manipulation [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] , or target humanoid-object interaction [ 2 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . HDMI [ 2 ] extracts human and object trajectories for co-tracking policies, while VideoMimic [ 1 ] reconstructs human-scene geometry for contextual skills. HumanX and SUGAR scale video-derived interaction learning [ 15 , 16 ] , but do not explicitly preserve task-specified global contact poses that can change at runtime. These systems primarily expand reference acquisition and policy learning; our focus is the intermediate geometric adaptation needed to keep sparse, task-defining contacts valid after embodiment transfer.

Kinematic imitation uses retargeted human motion as reference data for characters and robots [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . PHC [ 5 ] fits SMPL-style pose to a robot embodiment, and GMR [ 21 ] matches human pose through relative keypoint geometry. Video-to-humanoid systems such as HumanPlus and ResMimic use retargeted references for tracking [ 6 , 14 ] , but do not directly preserve global contacts or avoid task obstacles. OmniRetarget [ 3 ] preserves local human–object–terrain relations with an interaction mesh and hard joint, velocity, collision, and stance constraints. VICAR instead represents selected contacts as world-frame pose objectives and optimizes the whole clip to preserve source speed through contact. The distinction matters when collision avoidance admits several geometrically feasible solutions: in tabletop pickup, for example, entering and exiting the platform through different faces produces a discontinuous reference despite satisfying local clearance.

Monocular depth and segmentation provide useful but noisy scene geometry [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Video-to-robot pipelines also use body recovery, object reconstruction, 6D pose tracking, and registration to extract interaction priors [ 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 16 ] . Similar to VideoMimic [ 1 ] , we unproject depth and resolve scale from the human-scene geometry, but reconstruct only semantic regions likely to constrain the robot. This task-focused reconstruction avoids requiring a complete scene model while retaining the surfaces needed for collision and contact reasoning.

Interactive humanoid policies often track reference robot and object states [ 2 , 14 ] or reconstructed scene-conditioned references [ 1 ] . SUGAR [ 16 ] improves generalization with a hierarchical command generator after physics refinement. SceneBot [ 30 ] and ContactMimic [ 31 ] show that per-link or binary contact commands can condition the tracking policy directly when scene interaction is represented implicitly. This policy-level conditioning is sufficient when the controller can resolve the desired interaction from a motion and contact mode. In contrast, retargeting-layer anchors are needed when the world exogenously determines a specific SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) pose—such as a measured ball location or fixed ladder rung—that must first be embedded in the reference motion and interpolated across contact variants. VICAR places a contact-conditioned generator between retargeting and policy learning, separating geometric adaptation from low-level control.

2026-10-12.title: Towards Safer Cities: A Design Process for Perception Datasets in Urban Driving Scenarios
2026-10-12.authors: Alexander Kroth , Cristian Martinez , Steven Peters
2026-10-12.comment: . Submitted to 17. Uni-DAS e.V. Workshop Fahrerassistenz und automatisiertes Fahren. For details of the conference, see this https URL
2026-10-12.abstract: Urban environments present significant challenges for the perception systems of automated driving due to their high complexity, characterized by dense traffic, diverse obstacles, or a wide range of possible scenarios. While numerous automotive datasets exist, few focus on urban settings, and the majority are acquired exclusively on passenger cars and overlook other transport modalities such as heavy-duty trucks, busses and trams. In contrast to passenger vehicles, these platforms operate under different geographical and operational constraints; including traversing pedestrian zones or platform-specific tasks such as movement of trailer or winter service. In this work a method is proposed for a guided dataset creation based on an analysis of existing datasets using user-generated map data. Furthermore, representative truck-specific use cases are identified and exemplified to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed methodology and to support targeted acquisition planning.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Heavy-duty vehicles, buses and trams form the backbone of urban transportation for both goods and passengers. However, their operation is threatened by an already existing and growing shortage of qualified drivers [ 9 , 8 ] . Long-haul applications such as main-line rail or trucking are facing similar problems, but are already in the focus of both research and industry [ 19 ] . To tackle this issue automation is proposed as a possible solution. In main-line rail, this is reflected by the introduction of the European Train Control System (ETCS), which is already being tested in selected projects [ 4 ] . In the trucking sector, companies such as Torc and Aurora are pursuing to solve the hub-to-hub use-case, focused on highway operation [ 22 , 1 ] .

In contrast, great progress has been made in the research and adoption of automated driving in passenger cars. This is illustrated by both the large amount of available datasets and research based on them in this sector [ 10 ] . Furthermore, commercial services such as Waymo currently operate autonomous taxi fleets in multiple cities in the United States and are expected to expand to London in early 2026 [ 23 ] . Datasets form the basis for the development, training, and evaluation of both modular and end-to-end trained automated driving stacks. The scope of existing datasets closely aligns with automated driving solutions we see today.

This work demonstrates that current datasets only partially cover the requirements of truck and tram automation in urban environments. Based on an analysis of existing datasets and user-generated map data, relevant truck- and tram-specific scenarios are identified and used to derive Operational Design Domains (ODDs) for both platforms. Building on these findings, a methodology for targeted data acquisition is proposed to systematically address the identified gaps and support the creation of future urban truck and tram datasets.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Methodology

## 2.1 Dataset metrics

The accessibility of the different ODD elements in existing datasets and their suitability for planning future recordings is evaluated as shown in Table 1 . For most of the datasets, the recording vehicle is specified and the sensor setup is known, meaning that this information is directly available for acquisition. While information about Roadside Structures or the Road Network might be present in datasets, this can be extracted using the location of the recording and OpenStreetMap. Based on this information the acquisition can also be planned. Temporary Modifications are rarely explicitly annotated and are hard to plan for as they are not findable in a database similar to OpenStreetMap. While dynamic objects are the focus of most perception datasets and therefore are well annotated, their presence and distribution can’t be anticipated for a recording. The exact environmental conditions are also rarely annotated, at best a general indication is given. A rough estimate can be retrieved from Open-Meteo. For planning recordings the general weather can be taken into account, but also a detailed planning is difficult. Digital information, unless already annotated or directly captured, is not possible to acquire afterwards. For the planning stage most information can be known before. Overall Roadside Structures, Road Network and Vehicle Information are most promising to both gather information about existing datasets as well as to plan for new recordings.

## 2.2 Dataset Requirements and Acquisition Planning

As a first step towards the creation of new datasets, it is necessary to define the scenarios that should be captured. Based on representative use cases, individual scenarios are derived and decomposed into their constituent elements according to the six layer model, vehicle-specific characteristics, and the interactions between road users. The resulting set of requirements serves as a reference for evaluating the coverage of existing datasets and should therefore be as comprehensive as possible.

The analysis of existing datasets focuses on identifying which of these elements are already represented and which remain underrepresented. In particular, dynamic objects, roadside structures, road network characteristics, vehicle information, and scenario descriptions can be readily extracted from existing datasets and therefore provide a basis for comparison. This analysis enables the identification of dataset gaps and the prioritization of scenarios that should be targeted in future recordings.

Based on the identified gaps, an acquisition strategy can be defined. Layers 1 and 2 of the six layer model are largely represented in OpenStreetMap and can therefore be used to systematically identify candidate recording locations. Examples include roads with cobblestone surfaces, narrow intersections, height restrictions, or tram crossings. In contrast, temporary infrastructure modifications and dynamic traffic interactions are difficult to plan in advance and must be captured opportunistically. Environmental conditions can be partially targeted using weather services such as Open-Meteo, while vehicle-specific information can be directly controlled during recording. This process enables the systematic selection of recording locations and conditions that maximize the coverage of underrepresented scenarios.

Following data acquisition, the recorded data are evaluated with respect to the coverage of the previously defined ODDs. Any ODD elements that remain insufficiently represented are identified as open requirements for future recording campaigns. This iterative process is repeated until adequate coverage of all targeted ODDs has been achieved.

Submodular maximization provides an effective framework for such coordination, and resilient variants further account for robot failures or adversarial removals. However, existing methods typically overlook the impact of robot loss on the communication network, which may disconnect the surviving team and prevent continued coordination. To address this issue, we introduce Resilient k k -Connected Submodular Maximization, which jointly considers task performance, resilience, and communication connectivity. The resulting feasible family is not a matroid, preventing a direct application of classical curvature-greedy guarantees. We overcome this challenge through a Menger-based connectivity reduction, a connectivity-aware greedy algorithm with a feasibility-preserving fallback, and a new curvature-based analysis that captures the cost of enforcing connectivity through a single factor ρ \rho . Experiments on multi-robot target tracking validate the proposed method and characterize the practical impact of connectivity constraints.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Multi-robot systems provide scalable solutions to applications such as environmental monitoring, target tracking, search and rescue, and collaborative exploration [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . In many of these settings, the robots must coordinate their sensing or motion decisions to maximize a common team objective [ 5 ] . Submodular set functions provide a natural mathematical framework for such coordination by capturing the principle of diminishing returns: the marginal benefit of adding an additional robot decreases as more robots are already selected. Many commonly used objectives, including mutual information [ 6 ] , area coverage [ 7 ] , number of observed targets [ 8 ] , and sensor-measurement entropy [ 9 ] are monotone submodular [ 10 ] . This structure enables computationally efficient greedy algorithms with well-established constant-factor performance guarantees, as reviewed in Section II .

Classical submodular maximization, however, typically assumes that the selected robots remain available throughout execution. In practice, robots may be lost due to hardware failures, communication interference, denial-of-service attacks, or other adverse events. This has motivated resilient submodular maximization, where the team is selected so that the objective remains large even after a bounded number of robots are removed [ 8 , 11 , 12 ] . Existing resilient formulations primarily focus on preserving
submodular objective performance
after such removals. Yet, critically, robot loss can disrupt the communication network among surviving robots. A team might therefore retain high sensing or coverage capacity after failures while becoming disconnected and rendered unable to continue coordinated operation.

Communication connectivity and resilience have both been studied extensively, but largely as separate requirements. In this work, we consider them jointly and ask how to select robot actions so that the team achieves a high submodular objective while remaining connected even after adversarial robot removals. We refer to this problem as Resilient k k -Connected Submodular Maximization (see Fig. 1 ). The joint treatment is substantially more challenging than simply combining two existing constraints. Resilience requires accounting for the worst-case subset of removed robots, while connectivity is a global property whose feasibility depends on which robots survive.
This interaction also breaks key structures used in existing approximation analysis. In the resilient maximization framework of Tzoumas et al. [ 11 ] , robustness is achieved by constructing a sacrificial “bait” set of β \beta high-value robots together with a greedily selected remainder. Under a connectivity requirement, however, the adversary determines which robots are removed, and the worst-case removal need not coincide with the bait set. Consequently, enforcing connectivity only on the non-bait robots does not guarantee that the surviving team remains connected. Moreover, the constraint of selecting one trajectory per robot together with a global vertex-connectivity requirement does not form a matroid. As a result, classical curvature-based greedy guarantees cannot be applied directly and must be re-established for the connectivity-constrained resilient setting.

We make the following contributions:

We formulate resilient submodular maximization under a ( β + 1 ) (\beta{+}1) -vertex-connectivity constraint and show that the family of partial, connectivity-feasible selections is not a matroid (Proposition 1 ), identifying precisely why the classical greedy analysis fails to transfer.

We introduce a connectivity filter with a rigid-shift fallback across both bait and greedy stages, show it guarantees a feasible, ( β + 1 ) (\beta{+}1) -connected output that survives any removal of size at most β \beta regardless of composition (Proposition 2 ), and re-derive the curvature-greedy bound against a connectivity-respecting benchmark (Lemma 1 ), isolating the filter’s entire cost into a single interpretable constant ρ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \rho\in[0,1] .

We prove a resilient, connectivity-preserving approximation guarantee (Theorem 1 ) and empirically corroborate the algorithm’s feasibility, the price of connectivity, and the squared resilience factor (Section V ).

2026-10-12.title: CeDR-Nav: Cross-Embodiment Mapless Navigation via Offline Demonstration Recasting
2026-10-12.authors: Xianghui Wang , Xinming Zhang , Yiwei Qian , Siwei Cheng , Shanze Wang , Dan Zhang , Wei Zhang
2026-10-12.abstract:
Learning-based methods have demonstrated strong performance in mapless robot navigation. However, a learned policy remains restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. Many cross-embodiment navigation methods require time-consuming online training and can still underperform target-specific policies. In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for deriving a policy for each target embodiment, but the embodiment mismatch prevents these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target. In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a cross-embodiment demonstration recasting framework that trains a dedicated navigation policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online data collection. Geometry-consistent scaling with per-demonstration validity assessment converts the source demonstrations into target training data, and a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy generates feasible avoidance maneuvers for each target embodiment. Extensive quantitative simulations and real-world deployments
across multiple robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness
of CeDR-Nav, with an average success-rate gain of 13.8 percentage points
over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations and
target-specific policy training completed within seconds.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Autonomous navigation is a fundamental capability for mobile robots. In recent years, learning-based methods have emerged as effective approaches to mapless navigation in complex and cluttered environments [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . However, a learned navigation policy is commonly restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. In practice, the physical dimensions and sensor configurations of mobile robots not only vary across platforms, but also change within a single platform due to task requirements. When the robot’s embodiment changes, the original policy can suffer substantial performance degradation and may cause dangerous collisions. Whether learning from collected demonstrations or from agent–environment interaction, obtaining a navigation policy demands significant effort for every new embodiment [ 4 , 5 ] .

Existing methods address this challenge by adapting trained policies
at deployment [ 6 ] , training universal policies
across embodiment configurations [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] ,
or learning from multi-platform navigation experience [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . However, the conservative enclosure used by DVST can restrict
passage through otherwise traversable gaps when the target
and reference robots differ substantially in
shape [ 6 ] . Training universal policies across configurations, such as
DRL-DCLP [ 7 ] , requires time-consuming online
training with carefully designed environments, while the resulting
policy can underperform a dedicated target-specific policy. These data-driven approaches rely on multi-platform datasets
or scene-geometry estimation for experience augmentation [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] .

In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for each target embodiment. However, the geometric dimensions and velocity limits of the source embodiment prevent these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target embodiment [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . This raises the central question of this work: can source demonstrations be converted into valid target supervision without new demonstration collection, so that a dedicated navigation policy can be obtained for each target embodiment without additional online interaction?

In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a Cross-Embodiment Demonstration Recasting framework that obtains a dedicated policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online RL training . Specifically, CeDR-Nav first recasts source demonstrations into valid training data for the target embodiment through geometry-consistent scaling and validity assessment, ensuring that the recast trajectories remain geometrically consistent with the target embodiment. Subsequently, CeDR-Nav trains a target-specific policy using a Gaussian mixture model [ 20 ] to capture the multimodal action distribution in the recast demonstrations. Extensive cross-embodiment simulations and quantitative real-world experiments on multiple robot platforms demonstrate that CeDR-Nav derives effective navigation policies for diverse target embodiments from source demonstrations. The main contributions of this article are summarized as follows.

We introduce CeDR-Nav, an offline demonstration recasting framework for cross-embodiment mapless navigation that replaces target-specific online RL with offline learning from existing source demonstrations. It learns a navigation policy dedicated to each target embodiment, without requiring target-specific training-environment design.

It learns a navigation policy dedicated to each target embodiment, without requiring target-specific training-environment design.

We develop a geometry-consistent recasting method that produces valid training data for the target embodiment. Target-specific policy learning is then adopted to support effective obstacle avoidance on the target embodiment.

Extensive quantitative experiments in simulators and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms and navigation tasks validate the effectiveness of CeDR-Nav.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

Recent research has increasingly focused on cross-embodiment mapless
navigation. Existing works address the embodiment mismatch from two different
perspectives.

From the policy perspective, on the one hand, some works attempt to reuse
trained policies across robot configurations through perceptual
representations and deployment-time transformations. Early works developed
range-based representations to accommodate differences in sensing and robot
configuration [ 21 , 2 ] . Beyond perception, DVST adapts
a trained policy to robots with different dimensions through transformations
of both observations and actions at deployment, without retraining [ 6 ] . However, the conservative enclosure used by DVST can
lead to suboptimal behaviors when the target and reference robots differ
substantially in shape. On the other hand, other works train a universal
policy that accommodates multiple embodiments. These methods either
incorporate embodiment information into the observation representation [ 7 , 9 , 10 ] or randomize
embodiment parameters during training [ 8 ] . Despite their
applicability to multiple embodiments, reinforcement-learning-based methods
such as DRL-DCLP require carefully designed environments and extensive agent–environment interaction [ 7 ] . Moreover, performance may degrade on robot configurations outside the training distribution [ 22 ] . Other approaches, such as CE-Nav, learn target-specific policies through offline pretraining followed by online reinforcement-learning refinement [ 23 ] , which still requires online agent–environment interaction for each target embodiment.

From the data perspective, current methods address the embodiment mismatch
by learning from multi-platform navigation experience. Specifically,
navigation policies have been learned from data aggregated across multiple
robot platforms [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 16 ] .
In addition, robot-conditioned policies have been obtained by augmenting
visual navigation data with reconstructed scene
geometry [ 15 ] . However, these data-driven methods rely on multi-platform datasets
or scene-geometry estimation for experience
augmentation [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] .

In summary, existing approaches to cross-embodiment mapless navigation can
be limited by conservative policy transfer, training coverage, or the cost of
policy learning and multi-embodiment data preparation. CeDR-Nav focuses on
learning a dedicated policy for each target embodiment from existing demonstrations without additional online interaction.

2026-10-12.title: EgoReveal: Learning Active Vision and Object Manipulation under Partial Occlusions from Egocentric Demonstrations
2026-10-12.authors: Hiromu Kurihara , Kazutoshi Tanaka , Masashi Hatano , Tadashi Kozuno , Hideo Saito , Mariko Isogawa
2026-10-12.abstract:
Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) enables robots to learn object manipulation directly from human demonstrations.
In contrast to resource-intensive and labor-intensive teleoperation, egocentric demonstrations are easy to collect, enabling scalable data collection.
Manipulated objects are often partially occluded in everyday environments, yet prior egocentric demonstration-based methods that require no robots or specialized teaching devices do not explicitly address occlusions.
To fill this gap, we propose EgoReveal, a framework that learns viewpoint-repositioning together with manipulation actions from egocentric human demonstrations to reposition the viewpoint and obtain target visibility under partial occlusions.
EgoReveal instantiates this as two imitation policies: one predicts the future camera-arm pose sequence from the current view and camera-arm pose, and the other predicts the future control commands from object keypoints and a history of control commands.
EgoReveal switches between the two based on target visibility.
In experiments where the manipulated object is partially occluded initially, EgoReveal repositions the camera to obtain visibility and completes the task more reliably than fixed-camera baselines.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Learning from Demonstrations (LfD), such as imitation learning (IL), enables robots to learn object manipulation directly from human demonstrations [ 1 ] .
In LfD via teleoperation, a human operator remotely controls the robot while the system records the robot’s observations and actions, yielding directly usable action labels without requiring any mapping from the human body to the robot [ 2 , 3 ] .
Despite this advantage, teleoperation is resource-intensive and labor-intensive, since it requires specialized hardware and skilled operators, thereby limiting scalability to diverse, large-scale datasets.
Egocentric demonstrations are captured as first-person videos using an egocentric camera (e.g., smart glasses).
In contrast to teleoperation, egocentric demonstrations are easy to collect, enabling scalable data collection [ 4 , 5 ] .

Manipulated objects are often partially occluded in everyday environments by the hands, surrounding objects, or clutter, obscuring task-relevant visual cues.
In this study, we focus on the common case where the target remains in view but is partially occluded at the start of the episode.
Egocentric demonstrations capture naturally changing viewpoints, with humans adjusting their viewpoint when targets become hard to see, yet many egocentric demonstration-based methods assume a fixed camera viewpoint at inference time [ 4 , 6 ] .
This fixed-view assumption can cause the robot to fail the task by preventing access to task-relevant visual cues under occlusions.

To ensure access to task-relevant visual cues under occlusions, recent studies use Head-Mounted Displays (HMDs) and enable active vision by learning to move a robot-mounted camera from an operator’s viewpoint changes [ 7 , 8 ] .
These studies also rely on teleoperation or specialized teaching devices, increasing hardware costs and operational burden.

To fill this gap, we propose EgoReveal, a framework that learns viewpoint-repositioning together with manipulation actions from egocentric human demonstrations to reposition the viewpoint and obtain target visibility under partial occlusions.
EgoReveal instantiates this as two imitation policies: one predicts camera-arm pose trajectories from the current view and camera-arm state, and the other predicts end-effector actions from keypoints tracked in the actively moved camera view.
EgoReveal switches between the two based on target visibility.
In experiments where the manipulated object is partially occluded initially, EgoReveal repositions the camera to obtain visibility and completes the task more reliably than fixed-camera baselines.
L

The contributions of this paper are twofold:

Formulation: A problem setting for learning manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations without robotic teleoperation or handheld teaching devices, under partial occlusions.

EgoReveal: A framework for learning manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations that couples the Active Vision policy and the Manipulation policy via visibility-based switching to handle partial occlusions.
