2. EgoReveal: A framework for learning manipulation from egocentric human demonstrations that couples the Active Vision policy and the Manipulation policy via visibility-based switching to handle partial occlusions.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Learning Manipulation from Egocentric Demonstrations

Several works augment robot policy learning by pretraining on large-scale egocentric human demonstrations, using the demonstrator’s viewpoint to learn task-relevant visual representations and action structure, before grounding the model with a small amount of robot demonstrations.
Yang et al. proposed EgoVLA, which pretrains a vision-language-action model on egocentric human videos and then fine-tunes it with a small amount of robot demonstrations to obtain a robot policy [ 9 ] .
Kareer et al. presented EgoMimic, a full-stack framework that co-trains a unified policy on egocentric human data and robot data to scale IL across diverse manipulation tasks [ 10 ] .

Another line of work uses egocentric human demonstrations not as the primary supervision, but as complementary data during training, paired with robot demonstrations to broaden coverage.
Wang et al. proposed MimicPlay, which leverages large-scale human play videos to learn hierarchical plans and then trains low-level visuomotor control with a small amount of robot demonstrations for long-horizon manipulation [ 11 ] .
Lepert et al. proposed Masquerade, which edits in-the-wild egocentric human videos into robotized demonstrations and uses them to pretrain visual representations and co-train policies, before fine-tuning with a small amount of robot demonstrations for robust long-horizon manipulation [ 12 ] .

Human-only learning from egocentric demonstrations has also been explored, training policies purely from smart-glasses first-person human data and deploying them on real robots without requiring robot demonstrations.
Liu et al. proposed EgoZero, a minimal system that learns manipulation policies from Project Aria smart-glasses demonstrations with zero robot data [ 4 ] .
Gavryushin et al. presented MAPLE, which learns dexterous manipulation priors from egocentric videos by predicting contact points and detailed hand poses and transfers these representations to downstream manipulation policies [ 13 ] .
Guzey et al. presented AINA, which learns multi-fingered manipulation policies from first-person videos captured by smart glasses in everyday settings, without using any robot data [ 5 ] .

These egocentric-demonstration-based manipulation methods typically do not explicitly learn viewpoint control policies for handling partial occlusions, which is a key distinction from EgoReveal.

## II-B Learning Viewpoint Control from Demonstrations

Recent works learn visibility-aware viewpoint control from human demonstrations by coupling viewpoint control with manipulation to handle occlusions and limited visibility, collecting such demonstrations via on-robot teleoperation using a HMD.
Chuang et al. presented AV-ALOHA, an HMD-based teleoperation system that learns an active vision policy jointly with manipulation by mapping the operator’s head motion to a dedicated camera-arm to maintain task-relevant visibility [ 7 ] .
Xiong et al. proposed ViA, which learns task-relevant perceptual strategies such as search, tracking, and focusing from human demonstrations collected with an HMD using an actuated camera neck [ 8 ] .
These HMD-based teleoperation approaches collect demonstrations by operating the robot and explicitly teleoperating the camera viewpoint through an actuated viewpoint mechanism such as a dedicated camera-arm or an actuated camera neck.
Such robot-operated, HMD-based data collection is costly and labor-intensive, whereas EgoReveal learns viewpoint motions from passively collected, natural egocentric demonstrations without on-robot teleoperation.

Robot-free human demonstration frameworks have also begun to incorporate visibility-aware viewpoint control.
Zeng et al. presented ActiveUMI, a portable HMD-based teleoperation kit that records an operator’s head motion as supervision for viewpoint control while collecting end-effector commands using tracked, instrumented hand controllers that capture six-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) pose and discrete inputs [ 14 ] .
Yu et al. proposed EgoMI, which trains a memory-augmented policy to handle large viewpoint changes from synchronized head and hand trajectories captured using a HMD and tracked hand controllers [ 15 ] .
These works still rely on dedicated capture devices and specialized data-collection interfaces to record head/hand coordination and retarget it to robots, whereas EgoReveal learns viewpoint motions directly from lightweight smart-glasses recordings of natural human demonstrations without requiring such dedicated interfaces.

2026-10-12.title: Adaptive Whole-Body MPC with Optimal Posture Planning for Humanoid Robots under Unknown Payloads
2026-10-12.authors: Manh Cuong Nguyen , Duc Cuong Vu , Viet Anh Vu , Duc Tuan Pham , Toan Nguyen , Minh Hiep Phung , Ngo Anh Vien , Minh Nhat Vu
2026-10-12.comment: Accepted for presentation at the 25th IEEE RAS International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids2026)
2026-10-12.abstract:
Humanoid robots performing lifting and material-handling tasks must maintain balance despite unknown and varying payloads.
However, payload uncertainty significantly affects whole-body dynamics and may destabilize conventional controllers.
We propose an adaptive whole-body control architecture that integrates three components:
(i) a centroidal model predictive controller (MPC) that generates dynamically feasible reference motions,
(ii) an adaptive fuzzy balance controller that compensates for payload-induced model mismatch by generating corrective torques distributed across the supporting-leg joints,
and (iii) a waypoint-based optimal posture planner built on a triple-integrator model that produces smooth sit-to-stand and stand-to-sit trajectories satisfying center-of-mass (CoM) stability constraints, joint limits, and whole-body feasibility requirements.
Together, these components enable stable lowering, grasping, lifting, carrying, and placing behaviors under significant payload uncertainty.
Extensive simulation and hardware experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework improves balance robustness and reduces tracking degradation during posture transitions and lifting tasks compared to non-adaptive baselines.
2026-10-12.introduction:
In recent years, humanoid robots have attracted significant attention due to their versatility and potential to operate in human-centered environments [ 2 ] . Their comprehensive structure, which integrates mobility [ 1 ] , manipulation [ 21 ] , and perception [ 3 ] , enables them to perform a wide range of complex tasks and operate in modern manufacturing systems [ 6 ] . Unlike traditional industrial robots, which are typically designed for structured, repetitive tasks, humanoid robots are inspired by human morphology and motion, enabling them to operate in environments originally designed for human workers. This anthropomorphic configuration provides remarkable advantages in industrial scenarios that require flexibility, dexterity, and whole-body coordination, particularly in tasks involving physical interaction with the environment.

Among these applications, lifting and material handling of unknown payloads represent a critical and challenging problem [ 25 ] . Such tasks frequently arise in real-world industrial environments where the object properties, including mass, shape, and inertia, are not precisely known in advance. In these situations, the robot must maintain balance while adapting its posture and control strategy to ensure stability and safety. However, despite the promising capabilities of humanoid systems, several technical bottlenecks still limit their practical deployment in industrial lifting tasks. First, the dynamic stability of humanoid robots is highly sensitive to payload variations [ 23 ] , as unknown mass distributions can significantly alter system dynamics and shift the CoM, potentially leading to instability or failure. Second, posture transitions during lifting, such as squatting, grasping, and standing up, involve complex whole-body coordination and nonlinear dynamics, which remain difficult to model and control accurately [ 24 ] . Third, ensuring robustness and adaptability in the presence of uncertainties, external disturbances, and interaction forces remains a major challenge in humanoid control [ 20 ] . Therefore, developing adaptive and robust control frameworks capable of handling unknown payloads, maintaining balance, and optimizing posture during lifting remains a critical research challenge.

This paper proposes a comprehensive control architecture that integrates Centroidal MPC with a WBC framework [ 27 ] . The centroidal MPC layer generates dynamically feasible CoM motion and contact force references, while the WBC layer ensures accurate joint-space tracking under kinematic and dynamic constraints. To enhance robustness against unknown payload variations, an Adaptive Fuzzy Balance Controller is introduced to generate compensation torques for regulating the CoM and maintaining pelvic stability. The computed compensation torques are subsequently mapped into the joint space of the supporting legs through torque distribution within the whole-body control structure. This mechanism enables adaptive stabilization in the presence of external disturbances and load uncertainties. Furthermore, to ensure smooth and stable execution of sit-to-stand and stand-to-sit motions, a waypoint-based trajectory optimization formulation is proposed. The optimization problem generates dynamically consistent posture transition trajectories while explicitly satisfying CoM stability constraints and joint limits. The resulting motion guarantees stable pelvis balancing and posture transitions that are constraint-consistent.

Overall, our key contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

Firstly, this work presents a novel adaptive control structure that integrates centroidal MPC with fuzzy logic regulation, ensuring the stability of the overall system under unknown and varying payload conditions during posture and motion tasks.

Secondly, an optimization posture transition planning based on their triple-integration waypoint model is provided. This framework helps the robot change posture for the lifting task; the resulting trajectory is smooth, balancing the generated trajectory with joint limitations.

Finally, the simulation and experiment are conducted to validate the performance of the proposed method.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II presents the related work as well as the motivation of this study. Section III introduces the adaptive balancing control framework, including the robot model, centroidal dynamics, whole-body control, and the proposed method. Section IV describes the generation of optimal posture-transition motions using the waypoint model. Section V presents the experimental implementation and results. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper.

1. Firstly, this work presents a novel adaptive control structure that integrates centroidal MPC with fuzzy logic regulation, ensuring the stability of the overall system under unknown and varying payload conditions during posture and motion tasks.

2. Secondly, an optimization posture transition planning based on their triple-integration waypoint model is provided. This framework helps the robot change posture for the lifting task; the resulting trajectory is smooth, balancing the generated trajectory with joint limitations.

3. Finally, the simulation and experiment are conducted to validate the performance of the proposed method.

# II Related works

## II-A Posture transition for humanoid robot

Posture transition motions such as sit-to-stand and stand-to-sit are essential capabilities for humanoid robots operating in human-centered environments. These tasks require coordinated whole-body motion, multi-contact interaction, and robustness against model uncertainties and payload variations [ 12 ] . Recent studies have therefore focused on optimization-based approaches to generate dynamically feasible trajectories while explicitly accounting for balance and contact constraints, e.g., [ 24 ] . Several works have proposed unified centroidal and whole-body MPC formulations to simultaneously optimize contact forces, center-of-mass motion, and kinematic trajectories, enabling robust locomotion and posture [ 9 ] . Reduced-order models have also been introduced to improve computational efficiency while maintaining stability, allowing real-time implementation in balancing and posture control tasks [ 10 ] .

Despite these advances, most existing work focuses primarily on locomotion or assumes fixed payload conditions. Efficient and real-time trajectory generation for posture transitions under uncertain payloads remains a challenging problem. In particular, integrating waypoint-based trajectory modeling with MPC to generate smooth, dynamically consistent motions for posture transitions has received limited attention.

## II-B Adaptive Fuzzy Control (AFC) for humanoid robot

Fuzzy logic has been widely applied in humanoid robotics to address nonlinear dynamics and environmental uncertainties. A recent review highlights its effectiveness in balance regulation, gait stabilization, and disturbance rejection when precise models are unavailable [ 13 ] .

Fuzzy-based controllers have been successfully used to maintain stability during standing and walking by regulating CoM motion and ensuring the zero moment point containment under uncertainties [ 15 ] . Disturbance rejection performance has been further improved through fuzzy stabilization strategies [ 28 ] , while adaptive fuzzy approaches have enhanced dynamic walking robustness [ 5 ] . Fuzzy methods have also been extended to terrain adaptation and compliance regulation [ 8 ] , as well as payload-aware humanoid manipulation [ 16 ] . Despite their robustness, conventional fuzzy controllers rely on heuristic rule design and lack predictive optimization and constraint handling. In contrast, MPC enables systematic, constraint-aware torque generation [ 26 ] , but its performance may degrade under significant uncertainties.

To combine the strengths of both methods, we integrate Adaptive Fuzzy Control (AFC) with MPC-based Whole-body Control for the pose transition task of humanoids. The adaptive fuzzy component estimates torque compensation from tracking errors and augments the nominal MPC output, improving robustness while preserving the optimal structure of the predictive control framework.

The choice of a fuzzy compensator over classical model-based alternatives, such as disturbance observers (DOB) [ 32 ] , model-reference adaptive control [ 30 ] , or robust control [ 19 ] , is deliberate and follows from the nature of the payload uncertainty considered here. An unknown payload simultaneously perturbs the robot mass, center-of-mass location, and inertia tensor, so the induced model mismatch is a coupled, state-dependent nonlinearity rather than an additive bounded disturbance. Model-based robust and adaptive laws therefore require either an explicit parametric disturbance model, a reliable uncertainty bound, or online identification of the payload; on a full-scale humanoid these quantities are noisy and slow to converge, and conservative worst-case bounds sacrifice performance. In contrast, the proposed controller is estimation-free: it maps directly measurable balance signals, i.e., the capture-point deviation, the CoM velocity, and its integral, to a bounded compensation moment through an interpretable rule base, without ever estimating the payload mass or reconstructing the disturbance term. This yields three practical advantages. First, it removes the payload-identification loop and its convergence transients, which is critical when the load changes abruptly during grasping and placing. Second, the saturated, rule-bounded output provides an inherent safety envelope on hardware, unlike unbounded adaptive gains that risk parameter drift. Third, the fuzzy law is complementary to, rather than a replacement for, the predictive layer: the MPC retains full constraint-aware optimality for the nominal motion, while the fuzzy term only supplies model-free residual compensation, preserving the MPC structure.

2026-10-12.title: JoyInside-VLM-Agent: Product-Conditioned Multimodal Policy Learning for Embodied Agents
2026-10-12.authors: Gangyi Li , LuYao Wang , Jingfu Sun , Jingyi Yuan , Hang Liu , Hao Zong , Yujia Hu , Tingting Gao , Jianyong Wang , Xu Yang
2026-10-12.abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy’s parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Embodied agents deployed on robotic platforms and smart hardware must translate multimodal observations and user instructions into executable behavior. Across products ranging from bipedal, quadruped, and wheeled robots to AI-enabled plush toys, the appropriate response to a given request depends on the agent’s role, capabilities, and operating constraints. Changes in user goals, new visual evidence, and execution failures can further invalidate earlier plans. We study how to train a shared multimodal policy that adapts to product specifications and revises its decisions as interactions unfold. Figure 1 presents the training framework and deployment examples.

Multimodal training has demonstrated positive transfer across tasks and robotic embodiments [ 1 , 2 ] , while context-aware systems use user intent and environmental feedback to guide interaction [ 3 , 4 ] . However, reported failures include actions beyond device capabilities and descriptions that no longer match the user’s current scene or intent [ 3 , 4 ] . These observations motivate training policies that combine transferable capabilities with adherence to product constraints and sustained alignment with the user’s current goal.

This objective imposes two requirements on training. The data must cover diverse product configurations, goal revisions, and failure recovery while preserving the correspondence between actions and observations. The learning signal must reflect reasoning quality, compliance with product constraints, and progress toward the current goal. Trajectory-level rewards summarize these criteria but do not specify how to distribute credit across tokens. Using additional evidence during training therefore requires selecting an appropriate source for each token and controlling how that evidence affects policy updates.

We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned data construction and staged policy learning. Our pipeline combines product roles, workflows, and constraints with available tools and skills to build executable environments. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories, which undergo execution checks and semantic validation. Multi-source supervised fine-tuning establishes behavior consistent with product specifications, while multi-expert on-policy distillation integrates complementary language and visual capabilities. Reinforcement learning then refines the policy using interaction-specific rewards.

To guide reinforcement learning, we combine process-quality scores from a Generative Process Reward Model (GPRM), multi-judge rankings of the same candidate trajectories, and task-queue assessments of goal alignment and cross-turn continuity. For token-level policy optimization, we introduce DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing), building on RLSD’s sign-preserving advantage modulation [ 5 ] and DOPD’s dual-source routing [ 6 ] . A frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy’s parameters score tokens along the same student-generated trajectory. DPER selects evidence based on their disagreement and support for each sampled token. The selected evidence rescales token-level advantages while preserving their reward-derived signs. Privileged information is used only during training.

We evaluate JoyInside-VLM-Agent on public tool-use benchmarks and the proprietary JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics datasets. The model achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, outperforming the evaluated baselines. Case studies on a physical quadruped robot provide qualitative evidence of visually grounded search, replanning in response to execution feedback, and honest failure reporting.

Our contributions are as follows:

Product-conditioned trajectory construction. We compose executable product configurations and generate verified multimodal trajectories covering product variation, goal revisions, and failure recovery.

DPER for policy optimization. We route token-level evidence between two privileged sources to scale token advantages while preserving their reward-derived signs.

Multi-source interaction rewards. We combine process evaluation, multi-model rankings, and task-queue consistency into a learning signal for reasoning quality, adherence to product constraints, and alignment with evolving goals.

JoyInside-VLM-Agent and its evaluation. We integrate these components into a unified training framework and assess the resulting model through public benchmarks and proprietary evaluation sets and qualitative quadruped case studies.

1. Product-conditioned trajectory construction. We compose executable product configurations and generate verified multimodal trajectories covering product variation, goal revisions, and failure recovery.

2. DPER for policy optimization. We route token-level evidence between two privileged sources to scale token advantages while preserving their reward-derived signs.

3. Multi-source interaction rewards. We combine process evaluation, multi-model rankings, and task-queue consistency into a learning signal for reasoning quality, adherence to product constraints, and alignment with evolving goals.

4. JoyInside-VLM-Agent and its evaluation. We integrate these components into a unified training framework and assess the resulting model through public benchmarks and proprietary evaluation sets and qualitative quadruped case studies.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Embodied and Context-Aware Interaction

PaLM-E learns shared representations for robotic and vision-language tasks [ 1 ] , while Open X-Embodiment studies cross-platform transfer using pooled interaction data [ 2 ] . Context-aware assistants address how observations and user intent guide behavior: Sasha grounds smart-home requests in available devices and user feedback [ 3 ] ; GazePointAR combines gaze, pointing, and dialogue history to resolve references [ 7 ] ; and WorldScribe adapts visual descriptions to intent and environmental changes [ 4 ] . Together, these lines connect shared capabilities with decisions grounded in the current interaction.

Interactive benchmarks further make behavioral constraints explicit. τ \tau -bench evaluates conversations under domain policies [ 8 ] , while τ 2 \tau^{2} -Bench considers user–agent coordination in a shared environment [ 9 ] . WildToolBench covers intentions distributed across turns and transitions among tool use, conversation, and clarification [ 10 ] . These settings motivate evaluating whether behavior respects constraints and follows the current goal. Our work addresses the corresponding training problem across robotic platforms and smart hardware, conditioning a shared policy on each product’s role, capabilities, constraints, and interaction state.

## 2.2 Multimodal Trajectory Construction

Synthetic data methods expand agent training beyond available interaction logs. ToolACE constructs diverse function-calling dialogues with rule- and model-based verification [ 11 ] , and T3-Agent generates and verifies multimodal queries and tool-use trajectories [ 12 ] . Their focus on coverage and validity provides a basis for learning tool interaction. Training for dynamic tasks additionally requires representing the consequences of intermediate actions and the decisions that follow unexpected feedback.

Agent-R constructs revision trajectories through search and model-guided critique, connecting erroneous behavior to successful continuations [ 13 ] . Agent World Model builds executable, stateful environments for interaction and reinforcement learning [ 14 ] . These approaches expose learners to recovery behavior or environmental transitions. Our pipeline couples such execution feedback with compositional product specifications and visual observations, covering both recovery toward an existing goal and adaptation after the user changes it. We jointly vary product roles, workflows, constraints, and capabilities within executable environments.

## 2.3 Post-Training and Reward-Guided Optimization

AgentTuning and Agent-FLAN study how instruction tuning develops agent behavior from demonstrations [ 15 , 16 ] . Generalized knowledge distillation obtains teacher feedback on student-generated sequences, addressing the mismatch between fixed demonstrations and the learner’s behavior [ 17 ] . H-OPD combines vision-language and text-only teachers through visual-description transfer and token-level arbitration [ 18 ] . Agents-A1 integrates domain expertise through staged training and multi-teacher on-policy distillation [ 19 ] . RL Starts before RL studies OPD as preparation for reinforcement learning, reporting higher post-RL averages than direct RL and SFT-initialized RL in text and vision-language reasoning [ 20 ] . These methods inform capability acquisition and consolidation; our training additionally conditions expert transfer on product specifications and refines the resulting policy against interaction-specific rewards.

Reward modeling determines which behavior to encourage. Process supervision evaluates intermediate reasoning [ 21 ] , generative verifiers produce correctness judgments [ 22 ] , and PoLL aggregates assessments from multiple models [ 23 ] . Aggregation can retain shared errors [ 24 ] ; evaluation criteria must still be defined for the target behavior. Using these assessments in optimization is a separate question. RLSD uses privileged evidence to scale token advantages while preserving their reward-derived signs [ 5 ] . DOPD routes supervision between privileged teacher and student policies to address differences in token-level supervision [ 6 ] . DPER combines these mechanisms: it extends RLSD’s magnitude modulation to dual-source evidence selected through DOPD’s routing principle. Our multi-source rewards separately assess reasoning, product constraints, and goal consistency.

2026-10-12.title: Evo-World: A Lightweight Vision-Language-Action Model with Future Motion Prediction via Optical-Flow Supervision
2026-10-12.authors: Zile Zhong , Yuxin Du , Tao Lin , Haoxiao Wang , Wei Dai , Binhua Zuo , Bo Zhao
2026-10-12.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control, yet anticipating how the scene will evolve beyond the current observation can provide additional information for control. Action supervision alone does not explicitly encourage such anticipation, while future-image prediction entangles task-relevant motion with largely static appearance. To address these limitations, we introduce Evo-World , a lightweight VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision, thereby providing a task-relevant predictive signal focused on motion rather than appearance. We further design the training procedure to preserve these predictive representations during policy learning, regulating representation diversity while decoupling representation learning from action optimization. Across simulation benchmarks, Evo-World demonstrates strong performance, achieving a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1% on Meta-World MT50 , with a 13.0% relative improvement over the non-predictive baseline. On real-world AgileX robots, Evo-World outperforms the evaluated baselines across single-arm and bimanual manipulation tasks while using only 0.87B parameters and delivering lower GPU memory usage and higher inference efficiency. These results demonstrate that future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision provides an effective and lightweight approach to enhancing the predictive capabilities of VLA models.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control. By adapting pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge to action generation, they support a broad range of manipulation behaviors ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2026 ) . Successful manipulation also depends on anticipating how a scene should change as a task unfolds: grasping, placing, and opening require coordinated changes in the robot and its surroundings. Yet action supervision alone does not explicitly require a policy’s representations to anticipate these changes. Providing this predictive structure is therefore an opportunity to improve VLA policies beyond their understanding of the current observation.

Future-observation prediction offers temporal supervision for learning such anticipation ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Cheang et al., 2024 ) , but the prediction target determines which aspects of scene evolution the model must represent. Future RGB images entangle motion with appearance, including background textures and objects that remain largely unchanged. Preserving these details can support visual recognition, but it does not directly emphasize the changes needed for control. Optical flow provides a complementary target by describing image-space displacement while suppressing static texture. This motivates learning future motion representations that complement the policy’s visual and linguistic context, as illustrated in Figure 1 .

We introduce Evo-World , a lightweight VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision. Evo-World learns to anticipate motion from the current observation and task instruction, and uses this prediction to inform action generation. The key idea is to make scene change an effective learning target while retaining the appearance and semantics available to the vision-language backbone. Optical flow computed from demonstration videos supplies supervision during training; a compact predictive branch learns its latent representation.

For the predictive signal to remain useful, policy learning must preserve informative motion representations. We address two complementary requirements: maintaining representation diversity and preserving the motion-learning objective during action optimization. We adopt Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) from LeJEPA to discourage collapse of learned representations ( Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ) . We also separate the gradient paths for representation learning and action optimization, allowing the policy to learn how to use the motion features while the predictive branch is trained by its own objective.

Evo-World contains only 0.87B parameters, including its predictive branch. At deployment, it uses current camera observations, the instruction, and robot state; future observations and optical-flow estimation are unnecessary. Motion prediction operates in a latent space, avoiding the need to decode future images or flow fields during action generation. This design incorporates anticipation within a compact policy suitable for deployment on a physical robot.

We evaluate Evo-World on Meta-World MT50, RoboTwin, and three real-world manipulation tasks ( Yu et al., 2020 ) ( Chen et al., 2025a ) . It achieves 91.1% tier-averaged success on Meta-World, a 13.0% relative improvement over the non-predictive baseline, and 41.8% average success across Clean2Clean and Clean2Random on RoboTwin (Table 1 ). On an AgileX dual-arm robot, Evo-World outperforms OpenVLA-OFT and π 0 \pi_{0} on all three tasks, with 63.3% average success (Table 2 ). These tasks cover single-arm floral arrangement and bimanual collaboration in mug hanging and microwave placement. Component ablations support the training design: regularization counters representation contraction, and both regularization and gradient separation improve aggregate success in the tested setting.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce optical-flow-supervised future motion prediction into a lightweight VLA policy, providing a strong predictive signal that complements visual understanding and language grounding.

We introduce optical-flow-supervised future motion prediction into a lightweight VLA policy, providing a strong predictive signal that complements visual understanding and language grounding.

We combine distribution regularization with separate gradient paths to preserve predictive representations during policy learning, and integrate these representations into action generation through a compact conditioning module.

We conduct comprehensive experiments across simulation and real-world robotic manipulation tasks. With a compact 0.87B-parameter model, Evo-World achieves strong task performance while retaining low computational overhead.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision-language-action policies and efficient deployment

VLA models connect visual understanding and language grounding to robot control. RT-2 and OpenVLA adapt pretrained vision-language models by predicting action tokens ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) . For continuous control, Diffusion Policy learns action sequences through denoising ( Chi et al., 2025 ) and π 0 \pi_{0} integrates a flow-matching action expert with a vision-language backbone ( Black et al., 2026 ) . SmolVLA and Evo-1 emphasize compact architectures and efficient adaptation of multimodal features ( Shukor et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026d ) . These advances improve policy capacity and deployment practicality, but action supervision does not explicitly require anticipation of future scene changes.

## 2.2 Predictive learning for robot control

Predictive learning supplements action labels with supervision about how observations evolve. GR-1 and GR-2 learn future RGB observations alongside actions ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Cheang et al., 2024 ) . V-JEPA 2 learns video embeddings through masked prediction and action-conditioned latent dynamics for planning ( Assran et al., 2025 ) . Moto learns discrete motion tokens through conditional frame reconstruction and transfers motion priors to control ( Chen et al., 2025b ) . These methods connect visual prediction to control through both generative and latent representations. The prediction target determines which scene properties the model must preserve: RGB reconstruction couples motion with appearance, while learned representations inherit the structure of their supervision. Motion-specific targets offer a complementary way to emphasize displacement.

## 2.3 Motion supervision for manipulation

Motion guides manipulation through point trajectories ( Wen et al., 2023 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024 ) , predicted flow ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2026a ) , and motion-guided visual prediction ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) . Recent flow-supervised policies use this signal in different roles. Fang et al. (2025) augment VLA training with motion-image diffusion in a frozen VAE latent space. This auxiliary head supervises the shared VLM and is omitted from policy inference. FlowWAM jointly models RGB and flow latents, using generated flow for action prediction and supplied flow to condition world modeling ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . LaMP supplies future 3D motion priors through a frozen expert’s one-step denoising features, avoiding full motion reconstruction ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . TemporalFlow-VLA instead supervises execution-history queries with robot-surface flow derived from kinematics and camera calibration ( Yang et al., 2026a ) .

Evo-World predicts future motion by directly regressing learned embeddings of 2D optical-flow renderings from the current observation and instruction. These embeddings remain available to action generation without motion-denoising or flow-reconstruction objectives. The motion branch continues optimizing its prediction objective and distribution regularization ( Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ) , with action gradients blocked; bounded FiLM combines current and predicted embeddings to condition the policy ( Perez et al., 2018 ) . Its RGB-derived targets require neither depth nor robot-geometry labels.

2026-10-12.title: Sampling-based Kinodynamic Planning with World Models
2026-10-12.authors: Yitian Gao , Hanlan Yang , Zachary Kingston
2026-10-12.abstract:
Visual world models predict the consequences of actions from images, but planning with them is typically done by optimizers such as CEM and MPPI.
However, these optimizers stall on long-horizon tasks where progress requires motion the objective does not reward, such as moving around a block before pushing it.
This paper revisits kinodynamic sampling-based motion planning for world models, using the learned model as the propagator of a tree search in latent space.
Our key insight is that the sampling strategies devised for high-dimensional search in configuration space apply directly to the latent space of a world model, where they rapidly expand through intermediate states that myopic optimizers never sample.
We present two exploration strategies for the high-dimensional latent space, nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based KPIECE, with GPU-native batched expansion for efficient device utilization.
We evaluate with an off-the-shelf DINO-WM on four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task.
Our approaches match or exceed the success rate of CEM and MPPI at up to 13.8 × 13.8\times lower planning time in simulation, and improve the success rate by 20 % 20\% on the real robot.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Visual world models learn to predict the consequences of actions from images [ 11 ] .
Given a history of observations and a candidate action, the model predicts the next observation or latent state, and this prediction can stand in for a simulator when no analytical model of the task is available [ 12 , 13 , 39 , 2 , 1 ] .
For example, a robot pushing a block across a table has no exact closed-form model of the contact, but a world model trained on demonstrations can predict where the block will end up ( Sec. V-A5 b).
The remaining question is how to search through the model’s predictions to find actions that reach a goal.

Prior works [ 3 , 12 , 14 , 39 , 2 ] typically use closed-loop planning, i.e., they repeatedly generate plans with the Cross-Entropy Method (CEM) [ 4 ] or Model-Predictive Path Integral control (MPPI) [ 34 ] , then execute action prefixes with receding-horizon Model Predictive Control (MPC) [ 23 ] . However, gradient-free methods like CEM and MPPI require repeated rollouts for decision-making. Combined with costly inference on large-scale world models, this requires care to balance planning quality and computational cost. Additionally, CEM and MPPI perturb around a mean, leading them to focus exploration and become trapped in local minima. Variants reshape the sampling distribution [ 29 , 32 ] but keep the same search structure. With exact dynamics, tree search under a receding horizon has been shown to outperform CEM [ 19 ] ; others have proposed to use search methods such as Monte Carlo tree search [ 18 ] , but rely on an action prior. These gaps raise the question, are optimization-based approaches the right tools for exploring and planning in the latent space of world models?

On the other hand, classical search-based and sampling-based motion planning methods (SBMPs) excel in long-horizon planning for robotics [ 20 ] , as they maintain a tree or graph that guides exploration. However, they have not been widely adopted as planning methods with world models due to the curse of dimensionality. A large body of literature tackles this problem in robotics with more efficient sampling and exploration strategies designed for high-dimensional spaces [ 30 , 31 , 7 ] ; others use parallel hardware to speed up the planning process [ 27 , 37 , 36 , 16 ] . These advances motivate bridging the aforementioned research gaps in world model planning with classical planning methods.

Thus, we revisit kinodynamic SBMP for planning with world models.
Our key insight is that the sampling strategies devised for high-dimensional search in robot configuration space apply directly to the latent space of a world model.
Nearest-neighbor guidance (i.e., RRT [ 21 ] ) and projection-based coverage estimation (i.e., KPIECE [ 31 ] ) need only a compact descriptor of each state, while the world model propagates the full latent along each branch.
Batching propagation across candidate expansions amortizes the predictor’s cost, allowing our planner to match or exceed the success rate of CEM and MPPI at a fraction of their planning time, with a frozen, off-the-shelf world model. In this work, we present:

a kinodynamic tree planner that uses a visual world model as its propagator, with batched expansion;

a kinodynamic tree planner that uses a visual world model as its propagator, with batched expansion;

two exploration strategies for the world model’s latent space, nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based coverage guidance with KPIECE [ 31 ] ;

and an evaluation against CEM, MPPI, and MCTS [ 18 ] with DINO-WM on four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task, with ablations of exploration, refinement, and numerical precision.

Across the simulated domains, our planners match or exceed the success rate of CEM and MPPI with up to 13.8 × 13.8\times lower median planning time and an order of magnitude fewer world-model evaluations.
On the real robot, our planner solves 29 / 30 29/30 problems where CEM and MPPI solve 23 / 30 23/30 , and the gap is widest on tasks that require a detour before pushing, 9 / 10 9/10 versus 5 / 10 5/10 .

# II Related Work

Early work on visual prediction, such as Visual Foresight [ 6 , 5 ] , combined action-conditioned video prediction with model-predictive control (MPC) and demonstrated that a data-driven visual predictive model can guide control toward goals in manipulation tasks. Other recent work advances visual world models through large-scale pretraining of visual encoders or predictive models. iVideoGPT [ 35 ] pretrains an autoregressive model on human and robot manipulation trajectories and adapts it to action-conditioned prediction, visual planning, and model-based reinforcement learning. DINO-WM [ 39 ] learns action-conditioned dynamics over frozen DINOv2 [ 26 ] patch features, while V-JEPA2 [ 2 ] builds on pretrained video representations and demonstrates image-goal planning on physical robots. However, due to the fidelity gap, these world models typically use CEM to optimize action sequences within a receding-horizon MPC framework. WorldPlanner and STORM [ 18 , 22 ] use Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to guide planning.

Learned components have been integrated into SBMP at every stage, including samplers, steering, distance metrics, collision checking, and action proposals inside a kinodynamic tree [ 24 , 15 ] . In each case the learned component operates in a classical state space and the propagator remains a simulator or analytic model. One line of work instead plans in a learned latent. L2RRT [ 17 ] learns a compact state representation and a collision classifier, then constructs a search tree through sampled controls and learned forward propagation through latent dynamics. ELAST [ 10 ] extends this direction through exploration in learned visual representations, incorporating model uncertainty and transition density. VELAP [ 9 ] adds RRT-style expansion and prunes transitions by Q-ensemble disagreement. These methods train their latent on task data and construct compact representations for planning, yet sampling-based kinodynamic planning with the larger patch-feature latent representations used in contemporary visual world models remains underexplored.

Our approach draws inspiration from L2RRT and KPIECE [ 17 , 31 ] . While sharing the fundamental principle of constructing reachable trajectories through learned forward propagation, we focus on integrating established SBMP methods with existing visual predictors whose rich representations, temporal context, and inference costs impose different computational demands. Through this integration, we examine the practical value of established kinodynamic planning techniques for contemporary visual world models on long-horizon robotic tasks including contact-mediated manipulation.

2026-10-12.title: LeapBot-JAC: Joint Action Chains for World Action Models
2026-10-12.authors: Chenhao Zhu , Baibing Liu , Pei Liu , Rui Yang , Lang Zhang , Mingyue Feng , Yaonong Wang , Jun Ma
2026-10-12.abstract: Action-chunking policies predict future controls but execute only a prefix before replanning. How should a fixed action-token budget be organized to support execution? We propose LeapBot-JAC, which allocates sparse future-control references and dense execution targets within one shared action expert. Both chains are supervised by demonstrated controls and jointly denoised at aligned physical-time positions. Directed attention allows execution tokens to read reference tokens subject to the host’s visibility constraints. JAC adds neither action tokens nor parameters and retains the host’s world-modeling process; both chains participate in inference, while only the execution chain drives the robot. On LIBERO, JAC reaches 98.3% success with FastWAM and LeapBot-WA, up from 97.0% and 97.3%. On zero-shot LIBERO-Plus, their success rates improve from 53.5% to 70.4% and from 73.1% to 77.3%, respectively. RoboTwin and two real-world tasks provide additional deployment evaluations. Single-training-seed comparisons and FastWAM ablations support action-role organization as a practical design choice under a fixed action-token budget.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Action-chunking policies predict a sequence of future robot controls, but closed-loop deployment often executes only a short prefix before querying the policy again. ACT and Diffusion Policy exploit sequence generation for temporally coherent behavior while using temporal ensembling or receding-horizon execution to incorporate new observations ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) . Predictions beyond the executed prefix can still influence the current output through the model’s internal dependencies. The resulting design question is how to organize those predictions: should every token have the same temporal density and deployment role?

World action models (WAMs) couple robot control with learning environment dynamics. Motus supports multiple video–action modeling modes ( Bi et al., 2025 ) ; LingBot-VA uses causal video–action generation ( Li et al., 2026a ) ; Fast-WAM retains video co-training while omitting future-video generation at inference ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) . These approaches primarily organize world representations and their interaction with control. Within an existing action expert, the organization of a fixed number of control predictions remains a separate design choice.

We study action-role organization under a fixed action-token budget . Dense predictions preserve near-term control resolution, whereas sparsely sampled control targets span a longer interval using fewer tokens. Combining these roles provides a way to expose execution to a temporally extended reference without adding an action expert or expanding its token sequence. The reference consists of robot controls, not semantic subgoals or executable waypoints; its role is to condition the jointly generated execution chain.

We propose LeapBot-JAC (Joint Action Chains, JAC). A sparse reference chain R R and a dense execution chain A A share input projections, Transformer layers, an output head, and every action forward pass. Both chains are supervised by demonstrated controls and evolve together during denoising, with independent noise samples at a common noise level. Physical-time positions align the two target sequences. A directed role mask permits A A to read R R while blocking direct access in the reverse direction, subject to the host’s legal attention edges. Only the execution prefix is sent to the robot. This construction reorganizes action prediction while preserving the host’s world-modeling process.

Prior work already explores joint generation of high-level intent and executable actions ( Li et al., 2026b ; Hao et al., 2025 ) . JAC’s focus is more specific: directly supervised control references and dense execution coexist within one existing action expert at a fixed token budget. We assess task success across two hosts and examine how information-flow direction, reference weight, and reference stride affect performance.

Our contributions are threefold. (1) Action-role allocation: we formulate sparse reference and dense execution prediction within a fixed action-token budget, separating the supervision span from the executed prefix. (2) Shared-expert joint generation: we combine control-label supervision, physical-time alignment, and directed cross-chain access without adding action parameters, while retaining host visibility constraints. (3) Empirical evidence on two hosts: JAC improves LIBERO success for FastWAM and LeapBot-WA to 98.3%, and improves their LIBERO-Plus totals by 16.9 and 4.2 percentage points, respectively. Three FastWAM ablations characterize sensitivity to access direction, reference supervision, and temporal coverage.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

ACT improves fine manipulation through sequence generation and temporal ensembling ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) . Diffusion Policy represents multimodal action distributions with conditional diffusion and receding-horizon control ( Chi et al., 2023 ) . Play-LMP learns latent plans from play data for goal-conditioned behavior ( Lynch et al., 2019 ) . Dense Policy progressively expands sparse action keyframes into a dense sequence ( Su et al., 2025 ) . JAC instead retains simultaneous reference and execution roles at a fixed total token count. Hierarchical methods distinguish longer-term plans from local execution. CHD jointly diffuses high-level subgoals and low-level trajectories, allowing low-level feedback to refine subgoals ( Hao et al., 2025 ) . JAC allocates reference and execution roles inside one existing action expert; its directionality is evaluated as an architectural choice.

Motus combines multiple experts and modality schedules for different conditional generation modes ( Bi et al., 2025 ) . LingBot-VA jointly models video and control with causal blocks and history updates ( Li et al., 2026a ) . Fast-WAM separates video co-training from test-time future generation ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , while LeapBot-WA explores world anchoring in predictive semantic space ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . JAC preserves a host’s world objective and sampling process while changing targets and visibility within its action budget. Beyond joint action generators, DINO-WM optimizes actions through predicted visual features ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and V-JEPA 2-AC uses an action-conditioned latent world model for planning ( Assran et al., 2025 ) .

UniPi synthesizes text-conditioned video plans and extracts controls from them ( Du et al., 2023 ) ; CoTDiffusion generates visual subgoals to guide a low-level policy ( Ni et al., 2024 ) . These differ from JAC’s directly supervised control references. ECoT generates embodied reasoning about objects, end-effector states, and subtasks before actions ( Zawalski et al., 2024 ) . LAWA learns codebook-based transition targets from action-free video, jointly denoises separate latent-action and executable-action experts, and omits the future video branch at inference ( Li et al., 2026b ) . Its online latent intent evolves in a continuous embedding space. JAC shares the idea that execution can use evolving intent, but differs in supervision , taken directly from robot controls without a new video-action tokenizer; parameters and budget , reallocating a fixed token count inside an existing expert; and host integration , retaining the host world process while changing action-target organization and direct cross-chain access.

Robust-WAM aligns action-stream queries with future semantic features and their physical times ( Yan et al., 2026 ) . MaskWAM combines object-mask prompting and prediction ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , and MemoryWAM studies persistent history ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . These mechanisms address semantic, spatial, and historical conditioning. JAC complements these mechanisms by supervising intermediate robot controls.

Diffusion Forcing assigns independent noise levels to sequence tokens ( Chen et al., 2024 ) . JAC instead uses independent noise realizations at a common action noise level.

2026-10-12.title: TAME-Nav: Temporal Asymmetric Mixture-of-Experts Distillation for Agile and Versatile Robot Navigation
2026-10-12.authors: Lingjie Zhang , Jun Xue , Shanze Wang , Haoyu Xi , Xinming Zhang , Xiaoyu Shen , Wei Zhang
2026-10-12.abstract: Agile and reliable navigation is a core capability for embodied robots navigating complex spatial constraints and dynamic interactions. However, a single policy often struggles to accommodate the distinct decision-making demands of diverse scenarios. We present TAME-Nav, an asymmetric Teacher–Student navigation framework built around a temporal soft mixture of experts (Soft-MoE). The Teacher combines clean observations with causally maintained dynamic-obstacle tracks to construct privileged representations, while the Student learns complementary navigation features from corrupted observation histories through temporal encoding, soft expert routing, and latent distillation. Procedural scenario generation and parallel task-level simulation broaden training coverage, while deployment-informed asymmetric domain randomization supports sim-to-real transfer. Across in-distribution and unseen compositional scenarios, TAME-Nav achieves higher success rates, lower collision rates, and higher navigation scores than representative baselines. On a real quadruped robot, it completes all twenty trials across local-trap escape and narrow-passage navigation with sudden dynamic obstacles, with only one minor contact.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Reliable local navigation is a prerequisite for autonomous navigation in complex environments. A local navigation policy converts onboard sensory observations and a local goal into real-time motion commands, determining whether a planned route can be executed safely and continuously [ 1 ] . A capable local navigator can also reduce the burden on upstream modules by allowing them to provide sparser subgoals at a lower decision frequency [ 2 ] . Traditional model-based planners offer interpretable motion models and geometric constraints, but their performance often depends on manually designed objectives and short-horizon environment predictions [ 3 ] . Consequently, they may become trapped near concave obstacles, oscillate in narrow passages [ 4 ] , or exhibit overly conservative freezing behavior in dense, interacting crowds [ 5 ] . Learning-based methods can acquire richer interaction priors from demonstrations or environmental experience [ 6 ] , yet their performance remains strongly affected by the diversity of the training distribution and the expressiveness of the observation representation [ 7 ] . Learned policies may generalize poorly to unseen cluttered or confined environments [ 8 ] . Obstacle motion must be inferred from sensory histories, while explicit object-state inputs introduce deployment-time tracking dependencies [ 9 ] .

These raise two fundamental questions:

With only local observations, how can a single policy coordinate complementary navigation skills, including safe obstacle avoidance, narrow-passage traversal, and local-trap escape?

With only local observations, how can a single policy coordinate complementary navigation skills, including safe obstacle avoidance, narrow-passage traversal, and local-trap escape?

Can such coordination translate into higher task completion rates and lower collision risk in unseen compositional scenarios and real-world environments?

To address these questions, we present TAME-Nav, an asymmetric
Teacher–Student framework for agile and versatile robot navigation.
The Teacher fuses clean observation histories with causal dynamic-object
tracks, while a temporal Soft-MoE Student learns to match its privileged
navigation representation through latent distillation. Both branches
share an Actor that generates body-frame velocity commands. Using only
onboard observations and local goals, the deployed Student supports
obstacle avoidance, narrow-passage traversal, and local-trap recovery
without explicit object tracking or global-map inputs.

We further develop a massively parallel task-level simulator with
procedurally generated geometric layouts and dynamic interactions to
broaden training coverage. Deployment-informed randomization models
sensor degradation and velocity-response uncertainty: the Student
receives corrupted observations, while the Teacher and Critic retain
clean observations of the underlying simulated state.

Our evaluations demonstrate consistent gains in navigation success
and safety over SEA-Nav, NavRL, and DRL-DCLP under matched training
budgets. TAME-Nav improves in-distribution success by over 25 percentage
points over the strongest baseline and maintains its advantage across
unseen sequential and multiroom scenarios. Real-world experiments
further demonstrate its ability to escape local traps and negotiate
narrow passages with suddenly appearing obstacles: the quadruped
completes all trials in both scenarios, with only one minor contact
across the twenty trials.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows.

We propose TAME-Nav, an asymmetric Teacher–Student framework that transfers privileged navigation representations augmented with causal dynamic-obstacle tracks from a Teacher to a deployable temporal Soft-MoE Student, enabling a single policy to handle obstacle avoidance, constrained-space traversal, and local-trap escape.

We develop a massively parallel task-level simulator with procedural scene generation for diverse geometric and dynamic navigation challenges, together with deployment-informed asymmetric randomization that corrupts Student observations while preserving clean Teacher–Critic supervision.

We demonstrate improved navigation success and safety across
in-distribution and unseen compositional scenarios, and validate
reliable local-trap escape and narrow-passage navigation with
sudden dynamic obstacles on a real quadruped.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Learning-Based Local Navigation

Local navigation methods can be broadly categorized into model-based approaches and learning-based approaches. Classical methods such as DWA and TEB search for safe control commands online using explicit kinematic constraints and manually designed cost functions [ 3 , 10 ] . Although these methods are interpretable and computationally efficient, their performance in complex static–dynamic environments often depends heavily on environment modeling and parameter tuning. Reinforcement learning instead learns a direct mapping from observations, such as LiDAR measurements and goal states, to continuous velocity commands [ 11 ] . Subsequent studies have incorporated dynamic-agent modeling, velocity-obstacle priors, and temporal environment representations to improve anticipatory collision avoidance in crowded environments [ 12 , 1 ] . Recent work has also explored learning-based locomotion and navigation for quadruped robots in high-speed, cluttered, and open environments [ 13 , 14 ] . Nevertheless, existing methods are often limited by insufficient coverage of diverse local-navigation scenarios and the high cost of data collection in high-fidelity physics simulators.

## II-B Teacher–Student Reinforcement Learning

Teacher–Student reinforcement learning typically allows the Teacher to access privileged information during training and transfers the acquired capability to a Student that relies only on deployable observations, commonly through action imitation or latent-representation distillation [ 15 , 16 ] . Recent studies have further shown that excessive reliance on privileged information unavailable to the Student may lead the Teacher to develop behaviors that are difficult to imitate, highlighting the need to account for the Teacher–Student information gap during Teacher training [ 17 ] .

This paradigm has been widely adopted in legged locomotion, where privileged terrain information or full-state observations are used to train a Teacher, while the deployable Student operates using proprioceptive signals and observation histories [ 18 , 19 ] . Wu et al. [ 20 ] further incorporate a gated MoE Student into concurrent Teacher–Student learning to improve
proprioceptive locomotion across diverse terrains. In navigation, DiPCAN reconstructs privileged dynamic-environment representations from historical visual observations [ 21 ] , while the recent GPTS-Nav employs graph-structured privileged information to guide a LiDAR-based navigation policy in dynamic environments [ 22 ] . These studies demonstrate the value of privileged knowledge for action generation; however, most focus on observation asymmetry within the same simulation setting and employ a unified Student representation for a relatively specific class of navigation scenarios.

Our approach exploits a lightweight task-level simulator to achieve broader coverage of complex maps and failure cases. The Teacher–Student framework transfers privileged navigation knowledge to a deployable Student, while the Student’s mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture provides a structural basis for learning scene-dependent representations across heterogeneous local-navigation situations.

2026-10-12.title: Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning for Long-Tailed Robotic Policies
2026-10-12.authors: Weiwei Chen , Chenghao Xu , Meiling Yu , Xu Yang , Cheng Deng
2026-10-12.abstract: In the practical deployment of vision–language–action policies, handling long-tailed task distributions is a common challenge due to the highly imbalanced composition of robot demonstration datasets. To investigate this issue, we study the head-task action bias in shared robot policies, particularly focusing on its relationship with task-specific visual evidence. Our experimental analysis shows that, when the visual evidence required by a tail task is insufficient, the policy increasingly falls back on action patterns reinforced by data-rich head tasks, resulting in degraded performance on under-represented tasks. Motivated by this observation, we propose Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning, a training framework for long-tailed robot policies. Our method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence using instruction-related and action-related signals, and constructs counterfactual observations by removing the selected evidence. The resulting counterfactual predictions are used to strengthen the association among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with the supervision adaptively adjusted according to the number of demonstrations available for each task. The proposed framework requires neither additional training data nor region-level annotations and incurs no additional computation during deployment. Extensive experiments across simulated benchmarks, different VLA architectures, and real-world robot platforms demonstrate that our method robustly and consistently improves long-tailed robot policy learning, particularly for tail tasks, while maintaining reliable performance on head tasks.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Vision–language–action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising foundation for generalist robot policies, integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action generation within a unified framework ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . Robot demonstration datasets, however, can be highly imbalanced across manipulation skills ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2024 ) . Similar to the long-tailed category distributions observed in datasets such as iNaturalist ( Van Horn et al., 2018 ) , robot task distributions can be skewed toward a few data-rich head tasks, leaving many tail tasks with limited demonstrations ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) .

Long-tailed learning addresses unequal supervision through approaches such as resampling, loss reweighting, and decoupled representation and classifier learning ( Cui et al., 2019 ; Kang et al., 2019 ; Ma et al., 2022 ) . However, most of these methods are developed for classification and are difficult to apply directly to VLAs due to differences in task formulation and model architecture. Zhu et al. (2026) propose Approaching-Phase Augmentation (APA) for long-tailed VLA learning, but it relies on additional tools, such as object detection and image inpainting, increasing the complexity of the approach.Moreover, APA primarily mitigates the problem through data augmentation, without directly constraining VLAs’ reliance on head-task action bias.

However, comparing the results of policies trained on the balanced FULL dataset and the long-tailed LT dataset (see Appendix A ), we find that tail-task performance drops substantially under LT, as shown in Fig. 1 (a). Interestingly, some head tasks perform worse under FULL than under LT: more complete and diverse training data do not yield uniform improvements across all tasks. This leads us to consider whether the long-tailed multi-task learning problem is related to how different tasks jointly influence a shared policy. We further visualize the model’s attention during inference. Figures 1 (b) and (c) show that head tasks attend reasonably well to visual evidence associated with the target object, but may exhibit more dispersed visual attention due to cross-task interference. Tail tasks face a more severe problem: they struggle to establish reliable task-specific visual grounding. Through the toy experiment in Section 3.1 , we find that when such evidence is insufficient, the model must still produce an action, and the shared policy tends to fall back on frequent action patterns in the training data, giving rise to a head-task action bias . Thus, tail tasks do not merely suffer from insufficient data exposure; during decision-making, shared action priors associated with head tasks are more likely affect the visual evidence needed for the current task.

This finding raises a new question: how can we preserve reliable decisions on head tasks while preventing tail tasks from relying excessively on head-task action bias?

Thus, we introduce Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning (ECL) , Without requiring additional annotations or training data, ECL directly uses the original data and a relation-aware counterfactual branch to identify visual evidence relevant to decisions during rollouts. It constructs counterfactual samples by removing key relational tokens and strengthens the associations among task instructions, visual relations, and actions through counterfactual training. Crucially, evidence guides both counterfactual construction and supervision in ECL, which adaptively assigns weaker regularization to head tasks and stronger supervision to tail tasks according to the number of demonstrations.

Our contributions: 1) We reassess the conventional view that tail-task failures arise from data scarcity and show through a toy experiment that, when task-specific visual grounding is insufficient, tail-task predictions fall back on action bias shaped by head tasks. 2) We propose ECL, which suppresses tail tasks’ reliance on action priors via counterfactual supervised training to build their task-specific evidence, without requiring extra annotations or additional training data. 3) We evaluate ECL on two VLA policies in LIBERO-Core-LT and on two real-world robot platforms, Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, with macro-averaged gains and task-specific outcomes reported.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Long-Tailed Learning. Long-tailed recognition studies class imbalance that biases models toward head classes ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) . Representative approaches include class-balanced re-weighting ( Cui et al., 2019 ) , decoupled representation and classifier learning ( Kang et al., 2019 ) , and prior-based logit adjustment ( Menon et al., 2020 ) . LDAM adjusts classification margins according to class frequencies ( Cao et al., 2019 ) , Balanced Softmax addresses label distribution shift ( Ren et al., 2020 ) , and DisAlign combines adaptive score calibration with prior-based re-weighting ( Zhang et al., 2021 ) . Feature augmentation methods enrich tail classes through transferable class-generic variations ( Chu et al., 2020 ) , learned semantic augmentation directions ( Li et al., 2021 ) , or head-class feature displacements ( Wang et al., 2021 ) . Contrastive methods improve representation geometry: PaCo introduces learnable class-wise centers ( Cui et al., 2021 ) , while BCL balances inter-class contributions ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) . These methods primarily address discrete class imbalance rather than long-tailed state and behavior distributions in sequential robotic manipulation.

Robotic Foundation Models. Robotic foundation models build on large vision and language models ( Touvron et al., 2023 ; Zhai et al., 2023 ; Oquab et al., 2023 ) . PaLM-E integrates visual, state, and textual inputs for embodied reasoning and planning ( Driess et al., 2023 ) . Robot policies span autoregressive, diffusion-based, and continuous generative approaches. RT-1 ( Brohan et al., 2022 ) scales Transformer-based behavior cloning through action tokenization, while RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) transfers Internet-scale vision-language knowledge to robotic control. OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) combines a pretrained language model with SigLIP and DINOv2 features and trains on Open X-Embodiment demonstrations ( Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al., 2024 ) . MiniVLA ( Belkhale and Sadigh, 2024 ) adopts a lightweight Qwen2.5-0.5B backbone, while OpenVLA-OFT improves adaptation and inference through parallel decoding, action chunking, and continuous regression ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . Diffusion policies generate continuous actions through iterative denoising ( Chi et al., 2025 ) . Octo ( Team et al., 2024 ) trains a Transformer-based diffusion policy on diverse robot trajectories for adaptation to new observation and action spaces. π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) combines flow matching with a pretrained vision-language model for cross-embodiment control, while π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ) broadens task and environment coverage. SmolVLA uses a compact architecture and asynchronous inference for efficient training and deployment ( Shukor et al., 2025 ) . Despite these advances, training data can remain imbalanced across tasks, states, and behaviors, motivating further investigation into how long-tailed distributions affect visuomotor representations and action prediction.
