2026-10-12.title: VLMs are Native Action Models: Unleashing the Manipulation Capabilities of VLMs with Explicit Action-Space Grounding
2026-10-12.authors: Jingkun Yi , Shujie Zhang , Zirui Zhou , Haoxiao Wang , Haiyang Sun , Yuhang Dong , Xudong Xu , Xing Shen , Tao Zhang , Yong Liu , Jiangning Zhang
2026-10-12.abstract: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already exhibit strong visual, spatial and reasoning capabilities relevant to robotic manipulation. The key challenge in turning pretrained VLMs into generalist manipulation policies is to expose these capabilities through an appropriate action interface. Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified trainable policy, but typically introduce learned action tokens, action heads, or action experts whose semantics must be learned from robot data pretraining. In contrast, modular foundation-model-based manipulation methods can exploit pretrained VLM capabilities for zero-shot manipulation, but rely on external planning and control scaffolds that are not end-to-end trainable as a unified continuous-action policy. In this work, we introduce EASG , an E xplicit A ction- S pace G rounding framework that bridges these two paradigms. By projecting a tool center point (TCP)-centered action frame into the wrist camera observation and expressing actions in the form of VLM’s native textual generation interface, EASG makes the semantics of a continuous robot action space directly observable in the VLM’s perceptual context. This allows pretrained VLMs to directly generate executable robot actions using their existing visual-spatial reasoning capabilities, without robot-action pretraining or additional action modules. Besides, the same action interface supports direct fine-tuning with robot trajectories, allowing the models to continuously improve beyond their manipulation capabilities unleashed by EASG. Overall, EASG enables zero-shot manipulation and generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, while supporting effective fine-tuning in the same continuous action space. These results demonstrate that, given an appropriate action interface, pretrained VLMs can themselves serve as native action models for robotic manipulation.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Advances in large-scale multimodal pretraining have equipped vision-language
models (VLMs) with strong visual, spatial, and commonsense reasoning
capabilities [ 7 ] . Many of these capabilities are directly relevant to robotic
manipulation. Yet turning a pretrained VLM into an executable manipulation
policy requires an appropriate action interface that connects its
perceptual and reasoning capabilities to robot control. To make this, such an interface is expected to first specify to the policy how actions should be represented and generated, such as incremental end-effector translation, rotation, and gripper commands. Secondly, it’s necessary to clearly state the semantics of the action space to the VLM, including the reference frames and the physical meanings of parameterization. Existing vision-language-action (VLA) models construct such an interface by extending pretrained VLMs with robot-action representations learned from robot trajectories. A common strategy treats robot actions as additional
tokens [ 64 , 34 , 48 , 50 ] , while other
approaches introduce dedicated action modules, such as flow-matching or
diffusion-based action experts [ 4 , 44 ] and continuous action heads trained with regression or parallel decoding
objectives [ 32 ] . Alongside these architectural advances, VLA
training has increasingly scaled to large and diverse robot
datasets [ 47 , 31 , 55 , 6 ] . These
approaches provide a unified and trainable action policy and have led to impressive advances in generalist robotic manipulation.

However, the semantics of these robot action spaces are generally not directly available to the pretrained VLM before robot-action training. Robot trajectories must therefore teach the model not only what action to
take , but also how that action is defined in the physical world. First, the
model must infer in which coordinate frame an action is expressed and how it
is parameterized, since these conventions are typically only implicit in the
action labels. Second, precise control requires sufficiently accurate metric
geometry. The mapping from 2D visual observations to 3D physical motion is not
uniquely determined without camera geometry [ 22 , 61 , 29 ] : variations in camera intrinsics
and extrinsics can make visually similar observations correspond to different
robot physical displacements. Third, the policy must learn how embodiment-specific robot states relate to end-effector motion in Cartesian space, including the
relationship between robot configurations, end-effector states, and the
resulting visual changes. Learning these geometric and kinematic
correspondences jointly with manipulation behavior places a substantial burden
on robot data and model capacity. More fundamentally, it prevents the
manipulation-relevant capabilities already present in the pretrained VLM from being directly unleashed to generate executable task-space actions. Besides, extensive robot-action training may
further alter some of the visual-semantic and reasoning capabilities inherited
from the pretrained VLM [ 13 , 21 ] .

An alternative line of work exposes pretrained foundation-model capabilities
through explicit intermediate representations instead of learning the entire action interface from robot trajectories. These modular foundation-model-based manipulation methods generate policy programs [ 38 ] ,
spatial constraints over object parts [ 25 ] , composable 3D value
maps [ 28 ] or relational keypoint
constraints [ 27 ] , which are subsequently converted into robot
motion by downstream planners [ 35 , 57 ] , optimizers [ 54 ] or controllers [ 15 ] . By formulating manipulation problems in representations that pretrained foundation models can
already reason about, these methods can perform a range of tasks zero-shot without robot-action pretraining. However, the mapping depends on intermediate representations and external planning or execution modules without a unified action policy. Consequently,
the same VLM policy cannot be trained end-to-end in the continuous action space with robot trajectories through the interface that enables its zero-shot behavior.

The two paradigms therefore expose a complementary trade-off. VLA models
provide a unified and trainable action policy, but require the action interface
to be learned from robot data before the model can act. Modular
foundation-model methods can directly exploit pretrained capabilities for zero-shot manipulation, but externalize action generation across separate
representations, planners, and controllers. This raises a natural question: Given an appropriate action interface, can a pretrained VLM serve directly as a unified manipulation policy that acts zero-shot
and can be further improved through robot-data fine-tuning?

To answer this question, we introduce EASG , an E xplicit A ction- S pace G rounding framework that provides a unified action interface between pretrained VLM reasoning
and continuous robot control. EASG explicitly grounds the semantics of
a continuous robot action space in the VLM’s perceptual context by projecting
a tool center point (TCP)-centered action frame into first-person observations in the wrist view and providing metric information for action execution. Actions are expressed through the VLM’s native textual generation interface, so the pretrained model can directly map its existing visual-spatial reasoning to continuous robot
actions without adapting to a new robot-specific output modality.
Together, these designs allow pretrained VLMs to generate executable actions
without robot-action pretraining or auxiliary learned planning modules.
Crucially, the same action space and generation interface directly support robot-data fine-tuning, allowing the VLM to continuously improve the
manipulation capabilities initially unleashed by EASG .
To ensure reliable action generation through this native interface, we
further introduce grammar-constrained decoding, which restricts autoregressive
generation to valid action formats while preserving the pretrained VLM’s
original vocabulary and generation process.
Because the pretrained VLM itself generates robot actions through the same native
generation interface both before and after fine-tuning, we refer to it as a native action model .
To summarize, our key contributions are as follows:

We introduce EASG , an Explicit Action-Space Grounding framework that makes robot-action semantics directly accessible to
pretrained VLMs while preserving their native textual generation interface,
enabling them to act without large-scale robot-action pretraining.

enabling them to act without large-scale robot-action pretraining.

We show that the same action interface supports both zero-shot manipulation and robot-data fine-tuning.

We empirically demonstrate the capability of VLM-native manipulation:
a 27B-scale VLM with EASG achieves comparable zero-shot performance with
fine-tuned VLA models, while a 0.8B-scale VLM fine-tuned with EASG achieves
competitive performance with several VLA baselines.

# Related Work

Existing VLA models have explored discrete action tokens [ 64 , 34 , 2 , 48 , 63 , 50 ] or additional action modules [ 4 , 44 , 32 ] for better robotic action representation and generation. With these architectural advances, VLA pretraining has scaled to increasingly large and diverse robot datasets [ 5 , 47 , 31 , 55 , 6 ] . More recently, video or world-model-based policies also try to leverage pretrained video generators to provide future visual dynamic priors for action generation [ 33 , 58 ] . Despite these advances, the prevailing action-pretraining paradigm remains highly data-intensive, since it implicitly requires models to jointly infer action coordinates, depth information and inverse dynamics from robot data. We provide further discussion in Appendix A.1 .

Modular foundation-model-based manipulation methods leverage pretrained
foundation models for high-level perception and reasoning [ 26 , 60 ] , while mediating
robot action through explicit intermediate representations and downstream
planning or control modules [ 53 ] .
Code as Policies [ 38 ] generates executable programs that
compose predefined perception and control APIs, while subsequent methods use
structured representations such as 3D affordance maps in
VoxPoser [ 28 ] , spatial end-effector constraints in
CoPa [ 25 ] , and relational keypoint constraints in
ReKep [ 27 ] .
These methods enable zero-shot manipulation without robot-action pretraining,
and recent Robot-Use-Agent approaches further expose perception, planning, and control as callable tools or autonomously refine robot policies through execution
feedback [ 16 , 24 , 56 , 41 ] .
However, their perception-to-action mapping remains distributed across the
foundation model and external execution modules rather than forming a unified action policy within the model itself, preventing end-to-end optimization of the complete perception-to-action pipeline.
Further discussion is provided in Appendix A.2 .

A complementary line of work incorporates explicit 3D geometry into visuomotor policy learning [ 30 ] . PerAct [ 52 ] predicts 6-DoF actions from voxelized RGB-D scenes, while RVT [ 20 ] and RVT-2 [ 19 ] use virtual multi-view projections and coarse-to-fine prediction for efficient spatial reasoning. In contrast, EASG does not reconstruct the full 3D scene, but dynamically projects the z z -axis of the TCP-centered frame toward the manipulation target. This action-centric grounding with depth information enables pretrained VLMs to directly reason about 3D motion for zero-shot manipulation and subsequent fine-tuning.

2026-10-12.title: Cubic Spline Interpolation for Smooth Trajectory Generation in Autonomous Motion Systems
2026-10-12.authors: Aarush Mandayam , Sriram Aditya Gundla , Elliott Tammaro
2026-10-12.abstract: Trajectories for robots, drones, and other autonomous vehicles must pass through a sequence of prescribed waypoints while remaining physically realizable, meaning the underlying position signal should have continuous velocity and acceleration. Piecewise-linear interpolation between waypoints violates this requirement: velocity changes discontinuously at each waypoint, implying infinite acceleration. We describe a program that fits piecewise cubic splines to a set of waypoints specified as position-time pairs ( x i , t i ) (x_{i},t_{i}) , enforcing continuity of the function value, first derivative, and second derivative across segment boundaries. The spline coefficients are obtained by assembling the interpolation and continuity conditions into a single linear system and solving for the unknown coefficients directly, removing the need to derive the per-segment equations by hand. We demonstrate the approach on two illustrative tasks: generating smooth free-form paths from a sparse set of user-specified points, and reconstructing continuous digital traces of handwritten signatures from sampled pen positions. We discuss the computational cost of the direct linear-system approach relative to the classical tridiagonal (moment-based) formulation, and outline the extensions needed to apply this method to multi-axis robot and drone trajectories subject to velocity and acceleration limits.
2026-10-12.introduction:
A recurring problem in robotics, computer animation, and autonomous vehicle control is generating a trajectory that passes through a specified sequence of waypoints while producing motion that is physically executable. A naive solution connects consecutive waypoints with straight line segments (piecewise linear interpolation). This is simple to compute, but it is unsuitable for actuated physical systems: at each interior waypoint, the direction and often the magnitude of the velocity vector changes instantaneously. Since acceleration is the time derivative of velocity, a discontinuous velocity implies an infinite acceleration at that instant, which no real actuator, motor, or propulsion system can produce.

This limitation motivates the use of smoother interpolants. A trajectory that is C 1 C^{1} continuous (continuous position and velocity) removes the infinite-acceleration problem at the position level, but a trajectory that is C 2 C^{2} continuous (continuous position, velocity, and acceleration) is preferable for most physical systems, since acceleration commands are what feedback controllers on robots and drones ultimately track. Piecewise cubic polynomials are the lowest-degree polynomials that can be joined together to form a globally C 2 C^{2} curve while still leaving enough free parameters to interpolate an arbitrary sequence of waypoints; this is the classical cubic spline [ 1 ] .

In more demanding aerial robotics applications, still higher continuity (up to the fourth derivative, or “snap”) is used so that the commanded thrust and body rates vary smoothly, as in minimum-snap trajectory generation for quadrotors [ 2 ] . Cubic splines represent the simplest member of this family: they guarantee only C 2 C^{2} continuity, but they are correspondingly cheaper to compute and are sufficient for many ground robot, camera path, and animation applications where jerk and higher derivatives are not explicitly constrained.

In this work we describe a program that automates the construction and solution of the cubic spline interpolation problem for a set of waypoints given as ( x i , t i ) (x_{i},t_{i}) pairs. Rather than deriving the spline coefficients for each new set of waypoints by hand, the program assembles the full linear system of interpolation and continuity constraints, and solves for the coefficient vector directly. We apply the resulting tool to two tasks that are not typically framed as robotics problems, but which exercise exactly the same underlying interpolation machinery: (1) generating smooth free-form curves (“abstract drawings”) from a small set of user-supplied points, and (2) reconstructing a smooth digital trace of a handwritten signature from a sparse set of sampled points lying on the signature. Both tasks illustrate that once a program can turn an arbitrary list of waypoints into a C 2 C^{2} curve, the same machinery is directly reusable for generating feasible motion commands for physical autonomous systems.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Cubic spline interpolation is a classical topic in numerical analysis; de Boor’s text [ 1 ] remains the standard reference for both the theory (existence, uniqueness, and optimality properties of the interpolating spline) and the numerical construction of splines via divided differences and B-spline recursions. The formulation used in this paper follows the direct polynomial-coefficient construction described there, rather than the B-spline basis.

In robotics and aerial vehicle control, piecewise polynomial trajectories are widely used to convert a sequence of waypoints into a reference signal that a lower-level controller can track. Mellinger and Kumar [ 2 ] generate trajectories for quadrotors by minimizing the integral of the square of the fourth derivative (snap) of position, subject to waypoint and boundary constraints, using piecewise polynomials of higher degree than cubic. Their formulation illustrates the general pattern followed here: waypoint interpolation constraints plus derivative-continuity constraints at segment boundaries, assembled into a linear system whose solution gives the polynomial coefficients. Cubic splines correspond to the special case where only continuity up to the second derivative is required, which reduces the polynomial degree needed per segment from the degree required for minimum-snap trajectories, at the cost of not directly controlling jerk or snap.

Cubic splines and related low-order piecewise-polynomial curves have also been used outside of vehicle motion planning for exactly the same reason they are useful here: they turn a sparse set of sample points into a smooth, evaluable curve. In signature processing, cubic splines have been used to smooth the raw, jagged pen-position sequences captured by a digitizing tablet before further feature extraction [ 3 ] , and Bézier variants of piecewise cubics have been used to vectorize and reconstruct handwritten signature contours. This is directly analogous to the signature-digitization application described in Section 5 of this paper, where a small number of sampled points on a signature are used to reconstruct a continuous curve.

2026-10-12.title: LeWAM: End-to-End World and Action Modeling with JEPAs
2026-10-12.authors: Minghao Fu , Tavis Siebert , Eryk Halicki , Randall Balestriero
2026-10-12.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models without pixel reconstruction. Existing JEPA pipelines typically train visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics before adding a control policy or solver. We introduce LeWAM , an end-to-end JEPA for control with: (1) a joint training objective over next latent state prediction and action flow matching, and (2) an isotropic Gaussian constraint on the latent state, enabling a single model to support direct policy execution and efficient planning by evaluating sampled actions with its learned latent dynamics. Compared with prior JEPAs in visual planning, LeWAM improves success rate from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks, and plans 32.3 × 32.3\times faster. On behavior cloning tasks in simulation and physical robots, LeWAM is also competitive with established methods. Interpretability analyses show that LeWAM learns control-relevant representations and action distributions effectively guiding test-time planning and control.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Visual control requires autonomous agents to complete tasks by selecting actions based on visual observations of the world. World models address this challenge by predicting the consequences of candidate actions, allowing agents to anticipate how the world will evolve before executing them. Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) ( LeCun, 2022 ) offer a compact world modeling paradigm where future world states are predicted in latent space rather than by reconstructing pixels.
Recent works such as DINO-WM ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) and LeWorldModel (LeWM) ( Maes et al., 2026b ) demonstrate the promise of applying action-conditioned latent world models to downstream control. These pipelines obtain visual features from pretrained encoders ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) , or train representations from scratch with distributional regularizers such as SIGReg ( Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ; Maes et al., 2026b ) to prevent collapse. However, these methods alone do not reliably retain control-relevant information; JEPAs can favor temporally persistent distractors ( Sobal et al., 2022 ) , while action-conditioned dynamics may retain extraneous observation information ( Brandfonbrener et al., 2023 ) .

Control with these models typically requires an online solver such as the cross-entropy method (CEM) ( Rubinstein, 1999 ) or a separately trained action predictor. When initialized with a broad Gaussian prior over action sequences, CEM demands extensive rollouts to identify viable candidates, particularly as action dimensionality or planning horizon grows ( Huang et al., 2021 ) . Contact transitions also complicate local action optimization because the dynamics can switch between modes ( Pang et al., 2023 ) . A post-trained action predictor can provide direct control, as in GC-IDM ( Nguyen et al., 2026 ) , or guide action search, as in PRISM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Training these predictors on frozen JEPA embeddings leaves action supervision disconnected from visual representation learning.

We introduce LeWAM , an end-to-end JEPA that jointly learns
representation, action-conditioned dynamics, and a stochastic policy
in a single training stage (Figure 1 ). Training combines two ingredients: a joint training objective over next-latent-state prediction and action flow matching, and SIGReg ( Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ) to regularize the latent states. A Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) ( Liang et al., 2025 ) predictor uses clean actions for latent dynamics prediction and noisy actions for policy learning through flow matching, so both objectives train the shared visual representation. Consequently, LeWAM supports both direct policy execution and visual planning by refining action sequences sampled from its learned policy. Our contributions are threefold:

To our knowledge, the first JEPA that jointly learns representation, action-conditioned latent dynamics, and stochastic policy, using a joint prediction objective, one weight for latent-space regularization, and approximately 17M parameters.

A planning procedure that jointly imagines the consequences of actions and how to act in the resulting states, which samples candidate action sequences from the learned action distribution and refines them with gradient descent through learned dynamics.

Across ten heterogeneous simulated environments, LeWAM improves goal-reaching success over LeWM ( Maes et al., 2026b ) , particularly on contact-rich tasks. Four-task comparisons extend these gains to longer goal horizons and show faster planning. On goal-agnostic task completion in simulation and physical robot execution, LeWAM performs competitively with established baselines. Linear probes reveal decodable physical-state and action information, recorded-action rollouts visualize its learned dynamics, and planner ablations measure the gains from its stochastic action proposals.

1. To our knowledge, the first JEPA that jointly learns representation, action-conditioned latent dynamics, and stochastic policy, using a joint prediction objective, one weight for latent-space regularization, and approximately 17M parameters.

2. A planning procedure that jointly imagines the consequences of actions and how to act in the resulting states, which samples candidate action sequences from the learned action distribution and refines them with gradient descent through learned dynamics.

3. Across ten heterogeneous simulated environments, LeWAM improves goal-reaching success over LeWM ( Maes et al., 2026b ) , particularly on contact-rich tasks. Four-task comparisons extend these gains to longer goal horizons and show faster planning. On goal-agnostic task completion in simulation and physical robot execution, LeWAM performs competitively with established baselines. Linear probes reveal decodable physical-state and action information, recorded-action rollouts visualize its learned dynamics, and planner ablations measure the gains from its stochastic action proposals.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

World Models. World models ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ) learn environment dynamics to enable agents to simulate candidate action outcomes for planning and control. Early approaches like PlaNet ( Hafner et al., 2019 ) perform planning via latent rollouts, whereas TD-MPC ( Hansen et al., 2022 ) and TD-MPC2 ( Hansen et al., 2024 ) ground latent dynamics in reward and value predictions. Dreamer ( Hafner et al., 2020 ; Hafner et al., 2023 ) learns generative latent dynamics with pixel reconstruction, while VideoGPT ( Yan et al., 2021 ) and IRIS ( Micheli et al., 2023 ) model discrete visual tokens. LeWAM learns latent dynamics and a policy directly from offline trajectories, without reward supervision or pixel reconstruction.

Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures. JEPAs predict target states in representation space without pixel
reconstruction, using variance and covariance constraints ( Bardes et al., 2022 ) , momentum
targets ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) , or distributional
regularization ( Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) to prevent collapse.
For action-conditioned world modeling,
DINO-WM ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) and V-JEPA 2-AC ( Assran et al., 2025 ) build on pretrained representations, whereas LeWM ( Maes et al., 2026b ) leverages
SIGReg ( Balestriero and LeCun, 2025 ) to learn the encoder and latent dynamics from scratch.
Additional action prediction objectives attempt to make representations action-aware in PLDM ( Sobal et al., 2025 ) or as an anti-collapse signal in
SMWM ( Ivashkov et al., 2026 ) . LeWAM jointly trains action-conditioned latent
dynamics and policy in one predictor, so both consequence prediction and action supervision
shape the shared representation.

Control with Latent Dynamics. Conventional planning in latent world models uses population-based solvers, such as CEM ( Rubinstein, 1999 ) , iCEM ( Pinneri et al., 2021 ) , MPPI ( Williams et al., 2017 ) , or gradient-based methods ( Henaff et al., 2017 ; Huang et al., 2021 ) . Population-based search can require many model rollouts as the action dimension or horizon grows ( Pinneri et al., 2021 ; Huang et al., 2021 ) , and contact mode changes in manipulations also complicate local optimization ( Pang et al., 2023 ) (more discussion in Appendix E ). GC-IDM ( Nguyen et al., 2026 ) post-trains a goal-conditioned action predictor for direct control, whereas PRISM ( Wang et al., 2026 ) trains a Gaussian prior head on frozen world-model features; its predicted mean and standard deviation guide MPPI sampling. LeWAM jointly trains the latent world model and a flow-based action predictor, using its sampled actions for direct control or gradient-based planning.

World Action Models. These models couple world prediction with action prediction
(Table 13 , Appendix E ).
Built on pretrained video generative models, DreamZero ( Ye et al., 2026 ) jointly models future video and actions, while Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) retains video co-training but skips future video generation at inference. UVA ( Li et al., 2025 ) , UWM ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , and Cosmos 3 ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) specifically support both forward dynamics modeling (FDM) and policy learning, but optimize only one objective per sample, rather than both jointly on the same pass. LeWAM jointly trains its encoder and predictor end-to-end using latent-state prediction and action flow matching, without pixel reconstruction. Each training sample supplies
clean actions for FDM and noisy actions for stochastic policy modeling. LeWAM learns action-conditioned dynamics from expert and non-expert interactions and uses them to evaluate and refine actions at test time.

2026-10-12.title: Gamma: Grounded Multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit for Memory-Intensive Manipulation
2026-10-12.authors: Yudong Liu , Yueqian Lin , Zijia Tang , Yuxi Zheng , Yuan Li , Shuai Zhang , Yi Li , Taotao Jing , Shuangjun Liu , Dashan Gao , Ning Bi , Jingwei Sun , Yiran Chen , Hai Helen Li
2026-10-12.abstract:
Pretrained vision–language–action (VLA) policies fail on memory
tasks, behaviour that depends on events observed long before the
current frame, because their training data is overwhelmingly Markov and
mapping episodic memory directly to action chunks is hard. Yet the same policy, finetuned once to follow a privileged oracle’s
grounded-subgoal text, nearly solves these tasks: the difficulty lies
entirely in mapping memory to a grounded symbolic subgoal. Existing work entrusts this stage to a
single VLM that selects keyframes and reasons over raw frames, and falls
far short of the oracle: key identities and dynamics are buried in
noisy pixels, the reasoning spans hundreds of frames in an unbounded
context, and hallucination corrupts the memory itself. We instead present Gamma ( G rounded multi- A gent M emory with M echanical A udit), which builds the stage as a
collaborating two-agent memory system: a detector tool
(SAM-3) for spatial grounding, a VLM writer that distils each
replan window into one grounded text line, an append-only text
memory bank , and a VLM reasoner that reads the bank and emits
the next grounded subgoal at the oracle’s cadence, wrapped in a propose–verify harness that admits, defers, corrects, or
rejects every agent claim against mechanical visual evidence, at
training-corpus construction and at deployment alike. On a sixteen-task
memory-manipulation suite Gamma recovers a large fraction of the
oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several
tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) policies pretrained on large manipulation
corpora ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ) now solve a wide range of tabletop tasks
from a single language instruction. Their training data, however, is
overwhelmingly Markov : the correct action chunk is a function of
the current observation and the instruction. Robot tasks in homes and
factories are frequently not of this kind. An agent that watched a
demonstration must reproduce it after the visual evidence is gone; an
agent that saw a container shuffle must remember which container now hides
which object; an agent asked to press a button after the fourth
pass of a moving object must count. On a recent memory-manipulation
benchmark ( Dai et al., 2026 ) instantiating sixteen such tasks, the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policy ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) , finetuned end-to-end, succeeds on only
a small fraction of episodes (Table 1 ).

Two observations make this failure a well-posed problem. First,
finetuning the policy on the benchmark under the standard instruction
leaves success low even when a memory module injects past frames into
it ( 0.179 0.179 end-to-end, 0.445 0.445 for the best memory-VLA architecture;
Table 1 ): the mapping from a long episodic history
to an action chunk lies far from the distribution the policy was
pretrained on. Second, the benchmark ( Dai et al., 2026 ) ships the same
policy finetuned once to condition on a privileged oracle’s
grounded-subgoal text, one grounded sentence per action chunk such as “pick up the container at ⟨ 105 , 87 ⟩ \langle 105,87\rangle that hides
the green cube” , and it nearly solves the suite ( 0.841 0.841 ): a
grounded subgoal returns the data to the pretraining distribution,
Markov, simple and direct, since the behaviour is again a function of
the current observation and one instruction-like sentence.
Subgoal-to-action is thus solved by the pretrained VLA’s own low-level
control; learning memory-to-action directly would couple that control
with high-level memory reasoning, the hard part, whereas decomposing
the problem as

The natural candidate for this first stage is a single VLM over the
episode’s frames, as in keyframe-memory pipelines such as
MemER ( Sridhar et al., 2025 ) : select a small set of informative frames, then reason
over them to produce the next subgoal. Benchmark results show that this family
falls well short of the oracle
(Figure 1 ), and our tick-level analysis
(Section 5.4 ) explains why. (i) Keyframe selection
loses information : nothing guarantees the decisive frame survives
selection, the selector’s policy is opaque, and a dropped frame is
unrecoverable. (ii) VLMs are weak at precise spatial grounding :
grounded subgoals carry exact coordinates, and a ⟨ x , y ⟩ \langle x,y\rangle off by a few pixels sends the policy to the wrong one of N N identical
objects. (iii) Reasoning over raw frames is hard : the key object’s
identity and motion are buried in redundant background, and the
frame-token context grows without bound. (iv) VLMs hallucinate :
a VLM asserts what is plausible rather than what is
observed, uniquely damaging in a memory system, where one false fact
enters the record and poisons every decision downstream. The first three
failures share a root— pixels are the wrong medium for episodic
memory —and the fourth demands that whatever medium replaces them be
verifiable.

We therefore build the memory stage as Gamma , a grounded
multi-agent system rather than a single model
(Figure 2 ). A segmentation-based detector
(SAM-3 ( Carion et al., 2025 ) ), called as a tool on every frame, supplies the
precise coordinates a VLM produces unreliably. A VLM writer (agent-1)
runs once per replan tick and distils its window of sampled frames,
their detections, the memory so far and the planner’s expected next
subgoal into at most one grounded text line, or none when the window
shows no task-relevant change. The append-only text memory bank is the
only history carrier: faithful (every line is evidence-gated against
its own frames), compact (hundreds of steps become a handful of lines)
and transparent (every coordinate in it came from the detector). A VLM
reasoner (agent-2) reads the bank alone, without pixels, and emits the
next grounded subgoal, trained to match the oracle stream verbatim at
its cadence. Grounded text alone does not remove failure (iv): in
closed loop the finetuned writer completed actions on a learned
schedule rather than on evidence, and both agents cited coordinates
they could not know (Section 5.4 ). Because the bank is
symbolic and grounded, every such claim is checkable, and we therefore
wrap both agents in a propose–verify harness
(Section 4.2 , Algorithm 1 ): every claim

Across the full suite, Gamma recovers a large fraction of the

Vision–language–action policies. Imitation policies for

frame ( Mandlekar et al., 2021 ; Jang et al., 2025 ) . We treat the fixed
subgoal-conditioned policy (Section 3 ) as a competent
executor and study the memory stage above it.

Memory for embodied agents. Partial observability in control
has classically been met with architectural memory ( Hausknecht & Stone, 2015 ; Wayne et al., 2018 ; Parisotto et al., 2019 ; Grigsby et al., 2023 ; Bulatov et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2024 ; Cherepanov et al., 2025b ) : representations
that are latent, and so cannot be inspected, audited, or corrected at
deployment. In VLAs, recent work compresses past frames into the policy’s
context ( Jang et al., 2025 ) or attaches a memory module to the
backbone or recurrent queries ( Shi et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) ; a growing 2026
line gives VLAs explicit
memory ( Osterberg et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Ji et al., 2026 ) , audits show frozen
VLAs barely deploy the history they encode ( Liao et al., 2026 ) , and a

MemER ( Sridhar et al., 2025 ) keeps an episodic memory of VLM-selected keyframes
and reasons over the selection with a second VLM pass. We share the
decompose-to-subgoal philosophy but replace pixel memory with verified
grounded text and selection with per-tick writing: nothing is
discarded, and every remembered fact is a checkable sentence.

Benchmarks. Standard manipulation
suites ( Yu et al., 2019 ; James et al., 2020 ; Mees et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) evaluate

orders, swaps, and demonstrated routes, with a privileged

2026-10-12.title: Tactile Sensing-based Secure and Gentle Grasping of Unknown Objects
2026-10-12.authors: Feng Han
2026-10-12.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires maintaining a firm grasp while strictly avoiding both contact slip and structural damage to the object. Satisfying these inherent secure-and-gentle grasping constraints is challenging for unknown objects. We present a novel online data-driven predictive control framework for safe dynamic robotic grasping of unknown objects. The proposed system features a pair of compact, single-channel tactile-sensing modules that characterize the gripper-object dynamic interaction in real time, entirely bypassing the need for prior knowledge or offline training. A finite-state-machine-based grasping force probing mechanism is developed to establish the initial grasping force and explicitly identify grasping force constraints. Through online dynamics learning, a Gaussian Process (GP) model captures gripper-object interaction dynamics. The model uncertainties are further used to form robust grasping constraints, which are embedded into a model predictive control scheme. We demonstrate error convergence in a probabilistic sense. The proposed control framework runs at 100 Hz in real time to dynamically manipulate and handle objects rather than static holding. Extensive experimental evaluations across diverse contact surface topologies and various types of objects validate superior performance and efficiency compared to baseline strategies. The proposed method is able to manipulate objects ranging from delicate items, such as raw tofu and marshmallows, to rough objects, such as rocks.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Robotic grasping and manipulation offer great efficiency and dexterity across a broad spectrum of automated tasks. Notable examples include automated fruit harvesting in modern agriculture [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , dynamic food sorting and picking in the food industry [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , and the delicate and ultra-precise grasping and transporting of live organs during robotic surgery [ 7 , 8 ] . With prior knowledge and offline training, these grasping tasks can be achieved safely. However, reliable robotic grasping of unknown objects remains one of the most fundamental yet challenging objectives in autonomous robotics [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . When a robotic gripper interacts with unseen objects, the inherent but mathematically unknown grasping force constraints must be satisfied. The grasping force should provide secure but delicate contact to avoid contact slip, damage, or breakdown [ 9 , 12 , 13 ] . These constraints are related to the object’s mass, material compliance, friction, and contact interface topology, etc., which are completely unknown. Even the same object under different contact interface topologies with the same gripper will result in different interaction dynamics [ 14 ] . For instance, grasping a metal cube along diagonal portions or parallel edges requires significantly different forces.

Human grasping and manipulation of unknown objects take advantage of the coordination of vision and haptic-based force feedback [ 15 , 10 , 16 , 17 ] . The advanced biostructure of human fingers is capable of adapting to the object’s geometry, size, surface topologies, etc. When handling objects out of the line of sight, human manipulation can still achieve success by relying fundamentally on blind haptic reflexes [ 18 , 17 ] . During this process, humans learn the unseen object’s mechanical properties, “feel” the interaction mechanism online, and then adjust the applied force to reach a secure-and-gentle grasp [ 17 , 14 ] .

For robotic grasping, accurate sensing plays a significant role in characterizing the robotic gripper-object interaction mechanism and dynamic grasping control. Sensing technology can be categorized into contactless (i.e., vision-based) and contact (i.e., tactile/haptic-based) groups. Vision-based machine learning agents can recognize and label object types and prescribe a grasping force [ 19 , 16 , 20 , 9 , 13 , 21 ] . However, such pipelines heavily depend on a pre-trained network over massive object datasets [ 22 , 23 ] . Vision systems inherently suffer from critical degradation in occluded spaces and an inability to monitor visually unrecognized micro-slip at the interface [ 24 , 25 , 12 , 13 ] . Furthermore, the computational cost of vision-based grasping is usually demanding, and the real-time control frequency is relatively low [ 26 , 9 ] . For instance, in [ 26 ] , video processing is used to handle tactile sensing feedback, and the control frequency can only reach 1 1 Hz. Tactile sensing provides an alternative by perceiving physical interactions through direct contact [ 27 , 19 , 14 , 28 ] . Nevertheless, tactile sensing requires accurate calibration, and haptic feedback is inherently susceptible to distortions caused by complex contact surface topologies, localized stress concentrations, and vibrations [ 29 , 30 ] . The uncertainties in sensing propagate into interaction dynamics characterization and control design. Under dynamic grasping with a time-varying reference force, the control system design must respect secure-and-gentle grasping constraints [ 9 , 26 ] .

To overcome the challenges in unknown object grasping, we propose a multi-phase, vision-free interaction dynamics learning and predictive control architecture. The proposed tactile mechatronics can adapt to different contact interface topologies and detect potential object slip or yielding while preserving the fidelity of the measurement. Additionally, a Gaussian Process (GP)-based calibration model accurately captures the interaction force from raw measurements with bounded uncertainties. The case-specific interaction mechanism is characterized online through a haptic-based finite state machine (FSM). The object geometry, stiffness, and grasping force constraints are identified systematically. Through online dynamics learning, a GP-based non-parametric interaction dynamics model is constructed. Together with the identified constraints, we design a robust model predictive control (MPC) scheme by incorporating both calibration and modeling uncertainties, ensuring grasping force control convergence and strict constraint satisfaction. The proposed control is data-efficient and does not depend on prior knowledge or datasets. Compared to the low-frequency control of vision-tactile sensing, the real-time control frequency of the proposed control reaches 100 100 Hz.

Robotic grasping and manipulation encompass multifaceted innovations, including advanced gripper design, sensing and perception, actuation, modeling, and control. In the following, we review the most relevant work in the literature.

Robotic grasping has been used in various applications due to its dexterity, ranging from fruit harvesting in agriculture [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] and food-feeding in caregiving [ 15 , 31 ] to raw material picking in manufacturing. For different applications, various gripper mechanisms have been developed, including rigid [ 13 , 14 , 32 ] and soft grippers [ 27 , 28 ] . For instance, a compliant three-finger gripper is designed with embedded strain gauges in [ 19 ] , while the work in [ 3 ] designs a hybrid robotic gripper combining six soft auxetic fingers with a rigid exoskeleton. Soft grippers can provide direct lifting force, whereas parallel-jaw grippers usually apply a normal contact force, with lifting force generated indirectly through friction [ 14 ] .

Emerging tactile sensing technology provides direct information about the gripper-object contact interface at the interface [ 33 , 34 , 35 ] , which resembles advanced human grasping feedback. To provide rich contact information, multi-tactile sensing arrays have been designed and integrated into gripper systems [ 14 , 9 , 16 , 35 ] . However, the high nonlinearity of tactile sensors requires advanced calibration to address hysteresis, dead zones, saturation, etc. A popular approach in the literature is to use machine learning-based methods to interpret raw measurements and bypass the calibration process. Tactile sensing, in principle, measures pressure and is thus sensitive to the gripper-object contact profile, area size, slip, and vibrations, leading to inherent uncertainties and case-specific feedback [ 29 , 30 ] . Integrated with vision systems, visual-tactile sensing combines the advantages of both modalities, providing rich feedback information for decision-making and control design [ 9 , 13 , 26 ] . However, the computational costs become very demanding, resulting in a low real-time control frequency (i.e., less than 50 50 Hz).

A critical component in robotic grasping is contact force design and control. Since interaction dynamics are case-specific, most existing works either ignore the hidden nonlinear gripper-object interaction dynamics or embed them implicitly into the learning process [ 19 ] . The most popular approach designs the grasping force based on prior datasets [ 13 , 22 , 23 ] . Empowered by machine learning techniques, robotic grasping can perceive and recognize objects, with grasping forces designed accordingly to enable object-specific strategies. In [ 27 , 36 ] , raw tactile feedback is used for object recognition within a neural network. However, when grasping unknown, delicate objects, failures are commonly observed. Secure-and-gentle grasping requires adequate force without aggressive contact. The boundary grasping forces vary depending on the object’s mass, compliance, surface roughness, and contact topology [ 17 , 14 , 16 ] , and they must be identified online. Meanwhile, most works in the literature focus on object grasp-and-hold tasks [ 37 , 14 ] rather than dynamic grasping force control, which is critical in the presence of environmental uncertainties.

Additionally, PID, MPC [ 9 , 26 ] , and machine learning-based control strategies [ 27 , 19 , 38 , 39 , 16 ] have been proposed in the literature. Physical model-based control primarily focuses on gripper kinematic movement control rather than explicit gripper-object interaction dynamics [ 9 , 27 ] . The MPC approach enforces constraints on gripper movement and contact force to ensure safe and secure grasping. In [ 9 ] , an MPC is designed using gripper kinematics and vision-tactile sensing feedback. However, the constraints are only imposed on the kinematic movement of the gripper. Because the interaction dynamics remain unknown, there are no constraints involving the interaction force. Machine learning-based control is also popular given the complicated gripper-object interaction dynamics. In [ 27 ] , raw tactile sensing data are directly processed in a neural network without calibration. End-to-end reinforcement learning neglects interaction dynamics, and the grasping force is designed through reward shaping [ 19 , 38 ] . Learning from human grasping is another alternative [ 39 , 16 ] . However, these learning mechanisms rely on offline training and have low transparency and adaptation to unknown objects.

The major contributions of the proposed online grasping dynamics control framework are summarized as follows:

The proposed tactile sensing module is compact, containing only a single-channel thin-film force-sensitive resistor (FSR). The module does not require an advanced tactile sensing array design nor significant alteration of the grippers and supportive mechatronics. Through GP-based calibration, the tactile sensing provides high-fidelity measurements regardless of the tactile contact interface topologies.

The proposed novel finite-state machine safely and explicitly identifies the object’s geometry, compliance, and object-specific grasping force constraints online in real time, which lays a solid foundation for secure and gentle grasping control. During this process, no prior knowledge or vision inspections are needed.

We explicitly learn the gripper-object interaction dynamics online. An MPC-based controller ensures force control performance and robust constraint enforcement within the information-theoretic envelope of the dynamics learning uncertainties and tactile sensing uncertainties. We provide a comprehensive theoretical proof to establish probabilistic stability and convergence, bounding the true but unknown force control error within a compact residual set. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no previous work has explicitly identified and incorporated the secure-and-gentle grasping force constraints of unknown objects into control design.

We validate the framework through extensive experiments, demonstrating superior control accuracy, slip prevention, and structural protection over baseline architectures across diverse types of objects, ranging from raw tofu to metal blocks. The control system reaches a real-time 100 100 Hz frequency.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Sec. II outlines the system modeling and formalizes the robust dynamic grasping problem. Sec. III details the tactile sensor mechatronics design and calibration. Sec. IV identifies the initial grasping force and inherent secure-and-gentle grasping force constraints. Sec. V formulates the online interaction dynamics learning and robust MPC scheme and delivers the analysis for error convergence. Sec. VI presents the experimental setup, sensor configurations, and performance benchmarks. Finally, limitations and future research avenues are discussed in Sec. VII , and concluding remarks are provided in Sec. VIII .

2026-10-12.title: Multimodal Image-based Robotic Assistance and Guidance Environment (MIRAGE): A Novel Unified Framework for Surgical Navigation and Visualization
2026-10-12.authors: Ehsan Nasiri , Yi Zheng , Michael A. Kokko , Xiaoyao Fan , William R. Warner , Keith D. Paulsen , Ryan J. Halter
2026-10-12.comment: Submitted to the ASME Journal of Mechanisms and Robotics; currently under review
2026-10-12.abstract: This paper presents the computational architecture and quantitative preclinical evaluation of MIRAGE, a multimodal image-guided robotic surgery framework for real-time visualization and navigation. It integrates stereovision scene reconstruction, augmented-reality (AR) video overlay, quantified heads-up display (HUD) navigation, and intraoperative ultrasound within the da Vinci console’s TilePro display (Intuitive Surgical). Additional modules include optical/electromagnetic tracker registration, stereo calibration, fiducial rigid registration with RMSE feedback, and 3D point-cloud reconstruction. Video I/O and rendering run in a C++ backend, while a Python GUI coordinates calibration, registration, reconstruction, visualization, and user interaction through an in-process zero-copy binding layer. The framework formalizes spatial transforms, module states, and synchronization of heterogeneous video and tracking streams. Preoperative calibration uses synchronized checkerboard image pairs and optimization, with estimated intrinsics, extrinsics, and rectification reused intraoperatively. MIRAGE was validated in phantom experiments across da Vinci S,Si, Xi, and SP platforms. Across clinically relevant working distances, mean 3D reprojection error was 0.6mm, with best 0.1mm RMSE at 100mm on Xi. Results support MIRAGE as a preclinical technical-validation platform for accurate, responsive, and extensible multimodal surgical guidance.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Robotic surgery has been shown to improve patient outcomes, with lower morbidity rates compared to traditional open surgery [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
Image-guided surgery, also known as surgical navigation, is another form of computer-assisted intervention designed to give surgeons real-time intraoperative guidance. Its purpose is to enable precise and efficient access to target regions, support surgical planning, and minimize the risk of damage to surrounding critical structures [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] .
Imaging modalities integrated with surgical robots include fluorescence imaging, augmented-reality overlays, and navigational displays [ 10 , 11 ] . In urologic surgery for example, image-guided robotic systems employing near-infrared fluorescence imaging and augmented reality overlays have enhanced visualization of tumors and critical anatomy, improving surgical decision-making and functional outcomes [ 12 , 13 ] . Similarly, in transoral robotic (TORS) procedures, the introduction of intraoperative imaging and navigational augmented reality helps surgeons overcome confined operative spaces and the lack of haptic feedback, thereby increasing the accuracy of tumor resection and safety near vital structures [ 14 ] . These advances, underscore a broader trend toward more precise, image-enhanced robotic interventions that improve oncologic and functional results for patients [ 10 ] .

Recent development in image-guided and robotic surgery have explored a wide spectrum of visualization strategies, ranging from integral videography (IV) autostereoscopic displays for 3D overlays without head-mounted devices [ 15 ] to goggle-based and monitor-based augmented reality (AR) systems that project preoperative models into the surgical field [ 16 , 17 ] . In urology, numerous groups have applied computer vision and machine-learning techniques to automate 3D model registration during robotic partial nephrectomy [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] , while systematic reviews highlight the broader use of extended reality (AR/VR) tools for planning, navigation, and education [ 21 , 22 ] .
Similar approaches have been extended to TORS to assist with tumor localization [ 23 , 24 ] and to robotic prostatectomy, where AR improved anatomical orientation but remained hindered by organ motion [ 17 ] . Across these studies, the main benefits include enhanced depth perception, improved anatomical visualization, and reduced surgeon workload, whereas persistent drawbacks involve soft-tissue deformation, registration inaccuracy, high computational demands, hardware costs, and limited large-scale clinical validation.

Many image-guided robotic surgery systems are still evaluated as isolated demonstrations rather than integrated, time-synchronized navigation frameworks. This paper asks whether heterogeneous imaging, instrument tracking, modeling, reconstruction, and overlay streams can be synchronized, fused, and rendered within a unified robotic surgery framework while preserving measurable navigation accuracy and real-time responsiveness across multiple robotic platforms.

Prior multimodal guidance systems in robotic surgery (e.g., [ 25 ] ) have typically addressed only subsets of the sensing/visualization stack and left key integration gaps. In robotic prostatectomy, for example, Ukimura et al. [ 26 ] reconstructed TRUS-derived, patient-specific 3D models and displayed them on the da Vinci console via TilePro, reporting favorable margin outcomes but relying on preoperative data and static alignment. Samei et al. [ 27 ] integrated preoperative MRI with intraoperative 3D TRUS and live 2D TRUS in a “partial AR” scene shown beneath the endoscope feed on the surgeon’s console, improving situational awareness yet still constrained by registration quality and without optical/EM tracking fusion. Fusing optical and EM tracking instrument provides complementary robustness and tighter, continuous pose estimation of the endoscope and TRUS probe in a common frame, improving overlay accuracy under real operative dynamics. In [ 28 ] authors registered ultrasound/photoacoustic images to the da Vinci stereo camera via an arc-to-line optimizer and achieved sub-centimeter target registration error (TRE) in simulation/bench experiments, but the workflow remains preclinical and depends on photoacoustics hardware. Meza et al. [ 29 ] fused freehand ultrasound with structured-light surface capture (optically tracked) to one frame with sub-mm inter-modality error, demonstrating fusion accuracy but outside the robotic console and without endoscopic integration, so the surgeon is not able to see/fuse the modalities natively in the binocular console view. Classic stereo-vision pipelines (e.g., Stoyanov [ 30 ] ) deliver real-time 3D tissue reconstruction from robotic endoscopy but are vision-only and lack fusion with other modalities (e.g., without any alternative imaging/sensing modules). In contrast, we introduce a unified, integrated framework that fuses preoperative stereo calibration, dual optical–EM tracking within a heads-up display(HUD)-TilePro navigation-visualization interface, live 3D stereo reconstruction (point clouds), 3D AR overlay, and live ultrasound streaming. This integration supports dynamic intraoperative registration within a console workflow. Component calibration accuracy and end-to-end target accuracy are distinct endpoints, since the latter also depends on registration, tracking, motion, and temporal association.

The novelty of this work is not the individual use of stereo calibration, rigid registration, learned disparity estimation, or AR rendering, which are established in the literature. Instead, the contribution is a unified, time-aware, and quantitatively evaluated architecture that coordinates these components within a single console-attached robotic surgery workflow. By defining cross-modal states, timestamp association, transform propagation, buffer ownership, synchronization rules, and evaluation metrics, the framework enables reproducible testing of multimodal surgical guidance under realistic system-level constraints.

Recent consensus guidance recommends evaluating surgical robotics through staged translation rather than technical feasibility alone, spanning device performance, usability, patient acceptability, health-system impact, and long-term monitoring (IDEAL) [ 31 ] . This is directly relevant to multimodal image-based robotic assistance and guidance environment (MIRAGE), where value depends not only on accuracy and frame rate, but also on workflow integration, user trust, failure mitigation, and reproducible evaluation across platforms and procedures.

Prior systems that utilize C++-Python software frameworks largely follow three major patterns:
(1) Code-generated monoliths (e.g., large simulators) auto-generate both the C++ API and the pybind11 [ 32 ] glue to form a single expansive Python module; this scales to evolving engines but introduces a generator/continuous integration (CI) toolchain and is not tailored to low-latency, heterogeneous device streams [ 33 ] .
(2) Custom-designed interface over a single high-performance library deliver near–C++ speed, but typically bind one math-control stack rather than multiple device-module subsystems [ 34 ] .
(3) Thin Python fronts over real-time C++ processes (e.g., shared-memory or bursting-mode toolboxes) keep hard real-time loops out-of-process in C++ and expose a minimal Python API. This helps determinism but adds orchestration and deployment complexity beyond the process boundary [ 35 ] .

In the proposed multi-threaded multimodal system, most high-level modalities are implemented in Python, while video acquisition, rendering, calibration support, and selected hardware-facing modules are implemented in C++ and bound in-process via a custom-developed binding interface into a single Python orchestrator and GUI. The contribution is not the use of pybind11 alone, but the surrounding integration method: explicit buffer ownership, timestamped frame exchange, mutex-protected shared state, asynchronous worker management, and a unified state machine that coordinates C++ and Python modules. This design binds multiple heterogeneous C++ subsystems alongside Python-native modalities under one event loop, prioritizes in-process frame access over out-of-process shared memory, and exposes C++ frame buffers to Python through the buffer protocol when copy-free access is possible. Long-running C++ operations are isolated from the GUI event loop through worker threads and status callbacks. The system maintains a consistent timebase and timestamping policy to support Python-side data fusion and quantitative synchronization analysis.

The binding layer connects C++ acquisition and rendering to the Python interface through timestamped image and pose exchange, shared configuration, and worker-status callbacks.

The formulation brings the spatial transforms, timestamp association, and module interfaces into a common description of the integrated workflow. Registration and calibration use established methods [ 36 , 37 , 38 , 30 ] ; the integration analysis concerns their coupled spatial, temporal, and configuration dependencies.

Compared with general-purpose robotic middleware and application frameworks such as the robot operating system (ROS/ROS2), the da Vinci research kit (dVRK) or NVIDIA Isaac, MIRAGE is deliberately implemented as a single workstation, console-attached framework focused on image guidance rather than robot actuation. In our configuration, the robot is driven entirely by its native clinical console, while MIRAGE concentrates on integrating stereo video, tracking, and multimodal visualization-navigation on the same machine. Introducing an additional middleware layer
would add serialization, inter-process communication, and dependency-management overhead without clear benefit for this tightly coupled setup.The single-process design prioritizes direct frame access and a common application state on the console workstation. Related infrastructure includes OpenIGTLink for data exchange [ 39 ] , Plus for tracked-image acquisition and calibration [ 40 ] , 3D Slicer for extensible medical-image computing [ 41 ] , and ROS 2 for communication and component composition [ 42 ] . Table 1 compares these roles with the application scope of MIRAGE. These complementary roles motivate comparisons with equivalent tasks, hardware, data-transfer policies, and timing boundaries.

The contributions of this research paper are summarized as follows:

[1.] A novel time-synchronized multimodal robotic surgery architecture that formalizes the coupling among stereo video, optical/electromagnetic tracking, AR overlay, stereo reconstruction, ultrasound, HUD navigation, and surgeon-console visualization within one state-driven framework.

[2.] A novel cross-language real-time integration method that defines explicit function mappings, buffer ownership, synchronization invariants, thread-safety rules, and state-transition models between a C++ video/rendering backend and Python-based navigation, reconstruction, registration, and GUI modules.

[3.] A temporal association and interpolation strategy for heterogeneous surgical data streams operating at different update rates, including video frames, tracker poses, rendering loops, and GUI events.

[4.] A quantitative evaluation protocol for multimodal image-guided robotic surgery systems, including calibration/reprojection error, fiducial registration error, overlay reprojection error, stereo reconstruction error, end-to-end response time, synchronization error, and platform-specific repeatability.

[5.] A comparative system-level analysis against representative prior image-guided robotic surgery approaches, identifying which capabilities are integrated within MIRAGE and which remain limitations.

[6.] Preclinical validation with phantom experiments across the da Vinci S, Si, Xi, and SP platforms, demonstrating the feasibility of real-time multimodal guidance and defining the next evaluation steps needed for IDEAL-aligned translational assessment.

This study asks whether heterogeneous imaging, tracking, reconstruction, and rendering modules can be integrated into a time-consistent robotic surgery navigation framework while preserving geometric accuracy and real-time responsiveness.

The following hypotheses organize the evaluation of spatial accuracy, temporal association, frame access, and repeatability:

H1: A unified transform chain preserves sub-millimeter to millimeter-scale calibration and registration accuracy across platforms and working distances.

H2: Timestamped multimodal association aligns video, tracking, rendering, and GUI events across different stream rates.

H3: In-process C++/Python integration enables real-time frame access and module switching without unnecessary frame duplication.

H4: The system supports reproducible quantitative evaluation of calibration, registration, overlay accuracy, reconstruction error, synchronization error, and latency.

This study is a preclinical technical and workflow validation, not evidence of clinical superiority or improved patient outcomes. Under IDEAL robotics [ 31 ] , MIRAGE aligns primarily with stages 0–1, with early stage 2a elements, based on iterative development, integration with clinical robotic platforms, and phantom testing. Accordingly, evaluation focuses on integration, accuracy, real-time performance, reproducibility, and surgeon-facing visualization; clinical outcomes, learning curves, human factors, failure modes, health economics, and long-term surveillance remain future work.

2026-10-12.title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control
2026-10-12.authors: Taoyang Jia , Weikai Huang , Linxin Song , Jared Darlington , Jieyu Zhao , Yue Wang , Jiafei Duan , Zhongzheng Ren , Ranjay Krishna
2026-10-12.abstract:
Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision.
We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects.
We present Reflex , a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable.
In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers’ success at the same distances.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Humans routinely react to fast-moving objects with their entire body.
A goalkeeper shifts, dives, and braces for an incoming shot; a worker catches a box tossed from a truck; a person reaches for a falling cup while stepping to keep balance; another twists aside as a cart passes unexpectedly close.
These behaviors require more than tracking an object in motion. They require predicting where it will go, deciding how the body should meet or avoid it, and coordinating a whole-body response before contact, often within about a second. Humanoids have the morphology to perform such behaviors, but robust visually reactive whole-body control remains largely out of reach.

This capability couples three challenges. First, the robot must control the whole body: it must place its feet and torso, move its arms into position, absorb impact, and remain balanced. Second, it must reflexively react to fast object dynamics under latency. In our real-robot trials, a thrown box reaches the robot roughly one second after release, while camera-to-control latency alone has a median of 69 ms in our detector-based pipeline. The robot therefore cannot simply react to the latest observation; it must infer where the object is going and commit to an interception before contact.
Third, it must do so from egocentric vision. Because the camera moves with the robot, observed image motion combines object motion with self-motion, while the robot’s own arms increasingly occlude the object near contact.

We study catching thrown boxes as a representative test of all three challenges. Catching a box is more demanding than intercepting a ball with the hands: the robot must reposition its body, use the forearms and torso to form a support, absorb the box’s momentum, and retain the load without losing balance. At the same time, the box is an ordinary uninstrumented object observed only through onboard RGB-D cameras. The task is difficult even for people: across our trials, three human catchers succeed on only 28.3% of throws from 7 m.

Existing systems address only parts of this problem. Robotic manipulators can catch moving objects from fixed or wheeled bases, avoiding the challenge of whole-body balance and impact absorption [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Recent humanoid systems demonstrate dynamic interactions such as punching away a ball [ 4 ] or catching a basketball with the hands [ 5 ] , but rely on motion capture or retroreflective objects rather than grounding fast object motion from onboard vision.
As a result, whole-body control, fast prediction of object dynamics, and egocentric visual grounding have rarely been combined on a real humanoid.

We present Reflex , a three-stage framework for visually reactive whole-body control (see Figure 2 ). Stage 1 learns whole-body catching from privileged simulator state using reinforcement learning and human motion priors. Stage 2 learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed (20–60 ms latency) and incomplete observations of its position, velocity, orientation, size, and observation age, producing a latent representation that conditions the controller to react. Stage 3 learns to recover this same dynamics representation from egocentric RGB-D history and camera ego-motion while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. Our decomposition gives each capability a direct training signal and isolates expensive visual learning from reinforcement learning.

In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is vital for good performance; removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and 0.6 m-offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes on 65% and 40% of throws at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of the human success rate at the same distances (85.0% and 68.3%). Ablations further show that camera ego-motion matters for visual grounding, that regressing the learned latent works better than regressing the full privileged box state, and that action-matching initialization outperforms weight mapping by 5.2 points on average.

More broadly, our results suggest a path toward humanoids that can react to dynamic events directly from onboard vision, rather than relying on instrumented environments or task-specific perception systems. Catching is one instance of a broader class of visually reactive whole-body skills, including interception, avoidance, handoffs, and physical assistance. These everyday tasks require predicting how the world will change and coordinating the body before contact.

# II Related work

## II-A Catching thrown objects

Catching a thrown object requires predicting its trajectory and moving into position within a short time window. Early systems addressed this with fixed-base arms guided by vision [ 6 ] , with later work learning object dynamics and catching motions from demonstration [ 1 ] or planning impact-aware bimanual motions with fixed-base arms [ 7 ] . Learning-based approaches have since extended catching to whole-body model predictive control combined with policy learning [ 2 ] , dexterous and bimanual throw-and-catch [ 8 , 9 ] , and mobile manipulators [ 10 , 3 ] . More recently, bipedal humanoids have been trained to intercept balls as goalkeepers [ 4 ] and to catch basketball passes [ 5 ] . However, most of these systems observe the object with motion capture or fixed external cameras, with fewer relying on onboard sensing: humanoids have kicked and struck moving balls from onboard vision [ 11 , 12 ] , a legged manipulator plays badminton with a learned perception-error model [ 13 ] , and onboard catching has been shown on a wheeled humanoid [ 14 ] and a quadruped [ 15 ] , and concurrent work catches a thrown box on a humanoid from egocentric RGB without reporting real-robot success rates [ 16 ] . To address this, we train a humanoid to catch and retain a thrown box using onboard egocentric RGB-D.

## II-B Humanoid whole-body control and loco-manipulation

Human motion data has become a common foundation for humanoid whole-body control. This approach began in physics-based character animation with motion imitation [ 17 ] and adversarial motion priors [ 18 ] . Extending this to object interaction, Catch & Carry [ 19 ] paired a motor-primitive module learned from human demonstrations with an egocentric-vision policy trained by reinforcement learning to catch balls and carry boxes in simulation. These methods have since moved from simulation to hardware, where learned motion trackers provide general whole-body control on real humanoids [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . Recent loco-manipulation systems go further, lifting and carrying boxes and bulky objects through whole-body contact [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ] . In these tasks, though, the object is at rest when interaction begins, so the robot can approach and make contact at its own pace. Catching removes this freedom, since the body must already be in place when the box arrives. Like these methods, we build on human motion, but train a dedicated catching controller that reacts to the incoming box and coordinates interception and retention.

## II-C Privileged Learning and Visual Sim-to-Real

Policies trained in simulation can use information that is unavailable at deployment, such as the exact state of an object. Privileged learning exploits this by training a teacher with such information to supervise a student that uses onboard sensors [ 29 ] , typically alongside asymmetric critics [ 30 ] , domain randomization [ 31 ] , and on-policy data aggregation [ 32 ] . Legged robots adopted this approach early, with students that reproduce a teacher’s latent from observation history [ 33 , 34 ] or walk from egocentric depth [ 35 ] . Humanoids now use it to perform loco-manipulation, door opening, parkour, and ladder climbing from depth or RGB [ 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 ] . However, these students perceive static terrain or slow-moving objects. A thrown box instead moves quickly through the view of a moving camera. Following RMA [ 34 ] , we keep the action decoder fixed and train a visual model by latent regression to predict the privileged latent from RGB-D history and camera ego-motion.
