2026-10-12.title: Verifier-Mediated Multi-LLM Coordination for Multi-Robot Path Planning
2026-10-12.authors: Vivek Khatana , Zijian Song , Naira Hovakimyan , Petros Voulgaris
2026-10-12.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used for high-level multi-robot task planning, yet independently generated symbolic plans can become jointly infeasible after geometric grounding because of shared spatial and temporal constraints. We study execution-aware coordination of large-language-model (LLM) planners for multi-robot navigation. We compare a centralized architecture, in which one LLM jointly reasons over the robot team, with a decentralized multi-LLM architecture in which each robot independently proposes a task plan. A geometric verifier grounds the candidate plans into robot trajectories, detects predicted inter-robot conflicts, and converts conflict information into structured feedback for targeted replanning. This verifier-mediated architecture separates semantic task reasoning from execution-level feasibility while enabling iterative coordination among LLM planners. Experiments in CARLA and on Crazyflie aerial robots evaluate coordination performance as task complexity increases and characterize the trade-offs between centralized reasoning, decentralized verifier-mediated coordination, and physical executability.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Foundation models provide a flexible interface for semantic reasoning, task decomposition, and high-level planning in robotic systems. In multi-robot settings, however, a plan that is individually meaningful for each robot may still be jointly infeasible after geometric grounding. Independently generated routes can intersect in space and time, violate shared workspace constraints, or create execution conflicts that are not apparent at the symbolic planning level. These failures motivate an execution-aware coordination mechanism between foundation-model reasoning and physical robot motion. A key architectural question is whether multi-robot foundation-model planning should be centralized or decentralized. A centralized planner can reason over the complete team state and generate coordinated plans jointly, but its context and decision space grow with team and task complexity. In contrast, decentralized planners provide modularity and local reasoning, but they require an explicit coordination mechanism to resolve conflicts between independently generated plans. Recent multi-robot LLM frameworks coordinate robot teams through centralized or decentralized symbolic reasoning and inter-agent communication [ 1 , 2 ] . However, such symbolic coordination does not by itself ensure that the resulting plans remain physically feasible after geometric grounding.

This work studies verifier-mediated multi-LLM coordination . Each robot-level LLM proposes a symbolic task plan, which is grounded into an executable trajectory by a geometric planning layer. A shared execution-level verifier evaluates the grounded trajectories for obstacle and inter-robot conflicts. When a conflict is predicted, the verifier converts the failure into structured feedback —including the affected agents, conflict location, and conflict time—and returns this information to the appropriate LLM planner for targeted replanning. This creates a closed coordination loop between foundation-model reasoning and robot execution without requiring unrestricted natural-language negotiation. The framework is illustrated in Fig. 1 .

The main contributions of this work are:

We formulate centralized and decentralized LLM-based architectures for multi-robot task planning under shared execution constraints.

We introduce a verifier-mediated coordination mechanism that converts predicted geometric conflicts into structured feedback for targeted multi-LLM replanning.

We empirically study coordination and task completion performance across increasingly complex multi-robot tasks in CARLA [ 3 ] and demonstrate transfer of the planning–verification–execution framework to Crazyflie [ 4 ] aerial robots.

Relation to prior work. Recent work has explored centralized and decentralized LLM-based multi-robot symbolic reasoning and coordination [ 1 , 2 , 5 ] , as well as feedback and constraint-guided refinement of LLM-enabled robotic behavior [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Our focus is different: we use an external execution-level verifier to evaluate grounded multi-robot trajectories, detect physical conflicts, and return structured agent-specific geometric feedback for targeted multi-LLM replanning.

1. We formulate centralized and decentralized LLM-based architectures for multi-robot task planning under shared execution constraints.

2. We introduce a verifier-mediated coordination mechanism that converts predicted geometric conflicts into structured feedback for targeted multi-LLM replanning.

3. We empirically study coordination and task completion performance across increasingly complex multi-robot tasks in CARLA [ 3 ] and demonstrate transfer of the planning–verification–execution framework to Crazyflie [ 4 ] aerial robots.

2026-10-12.title: Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Driving in Road Construction Zones Using Human-in-the-Loop Driving Data
2026-10-12.authors: Shuo Zhang , Aman Sunesh , Semiha Ergan , Kaan Ozbay
2026-10-12.abstract:
Ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway work zones
remains an underexplored topic in autonomous-driving research, with limited dedicated data and systematic evaluation.
Roadway work zones involve temporary changes in the lane
layouts and connectivity of the roads, complicating
interactions with surrounding vehicles and workers.
These changes make future vehicle trajectories difficult
to predict. To address these challenges, we collect WZDrive-Data , a multimodal dataset comprising
1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers,
using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with
prerecorded worker animations and VR-controlled workers.
Driver control and gaze signals are recorded from human
participants, while vehicle trajectories and scene
information are obtained from the simulator. Our proposed multimodal ego-trajectory predictor, WZDrive , achieves a mean minADE 6 of 1.09 m
and minFDE 6 of 2.12 m. Compared with the best-performing state-of-the-art baseline for each metric in our benchmark,
WZDrive reduces minADE 6 by 7.18% and minFDE 6 by 13.18%. This research addresses a gap in autonomous-driving research on urban work zones by combining human-in-the-loop
data collection with multimodal learning from human
driving signals and in the context of work-zones. A project website with code and example data is available at https://shuo9898-zs.github.io/wzdrive/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Roadway work zones are essential for maintaining and upgrading
transportation and utility infrastructure, but they temporarily change the
conditions under which vehicles operate. Maintenance activities can narrow
or redirect travel lanes and require drivers to respond to surrounding
vehicles, temporary traffic-control devices, and roadway workers in
constrained spaces. These temporary changes can create safety-critical
conditions for drivers and workers. In the United States, an estimated
101,000 work-zone crashes occurred in 2023, resulting in roughly 39,000
injuries and about 900 fatalities ( Work Zone Safety Information Clearinghouse, 2026 ; National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, ) . As aging infrastructure and continuing utility work sustain the need for maintenance and rehabilitation ( Ullman et al., 2014 ) , roadway work zones will remain a recurring part of road travel and an important setting for studying how vehicles adapt to temporary road configurations.

Ego-trajectory prediction estimates a vehicle’s near-future
motion to support autonomous driving (AD) and advanced
driver-assistance systems (ADAS).
In work zones, these predictions can help AD systems
assess where the vehicle is likely to travel and plan
safer paths around workers and nearby traffic.
For ADAS, they can support hazard warnings and corrective
control when a driver’s actions may lead to unsafe motion.
However, temporary lane changes and interactions with
vehicles and workers make prediction challenging.
Limited road space in urban areas can restrict standard
traffic-control layouts, while short-term work zones
may provide less warning and protection, leaving drivers
less time to respond.

Dedicated work-zone datasets have advanced scene
understanding and navigation.
EPOSH focuses on perspective-view and bird’s-eye-view
segmentation ( Dwivedi et al., 2021 ) , while ROADWork
provides rich visual annotations and reconstructed
driving paths ( Ghosh et al., 2025 ) .
However, ROADWork’s pathway-prediction task uses
spatially sampled waypoints derived from video-based
reconstruction rather than directly recorded vehicle
states at fixed time intervals.
General driving datasets, including nuScenes,
Argoverse, and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset,
provide temporal trajectories and established forecasting
benchmarks ( Caesar et al., 2020 ; Chang et al., 2019 ; Ettinger et al., 2021 ) . Yet their collection and evaluation protocols are not
specifically organized around safety-critical work-zone
conditions. This leaves a need for dedicated trajectory data and systematic evaluation of vehicle motion under these
conditions.

Human signals offer a potential means of addressing
prediction challenges that trajectory history alone
cannot resolve.
Prior work has developed immersive platforms for
collecting human driving signals ( Silvera et al., 2022 ) and explored EEG-based feedback and attention-based
guidance for ADAS and autonomous driving ( Zhuang et al., 2026 ; Zhuang et al., 2025 ; Biswas et al., 2024 ) .
These studies motivate investigating human signals
as complementary information for predicting driving
responses in complex work-zone conditions.
We therefore propose a multimodal approach that combines
historical driver-control and attention signals with
vehicle trajectories, surrounding agents, lane geometry,
and temporary work-zone context. To address ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway
work zones, we recruited 33 participants to collect
driving data across six scenarios using a CARLA–SUMO-based
driving simulator with VR-controlled workers and
prerecorded worker animations ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2017 ; Lopez et al., 2018 ) .

Our contributions includes:

Dataset: We collect WZDrive-Data ,
comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments with
synchronized vehicle trajectories, driver signals,
and scene context across six scenario conditions.

Benchmark: We benchmark rule-based,
sequence, and state-of-the-art models for ego-trajectory
prediction in roadway work zones.

Model: We propose WZDrive ,
which combines multimodal encoding and stage-wise
refinement to improve ego-trajectory prediction
over the evaluated baselines.

1. Dataset: We collect WZDrive-Data ,
comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments with
synchronized vehicle trajectories, driver signals,
and scene context across six scenario conditions.

2. Benchmark: We benchmark rule-based,
sequence, and state-of-the-art models for ego-trajectory
prediction in roadway work zones.

3. Model: We propose WZDrive ,

2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2. Related Work

## 2.1. Trajectory Prediction

Trajectory prediction supports autonomous driving and navigation among
human road users by estimating future motion from observed histories
and scene context. Trajectron++ models multimodal agent behavior ( Salzmann et al., 2020 ) , while Social-STGCNN captures pedestrian
interactions through spatiotemporal graphs ( Mohamed et al., 2020 ) . Map-aware approaches incorporate lane
structure and agent interactions through lane graphs, graph traversals,
and hierarchical representations ( Liang et al., 2020 ; Deo et al., 2022 ; Zhou et al., 2022 ) .

Attention-based models jointly represent agents, time, and heterogeneous
scene inputs ( Yuan et al., 2021 ; Nayakanti et al., 2023 ) .
MTR, MTR++, and QCNet use query-based prediction and refinement ( Shi et al., 2022 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ) , while Forecast-MAE
pretrains representations through masked trajectory and lane
reconstruction ( Cheng et al., 2023 ) .
LAFormer combines lane-aware constraints with two-stage refinement ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , and DeMo separates directional intentions
from dynamic states ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) .
For ego-trajectory prediction, RouteFormer incorporates trajectory
history, egocentric imagery, and driver field of view ( Akbiyik et al., 2025 ) . These methods primarily address
general driving environments rather than the joint use of temporary
work-zone geometry and human-driver control signals.

## 2.2. Driving and Roadway-Work-Zone Datasets

General driving datasets, including nuScenes, Argoverse,
and the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, provide trajectories
and map context for motion forecasting ( Caesar et al., 2020 ; Chang et al., 2019 ; Ettinger et al., 2021 ) .
Driver-centered datasets additionally capture human
behavior and attention.
DR(eye)VE includes driving video, vehicle states,
and gaze ( Alletto et al., 2016 ) , while GEM,
introduced with RouteFormer, synchronizes egocentric
video, corrected ego locations, and gaze ( Akbiyik et al., 2025 ) .
Zhuang et al. collect EEG, gaze, and driver-control
data in VR driving simulations to support
human-informed autonomous vehicle control ( Zhuang et al., 2026 ) .
These resources support complementary aspects of
driving research but do not specifically target
human driving responses in roadway work zones.

Work-zone research spans perception, scene understanding,
and navigation.
Early work identified work-zone boundaries and traffic
changes from signs ( Seo et al., 2015 ) .
EPOSH provides perspective-view and bird’s-eye-view
semantic annotations ( Dwivedi et al., 2021 ) .
ROADWork adds object and sign annotations, scene
descriptions, and reconstructed driving paths ( Ghosh et al., 2025 ) .
More recently, Dash2Sim reconstructs metric,
geo-referenced 4D driving logs from dashcam videos
and introduces ROADWork4D-CL for closed-loop planning
evaluation ( Ghosh et al., 2026 ) .
Our dataset complements these resources by pairing
controlled human-driving trajectories with synchronized
driver signals and explicit work-zone geometry
for ego-trajectory prediction.

## 2.3. Human-in-the-Loop Simulation for Road-User Interaction

Immersive simulation enables controlled collection of interactions
that would be difficult or unsafe to reproduce in real traffic.
Weng et al. evaluated VR-based collection of pedestrian trajectories
and body poses in safety-critical interactions ( Weng et al., 2023 ) . JaywalkerVR and its CARLA-VR dataset
further support controlled studies of pedestrian behavior ( Mukoya et al., 2024 ) . Related VR frameworks investigate
human-driver–pedestrian interactions, trajectory and crossing
prediction, and coupled intentions and actions ( Crosato et al., 2024 ; Dang et al., 2024 ) .
Dang et al. additionally model bounded rationality in game-theoretic
vehicle–pedestrian decision making ( Dang et al., 2025 ) .

Driver-centered platforms demonstrate the feasibility
of immersive simulation for multimodal human-driving
research.
DReyeVR integrates CARLA with VR driving, eye tracking,
driver controls, and experiment replay ( Silvera et al., 2022 ) .
DualTake combines immersive simulation with gaze,
physiological, and vehicle signals to predict takeover
behavior across cars and micromobility ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) .
For roadway work zones, Zhang et al. combine VR–CARLA
simulation with eye tracking to study driver responses ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) , while VR-WISE integrates
CARLA–SUMO co-simulation with gaze and physiological
sensing to investigate driver awareness ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) .
These studies provide a methodological basis for
collecting human responses under controlled driving
conditions.

Work zones are not inherently safety-critical, but particular layouts,
environmental conditions, and worker interactions can increase conflict
potential. This motivates a trajectory-centered benchmark that
combines human-driving signals and the context of both work-zone under a matched
control condition and crash-informed, safety-critical configurations.

2026-10-12.title: StereoEngine: Scaling Stereo Bimanual Robot Data without Stereo Cameras
2026-10-12.authors: Jason Chen , I-Chun Arthur Liu , Gaurav Sukhatme , Daniel Seita
2026-10-12.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-12.abstract: Stereo vision is increasingly used for robotic manipulation with a growing body of work incorporating it into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, the scarcity of large-scale, real-world stereo datasets remains a fundamental bottleneck for scaling such policies. Recent generative monocular-to-stereo methods target settings such as VR content and autonomous driving. No prior work produces realistic synthetic stereo data for robotic manipulation where stereo supervision has come predominantly from simulation. We propose StereoEngine, which introduces two complementary methods to synthesize stereo data for robotic manipulation. In the first, we warp a monocular (left) video into the right view using estimated depth and inpaint the disoccluded regions with a video diffusion model which lifts monocular demonstrations into stereo pairs without training on real stereo. In the second, we render a stereo pair in simulation and jointly generate both photorealistic views which produces consistent left–right data without any real video as input. StereoEngine outperforms existing baselines in generated stereo quality, and using its synthetic data for policy mid-training or task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves downstream bimanual manipulation. Project website: https://stereoengine.github.io .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Imitation learning from teleoperated demonstrations has enabled increasingly capable bimanual manipulation systems [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Recent stereo-conditioned policies extend this by taking stereo observations as input and exploiting binocular views to improve spatial reasoning, including challenging cases such as transparent objects [ 4 , 5 ] . However, scaling these stereo-conditioned policies to the point where they can be used for large-scale general imitation learning remains difficult, as large-scale robot datasets are overwhelmingly monocular and single-arm [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . The few datasets captured with stereo cameras, such as DROID [ 9 ] , are single-arm which means no large-scale bimanual stereo dataset exists. Collecting stereo demonstrations at comparable scale would require expensive stereo rigs and costly re-teleoperation. This motivates scalable methods to synthesize stereo data without additional real-world collection [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] .

While monocular-to-stereo synthesis has emerged as a promising direction [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] , existing works target domains outside of robotic manipulation, such as VR/AR content [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] .
Reconstruction-based novel-view synthesis (e.g., NeRF [ 21 ] , 3D Gaussian Splatting [ 22 ] ) requires multi-view datasets and per-scene optimization on static scenes, unlike our dynamic single-view setting.
Methods that train on stereo pairs draw on simulation data that suffers from domain gaps or on only a small number of real pairs [ 23 ] . To our knowledge, no prior work synthesizes realistic stereo data directly from real robot video data.

To address the data bottleneck, we present StereoEngine, a scalable framework for synthesizing photorealistic stereo data for bimanual manipulation using video diffusion. StereoEngine provides two independent methods. When a real monocular demonstration exists, we convert it into a stereo pair by warping the left view and inpaint the disoccluded regions which are the surfaces that become visible in the right view but were never observed in the left. This preserves the appearance of the real data, though every generated pair remains tied to an existing demonstration. When no real video exists, we instead generate both views from a simulated trajectory, which allows data generation for entirely new tasks and configurations. Together, the two methods lift the abundant monocular data that already exists and generate new data where none exists, without ever training on real stereo correspondences.

We evaluate StereoEngine across 480 real-world rollouts spanning five bimanual manipulation tasks. See Figure 1 for a visualization of the diverse synthetic stereo pairs produced by StereoEngine.
Using ExStereo [ 24 ] and StereoVLA [ 5 ] as our downstream policies, mid-training [ 24 ] them on StereoEngine data—an intermediate stage between a policy’s large-scale pre-training and task-specific fine-tuning—or fine-tuning them on it directly, consistently improves manipulation performance and generalization over baselines.

The contributions of StereoEngine are:

StereoEngine-L, a monocular-to-stereo pipeline whose inpainter is trained without any real stereo pairs, using warp-derived masks, partial arm masks, and disparity dropout.

StereoEngine-S, which jointly generates both left and right views from simulation, needing no real video.

A large-scale bimanual robot stereo dataset released from both methods.

Real-world experiments showing that StereoEngine data improve stereo-conditioned policies through both large-scale mid-training (StereoEngine-L) and task-specific fine-tuning (StereoEngine-S).

2. StereoEngine-S, which jointly generates both left and right views from simulation, needing no real video.

3. A large-scale bimanual robot stereo dataset released from both methods.

4. Real-world experiments showing that StereoEngine data improve stereo-conditioned policies through both large-scale mid-training (StereoEngine-L) and task-specific fine-tuning (StereoEngine-S).
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Stereo Vision in Computer Vision

Stereo vision offers an efficient way of recovering 3D structure from image pairs where
depth is obtained by estimating the disparity between a rectified left–right pair. This means obtaining
3D information from ordinary RGB cameras without active depth sensors. Recent stereo matching has shifted toward general-purpose foundation models with strong
zero-shot generalization, largely by leveraging priors from monocular depth foundation models
to generalize across unseen domains and remain reliable on transparent, reflective, and
textureless surfaces [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] . These advances make stereo an accurate and deployable source of 3D
geometry well suited to robotics. In this work, we leverage these benefits for robot manipulation by generating large-scale stereo data so that stereo-conditioned policies can scale for training.

## II-B Monocular-to-Stereo Generation

Monocular-to-stereo generation synthesizes a right-eye view from a monocular left video, originally for immersive 3D content [ 28 ] . Most methods require stereo pairs for training, either from large-scale stereo datasets that are expensive to obtain or from synthetic renders with a large domain gap from real video [ 14 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] ; training-free [ 29 , 15 , 30 ] and recent self-supervised [ 16 ] variants relax this requirement. However, all of these only convert an existing left video and cannot produce stereo pairs where none exists. As summarized in Table I , StereoEngine addresses both limitations: it needs no stereo pairs, operates on real robot data, and jointly generates both photorealistic views without any real footage.

## II-C Stereo Vision in Robotics

Stereo perception offers a practical route to 3D geometry in manipulation, recovering
structure on materials where active depth sensors fail, such as transparent, specular, and
textureless surfaces. Stereo can also yield cleaner geometry than active depth sensors, as we show later in Section IV-A1 . Prior work adapts stereo depth estimation to these challenging
conditions [ 31 , 32 ] and uses stereo depth
for downstream grasping and tracking [ 33 ] . More recently, stereo has been integrated into imitation and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies. ActiveGlasses [ 34 ] reconstructs a point cloud from the stereo pair through a stereo matcher and feeds that to the policy, while StereoPolicy [ 4 ] and StereoVLA [ 5 ] consume the stereo images directly. All of these methods can benefit from large-scale stereo demonstrations, yet none address how such data can be obtained at scale. Stereo demonstrations can be teleoperated on a stereo rig, but this requires stereo hardware on every platform and teleoperation for every new task. StereoEngine instead generates the stereo data needed to train these policies without additional real-world collection.

## II-D Video Generation in Robotics

Video generation models have recently been used to scale robot data, either as world models that generate demonstrations for policy learning [ 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 ] or as data engines that augment existing demonstrations while keeping the robot trajectory fixed [ 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 ] .
A related group of methods conditions video diffusion on simulation to synthesize new configurations or diverse demonstrations [ 10 , 12 ] .
Closest to our setting is CRAFT [ 13 ] , which generates a video from Canny edges [ 44 ] of a simulated bimanual episode together with a real reference image.
However, all of these generate only monocular video, and StereoEngine is the first to extend video generation for robot data to stereo pair synthesis.

2026-10-12.title: Visual-Wi-Fi Navigation to Signal-Emitting Devices
2026-10-12.authors: Lihao Wang , Tianjian Xu , Tianmin Shu , Renjie Zhao
2026-10-12.abstract:
Indoor navigation to task-relevant targets remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, or visually indistinct.
Meanwhile, smart appliances, mobile devices, and IoT tags emit Wi-Fi signals during everyday communication, providing a pervasive but underused spatial cue.
We study visual–Wi-Fi navigation, where a robot reaches a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment using onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the device, without connecting to the device or modifying infrastructure.
Realizing this requires pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations during closed-loop policy learning and reliable spatial cues from bearing measurements corrupted by indoor multipath propagation on a moving robot.
We present WiFiSpaces , which extends the Habitat embodied simulator with online ray-traced Wi-Fi sensing, rendering Wi-Fi observations for a robot-mounted antenna array at continuous poses during policy rollouts.
On top of it, we build ViFiNav , a localization-aware navigation framework: an online source-localization algorithm exploits robot motion to disambiguate and robustly aggregate bearings from multiple viewpoints into a confidence-aware source estimate, and a learned policy fuses this evolving estimate with depth observations and learns to act on it as it is refined.
Experiments show that exploiting robot motion is key to accurate source estimates, and that fine-tuning on ray-traced Wi-Fi observations in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav . The policy transfers zero-shot to unseen scene datasets, and we deploy it on a real robot with a Wi-Fi sensor built from a commodity router, without any real-world training.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Navigation in unmapped environments often involves locating and reaching task-relevant targets, including everyday connected devices such as smart appliances and mobile devices.
While visual navigation has made substantial progress [ 38 , 20 , 19 ] , it remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, visually indistinct, or has no direct visual manifestation [ 46 ] . A vision-only agent then lacks an explicit spatial cue and must rely on weak semantic priors or broad exploration, producing inefficient trajectories.
Meanwhile, the growing prevalence of connected devices creates a new sensing opportunity: many indoor targets already emit wireless signals as part of their normal communication, which can be overheard by a robot-mounted receiver to provide complementary spatial cues.
As shown in Fig. 1 , we study visual–Wi-Fi navigation : in an unmapped environment, an embodied agent uses onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the target’s existing traffic to navigate to the physical location of a signal-emitting target device. The target is defined by the Wi-Fi source location and need not be visible.

Unlike audio cues, which require the target to actively and continuously emit informative sound and are susceptible to environmental noise [ 7 , 8 , 35 ] , wireless signals are emitted by ordinary devices as a by-product of communication and propagate through and around obstacles [ 16 , 29 ] , providing spatial cues beyond visual line of sight.
Among wireless technologies, we focus on Wi-Fi because it is the most pervasive: ultra-wideband (UWB) and Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) localization typically require dedicated anchors or tags to be deployed and calibrated [ 15 , 48 , 47 ] , whereas most household and personal devices, including IoT tags, already communicate over Wi-Fi (Fig. 1 ), and their packets can be overheard by a commodity Wi-Fi router without connecting to the device or its network [ 14 , 16 ] .
Wi-Fi is a deployment choice, not a requirement: the same setting arises for any wireless modality that carries spatial cues beyond line of sight.
However, autonomous navigation with Wi-Fi signals raises two key challenges.

The first challenge is to obtain pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations at scale for learning-based embodied navigation: during rollouts they must track the agent’s continuous pose, including heading, while reflecting the source location and the 3D geometry that shapes propagation, reflection, and blockage.
Precomputed radio maps do not fit: they tabulate the signal on a discrete grid and would have to be rebuilt every episode as the source moves, over poses that are policy-dependent and unknown in advance.
To address this, we propose WiFiSpaces , to our knowledge the first embodied navigation simulator to provide online Wi-Fi observations at the agent’s current pose, by extending Habitat with a Wi-Fi sensor built on physics-based ray tracing [ 1 ] ; synchronizing agent state with the wireless scene at every step and reusing scene geometry across episodes makes online ray tracing practical for closed-loop policy learning.

The second challenge is to turn noisy Wi-Fi measurements into reliable spatial cues on a moving robot. Each overheard packet yields channel state information (CSI) at the router, from which a bearing to the source can be estimated [ 23 , 16 ] , but indoor multipath makes single-vantage bearings heavy-tailed: in WiFiSpaces , about 10 % 10\% of raw bearings are off by more than 30 ∘ 30^{\circ} (Fig. 7(a) ), consistent with real deployments [ 23 , 40 , 11 ] , and acting on such an estimate commits the robot to the wrong part of the scene.
To address this, we present ViFiNav , a localization-aware visual–Wi-Fi navigation framework: an online Wi-Fi source localization algorithm resolves the directional ambiguity of the small antenna array using the robot’s natural motion and robustly aggregates multi-view bearings into a confidence-aware source estimate, and, rather than heuristically following each intermediate estimate, a learned multimodal policy fuses this evolving cue with visual observations and learns to act on it in closed loop.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

A complete system for visual–Wi-Fi navigation, which we formulate as reaching a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment from visual observations, odometry, and Wi-Fi packets overheard from its existing traffic, without modifying the target device or infrastructure.

WiFiSpaces , an embodied navigation simulator that provides online ray-traced Wi-Fi observations synchronized with continuous agent poses during policy rollouts.

An online Wi-Fi source localization algorithm coupled with a reinforcement-learned policy that learns to act on its evolving estimates.

Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment: fine-tuning in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav over the same policy without Wi-Fi fine-tuning, and the policy generalizes zero-shot across indoor scene datasets; the same policy is further deployed on a real robot with a commodity-router Wi-Fi sensor [ 14 , 16 ] , without any real-world training.

1. A complete system for visual–Wi-Fi navigation, which we formulate as reaching a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment from visual observations, odometry, and Wi-Fi packets overheard from its existing traffic, without modifying the target device or infrastructure.

2. WiFiSpaces , an embodied navigation simulator that provides online ray-traced Wi-Fi observations synchronized with continuous agent poses during policy rollouts.

3. An online Wi-Fi source localization algorithm coupled with a reinforcement-learned policy that learns to act on its evolving estimates.

4. Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment: fine-tuning in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav over the same policy without Wi-Fi fine-tuning, and the policy generalizes zero-shot across indoor scene datasets; the same policy is further deployed on a real robot with a commodity-router Wi-Fi sensor [ 14 , 16 ] , without any real-world training.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

Embodied navigation with vision and sound. Visual navigation has been widely studied, including PointGoal [ 32 , 39 , 43 , 38 ] , ObjectGoal [ 5 , 19 , 21 ] , ImageGoal [ 20 ] , and vision-language navigation [ 26 ] , but relies on target visibility or learned semantic priors and degrades to weakly guided exploration when the target is small, occluded, or has no visual manifestation.
Audio-visual navigation [ 7 , 8 , 35 ] adds sound cues, but requires the target to actively and continuously emit informative sound.
Wi-Fi signals, in contrast, are emitted by ordinary devices as a by-product of their normal traffic and provide spatial cues beyond visibility.

Wireless localization and navigation. Indoor localization with Wi-Fi [ 4 , 41 , 23 , 40 , 3 , 18 , 11 ] , UWB [ 15 , 48 ] , and BLE [ 47 ] is well studied; Wi-Fi is attractive for its commodity availability, but existing systems rely on site-specific data [ 4 , 3 ] or calibrated anchors [ 41 , 23 , 40 , 18 , 11 ] , limiting map-free use.
Robot motion has been exploited to synthesize larger apertures for angle-of-arrival (AoA) estimation [ 17 ] , but with active coordination with the Wi-Fi infrastructure [ 16 , 29 ] and for localization or tracking rather than closed-loop navigation.
Classical radio source seeking [ 37 , 6 ] couples an RF estimate with a model-based controller, but does not fuse it with visual observations in a learned policy or formulate the problem as an embodied navigation task with standardized episodes and metrics.
Prior navigation works using indoor mmWave cellular links [ 45 , 44 , 24 ] need dedicated base stations and suffer severe wall attenuation, require hard-to-obtain link-state labels, and train on precomputed radio maps rather than pose-dependent observations during closed-loop execution.

Wireless-aware simulation platforms. As summarized in Table I , embodied simulators [ 32 , 34 , 22 , 30 ] provide navigation tasks, visual observations, and policy-learning interfaces but do not model radio propagation, whereas wireless simulators [ 1 , 31 , 9 ] model propagation with high fidelity but are not embodied environments.
Recently, SimART [ 42 ] couples a robotics simulator with Sionna ray tracing for outdoor 6G sensing but does not target indoor navigation, and concurrent work [ 27 ] trains an RF-guided navigation policy with Habitat and Sionna but evaluates it only in simulation. WiFiSpaces instead embeds Wi-Fi sensing in the step loop of an embodied simulator: CSI for a robot-mounted antenna array is rendered at every agent pose in indoor scenes and exposed as an observation synchronized with visual observations and actions, so policies can be trained and evaluated closed-loop.

2026-10-12.title: REMM: Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation
2026-10-12.authors: Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran , Ruwan Wickramarachchi , Alessandro Oltramari , Jonathan Francis
2026-10-12.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. Retaining observations alone does not specify which completed conditions should be withdrawn after a disturbance or which obligations require repair. We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor. REMM separates an append-only evidence history from revisable task state and explicitly links derived relations and completed conditions to their supporting facts. When accepted evidence changes a supporting fact, it withdraws dependent conclusions and schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries without updating the executor. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall. Complementary video diagnostics show improved grounding of retained history into the next instruction, including comparisons with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -compatible high-level planner adaptations. These results support revisable memory as a practical interface for continued manipulation without policy retraining. Project: https://revanthsenthil.github.io/remm/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation requires more than executing a sequence of independent skills. Each action changes the world in which subsequent decisions are made, and information needed later may no longer be directly observable: which object was handled first, what remains inside a container, or where an object was placed before becoming occluded. Such tasks therefore require decisions that depend on interaction history under partial observability [ 1 , 2 ] . Yet retaining history alone is insufficient. A previously valid relation may cease to hold after a slip, human intervention, or environmental rearrangement. A robot must therefore preserve what happened while revising what is currently supported by the available evidence .

Generalist robot policies have substantially improved the execution of individual manipulation skills [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Recent models further extend language-conditioned control to long-horizon settings; in particular, G0.5 provides an autoregressive interface that interleaves reasoning and action generation within a single policy [ 7 ] . However, a capable executor does not by itself determine what should happen next when the relevant evidence is old, hidden, or contradicted by a subsequent physical intervention.

Recent work equips manipulation systems with temporal context through learned memory banks, sparse visual events, or retrieved keyframes [ 2 , 8 , 9 ] . Hierarchical systems instead place memory and reasoning above the motor policy: HiMe [ 10 ] maintains editable multimodal memory, while HyMeS [ 11 ] and BATON [ 12 ] steer reusable or frozen skills using external verification and transition-aware memory. These methods establish that memory can extend a policy beyond its immediate observation. They also sharpen a different question: after evidence changes, which earlier conclusions should change with it?

Closed-loop planners can incorporate success, scene, or human feedback into subsequent decisions [ 13 ] ; structured world representations encode relational scene state [ 14 ] ; and dynamic memories can add, delete, or modify stored relations as new evidence arrives [ 15 ] . Yet these capabilities do not explicitly track which physical relations support previously completed task conditions. If such a relation changes without revising its downstream consequences, the controller can retain an internally coherent but physically stale task state. We therefore consider an intervention-grounded process memory in which physical relations, derived scene state, and completed task conditions are connected through explicit support dependencies. When verified evidence changes an upstream relation, its affected consequences can be selectively withdrawn. These dependencies are supplied by task and physical semantics rather than learned through causal discovery; their use as recorded justifications is related to truth maintenance [ 16 ] , while remaining distinct from causal world models that learn or probabilistically infer manipulation outcomes [ 17 , 18 ] .

We introduce REMM , R evisable E mbodied M emory for M anipulation, a supervisory layer around a frozen G0.5 executor. REMM preserves an append-only evidence history while maintaining a separate projection of currently supported state. It records causal dependency links from physical relations to derived and completed task conditions; when verified evidence supersedes a parent relation, REMM invalidates affected descendants, identifies the broken task obligation, and schedules a bounded recovery instruction at the next verified stationary skill boundary. This produces an inspectable path from physical intervention to memory revision and changed control without REMM-specific parameter training.

We evaluate REMM on real-robot tasks involving transport disruptions, delayed sequence recall, and hidden-object rearrangement. The evaluation separates retention from revision : sequence and hidden-object tasks test whether decision-relevant history persists through delay and occlusion, while transport interventions test whether previously valid task state is correctly withdrawn and repaired after the world changes. Beyond end-to-end task success, we measure change acceptance, dependency revision, recovery timing and destination, physical repair, and the observed memory-to-control trace. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall, while completing all four of its hidden-object trials.

Our contributions are threefold:

a formulation of revisable embodied memory that separates recorded execution history from currently supported task state and represents intervention-sensitive dependencies from physical relations to derived and completed task conditions;

REMM, a supervisory system that propagates dependency invalidation and dispatches nominal or recovery instructions to a frozen G0.5 policy without REMM-specific parameter training; and

a controlled real-robot evaluation that traces observed changes through memory revision to subsequent control decisions across transport, sequence-recall, and hidden-object manipulation tasks.

1. a formulation of revisable embodied memory that separates recorded execution history from currently supported task state and represents intervention-sensitive dependencies from physical relations to derived and completed task conditions;

2. REMM, a supervisory system that propagates dependency invalidation and dispatches nominal or recovery instructions to a frozen G0.5 policy without REMM-specific parameter training; and

3. a controlled real-robot evaluation that traces observed changes through memory revision to subsequent control decisions across transport, sequence-recall, and hidden-object manipulation tasks.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Memory for Vision–Language–Action Control

Policy-integrated approaches make history part of action generation. MemoryVLA retrieves perceptual and cognitive tokens from a learned memory bank [ 2 ] ; EventVLA learns when to preserve sparse visual evidence [ 8 ] ; and Chameleon and ChainVLA propagate compact event or execution state across action queries [ 19 , 20 ] . These methods learn representations for retention and retrieval inside the policy. RoboMME shows that their benefit depends strongly on whether a task requires temporal, spatial, object, or procedural memory [ 1 ] . REMM uses a different boundary: it leaves G0.5 frozen, does not learn a memory-conditioned action model, and studies explicit revision of task state between bounded skills.

Hierarchical approaches place memory above the executor. MemER trains a high-level visual policy to select keyframes and predict subtasks for a separately trained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 9 ] . HiMe divides control among an Executor, a working-memory Sentry, and a Planner that retrieves and edits multimodal memory [ 10 ] . HyMeS uses executable memory-management heuristics and multimodal completion checks to steer a Markovian VLA [ 11 ] , while BATON uses a frozen VLA with subtask exploration and transition-aware memory [ 12 ] . These systems are the closest architectural context for REMM. Our question is narrower than general memory management: whether storing explicit parents for derived and completed task conditions allows a verified intervention to revise exactly the downstream obligations that no longer hold.

## II-B Closed-Loop State Revision and Recovery

Robotic planners have long used feedback to reconsider high-level action. Inner Monologue conditions an LLM planner on success detection, scene description, and human feedback [ 13 ] ; 𝒫 3 \mathcal{P}^{3} schedules emerging tasks using priorities, dependencies, interruption, and resumption [ 21 ] ; and PhyAgentOS couples persistent session state with verification and replanning [ 22 ] . These works establish closed-loop supervisory control, but their task scheduling or model-mediated replanning does not by itself expose which physical fact sustained a completed condition. REMM connects these levels explicitly and preserves the active atomic skill while inserting, deferring, or retargeting a recovery at a skill boundary.

Structured memories provide the complementary world-state representation. ReMEmbR indexes spatially and temporally grounded experience for navigation [ 23 ] ; ConceptGraphs builds open-vocabulary object–relation graphs for planning [ 14 ] ; and RoboMemory revises relevant neighborhoods of temporal, spatial, semantic, and episodic memory [ 15 ] . REMM does not claim the first relational memory or editable knowledge graph. It adds an append-only evidence ledger, an active projection, and typed links from physical relations to derived scene and task conditions.

Those links draw on two related traditions. Truth-maintenance systems retain justifications and withdraw conclusions when their support becomes inactive [ 16 ] . Causal manipulation work instead uses controlled interventions or causal Bayesian models to reason about action effects [ 17 , 18 ] . REMM does not discover a causal graph or predict general dynamics. It instantiates task-semantic causal dependencies whose operational meaning is intervention-sensitive: changing a required parent relation changes the validity of its descendant task condition and, through the controller, the selected continuation. The experiments therefore test both the stored revision and its downstream control effect rather than treating an edited memory record as sufficient evidence of recovery.

2026-10-12.title: FallGown: A Soft Pneumatic Wearable Device for Fall Prevention
2026-10-12.authors: Megan C. Coram , Haoran Lei , Steven H. Collins , Steve B. Cousins , Michelle Baldonado , Cynthia Sung , Allison M. Okamura
2026-10-12.abstract: Concerns about falling and potential resulting injuries prevent many older adults from participating in forms of health-improving exercise such as walking, dance, and tai chi. Existing passive devices like walkers require use of the arms for support, and active devices like exoskeletons and robotic frames are often rigid, bulky, and stigmatized, which limits their use. The FallGown is a soft wearable support structure consisting of pressurized pneumatic pouches within a fabric shell; it can support the full weight of a user’s body and aims to prevent falls. It is portable (6.9 kg and 0.051 m 3 when stored), minimally burdensome (7.24-20.8 N drag force depending on floor type and whether an optional rolling base frame is used), and convenient (less than 2.5 minutes on average to don and less than 0.5 minutes on average to doff). The optional rolling base lowers friction with the floor, but reduces portability and skirt deformation (which can be useful to fit through doors and other tight spaces). Fall prevention testing with a single user revealed a tradeoff between device size and stability against tipping; a skirt with 12 pneumatic pouches and a floor diameter of 1.4 meters with a base frame prevented all falls except in one case with a mechanical failure. On-board pressure sensors can sense the user’s weight distribution, providing an opportunity for monitored exercise and adaptive support.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Wheelchairs and walkers are traditional passive devices that support mobility for adults with weakness, poor balance, and other movement challenges. Robotic versions include autonomous wheelchairs [ 1 ] , frames [ 2 ] , and handles [ 3 ] . Exoskeletons reduce footprint and provide more versatile locomotor assistance in unstructured environments [ 4 ] . However, the rigidity of traditional robotic mechanisms can create discomfort, and their bulkiness can limit portability. In a recent review of the state-of-the-art of robotics to assist mobility, physiotherapists and patients highlighted the following needs: safety, a one-size-fits-all approach, ease of device use, weight and placement of the device, cost of the device, and appearance of the device [ 5 ] . Negative perceptions of the appearance of an assistive device can result in stigma and reduce adoption, even for occupational scenarios [ 6 ] . Another recent survey found that fall prevention was the most (according to clinicians) or second-most (according to older adults) important feature that a wearable assistive device could offer [ 7 ] .

Approaches using techniques from the field of soft robotics aim to make exoskeletons easier to wear and use, and potentially less noticeable. However, they can still be difficult to don and doff, and they are usually not able to support the user’s full body weight. Exosuits are one form of “soft” support; they have no rigid frame to bear compressive loads, rather they use fabrics and tensile elements, usually cables, anchored to the body to apply forces in parallel with the wearer’s own muscles [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Some exosuits pass applied loads through the user’s own joints, which could lead to painful changes in the magnitude and direction of joint loading. Inflatable support devices (sometimes referred to as exomuscles) have been designed to support a single joint in research projects [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] and commercial products like the torsional air-driven bladder used for knee support by Roam Robotics, Inc. The authors are not aware of any portable inflatable lower-body device that attempts full body-weight support.

We were inspired to create a new form of mobility support device based on the following challenge presented to our research team by a local older adult day care center: During individual or group low-impact exercises, such as dance and tai chi, older adults’ fear of falling will often cause them to opt out of physical activities or, if they choose to participate, keep them in a wheelchair or grasping a walker. Avoiding activity altogether for fear of falling can have negative impacts on long-term health [ 14 ] , but reliance on current assistive devices prevents users from performing whole body movements, which are important to maintain strength and coordination and key to the aesthetics of the performance. Hands-free walkers such as the LifeGlider and Merry Walker permit arm movement, but they may still encounter the same stigma as traditional walkers, which limits their adoption. To address this challenge, we aimed to combine features of existing passive mobility support devices with soft wearable robotics. We created FallGown (Fig. 1 ), an inflatable skirt that is donned via a conventional climbing harness and zippers, can support a user’s weight, and has a conical shape wide enough to resist falls for a variety of user movements. As a fashion statement, FallGown evokes a ball gown and is very noticeable; it counters the clinical aesthetic of prior assistive device designs.

The primary contribution of this work is a new inflated assistive wearable device that aims to support hands-free exercise for people with weakness, poor balance, and other movement challenges that limit beneficial exercise. A secondary contribution is a series of evaluation methods that address key assistive technology needs identified by patients and physiotherapists.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Design and Fabrication

The FallGown design is motivated by the need for a stand-alone device that is portable and comfortable, leaves the arms free, allows walking and knee bends, prevents falls, can adjust its level of support depending on user needs, and invokes fashion imagery rather than resembling a medical device. The primary design concept is that an inflated structure can provide body support while minimizing device weight. For portability, we constructed the device from thin, pliable textiles so that it can be easily folded up when deflated. For user comfort, we used soft cotton for the outermost layer of the device and made the harness adjustable. To free the arms, we designed the device to surround and support the body in all directions. To permit internal movement and promote stability, we made the base of the structure wide. For adjustable support and robustness, we made each pneumatic pouch individually inflatable. For an appealing appearance and durability, we top stitched the fabric seams.

Initial development investigated the potential of using discrete pressurized tubes to support the body. However, these thin tubes buckled too easily outwards, as shown in Fig. 2 A. Connecting the tubes together side-by-side resulted in the hollow cone shape. When compressed, the geometry is maintained by hoop stress. The first full-size prototype of the FallGown, pictured in Fig. 2 B, was made from a single layer of thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU)-coated ripstop nylon in order to make the device as lightweight as possible. However, complex corner seams caused wrinkling issues in the ultrasonic welding process and made airtightness difficult to achieve. The first version of the skirt was comprised of one contiguous air pocket, so small holes or tears anywhere on the device would cause the whole structure to deflate. To address these issues, the final version of the device was composed of two layers: simple discrete rectangular pneumatic pouches on the inside and a robust protective fabric shell on the outside. The pouches are airtight and create individually strong members, and the fabric shell creates the overall structure and prevents buckling of the individual members.

The components of the final version of the FallGown evaluated in the following section are laid out in Fig. 3 A. The clothing pattern shown in Fig. 3 C is sewn together into the 3-dimensional form illustrated in Fig. 3 D with two concentric cones linked axially along vertical lines. The fabric shell is made from lightweight cotton (AK Trading Co. Medium Weight Muslin), while the inner pouches are made from ultrasonically welded TPU-coated ripstop nylon (Quest Outfitters #1056). Each pouch, shown in Fig. 3 B, is inflated through a push-to-connect bulkhead connector and valve. Each pouch measures 145 cm by 51 cm when uninflated, which is oversized compared to the dimensions of the shell to ensure that the pouches can expand to fill the full interior volume of the shell. Wide zippers along vertical seams in the front of the device provide an easy access point for donning and doffing and permit the attachment of additional pneumatic pouches. A rock climbing style harness made of nylon webbing is worn at the hip and upper legs. It connects via side release buckles to the skirt to anchor it gently but securely to the body. We also developed a wheeled frame shown in Fig. 3 A that can be added to the base of the FallGown for increased rigidity of the conical structure and reduction of sliding friction with the ground. When the frame is not used, a loop of soft webbing is attached in its place underneath the skirt to help reduce the tension applied to the bottom of the zippers.

2026-10-12.title: Spa-Bench: A Real-Robot Benchmark for Spatial Grounding in Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-12.authors: Justin Tien-Smith , Matthew Pidden , Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
2026-10-12.comment: including appendices. Website: this https URL
2026-10-12.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising route toward general-purpose robotics by transferring semantic knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into language-conditioned control. However, most VLA evaluations emphasize aggregate manipulation success under changes in objects, instructions, or environments, leaving unclear how reliably these policies ground spatial descriptions in the physical scenes where they act. We therefore ask a sharper question: how reliably can current VLAs translate spatial descriptions into appropriate real-robot behavior? To investigate this, we introduce Spa-Bench, a real-robot benchmark that evaluates spatial grounding across six tabletop tasks covering Object State , Relative Size , Referential Description , Relational Placement , Ordinal Position , and Counting . Our primary evaluation compares in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) spatial configurations while retaining training support for the relevant objects, concepts, and actions, reducing object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure. Four diagnostic conditions further probe physical execution, sensitivity to wording, object-task associations, and recognition that no action is required. We release 4,092 episodes collected on the SO-101 robot arm: 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 real-robot evaluation rollouts from five state-of-the-art VLA policies. Across the three fully evaluated policies, success falls from 67.5–73.3% on ID spatial configurations to 40.7–52.0% on OOD spatial configurations, while matched direct instructions improve success by 28.3–40.0 percentage points. These results show that the evaluated VLAs can often execute the required manipulations but lack robust spatial grounding. Project materials, including videos, code, and benchmark data, are available at https://justintiensmith.github.io/Spa-Bench/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have emerged as a promising approach to general-purpose robot learning. By connecting pretrained vision-language representations to robot actions, these models can transfer semantic knowledge acquired from internet-scale data into language-conditioned control [ 1 , 4 , 10 , 12 ] . This transfer promises robots that can respond to new objects, instructions, and environments without requiring a separately trained policy for every behavior.

Policies evaluated on existing benchmarks have demonstrated increasingly broad manipulation capabilities, including generalization across objects, instructions, visual conditions, and task sequences [ 5 , 6 , 20 ] . Nevertheless, completing a manipulation task does not by itself establish that a policy has correctly interpreted the spatial structure of its environment. Spatial understanding in existing benchmarks is typically embedded within an overall task-success metric and is consequently entangled with object recognition, language interpretation, and motor execution. If a policy fails to place a green pen to the left of a red block, for example, the failure could arise from incorrect spatial grounding, failure to identify the objects, an unsuccessful grasp, or an inability to execute the required placement due to an inadequate number of demonstrations spanning the full workspace. Furthermore, benchmarks that introduce a fixed scene to mitigate some of these issues introduce a different problem: Success may result from memorizing recurring object locations or action patterns rather than from grounding the instructed spatial relation.

In this work, we use spatial grounding to describe the ability to map language about properties, positions, quantities, and relations in the current physical scene to an appropriate target, goal configuration, or decision not to act. We study this capability through the following question:

How reliably can current VLAs ground spatial descriptions into appropriate actions in the real world?

Answering this question requires more than measuring success on an ordinary held-out task. A test task that simultaneously introduces an unfamiliar object, instruction, spatial concept, or physical behavior cannot reveal which of these changes caused a failure. A diagnostic spatial benchmark should instead establish familiarity with the constituent objects, concepts, and manipulation behaviors before evaluating whether the policy can use the relevant spatial information in a different physical configuration.

We introduce the Spatial Grounding Benchmark (Spa-Bench), a controlled real-robot benchmark designed around this principle. Spa-Bench comprises six tabletop tasks evaluating the grounding of Object State , Relative Size , Relational Placement , Referential Description , Ordinal Position , and Counting . All tasks use the same robot embodiment, workspace, receptacle, and broad pick-and-place action family. The principal source of variation is therefore the scene-grounded rule that determines which object should be manipulated, where it should be placed, or whether movement is even required.

Spa-Bench evaluates policies in ID and OOD spatial configurations. ID configurations measure whether a policy has acquired the spatially grounded behaviors represented in its demonstrations. OOD configurations change the association between a spatial concept and its task argument while preserving training support for the relevant objects, physical actions, and spatial concepts. We implement this controlled split through a withheld-cell design: each component of an OOD evaluation configuration appears elsewhere in training, but their particular combination is reserved for evaluation (see Fig. 3 ). The purpose of this construction is to reduce object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure.

To characterize spatially grounded performance beyond the primary ID–OOD comparison, Spa-Bench includes four additional diagnostic conditions that probe complementary aspects of policy behavior. Direct-manipulation controls remove the need for spatial inference while preserving the requested robot motion. Prompt-paraphrase trials restate both OOD spatial and direct-manipulation instructions on the same scenes, testing whether their performance gap depends on exact wording. Cross-task-object rollouts vary the usual association between an object and task. Finally, no-intervention scenes test whether a policy can recognize when no action is required.

Spa-Bench contains 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations, with 200 demonstrations for each task. We evaluate five fine-tuned state-of-the-art policies that are drawn from four different VLA architectures: VLA-0, MolmoAct2, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , GR00T-N1.7 Frozen LLM (GR00T-N1.7 F-LLM), and GR00T-N1.7 Full Fine-Tune (GR00T-N1.7 F-FT). Three policies complete the full 900-rollout evaluation protocol, producing 2,700 evaluation episodes, while two partial baselines contribute 192 episodes. In total, we release 4,092 SO-101 episodes, including the demonstrations, rollout videos, task specifications, and documented scene layouts.

Across the three fully evaluated policies, ID spatial-configuration success ranges from 67.5% to 73.3%, but success decreases to 40.7%–52.0% in OOD spatial configurations. On the OOD spatial configuration matched scene subset, direct-manipulation instructions achieve 81.7%–89.2% success, showing that many of the physical behaviors are executable even when the policy fails under a spatially grounded instruction. Performance is strongly task dependent: all three policies fail every OOD Counting trial, almost always without acting; other tasks are dominated by target-selection or spatial-outcome errors. The direct manipulation advantage also persists when both instruction types are paraphrased, revealing that the state-of-the-art VLAs we evaluate do not exhibit robust spatial grounding. In summary, our core contributions are:

We introduce Spa-Bench, a six-task real-robot benchmark for evaluating spatial grounding across ID and OOD physical configurations.

We introduce Spa-Bench, a six-task real-robot benchmark for evaluating spatial grounding across ID and OOD physical configurations.

We develop a controlled evaluation protocol that combines a withheld-cell split with four diagnostics that probe physical execution, wording sensitivity, object context, and action gating.

# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Models

Vision-language-action models (VLAs) connect pretrained multimodal representations to robot actions with the goal of transferring semantic and visual knowledge into closed-loop control. RT-2 helped establish this formulation by representing actions as tokens and co-fine-tuning a vision-language model on web and robot data, demonstrating transfer to novel objects, instructions, and semantically specified behaviors [ 1 ] . OpenVLA subsequently introduced an open-source 7-billion-parameter VLA trained on large-scale robot data and designed for adaptation to downstream embodiments [ 2 ] . In parallel, π 0 \pi_{0} coupled a pretrained vision-language backbone to a flow-matching action expert for generating continuous action chunks across multiple embodiments [ 3 ] .

More recent VLAs have targeted open-world generalization, heterogeneous robot data, embodied reasoning, and practical deployment. π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} extends π 0 \pi_{0} through heterogeneous co-training on robot trajectories, verbal instructions, semantic predictions, and web data [ 4 ] . The GR00T-N1.7 family uses a dual-system architecture in which a vision-language module interprets the scene and instruction while a diffusion transformer produces continuous actions [ 10 ] . VLA-0 investigates whether continuous actions can instead be generated directly as numerical text without introducing a specialized action vocabulary or action head [ 11 ] . MolmoAct2 connects an embodied-reasoning vision-language model to a flow-matching continuous-action expert [ 12 ] . Because these models differ in pretraining data, training objectives, action representations, and fine-tuning procedures, Spa-Bench compares complete policy systems rather than isolating individual architectural choices. Each fine-tuned policy is evaluated under the same controlled spatial configurations and diagnostic conditions to characterize its spatial generalization.

## II-B Simulation and Reasoning Benchmarks

Simulation benchmarks have enabled scalable evaluation of language-conditioned robot behavior. RLBench provides a broad collection of vision-guided manipulation tasks and automatically generated demonstrations [ 14 ] , while ALFRED evaluates grounded instruction following over compositional household activities [ 15 ] . LIBERO studies declarative and procedural knowledge transfer across lifelong-learning task suites [ 16 ] . RoboCasa expands language-conditioned manipulation to diverse household activities in simulated kitchens [ 17 ] , and BEHAVIOR-1K targets long-horizon everyday activities involving physical and semantic state changes [ 18 ] . VLABench further evaluates semantic knowledge, spatial relationships, physical understanding, and long-horizon reasoning across numerous tasks and objects [ 5 ] . VIMA-Bench more explicitly separates forms of generalization, including a combinatorial split that evaluates unseen object–texture pairings whose individual components appear during training [ 13 ] . These benchmarks establish task breadth and scalable evaluation, but spatial grounding is generally one component of overall task success and therefore remains entangled with perception, planning, and execution.

A complementary line of work examines whether policy performance persists under controlled distribution shifts. The COLOSSEUM evaluates manipulation policies under systematic visual and physical perturbations [ 19 ] , while LIBERO-PRO varies manipulated objects, initial states, instructions, and environments, revealing that strong standard-benchmark performance can depend on memorized layouts and action sequences [ 6 ] . STAR-Gen organizes generalization along visual, semantic, and behavioral axes [ 20 ] . BeTTER applies targeted interventions, including spatial-layout shifts, together with kinematic isolation intended to separate reasoning failures from execution limitations [ 8 ] . Other benchmarks evaluate reasoning without requiring closed-loop physical execution. ManipBench probes low-level manipulation reasoning in vision-language models [ 21 ] , whereas MultihopSpatial evaluates compositional spatial inference and visual grounding over multi-hop relationships [ 22 ] . These evaluations provide fine-grained measures of reasoning, but correct visual or textual answers do not necessarily establish that the inferred relation can guide real-robot behavior.

## II-C Real-World Robot Evaluation

Real-world benchmarks address the complementary challenges of physical validity, reproducibility, and evaluation at scale. REALM evaluates manipulation policies under controlled perturbations in simulation and validates the resulting trends through physical experiments [ 7 ] . RoboChallenge provides infrastructure for evaluating embodied policies across multiple real robots and manipulation tasks [ 23 ] . RADAR focuses on real-world dynamics and spatial-physical intelligence while using automated three-dimensional success metrics [ 9 ] . ManipArena combines diverse real-robot tasks with task-specific OOD conditions, including unseen objects and held-out spatial, ordering, or procedural configurations of familiar objects [ 24 ] . VLA-REPLICA instead emphasizes low-cost cross-laboratory reproducibility through standardized hardware and evaluation on the SO-101 platform [ 25 ] .

Spa-Bench complements these efforts by isolating spatial grounding under closed-loop real-robot execution. It fixes the robot, workspace, object inventory, and broad manipulation behavior, and places the held-out combination specifically in the mapping between spatial concepts and task arguments. Thus, its OOD configurations preserve training support for the constituent objects, spatial concepts, and physical behaviors. Direct-manipulation controls test whether the relevant manipulation behavior remains executable when the task-specific spatial inference is removed. Prompt paraphrases test whether the performance difference between matched OOD spatial and direct instructions persists under alternative phrasings. Cross-task-object evaluations test sensitivity to familiar object–task associations, while no-intervention scenes test whether policies can correctly withhold action. Together, these diagnostics make Spa-Bench a targeted evaluation of how reliably current VLAs translate spatial descriptions into appropriate behavior in physical scenes.
