2026-10-12.title: Non-Prehensile Multi-Object Placement with Mobile Robots via Diffusion-Based Trajectory Planning
2026-10-12.authors: Lance Pharand , Megnath Ramesh , Mark Chiu , Yash Vardhan Pant , Stephen L. Smith
2026-10-12.abstract: Non-prehensile manipulation with mobile robots has primarily targeted placement in coarse goal regions. Precision placement has been studied with manipulators on benchmarks such as Push-T, where an omnidirectional end effector can readily re-approach an object from any side. For a mobile robot, correcting the same placement errors may require wide repositioning maneuvers around the object. We formalize multi-object pushing with a mobile robot as a multi-target assignment problem at tight tolerances. We propose a diffusion planner with a causal factorization: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the current clean robot estimate. This factorization allows us to sample multiple object outcomes for a single robot plan, capturing the multi-modality of pushing. We also design a set of pushing-specific costs for mobile robots, used for both guidance and best-of- N N sampling at inference. On Push-T, our planner attains the highest success rate of the methods we compare, while having the lowest rate of implausible object motion. Across three multi-box pushing environments resembling warehouse scenarios, it raises the fraction of boxes placed by 21.5 21.5 percentage points over an unguided baseline, and replans 1.8 × 1.8\times faster than a planner that denoises the two trajectories together. Lastly, we deploy the guided planner on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with object shapes absent from the training data, where it places 85.0 % 85.0\% of objects within tolerance against Diffusion Policy’s 37.5 % 37.5\% .
2026-10-12.introduction:
In this work, we focus on the problem of multi-object pushing with a mobile robot. Formally, this is a multi-target assignment problem, where each object must be placed inside a tight target configuration (Fig. 1 ). Successfully solving this problem would make mobile robots viable for warehouse tasks where they must push boxes or pallets to precise positions for downstream automation to take over. Precision pushing has been studied in the manipulator setting, where Push-T [ 1 , 2 ] is a popular benchmark [ 3 , 4 ] . Here, a robot with a circular end-effector must push a T-shaped block onto a goal pose, with success requiring near-complete overlap. In contrast, existing non-prehensile manipulation (NPM) work with mobile robots [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] only requires the object to land inside a target zone much larger than the object itself.

Two properties of the mobile robot setting make pushing an object to within a small tolerance of a target harder than it is in the manipulator setting. First, mobile robots typically have non-holonomic dynamics and cannot move sideways. Second, the robot’s contact face is typically a non-prehensile bumper fixed to the front, so changing the side of the object being pushed requires a wide reposition. Both aspects make it difficult to perform the small corrections needed to bring an object within a tight tolerance of its target. In contrast, the end effector in Push-T can move sideways, is omnidirectional, and can re-approach the object from any side. Planners and policies for the studied setting must account for the difficulty of these corrections, but existing mobile robot NPM methods are evaluated in settings where this is not necessary.

Diffusion-based planners have shown promise in solving difficult pushing problems [ 3 , 4 ] . Diffusion planners that predict object motion typically denoise the robot and object trajectories simultaneously [ 8 ] , which can yield object motion that is implausible given the robot’s actions. We instead factorize the joint trajectory distribution into a robot trajectory prior and an object trajectory conditional. Each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the current clean robot estimate (Fig. 2 ). As a result, guidance can be evaluated on a predicted object outcome that is a response to the current robot plan, and its gradient is backpropagated through that response to improve the robot plan. The Causal factorization also lets us sample several object outcomes for a single robot plan, which is beneficial as pushing is multimodal [ 9 ] . Our main contributions are:

We formulate and evaluate multi-object placement by a mobile robot under tight spatial tolerances, requiring each object’s footprint to lie within its target region and previously completed placements to remain undisturbed. We assess how placement tolerance affects execution success across multiple environments.

We formulate and evaluate multi-object placement by a mobile robot under tight spatial tolerances, requiring each object’s footprint to lie within its target region and previously completed placements to remain undisturbed. We assess how placement tolerance affects execution success across multiple environments.

We propose a diffusion-based planner that uses a Causal factorization of trajectory denoising for non-prehensile pushing. With this, each robot denoising step is followed by an object step that is conditioned on the current clean robot estimate. We also propose a guidance formulation for this factorization, together with a set of differentiable cost terms tailored to mobile robot pushing.

In this work, our evaluation spans the Push-T task, three unseen mobile robot pushing environments, and a hardware deployment on a TurtleBot 3 Burger, with analysis of the planner’s capabilities and limitations.

Diffusion-based trajectory planners have been applied to both short and long-horizon tasks, both of which arise in NPM. At short horizons, the planner samples a trajectory, executes a portion of it, and then replans [ 1 , 3 ] . Long horizon settings instead tend to rely on trajectory stitching, where a full plan is composed from sub-trajectories already present in the training distribution [ 8 , 10 ] . Closest to our proposed factorization is MBA [ 11 ] , which also splits robot and object denoising into two phases. However, MBA fully denoises the object trajectory first and conditions the robot denoising on that finished prediction, whereas our phases alternate within each denoising step. Diffusion Forcing [ 12 ] also orders denoising, but through per-token noise levels rather than separate phases, resolving lower-noise tokens first. Unlike our method, most of these planners do not apply guidance at inference, which can limit their ability to adapt to task settings outside their training distribution at deployment.

Guidance is applied to diffusion models across many domains such as image generation [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , autonomous driving, and robotics. Diffuser [ 16 ] steers plans by nudging the denoising process along the gradient of a learned return predictor. However, the performance of this learned model on novel scenes is dependent on its training distribution. Diffusion-ES [ 17 ] skips gradient-based guidance entirely. Instead, it samples trajectories from an unconditional diffusion model, scores them with a reward function, and projects elites back onto the data manifold. This keeps the trajectory distribution broader and improves robustness, but the search across iterations is expensive. Diffusion Planner [ 18 ] is a transformer-based driving planner that relies on hand-designed energy functions at inference, eliminating the need for an auxiliary model. Our work builds upon this concept in two ways. First, we extend these energy functions to have asymmetric penalties for precision pushing tasks. Second, we add a per-term gradient rescaling that lets each term’s contribution be tuned independent of its native scale and units.

Diffusion-based trajectory planners have been applied to pushing in non-precision settings, beyond just Push-T. CompDiffuser [ 8 ] reports encouraging results on AntSoccer, where a quadruped agent pushes a ball to a goal location, and HeRD [ 7 ] demonstrates similar gains in a multi-object box environment. Precision has instead been pursued through reinforcement learning by [ 19 ] , who train a recurrent policy that pushes single objects to within 1 cm of the goal. To the best of our knowledge, no diffusion-based planner targets multi-object NPM with a mobile robot at tight tolerances.

2026-10-12.title: Robust and Scalable UAV-UGV Planning for Aerial Monitoring under Energy and Precedence Constraints
2026-10-12.authors: Cahit Ikbal Er , Yasin Yazicioglu
2026-10-12.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-12.abstract: We consider planning for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) and unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) teams in aerial monitoring missions with ordering requirements on the monitoring points to be visited by the UAV. The system consists of multiple UAV-UGV teams, each comprising one UAV and one UGV. UAV energy limitations are modeled through endurance, defined as the maximum flight time on a full battery. The UGVs serve as mobile charging stations and transport the UAVs between consecutive aerial tours. Given a set of monitoring points subject to ordering constraints and the teams’ initial and terminal positions, the objective is to minimize mission completion time while satisfying UAV energy limits and the required visit order under bounded travel-time disturbances that may arise during execution. Unlike prior work, the plan jointly determines vehicle routes and their timing, allowing teams to slow down as needed to satisfy the ordering constraints. We develop a polynomial-time algorithm that generates efficient solutions to the underlying NP-hard planning problem. We establish feasibility guarantees, characterize the algorithm’s computational complexity, and evaluate its performance via numerical comparisons.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are used in various domains such as agriculture and environmental monitoring (e.g., [ 1 , 2 ] ). However, their limited energy restricts missions defined over large areas or long time-horizons. Using unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) as mobile charging stations addresses this limitation by providing a flexible alternative to fixed recharging infrastructure.
Recently, energy-constrained planning of UAV-UGV teams has gained significant attention (e.g., [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] ). However, these methods generally assume that points of interest may be visited in any order.

In practice, aerial monitoring missions may require some locations to be visited before others. In multi-robot task allocation, such ordering requirements are formalized as cross-schedule dependencies [ 10 ] . Exact methods have addressed vehicle-routing problems with temporal synchronization [ 11 ] , while polynomial-time sequencers handle task allocation under temporal and spatial constraints [ 12 ] ; however, these approaches generally do not model vehicle energy. Similarly, [ 13 ] schedules cooperative tasks using greedy construction and local search, but focuses on task scheduling rather than energy-constrained spatial planning. More recently, [ 14 ] computes optimal precedence-constrained plans for heterogeneous UAV teams under energy limits, though its computational complexity grows significantly with team size and recharging relies on static infrastructure.

In this paper, we propose a heuristic algorithm for robust UAV-UGV planning in aerial monitoring missions with precedence constraints. The goal is to minimize the overall mission completion time while respecting the energy constraints and the required visit order under bounded travel-time disturbances. We formulate this planning problem as a mixed-integer program, which is NP-hard. Our main contribution is an efficient heuristic (Alg. 1 ) that jointly determines vehicle routes and their timing, with formal guarantees on feasibility and worst-case time complexity (Theorem 1 ). We validate our approach via numerical comparisons against branch-and-cut, simulated annealing, and a heuristic baseline that assigns all locations that are weakly connected by precedence constraints to the same team.

# II Problem Formulation

We consider an aerial monitoring mission executed by multiple UAV-UGV teams. The energy-constrained UAVs must visit a set of monitoring points, supported by the UGVs which serve as mobile charging stations and transport the UAVs between take-off and landing locations. Two features distinguish this formulation from prior work (e.g., [ 8 , 9 ] ). First, precedence requirements constrain the order in which the monitoring points may be visited. Second, the plan selects not only where the vehicles go but how long each leg takes, allowing a team to slow down if needed rather than reroute to satisfy these ordering constraints.

2026-10-12.title: PriMoRetarget: Humanoid Motion Transfer Through Prioritized Motion Retargeting
2026-10-12.authors: Nicholas Ioannidis , Dun Yang , Max Smith , Tue Vu , Ziyu Zhang , Shayegan Omidshafiei , Xue Bin Peng
2026-10-12.abstract:
Motion retargeting is a critical preprocessing step for transferring human motion data to humanoid robots.
While existing methods are effective for single-character motions, interactions involving multiple characters and objects introduce additional contacts and spatial relationships that must be preserved.
Retargeting is commonly formulated as a weighted multi-objective optimization problem, where conflicting objectives can require careful tuning of relative weights and can still compromise important motion characteristics.
We introduce PriMoRetarget , a prioritized motion-retargeting framework that replaces relative objective weighting with an explicit priority hierarchy.
Lower-priority updates are constrained to preserve higher-priority objectives, allowing critical characteristics such as foot placement and interaction contacts to take precedence over lower-priority pose objectives.
The method is evaluated on four datasets spanning single-character motion, character–object manipulation, and character–character interactions.
The resulting motions better preserve task-relevant interactions and provide reference trajectories that can be tracked more reliably than those produced by widely used retargeting methods.
2026-10-12.introduction:
For humanoid robots, human motion-capture data provides a rich source of reference behaviors despite morphological differences between humans and robots.
Motion retargeting bridges this embodiment gap by transferring motion across embodiments while preserving the defining characteristics of the source motion.
A long line of prior work has studied retargeting single-character motions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
However, motions involving interactions with objects or other characters remain substantially more challenging, as successful retargeting must preserve not only individual body poses but also the contacts, spatial relationships, and coordinated movements that define the interaction.
Errors in these relationships can produce physically infeasible reference motions and increase the burden on downstream learning and control.

Many commonly used retargeting methods formulate these requirements as a multi-objective optimization problem, where each objective captures a characteristic of the source motion to preserve in the target motion [ 1 , 4 , 2 , 5 ] .
Such objectives may include matching source keypoints, preserving foot placement and interaction contacts, and respecting the robot’s joint limits.
Jointly optimizing these objectives is nontrivial because they can conflict: improving pose fidelity, for example, may degrade contact preservation or foot placement.
These conflicts become increasingly pronounced as additional characters and objects introduce more contacts and spatial relationships that must be preserved.
To resolve these conflicts, retargeting methods typically rely on carefully tuned objective weights that reflect task- and morphology-specific priorities [ 1 , 4 , 2 , 5 ] .
However, weighted objectives encode only relative preferences: improving a lower-weighted objective may still come at the expense of a higher-weighted objective.
Consequently, these weights do not guarantee that desired priority relationships between objectives are preserved.
Achieving the desired priority relationships therefore often requires careful manual tuning of the objective weights.

Two broad classes of methods address conflicting objectives without weight tuning:
(1) prioritized optimization methods, which organize objectives into a hierarchy [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] , and
(2) gradient-surgery methods, which modify interfering gradients across objectives [ 10 , 11 ] .
Our approach draws on both, using an explicit priority hierarchy to specify which objectives should take precedence and gradient projection to enforce these priorities during optimization.

In this work, we propose PriMoRetarget , a prioritized motion-retargeting framework that replaces soft objective weighting with an explicit priority hierarchy.
Lower-priority updates are restricted to preserve higher-priority objectives, allowing critical requirements to take precedence over lower-priority preferences.
We show that our method is compatible with commonly used motion-retargeting objectives and apply our framework to four datasets spanning multi-character and object interactions. We evaluate the resulting motions using a range of kinematic metrics and assess their effectiveness as reference trajectories for training reinforcement learning (RL) policies.
Our method substantially reduces common retargeting artifacts that compromise physical feasibility, including foot sliding and contact errors. The code and retargeted motion data will be publicly released upon publication.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

Motion retargeting is commonly posed as a constrained optimization problem [ 1 ] , often formulated as inverse kinematics (IK) to reconstruct source-motion features such as joint positions, orientations, and end-effector locations [ 1 , 12 , 2 , 3 ] .
While most methods assume similar source and target morphologies, prior work has also considered retargeting across different body structures, such as retargeting from humanoids to quadrupeds [ 13 , 14 ] .

Humans rarely act in isolation; instead, human motions often involve interactions with objects, terrain, and other actors.
Retargeting such interaction-rich motions therefore requires preserving not only individual poses, but also the relationships that define these interactions.
Early work represented interactions through relative spatial geometry [ 4 ] , with subsequent methods applying similar representations to bipedal robots [ 15 ] , terrain and object interactions [ 5 ] , and multi-character interactions [ 16 , 17 ] .
Trajectory optimization and simulation have also been incorporated into retargeting pipelines to improve dynamic feasibility [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 3 ] , though these methods typically rely on IK-based retargeting methods to provide a kinematic reference trajectory.

Despite their differences in their representation and optimization procedure, many modern retargeting methods formulate motion retargeting as a weighted multi-objective optimization problem.
When different objectives conflict, their relative importance is specified through weights.
These trade-offs can be difficult to tune and may need to be adjusted for different motions and target morphologies.
Our work alleviates the need for manual weight tuning by organizing multiple objective functions into a prioritized hierarchy, allowing higher-priority physical requirements to take precedence over lower-priority preferences.

As an alternative to optimization-based methods, data-driven retargeting methods learn mappings between different morphologies directly from motion data, without requiring explicitly defined motion retargeting objectives [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] .
By learning representations that disentangle motion from embodiment, these methods can support retargeting across substantially different skeletal structures [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] .
Contact-aware methods further incorporate geometric and contact information to improve the physical consistency of the retargeted motion [ 27 , 28 ] .

While data-driven retargeting can be effective, these methods are generally constrained by the motions and morphologies represented in their training data and may struggle to generalize beyond this distribution.
In contrast, optimization-based methods do not require motion- or morphology-specific training data and can therefore be applied more broadly across behaviors and embodiments.
As a result, optimization-based retargeting has thus far seen wider practical adoption than its data-driven counterparts.

Balancing competing objectives is a central challenge in multi-objective optimization.
Adaptive reweighting methods adjust loss weights during optimization [ 29 , 30 ] , while CAGrad accounts for worst-case objective performance [ 11 ] .
Gradient-surgery methods such as PCGrad [ 10 ] instead modify gradients to reduce interference.
However, these methods generally do not enforce an ordering of importance.
In motion retargeting, some objectives may require strict precedence; for example, preserving a foot contact may be high-priority than matching upper-body pose.
Prioritized optimization encodes such precedence through an explicit objective hierarchy.

Prioritized optimization has been widely used in robotics to exploit kinematic redundancy.
Higher-priority objectives often admit multiple solutions, leaving residual degrees of freedom available for lower-priority objectives.
Task-priority methods exploit this redundancy by restricting lower-priority optimization to solutions that preserve higher-priority objectives [ 31 , 6 , 7 ] .
This principle has been applied to IK for articulated characters [ 32 ] and whole-body humanoid control [ 33 , 9 , 34 , 8 , 35 ] .
Prior work has primarily considered online control and model-predictive settings.
In contrast, we show that prioritized optimization is also effective for motion retargeting and introduce techniques that enable its efficient application to long motion sequences, multiple interacting characters, and general non-quadratic retargeting objectives.

2026-10-12.title: Distributed Harmonic-Covariance Feedback for Hole Closure in Planar Robot Swarms
2026-10-12.authors: Jitian Liu , Subhrajit Bhattacharya
2026-10-12.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-12.abstract: We consider hole closure in a planar multi-agent system whose sensing disks form a time-varying Čech complex. We propose a harmonic-covariance feedback that uses harmonic edge signals to locate holes and converts those signals into agent forces. For distributed evaluation, we use a fixed-degree polynomial of the regularized Hodge Laplacian. This polynomial is evaluated through local operator applications. The closed loop has a unique global trajectory from every safe initial state. The model data and initial state are supplied with procedures for approximation to any requested accuracy with explicit error bounds. We assume that hole area is measurable and bounded, holes evolve continuously without splitting or merging, and only finitely many temporary new holes appear. Under these conditions, offline finite calculations produce rational lower bounds for the cumulative hole area on the time horizon without querying trajectory data. These bounds converge to that cumulative area, whether finite or infinite. If it is finite, holes close in the time-averaged sense: the average normalized hole area over every fixed-length time window tends to zero as time tends to infinity. In a 15-second numerical demo, all holes close by 9.9s and remain closed through the end.
2026-10-12.introduction:
In nature, among groups of animals such as bird flocks and fish schools, local interaction
rules can generate collective motions [ 1 , 2 ] . The same principle motivates
groups of mobile robots known as swarms . For multi-robot systems,
sensor coverage is a basic problem: each robot senses
a disk around its position, and together the robots should cover their
operating region. As the robots move, the covered set can develop holes: regions enclosed by the
sensing disks that receive no coverage at all. These holes are exactly the holes of the Čech complex built from the
current robot positions [ 3 , 4 ] .
The holes of a
moving cover are detected by persistent homology [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] and verified without localization or with switched higher-order
Laplacians [ 6 , 7 ] .

Related work on repair and coverage includes simplicial coverage repair for robot teams [ 8 ] , gradient descent on weighted
combinatorial Laplacians [ 9 ] , homology-based
repair of agricultural coverage [ 10 ] , conformal
mapping of domains with holes onto multi-hole disks [ 11 ] ,
and diffusive coverage of bounded domains [ 12 ] . Related tools include cellular sheaves, which generalize weighted
Laplacians for distributed coordination [ 13 , 14 ] ; simplicial filters for
processing on complexes [ 15 , 16 ] ; and
occupation-measure relaxations, which express dynamical constraints
and integral costs through measures and lead to linear optimization
problems over measures [ 17 , 18 ] .
The coverage-repair methods above do not provide a criterion for hole
closure based solely on the model and initial state. We derive such a
criterion for our distributed harmonic-covariance controller.
The contributions of this paper are as follows:

A feedback controller that converts the swarm Čech complex’s harmonic edge flows, which localize the holes, into locally Lipschitz force laws on the agents (such that the controlled trajectory is unique), together with a distributed realization of the controller (Sections III and IV ).

Under this paper’s controlled dynamics and assumptions, we construct an offline sequence of rational lower bounds { c T } T \{c_{T}\}_{T} . Each bound is produced by explicit finite calculations without querying trajectory data. The sequence converges to the cumulative hole area over the infinite time horizon. If its limit is finite, the hole area averaged over any fixed time window tends to zero as the window moves forward (Section IV ).

A numerical demo in which two holes close within 10 seconds under the regularized harmonic feedback controller (Section V ).

The paper is organized as follows. Section II sets up the task and model. Section III designs the controller and its distributed realization. Section IV proves uniqueness of the state space trajectory under the regularized controller, and constructs { c T } T \{c_{T}\}_{T} from the swarm’s initial state. Section V reports the numerical simulation. Appendix A records details to approximate the normalized hole areas in the swarm and the vector field yielded by the control law, whereas Appendix B supplies proofs to main theoretical results in this paper.

2026-10-12.title: Selectively Actuated Fiberbots for High-precision Minimally Invasive Surgery
2026-10-12.authors: Jinshi Zhao , Libaihe Tian , Alex Ranne , Qindong Zheng , Yue Li , Xiaotong Guo , Ziqi Yang , Ali Anil Demircali , Mohamed E. M. K. Abdelaziz , Bruno Gil Rosa , Ferdinando Rodriguez y Baena , Burak Temelkuran
2026-10-12.abstract: Long, slender instruments are essential for minimally invasive surgery (MIS), but achieving precise distal manipulation becomes increasingly difficult when actuation extends along the entire instrument. Here, we present an electrothermally actuated fiber-based robot designed for MIS procedures, in which Joule heating is concentrated in the distal active segment. The fiber is fabricated using a thermal drawing process and uses embedded metallic wires for thermal actuation. This robotic fiber, 1.9 mm in diameter and 1.2 m in length, can precisely manipulate surgical laser fibers with positional precision below 100 μ \mu m. The compact size of the fiber robot allows it to pass through the working channel of a flexible endoscope, while keeping both devices mechanically uncoupled to allow independent motion. A phantom demonstration combining the robotic fiber with a da Vinci instrument conceptually demonstrated its compatibility with existing endoscopic systems for clinical applications. Our robotic fiber enables precise distal motion and holds the potential to improve clinical outcomes by enhancing precision in MIS procedures.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Minimally invasive surgery (MIS) has reduced the need for large surgical incisions by enabling diagnostic and therapeutic procedures through small access ports or natural anatomical pathways. Laparoscopic, endoscopic, and catheter-based procedures have consequently expanded the range of lesions that can be reached with reduced damage to surrounding tissues. Robotic technologies can further enhance these procedures by improving instrument dexterity, motion precision, and operator control within confined anatomical environments [ 1 , 2 ] .

Many minimally invasive procedures require long and slender instruments to pass through access ports, flexible endoscopes, or tortuous anatomical pathways before reaching the target site. Although this geometry facilitates access to deep anatomical regions, it makes precise distal manipulation challenging. Conventional instruments are commonly controlled from their proximal ends, and their distal response can be affected by shaft deformation, friction, backlash, and interactions with the surrounding anatomy or the working channel of an endoscope. These effects become more pronounced as the instrument length and pathway complexity increase, limiting the ability to position or scan a small distal end-effector accurately. Miniaturized continuum and soft robotic instruments offer a promising means of introducing active steering and fine manipulation at the surgical site while retaining the flexibility required for minimally invasive access [ 3 ] .

In this paper, we present the next generation of electrothermally actuated fiber robots (Fiberbots). These robots take the form of a long (1.2 m in length) and slender (1.9 mm in diameter) catheter, with an electrothermally actuated tip capable of achieving sub-millimeter precision motion. A selective actuation mechanism was developed by localizing the high-resistance heating element to the distal active section. The fiberbot avoids dissipating substantial electrical power along mechanically passive portions of the shaft. Fiberbots are designed to fit through the working channels of off-the-shelf endoscopes, enabling seamless integration into an operating theater. In Sect. II , we begin by investigating common existing designs for laparoscopic robots used in MIS surgery, while highlighting their limitations that need to be addressed. Then in Sect. III , we present a new fiberbot design, highlighting its novelty in selective actuation. Using thermal fiber drawing technology, a bespoke polymer multi-lumen fiber was fabricated. This technique provides the capabilities to rapidly prototype devices with complex cross-sectional designs, while mitigating the difficulties faced by conventional extrusion or molding techniques. This section is followed by a summary of circuit assembly. Finally, in Sect. IV , we performed motion characterization to evaluate the fiberbot’s precision, repeatability, and reachable workspace. We also conducted temperature characterization to examine the temperature profile under different current levels and validate the efficiency and clinical viability of the selective actuation mechanism. To demonstrate system-level feasibility, we integrated the fiberbot with a da Vinci surgical instrument and used it to perform a moving task in an endoluminal phantom. The proposed selective-actuation architecture addresses a fundamental scaling limitation of electrothermally actuated fiberbots [ 4 ] . By localizing the high-resistance heating element to the distal active section, the fiberbot avoids dissipating substantial electrical power along mechanically passive portions of the shaft, thereby improving its suitability for high-precision minimally invasive surgery.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II RELATED WORKS

## II-A Manipulators for Minimally Invasive Surgery

Miniaturized manipulators for endoscopic and catheter-based interventions can be broadly distinguished by the location and type of their actuators. Tendon-driven systems use proximally located motors to transmit forces through cables along the instrument body. These systems have achieved substantial clinical maturity, but their distal response can be affected by tendon friction, wire slack, backlash, and hysteresis [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Concentric-tube robots generate three-dimensional motion by translating and rotating nested precurved tubes. Although they provide a compact structure, their behavior depends on tube interactions and elastic stability, and abrupt configuration changes can occur under certain designs and loading conditions [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] .

Magnetically actuated catheters place a magnetic component at the catheter body and generate steering forces using an externally applied magnetic field [ 14 , 15 ] . This approach removes mechanical transmission elements from the catheter body but requires dedicated magnetic-field-generation infrastructure.
Fluidic-driven catheters achieve bending by pressurizing internal chambers, which deforms the robot’s compliant structure [ 16 ] . These catheters can achieve large bending angles, although fabrication and control become increasingly challenging as channel dimensions decrease [ 17 , 18 ] . Shape-memory actuators operate through a temperature-induced phase transformation: heating drives the material toward its memorized shape, while cooling allows it to recover [ 19 ] . Although they offer a high force-to-volume ratio and compact construction, their nonlinear, temperature-dependent, and hysteretic behavior can complicate accurate open-loop positioning [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] .

## II-B Thermally Drawn Robotic Fibers

Thermal drawing enables the continuous fabrication of polymer fibers containing internal channels and embedded functional materials [ 23 ] . While it was originally introduced in the telecommunications industry to create silica-based optical fibers, researchers have recently adapted this method for prototyping medical devices [ 24 ] .

A previous study [ 4 ] developed a fiberbot for laparoscopic use by powering the entire 40 cm fiber length to generate precise motion at the distal tip, demonstrated in an in vivo porcine model. However, in that work, only the distal 12 cm contributed to motion, while the remaining length was clamped within a rigid tube to prevent unintended movement. This approach resulted in powering the entire length of the instrument. Here, we present an improved iteration of the system, consisting of a new device design that enables selective actuation by actuating a targeted length at the tip of the fiber rather than the entire device. This approach is more suitable for MIS applications that require long instruments, reducing the power required for actuation and Joule heating on the overall device.

2026-10-12.title: Image-Based Path-Planning for Navigation of Soft-Growing Robots in the Spinal Sub-Arachnoid Space
2026-10-12.authors: George Dimas , Panagiotis G. Kalozoumis , Panagiotis Vartholomeos , Dimitris K. Iakovidis
2026-10-12.abstract: Recently, soft robotic procedures are being developed aiming at achieving targeted minimally invasive operations or drug administration in specific locations in the human body. Accordingly, specialized path-planning algorithms need to be investigated for the estimation of efficient paths that would protect the delicate tissue structures and simultaneously satisfy a set of requirements for the efficient navigation of the robot. In this context, we propose an image-based 3D pathplanning algorithm, which is an extension of the A* algorithm, for the navigation of a soft-growing robot inside the spinal subarachnoid space (SSS). The proposed algorithm is capable of estimating a safe pathway towards the goal location, while ensuring the establishment of anchor points that facilitate the efficient steering of the soft robot. The algorithm is evaluated using a highly detailed model of the SSS with respect to its capacity to satisfy the robot movement requirements and path efficiency.

2026-10-12.title: Graph-Based Heuristics for Minimum Constraint Removal in Cluttered Robot Motion Planning
2026-10-12.authors: Antony Thomas , Fulvio Mastrogiovanni , Marco Baglietto
2026-10-12.abstract: Humanoid and service robots operating in clut- tered human environments may encounter motion planning problems that are infeasible when all surrounding objects are treated as fixed obstacles. The Minimum Constraint Removal problem, which we refer to as MCR, addresses this situation by identifying the minimum number of constraints, such as movable objects, whose removal enables a collision-free path. However, computing an optimal MCR solution is NP-hard. In this work, we propose a graph-based heuristic pipeline that combines bidirectional feasible-set generation with fixed- length searches over reduced MCR graphs. We further derive an extended feasible-set generator for instances in which the candidates produced by the first generator do not contain a complete optimal removal set. Across six benchmarks, the evaluated pipeline matches the exact solution in three cases and, in the remaining cases, selects at most 31.25% more obstacles than the optimum, while being between 3.4 and 33.7 times faster than exact search. In one of the benchmarks, involving a manipulation task amidst clutter, selecting two rather than seven obstructing objects reduces the combined MCR, inverse- kinematics, and motion planning time from 84.72 s to 30.59 s. These results indicate that the proposed approach provides a practical compromise between computational efficiency and solution quality for motion planning among movable obstacles.

2026-10-12.title: CASTER: Formalizing Zero-Shot Manipulation from Synthetic Videos as Constrained Optimization
2026-10-12.authors: Yinlong Dai , Homanga Bharadhwaj , Dylan P. Losey
2026-10-12.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-12.abstract:
Prior research on learning from humans often requires real human demonstrations.
But advances in video generation models offer a new paradigm: we can now prompt these generators to make synthetic videos of the task.
On the plus side, these synthetic videos take place in the robot’s current environment, and do not require actual human teaching.
However, while the generated videos appear to show plausible motions, they lack both physical consistency and robot grounding, and thus the robot cannot directly roll out the trajectory shown by the video.
In this paper we seek to formalize the process of going from synthetic video generation to real-world robot trajectories for zero-shot manipulation tasks.
We recognize that this problem is an instance of constrained optimization .
The object trajectories extracted from the synthetic video provide an initial guess at the correct motion, and the robot must refine these trajectories (for instance, within a digital twin) while enforcing physical feasibility and semantic consistency.
Our optimization-based formalism provides insights into the video generation properties necessary for success.
Specifically, we show that the video generation must probabilistically seed the search within a semantic basin of attraction where the trajectory can be locally modified without losing its task alignment.
Our analysis further reveals that state-of-the-art approaches can be viewed as instances of our unified formalism with key simplifications.
In our experiments we remove these simplifications to more closely match the underlying optimization, leading to more robust zero-shot trajectories from synthetic videos and improving average task success by 34.1% compared to the best-performing baseline.
See videos at our project website: https://collab.me.vt.edu/CASTER
2026-10-12.introduction:
Collecting robot-centric data is expensive [ 1 , 2 ] .
Videos of humans completing tasks are widely available, but these in-the-wild videos are often unstructured, and occur in settings that are unlike the robot’s context.
Video generation techniques can help bridge this gap.
By prompting video generators to create synthetic videos, we gather “human” data without actually requiring human demonstrations — plus, the resulting videos are set in the robot’s current environment.

Consider the example in Figure 1 .
The user prompts the system with a desired task.
Given this prompt and an initial image, recent video generation models can output a synthetic video of the task being performed by a human.
Ideally, the robot would be able to directly apply this video to guide its own motion. But there are two key limitations. First, while the synthetic video may appear visually plausible, it is not necessarily physically feasible.
Second, the generated video features a human doing the task, introducing kinematic and visual discrepancies between what the video shows and what the robot arm can actually do.

Our work focuses specifically on using pretrained video generation models at inference time to guide robot behavior.
That is, rather than using generated videos as offline data for policy training or fine-tuning a video generator on robot-specific data, we consider a setting where a general-purpose, frozen video generator produces task demonstrations during deployment.
Existing research searches for ways to address the above problems and unlock the promise of video generation models in this setting.
Common approaches typically fall along a spectrum in how much they post-process the video data.
At one extreme, the system simply learns to project the object’s motion in the synthetic video to real-world robot trajectories [ 3 ] .
At the other extreme, robots construct a digital twin to physically test and refine the proposed video behavior before applying the results in the real world [ 4 ] .
We view these methods as effective ad hoc solutions, but it remains unclear how to define the underlying problem .
For example: what should the robot optimize for when trying to map the synthetic video to real-world task performance?
And what characteristics does the video generation model need to have in order for this zero-shot transfer to be possible?

In this paper we seek to formalize the process of converting synthetic videos to real-world robot trajectories for zero-shot manipulation tasks.
Our key insight is that:

Formalizing this optimization provides three fundamental benefits.
First, we can unify existing approaches as instances of our optimization problem under different simplifying assumptions.
Second, we can use the optimization structure to define the characteristics of the video generation that are necessary for success.
Finally, we can develop new methods for zero-shot manipulation using video generation models by more closely approximating the underlying problem.
Overall, we make the following contributions:

Defining a Unified Formalism. We define a constrained optimization problem that inputs synthetic task videos and outputs trajectories for real-world execution.
This optimization must satisfy physical feasibility (i.e., the motion must be executable without accidental collisions) and semantic consistency (i.e., the motion must be aligned with the task).

Characterizing Video Generation. Building on our theoretical framework, we derive the properties and requirements for the video generation model.
We show that simultaneously enforcing feasibility and semantic constraints depends on generating videos that can be locally modified without losing their semantic meaning.
Intuitively, tasks with a larger basin of attraction around feasible motions (i.e., many initial guesses converge towards the same equilibrium) are more suitable for synthetic video frameworks.

Developing Approximate Solutions. We demonstrate that state-of-the-art approaches can be viewed as instances of our unified framework.
We then derive a new approach that more closely matches the underlying optimization problem by weighting trajectory features instead of matching every waypoint.
Our experiments show the pros and cons of these different solution methods.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

Robot Video Generation for Manipulation. Recent works have explored generating videos of robots performing tasks for learning manipulation policies and planning robot actions [ 5 ] .
Generating the robot directly reduces the differences in embodiment between the video demonstration and robot execution [ 6 ] .
UniPi [ 7 ] fine-tunes a pretrained video generator on robot data to predict language-conditioned visual plans, and uses an inverse-dynamics model to recover robot actions.
Video Policy [ 8 ] combines video and action diffusion, conditioning the action network on intermediate video features at each denoising step. VAG [ 9 ] jointly generates aligned video-action pairs, which can be used as synthetic training data or for learning world-action models.

Other works use generated robot videos to augment the data available for policy learning [ 10 , 11 ] .
DreamGen [ 12 ] generates synthetic trajectories and recovers pseudo-action labels for training robot policies.
Ctrl-World [ 13 ] predicts action-conditioned, multi-view robot rollouts and uses successful trajectories to fine-tune policies.
GE-Sim 2.0 [ 14 ] additionally predicts proprioceptive states and filters generated experience with a learned judge.
For humanoid manipulation, GenHOI [ 15 ] recovers contact-aware geometric constraints from generated interaction videos and optimizes trajectories for execution without task-specific policy training.

However, generating consistent robot videos zero-shot remains challenging for general-purpose video models, as robot behavior is sparsely represented in their training data. These models are trained on large amounts of human video and are better suited to generating human demonstrations in new scenes without fine-tuning [ 16 ] .
We therefore use human video generation to predict how a task can be performed, and translate the generated motion into robot actions.

Human Video Generation for Manipulation. Generated human videos can describe tasks across diverse objects and scenes, but do not directly specify executable robot actions.
Prior works extract motion from these videos for trajectory optimization or policy learning [ 17 ] , including approaches that generate object motion without a visible human.

One line of work recovers trajectories or keyframes and translates them into robot actions through retargeting or trajectory optimization [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] .
Dreamitate [ 23 ] tracks tool motion, while RiGVid [ 3 ] recovers object poses; both use these trajectories to determine robot end-effector motion.
NovaFlow [ 24 ] recovers 3D object flow, and NovaPlan [ 25 ] uses object and hand motion with closed-loop replanning.
RoboReact [ 26 ] reconstructs interaction keyframes, retargets them to the robot, and refines execution using feedback.

Other works learn policies that use generated videos or recovered motion [ 27 ] . Gen2Act [ 16 ] trains a closed-loop policy conditioned on generated human videos to perform tasks specified through video generation at deployment.
GenMimic [ 28 ] trains a physics-aware reinforcement learning policy to track recovered human motion.
Dream2Flow [ 29 ] reconstructs 3D object flow and uses a tracking objective for either trajectory optimization or reinforcement learning.
PhysWorld [ 4 ] uses reinforcement learning in a digital twin to obtain executable robot actions that track generated object motions.
We seek a generalized formulation that lets us study these prior approaches within a common framework, analyze when generated motion can successfully transfer to a robot, and explicitly bridge semantic intent and physical feasibility.

2026-10-12.title: What Should Embodied Agents Remember? Benchmarking and Evaluating Memory Modality for Embodied Agents
2026-10-12.authors: Junxiang Wang , Yuchen Liu , Yi Wu , Guofei Chen , Nir Pechuk , Tao Chen , Zackory Erickson , Yuzhe Qin , Tianyu Li
2026-10-12.abstract: Memory allows large language model (LLM) agents to use past experience, often stored as textual records, when responding to requests. For embodied agents that control robots, visual and spatial observations introduce a broader choice of memory modalities, affecting both the information available for subsequent tasks and the model inference costs of constructing and using memory. We introduce MeMoREval, a benchmark for studying this problem through a controlled experience-request protocol. Agents first experience a sequence of events without knowing the subsequent tasks, and subsequently they use memory to respond to information and action requests without receiving new observations. The benchmark comprises 53 tasks across four simulated indoor environments and measures task success alongside the inference costs of memory construction and use. Our reference evaluations reveal that storing frames outperforms storing generated descriptions at lower write-time inference cost for the primary model, while storing frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success for every tested model. Extensions to accumulated experience, selective frame retention, and visual input to memory writers demonstrate how the benchmark accommodates further memory-design investigations. Two physical-robot demonstrations establish the feasibility of applying its protocol beyond simulation.
2026-10-12.introduction:
A coding agent investigating a bug may uncover facts about a codebase that remain useful long after the immediate fix. Memory systems preserve such findings beyond the model’s current context ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Packer et al., 2023 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . For large language model (LLM) agents that control robots, what is worth preserving extends to camera frames, object locations, and whether physical actions succeeded. This experience can be retained as textual descriptions, raw images, structured spatial records, or combinations of these forms, and the choice affects both what survives and what memory costs.

A textual record might note that several mugs were on a counter while omitting the colors needed to later retrieve a particular mug. Generating a description requires selecting what to mention before the future task is known, and task-relevant details may be discarded. A stored camera frame retains visual details for interpretation once the task is known, while a structured spatial record makes object locations and relations directly available.

Decisions to remember certain information are particularly important for embodied agents because recovering forgotten information can require considerable physical action. A coding agent can often rediscover a fact by inspecting an available codebase again or inspecting an earlier version of the codebase, which incurs additional computation and latency, but the memory lapse is largely invisible to the user. For a robot, recovering missing information may require navigating between rooms, opening containers, or manipulating objects. Such recovery makes memory failures apparent through repeated searches and unnecessary physical actions, delaying task completion. Moreover, changes to the environment can make forgotten information irrecoverable: once objects have been moved or removed, their earlier spatial relationships may no longer be observable.

To study which forms of retained evidence best support subsequent recall and action, we introduce MeMoREval, a controlled Eval uation protocol and benchmark for studying Me mory Mo dalities of R obotic embodied agents. We distinguish the memory modality , which determines the form of retained evidence, from the memory backend , which organizes that evidence and makes it available to the agent. Our study addresses three questions: ( RQ1 ) How do memory modalities affect success on information and action requests across task categories and models? ( RQ2 ) How do these modalities trade off task success against write-time and read-time inference cost? ( RQ3 ) How can MeMoREval inform memory-design decisions for deploying embodied agents?

Our evaluation protocol constructs each task from two phases. In the experience phase, the robot follows a scripted sequence of events while the memory module records its observations. In the request phase, the agent starts from a fresh context and uses memory to answer information requests and plan action requests, as a robot would when a user poses a request. Plans are executed without returning new observations, so the agent cannot compensate for missing memory by searching again, which would reward exploration ability rather than memory. Experience phases can also be stacked to evaluate memory over longer histories.

We instantiate this protocol in 53 simulated tasks across four simulated indoor environments and seven categories of remembered information. MeMoREval supports textual records, generated image descriptions, camera frames, scene graphs, and their combinations. Using common recorded observations and a fixed agent implementation, we compare different memory configurations on task success as well as model inference costs, as both write-time and read-time costs are candidates to be optimized in embodied agent design.

Our reference evaluations show that storing camera frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success for every tested model. For the primary model, archiving frames achieves higher success and lower write-time inference cost than generating descriptions, while also yielding the lowest read-time inference cost per successful request. The benefits of individual modalities vary across models and task categories, demonstrating the value of evaluating representations together with the models that use them.

We further examine deployment-oriented variants that accumulate experience across tasks, let writers select which frames to retain, or provide images to writers during memory construction. These variants preserve the benchmark’s evaluation structure while extending the design choices under study. The resulting differences in task success, retention rates, and inference costs illustrate how MeMoREval can support investigations of memory organization, evidence selection, and writer inputs. Two demonstrations on a physical robot further establish that the protocol and memory interfaces can be instantiated using camera observations and an annotated spatial map.

We situate the memory-modality question within prior work on LLM and embodied agents and their evaluation (§ 2 ), then establish the agent model and memory terminology needed to study it (§ 3 ). We then introduce the design of our evaluation protocol and its instantiation in MeMoREval (§ 4 ). Our experiments address the three research questions and demonstrate the protocol on a physical robot (§ 5 ).

Our contributions are:

A controlled memory evaluation protocol for embodied agents that separates experience from subsequent information and action requests, supports accumulated histories, and measures write-time and read-time inference costs.

MeMoREval, a benchmark of 53 tasks across four simulated environments, with configurable memory modalities and backends and complementary demonstrations on a physical robot.

Reference evaluations across memory modalities, models, and backends that characterize trade-offs between task success and inference cost and identify opportunities for improving evidence retention and access in deployed embodied agents.

1. A controlled memory evaluation protocol for embodied agents that separates experience from subsequent information and action requests, supports accumulated histories, and measures write-time and read-time inference costs.

2. MeMoREval, a benchmark of 53 tasks across four simulated environments, with configurable memory modalities and backends and complementary demonstrations on a physical robot.

3. Reference evaluations across memory modalities, models, and backends that characterize trade-offs between task success and inference cost and identify opportunities for improving evidence retention and access in deployed embodied agents.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Agent memory systems organize retained experience in different ways: MemGPT pages information between the context window and an external archive ( Packer et al., 2023 ) , Mem0 extracts and updates facts ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ) , A-MEM links evolving notes ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , Reflexion and Agent Workflow Memory distill feedback and reusable procedures ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) , and filesystem memories let agents read and reorganize files through generic file tools ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) . Benchmarks such as LoCoMo and LongMemEval chiefly test recall across long conversations ( Maharana et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) , while MemLens and MemEye evaluate whether memory systems preserve visual evidence across extended multimodal interactions ( Ren et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . We study the corresponding design choice for embodied agents, comparing memory modalities with the agent and observations held fixed and repeating the comparison across memory backends.

Object-centric scene graphs are widely used for robot mapping and planning ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) , so we include them as one storage modality alongside text, generated descriptions, and frames. Other systems combine scene graphs with images ( Saxena et al., 2025 ) or record changing state through text and spatio-temporal relations ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Gorlo et al., 2026a ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . Retrieval and indexing methods improve the efficiency and accuracy of multimodal memory ( Anwar et al., 2025 ; Long et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) and are complementary to the choice of what to store. Surprise-gated memory addresses which observations to preserve ( Gorlo et al., 2026b ) ; we examine this selection question by comparing writer-selected image retention with archiving every frame.

Household benchmarks test long-horizon embodied interaction ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , but memory failures there are confounded with exploration, planning, and manipulation ability. Memory-focused evaluations test question answering ( Majumdar et al., 2024 ; Ginting et al., 2025 ) , memory-dependent action ( Yadav et al., 2025 ; Kwon et al., 2026 ) , or both ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , typically by comparing complete memory systems or agents. When the stored modality does vary, other factors vary with it: in OpenEQA, for example, caption- and scene-graph-based agents use a language model, whereas frame-based agents use a vision-language model ( Majumdar et al., 2024 ) . We design our protocol so that the stored modality is the main variable. Within each backend, the main memory conditions share the same recorded observations, agent, and writer input, and descriptions and frames are archived without passing through the writer. Requests start from a fresh context without new observations, so missing memory cannot be recovered by searching again. No-memory and full-information controls bound performance, information and action requests separate recalling a fact from acting on it, and write-time and read-time inference costs are measured separately.

2026-10-12.title: PanTact: Teaching Whole-Body Dexterity with a Wearable Contact Interface
2026-10-12.authors: Xiaomeng Xu , Han Zhang , Zhian Ruan , Xiaofeng Guo , Jinkun Cao , Ruihan Yang , Carmelo Sferrazza , Shuran Song , Guanya Shi
2026-10-12.abstract:
Humanoid robots have many degrees of freedom and contact surfaces, yet most loco-manipulation research restricts manipulation to the hands and avoids other body contacts with the environment.
To extend manipulation beyond the hands, we present PanTact 1 1 1 The name PanTact combines pan- (all) with tact- (contact, tactile), reflecting a humanoid that manipulates with any body surface. , a system that learns humanoid whole-body dexterity , the capability to manipulate with any suitable body surface, directly from robot-free human demonstrations. Our key idea is to use contact as manipulation-centric information that transfers across embodiments. Contact locations and timing specify the interactions needed to accomplish a task, while the robot chooses how to coordinate its body to realize them within its own physical constraints. Specifically, PanTact captures, learns, and executes whole-body contact via: 1) a wearable, robot-free data collection interface that augments egocentric vision and bimanual UMI grippers with whole-body modular contact patches to record body contact locations and states; 2) a visuomotor policy that mitigates the egocentric observation gap and predicts whole-body contact goals; and 3) contact-aware whole-body control formulations that realize active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces. We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without additional body contact sensors, demonstrating whole-body dexterity involving body support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing.
Website: https://pantact.github.io .
2026-10-12.introduction:
When humans interact with the physical world, we use more than just our hands: our arms and torso embrace bulky objects, our forearms sweep multiple items or brace against surfaces, and our knees push objects when our hands are full.
We call this capability whole-body dexterity ( Xu et al., 2025a ) : the ability to accomplish manipulation tasks using any suitable surface of the body.
Humanoid robots share the human body’s overall morphology, with dozens of actuated degrees of freedom and potential contact surfaces distributed across the body. Yet much of loco-manipulation research limits manipulation to the hands, reserving the rest of the body for locomotion and balance and typically avoiding other body contact with the environment. This leaves much of the humanoid body’s potential for manipulation unused.

Realizing this potential requires coordinating whole-body motion with contact sequences across body surfaces.
Human demonstrations provide natural examples of this coordination. We therefore ask: how can a humanoid learn whole-body dexterity directly from human demonstrations?

Advances in imitation learning and demonstration interfaces ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) have made learning manipulation from humans increasingly scalable.
However, these pipelines capture and imitate either end-effector (EEF) or joint trajectories,
and do not explicitly carry body-contact information from demonstration through policy prediction to robot execution. Extending these pipelines to whole-body dexterity introduces three connected challenges:

Capturing body contact in human demonstrations. Existing interfaces record only EEF motions or joint angles and do not directly measure where and when body contact occurs.

Preserving contact in human-to-robot policy transfer. EEF targets leave body contacts unspecified, while retargeting whole-body joints can alter contact locations because humans and robots differ in shape and proportions.

Executing contact with whole-body control. Controllers designed to track motion references or EEF targets lack an explicit objective for achieving contact goals on the body.
They must incorporate contact goals while maintaining motion tracking and balance.

To address the above challenges, our key observation is that contact provides manipulation-centric information
that can be separated from embodiment-specific motion. Contact location and timing describe the task-level physical interaction, whereas the body surface and joint configuration used to produce it depend on the robot embodiment.
Contact also identifies which parts of the demonstrated body motion need to be preserved during transfer, allowing the robot to learn task-critical contacts without necessarily matching free-space body motions.
We therefore use contact as a cross-embodiment interface : measuring contacts on the human, predicting their desired states and locations with the policy, and tracking active contact goals with the controller.
Tracking only active contact goals without assigning them to particular robot links allows the controller to choose a body configuration suited to the robot to make contacts and maintain balance.

We present PanTact, a system that learns whole-body dexterity from robot-free human demonstrations and deploys it on an off-the-shelf humanoid through three components:

Contact-complete, robot-free data collection system. We augment egocentric sensing and bimanual UMI grippers with modular contact patches , reconfigurable force-sensing tiles covering the demonstrator’s forearms and knees that provide contact timing, intensity and location.

Contact-predictive whole-body manipulation policy. The policy observes embodiment agnostic observations with body portions geometrically masked out from the egocentric view, and jointly predicts EEF trajectories and per-sensor contact goals, each specifying a contact state and position.

Contact-aware whole-body controller. We propose three formulations to achieve active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces under physical constraints: upper-body contact-aware IK, whole-body IK executed by a dense tracker, and direct sparse contact tracking.

We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without adding body contact sensors. Our tasks combine grasping and body support to move differently sized objects simultaneously, sweeping objects with arm surfaces, using the legs for non-prehensile manipulation and locomotion at the same time, and sequentially switching contact across different body parts. Result videos are best viewed on https://pantact.github.io .

1. Capturing body contact in human demonstrations. Existing interfaces record only EEF motions or joint angles and do not directly measure where and when body contact occurs.

2. Preserving contact in human-to-robot policy transfer. EEF targets leave body contacts unspecified, while retargeting whole-body joints can alter contact locations because humans and robots differ in shape and proportions.

3. Executing contact with whole-body control. Controllers designed to track motion references or EEF targets lack an explicit objective for achieving contact goals on the body.
They must incorporate contact goals while maintaining motion tracking and balance.

1. Contact-complete, robot-free data collection system. We augment egocentric sensing and bimanual UMI grippers with modular contact patches , reconfigurable force-sensing tiles covering the demonstrator’s forearms and knees that provide contact timing, intensity and location.

2. Contact-predictive whole-body manipulation policy. The policy observes embodiment agnostic observations with body portions geometrically masked out from the egocentric view, and jointly predicts EEF trajectories and per-sensor contact goals, each specifying a contact state and position.

3. Contact-aware whole-body controller. We propose three formulations to achieve active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces under physical constraints: upper-body contact-aware IK, whole-body IK executed by a dense tracker, and direct sparse contact tracking.

# 2 Related Work

Whole-body sensing for robots. Distributed range, force, tactile, and vision sensing has been used for collision avoidance, contact detection, and compliant whole-body interactions. Examples include range sensing for safe navigation and interaction ( Tanaka et al., 2015 ; Qi et al., 2022 ) , force and pressure sensing for compliant contact ( Kollmitz et al., 2018 ; Goncalves et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2025b ) , tactile sensing for contact feedback ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Dean-Leon et al., 2019 ; Jiang and Wong, 2024 ; Murooka et al., 2025 ; Jang et al., 2026 ) , and whole-body vision on serial and soft growing robots ( Xu et al., 2025a ; Qin et al., 2026 ) .
These systems primarily integrate whole-body sensing into the robot and acquire demonstrations through teleoperation. PanTact incorporates whole-body tactile sensing into a wearable interface, and uses human contact measurements to supervise policy contact goal actions, which the robot realizes without additional body sensors.

Data collection interfaces for robot learning. Teleoperation provides robot-native demonstrations, but it is slow, costly, and hard to deploy on humanoids in diverse environments ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Xiong et al., 2025 ) . UMI ( Chi et al., 2024 ) enables robot-free data collection with a portable handheld gripper, and its extensions add a head-mounted camera ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , gripper-centric tactile and force sensing ( Choi et al., 2026 ) , while humanoid-oriented interfaces additionally capture body or keypoint trajectories ( Nai et al., 2026 ) .
These motion-centric interfaces capture EEF and keypoint trajectories or joint angles, but none of them measure body contact signals.
PanTact adds contact sensing to preserve contact interactions during human to robot transfer.

Learning loco-manipulation from demonstrations. A common architecture combines a high-level policy that predicts task-space commands with a whole-body controller that executes them ( Nai et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Controllers use optimization ( Ferrolho et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) or learned motion tracking ( He et al., 2024 ; Dugar et al., 2024 ; Weng et al., 2025 ) , with demonstrations obtained from wearable devices ( Nai et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) , human video ( Bahety et al., 2025 ) , or simulation ( Li et al., 2025 ) , but the policy-to-controller interface typically specifies only motion targets.
Recent work introduces contact-conditioned motion tracking ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) , but assigns contacts to predefined body parts and does not integrate contact prediction by a high-level visuomotor policy.
PanTact integrates human contact sensing, a visuomotor policy that predicts contact goals, and contact-aware whole-body control into a complete system.
