2026-10-12.title: Fly-by-Code: Embodied Coding Agents for Aerial Manipulation with Active Visual and Physical Feedback
2026-10-12.authors: Jaewoo Lee , Jeongyeon Seo , Sihyun Cho , Gyeongrak Choe , Yutong Wang , Bavin Saravanan , Jia-Bin Huang , Furong Huang , Sebastian Scherer , Guanya Shi , H. Jin Kim , Seungjae Lee , Dongjae Lee
2026-10-12.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-12.abstract:
Embodied coding agents construct robot policies from natural-language instructions by generating executable programs and refining them from execution feedback. This refinement assumes that execution feedback reveals whether the task succeeded and, after a failure, provides sufficient evidence to guide program revision.
Aerial manipulation violates this assumption in two ways. Payload constraints restrict onboard camera coverage and leave task-critical outcomes outside the robot’s view (partial observability), while strong dynamic coupling and limited control margins make physical interactions fragile (limited interaction robustness) and leave failure causes unresolved. Re-examining the same feedback cannot recover observations that were never collected or separate failure causes that the available evidence does not distinguish. To acquire this missing evidence, we introduce Active Feedback (AF), an active “View and Probe” framework. When execution feedback leaves unresolved questions, the agent synthesizes a separate diagnostic program that runs in simulation to inspect unseen outcomes from informative viewpoints (View) or test hypotheses about failure causes through targeted physical interactions (Probe).
Across six simulated aerial manipulation tasks with 60 trials per condition, AF reduces false completion declarations from 25 to 5 and raises final task success from 31.7% to 75% compared with terminal feedback under the same coding-agent configuration and task-execution limit. Using shared robot APIs, task programs refined with AF in simulation run on a physical aerial manipulator without task-program source-code modification and complete multi-stage manipulation tasks in the real world. These results show that executable diagnosis fills gaps in execution feedback for embodied coding agents, improving both completion assessment and program refinement in aerial manipulation. Project Page: https://fly-by-code.github.io/
2026-10-12.introduction:
Embodied coding agents provide a promising approach to task-level coordination by translating natural-language instructions into executable programs that combine general control flow and computation with calls to robot perception and action APIs ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) . In an iterative refinement loop, the agent executes a program, examines execution feedback, and revises it until it determines the task is complete. This refinement implicitly assumes that execution feedback provides sufficient evidence to assess the task outcome and, when execution fails, to identify how to revise the program.

This assumption breaks down under two challenging conditions: partial observability and limited interaction robustness. Partial observability can leave task-critical outcomes outside the robot’s observations, while failures arising from physical interaction limitations can be difficult to distinguish from perception or manipulation errors. We refer to these two gaps in execution feedback as missing outcome observations and unresolved failure causes , respectively. Re-examining the same feedback cannot supply observations that were never collected or resolve failure causes that the available evidence does not distinguish. Effective refinement therefore requires the agent to identify what additional evidence is needed and how to acquire it.

Aerial manipulation amplifies both limitations of execution feedback. An aerial robot equipped with a manipulator must physically interact with the environment while maintaining flight ( Ollero et al., 2022 ) . Spatially extended tasks can exceed the coverage of a fixed external camera, leaving the agent dependent on egocentric onboard sensing whose viewpoint changes with robot motion. At the same time, limited control margin and disturbances from manipulator motion and interaction wrenches can produce failures ( Yadav et al., 2025 ; Hwang et al., 2025 ) that are difficult to distinguish from perception or manipulation errors. For example, an empty gripper after a placement attempt does not reveal whether the object reached the target, while a failed door-opening attempt may not reveal whether the grasp failed, the commanded motion was inappropriate, or the platform lacked sufficient physical capability.

Resolving these gaps requires new evidence: choosing a viewpoint that reveals an unseen outcome or performing a targeted physical interaction that tests a specific failure hypothesis. Motivated by this observation, we introduce Active Feedback ( AF ), an explicit post-execution diagnostic stage . Rather than immediately revising the task program based on existing execution feedback, AF first lets the agent generate and execute a separate diagnostic program to gather evidence for unresolved questions. Using the same robot APIs as the task program, the diagnostic program can move to informative viewpoints to acquire missing outcome observations ( View ) or perform targeted physical interactions in simulation to test hypotheses about unresolved failure causes related to interaction behavior or embodiment constraints ( Probe ). The resulting observations and measurements are returned to the same agent, providing additional evidence for both completion assessment and subsequent program revision.

Existing coding-agent systems obtain evidence through multimodal execution feedback ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , per-primitive traces ( Lu et al., 2026 ) , task-specific verification procedures ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) , or information-gathering actions embedded within task execution ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . AF instead synthesizes an attempt-specific diagnostic procedure after execution, separately from task evaluation. AF uses the same prompt across tasks, while the agent generates a diagnostic program for each attempt to investigate unresolved questions. By decoupling diagnosis from task progress, AF gives the agent freedom to select actions for their information value rather than their immediate contribution to task completion. Task outcomes are evaluated before diagnosis, and the environment resets before the next task attempt, so diagnostic actions contribute evidence without earning task credit.

Across six aerial manipulation tasks in two simulated environments, AF achieves 75% final task success, outperforming terminal (31.7%) and execution-trace (48.3%) feedback under the same agent configurations and execution limits. These results show that additional observations and interaction evidence improve program synthesis beyond existing execution-feedback baselines. We analyze task progress across refinement iterations, evaluate AF across models and interfaces, and examine how diagnostics inform program revisions.

Finally, we investigate the real-world transferability of our approach by deploying the synthesized programs on a physical aerial manipulator. Because simulation and hardware share task-level APIs, these programs run on our custom hardware without source-code changes, even though the underlying sensing and control implementations differ. The resulting programs repeatedly complete two multi-stage tasks, 2-Objects Pick-and-place and Cabinet, despite differences between the simulated and physical scenes and variations in initial robot position and heading across trials (Figure 1 ).

In summary, our work makes the following key contributions:

We characterize two limitations of execution feedback for embodied coding agents: missing outcome observations and unresolved failure causes , which hinder completion assessment and program revision.

We introduce Active Feedback (AF), a post-execution diagnostic stage within a simulation-based program-refinement loop. At this stage, the agent synthesizes an attempt-specific executable program to acquire evidence through informative viewpoints that supply missing outcome observations ( View ) and targeted physical interactions that test hypotheses about unresolved failure causes ( Probe ).

We evaluate AF in aerial manipulation. Across six simulated tasks, AF improves final task success to 75%, compared with 31.7% for terminal feedback and 48.3% for execution-trace feedback, while also improving completion assessment. We further demonstrate repeated physical execution of simulation-synthesized task programs through shared robot APIs without task-program source-code modification. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of embodied coding agents for aerial manipulation .

1. We characterize two limitations of execution feedback for embodied coding agents: missing outcome observations and unresolved failure causes , which hinder completion assessment and program revision.

2. We introduce Active Feedback (AF), a post-execution diagnostic stage within a simulation-based program-refinement loop. At this stage, the agent synthesizes an attempt-specific executable program to acquire evidence through informative viewpoints that supply missing outcome observations ( View ) and targeted physical interactions that test hypotheses about unresolved failure causes ( Probe ).

3. We evaluate AF in aerial manipulation. Across six simulated tasks, AF improves final task success to 75%, compared with 31.7% for terminal feedback and 48.3% for execution-trace feedback, while also improving completion assessment. We further demonstrate repeated physical execution of simulation-synthesized task programs through shared robot APIs without task-program source-code modification. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study of embodied coding agents for aerial manipulation .
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Code-as-policy and program-synthesis approaches represent robot behavior as executable programs that compose perception and control APIs ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Mu et al., 2024 ; Oelerich et al., 2025 ; Mower et al., 2026 ) . Recent work extends program generation through iterative refinement: CaP-X uses textual and visual execution feedback, ASPIRE leverages multimodal execution traces with reusable repairs and program search, ARCHITECT incorporates execution traces and human corrections into reusable skills, and ENPIRE constructs task-specific reset, safety, and verification interfaces ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) . Related methods explain failures from execution experience, generate recovery behaviors, or acquire missing physical information ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Schlesinger et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) . Active Feedback (AF) instead addresses cases where existing execution evidence is insufficient, synthesizing an attempt-specific diagnostic program to actively acquire visual or physical evidence for completion assessment and subsequent program refinement.

Active perception selects sensing actions to acquire task-relevant information ( Bajcsy, 1988 ; Bajcsy et al., 2018 ) , while interactive perception uses physical interaction to reveal information that is difficult to obtain from passive observation alone ( Bohg et al., 2017 ) . Recent robotic manipulation systems extend these ideas through task-driven viewpoint selection and coordinated perception–manipulation under occlusion ( Weng et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Xiong et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026a ) . Language-model-based agents can likewise select epistemic actions to acquire multimodal information under partial observability ( Zhao et al., 2023b ) . Whereas prior methods primarily acquire information to support ongoing perception or task execution, AF synthesizes a separate diagnostic program after each attempt to resolve uncertainties for completion assessment and program refinement.

Aerial manipulation brings together challenges in flight,
perception, and physical interaction, with research spanning
platform design, contact-aware control, whole-body motion planning,
and perception-driven manipulation ( Ollero et al., 2022 ; Bodie et al., 2021 ; Zhao et al., 2023a ; Guo et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Ubellacker et al., 2024 ; Bauer et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) . Learning-based approaches learn manipulation policies from
demonstrations or adapt pretrained policies to aerial platforms ( He et al., 2025 ; Gupta et al., 2026 ; Tucker et al., 2026 ) ,
while we focus on actively acquiring post-execution evidence
to assess and revise policies expressed as executable programs. Among language-guided approaches, AERMANI-VLM constrains high-level decisions to predefined
flight-safe skills to improve execution reliability ( Mishra et al., 2025 ) , while AeroGrab actively changes viewpoints to improve target observability under occlusion ( Singh et al., 2026 ) .

2026-10-12.title: Beyond the Snowflakes: Disentangling Weather Effects from Confounding Meta-Factors in LiDAR Object Detection
2026-10-12.authors: Yiming Yang , Jeremy P. Bos
2026-10-12.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-12.abstract: Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) is critical for autonomous perception, yet its performance is known to degrade in adverse weather. While existing literature models snow as atmospheric noise that degrades performance, our granular evaluation on the WADS-3D and CADC datasets reveals a counter-intuitive phenomenon: detection accuracy consistently improves as snow intensity increases. Through ablation study and meta-information analysis, we reconcile this by confirming that while falling snow acts as noise, its negative impact is outweighed by a dominant, concurrent factor: significantly increased object point count. We hypothesize that this object point count boost acts as a geometric enhancement, driven by snow accumulation increasing vehicle surface area and a shift from specular to diffuse reflectance. Our findings demonstrate that evaluating perception systems using broad weather-severity bins without accounting for correlated object-level data can lead to misleading conclusions about detector robustness. We conclude that accurate evaluation requires decoupling atmospheric noise from surface accumulation effects and outline future research to validate these physical models. The WADS-3D dataset is available at: https://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/wads-3d/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Lidar sensors are a cornerstone of perception for robotics and autonomous vehicles due to their high-resolution 3D measurement capabilities. In these systems, LiDAR enables critical tasks such as localization [ 1 ] , obstacle avoidance [ 2 ] , and object detection [ 3 ] , providing precise depth information where vision-only systems may struggle.

However, adverse weather conditions including rain, fog, and snow degrade LiDAR performance by introducing noise, occlusion, and false returns [ 4 ] . Snowfall, in particular, presents unique challenges: snowflakes act as scatterers that obscure objects and create transient noise points. For autonomous systems, these errors can propagate to downstream modules [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] , potentially leading to safety-critical failures.

Despite these risks, many perception algorithms are developed under ideal weather conditions, leaving a significant reliability gap in real-world, dynamic environments. While recent studies have begun investigating LiDAR performance in fog [ 8 ] , rain [ 9 ] , and snow [ 10 ] , snowfall research remains comparatively limited. Investigating snow is difficult due to its complex spatiotemporal characteristics [ 11 ] , the lack of controlled test environments [ 12 ] , and the high cost of data acquisition. Consequently, many studies rely on theoretical scattering models [ 13 ] or qualitative observations, leaving a gap in systematic, quantitative analysis across varying snowfall intensities.

To bridge these gaps, we introduce the WADS 3D Object Detection Dataset (WADS-3D), an extension of the Winter Adverse Driving Dataset (WADS) [ 14 ] . Leveraging multi-year data from Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, WADS captures snowfall intensities significantly higher than those typically reported in existing literature [ 15 ] , providing a unique benchmark for the most severe winter conditions. To ensure our findings generalize across different environments and sensor specifications, we further evaluate our results against the established Canadian Adverse Driving Conditions Dataset (CADC) [ 16 ] . By utilizing WADS-3D for extreme-case analysis alongside CADC for broader validation, we present a comprehensive evaluation of 3D object detection performance across a wide spectrum of winter severity. Our analysis reveals a counter-intuitive key finding: detection performance can improve with heavier snowfall. To explain this, we conduct
an ablation study, error matrix analysis, and a three-stage meta information analysis,
which demonstrates that the improvement is not a direct result
of the falling snow, but rather an artifact of confounding
variables. The model’s performance is mainly governed by
the object complexity rather than environmental complexity.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection

LiDAR-based 3D object detection identifies and localizes objects within sparse and irregular point clouds. Traditional approaches utilized geometry-based clustering (e.g., Euclidean [ 17 ] or Supervoxel [ 18 ] ) alongside hand-crafted features and simple classifiers [ 19 ] . Modern methods are dominated by deep neural networks, categorized by their data representation: Voxel-based methods [ 20 ] discretize space into 3D grids for efficient sparse convolutions (e.g., SECOND [ 21 ] , Voxel R-CNN [ 22 ] ); Pillar-based methods [ 23 ] simplify this into 2D vertical columns for faster processing; Point-based architectures [ 24 ] operate directly on raw points; and Hybrid models [ 25 , 26 ] integrate both voxel and point features. While sensor fusion with cameras [ 27 ] , radar [ 28 ] or 4D-radar [ 29 ] often achieves state-of-the-art results, this study focuses exclusively on LiDAR-only methods to isolate performance degradation specifically caused by snowy conditions.

## II-B Impact of Snow on LiDAR Perception

Snowfall disrupts LiDAR perception through three primary mechanisms: backscatter noise (false positives), occlusion [ 30 ] , and signal attenuation [ 13 ] . Studies utilizing physically-based simulations, such as Hahner et al. [ 10 ] , typically report a monotonic degradation in detection performance driven by these factors. However, these simulations primarily model airborne snow, neglecting the geometric effects of snow accumulation on object surfaces and the surrounding environment. In real-world evaluations, Sun et al. [ 31 ] quantified degradation on the MSP dataset, reporting vehicle detection drops of up to 50% under heavy snow. Yet, this analysis aggregated multiple heterogeneous datasets (Boreas [ 32 ] , CADC [ 16 ] , RADIATE [ 33 ] , and WADS [ 14 ] ) collected with varying LiDAR sensors. Merging such diverse data introduces sensor-specific domain shifts that are difficult to eliminate entirely, potentially confounding weather effects with sensor discrepancies. Complementing this, the CADC+ dataset [ 12 ] demonstrated that snow introduces both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, effectively acting as a distinct data domain.

## II-C Object- and Scene-Level Complexity Metrics

Complexity is a decisive factor in perception performance, yet metrics vary across benchmarks. At the object level, KITTI [ 34 ] and A*3D [ 35 ] use camera-centric properties like pixel height and occlusion. Conversely, the Waymo Open Dataset [ 36 ] employs LiDAR-centric metrics (e.g., object point counts), while nuScenes [ 37 ] relies on post-hoc error analysis (NDS) correlated against visibility and range. At the scene level, complexity is defined by task-based or geometric factors. SemanticKITTI [ 38 ] uses manual annotation effort as a proxy for complexity, while Abohassan et al. [ 39 ] quantify the computational load imposed on LiDAR systems by dense infrastructure. Geometric approaches include surface smoothness derivatives [ 40 ] , semantic occupancy grids (M-SOG) [ 41 ] , and information-theoretic measures such as LiDAR point cloud entropy [ 42 ] or aerial image delentropy [ 43 ] .

## II-D Analyzing the Influence of Meta-Information

The black-box nature of deep learning detectors poses challenges for safety certification. To improve transparency, researchers analyze how specific meta-information influences performance. While Zendel et al. [ 44 ] and Linnhoff et al. [ 45 ] identified hazard chains for LiDAR and cameras, but their work lacked quantitative deep-learning analysis. Ponn et al. [ 46 ] introduced a multivariate approach using Random Forest (RF) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) to analyze 2D camera-based detectors. Recently, Kuznietsov [ 47 ] applied Kendall’s Tau and SHAP to rank influencing factors for LiDAR-based pedestrian detection on nuScenes. By analyzing both False Negative (FN) and False Positive (FP) errors, they highlighted the importance of accounting for multivariate dependencies to improve analytical reliability.

## II-E Research Gap

Current literature on snowy LiDAR perception is limited by reliance on coarse weather categories and synthetic models that typically simulate atmospheric noise while ignoring surface accumulation. Furthermore, empirical studies often merge heterogeneous datasets collected with varying sensors, introducing domain shifts that obscure genuine physical trends. Consequently, simply measuring accuracy drops fails to distinguish whether performance changes stem from atmospheric occlusion, object-level geometric changes, or sensor inconsistencies. To address these gaps, this work provides the following contributions: (1) we introduce WADS-3D, a dataset featuring extreme snowfall intensities for LiDAR perception; (2) we conduct independent benchmarks on WADS-3D and CADC to validate performances across distinct environments and sensor configurations without domain-shift artifacts; and (3) we employ meta-information analysis to reveal that object complexity primarily drives detector performance in heavy snow.

2026-10-12.title: Tracking the Invisible: Self-Supervised Wheel Track Detection with Thermal-RGB Fusion
2026-10-12.authors: Yiming Yang , Jeremy P. Bos
2026-10-12.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-12.abstract: Accurate detection of drivable area is essential for autonomous driving and advanced driver assistance systems. While state-of-the-art methods focus on general traversability estimation, they prove inadequate for snow-covered roads where following existing wheel tracks offers crucial advantages: improved traction, predictable vehicle dynamics, and verified path stability. To address this, we propose a low-cost, self-supervised approach detecting safety-critical wheel tracks using synchronized RGB-I (RGB + Long-Wave Infrared) imagery. Our method automatically generates training labels by projecting future wheel trajectories from recorded GNSS data. A neural network is designed to identify wheel tracks with the 4-channel RGB-I images from challenging, white-out road surfaces. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in visually monotonous and featureless adverse environment, offering a robust and cost-effective alternative for winter autonomy. The newly introduced ThermalTrack dataset is available at: https://digitalcommons.mtu.edu/thermaltrack/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Autonomous driving in cold regions faces significant challenges on snow-covered roads, where lane lines and road structures are often obscured by snow. For traditional navigation systems, Ruotsalainen et al. [ 1 ] show that existing fusion and map-matching algorithms for vehicle localization are inadequate for navigation in Arctic environments. LiDAR and HD map-based perception systems also experience localization loss under snow-covered road conditions [ 2 ] . Furthermore, HD maps struggle in these conditions due to altered driving dynamics: vehicles carving new paths in the snow shift lane centers and modifying lane widths beyond their original boundaries, making pre-mapped data unreliable. Similarly, the dynamic nature of adverse environments, where features change or disappear, disrupts map consistency and localization. Vision-based navigation struggles also in colorless and featureless environments due to challenges in visual feature extraction, leading to failures in visual odometry and navigation [ 3 ] . Fig. 1 shows a white-out frame from Winter Adverse Driving dataSet (WADS) [ 4 ] , with the corresponding wheel-track probability map predicted by our method. LiDAR SLAM encounters difficulties in distinguishing between snow-covered surfaces and actual road features, leading to unstable localization and navigation errors [ 5 ] . These challenges highlight the need for robust perception systems capable of adapting to dynamic and unstructured environments.

In such unstructured environments, wheel tracks carved into the snow offer a viable alternative for navigation. Unlike obscured lane markings or transient visual features, wheel tracks provide physical guidance that persists even in heavy snow. Research has shown that aligning a vehicle’s wheels with existing ruts during off-road driving offers multiple advantages [ 6 ] . First, it enhances safety by reducing lateral slippage during turns, as the ruts provide extra lateral force to guide the vehicle along its path. It also prevents the ruts from acting as obstacles, which reduces undesirable vibrations and instability. It increases traction, particularly when traversing loose terrains such as mud, sand, and snow. This strategy also saves energy by reducing the energy wasted on compacting the ground.

Traversability estimation [ 7 ] , a critical component of indoor/outdoor navigation, has gained considerable attention and made significant progress, both in urban [ 8 ] and rural [ 9 ] environments. These methods typically focus on identifying drivable areas by classifying terrain as traversable or non-traversable, leveraging advances in machine learning, sensor fusion, and traveling experience. While they excel at detecting general drivable regions, they fall short in snow-covered driving scenarios: they fail to account for the unique driving behavior in snow, where drivers tend to follow existing wheel tracks for safer and more stable travel. This gap highlights the need for a more specialized approach that focuses on wheel track detection over generic drivable area estimation, ensuring more robust navigation in adverse conditions.

In this work, we propose a novel method for detecting wheel tracks on snow-covered roads by fusing RGB and thermal images. While wheel tracks are often indistinct in RGB images, thermal imaging reveals critical temperature differentials between compacted wheel tracks (higher thermal inertia, emitting more radiation) and loose snow (higher reflectivity, emitting less radiation). To overcome the lack of clear visual features, we introduce a RGB-thermal fusion based self-supervised learning framework that mitigates manual labeling by projecting recorded wheel track trajectories onto image frames.

We validate our approach using the WADS dataset, with experiments demonstrating robust wheel track detection under extreme visual degradation (snow occlusion, low contrast, and homogeneous textures). Our method shows consistent improvements across standard evaluation metrics compared to baseline approaches. This work advances winter autonomy by leveraging thermal sensing and integrating wheel track detection with state-of-the-art traversability estimation technology.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Self-supervised Traversability Estimation

Traversability estimation plays a vital role in enabling autonomous navigation across diverse environments. Early approaches relied on analyzing basic features like slope, roughness, elevation [ 10 ] , and vision [ 11 ] . The rise of deep learning has shifted focus toward semantic segmentation techniques, such as terrain classification [ 12 ] and image segmentation [ 13 ] . Despite their effectiveness, these methods depend heavily on annotated datasets, limiting their ability to adapt to unfamiliar or dynamic conditions [ 14 ] . This has driven the development of self-supervised techniques, which learn from real-world interactions without extensive labeling, offering greater robustness and adaptability in uncertain environments.

In paper [ 15 ] , Seo et al. introduced a one-class classification method to distinguish traversable from non-traversable areas in visually diverse environments. Other approaches, such as employing autoencoders [ 16 ] to identify low- and high-risk terrains based on reconstruction errors, or using normalizing flow [ 17 ] for traversability classification on multi-modal images, have also demonstrated strong performance.

## II-B Wheel Tracks Detection

LiDAR and cameras are widely used for wheel track detection, typically relying on geometry-based feature extraction. Ordonez [ 18 ] highlighted the advantages of rut tracking for off-road autonomous vehicles, designing a laser range finder based system to detect and follow ruts. Zhang [ 19 ] created a hand-crafted image-processing pipeline for identifying wheel tracks in wheat fields, incorporating feature filtering and extraction, curve and polynomial fitting. Fuentes et al. [ 20 ] introduced an automated LiDAR method for rut detection using digital elevation models. However, depending on manually made ruts could reduce its performance in actual challenging environments Seok et al. [ 21 ] proposed a LiDAR-based bump and dip detection method for paved road, which shows potential for wheel track detection but involves multiple processing stages and highly customized filtering and feature extraction process, limiting its generalizability across diverse winter conditions. For snow-covered environments, Goberville et al. [ 22 ] developed a supervised learning-based tire track detection system, using a custom-labeled dataset and convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture. This approach requires intensive manual annotation and lacks generalization. Kim et al. [ 23 ] proposed a YOLOv5-based system for snowy lane-keeping, using manually annotated tire tracks and geometric post-processing (BEV/Hough) for path generation, but it relies on labor-intensive annotations and produces suboptimal bounding boxes that requiring future refinement. While these methods demonstrate progress, they rely on traditional feature extraction and manual annotation, limiting their adaptability to dynamic and complex environments. This highlights the need to integrate cutting-edge technology from adjacent research fields to achieve robust, generalizable performance.

## II-C IR Thermal Camera based Navigation

IR thermal imaging provides a low-cost, safe, and effective solution for mobile robot perception. Xaud et al. [ 24 ] addressed sugarcane robot navigation by combining thermal imaging with CNN-based segmentation to identify crop rows and compute centerline offset, outperforming RGB methods and offering a cost-effective alternative to Lidar-based systems. To tackle nighttime autonomous navigation challenges, Aditya et al. [ 25 ] developed a system combining thermal cameras with model predictive control. By fusing thermal and visible modalities during training, their approach achieves performance comparable to daytime RGB-based systems while operating in low-light conditions. For research that leveraging thermal image in adverse weather conditions, Vachmanus et al. [ 26 ] introduced an RGB-thermal fusion framework for robust road and pedestrian segmentation in snow, achieving better performance than existing approaches via a dedicated fusion module and pyramid supervision. Renaux [ 27 ] et al. improved autonomous vehicle perception in harsh weather by integrating thermal imaging with RGB data. Their method fused thermal intensity analysis with YOLOv3-tiny detections for reliable person detection, while a modified MultiNet achieved accurate road segmentation with minimal training.

## II-D Research Gap

Existing research on wheel track detection has primarily focused on scenarios where wheel tracks exhibit relatively consistent and well-defined characteristics, such as those found in wheat fields or manually created tracks. However, detecting wheel tracks on snow-covered surfaces introduces unique challenges due to the highly variable and complex nature of the tracks. In snowy environments, wheel tracks often overlap, vary in depth, and exhibit irregular shapes due to factors such as human inaccuracy in following existing tracks, new snowfall, and wind effects. These problems, which are not typically encountered in more controlled environments demand advanced techniques to accurately identify and distinguish wheel tracks in such dynamic and visually ambiguous conditions.

2026-10-12.title: MARGoS: A Configuration-Driven Platform for Reproducible MARL Experiments in ARGoS
2026-10-12.authors: Tom Philipp Backert , Mohammad D. Soorati , Javad Ghofrani
2026-10-12.comment: Submitted version (prior to peer review) of a paper published in the VARIABILITY 2026 Satellite Events proceedings (Project Showcase Track), LNCS 17104, Springer.
2026-10-12.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) has become a prominent research direction, particularly within collective robotics, where the ARGoS simulator is widely used to study emergent swarm behavior. Yet despite this growth, systematic support for reuse and reproducibility in MARL-based swarm robotics remains limited and insufficiently standardized: a single experiment is assembled from manually aligned simulator files, training scripts, configuration values, paths, seeds, and environment details, so reuse and reproduction stay fragile even within one research group. To address this gap, we introduce MARGoS , a lightweight, configuration-driven platform developed in this project that elevates these experiment-defining inputs to first-class, platform-managed artifacts. MARGoS enables reproducible experimentation through configuration hashing, end-to-end seed propagation, frozen (immutable) configurations, structured logging, environment fingerprinting, and exportable experiment bundles that facilitate sharing, replay, and verification of results across machines and over time. A five-dimension evaluation (architecture, efficiency, reproducibility, usability, and collaboration) supports our claim that managing experiment variation as a platform responsibility makes ARGoS+MARL experiments easier to reuse, reproduce, and hand off. Our code is available at https://github.com/tombackert/margos .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is a prominent paradigm for training collective robot behavior, in which large numbers of simple, embodied agents produce group-level behavior through decentralized local interaction rather than through a central controller [ 16 , 6 ] . Because experimenting with physical swarms is costly and slow, this training is simulation-first, and ARGoS is a widely used modular simulator for exactly this setting [ 15 , 1 ] . Running MARL training on ARGoS, which we refer to as ARGoS+MARL, is therefore a natural and increasingly common way to study learned swarm behavior. Its experiment workflow, however, is largely manual: a single run is assembled by hand from separately edited scenario files, training code, parameters, seeds, output paths, and environment assumptions, so small drifts can silently redefine the experiment and reuse or reproduction stays fragile even within one research group. We present MARGoS , a small, configuration-driven platform built in this project to make reuse and reproduction of ARGoS+MARL experiments a managed property of the platform rather than a matter of user discipline.

The recurring inputs above are variant-bearing experiment artifacts: some define a run, while others capture the state needed to rerun and compare it. When they vary independently, configuration, reproduction, and handoff become manual coordination tasks rather than managed properties. MARGoS treats these experiment-defining inputs as first-class, platform-managed artifacts through configuration hashing, end-to-end seed propagation, frozen configurations, structured logging, environment fingerprinting, and exportable experiment bundles. It thereby turns unmanaged artifact variation into platform-owned managed variation and frames ARGoS+MARL experimentation as a configuration and reuse problem rather than an algorithmic one: the contribution is the platform and its integration of variation-control responsibilities, not a new learning algorithm or swarm behavior.

The gap this addresses is deliberately bounded. Among the adjacent platforms surveyed in Section 2 , none is both ARGoS-native and covers configuration → \,\to\, orchestration → \,\to\, logging → \,\to\, analysis → \,\to\, export and import as a single pipeline. MARGoS explores integrated experiment-lifecycle support for this stack by centralizing the variant-bearing artifacts, and it was completed as a small-scale university research project sized for meaningful evaluation rather than as a general-purpose product: enough infrastructure to measure workflow efficiency, self-reproducibility, analytical usability, and handoff. Section 2 positions the platform against those adjacent systems, Section 3 defines the evaluation it enables, and Section 4 reports the lessons it produced.

To show that this problem is real and that MARGoS addresses it correctly, we evaluate the platform along the five dimensions summarized in Table 1 , which states each guiding question and the evidence type. RQ1 is enablement-only, validated by whether the platform executes the RQ2-RQ5 evaluation protocols, while RQ2-RQ5 are the four empirically tested dimensions that recur in the evaluation design (Section 3 ) and the consolidated results (Section 4 ). Throughout, the evaluation is supporting evidence for the platform contribution, not the contribution itself.

The scope is deliberately narrow: collaboration means asynchronous bundle handoff between prepared environments, not cloud workspaces, shared state, or live co-editing. The project also excludes algorithmic contributions, unrestricted cross-lab portability, and new experiments for this paper, reusing the executed project evaluation only. Each exclusion keeps the evidence tied to managed variation rather than product breadth. The next section turns the variant-bearing artifacts introduced here into platform-owned managed variation.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Platform Overview

MARGoS is structured as a five-stage pipeline: configuration → \,\to\, orchestration → \,\to\, logging → \,\to\, analysis → \,\to\, export/import. Each stage centralizes one or more of the experiment-defining artifacts named in Section 1 . The pipeline is the concrete mechanism by which those unmanaged inputs become platform-managed variation: configurations define experiment state, orchestration executes it, logs and reports preserve observed behavior, and export/import turns a run into a handoff bundle.

To position this design, we compare it against representative recent platforms that combine multi-agent or multi-robot learning infrastructure with simulator integration. The comparison uses three criteria tied to the gap claim: whether the system is ARGoS-native, whether it covers the full configuration → \,\to\, orchestration → \,\to\, logging → \,\to\, analysis → \,\to\, export/import lifecycle, and whether export/import is part of the reproducibility or handoff path rather than a separate manual step. Five comparators cover adjacent multi-agent or multi-robot slices: distributed many-agent infrastructure on Alchemist [ 5 ] , JAX-vectorized learning on the Robotarium testbed [ 7 ] , IsaacSim-based MARL self-play [ 8 ] , Gazebo/ROS autonomous-driving MARL [ 9 ] , and AirSim/UE4 UAV swarms [ 10 ] . ORBIT [ 12 ] and IsaacLab [ 11 ] cover integrated single-robot learning. Against the three criteria, the surveyed systems provide useful related-work context but do not cover the complete ARGoS+MARL lifecycle evaluated here; the gap claim opened in Section 1 is therefore bounded to this comparator set rather than to the literature as a whole. ORBIT and IsaacLab are used only as adjacent feasibility evidence for integrated robot-learning infrastructure, while the MARGoS pipeline is derived from the research questions and evaluation metrics for ARGoS+MARL. The contribution claimed here is the RQ-driven integration of variation-control responsibilities for this stack.

The CLI is the user-facing entry point to the pipeline and exposes it as five commands: run , show , compare , export , and import . These commands are entry points into the pipeline rather than one-to-one stage labels: run spans configuration loading, seed propagation, run-state capture, orchestration, and per-iteration logging; compare operates over stored logs and configuration hashes; and show , export , and import operate on stored runs. At the orchestration boundary, ArgosToZoo provides the ARGoS-to-MARL bridge: ARGoS communicates through ZeroMQ with a PettingZoo-compatible Python environment that RLlib training scripts can consume. There is no separate reproduce command: where later metrics label a reproduction task, the platform path is import followed by run , with compare used to verify the rerun against the reference. All five commands are invokable with a single positional argument under a convention-over-configuration default, so the surface a user must traverse to move an experiment through the pipeline is fixed at a five-verb interface. This five-command surface is itself a design decision, and it is the user-facing measurement surface that the efficiency, usability, and collaboration evaluations in Section 4 measure against.

Configuration hashing, seed propagation, frozen configs, structured logs, environment fingerprints, and exported source copies are the core reusable assets through which the platform turns experiment variants into managed artifacts. The hash is computed over the normalized frozen configuration. Because that configuration contains file references rather than embedded file bodies, the config hash alone is not a source-file versioning mechanism. Local rerun identity therefore assumes unchanged referenced sources; the platform makes that boundary explicit rather than claiming content-level version control. Drift in referenced simulator files and training scripts is controlled at the bundle boundary: the completed run records the frozen config, integrity hash, environment fingerprint, and logs, while the exported bundle copies the scenario and training-script sources and import rewrites references to those bundled copies. A received bundle therefore reproduces the captured variant rather than resolving mutable paths in the sender’s working tree.

The asset-to-outcome mapping is deliberately narrow. Configuration hashing, seed propagation, and frozen configs support RQ3 same-hardware rerun identity; logs and summaries support RQ2 workflow-effort measurement and result inspection; the RQ4 analytical-usability claim comes primarily from the five-command surface and measured task paths rather than from logs alone; and export/import bundles assembled from frozen configs, logs, source copies, and fingerprints support the RQ5 handoff evaluation. Figure 1 summarizes this control and managed-artifact flow across the five pipeline stages, and Section 3 picks up the asset-to-outcome mapping as the input to the evaluation design.

2026-10-12.title: LAPT-Scale: Scaling Embodied Policies with Latent Action Pre-Training on Human Videos
2026-10-12.authors: Zhiyuan Xiang , Peidong Liu , Mingyang Li , Jiawei Li , Wenhow Li , Wenbo Ding , Xiang Deng
2026-10-12.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-12.abstract:
Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting
embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich
alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation
methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse
manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale , a scalable latent
action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions
in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action
pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific
post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a
continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction
dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment
signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on
23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action
supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and
improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video
scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen
visual conditions.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Scaling data drives progress in vision and language, but embodied intelligence
faces a sharper bottleneck: interaction data requires physical robots or
simulators, making it far more expensive than text or static images. Large-scale
human videos, especially egocentric ones, offer a promising way to relieve this
bottleneck [ 1 ] . They naturally record diverse everyday
interactions at a scale beyond robot-collected trajectories, and transforming
such videos into action-like supervision could complement robot-only
datasets such as Open X-Embodiment [ 2 ] .

The central challenge is that human videos lack robot action labels, and human
motion cannot be directly mapped to robot control spaces. Existing methods,
such as VITRA [ 3 ] , often convert human videos into pseudo-actions
through explicit motion estimation, where estimation errors can lead to noisy
action annotations;
simply adding more human video does not necessarily improve policies. Latent
Action Models (LAMs) offer an alternative: they infer implicit actions between
consecutive frames end-to-end, without predefined robot action
labels [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
Because these implicit actions are optimized to explain visual transitions, they
provide compact supervision for unlabeled videos.

Despite this potential, existing LAMs are limited by their architectural priors
and alignment signals. Many recent methods use Vector Quantized (VQ) latent
spaces [ 8 , 5 , 6 ] . While compact, a fixed
discrete codebook can over-compress the continuous changes that define
egocentric manipulation, weakening the supervision needed for fine-grained
policy learning. In addition, pixel-wise reconstruction signals such as MSE
are often dominated by large static regions, providing weak signals for small
but important hand-object interactions. As a result, learned latent actions may
miss transition-relevant structure needed for downstream embodied policies.

To address these limitations, we introduce LAPT-Scale , a scalable
latent action pre-training paradigm for embodied policy learning. LAPT-Scale
contains two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM , which constructs
human-derived supervision with a continuous Latent Action Model trained on
large-scale human videos, and LAPT-Scale-Policy , which uses this
supervision to train a VLA policy. The policy training follows three stages:
human-video latent-action pre-training, embodiment alignment with target-robot
data, and task-specific post-training in simulation and the real world. Unlike
discrete LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM parameterizes implicit actions in a continuous
space to preserve fine-grained transition dynamics. To make this space
perceptually grounded and temporally consistent, we train the LAM with
alignment signals beyond pixel reconstruction: perceptual alignment for local contact
fidelity [ 9 ] , semantic
alignment with self-supervised features for hand-object structure [ 10 ] ,
and optical-flow alignment for observed dynamics [ 11 ] .

We train LAPT-Scale-LAM on 23.3K hours of diverse egocentric videos and use
it to annotate a 5.1K-hour cleaned human-video subset for policy pre-training.
With 250 hours of self-collected robot data for embodiment alignment,
LAPT-Scale reaches 90.0%/89.3% success on RoboTwin Easy/Hard, 64.8% on
RoboCasa-GR1. Scaling LAM-annotated human video from 1K to 5K hours further
improves real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0%, suggesting that continuous
latent action annotation is a promising route for benefiting from larger
human-video corpora. On four harder real-robot tasks, it retains 70.0–75.0%
success under unseen position, illumination, and background shifts.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

LAPT-Scale-LAM: a continuous latent action model with perceptual,
self-supervised feature, and optical-flow alignment signals for learning a more
expressive latent action space from human videos.

LAPT-Scale-Policy: a three-stage framework for human-video
latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and downstream
post-training.

Real-robot scaling: increasing only Stage-1 human-video
pre-training data improves downstream real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0%.

1. LAPT-Scale-LAM: a continuous latent action model with perceptual,
self-supervised feature, and optical-flow alignment signals for learning a more
expressive latent action space from human videos.

2. LAPT-Scale-Policy: a three-stage framework for human-video
latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and downstream
post-training.

3. Real-robot scaling: increasing only Stage-1 human-video
pre-training data improves downstream real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0%.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-language-action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language
conditioning, and action generation for generalist manipulation. Recent systems
scale VLA policies with web knowledge, robot data, flow-based action modeling,
and cross-embodiment training [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] ,
while other work studies backbone, adaptation, spatial-representation, and
action-space choices [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] .
However, VLA training remains constrained by action-labeled robot trajectories.
Egocentric VLA methods such as VITRA and EgoScale reduce this bottleneck by
converting human videos into action-like targets before robot
alignment [ 3 , 25 ] , but such targets depend on
explicit motion estimation or retargeting signals. Simulation-mediated
pipelines also convert reconstructed human demonstrations into physically
checked robot-centered trajectories [ 26 ] . LAPT-Scale instead
annotates human videos with LAM-derived implicit actions.

Human video datasets provide broad coverage of physical interaction, from
object manipulation in Something-Something and EPIC-KITCHENS to daily-life
egocentric video in Ego4D [ 27 , 28 , 1 ] .
Recent resources expand scale and annotation density with paired ego-exo views,
factory videos, 3D/4D annotations, dexterous demonstrations, multimodal
interaction labels, and filtered Ego4D text/action annotations [ 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 ] .
These datasets are useful visual experience, but their human observations and
motion annotations do not directly specify robot-executable actions. LAPT-Scale learns latent actions to bridge this missing-label
gap before robot embodiment alignment.

Latent Action Models infer action-like variables from observation transitions,
making unlabeled videos useful for behavior learning. Related work learns compact
transition variables through inverse-dynamics, world-model, or latent-action
objectives and integrates them into VLA or world-model
pipelines [ 4 , 5 , 35 , 36 , 37 , 6 , 7 , 38 , 39 , 40 ] .
However, many LAMs rely on discrete or vector-quantized latents, which can
over-compress continuous egocentric manipulation dynamics [ 8 , 5 , 6 ] .
Reconstruction-only training can be dominated by static background regions.
LAOF augments reconstruction with optical-flow constraints to improve
robustness to visual distractors [ 41 ] . LAPT-Scale-LAM
therefore uses continuous latents together with perceptual, self-supervised
semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to preserve fine-grained implicit actions
for human-video policy pre-training [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] .

2026-10-12.title: Probabilistic Ship Trajectory Forecasting using Transformer Models on AIS Data
2026-10-12.authors: Frederik E. T. Schöller
2026-10-12.abstract:
Anticipation of vessel trajectories is an essential task when navigating at sea. This applies to both human navigators and autonomous surface vessels. Trajectory forecasting enables sub-routines such as collision avoidance to assess the situation and react accordingly in time. This paper investigates Transformer and Performer models for trajectory prediction of surface vessels in confined waters. Using widely available position data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), candidate models are trained and evaluated. Historical information on how other vessels have moved in the local area surrounding each agent is conveyed using positional heat maps. The heat maps are generated using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and encoded with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) before entering the Transformer models. The models are trained with quantile loss to efficiently obtain a model-aware prediction interval, as this is crucial for timely collision avoidance.
The proposed model architectures are shown to greatly outperform previous work while the inclusion of local heat maps enables the prediction of vessel movement that is not otherwise indicated from the previous positions.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Recently, autonomous surface vessels have gained notable research interest. Services such as decision support or full autonomy are envisaged to be a crucial part of the future of shipping. This, however, requires excellent situational awareness [ 1 , 2 ] .

Situational awareness is obtained through three main steps: perception, understanding of the environment, and anticipation of how the situation develops [ 3 ] . While nearby vessels can be detected on both radar and cameras [ 4 ] , estimation of future trajectories is needed if a short term path should be planned. A human navigator will use information about surrounding waters from the Electronic Chart Display and Information System (ECDIS) together with the past motion of vessels to assess the current situation. The past motion of nearby ships can be obtained e.g. by detection and tracking using radar [ 5 , 6 ] or tracking camera detections [ 7 , 8 ] . Commercial vessels and some large leisure crafts use Automatic Identification System (AIS) to broadcast current position, speed and heading among others.

Trajectory forecasting is a widely researched area, especially for pedestrian motion prediction. Many methods use Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks for motion prediction such as [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . While Recurrent neural networks (RNN) are commonly used for tasks such as time series forecasting and Natural Language Processing (NLP), Transformer networks, first described in [ 12 ] , have recently had immense success, especially for NLP, where models such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [ 13 ] , BART [ 14 ] and GPT-3 [ 15 ] outperformed previous LSTM models. Transformer networks have also shown their strengths in pedestrian trajectory forecasting [ 16 ] , where they were shown to outperform the previous LSTM state of the art. One drawback of Transformers is that the computational burden increases quadratically with input sequence length. Multiple recent studies have investigated methods to introduce Transformer models with linear complexity [ 17 , 18 ] , though these often do not match the performance of the original Transformer. One study introduced the Performer [ 19 ] that incorporates Fast Attention Via Positive Orthogonal Random Features (FAVOR+) and obtains linear complexity. Their Performer-ReLU model showed to outperform a similar Transformer configuration with quadratic complexity while being more efficient.

If a trajectory forecast is to be used for risk assessment in the area of short term path planning for autonomous vessels, it is crucial not to obtain a single prediction, but to produce a prediction interval in which the observed vessel could go. A prediction interval can be obtained in numerous ways. For example by using Monte Carlo dropout [ 20 ] , using Bayesian neural networks with probabilistic layer weights [ 21 ] or training the model as a conditional generative adversarial network (GAN) [ 22 ] . Common for these methods is that a prediction interval is not obtained directly from the network, but by running the network multiple times to approximate a prediction interval. This might result in a misleading prediction interval, as the network is trained to output a prediction close to the mean prediction and the prediction interval is approximated by drawing from a distribution. To circumvent these problems, this work utilizes quantile loss [ 23 ] to estimate prediction quantiles during training, which generates a model that is both aware of its prediction interval and can supply this in a single forward pass.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

A recent assessment of collision avoidance methods for marine vessels mentions different ways to anticipate the trajectory of a given vessel [ 24 ] . Here, the prediction schemes are categorized into physics-based, interaction-aware, and maneuver-based methods. Physics-based methods usually assume that the target vessel maintains a constant course and speed. A disadvantage of such assumptions lies in the lack of information about the curve of the underlying navigational channels.

Maneuver-based methods use the information contained within the COLREGs or available historical data, such as AIS. Hexeberg et al. [ 25 ] described a single-point neighbor search method for long-term trajectory prediction using AIS data. Here, data points within a set distance to the target vessel were used to estimate the course and speed for the next timestep if the used points had a similar heading. The method could therefore model the mean trajectory for a vessel. A drawback to such an approach is the difficulty of predicting a trajectory that differs from the usual fairways. Rong et al. [ 26 ] fitted a Gaussian process on AIS data for a southbound shipping route. The Gaussian process was used to predict the lateral movement at discrete time steps while historical acceleration data was used for longitudinal movement estimation. Murray et al. [ 27 ] used clustered AIS data to predict the future trajectory of a target vessel based on cluster points near that of the target. An autoencoder approach was utilized for the generation of future movement by exploring the latent space, thereby generating a prediction interval. By using unsupervised learning [ 28 ] developed a method for AIS data that proposes potential routes and endpoints for the target vessel. The proposed routes are given a probability that is updated iteratively during run time. Tang et al. [ 29 ] used a LSTM to forecast the future position of a marine vessel using AIS data. The LSTM was trained to output the parameters of a bivariate gaussian distribution, describing the potential position of a vessel at a chosen point in the future relative to the amount of input data used. Schöller et al. [ 30 ] used an LSTM-GAN to forecast marine vessel trajectories using AIS data. The network had an auxiliary input consisting of CNN features from an AIS heat map of the area surrounding the vessels. It was found that including information about how previous vessels had moved in a given area would increase performance significantly enabling the method to predict movement which would not otherwise be indicated in the previous positions.

In the domain of pedestrian trajectory prediction, [ 11 ] proposed a method for encoding interaction between agents called social pooling by including other agents within a grid. The pooling method was used in training an LSTM-GAN and enabled the generation of socially aware trajectories. Sadeghian et al. [ 10 ] extended this idea by modeling social interactions using attention. Furthermore, a CNN was included to model the physical features of the environment. The most recent addition to the social GANs, [ 9 ] , used a graph attention network [ 31 ] for social interaction which had the advantage of being invariant to the number of agents in the scene. Even though the methods with social interaction obtained better results than similar methods without social encoding, [ 16 ] argued that using the original Transformer network ( [ 12 ] ) for time series forecasting yielded better results, even without social modeling, obtaining state of the art results on common pedestrian trajectory data sets. Giuliari et al. [ 16 ] , obtained prediction intervals by using a quantized version of the Transformer that performed step classification instead of regression, thereby enabling probabilistic modeling from the softmax output.

The bottlenecks of current AIS-based vessel trajectory prediction schemes are several:
Some current methods only take characteristics of the investigated vessel into account, environmental factors such as water depth, land and navigational fairways are thus unknown and not modeled. Situations can therefore occur where a trajectory is predicted to go through land, which is infeasible. Other methods have the opposite problem. Clustering methods solely rely on the past movements of other vessels in the local area. The predicted trajectory will thus be some average of the trajectories of other similar vessels without directly taking the past movement of the investigated vessel into account.
Finally, existing models use sampling-based approaches to obtain probabilistic predictions, which drastically increase inference time.

This paper, therefore, proposes a hybrid approach using Transformer models that uses the movement characteristics of the individual investigated vessel while considering the positional probability distribution of the local area.
Most time-series-based approaches to ship trajectory prediction rely on recurrent neural networks such as LSTM [ 32 ] and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) [ 33 ] . Even though Transformer models have gained immense popularity in recent years, they have, to the best of the author’s knowledge, not been investigated in the context of trajectory prediction for marine vessels.
To forecast future trajectories, the proposed method uses a vessel’s past movements together with a novel approach to including spatial probability distributions in form of positional heat maps in Transformer model. A probabilistic output is supplied without the need for Monte Carlo sampling by using quantile loss. The model therefore directly outputs a prediction interval useful for risk assessment.

The rest of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 discusses the related work done in the area of trajectory forecasting. Section 3 introduces the data used in this research. Section 4 describes the model architectures investigated in this work and explains the difference between the Transformer and the Performer. Section 5 lists the training parameters used and introduces the loss function. Section 6 introduces the performance metrics used for evaluation and discusses the results. Finally, Section 7 presents the conclusions.

2026-10-12.title: MAGMA-Bench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Embodied Agents under Dynamic Tasks and Execution Failures
2026-10-12.authors: Loan Bernat (LAAS-GEPETTO), Matthieu Grard , Ariane Herbulot (LAAS-RAP), Florent Lamiraux (LAAS-GEPETTO)
2026-10-12.abstract: Long-horizon embodied agents must maintain task-relevant information, coordinate heterogeneous robots, and adapt their decisions as execution unfolds. Existing benchmarks investigate dynamic task execution and embodied multi-agent coordination, but provide limited evaluation of their intersection. We introduce MAGMA-Bench, an architecture-agnostic benchmark for persistent task reasoning in dynamic multi-robot environments. MAGMA-Bench evaluates agents across increasing task horizons and controlled online perturbations, including execution failures, task interruptions, and mission updates, with scenarios requiring coordination across robots with heterogeneous capabilities. It uses a structured skill-level interface to separate task-level reasoning from perception and low-level control. We evaluate locally deployable open-weight planners, multi-agent state-tracking strategies, and frontier models. Even the strongest evaluated models fail on a substantial fraction of clean episodes, and their success rates decrease further under online perturbations. Supervised adaptation greatly improves a small model, but performance remains substantially lower on longer and multi-robot missions. We release the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an architecture-agnostic expert-trace generation pipeline.

2026-10-12.title: A Local Agentic AI Framework to Generate Edge Case Scenarios for Safety Assurance
2026-10-12.authors: Victoria J. Hodge , Colin Paterson , Rob Alexander
2026-10-12.abstract: Generating edge case scenarios is crucial for training, testing and safety assuring autonomous systems. This identifies hazardous failures to increase system reliability and robustness, ensures the system can still function safely on the boundaries of its operational design domain and learns the expected system behaviour for these edge cases. The rapid advancement in the generation and analysis capabilities of language models (LMs) has expanded their applicability and recent work has investigated LM scenario generation. However, many recent approaches rely on human-in-the-loop or rule-based strategies. This restricts the LM’s ability to generate diverse and edge case scenarios; the long tail of the distribution. Our work uses local LMs in a laptop-based agentic AI framework for adaptive scenario generation. This is cheap, fully-controlled, ensures data privacy and security. It uses think, act, observe, update, and continue loops with lightweight JSON encoding to generate scenarios. We use the system requirements, system description and environment description as knowledge bases in contextual prompts for an LM to ensure scenario realism. A second, independent LM critiques each scenario using domain specific criteria so it can be refined. The refined scenarios are run in simulation and evaluation metrics collected. These metric scores are analysed and similar scenarios are created for edge cases (exploitation) or novel scenarios are generated to explore the scenario space. Post-hoc clustering using metric scores and thematic-type analysis of the rich-text scenario descriptions produced by the LM pinpoints functional gaps and their triggering conditions. This creates traceable evidence for the safety assurance case. Our work highlights the potential of a flexible and adaptive local agentic AI framework for automating edge case generation and producing traceable safety assurance evidence.
2026-10-12.introduction:
The impact of recent innovations in AI systems has changed how businesses and even economies function and changed how people interact with their environment. The emergence of AI-based autonomous systems is a major part of this innovation. An autonomous system is: “ a system involving software applications, machines, and people, that is able to take actions with little or no human supervision ’’ 1 1 1 https://tas.ac.uk/our-definitions/ (accessed 27 Sept 2026) . These systems have the potential to revolutionise daily life and their use is expanding rapidly, in particular in safety-critical domains. Safety-critical domains include autonomous road vehicles; medical, assistive, manufacturing and delivery robots; aerial vehicles; marine vehicles; underwater vehicles; wireless sensor networks used for monitoring; and components within systems such as an autopilot system in an aircraft [ 1 ] .

The development of autonomous systems that operate in safety-critical domains remains complex. Failures in such systems can cause harm to the environment, harm to people, or substantial economic loss [ 2 ] . As systems become more autonomous, the level of human oversight decreases [ 3 ] . Replacing humans with AI in these systems means that we can no longer rely on a suitably qualified human to respond to unusual situations in a safe manner. Instead, we are required to argue that, throughout its operational lifetime, the system will, autonomously, meet operational, safety, and regulatory standards under all anticipated operating conditions. However, such safety assurance requires rigorous and often expensive through-life safety assurance processes to ensure safety standards and regulations are met, and that the system is free from unacceptable risks. Autonomous systems that operate in open-world environments shift the focus of safe development and operation from guaranteeing against known operational parameters to effectively anticipating and mitigating novel inputs, unexpected situations and uncertainty. Furthermore, the system’s operational environment may be underspecified at design time [ 3 ] , or even unknown, which further increases the likelihood of unknown and unsafe scenarios. Arguing that the system is free from unacceptable risk is a complex and multifaceted process.

The required safety guarantees on the autonomous system that must be evidenced to argue its safety can be represented as g ⁡ ( 𝐀𝐒 ) g(\mathbf{AS}) and include requirements such as minimum obstacle clearance, minimum safe lighting level, or task completion time limits. An operational design
domain (ODD) specifies this operational environment within which an autonomous system is intended
to operate reliably and safely. The ODD effectively defines the parameters for system testing [ 4 ] . Systematic and comprehensive testing throughout development and operation is vital for ensuring the system will operate reliably and safely within its ODD. Scenario-based testing tests systems against meaningful scenarios and can be used during training and verification and validation of AI models to ensure robustness and provide evidence that g ⁡ ( 𝐀𝐒 ) g(\mathbf{AS}) will be met. There are three levels of scenarios for safety assurance testing in decreasing level of abstraction: functional (linguistic description), logical (range and distribution of parameters), and concrete [ 5 , 6 ] . Concrete scenarios θ \theta are sampled from the logical scenario distribution Θ \Theta and specify a value for each parameter. These concrete scenarios can then be sub-divided into typical, critical (safety risk present) and edge-cases [ 6 ] . Edge cases are statistical outliers [ 7 ] that are rarely encountered in normal operational activities and lie on the boundaries of the ODD. We do not consider these three classes to be mutually exclusive as typical scenarios may be critical and edge cases may be critical. Typical scenarios can be rapidly generated using methods such as random generation where ensuring coverage is the key. Critical scenarios can be targeted by random generation in conjunction with approaches such as fuzzy logic [ 8 ] and could fall under typical or edge case.

Modern safety standards for autonomous systems such as ISO 21448: safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF) [ 5 ] and PAS 8800 [ 9 ] require specification of spatial edge case scenarios. The wide operating context of autonomous systems means the parameter space of Θ \Theta is vast and the parameters have complex, non-linear relationships. Identifying the parameters θ \theta to describe realistic edge case is complex and challenging. For example, placing an obstacle in a specific location may only cause a hazard if other obstacles are placed in specific locations. ISO 21448 clause 7 requires us to identify triggering conditions such as specific environmental layouts that expose functional gaps and lead to hazardous events. Clause 8 considers residual risk and introduces principles such as ALARP (as low as reasonably practicable) to reduce risk until any further reduction would cost far more than the safety benefit. Clause 9 mandates developing a verification strategy so we can find and mitigate issues and clause 10 mandates verification of the known scenario space to argue that known hazards are handled cleanly. We need to consider clause 11 which mandates validation of the unknown scenario space using testing approaches such as simulation and randomized scenario scaling. As the operational design domain of autonomous systems is vast, testing is limited by the resources available so needs to be focused where it is most useful and the ODD specification, whether specified by text or as a model, may not fully capture every scenario possible. Humans can provide linguistic descriptions and specify parameters ranges and distributions but producing a comprehensive set of concrete edge case scenarios by hand is infeasible due to this vast parameter space. Classical scenario generation for autonomous navigation such as Monte Carlo sampling struggles with high-dimensionality and does not target edge cases. For safety assurance, we are particularly interested in finding critical edge cases so we can mitigate the risks. Finding these safety-critical edge cases and testing them can lead to design, ODD or algorithm refinements and demonstrates that functional gaps have been considered and any found have been mitigated.

To address the issues highlighted above we propose the use of a language model (LM) supported scenario generation and testing environment able to identify edge cases for autonomous systems testing in complex environments.
Figure 1 illustrates the proposed solution which uses agentic AI running on the laptop to programmatically convert safety requirements into structured JSON, hierarchical text-based encodings of scenarios, for stress-testing autonomous systems in simulation. JSON is lightweight and human-readable and is often used for data storage and exchange. The simulation outputs metrics in JSON format to describe how effective each scenario is for uncovering functional gaps in the system’s algorithm(s). These scenarios and metric analyses provide traceable evidence for safety assurance.

A programmatic mapping framework translating formal ISO 21448 and PAS 8800 safety specifications into JSON-based spatial coordinate schemas.

A programmatic mapping framework translating formal ISO 21448 and PAS 8800 safety specifications into JSON-based spatial coordinate schemas.

An iterative and closed loop scenario generation framework capable of dynamic improvement of edge case scenario quality.

Empirical validation in simulation demonstrating higher edge-case yield and hazard discovery rates compared to baseline generation techniques.

Integration of simulation outputs as verifiable evidence artefacts for safety assurance cases.

The agentic AI framework demonstrates that such technology is feasible for smaller companies and ordinary users as it can operate on consumer-grade hardware (laptop).

The remainder of this paper reviews relevant safety standards and the scenario-based testing literature in Section 2 , details and motivates the architecture of our framework in Section 3 , describes how the framework relates to formal safety requirements in Section 4 , describes our empirical analyses in Section 5 , with the results in Section 6 . We evaluate and discuss the analyses in Section 7 along with identified limitations, and Section 8 draws conclusions and identifies relevant future work to further validate and improve the system.

1. A programmatic mapping framework translating formal ISO 21448 and PAS 8800 safety specifications into JSON-based spatial coordinate schemas.

2. An iterative and closed loop scenario generation framework capable of dynamic improvement of edge case scenario quality.

3. Empirical validation in simulation demonstrating higher edge-case yield and hazard discovery rates compared to baseline generation techniques.

4. Integration of simulation outputs as verifiable evidence artefacts for safety assurance cases.

5. The agentic AI framework demonstrates that such technology is feasible for smaller companies and ordinary users as it can operate on consumer-grade hardware (laptop).
