# 2 Regulatory Background & Related Literature

## 2.1 Safety Assurance Standards and Frameworks

As the level of automation in autonomous systems increases, ensuring they are safe to operate in safety-critical domains requires safety assurance methodologies specifically targeted at this task. Traditional safety standards such as ISO 26262 [ 11 ] for functional safety were designed around deterministic software architectures and explicit boundary conditions pre-specified in the ODD. For AI-enabled systems, these standards exhibit clear gaps, in particular failing to account for performance gaps rooted in the high-dimensional input spaces of AI-based systems. The operating environment may be underspecified at design time, or even unknown, and the generalisation of design-time verification to run-time safety is problematic which all increase the likelihood of functional gaps [ 12 ] . Thus, autonomous systems lack well-understood safety guarantees and this can lead to unpredictability and ultimately hazardous failures [ 13 ] . Furthermore, current AI validation approaches rely on empirical performance metrics (such as recall and precision) evaluated over static datasets. This hides local performance failures and fails to quantify the AI model’s capacity for safe interpolation and extrapolation when encountering edge cases or out-of-distribution scenarios [ 1 ] in the ODD.

The newer ISO 21448 (SOTIF) [ 5 ] lifecycle prescribes procedures for identifying and controlling system risks so the residual risk shall be demonstrated to be below an acceptable level by gathering evidence from safety verification and validation. Further, SOTIF defines four areas based on two metrics; knowledge of the scenario and safety . It classifies all scenarios along using these two metrics as axes, knowledge (known/unknown) and hazard (safe/unsafe) where unsafe are the critical scenarios defined earlier. System verification focuses on area 2 (known/unsafe: boundary tests to pinpoint where a system transitions from failing to safe) and validation focuses on area 3 (unknown/unsafe: edge cases that are real-world situations that system engineers have not tested). Thus, identifying boundaries between safe and unsafe and identifying edge case scenarios to reduce their occurrence within the ODD is an urgent problem in safety verification and validation [ 14 ] and is the focus of this research. Edge cases have a Triggering Condition (SOTIF Clause 7) which represents a specific set of parameters (physical properties and environmental states) that cause a functional gap where system performance does not meet desired performance. They can be identified by system-level safety analysis, component-level failure analysis, fault trees, and simulation. Scenario generation tools coupled with simulation are designed specifically to combine parameters until a (functional gap) triggering condition occurs. [ 15 ] note the importance of scenario-based testing during the development lifecycle for assuring the safety of autonomous systems.

PAS 8800 (Road Vehicles - Safety and Artificial Intelligence) [ 9 ] complements ISO 21448 with a normative safety framework for managing the AI safety lifecycle. While PAS
8800 defines the necessary safety objectives and process requirements, it remains strictly
non-prescriptive regarding implementation mechanisms. PAS 8800 specifies what must be achieved
to ensure safety but leaves an open methodological gap regarding how these requirements
can be verified, quantified, and traceably validated in practice. While SOTIF testing identifies triggering conditions, PAS 8800 mandates that synthetic edge-case scenarios must be generated to identify data gaps, AI model gaps, non-deterministic behaviour and to validate the AI model’s generalisation and robustness boundaries [ 9 ] .

STAMP (System-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes) is a safety framework based on systems theory and STPA (System-Theoretic Process Analysis) is a hazard analysis method derived from STAMP [ 16 ] . Together they can generate scenarios [ 17 ] . However, the number of scenarios generated can be large which is ideal for ensuring scenario coverage but not for targetting edge cases as only a small portion of the scenarios generated will be edge cases (the long tail of the distribution). [ 17 ] use statistical model-checking to search the STAMP/STPA scenario space for critical scenarios (those likely to cause hazards). However, the approach requires specification of UML and statistical modelling templates which are bespoke to the application and not generalisable. Our approach would complement STAMP/STPA by supplementing it with targeted edge cases.

SACE (Safety Assurance of Autonomous Systems in Complex Environments) [ 18 ] is an eight-stage methodology to safety assure autonomous systems considering their operational domain. Within SACE, scenario generation is important for identifying hazardous interactions with the operational environment in stage 2 to discover risks, for boundary testing using edge-case scenarios in stage 7 and for verifying system behaviour in stage 8 using simulation and testing pipelines to generate the necessary evidence for a justified safety case. SACE encourages the use of simulation-based testing using a scenario coverage approach but provides little guidance as to how to do it.

## 2.2 Robotic Simulation & Virtual Testing

Simulation-based testing is vital to overcome the testing bottleneck as comprehensively testing autonomous systems across their operational domain is highly complex and computationally expensive. Simulation provides a secure and fully-controlled environment to test the scenarios generated including testing edge cases without risking human life, the environment or property. [ 19 , 20 ] survey and critique simulation of autonomous robots focusing on the technologies used and how simulation can ensure the safety, reliability and robustness of the robots.

We can test in simulation and then transition to real-world testing. This requires the simulation to accurately represent the real-world to ensure the simulation testing is valid. Simulations operate at different levels of fidelity. However, [ 21 ] show that even low fidelity simulation can unearth bugs in a robot’s navigation system. Popular robotic simulation environments such as Gazebo have been used for scenario analyses [ 22 ] . For higher fidelity, game engines such as Unity-3D can realistically simulate complex and dynamic environments, making them ideal for robotics and vehicle simulation. For example, [ 6 ] use the CARLA simulator which is based on the Unreal game engine and is aimed at road vehicle simulation and [ 23 ] show that Unity-3D game engine scales better, achieves better visuals and is more capable of real-time LiDAR simulation than a traditional robotic simulation environment such as Gazebo.

## 2.3 AI-Driven Scenario Generation

Scenario generation overcomes the data scarcity bottleneck for training AI components of autonomous systems by generating large numbers of scenarios from some more general specification of the scenario space (e.g. a description of the ODD). It can be targeted specifically at edge case scenarios to challenge the system’s safety boundaries and learn optimal behaviour through systematic testing. There is a range of techniques for scenario generation covering typical, critical and edge case scenarios.

[ 24 ] use Monte Carlo simulations to generate test cases from a parameterised representation. However, the Monte Carlo simulation is a random search and not targetting edge cases. [ 8 ] adopt a fuzzy-logic approach which combines human-like descriptions with degrees of membership to target critical scenarios. By using ISO 34504:2024’s tag-based scenario categorisation [ 25 ] the authors transform an abstract ODD into a concrete, parametrised model describing the possible operating conditions. This motivates an approach that can systematically organize environmental factors, the system description and requirements from the ODD and the task description to represent the combinatorial space of possible autonomous system scenarios.

Formal methods can use formal analysis and falsification tools to generate test scenario(s) and their safety properties described in a formal language such as SCENIC and the SCENIC scenarios can be executed in simulation and analysed [ 26 ] . [ 27 ] generate a statistical model of the system for testing scenarios and skew the model towards critical scenario generation. However, this modelling requires the robot’s behaviour to be accurately statistically modelled across its operational domain which is complex and difficult to capture.

Authors have used evolutionary and genetic algorithms for scenario generation [ 28 , 29 ] . [ 30 ] used a search-based evolutionary algorithm to automatically generate challenging obstacle avoidance scenarios, uncovering failures often missed by manual or random testing. The authors demonstrate that their scenario generation workflow can be integrated into a complex industrial robotics workflow. Their scenarios are similar to ours, laying out obstacles, waypoints and goals. Their workflow generates test scenarios, executes them in simulation, and analyses the results for potential weaknesses. These approaches use random mutations, need extensive configuration and use complex trial and error analyses.

[ 10 ] note that many of the current scenario generation approaches do not provide dynamic adjustment within the scenario generation lifecycle. [ 10 , 6 ] use dynamic adjustment of test scenarios through reinforcement learning based on observed behaviours, enabling the identification of edge cases and high-risk interactions that are often overlooked in static methods. However, RL does not have the world knowledge of LMs, and requires millions of epochs of training and complex reward specification.

There is a lack of automated, compute-efficient tools that map from high-level safety standards onto executable 3D scenarios specified using standardised formats. There has been a body of work generating scenarios for safety assurance using LLMs but many focus on generating visual scenes [ 31 , 32 ] and adversarial behaviour simulation [ 33 , 34 ] . [ 35 ] introduce a pipeline to generate safety-critical scenarios from crash reports and road network diagrams but this requires such datasets to be available. [ 36 ] introduce SERA an LLM pipeline to create targeted scenarios from failure cases by analysing performance logs to pinpoint failure patterns and then retrieving semantically aligned scenarios from a pre-existing database of scenarios. [ 37 ] developed a semi-automated pipeline that transforms operational design domain (ODD) descriptions (text) into executable CARLA simulation scenarios. They decompose the ODD description using structured prompt engineering and reasoning into structured scenario specifications which can be run on simulation platforms, such as CARLA. Their second stage uses a second LLM to refine the scenario using known simulation error patterns and corresponding corrections. They also note that this may require minor manual interventions and adjustments or compensation for missing assets in the simulation. PlannerForge [ 38 ] is also a semi-automated pipeline where the user describes their required scenario in an LLM prompt, the LLM converts this to JSON to systematically describe the user’s intent and creates a scenario using maps and simulated layouts which the user edits. Targeting critical scenarios would require the user to specify critical scenarios in advance.

Our approach is fully automated and does not require prior knowledge of errors, functional gaps or critical scenario examples. Its purpose is to uncover such errors and gaps.
In the following sections, we develop an agentic framework that focuses on edge cases, directly links the ODD to the scenario-generation, does not require prior knowledge of functional gaps or for the entire system and environment to be fully modelled, does not require extensive trial and error testing to fine-tune the scenario generation process, is fully automated and incorporates feedback and dynamic adjustment into the scenario generation process. It is directed by safety assurance processes as we decompose the ODD to a domain ontology with three sections: { environment description, system description, system requirements } and we also supply a { task description } for scenario generation. We represent these as knowledge bases (see Section 4.2 ) which provide information and context in the prompt.

2026-10-12.title: AlphaNIST: Emergent Assembly Skills from Binary Task Rewards
2026-10-12.authors: Octi Zhang , Iretiayo Akinola , Rosario Scalise , Mateo Guaman Castro , Patrick Yin , Tobias Widmer , Miles Macklin , Chris Amevor , Dylan Turpin , Dirk Van Gelder , Jan Carius , Ankur Handa , Gavriel State , Yunrong Guo , Yashraj Narang
2026-10-12.abstract:
The NIST Assembly Task Board #1 remains a challenging benchmark for learning-based methods in robotic manipulation.
Over short horizons, it demands precise, contact-rich control of small, tight-fitting parts.
Over long horizons, it requires recovery and coordination across extended action sequences.
Demonstrations, task decomposition, and dense progress rewards have enabled research advances by providing guidance on how to assemble.
But how much of the strategy must be specified?
The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero showed that RL at scale can discover superhuman strategies without prescribing how to win.
AlphaNIST asks whether a sparse binary task reward and task diversity admitted by this task-agnostic reward can similarly let a robot discover how to assemble.
In simulation, we train a single policy from scratch across all 20 assembly tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board #1, reaching 98.2% overall training success without demonstrations, progress shaping, scripted primitives, or per-task tuning.
The framework also trains policies to complete ten assembly pairs in a single episode without a prescribed order, with task success rewarded only when all ten pairs are simultaneously complete.
The learned policies discover dexterous and planning-like behaviors: choosing grasps for later assembly, using surrounding geometry to reorient parts, and preparing one part, assembling another, then returning to finish the first without an explicit planner.
For videos, see our website: https://alpha-nist.github.io/
2026-10-12.introduction:
Robotic assembly is a longstanding challenge, and the NIST Assembly Task Boards are a persistent benchmark [ 1 ] ; to the best of our knowledge, no learning-based approaches have solved all tasks on any of the boards. Assembly Task Board #1 (ATB1) consists of 20 assembly pair tasks (a part and its fixed mating geometry on the board) that are relevant for manufacturing, including peg insertion, gear meshing, electrical connector insertion, and nut threading.
Solving this task board is exceptionally challenging for three key reasons: (1) The sequence for solving the tasks might be unspecified, and not all sequences may be efficient or valid (e.g., solving task N may obstruct the robot from accessing the parts in task N + 1). (2) Each task is long-horizon, encompassing grasping, transport, and
contact-rich assembly [ 2 ] .
Parts may begin in a wide range of poses and require multiple
reorientations before grasping.
During transport, parts may need further reorientation in-hand or
through extrinsic contact.
During assembly, parts may slip, become misaligned, or
jam during insertion or threading [ 2 ] , requiring
robust recovery and reexecution. (3) Solving the tasks requires precise control during complex contact interactions. The parts themselves are small (as small as 4 mm in diameter), have high geometric detail (e.g., helical threads), and have tight clearances between mating surfaces (as low as zero).
Tasks such as nut threading involve learning helical motion during frictional contact between multiple mating surfaces, during which a nut can tilt, cross-thread, or jam instead of advancing along the bolt [ 2 ] .

Learning-free approaches typically rely on planning and strong human priors:
assembly sequence planning [ 3 ] ; customized fixtures,
adapters, and tooling [ 1 , 4 ] ; engineered
motion and force primitives [ 5 ] ; and tuned admittance,
impedance, or force-motion controllers [ 4 , 5 ] .

Learning-based approaches, on the other hand, can relax some of these constraints, but have shown progress only within a limited scope.
Most efforts have assumed a fixed assembly sequence, heavily constrained the initial poses of parts (e.g., beginning in an already-grasped state) [ 6 ] , assumed access to accurate pose estimates, learned specialist rather than multi-task policies [ 2 ] , addressed only a subset of tasks on the board [ 6 ] , and/or achieved only low-to-moderate success rates by industrial standards.
Success-Guided Sampling (SGS) [ 7 ] , for example, solves tasks one at a time, but requires a separate policy per task and is considerably less compute-efficient.

We draw inspiration from the landmark AlphaGo series in reinforcement
learning, which surpassed the strongest human Go players.
The progression from AlphaGo to AlphaGo Zero
showed that learning from a terminal task objective
could encourage superhuman decision-making over long horizons without human demonstrations [ 8 , 9 ] .
In this paper, we ask whether a similar approach is possible for robotics: can sparse binary task rewards, combined with appropriate training strategies, enable a robot to solve sequences of long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation tasks, perhaps leveraging dexterous behaviors that no human could feasibly specify or demonstrate?
To make learning from sparse task rewards more tractable, we take a seemingly
counterintuitive step: train jointly across heterogeneous assembly pairs differing in geometries, tolerances, and assembly requirements (a nut and its bolt, a gear and its gearshaft, a peg and its hole) from a broad coverage of
initial states, converting MDP diversity into a resource rather than a burden .

Guided by this insight, we develop AlphaNIST, a learning framework that
trains a single policy under sparse binary task rewards across all 20 tasks
on the NIST Assembly Task Board 1 (Fig. 2 ).
The policy handles an exceptional range of initial part poses, learns
from point-cloud inputs without first training specialist policies,
and achieves a 98.2% overall success rate.
Furthermore, the same framework can train policies to complete 10 assembly pairs in
sequence, with a task reward issued only when all pairs are assembled with no prescribed order .
In other words, the policy exhibits planning-like behavior.

Our contributions are the following:

A highly-effective multi-task RL framework consisting of a novel combination of the following components: A) generation of a cache of assembly-relevant reset states [ 10 ] over heterogeneous assembly pairs, B) success-guided sampling within the cache [ 7 ] , C) a unified sparse binary task reward, D) multi-GPU training at scale. These components are supported by careful ablations. All tasks share one training configuration, without per-task tuning or demonstrations.

The first multi-task RL policy capable of solving all 20 tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board 1 . The policy takes point clouds as input; initial part poses are sampled from a wide range, including adverse conditions (e.g., upside-down); and each task can be solved with near-perfect success rates. Positive transfer is observed, where multi-task policies can solve the 20 tasks with higher success rate than individual specialists, including three tasks that the specialists struggle to solve.

The first assembly policy capable of solving up to 10 diverse assembly pairs in sequence , without an explicit hierarchy or prescribed task order. Thus, this work demonstrates that sequencing behavior can emerge within a single low-level assembly policy.

We observe a repertoire of unique emergent behaviors including dexterous skills such as pushing and sliding (to singulate parts), in-hand pivoting, multiple sequential regrasps, extrinsic contact (to reorient parts prior to insertion), and single-gripper nut threading.
The single policy also exhibits long-horizon planning-like behavior such as bringing parts into reach, moving obstructing parts aside, and leaving a task partially-finished and then returning to it later. None of these skills and behaviors were specified.
We encourage readers to watch our supplementary videos 1 1 1 https://alpha-nist.github.io/ for additional examples of these emergent behaviors.
We plan to release our code following the review and revision period.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Scalable Learning for Contact-Rich Assembly

Parallel physics simulation supports experience collection at scale for
on-policy methods such as PPO [ 11 , 12 ] ,
with applications ranging from dexterous in-hand manipulation [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] to industrial assembly.
GPU-accelerated physics engines such as PhysX [ 17 ] and
Newton [ 18 ] support large-scale parallel simulation for robot learning.
For industrial assembly,
Factory [ 2 ] demonstrated real-time or faster simulation of
1,000 simultaneous nut-and-bolt interactions in Isaac Gym, later incorporated into Isaac Lab.
AlphaNIST uses this
simulation throughput to collect experience across heterogeneous assembly pairs.

OmniReset [ 10 ] addressed state coverage through diverse,
manipulation-centric resets, demonstrating long-horizon on-policy RL with fixed
algorithm hyperparameters and no curricula or human demonstrations.
Success-Guided Sampling (SGS) [ 7 ] addressed experience
allocation by concentrating simulation near the policy’s changing capability
frontier, scaling beyond one million parallel environments using sparse rewards.
In its reported assembly experiments, SGS trains a separate policy for
each single task. AlphaNIST retains SGS’s sampling rule but trains one
multi-task policy across all 20 ATB1 tasks under a common binary task reward.
Our experiments show that this shared policy learns assemblies that
remain unsolved in single-task training
(Fig. 5 ).

## II-B Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning

Multi-task RL aims to improve learning by sharing experience across tasks.
However, standard joint-training baselines have achieved lower success
rates than separately trained policies on multi-task manipulation
benchmarks [ 19 ] .
One approach to obtaining a single multi-task policy is to distill
multiple separately trained specialists into a shared
policy [ 20 ] .
Other approaches address the difficulty of joint training directly.
PopArt [ 21 ] addresses differences in reward scales
with a separate value output and normalization statistics for each task,
while PCGrad [ 19 ] removes conflicting components of task
gradients before combining them.
However, Kurin et al. [ 22 ] show that shared-network
baselines with standard regularization and stabilization can match
specialized multi-task optimizers.

AlphaNIST takes a simple approach to multi-task learning by exploiting
the shared structure of assembly: threading, gear meshing, and insertion
all receive the same binary task reward when assembly error falls below
a common threshold. Under this shared objective, we train one
geometry-conditioned policy and one value function with standard PPO
at scale, without task-specific value heads, gradient projection,
or specialist pretraining.

## II-C Learning-Based Robot Assembly

Prior learning-based assembly systems make exploration tractable by shortening
the task horizon or restricting initialization to staged, pre-grasped, or
local-insertion problems [ 23 , 24 ] .
Factory [ 2 ] trains separate pick, place, and screw
subpolicies, while AutoMate [ 20 ] combines
assembly-by-disassembly, imitation learning, and curriculum-based RL to obtain
specialist and generalist assembly policies.
Refinery [ 25 ] improves pretrained assembly specialists
through Bayesian-optimization-guided sampling of initial conditions during
fine-tuning and Gaussian-mixture-model-based initialization at deployment.
The refined policies can then be chained to complete multi-part assemblies.
For longer sequences,
ARCH [ 26 ] uses a high-level imitation-learned policy to select from
a library of RL and model-based primitives. These methods structure learning
through initialization, demonstrations, or prescribed subskills.
OmniReset [ 10 ] uses a generic dense objective with fixed
weights, including gripper–object and object–goal distance terms. Zhang et al. [ 7 ] present the first end-to-end RL solution to individual tasks from the NIST ATB1, but retain task-specific
auxiliary grasp- and gripper-related shaping. Such
terms can aid exploration and discourage reward exploitation, but their relative
influence can change with object size, geometry, and assembly motion. Even with
fixed coefficients, a new task family requires checking that the shaped reward
remains aligned with successful assembly.

AlphaGo Zero provides a broader motivation: terminal win/loss and
search-generated policy targets support strategy discovery without human game
data or intermediate reward shaping [ 9 ] . AlphaNIST asks
whether binary task success can similarly support strategy discovery in continuous,
contact-rich control, with one shared policy learning heterogeneous
assemblies end to end.

2026-10-12.title: NovaSplat: Model-Free 6D Object Pose Estimation via 3D Gaussian Splatting Onboarding and Refinement
2026-10-12.authors: Georgios Floros , Evangelos Sartinas , Orestis Vangelis , Maria Pateraki
2026-10-12.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-12.abstract: 6D pose estimation of novel objects without CAD models remains an open challenge: model-free methods must build the object representation from scratch during onboarding and have long trailed their model-based counterparts. We present NovaSplat, a model-free pipeline that closes this gap. From a short smartphone video captured at onboarding, we train a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model that serves both as a template source for detection and coarse pose estimation and as a differentiable backbone for pose refinement. Our refiner optimizes the object-to-camera pose with combined photometric and geometric losses under a continuous rotation parametrization free of gradient singularities. On a household-object benchmark, NovaSplat surpasses all model-based methods. On a challenging industrial benchmark with textureless and specular surfaces, it outperforms all model-free competitors while substantially narrowing the gap to model-based ones. We further introduce NovaSplat-Lite, an inference variant that is 3.1 × 3.1\times faster at negligible accuracy cost. Code will be made available at https://github.com/POSE-Lab/novasplat .
2026-10-12.introduction:
6D object pose estimation, recovering the full position and orientation of an object relative to a camera, is a core capability for robotic manipulation, augmented reality, and industrial inspection. The highest-performing methods rely on a 3D CAD model of the object: they render templates at many viewpoints and extract geometric point clouds, which are then matched against the query image using powerful frozen foundation models [ 35 , 5 ] . In practice, however, CAD models are rarely available outside controlled environments, making these approaches impractical for real-world deployment. This motivates the model-free setting: given only a short video of a novel object captured during an onboarding phase, estimate its 6D pose in new scenes without any 3D model.

Model-free methods face a fundamental reconstruction problem. Where model-based methods receive the object geometry by definition, model-free methods must recover it from video, a noisier and less complete substitute that degrades every downstream stage, from template rendering to correspondence matching. As illustrated in Figure 1 , this has historically resulted in a substantial performance gap between the two paradigms, limiting the practical utility of model-free approaches.

We propose NovaSplat , a complete model-free pipeline that closes this gap and in some cases reverses it. During onboarding, we reconstruct a dense 3D representation of the object from video and train a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. This representation serves two roles simultaneously: rendering high-quality templates for object detection and coarse pose estimation and acting as a differentiable backbone for gradient-based pose refinement. Our 3DGS refiner freezes the learned scene representation and directly optimizes the object-to-camera pose by jointly minimizing appearance and geometric losses, using a continuous rotation parameterization that avoids singularities. This joint optimization proves considerably more robust than geometry-only refinement under the noisy reconstructions typical of video-based onboarding.

We make the following contributions:

A complete model-free onboarding pipeline that produces a high-quality 3DGS object representation from a short video, enabling model-based pose estimation methods to operate without a CAD model.

A complete model-free onboarding pipeline that produces a high-quality 3DGS object representation from a short video, enabling model-based pose estimation methods to operate without a CAD model.

A novel 3DGS-based pose refiner that jointly optimizes appearance and geometry, advancing model-free pose refinement.

State-of-the-art results on two benchmarks spanning household and industrial objects, demonstrating that model-free methods can match and exceed model-based performance without CAD models.

1. A complete model-free onboarding pipeline that produces a high-quality 3DGS object representation from a short video, enabling model-based pose estimation methods to operate without a CAD model.

2. A novel 3DGS-based pose refiner that jointly optimizes appearance and geometry, advancing model-free pose refinement.

3. State-of-the-art results on two benchmarks spanning household and industrial objects, demonstrating that model-free methods can match and exceed model-based performance without CAD models.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Taxonomy of 6D Object Pose Estimation

Existing 6D object pose estimation methods can be broadly categorized by the level of prior object knowledge they require. Instance-based methods [ 14 , 47 , 43 ] leverage 3D object models during training to achieve high accuracy but are restricted to previously seen objects. Novel object methods [ 35 , 5 , 32 , 29 , 11 , 25 , 18 , 21 , 23 , 55 , 56 , 4 , 49 ] generalize to unseen objects and can be further divided into category-based [ 50 , 46 ] and unseen object approaches. Within the unseen object paradigm, model-based methods [ 35 , 5 , 32 , 28 , 29 , 44 ] require a CAD model at inference time, exploiting geometric priors from rendered templates and 3D point clouds, while model-free methods build an object representation from a short video sequence during an onboarding phase, without any 3D model. This work focuses on the model-free unseen object setting.

## 2.2 Model-Based Novel Object Methods

Several recent methods follow a correspondence-based pipeline over CAD-rendered templates. FoundPose [ 35 ] matches DINOv2 [ 34 ] descriptors between the query and rendered templates but relies solely on visual features. FreeZe [ 5 ] and FreeZeV2 [ 6 ] extend to depth input by fusing visual and geometric (GeDi [ 39 ] ) features for 3D-3D correspondence matching and refine the final pose using the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm, ranking among the top BOP methods. We build directly on FreeZeV2 as our coarse pose estimator. GigaPose [ 32 ] is fast and supports both model-based and model-free settings on single RGB frames, though lacking depth limits its performance on small or occluded objects. GenFlow [ 28 ] and its successor Co-op [ 29 ] refine poses via optical flow and semi-dense correspondences, respectively, the latter using a CroCo-based [ 53 ] ViT with a differentiable PnP layer. Pos3R [ 9 ] likewise matches over CAD-rendered templates, employing MASt3R [ 22 ] , a 3D reconstruction foundation model, to establish dense correspondences, select the best template by feature similarity, and recover pose via PnP-RANSAC, with optional refinement via render-and-compare. WALDO [ 36 ] extends the detect-segment-hypothesize-refine pipeline with dynamic non-uniform sampling, multi-hypothesis inference, and iterative refinement to exhibit robustness under occlusions. All these methods require a 3D CAD model at inference time. NovaSplat operates without one at any stage, replaces ICP with a differentiable 3DGS-based refiner, and surpasses those of them evaluated on HOPEv2 (Table 1).

## 2.3 Model-Free Novel Object Methods

Model-free methods can be organized into three categories. Visual localization approaches [ 44 , 11 ] apply Structure-from-Motion (SfM) during onboarding to build a sparse 3D point cloud, recovering pose via 2D-3D correspondences. They struggle, however, with low-texture objects and large viewpoint changes. Template-based methods [ 25 ] use viewpoint retrieval over posed reference images for a coarse hypothesis before refinement but are sensitive to detection and bounding box quality. Few-shot methods operate from only one or a handful of RGB or RGB-D images: [ 18 ] generate a geometry-aware encoding from a few RGB views, [ 24 ] compress a single RGB-D reference into a pose embedding via latent diffusion, and [ 21 ] combine 2D-3D alignment with render-and-compare refinement from a single RGB-D anchor. Despite their practical appeal, these methods rely on strong assumptions, such as symmetry priors or scale constraints, to compensate for limited onboarding data, restricting generalization across object geometries.

## 2.4 Neural Rendering for Object Pose Estimation

Neural rendering approaches encode objects into differentiable implicit representations for CAD-free novel-view synthesis. Early NeRF-based methods such as LatentFusion [ 38 ] and NeRF-Pose [ 23 ] use latent voxel grids and radiance fields, respectively. BundleSDF [ 55 ] builds a Neural Object Field on-the-fly from an RGB-D stream, concurrently optimizing pose and a 3D representation. FoundationPose [ 56 ] extends this into a unified foundation model supporting both model-based and model-free setups via large-scale synthetic training. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [ 19 ] has largely displaced NeRF-based representations owing to superior rendering quality and real-time speed. GS-Pose [ 3 ] , iG-6DoF [ 4 ] , and 6DOPE-GS [ 17 ] all leverage 3DGS for render-and-compare refinement or online tracking but evaluate primarily on simpler benchmarks (Linemod [ 13 ] , HO3D [ 10 ] , YCBInEOAT [ 54 ] ) without testing on challenging multi-object scenes such as HOPEv2. The work that is most closely related to ours is GFreeDet2 [ 49 ] , which combines a 3DGS onboarding pipeline with template-based coarse pose estimation but relies exclusively on visual features, lacking the geometric integration we show is critical for accurate pose estimation on challenging objects.

2026-10-12.title: Sonic-AMG: Streaming Human Motion Generation from Spatial Audio
2026-10-12.authors: Jingcheng Ni , Zekun Li , Zhiyang Dou , Xiaoyan Cong , Ziyao Zeng , Hongyang Du , Randall Balestriero , Taku Komura , Srinath Sridhar
2026-10-12.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Graphics (cs.GR); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO); Sound (cs.SD)
2026-10-12.abstract:
Modeling human reactions to spatial audio requires understanding both what is heard and where it comes from.
Prior work generates motion offline from complete acoustic and spatial input sequences.
Humans, however, react to sounds without knowing what they will hear next.
We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for streaming human motion generation from spatial audio.
The model encodes acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens.
Conditioned on these tokens, a causal transformer with a flow head generates continuous motion latents, from which a causal decoder reconstructs motion segments.
Standard teacher-forced training derives motion histories and body-relative source locations from ground-truth motion, whereas streaming inference relies on generated motion for both, resulting in a training–inference mismatch. To reduce this history discrepancy, we introduce rehearsal training , which combines full-sequence teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction along short autoregressive self-rollouts.
To keep spatial conditioning consistent with generated motion, we propose spatial feedback , which recomputes body-relative source locations from generated root poses during both rehearsal training and inference.
On SAM, Sonic-AMG achieves state-of-the-art FID and R-precision.
It further supports real-time online generation of coherent reactions across sound events and source locations.
Project page: https://jingchengni.com/sonic-amg/ .
2026-10-12.introduction:
Sound provides information about events beyond the visual field, making it an important cue for embodied interaction ( Chen et al., 2020 ; Chen et al., 2021 ) .
Human reactions to sound depend on both its content and the source’s location relative to the body.
For example, hearing a voice from behind may prompt a listener to turn toward the speaker before the utterance ends and adjust the movement as new acoustic information arrives.
As the listener turns, the source’s direction relative to the body changes. Generating such reactions therefore requires responding as audio arrives and updating spatial conditions as the body moves.

Recent work ( Xu et al., 2025 ) synthesizes complete motion sequences within predefined temporal windows, conditioned on fully observed acoustic and spatial inputs.
Requiring the full input window prevents it from responding causally to an incoming audio stream.
Autoregressive motion models provide a basis for streaming generation by predicting successive motion segments from preceding movements ( Shi et al., 2024 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) .
Extending autoregressive learning to spatial audio requires representations that capture both acoustic content and spatial cues.
Furthermore, streaming generation requires each motion prediction to incorporate the acoustic and spatial information currently available as the input evolves.

We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for streaming human motion generation from continuous spatial audio (Table 1 ).
Motion is represented in the continuous latent space of a pretrained causal temporal VAE ( Xiao et al., 2025 ) . Given a binaural audio stream and the world-space sound source location (SSL), the model
encodes acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens.
At each step, a causal transformer processes the incoming acoustic and spatial conditions together with preceding motion latents.
Its output conditions a flow-matching head that samples the next motion latent, and a causal decoder reconstructs the corresponding motion segment.
Repeating this process extends the motion as audio arrives, without requiring the full audio in advance or revising previously generated frames.

We treat acoustic content and spatial cues as distinct modalities of spatial-audio conditioning.
We hypothesize that early fusion introduces interference between them.
Sonic-AMG therefore encodes them as dedicated what and where tokens, respectively, and learns their interactions within the causal transformer.
With sound source geometry supplied separately, the acoustic branch can focus on sound content rather than a comprehensive description of the binaural signal.
For instance, simple log-mel features in our model yield better results than MOSPA’s 2,272-dimensional audio features ( Xu et al., 2025 ) .
To design the where token, we examine perceptual research to understand how body-relative SSL influences human reactions.
We develop an 11-dimensional spatial event representation inspired by studies of nearby auditory space ( Graziano et al., 1999 ) , sound-source motion ( Warren et al., 2002 ) , and looming ( Neuhoff, 1998 ) .

With acoustic and spatial representations in place, learning the causal generator further requires addressing two sources of training–inference mismatch .
The first concerns motion history: teacher-forced training uses ground-truth histories, whereas autoregressive inference relies on the model’s own predictions.
To reduce this mismatch, two-forward training replaces selected ground-truth inputs with predictions from a preliminary teacher-forced pass ( Mihaylova and Martins, 2019 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) .
However, these replacements are still predicted under ground-truth histories, where later replacements do not depend on earlier sampled outputs.
We introduce rehearsal training , which combines teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction on short histories generated autoregressively by the model.
Training on self-rollouts improves robustness to accumulated prediction errors, while teacher-forced supervision provides a stable learning signal across the full sequence.

The second mismatch arises in spatial conditioning. While acoustic content is directly supplied by the incoming audio stream, body-relative SSL depends on the root position and orientation.
MOSPA uses complete SSL sequences precomputed from recorded motion, which encode information about future ground-truth root motion.
Such conditioning is incompatible with causal streaming generation, which requires SSL to be updated from the generated root.
Training with SSL derived from ground-truth motion therefore creates a mismatch with the spatial conditions encountered at inference.
Our experiments show that this mismatch substantially degrades generation quality.
We therefore introduce spatial feedback , which recomputes body-relative source coordinates after each generated segment during both rehearsal training and inference.
The updated coordinates condition the next prediction, keeping spatial conditions consistent with the generated motion history.

On SAM ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , Sonic-AMG achieves state-of-the-art FID and R-precision.
It further supports causal and online motion generation from streaming spatial audio in real time.
Although trained on individual audio–motion clips, Sonic-AMG can generate coherent motion across successive sound events with varying content and source locations (Fig. Sonic-AMG: Streaming Human Motion Generation from Spatial Audio ), demonstrating robust streaming generation.
Our contributions are:

• We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for causal human motion generation from streaming spatial audio, with dedicated what and where tokens for acoustic content and spatial cues .

• We introduce rehearsal training to address the history mismatch between training and inference, combining teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction from histories constructed through short autoregressive self-rollouts.

• We propose spatial feedback to address the mismatch in spatial conditioning, updating body-relative source coordinates from generated motion during both rehearsal training and inference.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Audio-conditioned motion generation. Music-driven dance methods use autoregressive models to align motion with musical structure, either in pose space or through learned choreographic codes ( Li et al., 2021 ; Siyao et al., 2022 ) .
Diffusion-based approaches support diverse choreography, motion editing, and hierarchical synthesis of long dance sequences ( Alexanderson et al., 2023 ; Tseng et al., 2023 ; Luo et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024a ) .
Diffusion-based visual generation and prediction benefit from complementary conditioning modalities ( Zhang et al., 2023b ; Mou et al., 2024 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) .
Co-speech gesture models combine acoustic, textual, and speaker or style information to generate gestures that match speech content and rhythm ( Yoon et al., 2020 ; Ao et al., 2023 ) .
Diffusion models and learned motion priors capture gesture diversity while coordinating body-part movements ( Zhu et al., 2023 ; Ao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) .
Streaming systems extend these tasks to incoming music and speech ( Saleem et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Vu et al., 2026 ; Ji et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) .
MOSPA ( Xu et al., 2025 ) introduces the SAM dataset of human reactions to spatial audio and a diffusion model conditioned on binaural audio, source coordinates, and reaction style.
Its full-sequence conditioning requires future observations, precluding causal reactions to an incoming audio stream.
MoSAT ( Xu et al., 2026 ) conditions a latent flow-matching model on text, acoustic features, and an initial body-relative sound-source direction.
Streaming generation remains future work.
Sonic-AMG enables real-time causal motion generation from incoming spatial audio, with spatial feedback updating body-relative source geometry.

Causal motion generation. Autoregressive (AR) models use next-token prediction for language modeling ( Brown et al., 2020 ) and image synthesis with discrete visual tokens ( Esser et al., 2021 ) .
Continuous latent representations support diffusion-based and flow-based generation ( Li et al., 2024b ; Ren et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026 ) .
Autoregressive approaches pair a transformer with a conditional diffusion or flow head, including in multimodal language models ( Sun et al., 2026 ) .
In motion synthesis, discrete-token models predict quantized motion codes ( Zhang et al., 2023a ; Jiang et al., 2023 ) , whereas AR diffusion models sample successive frames or motion primitives ( Shi et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Tevet et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) .
Streaming generation in latent space requires decoding segments without future latents.
Systems combining causal decoding with transformer-conditioned generative heads support online text control, two-character interaction, and co-speech gestures ( Xiao et al., 2025 ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) .
Causal decoding alone does not resolve exposure bias: teacher forcing uses recorded histories, whereas inference relies on model predictions.
Diffusion forcing exposes models to contexts at varying noise levels ( Chen et al., 2024a ; Cai et al., 2026 ; Ji et al., 2026 ) , while other strategies introduce model-generated histories ( Bengio et al., 2015 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) .
Two-forward training preserves parallel computation using replacement inputs from a preliminary teacher-forced pass ( Mihaylova and Martins, 2019 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ) .
These replacements do not recursively depend on earlier sampled outputs.
Our rehearsal training retains teacher forcing alongside short autoregressive self-rollouts. The combined objective accounts for error propagation across generated segments while retaining sequence-wide supervision.

2026-10-12.title: What Visual Representations Do World Action Models Need?
2026-10-12.authors: Kai Liu , Jiangran Lyu , Tingyu Deng , Yixin Zheng , Jingtian Wan , Wenbo Cui , Mi Yan , Yizhou Zhou , Haoran Li , Dongbin Zhao , Zhizheng Zhang , He Wang
2026-10-12.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-12.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) inherit powerful priors from pretrained video generation models, but their variational autoencoder (VAE) representations are optimized for visual reconstruction rather than manipulation. Recent studies show that external visual representations improve manipulation performance and robustness. However, these methods select representations based on presumed capability gaps and use different integration mechanisms, making it difficult to disentangle the effects of representation choice and integration. To better understand how external representations strengthen WAMs, we conduct a systematic study through controlled comparisons of multiple visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations. Our study yields three main findings. First, strong general-purpose visual representations provide broader robustness gains and can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities. Second, channel-wise joint prediction achieves the highest average success rate; further analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and the action expert’s effective use of added visual information contribute to its gains. Third, additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they contribute beyond existing representations, as the same source can help one combination but harm another. However, even the best evaluated composition provides a smaller additional gain than the initial improvement from adding a strong general-purpose representation to the VAE-only baseline. We instantiate the resulting R epresentation R ecipe as R 2 -WAM. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop with an 84.7% success rate and reaches 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over the VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Taken together, these findings suggest that future work should prioritize stronger general-purpose visual representations and more effective mechanisms for integrating them into WAMs, with feature composition serving as a supplementary route to improvement.
2026-10-12.introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) adapt pretrained video generation models to robot control by jointly predicting future video and actions. This allows robot policies to draw on the visual structure and temporal dynamics learned through large-scale video pretraining, as demonstrated by DreamZero ( Ye et al., 2026b ) , LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026a ) , and Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Along with these priors, WAMs inherit the latent space of their variational autoencoders (VAEs).

The inherited VAE is optimized for visual reconstruction ( Wan Team et al., 2025 ) , but how well its representations support robot manipulation remains unclear. Its reconstruction objective does not explicitly prioritize manipulation-relevant information, such as object semantics and spatial relationships. Recent studies augment WAMs with external visual features and report improvements in manipulation performance and robustness ( Qiu et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2026a ) . However, these methods select different representations based on prior assumptions about which visual capabilities WAMs lack. Systematic comparisons across representation types remain limited, leaving unclear which visual representations best support robot manipulation in WAMs.

Beyond representation choice, WAM performance also depends on the mechanism used to integrate external features into the model ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . A further question is whether combining more representations leads to continued performance gains. External features can be integrated through representation alignment ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2026 ) , action conditioning ( Wang et al., 2026c ) , or joint prediction ( Yan et al., 2026a ) . Existing studies often couple selected representations with specific integration designs ( Qiu et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) , making the effects of representation choice and integration mechanism difficult to disentangle across methods. Besides, the diverse demands of manipulation—including semantics, geometry, object extent, motion, and interaction—suggest that different representations may be needed. Yet additional sources may also introduce redundant information or interference during optimization. Whether and when different feature combinations improve WAM performance therefore remains an empirical question.

To address these questions, we systematically study visual representations in WAMs, focusing on capabilities, integration mechanisms, and composition. Using a common WAM backbone built on a pretrained video generation model, we compare diverse visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and multiple source combinations under a shared training protocol. Our study addresses three research questions (RQs):

Which visual representations improve WAM performance?

Which feature injection mechanism yields the greatest performance gains from external features?

Does combining more feature sources consistently improve WAM performance?

Our controlled comparisons yield three findings that guide the selection, integration, and composition of external visual representations for WAMs. (1) General-purpose visual representations should be the default choice for augmenting WAMs. They can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities—even under perturbations relevant to those capabilities—while providing broader robustness gains. (2) Channel-wise joint prediction yields the largest average gains across matched sources. Our analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and effective use of the added visual information by the action expert contribute to these gains and should guide future integration designs. (3) Additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they add beyond the existing representations. The same source can improve one combination but provide little benefit or even reduce performance in another. Although feature composition can provide further gains, these are limited compared with the initial improvement. Feature composition should therefore serve as a supplementary route to improvement.

Our contributions are threefold:

A controlled study of visual representations in WAMs. We systematically compare representation sources, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations within a common WAM backbone and shared training protocol, enabling controlled comparisons of their effects on manipulation performance and robustness.

Empirical guidance for WAM representation design. We derive practical recommendations for selecting, integrating, and combining external visual representations. These findings motivate future research on stronger general-purpose visual foundation models and more efficient and effective mechanisms for integrating their representations into WAMs.

R 2 -WAM and validation beyond the controlled study. We instantiate these findings as a R epresentation R ecipe for WAMs, termed R 2 -WAM. We validate the effectiveness of the recipe across different WAM formulations on LIBERO-Plus, and further demonstrate improvements over the corresponding VAE-only baselines on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop and RoboTwin 2.0, as well as in real-world robot experiments.

1. A controlled study of visual representations in WAMs. We systematically compare representation sources, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations within a common WAM backbone and shared training protocol, enabling controlled comparisons of their effects on manipulation performance and robustness.

2. Empirical guidance for WAM representation design. We derive practical recommendations for selecting, integrating, and combining external visual representations. These findings motivate future research on stronger general-purpose visual foundation models and more efficient and effective mechanisms for integrating their representations into WAMs.

3. R 2 -WAM and validation beyond the controlled study. We instantiate these findings as a R epresentation R ecipe for WAMs, termed R 2 -WAM. We validate the effectiveness of the recipe across different WAM formulations on LIBERO-Plus, and further demonstrate improvements over the corresponding VAE-only baselines on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop and RoboTwin 2.0, as well as in real-world robot experiments.
2026-10-12.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

WAMs learn action prediction alongside future visual dynamics. DreamZero ( Ye et al., 2026b ) transfers a pretrained video diffusion backbone to joint video–action generation, and LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026a ) combines autoregressive diffusion with closed-loop visual feedback. Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) shows that video co-training can benefit control even when future video generation is omitted at inference. Other studies modify the visual prediction space or its supervision. LDA-1B ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) learns dynamics in DINO feature space, while LaWAM ( Chen et al., 2026a ) conditions action generation on predicted latent visual subgoals. RepWAM ( Wang et al., 2026b ) and LingBot-VA 2.0 ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) learn semantically aligned visual–action tokenizers. ST-WAM ( Wang et al., 2026c ) diagnoses failures under visual shifts and combines DINO future prediction and history retrieval with VAE dynamics. Robust-WAM ( Yan et al., 2026b ) aligns queries in the action stream with future semantic features while retaining the VAE generation pathway. Flex- π \pi ( Yan et al., 2026a ) jointly denoises RGB latents, 3D pointmaps, DINO features, and actions, supporting different combinations of input and prediction streams at deployment. These studies demonstrate the effectiveness of specific visual representations within their respective WAM designs, but systematic comparisons are still needed to identify which features complement the capabilities that WAMs inherit from pretrained video generators.

Pretraining objectives shape the information captured by visual representations. Visual self-supervision has produced encoders such as DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2026 ) , VC-1 ( Majumdar et al., 2023 ) , LingBot-Vision ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , VideoMAE V2 ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , and V-JEPA 2.1 ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) . Language-associated approaches include image–text models such as CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) and SigLIP 2 ( Tschannen et al., 2025 ) , as well as multimodal language models such as Qwen3.5 ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) . Other pretraining objectives target segmentation with SAM 3 ( Carion et al., 2025 ) , geometry with VGGT- Ω \Omega ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , and interaction-related information with HRP ( Srirama et al., 2024 ) and DynaFLIP ( Lee et al., 2026 ) . UniTok ( Ma et al., 2025 ) and C-RADIOv4 ( Ranzinger et al., 2026 ) further combine multiple learning objectives or teacher models within a single representation. These approaches provide different but overlapping visual capabilities, but how their pretraining emphases translate into manipulation gains in WAMs remains an empirical question.

2026-10-12.title: Reinforcement Learning via Fixed-point Flow Matching
2026-10-12.authors: Denis Blessing , Onur Celik , Gerhard Neumann
2026-10-12.abstract: In maximum entropy and behavior-constrained reinforcement learning (RL), the optimal policy is given by a Boltzmann distribution. Generating samples from this distribution can be challenging, as it is often complex and multimodal. While flow policies trained with flow matching provide a powerful framework for representing such distributions, they traditionally rely on access to training data, which is generally unavailable in online RL. To address this limitation, we propose fixed-point flow matching (FFM), a data-free procedure for training and fine-tuning flow policies in RL. FFM leverages the target flow identity to formulate the actor update as a fixed-point iteration, utilizing a flow-matching-style regression objective where the critic’s action gradients serve as regression targets. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that FFM effectively fine-tunes pretrained flow policies in the offline-to-online setting and enables efficient and accurate training of flow policies from scratch in online RL. These results establish fixed-point flow matching as a principled approach for learning expressive flow-based policies without requiring training data.

In maximum entropy RL, π ⋆ ​ ( x ∣ s ) ∝ exp ⁡ ( Q ⁡ ( s , x ) / λ ) \pi^{\star}(x\mid s)\propto\exp(Q(s,x)/\lambda) is optimal for the policy improvement step of soft policy iteration ( Ziebart et al., 2008 ; Haarnoja et al., 2017 ; Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) ; in KL-regularized and behavior-constrained RL, which includes offline-to-online fine-tuning, the same expression appears tilted by a reference policy ( Peters et al., 2010 ; Abdolmaleki et al., 2018 ; Peng et al., 2019 ; Nair et al., 2020 ) . This target distribution can be complex and multimodal whenever several distinct action choices are viable, but the classical actor–critic recipe projects it onto a Gaussian due to the simplicity of the resulting optimization problem and the tractability of the policy’s log-likelihood ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) . Flow and diffusion models ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Albergo & Vanden-Eijnden, 2023 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) remove this representational restriction and have become the policy class of choice wherever a dataset is available ( Chi et al., 2023 ; Reuss et al., 2023 ; Janner et al., 2022 ; Park et al., 2025b ) . Yet, the stable training objectives that are used to train these models are not directly usable for online RL due to a lack of samples from π ⋆ \pi^{\star} .
Existing methods for training flow and diffusion models in the on-policy RL setting often require backpropagating the critic through the integrator ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Ding & Jin, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Celik et al., 2025 ; Le et al., 2026 ) , whose memory cost grows with every integration step and quickly becomes prohibitive, or rely on importance-weighted regression ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) , whose exponential critic weights have high variance and lead to unstable training updates. Moreover, methods for fine-tuning flow models typically use stochastic optimal control, which requires converting the flow into a diffusion model in order to use the adjoint method ( Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ; Li & Levine, 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026b ) . The adjoint method stores each sampled trajectory and integrates an adjoint state backward along it, leading to complex and expensive update schemes.

In this work we ask whether a flow policy can be trained against a Boltzmann target with the same simple regression that makes flow matching stable, but without samples from the target. Our starting point is the target flow identity : for a Boltzmann target, the velocity field that generates the noised target is, up to a rescaling of the noisy action, a conditional average of the critic’s action gradients ∇ x Q ​ ( s , x ) \nabla_{x}Q(s,x) at clean actions. It replaces the data-derived regression target of flow matching by a critic-derived one, and the resulting objective, target flow matching , has the same minimizer as flow matching while reading its targets off the critic instead of a dataset. Since the objective still averages over samples of the target, we evaluate it with samples of the current policy and iterate. The resulting fixed-point flow matching (FFM) update, illustrated in Figure 1 , generates actions with the current flow, labels them with critic gradients, noises them, and regresses the velocity field onto the labels. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. The whole procedure is conceptually simple, easy to implement and requires neither backpropagation through the integrator nor importance weights or conversion into a diffusion model.

# 2 Related work

Diffusion and flow models entered RL through imitation learning and offline RL, where a dataset makes their standard training objectives applicable and the critic enters through weighting, guidance, or gradients through the sampling chain ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Hansen-Estruch et al., 2023 ; Lu et al., 2023 ; Kang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Ding & Jin, 2024 ; Park et al., 2025b ) . In online RL there are no samples of the target policy, and existing methods differ in how the critic drives the actor update. One line backpropagates the critic value through the sampling chain ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Ding & Jin, 2024 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) , which is memory-intensive and unstable for many integration steps. A second line uses critic-weighted regression, interpreting the denoising loss as a variational bound or as a mirror-descent step ( Ding et al., 2024 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2025 ) , and a third estimates policy gradients through the denoising process, typically under a trust region ( Ren et al., 2025 ; McAllister et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Le et al., 2026 ; Lv et al., 2026 ) . Closest to FFM are methods that use the action gradient of the critic: DIPO ( Yang et al., 2023 ) clones actions improved by gradient ascent on Q Q ; QSM ( Psenka et al., 2024 ) regresses the score onto ∇ x Q \nabla_{x}Q evaluated at the noisy action, a plug-in approximation of the target score identity that is exact only at the clean end; and RFM ( Li et al., 2026 ) estimates the exact posterior-mean target by self-normalized importance sampling, using Langevin–Stein control variates to interpolate between Q Q -weighted noise averages and Q Q -weighted averages of ∇ x Q \nabla_{x}Q , which allows it to train flow policies as well. Maximum entropy RL with generative policies additionally requires an entropy estimate: DACER ( Wang et al., 2024 ) fits a Gaussian mixture, DIME ( Celik et al., 2025 ) and MaxEntDP ( Dong et al., 2025 ) use a lower bound and numerical integration, respectively, Sanokowski & Patil (2025) augment the MDP with the denoising steps, FLAG ( Kim et al., 2026 ) uses importance sampling in the latent space of the flow, and AMDP ( Thilges et al., 2026 ) amortizes the entropy-regularized update with adjoint matching. FFM obtains the entropy from the divergence of the velocity field it trains, using the instantaneous change of variables.

Reward fine-tuning of pretrained diffusion and flow models has been cast as policy gradient over the denoising chain ( Fan et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) and as entropy-regularized stochastic optimal control ( Uehara et al., 2024 ; Domingo-Enrich et al., 2025 ) , with the KL divergence to the pretrained model as regularizer; Uehara et al. (2025) review the corresponding inference-time methods. The same behavior-tilted target governs offline-to-online RL with flow policies. FQL ( Park et al., 2025b ) distills the flow into a one-step policy that is trained by reparameterized critic gradients, DSRL ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) keeps the flow fixed and learns a policy over its latent noise, ReinFlow and FINO ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Shin et al., 2026b ) inject noise into the flow to obtain tractable likelihoods and exploration, and Q-Flow ( Doo et al., 2026 ) propagates terminal values to intermediate states of the flow. QAM ( Li & Levine, 2026 ) imports adjoint matching: the pretrained flow is converted into a memoryless SDE and critic gradients are transported backward along sampled trajectories by the lean adjoint ODE, and TRQAM ( Dong et al., 2026b ) stabilizes it with a path-space trust region. Concurrent work regresses velocity corrections onto critic gradients ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Ziakas et al., 2026 ) or steers a fixed flow policy at test time ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Ruan et al., 2026 ) . FFM fine-tunes the pretrained flow directly in velocity space, requires neither SDE conversion nor adjoint simulation, and its behavior-tilted target has the KL-regularized optimum as a fixed point ( Appendix E ).

Beyond the RL literature, FFM shares the fixed-point structure of the matching objectives used to train diffusion and flow models from unnormalized densities, and of adjoint matching; Appendix C discusses these methods, together with further critic-driven policy updates.

2026-10-12.abstract: Autonomous small-body proximity operations require continuous-thrust guidance under uncertain gravity, solar-radiation pressure (SRP), and stochastic disturbances. We combine iterative covariance steering (iCS) with ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} distributionally robust adaptive control ( ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} -DRAC) to provide risk-aware collision avoidance despite mismatch between the nominal planning model and the true dynamics. Iterative covariance steering plans a nominal feedback policy satisfying distributionally robust conditional value-at-risk keep-out constraints, while ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} -DRAC compensates for dynamics uncertainty and bounds the residual distributional mismatch through a Wasserstein radius used by the planner. In 𝟏𝟎𝟎𝟎 \mathbf{1000} paired Monte Carlo trials with gravity, SRP, and diffusion mismatch, ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} -DRAC adaptive control reduces the keep-out violation rate from 32.7 % \mathbf{32.7\%} to 0.2 % \mathbf{0.2\%} and the physical collision rate from 16.4 % \mathbf{16.4\%} to zero, without actuator saturation.

Small-body proximity guidance must accommodate weak nonlinear gravity, uncertain solar-radiation pressure (SRP), and strict collision-avoidance requirements. Covariance-steering methods have addressed stochastic small-body guidance using chance constraints and impulsive control [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , while sequential covariance steering has enabled continuous low-thrust guidance in cislunar dynamics [ 4 ] . These approaches, however, rely on a specified planning model and can lose their safety guarantees under persistent dynamics mismatch. architecture uses ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} -DRAC to compensate for uncertain dynamics and to bound the residual state-distribution
mismatch. This bound directly defines the Wasserstein ambiguity
radius used to robustify the iCS safety constraint.

2026-10-12.title: Mind the Temporal Gap: Evaluating Video Models for Temporal Understanding in Driving
2026-10-12.authors: Shiva Sreeram , Erfan Aasi , Tsun-Hsuan Wang , Alaa Maalouf , Daniela Rus
2026-10-12.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-12.abstract: Modern video-language models are increasingly treated as general-purpose video reasoners, yet it remains unclear whether they robustly capture temporal dynamics in safety-critical settings such as driving. We study this question through controlled ego-motion tasks that require identifying actions from driving videos. Across video-language models, we find that standard prompting, visual prompting, few-shot prompting, and chain-of-thought prompting remain unreliable and highly task- and model-dependent, with persistent class biases, although newer models show substantial task-specific few-shot gains. In contrast, lightweight LoRA finetuning and simple probes trained on intermediate visual features recover strong motion-discriminative performance, indicating that motion-relevant cues are often present inside the models but are not reliably used by the final video-to-language pathway. These results suggest that, in driving, current video-language models remain unreliable temporal reasoners and often behave more like frame-level, bias-driven recognizers than dependable temporal world models.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Video models have undergone a rapid transformation in the last few years: from task-specific action recognizers to large-scale, spatiotemporal encoders trained with increasingly general objectives [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . This evolution mirrors a central trend in modern machine learning: replacing narrowly engineered pipelines with large-scale models that can transfer across tasks, data regimes, and forms of supervision [ 4 , 5 ] . In the video domain, early progress established that attention-based architectures over space and time can rival, and in some cases outperform, classical 3D convolutional approaches for visual understanding [ 6 , 7 ] . Later, self-supervised pretraining, made video representations more data-efficient and transferable [ 2 ] , and more recent “video foundation” efforts aim to provide general-purpose spatiotemporal representations across diverse downstream tasks [ 3 ] . In parallel, aligning visual representations with language has produced large video-language models (VidLLMs) that can caption, answer questions, and follow instructions over video inputs in a largely open-ended manner [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] , leading to a direct trend of video understanding inherited applications [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] .

This progress has fueled a natural hypothesis: if VidLLMs can describe what happens in a video, do they serve as world models , i.e., internal predictive representations that capture how the world evolves over time [ 20 , 21 ] .
Indeed, benchmark suites such as MVBench, Video-MME, and MMBench-Video report steady improvements and have become standard instruments for measuring video-language understanding [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] .
However, a missing (and practically consequential) question remains: do today’s VidLLMs genuinely reason about temporal dynamics, or do they behave primarily as strong frame-based models whose outputs are only weakly constrained by time? Recent evidence suggests that commonly used video QA benchmarks can contain substantial spatial and textual shortcuts, where single frames, shuffled frames, or language priors can explain a surprising fraction of performance [ 25 ] .
Concurrently, new benchmarks targeting spatio-temporal grounded reasoning indicate that even strong models may fail to reliably align their reasoning with when and where evidence occurs [ 22 , 26 , 27 ] .

Autonomous driving makes this gap especially stark.
Driving scenes are fundamentally dynamic : safe behavior depends on inferring ego-motion (forward/backward, left/right), as well as acceleration and deceleration, from temporally evolving cues.
Large-scale driving datasets (e.g., nuScenes and Waymo Open Dataset) therefore emphasize sequential, time-synchronized sensing precisely because motion and interaction are central to the task [ 28 , 29 ] .
Motivated by the promise of natural-language interfaces for driving agents, recent work has begun integrating vision-language models into driving-centric reasoning and interaction pipelines [ 18 , 30 ] .
Yet, despite this momentum, it is still unclear whether general-purpose VidLLMs can robustly infer even basic ego-vehicle dynamics from videos—a prerequisite for treating them as reliable video reasoning engines in the loop.

This paper provides an experimental study of temporal motion reasoning in driving-focused video understanding. We design controlled prompts and evaluations that isolate basic ego-dynamics and ask whether VidLLMs can infer them from video segments. We then probe a spectrum of intervention levels—from basic prompting to adaptation (fine-tuning)—and complement behavioral evaluation with representation-level diagnostics.

Driving-focused temporal reasoning protocol. We propose a targeted evaluation suite for ego-motion primitives (forward/backward, left/right) and longitudinal dynamics (acceleration/deceleration) from third-person car video.

Finally, (7) we train small probing models on features extracted from different layers of the VidLLM as detailed next.

Where is motion information preserved or lost? We probe intermediate visual features and find that motion cues may be preserved, strengthened, or degraded across architectures. Several models retain highly discriminative representations immediately before the language model despite poor prompted predictions, pointing to a downstream reasoning and generation bottleneck.

A glimpse into our findings. Our main contribution is a striking set of empirical observations. Across the tested VidLLMs, we see a consistent pattern:

a. VidLLM ego-motion predictions remain highly model- and task-dependent under prompting , with persistent class biases and poor forward/backward discrimination .

b. More elaborate/sophisticated prompting including structured guided templates and step-by-step reasoning instructions, typically improves fluency (outputs become more coherent and confident) but does not universally improve temporal correctness , where some newer models can be elicited into much better performance, but the gain fails to transfer consistently across ego-motion categories.

c. Adaptation can unlock motion reasoning: lightweight LoRA fine-tuning can reliably turn these models into robust motion reasoners , suggesting that the underlying architectures can represent temporal cues and that a key bottleneck is the availability/quality of supervision (used data and training procedure) for dynamics.

d. Finally, layer-wise probing shows that motion information remains strongly decodable before the language model, yet is not reliably reflected in final predictions, indicating a gap between visual representation and language-based reasoning.

Together, these caution against treating off-the-shelf VidLLMs as reliable video world models for driving without explicit temporal grounding and dynamics-aware training.
