# II Probing via Different Levels.

## II-A Prompt-Level Probing Strategies

(1) Standard prompt probing. We provide a set of binary questions depending on the scenario where we simply query the model what type of motion is being taken by the car in the video. This follows prompting strategies in related probing works [ 31 ] to obtain the results.

(2) Visual prompting : Here we aim to guide the models’ reasoning by choosing a static object in every video and placing a green bounding box. The objective is to extend task prompting to the image domain which has shown success in foreground segmentation and single object detection [ 32 ] . This box is placed via open-set detection, tracking, and following [ 33 ] . This test reveals whether highlighting a stable spatial anchor helps the model correctly infer motion by focusing its attention on consistent visual reference points.

(3) Fusion of visual and text : Here we aim to improve the models’ capabilities by providing an example of two types of motions (i.e. forward and backward) before providing the final video. This is an application of few-shot learning, which aims to generalize reasoning from a few examples [ 34 ] . Here, we evaluate whether the model can internalize simple motion patterns from a small number of demonstrations and generalize them to unseen videos.

(4) Chain-of-thoughts : Here, we aim to guide the model through the scenario such that we ensure the model understands how changes in the background can be reasoned through via chain-of-thoughts [ 35 ] . This is combined with the few-shot approach where it is explained to the model the way in which the cases can be identified to be a specific type of motion. In our videos, we would observe the way in which the static object shifting through the scene can lead to the correct interpretation of the motion. For example, the size of a static object in the background increasing means that the object is getting closer, which means that the ego is moving forward. This test assesses whether explicit step-by-step reasoning enables the model to connect background changes to vehicular motion, thereby compensating for missing implicit temporal understanding.

(5) Chain-of-thoughts with visual prompting : This aims to combine all of the prompt level strategies in order to provide the best reasoning capabilities to the model. In essence, the visual prompting approach of surrounding a static object with a bounding box is provided, with chain-of-thoughts reasoning to guide the model in understanding the way in which the bounding box shifts enables understanding of the motion. For example, the size of the bounding box in the background increasing means that the static object is getting closer, which means that the ego is moving forward. Through this probing technique, we examine whether combining structured reasoning with a visual reference object yields synergistic improvements in motion understanding beyond what either cue provides alone.

(6) LoRA finetuning : To evaluate whether the video-language models possess latent representational structure that can be unlocked through lightweight adaptation, we apply Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) [ 36 ] to finetune the model on our driving-motion dataset. LoRA introduces trainable low-rank matrices into the attention and projection layers while freezing the original model weights, enabling efficient specialization without altering the underlying pretrained parameters. During training, each video is paired with its ground-truth label, and the LoRA modules update rank- r r adapters on top of pretrained weights.

Comparing the pre- and post-compression probes allows us to distinguish between two possible failure modes. If motion information is recoverable before compression but lost afterward, the visual-to-language compression stage itself may be discarding task-relevant information. Conversely, if ego-motion remains highly decodable after compression but the model still fails under natural-language prompting, this suggests that the information survives into the representation available to the language model but is not reliably accessed or converted into the correct linguistic prediction.

2026-10-12.title: Imagine the Future, Internalize the Gist: Efficient VLA Reasoning via Internalized Spatiotemporal Imagination
2026-10-12.authors: Shenglan Li , Zhendong Mi , Hengyi Zhu , Jingwu Luo , Chun Kit Chan , Geng Yuan , Yanzhi Wang , Pu Zhao , Shaoyi Huang
2026-10-12.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-12.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models increasingly incorporate intermediate reasoning to improve robotic manipulation, yet existing approaches primarily reason about observed states without explicitly anticipating future scene evolution. Extending such reasoning to explicit future rollouts at every inference step, however, introduces substantial computational overhead. We propose IG-VLA , a VLA reasoning framework that enables models to i magine the future and internalize the g ist . Our Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning learns to imagine task-relevant future scene evolution directly in visual representation space, guiding action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation. To further reduce inference overhead, we introduce Scene Gist Memory , which internalizes reasoning-derived scene–behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token, preserving the benefits of future reasoning while bypassing explicit future imagination at inference. Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of IG-VLA. On the LIBERO-Plus Language suite, both the reasoning and gist policies outperform the strongest baseline by nearly 6% in success rate. The gist policy also achieves up to 6.38 × 6.38\times speedup over baselines, reducing inference latency from 1,081 ms to 169.5 ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000 GPU. These results demonstrate that future spatiotemporal reasoning can be effectively internalized for efficient VLA deployment.
2026-10-12.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models enable general-purpose robotic manipulation by mapping multimodal observations and language instructions to actions Guan et al. (2025) ; Li et al. (2025a) ; Li et al. (2025b) ; Sapkota et al. (2025) ; Wang et al. (2025) .
However, learning an effective end-to-end mapping from multimodal perception to robotic actions requires extensive, high-quality demonstration data Liu et al. (2025a) ; Ma et al. (2026) .
To address this challenge, recent VLA models adopt a “think-before-acting” paradigm through Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning Guo et al. (2025b) ; Ye et al. (2025) ; Yin et al. (2025) .By reasoning over task goals, visual observations, and object relations before execution, these models decompose complex instructions and adapt action plans to environmental feedback.

Existing VLA paradigms
include language-based reasoning Zawalski et al. (2024) ; Lee et al. (2025) ; Qu et al. () ; Huang et al. (2026a) , which carry out reasoning in language domain and reasoning in vision ,
exemplified by CoT-VLA’s decomposition of predicted goals into visual subgoals Zhao et al. (2025a) and
VLA-Thinker’s repeated incorporation of intermediate state images Wang et al. (2026) .
As shown in Figure 1 (a), language-based reasoning loses fine-grained visual details and achieves lower success rates.
In contrast, incorporating updated visual information during reasoning can mitigate drift from the actual environment Wang et al. (2026) (Figure 1 (b)).

In general, existing approaches face two limitations: (i) reliance on observed states rather than future predictions, and (ii)
substantial computational overhead from repeated reasoning rollouts.
Specifically, existing approaches primarily reason over observed states and plan subsequent actions based on the current environment, without explicitly anticipating how the environment may evolve under different decisions. Meanwhile,
reasoning in VLA models need to perform full spatiotemporal reasoning rollouts repeatedly at every inference step, introducing substantial computation overhead.

To address these issues, we propose a visual reasoning framework for VLA models with two core mechanisms: latent spatiotemporal reasoning and scene gist memory .
Latent spatiotemporal reasoning
enables the model to imagine future scene evolution in visual representation space, exploring plausible action trajectories and their potential outcomes.
These imagined futures guide action selection, as shown in Figure 1 (b).
It is inspired by human reasoning process, which imagines how a scene might unfold under different candidate actions and makes decisions based on expected consequences Atance and O’Neill (2001) .
For example, when crossing a street, we consider multiple possible futures conditioned on our own actions such as crossing, waiting, or speeding up, then choose the safest action.
This anticipation
evaluates candidate behaviors through the imagined consequences rather than merely extrapolating scene evolution independently of actions Conti and Irish (2021) .

To reduce computational overhead, our proposed Scene Gist Memory internalizes reasoning-derived scene–behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token . This token captures general scene context and corresponding action patterns rather than preserving the complete future reasoning trajectory. During inference, the gist encoder predicts the Scene Gist directly from the current context, allowing the model to bypass the explicit future-reasoning pathway while retaining reasoning-derived behavioral guidance (Figure 2 ).
It’s inspired
by human behavioral psychology that repeated
experience
in familiar environments
helps consolidate learned behaviors into procedural memory involving the basal ganglia Wulf et al. (2010) ; Wood and Rünger (2016) .
This memory supports rapid responses with less deliberation, reducing cognitive effort and decision time.
For example, familiarity with a home allows a person to head directly to the kitchen for coffee without searching the entire house. Repeated experience reinforces the association between the familiar scene and the corresponding navigation behavior.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

Our framework incorporates Latent Spatiotemporal Reasoning , enabling VLA models to learn to imagine task-relevant scene evolution in visual representation space. These anticipated scene dynamics guide action prediction without costly pixel-level video generation.

We further introduce Scene Gist Memory , which internalizes reasoning-derived scene–behavior associations into a compact Scene Gist Token. It enables the model to
reuse this knowledge in corresponding scenarios, preserving reasoning benefits while bypassing explicit future imagination and full reasoning rollouts at inference.

Extensive experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and VLABench demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our framework.
For example, IG-VLA achieves an 85.6% success rate on LIBERO-Plus’s challenging Language suite, outperforming the strongest baseline by nearly 6%.
Meanwhile, the gist policy requires only 169.5 ms per action chunk on a single NVIDIA A6000, achieving 6.38 × 6.38\times , 1.78 × 1.78\times and 1.55 × 1.55\times speedups over FastWAM-IDM (1,081 ms), FastWAM (1-step) (302 ms) and ImageWAM (263 ms), respectively.

2026-10-15.title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
2026-10-15.authors: Shaoyuan Xie , Zihan Zhang , Jingxuan Wang , Jiashu Qu , Xiaoqing Liang , Lingdong Kong , Junchi Lu , Henrik I. Christensen , Qi Alfred Chen
2026-10-15.comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-15.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose \texorpdfstring \pdfxform 4 SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. \texorpdfstring \pdfxform 4 SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Autonomous driving has shifted from modular pipelines [ 78 , 90 , 63 ] to end-to-end (E2E) systems [ 27 , 34 ] , where the latest generation of E2E models, Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs), further widens the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions [ 68 , 86 , 117 , 115 ] . VLAs are also entering production vehicles: Li Auto has rolled out its VLA driver model to customer cars [ 46 ] , and NVIDIA is bringing its Alpamayo VLA [ 86 ] to production in the Mercedes-Benz CLA [ 45 ] . This progression reduces inter-module error accumulation and scales better with large driving datasets, but also removes the explicit safety mechanism that once resolved conflicts between the navigation signal and the local scenarios.

Shown in Fig. 1 , classical modular stacks routed the navigation signal through a rule-based behavior planner [ 90 , 17 , 71 ] that resolved it against local context, such as traffic lights and pedestrians, before making driving decisions. E2E systems instead internalize this judgment into the neural network, leaving the model to learn from data alone whether to follow or delay a given navigation signal. VLAs amplify this difficulty, as the navigation interface becomes an open-ended language space.

In this work, we present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, since a model that ignores every instruction looks safe on a conflict benchmark, while one that follows every instruction looks good on a following benchmark. It covers (i) navigation following (CARLA-F), a closed-loop CARLA benchmark with traffic disabled so every navigation signal should be executed; (ii) navigation-scene conflict (B2D-C and NavSim-C), unsafe instructions or commands triggered at safety-critical events; and (iii) adversarial instructions (B2D-Adv), unsafe under any circumstance. This split mirrors the helpfulness–harmlessness trade-off in LLM alignment [ 4 , 13 ] . Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes none of its language-instructed lane changes in closed loop despite an 83% open-loop rate [ 68 ] , and all models degrade drastically under conflicting signals, executing them without grounding in the scene.

Next, we propose \texorpdfstring \pdfxform 4 SafeDriveVLA, to our knowledge, the first driving VLA that (i) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (ii) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. First, we relabel every expert frame with a mode ( strict , cautious , or fallback ) for whether the expert executes, cautiously follows, or overrides the signal, and emit this mode token before the action tokens, so conflict reasoning is directly supervised rather than entangled with action generation. Second, unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, our world model dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing the model when following is safe and making it less conservative than with the mode token alone. \texorpdfstring \pdfxform 4 SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% over the best SimLingo variant, and decreases B2D-C collisions from 60 to 38. Our contributions are: (1) Benchmarks for navigation following and navigation-scene conflict awareness; (2) Design of explicit navigation-compliance modes that decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and of navigation-conditioned world model dreaming that shows when following is safe; and (3) Evaluation on Bench2Drive and all our benchmarks.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Language–Action Alignment for Autonomous Driving

VLAs extend VLMs with an action head, carrying semantic reasoning into driving models [ 35 , 25 ] and enabling instruction following beyond a fixed command set. DriveBench [ 92 ] shows that plausible language outputs can rely on textual cues or general knowledge without reliable visual grounding, motivating evaluation beyond answer fluency. Recent VLAs pursue instruction following through action dreaming [ 68 ] , driver-preference alignment [ 88 ] , scaled instruction-following data [ 117 ] , and related designs [ 74 , 94 , 31 , 83 , 103 , 10 , 18 , 113 , 115 ] . NoRD [ 67 ] explores data-efficient driving without dense reasoning annotations. We instead study both sides of this capability, training a VLA to reliably follow safe navigation signals and to recognize when a navigation signal conflicts with the surrounding scene.

Early language-driven systems already connect semantic reasoning with driving decisions. DriveGPT4 [ 97 ] interprets driving actions and predicts low-level control signals. Dolphins [ 59 ] studies grounded conversational reasoning and reflection, while DriveVLM [ 77 ] couples scene analysis with hierarchical planning. DriveMLM [ 12 ] maps multimodal reasoning into explicit behavioral planning states, and RDA-Driver [ 30 ] constrains the correspondence between reasoning traces and planning outputs. LinkVLA [ 85 ] further aligns language and action through a shared codebook and bidirectional supervision. These mechanisms address decision representation and consistency; our mode token explicitly indicates whether the requested maneuver should be executed, delayed, or overridden. DriveTeach-VLA [ 100 ] strengthens action-grounded visual representations, and complementary VLM/vision-only systems [ 1 ] exploit their different strengths across driving scenarios.

## 2.2 World Models and Prospective Action Reasoning

Driving world models split broadly into pixel-space generation [ 26 , 84 , 87 , 49 , 69 ] and latent-state prediction [ 75 , 58 , 50 , 47 , 109 , 56 ] . WorldLens [ 54 ] evaluates visual, geometric, physical, and behavioral fidelity, emphasizing that realistic generation alone does not establish reliable control. The agentic world-modeling taxonomy [ 11 ] further emphasizes action-conditioned simulation and decision-centric evaluation. Latent designs typically roll out under the offline-collected expert action: LCDrive [ 75 ] and Uni-World VLA [ 57 ] interleave world-state and action prediction inside a unified VLA, and OneVL [ 58 ] predicts latent futures before acting. A second line rolls out under candidate intentions drawn from the policy or a trajectory vocabulary [ 109 , 56 ] and evaluates the predicted future. Drive-JEPA [ 82 ] combines predictive video representations with multimodal trajectory distillation, while Vault [ 95 ] couples single-step latent trajectory generation with evaluator-guided training and candidate scoring. We condition the rollout on the action implied by the navigation signal to expose navigation–scene conflicts.

Recent methods reason about action consequences before execution. CF-VLA [ 65 ] revises proposed meta-actions using counterfactual reasoning over the visual context, while VLA-World [ 81 ] reasons over generated future images to refine trajectories. DriveWorld-VLA [ 32 ] integrates action-conditioned world states with the planner in a shared latent space. AD-R1 [ 98 ] trains a world-model critic on synthesized dangerous outcomes to reduce optimistic forecasts during policy refinement, and ExploreVLA [ 73 ] uses dense future prediction and uncertainty-based, safety-gated exploration. CoWorld-VLA and DriveDreamer-Policy [ 28 , 114 ] integrate complementary world representations or explicit geometry with action planning. CausalDrive [ 99 ] studies reactive, action- and text-conditioned video simulation for closed-loop evaluation and policy training. Our dreamed latents inform an explicit instruction-conflict decision before action generation. Action-conditioned forecasting does not by itself establish event-specific causal counterfactual prediction [ 105 ] ; we use dreaming as a prospective decision aid.

Generative distillation also studies supervision on model-generated states. DanceOPD [ 112 ] composes capability-specific velocity fields through distillation at student-induced states. DiffusionOPSD [ 111 ] constructs reward-guided targets for clean-output predictions during diffusion post-training. In \texorpdfstring \pdfxform 4 SafeDriveVLA, imagined states serve a decision-making role: a frozen predictor exposes the consequences of a navigation-conditioned action anchor to inform conflict reasoning.

## 2.3 Robust Perception and Safety-Aware Driving

Early safety work targeted perception-level robustness and adversarial attacks [ 70 , 80 , 8 , 93 , 38 , 91 ] . LargeAD [ 42 ] and multimodal data-efficient scene understanding [ 43 ] improve cross-sensor representations and reduce annotation dependence, while Pi3DET [ 53 ] and 3EED [ 48 ] study cross-platform 3D detection and language grounding. Complementary corruption benchmarks study HD map construction [ 22 ] and monocular depth estimation [ 40 ] . Physics-informed, geometry-grounded weather synthesis [ 66 ] provides a complementary approach to improving perception robustness through adverse-weather augmentation.

World modeling also extends to structured spatial representations: DynamicCity and DOME [ 6 , 20 ] study dynamic semantic occupancy generation and trajectory-controllable occupancy forecasting, respectively, LiDARCrafter [ 55 ] models temporal LiDAR sequences, and U4D [ 96 ] incorporates uncertainty into 4D LiDAR generation. Such representations complement image and latent prediction by capturing scene geometry and temporal structure. For instruction-conditioned driving, reliable perception supplies the evidence needed to interpret a maneuver in context: road layout, surrounding agents, and evolving hazards can determine whether the same request remains feasible. Improvements in scene representation therefore support conflict reasoning, although representation quality alone does not determine how a policy should respond to an unsafe request.

SafeAuto [ 106 ] verifies predicted actions against logic-encoded traffic rules. DriveSafe’s risk-detection framework [ 2 ] identifies scene-grounded hazards and generates safety suggestions, while VLM-AutoDrive [ 5 ] adapts VLMs to temporally localized collisions and near-collisions. A separate DriveSafe taxonomy [ 44 ] evaluates unsafe requests to LLM-based driving assistants. SafeDrive [ 36 ] evaluates fine-grained risks in trajectory-conditioned sparse worlds, while safety-case patterns for SimLingo [ 102 ] organize evidence for instruction-based driving safety. In robotic manipulation, SafeDojo [ 76 ] separates task rewards and safety costs during world-model-based policy learning. These settings cover complementary aspects of rule compliance, hazard recognition, and response safety.

## 2.4 Navigation and Grounded Driving Evaluation

Related embodied-navigation studies connect visual imagination with control. Language-conditioned world modeling [ 16 ] studies learning policies in imagined latent space and jointly predicting actions and observations, while UniWM [ 15 ] combines visual foresight with memory-augmented planning. These settings focus on reaching navigation goals; our benchmark explicitly tests whether a requested maneuver is safe in the current scene.

For driving VLAs, the same instruction can be safe or unsafe depending on the scene where it executes. LMDrive [ 72 ] injects misleading instructions uniformly along the route, and ICR-Drive [ 21 ] studies instruction counterfactual robustness. Our benchmarks place conflicting instructions at safety-critical events and measure the resulting driving behavior.

The RoboDrive and RoboSense challenges [ 41 , 39 ] extend robustness evaluation across adverse sensing conditions, language-grounded decisions, navigation, and platform shifts. Bench2Drive-Robust [ 107 ] tests closed-loop deployment perturbations, while ReactSim-Bench [ 108 ] measures surrounding agents’ responses to ego behaviors that differ from the recorded log. Existing benchmarks assess different links between visual evidence, reasoning, and action. LingoQA [ 60 ] measures the truthfulness of driving-video answers, while Reason2Drive [ 62 ] evaluates perception–prediction–reasoning chains. DriveBench [ 92 ] diagnoses reliability under visual and textual perturbations, and DriveAction [ 23 ] connects real driving operations with high-level action labels and action-rooted evaluation. MSSBench [ 110 ] , SCD-Bench [ 104 ] , and DSBench [ 61 ] assess situational safety or driving risks through model responses. These evaluations establish important tests of grounding and risk awareness, but a correct explanation or discrete action answer does not establish safe execution. We evaluate navigation following, navigation–scene conflict, and adversarial instructions through closed-loop CARLA driving and real-world NavSim data, measuring the consequences of the policy’s actions.

2026-10-15.title: Hierarchical Residual Policy Learning for Real-World Mobile Manipulation with Sparse Human Guidance
2026-10-15.authors: Zhefei Gong , Hefeifei Jiang , Zehao Wang , Jiachen Li
2026-10-15.comment: Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026); Project Website: this https URL
2026-10-15.abstract:
Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning remains a formidable challenge because of high-dimensional action spaces and intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules.
In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa ( Hi erarchical Re sidual Mo bile Ma nipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems.
At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy.
A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform’s physical hierarchy.
To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we propose Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20% training coverage
to reshape the critic’s value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors.
Extensive real-world experiments on the TIAGo++ platform demonstrate that HiRe-MoMa consistently enhances task performance with only around 30 minutes of online interaction, regardless of the base policy architecture.
To our knowledge, this is among the first frameworks to enable efficient on-robot fine-tuning for mobile manipulation in the real world, providing a practical paradigm for deploying complex robotic systems in dynamic, human-centric environments.
Further details can be found on our project website .
2026-10-15.introduction:
Mobile manipulation is a key step toward multi-purpose robotic systems that operate in human-centric environments.
Performing long-horizon and multi-object tasks, from domestic chores to industrial logistics, requires the coordinated operation of heterogeneous modules such as mobile bases, robotic arms, and sensory heads.
Despite its potential, autonomous mobile manipulation remains challenging due to high-dimensional action spaces, tightly coupled inter-module dynamics, and the non-stationarity of real-world deployment.
Recent advancements have leveraged Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for semantic reasoning [ 45 , 23 , 60 , 56 , 5 ] , generative modeling for robust imitation learning [ 25 , 12 ] , and simulation-to-real reinforcement learning for skill acquisition [ 18 ] .
However, a single-shot trained policy often fails to generalize to the stochasticity of diverse real-world deployment scenarios.
Post-training or fine-tuning is thus essential to bridge the performance gap. While fine-tuning has seen success in isolated manipulation or locomotion tasks [ 1 , 48 ] , its application to the coupled, high-dimensional domain of mobile manipulation remains largely unexplored.

Real-world fine-tuning, however, is shaped by a series of fundamental trade-offs.
Imitation learning (IL), particularly DAgger-based approaches [ 43 ] , offers a straightforward optimization objective but is constrained by inherent expert data scarcity and a lack of autonomous exploration, which often leads to limited generalization on out-of-distribution states and compounding errors at deployment.
Reinforcement learning (RL) enables broader state-space exploration [ 33 ] but faces significant obstacles when paired with modern generative base policies, whose intractable log-likelihoods preclude standard policy gradient methods [ 59 ] .
Residual RL offers a promising and practical middle ground by learning additive corrections atop frozen base policies for model-agnostic adaptation [ 24 , 3 ] , yet extending it to mobile manipulation introduces a distinct challenge: inter-module coupling .
As shown in Fig. 1 , a task as routine as grasping becomes difficult in the MoMa context: it requires tight spatiotemporal coordination between the mobile base and the arm, and any misalignment in the base’s approach rapidly propagates as a sizable pose error at the manipulator.
Without explicit structural priors, the high-dimensional action space and non-stationary inter-module dynamics often hinder convergence and ultimately prevent the precision required for physical interaction.

In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa ( Hi erarchical Re sidual Mo bile Ma nipulation), a framework for real-world fine-tuning of mobile manipulation systems, built around three components.
First, our Policy-Agnostic Residual Learning paradigm adds a learnable residual atop a frozen base policy, sidestepping the intractable log-likelihoods of generative architectures and allowing the same procedure to refine diverse pre-trained policies.
Second, to address this base-arm coupling specific to mobile manipulation, we introduce a Hierarchical Decoupling structure with unidirectional conditioning: the manipulator’s residual head is conditioned on the base’s correction, reflecting the system’s physical hierarchy.
Third, an Expert-Guided Value Alignment loss leverages sparse human interventions to reshape the critic’s value landscape toward expert-preferred behaviors, improving sample efficiency without overriding RL exploration.
HiRe-MoMa is realized as an asynchronous actor-learner system on a single robot:
an onboard rollout worker executes the policy
while a central learner optimizes the residual on a workstation,
enabling on-robot fine-tuning in the real world.

Overall, our main contributions are as follows: 1) Systematic Fine-tuning Framework : We present an asynchronous, model-agnostic framework for the real-world fine-tuning of mobile manipulation systems, enabling efficient adaptation in this high-dimensional and coupled robotic domain with 25–40 minutes of online interaction. 2) Hierarchical Residual Architecture : We introduce independent residual policies for distinct modules, coupled with a unidirectional conditioning mechanism to ensure stable and logically coherent coordinated control. 3) Expert-Guided Alignment : We develop an auxiliary human intervention alignment loss that leverages sparse expert guidance ( ≤ \leq 20% of collected data) to improve sample efficiency and accelerate convergence. 4) Empirical Validation on Diverse MoMa Tasks : We validate HiRe-MoMa on three real-world TIAGo++ tasks of increasing complexity, demonstrating consistent improvements across two distinct base policy architectures (Diffusion Policy and ACT).
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Real-World Reinforcement Learning offers a principled path to bridging the sim-to-real gap [ 55 ] , with sample efficiency as the central challenge.
The SERL framework [ 34 ] demonstrated the efficacy of off-policy RL for robot fine-tuning, inspiring subsequent residual correction methods [ 8 , 2 ] .
Existing residual and HIL systems [ 35 , 8 , 24 , 3 , 2 ] fine-tune fixed-base arms, where base–arm gradient interference does not arise;
HiRe-MoMa instead targets policy-agnostic, on-robot fine-tuning of a whole-body mobile manipulator,
without simulation-pre-trained latent action spaces [ 19 ] .

Policy Post-Training of base policies [ 9 , 63 ] via RL is hampered by intractable log-likelihoods, motivating surrogate objectives [ 59 , 6 , 51 , 36 ] or policy-agnostic RL [ 38 , 8 ] . Residual RL offers a practical middle ground by learning additive corrections atop frozen policies [ 2 , 16 , 52 , 13 , 11 ] , with human-in-the-loop variants [ 26 , 21 , 27 ] further mitigating distributional drift.
Yet simple residuals cannot address the cross-module coupling inherent in MoMa:
the spatiotemporal dependency between base and arm demands structured decoupling that flat residual methods do not provide.

Mobile Manipulation poses unique challenges owing to its high-dimensional action space and tight base-arm coupling [ 25 , 7 ] . Most RL methods still rely on simulation-pre-trained priors [ 18 , 61 ] or expensive skill-discovery phases [ 19 , 39 ] to bridge the sim-to-real gap. HiRe-MoMa instead operates directly in the raw action space of any pre-trained policy, modeling hierarchical inter-module dependencies under a sparse success-only reward without manual reward shaping.

Human-in-the-Loop corrections serve as safety buffers [ 35 , 1 ] , imitation data sources [ 32 ] , or auxiliary supervision signals [ 31 , 50 , 28 ] in robot RL. Beyond these roles, interventions implicitly encode expert value preferences [ 1 ] ; HiRe-MoMa exploits this by treating corrections as functional constraints on the critic’s value surface, directly reshaping the value landscape to reflect expert priorities.
A broader discussion of related work on these four topics is provided in App. E .

2026-10-15.title: Modeling and Understanding Neural Weights of Humanoid Policies with Diffusion
2026-10-15.authors: Huixuan Cheng , Bike Zhang , Shankar Sastry , Koushil Sreenath
2026-10-15.abstract:
Recent advances in robot learning have driven rapid progress in humanoid control, enabling increasingly agile behaviors in the real world. However, humanoid control networks are typically obtained through conventional training procedures, while comparatively little attention has been given to directly modeling the distribution of their learned weights and generating functional networks in weight space.
In this work, we investigate whether high-performing humanoid control networks can be generatively modeled directly through their weights. We adopt a latent diffusion framework that couples a linear autoencoder with a Diffusion Transformer. The autoencoder compresses actor network parameters into a compact latent space, and the Diffusion Transformer models the distribution of these latents. Trained on networks collected from reinforcement learning for the Unitree G1 robot, our approach generates deployable networks that perform various motions in the real world, including walking, dancing, and spin kick. Beyond generation, we further study the learned weight space to better understand the structure captured by these humanoid control networks. We identify a structural principle in the first-layer weights that consistently reflects the robot’s kinematic prior. Notably, this kinematic prior emerges under both Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Imitation Learning (IL) training, suggesting that it is not specific to a particular optimization process but may instead reflect common knowledge associated with humanoid embodiment. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of generative modeling in humanoid network weight space, while providing initial insights into the information encoded by their learned weights. Additional results are available on our project website .
2026-10-15.introduction:
Humanoid control has progressed rapidly in recent years, from locomotion to whole-body control, with increasingly agile and versatile motions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Highly dynamic humanoid motions can now be learned through imitation of human reference motions [ 4 ] .
Scaling such motions has further led to humanoid foundation models with broader capabilities [ 5 ] .
Together, these advances enable humanoid robots to interact with complex real-world environments.

Despite this progress, humanoid skills are still typically acquired by training separate control networks for different tasks, which are then maintained as individual expert policies.
An alternative is to directly model and generate these expert networks in weight space.
A generative model over network weights could serve as a policy generator, synthesizing control networks for different motions or tasks, potentially conditioned on task descriptors, reference trajectories, or other embeddings, and providing a compact and flexible representation of diverse humanoid skills.

Early approaches to weight generation, such as hypernetworks, used a learned generator conditioned on a task or context to produce the weights of a target network [ 6 , 7 ] .
More recent work has explored diffusion-based methods for modeling and generating network weights.
In the image domain, diffusion-generated weights can perform image classification, with recent extensions to language classification and tabular prediction [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] .
This direction has since extended to embodied control, where latent diffusion models conditioned on target behaviors or trajectories generate network weights for HalfCheetah and Walker in simulation [ 12 ] , with recent progress extending to manipulation tasks [ 13 , 14 ] .
Notably, weights for quadruped locomotion can also be sampled and deployed in the real world [ 15 ] .
Generative modeling of humanoid control networks, however, remains largely unexplored, in part due to their high-dimensional weight space.
Neural network weights are known to be substantially redundant, with an effective dimensionality far below the nominal parameter count [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] , suggesting that humanoid network weights may likewise be modeled through compact latent representations.

Beyond weight generation, a complementary question is what information is encoded in humanoid control network weights.
To date, weight space analysis has largely focused on the image domain, where features are comparatively easy to associate with individual layers, from low-level edges and colors to class-specific concepts [ 20 , 21 ] .
In robotics, by contrast, such analysis remains limited: existing studies mostly examine which weights matter, for instance using pruning to identify task-relevant inputs [ 22 ] .
A systematic understanding of what humanoid control networks encode in their weights therefore remains largely unexplored.
Such analysis could reveal regularities that inform more compact architectures, while structures shared across motions may guide transfer learning for acquiring new policies.

In this work, we address two gaps: generating humanoid control networks in weight space and interpreting the structure and information encoded in their weights.
We collect a large dataset of RL-trained networks for the Unitree G1 humanoid robot performing walking, dancing, and spin kick motions, and train a linear autoencoder together with a Diffusion Transformer [ 23 ] to model their weight distribution.
We evaluate the quality and diversity of generated networks in simulation and assess their sim-to-real transfer on hardware, as shown in Fig. 1 .
Alongside this generative modeling effort, we systematically analyze the collected humanoid networks, investigating the structure encoded by RL-trained networks and how different training paradigms, including imitation learning, and training configurations, such as domain randomization, affect their weight space distributions.

2026-10-15.title: CoWear: Towards Collaborative Wearable Inertial Localization with Multiple Smart Devices
2026-10-15.authors: Zhuoyuan She , Zhanpeng Zhang , Yapeng Chen , Jiale Wang , Xin Xie , Ming Xia
2026-10-15.abstract: Consumer smart devices observe the same human motion from different body locations, yet existing inertial-localization benchmarks rarely provide synchronized heterogeneous wearables with device-specific motion ground truth. We present CoWear, a dataset and reference framework for collaborative inertial localization using a smartphone, smartwatch, and smart glasses. The dataset contains over 30 participants, over 300 walking sessions, and more than 30 hours and 100 km of aggregate device trajectories, with each device individually tracked by motion capture. To enable collaboration across distinct body motions, we train role-specific estimators to predict the displacement of a common reference device over synchronized temporal windows. Their predictions are transformed to the world frame using gyroscope integration and fused according to learned uncertainty. Experiments using phone, glasses, and watch as reference targets show that multi-device fusion consistently improves both displacement and trajectory rollout accuracy over individual-device estimation. CoWear provides a dataset and reproducible baseline for studying collaborative inertial localization across heterogeneous consumer wearables.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Consumer devices such as smartphones, smartwatches, and smart glasses increasingly accompany users throughout daily activities and continuously measure motion with embedded inertial sensors. Their independence from external infrastructure makes them attractive for pedestrian localization in indoor and GNSS-denied environments, where learning-based inertial odometry has shown strong potential with low-cost IMUs [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Yet most existing systems localize from one sensing device at a time, even though a user may simultaneously carry several inertial devices at different body locations. This naturally raises the question of whether these heterogeneous devices can provide redundant observations of human locomotion and jointly improve localization.

A key difficulty is that the motion of a sensing device is not necessarily the motion that localization aims to recover. A handheld phone, wrist-worn watch, and head-mounted glasses share the same global locomotion but also undergo distinct local motions caused by arm swing, head motion, and changing carrying styles. This discrepancy is already present in common inertial-localization settings where the IMU and trajectory reference correspond to different physical carriers [ 4 , 2 ] . In such cases, device-specific motion is not directly supervised and must be implicitly absorbed by the estimator. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , a representative RIDI example highlights how substantial device motion can coexist with much smaller changes in the underlying human trajectory.

This observation motivates two design choices in CoWear. First, multiple wearables provide redundant but non-identical observations of the same locomotion, offering the possibility of reducing the influence of device-specific disturbances. Second, to study this redundancy explicitly, the motion of each sensing device itself must be observable. We therefore collect synchronized smartphone, smartwatch, and smart-glasses inertial data while independently tracking every device with motion capture. This produces device-specific 6-DoF ground truth and allows each wearable to be analyzed either as a motion source or as a common localization reference.

The remaining challenge is how to compare and combine observations from non-co-located body locations. For every synchronized temporal window, role-specific estimators predict the displacement of one selected reference device from each wearable. These estimates are transformed into a shared world frame using gyroscope integration and combined through learned uncertainty. This common-target formulation avoids averaging trajectories of different physical carriers. Experiments with phone-, watch-, and glasses-reference targets show consistent improvements from collaborative estimation over single-device inference.

Our contributions are as follows:

We introduce CoWear, a synchronized multi-device inertial dataset containing smartphone, smartwatch, and smart-glasses measurements with device-specific 6-DoF motion-capture ground truth.

We formulate collaborative localization across non-co-located wearables as common-reference displacement estimation from synchronized heterogeneous observations.

We provide a reproducible collaborative localization baseline that maps heterogeneous wearable observations to a common reference displacement and combines them through uncertainty-aware fusion.

1. We introduce CoWear, a synchronized multi-device inertial dataset containing smartphone, smartwatch, and smart-glasses measurements with device-specific 6-DoF motion-capture ground truth.

2. We formulate collaborative localization across non-co-located wearables as common-reference displacement estimation from synchronized heterogeneous observations.

3. We provide a reproducible collaborative localization baseline that maps heterogeneous wearable observations to a common reference displacement and combines them through uncertainty-aware fusion.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

Classical pedestrian dead reckoning constrains inertial drift using footfall timing, heading estimation, and stride models [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
IONet introduced short-window neural inertial odometry by directly regressing motion from inertial sequences, while RoNIN improved robustness to varying phone placements through learned velocity estimation [ 1 , 2 ] .
TLIO further predicts displacement together with uncertainty and integrates learned estimates into a filtering framework, whereas NILoc extends learned inertial reasoning toward scene-level localization [ 3 , 8 ] .
More recent methods explore stronger temporal modeling and geometric structure, including HNNTA, IMUNet, and equivariant inertial odometry [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] .
These approaches substantially advance single-device inertial localization, but generally formulate each sensing stream as an independent motion-estimation problem rather than exploiting simultaneous observations from heterogeneous wearables.

RIDI provides smartphone inertial measurements together with reference trajectories for learning pedestrian motion, while OxIOD further covers diverse carrying placements and motion modes for deep inertial odometry [ 4 , 12 ] .
RoNIN provides large-scale free-form smartphone inertial data with body-referenced motion supervision, and TLIO supports learning displacement and uncertainty for inertial odometry [ 2 , 3 ] .
ADVIO complements these datasets with challenging visual–inertial pedestrian navigation sequences [ 13 ] .
Although these datasets adopt different sensing and supervision configurations, in several common settings the IMU measurements and trajectory reference correspond to different physical carriers, leaving device-to-reference motion implicit.
In contrast, CoWear independently tracks every consumer device, pairing each IMU stream with the 6-DoF motion of the same physical carrier and enabling explicit analysis of device-specific motion.

Suite-IN studies inertial navigation using multiple Apple consumer devices, while Project Aria provides a head-worn multimodal sensing platform with globally aligned measurements and Aria Everyday Activities extends this setting to daily human activities [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] .
DIP reconstructs human pose from sparse body-mounted IMUs, and TransPose further estimates both pose and global translation from distributed inertial sensors [ 17 , 18 ] .
HelmetPoser investigates head-mounted inertial motion with corresponding motion ground truth [ 19 ] .
These works demonstrate the value of body-distributed sensing, but their primary goals differ from collaborative inertial localization across heterogeneous consumer devices.
CoWear instead focuses on preserving the distinct motion of each wearable while allowing multiple devices to jointly estimate a common localization target.

2026-10-15.title: PingpongDuo: Agile Humanoid Table Tennis Doubles with Safe Team Coordination
2026-10-15.authors: Haoran Jiang , Yichao Zhong , Kai Zhang , Cheng Liu , Yixuan Pan , Zhenjie Yang , Jingbo Wang , Tianyu Li , Li Chen
2026-10-15.abstract:
Unlike singles, humanoid table tennis doubles requires teammates
to strike in strict alternation while sharing a confined workspace.
Rapid repositioning can compromise striking accuracy, while
uncoordinated teammate movements introduce collision risks.
We present PingpongDuo, a hierarchical framework for agile
humanoid doubles with safe team coordination.
At the team level, a planner jointly selects positioning targets
and uses learned risk estimates to filter risky proposals,
preferentially preserving the current striker’s target.
At the individual level, separate footwork and striking skills
combine agile movement with precise racket control.
The skills are guided by human motion references, including
footwork collected from human doubles play, and trained from
states produced by one another to support rapid transitions.
A racket-arm residual further refines strikes after movement
using return feedback from a simulator calibrated with real
ball-flight and contact measurements.
In simulation, PingpongDuo improves the ball-return success rate
by 13.2% over the state-of-the-art baseline,
while achieving approximately 2 cm positioning error during clearance.
In real-world experiments, a robot completes a 2.15 m
clearance-and-recovery cycle in 2.4 s with a peak speed of
2.23 m/s, while two robots sustain more than 10 consecutive
strikes in strict alternation.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Recent advances in humanoid learning and control [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] have enabled
robots to perform dynamic interactions with fast-moving
balls [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] .
Racket sports combine rapid movement, precise contact
timing, and whole-body balance. Progress in these individual
capabilities provides a foundation for studying humanoid team
sports, where successful execution also depends on coordination
with other players.

Existing humanoid table tennis systems such as
HITTER [ 4 ] and SMASH [ 9 ] combine
strike planning with learned control to support balance
and consecutive ball returns. Their focus is on individual
striking performance. We study table tennis doubles with two
humanoid teammates on the same side of the table
( Fig. 1 ). Unlike singles, doubles requires teammates
to strike in strict alternation and share the space needed
to approach, strike, and recover.

However, doubles requires each robot to coordinate its movement
with its teammate while remaining ready for its next strike.
After each strike,
one robot must clear the central hitting area while its teammate moves
into position for the next shot. Insufficient clearance can
obstruct the teammate or cause collisions, whereas excessive
displacement increases the time needed for subsequent recovery.
At the individual level, robots must combine agile footwork with
precise striking. Unlike singles, where movement primarily serves
the incoming shot, doubles robot also requires clearance and recovery
movements that may conflict with the next strike. The robot must
therefore adapt its movement direction and speed while maintaining
accurate racket control.

We present PingpongDuo , a hierarchical framework for agile
humanoid doubles with safe team coordination. A team planner
jointly selects positioning targets, and a learned risk filter
adjusts risky proposals while preferentially preserving the
striker’s target. For agile movement and precise striking, we
train separate footwork and striking skills with human motion
references, including footwork collected from human doubles play.
Each skill is trained from states produced by the other to
support repeated transitions. A racket-arm residual further
adjusts the nominal strike to the current robot and ball states
using simulated return feedback. The system
demonstrates more than 10 consecutive alternating strikes and
a 2.15 m clearance-and-recovery cycle completed in 2.4 s in real-world deployment.

In sum, the contributions are:

A hierarchical framework for safe team coordination and
agile individual control in humanoid doubles, combining risk-aware
joint positioning with footwork and striking skills trained for
continuous execution.

An arm refinement policy that preserves striking
accuracy after rapid footwork by adapting nominal actions to
robot and ball states using simulated return feedback.

Simulation and real-world evaluations of individual agility
and team coordination, including the first
real-world demonstration of humanoid-humanoid teammates
completing more than 10 consecutive alternating strikes.

1. A hierarchical framework for safe team coordination and
agile individual control in humanoid doubles, combining risk-aware
joint positioning with footwork and striking skills trained for
continuous execution.

2. An arm refinement policy that preserves striking
accuracy after rapid footwork by adapting nominal actions to
robot and ball states using simulated return feedback.

3. Simulation and real-world evaluations of individual agility
and team coordination, including the first
real-world demonstration of humanoid-humanoid teammates
completing more than 10 consecutive alternating strikes.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Humanoid Racket Sports

Humanoid racket-sport research has advanced whole-body striking,
repositioning, and perception [ 4 , 9 , 7 , 5 , 10 ] .
Related studies in badminton also investigate coordinated
locomotion and perception [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
Moving beyond individual skills, these capabilities become increasingly important in multi-robot settings, where robots must remain agile while safely coordinating their motions and avoiding collisions with teammates. PingpongDuo further develops a low-level controller that supports agile footwork and striking skills.

Accurate racket-ball contact modeling and closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL) are essential for precise and robust strike performance [ 14 ] . Human motion references also guide tennis skill learning and
task-specific adaptation [ 5 , 10 , 15 ] . In the context of table tennis, the small size and high speed of the ball make accurate trajectory modeling particularly important for precise interaction. Ball trajectory and racket–ball interaction modeling support
accurate returns [ 14 , 16 ] . PingpongDuo adopts this trajectory-based formulation. By incorporating simulated return feedback into training, PingpongDuo closes the loop between interaction and striking.

## II-B Safe Multi-Embodiment Coordination

Coordination in dynamic sports has been studied in robot
teams [ 17 ] and human–robot table tennis
doubles [ 18 ] .
Simulated humanoid football [ 19 ] and cooperative quadrupedal
soccer [ 20 ] combine learned skills with team-level policies.
HCSP [ 21 ] jointly refines an event-driven team strategy and motor
skills for multi-drone volleyball. Vision-driven humanoid
soccer [ 22 ] learns reactive soccer skills while using a high-level
behavior tree to assign roles and coordinate behavior across the team.

Prior works typically deploy robots sparsely in large workspaces, while our table tennis doubles setting requires two humanoids to operate concurrently within a confined workspace. This makes multi-robot co-safety, particularly collision avoidance and motion obstruction, a critical requirement. ABS series [ 23 , 24 ] integrate agile and recovery policies with reachability estimation to achieve high-speed locomotion, while safe RL approaches [ 25 ] introduce cost functions and recovery policies to enforce safety constraints during learning. In contrast to these single-robot safety formulations, temporal-logic planning [ 26 ] and Control Barrier Functions [ 27 , 28 ] have also been explored for multi-robot coordination and safety. However, acquiring full observations and humanoid Jacobians in the real world is often infeasible. We therefore combine risk estimation with constrained RL [ 29 ] for co-safe coordination, while a role-weighted safety filter prioritizes the striker’s target and adjusts the non-striker’s planned position to maintain ball-striking performance.

2026-10-15.title: KinoGen: Customizable Humanoid Loco-Manipulation References via Kinematically Grounded Video Generation
2026-10-15.authors: Qi Wu , Lulu Zhao , Sanghyun Hahn , Rishi Yennu , Emmy Yang , Dingqi Zhang , Tao Pang , Jiuguang Wang , Kuan Fang
2026-10-15.abstract:
We present KinoGen, a framework that synthesizes customizable humanoid loco-manipulation references through kinematically grounded video generation. KinoGen conditions a pretrained video generator on calibrated renders of the target robot and object in a simulated task instance and recovers the reference by fitting the same models to the generated two-view video, so that the reference lies in the robot configuration space by construction without a human body proxy or retargeting. Body, hand, and object priors initialize the reconstruction, and direct optimization against cross-view evidence refines it. Since an edited keyframe is simply another rendered state, a user can prescribe a goal object pose, regenerate the video around the edited keyframe, and obtain a reference that satisfies the pose exactly. Across eight loco-manipulation tasks, KinoGen yields lower penetration and foot skating than video-based baselines and preserves over 90% of annotated contacts, and its customized references satisfy every prescribed target with substantially less penetration than direct interpolation. Tracking policies trained on the synthesized references are deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands.
Project webpage: https://kinogen-humanoid.github.io/ .
2026-10-15.introduction:
Humanoid robots can learn impressive whole-body skills by tracking a reference motion with reinforcement learning.
Whereas a locomotion reference specifies only the body motion [ 21 , 18 ] , a loco-manipulation reference must specify synchronized whole-body, hand, and object trajectories. Such references must vary with the interaction behavior and the scene layout, and each must match the kinematics of the target robot and the geometry of its task. Many tasks further require the object to reach a prescribed pose. Obtaining such references remains a central bottleneck. Human demonstrations must be reconstructed and retargeted to the robot, which introduces embodiment errors, and teleoperation requires substantial human effort to cover the variation in behaviors, objects, scenes, and goals.

Video generators offer a scalable alternative: text and image conditioning can produce diverse, scene-conditioned interaction behaviors without manually collecting every demonstration [ 12 , 17 ] .
For humanoids, recent methods either generate human–object interactions and retarget the recovered motion to the robot [ 22 , 31 ] or generate the target robot directly [ 1 , 32 ] . For the first family, since the behavior is generated and reconstructed through a human body proxy, the robot’s kinematics and the exact task instance constraints can only be satisfied after generation, which can cause penetration and drifting. The second family still relies on human-motion recovery and retargeting or a separately trained robot-specific pose detector, and recovers neither hands nor objects. Consequently, these pipelines do not directly recover complete whole-body, hand, and object references through the robot and object models that define the task instance.
Moreover, text- or image-conditioned generation is open loop with respect to metric task requirements.
The outcome may depict the intended behavior but cannot be revised to satisfy a prescribed configuration.
We need references that are generated for the target robot in the exact task instance and can be customized to satisfy a prescribed configuration.

Our key insight, as shown in Fig. 1 , is that a pretrained video generator and a physics simulator can be coupled through rendering and reconstruction using the same robot and object models. The generator supplies the interaction behavior, and the simulator supplies the exact embodiment and task geometry. Rendering the simulated task instance into the conditioning image places the generated behavior in the target embodiment and scene, and fitting the same models to the generated video returns the behavior to the simulator. We refer to this coupling as kinematic grounding. It has two consequences. The complete body, hand, and object reference is recovered directly in the robot configuration space and the object pose space by construction, without a human body proxy, retargeting, or a pose detector. In addition, a keyframe edited in simulation is simply another rendered state, so the same interface lets the generator regenerate the behavior around the edit while reconstruction enforces it exactly.

In this work, we present KinoGen , a framework that synthesizes customizable humanoid loco-manipulation references through kinematically grounded video generation. KinoGen first grounds generation by conditioning the video generator on renders of the task instance from two calibrated views, so that the generated clip depicts the target robot with dexterous hands in the specified scene. It then reconciles the generated video with body, hand, and object priors to initialize reconstruction with plausible motion. Next, it fits the robot and object models to both views by direct optimization in the configuration space to recover the complete reference. Finally, a user may prescribe a goal object pose, and KinoGen edits the corresponding keyframe in simulation, renders it back into the generator, and enforces it in constrained reconstruction to obtain a reference that satisfies the pose exactly.

We evaluate KinoGen on eight loco-manipulation tasks for a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands, spanning sitting, kneeling, mopping, and the lifting of boxes, baskets, chairs, dumbbells, and basketballs. Against three video-based reference pipelines, KinoGen yields the lowest penetration and foot skating, preserves over 90% of annotated contacts, and trains tracking policies with the highest success rate. Ablations show that the second view, point tracks, and motion priors each contribute to accurate and coherent reconstruction. In reference customization, KinoGen satisfies every prescribed target while incurring substantially less penetration than direct interpolation. Finally, tracking policies trained on the synthesized references execute four of the tasks on the physical robot.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

Humanoid loco-manipulation. Humanoid whole-body control has advanced rapidly through reinforcement learning and imitation from human motion [ 21 , 34 ] .
Meanwhile, dexterous humanoid loco-manipulation couples high-dimensional whole-body motion with contact-rich object interaction, requiring coordinated robot–object references [ 36 , 33 , 30 ] . Previous methods use references commonly originated from teleoperation or human motion capture [ 6 , 10 , 35 ] which limits coverage to captured interactions and can introduce retargeting errors.

Video generators for robot data synthesis. Video generators have been used as world models and a scalable source of demonstrations from which motion references can be recovered [ 12 , 17 ] .
For object-centric manipulation, RIGVid [ 23 ] extracts a 6D object trajectory from a generated demonstration.
For humanoid data synthesis, recent approaches either generate human or proxy interactions and retarget the recovered motion [ 22 , 37 , 31 ] , or depict the target robot but recover its motion through human-motion retargeting, a robot-specific pose detector, or sparse point guidance [ 1 , 32 , 4 ] . GRAIL [ 31 ] grounds its proxy in the scene, but still requires retargeting to recover robot motion.
Large-scale robot-video models such as Uni-Mo [ 19 ] and
OmniHumanoid [ 28 ] further demonstrate that embodiment-conditioned generation can scale across robots, but do not recover complete robot–object reference trajectories.
In contrast, KinoGen conditions generation on calibrated renders of the simulator state of the task instance, and fits those same models to multi-view evidence, following a render-and-compare formulation [ 16 ] . This directly recovers coordinated body, hand, and object trajectories, without a human body proxy or a separately trained robot-specific pose detector.

Customizable video generation and editing. Generated videos may express the intended task without satisfying a prescribed metric configuration. Prior work controls generated motion using event keyframes, edge maps, rendered trajectories, or cross-embodiment editing [ 11 , 3 , 15 , 7 ] ; other methods treat the video as fixed and ground its output through downstream optimization or simulation [ 8 , 38 , 9 ] .
GRAIL mentions terminal-frame conditioning but does not evaluate intermediate edits.
None of these methods regenerates motion from an edited reconstructed robot–object state and then enforces that state exactly in the recovered reference. Through kinematic grounding, KinoGen closes this loop by rendering an edited reconstructed robot–object keyframe for keyframe-conditioned regeneration and enforcing the complete keyframe as a hard constraint during reconstruction.

2026-10-15.title: EarlyCommit: Calibrated Word-by-Word Commitment for Robots Acting Before You Finish Speaking
2026-10-15.authors: Muhammad Haris Khan
2026-10-15.abstract:
Human listeners can often identify the intended object several words before an instruction ends. Robots, however, are typically designed to wait until the speaker has finished before deciding how to act.
We present EarlyCommit, an open-source tool that lets a robot commit to the intended object while the instruction is being spoken.
After every recognised word a fine-tuned text encoder scores each object in the scene. The robot acts when the calibrated probability of the best object reaches a threshold τ \tau set by the user, so 1 − τ 1-\tau is the accepted risk of choosing the wrong object.
Otherwise it waits or asks.
The tool includes a streaming speech front end, a scene and instruction generator with exact word-by-word ground truth, and scripts to train, calibrate and evaluate. On instructions containing words never seen in training, EarlyCommit commits correctly 1.6 to 2 times as often as keyword matching, is right at least 92% of the time when it commits at τ = 0.9 \tau=0.9 , and needs 31–35 ms per word on consumer GPUs.
2026-10-15.introduction:
A person asks a robot: "could you grab the red cup, the one on the left next to the laptop, and bring it over here, please". If only one red cup stands on the table, a human helper knows the answer at the word "cup", the sixth of 21 words, and starts to reach while the remaining 15 words, more than four seconds of speech, are still being said. A typical robot pipeline instead waits for the end of the utterance, transcribes it and then decides. This adds delay to every request, and the delay grows with every word the speaker adds.
Users prefer a robot to reply about one second after their request ( Shiwa et al., 2008 ) , and robots that act in anticipation finish shared tasks seconds faster than robots that only react ( Huang and Mutlu, 2016 ) .
Although acting early is useful, it is also risky.
For example, halfway through a sentence several objects can still fit, and a wrong grasp costs more than a short wait.
A robot that acts early therefore needs two things.
It must know after each word which object is meant, and it must know when that belief is reliable enough to move.

Prior work covers each need separately.
Incremental reference resolution scores scene objects word by word ( Schlangen et al., 2009 ; Kennington and Schlangen, 2015 ) , learns when a partial utterance is understood well enough to respond ( DeVault et al., 2009 ) , and lets robots act on partial utterances ( Brick and Scheutz, 2007 ) or show their uncertainty through their actions ( Hough and Schlangen, 2017 ) .
These systems do not tie the decision to act to a calibrated error rate, and their word-level models do not transfer to words outside their training vocabulary. Conformal methods let robots ask for help with statistical guarantees ( Ren et al., 2023 ) , and risk-controlled rules stop classification early on growing inputs ( Ringel et al., 2024 ) .
They work on complete instructions or on fixed label sets.
Concurrent work lets a vision-language-action policy act on partial instructions through a learned readiness threshold ( Park et al., 2026 ) . Speech research on turn-taking answers a different question ( Skantze, 2021 ) . Its silence-based, inter-pausal-unit and continuous models decide when the user’s turn ends so that the system can speak or give feedback, and incremental dialogue systems pass partial results between modules as words arrive. EarlyCommit uses such an incremental front end but asks what is meant: which object, and whether it is safe to move for it while the speaker is still talking. It never predicts the end of the turn, and its decision is an action whose error rate the user sets with τ \tau . A recent survey finds very little research on this kind of incremental decision making ( Kennington et al., 2025 ) .

EarlyCommit brings these pieces together as one reusable tool. We contribute
(1) a runtime pipeline that turns streaming speech into a word-by-word decision to commit, wait or ask, controlled by one interpretable threshold τ \tau ;
(2) an evaluation harness that generates scenes and instructions with exact ground truth after every word and tests robustness to unseen language;
(3) an evaluation showing when the threshold holds and a practical lesson on how to calibrate it.
Code, result files and demo videos are provided as anonymised supplementary material.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2. Purpose

EarlyCommit is a drop-in module for robots that take spoken requests: given the list of objects on the table and the words recognised so far, it returns after every word either an object to grasp, “wait”, or “ask”. It also lets researchers train, calibrate and evaluate this decision on their own scenes and vocabularies, with exact word-by-word ground truth and one threshold τ \tau that sets the accepted risk of a wrong grasp.
