2026-10-15.title: Investigating Behavior Cloning from Few Demonstrations for Autonomous Driving based on Bird's-Eye View in Simulated Cities
2026-10-15.authors: Eric Aislan Antonelo , Gustavo Claudio Karl Couto , Christian Möller , Pedro Henrique Fernandes
2026-10-15.comment: . Accepted manuscript (author version) of the paper published in the proceedings of BRACIS 2024 (34th Brazilian Conference on Intelligent Systems, Belém, Brazil, 17-21 November 2024). Project page: this https URL
2026-10-15.abstract:
This paper investigates the use of Behavior Cloning (BC) for autonomous driving from a bird’s-eye view (BEV) perspective in simulated urban environments.
BC uses supervised learning to mimic expert driving behaviors.
Previous works have applied BC in the CARLA simulator but did not fully address the challenges of traffic light compliance.
Our approach enhances BC by integrating a kernel density estimator to adjust training sample weights based on action density, thereby improving the learning of rare but critical actions such as stopping at red lights and accelerating at green lights, specially in scenarios of scarce number of expert demonstrations. Using BEV inputs, which provide an abstract top-down view of the driving environment, our method simplifies the policy learning process. The trained convolutional neural network (CNN) outputs steering and acceleration actions based on these BEV inputs and additional state variables. Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC.
This weighted approach proved to be crucial in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training, highlighting its potential for enhancing autonomous vehicle navigation.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Autonomous driving has traditionally been implemented using separate modules for perception, planning, and control, organized in a sequential pipeline [ 13 , 21 , 15 , 16 ] . However, learning-based approaches have been gaining popularity as they attempt to address the complexities of autonomous driving in various scenarios, whether in simulation or real-world environments.

Most of these learning-based approaches rely on Behavior Cloning (BC), which employs supervised learning on a collection of expert demonstrations gathered offline [ 3 , 19 , 2 , 6 , 7 ] . For example, a human driver generates a set of input (observations) and corresponding desired output pairs.

Codevilla [ 6 , 7 ] employed BC for autonomous driving in the CARLA simulator.
He collected a large dataset of human driving and augmented it using image processing techniques to train end-to-end policies conditioned on the desired route.
Further improvements in BC were introduced in [ 4 ] , where a large deep ResNet network was used for feature extraction.
This approach combined data from cameras, LiDAR, and radar to create comprehensive feature maps.
The work also incorporated a probabilistic motion planner to account for uncertainties in the trajectory.

Couto [ 11 ] has shown results on behavior cloning on the CARLA simulator, but the agent did not have to respect traffic lights. In this work, we investigate an approach where the agent is able to navigate the city while respecting traffic lights, i.e., breaking when the light is red, and crossing the traffic light when it is green.
Only relying on regular BC to train an agent is not enough in a scenario with limited amount of training routes and where the agent needs to break at the red light and accelerate from stillness when light turns to green. To solve that, we employ a kernel density estimator [ 18 ] to estimate the actions density from the expert dataset. Then, the training samples are weighted in the BC loss function individually by setting the weight equal to the inverse of the actions’ density. In this way, we can account for the underrepresented actions in the expert set, i.e., those happening at traffic light transitions. This weighting is needed because we are considering only eight routes as training data.

Instead of learning directly from raw camera pixels as in [ 11 , 12 ] , the agent in this work has structured image inputs that are more abstract and meaningful to the navigation task.
To decouple feature representation from policy learning [ 14 , 8 ] has its advantages as potentially easing up the learning task.
In our context, this decoupling is accomplished by using a mid-level representation of the vehicle’s raw camera images.
For example, Bird’s-Eye View (BEV) representations of the road ahead have been used as mid-level inputs for trajectory generation and motor control networks in [ 2 ] and [ 20 ] , respectively.
In BEV representation, the camera scene is projected onto a top-down view, segmenting areas of interest, like vehicle lanes and sidewalks, into different colors [ 21 ] .
By using BEV as input for the control policy, the learning process can focus on the navigation problem, leveraging a more abstract and simplified view of the road ahead. The policy here is represented by convolutional neural networks, mapping the BEV image to control actuators such as steering and acceleration.

Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC.
This weighted approach proved to be essential in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training.

In Section 2 , we present
the bird’s-eye view representation employed as input to the convolutional neural network, the behavior cloning loss for the agent, and the kernel density estimation used to generate the weights per sample for the modified loss function. The agent architecture is presented in Section 3 .
Finally, the experiments and conclusions are shown in Sections 4 and 5 .

2026-10-15.title: Atomic-WAM: Execution-Grounded Atomic-Motion Reasoning for World Action Models
2026-10-15.authors: Shijun Shi , Zhe Liu , Zhi Hou , Yinan Chen , Tao Zhang , Kai Hu , Yong Liu , Jiangning Zhang
2026-10-15.abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction.
However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection.
To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions.
Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk.
Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations.
To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success.
Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project
2026-10-15.introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) transfer visual and motion priors from video foundation models to robotic control by jointly predicting future visual states and actions [ 28 , 41 , 20 , 18 , 1 ] .
Through video pretraining, these models acquire rich dynamic priors for modeling physically plausible future evolution.
However, robot control further requires determining which local evolution is appropriate under the current task and state. Given a fixed task-level instruction, the object to manipulate, the current interaction phase, and the local motion to execute are often not explicitly specified.
Such task-level conditioning leaves two related requirements to the executor.
First, a semantic grounding gap arises when categories, relations, or desired outcomes must be translated into concrete object interactions.
For example, Put the red things in the bin requires identifying the relevant objects and deciding how to manipulate them.
Second, a temporal granularity gap arises because a task instruction can remain unchanged as execution progresses through approach, alignment, grasp, transport, and release [ 22 ] .
Descriptive video pretraining does not by itself establish how to resolve these decisions in closed-loop control.
Figure 1 illustrates the sensitivity of video predictions to language specificity, motivating a more explicit interface between task reasoning and motion execution.

To address these requirements, we introduce Atomic-WAM , an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to video–action generation through an atomic-motion language interface. Specifically, a vision-language model (VLM) reasoner uses the task instruction and visual context to describe the next local interaction, including its target and relevant spatial grounding.
A WAM then predicts the corresponding future video and action chunk. The reasoner revises its description as execution changes the scene, while the task-level objective remains fixed.

Learning such an interface requires temporally aligned atomic-motion supervision, which is rarely available in existing robot demonstrations.
We therefore build an automatic pipeline that partitions the DROID dataset [ 17 ] into semantically coherent atomic motions. The interface further allows us to improve grasp learning. To this end, we enrich the corresponding descriptions with visible contact details.
The resulting labels supervise both motion selection and execution at the same atomic-motion granularity.

Nevertheless, supervised atomic-motion learning alone does not guarantee that the selected motion is compatible with the learned executor [ 11 , 7 ] . Existing works introduce intermediate commands, subgoals, or semantic events to decouple high-level reasoning from low-level control [ 7 , 13 , 22 ] , yet such intermediate decision policies are typically not optimized directly from the downstream executor. We therefore introduce execution-grounded reasoner adaptation through EG-GRPO, which closes the loop between the reasoner and the executor: the reasoner selects atomic motions, the executor produces physical outcomes, and these outcomes serve as the learning signal to improve atomic-motion selection.

Building on these advances, Atomic-WAM achieves competitive performance in an out-of-distribution real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab [ 39 ] , with 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

We introduce Atomic-WAM , an understand-then-execute framework that connects high-level task reasoning to joint video–action generation through state-dependent atomic-motion descriptions.

We develop a scalable atomic-motion annotation pipeline that integrates displacement and gripper cues, multi-view evidence, and visual verification to provide temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision for both motion selection and execution.

We introduce execution-grounded reasoner adaptation via EG-GRPO, using physical outcomes from a fixed executor to improve atomic-motion selection through closed-loop optimization.

1. We introduce Atomic-WAM , an understand-then-execute framework that connects high-level task reasoning to joint video–action generation through state-dependent atomic-motion descriptions.

2. We develop a scalable atomic-motion annotation pipeline that integrates displacement and gripper cues, multi-view evidence, and visual verification to provide temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision for both motion selection and execution.

3. We introduce execution-grounded reasoner adaptation via EG-GRPO, using physical outcomes from a fixed executor to improve atomic-motion selection through closed-loop optimization.

# II Related Work

## II-A Embodied foundation models.

Recent embodied policies have benefited from two forms of large-scale pretraining: vision–language pretraining for vision-language-action (VLA) models and video generative pretraining for world action models (WAMs).
VLA models transfer pretrained vision–language representations to action prediction [ 5 , 19 , 4 , 32 , 3 , 34 , 36 ] .
Such models benefit from rich semantic priors for objects, scenes, and language-specified tasks, supporting generalization across diverse manipulation tasks.
However, vision–language pretraining primarily emphasizes visual–semantic alignment rather than action-conditioned temporal dynamics.
In contrast, WAMs leverage video generation to model environment dynamics and couple future visual prediction with robot action generation [ 41 , 1 , 20 , 18 , 2 , 37 , 43 , 24 , 12 , 35 ] .
Despite this strength, the textual supervision of video foundation models is largely descriptive and offers limited grounding for semantically specified robot tasks.
Atomic-WAM integrates the strengths of both forms of pretraining: a VLM reasoner progressively translates high-level task semantics into atomic motions, while the WAM predicts the physical evolution and robot actions.

## II-B Embodied reasoning for robot control.

High-level embodied reasoning enables robots to decompose tasks, assess progress, reason about object affordances, and derive spatially grounded plans from multimodal observations.
Recent VLMs have substantially advanced these capabilities [ 30 , 16 , 9 , 33 ] , but translating high-level reasoning into controllable robot behavior remains challenging.
A growing line of work therefore grounds reasoning into robot policies through richer intermediate representations.
Embodied Chain-of-Thought (ECoT) augments action prediction with intermediate reasoning over plans, subtasks, motions, and visually grounded features [ 42 ] .
Steerable Policies train VLAs to follow commands at multiple levels of abstraction, including subtasks, atomic motions, and spatially grounded instructions [ 7 ] .
Similarly, π 0.7 \pi_{0.7} conditions robot behavior on diverse language, metadata, and visual subgoals [ 13 ] , while WALL-WM organizes video–action learning around semantically coherent action events [ 22 ] .
HarnessWAM further incorporates execution evidence into task management, using progress feedback to support replanning and failure recovery [ 10 ] .
These approaches strengthen the interface between reasoning and execution, but execution outcomes are generally not used to directly optimize the high-level reasoner under a downstream policy.
Atomic-WAM closes this learning loop by executing candidate atomic motions with a frozen WAM and updating the reasoner from group-relative rewards that capture both motion appropriateness and execution success.

## II-C Robot simulation evaluation.

Real-world robot evaluation is difficult to reproduce because physical resets and environmental conditions vary across trials [ 23 ] .
By contrast, simulation offers repeatable task instances and controlled variations in scenes and instructions.
While conventional simulation benchmarks support scalable evaluation across diverse manipulation tasks [ 26 , 8 , 6 , 27 ] , substantial training–evaluation overlap can lead to benchmark saturation and provide limited evidence of out-of-distribution generalization.
Recent real-to-sim benchmarks instead evaluate policies trained on real-world data directly in simulation, providing a controlled setting for policy evaluation [ 23 , 39 ] .
Within this setting, SIMPLER studies whether simulated evaluation reflects real-world policy behavior, while RoboLab further targets out-of-distribution task generalization with 120 novel tasks spanning visual, relational, and procedural competencies
In this work, we adopt RoboLab to evaluate Atomic-WAM under this out-of-distribution real-to-sim setting.

2026-10-15.title: Enabling Tidying Tasks in Robotic Vacuum Cleaners via a Geometry-Induced Self-Locking Deployable Linkage
2026-10-15.authors: Eunseok Song , inwoong Kim , Sohee Lim , Taehyeong Kim , Yongkook Kim , Hyeontaek Lim , Hyungmin Son , Seungyong Hyung
2026-10-15.abstract: Robotic vacuum cleaners must extend their functionality within tight limits on size, cost, and durability. Deployable linkages with few actuators meet these limits, but their backdrivability makes it difficult to hold a load-bearing posture without continuous motor torque. We introduce a two-stage deployable linkage that is self-locking, in the sense used for toggle and singularity-based linkages, through its own geometry: at full deployment an internal three-link subchain approaches a collinear, near-singular configuration where the input–output transmission ratio approaches zero, so that plate loads produce a small residual back-driving torque, absorbed by drive-train friction and a lightweight magnetic detent. A single actuator performs deployment and locking, a passive chassis-mounted trigger releases the lock for retraction, and a second actuator adjusts only the deployment height. We integrate the mechanism into a commercial robotic vacuum cleaner and validate it through a 100-cycle repeatability test, a quasi-static load test in which the locked plate held 50 N with the motor de-energized, and 140 pushing-type tidying trials on seven household objects against a commercial arm-equipped vacuum robot under a documented protocol. We derive the analytical holding condition and discuss its limits as an intermediate design point between passive compliance and articulated manipulation.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Robotic vacuum cleaners are among the most widely deployed domestic robots [ 1 ] , and recent studies emphasize that they could be repurposed for simple assistance tasks during their substantial idle time [ 2 , 3 ] . Any such extension, however, must fit within a commercial product’s fixed footprint, low-profile chassis, battery budget, and bill-of-materials cost. Adding a multi-DoF arm is possible, as recent products demonstrate, but it brings grasp planning, payload limits, and cost that are disproportionate to the simple pushing and containment actions that most floor-level tidying requires.

A low-cost alternative is a deployable linkage with few actuators. Such designs reduce actuation cost and, in the underactuated case, provide passive adaptability [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Their well-known weakness is the converse: a backdrivable linkage cannot hold a posture under load without continuous actuator torque, which wastes battery energy, and it may collapse or deviate when pushing against objects [ 10 , 11 ] . The design challenge is therefore to obtain a rigid, load-bearing configuration on demand without adding locking hardware.

Three families of prior work are relevant. Locking devices add brakes, clutches, or ratchets to hold a joint once a configuration is reached [ 10 , 12 ] ; Hsu et al. [ 13 ] , for instance, combine a differential with a friction brake so that an underactuated gripper locks automatically once a grasp is formed. Non-backdrivable transmissions such as worm gears or high-friction differentials achieve the same effect intrinsically [ 14 ] . These are true self-locking solutions, but they add mass, cost, and, for worm gears, efficiency loss in both directions.

Toggle, over-center, and bistable mechanisms exploit linkage geometry instead. A toggle clamp obtains a large mechanical advantage as two links approach collinearity and is held by driving the joint slightly past dead-center against a hard stop [ 15 ] ; bistable compliant mechanisms store elastic energy to hold either of two states [ 16 , 17 ] . The proposed mechanism belongs to this family but stops before dead-center (Section II-C ): the plates must fold flush into a curved chassis, which leaves no room for a far-side hard stop or a preload spring.

Singularity-based stiffness is a classical principle of closed-loop kinematics: at an input singularity the output loses a degree of freedom and the mechanical advantage becomes unbounded [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] . Closest to our work, Jeon et al. [ 21 ] proposed a six-bar toggle linkage for a finger clamping unit that holds its clamping force at an over-singular configuration, using added linkage compliance. Our design differs in its stopping point (before, rather than past, the singular configuration, with no stored elastic energy), its object (a deployable sweeping plate), its topology (a six-bar whose ternary link is the output plate), its release strategy (passive, body-triggered, and kinematically decoupled from the load direction), and its integration into a commercial chassis without modification of the primary structural frame or the stowed external envelope. We claim no new mechanism-theoretic principle; the contribution is the design instantiation and its system-level validation.

Two simpler alternatives deserve comment. A fixed scoop cannot be stowed: it would enlarge the footprint, block the bumper and cliff sensors, prevent docking, and obstruct navigation. A single-stage two-finger gripper can be stowed, but its sweep width is limited to the plate length, whereas the two-stage linkage roughly doubles the deployed width from the same stowed length; it must hold objects against lateral loads with continuous motor torque or a brake, whereas the proposed linkage holds with the motor de-energized; and a straight plate cannot conform to the curved front housing when stowed. The proposed linkage is the option that satisfies stowability, sweep width, and zero-torque holding simultaneously within the existing chassis volume.

A compact two-stage deployable linkage, driven by a single deployment actuator, that transitions between backdrivable motion and a load-supporting near-singular configuration, integrated into a commercial robotic vacuum cleaner without modifying its primary structural frame, its stowed external envelope, or its navigation pipeline (a second actuator adjusts only the deployment height).

A compact two-stage deployable linkage, driven by a single deployment actuator, that transitions between backdrivable motion and a load-supporting near-singular configuration, integrated into a commercial robotic vacuum cleaner without modifying its primary structural frame, its stowed external envelope, or its navigation pipeline (a second actuator adjusts only the deployment height).

A kinematic and static analysis of the locking condition, consisting of the loop-closure model, the scalar input–output Jacobian, and an analytical holding condition that identifies what resists the residual back-driving torque and how the load direction and manufacturing tolerances enter.

Experimental validation of deployment repeatability (100 cycles), zero-torque load holding (50 N, in-plane), and pushing-type tidying on seven household objects, with a documented comparison protocol against a commercial arm-equipped vacuum robot.

# II DESIGN AND OPERATING PRINCIPLE

## II-A Mechanism Architecture

The mechanism is a single-DoF, closed-chain planar linkage with six moving links l 1 l_{1} – l 6 l_{6} and the chassis as the fixed frame, connected by revolute joints j 1 j_{1} – j 6 j_{6} (Fig. 2 a). Link l 1 l_{1} is the first-stage plate, driven at the frame joint j 1 j_{1} by the deployment actuator through the gear-train of Section III ; the gear-train lies on the input side and does not add mobility. Link l 2 l_{2} is the second-stage plate and a ternary link: it connects to l 1 l_{1} , to the internal transmission member l 6 l_{6} , and to the external structural member l 3 l_{3} ; the joints to l 1 l_{1} and l 3 l_{3} are coincident, forming the multi-branch joint at the l 1 l_{1} – l 2 l_{2} – l 3 l_{3} interface. The linkage is thus fully actuated in the kinematic sense, and what varies along the stroke is not the number of controlled DoFs but the transmission ratio from input to second-stage plate. The two ternary links are l 2 l_{2} and the frame, and they are not directly jointed, which is the defining property of the Stephenson chain (in the Watt chain the two ternary links share a joint) [ 15 ] ; the linkage is therefore a Stephenson-type six-bar rather than three binary links sharing a pin.

We use self-locking in the sense common to toggle and singularity-based mechanisms [ 15 , 21 ] : the linkage geometry, rather than an added brake, resists back-driving in a designated configuration. The single-DoF trajectory is traversed in three regimes (Fig. 2 ). Far from alignment, J = O ⁡ ( 1 ) J=O(1) and actuator rotation at j 1 j_{1} produces coupled motion of both plates. 2026-10-15.title: Tactile-Guided Robot Learning: From Representation Learning to Foundation Models
2026-10-15.authors: Kiyanoush Nazari , Luchen Li , Haoshu Fang , Nima Fazeli , Zhibin Li , Fumiya Iida , Thomas George Thuruthel
2026-10-15.abstract: Tactile sensing is becoming central to robust, adaptive, and dexterous robotic manipulation. Beyond its traditional role in contact detection and reactive control, touch is increasingly used to learn transferable representations, condition manipulation policies, and support embodied physical reasoning. Yet existing surveys largely emphasize tactile hardware and perception, leaving the rapid shift toward learning-based tactile manipulation insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews tactile-guided skill learning from a learning-centric perspective, organized by the functional role of touch across the learning and control pipeline. We examine tactile representation and policy learning, tactile foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and generalization across objects, tasks, sensors, embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Across these directions, we identify common design principles and remaining challenges in learning transferable physical representations, integrating semantic reasoning with contact-level control, and scaling tactile learning across heterogeneous data and hardware. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward tactile foundation and world models that can predict, reason about, and adapt physical interactions. Together, this review characterizes the transition of touch from a task-specific feedback signal toward a core modality for general-purpose embodied intelligence. An accompanying database of the reviewed literature and associated resources is available at paper web page .
2026-10-15.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation remains a major challenge in developing robots capable of human-level adaptability in unstructured environments ( Lepora, 2024 ) . Despite substantial advances in perception, planning, control, locomotion, and embodied AI, robots still struggle with everyday contact-rich tasks such as precision insertion, deformable-object manipulation, and assembly under uncertainty ( Billard and Kragic, 2019 ) . Unlike more structured robotic tasks, manipulation requires continuous regulation of physical interactions among the robot, objects, and environment ( Cui and Trinkle, 2021 ) . Successful manipulation therefore depends not only on detecting contact, but on estimating and regulating evolving contact locations, forces, friction, compliance, and interaction dynamics, often across multiple simultaneous contacts. These quantities are difficult to infer reliably from vision alone, particularly under occlusion and during fine manipulation, making tactile perception and tactile-guided control essential for robust and dexterous interaction ( Li et al., 2025a ) .

Recent tactile sensors can capture high-resolution contact geometry, force distributions, deformation, and slip ( Team, 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2025b ) , while advances in imitation learning ( Tsuji et al., 2025 ) , reinforcement learning ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , diffusion policies ( Chi et al., 2025 ) , Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models ( Ma et al., 2026b ) , and embodied AI ( Feng et al., 2026b ) have substantially expanded robots’ ability to learn complex manipulation skills from data ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ) . Yet these developments remain only partially connected, where modern policies are still predominantly vision-centric and often treat touch as auxiliary information ( Comanici et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ) . This limits their ability to reason about physical interactions in tasks where contact dynamics, rather than visual appearance alone, determine successful execution.

The role of touch in robot learning is consequently shifting from estimating low-level quantities such as contact, slip, force, and object properties ( Howe, 1993 ) toward providing physically grounded information throughout the learning and control pipeline. Tactile observations now support representation learning ( Higuera et al., 2024 ) , multimodal policy learning, physical reasoning ( Huang et al., 2025b ; Morissette et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) , adaptive decision making, and embodied world modeling ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . This shift reframes the central question from how robots can sense touch to how robots can learn from and act through touch .

Despite rapidly growing work across tactile sensing, robot learning, computer vision, and embodied AI, this literature remains fragmented. Existing surveys largely emphasize sensor hardware, sensing principles, classical tactile perception, or earlier tactile-guided manipulation and control ( Li et al., 2020 ; Kroemer et al., 2021 ) . Many also predate recent developments in foundation models and VLA systems and therefore do not capture the emerging role of touch within modern learning-based manipulation ( Lepora, 2024 ; Jin et al., 2023 ; Meribout et al., 2024 ; Mandil et al., 2023 ; Jahanshahi and others, 2025 ; Cho et al., 2024 ; Yu and Liu, 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2022 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2025 ; Xie and Correll, 2025 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Yao and Wang, 2024 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024b ; Man et al., 2022 ; Zhu et al., 2022 ; Kroemer et al., 2021 ) . A unified learning-centric account of how tactile information contributes across representation, policy learning, embodied reasoning, and generalization is therefore still lacking.

To address this gap, we organize the review according to the functional role of tactile information within learning-based manipulation (Fig. 1 ). We examine six research questions. RQ1 considers how tactile observations are represented, encoded, and fused with other modalities, covering self-supervised ( Dave et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025b ) , multimodal ( Cheng et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2026a ) , and cross-modal representation learning ( Fu et al., 2024a ) . RQ2 examines how touch conditions action generation through imitation learning ( Funk et al., 2026 ) , reinforcement learning ( Miller et al., 2026 ) , diffusion policies ( Xue et al., 2025 ) , and multimodal policy architectures. RQ3 investigates tactile-informed foundation and world models, including tactile-enhanced VLAs ( Hao et al., 2026 ) , multimodal world models ( Zhang et al., 2026d ) , and foundation controllers ( You et al., 2026 ) , where touch supports physically grounded reasoning and planning. RQ4 considers predictive and adaptive tactile control, where tactile feedback supports interaction-state estimation, feedback regulation, contact prediction, online optimization, and adaptation under uncertain physical interactions ( Yin et al., 2025a ; Xu and She, 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ; Nazari et al., 2025 ; Nazari et al., 2023 ) . RQ5 evaluates generalization beyond training conditions across objects, tasks, sensors, robot embodiments, environments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Finally, RQ6 synthesizes these developments to identify the remaining challenges and research directions toward scalable tactile foundation models, general-purpose manipulation, and lifelong tactile learning.

# II Tactile Representation Learning

## II-A Self-Supervised Tactile Representation Learning

Self-supervised learning enables tactile representations to be learned from unlabeled interaction data ( Gui et al., 2024 ; Lee et al., 2018 ) , avoiding physically motivated preprocessing such as marker tracking ( Li et al., 2023 ) , finite-element modeling ( Sferrazza et al., 2019 ) , or task-specific descriptors. Unlike vision, where large-scale datasets and pretrained models are readily available ( Russakovsky et al., 2015 ) , tactile data require physical interaction and remain strongly sensor-dependent. Recent approaches therefore exploit data collected through robotic exploration, demonstration, or in-the-wild interaction ( Yang et al., 2022 ) , using reconstruction, contrastive learning, self-distillation, masked modeling, or action-conditioned prediction ( Mandil et al., 2022 ) to learn reusable tactile features.

Reconstruction-based methods require an encoded latent state to retain sufficient information for recovering the original observation, or components removed from it. Given a tactile observation 𝐱 \mathbf{x} , an encoder f θ f_{\theta} produces 𝐳 = f θ ​ ( 𝐱 ) \mathbf{z}=f_{\theta}(\mathbf{x}) , from which a decoder g ϕ g_{\phi} reconstructs 𝐱 ^ = g ϕ ​ ( 𝐳 ) \hat{\mathbf{x}}=g_{\phi}(\mathbf{z}) :

where d ⁡ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) d(\cdot,\cdot) measures reconstruction error. Although scalable, this objective may preserve sensor-specific appearance rather than physically relevant interaction variables. Early work ( Murali et al., 2020 ) used a recurrent conditional autoencoder to encode fingertip-force sequences for vision-free grasping, transferring the representation to material recognition and grasp-stability estimation. UniT ( Xu et al., 2025b ) instead introduces vector quantization ( Van Den Oord et al., 2017 ) , using a VQGAN to encode tactile images as discrete tokens; despite pretraining on a single simple object, its structured latent space transfers zero-shot to unseen-object pose estimation and classification and to three real-world policy-learning tasks. Following masked modeling ( He et al., 2022 ) , TacMAE ( Cao et al., 2023 ) reconstructs masked tactile-image regions, achieving 71.4% zero-shot and 85.8% fine-tuned accuracy on unseen YCB objects. For structured 3D tactile arrays, ( Wu et al., 2025a ) reconstructs masked local forces from taxel coordinates, poses, and forces before transferring the encoder to a visuo-tactile Diffusion Policy. Finally, ( Li et al., 2025d ) represents tactile observations as modulated neural implicit functions using a shared SIREN trunk, substantially reducing storage while retaining information for downstream pose estimation. Collectively, these methods progress from reconstructing raw sequences and pixels toward discrete tokens, physical force fields, and continuous functions, introducing stronger structural priors to encourage more transferable representations.

Contrastive learning methods forgo reconstruction and instead enforce similarity between observations of the same interaction while separating distinct interactions. Given an anchor embedding 𝐳 i \mathbf{z}_{i} , the following InfoNCE-style ( Oord et al., 2018 ) objective increases its similarity to a positive embedding 𝐳 i + \mathbf{z}_{i}^{+} while reducing its similarity to negative embeddings 𝐳 j − \mathbf{z}_{j}^{-} :

Non-contrastive methods replace explicit negatives with consistency or prediction objectives (see Fig. 2 for architecture examples). BYOL- ( Grill et al., 2020 ) and DINO-style ( Caron et al., 2021 ) self-distillation align online and target networks across augmented views, while spatial and temporal predictive methods infer masked or future latent states from context. Their central challenge remains defining appropriate invariances, since variations in contact location or pressure may represent either nuisance or task-relevant physical information. T-DEX ( Guzey et al., 2023 ) uses BYOL to pretrain a tactile encoder on 2.5 hours of teleoperated play with distributed uSkin sensors, enabling nearest-neighbor action retrieval from a visuo-tactile latent space and data-efficient manipulation from few demonstrations. exUMI ( Xu et al., 2025a ) instead introduces Tactile Predictive Pretraining, using a Transformer with latent diffusion to predict future tactile states conditioned on context and actions; the frozen encoder is subsequently transferred to Diffusion Policies, preserving deformation and contact-transition information overlooked by static objectives.

Sparsh ( Higuera et al., 2024 ) provides a large-scale comparison of these paradigms, benchmarking masked autoencoding, DINO self-distillation ( Caron et al., 2021 ) , and I-JEPA/V-JEPA ( Assran et al., 2023 ) on more than 460,000 unlabeled tactile observations through a benchmark of six touch-centric tasks. The stronger transfer of DINO and I-JEPA indicates that reconstructing tactile appearance does not necessarily preserve the mechanical information required downstream. More broadly, reconstruction, contrastive, and predictive objectives differ primarily in what they define as physically relevant structure: force fields, cross-modal semantics, augmentation invariance, or action-conditioned contact evolution. Their effectiveness therefore depends not simply on scale, but on whether the learning objective preserves interaction variables relevant to downstream manipulation. These methods nevertheless primarily learn representations from individual tactile streams; we next consider representations learned jointly with complementary sensory modalities.

## II-B Multimodal Touch Representations

Multimodal representation learning exploits complementary information across sensing modalities, analogous to human perception where visual and haptic cues are integrated according to their reliability ( Ernst and Banks, 2002 ) . Vision provides global context but degrades under contact-induced occlusion, whereas touch directly captures local interaction states. Their fusion can be expressed as

The simplest approaches concatenate independently encoded modalities, as in the ACT-based framework of ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) for deformable-object tracing and the contact-phase VITAL controller of ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) . While being modular, concatenation leaves cross-modal correspondence to be learned implicitly. 3D-ViTac ( Huang et al., 2024a ) instead projects vision and touch into a common 3D frame, forming a unified visuo-tactile point cloud in which contact locations and forces are directly grounded in scene geometry; Section IV revisits this representation for diffusion-policy control.

Attention-based fusion learns cross-modal relationships without explicitly specifying geometry. ViTacFormer ( Heng et al., 2025 ) uses bidirectional cross-attention between visual and tactile features, together with future tactile-token prediction, improving bimanual manipulation under occlusion and sustained contact. Because high-bandwidth vision can otherwise dominate learning, ( Li et al., 2025b ) introduces force-guided attention with auxiliary future-force prediction, achieving 93% success across three contact-rich tasks while dynamically shifting attention toward touch during contact and vision during free motion. VHTformer ( Li et al., 2025c ) instead uses symmetric joint queries across vision, touch, and language to avoid structurally privileging any modality.

Multimodal tactile representations need not include vision. Sparsh-X ( Higuera et al., 2025 ) jointly models optical deformation, contact-microphone vibration, motion, and pressure from Digit 360, outperforming tactile-image-only representations on plug insertion and in-hand rotation. Overall, multimodal representations span simple feature concatenation, geometrically grounded fusion, learned cross-attention, and adaptive modality weighting, with their key distinction being how explicitly they encode correspondence and complementarity among sensory signals.

## II-C Cross-Modal Alignment and Grounding

Large pre-trained vision-language models provide shared embedding spaces into which additional modalities can be aligned ( Girdhar et al., 2023 ) , an approach increasingly extended to touch ( Yang et al., 2024 ; George et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024b ) . Unlike multimodal fusion (Sec. III-B), which combines simultaneous observations into a task-specific representation, alignment projects touch into a pre-trained semantic space. Given paired data ( T , x ) (T,x) , a tactile encoder f ϕ f_{\phi} is trained to match the embedding g ⁡ ( x ) g(x) of a frozen encoder, typically through an InfoNCE objective

Synchronized vision-touch pairs provide the most direct alignment signal ( Yang et al., 2022 ) . VITaL ( George et al., 2024 ) aligns visual and tactile observations so that touch shapes a visual representation that remains beneficial even when tactile input is removed at deployment. VITaMIn ( Liu et al., 2025 ) introduces temporal structure by aligning a masked current observation with the CLIP embedding of a future unmasked frame, thereby relating contact to subsequent outcomes. Tac-DINO ( Li et al., 2026a ) instead addresses spatial granularity: rather than aligning local touch with an entire image, it aligns touch with the corresponding visual patch, outperforming image-level alignment on over 20,000 contacts across 505 objects. Together, these approaches show that both the temporal target and spatial granularity of alignment determine what interaction structure is preserved.

UniTouch ( Yang et al., 2024 ) aligns touch with frozen image embeddings already connected to language and sound, indirectly transferring this broader semantic structure and enabling zero-shot material recognition, cross-modal retrieval, and touch-conditioned generation. Octopi ( Yu et al., 2024 ) instead maps tactile embeddings into tokens consumed by a frozen large language model, enabling open-vocabulary reasoning about material and physical properties without explicit tactile-text alignment, although its reasoning remains dependent on the backbone’s physical knowledge. Finally, FG-CLTP ( Ma et al., 2026a ) complements semantic descriptors with quantitative physical information by converting tactile deformation into 3D point clouds, discretizing force and contact geometry into numerical tokens, and jointly aligning them with point clouds and language. Its sensor-independent 3D representation additionally supports sim-to-real and cross-sensor transfer. Overall, these methods progressively extend tactile alignment from global semantic correspondence toward spatially localized, temporally predictive, multimodal, and physically grounded representations.

## II-D Transferability and Generalization

Recent work increasingly targets general-purpose tactile encoders rather than task-specific features ( Higuera et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ) , following the pre-training paradigm of vision and language, z = f θ ​ ( T ) , z=f_{\theta}(T), where T ∼ p src ​ ( T ) T\sim p_{\mathrm{src}}(T) .
Such pre-training is valuable only if representations remain informative under shifts from p src ​ ( T ) p_{\mathrm{src}}(T) to a target distribution p tgt ​ ( T ) p_{\mathrm{tgt}}(T) . This is particularly challenging for touch because measurements are tightly coupled to sensor hardware, with transfer failures occurring even between instances of the same sensor model due to manufacturing variation ( Gupta et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2025 ) .

Cross-sensor transfer follows three main strategies. First, joint multi-sensor pre-training seeks sensor-invariant structure from heterogeneous data. T3 ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) combines sensor-specific input encoders with a shared Transformer trained across 13 sensors and 11 tasks, while AnyTouch ( Feng et al., 2025 ) learns cross-sensor correspondence in dynamic interactions and ToucHD ( Feng et al., 2026a ) extends this toward hierarchical contact dynamics. These approaches produce reusable encoders but require large jointly curated multi-sensor datasets. Second, pairwise transfer learns mappings between particular sensors, GenForce ( Chen et al., 2026c ) translates heterogeneous observations into a shared marker representation while preserving source force labels; CTTP ( Rodriguez et al., 2025b ) aligns GelSlim and Soft Bubble through InfoNCE; and Touch2Touch ( Rodriguez et al., 2025a ) translates between them using diffusion. Such methods avoid large joint corpora but must be retrained for new sensor pairs. Third, SITR ( Gupta et al., 2025 ) explicitly conditions a modified Vision Transformer on calibration images, disentangling sensor-specific effects from contact geometry and thereby extending transfer to new sensors given a small calibration set.

These strategies trade data scale, transfer specificity, and deployment assumptions, where joint pre-training scales across sensors but requires heterogeneous corpora; pairwise methods reduce this requirement but scale poorly with sensor diversity; and disentanglement offers broader transfer at the cost of calibration. More importantly, transfer across tasks, objects, and robot embodiments remains comparatively underexplored at the representation level, and whether sensor-invariant features ultimately yield transferable manipulation policies remains an open question revisited in Section VII.

Across the paradigms reviewed above, no tactile representation is universally optimal. Representations grounded in physical quantities such as force, contact geometry, or action-conditioned dynamics can improve invariance by abstracting away sensor-specific measurements, but excessive abstraction may discard fine texture, deformation, slip, or other task-relevant cues. The central challenge is therefore to preserve information required for downstream prediction and control while suppressing nuisance variation. Evaluating this balance remains difficult because benchmarks are fragmented across sensors, tasks, and datasets, motivating standardized evaluation of representation quality, transfer, and downstream manipulation performance. The following section examines how these representations are used for action generation.

2026-10-15.title: HM3D-M3: A Benchmark for Multi-Agent, Multi-Modal, Multi-Object Goal Navigation
2026-10-15.authors: Hongyu Ding , Kanyu Xu , Mingjia Chen , Zixuan Chen , Jieqi Shi , Jing Huo , Yifan Zhang , Yang Gao
2026-10-15.abstract:
Rapid progress in AI agents and robotics makes it a matter of the near future that humans are served by a team of robots.
Such a team will receive several goals at once, each specified in whatever form is convenient for the human, such as a category name, a photo, or a spoken description.
Existing benchmarks study multi-agent, multi-modal, and multi-object goal navigation in isolation , and a benchmark that places all three in one episode is missing.
To fill this gap, we introduce HM3D-M 3 .
A team of K K agents starts at distributed locations in a photorealistic indoor scene and searches for an unordered set of M M object goals, each given as an open-vocabulary category, an instance image, or an instance description.
HM3D-M 3 provides 1,000 validation episodes over 3,926 goals from 379 open-vocabulary categories, 100K observation–assignment training samples, and two team-level metrics, goal-level SR and makespan-normalized SPL.
We further contribute two baselines.
HiGA is a trained hierarchical goal assigner on top of a frozen open-vocabulary navigation policy, and LaViRA-M 3 is a training-free team of VLM agents with shared mapping and progress analysis.
Adapted multi-robot and zero-shot methods reach 16–27% SR, while our baselines reach 38–41% with complementary strengths and distinct failure modes.
Furthermore, we deploy LaViRA-M 3 on a heterogeneous three-robot team.
Project page: https://robo-lavira.github.io/hm3d-m3/
2026-10-15.introduction:
Consider a home with several robots and a resident who asks them to find a nightstand, the couch in a photo, and “the plant by the sliding glass door”.
Nothing in this request is exotic.
Rapid progress in AI agents and robot hardware places such teams within the near future, and the request has the shape everyday instructions take: several goals at once, each given in whatever form is at hand.
What is missing is a way to measure how well a team handles it, since the goals have to be divided, recognized under three different specifications, and tracked jointly.

Standing in that future and looking back at the present, the landscape of navigation benchmarks is fragmented, as Table I summarizes.
Single-agent object-goal navigation asks for one instance of one category, recently from an open vocabulary [ 1 , 6 ] . Multi-object variants give one agent several category goals [ 3 , 10 ] . Multi-modal variants mix category, image, and language goals, but present them sequentially and score each sub-task on its own [ 7 ] .
Multi-robot semantic navigation evaluates teams, but on a single goal of a single modality, and grants success as soon as any robot arrives [ 11 , 12 ] .
Recent systems combine all three [ 13 , 14 ] , yet they are evaluated on episodes borrowed from single-agent benchmarks with per-sub-task scoring.
No benchmark defines the joint task, generates episodes for it, or measures the team as a whole.

The intersection is not a concatenation of its parts.
Allocation happens under partial observability, since who should pursue which goal depends on heterogeneous evidence that arrives as the map grows. Verification becomes instance-level, since an image or a description refers to one specific object. Completion is joint, since the natural cost is the team makespan, so an idle or redundant robot is not free.

To fill this gap, we present HM3D-M 3 , a benchmark for M ulti-agent, M ulti-modal, M ulti-object goal navigation in photorealistic scans of real buildings [ 15 , 16 ] , illustrated in Fig. 1 .
An episode places K K agents at distributed, jointly reachable start positions and gives the team an unordered set of M M goals from 379 open-vocabulary categories.
Each goal is specified as a category (ON), an instance image (IIN), or an instance description (TN).
A goal counts as found when an agent declares it while standing within 1 m of that instance, and every episode stores the oracle team makespan d ∗ d^{\ast} for budgeting and normalization.

We further contribute two baselines, one trained and one training-free.
HiGA, short for Hierarchical Goal Assigner, is a trained method in which a transformer reads the shared map, agent poses, and per-goal CLIP heat maps, assigns goals to agents, and hands each assignment to a frozen open-vocabulary navigation policy [ 6 ] . It is trained with behavior cloning and DAgger [ 17 ] from an oracle assigner.
LaViRA-M 3 is a training-free method that extends the vision-language model (VLM) navigation agent of LaViRA [ 18 , 19 ] to a team coordinated only through a shared map, a shared goal board, and shared natural-language progress analysis.
We also adapt four existing multi-robot and zero-shot methods [ 20 , 21 , 11 , 13 ] to the benchmark.

The results expose a task that is far from solved, with adapted methods at 16–27% SR, HiGA at 37.9%, and LaViRA-M 3 at 41.0%, and two baselines with complementary strengths.
HiGA is the strongest on category goals but weak on image goals and inefficient, whereas LaViRA-M 3 is the strongest on image and text goals and the most efficient.
Their failures differ, since LaViRA-M 3 mostly declares a goal from the wrong place, whereas HiGA mostly fails to detect or match it.

Our contributions are:

HM3D-M 3 , the first benchmark for multi-agent, multi-modal, multi-object goal navigation, with a standardized episode generator, a validation set of 1,000 episodes and 3,926 goals on 36 held-out scenes, a training set of 100K observation–assignment samples on disjoint scenes, and team-level metrics.

Two baselines, the trained HiGA and the training-free LaViRA-M 3 , plus adaptations of four existing methods, evaluated with ablations, scaling studies over K K and M M , and a per-goal failure attribution.

A real-world deployment of LaViRA-M 3 on a heterogeneous team of three robots running local VLMs, which complete mixed-modality goal sets in an office through the same coordination channels as in simulation.

1. HM3D-M 3 , the first benchmark for multi-agent, multi-modal, multi-object goal navigation, with a standardized episode generator, a validation set of 1,000 episodes and 3,926 goals on 36 held-out scenes, a training set of 100K observation–assignment samples on disjoint scenes, and team-level metrics.

2. Two baselines, the trained HiGA and the training-free LaViRA-M 3 , plus adaptations of four existing methods, evaluated with ablations, scaling studies over K K and M M , and a per-goal failure attribution.

3. A real-world deployment of LaViRA-M 3 on a heterogeneous team of three robots running local VLMs, which complete mixed-modality goal sets in an office through the same coordination channels as in simulation.

# II Related Work

Goal navigation benchmarks. Single-agent benchmarks have progressively enriched how a goal is specified, from a closed set of categories [ 1 , 2 ] to an open vocabulary [ 6 ] , and to a particular instance shown in an image [ 5 ] or described in language [ 7 ] .
Multi-object variants ask one agent for several goals, in a fixed order [ 3 ] or as an unordered set [ 10 ] , recently across several floors [ 9 ] , and lifelong multi-modal navigation chains 5–10 goals of mixed modality into one episode with per-sub-task scoring [ 22 , 7 ] .
The one multi-agent benchmark among them, Habitat-MAS [ 8 ] , targets language-specified household tasks for heterogeneous teams, with multi-object navigation limited to a closed vocabulary and a single modality.
HM3D-M 3 inherits the open vocabulary and the three goal modalities of this line, and adds a team of agents, an unordered goal set searched jointly, and a per-episode team optimum.

Multi-robot semantic navigation. After early work in synthetic scenes [ 4 ] , recent systems on photorealistic scans let a VLM allocate frontiers to robots [ 11 , 12 ] , and LLM agents have been coordinated on unordered multi-object missions in a single modality on small custom episode sets [ 23 ] .
Closest to our task are two very recent systems that run robot teams on multi-modal, multi-goal missions.
DM 3 -Nav [ 13 ] is decentralized, with agents that exchange local maps, task states, and intents within communication range and claim goals by broadcasting them, and it introduces a makespan-normalized SPL.
AnyGoal [ 14 ] is a training-free team in which a VLM guides exploration toward category, image, and language goals presented sequentially, as in GOAT-Bench.
Both are methods rather than benchmarks, evaluated on single-agent episodes with sub-task scoring, and neither defines a multi-agent episode distribution, a team budget, or team metrics, which HM3D-M 3 supplies.
We evaluate the official implementation of DM 3 -Nav on it and adopt its MSPL. The code of AnyGoal had not been released at the time of writing.

Trained and training-free navigation policies. Trained object-goal policies range from end-to-end RL and imitation [ 24 ] to the DAgger-trained open-vocabulary policy [ 6 ] that we use frozen as the lower level of HiGA.
Training-free methods pair explicit maps with foundation models [ 25 , 20 ] , unify category, image, and text goals by graph matching [ 26 ] , or let an LLM or VLM act as the navigation agent itself [ 27 , 18 ] .
LaViRA [ 18 ] and Uni-LaViRA [ 19 ] decompose each decision into a language, a vision, and a robot action. LaViRA-M 3 extends them to a team.

2026-10-15.title: FoveaVLA: Foveation Actions Replace the Wrist Camera in VLAs
2026-10-15.authors: Bingao Chen , Lihan Zha , C. Karen Liu , Guy Tevet
2026-10-15.abstract:
We present FoveaVLA, a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model that replaces the wrist camera with learned foveation actions. Wrist cameras provide close-up detail but restrict the view to the end-effector’s surroundings.
External cameras see the whole scene, but the policy receives them at low resolution, so the fine detail needed for manipulation is lost.
FoveaVLA recovers this detail by predicting, alongside each action chunk, the interaction region to observe at the next policy query. The policy then receives crops of these regions, taken from the original-resolution images, together with the full views. We build FoveaVLA on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} in two configurations, Single and Dual, using one or two external stereo cameras with full and foveal RGB and depth inputs, and post-train both on DROID with RoboInter interaction annotations. Across four real-world task suites, FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8 70.8 % success with one external RGB-D view, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1 77.1 %, versus 52.1 52.1 % for the wrist-equipped π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Both match the baseline on plain pick-and-place and improve success with distractors, cloth manipulation, and far-away objects.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Recent progress in robot manipulation has been driven by large models trained on diverse robot datasets [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Most of these models take a wrist camera as input [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , which provides close-up observations that learned policies often depend on [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . This close-up view comes at the cost of scene coverage: the camera moves with the end-effector, so distant targets and surrounding context can lie outside its view, more so when manipulation spans a larger workspace or involves a mobile robot. The wrist camera also adds hardware and creates an observation mismatch with human demonstrations recorded without a wrist view [ 10 , 11 ] . Can a policy get the close-up detail it needs from external observations alone, so that the robot no longer needs a wrist camera?

External cameras record high-resolution images, but resizing a whole scene to the policy’s low input resolution reduces the detail available for the gripper and object, and uniformly increasing the input resolution spends computation on background regions. External views also lack a consistent geometric frame: a wrist camera maintains a fixed pose relative to the end-effector, whereas an external view depends on the camera’s placement relative to the robot. Prior work reports lower success for policies learned without wrist observations [ 12 , 7 ] . We observe a similar gap on our four real-world task suites: π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} post-trained on two external RGB views alone achieves 25.0 25.0 % success, compared with 52.1 52.1 % with the wrist view.

Existing approaches obtain close-up observations through additional sensing or constructed viewpoints. Generative methods synthesize wrist images from external observations [ 13 , 14 ] . Others render virtual views from 3D scene representations [ 15 , 16 ] , or move a camera on a dedicated arm or neck [ 17 , 18 ] . Human-gaze-guided foveation is closer to our goal of selecting detail within an existing image [ 19 , 20 ] , but relies on gaze recorded during data collection. We instead learn where to crop from existing robot demonstrations, supervised by their interaction annotations.

Human vision allocates detail selectively. Peripheral vision provides scene context while central vision resolves the detail needed to grasp an object [ 21 ] , and gaze reaches the next contact point before the hand does [ 22 ] . We take the same approach in FoveaVLA, which replaces the wrist camera with a learned foveation action that selects where to look next. Cropping the predicted interaction region from the original-resolution image and resizing it to the same 224 × 224 224\times 224 encoder input devotes many more pixels to the gripper and object than the resized full view does. Feeding this crop alongside the full view gives the policy both the close-up detail it needs for manipulation and the layout of the whole scene.

We build FoveaVLA on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 23 ] . From the current observation, it generates a robot action chunk and predicts one bounding box per external view for the interaction region at the next policy query. The predicted boxes crop the newly captured images, and the crops are added to the next policy input alongside the full views. We derive supervision from RoboInter annotations [ 24 ] on DROID demonstrations [ 5 ] , constructing a bounding box around the components involved in each annotated skill, such as the gripper, object, and target region. Annotations at the next query provide targets for future-box prediction. We instantiate the method as FoveaVLA-Single and FoveaVLA-Dual, using one and two external stereo cameras, respectively, with full and foveal RGB images and aligned depth estimated from each stereo pair. Both operate without a wrist camera; Dual adds a second external viewpoint to the same foveation mechanism.

We post-train both configurations on DROID and evaluate them on the four real-world task suites. FoveaVLA-Single achieves 70.8 70.8 % success using one external RGB-D view, exceeding the wrist-equipped π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} at 52.1 52.1 %, and FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 77.1 77.1 %. The largest gains are on pick-and-place with distractors, where Single raises success from 25.0 25.0 % to 58.3 58.3 %, and on moving far objects, from 41.7 41.7 % to 75.0 75.0 %. On MolmoSpaces [ 25 ] , FoveaVLA-Dual achieves 22.4 22.4 % average zero-shot success versus 17.8 17.8 % for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -DROID [ 26 ] , outperforming it on seven of nine tasks.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

Wrist cameras in robot manipulation. Eye-in-hand cameras date back to visual servoing [ 27 ] and were adopted in learning-based manipulation after empirical studies showed their benefit [ 12 ] . Hsu et al. argued that the partial observability of the hand-centric view is an inductive bias that aids generalization [ 7 ] . Wrist cameras are now standard in bimanual hardware [ 4 ] , handheld collection devices [ 6 ] , datasets and benchmarks [ 5 , 28 , 25 ] , and generalist policies [ 23 , 29 , 30 ] .
Wrist-only observations can lack the scene context needed for manipulation, motivating a wide-angle fisheye lens in UMI [ 6 ] and an additional external view in MV-UMI [ 31 ] .
Policies also come to depend on this view: LIBERO-Plus finds that multi-view VLAs retain much of their performance with the external view masked [ 8 ] , and other studies find policies including π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} more sensitive to masking or perturbing the wrist view [ 9 , 32 , 33 ] .
FoveaVLA keeps the close-up that makes the wrist view valuable, without mounting a camera on the hand.

Constructed viewpoints and active vision. WristWorld generates wrist-view videos from anchor views [ 13 ] , while inference-time view synthesis supplies in-hand images to a trained policy [ 14 ] . WARPED renders wrist-aligned training observations from egocentric human videos but retains a physical wrist camera during execution [ 34 ] . Others re-render the scene from virtual viewpoints using 3D scene representations, zooming coarse to fine on point clouds [ 16 ] or selecting virtual views and applying 3D zoom within a VLA [ 15 ] . Physical active-vision systems instead control a camera using demonstrations [ 17 , 18 , 35 ] or task reward [ 36 ] . EyeVLA predicts pan, tilt, and zoom for a physical PTZ camera [ 37 ] . Such systems require camera actuation and supervision or rewards for camera control.
FoveaVLA uses fixed cameras and selects regions within the images they already capture.

Learned visual attention and foveation. Human vision resolves fine detail only in a small central region, and the eyes move this region to the grasp point before the hand arrives [ 38 , 21 , 22 ] .
Attention models learn glimpse actions [ 39 ] , and foveation also aids recognition [ 40 ] and gaze-conditioned generation [ 41 ] . VLMs retrieve local evidence through crops [ 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 ] to answer questions about a given image, whereas we use predicted regions to select the next robot observation. In manipulation, foveation has been supervised by human gaze, as a foveal crop fed to the policy [ 19 ] or gaze co-predicted with actions [ 20 ] , a signal recorded with eye trackers during collection and not provided by DROID. AtVLA corrects visual attention with register tokens and, when uncertain, crops a region chosen by attention rollout [ 46 ] . Another approach trains a policy that chooses which regions a sensor captures for frozen downstream models, including a manipulation policy [ 47 ] . FoveaVLA instead decodes a future interaction box alongside each action chunk. Prior VLAs also use localization supervision [ 23 ] , spatial traces [ 48 , 49 ] , or visual and textual affordances [ 50 ] , but only as auxiliary targets that help action prediction.
In FoveaVLA, the predicted box determines the crop the policy receives next, and its supervision comes from existing large-scale interaction annotations [ 24 ] .

2026-10-15.title: MorphAct: Robot Policies Morphing with the Worlds They Act In
2026-10-15.authors: Ziyan Liu , Jiting Liu , Weihong Zhong , Wenda Yu , Yeqiu Chen , Jason Li , Xiaojiang Peng , Shuyuan Hu , Kai Wang , Bo Zhao
2026-10-15.abstract:
Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions. However, existing robot policies use shared parameters that remain fixed across interaction contexts. When different operations favor competing parameter adjustments, fitting their mixture can leave individual operations insufficiently adapted. Our atomic-task diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both vision–language and action parameters, with source-improving updates increasing loss on other tasks. This motivates MorphAct 1 1 1 “Morph,” rooted in Greek morphē (“form”), means “to transform.” , a contextual parameterization framework that dynamically adjusts robot policy parameters as interaction contexts change. Two coupled generators produce context-dependent low-rank updates for the vision–language and action modules. Their coupling follows the policy’s computational dependency: vision–language updates shape the representations that condition action-side parameter generation. Both generators are trained jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets.
MorphAct improves performance across three VLA backbones on LIBERO and Meta-World, with gains of up to 16.30%. In real-world evaluation, it achieves gains of up to 14% over π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Ablations support the benefits of contextual parameter generation and representation coupling.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Progress toward general intelligence in the physical world requires scaling robot learning across diverse environments, operations, and interactions ( Driess et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2025 ) . This expansion brings together heterogeneous perceptual and control demands within a shared model. Such diversity arises not only across tasks but also within a single interaction: placing an object in a tray involves approaching it, establishing contact, transporting it, and positioning it precisely. These operations require different visual cues and control behaviors, often under an unchanged instruction. As environmental and operational coverage expands, a central challenge is how a shared model can effectively accommodate these heterogeneous demands.

Vision–language–action (VLA) models provide a promising foundation by combining pretrained multimodal representations with action prediction ( Brohan et al., 2023a ; Kim et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . However, conventional VLA policies execute diverse interactions using a shared, static parameter configuration. Context changes their activations and predicted actions, but their effective weights remain fixed, including after full fine-tuning or low-rank adaptation ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Kim et al., 2025a ) . Different operations must therefore be learned through shared parameters, even when their training signals favor competing updates—a source of interference in joint optimization ( Yu et al., 2020a ) . This raises the question of how effectively shared parameters reconcile the demands of different operations.

We investigate this question through operation-level diagnostics using demonstrations from the 65 atomic tasks in RoboCasa365 ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) . At a common policy checkpoint, we examine gradient alignment, the effect of a single update on other tasks, and the contributions of individual parameter groups. The diagnostics reveal competing update directions in both the vision–language and action modules. Every measured source-improving update also increases loss on batches from other tasks, while opposing parameter-group contributions can cancel within a module. These findings expose local adaptation trade-offs in shared parameter space. They motivate a shared parameter-generation mechanism whose outputs vary with the interaction context.

To address this challenge, we introduce MorphAct , a contextual parameterization framework that enables robot policies to morph with changing interaction contexts (Figure 1 ). MorphAct generates context-dependent low-rank parameter updates for the vision–language and action modules, allowing a shared policy to adjust its effective weights to the current interaction. Because vision–language adaptation changes the representations used for control, MorphAct couples the two generators by conditioning action-side parameter generation on the adapted representations. Both generators learn jointly through the native action objective, without operation labels or expert-adapter targets. Low-rank factors provide an efficient implementation of these contextual updates.

We evaluate MorphAct on X-VLA, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) using LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) and Meta-World ( Yu et al., 2020b ) , comparing each backbone’s baseline with MorphAct. Across the three backbones, MorphAct improves Meta-World average success by 7.57–16.30%; on LIBERO, X-VLA, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} gain 4.15%, 2.50%, and 1.75%, respectively. Real-world evaluation with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} further yields gains of 8.00–14.00% across four manipulation tasks. Controlled X-VLA ablations on LIBERO show that fixed generation conditions, single-module adaptation, and action-side generation conditioned on pre-adaptation features each reduce mean success. These results support contextual parameterization and representation coupling for accommodating diverse manipulation demands.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) We identify parameter conflicts as a challenge to scaling robot learning across diverse environments and interactions through operation-level diagnostic experiments. (2) We introduce MorphAct, whose representation-coupled generators produce context-dependent vision–language and action parameter updates and learn jointly through the native action objective. (3) We demonstrate success gains on three VLA backbones, two simulation benchmarks, and four real-world tasks, with ablations supporting contextual generation and representation coupling.

The within-task reference shows that update directions also vary
among episodes of the same task, while cross-task comparisons
produce negative alignment more frequently.
Competing adaptation demands therefore affect both the
representations used for control and the action mapping.

## 2.2 Cross-Task Interference from Parameter Updates

Gradient alignment describes local update directions; we next measure
the loss changes produced by an actual update.
For each source batch U i U_{i} , we take one full-parameter gradient step
and evaluate the target batches V j V_{j} , restarting from the common
checkpoint for every source.
Target observations, action targets, flow times, and noise remain
fixed before and after the step.
Across four rounds, all 260 updates reduce their source-batch loss,
with a mean relative reduction of 2.38%.
Yet each update increases loss on batches from 22–46 of the other

Every source-improving update thus has both helpful and harmful
effects on other tasks: improving the source does not produce

## 2.3 Conflicting Contributions Across Parameter Groups

The preceding comparisons summarize each module as a whole.
To examine the interactions within these summaries, we decompose
gradient alignment across 47 VLM groups and 19 action groups,
including individual Transformer blocks ( Shi et al., 2023 ) .
Each group’s gradient inner product is normalized by the same

Positive and negative contributions can offset one another.

For cross-task pairs, cancellation reaches 36.13% in the VLM

tasks and act on both representation and action parameters.
An update that serves one context can work against another,
