2026-10-15.title: Complementary Future Token Pruning for World Action Models
2026-10-15.authors: Baekseung Kim , Junhoo Lee , Sohyeon Hong , Suhyun Jeon , Minkyu Kim , Seungyeon Kim , Donghoon Han , Nojun Kwak
2026-10-15.abstract:
World action models (WAMs) jointly predict future visual states and robot actions, but processing dense future-frame tokens incurs
substantial inference latency. We propose CF-Prune , a training-free framework for pruning future-frame tokens in pretrained WAMs.
Our key insight is that future visual predictions support action
generation and therefore need not preserve every visual detail
required for high-fidelity video synthesis. CF-Prune combines
instruction and action attention to identify task-relevant tokens
during the initial denoising forward pass, even when future-frame
and action representations remain highly noisy. An entropy-based
phase identification mechanism further retains dense computation
during precision phases to mitigate pruning-induced performance
degradation. Experiments on RoboLab, RoboCasa, and real-world
manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent inference speedups.
At a 35% pruning ratio, CF-Prune achieves average speedups of 1.19 1.19 – 1.27 × 1.27\times while improving task success rates.
At a 50% pruning ratio, it achieves 1.29 1.29 – 1.33 × 1.33\times average
speedups on both simulation benchmarks, with overall success
rates within 1.0 percentage point of the baseline.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Extending foundation models to physical environments, particularly robotic manipulation, has recently attracted significant attention, due to their potential to enable robots to generalize across diverse tasks and environments. Vision-language-action (VLA) models represent a prominent approach ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) , while world action models (WAMs) based on video diffusion models have emerged to better capture scene geometry, physical dynamics, and future state evolution ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026b ) . However, deploying these models on real robots requires not only high task performance but also low-latency inference ( Black et al., 2025 ) . Since robotic manipulation requires repeated action generation throughout a task, inference latency accumulates across policy queries, delaying action execution and substantially increasing the overall task completion time. This problem is especially critical for WAMs due to the substantial computational overhead of video diffusion models, making efficient inference essential for their practical use in real-world manipulation.

WAMs jointly generate robot actions and multiple future frames, introducing dense spatiotemporal token grids that account for a substantial portion of the computation in the video diffusion backbone. While VLAs address a similar bottleneck by pruning observation tokens ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , directly pruning future-frame tokens is difficult because they constitute the model outputs in conventional video diffusion models and support action generation through future-state prediction in WAMs. Video diffusion acceleration therefore modifies attention masks ( Xi et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2025 ) , but the cost of determining effective masks can offset the gains in few-step WAMs. Existing WAM methods instead reduce denoising steps ( Ye et al., 2026b ) or redesign the model to bypass future generation ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) ; the former retains the per-step token burden, whereas the latter requires retraining. Consequently, existing WAM acceleration methods do not directly reduce future-frame tokens without additional training.

We propose CF-Prune ( C omplementary F uture token Prun ing), a training-free method for pruning future-frame tokens in WAMs. Our key insight is that, while video diffusion models are designed to generate high-fidelity videos, WAMs use future-frame prediction primarily as an intermediate reference for action generation. Therefore, as
illustrated in Figure 1 , future representations must preserve task-relevant semantics and dynamics but need not retain every fine-grained visual detail. Allocating a dense grid of tokens to future frames is thus unnecessarily redundant for action prediction, motivating selective pruning that retains only the tokens needed for action generation without retraining. Realizing this potential requires identifying which future-frame tokens matter for action prediction early in denoising, when their representations remain highly noisy and their relevance is not yet explicit.

Specifically, CF-Prune constructs an attention-based pruning criterion by analyzing the concentration of visual information with respect to action and instruction tokens, enabling effective token selection even when the action and future-frame latents remain highly noisy. Using only the initial forward pass, CF-Prune identifies redundant tokens early in the denoising process, thereby maximizing pruning efficiency while demonstrating that the internal representations available at the beginning of generation are sufficient to select future-frame tokens needed for action generation. Finally, CF-Prune introduces a phase identification mechanism that exploits entropy differences across camera views and temporal positions within the action sequence to identify precision phases and selectively relax pruning, mitigating performance degradation.
Across RoboLab ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , RoboCasa ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) , and real-world tasks, CF-Prune achieves consistent efficiency gains at a 35% pruning ratio: a 1.23 × 1.23\times speedup with a 1.3 percentage point success rate gain on RoboLab, a 1.19 × 1.19\times speedup with a 4.0 percentage point gain on RoboCasa, and a 1.27 × 1.27\times speedup with a 5.4 percentage point gain in real-world experiments. At a 50% pruning ratio, CF-Prune achieves at least a 1.29 × 1.29\times average inference speedup across both simulation benchmarks, while keeping success rates within 1.0 percentage point of the dense baseline.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We reconsider the auxiliary role of future frames in WAMs and formulate token pruning from the perspective of action prediction, exposing redundancy that is not considered in conventional video generation.

We propose CF-Prune, a framework requiring no additional training that identifies redundant future frame tokens from noisy initial latents using their information concentration with respect to action and instruction tokens, while selectively relaxing pruning based on cross-view and temporal attention-entropy contrasts.

We extensively evaluate CF-Prune on the RoboLab and RoboCasa simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in inference efficiency while preserving manipulation performance.

1. We reconsider the auxiliary role of future frames in WAMs and formulate token pruning from the perspective of action prediction, exposing redundancy that is not considered in conventional video generation.

2. We propose CF-Prune, a framework requiring no additional training that identifies redundant future frame tokens from noisy initial latents using their information concentration with respect to action and instruction tokens, while selectively relaxing pruning based on cross-view and temporal attention-entropy contrasts.

3. We extensively evaluate CF-Prune on the RoboLab and RoboCasa simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks, demonstrating consistent improvements in inference efficiency while preserving manipulation performance.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

World action models build upon video diffusion models to jointly predict robot actions and future visual states, transferring learned physical dynamics and predictive capabilities to robot control ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026b ; Agarwal et al., 2026 ) . Existing approaches either adapt pretrained video diffusion models through post-training on robot demonstrations ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026b ) or jointly denoise video, action, and other multimodal tokens within a unified generator ( Agarwal et al., 2026 ) . Other methods predict compact latent future representations or decouple video and action decoding for efficient action inference ( Zheng et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . More recent action-centered designs jointly train action prediction and future video generation ( Ye et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Across these approaches, future-state prediction serves as a key source of supervision or predictive context for action generation.

Although future prediction is a defining advantage of WAMs, it comes at substantial inference cost because generating numerous future-frame tokens significantly increases computation within the video diffusion backbone. Existing approaches reduce inference cost by using fewer denoising steps ( Agarwal et al., 2026 ) or enabling single-step inference through decoupled video and action noise schedules during training ( Ye et al., 2026b ) . However, these methods accelerate inference by reducing denoising steps rather than making each step faster. Other approaches replace explicit future-frame prediction with compact future-state representations ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) or avoid explicit future-video generation during inference ( Ye et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . These methods require changes to the model architecture or training objective, making them difficult to apply directly to existing pretrained WAMs without additional training. In contrast, our approach directly reduces the future-frame token burden through token pruning, with no further training required.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically combine a pretrained VLM backbone with an action prediction module to generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions. Because processing dense visual tokens through large VLM backbones incurs substantial inference costs, recent studies have adapted visual token pruning techniques ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) to VLA policies. Some methods select task-relevant and diverse visual tokens ( Yang et al., 2025 ) or jointly consider spatial and semantic importance ( Li et al., 2026 ) , while others adjust pruning intensity across manipulation phases using recent robot motion ( Pei et al., 2026 ) . Further approaches combine semantic and action-decoding attention ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , incorporate historical context into current token selection ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , or forecast deep-layer token importance from attention patterns stored at previous control steps ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . Overall, these methods extend VLM-based pruning to robotic policies, but are not directly applicable to noisy future-frame tokens, limiting their efficiency gains in WAMs where noisy future-frame tokens dominate computation.

2026-10-15.title: MUCO: A Mani-Unit-Structured Manipulation Framework for Compositional Long-Horizon Robot Tasks
2026-10-15.authors: Xiangyi Wei , Hanzhe Yao , Jingwen Shang , Zhenhong Wu , Yang Li , Changbo Wang
2026-10-15.abstract: Learning and executing long-horizon robot manipulation as complete task trajectories raises data-collection costs, limits capability reuse, and causes local failures to cascade into later task stages. We introduce manipulation units (MUs) as reusable operations, each defined by a local goal, an initiation condition, and observable success and failure criteria. MUs are learned and verified individually. During execution, consecutive MUs remain coupled through shared environment dynamics. We formulate MU-Structured Manipulation (MUSM) and realize it through MU-Centric Orchestration (MUCO). Given language and vision, MUCO constructs an MU sequence, matches each MU to compatible policy models in a frozen capability registry, and dispatches the model with the highest calibrated success rate. Visual verification checks MU outcomes against success and failure criteria and governs transitions, enabling retry or fallback to another model from the current state without re-executing verified MUs. Canonical keys enable checkpoint reuse for equivalent MUs across tasks without new demonstrations or updates. We evaluate MUCO on RLBench, RoboTwin 2.0, and five real-world tasks. MUCO achieves higher complete-task success and verified progress, stronger failure containment, and lower error propagation than baselines. Results demonstrate cross-task MU reuse and heterogeneous policy composition without joint training, shared backbones, or common action representations.

2026-10-15.title: Active Perception of Upper-Limb Functional Mobility through Human-Robot Handovers
2026-10-15.authors: Francesco Semeraro , Marta Lagomarsino , Alberto Ranavolo , Arash Ajoudani
2026-10-15.abstract: The reintegration of people in the workplace after an upper-limb injury is often a long process. Collaborative robots and humanoids operating in shared workspaces must adapt their behaviour to the physical capabilities of their human partners. Achieving this requires robots to autonomously estimate task-relevant human mobility during interaction, without relying on external clinical assessments. In this work, we formulate the estimation of upper-limb functional mobility as an active perception problem. We model task-available upper-limb functional ranges of motion through impairment coefficients that parameterise reductions of healthy joint limits, and integrate this representation into a human model used by the robot during interaction. Based on this formulation, we propose an online active perception pipeline in which the robot actively probes the user through repeated handover requests while progressively updating a Bayesian belief over the impairment coefficients. This enables the robot to continuously refine its internal model of the user’s joint-level capabilities through interaction rather than passive observation. The proposed framework was evaluated through simulation studies and a proof-of-concept physical validation with a robotic platform and enacted human impairments, demonstrating that the pipeline can accurately recover the impairment coefficients during real human-robot handovers.

2026-10-15.title: FOMI: A Force-Feedback Manipulation Interface for Teaching Contact-Rich Manipulation
2026-10-15.authors: Yishu Shen , Yiming Luo , Ruilin Wang , Bowen Yang , Shuai Yang , Fangyi Xu , Yujun Shen , Fu Zhang , Boyu Zhou , Yinghao Xu

2026-10-15.introduction:
Human demonstrations provide behavioral supervision for manipulation policy learning.
Teleoperation Wu et al. (2024) ; Zhao et al. (2023) collects demonstrations directly on the target robot but requires robot hardware, limiting data scale and diversity.
Robot-free collection with handheld interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) Chi et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2024) has therefore been widely explored for scalable demonstration acquisition in diverse real-world environments.
However, collecting contact-rich manipulation demonstrations with these handheld interfaces remains challenging because a lack of intuitive force feedback can limit human operators’ ability to perceive object interaction forces and adjust actions in real time Liu et al. (2025c) , resulting in more failed attempts and lower collection efficiency Wu et al. (2025) .

A key factor is the interface’s mechanical design, which determines how directly interaction forces are transmitted to the human operator.
Common handheld interfaces in robot-free demonstration collection employ trigger-driven rack-and-pinion mechanisms Chi et al. (2024) ; Choi et al. (2026) .
These mechanisms transmit object interaction forces through multiple intermediate components, where mechanical backlash weakens force feedback Wu et al. (2025) .
Alternatively, interfaces with active force feedback Zhang et al. (2025) ; Citron et al. (2026) combine force sensing with motorized actuation to convey interaction forces to operators, requiring additional sensing hardware, actuators, and feedback control.
These limitations motivate a mechanical interface that provides intuitive force feedback for real-time action adjustment during contact-rich demonstration collection without additional force sensors or active feedback actuators.

Inspired by the comfortable handling and intuitive force feedback of scissors, we design a scissor-shaped mechanism to support contact-rich demonstration collection.
Each handle forms a rigid assembly with its sector gear and actuation link, preserving a direct mechanical path for force transmission without additional transmission stages between the handle and the actuation link.
To match the target parallel gripper, the two identical sector gears mesh with each other, constraining the two branches to open and close symmetrically.

Building on this mechanical design, we introduce FOMI, a force-feedback manipulation interface, together with a demonstration collection system that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection of contact-rich demonstrations.
Through calibration and mapping, the system further converts sensor measurements of FOMI’s pose changes and gripper opening into robot end-effector pose targets and gripper width commands, enabling teleoperated demonstration collection with the same interface.
Our main contributions are as follows:

Mechanical design for intuitive force feedback: We design a scissor-shaped interface in which each handle is rigidly integrated with its actuation link, providing a direct force path for intuitive force feedback during robot-free collection, with meshing sector gears matching the symmetric motion of parallel grippers.

Mechanical design for intuitive force feedback: We design a scissor-shaped interface in which each handle is rigidly integrated with its actuation link, providing a direct force path for intuitive force feedback during robot-free collection, with meshing sector gears matching the symmetric motion of parallel grippers.

Demonstration collection system for teaching contact-rich manipulation: We build a collection system around FOMI that integrates sensor calibration, data acquisition, and synchronization for robot-free collection, and further supports teleoperation by mapping FOMI’s motion and gripper opening to robot commands.

Improved collection efficiency and policy evaluation: Compared with baseline interfaces in both collection modes, FOMI achieves the highest collection efficiency and improves completion rates.
Policies fine-tuned on FOMI demonstrations achieve high success rates on four contact-rich tasks.
Hardware designs, code, and datasets will be released.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Demonstration Collection Interfaces

Human demonstrations for policy learning are commonly collected through robot-free collection or teleoperation. In robot-free collection, UMI Chi et al. (2024) and its variants Choi et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2024) enable demonstration collection across diverse real-world environments. In teleoperation, leader-follower interfaces such as GELLO Wu et al. (2024) , ALOHA Zhao et al. (2023) , and Mobile ALOHA Fu et al. (2024) use joint-space mapping for arm control to collect demonstrations, whereas VR systems George et al. (2025) and smartphone systems Wang et al. (2023) ; Agarwal et al. (2026) provide end-effector pose control. Recent interfaces have been developed to support both robot-free collection and teleoperation Seo et al. (2025) ; Surendran et al. (2026) .

## 2.2 Force Feedback for Demonstration Collection

The interface’s mechanical design can influence force feedback and action adjustment during demonstration collection Georgadarellis et al. (2026) . Existing manipulation interfaces provide force feedback through mechanical transmission or active feedback. UMI Chi et al. (2024) and UMI-FT Choi et al. (2026) use trigger-driven rack-and-pinion mechanisms, while other handheld interfaces use trigger-driven linkages Fang et al. (2026) ; Liu et al. (2026) ; Xu et al. (2025) . These mechanisms transmit interaction forces to the hand, but multiple transmission stages and backlash may obscure force feedback. In contrast, finger-driven interfaces Ohkawa et al. (2026) ; Wu et al. (2025) transmit interaction forces to the actuating fingers, but supporting the interface with the actuating fingers may affect force perception and action adjustment. Alternatively, interfaces with active force feedback provide bilateral gripper force feedback Luo et al. (2026) or reflect interaction forces from the follower robot Liu et al. (2025b) ; Zhang et al. (2025) ; Citron et al. (2026) , requiring additional actuators and feedback control. FOMI integrates each handle with an actuation link to provide direct mechanical force feedback and handle support during robot-free collection. Table 1 compares the mechanical designs, force feedback, and support handles of representative interfaces.

## 2.3 Contact Sensing for Policy Learning

Recent manipulation interfaces incorporate additional tactile or force sensors to collect contact information for learning contact-rich manipulation. Some interfaces collect synchronized visual and tactile observations and use tactile representation learning to support visuo-tactile policies Xu et al. (2025) ; Liu et al. (2025a) ; Zhu et al. (2026) . Others record interaction forces to support force-aware policy learning and contact control Jang et al. (2026) ; Choi et al. (2026) . FOMI provides mechanical force feedback to human operators during robot-free demonstration collection, while the collected demonstrations support policy learning for contact-rich manipulation without tactile or force inputs to the policy.

2026-10-15.title: What Matters for World Modeling in Vision-Language-Action Models?
2026-10-15.authors: Qisen Ma , Yixiang Chen , Yuan Xu , Peiyan Li , Jiabing Yang , Kai Wang , Jianhua Yang , Jianlou Si , Jun Huang , Jing Liu , Nianfeng Liu , Yan Huang , Liang Wang
2026-10-15.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-15.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ) have achieved notable success in robotic manipulation by adapting pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to continuous physical control.
However, standard VLAs mainly predict actions from the current observation.
Without modeling how the scene evolves under robot interaction, they struggle in long-horizon tasks and fail to adapt to distribution shifts or dynamic environments ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Lyu et al., 2026 ) .

To overcome this limitation, a promising direction is to integrate world models into VLAs to anticipate world dynamics ( Cen et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025b ) .
By incorporating world dynamics, such models have demonstrated improved long-horizon execution ( Chen et al., 2026a ) , dynamic manipulation ( Fang et al., 2026 ) , environmental robustness ( Sun et al., 2026 ) , and sample efficiency ( Chen et al., 2026b ) .
Despite these empirical successes, existing studies adopt heterogeneous world representations, integration paradigms, and policy backbones.
Specifically, they combine representations ranging from pixel details to semantic latents with designs such as implicit alignment and explicit conditioning across different VLA backbones ( Zheng et al., 2025b ; Lv et al., 2025 ; Su et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) .
Consequently, the true sources of empirical gains remain obscured, leaving it unclear which design choices fundamentally matter when integrating world modeling into VLAs.

Among these challenges, four core questions stand out:
(1) World Representation : Is there a universally optimal world representation for robot policy learning, or is representation effectiveness fundamentally coupled with the integration paradigm?
(2) Integration Paradigm : What are the performance trade-offs among different integration paradigms, and is coupled or decoupled world modeling more effective?
(3) Backbone Generalization : Do world modeling integration paradigms remain effective across policy backbones, spanning models without robot pretraining and pretrained foundation VLAs?
(4) Comprehensive Performance : How do different world modeling integration paradigms perform under diverse task conditions?

In this work, we present the first systematic, controlled empirical investigation of world modeling in VLA policies, as shown in Figure 1 .
To isolate world modeling choices, we conduct our study under a unified pipeline with a shared policy backbone and training protocol within each comparison, systematically addressing the four core questions:
First, to answer World Representation, we examine diverse world representations spanning pixel details (ImageVAE ( Tian et al., 2024 ) , WanVAE ( Wan et al., 2025 ) ), 2D semantics (DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) , SigLIP ( Zhai et al., 2023 ) ), 3D spatial geometry (VGGT ( Wang et al., 2025 ) ), and spatiotemporal video dynamics (V-JEPA 2.1 ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) ).
Second, to answer Integration Paradigm, we formalize existing architectures into four integration paradigms defined by how world dynamics are conditioned on and decoupled from the policy, namely Implicit Future Alignment, Explicit Future Query, MoT Future Expert, and External World Predictor.
We instantiate these paradigms as representative designs within our unified framework.
Third, to answer Backbone Generalization, we benchmark world modeling paradigms across representative policy backbones spanning a standard VLM backbone (Qwen3-VL-2B ( Bai et al., 2025 ) ) and a dedicated robot foundation VLA ( π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ) ).
Finally, to answer Comprehensive Performance, we evaluate these integration paradigms across diverse settings spanning in-domain and out-of-domain distributions, long horizons, dynamic objects, few-shot data, as well as real-world experiments.

Our extensive experiments yield four primary findings corresponding to our core questions:
(1) World Representation :
No single world representation is universally optimal.
Pixel-level features do not consistently translate in-domain gains into OOD robustness, while geometric and spatiotemporal representations are sensitive to the integration paradigm. DINOv3 and SigLIP provide consistent gains across paradigms.
(2) Integration Paradigm :
No paradigm dominates across all settings, yet the decoupled MoT Future Expert offers competitive overall performance, particularly in OOD robustness.
Implicit Future Alignment is lightweight but less effective on dynamic tasks, while Explicit Future Query is more task-dependent.
The External World Predictor achieves the best low-data in-domain performance.
(3) Backbone Generalization :
Integration effectiveness differs across policy backbones.
World modeling generally benefits policies built on standard VLMs, whereas decoupled designs offer substantially better compatibility when adapting pretrained foundation VLAs.
(4) Comprehensive Performance :
World modeling provides clear gains over action-only policies, particularly on long-horizon and dynamic tasks.
We believe these systematic findings provide actionable design principles for integrating world modeling into VLA systems.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action Models. Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) build on pretrained Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to predict robotic actions from a language instruction and the current observation.
These models have shifted from autoregressive discrete token decoding ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) to continuous diffusion- or flow-based action heads ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ) .
To enhance policy capabilities, parallel efforts inject 3D priors ( Zhen et al., 2024 ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025b ; Li et al., 2025a ) , adopt dual-system architectures ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025a ; Cui et al., 2025 ) , insert chain-of-thought reasoning before action generation ( Zhao et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Zhong et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) , incorporate latent actions ( Bu et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026b ) , or train on heterogeneous data mixtures ( Bu et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026a ) .
Despite these advances, standard VLAs inherit the static image–text pretraining of VLMs, lacking the temporal and physical dynamics priors essential for complex manipulation.
This motivates recent efforts to integrate world modeling into policy learning.

World Modeling in VLAs. To overcome the limitations of reactive policies, recent works integrate world models to provide VLAs with physical dynamics.
Depending on how world dynamics are conditioned on and decoupled from the policy, existing approaches can be organized into four paradigms: (1) Implicit Future Alignment uses world representations as auxiliary supervision to refine the VLM backbone without feeding predictions directly to the action head ( Su et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2026a ) . (2) Explicit Future Query introduces dedicated query tokens into the VLM to predict future latents, serving as explicit context for action generation ( Zhang et al., 2025b ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Luo et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . (3) MoT Future Expert co-optimizes parallel action and future experts within a Mixture-of-Transformers architecture, conditioning action generation on the future expert’s intermediate hidden states ( Lv et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Bi et al., 2025 ; Won et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . (4) External World Predictor decouples prediction by employing a standalone world predictor, supplying predicted future states as visual subgoals for the policy ( Chen et al., 2026a ) .
However, the field still lacks a systematic and controlled comparison of these paradigms, leaving it unclear how different paradigms choices affect the effectiveness of world modeling in VLAs.

2026-10-15.title: Learning from Demonstrations meets Symbolic Control - A Supervisory Control Architecture for Formal Certification of Learned Motion
2026-10-15.authors: Ashok Kumar , Mahathi Anand , Angela Schoellig , Abdalla Swikir
2026-10-15.abstract: Dynamical system (DS)-based learning from demonstration generates flexible robot motions, but existing guarantees rely on certificate generation to obtain formal guarantees of safety and goal convergence. We propose a symbolic supervisory control architecture that automatically generates a fail-safe backup plan, certifying safety, reachability, and actuator feasibility directly from the robot’s dynamics, independent of the learned DS. A nominal controller tracks the learned DS, while the supervisory controller monitors safety and target convergence, providing non-conservative intervention when the nominal controller violates necessary constraints. Experimental results include simulations and real robot deployment with various 2D and 3D datasets, including handwriting datasets, validating the effectiveness of our approach in providing formal guarantees with learned motion even in complex, dynamic environments.
2026-10-15.introduction:
lfd ( lfd ) is an efficient paradigm to teach robots highly complex tasks directly through demonstrations [ 1 ] . A popular approach is the ds ( ds ) method [ 2 ] , where the demonstrations are encoded via a dynamical system. Here, a vector field governs the velocity of the desired trajectories and issues commands to the low-level controller to track. The key advantage is generalizability: the ds is a time-invariant state-feedback policy over the whole domain, it can be evaluated from any state, and can quickly react to runtime perturbations. Nevertheless, additional properties such as stability and safety need to be imposed in order to ensure goal reaching, robustness to perturbations, and collision avoidance. Moreover, the learned vector field is not guaranteed to generate feasible trajectories that satisfy velocity and actuator constraints, as these limits are only imposed implicitly through robot demonstrations, if at all.

In this paper, we propose a novel approach for safe and robust realization of learned trajectories via symbolic supervisory control. Agnostic to the method used to learn the ds , our framework operates at the control layer as a certified supervisor that verifies the safety, reachability, and realizability of the resulting motion at runtime. When the nominal tracking controller threatens these guarantees, a symbolic controller intervenes to produce a certified input respecting actuator limits. The resulting motion is guaranteed to reach the goal set within finite time, remain safe against (possibly dynamic) obstacles, and recover from deviations once the environment is clear.

Formal stability and safety guarantees on learned dynamical systems are typically certified through certificate construction — Lyapunov functions for asymptotic stability [ 3 ] and barrier functions for safety [ 4 ] . A common strategy is to synthesize these certificates concurrently with the ds [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . The synthesis strategy, and subsequently, the optimization tool used, vastly depends on the characterization of the ds . For instance, [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] learn a lpv ( lpv ) dynamical system, and use conservative quadratic Lyapunov candidates for certifying stability. On the other hand, [ 8 ] learn polynomial dynamical systems along with polynomial certificates using sum-of-squares [ 10 ] tools, while [ 9 ] propose neural network characterizations for the system and certificates.

Independent of parameterization, certificate search suffers from a fundamental trade-off between the expressiveness of the learned dynamics and the tractability of the underlying optimization. An alternative is to modify the learned stable dynamics at runtime [ 11 , 12 ] , eliminating certificate optimization for collision avoidance, or to pass the generated velocity through a safety filter via a quadratic program with hand-crafted control Lyapunov and barrier functions [ 13 ] . Our approach departs from these in three respects. First, rather than modifying the learned dynamics, we operate one layer below it, designing control inputs that track the ds closely and intervening only when obstacles block the desired path. Additionally, physical realizability is guaranteed through velocity and actuator constraint satisfaction. Second, while Lyapunov-based approaches guarantee only asymptotic convergence, we guarantee reachability of a neighborhood of the goal within finite time. Finally, our synthesis does not require any certificate functions, only finite state abstractions of the model.

Our work also borrows from symbolic control, where finite approximations of control systems inform controller synthesis through simple fixed point computations [ 14 , 15 ] . This has been applied primarily in the context of motion planning for mobile robots and autonomous vehicles [ 16 , 17 ] .
While [ 18 ] addresses motion planning for manipulators via symbolic control, we utilize symbolic control strategies for safely modifying controllers obtained via lfd .

The contributions of our paper are as follows:

Starting with a ds learned from demonstrations with a preferred method, we propose a novel supervisory architecture that functions in the control layer and (i) monitors the safety of the reference paths generated by the ds , and (ii) modifies it so the robot can still reach a small neighborhood of the goal, while ensuring collision avoidance against dynamic obstacles. The designed methodology avoids computation of certificate functions while retaining formal guarantees of reachability and safety under standard assumptions on the real world (c.f. Section III-C ).

Our architecture relies on finite state abstractions on the manipulator’s operational space dynamics through sample-perturbed-system representations. Based on the discretized system dynamics and regions of interest (i.e, goals and obstacles), a symbolic controller is constructed as a fail-safe certified backup plan. Synthesis is performed either offline , suited for static obstacles, or online at low frequencies for dynamic obstacles.

At runtime, a nominal tracking controller is designed to faithfully follow the paths generated by the ds , and ensures convergence to the desired paths in the presence of deviations. A certified control input, computed to provide less-conservative modifications based on a ranking scheme, overrides the nominal control action when it is rendered to be unsafe or not goal-reaching. A full overview of our approach is presented in Figure 1 .

We validate our approach through several simulation experiments (MuJoCo) for learning handwriting motion with static and obstacles, and particularly compare the performance of approach against the closely related-work [ 13 ] . The results show that our approach is competitive with SoA and excels with high task success rates and formal guarantees. Additionally, our robot experiments on dynamic 3 ​ D 3D environments emphasize the flexibility of our approach while demonstrating that formal guarantees hold even in the real world.

2026-10-15.title: Design and Characterization of a Unified Continuum Robot Actuation Platform
2026-10-15.authors: Yunti Xu , Aedan Mangan , Miheer Potdar , Alex Lu , Tania K. Morimoto
2026-10-15.abstract: Continuum robots enable dexterous access to confined spaces in applications such as minimally invasive surgery and industrial inspection. However, their actuation systems are often custom-designed for specific robot architectures and tasks, limiting reuse across publications, institutions, and applications. This paper presents a unified actuation platform that decouples actuation hardware and software from continuum robot design. The platform provides modular actuation across continuum robot classes, scales to a large number of degrees of freedom (DOFs), and integrates with conventional serial manipulators for hybrid architectures. We validate the platform on an open-sourced surgical robotic system and experimentally characterize the actuation modules, achieving sub-millimeter translational accuracy and less than 5 ∘ 5^{\circ} rotational error over ranges of 30 30 mm and 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} , respectively. We further demonstrate the platform in two surgical use cases: teleoperation of a continuum camera in a constrained environment and bimanual manipulation using 2.53 2.53 mm concentric-tube-robot-based forceps alongside a conventional wristed instrument. All hardware designs and ROS-based software are open-sourced to facilitate reuse and further research in continuum and surgical robotics.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Continuum robots, with their continuously bending structures and small size, are well suited for navigating constrained and cluttered environments [ 1 ] , making them promising platforms for minimally invasive surgery and industrial inspection [ 1 , 2 ] . However, researchers typically develop custom, proprietary actuation hardware and software for specific robot designs and tasks, limiting reuse across publications, institutions, and applications. For example, a study of concentric tube robots found that 61.1 % 61.1\% of prototypes appeared in only a single publication, with similar trends observed across other continuum robot classes [ 3 ] . The need for a generalized actuation platform is further highlighted by the diversity of existing continuum robot classes and configurations [ 1 ] , as well as hybrid systems that integrate continuum robots with conventional rigid manipulators [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . In this work, we present a unified, robot design-agnostic actuation platform for continuum robots that can easily integrate with other robotic systems.

Although the working principles of continuum robots can vary, their actuation commonly relies on a combination of three main modes: linear translation, axial rotation, and tendon-induced motion.
For tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs), tendon displacement can be generated directly using lead-screw mechanisms [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] or through capstan drives [ 15 , 16 , 5 , 4 ] . Concentric tube robots (CTRs) [ 17 , 18 ] are actuated through the relative translation and axial rotation of nested, pre-curved Nitinol (NiTi) tubes, typically with diameters on the order of 1 1 – 2 2 mm. These motions can likewise be realized using different mechanisms, including gear-based [ 19 , 20 ] , belt-based [ 21 ] , and screw-based [ 22 ] mechanisms for linear translation, and gear-based [ 19 , 21 ] , and pulley-based [ 22 , 23 ] mechanisms for axial rotation.

Different modes of actuation impose different actuation requirements. For TDCRs, small inaccuracies in tendon displacement can produce large unintended motions at the distal tip [ 24 , 6 , 15 , 16 ] , requiring accurate tendon displacement and sufficient actuation force [ 24 , 6 , 15 , 7 , 10 ] . For CTRs, high tube pre-curvature can generate substantial axial and torsional friction during relative translation and rotation [ 25 ] , requiring sufficient force and torque while maintaining positioning accuracy under load [ 19 ] . Together, these differences in actuation requirements and mechanism design make a custom actuation system developed for one continuum robot difficult to transfer directly to another.

Grassmann et al. [ 26 ] addressed this challenge with a modular actuation system built around a common rotational module. Mode-specific mechanisms convert rotational input into tendon displacement for TDCRs or tube translation and axial rotation for CTRs. This work uses the same drive modules to actuate a 4-DOF CTR, a 2-DOF planar TDCR, and a 3-DOF spatial TDCR, with minimal module hardware changes between robot classes. However, the number and arrangement of drive modules vary with the robot design, resulting in substantially different actuation architectures and physical footprints. Thus, while the drive modules themselves are reusable between actuation modes, the actuation architecture remains configuration-dependent and must be re-conceived for each robot design. This dependence makes scaling the actuation system to higher-DOF configurations more challenging and can limit its mechanical integration with other robotic systems.

To date, researchers have combined continuum robots with serial manipulators in both surgical and general robotics applications. For surgical applications, Ma et al. [ 4 ] and Zhang et al. [ 5 ] mounted TDCRs on serial manipulators for laparoscopic visualization, while Zhang et al. [ 6 ] and Qi et al. [ 7 ] developed TDCR-based instruments for neurosurgical and spinal applications. Dwyer et al. [ 8 ] and Francis et al. [ 9 ] integrated CTRs with serial manipulators for fetoscopy. Beyond surgery, Ma et al. [ 10 ] combined a TDCR with a 6-DOF movable base to investigate dexterity, manipulability, and obstacle avoidance, while Shentu et al. [ 11 ] incorporated a 6-DOF movable base into motion planning for a TDCR to improve follow-the-leader (FTL) behavior. Across these applications, the continuum robots ranged from two to nine DOFs and employed robot design-specific actuation assemblies. This variation highlights the need for a unified actuation platform that scales across different DOFs and configurations and integrates with conventional serial manipulators.

We present a unified actuation platform—including the mechanical, electrical, and software components—that decouples actuation from continuum robot design, enabling:

actuation of multiple classes of continuum robots with arbitrary DOFs,

deployment across many diverse use cases, such as a flexible camera or surgical instrument,

hybrid continuum–serial robot architectures.

2. deployment across many diverse use cases, such as a flexible camera or surgical instrument,

3. hybrid continuum–serial robot architectures.

# II Mechanical Design

## II-A Design Requirements and Overview

To accommodate different continuum robot classes and numbers of DOFs, the actuation assembly must provide modular and scalable actuation, supporting both linear translation and axial rotation while maintaining high positioning accuracy. A common motor controller must interface with all actuated DOFs to extend this modularity to the electrical hardware. In addition, to support diverse end-use applications, the assembly must independently actuate end-effectors such as graspers and forceps. Finally, for integration with hybrid continuum–serial manipulators, the assembly must be lightweight to avoid overloading the serial manipulator’s actuators, maintain a compact and slim form factor for mounting, and enable rapid attachment/detachment.

To meet the above design requirements, we have designed the actuation assembly to consist of modular units that collectively provide multiple DOFs (Fig. 2 ), with each module capable of linear translation and axial rotation. The modules are integrated in series on a common frame using a lead screw and alignment rails. This modular architecture allows users to scale the total number of DoFs to accommodate different tool requirements.
Complete assembly instructions, and sourcing information for off-the-shelf components are provided in Supplementary File 1, and the custom CAD files are hosted on 1 1 1 https://ucsdmorimotolab.github.io/unified-actuation/ . A video demonstration of the assembly process is available in Supplementary Video 2.

As a representative serial manipulator, we use the Patient-Side Manipulator (PSM) of the da Vinci Research Kit (dVRK), an open-source surgical robotic system for research. The PSM provides a remote-center-of-motion (RCM)-constrained arm with multiple DOFs, of which we use three—outer yaw, pitch, and insertion—to demonstrate integration with the proposed actuation platform.

## II-B Module Design

The translation mechanism (purple in Fig. 2 ) performs the insertion and retraction of each module relative to the others, enabling both tendon actuation and tube translation.
Linear bearings constrain the module housing, allowing the module to translate along the linear rails.
For tendon actuation, a tendon routes back to the module and attaches via an L -bracket (Fig. 2 ).
The tendon wraps around a bolt which is fastened down, enabling quick attachment while being able to exert high forces without slipping.
For tube actuation, the module interfaces with the tube through the coupling described in Section II-B2 , allowing tube insertion.

The rotation mechanism (light red in Fig. 2 ) enables continuous axial rotation of the instrument shaft or tubes about the insertion axis.
We use a worm gear mechanism to achieve rotation concentric to the working channel (orange in Fig. 2 ) while minimizing backlash.
An additional benefit of this design is that the worm gear is not back-drivable, allowing the motor to maintain position under load with reduced holding current, preventing motor overheating during extended working times (Section II-D ). A brushless DC motor (Maxon EC-max 16) with a 19:1 planetary gearbox (Maxon, 16 A) provides sufficiently high torque, low mass, and unlimited rotation.
The motor drives a 10:1 worm gear pair composed of an off-the-shelf worm (McMaster-Carr 57545K634) and a 3D-printed worm wheel (Tough 1500 Resin V2, Formlabs Inc.).
The rotating shaft interfaces with a shaft collar (Fig. 2 ) that
users can adjust to meet the size requirements of their continuum robot.
An essential element of the design is the hollow lumen maintained throughout the actuation assembly while rotating the instrument shaft about the insertion axis, which allows for a working channel (orange in Fig. 2 ) for cameras, graspers, or other end effectors depending on the use case.

To actuate tendon-driven instruments, such as forceps, we mount a push-pull actuation mechanism to the most proximal actuation module.
After passing through the working channel, the instrument’s tendons attach to a custom hex-nut adapter and couple to a BLDC-driven push-pull actuation mechanism dedicated to the tool. Details on the instrument actuation mechanism can be found in Supplementary Video 2.

## II-C Assembly and Attachment

We attach both linear rails and the lead screw described in Section II-B1 to a 3D-printed front frame (Bambu Labs PLA)(Fig. 2 ).
Each module aligns its linear bearings with the rails and inserts forward into position, repeating for the desired number of modules.
After installing all modules, the back frame attaches to complete the actuation assembly.
All frame components—including the rails, front frame, and back frame—have a combined mass of 312 312 g, minimizing overall system weight and enabling mounting on serial-link robotic arms. Table I summarizes the mass of each subassembly. The complete actuation assembly measures 400 × 98.6 × 40 400\times 98.6\times 40 mm (L × W × H), allowing it to fit on serial manipulators with a minimal footprint.

As an example use case in surgery, we designed a modified sterile adapter to attach the actuation platform to the dVRK’s Patient Side Manipulator (PSM). The front frame bolts directly to this adapter, which then mounts to the PSM through a quick-release mechanism that enables tool-free attachment and detachment in under one minute.
Since conventional wristed instruments weigh approximately 50 g [ 27 ] , our design incorporates a constant-force spring (McMaster-Carr 9293K114) that offsets the additional weight introduced by the actuation assembly. Empirical testing shows that the chosen spring supports a 3-tube CTR assembly with an instrument attached without exceeding the PSM insertion force limits of the PSM.

## II-D Electronics Design

We select a multi-axis controller board (Nanotec CM-CPB3-44-0005-1, 4-axis) that contains four independent motor controllers capable of driving either stepper or BLDC motors, thereby making the control hardware agnostic to any specific drive mechanisms used in the actuation assembly. Each controller supports multiple sensor modalities for low-level closed-loop control. Specifically, the BLDC motors employ Hall-effect sensors for position feedback, while steppers operate in open-loop (see Fig. 3 ). The internal current control loop runs at 20 kHz.

Depending on the total number of DOFs in the actuation assembly, multiple 4-axis boards can be daisy-chained via EtherCAT, with a single board interfacing with the host PC. The controller processes data at 1 kHz. Each board operates over a voltage range of 12–57.6 V, which encompasses the operating requirements of the selected stepper and BLDC motors, both of which can operate at 12 V. The maximum current rating per controller is 3 A, which exceeds the expected peak current draw of the selected stepper and BLDC motors (1 A and 0.762 A, respectively), providing safe current margin.

2026-10-15.title: Refine Actions If Needed: Adaptive Action Chunk Refinement for Robot Manipulation
2026-10-15.authors: Hanlin Liu , Zichen Zhou , Jiacheng Zhang , Liuyuan Na , Jin Jin , Guangyan Chen , Yufeng Yue , Gen Li , Fangqiang Ding
2026-10-15.abstract: Computationally lightweight manipulation policies predict executable actions with low inference latency, but prediction errors can limit task success. Iterative generative policies can achieve higher task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. Refining action proposals from computationally lightweight policies can combine these strengths, but the amount of refinement needed varies across states. We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed), a framework that predicts action errors at different refinement levels to decide whether and how much to refine each executable proposal, before performing any refinement. We train an ensemble to predict these errors by comparing action proposals and their refined versions with expert actions from offline demonstrations, without requiring explicit labels of refinement needs. Calibration balances uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. We evaluate RAIN on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6% success, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate with 5.71 × \times lower policy latency. On the real robot, success increases from 55.0% with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) to 72.5%, with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level with 26.6% fewer refiner evaluations.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Closed-loop manipulation policies must generate effective actions quickly enough to replan as the environment changes. Diffusion Policy (DP) and flow-matching (FM) policies commonly generate these sequences by transforming an unstructured noise sample into an observation-conditioned action trajectory through repeated network evaluations [ 1 , 2 ] . This iterative process can improve task success rates, but repeated network evaluations increase inference latency. To reduce inference latency, a computationally lightweight policy can first produce an executable action proposal for a generative model to refine. Instead of generating the entire action sequence from noise, the model can then focus on correcting errors in the proposal.

BRIDGeR and Action-to-Action (A2A) flow matching explore related approaches by replacing noise with policy samples or action-history representations [ 3 , 4 ] . However, improving the starting point does not by itself determine how much refinement is needed. For an executable proposal, the appropriate choice may range from direct execution to additional correction, depending on the current state. Figure contrasts direct generation, iterative generation, fixed refinement, and our policy with adaptive refinement. The problem is therefore to determine whether the expected improvement over direct execution justifies additional computation, before invoking the refiner.

Making this decision before refinement presents two challenges. First, predicting how much refinement will improve action quality requires assessing refined actions before they are generated. Proposal uncertainty alone does not establish whether the refiner can improve a proposal or how much correction is worthwhile, while evaluating alternative refinements online consumes the computation we seek to save. Second, offline demonstrations provide expert actions, but no direct labels for refinement needs or the benefit of each allocation. The router must therefore learn from demonstrations to predict action errors at different refinement levels, including no refinement. These predictions allow it to decide whether and how much to refine by weighing the expected reduction in error against the additional computation.

We introduce RAIN (Refine Actions If Needed) to address these challenges through offline comparative supervision and pre-refinement risk prediction. Here, risk refers to the predicted deviation of an action chunk from expert actions. At demonstration states, frozen proposal and refiner models generate candidates whose deviations from the same expert action chunk provide continuous surrogate targets for a risk ensemble. Offline calibration balances predicted risk, uncertainty, computation, and temporal consistency. The router then selects direct execution or only the chosen refinement, without online reward optimization or refinement probes. We instantiate this framework with Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [ 5 ] as the proposal policy and flow matching as the refiner.

We evaluate the framework on eight ManiSkill tasks [ 6 ] and four real-robot tasks. In simulation, our policy achieves 66.6% success at 0.322 ms/action of amortized policy latency, approaching the best evaluated diffusion-policy success rate. On the real robot, it improves success over ACT by 17.5 percentage points with comparable average successful completion time. Matched controls further show that dynamic routing maintains the strongest observed fixed-refinement success level while reducing policy latency by 15.7%.

The paper makes three contributions:

RAIN, an adaptive action-refinement framework that decides whether and how much to refine an executable action proposal before invoking a generative refiner, preserving a direct-execution path.

A demonstration-only learning procedure that predicts continuous candidate risks from expert-action deviations, with offline calibration of uncertainty, computation cost, and temporal consistency.

Evaluation on eight ManiSkill tasks and four real-robot tasks demonstrating the success–efficiency benefits of executable-proposal refinement, with matched controls isolating the additional computation savings from dynamic routing.

# II Related Work

Action policies and generative efficiency. Imitation policies model robot actions through direct prediction, implicit models, or tokenized representations. ACT predicts executable action chunks in one forward pass [ 5 ] , while implicit behavior cloning and behavior transformers offer alternative representations of complex action distributions [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Diffusion and flow-matching policies instead construct action sequences through iterative denoising or vector-field integration [ 1 , 2 , 10 ] . This expressive generation process requires repeated network evaluations at each control decision, motivating efforts to reduce inference cost.

Several approaches reduce this cost by shortening generation or reusing computation. Consistency Policy, One-Step Diffusion Policy, and FlowPolicy enable few-step or single-step prediction through distillation or consistency training [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Warm-start methods exploit temporal continuity or predict informative initial actions [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] , while streaming generation and improved flow couplings offer complementary efficiency gains [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . However, distillation can trade action accuracy or diversity for speed [ 17 ] , while temporal reuse alone may not ensure compatibility with the current state [ 16 ] . These trade-offs motivate starting from an executable proposal and allocating correction according to its predicted value.

Executable proposals and learned refinement. Informative starting points offer another route to efficient generation. BRIDGeR refines source-policy samples [ 3 ] , while A2A and Vision-to-Action (VITA) construct flow sources from action history and visual representations [ 4 , 20 ] . These methods show that generation need not begin from unstructured noise, but an informative source alone does not determine whether further refinement justifies its cost. When the source is already executable, refinement becomes optional. RAIN explicitly compares the predicted value and cost of correction against direct execution, making the proposal both a refinement starting point and an executable alternative.

Learning corrections to an existing policy is also central to residual-policy methods. Residual reinforcement learning, FISH, and ResiP improve base policies through environment interaction [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] , while TRANSIC obtains corrective supervision from human interventions during deployment [ 24 ] . These approaches improve existing behavior but require additional interaction or intervention data for correction learning. RAIN instead learns refinement and its allocation from offline demonstrations, using candidate deviations from expert actions to supervise relative correction value. This supports adaptive refinement without collecting online rewards or human corrections.

Adaptive computation for generative policies. Adaptive computation allocates different generation effort to different control decisions. AdaFlow adjusts integration using conditional variance linked to discretization error [ 25 ] , while ProbeFlow estimates trajectory complexity from initial and lookahead velocity vectors [ 26 ] . Prefix-Optimal Generative Policies (POGP) instead learn intermediate denoising values to stop when further generation offers little benefit [ 27 ] . These criteria adapt computation within generation but do not directly compare refinement against an independently executable proposal. RAIN makes this comparison before the first refiner evaluation, allowing direct execution when the predicted correction benefit does not justify its cost.

Other approaches learn computation allocation from observations. Dynamic Denoising Diffusion Policy (D3P) jointly trains a step adaptor and diffusion policy through reinforcement learning [ 28 ] , whereas RAIN learns refinement allocation from offline demonstrations. Difficulty-Aware Stochastic Interpolant Policy (DA-SIP) selects integration steps and solver configurations, while the Vision-Adaptive Diffusion Policy Framework (VADF) adjusts denoising schedules and execution lengths [ 29 , 30 ] . These methods adapt generation or execution; RAIN instead compares correction amounts for the same executable proposal, including no correction. Modality-Adaptive Robot Sampling (MARS) selectively invokes stochastic generation when behavioral diversity is needed [ 31 ] . Yet even a single-modal action can require precise correction. RAIN therefore predicts continuous candidate risks, preserving correction differences that can be weighed against uncertainty and computation cost.

for comprehensive and reliable prototyping, verification and validation (V&V) of control
systems. There, the combination of feedback loops across multiple
realities (e.g., simulations, physical setups) enables various forms of
experimentation with robots and autonomous systems.
However, the handling of multiple realities requires a more specific
support by the modelling techniques used in control engineering.
To streamline the latter in the system life cycle, we propose a
framework for mixing (i.e., fusing, defusing) control input and
feedback signals (i.e., stimuli, responses) in simultaneously operated
plants for multiple realities.

Co-simulation, in particular, DTs are used for comprehensive
prototyping as well as V&V of control systems. In this area,
the combination of feedback loops across multiple realities (e.g.,
simulations, physical setups) enables various forms of experimentation
with robots and autonomous systems.

For example, in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) engineering, stable flight depends heavily on
the accurate modelling and validation of all control loop elements.
Simulation is used before deployment in physical experiments to reduce
equipment damage and safety hazards. Simulation enables parameter
pre-tuning and pre-testing of controllers, while physical experiments
introduce further realism for validation.
Differences in dynamics, disturbance models, sensor noise, and timing
inconsistencies cause discrepancies between simulated and physical
behaviour. Controllers doing well in simulation may behave poorly on
a physical UAV. The simulation-to-reality (S2R) gap underlying such discrepancies
can reduce performance and stability of a controller validated on
actual hardware [ 10 ] . These issues
are exacerbated in multi-UAV applications.

Mixed reality (MR) environments [ 4 ] narrow the S2R gap by co-executing physical and virtual
experiments in real time. This way, sensor data can be observed in a
physical plant along with the evolution of virtual quantities in a
simulation. For example, disturbances (e.g., wind), perhaps infeasible
to apply on a physical UAV, can be handled in the simulator and
virtual (dynamic) obstacles prevent from collisions during physical
tests. MR environments combine advantages of both worlds for
precise, effective, and robust controller V&V.

Nevertheless, MR requires the handling of issues, such as
physical/virtual parameter mismatches caused by neglected disturbances
and sensor noise [ 8 ] . One cannot conclude
MR stability from the individual stability of the involved realities (i.e., processes, plants, twins). Physical/virtual
couplings require logical

model inaccuracies and de-synchronisation.
Moreover, clock synchronisation—establishing a global clock across

measurements. The latter might not match temporally because of
different sampling rates or disassociated parameters on either side.
Such issues obstruct the comparison and fusion of signals and
require additional alignment.
In our UAV example, the two twins in a UAV-DT need to
be aligned for controller V&V.

combined into an MR concept for controller design and
V&V. A naïve parameter union or vector concatenation lacks
flexibility, may reinforce inconsistencies, propagate errors in the
control loop, and lead to undesirable feedback. A framework for
handling MR parameter combinations is needed.

2026-10-15.title: Coordi-pi: Coordination-Aware Dual-Hand Action Representation for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation
2026-10-15.authors: Yiming Meng , Yanming Shao , Weijie Shen , Kunyang Lin , Jiayu Sun , Ping Luo , Yao Mu
2026-10-15.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong potential for general-purpose robotic manipulation, but extending them to bimanual dexterous manipulation introduces a high-dimensional and structured action space. Existing bimanual VLA policies commonly concatenate right- and left-side arm–hand actions at each control timestep, leaving cross-hand interactions implicit within a single action vector. We introduce Coordi- π \pi , a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Coordi- π \pi represents the right- and left-side arm–hand actions as individual action tokens and organizes them into an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence. To explicitly encode hand identity and temporal synchronization in this interleaved representation, a learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides, while sequence–control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE) separates sequence position from control timestep, allowing actions at the same control timestep to share a temporal coordinate while retaining distinct sequence positions. Across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo, Coordi- π \pi achieves state-of-the-art performance under both rand-obj and rand-full , improving the average success rate over π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} from 31.9% to 51.3% and from 18.3% to 32.3%, respectively. Coordi- π \pi also consistently outperforms π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} across four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have recently shown strong progress
in general-purpose robotic manipulation [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . While early generalist policies largely focused on single-arm manipulation with parallel-jaw grippers, recent work has extended VLA-based control to higher-DoF embodiments, including dexterous hands, humanoid robots, and dual-arm systems [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Bimanual dexterous manipulation further requires each side to control a high-DoF arm–hand system while coordinating actions across
the two sides [ 13 ] , substantially increasing both the
dimensionality and structural complexity of the joint action space.

Despite recent progress, action representation remains underexplored
for bimanual dexterous manipulation. Conventional approaches typically
concatenate the right- and left-side arm–hand actions at each control
timestep,

To address these representation issues, we introduce Coordi- π \pi , a structured action representation framework for bimanual dexterous manipulation, as illustrated in Fig. . Coordi- π \pi first represents each bimanual action chunk as an
interleaved sequence of right- and left-side arm–hand tokens. A learnable hand-identity embedding distinguishes the two sides within the shared action representation. We further introduce sequence–control-timestep factorized rotary positional encoding (RoPE), which assigns each action token both a sequence-position coordinate and a control-timestep coordinate. In this representation, R h R_{h} and L h L_{h} occupy different positions
in the token sequence while sharing the same control-timestep
coordinate, explicitly representing their temporal synchronization.

We evaluate Coordi- π \pi on five bimanual dexterous manipulation
tasks in DexJoCo [ 12 ] under both rand-obj and
the more challenging rand-full setting, and further evaluate
it on four real-world bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks.
Coordi- π \pi achieves state-of-the-art performance on DexJoCo,
improving the average success rate over π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} from 31.9 % 31.9\% to 51.3 % 51.3\% under rand-obj and from 18.3 % 18.3\% to 32.3 % 32.3\% under rand-full . Coordi- π \pi also outperforms π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} across all four real-world tasks. Ablation studies further show
complementary contributions from the interleaved action representation,
hand-identity embedding, and sequence–control-timestep factorized RoPE.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are threefold:

We propose Coordi- π \pi , a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation that represents right- and left-side arm–hand actions as individual tokens and organizes them in an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence.

We introduce a learnable hand-identity embedding and sequence–control-timestep factorized RoPE to represent hand identity and temporal synchronization in the interleaved action representation.

We show that Coordi- π \pi achieves state-of-the-art performance
across all five bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks in DexJoCo under both rand-obj and rand-full , and outperforms π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} across all four real-world tasks.

1. We propose Coordi- π \pi , a structured action representation for bimanual dexterous manipulation that represents right- and left-side arm–hand actions as individual tokens and organizes them in an interleaved sequence, explicitly exposing the two sides within the action sequence.

2. We introduce a learnable hand-identity embedding and sequence–control-timestep factorized RoPE to represent hand identity and temporal synchronization in the interleaved action representation.

# II RELATED WORK

Bimanual and Dexterous Manipulation. Recent work has advanced bimanual dexterous manipulation through
improved teleoperation, data collection, policy learning, and
evaluation. BiDex develops a high-DoF teleoperation system for
collecting bimanual dexterous demonstrations [ 14 ] , while
DexMimicGen generates large-scale demonstration data from a small
number of human demonstrations [ 15 ] . Related systems
such as Mobile ALOHA [ 16 ] , ALOHA
Unleashed [ 17 ] , and DexCap [ 18 ] further
explore scalable data collection and policy learning for complex
bimanual or dexterous manipulation. BiDexHands studies high-DoF
bimanual dexterous control in simulation [ 19 ] .
On the policy side, InterACT captures inter-dependencies between two
arms during action prediction [ 20 ] , and KStar Diffuser
incorporates spatial–temporal robot structure and kinematic
constraints into bimanual control [ 21 ] . RDT-1B develops a
diffusion foundation model for bimanual manipulation [ 22 ] ,
while Dexora targets high-DoF dual-arm dual-hand VLA
control [ 11 ] . DexJoCo provides a benchmark covering bimanual
coordination, tool use, and long-horizon dexterous
manipulation [ 12 ] . Coordi- π \pi focuses specifically on action representation for bimanual dexterous VLA control, where each side controls a
high-DoF arm–hand system.

Vision-Language-Action Policies. Vision-language-action policies leverage large-scale visual,
language, and robot data for general-purpose robot control.
PaLM-E [ 23 ] and VIMA [ 24 ] demonstrate early forms of
multimodal reasoning and prompting for embodied manipulation, while
RT-2 transfers vision-language knowledge directly to robotic
actions [ 2 ] . OpenVLA provides an open-source VLA pretrained on diverse robot demonstrations [ 5 ] , alongside the broader development of large-scale robot datasets such as DROID [ 25 ] .
For continuous action generation, π 0 \pi_{0} combines a pretrained
vision-language backbone with a flow-matching action
expert [ 6 ] , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} further extends this framework
toward open-world manipulation [ 7 ] . Recent work has also
extended VLA policies to more diverse robot embodiments. DexVLA
studies general robot control across single-arm, bimanual, and
dexterous-hand settings through a diffusion-based action
expert [ 10 ] . Coordi- π \pi builds on this line of VLA policies
but focuses on the action representation required for bimanual
dexterous control.

Action Representation and Sequence Modeling. Robot policies represent continuous actions in different forms. ACT predicts temporally extended action chunks [ 26 ] , while Diffusion Policy represents continuous action trajectories through conditional diffusion [ 27 ] . Within VLA policies, OpenVLA-OFT adopts continuous action prediction together with parallel decoding and action chunking [ 28 ] , while FAST and ActionCodec study tokenization of continuous robot actions [ 29 , 30 ] . SpatialVLA introduces spatially structured representations for robot actions [ 31 ] , and Ego-Pi adopts an interleaved action formulation for high-dimensional dexterous action prediction within a π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -based policy [ 32 ] . Positional structure in sequence models is commonly represented with RoPE [ 33 ] , while multimodal extensions such as M-RoPE and VideoRoPE factor positional coordinates across spatial and temporal dimensions [ 34 , 35 ] . Coordi- π \pi focuses on structured action representation for bimanual control, combining interleaved arm–hand tokens with explicit hand identity and control-timestep structure.
