2026-10-15.title: PolyMorph: Learning Locomotion Policy for Cross-Embodiment Adaptation
2026-10-15.authors: Hyunsik Oh , Seunghun Jeon , Donghoon Youm , Jungwoo Hur , Hyeongjun Kim , Jeong Hyun Lee , Moonkyu Jung , Jemin Hwangbo
2026-10-15.abstract: Reinforcement learning has enabled robust locomotion for legged robots, but learned policies are typically tied to a specific robot morphology and require additional engineering when the number of legs, actuators, or mechanical properties change. We present PolyMorph, a morphology-conditioned framework that learns a single locomotion policy for heterogeneous legged robots. PolyMorph converts each robot’s URDF into joint-link modules and combines a recurrent encoder, graph-based Transformer, and per-joint decoder to generate actions across variable leg counts and joint configurations. To improve training stability, PolyMorph uses morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization. We evaluate PolyMorph in simulation across bipedal, tripedal, and quadrupedal robots, including unseen morphology variants and platforms, and deploy the policy on real quadruped platforms operated in multiple configurations. The results show that a single PolyMorph policy generalizes across diverse robot morphologies without per-robot policy retraining.
2026-10-15.introduction:
In the field of robotics, significant progress has been made through various control methodologies, including Model Predictive Control (MPC) [ 22 ] and learning-based approaches such as imitation learning (IL) [ 16 , 23 ] and reinforcement learning (RL) [ 7 , 18 ] . Among these, model-free RL has become a powerful tool for legged robot control because it directly optimizes policies from environment interactions without requiring explicit dynamics models. This makes RL particularly effective for complex and underactuated systems, enabling robust locomotion over challenging terrains such as rough slopes, stairs, and deformable terrain [ 15 , 10 ] .

Most existing studies on legged locomotion focus on enabling a single platform to perform a specific task [ 9 , 14 ] . However, policies trained for one robot often fail to transfer to another due to differences in morphology, including degrees of freedom, link masses, inertias, and kinematic configurations. Adapting a policy to a new robot typically requires redesigning the environment, observations, action space, and reward functions, which demands substantial engineering effort. This motivates the development of general controllers that can operate across diverse legged robots.

In this work, we address the following question: Can we train a single locomotion policy that operates across legged robots with diverse morphologies, including different numbers of legs and actuators, and deploy it on real hardware without per-robot retraining? We argue that such a controller must not only observe the robot’s current state but also reason about its morphology, and that achieving this in practice requires addressing training-level imbalances that arise when robots with very different reward magnitudes and learning difficulties are trained together.

To this end, we propose PolyMorph, a cross-embodiment locomotion framework with a URDF-conditioned policy interface. As shown in Fig. 1 , the same policy is deployed across diverse legged morphologies on various rough terrains in both simulation and the real world. Each robot is represented as a sequence of joint-link modules parsed from its URDF, and padding with valid-action masking allows the same policy to handle variable leg counts, actuator numbers, and joint configurations without redesigning the action interface. The policy combines a recurrent state encoder that summarizes proprioceptive history, a Transformer that conditions on URDF-derived graph structure, and per-joint decoder heads that generate actions only for actuated joints.

A unified locomotion policy across heterogeneous morphologies can shorten the robot design-test cycle by allowing new designs or modified configurations to be evaluated without retraining a separate controller for each platform, which is particularly useful for rapid robot design workflows [ 11 , 1 ] . It also enables policy reuse across heterogeneous robot platforms and exposes the policy to broader morphology and dynamics variations.

Beyond designing a policy that can process robots with different kinematic structures, we observe that jointly optimizing across morphologies introduces training-level obstacles: reward magnitudes can scale with the number of joints and legs, biasing optimization toward certain morphologies; easy-to-learn robots can dominate uniform sampling and reduce the learning signal for harder morphologies such as bipeds; and manually tuned PD gains reintroduce per-platform engineering effort. Complementary to prior multi-embodiment methods that emphasize morphology-conditioned policy architectures, PolyMorph addresses these training-level obstacles through morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, URDF-derived PD-gain initialization, together with curriculum learning and domain randomization for robust training. The same policy parameters are shared across all robots, and only morphology-dependent inputs are derived from each robot’s URDF.

In summary, the main contributions of this work are as follows:

We identify and address training-level obstacles in cross-embodiment optimization, including reward-scale mismatch, sampling imbalance between easy and hard robots, and per-platform gain tuning, through morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization.

We adapt joint-link tokenization, embodiment-masked attention, recurrent proprioceptive encoding, and per-joint action decoding into a URDF-conditioned policy interface that handles variable leg counts, actuator numbers, and kinematic structures with shared parameters.

We validate PolyMorph on heterogeneous legged robots in simulation and demonstrate cross-morphology hardware deployment on two real quadruped platforms operated in quadrupedal, tripedal, and bipedal configurations, with additional ablations and comparisons against multi-embodiment baselines.

1. We identify and address training-level obstacles in cross-embodiment optimization, including reward-scale mismatch, sampling imbalance between easy and hard robots, and per-platform gain tuning, through morphology-normalized rewards, adaptive robot sampling, and URDF-derived PD-gain initialization.

2. We adapt joint-link tokenization, embodiment-masked attention, recurrent proprioceptive encoding, and per-joint action decoding into a URDF-conditioned policy interface that handles variable leg counts, actuator numbers, and kinematic structures with shared parameters.

3. We validate PolyMorph on heterogeneous legged robots in simulation and demonstrate cross-morphology hardware deployment on two real quadruped platforms operated in quadrupedal, tripedal, and bipedal configurations, with additional ablations and comparisons against multi-embodiment baselines.

# II Related Work

## II-A Transformer architectures for robot control

In legged robot control, Transformer-based policies have been used to process observation histories or sensory inputs for locomotion [ 17 ] . Beyond such temporal use, Transformers also model relationships among input tokens through self-attention [ 20 ] , making them suitable for control problems where multiple body parts must interact. This spatial formulation is particularly attractive for multi-embodiment locomotion, since variable-length token sequences naturally correspond to robots with different numbers of joints. However, standard Transformers do not explicitly encode the physical structure of the robot and must infer morphology-dependent relationships only from data, which can be sample-inefficient when training across heterogeneous robots. Body Transformer [ 19 ] uses the robot’s adjacency graph as an attention mask to inject structural bias for a fixed morphology. PolyMorph adopts this structural prior in a policy shared across heterogeneous morphologies, where URDF-derived morphology inputs and attention masks vary across embodiments and are combined with recurrent state encoding.

## II-B Cross-embodied policy learning

Cross-embodied policy learning aims to train a single policy that can operate across different robot embodiments. In legged robotics, Metamorph [ 5 ] uses a Transformer to control modular robots but is evaluated only in simulation. GenLoco [ 4 ] achieves real-world transfer through morphology randomization but focuses on quadrupeds. URMA [ 2 ] learns multi-embodiment locomotion across quadrupedal and bipedal robots with an attention-based encoder–decoder. Graph neural networks [ 21 ] encode robot morphology as graphs. GCNT [ 13 ] further combines graph-based morphology encoding with Transformer communication to learn controllers across different robot structures. LocoFormer [ 12 ] takes a different approach, combining large-scale procedural training with long-context adaptation to generalize locomotion across unseen embodiments. While these works have advanced policy architectures, the training-level aspects of jointly optimizing heterogeneous legged robots have received less attention. PolyMorph also targets them directly. Beyond locomotion, Chen et al. [ 3 ] and Gupta et al. [ 6 ] study cross-robot transfer from demonstrations through intention-aligned representations and kinematics-aware policy synthesis, respectively.

2026-10-15.title: ForceBench: Benchmarking Force Integration for Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-15.authors: Xuan Han , Zinuo Jin , Tianlin Li , Yunfan Lou , Xin Liu , Yuchen Xue , Yuanpeng He , Boxian Yao , Shuhan Zhan , Ruihai Wu , Zhibo Pang
2026-10-15.abstract:
Force feedback provides vision-language-action (VLA) policies with
physical observations that can guide action selection and execution.
However, differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings
across existing systems hinder reliable comparisons of force integration
designs. We introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark for evaluating
six-axis wrist-force integration under a unified protocol.
ForceBench combines eight tasks spanning physical-property inference,
resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly with
1,600 synchronized demonstrations and task-specific success criteria.
We compare one no-force baseline and six force integration designs on
a shared π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} backbone. Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success
of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the baseline, and improves
success rates across all three task categories.
Predictive and temporal gains in simulation concentrate on
physical-property inference, while both temporal designs
underperform the baseline on assembly.
Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports
the main qualitative trends: Prompt Fusion and Dual-Path Fusion
achieve 63.00% mean success, compared with 40.00% for the baseline,
but only Prompt Fusion improves every task.
These findings support ForceBench’s practical value for identifying
the benefits and limitations of force integration across
manipulation demands.
The project page is available at https://forcebench-platform.github.io/ .
2026-10-15.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual and language pretraining
to robotic action, enabling a shared backbone to learn diverse manipulation
skills [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
Physical interaction additionally requires responding to properties and
conditions revealed through action, such as object mass and resistance.
Learning-based policies increasingly exploit such feedback, extending
diffusion-based visuomotor policies [ 5 ] with compliance-
or force-aware learning [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] and
incorporating force into VLA models. Wrist force provides a six-dimensional
observation of these interactions, combining three force and three torque
components. These measurements can refine a visually specified motion or
inform decisions about conditions that appearance alone does not reveal,
supporting both action selection and execution.

Existing systems incorporate force into action generation through adaptive
fusion of force tokens with vision–language
features [ 9 ] or temporal force encoding
with high-frequency feedback [ 10 , 11 ] .
Force also supports reactive execution through contact prediction that
regulates feedback usage [ 12 ] , while joint action–wrench
modeling supports reinforcement-learning post-training [ 13 ] .
Other work removes the force sensor
at deployment by distilling force knowledge into vision [ 14 ] .
Although standardized data and benchmarks have matured for vision-based
manipulation [ 15 , 16 ] ,
differences in tasks, demonstrations, and control settings across
force-aware systems hinder direct comparisons. Moreover, aggregate
success rates can obscure differences across physical-property inference,
resistance-dependent interaction, and contact-rich assembly. We therefore
ask how force integration designs can be reliably compared under a unified
protocol, and how their benefits vary across manipulation demands.

To address this gap, we introduce ForceBench, a simulation benchmark
dedicated to comparing six-axis wrist-force integration in robotic
manipulation (Fig. ). ForceBench combines parameterized
physical conditions, 1,600 synchronized multimodal demonstrations,
a shared observation–action interface, and evaluation on task instances
initialized with shared seeds. Seven tasks vary physical properties and
resistance conditions to examine behavior beyond object appearance;
a complementary contact-rich assembly task tests geometrically
constrained execution. Task-specific success criteria and category-level
metrics support comparison across these manipulation demands. We further
assess the practical relevance of the benchmark through real-world
experiments.

Using this framework, we compare a no-force baseline and six force
integration designs on a shared π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} backbone, using the same task
demonstrations and training protocol. The six designs comprise three
current-sample conditioning interfaces—Token Fusion, Prompt Fusion,
and Cross-Attention—a Token Fusion variant with auxiliary future-force
prediction, and two temporal reference systems, Temporal Prompt and
Dual-Path Fusion. ForceVLA provides an external comparison.
Prompt Fusion achieves the highest observed mean simulation success
of 35.31%, compared with 23.25% for the no-force baseline, and provides
the most consistent improvements across task categories.
In simulation, predictive supervision and temporal representations
provide task-dependent gains that concentrate on physical-property
inference, while both temporal designs underperform the baseline on
contact-rich assembly.

Real-world evaluation of eight systems across five tasks supports the
main qualitative trends. Prompt Fusion raises mean success from 40.00%
to 63.00%, tying Dual-Path Fusion overall while exceeding the no-force
baseline on every task. Both temporal designs achieve higher
physical-property inference success than current-sample Prompt Fusion,
but lower assembly success than the no-force baseline. These results
show that similar overall success rates can conceal different tradeoffs
across manipulation demands, supporting ForceBench’s practical value for
comparing force integration designs.

Our contributions are threefold:

A unified benchmark for force integration. ForceBench provides eight tasks with parameterized physical conditions,
1,600 synchronized multimodal demonstrations, and shared evaluation
with task- and category-level outcomes for six-axis wrist-force
integration.

A systematic comparative study. We evaluate observation conditioning, auxiliary predictive
supervision, and temporal force representations on a shared VLA
backbone, characterizing their benefits and limitations across
physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction,
and contact-rich assembly.

Real-world evaluation of benchmark findings. We evaluate eight systems across five real-world tasks in 800 trials.
The results support the main qualitative trends observed in
simulation and reveal task-dependent tradeoffs that overall success
rates alone can obscure.

1. A unified benchmark for force integration. ForceBench provides eight tasks with parameterized physical conditions,
1,600 synchronized multimodal demonstrations, and shared evaluation
with task- and category-level outcomes for six-axis wrist-force
integration.

2. A systematic comparative study. We evaluate observation conditioning, auxiliary predictive
supervision, and temporal force representations on a shared VLA
backbone, characterizing their benefits and limitations across
physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction,
and contact-rich assembly.

3. Real-world evaluation of benchmark findings. We evaluate eight systems across five real-world tasks in 800 trials.
The results support the main qualitative trends observed in
simulation and reveal task-dependent tradeoffs that overall success
rates alone can obscure.

# II Related Work

Force-Aware Policies for Robotic Manipulation. Token-based approaches incorporate force or tactile observations into
policy representations [ 9 , 17 ] .
Text-based conditioning includes proprioceptive discretization in π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 3 ] and stage-specific force prompts in ForceVLA2 [ 18 ] .
ManipForce and FAVLA use cross-attention [ 19 , 10 ] ,
while FoAR regulates visual–force fusion using predicted
contact [ 12 ] .
TA-VLA and ForceFlow incorporate future torque or force
prediction [ 20 , 21 ] , and MoSS combines
sensory streams with cross-modal attention and predictive
supervision [ 22 ] .
FAWAM couples action–force prediction with online residual
correction [ 23 ] ; our auxiliary prediction head is used
only during training.
ForceMimic links force-aware demonstration collection to hybrid
force–position imitation learning [ 24 ] .
Recent work extends tactile policies with predictive world
models [ 25 ] ,
while ContactWorld examines their visuo-tactile
representations [ 26 ] .

Benchmarking and Evaluation of Robotic Manipulation. RLBench, Meta-World, CALVIN, and LIBERO provide task
suites and evaluation protocols for vision-based
manipulation [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 ] .
RoboCasa, RoboTwin 2.0, DOMINO, and AutoBio extend coverage to
household, bimanual, dynamic, and laboratory
settings [ 31 , 32 , 15 , 16 ] .
SIMPLER studies correspondence between simulated and real-world
policy evaluations [ 33 ] ,
and UniVTAC benchmarks visuo-tactile perception and
interaction [ 34 ] .
ForceBench complements these resources with shared demonstrations
and a unified protocol for comparing six-axis wrist-force integration
across physical-property inference, resistance-dependent interaction,
and contact-rich assembly.

# 2 Introduction

Recent vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on robot manipulation, particularly for the tasks that can be completed within a local tabletop ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ; Wen et al., 2025 ) . Agentic systems further extend these capabilities to long-horizon mobile manipulation, through high-level planning, execution feedback, and tool use ( Ichter et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Fu et al., 2026 ) .
Yet mobile manipulation exposes a striking gap between solving individual subtasks and reliably composing them over time. Unlike tabletop manipulation, a mobile robot is required to move across workspaces while maintaining task progress, and every movement changes the viewpoint and base configuration from which the next manipulation is executed ( Yenamandra et al., 2023 ; Fu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . As a result, strong local manipulation do not necessarily translate into reliable long-horizon mobile manipulation.

The gap is surprisingly large. As shown in Figure 1 , a pretrained subtask VLA achieves 80% success rate on atomic manipulation tasks, yet the corresponding agentic baseline achieves only 19% on long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks.
This discrepancy suggests that the central challenge is not simply whether the robot knows how to manipulate, but whether it can reliably carry a manipulation skill through the sequence of decisions and physical states required by mobile manipulation tasks.
Specifically, a long-horizon task can fail even before manipulation begins: the planner may select the wrong target or lose track of task progress; navigation may reach the correct workspace but leave the robot in an unusable base pose; and even from a seemingly appropriate configuration, small errors in localization or end-effector alignment can derail the final interaction ( Yenamandra et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024a ; Huang et al., 2023b ) .
In this sense, what reliable mobile manipulation requires is not simply making a local skill stronger, but identifying where the execution pipeline breaks down.

This leads to a fundamental question: Where does mobile manipulation actually fail over long-horizon tasks, and how can an agent intervene at the bottleneck? We answer this question by cracking the failure structure of mobile manipulation.
Starting from a pretrained VLA that already performs individual tabletop subtasks well, we systematically analyze its failures when these subtasks are composed together. Our analysis reveals three dominant failure regimes that form a natural progression through the execution: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation.

Planning errors prevent the robot from pursuing the correct subtask, while navigation errors prevent it from reaching an executable configuration. And manipulation errors remain after the robot has successfully reached the intended workspace.
This diagnosis motivates a simple but powerful principle: intervene where the current system breaks, rather than uniformly increasing the capability of the underlying policy.

Guided by this principle, we develop a failure-guided agentic framework that progressively adds targeted interventions around a fixed subtask VLA.
For planning, in-context guidance from video demonstrations provides explicit task procedures ( Zhong et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , while adaptive visual memory retains what has already been accomplished and what remains to complete ( Yoneda et al., 2024 ; Sridhar et al., 2026 ) .
For navigation, an accessibility check evaluates whether the current robot configuration is suitable for the upcoming manipulation, followed by base adjustment when the approach is geometrically inadequate.
Finally, for local execution, end-effector adjustment refines the interaction pose to compensate for residual spatial misalignment.
These components are not independent add-ons: each is directly motivated by a diagnosed failure mode, transforming failure analysis into targeted agentic intervention.

We evaluate the resulting agentic system on all mobile manipulation composite tasks in RoboCasa365 ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) . Despite 80% success rates on atomic tasks, the agentic baseline achieves only 19% task success in the long-horizon tasks.
Progressively introducing the proposed interventions raises success rate to 47% .

This remarkable gain generalizes to held-out episode seeds, improving baseline from 18% to 49% success rate.
The same design also improves performance beyond RoboCasa365, raising the task success rate from 14% to 37% on five BEHAVIOR-1K tasks ( Li et al., 2023 ) and from 5/20 to 13/20 on two real-robot tasks.
Taken together, these results suggest a different way to approach long-horizon mobile manipulation. Rather than treating the robot as a monolithic policy whose capability must be scaled uniformly, we view it as an agentic system whose reliability can be improved by diagnosing bottleneck and intervening it precisely.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

A systematic failure diagnosis of mobile manipulation. We analyze the gap between strong subtask-level manipulation and long-horizon mobile manipulation, identifying three dominant failure regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. The analysis turns overall success gap into a concrete, stage-wise failure structure.

A systematic failure diagnosis of mobile manipulation. We analyze the gap between strong subtask-level manipulation and long-horizon mobile manipulation, identifying three dominant failure regimes: task planning, navigation and base positioning, and local manipulation. The analysis turns overall success gap into a concrete, stage-wise failure structure.

A failure-guided agentic intervention framework. Based on the diagnosed bottlenecks, we introduce targeted interventions around a fixed subtask VLA, including demonstration-based planning guidance, adaptive visual memory, accessibility-aware base adjustment, and local end-effector adjustment.

Agentic intervention consistently improves the performance of mobile manipulation. The proposed interventions improve the success rate from 19.0% to 47.0% on RoboCasa365. Our experiments further demonstrate consistent gains on held-out RoboCasa365 episodes, BEHAVIOR-1K tasks, and a real dual-arm mobile manipulator.

2026-10-15.title: RoboSpan: Learning Modular Coordination Policies for High-DoF Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation with Teleoperation
2026-10-15.authors: Keqiang Ren , Xuecheng Ye , Hanyu Liu , Zhihua Wang , Tao Jian , Yunsheng Ma , Jiayi Wen , Xinran Li , Zhigong Song
2026-10-15.abstract: Whole-body mobile manipulation suffers from two fundamental challenges: inherent motion heterogeneity across locomotion, arm, and hand modules, and progressive error accumulation over long-horizon multi-stage tasks. Existing teleoperation platforms also lack integrated dexterous tactile sensing to support coordinated whole-body decision-making. This paper presents RoboSpan, a high-DoF whole-body teleoperation and demonstration platform, and the Hierarchical Modular Framework (HMF) for learning modular coordination policies. HMF functionally decouples the 29-DoF action space into fine hand manipulation, arm pose adjustment, and mobile-base spatial configuration branches, and introduces the Coordinated Modular Embodied Transformer (COMET) with inter-modular cross-attention to enable dynamic information exchange and action coordination. Vision-language model driven hierarchical task decomposition structurally suppresses temporal error propagation, while a full-palm 2D tactile representation encodes distributed contact signals for cross-module tactile empowerment. Experiments on a physical 29-DoF robot demonstrate that the proposed method achieves over 20% higher task success rate than mainstream baselines across a range of long-horizon whole-body tasks, markedly improving stability and robustness in contact-rich manipulation.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Imitation learning, which acquires manipulation skills from human demonstrations, offers a core route for robots to rapidly learn complex interactive capabilities [ 1 , 2 ] . Driven by the demands of unstructured real-world scenes, robots are increasingly moving beyond fixed workbenches toward whole-body mobile manipulation systems that integrate mobile navigation, bimanual manipulation, and multimodal perception [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . This evolution also raises two core challenges: motion coordination among heterogeneous body modules and error accumulation in long-horizon complex tasks.
A whole-body mobile manipulation robot typically comprises a mobile base, manipulators, and dexterous hands, which differ markedly in action-space dimensionality, motion scale, control period, and optimization objective [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] : the base handles large-range locomotion and global pose adjustment with a long control period, whereas the arms and hands perform close-range, high-precision fine manipulation [ 5 , 6 ] . Modeling all modules jointly within a single policy sharply expands action dimensionality, increasing learning difficulty while masking the motion characteristics of each module and degrading per-module control precision [ 9 ] . Realizing efficient inter-module information exchange and coordination while preserving each module’s specialized control capability is thus a central problem for whole-body embodied intelligence, since forcing heterogeneous modules into one shared output space inevitably trades global mobility for local dexterity and ultimately limits real-world deployment.
Expanding the workspace also complicates task workflows and lengthens execution time. Methods designed for short-horizon, single-scene tasks are prone to cumulative error over multi-stage, long-cycle real-world tasks, causing a steep decline in the middle and late stages [ 10 ] . Vision-language models (VLMs) can decompose high-level natural-language instructions into executable sub-task sequences through semantic understanding [ 11 , 12 ] , offering new possibilities for hierarchical long-horizon execution. However, combining hierarchical task decomposition with low-level body-module coordination into a complete pipeline from semantic instructions to whole-body actions still lacks a systematic solution, which is the gap this work aims to close.
At the manipulation level, existing platforms mostly employ simple grippers or suction cups inadequate for complex dexterous interactions [ 13 , 14 ] . Bionic dexterous hands add DoFs and manipulation flexibility, yet without contact-state feedback they still suffer from unstable grasping and poor precision under vision-limited conditions. Distributed tactile sensing captures contact-force distribution and slip trends that vision cannot, offering an important route to improving fine manipulation [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] Most tactile studies, however, target hand manipulation itself; how tactile information propagates across modules to assist the coordinated decisions of the arms and the mobile base remains largely unexplored.
To address these issues, this paper proposes HMF, a hierarchical modular learning framework for high-DoF whole-body mobile manipulation, together with the companion teleoperation and demonstration platform RoboSpan. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

1) A high-DoF whole-body teleoperation and demonstration-collection platform: : RoboSpan integrates mobility, manipulation, and multimodal perception with 29 control DoFs in total, and a foot-IMU-based locomotion/elevation interface enables synchronous multi-module teleoperation and time-aligned data collection.

2) Full-palm distributed tactile sensing and 2-D representation: a full-palm sensing scheme with a 2-D image representation preserves the distribution of contact pressure and yields a tactile–visual isomorphic representation, providing a unified feature basis for cross-module tactile empowerment.

3) The HMF framework and COMET policy: HMF suppresses long-sequence error accumulation through VLM-driven stage decomposition, while COMET uses inter-modular cross-attention to improve whole-body coordination and task success while preserving per-module control precision.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Teleoperation and Demonstration Collection for Whole-Body Mobile Manipulation

Teleoperation is a core approach for acquiring high-quality human demonstrations and a key data-collection means for imitation learning [ 18 , 19 ] . As robotic tasks expand from fixed workbenches to large spaces, teleoperation systems have evolved from single-manipulator control toward coordinated control of multiple whole-body modules.
Early work targeted fixed-base upper-limb manipulation, mapping arm and hand motion through motion capture, exoskeletons, or VR interfaces. Open-TeleVision [ 18 ] and OPEN TEACH [ 19 ] built immersive VR-based bimanual systems for upper-limb fine manipulation, while Dexora [23] combined a vision-language model with an exoskeleton interface for more natural dexterous-hand teleoperation. These systems excel at desktop fine manipulation but are constrained by a fixed base and cannot support cross-space mobile manipulation.
To expand the robot workspace, mobile bases were introduced into teleoperation systems. Mobile ALOHA [ 20 ] realized bimanual mobile-manipulation control with leader–follower arms and a movable base; BEHAVIOR Robot Suite [ 21 ] combined dual manipulators with a mobile base for everyday household tasks; and RoboMatch [ 12 ] proposed a cockpit-style architecture supporting continuous long-horizon demonstration collection. As Table I summarizes, however, these platforms mostly use simple grippers or suction cups and lack high-DoF dexterous hands and distributed tactile sensing; their locomotion and upper-limb channels are also mutually independent, making it hard to adjust the base while sustaining continuous bimanual fine manipulation, which compromises multi-module demonstration synchronization.

## II-B Distributed Tactile Sensing for Dexterous Manipulation

Tactile sensing is a core technology for obtaining contact-state information and improving fine-manipulation robustness [ 24 , 25 ] . In complex interactions, vision alone cannot capture contact-force distribution, object slippage, or local deformation, and fusing vision with touch can effectively improve grasping stability and manipulation precision [ 26 , 27 ] .
Tactile hardware and algorithms have both advanced: flexible tactile arrays and electronic skins enable multi-region contact-force detection on dexterous-hand surfaces [ 14 ] , while ViTacFormer [ 27 ] and 3D-ViTac [ 28 ] learn visuo-tactile feature fusion that improves contact-rich performance and TACT [ 16 ] introduced the tactile modality into whole-body humanoid control.
Most existing work, however, treats touch as a local signal for hand-centric tasks such as grasping and in-hand manipulation [ 29 , 30 ] . In whole-body mobile systems its value remains underexploited: contact states can also constrain arm-pose adjustment and base-position calibration, and how tactile information propagates across modules to drive coordinated whole-body decisions still lacks systematic study.

## II-C Modular Imitation Learning and Long-Horizon Task Policies

Imitation learning is the dominant paradigm for robots to acquire complex manipulation skills from human demonstrations [ 31 , 32 ] . Transformer- and diffusion-based policy-learning methods have markedly improved performance and generalization on complex manipulation tasks [ 33 , 34 ] , and follow-up work has further extended policy learning through latent action representation, vision-language perception, and consistency distillation to enhance deployment efficiency and fine-manipulation capability across scenarios [ 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 ] .

For whole-body mobile manipulation, existing studies follow two main routes. Unified policy modeling integrates the action spaces of all body modules into a single output [ 6 , 9 ] , but sharply expands action dimensionality and makes it hard to balance the motion characteristics and control precision of different modules. Modular decomposition instead designs independent controllers per body module [ 7 , 8 ] , reducing learning difficulty but lacking dynamic inter-module information exchange and thus whole-body coordination in complex tasks. Most modular studies target single-module manipulation in a fixed workspace, such as standalone manipulators and end-effectors [ 39 , 40 , 41 ] ; for example, InterACT [ 41 ] introduces hierarchical attention for action chunking in bimanual manipulation, yet remains limited to fixed-base settings without whole-body mobility.
Long-horizon multi-stage tasks pose another major challenge for imitation learning, as conventional single-step policies accumulate error over long cycles and degrade substantially toward the end of a task [ 10 ] . Real-world mobile manipulation combines spatial locomotion, multi-stage manipulation, and long-horizon decision-making, which conventional desktop policies cannot directly handle [ 42 ] . Relay Policy Learning [ 10 ] mitigates this through policy chaining but relies on manual stage partitioning, while VLMs enable automatic semantic decomposition into sub-task sequences [ 11 , 12 ] , offering a new route for long-horizon execution. Existing studies, however, largely separate task decomposition from low-level control policies and fail to integrate hierarchical task structure with modular body coordination, leaving no complete pipeline from high-level semantic instructions to low-level whole-body actions.

2026-10-15.title: Back on Track: Deployment-time Policy Improvement via World Model Planning
2026-10-15.authors: Colton Crosby , Hao Wang , Mac Schwager , Somil Bansal
2026-10-15.abstract:
State-of-the-art visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet can fail during deployment in ways they cannot predict or recover from on their own. Improving their performance and robustness typically requires collecting more data, retraining, or modifying the policy architecture, all of which are time- and resource-intensive in practice.
We instead propose an offline-trained monitoring-and-intervention framework that improves a policy during deployment using only black-box query access. From a limited set of labeled on-policy rollouts, we learn a policy-conditioned liveness value that measures the nominal policy’s progress toward task completion; we additionally train a compact latent world model using these rollouts together with play data. At deployment, the liveness value continuously monitors execution. When it detects a loss of progress, a short-horizon planner searches the world model for corrective actions using the same value as its planning objective, after which control returns to the nominal policy. We evaluate our method on the LIBERO-Goal task suite and on a Franka Panda manipulator, using the vision-language-action model π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and a diffusion policy as nominal policies, and demonstrate significant improvements in task success rates, while supporting real-time control.
Additional results and videos are available on the project website .
2026-10-15.introduction:
Visuomotor policies are increasingly capable of complex tasks from rich sensory observations [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , yet they remain brittle at deployment and can fail in ways they cannot recover from on their own.

The dominant response is to scale policy learning itself, with more data, more compute, and larger architectures [ 4 , 5 ] .

While effective, these approaches are expensive and require access to the policy’s parameters and training pipeline — access a practitioner increasingly does not have, since strong policies are increasingly served as inference APIs or shipped with closed weights. When the weights are out of reach, deployment-time correction is a promising avenue.

We therefore ask how a policy that has already been trained and deployed can be improved without modifying the policy itself. We assume only black-box access: the parameters, architecture, and action-generation procedure are unknown, and the policy can only be queried for actions. Fine-tuning and methods that steer the policy’s internal sampling are therefore inapplicable, and improvement must come from an external wrapper that monitors execution and intervenes through actions alone. Two requirements make this demanding: policy rollouts are costly, so the wrapper must be learned from few labeled on-policy executions, and all monitoring and planning must keep pace with the control loop while the policy executes.

Our approach is based on monitoring-and-intervention, or filtering [ 6 , 7 ] , which in control theory most often enforces safety: a filter watches the nominal policy and overrides it only when a constraint would be violated [ 8 , 9 ] . We instead filter for task completion. Rather than characterizing and avoiding every failure mode, an intervention seeks to return the system to a state from which the nominal policy can complete the task. The intuition is that a capable policy need not be replaced or retrained when it falters; a short corrective action is often enough to put it back in its basin of success.

The framework has two components. A monitor tracks the nominal policy’s execution and detects when it is no longer progressing toward task completion; we instantiate it with a policy-conditioned liveness value function [ 10 ] , learned from on-policy rollouts with sparse episode-level outcome labels, that estimates how close the policy is to completing the task. When the value indicates a loss of progress, a planner briefly overrides the policy and searches a compact latent world model — trained on the same rollouts plus auxiliary play data — for a short corrective action sequence, then hands control back.

Critically, the same value that triggers intervention also scores the futures the world model imagines, directing the planner toward states from which the nominal policy can recover.

Methods that generate video futures report seconds-scale intervention times [ 11 , 12 ] , forcing either a pause or a control rate too low for responsive manipulation. We therefore design around deployment latency: the world model is compact, candidate futures are evaluated in parallel, and planning emits an action chunk rather than a single action. In our hardware experiment a planning cycle takes 108 108 ms, which, amortized over the chunk, keeps the monitor–planner loop above 10 10 Hz.

We summarize our contributions as follows. First, we formulate deployment-time improvement of visuomotor manipulation policies under a strict black-box access model and cast it as liveness filtering: an external wrapper intervenes briefly to return a fixed nominal policy to its basin of success. Second, we present a real-time instantiation in which a single policy-conditioned liveness value both monitors execution and guides corrective planning in a compact latent world model, with a data-informed action proposal that makes the search efficient. Third, we validate it across policy classes: on the ten-task LIBERO-Goal suite our method improves π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 13 ] from 72.6 % 72.6\% to 81.5 % 81.5\% , outperforming offline-RL and safety-filtering baselines, and on a Franka Panda manipulator it improves a diffusion policy [ 14 ] from 40 % 40\% to 60 % 60\% while operating within the policy’s control loop.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

We group prior work by the access and supervision it assumes, noting in each case how our problem setting differs. One line of work intervenes inside the policy’s action-generation process, requiring white-box access to the policy. Latent Policy Barrier [ 15 ] treats the latent embeddings of expert demonstrations as a barrier separating in- from out-of-distribution states, using a learned dynamics model to steer a diffusion policy’s denoising noise back toward the expert distribution at inference, equating in-distribution behavior with task success. VLS [ 16 ] steers a pretrained policy’s denoising process with guidance from a vision-language model; and [ 17 ] replaces a diffusion policy’s Gaussian sampling noise with a distribution learned via reinforcement learning (RL).
These methods intervene directly in action generation, but rely on the policy’s internal representations or sampling procedure and so do not apply when the nominal policy is only a black box.

A second class of methods treats the nominal policy as a black box and intervenes only through its inputs or outputs. RoboMonkey [ 18 ] and Steer Your Generalists [ 19 ] rerank action candidates sampled from the policy. This avoids modifying the policy’s weights, but requires multiple policy queries at every decision point, which is prohibitive for real-time control: a single diffusion-policy query alone takes 180 180 ms in our hardware setting. We instead query π b \pi_{b} once per intervention and obtain candidate diversity from our own proposal distribution rather than from the policy’s sampler.

Most closely related to our work are methods that use a learned world model to improve a fixed policy at deployment. Latent Policy Steering [ 20 ] continuously searches a latent world model for improved action sequences. In contrast, our monitor invokes planning selectively and returns control to the nominal policy after a short correction, limiting unnecessary computation and intervention when the nominal policy is progressing successfully.

DreamAvoid [ 12 ] ranks futures from a pretrained video world model at annotated critical phases, and VLA-in-the-Loop [ 11 ] specializes the paradigm to grasping, rolling back to an earlier state on a predicted grasp failure. Both are scoped to predefined critical events and to supervision we do not assume: access to the VLA’s sampling procedure plus critical-phase, progress, and failure-boundary labels for the former, grasp-feasibility labels and state rollback for the latter. We assume only black-box access and learn a policy-conditioned liveness value from sparse episode-level outcomes; the same value both detects loss of progress and guides planning, so intervention is not confined to predefined events, such as the wrong-task behavior in Fig. 2 . Their video models are also slower at deployment, reporting 2 2 s (DreamAvoid) and 20 20 s (VLA-in-the-Loop) per intervention against our 108 108 ms planning cycle.

Monitoring-and-intervention filters have a principled basis in reachability analysis [ 8 ] , which formalizes intervention under known dynamics: a filter overrides the policy only when needed to keep the system within a desired set of states. This machinery supports the dual objectives of safety (avoiding a failure set) and liveness (reaching a goal set [ 7 ] ). We focus on the latter.

Classical liveness filtering computes the reachable set exactly via dynamic programming [ 7 ] , but this is intractable for high-dimensional visual observations and the contact-rich dynamics of manipulation. We therefore build on the learned policy-conditioned liveness value of [ 10 ] , which can be estimated from limited policy-rollout data with sparse, episode-level outcome labels. Whereas that prior work uses the liveness value for offline policy evaluation, we use it here both to detect loss of progress during execution and, critically, to guide corrective planning in a learned world model.

World models differ in what they predict, and that choice sets the deployment cost. Video-generation models synthesize pixels, which is expensive enough to put them at seconds-scale latency; DreamerV3 predicts distributions over discrete latent codes [ 21 ] ; feature-prediction models forecast the patch-level features of a pretrained visual encoder, as in DINO-WM [ 22 ] . We take the last approach and keep the model compact, since each intervention must evaluate many imagined action sequences within a real-time budget.

2026-10-15.title: GS-PRM: Gaussian Visual Roadmap for Image-Goal Navigation
2026-10-15.authors: Ashraf Siddique , Kyung Min Han , Young J. Kim
2026-10-15.abstract:
Image-goal navigation requires a global planner that connects visually specified endpoints while providing observations that a local policy can follow. Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) provides map-registered RGB, opacity, and depth renderings, but does not explicitly encode navigable topology. We introduce GS-PRM, a Gaussian visual roadmap whose milestones, local connections, and visual references are constructed directly through 3DGS rendering without deriving an occupancy grid or signed distance field. We define render-based collision-free (RC-free) configurations and paths. Panoramic depth supplies conservative clearance for milestone validation and adaptive coverage, while edge-aligned orthographic rendering tests the robot’s swept volume.
We establish conditional soundness and sufficient conditions for deterministic query completeness and probabilistic construction completeness of GS-PRM.
To validate the performance of GS-PRM, we conduct experiments in both simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating long-horizon navigation using goal-conditioned policies guided by GS-PRM. Compared with a state-of-the-art 3DGS-based navigation system, our GS-PRM-based navigation system achieves up to a twice higher average success rate and reduces travel time by up to 57.2% when both systems complete the navigation task.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Image-goal navigation is a visual navigation problem that requires an agent to navigate to the location represented by a given goal image [ 1 ] . The image conveys appearance, but neither the goal pose nor a traversable route, and the destination is usually outside the current camera view. A goal-conditioned visual policy can reliably act only toward a nearby, recognizable observation within its training and control horizon. Long-horizon navigation, therefore, requires a persistent global topology that connects the localized query images and decomposes the route into reachable visual subgoals. It must also provide map-registered observations for repeated pose correction, since odometric drift can otherwise cause the physical robot to deviate from the planned route.
This task requires two forms of persistent scene information: a global planner needs the connectivity of traversable space, whereas the online robot needs map-registered visual observations for localization and feedback.

Probabilistic roadmaps (PRMs) construct a reusable graph by sampling collision-free milestones and connecting them through geometrically validated local paths [ 2 , 3 ] . However, conventional PRMs assume sufficiently accurate workspace geometry for collision checking, which can require many expensive collision tests. For physical robots, reconstruction and localization errors can further invalidate these geometric tests. Moreover, conventional PRMs lack the visual observations needed for image-based localization and feedback.

Three-dimensional Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is attractive in this setting because it represents metric, map-registered appearance and supports fast rendering of RGB, opacity, and depth from arbitrary viewpoints [ 4 ] . These renderings can provide visual references for localization and geometric evidence for planning through a common scene representation.
However, since raw Gaussian primitives are optimized for view synthesis and do not directly correspond to physical obstacles, a render-native planner must explicitly define what its renderer certifies.

Existing Gaussian-map planners take several approaches to this problem. SplatNav performs collision checking against Gaussian confidence ellipsoids and constructs safe volumes [ 5 ] . GaussNav and related systems derive voxel, bird’s-eye-view, or other planning maps from a Gaussian scene [ 6 , 7 ] . Other work directly renders visual subgoals for a learned navigation policy [ 8 ] . These methods demonstrate that 3DGS is useful for navigation. Still, they do not provide a persistent coverage-induced roadmap in which the same rendering interface defines milestone validity, local connectivity, image queries, and visual route references.

We address these limitations with GS-PRM , a coverage-driven Gaussian visual roadmap. PRM provides a persistent multi-query topology, while 3DGS provides map-registered observations that are absent from a conventional roadmap.
Using a single rendering interface, GS-PRM evaluates milestones and local connections, attaches image-defined endpoints, and generates visual references along the selected route.
We introduce the concept of render-based collision-free (RC-free), a conservative notion of free configuration space under some rendering assumptions,
providing a relationship between rendered evidence and planning. Clearance-adaptive coverage then reduces redundant
milestones in open areas while retaining finer resolution near constrained
regions.

The contributions of this work are:

We construct a Gaussian visual roadmap from the same map-registered 3DGS renderings used for planning, localization, and image-goal guidance, without deriving a separate occupancy or distance-field planning map.

We define RC-free milestones and local connections using conservative, thresholded depth, and state the assumptions under which their accepted configurations and paths lie within physical free space.

We construct a connected roadmap from certified clearance-adaptive regions and establish sufficient conditions for probabilistic construction completeness and deterministic query completeness of a completed roadmap.

For long-horizon visual navigation, we integrate image-based endpoint localization, validated roadmap attachment, and rendered visual subgoals for a goal-conditioned local policy.

We conducted a diverse set of experiments in both simulated and real-world
environments, demonstrating the effectiveness of GS-PRM for long-horizon
navigation. In particular, DevGRU combined with GS-PRM achieves a 50%
success rate, whereas standalone DevGRU achieves a 0% success rate.
Compared with another 3DGS-based planner, SplatNav, our GS-PRM combined with straight-line planner (SLP) also
achieves up to twice higher success rate and a 57.2% reduction
in travel time.

2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Probabilistic Roadmaps for Navigation

The classical PRM separates an offline learning phase, in which sampled milestones and locally feasible connections approximate free-space connectivity, from an online query phase [ 2 ] . Uniform, obstacle-based, bridge, Gaussian, visibility, and deterministic sampling strategies trade construction cost against narrow-passage discovery and dispersion; an overview is provided by LaValle [ 3 ] . PRM variants have subsequently been adapted to navigation. T-PRM predicts the temporal availability of roadmap vertices in the presence of moving obstacles [ 9 ] . PRM-RL accepts edges by rolling out a learned short-range policy rather than relying solely on a straight-line local planner [ 10 ] .

These methods exploit metric relationships among configurations but normally assume a geometric or state representation on which collision checking is defined. GS-PRM instead defines roadmap validity and coverage through 3DGS rendering and associates the resulting roadmap with visual observations for online navigation.

## II-B 3D Gaussian Splatting for Robot Navigation

3DGS combines an explicit set of spatial primitives with fast novel-view
synthesis [ 11 ] . Gaussian Splatting SLAM demonstrates that a Gaussian scene can jointly support online mapping, camera tracking, and novel-view rendering, while GSplatLoc estimates camera pose by aligning observed and rendered depth [ 12 , 13 ] . These works
establish 3DGS as a map-registered visual representation, but do not supply the persistent traversability graph required for multi-query planning.

Gaussian-map planners differ in how they obtain collision geometry. GaussNav constructs a semantic Gaussian map for image-goal matching and converts it to a grid for path planning [ 6 ] ; SplatBlox similarly derives a planning-oriented spatial representation [ 7 ] . SplatNav instead checks collisions against Gaussian confidence ellipsoids and constructs safe volumes [ 5 ] .
These methods either derive auxiliary planning geometry or reason directly about Gaussian primitives.

Rendering has also been used as the interface to a visual policy. GSplatVNM synthesizes intermediate point-of-view images that bridge gaps in a sparse image database [ 8 ] , and 3DGSNav renders informative views from a persistent Gaussian memory for long-horizon object navigation [ 14 ] . In contrast, GS-PRM builds a reusable coverage roadmap whose milestone test, connection test, image-query interface, and visual route references are all defined through rendering.

Rendered depth is not automatically a conservative collision oracle. It may be affected by missing surfaces, low accumulated opacity, depth blending, thin objects, finite raster resolution, and view dependence. We therefore make the relationship between rendered evidence and physical collision freedom an explicit assumption and evaluate it separately from roadmap connectivity.

## II-C Goal-Conditioned Visual Navigation

Image-goal policies infer short-horizon motion or waypoints from the current observation and a goal image. GNM learns this interface from heterogeneous robot datasets, and ViNT scales it into a reusable navigation model that generalizes across environments and embodiments [ 15 , 16 ] . NoMaD further models multimodal action sequences using a goal-masked diffusion policy and supports both goal-reaching and exploration [ 17 ] . Related approaches combine learned local control with topological memory or high-level goal proposal for longer-horizon navigation [ 18 , 19 ] .

These policies remain local and require a reachable, visually informative goal. GS-PRM supplies a render-validated global graph in which pose-indexed observations serve as subgoals and localization references, extending the policy horizon without requiring a densely recorded image graph.

2026-10-15.title: Dual-arm Cooperation for Tabletop Wiping with Temporal Object Removal
2026-10-15.authors: Pengqi Zhang , Longchang Yu , Daohan Li , Liang Yan , Hangxin Liu
2026-10-15.abstract: We devise a dual-arm cooperative planning framework for wiping table surface in the presence of scattered objects. Unlike conventional surface-cleaning strategies that only cover free areas and detour around obstacles, our framework explicitly assigns one arm to rearrange objects while the other performs coverage wiping, thereby enabling access to previously obstructed regions. Specifically, we first construct a set of wiping and object-rearrangement action primitives. Based on these primitives, we introduce Geo-MILP, a geometry-aware task planner formulated as milp ( milp ). By integrating lbbd ( lbbd ), Geo-MILP iteratively optimizes action sequencing and timing to resolve geometric conflicts, promoting efficient cooperation between wiping and object rearrangement. We then employ komo ( komo ) to generate smooth, collision-free motions to ensure feasible execution. Simulation and physical experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework not only increases reachable coverage by enabling access to obstructed areas, but also significantly improves time efficiency compared to tamp ( tamp ) baselines, reducing planning time by up to 9 × 9\times and execution makespan by approximately 40 % 40\% .
2026-10-15.introduction:
Wiping a tabletop surface to remove dust, stains, or liquid spills is a common domestic chore, and automating this task with service robots is highly desirable [ 1 , 2 ] . Effective wiping requires the robot’s end effector to thoroughly cover the entire planar surface. This could be accomplished by solving a coverage problem [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] in robotics, which has been extensively studied in the cpp ( cpp ) literature [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . CPP-based methods have achieved great success in applications such as robotic vacuum cleaning [ 10 , 7 , 8 ] , surface inspection and polishing [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] , where obstacles are typically modeled as static occupancy to be avoided.

However, in real-world domestic settings, desks, kitchen counters, and workbenches are often scattered with everyday objects that partially occlude the tabletop surface. When standard CPP is directly applied in such situation, the robot’s end effector is instructed to detour around objects, leaving large portions of the surface uncleaned (see Fig. 1(a) ). Moreover, such detouring motions increase the risk of collisions and lead to inefficient trajectories. As a result, achieving complete, safe, and efficient surface coverage in cluttered tabletop environments remains a challenging open problem.

To address this problem, we leverage a dual-arm robot that incorporates temporary object removal to clear obstructions. In particular, one arm performs coverage wiping while the other temporarily removes obstructing objects by picking them up and placing them back after the corresponding surface region has been wiped. This cooperated behavior enables the robot to reach regions that would otherwise be inaccessible. In principle, such behavior can be formulated within a tamp ( tamp ) framework [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] , where symbolic actions such as pick, place and others are defined at the task level and instantiated into continuous motions after proper sequencing.

However, directly applying conventional TAMP to this problem is often suboptimal for tabletop wiping. Standard TAMP frameworks typically focus on generating feasible sequences of symbolic actions, relying heavily on the assumption of atomic actions and instantaneous state transitions. Under this discrete modeling paradigm, the system state is updated instantaneously between action steps, making it especially difficult to represent the continuous temporal overlap required for coordinated execution. Consequently, without an explicit mechanism to coordinate motion duration, the two arms are forced to operate sequentially rather than concurrently [ 18 , 19 , 17 ] , leaving one arm idle while the other performs its task, as shown in Fig. 1(b) . This not only increases the overall task completion time but also prevents the robot from fully exploiting the advantages of bimanual cooperation. Although TAMP provides a natural formalism for dual-arm tabletop wiping, an additional mechanism is required to coordinately plan bimanual actions to achieve efficient and complete surface coverage.

In this work, we propose a dual-arm cooperative planning framework that explicitly reasons about concurrent wiping and temporary object removal to achieve efficient and complete tabletop cleaning. Our approach first constructs a set of primitive actions for wiping and object handling, and formulates a milp ( milp ) problem to optimize their sequencing and temporal coordination, promoting concurrency between the two arms (see Fig. 1(c) ). Crucially, to ensure physical feasibility in cluttered environments, we incorporate a lbbd ( lbbd ) strategy that iteratively refines the MILP schedule using geometric feedback from the motion planner. The resulting high-level plan is then refined using komo ( komo ) to generate smooth, collision-free motions that are physically feasible for execution on a real robot. The simulation and physical experiment demonstrate that our framework achieves significantly larger surface coverage while reducing task completion time compared to conventional TAMP approaches.

Surface cleaning has long been studied as a coverage problem in robotics. Classical cpp has succeeded in static surface cleaning tasks like floor and window wiping [ 6 , 7 ] . However, tabletop wiping introduces manipulable clutter. Existing approaches predominantly treat obstacles as immutable constraints, focusing on passive collision avoidance that inevitably leaves occluded regions uncleaned [ 8 , 20 , 21 , 3 , 10 ] . To guarantee maximal coverage, our formulation integrates CPP with active, reversible object rearrangement to explicitly recover obstructed workspace.

Bimanual Manipulation research has extensively explored safe motion synchronization [ 22 , 1 ] and compliance [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] , but it primarily focuses on collision-free execution. Relying solely on low-level coordination limits overall efficiency due to the lack of proactive action scheduling [ 26 , 27 ] . To overcome the limitations of purely reactive coordination, our approach elevates dual-arm synchronization to the task planning level. By explicitly optimizing the timing of wiping and rearrangement, we maximize bimanual concurrency rather than merely avoiding collisions.

Task and Motion Planning seeks to formally integrate discrete high-level reasoning and continuous low-level control [ 16 ] . In standard TAMP implementations, the task planning layer typically relies on symbolic planners (e.g., PDDL-based [ 18 ] , VKC-based [ 17 ] ) to resolve causal dependencies [ 28 , 29 ] .
However, a fundamental limitation of these approaches is the assumption of atomic actions and instantaneous state transitions. Since they optimize for logical plan length rather than continuous execution time, standard planners lack the intrinsic metric to seek concurrency, typically converging to sequential solutions. To address temporal reasoning, planners such as POPF [ 30 ] and LPG [ 31 ] introduce durative actions and heuristic search over temporal action graphs, enabling partial concurrency. However, they primarily operate in a symbolic domain and do not explicitly incorporate continuous geometric feasibility during planning.
More recent work on multi-arm and makespan-aware planning considers coordination across multiple manipulators [ 32 ] and explicitly optimizes execution time under coupled task constraints [ 33 ] , highlighting the importance of temporal coordination in multi-robot systems.
In contrast, our work focuses on a task-specific dual-arm tabletop wiping problem with temporary object removal. We emphasize coordination between coverage wiping and object rearrangement under fixed primitive abstractions, where geometric feasibility is handled by an external motion optimization module.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: (i) We propose a hierarchical dual-arm planning framework that integrates coverage wiping with active, reversible object removal, enabling complete access to occluded regions that are unreachable by conventional collision-avoidance strategies. (ii) We introduce Geo-MILP, a task planner that explicitly optimizes the temporal coordination of dual-arm actions, and combine it with a lbbd scheme to iteratively refine the schedule with geometric feedback, ensuring that the generated concurrent plans are not only time-efficient but also physically executable. (iii) We validate the proposed framework which achieves near-complete cleaning coverage in cluttered environments through extensive simulations and physcical experiments.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II provides a high-level system overview of the proposed coordinated framework and its hierarchical modules. Section III details the formulation of Geo-MILP task planner, and the LBBD-based geometric feedback mechanism. Section IV describes the KOMO-based motion planner used for trajectory generation and feasibility verification. Section V presents the simulation and physical experimental results. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper with discussions.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Coordinated Framework

## II-A CPP: Tabletop Coverage Path Generation

We first discretize the tabletop region into occupancy grids and construct a graph over the resulting cells. CPP then computes a coverage-efficient visiting order of waypoints for the wiper to achieve complete surface coverage. At this stage, clutter objects are treated as blocked nodes in the graph: we only identify occluded waypoints but do not generate any interaction or detouring logic. Accordingly, the output of CPP is a coverage-oriented abstraction, including the visiting sequence, adjacency relations, and the subset of occluded waypoints that are infeasible to wipe without manipulation.

## II-B MILP-based Task Planner: Temporal Scheduling and Dual-Arm Coordination

Taking the coverage path and blocked-waypoint information produced by CPP as input, we formulate dual-arm coordination as a milp problem. The MILP assigns obstacle-handling primitives to the left arm (e.g., pick , place , and reversible actions that return objects to their original locations) and jointly schedules them on a timeline alongside the right arm’s wiping sequence. Its primary goal is to produce a geometrically feasible, time-optimal action schedule that minimizes the makespan under logical precedence and synchronization constraints. To efficiently solve the spatial temporal coupling, we formulate this layer using an optimization-based architecture rooted in lbbd . Specifically, the MILP acts as the Master Problem proposing a feasible schedule, while a geometric sub-problem iteratively verifies feasibility and injects logic-based cuts to prune invalid solutions. Through this iterative constraint injection, the task planner refines the schedule until a valid, collision-free task skeleton is found. The solver outputs a time-indexed dual-arm action sequence that balances sequencing and concurrency, avoiding conservative sequential execution.

## II-C KOMO-based Motion Planner: Trajectory Generation

The discrete actions scheduled by the MILP is passed to the motion planner. We employ komo to translate each scheduled primitive into continuous constraints (e.g., end-effector pose targets for wipe and remove / place conditions) and jointly optimize the resulting trajectories. KOMO handles the robot’s kinematic constraints and the scene geometry, enforcing collision avoidance between the arms, the environment, and objects. By solving a trajectory optimization problem, KOMO produces smooth, physically executable, and collision-free trajectories for the scheduled action.

2026-10-15.title: Dungeon and Visibility World Generator
2026-10-15.authors: Edwin Mériaux , Antonio Loría , Gregory Dudek
2026-10-15.comment: This points to our git repo used in our many projects for standardization and reproduction of scientific work
2026-10-15.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-15.introduction:
Robotic exploration, coverage and deployment algorithms require reproducible
environments whose geometry and visibility can be varied independently of
the algorithm. This work provides a configurable generator for two- and
three-dimensional worlds, with continuous free-space geometry, discrete
occupancy grids and geometric line-of-sight queries. It supplies benchmark
worlds and observations, rather than exploration policies.

The generator supports six geometry classes (orthogonal,
polygonal/polyhedral and curvilinear in 2D and 3D) and six construction
families (scattered rooms, clusters, winding passages, caverns, branches
and loops). Room and passage dimensions, obstacle configurations and
placement can be controlled through fixed values, uniform ranges or
probability distributions. Configurations, seeds, geometries and visibility
results are saved for reproducible comparisons.

The implementation is available at https://github.com/EdwinMeriaux/Dungeon_and_Visibility_World_Generator .

Let d ∈ { 2 , 3 } d\in\{2,3\} . A continuous world occupies a bounded domain D ⊂ ℝ d D\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} , with free space 𝒲 ⊆ D \mathcal{W}\subseteq D . Positions have
real-valued coordinates: ( x , y ) (x,y) in two dimensions and ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) in
three dimensions. Let R R be the combined room region, P P the
combined passage region, and O O the combined obstacle region. Then 𝒲 = ( D ∩ ( R ∪ P ) ) ∖ O . \mathcal{W}=\bigl(D\cap(R\cup P)\bigr)\setminus O.

This combines rooms and passages, keeps them inside the domain, and
removes obstacles.
The continuous representation describes wall locations without imposing a
grid. In 2D, the saved geometry is a polygon; enclosed obstacles appear as
holes, and curved boundaries are approximated by short straight segments.
In 3D, rooms and passages are combined into a solid free region, with
obstacles removed. A surface mesh is also saved for visualization, while
the solid itself is used for geometric checks.

# 2 Discrete representations and visibility

## 2.1 From continuous geometry to a discrete grid
