2026-10-15.title: HiFun: a Hierarchical Framework for Efficient Functional Dexterous Manipulation Learning
2026-10-15.authors: Linyi Huang , Guowei Huai , Weibin Liu , Shulong Jiang , Ping Tan , Weixuan Zhang , Hui Zhang , Jie Song
2026-10-15.abstract:
While multi-fingered dexterous robot hands have the potential to provide human-level dexterity, using them for functional manipulation remains difficult because task success depends on precise contact, coordinated arm-hand motion, and reactive recovery from execution errors.
Precise contact depends on complex contact dynamics that are difficult to model accurately in simulation, motivating real-world learning.
However, real-world demonstrations in the full arm-hand control space are costly and noisy because each trajectory must coordinate arm motion with high-DoF multi-finger contact.
Small execution deviations can further cause slipped contact or premature force application, making recovery from off-nominal contact states important for robust execution.
To deal with these challenges, we propose HiFun, a hierarchical real-world RL framework for functional dexterous manipulation tasks.
Our key insight is to decouple the control complexity into a functional hand skill for precise contact execution and an arm-hand coordination policy for arm control and hand-skill activation.
This design enables effective real-time human intervention for reactive recovery learning and efficient data collection with Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) augmentation.
Across six real-world tasks on two dexterous hands, HiFun achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training and remains robust to dynamic disturbances.
The project page is available at https://hly-123.github.io/HiFun/ .
2026-10-15.introduction:
Functional dexterous manipulation is central for robot applications from factories to homes.
We study this setting through representative tasks in precise tool use, contact-rich rotation, and constrained-space manipulation.
For example, Thin-Handle Tool Retrieval (Fig. 1 C) requires extracting a foam-embedded handle through a narrow opening where direct grasping is blocked.
The robot must place fingertip contact on the exposed handle, coordinate arm motion with multi-finger levering to create access, and form a precision grasp without losing contact.
Small contact errors can cause slipping, trapping, or collisions with the opening.
These stages require precise contact, high-DoF arm-hand coordination, and recovery from contact errors, making functional dexterous manipulation challenging to learn and execute.

Specifically, precise contact requires the robot to place fingertips on task-relevant regions and regulate force as local contact changes.
High-DoF arm-hand coordination requires arm motion, multi-finger contact, and contact timing to be synchronized within one execution sequence.
Because fine-grained contact tasks are sensitive to small deviations, policies must recover from slipped contact, missed insertion, partial progress, or premature force application rather than only reproduce nominal successful trajectories.

Existing learning routes have made substantial progress, but these challenges remain only partially addressed for functional dexterity.
Precise contact can be explored at scale in simulation, enabling robust dexterous manipulation performance [ 30 , 5 , 52 , 35 , 51 , 32 ] . However, sim-to-real transfer is difficult for functional manipulation due to its intricate contact dynamics.
High-DoF arm-hand behaviors can be represented by imitation learning (IL) and pretrained visuomotor policies from demonstrations and robot datasets [ 8 , 56 , 3 , 31 , 18 , 2 , 48 ] .
However, collecting real-world demonstrations for functional dexterity remains costly and noisy because each trajectory must jointly specify arm motion, multi-finger contact, and contact timing, which are difficult for an operator to perform at the same time, especially considering the embodiment gap between human and robotic hands [ 13 , 36 ] . Furthermore, these demonstrations usually focus on successful cases, providing limited evidence for recovery after failures.
Recovery from execution errors can be improved by real-world RL from online physical outcomes [ 21 , 24 , 26 ] , but direct exploration and human correction in the full arm-hand action space are inefficient for learning reactive recovery.

To address these limitations, we propose HiFun, a hierarchical real-world RL framework for functional dexterous manipulation.
For fine-grained finger control and precise contact execution, HiFun adapts kinesthetic hand-motion priors with residual RL and real contact feedback, producing functional hand skills grounded in physical interaction.
To improve exploration efficiency in high-DoF arm-hand coordination, HiFun freezes the hand skills as action primitives and trains a coordination policy over arm motion and skill activation, with DMP-augmented rollouts providing initial coverage.
During online fine-tuning, human corrections are provided through the hand-skill interface to make interventions more consistent and effective, while a multi-head critic improves temporal coordination and intervention advantage weighting (IAW) prioritizes useful corrections for reactive recovery.
Together, this factorization reduces the burden of full arm-hand demonstrations, exploration, and correction, enabling reliable functional dexterous manipulation with efficient online training.
We evaluate HiFun on six functional dexterous tasks across two dexterous hands, as shown in Fig. 1 .
HiFun achieves 98.3% average success within one hour of online training, outperforms IL and flat human-in-the-loop RL baselines, and remains robust to disturbances, while ablations verify the contributions of the hand-skill and coordination components.

In summary, our contributions are: (1) a hierarchical real-world RL framework that decouples high-DoF arm-hand control into functional hand-skill learning and skill-conditioned coordination, enabling efficient real-world learning of functional dexterous tasks; (2) residual-RL hand-skill learning that adapts kinesthetic priors with real contact feedback for fine-grained contact execution;
(3) skill-conditioned coordination that uses hand skills as action primitives, DMP-augmented rollouts for efficient initial coverage, a multi-head critic for temporal coordination of arm motion and hand activation, and IAW for sample-efficient online recovery learning.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Dexterous Manipulation. Model-based control plans stable dexterous grasps from explicit object and contact models [ 27 , 37 ] , but functional manipulation depends on contact-rich dynamics that are difficult to model accurately.
Large-scale simulation has enabled robust dexterous grasping [ 55 , 7 , 15 , 23 , 41 , 54 ] and in-hand rotation [ 30 , 5 , 34 , 22 , 53 ] , yet functional contact dynamics involving deformation, friction variation, and fine-grained force feedback remain difficult to simulate [ 44 , 14 ] , causing precise contact behaviors to transfer unreliably.
IL and pretrained visuomotor policies can represent high-DoF arm-hand behaviors from demonstrations via diffusion-based policies [ 8 , 49 ] , transformer policies with action chunking [ 56 , 4 ] , and vision-language-action models [ 3 , 2 , 18 ] .
For dexterous arm-hand systems, however, such demonstrations require specialized teleoperation or capture interfaces [ 13 , 36 , 43 , 46 , 10 ] , and human-to-robot retargeting can introduce contact noise under morphology mismatch [ 47 ] .
Thus, demonstrations for functional dexterity remain costly and noisy, struggle to cover fine-grained finger contacts and dynamic arm-hand coordination, and provide limited recovery evidence.
HiFun instead obtains hand-motion priors through kinesthetic teaching [ 50 ] , adapts them into contact-aware skills with residual RL, and uses these skills to collect downstream coordination data, reducing direct teleoperation of all dexterous-hand DoFs.

Real-World Reinforcement Learning. Real-world RL learns directly from physical interactions, capturing hardware dynamics and contact physics that are difficult to simulate [ 21 , 25 , 1 ] .
Human-in-the-loop (HIL) methods improve sample efficiency by incorporating online corrections during training [ 26 , 16 , 39 ] , and HIL-SERL achieves near-perfect success on precise gripper tasks with demonstrations and real-time guidance [ 26 ] .
For functional dexterous manipulation, however, the high-dimensional arm-hand system degrades data precision and efficiency while increasing exploration burden, and coupled finger joints make consistent real-time correction across all DoFs difficult [ 57 ] .
Hierarchical and skill-based methods reduce exploration complexity by reusing lower-level behaviors or guiding policy search.
Prior work chains dexterous sub-policies for long-horizon manipulation [ 6 ] , reuses learned rotation skills for harder in-hand reorientation [ 35 ] , and guides RL exploration with simple sub-skill controllers [ 17 ] .
We adopt a hierarchical framework that decouples hand primitive skills from arm-hand coordination, shifting online learning from full arm-hand exploration to skill-conditioned coordination and recovery.

2026-10-15.title: Robota-Embed: Unified VLA Embeddings for Robot In-Context Learning and Evolution
2026-10-15.authors: Yunze Liu , Jing Wang , Shenrui Wu , Wenkun He , Guanqi Zhan , Xianzheng Ma , Junyu Chen , Wenhang Ge , Haozhan Tang , Yuchao Gu , Zhuoyang Zhang , Zekai Wang , Dantong Niu , Zhen Dong , Yuke Zhu , Trevor Darrell , Linxi "Jim" Fan , Song Han , Han Cai
2026-10-15.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-15.abstract:
Retrieving useful context for a robot requires matching not only its task,
but also its current stage of execution and the continuation that should
follow. We introduce Robota-Embed, to our knowledge the first
vision–language–action (VLA) embedding model to jointly encode all three
modalities in both current-state queries and recorded future continuations.
Predictive retrieval training aligns these endpoints for physical-experience
retrieval, and the resulting representation retrieves historical
continuations as context at inference time. We construct a multi-source corpus
of 1,695,684 cleaned training anchors and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench, which
evaluates 4,000 queries against a shared 8,000-entry gallery. Our model achieves
47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level R@1, surpassing action-free Gemini
Embedding 2 by 22.09 and 33.47 percentage points. Across controlled retrieval
studies, removing native action degrades retrieval more than removing vision,
indicating that execution information is a central part of the retrieval key.
We then study how this shared retrieval space transfers beyond retrieval
metrics through two complementary applications. Embed2ICL uses
retrieved experience for training-free and training-based policy conditioning,
increasing success from 47.0% to 56.3% in DROID-Sim and from 86.4% to 92.8%
on the LIBERO difficult subset. Both interfaces also improve task progress in
real-robot evaluations. Embed2Evolve uses execution feedback to grow
task-local memory and refine how retrieved context is used around a frozen
GPT-6 Astra policy. Across five ManiSkill tasks, it achieves 68% success,
compared with 24% for GPT-6 Astra Direct and 33% for a harness independently
evolved with Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B under the same protocol. Relative to the
latter, it uses approximately 79.5% fewer policy tokens per test rollout.
Together, these results show that a unified, action-aware retrieval space can
support both robot in-context learning and task-local context evolution.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Robot policies increasingly use experience supplied in context.
GEN-1.5 [ 1 ] and S1 [ 2 ] demonstrate
Robot In-Context Learning from sensorimotor or video examples. In our experiments,
GPT-6 Astra [ 3 ] generates robot actions from observations and execution
history. These capabilities make experience selection part of the control problem.
Demonstration-conditioned world action models (WAMs) need useful existing
examples; policies acting repeatedly must organize accumulated experience.
Both raise a representation question: how should physical experience be represented for task- and stage-sensitive retrieval?

Task similarity alone is insufficient. Reaching toward a bowl and withdrawing
after placement can share objects and an instruction yet require different
continuations. Language specifies the goal, vision the
interaction state, and native action the ongoing motion. The retrieval endpoints
have different temporal roles: the query describes the present, whereas a
candidate records what followed an earlier interaction. Predictive retrieval therefore requires sensitivity to task intent and execution stage: the goal is
an appropriate recorded continuation, not simply a similar scene.

General-purpose embeddings align vision and
language [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , while
action-aware metric learning connects perception or language with
behavior [ 7 , 8 ] .
We introduce Robota-Embed , a unified vision–language–action
(VLA) embedding model for physical-experience retrieval. To our knowledge, it is
the first to jointly encode all three modalities in both current-state queries
and recorded continuations. Each endpoint yields one vector, so native action
informs retrieval itself. Source-specific projectors handle
heterogeneous action formats.
Retrieval training combines predictive alignment, multimodal grounding and
discrimination, and representation regularization.

We construct a multi-source training corpus and introduce Robota-Embed-Bench,
with 4,000 queries and 8,000 gallery candidates spanning human, simulated,
and real-robot experience. Nearby same-episode clips distinguish finding the
right experience from locating its recorded continuation. Across four sources,
Robota-Embed achieves 47.33% clip-level and 81.77% episode-level
R@1. Native action adds information beyond text and images: with backbone,
data, and training budget matched on DROID, adding action raises clip-level
R@1 from 59.8% to 78.7%. Complementary retraining and query-masking studies
examine which information the representation learns and uses.

Figure 1 connects retrieval to demonstration conditioning and
memory-based interaction. Embed2ICL supports robot in-context learning
through two policy interfaces. For
DreamZero [ 9 ] , retrieved videos initialize the visual
cache without policy updates. For Fast-WAM [ 10 ] , we
fine-tune the policy to condition on precomputed Context Tokens from retrieved
demonstrations. Both interfaces improve simulation task success and real-robot
task progress. Random-reference controls show that useful context depends on
reference selection.

Embed2Evolve extends retrieval to context management for agentic
robots. Repeated attempts grow task-local memory, while execution feedback
refines retrieval, refresh, and retained-history settings around a frozen
GPT-6 Astra policy. Policy and embedding weights remain fixed. Across five
ManiSkill tasks, the selected context harness raises success from 24% with
Direct to 68%, using 43.7% fewer policy tokens per test rollout. To examine
the retrieval model’s role, we independently repeat evolution with
Omni-Embed-Nemotron-3B from the same initial memory under the same search
protocol. Its harness reaches 33% success; Embed2Evolve uses approximately
79.5% fewer tokens than this baseline. Token averages include failed tests
and exclude development.

We make four contributions.

Robota-Embed. A unified embedding model that jointly
encodes vision, language, and native action at both endpoints for predictive
physical-experience retrieval.

Data and evaluation. A multi-source training corpus,
Robota-Embed-Bench, and controlled studies of temporal precision, representation
learning, and native action’s contribution beyond vision and language.

Embed2ICL. Training-free and training-based interfaces that
turn retrieved demonstrations into useful policy context, evaluated in
simulation and on real robots.

Embed2Evolve. Embedding-guided memory and context evolution
around a frozen policy, improving success and token efficiency under matched
comparisons of retrieval embedding models.

1. Robota-Embed. A unified embedding model that jointly
encodes vision, language, and native action at both endpoints for predictive
physical-experience retrieval.

2. Data and evaluation. A multi-source training corpus,
Robota-Embed-Bench, and controlled studies of temporal precision, representation
learning, and native action’s contribution beyond vision and language.

3. Embed2ICL. Training-free and training-based interfaces that
turn retrieved demonstrations into useful policy context, evaluated in
simulation and on real robots.

4. Embed2Evolve. Embedding-guided memory and context evolution
around a frozen policy, improving success and token efficiency under matched
comparisons of retrieval embedding models.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

CLIP aligns images with language [ 4 ] ;
Perception Encoder and InternVideo2 extend vision–language representation
learning to video [ 11 , 12 ] .
Unified vision–language embeddings support image and video retrieval in one
space [ 13 , 6 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] ; ImageBind [ 5 ] includes additional sensory modalities.
Deep Multimodal Embedding [ 7 ] and
CLASP [ 8 ] align language or perception with action.
VLA-R [ 17 ] embeds visual–language queries and action-token
candidates in a shared space, while RADAR [ 18 ] reuses VLA-policy features for
retrieval. Robota-Embed jointly encodes vision, language, and native
action at both retrieval endpoints: the current state and the recorded future clip.

Action can enter the retrieval key or the content returned to the policy.
ROSER [ 19 ] searches proprioceptive sequences;
RAEA [ 20 ] , REGENT [ 21 ] , and
RICL [ 22 ] return actions selected through action-free keys.
Zeva [ 23 ] indexes action–effect evidence, whereas
RADAR [ 18 ] uses policy features.
MemER [ 24 ] selects rollout keyframes;
Retrieve-Reason-Act [ 25 ] indexes visual manuals.
Robota-Embed includes native action in both query and candidate keys,
so motion informs the similarity comparison itself
(Table 33 ).

GEN-1.5 [ 1 ] conditions on a sensorimotor example;
S1 [ 2 ] , Zero-WAM [ 26 ] , and
HOST [ 27 ] use supplied video. R+X [ 28 ] retrieves human-video clips and converts them into keypoint and hand-trajectory
context. Embed2ICL uses Robota-Embed to select experience for
training-free and training-based WAM conditioning.
Reflexion [ 29 ] stores verbal reflections in episodic
memory, using feedback to improve later trials without updating model weights.
In robotics, Zeva [ 23 ] retrieves action–effect evidence across
retries within an episode, resetting memory for each new episode.
Embed2Evolve performs in-context evolution :
it grows task-local memory across development episodes and refines retrieval,
refresh, and history settings around a frozen policy. Evaluation uses the selected
memory and context settings without further changes on fresh task initializations.

2026-10-15.title: IMU-Bench: Benchmarking Wrist IMU Representations Across Kinematic, Semantic and Clinical Tasks
2026-10-15.authors: Yiquan Li , Aidan Bradshaw , Chenfeng Gao , Karan Ahuja
2026-10-15.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-15.introduction:
Wrist-worn inertial measurement units (IMUs) provide a common sensing modality for studying human movement. Embedded in everyday smartwatches, accelerometers and gyroscopes capture motion relevant to activity recognition [ 78 ] , clinical motor assessment [ 65 ] and human–computer interaction [ 33 , 71 ] , with additional cues for articulated pose estimation and inertial odometry. Like the shadows in Plato’s allegory of the cave [ 50 , Book VII, 514a–517a] , different downstream tasks reveal distinct aspects of the same underlying human motion, each offering only a partial view [ 28 ] . These perspectives raise the question of whether these views share a representation.

Self-supervised learning has demonstrated substantial reuse of unlabeled wearable recordings. Yuan et al. [78] show transfer from large-scale free-living accelerometry to activity recognition across datasets and populations. Inertia-1 examines objectives, architectures, scale and sensing configurations across activity recognition, freezing-of-gait detection and disease prediction [ 75 ] . These studies establish transfer across classification tasks and sensing conditions, while leaving less understood how the same representations support articulated joint rotations, metric velocity and motion–language correspondence.

These targets also allow us to examine whether different forms of motion supervision are complementary. Task-transfer studies in vision provide a precedent for measuring such relationships [ 79 ] . For wrist IMUs, we ask both how broadly pretrained features transfer and whether supervision for one motion target improves or compromises their usefulness for others.

We present IMU-Bench, a benchmark of ten tasks from eight datasets addressing these questions (Figure 1 ). We compare six self-supervised methods pretrained on unlabeled activity and daily-living recordings together with simulated wrist motion. Evaluation spans classification, pose and velocity estimation, and IMU–language retrieval, using six-channel inputs from a single wrist. Beyond frozen probing and fine-tuning, we examine supervised source-task transfer and selected joint-training pairs. The results reveal a distinction between broadly useful pretraining and compatible task supervision. Full-body pose and odometry improve over training from scratch after fine-tuning, and each kinematic task’s best frozen source is another kinematic task, whereas under frozen probing no supervised source approaches the pretrained encoder on language retrieval. Five of the six kinematic transfers survive, at about half their size, when the tasks are evaluated on disjoint participants, and the observed trade-offs show why individual-task performance alone is insufficient to characterize a shared wrist representation.

We make three contributions:

A benchmark and comprehensive evaluations. IMU-Bench brings together ten tasks across six families to evaluate wrist-IMU representations through categorical, kinematic and motion–language prediction targets. We compare six self-supervised methods under matched encoder capacity and common task protocols, alongside training from scratch and retrained task-specific systems.

A benchmark and comprehensive evaluations. IMU-Bench brings together ten tasks across six families to evaluate wrist-IMU representations through categorical, kinematic and motion–language prediction targets. We compare six self-supervised methods under matched encoder capacity and common task protocols, alongside training from scratch and retrained task-specific systems.

A reusable pretrained wrist-IMU model. We provide InrtlWrist, a masked autoencoder pretrained on unlabeled recorded and simulated wrist motion. Among the six controlled methods, it achieves the best or joint-best frozen-probe performance on nine of ten tasks. Fine-tuning improves on training from scratch on nine of the ten tasks, including full-body pose, odometry and IMU–language retrieval.

An analysis of cross-task transfer and complementarity. We measure how source-task supervision and joint training affect other prediction targets. The experiments distinguish beneficial transfer between kinematic tasks from the gap that remains to the pretrained encoder on motion–language retrieval under frozen probing, and identify joint-training gains that come at the expense of the paired task. Additional analyses examine pretraining volume and motion coverage.

The benchmark code and the leaderboard are available on the project website, https://spicexlab.github.io/imubench/ ; pretrained models will be released there.

IMU-Bench brings together ten tasks across six families to evaluate wrist-IMU representations through categorical, kinematic and motion–language prediction targets. We compare six self-supervised methods under matched encoder capacity and common task protocols, alongside training from scratch and retrained task-specific systems.

2. A reusable pretrained wrist-IMU model. We provide InrtlWrist, a masked autoencoder pretrained on unlabeled recorded and simulated wrist motion. Among the six controlled methods, it achieves the best or joint-best frozen-probe performance on nine of ten tasks. Fine-tuning improves on training from scratch on nine of the ten tasks, including full-body pose, odometry and IMU–language retrieval.

3. An analysis of cross-task transfer and complementarity. We measure how source-task supervision and joint training affect other prediction targets. The experiments distinguish beneficial transfer between kinematic tasks from the gap that remains to the pretrained encoder on motion–language retrieval under frozen probing, and identify joint-training gains that come at the expense of the paired task. Additional analyses examine pretraining volume and motion coverage.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2. Related Work

Wearable-IMU representations are mostly evaluated on activity recognition: pretraining objectives [ 22 , 12 ] , cross-dataset generalization [ 26 ] and foundation models on activity and health outcomes [ 78 , 46 , 1 , 75 , 62 ] ; SlotFM adds gesture, gait and sports [ 49 ] , NormWear physiological signals [ 40 ] . Sparse-IMU pose [ 27 , 77 , 76 , 29 , 43 , 74 ] and inertial odometry [ 14 , 24 , 38 , 52 ] are studied apart, though label-free physical decoders now link them to self-supervised learning [ 34 ] . Task-specific systems for activity [ 48 ] , gestures [ 71 , 33 , 7 ] , Parkinson’s disease [ 9 , 65 ] and IMU–language alignment [ 80 , 44 , 83 ] are our reference points (Appendix B ). None measures how supervision on one task affects the others, which IMU-Bench adds.

Pretext tasks for wearable IMUs include transformation prediction [ 55 , 78 ] , self-training [ 61 ] , masked reconstruction [ 21 , 72 , 23 ] , masked modeling with contrast [ 18 ] , factorized multimodal contrast [ 37 ] , relative contrast [ 73 ] and video and text supervision [ 16 ] ; language models can also synthesize virtual IMU [ 35 ] . Each came with its own backbone, data and protocol, so we compare five with masked autoencoding under one corpus and matched capacity (Section 4.2 ). Transformers for multivariate series encode channels independently [ 47 , 19 ] , as whole-channel tokens [ 39 ] or in separate time and variate stages [ 82 ] ; the first loses the accelerometer–gyroscope coupling and the second the patch-level resolution pose and odometry need, hence the alternating frame-wise and global attention of InrtlWrist, adapted from VGGT [ 69 ] (Section 4.1 ).

Task relationships have been measured by transferring supervision [ 79 , 66 , 2 ] , by choosing tasks to train together [ 13 , 59 ] and by comparing representations directly [ 31 , 28 ] ; we take the transfer route for wrist IMUs (Section 6 ). Because probe accuracy reflects the probe as well as the representation [ 3 , 25 ] , we fix light decoders and add untrained-encoder and raw-input controls (Section 4.3 ). Scaling laws and data pruning [ 30 , 58 ] motivated wearable studies of data volume and participant count [ 46 , 75 ] ; we vary motion coverage at matched volume (Section 7 ).

2026-10-15.title: Active Generative Simulation: Meta-Learning What to Simulate for Sim-and-Real Policy Co-Training
2026-10-15.authors: Liqian Ma , Vaibhav Saxena , Utkarsh Aashu Mishra , Shuo Cheng , Yongxin Chen , Danfei Xu
2026-10-15.abstract:
Sim-and-real co-training is an effective way to scale robot learning by augmenting limited real-world demonstrations with simulation data. However, existing approaches typically treat simulators as fixed data sources, relying on uniform generation, offline retrieval, or manual parameter alignment by domain experts. We formulate Active Generative Simulation : optimizing a simulator’s data-generation distribution to maximize downstream real-world performance. To solve this problem, we propose MetaGenSim , a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to automatically discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified simulation parameter space, without manual parameter alignment. Across simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and retrieval baselines, achieves a 150 % 150\% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation, and matches expert manual alignment. We further show that distributions curated with a lightweight proxy policy transfer to VLA fine-tuning, and that MetaGenSim can exploit partial alignment through atomic skill stitching and object-receptacle composition when exact sim-and-real task alignment is unavailable.
Project website: https://meta-gensim.github.io/
2026-10-15.introduction:
While recent large-scale real-robot datasets have advanced generalist policies [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , relying exclusively on real data remains expensive, labor-intensive, and safety-constrained. Generative simulation offers a scalable alternative data source by procedurally synthesizing scene layouts, assets, and tasks [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . We refer to the variables controlling these environments, such as camera poses, object arrangements, visual appearance, and task goals, as data generation parameters .

Given data generation parameters, a generative simulator can instantiate environments and generate large numbers of demonstrations with minimal human intervention [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . However, the utility of simulation data remains limited by the sim-to-real gap. Domain randomization and system identification can mitigate this mismatch, but often require substantial human effort and cannot eliminate residual gaps [ 14 ] . A promising alternative is sim-and-real co-training , where real demonstrations anchor learning to the deployment domain while simulation provides scale and diversity [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . Co-training can outperform training on real data alone [ 17 , 16 , 20 ] , but not all generated data is useful: misaligned camera poses, object layouts, visual factors, or task goals can provide little benefit, and exact alignment may be impossible when the simulator lacks the target setting. This raises a central question: Among the vast space of possible simulation environments, which data should be generated to maximize the performance of a sim-and-real co-trained policy?

Current simulation data-generation strategies largely rely on manual heuristics [ 21 , 22 ] or uniform randomization [ 23 , 24 ] . Overly broad training distributions can degrade policy learning when many samples are irrelevant to the target task [ 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] . Prior work suggests that task-aware alignment helps [ 16 ] , but manually tuning high-dimensional generation parameters is laborious, requires expert knowledge, and can be misleading when exact alignment is impossible.

In this work, we formulate Active Generative Simulation : determining a distribution over simulation parameters such that co-training on the resulting synthetic data maximizes target-task performance. To efficiently tackle this problem, we propose MetaGenSim , a meta-learning framework that uses a sparse probing dataset to train an auxiliary rater network , which assigns utility scores to simulation samples based on their contribution to real-world validation performance, automatically guiding the active generation of a targeted synthetic dataset.
In summary, our core contributions are:

We formulate Active Generative Simulation , shifting simulation data generation from fixed distribution to controllable and targeted synthesis.

We introduce MetaGenSim , a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified parameter space, without manual parameter alignment.

We show that MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and offline retrieval, achieving a 150 % 150\% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation while matching the performance of manual expert alignment.

We demonstrate scalability and generalization of MetaGenSim : proxy-curated datasets transfer to fine-tuning π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and MetaGenSim can exploit partially aligned data when exact task alignment is unavailable.

2. We introduce MetaGenSim , a meta-learning framework that trains an auxiliary rater network via meta-gradients to discover high-utility data-generation distributions within a user-specified parameter space, without manual parameter alignment.

3. We show that MetaGenSim outperforms uniform generation and offline retrieval, achieving a 150 % 150\% relative improvement in real-world full-task success over uniform generation while matching the performance of manual expert alignment.

4. We demonstrate scalability and generalization of MetaGenSim : proxy-curated datasets transfer to fine-tuning π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and MetaGenSim can exploit partially aligned data when exact task alignment is unavailable.

# 2 Related Works

Generative simulation. Recent progress in generative modeling [ 30 , 31 ] , motion synthesis [ 9 , 32 , 33 ] , and procedural environment generation [ 4 , 5 ] has enabled automated simulation pipelines that scale synthetic robot data [ 34 , 7 , 35 , 23 , 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 ] . These systems can generate assets, tasks, scenes, and demonstrations with limited human intervention. However, most synthesize feasible data passively without optimizing which specific samples best improve a downstream policy. In contrast, MetaGenSim leverages a small set of target-task data to actively guide simulation data generation toward high-utility parameter regions.

Sim-and-real alignment and policy co-training. To leverage simulation data for real-robot deployment, policies must overcome the sim-to-real gap [ 24 , 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 , 16 , 23 , 17 , 18 ] . Domain randomization perturbs visual and physical properties to encourage robustness [ 24 , 41 , 42 ] , while system identification tunes simulator parameters to match real-world dynamics or appearance [ 46 , 43 , 45 ] . These approaches assume there exist high-fidelity alignments, but tighter matching does not necessarily translate to better policy learning when residual gaps remain [ 44 ] . Recent sim-and-real co-training methods instead mix simulated and real demonstrations, showing strong empirical gains [ 16 , 23 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . MetaGenSim builds on this co-training paradigm but treats the generative simulator as a controllable distribution, actively optimizing data synthesis rather than manually tuning the simulator to match the real world.

Data attribution and retrieval in robotics. Recent work shows that heterogeneous robot datasets can cause negative transfer on specific tasks [ 26 , 28 , 25 , 29 , 47 , 48 , 49 ] . Retrieval and attribution methods address this by selecting useful samples from existing datasets using embedding similarity [ 29 , 50 , 47 , 49 ] , rollout outcomes [ 26 ] , or validation loss [ 25 ] . However, these methods are fundamentally limited by the coverage of the static prior dataset and cannot synthesize new target-relevant data. MetaGenSim is complementary: it uses utility estimation to generate new simulation data tailored to the target task.

2026-10-15.title: Spacecraft Pose Tracking via Kinematic Prediction and Selective Event Correction
2026-10-15.authors: Yonglong Zhang , Guanning Yao , Shuo Zhang , Yifan Yang , Yang Liu† , Zongwu Xie
2026-10-15.abstract: In initialized spacecraft tracking, a short-horizon motion prediction remains available as event support changes. Observation-Aligned Event Innovation (OA-EI) uses events to correct selected components of this prediction. A constant-body-twist model propagates the complete pose; the event encoder proposes rotational and normalized image-plane translation corrections, retaining propagated axial depth. Candidate magnitudes come from a bounded Scale Gate and a deterministic activity factor, with empty windows returning the prediction unchanged. Evaluation uses four FRESH physical-event trajectories, twenty rollout starts, and three training seeds. Each rollout starts from two reference poses and then uses self-fed estimates. At 7.7 seconds, rotation and translation errors fall from 41.63 ∘ 41.63^{\circ} /57.28 mm for prediction alone to 15.73 ∘ 15.73^{\circ} /22.41 mm for OA-EI, reductions of 62.2% and 60.9%. Failure rates fall from 20.0% to 1.67%. Matched ablations favor the rotation–bearing interface for overall pose accuracy; combining scaling with activity support gives the lowest errors at every tested event-retention level. On Jetson Orin Nano, the measured in-memory update takes 44.56 milliseconds at the median and 58.77 milliseconds at P95.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Event cameras record brightness changes asynchronously, offering fine temporal sampling and a wide dynamic range [ 1 ] . For spacecraft tracking, the projected structure changes with motion and illumination, and event support varies in both amount and spatial coverage. Relative navigation, inspection, and robotic servicing require continuous estimates of target orientation and translation through these changes. Sparse observations can coincide with motion that is still predictable over a short interval.

Most spacecraft perception pipelines recover pose from current image evidence. SPEED and SPEED+ benchmark image-based estimation [ 2 , 3 ] ; SPADES and FRESH extend evaluation to synthetic and physical event recordings [ 4 , 5 ] . Event-based approaches recover geometric keypoints for pose estimation, then use smoothing or optimization to improve temporal consistency [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Initialized tracking also has recent pose history. A short-horizon motion model can predict the complete next state before the current event window is used for correction.

With that prediction available, the event branch must decide which components to correct and how much correction to inject. Full-pose re-estimation includes components already represented by the motion model; a selective update leaves the remaining components to the prediction. The magnitude matters beyond the current timestamp. An inaccurate correction enters the pose history used for later predictions, coupling state selection with update scaling throughout the rollout.

Observation-Aligned Event Innovation (OA-EI) applies this selective update to a complete six-degree-of-freedom prior from constant-body-twist propagation. The event branch predicts rotational and normalized image-plane translation candidates relative to the prior, while axial depth stays with propagation. Translation is thus split into bearing correction and depth prediction. Two scale coefficients, learned from error-minimizing scales along frozen candidates, set the correction magnitudes. Event count and spatial activity supply a deterministic support factor. The corrected pose becomes part of the next prediction history; with an empty window, the current prior is returned exactly. Neither CAD geometry nor keypoints are required by the event branch.

Prediction alone, full candidate injection, and OA-EI are evaluated under a common recursive protocol. Matched state-update and injection ablations examine state selection and correction scaling separately from this main comparison.

The contributions are:

The event-to-pose interface corrects rotation and bearing while retaining axial depth from the complete kinematic prediction.

Candidate-scale supervision is combined with event-activity support to bound injection. Empty event windows give an exact prediction fallback.

Multi-start self-fed evaluation on physical event recordings shows reduced recursive pose errors and improved accuracy under severe event sparsification. Matched ablations examine state selection and injection scaling.

1. The event-to-pose interface corrects rotation and bearing while retaining axial depth from the complete kinematic prediction.

2. Candidate-scale supervision is combined with event-activity support to bound injection. Empty event windows give an exact prediction fallback.

3. Multi-start self-fed evaluation on physical event recordings shows reduced recursive pose errors and improved accuracy under severe event sparsification. Matched ablations examine state selection and injection scaling.

# II Related Work

## II-A Spacecraft Pose Sensing

Direct pose regression and image keypoints followed by perspective- n n -point (PnP) geometry are the main routes to monocular spacecraft pose estimation [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Both recover the complete pose from an image, but keypoint pipelines retain an explicit link to known object geometry rather than learning the whole image-to-pose mapping. SPEED and SPEED+ benchmark these approaches in synthetic and laboratory domains [ 2 , 3 ] .

For event-based estimation, SPADES provides synthetic sequences [ 4 ] , and FRESH supplies aligned physical event and RGB recordings under harsh illumination [ 5 ] . FRESH’s event-only baseline forms keypoint measurements for PnP; its full fusion method combines event and RGB evidence. Compact event-frame keypoint networks have also been coupled with neuromorphic hardware by Rathinam et al. [ 6 ] . Temporal refinement takes different forms: PASAN and IRIS use polarity-aware temporal features with kinematic smoothing [ 7 ] , and the cascaded method in [ 8 ] adds geometric pose optimization and a motion-constrained backend. OA-EI starts its event update from the historical pose prediction, treating that prediction as the state to refine.

## II-B Event-Based Motion Processing

Grid representations allow convolutional networks to process asynchronous events [ 12 ] . Other motion-processing approaches work through event alignment, as in contrast maximization [ 13 ] , or image displacement, as in motion-compensated optical flow [ 14 ] . Geometric odometry [ 15 , 16 ] and learned odometry [ 17 ] recover camera motion from event streams. Event6D instead tracks novel objects in six degrees of freedom using events and depth [ 18 ] . For target-relative correction, OA-EI uses polarity-separated voxels and normalized image-plane translation, with axial depth supplied by the pose predictor.

## II-C Prediction and Observation Updates

Adaptive unscented Kalman filters for spacecraft tracking fuse neural pose measurements with motion predictions and adjust noise models or measurement uncertainty [ 19 , 20 ] . KalmanNet introduces recurrent learning into the filter when dynamics are partially known [ 21 ] ; latent Kalman filtering performs spacecraft pose prediction and learned observation fusion in feature space [ 22 ] . These estimators combine prediction and observation to address measurement noise and model mismatch. OA-EI places its learned correction in a selected pose subspace: rotational and bearing-space candidates have separate scale coefficients, and event activity supplies an additional support factor.

2026-10-15.title: Paraphrase Consensus Is Not Self-Consistency: Instruction Reliance and Robustness in VLA Policies
2026-10-15.authors: Hanlong Li , Sihan Tan , Takeshi Ashizawa , Benjamin Yen , Kazuhiro Nakadai
2026-10-15.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies fine-tuned on LIBERO are trained and evaluated on the same ten instruction strings, and rewording the instruction changes base OpenVLA’s success by − 38.0 -38.0 points. Test-time prompt ensembling, which improves language models, does not recover this loss in any setting we ran. Paraphrase consensus (the medoid action over K K paraphrases) costs base OpenVLA 16.8 16.8 points when the training instruction is a member. Without it, the medoid of the paraphrases scores − 32.4 -32.4 points relative to the training instruction, and confidence-based selection scores − 28.0 -28.0 . The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase improves on greedy decoding but stays − 27.6 -27.6 points below the training instruction, consistent with aggregation reducing variance without removing the bias the paraphrases share. A wrong-instruction probe measures how much of a policy’s success depends on the instruction. Across three policies and four suites, paraphrases cost a policy only where this share is high, and the stronger policies lose a much smaller fraction of it than base OpenVLA. LoRA post-training on paraphrased instructions reduces the one-paraphrase effect to + 2.0 +2.0 points, against − 32.0 -32.0 for a matched control, reproduces across two seeds and on OpenVLA-OFT, transfers to withheld phrasings, and leaves the policy’s reliance on the instruction unchanged.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies map a camera image and a natural-language instruction to robot actions ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ) . Many are language models fine-tuned to emit actions. OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , for example, is a 7B Llama-2 model that outputs actions as vocabulary tokens. On LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , the standard simulation benchmark for these policies, each released checkpoint is fine-tuned on exactly ten instructions, one fixed string per task, and evaluated on the same ten strings, character for character ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , which in NLP terms is an extreme case of single-template instruction tuning. Users will not phrase a request exactly as the training data did, and language models are sensitive to how a prompt is worded ( Sclar et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Sun et al., 2024 ; Mizrahi et al., 2024 ) , so a benchmark score says little about what happens when the instruction is reworded. We ask how much rewording costs such a policy, and whether that loss can be recovered at test time, without retraining, the way prompt ensembling and self-consistency recover accuracy for language models.

The natural test-time remedy comes from language models. Self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) samples several answers and keeps the majority, and prompt ensembling ( Jiang et al., 2020 ) aggregates answers over rewordings of a query. The VLA analogue is paraphrase consensus : rephrase the instruction K K ways, query the policy once per phrasing, and execute the medoid, the action closest to all the others, a continuous majority vote that always returns one of the policy’s own actions. It needs no training or verifier, and test-time selection over sampled actions already helps VLAs ( Kwok et al., 2025 ; Jang et al., 2026 ) . Prompt ensembling, however, works for language models pre-trained on many phrasings, where rewordings are comparably good prompts. A VLA fine-tuned on one string per task has seen only one good prompt, and every paraphrase may be a worse one. We implement paraphrase consensus (LCC, Language-Consensus Control) with paired, per-step logging and run it on OpenVLA-OFT (LIBERO-Spatial with and without a distractor object, and Goal) and base OpenVLA (Spatial and Long). For these two policies and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on all four suites, we also measure how much of each policy’s success needs the instruction at all. We find that unweighted consensus does not help. The per-step logs trace the failure to the members themselves, which points to a fix at training time.

Test-time consensus does not recover what a paraphrase costs. One paraphrase, held for the episode, changes base OpenVLA’s success by − 38.0 -38.0 points. Consensus with the training instruction among the members costs base OpenVLA 16.8 16.8 points and OFT 4.0 4.0 on Goal; without it, neither the medoid of the paraphrases nor the paraphrase the policy is most confident in comes close to the training instruction ( − 32.4 -32.4 , − 28.0 -28.0 ). The reason is that paraphrases are not exchangeable. Self-consistency aggregates K K draws from one conditional, whereas K K paraphrases are K K conditionals, only one of which the policy was fit to. The same medoid over samples of one paraphrase does reduce variance, beating greedy decoding by + 10.4 +10.4 , yet stays − 27.6 -27.6 below the training instruction (§ 4.3 ).

A paraphrase costs a policy only where its success needs the instruction. A wrong-instruction probe, a partial-input baseline ( Poliak et al., 2018 ; Gururangan et al., 2018 ; Kaushik and Lipton, 2018 ; Thomason et al., 2019 ) , gives another task’s instruction in the same scene. Base OpenVLA needs the instruction for nearly all of its success on every suite. OpenVLA-OFT and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Black et al., 2025a ) pay a paraphrase cost only on LIBERO-Goal, where all of their success needs the instruction, and lose a far smaller fraction of it than base OpenVLA does (§ 4.4 ). This qualifies LIBERO-Plus’s conclusion that fine-tuned VLAs “degenerate into vision-action models” ( Fei et al., 2026 ) .

The fix is at training time. LoRA post-training on the same demonstrations with paraphrased instructions moves the one-paraphrase effect from − 38.0 -38.0 to + 2.0 +2.0 , while a matched control trained on the original instructions stays at − 32.0 -32.0 . The result holds for a second seed, transfers to phrasings withheld from training, carries to OpenVLA-OFT on Goal, and leaves the policy reading its instruction. It costs about an hour of training once, whereas consensus queries four instructions at every step (§ 5 ).

Contributions. (i) A paired, per-timestep measurement of paraphrase consensus on two policies in five settings, with the mechanism read from the logs and tested by an exchangeable-sampling control and a confidence-weighted selector. (ii) An instruction-reliance probe on all LIBERO suites, a partial-input baseline for embodied models, and the finding that paraphrase cost appears only where reliance is high, across twelve policy–suite pairs from three policies. (iii) The established remedy, training on paraphrases ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) , measured with three controls we did not find reported for prior remedies ( Hou and Zhao, 2026 ; Yin and Zhang, 2026 ) : a matched training control, transfer to withheld phrasings and types, and a grounding check.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

VLAs and their language robustness. Large pretrained policies map images and language to actions ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ) . OpenVLA-OFT adds parallel decoding, a continuous action head and chunking ( Kim et al., 2025 ) . LIBERO’s perturbation suites reach opposite conclusions on language: LIBERO-Plus finds fine-tuned VLAs largely ignore the instruction ( Fei et al., 2026 ) , LIBERO-PRO reports collapse under minimal rewording ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and LIBERO-Para quantifies the collapse at 22 22 – 52 52 points under paraphrase across seven VLAs, attributed to surface-level matching rather than semantic grounding ( Kim et al., 2026 ) . Xing et al. (2025) attribute language-ignoring to shortcut learning, and LangGap shows π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} largely ignores instructions when one task per layout lets it ( Hou and Zhao, 2026 ) . LIBERO-Para is built on LIBERO-Goal, where its paraphrases cost OFT about 33 33 points. Ours cost it − 10.4 -10.4 there and base OpenVLA − 36.8 -36.8 . Our generator preserves every object reference, and LIBERO-Para attributes most of its drop to object-level lexical variation. What these diagnostics do not ask is whether test-time aggregation recovers the loss, or how the penalty relates to how much of a score needs the instruction at all (§ 4.4 ).

Perturbation ensembles and failure detection. Ensemble disagreement ( Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017 ; Ovadia et al., 2019 ; Menda et al., 2019 ; Hoque et al., 2021 ; Römer et al., 2025 ; Lee and Har, 2026 ; Shanmugam et al., 2021 ) and runtime monitors ( Agia et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Seligmann et al., 2026 ; Karli et al., 2025 ) are compared with paraphrase on identical trajectories in App. F and E .

Prompt sensitivity, self-consistency and test-time scaling. LLMs are sensitive to how a prompt is worded: formatting ( Sclar et al., 2024 ) , example order ( Lu et al., 2022 ) and paraphrased instructions ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Mizrahi et al., 2024 ) move accuracy by many points. Prompt ensembling ( Jiang et al., 2020 ) , self-consistency ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , semantic entropy ( Kuhn et al., 2023 ; Farquhar et al., 2024 ) and paraphrase-based uncertainty ( Gao et al., 2024 ; Khan and Fu, 2024 ) aggregate over samples or prompts in discrete output spaces. The medoid is minimum-Bayes-risk selection, of which self-consistency is a special case ( Bertsch et al., 2023 ) , and MBR over several prompts’ outputs helps text generation ( Heineman et al., 2024 ) . For VLAs, RoboMonkey scores sampled actions with a verifier ( Kwok et al., 2025 ) and MG-Select scores against a condition-masked reference ( Jang et al., 2026 ) , and both sample the action axis from one prompt. Paraphrase consensus samples the instruction axis. Aggregators built for prompts of unequal quality weight members by held-out accuracy ( Jiang et al., 2020 ; Arora et al., 2023 ) or zero-shot scores ( Allingham et al., 2023 ) , and lower-perplexity prompts work better ( Gonen et al., 2023 ) . With one member known to be the training instruction, that weighting degenerates to selecting it, which is the canonical controller. § 4.3 shows the difference between the two axes is decisive.

Remedies. Training on more phrasings is an established remedy. DIAL relabels demonstrations with VLM-generated instructions to broaden what a policy can follow ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) , SPRINT relabels for pre-training ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and RT-1 trained on diverse phrasings ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) . LangGap closes its language gap with targeted training-time augmentation ( Hou and Zhao, 2026 ) , and GSR argues the brittleness is architectural and retrains an action expert on separately extracted task semantics ( Yin and Zhang, 2026 ) . In NLP, multi-template instruction tuning ( Wei et al., 2022 ; Sanh et al., 2022 ) , consistency training under back-translation paraphrases ( Xie et al., 2020 ) , and prompt- and paraphrase-consistency objectives ( Zhou et al., 2022 ; Elazar et al., 2021 ; Sun et al., 2024 ) are the precedents for training on rewordings, and our paraphrase types are CheckList-style invariance tests ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ) for an embodied model. § 5 adds three measurements we did not find in these works: a matched training control that separates the phrasings from the extra steps, transfer to withheld phrasings, and a check that the remedy does not work by ignoring the instruction.

2026-10-15.title: $S^3$-Nav: Structured Spatial-Semantic Decision Making for Language-Guided Robot Navigation
2026-10-15.authors: Chaemin Lee , Hae Min Cho
2026-10-15.abstract:
This paper presents S 3 -Nav, a structured spatial-semantic decision-making framework for language-guided robot navigation under partial observability.
Rather than assuming a complete environment representation in advance, S 3 -Nav incrementally constructs persistent spatial-semantic state while exposing only a capacity-controlled, task-conditioned view to the high-level policy.
This separation decouples what the robot must retain from what the policy needs to inspect, allowing decision complexity to be controlled without discarding grounded evidence required for subsequent reasoning and validation.
High-level navigation outputs remain provisional and are independently grounded and validated against persistent semantic evidence and current geometric observations before physical execution or task termination.
Evaluations across multiple environments and object- and relation-goal tasks demonstrate that separating persistent state, decision-facing evidence, and execution authority improves closed-loop navigation reliability while reducing policy reasoning cost.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Autonomous mobile robots operating under partial observability must repeatedly make decisions from incomplete observations while retaining task-relevant environmental evidence accumulated over time.
A central question is therefore how persistent decision state, decision-facing evidence, and execution authority should be organized within a closed-loop decision process.
Language-guided mobile-robot navigation requires a robot to connect natural-language goals with spatial evidence accumulated over an extended trajectory.
A mobile robot may need to explore multiple regions before the requested target becomes observable, while relational instructions such as “find a chair next to a plant” require more than detecting the target category.
The robot must preserve observations, associate them with persistent object identities, and verify the requested relation before accepting a terminal state [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
As illustrated in Fig. 1 , navigation therefore requires both task-relevant spatial-semantic memory and a mechanism for connecting accumulated evidence to grounded decisions and stopping conditions.

Existing approaches separately address semantic reasoning, persistent spatial-semantic memory, and hierarchical control [ 5 , 2 , 6 ] .
However, combining these capabilities in closed-loop navigation introduces three distinct design challenges.
First, the robot may need to preserve observations for future grounding and relational verification even when much of that retained evidence is irrelevant to the current high-level decision.
Directly exposing all accumulated evidence to the policy increases the amount of information that must be inspected at every decision, whereas discarding persistent evidence solely to simplify policy reasoning can remove information required later in the episode.
Second, evidence sufficient to select or approach a plausible target is not necessarily sufficient to establish task completion.
A policy may select a target from remembered semantic evidence even when the requested relation has not yet been confirmed or when fresh target-associated geometry is unavailable for terminal validation.
Third, language-guided navigation should not assume that a complete map or spatial-semantic representation of the environment is available in advance.
Under partial observability, the robot must incrementally construct its spatial-semantic state from online observations while deciding where to explore and reasoning over previously accumulated evidence.
These challenges motivate a closed-loop decision formulation that incrementally constructs persistent spatial-semantic state while separating state retention, decision-facing evidence, and execution authority into distinct but interacting roles.

We propose S 3 -Nav, a structured spatial-semantic decision-making framework that addresses these challenges by incrementally constructing persistent spatial-semantic state, decoupling state retention from the task-conditioned evidence exposed to the high-level policy, and retaining independent authority over grounded execution and termination.
A capacity-controlled decision-facing view is constructed from the persistent spatial-semantic state while preserving grounded references to the underlying records, allowing the amount of structured evidence presented for policy-level reasoning to be controlled without pruning information required for later grounding or validation.
The resulting high-level outputs remain provisional and are resolved by a deterministic validation and execution layer against persistent semantic evidence and current geometric measurements before physical execution or terminal acceptance.
An overview of S 3 -Nav is provided in Fig. 2 .

The main contributions of this work are:

A structured spatial-semantic decision-making formulation that incrementally builds persistent state while decoupling retained evidence from the task-conditioned evidence exposed to the high-level policy, enabling decision complexity to be controlled without pruning the underlying grounded state.

A grounded decision-to-execution mechanism in which high-level navigation intents remain provisional, while deterministic execution retains authority over semantic, relational, geometric, and terminal validity using persistent and current evidence.

A cross-environment evaluation that systematically examines how decision policy, record capacity, persistent memory, localization quality, and reasoning cost affect closed-loop navigation.

1. A structured spatial-semantic decision-making formulation that incrementally builds persistent state while decoupling retained evidence from the task-conditioned evidence exposed to the high-level policy, enabling decision complexity to be controlled without pruning the underlying grounded state.

2. A grounded decision-to-execution mechanism in which high-level navigation intents remain provisional, while deterministic execution retains authority over semantic, relational, geometric, and terminal validity using persistent and current evidence.

3. A cross-environment evaluation that systematically examines how decision policy, record capacity, persistent memory, localization quality, and reasoning cost affect closed-loop navigation.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Spatial-Semantic Mapping and Memory

Persistent geometric and semantic representations are fundamental to long-horizon robot navigation because relevant environmental evidence often extends beyond the current observation.
Semantic mapping systems such as SemanticFusion and object-centric representations such as ConceptGraphs illustrate how persistent maps can be enriched with semantic labels, object identities, and spatial relationships [ 7 , 2 ] .
More broadly, SLAM, semantic mapping, and object-memory approaches have progressively improved what environmental information a robot can retain over time [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] .
These methods primarily address what information should be represented and retained, but do not necessarily distinguish the capacity of the persistent representation from the amount of evidence exposed to the high-level policy at each decision step.
S 3 -Nav treats these as separate system variables: the persistent state remains available for grounding and verification, while the decision-facing evidence view is independently capacity controlled.

## II-B Object-Goal and Language-Guided Navigation

Object-goal and language-guided navigation require robots to search beyond the current field of view and translate semantic goals into grounded navigation decisions.
Approaches such as LM-Nav and SG-Nav demonstrate how language-model reasoning can guide target selection and high-level navigation, alongside broader work on exploration, semantic search, vision-and-language navigation, and pretrained vision–language models [ 13 , 4 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 6 , 20 , 21 ] .
These advances improve where the robot should search or move, but relational goals introduce an additional requirement because evidence needed to justify a decision may have been accumulated across different observations.
A decision policy must therefore reason from task-relevant evidence without losing the persistent information needed to resolve targets, verify relations, and determine whether the task is actually complete.
S 3 -Nav instead considers how accumulated spatial-semantic state should be converted into a bounded, task-conditioned decision view without discarding the underlying evidence required later in the episode.
This separates the information used for high-level selection from the persistent evidence retained for grounding, relational verification, and terminal validation.

## II-C Grounded Language-Model Reasoning

Grounded language-model control commonly separates high-level semantic reasoning from feasibility checking and physical execution.
Systems such as SayCan and Inner Monologue illustrate this separation by combining language-based reasoning with independent mechanisms for feasibility assessment or interaction with the environment [ 22 , 23 ] .
A similar hierarchy appears in language-guided navigation, where pretrained models select high-level actions and lower-level modules execute them [ 13 , 6 , 19 ] .
This conventional planner–controller boundary determines how a selected high-level action is executed, but does not by itself distinguish what the system persistently retains from what evidence the policy should inspect at each decision step.
Nor does high-level target selection alone establish whether the accumulated semantic and current geometric evidence are sufficient to authorize terminal execution.
S 3 -Nav therefore separates the persistent spatial-semantic state from the evidence presented to the high-level policy, in addition to separating policy output from physical execution.
The policy produces provisional grounded intents from a task-conditioned evidence view, while deterministic execution resolves those intents against the persistent state and retains authority over semantic, relational, geometric, and terminal validity.

2026-10-15.title: From Failures to Learnable Worlds: Policy-Conditioned Environment Generation for Navigation Agents
2026-10-15.authors: Yue Zhang , Han Lin , Zun Wang , Yidong Huang , Zaid Khan , Mohit Bansal
2026-10-15.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-15.abstract:
Simulated environments enable scalable training data generation for embodied agents, but more data does not necessarily provide what a particular agent needs to learn. Existing environment-generation pipelines largely optimize generic properties such as realism, diversity, or task coverage, while different pretrained policies can fail for different environmental reasons, with some struggling when targets are hard to see and others when navigation requires long blind paths or multiple room transitions.
We therefore introduce Wedge , a framework for weakness-guided navigation learning in which the failure modes of a pretrained agent guide the generation of training environments at each adaptation round.
Rather than assuming a predefined set of tasks or skills to improve, Wedge derives its generation targets from the policy’s own success and failure patterns within the same task.
Given a pretrained policy, Wedge uses an LLM to propose executable weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, automatically validates them on the diagnostic set, and selects the strongest validated weakness based on its success-rate gap.
The validated weaknesses are then mapped to the environmental factors that control them, such as target placement, start configurations, and scene layouts. Wedge varies these factors to construct environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles, producing targeted training experience for adaptation.
Across three navigation agents with different adaptation mechanisms, we find
that policies exhibit distinct weakness profiles and benefit from different
training environments.
Weakness-conditioned adaptation consistently outperforms matched random and
hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR, while the resulting gains for Uni-NaVid
and Gemini also extend to HM3D after ProcTHOR adaptation.
Iterative re-diagnosis further shows that dominant weaknesses can persist or
shift as the policy improves, providing updated guidance for subsequent
environment construction.
Together, these results show that policy failures are not only diagnostic
signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that
target a policy’s current weaknesses 1 1 1 Website: https://zhangyuejoslin.github.io/WEDGE Code: https://github.com/zhangyuejoslin/WEDGE .
2026-10-15.introduction:
Simulated environments have become an important source of scalable training data for embodied agents ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Seed, 2025 ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Deitke et al., 2022 ; Chang et al., 2017 ; Ramakrishnan et al., 2021b ) , offering controllable worlds, inexpensive interaction, and access to situations that are difficult to collect in the real world. Accordingly, recent environment-generation pipelines have progressed from improving realism and diversity ( Yang et al., 2024b ; Pan and Liu, 2026 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2024 ) to task-conditioned generation, where environments are constructed to support specific embodied tasks ( Xia et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Zala et al., 2024 ) . However, these approaches primarily condition generation on predefined properties of the environment or user-specified embodied tasks (e.g., “Find the mug.”), with limited consideration of what the current policy has already mastered and where it still struggles.
As a result, the same training environment may be useful for one policy but redundant or overly difficult for another. This raises a central question: how can we generate environments that target what a particular agent has not yet mastered?

This distinction is particularly important when continuing to train a pretrained embodied agent, whose capabilities may already vary substantially across environmental conditions.
The same training environment may therefore be redundant for an agent that has already mastered the relevant behavior, informative for another that still struggles with it, or too difficult to provide a useful learning signal. As illustrated in Fig. 1 (top), two agents solving the same navigation task can fail for very different reasons: one may struggle when navigation requires traversing multiple rooms, while another may fail primarily when the target is poorly visible.
Generating environments that are simply more realistic, diverse, or difficult does not necessarily address either weakness. Task-conditioned generation provides a stronger form of control by constructing environments around the requirements of a given task, but it does not distinguish why different policies fail within that task. As a result, environments generated for the same task may still target conditions that one policy has already mastered while overlooking those that another policy struggles with. We therefore argue that training environments for continued learning should be generated relative to the current policy.

We introduce Wedge ( W eakness-guided E nvironment D esign, G eneration, and E valuation), a framework for procedural
environment generation that closes the loop between policy diagnosis,
environment construction, and policy adaptation for object navigation tasks.
Given a pretrained navigation policy, we first contrast its successful and failed episodes to identify environmental factors that systematically characterize where the policy struggles. An LLM instantiates these hypotheses as programmatic weakness features, such as target_visibility , blind_path_ratio , and room_hops , which can be computed over individual environments and directly connected to controllable simulator factors ( Fig. 1 (a)). We evaluate each proposed feature on the full diagnostic set and retain only those that provide sufficiently broad, non-redundant, predictive, and complementary signals of policy failure. These validated weaknesses then serve as actionable specifications for generation, determining which environmental factors should be varied and which failure-associated regimes should be targeted ( Fig. 1 (b)).
A key aspect of Wedge is that its generation targets are derived from the current policy’s own failure patterns rather than specified in advance. By identifying the environmental conditions associated with failures within the same task, Wedge determines which aspects of the environment should be modified and which regimes should be targeted during generation.
We then roll out the current policy in each candidate environment and select those that fall within the diagnosed weak regime while remaining challenging but solvable. The selected environments are then used to adapt the policy with its original learning mechanism.
We study this framework in 3D indoor navigation, where agents must continuously perceive, navigate, and act in complex environments over long horizons. We further show that weakness-targeted adaptation in ProcTHOR ( Deitke et al., 2022 ) transfers to HM3D ( Ramakrishnan et al., 2021a ) , demonstrating generalization beyond the simulator used for generation.

We evaluate Wedge across three navigation agents with different model architectures and adaptation mechanisms: a ProcTHOR ( Deitke et al., 2022 ) -trained DD-PPO policy ( Zeng et al., 2024 ) , an HM3D ( Ramakrishnan et al., 2021a ) -trained Uni-NaVid policy ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and a general-purpose VLM agent (Gemini-3.8-flash ( Google DeepMind, 2026 ) ).
Despite solving the same navigation task, the agents exhibit different weakness profiles, confirming that useful training environments depend on the current policy rather than the task alone.
Across all three agents, weakness-conditioned adaptation consistently outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR.
For Uni-NaVid and Gemini, the gains also extend to HM3D after ProcTHOR adaptation, showing that the resulting improvements are not confined to the environment used for training.
Iterative re-diagnosis shows that the dominant weakness may persist or shift after adaptation, and using the updated diagnosis to guide a second round of environment generation yields further performance gains. Our additional analysis shows that gains are concentrated in weakness-related cases and that rollout calibration focuses training on environments within the policy’s learning range.
Together, these results show that policy failures provide not only diagnostic signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that target the policy’s remaining weaknesses.

# 2 Related Work

Environment Design for Embodied AI. Environment design for embodied AI increasingly combines scalable scene construction with controllable, simulation-ready generation ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . Procedural generation and curated synthetic scenes expand environmental diversity and realism ( Deitke et al., 2022 ; Khanna et al., 2024 ; Raistrick et al., 2024 ; Paschalidou et al., 2021 ; Tang et al., 2024 ) , while language-guided and task-conditioned pipelines automate scene composition and robotic training environments ( Feng et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Wang et al., 2023a ; Fu et al., 2024 ) . Physical and interactive constraints further improve scene usability ( Yang et al., 2024a ) , and recent agentic pipelines refine generated environments through visual critique, physical validation, and semantic feedback ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2026 ) .
Simulation provides scalable training experience for embodied navigation across a broad range of tasks ( Savva et al., 2019 ; Shen et al., 2021 ; Wijmans et al., 2019 ; Huang et al., 2026b ; Deitke et al., 2022 ; Khanna et al., 2024 ) . Prior work scales this experience through procedurally generated or high-fidelity environments, augmented task configurations and trajectories, synthetic demonstrations, and curriculum-based sampling ( Maksymets et al., 2021 ; Kotar et al., 2023 ; Ehsani et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2021 ; Yadav et al., 2022 ; Morad et al., 2021 ) . Other efforts improve robustness and transfer through controlled perturbations, domain adaptation, target-conditioned simulation, and synthetic instruction–trajectory data ( Chattopadhyay et al., 2021 ; Deitke et al., 2020 ; Zhu et al., 2019 ; Truong et al., 2021 ; Deitke et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024b ; Xu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023b ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . These works improve the scalability and controllability of training environments, while our focus is to determine what environments to construct based on the diagnosed weaknesses of a particular pretrained policy.

Failure-Driven Learning and Adaptive Data Generation. Adaptive curricula and unsupervised environment design use learner feedback to prioritize, generate, and edit training environments ( Wang et al., 2020 ; Dennis et al., 2020 ; Jiang et al., 2021 ; Parker-Holder et al., 2022 ; Chung et al., 2024 ) .
Recent approaches extend this principle through LLM-based environment configuration and code generation ( Zala et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2024 ; Faldor et al., 2025 ) , performance-adaptive navigation curricula ( Kang et al., 2026 ) , and trajectory-informed scene editing ( Yeo et al., 2026 ) .
Related work targets grounding errors through counterfactual scene edits ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) or synthesizes and validates environment wrappers from behavioral diagnoses ( Huang et al., 2026a ) .
Our approach extends adaptive environment generation from predefined task-level adaptation to policy-specific failure diagnosis in 3D indoor navigation: rather than assuming known skills or weakness categories, Wedge identifies measurable environmental conditions associated with failures within the same task and validates them as policy-specific weaknesses.
These diagnosed weaknesses determine which environmental factors to modify and which regimes to target during 3D environment construction.
Policy rollouts then calibrate the generated candidates, retaining environments that expose the diagnosed weakness while remaining learnable for the current policy.
