2026-10-15.title: A VR Training System for Robot-Assisted Vascular Intervention with Dual-Mode Control and Model-Based Interaction Response
2026-10-15.authors: Yining Shang , Shuxiang Guo , Sheng Cao , Pengcheng Li , Bin Wang , Mingchao Ding
2026-10-15.abstract: Virtual reality training for robot-assisted vascular intervention requires accurate robotic control and effective feedback on guidewire–vessel interactions. This paper presents a VR training system combining asynchronous dual-mode command mapping with sensorless interaction estimation. The system supports velocity-controlled navigation and position-driven incremental manipulation. Guidewire deformation and a Hunt–Crossley-type contact response are combined and temporally filtered to estimate interaction intensity, while trajectory-based visualization supports post-procedure review. Tests confirmed distinct command-dispatch patterns across three velocity gears and the position mode. During hybrid-scene navigation, the estimated response remained low during straight insertion and increased as the guidewire bent within the vascular model. Trajectory analysis yielded a model-derived cumulative trauma work (CTW) value of 15.166 in normalized units and localized regions of elevated interaction. In a preliminary study with 15 novices, physical-phantom task success increased from 53.3% to 93.3% after VR training, while mean completion time decreased from 132.4 s to 96.7 s. These results demonstrate the system’s dual-mode operation, deformation-sensitive feedback, and potential to improve subsequent physical-phantom task performance.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Vascular interventional surgery (VIS) enables
minimally invasive treatment of cardiovascular and cerebrovascular
diseases. Robot-assisted VIS (RA-VIS) can improve manipulation
precision and reduce occupational radiation exposure [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . However, navigating flexible guidewires through
tortuous vessels remains demanding because operators must coordinate
instrument motion while interpreting guidewire–vessel interactions.
This creates a need for training systems that reproduce the control
characteristics of robotic platforms and provide interpretable
interaction feedback.

Previous studies have investigated robotic delivery [ 4 ] , force- and torque-feedback interfaces [ 5 ] ,
virtual-to-real autonomous navigation [ 6 ] , curvature-aware
delivery control [ 7 ] , and catheter interaction simulation [ 8 ] . Simulation and extended-reality environments have also
been investigated for endovascular training and performance assessment [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Although these studies have advanced individual aspects of robot-assisted intervention, few have established an integrated physical-leader–virtual-follower framework that connects robotic manipulation, virtual vascular simulation, interaction feedback, and post-procedure spatial review within one VR training workflow.
In particular, reproducing the visual workflow alone does not ensure
that inputs from a robotic leader-side device are consistently mapped
to virtual guidewire motion or that trainees can interpret the effects
of their manipulation.

Two technical gaps remain. First, operator input, command dispatch,
physics simulation, and visual rendering may operate at different
update rates. Feedback-control and haptically enhanced interfaces have
been studied for intervention teleoperation [ 13 , 14 ] , but direct
event-by-event forwarding in a hardware-connected simulator may produce
uneven actuation under asynchronous execution. This issue becomes more
complex when continuous velocity commands and discrete position
increments coexist within the same procedure.

Second, interaction feedback in vascular intervention training is
difficult to obtain without dedicated force sensors. Guidewire
deformation and tip–vessel proximity provide complementary cues, but
both are affected by numerical noise, sliding motion, and intermittent
contact. Existing deformable-body simulation, catheter interaction
modeling, and surgical haptic-feedback methods [ 15 , 16 , 8 , 17 ] provide useful foundations, but they do not
directly provide a unified sensorless interaction representation for
training. Moreover, instantaneous feedback alone does not record where
interaction occurred along the trajectory or quantify its accumulated
burden for post-training review. Mixed-reality visualization studies [ 18 ] motivate such spatially linked feedback.

To address these gaps, this paper presents an integrated
physical-leader–virtual-follower VR training framework for
robot-assisted vascular intervention. The framework reproduces the
manipulation workflow of the robotic platform, provides sensorless
interaction feedback during guidewire navigation, and supports
post-procedure spatial review. Within this framework, a multi-cue
interaction representation method combines distributed guidewire
deformation with local guidewire–vessel proximity to estimate relative
interaction intensity without a force sensor. The main contributions of this paper are:

framework with asynchronous dual-mode command mapping. The framework
connects physical manipulation, virtual instrument simulation,
velocity-controlled navigation, position-driven incremental
manipulation, and real-time interaction feedback within a unified
training workflow.

training workflow.

guidewire deformation with local guidewire–vessel proximity and a
nonlinear virtual contact response to provide relative
interaction-intensity feedback without requiring a force sensor.

A trajectory-linked post-procedure analysis function that
records estimated interaction intensity together with guidewire-tip
positions and visualizes its spatial distribution along the vascular
geometry.

# II Teleoperation Platform

The physical robotic platform adopts a leader–follower teleoperation
architecture. The leader-side console contains two horizontally arranged joystick interfaces for catheter and guidewire manipulation, respectively. These interfaces reproduce the relative
arrangement of the instruments on the operating table and allow the
operator to generate advancement, withdrawal, rotation, and combined
translation–rotation commands. The console can be connected either to
the physical follower robot for robotic intervention or to the computer
running the proposed VR training system. The physical follower robot is
therefore not required during VR training.

The physical follower robot uses four drive units to manipulate as many
as three catheters and one guidewire. Axial instrument motion is produced
by paired friction and pinch rollers. Catheter rotation is transmitted
through a geared Y-valve mechanism, whereas guidewire translation and
rotation are generated by dedicated roller assemblies. This arrangement
supports coaxial catheter–guidewire manipulation and rapid instrument
exchange. Although the simulation platform implements control switching
between the catheter and guidewire, the interaction-estimation method
and quantitative evaluation presented in this study focus primarily on
guidewire–vessel interaction.

The leader-side control interfaces support velocity and position modes.
In velocity mode, the instrument advances or withdraws at one of five
predefined speed levels: 2, 5, 10, 30, and 60 mm/s for Gears 1–5,
respectively. In position mode, the displacement of the control interface
is reproduced as a corresponding displacement of the virtual instrument,
enabling fine adjustment in tortuous branches, near bifurcations, and
within delicate anatomical structures. These control characteristics
form the basis of the velocity and position modes implemented in the VR
training system.

The virtual follower side is implemented using the Simulation Open
Framework Architecture (SOFA), an open-source framework for real-time
interactive mechanical simulation with an emphasis on biomechanics and
medical simulation, rather than the physical follower robot. The catheter and
guidewire are represented as deformable virtual instruments within a
surface-based vascular model. Commands acquired from the leader-side
console are mapped to virtual advancement, withdrawal, and rotation.
During simulation, SOFA updates the instrument configurations under
vascular constraints and provides the guidewire centerline nodes and
instrument-tip positions required for interaction estimation. In the
present implementation, guidewire deformation and tip-to-wall proximity
are used to estimate guidewire–vessel interaction, while catheter motion
is retained as part of the virtual procedural workflow.

Operators must learn to coordinate control modes while interpreting
guidewire bending, intermittent contact, and sliding.

An effective VR system should reproduce these interactions and the
teleoperation control characteristics while maintaining stable command
execution across asynchronous input, simulation, and rendering updates.
The following framework addresses these requirements through dual-mode
command mapping and model-based interaction estimation.

2026-10-15.title: Topology-Preserving Multi-Usage Pipe Centerline Refinement under Permanent Tubular Occupancy
2026-10-15.authors: Deng Quan
2026-10-15.abstract: Discrete multi-group pipe routers place channels on a grid or coarse graph. The resulting centerlines are topologically feasible but typically contain many axis-aligned corners. For permanently occupied fluid tubes---as in additively manufactured hydraulic manifolds---those corners are undesirable: they degrade geometric fairness and, in practice, flow quality. This technical report studies the downstream geometric stage that starts from a fixed routing topology and a feasible coarse layout, and refines tubular centerlines under permanent clearance. Unlike classical robotic path smoothing, which usually fair one temporary open trajectory, our setting is a branched manifold with declared terminal usages, finite tube radii, and static cross-group occupancy. We formalize the refinement problem, highlight the multi-usage junction conflict that a single shared branch point cannot resolve, and outline a hybrid trunk-share / junction-split parameterization with soft geometric costs and hard clearance acceptance. On a multi-group suite ($8$ groups $\times$ $8$ terminals, $r{=}2$) with capsule clearance, the refine reaches full hard-accept success, $\kappa r\lesssim 1$, and about a $95\%$ relative drop in the soft objective. Physics-based pressure-drop optimization is intentionally deferred to a later PDE stage; here the objective remains geometric.

2026-10-15.title: A Master-to-Simulation Interface with Demonstration-Trajectory Guidance for Vascular Intervention
2026-10-15.authors: Mingyu Zou , Shuxiang Guo , Sheng Cao , Pengcheng Li , Jian Guo , Bin Wang , Mingchao Din
2026-10-15.abstract: Robotic vascular intervention can reduce radiation exposure to physicians and improve manipulation stability, but effective guidance remains challenging because conventional fluoroscopic images provide limited spatial information. This paper developed a vascular intervention interactive system that connects a real robotic master controller with the SOFA(Simulation Open Framework Architecture) physical simulation platform and reused successful operation trajectories as visual guidance in physical phantom experiments. Experiments were conducted to validate the master-to-SOFA control loop and to compare three guidance conditions: no guidance, centerline guidance, and successful-trajectory guidance. The control validation results showed reliable command delivery under velocity-mode operation. In the physical phantom experiment, centerline guidance showed no obvious improvement over no guidance. In contrast, successful trajectory guidance provided a clear performance benefit. Compared with the no-guidance condition, it reduced task completion time, collision number, rollback number, and rotation number by approximately 66.8 % 66.8\% , 34.3 % 34.3\% , 55.6 % 55.6\% , and 66.7 % 66.7\% , respectively. These results indicate that successful trajectories obtained under instrument-vessel interaction can provide practical guidance cues, offering a simple and effective visual assistance strategy for robotic vascular intervention experiments.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Intravascular intervention has become an effective treatment for cardiovascular and cerebrovascular diseases, owing to its advantages of minimal trauma, reduced postoperative complications, and rapid recovery [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . During such procedures, catheters and guidewires are advanced through narrow and tortuous vessels to reach target lesions under fluoroscopic or digital subtraction angiography (DSA) guidance. However, conventional manual intervention highly depends on the operator’s experience, tactile sensitivity, and hand-eye coordination. Maintaining stable and precise manipulation during long procedures remains challenging. In addition, interventional physicians are exposed to ionizing radiation for prolonged periods, which poses non-negligible occupational health risks [ 5 , 6 ] . To address these limitations, vascular interventional robotic systems have been developed. By allowing operators to manipulate instruments from a remote console behind radiation shielding, robotic systems can reduce radiation exposure, improve motion stability, and enhance manipulation precision [ 7 ] .

Although robotic systems can improve the stability and repeatability of catheter and guidewire manipulation, physicians still need to interpret fluoroscopic or digital subtraction angiography images and continuously determine the spatial relationship between the instruments and the surrounding vasculature. Reinok et al [ 8 ] . proposed an automated passive tracking method for MR-guided endovascular interventions that detects discrete passive markers on an MR-visible guidewire in real time. The detection results are integrated into a custom software interface, offering a cost-effective, radiation-free, and near-real-time guidance assistance method for MR-guided interventions. Zhang et al [ 9 ] . proposed HDCAR, a 3D-2D registration network for abdominal aortic vessels that aligns preoperative CTA-based 3D vascular models with intraoperative DSA images. This method effectively compensates for missing vascular structures in single-frame DSA images, providing more precise imaging guidance and assistance for endovascular aneurysm repair procedures. However, these methods do not provide a structured opportunity for less experienced operators to explore and practice surgical measures in advance. The experience gained from successful virtual surgeries has not been transferred to subsequent actual surgeries. This limitation is important for young or less experienced physicians. Before performing an actual surgery, they may need to understand not only the anatomical route, but also how the guidewire and catheter should be advanced, rotated, retracted, and coordinated when passing through difficult vascular regions.

A successful surgical trajectory is more than a geometric curve. It implicitly records the physical response of the instrument during guidewire-vessel interaction, including bending, contact-induced deviation, passive compliance, and feasible advancement direction under operational constraints. If such successful trajectories can be collected and reused, they may provide operators with prior knowledge that is unavailable from vessel geometry alone. This successful trajectory containing prior knowledge can serve as a practical guidance reference, reflecting not only where the guidewire should go, but also how a successful route progresses through the vascular structure under physical constraints.

This study aims to enable doctors to conduct virtual training before actual surgery and transform successful operational experience into interpretable visual references. The main contributions are summarized as follows. First, a vascular intervention interactive system is developed by connecting a real robotic master controller with the SOFA physical simulation platform, enabling real-time guidewire/catheter manipulation and complete trajectory recording. Second, a successful trajectory acquisition and reuse method is proposed, in which successful trajectories containing instrument-vessel interaction information are used as visual guidance, mapping the recorded 3D successful trajectory onto real-time images of a physical vascular phantom. Finally, comparative experiments are conducted under the same vascular model, including no-guidance operation, centerline-guidance operation, and successful-trajectory-guidance operation, to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed guidance strategy.

# II SYSTEM DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION

## II-A Robotic Master manipulator

The vascular interventional robot used in this study is illustrated in Fig.2. The system is designed to support remote manipulation of interventional instruments while separating the operator from the radiation field. During operation, the physician controls the master manipulator outside the X-ray exposure area, and the follower robotic unit drives the catheter and guidewire at the operating side. This configuration reduces occupational radiation exposure and can also lessen the physical burden associated with wearing heavy lead protection during long procedures.
The platform consists mainly of a master controller and a follower delivery robot. The master side is designed according to the manipulation habits of interventional physicians. Instead of using a conventional joystick or knob-based interface, it adopts a dual push-pull lever structure to reproduce the advancing, retracting, and cooperative manipulation of catheters and guidewires. The follower robot is responsible for executing the commands from the master manipulator and delivering multiple interventional instruments in a coordinated manner [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] .

The master manipulator was used as the human-machine input device for the proposed guidance framework. The operator performed guidewire and catheter manipulation on the real master device, while the corresponding commands were transmitted to the virtual vascular intervention scene constructed in SOFA. In this way, successful guidewire movements generated under realistic master-side operation could be recorded in the simulation environment.

The master manipulator communicates through the Controller Area Network (CAN) protocol. To connect the physical master manipulator with the SOFA-based simulation program, CAN messages were converted into TCP packets through a CAN-to-Ethernet gateway. The converted data were then transmitted via a standard Ethernet interface. This communication structure allowed the physical robotic controller and the simulation environment to exchange control commands and instrument states in real time.

## II-B SOFA-based Vascular Intervention Simulation

The virtual intervention environment was developed using SOFA with the BeamAdapter plugin. SOFA provides a modular physical simulation framework suitable for interactive medical simulation, while BeamAdapter enables slender flexible instruments to be modeled using beam theory. In the proposed system, the guidewire and catheter were represented as deformable beam structures, allowing bending, twisting, and contact response during vascular intervention procedures to be simulated.

The vascular model was imported into SOFA as a rigid triangular mesh and used as the anatomical constraint for the intervention task. Collision response between the instruments and the vessel wall was enabled through triangle, line, and point collision models. The guidewire and catheter were modeled using Cosserat-beam-based components. Their mechanical behavior was solved using an implicit integration scheme, and the InterventionalRadiologyController was used to map external motion commands into instrument advancement, retraction, and rotation. Through this setup, the simulated guidewire could respond to vessel geometry and contact constraints rather than following an idealized geometric trajectory.

During each simulation step, the three-dimensional positions of the guidewire and catheter tips were recorded together with their command events. The trajectories of the two instruments were stored separately in CSV files, while command events were recorded with their timestamps, instrument identities, and action labels. These synchronized records enabled each trajectory sample to be associated with its corresponding instrument action. After a complete successful trial is obtained, the recorded historical data are processed to generate the reference trajectory used in subsequent visualization.

## II-C Master-to-SOFA Communication Middleware

In this study, a communication middleware was developed to connect the real robotic master controller with the SOFA-based vascular intervention simulation platform. The middleware acts as a bidirectional bridge between physical manipulation signals and virtual instrument motion. Its main functions include master-side signal acquisition, CAN frame parsing, command semantic mapping, SOFA window control, and real-time image display.

The overall workflow of the middleware is shown in Fig.2. First, the physical master controller generates CAN messages according to the operator’s push-pull and rotational manipulation. The CAN data are collected from the master-side device through a remote CAN wrapper. In the implementation, an SSH connection is established to the master device, and a ZMQ-based communication client subscribes to the CAN message stream. ZMQ is a lightweight asynchronous messaging library that enables efficient communication between distributed processes. The raw CAN frames are then transmitted to the local computer through TCP-based ZMQ communication.

## II-D Reference Trajectory Generation

The recorded data were converted into a reference trajectory after a successful simulation trial was completed. The procedure was applied independently to the guidewire and catheter. 2026-10-15.title: Beyond Kinematic Tracking: Preserving Expressive Characteristics in Humanoid Whole-Body Control
2026-10-15.authors: Lingfan Bao , Hanshang Zhu , Yan Pan , Jincheng Wang , Jingyang Yu , Tianhu Peng , Yiyang Jia , Dimitrios Kanoulas , Chengxu Zhou
2026-10-15.abstract: Whole-body control plays a crucial role in enabling humanoid robots to execute expressive motions. Faithful execution requires preserving both the intended action and its expressive characteristics. Existing whole-body trackers typically balance joint and keypoint tracking with physical stability across diverse motions, but these objectives do not necessarily prioritize the expressive characteristics of each action. Our analysis shows that lower average positional tracking error does not guarantee better preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics. To address this gap, we propose a residual learning framework with compensation objectives targeting amplitude, energy, body expansion, body lean, and pelvis height. To concentrate compensation while limiting interference with the underlying tracking behavior, motion-aware gating allocates correction capacity according to body-part activity, preserving larger correction ranges in more active parts and restricting them elsewhere. For each frozen tracker, we train motion-specific residual policies and distill them into a unified policy shared across motion categories. Simulation and physical experiments on the Unitree G1 across eight motion categories demonstrate superior preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics compared with the corresponding baselines.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Whole-body motion allows humanoid robots to convey intent and express themselves through physical behavior. Gestures and movements carry meaning through both the actions performed and how they unfold. Movement dynamics and posture are thus integral to the behaviors a robot seeks to reproduce. Bringing such expressiveness to physical humanoids requires whole-body control that coordinates movement while maintaining balance [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .

Recent advances in whole-body control have enabled humanoids to reproduce a broad repertoire of reference motions with a shared tracking policy [ 3 , 4 ] . Maintaining balance and satisfying physical constraints, however, may require deviations from the reference motion [ 7 ] . While aggregate tracking errors measure whole-body motion fidelity, expressiveness may depend on particular postural and dynamic features, such as hand movement amplitude during waving or forward lean during bowing [ 8 , 9 ] . These features may be diminished despite low overall tracking error.

This raises two questions. How are expressive motion characteristics altered during physical execution? How can we recover these characteristics while maintaining stable execution and accounting for tracking accuracy?

Previous work has leveraged residual learning to improve tracking and adapt pretrained controllers to challenging motions [ 10 ] , object interaction [ 11 ] , and deployment differences [ 12 ] . Residual policies refine execution by correcting nominal actions while retaining the underlying controller. This offers a way to address expressive characteristic discrepancies while keeping the pretrained tracker fixed.

To this end, we propose a residual learning framework for preserving expressive motion characteristics. Inspired by analyses of expressive movement [ 13 , 9 ] , we characterize dynamics through amplitude and energy, and posture through body expansion, body lean, and pelvis height. Discrepancies in these characteristics guide compensation by a unified residual policy shared across motion categories for each frozen tracker. To accommodate both postural and dynamic corrections, we introduce motion-aware gating that allocates larger correction bounds to more active body parts while retaining correction capacity in less active regions. Tracking constraints and bounded corrections further balance expressive preservation with tracking accuracy and stable execution.

Our contributions are threefold.

We analyze postural and dynamic deviations across motions and trackers, revealing that lower mean positional error does not necessarily correspond to better preservation of expressive motion characteristics.

We propose a motion-aware residual learning framework that augments a frozen whole-body tracker with a unified policy to recover expressive motion characteristics.

We conduct extensive evaluations across eight motion categories in simulation and on the physical Unitree G1. Results demonstrate that our framework outperforms the corresponding baselines in preserving dynamic and postural motion characteristics.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Expressive Motion Analysis

Human movement studies relate expressive qualities to movement dynamics and body posture, including trunk and arm configuration, movement direction, and intensity [ 13 , 9 ] . Research on bodily expression organizes these aspects into interpretable motion factors and quantitative measures [ 14 ] . Laban-based studies associate combinations of movement elements with emotions elicited through movement [ 15 ] , while computational approaches combine spatial body representations with energy-based temporal features for emotion recognition [ 16 ] . Dynamic and postural features have also been examined in virtual avatars. Head inclination, head position, body openness, and joint velocities have been used to extract representative static poses from expressive walking, with perceptual evaluations supporting the transfer of expressive information [ 17 ] . Extending expressive movement to robots requires accounting for task requirements and physical embodiment. Work in this direction has explored learning expressive motion objectives from human feedback [ 18 ] and combining human motion style transfer with physics-aware generation and whole-body tracking [ 19 ] . Drawing on these studies, we focus on the dynamic and postural characteristics that contribute to each motion’s expressive qualities and use them to define explicit compensation targets for humanoid motion execution.

## II-B Whole-Body Motion Tracking and Residual Adaptation

Whole-body motion tracking enables humanoids to reproduce diverse reference motions while maintaining balance [ 20 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 21 , 22 ] . Expressive control has progressed from coordinating upper-body imitation with velocity-controlled locomotion [ 6 ] to reproducing dynamic full-body motions [ 7 ] . Recent residual and adapter-based methods further extend pretrained controllers to challenging motion distributions [ 10 , 23 ] , object interaction [ 11 ] , and changing task requirements [ 24 ] . Related approaches address dynamics mismatch [ 25 ] and deployment-interface differences [ 12 ] . In contrast to these adaptation objectives, our work focuses on preserving expressive motion characteristics by explicitly compensating for deviations in posture and movement dynamics.

2026-10-15.title: Probabilistic Physics Digital Twin for Human-Robot Interaction
2026-10-15.authors: Yushen Hu , Harshvardhan Chandirasekar , Apurv Kushwaha , Jonathan King , Zhu-Tian Chen
2026-10-15.abstract: Digital twins are increasingly used in robotics to simulate interactions, predict action outcomes, and support planning. However, constructing accurate digital twins requires precise estimates of physical properties such as mass, friction, and center of mass, which are often difficult to obtain in real-world environments. We propose probabilistic digital twins, which represent uncertain physical properties as probability distributions rather than fixed values. By simulating actions across these distributions, the twin predicts a range of possible outcomes and their likelihoods. These probabilistic simulations can guide both human and robot actions by identifying actions that are effective despite physical uncertainty. We demonstrate this framework through human-robot interaction scenarios, including interfaces that communicate simulated outcomes to users and robot planning strategies that explicitly account for uncertainty.

2026-10-15.title: Learning Keypoint Constraints from Visual Demonstrations for Safe Motion Planning
2026-10-15.authors: Zheng Qiu , Zhouyu Zhang , Ninghan Zhong , Glen Chou
2026-10-15.abstract: We present Keypoint Constraint Learning (KCL), a framework for learning task-relevant motion constraints from visual demonstrations and for planning safely with the extracted constraints. To make constraint learning tractable from RGB-D observations, we represent demonstrations using sparse 3D object-centric keypoints and semantic mask centroids extracted through segmentation, visual feature clustering, and point tracking. In this reduced geometric space, we learn keypoint dynamics and infer distance- and orientation-based constraints that make the expert trajectories feasible and approximately locally optimal by enforcing KKT optimality conditions in the reduced state space. We then plan with the learned constraints under uncertainty, using robustness margins derived from accumulated prediction error, and provide a theoretical analysis of how keypoint perception error and learned dynamics error affect the recovered constraints. We evaluate KCL on visual demonstrations from navigation to rigid/deformable manipulation, showing that it recovers multi-stage geometric constraints and outperforms baselines in downstream safe planning.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Robotic behaviors depend on objectives and safety constraints that are often difficult for end users to specify.
Constrained inverse optimal control (CIOC) methods can learn constraints and objectives from locally optimal human demonstrations [ 1 ] , enabling safe downstream planning and control.
Despite success in navigation and obstacle avoidance, most CIOC methods require labeled state-action demonstrations and analytical dynamics. This limitation is particularly important when accurate state estimates or representations are unavailable, as in deformable object manipulation. Video demonstrations offer a practical alternative with rich visual data and without heavy instrumentation, but raw images are high-dimensional and difficult to scale for control. Moreover, CIOC requires generalizable constraints and objectives that are difficult to define in pixel space. This creates a gap between vision and CIOC, motivating a visual representation that is structured enough for constraint learning.

To close this gap, we use keypoints as an intermediate representation between images and CIOC. Keypoints provide a low-dimensional object-centric scene description that preserves constraint-relevant environment geometry, unlike unstructured latent representations [ 2 ] . Their physical interpretability simplifies nominal keypoint-space objectives, such as minimizing displacement, which regularize CIOC while allowing constraints to be inferred solely from safe expert demonstrations. We propose KCL, a framework for K eypoint C onstraint L earning from visual demonstrations. KCL extracts and tracks keypoints and semantic masks from paired RGB-D image-control demonstrations, and lifts them to the 3D world frame via depth maps.
We represent the state using keypoints and mask centroids, learn dynamics in this visual space, and infer constraints from these trajectories. Assuming demonstrations noisily optimize a task objective while satisfying constraints, we enforce the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions to recover consistent constraints.
We analyze learning error from imperfect keypoints and plan robustly using margins derived from accumulated prediction error.

Our contributions are: (i) a keypoint–mask representation for visual
constraint learning; (ii) KKT-based inference of geometric constraints with
learned dynamics and sensitivity bounds; (iii) a robust feedback planner; and
(iv) simulation and hardware validation on navigation and multi-stage
rigid/deformable manipulation, outperforming baselines in safety and success.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

Keypoints for Robotics. Keypoints are widely used as compact interfaces between perception and control [ 3 ] , enabling semantic 3D goal specification via geometric costs and constraints [ 2 ] , especially for deformable objects [ 4 ] and multi-stage manipulation [ 5 ] .
To power keypoint-based control, many methods use VLMs to propose keypoints or spatial constraints from language and vision [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . In contrast, we infer constraints from visual demonstrations via inverse optimality, without a retrieval database, language specification, or VLM-proposed test-time constraints, reducing hallucination and prompt errors while grounding constraints in expert behavior. VLM-free alternatives infer geometric equality constraints from demonstration variance [ 9 ] , but require manual skill and keypoint annotation [ 10 ] , or learn keypoint-space costs for goal reaching [ 11 ] without considering constraints. Our method instead learns interpretable keypoint-mask inequality constraints for safety and task requirements without VLMs or manual keypoint annotations.

Constraint Learning. We build on CIOC, which infers inequality constraints from demonstrations using KKT optimality conditions [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . CIOC is data-efficient because it exploits local optimality [ 13 ] , but assumes known differentiable dynamics, predefined state representations, and full state-control observations [ 13 , 15 , 1 ] . Other geometric constraint-learning methods require fiducial markers or focus on equality constraints [ 17 , 18 ] . Thus, existing CIOC methods are difficult to apply to visual settings without compact state representations, such as for deformable objects.
Inverse constrained RL (ICRL) is an approach for inferring constraints from demonstrations in constrained MDPs [ 19 ] . Unlike CIOC, it usually assumes simulator access rather than closed-form dynamics and can handle unknown dynamics [ 20 ] . However, existing ICRL methods still assume known, fully-observed states. We instead learn from vision and provide bounds on satisfying learned constraints under imperfect keypoint detection and dynamics.

2026-10-15.authors: Mohamed Abouagour , Junhyun Nam , Wonse Jo , Byung-Cheol Min
2026-10-15.abstract: Robots following persistent language instructions must decide which cached room judgments remain valid as their environment changes. We present MIND (Maintenance via INstruction-conditioned Dependencies), a framework for maintaining target-room decisions without re-evaluating every room after each event. A language model compiles each instruction into dependencies for semantic qualification and target selection. The controller intersects semantic dependencies with event footprints, refreshes affected judgments, and updates reachability and selection separately. For fixed deterministic evaluation, planning, and selection, conservative dependency and footprint coverage preserves the decisions of full recomputation. On 240 240 five-event ProcTHOR sequences with an exact benchmark predicate, MIND reduces mean semantic evaluations from 30.6 30.6 to 11.2 11.2 while preserving all 1,200 1{,}200 post-event decisions. Frozen-evaluator experiments with Phi-4 and Qwen3-14B also preserve all 1,200 1{,}200 decisions, without improving the evaluators’ underlying task accuracy. In 32 32 closed-loop AI2-THOR episodes using exact-predicate qualification and metadata-derived footprints, MIND matches the final target decision of full recomputation in every episode. Unitree G1 experiments demonstrate target reuse and reselection across room transitions without additional semantic evaluations under MIND, and abstention after a barrier and an object removal at 4 4 evaluations against 15 15 to 18 18 . Additional materials are available at https://mind-icra27.github.io/ .
2026-10-15.introduction:
A robot may continue following the same instruction while its environment changes. For “bring me the nearest mug,” entering another room, closing a doorway, or removing an object can alter the appropriate target in different ways. The robot has already evaluated which rooms satisfy the instruction, yet those cached judgments need not all become invalid together. Re-evaluating every room discards reusable computation; retaining every judgment can preserve a stale target. Each room judgment is a language-model call, which on a robot shares the GPU with perception and on a hosted model is billed, so the calls avoided are the resource at stake. We ask: after a world change, which room judgments must the robot check again?

The event alone does not determine the required update. For the nearest chair , robot motion can change the selected room without changing which rooms contain chairs. For a chair in the room I am in , the same motion changes which rooms qualify. The same variable thus enters qualification or selection depending on the instruction, and its stage decides whether semantic re-evaluation is needed.

Fig. 1 illustrates the distinction within one persistent instruction. Moving to another room changes the ranking of candidates but not their inventory-based qualification, so no room judgment needs refreshing. Removing the kitchen mug instead requires rechecking the kitchen while retaining the other judgments.

Dependency-based reuse is well established in incremental computation, where dependencies may be declared in program or query structure or discovered during execution [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . In our setting, the state dependencies relevant to maintenance are implicit in a language instruction and differ between qualification and selection. MIND infers these instruction-specific dependencies from language, separately for qualification and selection, to determine which cached judgments require updating. We therefore study decision-preserving maintenance of a given grounding pipeline, rather than replacing its semantic evaluator or replanning the entire task after every event.

We present MIND (Maintenance via INstruction-conditioned Dependencies), a framework for instruction-conditioned incremental grounding . Before execution, a language model compiles the instruction into separate dependency sets for room qualification and target selection. After an event, the controller intersects the semantic dependencies with a footprint of reported state changes to identify which cached judgments to refresh. Reachability and deterministic selection are maintained separately, allowing a target to change without unnecessary semantic evaluation. Under the fixed-evaluator and conservative-coverage assumptions of Section IV , MIND preserves the decisions of full recomputation. Over-approximation may increase work, whereas missing coverage can leave stale judgments; the guarantee does not certify the compiler’s predictions or the evaluator’s accuracy. We contribute:

Instruction-conditioned, stage-specific dependency signatures combined with region-scoped event footprints, separating semantic refresh, reselection, and reuse.

# II Related Work

Grounded planning and dynamic revision. Language-conditioned robots ground instructions in affordances and scene graphs [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] , revise plans from feedback [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] , and abstain or relax infeasible goals [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Other systems maintain contextual or task memory for replanning [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] ; Event-Grounding Graph represents spatial structure and events [ 18 ] , while LINGO-Space updates location distributions as referring expressions arrive [ 19 ] . These approaches motivate maintaining useful world knowledge, but stored information can become stale [ 20 ] . MIND addresses the validity of cached room-qualification judgments under a persistent instruction: which judgments a world change requires the controller to refresh, and when selection alone must be reconsidered.

Incremental computation and embodied reuse. Self-adjusting computation, view maintenance, build systems, and truth maintenance reuse outputs through dependencies on changed inputs [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Dependencies may be declared in formal descriptions or tracked during execution. KEEP manages model-state reuse, whereas AgenticCache caches and validates planning transitions [ 21 , 22 ] . MIND shares the dependency-based reuse principle but caches regional semantic verdicts rather than model states or plan transitions: instruction-conditioned signatures separate qualification inputs from selection inputs, regional footprints scope the invalidation, and the rule preserves a fixed pipeline’s decisions when both conservatively cover the required updates.

Dependencies derived from language. LiP-LLM, DeComplex, and DART-LLM infer precedence among subtasks [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] ; incremental parsing repairs grammar or lexical knowledge after parsing or planning failures [ 26 ] . LG-TAP constructs temporally compact world models through backward observation search and uses efficient graph updates to reuse grounding computations by selectively recomputing world-dependent factor features [ 27 ] . MIND applies dependency-based reuse to a different update unit: cached room-qualification verdicts supporting a persistent target decision. It infers separate qualification and selection dependencies and combines them with event footprints, yielding explicit conditions for decision-preserving regional updates under conservative estimates.

2026-10-15.title: Full-Order Safety for Nonlinear Reduced-Order MPC
2026-10-15.authors: Luis Pabon , Johannes Köhler , Revant Kasichainula , Marco Pavone
2026-10-15.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
2026-10-15.abstract:
Reduced-order models (ROMs) make model predictive control (MPC) of high-dimensional nonlinear systems tractable, but the resulting modeling error can lead to constraint violations on the real system. We introduce CoRE-MPC, a robust MPC formulation that plans with a nonlinear ROM and guarantees recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction for the full-order system. It can be applied with a broad class of nonlinear model reduction techniques and the resulting MPC does not require evaluating the full-order model online, thus ensuring computational efficiency.
The key insight is in how the ROM affects the dynamics of the prediction error. We account for this with two error radii that are propagated alongside the ROM and provide a guaranteed bound on the prediction error.
The approach is validated in simulation on an 80 80 -state oscillator chain, a Burgers equation, and a 9,768 9{,}768 -state finite-element soft robot, where a two-state ROM with data-driven bounds keeps all 1,628 1{,}628 nodes clear of a wall at a median solve time below 1 ​ ms 1\,\mathrm{ms} for a 20 ​ ms 20\,\mathrm{ms} control period. Across these examples, CoRE-MPC is 13 13 to 61 61 times faster than full-order robust MPC at only 27 27 to 35 % 35\% higher closed-loop cost, whereas existing certified schemes are either infeasible or at least twice as conservative. 2026-10-15.introduction:
Reduced-order models (ROMs) enable computationally tractable predictive control for high-dimensional nonlinear systems such as fluid flows, flexible structures, soft robots, and humanoids [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Safety, however, is a property of the real system, whose trajectory the ROM only approximates, and the two can differ significantly. For example, a ROM can predict a collision-free trajectory while the physical robot still hits an obstacle (Fig. 1 ). In practice, this mismatch is absorbed by hand-tuned constraint margins or by a larger ROM, which trade performance and computation for safety without guaranteeing it.

Robust MPC accounts for model error by bounding it as a function of the measured state and input and propagating the bound as a tube along the plan [ 5 ] . The prediction error of a ROM is different: it depends on the full state, of which only the reduced coordinates are measured, so its unmeasured part evolves with its own dynamics and feeds back into the reduced prediction.

For linear FOMs, the error dynamics are linear and reduced-order MPC with full-order guarantees is well developed, with uniform [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] or input-dependent [ 10 , 11 ] error bounds. Treating the nonlinearities as additional bounded disturbances extends these approaches to nonlinear dynamics, which is, however, prohibitively conservative (cf. Section V-A ). Nonlinear ROMs, such as proper orthogonal decomposition (POD)–Galerkin projections [ 12 , 2 ] , quadratic manifolds [ 13 ] , and spectral submanifolds [ 14 ] ,
can provide a more accurate ROM for nonlinear dynamics.
However, using these ROMs directly in an MPC formulation can only guarantee constraints on the ROM prediction, not the real system. Applying a standard nonlinear robust MPC [ 5 ] to ROMs treats the unmodelled dynamics as an independent model mismatch, resulting in overly conservative or even infeasible operation. To the best of our knowledge, the robust nonlinear reduced-order MPC (RN-ROMPC) in [ 15 ] is the only scheme that certifies full-order constraints using only ROM prediction. However, its application requires an invariant manifold, which is available only for specific systems near an equilibrium. Thus, there exists no MPC scheme that can ensure constraint satisfaction using the nonlinear ROMs that are common in high-dimensional soft robots.

Contribution: We present CoRE-MPC, a reduced-order MPC that enforces constraints on the full-order system for a general class of nonlinear ROMs. The prediction error within the reduced coordinates is measured, and can thus be reset at every update, but the error outside them is not. CoRE-MPC therefore bounds the two separately, as a tangential and a transverse error, together with their coupling.

Error bound : A coupled reduction-error certificate (CoRE, Thm. 1 ) bounds the prediction error for general ROMs using a two-dimensional comparison system.

Theoretical guarantees : Online, CoRE-MPC propagates two error radii with the ROM, at a computational cost comparable to nominal ROM-MPC with two extra states, and guarantees recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction for the original full-order system (Thm. 5 ).

Numerical experiments : We demonstrate CoRE-MPC on an oscillator chain, a Burgers equation, and the 9,768 9{,}768 -state finite-element soft robot of Fig. 1 , where nominal ROM-MPC violates the constraints. On the oscillator chain, all assumptions of Theorem 5 are satisfied. Compared to full-order robust MPC, CoRE-MPC is 13 13 to 61 61 times faster at 27 27 to 35 % 35\% higher closed-loop cost. Even when invariant-manifold assumption of RN-ROMPC [ 15 ] holds, CoRE-MPC incurs less than a quarter of its excess closed-loop cost. On the soft robot, where full-order robust MPC is computationally prohibitive, CoRE-MPC keeps all 1,628 1{,}628 nodes clear of the wall at a median solve time below 1 1 ms.

Outline: Section II states the problem, Section III derives the error certificate, Section IV presents CoRE-MPC and its closed-loop guarantees, and Section V reports the experiments.

2026-10-15.title: PACER: Process-Aware VLA Policy Learning from Human Corrections for Robotic Disassembly
2026-10-15.authors: Chang Liu , Sibo Tian , Litian Gong , Zhiwen Fan , Jiachen Li , Xiao Liang , Minghui Zheng
2026-10-15.abstract: Robotic disassembly of end-of-life (EoL) products requires robots to accommodate product variation, follow prerequisite sequences, and approach components precisely for contact-rich manipulation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides a practical path for adaptation, but limited and costly disassembly data cannot capture the distribution shifts arising from changing environments and product uncertainties. The policy’s own rollouts record its approach attempts, and human corrections demonstrate recovery from its errors, but turning these experiences into better policy performance remains challenging. We introduce PACER, a Process-Aware Correction and Evidence Reweighting framework that learns from these experiences through SFT, using progress toward the target and each trace’s source and outcome to weight valid action chunks in the native supervised action loss. PACER trains one policy per weighting setting and selects one of the resulting policies through held-out validation. We evaluate PACER on UR5e motherboard disassembly across five component classes, where it achieves 87/100 successful approach-and-handoff trials on the held-out benchmark, compared with 54/100 for vanilla post-SFT.
2026-10-15.introduction:
“The search for truth is more precious than its possession.”

The rise of vision-language-action (VLA) models offers a promising direction for enabling robots to learn from operational data end-to-end [ 15 , 39 , 6 ] . In the disassembly setting, they are used to identify actionable components in complex environments as tasks, plan motions to approach them, and execute precision contact-rich manipulations. However, these tasks differ from the daily-life tabletop tasks on which most current state-of-the-art VLA models are trained.

Adapting VLA models to industrial disassembly requires domain post-training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the most direct approach, but its effectiveness is limited by the scarcity and narrow coverage of real disassembly demonstrations [ 21 , 26 ] . While several agentic systems use VLAs primarily as planners or motion proposers rather than full executors to reduce complexity during contact-rich manipulation [ 27 , 7 ] , these models still suffer from distribution shift. A policy trained on nominal demonstrations can reach unfamiliar states through its own decisions during deployment. Autonomous rollouts record successful approaches, partial progress, and the states reached during failed attempts. Human corrections collected during rollouts provide recovery actions from policy-induced failure states that clean trajectories may not cover.

However, the value of robots’ own rollout data and human corrections is obscured when they are simply added to fine-tuning datasets. Clean demonstrations, expert recoveries, autonomous successes, near misses, and failed rollouts differ in reliability and in how they should influence the policy update for better performance. A binary success-or-failure label is also too coarse to explain which parts of a rollout were useful, while asking humans to annotate every step in real-world rollouts is costly. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a formal mechanism for credit assignment from trial experience to drive improvement, and recent work uses it to seek gains beyond SFT baselines in VLA post-training [ 18 , 3 ] . However, direct RL in industrial disassembly is costly because contact-induced physical changes are difficult to simulate accurately and efficiently, and learning on real hardware is slow, costly, and safety-sensitive [ 20 ] . Online RL obtains feedback through continued interaction, whereas offline RL learns from existing records using reward signals, value estimates, or advantage estimates [ 43 , 16 , 34 ] . Additionally, both RL routes require task-relevant reward specification and may involve adapting the optimization method to the VLA action head [ 3 ] . We therefore investigate whether SFT can learn more from autonomous experience and human corrections through a unified framework that retains the model’s native supervised action loss.

We introduce PACER, a process-aware correction and evidence reweighting framework for VLA post-training in robotic disassembly, as shown in Figure 1 . PACER learns from autonomous rollouts, human corrections, and supplementary clean demonstrations. It assesses progress toward the intended target within each trace and uses the trace’s role to judge which recorded actions provide useful supervision. These assessments translate into bounded weights that scale each valid action chunk’s contribution to the native supervised action loss. Different weighting settings specify how process evidence and trace roles are combined to determine these weights. PACER fine-tunes the same reference policy under each setting and selects one of the resulting policies through offline validation. We evaluate the selected policy on real UR5e motherboard disassembly across five component classes. PACER achieves 87/100 successful approach-and-handoff trials on the held-out benchmark, compared with 79/100 for fixed-geometry reweighting and 54/100 for vanilla post-SFT.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-language-action models. Vision-language-action (VLA) models reason over multimodal inputs, including task instructions, enabling the system to use the visual state, understand language prompts, and generate executable actions for robot control in a single model [ 36 , 12 , 5 ] . Systems such as RT-2 [ 2 ] , Octo [ 39 ] , OpenVLA [ 15 ] , OpenVLA-oft [ 14 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 11 ] , and π 0.7 \pi_{0.7} [ 9 ] show that visual robot policies can transfer across tasks, embodiments, and instructions when trained on large robot datasets. DROID [ 13 ] provides real-world manipulation data, while LIBERO [ 23 ] benchmarks knowledge transfer in lifelong robot learning. However, most of these models are trained on and targeted at daily-life tabletop tasks under a general manipulation setting. Industrial practice, like disassembly, introduces a different regime in which the policy must operate amid product variation, limited demonstrations, contact-rich execution, and costly real-world evaluation [ 21 , 42 ] .

VLA post-training and learning from human corrections. Post-training is the standard mechanism for adapting a pretrained VLA to a specific deployment domain and enhancing task performance [ 41 ] . Advantage-weighted regression and AWAC use exponentiated estimated advantages as nonnegative weights on a behavior-cloning loss [ 34 , 32 ] . L2RW updates minibatch example weights through validation-based meta-gradients, whereas Meta-Weight-Net uses validation feedback to learn a loss-to-weight function [ 35 , 37 ] .

Reinforcement learning (RL) extends this principle from supervised reweighting to interactive credit assignment with rollouts and reward signals [ 18 , 28 ] . Recent VLA models employ online policy-gradient post-training under sparse success rewards [ 38 , 29 , 44 ] , and extend this approach to deployment settings in which teleoperated interventions are fused with autonomous rollouts through advantage-conditioning, as exemplified by RECAP in π 0.6 ∗ \pi^{*}_{0.6} and SOP [ 10 , 33 ] . For learning from human corrections, HandITL and DexHiL embed low-latency
arm-hand intervention and prioritize corrective segments during training [ 8 , 22 ] . Action preference optimization converts intervention trajectories into preference pairs or language-grounded latent edits [ 40 ] . Hi-ORS applies reward-threshold rejection sampling and reward-weighted supervision to accepted rollouts [ 30 ] , and a VLM-based reflective post-training combines PPO guided by dense rewards from failure analysis with supervised fine-tuning on successful experience [ 17 ] . Flow-matching VLA heads do not directly expose tractable action log-likelihoods, complicating likelihood-based policy-gradient updates [ 3 ] . Existing approaches enable policy optimization through stochastic denoising reformulations [ 3 ] or perform RL in noise space with a frozen flow-matching decoder [ 31 ] . Offline and reward-verified variants can reduce the need for live rollouts but still rely on value estimates or reward supervision [ 43 , 4 , 19 ] .

2026-10-15.title: End-to-End Vision-Language-Action Policies for Autonomous Lunar Rover Docking
2026-10-15.authors: Sitan Huang , Grace Gao
2026-10-15.abstract:
Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances.
While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components.
End-to-end learned policies are an alternative approach to navigation, which maps observations directly to control actions without intermediate components.
Vision-language-action models, in particular, have driven significant breakthroughs in robotics and autonomous vehicle research.
By leveraging internet-scale vision-language pretraining, these models can be exploited for their commonsense reasoning and visual understanding to provide robust generalization with limited task-specific data.
However, their applicability and performance have yet to be characterized for lunar surface operations.
In this study, we design a vision-language-action policy for autonomous lunar rover docking and characterize its performance relative to a modular navigation pipeline.
We develop a scalable training framework that generates safety-aware expert demonstrations in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment.
In closed-loop evaluations, our policy performs competitively relative to the modular baseline under perceptual disturbances unseen during training.
To address the tradeoff between compute consumption and closed-loop safety,
the policy adapts its execution horizon by determining how far the rover may safely travel in open loop.
Adaptive-horizon execution reduces inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates relative to fixed horizons in the evaluated scenarios.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Following the crewed Artemis II lunar flyby in 2026, sustained human exploration on the lunar surface is expected in the upcoming decade.
Large-scale surface missions will require substantial autonomy to limit operational costs and shorten mission cycles, using vehicles that autonomously offload, stage, relocate cargo, and dock with surface assets prior to crew arrival [ 1 , 2 ] .

The lunar environment presents unique challenges for navigation.
Communication delays
and signal occlusion due to terrain make continuous ground control poorly suited for this task.
Lunar rovers must also operate in unmapped terrain with limited localization infrastructure. While proposed systems such as ESA’s Moonlight constellation will improve absolute positioning, local-relative navigation is necessary for hazard avoidance and safely maneuvering near astronauts and other vehicles.
Harsh lighting contrasts, long shadows, and feature-sparse terrain further complicate perception and navigation.

Planetary rover autonomy has traditionally employed modular perception, mapping, and planning pipelines [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . This provides interpretable intermediate representations and explicit safety constraints but can propagate perception errors into downstream planning [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] .
End-to-end policies instead learn a direct mapping from perceptual inputs to control actions.
Because perception and control are optimized jointly, these policies need not produce explicit intermediate outputs, thus reducing failures at component interfaces.
However, deployment-time lighting and terrain appearance can differ from learned visual features and degrade performance [ 10 , 11 ] .
Mitigating this typically requires training on sufficiently large and diverse datasets [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies offer an alternative
by finetuning vision-language models (VLMs) trained on internet-scale image-text corpora for closed-loop control.
Such pretraining provides robust generalization over unseen scenarios [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] . In low-data regimes, improved data efficiency is associated with vision-language pretraining [ 17 , 18 ] .
To date, the application of end-to-end VLA policies to lunar surface navigation has yet to be investigated.
In this paper, we consider the scenario of autonomous docking between a lunar transport rover and a landing module.
We study whether VLA policies provide a robust alternative to modular pipelines in this context.

Despite vision-language pretraining, policy learning still requires high-quality demonstrations of safe navigation.
This is challenging first due to the infeasibility of large-scale data collection on the lunar surface; second, while physical testbeds and digital environments exist to simulate lunar conditions, collecting human-driver trajectories is costly and difficult to scale.
We therefore adopt the Learn-by-Cheating (LBC) paradigm [ 19 ] using privileged simulator information to generate expert demonstrations.
Our safety-aware expert encourages clearance from terrain and dynamic hazards while avoiding poorly illuminated regions.
Using this scalable data generation pipeline, we train a VLA policy that autonomously docks a lunar rover with a landing module, using visual observations from a single monocular camera, without prior maps of the environment.

Onboard computation is a constrained resource for lunar rovers. Reducing model inference frequency is attractive to limit computational demand and power consumption.
Our VLA policy adopts action chunking [ 20 ] to predict multiple navigation waypoints into the future.
We further introduce a physically grounded adaptive-horizon execution strategy that estimates how far the rover can safely travel in open loop.

Accurate and fine-grained trajectory corrections are necessary during final docking alignment.
To improve the policy’s docking precision, we introduce a new technique, geometric temporal ensembling , which aggregates multiple trajectory candidates within a single inference and across successive inferences.

We construct a modular navigation baseline and compare its performance with that of the VLA policy, using the same underlying planner used for policy training but operating on online-estimated hazard information without privileged ground truth.
We evaluate both systems in simulation under nominal conditions and under sensor disturbances unseen during training.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We design a VLA navigation policy for autonomous lunar rover docking.

We introduce an adaptive-horizon execution strategy to reduce inference frequency while maintaining closed-loop safety.

We introduce geometric temporal ensembling to improve the precision of rover docking through inference-time trajectory ensembling.

We benchmark the VLA policy in closed loop against a modular autonomy baseline under nominal conditions and lunar-motivated sensor disturbances.

1. We design a VLA navigation policy for autonomous lunar rover docking.

2. We introduce an adaptive-horizon execution strategy to reduce inference frequency while maintaining closed-loop safety.

3. We introduce geometric temporal ensembling to improve the precision of rover docking through inference-time trajectory ensembling.

4. We benchmark the VLA policy in closed loop against a modular autonomy baseline under nominal conditions and lunar-motivated sensor disturbances.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Policies for Navigation

Vision-language-action models have been applied to terrestrial robot navigation in unstructured environments [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] .
Terrestrial navigation policies benefit from abundant and heterogeneous data sources.
Non-robot data can be crowdsourced from egocentric cameras mounted on pedestrians and bicyclists, or repurposed from YouTube tour videos [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] . Multi-robot datasets can be aggregated [ 12 , 23 ] for training robust policies across different embodiments.
No comparably large and diverse body of training data is currently available for lunar surface navigation.
Policies trained exclusively on terrestrial imagery may not generalize to the lunar environment.

## II-B Learning Navigation from Privileged Experts

Imitation learning trains end-to-end policies using expert demonstrations, but collecting task- and environment-specific human demonstrations can be costly [ 27 , 28 ] .
To reduce dependence on human demonstrations, LBC [ 19 ] uses privileged simulator information to construct automated experts that generate training data at scale [ 28 , 29 , 30 ] .
Importantly, privileged information need not be recoverable from deployment-time sensor observations.
In SPOC [ 31 ] , a learner policy trained from a privileged shortest-path planner exhibits robust closed-loop behaviors and outperforms one trained from an expert restricted to observable information.
However, shortest-path demonstrations do not account for deployment-time perceptual uncertainties and imperfect trajectory following.
Our expert generates demonstrations that encourage hazard clearance and avoid perceptually uncertain terrain, providing margins against both trajectory-following errors and perceptual uncertainty.

## II-C Action Chunking and Adaptive-Horizon Execution

Action chunking predicts a sequence of future actions per inference.
This reduces the effective decision frequency and can mitigate learner-induced compounding errors in imitation learning [ 20 ] .
To preserve closed-loop responsiveness, recent VLA methods adapt the execution horizon using online reinforcement learning [ 32 ] , model uncertainty [ 33 ] , attention structure [ 34 ] , action consistency [ 35 ] , or observed execution drift [ 36 ] .
While these signals estimate the reliability of a predicted sequence, they do not ground the horizon to the physical geometry of the environment.
Our VLA policy predicts curvature-conditioned execution horizons from visual observations and uses this prediction to determine the execution horizon.

## II-D Modular Planetary Rover Navigation

Several works have sought to improve the robustness of individual components in modular navigation pipelines by replacing hand-engineered estimators with machine-learning models for localization and traversability assessment [ 37 , 38 ] .
In prior work [ 39 ] , we have developed and validated a lunar rover autonomy stack for hazard mapping and localization under lunar conditions.

2026-10-15.title: A Mode-Unified, Continuous, and Biomimetic Control Strategy of a Robotic Lower Limb Prosthesis
2026-10-15.authors: Hanjun Kim , Sixu Zhou , John Shim , Xinyuan Guo , Kinsey R. Herrin , Aaron J. Young
2026-10-15.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
2026-10-15.abstract: Existing biomimetic lower-limb prosthesis controllers are commonly designed for discrete locomotion modes, requiring separate parameterizations for level walking, ramps, and stairs. We present a mode-unified prosthesis control framework that represents knee and ankle biomechanics continuously as functions of terrain slope and gait phase across those locomotion conditions. Locally optimized ascent and descent polynomial models were unified using radial basis function (RBF) interpolation, preserving the accuracy of the partitioned models while outperforming a global polynomial representation. The resulting biomechanics were transformed into continuous and slope-dependent impedance parameters and implemented within a single finite-state-machine (FSM) controller using bilateral sensing for gait-state estimation. Experiments with 10 individuals with transfemoral amputation demonstrated terrain-adaptive locomotion from level walking through ramps and stairs up to 35 degrees, including 13 degree ramp and 15 degree stair conditions absent from the underlying able-bodied (AB) dataset. Experimental results reproduced the principal slope-dependent biomechanical trends predicted by the unified model, with high agreement for knee-related measures (r-square = 0.82 - 0.99) and ankle kinematics (r-square= 0.78 - 0.96). These findings demonstrated that unified biomechanical parameterization enables a prosthesis control architecture across diverse terrain conditions while preserving key features of AB biomechanics without requiring independently tuned impedance parameter sets for each locomotion mode.

2026-10-15.title: FACT: A Multimodal Force-Action-Track Foundation Model for Human-to-Robot Dexterity
2026-10-15.authors: Zhi Cao , Yining Hong , Jiaolong Yang , Yejin Choi , Li Fei-Fei , Jiajun Wu , Huang Huang
2026-10-15.abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative to costly robot data collection for dexterous manipulation, but most human datasets lack force measurements. Dexterous manipulation requires not only visual and proprioceptive understanding but also the ability to anticipate and regulate interaction forces. To scale force-aware human–robot co-training, we introduce EgoForce , a large-scale human tactile dataset capturing force-rich manipulation experience, and combine it with robot demonstrations for pretraining. We present FACT , a robot foundation model that cascades from prospective visual planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation. FACT comprises two jointly trained components. A Track-Guided Coarse Planner jointly predicts actions, future video, and visual tracks. Future video and visual tracks also provide a shared task representation that facilitates cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and coarse action generation. Building on this coarse plan, a Force–Action Joint Refiner jointly predicts future force and refines the coarse action, allowing anticipated force and action to shape each other during refinement. We evaluate the model on ten tasks requiring fine-grained coordination and force feedback, including tool use, musical instruments, and precision laboratory procedures. Using as few as 10 robot trajectories with 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning, FACT outperforms both baselines, with success-rate gains of up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex. Ablations show that force supervision in human pretraining data is crucial for downstream robot performance after fine-tuning, while visual track prediction and training with future-force prediction improve dexterous execution. Experiments varying the human–robot data ratio during fine-tuning further suggest that FACT learns from human demonstrations nearly as effectively as from robot demonstrations.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Collecting diverse robot demonstrations for dexterous manipulation at scale is expensive, making human demonstrations an attractive source of manipulation experience. Most human manipulation datasets capture vision and motion without measuring contact forces. However, contact-rich dexterous manipulation often requires both prospective visual planning and force-aware refinement [ 1 , 2 ] : where the hands go is guided by vision and task context, while how the fingers finish the motion is shaped by contact forces. The former determines the coarse structure of the motion; the latter governs its fine-grained execution. Force measurements can provide supervision for how hand motion and physical interaction evolve together, allowing human experience to better support force-aware robot learning.

To support force-aware learning at scale, we develop a collection platform combining three egocentric views, bimanual tactile gloves, and automated force calibration to capture synchronized vision, hand motion, and tactile force during natural manipulation. Using this platform, we collect EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dataset comprising approximately 2k hours of manipulation across 40k episodes, 1k tasks, and 1k demonstrators.

To transfer this force-rich human experience to robots, we introduce FACT , a dexterous foundation model that
cascades from prospective visual motion planning to force-aware refinement for human-to-robot dexterity ( ). The model comprises two jointly trained components for coarse motion planning and fine-grained force-aware execution.
The Track-Guided Coarse Planner jointly predicts future video, visual tracks, and an action chunk. Building on the coarse plan, a Force–Action Joint Refiner takes the partially denoised action together with observed tactile signals and co-denoises the remaining action and future fingertip force through bidirectional self-attention, allowing action and force to reciprocally condition one another for action refinement. Future video and visual track prediction not only ground coarse action generation in anticipated visual motion but also provide an embodiment-agnostic task representation that encourages knowledge transfer between humans and robots.

We pretrain FACT on our large-scale EgoForce dataset together with a small set of robot
demonstrations. We then fine-tune and evaluate it across 10 real-world
tasks, spanning everyday skills such as tying shoelaces, precision laboratory
procedures such as pipetting and microcentrifuge-tube manipulation, as well as
tool use and musical instruments. Our ablations show that force supervision in human pretraining data provides the largest gains on tasks demanding precise contact and force control, while visual track prediction and training with future-force prediction improve dexterous execution. Experiments with different human–robot data ratios during fine-tuning suggest that human demonstrations can contribute nearly as much as robot demonstrations to policy learning, supporting human experience as a scalable source of dexterous manipulation skills.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce FACT , a dexterous foundation model that cascades from track-based visual motion planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation.

We introduce EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dexterous manipulation dataset and scalable collection platform for pretraining.

Across ten real-world tasks, we show the benefits of force supervision in human pretraining data and visual track and future-force prediction during training, together with the effectiveness of FACT in using human data for fine-tuning.

1. We introduce FACT , a dexterous foundation model that cascades from track-based visual motion planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation.

2. We introduce EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dexterous manipulation dataset and scalable collection platform for pretraining.

3. Across ten real-world tasks, we show the benefits of force supervision in human pretraining data and visual track and future-force prediction during training, together with the effectiveness of FACT in using human data for fine-tuning.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# II Related Work

Large egocentric corpora [ 3 , 4 ] have enabled robot learning from human
experience through pretrained visual representations [ 5 ] ,
imitation from human play [ 6 ] , portable in-the-wild
capture systems [ 7 , 8 ] , egocentric co-training [ 9 , 10 ] , and human–robot mixtures in VLA
pretraining [ 11 ] . These sources are largely force-blind, capturing hand motion without contact forces. EgoForce ( Section III ) closes this gap with 2,000 hours of human manipulation paired with calibrated tactile force.

Learning from this experience requires policies that use touch to guide dexterous execution. Tactile sensing has supported robot manipulation through vision-based skins [ 12 , 13 ] , learned touch representations [ 14 , 15 ] , in-hand control [ 16 ] ,
and tactile-aware imitation and VLA policies [ 17 , 18 ] . Related work has explored
force-centric demonstration capture [ 19 ] and auxiliary
future contact or force prediction [ 20 ] .
Hierarchical manipulation further separates planning from fine-grained control through
explicit action hierarchies [ 21 , 22 ] , staged
VLA post-training [ 23 ] , and slow-fast tactile refinement [ 24 , 11 ] . T-Rex [ 11 ] combines low-frequency visuomotor action generation with asynchronous tactile refinement, conditioning coarse actions on vector-quantized force history [ 25 ] . Force remains an input, leaving action–contact dynamics implicit and refinement dependent on the contact information preserved by compression. FACT instead jointly denoises continuous future force and action, allowing them to shape one another during refinement.

Future video and visual track prediction support human-to-robot transfer through a shared representation of anticipated scene motion across different action spaces. Work coupling action generation with future visual prediction includes video pretraining for
manipulation [ 26 ] , policy-as-video [ 27 ] , and
interactive world simulators [ 28 , 29 ] .
Visual point tracks provide an explicit, embodiment-agnostic description of scene motion. They have served as policy
interfaces [ 30 ] , transfer media from human video [ 31 , 32 , 33 ] , and cross-domain motion
representations [ 32 ] , enabled by general-purpose trackers [ 34 ] . Similar to [ 33 ] , FACT jointly predicts actions, future video, and visual tracks in its Wan2.2-based coarse planner [ 35 ] . These shared prediction targets let human demonstrations supervise motion representations that ground robot action generation in anticipated visual motion.
