2026-10-15.title: $λ_0$: Scaling Open-World Egocentric Human Data for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
2026-10-15.authors: Lambda-humanoid Team
2026-10-15.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-15.abstract:
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated whole-body interaction with the physical world, yet collecting robot demonstrations at scale remains costly.
Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, but existing egocentric human supervision often omits locomotion and posture, while embodiment differences and controller dynamics hinder accurate end-effector execution.
We introduce HumanVerse , a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion.
Our human-to-humanoid pipeline aligns camera viewpoints and arm appearance, and refines motion references and controller inputs offline to reduce end-effector errors while preserving whole-body coordination.
We validate the pipeline through zero-shot transfer to Unitree G1 on representative whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation tasks, without target-task robot demonstrations.
Building on this pipeline, we develop λ 0 \lambda_{0} 1 1 1 λ \lambda resembles “人” (human in Chinese), symbolizing learning from everyday human experience. , a humanoid foundation model for whole-body loco-manipulation, with robot-aligned human demonstrations providing supervision for mid-training.
Increasing whole-body human data consistently improves downstream task progress. λ 0 \lambda_{0} achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across real-world loco-manipulation tasks.
We expect this study to guide scalable whole-body human data collection toward humanoid foundation models for richer interaction with the physical world.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Learning humanoid loco-manipulation across tasks and environments requires demonstrations that capture coordinated locomotion, posture, and manipulation ( Jiang et al., 2026a ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026b ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Figure AI, 2026a ; Figure AI, 2026b ) .
Whole-body teleoperation provides visual observations paired with robot actions, but requires operators to guide a physical humanoid through each demonstration ( Fu et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026b ; GEAR Team et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026b ) .
This dependence on robot availability and operation makes broader task and environment coverage costly to obtain ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Punamiya et al., 2026 ) .
Scaling humanoid learning motivates a source of whole-body interaction experience that can grow beyond robot-operated collection.

Egocentric video records people’s everyday interactions across tasks and environments without requiring robot operation ( Grauman et al., 2022 ; Kareer et al., 2025 ; Hoque et al., 2026 ; Punamiya et al., 2026 ; Figure, 2026 ) .
Recent methods recover wrist and hand trajectories from these videos, turning observed interactions into action supervision for robot learning ( Li et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026a ) .
Pretraining on these action-labeled videos can improve downstream manipulation ( Zheng et al., 2026c ; Punamiya et al., 2026 ) .
For humanoid loco-manipulation, however, wrist and hand trajectories alone omit the locomotion and postural changes that support whole-body interaction ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) .
Recording synchronized body and hand motion captures this coordination, but motion retargeting and whole-body tracking can still leave end-effector errors due to geometric mismatch and imperfect execution ( Araujo et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026b ) .
These errors can compromise grasping and contact.
This raises our central question: Can egocentric whole-body human experience provide supervision that is both transferable to humanoids and practical to acquire at scale?

We develop a human-to-humanoid alignment pipeline that captures human demonstrations without a robot and aligns their observations and actions to the downstream humanoid (Sec. 3.4 ).
We match the camera and capture height to the robot setup, then remove human forearms and trackers from the images and composite rendered G1 arms.
Action alignment refines motion references and controller inputs offline to improve end-effector accuracy, producing robot-compatible state–action supervision.
We evaluate policies trained with this supervision on Unitree G1 across seven representative tasks spanning coordinated whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation (Sec. 5.1 ).
Using task-specific human demonstrations without target-task robot demonstrations, the evaluations achieve mean progress of 51.7% and 76.2%, respectively.

Using this capture setup, we build HumanVerse , a 500-hour corpus of human loco-manipulation spanning open-world scenes and tasks.
We record egocentric video and body motion with lightweight wearable sensors, synchronize the streams, and reconstruct hand motion from video.

We develop λ 0 \lambda_{0} , a whole-body humanoid vision–language–action policy that learns from scalable human experience and progressively adapts it to humanoid control (Fig. 1 ).
Egocentric hand-motion pretraining draws on diverse human interaction videos.
Mid-training on HumanVerse then provides a scalable, robot-free source of supervision for learning coordinated body and hand actions, bridging video pretraining and limited, costly robot demonstrations.
Robot post-training adapts the learned behaviors to the target humanoid.

Increasing whole-body human data reduces validation loss and raises real-world task progress monotonically from 59.9% without whole-body mid-training to 80.4% with the full corpus.
Ablations identify whole-body mid-training as the larger contributor to real-world success among the two human-data stages.
The full λ 0 \lambda_{0} policy achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across four real-world loco-manipulation tasks, improving over the strongest evaluated baselines by 3.9% and 22.5%, respectively.
Human-data training also improves progress on robot-unseen object instances observed in human demonstrations.
Our contributions are:

We develop a human-to-humanoid alignment pipeline for whole-body skill transfer and evaluate its collection efficiency and zero-shot transfer on G1 without target-task robot demonstrations.

We introduce HumanVerse , a 500-hour dataset pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion across open-world scenes and tasks.

We develop λ 0 \lambda_{0} to progressively adapt egocentric human interaction experience to humanoid control, and demonstrate that scaling human data with whole-body supervision improves downstream loco-manipulation.

1. We develop a human-to-humanoid alignment pipeline for whole-body skill transfer and evaluate its collection efficiency and zero-shot transfer on G1 without target-task robot demonstrations.

2. We introduce HumanVerse , a 500-hour dataset pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion across open-world scenes and tasks.

3. We develop λ 0 \lambda_{0} to progressively adapt egocentric human interaction experience to humanoid control, and demonstrate that scaling human data with whole-body supervision improves downstream loco-manipulation.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Generalist Robot Policies

Large-scale robot datasets combine demonstrations across tasks and embodiments, supporting the development of generalist policies ( Dasari et al., 2020 ; Jang et al., 2022 ; Walke et al., 2023 ; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2024 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ; Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026b ) .
These policies learn from diverse demonstrations within a shared model ( Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) , motivating more scalable ways to collect training data.
Advances in teleoperation and portable demonstration interfaces reduce collection effort ( Dass et al., 2023 ; Qin et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Fu et al., 2025b ; Chi et al., 2024 ) .
UMI on Legs extends robot-free hand-held demonstrations to quadruped manipulation by coupling a task-level manipulation policy with a simulation-trained whole-body controller ( Ha et al., 2025 ) .
Robot-based collection depends on hardware availability and repeated resets, while portable interfaces have limited action spaces.

## 2.2 Learning from Human Videos

Human video datasets capture diverse activities, objects, and environments, providing rich experience for robot learning ( Grauman et al., 2022 ; Damen et al., 2022 ; Goyal et al., 2017 ; Grauman et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2023b ; DeTone et al., 2026 ; Lightwheel AI, 2026 ) .
Learning from it requires connecting observations to actions.
Nymeria pairs synchronized multimodal egocentric recordings with full-body motion across 300 hours of daily activities in the wild ( Ma et al., 2024 ) , providing a foundation for studying context-dependent human motion.
Temporal and geometric annotations describe when interactions occur and how hands and objects move ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Sener et al., 2022 ; Ragusa et al., 2021 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Banerjee et al., 2025 ) , while motion tracking and reconstruction provide human trajectories for action learning ( Hoque et al., 2026 ; Punamiya et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Zheng et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2026a ) .
OpenEgo standardizes hand-pose annotations and temporally localized action descriptions across egocentric datasets ( Jawaid & Xiang, 2025 ) .
Human videos also support visual representation learning ( Nair et al., 2023 ; Sontakke et al., 2023 ; Kumar et al., 2020 ) and robot control through imitation and alignment ( Mandlekar et al., 2022 ; Shao et al., 2020 ; Bahl et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023a ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2023 ; Kareer et al., 2025 ; Lepert et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026b ) .
HAT unifies human and humanoid state–action spaces for co-training on aligned PH2D demonstrations ( Qiu et al., 2025 ) , while DexWild combines wearable human interaction data with robot demonstrations for dexterous manipulation across environments ( Tao et al., 2025 ) .
EgoZero learns closed-loop manipulation from smart-glasses demonstrations without robot data using morphology-agnostic representations ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , while HumanEgo uses hand–object interaction representations to learn robot-data-free policies from short human recordings ( Wang et al., 2026b ) .
Beyond stationary manipulation, EMMA co-trains human full-body mobile manipulation demonstrations with static robot data, avoiding mobile robot teleoperation and reporting improved performance as human data increases ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) .
We use synchronized body and hand motion as action supervision for bipedal humanoid loco-manipulation, and measure the benefit of increasing this data while holding robot demonstrations fixed.

## 2.3 Humanoid Whole-Body Control

Humanoid whole-body control coordinates locomotion, posture, and manipulation to support complex physical interactions ( Fu et al., 2025a ; He et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026b ) .
Motion retargeting is a key interface: GMR studies how retargeting artifacts affect downstream tracking ( Araujo et al., 2026 ) , and Human2Humanoid combines morphology-invariant trajectory alignment with physics-aware feasibility constraints ( Huang et al., 2026 ) .
Humanoid policies learn task-level behaviors from human experience through latent video actions, geometric pretraining, or joint training on human and robot demonstrations ( Jiang et al., 2026a ; Wei et al., 2026b ; Shi et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026a ) .
ZeroWBC generates and tracks whole-body motion from an initial egocentric image and language instruction without robot teleoperation demonstrations ( Yang et al., 2026a ) ; HALOMI couples egocentric demonstration capture with view alignment and controller-aware reference adaptation for active-perception loco-manipulation ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) .
Simulation provides another route from human video to control: VideoMimic reconstructs human motion and scenes for contextual control ( Allshire et al., 2025 ) , and SUGAR physically refines human-video interaction priors before distilling autonomous policies ( Wu et al., 2026 ) .
GRAIL instead synthesizes interactions from 3D assets and video priors to train visual policies through simulation ( Xie et al., 2026 ) .
LEGS combines procedurally generated demonstrations with photorealistic Gaussian-splatting scene backgrounds to fine-tune humanoid loco-manipulation VLAs without teleoperation ( Kim et al., 2026 ) .
Predictive models and integrated whole-body systems offer complementary ways to connect perception, motion, and control ( Li et al., 2026b ; Symbiosis Robotics, 2026 ; Figure AI, 2026a ; Parada, 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2026a ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) .
Our alignment pipeline addresses both geometric mismatch in motion references and controller execution error, so that recorded human motions can supervise the action interface used by G1.

Supplementary Table 5 compares human-data interfaces, training strategies, and scaling studies.

2026-10-15.title: AdaRSI: On-Demand Recursive Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
2026-10-15.authors: Peidong Wang , Ying Chang , Zhiming Ma , Xiaocui Yang , Shi Feng , Daqi Liu , Yuzhe Yang , Xu Cao , Chuang Wang , Jian Su , Daling Wang
2026-10-15.abstract:
Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks.
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do.
We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents.
A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks.
On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%.
Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) [ 21 , 11 , 1 ] can perform a wide range of manipulation tasks in diverse environments.
Recent models have also made progress on long-horizon tasks [ 27 , 22 ] .
Yet on unseen multi-step tasks they still often fail midway.
A robot may approach the wrong target, misjudge whether a step has succeeded, or fail to execute a required motion.
Some of these failures lie in how the VLA, acting as the executor, is called and others in what it can do, and the failure itself does not tell which.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system turns its own experience into persistent changes that make it better [ 4 , 37 , 3 ] , offers a way to repair such failures without collecting human demonstrations for every new task.
An embodied system, made of a coding agent, its skills and harness, and a low-level executor such as a VLA, can improve itself at two levels.
The harness, comprising the agent’s skills, its tools and the procedure that composes them, decides how the executor is called, while the executor’s weights decide what it can do.

Harness-level methods refine the agent’s skills and tools while keeping the executor frozen [ 16 , 6 , 18 , 31 , 33 , 38 , 30 , 26 , 17 , 25 ] .
Their changes are cheap, readable and easy to revert, but they stall when a task requires a motion the executor cannot perform [ 33 , 29 ] .
Policy-level methods instead update the executor’s weights [ 12 , 9 , 34 , 5 , 15 , 10 ] , some of them directing training toward tasks with low recent success [ 5 ] or toward high-risk scenarios [ 9 ] , and systems that act on both levels train on the data that a refined harness produces [ 32 , 7 ] .
None of these methods asks whether a persistent failure lies in how the executor is called or in a motion it lacks, although the two call for different remedies.
Training on a failure that lies in how the executor is called is not only costly but also risky, as a fine-tuned policy can perform a sub-step worse than the executor it started from.

This raises a question that current embodied RSI leaves open: when should a self-improving system change the weights of its executor?
We argue that the answer is a matter of attribution.
The weights should change only for a sub-step that stays unreliable after the agent has tried other ways of calling the executor, such as other instructions, robot poses or approaches.
Refining the harness first therefore does more than fix the failures that lie in how the executor is called.
It also sets the states from which the executor is called, so that a policy trained afterwards learns the motion that is actually missing, from the states in which it will be used.

We answer this question with AdaRSI , an on-demand recursive self-improvement framework for embodied agents.
The agent first refines its harness from execution feedback, so that the harness absorbs the failures that better calling can fix without any training.
It then attributes the failures that persist, retrying a failing sub-step from a saved simulator state under different instructions and approaches, which separates a poor way of calling the executor from a motion it cannot make.
For the sub-steps that no such retry makes reliable, the agent collects demonstrations in simulation and fine-tunes a sub-step policy from the states its harness reaches.
Each new policy is evaluated on held-out start states, and the procedure calls it only where these measurements show that it helps, so a weight change enters the system only after it has been both attributed and validated.
Improvements accumulate over rounds, each starting from the system that the previous round produced.
Experience and a training budget derived from earlier tasks guide later ones, so the system improves not only itself but also the way it improves.
No human demonstrations are used, and privileged simulator state serves only to generate and label data, never at test time.

We evaluate on all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365 [ 19 , 20 ] under the official protocol, with GR00T N1.5 [ 21 ] as the executor.
AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites, most of all on unseen composite tasks, where it raises success from 4.6% to 13.8%, about three times the base rate.
The harness provides most of this gain, and fine-tuning, which executes only 15% of the manipulation steps, carries the tasks that the harness alone could not solve, such as one that requires opening a microwave door the VLA never opens on its own.
In paired tests from identical states, fine-tuning teaches motions that the executor lacks, but it can degrade sub-steps that the executor already completes.
Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step and calling the new policies by default, AdaRSI reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations.
Fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less, and its deployed system calls few of the policies it trained.
Training instead the sub-steps on which the executor succeeds least, under the same budget, gains nothing over the harness alone, even though most of the sub-steps it trains are the same, as attribution also tells the agent from which states a missing motion should be learned.

Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate on-demand recursive self-improvement for embodied agents, in which the decision to change the executor’s weights rests on attributing each persistent failure to the harness or to the executor, and instantiate it as AdaRSI.

We find that the harness decides whether training pays off, as it absorbs failures that would otherwise be trained on and sets the states from which policies are trained and called, while fine-tuning teaches motions the executor lacks but can degrade sub-steps it already completes.

We show on all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, without any human demonstration, that training on demand improves a pretrained VLA on every suite at a fraction of the training cost of fine-tuning every sub-step.

1. We formulate on-demand recursive self-improvement for embodied agents, in which the decision to change the executor’s weights rests on attributing each persistent failure to the harness or to the executor, and instantiate it as AdaRSI.

2. We find that the harness decides whether training pays off, as it absorbs failures that would otherwise be trained on and sets the states from which policies are trained and called, while fine-tuning teaches motions the executor lacks but can degrade sub-steps it already completes.

3. We show on all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, without any human demonstration, that training on demand improves a pretrained VLA on every suite at a fraction of the training cost of fine-tuning every sub-step.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

VLAs map images and language instructions directly to robot actions [ 11 , 1 , 21 ] .
Trained on large and diverse data, they follow instructions in new environments [ 23 , 8 ] , carry out long-horizon tasks with memory [ 27 , 22 ] , and can be paired with a high-level model that decomposes a task [ 24 ] .
Yet they still generalize poorly to tasks outside their training distribution [ 20 , 39 ] .
We keep a pretrained VLA as the executor and let the embodied system built on it improve itself.

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) refers to systems that turn their own experience into persistent changes that make them better [ 4 , 3 ] , as language-model agents have done by rewriting their own code, harness and skills [ 37 , 13 , 36 , 14 ] .
Most embodied methods refine the agent’s skills and harness while the executor stays frozen [ 16 , 6 , 18 , 31 , 33 , 38 , 30 , 26 , 17 , 25 ] .
They change how and when the executor is called, but not what it can do [ 29 ] .
Other methods improve the executor itself by training policies on self-collected data [ 12 , 9 , 34 , 5 , 35 , 15 , 10 ] .
Some of them choose where to train, practicing tasks with low recent success [ 5 ] or collecting high-risk scenarios for a specialist that a gate calls in place of the nominal policy [ 9 ] , and a few act on both levels [ 32 , 7 ] , for example fine-tuning the policy on data that an evolved harness collects [ 32 ] .
These methods choose which failures to train on, but not whether a failure lies in how the executor is called, which a harness change can fix, or in a motion the executor lacks, which calls for new weights.
We instead attribute each persistent failure to one of the two levels before training, and change the weights only for the sub-steps that remain unreliable after the harness has been refined.

2026-10-15.title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning
2026-10-15.authors: Sayan Bandyapadhyay , William Lochet , Saket Saurabh , Jie Xue
2026-10-15.subjects: Computational Geometry (cs.CG) ; Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-15.abstract:
We study multi-robot Motion Planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots.
The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain 𝒲 \mathcal{W} with n n vertices and k k robots R 1 , … , R k R_{1},\dots,R_{k} translating in 𝒲 \mathcal{W} each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity.
Given a source configuration 𝐬 \mathbf{s} and a target configuration 𝐭 \mathbf{t} of the robots in 𝒲 \mathcal{W} , the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from 𝐬 \mathbf{s} to 𝐭 \mathbf{t} that is shortest with respect to some cost function.
Here a plan is called collision-free if all the robots stay inside 𝒲 \mathcal{W} and no two robots collide with each other during the plan.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Coordinating the motion of multiple robots that share a common workspace is one of the
oldest and most fundamental problems in algorithmic robotics. Autonomous warehouse
fleets, fleets of cleaning or inspection robots, swarms of drones, and automated
manufacturing cells all require a planner that can move many physical agents from
their initial locations to specified destinations without the agents colliding with
one another or with the static obstacles of the environment. Beyond mere feasibility,
practitioners care about the quality of the resulting motion: a plan that
wastes battery, time, or wear-and-tear on the robots is far less useful than one that
moves the robots efficiently.
Despite decades of study, the understanding of
how to compute, or even efficiently approximate, cost-optimal multi-robot motion
plans has remained remarkably incomplete, in sharp contrast with the
single-robot case, for which shortest collision-free paths can be computed exactly in
polynomial time. This gap between the single-robot and multi-robot settings is the
starting point of our work.

A setting of the multi-robot motion planning problem commonly considered in the literature is as follows.
We essentially follow the terms in the previous work [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] .
Let 𝒲 \mathcal{W} be a polygonal domain in ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} with n n vertices, referred to as the workspace .
We are given a collection of k k robots R 1 , … , R k R_{1},\ldots,R_{k} , each of which is typically an axis-parallel unit square (or more generally, a polygon of constant complexity).
In most of the previous work, the robots are required to be identical, but we do not make this assumption in this paper.
A placement of a robot R i R_{i} in 𝒲 \mathcal{W} is given by a vector 𝐩 ∈ ℝ 2 \mathbf{p}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} such that 𝐩 + R i ⊆ 𝒲 \mathbf{p}+R_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{W} .
Here 𝐩 + R i \mathbf{p}+R_{i} denote the translate of R i R_{i} with the offset vector 𝐩 \mathbf{p} .
The set of all placements of R i R_{i} in 𝒲 \mathcal{W} is its free space , denoted by ℱ i ⊆ 𝒲 \mathcal{F}_{i}\subseteq\mathcal{W} .

A configuration is a k k -tuple ( 𝐩 1 , … , 𝐩 k ) ∈ ∏ i = 1 k ℱ i (\mathbf{p}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{p}_{k})\in\prod_{i=1}^{k}\mathcal{F}_{i} ,
where 𝐩 i \mathbf{p}_{i} specifies a placement of robot R i R_{i} in 𝒲 \mathcal{W} .
We say a configuration is feasible if the placed robots are interior-disjoint (or collision-free).
Formally, if we write [ k ] = { 1 , … , k } [k]=\{1,\dots,k\} and denote by int ⁡ ( R ) \operatorname{int}(R) the interior of a region R R , then

A motion plan refers to a scheme that translates the k k robots inside 𝒲 \mathcal{W} from one feasible configuration to another one, while keeping the robots collision-free.
Some variants of the problem may care about the time cost of a motion plan.
As such, there is usually an extra unit-speed constraint in the definition of motion plans: each robot can move with a maximum speed 1 1 during the plan.
Formally, we define motion plans as follows.
Let L 2 ​ ( ⋅ , ⋅ ) L_{2}(\cdot,\cdot) denote the L 2 L_{2} -metric (i.e., Euclidean metric) and π i : ( ℝ 2 ) k → ℝ 2 \pi_{i}:(\mathbb{R}^{2})^{k}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2} be the projection function defined as π i ​ ( 𝐩 1 , … , 𝐩 k ) = 𝐩 i \pi_{i}(\mathbf{p}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{p}_{k})=\mathbf{p}_{i} , for i ∈ [ k ] i\in[k] .
Given a source configuration 𝐬 ∈ 𝐅 \mathbf{s}\in\mathbf{F} and a target configuration 𝐭 ∈ 𝐅 \mathbf{t}\in\mathbf{F} , an ( 𝐬 , 𝐭 ) (\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}) -plan is defined as a continuous 1 1 1 Here 𝐅 \mathbf{F} is viewed as a subspace of ( ℝ 2 ) k (\mathbb{R}^{2})^{k} with the subspace topology. map γ : [ 0 , λ ] → 𝐅 \gamma:[0,\lambda]\rightarrow\mathbf{F} for some λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 such that γ ⁡ ( 0 ) = 𝐬 \gamma(0)=\mathbf{s} , γ ⁡ ( λ ) = 𝐭 \gamma(\lambda)=\mathbf{t} , and L 2 ​ ( π i ​ ( γ ⁡ ( b ) ) , π i ​ ( γ ⁡ ( a ) ) ) ≤ b − a L_{2}(\pi_{i}(\gamma(b)),\pi_{i}(\gamma(a)))\leq{b-a} for all i ∈ [ k ] i\in[k] and all 0 ≤ a < b ≤ λ 0\leq a<b\leq\lambda .
Here the last condition is the unit-speed constraint guaranteeing that the maximum speed of each robot is at most 1 1 during the plan.
The general form of the Motion Planning problem is the following.

Let γ : [ 0 , λ ] → 𝐅 \gamma:[0,\lambda]\rightarrow\mathbf{F} be an ( 𝐬 , 𝐭 ) (\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}) -plan.
For each i ∈ [ k ] i\in[k] , π i ∘ γ \pi_{i}\circ\gamma is a plane curve describing how the robot R i R_{i} moves in the plan.
We denote by | π i ∘ γ | |\pi_{i}\circ\gamma| the length of the curve, i.e., the traveling distance of R i R_{i} in the plan.
Two commonly studied cost functions for evaluating the quality of an ( 𝐬 , 𝐭 ) (\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}) -plan in multi-robot motion planning are the sum-cost and the max-cost , defined as

When the number of robots, k k , is part of the input, even deciding whether there exists an ( 𝐬 , 𝐭 ) (\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}) -plan (without any optimization objective at all) is already a hard algorithmic problem.
Schwartz and Sharir [ 19 ] gave one of the first algorithms for coordinating disk-shaped robots among polygonal obstacles, running in time polynomial in the complexity of the obstacles but exponential in k k .
Soon after, Hopcroft, Schwartz, and Sharir [ 13 ] showed that this exponential dependence on k k is in a precise sense unavoidable: they proved that deciding the existence of ( 𝐬 , 𝐭 ) (\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}) -plans for an arbitrary number of unit-square robots translating in a rectangular workspace is PSPACE-hard, a result later strengthened and extended in several directions [ 1 , 7 , 12 , 14 ] .
Around the same time, Spirakis and Yap [ 20 ] showed that the problem for unit-disk robots is strongly NP-hard.
These hardness results already rule out, under standard complexity assumptions, an algorithm with time
polynomial in both n n and k k for testing the existence of ( 𝐬 , 𝐭 ) (\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}) -plans, let alone for the optimization variants.

Given that the general problem for unbounded k k is provably intractable, most
algorithmic results restrict attention to a small, constant number of robots, i.e., treat k k as a parameter rather than part of the input.
For Motion Planning with a single robot ( k = 1 k=1 ), an exact optimal solution can be computed in polynomial time using classical
techniques for shortest paths amid obstacles [ 9 , 17 , 18 ] , which already indicates that the difficulty of the motion-planning problems stems from the interaction between robots rather than from planning for a single robot alone.

For k = 2 k=2 , Motion Planning is already quite challenging, and positive results have been known only very recently.
When the workspace 𝒲 \mathcal{W} is rectilinear and the cost is evaluated under the L 1 L_{1} -metric, Agarwal, de Berg,
Holmgren, Steiger, and Struijs [ 2 ] considered the problem with two unit-square robots.
In this setting, they gave an exact O ⁡ ( n 4 ​ log ⁡ n ) O(n^{4}\log n) -time algorithm for the min-sum variant and proved that the min-makespan variant is NP-hard.
In a general polygonal workspace 𝒲 \mathcal{W} under the Euclidean metric, however, it is open whether the problem is NP-hard or polynomial-time solvable for any of the cost functions.
The best known result with two unit-square robots is a ( 1 + ε ) (1+\varepsilon) -approximation algorithm, in fact an FPTAS, for the min-sum objective, due to Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, and Steiger [ 4 ] .
Their algorithm crucially exploits the fact that, for two robots, there is always a near-optimal plan in which the robots
move one at a time; for k > 2 k>2 robots this property provably fails, since one can construct instances in which every near-optimal plan must move several robots simultaneously, which makes the generalization beyond two robots difficult.

For k ≥ 3 k\geq 3 , the only known result so far is due to Agarwal, Holmgren, and Steiger [ 5 ] , who gave a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for Min-Sum Motion Planning with k k unit-square robots, with running time ( k / ε ) O ⁡ ( k 2 ) ​ n O ⁡ ( k ) (k/\varepsilon)^{O(k^{2})}n^{O(k)} , in the sense that the solution returned by the algorithm is an ( 𝐬 , 𝐭 ) (\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}) -plan γ \gamma satisfying that 𝖼𝗈𝗌𝗍 + ​ ( γ ) ≤ ( 1 + ε ) ⋅ 𝗈𝗉𝗍 1 + ε + ε \mathsf{cost}^{+}(\gamma)\leq(1+\varepsilon)\cdot\mathsf{opt}_{1+\varepsilon}+\varepsilon , where 𝗈𝗉𝗍 1 + ε \mathsf{opt}_{1+\varepsilon} denotes the cost of a min-sum ( 𝐬 , 𝐭 ) (\mathbf{s},\mathbf{t}) -plan with ( 1 + ε ) × ( 1 + ε ) (1+\varepsilon)\times(1+\varepsilon) square robots.
Note that 𝗈𝗉𝗍 1 + ε \mathsf{opt}_{1+\varepsilon} is in general not bounded by any function of the actual optimum, and the bound also has an additive error ε \varepsilon , which can be removed if 𝗈𝗉𝗍 1 + ε ≥ 1 \mathsf{opt}_{1+\varepsilon}\geq 1 [ 5 ] .
An equivalent view of the algorithm in [ 5 ] is that it shrinks each robot by a factor of 1 + ε 1+\varepsilon and computes the approximation solution with the shrunk robots.
The arguments in [ 5 ] relied heavily on this shrink operation, making it difficult to transform the bicriteria-approximation algorithm to an actual FPTAS.
Furthermore, it is not clear whether the approximation algorithms in [ 4 ] and [ 5 ] can be applied to the min-max and min-makespan objectives as well.

Given the aforementioned approximation algorithms in [ 4 , 5 ] , the most natural question to be asked now is about the approximability of the problems for a general (fixed) k k .
Specifically, the question below has been mentioned in the previous work [ 4 , 5 ] as an open question.

In this paper, we resolve (in a stronger form) the above open question, by giving the first FPTAS for Min-Sum/Min-Max/Min-Makespan Motion Planning with general polygonal robots (of constant complexity) for any fixed k ∈ ℕ k\in\mathbb{N} .
Specifically, we prove the following theorem.

Min-Sum Motion Planning , Min-Max Motion Planning , and Min-Makespan Motion Planning with polygonal robots admit ( 1 + ε ) (1+\varepsilon) -approximation algorithms of running time f ⁡ ( k , ε ) ⋅ n O ⁡ ( k 2 ) f(k,\varepsilon)\cdot n^{O(k^{2})} , for some function f ⁡ ( k , ε ) = k O ⁡ ( k 2 ) ​ ( 1 ε ) O ⁡ ( k ) f(k,\varepsilon)=k^{O(k^{2})}(\frac{1}{\varepsilon})^{O(k)} .
In particular, for any fixed number k ∈ ℕ k\in\mathbb{N} of robots, the three problems admit FPTAS.

We remark that the polygonal robots in Theorem 1 are not required to be identical.
In fact, there is no assumptions on the polygons representing the robots, except the constant complexity.
However, for technical reasons, our result does not generalize (without new ideas) to robots with non-linear boundaries, while the bicriteria-approximation in [ 5 ] works for unit-disk robots.

Interestingly, our algorithm in Theorem 1 is not restricted to Motion Planning in the plane, but directly generalizes to Motion Planning in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} for any fixed d ∈ ℕ d\in\mathbb{N} with polytope workspace and polytope robots.
To the best of our knowledge, the problem in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} for d > 2 d>2 is widely open.

In terms of the techniques, our algorithms are substantially simpler than the previous approximation algorithms [ 4 , 5 ] .
The proof of Theorem 1 is essentially self-contained and only uses classic techniques in computational geometry and algorithmic graph theory.
Surprisingly, our proof does not rely on any structural results developed in the previous work [ 2 , 4 , 5 ] .

All of the min-sum, min-max, and min-makespan variants are solved within a single unified framework.
This unified treatment is, we believe, of independent interest, since it suggests that the three common objective functions for multi-robot motion planning are algorithmically much closer to one another than their rather different behavior in the discrete multi-agent path finding setting might suggest [ 11 , 22 , 21 ] .
To explain the unified framework, we need to introduce an α \alpha -restricted version of the problem.

The first component is a sub-routine that can estimate the optimum of the problem instance, 𝗈𝗉𝗍 \mathsf{opt} , with a multiplicative error ( k ​ n ) O ⁡ ( k ) (kn)^{O(k)} .

For simplicity of exposition, we present our algorithms for Motion Planning in the plane.
The generalization to higher dimensions is straightforward.
In Section 2 , we introduce the basic notions and preliminaries needed for our result.
Section 3 presents the high-level framework of our algorithms.
Section 4 proves the existence of an optimal solution with certain nice properties.

2026-10-15.title: Why 3D Reconstruction Breaks Down on Under-Ice AUV Video, and How to Predict It
2026-10-15.authors: Ana-Ştefania Kogălniceanu , Klára Orbán , Ashwin Nedungadi , Stefan Lüdtke , Kuderna-Iulian Benţa
2026-10-15.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-15.comment: Short paper presented at the 2nd Workshop on Marine Vision, ECCV 2026, Malmö, Sweden, September 8, 2026. Published on OpenReview: this https URL
2026-10-15.abstract: Reconstruction of 3D structures using under-ice AUV video footage has been inaccurate, although it is not certain whether this is due to shortcomings in the methods or an inherent deficiency of the capture system. We test four different models for reconstruction on the same Antarctic under-ice AUV video (Icefin, Kamb Ice Stream): classical feature matching SfM, differentiable photometric splatting, volumetric depth fusion, and a pose-free feed-forward foundation model. All four fail, each in a distinct way: near-total registration yielding almost no structure, geometrically broken output despite healthy photometric metrics, a persistent coverage artifact, and unstable cross-chunk scale. We show that all four are consistent with the same capture regime, a small camera-baseline-to-scene-depth ratio. Following our analysis, we propose a detection system that flags this type of failure in minutes, rather than hours of wasted compute.
2026-10-15.introduction:
3D reconstruction from under-ice AUV video is persistently unreliable: turbidity and backscatter flatten contrast, while the ice underside is often smooth and weakly textured [ 1 , 8 ] . Although mitigations exist, it remains unclear whether the residual failures reflect the shortcomings of any one method or a deeper limitation of the capture geometry itself. Slow-moving AUVs sampled at low frame rates produce near-converging camera trajectories with limited translation between viewpoints, unlike the wide-baseline, well-distributed views on which most reconstruction pipelines are designed and validated. In practice, researchers face large collections of such footage where reconstruction success is difficult to anticipate, and substantial compute is routinely spent on batches that converge to geometrically fragmented output, with the failure only apparent after the fact.

Prior work in this space has largely evaluated individual pipelines in isolation [ 11 , 5 , 13 ] , without asking whether failures across structurally
different methods share a common, measurable cause. This distinction matters: if
failure is method-specific, the fix is method-specific tuning; if failure is
geometric, the fix is a single early warning system that generalizes across
pipelines.

This work tests four structurally unrelated reconstruction approaches: classical feature-matching SfM, differentiable photometric splatting, volumetric depth fusion, and a pose-free feed-forward foundation model – on the same under-ice AUV footage (Icefin, Kamb Ice Stream, USAP-DC 601975 [ 15 ] ), and shows that all four fail for reasons traceable to the same capture regime. The main contributions of this work are:

identification of a single quantified geometric predictor: a narrow camera baseline-to-scene-depth ratio that explains the distinct failure modes of four structurally different reconstruction methods on the same footage,

a lightweight baseline-to-depth check, derived directly from foundation-model camera poses, that flags likely failure in minutes rather than hours,

a negative control against the competing hypothesis that reconstructability is predictable from image content, rather than capture geometry: a texture-usability score, tested against altimeter ground truth, did not hold up.

# 2 Related work

Classical Structure-from-Motion methods such as COLMAP [ 11 ] recover camera poses and sparse structure through incremental feature matching and bundle adjustment, with dense surfaces typically obtained through volumetric depth fusion into a signed-distance field [ 3 ] . While these pipelines are well validated for wide-baseline, well-distributed captures, their behavior under narrow-baseline, near-converging viewpoints remains comparatively unexplored. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [ 5 ] replaces explicit correspondence search with differentiable photometric optimization, achieving high-quality novel-view synthesis without directly guaranteeing geometric consistency, a limitation that underwater adaptations have had to address [ 16 ] . Feed-forward foundation models such as DUSt3R [ 14 ] and its more scalable successor VGGT [ 13 ] instead predict camera poses and dense point maps directly from images, avoiding iterative optimization but introducing a different failure mode: maintaining consistent scale and pose across inference chunks.

AUV-based seafloor mapping has similarly reported reconstruction gaps and weakly reconstructed regions caused by platform motion and uneven illumination [ 12 ] . Icefin-based surveys demonstrate the scientific value of under-ice observation [ 6 ] , but the reliability of 3D reconstruction from such footage remains largely unaddressed. A smaller body of work has explored predicting reconstruction quality before running a full pipeline, including models linking UAV image characteristics such as blur, exposure, and noise to point-cloud accuracy [ 7 ] , no-reference image-quality measures based on photogrammetric descriptors [ 10 ] , and preprocessing strategies for blurred or texture-poor imagery [ 4 ] . However, these approaches primarily assess 2D image quality rather than 3D capture geometry.

2026-10-15.title: HyperLoop: Hyperspectral-Assisted Loop Closure Detection in 3D-SLAM for Planetary Exploration
2026-10-15.authors: Annie Bhalla , Dennis Rotondi , Riccardo Giubilato , Kai O. Arras , Wolfgang Stuerzl
2026-10-15.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-15.comment: Paper accepted at International Astronautical Congress 2026, IAC-26, A3, IP, 163, x107111
2026-10-15.abstract:
Autonomous navigation of planetary rovers remains a fundamental challenge in space
exploration, particularly in environments that are featureless, poorly illuminated,
or visually repetitive. Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) systems based
on 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) offer promising dense mapping capabilities; however,
their loop closure modules rely on RGB appearance descriptors that degrade under
perceptual aliasing–a common failure mode in extraterrestrial terrain where
physically distinct locations appear visually identical to optical sensors.
This paper presents HyperLoop, the first framework integrating hyperspectral imaging
(HSI) into the loop closure module of a 3DGS-based SLAM system.
Hyperspectral descriptors encode material-level spectral signatures that complement
RGB appearance features, providing a modality inherently robust to illumination
changes and visual repetitiveness.
Two HSI descriptor families are introduced: the Bag-of-Spectral-Words (BoSW)
model, which encodes spectral material distributions via TF-IDF weighted
frequency histograms, and the PCA-K VLAD (PCAK-VLAD) model, which captures
first-order residual statistics of PCA-compressed spectral signatures.
Both are evaluated in combination with SIFT-VLAD and NetVLAD RGB descriptors
under Strict-AND and Weighted decision-level fusion strategies.
The framework is assessed on a custom multi-modal dataset collected at the
Moon-Mars Outdoor Test Site (MMOTS) of the German Aerospace Center (DLR),
comprising synchronized RGB-D and hyperspectral sequences totalling 65.5 m
across four planetary analog traverses, with evaluation conducted on the
MMOTS-WS loop sequence (8 m).
A key empirical finding is that the sensor’s Red-NIR spectral range (600–860 nm)
provides limited discriminability for planetary analog rock terrain: the best fusion configuration (SIFT-VLAD + BoSW, Strict-AND) achieves
5.04 cm aligned ATE RMSE, within 1.8% of the best RGB-only configuration
(4.95 cm, SIFT-VLAD alone). The improvement over the NetVLAD baseline (8.81 cm) is attributable
entirely to replacing NetVLAD with SIFT-VLAD, not to HSI fusion;
the sensor’s Red-NIR spectral range is identified as the primary
limiting factor for the HSI contribution.
This motivates future adoption of shortwave infrared (SWIR) sensors,
which capture diagnostic mineral absorption features absent from the
600–860 nm range, for planetary SLAM missions.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM)—the joint estimation of a
robot’s pose and a map of its surroundings from on-board sensor data—has
reached remarkable maturity over the past two decades [ 1 ] .
Classical geometrically-grounded pipelines now achieve centimetre-level
accuracy in structured environments, while recent semantic extensions such as
3D scene graph representations [ 2 ] further enrich
these maps with object-level and spatial reasoning. Yet this progress has
been concentrated in information-rich, feature-dense settings: urban streets,
indoor offices, and structured facilities where visual cues are abundant and
predictable. Mapping in extreme environments —planetary surfaces
dominated by featureless regolith, visually repetitive craters, and
mineralogically diverse rocks—remains a frontier where classical SLAM
assumptions break down.

Autonomous navigation of planetary rovers must contend with exactly these
conditions. Rovers must navigate unknown, unstructured terrain autonomously,
performing in-situ scientific analysis while building consistent environmental
representations. Unlike the structured, feature-rich urban environments common
on Earth, extraterrestrial terrain is dominated by craters, regolith, rocks,
and dust that create a visually repetitive landscape. This causes perceptual aliasing : distinct locations appear nearly identical to
optical sensors. In SLAM, this directly impairs loop closure detection :
the critical process of recognising a previously visited location to correct
accumulated odometric drift. Failed loop closures produce corrupted maps and
irrecoverable trajectory divergence, threatening mission success.

Despite visual similarity, planetary terrain is often mineralogically
diverse. Rocks of different composition, regolith with varying particle
distributions, and exposed bedrock exhibit distinct spectral signatures
in the infrared range, differences entirely invisible to conventional
RGB cameras. Hyperspectral imaging (HSI) captures tens to hundreds of
narrow spectral bands per pixel, encoding material composition and
chemical properties as a high-dimensional fingerprint. These signatures
reflect what a surface is made of rather than how it appears,
and are inherently more robust to illumination changes.

Recent advances in 3DGS [ 3 ] have transformed dense visual
SLAM by enabling efficient, photorealistic scene representations.
LoopSplat [ 4 ] , the first 3DGS SLAM system with explicit
loop closure, demonstrates compelling performance in structured indoor
environments using NetVLAD [ 5 ] descriptors. However,
its reliance on RGB appearance limits applicability to the visually
uniform terrain of planetary environments.

This paper introduces HyperLoop , extending LoopSplat by
integrating hyperspectral sensing into its loop closure module.
The key contributions are:

A 3DGS-SLAM architecture integrating HSI loop closure detection, the
first such combination, to the best of our knowledge.

Two HSI descriptor families: BoSW and PCAK-VLAD, adapted from
visual retrieval literature to spectral signatures.

Evaluation of Strict-AND and Weighted decision-level fusion
strategies combining RGB and HSI descriptors.

The first empirical analysis of hyperspectral loop closure on
a planetary analog dataset, yielding an empirically motivated
spectral range hypothesis for future mission hardware selection.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows:
Section 2 covers relevant background;
Section 3 reviews related work;
Section 4 describes the HyperLoop methodology;
Section 5 presents the experimental setup;
Section 6 analyses descriptor performance;
Section 7 reports trajectory and loop closure results;
Sections 8 and 9 discuss findings and conclude.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Background

## 2.1 SLAM and Loop Closure

SLAM jointly estimates a robot’s pose trajectory and map from on-board
sensor data [ 1 ] . Sensor noise causes odometric drift ;
loop closure corrects it by recognising a previously visited location,
inserting a constraint, and triggering Pose Graph Optimisation (PGO) [ 6 ] .
The pipeline comprises (1) place recognition via descriptor similarity
and (2) geometric verification via spatial consistency checks.
In planetary terrain, both stages are challenged: perceptual aliasing
degrades appearance-based retrieval, and surface planarity limits geometric filtering.

## 2.2 3D Gaussian Splatting and LoopSplat

3DGS [ 3 ] represents a scene as a collection of anisotropic
3D Gaussian primitives, each parameterised by position 𝝁 \boldsymbol{\mu} ,
covariance 𝚺 \boldsymbol{\Sigma} , opacity α \alpha , and view-dependent
colour encoded via spherical harmonics (SH, a basis for view-dependent appearance).
Differentiable splatting projects each 3D Gaussian as a 2D Gaussian; overlapping
splats are composited via depth-sorted alpha-blending, enabling gradient-based
optimisation of all parameters.

LoopSplat [ 4 ] implements a real-time dense RGB-D SLAM
system on 3DGS with explicit loop closure. It maintains submaps (groups of keyframes) for computational tractability. Tracking minimises
photometric and geometric losses. Loop closure candidates are retrieved
via NetVLAD cosine similarity and verified by computing the geometric
overlap of Gaussian splats between candidate submaps. Confirmed loops
trigger submap registration in Gaussian space followed by PGO.

## 2.3 Hyperspectral Imaging

A hyperspectral image is a data cube H × W × B H\times W\times B , where B B is the number of spectral bands. Each pixel stores a spectral
signature : reflectance at B B wavelengths, encoding material
composition. Raw measurements are converted to reflectance via
calibration [ 7 ] :

## 2.4 Multi-Modal Sensor Fusion

Multi-modal sensor fusion combines information from heterogeneous
sensors to improve robustness beyond what any single modality
can achieve [ 8 ] .
Three levels of fusion are commonly distinguished. Early (data-level) fusion merges raw sensor measurements
before any feature extraction, requiring tight spatial and temporal
alignment between modalities. Feature-level fusion concatenates or projects intermediate
representations into a shared embedding space, and is applicable
when modalities share a common field of view. Decision-level (late) fusion combines independent
per-modality decisions or scores, and is applicable even when
modalities have mismatched resolutions, fields of view,
or update rates–making it the most flexible strategy for
heterogeneous sensor pairs.

2026-10-15.title: What Happens to the Goal? Distinct Failures of Policy Alignment in Goal Misgeneralization
2026-10-15.authors: Julia Barth , Armin Sommer , Kunvar Thaman , Jannik Schilling
2026-10-15.comment: main text, total. Code: this https URL
2026-10-15.abstract:
Goal misgeneralization is a common failure mode in which an agent behaves competently out of distribution but does not pursue the intended goal. However, we still have a weak understanding of what happens to the intended goal in misgeneralizing agents.
Across three Procgen environments and five robot tasks, we find three distinct forms of policy–goal misalignment: (1) functional target substitution, where behavior follows an alternative goal, (2) a policy shortcut, where behavior follows a learned action strategy, and (3) cue competition between intended and proxy goal cues.
We distinguish these regimes by tracing where goal information remains available internally, how strongly it influences the policy, and what role it plays in action selection, and find that the goal is lost at different depths.
Where the goal reaches the decision, as in cue competition, steering redirects the policy to the goal’s location, raising intended-goal reach from 16.0 % 16.0\% to 95.3 % 95.3\% . Where it reaches the policy but not the decision, only new downstream wiring recovers goal reach, from 31.6 % 31.6\% to 84.3 % 84.3\% in the environment with the action shortcut. Where it is inert, neither works.
Our results show that goal misgeneralization is not a single failure of goal representation, but distinct failures of policy alignment at different depths, tightly connected to which recovery works.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Reinforcement learning specifies the intended goal only indirectly, through rewards that mark it.
Whenever a proxy co-occurs with the goal during training, the rewards cannot tell the two apart, and the agent can learn the proxy in its place.
This is why goal misgeneralization is common in reinforcement learning, and it is dangerous because the agent stays competent and its misalignment only becomes visible once the co-occurrence breaks.

So far, goal misgeneralization has mainly been characterized behaviorally, in large language models ( Shah et al., 2022 ; Maniyar et al., 2026 ) , in toy reinforcement-learning environments such as Procgen ( Langosco et al., 2022 ; Ramanauskas & Şimşek, 2023 ) and in large pretrained control policies ( Jucys et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) .
Interpretability work has studied individual agents in these environments ( Mini et al., 2023 ; Trinh et al., 2024 ) , mostly to understand how they navigate or represent their goal, but not goal misgeneralization itself, and mitigation attempts intervene broadly during training ( Langosco et al., 2022 ; Abdel Sadek et al., 2025 ; Nait El Barj & Sautory, 2024 ; Armstrong et al., 2023 ; Trinh et al., 2024 ) rather than after it.
Studying goal misgeneralization in depth, from the inside and the outside, closes the gap between these lines of work, and we additionally carry it into a new and wider domain, robot control.
The leading question we ask is therefore quite direct: what actually happens to the true goal in misgeneralized agents?

To answer it, we trace the goal through the agent from the outside and the inside, asking whether the goal is represented, whether the policy reads it, whether behavior is organized around it, and whether goal-directed behavior can be recovered at test time.
We analyze three classic goal-misgeneralization environments from Procgen, Maze , Coin and Maze II, which we call Attribute Maze , and five new robot tasks on a simulated arm and quadruped, such as PushToMarker (Figure 1 , Figure 13 ).

What looks like one failure from the outside is three distinct failures of policy alignment, target substitution, a policy shortcut and cue competition, and the goal gets lost at different depths of the agent.
We find that in Maze , replicated in a simulated arm task, the goal is inert to the policy and a place substitutes for it.
In PushToMarker a place substitutes for the goal as well, but the goal still reaches the policy weakly, which reacts to it without following it.
This is the same depth at which an action shortcut bypasses the goal in Coin .
In Attribute Maze , replicated in three more robot tasks, the goal reaches the decision as a cue or an object that competes with the proxy and loses.
We find that which repair works follows the depth, not the failure type.
Steering the existing policy redirects it to the goal’s location only where the goal reaches the decision.
Relearning the readout recovers goal-directed behavior wherever the goal still reaches the policy, and where the goal is inert, neither repair works.
Misgeneralized agents therefore cannot be understood from their behavior alone, as only knowing where the goal is lost tells us which repair can bring it back.

Our main contributions are:

We trace the intended goal through misgeneralized agents in eight environments and find three distinct failures of policy alignment at three depths, including the first internal characterization of cue and object competition and its geometry (Section 3 ).

We add an internal view and deepen the behavioral one to better understand goal misgeneralization. We propose the Fisher information of the policy with respect to its internal representations to isolate a policy-directed view of the internals, which lets us characterize, for example, different styles of competition. It also sharpens a proxy characterization of Langosco et al. (2022) , as the Maze agent follows the top-right extreme of the current maze rather than a fixed corner.

To our knowledge, we are the first to relate which repair succeeds to where the goal is lost, and to recover goal-directed behavior at test time without further reinforcement learning or retraining the representation (Section 4 ).

We are the first to induce goal misgeneralization systematically in reinforcement learning for robot control and diagnose it in five simulated arm and quadruped tasks, where the failures recur.

2026-10-15.title: VLRLA: Deployment-Time Adaptation of Vision-Language-Action Models through In-Context Reinforcement Learning
2026-10-15.authors: Diyuan Shi , Yiqi Tang , Hongyin Zhang , You Wu , Donglin Wang
2026-10-15.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual perception and language understanding with robot control, providing a foundation for instruction-conditioned manipulation. However, conventional pretrained VLA policies lack a mechanism for gradual adaptation through accumulated interaction experience during deployment. We therefore propose VLRLA, a general framework that equips existing VLA models with in-context reinforcement learning capabilities for deployment-time adaptation. Our approach augments a VLA model with a reinforcement learning module that learns from historical observations, actions, rewards, and termination signals. During deployment, the policy gradually refines its action generation and progressively improves task success while keeping model parameters fixed. Our approach is also designed for general applicability and compatibility with diverse learning history construction strategies and model training pipelines. Finally, through extensive experiments, we systematically investigate the learning properties of VLRLA in simulation and demonstrate its ability to adapt to unseen scenarios during real-world deployment.
2026-10-15.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions, enabling robots to interpret their surroundings and carry out user requests. Their potential applications span household assistance, warehouse logistics, and industrial manipulation ( Collaboration et al., 2023 ; Intelligence et al., 2025b ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Ai et al., ; Xu et al., 2026 ) .

Conventional VLA methods learn from collected demonstrations and could generalize to new situations. However, demonstration-based training alone does not provide a mechanism for gradual adaptation after deployment. A robot may encounter an unfamiliar camera viewpoint, lighting condition, or instruction phrasing, each of which hinders task performance. The central limitation is therefore the inability to turn accumulated deployment experience into adaptive behavior.

Online Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) or interactive Imitation Learning (IIL) provide routes to deployment-time adaptation through parameter updates, using reward feedback or corrective actions, respectively ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ; Intelligence et al., 2025a ; Pan et al., 2026 ) . However, these approaches have several drawbacks: 1) Collecting the samples needed for policy updates takes tens of minutes to hours and involves substantial human effort; 2) They typically require task-specific hyperparameter tuning; and 3) They update policy in each deployment environment, making it difficult to scale to multi-task settings. These motivate us to explore an adaptation mechanism that uses deployment feedback without parameter updates.

In this work, we propose VLRLA, a framework for equipping VLA models with in-context Reinforcement Learning (RL) capabilities. The framework augments a VLA model with a RL module that learns to use past interactions for adaptation. During deployment, action generation is conditioned on a memory of previous interactions and reward feedback, while model parameters remain fixed. As experience accumulates, this memory informs refinements to subsequent behavior, helping policy adapt to the deployment environment. The intended result is gradual improvement in task success through continued interaction during deployment and no parameter updates.

Existing VLA works vary across training datasets, policy architectures, and deployment tasks, we aim to develop a general VLRLA framework that accommodates various learning history construction strategies, policy instantiations, and integration strategies. Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate deployment-time adaptation in VLA models as an in-context reinforcement learning problem, using accumulated interactions and reward feedback to inform subsequent decisions while keeping model parameters fixed.

We propose a general framework that unifies learning history construction and adaptation-module integration to equip pretrained VLA models with in-context reinforcement learning capabilities across diverse data construction settings, model architectures, and deployment tasks.

We conduct extensive experiments in simulation and on real-world robots to demonstrate the effectiveness of VLRLA. Our results show adaptation across multiple pretrained backbones and improved task success with accumulated experience, including on challenging unseen tasks.

1. We formulate deployment-time adaptation in VLA models as an in-context reinforcement learning problem, using accumulated interactions and reward feedback to inform subsequent decisions while keeping model parameters fixed.

2. We propose a general framework that unifies learning history construction and adaptation-module integration to equip pretrained VLA models with in-context reinforcement learning capabilities across diverse data construction settings, model architectures, and deployment tasks.

3. We conduct extensive experiments in simulation and on real-world robots to demonstrate the effectiveness of VLRLA. Our results show adaptation across multiple pretrained backbones and improved task success with accumulated experience, including on challenging unseen tasks.
2026-10-15.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action Models. VLA models integrate visual and language representations with action prediction to support generalist robotic manipulation. Progress in this direction has centered on expanding the data and representations learning for training robot policies. The RT series ( RT1, 2022 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ; Collaboration et al., 2023 ) advances generalist robot control through multi-task learning, web-scale vision-language knowledge transfer, and training across robot embodiments. OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) makes VLA modeling accessible through an open-source model trained on diverse robot demonstrations and designed to support efficient fine-tuning. π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Intelligence et al., 2025b ) pursues open-world generalization by co-training on heterogeneous robot and web data, combining semantic subtask prediction with robot control. LingBot-VLA ( Wu et al., 2026 ) further explores large-scale pretraining across multiple dual-arm robot configurations, releasing a model, training infrastructure, and evaluation data to support adaptation across tasks and platforms. In this work, we study how to equip existing VLA models with in-context Reinforcement Learning capabilities for deployment-time adaptation.

Deep Reinforcement Learning. DRL enables policies to improve through trial-and-error. Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) uses a policy-gradient surrogate objective to learn from on-policy rollouts. Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) ( Haarnoja et al., 2019 ) combines off-policy actor–critic learning with an entropy maximization framework for continuous control. Recent studies apply these policy optimization principles to finetune pretrained VLA models. Examining the generalization benefits of RL fine-tuning, Liu et al. (2026) report that PPO-based OpenVLA fine-tuning improves semantic and execution generalization over supervised fine-tuning. SimpleVLA-RL ( Li et al., 2025 ) also combines parallel trajectory collection with VLA-specific training optimizations to scale reward-based RL for OpenVLA-OFT. Other methods focus on online DRL fine-tuning directly in real-world tasks: RLToken ( Xu et al., 2026 ) uses a compact representation from a pretrained VLA for sample-efficient online DRL fine-tuning. Similarly, DSRL ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ) learns an RL policy over the latent-noise input of a frozen diffusion or flow policy. These methods require parameter updates during RL fine-tuning, whereas our work studies in-context adaptation with all parameters fixed.

In-Context Learning. Recent robotics research explores how demonstrations, prompts, and interaction histories can guide action generation at inference time for VLA models. For adaptation from demonstrations, In-Context Robot Transformer (ICRT) ( Fu et al., 2024 ) predicts actions from sensorimotor trajectories, allowing new tasks to be specified through demonstration prompts without parameter fine-tuning. π 0.7 \pi_{0.7} ( Ai et al., ) combines language, subgoal images, and episode metadata to steer task execution, highlighting the role of multimodal context in generalization. In concurrent work, RoboTTT ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) compresses visuomotor context into recurrent fast weights through test-time training, focusing on one-shot imitation from human videos and online corrections learned through DAgger ( Ross et al., 2011 ) distillation. Specifically, reward-driven adaptation is addressed by Algorithm Distillation (AD) ( Laskin et al., 2022b ) which performs in-context RL in discrete simulation environments. In contrast, our work focuses on designing a general framework to equip existing VLA models with in-context RL capabilities across diverse learning history construction strategies and model settings with validated effectiveness in both simulation and real-world continuous robot control tasks.

2026-10-15.title: Seeing, Maintaining, and Learning: The Evolution of Multimodal Agent Memory
2026-10-15.authors: Minghao Guo , Qingyue Jiao , Xiujin Liu , Jianhong Pang , Ruimeng Yang , Naihao Xu , Liwei Che , Haochen Xue , Ziqi Wang , Xinying Cai , Jiaxuan Luo , Jiaxin Deng , Xuesong Ye , Jintao Qu , Wenyao Gao , Jingwen Gu , Chenyang Zhao , Shichun Liu , Guibin Zhang , Zefang Liu , Siyin Wang , Wujiang Xu , Danrui Li , Zeru Shi , Woongyeong Yeo , Shuang Liu , Wei-Chieh Huang , Weizhi Zhang , Tianyu Yang , Kangsan Kim , Yebowen Hu , Bowen Wen , Bowen Jiang , Haohao Su , Ming Yin , Sheldon Yu , Mian Zhang , Yuyan Chen , Hanrong Zhang , Kai Mei , Zihao Zhang , Mingyu Jin , Xi Zhu , Hengyi Wang , Tianxin Wei , Linyong Nan , Zhenwen Liang , Zhendong Chu , Ziqi Huang , Yongye Su , Sixun Dong , Shujian Liu , Kaiqu Liang , Jiaojiao Han , Zhaoye Fei , Kun Wang , Shihan Dou , Zhichun Guo , Xingjian Diao , Zeqi Gu , Heng Wang , Tao Feng , Cheng Qian , Hamid Palangi , Silei Xu , Xi Yun , Yi Zhu , Shilong Liu , Qingsong Wen , Sung Ju Hwang , Zuxuan Wu , Yu-Gang Jiang , Yiyu Shi , Dimitris N.
