2026-10-16.title: Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards
2026-10-16.authors: Helena Merker , Nick Walker , Andreea Bobu
2026-10-16.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-16.comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin, TX.
2026-10-16.abstract:
Reward learning typically assumes the human’s input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features—or aspects of the task—better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot.
Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn’t know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human’s attention on exactly those features.
In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to 30.8 % 30.8\% in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.
2026-10-16.introduction:
When a human teaches a robot how to do a task, not every relevant aspect of the task—or feature —gets equal attention. For instance, while teaching a robot how to carry a knife across your cluttered kitchen, you might do a good job avoiding the hot stovetop or the rack hanging overhead, but struggle to consistently keep the knife away from every person or obstacle. Because humans have limited working memory and can’t focus on everything at once [ 1 , 2 ] , some features get carefully attended to while others are left underspecified . Recent work shows how the robot can detect, directly from its teaching data, which features were poorly supervised or entirely irrelevant to the task [ 3 , 4 ] . We go a step further and ask: how should the robot work with the human to resolve that underspecification?

One approach is to ask the human for more demonstrations focused on the underspecified features [ 3 ] . But this places the burden on the human, who already struggled with attending to those features. We propose to shift this burden onto the robot: rather than ask the human to try again, the robot should itself ask targeted questions that resolve what it is uncertain about.

Preference queries, where the robot generates behavior options and the human just picks their preferred one, offer this kind of low-effort channel [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . Active learning approaches select queries to maximally reduce uncertainty under a distribution over the human’s reward [ 6 ] . But when that distribution is initialized from imperfect teaching data [ 8 ] , it inherits not just what the feedback got right but also its errors on the underspecified features. The robot then spends its early queries correcting a misaligned distribution before it can make progress on what it actually needs to learn.

Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn’t know can help it ask better questions . The robot’s diagnosis of what past teaching missed serves two roles. First, we use it to build an informed prior over the human’s reward: a Gaussian that is confident on the well-supervised features, flat on the underspecified ones, and near zero on irrelevant ones. This ensures preference queries are automatically directed at what needs resolving.
Second, we use it to supplement each query with an explanation that tells the human which features to focus on when answering, making the robot’s learning process transparent [ 9 ] .
In Fig. 1 , the robot communicates uncertainty about distance to human, and its query presents two options that vary along that feature. Together, these two components align what the robot asks with what the human attends to.

Our contributions are: (1) an informed prior for active preference learning that corrects what the teaching data got wrong, automatically targeting queries at the underspecified features; (2) an explanation mechanism that directs the human’s attention to those same features when answering, aligning what the robot asks with what the human attends to; and (3) empirical validation in two simulated 7-DoF manipulation domains and a user study, where both components independently improve reward recovery and amplify each other, with the largest gains in the low-query regime.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Reward learning from human feedback typically assumes the teacher is optimal or noisily optimal [ 10 , 11 ] , but human input is routinely suboptimal. Some methods build richer models of the human, capturing systematic or structured deviations from optimality [ 12 , 13 ] . Others treat suboptimality as localized failures of supervision rather than uniform noise: the robot reasons about how well its hypothesis space explains the human’s input and flags what it cannot account for [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] , or detects from the teaching data which features were well-supervised versus underspecified [ 3 , 4 , 17 ] .
Rather than resolving the diagnosed gap by requesting more data, we use the diagnosis to drive active preference queries, shifting resolution onto the robot.

Preference queries, which ask the human to choose between trajectories, are a low-effort channel for reward learning. The robot can select each query to maximize information gain, minimizing the comparisons the human must answer [ 6 ] . Prior work extends this loop in various ways: warm-starting the reward belief from demonstrations [ 8 ] , enriching queries to ask which features make a trajectory preferable [ 7 ] , and using language models to select queries and ease answering [ 18 ] .
From Biyik et al. [8] we inherit the initialization of the reward belief from demonstrations. But rather than treating all features alike, we shape that belief to encode where teaching was reliable, letting the information-gain criterion target the underspecified features.

2026-10-16.title: Safe and Fuel-Efficient Motion Planning for Lunar Propulsive Drones
2026-10-16.authors: Elena Wittemyer , Graco Gao
2026-10-16.comment: This work has been submitted to the 2027 IEEE Aerospace Conference
2026-10-16.abstract: Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC.
2026-10-16.introduction:
In a 2028 mission titled “MoonFall”, NASA plans to send a team of four propulsive drones to the Moon’s south pole to rapidly scout the lunar surface [ 1 ] . The drones will use their propulsion systems to complete short ‘hops’ across the surface of the Moon. In-flight, they will use multiple high-definition optical cameras to capture images of terrain that would be challenging to reach from the ground. With these images, the drones seek to build high-resolution models of the lunar surface, which are a critical resource for safe exploration of the Moon.
Scientists have developed terrain models for most of the lunar surface using orbital measurements [ 2 ] . At best, these digital elevation models (DEMs) have a resolution of about 1-5 m/pix; at worst, their resolution is about 60 m/pix [ 3 ] . Even the best DEMs do not have sufficient resolution to resolve smaller rocks or craters. Lunar landers often rely on these terrain models for choosing a landing site; these low-resolution models cannot provide enough information, so lunar landers must rely on sensor measurements moments before landing. Propulsive drones will generate terrain models at sub-meter resolutions, enabling safe landings for future spacecraft and supporting a sustained presence on the lunar south pole.

In this work, we consider the problem of autonomous motion planning for propulsive drone-based exploration of the lunar south pole. The first key challenge in motion planning for propulsive drones is landing site safety. At the moment a drone begins a hop, it does not know in advance where it is safe to land. Mid-flight, the drone must be able to identify a site that is not only free of obstacles like rocks or craters, but is also reachable under its dynamics model. It must then calculate and follow some feasible trajectory to reach this safe site. Moreover, it is important that each hop the drone completes is fuel efficient. The planned MoonFall drones have a limited fuel supply and are not designed to refuel; once they are low on fuel, the drones will permanently land and deploy a long-duration payload [ 1 ] . The more fuel efficient a drone’s hops are, the more terrain it can cover during its short flying lifespan. Critically, the drone must be able to determine landing site safety/reachability online and track efficient hop trajectories in real-time. We present a robust motion planning framework for propulsive drones which tackles the aforementioned challenges. Our motion planning framework begins with a series of global waypoints, which are chosen using low-resolution existing DEMs of the moon. Our optimal trajectory planner then generates hops between these waypoints. Midway through each hop, we calculate the set of landing sites that are both reachable and obstacle-free. If the next global waypoint is not reachable or safe, we calculate an optimal trajectory to the nearest valid landing site. This motion planning process is illustrated in Fig. 1 . We test our motion planning framework in a high-fidelity lunar simulation developed by the Stanford NAVLab [ 4 ] .

Our main contributions are as follows:

We design a motion planning architecture for fuel-efficient hop trajectories that are rapidly tracked using model predictive control.

We propose a strategy for calculating the set of reachable landing sites under the drone’s dynamics model in real-time.

We develop a lightweight semantic segmentation model trained on aerial images of simulated lunar terrain to identify rocks and craters in real-time.

1. We design a motion planning architecture for fuel-efficient hop trajectories that are rapidly tracked using model predictive control.

2. We propose a strategy for calculating the set of reachable landing sites under the drone’s dynamics model in real-time.

3. We develop a lightweight semantic segmentation model trained on aerial images of simulated lunar terrain to identify rocks and craters in real-time.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Hopping Robots for Extraplanetary Exploration

There are a number of existing works on
hopping robots for extraplanetary exploration. Hopping robots are capable of exploring terrain that ground-constrained robots, like rovers, would struggle to reach. Unlike traditional rotorcraft or drones, hopping robots can traverse extraplanetary environments that do not have an atmosphere. Many works focus on hopping robots for exploration of small Solar System bodies [ 5 ] [ 6 ] [ 7 ] . We build off of some of the control strategies in these works, but we also incorporate vision and existing terrain models into our approach to deal with the complexity of the lunar surface. There are also a number of existing works on hopping robots for the Moon. [ 8 ] proposes a multi-stage ballistic hopping control framework for a spherical robot to explore lunar pits. The spherical robot is designed to hop short distances and uses geometric analysis to identify obstacles. [ 9 ] also presents a hopping robot designed for short-distance traverses, though this robot is made to image the lunar surface rather than explore the lunar subsurface. [ 10 ] presents a long-range, thruster-based Tensegrity robot for exploration of hilly terrain. However, this work uses fixed landing positions and thus does not consider the safety of a potential landing site in the path planning process.

There are also a few existing works on the design and/or control of a propulsive drone for lunar exploration. In [ 11 ] , the author proposes a small, cold gas propulsion-based flying vehicle; this work primarily focuses on the design of the propulsion system and not optimal trajectory planning, utilizing a simple ballistic hop. [ 12 ] presents the design of a larger lunar reconnaissance drone for mapping the lunar surface. For planning the hop, the authors combine a fuel-efficient ballistic trajectory with a constant-altitude hovering trajectory. Their work does not consider landing site safety or mid-flight diversions to new terrain. The closest existing work to ours is [ 13 ] , which proposes a linear quadratic tracking (LQT)-based optimal control strategy for lunar hoppers. The authors use reinforcement learning to dynamically plan an obstacle-avoidant reference trajectory that they track with LQT. This work uses a simplified lunar environment and directly queries the distance to the nearest obstacle, rather than solving for this distance from sensor information. To the best of our knowledge, our work is the first vision-based optimal trajectory planning framework for lunar hoppers.

## II-B Safe and Feasible Autonomous Landing

Our approach to generating a safe and feasible landing trajectory is based on existing literature on lunar landers and autonomous extraplanetary aerocraft. There are a number of works on calculating reachable landing trajectories for lunar landers. [ 14 ] proposes an algorithm for calculating the reachable and controllable states for a planetary landing vehicle; we directly build off of this work to calculate a reachable landing site. The real-time re-targeting policy used for the Chandrayaan-3 lunar landing mission is given in [ 15 ] . This work presents a data-driven re-targeting policy that uses the controllable set given by some baseline policy to find an optimal landing state. While this work is constrained to some base policy, our work uses a precomputed representation of the reachable set and thus does not require some base guidance policy. [ 16 ] presents a guidance policy for a lunar lander to complete a feasible trajectory diversion in the event of hazard detection at a nominal landing site. Similar to this work, the authors of [ 16 ] use [ 14 ] to calculate a reachable set of landing sites; however, the authors use LiDAR to detect potential hazards. Our work purely uses vision for hazard detection, as future lunar propulsive drones will not necessarily have access to depth sensors like LiDAR.

On the note of vision-guided hazard avoidance, the Mars Ingenuity Helicopter also used vision when planning its autonomous landings. Though its early landing sites were planned by human scientists, following a software update [ 17 ] , the helicopter was able to use its downward-facing camera to detect and avoid risky terrain before landing. Our work builds on this idea, detecting obstacles mid-flight and planning trajectories that touch down in the nearest safe region to the nominal landing site. Unlike the Ingenuity helicopter, it is not possible for our drone to hover in place while making decisions; instead, it quickly identifies safe sites and plans new trajectories while in motion.

2026-10-16.title: MOSS: Mode-Oriented Source Shaping for Robot Flow Matching Policies
2026-10-16.authors: Zirun Ma , Jindou Jia , Tuo An , Jiaqi Bai , Jiahua Dong , Jianfei Yang
2026-10-16.abstract: In robotic manipulation, the same observation often admits multiple feasible actions. Generative policies such as diffusion and flow matching naturally capture such multimodal behaviors, yet which mode is executed is left to random sampling and cannot be actively controlled. We propose M ode- O riented S ource S haping ( MOSS ), which turns mode selection into an explicit choice of where generation starts. We first reveal, both empirically and theoretically, that deterministic flow transport induces mode-dependent structure in the source space. Under ideal deterministic ODE transport, distinct behavioral modes have distinct source-space preimages, while practical approximation errors can blur their boundaries due to imbalanced data, limited model capacity, and few inference steps. Motivated by this source-space structure, MOSS constructs semantically aligned mode-specific Gaussian sources that encode mode identity in the initial noise. A modality-strength estimator predicts the local degree of multimodality, which adaptively controls the geometry of the mode-specific sources. It contracts them toward a shared Gaussian where behaviors are similar and separates them near behavioral branching points. During deployment, the desired behavior is selected at inference simply by sampling from the corresponding component. Across 6 6 simulated and 3 3 real-world manipulation tasks, MOSS steers to the target mode up to 100 % 100\% of the time with high task success, recovers minority modes at over 90 % 90\% guidance rate under a : 90 10\!:\!90 imbalance dataset, and surpasses mode-conditioned flow policy by 43.3 43.3 points of guidance rate on real robots.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Generative models have recently become a prominent paradigm in robot imitation learning ( Pearce et al., 2023 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ) . Unlike conventional policies that regress toward an optimal action, representative approaches such as Diffusion Policy (DP) ( Chi et al., 2023 ) and Flow Matching (FM) ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Bai et al., 2026 ) generate action trajectories from random noise, allowing them to represent multiple feasible behaviors under the same observation, i.e., multimodal behaviors ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) . Here, a behavior mode denotes a semantically coherent family of action sequences that follow the same qualitative strategy for accomplishing the task ( Chi et al., 2023 ) . For instance, a robot may approach the same object from the left or the right, or interact with different targets in different orders, while still completing the task successfully. However, in existing generative policies, which mode is ultimately executed is largely determined implicitly by random sampling ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . This limits their applicability in settings that require user-specified preferences, test-time constraints, or human intervention ( Zoellner et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2025 ) .

Existing solutions fall into two categories. The straightforward one explicitly conditions the generative model on a mode indicator, in practice most often a language instruction, so that different conditions induce different action distributions ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhang and Gienger, 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Such conditioning, however, often fails to steer the policy reliably when the training data are imbalanced ( Fang et al., 2026 ) , since high-dimensional visual scenes are strongly correlated with task execution, the model tends to learn scene-action shortcuts that bypass the weaker, low-dimensional language condition ( Ren et al., 2026 ) . The other line instead operates on the source distribution of FM, controlling multimodal behaviors by implicitly learning a set of Gaussian priors ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Machado et al., 2026 ) . These priors, however, carry no explicit semantic correspondence to behavioral modes, so aligning them with user-defined modes still demands additional networks and laborious post-alignment ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) .

Toward a more reliable handle on mode selection, we first analyze how a well-trained FM policy behaves on multimodal tasks. We find that, even with a standard isotropic Gaussian source, the final behavior does not arise randomly from the entire noise space. Under deterministic Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) transport, different behavioral modes tend to occupy distinct, albeit noticeably entangled, regions of the source space. We further show theoretically that, under ideal transport conditions, such mode-specific initial-noise regions are guaranteed to be implicitly separated. In practice, however, imbalanced mode distributions, limited model capacity, and a restricted number of inference steps leave these partitions interleaved, weakly separated, or severely imbalanced, sometimes resulting in mode preference or even mode collapse ( Zhai et al., 2025 ; Mazza et al., 2026 ) . This raises a natural question: can we make the existing partitioning more explicit, and steer behavior directly through the initial distribution?

Based on this insight, we propose M ode- O riented S ource S haping, termed MOSS , which enables controllable multimodal generation by dynamically shaping the source distribution of FM, as shown in Figure 1 . Specifically, we first construct semantically defined mode-specific Gaussian sources, explicitly encoding mode identity into the initial noise and making the resulting control more robust to imbalanced mode distributions, limited model capacity, and limited inference steps. Since multiple modes typically arise only during certain critical phases rather than throughout the entire task ( Jia et al., 2026a ) , a modality-strength estimator then predicts the local degree of multimodality from previous observation and action history, and uses it to continuously modulate the separability of the Gaussian components. When demonstrations from different modes behave alike, the components contract toward a shared Gaussian and maximize data sharing. As the robot approaches a behavioral branch, they gradually separate and give the initial noise a clear, stable mode identity.

MOSS provides several practical advantages beyond explicit mode selection. First, when different modes in the training demonstrations are highly imbalanced, the generation probabilities of standard FM tend to inherit the empirical data distribution. In contrast, our method can directly adjust the deployment probability of each mode by changing the source sampling distribution. Second, for data-scarce modes, we find that the proposed strategy can effectively leverage shared trajectory data from other modes, allowing the policy to learn more stable common motion structures while preserving clear mode boundaries, thereby improving both sample efficiency and task success for minority modes. Finally, compared with methods that apply strong guidance to shift the learned vector field at inference time, mode-specific sources still initialize transport from regions already established during training. This can potentially reduce trajectory-quality degradation caused by inference-time guidance ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , while naturally extending to currently emerging one-step denoising algorithms that do not support guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ; Jia et al., 2026b ) .

We systematically evaluate our method on multiple robotic manipulation tasks with multimodal structure, including 6 6 simulation tasks and 3 3 real-world robot tasks. Compared with standard FM ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) , explicit mode-conditioned FM ( Lei et al., 2026 ) , and source-based methods ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) , MOSS achieves up to 100 % 100\% target-mode steering while maintaining high task success rate (SR). Even under a highly imbalanced mode distribution ( 10 : 90 10:90 ), our method can reliably recover the minority mode, achieving over 90 % 90\% guidance rate (GR). Ablations show that adaptive source geometry improves GR over fixed Gaussian separation by 12 12 - 14 14 percentage points in average GR at the same training budget. On real-world tasks, MOSS achieves an average GR/SR of 84.2 % / 85.3 % 84.2\%/85.3\% , outperforming mode-conditioned FM by 43.3 43.3 and 12.0 12.0 percentage points in average GR and SR, respectively. These results validate the effectiveness of source-space control under visual noise, limited demonstrations, and execution errors.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Generative policies such as diffusion ( Chi et al., 2023 ) and FM ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) naturally model multimodal action distributions through stochastic generation. However, different behavioral modes can still become entangled or collapse during generation ( Zhai et al., 2025 ; Mazza et al., 2026 ) . Recent methods improve multimodal modeling through additional structure. VFP ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) combines a variational latent prior, optimal transport, and a MoE decoder to better separate action modes, while MARS ( Jia et al., 2026a ) adaptively switches between stochastic and deterministic generation according to multimodality degree. None of these methods can actively control multimodality.

Standard FM-based policies ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) commonly initialize transport from a simple Gaussian source. Recent works instead design the source distribution to improve efficiency or structural alignment. A2A ( Jia et al., 2026b ) initializes flow from action-history representations to enable shorter transport and one-step inference; VITA ( Gao et al., 2026 ) uses visual latents as the flow source; and LAFM ( Machado et al., 2026 ) selects learned source priors according to latent actions. These methods primarily target efficient or better-aligned transport rather than explicit mode-level control. More recently, SL-FM ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) separates behavioral branches through orthogonal source lifting while retaining a shared velocity field. MOSS similarly controls behavior through the source space, but explicitly aligns source components with semantic behavior modes and adaptively adjusts their separation according to local multimodality.

Explicit conditioning provides a direct mechanism for controlling multimodal action generation by injecting the desired behavioral intent into the policy. Large VLA models such as RDT and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) use language and visual-semantic conditions to guide action generation. Lightweight generative policies can instead introduce explicit discrete mode variables; for example, PF-DAG ( Lei et al., 2026 ) predicts a primary mode and generates continuous actions with a mode-conditioned MeanFlow policy. While effective, such explicit conditioning may introduce shortcut solutions, where the policy relies heavily on the injected mode signal rather than organizing multimodal behaviors intrinsically. In contrast, MOSS controls behavior through the source distribution without exposing the mode variable to the policy itself, and our experiments show source-based mode control yields stronger controllability than directly injecting the mode variable into the velocity-field condition.

2026-10-16.title: Whole-Body Dexterity
2026-10-16.authors: Conor Mc Gartoll , An Dang , Pranay Thangeda , Arjun Gupta , Carolina Higuera , Nima Fazeli , Mustafa Mukadam , Manikantan Nambi
2026-10-16.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-16.abstract: Current humanoid dexterous manipulation remains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans’ ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot’s body and appendages as contact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects. Our sim-to-real pipeline first generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, then trains reinforcement-learning experts on a general any-to-any repositioning objective by sampling initial and goal grasps from the dataset, and distills these experts into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry. We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes a long-horizon task that stows a box under one arm, carries it from a shelf to a table, and places it. The controller operates interactively, steered by coarse motion references from a human teleoperator. Across real-world whole-body manipulation tasks, the distilled controller completes 90% of trials, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.
2026-10-16.introduction:
People rarely manipulate with their hands alone. We brace a box against the chest, cradle a basket across both arms, or tuck an object under one arm to free the other. These actions use the limbs and torso as a single highly dexterous manipulator.
We call this ability to reposition objects by continually changing supporting body contacts whole-body dexterous manipulation and apply it directly to humanoids.

Prior humanoid work has used this term for specific settings, such as coordinated whole-body control for manipulation with the hands [ 1 , 2 ] , while related loco-manipulation confines dexterity to the end-effectors [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] or to a sustained arm grasp on a bulky object [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . None treats it as a general capability in which contact is established and released with any link to move an object across diverse regions of the body.

Viewed through this lens, whole-body dexterous manipulation has a useful parallel in dexterous hands, with the limbs and torso taking the roles of fingers and palm. Recent dexterous-hand work shows that strong capabilities emerge from learning to move objects through dense sequences of intermediate targets, whether by pre-training on anygrasp-to-anygrasp transitions [ 11 ] or by tracking hand–object subgoals from human motion through regrasps and finger gaiting [ 12 ] .
Extending this principle to humanoids introduces a challenge: a dexterous hand with many fingers can often reposition some fingers while the others support the object [ 13 , 14 ] , whereas a humanoid using two arms has fewer independent supports. Releasing one arm may require the other to brace the object against the torso, and changing grasps can require rapid reconfiguration and rolling or sliding contact.
This additional complexity calls for a different approach to repositioning across body regions than these existing methods.

We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD) , a framework for learning whole-body dexterous manipulation through mode-constrained re-grasping ( Fig. 2 ) and deploying it on a real humanoid. We first generate a diverse set of whole-body grasps, then use them to initialize reinforcement-learning experts, WBD-EX . Experts learn to move objects between grasps toward goals specified by an object position and a target grasp mode: a left-arm, both-arm, or right-arm grasp. Transitions allow brief contact loss during movement but require a stable hold in the target mode at goals, so the experts learn how to hand off objects between arms, enabling repositioning across difficult regions such as behind the back and on top of the shoulders.
We distill expert trajectories into a controller that uses an object geometry descriptor to refine motion commands into stable whole-body object repositioning, without privileged object state.
Our main contributions are:

A whole-body grasp generation method defined over mode-typed contact configurations, formulated for arbitrary open-link articulated rigid-body systems and demonstrated on a humanoid robot.

A whole-body grasp generation method defined over mode-typed contact configurations, formulated for arbitrary open-link articulated rigid-body systems and demonstrated on a humanoid robot.

WBD-EX , per-object repositioning experts built on a mode-constrained re-grasping formulation that uses the diverse grasp dataset.

A distillation procedure that turns these experts into a controller conditioned on proprioception and object geometry, refining coarse commands into dexterous manipulation of diverse objects in simulation and on a real humanoid.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Work

Whole-Body Manipulation. In this paper, we advance whole-body dexterous manipulation, in which objects are held and repositioned through contact anywhere on the robot’s body rather than only at designated end-effectors or links. The closely related term, whole-body dexterity, was defined for a snake-like robot arm that manipulates with its entire body surface [ 18 ] . Related in spirit, a humanoid can manipulate
from onboard proprioception alone, since joint-encoder readings under compliant
contact act as a coarse whole-body tactile channel [ 19 ] . Several methods manipulate bulky objects that exceed the hand’s size and payload by
grasping them with the arms and torso and distributing contact across the
body [ 8 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . Other work uses upper-body tactile sensing to
hold boxes against the arms and chest on a real humanoid [ 9 ] .
Closest to our setting,
reinforcement learning on a large soft robotic torso lifts cuboids of varying
sizes and masses and performs recovery re-grasping in front of the torso [ 23 ] , but without standing or walking and
without moving the object to other regions of the body.

Classical model-based work
formulates this as optimization over contacts placed anywhere on the body
surface [ 24 , 25 ] and plans holding manipulation as a
transition graph over object motion and contact states [ 26 ] , though
typically under planar, quasi-static, or box-shaped assumptions; recent
learning-based methods instead expose whole-body contact as an explicit,
commandable interface [ 27 ] or imitate whole-body
human-object interactions in simulation from motion-capture demonstrations [ 28 , 29 ] . Evidence that the hand and the humanoid
form a structural continuum comes from reconfigurable hardware [ 30 ] and
from commercial humanoids that already tuck containers under one arm, drape cloth over a shoulder,
and lift appliances during everyday tasks [ 31 , 32 ] .
Humanoid loco-manipulation couples locomotion with manipulation, enabling
dynamic behaviors such as climbing and wall flips alongside picking, placing, and pushing
objects [ 5 , 4 , 33 , 34 , 35 ] , including humanoid pushing in simulation [ 36 ] .
We instead focus on general object manipulation across body regions.

Teleoperation is a direct route to whole-body manipulation and is well developed as motion transfer, through real-time human-to-humanoid retargeting and shadowing [ 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 ] and tracking controllers that follow whole-body targets [ 41 , 42 , 3 , 43 ] . However, without force or tactile feedback, it is difficult for the operator to tell whether an object is pinned or slipping, which largely limits teleoperation to hand-only pick-and-place behavior.

Dexterity as Contact Sequencing. In-hand manipulation can be framed as re-grasping: an object is carried through
a sequence of grasps by repeatedly breaking and remaking finger contacts, a process
known as finger gaiting [ 14 , 13 , 44 ] .
Using this idea, prior work trains dexterous-hand controllers that high-level policies or teleoperators steer with motion commands [ 11 , 12 ] .
Related goal-conditioned approaches learn grasping and reorientation
across procedurally generated tools [ 45 ] or pre-train object reposing before adapting to downstream manipulation
tasks [ 46 ] . Similar in mechanism to our own
approach, a constrained sampler over feasible contact-rich states can guide goal-conditioned
manipulation RL directly [ 47 ] . We lift this re-grasping principle from dexterous hands and arms to the whole humanoid.

2026-10-16.title: REKI: Registering Knowledge in VLAs
2026-10-16.authors: Juliette Marrie , Paul Pacaud , Adrien Ramanana Rahary , Shizhe Chen , Moritz Böhle
2026-10-16.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-16.abstract:
We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size.
REKI consists of a vision–language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision–language data.
Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert’s cache.
This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer.
REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference.
We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: github.com/kyutai-labs/reki .
2026-10-16.introduction:
Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have become an effective paradigm for language-conditioned robot control.
A pretrained vision–language model (VLM) encodes camera views and instruction, based on which a smaller action expert predicts the next actions ( Black et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Shukor et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) .

The strongest VLAs today are pretrained partly on proprietary data, and neither these data nor the pretraining pipelines are released ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) , making it hard to reproduce their results. Since each new model changes architecture, data and training recipe at once, gains cannot be traced back to a single choice.
With REKI, we release the full pipeline, from data curation to deployment.
REKI has a simple design, is pretrained on public data only and sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size.
It pairs a VLM with a flow-matching action expert, and a memory mechanism gives the policy access to its recent past.

Preserving past context can improve control ( Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) , yet most VLAs predict actions from the current observation alone ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Shukor et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) .
Existing ways of incorporating such context, however, often introduce substantial overhead ( Fig. 2 ): feeding past frames to the VLM adds their image tokens to every VLM pass ( Jang et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) , recurrent methods require sequential training ( Cherepanov et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) , and others introduce additional, dedicated memory modules to the policy ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Koo et al., 2026 ) .

REKI summarises past context through a small set of registers ( Darcet et al., 2024 ) in the action expert.
The registers of each frame are cached across chunks ( Fig. 3 ).
Each frame is thus encoded only once and no separate module, sequential unroll during training or test-time update mechanisms are necessary.
This yields clear gains at almost no overhead, and our 2.4B model REKI ranks first among VLAs pretrained on public data on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365 ( Fig. 1 ), and generalises to real robots.

Our ablations show that memory consistently improves performance, with the most pronounced gains for the first past frame ( Fig. 5 ).
Beyond task success, we find that memory stabilises action generation: without memory, the policy often oscillates between poses across action chunks, while with memory, such oscillations are about four times rarer ( Fig. 5 ).

Our contributions are thus three-fold : (i) We introduce REKI, a 2.4B-parameter VLA pretrained on public data, which sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size. (ii) We introduce register tokens in the action expert to act as a memory, which can be cached efficiently, and analyse how this reduces the failure modes of the memoryless policy. We hope REKI serves as a strong and accessible baseline for future VLA research. To foster VLA research, we release the model weights and our optimised training and inference code, from data curation to deployment on a real robot.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Open pretraining. Many VLAs release their weights, and often their finetuning code, but not the code or the exact data mixture used for pretraining ( Physical Intelligence, 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) .
The strongest VLAs are pretrained partly on proprietary data, collected ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026 ) or synthesised ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , and several have no public weights ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) .
OpenVLA, Octo and RDT-1B released their full pipeline on public data such as Open X-Embodiment ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , followed by SmolVLA, MolmoAct and MolmoAct2, which also releases bimanual data collected by its authors ( Shukor et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) .
These releases have helped the research community pretrain models again, change their data or design, and compare them under the same conditions.
Models pretrained on larger in-house data, with more recent design choices, have nonetheless kept a lead on most benchmarks.
Building on this line of work, REKI is pretrained on a broad mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision–language data, and released in full, from data curation to deployment on a real robot.
It reaches the best results among VLAs pretrained on public data on three benchmarks ( Section 6.1 ), and is optimised for fast inference ( Section 6.3 ).

Memory in VLAs. Most of these models act on the current observation alone, yet past context helps a policy identify the task state and recover from failed attempts ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Torne et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) , and methods differ in where they pay for it ( Fig. 2 ).
The most direct approach stacks or compresses past frames in the VLM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Torne et al., 2026 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ; Jang et al., 2025 ) .
Its cost then grows with the window, at least in the vision encoder ( Koo et al., 2026 ) .
A recurrent state ( Cherepanov et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) or fast weights ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) keep the input short, but must be unrolled step by step in training.
Others store past features or keyframes in an extra module ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Koo et al., 2026 ; Mark et al., 2026 ; Sridhar et al., 2026 ) .
Like μ \mu VLA and HAMLET, REKI carries the past in a few learnable tokens, but as registers ( Darcet et al., 2024 ) in the action expert.
The VLM encodes each frame once, a training window is one batched pass, and at inference memory adds under 1% to the prediction time of a model without memory ( K = 1 K\mkern 1.25mu{=}\mkern 1.25mu1 , Section A.1 ).
Without memory, a policy can also switch between modes at each new action chunk ( Agarwal et al., 2026 ; Lian et al., 2026 ) , which is attributed to perceptual aliasing in reinforcement learning ( Whitehead & Ballard, 1991 ; Singh et al., 1994 ; McCallum, 1996 ) .
In REKI, memory makes such switches about four times rarer ( Section 6.2 ), without the extra policy queries of temporal ensembling or bidirectional decoding ( Zhao et al., 2023b ; Liu et al., 2024b ) .

2026-10-16.title: Inertially Significant Humanoid Teleoperation via Whole Body Model Predictive Control and Online Parameter Estimation
2026-10-16.authors: James Foster , Beomyeong Park , Luigi Penco , Robert Griffin
2026-10-16.abstract: The effective deployment of humanoid robots in practical tasks of interest will require a capability of sensing and adapting to variations in inertial parameters, as occurs during heavy tool use or when carrying significant payload. Such payloads constitute a significant proportion of the combined payload-robot system, the effects of which cannot be ignored by delegating to feedback control. This paper showcases a general solution to this problem by integrating a whole body model predictive controller (WB-MPC) with an extended Kalman filter (EKF) for online estimation of fully physically consistent time-varying inertial parameters. These estimates are fed through to the WB-MPC’s full rigid body dynamics model, resulting in more accurate feedforward torques for task demands under external load. Additionally, a virtual reality (VR) interface is provided that enables an operator to provide task-specific references without regard to payload while delegating dynamic balance to the WB-MPC. The framework is validated with simulation and hardware experiments on a humanoid system.
2026-10-16.introduction:
A key promise of humanoid robots lies in performing tasks that involve exerting significant force to manipulated objects, such as lifting a heavy tool or carrying a payload. In many such tasks, the inertia of the manipulated object is a significant fraction of the robot’s own.

A promising candidate solution is whole body model predictive control (WB-MPC), which iteratively solves a trajectory optimization over the robot’s full rigid body dynamics. It was first demonstrated on a humanoid in [ 1 ] , and subsequent humanoid implementations have largely targeted locomotion [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Far fewer works apply WB-MPC to manipulation [ 5 ] , and fewer still to objects whose inertia is significant relative to the robot. The closest is [ 6 ] , which remains in simulation and estimates a modest payload inertia only after task execution. Other model-based approaches either add the load to a centroidal model explicitly [ 7 ] , or absorb it implicitly through direct adaptive control laws bound to a reference model [ 8 , 9 ] . Reinforcement learning (RL), meanwhile, has produced increasingly robust humanoid locomotion and manipulation [ 10 , 11 ] , but typically absorbs load variation in one of two ways. The first is domain randomization [ 12 , 13 ] , which trades nominal performance for robustness and tends toward conservative behavior; the second is a learned “extrinsics” estimator, whose abstract signals are tightly coupled to the policy that consumes them [ 14 ] . MPC and RL have recently been combined in [ 15 ] , where a massively parallelized nonlinear centroidal MPC embedded inside policy training yields robust loco-manipulation.

A WB-MPC over the full rigid body dynamics can in principle directly command the feedforward effort an added payload demands, but only insofar as its rigid body dynamics model accurately captures the manipulated inertia [ 16 ] . A structure that underpins most identification methods for rigid body inertial parameters is that the inverse dynamics are linear with respect to the inertial parameters [ 17 ] . The system identification literature usually focuses on offline identification [ 18 ] ; control-oriented online work has instead tended to focus on estimating gross quantities such as the center of mass and momentum [ 19 ] , or a payload from previously identified dynamics coefficients [ 20 ] or a momentum observer [ 21 ] . For an estimate to be safely fed into a downstream controller, it must be fully physically consistent [ 22 ] , which can be enforced via semidefinite programming [ 23 ] , smooth nonlinear reparameterizations of the inertial parameters [ 24 ] , or geometric methods [ 25 , 26 ] .

Model bias is also problematic when operating the robot via a virtual reality (VR) interface. VR provides operators with an intuitive control interface [ 27 ] , and has become common both as a primary operation method and for data collection of learned control policies [ 28 ] . With some exceptions, VR operators typically do not have access to force feedback indicating a payload, and so may compensate to mitigate tracking offset, which is burdensome and deleterious to task performance. One such exception is the impressive but complex VR/haptic teleoperation suite in [ 29 ] , where online inertial estimates are used to adjust the posture of a wheeled humanoid modeled as a cart-pole system, allowing the manipulation of heavy payloads relative to robot weight.

In this paper we propose a framework coupling three components to enable intuitive VR teleoperation of humanoids manipulating significant loads via WB-MPC. Firstly, a WB-MPC trades off dynamic balance objectives with tight tracking of operator-specified taskspace objectives. Secondly, an extended Kalman filter (EKF) coupled in closed-loop with the WB-MPC estimates fully physically consistent inertial parameters online and passes them to the WB-MPC’s rigid body dynamics model, allowing feedforward torque compensation of a priori unknown loads. We include EKF extensions that increase numerical robustness and aid interpretation: we regularize the estimate through a fictitious nominal measurement that keeps the estimate well-conditioned under the weak excitation of teleoperated motion, and estimate deviations from a well-characterized nominal body using a generalized log-Cholesky parameterization [ 24 , 30 ] . Lastly, a minimal VR teleoperation interface, combined with the aforementioned WB-MPC and EKF, allows an operator to command desired motion without the burden of compensating for added payload, while dynamic balance control is delegated to the WB-MPC. We validate the framework on loaded trajectory tracking and balance tasks in simulation, and showcase VR teleoperation under load on hardware for a 23 23 degree of freedom humanoid system (Fig. 1 ).

2026-10-16.title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-16.authors: Jiuyi Xu , Chengyuan Qian , Zhengzhong Tu , Yang Sui , Yangming Shi
2026-10-16.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency.
Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens.
We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework.
At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration.
We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot.
In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59% and action latency by 9-32% (a 1.09 × \times -1.46 × \times speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines.
On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20% (1.25 × \times speedup) at comparable success.
Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA .
2026-10-16.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a compelling paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, enabling policies to predict low-level actions conditioned on natural-language tasks and visual observations [ 30 , 15 , 3 , 22 , 6 ] .
By leveraging large-scale pretraining and large vision-language backbones, VLAs demonstrate strong generalization across objects, scenes, and task specifications, making them increasingly attractive for deployment in versatile manipulation systems.
Despite their impressive capabilities, deploying these models in closed-loop control is often limited by inference efficiency [ 8 ] .
At every control step, high-resolution (e.g., 224 × \times 224) and frequently multi-view observations are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens [ 14 , 10 ] that dominate the compute and latency of the vision-language-model (VLM) backbone during action prediction, far outweighing the few text tokens of a short task.

Yet not all visual tokens contribute equally to action prediction.
In a typical manipulation step, only a small subset of tokens carries decision-critical information (e.g., the target object/place or the gripper–object contact region), while the rest are redundant or even distracting [ 26 , 27 , 11 ] .
Reducing the number of visual tokens processed by the large-language-model (LLM) backbone, without sacrificing task performance, has therefore become a key direction for accelerating VLA inference [ 20 , 21 , 25 ] .

However, directly applying VLM-specific token compression methods [ 4 , 7 , 29 ] to robotic control is often suboptimal, because these methods are designed for single-shot vision-language understanding, where the objective is to preserve global semantic content for perception tasks such as detection, captioning, or generation.
Unlike image-based VLMs that process a single image, or video-based VLMs that encode a fixed sequence of frames, a VLA interacts with the environment through actions that directly shape its subsequent observations: at each step the agent receives a new observation conditioned on its previous action and predicts the next one.
Visual tokens are thus not representations of a static scene but components of a sequential decision process , which sets token compression for VLA apart from its VLM counterpart in two respects.
The first is that token relevance is governed by the task rather than by generic visual saliency (now standard practice in language-guided pruning), which we adopt as our importance signal rather than claim as a contribution.
The second, and the focus of this work, is that the amount of decision-critical visual information varies drastically across control steps: some steps (e.g., target localization) rely on broad scene context, whereas others (e.g., grasping or contact) depend on a small, localized region.
A single fixed compression rate is therefore inherently mismatched, wasting computation when the useful information is concentrated, and discarding necessary context when broader information is required.

Motivated by this, we propose FastVLA, a training-free visual token compression framework for efficient VLA inference whose core is a temporally adaptive, per-step compression rate .
At each step, FastVLA scores visual-token importance with task-to-vision attention which is a training-free signal that a controlled comparison shows is more reliable for action prediction than vision-only or fused attention and then, crucially, decides how many tokens to keep from the shape of the resulting importance distribution.
Specifically, it estimates the effective number of tokens the decision depends on via an inverse-Simpson uniformity measure, and maps this quantity through an online sliding-window calibration to a timestep-dependent compression rate: when the current step concentrates on few tokens relative to its recent history it prunes aggressively, and when the decision draws on broader context it prunes conservatively.
By allocating the token budget where each decision needs it, FastVLA reduces LLM-backbone computation, speeds up action prediction, and improves closed-loop responsiveness, without caches or training.

We evaluate FastVLA on three open-source VLA models including OpenVLA [ 15 ] , OpenVLA-OFT [ 14 ] , and CogACT [ 16 ] , across the widely used LIBERO [ 18 ] and SIMPLER [ 17 ] benchmarks, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot.

On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20% ( 1.25 × 1.25\times speedup) and raises the control frequency by up to 25% at comparable success.

We propose FastVLA, a training-free, plug-and-play visual token compression framework that accelerates closed-loop VLA inference.

We design a step-adaptive compression policy that sets a timestep-dependent token budget from the inverse-Simpson uniformity of the importance distribution under online sliding-window calibration.

We validate FastVLA on OpenVLA/OpenVLA-OFT (LIBERO), CogACT (SIMPLER), and a physical Franka Research 3 robot, achieving substantial compute and latency reductions in simulation and a 1.25 × 1.25\times real-robot speedup with comparable task success.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision-Language-Action Models for Robot Manipulation

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a general-purpose paradigm for robot manipulation, predicting actions directly from natural-language tasks and visual observations and generalizing across objects, scenes, and task specifications.
Early work such as SayCan [ 1 ] combines language-conditioned planning with learned low-level skills, while RT-1 [ 5 ] and RT-2 [ 30 ] scale language-conditioned visuomotor learning with large robot datasets and web-scale vision-language pretraining.
In parallel, PaLM-E [ 9 ] and Octo [ 23 ] highlight the benefits of large pretrained representations across tasks and embodiments.
More recently, foundation VLA models including OpenVLA [ 15 ] and OpenVLA-OFT [ 14 ] , CogACT [ 16 ] , and π 0 \pi_{0} [ 3 ] / π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 10 ] demonstrate strong robustness and open-world generalization via heterogeneous multi-robot data and transformer backbones.
Despite their capabilities, these models are typically billion-scale and rely on high-resolution (often multi-view) observations that are encoded into long visual-token sequences and processed by large transformers at every control step.
This incurs substantial computation and end-to-end latency in closed-loop control, motivating inference-time methods that reduce redundant visual tokens while preserving task-critical information.

## 2.2 Visual Token Compression for Efficient VLA Inference

Because most VLA models [ 15 , 14 , 16 , 3 , 10 ] adopt VLM-style architectures, training-free token compressors built for VLMs are broadly applicable: they prune or merge visual tokens by token similarity (ToMe [ 4 ] ), shallow-layer or cross-modal attention (FastV [ 7 ] , SparseVLM [ 29 ] , VisPruner [ 28 ] ), or token diversity (DivPrune [ 2 ] ). However, these methods are designed for single-image inference and apply a static pruning policy, so transferring them directly to VLA often degrades control performance.

Recent work therefore targets VLA inference along three lines: reuse- and cache-based methods that exploit cross-step temporal redundancy (VLA-Cache [ 26 ] , FlashVLA [ 21 ] ); importance-estimation methods that add task-, phase-, or motion-aware cues (SpecPrune-VLA [ 25 ] , ADP [ 20 ] , VLA-Pruner [ 19 ] ); and hybrid or learned schemes that go beyond pruning (EfficientVLA [ 27 ] , LightVLA [ 11 ] ).

These methods still share limitations that FastVLA overcomes. Reuse and caching introduce cross-step state and cache-management overhead, so wall-clock gains can lag FLOP reductions; learned schemes such as LightVLA require training and are tied to a specific backbone, although at equal success they can reach a better compute–latency point than training-free methods. In addition, some VLM/VLA compression algorithms commit to a fixed compression ratio, adapting (if at all) only through auxiliary external signals such as end-effector motion.
FastVLA differs on three axes: it is training-free, pruning independently at each step without caches; it conditions token importance on the language task; and, crucially, it makes the compression rate itself adaptive, reading the per-step concentration of task-relevant evidence via an inverse-Simpson uniformity signal calibrated against a short temporal window, spending tokens where the decision needs them and pruning harder where it does not.

2026-10-16.title: Compliant GMT: Making General Motion Tracking Compliant via Residual Reference Adaptation
2026-10-16.authors: Venki Parsuram , Michelle Wang , Jin-Hyuk Hong , Pulkit Agrawal
2026-10-16.abstract:
We propose Compliant GMT (C-GMT), a modular framework for full-body compliant responses in general motion tracking. As humanoid robots move into real world deployment, they not only need to perform any motion but also respond safely and robustly to interaction forces. Existing general motion tracking policies can imitate diverse motions but are trained to be stiff, leading to unexpected and unsafe behaviors under disturbance. Prior work in compliant humanoid control trades off compliance and generality. There exist examples of full-body compliant responses, but these are heavily curated to single-reference policies. On the other hand, general motion trackers (GMT) are trained to rigidly imitate massive motion capture datasets. Our key insight is to leverage the generality of pretrained GMTs for motion tracking while introducing compliance from a residual adapter that conditions on a history of proprioception. This enables our approach, C-GMT, to achieve both general motion tracking and whole-body compliant responses. Compared to state-of-the-art general motion trackers and single-motion compliant policies, C-GMT demonstrates competitive performance in both motion tracking accuracy and compliance adherence. We further demonstrate improved safety, robustness, and error tolerance in simulation and real-world G1 experiments.
Project website: https://venki1899.github.io/c-gmt/
2026-10-16.introduction:
As humanoid robots move toward operation in human-centered environments, they must combine agile and robust whole-body control with the ability to interact safely and effectively with people and objects. General motion tracking (GMT) has emerged as the predominant approach for humanoid whole-body control, using a single policy trained on massive human motion capture datasets to imitate diverse and highly dynamic motion references while rejecting external disturbances [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Although this stiffness is desirable for free-space motion tracking, unexpected contacts during physical interaction will cause the policy to forcefully drive the robot toward its reference position, potentially damaging the robot or environment. This is a fundamental barrier to deploying humanoids alongside people.

A compliant robot mitigates these effects by yielding appropriately to external forces, improving safety and robustness. However, recent work on learned compliant humanoid control trades off generality and compliance. Works that demonstrate coordinated full-body compliant responses are restricted to single motion imitation [ 4 ] or command the lower body only with base velocity and height [ 5 ] . Alternatively, other works perform general motion tracking but restrict compliant responses to the upper-body [ 6 , 7 ] . These approaches jointly train motion tracking and compliance within the same policy, requiring the agent to simultaneously follow the commanded motion, maintain balance, infer external wrenches, and learn to respond compliantly. Consequently, single-stage training poses significant challenges with long training times, many infeasible force events, and sensitive reward tuning. Our key insight is that we can achieve both competitive generality and compliance in a single policy by exploiting the capabilities of pretrained general motion trackers and introducing compliance through a residual adapter conditioned on a proprioception history.

We introduce Compliant GMT (C-GMT), the first framework for general motion tracking with unified full-body compliant responses. Rather than asking the motion tracking policy itself to learn both tracking and compliance, we formulate compliance as a reference adaptation problem. This decomposition separates the two objectives: a force-robust GMT based on [ 3 ] is responsible for faithfully executing the commanded motion and maintaining balance under disturbances, while a learned residual adapter modifies the reference motion to realize the desired compliance. To generate compliant reference motions for the downstream GMT, we construct an analytical teacher that observes the applied external force and uses a spring law and an inverse-kinematics (IK) solver to compute compliant adaptations. We can use the teacher and pretrained GMT to tune the desired response and verify its feasibility before training the adapter. To learn to estimate force and react appropriately at deployment time, we distill the compliant behavior into a residual adapter conditioned on proprioception that provides compliant references to the GMT. Our contributions are twofold:

1. We introduce Compliant GMT, a modular framework that unifies general motion tracking with adjustable whole-body compliance through residual reference adaptation. We propose a proprioceptive residual adapter distilled from a force-privileged teacher to generate compliant references.

2. Through simulation and real world experiments on the Unitree G1, we show that C-GMT matches both the compliance adherence of previous compliant single-motion tracking policies [ 4 ] and maintains tracking performance comparable to state-of-the-art GMTs. We further demonstrate C-GMT’s novel advantages of compliance during highly dynamic whole-body motions and coordinated whole-body compliant responses.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A General Motion Tracking

Advances in sim-to-real reinforcement learning [ 8 , 9 ] , motion retargeting [ 10 , 11 ] , and large-scale human motion capture datasets [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] have enabled impressive humanoid general motion tracking policies capable of playing back diverse dynamic motions in the real world. GMTs convert target trajectories of joint or keypoint positions from a reference motion clip or planner output into physically feasible joint motor commands [ 2 , 15 , 1 ] . They have formed the critical foundation of humanoid visuomotor policy training as both a teleoperation interface for data collection [ 16 , 3 ] and the module responsible for physically executing vision-language-action (VLA) model outputs [ 17 ] . Recent work has used LoRA [ 18 ] to finetune open-sourced GMTs [ 3 ] for perceptive control [ 19 ] and cross-embodiment transfer [ 20 ] . Currently, leading GMTs are trained to stiffly track target positions, exerting large, uncontrolled forces [ 21 ] when the robot deviates from its reference. This problem is exacerbated when reference motions are generated by higher-level systems with delayed, imperfect feedback [ 22 , 23 ] and performed by a GMT that may introduce subtle, hard-to-model tracking error [ 24 ] . These issues can be alleviated by a compliant GMT that yields to unexpected forces, reducing the necessary precision and reactivity of a higher-level control system. Motivated by these observations, we propose a compliant GMT based on SONIC [ 3 ] which supports plug-and-play integration with open-source teleoperation systems and VLAs.

## II-B Learned Compliant Humanoid Control

Reinforcement learning is a promising method for training compliant control policies in simulation [ 25 ] and deployed on real legged robots [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] . A common approach in both classical [ 30 , 31 ] and learning-based methods is to model the end effector as a spring-mass-damper system and alter reference trajectories based on force feedback. For humanoids, balancing force interaction, motion tracking, and stability objectives to achieve compliant responses is nontrivial, and recent learning-based methods approach this problem by trading off generality and compliance. CHIP [ 7 ] and GentleHumanoid [ 6 ] are built on trained-from-scratch, whole-body motion-tracking policies, but only the upper body participates in compliant responses. SoftMimic [ 4 ] demonstrates coordinated whole-body compliant responses, but trains a separate policy for each reference motion. More recently, LAC [ 5 ] learns to respond compliantly with coordinated whole-body responses, but only supports base velocity and height commands for the lower body. C-GMT is the first system to achieve state-of-the-art performance in both general motion tracking and coordinating compliant responses across the whole body.

## II-C Residual Models for Humanoid Robotics

It is very appealing to enable compliant behaviors without retraining foundational GMTs from scratch. Prior work in residual policy learning adds corrective residual layers over frozen base controllers [ 32 ] . Recent work in humanoid whole body control continues to use residual models to preserve the base motion tracker’s stability and generality while enabling dynamic trajectory modification based on sensory feedback [ 33 , 34 , 24 ] . Notably, Huang et al. apply learned residual offsets to stabilize payloads upstream at the kinematic reference layer before the motion tracking policy [ 35 ] . To make modifications without onboard force sensors, teacher-student distillation is commonly used to infer dynamic and environmental properties from joint position and velocity histories [ 36 ] .
Drawing from these works, C-GMT uses a lightweight residual adapter that computes an adapted reference from proprioception and passes it to a pretrained general motion tracker to execute.
