2026-10-16.title: Perceptual Comparisons of Viscoelastic Renderings: Fractional- vs Integer-Order Models
2026-10-16.authors: Gorkem Gemalmaz , Harun Tolasa , Volkan Patoglu
2026-10-16.comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Haptics for possible publication.
2026-10-16.abstract: Realistic haptic rendering of viscoelastic materials requires reproducing time-dependent behaviors such as creep and stress relaxation, which arise from the material’s inherent memory effects. Fractional-order viscoelastic models have been shown to capture these dynamics accurately and compactly, but it remains unclear whether their increased fidelity translates into perceptual benefits during haptic interaction. In this work, we investigate whether users perceive fractional-order models as more realistic than conventional integer-order models while rendering viscoelastic materials. We compare the fractional-order standard linear solid (FO-SLS) model with two integer-order alternatives: the 3-parameter SLS model and the 5-parameter generalized Maxwell model. We consider two complementary approaches to optimal parameter selection to evaluate rendering realism from both objective and perceptual perspectives: In the first approach, we determine the model parameters via least-squares based system identification of physical viscoelastic reference materials to establish evaluation baselines. In the second approach, we determine population-level perceptually optimal parameters using a qualitative-feedback-based human-in-the-loop optimization and aggregation method. This method establishes model parameters that maximize perceived realism of viscoelastic behaviors through qualitative evaluations. Human-subject experiments indicate that the FO-SLS model is perceived as significantly more realistic than both integer-order alternatives under both parameter selection approaches. Overall, this study provides experimental evidence that fractional-order viscoelastic models are not only theoretically well-motivated, but also perceptually relevant for realistic haptic rendering of creep- and relaxation-dominated behaviors of viscoelastic materials.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Viscoelastic materials, including biological tissues and polymers, show inherently time-dependent mechanical behavior. In particular, these materials exhibit phenomena such as creep and stress relaxation, which arise from the dependence of the response on the deformation and loading history. Accurately capturing these behaviors is important for applications involving physical interaction with soft materials, particularly in haptic medical and surgical training simulators [ 1 ] . For instance, palpation can detect changes in tissue viscoelasticity associated with abnormalities such as tumors, and haptic medical simulators may assist in training for diagnosing such tumors [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Therefore, realistic rendering of viscoelastic tissue behavior is essential for applications involving physical interaction with soft biological materials.

Selecting an appropriate model for viscoelastic haptic rendering requires considering both how accurately the model captures the physical material response and how realistic the resulting interaction is perceived by users. Classical compliance models based on integer-order (IO) spring-damper networks, including the standard linear solid (SLS) model and the generalized Maxwell (GM) model, approximate these behaviors, but fail to represent long-term memory effects and frequency-dependent dynamics accurately [ 3 ] . Fractional-order (FO) viscoelastic models provide an appealing alternative, as non-integer derivatives naturally encode memory-dependent dynamics and can represent complex viscoelastic responses with relatively few model parameters [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] .

Despite these modeling advantages, it remains unclear whether the improved descriptive performance of FO models necessarily translates into perceptually more realistic haptic rendering. Model accuracy is commonly evaluated through physical characterization, by assessing how well a model fits measured response in a least-squares sense. On the other hand, during haptic rendering, an accurate physical description of the reference does not necessarily correspond to the most realistic percept during physical interactions [ 8 , 9 ] .

This distinction is particularly relevant for viscoelastic rendering, where the perceived response depends on the combined perception of stiffness, damping, and the interaction history provided by the haptic interface. Consequently, comparing viscoelastic rendering models only through system-identification error or model complexity is insufficient to determine which model provides the most realistic haptic experience. A fair comparison among viscoelastic rendering models requires not only determining optimal parameters for each model to capture the same physical reference material, but also evaluating whether users perceive the resulting renderings as realistic.

Determination of optimal parameters can be achieved through system identification or human-in-the-loop (HiL) optimization of perceived realism [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . While tuning the model parameters through HiL optimization, different model structures introduce different trade-offs. A lower-dimensional IO model is relatively easier to tune and interpret, whereas a higher-dimensional IO model can represent richer dynamics at the cost of a larger parameter space. An FO model can capture memory-dependent behavior more compactly with fewer parameters, but the coupling among its parameters makes their individual perceptual effects harder to predict.

In this study, we investigate whether the modeling differences and trade-offs between FO and IO viscoelastic models are also reflected in their perceived realism during haptic rendering.
In particular, we evaluate whether the compact representation of memory-dependent behavior provided by the FO-SLS model results in higher perceived realism than its IO counterparts, and whether increasing the number of parameters in an IO model provides sufficient improvement in perceived realism to compensate for the added complexity.

Accordingly, we compare the rendering performance of the 4-parameter FO-SLS model with two integer-order alternatives of different model complexities: the 3-parameter IO-SLS model and the 5-parameter IO-GM model. We perform such comparisons under two complementary optimal parameter-selection approaches. First, we compare model parameters identified through physical characterization of the reference viscoelastic materials. Second, we compare population-level perceptually optimal parameters determined from participants’ qualitative feedback through HiL optimization experiments conducted according to [ 12 ] . This way, we evaluate the effects of model structure and complexity on perceived realism under both physically and perceptually optimized parameter sets.

The main contribution of this paper is a human-subject comparison of FO and IO viscoelastic rendering models under various optimal parameter selection settings. By comparing the FO model with IO models of increasing complexity, using qualitative participant evaluations, we provide experimental evidence indicating that rendering viscoelasticity with FO-SLS models results in perceptually more realistic interactions than conventional IO alternatives. Overall, this study shows that FO models are not only theoretically more suitable for describing viscoelastic materials but also that users perceive these modeling advantages while rendering viscoelasticity.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Viscoelastic Models for Haptic Rendering

Creep and stress relaxation arise from internal memory [ 13 ] : creep captures gradual deformation under constant stress, while stress relaxation models force decay under constant strain. These effects are crucial for capturing the response of soft biological tissues and polymeric materials and cannot be adequately represented by purely elastic models [ 14 ] . Common IO viscoelastic representations include the Kelvin–Voigt, Maxwell, SLS, and GM models. These models differ in their ability to capture creep and relaxation behavior.

Classical IO viscoelastic models are easier to interpret and computationally convenient since they are built from networks of ideal springs and dampers. The Kelvin-Voigt model can capture bounded creep, but is inadequate to represent stress relaxation [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] , while the Maxwell model captures stress relaxation but results in unbounded creep [ 18 , 19 ] . The SLS model (Fig. 1 (a)) improves on these limitations by more accurately representing both creep and stress relaxation; however, its single relaxation time constant limits its fidelity when modeling materials with broader relaxation spectra [ 20 , 21 ] . GM models (Fig. 1 (c)) further increase expressiveness at a cost of model complexity by adding several Maxwell branches with different relaxation time constants [ 22 , 23 ] ; however, a finite number of such branches cannot fully account for the history dependence underlying viscoelasticity [ 22 , 23 ] .

Fractional-order (FO) viscoelastic models (Fig. 1 (b)) offer a compact alternative by replacing classical damping with a fractional-order one. Since fractional derivatives depend on the full history of the signal, FO models can naturally capture memory-dependent behavior, such as intermediate viscoelastic responses between solid-like and fluid-like behaviors in materials exhibiting creep and relaxation characteristics [ 21 , 24 , 25 ] . For instance, the FO-SLS model can model broad relaxation behavior that would otherwise require infinitely many IO branches in the GM model; that is, the GM model converges to an FO-SLS model in the limit, as the number of Maxwell branches approaches infinity [ 17 , 26 ] . This property makes the FO-SLS model attractive for haptic rendering, where realistic time-dependent behavior must be captured with a manageable number of model parameters [ 24 , 27 , 28 ] .

On the other hand, theoretical modeling advantages do not necessarily translate into higher perceived realism during physical interactions with a haptic interface. A low-parameter IO model, as in Fig. 1 (a), is easier to tune; a higher-parameter IO model, as in Fig. 1 (c), may approximate richer dynamics with additional parameters, while an FO model, as in Fig. 1 (b), can capture memory effects compactly but with less intuitive parameters that display frequency-dependent couplings.

## II-B Perceptual Evaluation of Viscoelastic Haptic Rendering

Perceived realism is commonly evaluated through human judgments of similarity, preference, or naturalness with respect to interactions with a physical reference object [ 29 , 30 , 31 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Studies in the literature indicate that physical model accuracy alone is insufficient to evaluate the realism of haptic rendering, and that when the target outcome is the perceived realism , human evaluation constitutes the gold standard [ 32 ] .

Qualitative user evaluations have therefore become an important complement to quantitative physical characterizations. Data-driven rendering studies have shown that while measured interactions can capture complex responses, perceptual validations are still required to determine whether the rendered interaction feels similar to the physical material [ 33 , 34 ] .

This is particularly relevant for rendering viscoelasticity, since the perception of the material depends on multiple exploratory cues that are time-dependent, including stiffness, damping, creep, relaxation, and other kinesthetic force-motion relationships [ 35 , 36 , 37 ] . Psychophysics studies have established systematic means of evaluation when the quantity of interest is perceived similarity or realism [ 38 , 39 , 10 , 40 , 12 ] .

Earlier works on the perceptual evaluation of haptic rendering of viscoelasticity
have focused on physical modeling with perceptual experiments, and relied on user-centered evaluation of realism to verify the results [ 41 , 12 , 42 , 37 ] . However, none of these related works addressed whether different viscoelastic model families produce different perceived realism for the same material. In this study, we address this gap by directly comparing the FO-SLS models with low- and high-parameter IO models, using both physically characterized and population-level perceptually optimized parameters for each model. Accordingly, we test whether users can perceive the modeling advantages of FO models while rendering viscoelastic behavior.

2026-10-16.introduction:
In-space servicing, assembly and manufacturing (ISAM) could support structures
whose dimensions are not constrained by a single launch-vehicle fairing and
could allow spacecraft to be repaired or upgraded in orbit [ 1 , 2 ] . Realising either depends on a
capability that remains largely unqualified for flight: permanent, load-bearing
metal joining. Mechanical fasteners and adhesives cover part of the design space,
but neither restores parent-metal continuity in a pressure boundary or a primary
structural member, and both introduce additional mass. Ground demonstrators have
examined high-degree-of-freedom
robotic assembly of structures too large for single-launch deployment [ 3 ] .

Figure 1 illustrates the representative on-orbit joining
scenario considered in this study.

Fusion welding is one candidate and has been tested in space. The Skylab M551
experiment produced electron-beam melts on 304 stainless steel, 2219-T87
aluminium and commercially pure tantalum in 1973, providing a rare in-space
fusion-welding dataset on structural alloys [ 5 ] . Soviet
work established that an arc can be sustained in vacuum, while also documenting
its instabilities [ 6 ] . Recent campaigns have
investigated laser beam welding in parabolic-flight and thermal-vacuum
demonstrations on AISI 316L [ 7 , 8 ] .
Taken together, these studies do not report a qualified welding procedure or a
validated operating envelope spanning the gravity and pressure conditions
relevant to a mission.

Establishing that envelope experimentally is resource intensive. Reduced-gravity
access is limited to short parabolic-flight intervals, thermal-vacuum testing is
costly, and each run covers only a small part of the parameter space. The
coupled process physics therefore make exhaustive empirical mapping impractical.

A physics-based computational model can screen this operating space before
hardware tests, but a three-dimensional weld-pool calculation requires minutes
of computation per operating point. This cost prevents direct use at robotic
control rates and makes dense exploration of a five-dimensional design space
impractical. A faster surrogate model is therefore required.

This paper develops a reduced thermal weld-pool model parameterised by the CMT
operating condition and effective local-pressure parameter, compares Gaussian-process
and neural-network surrogates, and couples the GP surrogate to a
six-degree-of-freedom manipulator simulation. Gravity is sampled to check numerical
invariance and enters a separate hydrostatic-to-capillary pressure ratio, but is
absent from the implemented thermal energy equation. The
contributions are:

A finite-volume thermal model applied here to 1 mm 316L
stainless-steel sheet, with explicit numerical convergence and
field-quality criteria; extension to the 2 mm coupon configuration is
not evaluated in this paper.

stainless-steel sheet, with explicit numerical convergence and
field-quality criteria; extension to the 2 mm coupon configuration is
not evaluated in this paper.

and deterministic boundary cases, with empirical interval coverage and
measured inference latency.

A model-based closed-loop study in which a controller adjusts the
synergic power-source setting in response to a trajectory-imposed change
in travel speed.

A sensitivity analysis that separates conclusions supported within the
reduced model from gravity-dependent free-surface and metal-transfer
mechanisms that still require experiments and higher-fidelity models.

Verification concerns the numerical solution of the governing equations,
whereas validation assesses agreement with physical observations.
This paper reports
numerical quality-control criteria, quantified
surrogate fidelity to the finite-volume model, and literature-informed parameter
priors. A formal grid-convergence study is still required before discretisation
uncertainty can be quantified. The paper does not claim
experimental validation: the targeted literature review identified no bead-
geometry dataset for 1–2 mm 316L in the relevant travel-speed range, and
validation against the ISPARK coupons is unavailable in this study.

Section 2 sets out the framework architecture and its latency
budget. Section 3 gives the weld-pool formulation, and
Section 4 its convergence and numerical-quality criteria.
Section 5 describes literature-informed parameter priors.
Section 6 reports surrogate fidelity and speed-up, and
Section 7 the model-based closed-loop study.

# 2. The ISPARK digital-twin architecture

The proposed architecture is organised into four layers with explicit interfaces. This
separation allows the finite-volume model to generate data offline while the
surrogate supplies predictions at control-loop rates.

Physics model. A finite-volume thermal weld-pool model
(Section 3 ) solving enthalpy transport with solid–liquid phase
change and driven by a time-averaged arc heat input. The effective local-pressure
parameter enters the surface-loss model. Gravity is carried as a design
variable for an explicit invariance check and enters the separate
hydrostatic-to-capillary pressure ratio, but not the thermal energy equation. Cost is of order 10 2 10^{2} – 10 3 10^{3} s per operating point.

Surrogate layer. Gaussian-process and neural-network emulators trained
on solver sweeps (Section 6 ), mapping a five-element process
and environment vector to weld-pool geometry, peak temperature and evaporation
rate. Each GP output has a nominal predictive interval. Cost is of order 1.1 × 10 − 4 1.1\times 10^{-4} s for a single target and 2.5 × 10 − 4 2.5\times 10^{-4} s for the three outputs queried by the control loop, measured on the
deployed predictor including input scaling and predictive variance.

Robotic coupling. A six-degree-of-freedom manipulator with inverse
kinematics following the seam and querying the surrogate at each control step.
The controller adjusts the synergic power-source setting; travel speed is
prescribed by the motion plan (Section 7 ). Related work combines
learned vision and manipulator trajectory generation in a spacecraft guidance,
navigation and control architecture for on-orbit manipulation [ 9 ] .

Sensing interface. The path by which measurements would update model
states and parameters
(Section 9 ). In this paper the interface is specified and the
assimilation structure defined, but the loop is not closed against hardware.

The thermal model generates surrogate training data offline. Within the online
control loop, the surrogate must provide sufficiently accurate predictions
within the available computation time. Measurement updates are part of the
proposed architecture but are not implemented in this study. The present
implementation is therefore a model-based control prototype within the proposed
architecture, not a hardware-connected digital twin.

The software interfaces could in principle support a different process model,
but transfer is not automatic. We infer from the process-specific diagnostics
and operating conditions used in recent laser-welding studies [ 7 , 8 ] that a laser- or
electron-beam implementation would require its own heat-source model, inputs,

2026-10-16.title: TS-WAM: Temporal Latent Actions and World-Action Coupling for Vision-Language Robot Control
2026-10-16.authors: Menghao Yin , Jiaju Yin , Xiyue Dong , Lixin Xu , Zhenhui Zhang , Ke Zhang , Yating Feng , Renjing Xu
2026-10-16.abstract:
Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot
demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual
states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can
encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization
and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action
Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal
learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from
heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human
videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained
external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to
predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses
them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at
inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes
temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without
a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target
branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight.
Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world
manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate
that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and
robustness.
2026-10-16.introduction:
A robot must convert a language instruction and a changing visual scene into a
temporally coherent sequence of actions. Recent vision-language-action (VLA)
systems use a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) as a semantic backbone
and attach a diffusion or flow-matching action decoder [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
This recipe gives strong instruction following, but
the action interface is commonly learned directly from robot trajectories. The
resulting hidden state need not represent the short-horizon visual change that
an action is intended to cause. Consequently, the policy has no explicit
internal prediction of what its action will do before it is executed.

At the same time, large video collections contain abundant information about
how objects and hands move, but generally do not provide robot actions. Latent
action models (LAMs) address this gap by compressing temporal changes into a
compact code [ 5 ] . Existing systems, however, often pretrain a
LAM or a latent world model separately and subsequently adapt it to a robot
policy. This multi-stage procedure introduces an additional checkpoint and
optimization boundary, and it does not guarantee that the learned latent is
useful to the final action decoder.

We propose TS-WAM (Teacher-Student World-Action Model), a task-adaptation
architecture that makes temporal prediction the central interface of a VLA
policy without requiring a separately pretrained latent-action model. The
model uses an asymmetric pair of VLM branches.

The online X X -VLM
receives only the current observation and language instruction. It produces
latent- X X tokens that a small transformer predictor maps to a predicted latent
action. The EMA Y Y -VLM receives the current and future observations and reads
the corresponding target latent action. This temporal information asymmetry
turns future visual evidence into a training-only teacher signal while keeping
the deployed policy causal.

The latent action is coupled to visual dynamics and control. A frozen DINO
encoder represents the current and future images as spatial feature grids. A
newly initialized latent world decoder predicts the feature displacement Δ ​ F t = F t + 1 − F t \Delta F_{t}=F_{t+1}-F_{t} conditioned on the current feature and latent action.
The predicted future feature F t + Δ ​ F ^ t F_{t}+\widehat{\Delta F}_{t} is passed to a
conditional flow-matching action head together with VLM context and robot
state. The policy therefore follows an explicit chain: infer a latent intent,
predict its visual consequence, and ground that consequence into an action
chunk.

The same training procedure can mix robot demonstrations and action-free human
videos. Human clips contribute current–future visual pairs to the teacher and
world-model objectives, whereas robot clips additionally provide state and
action supervision for the flow head. Thus, action-free data expands temporal
supervision without providing embodiment-specific action labels. The
task-specific world decoder is initialized from scratch and co-adapts with the
VLM and policy.

This joint objective keeps temporal prediction aligned with the downstream
control interface throughout task adaptation. At deployment, the resulting
policy uses only the current observation while retaining visual anticipation
learned from both data sources.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce vlm-jepa, a self-supervised framework for learning
temporal latent-action representations from robot demonstrations and
action-free human videos.

We propose TS-WAM, a lightweight world-action model that unifies
temporal representation learning, visual prediction, and action generation
through end-to-end training. It anticipates action consequences to guide
control, without separate latent-action or world-model pretraining.

Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with
real-world evaluations on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate
TS-WAM’s strong manipulation performance.

temporal latent-action representations from robot demonstrations and
action-free human videos.

2. We propose TS-WAM, a lightweight world-action model that unifies
temporal representation learning, visual prediction, and action generation
through end-to-end training. It anticipates action consequences to guide

2026-10-16.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

Vision-language-action policies. VLA methods adapt large multimodal models to robot demonstrations and decode
continuous action chunks with autoregressive, diffusion, or flow-based heads [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
Their pretrained semantic representations are useful for language grounding,
as demonstrated by recent generalist policy and multimodal-control systems [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] ,
but the action decoder is typically the only component trained to model robot
dynamics. TS-WAM retains the VLM as a semantic context encoder while adding an
explicit temporal latent-action and future-feature interface.

Latent actions and world models. World models learn compact dynamics for planning and control [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 7 , 14 ] .
Reconstruction-free models such as DINO-WM predict features from a frozen
visual representation [ 15 , 16 ] , avoiding the cost of pixel
prediction. Existing approaches commonly first pretrain on large-scale video
or interaction data to obtain latent-action or dynamics supervision, and then
fine-tune on robot demonstrations for embodiment-specific control [ 5 , 17 ] . This two-stage pipeline incurs substantial
additional computational cost and resource demands. TS-WAM instead
jointly optimizes a causally predicted latent action and world-action model
within the deployed VLM.

Joint-embedding predictive architectures. JEPA methods learn by predicting the representation of a target region or
future observation from an encoded context, rather than reconstructing the
input in pixel space. A context encoder and predictor estimate the target
embedding, which is provided by a separately encoded target. The target
encoder is commonly updated by an exponential moving average, providing a
stable regression target without explicit negative samples. This objective
emphasizes predictable semantic and temporal structure. I-JEPA and V-JEPA
apply this principle to images and videos, respectively [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] .
Their EMA target encoders provide stable self-supervision for visual
representation learning.
TS-WAM transfers this principle to VLA: the target is a latent action extracted
from a future-aware VLM, while the student is restricted to current
observations, making the learned representation directly usable for control.

Learning from heterogeneous video. Self-supervised video learning extracts temporal representations without action
labels [ 22 , 19 ] , but they must still be grounded
in embodiment-specific robot actions. LAPA and UniVLA address this gap by
learning latent actions from videos and adapting them to robot control [ 5 , 17 ] . TS-WAM uses unlabeled human videos for temporal
supervision while jointly optimizing robot actions. Its shared latent-action and
future-feature interfaces align video-derived representations with the robot
objective throughout adaptation.

A second challenge is retaining video-derived knowledge during robot adaptation.
Sequential objectives can cause catastrophic forgetting [ 23 ] , motivating continued video supervision during
robot adaptation. TS-WAM retains
ego-video supervision while learning the robot action objective, anchoring the
shared temporal representation to both visual domains. This joint training is
intended to mitigate forgetting; verifying skill retention requires dedicated
evaluation.

2026-10-16.title: What Should Robot Policies Learn to Predict? Rethinking Supervision Targets in Vision-Language-Action Learning
2026-10-16.authors: Haitao Shen , Hanyu Liu , Yihan Lin , Huiping Liu , Junbo Cui , Daoheng Li , Yang Li , Jing Zhang , Wenxin Li , Yuan Yao
2026-10-16.comment: . Haitao Shen and Hanyu Liu contributed equally
2026-10-16.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are typically trained with action
prediction as the primary supervision signal, since robots ultimately execute
actions. Auxiliary objectives such as latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV)
prediction are often added to improve policy learning, yet they compete with
action prediction for the same training budget. We ask whether, under a fixed
budget, allocating a substantial share of training samples to such objectives,
rather than to further action prediction, can improve policy learning. We build
a unified VLA framework that couples a two-stream multimodal diffusion
transformer (MMDiT) with a sample-level router, which assigns each training
sample to either action prediction or an auxiliary objective and thus makes
supervision allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA
targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based
on DINOv3, V-JEPA 2, and Wan2.2 representations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and
four real-robot tasks, suitable LA and FV supervision outperforms action-only
training under the same budget, even when action prediction receives no more
than half of the training samples. FV generally outperforms LA, although the
strongest LA target remains competitive on CALVIN. Diagnostic analyses suggest
that DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets
emphasize absolute position and task identity. We therefore argue that what
robot policies learn to predict, and how training is allocated among these
targets, should be treated as explicit design choices rather than defaulting
to action-dominant training.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for robot learning, achieving strong performance across many manipulation tasks ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2025a ) . Beyond direct action supervision, recent studies increasingly introduce additional learning objectives into VLA training, including geometric representation alignment and spatial or 3D structure prediction ( Li et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . Among these, latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction have become two representative forms of supervision. Latent action abstracts visual transitions into compact tokens that characterize how the scene changes over time ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , whereas future vision encourages the policy to predict future representations, providing supervision about how the scene is expected to evolve ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) .

Because executable actions are the ultimate outputs of robot policies, direct action prediction is typically treated as the dominant training objective, while LA and FV prediction are introduced as auxiliary supervision. Prior studies have examined latent-action formulations and integration strategies ( Lin et al., 2026 ; Bu et al., 2026 ) , showing that such supervision can benefit downstream policy learning. More importantly, LA and FV are not merely auxiliary in effect: by providing learning signals about state changes and task structure, they directly shape the same policy during optimization. Yet, showing that an additional target is useful does not establish that direct action prediction is itself the most effective supervision. We therefore ask (Figure 1 ): under a fixed training budget, what should robot policies learn to predict, and can assigning LA or FV prediction an equal or larger share of training samples than direct action prediction improve action execution?

To investigate this question, we build a unified VLA framework that places a two-stream MMDiT on top of a pretrained VLM, with separate action and auxiliary experts interacting through joint self-attention. We further introduce a sample-level router that assigns each training sample to either action or auxiliary supervision under a fixed training budget, making their relative training allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets and three FV targets: LA predicts discrete latent tokens extracted by different encoders, whereas FV predicts future features in different visual representation spaces. This unified setup enables a controlled comparison of how different supervision targets shape policy learning, with source-matched controls that change only routing for each FV target; FV prediction still conditions on demonstrated actions.

We evaluate our framework on two simulation benchmarks (LIBERO and CALVIN) and four real-robot manipulation tasks, and obtain three main findings. First, suitable LA and FV supervision can outperform action-only training under the same training budget, even when direct action prediction receives only half or fewer of the training samples. Second, FV generally performs better than LA across both simulation and real-robot tasks, while the strongest LA configuration remains competitive on CALVIN. Third, our analyses suggest that LA and FV shape policy learning in different ways : DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets better capture absolute position and task identity, and both can alter policy attention toward task-relevant regions.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) We revisit the dominant role of direct action prediction in VLA training and investigate how allocating supervision to LA and FV affects policy learning. (2) We introduce a unified VLA training framework with a sample-level training router that explicitly controls the allocation of action and auxiliary supervision under a fixed training budget, enabling controlled comparisons across multiple LA and FV targets. (3) We conduct extensive experiments on LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot manipulation tasks, together with representation and attention analyses, and derive systematic findings on action-supervision allocation, the performance differences between LA and FV, and their representation characteristics.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Robot learning draws on supervision beyond action labels, including visual
reconstruction and language generation ( Karamcheti et al., 2023 ) , vision-language
co-training ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ) , and geometric
alignment ( Li et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . We focus on two
demonstration-derived targets, LA and FV, and study both which target to
predict and how to allocate training samples between it and direct action
prediction.

LAPA and UniVLA pretrain policies with latent actions derived from visual
transitions ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) . The villa-X framework jointly models
latent and robot actions, using latent plans to support action
generation ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Analyses examine controllable changes and
exogenous noise ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , while LARYBench ( Nie et al., 2026 ) finds that
general visual encoders can outperform specialized latent-action models on its
semantic and physical-action probes. Empirical studies compare latent-action
formulations, integration strategies, and loss weights ( Lin et al., 2026 ) ,
and examine links between representation-quality proxies and downstream policy
performance ( Bu et al., 2026 ) . Rather than reweighting losses on every
sample, we route each sample to a single objective, and we probe LA and FV
sources with the same absolute- and relative-motion readouts.

GR-1, GR-2, UWM, and DreamZero jointly model future images or videos and robot
actions ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Cheang et al., 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . Seer and VPP guide action
generation with predicted visual states or features ( Tian et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ) .
FLARE enhances policy learning through future-representation alignment and
compares against an action-only baseline trained for longer ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) .
We instead compare against action-only training with the same total budget,
vary the action share, and add source-matched FV controls, including
allocations where auxiliary prediction receives most samples.

2026-10-16.title: Sub-Millisecond Reflexes for Continuous Physical Human-Robot Interaction
2026-10-16.authors: Jon Škerlj , Sami Haddadin
2026-10-16.comment: Submitted to IEEE, source code available at: this https URL
2026-10-16.abstract: Continuous physical human-robot interaction requires robots to rapidly adapt their control behaviour without interrupting task execution. However, existing ROS 2 control architectures rely on stop-to-switch mechanisms that introduce substantial delays and interrupt execution. We present an open-source, sub-millisecond reflex engine based on an enhanced ROS 2-compatible multimode controller that enables deterministic switching between control modalities and integrates reflex behaviours for mitigating contact hazards and kinematic limit violations. Experiments on a Franka Robotics manipulator demonstrate switching delays below 0.1 ​ ms 0.1\>\text{ms} , more than four orders of magnitude faster than conventional ros2_control , while maintaining continuous operation during safety-critical events. In a multi-stage manipulation task, the proposed framework reduced execution time by 3.5 % 3.5\% and peak trajectory jerk by more than threefold. By eliminating runtime middleware overhead, controller transitions are implemented as lock-free pointer operations, enabling reflex-level responsiveness within an open-source robotics framework.
2026-10-16.introduction:
The deployment of service robots in domestic and home environments creates a need for physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) that is inherently safe and robust [ 1 , 2 ] . Unlike a structured lab environment or an industrial cell, a home is a dynamic and unpredictable setting. While future humanoid service robots are expected to operate with human-level capabilities to execute complex, contact-rich manipulation tasks [ 3 , 4 ] , there is still work to be done, with current state-of-the-art systems primarily serving as research platforms [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] .

During operation in such surroundings around humans, unforeseen collisions become inevitable [ 10 ] . Actively mitigating the severity of injuries during these collisions requires torque-controlled systems capable of rapid, low-latency reactions [ 11 , 12 ] . While safety standards specify the high-rate measuring frequencies, such as 1 kHz (ISO 10218 [ 13 ] , ISO 13482 [ 14 ] ), for collision detection, a major gap remains in translating advanced safety and interaction algorithms to modular, open-source architectures [ 10 ] .

In addition, the selected range of diverse domestic tasks, e.g., surface cleaning, folding clothes, or close-proximity physical assistance, directly dictates the requirements of the system’s real-time control architecture. Different phases of these tasks often impose conflicting control objectives, such as accurate free-space motion, compliant interaction, force regulation, or safety-oriented recovery behaviours [ 15 ] . While unified control formulations can address several of these objectives at once [ 16 , 17 ] , no single control strategy is universally optimal for all phases of service robotic tasks. Different approaches may prioritize accuracy, compliance, force regulation, or rapid safety reactions, requiring distinct control characteristics and tuning objectives. Hence, enabling service humanoids to execute these multifaceted routines successfully requires the capability to dynamically and instantaneously switch their control behaviour according to task demands and environmental conditions [ 16 , 15 , 18 ] .

Nowadays, the prevalent state-of-the-art open-source middleware like Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2) [ 19 ] and its hardware-agnostic control framework ros2_control are constrained by their reliance on lifecycle node state transitions with a conservative “stop-to-switch” implementation [ 20 ] . This introduces timing inconsistencies and additional communication overhead [ 21 ] , which fails to fulfill the real-time requirement and introduces time delays for long-horizon tasks. Consequently, conventional safety mechanisms may completely halt the robot’s motion upon safety-critical events. By doing so, these approaches sacrifice fluid physical manipulation and system autonomy for functional safety [ 10 ] .

Having established the need for multi-modal control, safety requirements of low-latency interactions, and the limitations of the middleware “stop-to-switch” bottleneck, as visualized in Fig. 1 , the novel contributions of our work are:

A real-time, sub-millisecond controller switching architecture for smooth continuous task execution compatible with existing ROS 2 ecosystems.

A reflex engine built upon the proposed switching architecture, enabling rapid reactions to contact hazards, joint limits, and excessive velocities before manufacturer safety stops are triggered.

Continuous execution of multistage manipulation tasks through seamless transitions between control behaviours, eliminating the traditional stop-to-switch interruption.

Empirical validation on a physical Franka Robotics manipulator, demonstrating switching latencies below 0.1 ​ ms 0.1\>\text{ms} , successful hazard mitigation, and uninterrupted task execution.

# II State of the Art

## II-A High-Frequency Torque Control

The groundwork for robots to be able to work side by side with humans today was established with the introduction of force and torque control [ 22 ] . The early work in this area supported control frequencies of 60 Hz [ 23 ] and 120 Hz [ 24 ] , which prevented them from detecting higher oscillations at around 280 Hz. With the rapid technological advancement in recent decades, the current safety standards, e.g., ISO 10218 [ 13 ] , require 1 kHz control and measurement frequencies to detect collisions and minimize injury risks during pHRI tasks. This torque command loop frequency enables utilization of Lagrangian dynamics for modelling, so that the joints can be treated as ideal torque sources by higher-level controllers [ 25 ] . Consequently, we have seen a prevalent increase in available collaborative robots (cobots), such as the DLR Lightweight Robot Series [ 26 ] , Franka Emika Panda [ 25 ] & FR3 [ 27 ] , KINOVA Gen 3 [ 28 ] , etc.

## II-B Reflex Behaviours

A continuous, deterministic 1 1 kHz torque-control loop provides the necessary sensory readings for collision detection by estimating external contact wrenches, ℱ ext \mathcal{F}_{\text{ext}} , via proprioceptive observers [ 29 , 30 ] . However, translating these torque observations into safe physical interaction requires a structured control response tailored to the physical evolution of a collision [ 10 ] . In the literature, physical human-robot impacts are categorized into four distinct temporal phases [ 10 ] :

Pre-Collision Phase: Anticipatory measures (velocity scaling, posture optimization) bound kinetic energy before contact [ 11 ] .

Impact Phase I (Transient): Open-loop dynamics ( 10 10 – 20 ​ ms 20\>\text{ms} ) governed by structural inertia. Feedback control cannot attenuate initial peak forces [ 31 , 30 ] .

Impact Phase II (Quasi-Static): Slower contact dynamics where low-latency control eliminates residual crushing forces and clamping [ 32 , 11 ] .

Post-Collision Phase: Reaction termination, secondary hazard management, and task recovery [ 33 , 10 ] .

Task-Preserving Reflexes: e.g., by adjusting execution timing ( Δ ​ t \Delta t ) along the nominal path without altering spatial geometry [ 30 ] .

Task-Relaxing Reflexes: e.g., by permitting transient path shifts before resuming normal tracking [ 10 ] .

Task-Abandoning Reflexes: e.g., by suspending tracking upon reaching the safety limits [ 10 ] .

Beyond reactive control, monitoring and recording frameworks have been proposed to capture robot and human states during pHRI, allowing safety-critical interactions to be analyzed and reconstructed [ 34 , 35 ] . Such approaches provide complementary observability and traceability, whereas the present work focuses on closing the safety loop online through low-latency detection, reflex activation, and recovery.

## II-C Existing Robotics Middlewares

Modular robotics middlewares, primarily ROS 2 [ 19 ] and its hardware-agnostic control framework ros2_control [ 20 ] , have greatly simplified robotics development utilizing component-based architectures. However, this modularity introduces significant communication and scheduling bottlenecks. Standard distributed multi-process configurations suffer from quadratic memory growth ( 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 2 ) \mathcal{O}(N^{2}) ) due to DDS network participant discovery [ 36 ] ; meanwhile, serialization overhead and default executor scheduling models introduce timing jitter and latency [ 19 , 36 ] . To address these problems, ROS 2 introduced node composition and intra-process communication, which uses smart pointers to achieve stable microsecond-level latencies ( ≈ 40 ​ μ ​ s \approx 40\;\mu\text{s} ) [ 36 ] .

Despite these optimizations, the standard ros2_control architecture remains heavily constrained by relying on standard lifecycle node transitions and a conservative “stop-to-switch” paradigm that involves various service calls and resource allocations [ 20 ] that block the real-time loop. To minimize velocity discontinuities during controller switching, some approaches use predefined transition zones to blend from one controller to another [ 37 ] . Unfortunately, this approach could lead to dangerous outcomes in contact-rich pHRI tasks where potential transition zones are almost non-existent. Conversely, the multipanda_ros2 addressed this issue to a certain degree, taking advantage of referencing and shared memory [ 18 ] . However, the reported values still showed an average switching delay of approximately 2 ​ ms 2\>\text{ms} , which still does not satisfy strict ISO-defined requirements for collision detection [ 13 , 14 , 38 ] .

On the other hand, high-performance platforms, to this day, usually rely on proprietary or in-house built frameworks to achieve deterministic execution. For instance, the DLR humanoid Rollin’ Justin uses custom-built controllers for real-time control [ 3 ] . Similarly, the OROCOS framework integrates specialized toolkits to guarantee deterministic execution [ 39 , 40 ] . While these custom solutions meet the strict timing constraints, they lack plug-and-play modularity, adaptability, and generalizability found in modern open-source ecosystems. This forces an unwanted trade-off between the flexibility of general-purpose middlewares and the rigid determinism of platform-specific architectures [ 40 , 19 ] .

2026-10-16.title: MAGMA: Multiplier-Augmented Geometric Motion Algorithm
2026-10-16.authors: César E. Ramos Chuquiure , Vansh Thakur , Challen Enninful Adu , Ram Vasudevan
2026-10-16.abstract:
Solving optimal control problems for high-dimensional mechanical systems subject to constraints remains challenging due to nonlinear dynamics and non-convex feasible sets.
This paper introduces MAGMA (Multiplier–Augmented Geometric Motion Algorithm), an Affine Geometric Heat Flow (AGHF)–based trajectory optimizer that incorporates an augmented Lagrangian framework solved via a primal–dual flow.
A theoretical characterization of the primal-dual AGHF is provided, establishing that MAGMA is a gradient flow on an appropriately defined energy. MAGMA is validated across a variety of challenging trajectory generation problems with obstacles, state limits, and actuation limits.
Comparative evaluations against state-of-the-art solvers demonstrate that MAGMA achieves high quality solutions with significantly reduced tuning effort on the hardest problems.
2026-10-16.introduction:
For practical deployment, an optimal control algorithm must satisfy several requirements: (1) computational efficiency for online or near real-time planning, (2) scalability to high-dimensional systems, (3) compatibility with nonlinear constraints, and (4) reliable convergence from a wide range of initializations.
Existing optimal control methods struggle to simultaneously satisfy these criteria.

Existing methods can be grouped into Dynamic Programming (DP) and Variational methods .
DP-based approaches leverage Bellman’s Principle to compute optimal policies.
Global approaches that solve the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) PDE provide strong optimality guarantees, but require discretizing the entire state space, rendering them intractable beyond moderate dimensions [ 1 ] .
Local variants such as Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) [ 2 ] improve scalability, but suffer from poor convergence when initialized far from the optimum and require careful treatment of inequality constraints.
Variational methods provide an alternative route.
Direct methods such as collocation-based nonlinear programming [ 3 , 4 ] can incorporate complex constraints, but incur high computation times and exhibit sensitivity to discretization and initialization.
Parameterized approaches such as [ 5 ] improve robustness and speed, but still struggle with convergence.

One can also perform trajectory optimization by computing the solution to the Affine Geometric Heat Flow (AGHF) PDE [ 6 ] .
AGHF evolves an initial, potentially infeasible trajectory toward dynamic feasibility by minimizing control effort over a two-dimensional domain , enabling scalability beyond HJB-based approaches.
More recent implementations [ 7 , 8 ] demonstrate that AGHF-based solvers can rapidly produce trajectories for high-dimensional systems.
However, these methods rely on penalty and barrier formulations to enforce constraints, leading to two key limitations: (i) hyperparameter tuning to balance task costs and feasibility and (ii) degraded convergence when constraints compete with the objective.
A recent formulation of the AGHF [ 9 ] casts the problem as a primal-dual flow by introducing Lagrange multipliers associated with the equality constraints.
This remedies the shortcomings of penalty and barrier functions while enforcing constraints.
However, this formulation has only been demonstrated for kinematic constraints and while considering just a single type of cost function.

The key observation underlying our approach is that the AGHF can be identified as a gradient flow in an appropriate function space.
This identification allows classical augmented Lagrangian primal-dual schemes to be lifted directly to the AGHF setting.
Building on this idea, this paper introduces the Multiplier-Augmented Geometric Motion Algorithm (MAGMA) , a new AGHF-based trajectory optimization framework that incorporates an augmented Lagrangian structure solved via an augmented primal–dual geometric flow .
Unlike penalty-driven AGHF variants, MAGMA automatically balances constraint satisfaction and optimality by evolving primal and dual variables.
In contrast to Kim and Park [ 9 ] , MAGMA considers arbitrary nonlinear constraints and cost functions.

The primary contributions of this paper are: (i) a theoretical connection between gradient flows and the AGHF, and (ii) a formulation (MAGMA) of an augmented primal-dual flow based on the AGHF  for nonlinear constraints. 
All code is made available at https://github.com/roahmlab/MAGMA .

2026-10-16.title: Time-Optimal Ergodic Retrieval
2026-10-16.authors: Christian Sulana , Christian Hughes , Ian Abraham
2026-10-16.abstract:
Retrieval tasks are a form of search task where a robot must explore, find an object, and return with it as quickly as possible.
Recent work in ergodic control has demonstrated time-optimal path planning for search tasks where visitation is proportionally matched, within some tolerance, to a given target distribution.
However, these planners minimize the duration of a full deterministic search, while retrieval missions end their search at an unknown point in the trajectory and must return to a given base.
In this work, we propose a new formulation of the time-optimal ergodic search problem that models detection as a Poisson process and minimizes total mission time by including the return phase in the objective.
Experimental results show that time-optimal ergodic retrieval (TOER) achieves up to 19 % 19\% shorter mission durations relative to ergodic baselines and that this advantage grows as the return phase becomes more costly.
Simulation and hardware implementations validate TOER’s compatibility with environments of non-convex geometry as well as both 2D and 3D search domains.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Retrieval tasks are common in search-and-rescue, logistics, and inspection tasks, where a robot must locate an object and bring it to a given destination [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Such missions do not end when the object is found, but rather when it is delivered back to base.
Because detection is uncertain, the point of transition from search to return is a random variable unknown at the time of planning.
A planner that optimizes only up to the moment of detection therefore optimizes a fraction of the total mission which is smallest when the object is hardest to find.
In this work, we address the question: How should a robot order its search when the cost of completing the mission depends on where the search ends?

Ergodic search methods plan single-shot trajectories whose time-averaged visitation is proportional to a given target distribution on the domain [ 4 , 5 ] .
Kernel-based formulations have extended these guarantees to non-Euclidean domains via the Maximum Mean Discrepancy metric [ 6 ] , while time-optimal ergodic search methods (TOES) invert the classical objective to minimize terminal time subject to an ergodic inequality constraint to produce the fastest trajectory that still covers the domain to a chosen tolerance [ 7 ] .

However, these formulations do not currently represent that the search outcome is stochastic.
The optimized horizon is the duration of the full planned search, while retrieval missions end at a random point in the path where the target is detected.
Since the robot rarely executes the entire plan, minimizing the terminal search time generally optimizes an incorrect duration.
In addition, while current time-optimal formulations define a terminal boundary constraint to force the trajectory to end at a base, this hard constraint fixes the final pose even when detection occurs at an earlier segment.

In this paper, we propose time-optimal ergodic retrieval (TOER), which minimizes the expected duration of the full search-and-return mission subject to an ergodic constraint.
We model detection along a trajectory as an inhomogeneous Poisson process whose rate is set by the sensor’s response to a given target distribution such that the probability that the robot is still searching decays with accumulated detection pressure.
The objective sums the expected search time with an expected return time charged from the node at which detection occurs.
We retain ergodicity as a constraint to preserve the coverage guarantees of time-optimal ergodic search and eliminate the degenerate solution of immediately abandoning the search.

We show that the return may be modeled by any lower bound on the return cost, including a straight-line estimate that ignores obstacles, and that the resulting plan carries a computable certificate of ε \varepsilon -optimality.
Constraining the survival probability at the horizon certifies that the target is detected with at least the given probability.
We prove that ergodic coverage guarantees transfer unchanged, and that the value of return-awareness scales predictably with the difficulty of the return toward a computable ceiling fixed by domain geometry, coverage tolerance, and the target distribution.

In summary, the contributions of this work are:

A novel formulation of ergodic retrieval that minimizes the expected duration of a search-and-return mission by charging the return from an unknown detection point;

Derived guarantees that any admissible lower bound on the return yields a certifiably ε \varepsilon -optimal plan, that ergodic coverage guarantees hold in this formulation, and that return-awareness’ advantage grows with return discrepancy toward a fixed ceiling;

Validation in 2D and 3D domains in simulation and on hardware, including isolation of the return term against a search-only reference.

1. A novel formulation of ergodic retrieval that minimizes the expected duration of a search-and-return mission by charging the return from an unknown detection point;

2. Derived guarantees that any admissible lower bound on the return yields a certifiably ε \varepsilon -optimal plan, that ergodic coverage guarantees hold in this formulation, and that return-awareness’ advantage grows with return discrepancy toward a fixed ceiling;

3. Validation in 2D and 3D domains in simulation and on hardware, including isolation of the return term against a search-only reference.

# II Related Work

## II-A Search Under Detection Uncertainty

Search under uncertainty has classically been posed as an allocation of limited effort to maximize the likelihood of detection.
Search theory models a sensor’s chance of finding a target through an exponential detection law whose exponent accumulates with the effort applied in a region [ 8 ] .
Recent work uses a Poisson structure to tie search effort to the probability that an object remains undetected [ 9 ] .
This approach gives a principled notion of how detection likelihood accumulates during search, but is posed over the allocation of sensing effort instead of a trajectory.

Information-driven exploration instead scores uncertainty directly and drives a robot to reduce it [ 10 ] .
Existing work leverages uncertainty metrics such as expected information gain [ 11 ] , the posterior variance of a Gaussian process [ 12 ] , or learned predictions of unobserved regions from sparse samples [ 13 ] .
These scores are used greedily [ 12 ] or over a short lookahead planned via Bayesian optimization [ 14 ] .
However, since the decision horizon is often short, the resulting paths are locally efficient but make no guarantees regarding the coverage that the trajectory induces over the domain.

## II-B Ergodic Search Methods

Ergodic search methods resolve the short-horizon problem of greedy methods by constructing trajectories whose time-averaged visitation proportionally matches a given target distribution [ 4 , 5 ] .
Traditional ergodic metrics are defined over Fourier spectral modes, which fix the approach to a rectangular coordinate structure.
However, recent work has shown that kernel-based formulations such as Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) extend ergodic coverage to domains of arbitrary geometry [ 6 ] and scale [ 15 ] , as well as flow-evolved search spaces [ 16 ] .

Time-optimal ergodic search inverts the classical ergodic problem by minimizing overall search time t f t_{f} subject to an ergodic constraint ℰ ≤ γ \mathcal{E}\leq\gamma [ 7 ] .
The resulting trajectory is the fastest path that still reaches a chosen level of coverage, as characterized through Pontryagin’s conditions of optimality.
However, these formulations fix the final trajectory point via a terminal constraint and treat the search horizon as fixed once planned, which is incompatible with retrieval mission priorities.
Because object detection can happen at any segment of the search trajectory, minimizing t f t_{f} optimizes a duration that is rarely realized, and when the search ends early, the terminal constraint is fixed to a trajectory point that the robot never reaches.

## II-C Return-Aware Planning

Planning that accounts for a return trip is well-studied when the destination is known in advance.
Orienteering and prize-collecting formulations select which locations to visit under a budget that must accommodate the trip back to base [ 17 ] , and coverage planners for energy-limited platforms impose a return-to-base condition on the terminal state [ 18 ] .
In mobile manipulation, search-and-return pipelines typically decompose the task into separate search and transport phases that execute sequentially once the object has been located [ 19 ] .
However, each of these approaches assumes that the return originates from a location that is either fixed or chosen by the planner.
In retrieval under detection uncertainty, the return instead originates from wherever detection occurs, which is a random variable induced by the search trajectory.
In this work, we compute a mission’s return as the expected return cost from each trajectory point to account for the unknown target location.

2026-10-16.title: Cross-Embodiment Causal Transfer from Human Videos to Robot Manipulation
2026-10-16.authors: Xingyu Zhang , Yingchao Li , Peizheng Guo , Jie Hu , Changwen Zheng , Wenwen Qiang
2026-10-16.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation models requires large amounts of interaction data, yet collecting diverse real-robot experience remains costly. Human manipulation videos, in contrast, provide abundant and diverse task experience that could potentially benefit robot learning. However, differences in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms make human motions unsuitable as direct supervision for robot actions, raising a scientific question: what knowledge in human videos should be transferred across embodiments to robot manipulation? To address this question, we analyze subtask transfer through the lens of causal beams, focusing on which contextual conditions and interaction dependencies should be retained to support local task effects. Based on this perspective, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST learns manipulation-related representations from human videos and grounds them in task-level semantic variables using robot demonstrations. Within a predefined manipulation model, causal-beam constraints guide contextual information selection by requiring retained assignments to sustain local mechanism outputs while preserving nontrivial responsiveness to retained inputs. The selected semantic information conditions a world-action model, allowing the robot to generate actions from its own observations without requiring human–robot motion correspondence. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show improvements in task success over the corresponding world-action model baselines.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Recent robot manipulation models are evolving toward World Action Models (WAMs) that jointly model future scene evolution and robot behavior, enabling predictions of interaction outcomes ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . However, scaling real-world robot data requires dedicated hardware, human operation, and physical deployment, making broad coverage of tasks, objects, and scenes expensive. In contrast, human manipulation videos are abundant and capture diverse task processes and object interactions, making them an attractive source of additional experience for robot learning ( Khazatsky et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . Yet humans and robots differ substantially in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms, so concrete human actions cannot be directly reused as robot supervision ( Bahl et al., 2022 ; Xu et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025a ) . This leads to the central question of this work: what knowledge in human manipulation videos should be transferred across embodiment differences to robot manipulation?

A complete human manipulation sequence contains two types of information: object-interaction relations that support task progress, and concrete motion realizations that are closely tied to the human embodiment. For long-horizon manipulation tasks, we first organize continuous execution into local task processes using temporally extended subtasks, thereby avoiding the requirement that the robot reproduce human motion step by step. However, defining a subtask only specifies the local scope within which transfer takes place; it does not further determine which information within that scope should be preserved together with the task experience. Retaining only the task intention or boundary states of a subtask may discard the conditions and interaction relations that determine how a local effect is realized, whereas retaining the complete human execution trajectory reintroduces substantial embodiment-specific motion details.

We study this selective information-preservation problem through the lens of causal beams ( Pearl, 2009 ) . Given a structural model and a specific context, a causal beam allows part of the inputs to be projected out in a context-dependent manner, while requiring the actual values of the retained variables to sustain the actual outcome of the current mechanism and the projected mechanism to retain nontrivial responsiveness to its retained inputs. This perspective motivates separating task-level abstraction from contextual information selection. Task-level variables provide an abstraction of execution, while causal-beam conditions constrain which semantic dependencies are retained within a specified model.

Based on this, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST first learns manipulation-related temporal representations through human-video pretraining and grounds them, under robot demonstration supervision, into a candidate SCM instantiated from shared manipulation templates. A contextual subtask-conditioning module then selects a contextual causal beam from the candidate SCM according to the current execution context, producing the local task effect, relevant conditions, and their effect-relevant dependencies. This structural information conditions the target robot WAM, while concrete actions are still generated from the robot’s current state and its own action space. CBST therefore combines human-video representation transfer with causal-beam-constrained selection of contextual subtask information for robot execution.

Our contributions are summarized as: ( 1 ) We study human-to-robot learning from the perspective of cross-embodiment transfer, focusing on which task-progress structures should remain transferable after embodiment-specific motion is discarded; ( 2 ) We propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST) , which combines a shared candidate manipulation SCM with learned contextual causal beams to preserve effect-relevant conditions and dependencies for conditioning robot WAMs; ( 3 ) We systematically evaluate CBST on WAMs including LingBot-VA and Cosmos Policy, examining the contributions of human video pretraining, context-specific causal selection, and their effects on robot control.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Human-to-robot transfer aims to exploit abundant human demonstrations while addressing the embodiment gap between human and robot execution. Motion-oriented approaches seek representations that remain useful across embodiments while retaining execution information. WHIRL aligns human and robot videos to infer task intent and initializes robot policy learning from third-person human demonstrations ( Bahl et al., 2022 ) , while EgoMimic uses egocentric human videos with 3D hand tracking, cross-domain alignment, and joint training on human and robot demonstrations ( Kareer et al., 2024 ) . Latent Action Pretraining (LAPA) instead learns discrete latent actions from videos without robot action labels and subsequently maps them to robot actions using limited robot data ( Ye et al., 2025 ) . Other approaches move toward higher-level transferable representations. MimicPlay learns latent plans from large-scale human play videos and uses them to guide a low-level robot controller ( Wang et al., 2023 ) ; XSkill discovers cross-embodiment skill prototypes from unlabeled human and robot videos and maps them to robot actions with a conditional policy ( Xu et al., 2023 ) ; Translating Robot Skills learns unsupervised correspondences between skill sequences across morphologically different agents ( Shankar et al., 2022 ) ; and UniSkill learns embodiment-agnostic skill representations that allow skills extracted from human video prompts to guide robot policies trained on robot data ( Kim et al., 2025a ) . More recently, Gen2Act generates human future videos for novel tasks and conditions a robot policy on the generated motion information ( Bharadhwaj et al., 2024 ) .

Temporal abstraction organizes long-horizon behavior into reusable units beyond primitive actions. The options framework formalizes temporally extended policies through initiation sets, internal policies, and termination conditions ( Sutton et al., 1999 ) , while later robotic methods model skill feasibility and composition, such as SayCan ( Ahn et al., 2022 ) and relational skill-precondition learning. Another line of work represents task progress through intermediate subgoals: Video Language Planning generates hierarchical visual and language plans ( Du et al., 2023 ) , TaKSIE conditions visual subgoal generation on task progress ( Kang and Kuo, 2024 ) , and Latent Space Backward Planning recursively constructs intermediate latent goals from the final task goal ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . More recent world-model methods integrate such temporal abstraction directly into planning: Hierarchical Planning with Latent World Models learns dynamics at multiple temporal scales and uses high-level latent subgoals to guide low-level planning ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , while SAGE similarly exploits temporally extended latent subgoals for action-sequence generation ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) .

World models learn predictive dynamics to support action selection and planning. Early latent-dynamics approaches such as PlaNet perform planning directly in learned latent spaces ( Hafner et al., 2019 ) , while more recent methods extend this idea to visual robot manipulation: DINO-WM predicts future visual features for zero-shot planning ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , V-JEPA 2-AC learns action-conditioned latent dynamics for model-predictive control ( Assran et al., 2025 ) , and IRASim models fine-grained action-conditioned visual futures for simulation and planning ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) . Recent World-Action Models further unify future prediction with action generation. WorldVLA jointly models visual and action tokens in an autoregressive framework ( Cen et al., 2025 ) ; Cosmos Policy generates robot actions together with future-state images and value estimates ( Kim et al., 2026 ) ; LingBot-VA jointly learns future-frame prediction and policy execution in a shared visual–action latent space ( Li et al., 2026 ) ; and τ 0 \tau_{0} -WM further combines video prediction, action generation, and action evaluation within a unified model ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) .
