2026-10-16.title: Trajectory-based Diffusion from One-shot Human Video for Generalizable Manipulation
2026-10-16.authors: Guoping Pan , Xinmiao Yu , Wannan Cao , Jincheng Li , Baolin Jiang , Yizhe Li , Yi Cheng , Houde Liu
2026-10-16.abstract: Imitation learning enables robots to perform complex tasks by leveraging human-collected demonstrations. However, most existing approaches require labor-intensive data collection with additional teleoperation systems, which hinders scalability. Human videos represent a natural source of data that implicitly contain knowledge of manipulation behaviors. However, transferring them to robots remains challenging due to the visual domain gap and the absence of explicit action labels. In this work, we introduce TDV, a trajectory-based framework that leverages data generation to enable generalizable manipulation. TDV focuses on task-relevant objects by leveraging plug-and-play 6D pose estimation techniques to extract object trajectories from human videos, thereby mitigating the impact of irrelevant backgrounds and varying viewpoints. As a modality-agnostic intermediate representation, trajectories are inherently independent of the visual domains and different embodiments, enabling efficient data generation. Our method outperforms previous approaches on RLBench simulation tasks, achieving near 100% success rates across seven tasks. In real-world experiments, TDV enables cross-embodiment generalization manipulation from one-shot human demonstrations by leveraging efficient trajectory generation techniques.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Imitation learning enables robots to perform complex tasks without the need for manually configured heuristic rules. Most existing imitation learning approaches rely on proprioceptive states and visual data collected directly from the robot system, typically obtained through additional teleoperation systems operated by humans [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . However, this approach is inefficient and presents significant challenges in scaling up data collection. In addition to images and text, there is a vast amount of human demonstration videos available on the internet, which inherently encode procedural knowledge for performing various manipulation tasks. Nevertheless, extracting meaningful perceptual information and actions from these videos for robot manipulation remains a non-trivial challenge.

This problem involves two main aspects: the significant gap in visual domains and the lack of robot action information. To address the visual domain gap, the most straightforward approach is to leverage image editing techniques, replacing the human with a robot in the images or erasing the human entirely [ 4 , 5 ] . However, this method heavily depends on the editing quality, and there is currently a lack of studies that ensure both good consistency and compliance with physical laws. Some studies utilize flow as an intermediate representation [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] , which captures the motion trends of task-relevant objects and exhibits robustness to visual discrepancies introduced by different embodiments. However, these methods require the camera viewpoint during deployment to be consistent with the one used during data acquisition, which limits their scalability in practical applications [ 10 ] . For manipulation tasks, the primary focus is on the state changes of task-relevant objects, rather than the agent executing the actions, thereby enabling cross-embodiment deployment. We find that object-centric representations, such as 6D object pose [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] , can effectively capture the real-time state of the object while mitigating the effects of irrelevant background and different viewpoints. A trajectory composed of a sequence of 6D object poses encapsulates the state transitions during the manipulation process. The previous method [ 12 ] requires pre-generated grasp poses for the object and fails to fully exploit the advantages of trajectory representations in scaling datasets [ 14 ] , which is crucial for enhancing the generalization of manipulation.

To overcome these shortcomings, we propose a trajectory-based diffusion framework, TDV, which enables generalizable manipulation across different embodiments from one-shot human demonstrations, as shown in Fig. . Our framework is structured into three stages.
First, we parse human videos to extract motion trajectories relevant to the manipulation task. The full trajectory is then divided into multiple subtask segments according to changes in the moving entity or the reference object. Based on the type of moving entity, we categorize each subtask segment into two types, as illustrated in Fig. 2 : hand tasks , where the motion is dominated by the hand itself, and object tasks , where the motion corresponds to manipulated objects. For example, in the pouring task, grasping the kettle is treated as a hand task, while the subsequent pouring action is treated as an object task. In hand tasks, we employ a hand pose estimation model [ 15 ] to reconstruct human hand trajectories. For object tasks, we adopt a plug-and-play 6D pose estimation model [ 16 ] to extract object trajectories. To eliminate the influence of viewpoint changes, we represent trajectories relative to the reference object frame. Then, the resulting trajectories provide a modality-agnostic intermediate representation, enabling efficient data augmentation through simple trajectory scaling and interpolation. Finally, we then use the augmented dataset to train a trajectory-based diffusion policy, which achieves robust generalization across diverse manipulation tasks and supports multi-procedure execution conditioned on high-level task descriptions. During deployment, the pose of the moving entity is detected in real time and fed into the history sequence of the diffusion policy, enabling closed-loop execution.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We propose a trajectory-based diffusion framework (TDV) that learns manipulation policies solely from human videos, significantly improving data collection efficiency and enabling scalable policy learning across diverse tasks.

We leverage an object-centric intermediate representation based on trajectories to enable effective learning and cross-embodiment generalization.

Our experiments demonstrate that TDV achieves strong spatial generalization and remains robust under complex backgrounds and diverse camera viewpoints.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Learning from Human Videos

Many efforts have been made to learn scalable manipulation policies from non-robotic data, particularly human videos [ 8 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . The main idea is to extract meaningful representations from massive visual data and transfer them to robotic tasks. For instance, R3M [ 20 ] and MVP [ 21 ] pretrain visual representations on the large-scale internet human video dataset Ego4D [ 22 ] , aiming to extract manipulation knowledge beneficial for robot learning from first-person perspective videos. However, due to the heterogeneous nature of the data sources and significant domain gaps, transferring pre-trained representations to specific manipulation remains challenging. To address this issue, some methods [ 23 , 24 ] leverage in-domain human videos, where humans and robots perform the same manipulation tasks in identical environments. Another approach leverages transferable representations, such as affordances [ 25 , 5 ] and flows [ 6 , 8 , 7 ] , combined with additional action policies.

## II-B Object-Centric Manipulation

To exclude background and task-irrelevant objects, many researchers focus on developing effective object-centric representations, which possess visual robustness and cross-scene generalization capabilities. The primary representation include point clouds [ 26 ] , Gaussian splatting [ 27 ] , 6D object pose estimation, neural implicit fields [ 28 ] , and other related methodologies [ 29 , 6 , 30 , 12 ] . Owing to the development of visual foundation models, previous work [ 26 ] has segmented the object point cloud from the scene point cloud in a modular manner and used it as input for the imitation policy, which are robust to background changes. Rather than directly using point clouds, Kerr et al. [ 29 ] combined 3D Gaussians with object part motion to construct a 4D Differentiable Part Model. Among object-centric representations, the 6D object pose is comparatively straightforward and efficient. Pan et al. [ 13 ] instructed the LLM to construct constraint relations based on the coordinate of task-relevant objects, and performed real-time 6D pose tracking during closed-loop execution to optimize the trajectory.

2026-10-16.title: Comfortably Stuck: Evaluation Pitfalls in Bench2Drive's Closed-Loop Protocol
2026-10-16.authors: Thomas Schwarzfischer , Emad Aghajanzadeh , Moritz Thoma , Nael Fasfous , Manoj Rohit Vemparala , Pierpaolo Mori , Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder , Ulf Schlichtmann
2026-10-16.abstract: Closed-loop evaluation is widely regarded as a more faithful way to assess end-to-end (E2E) driving models than open-loop evaluation, and Bench2Drive, built on the CARLA simulator, has become the dominant benchmark for it. We show that its evaluation protocol itself contains pitfalls that can misrepresent the models scored on it. Bench2Drive’s comfort metric, adapted from nuPlan, has several implementation errors and a segmentation scheme that rewards standing still, so it mostly measures how long a vehicle stays stationary, correlating with stationary time at r = 0.97 r=0.97 across eight models. We propose a corrected, distance-based metric that cuts that correlation to r = 0.06 r=0.06 . Under it, the strong driving-score/comfort tradeoff the original metric reports is no longer detectable once models are compared at matched driving speed, which suggests that comfort trades against how fast a model drives rather than against how well it drives. We also uncover two pitfalls in how the harness supplies navigation signals: the default controller can replace a model’s own steering with an angle toward the route target point, and the target point supplied at evaluation time can differ substantially from what a model saw in training. We demonstrate both on UniAD and VAD, where their effects differ sharply, and argue that future closed-loop evaluations should check for them. We will release all fixes as standalone code, so corrected comfort scores can be obtained from logged trajectories without re-running closed-loop simulation.
2026-10-16.introduction:
End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving models have recently attracted substantial attention, and as the space grows, reliable evaluation becomes essential for directing research and comparing models fairly [ 1 , 2 ] . Closed-loop evaluation, in which a model reacts to the consequences of its own past decisions rather than replaying a fixed expert trajectory, is a more faithful proxy of real-world driving quality than open-loop evaluation [ 3 , 2 ] . CARLA [ 4 ] is the most widely used platform for closed-loop testing, and Bench2Drive [ 2 ] builds on it with a curated set of edge-case routes to standardize closed-loop evaluation across the field. We show that the Bench2Drive protocol itself contains issues that can lead to large misinterpretations of E2E models along two axes: driving comfort and driving behavior.

Comfort: Bench2Drive adapts nuPlan’s comfort check [ 5 ] , which tests six kinematic quantities, among them lateral and longitudinal acceleration, jerk and yaw rate, against thresholds calibrated on human driving logged at 10 ​ Hz 10\,\mathrm{Hz} with angles in radians. Ported to CARLA’s 20 ​ Hz 20\,\mathrm{Hz} logs, the implementation gets the sampling rate, the smoothing window, the angular units and the yaw derivative wrong, and together these errors inflate the measured jerk and yaw terms enough that segments in which the vehicle is genuinely driving fail thresholds a human driver would pass. Worse, comfort is scored over fixed one-second chunks rather than distance travelled, so a vehicle that simply stops satisfies every threshold for free and keeps banking comfortable segments for as long as it stands there. The resulting score measures how long a model stands still rather than how smoothly it drives, correlating with stationary time at r = 0.97 r=0.97 across eight models and ranking the models that most often get stuck as the most comfortable. Fixing the implementation alone does not help, because time-based segmentation rewards standing still by construction. We therefore propose a distance-based metric that scores comfort per meter driven, which cuts that correlation to r = 0.06 r=0.06 and moves VAD and SimLingo sharply down the comfort ranking. Measured this way, the strong tradeoff between driving score and comfort that prior evaluations report is no longer detectable once models are compared at matched driving speed, so comfort trades against how fast a model drives rather than against how well it drives.

Navigation signals: E2E models rely on a high-level navigation signal, a discrete command or a continuous target point, to know where the route leads. Prior work studies how best to integrate that signal into the architecture [ 6 , 7 ] ; we instead study how the harness supplies it, and find two issues. First, Bench2Drive’s default controller replaces the model’s own predicted steering with an angle toward the route target point, a behavior we call steering overruling (SO), in more than half of all frames in some scenarios. This masks whether a model can correct its own drift or react to a sudden obstacle, and it affects models so unevenly that scores obtained under the default controller are not comparable across models. Second, the target point supplied at evaluation time can differ substantially in density and distance from what a model saw during training, pushing it toward out-of-distribution inputs. We propose fixes for both: a controller that never overwrites the model’s steering, and a route planner whose target-point sampling matches the training distribution.

Our contributions are as follows:

We show that Bench2Drive’s comfort metric is dominated by a bias toward standing still, and propose a corrected, distance-based metric that removes it while staying faithful to nuPlan’s thresholds.

We uncover two protocol-level pitfalls in how Bench2Drive supplies navigation signals, a controller that overwrites the model’s steering and a train-deployment mismatch in the target point, and propose fixes for both.

We re-benchmark comfort across eight recent E2E models under the corrected metric and demonstrate the navigation fixes on UniAD and VAD. We will release all fixes as standalone code, so corrected comfort scores can be obtained from existing logs without re-running closed-loop simulation.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A End-to-end driving architectures

End-to-end (E2E) driving replaces the hand-designed interfaces of the modular stack with a single network trained toward the final planning task [ 8 , 9 ] . In E2E design, modules exchange information with dense features which preserves scene information and limits error accumulation [ 10 ] . UniAD [ 9 ] and VAD [ 11 ] pioneered this direction. Both chain perception, prediction, and planning through task queries over a shared bird’s eye view (BEV) representation, and VAD swaps the costly rasterized scene for a vectorized one. Transfuser [ 12 ] fuses camera and LiDAR modalities into a dense BEV with transformer attention, and TFv6 [ 6 ] is the latest variant of it that further enhances its planning head design. Models also differ in how the plan itself is produced. Hydra-MDP [ 13 ] and SparseDriveV2 [ 14 ] score a fixed trajectory vocabulary instead of regressing a single trajectory, the latter from a sparse scene representation. SimLingo [ 3 ] and Orion [ 15 ] put a language model in the loop: SimLingo outputs reasoning and action directly from a Qwen model [ 16 ] , while Orion decodes language reasoning features into actions with a generative planner.

## II-B Evaluation of End-to-end models

E2E models are evaluated either open-loop or closed-loop [ 1 , 17 , 2 ] . Open-loop evaluation replays pre-recorded expert data and measures how closely the model imitates it. It is cheap and needs no simulator, but it never confronts the model with the consequences of its own actions. Real driving is closed-loop: every scene a driver meets follows from what it did before, including its errors. Closed-loop evaluation is therefore the more faithful measure of driving quality, and safety confines it to simulation. Real data supports it only partially. NAVSIM [ 1 ] rolls a predicted trajectory out for four seconds against replayed actors, and NAVSIMv2 [ 17 ] adds perturbed restarts to probe recovery, but both query the policy once and score a plan it never revises. HUGSIM [ 18 ] goes further, reconstructing recorded scenes with Gaussian splatting so the ego can leave the logged path and still be rendered from novel views, yet its HD-Score is inherited from NAVSIM and still scores the predicted trajectory rather than the path actually driven [ 19 ] .
CARLA [ 4 ] closes the loop fully. The simulator reacts to the policy at every step, and renders the future scene sensors necessary for E2E models, different than planning-only benchmarks like NuPlan [ 5 ] . Bench2Drive [ 2 ] design 220 driving routes, each built around one edge-case scenario and one driving ability, scored by driving score, success rate, efficiency, and comfort. It is now the default closed-loop benchmark for E2E driving [ 20 , 14 , 15 , 3 , 21 ] .

E2E policies need a high-level navigation signal to know where the route leads. It arrives either as a discrete navigation command [ 9 , 11 , 15 ] or as a continuous navigation target point from a route planner [ 3 , 6 ] . Jaeger et al. [ 22 ] show that target-point-conditioned models learn to follow the point as a shortcut for lateral control, so gains credited to architecture partly reflect that bias [ 6 ] . That bias is acquired from training data. We study the evaluation side instead. First, the harness supplies its own target point at test time, and its distribution need not match the training one. Fixing the distance to a constant does not resolve this: the point lies ahead on the route, so its distance shrinks as the ego approaches and jumps when the next point activates. What the harness controls is route sampling density, and every spacing induces a different distance distribution. Second, the harness does more than pass the signal on. Bench2Drive’s controller steers toward the target point itself, overruling the model ( section III-A ).

nuPlan [ 5 ] defines an ego comfort check over six kinematic quantities: longitudinal and lateral acceleration, yaw rate, yaw acceleration, longitudinal jerk, and jerk magnitude. It is all-or-nothing. Every quantity must stay within its threshold on every frame, so one violation fails the whole trajectory. The thresholds [ 23 ] are fit empirically on expert driving, given in SI units with angles in radians, and calibrated for a 10 ​ Hz 10\,\mathrm{Hz} sampling rate together with the smoothing windows applied at that rate.
The formulation spread beyond nuPlan. NAVSIM [ 1 ] scores comfort against the same style of thresholds, following PDM-Closed’s weighting scheme [ 24 ] , and Bench2Drive [ 2 ] adopts them for CARLA. Comfort is thus shared across open-loop, pseudo-closed-loop, and closed-loop protocols rather than specific to any one of them.

Human-perception studies justify the ingredients. de Winkel et al. [ 25 ] tie discomfort to acceleration and jerk, and show it depends on the direction of motion as well as its magnitude. Hu et al. [ 26 ] score comfort from jerk on Bézier-interpolated trajectories and add energy consumption. None of this work asks whether such a check still measures what it was calibrated for once it is ported into a closed-loop harness. We show that it does not: implementation details and the choice of segmentation dominate the score.

2026-10-16.title: Uni-PNP: Unified Prehensile and Non-prehensile Policy Learning for Generalizable Object Pose Reaching
2026-10-16.authors: Wenxuan Zhu , Yuze Wang , Jiangran Lyu , Jiayi Chen , Yixin Zheng , Mi Yan , Li Yi , Zhizheng Zhang , He Wang
2026-10-16.abstract: Object manipulation often requires combining non-prehensile actions with grasping. However, existing approaches typically develop these capabilities separately and integrate them by sequencing distinct primitives through prescribed intermediate objectives, limiting the coordination of contact motions and grasping. Their integration also remains sensitive to object and gripper geometry and depends on particular environmental supports, complicating real-world deployment. We present Uni-PNP, a unified policy that jointly learns prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation for object pose reaching across diverse objects and grippers. To achieve this, we first pretrain a geometry encoder to predict contact-induced object motion using a contact-dynamics dataset constructed from simulated interactions between diverse objects and grippers. We then train the policy in a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum from graspable objects to ungraspable peers, encouraging the discovery of non-prehensile interactions and their integration with grasping. Experiments show 76.39% success on hundreds of seen objects with grippers, and 57.91% on unseen peers, outperforming the strongest pose-reaching baseline by 20.52 and 17.79 percentage points, respectively. We also analyze emergent behaviors, including nonprehensile and prehensile repositioning, grasp acquisition that requires grasping after tipping, and table-assisted reorientation while grasping, and transfer to the real-world scenario. Project page available at lgswdn.github.io/Uni-PNP .
2026-10-16.introduction:
Robotic manipulation can be broadly divided into prehensile and nonprehensile modes. Prehensile manipulation moves an object while holding it in a stable grasp. Nonprehensile manipulation moves an object without grasping, through actions such as pushing or tipping. We often combine these skills in everyday activities. For instance, a phone lying flat on a table leaves little clearance for a direct grasp. We slide and tilt the phone while closing our fingers, creating room to secure and lift it. Nonprehensile contact creates access for grasping, while a secure grasp enables controlled lifting and repositioning. However, prior work typically develops prehensile and non-prehensile capabilities separately, and combines them either by preparing objects for a grasp using non-prehensile manipulation [ 1 , 2 ] , or by planning sequences of prehensile and non-prehensile primitives [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Treating the two modes as separate skills limits their ability to learn unified manipulation behaviors.

Moreover, prior methods depend strongly on the geometry of the environment, object, and gripper. Several grasp-preparation strategies exploit environmental features such as edges and walls to obtain extrinsic dexterity [ 6 , 1 , 7 ] , requiring suitable environmental supports. GOMP [ 2 ] uses a learned graspability field to guide non-prehensile manipulation toward configurations suitable for subsequent grasp execution. Furthermore, these methods are constrained to the gripper geometry seen in training, which is inconvenient for real-world deployment. Cross-gripper policies learn grasp poses from grasp synthesis [ 8 , 9 ] . However, geometry influences manipulation beyond grasp pose selection: it also determines the contact interactions and resulting object motions. These geometry-dependent effects motivate jointly learning prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation across diverse objects and grippers.

We present Uni-PNP, a unified policy for prehensile and non-prehensile (PNP) object manipulation. Our policy reaches target object poses across diverse objects and grippers. To achieve this, we first construct a contact-dynamics dataset by sampling object–gripper contact configurations and recording the resulting object motions under gripper actions. We then pretrain a compact geometry encoder to predict these motions, learning a representation of geometry-dependent contact dynamics for the policy. Finally, we train the policy on these features through a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum. The policy first learns grasping and repositioning with smaller, readily graspable objects. Training then continues on an object set whose initial configurations are challenging for direct grasping, encouraging the policy to discover non-prehensile interactions and combine them with grasping.

We evaluate Uni-PNP in simulation on 1,218 objects from this challenging set and 249 unseen objects from a different distribution, using grippers drawn from a training catalog of 200 geometries and the unseen Panda gripper. Uni-PNP achieves 76.39% pose-reaching success on training objects and grippers, and 57.91% on unseen objects with the unseen Panda gripper, outperforming the pose-reaching baselines across all settings. We complement these benchmarks with real-world experiments and an analysis of emergent manipulation skills, including tip-assisted grasping and table-assisted reorientation.

Our contributions are:

We introduce Uni-PNP, a unified policy that learns prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation jointly for object pose reaching.

We construct a contact-dynamics dataset and propose motion-prediction pretraining to learn a compact geometry representation across varied objects and grippers.

We demonstrate effective object pose reaching and generalization to unseen objects and grippers in simulation and real-world experiments.

1. We introduce Uni-PNP, a unified policy that learns prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation jointly for object pose reaching.

2. We construct a contact-dynamics dataset and propose motion-prediction pretraining to learn a compact geometry representation across varied objects and grippers.

3. We demonstrate effective object pose reaching and generalization to unseen objects and grippers in simulation and real-world experiments.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Learning-based Non-Prehensile Manipulation

Non-prehensile manipulation changes an object’s pose through contacts such as pushing and pivoting [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Recent learning-based methods unify non-prehensile manipulations by directly mapping geometric observations to actions [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . CORN [ 13 ] and HACMan [ 17 ] improve generalization across object shapes through contact-aware representations and end-to-end interaction learning, while other methods use parameterized primitives or policy decomposition [ 18 ] . Nevertheless, these approaches focus on non-prehensile repositioning itself; a non-prehensile policy alone does not secure the object for stable lifting. Grasp and post-grasp repositioning therefore remain separate objectives in most existing systems.

## II-B Combining Prehensile and Non-Prehensile Manipulation

Grasp-Oriented Preparation and Affordance-Guided Manipulation. Many methods treat non-prehensile actions primarily as grasp preparation. Push–grasp systems coordinate pushing and grasping to improve grasp accessibility [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] . Affordance-based methods predict regions or object configurations that support a subsequent grasp [ 1 , 2 ] , with language-conditioned affordances extending this idea to task-specific manipulation [ 22 ] . GOMP [ 2 ] learns a graspability field and directs non-prehensile motion toward configurations suitable for grasp execution. Several approaches obtain extrinsic dexterity from walls, edges, slots, or slopes [ 6 , 1 , 7 ] , making execution dependent on suitable support geometry. Separating preparation from grasp execution introduces a handoff between the two stages, whose effectiveness depends on the intermediate object configuration and available support.

Explicit Integration of Prehensile and Non-Prehensile Skills. Another line of work explicitly plans contact modes or sequences of manipulation skills. External pushes, shared grasping, and contact-mode planning coordinate finger contacts with environmental support [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . HACMan++ [ 3 ] selects spatially grounded motion primitives, AdaptPNP [ 5 ] revises primitive sequences and intermediate object poses using execution feedback, and SPIN [ 4 ] learns connectors between independently trained skills before distilling their planned trajectories into a policy. For skill-library approaches, the available primitives and transition conditions constrain the behaviors that can be composed. Contact-mode planners instead explore modeled contact interactions without necessarily requiring a predefined skill library. In contrast, Uni-PNP learns coordinated arm and gripper actions through a unified policy.

## II-C Geometry Representations for Contact-Rich Control

Point-cloud encoders such as PointNet [ 28 ] provide geometric features for downstream learning. Self-supervised pretraining develops these features through correspondence matching [ 29 ] , completion of occluded geometry [ 30 ] , and masked prediction of discrete tokens, point geometry, or latent representations [ 31 , 32 , 33 ] . For robotic control, PointPatchRL [ 34 ] combines masked reconstruction with reinforcement learning, while 4D visual pretraining learns features through future prediction [ 35 ] . These objectives do not explicitly supervise the object motion induced by gripper contact.

Contact-based representations focus on the geometry through which forces can be applied. CORN [ 13 ] predicts contact between an object and the gripper, while UniCORN [ 14 ] extends contact prediction to pairs of arbitrary geometries. Their supervision identifies where contact occurs but does not specify the motion it produces. DAPL [ 16 ] incorporates physical attributes and action-conditioned dynamics prediction to represent contact-induced scene motion. Its encoder is refined using trajectories collected by the RL policy, tying the learned representation to the task-specific interaction distribution explored during training.

2026-10-16.title: MAIA: Anticipating Interaction Anomalies in Contact-Rich Manipulation via Multimodal World Models
2026-10-16.authors: Yi Qiao , Maolin Zheng , Haoran Sun , Lujia Dong , Wenzhao Lian
2026-10-16.abstract:
Reliable contact-rich manipulation requires detecting execution deviations early enough for corrective action. Yet most monitoring methods are reactive, identifying anomalies only after they become observable. Anticipating such anomalies is challenging because visual observations only partially reveal physical interaction, while planned actions describe intended motion rather than their actual physical consequences.
We address this problem with MAIA, a multimodal framework for anomaly anticipation. Its vision–action–force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts the visual and force responses of planned actions, while a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending interaction anomalies.
To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset of 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution.
Experiments on both seen and novel tasks show that MAIA achieves more accurate anomaly discrimination than representative baselines while providing earlier warnings, with bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 and median anticipation lead times of 28.0 and 25.1 steps, respectively. Moreover, using these predictions for anomaly-aware action selection improves end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5% without retraining the underlying manipulation policy.
These results highlight the value of modeling future physical consequences for proactive anomaly anticipation.
View our project in https://joringell.github.io/MAIA/
2026-10-16.introduction:
Modern robot manipulation policies can plan and execute increasingly complex behaviors, yet even strong policies cannot eliminate execution uncertainty during physical interaction [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
While policy-generated actions appear reasonable, perception errors, imperfect alignment, object constraints, and environmental variations can cause the resulting interaction to deviate from the intended trajectory.
This uncertainty is especially pronounced in contact-rich manipulation, where similar actions can lead to substantially different physical outcomes depending on how the interaction unfolds [ 4 , 5 ] .
Reliable execution therefore requires monitoring the evolving robot–environment interaction and responding to deviations before they escalate and compromise task progress.

Existing approaches to robot execution monitoring predominantly focus on reactive detection of failures and anomalies [ 6 , 7 ] . By identifying deviations only after observable evidence emerges, they leave little window for intervention. This is particularly limiting for anomalous interactions, which may emerge locally and evolve without producing clear task-level failure signals.
Modern manipulation policies, however, often generate action sequences over a future horizon, enabling evaluation of their potential consequences in advance [ 1 , 2 , 8 ] .
This motivates anomaly anticipation, which assesses whether planned actions are likely to induce anomalous interactions before they occur, thereby providing an early warning for intervention or replanning, as illustrated in Fig. MAIA: Anticipating Interaction Anomalies in Contact-Rich Manipulation via Multimodal World Models .

A central challenge in predicting anomalous interactions stems from the partial observability of underlying physical dynamics.
While visual observations provide valuable geometric context and task progress, they offer only indirect evidence of contact forces, friction effects, resistance, and mechanical constraints.
Planned actions specify the robot’s intended motion, yet do not reveal how the environment will physically respond.
Thus, similar visual states and actions can lead to substantially different interaction outcomes.
Force–torque feedback reduces this ambiguity by providing direct measurements of physical responses.
This calls for modeling future multimodal physical responses under planned actions to anticipate anomalous interactions.

Driven by these insights, we formulate contact-rich anomaly anticipation as prospective action evaluation: predicting whether planned actions will cause the robot–environment interaction that deviates from its expected dynamics.
We instantiate this formulation in MAIA , a framework for M ultimodal A nticipation of I nteraction A nomalies.
At its core, the vision–action–force world model learns expected interaction dynamics from nominal executions and predicts future visual and force responses under planned actions. A lightweight anomaly head then integrates the resulting predictive representations to estimate whether an anomaly will occur and its temporal prevalence over the future horizon.

However, evaluating anomaly anticipation requires temporally localized supervision indicating when an anomaly begins and how it evolves, which is not provided by conventional failure-oriented datasets. Thus, we introduce CRIA , a real-world multimodal dataset for C ontact- R ich I nteraction A nomaly anticipation. CRIA comprises 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, covering nominal and anomalous executions. It provides temporally aligned visual, action, and force/torque signals with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution.

Built on this data, MAIA learns interaction dynamics rather than task-specific failure templates. This interaction-centric representation captures shared dynamics across diverse contact regimes while remaining sensitive to task-specific deviations, supporting transfer to novel tasks with limited adaptation.
Additionally, because model predictions are conditioned on planned actions, MAIA can evaluate candidate action sequences before execution, extending anomaly anticipation from passive monitoring to proactive action selection.

Our key contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate contact-rich anomaly anticipation as prospective action evaluation and introduce MAIA, a vision–action–force framework for anticipating anomalous interactions.

We introduce CRIA, a real-world aligned visuo-action-force dataset for contact-rich manipulation, comprising 2,852 trajectories across 18 tasks with fine-grained temporal anomaly annotations.

We demonstrate that MAIA learns transferable predictive interaction representations across diverse contact regimes, achieving bACC of 0.765 on seen tasks and 0.710 on novel tasks. MAIA further enables anomaly-aware action selection, improving real-robot success from 52.6% to 61.5% without policy retraining.

1. We formulate contact-rich anomaly anticipation as prospective action evaluation and introduce MAIA, a vision–action–force framework for anticipating anomalous interactions.

2. We introduce CRIA, a real-world aligned visuo-action-force dataset for contact-rich manipulation, comprising 2,852 trajectories across 18 tasks with fine-grained temporal anomaly annotations.

3. We demonstrate that MAIA learns transferable predictive interaction representations across diverse contact regimes, achieving bACC of 0.765 on seen tasks and 0.710 on novel tasks. MAIA further enables anomaly-aware action selection, improving real-robot success from 52.6% to 61.5% without policy retraining.

# II Related Work

## II-A Robot Failure and Anomaly Detection

Robot execution monitoring aims to detect deviations that may indicate anomalous interactions or impending task failures.
A common line of work formulates failure monitoring as out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, learning representations of nominal execution and detecting departures from the learned distribution [ 6 , 9 , 10 ] .
With the emergence of vision-language-action policies, recent methods exploit temporal action consistency [ 11 , 12 ] , internal policy representations [ 7 , 13 ] , and semantic reasoning [ 14 ] for runtime monitoring and failure characterization.
More recently, predictive methods have begun to assess the consequences of planned actions through learned future representations or world-model rollouts, offering earlier evidence of potential failures [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] .
However, these approaches seldom explicitly model physical interaction dynamics under future actions. In contrast, we anticipate anomalies by modeling how the interaction is expected to evolve from visual observations, planned action sequences, and force-torque feedback.

## II-B World Models for Robot Interaction

World models learn predictive representations of robot-environment interactions to support planning and control, modeling future observations in pixel space or latent dynamics space [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] .
Building on these predictive capabilities, recent methods leverage imagined futures to guide action generation, evaluation, and selection [ 3 , 17 , 22 , 23 ] .
To better capture contact-rich physics, multimodal world models have increasingly incorporated force or tactile sensing alongside visual inputs [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ] .
However, existing approaches predominantly focus on predicting future visual scenes or generating next actions, rather than explicitly modeling the physical consequences resulting from planned actions. We instead forecast future visual and force responses conditioned on these actions, revealing how the physical interaction is expected to evolve and enabling anomaly anticipation before deviations become
fully observable.

2026-10-16.title: Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering: Improving Imitation Learning Policy Robustness through Expert Hidden-State Geometry
2026-10-16.authors: KwangBin Lee
2026-10-16.abstract:
Small observation or action errors can compound during closed-loop execution and disrupt a trained imitation learning policy.
We study whether the original expert demonstrations can improve robustness through test-time hidden-state steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining.
Our analysis of a trained policy finds that expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in relatively few dimensions, while the directions capturing this variation differ across regions.
Motivated by this geometry, we propose Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states obtained by replaying the demonstrations through the frozen policy.
DHS attenuates coordinates with low expert variance more strongly than those with high variance, then maps the modified coordinates back to hidden-state space.
This allows steering directions to vary with the current hidden state while retaining every coordinate.
Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over the unmodified Transformer policies.
Controlled comparisons yield higher mean success with learned nonlinear coordinates than with linear coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling.
Combining DHS with action smoothing improves mean success rate under observation noise in certain tasks compared with action smoothing alone.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Imitation learning (IL) trains robot policies from expert demonstrations, but the observations encountered during execution also depend on the policy’s own actions.
Observation noise or action errors can therefore take the policy into conditions poorly represented in the demonstrations, where further errors can compound and disrupt task execution.
DAgger addresses this distribution mismatch by obtaining expert actions on learner-visited states, while DART collects demonstrations that include recovery from disturbances [ 1 , 2 ] .
Online reinforcement learning can also improve pretrained robot policies by updating their parameters using reward feedback from interaction [ 3 ] .
These approaches all require information beyond the original demonstration set, such as new expert labels, additional demonstrations, or reward feedback from interaction.
This motivates a complementary question: whether the original demonstrations alone can improve the closed-loop robustness of a trained IL policy without additional demonstrations or policy retraining.

A neural IL policy processes observations into hidden states, which its later layers use to generate actions.
Replaying the original demonstrations through the frozen policy exposes the hidden states associated with expert behavior, providing a policy-specific reference that can be reused during deployment without additional supervision.
Intermediate hidden states therefore provide a natural intervention point: modifying one during execution can change the action while leaving the policy parameters fixed. We refer to this operation as test-time hidden-state steering .
Prior work learns hidden-state correction modules jointly with the task network [ 4 ] , or steers trained robot policies using conceptors fitted to successful and failed roll-out activations [ 5 ] .
In our demonstration-only setting, the steering reference instead consists solely of expert hidden states collected from the original demonstrations.
The resulting challenge is how to use the structure of these expert hidden states to suppress undesirable deviations while preserving the variation needed for action generation.

Our empirical analysis finds that expert hidden states vary predominantly within relatively few dimensions, while linear subspaces fitted to different clusters of expert hidden states differ in orientation (Section IV-A ).
These observations motivate viewing the expert distribution as concentrated near a low-dimensional manifold, with broad variation along local tangent subspaces and narrow variation along local normal subspaces.
Variation along this structure can reflect differences between demonstrated situations that require different actions.
The steering problem can therefore be viewed as reducing departures from the structure while limiting changes to the variation needed for action generation.

One way to pursue this goal is to attenuate components along directions with low expert variance more strongly than those along directions with high variance.
A linear filter can implement this rule using globally fitted directions and attenuation factors [ 6 ] .
Under the manifold view, however, local tangent and normal subspaces can change orientation with location.
A fixed linear filter may therefore attenuate tangential expert variation as well as normal deviations, motivating steering directions that adapt to the local geometry.

Our key idea is to use nonlinear expert coordinates for selective attenuation, limiting changes to high-variance coordinates while attenuating low-variance coordinates more strongly.
We implement this idea with Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns a diffeomorphic coordinate map, or chart , from expert hidden states.
DHS builds on score-based pullback Riemannian geometry (SPRG) [ 7 ] to learn the chart and an anisotropic Gaussian model of expert variation in its coordinates.
Under the manifold view, high and low-variance coordinates serve as proxies for tangential variation and normal deviations, respectively.
The inverse chart provides location-dependent coordinate directions for selective attenuation in hidden-state space.
At test time, DHS maps the current hidden state to chart coordinates, rescales them according to their fitted expert variances, and maps the result back before the remaining policy layers generate an action (Fig. 1 ).

Our contributions are as follows:

We characterize expert hidden-state geometry in a trained IL policy, observing concentrated variation and differences in the orientation of linear subspaces fitted to different clusters of expert hidden states.

We introduce DHS, a full-rank nonlinear steering operator that uses expert hidden-state geometry to attenuate low-variance chart coordinates while limiting changes to high-variance coordinates in a frozen IL policy.

We demonstrate that DHS achieves higher mean success than the unmodified policy under observation noise across four simulated manipulation tasks.
Also, learned nonlinear coordinates yield higher mean success than linear coordinates from principal component analysis (PCA) under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling.

1. We characterize expert hidden-state geometry in a trained IL policy, observing concentrated variation and differences in the orientation of linear subspaces fitted to different clusters of expert hidden states.

2. We introduce DHS, a full-rank nonlinear steering operator that uses expert hidden-state geometry to attenuate low-variance chart coordinates while limiting changes to high-variance coordinates in a frozen IL policy.

3. We demonstrate that DHS achieves higher mean success than the unmodified policy under observation noise across four simulated manipulation tasks.
Also, learned nonlinear coordinates yield higher mean success than linear coordinates from principal component analysis (PCA) under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Hidden-State Steering and Filtering

Hidden-state steering can be learned jointly with a task network or derived from the statistics of reference activations.
State-Reification Networks jointly train denoising or attractor modules with the task network to improve generalization, and combine state reification with adversarial training to improve adversarial robustness [ 4 ] .
The statistical approach underlies conceptor filters, which use second moments of recurrent activity to preserve characteristic patterns and control their generation [ 6 ] .
COAST applies this principle to robot policies by combining conceptors fitted to successful and failed roll-out activations [ 5 ] .
Each fitted conceptor applies a linear map in hidden-state space. DHS uses nonlinear expert coordinates whose induced coordinate basis can vary with the current hidden state, allowing variance-dependent steering to follow the learned geometry.

## II-B Representation Geometry and Nonlinear Steering

Studies of intrinsic dimension in image classification networks [ 8 ] and representation geometry in protein and image Transformers [ 9 ] motivate examining how expert variation is organized within robot policies.
A constructive approach to such geometry is provided in [ 7 ] : anisotropic flows yield tractable pullback geometry and a Riemannian autoencoder that reconstructs data after retaining high-variance coordinates.
DHS builds on this coordinate construction for full-rank selective attenuation during policy execution.

Geometry also affects how interventions move between represented behaviors.
Interpolation along fitted activation manifolds is examined in Manifold Steering through behavioral transitions in structured language tasks and a visual world model [ 10 ] .
For targeted behavioral changes, Curveball Steering applies contrastive shifts in polynomial kernel PCA coordinates, using approximate inversion and restoring the reconstruction residual [ 11 ] .
These approaches establish precedents for nonlinear geometric intervention; our focus is how expert variation can guide corrective attenuation steering while preserving execution of an existing robot task.

## II-C Predictive Guidance and Activation Feedback

Guidance can also be derived from an action’s predicted consequences.
Proximity to expert observation embeddings supplies the objective in Latent Policy Barrier, where dynamics learned from expert data and policy roll-outs guide action denoising through predicted future embeddings [ 12 ] .
Predicted future state values provide another criterion: Cosmos Policy learns action, state, and value predictions by fine-tuning a video model, and uses these values to select action proposals in its planning mode [ 13 ] .
Feedback can instead operate across network depth, as in WA-LQR, which locally linearizes diffusion Transformer blocks to track contrastive robustness feature targets [ 14 ] .
For DHS, the correction reference is the fitted distribution of expert hidden states: coordinate variances determine the attenuation directly, without future state prediction or contrastive feature tracking.

2026-10-16.title: SPEAR: Selective Preference Elicitation with Adaptive Rewards for VLM-Guided Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-16.authors: Zewen Wu , Ruizhe Liu , Pei Zhou , Feng Chen , Yanchao Yang
2026-10-16.comment: . Accepted at IROS 2026. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-16.abstract:
Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
enable automated preference labeling
for robotic manipulation,
yet their deployment
remains impractical since each query incurs
substantial inference cost,
while VLMs frequently abstain on visually challenging comparisons.
We propose SPEAR ,
a framework that transforms
VLMs into efficient preference oracles
via two synergistic mechanisms.
First, we design distinguishability-aware query selection to reduce abstention rates by targeting only informative and distinguishable comparisons.
Second, we deploy an adaptive reward transition that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized guidance before preference-based refinement.
Experiments on the manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that SPEAR achieves 88.9% average success, outperforming baselines by 23.3 percentage points, while significantly reducing abstention and wall-clock training time on contact-rich tasks. SPEAR learns three Mobile ALOHA manipulation tasks fully online on real hardware, demonstrating end-to-end real-world applicability.
By addressing query efficiency
and exploration challenges, SPEAR establishes VLMs
as practical preference oracles
for scalable robot learning without manual reward engineering. Project page: https://zevinwu.github.io/spear-project .
2026-10-16.introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL)
offers a principled way to
acquire robotic manipulation skills in demonstration-scarce settings, yet practical deployment remains constrained by reward specification.
Preference-based Reinforcement Learning (PbRL)
addresses this by learning from pairwise trajectory comparisons rather than numerical rewards [ 1 , 2 ] .
However, the scalability of PbRL is constrained by the need for frequent human-in-the-loop preference queries.
Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs)
present an appealing solution:
modern VLMs can naturally serve as automated preference oracles [ 3 ] due to their encoding of extensive world knowledge and robust visual-language grounding.
This enables automated robot learning from online interaction and language goals,
without relying on demonstrations, manually designed rewards, or ongoing human labeling.

However,
VLMs introduce a notable computational constraint –
each preference query incurs a significant inference cost.
This makes query efficiency critical,
yet existing VLM-guided PbRL methods waste considerable budgets due to two fundamental inefficiencies. First, VLMs are frequently incapable of providing valid preferences for visually similar or indistinguishable trajectories, i.e., returning abstention.
Naive query selection
could misuse a significant portion
of expensive queries
on comparisons that yield zero learning signal.
Across backbones, higher visual distinguishability leads to both lower abstention and higher preference accuracy, motivating abstention-aware acquisition as a core design target. Second, meaningful preferences
require behaviorally task-related trajectories,
yet initial random policies produce only aimless motions.
This creates a bootstrapping paradox:
generating task-related behaviors requires rewards that need to be learned from comparing task-related behaviors. Together, these dilemmas make VLM-guided preference learning inefficient for automated learning.

We present SPEAR ( S elective P reference E licitation with A daptive R ewards),
a framework that addresses both challenges with two synergistic mechanisms designed specifically for VLM-based preference learning under computational constraints. To overcome the query efficiency challenge,
we develop Distinguishability-Aware Query Selection that predicts VLM response likelihood before querying.
Our approach combines global semantic embeddings with local spatial patterns,
and further trains a calibrated distinguishability prediction model.
By weighting information gain with predicted distinguishability,
we ensure computational resources target only answerable and informative comparisons, while enhancing learning efficiency. To resolve the exploration bootstrapping challenge,
we introduce Adaptive Reward Transition that leverages VLM-synthesized rewards to jumpstart exploration before transitioning to refined preference-based learning.
While VLM-synthesized rewards lack precision for task completion,
they successfully guide initial exploration toward semantically task-relevant regions.
Combined with relay exploration that maintains distributional coverage,
this mechanism ensures continuous generation of diverse yet task-relevant trajectories that are necessary for meaningful preference comparisons.

We evaluate our approach on six diverse manipulation tasks from Meta-World [ 4 ] . SPEAR achieves an 88.9% average success rate, surpassing the strongest VLM-based baseline by 23.3 percentage points, with substantially fewer wasted oracle queries and reduced wall-clock training time.
Beyond simulation, we further validate SPEAR on a real Mobile ALOHA robot by running the full online pipeline directly in the real world, demonstrating VLM-guided preference learning can bootstrap manipulation skills from scratch under realistic sensing and actuation constraints.
The ablation studies confirm that both mechanisms are essential for efficient online PbRL. Our contributions are threefold:

First, we propose a distinguishability-aware query selection mechanism that predicts VLM answerability through multi-scale visual features and online-adapted modeling, effectively reducing wasted queries.

Second, we introduce an adaptive reward transition strategy
that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized reward before transitioning to preference-based learning, ensuring the collection of informative trajectories.

Third, we demonstrate substantial improvements across diverse manipulation tasks and on a real robot,
validating that addressing query efficiency and exploration bootstrapping enables practical VLM-guided preference learning under realistic computational constraints.

1. First, we propose a distinguishability-aware query selection mechanism that predicts VLM answerability through multi-scale visual features and online-adapted modeling, effectively reducing wasted queries.

2. Second, we introduce an adaptive reward transition strategy
that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized reward before transitioning to preference-based learning, ensuring the collection of informative trajectories.

3. Third, we demonstrate substantial improvements across diverse manipulation tasks and on a real robot,
validating that addressing query efficiency and exploration bootstrapping enables practical VLM-guided preference learning under realistic computational constraints.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A VLM-guided Robot Policy Learning.

The difficulties in hand-crafting
dense reward functions
for robotic control
have motivated a new paradigm leveraging recent large-scale models for reward specification or generation [ 5 , 6 , 3 ] .
A typical current approach
utilizes Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] as direct, zero-shot reward models (VLM-RMs) [ 5 ] by calculating the cosine similarity
between the visual and the goal text embedding.
This strategy has also been explored
in works using CLIP-style models [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
Other works, exemplified by Text2Reward [ 6 ] ,
use Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate executable dense reward programs grounded in environment APIs [ 15 , 16 ] .
An alternative paradigm,
which our work adopts,
avoids direct reward specification. Instead, it leverages VLMs as automated preference oracles within a Preference-based Reinforcement Learning (PbRL) framework.
For instance,
RL-VLM-F [ 3 ] queries a VLM to provide preference labels for pairs of image observations, and then learns a reward function from this feedback.
Our approach builds upon this VLM-driven preference-based paradigm,
focusing on the query efficiency and effective preference elicitation under costly, abstaining VLM oracles.

## II-B Preference-based Reinforcement Learning.

PbRL [ 1 , 2 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] learns an implicit reward function from pairwise comparisons provided by an expert, often based on the Bradley-Terry model [ 23 ] .
Traditionally, these comparisons are sourced from human experts [ 1 , 24 , 25 ] . However, this process is notoriously costly and slow, creating an annotation bottleneck that hinders scalability. Meanwhile, many existing PbRL systems and benchmarks assume access to an idealized scripted teacher.
This oracle computes preferences by using privileged access to the ground-truth environment reward signals [ 19 ] , an approach that constitutes an unrealistic training regime and contradicts the PbRL desideratum.
The concurrent advancement of VLMs offers a promising direction, positioning VLMs as natural candidates to serve as automated preference oracles [ 3 ] .
Moreover,
AI feedback (RLAIF) has also been explored for aligning models [ 26 , 27 ] .
While this paradigm shift addresses the expertise bottleneck,
it introduces new, open problems:
how to query these powerful but fallible and non-negligibly costly VLM oracles efficiently and effectively remains challenging.

2026-10-16.title: Training-Free Target-Aware Refinement of 3D Gaussian Language Map
2026-10-16.authors: Sibaek Lee , Kyeongsu Kang , Seongbo Ha , Yewon Jeon , Joonyeol Choi , Daegeol Ko , Jaehyuk Hur , Taemin Choi , Minsu Kim , Hyungjoo Ahn , Wonsok Yoo , Hyeonwoo Yu
2026-10-16.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-16.abstract:
Distilling vision-language features into 3D Gaussian Splatting yields a language map that can be queried with arbitrary text. In deployment, however, a small set of user-specified targets must be reliably located, which current distilled maps often miss, while open-vocabulary queryability for other words must remain intact. We propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Guided by a text-promptable segmenter, the visual embedding inside each detected target region is blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient sets the amount of injected prior, while non-target regions are left untouched. Injecting too much overwrites appearance cues and general queryability, so we seek, for each target, the smallest coefficient that still lets it win, and we obtain every coefficient in closed form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. We further identify a failure mode of injection in language-goal localization. Text embeddings share a common component, and injecting them makes the standard cosine read-out query-agnostic, which a centering step in the read-out removes. Across three benchmarks, the refinement consistently improves open-vocabulary segmentation, roughly doubling the base mIoU on Replica, and localizes language goals more reliably than the base map. It also transfers as a plug-in to off-the-shelf field-based and object-level language maps and supports a real-world demonstration in which a legged robot navigates to natural-language goals.
Project page and code: https://lab-of-ai-and-robotics.github.io/target-aware-langmap/
2026-10-16.introduction:
A reliable spatial representation is central to robotic autonomy, since a robot must understand its environment before it can act within it across tasks such as localization, navigation, and manipulation. The recent emergence of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [ 21 ] and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [ 12 ] has made photorealistic spatial representation possible. Moreover, by combining these representations with vision language models [ 25 ] , a scene is no longer restricted to a fixed set of semantic labels, and open-vocabulary NeRF and 3DGS representations [ 13 , 37 , 24 ] have become possible, allowing the space to be queried with arbitrary natural language.

However, existing methods for building such language maps tend to fall toward one of two ends of a spectrum, and we instead pursue the practical middle ground, precise localization of user-specified targets without giving up open-vocabulary generality. Closed-set methods are trained per scene with semantic supervision [ 18 , 38 ] and are accurate on their predefined labels, but cannot be queried with any word outside that set. Open-vocabulary methods instead distill vision-language features and respond to arbitrary text [ 13 , 24 , 37 ] . Yet because the distillation blends surrounding context into each feature, the resulting relevancy can be spatially diffuse, so a query often yields a plausible heatmap whose peak is not always precise enough to serve directly as a navigation goal. We first tried to sharpen such maps with a training-free post-processing, but found that the limitation is already present in the 2D features themselves, whose top-ranked retrieval is often wrong before any lifting to 3D. Purely post-hoc processing is therefore insufficient, which motivates injecting the target text directly into the features.

To this end, we propose a training-free, target-aware refinement of an already-distilled language map. Given a small set of user-specified target words, we localize each target in every training view with a text-promptable segmenter, retain the open-vocabulary base from a class-agnostic segmenter, and encode both with a vision-language model. Within each target region the visual embedding is then blended with the target text embedding, a convex combination whose coefficient decides how much prior is injected, while non-target regions are left untouched. Such coefficients are conventionally treated as hyperparameters, swept over a grid or set by heuristics. Injecting too much overwrites the region’s visual embedding and erodes the appearance cues and general queryability that make the map open-vocabulary. We therefore formulate the problem as finding the smallest coefficient that still lets each target win, and we solve it in closed form. Each detection yields this minimum as a flip point, and the per-target strength is read off the knee of the capture curve that the flip points form, leaving no hyperparameters to tune. This minimal injection, together with the untouched non-target regions, is what keeps the refined map open-vocabulary.

Because the refinement acts only on the 2D features before distillation, it is pipeline-agnostic and drops into different language maps as a plug-in module, from dense feature fields to object-level maps. It also carries over to language-goal localization, where the map must turn a query word into a 3D goal position. We observe a failure mode rooted in the geometry of contrastive vision-language embeddings [ 19 , 22 ] . Text embeddings cluster around a shared direction, so injecting them plants this common component in the map, and under the standard cosine read-out every query then retrieves the same dominant regions. A centering step in the read-out removes this common mode. Notably, centering barely changes the base map but is decisive on the refined one, after which the refined map localizes goals more reliably than the base across Replica [ 30 ] , ScanNet [ 3 ] , and HM3D-Semantics [ 35 ] . We summarize our contributions as follows:

A training-free, target-aware refinement that makes user-specified targets reliably retrievable while keeping the map open-vocabulary, with each target’s injection strength obtained in closed form instead of tuned.

A centered read-out that identifies and removes the query-agnostic bias of injection, turning the refined map into a reliable source of language-goal locations.

Consistent gains in segmentation and localization on three benchmarks, plug-in transfer to field-based and object-level maps, and a real-world demonstration on a legged robot.

1. A training-free, target-aware refinement that makes user-specified targets reliably retrievable while keeping the map open-vocabulary, with each target’s injection strength obtained in closed form instead of tuned.

2. A centered read-out that identifies and removes the query-agnostic bias of injection, turning the refined map into a reliable source of language-goal locations.

3. Consistent gains in segmentation and localization on three benchmarks, plug-in transfer to field-based and object-level maps, and a real-world demonstration on a legged robot.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related work

## II-A Open-vocabulary 3D language maps

Semantic mapping has long attached labels to reconstructed geometry, but classical systems remain closed set, recognizing only the categories their segmenters were trained on [ 20 ] . Open-vocabulary maps remove this limit by distilling vision-language embeddings into 3D, first over point clouds and implicit fields [ 23 , 9 , 13 ] and more recently into 3D Gaussian Splatting [ 24 , 37 , 33 ] , with closed-form solvers reducing the distillation cost [ 34 , 10 ] and online variants embedding language during SLAM [ 15 , 6 ] . Dedicated benchmarks now track the open-vocabulary quality of such maps [ 11 ] . All of these works concern how to build the map, and to our knowledge none refines the language field of an already-built one, so our training-free, target-aware refinement is complementary to all of them.

## II-B Language-goal localization and navigation

A language map supports many downstream tasks, and this work concerns the one closest to deployment, turning a query word into a navigation goal. Spatial memories built from vision-language features have enabled language-driven navigation over grids and implicit fields [ 7 , 28 , 16 ] , zero-shot object search [ 4 ] , scene graphs queried through language model reasoning [ 32 , 5 ] , and Gaussian memories for goal retrieval [ 36 ] , evaluated under object-goal navigation protocols [ 1 , 14 ] . Across these systems the goal is typically read out by raw cosine similarity between the query embedding and the stored features. We show that this standard read-out breaks once text embeddings are injected into the map, and that a centering step in the read-out restores and then surpasses the base retrieval.

2026-10-16.title: A Flow-Theoretic Multimodal Control Framework Fusing Mental and Physical Engagement for Upper-Limb Rehabilitation
2026-10-16.authors: Jun Leng , Pengcheng Li , Hanze Wang , Shuxiang Guo , Junlin Jiang
2026-10-16.abstract: While Assist-as-Needed (AAN) control aims to maximize user participation in robot-assisted training, existing methods relying solely on physical metrics cannot distinguish muscular inability from mental disengagement, leading to suboptimal interventions. To address this ambiguity, a Flow-theoretic multimodal AAN framework is proposed, fusing EEG-based mental engagement and sEMG-based physical engagement into an adaptive impedance control strategy. A four-quadrant fuzzy decision engine translates these dual physiological metrics into continuous control policies. This enables the upper-limb exoskeleton to inject feedforward assistance during intent-execution mismatch (e.g., motor output attenuation despite mental focus) and escalate guiding stiffness to penalize mental distraction. The framework was validated with healthy participants against a state-of-practice sEMG-only AAN baseline. Kinematically and mechanically, the proposed framework reduced robotic energy expenditure by 71.9% while maintaining precise trajectory tracking, confirming it elicited greater voluntary human effort. Physiologically, the system increased the time spent in the neuroplasticity zone (Flow State Ratio) from 4.6% to 42.8%. These results validate that decoupling and jointly regulating mental and physical states enhances the selectivity of robotic assistance, mitigating user passivity and sustaining the engagement crucial for motor learning.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Upper limb movement dysfunction caused by neurological injuries, such as stroke, severely impairs an individual’s ability to perform Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) and significantly reduces quality of life [ 1 ] . Modern neurorehabilitation relies on promoting patients’ active participation in high-intensity, repetitive training to stimulate neuroplasticity and facilitate functional recovery [ 2 ] . To address these rigorous demands, robot-assisted therapy provides consistent, quantifiable training that directly complements traditional therapist-led methods [ 3 , 4 ] . These systems offer precise physical guidance while reducing the labor burden on clinicians, making them essential for delivering the high-dosage therapy required for motor learning.

To maximize therapeutic outcomes, the field has widely adopted the “Assist-as-Needed” (AAN) paradigm. The core principle of AAN is to minimize robotic intervention, providing assistance only when the user cannot complete the movement independently. This approach aims to ensure maximal active effort [ 5 ] . However, accurately inferring the user’s true “need” remains a critical challenge. Traditional AAN strategies rely heavily on physical performance metrics, such as kinematic error or interaction force. For instance, Han et al. [ 6 ] proposed an adaptive control method that infers movement intention by decomposing real-time interaction forces. The system then adjusts the robot’s impedance parameters to promote active participation. More recently, researchers have integrated surface Electromyography (sEMG) to incorporate physiological effort into the control loop. Xu et al. [ 7 ] , for example, developed a framework that adapts training trajectories and robotic assistance based on sEMG-derived muscle activation. This system encourages patient participation by modulating feedback gains. However, while such approaches successfully measure mechanical or muscular execution, they still fail to capture user’s mental focus. Although high-amplitude sEMG quantifies physical exertion, it cannot differentiate genuine task engagement from pathological co-contraction or abnormal compensatory synergies. Execution-level metrics alone fall short in revealing the user’s mental intent. Without monitoring mental focus, purely physical assistance strategies often fail to maintain an optimal training challenge, eventually leading to user passivity.

To resolve this ambiguity, integrating electroencephalography (EEG) into the control loop is essential for providing a direct measure of task-related attentional focus [ 8 ] . While EEG is widely applied in robotic rehabilitation, current paradigms mostly use it within Motor Imagery-based Brain-Computer Interfaces (MI-BCI) to decode discrete movement intentions [ 9 ] , [ 10 ] .

This paper introduces an adaptive control framework grounded in Flow Theory to map these multidimensional physiological signals into actionable robotic interventions. Classic Flow Theory defines an optimal mental state as a balance between external task challenge and intrinsic user skill [ 11 , 12 ] . The modern four-quadrant extension categorizes user experience into Flow, Anxiety, Boredom, and Apathy based on these misalignments [ 13 ] . In robot-assisted training, keeping users within this flow state mitigates both task-induced anxiety and under-stimulated boredom [ 14 , 15 ] . This equilibrium sustains intrinsic motivation and facilitates motor learning [ 16 ] .

Most existing flow-aware systems rely on predefined task difficulties or intermittent self-reporting, limiting their real-time adaptability. Directly quantifying the abstract Challenge and Skill axes in real-time is also highly impractical during dynamic robot-assisted training, as the user’s motor capabilities fluctuate continuously due to fatigue and varying physical demands. To address this gap, the proposed framework bypasses the direct measurement of classic Flow coordinates. It instead establishes a two-dimensional physiological diagnostic space using mental engagement ( s me ∗ s^{*}_{\text{me}} , via EEG) and physical engagement ( s pe ∗ s^{*}_{\text{pe}} , via sEMG) as continuous proxies. By continuously monitoring the congruence or mismatch between cognitive intent and motor execution, the system inversely infers the user’s psychological state. This diagnostic mapping directly drives the real-time, closed-loop interventions. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

A multimodal, mental-physical aware exoskeleton system is developed to fuse real-time EEG and sEMG signals, enabling the continuous monitoring of the user’s mental and physical engagement during robot-assisted training.

A Flow-grounded fuzzy decision engine, coupled with a sensorless variable impedance controller, is proposed. By estimating the user’s Flow state, the system dynamically adjusts guiding stiffness and feedforward assistance to mitigate physical passivity, address the mismatch between mental intent and physical execution, and optimize the AAN interaction.

# II System Overview and Hardware Platform

## II-A CURE Exoskeleton

The CURE system targets home-based rehabilitation (Fig. 1 (a), (b)). A Bowden-cable transmission spatially separates the actuation unit from the wearable arm brace, relocating the heavy components to a backpack. This configuration reduces the distal arm mass to approximately 0.7 kg, which lowers interaction inertia and delays user fatigue. Although the robot supports three degrees of freedom (DoFs) across the elbow and wrist, this study validates the control strategy on the 1-DoF elbow joint.

A high-torque DC motor (GO-M8010-6, Unitree, China) actuates this joint. Motor encoders and Inertial Measurement Units (IMUs, JY901, WitMotion, China) measure joint kinematics (angular position q q and velocity q ˙ \dot{q} ) to provide high-frequency state feedback for the closed-loop controller. A backpack-mounted emergency stop button provides a hardware safety override.

## II-B Multimodal Sensing Interface

A multimodal sensing interface (Fig. 1 (c)) is integrated to close the human-in-the-loop control. A wireless 8-channel EEG system (OpenBCI Cyton, USA) captures real-time neural activity, with dry electrodes positioned at Fp1, Fp2, F3, F4, Fz, Cz, Pz, and Oz. This montage targets frontal and parieto-occipital regions to decode mental engagement. Bipolar sEMG sensors (Sichiray, China) attached to the Biceps and Triceps Brachii quantify physical engagement by monitoring agonist voluntary effort and antagonist co-activation. A central PC manages the entire system, acquiring physiological streams via LSL and serial interfaces and synchronizing them with the robot’s low-level torque controller at a 100 Hz loop rate.
