2026-10-16.title: Policy-Aligned Predictive Verification for Adaptive VLA Action-Chunk Execution
2026-10-16.authors: Minkyu Kim , Junhoo Lee , Seungyeon Kim , Suhyun Jeon , Baekseung Kim , Donghoon Han , Nojun Kwak
2026-10-16.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate action sequences that reduce repeated inference, but deciding how much of each sequence to execute is critical to task success. Existing adaptive methods make this decision using generation stability or prediction agreement, yet these signals do not establish whether executing a candidate prefix preserves the ability to complete the task. We introduce a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that anticipates the consequences of candidate action prefixes and evaluates their compatibility with successful continuation before execution. Rather than using future prediction to generate actions, our method evaluates existing proposals in the VLA’s internal task-conditioned representation space. To learn local judgments from terminal task outcomes, we combine trajectory-level survival supervision with a localization prior that preserves useful behavior within failed rollouts. The resulting validity scores guide execution-horizon selection. Evaluations with π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success–query trade-offs. These findings point toward a different role for future prediction in robotics, using it to assess how far to trust a policy’s proposed actions rather than to generate new ones.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong performance in generating robot actions from visual observations and language instructions ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Miao et al., 2026 ) . Yet querying a large VLA policy at every control step is costly, while robot behavior requires coordinated motion over multiple steps. Action chunking addresses both demands by generating a sequence of future actions in one query, supporting temporal coherence with fewer policy calls. However, executing an entire chunk without new observations limits responsiveness to environmental changes and allows execution errors to accumulate. Many systems therefore use a shorter execution horizon to execute only an initial prefix of each chunk before replanning from new observations. Adapting this horizon is thus central to retaining the efficiency of action chunking while remaining responsive to feedback.

Adaptive execution seeks the longest prefix of each action chunk that still allows the policy to complete the task successfully. Identifying this prefix requires anticipating how the proposed actions will affect the policy’s ability to complete the remaining task. Because the effects of a candidate prefix on task success are not directly observable before execution, existing approaches rely on indirect signals to guide execution. Some methods use generation stability as this indirect signal, drawing on internal policy information to select an execution horizon ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Others use prediction agreement, comparing action-conditioned predictions with incoming observations to guide correction or replanning during execution ( Pan et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . Generation stability and prediction agreement alone, however, do not establish whether a candidate prefix preserves compatibility with successful task completion. As illustrated in Figure 1 , an action proposal can be consistently generated and its consequences accurately predicted, yet executing it can still lead to a missed grasp and task failure.

To assess this compatibility directly, we introduce proposal validity , which estimates the probability that the policy can successfully complete the task after executing a candidate prefix. This probability depends on the state reached after executing the prefix, because the policy must complete the remaining task from that state. We therefore predict this future state to evaluate whether it supports successful continuation under the policy. World models and World Action Models have demonstrated this capability, building on pretrained visual representations or video models to predict future observations or latent states for planning and action generation ( Seo et al., 2022 ; Du et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . However, because VLA policies already generate effective action proposals, we use this predictive capability to evaluate those proposals rather than to generate new actions. To ground this evaluation in the same information used for action generation, we predict the effects of each prefix in the VLA’s task-conditioned representation space, which integrates visual observations and language instructions.

We therefore propose a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that assesses each action extension’s compatibility with successful continuation from predicted VLA representations. These extension-level assessments provide local validity estimates used to select execution horizons. To learn these local judgments, however, we must rely on rollouts that provide only terminal task outcomes. These outcomes do not reveal the validity of individual extensions, since even a failed rollout may contain valid action prefixes. We therefore treat extension-level validity as latent and supervise its accumulated product using the terminal outcome. However, the model can fit a failed rollout by slightly lowering validity scores across the rollout, including those of valid extensions. We therefore introduce a localization prior that encourages the model to concentrate these reductions in fewer extensions. At inference time, we combine the local validity scores to evaluate each candidate prefix, accounting for its length. We use these prefix-level scores to decide how many actions to execute before obtaining a new observation and querying the policy again.

Our experiments with π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks assess whether proposal validity selects execution horizons that improve success with fewer policy queries. To examine the basis for these decisions, prediction tests assess action sensitivity, while ablations examine future prediction, policy alignment, and the contributions of individual loss terms. Predicting future VLA representations achieves higher success with fewer queries than direct verification or prediction in generic visual features.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Adaptive Execution of Action Chunks

Action-sequence policies such as ACT and π 0 \pi_{0} generate future action chunks ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ) . A fixed execution horizon uses the same prefix length across proposals and states, trading fewer queries for later feedback. Adaptive execution instead adjusts when to request a new proposal. One line of work uses internal policy signals to assess generation stability and guide horizon selection. AutoHorizon estimates an execution limit from action self-attention ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , while A 3 A^{3} selects an execution horizon using action consensus and re-decoding stability ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Another line of work assesses prediction agreement from observations during execution. VLA-Corrector truncates and replans when predicted and observed visual dynamics persistently diverge, whereas CheckVLA relates prediction-observation discrepancies to failure risk and latency-aware suffix repair ( Pan et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . These approaches use generation stability or prediction agreement to guide execution, whereas our verifier predicts the consequences of candidate prefixes and evaluates their compatibility with successful continuation before execution. To our knowledge, we are the first to combine prefix-conditioned future prediction with proposal-validity estimation for adaptive action-chunk execution.

## 2.2 World Models and Predictive Representations

World models capture action-conditioned dynamics over future observations or latent states ( Chua et al., 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2019b ; Hansen et al., 2022 ; Hansen et al., 2024 ) . Dreamer learns behavior from imagined latent trajectories ( Hafner et al., 2019a ) , DINO-WM predicts pretrained visual features for goal-directed planning ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and World Action Models such as DreamZero jointly predict future video and actions ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . Value Prediction Networks evaluate imagined futures through rewards and values ( Oh et al., 2017 ) , while Diffuser generates trajectories for planning ( Janner et al., 2022 ) . Beyond these uses, prediction can support proposal verification. Given a VLA proposal, future prediction anticipates the consequences of executing candidate prefixes. Assessing these consequences requires representations that retain information relevant to control. DeepMDP and bisimulation-based learning connect representations to rewards and transitions ( Gelada et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2020 ) , while VIP learns visual representations through goal-conditioned value learning ( Ma et al., 2022 ) . We therefore predict prefix-induced futures in the action-generating policy’s internal representation space, retaining the joint observation and instruction context for outcome-based proposal verification.

## 2.3 Learning from Trajectory-Level Outcomes

Learning prefix-level validity from terminal outcomes is related to multiple-instance learning, where collection-level labels leave individual instance labels unobserved ( Dietterich et al., 1997 ; Ilse et al., 2018 ) . Here, rollout outcomes supervise temporally ordered prefix extensions without identifying which extension caused a failure. Reward redistribution similarly derives local learning signals from delayed returns or demonstrations ( Arjona-Medina et al., 2019 ; Ren et al., 2021 ; Patil et al., 2020 ) . A related credit-assignment problem arises in language-model reinforcement learning ( Chan et al., 2024 ) , where RED derives token-level rewards from holistic response feedback ( Li et al., 2025 ) . These approaches recover local information from global outcomes ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) , but we use this supervision to verify proposed execution and select horizons rather than optimize the action-generating policy.

2026-10-16.title: MuSTMM: Learning Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation across Multiple Scenes
2026-10-16.authors: Hao Ju , Feng Yan , Zhihao Zhong , Heng Yang , Shaofei Huang , Zhedong Zheng
2026-10-16.abstract:
Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (STMM) requires robots to respond to sound events by navigating to the associated objects and performing appropriate physical interactions.
Existing STMM evaluations primarily vary object layouts within limited architectural structures, leaving challenges to unseen scenes insufficiently explored.
We introduce Multi-scene Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (MuSTMM) , a dataset that combines spatial audio rendering and physical interaction across 31 scenes with diverse architectures and object layouts.
MuSTMM contains 14.36 million precomputed binaural Room Impulse Responses (RIRs) and a scene-disjoint split for evaluating single-event and multi-event settings in unseen scenes.
We further augment the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory that complements acoustic cues with observed geometry.
Specifically, we accumulate pose-aligned depth observations in a shared coordinate frame and project this memory into an egocentric Bird’s-Eye View (BEV) occupancy map.
Fusing map features with sound context produces a goal descriptor that provides both target-location and scene-structure priors, guiding navigation to the target region required for subsequent physical interaction. This policy achieves a 3.81% success rate boost over existing methods, while component ablations further support the effectiveness of spatial memory.
MuSTMM and the navigation policy provide a testbed for the new challenge of studying sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes. The code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Sound events provide a natural trigger for robots to perceive their surroundings and interact with physical objects.
Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (STMM) ( Ju et al., 2026 ) studies this capability by requiring a robot to respond to sound events, navigate to the associated objects, and perform appropriate physical interactions.
These interactions include relocating sounding rigid objects and changing the states of articulated objects, either for a single event or sequentially for multiple events.
Existing benchmarks provide only partial challenges of different scene structures and object layouts.
Audio-visual navigation benchmarks, such as SoundSpaces ( Chen et al., 2020a ) and SAVi ( Chen et al., 2021 ) , support sound rendering across multiple scenes but do not include the physical interactions required by STMM.
Conversely, mobile manipulation benchmarks, such as Habitat-M3 ( Gu et al., 2023 ) and ManiSkill-Hab ( Shukla et al., 2025 ) , support physical interaction in a limited structure variation without sound rendering.
STMM ( Ju et al., 2026 ) brings these capabilities together, but evaluates object-layout variation within limited scene structures.
Although varying object placements brings partial layout variation, it does not evaluate whether agents can perceive and respond to sound events in unseen structures.
This motivates a benchmark that combines structural diversity with both sound rendering and physical interaction.

To address this gap, we introduce MuSTMM , a multi-scene benchmark that supports sound rendering and physical interaction across 31 scenes from HSSD ( Khanna et al., 2024 ) (see Figure 1 ).
MuSTMM expands variation at two complementary levels. Structure variation covers differences in scene architecture, including room geometry and spatial connectivity. Layout variation combines episode-specific placements of sounding targets and silent source-capable distractors with scene-specific arrangements of non-source background furniture.
To support sound rendering across these scenes, we leverage SoundSpaces ( Chen et al., 2022 ) to densely precompute 14.36 million binaural Room Impulse Responses (RIRs), providing scene-specific sound rendering.
A scene-disjoint split, with 23 training scenes and 8 held-out test scenes, enables evaluation of both single-event and multi-event tasks in unseen scenes.
The accompanying configurable simulator and data-generation pipeline also supports extensions with additional scenes, assets, and task configurations.

We study MuSTMM with a hierarchical framework in which a Sound-triggered Task Planner uses the initial RGB and audio observations to predict an ordered skill chain, which is executed by the corresponding skill-specific policy models.
Among the low-level policy models, sound navigation policy brings the robot to the target region required for subsequent interaction, providing the spatial precondition for executing the next skill.
This cross-scene setting motivates a closer examination of how navigation policies estimate and represent sound-source goals.
Binaural sound supplies directional cues about the source but contains limited geometry information of the observed scene.
Instead, vision observations contain rich geometry priors.
However, this geometric context is distributed across observations acquired at different viewpoints and time steps.
Previous methods encode vision and sound observations into temporal memories ( Zeng et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2021 ) . But the geometry information of the scene may misalign across different time steps in this way.
To this end, we augment memory-based goal estimation with explicit spatial memory.
Rather than relying on compressed observation history alone to represent observed geometry, we accumulate depth observations in a shared coordinate frame, and project them into an egocentric BEV occupancy map.
The map records occupancy and exploration status, while its features are fused with acoustic and temporal context to form a goal descriptor.
In this way, the explicit spatial memory contains both goal-related cues and observed scene structure, providing priors for the navigation policy.

We evaluate MuSTMM under a scene-disjoint protocol in single-event and multi-event settings.
Results identify navigation as a major execution bottleneck in held-out scenes, even when ground-truth skill chains are provided.
Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory achieves a navigation success rate of 75.28%, outperforming existing methods.
Memory ablations further show that combining explicit spatial memory with compressed spatio-temporal memory outperforms either component alone, highlighting their complementary roles in across-scene sound navigation.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce MuSTMM , a multi-scene benchmark that combines spatial audio rendering and physical interaction with architectural structure variation and object layout variation. MuSTMM consists of 30.11k episodes. The scene-disjoint evaluation protocol and configurable data-generation pipeline support the study of sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes.

We augment the Goal Descriptor Branch of the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory accumulated from depth observations. By integrating observed geometry with sound context, the resulting goal descriptor provides target-related and structural priors for the navigation policy model and ensures subsequent interaction.

We systematically evaluate baselines in held-out scenes under both single-event and multi-event settings. Navigation comparisons and memory ablations show that explicit spatial memory complements compressed observation history to improve sound-source navigation. Despite these gains, results of the Oracle baseline identify navigation as a major bottleneck in unseen scenes, highlighting a key direction for future research.

MuSTMM consists of 30.11k episodes. The scene-disjoint evaluation protocol and configurable data-generation pipeline support the study of sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes.

2. We augment the Goal Descriptor Branch of the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory accumulated from depth observations. By integrating observed geometry with sound context, the resulting goal descriptor provides target-related and structural priors for the navigation policy model and ensures subsequent interaction.

3. We systematically evaluate baselines in held-out scenes under both single-event and multi-event settings. Navigation comparisons and memory ablations show that explicit spatial memory complements compressed observation history to improve sound-source navigation. 2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Embodied Navigation and Manipulation Benchmark. Audio-visual navigation and mobile manipulation benchmarks provide complementary capabilities for embodied agents.
SoundSpaces ( Chen et al., 2020a ; Chen et al., 2022 ) support spatial audio rendering across diverse indoor scenes, while SAVi ( Chen et al., 2021 ) introduces semantic sound events for target navigation.
These benchmarks require agents to reach sound sources but do not include the subsequent physical interactions.
In parallel, Habitat-M3 ( Gu et al., 2023 ) studies mobile manipulation for household rearrangement, while ManiSkill-HAB ( Shukla et al., 2025 ) emphasizes GPU parallelism in home rearrangement tasks.
Their ReplicaCAD-based evaluations vary furniture layouts and object placements within a shared architectural structure, providing layout variation but limited structure variation.
HomeRobot ( Yenamandra et al., 2023 ) evaluates open-vocabulary mobile manipulation across diverse indoor scenes, with scene-disjoint splits to assess generalization to unseen scenes.
However, these mobile manipulation benchmarks do not incorporate spatial sound rendering.
STMM ( Ju et al., 2026 ) combines sound rendering and physical interaction through Habitat-Echo, requiring robots to respond to sound events by navigating to and manipulating the associated objects.
However, the evaluation primarily varies object configurations within limited architectural structures, leaving performance in unseen scenes under-explored.
The proposed MuSTMM introduces architecturally distinct scenes together with object-layout variation, preserving both sound rendering and physical interaction at the same time.
The scene-disjoint evaluation protocol supports the study of sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes.

Embodied Navigation. Explicit spatial representations have long been used to accumulate observations and support planning in visual navigation ( Chaplot et al., 2020 ; Gupta et al., 2017 ; Ramakrishnan et al., 2020 ) .
Trans4Map ( Chen et al., 2023 ) aggregates egocentric visual features into allocentric memory for Bird’s-Eye-View (BEV) semantic mapping.
GridMM ( Wang et al., 2023 ) and BSG ( Liu et al., 2023 ) organize historical observations into grid-based memory and BEV scene graphs, respectively, supporting spatial reasoning and navigation decisions.
VLN-Game ( Yu et al., 2026 ) uses object-centric spatial maps for language-guided target search, while NavA 3 ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) exploits top-down scene representations for target-region reasoning and navigation.
Audio-visual navigation similarly benefits from structured spatial information, but requires agents to infer goals from acoustic observations ( Gan et al., 2020 ) .
AV-WaN ( Chen et al., 2020b ) incorporates spatially grounded acoustic memory into waypoint-based navigation.
SAVi ( Chen et al., 2021 ) introduces a goal descriptor capturing the target’s spatial and semantic properties, together with persistent multimodal memory.
MAGNet ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) further combines auditory cues, self-motion information, and episodic memory to maintain goal estimates over time.
Our method complements memory-based goal estimation with explicit geometry accumulated from pose-aligned depth observations.
The goal descriptor provides both target-related and structural priors for the policy branch, supporting navigation to the target region required for subsequent interaction.

2026-10-16.title: Modular Inverse Dynamics and Wrench Recovery for Closed-Chain Mechanisms Using Path Assembly
2026-10-16.authors: Mohammad Dastranj , Jouni Mattila
2026-10-16.abstract:
Rigid closed chains can admit indeterminate internal reactions
even when their motion is fully specified. This paper develops
a modular inverse-dynamics workflow that combines path-based
motion reconstruction with recovery of uniquely determined
actuator and joint-wrench outputs. Analytical second-order
differentiation of assembled transformation paths supplies
passive velocities and accelerations on a regular closure branch.
Spatial Newton–Euler balances are then assembled over the
physical body-and-joint graph. Established nullspace and dual
criteria identify and recover unique outputs, while balance,
ideal-joint admissibility and affine-family diagnostics assess
nonunique reference reactions. Evaluation against Simscape
Multibody uses prescribed motion of a seven-degree-of-freedom
heavy-duty hybrid serial–parallel manipulator under common
rigid-body, ideal-joint assumptions. The results show close agreement with the reference for passive positions, actuator efforts and uniquely recoverable constraint-wrench components. Reaction diagnostics support compatibility with the admissible numerical load family.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Modular modeling supports the reuse of submechanism descriptions
while preserving their kinematic and dynamic coupling.
Systematic treatments of closed chains include modular dynamics
for parallel manipulators with hybrid limbs [ 1 ] and constraint embedding for recursive dynamics with local
loops [ 2 ] .
Virtual Decomposition Control (VDC) likewise requires compatible
motion and wrench quantities for its virtual-power-flow
analysis [ 3 ] ;
applications include heavy-duty hydraulic
manipulators [ 4 , 5 ] and, more recently, hydraulic
robot legs with triangular closed chains [ 6 ] .
These developments motivate reusable motion and load descriptions
for closed-chain modules.

Closure-consistent motion, however, does not imply that every
joint load is uniquely determined. Redundant rigid constraints
can admit multiple reaction distributions while selected
components remain unique [ 7 ] .
Free-body-diagram [ 8 ] and constraint-matrix [ 9 ] approaches have been
developed for analyzing reaction and driving-force uniqueness,
with subsequent
developments within the divide-and-conquer
framework [ 10 ] .
Consequently, load recovery requires identifying which requested
outputs are invariant across the admissible solutions of the
balance equations.

Path-Assembled Closure Differential Mapping (PACDM) provides
closure resolution and local active-to-passive mappings from
ordered transformation paths [ 11 ] .
This representation has also been connected to actuator-port
mappings, acceleration reduction, and reduced inverse and forward
dynamics [ 12 ] . However, integrating reaction-uniqueness analysis into PACDM-based inverse dynamics for physical actuator and joint-wrench recovery remains to be demonstrated.
Building on these developments and established body-balance and
reaction-uniqueness formulations [ 8 , 9 , 13 ] ,
the present work develops a path-assembly workflow for motion
reconstruction and recovery of uniquely determined actuator and
joint-wrench outputs in the presence of indeterminate internal
reactions. Here, modularity refers to module-local closure reconstruction and assembly of body-level balance equations; the coupled load-recovery problem is solved globally.

The workflow extends the inherited kinematics through analytical
second-order path differentiation, reconstructing passive
velocities and accelerations on a regular closure branch.
Spatial Newton–Euler balances are assembled over an explicitly
specified physical body-and-joint graph, with each body’s
inertia included once. The established nullspace criterion
and its dual formulation recover each determined output,
subject to numerical consistency and rank checks.
Reference reactions that are nonunique are assessed through
body balance, ideal-joint admissibility and distance to the
normalized affine solution family.
Together, these elements retain the modular path description
while separating uniquely recoverable loads from indeterminate
reaction distributions.

The formulation is evaluated against Simscape Multibody under
prescribed motion of a 7-degree-of-freedom heavy-duty
hybrid serial–parallel manipulator with two closed-chain modules.
Simulation provides reference constraint forces and torques that
are difficult to measure comprehensively in
hardware [ 13 ] .
The common rigid-body, ideal-joint setting isolates reconstruction
and load recovery from measurement noise and unmodeled physical
disturbances.

2026-10-16.title: Fast-VLA: You Only Think Once for Robot Manipulation
2026-10-16.authors: Kehong Gong , Guanli Hou , Xiaoxu Zheng , Qi Wang , Mingxi Xu , Anbang Zhai , Xiaoyu He , Mingyuan Zhang , Michael Bi Mi
2026-10-16.abstract:
Vision–language–action (VLA) policies commonly place a multi-billion-parameter
model inside the feedback loop, repeatedly recomputing task context whenever
they predict a new action chunk. Yet task understanding changes far more slowly
than the robot state. We introduce Fast-VLA, which invokes a frozen 4B
VLM once per episode to contextualize the instruction and
initial views as fixed, multi-layer key–value task memory. During execution, a
lightweight online actor fuses learned time- and arm-indexed queries with
current visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task
context from the fixed memory and predict action chunks without re-running the
foundation model. Fast-VLA achieves 92.46% and 92.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0
Clean and Randomized, and 95.95% and 79.11% on LIBERO and
LIBERO-Plus evaluation. Against three continually conditioned baselines on the
same hardware, it reduces RoboTwin amortized policy inference time by
10.9–17.1 × \times and requires 1.22 GiB of post-prefill online resident
memory. Task-memory swaps further show that the actor relies on episode-matched task
memory. These results show that task context can be established once while
closed-loop control remains responsive throughout execution.
Project page: https://garfield-kh.github.io/FastVLA .
2026-10-16.introduction:
VLA models bring the semantic knowledge of large
pretrained VLMs into robot control, enabling a single policy
to follow diverse instructions across objects and scenes ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . This capability, however, is commonly coupled to
repeated backbone execution: each action chunk re-encodes the current images
and language instruction with a large model. The robot must continuously
observe the environment and revise its actions, but the instruction and overall
task remain largely unchanged. Must the large VLM backbone also be
re-run at every control decision?

When manipulating objects, people typically work out the goal and identify the
relevant objects before acting. As they reach, grasp, and place, they adjust
their movements from what they see and feel without reinterpreting the whole
task before every small action. This suggests two timescales: task
understanding can remain stable, while control must respond continuously to
changes in the scene. This motivates a policy that establishes task context once and then stays
responsive to live observations throughout execution.

Prior work reduces VLA inference cost by changing action representations or
generation procedures ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . These improvements leave a
separate question: must a large model recompute task context for every action
chunk? Can a VLA think once about the task and still manipulate effectively as
the scene changes throughout an episode?

A fixed memory cannot represent the current world state: objects and arms
move, and the visible scene changes during execution. The central challenge
is to use live observations to query fixed task context at every control
decision. We address this with Fast-VLA— You Only Think Once . A frozen
4B VLM encodes the instruction and initial multi-camera
views into layer-wise key–value task memory at the start of an episode, then
leaves the repeated control loop.

The online actor continually processes current camera views and
proprioception, with short visual history in the RoboTwin configuration.
Query fusion combines learned time- and arm-indexed queries with current arm
state and wrist-view features to form action queries. The action decoder uses
these queries to read visual tokens and task memory, and an action head
predicts an action chunk in one forward pass. The memory remains fixed, but the observations and predicted
actions change at every control decision. The policy therefore remains
closed-loop even though its task memory is fixed.

We evaluate Fast-VLA on RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , and LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) . On RoboTwin 2.0, it reaches
92.46% success in the Clean setting and 92.40% under domain randomization. Fast-VLA obtains 95.95% on standard LIBERO and 79.11% on the
LIBERO-Plus protocol. On RoboTwin, same-hardware measurements against
Faster-WAM (HUST), DM0.5, and Fast-WAM show a 10.9–17.1 × \times reduction in amortized policy inference time after including its one-time
initial call, and its post-prefill online resident memory is 1.22 GiB.
Task-memory swaps cause large performance drops, showing that the actor
depends on episode-matched memory in our evaluation.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce an episode-level VLA architecture that represents
one-time task understanding as fixed, multi-layer memory, moving a frozen
4B VLM outside the repeated control loop.

We develop an online actor that fuses learned queries with live
visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries
retrieve task context across VLM depths, enabling action-chunk prediction
in one forward pass.

Across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, we show that this
separation preserves competitive closed-loop performance while reducing
RoboTwin amortized inference cost by 10.9–17.1 × \times ; controlled memory
interventions verify that the actor uses episode-matched context.

1. We introduce an episode-level VLA architecture that represents
one-time task understanding as fixed, multi-layer memory, moving a frozen
4B VLM outside the repeated control loop.

2. We develop an online actor that fuses learned queries with live
visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries
retrieve task context across VLM depths, enabling action-chunk prediction
in one forward pass.

3. Across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, we show that this
separation preserves competitive closed-loop performance while reducing
RoboTwin amortized inference cost by 10.9–17.1 × \times ; controlled memory
interventions verify that the actor uses episode-matched context.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Generalist VLA policies couple pretrained VLM representations
with action generation through autoregressive tokens, flow matching, or
specialized action heads ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ) . Recent work reduces the cost of
each policy invocation through parallel continuous-action decoding and action
chunking ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , or through more compact action tokenization ( Pertsch et al., 2025 ) . These methods primarily optimize action generation while
retaining repeated processing of new observations by the VLM
backbone. Our focus is instead the frequency of backbone invocation: Fast-VLA removes the frozen VLM from the control loop after one episode-level prefill.
HyperVLA amortizes task conditioning by encoding the instruction and initial
image into the generated parameters of a compact base policy, which then maps
each current observation to an action ( Xiong et al., 2025 ) . Fast-VLA instead keeps
the online actor shared across episodes and retains task context as explicit,
layer-wise key–value task memory; at every control decision, query fusion
combines learned queries with current feedback to form action queries that
retrieve from this fixed memory.

VLA-Cache reuses representations of visually stable tokens between adjacent
observations while selectively recomputing changed or task-relevant content ( Xu et al., 2025 ) . World-action models reduce online cost by omitting test-time
future generation ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , sparsifying video–action interaction ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , or attaching a shallow action module to a deep video
backbone ( Ma et al., 2026 ) . These approaches reduce the work performed at
each online call, but retain a large visual or video backbone in the repeated
control path. Fast-VLA instead fixes task context at episode start and delegates
changing-state estimation entirely to a lightweight online actor.

2026-10-16.title: From Optical Flow to Safety: Visual Safety Certification via Scale-Free Relative Motion
2026-10-16.authors: Bazeela Banday , Jishnu Keshavan
2026-10-16.abstract:
Safe autonomous navigation using monocular vision remains challenging
because explicit obstacle states are not directly observable. This
letter introduces a visual safety-certification paradigm that uses
scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion encoded by monocular
optical flow as the representation for collision-risk certification,
without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or a
metric world model. Unlike conventional optical-flow-based navigation approaches that rely on image motion to shape avoidance behavior, the proposed framework directly encodes collision-cone geometry and safety constraints in this relative-motion representation. An online Concurrent
Learning observer estimates the normalized relative velocity and
provides a computable estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is
propagated into the collision cone through angular inflation and a
monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding a Robust Vision-Based
Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C 3 BF). An optimal-decay
CBF quadratic program minimally modifies the nominal control input to
enforce the resulting robust safety constraint under the stated
assumptions. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a TurtleBot3 in cluttered environments with static and dynamic obstacles demonstrate collision avoidance using
only monocular vision and onboard proprioception, with the estimation-error bound containing the measured error in 98.3 % 98.3\% of simulation samples and the robot achieving collision-free navigation in 93 93 of 100 100 real-world trials.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Safe autonomous navigation in dynamic and unstructured environments
requires robots to reason about collision risk despite incomplete
knowledge of their surroundings. Monocular cameras offer a lightweight
sensing modality for mobile robots but do not directly provide metric
depth or explicit obstacle states. Optical flow, however, encodes
scene motion relative to the camera without requiring explicit
three-dimensional reconstruction [ 1 ] .
This raises a fundamental question: can collision risk be formally
certified directly from optical flow, without reconstructing a metric
representation of the environment?

Optical flow has long been used to guide collision-avoidance
behavior in autonomous systems [ 2 , 3 ] . However, its use as a
representation for formal safety certification remains largely
unexplored. Existing optical-flow-based methods primarily use image
motion to generate or condition avoidance actions, rather than to
construct explicit safety constraints. This work addresses this gap by
introducing a visual safety-certification paradigm that bypasses
obstacle-state reconstruction and constructs collision geometry and
robust safety constraints directly from the scale-free relative motion
encoded by optical flow.

Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) provide a formal framework for
enforcing safety through optimization-based control filters [ 4 ] . Collision Cone Control Barrier Functions
(C 3 BFs) characterize collision risk through relative-motion
direction [ 5 ] , but typically rely on explicit
obstacle states or geometric information. Recent vision-based CBF
approaches use RGB-D sensing [ 6 ] , dense point clouds [ 7 ] , vision-language models [ 8 ] ,
or learned multi-camera perception [ 9 ] .
Measurement-robust CBFs account for perception uncertainty [ 10 , 11 ] , but require uncertainty
bounds defined over an explicit measurement representation. Thus, existing approaches either rely on explicit geometric models or use image motion without formal safety certification.

The key insight is that collision-cone reasoning fundamentally depends
on relative-motion direction rather than metric obstacle state. Under
perspective projection, translational optical flow is directly related
to depth-normalized relative velocity, preserving its relative-motion
direction while eliminating metric scale. Together with the
line-of-sight direction, these quantities provide the information
required to construct collision-cone geometry. Thus, monocular optical
flow, combined with onboard proprioception, provides a scale-free
representation in which collision risk can be certified directly,
without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or
a metric world model. Rather than treating optical flow merely as a cue for
avoidance behavior, we use it as the underlying representation for
formal collision-risk certification.

Building on this representation, we develop the estimation and safety
machinery required to make the certification robust to visual estimation
errors. An online Concurrent Learning (CL) observer estimates the
depth-normalized relative velocity and provides a computable
estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is propagated into the
collision-cone geometry through angular inflation and combined with a
monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding the Robust Vision-Based
Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C 3 BF). An optimal-decay
CBF quadratic program (QP) [ 12 ] then enforces the
resulting robust safety constraint while minimally modifying the nominal
control input. The complete framework is implemented onboard a TurtleBot3
and validated in cluttered environments containing both static and
dynamic obstacles.

The main contributions are:

A visual safety-certification paradigm showing that
scale-free relative motion, naturally encoded by monocular optical
flow, is sufficient for collision-cone safety certification without
explicit obstacle-state or geometric world-model reconstruction.

An online Concurrent Learning observer that relies on a finite-time excitation condition to estimate the
depth-normalized relative velocity in this representation and
provide a computable estimation-error bound.

The RV-C 3 BF that propagates representation uncertainty and a
monocular robot-footprint margin into the collision-cone constraint
for robust safety enforcement.

Extensive simulation and real-world validation on a TurtleBot3 navigating cluttered environments populated with static and dynamic obstacles using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception.

1. A visual safety-certification paradigm showing that
scale-free relative motion, naturally encoded by monocular optical
flow, is sufficient for collision-cone safety certification without
explicit obstacle-state or geometric world-model reconstruction.

2. An online Concurrent Learning observer that relies on a finite-time excitation condition to estimate the
depth-normalized relative velocity in this representation and
provide a computable estimation-error bound.

3. The RV-C 3 BF that propagates representation uncertainty and a
monocular robot-footprint margin into the collision-cone constraint
for robust safety enforcement.

4. Extensive simulation and real-world validation on a TurtleBot3 navigating cluttered environments populated with static and dynamic obstacles using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception.

2026-10-16.title: LTM: Latent Transition Based In-Context Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-16.authors: Qixin Sun , WenLong Gao , Xiansheng Chen , Zhongyuan Wang , Si Liu , Pengwei Wang
2026-10-16.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-16.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine pretrained visual and linguistic representations with action generation to follow diverse manipulation instructions ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Yet the current observation may omit information needed for the next action. A robot placing three objects into a bag must remember completed transfers; one tracking an occluded object must retain the effects of earlier interactions. Similar scenes can therefore require different actions depending on the preceding history, motivating explicit memory for robotic control ( Dai et al., 2026 ; Chung et al., 2026 ) .

Existing memory designs retain visual observations, summarize experience in language, or update a recurrent state ( Shi et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2026 ; Torne et al., 2026 ; Cherepanov et al., 2026 ) . Dense visual histories consume substantial context, whereas sparse sampling can omit intermediate interactions. Language summaries abstract away visual detail but may miss fine-grained motion. Recurrent representations support compact updates but must continually decide what to preserve in a bounded state.

These trade-offs raise a representational question: what should a VLA remember about its past interactions?

For many manipulation tasks, the relevant history is the sequence of changes induced by robot–environment interactions. Latent action models encode an observation pair into a compact code from which the later observation can be reconstructed conditioned on the earlier one ( Bruce et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2024 ) . This objective encourages the code to capture temporal changes. While latent actions have been used for policy pretraining and world-model control ( Ye et al., 2024 ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026a ) , we study their use as an ordered episodic memory for action generation.

We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM) , which encodes consecutive observations with a frozen latent action model and projects each code into one memory token. The policy receives a delayed transition prefix alongside the instruction and current observation. Each code depends only on an adjacent observation pair, allowing encoding to overlap action execution. We instantiate LTM on π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} as LTM- π \pi , with a lightweight adapter and causal attention that permits persistent KV caching. Sparse initial-frame anchors provide visual grounding for video-conditioned tasks. The policy and adapter learn from robot demonstrations without memory-specific semantic annotations. At inference, the frozen encoder supplies transition codes directly to the policy, without an external reasoning model or intermediate language generation.

We evaluate LTM- π \pi with two frozen latent encoders, CD-LAM and DreamDojo, on RoboMME and LIBERO-Mem. With the original benchmark data, the DreamDojo variant reaches 58.54% average success on RoboMME, compared with 17.93% for the reported memory-free π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} baseline, and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem, compared with 42.5% for the strongest baseline included in our comparison. We then isolate the effects of memory content and inference lag. Replacing observation-dependent latent transitions with fixed random representations reduces RoboMME success from 57.67% to 44.50%, supporting the contribution of transition-specific content beyond temporal-progress cues. Using a five-step lag reduces estimated latent-encoder blocking from 114.25 ms to 9.47 ms relative to zero lag, with a small change in success (57.88% to 57.67%).

We next test how LTM benefits from broader demonstration coverage. We expand RoboMME from 100 to 1,000 episodes per task family and increase training from 40K to 120K steps. With the same encoder and policy architecture, success rises from 57.67% to 87.50% (Figure 1 ). All four tracks improve; Reference, the weakest base-data track, gains 47.50 percentage points. Extending training to 120K steps on the original data alone yields no appreciable gain, supporting the benefit of broader demonstration coverage. LTM- π \pi exceeds the reported PonderPounce result with 9 × 9\times data by 11.96 points overall, under different data budgets and supervision assumptions.

Scaling does not fully resolve the challenge of composing local transitions into persistent object states: VideoUnmaskSwap and ButtonUnmaskSwap reach 74% and 62%, versus 100% for their non-swap counterparts. In a Cup Swap diagnostic, process supervision achieves 97.93% final-state recovery from latent transitions, compared with 2.40% under final-state-only supervision. These results demonstrate that latent transitions preserve recoverable multi-step interaction information and highlight the importance of intermediate supervision, motivating language-guided reasoning and process supervision to address remaining temporal-composition challenges.

To bound execution-memory growth, we merge the most similar adjacent projected tokens under the same quota during training and inference. On RoboMME-10x, a 200-token budget retains 84.00% success versus 87.50% uncompressed and reduces mean transition-token count by at least 38.26% on profiled training queries.

Finally, we evaluate LTM- π \pi on a Galbot G1 robot in a real-world repeated pick-and-place counting task. LTM- π \pi improves average success from 11.25% for the memory-free π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} baseline to 82.50%, demonstrating that transition memory also helps track completed interactions during physical manipulation.

Our contributions are threefold:

We propose Latent Transition Memory (LTM) , a memory representation that uses compact latent transitions between consecutive observations as historical context instead of retaining the full visual history. This focuses memory on interaction-induced changes and enables the policy to use past experience without external reasoning-model calls or memory-specific semantic annotations.

We develop LTM- π \pi , integrating transition memory into π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s inference context through a lightweight adapter. Causal attention, persistent KV caching, and asynchronous transition encoding support efficient online control. Experiments on RoboMME and LIBERO-Mem demonstrate strong memory-dependent manipulation performance, with a measured policy inference time of 66.71 ms on an H100.

We characterize transition-memory information, data scaling, and context-budget trade-offs . Ablations distinguish transition content from temporal cues; tenfold RoboMME data expansion raises success from 57.67% to 87.50%; process-supervised Cup Swap decoding recovers final states with 97.93% accuracy; and a 200-token budget retains 84.00% success. Finally, real-robot counting experiments improve success from 11.25% to 82.50%.

# 2 Related Work

VLA models transfer pretrained visual and linguistic representations to robotic control. RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) predicts tokenized actions, and OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) provides an open-source generalist policy. π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2024 ) introduces flow matching for continuous action generation; π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) and LingBot-VLA ( Wu et al., 2026 ) extend generalization through heterogeneous co-training and multi-embodiment data. These advances do not remove partial observability: the appropriate action may depend on events absent from the current observation. RoboMME ( Dai et al., 2026 ) and LIBERO-Mem ( Chung et al., 2026 ) evaluate this need for execution memory.

RoboFlamingo ( Li et al., 2023 ) models history through a sequential policy head; HAMLET ( Koo et al., 2025 ) and μ \mu VLA ( Cherepanov et al., 2026 ) use learned memory tokens. MemoryVLA ( Shi et al., 2025 ) and LaMem-VLA ( Qu et al., 2026 ) retrieve evidence from explicit memory banks. SAM2Act+ ( Fang et al., 2025 ) extends a multi-view manipulation policy with a spatial memory bank, encoder, and memory attention. Object-centric approaches retain a different unit of history: SlotVLA ( Hanyu et al., 2025 ) models object slots and their relations, while E-SlotSSM ( Chung et al., 2026 ) studies the progression of object-centric memory states. GMP ( Gao et al., 2026b ) learns when to activate cross-attention over cached image and action tokens. RoboMME also compares symbolic, sampled-frame, and recurrent memories with several policy interfaces ( Dai et al., 2026 ) . LTM instead retains an ordered sequence of changes between observations, rather than appearance tokens or a recurrent summary of the episode. Temporal prediction also informs memory-based control: HiF-VLA ( Lin et al., 2025 ) incorporates motion representations, MemoryVLA++ ( Shi et al., 2026 ) combines retrieved history with imagined futures, and MemoryVAM ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) injects compressed visual memory into both video prediction and action decoding.

MEM ( Torne et al., 2026 ) combines recent video with long-term textual memory, HiMe ( Ji et al., 2026 ) separates working memory from long-term planning, and WeaveLA ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) passes latent summaries of completed segments to subsequent subtasks. MemER ( Sridhar et al., 2025 ) retrieves keyframes for a high-level vision-language model that generates instructions for a low-level policy. PonderPounce ( Choi et al., 2026 ) uses a separate pretrained multimodal context model to asynchronously supply continuous cognition tokens to its action model. Its RoboMME training recipe includes transition, subgoal, and demonstration-reasoning supervision. In 2AM ( Hu et al., 2026 ) , an agent maintains episodic memory and guides an episodically stateless action model through subtask language and optional 2D spatial hints. These designs delegate historical interpretation to a higher-level model or interface. LTM instead exposes observed transitions directly to the action policy, without invoking a separate reasoning model or generating intermediate language during control.

SimpleMemVLA ( Yin et al., 2026 ) retains timestamped video in its VLM’s native context and reuses the prefix cache through streaming prefill. Its action head receives representations of generated subtask text, with subtask annotations produced offline by a cloud VLM. This is a training-time annotation dependency, rather than a requirement for cloud-model calls during control. T 2 Mem ( Liu et al., 2026 ) places a fast-weight memory between the VLM and action expert and updates it through self-supervised test-time gradients. Like LTM, it learns from action demonstrations without an external reasoning model or memory-specific annotations. Our distinction is therefore the memory representation and update rule: LTM appends frozen pairwise transition codes to a persistent sequence, without test-time gradient updates. Its causal attention and delayed prefix support incremental inference while preserving access to the current observation.

LAMs infer compact transition codes from observation pairs, typically using reconstruction without action labels ( Bruce et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2024 ) . Genie ( Bruce et al., 2024 ) uses discrete codes for controllable video generation, LAPA ( Ye et al., 2024 ) uses them for policy pretraining, and CLAM ( Liang et al., 2025 ) and UniVLA ( Bu et al., 2025 ) extend latent actions to continuous and cross-embodiment control. DreamDojo ( Gao et al., 2026a ) uses latent actions for world-model pretraining; CD-LAM ( Wei et al., 2026 ) reduces visual confounding in such codes. We use pretrained LAMs only to encode observed transitions into episodic memory; the deployed policy does not need to reconstruct past frames or generate future videos.

2026-10-16.title: Hierarchical Building-Floo-Room Framework for Privacy-Preserving Autonomous Delivery in Large-Scale Buildings
2026-10-16.authors: Xu Xiaoji , Luo Rui , Chen Jinhua , Xiang Changying , Zhang Leihan , Liao Zhongyuan
2026-10-16.abstract: Autonomous delivery in large-scale buildings requires coordinated planning across multiple spatial levels, including building, floor, and room, while ensuring scheduling efficiency. Existing methods often focus solely on algorithmic development, neglecting integration with physical robotic platforms, and rarely validate performance in real-world scenarios. Many approaches also overlook hierarchical building structures and room-level privacy constraints, limiting practical applicability. To address these challenges, this paper presents a hierarchical delivery framework based on a Building–Floor–Room abstraction, which decomposes the problem across multiple levels to significantly reduce optimization complexity. We formulate a building-aware extension of the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) that explicitly models inter-building and inter-floor connectivity, room-level access constraints, and privacy-sensitive areas, enabling globally feasible and privacy-compliant task assignment and routing. Based on this hierarchical model, the framework can evaluate delivery efficiency across different building layouts and optimize depot placement for specific configurations. At the execution level, we introduce a novel hardware design for non-interactive, privacy-preserving delivery, supported by reachability-aware distances and a closed-loop mapping, localization, and navigation system, ensuring consistency between planned routes and physical navigation. The proposed framework is validated on a real multi-sensor robotic platform, demonstrating reliable multi-floor delivery with improved path rationality and overall efficiency.
2026-10-16.introduction:
The increasing demand for last-mile delivery in building complexes, campuses, and large residential communities necessitates mobile robots capable of executing multi-goal delivery tasks in real-world indoor environments [ 34 ] . Unlike conventional indoor navigation, which often focuses on a single floor or building, real-world facilities exhibit a three-level hierarchical structure — building, floor, and room —each posing distinct operational challenges [ 24 ] :
(1) Building-level , where physical separation and sparse inter-building connections make inter-building travel costly and planning-sensitive;
(2) Floor-level , where vertical mobility relies on elevators with vertical transfer cost and nontrivial waiting times, creating significant scheduling constraints;
(3) Room-level , where each floor features complex 2D topologies, branched corridors, diverse room layouts, and privacy-restricted zones, complicating local path planning and reachability.

Such hierarchical structures pose fundamental challenges to classical Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) formulations. VRP typically relies on ideal Euclidean distances and metric properties (e.g., symmetry and triangle inequality), assumptions fundamentally violated by non-Euclidean path distances, elevator access costs, and time-varying vertical transfers. Furthermore, while the base Capacitated VRP (CVRP) is already known to be NP-hard [ 1 ] , constructing a unified graph spanning all building, floor, and room levels exacerbates this complexity. This unified modeling leads to a combinatorial explosion of the state space, rendering the global hierarchical routing problem intractable for real-time operation and preventing timely responses to dynamic delivery requests [ 7 ] .

Beyond structural complexity, reliable multi-goal delivery in real-world deployments is further hindered by three key practical challenges.

(1) Lack of effective large-scale cross-building optimization models. Most existing approaches focus on single-building or small-scale routing problems, and do not scale to delivery scenarios involving multiple buildings and heterogeneous inter-building distances. As a result, cross-building delivery decisions are often handled by ad hoc heuristics, leading to suboptimal capacity utilization and excessive depot returns.

(2) Dynamic environments and sensing limitations. Real-world indoor environments are highly dynamic, with moving pedestrians and time-varying layouts that disrupt stable perception and localization. These factors introduce uncertainty into navigation and execution, necessitating robust odometry and sensor fusion methods to maintain reliable operation [ 40 ] .

(3) Plan–execution mismatch in decoupled systems. Global VRP solutions are typically computed on idealized maps and assume perfect execution. In practice, however, discrepancies between planned routes and feasible robot trajectories frequently arise. Moreover, mapping, localization, scheduling, and navigation modules are often designed and optimized independently, preventing closed-loop coordination and resulting in inconsistent end-to-end performance.

Moreover, with the increasing adoption of autonomous delivery systems and the rising cost of manual labor, delivery efficiency has become an important consideration in residential building design. In many communities, building layout and depot placement directly affect the feasibility and performance of unmanned delivery. Therefore, it is also essential to use quantitative models to guide building layout design toward better support for autonomous delivery.

To address these challenges, a hierarchical autonomous delivery system tailored to the Building–Floor–Room structure is proposed. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A hierarchical Building–Floor–Room model and a building-aware CVRP formulation are introduced, accounting for inter-building and inter-floor connectivity, room-level access, and privacy-sensitive areas, which reduces optimization complexity while enabling globally feasible and privacy-compliant routing.

A hierarchical Building–Floor–Room model and a building-aware CVRP formulation are introduced, accounting for inter-building and inter-floor connectivity, room-level access, and privacy-sensitive areas, which reduces optimization complexity while enabling globally feasible and privacy-compliant routing.

A unified mapping and autonomous navigation system integrated with a non-interactive, privacy-preserving robot design is developed, ensuring consistency between hierarchical planning and real-world execution.

A layout evaluation and depot optimization method is proposed, allowing quantitative assessment of delivery efficiency across different building configurations and optimal depot placement.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Hierarchical and Semantic Environmental Modeling for Navigation

Autonomous navigation fundamentally relies on accurate environment representation.
Pioneering works established metric-based grid maps and early topological graphs [ 33 ] to represent planar environments.
Modern facilities, however, demand multi-level abstractions that can explicitly capture building-scale structure and semantics. Han et al. [ 9 ] and Palacín et al. [ 20 ] model robots navigating multi-floor buildings, explicitly considering elevator and stair nodes.
To this end, hierarchical environment models and graph-based representations have been proposed to manage spatial complexity,
ranging from extended hierarchical building graphs for design and engineering [ 30 ] ,
to hierarchical attributed graphs for facade and building component modeling [ 36 ] ,
and indoor navigation graphs that explicitly encode multi-storey visibility and connectivity [ 44 ] .
Such hierarchical mapping structures often segment the environment into connected regions or levels [ 12 , 37 ] ,
enabling scalable reasoning across floors and functional spaces.
As environment scale increases, optimizing large unified graph structures becomes computationally expensive.
Hierarchical or multi-level graph representations can significantly improve efficiency; however, designing effective hierarchical models that balance geometric fidelity, semantic richness, and computational tractability remains an open research problem.

With the prevalence of 3D sensing, research has moved towards dense 3D reconstruction using methods like TSDF [ 13 , 5 ] , and scalable volumetric maps [ 41 ] . Concurrently, semantic mapping has gained traction, enriching geometric models with object and place labels. Recent systems, including Kimera [ 23 ] and Hydra [ 11 ] , represent the environment using 3D Scene Graphs, unifying metric and semantic information. Gu et al. proposed ConceptGraphs, an open-vocabulary graph-structured representation for 3D scenes [ 8 ] . While these semantic approaches provide rich contextual representations, they mainly focus on scene understanding or geometric reconstruction. Meanwhile, with the growing emphasis on user privacy, explicitly modeling privacy-sensitive areas (e.g., restricted offices or sensitive zones) has become increasingly important. Existing privacy-preserving efforts, such as the multi-factor authentication framework proposed by Yang et al. [ 42 ] , primarily protect identities and communication security in robotic delivery systems rather than spatial semantic representations. As a result, few semantic environment models explicitly incorporate privacy constraints into their spatial abstractions. Our work addresses this gap by integrating semantic connectivity, privacy-sensitive regions, and cost modeling into a unified Building–Floor–Room hierarchical graph optimized for delivery and navigation tasks.

## 2.2 Vehicle Routing Problems with Indoor and Dynamic Constraints

The Vehicle Routing Problem (VRP) is the core of multi-goal delivery, with foundational theory well-documented in classical works [ 35 ] . Standard VRP formulations rely on metric assumptions, such as symmetric and Euclidean distances, which fail dramatically in structured indoor settings [ 29 ] .

Efforts to adapt VRP to robotic systems have focused on incorporating physical constraints. The VRP with Time Windows (VRP-TW) [ 31 ] is relevant for timed deliveries, while stochastic VRP addresses uncertainty in service times. For indoor logistics, the primary challenge is the non-Euclidean topology and the asymmetric cost induced by vertical movement. Studies have attempted to model elevator waiting times [ 21 ] and integrated multi-floor scheduling with localization [ 14 , 16 ] . Furthermore, optimizing for energy (Green VRP) [ 26 ] is crucial for battery-powered AMRs. From an algorithmic perspective, both metaheuristics like Ant Colony Optimization [ 32 ] and emerging learning-based approaches [ 2 ] have been applied to VRP variants. In addition to single-robot navigation, multiple robots must be coordinated to optimize overall delivery efficiency. Multi-trip vehicle routing problems (MTVRP) are used in [ 9 ] to schedule multiple robots across multiple floors while minimizing total travel cost. However, existing VRP applications for robotics generally operate on idealized graphs. They lack a mechanism to dynamically incorporate SLAM-derived reachability and consistency information, leading to the persistent plan–execution mismatch when transitioning between different building levels. We overcome this by formulating a hierarchical CVRP whose distance matrix is derived directly from a reachability-aware map pipeline.

## 2.3 LiDAR SLAM, Fusion, and Closed-Loop System Integration

Reliable autonomy hinges on robust Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). The progression from 2D methods like Cartographer [ 10 ] to 3D LiDAR SLAM, starting with LOAM [ 43 ] , has been critical. Contemporary systems like LIO-SAM [ 27 ] , Invariant-DLIO [ 4 ] , and the highly efficient FAST-LIO2 [ 39 ] use tight LiDAR-Inertial fusion to maintain accuracy over long trajectories. For additional robustness, visual-inertial odometry (VIO), pioneered by systems like VINS-Mono [ 22 ] and DSO [ 38 ] , and full Lidar-Visual-Inertial fusion (LVI-SAM [ 28 ] , R3LIVE [ 18 ] ) have been developed to mitigate drift in feature-poor or geometrically degenerate environments. Graph-based SLAM systems are also critical for global consistency and loop closure [ 15 , 19 ] .

Despite the sophistication of these modules, they often operate in isolation. The widely used navigation architecture consists of global planning feeding into local planners like the Dynamic Window Approach (DWA) [ 6 ] or the Time-Elastic Band (TEB) [ 25 ] . Crucially, this setup inherently suffers from decoupling: the high-level VRP scheduler (Section 2.2) is blind to real-time SLAM consistency and execution challenges (e.g., elevator localization degradation). While theoretical work has outlined the necessity of integrated systems [ 3 , 17 ] , few deployable architectures have achieved true closed-loop integration. Our work represents a significant step by implementing a closed-loop system that leverages Fast-LIO for high-fidelity state estimation and feeds real-time spatial information directly back into the hierarchical task scheduler, thereby ensuring global-local plan consistency.

2026-10-16.title: A Black-Box Positioning Solution for Effortless Integration in Wearable Navigation
2026-10-16.authors: Anh-Van Vu , Changmin Sung , Dongsoo Han
2026-10-16.abstract: Accurate localization is critical for a wide range of applications, including navigation, augmented reality, safety management, and healthcare. However, achieving accurate positioning remains challenging, especially in GPS-degraded environments. Pedestrian Dead Reckoning (PDR), which estimates position based on inertial sensor data, offers a promising alternative but typically demands substantial effort in algorithm design and system integration. This complexity often leads to prolonged development timelines and elevated costs. To address these challenges, we present the PDR Sensor (PDRS), a plug-and-play, black-box PDR module optimized for seamless integration into wearable and IoT platforms. PDRS integrates a microprocessor and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) within a compact, low-power module. It executes real-time sensor fusion onboard, providing position updates via standard interfaces (I²C, SPI, UART). Experimental evaluations demonstrate its high robustness, achieving a step detection error of just 0.16% over 1250 steps and a traveled distance error of 1.87% under diverse conditions. The system further exhibits low latency (2.5 ms) and modest power consumption (52.35 mA). Unlike conventional studies, the PDRS leverages a holistic co-design of hardware and software to enhance performance and integration aspects, simplifying adoption without requiring deep expertise. By lowering technical barriers, PDRS enables developers and researchers to prioritize innovation in IoT and wearable technologies, accelerating prototyping, reducing development time, and advancing industry progress. Future work aims to enhance accuracy, reduce power usage and module size, and integrate AI-driven techniques to better mitigate drift.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Indoor positioning, crucial for diverse applications ranging from navigation in complex environments (e.g., airports, shopping malls) to augmented reality and healthcare [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , relies heavily on PDR. Its infrastructure-free nature, utilizing only inertial sensors (accelerometers and gyroscopes) to track user movement, offers a significant advantage where satellite or RF methods are ineffective [ 4 , 5 ] . This autonomy, achievable with compact IMUs integrated into modern smartphones and wearables [ 6 , 7 ] , has fueled extensive research resulting in numerous PDR algorithms and system designs [ 8 , 6 , 7 , 9 , 10 ] . Therefore, it is now an essential component of most indoor localization systems [ 11 , 4 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] .

Despite significant advancements, deploying practical PDR systems remains challenging. PDR is a relative positioning method prone to cumulative drift errors over time [ 15 , 8 , 6 , 16 ] , where even minor sensor biases or step length inaccuracies compound, causing trajectory divergence. Consequently, standalone PDR is unsuitable for long-term tracking, necessitating fusion with external references or additional sensors (e.g., magnetometers, barometers, UWB, map constraints) to mitigate drift [ 16 , 11 , 4 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] . However, such multi-sensor fusion increases system complexity, power consumption, and cost, undermining PDR’s inherent simplicity. Practical indoor positioning demands ease of implementation, affordability, and minimal computational complexity [ 17 ] , criteria often unmet by research prototypes requiring specialized hardware or extensive calibration.

Another key challenge involves the significant expertise and development effort required to create robust PDR solutions. Building a PDR system necessitates real-time coordination of numerous components on resource-constrained hardware: sensor data acquisition, signal processing (step detection, orientation and distance estimation), and error correction. As Nilsson et al. observe, although “dead reckoning is not rocket science,” the number of hardware/software components that must work in harmony is large, and achieving a well-performing embedded implementation is far from trivial [ 18 ] . Careful selection of an embedded processor with sufficient processing power and algorithmic optimization for low latency and energy consumption is crucial.

Further complexities arise from the need for small form factors and mechanical reliability (for wearable or mobile applications), with few readily available modular, reusable hardware-algorithm solutions [ 18 ] . Commercial solutions, such as Bosch Sensortec’s BHI160B and BHI260AP, can fulfill these requirements but require specialized PDR-enabled firmware, which is often publicly unavailable [ 19 ] . This necessitates significant custom integration, increasing development time and costs for solutions seeking to utilize PDR. Therefore, despite the ubiquity of low-cost MEMS sensors, the barrier to entry for deploying PDR systems remains high. This gap between algorithmic research and deployable products, highlighted in recent literature [ 17 ] , emphasizes that accuracy alone is insufficient; stability, real-time capability, energy efficiency, and easy integration are equally critical for widespread adoption.

This paper addresses the challenges of deploying PDR systems by introducing the PDR Sensor (PDRS), a compact, low-power hardware module integrating a microcontroller unit (MCU), an inertial measurement unit (IMU), and an onboard adapted PDR algorithm. Designed as a plug-and-play solution, the PDRS encapsulates complex sensor fusion and computation logic, providing real-time position updates via standard interfaces (I²C, SPI, UART). Our module can be treated as an off-the-shelf component – effectively a “black box” PDR unit – that researchers, and system designers can drop into their prototypes or products with minimal effort. This hardware-software co-design contrasts with previous research primarily focused on algorithmic accuracy within high-end processing environments [ 9 , 8 , 6 , 16 ] . By offloading computational complexity and sensor management, the PDRS enables developers to obtain accurate step counts, heading, and displacement estimates without specialized signal processing or inertial navigation expertise. Utilizing inexpensive, commercially available, reproducible components, the PDRS achieves competitive accuracy (0.16% step detection error, 1.87% travel distance estimation error) with low latency (milliseconds) and power consumption (tens of milliamps), suitable for numerous real-time positioning applications. This simplified PDR integration significantly lowers the barrier to entry for indoor localization, accelerating adoption in applications ranging from IoT devices to assistive wearables, where a self-contained inertial positioning module unlocks new functionality without added cost or complexity.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section III details the hardware and software co-design of the PDRS. Section IV describes the adapted PDR algorithm and bias mitigation technique. Section V presents evaluations of positioning accuracy in different environments, real-time latency, power consumption, and thermal characteristics. Finally, Section VI concludes and outlines future works.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Works

PDR has long been studied as a viable solution for indoor positioning when external signals are unavailable. Early work by Beauregard and Haas [ 20 ] established the basic framework of PDR—leveraging step detection, stride estimation, and heading determination from wearable sensors. Their approach, however, required careful calibration to accommodate individual gait variations and stable sensor mounting, underscoring intrinsic limitations that would drive subsequent research.

A key challenge in PDR is drift caused by sensor biases and noise. Ojeda and Borenstein [ 5 ] addressed this using zero-velocity updates (ZUPT), exploiting the foot’s stationary phase to reset errors and improve short-range tracking accuracy. Nilsson et al. [ 18 ] further advanced this concept with OpenShoe, embedding an IMU and microcontroller in footwear for continuous ZUPT-aided inertial navigation. Despite effectiveness, these foot-mounted systems remained sensitive to sensor placement, requiring robust stationary-phase detection, prompting refinements through probabilistic filtering methods like Extended Kalman Filters (EKF) and heuristic drift-reduction techniques [ 7 , 8 ] . Moreover, the reliance on precise placement and individual calibration highlighted the gap between research prototypes and practical, user-friendly solutions.

Beyond foot-mounted systems, smartphone-based and wearable PDR solutions have expanded to integrate a broader sensor array [ 9 , 7 ] . Modern approaches typically fuse accelerometer, gyroscope, and magnetometer data to estimate displacement and heading. Hou and Bergmann [ 7 ] reviewed various wearable PDR systems, noting that although sensor fusion enhances accuracy, indoor magnetic disturbances and variable sensor orientations often require frequent recalibration. Many systems mitigate these issues by periodically incorporating external references or adaptive filtering, yet these methods increase complexity and computational overhead.

Recent advancements have explored data-driven and AI-based approaches to further enhance PDR performance [ 21 , 22 ] . Saha et al. [ 21 ] introduced TinyOdom, a framework that employs temporal convolutional networks (TCNs) to process raw IMU data and output displacement estimates in real time. By integrating learned motion patterns with physics-based constraints, TinyOdom achieved competitive accuracy on resource-constrained devices, demonstrating that neural models can complement traditional signal processing. However, the necessity for extensive training data and computational complexity remains a challenge for widespread deployment in consumer devices.

Industrial developments further underscore the trend toward integrated, user-friendly PDR solutions. Companies like STMicroelectronics have developed turnkey PDR engines optimized for smartphones, providing developers with Android and iOS libraries that fuse data from ST’s MEMS sensors to automatically adjust for sensor error, offering PDR as well as contextual awareness [ 23 ] . Similarly, Bosch Sensortec’s BMI270 [ 24 ] and ST’s LSM6DS3 [ 25 ] incorporate on-chip algorithms for step counting and activity recognition, offering low-power, plug-and-play functionality that simplifies integration for wearables. Although these sensors alleviate some computational burdens, they typically deliver only partial functionality (e.g., step detection without full trajectory estimation). More recently, several smart sensors from Bosch Sensortec, including BHI160B and BHI260AP [ 26 ] , have been promoted as fully PDR-capable. However, these capabilities require dedicated PDR-enabled firmware, which remains unavailable [ 19 ] .

In summary, prior research has made significant strides in reducing drift, integrating sensor fusion, and applying AI to enhance PDR capabilities. Foot-mounted systems offer high accuracy with ZUPT but demand careful calibration, while smartphone-based solutions use multi-sensor fusion at the cost of increased complexity. Recent industry efforts have shifted toward integrated sensor solutions, though these often address only parts of the broader PDR problem. Our work tackles these gaps with a compact, black-box PDRS that encapsulates PDR complexities within a low-power module, enabling seamless integration into wearables and IoT devices without requiring specialized expertise. By aligning and extending recent advances, the PDRS provides a robust, accessible solution bridging high-performance academic prototypes and commercially viable systems.
