2026-10-16.title: CQDC-Warp: GPU-Accelerated Differentiable Quasi-Dynamic Simulation for Contact-Rich Manipulation
2026-10-16.authors: Yanchen Ding , Jiayi Chen , Jianfeng Xu , Wei Zhao , Li Yi , He Wang
2026-10-16.abstract:
Efficient synthesis of contact-rich manipulation trajectories is essential for
downstream robot learning. Gradient-based planning offers a promising approach,
but jointly optimizing motion and contact decisions remains challenging.
Meanwhile, many existing planners run on CPUs with limited throughput.
We present CQDC-Warp , a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic
simulator for batched model predictive control (MPC). We use it to study
contact-guided trajectory optimization, in which intended robot–object
contacts are specified before planning and encouraged through soft costs,
while the simulated dynamics
determine contact geometry and frictional response without a prescribed
contact-mode schedule. Across 17,408 17{,}408 trials on the 17 17 -object Allegro in-hand rotation benchmark, our
framework achieves 79.8 % 79.8\% success, compared with 73.7 % 73.7\% for CFree and 65.2 % 65.2\% for IMPACT, and reduces mean trajectory-generation time by
factors of 27.0 27.0 and 50.2 50.2 , respectively. On a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with 2,048 2{,}048 parallel worlds, forward and backward throughput reach 2.06 × 10 5 2.06\times 10^{5} and 2.25 × 10 5 2.25\times 10^{5} world-steps per second, respectively.
Further experiments cover manipulation with LEAP and Shadow hands,
environmental contact exploitation, bimanual manipulation, whole-body control,
and real-world trajectory replay on a Sharpa hand.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Contact-rich dexterous manipulation is a central capability for
general-purpose embodied intelligence. Modern robot learning increasingly
relies on large, diverse, and high-quality datasets of robot
behavior [ 14 ] . Collecting such data for dexterous hands is
particularly challenging due to the high cost and complexity of teleoperation,
as well as differences between human and robot
embodiments [ 15 , 16 ] . Scalable generation of
physically plausible dexterous trajectories could therefore support both
task execution and demonstration collection for downstream robot learning.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated impressive dexterous manipulation
behaviors [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] covering a broad range of objects [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . However, acquiring these behaviors with
model-free RL typically requires extensive trial and error guided by
task-specific rewards. The underlying dynamics are treated as a black box:
policy updates rely on sampled experience rather than derivatives of the
physical dynamics. Moreover, learned policies remain sensitive to their
training distributions, which can limit their reuse across contact-rich
tasks and scenes.

Gradient-based planning provides another route, exploiting dynamics
derivatives to efficiently refine action
sequences [ 23 , 24 ] . Within this paradigm,
contact-implicit trajectory optimization is an active and promising research
direction: it jointly optimizes state and control trajectories and contact
interactions without prescribing intended contact in advance [ 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] .
However, this generality also introduces strong coupling between motion and
contact decisions, resulting in large, nonconvex optimization problems that
can be difficult to solve reliably. Yet, from a practical standpoint, an even
more basic question remains open: given a suitable initialization and intended
contacts specified in advance, can existing tools reliably optimize action
sequences across diverse robot platforms and contact-rich tasks? Here, intended contacts
specify which robot link should touch the object, rather than prescribing a complete
contact-mode schedule; their exact geometry and frictional response are still determined
by the simulated dynamics. This assumption is practical in many manipulation settings,
where intended contacts can be inferred from task structure, grasp or trajectory initialization,
or human demonstrations with tactile gloves.

Differentiable simulation supports such local optimization by providing
gradients through simulated rollouts. Existing differentiable contact
simulators, however, face several limitations. Some methods introduce
force-at-a-distance through smoothing [ 5 ] or neglect coupling
between contact constraints [ 8 ] . Many implementations run on CPUs
or optimize only one trajectory at a time [ 8 , 30 , 29 ] , limiting throughput. GPU-based differentiable simulators are
available [ 9 , 12 , 13 ] ,
but their published evaluations typically cover only one or two robot
embodiments and a limited set of tasks. Efficient trajectory generation across
diverse robot platforms and contact-rich tasks remains less explored.

In this work, we propose CQDC-Warp , a GPU-accelerated differentiable
simulator that extends the Convex Quasi-Dynamic Contact (CQDC) model in three
respects. First, we introduce compliant frictional contact to regularize the
contact solve and revise the inertial model to retain coupling between
actuated and unactuated coordinates. Second, we provide implicit derivatives
of the contact dynamics and sampled surrogate derivatives of contact geometry.
Third, we develop an efficient GPU implementation built on MuJoCo-Warp’s
batched pipeline [ 31 ] , enabling parallel model predictive
control (MPC) across independent simulation worlds. Experiments demonstrate
in-hand manipulation, environmental contact exploitation, bimanual
manipulation, and whole-body control across dexterous hands, quadrupeds, and
humanoids, as well as a trajectory replay in the real world.

Our main contributions are:

CQDC-Warp, a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic contact simulator,
integrated into a batched MPC framework.

A contact-guided trajectory optimization setting in which intended
contacts are specified before planning, while the exact contact realization
remains implicit.

Experimental validation across diverse robots and
contact-rich tasks, including simulation benchmarks and
real-world trajectory replay.

1. CQDC-Warp, a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic contact simulator,
integrated into a batched MPC framework.

2. A contact-guided trajectory optimization setting in which intended
contacts are specified before planning, while the exact contact realization
remains implicit.

3. Experimental validation across diverse robots and
contact-rich tasks, including simulation benchmarks and
real-world trajectory replay.

# II Related Work

## II-A Rigid-Body Contact Models

Classical penalty models prescribe local contact forces that penalize
penetration, typically using spring–damper laws for the normal response
and regularized friction [ 1 , 9 ] .
Larger penalty stiffness reduces penetration but can worsen numerical
conditioning [ 1 ] .
Complementarity-based formulations instead express rigid frictional contact
as a nonlinear complementarity problem (NCP), combining the Signorini
condition, Coulomb friction, and
maximum dissipation [ 32 , 3 , 4 , 6 , 7 , 9 ] .
Polyhedral approximations of friction cones yield linear complementarity
problems (LCPs) [ 33 , 2 , 11 ] .
Cone complementarity problems (CCPs) retain the circular friction cones but
relax normal complementarity, enabling convex optimization at the cost of
possible gliding artifacts [ 34 , 32 ] ;
this formulation underlies CQDC [ 5 ] .

## II-B Differentiable Contact Simulation

Dynamics gradients can be obtained through automatic differentiation (AD),
which applies the chain rule to the simulator’s computational
graph [ 9 , 12 ] .
For iterative contact solvers, unrolling makes differentiation cost grow
with the iteration count [ 6 ] .
Implicit differentiation instead linearizes the contact equations or
optimality conditions at the converged solution and solves a sensitivity
system, avoiding differentiation through solver
iterations [ 2 , 3 , 1 , 5 , 6 ] .
CQDC-Warp follows this implicit approach.

Geometry gradients describe how contact points, normals, and gaps change
with body poses. Signed distance fields (SDFs) provide distances and
surface normals through field values and spatial derivatives, supporting
differentiable contact with nonconvex shapes [ 11 ] .
However, constructing and storing an SDF adds preprocessing and
memory overhead, and geometry edits may require rebuilding the
field [ 35 ] .
For triangle-based collision queries, analytic derivatives
and direct AD capture variation within a triangle but not transitions
between triangles [ 2 , 36 ] .
Silico obtains implicit geometry gradients by jointly solving geometry
and dynamics, but embedding geometric variables and constraints enlarges
the coupled system [ 4 ] .
Sampling-based surrogate gradients aggregate information across neighboring
surface features, providing informative local gradients beyond a single
triangle [ 37 , 36 ] .
CQDC-Warp adopts this surrogate approach.
Table I summarizes these
differentiation choices across simulators.

## II-C Contact-Rich Trajectory Optimization

Trajectory optimization commonly uses single shooting, multiple shooting,
or direct collocation [ 23 ] .
Single shooting optimizes control sequences through a complete rollout;
multiple shooting introduces intermediate states and continuity constraints
between shorter rollouts [ 26 , 27 ] .
Direct collocation represents trajectories with piecewise polynomials and
enforces dynamics at selected nodes [ 23 ] .
The latter two allow direct state-trajectory initialization and expose
temporal sparsity, at the cost of additional variables and constraints.
Differentiable simulation also enables gradient-based single-shooting MPC
on GPUs [ 13 ] .
CQDC-Warp follows this route, optimizing command sequences through
GPU-batched differentiable rollouts.

A separate design choice is how much contact structure is prescribed.
Crocoddyl [ 38 ] optimizes motion given a predefined
contact-mode sequence and enforces the corresponding contact constraints.
Contact-implicit methods instead optimize motion and
contact interactions jointly without requiring such a
sequence [ 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] .
Our contact-guided setting uses an intermediate level of contact prior.

2026-10-16.title: MR-MPCC: Model Predictive Contouring Control for Robotic Manipulator Tracking under Moving Reference Frames
2026-10-16.authors: Chonghao Cheng , Tiancheng Li , Jonathan Woolfrey , Liang Zhao , Shoudong Huang
2026-10-16.comment: Accepted by The IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems 2026 (IROS 2026)
2026-10-16.abstract: Maintaining small path-tracking errors under moving reference frames is essential for robotic manipulation tasks with tight execution tolerances, such as machining and surgical automation. Conventional time-indexed controllers, including tracking Model Predictive Control (MPC), rely on a fixed temporal correspondence with the reference trajectory and may therefore accumulate path-relative error under abrupt reference-frame motion or timing mismatch. This paper presents MR-MPCC, a Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) framework for velocity-controlled robotic manipulators with 6-DoF end-effector pose regulation under Moving-Reference disturbances. A hierarchical control architecture is adopted, in which an upper-level MPCC optimizes path progress while penalizing contouring and orientation errors, and a constrained resolved motion rate control (RMRC) layer maps the commanded Cartesian twist to feasible joint velocities under joint-level and safety constraints. MR-MPCC is implemented in a ROS2–MuJoCo pipeline and validated on a UR5e platform under moving-reference disturbances, where the path frame is perturbed and tracked by electromagnetic sensors. Compared with PI control and time-indexed tracking MPC under matched disturbance, MR-MPCC achieves lower geometric path-following error and smaller deviations in the moving path frame, demonstrating improved path-following performance under reference-frame motion.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Accurate end-effector motion control is fundamental to robotic
manipulation in industrial assembly, surgical automation, and machining [ 1 , 2 ] .
In such tasks, performance is usually determined by geometric fidelity to a prescribed path rather than by strict adherence to a preassigned timing law [ 3 ] . The control objective is therefore to minimize spatial deviation
from the path in the presence of disturbances and modeling uncertainty.

Conventional controllers such as proportional–integral–derivative (PID) control provide intuitive and computationally efficient solutions [ 4 ] , but do not explicitly predict future system evolution or systematically handle state and input constraints.
Model Predictive Control (MPC) addresses these issues by optimizing
future control actions over a finite horizon [ 5 , 6 ] .
However, standard MPC formulations are time-indexed and rely on a fixed
time parameterization of the reference [ 7 ] . Under disturbances that induce
timing mismatch or abrupt motion of the reference frame, time-indexed
tracking can accumulate geometric error, leading to degraded robustness,
especially when simultaneous position and orientation regulation is
required.

Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) offers an alternative by reformulating tracking relative to the reference path [ 8 ] . It decomposes the tracking deviation into a contouring component orthogonal to the path and a lag component along the path, allowing geometric path-following accuracy and path progress to be regulated separately.
Despite these advantages, its application to robotic manipulators remains in its infancy, with only a small number of recent works beginning to explore this domain [ 9 ] .

Extending MPCC to robotic manipulators is challenging because nonlinear kinematics, and joint-level constraints complicate real-time task-space control [ 10 ] . The challenge increases when the reference frame moves abruptly, since stable joint-level control does not necessarily ensure small path-relative errors. In applications such as surgical milling and high-accuracy assembly, these errors can affect task quality and safety. This motivates direct regulation of path-relative error under reference motion and joint constraints.

This paper presents MR-MPCC, a task-space MPCC framework for velocity-controlled manipulators with full 6-DoF end-effector pose regulation. The method combines MPCC with constrained RMRC to generate feasible joint-velocity commands in real time. It is implemented in a ROS2–MuJoCo pipeline (Fig. 1 ) and validated on a physical UR5e, where reference-frame motion is measured using electromagnetic tracking and the controller operates at 500 Hz. Under matched paths and disturbance, MR-MPCC achieves lower contouring error than PI control and time-indexed tracking MPC in both simulation and physical experiments.

The main contributions are:
(i) a task-space MPCC formulation for full 6-DoF manipulator path following under moving reference frames;
(ii) a unified simulation and physical evaluation pipeline for reference-frame disturbances; and
(iii) a comparison with PI control and time-indexed tracking MPC of contouring, lag, and rotational tracking errors.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Manipulator Control and Disturbance Rejection

Robotic manipulators are subject to modeling uncertainties and external disturbances that can degrade
tracking accuracy and closed-loop stability. Classical controllers such as PID and feedback linearization
provide reliable baseline performance, but disturbance attenuation often depends on careful tuning and
model fidelity [ 4 ] .

Robust control techniques explicitly shape uncertainty margins to improve disturbance rejection, including
sliding-mode control [ 11 ] and H ∞ H_{\infty} designs [ 12 ] .
In practice, these methods can trade tracking smoothness or responsiveness for robustness, and they do not
directly address the timing sensitivity induced by a time-parameterized reference.

Iterative learning control leverages task repetitiveness to reduce tracking errors across
repeated executions, which has been widely adopted in machining and contouring applications [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] .
However, its effectiveness diminishes when disturbances are non-repetitive or when the task
conditions change rapidly between trials.

Overall, these approaches strengthen robustness via feedback compensation or repetition-based
error refinement, but they do not explicitly optimize future motion under constraints.
This motivates predictive control formulations that can incorporate constraints
and anticipate disturbance effects.

## II-B MPC for Manipulators

MPC is attractive for manipulator systems since finite-horizon optimization can explicitly encode multivariable dynamics, actuation limits, and safety constraints, enabling motion objectives to be pursued subject to requirements such as joint-limit enforcement, collision avoidance, and pose-constrained path or tunnel following [ 16 , 5 , 17 ] .

Robust MPC variants, including tube-based designs, further account for model uncertainty and external
disturbances. For instance, Yao et al . [ 18 ] combined disturbance observers with tube MPC to improve
tracking robustness under uncertainty and input constraints, while Kang et al . [ 19 ] developed a sliding-mode adaptive tube MPC to enhance robustness and constraint satisfaction
under dynamic uncertainties.
Learning-augmented MPC [ 6 ] has also been studied to improve model fidelity in unstructured settings.

A recurring limitation of time-indexed MPC is sensitivity to timing mismatch and reference-motion effects:
execution delays or moving-reference disturbances can preserve time alignment while accumulating spatial
deviation from the underlying geometric path. Spatially aware formulations such as MPCC mitigate this issue
by directly penalizing contouring and lag errors relative to the path parameterization, decoupling path fidelity
from time parameterization.

## II-C Evolution of MPCC

MPCC [ 8 ] was introduced to balance geometric path accuracy
against traversal progress in contouring systems by formulating tracking in path coordinates
and explicitly penalizing contouring and lag errors.
Subsequent studies [ 20 ] extended the formulation to multi-axis motion platforms to achieve
high-precision contour tracking under actuation constraints.

MPCC later gained traction in robotics for high-performance trajectory tracking [ 21 ] , where optimizing
the path progress online enables adaptive speed regulation while directly minimizing geometric
deviation from the reference path.
To support general spatial motion, recent works [ 22 , 23 ] formalized consistent contouring and lag error
definitions in three dimensions, enabling MPCC on arbitrary 3D paths.
Constraint-aware variants have further incorporated safety structures into the optimization,
such as corridor-constrained MPCC [ 24 ] for aggressive flight along spatial paths.

The application of MPCC to robotic manipulators remains relatively limited. Yoon et al . [ 9 ] proposed a reactive MPCC formulation augmented with control barrier functions for obstacle avoidance, self-collision prevention, and singularity handling, and demonstrated real-time performance on a 7-DoF Panda manipulator. Their work primarily addresses safe and feasible path following in constrained environments. In contrast, this paper focuses on accurate manipulator tracking when external disturbances alter the reference frame, requiring online compensation for relative robot–reference motion.

2026-10-16.title: LICOA: Learning Instruction-Conditioned Optical Actions for Mobile Spatial Augmented Reality
2026-10-16.authors: Yuchen Deng , Shunkai Zhou , Ruixuan Zhu , Haibin Ling , Bingyao Huang
2026-10-16.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-16.abstract: Spatial augmented reality (SAR) augments physical environments with projected content, but most systems assume that the projector pose, target region, or motion path has been fixed or specified. We instead make projected light an embodied action: given a language instruction and current visual observations, a system must decide how to move and where and at what scale to place the projection. We introduce LICOA to realize this capability. Its differential-drive chassis provides room-scale approach and repositioning, while a steerable mirror with two degrees of freedom (2DoF) and projection scale provide rapid local control of the beam. A shared interface maps synchronized external and onboard RGB cameras with robot control state to physical optical actions across pretrained action models. Because instruction-conditioned optical action lacks dedicated training data and a common evaluation protocol, we construct a matched simulation embodiment and a corpus with 150 150 tasks and 7,500 7{,}500 rendered episodes, then evaluate models trained only on this corpus in previously unseen real-world environments. Across 480 480 complete closed-loop real-world execution trials (rollouts) on 12 12 tasks, the best adapted action model achieves a 57.50 % 57.50\% success rate and 40.64 % 40.64\% success weighted by path length, compared with 8.33 % 8.33\% and 5.15 % 5.15\% for the same architecture trained from scratch. A further 150 150 real-world ablation rollouts support the need for both camera views and coordinated control of the chassis and mirror. These results establish a physical platform, shared perception and optical action interface, corpus, and real-world evaluation protocol for treating projected light as an embodied action.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Spatial augmented reality (SAR) overlays digital visual content directly onto physical environments using projectors [ 2 , 22 , 35 ] . Unlike head-mounted or handheld displays, projection requires no worn or held device, supports shared viewing, and presents spatial cues for navigation, object localization, and collaborative work [ 47 , 49 , 24 , 69 ] . Yet useful projection also requires placing light at the intended location,
direction, and scale. Most existing SAR systems rely on fixed projector setups and predefined projection regions. Such configurations provide geometric calibration [ 62 , 32 , 14 ] and support diverse projection mapping applications [ 54 , 1 , 30 , 31 , 17 , 18 , 45 , 12 ] , but restrict the workspace to surfaces visible from a predetermined projector pose. Mobile and steerable systems expand the reachable workspace, but their targets, paths, or control rules are commonly predefined [ 53 , 42 , 64 , 19 , 63 , 24 , 69 , 57 ] . They therefore do not address a general case in which a system enters an unfamiliar environment, interprets a language instruction, and decides both how to move and where to place light. Achieving this capability requires treating the placement of projected light as part of the system’s physical action. A language instruction such as “project onto the bear” specifies a desired physical effect rather than a target robot pose or a preselected display surface. The system must identify the referenced region, approach a feasible projection pose, redirect the beam, adjust its scale, and determine when placement is complete.

We call this task instruction-conditioned optical action . Throughout, physical describes tangible entities and actuator-level quantities, such as scene objects, the platform, and its actions, whereas real-world denotes the non-simulated deployment and evaluation domain. Realizing this capability introduces three practical challenges.
First, room-scale coverage and local beam placement require different controls. Moving the projector offers broad reach but is slow and changes the sensing viewpoint, whereas beam steering is fast but locally bounded. Multi-projector installations provide coverage at the cost of fixed infrastructure and calibration [ 11 , 56 , 36 ] , while arm-mounted systems provide local pose flexibility with a more complex mechanism and a workspace bounded by the arm [ 47 , 7 , 49 ] . A mobile SAR
platform must therefore combine broad repositioning with fast local optical control in one action space.
Second, pretrained action models target embodiments such as manipulators and grippers, with different camera inputs, state dimensions, action outputs, and training objectives [ 6 , 51 , 21 , 41 , 4 , 3 ] . Training from scratch must learn both general vision-language grounding and optical action semantics from task-specific data. We therefore ask whether pretrained models can retain their grounding and action-generation knowledge while learning optical action from task-specific demonstrations [ 5 , 51 , 3 ] .
Third, pretraining does not remove the need for task-specific data and evaluation. No existing corpus pairs spatial instructions and external and onboard RGB images with coordinated commands for the differential-drive chassis, a steerable mirror with two degrees of freedom (2DoF), and projection scale, plus episode termination outputs, and no common evaluation protocol assesses their physical outcomes. This absence is the underlying data problem; simulation is our means of addressing it. A useful real-world evaluation protocol must match the physical embodiment and sensing roles and test whether models trained without real-world demonstrations can act in unseen real-world settings.

To address these challenges, we introduce LICOA (Learning Instruction-Conditioned Optical Actions), a mobile SAR system that makes projected light an embodied action, as summarized in \cref fig:teaser. First, its differential-drive chassis provides coarse room-scale approach and repositioning, whereas its 2DoF steerable mirror provides rapid local beam redirection and projection scale controls the footprint. The resulting action components jointly determine where light is placed. Second, LICOA combines timestamp-synchronized external and onboard RGB images with the robot control state in a shared perception and optical action interface. This interface maps the observations and action output of different pretrained action models [ 3 , 52 , 68 ] to the same physical embodiment. Third, we reproduce the embodiment in simulation [ 20 , 59 ] and construct 150 150 spatial placement tasks with 7,500 7{,}500 rendered episodes. Models are fine-tuned only on this corpus and evaluated through real-world rollouts with new scenes, targets, instructions, and initial configurations.
Experiments evaluate three action-generation paradigms, isolate pretraining with a scratch version of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 3 ] , and ablate the camera views and action components. Across 480 480 complete closed-loop real-world executions (rollouts), adapted π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} achieves 57.50 % 57.50\% success and 40.64 % 40.64\% success weighted by path length, compared with 8.33 % 8.33\% and 5.15 % 5.15\% for the scratch control; another 150 150 rollouts support the ablations.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We formulate projected light as an instruction-conditioned optical action and realize it with a mobile optical platform whose differential-drive chassis, 2DoF steerable mirror, projection scale, and episode termination output form a coupled physical action space.

We define a shared perception and optical action interface comprising external and onboard RGB images, the robot control state, action chunks, and physical action components, and instantiate it with pretrained action models based on continuous action generation, autoregressive action tokenization, and world-action modeling.

We establish a matched simulation corpus and real-world evaluation protocol for this new task, including 150 150 spatial placement tasks, 7,500 7{,}500 rendered episodes, fine-tuning only in simulation, a real-world evaluation task set of 12 12 previously unseen real-world tasks with 480 480 real-world evaluation rollouts, and 150 150 ablation rollouts that test the sensing and hardware design.

2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Spatial augmented reality and mobile projection

Spatial augmented reality (SAR) overlays digital information directly onto physical surfaces and supports shared viewing without worn or handheld displays [ 2 , 22 , 35 ] .
To place an augmentation correctly, an autonomous SAR system must perceive candidate surfaces and semantic targets in the scene.
If projected content is visible in the camera input, the system must also distinguish it from the underlying scene. Most projector-camera systems (ProCams) pipelines focus on geometric and photometric perception under a fixed, calibrated setup [ 62 , 32 , 14 ] . Temporal [ 34 , 60 ] or spatial [ 40 , 32 ] structured light patterns establish dense correspondences for calibration, shape recovery, and appearance control [ 39 ] , while high-speed and infrared capture reduce motion-to-photon error on moving faces and hands [ 1 , 18 ] . Recently, ProCap extends SAR perception from geometry and photometry to semantics by separating the physical scene from projected content and describing the two layers independently [ 8 ] . It therefore exposes the virtual-physical ambiguity relevant to visually guided SAR, but stops at scene description rather than selecting and executing a projection action. Once the scene and projector response are known, a complementary line of work determines what a configured projector should emit. Per-pixel correction and learned visual models compensate for geometric and photometric distortions [ 55 , 10 , 23 , 33 , 48 , 29 , 28 , 31 ] . Neural rendering, path tracing, and Gaussian splatting model projector-camera light transport for relighting, compensation, or optical simulation [ 30 , 17 , 45 , 12 ] . Application-specific systems edit perceived softness, faces, glossy objects, or hands [ 54 , 1 , 39 , 18 ] , while neural deblurring and alternative optical paths address defocus, shadowing, and ambient illumination [ 37 , 38 , 43 , 25 , 67 ] . LAPIG further maps language prompts to surface-adapted, stylized content, but still assumes a calibrated projector and a given target surface [ 13 ] . Together, these perception and appearance methods define fixed ProCams represented by the first row of \cref tab:embodied_device_comparison, but they do not expose physical controls for deciding where light should be placed.

To distinguish configured projection from autonomous placement, \cref tab:embodied_device_comparison compares architecture classes along five requirements: projector-origin mobility, exposed action components, spatial instruction, learned closed-loop control, and a matched simulation interface. Fixed multi-projector systems enlarge an installed workspace by coordinating calibrated units, but their origins and coverage remain predetermined [ 11 , 56 , 36 , 58 , 50 ] . Fixed beam-steered systems add rapid local redirection through a rotating mirror or pan-tilt mechanism, yet cannot approach targets outside the useful range of their installed origin [ 53 , 42 , 64 ] . Arm-mounted projectors add local pose flexibility for gesture interaction, target tracking, or expressive movement, while remaining bounded by the arm workspace and mechanism complexity [ 47 , 7 , 49 , 27 ] . Mounting a projector on a chassis makes its origin room-scale. With fixed optics, mobile systems detect suitable surfaces or visualize a planned navigation path, but the beam direction remains coupled to the chassis pose [ 19 , 24 ] . Adding pan-tilt or gimbal actuation decouples local beam direction from chassis orientation: prior systems use this combination for marker-based tracking, scripted near-object overlays, or semantic-map and geometry-based surface search [ 63 , 69 , 57 ] . These systems establish the mechanical ingredients of mobile projection, but their spatial targets and motion are supplied by detected planes, markers, planned paths, scripts, maps, or scoring rules. None jointly learns closed-loop optical actions from current RGB observations and a natural-language spatial goal, and the optical simulators used by some fixed ProCams methods do not reproduce the mobile embodiment, camera roles, robot control state, and action interface.

LICOA instead connects a natural-language spatial goal and current observations to learned placement actions for a room-scale chassis, 2DoF steerable mirror, and projection scale. As summarized in \cref tab:embodied_device_comparison, its distinction lies in the learned closed-loop optical action interface and matched embodiment.

## 2.2 Generalist action models for optical action

The hardware comparison in \cref tab:embodied_device_comparison identifies learned closed-loop control as a principal capability missing from prior mobile projection systems. LICOA addresses this gap not by designing another action-model backbone, but by adapting pretrained generalist action models to a new optical embodiment. This adaptation is nontrivial: unlike conventional manipulation, the model must coordinate differential-drive velocities, absolute mirror pan and tilt targets, projection scale, and termination from external and onboard RGB observations and the current robot control state. We therefore use generalist action models to study whether pretrained representations and diverse action-generation mechanisms transfer to instruction-conditioned optical action.

Vision-language-action models. Vision-language-action (VLA) models learn mappings from visual observations and language instructions to executable controls. RT-1 and RT-2 established scalable language-conditioned robot policies and the transfer of semantic knowledge from vision-language pretraining, while Open X-Embodiment, Octo, and OpenVLA extended this direction through cross-robot data and open generalist policies [ 6 , 5 , 51 , 21 , 41 ] . For LICOA, two action-generation paradigms are particularly relevant. π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} uses a continuous flow-matching action expert, providing a direct mechanism for generating coupled optical action chunks [ 4 , 3 ] . FAST instead compresses continuous action sequences into discrete tokens, allowing π 0 \pi_{0} -FAST to generate action chunks autoregressively [ 52 ] . Instantiating both through the same optical action interface tests whether LICOA depends on one particular action representation. Comparing the adapted and scratch versions of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} additionally isolates whether pretrained visual-language and action representations transfer to optical placement.

World-action models. World-action models (WAMs) use visual dynamics as an additional learning signal. Earlier video-based robot models generate or encode possible visual futures and convert them into actions through inverse dynamics or downstream control [ 15 , 16 , 70 ] . More recent models jointly learn video evolution and robot actions, including GR-1, GR-2, Video Prediction Policy, Unified Video Action Model, and Unified World Models [ 65 , 9 , 26 , 46 , 71 ] . Fast-WAM retains this video-action co-training signal but predicts actions without explicitly generating future video at inference [ 68 ] . We include it as a third instantiation to test whether a video-derived dynamics prior transfers to optical action while remaining compatible with LICOA’s closed-loop replanning interface.

Taken together, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , π 0 \pi_{0} -FAST, and Fast-WAM are not presented as an exhaustive survey or as directly comparable pretrained architectures. They instantiate three action-generation paradigms: continuous flow matching, autoregressive action tokenization, and video-action co-training. LICOA supplies each model with the same instruction, external and onboard RGB images, and robot control state, and maps its predictions to the same chassis, mirror, projection-scale, and termination actions. This controlled interface allows the experiments to test model transfer and interface compatibility across action-generation paradigms without changing the physical task or embodiment.

2026-10-16.title: CLIS-MPPI: Closed-Loop Model Predictive Path Integral Control With Initial-State Sampling Under Execution Delay
2026-10-16.authors: Zidong Liu , Xu Chen
2026-10-16.comment: 65th IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC 2026)
2026-10-16.abstract:
Sampling-based motion planning such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control has become attractive for robotics due to its ability to handle nonlinear dynamics and non-smooth objectives without gradient information, while leveraging parallel rollout computation for real-time performance. However, in real-world robotic systems, the optimized control input is often applied after a non-negligible planning delay, causing a mismatch between the state used in forward simulation and the actual state at control execution, which can significantly degrade planning accuracy and may even lead to unsafe behavior such as collisions. This paper proposes Closed-Loop MPPI with Initial-State Sampling (CLIS-MPPI), which explicitly addresses execution-time state mismatch by modeling planning delay as a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, performing rollout optimization from sampled initial states, and applying a rollout-based local feedback correction during control execution.
The proposed method is validated through real-world experiments on a 6-DoF UR5e manipulator in a narrow-passage task involving obstacle avoidance and end-effector target reaching.
Across 5 real-world runs of the same task, standard MPPI collided in 2 runs, whereas CLIS-MPPI remained collision-free in all 5 runs. Averaged over all collision-free runs for each method (3 for MPPI and 5 for CLIS-MPPI), CLIS-MPPI reduced the average task completion time from 25.4 s to 24.4 s and the average end-effector path length from 0.456 m to 0.425 m. It also reduced the overall joint-position and joint-velocity root mean square errors (RMSEs) from 0.100 rad and 0.108 rad/s to 0.017 rad and 0.011 rad/s, respectively. These results demonstrate improved safety, planning-execution consistency, and motion smoothness.
2026-10-16.introduction:
With the rapid growth of computing hardware, sampling-based motion planning methods [ 1 , 2 ] , especially Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control [ 3 ] , have emerged as a powerful framework for real-time robotic motion planning and control. MPPI repeatedly samples stochastic control rollouts, performs forward simulation, evaluates trajectory costs, and refines the control sequence through a path-integral weighted update over a receding horizon. Compared with traditional gradient-based model predictive control (MPC) [ 4 ] , MPPI does not require differentiable cost functions, making it particularly suitable for robotic systems with nonlinear dynamics, obstacle-rich environments, and complex non-smooth objectives [ 5 ] . Furthermore, unlike learning-based methods such as reinforcement learning [ 6 ] , which typically depend on large-scale offline training, MPPI is a fully online planning method and can leverage GPU-parallelized rollout computation [ 7 ] to enable real-time decision-making.

Despite these advantages, the performance of MPPI in real-world robotic systems can be significantly degraded by execution-time delay. In particular, the quality of MPPI critically depends on the accuracy of its forward simulation and cost evaluation, since both are used to determine the control update at each planning cycle. However, forward simulation is typically the most computationally expensive step in MPPI, and the resulting planning latency can introduce a substantial mismatch between the state used for optimization and the state at which the optimized control is actually applied. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , at planning time t i plan t_{i}^{\mathrm{plan}} , MPPI starts forward simulation from the measured robot state x i ref x_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}} , and the rollout costs are evaluated based on this state. During the planning interval τ i \tau_{i} , however, the robot continues executing the previous control command u i − 1 u_{i-1} . Consequently, when the newly optimized control u i u_{i} becomes effective at t i send t_{i}^{\mathrm{send}} , the actual robot state has already evolved to x i apply ≠ x i ref x_{i}^{\mathrm{apply}}\neq x_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}} . As a result, the control command u i u_{i} is no longer applied to the state on which it was optimized, leading to a delay-induced state mismatch. This issue becomes particularly critical in high-frequency control settings or when the robot operates with large control actions, where even a small planning delay may produce a significant state deviation. In safety-critical tasks such as obstacle avoidance in narrow spaces, such mismatch can cause severe performance degradation and even collisions, despite the fact that the planned rollouts themselves are collision-free during forward simulation.

To address the delay-induced state mismatch, we propose closed-loop MPPI with initial-state sampling (CLIS-MPPI), as illustrated in Fig. 2 . The key idea is to explicitly convert execution delay into an initial-state uncertainty at each planning cycle, and to compensate for the resulting mismatch through a closed-loop control update. Instead of assuming that the control optimization starts from a single measured state, CLIS-MPPI samples a distribution of perturbed initial states around the currently measured state to represent the possible system evolution during the planning interval. For each sampled initial state, perturbed control sequences are generated and parallel forward simulations are performed to obtain rollout trajectories and their associated costs. Based on the weighted rollout distribution, a nominal state-control trajectory is constructed, from which a local feedback gain is further extracted in a rollout-based manner. The final control input is then computed as a closed-loop combination of the MPPI feedforward update and a state-feedback correction term. In this way, the proposed method enables the applied control command to better match the actual robot state at execution time, thereby improving consistency between planning and execution, motion smoothness, and safety in delay-sensitive real-world tasks.

In contrast to standard MPPI, which assumes immediate actuation after planning and samples only control perturbations from a single planning state, CLIS-MPPI replaces this assumption with a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, jointly samples both initial-state and control perturbations, and augments the control update with rollout-based feedback correction.

MPPI was originally introduced for aggressive autonomous driving tasks, where its sampling-based formulation demonstrated strong capability in handling high-speed, nonlinear systems under complex objectives [ 3 ] . Since then, MPPI has been extended to a wide variety of robotic platforms, including robotic manipulators [ 5 , 8 , 9 ] , aerial robots [ 10 ] , and legged systems [ 11 ] . In robotic manipulation, STORM [ 5 ] and RAMP [ 8 ] showed that GPU-accelerated MPPI can achieve real-time obstacle avoidance and goal-reaching on 6–7 Degrees of Freedom (DoF) manipulators in cluttered environments. For dynamic environments, Zhou et al. [ 9 ] proposed a parallel MPPI framework for manipulators that improves computational efficiency and incorporates a gradient-velocity modulated signed distance field cost for dynamic obstacle avoidance. Zhai et al. [ 10 ] developed a perception-aware MPPI method for quadrotor navigation in unknown environments, where perception-driven objectives are integrated into the planning process to promote exploration and path recovery under occlusion.

Delay-induced state mismatch causes the optimized control input to be applied to a state that is no longer consistent with the one used during planning, which may lead to degraded performance and even unsafe behavior. To improve the safety of MPPI, several works have combined MPPI with control barrier functions (CBFs) [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . Tao et al. [ 12 ] proposed SCBF-MPPI, which constrains the sampling distribution using stochastic control barrier function conditions to improve probabilistic safety and sample efficiency. Parwana et al. [ 13 ] combined an MPPI planner with a CBF-based safety filter so that MPPI handles task planning while the CBF layer enforces safe execution. Rabiee and Hoagg [ 14 ] proposed GS-MPPI, which incorporates a composite CBF into the system dynamics and enables MPPI to optimize only over guaranteed-safe trajectories. In a different direction, Belvedere et al. [ 15 ] proposed Feedback-MPPI, which augments MPPI with local feedback gains extracted from rollout sensitivity analysis to improve closed-loop responsiveness. However, these methods mainly focus on safety filtering or high-frequency feedback enhancement, and do not explicitly address the execution-time state mismatch caused by planning delay.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

We propose CLIS-MPPI, a novel MPPI formulation that explicitly compensates for execution-time state mismatch. Unlike standard MPPI, which implicitly assumes immediate actuation after the planning stage, CLIS-MPPI models planning delay as a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, jointly samples both initial-state and control perturbations, and computes the applied control input using a closed-loop combination of the MPPI feedforward update and a rollout-based local feedback correction.

We validate CLIS-MPPI through real-world experiments on a UR5e manipulator in a narrow-passage task involving both obstacle avoidance and end-effector target reaching. Across 5 real-world runs of the same task, standard MPPI collides with the environment in 2 runs, whereas CLIS-MPPI remains collision-free in all trials. Averaged over all collision-free runs for each method (3 for MPPI and 5 for CLIS-MPPI), CLIS-MPPI reduced the average task completion time from 25.4 s to 24.4 s and shortened the average end-effector path length from 0.456 m to 0.425 m. In addition, the overall joint-position and joint-velocity root mean square errors (RMSEs) were reduced from 0.100 rad and 0.108 rad/s under MPPI to 0.017 rad and 0.011 rad/s under CLIS-MPPI, corresponding to reductions by factors of approximately 5.9 and 9.7, respectively.

2026-10-16.title: Vision-Guided Closed-Loop Autonomous Navigation of Light-Driven Janus Microbots
2026-10-16.authors: Kanhu Charan Andia , Harsh Prashant Katole , Parth Nitinkumar Bhosale , Hemant Kumar , Dhruv Pratap Singh
2026-10-16.abstract: Artificial microbots capable of precise and autonomous navigation could provide versatile platforms for microscale transport, manipulation, and task execution in complex environments. However, reliable navigation becomes increasingly challenging at the micrometre scale, particularly when the surrounding environment changes dynamically. Here, we develop a vision-guided closed-loop navigation framework for light-driven cube-shaped hematite/TiO2 Janus microbots with a characteristic size of approximately 3 {\mu}m. Real-time visual localization using a custom-trained YOLOv11 object-detection model is integrated with discretized waypoint-based magnetic steering to enable precise navigation along complex prescribed trajectories, with more than 90% of the measured trajectory deviations remaining below 6 {\mu}m across the tested path geometries. The framework further enables arbitrary user-defined free-hand trajectories and autonomous navigation through a physically confined maze. In dynamically changing environments, A* path planning enables real-time path replanning while avoiding multiple independently swimming 5 {\mu}m spherical Janus micromotors. Finally, the microbot selectively captures multiple cargo particles and autonomously transports and delivers them to a predefined location while simultaneously avoiding dynamic obstacles. These results establish an integrated platform combining programmable trajectory control, autonomous path planning, real-time environmental adaptation, and task execution within a single light-driven Janus microbot system.

2026-10-16.title: An Agentic Framework for Proactive Robots with Procedural Assistance Memory
2026-10-16.authors: Dohyun Lee , Minho Park , Jeonghoon Park , Dongyoon Hwang , Junha Hyung , Sungwon Hwang , Byungkun Lee , Jaegul Choo
2026-10-16.comment: Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-16.abstract:
Proactive robots should anticipate user needs and provide assistance before being explicitly asked. A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance.
We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions.
Based on this, we propose a memory-based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor
reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation
to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task.
PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance
rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day’s
interaction trace without weight updates or retraining.
In our 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, memory-free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks.
Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest
precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds
on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5.
Our approach also adapts to changes in the user’s routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory–routine misalignment after a single memory update.
The project page is available at https://DAVIAN-Robotics.github.io/PAM .
2026-10-16.introduction:
A truly useful assistant in everyday life does not only respond to requests, but also anticipates when help would be valuable.
This may involve handing over an object at the right moment, putting away an item after it has been used, or preparing something that will be needed in the next step.
By contrast, robot assistants are still commonly evaluated as systems that execute explicit user commands [ 1 , 2 ] .
For robots to play the role of capable assistants in household, and home-office settings, they must move beyond waiting for instructions and learn to recognize when intervention would be helpful.
This has motivated growing interest in proactive robot assistance : robots that infer when help may be useful and act in advance of explicit commands.

One line of work in proactive robot assistance predicts task progress in structured sequential tasks [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . However, these approaches are largely confined to robots that perform a single task by following a fixed protocol (e.g., chair assembly), and are ill-suited to generalist robots tasked with open-ended housekeeping. Recently emerging generalist Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) [ 1 , 6 , 7 , 2 ] may appear to offer an alternative, but robotics datasets remain scarce across the diverse scenarios such settings demand. As a result, end-to-end models that map perception directly to action face clear limitations even when equipped with reasoning, and proactive tasks, where intent is often underspecified, have received little attention.
In response, recent work has adopted a System 1–2 design [ 8 ] that explicitly separates a high-level reasoning module from a VLA that executes atomic tasks [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] .
This separation simplifies learning, since the VLM decides when and what to help with while the VLA need only carry out the prescribed action. We adopt this structure, which in turn places the burden of proactivity squarely on the high-level VLM.

The central challenge, then, is accurately predicting human intention at the high level [ 13 ] , and recent approaches leverage pretrained, large-scale VLMs to do so in open-ended settings [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] .
Yet zero-shot prediction remains unreliable when the same observable behavior corresponds to different desired outcomes across users: one person setting out a mug wants coffee, another wants hot water for tea ( Figure 1 ).
A fixed, pretrained predictor cannot resolve such ambiguity, because the missing information is not in the scene but in the individual user’s habits.

Crucially, this missing information can be learned during deployment. In housekeeping settings, an individual’s behavior is highly repetitive, so even a handful of past interactions reveal stable preferences, and corrective feedback gathered once can be reused whenever a similar situation recurs. This suggests that a proactive robot should not treat each deployment as zero-shot, but should accumulate experience about its specific user over time. We therefore investigate a test-time learning approach for the high-level VLM, building a robot that personalizes quickly from few interactions, continues adapting after deployment, and carries user feedback forward into future behavior.

To this end, we introduce Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM), a continually updated deployment-time memory that records when assistance is needed and what assistive task should be issued for a particular user.
PAM structures this memory as a finite-state machine over the user’s activity, where states represent activity phases, transitions represent progress between phases, and per-state assistance entries store the assistive opportunities associated with each phase.
In our five-day scenario, the user repeatedly performs a daily activity; PAM is updated across these days so that the robot can provide increasingly appropriate assistance. Our contributions are threefold:

We propose a memory-based agentic framework for proactive robot assistance.
By conditioning the high-level VLM on user-specific routine context, it decides both when to assist and what task to issue without explicit user requests.

We propose a memory-based agentic framework for proactive robot assistance.
By conditioning the high-level VLM on user-specific routine context, it decides both when to assist and what task to issue without explicit user requests.

We propose Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM), a memory following a finite-state-machine structure with activity phases, transitions, and per-state assistance entries.
It uses user and activity context to reduce ambiguity in assistance needs.

We develop a self-evolving memory loop whose reflector revises PAM offline after each day using observed behavior and user feedback.
This enables the robot to learn the user’s routine, adapt to changes, and incorporate user feedback without retraining.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision-Language-Action Models

Robot manipulation has advanced through visuomotor imitation-learning policies [ 17 , 18 ] and generalist VLAs [ 1 , 7 , 2 , 6 ] , with subsequent work exploring chain-of-thought reasoning [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] , spatial grounding [ 22 , 23 ] , and world-model predictions [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] .
However, jointly optimizing action execution and high-level reasoning in a single network causes the two objectives to compete under limited robot data.
In response, recent work adopts a System 1–2 design [ 8 ] that explicitly separates a slow reasoning module from a fast action executor [ 12 , 10 , 11 , 9 , 6 ] . The reasoning module interprets the scene and reasons about how to solve the task, while the executor generates low-level actions for robot control conditioned on the high-level outputs. We build on this division of roles, using a VLM to predict proactive tasks and a VLA to execute the selected atomic skills.

## 2.2 Proactive Assistance in Embodied HRI

A prominent line of work on proactive robots studies assistance in structured sequential tasks, where the human activity is already organized into known subtasks.
In these settings, robots estimate task progress or subtask completion to provide help at the right moment [ 4 , 5 ] , such as handovers in assembly [ 3 ] or ingredient delivery in cooking [ 27 ] .
This direction is especially effective when the task sequence, progress measure, and assistance opportunities are known in advance.
Another line of work models object usage patterns in daily environments to anticipate future assistance needs [ 28 , 29 , 30 ] .
These methods move beyond single structured tasks, but they typically require substantial interaction logs or curated observations for training, limiting their flexibility across diverse everyday routines and rapidly changing user behavior.

With the recent progress of foundation models, proactive assistance has begun to move toward more general intent inference.
Some systems rely on non-verbal cues such as visual scene changes [ 14 ] , human-object interactions [ 31 , 32 ] , or gaze [ 33 , 34 ] to infer assistive intent, while others draw on verbal cues such as indirect instructions [ 16 ] , speech [ 15 ] , or dialogue [ 35 , 36 ] .
However, intent inference from momentary cues alone remains ambiguous: the same cue can imply different assistance needs depending on the user, context, and activity history.
We address this by conditioning the proactive decision on a user-specific memory accumulated across days, so that assistance is grounded not only in the current cue but also in how this user has typically acted and been assisted.

## 2.3 Evolving Memory for Test-Time Adaptation

Recent LLM-agent systems use external memory to support test-time adaptation without weight updates, allowing an agent to accumulate and reuse experience across episodes.
These works span verbal self-reflection [ 37 ] , reusable skill libraries [ 38 ] , workflow or experience extraction [ 39 , 40 ] , and long-term memory [ 41 , 42 ] .
However, their memories are generally designed for text-centric agents, games, or instruction-following tasks, rather than for deciding when a robot should proactively assist during an evolving human activity.
PAM organizes assistive opportunities into activity phases, per-state assistance entries, and transitions, preserving the context in which each opportunity arises. The task predictor uses this context to decide when assistance is needed and what assistive task should be issued given the user’s current activity and learned routine.

2026-10-16.title: LIN-SLAM: Lightweight LiDAR--Inertial Neural SLAM for Real-Time Onboard Navigation
2026-10-16.authors: Shiqi Che , Yijie Liu , Shuo Wang , Wenxin Liu
2026-10-16.comment: submitted to Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
2026-10-16.abstract:
Geometric light detection and ranging (LiDAR)–inertial simultaneous
localization and mapping (SLAM) provides efficient state estimation but lacks the continuous map representation and global
refinement capabilities of neural implicit SLAM, while neural implicit methods remain computationally expensive. We propose Lightweight LiDAR–Inertial Neural SLAM (LIN-SLAM), a hybrid method that couples
high-rate geometric LiDAR–inertial estimation with neural implicit
tracking, continual mapping, and global refinement for accurate real-time
onboard SLAM. Experiments on twelve representative sequences from three datasets spanning 32-, 64-, and 128-channel LiDAR configurations show that LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest overall mean absolute trajectory error (ATE) among the evaluated state-of-the-art geometric and neural implicit methods, while substantially reducing runtime compared with existing neural implicit SLAM methods. On a Unitree Go2 equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and a 16-channel LiDAR, LIN-SLAM sustains real-time localization and neural mapping over a 1.47-km indoor trajectory through challenging repetitive corridor environments, with an endpoint closure error of only 0.141 m.
To the best of our knowledge, LIN-SLAM is the first LiDAR–inertial SLAM system with a neural implicit backend to achieve real-time online operation on a mobile robotic platform while maintaining state-of-the-art localization accuracy. The code will be released upon acceptance.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Mobile robots require real-time state estimation and globally
consistent mapping within limited onboard computational and memory
budgets.
Geometric LiDAR–inertial odometry (LIO)
provides efficient local
motion estimation through point registration and inertial
fusion [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . However, its local motion
constraints provide limited correction of accumulated drift and
inconsistencies across revisited locations, motivating map-level
refinement.
Neural implicit SLAM integrates
continuous surface representations with
map-based tracking, continual reconstruction, and global map
refinement [ 4 , 5 ] . However, these capabilities
require repeated signed distance field (SDF) queries, gradient
evaluation, and online optimization, introducing substantial computational
and memory overhead. Sustaining this workload alongside responsive
state estimation is particularly challenging on resource-constrained
onboard platforms. Achieving the accuracy and map consistency of
neural implicit SLAM while maintaining low computational cost within
onboard resource constraints therefore remains an open challenge.

We present LIN-SLAM, a hybrid framework that combines the best of both worlds: the computational efficiency of traditional geometric methods with the map consistency and high accuracy of neural implicit approaches.
LIN-SLAM consists of three complementary components.
The geometric frontend provides responsive motion estimates and
posterior-consistent scans. The keyframe interface transfers geometry,
motion, and uncertainty to the neural implicit backend. The neural implicit backend refines
poses, continually learns a continuous map, and maintains global
consistency, while asynchronous operation supports real-time
onboard execution.

The geometric frontend further improves neural implicit tracking and
mapping by providing posterior-conditioned geometry, relative motion,
and uncertainty. These outputs provide better-aligned observations and
reliable initialization for the neural implicit backend, reducing
trajectory estimation error and improving map reconstruction quality.
In return, the accepted global map revisions correct the high-rate frontend tracking through the map-to-odometry transform without interrupting the local estimator.
We evaluate our hybrid framework on twelve public sequences from Newer College Stereo-Cam, Newer College Multi-Cam, and M2DGR, spanning 32-, 64-, and 128-channel LiDAR configurations. The results show that LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest overall mean ATE among all evaluated geometric and neural implicit methods.

We further optimize our hybrid approach for computational efficiency, enabling real-time performance on resource-constrained edge computing platforms.
We successfully deploy LIN-SLAM on a Unitree Go2 equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and a Hesai 16-channel LiDAR, demonstrating real-time localization and neural mapping over kilometer-scale trajectories in challenging indoor environments with low endpoint closure error. In contrast, the evaluated geometric baselines accumulate substantial drift or diverge on the challenging onboard trajectories, while the evaluated neural implicit baselines cannot execute the complete SLAM pipeline under the same onboard resource constraints. To the best of our knowledge, LIN-SLAM is the first LiDAR–inertial SLAM system with a neural implicit backend to achieve real-time online operation on a resource-constrained mobile robotic
platform.

Our contributions are threefold:

A hybrid framework for LiDAR–inertial neural implicit SLAM. We integrate high-rate geometric LiDAR–inertial estimation with neural
tracking, mapping, and global refinement through bidirectional
frontend–backend information exchange. LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest
overall mean ATE across the evaluated public sequences and endpoint closure errors below 0.15 m over two real-time onboard trajectories.

A hybrid framework for LiDAR–inertial neural implicit SLAM. We integrate high-rate geometric LiDAR–inertial estimation with neural
tracking, mapping, and global refinement through bidirectional
frontend–backend information exchange. LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest
overall mean ATE across the evaluated public sequences and endpoint closure errors below 0.15 m over two real-time onboard trajectories.

Lightweight optimization for real-time onboard deployment. We decouple geometric estimation and neural implicit processing into asynchronous threads to preserve estimation accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. Selective neural-backend processing together with an optimized implementation in C++ and CUDA substantially reduces complete-system processing cost, enabling real-time onboard operation.

An open-source implementation of LIN-SLAM. We will release LIN-SLAM as open-source software to facilitate reproducibility, real-world deployment, and further research on lightweight neural implicit SLAM.

# II RELATED WORK

LiDAR–inertial odometry has progressively moved toward tightly coupled estimation with higher update bandwidth
and more accurate motion compensation. FAST-LIO [ 6 ] formulates LiDAR–inertial fusion within an iterated Kalman-filter
framework, where geometric LiDAR observations update the inertially propagated state, while FAST-LIO2 [ 1 ] further removes
explicit geometric feature extraction and directly registers raw LiDAR measurements to an incrementally maintained
map, providing an efficient tightly coupled formulation applicable to different LiDAR scanning patterns.
Point-LIO pushes the estimation bandwidth further through point-wise state updates at the actual
sampling time of each LiDAR measurement, thereby avoiding accumulation and providing high-frequency
odometry under aggressive motion [ 7 ] . Together, these methods establish tightly
coupled geometric LiDAR–inertial filtering as an effective basis for high-bandwidth state estimation.

Another line of work focuses on the temporal structure and motion distortion within LiDAR scans.
DLIO constructs analytical continuous-time trajectories for point-wise motion correction and combines
them with direct scan-to-map registration, targeting accurate yet lightweight odometry under aggressive
motion [ 8 ] . SLICT similarly models the LiDAR–inertial trajectory in continuous time and
employs surfel-based registration to exploit geometric constraints throughout the scan acquisition
interval [ 9 ] . For spinning LiDARs, LLOL reduces sensing latency by processing partial
sweeps as a continuous stream instead of waiting for complete physical revolutions [ 2 ] .
Its local trajectory is repeatedly propagated during iterative registration, enabling pose updates at
rates substantially higher than the LiDAR revolution frequency. These approaches demonstrate
the benefits of high-rate estimation, continuous-time motion modeling, and partial-sweep processing
for reducing the latency and motion distortion inherent in frame-based LiDAR estimation.

More recently, neural implicit representations have been introduced into LiDAR SLAM to provide continuous geometric modeling while improving odometry and map consistency.
SHINE-Mapping [ 10 ] demonstrates large-scale incremental reconstruction with sparse implicit features, while NeRF-LOAM [ 11 ] extends neural SDFs to joint LiDAR odometry and mapping.
PIN-SLAM further develops a unified point-based implicit representation for correspondence-free tracking, continual mapping, loop detection, pose-graph optimization, and map deformation [ 4 ] . Its elastic neural map enables globally consistent dense reconstruction and accurate tracking. NDF-SLAM [ 12 ] and S 2 KAN-SLAM [ 13 ] use neural distance fields and SDF submaps, respectively. However, these methods primarily operate on LiDAR measurements alone, and typically rely on discrete GPU computation, posing challenges for real-time deployment on resource-constrained onboard platforms.

Neural implicit SLAM has also been extended to incorporate inertial measurements for more robust state estimation. CLID-SLAM tightly couples neural SDF representations with LiDAR–inertial estimation by introducing neural-SDF observations into an iterated error-state Kalman filter (IESKF) and employing region-specific supervision for geometric modeling [ 5 ] . While such tight coupling improves the integration of neural mapping and motion estimation, neural-field evaluation is directly involved in the measurement update, introducing additional computational overhead into the estimation pipeline. Moreover, its evaluation focuses on workstation-class discrete-GPU platforms, leaving real-time deployment on resource-constrained onboard hardware largely unexplored.

2026-10-16.title: Evo-DexBench: Benchmarking Generalization across Related Tasks for Dexterous Manipulation
2026-10-16.authors: Bing Cheng , Yiran Mao , Zewei Ye , Yifan Jin , Xinyi Chen , Ruifeng Tu , Shuhuai Wang , Tao Lin , Zhimu Zhou , Yuxin Du , Fangwei Zhong , Junchi Yan , Bo Zhao
2026-10-16.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-16.introduction:
General dexterous manipulation requires policies to learn shared manipulation patterns from existing tasks and transfer functional interactions to new tasks with only a few demonstrations [ 9 , 27 ] . Recent progress in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [ 20 , 16 , 43 , 38 ] and World Action Models (WAMs) [ 36 , 11 , 13 ] makes it possible to learn reusable functional interactions from multi-task demonstrations. Many tasks use different objects and scenes but share the same functional interaction. For example, turning a knob, opening a bottle cap, and twisting a tool all require a stable grasp and proper contact. Success should not come from memorizing specific objects, trajectories, or instructions. Instead, a policy should learn reusable object-use behaviors.

A key test of general dexterous manipulation is whether a policy can transfer interaction knowledge from related tasks to new ones, yet existing evaluations struggle to measure this ability. Dexterous hands have many degrees of freedom and require coordinated finger movements. Task success therefore depends not only on the end-effector trajectory, but also on finger configurations and contact relationships [ 42 , 30 ] . When the target object changes, the policy must preserve the functional interaction requirements while adapting its finger and arm motions. Collecting many demonstrations for every new task is costly. Transferring interaction knowledge from related tasks is therefore essential for scaling to a broader range of everyday manipulation skills [ 1 , 12 ] . However, current evaluations [ 14 , 35 ] often make this ability difficult to assess: Too many target-task demonstrations may allow a model to rely on task memorization. If the source and target tasks differ too much, it is difficult to determine whether performance differences result from functional interaction transfer or other factors.

To address these issues, we propose Evo-DexBench, a benchmark for evaluating generalization across related tasks, in addition to robustness to scene variations. Given source tasks that share functional interaction requirements with a target task, Evo-DexBench changes the object instances and scene conditions and gives the policy only a few target demonstrations. By controlling how much the target task is directly exposed, we test whether the policy learns reusable knowledge from related source tasks and whether experience with more related tasks leads to better performance.

Our contributions can be summarized as:

We introduce Evo-DexBench, which evaluates the generalization of dexterous policies across related tasks. It follows the Core-Gen design principle: each evaluation unit is a core-task-set–gen-task pair with shared functional interaction. We provide only a few target demonstrations and measure how well a policy transfers interaction knowledge to new tasks.

We build an integrated simulation environment and a VR teleoperation data collection pipeline. For each task, we create three everyday scenes. We also equip simulated Shadow Hands with 123 taxels per hand and collect 1,248 multimodal demonstrations. These resources provide the data needed for evaluation.

We systematically evaluate representative models on Evo-DexBench. We compare few-shot adaptation strategies, Core sources of different relatedness and breadth, and the effect of tactile input. The best mean success rate is only 38.5%, and functionally matched Core data tends to yield larger gains than mismatched data. These results show that current methods still struggle to extract and reuse functional interaction knowledge.

2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Existing manipulation benchmarks mainly assess generalization to unseen environments [ 17 , 41 , 5 ] . Others evaluate policies on held-out tasks, such as the ML10/ML45 splits of Meta-World [ 37 ] and the ML4 split of Bi-DexHands [ 6 ] , or on knowledge-partitioned
task suites in LIBERO [ 14 ] . However, these splits are defined by task identity rather than by shared functional interaction, leaving source–target relatedness uncontrolled. These methods then adapt to the target either from rewards alone via meta-reinforcement learning or from abundant demonstrations (50 per task in LIBERO). Where2Act [ 18 ] and VAT-Mart [ 32 ] learn reusable interaction structures, but only for individual articulated objects.

Table 1 shows that benchmarks for dexterous manipulation cover functional grasping, manipulation of unseen objects and bimanual coordination [ 3 , 8 ] . DexCraft [ 39 ] scales grasp pretraining toward tool-oriented manipulation; DexJoCo [ 30 ] targets task-oriented functional manipulation; and DexVerse [ 35 ] emphasizes multi-task, multi-embodiment operation. These efforts extend evaluation beyond single-step grasping, but they typically ask whether a policy can complete predefined tasks, rather than whether contact-level interaction knowledge transfers across tasks.

Prior work has advanced vision-based dexterous manipulation and generalization to unseen objects and scenes [ 25 , 2 , 21 , 34 , 28 , 22 , 15 ] ,
while other studies have scaled up human demonstration data and incorporated tactile information [ 23 , 29 , 40 ] . More recent models such as DexVLA [ 31 ] , DexGraspVLA [ 44 ] , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 10 ] seek behavior priors across tasks, objects, and embodiments. Despite this progress toward reusable knowledge, most benchmarks still mainly measure task success and do not systematically control source–target task relatedness. They therefore struggle to distinguish transferable interaction knowledge from target-task memorization. Evo-DexBench addresses this gap by evaluating transfer from multiple related source tasks to a new target task with only a few demonstrations.
