2026-10-16.title: When to Ask for Help: A Decision-Theoretic Account and Measurement Standard for Slow-Module Scheduling in Dual-System Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-16.authors: Shilin Zhang (North China University of Technology)
2026-10-16.abstract:
Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency
fast policy with a slow, more expensive module, and differ both in how the module intervenes (latent refreshing, value-guided
resampling, action-suffix reuse) and in when it is invoked.
The invocation question has just begun to be mechanized by trigger
mechanisms, but these come with no shared objective, no measured
costs, and no evaluation standard that separates schedule quality
from slow-module quality. We provide the missing account. We
formalize invocation as a calibrated decision problem under a query
budget, show that fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated
scheduling are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of
Intervention (VoI), and prove a renewal baseline that locates the
economics: under state-independent collapse the optimal schedule is
periodic, and the gain of any adaptive trigger is governed by the
cost ratio ρ = c slow / c fast \rho=c_{\text{slow}}/c_{\text{fast}} and the temporal
dispersion of collapse. Published systems span an order of magnitude
on ρ \rho ; measuring FiS-VLA on one RTX 4090
places it at the low end, one slow refresh costing 52 52 ms, about
one fast action ( 55 55 ms) or 3.8 3.8 denoising steps, which explains
why its hand-tuned 1 : 4 1{:}4 cadence is reasonable and bounds what any
trigger can gain there. A direct test confirms the prediction: on a
controlled testbed the calibrated advantage over the fixed cadence
vanishes under homogeneous collapse and grows monotonically with
collapse heterogeneity. A calibrated router instantiates the account:
on a synthetic testbed with matched budgets it Pareto-dominates all
three baseline families ( 0.825 ± 0.002 0.825\pm 0.002 vs. 0.762 ± 0.002 0.762\pm 0.002 success
at a 0.25 0.25 query rate), and we characterize its boundary, not only
its wins: the advantage is insensitive to estimator variance but
vanishes once the estimator loses validity on most steps, the
requirement any trigger mechanism must meet to pay. Finally, we
contribute a four-measure protocol with an explicit leak-free rule;
on 929 deployment traces from RoboICL the rule is load-bearing,
cutting the apparent early-warning AUC of schedule statistics from 0.93 0.93 post hoc to 0.62 0.62 ( p = 0.010 p=0.010 ), and failure attribution
reverses across task categories, so no single fixed ratio can exploit
the signal. A detection-limited frontier theorem converts such
early-warning AUC into a schedulability statement: rescoring 33,443 33{,}443 RoboICL decision points leak-free, a threshold router
reaches the deployed reuse gate’s 33 33 – 48 % 48\% call-reduction regime
at an explicit missed-failure price, and the release’s reported API
costs anchor the continuum’s high-asymmetry end at ρ ≈ 10 3 \rho\approx 10^{3} , three orders of magnitude above FiS. We close the loop on
the released system itself:
fine-tuning FiS-VLA on RLBench, we measure the freshness value
function of the slow latent directly and find it nonpositive over
ages up to eight fast steps while amortized latency falls 2.1 × 2.1\times ; the latent drifts with the δ \sqrt{\delta} law of a
Wiener process, yet the action map is locally insensitive to it; and
a negative closed-loop result, realized under two fine-tuning
regimes, isolates the failure mechanism and yields a
competence-conditioned criterion for when success-level scheduling
comparisons are informative at all. A compilation loop completes the
account: on controlled task families the per-task period compiled
from the measured value function tracks the closed-loop oracle
within 2.4 % 2.4\% , and the released checkpoint compiles to the boundary
its nonpositive value function dictates. Closed-loop arms on LIBERO
instantiate the account where the economics are contested
( ρ = 1.53 \rho=1.53 ): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly
as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel
cannot convert them into success on either of two task suites,
while a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only
intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and
LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to
forty-two points. Together these results turn slow-module
invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) systems increasingly adopt a dual-system
architecture: a fast policy executes at control frequency, while a
slower, more expensive module intervenes occasionally to correct or
re-plan. This pattern appears in trained systems, where the slow layer
is a large VLM conditioned on the fast policy’s latents
(Fast-in-Slow ( Chen et al., 2025 ) ) or performs value-guided best-of- N N resampling (Hume ( Song et al., 2025 ) ), and in zero-training systems built
on frozen LLMs, where a gate decides when to reuse predicted action
suffixes (RoboICL ( Liu et al., 2026 ) ).

These systems differ in how the slow module acts. Our starting
observation is that they also differ in when it acts, and that
this second choice has just begun to be mechanized: OneTwoVLA learns a
decision token that toggles between reasoning and acting; the
concurrent TUD trigger invokes the generalist on high predictive
uncertainty ( Yang et al., 2026 ) ; System Switch
defers to a reasoning model on low
confidence ( Bailo, 2026 ) . What these mechanisms lack
is an account of the problem they solve: no shared objective, no
measured costs, no evaluation standard that separates schedule
quality from slow-module quality, and no prediction for when
adaptivity beats a hand-tuned fixed ratio at all.

We give that account
(Figure 1 ). We model slow-module invocation as a
calibrated decision problem under a query budget; show that existing
fixed schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value
of Intervention (VoI); and locate the economics of the problem on a cost-asymmetry continuum ρ = c slow / c fast \rho=c_{\text{slow}}/c_{\text{fast}} that spans three orders of magnitude across published systems and
that we measure at both ends ( ρ = 0.95 \rho=0.95 on FiS-VLA hardware, ∼ 10 3 {\sim}10^{3} from the RoboICL deployment’s reported API costs). This
yields four contributions.

A decision-theoretic account with a cost baseline. We
define VoI as the expected quality gap between the slow-corrected and
fast-only actions, weighted by the probability that the fast policy
collapses in state s s (Section 3 ). Fixed-ratio,
fixed-budget, and history-gated scheduling are degenerate cases of VoI
routing (Propositions 1 – 3 ). A renewal
baseline (Proposition 4 ) then locates the regimes:
under state-independent collapse the optimal schedule is periodic with

ratios are hard to beat at low ρ \rho and low collapse heterogeneity,
while adaptivity pays as either grows. This explains why hand-tuned
cadences are reasonable on embedded-latent systems and why triggered
invocation concentrates on separate-VLM systems.

cadences are reasonable on embedded-latent systems and why triggered
invocation concentrates on separate-VLM systems.

A calibrated router with its boundary characterized. A
lightweight router estimates VoI online and queries the slow module
only when the estimate exceeds the query cost. We characterize where
this construction breaks, not only where it works: the advantage is
insensitive to estimator variance but vanishes when the estimator
loses validity on most steps, which is the requirement any trigger
mechanism must meet to pay (Sections 5.2 – 5.3 ).

A leak-free measurement standard. We contribute
staleness curves, routing frontiers, failure attribution, and
calibration reliability as a four-measure battery for slow-query
policies (Section 4 ), with an explicit leak-free
rule. On 929 deployment traces from the RoboICL release the rule is not decoration:
the same features reach AUC 0.93 0.93 post hoc but 0.62 0.62 ( p = 0.010 p=0.010 )
leak-free, so without it the early-warning capability of schedule
statistics would be overstated by roughly 1.5 × 1.5\times . The traces
also fix the precision of frontier claims themselves: skip decisions
cluster by episode at design effects of 8 8 – 18 18 , so a frontier
estimate over 16,000 16{,}000 decision points carries the information of
about one thousand episodes
(Proposition 8 ).

Schedule compilation. The measured quantities are not
only diagnostic. A renewal compiler turns a task’s measured staleness
value function into a per-task refresh period; on controlled task
families the compiled period tracks the closed-loop oracle at a cost
gap of at most 2.4 % 2.4\% , the compilation is a sample-average
approximation whose optimality gap admits a statistical
certificate ( Mak et al., 1999 ) , and the underlying trade-off inherits
the cost flatness of the Harris–Wilson order-quantity
problem ( Harris, 1913 ) , so moderate cost-estimate errors degrade
the achieved schedule only at second order; and the validation
budget itself has an optimal allocation, concentrated on the
near-ties of the cost bowl, which roughly doubles the probability
of recovering the oracle period at a fixed budget
(Remark 4 ). On the FiS backbone the
compiler sends every task to the boundary its measured (nonpositive)
value function dictates (Section 5.9 ). Adaptive
triggers, fixed periods, and compiled schedules become commensurable
as different amounts of measurement invested in the same cost
functional.

On a synthetic testbed with matched query budgets, calibrated routing
dominates the Pareto frontier of the fixed-ratio, always-query, and
reuse-gate baselines
(Section 5.1 ). On real systems, we apply the
protocol to all 929 deployment traces released by RoboICL
(Section 5.4 ): failed episodes query the slow module 25 % 25\% less densely and run with greater staleness, and the effect is
category-dependent, so no single fixed ratio can exploit it. On
hardware we instantiate the cost side of the continuum with
FiS-VLA: one slow refresh costs 52 52 ms, about one fast action
( 55 55 ms), or 3.8 3.8 denoising steps, on a single RTX 4090
(Section 5.6 ), placing embedded-latent dual
systems at the ρ ≈ 1 \rho\approx 1 end, opposite the separate-VLM
systems at ρ \rho of 10 10 – 20 20 that trigger-based invocation
targets, and the frozen-LLM API systems at ρ ≈ 10 3 \rho\approx 10^{3} measured from the same release’s reported costs
(Section 5.5 ): three orders of magnitude with both
ends anchored on hardware measurement or audited cost reports
(Table 5 ). A closed-loop dual system placed at the
continuum’s middle ( ρ = 1.53 \rho=1.53 : OpenVLA-7B as the fast policy and
Qwen2.5-VL-7B as the slow module on LIBERO-Spatial) then tests the
account where the economics are contested. Fourteen closed-loop arms
at matched seeds, initial states and budgets, eleven on LIBERO-Spatial
and a three-arm replication on LIBERO-Goal with an LLM slow endpoint,
sweep the two layers the
account separates: the adaptive trigger allocates its queries
exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet a subgoal-rewrite
channel cannot convert them into success, and neither can the
screened, faster or slower variants of that channel, whose pooled
rate sits at 43 % 43\% against fast-only’s 58 % 58\% with no dose axis in
sight. The failure is the channel’s, not the schedule’s: replacing
the language channel with action ranking, or adding an actuator that
undoes an unhelpful rewrite, changes the outcome’s risk profile
rather than its mean, and the revert arm produces the table’s only
direction-consistent positive contrast ( 15 15 vs. 4 4 discordant
pairs, nominal p = 0.019 p=0.019 , null under family correction), landing
on exactly the tasks the risk coordinate predicts. The cross-suite
replication keeps the ordering: the rewrite channel’s deficit
deepens to 42 42 points on the second suite while the revert arm
tracks fast-only exactly ( 48 / 100 48/100 against 48 / 100 48/100 ). The operating
point is thus a boundary case in which the deployment, not the
module, sets the value of asking
(Section 5.10 ).

This is a methodology contribution: a decision-theoretic account, a
constructive router with characterized boundaries, and a measurement
standard. Third-party systems enter only as measurement subjects:
they anchor the continuum’s two ends and stress-test the standard;
no contribution depends on their internals or on access beyond
public artifacts. The account’s low- ρ \rho prediction is tested directly: on
the testbed, the calibrated advantage vanishes under homogeneous
collapse and grows monotonically with collapse heterogeneity, exactly
as the renewal baseline predicts
(Section 5.7 ). Fine-tuning the open checkpoint
on four consumer GPUs and measuring its staleness frontier directly
confirms the prediction’s transfer to the deployed FiS system
(Section 5.8 ).
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work: Three Families, One Design Space

We group dual-system VLA work by the mechanism that connects the fast
policy to the slow module, and summarize the comparison in
Table 1 .

Fast-in-Slow ( Chen et al., 2025 ) trains a single 7B backbone whose slow
path conditions the fast path through latents refreshed every k k steps; the ratio 1 : 4 1{:}4 is selected by ablation over 1 : 1 1{:}1 to 1 : 8 1{:}8 . The schedule is fixed at deployment regardless of task
difficulty. We emphasize a nuance for later comparisons: the slow
layer here is a refresh cadence on a latent condition, not an
independent low-frequency process; the reported 21.9 21.9 Hz control
rate is the whole system, and the effective slow refresh tick is 21.9 / 4 ≈ 5.5 21.9/4\approx 5.5 Hz.

Hume ( Song et al., 2025 ) pairs a VLM System-2 ( 4 4 Hz) with a lightweight
diffusion System-1 ( 90 90 Hz) and samples N N action candidates,
selecting by a Cal-QL-trained value head. The schedule question
becomes the budget N N , which is fixed. The value head is the closest
published antecedent of our calibration measure, but it is trained per
system and used for selection, not for deciding whether to
consult the slow module at all.

RoboICL ( Liu et al., 2026 ) shows that a frozen LLM can act as a robot
policy via typed in-context programs. Its Jev gate suppresses
redundant LLM calls by reusing predicted action suffixes, cutting
calls by 33 33 – 48 % 48\% . Two facts from the source matter here. First,
the main benchmarks run without the Jev gate; it is an
auxiliary study. Second, the gate is history-based and its task
success is uneven (it degrades some benchmarks), which we analyze as a
missing-calibration failure mode.

While this paper was in preparation, the scheduling question has begun
to be mechanized. OneTwoVLA learns a decision token that toggles the
system between reasoning and acting modes, at the cost of manually
annotated phase boundaries ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . The concurrent TUD
trigger measures the cross-step dispersion of the specialist’s action
re-predictions under the cached generalist context and invokes the
generalist when dispersion crosses a threshold, reporting higher
success at matched call budgets and a 75 % 75\% call reduction on a real
robot ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . System Switch defers decisions from a fast
actor to a reasoning VLM on low confidence and shows the gain tracks
the actor’s calibration quality ( Bailo, 2026 ) . These
mechanisms are complementary to our contribution rather than
competing with it: each is a particular estimator of the
collapse-probability factor of VoI, deployed at the high-asymmetry
end of the continuum (separate VLM generalists), and none reports the
measured query costs, the collapse heterogeneity, or the leak-free
evaluation that determine whether a trigger can pay
(Section 3.4 ).

The scheduling question we pose has a classical upstream in the
age-of-information and remote-estimation literature: a monitor must
decide when to pay for a fresh sample of a drifting
signal ( Yates and Kaul, 2019 ; Yates et al., 2021 ) . Sun, Polyanskiy, and
Uysal prove that the optimal sampling policy for a Wiener process under
a sampling-rate constraint is a threshold rule whose period scales with
the square root of the cost-to-drift ratio ( Sun et al., 2020 ) , and ( Sun et al., 2017 ) shows the same trade-off in the
generate-at-will model, where eager sampling can be strictly worse
than waiting. These results are derived for scalar signals and
communication channels; none has been applied to embodied systems,
where the signal is a learned latent, the cost is wall-clock latency of
a 7B model, and the consumer is a diffusion policy. Our contribution
relative to this literature is transport and measurement:
Proposition 4 is the Bernoulli-collapse instance of
the same family, and Section 5.8 measures both
factors of the threshold rule, query cost and latent drift, on the
FiS-VLA system rather than assuming them.

Web-caching theory is a third upstream that prices the same object:
a TTL-based cache holds a stale copy and pays an age-dependent miss
penalty, the cache-side instance of the freshness value V V ; Cohen
and Kaplan quantify how miss rates depend on the age of cached
copies ( Cohen and Kaplan, 2001 ; Cohen et al., 2005 ) . What the caching and
status-update literatures leave open, and what the continuum
addresses, is the regime where the refresh is not a disk read but a
multi-second VLM call, three orders of magnitude past the cost
asymmetries those literatures were built for.

Adaptive computation in language models reduces cost within a single
model by early exiting ( Teerapittayanon et al., 2016 ) , adaptive
depth ( Elbayad et al., 2020 ) , or token
pruning ( Kim et al., 2022 ) , while action
chunking ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) amortizes policy calls over predicted
horizons. These address budget questions inside one model; our
question is the budget for consulting a separate slow module inside a dual-system VLA. Calibrated confidence
estimation ( Guo et al., 2017 ) underpins our collapse estimator,
and offline RL value heads ( Nakamoto et al., 2023 ) are the closest
published antecedent of the calibration signal we rely on, though they
are trained for selection rather than for scheduling. Prior and
concurrent work thus supplies trigger mechanisms ; none supplies
the decision-theoretic account that subsumes the fixed schedules these
mechanisms improve on, the measured cost economics that decides
whether any mechanism can pay, or a leak-free standard for comparing
them across system families. That account and standard are what we
contribute.

2026-10-16.title: KODA: Kinematics--Observation Data Alignment for Humanoid Learning from Human Egocentric Demonstration
2026-10-16.authors: Zibo Zhou , Yueru Chen , Junsong Wu , Weiji Xie , Qingyao Xu , Sheng Yin , Shiqing Wang , Jiyuan Shi , Siheng Chen , Chenjia Bai , Xuelong Li
2026-10-16.abstract:
Training humanoid whole-body vision–language–action (VLA) policies requires
costly robot demonstrations with aligned robot-view observations and
controller-compatible whole-body state–action labels. Egocentric human
demonstrations offer scalable supervision but have misaligned views and
sparse motion cues. Existing approaches either pretrain policies that still
require robot data for adaptation or generate controller-specific commands
that limit reuse. Conversion also requires robot-view observations aligned
with the generated whole-body motion. We present KODA
(Kinematics–Observation Data Alignment), which converts egocentric RGB
demonstrations into whole-body VLA training data using a reusable canonical
trajectory to guide robot-view synthesis and generate controller-specific
whole-body state–action supervision. KODA first generates a
simulator-checked whole-body trajectory using a sparse tracker with
sampling-based command optimization. This generated trajectory directly
determines the onboard camera poses used to synthesize corresponding
robot-view observations. The motion, observations, and task instruction form

2026-10-16.title: Manifold Generative Annealing for Contact Constraint-aware Impedance Control with Reinforcement Learning Prior
2026-10-16.authors: Zhilin He , Guoquan Qi , Changliu Liu
2026-10-16.abstract: Contact-rich robotic tasks require coordinated motion and impedance under uncertain interaction dynamics and physical constraints. While recent methods on learned policies provide useful interaction strategies, they may fail when contact conditions differ from those encountered during training. Model-based generative methods show promising receding-horizon trajectories optimization results, but often lack structured behavioral guidance and refinement that jointly accounts for constraint geometry and actual contact responses. To this end, we propose Manifold Generative Annealing ( MGA ) , a joint model-free and model-based generative framework for motion–impedance optimization. MGA first organizes pretrained reinforcement learning policies into structured sequence proposals, retaining task-specific interaction strategies without committing to their execution. It then evaluates these proposals alongside exploratory samples through model-based rollouts for refinement or separate execution selection. Crucially, realization-aware manifold refinement aligns updates from the refinement bank with both task constraints and locally achievable physical responses, allowing learned experience to guide online adaptation under changing contact conditions. Experiments cover surface scanning, peg insertion, and humanoid pushing, with improved safety success rate of impedance control under nominal and sensing-shift conditions. 2026-10-16.introduction:
Contact-rich tasks such as surface scanning, peg insertion, and whole-body pushing require robots to coordinate motion with compliant interaction while respecting physical constraints. Impedance learning and control provide an interface for regulating the relationship between motion and interaction forces ( Hogan, 1984 ; Buchli et al., 2011 ; Martín-Martín et al., 2019 ) . Selecting these commands remains challenging due to multimodal interaction behaviors, uncertain physical responses, and safety-critical execution, requiring their joint optimization to sustain task progress under changing contact conditions ( Abu-Dakka and Saveriano, 2020 ; Tsuji et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) .

Safe Reinforcement Learning (RL) combines learned task policies with stiffness adaptation, recovery mechanisms, or action safeguards ( Zhao et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) , providing behavioral structure for contact-rich decisions. Beyond individual policy outputs, the same learned experience can define distributions over candidate behaviors. Model-free diffusion planners provide this generative extension by representing multimodal trajectory distributions, while constrained variants incorporate model-based projections and primal–dual sampling to enforce deployment-time constraints ( Römer et al., 2025 ; Christopher et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Blanke et al., 2026 ) . These learned distributions can therefore supply task-informed candidates that reduce unguided search. However, they remain proposals rather than reliable plans because their relevance is inherited from the training distribution and may deteriorate as task or contact conditions change.

Model-Based Diffusion (MBD) ( Pan et al., 2024 ) offers a way to revise sequences through their predicted consequences: it casts trajectory generation as optimization using objective-weighted dynamics rollouts without a learned denoising score. Constrained extensions ( He et al., 2026b ; He et al., 2026a ) improve feasibility through Control Barrier Function (CBF) ( Ames et al., 2019 ) or Convex Feasible Set (CFS) ( Liu et al., 2018 ) with adaptive scheduling. Building on this trajectory-optimization view, DIAL-MPC brings diffusion-style annealing to short-horizon model predictive control for online refinement ( Xue et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . With a limited rollout budget, learned proposals can focus this search on useful contact strategies, and model-based evaluation can reassess them under current conditions. However, weighting promising candidates does not ensure that their combined sequence preserves nonlinear task relationships. Evaluation therefore leaves a second problem: how to correct the update it produces.

Constraint geometry provides local information for correcting such updates. ATACOM constructs safe actions in the tangent space of constraint manifolds ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , while geometry-aware generative optimization uses active constraints to shape refinement and exploration ( He et al., 2026c ) . Geometric impedance control further exploits SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) structure in learned variable-impedance policies for contact-rich manipulation ( Seo et al., 2023 ) . Under compliant contact, jamming, or switching, however, displacement commands may produce deformation or force, and stiffness changes the local response. Refinement must therefore account for measured tracking and contact responses when defining the task residual. Shaping the update can reduce the normal response it introduces, but residuals already present or left after a finite step require a further correction. These two operations connect model-based reassessment to continued contact execution.

We propose M anifold G enerative A nnealing ( MGA ), a short-horizon controller that organizes learned behavioral structure, model-based reassessment, and feedback-conditioned geometric correction in the same motion–impedance sequence space. Rollout weighting determines which candidates inform the update. Geometry shaping adjusts its direction. Local residual correction then revises the updated sequence. The proposal and evaluation stages supply task-informed candidates for refinement or separate execution selection. Our C ontributions are three-fold:

C1 : We organize model-free learned action policies into structured short-horizon motion–impedance proposals, supplying task-specific interaction behaviors alongside Gaussian exploration in a common sequence space.

C2: We integrate these candidates with model-based generative annealing (online optimization) through common closed-loop evaluation, reassessing their relevance under current task and contact conditions through bank weighting or separate expert selection.

C3: We develop realization-aware manifold refinement that adjusts update directions and corrects remaining task residuals. Contact feedback updates the task references, while response reliability controls the refinement strength. We analyze how the normalized core suppresses encoded normal responses and reduces local residuals.

Contact feedback updates the task references, while response reliability controls the refinement strength. 2026-10-16.title: Slip-Induced Fall Suppression During Cornering for a Remotely Operated Motorcycle with a Rear-Wheel-Swing Mechanism
2026-10-16.authors: Tadashi Sumioka , Kazushi Akimoto , Takuya Tsujimura , Sho Takayanagi , Kineo Tomura
2026-10-16.abstract: Slip-induced falls when riding motorcycles are difficult to avoid even for expert riders and represent a major cause of single-vehicle accidents. Despite their prevalence, no practical solution has yet been proposed to suppress this phenomenon. We previously introduced a motorcycle model applicable to systems with both front- and rear- wheel steering. In this paper, we extend that model and formulate the suppression of slip-induced falls as an optimization problem that distributes assistive control inputs according to vehicle speed and road surface conditions. To evaluate the proposed method, we developed a remotely operated motorcycle and conducted experiments under two scenarios: slalom driving on a low-friction surface at 5.5 m/s, and turning maneuvers on synthetic ice to simulate driving over manholes on rainy days. The results demonstrate that our approach successfully suppresses falls under these challenging conditions.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Motorcycles are attractive vehicles because they are small, highly maneuverable, and environmentally friendly.
However, when a motorcycle falls over, it can cause serious injury to the rider.
A lot of research has thus been conducted on the dynamic performance of motorcycles (e.g., [ 1 ] , [ 2 ] , [ 3 ] ), particularly on the suppression of falls.

The causes of motorcycle falls can be divided into two categories depending on the vehicle speed. When a motorcycle is stopped or moving at an extremely low speed,
falls are due to the fundamental lack of stability of motorcycles. Many methods have thus been developed to improve stability, such as those that add flywheels or movable axles (e.g., [ 4 ] , [ 5 ] , [ 6 ] , [ 7 ] , [ 8 ] ).
Although there are still issues to be addressed, such as the coordination between the rider and fall suppression control and implementation costs, progress has been made in terms of fall prevention.
When a motorcycle is moving at a normal speed, falls are often caused by a loss of traction.

Falls that occur at normal speeds can be further divided into falls that occur while going straight and falls that occur while turning.
Technologies for suppressing slippage and falls while going straight include an anti-lock
braking system [ 9 ] , which prevents the wheels from locking during braking, and a traction control system [ 10 ] , which prevents the rear wheels from spinning due to an excessive driving force.
These two technologies, which are used in many mass-produced motorcycles, detect the longitudinal slip ratio of each wheel and control the braking and driving force such that the slip ratio does not become excessive.
In contrast, there is little research on preventing motorcycle slips and falls while turning.
A slip and fall avoidance method developed by Bosch [ 11 ] uses gas injection to generate a restoring moment; however, this makes the method difficult to use in mixed traffic situations involving cars, motorcycles, and pedestrians.
The present study proposes an extension of a previously developed front- and rear-wheel steering control method [ 8 ] to achieve slip-induced fall suppression while preserving the fundamental characteristics of the motorcycle structure.

Considering rider safety, it is difficult to test a motorcycle in terms of slipping and falling while turning.
Furthermore, although tire–road interaction modeling has been investigated in works such as [ 2 ] , the behavior in limit conditions—e.g., rollover—does not match real vehicle dynamics, making simulation-based verification difficult.
To overcome the above problems, experiments can be conducted using a remotely operated motorcycle.
Riderless motorcycles have been investigated mostly using simulations; few studies have verified their effectiveness using actual vehicles (e.g., [ 12 ] – [ 16 ] ).
BMW [ 17 ] and Yamaha [ 18 ] have developed actual autonomous motorcycles, but neither has published a related study.
Miyagishi et al. [ 19 ] used an actual autonomous motorcycle in their study. Their stabilization control method outputs a front-wheel steering angle that makes the roll angle track the target roll angle, as done in self-driving bicycles [ 20 ] . However, there are no reports on the behavior when slippage occurs.

Although autonomous bicycles using gyroscopes—such as those described in [ 21 ] —have been proposed, this approach is not practical for slip‑induced rollover avoidance in motorcycles operating in normal speed ranges. This is because a significantly larger restoring roll moment is required, and the associated actuator output and power demand become impractically high.

In this study, we propose a method for suppressing slips and falls while turning and verify it using a remotely operable motorcycle, shown in Fig. 1 .

Based on a previously developed vehicle [ 8 ] , we propose an optimal front- and rear-wheel assist method that takes into account vehicle speed and the road surface friction coefficient for driving speeds that range from extremely low to 5.5 m/s while maintaining the divergent component of motion (DCM) feedback control, which is the best regulator in terms of stabilization.
In order to establish a fall‑prevention method safely, rider-on-board experiments are beyond our present scope. However, when a rider is on board, assist control is expected to require additional rider–machine cooperative control methods, as suggested in [ 8 ] . Therefore, future work will extend this approach toward systems capable of interacting with a rider.

2026-10-16.title: MoCaP: Mobile Code-as-Policies for Zero-Shot Mobile Manipulation from Passive Human Videos
2026-10-16.authors: Yiyang Cai , Tatsuya Kamijo , Ninghao Lu , Zijin Hu , Sherry Yang
2026-10-16.abstract:
Passive human videos of everyday activity offer robots access to a massive amount of human experience without requiring a demonstration for each task. However, using this experience requires recovering knowledge from unstructured video recordings and adapting it to a different body (i.e., the robot). To overcome these challenges, we present mobile code-as-policy (MoCaP), an agentic framework that turns passive human video recordings into guidance for an end-to-end mobile manipulation policy. MoCaP extracts spatial memory and cues of how people prepare to interact with objects, which inform navigation and the search for a manipulation-ready configuration. Guided by passive human experience and current observations, MoCaP uses a closed-loop code-as-policy to coordinate planning and tool use primitives to solve motions under the robot’s geometry and kinematic constraints.
On a real mobile manipulator, MoCaP achieves 80% success on each of two mobile manipulation tasks in an indoor environment whereas existing approaches cannot succeed at the task. Video-derived spatial memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, and human approach prior raises the rate of finding a reachable base pose from 0% to 100% at an unfavorable start location.
Videos and code are available on the project website .
2026-10-16.introduction:
Household robots should be able to assist different users in a wide range of homes, responding to everyday requests without requiring users to specify every action. Open-vocabulary mobile manipulation moves toward this goal by enabling robots to act on natural-language instructions involving diverse objects and environments [ 1 ] . To fulfill a request such as “bring the cup back,” a robot must determine which objects and places are relevant, locate them, and decide how to act. Supporting this ability across homes and users motivates learning from experience beyond the robot’s own interactions.

Passive recordings of human activity offer a potentially abundant source of such experience. Wearable cameras can capture how people interact with objects and their surroundings during everyday life, without requiring robot teleoperation or prescribed demonstrations [ 2 ] . We investigate how robots can draw on this accumulated human experience for open-vocabulary mobile manipulation. We consider the setting where a collection of human activity videos is passively recorded through people’s daily lives capturing diverse activities that may be requested of a robot. Rather than reproducing a particular demonstration, the robot must use relevant experience from the collection to guide its actions in its current environment.

However, passive recordings of egocentric human data do not directly provide the information a robot needs to act. Specifically, using passive human experience for robots presents three challenges.

First, the recorded experience lacks explicit spatial structure. A video supplies neither object coordinates nor labeled places and traversable connections. Relevant observations are distributed over time, with objects and regions reappearing from different viewpoints. Searching beyond the current view requires connecting objects to their spatial context.

Second, human and robot sensing and morphology differ. Camera height and viewing angle change the visible scene, while different cameras introduce further differences in intrinsics, field of view, resolution, and color response. These visual discrepancies complicate matching recorded experience to the robot’s current observations. Body dimensions, joint structure, and available motions also determine which actions can be executed: a person can turn sideways through a narrow passage or manipulate an object with a dexterous hand, whereas a mobile manipulator has a different footprint and gripper. Transferring experience therefore requires interpreting observations across cameras and viewpoints and grounding actions in the robot’s own geometry and kinematics.

Third, navigation and manipulation are not explicitly separated in human activity. People naturally adjust their approach and position as they get ready to interact, without marking when navigation ends and manipulation begins. For a robot, reaching the vicinity of an object does not ensure that it can manipulate it. The recording does not explicitly reveal which movements simply bring a person closer and which make the subsequent interaction possible.

To overcome these challenges, we present MoCaP , which turns passive human video into guidance for mobile navigation and manipulation (Fig. 1 ). MoCaP extracts spatial memory about a place together with records of where people stood when they reached for objects. During task execution, the spatial memory helps locate the requested object, and the human approach prior guides the robot to approach the object in the right way. A code agent uses this guidance together with current observations to coordinate navigation and manipulation primitives. The primitives solve and check motions for the robot’s embodiment, returning execution feedback that lets the agent revise subsequent actions.

Our contributions are:

A unified Code-as-Policy system for mobile manipulation. MoCaP flexibly coordinates navigation and manipulation through executable code, without a predefined division into navigation and manipulation stages. The agent selects and revises actions using prior human experience, live observations, and feedback from robot-grounded primitives.

Reusable spatial memory from passive human video. We develop a fine-grained spatial memory pipeline that draws on the abundance of everyday human activity recordings to extract object relations, landmarks, and place connectivity for subsequent robot search and navigation. This video is task-independent and can be reused to different tasks.

Human-guided base placement for manipulation. We infer the direction to approach object from how a person positioned themselves before manipulation in passive human videos, then search nearby base poses under the robot’s own reachability and collision constraints. A poor arrival side can leave no feasible pose within reach of local adjustment, and this guidance is designed to turn such arrivals into graspable configurations, using only video that accumulates from everyday activity.

We evaluate MoCaP on a real mobile manipulator in an indoor environment through an object-navigation task and two mobile manipulation tasks. MoCaP achieves 80% success on each manipulation task, whereas existing methods [ 3 ] cannot succeed at the task. To examine the contributions of video-derived guidance, we separately evaluate spatial memory for object search and human approach priors for base placement. Spatial memory increases navigation success from 70% to 100%, while controlled comparisons suggest that human approach priors improve manipulation readiness from unfavorable initial base configurations.
Base placement guided by the human prior found a reachable pose in 5 of 5 trials whereas a naive proximity-based docking failed in all five.
Together, these results suggest that passive human video can help robots complete mobile manipulation tasks by guiding both object search and the approach to manipulation.

The agent selects and revises actions using prior human experience, live observations, and feedback from robot-grounded primitives.

# II Related Work

## II-A Human Video as Scene and Interaction Experience

Using past observations to guide future action is a central motivation for persistent scene representations. Spatial-semantic maps and scene graphs associate objects with locations, appearance, and spatial relations, supporting queries and planning beyond the robot’s current
view [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . More recently, recorded video has provided another source of scene experience: relational video memories support later scene questions [ 7 ] , while tour-conditioned navigation retrieves goal views for graph-based execution [ 8 ] or generates route instructions for a downstream navigator [ 9 ] . Together, these approaches establish how earlier observations can help an agent determine where to search. For mobile manipulation, however, locating the relevant workspace is only part of the problem: the robot must also approach it from a
configuration that permits interaction.

Human activity video offers complementary information about how
interaction is prepared and performed. Prior work transfers predicted
hand trajectories into robot actions [ 2 ] , or extracts
contact locations and subsequent motion as visual affordances for robot learning [ 10 ] . SafeMimic adapts demonstrated actions through safety-checked search [ 11 ] , and HoMMI learns hand-eye trajectories realized by whole-body control [ 12 ] .
These approaches motivate using human behavior as more than a record of object locations. MoCaP focuses on a complementary cue: the position from which a person prepares to interact. It combines this cue with spatial memory from the same passive recordings, using scene experience to guide search and pre-contact positioning to guide approach. The recordings are processed before downstream requests are supplied and can support multiple tasks without a prescribed demonstration of each requested robot behavior.

## II-B Language-Guided Mobile Manipulation

Language-guided robot systems connect high-level requests to executable behavior through perception and action interfaces. Skill-based approaches use language or vision-language models to select and parameterize robot capabilities [ 13 , 14 ] ; Code as Policies extends this interface to executable programs that compose perception and control APIs into executable programs [ 15 ] . Incorporating execution feedback enables these systems to revise plans and recover from failures [ 16 , 17 ] , while ASPIRE turns validated program repairs into reusable skills [ 18 ] . For mobile manipulation, integrated systems bring object search, navigation, and manipulation into a common execution pipeline [ 1 , 19 ] .

CaP-X provides a closely related foundation for composing perception and control primitives, with its real-robot evaluation centered on tabletop manipulation [ 3 ] . Its mobile manipulator interface selects base poses by geometric heuristics and relies on the simulator’s planner to reject infeasible ones. MoCaP adopts the CaP-X program interface but grounds base motion in the real robot: docking goals are validated against the online costmap and executed by a classical navigation stack [ 20 ] , and arrival is verified with fresh perception before manipulation proceeds. Moving to mobile manipulation also introduces a coupled problem beyond collision-free motion: the robot must decide where to search and from which side to approach for manipulation. A code-based control interface enables these decisions but does not itself supply the scene and interaction experience needed to guide them, failing the tasks. MoCaP draws this guidance from passive human video, using spatial memory to guide search and pre-contact positioning to guide approach, while robot-specific primitives determine executable motions.

## II-C Base Placement for Mobile Manipulation

Whether a mobile manipulator can execute a manipulation task heavily depends on where it stops.
Classical methods precompute a voxelized map of the arm’s reachable workspace [ 21 ] and invert it to obtain the base poses from which a target is reachable [ 22 ] .
These maps depend only on kinematics, so they are nearly symmetric around the target and cannot tell which side of a table is free or which way a door opens.
Learning-based methods recover that context from successful rollouts [ 23 ] , reinforcement learning with reachability prior [ 24 ] , at the cost of robot trials in each new environment.
Welschehold et al. [ 25 ] initialized base poses from observed human torso poses, yet their demonstrations are specific to target task.
We instead use passive egocentric video, detecting the transition from walking to reaching and using the recorded human standing position as a good prior to order the search over base poses.

2026-10-16.title: When a robot can trust reversing wind to find an odour source
2026-10-16.authors: Junlong Shen , Shunsuke Shigaki
2026-10-16.abstract:
A wind-derived heading can guide a robot towards an odour source even after the wind reverses, but its reliability depends on the plume’s transport history.
On a quadruped initially facing the source, holding the initial heading reached it in every reversing-wind trial, whereas comparison controllers never settled there. An exact geometric condition links heading correctness to net odour transport, and simulations separate sensing error from departures from nominal flow.
Where the alternating wind directions are too close for reversal alone to produce wrong-side headings, the wrong-side rate rises from 1.0% under uniform transport to 4.7% in a stochastic flow. Re-acquiring headings from new odour contact improves simulated search when contact is intermittent.
These results identify distinct requirements for wind-guided search: a heading supported by the transport geometry and sufficient intermittent contact to replace it.
2026-10-16.introduction:
A robot searching for a gas leak detects intermittent filaments of odour, thin strands separated
by clean air [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
Many search strategies follow an insect-inspired rule: surge upwind during contact and cast
crosswind after contact is lost [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
Robotic implementations include underwater plume tracers [ 11 , 12 ] and time-varying moth strategies [ 13 ] . These strategies use the current wind
as a cue to the source direction. A reversal can invalidate that cue while previously released
odour is still arriving.

Holding an earlier heading can protect a searcher from this error. On a Unitree Go1 quadruped
searching for ethanol between alternating fan banks, a held heading reached the source while
the comparison controllers failed to settle there (Fig. 1 ). However, the robot
started facing the source, so its initial upwind heading was favourable. The demonstration
motivates a separate question: under what conditions does a wind-derived heading point toward
an unknown source?

The answer starts with transport. A packet detected now has accumulated displacement under the
wind along its path. The source lies back along that displacement, whereas a wind sensor reports
only the local wind now. Their agreement depends on the packet’s history and on how the plume
departs from the nominal flow. We call storing a world-frame heading from the sensed wind a commitment . Its sign is correct when the heading lies within a right angle of the true
source bearing. Correct sign is weaker than accurate alignment or eventual arrival.

We separate these requirements using physical trials and controlled simulations. The robot
tests whether a held heading survives real reversals and sensor limitations. Simulations expose
packet release times and transport, and allow plume models to change while retaining the same
robot and sensing parameters. WindReacquire ( WR-G in Methods and the Supplementary Information) supplies the test
controller: it stores an upwind heading on odour contact, rejects conflicting wind readings, and replaces
the heading after odour contact is lost. The contribution is a diagnosis of when these rules
work. Three findings carry the argument:

A held heading reaches the source through real wind reversals from a favourable start
(§ 2.1 ).

Transport geometry gives an exact sign condition; controlled plume comparisons identify
errors that nominal wind histories alone miss (§ 2.3 –§ 2.6 ).

Re-acquisition improves simulated search when odour contact is intermittent
(§ 2.8 ).

# 2 Results

## 2.1 Reversing wind defeats wind-following on a legged robot

Holding the initial heading preserved source arrival through wind reversals on the Go1.
We compared five controllers under steady and reversing wind, with three runs per condition. On the robot, WindReacquire ran with its discard rule disabled, so it held its first heading for
the whole run (the no-discard variant; Methods).
An overhead camera scored the runs without supplying observations to the controllers (Methods).
The steady condition checked that each controller could solve the task before reversal was
introduced. The comparison controllers were surge-cast, a published moth model [ 14 ] , reliability-modulated
surge [ 15 ] , and infotaxis [ 16 ] .

The steady condition passed: all five controllers reached the source in all three runs
(Table 1 ). Under reversal the outcome split cleanly. WindReacquire’s settled
distance was 0.31 m 0.31\text{\,}\mathrm{m} on average and within 0.39 m 0.39\text{\,}\mathrm{m} in every run, while the four wind-following controllers settled between 1.05 m 1.05\text{\,}\mathrm{m} and 1.90 m 1.90\text{\,}\mathrm{m} on average, and no run of theirs settled closer than 0.76 m 0.76\text{\,}\mathrm{m} . Each WindReacquire run finished closer than any run of each comparison controller.
The one-sided exact permutation test gives p = 0.05 p=0.05 per comparison, before correction for the four comparisons. This small sample supports a demonstration, with limited precision on
the size of the benefit. Fig. 1 d shows the failure pattern: the comparison controllers
initially approach the source and lose ground after a reversal. WindReacquire continues closing
range. Its conflict gate,
the rule that overrides the live wind when it disagrees with the held heading by more than π / 2 \pi/2 , was active on 34.3 – 37.1 % 34.337.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of control ticks in every reversing-wind run. Gate activation followed each fan switch after the flow settled. The trials show the rule
engaging on hardware. Its contribution under continuous and intermittent detection is isolated
in § 2.8 .

The rig measurements define the physical conditions behind this result.
The fan-bank directions differ by 146.5 ° 146.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} . The wind did not jump; it rotated. In 29 29 of the 40 40 reversals followed by at least 8 s 8\text{\,}\mathrm{s} of wind record, the sensed wind settled within 30 ° 30\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} of its new direction after a median of 10.7 s 10.7\text{\,}\mathrm{s} , always within the 20 s 20\text{\,}\mathrm{s} reversal interval; in the other 11 11 it did not stay within 30 ° 30\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} before the next reversal or the end of the run. The rig’s own anemometer updated at 1.96 Hz 1.96\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} with a direction scatter (circular standard deviation) of 21.3 ° 21.3\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} at rest, coarser than the anemometer the simulator models. The gas sensors also reported odour on every control tick of all thirty runs,
so on this rig odour worked as an on/off gate and every controller in fact steered by wind.
We vary wind separation in simulation (§ 2.4 ) and isolate its effect on arriving
bearings (§ 2.6 ). Rig-matched simulations test re-acquisition under continuous
detection (§ 2.8 ).

The demonstration has a favourable initial condition. The robot started from one
pose facing the source-side fan bank, and its heading froze within the first second.
On this rig the held heading was therefore the first
upwind bearing, which pointed at the source. The trials therefore test persistence of a useful
heading. They do not test the criterion of § 2.3 , which requires packet
transport information unavailable on the robot. We adopted settled distance as the score after
one infotaxis reversing-wind run passed within 0.27 m 0.27\text{\,}\mathrm{m} of the source and then walked away. By closest approach, infotaxis reaches in one of three reversing-wind runs and
WindReacquire in three of three; Table 1 reports both scores. Reversal exposure also differs because runs differed in length; Table 1 lists the
number encountered in each run.

A rig-matched simulation started each episode as the robot started, facing the source with the
first reversal 14.6 s 14.6\text{\,}\mathrm{s} after release. Over 200 episodes per controller it reproduces the controller ordering (Methods). The held heading reaches the source in 86.0 % 86.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of episodes ( 95 % 95\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} interval 80.5 – 90.1 % 80.590.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} ) after a median of three reversals, consistent with the physical demonstration. The surge-cast, moth-model and
reliability-modulated controllers reach it in none (Holm-adjusted p = 8.4 × 10 − 52 p=8.4\times 10^{-52} against the held heading). When both initial heading and reversal phase are randomized, the held heading reaches the source in 42.5 % 42.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the same episodes (95 against 8 discordant episodes, one-sided exact McNemar p = 2.6 × 10 − 20 p=2.6\times 10^{-20} ). The robot’s start therefore roughly doubles the held heading’s success, while following the current wind fails from either start. The simulated infotaxis also fails under steady wind, where
the robot’s infotaxis runs reached the source, so the simulation does not model those runs.

## 2.2 Simulation reproduces the collapse and isolates it

Releasing the robot with the source bearing unknown tests whether a heading is reliable rather
than merely favourable.
In the fixed source geometry of the silkmoth virtual-reality
paradigm [ 14 ] , a straight-line policy can solve the task without
interpreting the wind. We instead hide the source bearing and reverse the wind. An episode releases the simulated
robot at a random pose with the source bearing unknown, in a wind that alternates between two
nominal directions separated by σ \sigma (antipodal unless stated), with an interval T 1 / 2 T_{1/2} between reversals. We call these directions the two wind legs. The
simulated robot carries two gas sensors, a two-dimensional anemometer and a heading estimate,
with a quadruped gait model; it has no map, no odometry and no knowledge of the source
(Methods). There the reactive family, five controllers that steer by the currently sensed wind,
collapses to 0 – 5 % 05\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} success across the tested release conditions (Methods). Infotaxis is an exception to this collapse: in simulation it does not collapse at
reversal, and its standing depends on where its prior over the source position is placed
(Supplementary Table S1). Its physical-trial outcome does not establish a general failure of infotaxis.

Two plume models driven by the same nominal wind process isolate the role of plume transport. pompy [ 17 ] is a published
implementation of the filament model [ 18 ] . Its wind is a stochastic grid
field that relaxes toward the nominal direction, so an odour packet’s transport is not the nominal transport. Our own env-A is a discrete-puff model in the style
of [ 18 ] whose puffs move with the nominal wind. Below, stochastic
field refers to pompy and nominal advection to env-A. On both plumes the simulated
anemometer samples the nominal wind through the same motion, lag and noise model; only packet
transport uses pompy’s stochastic field. The comparison therefore changes transport while holding
the wind sensing fixed.

## 2.3 When a wind-derived heading faces the source

Net packet displacement gives an exact geometric test for heading correctness. Consider a
point packet emitted from a stationary source and detected at the robot at time t t . Its net
displacement is 𝐓 \mathbf{T} , so the source lies along − 𝐓 -\mathbf{T} . With perfect sensing,
an upwind heading is − 𝐮 ⁡ ( t ) -\mathbf{u}(t) , where 𝐮 ⁡ ( t ) \mathbf{u}(t) is the wind at detection.
The heading points to the source’s side precisely when

A simpler approximation places the source on the upwind axis at emission. Under antipodal
reversals it labels a heading correct when the current and emission winds agree, or equivalently
when an even number of reversals occurred during transit. This approximation can disagree with
Eq. ( 1 ): the wind directions at the ends of a journey do not specify how long
the packet travelled in each direction. We distinguish this emission-heading approximation
from the exact transport condition throughout.

In a synthetic uniform-flow check, the transport condition agrees with the point-packet
geometry in 1.0000 1.0000 of cases. Agreement is 0.9902 0.9902 for concentration-weighted packet mixtures in the same diagnostic. These checks establish implementation consistency in the ideal setting. The emission-heading approximation also has unexplained ensemble-fit behaviour, reported in
Supplementary Fig. S1 and Table S2 (Methods).

## 2.4 Sign error persists at small wind separations

Small wind separations isolate errors that nominal reversal alone cannot explain.
Under uniform advection, any mixture of two wind directions separated by σ < π / 2 \sigma<\pi/2 has a positive projection onto either direction (Fig. 2 b).
Equation ( 1 ) then predicts P ⁡ ( sign ​ ok ) = 1 P(\mathrm{sign\ ok})=1 for an ideal upwind heading.
Measured sign errors must come from departures from that flow or from perfect sensing.

Each simulated measurement runs on a seed block, a disjoint range of random seeds that is never
reused between selection and testing (Methods).
On the first test block, 677 677 of 708 708 commitments are sign-correct at the tested separations below π / 2 \pi/2 .
The rate is P ⁡ ( sign ​ ok ) = 0.9562 P(\mathrm{sign\ ok})=0.9562 , with upper 95 % 95\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} Wilson bound 0.969 0.969 , below the prespecified 0.99 0.99 bar. Thus 4.38 4.38 percentage points (pp) of sign error remain where nominal reversal alone predicts none.

We separated sensing error from plume geometry by varying the plume model while holding the
sensing model fixed. Both models use the same anemometer noise and lag, gait model and
heading drift. Matched episode indices also fix release pose, heading, reversal phase and seed.
An attribute-by-attribute check found no mismatch over 1200 1200 indices.

The models nevertheless give different error rates. Pooling the seven matched separations
from 30 ° 30\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} to 75 ° 75\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} , the sign-error rate is 4.70 4.70 pp on the stochastic field ( n = 1171 n=1171 commitments, Wilson 95 % 95\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} interval 3.6 – 6.1 pp 3.66.1\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{p} ) against 1.03 1.03 pp under nominal advection ( n = 1065 n=1065 , 0.6 – 1.8 pp 0.61.8\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{p} ); a two-proportion test gives z = − 5.11 z=-5.11 (one-sided p = 1.6 × 10 − 7 p=1.6\times 10^{-7} ). two plume models give nearly equal rates, 1.59 1.59 against 1.60 1.60 pp. The no-reversal condition supplies a common baseline. Rotating the wind separates the plume
models while the sensing model stays the same. This pattern implicates the flow’s effect on
the relation between wind direction and source bearing.

On two disjoint stochastic-field blocks, the kernel prediction outperforms a baseline that

The uncorrected emission-heading prediction also over-predicts sign correctness along the

## 2.6 General across wind processes, specific to flow fields

The kernel prediction transfers across tested wind schedules but fails across flow fields. Wind processes. We tested asymmetric dwell times and a Poisson reversal train.
Neither requires a periodic wind: the endpoint rotation Ψ ⁡ ( Δ ) \Psi(\Delta) uses the realized
wind history. Across these conditions, it predicts P ⁡ ( sign ​ ok ) P(\mathrm{sign\ ok}) at a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0165 0.0165 , against 0.0336 0.0336 on the square wave it was built on (Table 3 ). This beats a baseline that predicts the mean rate across tested
conditions by 5.2 5.2 times in MAE. Given each Poisson condition’s mean timescale as a matched square wave, the same predictor
is 17.6 17.6 times worse in MAE: it uses the wind’s actual history, not its rate.

Flow fields. The same construction fails on nominal advection, even with that model’s
own no-reversal kernel. It predicts 12.04 12.04 pp of sign error at σ = 82.5 ° \sigma=$82.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}$ , where this sweep’s own fresh block shows 0.62 0.62 pp, and it loses to a constant-rate baseline (Table 4 ). On the seed block behind

by σ \sigma . We tested that assumption by splitting commitments according to the age-implied
emission leg. At σ = 82.5 ° \sigma=$82.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}$ the difference in mean angular error is 43.99 ° 43.99\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} on the stochastic field and 17.56 ° 17.56\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} under nominal advection (Table 4 ). The stochastic-field distribution extends farther across the sign boundary.
The measured gains explain a limitation of the emission-heading approximation: it assumes
the full wind rotation transfers to the arriving bearing, while both fields transmit only a
fraction. A condition based on actual transport can be exact while this approximation fails.

Independent dispersion engine. We tested the same account on
GADEN [ 19 , 20 ] , a published three-dimensional filament
simulator with independent dispersion dynamics (Methods). We supplied a spatially uniform
wind map, placing this test at the nominal-advection end of the comparison.
It tests another engine under uniform wind, rather than another flow field.
The pooled error rate below σ = π / 2 \sigma=\pi/2 is 0.67 0.67 pp (Wilson 95 % 95\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} interval 0.3 – 1.3 pp 0.31.3\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{p} , n = 1201 n=1201 commitments), below pompy’s 4.70 4.70 pp and inside env-A’s band. The measured gain is 8.1 % 8.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of σ \sigma ( 95 % 95\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} bootstrap interval − 1.2 – 18.0 % -1.218.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} ). Above σ = π / 2 \sigma=\pi/2 the emission-heading prediction over-predicts sign error, as under nominal
advection, predicting 0.55 0.55 sign-correct at σ = 180 ° \sigma=$180\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}$ where 0.91 0.91 occurs. The prediction was fixed before the block was run, so this is a registered miss. It reproduces the flow-field dependence on an independent engine.

## 2.7 From a correct heading to reaching the source

A correct sign was necessary for success on the hold-only variant, which never discards its
heading. All 1074 1074 episodes with a wrong-sign first commitment failed across the fourteen
conditions of release distance, separation and reversal period. Episodes without a commitment also failed. Observed success therefore factorises as p commit ⋅ p sign ⋅ q p_{\mathrm{commit}}\cdot p_{\mathrm{sign}}\cdot q : the probability of committing,
the conditional probability of correct sign, and the fraction q q of correct-sign episodes
that reach the source. This is an empirical identity on that variant.
The emission-heading prediction carries the order of success across
conditions and not its level , because q q varies by a factor of 8.3 8.3 across the sweep and moves with release distance and separation. Sign prediction alone is therefore insufficient to predict success. Table 5 summarizes the headings and arriving ages on the same controller.

## 2.8 Re-acquiring the heading pays, given intermittent contact

WindReacquire adds one rule to a held heading, and the rule needs intermittent odour contact. The
controller freezes an upwind heading at the first accepted odour detection (detections count only
while sensed upwind lies within 120 ° 120\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} of the robot’s heading), discards it after a fixed time without accepted detection,
and re-acquires from the next such detection (Methods). The primary benchmark releases the robot
on either side of the source (Methods). There
re-acquisition is worth + 46.5 +46.5 pp with the conflict gate on and + 44.0 +44.0 pp with it off, and + 40.0 +40.0 pp on a disjoint confirmation block (Table 6 , Supplementary Table S3). The gate’s measured differences are + 3.0 +3.0 and + 0.5 +0.5 pp, with no resolved benefit on this benchmark. On the confirmation block, however, the gate added 11.0 11.0 pp with re-acquisition on, so its registered null did not hold there (Supplementary Table S3).
Re-acquisition needs time to repay its cost. At a 30 s 30\text{\,}\mathrm{s} horizon it costs 8.5 8.5 pp ( 95 % 95\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} interval 3.5 – 13.5 pp 3.513.5\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{p} , McNemar p = 0.002 p=0.002 ), and the + 46.5 +46.5 pp is read at the 300 s 300\text{\,}\mathrm{s} cap. The replacement must also use the odour cue. Re-acquiring from odour beats two controls that, on contact loss, replace the heading with a random
direction or a random sign, by 27.5 27.5 to 34.2 34.2 pp across the four control–plume pairs, fully paired on one 400-episode block. On pompy, fixed-interval and path-length triggers match the detection-loss trigger under the
same tuning budget. This comparison supports cue-informed replacement without attributing
its benefit to one trigger form.

Re-acquisition also helps on GADEN, by + 40.25 +40.25 pp: 78.50 % 78.50\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} against 38.25 % 38.25\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} (179 episodes succeed only with re-acquisition and 18 only without, exact one-sided p = 7.7 × 10 − 35 p=7.7\times 10^{-35} , 400 paired episodes). Arriving odour is younger there ( Δ / T 1 / 2 = 0.51 \Delta/T_{1/2}=0.51 ), so the reversal matters less than on pompy.

The hardware and simulation tests address different rules. The robot’s gas channel read odour
on every tick, but its deployed controller also had discard disabled by configuration.
The robot therefore tested a held heading plus the conflict gate; it cannot establish whether
continuous detection would disable an enabled re-acquisition rule.
The rig-matched component comparison tests that rule explicitly.
With continuous detection, the conflict gate adds + 11.0 +11.0 pp and re-acquisition + 0.5 +0.5 pp (200 paired episodes; all 22 discordant episodes favour the gate, McNemar p = 4.8 × 10 − 7 p=4.8\times 10^{-7} ). Replacing continuous detection with plume-driven gas at the rig’s range does not bring the
mechanism back. It makes it harmful, 0.0 % 0.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} with re-acquisition against 26.0 % 26.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} without, because at that range contact is so rare that a discarded heading is never replaced. The benefit therefore depends on contact conditions. Measured on a
stationary probe that runs no controller, the crossover lies between 3.3 3.3 and 4.7 % 4.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of ticks with odour: re-acquisition is worth + 9.5 +9.5 pp at 4.7 % 4.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} (McNemar p = 0.001 p=0.001 ) and is unresolved at 3.3 % 3.3\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} . These measurements identify a useful operating band in the tested configuration.
A stationary survey can detect continuous or sparse contact, but the measured duty-cycle
bracket is not a transferable guarantee of benefit. During search, a 20 s 20\text{\,}\mathrm{s} window cannot distinguish persistently sparse contact from a recent loss of the plume.

2026-10-16.title: SOMA: Stack-of-Objects Manipulation using a Quadruped Robot
2026-10-16.authors: Stergios E. Bachoumas , Panagiotis Artemiadis
2026-10-16.abstract: Executing heavy-duty physical manipulation in unpredictable environments remains a major challenge for quadrupedal robots lacking dedicated manipulators. This paper presents SOMA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for whole-body non-prehensile manipulation of multi-object stacks using a quadruped robot. Unlike traditional methods restricted to two-dimensional planar pushing, SOMA integrates explicit robot base-height control, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This capability enables the quadruped to manipulate complex payload stacks as a unified system while preventing relative sliding or tipping of upper layers. The architecture factorizes control into a high-level manipulation policy using a Simplified Structured State Space Sequence (S5) encoder to reason over long-horizon temporal history and predict bounded target tracking commands via Beta distributions, and a low-level locomotion policy that dynamically adapts leg stance configurations. In extensive simulation benchmarks, SOMA achieves a 90.3 % 90.3\% success rate for single-object reposing and up to 90.1 % 90.1\% for dynamic two-box stacks under stringent error margins ( 0.05 ​ m 0.05\text{ m} position error, 1 ​ ° 1\degree orientation error). Finally, we validate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot across diverse payload masses and geometries, demonstrating active base-height adjustments to maintain traction and balance during heavy pushing tasks.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Recent work on quadrupedal locomotion has enabled significant maneuverability across diverse and complex terrains [ 11 , 13 ] , and has also enabled gymnastic-style maneuvers such as a running backflip [ 15 ] . However, these platforms still exhibit limitations when executing tasks that require close physical interaction with the environment. Truly autonomous robotic systems must physically interact with their environment and thus act as mobile manipulators [ 23 ] . Recently, the robotics community has increased efforts in this direction, with promising work combining locomotion and manipulation for quadruped robots, commonly referred to as loco-manipulation.

Unlike bipeds, quadrupedal platforms inherently lack dedicated end-effectors for physical interaction.
Nevertheless, in [ 33 , 4 , 16 , 2 ] , the authors used pedipulation, i.e., manipulation using the legs of a quadruped as an on-demand manipulator, to accomplish tasks such as opening spring-loaded doors, pushing lightweight objects out of the way, doing laundry, pushing switches, and even collecting rock samples in the wild. While these strategies prove effective for versatile manipulation, most prior work [ 4 , 2 ] strictly constrains the robot’s mobility by prioritizing base static stability, with the notable exceptions of [ 16 , 33 ] .

To overcome this limitation, a prominent body of work has successfully integrated robotic manipulators onto quadruped bases, achieving significant progress in mobile prehensile loco-manipulation [ 7 , 20 , 6 , 8 , 17 , 22 , 31 , 33 ] .
Despite these advancements, dedicated manipulator-base systems face severe physical constraints when deployed in complex environments. The increased spatial footprint and payload capacity limits of mounted arms hinder operation in tightly confined spaces and restrict the maximum load the system can manipulate. This gap becomes particularly critical in search-and-rescue operations, where robots must navigate narrow passages and interact with heavy, unstable debris under shifting dynamic loads. Consequently, achieving heavy-duty physical manipulation within highly constrained, unpredictable, and hazardous environments remains an open challenge.

Quadrupedal robots can manipulate objects without dedicated arms either by deploying individual limbs or by leveraging their entire body for pushing interactions. While limb-based manipulation enables fine control over lightweight objects, whole-body pushing provides a compelling mechanism for transporting heavy or bulky payloads. Although non-prehensile pushing was historically underexplored [ 14 ] , foundational work by Mason established the underlying mechanics and motion planning challenges of contact-driven manipulation [ 19 ] . Modern optimization-based techniques have since made this problem more tractable by formulating pushing as a multi-contact planning problem [ 9 ] . Recently, these optimization frameworks have been extended to quadrupedal platforms to enable body-pushing behaviors [ 24 , 29 ] . However, planning through contact remains inherently difficult [ 19 ] , and current optimization methods rely heavily on pre-specified environmental models and fixed robot parameters. We extend prior work by incorporating explicit control over the robot’s base height, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This vertical degrees-of-freedom integration enables the quadruped to intelligently manipulate and reconfigure complex stacks of objects from arbitrary initial states to target poses.

Our approach incorporates direct robot base height commands, enabling full 3D pushing strategies—a crucial component missing from previous methods that restrict the robot to a predefined height and, consequently, to 2D planar pushing strategies.

## II-D SOMA: Training, Domain Randomization, and Deployment

SOMA is a full-stack framework for the manipulation of multi-object stacks using a quadruped robot. It contains the complex training pipeline, the custom domain randomization procedure, and the hardware deployment implementation. For control-system training, we use Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [ 26 ] in three stages. Because we train the policies in simulation, we use domain randomization at each stage to ensure the system generalizes well to different objects and physical properties in the real world.

In the first stage, only the low-level locomotion policy is trained to track random locomotion commands. At the start of each episode, a random target locomotion command is generated and then resampled every 4 ​ s 4\,\text{s} . To make the policy robust against payloads, we sample a robot base link mass variation in the range [ − 1 , 3 ] ​ kg [-1,3]\,\text{kg} from its nominal mass. To improve the policy’s disturbance-rejection capabilities, we apply simulated velocity disturbances. Specifically, we sample linear velocity disturbances in the range [ − 0.5 , 0.5 ] ​ m/s [-0.5,0.5]\,\text{m/s} for the forward and lateral directions and [ − 0.4 , 0.4 ] ​ m/s [-0.4,0.4]\,\text{m/s} for the vertical direction of the robot. For the angular velocity disturbances, we sample for all main axes in the range [ − 45 , 45 ] ​ ° ​ /s [-45,45]\,\degree\text{/s} . The disturbances are applied to the base link every 1 − 3 ​ s 1-3\,\text{s} [ 25 ] . Finally, to facilitate sim-to-real transfer, we inject synthetic additive Gaussian noise into the locomotion policy’s observation 𝐱 t \mathbf{x}_{t} .

In the second stage, we freeze the low-level policy parameters and train the high-level manipulation policy using a single object (box). The robot’s task is to push the box to a goal pose with position error less than 0.05 ​ m 0.05\,\text{m} and orientation error less than 1 ​ ° 1\degree . To encourage policy generalization, we randomly sample each dimension of the box independently from the range [ 0.35 , 0.45 ] ​ m [0.35,0.45]\,\text{m} at the start of each episode. We also sample the box mass uniformly from [ 6 , 10 ] ​ kg [6,10]\,\text{kg} , which remains constant for the duration of the episode. Crucially, we also randomize the sliding friction coefficient between the box and the ground, sampling it uniformly from [ 0.3 , 1.5 ] [0.3,1.5] at the start of each episode.

The task is then extended to a stack of two box-shaped objects. The top object is unconstrained and free to move or slide relative to the bottom object. The robot must complete the same re-posing task as in Stage 2, but with the added requirement of keeping the stack stable, i.e., the top object must always remain on top of the bottom object.
