2026-10-16.title: Line-Augmented cuVSLAM: Robust Visual Odometry in Low-Texture Environments
2026-10-16.authors: Dara Molloy , Terry Wu , Wonju Lee , Abhilash Nand Kumar , David Adley , Conor Ferguson , Hesam Rabeti
2026-10-16.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-16.abstract:
Autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) in warehouses and production facilities operate in
precisely the environments that defeat point-feature visual odometry: featureless
aisles, uniform walls, repetitive racking and specular floors. Such environments are,
however, rich in straight-edge structure: rack uprights, door frames, wall
junctions and cabinet outlines present high-contrast linear edges stable across wide
viewpoint changes. A line-feature extension to cuVSLAM [ 1 ] ,
a CUDA-accelerated visual-SLAM system, is presented that recovers this
signal. Lines are parameterised as Plücker coordinates for geometric transport
and as the minimal 4-DOF orthonormal representation of Bartoli and Sturm [ 2 ] for optimisation; a Cauchy-robust point-to-line residual with analytic Jacobians is
folded directly into cuVSLAM’s per-frame Gauss–Newton pose solve, and the same line
state is jointly refined in the Schur-complement sliding-window bundle adjustment. An
adaptive information weight causes lines to assume more of the estimation burden exactly
as point features become scarce, and the extension adds residual blocks to existing
solvers rather than introducing a second estimator, reducing exactly to the unmodified
point pipeline when disabled. Evaluated in RGB-D mode under SE(3) Umeyama alignment with
no scale correction, line features reduce mean absolute trajectory error by
38.5% over the 22 sequences of the TUM RGB-D freiburg3 collection and by
30.1% over the 8 Replica room and office sequences, where median
translation error falls by 38.9% and median rotation error by
66.4%, with zero tracking failures in any configuration tested.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Cameras are inexpensive, compact and information-dense, making visual odometry an
attractive alternative to LIDAR-based localisation for autonomous mobile robots,
provided it can match LIDAR’s robustness in the industrial
environments where point-feature tracking degrades.
cuVSLAM [ 1 ] represents a modern, state-of-the-art
visual-SLAM system: CUDA-accelerated, supporting up to 32 cameras across RGB,
depth and stereo-inertial pipelines, and running in real time on NVIDIA Jetson
edge hardware.
As in ORB-SLAM3 [ 3 ] , VINS-Mono [ 4 ] and other
deployed visual or visual-inertial odometry (VIO) systems, its front end tracks sparse
point features: corners and textured patches carried across frames by descriptor
matching or optical-flow tracking. cuVSLAM’s own point path uses the latter: GFTT
corner detection followed by GPU Lucas–Kanade optical-flow tracking with
normalised-cross-correlation validation, not descriptor re-matching.

Point features are precisely the primitive that indoor structured environments lack. A
warehouse aisle or production facility presents long stretches of uniformly painted wall,
repetitive shelving, specular flooring and low-contrast or distant ceiling structure. Corner
detectors yield few correspondences in these conditions, and the surviving matches are
often poorly conditioned or attached to moving inventory.

These environments are, however, rich in straight-edge structure. Rack uprights, door
frames, wall–floor junctions, pallet edges and cabinet outlines are abundant,
high-contrast and stable across wide viewpoint changes. A line is also a
better-conditioned measurement than a point in these scenes, as it aggregates gradient
evidence along its full length, which increases robustness to noise, motion blur and
partial occlusion relative to a small tracked point patch. The point-line VIO
literature converges on this observation, reporting that line features yield the
largest gains in degenerate, low-texture and structured
scenes [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] .

This paper carries the point-line VIO formulation established by
PL-VINS [ 5 ] and its lineage into cuVSLAM’s CUDA-accelerated pose
solve and bundle adjustment, and extends it with five departures aimed at the
industrial degradation regime above. The extension augments rather than replaces the
point pipeline and preserves the low-latency front end/back end separation that makes
cuVSLAM deployable on edge hardware. The contributions are:

A persistent, cross-window line landmark registry that keeps a landmark alive after its originating frame
leaves the bundle-adjustment sliding window, so an early, wide-baseline observation
can still be paired against a much later one for triangulation, in place of
PL-VINS’s window-scoped landmarks, which are deleted outright once their originating
frame marginalises out.

A persistent, cross-window line landmark registry that keeps a landmark alive after its originating frame
leaves the bundle-adjustment sliding window, so an early, wide-baseline observation
can still be paired against a much later one for triangulation, in place of
PL-VINS’s window-scoped landmarks, which are deleted outright once their originating
frame marginalises out.

# II Related Work

Early visual-SLAM systems were formulated as recursive filters, with camera poses and map
features maintained in a state updated around a local linearisation [ 8 ] . Nonlinear factor-graph optimization subsequently became
standard, with bundle adjustment providing a sparse pose-landmark formulation for joint
refinement [ 9 ] . Keyframe-based systems such as ORB-SLAM3 [ 3 ] established this point-centric paradigm across monocular,
stereo, RGB-D, and visual-inertial configurations. cuVSLAM [ 1 ] extends this lineage to CUDA-accelerated, multi-camera, real-time edge deployment.

Early point-line systems commonly represented a mapped segment by two 3D endpoints.
In the original PL-SLAM implementation [ 10 ] , the endpoint
coordinates were optimized directly, and the residual was formed from the projected
endpoints and the corresponding observed infinite image line. This representation
simplified initialization and association, but endpoint locations remained sensitive to
occlusion, contrast variation, and partial visibility. Metric depth does not remove this
issue in RGB-D systems, because endpoint locations remain affected by image truncation.
Later formulations replaced endpoint coordinates with geometric line states while
retaining endpoint-to-line reprojection constraints, as in PL-VIO [ 6 ] .

The geometric foundation was provided by the Plücker representation, which supports
rigid transport and projection but uses six coordinates subject to the Klein constraint.
A minimal four-degree-of-freedom orthonormal representation was established for line
reconstruction and bundle adjustment by Bartoli and Sturm [ 2 ] . Plücker coordinates can consequently be retained for
transport while the orthonormal chart is used for optimization, avoiding the rank
deficiency of direct constrained optimization. This representation was incorporated into
tightly coupled point-line estimation by PL-VIO [ 6 ] and PL-VINS [ 5 ] . Line measurements complement point measurements but do not remove
the underlying unobservable directions [ 11 ] .

The Plücker–orthonormal formulation has been implemented in visual-inertial estimation [ 12 ] , wheel-odometry-aided odometry [ 13 ] , and RGB-D SLAM [ 14 ] . Structural-prior methods
such as StructVIO [ 7 ] obtain additional constraints from Manhattan-world regularity; no such axis-alignment
assumption is imposed here.

In this work, the established line geometry is integrated into cuVSLAM’s
CUDA-accelerated frontend and backend, with PL-VINS serving as the principal
architectural reference. Three limitations of the inherited design motivate corresponding
extensions for persistent line estimation in low-texture, structure-rich environments:

Landmark persistence Line landmarks are scoped to the active sliding
window. When the frame associated with a landmark is marginalized, its identity is not
retained for later re-association; a subsequent observation of the same edge is therefore
treated as a new landmark. Long-lived structural edges cannot consequently accumulate
observations across successive windows.

Landmark persistence Line landmarks are scoped to the active sliding
window. When the frame associated with a landmark is marginalized, its identity is not
retained for later re-association; a subsequent observation of the same edge is therefore
treated as a new landmark. Long-lived structural edges cannot consequently accumulate
observations across successive windows.

Multi-view reconstruction In the inherited monocular formulation, a line
landmark is initialized from a selected observation pair and subsequently refined as a
free bundle-adjustment variable. No separate multi-view fusion step is applied, so an
erroneous association or poorly conditioned reconstruction can influence the landmark
state.

Residual weighting Point and line residuals share a fixed information
matrix under a Huber norm [ 15 ] , without a relative point-line
weight. Their relative authority therefore remains constant as point support varies.

Sections V-B and IV-D address these three points in
turn.

LSD [ 16 ] is used for its subpixel localization and false-detection
control; EDLines [ 17 ] and ELSED [ 18 ] provide
alternative accuracy–runtime trade-offs. Detection is exposed through an interchangeable
interface (Section V-A ), and association is performed with the Line Band
Descriptor [ 19 ] , as in the PL-VIO/PL-VINS lineage [ 6 , 5 ] .

2026-10-16.title: Adaptive Prescribed Performance Trajectory Tracking for Uncertain Autonomous Underwater Vehicles With Input Saturation
2026-10-16.authors: Athanasios K. Gkesoulis , Christos Vlachos , George K. Fourlas , Charalampos P. Bechlioulis , George C. Karras
2026-10-16.comment: . Supplementary video included as ancillary material
2026-10-16.abstract: Accurate trajectory tracking is essential for autonomous underwater vehicles operating with uncertain hydrodynamics and limited thruster authority. This paper develops a low-complexity adaptive prescribed performance controller for uncertain underwater vehicle dynamics with coupled and saturated inputs. The proposed method adapts the performance functions directly through the mismatch between the requested and saturated control inputs, enlarging the performance funnels only when the available actuation cannot meet the nominal specifications. A coupled invariant-set analysis establishes boundedness of all closed-loop signals, prescribed bounds on the filtered tracking errors, and explicit feasibility conditions. Comparative simulations on a BlueROV2 underwater vehicle show that the adaptive design maintains prescribed performance during a figure-eight maneuver, whereas conventional prescribed performance control loses feasibility under input limits. A real-time pool experiment further demonstrates stable trajectory tracking and the practical implementation of the proposed method on an underwater robotic platform.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are increasingly expected to execute inspection, mapping, intervention, and environmental monitoring missions under limited actuation authority. In these operations, trajectory tracking accuracy is a robotic mission requirement: large transient deviations may compromise sensor coverage, vehicle safety, or the quality of collected data. Underwater vehicles also operate with uncertain hydrodynamics, restoring forces, disturbances, and hard thruster limits whose effects propagate through control allocation and coupled body motion. Experimental prescribed performance tracking of underwater robots [ 1 ] and open-water funnel control under input saturation [ 2 ] reinforce the need to jointly address tracking performance and actuation limits.

Prescribed performance control (PPC) imposes transient and steady state tracking specifications through designer-selected performance envelopes [ 3 ] , while funnel control achieves the same following a different design [ 4 ] . Barrier-like transformations of normalized errors can enforce convergence rate, overshoot, and residual error requirements without exact model identification. Actuator saturation, however, creates a feasibility conflict whenever a fixed performance envelope demands more control authority than the vehicle can deliver, particularly during aggressive maneuvers or in the presence of strong currents and other disturbances.

Input constraints have been studied through adaptive, robust, neuroadaptive, finite-time, and sliding-mode control [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Saturation-aware PPC and funnel designs include adaptive-gain and MIMO funnel controllers [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] , bang-bang designs [ 13 , 14 ] , disturbance-regularity and bounded-gain methods [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] , and approximation-free constrained PPC [ 18 ] . Flexible envelopes, switching mechanisms, auxiliary dynamics, observers, and neural or fuzzy approximators have also been employed [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Recent underwater-vehicle work combines prescribed performance with dynamic compensation, neural approximation, filtering, and velocity observation to handle saturation and uncertainty [ 25 ] . Although effective, the use of such structures increases implementation complexity on robotic platforms that usually operate with limited computational capabilities.

Among low-complexity alternatives, an adjustable outer funnel is employed in [ 26 ] , adaptive performance bounds are adopted in [ 21 , 27 ] , and desired-motion modification is considered in [ 28 , 29 ] to recover feasibility. The MIMO adaptive performance design of [ 21 ] exploits the available control authority across the input channels. However, its adaptation mechanism contains the saturation mismatch divided by the normalized error | ξ i | < 1 |\xi_{i}|<1 , together with user-selected cross-channel coupling parameters. Consequently, its saturation-induced relaxation contains a term of order 𝒪 ⁡ ( | Δ ​ τ i | / | ξ i | ) \mathcal{O}(|\Delta\tau_{i}|/|\xi_{i}|) , where Δ ​ τ i \Delta\tau_{i} denotes the mismatch between the saturated and required unsaturated input. The scalar design of [ 27 ] instead adapts the performance envelope directly through | Δ ​ τ i | |\Delta\tau_{i}| , avoids divisions by the normalized error, and yields an 𝒪 ⁡ ( | Δ ​ τ i | ) \mathcal{O}(|\Delta\tau_{i}|) degradation bound, but it does not address coupled MIMO dynamics. Reference modification methods preserve the nominal performance funnel by altering the commanded motion. In particular, [ 30 ] treats uncertain MIMO systems with coupled and constrained inputs and obtains a mismatch-dependent tracking bound through reference adaptation rather than performance adaptation. In contrast, [ 28 ] does not consider the state-dependent cross-channel input coupling induced by the inverse inertia matrix. Therefore, to the best of the authors’ knowledge, no low-complexity adaptive performance result has yet considered direct mismatch-proportional adaptation of the performance bounds and an explicit treatment of the coupled input action of uncertain Euler–Lagrange underwater vehicles. This combination is challenging because the inverse inertia matrix maps each saturated generalized input into multiple acceleration channels. Saturation in one channel can thus affect all filtered errors, invalidating the decoupled invariant-set arguments employed in the scalar case [ 27 ] .

Motivated by the aforementioned discussion, we develop an adaptive PPC framework for uncertain AUV Euler–Lagrange dynamics with coupled and saturated inputs. Each performance function is driven directly by the corresponding saturation mismatch and recovers its prescribed form exponentially when saturation is inactive, while the desired trajectory remains unchanged. To overcome the coupling challenge, we construct a coupled invariant set and a saturation-aware auxiliary Lyapunov function whose cancellation structure exploits the positive definite symmetric part of the inverse inertia matrix. This establishes boundedness of all closed-loop signals, explicit feasibility conditions, and a tracking degradation bound that is linear in the saturation mismatch, without the normalized-error denominator appearing in [ 21 ] .

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a low-complexity adaptive prescribed performance trajectory tracking controller for uncertain AUV Euler–Lagrange dynamics with saturated generalized inputs and coupled error channels, without reference modification, dedicated controller-side observers, regressors, neural networks, or fuzzy approximators.

We establish boundedness and adaptive prescribed performance through a coupled invariant-set argument and an auxiliary Lyapunov function tailored to the saturation mismatch.

We derive explicit sufficient feasibility conditions linking the required saturation levels to the performance envelopes, controller gains, uncertain dynamics, and the positive definite symmetric part of the inverse inertia matrix, together with a mismatch-dependent tracking degradation bound.

We validate the design through comparative BlueROV2 simulations and a real-time pool experiment.

The analysis explicitly accommodates coupled MIMO dynamics and constrained generalized inputs while retaining the commanded trajectory and adapting only the performance functions.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II states the AUV model, assumptions, and control objective. Section III presents the adaptive PPC design and the stability and performance analysis. Section IV reports comparative simulations and experimental validation, and Section V concludes the paper.

1. We propose a low-complexity adaptive prescribed performance trajectory tracking controller for uncertain AUV Euler–Lagrange dynamics with saturated generalized inputs and coupled error channels, without reference modification, dedicated controller-side observers, regressors, neural networks, or fuzzy approximators.

2. We establish boundedness and adaptive prescribed performance through a coupled invariant-set argument and an auxiliary Lyapunov function tailored to the saturation mismatch.

3. We derive explicit sufficient feasibility conditions linking the required saturation levels to the performance envelopes, controller gains, uncertain dynamics, and the positive definite symmetric part of the inverse inertia matrix, together with a mismatch-dependent tracking degradation bound.

4. We validate the design through comparative BlueROV2 simulations and a real-time pool experiment.

5. The analysis explicitly accommodates coupled MIMO dynamics and constrained generalized inputs while retaining the commanded trajectory and adapting only the performance functions.

2026-10-16.title: LEAP: Gradient Flow Augmented Lagrangian Trajectory Optimization for Contact Constrained Robots
2026-10-16.authors: César E. Ramos Chuquiure , Ryan Tsai , Yutong Zhou , Zihang Huang , Vansh Thakur , Akshunn Trivedi , Zachary Lin , Pearl Lin , Ruikai Yang , Challen Enninful Adu , Ram Vasudevan
2026-10-16.abstract:
Generating dynamically feasible motions for legged and manipulating robots requires solving a large, nonlinear, non-convex optimal control problem (OCP) in which contact wrenches must satisfy friction-cone constraints throughout the motion, not only at isolated instants.
Existing solvers are sensitive to the initial guess and scale poorly with the number of joints.
This paper introduces LEAP , which transcribes the OCP with pseudospectral collocation and, instead of a Newton or SQP solve, integrates a primal–dual gradient flow of a Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar augmented Lagrangian to compute a solution.
Because the flow is stiff, this paper designs a linearly implicit integrator with a Gauss–Newton metric, momentum, and a merit-based step controller that keeps the augmented Lagrangian monotone.
Across locomotion benchmarks on five robot platforms, from planar hoppers to 32-joint humanoids, LEAP is the only method to solve every tested problem, achieves substantial speedups over Crocoddyl and Aligator on several benchmarks, and reaches trackable references at smaller compute budgets.
The resulting trajectories are validated by tracking them in a high-fidelity simulator and on hardware.
We will make the code public upon final acceptance of this paper.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Robots interact with the world through contact: a humanoid walks by planting and lifting its feet, a manipulator pushes, grasps and releases objects, and a quadruped climbs by loading and unloading its limbs.
Planning such motions means choosing joint torques and contact forces that respect the robot’s dynamics, its actuation limits, and the physics of contact, which requires the contact wrench to stay inside a friction cone at every instant.
Trajectory optimization formalizes this as an Optimal Control Problem (OCP) over hybrid dynamics: minimize a cost, subject to the equations of motion in each contact mode, and the constraints above.

Solving this OCP is difficult for three reasons.
The dynamics are nonlinear and change discontinuously across contact modes.
The constraints, in particular the friction cones and the dynamics themselves, are nonlinear and non-convex, and any solver must decide how to enforce them and where in time.
And the resulting problem is non-convex in the decision variables, so the outcome depends on the initial guess, and a good one is often unavailable for a new behavior or a new robot.
We refer to these as the dynamics, constraint, and initialization challenges.

State-of-the-art solvers exploit the temporal structure of the dynamics to make each iteration cheap.
Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP) methods such as Crocoddyl [ 17 ] and Aligator [ 11 ] combine quadratic approximations of the value function with multiple shooting, and direct methods such as acados [ 24 , 26 ] transcribe the OCP into a nonlinear program (NLP) with banded structure.
In both families each iteration is a Newton-type step, and this is what makes the constraint and initialization challenges persist.
A Newton step is only meaningful near a solution, so these solvers rely on a good warm start and on line-search or trust-region globalization whose parameters must be tuned per problem.
Constraints are handled by penalties, by projection onto a box, or by an augmented Lagrangian inside the Riccati recursion, and they are enforced only at discrete knots, so the friction cone can be violated between them. In Section V illustrates that, on the contact-constrained problems, these solvers scale poorly with the number of joints and their performance depends strongly on hyper-parameters.

Gradient flows (GF) offer a different way to handle the initialization challenge.
Instead of taking Newton steps, the trajectory is deformed continuously in a pseudo-time until it becomes stationary for an action functional.
Every step of the flow is a descent step that is well defined anywhere, not only near a solution, so the method tolerates poor initial guesses and admits continuation naturally. [ 15 ] and [ 14 ] introduced the Affine Geometric Heat Flow (AGHF), whose steady state solves the OCP, and [ 6 ] , [ 16 ] and [ 7 ] extended it to free boundary conditions and to low-dimensional legged systems. [ 1 ] and [ 2 ] improved the numerics to reach higher-dimensional systems, and [ 13 ] extends the idea to extended Lagrangians.
What these methods gain on initialization they give back on the other two challenges.
Constraints enter as quadratic penalties, so they are never satisfied exactly, and raising the penalty to reduce the violation makes the flow stiffer.
The stiff flow is then integrated with general-purpose solvers whose error control is unaware of the optimization structure, so the dynamics challenge reappears as a numerical one.

This paper introduces LEAP , a gradient-flow trajectory optimizer for robots in contact under a prescribed contact sequence, together with a numerical scheme designed for that flow.
It keeps the robustness to initialization of gradient flows while resolving the aforementioned constraint and stiffness problems.
Our contributions are four-fold:
First, we utilize a Powell–Hestenes–Rockafellar (PHR) augmented Lagrangian formulation and derive a two-time-scale primal–dual flow to enable exact constraint handling (Section III ).
Second, we describe how to extend this approach to hybrid dynamical systems and illustrate how to ensure that wrench feasibility is satisfied for all timein Lemma 2 .
Third, we develop a linearly implicit solver to ensure that the augmented Lagrangian monotonically decreases along the numerical solution to the primal-dual flow (Section IV ).

Finally, we compare LEAP against Crocoddyl and Aligator on solve time and terminal tracking accuracy under a time budget across two tasks and five robots with two to thirty-two joints with solution quality judged by a whole-body tracking controller in a high-fidelity simulator (Section V ).

A hopscotch trajectory is executed on a Unitree Go2 quadruped (Section VI ).

2026-10-16.title: Planning to Learn: Real-Time Robust Adaptive Control on the GPU with Guaranteed Future Learning
2026-10-16.authors: Anutam Srinivasan , Siddhant Panse , Glen Chou
2026-10-16.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
2026-10-16.abstract: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Robots operating in unstructured environments must act safely despite uncertainty in their dynamics and surroundings. Robust control is one approach to achieve this, providing worst-case guarantees by treating uncertainty as persistently adversarial, propagating reachable tubes over admissible uncertainty, and tightening constraints accordingly. While this is appropriate for irreducible aleatoric uncertainty, it can be overly conservative for epistemic uncertainty arising from unknown but learnable physical parameters such as mass, friction, wind, or motor damage. Because this structured uncertainty can be reduced through interaction, robust adaptive control can become less conservative as parameter estimates improve online. As data is collected and parameter uncertainty shrinks, controllers can safely exploit the reduced uncertainty to improve performance. Moreover, because the rate of learning depends on how informative the chosen trajectory is, control actions can directly influence future parameter uncertainty, creating a tradeoff between performance, robustness, and information gathering.

However, designing robust adaptive controllers for robotics remains an open problem, with two central challenges. First, synthesizing adaptive controllers while jointly reasoning about estimation error, aleatoric uncertainty, and parametric uncertainty is computationally expensive for long-horizon, high-dimensional nonlinear systems, yet practical robotic systems require real-time learning, verification, and controller adaptation. Second, many existing methods update parameter estimates online but plan using the current parameter uncertainty set, incorporating newly learned information only reactively after measurements are collected. As a result, they cannot exploit guaranteed future uncertainty reduction during planning and may produce unnecessarily large reachable tubes even along informative trajectories. For example, a drone traversing an uncertain but learnable wind field should be able to plan knowing that it can measure, estimate, and compensate for the wind during execution. Ignoring this future learning can degrade performance or prevent task completion, while also leading to myopic planning that fails to seek informative trajectories that accelerate uncertainty reduction. Addressing these challenges requires jointly modeling the state and parameter-estimate dynamics while efficiently forecasting the worst-case learning guaranteed under all admissible uncertainties.

In this work, we close these gaps with A-SLS, a scalable robust adaptive policy optimization framework that explicitly accounts for future learning during planning. Building on system-level synthesis (SLS) [ 1 ] , we augment the physical state with the online parameter estimate so that estimator evolution becomes part of the closed-loop dynamics. We propagate bounded parameter uncertainty and parameter-estimate shifts over the planning horizon, while adaptive SLS responses preserve correlations among process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tighter reachable tubes. Crucially, this enables assured future learning : for each candidate trajectory, we forecast the parameter uncertainty guaranteed to remain after future observations, allowing the optimizer to exploit worst-case future tube contraction without assuming favorable measurements. Because informativeness depends on the trajectory, the same formulation can also favor motions that accelerate uncertainty reduction. Finally, the structured SLS policy class admits efficient parallel reachability and robust constraint tightening, enabling GPU-parallel optimization for long-horizon, high-dimensional nonlinear systems. Our contributions are:

We formulate learning-aware robust adaptive control as an SLS problem that augments the state with the online parameter estimate, returning policies that adapt to online data while remaining robust to residual uncertainty.

We derive reachable sets that preserve correlations between disturbances, parameter error, and estimate shifts, enabling tightened robust tubes that account for and guarantee future learning. These information-sensitive tubes also enable planning that favors informative trajectories that reduce uncertainty and improve performance.

We develop a GPU-parallel solver that enables real-time long-horizon control on high-DoF nonlinear systems.

We evaluate safety, tube tightness, parameter learning, active information gathering, and scalability on high-dimensional nonlinear robotic systems and hardware.

These information-sensitive tubes also enable planning that favors informative trajectories that reduce uncertainty and improve performance.

# II Related Work

Classic robust adaptive control [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] establishes stability guarantees under disturbances and parametric uncertainty. Recent work extends these ideas to nonlinear and unmatched uncertainty using contraction theory [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] and ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} -LPV control [ 11 ] . Other approaches develop SLS-based robust control under parametric uncertainty [ 12 ] and robust adaptive control for linear systems [ 13 ] . While these methods provide strong stability guarantees, they generally do not optimize long-horizon constrained trajectories or anticipate how planned actions reduce uncertainty; contraction-based approaches also require challenging metric synthesis and online geodesic computation. In contrast, our method uses SLS for robust adaptive nonlinear trajectory optimization, coupling closed-loop reachability with guaranteed future learning and real-time GPU-parallel synthesis.

Other methods incorporate adaptation into safety-critical control. Adaptive and robust-adaptive control barrier functions (CBFs) provide forward-invariance guarantees under parametric uncertainty [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] , with later applications to robotics [ 17 , 18 ] . Many reduce online control to small QPs or impose Lyapunov conditions within MPC. However, synthesizing adaptive CBFs/CLFs can be challenging, and these methods typically provide pointwise invariance or stability guarantees without explicitly planning trajectories to improve parameter learning. Our approach instead couples closed-loop reachability and planning through shared uncertainty sources affecting physical states and future parameter estimates, yielding tighter robust tubes while making information gathering part of the trajectory optimization.

Robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) combines online model learning with constrained planning. Early work used conservative constraint tightenings or separate robust safety and learned performance models [ 19 , 20 ] . Set-membership identification was later integrated with robust MPC for linear [ 21 ] and nonlinear systems [ 22 , 23 ] , with extensions addressing convergence [ 24 ] , safety certification [ 25 ] , ℒ 1 \mathcal{L}_{1} adaptation [ 26 ] , contraction [ 27 ] , and distributed control [ 28 ] . However, most methods exploit learning only after uncertainty updates are observed rather than anticipating guaranteed future estimator evolution, and can be computationally demanding online. Our adaptive SLS formulation instead jointly propagates parameter-estimation and disturbance dynamics, preserves their correlations for tighter tubes, and enables real-time GPU-parallel synthesis.

Finally, dual and active-learning MPC recognize that control affects both task execution and future model quality [ 29 ] . Persistent-excitation constraints can promote parameter convergence in RAMPC [ 30 ] , while [ 31 ] embeds predicted set-membership updates in linear MPC for informative exploration. These methods closely align with our planning-to-learn objective. However, persistent excitation is an indirect proxy for task-relevant uncertainty reduction, while exact future set-membership reasoning can be expensive and difficult to scale. Our method instead optimizes worst-case parameter-estimation dynamics within a scalable SLS framework, exploiting assured future tube contraction while retaining robust nonlinear constraints and GPU-parallel computation for long-horizon, high-dimensional systems.

2026-10-16.title: EgoJEPA: Beyond Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation from Egocentric Videos
2026-10-16.authors: Meng Cao , Can Zhao , Jinjie Wei , Haonan Zhao , Yulong Zhang , Duo Han , Xiaofan Li , Ziwu Song , Rongtao Xu , Ruyi Gan , Hao Wang , Qian Wang , Daolin Ma , Ian Reid , Xiaodan Liang
2026-10-16.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-16.abstract: Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative to costly robot demonstrations, yet transferring their manipulation priors to robot control remains challenging. The commonly adopted retargeting-based approaches convert human wrist and finger poses into embodiment-specific action commands through hand-crafted geometric mappings. However, such mappings require meticulous recalibration across different embodiments and risk propagating hand-tracking errors into downstream robot control pipelines. To this end, we propose EgoJEPA , a three-stage framework that learns embodiment-agnostic representations from egocentric human videos without rule-based human-to-robot retargeting: 1) Human-action pre-training learns effect-aware latent actions through JEPA-style visual prediction conditioned on hand-motion differences; 2) Latent-action-based world modeling jointly predicts future visual dynamics and latent actions, which decouples human prior pre-training from robot-specific control parameterizations; 3) Embodiment-specific tuning adapts the pretrained model to diverse robots through lightweight action adapters. Experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of EgoJEPA. It achieves a 74% average success rate under the out-of-domain evaluation, compared with 65% for the retargeting baseline, while reducing cumulative cross-embodiment wall-clock cost by 47.2%, from 743.2 to 392.7 hours.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Despite recent advances in robotic manipulation policies ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) , scaling such systems remains constrained by their reliance on task-specific robot demonstrations, typically obtained through teleoperation or specialized capture systems ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ; Chi et al., 2024 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Collecting these demonstrations is costly, labor-intensive, and time-consuming, posing a significant bottleneck to scalable robot learning. In contrast, egocentric human videos provide a scalable supervision source for transferring manipulation skills from human hand-object interactions to robotic systems ( Ma et al., 2026b ; Feng et al., 2026 ) .

Earlier action-free methods operate without explicit hand-pose annotations, instead learning latent action representations directly from inter-frame visual dynamics ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024 ) . However, the resulting representations may capture generic visual variations rather than action-induced physical effects, limiting their interpretability and transferability to robot control. To move beyond learning solely from visual supervision, recent approaches explicitly leverage human hand-pose annotations and adopt a retargeting-based pipeline ( Kareer et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Tao et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026c ) . Specifically, human hand motions, such as wrist and finger poses, are captured using specialized devices ( e.g . , Leap Motion ( Weichert et al., 2013 ) or Aria glasses ( Engel et al., 2023 ) ) and subsequently mapped to a target robot action space through hand-crafted rules for policy pre-training or human-robot co-training.

Despite the intuitive formulation, the retargeting pipeline suffers from two key limitations: 1) Embodiment-specific mapping . Retargeting relies on low-level geometric or kinematic mappings tailored to a particular robot embodiment, rather than learning transferable action semantics. Consequently, such mappings are tightly coupled to the robot morphology and typically require meticulous recalibration whenever either changes. As shown in Figure 1 (a), human–robot calibration alone takes 52.1 hours, accounting for 25.2% of the total pipeline time. Figure 1 (b) shows that this cost compounds when scaling to multiple robots, i.e . , retargeting must repeat the embodiment-specific human-robot calibration and pre-training whenever the robot morphology changes, which causes the cumulative wall-clock time to grow rapidly. 2) Noise propagation . Retargeting is highly sensitive to errors in estimated human motion. Hand-pose estimation noise caused by occlusions, viewpoint variations, or temporal jitter can propagate through the retargeting process, resulting in physically infeasible robot actions. As a concrete stress test, we inject Gaussian noise into human action annotations while keeping robot training unchanged. As shown in Figure 6 (a), under a mild per-axis position noise of σ = 10 \sigma=10 mm, the retargeting pipeline on the task of bottle cap unscrewing drops drastically from 60% to 30% success rate, showing that annotation errors are directly amplified into downstream robot control failures.

To this end, we propose EgoJEPA , an Ego centric instantiation of the J oint E mbedding P redictive A rchitecture ( Assran et al., 2023 ) that learns embodiment-agnostic latent action representations from human videos. As shown in Figure 1 , EgoJEPA comprises three stages: 1) Human-action pre-training learns generic effect-aware latent actions through human-motion-conditioned visual prediction; 2) Latent-action-based world modeling jointly predicts future visual dynamics and the latent actions learned in Stage 1 via joint flow matching, rather than embodiment-specific robot commands; and 3) Embodiment-specific tuning adapts the pre-trained world model to robot action spaces through lightweight adapters. Evaluated on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments (two dexterous hands and a gripper), EgoJEPA achieves the highest average success rate of 74% under the out-of-domain evaluation, outperforming the action-free method LAPA ( Ye et al., 2025 ) , the retargeting pipeline, and the prior egocentric human-video method DexWild ( Tao et al., 2025 ) . In addition, EgoJEPA significantly reduces the cost of scaling across robot embodiments. By reusing Stage 1–2 models and adapting only Stage 3 for each new robot, EgoJEPA reduces cumulative wall-clock cost from 743.2 to 392.7 hours over retargeting ( c.f . Figure 1 (b)).

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose EgoJEPA, a JEPA-style framework that eliminates the need for rule-based human-to-robot retargeting by learning embodiment-agnostic representations from human videos.

We introduce effect-aware latent actions as a transferable interface between human motion priors and robot control, enabling efficient policy adaptation across diverse embodiments via lightweight action adapters.

Extensive experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and cross-embodiment scalability of EgoJEPA.

1. We propose EgoJEPA, a JEPA-style framework that eliminates the need for rule-based human-to-robot retargeting by learning embodiment-agnostic representations from human videos.

2. We introduce effect-aware latent actions as a transferable interface between human motion priors and robot control, enabling efficient policy adaptation across diverse embodiments via lightweight action adapters.

3. Extensive experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and cross-embodiment scalability of EgoJEPA.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

WAMs for Dexterous Manipulation. WAMs move beyond action-only policies by incorporating future state prediction into the action learning process, thereby modeling the coupled evolution of visual dynamics and action control ( Wang et al., 2026a ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . While early WAMs mainly target low-DoF gripper manipulation, recent works have extended this paradigm toward dexterous manipulation ( Goswami et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., ) . DexWM ( Goswami et al., 2025 ) conditions latent-state prediction on fine-grained hand keypoint displacements for dexterous interaction modeling. DWM ( Kim et al., 2026 ) simulates dexterous behaviors using scene-action-conditioned video diffusion without explicitly decoding robot actions. However, existing dexterous WAMs rely on embodiment-specific robot demonstrations, limiting cross-embodiment transfer and scalability. EgoJEPA instead learns transferable manipulation priors from egocentric human videos, enabling efficient adaptation to diverse robots.

Robot Learning from Human Videos. Due to the high cost of teleoperated robot demonstrations, recent work has increasingly turned to human-centric robot learning, which leverages abundant human videos as scalable semantic and physical priors ( Ma et al., 2026b ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . Existing approaches can be broadly grouped into two categories. 1) Latent-based methods learn action-related representations from action-free videos by encoding inter-frame changes ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) or future visual dynamics ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Cheang et al., 2024 ; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024 ) . However, lacking explicit action grounding, such latents may conflate controllable hand motion with camera motion and passive scene dynamics, making them less interpretable as action representations. 2) Retargeting-based methods recover explicit human motion, e.g . , wrist poses and finger poses captured by devices like Leap Motion or Aria glasses, and map them to robot-specific action spaces for pre-training or co-training ( Kareer et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Tao et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026c ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Although these approaches provide more structured supervision, they remain tied to embodiment-specific geometric mappings and are sensitive to hand-tracking noise. To this end, EgoJEPA encodes explicit human hand motions into effect-aware latent actions, enabling transfer to robot control without rule-based retargeting while improving robustness to hand-tracking noise. While concurrent work such as Being-H0 ( Luo et al., 2025 ) adopts a similar spirit by discretizing MANO trajectories into motion tokens via a VQ-VAE structure, its motion tokens rely exclusively on isolated hand-pose sequences without grounding the tokenizer in the visual context. Consequently, such tokenizers are agnostic to visual interaction semantics, failing to capture the critical contact dynamics and spatial alignment between hands and target objects.

Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures. JEPAs formulate latent world modeling by predicting the future evolution of a system in a compact representation space rather than reconstructing raw observations ( LeCun and others, 2022 ) . Early works apply JEPA to self-supervised representation learning, where models learn semantic representations by predicting latent embeddings of masked image or video patches ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) . Recent studies further explore JEPA for action-conditioned latent world modeling ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . LeWorldModel ( Maes et al., 2026 ) extends JEPA into an end-to-end action-conditioned world model via SIGReg regularization ( Bardes et al., 2021 ) . DINO-WM ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) instead leverages pretrained visual representations to learn latent dynamics by predicting future semantic features. Following this spirit, EgoJEPA investigates how human motion can serve as a physical condition for latent world modeling, which enables adaptation to diverse robot embodiments.

2026-10-16.title: TGrasp6D: Task-Informed Vision-Language Priors and Pose Refinement enable Zero-Shot Task-Oriented 6DoF Grasping
2026-10-16.authors: Manav Kulshrestha , Apoorva Vashisth , Damon Conover , Aniket Bera
2026-10-16.abstract:
Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation.
Given the task of using a knife to “slice bread,” a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for “hand[ing] the knife over,” it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff.
Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs. To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner.
Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task-informed prior.
This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency.
Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%.
We also deploy our approach on a Franka Research 3 robot to demonstrate zero-shot generalization to real world objects.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Robotic manipulation, and specifically robotic grasping, is a fundamental capability for enabling robots to physically interact with, and operate, in the real world [ 23 , 12 ] .
Recent methods have significantly advanced this field [ 11 , 1 , 10 ] by prediction of stable grasps for diverse objects.
However, a stable grasp solves half the problem: it does not consider whether the resulting hand-object configuration will support the intended task.
Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) captures this coupling between grasp and intent, requiring joint reasoning over object affordances and task semantics, rather than treating grasp selection as a purely geometric problem.
This matters wherever robots operate around humans or chain manipulation steps together – an assistive robot handing over a tool, or an industrial arm that must re-grasp a part differently depending on whether it’s inserting or fastening.

Various methods have been proposed for TOG.
Training-based approaches [ 20 , 19 , 4 , 14 ] rely on large human-annotated datasets of object-task-grasps labels [ 14 ] .
However, due to the boundedness of these datasets in the space of valid grasps and possible tasks, even large annotation efforts [ 4 ] yield sparse coverage.
Hence, their performance [ 20 , 19 , 4 , 14 ] is capped by the dataset size, and generalization to novel task-object combinations remains limited.
Many approaches [ 20 , 19 , 5 , 8 , 22 ] attempt to bypass the generative aspect of grasp synthesis by coupling with a task-free generator [ 18 , 26 , 6 ] and then scoring the resulting grasps for the given task, essentially reducing the problem to that of score regression.
By injecting task semantics onto task-agnostic grasp priors, these methods are bottlenecked by the coverage of the upstream generator: if no candidate near the task-relevant region was proposed, no downstream semantic reasoning can recover it.
Finally, planar-grasp methods [ 24 , 7 , 21 , 13 ] restrict prediction to the image plane, discarding a broad class of feasible grasps with out-of-plane approach directions.

In contrast, large vision-language models offer a different foundation for TOG.
Pretrained on internet scale image-text corpora, they encode priors over object semantics and functional affordances without requiring the exhaustive supervision that prior TOG methods depend on.
These priors, however, are expressed in the image and text modalities that the models were trained on.
Extending their reasoning requires situating the model in the three-dimensional, geometric space where manipulation actually occurs.

Hence, we present TGrasp6D, a framework that leverages VLMs to synthesize 6DoF task-oriented grasps in a zero-shot manner, requiring no task-specific training or fine-tuning.
Given a single RGB-D observation of an object and a natural language task instruction, TGrasp6D first reasons jointly over the object’s geometry and semantics to identify the task-relevant grasp affordance, then localizes this affordance within the image.
To bridge the resulting image-space localization into 3D, we lift it into a plane consistent with the camera’s projective geometry, yielding a task-informed grasp prior around the localized affordance.
Candidate grasps sampled within this prior are then refined through pose optimization that trades off collision avoidance against consistency with the task-relevant region, yielding grasps that are simultaneously geometrically feasible and appropriate to the task at hand.
In summary, we make the following four contributions:

We introduce TGrasp6D , a zero-shot framework for task-oriented 6DoF grasping from a single RGB-D observation and natural-language task instruction.

Our VLM-guided grasp synthesis pipeline grounds task-relevant affordances in image space, lifting them into 3D task-informed grasp priors, and refining candidate grasps through collision-aware pose optimization.

TGrasp6D achieves a 94% success rate on the TaskGrasp benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline by ∼ 𝟐𝟎 % \mathbf{\sim 20\%} .

We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to real-world manipulation on a Franka Research 3 robot across novel objects and task instructions.

1. We introduce TGrasp6D , a zero-shot framework for task-oriented 6DoF grasping from a single RGB-D observation and natural-language task instruction.

2. Our VLM-guided grasp synthesis pipeline grounds task-relevant affordances in image space, lifting them into 3D task-informed grasp priors, and refining candidate grasps through collision-aware pose optimization.

3. TGrasp6D achieves a 94% success rate on the TaskGrasp benchmark, outperforming the strongest baseline by ∼ 𝟐𝟎 % \mathbf{\sim 20\%} .

4. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer to real-world manipulation on a Franka Research 3 robot across novel objects and task instructions.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Task-Agnostic 6DoF Grasp Synthesis

Early methods [ 18 , 6 , 26 , 10 , 1 , 11 ] focused on generating stable 6DoF grasps conditioned only on object geometry, regardless of the downstream task. Sundermeyer et al. [ 18 ] root grasp contact points directly in the observed point cloud to reduce the search space for cluttered-scene grasping. Fang et al. [ 6 ] learn dense, temporally-consistent grasp perception from large-scale supervision, incorporating object center-of-mass to improve stability. Yuan et al. [ 26 ] unify grasping and placement in a single transformer that can optionally condition on a language goal, though this selects which object to act on rather than where on it to grasp. Iwase et al. [ 10 ] instead couple grasp prediction with 3D shape reconstruction, arguing that reasoning jointly about occluded geometry benefits both. Bukhari et al. [ 1 ] learn a probabilistic latent space over object shapes and use the inferred features to guide 𝕊 ​ 𝔼 ​ ( 3 ) \mathbb{SE}(3) diffusion-based grasp synthesis, improving robustness to noisy or partial observations over deterministic shape encoders. Most recently, Kulshrestha et al. [ 11 ] removes the need for grasp-specific training by querying a VLM to generate a candidate antipodal axis in image space, then lifting it into 3D via depth alignment. While these methods differ in representation and supervision, all optimize purely for stability and feasibility; we instead condition the search for a feasible pose on a task-relevant region identified before optimization begins.

## II-B Task-Oriented Grasping

A first line of work learns task-conditioned grasp selection from annotated data. Murali et al. [ 14 ] introduce TaskGrasp, the largest TOG benchmark to date, and propagate a semantic knowledge graph over objects and tasks to generalize to held-out instances. Tang et al. [ 20 ] replace this closed-world graph with open-ended knowledge queried from an LLM to generalize to novel concepts, and [ 19 ] extends the idea to both LLMs and VLMs over an expanded dataset. Deshpande et al. [ 4 ] scale data rather than knowledge sources, fine-tuning a VLM on a large synthetic corpus of cluttered, realistically-instructed scenes. Chu et al. [ 3 ] instead incorporate explicit physical-property reasoning over multi-step, flexible language instructions to condition 6DoF grasp generation. Since each method depends on a bespoke annotated or synthesized TOG corpus, generalization is bounded by that corpus’s coverage of the object-task-grasp space.

A second line of work couples task reasoning with an existing task-agnostic generator, applying semantics only after a candidate set has been produced. Dong et al. [ 5 ] retrieve grasp constraints from human demonstration videos and use them to filter task-agnostic candidates. Huang et al. [ 8 ] fold similar human-derived constraints directly into a guided diffusion sampler rather than filtering after the fact, while Tang et al. [ 22 ] use a VLM to ground task-relevant affordance regions but still select among poses returned by a fixed generator [ 6 ] . Because semantics are applied downstream of an already-fixed candidate distribution, a task-appropriate grasp the generator never proposed cannot be recovered by any amount of subsequent reasoning.

A third line of work restricts prediction to the image plane. Vuong et al. [ 24 ] treat grasp detection as a diffusion-based generative problem conditioned on language, Holomjova et al. [ 7 ] predict a task-relevant grasp rectangle via one-shot learning, Tang et al. [ 21 ] ground task and object jointly through a 2D vision-language model restricted to top-down grasping, and Li et al. [ 13 ] decompose objects into convex parts for LLM-guided part selection but likewise execute largely top-down grasps. A task-relevant affordance need not lie in the image plane, so planar prediction structurally excludes a broad class of otherwise feasible grasps. TGrasp6D avoids all three limitations, requiring no task-specific dataset, no upstream task-agnostic generator, and no restriction to the image plane.

## II-C Vision-Language Models for Affordance Reasoning in Manipulation

Beyond grasping, VLMs increasingly ground task-level affordances for general manipulation. Huang et al. [ 9 ] show an LLM can infer free-form affordances and, by querying a VLM, compose them into 3D value maps that a planner optimizes over, demonstrating that language-model priors transfer zero-shot to full trajectory synthesis. Yuan et al. [ 25 ] instruction-tune a VLM to output image keypoint affordances directly, generalizing across navigation, manipulation, and augmented reality, though the output remains a 2D point requiring a separate module to become an executable action. Qian et al. [ 16 ] use a VLM’s contextual reasoning to decide which occluding objects to remove in clutter, reasoning at the level of object visibility rather than part-level grasp selection on the target itself. [ 22 ] and [ 4 ] , discussed above, are the closest prior instances of VLM reasoning applied specifically to grasp affordances, but the former delegates pose synthesis to a task-free generator and the latter requires fine-tuning on a large synthetic corpus. We instead use a VLM purely to localize the task-relevant affordance, then lift and refine that region directly into a feasible 6DoF grasp through geometry-aware pose optimization.

2026-10-16.title: BubbleCBF: Constructive Safety for Second-Order Systems and Application to Autonomous Robot Navigation in Unknown Environments
2026-10-16.authors: Mani Amani , Mohammed Alyaseen , Zhirui Dai , Ki Myung Brian Lee , Nikolay Atanasov , Jorge Cortes
2026-10-16.abstract: Satisfying safety constraints for systems with second-order dynamics is challenging because a position constraint may require infeasible deceleration. Higher-order control barrier functions (CBFs) provide an approach for expressing safety conditions for such systems but feasibility depends on the system dynamics and available control authority. We develop a constructive approach for designing feasible safety constraints for second-order control-affine systems. Starting from a signed distance function (SDF), we construct collision-free spheres, i.e., bubbles , in position space, and use their quadratic geometry and overlap to construct a velocity-dependent safety constraint. The associated safe set is represented as a union of intersections and enforced through a quadratic-program safety filter. Under mild assumptions on the dynamics, bubble overlap, and design parameters, we prove that the quadratic-program-based controller is well defined, continuous in the system state, and renders the set forward invariant. We also derive sufficient conditions for feasibility under bounded inputs. We demonstrate that our BubbleCBF , applied to a differential-drive robot, achieves safe autonomous navigation in unknown environments. Videos and results are available at: https://existentialrobotics.org/bubblecbf/ .
2026-10-16.introduction:
Autonomous navigation in unknown environments requires a robot to simultaneously build a map of its surroundings and execute actions that avoid collisions.
Beyond representing obstacle-free space, robots with second-order dynamics must ensure that feasible actions exist to enforce safety constraints. Since actuation enters at the acceleration level, a robot may remain positionally safe while approaching the boundary too quickly for any admissible input to prevent escape.

Control barrier functions (CBFs) [ 1 ] provide a principled approach for safe control design. A CBF limits how quickly the safe set boundary may be approached with rate dependent on the barrier value.
Far from the boundary, the barrier value may decrease more quickly, while near the boundary, the permitted decrease becomes increasingly restrictive. Signed distance functions (SDFs) are natural CBF candidates because they encode free space using the distance to the nearest boundary [ 2 ] . SDF models of the environment can be estimated from point-cloud observations using data-driven and probabilistic approaches, including neural implicit methods [ 3 ] and Gaussian-process methods [ 4 ] . However, for second-order systems, a position-dependent safety constraint has relative degree two and cannot be enforced by formulating CBF constraints directly from SDF values. Higher-order CBFs (HOCBFs) [ 5 ] formulate safety constraints for high-relative-degree systems but do not by themselves guarantee the existence of feasible control inputs. A key challenge in safe control synthesis for second-order systems is therefore to construct valid safe sets in the joint position-velocity space whose invariance can be enforced with admissible inputs.

To address this challenge, we develop BubbleCBF , a safe control method for second-order control-affine systems. Starting from an SDF representation of the obstacles, we derive a velocity-dependent safe set from overlapping collision-free spheres, i.e., bubbles , illustrated in Fig. 1 . Our design extends the union-of-intersections CBF approach of [ 6 ] to quadratic constraints and guarantees forward-invariance of the safe set and feasibility under input constraints. Our contributions are summarized as follows.

We develop BubbleCBF , a safe control method for second-order control-affine systems that constructs velocity-dependent CBFs from position-space bubbles.

We develop BubbleCBF , a safe control method for second-order control-affine systems that constructs velocity-dependent CBFs from position-space bubbles.

Under mild assumptions on the system dynamics, bubble overlap, and input constraints, we prove that the quadratic program (QP) for BubbleCBF is feasible over the safe set, and renders the set forward invariant.

BubbleCBF enables safe autonomous navigation with a Clearpath Jackal robot in real-world environments, achieving a 100% success rate, compared to 50% for an SDF-CBF baseline, while increasing average obstacle clearance by 4.8%.

1. We develop BubbleCBF , a safe control method for second-order control-affine systems that constructs velocity-dependent CBFs from position-space bubbles.

2. Under mild assumptions on the system dynamics, bubble overlap, and input constraints, we prove that the quadratic program (QP) for BubbleCBF is feasible over the safe set, and renders the set forward invariant.

3. BubbleCBF enables safe autonomous navigation with a Clearpath Jackal robot in real-world environments, achieving a 100% success rate, compared to 50% for an SDF-CBF baseline, while increasing average obstacle clearance by 4.8%.

# II Related Work

CBFs have become a popular tool for safety-critical robot control [ 1 , 7 , 8 ] . For collision avoidance, SDFs [ 2 ] are a natural candidate to form safety constraints because they measure the minimum distance to occupied space. However, using an SDF to define a CBF constraint directly leads to challenges because SDF are often nonsmooth and can result in high relative degree constraints for high-order systems.

Existing work addresses these challenges in several ways. In [ 9 ] , dual variables are used to formulate CBF constraints for nonsmooth distance functions between polytopes. Other approaches construct smooth approximations of distance functions [ 10 ] , while nonsmooth CBF theory handles nonsmooth barrier compositions directly [ 11 ] . High relative degree is addressed using exponential and higher-order CBF constructions [ 12 , 5 ] . Long et al. [ 13 ] learn SDF approximations online and use them to construct robust CBF constraints for safe navigation in unknown environments. Barbosa and Tumova [ 14 ] address both nonsmoothness and high relative degree by constructing a smooth approximation of the distance field and its derivatives and applying higher-order CBF techniques.
In contrast, we neither smooth nor differentiate the SDF. We use only SDF queries to construct collision-free balls [ 15 ] , whose quadratic geometry allows us to construct a velocity-dependent safe subset of their union for second-order systems.

Regularity is especially challenging for nonsmooth safe sets composed of multiple barrier functions [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] . Alyaseen et al. [ 6 ] address this by enforcing componentwise CBF constraints with state-dependent relaxation, avoiding explicit switching between active components and yielding a continuous optimization-based controller. We extend this approach to a union of bubble intersections and derive the corresponding quadratic barriers and feasibility conditions for second-order dynamics and bounded inputs.

Bubble-based representations have also been used in robotics to cover collision-free configuration space with overlapping local regions [ 19 , 15 ] . Sampling-based neighborhood graphs (SNG) [ 20 ] cover free configuration space with overlapping neighborhoods, such as balls, and construct feedback navigation functions over the resulting graph. Invariant configuration-space bubbles [ 21 ] lift configuration-space bubbles to control-invariant subsets of the state space and enforce invariance using a command governor. In contrast, we construct a CBF over a union of overlapping bubbles and enforce it using a continuous QP safety filter for general second-order systems.
Moreover, we show that this QP is always feasible within the safe set, and hence guarantees forward invariance of the safe set. Geometry-aware mixed-integer linear programming model predictive control (MILP-MPC) [ 22 ] combines long-horizon planning with Minkowski-based CBFs, accounting explicitly for robot geometry and environment topology at the cost of mixed-integer optimization. Our approach instead operates on an SDF-derived bubble cover, enabling online safety filtering in unknown environments without mixed-integer planning or exact robot-obstacle distance computations.

2026-10-16.title: Optimally Trading Energy for Information through Speed Trajectory Optimization of Sustainably Powered Mobile Robots
2026-10-16.authors: Kavin M. Govindarajan , Dimitra Panagou , Chris Vermillion
2026-10-16.abstract: Sustainably powered mobile robots enable long-duration observational missions by harvesting energy from the environment. However, effective autonomy requires the robots to make decisions as to how to allocate this energy to maximize information quality over time. In this paper, we study a persistent (infinite-horizon) speed trajectory optimization problem that is posed as a periodic optimal control problem in which a robot repeatedly traverses a fixed closed path, coupling a super-linear propulsion cost with dynamic information gain and decay. Using the information-theoretic quantity of clarity as an information metric, we first derive the necessary conditions for optimal control. We then derive a number of specialized follow-on properties, which characterize (i) the nature of the optimal control when points on the path are of varying importance and when they are of equal importance, along with (ii) a high-speed information limit that is approached when energy reserves approach infinity. We illustrate the information-optimal speed trajectories on a simple example in order to showcase key trends that are followed under the optimized speed profile. This is followed by a simulation study based on the persistent characterization of salinity in the Chesapeake Bay, illustrating the practical merit of applying the results from this work.

2026-10-16.title: Race to Recovery: Designing Advanced Safety Systems for Autonomous Driving via Learning Autonomous Racing

2026-10-16.abstract: Vehicles that lose control at the handling limit through icing, hydroplaning, or an abrupt evasive maneuver fall outside the operating envelope of production safety systems such as electronic stability control, which focus on preventing instability rather than recovering from it. Expert drivers regain authority in these conditions by drifting. Existing autonomous recovery approaches are validated on idealized scenarios, define “recovered” states empirically and inconsistently, or rely on offline-planned trajectories rather than acting online. We address these gaps by first training a racing policy with reinforcement learning that learns drifting as a time-optimal maneuver, then adapting it to recovery through continued training with a minimum-time reward. We define recovery relative to a phase-plane-grounded stable equilibrium and introduce Gym-Khana for controller training and evaluation. Across 294 initial loss-of-control states, the transferred policy improves recovery by 186.8 % 186.8\% over a Stanley path tracker and outperforms both a nonlinear model predictive controller and a recovery-only policy trained from scratch, while also recovering faster on states the baseline can already handle. An ablation shows that racing pretraining, rather than broader initial-state exposure alone, drives this gain. Deployed on a physical 1:10-scale F1TENTH vehicle using system identification, actuator-lag modelling, and domain randomization, the transferred policy outperforms Stanley on every tested loss-of-control state, including recovering 50 % 50\% of the time from a hard state the baseline never recovers from.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Usually, driving takes place in the linear tire regime, where manual inputs or conventional controllers perform well. Controlling a vehicle safely at the limit of handling remains an open challenge. Events that could cause loss of control, such as driving on ice, high-speed hydroplaning, or a sudden evasive maneuver, are rare but dangerous, and excessive speed alone is a factor in roughly a third of all traffic fatalities [ 1 ] . They are also the events an advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) is least able to help with. Production systems such as electronic stability control (ESC) are designed to keep the vehicle inside a conservative, linear-tire handling envelope, braking individual wheels to suppress the onset of tire saturation. That design is well suited to preventing a loss of control, but not to act once one has occurred: beyond this stable envelope, suppressing instability is no longer the same problem as recovering from it.

Expert rally and drift drivers, by contrast, routinely operate at the limit by “drifting”, where they intentionally saturate the tires to sustain large sideslip angles. Saturation decouples the direction the vehicle points from the direction it travels, giving the driver direct lateral control through two inputs, steering and throttle, rather than one, enabling more agile vehicle control [ 2 ] . This is the authority an expert exploits when control is lost, while current production safety systems cannot. Recent research has begun to reproduce this capability autonomously in the service of active safety, using drift-based control to regain control of the vehicle in scenarios where conventional safety systems fall short [ 3 , 4 ] . We call this task recovery : returning an out-of-control vehicle to a stable driving state while keeping it on its intended path. We aim to develop a controller that recovers from the broadest possible set of loss-of-control states and recovers in the least time while remaining within the track. Our motivation is to endow an ADAS with the recovery skill of an expert driver.

Existing autonomous approaches to recovery, however, leave three elements unresolved. Each addresses a single narrow, idealized scenario from a fixed initial condition, so nothing is established about the range of loss-of-control states from which a controller can recover [ 5 , 6 ] . Each defines the “recovered” state empirically, and differently, so no two results are comparable. And the one method validated on a real vehicle relies on a trajectory planned offline in advance [ 3 ] , whereas an intervention must act online, from whatever state the vehicle is in.

A recovery controller that closes these gaps must therefore act online, without a precomputed plan, across a broad domain of loss-of-control states in the saturated-tire regime. That is the regime of racing and drifting at the limit of handling, where reinforcement learning (RL) has been shown to outperform state-of-the-art model predictive control (MPC) [ 7 , 8 ] .
We therefore derive the controller with RL, focusing on the control task in particular, assuming knowledge of the vehicle state, and leave perception, state estimation, and planning out of our scope. The open question is how to set up training.

Our central insight is that the answer lies in racing. The recovery task has much in common with drifting: both are defined primarily by a large sideslip angle and yaw rate, but where a racing driver produces the drift state intentionally, a loss of control is an unwanted drift that can lead to a collision. A policy that has learned to race by drifting has, in the process, learned to manage saturated tires and large sideslip angles across the whole regime, which is precisely the competency that recovery requires. We therefore investigate the following hypothesis: a policy first trained to race with drifting, and then adapted to recovery, recovers control more reliably than a policy trained on recovery alone, and more reliably than classical control baselines. To test it, we train a racing policy in Gym-Khana, a simulator we built for prototyping vehicle control at the limit, adapt it to recovery by continuing training under a minimum-time recovery reward, and deploy the result on a 1:10-scale F1TENTH vehicle [ 9 ] .

In summary, our contributions are:

A racing-to-recovery transfer learning method, which builds a recovery controller by pretraining a policy to race with drifting and then adapting it to recovery. Over a grid of 294 294 initial states spanning conditions more extreme than any seen in training, the transferred policy recovers 186.8 % 186.8\% more than a Stanley path tracker, and outperforms both a model predictive controller and a recovery-only policy trained from scratch.
Additionally, we demonstrate that even non-specialized racing policies recover competently with no recovery-specific training (Sections IV-C and V-C ).

Gym-Khana, a simulator for prototyping vehicle control at the limit of handling, built around the drift-capable single-track model used here, on which both the racing and recovery policies are trained (Section IV ). It is released open-source, with online documentation. 1 1 1 Gym-Khana simulator: https://github.com/TeoIlie/Gym-Khana ; documentation: https://gym-khana.readthedocs.io

A rigorous, phase-plane-grounded definition of vehicle recovery that formalizes the “recovered” state as a tolerance region about a stable equilibrium, together with a set of experimental recovery metrics that make recovery controllers comparable over a common domain of loss-of-control states (Sections III-B and V-A ).

Validation on a physical F1TENTH vehicle, enabled by a sim-to-real pipeline of system identification, actuator-lag modelling, and domain randomization. Over 179 179 runs from three real loss-of-control initial states of increasing difficulty, the transferred policy outperforms the Stanley baseline on every state (Section VI ).
