2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Control at the Limit of Handling: From MPC to RL

Control at the limit of handling has historically been approached with optimal control, most commonly MPC. The model predictive contouring control (MPCC) formulation, which maximizes progress along a reference centreline subject to track constraints, has been applied successfully to both autonomous drone and vehicle racing [ 10 , 11 ] , and model-based methods have achieved controlled drifting on full-scale vehicles [ 2 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] . The cost of the paradigm is a nonconvex optimization over combined-slip tire forces at every step of the control loop, which bounds model fidelity, horizon length and control rate even with efficient modelling and solver tooling [ 15 , 16 ] , and a cost function that must be hand-tuned.

RL has since overtaken these methods at the limit. In the highly realistic Gran Turismo racing simulator, a policy was the first to achieve superhuman lap times, learning from a reward of centreline progress and a wall-collision penalty—the MPCC objective, optimized directly rather than through a planner [ 17 ] . Two years later, “Swift” became the first system to outperform champion human pilots at drone racing, using onboard sensing alone [ 18 ] . A companion study compared RL against optimal control on the same task, found RL to outperform it, and identified the reason: the fundamental advantage of RL is “not that it optimizes its objective better but that it optimizes a better objective” [ 7 ] —it optimizes the objective of interest directly, rather than through a planner and a limited intermediate representation.

The same progression has played out in drifting. Early work learned drift control in simulation [ 19 , 20 ] and transferred a policy rewarded for path tracking and sideslip onto a 1:10-scale car using domain randomization on tire friction [ 21 ] ; more recent work has reached full-scale vehicles and increasingly fuses learning with physics-based structure [ 22 , 23 ] . Czechmanowski et al. [ 8 ] brought the two threads together with a policy trained on a single-track model with combined-slip Pacejka tires and deployed zero-shot on a 1:8-scale car, the first controller to outperform both expert human drivers and a state-of-the-art MPC at racing. Drifting emerged there organically , as the fastest way around the track, from nothing more than a progress reward and an out-of-bounds penalty. Sim-to-real transfer combined actuator-lag modelling, learning-based system identification and targeted domain randomization—the three ingredients we build on in Section IV-D .

Across racing and drifting, then, RL is the strongest demonstrated approach to control at the limit of handling, outperforming both expert humans and state-of-the-art MPC. We adopt it on that evidence, and scope our own baseline claim accordingly in Section V-A .

## II-B Drifting for Active Safety and Recovery

An emerging body of work explores safety applications of drift-like maneuvers. Yin et al. [ 5 ] applied deep RL to stabilizing yaw motion following a high-speed rear-end collision in simulation, improving over a baseline of no stabilization but with no comparison against alternative controllers; an episode counted as safely completed when the vehicle came to a stop. Li et al. [ 3 ] planned a drift-based U-turn to prevent a head-on collision with an obstacle and demonstrated it on a real vehicle, where it recovered in conditions that defeat automatic emergency braking and steering; its trajectory is computationally intensive enough to require offline pre-planning, so the method cannot run in real time. A nonlinear MPC has been used for path tracking with drifting to avoid a collision at a T-junction, outperforming an anti-lock braking baseline and a feedback-feedforward steering controller [ 4 , 24 ] . Most recently, Lee and Cong [ 6 ] learned a policy from sub-optimal demonstrations that recovers from excessive oversteer while avoiding obstacles, outperforming both pure RL and behaviour cloning. Loss of control is induced by a virtual kick plate, and recovery is defined there as maintaining less than 1 ∘ 1^{\circ} of sideslip for 100 timesteps [ 6 ] .

Together these works exhibit the three gaps that our work addresses, set out in Section I : highly specific task constructions lacking general applicability, a recovered state defined differently and empirically by each, and one real-vehicle validation that depends on an offline plan.

2026-10-16.title: Clarity-Driven Adaptive Mission Planning for a Solar-Powered Autonomous Surface Vessel
2026-10-16.authors: Kavin M. Govindarajan , Kaleb Ben Naveed , David Li , Devansh R. Agrawal , Mary Maceda , Matthew Bryant , Dimitra Panagou , Chris Vermillion
2026-10-16.abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive methodology, backed by simulation and experimental results, for an adaptive mission planning strategy that is mathematically grounded in the maximization of the information-driven quantity of clarity . In particular, the methodology introduced in this work addresses the use of sustainably powered autonomous surface vessels (ASVs) to perform scientific missions that prioritize locations of maximum interest. Because these locations of maximum interest are not known a priori but are rather identified based on in-situ measurements, online adaptation is essential for mission planning. Furthermore, the reliance on a limited-power renewable resource requires an adaptation strategy that maximizes information gathering subject to mobility restrictions imposed by the renewable resource. Our approach addresses these challenges through a clarity-driven ergodic search, where clarity represents a mathematical quantity that has been rigorously linked to differential (information) entropy. In our approach, a target clarity map is adapted online to reflect the prioritization of certain areas based on in-situ measurements, and an ergodic path planner continually re-plans based on the target clarity map and ASV speed limitations (driven by the renewable propulsion source). Focusing on a solar-powered ASV, we present simulations and experiments conducted at Jordan Lake, North Carolina, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
2026-10-16.introduction:
The collection of spatiotemporally varying data is critical for many environmental and engineering applications: characterizing wind and ocean currents enables the identification of energy-harvesting sites [ 1 ] , surface temperature data supports improved weather forecasting [ 2 ] , and salinity data enhances understanding of climate-driven processes [ 3 ] . While fixed platforms (e.g., moored sensor arrays [ 4 ] and high-frequency radar [ 5 ] ) enable data acquisition over extended periods, there has been recent emphasis on using mobile observational platforms that can adjust their physical locations to target areas of interest, which are often unknown a priori and can change over time. Mobile observation can be accomplished through vessels equipped with finite amounts of energy (e.g., diesel-powered research vessels [ 6 ] and undersea gliders [ 7 , 8 ] ) or through renewably powered platforms (e.g., sailing drones, wave gliders, or solar-powered autonomous surface vessels (ASVs)) that enable longer-term missions. Example applications include tracking plumes of pollutant or contaminant dispersion [ 9 , 10 ] , adaptive front-following for estimating transport and mixing processes [ 11 , 12 ] , and resource measurement (e.g., wind or ocean current) for siting energy-harvesting devices [ 13 , 14 ] .

Regardless of the motivation for adaptation or whether the mobile observational platform at hand is powered by a finite or renewable resource, the basic objective is the same: maximize the collection of useful scientific information under a limited energy resource . In the case of a finite energy resource, the limitations map to a restricted range that is influenced by the device’s velocity profile. In the case of a renewable energy resource, the total range is not limited, but the achievable velocity profile is constrained by the available power. In either case, both the energy and information resources evolve over time. Notably, the information known about the scientific resource at any given location can increase due to sensor measurements but can also decay if that point goes unvisited for a long time. Ultimately, therefore, a unified framework for adaptive mission planning should satisfy three features:

Rigorous consideration of an evolving information field (where information is gained through observation but will also decay over time at points that go unvisited), based on observations taken;

Explicit consideration of an evolving battery state of charge, based on the environmental (solar) energy input and energy used for mobility;

Real-time adaptation based on in-situ scientific measurements.

Information-driven planning has been heavily popularized (see [ 15 , 16 ] ), with efforts often tying information measures to statistical quantities like entropy. To capture complex spatial fields, recent robotic information gathering frameworks employ nonstationary spatiotemporal models for autonomous surface vehicles [ 17 ] . However, energy constraints in such formulations are typically imposed as simplistic “budgets” [ 18 ] (e.g., total distance, time, or control effort as a surrogate [ 19 ] ) without accounting for vehicle power dynamics or state of charge (SOC) [ 20 ] . Furthermore, standard IPP formulations generally assume non-decaying information, optimizing over truncated horizons for one-off coverage. Consequently, these approaches are prone to local extrema and struggle to sustain long-term tracking of dynamic scientific resources where unvisited locations decay in certainty over time.

A notable exception addressing this limitation is the information-theoretic quantity clarity [ 21 ] , derived from differential entropy [ 22 ] , which explicitly models time-varying certainty decay. A natural planning strategy for clarity is ergodic search [ 23 ] . By matching the Fourier coefficients of the vehicle’s trajectory statistics to a target spatial distribution (TSD), ergodic control inherently balances exploration and exploitation over long horizons without heuristic switching. Recent efforts have begun incorporating energy awareness into ergodic control: Seewald et al. [ 24 ] integrated battery models for multi-agent coverage, while Naveed et al. [ 25 ] introduced clarity-driven ergodic search under SOC constraints. However, existing energy-aware ergodic methods rely on static target distributions defined offline, or achieve persistence through multi-agent duty cycling to fixed charging stations rather than optimizing trajectory-level energy dynamics for continuous operation of a single sustainably powered vehicle. In contrast, our work enables real-time, online adaptation of the target clarity map based on in-situ scientific measurements, allowing the planner to dynamically re-prioritize informative regions while explicitly controlling speed to satisfy energy constraints.

The present work extends the framework of [ 25 ] by (i) enabling online adaptation according to in-situ measurements, (ii) augmenting the ergodic adaptive mission planner with energy-informed speed control, and (iii) validating the integrated framework experimentally. In particular, we utilize a spatiotemporal Gaussian Process Kalman Filter (STGPKF) to maintain real-time estimates of the prediction means and variances of the scientific quantity of interest, based on real-time, in-situ measurements. From the prediction mean and variance models, we generate both an actual clarity map and a target clarity map . These maps jointly define the ergodic objective, allowing the controller to prioritize scientifically meaningful regions as the environment evolves. Additionally, following our earlier work [ 26 ] that established the optimality of piecewise constant speeds when the battery state of charge did not satisfy tightened saturation limits at equality, this speed control approach is incorporated into the ergodic planning problem.

To ground the problem in a real deployment scenario, we focus on a solar-powered ASV, namely the SeaTrac SP-48 (shown in Fig. 1 ). Both simulation and field trials consider a mission domain in Jordan Lake, North Carolina, where the scientific objective is to characterize the evolving wind resource. Motivated by wind turbine siting studies, wherein regions with wind speeds close to a rated value are of primary interest, we construct the target clarity map from the STGPKF wind speed estimates and their deviation from the rated speed.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows:

We develop an energy-aware, adaptive clarity-driven ergodic control framework that unifies a statistically rigorous information metric with energy-aware speed control.

We introduce an STGPKF-based method that generates real-time actual and target clarity maps from online measurements, enabling fully adaptive, science-aware planning.

We validate the complete framework using both simulations and field experiments on the SeaTrac SP-48 ASV at Jordan Lake, demonstrating that the system actively targets informative regions while respecting energy and speed constraints.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the information (clarity) and energy models used throughout this work. Section III presents the problem formulation and proposed control framework. Section IV evaluates performance in simulation. Section V presents field results from a wind characterization mission on the SeaTrac ASV. Section VI concludes and outlines future research directions.

2026-10-16.title: A Phenomenology of Neural Geometry in Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-16.authors: Mozes Jacobs , Aiden Swann , Mathilde Papillon , Siddharth Boppana , Fenil R. Doshi , Usha Bhalla , Thomas Icard , Matt Feiszli , Thomas McGrath , Vasudev Shyam , Demba Ba , Leon Bergen , Nina Miolane , Owen Lewis , Jack Merullo , Ekdeep Singh Lubana , Atticus Geiger , Matthew Kowal , Thomas Fel

2026-10-16.abstract:
Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it?
Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional.
Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models.
We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp.
The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation.
We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes.
Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept’s shape carries as much importance as its readability.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric. Robotic systems operate in three-dimensional space through articulated kinematic structures, while the objects they manipulate and the tasks they perform have their own geometric organization, including symmetries, constraints, and phases of interaction. Any general manipulation policy must contend with this structure, and vision-language-action (VLA) models have become the dominant paradigm for building such policies ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025b ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ; Deshpande et al., 2026 ) .
VLAs inherit visual and semantic priors from backbones pretrained on internet-scale data, including vision encoders ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Oquab et al., 2024 ; Zhai et al., 2023 ) , language models ( Touvron et al., 2023 ; Gemma Team et al., 2024 ) , and full vision-language models ( Driess et al., 2023 ; Beyer et al., 2024 ; Deitke et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2024 ) .
This data has grown by orders of magnitude in volume and diversity ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ; Walke et al., 2023 ; Bu et al., 2025 ; Deshpande et al., 2026 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) , with generalization improving along power-law-like trends ( Lin et al., 2025 ) .
The resulting systems are increasingly capable, general, and even deployed in the real world ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025b ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025a ; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025 ; Figure AI, 2026 ; Gemini Robotics Team, 2026 ; Figure AI, 2025b ; Figure AI, 2025a ) .

How such competence is reflected in the representations of these VLAs is the subject of a nascent literature ( Qi et al., 2025 ; Qi et al., 2026 ; Swann et al., 2026 ; Buurmeijer et al., 2026 ; Häon et al., 2025 ; Bhardwaj et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Molinari et al., 2025 ; Khan et al., 2025 ; Grant et al., 2026 ; Goyal, 2026 ; Yang and Mokalla, 2026 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) .
In particular, one line of work uses probes, testing whether a quantity of interest can be read out from the model’s activations ( Joseph et al., 2026 ; Buurmeijer et al., 2026 ; Bhardwaj et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ; Molinari et al., 2025 ; Grant et al., 2026 ; Yang and Mokalla, 2026 ) .
A second trains sparse autoencoders (SAEs) ( Cunningham et al., 2024 ; Bussmann et al., 2024 ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024b ; Fel et al., 2025 ; Costa et al., 2025 ; Hindupur et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ; Lubana et al., 2026 ; Bhalla et al., 2026b ; Templeton et al., 2024 ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024a ; Lieberum et al., 2024 ; Thasarathan et al., 2025 ; Makhzani and Frey, 2014 ) to discover concepts without supervision ( Swann et al., 2026 ; Khan et al., 2025 ; Grant et al., 2026 ) , and the discovered features even provide control over the policy via steering Joseph et al. (2025) .

Both lines of work share a limitation. A probe can ensure that a variable is decodable, yet says nothing about the structure through which the model “realizes” it, and an SAE inherits the linear representation hypothesis (LRH) ( Park et al., 2024 ; Costa et al., 2025 ) , which casts each concept as a single direction in activation space and therefore fixes that structure in advance.
Interpretability for language and vision models, conscious of this limitation, has moved beyond the single direction to multi-dimensional features and curved geometry ( Modell et al., 2025 ; Feucht et al., 2026 ; Wurgaft et al., 2026 ; Bhalla et al., 2026a ; Fel et al., 2026b ; Fel et al., 2026a ; Engels et al., 2025 ; Lubana et al., 2026 ; Karkada et al., 2026 ; Dooms and Gauderis, 2025 ; Kantamneni and Tegmark, 2025 ; Gurnee et al., 2026 ; Yocum et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2025a ; Sarfati et al., 2026 ; Costa et al., 2025 ; Pearce et al., 2025 ; Diego-Simón et al., 2024 ; Chung et al., 2018 ; Cohen et al., 2020 ; Hosseini et al., 2026 ; Dhimoila et al., 2026 ; Fel et al., 2025 ; Gorton, 2024 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Tvetkova et al., 2025 ; Park et al., 2025b ; Park et al., 2026 ) , a line of work now gathered under the name of Neural Geometry ( Geiger et al., 2026 ) .

Do VLAs realize their variables through similarly rich geometry? Two facts suggest they might.
First, vision models, including the backbones VLAs inherit, already carry colors, shadows, and position as multi-dimensional features rather than single directions ( Fel et al., 2026b ; Fel et al., 2026a ; Pach et al., 2026 ; Uselis et al., 2026 ) .
Second, representations tend to inherit the symmetries of their training data, so that cyclic concepts, for example, come to be arranged on circles ( Karkada et al., 2026 ) .
The variables a manipulation policy must track, such as poses, distances, contacts, and task phase, are geometric objects with symmetries of their own before the network ever represents them.

We take up this question and make the following contributions:

Realized geometry as a lens for VLA interpretability. We formalize the distinction between concept realization —the capacity to extract information about a concept under a given readout—and its realized geometry —the structure activations trace as the concept varies. Linear readability establishes only that a concept is present, while its realized geometry determines how its values are structured and whether they can be manipulated.

Realized geometry as a lens for VLA interpretability. We formalize the distinction between concept realization —the capacity to extract information about a concept under a given readout—and its realized geometry —the structure activations trace as the concept varies. Linear readability establishes only that a concept is present, while its realized geometry determines how its values are structured and whether they can be manipulated.

A taxonomy of realized geometry in MolmoBot. Combining controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we chart the realized geometry of seven control concepts: gripper state, end-effector position, distance to the target, target object position, contact, task phase, and wrist orientation. We find this geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts: joint limits leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, while the numerical precision of the embedding splits distance into orthogonal coarse (meter-scale) and fine (centimeter-scale) rulers.

Real-world transfer. We reproduce these geometries in π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025b ) and MolmoAct2 ( Fang et al., 2026 ) on the real-world DROID dataset ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) , indicating they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation.

2026-10-16.title: Persistent Profile-Guided Reset-Free Recovery Improves Final Gait Selection after Irreversible Leg Damage
2026-10-16.authors: Minjoong Kim
2026-10-16.abstract: Damage-recovery algorithms often rank gaits from short trials, yet a gait that performs well briefly may not remain effective during continued execution. In reset-free recovery, each trial also changes the physical state inherited by the next. We introduce persistent profile-guided reset-free recovery (PGRR), which predicts multiple outcomes over repeated gait execution and uses conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot. Across 108 matched MuJoCo tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock, PGRR improves final quality by 0.106 and slot-averaged recovery quality (SRQ) by 0.044 relative to an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline, while reducing low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points. Final-quality gains occur in all three damage classes. Against no adaptation, PGRR also improves final quality and reduces low-quality failures, whereas the aggregate SRQ difference is inconclusive. Development ablations identify conservative uncertainty handling as the clearest supported contributor to the observed gains. These results show that PGRR can identify stronger post-damage gaits under continuous physical state and that final-gait quality and recovery-summary performance provide complementary evidence for evaluating reset-free recovery.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Robots enable monitoring and inspection in environments that are difficult or hazardous for people to access. Deployments in nuclear facilities and underwater survey and inspection illustrate the value of performing these tasks remotely or autonomously [ 1 , 2 ] . As missions extend from individual inspections to repeated operation over days or weeks, maintaining mobility with limited human intervention becomes increasingly important [ 1 ] . For a legged robot, structural damage creates a direct obstacle to continued operation because a gait developed for an intact body may no longer produce effective locomotion. Recovering useful motion with the remaining limbs is therefore an important step toward sustained autonomy [ 3 , 4 ] .

Post-damage adaptation has advanced through self-modeling, which revises a robot’s body model after component loss [ 3 ] , and Intelligent Trial and Error (IT&E), which uses a library of behaviors computed offline to guide a small number of online tests [ 4 ] . Reset-free Trial and Error (RTE) further accounts for the physical state left by each preceding attempt [ 5 ] . RTE evaluates recovery while successive trials inherit the state produced by earlier ones, but this does not by itself characterize how well the finally selected gait performs when executed separately after adaptation. This distinction matters because every attempted gait changes the robot’s pose, velocity, and contacts. A search may eventually identify an effective gait even if some intermediate trials perform poorly, while a gait that appears promising during a short test may deteriorate during continued execution.

To address this distinction, we propose persistent profile-guided reset-free recovery (PGRR). In an offline stage, candidate gaits are repeatedly executed to learn how their performance changes beyond an initial short trial. These profiles describe survival, early-to-late locomotion quality, final quality, path-related performance, and energy use over continued execution. After damage, PGRR uses these profiles and their predictive uncertainty to select a promising gait for a short online probe. The observed performance is then used to update the predictions, while the best gait identified so far is executed between probes as the incumbent bridge. The robot is not reset between trials: each new probe starts from the physical state left by the preceding motion. In this way, PGRR uses short online tests to search for a gait that is expected to remain effective during continued execution while preserving the robot’s physical state throughout recovery.

We implement PGRR on a simulated hexapod and evaluate it on a frozen holdout of 108 matched condition–seed tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock. Locomotion quality combines forward motion, path tracking, energy use, and transition stability. We report both SRQ, which summarizes recovery under a fixed scoring budget, and the quality of a separate 3-s execution of the selected gait. Relative to the tested IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline, PGRR improves final quality by 0.106 and SRQ by 0.044, while reducing low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points. Final quality improves in all three damage classes.

This work makes three contributions. First, we distinguish final-gait quality from the overall recovery summary in reset-free damage recovery. Second, we introduce PGRR, which combines repeated-execution profiles, conservative uncertainty-aware selection, short online probes, and incumbent bridging without resetting the robot. Third, we evaluate the method on 108 matched MuJoCo tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock. PGRR improves final-gait quality and reduces low-quality failures, while SRQ gains depend on the comparison baseline. These results show that final performance and recovery-summary performance capture complementary aspects of reset-free recovery.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Work

Quality-diversity methods construct collections of distinct, high-performing behaviors [ 6 , 7 ] . These collections allow a damaged robot to search among previously generated options rather than learn every movement from scratch. Work following IT&E examines repertoire size in hexapods [ 8 ] , chooses among libraries suited to different situations with APROL [ 9 ] , and uses hierarchical libraries for simulated and physical damage recovery [ 10 , 11 ] . PGRR instead emphasizes how a candidate is expected to behave across repeated execution and how observations revise those expectations during recovery. Its experiments compare policies using a shared candidate pool and trial budget; the specific IT&E-inspired implementation is defined in the experimental protocol.

Rapid motor adaptation adjusts locomotion to changing terrain and payload [ 12 ] , whereas the present study concerns permanent loss or immobilization of leg components. Risk-sensitive methods also inform the choice of adaptation trials. Safe Bayesian optimization uses probabilistic performance models to seek improvement while enforcing safety constraints under stated assumptions [ 13 , 14 ] . Safety-aware damage recovery can initialize these models with behavior predicted in simulation [ 15 ] . PGRR uses uncertainty penalties and observed viability thresholds to select and extend trials, without claiming the formal safety guarantees of those methods. We examine both the quality summarized across recovery and the motion produced by the final selected controller in a separate execution interval.

A mesh of interceptors defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted
arrival point of an approaching object. This is a recurring task in multi-agent
robotics: N N agents, each covering a disc of radius r r , spread over a
probability density so that a point drawn from it falls within some agent’s
disc. We give closed forms for the quantities that bound performance before any
policy is chosen, and validate each by Monte Carlo. The uncertainty of a point
predicted by extrapolating a noisy linear track follows from least-squares
variance propagation plus a delta-method term for the uncertain arrival time,
agreeing with simulation to within 1.8 % 1.8\% . The coverage probability of a
packed mesh admits a closed form accurate to 0.007 0.007 absolute, with a
volumetric analogue. A naive area ratio misses a ceiling: while agents stay at
least 2 ​ r 2r apart, no mesh exceeds 90.69 % 90.69\% coverage in the plane or 74.05 % 74.05\% in a volume. This ceiling belongs to the separation constraint, not to the
problem — permitting overlap substitutes Kershner’s thinnest-covering density
and removes it, the better regime above a crossover at p = 0.80 p=0.80 . Hexagonal
packing is optimal among five arrangements; the centroidal-Voronoi
configuration coverage control supplies reaches only half its coverage at small
budgets. The Gaussian assumption is conservative under heavy tails and
anisotropy but fragile under bias: a one-sigma aim-point offset costs 14 14 points of coverage. A repositioning team must also choose a commit time, and
the admissible window can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic
placement attains 85 % 85\% of what the configuration permits while centralised
PPO averages 15 % 15\% over three trainer seeds, with a paired bootstrap against a
null policy containing zero at every seed. We argue such ceilings should be
computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.
2026-10-16.introduction:
A fixed site is approached by an airborne object on a ballistic or
near-ballistic course. A sensor tracks the object and predicts where it will
cross a defensive plane standing off from the site, with an error that shrinks
as the track lengthens. A mesh of small interceptors, each able to engage
whatever comes within a radius r r of it, must spread itself across that
predicted crossing point and be on station before the object arrives. Three
questions decide whether the concept is viable at all, and none of them is
about control: how many interceptors the prediction’s uncertainty demands, how
early the mesh must commit to a position, and whether any commit time satisfies
both the sharpness of the prediction and the distance the vehicles must fly.
All three can be answered from geometry, before a controller exists.

We strip the application to that geometry. Consider a team of N N agents
constrained to a plane, each able to cover a disc of radius r r centred on
itself. A point of interest will arrive somewhere in that plane at a known
future time; the agents hold a noisy prediction of where.
The team must distribute itself so that the arriving point falls inside some
agent’s disc. This is a coverage problem in the sense of Cortés et al. [ 1 ] , specialised in two ways that turn out to
matter a great deal. The density is a prediction with a quantified and
time-varying error rather than a static importance map. And success is binary
and instantaneous — a point either lands within r r of some agent or it does
not — rather than an integrated sensing cost.

Tasks of this shape invite a multi-agent reinforcement-learning treatment, and
the recipe is easy to follow: define an environment, shape a reward, train a
policy, report a success rate. The difficulty is that a bare success rate on a
hand-designed task carries almost no information. Whether 16 % 16\% is a failure
or a near-optimal result depends on what the configuration permits, and that
quantity is rarely computed. Henderson et al. [ 30 ] ,
Colas et al. [ 31 ] and Agarwal et al. [ 32 ] have each documented how fragile deep
reinforcement-learning comparisons are to precisely this kind of missing
context — unreported baselines, too few seeds, and point estimates quoted
without dispersion.

This paper supplies the missing context for the coverage task above, in closed
form, and then validates the assumptions the closed form rests on. We
contribute:

the uncertainty σ \sigma of the predicted arrival point, propagated from
per-fix sensor noise through a least-squares track fit, with a
delta-method term that a common heuristic omits at a cost of up to 9.5 × 9.5\times (Section IV );

the uncertainty σ \sigma of the predicted arrival point, propagated from
per-fix sensor noise through a least-squares track fit, with a
delta-method term that a common heuristic omits at a cost of up to 9.5 × 9.5\times (Section IV );

the coverage probability attainable by N N agents at given σ \sigma and r r , in the plane and in a volume, including a ceiling no mesh can exceed
at any size (Section V );

an empirical check that hexagonal packing is the right arrangement, and a
quantification of how far the standard coverage-control answer falls
short of it on this objective (Section VI );

a robustness study of the Gaussian assumption, separating departures that
make the law conservative from the one that breaks it
(Section VII );

the admissible window of commit times for a team that must physically
reposition, which can be empty (Section VIII ).

Section X reports what happened when a learned placement
policy was trained on this task, across three trainer seeds, and argues that
the outcome is better explained by these bounds than by any property of the
learner. Section XI states what the analysis omits.

Each individual result applies standard material — ordinary least squares,
the delta method, densest packing of equal spheres. The claim is that
computing them first , and reporting them alongside learned
results, changes what those results mean, and that this is not current
practice.

# II Related Work

## II-A Coverage control

The canonical formulation distributes agents over a density to minimise an
integrated sensing cost, and is solved by Lloyd-type descent to a centroidal
Voronoi configuration [ 1 , 2 ] . The framework has been extended
to agents that learn the density online [ 3 ] and developed into
a general theory of distributed robotic networks [ 4 ] . More
recently, graph neural networks have been used to let agents exploit multi-hop
information and beat the purely local classical controller [ 5 ] .

The objective in all of this work is continuous: a weighted integral of the
distance from each point to its nearest agent. Our objective is the probability
that a single draw lands within a fixed radius of some agent. The two are not
equivalent, and Section VI measures the gap: at small
budgets, the centroidal Voronoi configuration attains barely half the coverage
of a packed one, because minimising mean squared distance rewards spreading
into the tails while binary containment does not.

## II-B Packing bounds

That the densest packing of equal circles in the plane has density π / 12 \pi/\sqrt{12} is classical, due to Thue and developed by Fejes
Tóth [ 6 , 7 ] ; the volumetric analogue π / 18 \pi/\sqrt{18} is the Kepler conjecture, proved by Hales [ 9 ] and later verified
formally by machine [ 10 ] . We use these as the ceiling on what any
non-overlapping arrangement of covering discs can achieve — a qualification
that matters, and which Section V-E makes explicit by showing
what happens when the non-overlap constraint is dropped. To our knowledge
this ceiling is not usually stated in the multi-agent coverage literature,
where it is natural to write down an area ratio that tacitly assumes perfect
tiling and therefore permits coverage probabilities that are unattainable at
any team size.

## II-C Track prediction and manoeuvre models

Propagating measurement noise through a least-squares trajectory fit is
standard estimation practice [ 12 ] , as is the recursive
alternative [ 11 ] . We use the batch closed form rather than a
filter because the quantity wanted is not a running state estimate but the
error covariance of an extrapolation to a fixed plane, and because a closed
form keeps the resulting sizing law analytic end to end. The delta method used
for the uncertain arrival time is likewise textbook [ 15 ] .

The straight-line assumption is the weak point, and the tracking literature has
long known it. Singer [ 13 ] models target acceleration as a
correlated random process precisely because constant-velocity fits degrade
badly under manoeuvre, and Li and Jilkov [ 14 ] survey several decades
of successors. Section VIII uses a deliberately crude version of
this idea — an independent per-axis acceleration with fixed standard
deviation — and finds that it dominates the sensor term by two orders of
magnitude at realistic lead times. A Singer-type correlated model would refine
the constant; it would not change which term binds.

## II-D Assignment

Allocating agents to positions at minimum total travel is a linear assignment
problem, solved exactly by the Hungarian method [ 16 ] in O ⁡ ( N 3 ) O(N^{3}) .
Distributed alternatives exist where centralised computation is
unavailable [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . This matters below
because assignment is one of two classical sub-problems that an end-to-end
policy is implicitly asked to rediscover, and the only one with an exact
polynomial solution.

## II-E Interception and pursuit

Coverage of a predicted arrival point is adjacent to pursuit-evasion, surveyed
for mobile robotics by Chung et al. [ 20 ] . The distinction
is that the team here does not pursue: it positions itself ahead of the
arrival and lets the geometry do the rest, which converts a speed problem into
a placement problem. That is also why packing, rather than pursuit strategy, is
the governing mathematics.

## II-F Multi-agent reinforcement learning and its evaluation

PPO [ 21 ] remains a common default for continuous multi-agent
control, and is a strong baseline in cooperative settings when implemented
carefully [ 22 ] ; we use the Stable-Baselines3
implementation [ 23 ] . Permutation-equivariant
architectures [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] are the standard
remedy for policies whose action space treats interchangeable agents as
unrelated output dimensions. Our negative result in
Section X concerns an unstructured centralised baseline, and
we are explicit that it does not settle the structured case.

Reward-specification pathologies are well understood in
principle [ 27 , 28 , 29 ] ; what we add is a concrete
instance in which two of them produced the same observable symptom as a genuine
learning failure, and were diagnosed only after the fact. On evaluation, we
follow the recommendations of [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] in
reporting multiple seeds with interval estimates rather than point estimates,
using the percentile bootstrap [ 33 ] .

2026-10-16.title: Navigation by Skylight Polarization via Rayleigh Model Optimization on a Road Vehicle
2026-10-16.authors: Ben Potter , Eslam Mounier , Aboelmagd Noureldin , Yahia Antar , Muhammad Alam
2026-10-16.abstract:
Reliable absolute heading estimation is critical for road-vehicle navigation, particularly when magnetic, inertial, or GNSS-based references are degraded.
This paper presents a skylight-polarization navigation method that estimates vehicle heading by globally optimizing a Rayleigh sky model against measurements from a division-of-focal-plane polarimetric camera.
The proposed framework combines a pinhole camera model, a single-scattering Rayleigh polarization model, and a solar position algorithm to synthesize the expected full-image angle-of-polarization distribution for candidate vehicle states.
A degree-of-polarization-weighted root-mean-square error objective function compares measured and simulated polarization patterns, allowing the estimator to use all available sky information while attenuating low-confidence pixels caused by clouds, buildings, foliage, and other depolarizing occlusions.
Experimental evaluation is performed using three urban road-vehicle trajectories collected with a roof-mounted polarimetric camera and a high-precision dual-antenna GNSS/INS reference system.
Results show sub-degree RMS yaw error across all trajectories, ranging from 0.718 ° 0.718\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} to 0.889 ° 0.889\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} .
Compared with representative feature-based and model-based polarization navigation methods, the proposed approach reduces RMS heading error by up to 87 % 87\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} and demonstrates improved robustness to partial sky occlusion.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Modern mobile platforms spanning driver assistance systems, manned tactical vehicles, autonomous road transportation, and industrial robotics depend on accurate, continuous, and highly resilient navigation systems for safe and reliable operation.
Among the core parameters governing vehicle state estimation and trajectory control, absolute heading determination plays a pivotal role.
In dynamic, real-world operational environments, maintaining an uncompromised orientation reference is essential to prevent cumulative dead-reckoning drift, ensuring operational continuity and human safety, particularly when external positioning infrastructure is degraded or unavailable.

Despite significant advances in navigation instrumentation, conventional sensors utilized for absolute heading determination suffer from severe physical and environmental limitations.
Gyrocompasses and inertial measurement units provide self-contained dead-reckoning capabilities, but their orientation estimates suffer from unbounded error integration over time [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , and a loss of power permanently destroys the reference orientation.
Magnetic compasses provide absolute heading but are highly susceptible to local electromagnetic interference [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , structural ferromagnetic distortion from the vehicle chassis [ 7 , 8 ] , and ambient anomalies in the Earth’s magnetic field [ 9 , 10 ] .
Dual-antenna global navigation satellite system configurations can deliver high-precision heading solutions under open skies; however, their performance degrades in complex operational environments.
Natural and artificial obstructions such as tall buildings and dense foliage cause signal multipath and line-of-sight shadowing [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
Furthermore, global navigation satellite system signals are increasingly vulnerable to deliberate radio frequency jamming and spoofing [ 14 , 15 ] , which poses failure risks in high-reliability civilian and defense scenarios.
Although multi-sensor fusion strategies aim to combine complementary sensor modalities to mitigate individual weaknesses, effective fusion relies on the availability of a passive, drift-free, and infrastructure-independent absolute orientation reference.

Skylight polarization offers a compelling physical foundation for self-contained, passive, and drift-free navigation.
As unpolarized sunlight enters the Earth’s atmosphere, atmospheric scattering interactions impart a predictable, structured linear polarization pattern across the sky.
The spatial distribution of this polarization pattern depends solely on the solar position relative to an observer on the Earth’s surface.
Biological organisms, including desert ants [ 16 , 17 ] , honeybees [ 18 , 19 ] , desert locusts [ 20 , 21 ] , and monarch butterflies [ 22 ] , exploit this skylight polarization pattern via specialized optical structures to perform long-distance navigation with remarkable precision [ 23 ] .
Inspired by these biological visual systems, polarization-based navigation systems measure skylight polarization parameters across observed sky points to infer the absolute orientation of the observer.

Recent developments in polarimetric imaging, particularly division-of-focal-plane polarimeters, have enabled real-time, high-resolution capture of spatial polarization patterns.
Traditional polarization navigation algorithms predominantly rely on extracting specific geometric landmarks, such as the solar meridian line or neutral points, using line-fitting or transformation techniques such as the Hough transform [ 24 ] .
However, these local feature-based methods suffer from three primary drawbacks when applied to ground vehicle navigation.
In urban canyons, buildings, bridges, and tree canopies obscure significant portions of the sky. When local geometric features (e.g., the solar meridian) are occluded, feature-based algorithms experience performance degradation or failure.
Existing studies often assume a strictly horizontal polarimeter orientation. In mobile vehicle applications, dynamic pitch and roll motions introduce non-horizontal measurement tilts. Transforming angle of polarization measurements from the sensor frame into ray coordinate frames under non-horizontal conditions incurs systematic errors that are rarely modeled or compensated in literature.

To overcome these challenges, this paper presents a global model optimization framework for absolute heading determination on road vehicles using a wide-field division-of-focal-plane polarimetric camera.
Rather than relying on local feature extraction, our method formulates heading estimation as an optimization problem evaluated over the full polarimetric image.
By integrating a pinhole camera model with single-scattering Rayleigh sky theory and an accurate solar position algorithm (Plataforma Solar de Almeria) [ 25 , 26 ] , we simulate superpixel-level expected angle of polarization distributions for candidate vehicle poses.
We construct an objective function that compares simulated and measured angle of polarization distributions, weighted by the degree of polarization, across all visible sky pixels.
The degree of polarization weighting naturally attenuates low-polarization noise from depolarizing cloud cover and solid occlusions.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We develop a full-image polarimetric camera simulation combining a pinhole camera model with the Rayleigh sky model to synthesize expected superpixel-level angle of polarization distributions for division-of-focal-plane sensor hardware under arbitrary camera orientations and solar positions.
Additionally, we formulate our simulation based exclusively on the state (i.e., position, time, orientation) of a virtual polarization camera in the horizontal coordinate system, which enables its application to conventional trajectory data where the position of the sun is not immediately recorded.

We formulate a coordinate transformation between the division-of-focal-plane measurement coordinate system and individual ray coordinate systems used by the Rayleigh sky model.
We explicitly account for non-horizontal camera tilt and document the errors incurred from such tilted measurements in vehicle-mounted schemes.

We propose a weighted root mean squared error objective function for heading extraction that evaluates global skylight polarization patterns and incorporates degree of polarization weighting to suppress measurement noise and depolarizing occlusions such as cloud cover, buildings, and foliage.

We perform experimental evaluations on an urban vehicle dataset collected under dynamic road conditions using a high-precision dual-antenna global navigation satellite system/inertial measurement unit reference system. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves up to an 87 % 87\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} decrease in the root mean squared error of the heading estimate compared with traditional Hough transform-based methods and up to a 73 % 73\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} decrease compared with other model optimization methods.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows.
Section II provides a review of relevant literature on bio-inspired skylight polarization navigation.
Section III presents the physical theory of skylight polarization, representations of linearly polarized light, and the Rayleigh sky model.
Section IV details the proposed model optimization framework, objective function formulation, camera projection model, and polarimetric measurement scheme.
Section V describes the experimental vehicle instrumentation and the urban trajectory dataset.
Section VI presents the experimental results, performance evaluations, and comparative analyses against existing methods.
Finally, Section VII concludes the paper and highlights directions for future research.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# II Related Work

Methods for heading estimation from polarized skylight measurements fall into two major categories.
The first category relies on the extraction of heading from geometric landmarks, such as the solar merdian and neutral points, present in images of the skylight polarization.
The Hough transform was introduced as a method of line-fitting the solar meridian by Lu and collaborators [ 24 ] , and has been implemented on diverse hardware [ 27 ] .
Other works have used the Hough transform method as a benchmark for their datasets.
Unsupervised learning methods, such as the support vector machine, have been suggested for solar merdian detection, too [ 28 ] .
The neutral points have been used for full attitude determination by Jue et al. [ 29 ] .
Such geometric landmark identifiers suffer from performance degradation when regions of the polarization measurement are occluded.
While these methods show promise on static datasets collected with rotational stages, they begin to suffer under the dynamic conditions of realistic road trajectories with occlusions from buildings, foliage, and adverse weather.

The second category uses an analytic model of the skylight polarization pattern to resolve the heading estimate.
Wang et al. established the application of the orthogonality of the e-vector and solar vector predicted by the Rayleigh model using the Lagrange multiplier method to determine the solar vector given a set of measured e-vectors [ 30 ] .
Kronland-Martinet et al. use the distribution of the degree of polarization to determine heading [ 31 ] .
Zhou et al. use the additivity of the e-vectors in circles about the zenith [ 32 ] .
He et al. apply the Berry model to optimize the solar vector using the particle swarm optimization algorithm [ 33 ] .
While such methods have explored sky model optimization as a technique for heading determination, additional research is required for improved performance in realistic scenarios.

Model-based methods for preprocessing measured polarization data have also received significant research attention.
Optical path modelling, via frameworks like the pinhole camera model, has been used for calibration [ 34 , 35 ] and noise suppression [ 36 ] .
Other methods use a sky model to resolve the angle of polarization in occluded regions of the polarization measurement [ 37 , 29 , 38 ] .
Typically, such restoration of the angle of polarization data is followed by the application of an existing heading extraction method: [ 38 ] uses the Lagrange method from [ 30 ] and [ 37 ] uses the Hough transform method from [ 24 ] .
Our proposed method combines the strength of the sky model under occluded settings with the heading estimation algorithm directly, which reduces the importance of such preprocessing schemes.

2026-10-16.title: Multi-Dimensional Featurizers Yield Fine-Grained Steering and Data Shaping in Robot Foundation Models
2026-10-16.authors: Aiden Swann , Mozes Jacobs , Mathilde Papillon , Siddharth Boppana , David Chanin , Dron Hazra , Usha Bhalla , Curt Tigges , Mac Schwager , Owen Lewis , Jack Merullo , Ekdeep Singh Lubana , Atticus Geiger , Thomas Fel , Matthew Kowal
2026-10-16.abstract:
Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn.
We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model’s computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than 1.4% of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.
2026-10-16.introduction:
A vision-language-action (VLA) model maps visual observations, language instructions, and robot state to actions in the physical world ( Black et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Deshpande et al., 2026 ) . Although today’s VLAs rarely perform consequential real-world tasks, fully learned robotics models may soon see widespread deployment. Yet little is known about the computations underlying their actions. Understanding these internal representations will be essential for safe deployment.

One way to understand the internal representation of a learned model is through the perspective of features , which are recurring internal variables that encode concepts, states, relationships and ultimately underlie the process by which the model converts input to output. A promising line of work, e.g., sparse autoencoders (SAEs), leverages the linear representation hypothesis (LRH) ( Park et al., 2023a ; Huben et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Elhage et al., 2022 ) and assume that activations are composed of a sparse set of vectors. These methods have been well studied in language and vision modalities ( Huben et al., 2024 ; Templeton et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) . Examining models in the basis of the features that they express is useful for a plethora of problems, such as to study generalization ( Gallifant et al., 2025 ; Olson et al., 2025 ) , steer model behavior ( Templeton et al., 2026 ; Prasad et al., 2026 ; Turner et al., 2023 ; Rimsky et al., 2024 ) , attribute behaviors to training data ( Kowal et al., 2026 ; Bergen et al., 2026 ; Koh & Liang, 2017 ) , and identify safety-relevant computation ( Templeton et al., 2026 ; Marks et al., 2025 ) .

However, a featurizer is ultimately a hypothesis about the data-generating process of the activations ( Fel et al., 2026a ) . The LRH is particularly questionable for visual domains involving perception, since continuous factors such as viewpoint, illumination, position, and motion naturally generate low-dimensional manifolds that are reflected in learned representations ( Cohen et al., 2020 ; Kvinge et al., 2024 ; Fel et al., 2026a ; Engels et al., 2025 ; Michaud et al., 2025 ) . Despite this, the majority of work in VLA interpretability assumes the LRH, with varying degrees of success. Early studies showed that specific MLP directions can offer limited control of variables like speed and height ( Häon et al., 2025 ) . Complementary studies use linear probes and activation interventions to characterize the contributions of visual, language, and action pathways and identify representations of environmental dynamics and task progress ( Molinari et al., 2025 ; Grant et al., 2026 ; Bhardwaj et al., 2026 ; Buurmeijer et al., 2026 ) . More recently, SAEs have been applied to recover semantic concepts, motion primitives, task structure, and episode-specific memorization, demonstrating that interventions on individual features can alter policy behavior ( Swann et al., 2026 ; Khan et al., 2025 ; Jin et al., 2026 ; Grant et al., 2026 ) .Prior work has improved our understanding of VLA policies, but precise behavioral steering remains challenging, with interventions often producing inconsistent, off-target, or weak effects. Much of this work relies on pooled visual activations or small activation corpora, leaving open whether training SAEs on individual token activations at greater scale improves feature discovery and steering.

In this work, we apply recent methods for multi-dimensional feature discovery—block-sparse featurizers (BSFs) ( Fel et al., 2026a ) —to frontier open-source VLA models, training BSFs and baseline SAEs on the largest corpora of unpooled VLA token activations to date. BSFs represent features as sparse low-dimensional blocks ( Yuan & Lin, 2006 ; Eldar & Bölcskei, 2009 ; Jenatton et al., 2010 ; Bach et al., 2012 ) rather than single directions, making them a natural fit for robotic representations. Across models and layers, we recover a broad vocabulary of task-relevant features spanning visual perception, language, proprioceptive state, task variables and episode progress. BSFs outperform matched SAEs on recovering and intervening on task-relevant structure, suggesting that the additional geometry is useful rather than simply excess representational capacity. We then causally validate them through fine-grained steering experiments across multiple layers, inducing targeted changes at several stages of the policy: what is perceived in the observation, which object is selected, where that object is localized. Finally, we perform feature-based attribution to connect interpretable behaviors directly to the episodes in the fine-tuning dataset that shaped them. Related robot data-curation methods select demonstrations with datamodels, influence estimates, or mutual information ( Dass et al., 2026 ; Agia et al., 2025 ; Hejna et al., 2025 ) . Using a ‘failure-recovery’ feature as as case-study, we isolate fewer than 1.4% of fine-tuning tokens in DROID whose influence is disproportionately associated with this behavior.
Our contributions are:

Comparing block-sparse and linear featurizers for VLAs. We systematically compare BSFs and SAEs in VLAs. BSFs recover features spanning perception, language, proprioception, task state and episode progress, better capturing computational geometry qualitatively and quantitatively. We also strengthen VLA SAE baselines with substantially larger, unpooled activation corpora to better evaluate multidimensional features.

Causal validation through fine-grained steering. Across multiple layers, and computational regimes, we causally validate recovered features by steering perception, semantics, target-object selection, geometric localization, and downstream robot behavior.

Feature-based dataset attribution and shaping. We trace behaviors captured by BSF features to the data that caused them. For failure recovery, masking ∼ 1.4 % \sim 1.4\% of fine-tuning tokens qualitatively transforms robot behavior, demonstrating precise control over robot datasets and learned policies.

2026-10-16.title: Causal Analysis of Robot Foundation Models Enables Efficiency Gains
2026-10-16.authors: Aiden Swann , Mathilde Papillon , Mozes Jacobs , Siddharth Boppana , Tal Haklay , Eric Bigelow , Andrew Lee , Conor Watts , Thomas Icard , Mac Schwager , Owen Lewis , Jack Merullo , Ekdeep Singh Lubana , Atticus Geiger , Thomas Fel , Matthew Kowal
2026-10-16.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. While the internal computation of vision-language models, which compose the backbone of VLAs, has been studied extensively, less is known about how their perceptual and semantic representations are transformed into action in VLA models. We study this question mechanistically in three frontier VLA models ( π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot) by analyzing the causal pathways through which the input image and the instruction shape actions. Across the three models, activation patching shows that causally relevant information influences the action expert (AE) through a narrow band of mid-to-late cross-attention layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface . The content of this information changes with token and layer within the model. Early-to-mid layer representations of the target noun token determine which object is selected, whereas mid-to-late layers carry the spatial information in text tokens that redirects the movement when patched. Where spatial information is stored in prompt tokens various based on the architecture. In MolmoAct2 the model forms task-conditioned representations at the text positions that follow the instruction, whereas π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} additionally stores this information at image token positions. We show that these findings can be translated directly into improving model efficiency. We find that restricting MolmoBot’s action expert conditioning to only 3 out of 36 layers reduces inference FLOPs by up to 33 % 33\% while maintaining comparable task success with the default model across 3,000 evaluation episodes (46.7% vs. 46.9%), and the same principle carries over to real-robot deployment of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} .
2026-10-16.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising route to achieve general-purpose robot manipulation. By adapting large pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) to action ( Driess et al., 2023 ; Beyer et al., 2024 ; Deitke et al., 2025 ) , VLAs combine broad visual and semantic knowledge with continuous control and increasingly handle manipulation tasks across objects, environments, and robot embodiments ( Brohan et al., 2022 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) .

Architecturally, VLAs typically combine a pretrained VLM backbone ( Chi et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Deshpande et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026 ; Wen et al., 2025a ; Wen et al., 2025b ) with a separate diffusion or flow-matching action expert that produces continuous control. The two modules are typically joined through a dense, layer-wise interface that conditions the expert on the backbone at every layer. Despite their growing real-world efficacy and partially due to the multi-modal architecture design, these models remain black boxes. VLAs transform thousands of image, language, and proprioceptive tokens through billions of parameters before producing a small set of continuous action tokens, leaving the internal mapping from perception to action an open area of study.

We study three frontier open-source VLAs: π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , MolmoBot, and MolmoAct2 ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Deshpande et al., 2026 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . Across all three models, we find that perception and action communicate through a surprisingly narrow channel (1-3 cross-attention layers). Causal influence concentrates in a middle-to-late band of VLM layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface . This suggests that the action expert ingests representations which already encode task-relevant spatial information, rather than depending equally on every stage of backbone computation.

We apply our findings of the narrow action-conditioning interface between the AE and VLM to improve VLA efficiency. Many prior works have attempted to reduce VLA computation, by skipping or exiting backbone layers ( Yue et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) , pruning redundant layers or parameters ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) , or conditioning the action head on only a subset of backbone layers ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Shukor et al., 2025 ) . These methods decide what to remove using heuristics such as representational similarity or benchmark success. We offer a more mechanistic account of why these designs work. Our results show that the representations necessary for action are stored sparsely across tokens and layers.

In this work we show that by leveraging causal analysis we can choose exactly the relevant areas of the model to prune. Restricting conditioning to the causally important layers removes 92 % 92\% of MolmoBot’s cross-attention parameters and reduces the estimated VLM–action-expert floating-point operation count by up to 33 % 33\% with a similar change in real world measured latency. The simplified architecture achieves task success comparable to the vanilla policy across 3,000 evaluation episodes. The same approach carries over to preliminary trials on a real robot, where sparse and dense π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policies achieve comparable success rates (67 and 64 of 100 trials). We view these results as a step toward intentional design ( McGrath, 2026 ) of VLA models, where the internal mechanisms connecting perception to control directly inform how robot policies are built and trained.

Beyond just leveraging the action-conditioning interface we seek to understand and explain it. There are many promising approachs to understanding VLA computation via mechanistic interpretability ( Grant et al., 2026 ; Bhardwaj et al., 2026 ; Molinari et al., 2025 ; Khan et al., 2025 ; Goyal, 2026 ; Yang & Mokalla, 2026 ) . In particular, activation patching ( Vig et al., 2020 ; Geiger et al., 2021 ; Zhang & Nanda, 2024 ; Heimersheim & Nanda, 2024 ) approaches aim to measure the causal role of an internal representation by replacing the target representation from one rollout with a donor from another rollout, while measuring the resulting change in behavior. In language models, such interventions have localized the computations behind factual recall and uncovered computations underlying numerous tasks ( Meng et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ; Geiger et al., 2023 ; Mueller et al., 2026 ) , helping elucidate the causal relationships between internal model representations and behavior.

Recent work has begun to apply such tools to VLAs, identifying internal directions that steer movement, recovering sparse features tied to semantic concepts, and manipulating observable features to control behavior ( Häon et al., 2025 ; Swann et al., 2026 ; Buurmeijer et al., 2026 ) . Closest to our work, Grant et al. (2026) performed activation-injection experiments and showed that patching representations into a VLA can redirect movement toward the spatial location of a donor task. Shi et al. (2026) used attention knockout ( Geva et al., 2023 ) , which blocks attention from selected token positions (such as all image or all language tokens) at chosen layers and measures how the output changes, to characterize which modalities and layers action generation depends on. Together, these results establish that individual VLA representations can be causally manipulated. However, they do not address how task-relevant information is composed across the depth of the backbone and how it reaches the action expert.

We answer these questions with counterfactual comparisons that test visual, semantic, and geometric hypotheses at the interface and within the backbone. We trace how the representations read by the expert reveals a progression across depth, from transferable object selection to spatially grounded action information. The two kinds of information also reside on different tokens: semantic content is carried by the noun token of the instruction, while geometric content is spread across the other prompt tokens and, in π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , the image tokens.

Our contributions are as follows:

Discovery of a narrow action-conditioning interface. Across π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot, we identify a narrow middle-to-late region through which the backbone conditions action generation. We show that this interface mediates geometric information about the target object.

Mechanistically informed architectural improvements. We use the identified interface to design substantially sparser VLM–action-expert connections, preserving observed closed-loop performance while reducing the estimated combined operation count by up to 33 % 33\% . We validate the simplified architecture through direct training and adaptation in simulation, and demonstrate real-robot deployment with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} .

A causal account of the information supplied to the interface. We build a counterfactual dataset with over 156 counterfactual pairs across sets of household objects. We run over 775,000 activation patching interventions across π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot specifically designed to differentiate representations within the backbone. Visual information influences behavior through early image tokens, semantic information through the early target noun, and geometric information through later text and readout positions.

2026-10-16.authors: Zirui Wu , Chen Guo , Tianjian Jiang , Zeren Jiang , Zeming Li , Lingchen Yang , Longteng Duan , Ying Xue , Handi Yin , Shenyuan Gao , Martin R. Oswald , Jun Zhang , Ping Tan , Jie Song

2026-10-16.abstract:
We introduce P 3 -WAM, a unified world action
model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that learns
3D perception, action-conditioned prediction, and goal-directed planning through three complementary
modes: Perceive , which reconstructs articulated
hand motion and camera trajectories from video; Predict , which generates visual futures under
prescribed actions; and Plan , which jointly
generates action trajectories and their anticipated visual consequences conditioned on an initial image, a language instruction, and an optional visual goal.
Our model integrates a compact, structured 3D action representation into a pretrained video diffusion transformer through a mixture-of-transformers architecture with shared base weights, modality-specific adaptation, and bidirectional visual–action attention.
Randomized modality visibility lets video and 3D actions
serve as either conditioning context or prediction targets across the three modes.
Experiments show that unified training improves all three
capabilities over single-mode training, including gains in planning quality under a vision–language model evaluation.
Through unified training, our model outperforms specialized
baselines on 3D hand reconstruction and action-conditioned
video prediction across four datasets, while producing
goal-directed manipulation videos with stronger instruction
adherence and action progression than video-generation
baselines.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation requires more than mapping pixels directly to actions. An embodied model must answer three complementary questions: What happened in an observed interaction? What will happen under a specified action? What should be done to accomplish a desired goal? These questions correspond to three fundamental capabilities: perceiving the 3D motion underlying observed interactions, predicting action-conditioned world dynamics, and planning actions together with their anticipated consequences. Infants can use what they learn from observing adults’ actions to guide their own behavior ( Hauf & Aschersleben, 2008 ) . Through their own interactions, they learn to predict action outcomes and use those expected outcomes to select actions ( Verschoor et al., 2013 ) and organize movements toward a goal ( Claxton et al., 2003 ) . Together, these findings suggest that perception, prediction, and planning are linked by knowledge of actions and their consequences.

Despite these connections, prior work on egocentric manipulation has developed along three closely related but largely separate lines. Egocentric reconstruction methods recover structured 3D interaction information, such as hand motion and camera trajectories, from observed videos ( Pavlakos et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) . Action-conditioned world models predict future observations under prescribed motion trajectories ( Hao et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . World action models jointly generate actions and future observations for goal-directed control ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . These capabilities, however, are still largely learned in isolation or coupled only in subsets.

To close this loop, we introduce P 3 -WAM, a unified world action model for egocentric dexterous manipulation that integrates three complementary modes: 3D interaction reconstruction ( Perceive ), action-conditioned world prediction ( Predict ), and joint action–future planning ( Plan ). Reconstruction develops the model’s capacity for 3D perception by recovering 3D motion from observed interactions. Prediction teaches the model to anticipate the visual consequences of prescribed actions. Together, these capabilities provide the foundation for world–action planning, in which the model learns to jointly generate goal-directed hand action trajectories and their anticipated visual futures. We learn all three modes through unified training. Figure 1 illustrates these three modes.

We build P 3 -WAM on a pretrained video diffusion transformer ( Wan et al., 2025 ) to draw on its rich visual and motion priors. We represent each action by the articulated poses of both hands and the camera pose, and encode these states as compact tokens alongside the video tokens. We integrate this representation into the video backbone through a mixture-of-transformers (MoT) architecture with a dedicated action expert, which shares the backbone’s base weights while incorporating modality-specific low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . To train this architecture across all three modes, we randomly vary the visibility of visual observations and actions: providing video while withholding actions supports perception, providing actions while withholding future video supports prediction, and withholding actions and video supports joint action–future planning, exposing the model to complete modes and partially observed interactions. Over long sequences, successive visual subgoals specify the target arrangement for each planning window.

Unified training improves all three modes over single-mode training. Our model outperforms the evaluated baselines in Perceive and Predict . Its Plan videos receive higher VLM scores for action process and instruction adherence. Robot demonstrations illustrate how generated human-hand motion can be transferred to a dexterous robot. Our main contributions are:

A unified world action model, P 3 -WAM, for egocentric
dexterous manipulation that integrates 3D interaction reconstruction,
action-conditioned world prediction, and goal-guided
world–action planning. We will release our code and model checkpoints.

# 2 Related Work

Action-conditioned world models predict single images ( Sudhakar et al., 2024 ) or roll out videos ( Akkerman et al., 2025 ; DreamX Team et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2026a ) . Wan ( Wan et al., 2025 ) and Cosmos 3 ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) provide pretrained video priors. For action representation, Dexterous World Models ( Kim et al., 2026 ) uses rendered scenes and hand-mesh trajectories, while DreamDojo ( Gao et al., 2026b ) learns latent actions from human videos for robot-world rollouts. Explicit scene and camera geometry can also help maintain spatial consistency. EgoSim ( Hao et al., 2026 ) combines video generation with an updatable 3D scene and shared human–robot keypoints, and EgoGenesis ( Yan et al., 2026b ) uses camera-aware 3D action embeddings and online projective memory for autoregressive rollout.

World action models generate actions alongside anticipated visual dynamics through causal video prediction and inverse dynamics, as in LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026a ) , or joint video–action flow matching, as in DreamZero ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , Foresight Without Seeing ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , and RIFT ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) study predictive visual information for control without a complete iterative visual rollout at deployment.

Recovering 3D hand motion from video requires estimating hand articulation while accounting for a moving camera. Single-image methods provide hand pose and shape estimates: HaMeR ( Pavlakos et al., 2024 ) scales transformer capacity and heterogeneous training data, while WiLoR ( Potamias et al., 2025 ) integrates localization, handedness estimation, and image-aligned mesh refinement. For egocentric sequences, HaWoR ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and Dyn-HaMR ( Yu et al., 2025 ) combine hand-motion estimation with SLAM to recover global trajectories, using temporal infilling or interacting-hand priors and optimization. Concurrent work MINT ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) jointly estimates camera and hand motion.

Video generative models offer another source of information about hand motion. Concurrent works ViDiHand ( Wang et al., 2026a ) and ACE-Ego-Hand ( Liu et al., 2026 ) use video diffusion features for hand motion recovery. We train reconstruction jointly with future prediction and planning, allowing the model to learn from how hand interactions unfold as well as from observed video. This joint training improves 3D hand reconstruction in our single-mode comparison (Sec. 4.1 ).

A shared model can connect these tasks by changing which modalities are observed and which are generated. Unified World Models ( Zhu et al., 2025a ) couples video and action diffusion for forward, inverse, policy, and video inference. Language provides a further interface for world modeling and control: Motus ( Bi et al., 2026 ) combines language, video, and latent actions, while MotuBrain ( MotuBrain Team et al., 2026 ) jointly models text, video, and embodiment-specific actions. Geometric modalities extend this shared formulation to spatial reasoning. Flex- π \pi ( Yan et al., 2026a ) includes pointmap and feature streams alongside RGB and actions, and Aether ( Zhu et al., 2025b ) unifies 4D reconstruction, camera-conditioned prediction, and goal-image-conditioned visual planning. P 3 -WAM applies joint reconstruction, prediction, and planning to articulated hand interaction. It plans hand and camera trajectories together with video and supports visual goals to preserve spatial targets across a task.
