2026-10-16.title: SHRED: Self-Play for Heterogeneous Road-Users without Expert Demonstrations
2026-10-16.authors: Wei-Jer Chang , Zhouchonghao Wu , Akshay Rangesh , Weixin Li , Masayoshi Tomizuka , Wei Zhan
2026-10-16.abstract:
Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction.
On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Developing autonomous vehicles that operate safely alongside human road users requires scalable and realistic closed-loop traffic simulation. Real-world traffic, however, is inherently heterogeneous: beyond vehicles, it includes pedestrians, cyclists, and other agents with distinct physical dynamics, motion constraints, and behavioral patterns. These differences shape how agents respond to one another and how their interactions unfold over time. A pedestrian or scooter yielding at a crosswalk and a vehicle merging into traffic follow fundamentally different rules of engagement. Capturing such heterogeneous interactions is therefore central to realistic closed-loop simulation. It is equally central to autonomous planning, where the ego vehicle must anticipate how diverse agents will react to its own actions.

Recent advances in traffic simulation and autonomous planning have widely adopted data-driven learning, leveraging large-scale human driving datasets to model traffic behavior and train driving policies. Tokenized and generative simulation models reproduce realistic traffic behaviors and achieve strong performance on large-scale simulation benchmarks ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Philion et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) . However, these approaches often rely on computationally expensive centralized models, limiting throughput in large-scale closed-loop simulation ( Chang et al., 2026 ) . In parallel, learning-based planning methods have increasingly leveraged large-scale driving datasets to learn scene representations, model interactions, and optimize driving decisions, achieving strong performance across challenging driving scenarios ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ; Tan et al., 2025 ) . Despite their different objectives, both lines of work remain widely dependent on logged human driving data for learning realistic and effective interaction behaviors.
Their behavior remains tied to the interaction distributions in logged datasets, which can make coverage of diverse heterogeneous interactions and cross-dataset transfer more challenging. Large-scale demonstration datasets are also expensive to collect and may not fully capture the diversity of reactive multi-agent behaviors observed in real-world traffic.

Self-play reinforcement learning offers a complementary direction: it can learn through online interaction without trajectory supervision, scales naturally to large numbers of agents, and enables diverse multi-agent interactions to emerge through closed-loop rollouts.
Recent work has shown that self-play can produce robust driving policies at unprecedented scale ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ) and achieve competitive realism when anchored to pretrained reference models ( Chang et al., 2026 ) . However, prior self-play systems focus on vehicle policies or homogeneous dynamics and rewards across road-user types despite fundamentally different motion characteristics. Scalable, fully reactive heterogeneous self-play across vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists without relying on logged trajectory data or pretrained imitation-policy anchors therefore remains largely unexplored.

To address these challenges, we propose SHRED ( S elf-Play for H eterogeneous R oad-Users without E xpert D emonstrations), a scalable framework for learning heterogeneous traffic behavior through large-scale self-play. SHRED jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists from random initialization, with type-specific dynamics, objectives, and action spaces that reflect their distinct modes of interaction. Procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization of dynamics and reward parameters expose agents to diverse traffic configurations and behaviors throughout training. This enables a compact decentralized policy to learn realistic heterogeneous multi-agent behaviors entirely through self-play, without demonstration supervision.

We show that demonstration-free self-play can achieve both realistic
heterogeneous traffic simulation and strong interactive planning. For
simulation, we evaluate on the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge
(WOSAC) ( Montali et al., 2023 ) while jointly controlling vehicles, pedestrians,
and cyclists. SHRED outperforms the closest demonstration-free self-play
baseline, while controlled ablations show that heterogeneous self-play
substantially improves traffic realism, including the behavior of vehicles
themselves. For planning, we evaluate SHRED on
InterPlan ( Hallgarten et al., 2024 ) , where it outperforms all compared planners
on interaction-heavy closed-loop scenarios. Complementary planning ablations
show that heterogeneous self-play substantially outperforms vehicle-only
self-play, with the largest gains on scenarios involving concentrated
interactions with other road users. Beyond these benchmarks, policies trained
on nuPlan maps transfer zero-shot to Waymo, while behavioral analyses show
that self-play produces diverse, plausible alternatives to logged trajectories
(Figure 1 ).

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce SHRED, a demonstration-free heterogeneous self-play framework that jointly learns vehicle, pedestrian, and cyclist behaviors with distinct dynamics and objectives, entirely without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay.

We develop the key components for scalable heterogeneous self-play, including procedural scenario and goal generation, per-agent randomization of dynamics and objectives, and type-specific policy components that support joint learning across diverse road-user types.

We show that demonstration-free self-play is effective across both simulation and planning: SHRED achieves strong sim-agent realism on WOSAC, the highest score among compared planners on the official 80-scenario InterPlan split, and zero-shot map transfer from nuPlan to Waymo.

1. We introduce SHRED, a demonstration-free heterogeneous self-play framework that jointly learns vehicle, pedestrian, and cyclist behaviors with distinct dynamics and objectives, entirely without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay.

2. We develop the key components for scalable heterogeneous self-play, including procedural scenario and goal generation, per-agent randomization of dynamics and objectives, and type-specific policy components that support joint learning across diverse road-user types.

3. We show that demonstration-free self-play is effective across both simulation and planning: SHRED achieves strong sim-agent realism on WOSAC, the highest score among compared planners on the official 80-scenario InterPlan split, and zero-shot map transfer from nuPlan to Waymo.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2. Related Work

## 2.1. Data-Driven and Heterogeneous Traffic Simulation

Imitation from human driving logs has become the dominant paradigm for
realistic traffic simulation.
Tokenized autoregressive
models ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Philion et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) and diffusion-based
approaches ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) have driven strong performance
on WOSAC ( Montali et al., 2023 ) , while closed-loop fine-tuning,
promptable rollout, and RL/RLHF post-training further improve rollout
realism and controllability ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Tan et al., 2024 ; Peng et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Cao et al., 2024 ; Pei et al., 2026 ) .
RLFTSim ( Ahmadi et al., 2026 ) fine-tunes a pretrained traffic simulator with a distribution-alignment reward. DecompGAIL ( Guo et al., 2026 ) combines a SMART-based model with decomposed adversarial imitation learning. Both methods use a trajectory-model prior; SHRED instead studies heterogeneous recurrent self-play without one.
Pedestrian and cyclist behavior has additionally been studied through
rule-based crowd dynamics ( Helbing and Molnár, 1995 ; Helbing et al., 2005 ; van den Berg et al., 2011 ) , multimodal trajectory forecasting
models ( Alahi et al., 2016 ; Gupta et al., 2018 ; Salzmann et al., 2020 ; Xu et al., 2022 ; Rasouli and Kotseruba, 2023 ) , and multi-agent driving
simulators ( Suo et al., 2021 ; Vinitsky et al., 2022 ; Gulino et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Kazemkhani et al., 2025 ; Rowe et al., 2024 ) .
However, realistic heterogeneous interaction behavior is typically
learned implicitly from demonstrations, while learned closed-loop
control remains largely vehicle-centric or relies on shared dynamics
across all road users.
Our work instead studies whether realistic heterogeneous traffic can
emerge from demonstration-free self-play with type-specific dynamics,
rewards, goals, and policy components for vehicles, pedestrians, and
cyclists jointly.

## 2.2. Self-Play Reinforcement Learning for Driving

Self-play has driven landmark results in game
playing ( Silver et al., 2017 ; Vinyals et al., 2019 ; Berner et al., 2019 ; Jaderberg et al., 2019 ) and has recently been adopted for
traffic simulation.
Gigaflow ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ) is the closest demonstration-free
precedent, training a unified policy for vehicles, pedestrians, and
cyclists through massively parallel self-play.
However, all agents share the same jerk-actuated bicycle dynamics and
goal-generation mechanism, with diversity induced primarily through
conditioning variables inside a shared backbone.
Other self-play systems explore complementary directions: Cornelisse et al. (2025) scale vehicle-only PPO
from logged WOMD initial states, while HR-PPO ( Cornelisse and Vinitsky, 2024 ) and SPACeR ( Chang et al., 2026 ) regularize self-play with
behavior-cloned or tokenized policy anchors.
NOMAD ( Wang et al., 2026 ) studies map-transfer through self-play, and
GPUDrive ( Kazemkhani et al., 2025 ) provides a GPU-resident substrate
for large-scale simulation.
TerraTransfer ( Xiong et al., 2026 ) aligns a self-play policy with a
pretrained vision backbone to obtain end-to-end driving policies without
expert demonstrations.
In contrast, we jointly train vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists from
fully procedural initialization, without trajectory supervision, pretrained imitation-policy anchors, or logged-trajectory replay, using type-specific dynamics,
rewards, and goal generation.

## 2.3. Heterogeneity in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning

Most heterogeneous multi-agent RL methods are developed for cooperative
settings with shared rewards, including QMIX ( Rashid et al., 2018 ) ,
MAPPO ( Yu et al., 2022 ) , and HAPPO/HATRPO ( Kuba et al., 2022 ; Zhong et al., 2024 ) . Several of them rely on sequential per-agent updates
(HAPPO/HATRPO) or separate per-agent policies, which become costly in
traffic scenes containing dozens of agents with different dynamics and
action spaces.
Recent modular and role-conditioned approaches such as
SePS ( Christianos et al., 2021 ) , ROMA ( Wang et al., 2020 ) ,
RODE ( Wang et al., 2021 ) , and MoE-based RL
architectures ( Yang et al., 2020 ; Obando-Ceron et al., 2024 ) reduce
interference through selective parameter sharing or latent routing, but
remain primarily focused on cooperative domains.

Our setting is instead mixed-motive: each road user optimizes its own
goal under type-specific rewards and dynamics without a shared team
objective.
We therefore organize policies by physical agent type rather than agent
identity, sharing perception while maintaining separate recurrent,
actor, and value heads for vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists.

2026-10-16.abstract: In response to the reply presented in [ Muñoz-Vázquez and Sánchez-Torres(2026) ] , this technical report extends the experimental evaluation of position-feedback velocity observers and adaptive tracking controllers for a pendular system with nonlinear friction reported in [ Cervantes-Pérez et al.(2026) ] . The immersion-and-invariance (I & \& I) adaptive control scheme proposed in [ Romero et al.(2025) ] , whose gains are tuned according to the guidelines presented in [ Ortega et al.(2025) ] , is compared with a control scheme employing the adaptive modified super-twisting observer of [ Dávila et al.(2006) ] , whose observer gains are selected according to the guidelines proposed in [ Muñoz-Vázquez and Sánchez-Torres(2026) ] . Although these “tuning guidelines” attenuate chattering in certain scenarios, the experimental results reported here show that they do not eliminate it in general.

This section introduces the experimental platform used to conduct the comparative study and outlines the scope of the reported tests. The testbed consists of a direct-drive pendular device with a single vertical link, designed and built at the La Laguna Technological Institute, Mexico. A picture of the pendular device is shown in Figure 1 , whereas its schematic diagram is presented in Figure 2 , where q q denotes the angular position of the actuated joint.

The joint is actuated by a direct-drive motor manufactured by Yokogawa Electric Corporation, model DM1A200G . The motor operates in torque mode, providing a maximum torque of ± 200 ​ [ Nm ] \pm 200~\mathrm{[Nm]} . It is also equipped with a relative encoder offering a resolution of 1,024,000 1{,}024{,}000 pulses per revolution. The proposed controller was implemented digitally in MATLAB using the Simulink Desktop Real-Time environment, with a sampling period of 1 ​ [ ms ] 1~\mathrm{[ms]} . The experiments were conducted on a PC running Windows 10, equipped with an Intel Core i5-14600K CPU, 32 ​ GB 32~\mathrm{GB} of RAM, an RTX 3060 GPU, and a 512 ​ GB 512~\mathrm{GB} M.2 SSD. Communication between the PC and the robot was established through a Sensoray 626 data acquisition card (DAQ) installed in the PCI port of the motherboard. The DAQ interfaced with the motor driver (PARKER COMPUMOTOR model DMG3-1200A) by sending analog voltage signals corresponding to the control torques. In turn, the driver transmitted pulse trains replicating the motor encoder signals to the DAQ digital inputs. The physical parameters of the link are listed in Table 1 , as originally reported in [ Gamez-Herrera et al.(2025) , Gandarilla et al.(2022) ] . The table summarizes the meaning of the parameters and their numerical values, where l l denotes link length, and ‘Dist.’, ‘Inert.’, and ‘com’ stand for distance, inertia, and center of mass, respectively.

2026-10-16.title: Robotic-supported Data Loss Detection in Android Applications
2026-10-16.authors: Davi Freitas , Breno Miranda , Juliano Iyoda
2026-10-16.abstract: Smartphones have become integral to modern life due to their diverse applications. However, the development of applications for these devices faces significant challenges, primarily due to two factors: (i) the diverse hardware and operating system versions that require testing across multiple configurations; and (ii) the imperative activity of testing the smartphone in a non-invasive way (similar to an end-user interaction), which is expensive, tedious and error-prone as it is usually carried out manually. In this context, robotic automation has emerged as an effective solution for addressing the diversity of smartphone systems and versions, and in performing some testing tasks non-invasively. In addition, automated robots facilitate quick, accurate, and repetitive testing, thus enabling developers to validate their applications across various configurations effectively. This results in a less invasive verification and in a significant reduction in time spent on manual testing, thus accelerating the development cycle. Our work proposes R-DLD (Robotic-supported Data Loss Detection), a robot-assisted infrastructure for data loss detection in Android applications, offeringless invasive and more realistic tests by interacting directly with smartphone sensors. The robot is constructed using cost-effective materials, facilitating its adoption in testing environments. In our empirical evaluation R-DLD successfully identified 341 data loss issues in 77 randomly selected apps from an Android store. All reported bugs received responses from the developer, with 89.55% confirming the data loss problems, while 35.82% have being subsequently fixed.

2026-10-16.authors: Abdullah Al Maruf , Md. Sajedul Islam , Tanmoy Mridha , Irfan Hossain Bhuiyan
2026-10-16.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-16.comment: Accepted at the ECCV 2026 Workshop on Safe and Defensive Autonomous Driving (SDAD).
2026-10-16.abstract:
Vision-language models are increasingly used for driving-scene
understanding, yet their defensive reasoning under weakly structured
Global South traffic remains unclear. We introduce BD-HazardVLM , a
diagnostic benchmark of 500 Bangladesh road-scene images—375 from
RSUD20K and 125 from TFP-BD—annotated for hazard presence, primary
hazard category, risk timing, severity, defensive actions, visible
evidence, and hallucination- and Western-road-bias traps. We evaluate
Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B, and MiniCPM-V-4.6 using a shared zero-shot task definition and structured output schema. Binary hazard-presence accuracy ranges from 88.0% to 89.2%,
essentially matching the 89.0% majority-class baseline. Fine-grained
reasoning is substantially weaker: category accuracy remains below 40%,
risk-timing accuracy ranges from 1.6% to 12.4%, and exact
defensive-action matching remains below 2%. Although InternVL3-8B achieves
the highest severity accuracy at 61.2%, it has zero recall on the 58
high-severity cases. Qwen exhibits severe category mode collapse, while all models show weak
latent-hazard anticipation and near-zero self-reported trap recognition. For the
evaluated models, these findings show that coarse hazard recognition does
not imply reliable fine-grained defensive-driving reasoning and motivate
geographically diverse safety evaluation.
2026-10-16.introduction:
Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used for interpretable
driving-scene understanding, visual question answering, planning, and
language-guided control [ 23 , 13 , 14 , 16 ] .
Their ability to describe visible road users is promising, but
safety-critical driving requires more than object recognition. A
defensive driver must identify which element constitutes the primary
hazard, estimate whether the risk is immediate or may emerge later,
assess its severity, and select a suitable preventive action.

This distinction is particularly important for latent hazards .
A pedestrian partly hidden behind a vehicle, a bus blocking the forward
view, an unstable mixed-traffic interaction, or a roadside crowd may not
represent an immediate collision threat in a single frame. Nevertheless,
the scene may require slowing down, maintaining distance, avoiding an
overtake, or preparing to brake before the danger becomes explicit.
Existing driving-VLM benchmarks increasingly examine corner cases and
model reliability [ 3 , 21 , 22 ] , but
fine-grained defensive reasoning under weakly structured traffic remains
underexplored.

Bangladesh road scenes present a demanding test environment. They often
contain heterogeneous vehicles, rickshaws and easybikes, CNG
auto-rickshaws, motorcycles, informal pedestrian crossings, roadside
markets, large-vehicle occlusion, damaged surfaces, waterlogging, and
limited lane organization. South Asian datasets such as IDD and IDD-3D
have established the importance of evaluating perception beyond
well-structured Western road environments [ 17 , 4 ] . Bangladesh-specific datasets such
as RSUD20K and TFP-BD provide geographically relevant imagery [ 27 , 8 ] , but their original annotations
do not directly evaluate hazard timing, severity, or defensive action
selection.

Geographic mismatch may also encourage unsupported assumptions. A VLM
may infer zebra crossings, formal lane boundaries, sidewalks, traffic
signals, or organized road behavior even when such evidence is absent.
Prior studies demonstrate that multimodal models can hallucinate visual
content and exhibit systematic geographic or contextual biases [ 9 , 6 , 7 ] . Such errors
are especially concerning in driving, where a plausible but visually
ungrounded explanation may conceal unsafe reasoning.

To study these limitations, we introduce BD-HazardVLM , a 500-image
Bangladesh-centric benchmark with structured annotations for hazard presence,
primary hazard category, risk timing, severity, defensive actions, visible evidence,
hallucination traps, and Western-road-bias traps. We evaluate Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL3-8B,
and MiniCPM-V-4.6 using a shared zero-shot task definition and structured output schema.

Our results show that binary hazard-presence accuracy is misleading:
a trivial majority-class predictor reaches 89.0%, essentially matching
all evaluated models. Fine-grained reasoning is substantially harder.
Hazard-category accuracy remains below 40%, risk-timing accuracy ranges
from 1.6% to 12.4%, and exact defensive-action matching remains below
2%. Moreover, InternVL3-8B, despite achieving the highest aggregate
severity accuracy, fails to identify any of the 58 high-severity cases.
The models also exhibit category mode collapse and near-zero self-reported recognition
of hallucination- and Western-bias-prone scenes.

Our main contributions are:

We introduce BD-HazardVLM , a 500-image diagnostic benchmark for
defensive-driving reasoning in Bangladesh mixed-traffic scenes.

We introduce BD-HazardVLM , a 500-image diagnostic benchmark for
defensive-driving reasoning in Bangladesh mixed-traffic scenes.

We define a structured taxonomy covering twelve locally
relevant hazard categories, temporal risk, severity, defensive
actions, visible evidence, and scene-level hallucination and
Western-road-bias traps.

We provide a controlled zero-shot evaluation of three open
VLMs using the same 500 images, semantic task definition, output
schema, and per-image statistical comparisons.

We identify systematic failures in category selection, latent
hazard anticipation, high-severity recognition, context-specific
action recommendation, and self-reported trap awareness.

1. We introduce BD-HazardVLM , a 500-image diagnostic benchmark for
defensive-driving reasoning in Bangladesh mixed-traffic scenes.

2. We define a structured taxonomy covering twelve locally
relevant hazard categories, temporal risk, severity, defensive
actions, visible evidence, and scene-level hallucination and
Western-road-bias traps.

3. We provide a controlled zero-shot evaluation of three open
VLMs using the same 500 images, semantic task definition, output
schema, and per-image statistical comparisons.

4. We identify systematic failures in category selection, latent
hazard anticipation, high-severity recognition, context-specific
action recommendation, and self-reported trap awareness.
2026-10-16.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision-Language Models for Autonomous Driving

Recent work has explored language-conditioned driving systems for scene
understanding, explanation, planning, and control. DriveGPT4 combines
multi-frame visual input with language generation and low-level control
prediction, while LMDrive studies language-guided closed-loop driving with
multi-view sensors and natural-language instructions [ 23 , 13 ] . DriveLM organizes perception,
prediction, and planning questions as a graph-structured reasoning task,
and DriveVLM decomposes scene description, analysis, and hierarchical
planning into language-mediated modules [ 14 , 16 ] . OmniDrive extends this direction
toward 3D grounding and counterfactual reasoning for decision making and
planning [ 19 ] .

These systems demonstrate the potential of language models for
interpretable driving, but most are designed around full-stack driving,
trajectory prediction, question answering, or closed-loop control. Their
benchmarks are also largely built from datasets such as nuScenes, CARLA,
or BDD-X, whose visual and infrastructural assumptions differ from dense,
weakly structured Bangladesh mixed traffic. In contrast, BD-HazardVLM isolates image-level defensive reasoning and evaluates whether a model can
identify the primary hazard, distinguish latent from immediate risk,
estimate severity, and recommend an appropriate defensive response.

## 2.2 Hazard, Corner-Case, and Reliability Evaluation

Driving corner cases have increasingly been used to test whether VLMs are
visually grounded and safety-aware. CODA-LM evaluates large VLMs on
self-driving corner cases through general perception, regional
perception, and driving-suggestion tasks [ 3 ] .
DriveBench evaluates reliability under clean, corrupted, and text-only
inputs and shows that plausible driving answers may arise from textual
priors or general knowledge rather than visual evidence [ 21 ] . AutoTrust broadens evaluation to trustfulness,
safety, robustness, privacy, and fairness in driving VLMs [ 22 ] .

BD-HazardVLM is complementary to these efforts. It does not evaluate
end-to-end control or generic trustworthiness across many attack types.
Instead, it targets a narrower defensive-driving question: whether a VLM
can reason about locally relevant hazards before they become immediate.
Its structured labels separate hazard identity, temporal risk, severity,
and defensive action, enabling diagnosis of failures that may be hidden
by a single overall score or by binary hazard detection. Recent benchmarks examine complementary safety-reasoning capabilities.
DRAMA-X evaluates vulnerable-road-user intent, risk, and ego-action
suggestions, while SCD-Bench studies safety cognition under ambiguous,
misleading, or unsafe driving instructions [ 5 , 25 ] . NuScenes-SpatialQA and
RoadSceneBench instead emphasize spatial and relational road-scene
reasoning [ 15 , 10 ] , whereas
INSIGHT improves hazard localization and reasoning through supervised
alignment [ 2 ] . In contrast, BD-HazardVLM evaluates
zero-shot, image-level defensive reasoning in Bangladesh mixed traffic
with explicit labels for hazard identity, timing, severity, and action.

## 2.3 South Asian and Bangladesh Road-Scene Datasets

Geographic coverage remains a central limitation of autonomous-driving
data. The Indian Driving Dataset (IDD) introduced pixel-level annotations
for unconstrained road environments, while IDD-3D added multi-camera and
LiDAR data for 3D detection and tracking in unstructured Indian traffic [ 17 , 4 ] . These datasets established the need
to evaluate perception under heterogeneous vehicle types, weak lane
discipline, dense traffic, and road layouts that differ from those in
widely used Western benchmarks.

For Bangladesh, RSUD20K provides more than 20,000 driving-perspective
images with object-detection annotations for locally relevant road users
and vehicles [ 27 ] . TFP-BD contains 23,678 images from
urban Dhaka traffic videos, including irregular pedestrian movement,
different road configurations, and varied environmental conditions [ 8 ] . Both datasets are valuable sources of
geographically relevant visual data, but their original annotations
target object detection, traffic flow, or pedestrian analysis rather than
defensive-driving reasoning. BD-HazardVLM builds on their imagery by adding
image-level hazard categories, risk timing, severity, recommended
actions, and scene-level hallucination and geographic-bias traps.

## 2.4 Hallucination and Geographic Bias in VLMs

Large VLMs can generate objects or attributes that are unsupported by the
image. POPE introduced systematic object-hallucination probing, while
HallusionBench evaluates entangled language hallucination, visual
illusion, and logical inconsistency [ 9 , 6 ] . Bias benchmarks further show
that multimodal models can exhibit systematic response disparities across
social and geographic contexts [ 20 ] . Recent
geographic evaluation also reports weaker VLM performance for less
wealthy and sparsely represented regions, together with systematic
location over-prediction [ 7 ] .

In driving scenes, such failures may appear as unsupported assumptions
about lane markings, zebra crossings, sidewalks, traffic signals, or
other infrastructure that is common in highly represented training
regions but absent from the image. BD-HazardVLM therefore annotates hallucination traps and Western-road-bias traps . These labels
describe scene susceptibility, not verified hallucinations in a model’s
complete response. Accordingly, our evaluation measures whether a model
recognizes that unsupported reasoning is possible; direct hallucination
measurement would require separate evidence-based human adjudication. Unlike NOPE and DO-Bench, which directly evaluate unsupported object
existence claims and diagnose perceptual versus prior-driven failures [ 11 , 18 ] , our trap fields measure whether a
model self-reports that a scene is susceptible to unsupported reasoning.

2026-10-19.title: Blind Precise Assembly: Proprioceptive Sim-to-Real Peg-in-Hole for Diverse Parts
2026-10-19.authors: Antonia Bronars , Younghyo Park , Kushal Kedia , Pulkit Agrawal
2026-10-19.comment: . Antonia Bronars and Younghyo Park contributed equally. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-19.abstract:
Every robot already carries high-resolution contact sensors: its own joints.
Legged robots and humanoids exploit them to walk, run, and track whole-body
motions without vision, but there the contacts are large and forceful. Is joint sensing also enough for precise, contact-rich assembly, where the robot must
find a millimeter-scale opening, mesh gear teeth, or catch a thread through light
contact? We study this question by training blind assembly policies that observe
only a short history of joint positions, velocities, and their own actions, without
visual, force, torque, or tactile sensing. The poses of both the fixture and the part
are unknown to the policy, and the grasp is randomized substantially. The policy must
therefore assemble the parts through contact, sensed exclusively through its own
proprioception. Trained with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation over
randomized parts, grasps, and contacts, such policies learn peg insertion, gear
meshing, and nut threading. The peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to the real
world and inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in 73% of trials.
Controlled comparisons with matched visual policies in simulation show that blind policies generalize far better to unseen part shapes and sizes, though they can be slower.
Training such policies needs thousands of different assemblies, each
simulated with its clearance intact, so we also release an
open-source generator that builds them procedurally from exact convex pieces
for MuJoCo; it is more accurate and faster than convex decomposition or
MuJoCo’s signed-distance collision. Videos and interactive simulations are at younghyopark.me/blind-proprioceptive-assembly/ .
2026-10-19.introduction:
A force applied anywhere on a robot’s body travels through its links to the
joints, which then move differently from what their commands alone would
produce. The encoders record that difference, so the joints of every arm and
leg double as contact sensors. Legged robots exploit this proprioceptive
signal to walk, run, and climb stairs blind ( Lee et al., 2020 ; Siekmann et al., 2021a ; Siekmann et al., 2021b ; Kumar et al., 2021 ) ,
and humanoids to walk and track whole-body motions ( Radosavovic et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024 ) . In these
settings, however, contacts are large and forceful, and joints often comply meaningfully while recording measurable deviations. Can robots exploit the same signal for precise, contact-rich assembly?

Precise assembly with a robotic arm occupies the opposite regime: the robot must
find an opening with a millimeter or less of clearance, bring gear teeth into mesh, or
catch a thread, through light contact whose effect on the joints is easy to miss. We
study this question by training blind assembly policies that have no
information outside of their own joint sensing, and verify that proprioception
contains enough information for three such tasks: peg insertion, gear meshing, and
nut threading (figure 2 ). In the real world, our peg insertion policy
inserts eight pegs of different cross-sections, three of them outside
its training distribution, with 0.5–1.5 mm of clearance per side, in
73% of 237 trials, without being
given the hole’s location, the peg’s pose in its grasp, the part’s size, or
its clearance (section 3.4 ). To our knowledge,
this is the first such demonstration.

We train our policies entirely in simulation with reinforcement learning and
deploy the peg insertion policy in the real world without fine-tuning
(figure 1 ). Training
randomizes part geometry, contact properties, fixture poses, and grasps, which can
hold the part off-center on the finger pads and tilted in the grasp. The policy
observes a 0.6 s history of joint positions and velocities, the gripper
pose and twist computed from them, and its own previous actions. It receives
no image and no force signal, so it can perceive contact and find the hole, shaft,
or bolt only through its own motion (section 2 ).

On all three tasks, probing the blind policies’ learned representations and comparing them with matched visual policies revealed two interesting properties of visually blind behaviors:

Visually blind yet intelligent. The learned behavior is not an open-loop pattern: its learned representation encoding its own proprioceptive inputs contains meaningful task-relevant information that the policy itself heavily relies on to adjust its behavior (section 3.2 ).

Proprioception generalizes better. Because a blind policy depends on the part only through its contacts, it degrades far less than vision on part shapes and sizes it has not seen during training (section 3.3 ).

Training for this robustness requires diverse parts: thousands of different
assemblies, generated procedurally and simulated in parallel, each with its
millimeter clearance intact. In MuJoCo ( Todorov et al., 2012 ) , building
holes from convex primitives by hand does not scale to random shapes, and the
automatic alternatives, convex decomposition and signed-distance-field (SDF)
collision, are less accurate and slower at these clearances. We therefore
built mjfit , which procedurally generates pegs and holes from any planar outline, as well as threads and gears, out of exact convex prisms. To summarize, our contributions are:

Blind policies, trained purely in simulation, that learn peg insertion,
gear meshing, and nut threading from proprioception alone, given no fixture pose,
grasp, or part model
(section 3.1 ), with analyses showing that
on all three tasks they search reactively,
acting on the contact state their joint histories encode rather than following a
fixed pattern (section 3.2 ), and that they generalize to unseen part shapes and
sizes better than matched visual policies (section 3.3 );

Blind policies, trained purely in simulation, that learn peg insertion,
gear meshing, and nut threading from proprioception alone, given no fixture pose,
grasp, or part model
(section 3.1 ), with analyses showing that
on all three tasks they search reactively,
acting on the contact state their joint histories encode rather than following a
fixed pattern (section 3.2 ), and that they generalize to unseen part shapes and
sizes better than matched visual policies (section 3.3 );

The first sim-to-real policy for precise insertion from proprioception alone:
trained only in simulation, the peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to a real
robot and inserts pegs of different cross-sections, including pegs outside its
training distribution (section 3.4 );

mjfit , an open-source procedural generator of assemblies for MuJoCo
(pegs and holes, threads, and gears) with exact convex collision geometry,
which supplies the thousands of different training assemblies, and a
benchmark against analytic ground truth in which it is more accurate and
faster than convex decomposition and MuJoCo’s SDF collision
(section 2.2 ).

1. Visually blind yet intelligent. The learned behavior is not an open-loop pattern: its learned representation encoding its own proprioceptive inputs contains meaningful task-relevant information that the policy itself heavily relies on to adjust its behavior (section 3.2 ).

2. Proprioception generalizes better. Because a blind policy depends on the part only through its contacts, it degrades far less than vision on part shapes and sizes it has not seen during training (section 3.3 ).

# 2 Learning blind assembly

## 2.1 Tasks

In all three tasks (figure 2 ), a 7-DOF robot arm equipped with a parallel jaw gripper holds a part
and must assemble it with a fixture that can sit almost anywhere in its workspace, and tilted (figure 3 a). The part’s geometry, its
pose in the grasp (figure 3 b), and the contact properties are randomized and not observed by policy (Table 1 ). Episodes
start with the part touching the fixture but misaligned, and succeed once it is
fully assembled. This requires the policy to both search for alignment through contact, and then perform the assembly, based on its joint position feedback alone.

Peg insertion: the pegs are prisms with varying cross-section, size,
aspect ratio, mass, and length, with 1.0–1.5 mm of clearance per side
(Appendix A ). Pegs start typically around 2 cm from the hole,
tilted far more than the clearance admits, and succeed when the peg is seated in the
hole.

Gear meshing: spur gears of varying size and tooth count must slide down a
shaft into mesh with one or two anchor gears that turn on their own axles, with
0.2–0.6 mm of backlash. Episodes start with the gear in contact with the shaft tip, but misaligned and with its teeth out of phase with the anchors’, and succeed when the gear
is seated on the shaft with teeth meshed.

Nut threading: metric nuts from M24 to M42 must thread onto a bolt with 0.05–0.2 mm of thread clearance. Episodes start with the nut resting on the bolt’s
tip, off its axis and tilted, and succeed a quarter turn after the thread catches.

## 2.2 Simulating tight insertion at scale

Training on this distribution means simulating thousands of parallel worlds
that each hold a different, randomly generated assembly, with per-side
clearances down to 0.5 mm. MuJoCo collides meshes
through their convex hulls, so a concave hole must be given an SDF or built
from convex pieces, which simulation benchmarks assemble from boxes by hand ( Zhu et al., 2020 ; Tao et al., 2024 ; Zakka et al., 2025 ) .

mjfit automates the hand-built hole
and generalizes it to arbitrary outlines. Given the planar outline of a hole,
optionally with islands such as connector pins, it emits a ready-to-simulate
MJCF model in which every contact surface is a MuJoCo primitive or a convex
prism (figure 4 ). The plate around the hole is split into convex
polygons and extruded; the peg is the hole outline offset inward by the
clearance, so every peg edge sits exactly the clearance from its hole edge,
and islands become pockets in a hollow peg. Curves are tessellated by a circumscribed polygon, so the wall never intrudes into the true hole,
as it does in rings of boxes that inscribe the circle ( Zhu et al., 2020 ) ; the only error is extra play at the corners, c ⁡ ( 1 / cos ⁡ ( π / n ) − 1 ) c\,(1/\cos(\pi/n)-1) for a circle of n n sides at radial clearance c c .
Because the construction knows which region must stay empty, the user
specifies the clearance directly rather than tuning a concavity tolerance and
checking the result. Companion generators apply the same idea to bolt–nut
pairs and spur gears, and a sampler draws random outlines, islands, and
dimensions, so one training run can hold thousands of different assemblies.

We compare against the three automatic ways to give
MuJoCo a concave hole: CoACD ( Wei et al., 2022 ) , V-HACD ( Mamou & Ghorbel, 2009 ) , and MuJoCo’s native mesh SDF, each swept over its
granularity setting. The test is a 16 mm round or square hole with clearance
down to 20 µm; we measure
each method’s error against its time per step, on CPU and on GPU with MuJoCo
Warp ( Google DeepMind and NVIDIA, 2025 ) (figure 6 ; Appendix B ).
Approximate decomposition tolerates concavity far larger than an assembly’s
clearance, so it leaves wall material inside the hole (figure 5 );
refining it narrows the error but never closes it (figure 6 a).
Mesh SDF misses contacts and rounds the rim. These errors change outcomes: a
centered peg stops on the rim or jams on every baseline’s default plate, but
falls cleanly through ours (figure 6 c). mjfit is also an order of
magnitude faster than mesh SDF on CPU at equal or better accuracy
(Table 4 ), and has the best speed–accuracy trade-off on GPU
(figure 6 b). Each assembly is only a few dozen convex pieces, so
every one of our 12,288 parallel training worlds ( Zakka et al., 2026 ) can hold a
different one.

## 2.3 Policy and training

At each step, the actor (figure 7 ) observes its
joint positions and velocities, the gripper pose and twist computed from them
by forward kinematics, and its previous action. It never receives the hole
pose, the part geometry, a wrench estimate, or an image. A temporal
convolutional encoder compresses the last 0.6 s of observations into a
latent, and an MLP maps the latent and the current observation to
joint-position increments. A joint impedance controller tracks them on an arm model
whose armature, damping, and friction were identified from real-world measurements.
Additional training details in Appendix A .

We use PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) with a sparse
reward: a bonus on success and one-time bonuses for intermediate milestones, such
as the peg’s first capture by the opening (Appendix A.1 gives the
gear’s and nut’s). Two training-only signals speed up learning from the sparse reward
without giving the actor privileged information: an asymmetric critic ( Pinto et al., 2018 ) that also sees the part’s pose relative to the fixture
and the true contact labels, and the contact supervision described next.
Randomizing dynamics and geometry ( Tobin et al., 2017 ; Peng et al., 2018 ) covers
the ranges of Table 1 .

A blind policy has to infer contact from how
the arm moves. To give that inference a dense training signal, we supervise
the actor’s latent with the contact state it cannot observe. At every step,
the simulator labels points sampled on the mating features of the part and fixture, as free, touching but misaligned, or aligned
(figure 7 , top; Appendix A details each task’s labels).
A small contact decoder predicts these labels
from the latent z t z_{t} , and its class-weighted cross-entropy is added to the
PPO loss ( Jaderberg et al., 2017 ) . The gradient of this loss trains the
encoder, but the prediction never enters the policy, so nothing privileged
reaches the actor and the decoder is dropped at deployment.

To isolate the sensing modality, we train
visual policies with the same task, resets, randomization, reward, actions,
and success check. A camera rigidly mounted on the wrist renders a
64 × \times 64 RGB image of the held part and the fixture. The visual policy sees only
images, over the same 0.6 s history, through a compact CNN.

2026-10-19.title: MOSS: Multimodal Origami Swamp Robot System
2026-10-19.authors: T. Lan , A. Babgei , L. Romanello , M. Kovac , S. F. Armanini
2026-10-19.comment: submitted to ICRA 2027
2026-10-19.abstract: Robotic systems for environmental monitoring and ecological surveying in wetlands and swamps must operate across diverse terrestrial and aquatic conditions. Conventional fixed-geometry wheels cannot adapt their contact geometry to these varying conditions. This work presents MOSS (Multimodal Origami Swamp Robot System), a compact amphibious robotic platform with 3D-printed origami wheels. The compact crank mechanism switches the wheel between contracted and expanded configurations, changing its width, body diameter, and fin orientation simultaneously. The contracted configuration is better suited to efficient rolling on firmer ground, whereas the expanded configuration provides greater contact and terrain engagement on softer surfaces. MOSS was evaluated on soil, sand, mud with varying water content, and water, in addition to in-motion morphing and terrestrial-aquatic transition tests. The more energy-efficient wheel configuration depended on terrain. The contracted configuration achieved a lower cost of transport on firmer soil and mud, whereas the expanded configuration performed better on wetter mud, sand, and water, reducing the cost of transport by up to 29%. Expanded wheels also reduced slip in wet mud and reduced both slip and hub sinkage in sand. MOSS successfully completed configuration changes in 1.95 ± 0.11 s and demonstrated continuous locomotion across soil–mud–water transitions. Outdoor trials further demonstrated operation across natural deformable terrain and water. These results show that adaptive wheel geometry provides terrain-dependent locomotion benefits and enables a single compact platform to traverse substantially different terrestrial and aquatic conditions.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Environmental change and habitat loss motivate long-term, low-disturbance ecological monitoring for conservation and ecosystem management [ 1 , 2 ] . Swamps support diverse communities, regulate water, and store carbon [ 3 ] . Yet biodiversity observations remain spatially and temporally uneven, while seasonal changes in water level and soil condition make repeated surveys difficult [ 4 ] . Robotic platforms can reduce the need for repeated human access while collecting observations in challenging environments [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] .

However, swamp environments often combine firm ground, sand, soil, mud, and water. These surfaces differ in how they support the robot and provide traction, and soft ground can also lead to wheel sinkage [ 10 ] . Firm ground favours low rolling resistance, whereas deformable terrain requires sufficient contact area and shear engagement to limit slip and sinkage. Fixed-geometry wheels cannot change their diameter, width, or contact geometry as these requirements change. Previous studies have shown that transformable and origami-inspired wheels can reconfigure their geometry to adjust ground contact across different terrains [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Although these studies establish the feasibility of wheel morphing, integrating axial reconfiguration, terrain-interacting fins, and drive-torque transmission into a single compact mechanism remains challenging. More importantly, the locomotion performance of such multimodal morphing wheels remains insufficiently characterised across swamp-relevant terrestrial and aquatic conditions. To address these gaps, this work presents MOSS (Multimodal Origami Swamp Robot System), an origami wheel mobile platform developed for locomotion across swamp-relevant deformable terrains. With MOSS, a systematic experimental evaluation is conducted across representative terrestrial and aquatic environments to determine how morphing between contracted and expanded configurations alters wheel–surface interactions and delivers terrain-specific locomotion benefits.

The main contributions of this work are:

Design and fabrication of a 3D-printed origami morphing wheel with integrated fins for wetland locomotion.

Design and fabrication of a 3D-printed origami morphing wheel with integrated fins for wetland locomotion.

Integration of the morphing wheels into a compact amphibious robot, using telescopic drive shafts that transmit drive torque while enabling axial reconfiguration.

Laboratory tests showing contracted wheels are more efficient on firmer ground and expanded wheels on softer ground and water, plus outdoor demonstrations.

1. Design and fabrication of a 3D-printed origami morphing wheel with integrated fins for wetland locomotion.

2. Integration of the morphing wheels into a compact amphibious robot, using telescopic drive shafts that transmit drive torque while enabling axial reconfiguration.

3. Laboratory tests showing contracted wheels are more efficient on firmer ground and expanded wheels on softer ground and water, plus outdoor demonstrations.

# II Morphing Wheel Design and Manufacturing

## II-A The Origami Wheel

The wheel was designed to change the axial width, body diameter, and terrain-contact geometry through a single morphing motion. Its folding pattern was adapted from the rotational-sweep Origami Sphere proposed by Mitani [ 17 ] , but was modified for thick-panel additive manufacturing. The resulting origami pattern is shown in Fig. 2 (a). Each wheel is made from two identical 3D-printed patterns bonded into a ring. The ring is then folded by hand along the designed crease lines to form the wheel structure. Unlike an ideal paper model, a printed wheel must accommodate finite panel thickness, crease interference, limited folding clearance, and repeated contact loading [ 18 , 19 ] . The pattern therefore uses three local thicknesses of 0.1 0.1 , 0.2 0.2 , and 0.7 ​ mm 0.7~\mathrm{mm} , as indicated by the colours in Fig. 2 (a). The thinner regions provide folding compliance, whereas the thicker panels provide the load-bearing and wear-resistant structure. The central crease region is widened to reduce interference during deformation.

Compared with conventional multilayer fabrication [ 14 , 13 ] , printing each flat pattern as a single piece reduces the number of parts and avoids cutting, stacking, and aligning multiple layers, as well as many assembly steps. Digital fabrication allows local thicknesses, crease features, and geometry to be modified directly, accelerating design iteration. The resulting patterns improve geometric consistency between wheels and reduce assembly errors while preserving the intended folding sequence and final wheel configuration.

However, PLA has limited ductility. Thinning the folding regions improves their flexibility but reduces their load-bearing capacity and durability during repeated deformation. Compliance cutouts (Fig. 2 a) were therefore introduced in selected regions and bridged with soft textile tape. The tape provides local flexibility, while overlapping segments arranged like pillbug plates (Fig. 2 b) preserve the wheel’s circumferential load path [ 16 ] . The same tape reinforces the exposed segment tips and reduces wear during ground contact. Together, these features support repeated morphing while retaining the stiffness required for locomotion.

The resulting transformation couples wheel width and body diameter. In the prototype, the contracted configuration is approximately 27 ​ mm 27~\mathrm{mm} wide with a 95 ​ mm 95~\mathrm{mm} body diameter, whereas the expanded configuration is approximately 53 ​ mm 53~\mathrm{mm} wide with a 73 ​ mm 73~\mathrm{mm} body diameter. The wheel width nearly doubles during reconfiguration. These dimensions describe the wheel body without the fins and were selected based on the available chassis envelope, actuator stroke, linkage packaging, and manufacturing constraints.

## II-B Integrated Fins and Coupled Morphing

As shown in (Fig. 2 a), fin-like features inspired by mudskipper pectoral appendages were integrated directly into the printed pattern [ 20 ] . During contact, the fins penetrate deformable terrain, increase tangential shear resistance, and distribute load over additional contact points. This design increases available traction and helps reduce local sinkage. The fins therefore form part of the wheel structure rather than a separately actuated attachment. Their orientation changes passively as the inclined origami panels rotate. In the contracted configuration, the fin edges are approximately parallel to the ground, corresponding to α ≈ 85 ∘ \alpha\approx 85^{\circ} under the geometric convention used here. As the wheel expands, α \alpha decreases below 85 ∘ 85^{\circ} , which may improve shear engagement and load distribution on deformable terrain such as sand and mud. The fins are considered an integral part of the morphing wheel, so their individual contribution is not isolated.

## II-C Crank Actuation and Shape Retention

The wheel is morphed by a centrally mounted actuator and crank linkage (Fig. 2 c). The inner wheel sides remain fixed to the axle, while the linkage pulls the outer sides inward or pushes them outward. This changes the wheel’s axial width and body diameter without changing the wheel-axle interface. The contracted and expanded configurations are defined by target positions of the morphing actuator and are used as the two locomotion conditions in this study. In position mode, the actuator actively maintains the selected wheel configuration without a separate mechanical lock.

2026-10-19.title: Not All Actions Contribute Equally: Learning Precise Progress Estimation from Imprecise Demonstrations
2026-10-19.authors: Huanqian Wang , Boshi Tang , Botong Xiao , Jie Zhang , Yang Yue , Danhua Tao , Shiji Song , Gao Huang
2026-10-19.abstract:
Progress estimators play an essential role in providing dense reward signals for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation, but accurately assessing task progress can be much challenging.
Existing methods heavily rely on expert data and naively assume that all actions within a demonstration contribute to task success.
This assumption often breaks down in real-world scenarios, especially in high-precision manipulation, where subtle geometric errors can lead to task failure.
Therefore, these methods can erroneously interpret human mistakes as meaningful progress, further corrupting progress learning.
We argue that a key limitation is the lack of a global prior regarding task evaluation criteria, which is crucial for distinguishing meaningful progress from human mistakes.
To this end, we propose PRIME, a novel progress estimator capable of learning precise progress estimation from imprecise demonstrations by aggregating experience across trajectories.
PRIME constructs a weighted graph over observed states, connecting states across trajectories based on spatial proximity and visual consistency. Edge weights encode spatial distances as transition costs, and shortest-path search approximates the geodesic distance to success. Changes in this distance naturally distinguish advancement, stagnation, and setbacks without assuming monotonic progress over time.
Extensive experiments in both simulation and real world on precise manipulation tasks show that PRIME is consistently effective across diverse tasks, and robust to data with varying degrees of suboptimality.
Notably, the advantage of PRIME gets more pronounced in higher-precision scenarios, yielding up to a 5 × 5\times improvement in policy success rate over the SFT baselines on charger insertion.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Real-world Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as an indispensable paradigm for advancing robotic manipulation from simple, repetitive actions to highly complex, precise skills [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
However, mastering these high-precision tasks demands feedback that goes beyond binary success signals to identify and rectify the inevitable imperfections within human-collected demonstrations and policy rollouts [ 1 , 2 , 5 ] .
To bridge this gap, progress estimators have garnered extensive attention in the research community [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
Despite recent progress, faithfully capturing subtle advancement, stagnation, and setbacks remains challenging for progress estimators, particularly in high-precision manipulation [ 11 , 12 ] .

The inefficiency of existing methods in high-precision tasks stems from their inability to distinguish genuine task progress from suboptimal behaviors such as drifting, overshooting, and idling (Fig. 1 , Bottom). These methods rely on a simple yet flawed assumption that all actions within a trajectory contribute equally to eventual task success [ 8 , 9 ] . Consequently, they depend heavily on expert data and discard a substantial proportion of collected demonstrations that fail to meet the required precision threshold.
However, discarding low-quality demonstrations is costly and overlooks that, in high-precision settings, even high-quality demonstrations may contain steps that do not advance the task. Although trajectory-level filtering improves the policy success rate by 16.7 percentage points in our SFT experiments (Fig. 1 , top), suboptimal behaviors within the retained demonstrations can still confound progress estimates. This motivates finer-grained, step-level progress estimation.

Our key observation is that accurate progress estimation can be achieved only if the underlying progress structure captures holistic task priors. Such priors cannot be obtained from a single trajectory.
For example, when learning to operate an entirely new machine, the human operators cannot determine whether the current operation is optimal and can only attempt to faithfully follow the demonstration.
However, after observing multiple demonstrations, the operator can distinguish between suboptimal and optimal actions and thus estimate the progress of the current operation.
Thus, we incorporate this holistic information into our progress labels by leveraging the collective experience across multiple demonstrations, rather than relying solely on the temporal position within an individual trajectory.

Building on this observation, we propose PRIME ( PR ecise progress estimation from IM precise d E monstrations), a progress estimation method extracting collective experience from the collected suboptimal demonstrations to assess step-level quality. We adopt a graph search framework to approximate geodesic distances over the feasible manifold.
Each node represents an observed state comprising the robot configuration and multi-view visual observations.
Edges are established based on configuration proximity and visual consistency, while edge weights quantify geometric changes in robot configuration, which allows for transitions to alternative trajectories with only a fine-grained distance penalty. Shortest-path search on the resulting graph estimates the geodesic distance to success. Changes in this distance naturally distinguish advancement, stagnation, and setbacks without assuming monotonic progress over time.

We validate the effectiveness of PRIME through extensive experiments in both real-world and simulation scenarios, which demonstrate that a policy trained with PRIME significantly improves the success rate across diverse tasks and is robust to data with varying degrees of suboptimality.
In real world experiments, PRIME achieves consistently superior success rates especially on higher-precision tasks, outperforming the standard SFT baseline by up to 2.2 × − 5 × 2.2\times-5\times across 3 high-precision tasks: peg-in-hole (73.3% v.s. 33.3%), peg-in-hole Hard (70.0% v.s. 20.0%), and charger insertion (50.0% v.s. 10.0%).
We further construct a diagnostic benchmark covering stage understanding, local precision, and progress continuity. PRIME achieves 92.5% accuracy in local-precision discrimination, substantially outperforming the best baseline at 70.0%.
In the simulation environment, we evaluate PRIME (see Sec. IV-A ) via online reinforcement learning. Specifically,
our method achieves relative improvements of 10.9% in InD success rates (0.674 v.s. 0.608) and 13.5% in OOD success rates (0.353 v.s. 0.311), demonstrating its effectiveness in guiding policy learning.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Progress estimation in robotics

Obtaining an effective reward function is fundamental in robotic reinforcement learning to guide policy optimization and efficient exploration. This is especially crucial for high-precision tasks, where sparse feedback often leads to optimization collapse due to long credit-assignment horizons [ 1 ] .
To derive dense rewards from demonstrations, existing methods commonly construct progress estimation from the temporal structure of trajectories.
Early approaches adopt linear temporal progress, such as normalized remaining-step estimation or linear interpolation over execution time [ 13 , 9 , 8 , 6 , 14 ] .
More recent approaches introduce structured, non-uniform progress estimation [ 15 , 16 ] . SARM [ 7 ] introduces subtask-level progress allocation with linear interpolation within each subtask, while ProcVLM [ 17 ] further refines it by redistributing intra-subtask progress according to visual changes.
ARM [ 16 ] learns from human-annotated progress directions, which incurs substantial time and labor costs.
Although these designs relax the uniform-rate assumption of linear interpolation, their progress targets are still largely derived from temporal ordering in demonstrations, enforcing progress to increase monotonically along the trajectory. Such temporal monotonicity does not necessarily reflect effective progress in high-precision manipulation. Demonstrations may contain hesitation, overshooting, or redundant adjustments where later observations can be temporally closer to task completion yet physically farther from a successful state.

## II-B Learning precise manipulation

Reinforcement learning in high-precision tasks has enabled remarkable breakthroughs, such as screw installation [ 1 ] , shoelace tying [ 2 ] , in-hand manipulation [ 18 , 19 ] , band tying [ 20 ] , belt assembly [ 21 ] , and deformable object handling [ 22 ] .
While these works improve precise manipulation, reliable dense progress supervision from offline demonstrations remains unaddressed.
Beyond these methods, researchers are also exploring efficient strategies for learning high-precision tasks.
Compared to these works that achieve high-precision manipulation with reweighted behavior cloning [ 20 , 2 ] or pure reinforcement learning [ 2 , 18 , 19 , 21 , 1 ] , PRIME distinguishes itself by focusing on accurate progress estimation learning, which further drives high-efficiency reinforcement learning.

2026-10-19.title: Learning Robot Metareasoning: Adaptive Computation Budgets for Real-Time Control
2026-10-19.authors: Lorenzo Magnino , Antonio Marino , Michael Amir , Daigo Shishika , Amanda Prorok
2026-10-19.abstract:
Planning while moving faces an historical trade-off between deliberation and reactivity.
A planner running concurrently with execution needs time to compute, so the robot must commit to an open-loop action chunk for that duration: a longer commitment buys a better plan at the cost of feedback frequency. Existing controllers fix this action commitment, and consequently the computation budget, before deployment. However, the optimal computation time is highly state-dependent (due to factors such as unmodeled dynamics, safety constraints, and marginal optimisation gains), i.e. dynamic, therefore offline static tuning risks leaving systems blind during critical maneuvers or unable to find global effective solutions.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Deciding how much to think is as hard as the thinking itself (e.g., deciding
what to do) [ 1 ] . Biological agents dynamically arbitrate their cognitive resources, continuously balancing rapid, reactive responses against slower, deliberate reasoning based on environmental uncertainty and temporal constraints [ 1 , 2 ] . This adaptive allocation represents a fundamental speed-optimality trade-off where extended deliberation is penalized by elapsed time [ 3 , 4 ] .
The value of computation (VOC) formally characterizes this trade-off between the marginal gain in decision optimality and the cost of deliberation [ 5 , 6 ] . Traditional metareasoning frameworks assume a frozen world state during planning, requiring an explicitly defined cost function to penalize extended computation, a paradigm we refer to as the economic value of computation. Embodied autonomous agents, conversely, operate in continuous time where this assumption fails. Because the robot and its environment evolve concurrently with the planner’s execution, heuristic timing penalties are unnecessary. Instead, the physical dynamics inherently penalize computational delay through unmitigated state drift, thereby hindering high-frequency reactivity and reducing safety margins. We introduce this dynamic trade-off as the physical value of computation, formalized in Sec. III .

As standard for computational efficiency, robots typically plan in receding-horizon: the system optimizes a trajectory over a finite horizon, executes the initial segment, and subsequently replans from the evolved state. Model predictive control (MPC) [ 7 , 8 ] commits to a single control step, resolving the problem at every control period, providing high-rate feedback around a
nominal trajectory.

Alternatively, action-chunking architectures generate a sequence of actions
to execute in open-loop while the next plan is produced. This commitment can improve motion smoothness and sample efficiency [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] , yet fundamentally limits the system’s ability to react to high-frequency disturbances or environmental changes. In both paradigms, the solver’s computational budget and execution horizon are statically defined prior to deployment. Consequently, the robot lacks a principled mechanism to dynamically arbitrate when a state warrants extended deliberation for trajectory optimality versus when it necessitates rapid, reactive feedback (Fig. 1 ) .

Identifying an optimal static computation budget cannot be resolved via offline tuning. It is fundamentally a state-dependent quantity, dictated by the unmodelled dynamics , the proximity to state-space constraints , and the marginal optimality gained through additional solver iterations. Moreover, the budget choice cannot be assessed from the current state alone: its consequences propagate to future states throughout the episode, where they may influence later decisions and outcomes.

We address these challenges by formulating adaptive computation budgets for real-time control
as a semi-MDP over decision epochs. At each epoch, one decision sets both the
open-loop execution horizon and the parallel computational resources allocated to solver. We then learn this decision from experience with an RL policy
(Fig. 2 ).

Our contributions are the following:

We review the work most closely related to our setting.

Because a chunking policy emits several actions at once, a mechanism is required to cover the gap
while the next chunk is generated. RTC [ 12 ] keeps execution smooth
across that gap by conditioning the new chunk on the actions still running, and
DEFLECT [ 13 ] instead trains the policy to tolerate acting on
observations that have gone stale; both leave the chunk length fixed. [ 14 ] makes that length adaptive, while [ 15 ] pre-computes several candidate
chunks and follows whichever best matches the realised state. Unlike our approach, none of these methods couples the execution length with the solver’s computation budget, so a larger commitment cannot be leveraged to compute a better plan.

Event- and self-triggered MPC frameworks dynamically determine when to replan rather than solving at every control step, preserving feasibility and stability of the system [ 16 ] . Alternative approaches dictate the replanning interval based strictly on safety, defining it as the maximum duration the current trajectory can be executed while a collision-free fallback remains available [ 17 ] . However, these triggering mechanisms are designed fundamentally to conserve computation subject to a baseline guarantee, treating the underlying optimizer as an oracle whose solution quality does not improve with additional allocated time.

Metareasoning prices computation by the improvement in the decision quality it produces, net of the cost of running it [ 5 , 6 ] . This principle underlines anytime
algorithms, deliberation scheduling [ 18 , 19 ] , and learned computation budget [ 20 ] . In these conventional formulations, the world is treated as frozen while the agent deliberates, so the cost of thinking is an explicit penalty chosen by the designer to trade against the expected benefit.

Closest to our work, [ 21 ] learns how long to deliberate
in real time and casts the decision as a semi-MDP over budgeted options.
Their setting, however, is restricted to discrete game examples and therefore does not expose uncontrolled variation that arises when acting in the
real world. Furthermore, their method requires a separate reflex policy that acts in the open-loop phase, an assumption that our framework does not need.

# II Preliminaries

Given a Markov Decision Process (MDP) defined by the tuple ℳ := ( 𝒮 , 𝒜 , 𝒫 , r , γ ) \mathcal{M}:=(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},r,\gamma) , let 𝒮 ⊆ ℝ n \mathcal{S}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} be the state space, 𝒜 ⊆ ℝ m \mathcal{A}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{m} be the action space. We define 𝒫 : 𝒮 × 𝒜 → 𝒮 \mathcal{P}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{S} as a transition kernel (dynamics model) yielding transition probabilities 𝒫 ⁡ ( s t + 1 | s t , a t ) \mathcal{P}(s_{t+1}|{}s_{t},a_{t}) . Moreover, let r : 𝒮 × 𝒜 → ℝ r:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} and g : 𝒮 → ℝ g:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be, respectively the one-step and the goal-conditioned reward functions. At any time t t the set of goals will be denoted by G t ⊆ S × 𝒜 G_{t}\subseteq S\times\mathcal{A} . We work throughout in discrete time with continuous state : where the index t ∈ ℤ ≥ 0 t\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} advances at the fixed control period d ​ t dt .

The objective of ℳ \mathcal{M} is to determine a sequence of actions (control inputs), that drives the system into a desired state, solving the following infinite-horizon goal-conditioned control problem.

To solve 1 online in a receding horizon, we utilize a monotonic-improving optimizer, ψ \psi . A defining characteristic of such a solver is that its solution monotonically improves with the computational budget it is allocated. However, allocating more computation time introduces a temporal cost: the physical system must continue to operate while the solver thinks. To afford a computational budget of h h control periods, the solver must therefore commit to generating a sequence of actions (a chunk) of length h ∈ { 1 , … , 𝔥 max } = ℋ h\in\{1,\dots,\mathfrak{h}_{\mathrm{max}}\}=\mathcal{H} , where 𝔥 max ∈ ℕ + \mathfrak{h}_{\mathrm{max}}\in\mathbb{N}^{+} . We define this solver as a mapping ψ h : 𝒮 → 𝒯 h \psi_{h}:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathcal{T}_{h} , where 𝒯 h = 𝒜 h \mathcal{T}_{h}=\mathcal{A}^{h} is the space of action sequences. By committing to this extended sequence, the robot executes the chunk open-loop, explicitly buying the required time window for the solver to concurrently compute the subsequent plan. While classic MPC formulations restrict this mapping to a single step ( h = 1 h=1 ), our formulation extends h h to leverage the solver’s monotonic improvement at the expense of delayed reactivity. We evaluate this framework using Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) and the Cross Entropy Method (CEM), two standard sampling-based receding horizon solvers, though our method accommodates any monotonic-improving optimizer.

Two fundamental difficulties arise when solving 1 online with a receding horizon time-monotone solver ψ h \psi_{h} whose computation time is non-negligible and proportional to the action chunk length h h :

Because the solver’s computational budget scales with the chunk length h h , the problem formulation inherently couples how deeply the solver reasons with how frequently the system observes. A small h h enables rapid feedback to counter the disturbances described in (C1), but heavily restricts the computational budget, resulting in myopic and suboptimal planning. Conversely, a large h h allocates sufficient budget for deep, long-horizon deliberation but forces the system to remain open-loop for extended periods. A static h h therefore forces a rigid compromise between optimality and robustness, failing to exploit the fact that different states in the MDP require different levels of deliberation versus reaction .

We take up these challenges by adopting real-time chunking, which makes (C1) explicit rather than assuming it away, and by adapting the commitment length h h (and consequentially budget of the solver) online through an RL policy learnt from experience, which turns the design constant of (C2) into a decision.

2026-10-19.title: TransNav: Transformer-Based End-to-End Navigation Method for Static and Dynamic Quadrotor Obstacle Avoidance
2026-10-19.authors: Jianghan Zhu , Zhuo Li , Yanjun Zhang , Jian Sun
2026-10-19.comment: . Published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
2026-10-19.abstract: Obstacle avoidance for autonomous quadrotors in cluttered environments remains challenging, especially when both dense static obstacles and moving obstacles are present. Existing methods are often tailored to either static or dynamic settings, which always limit their adaptability across diverse environments. This paper presents TransNav, a transformer-based end-to-end navigation method for quadrotor obstacle avoidance in both static and dynamic environments. TransNav employs a patch-based point-cloud encoding scheme that combines local feature extraction with global contextual modeling, enabling compact yet informative environment representation. The method integrates perception and navigation in a single architecture and directly predicts a finite-horizon action sequence, from which the first action is executed. Moreover, we develop an unsupervised learning strategy by incorporating a lightweight point-mass dynamics model, which directly optimizes trajectory-level costs over the predicted sequence through numerical gradient propagation. Thus, the policy can be efficiently trained without expert demonstrations. Simulation and real-world experiments show that the proposed method achieves strong performance in dense static environments and competitive obstacle-avoidance capability in dynamic scenarios, while maintaining low inference cost for onboard deployment.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Autonomous drones are widely deployed in scenarios such as exploration [ 1 ] , search and rescue [ 2 ] , and inspection [ 3 ] . These environments are filled with densely distributed small obstacles and randomly moving dynamic obstacles, which require drones to perceive their surroundings in real time and generate immediate control commands to navigate safely. Traditional methods typically rely on manually designed perception-decision-control pipelines, where computational delays and cumulative errors severely degrade performance. In contrast, learning-based end-to-end navigation methods directly map raw sensory input to control commands, enabling high-performance real-time flight [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Recent studies using depth images [ 6 ] , optical flow [ 7 ] , or 3D LiDAR point clouds [ 9 ] as perception data have demonstrated outstanding results in dense environments.

Achieving a good balance between static-scene navigation and dynamic-obstacle avoidance remains difficult. Approaches designed for static environments [ 6 ] , [ 9 ] react insufficiently to rapidly moving obstacles, while a few methods [ 10 ] tailored for dynamic scenarios tend to overfit to motion features, leading to degraded performance in dense static environments. Moreover, training strategies of the navigation policies in [ 10 ] , [ 11 ] rely heavily on training settings dominated by dynamic obstacles, which increase computational burden and fail to cover the full diversity of real-world obstacle motions, resulting in limited generalization. These limitations make it difficult to deploy an end-to-end policy reliably across a wide range of realistic conditions.

To address these limitations, we propose TransNav, a transformer-based end-to-end navigation method for quadrotors using LiDAR point clouds. TransNav is designed to provide a more general policy for obstacle avoidance across both settings. On the one hand, to overcome the insufficient response speed of existing static-scene methods to moving obstacles, TransNav predicts a finite-horizon action sequence at a high frequency, achieving more effective reactions to obstacle motion. On the other hand, to ensure navigation performance in dense static environments, TransNav employs a patch-based LiDAR representation that preserves local geometric details while allowing global spatial context to be modeled compactly. Specifically, raw point clouds are first converted into a high-resolution distance map and then partitioned into patches inspired by vision transformers. A lightweight CNN and self-attention mechanism are further used to jointly encode local obstacle structure and longer-range spatial dependencies. In addition, an efficient unsupervised training strategy is introduced to directly optimize trajectory-level costs over a finite prediction horizon. By integrating a lightweight point-mass dynamics model into the learning pipeline, gradients of the full action sequence can be backpropagated directly without expert demonstrations or critic networks. This design enables fast convergence while maintaining strong sim-to-real generalization. The quadrotor used in real-world environments is shown in Fig. 1 .

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

A transformer-based end-to-end navigation architecture is proposed for quadrotors, which fuses patch-based LiDAR distance-map representations with sampled reference-trajectory states to predict a finite-horizon action sequence within a unified framework.

A lightweight perception-to-action pipeline is developed, which predicts action sequences for high-frequency receding-horizon execution. It improves the response ability of the policy to moving obstacles while maintaining strong navigation performance in dense static environments.

An efficient unsupervised training strategy for the proposed action-sequence policy is developed, which incorporates a lightweight point-mass dynamics model to directly optimize trajectory-level costs over the predicted action sequence without expert action labels.
