2026-10-19.title: Reinforcement Learning Based Multi-Terrain Adaptive Whole-Body Control for a Quadruped Manipulator
2026-10-19.authors: Yanzhou Jin , Fei Suo , Chang Liu , Yasuhisa Hasegawa , Liming Chen , Yusuke Iwasawa , Yutaka Matsuo , Yaonan Zhu
2026-10-19.abstract:
Legged robots equipped with manipulators offer promising capabilities for loco-manipulation tasks in unstructured environments. However, achieving task-consistent end-effector behavior during locomotion remains challenging due to terrain-induced disturbances and the strong coupling between locomotion and manipulation, particularly for small-scale quadruped platforms. A reinforcement-learning-based whole-body control framework is proposed for quadruped loco-manipulation on complex terrain.
The proposed framework combines a hybrid task representation with task-prioritized whole-body learning to coordinate locomotion and manipulation while preserving task-consistent end-effector behavior. A lightweight quadruped manipulator platform is further developed to validate the proposed framework on a small-scale quadruped system.
Real-world experiments demonstrate successful deployment on complex terrains such as slopes up to 30 degrees, stairs, and deformable terrain. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying a learned whole-body control policy for quadruped loco-manipulation in real-world environments and highlight the importance of task-consistent whole-body coordination for terrain-adaptive loco-manipulation.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Recent advances in quadruped locomotion have enabled robust traversal across challenging terrains. By integrating onboard manipulators, quadruped robots are expected to perform loco-manipulation tasks that require both mobility and object interaction, such as inspection, maintenance, search-and-rescue, and operation in unstructured environments. However, combining locomotion and manipulation introduces strong coupling between base motion and end-effector (EE) behavior, making precise task execution substantially more challenging than pure locomotion [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .

Compared with larger mobile manipulators, small-scale quadruped manipulators operate under significantly tighter payload constraints [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Commercially available arms used on such platforms can occupy a substantial portion of the quadruped payload capacity and act as moving loads during locomotion [ 7 , 8 ] . Their static mass, configuration-dependent center-of-mass shifts, and dynamic reactions may increase leg actuator demands and reduce the performance of terrain traversal.
Conversely, terrain irregularities and changing foothold contacts can induce body motions that are transmitted to the end effector, thereby compromising manipulation performance [ 3 ] .
Existing loco-manipulation systems often adjust body posture to expand the manipulator workspace and improve end-effector reachability [ 9 , 10 ] . Although effective on flat terrain, such posture adjustments may conflict with the body regulation required for terrain traversal [ 11 ] , whereas body motions required for terrain adaptation may disturb end-effector tracking [ 12 , 13 ] . Accordingly, maintaining task-relevant end-effector behavior while preserving locomotion feasibility on challenging terrain remains a central challenge for quadruped loco-manipulation.

Reliable locomotion requires adequate body regulation [ 11 ] , while manipulation depends on maintaining locomotion feasibility. These dependencies motivate the state-dependent prioritization of body regulation, locomotion, and manipulation. Existing loco-manipulation approaches commonly coordinate locomotion and manipulation through unified optimization frameworks [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] , hierarchical locomotion-manipulation architectures [ 17 ] , or learning-based whole-body control (WBC) policies [ 18 , 19 ] . Optimization-based approaches can explicitly incorporate whole-body dynamics and physical constraints [ 20 ] , but their application to rough terrain depends on sufficiently accurate modeling of coupled robot dynamics, changing contacts, and terrain interactions, together with repeated online optimization. Reinforcement-learning (RL) is well suited to this setting because it allows closed-loop whole-body coordination to be optimized offline over randomized terrain, contact, and loading conditions, while deployment requires only fixed-cost policy inference. Recent learning-based studies have demonstrated whole-body trajectory tracking [ 8 ] , object interaction [ 21 , 22 ] , and mobile manipulation [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] . However, explicit state-dependent coordination among body regulation, locomotion, and manipulation has received limited attention, particularly regarding how manipulation should be modulated when body regulation or locomotion deteriorates. Incorporating these objective dependencies into a unified learned policy therefore remains an open challenge for rough-terrain loco-manipulation.

Beyond objective coordination, end-effector position and orientation play different roles in manipulation tasks. Positional deviations can often be compensated through robot repositioning or locomotion planning, whereas orientation tracking frequently has a direct impact on task execution. Examples include container transportation, tool manipulation, and other disturbance-sensitive tasks in which the end-effector orientation must remain consistent relative to the environment [ 26 ] . Consequently, treating end-effector position and orientation identically may lead to unnecessary compromises between task consistency and locomotion feasibility. Effective task representations that balance these competing requirements, therefore, remain another key challenge for rough-terrain loco-manipulation.

To address these challenges, a reinforcement-learning-based whole-body loco-manipulation framework combining task-prioritized learning with a hybrid task-space representation is proposed. The policy is optimized using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO [ 27 ] ) because its clipped update objective supports stable training, while its rollout-based formulation is compatible with large-scale parallel simulation for continuous 18-DoF control under randomized terrain and contact conditions. Task-prioritized learning modulates the contributions of lower-priority objectives according to the current performance of body regulation and locomotion. The hybrid representation regulates end-effector orientation relative to gravity to preserve task consistency, while expressing end-effector position in the body frame to maintain tracking feasibility under terrain-induced body motions. A lightweight quadruped manipulator is further constructed by integrating a custom-designed 1.5-kg Lite Arm with a Unitree Go1 (Fig. 1 ). The lightweight design reduces manipulator-induced loading, while the whole-body policy coordinates the arm and base under the remaining configuration- and motion-dependent coupling. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate consistent end-effector tracking on challenging terrains, including slopes, stairs, and deformable surfaces.
The contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A lightweight quadruped manipulator platform integrating a custom-designed Lite Arm and a Unitree Go1 is developed, together with a hybrid task-space representation that enables rough-terrain loco-manipulation while preserving task-consistent end-effector behavior.

A lightweight quadruped manipulator platform integrating a custom-designed Lite Arm and a Unitree Go1 is developed, together with a hybrid task-space representation that enables rough-terrain loco-manipulation while preserving task-consistent end-effector behavior.

A reinforcement-learning-based whole-body control framework with task-prioritized learning is proposed, enabling coordinated loco-manipulation while maintaining end-effector task tracking under challenging terrain. A systematic ablation study validates the effectiveness of the proposed objective hierarchy.

The proposed whole-body control framework is validated through simulation and real-world experiments on challenging terrains, including slopes, stairs, and deformable surfaces. The controller is further integrated into an autonomous loco-manipulation pipeline, demonstrating practical deployment in real-world tasks.

2026-10-19.title: FLoTS-SLAM: Optical Flow-Derived Uncertainty for Monocular Dynamic SLAM with Two-Stage Optimization
2026-10-19.authors: Haorui Du , Lipu Zhou
2026-10-19.abstract:
Monocular simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) remains challenging in
dynamic environments. Thus, real-time dynamic object identification in
such environments is a critical problem. Recent approaches estimate per-pixel
uncertainty from rendering residuals or multiview feature inconsistency to
identify dynamic regions. These methods lack direct motion
evidence, and their accuracy may degrade when reconstruction is inaccurate or
features are ambiguous. In addition, such uncertainty merely downweights
pixels in bundle adjustment (BA), so inaccurate uncertainty estimates can
still impair camera pose estimation and 3D reconstruction. Accordingly, we
present a monocular RGB SLAM system for dynamic scenes. Specifically, a
motion uncertainty estimation method is proposed to derive
uncertainty from the residual between optical flow and
camera motion induced flow, directly reflecting object motion. The estimation
varies with frame alignment accuracy, reducing false detections and yielding accurate
pixel-level masks of dynamic regions. To make BA more robust, we estimate camera poses from high confidence pixels. These poses are then used to reproject
dynamic pixels during joint refinement of poses and depth, reducing
the influence of object motion on both pose and depth updates. Moreover, we
provide a quantitative evaluation of dynamic masks and analyze how
these masks affect the downstream tracking and reconstruction of dynamic
objects. Our approach improves the mean dynamic mask IoU by 35% over a
state-of-the-art baseline on DAVIS, and reduces the average ATE by
59% on Bonn and 19% on TUM relative to the SLAM backbone used in our system.
The source code will be made publicly available.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Monocular simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) is a
fundamental problem in robotics, with broad applications in autonomous
navigation [ 1 ] , augmented reality [ 2 ] , and virtual reality [ 3 ] .
However, dynamic objects disrupt the geometric consistency across views and may
introduce erroneous correspondences. Such correspondences
degrade camera pose estimation and 3D reconstruction, reducing SLAM accuracy
and robustness in real-world scenes. Dynamic environments therefore remain a
challenge for reliable SLAM. This paper focuses on monocular SLAM
in such environments.

Identifying dynamic objects underpins subsequent camera tracking and 3D scene
reconstruction. Moving object segmentation (MOS) models [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] can identify dynamic objects in video, but these models typically have prohibitive inference costs for real-time tasks.
Earlier dynamic SLAM methods instead use lightweight semantic segmentation or
object detection models [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] , which infer motion from
semantic categories rather than actual motion. As a result, they fail to
recognize moving objects from unseen classes. For known classes, they may
mistake static objects for dynamic ones and moving ones for static.
Open-vocabulary segmentation [ 10 ] broadens object coverage but
leaves this semantic basis unchanged. Fig. 1 illustrates
the potential errors of the detection-based method NGD-SLAM [ 11 ] .

Recent works [ 13 , 14 ] estimate per-pixel uncertainty for
dynamic regions, independent of object categories. This uncertainty is
predicted from DINO [ 15 ] features with a shallow
multilayer perceptron (MLP), supervised online by the discrepancy between
input images and current renderings. The estimates degrade when the
map is inaccurate. DROID-W [ 12 ] avoids this dependence
on reconstruction accuracy by using multiview feature inconsistency.
However, the feature inconsistency provides indirect evidence of motion
and may be unreliable in semantically complex or weakly textured regions,
as shown in the second row of Fig. 1 .

Optical flow captures interframe motion directly, and several
SLAM systems use it to detect dynamic regions [ 16 , 8 , 17 ] . In these systems, however, the flow comes
from a dedicated estimator, adding computational overhead and increasing
per-frame processing time [ 18 ] .
In addition, the identification scheme for
marking a pixel as dynamic is fixed in advance [ 16 , 19 , 20 ] . Consequently, pose and depth errors
may cause static pixels to be misclassified as dynamic.

Apart from dynamic object identification, how the estimated uncertainty is used in
optimization also affects system robustness. Existing uncertainty-aware
systems [ 13 , 12 ] apply uncertainty estimates in
bundle adjustment (BA) as per-pixel weights, and refine poses and depths
jointly under that weighting. However, motion residuals from dynamic pixels
that are not fully suppressed still impact both depth estimates and keyframe
poses. All pixels are used in BA, so inaccurate uncertainty at any pixel can affect
the estimation.

Motivated by the above observations, we present a monocular RGB SLAM system for dynamic scenes built on FL ow-derived uncertainty and T wo- S tage optimization (FLoTS-SLAM).
Optical flow measures motion directly and is obtained from the existing
correspondence predictions of the system tracker without additional computation.
To identify dynamic objects accurately, we design a motion uncertainty
estimation method based on optical flow residuals.
In addition, uncertainty weighting alone may not fully suppress the influence
of dynamic pixels on pose and depth estimation, and removing these pixels
would reduce the number of constraints for optimization. We therefore perform
optimization in two stages to improve robustness.
In the first stage, depth is fixed and poses are estimated from high confidence pixels.
In the second stage, poses and depth are jointly refined,
using the first-stage poses to predict where dynamic pixels would appear if the scene were static.
Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a motion uncertainty estimation method
to improve the accuracy of dynamic object identification. It
derives uncertainty from the residual between optical flow and
camera motion induced flow, and adapts to frame alignment accuracy.

to improve the accuracy of dynamic object identification. It
derives uncertainty from the residual between optical flow and
camera motion induced flow, and adapts to frame alignment accuracy.

We introduce a two-stage optimization method to reduce the influence of
object motion on pose and depth updates, and improve tracking
robustness.

We conduct extensive experiments.
FLoTS-SLAM attains state-of-the-art camera localization on Bonn
and TUM, reducing the average ATE of its DROID-SLAM backbone by 59%
and 19%. We also introduce
Dynamic Mask IoU (DM-IoU) to quantitatively evaluate dynamic identification
across methods. On DAVIS, our method improves the mean DM-IoU by 35%
over a state-of-the-art baseline.

We will make the source code publicly available to facilitate future research.

2026-10-19.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Moving Object Segmentation

Moving object segmentation (MOS) aims to identify dynamic objects in a video and produce masks for each frame.
Early learning-based methods group pixels whose motion is coherent across
frames [ 21 , 22 ] , and later work adds complementary cues such as
layered representations, residual-flow modeling, and appearance
features [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] . Recent methods instead inherit the generic priors
of foundation models [ 4 ] or ground segmentation in
pretrained 4D geometry [ 5 , 6 ] . All of them, however, run a
dedicated network over a multi-frame window, and their inference costs are
prohibitive for real-time systems.

## II-B Traditional Dynamic SLAM

Dynamic objects produce correspondences that rigid camera motion cannot explain,
degrading camera pose estimation and 3D reconstruction in conventional visual
SLAM [ 26 , 27 ] . Many dynamic SLAM methods therefore detect
dynamic regions and exclude them from optimization, reconstructing the static
scene alone. Such regions are identified from geometric consistency across
frames [ 28 , 29 ] , from semantic priors on movable
categories [ 8 , 9 ] , or from a combination of the two.
DynaSLAM [ 7 ] , for instance, segments movable instances with Mask
R-CNN [ 30 ] and verifies them by multiview reprojection consistency.

## II-C Dynamic NeRF- and 3DGS-based SLAM

Recent SLAM methods based on neural radiance fields (NeRFs) [ 31 ] and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [ 32 ] incorporate dynamic region
identification to handle moving objects. Dynamic extensions such as
PG-SLAM [ 33 ] , NID-SLAM [ 34 ] , and SDD-SLAM [ 35 ] obtain motion masks from segmentation networks. The masks, however,
follow object category rather than observed motion, and
cover only the classes the network has seen.

Another group of methods replaces category priors with a per-pixel uncertainty
map [ 36 ] . WildGS-SLAM [ 13 ] and UP-SLAM [ 14 ] extend it to SLAM by regressing uncertainty from DINOv2 [ 15 ] features,
supervised by the discrepancy between the input image and the current rendering.
The estimate may degrade when the rendering is inaccurate. DROID-SLAM in
the Wild [ 12 ] instead derives uncertainty from multiview feature
inconsistency, requiring neither a rendered map nor a learned prior. However, all
of these methods rely on appearance cues, which provide only indirect evidence of
object motion. So our method derives uncertainty from the residual between
optical flow and camera motion induced flow, which measures motion directly.

## II-D Optimization in Dynamic SLAM

Optimization in dynamic scenes should account for moving objects.
Early methods such as DynaSLAM [ 7 ] exclude detected
dynamic regions from tracking and mapping.
DynoSAM [ 37 ] jointly estimates camera poses, scene
structure, and rigid-object motion within a factor graph.
BA-Track [ 38 ] learns to isolate camera-induced motion
from observed point trajectories, providing correspondences for BA.
Recent methods [ 13 , 12 ] use per-pixel uncertainty to weight residuals
during joint pose and depth refinement.
However, inaccurate weights may insufficiently suppress
motion-induced residuals, compromising estimation accuracy.
We therefore introduce a two-stage optimization method
for more robust and accurate pose and depth estimation.

2026-10-19.title: HexaShell: A Thin Harness for Exploring the Limits of VLM Agents as Robot Coding Agents
2026-10-19.authors: Hongcheng Gao , Alex Zhou , Jay Zhu , Zelin Zheng , Shijia Ge , Xiping Li , Di Wu , Yazhe Wang , Jianshu Zeng , Xuan Shangguan , Yongli Wang , Yexing Wan , Lingyu He , Zhiqi Jia , Sihang Wu , Xiao He
2026-10-19.comment: Code: this https URL
2026-10-19.abstract: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin: it only turns the agent’s commands into robot motion. The agent drives a robot with two arms through one command line. It sees three RGB cameras and knows their calibration. After each failed attempt, the agent reads the log, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools. In this way it keeps what it learns as code, as a coding agent does when it fixes a failing test. The tools may use only what the robot observes. They use triangulation to find where objects are, relative to each other and to the gripper. If two cameras see the same point, the point lies where the two camera rays meet. If a point lies on a known plane, such as the table or the top of a block, it lies where its ray meets that plane. When the head camera is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get a second view. We build the tools on only ten layouts of one seed per task, then freeze them and test them on ten new layouts of the same seed. We use Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. On all 42 RoboDojo tasks, HexaShell reaches a success rate of 39.7% and a progress score of 48.0, averaged in the same way as the leaderboard. This is a new state of the art on RoboDojo. The limit is contact, not reasoning: pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. When the agent fails, it usually sees the failure but cannot make the motion work. We open source the tools evolved so far at https://github.com/HexaFuture/HexaShell .
2026-10-19.introduction:
Robot manipulation leaderboards have been led by learned policies. Vision language action models and world action models learn from large sets of demonstrations and output the robot’s actions directly [ 35 , 4 , 7 ] . Agents built on vision language models have now started to compete. On RoboDojo [ 14 ] , the model we use reaches 22.5% without tools of its own, choosing gripper targets through a fixed harness written by the benchmark’s authors [ 69 ] .

Coding agents suggest another route. In a software repository, a coding agent reads the code, runs it, reads the error and fixes the code, and the fix stays. Recent work has begun to let coding agents write and revise robot tools and programs [ 26 , 25 , 40 , 34 ] . We ask how far a coding agent can go when it works on a robot in the same way, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin. The agent gets one command, robo, three RGB images with their calibration, and a manual of one page. The harness turns commands into joint motion and does nothing else. What the agent learns is kept as tools, small programs that add commands to robo and may use only what the robot observes. An acting agent tries a layout with the current tools. After a failure, an optimizer agent of the same model reads the episode as it would read a failing test, writes or fixes a tool with its unit tests, and the layout is tried again ( Fig. 3 ). Both agents are Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort.

The hard part is turning pixels into positions. In a repository, everything the agent works on is text it can read exactly. On a robot, the agent sees objects as pixels, but every command needs a position in the world, to about a centimetre for a grasp. Vision language models are known to judge such distances poorly [ 9 , 16 ] . The standard observation has no depth. A monocular depth network can estimate depth from one image, but on RoboDojo scenes Depth Anything V2 [ 65 ] is off by a median of 41 mm at the head camera and about 100 mm at the wrists, even after we fix its scale with the table. Our tools use triangulation instead. The cameras are calibrated, and the robot knows where its wrists are. A point that two cameras see lies where their rays meet, and a point on a measured plane, such as the table, lies where its ray meets that plane [ 27 ] . When one view is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get another. This is active perception [ 3 ] , and on a benchmark it has a price: the motion uses action steps, and every task has a step limit.

We build the tools on ten layouts of each task, freeze them, and test them on ten new layouts. On all 42 tasks, HexaShell reaches 39.7% success and a progress score of 48.0 on the leaderboard’s metric, a new state of the art on RoboDojo ( Fig. 2 ). It does best where the right action follows from measured geometry, and it stops at contact: tight insertion stays low. The paper makes three contributions.

A thin harness and a short repair loop for robot coding agents. The harness gives an unchanged coding agent one command line to the robot and makes no decisions for it. All that the agent learns is kept as small tools with unit tests, which the next episode loads. After a failure, a second agent of the same model edits one tool and the same layout runs again. A repair round takes a median of 6.3 minutes, and no robot data, training or change to the model is needed ( Section 3 ).

The finding that triangulation locates objects more reliably than a depth network, and so lifts what a VLM agent achieves on a robot. The model picks a pixel on the target, and the tool turns it into a position. With the same harness, loop and model, on the same layouts, triangulation scores 8.7 points higher than Depth Anything V2; paired by layout, it wins 57 layouts and loses 23 ( Table 1 ). # 2 Related Work

Language models have written robot code before. Code as Policies [ 37 ] emits executable programs over perception and control primitives, ProgPrompt [ 54 ] and Inner Monologue [ 29 ] plan with a language model and feedback, VoxPoser [ 30 ] writes value maps for a planner, ReKep [ 31 ] and MOKA [ 39 ] let a vision model mark keypoints that code then optimises, RoboCodeX [ 45 ] and RoboScript [ 10 ] generate manipulation code from images and text, language models write reward functions for policy learning [ 66 , 44 ] , and SayCan [ 1 ] grounds language in a fixed skill library. In each, the program is produced per instruction and discarded, and people write the primitives. HexaShell inverts this division of labour: the agent writes the primitives, they persist across episodes and are what is optimized, and the per-episode program is short. Concurrent work moves the same way: URAI pairs a programming agent that writes motion tools with an execution agent that calls them [ 26 ] , Gao et al . [ 25 ] treat tools, traces and memory as code that a physical coding agent revises, CaP-X benchmarks coding agents on manipulation [ 23 ] , RLE-Bench tests them as robot learning engineers [ 43 ] , LIBERO-Agent tests general agents that act on the robot directly [ 18 ] , and MEMENTO evolves code policies with a memory of past programs [ 56 ] . We measure, on one full benchmark, how far such tools reach and where they stop.

Frontier models have also been used as policies without tools of their own. Zhang et al . [ 69 ] evaluate GPT-6-Astra on RoboDojo through a fixed end-effector harness with no learned policy in the loop, and in a case study the model writes a piano controller that transfers across tempo but not key geometry. Show-Harness [ 15 ] , Agent as Policy [ 32 ] , VIA [ 28 ] and World Action Agent [ 70 ] drive robots through a vision language agent and a fixed interface, and a line of recent work builds harnesses in which coding agents program, test and improve robot skills [ 21 , 42 , 63 , 59 , 19 , 57 , 11 ] , sometimes starting from a few human demonstrations [ 40 , 34 ] . We keep the model and benchmark and change one thing, letting the agent write, keep and repair tools ( Section 5.1 ).

Agents that build their own tools are the closest family. Coding agents that read a repository, run the tests and fix the code [ 12 , 33 , 64 , 62 ] are the starting point of this paper. Voyager [ 58 ] grows a skill library of JavaScript functions while playing Minecraft, Toolformer [ 52 ] learns when to call existing tools, LATM [ 8 ] and CRAFT [ 67 ] have language models write and retrieve tools, and self-improving coding agents [ 68 , 47 , 41 ] modify their own scaffolding or programs and keep edits that improve a score. Our loop belongs to this family but holds the agent’s scaffold, prompt and base interface fixed and changes only task tools. We are able to diagnose faults in one round, while ensuring that the tools stay runnable under the official client. Like Reflexion [ 53 ] and Eureka [ 44 ] , the optimizer iterates on code from traces, but acceptance is a fresh execution of the same layout rather than self-assessment.

Our tools measure 3D positions from RGB images. Monocular depth networks predict depth from one image [ 65 , 5 , 60 , 61 ] , but their scale must be fixed from outside and their errors are several centimetres on our scenes ( Section 4.4 ). Vision language models judge metric distances in an image poorly, and SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT train them on spatial data to improve this [ 9 , 16 ] . Multiple view geometry recovers a point from two calibrated views [ 27 ] , and plane sweep tests candidate depths by warping one view into another [ 17 ] ; both are standard in OpenCV [ 6 ] . Active perception moves the sensor to get a better view [ 3 , 2 ] . Our tools combine these ideas and charge each extra view to the robot’s action budget, which a benchmark with a step limit makes explicit ( Section 4.5 ).

The baselines we compare against are mostly learned manipulation policies. Vision language action models [ 7 , 35 , 49 , 4 , 50 , 48 , 73 ] , trained on demonstrations collected with low cost hardware [ 71 ] , are evaluated on suites such as LIBERO [ 38 , 22 ] , RoboCasa [ 46 ] , RoboTwin [ 13 ] and SIMPLER [ 36 ] , or in autonomous real-world evaluation [ 72 ] . RoboDojo [ 14 ] adds a fixed action budget per task, a multi-seed evaluation, and paired clean and cluttered layouts, which let us separate geometric competence from appearance memorisation ( Section 4.3 ).

2026-10-19.title: No Eyes, No Problem: What Does Touch Contribute to Blind Baoding Ball Manipulation?
2026-10-19.authors: Ayush Deshmukh , Nalin Agarwal , Elle Miller , Sethu Vijayakumar
2026-10-19.abstract:
Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, achieving sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can generate sophisticated blind manipulation policies in simulation, transferring them to a real dexterous hand remains hindered by continuously changing contacts, motion-induced tactile information drift, and the gap between simulated and physical dynamics. We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback as observations. We achieve successful zero-shot transfer through a combination of a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels. On the physical hand, the policy achieves sustained blind Baoding rotation, completing 225 consecutive 𝟏𝟖𝟎 ∘ \mathbf{180^{\circ}} rotations (112.5 full rotations) at ∼ 0.36 ​ rot/s \sim 0.36\;\text{rot/s} in a single continuous trial without any vision or object-state information. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of tactile sensing relative to proprioception alone and identify the hand regions where tactile information is most important.
This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, irrespective of the sensing modality used. By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.
2026-10-19.introduction:
In-hand manipulation requires continuous control of contact, with fingers making, breaking, and re-establishing contact as the object moves relative to the hand. The hand is simultaneously the actuator and the sensor, so each corrective motion changes the contact state from which the next correction is made. This intermittent contact and discontinuous dynamics make in-hand manipulation difficult to model and control. Most approaches address this challenge by supplying object state externally, through cameras, markers, or privileged simulator information. These observations provide explicit information about object pose and geometry, yet humans can reorient objects in the hand without continuously observing them, relying instead on contact during manipulation.
This raises a fundamental question: can contact alone stand in for explicit object state, as it does for humans?

We take this question literally. Unlike prior systems that rely on
cameras [ 1 , 2 ] ,
motion-capture markers [ 3 ] , or privileged
simulator state distilled into a student
policy [ 4 , 5 ] , our policy receives none
of these; it observes only joint encoders and 16 binary contact
signals, a representation shown to be sufficient in
simulation for single-object
rotation on hardware [ 6 ] .
While most existing real-world in-hand manipulation studies focus on reorienting a single object via reinforcement learning (RL) [ 3 , 7 , 1 , 6 , 2 , 5 ] , we choose to study Baoding ball manipulation as a more challenging instance of in-hand dexterity: two objects circulate simultaneously, interact with each other as well as the fingers, and are manipulated here on only a four-fingered Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite. The phase relationship between the two objects must be maintained without being directly observed.

Prior approaches that attempt Baoding ball rotation have typically used external object-state information or tactile sensing to demonstrate rotation [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . However, sustained zero-shot transfer of a blind policy from simulation to physical hardware remains an open challenge.
More recently, dexterous Baoding ball rotation was demonstrated in simulation across multiple robotic hands using only proprioception and binary contacts [ 11 ] . It was shown that combining RL with self-supervision (e.g. latent multi-step forward dynamics) learned implicit representations of the manipulated object(s) state, which led to superhuman simulated blind dexterity [ 12 ] . Yet, these works did not provide any hardware results, so the transferability of these results was unknown.

In this work, we achieve zero-shot sim-to-real transfer of Baoding ball rotation using only proprioceptive and binary contacts as observations, extending upon the simulation results in [ 12 , 11 ] . We construct a simulation embodiment that reproduces the physical tendon coupling and tactile sensor layout used on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, and introduce per-channel tactile calibration, command slew-rate randomisation and Stuck-AT Taxels (STAT) to improve robustness to hardware discrepancies. We show that a policy trained entirely in simulation can complete 225 consecutive 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} rotations (112.5 full rotations) at ∼ 0.36 ​ rot/s \sim 0.36\;\text{rot/s} in a single continuous trial on a physical Shadow Hand Lite from touch and proprioception alone. Our main contributions are as follows:

A hardware-aligned Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite simulation with matched tactile sensor sites and action mapping that reproduces the physical tendon coupling.

A hardware-aligned Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite simulation with matched tactile sensor sites and action mapping that reproduces the physical tendon coupling.

A per-channel hysteresis-based tactile calibration to mitigate sensor noise.

Two episode-level randomisations, Slew-rate Domain Randomisation (SlewDR) and Stuck-AT Taxels (STAT), that encourage smoother policy outputs and reduce reliance on individual tactile channels.

Rigorous benchmarking of Baoding ball rotation across increasing levels of feedback information and cumulative randomisation ablations.

Zero-shot transfer of a blind Baoding policy to the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, sustaining rotation from proprioception and binary contact, with tactile feedback substantially improving performance and long-horizon recovery.

1. A hardware-aligned Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite simulation with matched tactile sensor sites and action mapping that reproduces the physical tendon coupling.

2. A per-channel hysteresis-based tactile calibration to mitigate sensor noise.

3. Two episode-level randomisations, Slew-rate Domain Randomisation (SlewDR) and Stuck-AT Taxels (STAT), that encourage smoother policy outputs and reduce reliance on individual tactile channels.

4. Rigorous benchmarking of Baoding ball rotation across increasing levels of feedback information and cumulative randomisation ablations.

5. Zero-shot transfer of a blind Baoding policy to the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, sustaining rotation from proprioception and binary contact, with tactile feedback substantially improving performance and long-horizon recovery.

# II Related Works

In-hand manipulation involves contacts that continuously form, break, and shift
as the object moves relative to the hand. RL in simulation
with domain randomization has made such skills practical, from block
reorientation [ 3 ] and Rubik’s cube
manipulation [ 13 ] on the Shadow Hand to agile cube
reorientation on the Allegro Hand [ 1 ] . Later work
generalized across object shapes and sensing modalities, using object pose and
point clouds [ 4 ] , a single depth camera [ 2 ] ,
or vision combined with dense touch [ 14 ] . These methods obtain
object state from outside the hand, even though the object is often occluded
once the fingers enclose it.

Blind in-hand manipulation relies on the hand’s own sensing rather
than external perception. Proprioception has
enabled single-object rotation [ 5 ] , and joint position and
torque sensing has enabled sustained cube rotation and
reorientation [ 7 , 15 ] . However, light objects
produce only small changes in the hand state [ 12 ] , which motivates direct contact
sensing. Dense and optical tactile representations provide richer contact
information but are harder to simulate and
calibrate [ 16 , 17 ] , whereas binary contacts are
compact and transfer more readily [ 6 , 18 ] . Existing blind hardware results with sustained manipulation involve a single object.

Baoding ball manipulation extends blind in-hand manipulation to the coordination of multiple free objects, requiring two balls to be coordinated through both ball–hand and ball–ball contacts, making it more challenging than single-object manipulation. Prior
hardware results (Table II ) rely largely on external object
information. Nagabandi et al. [ 8 ] used stereo vision with model
predictive control on a Shadow Hand, while Yuan et al. [ 9 ] fused
depth point clouds with binary FSR sensing on an Allegro Hand. Blind hardware
evidence remains limited. Yang et al. [ 10 ] estimated ball positions
from a 653-taxel tactile array using a graph network, but reported only a single
qualitative half-rotation on hardware.
RoTO [ 12 ] and RoTO 2.0 [ 11 ] used binary tactile sensing,
including on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, but remain in simulation. Moreover, none of these hardware works demonstrates rapid rotation sustained
over several minutes. We address this gap through zero-shot transfer of a blind policy to the
Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile
sensing, and show sustained rotation on hardware.

2026-10-19.title: AWAM: Active Trajectory-Conditioned View Imagination for Robust Robot Manipulation
2026-10-19.authors: Jiawei Geng , Zhenyang Liu , Yuzheng Wu , Yanwei Fu
2026-10-19.abstract: Rapid progress in embodied intelligence has enabled increasingly capable robots to follow language instructions and manipulate diverse objects. However, strong results in structured environments do not automatically transfer to open-world conditions, where clutter, occlusion, and changing viewpoints can obscure the spatial relationships required for action. To address this perceptual gap, a virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced. AWAM, an Active World-Action Model actively plans where to observe and imagines what will be seen along the planned trajectory before acting. Task-related virtual camera motion is predicted and used as a structured query into a geometry-conditioned world model, producing a reusable spatial prior for manipulation, which is later compressed into a fixed memory and fused with live observations through cross-attention for diffusion-based action prediction. AWAM achieves competitive success rates with 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. These results support improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts, addressing part of the gap between structured manipulation and less controlled environments.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Embodied intelligence has advanced rapidly through large-scale robot learning, vision–language pretraining, and generative action modeling. Increasingly capable policies can translate language goals and visual observations into manipulation behaviors across diverse tasks ( Brohan and others, 2022 ; Brohan and others, 2023 ; Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) .

However, much of this progress is evaluated in relatively structured settings in which camera configurations, scene layouts, and task-relevant objects remain sufficiently observable. Occlusion-focused and distribution-shift benchmarks expose a complementary limitation: once deployment becomes less structured, an unfavorable camera pose, clutter, or a shifted layout can hide the target or interaction region and remove the evidence required for control ( Li et al., 2026 ; Fei et al., 2026 ; Bai et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025c ; Liu et al., 2025d ) . This creates a perceptual bottleneck rather than only an action-modeling bottleneck. More expressive action models alone cannot directly recover scene evidence that is absent or highly ambiguous in the input, so performance gains obtained under well-observed scenes may not transfer to open-world conditions with incomplete visibility.

Several lines of work have begun to address this problem. Physical active perception acquires additional evidence by moving the camera or robot, but introduces extra execution steps and can alter the robot or scene state. Virtual-view methods avoid this cost by selecting or synthesizing complementary observations. Candidate-view approaches choose from predefined cameras ( Liu et al., 2026b ; Xu et al., 2026 ) ; TVVE predicts task-conditioned virtual poses and re-renders reconstructed geometry ( Bai et al., 2026 ) ; and world-action models such as Motus and Fast-WAM exploit predictive visual modeling to strengthen action representations ( Bi et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) . These directions establish the value of additional visual context, yet the underlying limitation is not fully resolved: virtual perception is often restricted to isolated views, reconstruction-based rendering cannot reveal surfaces absent from the initial geometry, and predictive world models are commonly organized around action-induced futures rather than deliberate viewpoint queries.

To address these questions, task-conditioned virtual active perception is formulated as trajectory-conditioned view imagination. Instead of selecting a single view or a small set of independent poses, a virtual camera trajectory specifies how perception should evolve to expose task-relevant evidence. Such a trajectory can reorient toward a target, approach fine interaction geometry, or move around an occluder when no single viewpoint is sufficient. Importantly, the predicted trajectory is never physically executed; it serves only as a sequence of virtual queries, thus retrieving the available evidence and learned spatial priors into a representation that better supports control, separating perceptual exploration from robot motion.

Based on this formulation, AWAM is introduced as an Active World-Action Model that realizes the virtual-perception process before closed-loop control. A task-conditioned trajectory predictor first produces virtual camera poses for better observation from the initial RGB-D image and language instruction. The calibrated observations are then back-projected into coarse 3D geometry and rendered along the predicted path. A geometry-conditioned world model fills unsupported regions and produces multi-view latent features, which are compressed into a persistent world memory. During manipulation, live static- and wrist-camera observations retrieve relevant predictive context from this memory, and a diffusion policy generates short-horizon action chunks in closed loop. The resulting design uses world modeling as an internal perceptual mechanism for asking where to look and what would be seen, rather than as a prediction of the robot’s executed future.

Evaluation is conducted across three simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation. Success reaches 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5 ± 1.1 76.5\pm 1.1 % on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. On LIBERO-Occ, removing the entire predictive-memory branch reduces average success by 11.5 percentage points, and replacing learned task-conditioned virtual trajectory with sampled viewpoints reduces it by 5.7 points. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of learned virtual camera motion and persistent predictive memory for manipulation under incomplete visibility. The contributions are threefold:

A trajectory-conditioned virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced for manipulation, replacing isolated or physically executed viewpoint acquisition with a continuous sequence of task-directed virtual queries.

A trajectory-conditioned virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced for manipulation, replacing isolated or physically executed viewpoint acquisition with a continuous sequence of task-directed virtual queries.

AWAM is proposed to transform the predicted observation trajectory into geometry-consistent multi-view representations and compress them into persistent world memory as a reusable spatial prior for manipulation under partial observability.

Extensive evaluations across three challenging simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation demonstrate strong performance under occlusion and distribution shifts and confirm the benefits of learned camera motion and predictive memory through ablations.

1. A trajectory-conditioned virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced for manipulation, replacing isolated or physically executed viewpoint acquisition with a continuous sequence of task-directed virtual queries.

2. AWAM is proposed to transform the predicted observation trajectory into geometry-consistent multi-view representations and compress them into persistent world memory as a reusable spatial prior for manipulation under partial observability.

3. Extensive evaluations across three challenging simulation benchmarks and real-world manipulation demonstrate strong performance under occlusion and distribution shifts and confirm the benefits of learned camera motion and predictive memory through ablations.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Large-scale robot policies map visual observations and language instructions directly to actions. Recent VLA models and diffusion-based policies improve generalization, action representation, and efficient decoding through large-scale pretraining and expressive generative objectives ( Brohan and others, 2022 ; Brohan and others, 2023 ; Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Chi et al., 2025 ; Pertsch et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Liu et al., 2025b ) . These methods primarily focus on how actions are represented and learned from available observations. In contrast, AWAM targets the perceptual evidence supplied to the policy, constructing additional task-conditioned spatial context when relevant scene information is poorly observed or occluded.

Occlusion can be mitigated by acquiring or synthesizing complementary visual evidence through multiview perception, viewpoint selection, and imagined views ( Liu et al., 2026b ; Bai et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) . Existing approaches typically rely on additional sensing, reconstructed views, or a small fixed number of generated observations. AWAM instead predicts a task-conditioned virtual camera trajectory and consolidates the generated multi-view sequence into persistent world memory for closed-loop manipulation. This formulation turns occlusion handling into trajectory-conditioned predictive perception, where the model jointly reasons about where to observe, what would be observed, and how this information should support subsequent control.

Recent video diffusion and world models have shown strong capability in modeling long-horizon visual dynamics, while text-, action-, and camera-conditioned variants further enable controllable prediction of future or novel observations ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ) . Predictive world models provide representations of how visual observations may evolve and have increasingly been integrated with robot control. Video Prediction Policy ( Hu et al., 2025 ) conditions control on features learned from predictive video modeling. Motus ( Bi et al., 2026 ) unifies visual understanding, video generation, inverse dynamics, and action prediction within a latent world-action model. Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) separates the benefits of video co-training from explicit test-time future generation and shows that strong action prediction can be retained without iterative future-video rollout. Unlike approaches centered on predicting the future scene induced by robot actions, AWAM uses world modeling as a form of active perception. A task-conditioned camera trajectory specifies where the current scene should be queried, and a geometry-conditioned world model predicts visual representations along this trajectory. These representations are consolidated into a compact world memory and reused throughout manipulation rather than interpreted as the robot’s executed future.

2026-10-19.title: Look Before You Act: Bridging Active Perception and Vision-Language-Action Models via Observation-Aligned Data Adaptation
2026-10-19.authors: Jiawei Geng , Zhenyang Liu , Yuzheng Wu , Yongchong Gu , Yanwei Fu
2026-10-19.abstract: Robots manipulating objects in clutter must decide not only how to act, but also where to look. Although active camera motion can expose an occluded target, it may move the robot into an initial observation–state distribution that differs from the manipulation policy’s training distribution. We identify this problem as first-frame distribution sensitivity : under perturbed starts in LIBERO, naively prepending camera repositioning to π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} reduces success from 46.3% to 11.5%. We introduce ActiveAlign , a data-adaptation framework that trains a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy from the states at which active perception terminates. A learned viewpoint module first generates a camera trajectory. Offline, ActiveAlign uses closed-loop alignment to connect the trajectory endpoint to an existing demonstration, replays the remaining manipulation trajectory, and retains successful continuations for fine-tuning. At deployment, the same viewpoint module precedes the adapted VLA without modifying its architecture. Across 40 LIBERO tasks, ActiveAlign achieves 70.7% success with π 0 \pi_{0} and 72.7% with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , outperforming their standard-training baselines by 40.0% and 26.4% respectively. Matched-state and data-matched controls support gains beyond prefix shortening and generic viewpoint augmentation; OpenVLA and GR00T N1 also show the same trend. Success rate under physical occlusion in real world increases from 35/90 to 83/90. These results show that active perception benefits manipulation when policy training is aligned with the observation and robot-state distribution induced by viewpoint selection.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Effective manipulation begins with an observation that supports the intended action [ 1 , 2 ] . A robot asked to retrieve fruit from a container or grasp a cup behind clutter may need to move its camera before it can see a useful approach direction. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] provide a powerful interface from visual observations and language to robot actions, but their input is still determined by where the robot looks. Repositioning an existing wrist camera is an appealing way to expose the target before manipulation. The resulting system must therefore solve two connected problems: selecting an informative view and continuing the task from the state produced by that selection.

The most direct composition is to let an active-perception (AP) module improve the view, then hand control to a VLA trained on conventional demonstrations. Our experiments reveal a counterintuitive outcome: this composition can substantially reduce task success. Under a shared perturbed-start LIBERO protocol, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} falls from 46.3% to 11.5% average success after camera repositioning, and π 0 \pi_{0} falls from 30.7% to 7.0%. The qualitative examples in Fig. 1 illustrate the tension: a policy can act from a familiar but occluded view, yet struggle to exploit a view selected to reveal the target. Improving the observation and making it usable by the action policy are distinct requirements.

We study this interface through first-frame distribution sensitivity . Here, the first frame is the observation at the handoff from active perception to manipulation. Wrist-camera motion changes image location, scale, and occlusion together with arm configuration and the relationship to the remaining task. A policy must consequently infer a suitable continuation from a different combination of visual and proprioceptive cues. Action chunking [ 8 , 9 ] can propagate an early error through the actions executed before the next observation, even when later decisions use fresh images. This motivates examining the joint observation–action interface; a difference between first-frame image distributions alone does not establish the cause of every failure. Our experiments therefore pair the failure observation with controls that separate viewpoint information from robot-state progress and data volume.

The central design insight is that the deployment viewpoint policy is available during data construction. Rather than requiring a manipulation learner to accommodate arbitrary sensing motions, we can expose it to successful continuations from the endpoints of the very module it will encounter at inference. This turns the composition problem into a question about supervision: how can existing demonstrations be made to begin where active perception stops? Demonstration-generation methods such as MimicGen and DemoGen [ 10 , 11 ] motivate reusing recorded behavior, while the present setting adds a specific constraint: the starting observation and state are chosen by a task-conditioned camera policy. Visual augmentation alone does not supply the actions needed to continue from that state.

ActiveAlign constructs these continuations offline. Given scene RGBD and a language instruction, a learned module predicts a wrist-camera trajectory. In a restored environment, we execute the trajectory and match its endpoint to a nearby end-effector state in an early demonstration prefix. Closed-loop alignment bridges the residual gap, after which the recorded manipulation suffix is replayed. Successful alignment-and-replay trajectories become training data for the VLA. The active approach replaces part of the original demonstration, while the recorded continuation teaches the policy how to proceed after that approach. At deployment, the same viewpoint module runs once before object contact; the adapted VLA then manipulates using fresh observations. The procedure changes training data and policy weights while preserving the VLA architecture.

Replay feasibility is essential to this construction. End-effector proximity does not ensure that object and contact states agree, so nearest-state matching alone cannot validate a continuation. Successful replay filters the candidate endpoints and limits the training distribution to states for which usable supervision can be reconstructed. ActiveAlign consequently applies to resettable simulators and reconstructable physical workcells. This requirement belongs to offline data collection: deployment requires neither scene reset nor expert replay. The resulting scope is pre-manipulation view selection, with longer-horizon tasks testing the lasting value of that initial view rather than continuous response to moving occluders.

Our evaluation follows this reasoning from composition failure to controlled explanation and physical validation. On LIBERO Spatial, a matched-state camera-extrinsics control holds the demonstration step and manipulation suffix fixed and reaches 54.6%, compared with 78.2% for ActiveAlign. Data-matched random views and broad viewpoint jitter reach 58.0% and 61.4%, respectively. These comparisons support a benefit from the informative, deployment-matched observations beyond shorter demonstrations and generic coverage. Across four suites, ActiveAlign improves π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} by 40.0 and 26.4 percentage points; OpenVLA and GR00T N1 extend the evidence to different action formulations. Initial-occlusion simulation tasks, diverse physical tasks, and endpoint perturbations further characterize when the construction is useful and where it breaks down.

Our contributions are threefold:

We characterize the failure of naive composition of active perception and VLAs, and test competing explanations through matched-state and data-matched controls.

We introduce observation-aligned demonstration adaptation, connecting active-view endpoints to successful manipulation through prefix matching, closed-loop alignment, and replay filtering.

We evaluate the construction across four VLA backbones, 40 LIBERO tasks, initial occlusion, and physical manipulation, with sensitivity studies that quantify the feasibility–diversity trade-off and endpoint error tolerance.

1. We characterize the failure of naive composition of active perception and VLAs, and test competing explanations through matched-state and data-matched controls.

2. We introduce observation-aligned demonstration adaptation, connecting active-view endpoints to successful manipulation through prefix matching, closed-loop alignment, and replay filtering.

3. We evaluate the construction across four VLA backbones, 40 LIBERO tasks, initial occlusion, and physical manipulation, with sensitivity studies that quantify the feasibility–diversity trade-off and endpoint error tolerance.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

Vision-language-action policies. Large-scale language-conditioned robot policies such as RT-1 and RT-2 established a general interface from visual observations and language instructions to robot actions [ 12 , 13 ] . Recent VLA models instantiate this interface with different action representations: π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} use flow matching [ 3 , 5 ] , OpenVLA predicts discrete action tokens [ 4 ] , and GR00T N1 uses a diffusion-transformer action module [ 14 ] . Diffusion policies and alternative action tokenizations provide additional formulations for visuomotor control [ 9 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] . Despite these architectural differences, each policy depends on the observation–state distribution represented in its training demonstrations. ActiveAlign is orthogonal to these action parameterizations: it preserves the policy architecture while adapting the fine-tuning distribution to the states induced by a deployment-time viewpoint module which offers a more informative view.

Active and multi-view perception. Active perception [ 18 , 19 ] and next-best-view methods [ 20 , 21 ] select sensing actions that improve downstream decisions. Multi-view manipulation methods aggregate or render observations from multiple viewpoints to improve spatial reasoning [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] , while SAM2Act, VISO-Grasp, and ViewActive explore related mechanisms for visual representation and viewpoint selection [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] . Our approach, instead, physically repositions a wrist camera before invoking a separately adapted VLA, thus studying physical wrist-camera motion, which changes not only the visual input but also the robot configuration from which manipulation begins. Its focus is therefore the compatibility between a selected better viewpoint and the downstream policy’s manipulation distribution.

Recent robotic systems learn physical sensing motion together with manipulation. Vision in Action couples sensing and bimanual behavior using a 6-DoF neck and VR teleoperation [ 29 ] ; HoMMI combines egocentric human demonstrations, hand–eye policies, and whole-body control [ 30 ] ; and ActiveGlasses uses a dedicated perception arm to coordinate camera and manipulation motion [ 31 ] . These systems collect or learn paired sensing and manipulation behavior for specialized active-vision embodiments. In contrast, ActiveAlign uses an existing wrist camera for a single pre-manipulation viewpoint trajectory and connects it to an independently trained VLA through offline demonstration adaptation, without altering the VLA architecture or requiring continuous gaze control. GenDoP [ 32 ] studies related autoregressive RGBD-and-language camera trajectory generation [ 33 ] ; our contribution concerns the robot-data adaptation interface.

Demonstration adaptation and distribution shift. DAgger [ 34 ] addresses policy-induced state mismatch through iterative collection. Domain randomization and augmentation broaden visual coverage [ 35 , 36 , 37 ] , including through generated images [ 38 , 39 , 40 ] . ActiveAlign targets a different source of shift: the handoff states produced by a separate viewpoint policy used at deployment. Demonstration-generation methods reuse recorded behavior to expand the training distribution. MimicGen transforms demonstrations across object configurations [ 10 ] , while DemoGen adapts trajectories and point-cloud observations for spatial generalization [ 11 ] . ActiveAlign instead adapts demonstrations to the physical endpoints induced by a task-conditioned viewpoint policy. Because camera motion changes both arm configuration and visual observations, geometric endpoint matching alone does not guarantee a valid manipulation continuation. ActiveAlign therefore uses closed-loop alignment and successful replay to validate supervision. Our matched-state and data-matched controls further compare this targeted, deployment-matched adaptation with shorter manipulation suffixes and broader random-view or viewpoint-jitter coverage.

2026-10-19.title: Beyond Success Rate: Interventional Evaluation of Memory in Vision-Language-Action Systems
2026-10-19.authors: Keyuan Luo , Yi Xie , Wanyun Ling , Yuanzhe Li , Ziyue Li , Zhuoqi Zeng
2026-10-19.comment: including references and appendices
2026-10-19.abstract:
When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role?
Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they
change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide
offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation
Protocol (IMEP) for vision–language–action (VLA) systems to address four
questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does
memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects
specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we
compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal
numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness
separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode,
cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments,
a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation
procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect
over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce
ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in
current observations. The full memory configuration raises task
success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under
shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support
robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit
requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.
2026-10-19.introduction:
A robot’s current observation may omit information needed to act: an earlier
visual cue, a previous episode’s experience, or a fact retained across tasks.
Vision–language–action (VLA) systems therefore augment policies with memory
banks, event keyframes, or temporal representations ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ; Koo et al., 2026 ) , experience retrieval ( Sridhar et al., 2026 ) , and external
text records ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . These mechanisms aim to turn history into
useful evidence for current decisions. Their value is often evaluated through
memory ablations and task success ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) . Such gains show
improved performance, but do they establish use of task-relevant stored facts
(Figure 1 a)?

Three distinctions prevent that inference. First, enabling memory can change
both information and computation. Second, an unchanged success rate can hide
gains on some trials and losses on others ( Milani Fard et al., 2016 ) . Third, changing memory can alter
behavior even when a replacement preserves the target fact or introduces only
a small numerical perturbation. History can also support shortcuts, as shown
by causal confusion and copycat behavior in imitation learning ( de Haan et al., 2019 ; Wen et al., 2020 ) . Behavioral sensitivity alone does not
establish use of task-relevant facts. Conversely, an undetected net gain does not imply
that memory has no effect. Interpretation also depends on whether current
observations already reveal the answer, whether an intervention reaches the
reader, and whether stored facts remain valid.

We introduce the Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) to
separate net benefit (Q1), conditions for memory to help (Q2), outcome
sensitivity (Q3), and fact specificity (Q4). At a fixed retrieval interface,
IMEP compares replacements that change the target fact with those that preserve
it. On matched units, it records outcome flips alongside aggregate success
and scores decisions separately from execution where observable.
Section 3 defines the protocol; Section 2 discusses related work.

In the evaluated learned banks, memory interventions change outcomes without
establishing fact specificity. Remember Color’s one-unit-in-the-last-place
(ULP) control, including installation, changes 11.9 % 11.9\% of paired outcomes;
different-fact replacements, as delivered, produce no clear additional effect
over same-fact replacements. No detected learned-bank gain meets a registered net-benefit
criterion. On ChainBench, full memory achieves perfect decision accuracy on
202 chains and raises task success from 39.1 % 39.1\% to 74.3 % 74.3\% , matching the
oracle under shared recorded executions. A separate
experiment supports fact specificity for a scripted reader on curated records.

Our contributions are:

IMEP , a four-question protocol using fact-changing and
fact-preserving substitutions, exact repeats, and one-ULP controls, with
separate decision and execution readouts.

ChainBench , a LIBERO benchmark of multi-episode chains requiring
historical facts absent from current observations, with decisions scored
separately from motor execution.

An evaluation of within-episode, cross-episode and agentic
memory , finding outcome sensitivity without established fact specificity in
learned banks, and task success at the motor-execution ceiling for the evaluated
ChainBench configuration under shared recorded executions.

1. IMEP , a four-question protocol using fact-changing and
fact-preserving substitutions, exact repeats, and one-ULP controls, with
separate decision and execution readouts.

2. ChainBench , a LIBERO benchmark of multi-episode chains requiring
historical facts absent from current observations, with decisions scored
separately from motor execution.

3. An evaluation of within-episode, cross-episode and agentic
memory , finding outcome sensitivity without established fact specificity in
learned banks, and task success at the motor-execution ceiling for the evaluated
ChainBench configuration under shared recorded executions.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

VLA memory methods augment policies with learned banks, temporal representations,
or retrieved experience ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Koo et al., 2026 ; Sridhar et al., 2026 ) .
Robotic benchmarks test history dependence ( Cherepanov et al., 2026 ; Dai et al., 2026 ) ,
while MemoryAgentBench tests fact updating ( Hu et al., 2026 ) .
ChainBench separates decision and execution readouts when query observations
omit the deciding fact.

Causal scrubbing and activation patching probe behavioral dependence on internal
variables ( Chan et al., 2022 ; Zhang & Nanda, 2024 ) . PoPE uses placebo controls to
distinguish useful error content from presentation effects in code-model
self-repair ( Iscan, 2026 ) . IMEP adapts these principles to embodied memory through
fact-changing and fact-preserving interventions at a specified retrieval interface,
paired outcome flips, and delivery checks. Appendix J expands
these connections and their limits.
