2026-10-19.title: LAW: Unifying Language, Action, and World Modeling for Agentic Physical Intelligence
2026-10-19.authors: Jiajun Cao , Kai Tang , Bohua Zhang , Zezhong Qian , Ying Li , Xiaozhu Ju , Xiaobao Wei , Jiaming Liu , Yang Ding , Sixiang Chen , Yiding Sun , Siyuan Qian , Tinghao Wang , Jixian Wu , Yichen Guo , Yi Zhang , Shilong Zou , Yong Dai , Jian Tang , Shanghang Zhang
2026-10-19.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-19.introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation is a sequence of semantic subtasks, not merely a longer sequence of motor commands. After reaching for an object, a robot must decide whether the grasp actually succeeded; after a successful grasp, it must recognize that the task has entered a new stage; before executing the next motion, it must choose among several physically plausible actions according to the current objective [ 23 , 22 ] . Errors in any of these decisions compound over time. Consequently, local action quality alone does not determine task success. A capable agent must maintain a persistent account of task progress, connect that account to action generation, and revise its decisions when execution departs from expectation [ 35 , 44 ] .

Vision-language-action policies connect semantic representations to control [ 60 , 26 , 8 ] , while world-action models learn action-conditioned scene evolution and executable behavior [ 59 , 57 , 27 , 51 ] . These models substantially improve action generation, but long-horizon deployment exposes a complementary systems problem: reasoning and control must remain aligned as the task evolves. A language plan generated once at the beginning cannot determine whether its intermediate steps were completed [ 22 ] , and an action generator conditioned only on the current observation may not know which visual changes matter to the larger goal [ 41 ] . Placing a planner before a policy therefore leaves three interfaces underspecified: how execution progress updates the plan, how candidate actions are judged against the current semantic objective, and how relevant history is retained without overwhelming either model.

Our premise is that semantic subtask progress should serve as the temporal interface between language reasoning and world-action modeling. Subtasks provide more than a decomposition of the instruction: they define when the agent should advance its plan, which outcomes a candidate action should optimize, and which observations should remain salient in memory. This view reveals that computations occur at different rates. State assessment should run continuously without blocking control, candidate evaluation should occur whenever the WAM proposes a new action chunk, and planning should operate at the semantic task scale rather than at every control step. The challenge is coordinating reasoning and control, rather than invoking a larger reasoner at every step.

We instantiate this principle in LAW, a closed-loop VLM–WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress, as summarized in Fig. 1 . The LAW agent uses a hybrid-expert VLM with role-selected planner, state, and value experts on a shared frozen backbone. The planner predicts the remaining semantic subtasks; conditioned on the current subtask, the WAM generates diverse action chunks; the value expert ranks and fuses them; and execution status is assessed asynchronously to determine subtask completion. Once the current subtask is completed, the planner predicts the next subtask and the agent switches to it; otherwise, the agent continues executing the current subtask. The LAW agent coordinates planning, action selection, and execution monitoring at different frequencies, using feedback to continue or switch subtasks.

To strengthen joint world and action modeling, we introduce Mixture-of-Transformer Experts (MoTE) into the WAM, yielding MoTE-WAM. MoT projects video and action features into a common attention space to exchange cross-modal information, but their subsequent transformations remain modality-specific. MoTE introduces shared experts to further transform these cross-modal representations, alongside video-private and action-private experts that preserve modality-specific computation. The shared experts learn common temporal and physical structure across predicted scene dynamics and robot actions, strengthening video–action joint modeling beyond information exchange through attention alone. Long-horizon execution also requires memory aligned with subtask transitions. Separate hierarchical memory streams for the VLM and WAM retain recent observations and full-resolution states at subtask boundaries, while compressing older history to preserve relevant context across subtasks. To better exploit failed trajectories when training the value expert, we introduce subtask-local value learning, which terminates returns at semantic boundaries. This preserves positive supervision from successfully completed subtasks within failed episodes, rather than assigning zero value to all their actions.

We evaluate LAW on 50 RoboTwin [ 13 ] tasks, the RoboDojo [ 12 ] capability benchmark, and three long-horizon real-robot tasks containing up to nine semantic subtasks. LAW achieves 94.21% average success on RoboTwin, 2.38 percentage points above Fast-WAM, without robot-data pretraining. Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM- α \alpha further raises the average success rate to 95.56%, establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High within the same LAW framework. On RoboDojo, LAW achieves leading performance across capability dimensions among methods without additional robot-domain or embodied-interaction pretraining. On the three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65% average success, compared with 28.33% for π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and 25% for Fast-WAM. We also conduct extensive ablation studies to validate the effectiveness of each component. Our contributions are:

We introduce LAW, a closed-loop VLM–WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. The LAW agent coordinates planning, asynchronous completion assessment, and value-guided action fusion for long-horizon execution.

We introduce MoTE, dual-stream hierarchical memory, and subtask-local value learning to support progress-aware control: MoTE strengthens joint video–action modeling through shared and modality-specific experts; dual-stream hierarchical memory preserves task-relevant history and subtask-boundary observations; and subtask-local value learning retains positive supervision from completed stages of failed trajectories.

We demonstrate LAW’s effectiveness on RoboTwin, RoboDojo, and long-horizon real-world manipulation through extensive experiments and ablation studies. Integrating OpenWAM- α \alpha achieves 95.56% average success on RoboTwin, establishing a new open-source state of the art and demonstrating LAW’s extensibility to stronger pretrained WAMs.

1. We introduce LAW, a closed-loop VLM–WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. The LAW agent coordinates planning, asynchronous completion assessment, and value-guided action fusion for long-horizon execution.

2. We introduce MoTE, dual-stream hierarchical memory, and subtask-local value learning to support progress-aware control: MoTE strengthens joint video–action modeling through shared and modality-specific experts; dual-stream hierarchical memory preserves task-relevant history and subtask-boundary observations; and subtask-local value learning retains positive supervision from completed stages of failed trajectories.

3. We demonstrate LAW’s effectiveness on RoboTwin, RoboDojo, and long-horizon real-world manipulation through extensive experiments and ablation studies. Integrating OpenWAM- α \alpha achieves 95.56% average success on RoboTwin, establishing a new open-source state of the art and demonstrating LAW’s extensibility to stronger pretrained WAMs.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Vision-Language-Action Models for Robot Control

Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) provide semantic representations that vision-language-action (VLA) policies connect to executable control [ 14 , 60 , 28 , 26 , 8 ] , supported by heterogeneous robot datasets and generalist pretraining [ 39 , 17 ] . RT-2 and OpenVLA represent actions as tokens, whereas π 0 \pi_{0} couples a VLM with a flow-matching expert for continuous action generation [ 60 , 26 , 8 ] . Beyond action parameterization, CoT-VLA predicts intermediate visual subgoals [ 54 ] , while VEGA aligns visual-encoder outputs with geometry-aware features before vision-language fusion [ 45 ] . These approaches strengthen semantic transfer and spatial grounding, motivating complementary mechanisms for coordinating instructions, execution progress, and action selection over extended tasks.

Language-guided systems connect reasoning to execution through affordance-based skill selection, environmental feedback, action hierarchies, and spatial value maps [ 23 , 22 , 4 , 21 ] . SayCan grounds language plans in learned affordances, whereas VoxPoser translates language-specified objectives and constraints into spatial maps for trajectory optimization [ 23 , 21 ] . In navigation, NavCoT structures decisions through future imagination and observation matching [ 33 ] , while Memoir retrieves environmental and behavioral experience using imagined states [ 47 ] . Although navigation differs from continuous manipulation, these studies illustrate how intermediate reasoning and selective memory access support sequential decisions. For long-horizon robot policies, the corresponding challenge is to retain task-relevant history and execution feedback when semantic stages extend beyond individual action chunks [ 41 , 44 ] .

## 2.2 World Action Models and Video-Based Policy

World models support control through action-conditioned visual prediction or latent dynamics [ 15 , 19 , 58 , 1 , 3 ] , while video generators also enable synthetic robot training trajectories [ 24 ] . Visual Foresight optimizes actions through predicted observations, whereas Dreamer learns behavior through latent imagination, providing two complementary uses of predictive dynamics [ 15 , 19 ] . Recent world-action models (WAMs) connect future visual modeling with executable action generation through joint diffusion or future-latent alignment [ 59 , 57 , 30 , 32 , 27 , 51 , 53 ] . Their designs differ in how predictive information is used during deployment: LingBot-VA combines causal video–action modeling with observation feedback and asynchronous execution [ 27 ] , whereas Fast-WAM retains video co-training but omits test-time future prediction [ 51 ] . WAM4D further introduces geometric supervision through spatial register tokens and modality-specific causal attention [ 29 ] . These developments distinguish predictive supervision benefits from the cost of generating future observations online.

Reliable world-model-based control also requires faithful action consequences and informative evaluation signals. WorldEcho diagnoses failures to follow off-expert actions, and WorldSync improves action-conditioned generation through broader coverage and explicit action-effect alignment [ 11 ] . Cosmos Policy jointly generates actions, future states, and values for planning [ 25 ] ; MV-WAM integrates progress-value estimation with value-guided rollback [ 10 ] ; and SafeDojo optimizes VLA policies using imagined trajectories with separate task-reward and safety-cost estimates [ 42 ] . LAW builds on these ingredients by coordinating semantic planning, asynchronous state assessment, and value-guided WAM candidate selection, supported by hierarchical visual memory. Its modality-specific and shared experts strengthen video–action interaction, while separate hierarchical memory streams preserve temporal context for language-level reasoning and continuous robot action generation. Unlike the trajectory-level returns used by MV-WAM [ 10 ] , LAW terminates value targets at semantic subtask boundaries, preserving supervision from completed prefixes of unsuccessful episodes. This links local action evaluation to progress-aware action selection and planning grounded in semantic subtasks.

2026-10-19.title: From Sliding Windows to Self-evolving Lifelong Memory: A Dual-perspective Survey of Memory Paradigms for Long-Horizon Robotics VLA Models
2026-10-19.authors: Yong Wang , Boyu Shen , Xinwei Zhang , Yizheng Li , Keyuan Luo
2026-10-19.abstract: Long-horizon robotic tasks expose a fundamental limitation of current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models because their restricted temporal context pre-vents effective accumulation and reuse of past experiences. As a result, memory has become a fundamental component for enabling embodied agents to perform long-horizon reasoning and adaptive decision-making. This survey presents a systematic taxonomy of VLA memory mechanisms based on memory scope and persistence, categorizing existing approaches into five representative paradigms and one emerging frontier. Based on this taxonomy, we compare representative VLA memory systems in terms of memory characteristics, architectural com-plexity, and open-source maturity, revealing a clear trade-off in which increasing architectural complexity is generally accompanied by decreasing open-source ma-turity. Finally, we discuss the key challenges in building full-lifecycle memory systems, including efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolu-tion. Overall, this survey provides a unified perspective on memory architectures for VLA agents and offers insights into the development of lifelong embodied in-telligence.

2026-10-19.title: SkyAgent: Revisable Target Memory for Continuous Aerial Search
2026-10-19.authors: Kaibo Yang , Xingyu Wu , Enze Zhu , Yajie Chai , Xuyang Li , Jiahui Cui , Xiaoxuan Liu , Lei Wang , Zhan Chen
2026-10-19.abstract:
Continuous aerial search builds target hypotheses from sparse,
viewpoint-dependent observations.
When later evidence contradicts a stored hypothesis, however, the
candidate can remain available to the planner and continue triggering
approach or verification actions.
We call this trajectory-level failure false candidate persistence (FCP).
We equip SkyAgent with Revisable Target Memory (RTM),
which associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts
correlated views, and revises each candidate through Tentative , Confirmed , and Rejected states.
The key interface binds every generated waypoint to its source candidate:
rejection therefore invalidates stale goals, while conservative
reactivation protects temporarily occluded targets. Across four splits from the CityAVOS, UAV-ON, and OpenUAV benchmarks, our SkyAgent equipped with RTM outperforms all competitors, improving SR by 2.90–6.31 points while substantially reducing Behavior-FCP and post-contradiction travel with a low false-rejection rate. Across 35 matched real-world DJI scenarios per method, RTM consistently improves task success and behavioral reliability, further validating its state-to-action correction under physical deployment conditions.
2026-10-19.introduction:
In a representative aerial search, a distant rectangular region is logged
as a target candidate.
A later side-angle view reveals that the region is a facade reflection,
not the target.
This revision problem is central to continuous aerial object search: the
physical target is static, but evidence about each candidate shifts
as the vehicle approaches, changes viewpoint, or encounters occlusion ( Ji et al. 2026 ; Xiao et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2025 ) .
The agent rarely sees decisive evidence in a single frame; a distant
shape, a brief gap in foliage, or an intermittent specular return may be
all that a long trajectory provides.

Existing aerial agents have made progress on two fronts. Memory-based methods retain observations across frames through
asynchronous maps, octree representations, or filtered
write-in ( Zhang et al. 2026a ; Zhou et al. 2026 ; Ji et al. 2026 ) . Verification-based methods seek additional viewpoints before
committing to a stop or reconsider a selected snapshot before
executing it ( Jang and Kim 2026 ; Cao et al. 2025 ; Ren et al. 2024 ; Wang et al. 2026a ) .
Both fronts focus on the forward direction: building or validating
confidence before a decision is made.
We focus on what happens after : when a later view contradicts
a candidate already sitting in persistent memory, can the system
actually change that memory and cancel the goals it generated?
In the systems we study, the answer is often no—the candidate remains
available to planning even after a closer view proves it wrong.

We define false candidate persistence (FCP) as a trajectory-level
failure: after a candidate receives sufficient reference contradiction,
it stays in the active plan (State-FCP) or again induces approach,
revisit, or confirmation actions (Behavior-FCP).
FCP is not a transient detector error, which is a wrong observation in
a single frame; it is a known-wrong hypothesis that continues to consume
distance, time, and planning cycles through stale memory state.
Figure 1 illustrates this failure and its correction.

The fix is not more storage.
It is different memory semantics: candidates should be revisable
hypotheses, not committed facts.
A candidate must retain both supporting and opposing evidence, discount
redundant adjacent frames, and expose an explicit lifecycle state to
the planner.
Changing a score alone is not enough; when a candidate is rejected,
every pending waypoint it sourced must be invalidated before the next
planning cycle.
At the same time, rejection must not be permanent, because temporary
occlusion and low-quality frames can produce misleading negative evidence.

We equip the SkyAgent execution backbone with Revisable Target Memory (RTM). Candidate Evidence Memory associates observations with persistent
candidates, groups them by independent viewpoint, and accumulates
signed evidence. Revise-and-Suppress maps accumulated evidence to lifecycle states
through a state-dependent transition function and cancels all stale
waypoints on rejection.
The existing fast search policy, event trigger, inspection skills, and
safety-projected controller remain as execution infrastructure;
candidate truth state is managed exclusively through RTM.

Our contributions are three:
(1) we identify false candidate persistence (FCP) as a trajectory-level
failure distinct from transient detection errors, and introduce
complementary state-, behavior-, and cost-level measures that separate a
stored false hypothesis from one that still affects flight;
(2) we propose Revisable Target Memory (RTM), which couples candidate
lifecycle revision to planner binding: rejecting a candidate invalidates
every unexecuted goal it sourced, while conservative reactivation permits
recovery after new independent positive evidence;
(3) we evaluate RTM through natural FCP prevalence, controlled comparisons
and mechanism ablations on three aerial benchmarks, and 35 matched DJI
scenarios per method (Table 1 ).
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Classical aerial target-search systems improve coverage through
visibility-aware viewpoint selection, hierarchical planning, probabilistic
target beliefs, or sparse history maps ( Luo et al. 2024 ; Ray et al. 2024 ; Hou et al. 2026 ) .
Semantic aerial navigation has since moved from instruction-following
benchmarks such as AerialVLN, OpenUAV, and CityNav ( Liu et al. 2023 ; Wang et al. 2025 ; Lee et al. 2025 ) to city-scale planners with topo-metric, annotated-map, hierarchical-memory,
and VLM reasoning modules ( Gao et al. 2024 ; Zhang et al. 2025a ; Zhang et al. 2025b ; Cai et al. 2025 ) .
Training-free aerial frameworks include SPF’s image-space waypoint grounding
and PSC-AVDN’s parsing–search–confirmation with structured spatial memory;
HTNav and LookasideVLN instead learn tiered or direction-aware policies ( Hu et al. 2025 ; Qi et al. 2026 ; Fan et al. 2026 ; Ning et al. 2026 ) .
The adjacent aerial object-goal line introduces open-world target
descriptions and long-horizon search in UAV-ON and CityAVOS ( Xiao et al. 2025 ; Ji et al. 2026 ) , with APEX, OctMem-Agent, NavFoM, and
RAVEN scaling retrieval through asynchronous maps, octrees, foundation-model
memory, or voxel–ray representations ( Zhang et al. 2026a ; Zhou et al. 2026 ; Zhang et al. 2026b ; Kim et al. 2025 ) .

Persistent memory is also central to ground ObjectNav and lifelong
navigation.
VLMaps and ConceptGraphs attach open-vocabulary semantics to metric maps or
3D scene graphs ( Huang et al. 2023 ; Gu et al. 2024 ) ;
MemoNav, 3D-Mem, and AstraNav-Memory compress observations into working,
snapshot, or image-centric long-term memories ( Li et al. 2024 ; Yang et al. 2025 ; Hu et al. 2026 ) .
GOAT-Bench explicitly evaluates memory across a sequence of heterogeneous
goals, while TrajRAG retrieves geometric–semantic experience accumulated
across episodes ( Khanna et al. 2024 ; Wang et al. 2026b ) .
These methods chiefly improve representation, retention, retrieval, or
coverage.
RTM addresses a downstream failure mode: after new evidence contradicts a
stored candidate, whether that candidate remains available to the planner
and what happens to every goal it already generated.

Active perception acquires informative views before committing to a
decision ( Bajcsy 1988 ) ; APRR applies this principle to refine the
last-mile viewpoint for precise ObjectNav ( Qin et al. 2025 ) .
Recent navigation agents verify different objects of uncertainty.
PSC-AVDN confirms a candidate region after a structured search ( Qi et al. 2026 ) ; Context-Nav scores memory-conditioned viewpoints,
CogNav models a cognitive action process, and SCOPE revisits promising
locations before committing ( Jang and Kim 2026 ; Cao et al. 2025 ; Wang et al. 2026a ) .
UniGoal uses graph matching for goal-conditioned aerial decisions, while
WMNav corrects short-horizon actions through a learned world model ( Yin et al. 2025 ; Nie et al. 2025 ) .
Explore-Until-Confident calibrates stopping in embodied question answering
rather than target navigation ( Ren et al. 2024 ) .
CARe is especially close: it combines confidence and multi-view consistency
to replan decisions induced by an erroneous pre-explored semantic map ( Ko et al. 2025 ) .
Classical multiple-hypothesis tracking provides a related probabilistic
view of preserving alternatives under ambiguous association ( Blackman 2004 ) .
RTM does not claim candidate lifecycles or replanning in isolation.
Its distinction is a candidate-local revision contract: every waypoint
records its source candidate, and rejection invalidates all unexecuted
goals sourced from that candidate rather than only reconsidering the next
action.

VLM self-correction can revise semantic grounding errors under targeted
prompts ( Liao et al. 2025 ) , while Reflexion converts task
feedback into linguistic episodic memory for later trials ( Shinn et al. 2023 ) .
Neither mechanism specifies how a continuously acting navigation system
should retract the downstream commitments of a disproved perceptual
hypothesis.
RTM instead operates online and candidate-locally: it retains supporting and
contradicting observations for audit, changes a candidate’s availability to
planning during the same episode, cancels its still-pending waypoints, and
permits recovery only after independent positive views arrive.

2026-10-19.title: CoEvolve: Self-Evolving Code Policies from Skills to Strategies for Humanoid Robots
2026-10-19.authors: Zicheng Liu , Haochen Wu , Jiawei He , Suyun Zhao , Huan Yang , Cheng Chi , Hao Tang
2026-10-19.comment: Under review at ICLR 2027
2026-10-19.abstract:
Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action
Models (WAMs) have expanded the manipulation and whole body capabilities of
individual robots. Yet a single robot remains limited by its embodiment, and
many real world tasks require capabilities that can only emerge through
cooperation. Existing multi robot frameworks largely emphasize task
decomposition, allocation, and replanning, while providing limited support
for adapting executable coordination when physical execution deviates from
the intended behavior. We present CoEvolve , a framework that represents
team coordination as executable code over fixed robot motor skills. CoEvolve introduces Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, where a
multimodal foundation model instantiates coordination strategies through
motion primitives, semantic objectives, temporary robot roles, and bounded
execution parameters. Physical verification evaluates each executed
transition, rejected behaviors trigger structured coordination revision from
an accepted checkpoint, and verified experience is retained to guide
subsequent decisions. We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1
humanoids transporting a freely supported rigid payload through constrained
corridors. Across 15 base task runs with three multimodal backbone families, CoEvolve completes 8 tasks, with every backbone achieving end to end
success. Additional evaluations yield verified placement on two additional
corridor layouts and after both same-backbone and cross-backbone experience
initialization, while exposing persistent limitations in motion precision and
contact stability. These results support executable coordination as a
practical interface for adapting long horizon multi robot collaboration under
shared physical constraints. Our code will be available at https://github.com/Innovationlzc/CoEvolve .
2026-10-19.introduction:
Recent advances in robot foundation models have equipped individual robots
with increasingly general visuomotor capabilities, enabling them to follow
language instructions and perform diverse manipulation
tasks ( Brohan et al., 2022 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) .
Yet some physical tasks require capabilities that cannot be provided by one
robot alone. Transporting an extended object through a constrained environment, for
example, requires coordinated support, relative motion, corner negotiation,
and placement ( De Vincenti and Coros, 2023 ; Pandit et al., 2025 ) .
Collaboration is therefore not simply the aggregation of individual skills.
Robots that can independently walk, turn, and move laterally must still
determine how to combine these capabilities while carrying a shared object.
We view this formation of team behavior as a form of co-becoming :
effective cooperation is realized through the changing relationship between
individual capabilities and the shared physical state.

This motivates our central question: given fixed individual motor
skills, how can an agent instantiate and revise executable team coordination
as a shared physical task unfolds? Multi-robot planning methods address task decomposition, allocation, and
collaboration through structured and language-model planning ( Cai et al., 2025 ; Mandi et al., 2024 ; Kannan et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) ,
while learned coordination methods optimize joint or decentralized policies
through training ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Doshi et al., 2026 ) . In parallel, agents improve
textual skills, memory systems, and executable implementations through
feedback and experience
sharing ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Weng et al., 2026 ) .
Code as Policies and subsequent robot programming systems also generate and
revise executable behaviors through
interaction ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Fu et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) .
We study a complementary challenge: revising coordination when robots are
physically coupled through a shared payload. In this setting, an individual
action can alter both a teammate’s support conditions and the feasibility of
subsequent joint motion. As a result, a valid task plan does not guarantee
that the current coordination pattern remains executable. The key challenge
is therefore to instantiate joint behavior from fixed motor skills and revise
the relevant coordination relation when physical execution deviates, for
example when unequal displacement disrupts formation or a constrained turn
requires temporary support and mover roles.

We introduce CoEvolve , a framework for adapting executable team
coordination during shared physical tasks. Figure 1 summarizes
the motivation and overall interaction loop. CoEvolve separates fixed
individual motor capabilities from the coordination strategy that composes
them for the current task phase. Rather than selecting from a library of
complete strategies, the agent instantiates coordination through motion
primitives, semantic objectives, temporary roles, coordination modes, and
bounded execution parameters. The evaluated setting provides simulator
measurements and route references, while the model determines how these
capabilities should be combined within the resulting physical constraints.

Our Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution mechanism uses physical execution
evidence to determine which aspects of coordination should change. A rejected
transition triggers a revision to the maneuver, the relationship between
robot roles, or the execution parameters. Revised policies are evaluated
after restoration of the latest accepted simulator checkpoint. Verified
outcomes also contribute complementary forms of experience: abstract
coordination records guide subsequent decisions, while accepted executable
examples inform code generation. Foundation model and motor policy weights
remain fixed. The adaptation concerns the task plan, instantiated
coordination strategies, and stored experience rather than the acquisition
of new motor skills.

We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids carrying a
freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors. The base
evaluation contains eight complete tasks across fifteen runs and three
foundation model families. We further compare against four adapted external
baselines and two component variants, evaluate additional corridor layouts,
and study reuse of verified cooperative experience across foundation model
backbones. These experiments distinguish demonstrated execution capability
from causal component effects: some comparison, scene, and transfer records
differ in runtime configuration, interaction budget, or continuation
conditions. Our contributions are:

We introduce an executable representation of team coordination
that separates fixed individual motor capabilities from the cooperative
strategy instantiated for the current physical situation.

We introduce an executable representation of team coordination
that separates fixed individual motor capabilities from the cooperative
strategy instantiated for the current physical situation.

We propose Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, which combines
physical verification, structured strategy revision, and reusable
cooperative experience to adapt coordination during execution.

We provide an extensive evaluation across three foundation model
families, adapted multi robot and code policy baselines, additional corridor
layouts, and cross-model experience reuse, while analyzing the execution and
contact limitations that remain.

that separates fixed individual motor capabilities from the cooperative
strategy instantiated for the current physical situation.

2. We propose Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, which combines
physical verification, structured strategy revision, and reusable

3. We provide an extensive evaluation across three foundation model

2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Self-evolving agents adapt multiple components of an agent system.
Building on feedback accumulation and skill reuse in Reflexion and
Voyager ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) , SkillOpt optimizes textual
skills for frozen agents, while MemEvolve evolves the memory architecture
itself ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Continual Harness adapts
prompts, sub-agents, skills, and memory within an ongoing episode, and
Hyperagents additionally makes the improvement procedure
editable ( Karten et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ) . Related systems automate the design or modification of the agent itself,
including Automated Design of Agentic Systems and the Darwin Gödel
Machine ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . Group-Evolving Agents (GEA) enables experience sharing among evolving coding
agents, whereas CORAL supports autonomous multi-agent search through shared
persistent memory ( Weng et al., 2026 ; Qu et al., 2026 ) . These approaches concern
agent implementations, knowledge, or search processes. CoEvolve instead
studies online revision of executable inter-robot coordination during a
shared physical task, with motor skills and runtime contracts fixed.

REMAC revises multi-robot task plans through reflection, while HyCodePolicy
and Act-Observe-Rewrite revise executable robot programs from execution
feedback ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025b ; Kumar, 2026 ) .
ASPIRE combines multimodal failure diagnosis, program repair, and reusable
skill discovery, including bimanual manipulation; ENPIRE automates policy
improvement through real-robot experimentation and
reset ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) . These works already connect
program revision with physical experience. CoEvolve focuses on
physically coupled humanoid transport, where failures can require changes
to the selected maneuver or temporary support roles. It combines structured
coordination revision with physical transition checks, checkpoint recovery,
and sequential retrieval of strategy records and accepted code exemplars.

2026-10-19.title: LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300: Prediction-Guided Action Selection with a Graph Dynamics Model
2026-10-19.authors: TianLiang Ma , Ting Ma , ZhongYuan Ma
2026-10-19.comment: . Technical report. Code and evaluation materials: this https URL
2026-10-19.abstract: We present LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300, a policy that combines a Human300-fine-tuned GR00T-N1.5 action generator, an action-conditioned graph dynamics model, and a learned binary state-reward scorer. At inference, the policy samples four action chunks, predicts the future latent features and robot state for each, and executes the candidate with the highest predicted-state reward logit. Predictions therefore influence the actions sent to the environment. The evaluated system uses a 16-step prediction horizon and keeps all three components frozen during evaluation. In the local evaluation on 50 RoboCasa 1.0.1 tasks in the pretrain kitchen split, with 50 episodes per task, the system records 207/2,500 successes (8.28%), compared with 181/2,500 (7.24%) in the historical self-trained GR00T-N1.5 baseline. The observed difference is 26 successes, or 1.04 percentage points. The atomic group improves from 141/900 to 150/900. Separately, the RoboCasa maintainers re-evaluated the submission and reported 354/1,500 successes (23.6%) across 50 tasks, with leaderboard rates of 48.3%, 16.3%, and 3.1% for Atomic-Seen, Composite-Seen, and Composite-Unseen. The local and official results are reported separately; their difference is not attributed to a model improvement. Recorded local audits identify 212,700 changed environment-input chunks, including 28,223 in atomic tasks. We describe the actual training stages, implemented inference mechanism, evaluation provenance, and public reproduction entrypoints. These results document an active prediction-and-selection system and a positive historical difference.

2026-10-19.title: NestedVLA: Learning to Consolidate and Generate Skills for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-19.authors: Guodong Du , Wanyu Lin
2026-10-19.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. . Code: this https URL
2026-10-19.abstract:
Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic
agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and
environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across
platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model
merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural
changes. We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned
independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose NestedVLA , which replaces parameter aggregation with parameter generation : a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the
target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose
with a frozen base VLA. Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained
separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse
while mitigating interference. Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld,
ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging
baseline by 41 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing
toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation. Code is available
at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA .
2026-10-19.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models combine visual and language understanding
with embodied control [ 2 , 71 , 26 , 1 , 40 ] . Independently
fine-tuning a common backbone produces policies specialized for different
robotic benchmarks, but storing one full checkpoint per benchmark duplicates
most parameters. Joint multi-task training can avoid this duplication when
data from all benchmarks can be pooled. We instead study post-hoc
consolidation of policies independently fine-tuned from the same backbone.
We seek to consolidate their task-specific parameter updates into a compact
representation without pooling the original training data.

A natural post-hoc approach is to merge the parameter updates of the
fine-tuned policies into a single checkpoint. In VLA models, however,
independently learned updates can interfere strongly when combined: in our
experiments, simple averaging loses most of the performance of the separate
policies. Our weight-space analysis finds weak alignment across major
parameter groups, an incompatibility that is particularly consequential in
the action expert because it directly governs control
(Appendix E ). This observation is consistent with
MergeVLA [ 16 ] , which likewise identifies dependencies
distributed across action-expert layers as a major obstacle to cross-skill
merging. These findings motivate a consolidation strategy that preserves
policy-specific parameter structure rather than collapsing all updates into
one set of weights.

We propose NestedVLA , a framework that shifts the paradigm from
parameter aggregation to parameter generation. A hypernetwork embedded in
the VLA generates sparse action-expert updates conditioned on the target
task, while compressed task-specific VLM residuals are retained separately.
The selected updates compose with a shared base to instantiate a
task-specific VLA without changing its forward architecture or introducing
routing supervision. We evaluate NestedVLA on MetaWorld [ 35 ] ,
ManiSkill [ 45 ] , and CALVIN [ 36 ] using the open-source π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 40 ] backbone. NestedVLA outperforms the strongest
model-merging baseline by 41 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning
within 1 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Recent VLAs cast robotic control as instruction-following on top of
pretrained vision-language backbones [ 2 , 71 , 26 , 24 , 1 , 40 ] . OpenVLA [ 26 ] discretizes actions into rare
vocabulary tokens for autoregressive prediction; π 0 \pi_{0} [ 1 ] pairs the VLM with a separate action expert trained via flow
matching for continuous action chunks; π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 40 ] extends this design to interleave sub-task narration and low-level
control. Lighter variants such as VLA-Adapter [ 51 ] preserve multi-task competence at sub-billion-parameter scales. VLAct
uses representation-centric continued pre-training to preserve VLM priors
and promote shared action semantics across
embodiments [ 63 ] . Across this family, multi-task ability
is learned from pooled data, requiring co-located datasets and predefined
skills. We target the regime where these assumptions break: skills are
acquired independently and consolidated after the fact .

Prompt- and adapter-based methods offer lightweight alternatives to full
fine-tuning of vision backbones. Recent work makes prompts instance-aware,
injects structured visual semantics, or searches for layer-specific prompt
fusion rules [ 57 , 58 , 59 ] .
Structured low-rank adaptation further filters task-irrelevant directions
and coordinates updates across layers [ 61 ] , while visual
alignment methods address over-reliance on language priors in multimodal
models [ 60 ] . Meng et al. [38] propose AHRA, a
hierarchical shared–private expert framework that aligns semantic levels
while preserving modality-specific evidence. Such methods adapt or organize
multimodal representations; NestedVLA instead starts from independently trained
VLA policies and consolidates their parameter updates post hoc.

Using one network to predict the parameters of another dates back to
HyperNetworks [ 20 ] , with later applications to
continual learning [ 46 ] and multi-task
NLP [ 25 ] . Recent parameter generators use latent
diffusion to synthesize neural-network weights [ 48 ] , scale
this process to full models with recurrent generation [ 49 ] ,
map task prompts directly to LoRA weights [ 31 ] , or produce
instance-conditioned weight updates as functional memory [ 56 ] .
NestedVLA inherits this task-conditioned generation premise, but targets a
sparse top- K K delta on a frozen billion-scale VLA backbone via patch-based
tokenization, and consolidates independently fine-tuned RL policies rather
than learning skills from scratch.

Related work on language models compresses full-model task updates into
modular SkillPacks for heterogeneous knowledge fusion and multi-domain
specialization [ 13 , 30 ] . HoE instead extracts
LoRA-form experts from task vectors and routes them for multi-objective
alignment [ 29 ] . These studies concern text-only language models
and retain or select task modules. NestedVLA studies closed-loop VLA policies
and generates the action-expert update with an embedded hypernetwork.

Model merging combines independently trained checkpoints into a single
deployable model. Recent surveys organize model fusion across parameter,
representation, and behavior levels [ 3 , 69 , 70 ] . Static merging produces one fixed delta via
weighted averaging [ 55 , 34 , 22 , 11 ] ,
conflict-handling [ 62 , 65 , 5 , 10 , 14 ] , or low-rank
sub-spaces [ 17 , 44 , 33 , 32 , 12 ] , with adapter
counterparts [ 66 , 68 ] . Dynamic
merging retains per-task masks, scalars, residuals, or
frequency-domain corrections at inference [ 47 , 21 , 67 , 27 , 7 ] . Recent adaptive methods build reusable
component-level expert libraries for input-aware recombination [ 42 ] or evolve experts with manifold-aware, training-free routing for continual
merging [ 43 ] . Across both regimes the operative verb is select : every output value is an interpolation, mask, or
projection of values already present in { θ m − θ 0 } m \{\theta_{m}-\theta_{0}\}_{m} .
Complementary studies make expert training merge-aware [ 19 ] ,
calibrate or quantize post-merge models [ 18 , 50 ] ,
and analyze scaling laws or expert-read budgets for weight-space
merging [ 53 , 52 ] .
NestedVLA generates the per-skill delta from a single shared
hypernetwork instead. Embodied applications of merging remain largely
unexplored; ReVLA [ 6 ] mitigates single-skill domain
forgetting rather than multi-skill consolidation.

2026-10-19.title: Expand-and-Prune: Test-Time Candidate-Space Adaptation for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
2026-10-19.authors: Fabian Schmidt , Karol Fedurko , Markus Enzweiler , Abhinav Valada
2026-10-19.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-19.comment: Accepted to IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) 2027
2026-10-19.abstract:
Candidate-based end-to-end driving planners reason over a finite set of trajectory hypotheses. However, for sparse planners, a limited candidate set may provide insufficient support for scene-relevant maneuvers, while fixed downstream candidate budgets do not account for prediction uncertainty.
To address these challenges, we introduce Expand-and-Prune , a test-time framework that jointly adapts candidate support and capacity without updating learned parameters.
The framework expands the native candidate set using semantic driving intent and temporally propagated predictions and then uses uncertainty in intermediate trajectory scores to adaptively prune the resulting candidates.
Across four heterogeneous candidate-based planners and four benchmarks, Expand-and-Prune consistently improves planning performance.
It achieves state-of-the-art results on LangAuto, increasing the Driving Score from 68.2 68.2 to 75.9 75.9 , while providing further improvement on Bench2Drive, Fail2Drive, and NAVSIMv2, with particularly strong improvements in out-of-distribution scenarios.
Moreover, in its full instantiation, 72.5 % 72.5\% of selected trajectories originate from the newly introduced intent-guided or temporal candidates, confirming that candidate-space expansion provides useful hypotheses beyond those generated natively by the planner.
The code is available at https://github.com/iis-esslingen/Expand-and-Prune .
2026-10-19.introduction:
End-to-end planning has become a prominent paradigm for autonomous driving, directly mapping sensor observations and contextual information to future ego motion [ 2 , 8 , 11 , 21 ] .
Rather than predicting only a single trajectory, many recent planners capture multimodal driving behavior through a finite set of motion hypotheses.
These candidates may originate from offline precomputed trajectory vocabularies or clustered anchors [ 14 , 17 , 34 , 27 ] , or be generated and refined online through learned queries, diffusion, or related generative mechanisms [ 13 , 5 , 18 , 41 , 22 ] .
The planner subsequently scores or refines these hypotheses before selecting a trajectory for execution [ 17 , 34 , 27 ] .

Despite advances in candidate generation, how motion hypotheses are constructed and how many are propagated downstream remains largely prescribed by the planner’s inference design.
First, for sparse anchor- or proposal-based planners [ 18 , 19 ] , a limited number of hypotheses must cover a broad motion space and may therefore provide only limited support for the maneuver currently favored by the scene.
For example, a generic candidate set may contain only a few hypotheses matching a sharp turn even when the current semantic belief strongly favors that maneuver.
Second, a fixed downstream candidate budget, often implemented through static Top- K K selection, treats confident and ambiguous scenes alike, propagating the same number of hypotheses regardless of how many plausible alternatives remain [ 34 , 27 ] .
Such limitations may become particularly consequential over longer closed-loop horizons and under distribution shift, where the planner may encounter scene configurations and maneuvers that are poorly represented by its training distribution and native candidate set.

Learned scene-adaptive proposal mechanisms [ 35 , 36 ] can improve candidate generation, but require planner-specific training. Other methods operate at test time [ 25 , 32 ] , either updating model parameters or optimizing trajectories using the planner’s scores as an objective. In contrast, we keep the pretrained planner entirely fixed and adapt its candidate space at inference time, leaving both the model parameters and the scoring procedure unchanged. Thus, we enable adaptation of pretrained planners without specific retraining or modification of their native scoring pipeline.

Building on this principle, we introduce Expand-and-Prune , which dynamically reshapes the planner’s candidate space through complementary expansion and pruning, cf. Fig. 1 .
Intent-guided candidate expansion and entropy-adaptive temporal memory augment the native candidate set with semantically and temporally relevant hypotheses.
Uncertainty-aware adaptive pruning regulates downstream candidate capacity.
Expansion therefore adapts where candidate support is allocated, while pruning adapts how many hypotheses receive further computation.
Both mechanisms operate at existing candidate-processing boundaries, enabling their integration into different candidate-based architectures.

We evaluate Expand-and-Prune using LAD-Drive [ 22 ] on LangAuto [ 23 ] as our primary testbed. Expand-and-Prune achieves state-of-the-art performance, increasing mean Driving Score from 68.2 68.2 to 75.9 75.9 , with particularly strong improvements on longer routes.
We further evaluate the transferability of our framework across three additional heterogeneous candidate-based planners.
For each architecture, we instantiate the components that are compatible with its native candidate representation and processing pipeline, using the established evaluation settings: BridgeDrive [ 19 ] on Bench2Drive [ 9 ] , and DriveSuprim [ 34 ] and SparseDriveV2 [ 27 ] on NAVSIMv2 [ 1 ] .
Across these planners and benchmarks, the proposed adaptations consistently improve planning performance.
We additionally evaluate our candidate-space-adapted BridgeDrive on Fail2Drive [ 6 ] , where the gains become particularly pronounced in out-of-distribution scenarios.
Candidate-provenance analysis on LAD-Drive further reveals that 72.5 % 72.5\% of selected trajectories originate from the added intent-guided or temporal candidates, indicating that the additional hypotheses frequently influence the planner’s final decision.

Our main contribution is Expand-and-Prune , a test-time framework for adapting the candidate support and downstream capacity of pretrained candidate-based driving planners without updating their learned parameters or modifying their scoring procedure.
We demonstrate the generality of this principle across sparse diffusion and dense selection-based planners, complemented by analyses of candidate provenance, adaptive capacity, and computational efficiency.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Candidate-based end-to-end planning . Many end-to-end driving systems directly predict a single ego trajectory or waypoint sequence from sensor observations [ 2 , 30 ] , without explicitly representing multiple plausible future behaviors.
More recent approaches model several trajectory hypotheses using offline trajectory vocabularies, clustered anchors, or learned query-based proposal generators [ 14 , 15 , 17 , 16 , 10 , 7 , 27 , 34 , 13 , 5 ] .
For instance, DrivoR [ 13 ] decodes candidates from learned trajectory queries and evaluates them using a separate scoring decoder.
Another line of work progressively refines trajectory hypotheses using diffusion, flow matching, or diffusion bridges [ 18 , 41 , 31 , 19 , 22 , 36 , 26 ] .
HAD [ 35 ] generates structured local variations around selected intention anchors, while DiffRefiner [ 36 ] adjusts predefined anchors using a learned proposal decoder before applying scene-conditioned diffusion.
Although these methods generate scene-aware hypotheses, their candidate generation and refinement are tightly coupled to model-specific architectures trained jointly with the planner.
In contrast, our framework modifies the candidate collection of an already trained planner directly at inference time.

Test-time planning adaptation . Deployment-time methods improve planning through online parameter updates, iterative trajectory search, score adaptation, or output-level safety mechanisms.
Centaur [ 25 ] updates planner parameters using gradient steps driven by a cluster-level entropy objective.
TOAD [ 32 ] keeps the planner frozen and treats its scoring module as a reward for iterative Cross-Entropy Method optimization in continuous control space.
Diffusion-ES [ 33 ] combines a trained diffusion model with gradient-free evolutionary search, iteratively selecting and mutating trajectory populations according to a black-box reward.
DrivoR [ 13 ] adapts driving behavior by reweighting predicted trajectory sub-scores at inference.
UniAD [ 8 ] and SafetyNet [ 28 ] employ occupancy-aware trajectory refinement and rule-based safety validation with fallback behavior, respectively.

Our work considers a complementary paradigm: test-time candidate-space adaptation .
Rather than updating planner parameters, modifying only the final scoring objective, or introducing an external iterative trajectory optimizer, we adapt the candidate collection within the planner’s native inference pipeline.
Candidate support is expanded using semantic intent and temporal memory, while uncertainty in intermediate trajectory scores adapts the downstream candidate capacity.
All learned planner parameters remain unchanged.

2026-10-19.authors: Lingyi Hong , Weiren Cai , Jiayu Chen , Xinyu Zhou , Bailin He , Yunfei Guo , Qiao Sun , Boyu Ma , Jianfei Yang , Wenqiang Zhang

2026-10-19.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to ground language in visual observations and make long-horizon decisions. Existing methods often address these demands through task-specific architectures. At the formulation level, SimpleVLN combines single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global–local memory to efficiently use navigation history without unbounded context growth, while action chunks enable efficient output of multiple primitive actions per model invocation. For data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent DAgger experience and develop a scalable synthesis pipeline that generates large-scale tasks for reinforcement learning. At the optimization level, a progressive IL–DAgger–RL pipeline advances from action imitation to task-level outcome optimization. 2026-10-19.introduction:
Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to follow natural-language instructions in unseen environments ( Anderson et al., 2018 ; Ku et al., 2020 ) , combining visual understanding, language grounding, spatial reasoning, and long-horizon decision making. Existing methods have advanced through task-specific designs for perception and spatial reasoning ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , graph-based modeling ( Chen et al., 2022 ) , and hierarchical or dual-system decision making ( Wei et al., 2026 ) . These architectures are effective, while multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer strong general-purpose visual understanding, reasoning, and instruction following ( Bai et al., 2025 ) . However, the performance of augmented MLLM systems reflects both the backbone and task-specific components, leaving the capability of a native MLLM alone unclear. This raises an underexplored question: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? To answer it, we investigate how far native MLLMs can be advanced for VLN without architectural modifications.

Preserving the architecture still requires adapting the MLLM to sequential navigation. We develop SimpleVLN by studying three aspects: formulation, data construction, and optimization (Figure 1 ). First, at the formulation level, we combine single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global–local memory to prevent unbounded context growth while efficiently using navigation history. Action chunking further enables efficient action output by predicting multiple primitive actions per model invocation. Second, for data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent experience collected through DAgger ( Ross et al., 2011 ) . We further develop a scalable task-synthesis pipeline to generate large-scale navigation tasks for reinforcement learning. Third, at the optimization level, we investigate a progressive IL–DAgger–RL training pipeline. IL initializes the policy through action imitation, DAgger adapts it to policy-induced states, and RL directly optimizes task-level outcomes, progressively improving navigation accuracy.

Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these three aspects. We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple MLLM backbones and model sizes, demonstrating its generality. SimpleVLN achieves 76.7 % 76.7\% and 80.1 % 80.1\% SR on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE val-unseen splits, respectively, substantially outperforming existing methods. These results demonstrate that the navigation capabilities of native MLLMs can be effectively unlocked without task-specific architectural designs.

Our contributions are threefold:
(1) We introduce SimpleVLN, an architecture-preserving framework that adapts native MLLMs to VLN through single-turn decision inputs, managed visual history, and action-chunk prediction, without task-specific architectural modules.
(2) We construct training data from expert demonstrations, policy-dependent DAgger experience, and scalable RL task synthesis, and develop a progressive IL–DAgger–RL pipeline for improving navigation accuracy.
(3) We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple backbone families and model sizes, achieving strong performance on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, while extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of its formulation, data construction, and optimization.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-and-Language Navigation. Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow natural-language instructions grounded in visual observations ( Anderson et al., 2018 ; Ku et al., 2020 ) . While early VLN operates over predefined discrete viewpoints, VLN-CE ( Krantz et al., 2020 ) extends navigation to continuous environments with low-level actions.

Multimodal Large Language Models for VLN. Recent VLN methods leverage multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for vision–language understanding ( Zhang et al., 2024b ; Cheng et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024a ) , while introducing streaming contexts ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , 3D geometry encoders ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , dual-system architectures ( Wei et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Xin et al., 2026 ; Team, 2025 ) , or explicit chain-of-thought reasoning ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) for long-horizon navigation. In contrast, SimpleVLN directly adapts a pretrained MLLM without architectural modifications, retaining compatibility with existing MLLM inference frameworks.

Training Paradigms for Navigation. Imitation learning trains navigation policies from expert trajectories ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , but suffers from distribution shift under policy execution. DAgger ( Ross et al., 2011 ) mitigates this issue using supervision on model-induced states ( Wei et al., 2025 ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) , while RL ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) directly optimizes task-level outcomes. SimpleVLN combines them in a progressive IL-DAgger-RL pipeline from expert supervision to task-completion optimization.

2026-10-19.title: ORD-WM: Learning Object-Centric Rigid Dynamics for 3D World Modeling in Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-19.authors: Yueyang Weng , Xiaopeng Zhang , Yuxi Ou , Yongjin Mu , Chengzhi Zhao , Yanjie Li
2026-10-19.abstract: World models provide robots with a predictive mechanism for reasoning about how actions change object states in manipulation tasks. However, existing image-based and dense 3D world models do not explicitly impose object-level rigid motion, leaving rigid-object geometry preservation to be learned implicitly and making multi-step rollouts susceptible to shape drift or object-level motion inconsistency. To address this, we propose ORD-WM, a 3D world model that learns object-centric rigid dynamics for robotic manipulation. ORD-WM learns a vector-neuron variational autoencoder supervised by signed distance fields, which encodes each object point cloud as a geometry-aware latent representation composed of 3D vector features, and uses an action-conditioned dynamics model to predict object-wise SE(3) motion increments. Rather than generating unconstrained next latent states, ORD-WM analytically applies predicted object-wise rigid transformations to the current latent states, separating persistent object geometry from pose changes. Experiments show that ORD-WM enables stable, geometry-preserving multi-step prediction and supports efficient real-time replanning for closed-loop model predictive control in simulated and real-world manipulation scenarios.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Humans can anticipate how physical scenes evolve and how actions change object states, which is fundamental to everyday interaction with the physical world. Endowing robots with a similar predictive ability is an important step toward more capable manipulation: before pushing, grasping, or rearranging objects, a robot should reason about how its actions may move and transform the objects in a scene. World models provide a natural framework for acquiring such capability by learning action-conditioned dynamics and rolling out future states internally, enabling robots to evaluate candidate actions and plan toward desired object configurations without relying solely on trial-and-error interaction in the real world [ 14 , 18 ] .

Recent robotic world models have explored several forms of action-conditioned prediction. Video-based models roll out future visual observations and can capture rich visual changes in robot-object interaction [ 33 ] .
However, because prediction is performed in image or visual latent space, these models lack an explicit metric 3D state. As a result, visual plausibility alone does not guarantee temporally consistent object geometry or physically plausible interactions during rollout [ 23 , 56 ] .
Dense 3D world models based on point clouds, particles, or Gaussian scene representations move prediction closer to physical space by forecasting the motion of 3D elements [ 1 ] . However, when modeling rigid object motion through local element-wise updates, these models must coordinate local motions to produce globally consistent object transformations, which may accumulate into shape distortions or object-level drift during multi-step rollout [ 22 ] .

For manipulation tasks involving rigid or approximately rigid objects, prediction should preserve object geometry while allowing object poses to change through interaction. Rigid-body simulators [ 41 ] offer a useful abstraction for this setting: they represent scenes as collections of bodies with persistent geometry and update object states through constrained body-level motion, rather than by independently moving dense visual or geometric elements. This separation between geometry and motion suggests a natural inductive bias for learned world models of rigid-object manipulation.

Building on this perspective, we propose ORD-WM, a 3D world model that learns object-centric rigid dynamics for robotic manipulation (Fig. 1 ).
ORD-WM represents a manipulation scene as a collection of geometry-aware object states and evolves them through object-wise rigid motion. To obtain such states, ORD-WM trains a signed-distance-field (SDF)-supervised vector-neuron (VN) [ 7 ] variational autoencoder (VAE) [ 26 ] , denoted SDF-VNVAE. Its encoder maps each object point cloud to a geometry-aware latent state composed of 3D vector features that capture object geometry and can be analytically transformed by rigid motions in latent space. Instead of predicting unconstrained next latent states, ORD-WM predicts object-wise SE(3) 1 1 1 SE(3) denotes the Special Euclidean group in three dimensions, representing 3D rigid transformations consisting of a rotation R ∈ S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) R\in SO(3) and a translation t ∈ ℝ 3 t\in\mathbb{R}^{3} . motion increments conditioned on the current scene state and robot action, and applies these transformations directly to the object states.

Together, these design choices yield an object-centric 3D world model in which object geometry is maintained as a persistent latent structure and future states are generated through structured rigid updates. We evaluate ORD-WM on multi-step dynamics prediction and model predictive control (MPC) for object pushing and pick-and-place, showing that its object-centric SE(3)-structured rollout improves geometric consistency and supports downstream model-based control.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

World Models for Robotic Manipulation. World models [ 14 ] learn action-conditioned predictions of future states or observations, providing a predictive substrate for planning and policy learning in imagination [ 18 , 17 , 16 , 19 ] .
Recent robotic world models extend this paradigm by learning action-conditioned predictors from large-scale video and robot interaction data. These models forecast future images [ 49 , 57 , 59 ] or visual latents [ 3 , 2 ] , supporting policy learning [ 50 , 60 ] , policy conditioning [ 20 ] , visual model-based control [ 12 , 9 ] , and policy evaluation [ 37 , 42 ] .
However, prediction in image or visual-latent spaces does not by itself impose physical consistency: visually plausible rollouts may still fail to preserve object geometry, identity, or rigid-body motion over time. Another line of work grounds prediction in 3D, using point clouds [ 22 , 21 ] , particles [ 28 , 39 ] , or Gaussian scene representations [ 31 , 32 ] to model physical scene evolution. While these representations move prediction closer to physical space [ 52 ] , dense element-wise motion still leaves rigid consistency to be learned implicitly: all points of a rigid object must agree with a single object-level transformation [ 5 ] . ORD-WM targets this rigid-object regime by evolving object states through object-wise SE(3) motion increments rather than future frames or dense point flows.

Object-Centric Representations for Dynamics Modeling. Object-centric representations factorize a scene into entities rather than representing the entire scene with a single holistic latent, providing a natural structure for learning compositional dynamics [ 1 , 4 , 47 , 27 ] . This factorization mirrors physical scenes, where objects move independently, interact relationally, and form new configurations across contexts [ 45 ] . Object-centric dynamics have been shown to benefit prediction [ 47 ] , planning [ 54 ] , model-based reinforcement learning [ 10 , 46 ] , and relation-aware manipulation [ 34 ] by making dynamics more modular and interpretable. However, existing methods typically use abstract object representations that support compositional reasoning but do not explicitly encode object geometry or constrain transitions to follow rigid-body motion [ 27 , 34 , 30 ] . As a result, rigid geometry preservation remains an implicit property to be learned from data. ORD-WM builds on this object-centric view, but represents each object with a geometry-aware latent state composed of 3D vector features and updates the latent state through explicit rigid transformations, thereby imposing rigid structure directly on the latent transition.

Implicit 3D Object Representations. Implicit 3D object representations, such as SDFs and occupancy fields, model object shape as continuous functions and provide geometric information beyond discrete surface samples [ 24 , 51 ] .
In robotics, SDFs have been widely used for collision-aware motion planning, where reasoning about geometry and spatial proximity is essential [ 61 , 11 , 44 , 8 ] .
Learning-based SDF methods use signed distance supervision to learn object shape representations for reconstruction [ 36 ] , perception [ 43 , 40 , 53 ] , and manipulation planning [ 25 , 15 ] .
ORD-WM trains a VNVAE with an SDF reconstruction objective, producing geometry-aware latents composed of 3D vector features that serve as object states for rigid, geometry-preserving rollout.

2026-10-19.title: SCOPE: Selective Certification of Program Edits for Embodied Heuristic Learning
2026-10-19.authors: Junyang Shu , Bingqing Wei , Jishuo Li , Zheqi He , Yongtao Wang
2026-10-19.abstract:
Embodied heuristic learning must balance strategic adaptation with the
preservation of previously successful behavior. Local repairs may leave
structural failures unresolved, whereas broader revisions can introduce
regressions that are costly to detect through repeated environment interaction.
We introduce SCOPE (Selective Certification Of Program Edits), which uses
failed and successful executions as complementary evidence for program revision.
Frontier-guided program search annotates a shared diagnostic graph with
execution evidence to distinguish supported progress from unresolved checks.
Selective behavioral certification
uses stateful API replay to restore recorded responses and mutations, checking
whether edits preserve selected historical successes. Diagnosis and certification feedback,
supplemented by sparse environment diagnostics, guide consecutive repairs
across configurations. SCOPE outperforms the strongest baseline
in both simulation and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-PRO and Robosuite,
it achieves mean success rates of 80.66% and 84.48%, with respective gains
of 6.51 and 3.48 percentage points.
Our code is available at https://github.com/VDIGPKU/SCOPE .
2026-10-19.introduction:
Robot control programs provide an explicit representation of how perception,
decisions, and actions compose into task behavior. Language models can
generate these programs from natural-language instructions, using control
flow and API calls to express policies and situated task
plans ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2023 ) . Environment feedback then
provides a basis for adapting behavior when execution departs from the
plan ( Huang et al., 2023b ) . This supports embodied heuristic learning,
in which interaction improves task-specific decision rules while
language-model parameters remain fixed. The resulting program must work across
configurations, so learning requires more than solving the latest observed
failure.

Execution-driven systems build on this approach through iterative program search.
CaP-X studies coding agents that compose robot APIs and revise programs
through interactive execution, while RHO optimizes policy repositories
using execution feedback and validation-based candidate
selection ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Elmaaroufi et al., 2026 ) . Reusable knowledge provides
another source of improvement. Playful Agentic Robot Learning acquires code
skills through self-directed exploration, and ASPIRE combines multimodal
execution traces, validated repair knowledge, and evolutionary program
search ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) . These approaches establish
execution as both a source of learning evidence and a means of evaluating
candidate programs. As revisions accumulate, the effects of each edit on
previously successful behavior become an additional concern.

The difficulty is that a failure reveals where execution broke down, but
the required change may extend beyond that point. A failed lift, for
example, may originate in an unstable grasp, requiring the grasping stage
to be redesigned rather than the lifting height to be adjusted. Local
repairs can leave such structural failures unresolved, whereas broader
revisions can alter decisions that supported success in other
configurations. Success on the current configuration provides no direct
evidence about those earlier behaviors. Repeating environment execution
across historical successes can assess the change, but spends interaction
budget on checking old behavior as well as discovering new behavior.
Effective search therefore needs evidence to guide the extent of a repair
and assess its consequences for prior successes.

Our central insight is that failed and successful executions provide
complementary evidence for program revision. Failed traces guide diagnosis
and revision planning, while successful traces can be replayed to assess
whether earlier behavior is preserved after an edit. By executing a revised
program against the exchanges recorded in a successful trace, we can check
whether it makes the same API requests and consumes the full trace with
normal termination.
Under faithful recording and deterministic execution, with all relevant
external interactions captured at the API boundary, a complete match
certifies success on the recorded instance. A divergence instead identifies
where behavior changes and provides a target for further environment
diagnosis. This turns historical interaction into feedback for subsequent
program edits.

We introduce SCOPE (Selective Certification Of Program Edits), which couples
frontier-guided program search with this selective certification feedback.
SCOPE first constructs a shared diagnostic graph whose checks describe
observable task progress and whose edges encode prerequisites. Execution
evidence annotates the graph to identify a failure frontier consisting of
unresolved checks with supported prerequisites. This frontier and its dependencies
guide repair planning, allowing the model to select among local repair,
stage redesign, and strategy regeneration. Revisions accumulate in a shared
working program across development configurations.

SCOPE accepts the working program whenever it succeeds on a configuration.
If this changes the accepted source, SCOPE
samples historical successes for stateful full-trace API replay.
Replay preserves recorded responses and public-state
mutations, allowing later program decisions to depend on the same effects
as in the original execution. For selected configurations that remain
uncertified, sparse environment diagnostics provide fresh outcomes and
failure evidence. These observations feed back into the same repair loop.
Certification thus informs subsequent search through evidence of preserved
behavior and changed interactions.

We evaluate the frozen programs on held-out configurations in
LIBERO-PRO ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) and
Robosuite ( Zhu et al., 2020 ) . SCOPE achieves mean success rates of
80.66% and 84.48%, exceeding the strongest baseline on each benchmark
by 6.51 and 3.48 percentage points, respectively. Component ablations
support the roles of failure-frontier guidance, certification feedback,
and explicit revision-level planning. Across the reported settings,
full-trace replay takes 4.62–6.59% of the corresponding original
environment execution time, demonstrating the low cost of obtaining
behavioral evidence from recorded interactions.

Our contributions are:

A program-search framework that uses execution evidence to
localize failure frontiers and plan repairs at different revision
levels, integrating historical-success feedback into consecutive
repair.

A selective certification mechanism based on stateful full-trace
API replay, with an instance-specific success guarantee under the
stated execution assumptions and sparse diagnostics for further repair.

An evaluation on LIBERO-PRO and Robosuite showing improved
mean held-out success over the strongest baseline on each benchmark,
together with real-world experiments demonstrating strong performance
on tasks requiring base–arm coordination, bimanual coordination,
and fine manipulation.

1. A program-search framework that uses execution evidence to
localize failure frontiers and plan repairs at different revision
levels, integrating historical-success feedback into consecutive
repair.

2. A selective certification mechanism based on stateful full-trace
API replay, with an instance-specific success guarantee under the
stated execution assumptions and sparse diagnostics for further repair.

3. An evaluation on LIBERO-PRO and Robosuite showing improved
mean held-out success over the strongest baseline on each benchmark,
together with real-world experiments demonstrating strong performance
on tasks requiring base–arm coordination, bimanual coordination,
and fine manipulation.
