2026-10-19.title: BeJEPA: A Goal-Conditioned Humanoid Behavior World Model via Unsupervised RL
2026-10-19.authors: Liyun Yan , Haoyang Li , Yang Zhang , Jialing Zhu , Zhanxiang Cao , Zihao Zhou , Keqi Zhu , Yizhi Chen , Huang Chuxuan , Shengcheng Fu , Zhong Jiangwei , Qiao Sun , Chen Zhang , Yue Gao
2026-10-19.abstract:
Humanoid control requires coordinating whole-body posture with position and heading in the world frame.
Mainstream controllers imitate trajectories in the root frame, but struggle to regain the target world pose after displacement.
We introduce BeJEPA , a goal-conditioned Behavior World Model learned through unsupervised
reinforcement learning from human motion priors and robot interaction.
BeJEPA learns a shared representation of body configuration and world placement
through a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA).
A Dynamic Predictor predicts the next state embedding under an action, while a Successor Predictor
summarizes a goal-conditioned policy’s expected discounted future state embeddings in a single vector.
During joint training, Dynamic grounds the initial representation in observed physical transitions,
while Successor increasingly organizes it around long-term behavior.
Their composition guides policy improvement through one physical prediction and one behavioral summary,
without long imagined rollouts.
In 20-second motion-tracking experiments, BeJEPA with online action refinement using Dynamic outperforms
all evaluated baselines in global body-position error, reducing it on AMASS
by 61.7% relative to BFM-Zero with world-pose inputs and 58.7% relative to SONIC.
Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates joint attainment of posture, world position,
and heading goals, recovery from the ground, and closed-loop return after disturbances and goal changes.
Project page: https://ylyem9x.github.io/BeJEPA-project/ .
2026-10-19.introduction:
Whole-body control (WBC) is the physical foundation of humanoid applications, enabling manipulation, expressive motion, and the execution of higher-level commands ( Ben et al., 2025 ; Wei et al., 2026 ) .
It translates desired robot states into coordinated actuator commands.
For world-coordinate tasks, the desired body posture must be reached together with the requested base position and heading.
Existing motion-centered controllers can reproduce a posture while remaining displaced from its intended location.
Correcting this displacement requires the robot to step, temporarily departing from the requested posture before reaching it at the right place.
Whole-body control must therefore judge a movement by the goal it helps achieve, even when that movement initially worsens posture matching.

Human motion references show coordinated movement, making imitation a practical starting point for learning WBC ( Peng et al., 2018 ; He et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2026 ) .
However, tracking a given trajectory does not explain how to reach a new goal when no trajectory is provided.
This motivates reinforcement learning (RL), through which the robot can discover intermediate movements and evaluate how they help it reach the goal.
Meta Motivo and BFM-Zero use unsupervised RL to learn reusable behaviors ( Tirinzoni et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) .
Given a reward that is linear in the learned state features, these methods can select behaviors to maximize return without specifying intermediate states.
BFM-Zero uses body-relative features, so its learned objective focuses on posture and excludes absolute position and heading.
To control posture and world placement together, the robot must learn how actions change its body and how the resulting behavior brings it closer to the goal.

We introduce BeJEPA , a goal-conditioned Behavior World Model for humanoid control, learned through unsupervised RL from human motion priors and robot interaction.
Its shared representation encodes body configuration, world position, and heading.
A goal-independent Dynamic Predictor models one-step action consequences, while a goal-conditioned Successor Predictor summarizes the policy’s expected future state features.
Early in joint training, Dynamic provides physical supervision that helps preserve useful features despite the unskilled policy’s noisy long-term targets.
As the policy improves, Successor organizes these features around long-term behavior.
Their composition trains the actor to choose movements by their future goal alignment, including steps that temporarily worsen posture matching, without long imagined rollouts.
Dynamic also supports online action refinement for time-indexed tracking.

Our contributions are threefold:

A goal-conditioned Behavior World Model for humanoid control. BeJEPA learns a shared representation of posture and world placement through unsupervised RL, supporting goal reaching and motion tracking.

A Dynamic–Successor predictor decomposition. We compose immediate dynamics with a goal-conditioned prediction of future state features, jointly learning the representation and guiding long-term policy improvement without long imagined rollouts.

World-anchored control in simulation and on hardware. The learned actor improves global body alignment on AMASS and LAFAN. G1 demonstrates joint posture and world-pose control, ground recovery, and closed-loop return after disturbances and goal changes.

1. A goal-conditioned Behavior World Model for humanoid control. BeJEPA learns a shared representation of posture and world placement through unsupervised RL, supporting goal reaching and motion tracking.

2. A Dynamic–Successor predictor decomposition. We compose immediate dynamics with a goal-conditioned prediction of future state features, jointly learning the representation and guiding long-term policy improvement without long imagined rollouts.

3. World-anchored control in simulation and on hardware. The learned actor improves global body alignment on AMASS and LAFAN. G1 demonstrates joint posture and world-pose control, ground recovery, and closed-loop return after disturbances and goal changes.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Motion imitation is a dominant route to humanoid behavioral foundation models ( Peng et al., 2018 ; He et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2026 ) .
SONIC and Humanoid-GPT scale tracking accuracy and generalization across motions while retaining a reference-sequence interface ( Luo et al., 2026 ; Qi et al., 2026 ) .
Isolated or abruptly changed goals thus need an additional mechanism for intermediate motion.
Hierarchical systems supply this motion with a separate planner ( Tevet et al., 2025 ) .
Generated motions must remain within the tracker’s capabilities, while replanning frequency trades motion consistency against responsiveness ( Huang et al., 2025 ) .
Meta Motivo and BFM-Zero instead infer behaviors directly through unsupervised RL ( Tirinzoni et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) .
However, BFM-Zero’s body-relative formulation leaves world position and heading outside its learned goals.
BeJEPA learns world placement through both physical and behavioral prediction, outperforming BFM-Zero retrained with world-pose inputs (Section 4.2 ).

Reconstruction-based models such as PlaNet and Dreamer allocate representation capacity to observation detail, including variation irrelevant to control ( Hafner et al., 2019b ; Hafner et al., 2019a ; Hafner et al., 2025 ) .
Dreamer and the decoder-free TD-MPC family limit rollout horizons and estimate the remaining return with learned values ( Hafner et al., 2019a ; Hansen et al., 2022 ; Hansen et al., 2024 ) .
These values depend on training rewards, so their long-term predictions do not automatically transfer to newly specified objectives.
Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn by predicting state embeddings, allowing abstraction from unpredictable observation detail ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) .
Yet planning with latent dynamics, as in DINO-WM and LeWorldModel, composes transitions and risks accumulating prediction error ( Zhou et al., 2024 ; Maes et al., 2026 ) .
BeJEPA combines feature prediction with a directly learned, goal-conditioned summary of future state features, enabling long-term policy improvement without extended dynamics rollouts or downstream reward supervision.

Successor features summarize a policy’s expected discounted future state features, separating behavioral prediction from reward readout ( Barreto et al., 2017 ) .
Forward–Backward representations learn this structure to infer policies for new rewards and goals ( Touati and Ollivier, 2021 ; Touati et al., 2022 ) .
TD-JEPA introduces joint-embedding learning of these long-term predictions from offline transitions ( Bagatella et al., 2026 ) .
Acquiring informative transitions online remains a separate problem, motivating dedicated FB exploration strategies ( Urpí et al., 2025 ) .
In online humanoid learning, the policy and its long-term prediction targets evolve together.
Early movements may reveal little about how to reach a distant goal, although each executed action already provides an observed physical transition.
BeJEPA learns these two timescales jointly: observed one-step transitions directly supervise the encoder while goal-conditioned continuation organizes the same representation over longer horizons.

2026-10-19.title: GRASP: Global-Local Representation Alignment and Spatial-Physical Grounding for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-19.authors: Zeyuan Ren , Guanxun Zhao , Qi Li , Hao Wang , Wenlong Liao , Keyi Luo , Xijing Zhang , Zhiyuan Zhang , Jingye Cui , Qibin Gu , Zhichen Wang , Yucheng Hu , Liqiao Xia , Nan Bu , Zhengde Ma , Rankun Li , Xue Yang , Wende Xie
2026-10-19.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly regress joint-space actions avoid the deployment-time cost of inverse kinematics. However, their training objectives remain misaligned with task success, as joint-space losses ignore the unequal physical consequences of joint errors and visual conditioning lacks explicit focus on hand-object interaction regions. To address these issues, we propose a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation. First, a physics-grounded flow-matching loss maps the implicit clean-action estimate at every noise level through differentiable forward kinematics (FK) and supervises the resulting Tool Center Point (TCP) pose and inter-arm relative pose, with a bounded noise-level weighting that compensates gradient decay. Second, we introduce a global prediction query group distilled from a frozen DINOv3 teacher through future-frame feature prediction, together with a local interaction query supervised by Grounding DINO at the attention level. Both teachers are removed at inference, and the deployment pipeline is that of a standard joint-space flow policy, adding only the learned query pathway. Simulation and real-robot experiments on long-horizon bimanual tasks show that the two priors are complementary across different deployment settings. The full model excels in in-distribution deployment, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action models have made significant progress in general robot manipulation, with models such as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , OpenVLA, and LingBot-VLA 2.0 [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] demonstrating strong manipulation capabilities. Flow-based policies such as π 0 \pi_{0} generate continuous action sequences through conditional flow matching [ 4 , 5 ] . Such models either predict the End-Effector Pose (EEP) in task space, requiring a real-time Inverse Kinematics (IK) solver that may yield unreachable poses and discontinuous trajectories due to the one-to-many mapping [ 6 ] , or directly regress the joint configuration, which avoids these issues but may misalign the normalized joint-space loss with physical-space task success. Specifically, standard joint-space regression losses do not explicitly account for the configuration-dependent effects of joint errors on end-effector motion. As a result, similar errors in joint space can lead to substantially different task-space deviations after forward-kinematic propagation. Meanwhile, visual conditioning in VLA models is often learned indirectly from the action objective, which may limit consistent attention to fine-grained hand-object interaction regions.

To address these issues, this paper proposes a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation, along two dimensions: action supervision and visual conditioning.

First, rather than applying kinematic regularization to final actions, we supervise the implicit clean-action estimate throughout the flow trajectory: the estimated clean actions at each noise level are mapped through differentiable forward kinematics, and a geometric loss over TCP pose and inter-arm relative pose ties each penalty to its physical consequence. This loss is training-only, and the policy still outputs joint commands directly at inference.

Second, we append a global query group Q G Q_{G} and a local interaction query Q P Q_{P} to the input sequence, supervised respectively by predicting the dense future-frame features of a frozen DINOv3 teacher [ 7 ] and by attention-level KL divergence distillation using interaction regions derived from Grounding DINO [ 8 ] , explicitly guiding the model toward hand-object interaction regions. Both teachers are removed at inference.

In our evaluation, we conduct both simulation and real-robot experiments, and show that the proposed framework exhibits a number of desirable properties for fine-grained bimanual manipulation:

Simulation benchmark: on 50 bimanual tasks from the RoboTwin 2.0 [ 9 ] benchmark, our full model improves the average success rate over the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -SFT baseline by 15.1 percentage points in clean settings, while the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -Global+Local Query variant improves it by 29.0 percentage points under domain randomization.

Real-robot evaluation: on four long-horizon real-world tasks, including make watermelon juice, soda bottle opening, beverage mixing, and clothes folding, our method improves the average success rate by 14.2 percentage points over the baseline.

Physically accurate execution: supervision in physical space reduces TCP position error compared with joint-space-only training, confirming that the geometric loss better aligns the optimization objective with physical execution.

Interaction-aware perception: the decoupled global–local queries improve manipulation performance under randomized scenes and unseen-language instructions by guiding the policy toward task-relevant interaction regions.

In summary, our core idea is to compress task-space physical constraints and visual-teacher spatial priors into the training phase. Experiments in both simulation and real-world settings on long-horizon bimanual tasks show consistent improvements in accuracy and robustness.

1. Simulation benchmark: on 50 bimanual tasks from the RoboTwin 2.0 [ 9 ] benchmark, our full model improves the average success rate over the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -SFT baseline by 15.1 percentage points in clean settings, while the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -Global+Local Query variant improves it by 29.0 percentage points under domain randomization.

2. Real-robot evaluation: on four long-horizon real-world tasks, including make watermelon juice, soda bottle opening, beverage mixing, and clothes folding, our method improves the average success rate by 14.2 percentage points over the baseline.

3. Physically accurate execution: supervision in physical space reduces TCP position error compared with joint-space-only training, confirming that the geometric loss better aligns the optimization objective with physical execution.

4. Interaction-aware perception: the decoupled global–local queries improve manipulation performance under randomized scenes and unseen-language instructions by guiding the policy toward task-relevant interaction regions.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Kinematic constraints in the control of dual-arm robots

Two common action representations for bimanual manipulation policies are task-space end-effector poses and joint-space configurations. One paradigm predicts the end-effector pose and relies on a cascaded IK solver, but numerical solvers tend to produce discontinuous trajectories near singular configurations. Generative IK methods alleviate this issue through learning [ 10 ] , yet they keep kinematic constraints outside the policy. The other paradigm directly regresses the joint configuration, but dimension-wise regression losses ignore the non-uniformity of the physical consequences of errors propagated through the kinematic chain. Ma et al. [ 11 ] introduced joint supervision over joint-space and task-space representations, while Lv et al. [ 6 ] incorporated differentiable forward kinematics to regularize pose learning. Different from these formulations, this paper embeds differentiable forward kinematics directly into the training objective of a joint-space policy, unifying TCP pose and inter-arm relative pose into a geometric loss, requiring no inverse-kinematics solver at inference.

## II-B Visual Query and Distillation Supervision in VLA models

Many existing vision-language-action models encode multi-camera observations into dense visual tokens, while the allocation of visual attention is largely learned implicitly from the downstream action objective. Among existing approaches, two directions are particularly relevant. One line introduces learnable query tokens distilled from frozen visual teachers, for example, predicting future scene representations or kinematic evolution from current observations [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . Such supervision remains at the feature level, without explicitly constraining the spatial allocation of attention. The other line injects spatial priors into attention via open-vocabulary detectors [ 15 ] , but does not distinguish the responsibilities of global scene semantics from local interaction details. In contrast, this paper introduces two dedicated query sets, a global query group and a local interaction query. The former is supervised by predicting the dense features of future frames produced by a self-supervised vision model [ 7 ] , while the latter is supervised through attention-level distillation from attention distributions derived from detection boxes [ 8 ] . This explicitly guides the model to focus on the hand-object interaction region, with the detector used only during training.

2026-10-19.title: InstAgent: A Recursively Self-Improving Agent Operating System for Heterogeneous Robot Collaboration
2026-10-19.authors: Haoyang Luo , Junhao Qin , Jingyan Cao , Yi Huang , Guangjie Yang , Xiaoyu Chen , Haotao Lu , Tianxiang Gui , Ye Shi , Jingya Wang
2026-10-19.abstract: Heterogeneous robot teams enable complex, long-horizon tasks by combining complementary sensing, mobility, and manipulation capabilities across multiple embodiments. Yet existing systems struggle to retain execution-time corrections as reusable experience, maintain task-relevant context memory across space and time for reliable handoffs, and explicitly represent the inter-robot dependencies required for structured collaboration. In order to address these challenges, we present InstAgent , a recursively self-improving (RSI) Agent Operating System for heterogeneous robot collaboration. InstAgent organizes team behaviors as agentic behavior trees(BTs) that explicitly model capability assignment, inter-robot dependencies and handoff checks. The RSI mechanism updates these collaboration programs from execution feedback and preserves successful revisions for reuse in future tasks, while shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory provides context for planning and handoff validation. Experiments on 20 real-world multi-robot tasks with three high-level models show consistent gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Heterogeneous robot teams combine complementary capabilities in perception,
mobility and manipulation, enabling long-horizon tasks which are
difficult for a single embodiment to complete. Such tasks, however, require much more than assigning individual skills to different robots. Robots operate
across different locations and stages, and the outcome of one robot may
determine whether another can proceed. Recent large-language-model-based agentic
systems provide a promising abstraction for this setting by connecting
high-level reasoning, heterogeneous skill invocation, multimodal perception,
and execution feedback in a closed loop. This makes them particularly suitable
for long-horizon heterogeneous collaboration, where task procedures cannot
always be fully specified in advance.

Despite this promise, three challenges remain. First, complex physical tasks
rarely succeed from an initial plan alone, yet execution corrections are often
task-specific rather than accumulated as reusable executable experience. Existing
work has explored reflection, skill reuse, and feedback-driven adaptation [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] , but collaboration procedures corrected during execution
are not always retained in a form that later tasks can inherit and further
improve. Second, long-horizon collaboration requires persistent
spatio-temporal context beyond current local observations, which helps heterogeneous robots plan and act accordingly. Existing memory
systems support spatial and temporal retrieval [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] , but
historical observations must still be connected to current physical checks
before inter-robot handoffs. Third, treating heterogeneous robots as a flat
collection of callable skills under-specifies collaboration structure.
Reliable execution requires explicit inter-robot dependencies, handoff
conditions, and recovery logic, rather than isolated skill invocation alone [ 9 , 10 ] .

To address the aforementioned challenges, we present InstAgent , a recursively self-improving Agent Operating System designed to enable instant adaptation and deployment of heterogeneous robot teams across diverse and complex scenarios. As shown in Fig. , InstAgent represents
collaboration as an executable behavior-tree (BT) program that can be grounded
in shared environmental context, verified during physical execution, and
improved through accumulated experience. Its BT-based recursive
self-improvement (RSI) revises failed collaboration structures from execution
feedback and retains validated revisions for inheritance and further
adaptation. Shared Multimodal Spatio-Temporal Memory with Agent-Driven
Retrieval (SMAR-T) provides task-relevant observations with spatial,
temporal, and source information, while current observations verify physical
handoff conditions. InstAgent further composes heterogeneous capabilities into
BTs that explicitly encode inter-robot dependencies, handoff conditions, and
recovery branches. Together, these components form a closed loop of
composition, execution, verification, revision, and reuse.

We evaluate InstAgent on real-world embodiments across 20 heterogeneous
multi-robot tasks and three high-level models. Compared with BT execution without cross-task procedural
experience, feedback-updated experience improves task success by 15–25
percentage points across the three models, while increasing first-attempt
success and reducing recoveries. In the meanwhile, RAVEN-QA independently evaluates task-relevant
environmental observation retrieval.

Our main contributions are:

An agentic OS for heterogeneous multi-robot collaboration that
organizes robot capabilities and inter-robot dependencies
into executable BTs for structured coordination and execution.

An RSI mechanism that revises collaboration programs from
execution feedback and retains validated revisions for reuse, supported
by shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory (SMAR-T).

Extensive real-robot evaluations across heterogeneous platforms,
tasks, and high-level models, demonstrating consistent improvements in
task success and execution performance.

1. An agentic OS for heterogeneous multi-robot collaboration that
organizes robot capabilities and inter-robot dependencies
into executable BTs for structured coordination and execution.

2. An RSI mechanism that revises collaboration programs from
execution feedback and retains validated revisions for reuse, supported
by shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory (SMAR-T).

3. Extensive real-robot evaluations across heterogeneous platforms,
tasks, and high-level models, demonstrating consistent improvements in
task success and execution performance.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Physical Agents and Embodied Execution

Physical-agent systems connect language reasoning with physical execution
through programs, robot interfaces, and environmental feedback.
Code as Policies [ 11 ] generates robot programs
that compose perception and control APIs. Inner Monologue [ 12 ] uses execution feedback for closed-loop planning. ROS-LLM [ 13 ] integrates language models with ROS for multiple execution representations,
skill extension, and feedback-driven reflection. RoboClaw [ 14 ] uses a VLM to orchestrate learned policy primitives.
Recent AgentOS frameworks further combine spatial memory, heterogeneous
capability scheduling, and runtime management:
HoloAgent-0 [ 7 ] supports 3D spatial memory and cross-robot execution,
ABot-Claw [ 8 ] provides shared cross-embodiment memory and feedback-driven
correction, and ABot-AgentOS [ 15 ] stores environmental and task context in a
source-grounded multimodal graph.
These systems support cross-robot coordination and feedback-driven
recovery. Table I summarizes the
capabilities of representative agentic robotic systems, including
collaboration, spatial memory, and the two forms of RSI considered in
this work. Despite these advances, mechanisms for turning
collaboration failures into reusable handoff checks and recovery rules
remain under-specified.
InstAgent combines shared observations with collaboration BTs to revise
inter-robot dependencies and handoff conditions using execution
feedback and retain effective revisions for subsequent tasks.

## II-B Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Collaboration

LLM-based multi-robot systems organize joint actions through dialogue
negotiation or hierarchical task allocation.
RoCo [ 16 ] negotiates task plans through inter-robot dialogue and refines
execution using motion planning and environmental
feedback.
Chen et al. [ 17 ] further compare centralized,
decentralized, and hybrid communication architectures in terms of
task success and communication efficiency.
These approaches support flexible and interpretable coordination,
although communication and context requirements increase with team
size and task horizon.
Hierarchical methods separate global coordination from local
execution [ 18 ] .
COHERENT [ 9 ] , for example, uses a centralized
task assigner to match heterogeneous capabilities and adjusts
plans through feedback from robot executors.

Executing the allocated tasks also requires organizing action
dependencies and recovery procedures.
In robotics, behavior trees (BTs) provide a control structure for
this purpose [ 19 , 20 ] ,
combining reactivity and modularity with ease of modification
and interpretability [ 21 , 22 ] .
LLM-HBT [ 10 ] integrates this structure with task
allocation, using condition checks, local subtree extension,
and inter-robot task reassignment to recover from failures.
These methods improve coordination and runtime adaptation, but leave
under-specified how corrected handoff conditions and recovery
dependencies are validated, persistently retained, and inherited
for further revision across tasks.
InstAgent retains validated handoff checks and recovery logic as reusable
collaboration subtrees, enabling subsequent tasks to inherit and
further improve effective revisions made during execution.

## II-C RSI and Executable Experience

Existing embodied-agent research has explored how execution feedback can
be converted into reusable experience.
Reflexion [ 1 ] stores feedback as verbal reflections and represents
Experience-Context RSI, whereas Voyager [ 2 ] and LRLL [ 3 ] convert
experience into retrievable, composable, and executable skills,
representing Structured-Program RSI.
However, these methods primarily target a single agent or single-robot
skills and do not represent role bindings, handoff conditions, or
recovery dependencies in heterogeneous teams.

In the context of physical AgentOS systems, PhyAgentOS [ 4 ] organizes
execution, verification, diagnosis, revision, re-verification, and
experience consolidation into a self-evolution loop.
ABot-AgentOS [ 15 ] uses failure-driven self-evolution to improve memory writing,
retrieval, and evidence-selection policies.
These systems primarily represent
Experience-Context RSI, rather than directly revising heterogeneous multi-robot
collaboration programs.

Experience-Context RSI is flexible, but translating experience into
concrete execution still depends on the Agent’s current reasoning and
does not inherently preserve stable execution orders and explicit
dependencies.
Structured-Program RSI retains conditions, execution orders, and
recovery branches in the program structure, making it better suited to
repeated or structurally similar collaboration tasks.
InstAgent combines both forms of RSI:
Experience-Context RSI uses experience documents, failure feedback, and
shared observations to guide revisions, while Structured-Program RSI
stores validated revisions as collaboration BT subtrees for subsequent
inheritance, rebinding, and improvement.

2026-10-19.title: Bio-Inspired Magnetic Navigation Using Gradient Descent With Rao-Blackwellized Particle Filtering
2026-10-19.authors: Zayed Herma , Andrea Vassilev , Philippe Cardin , Jean-Michel Leger
2026-10-19.abstract: Navigation in GPS-denied environments is commonly based on magnetic maps, which are used to correct trajectory drift and enable relocalization. However, such navigation systems suffer from a strong dependence on magnetic maps that are complex, heavy, and costly to construct. Bio-inspired magnetic navigation (BIMN) does not rely on magnetic maps, making it simpler and more frugal. In this paper, we present a gradient descent BIMN method based on the Rao-Blackwellized particle filter (RBPF) for local gradient estimation. We show that magnetic navigation can be performed without magnetic maps, as gradient descent naturally attracts the system toward the destination, resulting in a simple and memory-efficient approach.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Modern low-cost, passive navigation methods for GPS-denied environments typically rely on high-precision, pre-constructed magnetic maps. These methods use map matching, in which the measured magnetic parameters are compared with the map to estimate the most probable measurement location and reconstruct the navigation path [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] .

The main challenge of this magnetic map–based approach is the requirement for a pre-constructed magnetic map. Such a map must be constructed a priori using a dedicated mapping method [ 7 , 8 ] . Once constructed, the map must be stored and continuously accessed by the navigation system, which results in significant memory consumption. In addition, magnetic maps must be regularly maintained and updated to preserve localization accuracy, further increasing system complexity and operational cost.

These issues become especially pronounced in large-scale environments, where building, storing, and processing high-resolution magnetic maps is computationally intensive and expensive. As a result, the practical utility of magnetic map–based methods is generally limited to relatively small areas, making this approach unsuitable for large-scale navigation, for which constructing and maintaining such maps
would be extremely challenging.

This is why drawing inspiration from animals that navigate long distances using the Earth’s magnetic field could help overcome the complexity of using such magnetic maps. These animals have been demonstrated to navigate without relying on pre-constructed maps or external infrastructure, using mechanisms that are robust, efficient, and probably simple [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . For example, the long-distance migration of sea turtles across vast expanses of seemingly featureless ocean suggests that these animals rely on the Earth’s magnetic field for navigation [ 13 , 14 ] . It has been shown that these animals memorize and store only the magnetic parameters of their destination, not an entire magnetic map. As they travel, they continuously measure local magnetic parameters and compare them with stored destination parameters to determine the correct direction toward the destination, as illustrated in Fig. 1 [ 15 , 16 ] .

This has led to the development of many bio-inspired magnetic navigation (BIMN) methods [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . In these studies, the gradient (representing the first-order variation of magnetic parameters) is explicitly and manually estimated to guide the agent. This estimation typically requires executing multiple maneuvers in different directions to acquire the necessary gradient information. To compensate for inaccurate or delayed gradient estimates, complex techniques (such as evolutionary optimization, predictive control, and data-driven approaches) are often employed, leading to oversized and computationally expensive solutions.

In this paper, we propose a navigation method that is fusion-based in the sense of performing online joint estimation of the local magnetic gradient and the agent’s position during navigation toward the destination. The proposed approach formulates gradient and position as coupled states and estimates them using the Rao-Blackwellized particle filter (RBPF). The estimated local gradient is then exploited to compute the direction of motion via a gradient-descent strategy. The main contributions of this paper can be summarized as follows:

Formulating the BIMN problem as a gradient-descent optimization approach (see Section II ).

Jointly estimating the local gradient and the agent’s position using the RBPF (see Section III ).

The proposed approach is compared with a representative state-of-the-art method [ 23 ] , which assumes a constant gradient. This baseline method is selected for its conceptual simplicity and bio-inspired nature. The proposed method introduces only minimal additional estimation to handle a spatially varying gradient.

The comparison highlights the limitations of constant-gradient assumptions and demonstrates the benefits of online local gradient estimation, particularly in long-range navigation scenarios where magnetic gradients vary spatially. The results show that the local gradient is estimated along the navigation path, with uncertainty that is smaller in the direction of motion, which is the direction of attraction governed by gradient descent. Consequently, estimating the gradient in all directions is unnecessary: only the component of the gradient projected onto the direction of motion matters for effective descent (see Section IV ). We also show that the developed method uses the same locally estimated gradient to correct the position and attenuate drift in the integrated trajectory, as if a local map were available.

1. Formulating the BIMN problem as a gradient-descent optimization approach (see Section II ).

2. Jointly estimating the local gradient and the agent’s position using the RBPF (see Section III ).

2026-10-19.title: Foundation Models for Autonomous Space Robotics: Architectures, Physical Adaptation, and Validation
2026-10-19.authors: Zizhe Wang , Jia Deng , Xin Lu , Zehao Jia , Yi Huang , Yao Zhu , Jianing Li
2026-10-19.comment: . Critical review. Ancillary files include source inventory and evidence documentation
2026-10-19.abstract: Space robots must interpret tasks and act despite unfamiliar dynamics, difficult sensing conditions, and limited opportunities for human intervention. Foundation models offer reusable perceptual and behavioral knowledge, but their value depends on how that knowledge reaches physical execution. This critical review follows space-specific requirements through perception, prediction, planning, and action to deployment and validation, emphasizing orbital manipulation and proximity operations. Terrestrial comparisons establish benefits of particular pretraining stages and model interfaces; their transfer to space dynamics and constrained onboard operation remains insufficiently tested. Event cameras offer timely motion observations across strong illumination contrasts, while spiking neural networks provide possible routes to sparse local computation. We examine how sensor degradation, state estimation and computing choices affect feedback and recovery. Higher action throughput need not yield fresher feedback; lower processor power can also coexist with higher energy per inference. We organize validation as an iterative sim-to-ground-to-space pathway, connecting physical tests with telemetry-based diagnosis and closed-loop revalidation. A satellite-capture example links observations to approach, contact and recovery, while a corresponding protocol separates generalization from adaptation with limited target-domain interaction. These comparisons identify what models already contribute and the physical evidence needed to support autonomous space operation.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Space robots must interpret tasks and act with limited human intervention. Tracking or control errors can cause collisions; repair may be impossible. Satellite capture couples tracking, approach, contact, and stabilization; surface sampling connects terrain assessment to tool–material interaction; cabin maintenance requires manipulation in confined, shared workspaces. These operations rely on established dynamics, estimation, planning and supervisory autonomy [ 1 , 2 ] . Foundation models offer reusable knowledge and behavior when task-specific interaction data are scarce. Can reuse remain useful under changed dynamics, sensing and computation?

We define a foundation model by broad pretraining and downstream reuse through a shared model or backbone. Size or architecture alone does not establish this status [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . We include space applications reusing identifiable foundation models and robot models with documented pretraining and reuse, assessing transfer to held-out tasks separately.

Vision–language models (VLMs) connect visual observations to linguistic or structured outputs; vision–language–action models (VLAs) extend this interface to actions. World models predict action consequences and qualify as foundation models when their pretraining and reuse support that description. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) use spikes for computation; their generality depends on training and reuse. SNNs, event cameras, task-specific reinforcement learning and conventional control inform adaptation, deployment and evaluation of pretrained components.

We emphasize orbital manipulation and proximity operations, using intravehicular and selected planetary studies to compare shared problems and physical requirements. Remote sensing and scientific question answering enter only when relevant to robot operation. We distinguish stabilized spacecraft, free-floating manipulators, pressurized cabins and lunar rovers.

Existing surveys frame this discussion (Table 1 ). AI-SRO connects physics, model/control interfaces, simulators, deployment resources and progressive validation [ 6 ] . The multimodal space-robot review organizes work by task planning and end-to-end control; our comparison is limited to its original abstract [ 7 ] . The closed loop is a shared organizing principle.

We examine how experiments distinguish reused components’ contributions from task-specific adaptation and surrounding control, including timing, energy demands, new tasks and physical conditions. Within-study comparisons trace reused components, target-domain updates and tested conditions. Event cameras and SNNs receive particular attention because observation timing and sustained local computation connect model capability to physical feedback [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . We organize validation into a sim-to-ground-to-space pathway and propose a capture protocol separating held-out generalization from adaptation under a fixed interaction budget.

This critical narrative review considers works available by 14 October 2026. Initial searches were followed by targeted retrieval and source checks on 15 October, retaining the original eligibility cutoff. Surveys seeded citation tracing, and web searches led to primary sources through arXiv, publishers, proceedings, institutions, and space agencies. Selection favored distinct operational interfaces, physical mechanisms, or validation settings; terrestrial studies explain transferable methods. Titles, DOIs, and versions supported deduplication.

The ancillary inventory records the search history, versions, and reading scope of all cited works. Mechanism comparisons use methodological passages; abstract-only sources support only their stated claims. Unresolved candidates and a local unpublished survey were excluded. Purposive selection limits completeness, and differences between tasks preclude pooled performance rankings.

The review proceeds from space requirements through the embodied closed loop to adaptation, validation and cross-study conclusions.

# 2 From space operating conditions to technical requirements

## 2.1 Dynamics and contact

A fixed-base terrestrial arm can often treat its base frame as stationary. A free-floating arm exchanges momentum with the base, changing the base attitude, the robot’s reachable configurations and the required control effort. Figure 2 illustrates why the same joint motion can produce a different end-effector motion. Capture changes mass distribution and motion. ETS-VII experiments and the manipulation literature establish these effects independently of learned policies [ 16 , 1 ] .

Rendezvous requires relative states and orbital dynamics [ 17 , 18 ] ; capture adds base–target coupling and contact. State and dynamics models must follow the mission stage.

For orbital manipulation, relevant state includes joint configurations, base attitude and velocity, target-relative motion, and contact mode. Active attitude control also introduces actuator and propellant constraints. Task-specific space reinforcement learning illustrates these state requirements [ 19 , 20 ] . Surface interaction poses a different problem: reduced gravity changes both robot loading and granular-medium behavior. Parabolic-flight wheel–soil experiments found reduced traction and increased sinkage relative to ground tests at matched wheel loads [ 21 ] . Reducing the robot’s supported weight therefore does not reproduce all relevant soil effects.

## 2.2 Perception and hardware constraints

Illumination extremes and specular reflections can obscure spacecraft features, as the physical images in SPEED+ illustrate [ 22 ] . Thermal changes also perturb measurement geometry: MESSENGER images reveal temperature-dependent focal length [ 23 ] . Proton irradiation of CMOS imagers produces increased dark current and switching pixel defects [ 24 ] . Missing or displaced keypoints can then bias pose estimates or interrupt tracking. The resulting requirement is to expose calibration state and measurement validity to the estimator and learned policy, alongside coordinate frames and timestamps.

Temperature-dependent calibration, dark-signal correction, and bad-pixel masks address characterized errors; learned compensation should be evaluated by pose and tracking accuracy. Neither calibration nor a plausible reconstruction restores a unique measurement where saturation or occlusion has removed it. The robot may need a new exposure, viewpoint, or modality. Event sensing improves temporal sampling [ 8 ] , while force, touch, and proprioception supply contact or body-state information [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] ; their value depends on the state uncertainty and feedback deadline.

Sustained computation depends on power and heat rejection. External vacuum removes ambient convective cooling, making structural conduction and radiation central; pressurized cabins and planetary atmospheres differ. Mounting, conductive paths, duty cycle, and thermal-control capacity determine feasible computation [ 14 ] . Model deployment must fit the spacecraft’s peak and sustained power, allowable temperature, and task-energy budgets.

Radiation can disrupt computation and storage through single-event effects and accumulated dose [ 15 ] , requiring error detection, redundancy, recovery, and appropriate devices. Proton and neutron tests measure device responses beyond what image-domain adaptation can establish [ 28 , 29 ] . Redundancy also consumes power and may remain vulnerable to common failures, so protection and computational efficiency must be assessed together.

## 2.3 Communication and limited interaction data

Communication delay, jitter, and outages limit reliance on human intervention. SUPVIS Justin demonstrated task-level supervision by ISS astronauts while a ground robot planned and executed locally [ 30 ] . Collision avoidance and contact response need local feedback; Section 5 examines the division of authority.

Hardware access and the consequences of failure restrict interaction data. Terrestrial pretraining supplies object semantics and action structure, but representative floating-base contacts and recovery trajectories remain difficult to acquire. Studies should identify physical variations absent from pretraining and the new interaction needed to handle them [ 3 , 31 ] .

## 2.4 Connecting requirements to a task

Consider satellite capture. Visual pretraining may identify a grasp feature, but its location at contact depends on target-relative motion and observation age. Approach needs pose tracking and uncertainty propagated to the intended action time [ 18 ] ; closing the gripper adds contact evidence, and stabilization requires the coupled base–target state [ 1 ] . Degraded or stale observations can therefore require a slower approach or reacquisition before engagement. Adaptation data and performance across targets assess reuse; contact loads, base disturbance, and stabilization assess execution. This task connects the following architecture to the evaluation in Section 8 .

2026-10-19.title: Unifying Embodied Foundation Models via a Model-to-Policy Formulation
2026-10-19.authors: Xinyi Hong , Mingyang Ren
2026-10-19.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as promising approaches to robot learning and control. These models integrate multimodal perception and action generation, but differ in their architectures, output representations, and learning objectives. In this paper, we present a unified, architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models based on stochastic kernels. Our formulation has two key components: (i) we characterize embodied foundation models through conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels, which together induce task-conditioned robot policies; and (ii) we connect pretraining and post-training to policy deployment, accommodating model-specific pretraining objectives and offline or online post-training strategies. We instantiate the formulation for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Robot learning is moving from task-specific controllers toward embodied AI systems that learn reusable perception-to-action policies across tasks and embodiments ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ; Team et al., 2024b ) . At its current stage, embodied AI largely adapts the broader foundation-model development pipeline to physical interaction ( Driess et al., 2023 ) . This pipeline combines a shared architectural core with three stages: pre-training, post-training, and deployment. The shared architectural core is typically based on the Transformer family, with modality-specific encoders, tokenizers, or output heads added (if needed) ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ; Brown et al., 2020 ; Team et al., 2024a ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Team, 2026 ) . First, pre-training learns general representations from large-scale corpora and multimodal collections through model-specific objectives ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Team et al., 2024a ; Team, 2026 ) . Specifically for LLMs, the resulting next-token loss follows predictable power-law relations in model size, data, and compute (similarly rigorous scaling laws are less established for other foundation models) ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ; Hoffmann et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) . Second, post-training adapts the pretrained model to follow instructions, align with human or verifiable preferences, and improve downstream task performance ( Wei et al., 2021 ; Ouyang et al., 2022 ) . Common approaches include supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference optimization (e.g., DPO and KTO) ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Rafailov et al., 2023 ; Ethayarajh et al., 2024 ) . Other routes use reinforcement learning (e.g., RLHF and RLVR, often implemented with PPO or GRPO) or on-policy distillation (OPD) ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Schulman et al., 2017 ; Shao et al., 2024 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Agarwal et al., 2024 ) . Finally, deployment turns the trained model into a reusable inference and reasoning core. The above foundation-model pipeline has shown broad effectiveness across scales and modalities, underpinning recent language and reasoning models (e.g., GPT-5.6 and DeepSeek-V4), multimodal or omnimodal models such as MiniMax M3 and Qwen3.5-Omni, and generative models including FLUX.2 ( Achiam et al., 2023 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Team, 2026 ) . The resulting models can also serve as reasoning and perception cores for agents ( Hong et al., 2026a ) . Such agents support tool use, coding, digital-environment interaction, and multi-agent coordination ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Schick et al., 2023 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2023 ) . Can the success of large foundation models be carried into the physical world? The above non-embodied foundation models generally learn a mapping f θ : 𝒳 → 𝒴 f_{\theta}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y} from input data to predictions or generated content ( Hong et al., 2026b ) . However, for robot learning, embodied foundation models aim to induce a task-conditioned policy π θ : 𝒯 × 𝒞 → 𝒫 ⁡ ( 𝒜 ) \pi_{\theta}:\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}) that maps the available interaction history and task condition to a probability distribution over robot actions. Fitting a fixed data distribution is insufficient, since a policy must also perform well on the trajectories induced by its own actions ( Kaelbling et al., 1998 ; Ross et al., 2011 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ) .
Vision-language-action (VLA) models pursue this policy-learning objective by combining visual observations and language instructions to generate robot actions. The Robotics Transformer (RT) series develops this approach from RT-1’s discretized action prediction to RT-2’s transfer of internet-scale visual-semantic knowledge through autoregressive action-token prediction ( Brohan et al., 2022 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ) . OpenVLA likewise adapts a pretrained vision-language backbone with an action-token cross-entropy objective, while π 0 \pi_{0} couples such a backbone to a flow-matching action expert that generates continuous action chunks ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) . Scaling their robot pre-training is constrained by the difficulty of collecting real robot trajectories across diverse tasks, environments, and embodiments ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) . Video pre-training offers a complementary route to learning motion and scene dynamics from internet-scale data without robot action labels, reducing reliance on embodiment-specific trajectories for acquiring these priors ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . For control, the value of this pre-training lies in acquiring transferable regularities of physical interaction that support action, rather than visual realism alone ( Assran et al., 2025 ) . Such priors support control through predictive world models, as in UniPi, which uses inverse dynamics to extract robot actions from generated video plans ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Du et al., 2023 ) . World-action models (WAMs) couple these visual predictions with action generation under language conditioning, as in DreamZero, which adapts a pretrained video diffusion backbone to jointly generate future video and robot actions ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . Conditioned on visual history and proprioception, DreamZero uses flow matching within chunks and autoregressive generation across chunks ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . Real robot trajectories ground these pretrained representations in embodiment-specific commands and physical transitions, supporting transfer across tasks, environments, and embodiments ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Adapting these representations to downstream control can also change the model’s outputs, as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} adds a continuous action expert during post-training after discrete-token pre-training ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . The resulting outputs must then be converted into executable actions through decoding and action selection or scheduling ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . These actions change the observations conditioning subsequent predictions, so the deployed policy depends on both the learned output distribution and its realization in closed-loop interaction. A common description must therefore connect these two components with the objectives and data used in pre-training and post-training.

Motivated by this connection, we develop an architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation based on stochastic kernels. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first formulation that explicitly connects model output distributions and action realization with pre-training, post-training, and closed-loop robot interaction for both VLAs and WAMs. We instantiate it for OpenVLA and DreamZero.

2026-10-19.title: PASS: A Trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System for CAT III Integrity Algorithm Development
2026-10-19.authors: Lang Zhu (1), Xin Zhang (1), Yulong Sun (1), Nan Liu (2), Jiahe Shen (2), Xiaodong Zhang (2), Xingqun Zhan (1) ((1) Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China, (2) Flight Automatic Control Research Institute, Xi'an, China)
2026-10-19.abstract: For fixed-wing aircraft, reliable localization during approach and landing is critical to flight safety. Visual–inertial navigation is promising, but aircraft navigation also requires integrity: trustworthy outputs and timely warnings when they should not be used. Real approach data are costly to collect, while many visual errors and failures required for integrity algorithm development are difficult to reproduce safely. We present PASS , a trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System for CAT III integrity algorithm development. In a unified temporal and geometric framework, PASS integrates configurable airport environments, prescribed trajectories, inertial simulation, calibrated stereo images, and continuous runway-relative ground truth. It supports navigation and integrity research through controllable sensor errors and environmental variations, computable visual projection errors, deterministic runway geometry priors, and condition-labeled data for statistical error modeling. We further propose Sim-to-Real Scene Trustworthiness ( SRST ), a measure based on DINOv2 feature distributions and UMAP, to quantify sim-to-real closeness. Experiments with representative stereo–inertial estimators demonstrate the usability of the generated sequences and quantify localization errors across algorithms and environments. PASS provides a controllable foundation for developing and evaluating visual–inertial navigation and integrity algorithms for fixed-wing precision approaches up to CAT III requirements.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Reliable runway-relative localization is essential for autonomous fixed-wing approach and landing, particularly when conventional landing aids or Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals are unavailable, degraded, or unreliable. Cameras and inertial sensors provide complementary geometric and motion information, making visual–inertial navigation a promising solution for runway perception, aircraft pose estimation, and approach navigation Marianandam and Ghose (2014) ; Tsapparellas et al. (2024) ; Ferreira et al. (2025) . In safety-critical aircraft navigation, however, positioning accuracy alone is insufficient. Navigation integrity is also required to determine whether an estimated state can be trusted and to identify misleading information before it compromises the operation. As visual measurements become increasingly involved in aircraft localization, integrity monitoring for vision-aided navigation is therefore receiving growing attention Sun et al. (2026) .

Developing visual–inertial navigation and integrity algorithms requires more than synchronized sensor measurements. Navigation algorithms depend on continuous imagery, inertial measurements, calibration parameters, and reliable trajectory references, whereas integrity algorithms additionally require controllable error excitation, truth-referenced visual errors (differences between detected runway features and their projections from independent pose and runway geometry truth), deterministic geometric priors, and condition-labeled observations for uncertainty modeling and error bounding. These reference errors are needed to characterize and bound visual-measurement uncertainty for downstream computation of navigation integrity risk; PASS provides the requisite data rather than calculating that risk itself. Acquiring this information from real fixed-wing approaches is costly and constrained by operational and safety requirements. In particular, adverse visual conditions, sensor disturbances, prior information inconsistencies, and rare failure events cannot be introduced freely or reproduced systematically during flight tests. Existing runway-oriented datasets such as LARD and BARS improve access to labeled approach imagery, but primarily provide individual images and two-dimensional annotations rather than continuous calibrated visual–inertial sequences Ducoffe et al. (2023) ; Chen et al. (2023) . They also lack the controlled disturbances, independent error references, runway priors, and condition labels needed to model measurement covariance, assess residual consistency, construct conservative error bounds, and determine the operating conditions under which a visual error model remains trustworthy. Existing resources are therefore insufficient for reproducible research that connects runway perception with visual–inertial navigation and integrity evaluation throughout fixed-wing precision approaches.

Simulation provides a practical means of generating repeatable sensor observations and exact geometric references under controllable airport, environmental, and sensor conditions. Nevertheless, two related questions must be addressed before simulated data can support downstream integrity analysis. First, fully simulated system must expose the information needed to construct and evaluate integrity models rather than merely reproduce nominal visual–inertial measurements. Second, the generated observations must be sufficiently trustworthy with respect to real approach imagery, because visually plausible rendering alone does not establish the applicability of an error model developed in simulation. The rendered stereo images, inertial measurements, calibration parameters, coordinate transformations, runway geometry, and trajectory ground truth must therefore remain mutually consistent, while the remaining sim-to-real discrepancy must be quantified explicitly.

To address these requirements, we present PASS : A Trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System designed to support CAT III integrity algorithm development. PASS couples prescribed approach trajectories and inertial simulation based on the Precise Strapdown Inertial Navigation System (PSINS) toolbox Yan (2024) with configurable multi-airport environments and calibrated stereo imaging in Unreal Engine. A shared time base and an explicit transformation chain connect the global, runway, aircraft, inertial, camera, and image frames, allowing the system to generate continuous visual–inertial observations together with traceable runway-relative ground truth. PASS is not itself an integrity monitoring or navigation algorithm and does not directly output a protection level. Instead, it provides a controlled simulation and data interface through which navigation algorithms can be exercised and the information required by downstream integrity models can be generated, measured, and statistically characterized.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We develop PASS : A Trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System that integrates PSINS-based trajectory and inertial simulation, configurable airport environments, and calibrated stereo-image generation. Its modular architecture, shared temporal basis, traceable sensor configuration, and explicit coordinate transformation chain maintain consistency across the generated multimodal data while allowing airport, trajectory, environment, and sensor parameters to be configured independently.

We develop PASS : A Trustworthy Precision Approach Simulation System that integrates PSINS-based trajectory and inertial simulation, configurable airport environments, and calibrated stereo-image generation. Its modular architecture, shared temporal basis, traceable sensor configuration, and explicit coordinate transformation chain maintain consistency across the generated multimodal data while allowing airport, trajectory, environment, and sensor parameters to be configured independently.

We enable PASS to provide structured support information for the development and evaluation of visual–inertial navigation integrity algorithms. This information comprises controllable sensor error excitation and environmental variation, computable visual projection errors referenced to ground truth, deterministic runway geometry priors, and condition-labeled data for statistical error modeling. Together, these capabilities support visual error distribution modeling, dynamic covariance estimation, residual construction, conservative error bounding, and integrity analysis across operating conditions while keeping the downstream integrity algorithm independent of the simulation framework.

We introduce Sim-to-Real Scene Trustworthiness (SRST), a stage-conditioned measure for small samples of real and simulated images acquired during airport approach. The measure is designed to mirror a human comparative scene judgment: a simulated image is assessed against both the corresponding category in the real-image set and competing categories. Using frozen DINOv2 features and a joint two-dimensional UMAP representation constructed separately for each approach stage, SRST quantifies category-relative scene correspondence across coastal, mountainous, desert, and urban airports without requiring image-level pairs.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews datasets and simulation resources relevant to fixed-wing runway perception, visual–inertial navigation, and downstream integrity algorithm development. Section 3 presents the PASS architecture, its modular simulation subsystems, and the integrity support information provided by the framework. Section 4 evaluates the functional usability of the generated sequences using representative stereo–inertial estimators. Section 5 concludes the paper.

The PASS dataset will be made publicly available upon publication at https://github.com/zhulang195/PASS_dataset .

2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

The value of an approach dataset for navigation integrity depends both on the information it provides and on the credibility of its simulated observations. Synchronized stereo images and inertial measurements must be accompanied by trustworthy sensor parameters, runway-relative trajectory references, and explicit runway geometry to connect perception with navigation-state estimation. Developing downstream integrity algorithms additionally requires controllable error sources, independent truth references, deterministic geometric priors, and condition-labeled observations from which measurement error distributions, dynamic covariance models, residual tests, and conservative error bounds can be constructed Sun et al. (2026) . Sim-to-real assessment addresses a complementary question: whether the visual organization of simulated approach scenes corresponds to that of real imagery under the available reference information. This section therefore reviews both runway and navigation datasets and methods for assessing simulation credibility.

Runway-oriented image datasets are closely related to the visual conditions encountered during fixed-wing approach. LARD provides predominantly synthetic front-view runway images with automatically projected runway-corner labels and supplements them with manually annotated real images Ducoffe et al. (2023) . LARD 2.0 extends this concept through multiple virtual globes and flight simulators, incorporates complex multi-runway airports, and introduces an operational-design-domain-aware detection benchmark Bougacha et al. (2026) . BARS and RLD similarly provide runway imagery and instance-level segmentation annotations under different terrain, weather, and viewing conditions Chen et al. (2023) ; Wang et al. (2024) . These datasets have advanced runway detection, segmentation, and keypoint estimation, particularly under small-target, perspective-change, and adverse-appearance conditions. Their published data units, however, are primarily individual images and two-dimensional annotations. They do not provide continuous calibrated stereo–inertial measurements, runway-relative aircraft states, or time-aligned error references. Consequently, they can support runway perception but cannot independently support continuous visual–inertial navigation or integrity analysis throughout an approach.

Synthetic datasets and simulation platforms provide an alternative means of generating repeatable observations under controllable conditions. UnrealCV enables programmatic camera control and ground-truth extraction in Unreal Engine, while AirSim provides configurable vehicles, sensors, and hardware-in-the-loop interfaces Qiu and Yuille (2016) ; Shah et al. (2017) . Mid-Air releases simulated camera, inertial, positioning, depth, and semantic data under multiple climate conditions, whereas TartanAir provides stereo imagery, camera poses, depth, segmentation, and optical flow across diverse environments and motion patterns Fonder and Van Droogenbroeck (2019) ; Wang et al. (2020) . These resources demonstrate the scalability of synthetic-data generation. Nevertheless, their scenes, trajectories, coordinate frames, and reference quantities are designed primarily for general visual navigation or low-altitude multirotor operation rather than integrity evaluation, the standard compulsory procedure for precision approach. Although some platforms are configurable at the simulator level, their released data and interfaces do not natively organize runway geometry, runway-relative states, calibrated stereo–inertial sensing, controllable prior information inconsistencies, and in particular, truth-referenced visual errors within a single approach-oriented framework. Substantial redevelopment would therefore be required to use them for systematic visual error modeling and navigation integrity studies. Moreover, visual plausibility alone cannot establish simulation credibility; the internal consistency of the sensor models and the remaining discrepancy between simulated and real approach imagery must also be evaluated explicitly.

Having the dataset for integrity evaluation, a natural question is the trustworthiness of the simulator. Quantitative assessment of visual sim-to-real correspondence is commonly formulated as a comparison between real and synthetic image distributions in a fixed feature space. The Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) approximates inception features by Gaussian distributions and compares their means and covariances Heusel et al. (2017) , whereas the Kernel Inception Distance (KID) applies a polynomial-kernel maximum mean discrepancy to the same feature family Bińkowski et al. (2018) . More generally, maximum mean discrepancy provides a kernel-based two-sample statistic without requiring an explicit parametric distribution model Gretton et al. (2012) . Recent work has replaced inception features with representations from more broadly pretrained visual encoders; for example, CMMD combines CLIP features with a Gaussian-kernel discrepancy Jayasumana et al. (2024) , while sim-to-real studies have also used distances between fixed pretrained features to characterize appearance gaps and their relationship with downstream performance Vanherle et al. (2024) . These approaches make distribution-level comparison possible for unpaired images. Their values, however, depend on the feature extractor, preprocessing, sample composition, and discrepancy definition. FID additionally exhibits finite-sample bias Chong and Forsyth (2020) , and a low aggregate discrepancy does not by itself show that the synthetic data preserve individual scene categories or cover the relevant variation in the real domain.

Distributional proximity should therefore be distinguished from conditional correspondence, spatial correspondence, and task-level predictivity. Feature-space precision and recall separate the extent to which generated samples remain within the support of real data from the extent to which they cover real-data variation Kynkäänniemi et al. (2019) . Conditional evaluation further addresses cases in which images may appear realistic overall while remaining inconsistent with their intended conditions Soloveitchik et al. (2021) . Stronger forms of correspondence require additional reference information. Perceptual distances such as Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) assume images with sufficiently comparable content or viewpoint Zhang et al. (2018) , whereas visual place-recognition measures such as Recall@K require reliable place identities and a cross-domain retrieval gallery Keetha et al. (2024) . Downstream task accuracy and sim-to-real predictivity provide more direct evidence of application utility, but require a defined perception or navigation system that can be evaluated in both domains Kadian et al. (2020) . These evaluation modes consequently answer different questions and cannot be interpreted as interchangeable measures of simulation credibility.

The remaining research gap is therefore twofold. First, existing runway-image datasets and general-purpose synthetic navigation resources do not jointly provide the calibrated visual–inertial observations, continuous runway-relative ground truth, deterministic geometric priors, controllable disturbances, and condition-labeled error references required for integrity algorithm development. Second, the inclusion of visually plausible synthetic imagery is rarely accompanied by an explicit evaluation of how its scene organization corresponds to real fixed-wing approach imagery under the available category and approach-stage information. Reporting synthetic and real examples, or demonstrating simulator configurability, does not by itself resolve either requirement.

PASS addresses these complementary gaps within a common precision approach framework. It integrates calibrated stereo–inertial observations, runway-relative state truth, configurable operating conditions, integrity support information, and an explicit stage-conditioned assessment of sim-to-real scene trustworthiness. Table 1 summarizes these distinctions. PASS does not implement a particular navigation or integrity monitoring algorithm, and SRST is not presented as a universal measure of visual realism or a certified safety threshold. Instead, the system provides controlled observations and traceable reference information through which navigation and integrity algorithms can be developed and evaluated, while SRST supplies bounded evidence that the simulated visual observations preserve the intended category-level organization of the evaluated real approach scenes.
