2026-10-19.title: VLA-Fabric: Learning Interaction for Composable Multi-Arm VLA Agents
2026-10-19.authors: Chenglong Zhang , Shuaijun Liu , Feiyang You , Shuyang Hao , Chengyu Wu , Ningxin Su
2026-10-19.comment: including references and appendices. Project website: this https URL
2026-10-19.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are rapidly expanding what individual
robots can accomplish, yet many real-world manipulation settings require
multiple arms to operate as a coordinated system. Existing approaches organize
multi-arm coordination in different ways, including centralized joint policies,
high-level task or role assignment, and locally executed policies that react
to teammates. However, how complete action-producing VLAs should explicitly
interact with one another during action generation remains largely unexplored.
We introduce VLA-Fabric, which organizes one complete VLA per arm while
preserving local perception and action ownership, and enables coordination
through learned interaction across policy boundaries. We first systematically
study where such interaction should occur, how peer information should be
aggregated, and how the interaction should be learned, revealing complementary
coordination functions spanning shared context, peer-specific latent
information, and action-stage interaction. We then re-instantiate these
functions in a structurally different VLA architecture, showing that the
coordination principle is not tied to a particular tensor layout or backbone
implementation. Finally, we compose teams of three and four arms
and evaluate them in simulation and physical experiments.
On all four physical tasks, Full interaction improves success over
independently trained local policies by 16–40 percentage points.
Together, these results suggest that explicit interaction among complete VLA
policies offers a scalable path toward networked embodied intelligence.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are advancing the capabilities of individual
robots by connecting visual and language understanding with learned action
generation ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Many important robotic applications,
however, require several manipulators to contribute to a common physical
objective. Cooperative manufacturing, multi-part assembly, shared-load handling,
and flexible robotic workcells motivate systems in which multiple arms work
together ( Dio et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2025 ) . As pretrained VLAs become more
capable, their progress creates an opportunity beyond improving a single robot:
organizing multiple action-producing policies into a collaborative system.
The ability of each constituent model to perceive and act does not, by itself,
specify how those models should work together.

Recent multi-arm VLAs pursue this goal through different organizations.
RDT-1B, ET-VLA, TwinVLA, and Dexora place cross-arm dependencies within a joint
policy ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Li and Peng, 2025 ; Im et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) .
Other approaches coordinate at different levels: MA-VLA assigns
atomic behaviors to individual arms ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , while CHORUS demonstrates
implicit decentralized coordination through locally executed policies that
observe and react to teammates without runtime messages ( Doshi et al., 2026 ) .
These approaches establish effective collaboration, with coordination inside a
joint policy, above the action policy through behavior assignment, or indirectly
through observations of teammates. This raises an organizational challenge as
the number and roles of manipulators grow. How can a multi-arm system remain
modular at the level of individual manipulators while still supporting tightly
coupled collaboration?

A natural way to obtain such modularity is to organize the system around
complete arm-local policies rather than a growing joint policy. We therefore
treat each manipulator and its complete VLA as a self-contained execution unit
that perceives its local context and produces its own actions.
Local information can remain with the policy that uses it,
and larger teams can be formed by composing additional execution units.
Crucially, local does not mean isolated . Policies participating in the
same physical task still need to adapt their actions to one another. The key
challenge is to connect these local policies through explicit interaction
without giving up their local action ownership.

To realize this local-but-connected organization, we introduce
VLA-Fabric 1 1 1 Project website and code: https://nebulis-lab.com/VLA-Fabric/ . ,
a multi-VLA coordination architecture connecting complete arm-local policies
through learned internal representation interaction
(Figure 1 ). Each VLA retains local perception and action
generation while selected peer representations condition its computation
through explicit policy interaction. VLA-Fabric thus makes coordination
among complete policies an explicit learning and architecture problem instead
of absorbing all cross-arm dependencies into a joint policy.

First, we establish an effective VLA-Fabric interaction architecture through a
broad controlled study. Starting from a decomposable bimanual VLA with
pretrained single-arm streams ( Im et al., 2026 ) , we separate its original cross-arm
dependencies. We systematically explore a combinatorial design space covering
interaction entry points, aggregation operators, and fine-tuning strategies.
The study shows that exposing more peer information does not by itself ensure
coordination; interaction structure and adaptation determine how effectively
local policies use one another’s information. This exploration identifies
complementary interaction at shared-context, peer-specific intermediate, and
action-generation stages.

Second, we demonstrate that the same VLA-Fabric interaction paradigm can be
re-instantiated in substantially different VLA architectures. We use π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) as a second realization, whose multimodal processing and action
generation differ markedly from the Eagle2 VLM-based SingleVLA used in our
initial study. Accordingly, the same coordination functions are realized at
architecture-appropriate computational boundaries while preserving complete
local policies with explicit policy interaction. The resulting π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -Fabric system enables multiple complete π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policies to
interact and achieves strong performance across several
bimanual tasks. Its stronger results suggest that advances in the constituent
VLA may translate into stronger collaborative systems. This observation is
consistent with the value of pretrained single-arm capabilities demonstrated
by TwinVLA ( Im et al., 2026 ) .

Third, we establish the extensibility of VLA-Fabric from bimanual coordination
to larger teams of complete VLA policies. Additional manipulators are
incorporated by composing additional local policies and extending their
interaction. We instantiate three- and four-arm VLA-Fabric teams and evaluate
them on simulation tasks with different coordination demands.
We further validate the same organization on four physical
three- and four-arm tasks, where Full interaction consistently improves over
independently trained local policies.
Our contributions are:

VLA-Fabric interaction architecture. We introduce VLA-Fabric, which organizes complete arm-local VLAs as the execution
units of multi-arm collaboration and connects them through learned
representation interaction. A broad controlled architecture study establishes
effective interaction structure, aggregation, and adaptation for coordinated
action generation.

Cross-architecture transfer of VLA-Fabric. We re-instantiate the same interaction paradigm in Eagle2 VLM-based SingleVLA
and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} despite their substantially different policy computations.
The resulting systems demonstrate a common coordination organization across
distinct VLA architectures.

Composable multi-arm scalability. We scale VLA-Fabric from two complete VLA policies to teams of three and four
while preserving local action generation and explicit policy interaction.
We validate the resulting organization across simulation and physical
multi-arm tasks with differing coordination demands.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Multi-arm robotics has studied coordinated transport, cooperative assembly,
and learned dual-arm manipulation under shared physical constraints ( Dio et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2025 ) . These settings require compatible
arm motions under a shared load or coordinated holding, alignment, and
placement during assembly. Planning and control address the resulting task
and motion dependencies. Our work studies the complementary policy-level
problem of organizing complete learned VLAs into a collaborative system.

Multi-arm VLAs organize coordination through several mechanisms.
RDT-1B, ET-VLA, TwinVLA, and Dexora resolve cross-arm dependencies within
joint bimanual policies ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Li and Peng, 2025 ; Im et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) .
MA-VLA uses high-level behavior assignment ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) , while CHORUS
coordinates locally executed policies through teammate observations
without inference-time communication ( Doshi et al., 2026 ) .
VLA-Fabric studies explicit learned interaction between complete arm-local
VLA policies during action generation.

LatentToM combines ego and consensus representations in decentralized
diffusion policies and supports explicit consensus exchange for cooperative
manipulation ( He et al., 2025 ) . Its no-message variant instead infers teammate
behavior from local observations.
CommNet, DIAL, and TarMAC establish broader foundations for learning
communication jointly with agent policies ( Sukhbaatar et al., 2016 ; Foerster et al., 2016 ; Das et al., 2019 ) .
Here, each agent is a complete pretrained VLA containing perception,
multimodal reasoning, and action generation. We study which internal
coordination functions should connect these policies and whether the resulting
interaction organization transfers across substantially different VLA
architectures.

2026-10-19.title: What Makes a Good Symbol for Hybrid Discrete-Continuous Planning?
2026-10-19.authors: Yiyuan Pan , Changliu Liu , Jiayuan Mao
2026-10-19.abstract: The physical world has continuous state and action spaces, yet robot planning often benefits from hybrid discrete-continuous formulations that explicitly expose combinatorial structure, such as contact modes or discrete primitive actions. Existing methods typically rely on human-defined symbol sets or symbols derived from language supervision, without asking what makes a symbol computationally useful . In this paper, we take an inference-algorithm–centric view to define usefulness : a good symbol should expose the discrete commitments that simplify solving the original planning problem. We first introduce the concept of solver-sufficient symbolization by studying finite-horizon piecewise-affine systems, for which solver sufficiency can be precisely characterized, and develop a counterexample-guided algorithm for symbol invention. We then extend this principle to invent symbols for optimization objectives parameterized by general neural networks as energy functions, showing that solver-sufficient symbols can nevertheless be induced from their continuous optimization landscapes. Experiments on simulated and real-robot tasks show that the resulting symbols reduce solving cost while preserving solution quality, while also improving interpretability and steerability. Furthermore, our theoretical and algorithmic insights help explain why certain human-defined symbols are computationally useful.
2026-10-19.introduction:
The physical world has continuous state and action spaces, yet planning often benefits from hybrid discrete–continuous formulations that explicitly expose combinatorial structure, such as contact modes in manipulation (e.g., fixed and sliding contact s) [ Posa et al., 2016 ; Cheng et al., 2022 ] and symbolic relational states (e.g., holding , in ) [ Garrett et al., 2021 ] . From a resource-rational perspective in cognitive science, a useful symbol can expose key commitments and abstract away details to support efficient planning under bounded computation [ Lieder and Griffiths, 2020 ; Ho et al., 2022 ] : When a person wants to go to the office with a bag, the motion of the person and the bag must initially be considered jointly. Once “the bag is being carried” is established as a symbolic commitment, the bag’s motion can be abstracted away when planning the person’s path.

While humans can invent symbols to reduce the complexity of decision-making, deep learning–based solutions to decision-making often choose to encode the full decision landscape within a single continuous-space model [ Chi et al., 2025 ; Janner et al., 2022 ] . They remove the need to declare discrete modes and dependencies a priori , but fundamentally cannot remove the underlying combinatorial structure of the problem. For example, for neural-network–parameterized dynamics models, basins and barriers appear in the optimization landscape. This makes planning or optimization hard as tasks and horizons grow [ Florence et al., 2022 ] .
To this end, researchers have considered exposing symbol commitments explicitly as state variables, such as the object relation of person-carrying-bag, to break much of the global coupling in planning.
The symbol invention problem studies inducing these symbols from data, but typically from predefined grammars and labels [ Silver et al., 2023 ; Athalye et al., 2025 ] . Such symbols are often interpretable and descriptive, yet their construction typically relies on heuristics about the problem structure, such as sparsity and locality. As a result, they may hinder rather than simplify planning. In this paper, we address this fundamental question:

Our definition of a useful symbol comes from the perspective of inference-time solving. We consider a general family of hybrid discrete-continuous planning algorithms based on search-then-optimize [ Geoffrion, 1972 ; Dechter, 1990 ] : symbols partition the entire decision space into conditioned subproblems, within which continuous-space optimization is performed. Let x ∈ 𝒳 x\in\mathcal{X} denote all decision variables and h h the planning objective. Our goal is to solve the hybrid optimization problem:

To put these in practice, we begin with simple piecewise affine (PWA) systems [ Rodrigues and How, 2003 ] , where the solver sufficiency and complexity can be studied exactly using TU-dimension tools [ Hoffman and Kruskal, 2010 ] . We then extend this perspective to general settings involving neural networks, focusing on energy-based formulations which include frameworks such as diffusion and flow-matching policies [ Chi et al., 2025 ; Lipman et al., 2022 ] . In both settings, we develop algorithms for
both symbol invention and symbol-guided planning. Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce solver-sufficient symbolization, in which symbolic commitments preserve optimality while reducing grounded solving cost. This formalizes the symbolic invention problem as an optimization problem rather than a purely descriptive interface.

We introduce solver-sufficient symbolization, in which symbolic commitments preserve optimality while reducing grounded solving cost. This formalizes the symbolic invention problem as an optimization problem rather than a purely descriptive interface.

We provide a mathematical foundation for analyzing why certain human-defined concepts are useful in robotic planning, and characterize task hardness by the amount of irreducible discrete structure that must remain explicit for faithful solving.

We develop and evaluate a symbol invention and hybrid planning framework that retains key advantages of symbolic planning, including interpretability and behavior steerability.

In search-then-optimize planning [ Geoffrion, 1972 ; Audet et al., 2026 ] , the key step is to choose a conditioned subproblem, such as mode assignments in MILPs [ Marcucci and Tedrake, 2020 ; Cauligi et al., 2021 ] and energy-based model inference with multi-seed initialization [ Florence et al., 2022 ; Chi et al., 2025 ] . This choice is hard because decisions are coupled. Researchers have formalized such coupling in AI planning problems [ Chen and Giménez, 2007 ; Mao et al., 2023 ] . Hybrid discrete-continuous planners aim to address this by introducing symbols [ Konidaris et al., 2018 ; Garrett et al., 2020 ] , but their symbols come from labels or simple algebraic combinations of state variables [ Silver et al., 2023 ; Athalye et al., 2025 ] . We instead derive symbols from the solver itself: the commitments required before make the conditioned problem cheap to solve, and the commitment number measures the problem’s coupling and irreducible combinatorial hardness. We include a more comprehensive discussion of related work in Appendix A .

1. We introduce solver-sufficient symbolization, in which symbolic commitments preserve optimality while reducing grounded solving cost. This formalizes the symbolic invention problem as an optimization problem rather than a purely descriptive interface.

2. We provide a mathematical foundation for analyzing why certain human-defined concepts are useful in robotic planning, and characterize task hardness by the amount of irreducible discrete structure that must remain explicit for faithful solving.

3. We develop and evaluate a symbol invention and hybrid planning framework that retains key advantages of symbolic planning, including interpretability and behavior steerability.

2026-10-19.title: Robotic Spatiotemporal Editing: A Unified Interface for Controllable Action Generation via Masked Action Reconstruction
2026-10-19.authors: Yanbang Li , Bu He , Yi Tian , Yu-Chiao Huang , Chenyu Zhang , Ruoqu Chen , Yuanzhe Liu , Yuxiang Gao , Mengdi Xu
2026-10-19.abstract:
Generative policies can synthesize robot behaviors, yet controlling and editing them through diverse spatiotemporal references remains challenging.
Real-world manipulation requires robots to satisfy user-specified constraints on where, when, and how actions are executed.
Our key insight is that spatiotemporal control references, such as keypoints, flows, orientations, and keyposes, can be viewed as partial specifications of the same temporal Cartesian action space.
We introduce the MAP (Masked Action Space) interface to unify these action references and formulate controllable manipulation as an action inpainting problem.
Our Inpainting Policy (IP) reconstructs missing action dimensions of the end-effector, combining progress-guided alignment with multi-mask training to support unseen action constraint combinations.
We further adopt a training-free RePaint variant that iteratively inpaints the action during denoising to reduce control error.
On ManiSkill and LIBERO-10, our policy achieves average task success rates of 92.67 % 92.67\% and 64.67 % 64.67\% , respectively.
Real-world experiments demonstrate spatiotemporal control with average positional and rotational errors of 44.3 ​ mm 44.3\,\mathrm{mm} and 7.8 ∘ 7.8^{\circ} , respectively.
Project page: https://robotic-spatiotemporal-editing.github.io/rose.github.io/ .
2026-10-19.introduction:
Generative models have recently demonstrated remarkable progress in robotic manipulation, enabling policies to synthesize complex robot behaviors from visual observations and task descriptions ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2026 ; Brohan et al., 2023 ) .
However, generating plausible behaviors alone is insufficient for deploying robots in the physical world.
Real-world tasks require robots not only to decide what to do but also to satisfy constraints on where, when, and how to execute an action ( Rempe et al., 2026 ) .
Moreover, humans and intelligent systems often need to refine, modify, and compose robot behaviors by adding spatiotemporal constraints.
For example, when tidying a table, a user may use a hand gesture or a sketch instruction ( Li et al., 2025b ) to specify where an object should be placed, rather than merely asking the robot to tidy the table.
While generative models can create robot behaviors, the next challenge is enabling humans and intelligent systems to control and edit them.

Meanwhile, robotics is gaining access to diverse spatiotemporal references from world models, 3D/4D videos, advanced agents, grasp models, and human demonstrations ( Jang et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Murali et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2025b ) , including keypoints ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , flow ( Xu et al., 2024 ) , keyposes ( Yu et al., 2024 ) , and grasp proposals ( Fang et al., 2023 ; Hao et al., 2025 ) (see Figure 1 (A)).
These representations are physically grounded and low-dimensional, but they only provide partial information on future robot motion rather than complete executable actions.
Existing approaches typically address this gap with signal-specific policies or conditioning mechanisms.
This motivates the need for a unified action interface that can transform diverse spatiotemporal references into controllable robot behaviors.

Our key insight is that heterogeneous spatiotemporal control are not different control problems, but partial action tokens of the same underlying Temporal Cartesian Action Space.
We design Masked Action Space (MAP) as a shared interface that represents these references through partially specified action tokens and a binary mask (see Figure 1 (B,C)).
We formulate controllable action generation as a masked action inpainting problem , and we propose Inpainting Policy (IP) to reconstruct masked components in MAP and turn them into a complete executable trajectory (see Section 3.3 ).

To enable this formulation, we design three components. (1) A progress-guided sliding window aligns control references with the current task stage using estimated progress value ( Chen et al., 2026a ) rather than raw execution timesteps (Section 3.2 ). (2) A two-stage joint-training strategy uses random masks in the first stage and structured masks in the second stage to learn robust control over diverse and unseen control references (Section 3.4 ). (3) As a training-free alternative, we also adopt a RePaint-style inpainting strategy that can be applied during the inference-time denoising process of an off-the-shelf policy.
We conduct experiments on 15 tasks across the ManiSkill, LIBERO-10, and real-world environments, covering six standard control references and randomly structured references.
In sum, our method demonstrates several capabilities:

Versatile controllability. Inpainting Policy supports diverse spatiotemporal references, including keypoints, flows, orientations, poses, and combinations of these reference types.
In real-world experiments, it attains mean position and rotation errors of 44.3 ​ mm 44.3\,\mathrm{mm} and 7.8 ∘ 7.8^{\circ} , respectively.
Meanwhile, our method improves the success rate on LIBERO-10 by 4.67 percentage points compared with the baseline.
This proves that our policy enables arbitrary spatiotemporal controllability without compromising task completion.

Versatile controllability. Inpainting Policy supports diverse spatiotemporal references, including keypoints, flows, orientations, poses, and combinations of these reference types.
In real-world experiments, it attains mean position and rotation errors of 44.3 ​ mm 44.3\,\mathrm{mm} and 7.8 ∘ 7.8^{\circ} , respectively.
Meanwhile, our method improves the success rate on LIBERO-10 by 4.67 percentage points compared with the baseline.
This proves that our policy enables arbitrary spatiotemporal controllability without compromising task completion.

Interpretability. MAP (Masked Action Space) provides a human-readable and editable interface that bridges multi-dimensional spatiotemporal information from the physical world with robotic manipulation actions via the masked temporal Cartesian space.
It explicitly indicates which timesteps and action dimensions are constrained.

Practicality. Our method can be directly applied to diffusion- or flow matching-based policies in simulated or real-world environments.

# 2 RELATED WORK

## 2.1 HETEROGENEOUS SPATIOTEMPORAL SIGNALS FOR ROBOT CONTROL

Robotic manipulation increasingly uses spatially grounded intermediate representations, including keypoints, trajectories, and keyposes, to guide action generation.
Point-based methods provide sparse spatial guidance ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , while KALM uses task-relevant keypoints to define object-relative frames for action prediction ( Fang et al., 2025 ) .
BiKC predicts keyposes to guide a low-level trajectory generator, and AnyGrasp provides grasp-pose proposals for downstream execution ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Fang et al., 2023 ) .
Gemini Robotics-ER supports spatial reasoning and trajectory prediction, while RoboBrain and A0 produce affordance and trajectory predictions to guide manipulation ( Team et al., 2025 ; Ji et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) .
Beyond sparse references, trajectory-based interfaces provide denser motion guidance for downstream action policies ( Xu et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2024 ; Gu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) .
Video-based models offer another route to control: V-JEPA 2-AC plans toward image goals through action-conditioned prediction in latent space, while UVA jointly learns video and action prediction ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ) .

Our work focuses on unifying heterogeneous control references as specified entries in a shared Cartesian action representation, allowing a single policy to reconstruct the remaining action entries across different reference types and their combinations.

## 2.2 INPAINTING FOR ROBOT CONTROL

Visual masking and inpainting support several aspects of robot learning.
ROSIE augments robot observations through text-guided inpainting, while Mirage modifies robot appearance through cross-painting for embodiment transfer ( Yu et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) .
Cloak masks the end-effector in wrist-camera observations without generative inpainting, whereas Masked Visual Actions uses partially revealed video trajectories for forward and inverse world modeling ( Piseno et al., 2026 ; Alzayer et al., 2026 ) .
In motion generation, Kimodo supports pose-feature completion, Scheduled Inpainting balances motion preservation and editing, and MotionBricks performs latent in-betweening ( Rempe et al., 2026 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) .
In action space, RTC and DiscreteRTC preserve committed action prefixes while generating subsequent actions, enabling asynchronous execution through inpainting ( Black et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) .
HDP and DISCO use inpainting to impose trajectory-endpoint and semantic-keyframe constraints, respectively ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Hao et al., 2025 ) .

2026-10-19.title: GR-VIP: Geometric representation conditioning for precise visuomotor policy
2026-10-19.authors: Chanhwi Lee , Jiwon Seong , Eunje Choi , Hohyung Lee , Jongsoo Lee , Junyeong Bae , Inveom Kwak , Woosang Shin , Soohee Han
2026-10-19.comment: Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). . This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
2026-10-19.abstract: Achieving precise terminal position and heading alignment remains a significant challenge for learning-based mobile robot control. Recent vision-based learning methods have shown promise for precise target-relative control and generalization to unseen environments with pretrained visual encoders, but general-purpose visual representations are not specifically designed to capture the fine-grained spatial differences between current and goal views required for precise control, and real-world demonstrations combining millimeter-scale terminal accuracy with zero-shot transfer across environments remain limited. To address these challenges, we propose Geometric Representation Conditioning for Precise Visuomotor Policy (GR-VIP), a goal-conditioned visuomotor policy that leverages a visual encoder pretrained for relative camera pose estimation. Rather than using the final relative-pose estimate, GR-VIP conditions action prediction on the dense relational features produced before pose regression, preserving fine-grained cross-view information for learning corrective actions from demonstrations. We evaluate GR-VIP on a real-world docking task and demonstrate high docking success rates and millimeter-scale terminal accuracy in both the training and unseen environments, without additional training for transfer. Furthermore, supplementary experiments illustrate the policy’s ability to align with non-docking targets and complete docking under a tested low-light condition.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Learning-based methods enable mobile robot behaviors to be learned directly from data, rather than relying on manually designed control strategies [ 1 , 2 ] .
These approaches have been applied to a wide range of mobile robot tasks, including navigation [ 3 , 4 ] , trajectory tracking [ 5 , 6 ] , and visual servoing [ 7 , 8 ] . However, achieving precise terminal alignment remains challenging in applications such as docking, inspection, and manipulation-ready base positioning, where successful operation requires accurate positioning and orientation relative to a target [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] .

Recent vision-based learning methods have explored precise target-relative positioning for mobile robots [ 10 , 12 ] . These approaches have demonstrated promising performance in precise positioning and generalization to unseen objects or conditions. However, precise control requires the policy to distinguish fine-grained spatial differences between the current and desired configurations and translate them into appropriate corrective actions. General-purpose visual representations are not explicitly pretrained to encode goal-relative geometric relationships, and existing approaches often introduce additional geometric or target-specific processing to support precise control.
Despite these advances, real-world demonstrations that combine millimeter-scale terminal accuracy with zero-shot transfer across environments remain limited.

To address these challenges, we propose Geometric Representation Conditioning for Precise Visuomotor Policy (GR-VIP), a goal-conditioned visuomotor policy that uses a visual encoder pretrained for relative camera pose estimation. We hypothesize that geometry-aware cross-view representations provide a suitable prior for precise goal-relative control, rather than relying on the final relative-pose estimate. GR-VIP therefore retains dense relational features before pose regression and uses them for policy conditioning. This allows the policy to exploit fine-grained geometric information while learning appropriate corrective actions from demonstrations.

We evaluate GR-VIP on a real-world mobile robot docking task requiring precise terminal position and heading alignment. We compare our method with baselines using alternative visual representations in the training environment and under unseen background and target conditions.
Our experiments show that GR-VIP achieves millimeter-scale terminal accuracy and a high docking success rate in the training environment, while maintaining high success rates and millimeter-scale accuracy in unseen environments without additional training.
Furthermore, additional experiments illustrate alignment to configurations specified by non-docking goal images and successful docking under a low-light condition. Fig. 1 provides an overview of GR-VIP’s capabilities.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Precise Docking Systems

Precise mobile robot docking requires accurate terminal position and heading alignment for successful physical engagement [ 13 , 14 ] . A common approach is to estimate the relative pose between the robot and the docking target and use this estimate to control the final approach and alignment [ 14 ] . Marker-based methods use fiducial markers installed on the docking target as visual references to estimate relative position and orientation for precise docking [ 15 , 16 ] . Laser-based methods have also been proposed to detect charging stations and guide the docking process [ 17 ] .
Registration-based approaches instead exploit the geometric structure of the target directly. Gutierrez et al. [ 18 ] extract line features from sparse point clouds and use the geometry of the docking station for global registration, estimating the poses of both the robot and the station with millimeter-level positioning accuracy. Although these approaches can achieve precise docking, repositioning maneuvers to correct misalignment are less commonly addressed. In contrast, GR-VIP is trained on demonstrations that include such maneuvers, enabling the policy to learn repositioning behavior directly from data.

## II-B Goal-Conditioned Navigation for Precise Local Alignment

Image-goal navigation provides a flexible formulation in which a destination is specified by a goal image rather than accurate target information [ 19 , 20 ] . ViNT [ 21 ] and NoMaD [ 22 ] learn transferable goal-conditioned navigation policies from data collected across diverse robots and environments. However, these methods primarily focus on long-horizon goal reaching and do not directly address the precise terminal position and heading alignment required for physical docking. More recent work has explored spatial relationships between current and goal observations for precise local alignment.
AnyImageNav [ 23 ] adopts a learning-free approach that treats the goal image as a geometric query, matches it against accumulated observations, and recovers the 6-DoF pose of the goal viewpoint for navigation. Lee et al. [ 12 ] ground the target object and use object-centric spatial correlations between the current and goal views for manipulation-ready positioning. Aim My Robot [ 10 ] explicitly specifies the desired spatial relation as a target-relative base pose and predicts a trajectory toward that pose using RGB-D and LiDAR observations. While these approaches advance precise local alignment, they often incorporate additional sensing or explicit target-related processing beyond the goal image. Moreover, the combination of millimeter-scale terminal accuracy and zero-shot transfer across real-world environments remains underexplored. In contrast, GR-VIP performs precise local alignment using monocular RGB observations and proprioceptive information, while achieving millimeter-scale accuracy and transfer to unseen environments without additional training.

## II-C Visual Representations for Visuomotor Control

In visuomotor control, the representation used to encode visual observations can substantially affect downstream control performance [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] . Accordingly, a wide range of visual representations have been explored for visuomotor policies.
R3M [ 27 ] transfers representations pretrained on diverse human videos to manipulation policies. MVP [ 28 ] uses masked visual pretraining on large-scale real-world images to provide representations for downstream motor control.
General-purpose visual representations such as DINOv2 have also been adopted in visuomotor policies [ 29 ] .
More recent approaches incorporate spatial or geometric information into visuomotor policies. DP3 [ 30 ] conditions a diffusion policy on 3D representations extracted from sparse point clouds, while VGGT-DP [ 31 ] integrates geometric priors from a pretrained 3D perception model with proprioceptive information. In contrast, GR-VIP uses dense relational features extracted from current–goal image pairs by an encoder pretrained for relative camera pose estimation, providing a pairwise representation tailored to goal-relative control.

2026-10-19.title: Hardware-as-Regularization: Enhancing Data Consistency in Imitation Learning via an Adjustable Passive Compliant Leader Arm
2026-10-19.authors: Hideyuki Ichiwara , Yushi Kaida , Hirokazu Ishida
2026-10-19.abstract:
Low-cost passive leader arms enable scalable data collection for imitation learning, but their lack of restoring forces leaves redundant joints unconstrained, yielding highly inconsistent joint-space trajectories.
We address this with a low-cost passive joint module (an adjustable mechanical clutch and a 3D-printed spiral spring) that pulls each joint toward a user-defined neutral posture.
This passive restoring force acts as a physical prior equivalent to joint-space L 2 L_{2} regularization (“Hardware-as-Regularization”), improving kinematic consistency with shorter completion time than an unregularized arm and preserved movement smoothness.
Experiments show substantial variance reduction over a naive passive arm, trajectory consistency on par with an active virtual spring of the same actuator class, and substantially higher downstream success rates (e.g., 73.3% vs. 36.7% on Block Stacking); a stiffness sweep shows consistency degrading monotonically as stiffness decreases, confirming that mechanical stiffness behaves like a regularization weight.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Modern robot manipulation research is increasingly driven by large-scale imitation learning and deep visuomotor policies [ 17 , 18 , 6 ] .
To acquire the necessary demonstration data at scale, the community has rapidly adopted low-cost, 3D-printable passive leader arms (e.g., ALOHA [ 24 , 13 ] and GELLO [ 21 ] ).
However, this architectural simplification introduces a severe mechanical vulnerability: the complete absence of restoring forces leaves redundant degrees of freedom (DoFs) unconstrained.
Operators naturally allow their posture to drift arbitrarily in the null-space, inducing severe kinematic inconsistency : highly multimodal joint-space trajectories that degrade the optimization landscape and sample efficiency of downstream imitation learning [ 5 , 11 ] .

In classical robotics, kinematic redundancy is resolved via active impedance control.
While utilizing high-end, expensive actuators can easily yield high-fidelity virtual stiffness, this fundamentally contradicts the community’s core objective of scalable, democratized data collection.
Conversely, synthesizing active virtual stiffness on modern, low-cost telemetry rigs inherently risks high-frequency instability due to control loop latency [ 8 ] , requiring heavy artificial damping that degrades operational transparency.
To bridge the gap between the necessity for kinematic consistency and the physical limits of low-cost hardware, we introduce the paradigm of Hardware-as-Regularization (Fig. 1 ). Drawing inspiration from passive haptics [ 1 ] , we propose a novel, purely mechanical compliant joint module featuring a Hirth coupling and a 3D-printed spiral spring. Operating in continuous time with zero latency, this spring is passive: it injects no active energy into the system.
Mathematically, it acts as a physical structural prior, applying L 2 L_{2} regularization directly in the joint space to continuously guide the operator’s posture toward a user-defined neutral point.

The main contributions of this paper are threefold: (1) a low-cost, passive (no active energy injection) joint mechanism using a 3D-printed spiral spring and an adjustable clutch; (2) the concept of Hardware-as-Regularization , showing that physical compliance naturally resolves kinematic inconsistency in redundant teleoperation; and (3) empirical evidence that our hardware reduces joint-space variance in demonstrations, yielding downstream success rates substantially higher than a naive passive arm and comparable to an active virtual spring system of the same actuator class. Videos are available on the project page 1 1 1 https://sbintuitions.github.io/hardware-as-regularization/ , where the design file (STEP) will also be released.

# 2 Related Work

Low-Cost Teleoperation and Imitation Learning: Recent advancements heavily rely on scaling visuomotor policies via low-cost passive leader arms like ALOHA and GELLO [ 18 , 21 ] .
While democratizing data collection, their simplified structures introduce massive stochastic variance in the null-space, leading to state-distribution shifts that degrade Behavioral Cloning [ 5 , 14 ] .

Generative Policies and the Variance Bottleneck: State-of-the-art architectures like Diffusion Policy [ 7 ] and FlowPolicy [ 22 ] effectively model diverse behaviors.
However, they remain bottlenecked by the unconstrained kinematic noise of purely passive data collection, expending network capacity merely to fit variance.
This vulnerability is especially acute in joint-space representations, which are vital for control stability [ 11 ] .

Passivity and Virtual Fixtures in Redundant Control: Synthesizing active virtual stiffness fundamentally violates discrete-time passivity bounds [ 8 ] , inevitably leading to unstable oscillations.
To mitigate this, researchers have explored passive haptic exoskeletons utilizing mechanical brakes or springs [ 16 , 23 ] .
Building on these paradigms, we embed physical compliance directly into the hardware to mechanically regularize action divergence at the source.

Operator Effort in Teleoperation: Classical models of human motor control indicate that voluntary arm movements are organized to optimize smoothness- and effort-related criteria [ 12 , 20 ] .
This supports our modeling assumption that, in the presence of an elastic restoring force, a teleoperator tends to settle into postures minimizing physical exertion (Section 3.1 ); we rely on behavioral proxies (completion time and smoothness) rather than direct workload measures.

2026-10-19.title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-19.authors: Khuyen Pham , Tran Nguyen Le , Edoardo Fazzari , Cesare Stefanini

2026-10-19.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a 10 × 10\times smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by 64.8 % 64.8\% on LIBERO and 58.8 % 58.8\% in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by 1.08 1.08 percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct .
2026-10-19.introduction:
Recent flow-matching VLAs such as π 0 \pi_{0} [ 1 ] and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 2 ] achieve strong manipulation performance, but their iterative action-generation process introduces substantial inference cost. At every policy query, the visual-language prefix can be computed once, whereas the action expert must be evaluated repeatedly across multiple flow-matching denoising steps. As a result, action generation can become the dominant source of latency even when the visual-language backbone itself is relatively compact.

Recent efforts to improve VLA efficiency have largely reduced this cost by decreasing the number of sampling steps, compressing or pruning pretrained networks, reducing visual-token processing, or redesigning the policy around smaller architectures. While effective, these approaches primarily accelerate inference by reducing how often existing components are evaluated or by simplifying the visual-language pathway and overall model. In contrast, the architecture of the repeatedly evaluated action expert itself remains comparatively underexplored as an efficiency axis. This motivates us to ask whether flow-matching inference can instead be accelerated by replacing the action-generation module while preserving the pretrained visual-language representations and standard flow-matching formulation.

We address this question with MambaAct , a compact Mamba [ 3 ] action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} visual-language encoder and replaces its large Transformer-based action expert with a lightweight Mamba sequence mixer. Mamba is attractive in this setting because its selective state-space formulation provides a compact inductive bias for modeling ordered, strongly correlated action sequences. As we show empirically, this design enables aggressive action-expert compression while preserving policy performance. To efficiently condition the newly initialized expert on the pretrained VLM, we introduce a Context Compressor and gated FiLM [ 4 ] interface that transform the visual-language prefix into a compact representation reused throughout flow-matching denoising. The resulting expert contains only 29.7 29.7 M parameters, compared with 311.5 311.5 M for the original π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} action expert.

Our main contributions are:

We introduce MambaAct , establishing action-expert replacement as a complementary efficiency axis for flow-matching VLAs. MambaAct replaces the repeatedly evaluated Transformer action expert with a compact Mamba expert while retaining the pretrained visual-language backbone and standard flow-matching formulation, without additional pretraining or distillation.

We show that Mamba enables aggressive action-expert compression: MambaAct uses over 10 × 10\times fewer action-expert parameters than π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} while improving mean LIBERO [ 5 ] success by 1.08 1.08 percentage points across three fine-tuning seeds.

Through controlled ablations, we examine the contributions of the Mamba action mixer and conditioning interface to the efficiency-performance trade-off. We further demonstrate that MambaAct composes with VLM-depth reduction and transfers to SmolVLA [ 6 ] , indicating that action-expert replacement generalizes across flow-matching VLA backbones.

2026-10-19.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models

The growing computational cost of VLA models has motivated a range of approaches that reduce inference cost at different stages of the policy. One direction focuses on accelerating iterative action generation. SnapFlow [ 7 ] , for example, uses progressive self-distillation to compress iterative flow matching into a single action-expert evaluation, thereby reducing the number of sampling steps required at inference time. Complementary approaches instead reduce the cost of each network evaluation by simplifying the underlying architecture. Shallow- π \pi [ 8 ] distills shallower visual-language and action transformers, while CLP [ 9 ] identifies and removes redundant layers from pretrained VLA models.

Another line of work targets the visual-language pathway, where long visual-token sequences can dominate computation. General VLM pruning methods such as FastV [ 10 ] and DivPrune [ 11 ] preserve early visual processing while removing redundant tokens before later transformer layers, and have subsequently been evaluated in VLA policies [ 9 ] . VLA-specific methods further adapt this idea to robotic control: LightVLA [ 12 ] , ADP [ 13 ] , and SpecPrune-VLA [ 14 ] selectively reduce visual tokens while retaining task-relevant information for action prediction. Beyond pruning individual components, several works pursue efficiency through compact architectures or coordinated reductions across multiple computational axes. SmolVLA [ 6 ] reduces the overall model scale, whereas CogVLA [ 15 ] combines instruction-conditioned visual aggregation, token sparsification, and a redesigned action decoder. Similarly, EfficientVLA [ 16 ] combines token and layer reduction with feature reuse across action-generation steps.

MambaAct targets a different design point: it retains the pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} backbone and standard flow-matching formulation, but replaces the transformer action expert with a compact Mamba-based expert trained jointly during task fine-tuning, without teacher models, distillation objectives, or additional pretraining.

## II-B Mamba in Vision-Language-Action Models

Mamba [ 3 ] replaces pairwise self-attention with selective state-space recurrence, providing a compact mechanism for modeling ordered sequences. This makes it attractive for repeatedly evaluated action experts operating under tight parameter budgets. Mamba has been explored across sequence modeling and computer vision [ 17 ] , with recent extensions to robotic perception and control [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] .
Within VLA modeling, RoboMamba [ 18 ] uses Mamba primarily as the multimodal visual-language reasoning backbone, targeting efficient perception and reasoning rather than dense continuous action generation.

Mamba has also been explored for continuous control. Mamba Policy [ 19 ] applies Mamba to continuous-action diffusion, demonstrating selective state-space models as compact action-denoising networks. However, it is not designed as an action expert conditioned on representations from a pretrained vision-language backbone. More recently, SUREFlow [ 20 ] develops a lightweight Mamba-based multimodal policy with uncertainty-aware residual flow matching, jointly predicting action velocity and uncertainty to selectively refine unreliable actions. Unlike MambaAct, SUREFlow constructs a compact end-to-end multimodal policy rather than preserving a pretrained foundation VLM and replacing only its action expert.

MambaAct targets this complementary setting: accelerating the action-generation pathway of a pretrained flow-matching VLA while preserving its learned visual-language representations. It retains the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} VLM and standard flow-matching objective, while replacing only the repeatedly evaluated Transformer action expert with a compact Mamba expert conditioned through compressed VLM context and gated FiLM modulation. We further show that this action-expert replacement transfers to SmolVLA.

2026-10-19.title: Ego2Contact: Predicting Touch from Egocentric Human Video for Contact-Rich Robot Manipulation
2026-10-19.authors: Qianqian Yang , Dayou Li , Bangya Liu , Zihao Zhu , Nuo Chen , Siyuan Xu , Hezhen Hu , Chen Yu , Rebecca Friesen , Minghui Zheng , Cynthia Hipwell , Xiaoning Qian , Kenji Shimada , Zhiwen Fan
2026-10-19.abstract: Contact locations and interaction forces are critical for contact-rich robot manipulation but are often ambiguous from vision alone. Measuring them on robots requires specialized tactile hardware and platform-specific data collection, which keeps robot tactile data scarce. Human egocentric video is far easier to scale but lacks touch. Recent predictors trained on egocentric recordings paired with tactile-glove measurements can predict this missing signal from video alone. These predictors, however, remain confined to human hands, which differ from robot hands in appearance and tactile layout. We present Ego2Contact, which learns a visual-tactile prior from human interactions and transfers it to robot hands. Its predictor fuses temporal scene context with hand-local visual features to infer bimanual tactile fields from the RGB video. Anatomical region correspondences align varying robot tactile layouts with the predictor’s canonical grid, turning robot measurements into fine-tuning targets and predictions into policy inputs. Ego2Contact outperforms prior tactile predictors on human data, including unseen objects, and on robot data after adaptation. The adapted predictor provides tactile inputs for both simulated reinforcement learning and real-robot policy post-training. In simulation, policies using predicted touch outperform non-tactile baselines and recover part of the benefit of ground-truth tactile sensing. These results show that human-learned tactile priors can supply touch when direct tactile sensing is limited.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Reliable contact-rich robot manipulation depends on understanding where physical contact occurs and how interaction forces evolve. Dexterous behaviors, from regulating grip force against slip to detecting contact onset under occlusion, rely on contact information that is often ambiguous from visual observations alone [ 1 , 2 ] . Tactile sensors provide direct measurements of these interactions, yet collecting large-scale visual-tactile data on robots remains challenging. Tactile skins and optical sensors require specialized hardware that is difficult to integrate and tightly coupled to specific end-effector geometries [ 3 , 4 ] . Consequently, tactile recordings are costly to collect and difficult to reuse across platforms, leaving tactile measurements largely absent from large-scale cross-embodiment datasets [ 5 ] .

Human egocentric video, by contrast, is far easier to collect at scale [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] but lacks touch. Recent datasets recorded with sensing gloves pair egocentric RGB video with dense full-hand pressure measurements [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Training a predictor on such data makes it possible to recover this missing signal directly from visual observations, without a tactile sensor at inference time. However, existing visual-tactile predictors are developed and evaluated exclusively within the human domain [ 12 , 10 , 11 ] , and they do not show that inferred touch can drive robot policies. In contrast, robot-centric approaches that imagine or predict tactile signals learn entirely within a single robot’s native sensor space and do not draw on human interaction data [ 13 , 14 ] . Methods that do transfer human tactile priors to robots entangle tactile estimation with a specific policy architecture or action space [ 15 , 16 ] . What remains missing is a unified mechanism that extracts a generalizable visual-tactile prior from human interactions and delivers it to heterogeneous robots as explicit tactile observations that their policies can consume.

Establishing this human-to-robot bridge involves two fundamental challenges. The first is to resolve the visual ambiguity during contact inference. Since the interacting surfaces are routinely occluded by the hand, a static image or an estimated 3D hand pose does not uniquely determine the underlying pressure distribution. Identical hand configurations can exert vastly different forces depending on the task phase. Therefore, reliable inference demands integrating the temporal dynamics of the scene with fine-grained local hand appearance. The second challenge is to overcome the morphological and sensory discrepancy between human and robot hands. Robot hands differ visibly from gloved human hands, which shifts the visual input away from the human training distribution. A predictor trained on human gloves also produces pressure on a human-centric layout, whereas the downstream robots may rely on sparse rigid-link force readings in simulation or high-density taxel arrays in the real world. Without a structured interface, predictions in human space cannot be supervised by robot measurements or consumed by robot control policies.

We introduce Ego2Contact , a framework that learns a visual-tactile prior from human egocentric video and transfers it to robot hands, where it provides tactile observations for robot learning (Figure 1 ). Ego2Contact formulates tactile estimation as conditional flow-matching generation over a canonical 2D hand-grid representation [ 10 ] . To address the visual ambiguity, our diffusion transformer is conditioned on a cross-attentive fusion of temporally aggregated scene tokens and hand-local visual features. The canonical grid organizes tactile signals into explicit anatomical regions, so it naturally serves as a cross-embodiment interface. By establishing region-level correspondences between this grid and a target robot’s physical sensing zones, we map distinct robot tactile recordings into the canonical space for fine-tuning and decode the generated grid predictions into policy-compatible tactile inputs. Fine-tuning on paired robot video also adapts the predictor to the robot’s visual appearance. Because the predictor outputs explicit tactile observations, it remains decoupled from the downstream policy and serves both reinforcement learning and vision-language-action (VLA) post-training.

We validate Ego2Contact across the perception-to-action loop. In tactile prediction, our method outperforms regression and pose-conditioned baselines across seen and unseen objects on human data, as well as after adaptation to collected robot data. More importantly, the adapted predictor functions as a virtual tactile sensor that provides link-level contact features for reinforcement learning in simulation, and it generates dense tactile images from demonstration videos to post-train a VLA policy on a real dexterous hand. In simulation, policies consuming predicted touch improve over non-tactile baselines and recover part of the benefit of ground-truth tactile sensing.

In summary, this work has the following contributions.

We propose Ego2Contact, a conditional flow-matching visual-tactile generator that fuses temporal scene context with hand-local visual features to synthesize accurate bimanual pressure fields from egocentric video.

We establish an anatomical adaptation interface that aligns human tactile priors with different robot sensor topologies, turning robot measurements into fine-tuning targets and canonical predictions into policy-compatible inputs.

We evaluate Ego2Contact from human tactile prediction to simulated reinforcement learning and real-robot VLA post-training, showing in simulation that vision-inferred touch improves the success rate of contact-rich manipulation over non-tactile baselines and recovers part of the benefit of real tactile sensing.

# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Based Contact and Pressure Estimation

Predicting physical interaction from images has progressed from localizing contact to estimating continuous pressure. Early datasets capture where contact occurs on object or hand surfaces [ 17 , 18 ] , and dense predictors estimate the binary hand-surface contact [ 19 ] . A parallel line regresses hand pressure from RGB, from planar touchpads [ 12 , 20 ] to egocentric observations with pose and mesh-space pressure [ 21 , 22 ] . Recent work scales this to full-hand tactile fields by pairing egocentric video with wearable-glove measurements [ 10 , 11 , 23 , 9 , 24 ] , and estimates contact and 3D force jointly from monocular input [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] . Among these, TouchAnything introduces the EgoTouch dataset and a bimanual predictor whose 21 × 21 21\times 21 canonical layout we adopt [ 10 ] . These methods show that dense touch is visually predictable, but they operate and are evaluated within the human domain.

## II-B Tactile Sensing and Imagination for Robot Manipulation

Tactile feedback improves contact-rich control when vision is ambiguous. Policies combine visual and tactile observations to select regrasping actions [ 2 ] and to react to force feedback during execution [ 28 ] . Multimodal visual-tactile representations support contact-rich tasks [ 29 ] , and tactile sensing has enabled dexterous skills such as in-hand object rotation from vision and touch [ 30 , 31 ] . Since tactile hardware is not always available at deployment, a line of work predicts tactile signals within the robot’s own domain. TacImag learns a vision-to-touch model from paired robot demonstrations and supplies imagined tactile to sensor-free policies [ 13 ] , while ViTacWorld learns an action-conditioned visuo-tactile world model from robot trajectories for rollout generation and policy learning [ 14 ] . These approaches rely on robot-collected tactile data and do not leverage the scale of human interaction data.

## II-C Transferring Human Priors to Robot Tactile Learning

Beyond extracting visual representations [ 32 ] or motion trajectories [ 33 , 34 , 35 ] from egocentric datasets [ 36 , 37 , 38 ] , recent efforts have begun transferring human tactile priors to robots. VTDexManip [ 15 ] pretrains visual-tactile representations from human demonstrations to accelerate dexterous reinforcement learning, whereas H-Tac [ 16 ] learns a joint tactile-action latent space that transfers to robots via post-training. In particular, both paradigms entangle tactile estimation with a specific policy architecture or action space. Ego2Contact instead decouples perception from control, learning a dense pressure predictor from human video and bridging robot sensor layouts via anatomical correspondences. The predictions are evaluated as observations for both simulated and real-world policy training.

2026-10-19.title: SenseSwarm: Swarm Exploration via Neural Structure Estimation with Shared World-Anticipation for Rapid Mapping
2026-10-19.authors: Haohua Que , Haojia Gao , Mingkai Liu , Hoiian Au , Qian Zhang , Jiayue Xie , Yule Cai , Bokui Chen , Xueqian Wang , Fei Qiao
2026-10-19.abstract: A robot swarm covers a building faster with more robots, but the map is only as complete as the space the robots have physically visited. We target the amount of an unknown building a decentralized swarm knows at each instant, ahead of physical coverage. SenseSwarm serves a lightweight learned map predictor on the swarm’s shared occupancy map and folds the predicted structure back into a stigmergic guidance field. Its 709K-parameter predictor is fine-tuned on the swarm’s own multi-front observations, which we show is necessary: a single-robot predictor collapses on such views. We build a benchmark of twelve real building floors from HouseExpo, HKUST, and KTH, up to 24,000 square meters, and run 1,620 simulations across nine coordination methods, swarm sizes 32 to 512, and three seeds. On physical coverage the swarm is near parity with a greedy frontier planner, as expected. On map reconstruction, every non-predictive baseline needs 1.3 to 1.9 times longer to reach an 80 percent known map, and SenseSwarm holds an equal-time area lead of about 670 square meters, up to 1,359. Folding the prediction into the shared field matters: the same predictor applied per robot matches our speed but suffers a 6.9 times higher inter-robot contact rate at 512 robots. The prediction is computed once per shared map, so its cost stayed flat from 32 to 512 robots.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Multi-robot exploration of an unknown building is a core capability for search and rescue, inspection, and mapping [ 1 ] . A larger team explores faster, yet the useful output is the map, and the map is only as complete as the space the robots have physically sensed: every unentered room stays blank until a robot walks up to it. We target this ceiling and ask how much of the building a swarm can know at each instant, ahead of physical coverage, rather than how fast it can walk every cell.

Prior work optimizes traversal. Frontier methods drive robots to the known-unknown boundary [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] , next-best-view planners select informative viewpoints [ 7 ] , decentralized systems such as RACER and TARE coordinate teams to high efficiency [ 8 , 9 ] , and benchmarks standardize the metrics [ 10 ] . All report how fast the robots cover the space; to our knowledge, none reports how fast a decentralized swarm reconstructs the map when unseen structure is predicted rather than visited.

Map prediction closes exactly this gap, but for single robots: generative networks predict unknown structure and planners act on it [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] , MapEx inpaints the global grid [ 17 ] , PIPE Planner adds pathwise information gain [ 18 ] , and SenseMapNet with SenseExpo distill a lightweight local predictor [ 19 , 20 ] . For multiple robots, 4CNet runs a per-robot diffusion predictor conditioned on teammate trajectories, demonstrated on three robots [ 21 ] . No method reports a map-reconstruction speedup for a decentralized swarm. That slot is empty, and it is the one we fill. 1 1 1 Videos of every run, the benchmark maps, and the construction scripts: https://que121.github.io/senseswarm-site/

Reaching it requires a predictor that runs at swarm scale, stays accurate on what a swarm actually observes (thin multi-front strips of a shared map, not a single robot’s connected blob), and guides the swarm without central control. SenseSwarm answers with one predictor served on the shared map, tiled so the cost tracks the frontier and not the robot count, fine-tuned on the swarm’s own observations, and deposited as a stigmergic field that each robot reads only locally.

We evaluate in ARGoS [ 22 ] on twelve real floors [ 23 , 24 ] with 32 to 512 robots, against seven baselines covering every non-predictive decentralized family [ 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ] plus an integration ablation that runs the same predictor per robot, standing in for the 4CNet mechanism at swarm scale.
Our contributions are threefold.

The first swarm-scale exploration benchmark on real super-large buildings, to our knowledge. Twelve real floors up to 24,000 square meters, in a 1,620-run matrix [ 10 ] .

Predictive stigmergy. One predictor serves the shared map and becomes a stigmergic field read only locally, so the cost tracks the frontier, not the robot count. It must match the swarm’s observation distribution: trained for a single robot, the same architecture drops from 0.85 to 0.34 IoU.

Reconstruction is where prediction pays. Every non-predictive baseline needs 1.3 to 1.9 times longer to reach an 80 percent known map, and folding the prediction per robot costs 6.9 times the contacts at 512 robots.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# II Related Work

Multi-robot exploration. Frontier exploration sends robots to the known-unknown boundary [ 2 , 3 ] , coordinated variants assign frontiers across a team [ 4 , 5 ] , information-theoretic planners maximize expected gain [ 6 , 7 ] , and recent decentralized systems reach high efficiency [ 8 , 9 ] . All report coverage time, treating the map as the set of visited cells; SenseSwarm keeps a greedy frontier drive and adds a reconstruction objective prior work does not measure.

Learned map prediction. Predicting unseen structure lets a robot act on a map larger than what it has sensed [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] : MapEx inpaints the global grid with an ensemble [ 17 ] , PIPE Planner adds pathwise gain [ 18 ] , and SenseMapNet with SenseExpo distill a lightweight local predictor for a single explorer [ 19 , 20 ] . 4CNet runs a per-robot diffusion predictor conditioned on shared trajectories [ 21 ] , accurate but seconds per robot per cycle and demonstrated on three robots. SenseSwarm instead predicts once on the shared map, is fine-tuned on the swarm observation distribution, and reports a reconstruction speedup at swarm scale.

Stigmergic swarm coordination. Robot swarms reach thousand-robot scale in hardware [ 14 ] , and social insects coordinate without central control through stigmergy, signals deposited in the shared environment [ 29 ] . Pheromone-inspired robotics uses shared fields for dispersion and coverage [ 30 ] , recent methods refine the potential shaping [ 27 ] and the stigmergic gradient itself [ 28 ] , and dense swarms are known to congest past an optimal size [ 31 , 32 , 33 ] . We run representatives of both recent families as baselines. Unlike prior stigmergic explorers, SenseSwarm injects a learned predictive signal into the field, pulling the swarm toward structure it has not yet sensed.

2026-10-19.title: Structured Perception Representations for Off-road Dynamics Learning
2026-10-19.authors: Micah Nye , Samuel Triest , Matthew Sivaprakasam , Isaiah Adu , Sebastian Scherer , Wenshan Wang
2026-10-19.comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026.
2026-10-19.abstract: Autonomously navigating off-road terrain at high speed demands accurate control, which often relies on dynamics models that capture complex interactions between the robot and terrain. In off-road regimes, terrain interaction is a major component of the vehicle’s dynamics. Prior work attempts to capture this effect by training learned models of the vehicle’s dynamics, conditioned on its perception of the local environment. However, said conditioning is often overly simplistic, ignoring the spatial structure of the dynamics problem. Our approach, SpatialBEV, exploits this spatial structure. At each step, we query the bird’s-eye-view (BEV) features around the predicted state, conditioning the next prediction on current geometric and semantic cues. We additionally present a benchmarking approach that mines a dataset’s most difficult scenarios. On datasets collected across seasons, SpatialBEV reduces prediction error by 17.1%, compared to physics-based and learned baselines. We further evaluate on hardware on high-speed ( ≥ \geq 10m/s) and geometrically challenging courses with a 25.3% reduction in maximum cross-track error. More details can be found at https://theairlab.org/spatial-bev-dynamics.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Autonomous navigation in unstructured, off-road environments at high speeds remains a significant challenge for model-predictive control (MPC) frameworks. MPC is a well-established method in control theory; however, its success depends on accurate dynamics models for forward prediction. Traditional methods rely on simplified physics models [ 18 , 50 , 20 , 15 , 25 ] that struggle to capture complex terradynamics induced by challenging terrains like loose gravel, deep snow, or standing water. High speeds exacerbate these unmodeled interactions which may lead to task failure.

While learned dynamics models have emerged as a potential solution due to their expressivity, they often neglect environment observation [ 41 , 7 ] . When a robot commands identical actions under identical initial conditions on different surfaces with differing geometry or friction, the resulting trajectory varies significantly [ 12 , 5 ] . In state-only models, this variance is captured as an unmodeled disturbance term or stochastic noise term. However, this uncertainty is largely epistemic; it is a direct consequence of the model’s inability to observe the environmental physics imposed on the robot during interaction.

Motivated by this shortcoming, we propose a dynamics representation that conditions its prediction on environment geometry and visual semantics. We use birds-eye-view (BEV) representations which provide a spatially-aligned structure for environment attributes such as terrain elevation and Visual Foundation Model (VFM) features. While prior works encode BEV features as a fixed contextual prior at the beginning of a prediction pass [ 47 , 30 , 35 ] , this leaves the spatial representation underutilized. Instead of treating the BEV information as a single prior, we make full use of its spatial structure by treating it as a continuous source for incremental feedback and state correction at every prediction step. This explicit architecture ensures the most relevant BEV features are queried at each step. This is especially important at high speed, where a robot traverses large distances and fixed-prior approaches condition every prediction step on the same initial encoding, rather than the features local to the robot’s current position.

We demonstrate the efficacy of this representation through extensive evaluation. We also introduce a systematic testing methodology that clusters similar actions to isolate high-variance regimes, specifically targeting the scenarios where current models are likely to fail and where environment context is necessary for accurate dynamics prediction. Our results span both offline evaluation on aggressive driving data around multiple test sites as well as online hardware deployment on high speed ( ≥ \geq 10m/s) and geometrically challenging courses. Through all experiments, we show that our spatial representation for incremental conditioning reduces forward prediction error and improves closed-loop tracking. Specifically our work provides three key contributions:

A new method for leveraging structured perception representations for environment context in dynamics modeling

A benchmarking approach to mine the most challenging sequences of dynamics datasets

Extensive offline experiments and online hardware experiments at high speeds ( ≥ \geq 10 m/s), demonstrating the efficacy of our approach
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Both the learning objective and representations for the dynamics model are critical for robust control on varying terrains. Djeumou et al. [9] choose to learn the parameters of a tire model, which grants a structured learning paradigm with natural saturation in physically infeasible regimes, but also hinges on the accuracy of this physical assumption. Such models struggle on off-road terrains, with difficult-to-model nonlinearities imposed by undulated terrain surfaces, which Gibson et al. [14] address by learning the force residual to a tire model. Dynamics residual learning supplements the physics model by learning any unmodeled disturbances and is used widely in literature for off-road platforms [ 15 , 35 , 30 , 31 , 41 , 36 ] , on-road platforms [ 65 , 10 ] , and aerial vehicles [ 39 , 42 ] , among other embodiments. Yet, these approaches depend on the physics model accuracy, require ample time to tune the physics model, and restrict the model to an explicit physical form factor.

Thus, much like model-based reinforcement learning [ 59 , 24 , 40 ] , it is common to learn the forward states directly, without any physics-informed prior [ 56 , 29 , 60 , 22 , 2 , 44 , 21 , 54 ] . These state representations can be further formulated probabilistically [ 13 , 7 , 67 , 28 , 50 , 8 , 32 , 11 ] . To improve terrain awareness, dynamics models can be augmented with geometric and semantic inputs using perception representations. Prior work conditions dynamics models on first-person-view (FPV) images [ 24 , 3 , 16 , 6 ] , point clouds [ 26 ] , or BEV representations, specifically elevation maps [ 47 , 14 , 30 ] , RGB maps [ 43 , 36 ] , or VFM feature maps [ 35 , 14 ] .
However, most prior work treats perception as a fixed context, encoded into the latent state once at rollout start [ 47 , 35 ] . Lee et al. [30] reduce the encoder load via a BEV crop around a conservative feasible motion extent. Most similar to our approach, Gibson et al. [14] query features at tire points along the rollout; however, they use this context as a physics residual and no further. In contrast, our approach takes full advantage of the context by using it for both state prediction and correction , which contributes substantially to prediction accuracy. Beyond the architecture, we formalize this spatially-grounded representation and isolate its benefit through extensive ablations and quantitative & qualitative evaluations.
