2026-10-19.title: Micro-Localization: High-Precision Mobile Robot Localization Using Microscopic Ground Texture
2026-10-19.authors: Aaron Wilhelm , Marina de Albuquerque Marcon , Emith Uyanwatte , Nils Napp
2026-10-19.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-19.abstract:
We demonstrate high-precision global localization using natural ground texture viewed through microscope optics, achieving localization in the tens-of-micrometers regime.
For the planar ground texture localization problem considered here, we relate optical magnification and image-space localization uncertainty to physical localization precision.
Leveraging this relationship, we then develop a microscope-based localization system that addresses the calibration, camera-modeling, and focus challenges introduced by high-magnification imaging.
We evaluate this system across several surface textures using a calibrated precision gantry.
Across 1,007 held-out queries per surface, the system localizes every query and achieves translation RMSEs of 28–73 μ \mu m.
Independent photometric registration agrees with the feature-based localization estimates to within approximately 9 μ \mu m RMSE.
We further demonstrate localization on a low-cost mobile robot using the gantry-collected maps, and also show that the system can resolve micrometer-scale
displacement caused by thermal expansion.
These results show that microscopic natural surface texture can bring mobile localization into a precision regime typically associated with fixed positioning systems.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Mobile robots offer a compelling way to bring inspection, manipulation, and fabrication capabilities to large or reconfigurable workspaces.
However, many of these tasks require positioning accuracy far finer than that needed for navigation.
Precision manufacturing systems such as CNC machines can achieve micrometer-scale positioning, but their rigid mechanical structure confines them to a fixed work envelope.
In many mobile applications, such precision may only be needed near the task, motivating localization methods that provide high accuracy locally while preserving the flexibility of a mobile platform.

Ground texture localization provides a promising basis for this capability.
Rather than relying on sparse landmarks or installed fiducials, these methods use the natural surface texture beneath a robot as a global reference.
Because the surface is viewed at close range, a given planar displacement produces a larger displacement of the texture in the native sensor image than it would under a more distant viewing geometry, helping enable high physical localization precision.
We refer to this relationship between physical displacement and the resulting image displacement as the geometric sensitivity of the imaging system.
Building on this principle, we use microscope optics to substantially increase optical magnification to target globally referenced localization in the tens-of-micrometers regime.

High optical magnification provides a second benefit beyond increased geometric sensitivity: it can reveal natural surface structure that is not readily visible or distinctive at conventional imaging scales.
Surfaces that appear weakly textured at the macro scale can expose rich microstructure, while surfaces with visible macroscopic patterns can reveal additional fine-scale structure under microscopic observation.
Figure 2 illustrates this change in appearance for the surfaces considered in this work.
We use this naturally occurring microtexture as a visual reference for localization without modifying the surface with artificial landmarks.

Using this sensing configuration, we show that natural microscopic surface texture supports globally referenced planar localization in the tens-of-micrometers regime across multiple surfaces.
At this scale, localization errors are a fraction of the diameter of a human hair.
This precision is achieved with a localization pipeline built on an established ground texture localization method, without requiring a localization algorithm specialized for micrometer-scale operation.

We envision this level of precision for localized high-precision work regions, where such accuracy is needed near the task rather than throughout the broader environment.
The system is therefore not intended to replace general-purpose navigation across an entire factory or building.

The primary contributions of this work are:

A geometric formulation relating optical magnification, image-space localization uncertainty, and physical localization precision, motivating the use of microscopic surface texture for high-precision localization

A microscope-based ground texture localization system that addresses the calibration, camera-modeling, and focus challenges introduced by high-magnification optics

A demonstration of tens-of-micrometers global localization on a low-cost mobile robot using a surface map collected independently with a precision gantry

We validate these contributions across three distinct surface types using a calibrated gantry reference system and further demonstrate our system’s ability to measure micrometer-scale displacement by observing the thermal expansion of an aluminum beam.
We will release the resulting high-resolution microscopic ground texture datasets and accompanying code.

1. A geometric formulation relating optical magnification, image-space localization uncertainty, and physical localization precision, motivating the use of microscopic surface texture for high-precision localization

2. A microscope-based ground texture localization system that addresses the calibration, camera-modeling, and focus challenges introduced by high-magnification optics

3. A demonstration of tens-of-micrometers global localization on a low-cost mobile robot using a surface map collected independently with a precision gantry

# II Related Work

## II-A Conventional Robot Localization

Modern mobile robots commonly use visual, LiDAR, visual-inertial, or multimodal localization and SLAM methods based on macroscopic environmental structure [ 1 , 2 ] .
These approaches support robust localization across diverse environments, but their physical accuracy generally remains in the centimeter-to-millimeter regime, substantially coarser than the tens-of-micrometers precision considered here.
Applications requiring substantially finer positioning therefore motivate sensing and positioning approaches designed for a different precision regime [ 3 , 4 ] .

## II-B Surface Texture as a Visual Reference

Ground texture localization uses the appearance of the surface beneath a robot as a visual reference.
Early work showed that floor appearance mosaics could support robot localization, establishing that the ground surface itself can serve as a map [ 5 ] .
More recent work has pushed this idea toward higher precision, including the HD Ground benchmark, where localization methods demonstrated sub-millimeter accuracy using high-resolution ground imagery [ 6 ] .
L-GROUT demonstrated lightweight global metric localization on this benchmark using local visual features and geometric voting [ 7 ] , and GTBoW further showed that ground texture can support place recognition across long time intervals [ 8 ] .
These methods operate at fine spatial scales for robot localization, but use surface imagery at a coarser physical scale than the microscopic imagery considered here.

Related work on physical fingerprints further shows that natural materials contain distinctive visual structure at fine spatial scales.
Microscopic arrangements of fibers and other surface features have been used to identify nominally similar pieces of paper and other materials through physically unclonable visual signatures [ 9 , 10 ] .
Although this literature addresses identification rather than localization, it demonstrates that natural surface microstructure can provide distinctive visual information.

Digital image correlation (DIC) provides a related optical approach for high-precision displacement and strain measurement by correlating surface appearance between images [ 11 ] .
Conventional 2D DIC estimates in-plane deformation of approximately planar surfaces and commonly uses applied speckle patterns, although natural surface texture can also provide sufficient image structure.
For example, small local strains have been measured directly from the natural texture of concrete [ 12 ] .
Unlike DIC, which typically measures deformation between corresponding images of the same region, our objective is to globally localize a query image within a prebuilt microscopic surface map.

## II-C High-Precision Positioning Systems

At finer precision scales, positioning is commonly achieved using dedicated mechanical or metrology systems.
CNC machines and precision gantries achieve micrometer-scale positioning through rigid mechanical structures and accurate proprioceptive feedback, but their precision is tied to a fixed work volume [ 13 ] .
Coordinate Measuring Machines similarly use rigid frames and precision probing for highly accurate dimensional measurement [ 14 ] .
These systems provide substantially greater precision than conventional robot localization, but depend on specialized hardware and mechanically constrained workspaces.

Artificial references provide another route to globally referenced positioning.
Fiducial markers and other calibrated visual landmarks simplify pose estimation by introducing detectable references at known locations and have been used for robot localization and docking [ 15 ] .
Such approaches can provide precise localization, but require placing and calibrating references in the environment.
In contrast, our approach uses natural surface appearance as the global reference and investigates whether microscopic imaging can extend ground texture localization to a finer precision regime.

2026-10-19.title: When Plans Change, Remember: Replanning-Guided Visual Memory for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-19.authors: Victoria Smelova , Daniil Kazachkov , Georgiy Kazantsev , Iuliia Tsvetkova , Egor Cherepanov , Nikita Kachaev , Artem Latyshev , Aleksandr I. Panov , Alexey K. Kovalev
2026-10-19.abstract:
Long-horizon, multi-stage Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies often require
visual information that is no longer present in the current observation.
Retaining the complete observation history is computationally expensive and
highly redundant, motivating selective visual memory. We introduce RePlanMem-VLA ( Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA ), which turns a policy’s own plan revisions into an online memory-write signal. Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions. RePlanMem-VLA treats unusually large disagreement between these temporally aligned predictions as evidence of a task-relevant event. We first compare 35 disagreement measures across single-task autoregressive decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformers trained from scratch, then validate the selected signals on pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policies over MIKASA-Robo-VLA tasks. The resulting detectors achieve ROC-AUC of
0.981–0.997. We then use the selected signals in RePlanMem-VLA to trigger updates to a bounded visual memory, with a robot-masked write filter suppressing redundant frames. In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision point in 100 % 100\% of episodes. Real-robot replay data further show that event selection and redundancy suppression extend beyond simulation. These results establish plan revision as a policy-internal signal for controlling what a VLA remembers.
Website: https://vika787.github.io/RePlanMem/ .
2026-10-19.introduction:
Long-horizon manipulation often requires Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies to use visual information
that has left the current observation, including object properties ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Shi et al., 2026 ) ,
earlier environment states ( Chen et al., 2026a ; Shi et al., 2026 ) , and task
progress ( Buamanee et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) .
Retaining the full history preserves these cues but increases context length and
computation while adding visual redundancy ( Jang et al., 2025 ; Qiu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) .
We therefore seek a small set of informative observations.

We call these observations keyframes : they preserve cues needed
later ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Lei et al., 2026 ) or mark task-phase
transitions ( Buamanee et al., 2026 ; Yi et al., 2026 ) . Prior work
selects them with vision-language models ( Lei et al., 2026 ) , waypoint
heuristics ( Shi et al., 2023 ) ,
learned retrieval ( Sridhar et al., 2026 ) , progress estimates ( Liu et al., 2026 ) ,
or event detectors ( Zeng et al., 2026b ) . We investigate whether the policy’s own plan revisions can provide an online signal for selecting these observations.

Under receding-horizon execution, consecutive action chunks predict some of the same future actions, while the new plan incorporates
the latest observation (Fig. 1 ). Comparing these temporally aligned predictions reveals how the policy revises its intended behavior after receiving new visual information. Our central hypothesis is that task-relevant observations induce unusually large revisions in predictions for the same future
actions. This motivates using plan disagreement as a policy-internal signal to identify candidate keyframes for visual memory.

We introduce RePlanMem-VLA ( Replanning-Guided Keyframe Memory for VLA ), which derives its selection
signal from revisions between overlapping action predictions already produced
during normal replanning. Selected keyframes become part of the policy’s visual context,
keeping past observations available for subsequent action prediction, while a robot-masked write filter suppresses redundant frames, reducing repeated overwrites. At deployment, the trigger requires neither keyframe annotations nor privileged simulator state.

Our experiments are conducted on MIKASA-Robo-VLA ( Cherepanov et al., 2026b ) , an extension of MIKASA-Robo ( Cherepanov et al., 2026a ) for evaluating memory-intensive manipulation with VLA policies. We first screen 35 disagreement metrics using autoregressive decoder-only and
Flow-Matching Transformers ( Lipman et al., 2023 ) trained from scratch. We then evaluate detectors based on the selected signals with
pretrained OpenVLA-OFT ( Kim et al., 2025 ) and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) policies, obtaining ROC-AUC of
0.981–0.997.
In the evaluated memory-retention experiments, RePlanMem-VLA
preserves task-relevant observations until the later decision
point in 100 % 100\% of episodes, while robot-masked filtering
reduces redundant overwrites.
Real-robot replay data further support its event-selection and
redundancy-suppression behavior beyond simulation
(Fig. 2 ).

Our main contributions are as follows:

We introduce RePlanMem-VLA , which identifies keyframes from
policy-internal revisions of predictions for the same future actions across
consecutive replanning steps (Section 3.3 ).

We introduce RePlanMem-VLA , which identifies keyframes from
policy-internal revisions of predictions for the same future actions across
consecutive replanning steps (Section 3.3 ).

We identify disagreement measures that best align with keyframe events through systematic analysis across decoder-only and Flow-Matching Transformer policies, and verify their transfer to pretrained OpenVLA-OFT and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} policies
(Sections 4.1 and 4.2 ).

We develop a bounded visual-memory mechanism where plan disagreement determines when to write and redundancy-aware filtering, including robot-masked clustering, determines what to retain, substantially reducing redundant updates while preserving task-relevant observations (Sections 3 and 4.3 ).
2026-10-19.related_work:
Long-horizon manipulation often requires access to information from earlier in
the episode. Recent VLA work addresses this through
recurrent or belief-state
latents ( Cherepanov et al., 2026c ; Li et al., 2026a ) ,
explicit memory representations ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) , long-context or
compressed multi-frame conditioning ( Jang et al., 2025 ) , and retrieval- or structure-based memory ( Sridhar et al., 2026 ; Haresh et al., 2026 ; Chung et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) .
Memory-dependent manipulation is also studied in dedicated benchmarks ( Cherepanov et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Lei et al., 2026 ) . These works study how historical information is represented or retrieved, whereas our focus is on when an observation should be admitted to a bounded memory.

Existing approaches identify important observations using motion or
bottleneck-pose heuristics ( James et al., 2022 ) ,
learned frame scoring ( Mark et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026c ) ,
progress, value, or critic signals ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Yi et al., 2026 ; Buamanee et al., 2026 ) ,
trajectory annotation ( Feng et al., 2026 ) , or dedicated event detectors ( Zeng et al., 2026b ) — each
relying on a separate selector or external signal. We instead derive the selection signal directly from changes in the acting policy’s own predicted action plans.

Action-chunking policies predict short action sequences and under receding-horizon
execution successive chunks overlap on predictions for the same future actions ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Prior work mainly uses this overlap to improve consistency ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) or studies the trade-off between open-loop execution and replanning ( Lazzati et al., 2026 ; Zeng et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Jing et al., 2026 ) .
We instead use disagreement between overlapping predictions as a signal that the
new observation has changed the policy’s intended behavior.

Memory representation, keyframe selection, and plan consistency are typically
studied separately, whereas we connect them by using plan disagreement as a
policy-internal signal for memory updates.

2026-10-19.title: RTISSLAM-3D: Full 6-DoF SLAM With an In-Air 3D Imaging Sonar
2026-10-19.authors: Jan Steckel , Vincent Katter , Wouter Jansen
2026-10-19.abstract: Echolocating bats navigate dense forests using sonar alone, and in-air 3D imaging sonars now capture the entire frontal hemisphere with every pulse. Sonar SLAM, however, has so far been planar: current systems estimate a 2D trajectory and discard the elevation information in the sonar images, an assumption that does not hold on rough and sloped terrain such as a forest floor. In this paper, we introduce RTISSLAM-3D, a novel 6-DoF SLAM system for a wheeled robot that carries an in-air 3D imaging sonar, an IMU and wheel encoders. A CFAR detector on the sphere reduces every sonar image to a sparse set of 3D detections, which we use for a 3D acoustic odometry that models the shape of the sonar beam, for place recognition with polar submap descriptors, and for the verification of loop closures by 3D registration, all combined in a 6-DoF pose graph with attitude factors. We evaluated RTISSLAM-3D on a 545 m 545\text{\,}\mathrm{m} drive through a forest, with a 3D lidar SLAM as reference. The loop closures reduced the horizontal error of the acoustic odometry from 1.74 m 1.74\text{\,}\mathrm{m} to 0.28 m 0.28\text{\,}\mathrm{m} , with a height error of 0.12 m 0.12\text{\,}\mathrm{m} , and 94.6 % 94.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the resulting 3D sonar map lies within 0.3 m 0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{m} of the lidar map.
2026-10-19.introduction:
Sonar was one of the first sensors with which mobile robots built maps [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , and in-air sonar keeps working in exactly those conditions in which cameras and lidar struggle: in darkness, smoke, dust and fog, and next to glass [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Indeed, ultrasonic sensors are cheap, small and robust, and the embedded 3D imaging sonars of the last decade, such as the eRTIS [ 5 , 6 ] , turn the echoes of a single broadband pulse into an image of the reflected energy as a function of range and direction over the complete frontal hemisphere, the so-called energyscape [ 4 ] . With nonlinear beamformers such as Delay-Multiply-And-Sum (DMAS) with a coherence factor [ 7 ] , these images have become sharp enough to be used for more than obstacle avoidance and reactive control [ 8 , 9 ] .

In two recent papers, we have shown how such sonar data can drive a modern, robust SLAM back-end. BatSLAM 2.0 [ 10 ] combined sequence-verified place recognition on the echoes of a binaural bat-like sonar with a factor-graph back-end [ 11 , 12 ] , and produced reliable topological maps in strongly aliased environments. RTISSLAM [ 13 ] replaced the binaural sensor by an eRTIS imaging sonar and used its energyscapes as place descriptors. Furthermore, the system extracts acoustic odometry from the sequence of the data, and anchored an occupancy grid to the nodes of the pose graph, so that a metric map is constructed, updated by every loop closure. Both systems, however, are operating in a strict 2D assumption: they estimate the position and heading of the robot on a plane, and they use the 3D imaging capability of the sensor only to build a 2D map, by suppressing the elevation dimension of the energyscape (looking at a horizontal slice). This is a reasonable choice in an office or a warehouse with flat floors, but it throws away a significant portion of what the sensor measures. Furthermore, this approach breaks down as soon as the robot leaves the flat floor, as is common in offroad scenarios, and for UAV navigation.

Outdoors, and in particular in a forest, the ground is neither flat nor level, and the robot rolls and pitches as it drives over roots and stones. The relevant structure (tree trunks, shrubs, fallen branches) is best represented in 3D, and a planar slice through it at the height of the sensor depends on the attitude of the robot. Furthermore, a forest is a notoriously difficult environment for place recognition as it can be strongly self-similar. In our own first experiments with the 2D RTISSLAM on real forest data, the recall of single-view place recognition at a useful precision was close to zero, and loop closures could only be found by restricting the search to the vicinity of the current pose estimate.

In lidar SLAM, the step from 2D to 3D has long been made: 3D point clouds are registered with point-to-point or point-to-distribution ICP variants [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] , places are recognized with egocentric polar descriptors of the 3D structure [ 17 ] , and maps are stored as 3D occupancy grids [ 18 ] . Underwater, multibeam and imaging sonars have been used to build volumetric submaps [ 19 ] . For in-air sonar, however, a full 3D SLAM system, estimating the 6-DoF trajectory of the robot and a 3D map from the sonar, has, to the best of our knowledge, not been demonstrated on a real robot. The data of an in-air imaging sonar is quite different from a lidar scan: a capture yields at most a few dozen detections within a range of a few meters, the angular resolution is a few degrees, often with anisotropy in azimuth and elevation, specular surfaces are only seen near normal incidence, and the ground returns both a direct echo and a mirror image through ground multipath. A sonar SLAM system needs to take all of these peculiarities into account when trying to succesfully build a spatial map.

In this paper, we propose RTISSLAM-3D, a novel full 6-DoF SLAM system for an in-air 3D imaging sonar on a wheeled robot, which uses the sonar’s 3D images for every part of the localization: for odometry, for place recognition and for the metric verification of loop closures. Only an IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) and the wheel encoders complement the sonar, and no learned components are used in the whole pipeline. In our approach, every capture is imaged over the full frontal hemisphere and turned into a sparse set of 3D detections by a CFAR detector that operates on the sphere, efficiently implemented through the heat kernel of a graph Laplacian, which is in effect a Gaussian blur over a set of irregular directions on a sphere. The ground echoes give the height and tilt of the sensor above the local ground and reveal the multipath mirror images, which are removed. A 3D acoustic odometry registers every detection set to a local 3D submap, with the beam-shaped uncertainty of each detection, and takes the rotation from the gyroscope. Keyframes enter a 6-DoF pose graph with IMU attitude factors, loop closures are proposed by a polar descriptor of the 3D submap and verified by a 4-DoF registration of the two submaps, and a 3D log-odds occupancy map is built on the optimized poses.

We evaluate RTISSLAM-3D on a 545 m 545\text{\,}\mathrm{m} drive through a forest in Trondheim, Norway, with a gravity-aligned 3D lidar SLAM as reference, and we show that it reduces the horizontal trajectory error of the wheel and gyroscope odometry from 2.40 m 2.40\text{\,}\mathrm{m} to 0.28 m 0.28\text{\,}\mathrm{m} , with a height error of 0.12 m 0.12\text{\,}\mathrm{m} , closes 233 loops of which none is off by more than 0.5 m 0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m} , and builds a 3D map in which 94.6 % 94.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the occupied voxels lie within 0.3 m 0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{m} of the lidar ground-truth map.

The contributions of this paper are as follows: (1) a 3D imaging and detection chain for in-air sonar over the full frontal hemisphere, with a CFAR detector on the sphere and the removal of ground multipath through a fitted ground plane, (2) a 3D acoustic odometry that registers sparse sonar detections with their beam-shaped uncertainty, (3) 3D place recognition for sonar, with candidates proposed by a polar submap descriptor and verified by submap registration, (4) the complete 6-DoF SLAM system and a 3D occupancy map with beam-shaped evidence and free-space carving, and (5) an evaluation on real data against a gravity-aligned 3D lidar reference, with ablations of every component. The complete pipeline, from the raw recording to the map and the videos, runs with a single command and will be made available as open source.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows. First, we give an overview of RTISSLAM-3D in section II . Next, we detail the imaging and detection chain, the acoustic odometry, the place recognition, the pose graph and the mapping in section III . Section IV describes the robot, the recording and the reference, after which section V presents the results. We discuss the limitations of our work in section VI and conclude the paper in section VII .
2026-10-19.related_work:
# II Overview of RTISSLAM-3D

Figure 1 shows the processing flow of RTISSLAM-3D. For every pulse, the eRTIS records the echoes with its N = 32 N=32 microphones, which are beamformed with fifth-order DMAS with coherence factor (CF) into an energy volume P ⁡ ( r , ψ ) P(r,\psi) over M = 2293 M=2293 directions ψ \psi that sample the frontal hemisphere uniformly (section III-A ). A CFAR detector on the sphere and a peak threshold turn every volume into a sparse set of 3D detections, after which a ground plane is fitted to the near-field ground echoes and the multipath mirror images below it are removed (section III-B ). Each detection set is registered to a local submap of the previous captures, with the wheel distance and the gyroscope rotation as prior, which yields the 3D acoustic odometry (section III-C ). After every 1 m 1\text{\,}\mathrm{m} of travel, a keyframe is created: a 6-DoF node in the pose graph, connected to the previous keyframe by the acoustic odometry and to the direction of gravity by an IMU attitude factor (section III-D ). The keyframe also stores its submap, the detections of the last 4 m 4\text{\,}\mathrm{m} of travel expressed in a level frame, together with a polar descriptor of that submap. Keyframes that were visited at least 20 m 20\text{\,}\mathrm{m} of travel earlier and lie close to the current estimate are ranked by their descriptor, and the best candidates are verified by registering the two submaps; a verified revisit becomes a robust loop closure factor (section III-E ). Finally, a 3D log-odds occupancy map is built from the detections on the optimized poses (section III-F ). As in RTISSLAM [ 13 ] , the information flows in one direction: the map is built from the pose graph, but map information never feeds back into the pose-graph construction, which is a deliberate choice based on the peculiar reflection dynamics of ultrasound sensing [ 13 ] .

2026-10-19.title: Scaling Online Exploration for Robot Agents
2026-10-19.authors: Runhan Huang , Xiangcheng Zhang , Haoyu Chen , Yitong Li , Yen-Jen Wang , Bohan Lyu , Haotian Ye , Chuye Hong , Yixuan Wang , Chloe Su , Haoyu Xiong , Yangzhen Wu , Enze Xie , Travis Manderson , Stefano Ermon , Pieter Abbeel , Antonio Torralba , Dawn Song , Weirui Ye , Yilun Du

2026-10-19.abstract: Robot learning has advanced significantly by scaling demonstration datasets and model capacity; however, deploying a new robot embodiment or task typically necessitates a dedicated teleoperation corpus. Furthermore, resulting policies remain bounded by their imitation distributions, limiting generalization and continual self-improvement. We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration) , an open-source framework for robot agents centered on scaling exploration : enabling agents to improve by acquiring online experience and synthesizing executable programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent generates robot control code directly, operating without action demonstration data, hand-engineered action primitives, or value-function guidance. Through online exploration, the agent identifies decision sequences that achieve task goals and compiles them into modular programs encapsulating the full perception-planning-control loop for fast inference. Using RAX, we present a systematic multi-embodiment study on scaling online exploration across fine-grained precision and long-horizon manipulation tasks using single-arm, bimanual, dexterous, mobile, and humanoid systems in simulation and on real robots. Generalization performance on unseen environments improves consistently as exploration scales. In simulation, RAX outperforms top baseline models by + 37.4 % +37.4\% on average. On real robots, RAX autonomously learns memory-dependent, articulated, high-precision, deformable, and long-horizon mobile manipulation tasks without human demonstrations, continually improving performance by composing verified skills from prior exploration sessions. As exploration scales, we observe emergent system capabilities including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and human-robot agent collaboration. We open-source RAX as a generalist robot-agent platform that allows new robot embodiments to be integrated solely via API interfaces, bypassing teleoperated data collection and policy training entirely. More details are available on our project page at robot-agent-exploration.com .
2026-10-19.introduction:
“We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what
we have discovered. Building in our discoveries only makes it harder to see how the
discovering process can be done.”

“We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what
we have discovered. Building in our discoveries only makes it harder to see how the
discovering process can be done.”

— Richard S. Sutton, The Bitter Lesson ( 2019 )

Robot learning has made substantial progress by scaling demonstration data and model capacity with imitation learning, aiming to replicate the training recipe that transformed language modeling ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) . Vision-language-action (VLA) models and World-Action models (WAMs) fine-tune pretrained VLMs and video generation models, respectively, using large teleoperation corpora ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) . However, deploying a new robot or task still requires a dedicated teleoperation corpus of its own ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ; Team et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026e ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Bi et al., 2026 ) . Furthermore, the knowledge of such policy models is inherently bounded by the demonstrations they imitate. Consider a mobile robot tasked with loading a car in an unfamiliar house: while opening doors, grasping bags, and placing objects may each be familiar skills, the robot must adapt to novel scenes, visual appearances, and task compositions while discovering new approaches. This adaptation and discovery process is absent during imitation learning on static teleoperation data. Consequently, these policies struggle to generalize and self-improve, even when provided with environment interactions and test-time compute. This limitation motivates a central question: can robots self-improve and learn to discover new skills through autonomous online experience and active exploration?

Humans learn physical skills by attempting a task, observing the outcome, diagnosing failures, and practicing until their behavior becomes reliable. LLM agents exhibit a similar pattern in software domains: they explore unfamiliar systems by executing programs, inspecting outputs, and revising their work ( Yang et al., 2024 ) . Instead of training policies exclusively on teleoperated demonstration data, we let agents program robots directly ( Lozano-Perez, 1983 ) without hand-designed action primitives. The agent explores online to discover decisions that drive task success, then automates these decision-making principles into modular robot programs that integrate perception, planning, and control. It continuously debugs and tests these programs through online execution. These programs encode the agent’s underlying principles for how to generate successful actions based on environment perception, rather than merely mimicking the actions themselves, thereby enabling more robust generalization. Furthermore, the agent can compose, modify, and update these programs when confronting increasingly complex scenes and tasks, continually improving through online experience.

We introduce RAX (Robot Agent eXploration) , a cognitive architecture for robot agents. Its core organizing principle is scaling exploration : robot agents should improve by gathering their own online experience and optimizing their programs. In RAX, a general-purpose coding agent receives a natural-language instruction, at most a few goal images or visual demonstrations, and a budget of exploration episodes. It interacts directly through the robot’s perception and control interfaces without requiring human teleoperation or value function guidance. The underlying language model parameters remain fixed and no policies are trained; instead, learning updates a persistent workspace of programs, notes, and verified skills. The agent converts successful interactions into autonomous code programs and stores reusable knowledge for subsequent episodes and tasks.

As exploration scales, we observe several emergent system capabilities: the agent constructs task-relevant 3D perception models, plans actions via pose search in 3D joint space, generates fully automated programs with closed-loop visual and force feedback, and adapts its programs when encountering novel task conditions. Furthermore, we observe agentic behaviors on real robots, including active perception, error recovery, safety guardrails, and active human-robot interaction. For example, the robot executes end-effector contact probing for precise localization when depth measurements are inaccurate. In mobile manipulation experiments, following an initial collision with a cabinet, the agent automatically instantiates a safety check to verify workspace clearance before every base rotation. To test code robustness, the agent actively requests the human operator to vary object layouts, systematically testing the spatial generalization of the autonomous program.

In RAX, we equip the agent with rich multimodal sensing by exposing metric depth and force signals through the robot interface. A unified architecture supports tabletop bimanual arms, dexterous hands, mobile household robots, and humanoids through interfaces to each robot’s sensors, controllers, and kinematic models ( Section 4 ). Unlike standard VLAs or WAMs operating on RGB images alone, the agent autonomously leverages these rich sensing signals to construct 3D point clouds and fit object models directly from perception. It then searches for actions to manipulate these 3D models while accounting for their unique shapes and affordances. Force feedback further enables the agent to resolve spatial uncertainty through contact and enable close-loop control on force signals in insertion tasks. Such multimodal world modeling have been largely absent from generalist policy models, yet naturally align with human cognitive processes.

To enable high-frequency closed-loop control, the agent compiles its decision-making process into executable Python programs that generate actions directly from sensor signals. Unlike prior approaches that rely on human-designed action primitives or policies trained on demonstrations ( Lu et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) , our approach directly generates robot control programs that encapsulate the full perception-planning-control loop, whereas standard policies discard the underlying decision-making process essential for generalization. In practice, we observe the agent writing programs that automatically segment and identify objects in 3D using point-cloud fitting and hue-based identification, then plan actions grounded in this 3D world model, with retry loops and exception handling naturally incorporated into the code. Because actions are planned directly on perceived 3D objects rather than learned through imitation, this approach generalizes to far more diverse object layouts and domain variations than standard VLAs or WAMs. For semantically rich perception in open-world environments, the agent can program direct API calls to LLMs (such as Gemini) within the code to assist with object identification, while incorporating checkpoints and exception handling to step in and verify progress. Over the course of exploration, both action inference latency and token counts decrease as an increasing fraction of decisions becomes automated through code.

As experience scales with exploration, RAX maintains an intra-task memory file system across episodes to record failure lessons and successful strategies, allowing the agent to continually refine its programs. Across multiple tasks and sessions, we maintain a repository of modular programs as verified skills for various tasks and manipulation primitives. Each skill includes the executable code for a specific task, accompanied by execution logs from successful runs, clear preconditions, and verification checkpoints, allowing skills to be composed and reused for complex downstream tasks. In real-world mobile manipulation experiments in household settings, the agent practices individual tasks, each in its own exploration session, such as picking and placing boxes or tucking in office chairs, and commits them as verified skills. When subsequently evaluated on a composite, long-horizon task involving more than six sequential object manipulations, the agent achieves substantial automation and efficiency gains by reusing these stored skills. We envision agents practicing skills in a distributed, parallel fashion to build a rich repository of diverse capabilities, thereby enabling continual lifelong learning.

Using RAX, we conduct the first large-scale, multi-embodiment, systematic study of
scaling exploration for robot agents , spanning fine-grained precision and long-horizon tasks
across LIBERO, LIBERO-Pro, RoboDojo, DexJoCo, BEHAVIOR-1K, and HumanoidArena in simulation and
on two real robots. We evaluate the resulting policies on unseen scenes, separating
exploration from evaluation. Performance grows steadily with exploration, and on
fine-grained and long-horizon tasks on which state-of-the-art methods rarely succeed, RAX achieves high success rates, surpassing the strongest prior models by +37.4 on average over
five benchmarks ( 1 , Section 13 ). Without any expert action trajectories, RAX sets a new
state of the art on RoboDojo (+53.4), BEHAVIOR-1K (+38.3), DexJoCo (+31.4), and
LIBERO-Pro (+21.2). On HumanoidArena, it sets a new state of the art (+7.9) with three
teleoperated demonstrations per task, where every baseline uses 100. On real Franka and Rainbow RB-Y1
robots, RAX masters five complex tabletop manipulation tasks and a long-horizon mobile
manipulation task with zero demonstrations, and verified skills accumulated across sessions let
later sessions build on earlier ones.

We summarize our contributions below:

We introduce RAX and establish scaling online exploration as a foundational principle for agentic robotics. In RAX, the agent operates directly through perception and robot control interfaces without policy training, compiling successful decision sequences into executable code programs that run autonomous execution loops.

Using RAX, we conduct the first systematic, multi-embodiment study of scaling online exploration across simulation and real robot environments. RAX acquires diverse manipulation capabilities solely through autonomous exploration, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines by + 37.4 +37.4 points on average across five simulation benchmarks, while solving high-precision, deformable, articulated, and long-horizon manipulation tasks on real robots without human demonstrations.

We demonstrate rapid adaptation and continual learning on real robots, showing that generated programs can be selectively updated in response to environmental and task shifts while retaining verified skills in a persistent repository for composition and reuse in complex tasks.

1. “We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what
we have discovered. Building in our discoveries only makes it harder to see how the
discovering process can be done.”
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

A substantial body of work uses pretrained language models as high-level planners or program
generators for robots. SayCan grounds language-model plans in learned
affordances ( Ahn et al., 2022 ) , Inner Monologue folds environment feedback into iterative
replanning ( Huang et al., 2022 ) , and Code as Policies, ProgPrompt, and VoxPoser synthesize
executable programs, situated task plans, or 3D value maps directly from
instructions ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2023 ) . These methods
typically invoke the model zero-shot or with a few in-context examples, producing a plan or a
program that is executed with little opportunity to improve from experience. RAX instead treats the language model as a learner : it interacts with the robot over many
episodes and revises its perception and control programs according to what it observes.

More recently, several works let coding agents improve robot behavior through interaction.
ENPIRE runs agents in a closed loop of automatic reset, rollout, and policy training on a
fleet of bimanual arms, and accelerates discovery by scaling the fleet ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) ;
FAEA and Encore refine policy programs from execution feedback, the latter starting from a few
teleoperated demonstrations ( Tsui et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2026 ) ; Baton explores long-horizon
tasks subtask by subtask with transition-aware memory ( Xu et al., 2026 ) ; SimEX develops robot
skills in a simulator reconstructed from the physical workspace before a few trials on the
real robot ( Hu et al., 2026 ) ; RPG practices in simulation on tasks derived from an offline
trajectory dataset and refines a library of reusable skills ( Wang et al., 2026d ) ; EmbodiedSWE
turns coding-agent solutions into training data for vision-language-action
models ( You et al., 2026 ) ; and CaP-X benchmarks coding agents on
manipulation ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . These works establish that agents can improve robot behavior
through interaction, and have so far demonstrated it mainly in tabletop manipulation with
parallel-jaw
grippers ( Xiao et al., 2026 ; Tsui et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026d ) ,
often on a single platform ( Xiao et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026d ) , with humanoid and
mobile settings explored through pretrained locomotion ( You et al., 2026 ) or short
pick-up tasks ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . Several also draw on demonstrations ( Kang et al., 2026 ) ,
offline datasets ( Wang et al., 2026d ) , reconstructed simulators ( Hu et al., 2026 ) , or neural
policy training ( Xiao et al., 2026 ) . RAX complements these efforts: it learns each
task on the robot itself, from its own exploration, and does so across single-arm and bimanual
manipulators, dexterous hands, mobile manipulators performing long-horizon household
activities, and legged humanoids whose locomotion the agent constructs itself, on established
benchmarks and on real robots. On this basis, it studies systematically how performance scales
with exploration, with 3D perception, and with accumulated memory.

Vision-language-action models ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) and imitation
learning methods ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) improve robot capability by scaling
demonstration data and model size, and world action models extend this recipe by learning to
predict how the scene evolves together with the actions that produce
it ( Wang et al., 2026e ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ; Bi et al., 2026 ) . To cover multiple embodiments, generalist
policies pool demonstrations across robots into a single training
mixture ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ; Team et al., 2024 ; Doshi et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) ,
and a robot outside this mixture requires data of its own and further fine-tuning. In language
modeling, computation spent at inference has emerged as a further scaling
axis ( Guo et al., 2025 ; OpenAI, 2024 ) . RAX instead studies how robot
capability grows with online experience acquired and organized by the agent itself, without
additional demonstrations or parameter updates. Because this experience is gathered on the
robot at hand, RAX extends to a new embodiment without pooled data, and adapts to it within a
few episodes of exploration.

Language agents can retain experience as explicit memory: Voyager grows a library of code
skills through open-ended exploration in a game ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , and Reflexion and
ExpeL distill feedback into textual lessons that improve later
attempts ( Shinn et al., 2023 ; Zhao et al., 2024 ) . At a broader level, classical cognitive
architectures such as Soar and ACT-R structure intelligent behavior around perception,
memory, and deliberation ( Laird et al., 1987 ; Anderson et al., 2004 ) , CoALA revisits this structure
for language agents ( Sumers et al., 2023 ) , and Sutton’s common model of the intelligent
agent ( Sutton, 2022 ) and OaK architecture ( Sutton et al., 2022 ) hold that all
task-specific knowledge should be acquired at runtime from the agent’s own experience, a view
developed further as the era of experience ( Silver and Sutton, ) . RAX brings this
view to physical robots, where every skill is executable control code that enters memory only
after it succeeds without supervision.

2026-10-19.title: Has GPT-6-Astra Achieved Embodied Intelligence?
2026-10-19.authors: SenseNova , Joint Research Team : Zhongang Cai , Ziang Cao , Tailai Chen , Han Chong Chua , Linjun Dai , Hanming Deng , Hokin Deng , Haiwen Diao , Chenjing Ding , Weichen Fan , Xiao Fu , Zerui Gong , Chenyang Gu , Zexin He , Zhi Hou , Bo Li , Qinyue Li , Quanzhou Li , Xiaowan Li , Zhichao Liao , Dahua Lin , Zilong Lin , Bo Liu , Chunxiao Liu , Pengfei Liu , Tianqi Liu , Ziwei Liu , Chen Change Loy , Lewei Lu , Jiapeng Luo , Yuexiao Ma , Liang Pan , Xingang Pan , Oscar Qian , Ziyi Shang , Yuyao Shao , Dawei Su , Dacheng Tao , Qingyi Tao , Quan Wang , Ruisi Wang , Xiaogang Wang , Ziyi Wang , Beichen Wen , Donghao Wu , Jiaxu Wu , Silei Wu , Xiaoming Wu , Zhonghua Wu , Hongcan Xiao , Weiye Xu , Atsushi Yamashita , Lei Yang , Zhe Yang , Baiqiao Yin , Wanqi Yin , Hanfei Zhao , Tianbo Zhong , Long Zhuo , Jing Zuo
2026-10-19.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Multimedia (cs.MM)

2026-10-19.abstract:
GPT-6-Astra demonstrates a level of competence in robotic manipulation and navigation that challenges the conventional paradigm of building specialized models for individual tasks and embodiments. In this report, we ask not only how capable GPT-6-Astra is, but what its capabilities imply for the field. First, we probe the limits of standalone GPT-6-Astra. We conduct a large-scale evaluation across 12 representative benchmarks spanning tabletop manipulation, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under a unified protocol that allows in-context learning (ICL) from training-set demonstrations and substantially increases the number of execution steps, GPT-6-Astra achieves unprecedented performance ( Fig. 1 ). Our analysis suggests that future research should increasingly focus on improving
1) the generality of in-context learning
2) cost and execution time,
3) physical-state verification,
4) recovery from irreversible failures, and
5) long-horizon preservation of progress. Second, we study the agentic harness for embodied control. Besides exploring the ideal action representation and chucking parameters, we identify that close-loop coordination between a high-level "System 2" reasoner ( i.e. , GPT-6-Astra) and a low-level "System 1" controller ( e.g. , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ) is costly but effective. Third, we examine GPT-6-Astra on real-world deployment. Our experiments on 8 robot configurations reveal substantial gaps: 1) robot demonstrations required for in-context learning are expensive to collect, and 2) it is implausible to trade longer execution for higher success rates with physical constraints. Fourth, we envision the next generation of embodied benchmarks. We develop a prototype that 1) derives tasks from real-world needs rather than current robot capabilities, 2) provides no in-domain demonstrations, and 3) judges agents on a world clock that keeps running while they deliberate.
Taken together, our results suggest that GPT-6-Astra has largely crossed the threshold of embodied competence, but not yet that of practical embodied intelligence. The key remaining challenge is to translate benchmark success into reliable, efficient, and scalable real-world deployment.
2026-10-19.introduction:
The advent of GPT-6-Astra marks a major shift in embodied intelligence: a general-purpose model can now tackle robotic manipulation and navigation tasks that have traditionally been dominated by specialized models, such as VLAs and WAMs, while exhibiting capabilities including zero-shot generalization, in-context learning, and failure recovery.
In this technical report, we use GPT-6-Astra as a lens to examine a broader question: what does this new level of embodied capability mean for the research community, and where should the field go next? We first conduct a large-scale evaluation across diverse embodied tasks to characterize the extent of its capabilities and identify which problems are already approaching saturation. We then study harness design to understand the performance–cost trade-offs involved in translating these capabilities into effective control. Next, we validate our findings on real robots, asking how far benchmark success carries over to physical deployment and what gaps remain.Finally, we revisit benchmark design and envision what the next generation of embodied benchmarks should look like.

First, we probe the upper bound of GPT-6-Astra’s embodied capabilities under a unified protocol. We conduct a large-scale study across 12 representative benchmarks, covering tabletop robotic arms, humanoids, mobile platforms, and dexterous hands. Under this protocol, GPT-6-Astra outperforms existing methods by substantial margins, including recent agentic approaches that also build on GPT-6-Astra. Notably, as shown in Fig. 1 , it approaches saturation on the LIBERO series and SIMPLE, while achieving 81.9% on RoboDojo and 87.3% on DexJoCo. The protocol follows two simple and well-motivated principles:

1) We allow in-context learning (ICL) from the training set whenever successful demonstrations are available, which we consider reasonable since such demonstrations are conventionally accessible when training smaller task-specific policies. GPT-6-Astra studies the available training data and constructs a frozen knowledge package containing task guidance, motion and visual references, executable helpers, recovery procedures, and metadata. At test time, it retrieves and adapts these resources to the current scene. This substantially improves performance when the demonstrations closely cover the test distribution, but the benefit weakens as tasks move away from the data used to build the package.

2) We extensively increase the execution budget , allowing up to 10 × \times more interaction steps than the official setting. We find that standard step limits can significantly underestimate GPT-6-Astra’s capabilities. Additional interaction yields large gains on tasks that benefit from repeated correction, such as RoboDojo and Bench2Dex, because GPT-6-Astra can detect failed actions, revise its strategy, and recover through further interaction. This emerging failure-recovery capability is the key mechanism that allows a larger execution budget to translate into higher success rates.

Our strong empirical results put us in a position to identify the remaining limitations of GPT-6-Astra more clearly. Specifically, we find that:
i) in-context learning transfer poorly beyond the tasks from which the demonstrations are drawn;
ii) even simple tasks incur inference cost and execution time far beyond what would be practical for commercial deployment;
iii) GPT-6-Astra often struggles to verify physical success and identify which task condition remains unmet;
iv) GPT-6-Astra often struggles to identify the cause of task failure;
v) it cannot reliably recover from consequential or irreversible failures; and
vi) long-horizon execution remains difficult, as the model struggles to preserve and track progress across many subtasks.

Second, we ablate the harness design and find that effectively unleashing GPT-6-Astra’s embodied performance depends critically on both the collaboration protocol and the action interface. We first study the interaction between “System 2” ( i.e. , GPT-6-Astra) and “System 1” ( e.g. , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 13 ] ). Closed-loop collaboration, where GPT-6-Astra reviews and refines VLA-proposed actions before execution, substantially improves performance over standalone or open-loop execution, but frequent System-2 supervision incurs significant token cost. Reviewing longer action sequences improves this trade-off, while combining closed-loop collaboration with ICL yields the strongest performance at the highest cost.
We further study action representation and chunking, and identify a representation gap between multimodal reasoning and low-level robot control. Direct joint-angle control underperforms, while more semantically aligned end-effector commands work better; adaptive action chunking further improves performance while reducing unnecessary model calls. Together, these findings suggest that harness design should expose action spaces aligned with the model’s reasoning capabilities while delegating precise execution to lower-level controllers, with adaptive interaction to balance performance and inference cost.

Third, we validate GPT-6-Astra on real-world robots spanning single and dual robotic arms, grippers, dexterous hands, a wheeled mobile manipulator, and a humanoid. Our study reveals three key findings.
1) GPT-6-Astra operates effectively across a wide range of embodiments, but its success rate remains highly task-dependent. It performs particularly well on tasks such as tabletop grasping, while deformable-object manipulation, precise contact, and long-horizon tasks remain challenging.
2) GPT-6-Astra demonstrates surprising active-vision capabilities, intentionally repositioning the camera to obtain observations needed for subsequent actions.
3) GPT-6-Astra shows that a slow “System 2” model can directly collaborate with a high-frequency “System 0” locomotion controller to perform humanoid manipulation that requires high-frequency local control.
At the same time, real-world deployment introduces challenges that are largely absent from simulation.
GPT-6-Astra can no longer easily trade additional execution steps for higher success rates, due to safety constraints, mechanical limits, and real-time requirements.
Moreover, successful trajectory demonstrations, which are central to our ICL setup in simulation, are often expensive or unavailable in real-world applications.

Fourth, we showcase a prototype of what we envision as the next generation of benchmarks for embodied intelligence.
We propose three principles.
1) Tasks should be derived from human needs and expressed as people would naturally state them, with evaluation based on the utility of the outcome rather than a fixed goal state.
2) No in-domain training episodes or scene-specific demonstrations should be provided; instead, agents should acquire experience during deployment.
3) The world should continue to evolve while the agent deliberates, making reasoning time and its physical consequences part of the evaluation.
The prototype makes several remaining limitations more apparent in a deployment-oriented setting:
i) GPT-6-Astra focuses on the current step but can lose track of other changes it has caused in the environment, such as leaving a refrigerator open;
ii) without demonstrations, it struggles to figure out how unfamiliar objects and mechanisms work, or how to position its own body to interact with them; and
iii) because the world continues to change while it reasons, its observations can become outdated before the resulting action is executed.
Building such benchmarks also raises practical challenges in reliable judging, simulation fidelity, real-time evaluation, and evaluation cost.

In summary, by pushing GPT-6-Astra toward its capability limits, dissecting the harness that enables this performance, validating its behavior on real robots, and rethinking how embodied intelligence should be evaluated, we aim to clarify both what has changed and what remains fundamentally unsolved.
2026-10-19.related_work:
# 2 Large-Scale Study under A Unified Protocol

## 2.1 Protocol

Our study covers twelve evaluation settings, grouped into five categories: tabletop manipulation (RoboDojo [ 26 ] , RoboLab [ 161 ] , LIBERO-Long++ and LIBERO-Ultra-Long [ 162 ] , and LIBERO-PRO [ 183 ] ), dexterous manipulation (Bench2Dex [ 163 ] and DexJoCo [ 144 ] ), humanoid loco-manipulation (SIMPLE [ 152 ] ), long-horizon household activities (BEHAVIOR [ 8 ] ), and vision-language navigation (VLN-CE R2R and RxR [ 87 ] , and LHPR-VLN [ 134 ] ).

We evaluate GPT-6-Astra under a demonstration-informed protocol with two interaction budgets (1 × \times and 10 × \times ), as illustrated in Fig. 2 . The protocol separates preparation using training demonstrations from test-time interaction. We report performance under the standard budget and an extended budget that allows more interaction steps for execution and recovery.

Motivation. Learned robotic policies are commonly trained or fine-tuned on demonstrations provided by the benchmark. Evaluating GPT-6-Astra without access to these demonstrations would therefore measure its performance under a different information regime. We use in-context learning (ICL) to investigate how effectively GPT-6-Astra can exploit the available training demonstrations without updating its model weights. Our objective is to characterize its capabilities when the task-relevant information used to train conventional policies is also available to it through contextual preparation.

We additionally investigate the effect of the interaction budget. In our evaluations, GPT-6-Astra often identifies unsuccessful actions, revises its strategy, and recovers through further interaction. A strict step limit can terminate this process before recovery succeeds. We therefore evaluate under two budgets. The standard budget ( 1 × 1\times ) is the interaction budget prescribed by each benchmark and measures performance under its intended conditions; the extended budget ( 10 × 10\times ) allows up to ten times as many action steps and measures how task completion improves when the policy has more opportunities to correct mistakes.

In-context learning preparation. Before testing, GPT-6-Astra undergoes a separate ICL preparation phase for each task, using the available training demonstrations represented through benchmark-appropriate observations and demonstrated actions. During preparation, GPT-6-Astra may analyze the demonstrations and develop task-specific notes and reusable code. These materials form a knowledge package, which is frozen before evaluation and provided to every test episode of that task. GPT-6-Astra’s model weights remain unchanged. Preparation excludes held-out test episodes and evaluator-private information.

Episode evaluation. Each test episode begins in a fresh, isolated session with the task instruction, the frozen knowledge package, and the permitted observation and action interfaces. At each decision point, GPT-6-Astra examines the current observations and specifies the next action or action sequence. The environment executes these actions and returns new observations, which GPT-6-Astra uses to assess the outcome and determine its next action. The interaction history is retained within the episode, allowing GPT-6-Astra to diagnose mistakes and attempt recovery. Neither the knowledge package nor the model weights are updated during testing, and information from one test episode is not transferred to another. Observation access, robot-control action semantics, control frequency, and success criteria remain fixed across budget conditions.

Extended interaction budget. The extended budget allows ten times as many action steps as the standard budget. We report outcomes at 1 × 1\times and at cumulative cutoffs of 2 × , … , 10 × 2\times,\ldots,10\times the standard budget, using the same initialization, policy configuration, and success criterion. An extension continues the same episode, preserving its interaction history and accumulated environmental consequences; additional attempts occur within that episode rather than through resets. Episodes terminate upon verified success, an applicable terminal failure, or exhaustion of the allotted budget. Reporting success across these cutoffs quantifies the contribution of additional interaction while retaining the standard-budget result as a separate comparison point.

## 2.2 In-context Learning

With in-context learning, GPT-6-Astra achieves strong performance across embodied benchmarks without any update to its model weights. Figure 1 compares GPT-6-Astra with the best published result (SOTA) and the best published agentic method (Agentic SOTA) on all 12 settings, both reported under the standard budget. Already at the standard ( 1 × 1\times ) budget, GPT-6-Astra matches or exceeds the strongest published result on most settings, with the largest margins on LIBERO-Ultra-Long and DexJoCo, where it nearly doubles the best published success rate. To isolate the contribution of ICL, we compare zero-shot and ICL conditions on SIMPLE: task-level ICL raises standard-budget success on the four common tasks from 70.8% to 90.8% and shortens successful episodes (Table 12 ). The benefit of ICL, however, depends on how closely the training data covers the test tasks. Where test tasks closely follow the training distribution, as in the LIBERO family, SIMPLE and VLN-CE, the package can retrieve and adapt demonstrated motions or routes almost directly, and success approaches saturation. DexJoCo’s contact-rich dexterous tasks are demanding, but phase-indexed motion references and controller helpers cover them well. RoboLab, in contrast, provides no training set from which a task-level package can be built, and its success remains moderate; Sec. 2.4 discusses this limitation further.

Package contents. Each knowledge package is organized around six recurring components (Fig. 3 ): task guidance, motion references, visual references, executable helpers, checks and recovery, and metadata and provenance. This structure is not prescribed. During ICL preparation, GPT-6-Astra independently chooses what to inspect and retain within each benchmark’s permitted training data and tool interfaces, and we do not specify which demonstrations, frames, or state/action records it should examine or save; the six components nonetheless recur across benchmarks.

Task guidance. Written instructions describe task goals, execution stages, and strategies. They specify subtask ordering, object roles, and constraints that guide the selection and use of stored references.

Task guidance. Written instructions describe task goals, execution stages, and strategies. They specify subtask ordering, object roles, and constraints that guide the selection and use of stored references.

Motion references. Demonstration-derived trajectories, grasp configurations, and phase anchors provide numerical examples of how actions unfold. The agent retrieves relevant segments or poses and adapts them to the current scene and robot state.

Visual references. Selected demonstration frames and contact crops illustrate object appearance, grasp regions, and intermediate task states. These examples support interpretation of the stored motions and comparison with current observations.

Executable helpers. Reusable Python programs support forward and inverse kinematics, reference retrieval, and action generation. They convert stored references and current geometric estimates into candidate actions.

Checks & recovery. Completion tests describe observable evidence that a grasp, subtask, or overall task has succeeded. Recovery procedures associate failure symptoms with corrective actions, such as adjusting an approach or selecting an alternative grasp.

Metadata & provenance. Robot specifications and interface conventions define how stored states and actions should be interpreted. Source records and validation notes document the origin of the retained material and the scope of its offline checks.

Within this shared structure, the retained information reflects each benchmark’s demands. Bench2Dex [ 163 ] and DexJoCo [ 144 ] emphasize hand configurations, phase-indexed motion examples, and helpers for dexterous control. LIBERO-Long++ and LIBERO-Ultra-Long [ 162 ] organize selected demonstrations around composable atomic skills, while LIBERO-PRO [ 183 ] primarily retains textual strategies and recovery knowledge from exploration. SIMPLE [ 152 ] preserves complete numerical training trajectories and helpers for extracting and modifying candidate action chunks under current feedback. LHPR-VLN [ 134 ] and VLN-CE [ 87 ] retain navigation strategies, landmark references, stopping guidance, and recovery notes from training-scene practice. BEHAVIOR [ 8 ] emphasizes object-specific grasping affordances, bimanual and tool-contact geometry, and conditional verification and recovery procedures.

Package usage. Retrospective usage analyses reveal a common workflow on every benchmark we audited: GPT-6-Astra reads the task guidance, retrieves a candidate motion through a prepared helper, and checks its execution against the visual references. Numerical demonstrations are frequently loaded internally by these helpers, linking stored examples directly to action generation; on DexJoCo, controllers and visual references are used repeatedly during both initial execution and continuation. Rather than replaying demonstrations, GPT-6-Astra adapts them to the current scene. In Bench2Dex Ball Box Loading, it remaps reference joints and compensates for a 4–5 cm difference in workspace height while preserving the demonstrated bimanual support geometry; in DexJoCo Photograph, it selects an alternative reference pickup after a slip. The packages thus serve as reusable resources for proposing, adapting, and revising actions under feedback, although these analyses do not isolate the causal contribution of individual components.

## 2.3 Extending Interaction Budget

Beyond the coverage of training data (Sec. 2.2 ), the demands of the tasks themselves limit performance at 1 × 1\times , leaving four benchmarks far from solved even with ICL: RoboDojo, Bench2Dex, BEHAVIOR, and LHPR-VLN. RoboDojo and Bench2Dex require precise bimanual or dexterous manipulation, often involving repeated corrections. BEHAVIOR and LHPR-VLN require long sequences of household manipulation or navigation, with subgoals tracked across many stages, and have the lowest success rates of all settings.

To assess how much the standard step limit contributes to these shortfalls, we extend the budget to 10 × 10\times while keeping model weights and ICL packages fixed (Figs. 1 and 4 ). Additional interaction yields large gains on RoboDojo and Bench2Dex. On RoboDojo, success roughly triples, and about three quarters of the episodes unfinished at 1 × 1\times are completed, with the Precision group gaining most. Success on Bench2Dex more than doubles. These gains indicate that the standard budget can interrupt productive execution and recovery, while additional interaction allows GPT-6-Astra to complete further corrective attempts.

On LHPR-VLN, however, the extended budget yields only a modest gain, and success remains the lowest of all settings. This suggests that the demands of long-horizon navigation, including tracking subgoals across many stages, are not resolved by additional interaction alone (Sec. 2.4 ). We do not extend the budget on BEHAVIOR, whose standard budget is already long.

Benchmarks that already perform well at 1 × 1\times also benefit from additional interaction. DexJoCo and VLN-CE reach success rates of around 90%, while the LIBERO family and SIMPLE exceed 95% and approach saturation (Fig. 1 ).

## 2.4 Limitations and Failure Modes

Despite the substantial gains from ICL and the extended budget, several limitations and recurring failure modes remain. We first discuss two limitations of the approach, transfer and cost, and then three behavioral failure modes identified from episode videos and agent logs (Fig. 6 ). Infrastructure interruptions remain scored as failures but are considered separately from the behavioral analysis.

ICL packages are largely task-specific, which limits transfer. Although ICL packages substantially improve performance across benchmarks, they are built from each benchmark’s training data and mostly encode task-level guidance, motion references, and helpers, so their benefit weakens when test tasks move away from the data they were built from. In the RoboDojo Open group, which has no task-specific demonstrations and relies on a package studied from the other four groups, GPT-6-Astra + ICL still benefits from additional interaction but attains the lowest success among all groups (Appendix 9.3 , Table 5 ). Similarly, RoboLab provides no training set from which a package can be built; GPT-6-Astra leads the listed baselines there, yet its absolute success remains moderate (Table 6 ). Building packages that generalize beyond their source tasks remains an open direction.

Time and cost remain high. Strong performance comes at a substantial cost in tokens and wall-clock time, even on benchmarks that GPT-6-Astra nearly solves (Fig. 5 ). On LIBERO-Long++, where success at the standard budget already exceeds 97%, each episode still consumes about a million tokens and nearly an hour of inference and tool use; on LIBERO-Ultra-Long, these costs rise to roughly nine million tokens and nearly two hours (Table 4 ). Extending the budget increases the cost further, and much of the additional cost is concentrated in difficult episodes that often still fail: on RoboDojo, a single episode under the extended budget takes more than three hours on average. Since the 10 × 10\times setting only caps the number of action steps and episodes may end earlier upon success or terminal failure, these costs reflect the steps actually executed. Because inference latency is not counted in the action-step budget, this cost also limits deployment in settings that require real-time control.

Verifying physical success. GPT-6-Astra can detect that a task is not yet complete without identifying which physical condition remains unmet; consequently, its correction process fails to converge (Fig. 6 (a)). In Bench2Dex Jigsaw Puzzle Assembly, it reports that all four pieces form the required rectangle while noting that the episode has not ended, and continues to adjust the residual offsets, but its corrections pull the pieces apart again instead of closing the remaining gaps. In RoboDojo Hang mugs, GPT-6-Astra takes an overlap between a mug’s handle and the peg in its head camera as evidence that the mug is hung, without confirming that the peg passes through the handle; the mug ends up on the table, and in its later regrasps the closing of its fingers is likewise taken as contact that has not occurred. In RoboDojo Fill egg holder, GPT-6-Astra moves all four eggs from the basket into the holder and reports that they remain seated after it withdraws, yet the episode ends as a failure with only partial credit. Visual plausibility and self-reported progress can therefore diverge from the task’s actual completion conditions, sustaining repeated correction or premature confidence. Reliable execution requires checks that resolve the task’s actual contact, support, and alignment constraints.

Recovering from consequential actions. Each attempt changes the state from which recovery must proceed, and some changes cannot be undone (Fig. 6 (b)). In RoboDojo Pour liquid into cup, the cup tips over early in the episode and the liquid spills onto the table; GPT-6-Astra rights the cup and resumes pouring, but the spill cannot be reversed, and the episode ends with most of its budget unused. In DexJoCo Assembly, a peg slips from the grasp and falls to the floor; GPT-6-Astra judges it unreachable and parks the arms with most of the budget remaining. Recovery is also costly when the failed step is a prerequisite for later ones, such as opening a container or securing an object: until it succeeds, downstream subtasks cannot proceed, and repeated retries consume the budget without advancing the task. Such dependencies are especially prevalent in long-horizon benchmarks like BEHAVIOR and LHPR-VLN, where a single unresolved subtask can stall progress toward the overall goal. In LHPR-VLN, for example, an agent may become stuck trying to reach an intermediate destination, lose track of its navigation plan, and resort to aimless exploration without making meaningful progress. Additional budget therefore helps only when a recovery path still exists, and successful recovery usually involves a meaningful change of strategy rather than repetition. In DexJoCo Fold Glasses, for example, GPT-6-Astra switches to a side approach, verifies the grasp with a test lift, and completes the task after exceeding the standard budget.

Preserving progress over long horizons. Long-horizon tasks require earlier progress to remain intact while later actions are executed, and small deviations compound across stages (Fig. 6 (c)). In RoboDojo Store laptop and headphones, GPT-6-Astra has already stored the laptop and hung the headphones on their stand, then returns to adjust one earcup; the correction pulls the headband off the stand, and the headphones are not re-hung before the budget runs out. In BEHAVIOR can_meat, a jar that is already held beside the counter tilts during the next motion and falls to the floor, so progress has to be rebuilt before the task can continue. Beyond such direct disruptions, small errors in grasping, placement, or navigation accumulate over successive stages and alter the conditions for later actions, forcing GPT-6-Astra to re-localize and correct earlier mistakes. Reliable long-horizon execution therefore requires tracking and rechecking conditions established earlier, rather than treating completed subgoals as permanently resolved.

These observations motivate task-relevant verification, recovery strategies that account for irreversible consequences and prerequisite dependencies, and persistent tracking of earlier progress. They suggest that further progress depends on how effectively the agent uses additional interaction to revise its strategy and verify the resulting state.

2026-10-19.title: Mothership: A Two Tier Autonomous Refuse Collection System for Pedestrian Campuses
2026-10-19.authors: Wei Wang , Yiru Veronika Wang , Yihan Wang , Zihao Li , Xiaohui Liang (Robostreet research team. Cambridge, MA, USA)
2026-10-19.abstract: Refuse collection in pedestrian campuses, parks and mixed-use districts remains manual because compaction trucks cannot reach bins located on walkways, courtyards and building service doors. This paper presents Mothership, a two-tier autonomous refuse collection system in which an electric compaction truck (the mothership) carries two low-speed sidewalk robots (RoboCarts) that fetch standard two-wheel bins, deliver them to the truck, return the empty bins to their original positions and re-dock on the truck for charging. The architecture separates responsibilities by scale: the truck performs road driving, compaction, lifting and energy supply, while the carts perform only sidewalk transport and bin grasping. This split removes the lift-and-tip mechanism from the sidewalk vehicle, keeping it light and low, and relaxes cart-to-truck docking tolerance to the +/-100 mm capture window of a standard automated lifter. We describe the system architecture, the bin-handling and docking interfaces, and a mission-planning formulation that decomposes a route into truck stop points and cart tasks. A discrete-event simulation over synthetic campus layouts with 2-16 bins/ha quantifies throughput as a function of bin density, cart count and stop-point radius. A two-cart configuration serves 20-29 bins/h. Throughput is governed by an interaction between cart count and stop-point radius: a single cart performs best with many close stops, whereas three or four carts need wide stops (80 m) to stay busy, reaching 35-49 bins/h at moderate-to-high densities. The best stop radius therefore has to be chosen together with the fleet size, not fixed in advance.
