2026-10-20.title: Physical Words: A Vocabulary for Structuring Latent Reasoning in Robot Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Jiaming Liu , Xinghao Zhu , Yiming Zhang , Shanghang Zhang , Yinxi Wang , Yichu Yang , Zhuoyang Liu , Dantong Niu , Soha Pouya , Juekun Li , Yan Chang
2026-10-20.abstract: Abstract: Multimodal reasoning provides robotic foundation models with predictive context needed for reliable action generation. However, language-based reasoning captures task semantics but struggles to express fine-grained physical dynamics, while latent reasoning models future state evolution but offers limited structure for organizing these dynamics into reusable reasoning primitives. To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysWord , a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words , which use atomic action verbs as shared semantic anchors for continuous representations of physical dynamics. Specifically, PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations. Building on these primitives, we construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and optional tactile variants of each action word. Autoregressively predicting Physical Words across future timesteps captures transitions between execution stages, providing structured multimodal context for action generation. PhysWord achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 90.3% on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6% on vision-based LIBERO-Long, and outperforms competing methods on real-world tasks using bimanual grippers and dexterous hands. Further evaluations demonstrate that our structured latent reasoning framework generalizes to unseen scenarios and enables long-horizon manipulation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising foundation for general-purpose robotic manipulation [ 1 , 2 ] , integrating the semantic knowledge of pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] with robot action learning. Reliable manipulation, however, requires anticipating how the physical environment evolves as the robot acts.
This need has motivated reasoning-before-acting VLA approaches [ 6 , 7 ] , which generate intermediate task plans or predictive context to guide action generation.
World Action Models (WAMs) further integrate future world prediction with action generation, enabling policies to leverage dynamics knowledge learned from video and manipulation data. These advances highlight the value of multimodal reasoning in providing predictive context that aligns robot actions with evolving environments.

Existing reasoning approaches differ in how they represent predictive context.
On the one hand, some VLA models adopt the reasoning paradigm of pretrained VLMs, using language to decompose tasks and express task-level action semantics [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . However, linguistic descriptions remain physically coarse, as a verb such as “rotate” identifies an operation without fully conveying its fine-grained dynamics.
On the other hand, WAMs [ 11 , 12 ] and latent reasoning methods [ 7 , 13 , 14 ] model future state evolution, providing rich predictive representations of interaction dynamics. Yet these approaches do not necessarily organize their representations around shared action semantics. Since the same manipulation skill can be applied across different objects and scenes, a useful reasoning representation should preserve shared semantics while capturing context-specific physical dynamics. This raises a central question: Can atomic action semantics organize physical latent representations into reusable reasoning primitives?

To this end, we introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as semantic anchors for continuous latent dynamics. We assemble a vocabulary of atomic action verbs, such as “pick,” “rotate,” and “push,” based on the action taxonomy of prior work [ 15 , 16 ] .
As shown in Figure Abstract (a), PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words from the current observation context and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations.
Joint semantic and latent supervision encourages these representations to capture shared action semantics while retaining action-related physical dynamics.
To capture how these dynamics evolve during execution, we organize Physical Words at multiple future timesteps within the action-chunk horizon, forming a temporally structured PhysWord space.
Within this space, we use separate visual and tactile variants of each action word to capture complementary motion and contact dynamics, including tactile variants only for tactile-enabled tasks.
By autoregressively predicting these Physical Words, PhysWord captures changes in action semantics and physical dynamics across execution stages, providing structured multimodal predictive context for long-horizon manipulation.
This token interface adapts to the available sensory modalities, bringing demonstrations with and without tactile observations into a unified training formulation. This flexibility enables us to jointly pretrain PhysWord on approximately 7,000 hours of real-robot and human-hand demonstrations.
Across this corpus, we use a VLM [ 17 ] to automatically segment trajectories into atomic action stages and align the resulting atomic verbs with the corresponding observations.

As shown in Figure Abstract (b), PhysWord achieves success rates of 90.3% on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6% on vision-only LIBERO-Long, outperforming prior SOTA methods.
Real-world experiments on bimanual gripper and dexterous-hand platforms with visual and tactile sensing further demonstrate its effectiveness in contact-rich, precise, and long-horizon manipulation.
To assess reusability, we evaluate both unseen scene configurations and extended task sequences absent from training.
PhysWord outperforms competing methods under unseen backgrounds, object instances, and object positions on Powered Screw Driving and Pick A4 Paper , and successfully executes extended manipulation sequences, supporting reuse across both scenarios and task stages.
To assess the predictive value of its tactile representations, we replace measured tactile inputs with predicted latents at inference.
Remarkably, the resulting policies retain strong performance with only modest degradation, suggesting that semantic structuring preserves contact information needed for control and enables deployment without online tactile sensing. Our contributions:

We introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as semantic anchors for continuous physical dynamics by directly supervising their contextual hidden states with future latent targets.

We construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and tactile variants of atomic action words, capturing evolving motion and contact dynamics for action generation.

PhysWord achieves 90.3% on UniVTAC and 99.6% on LIBERO-Long, outperforming prior SOTA methods. Experiments on real-world tasks demonstrate superior performance, stronger generalization, and long-horizon manipulation through sequential reuse of Physical Words.

# 2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models. VLA models [ 1 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 2 , 21 ] adapt pretrained VLMs to generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions.
Reasoning-before-acting VLAs introduce intermediate reasoning to anticipate task progression.
Language-based approaches, including subtask prediction, embodied chain-of-thought (CoT), and motion descriptions [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 22 ] , convey task semantics and subtask plans but struggle to express fine-grained dynamics.
Beyond language, recent methods predict future visual observations [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ] or incorporate anticipated signals from multiple modalities [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] .

Latent Reasoning and World Action Models (WAMs). Latent CoT represents intermediate reasoning through continuous latent states in LLMs and VLMs [ 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 ] .
ATLAS [ 36 ] further highlights the importance of LLMs’ native language-based CoT for general reasoning tasks.
In robotics, recent VLA models adopt latent reasoning to guide control using compact representations of future physical dynamics [ 37 , 6 , 38 ] .
Subsequent work incorporates reinforcement learning [ 39 ] and latent alignment between human and robot demonstrations [ 40 ] .
Related WAMs jointly model video and action sequences [ 41 , 42 , 11 , 12 ] .
Several approaches condition action generation on latent representations of predicted future states [ 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 , 47 ] .
Although these approaches capture rich future dynamics, their latent representations are not structured around shared action semantics.
PhysWord introduces this structure by anchoring future dynamics to atomic action verbs, forming reusable reasoning primitives that provide predictive context for action generation.

2026-10-20.title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
2026-10-20.authors: Zehao Wang , Jianpeng Yao , Yuping Wang , Yiping Li , Jiaqi Li , Zhixu Li , Kanghoon Lee , Jinfeng Wang , Cong Liu , Zhaowei Tan , Jinkyoo Park , Jiachen Li
2026-10-20.comment: Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026); Project Website: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/ .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Safely navigating among humans is fundamental to deploying mobile robots in real-world shared spaces such as hospitals, offices, and warehouses [ 18 , 33 , 27 , 3 ] . Multiple robots may operate simultaneously in these constrained spaces while pedestrians move unpredictably through narrow corridors, blind corners, and cluttered layouts. Navigation decisions are shaped by both static geometry and dynamic human motion. Reinforcement learning (RL) and multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) support reward-driven policy learning and preference-based refinement [ 48 , 16 ] , provide fast decision-making, and have shown promising performance in multi-robot socially-aware navigation [ 6 , 13 , 26 , 41 , 5 , 9 , 4 , 30 , 43 ] .
Previous studies have shown that prediction-aware policies can help robots shape their decisions on future human motion [ 24 , 22 , 1 , 40 , 31 ] . While trajectory prediction is widely used to represent pedestrian futures, it often focuses on dynamic agents alone and does not model the surrounding static geometry that is crucial in constrained spaces. Occupancy grid maps (OGMs) [ 34 , 45 ] provide a more unified representation, encoding static obstacles, free space, and human motion within the same spatial structure. This makes OGMs suitable for social navigation in cluttered and partially observable environments.

However, forecasting future occupancy remains challenging in environments with evolving pedestrian intentions, diverse motion patterns, denser crowds, and unseen occlusion-heavy regions. Learning-based policies often degrade under such out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, since distribution shifts can introduce prediction errors and severely mislead planning. This challenge is pronounced when multiple robots operate in constrained environments shared with pedestrians, where each individual robot may overlook risks caused by occlusions or inaccurate predictions. Therefore, effective cooperation among robots is essential to ensure safety, efficiency, and human comfort.
Moreover, to ensure robust and adaptive navigation, robots need not only to predict future states but also to estimate the uncertainty of predictions. Such uncertainty indicates when a prediction is reliable and when the policy should adapt its behavior.
For instance, as shown in Figure 1 , a robot may get stuck in a confined area due to static obstacles or fail to detect pedestrians hidden behind a wall when turning a corner. In contrast, cooperative multi-robot systems can coordinate planning and exchange information to improve task execution and situational awareness [ 12 , 20 , 47 ] . By sharing spatiotemporal features when a nearby robot detects a pedestrian in an occluded region, robots can make more informed and proactive decisions, improving safety, efficiency, and human comfort under challenging distribution shifts.

To this end, we propose CoopUQ , a multi-robot social navigation framework. CoopUQ forecasts future OGMs and estimates uncertainty maps by modeling the stochasticity of future occupancy over cross-robot spatiotemporal features, improving prediction quality over raw-LiDAR or prediction-level fusion. Beyond using uncertainty as an extra observation, we employ constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning (CMARL) [ 11 ] to explicitly guide risk-aware control, allowing robots to avoid ambiguous regions under distribution shifts while maintaining efficiency in well-observed areas.
Our main contributions are three-fold. First, CoopUQ leverages uncertainty as a bridge between stochastic cooperative forecasting and robust decision making. Second, we design a deviation-guided cross-robot fusion module that adaptively aggregates complementary features in regions affected by occlusions or cross-robot disagreement. Third, we introduce a risk-aware safety cost in CMARL to explicitly guide the navigation policy. Extensive Unity3D simulations and real-robot experiments demonstrate safer and more robust navigation across in-distribution and OOD scenarios.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Social Robot Navigation. Mobile robots that navigate in spaces shared with humans should adhere to social norms [ 28 , 3 , 49 , 39 , 2 , 32 ] . Social navigation is often modeled as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process, where agents act based on incomplete local observations [ 28 ] .
A key challenge is modeling partial and uncertain observations in real-world environments [ 15 ] .
Many prior works focus on predicting trajectories of dynamic obstacles, modeling pedestrians as simple position-radius tuples. These rule-based or learning-based methods perform well in simulation [ 24 , 22 , 41 , 6 , 13 , 26 , 8 ] , but often assume full visibility in open spaces and overlook static obstacles, limiting their applicability in occluded or cluttered environments.
In contrast, we adopt OGM forecasting with uncertainties as a holistic spatiotemporal representation and aggregate complementary observations through multi-robot cooperation, enabling safer decisions in constrained environments.

Occupancy Grid Map (OGM) Forecasting. Predicting the future environment remains challenging due to its inherent stochasticity and uncertainty. OGM is an effective spatial representation that unifies both static and dynamic obstacles.
Since OGMs can be treated as images, multi-step forecasting is often formulated as a video prediction problem [ 29 , 14 , 36 , 19 , 37 ] . Recent studies use OGMs to model dynamic human crowds [ 7 , 44 ] .
However, individual OGM forecasting remains challenging in constrained environments, where occlusions can lead to incomplete or less accurate predictions.
In contrast, cooperative forecasting allows multiple robots to fuse spatiotemporal features and produce uncertainty-aware predictions, constructing more reliable guidance for downstream navigation.

Cooperative Perception and Prediction. Cooperative perception and prediction are crucial for addressing partial observability and perceptual limitations, particularly in environments with occlusions [ 21 ] .
By sharing sensor data, intermediate features, or predictions, multiple agents can construct a more comprehensive scene understanding, enhancing detection and motion prediction in occlusion scenarios [ 46 , 42 , 10 , 23 ] .
In this work, we bridge cooperative occupancy forecasting with uncertainty-aware planning for multi-robot social navigation, allowing robots to leverage predictions and their corresponding uncertainties to make more robust decisions under occlusion and distribution shifts.

2026-10-20.title: Where is Physical RSI capability from? An Observational Scaling Law of LLM-as-policy
2026-10-20.authors: Zekai Li , Jiayi Yu , Jinlu Zhang , Luyang Niu , Zekun Qi , Jun Zheng , Xuchuan Chen , Dairu Liu , Yintianrun Zhang , He Wang , Li Yi
2026-10-20.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-20.abstract:
In this paper, we systematically investigate the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and generalization of physical Recursive self-improvement.
We introduce PhysRSI-eval to quantify physical RSI through a five-axis metric: First-Attempt Performance, Efficiency, Success, Budget and Improvement from failure. Different VLMs are evaluated on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget.
The analysis of experimental results motivates the Physical Barrel Hypothesis : different capabilities may constrain different parts of improvement. Systems with similar public benchmark averages can still differ widely on the five axes, and a system that reaches a high final score may improve late or consume more of its budget. We study observational scaling from two perspectives: predicting the relative performance of VLM agents from their public capabilities, and forecasting later progress from early physical feedback. Together, these analyses ask how quickly and how far an agent can improve.
Moreover, we conduct workspace interventions and then analyze what improvement leaves behind. Removing history reduces late-round success, frozen workspaces remain useful on unseen layouts, and three cross-task cases achieve success earlier. The results suggest that scene-specific adaptation and reusable experience can coexist.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Frontier LLM agents demonstrate remarkable capabilities in directly generating actions for robotic manipulation.
Through iterative trial and error, they continually improve manipulation ability by updating skills, generating code, and using tools. [ 22 , 9 ] We call this process physical recursive self-improvement, or physical RSI.
In this work, rather than further demonstrating the impressive capabilities of frontier LLM agents, we pose three more fundamental questions: What is the origin of physical RSI capabilities? What scaling laws govern this process? Do the resulting improvements reflect overfitting or generalization?

What allows an agent to turn physical feedback into a better policy? Perception helps it interpret outcomes, spatial reasoning relates observations to actions [ 31 ] , and coding and harness use allow it to implement and test revisions. These capabilities may play different roles. We ask whether strengths behind a good first attempt also explain improvement after feedback.

We introduce PhysRSI-eval to study these questions under a common protocol ( Figure 2 ). Six systems revise persistent code, tools and notes across 18 manipulation tasks, with frozen model weights and a fixed physical interaction budget. Gemini 4 is reported separately on ten tasks.

An exploratory comparison of four public capability profiles on the 18 tasks associates spatial reasoning most strongly with initial performance, and perception with attained performance and recovery ( Figure 4 ). This pattern motivates the Physical Barrel Hypothesis : the capability that limits an agent may depend on which aspect of improvement we measure. Starting well and learning from failure may require different strengths. These associations suggest candidate bottlenecks, not causal requirements.

An endpoint score alone cannot quantify physical RSI. It says little about when gains occur or what they cost. Repeated attempts can also increase the chance of success without useful revision. Our five-axis metric separates initial performance, gain timing, attained score, physical budget savings and recovery from failure ( Section 3.4 ). These axes reveal different strengths. Opus 5.5 attains a higher score than GPT-6.1 Sol, but has lower gain-timing and budget-savings scores. Higher scores need not mean improving earlier or using fewer physical interactions.

With these outcomes defined, we study observational scaling across model capabilities and physical interaction budgets. Following Ruan et al. [34] , we first ask whether public capability scores can predict the relative order of held-out systems, in attained performance and gain timing ( Section 5.2 ).

We then ask whether early physical progress predicts the gains from a larger interaction budget. This connects physical RSI to the study of learning curves [ 19 , 12 ] , with the interaction round as our budget variable. Calibrating the improvement shape of a reference model to a few early rounds forecasts the rest of a related model’s trajectory ( Figure 8 ). The two analyses address complementary questions: what improvement to expect from a model’s capabilities, and how much further it may progress after its first attempts. Both remain exploratory.

Does the agent acquire a reusable procedure, or adapt to its practice scene? A rising score alone cannot answer this question. We first remove history to test whether retained experience helps beyond repeated attempts. We then freeze workspaces on unseen layouts and transfer them across tasks.

In a six-task Astra ablation, removing history lowers late-round success from 41.7% to 8.3% ( Table 8 ). With further revision disabled, frozen workspace files support success in 25 of 60 trials on unseen layouts ( Table 9 ). Three cross-task cases also reach first success earlier when initialized from other tasks’ workspaces ( Figure 9 ). These results support a role for retained experience and show that some artifacts remain useful beyond the scenes where they were refined. Scene-specific gains and useful transfer can coexist. Explaining which retained skills or memories enable transfer connects this question back to the origins of physical RSI.

Our contributions follow this progression:

Five-axis evaluation and capability diagnosis. A fixed-budget protocol separates five physical RSI outcomes and relates them to four capability profiles, motivating the Physical Barrel Hypothesis.

Observational scaling and prediction. Cross-model rank prediction and early-round forecasting probe how model capabilities and interaction budget relate to physical improvement.

Specialization and generalization. Ablations, frozen-workspace tests and cross-task adaptation examine whether gains depend on retained experience and whether that experience remains useful elsewhere.

1. Five-axis evaluation and capability diagnosis. A fixed-budget protocol separates five physical RSI outcomes and relates them to four capability profiles, motivating the Physical Barrel Hypothesis.

2. Observational scaling and prediction. Cross-model rank prediction and early-round forecasting probe how model capabilities and interaction budget relate to physical improvement.

3. Specialization and generalization. Ablations, frozen-workspace tests and cross-task adaptation examine whether gains depend on retained experience and whether that experience remains useful elsewhere.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 LLM-as-policy Agents and Embodied Evaluation

LLMs can act as robot policies by writing programs over perception and control tools [ 22 ] . Feedback lets them revise plans or reward code [ 39 , 14 , 26 ] . Recent benchmarks evaluate these policies through controlled robot interfaces [ 7 , 24 , 5 , 57 , 52 ] , while others give coding agents extended simulator access and assess the resulting programs [ 35 , 25 ] . These evaluations typically summarize outcomes per episode, across independent trials or within a time budget. A reported Astra case, where a self-written fix succeeded once and failed on repetition, highlights the gap between finding a solution and retaining reliable behavior [ 9 ] . PhysRSI-eval tracks judged physical attempts connected by a persistent workspace, measuring both progress and physical cost under a fixed budget.

## 2.2 Agent Self-Improvement

Agents can accumulate skills and reflections without updating their model weights [ 43 , 37 , 27 ] . Recent benchmarks examine whether changes to the harness or retained experience improve later performance [ 13 , 46 , 38 , 58 ] . Producing an update and benefiting from it are distinct questions [ 23 ] . Related designs test memory, transfer and gains relative to cost [ 36 , 49 , 10 , 17 , 20 , 47 ] . AI-R&D benchmarks address research engineering under time or compute budgets [ 45 , 1 , 40 , 32 , 4 ] . These designs motivate separating initial ability, improvement and cost, and testing retained experience against repeated attempts. PhysRSI-eval brings these questions to physical interaction. Native task scores evaluate each attempt, while workspace interventions test what the agent retains. Clearing the workspace tests whether accumulated experience helps; freezing and transferring it test whether its benefits extend to new layouts and tasks.

## 2.3 Capability Benchmarks and Observational Scaling

Public benchmarks provide candidate measures of perception [ 8 , 54 , 33 ] , spatial reasoning [ 2 , 50 , 6 , 16 ] , coding and tool use [ 18 , 44 , 15 , 28 , 48 , 53 ] , and broader reasoning and work performance [ 30 , 42 , 29 ] . Embodied benchmarks and VLA models address planning and physical reasoning [ 51 , 21 , 11 , 56 , 41 ] , but do not track policy revision from graded attempts. Observational scaling relates benchmark-derived capability factors to agent performance across models [ 34 ] . We predict the relative order of physical improvement, in both extent and timing, from public scores. We also forecast later gains from early physical performance. With few closed systems and no training-compute data, these analyses remain observational and exploratory.

2026-10-20.title: GPT-6 Astra Is a Native Visuo-Tactile Policy for Contact-Rich Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Chen Yang , Linzhe Shi , Hang Zhang , Mu Xu , Jiansheng Fan , Chen Wang
2026-10-20.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-20.introduction:
Recent studies show that GPT-6 Astra can translate visual observations and instructions into robot actions, challenging the assumption that effective manipulation requires a separately trained policy. GPT-as-Policy ( Su et al., 2026 ) , RoboProbe ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , RoboDawn ( Guo et al., 2026 ) , and RoboICL ( Liu et al., 2026 ) explore this capability through different control interfaces and forms of contextual feedback. GPT-Policy and broader embodied evaluations further examine how demonstration following and task decisions translate into physical execution ( Cheng et al., 2026 ; Galbot Team et al., 2026 ) . These advances shift the question from whether general models can control robots to which capabilities still distinguish specialist policies.

Contact-rich manipulation is a prominent candidate. Precise insertion, stable grasping, and material discrimination depend on local geometry, slip, and physical properties that scene images may not reveal. Motions that work in free space can fail after contact, while a stronger grasp can damage a fragile object. These demands motivate tactile pretraining and learned visual–tactile integration, including FTP-1 ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) , OpenVTLA ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , and SimpleTouch ( Yang et al., 2026a ) . Can Astra directly use contact evidence for these decisions, or do such interactions require specialist training?

Vision-based tactile sensing makes this question especially relevant. Sensors such as GelSight encode contact geometry and deformation as images ( Yuan et al., 2017 ) , exposing touch through the same interface that supports general visual understanding. Few-shot demonstrations relate local deformation to preceding actions, grasp conditions, and resulting object motion. We explore whether Astra can interpret these relationships and use tactile evidence to guide a new interaction, extending visual competence to contact understanding.

We investigate Astra’s direct tactile-image understanding on UniVTAC ( Chen et al., 2026a ) and OpenViTac ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . Tactile RGB images enter through the model’s existing visual interface, allowing us to compare vision-only and visuo-tactile control on the same sampled scenes. We connect task outcomes to recorded contact inference, corrective actions, and recovery. Our contributions are threefold:

Direct tactile-image understanding and control. To our knowledge, we provide the first demonstration of Astra directly interpreting vision-based tactile images and using their contact cues for manipulation. We investigate this capability on nineteen tasks and 210 sampled scene seeds per input setting.

Leading contact-rich manipulation results. Astra reaches 93.8% and 81.8% mean success, exceeding the strongest reported specialist means in our comparison by 22.9 and 13.1 percentage points (Figure 1 ). It outperforms FTP-1 and SimpleTouch on UniVTAC and OpenVTLA on OpenViTac; vision-only performance also leads these baselines at 76.3% and 80.6%.

An analysis of contact understanding and visual compensation. We connect task-level outcomes to contact-guided probing, fine adjustment, and recovery, and identify subtle visual cues that compensate for missing touch. This analysis reveals both Astra’s tactile competence and its remaining perceptual and control limitations.

Together, these results challenge the presumed moat of specialist contact-rich policies and connect tactile sensing to the development of more capable general models.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2  Related Work

Code as Policies and VoxPoser use general models to generate robot programs and spatial objectives ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2023 ) . Recent Astra-based work brings the model closer to direct control: GPT-as-Policy compares direct and hybrid policies ( Su et al., 2026 ) ; RoboProbe and systematic evaluations examine manipulation and execution limits ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Galbot Team et al., 2026 ) ; and RoboDawn and GPT-Policy ground control in demonstrations ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) . RoboICL unifies demonstrations and online experience through an observation–action–receipt–observation grammar, preserving distributed interactions alongside recent feedback ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . Tactile feedback has also been studied in Astra-based peg insertion ( Tanaka, 2026 ) . This line complements learned action-chunking, diffusion, and pretrained VLA policies ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Our study centers on Astra’s direct interpretation of tactile RGB images and their role in contact-rich control.

VITaL, 3D-ViTac, and ViTacFormer learn visual–tactile representations for manipulation ( George et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Heng et al., 2025 ) . Tactile-VLA, VLA-Touch, and AT-VLA incorporate tactile feedback into pretrained VLAs ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . FTP-1 pretrains tactile policies across sensors ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) ; OpenVTLA studies tactile representations and integration within OpenViTac ( Wu et al., 2026 ) ; and SimpleTouch adds a tactile expert with predictive contact features, without additional tactile policy pretraining ( Yang et al., 2026a ) . TacDyn-WAM models implicit tactile dynamics by predicting future representations within a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Sparsh, AnyTouch, and T3 provide reusable sensory representations across sensing configurations and tasks ( Higuera et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . We examine how much tactile competence a general model can access directly through its visual interface, using demonstrations that relate contact images to actions and outcomes.

LIBERO, ManiSkill3, and RoboDojo evaluate manipulation learning, transfer, and generalist control ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Tao et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) ; Bench2Dex extends evaluation to visuo-tactile bimanual manipulation across dexterous hands ( Yang et al., 2026b ) . UniVTAC unifies tactile data generation, learning, and benchmarking ( Chen et al., 2026a ) , supporting established comparisons across grasping, classification, placement, and insertion ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) . The more recent OpenViTac provides a complementary sim-and-real framework for property discrimination and precise contact manipulation ( Wu et al., 2026 ) . Our evaluation spans both suites and examines whether texture, contour, and visible slip can support nominally tactile judgments, helping distinguish fine-grained visual competence from understanding of genuinely unobservable physical properties.

2026-10-20.title: Bio-inspired Thrust-Assisted Trotting on a legged-Aerial Robot via Real-Time QP-MPC
2026-10-20.authors: Shreyansh Pitroda , Eric Sihite , Alireza Ramezani , Morteza Gharib
2026-10-20.comment: To be published in IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
2026-10-20.abstract: This paper presents the hardware implementation of a quadratic program-based controller on Harpy: thruster-assisted bipedal robot to perform thruster-assisted trotting. This is inspired by wing-assisted locomotion observed in birds such as the chukar partridge, which employ thrust vectoring to manipulate the ground reaction force. The proposed controller formulates the thruster-assisted spring-loaded inverted pendulum dynamics as a condensed QP-based model predictive control problem, enabling simultaneous regulation of ground contact force and active thrust vectoring at 500 Hz. A decoupled control architecture is used, where the robot’s sagittal dynamics are controlled using QP-MPC while the frontal dynamics is regulated using a cascade orientation stabilization controller. Two experiments were conducted with different forward reference velocities of 0 m/s and 0.1 m/s. While the instantaneous velocity oscillates, the mean velocities can track their respective reference. Additionally, joint tracking error remains within ± 1 ∘ \pm 1^{\circ} while tracking the desired leg length given by the leg trajectory controller and desired swing trajectory given by Raibert’s heuristic. The QP-MPC problem is consistently solved with 0.18ms, which is well within the 2ms computation budget while satisfying the GRF friction cone constraint.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Birds are capable of using their wings to fly and also use their feet to walk on the ground, perch, and grabbing objects. Additionally, birds such as chukar’s wing-assisted incline running [ 2 ] and widowbirds’ controlled flapping descent [ 12 ] can use their wings while walking over a steep slope or during a rapid descent to stabilize their upper body orientation and velocity. We aim to take inspiration from and mimic the biological counterparts by combining both ground and aerial locomotion modes to achieve a versatile legged-aerial multi-modal robot.

There are several studies focused on multi-modal locomotion, specifically ground-aerial robots showing their versatility in traversing various terrains. Some of these studies focus more on transitioning between locomotion modes instead of using all available actuators at the same time.
Some robot design requires transformation to switch mode of locomotion, such as [ 31 , 30 ] , which transitions between terrestrial and aerial locomotion by morphing its appendages, [ 35 ] is a quadrupedal robot with propellers attached to its knee-axis and can perform flight after transforming into a quadrotor configuration.
On the other hand, some robot design with a fixed configuration such that they can perform ground and aerial locomotion without transforming, such as a jet powered bipedal robot capable performing large vertical jumps [ 19 ] , pogo-stick mechanism with quadrotor dynamics [ 40 ] , a bipedal robot [ 13 ] and a quadrupedal robot [ 17 ] with quadrotor style propulsion attached to its torso.

A multi-modal robot can utilize both ground and aerial actuators at the same time if the design allows it, making it possible to augment a mode of locomotion or perform a gait that can’t be done by using either ground or aerial actuator by themselves. This work explores the capability of our legged-aerial Harpy platform, shown in Fig. 1 , in performing a trotting gait using both the legs and thrusters at the same time. Bipedal robot locomotion requires a regulation of ground reaction force (GRF) so that the foot does not slip. The addition of thruster forces during walking will impact the resulting GRF and must be regulated together with the walking gait. Simulation studies have laid a theoretical groundwork for using both legs and thrusters at the same time to augment the legged locomotion to perform difficult maneuvers, such as narrow path walking [ 37 , 16 ] and steep incline walking [ 15 , 18 , 17 , 34 , 14 ] . Building on this foundation, the Harpy platform has also been validated in simulation across various locomotion tasks, such as jumping [ 6 , 32 ] , walking [ 21 , 23 , 24 , 36 ] , and inclined slope walking [ 22 ] . However, unlike in simulations, the practical usage of the algorithm in a real-time controller requires an approach that can be solved quickly and efficiently.

A common solution for GRF regulation for legged robot uses an optimization method, such as quadratic programming (QP) or nonlinear model predictive control (MPC), by modeling the robot’s dynamics and implementing the foot no-slip condition (the friction cone constraint) as constraints in the optimization. The optimization problem needs to be solved quickly to be feasible for a real-time implementation, where a reduced order model (ROM) is often used to reduce the model complexity and computational time.

The reduced-order modeling tool, such as the Linear inverted pendulum (LIP) and the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP) model, captures the essential dynamics of walking or running [ 1 , 8 ] . The SLIP model, first formalized by [ 1 ] and validated through extensive biomechanical studies [ 7 , 8 ] , has emerged as the canonical template for understanding and controlling such dynamic gaits. The SLIP model’s elegance lies in its simplicity: a point mass connected to a massless spring leg model, where the ground contact forces is applied alternatively between stance and flight phases. The reduced-order representation has proven remarkably effective in describing the locomotion of diverse running animals [ 10 ] and has guided the development of numerous robotic systems, from Raibert’s pioneering hopper [ 27 ] to modern dynamic bipeds [ 26 , 11 , 9 , 3 , 39 , 33 , 38 , 28 , 29 ] .

In this paper, we formulated an MPC optimization problem into a QP, and implemented it in our Harpy robot to satisfy ground constraints to perform a thruster-assisted trotting gait. The QP is formulated using a Thruster-SLIP (TSLIP) model, where thrusters are incorporated in the SLIP reduced order model, which then is implemented on hardware and solved in real-time using the qpSWIFT [ 20 ] algorithm at 500 Hz control loop frequency. This controller is then tested on hardware during the thruster-assisted trotting gait, where the experimental results showed the controller’s feasibility and performance. The contributions of this paper is listed as follows: 1) the derivation of the dynamic Thruster-SLIP model of a legged-aerial robot, 2) implementation of the QP-SLIP model on hardware, and 3) experimental validation of the controller performance showing the satisfaction of the GRF constraints in real-time. This paper is organized as follows: the robot design overview, followed by dynamic modeling, controller design and formulation, leg trajectory controller. Then, we present the experimental results, discussions, concluding remarks, and future work.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Robot Overview

Harpy [ 25 , 4 , 5 ] is designed with three joints for each leg: hip frontal joint, hip sagittal joint, and knee joint. The lower leg forms a parallelogram linkage, where a shock absorber spring is attached to the rear lower linkage to reduce the impulsive force on leg touchdown. There are four electric ducted fans (EDFs) attached to the torso: a high-powered EDF at each side of the robot, and two smaller upper EDFs with front/rear-facing orientation. Each larger and smaller EDF can generate a maximum thrust of 5kgf and 0.9kgf, respectively. The total weight of the robot is 7.1kg. Each joint is made with 3D printed material with embedded components. Joints are further connected using oval shape 2mm thickness carbon-fiber tube. The robot is equipped with STM32 F429ZI, which acts as a communication hub between ICM-20948 (IMU), OptiTrack data received over Wi-Fi using ESP32, and the xPC target machine.

2026-10-20.title: HandsOn: A Large-Scale Simulation Benchmark for Generalizable Dexterous Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Tianwei Luo , Yiming He , Hongjin Wu , Ting Pan , Debin Ren , Haorui Guo , Junlin Yang , Yuxin Zuo , Zhehao Kou , Kaisen Yang , Zhuoqun Lai , Yi Ding , Jiale Yu , Yuchen Zhang , Zijie Qiu , Haozhan Li , Ning Ding
2026-10-20.abstract:
General-purpose manipulation requires reliable behavior across embodiments, objects, and task demands.
We introduce HandsOn, a composable simulation platform and benchmark for cross-embodiment dexterous manipulation.
It supports five robotic arms, six dexterous hands, and approximately 200 rigid, articulated, and deformable assets in randomized scenes.
The benchmark pairs 18,000 curated human demonstrations with 66 human-verified tasks: Core-50 supports demonstration-based learning and execution tests, while Transfer-16 evaluates asset and relation transfer, skill composition, and deformable manipulation without target-task training demonstrations.
Qualitative real-robot rollouts illustrate sim-to-real transfer.
Across diffusion, vision-language-action, world-action, and prompted VLM-based methods, the best trained multi-task policy achieves 29.1% Core-50 success.
Without benchmark finetuning, GPT-6 using move_eef for palm-and-finger control achieves 5.2% on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16 over 660 trials.
Trained-policy stage diagnostics expose failures in contact establishment, action coordination, and maintaining achieved goals, with additional sequencing errors in composed tasks.
HandsOn provides a shared basis for investigating manipulation generalization and the limits of reliable physical interaction.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation requires controlling how contacts change during an
operation. Moving a mouse must not trigger a premature click; setting two
knobs requires both knobs to remain at their target settings simultaneously;
and placing a lid requires preserving alignment while releasing it. Evaluating
these capabilities requires demonstrations of varied interactions and diagnostics
that distinguish initial progress from reliable functional completion.
Recent dexterous benchmarks broaden task and embodiment coverage [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] , but their
human-demonstration sets are small and their tasks rarely include ones
reserved for evaluation.

HandsOn provides 18,000 curated simulation demonstrations, approximately
56 hours of interaction with three synchronized camera views. This is
5.7–16.4 times the human trajectory count of representative dexterous
benchmarks under the convention in Table 1 .
High-fidelity re-rendering produces varied observations of recorded
behavior while preserving state/action supervision. Visual domain
randomization and meaning-preserving prompt randomization broaden
appearance and language coverage around task-specific configurations.
Figure 1 summarizes the asset collection, environment
and interaction diversity, demonstration scale, and Core-50 results.
Figure 2 connects this data pipeline to evaluation and
illustrates correspondence with the physical system.

The benchmark comprises two complementary suites: Core-50 ,
50 tasks with demonstrations for policy learning and fresh-rollout evaluation,
and Transfer-16 , 16 tasks reserved for generalization evaluation.
Core-50 tasks combine functional and numerical understanding,
articulation, spatial relations, precise contacts, and bimanual execution
(Figure 3 ). Transfer-16 tests new asset relations and
skill combinations, including three deformable interactions without
deformable-task demonstrations in this dataset. The simulated embodiment
follows a physical platform, and real-robot rollouts of
simulation-trained checkpoints are shown in the accompanying videos.

Our Core-50 study compares ten methods: five VLA models, three WAM models,
single-task Diffusion Policy, and the prompted VLM controller GPT-6.
The best trained multi-task score is 29.1%. Across the trained checkpoints,
tool use and precision fits are nearly unsolved, and skill-group gaps persist after
adjusting for demonstration count and expert duration. Two VLA checkpoints
barely condition on which object the instruction names. Failures concentrate
where closing the grasp fires a button, where both hands must hold their
targets together, and where reached goals must be kept. These findings
motivate evaluating what happens after acquisition, alongside aggregate
success.

We additionally study GPT-6 as a prompted multimodal controller, using
RGB observations, measured robot state, and the move_eef palm-and-finger
control interface without HandsOn finetuning. This supplementary experiment
achieves 5.2% success on Core-50 and 1.9% on Transfer-16 over 660 trials.
Success appears on only 12 of the 66 tasks. Qualitative action traces
suggest task-level planning potential and motivate richer interfaces
between that planning and high-dimensional dexterous execution. Its
observation interface, trial count, and model-call budgets are disclosed
alongside the trained-policy comparison.

Our contributions are:

A large human-demonstration dataset, re-rendered with visual and
prompt randomization.

Core-50 and Transfer-16: 50 demonstration-backed tasks and 16
evaluation-only asset, skill-composition, and deformable tasks, scored by
native stage checkers.

A comparison of DP, five VLA, and three WAM policies with a
covariate-adjusted skill analysis and a language-conditioning probe,
locating failures at three hand transitions and, in compositions, at
step order and completion, together with a 660-trial GPT-6 move_eef evaluation without benchmark finetuning.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

DexJoCo, DexVerse, Bench2Dex, and LabDex cover functional and bimanual
manipulation with diverse embodiments [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
DexMimicGen expands human seeds through automated trajectory generation,
whereas SPD studies simulation pretraining and real-data adaptation [ 5 , 6 ] . Table 1 compares data scale, randomization, policy coverage, and evaluation protocols.
HandsOn evaluates DP, five VLA models, three WAM models, and a prompted
VLM controller, GPT-6 with move_eef , across a demonstrated task
suite and a separate dexterous task-transfer suite.

LIBERO, CALVIN, DexArt, RoboDojo, and RoboTwin motivate transfer,
capability evaluation, and randomization [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] .
Earlier dexterous suites learn mainly by reinforcement or from small
demonstration sets [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] ;
large simulated and real manipulation corpora are dominated by grippers [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] .
Dexterous teleoperation and motion capture [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] collect human data outside a benchmark; HandsOn records it in the
evaluation simulator. Dexterous sim-to-real learning precedes HandsOn [ 23 , 24 ] .
Section 4.2 describes the dataset counting conventions.
Appendix F presents qualitative real-robot
rollouts, and Appendix B.5 specifies the proposed
matched evaluation protocol.

2026-10-20.title: DexOAK: Object-Aware Kinematic Retargeting
2026-10-20.authors: Federica Spinola , Robert Katzschmann , Cordelia Schmid
2026-10-20.abstract:
We introduce DexOAK , a learning-based object-aware kinematic retargeting framework for generating contact-consistent robot hand references from human motion-capture data. DexOAK first minimizes an interaction-graph Laplacian objective over a joint hand–object graph, so the robot reproduces the demonstrated object-relative interaction geometry rather than the human hand pose alone.
These per-frame solutions form seed retargeted references, from which a feed-forward network conditioned on human keypoints and object point clouds learns the retargeting function. Object-aware fine-tuning then refines the network under contact, non-penetration, and self-collision losses that position the fingers on the demonstrated contacts and reduce artifacts destabilizing physics-based refinement.
Once trained, the network transfers to unseen data by inference alone, without per-frame optimization.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Progress in robot manipulation increasingly comes from learning at scale, yet the resulting policies [ 1 , 2 ] remain bounded by scarce robot interaction data. It cannot be scraped from the web like the image and text corpora behind vision and language models, and teleoperation, the most reliable alternative, is slow and costly. The gap is widest for dexterous manipulation, where multi-fingered hands are hard to teleoperate [ 3 ] , leaving contact-rich interaction especially scarce. Abundant clips of people handling objects, increasingly annotated with hand and object pose [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , are a natural source of the dexterous interaction data that robots lack.
Such data supports robot learning through representation learning [ 7 ] , policy pretraining [ 8 ] , imitation learning [ 9 ] , or retargeting [ 10 ] . We focus on retargeting because it directly converts human demonstrations into dynamically feasible robot trajectories [ 11 , 12 ] , bypassing teleoperation entirely.

A human-to-robot retargeting pipeline has two stages. Kinematic retargeting sets where the robot hand goes relative to the environment, and dynamic retargeting sets how it actuates to interact with the object.
Kinematic retargeting most often matches the robot and human vectors between hand keypoints [ 13 , 14 ] , fitting hand shape alone and ignoring the object. Yet human and robot hands differ in degrees of freedom (DoF) and embodiment geometry, so shape similarity does not guarantee task-equivalent interaction.
Instead, recent work [ 15 ] preserves robot–environment relations with per-frame interaction-graph optimization, but targets whole-body loco-manipulation rather than dexterous finger-level contact.

We argue that kinematic retargeting should preserve task function rather than hand-pose fidelity. What matters is the human–object interaction: object-relative fingertip placement, grasp approach, and object motion. Prior pipelines introduce object and contact information only during physics-based refinement [ 12 , 11 , 10 ] , and never refine the kinematic reference itself under contact objectives.
We therefore propose DexOAK , which learns object-aware kinematic references
before dynamic refinement.
Every reference still requires physics refinement, but its quality determines how much error the dynamic stage must correct. We hypothesize that object-aware references let it focus on dynamics rather than inferring contact locations, improving performance.

DexOAK is a two-stage pipeline that turns human hand–object motion-capture demonstrations into kinematic robot trajectories. An optimization-based retargeter builds paired human–object and robot–object
interaction graphs [ 15 ] and solves for robot wrist pose and joint angles matching their Laplacian coordinates.
Solving these per-frame nonlinear programs sequentially yields object-aware kinematic references, our seed retargeted references . However, this optimization is sensitive to initialization [ 16 ] as contact and collision terms would make
the objective more non-convex.
We therefore train a differentiable network, sharing structure across tasks, to reproduce the seed references with one forward pass per frame instead of
per-frame optimization. This supervised amortization initializes object-aware fine-tuning , whose surface-contact,
object-part, and contact-direction losses improve robot finger placement beyond
the optimizer outputs. Importantly, the fine-tuned
network transfers to unseen data without a single per-frame solve. DexOAK ’s kinematic references act as the base action for a residual
reinforcement learning (RL) stage [ 17 , 11 ] that corrects the remaining dynamics gap. Successful simulation rollouts are then replayed open-loop on hardware, demonstrating physical executability and yielding real-robot trajectory data from human motion-capture data inputs ( Fig. 1 ).

This paper makes three contributions: (i) We present DexOAK , a kinematic retargeting pipeline that preserves the hand–object interaction rather than hand pose alone, pairing an interaction-graph Laplacian optimizer with a feed-forward network that amortizes the seed retargeting and is refined under object-aware contact losses. (ii) We show that object awareness at the kinematic stage improves downstream RL, raising success from 20.6% to 48.2% over hand-only references. The learned retargeter transfers to an unseen dataset zero-shot or with light fine-tuning, without repeating optimization or amortization. (iii) We surpass state-of-the-art (SOTA) on OakInk-v2 [ 6 ] and ARCTIC [ 5 ] with Allegro [ 18 ] and Inspire [ 19 ] hands, and achieve 46/56 successful hardware replays across 5 tasks.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Learning manipulation from human data. Generalist robot policies [ 1 , 2 ] draw action supervision from large,
costly robot-trajectory datasets tied to particular hardware.
Human data offers an abundant alternative and enters robot learning at two levels. At the representation level, it pretrains visual features, latent plans, or human–robot aligned embeddings [ 7 , 9 , 20 ] , without ever mapping motion to the robot. At the action level, methods predict human actions that are retargeted to the robot [ 8 ] , or learn policies and controllers from reconstructed videos and kinematic human–object references [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] , which first requires expressing the demonstration in the target embodiment. DexOAK supplies that step, generating the object-aware references these pipelines consume.

Retargeting from human data. Kinematic retargeting maps human motion to robot configurations without physics.
Hand-centric DexPilot [ 14 ] and AnyTeleop [ 13 ] optimize keypoint
vectors, while GeoRT [ 25 ] learns a direct map from human finger keypoints to
robot joints through geometric objectives. None constrains object-relative contact.
OmniRetarget [ 15 ] instead preserves body–object–terrain relations through an interaction mesh and sequential constrained optimization, but targets humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation. Dynamic retargeting enforces physical executability. ManipTrans [ 11 ] pairs a hand-motion imitator with task-specific residual RL driven
by object-tracking and contact rewards. DexMachina [ 12 ] learns object-state tracking with RL under a curriculum
that progressively removes virtual object-control assistance, guided by explicit motion
and contact rewards. SPIDER [ 10 ] instead uses sampling-based optimization,
refining simulated control sequences through annealed sampling with virtual contact
guidance. These recover physical plausibility, but receive an object-agnostic reference and must discover contacts themselves. DexOAK instead places the object in the kinematic stage so the dynamic stage starts from a reference carrying the demonstrated contact geometry.

Concurrent pipelines [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] preserve hand–object structure with Laplacian objectives, but re-optimize each new frame or demonstration before RL. DexOAK instead uses optimization only for training seed references. Its reusable retargeter is fine-tuned dataset-wide with object-aware losses to retarget new inputs without further optimization.

Hand–object interaction. DexYCB [ 4 ] , ARCTIC [ 5 ] , and OakInk-v2 [ 6 ] support
contact-aware reconstruction and synthesis. ContactOpt [ 29 ] refines human pose
with predicted contact. Grasp’D [ 30 ] synthesizes human and robot grasps through
differentiable contact. ArtiGrasp [ 31 ] uses physics-based RL for bimanual
grasping and articulation. Unlike these reconstruction and synthesis methods, DexOAK uses contact attraction, contact direction, and penetration objectives for human-to-robot
trajectory retargeting.

2026-10-20.title: Tactile In-Hand Object Rotation: A Comparative Study of Hand Morphology in Simulation and Hardware
2026-10-20.authors: Wenhao He , Max Yang , Chenghua Lu , Yijiong Lin , David A.W. Barton , Nathan F. Lepora
2026-10-20.abstract:
Continuous in-hand rotation requires coordinated contact
maintenance and renewal, linking manipulation performance to
both hand geometry and tactile feedback. We investigate these
relationships through rotational progress, finger participation,
and fingertip loading on two versions of the low-cost LEAP Hand with
anthropomorphic and symmetric finger arrangements. Both hands are integrated with
TacTip vision-based tactile sensors and use a shared reinforcement learning
framework. Simulation evaluates full tactile, binary touch, and
proprioception-only observations on 12 unseen objects; hardware
experiments evaluate full tactile policies on ten objects under
multiple hand orientations. In simulation, full tactile
observations increase mean normalized rotation per
episode over proprioception alone by 94.8% for the
anthropomorphic hand and 66.9% for the symmetric hand, with
longer mean episode durations and lower mean total fingertip
loads. Hardware contact measurements reveal more differentiated
finger participation in the anthropomorphic hand, while
cumulative loading is more evenly distributed across the
symmetric hand’s fingers. Overall, the symmetric hand achieves a 32.0%
higher mean rotation count and a 25.8% higher aggregate
rotation rate, together with longer manipulation duration.
Additional hardware force recordings show a 19.9% lower
mean total fingertip load for this layout. These findings
relate finger arrangement to contact organization and load
sharing, and show that richer tactile information supports
greater task progress at lower mean loading in both
simulated embodiments.
2026-10-20.introduction:
A robotic hand’s geometry determines where its fingertips
can reach and how they approach an object. During sustained
rotation, these geometric constraints interact with the need
to support the object, permit motion, and renew contact under
different gravity directions. The forces carried by the
fingertips and the distribution of contact changes across
fingers characterize how these interactions develop during
manipulation. Learning-based controllers have enabled
continuous fingertip rotation using proprioceptive and tactile
observations [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , providing an experimental basis for
examining these relationships across hand layouts.

The question considered here is how finger arrangement
changes both the organization of fingertip contact and loading
and the benefit obtained from tactile feedback. Similar task
scores can arise from different distributions of persistent
contact, contact-state changes, and accumulated fingertip load.
Examining these quantities together provides a basis for
interpreting how each layout performs the task. Comparing full
tactile, binary touch, and proprioception-only observations
then establishes how task progress, duration, and average
loading change as more local contact information becomes
available.

We study anthropomorphic and symmetric configurations of
the low-cost LEAP Hand [ 4 ] , each with 16 actuated joints and
4 integrated vision-based (TacTip) tactile fingertips [ 5 ] . We adopt the task and
reinforcement learning framework of AnyRotate [ 3 ] as a shared experimental protocol. The comparison uses a common
tactile observation interface and learning procedure to examine
differences across finger arrangements and observation
conditions. Simulation evaluates the three observation
conditions on 12 unseen objects with randomized hand
orientations and rotation axes. Hardware experiments evaluate
full tactile policies on ten objects under multiple hand
orientations, with additional force recordings following the
corresponding evaluation settings.

The results associate the two layouts with distinct patterns
of finger participation and cumulative loading. On hardware,
the anthropomorphic thumb and middle finger maintain contact
more persistently and contribute a larger share of accumulated
load, with more frequent contact changes at the index and
little fingers. The symmetric hand distributes participation
more evenly, and its cumulative loads are more uniformly
shared in both simulation and hardware. In the simulation comparison, richer tactile observations improve mean normalized rotation and manipulation duration while reducing mean fingertip loading in both hands.

The main contributions of this work are:

We compare two hand morphologies under three observation
conditions, quantifying changes in normalized rotation,
manipulation duration, and mean fingertip loading on unseen
simulated objects.

We relate fingertip workspace arrangement to hardware
contact persistence and transitions, and to cumulative load
sharing in simulation and hardware, identifying differentiated
and more evenly distributed patterns of finger contribution.

We implement two low-cost LEAP–TacTip hand configurations
and evaluate their continuous fingertip rotation on ten physical
objects under multiple hand orientations, combining manipulation
outcomes with complementary contact and loading measurements.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Tactile Feedback for Robotic Manipulation. Tactile manipulation spans explicit feedback control and learned policies. Li et al. use pressure-array features for tactile servoing [ 6 ] , while van Hoof et al. learn object rolling with distributed tactile feedback on the compliant ReFlex hand [ 7 ] . On the torque-controlled DLR Hand-II, joint sensing supports cube manipulation [ 8 ] and shape-conditioned reorientation of diverse objects [ 9 ] . Distributed binary contact on Allegro hands enables unseen-object rotation [ 10 ] and, in DexTouch, object seeking and manipulation without vision [ 11 ] . Optical sensors such as the TacTip family infer local interaction from deformation of a compliant sensing surface [ 12 , 5 ] . Tactile Gym 2.0 compares TacTip, DIGIT, and DigiTac sensors under a common sim-to-real learning framework for object pushing, edge following, and surface following [ 13 ] . These systems differ in sensing coverage, information content, and robot mechanics.

Learning Continuous In-Hand Rotation. Simulation-trained policies support dexterous reorientation on the Shadow Hand [ 14 ] and across diverse object geometries [ 15 ] . For continuous rotation, rapid motor adaptation uses proprioceptive history [ 1 ] , whereas RotateIt combines vision, optical tactile information, and proprioception [ 2 ] . AnyRotate introduces gravity-invariant multi-axis rotation with contact-pose and force features, teacher–student training, and curricula [ 3 ] . It also evaluates tactile observation variants and analyzes reactive contact behavior on an Allegro hand. These observation choices distinguish information about fingertip
engagement from more detailed descriptions of contact geometry and
loading. We examine how the gains from these successive levels of
information vary with finger arrangement during sustained rotation.

Hand Design and Comparative Evaluation. Comparative studies assess in-hand dexterity through manipulation tasks and measures of hand capability. The Elliott and Connolly Benchmark provides a common set of in-hand manipulation tasks [ 16 ] , while KaRMA compares feasible translation and reorientation through rolling contact in a two-finger pinch across 16 hand designs [ 17 ] . Complementing these evaluations, Almeida et al. investigate how tactile feedback from different finger and palm regions affects reorientation on a simulated Shadow Hand [ 18 ] . Kinematic capability and executed manipulation provide complementary
views of hand design. Reachable motions describe the opportunities
afforded by geometry; contact persistence, contact changes, and
accumulated loading describe how the fingers participate as a task is
performed. This distinction motivates assessing workspace arrangement
together with measured interaction and task outcomes.

2026-10-20.title: Robot Learning with Vision-Language-Action Models for Agricultural Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Hamid Hafezi , Javad Mohammadpour Velni , Mohammadreza Davoodi
2026-10-20.abstract:
Robotic manipulation in agricultural environments remains challenging due to variations in plant geometry, occlusion, and camera viewpoints. Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) and generalist robot policies offer a promising approach to addressing these challenges by learning manipulation behaviors from multimodal observations and language instructions. However, adapting these policies to agricultural tasks requires domain-specific demonstrations, which are costly and time-consuming to collect on physical robots.
In this work, we develop a simulation-to-real robot-learning framework for agricultural reaching and grasping that integrates task-specific demonstration collection and
pretrained policy adaptation. A MuJoCo-based agricultural environment is developed with diverse tomato plant structures to support demonstration collection and controlled evaluation. Expert demonstrations are collected through joystick teleoperation using a low-level controller that executes the learned policy actions. Two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , are adapted using simulated demonstrations, followed by further fine-tuning on a physical Franka Research 3 manipulator using real-robot demonstrations.
The adapted policies are evaluated under in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, followed by physical-robot experiments. The influence of proprioceptive information on policy performance is also investigated. Results show that π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} achieves higher task-performance scores than Octo and exhibits less degradation under distribution shifts.
These findings demonstrate the potential of integrating pretrained generalist policies with task-specific demonstration learning for agricultural manipulation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Many agricultural operations remain labor-intensive and physically demanding, making them a compelling domain for robotic automation. Robotic manipulators are increasingly being explored for tasks such as harvesting, planting, monitoring, weeding, and spraying in greenhouses, open fields, and orchards [ 1 , 2 ] .
However, agricultural environments are substantially less structured than typical industrial settings. Crops exhibit significant variations in geometry, orientation, and height,
while leaves, branches, and other plant structures can occlude
targets and constrain manipulator access [ 3 , 4 ] .
These characteristics make target localization, motion planning, and reliable robotic manipulation complicated.

Conventional agricultural manipulation systems commonly employ
a modular architecture in which perception, planning, and control
are implemented as separate components [ 1 ] .
On the perception side, the literature commonly relies on vision or multi-sensor processing to detect crops and estimate 3D target locations, often requiring careful camera placement, calibration, and coordinate-frame alignment to achieve reliable target estimates under occlusion and clutter [ 5 , 6 ] . For example, in [ 7 ] , a tomato-harvesting system combines YOLOv5 with image processing and depth information to recognize tomato clusters and localize stems, transforming image-based estimates into spatial coordinates for robot motion. Similarly, in [ 6 ] , a dual-arm fruit-harvesting framework combines YOLOv5 and object tracking with RGB-D measurements to estimate fruit positions, while image processing identifies the tree trunk.
In these systems, learning-based perception serves as a front-end component that provides geometric targets and information about the surrounding scene for downstream motion generation.

Using these target estimates and a representation of the workspace, the planning module generates feasible motions that account for the robot’s kinematics, reachability, and surrounding obstacles.
In agricultural applications, [ 3 ] combines manipulator placement optimization with an improved RRT* planner to generate collision-free trajectories for tomato harvesting.
Other fruit-picking systems modify the RRT* sampling strategy to improve path generation in cluttered environments containing branches and leaves [ 4 ] . During motion execution,
feedback control can improve positioning accuracy and interaction safety. In [ 8 ] , visual feedback is used to refine the end-effector position, while estimated contact forces are monitored to prevent unsafe interaction with workers or plants. In [ 9 ] , localized fruit positions
are used by a neural control framework to generate coordinated reaching and cutting motions while accounting for robot constraints. These studies illustrate how conventional
agricultural manipulation systems integrate perception, planning, and control through a modular architecture.

Although such modular approaches benefit from mature robotics tools and explicit handling of constraints, their performance depends on the accuracy and completeness of the information exchanged between components.
Errors in target localization or incomplete representations of surrounding plant structures can affect motion generation and execution. Reported challenges include occluded targets, unmodeled branches, and fruit displacement during interaction [ 6 ] .
Changes in lighting and crop arrangement may also require adjustments to perception and target-access strategies [ 7 ] .
Moreover, many agricultural robotic systems are developed for specific crops, environments, and tasks, and adapting them to new agricultural settings may require additional development
and validation [ 1 , 2 ] .
These limitations motivate the investigation of learning-based approaches that map observations more directly to robot actions while retaining feedback and low-level control
for execution.

Robot learning provides a framework for acquiring manipulation behaviors from data and interaction rather than relying solely on manually designed models and controllers [ 10 , 11 ] .
Two major paradigms are reinforcement learning (RL),
which learns behaviors through interaction and reward
feedback [ 12 ] , and learning from
demonstration (LfD), which learns from expert demonstrations [ 10 ] . Recent advances in machine
learning and the growing availability of large-scale robot
datasets have significantly expanded both paradigms [ 13 ] . In particular, pre-collected datasets
have enabled offline RL, while large and diverse
demonstration datasets have supported the development
of generalist policies that can transfer across tasks,
environments, and robot embodiments. While offline RL
typically relies on reward information associated with
collected trajectories, specifying appropriate reward
functions for complex manipulation tasks can be challenging. In contrast, LfD enables policies to be learned directly from expert demonstrations without requiring explicit reward labels [ 14 ] .

Previous research has explored a wide range of LfD approaches for acquiring robot manipulation skills. One class of methods focuses on representing and generalizing demonstrations at the trajectory level (e.g., joint-space or end-effector motion) using structured movement representations such as probabilistic and neural network-based movement primitives [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . A second class instead learns policies that directly map robot observations, such as RGB/depth images and proprioceptive states, to robot actions, including joint-space, end-effector, or gripper commands. Representative examples include implicit policies formulated as energy-based models [ 21 ] , diffusion-based visuomotor policies [ 22 ] , and Transformer-based behavior cloning approaches such as the Behavior Transformer [ 14 ] . Although these methods have demonstrated strong performance, many are developed for specific tasks and trained on datasets with limited diversity. More recently, large-scale multi-task robot datasets such as Open X-Embodiment [ 13 ] have accelerated interest in generalist robot policies, which use large Transformer backbones to scale across
tasks and embodiments. Some of these policies, such as RT-1 [ 23 ] and Octo [ 24 ] , are trained primarily on robot data with lightweight vision and language encoders. Others, referred to as vision-language-action (VLA) models, build on
vision-language models pretrained on web-scale data and adapt them to predict robot actions; examples include RT-2 [ 25 ] , OpenVLA [ 26 ] , π 0 \pi_{0} [ 27 ] , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 28 ] . Both families have demonstrated broad transfer and, in some settings, zero-shot or few-shot
generalization to novel tasks.

Recent studies have also investigated learning-based and vision-language models (VLMs) for agricultural robotics, including task-specific imitation learning for outdoor pepper harvesting [ 29 ] , VLM-guided task planning for crop monitoring through navigation and active-vision tools [ 30 ] , and scene-graph-grounded vision-language reasoning for greenhouse manipulation through predefined basic actions [ 31 ] .

Despite these advances, adapting pretrained generalist
policies to agricultural manipulation remains limited and
challenging due to differences between pretraining and
agricultural environments, while collecting task-specific
demonstrations across diverse plant configurations on
physical robots is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, understanding how these adapted policies perform
under variations in plant structure, camera viewpoint, and robot configuration remains an important research question.

To address these challenges, we develop a simulation-to-real robot-learning framework that integrates demonstration collection, pretrained policy adaptation, and low-level
manipulator control. The framework includes a MuJoCo-based agricultural simulation
environment for scalable demonstration collection and controlled evaluation, together with a joystick-based teleoperation system and a damped, null-space-based inverse-kinematics controller for demonstration collection and learned-policy execution.
Two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , are adapted to a tomato reaching-and-grasping task through fine-tuning on simulated demonstrations, followed by further fine-tuning using demonstrations collected on a physical Franka Research 3 (FR3) robot. We further evaluate the adapted policies under in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, followed by physical-robot experiments, while investigating the influence of proprioceptive information on policy
performance. The overall learning and deployment workflow is illustrated in Fig. 1 .

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

A MuJoCo-based agricultural manipulation environment
with diverse tomato plant structures, integrated with a
joystick-based teleoperation and low-level inverse-kinematics
control framework for demonstration collection and
learned-policy execution.

A simulation-to-real adaptation of two pretrained
generalist robot policies, Octo and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , for
agricultural reaching and grasping, using simulated
demonstrations followed by further fine-tuning with demonstrations collected on a physical Franka
Research 3 (FR3) robot.

A comparative evaluation of the adapted policies under
in-distribution, viewpoint/spatial-shift, and
out-of-distribution conditions in simulation, together
with real-robot experiments investigating their performance
and the influence of proprioceptive information.
