# II Task Formulation and Preliminaries

## II-A Agricultural Manipulation Task Formulation

We consider a robotic reaching-and-grasping task in which
a manipulator must approach and grasp a target ripe tomato
under variations in plant geometry, fruit location, and
visual occlusion. At each time step t t , the policy receives
visual observations from a primary (third-person) camera and a wrist-mounted camera, together with a natural language task instruction and, depending on the experimental configuration, proprioceptive information. Based on these
inputs, the policy predicts a sequence of end-effector
motion and gripper commands to accomplish the task.
This task is representative of agricultural manipulation because
it requires target localization, precise end-effector positioning,
and interaction in cluttered and partially occluded environments.
These capabilities are also relevant to other agricultural
operations, such as pruning, monitoring, and spraying.
We investigate the adaptation of two pretrained generalist
robot policies, Octo and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , to this task. The following subsections
introduce the general VLA formulation and the
architectures of the two models. Section III presents the MuJoCo simulation environment
and experimental setup, including demonstration collection
and evaluation scenarios, while Section IV describes
the policy fine-tuning procedures, experimental evaluation,
and results.

## II-B Vision-Language-Action Models

VLA models are robot policies that map multimodal observations and natural language instructions directly to robot actions. They are commonly trained through behavior cloning using demonstrations collected from human operators, scripted controllers, or previously trained policies. In contrast to conventional modular pipelines, where
perception, planning, and control are designed separately,
VLA policies learn an observation-to-action mapping from
demonstration data while relying on a low-level controller for execution. This approach is particularly relevant to
agricultural manipulation, where variations in plant
structure and fruit placement can complicate explicit
perception and motion planning.

Let 𝒟 = { ζ i } i = 1 N 𝒟 \mathcal{D}=\{\zeta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N_{\mathcal{D}}} denote a dataset of expert demonstrations, where ζ i = { ( o t i , l i , a t i ) } t = 0 T i − 1 \zeta_{i}=\{(o^{i}_{t},l^{i},a^{i}_{t})\}_{t=0}^{T_{i}-1} represents the i i -th trajectory of length T i T_{i} . A VLA policy generates the robot action a t ∈ ℝ d a a_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} conditioned on an observation history o t − H o + 1 : t o_{t-H_{o}+1:t} of length H o H_{o} and a natural language instruction l l , expressed as a t ∼ π ( ⋅ | o t − H o + 1 : t , l ) a_{t}\sim\pi(\cdot|o_{t-H_{o}+1:t},l) .
The robot observations o t o_{t} may include camera images I t I_{t} and proprioceptive state s t s_{t} , which contains low-dimensional information such as joint positions, joint velocities, and end-effector pose.
The language instruction l l is a text-based input that specifies the desired task. The robot action a t ∈ ℝ d a a_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{a}} denotes the continuous command applied through the robot control interface, which may represent joint-space commands, Cartesian end-effector commands, or gripper actions, depending on the application. However, in many robot-learning datasets, actions are represented as incremental changes in joint configurations or end-effector poses. Recent robot policies also employ action chunking [ 32 ] , in which a sequence of H a H_{a} consecutive actions, a t : t + H a − 1 a_{t:t+H_{a}-1} , is predicted instead of a single action a t a_{t} . Predicting action sequences can help reduce compounding errors during sequential execution [ 32 , 33 ] . Recent VLA models employ diffusion or flow-matching methods to jointly generate continuous action chunks rather than predicting actions sequentially.

Despite architectural differences, many VLA models share a common three-component structure, as illustrated in Fig. 2 : (i) modality-specific tokenizers/encoders that map the language instruction and each observation into a shared embedding space; (ii) a Transformer backbone that fuses multimodal tokens; and (iii) an action head that generates an action chunk a t : t + H a − 1 a_{t:t+H_{a}-1} . Beyond this shared structure, models differ in several
key aspects. Some models train their Transformer backbones primarily from scratch on robot demonstration data, whereas others initialize them from VLMs pretrained on web-scale image-text data and thus inherit broader semantic priors. Models also vary in scale, from relatively compact policies to architectures with billions of parameters, with larger models generally requiring more computational resources.
They further differ in their tokenization strategies and action-generation mechanisms. In this work, we study two pretrained generalist robot policies, Octo and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , which differ in their architectures and pretraining strategies.

The model is pretrained in a single stage on a mixture

and action commands.

π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 28 ] is a larger VLA than Octo and, unlike Octo, is built on a
pretrained VLM backbone. It uses a 3B-parameter PaliGemma VLM [ 35 ] , augmented with a separate

training example, these tokens represent semantic outputs,

For post-training, the autoregressive token-prediction

introduced and trained to generate continuous action chunks.
Thus, during post-training, the model learns to predict
action chunks in both discrete and continuous forms.

2026-10-20.title: Robotic Physical Comparison of Biologically Motivated and Counterfactual Sensory Arrangements using Biomimetic Skin
2026-10-20.authors: Akihiro Miki , Shun Hasegawa , Yoshimoto Ribayashi , Yuta Sahara , Kento Kawaharazuka , Kei Okada
2026-10-20.comment: Published in Bioinspiration & Biomimetics (IOP Publishing). Project page: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract:
Human skin contains diverse mechanoreceptors, including Merkel cells and Pacinian corpuscles, each localized in specific regions.
Although their spatial organization is known to be shaped by molecular signaling and neural induction during development, experimentally examining its functional significance under controlled conditions in living systems remains challenging.
In particular, physically comparing alternative receptor arrangements that do not occur biologically is difficult.
In this study, we developed a layered biomimetic robotic skin designed to mimic key structural features of human skin tissue by embedding receptor-analog sensors within compliant soft media.
Using this platform, we implemented both biologically motivated and counterfactual sensory arrangements and quantitatively evaluated their performance across three passive tactile tasks: detection of weak contacts, a two-point discrimination-like assessment, and texture identification.
Arrangements reflecting key features of the biologically motivated sensory organization exhibited higher performance than the alternative configurations examined.
This study addresses a biological question concerning how spatial organization influences tactile function by presenting a biomimetic robotic approach that enables physical and empirical comparison of biologically motivated and counterfactual sensory arrangements that are difficult to investigate in living systems.
2026-10-20.introduction:
The skin is composed of three layers: epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous tissue (hypodermis) [ 1 ] .
The epidermis, the outermost layer, consists mainly of keratinocytes and serves as a protective barrier against the external environment.
Beneath it lies the dermis, which contains connective tissues such as collagen and elastin.
The deeper subcutaneous tissue comprises adipocytes, blood vessels, and nerves, contributing to thermoregulation and absorption of mechanical impact.

Within these skin tissues, a variety of sensory receptors—including Merkel cells, Pacinian corpuscles, Ruffini endings, and Meissner corpuscles—are distributed at different depths and regions depending on the nature of the stimulus.
These receptors enable precise detection of pressure, vibration, slip, and skin stretching.
For example, Merkel cells are located in the basal layer of the epidermis and respond to sustained pressure [ 2 ] .
Meissner corpuscles reside at the dermal–epidermal junction and are sensitive to light touch and slip [ 3 ] .
Ruffini endings, found in the dermis, are thought to detect skin stretching, although morphological evidence for their structure remains limited [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
Pacinian corpuscles are distributed from the deep dermis into the subcutaneous tissue and respond to high-frequency vibrations with a peak sensitivity approximately 200 Hz [ 7 ] .
Collectively, these receptors are arranged according to their functional properties at distinct depths and regions within the skin, thereby enabling the integration of diverse tactile information [ 8 , 9 ] .

Studies in developmental biology and neuroscience have demonstrated the involvement of molecular signals and neural induction in the formation of sensory receptor arrangements.
For instance, Merkel cells are epithelial cells that differentiate from a subset of the epidermis during embryogenesis, and their patterning is regulated by the spatial and temporal actions of diverse developmental signals such as Wnt, Shh, and BMP [ 10 , 11 ] .
The formation of Pacinian corpuscles also involves multiple molecular factors, among which the GDNF family ligand neurturin (NRTN) and its receptors GFR ​ α ​ 2 / Ret \text{GFR}\alpha 2/\text{Ret} play a critical role [ 12 ] .
In addition, several neurotrophins—including nerve growth factor (NGF), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and neurotrophin-3 (NT3)—have overlapping roles, as evidenced by reduced numbers of Pacinian corpuscles in knockout mice for each of these factors [ 13 ] .
Collectively, these findings indicate that diverse molecular signals, acting through interactions between skin cells and the nervous system, contribute to the formation of sensory receptors, and the mechanisms underlying the construction of tactile function are gradually being elucidated [ 14 ] .
Moreover, recent studies have shown that the Piezo2 channel mediates coordinated mechanotransduction between Merkel cells and sensory neurons, further advancing our understanding of the mechanisms underlying mechanosensory neuron activation [ 15 , 16 ] .

Despite substantial progress in understanding the developmental mechanisms underlying mechanoreceptor formation, it remains unclear how the spatial organization of these receptors influences tactile function.
In particular, because receptor configurations are largely fixed during development, it is experimentally difficult to systematically compare alternative arrangements in living systems.
To address this limitation, this study proposes a biomimetic robotic framework that enables physical comparison between biologically motivated and counterfactual sensory arrangements by mimicking the layered structure of skin at the tissue level.
Here, “biologically motivated” refers to configurations designed to preserve qualitative organizational principles observed in biological receptor arrangements under physical constraints, rather than strict quantitative anatomical reproduction.
Specifically, we construct a biomimetic skin in which receptor-like sensors can be embedded in different configurations, thereby providing an experimental platform that allows comparative investigation of functional consequences, including configurations that are difficult to isolate and evaluate in biological systems.
This study aims to present an approach that enables empirical investigation, from a biomimetic robotics perspective, of how differences in spatial organization influence tactile function under controlled conditions.

Within this experimental framework, this study adopts physical experiments rather than simulation-based approaches.
This is because tactile phenomena such as sliding interactions involving stick–slip dynamics are difficult to model accurately.
In addition, another reason is that this study emphasizes a constructive approach in robotics, which assumes that certain system-level properties may only become apparent through physical implementation and experimental validation.

The skin is an organ that covers the entire body, from the trunk to the hands and plantar surfaces.
Although the density and functional properties of mechanoreceptors vary across different regions, several major types of mechanoreceptors are distributed across multiple skin areas and exhibit characteristic spatial organization corresponding to the layered structure of the skin.
In this study, we focus on representative mechanoreceptors that are present in both trunk and distal regions, namely Merkel cell complexes and Pacinian corpuscles, and examine their spatial arrangements to discuss aspects of sensory organization in the skin.

Numerous approaches have been developed in robotics and haptics research to achieve highly accurate tactile sensing through the integration of various technologies.
For example, BioTac, a fingertip sensor inspired by human tactile function [ 17 ] , consists of a flexible elastomeric skin filled with conductive fluid and equipped with multiple electrodes on its surface, and has been applied to studies of object recognition [ 18 , 19 ] .
Other examples include fingertip sensors embedded with strain gauges and PVDF films in random distributions [ 20 ] , and designs that place force sensors in deeper layers and accelerometers in more superficial layers [ 21 ] .
Advances have also been made in modular skin systems designed to cover the entire body of a robot, including conformable modules [ 22 ] and large-scale tactile sensing arrays composed of interconnected triangular or hexagonal modules [ 23 , 24 ] .
More recently, research on flexible sensors based on novel materials such as conductive polymers, gels, and liquid metals has accelerated [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] , and new sensing modalities, including electrical impedance and acoustic tomography, have also been proposed [ 28 ] .

However, most of these studies have focused on achieving advanced tactile functions or improving technical performance, and few have strictly mimicked the spatial arrangement of sensory receptors found in biological skin.
As a result, it has been difficult to deepen our understanding of biological sensory systems in ways that depend on how information changes with receptor placement.
For example, impedance tomography techniques, which measure electrical data between multiple electrodes, reconstruct the shape deformations of the skin but do not directly capture forces or strains at specific depths.
In contrast, this study emphasizes the spatial arrangement of the receptors and their corresponding mechanoreceptive properties.
We constructed a biomimetic skin that incorporates not only biological structures but also modified arrangements based on them, with the goal of advancing our understanding of sensory systems.
In particular, the fabricated biomimetic skin was quantitatively evaluated through tasks such as discrimination analogous to the two-point threshold, detection of fine pressure contacts, and recognition of different textures, thereby empirically verifying the impact of sensory receptor arrangements on tactile function.
Previous studies have often focused on the characteristics or developmental mechanisms of single types of receptors, and very few have addressed the functional significance of arrangements comprising multiple receptor types.
In contrast, this study considered the spatial distribution of multiple receptor types and comprehensively examines their functional effects.

This study is expected to provide insights from a biomimetic robotics perspective for the design of multimodal sensing systems by emulating and examining biologically motivated sensory arrangements that are thought to support interaction with the environment.
In addition, this work presents a biomimetic robotic approach to biological questions, in which physical models are used instead of living systems to enable comparative investigation not only of biologically motivated configurations but also of counterfactual configurations that are difficult to realize in vivo.
Such an approach may offer a constructive perspective for exploring functional constraints and possible adaptive factors underlying body organization, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of sensory arrangement in human skin and facilitating interdisciplinary research.

# 2 Material and Methods

## 2.1 Design and Implementation of the Biomimetic Skin

In this section, we describe a method for constructing a biomimetic skin using robotic techniques and the design principles of sensory receptor arrangements.
In biological skin, sensory receptors are primarily mechanoreceptors that respond to stimuli transmitted through the skin tissues.
To understand the organization of these receptors, it is essential to reproduce the layered structures of tissues through which mechanical stimuli propagate.
Accordingly, in this study, we constructed biomimetic skin at the tissue level using rubber and silicone, with an emphasis on replicating the layered architecture and elastic variations of biological skin.
Within this artificial skin, sensory elements were embedded not only in biomimetic configurations resembling biological arrangements, but also in modified arrangements, thereby enabling deeper investigation of sensory system organization.

Human skin is composed of three layers: epidermis, dermis, and subcutaneous tissue, and exhibits a gradient in stiffness, with outer layers being stiffer and inner layers softer.
However, owing to substantial inter-individual and regional variation, skin stiffness cannot be precisely represented by a single Shore hardness value [ 29 ] .
Based on previous biomimetic sensor studies [ 17 , 20 ] , we adopted silicone materials for the epidermis and selected a formulation with hardness comparable to that used in BioTac [ 17 ] .
Softer materials were selected for the deeper layers to reproduce the gradual reduction in stiffness.
The final materials used for each layer are as follows:

Epidermis: Dragon Skin 30 (silicone rubber, Shore hardness 30A, Smooth-On, Inc.)

Dermis: Ecoflex Gel 2 (silicone gel, Shore hardness 000–34, Smooth-On, Inc.)

Subcutaneous tissue: Soma Foama 15 (foamed silicone sponge, density 240 kg m − 3 240\text{\,}\mathrm{kg}\text{\,}{\mathrm{m}}^{-3} , Smooth-On, Inc.)

The cutaneous mechanoreceptors are extremely small and densely distributed [ 37 ] .
It is technically infeasible to reproduce all receptor types at the same density as that in human skin because of spatial constraints and current sensor limitations.
Therefore, in this study we focused on two receptor types that are broadly distributed across both trunk and fingertip skin: Merkel cells, which detect static pressure, and Pacinian corpuscles, which detect vibrations.
We aimed to enable macroscopic verification by constructing a simplified biomimetic skin incorporating these two receptors.
For Merkel cells, which are associated with slowly adapting type I (SA1) afferents and respond to sustained pressure, we used strain gauge sensors (General-purpose Foil Strain Gages, KYOWA ELECTRONIC INSTRUMENTS CO., LTD, Tokyo, Japan) whose resistance varies with applied pressure.
For Pacinian corpuscles, which are associated with rapidly adapting type II (RA2) afferents and respond exclusively to dynamic stimuli, we used MEMS accelerometers (MC3479, Memsic Inc., Shanghai, China).
By embedding these surrogate receptors within the biomimetic skin, we were able to acquire and analyze sensory signals specific to each arrangement (Fig. 1 c, Fig. 1 d).
Ruffini endings were excluded because morphological evidence remains limited [ 5 , 6 ] and they are thought to primarily encode skin stretch.
Meissner corpuscles were also excluded, as they are scarce outside the glabrous skin of the fingertips and soles [ 38 , 39 ] , and fine texture discrimination is known to be achievable via Pacinian corpuscles [ 40 ] .
Furthermore, the frequency response of the Meissner corpuscles is limited to approximately 50 Hz 50\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} , which predominantly contributes to slip detection, a range already covered by the accelerometers used here.

The strain gauges were 5 mm 5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} long, 1.4 mm 1.4\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} in width, and 14 µ ​ m 14\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} in thickness, and were connected to an Arduino MEGA [ 41 , 42 ] via a dedicated voltage divider circuit.
The accelerometers consisted of MEMS chips measuring 2 mm 2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} × \times 2 mm 2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} × \times 0.92 mm 0.92\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} , mounted on 10 mm 10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} square circuit boards, which were directly embedded in the skin.
Sensor data were transmitted from the Arduino MEGA to a PC via serial communication using Robot Operating System (ROS) middleware [ 43 ] .
The final sampling frequencies were approximately 360 Hz 360\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} for the strain gauges and 500 Hz 500\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} for the accelerometers, both of which encompassed the peak response ranges of the corresponding biological receptors.

In designing the sensory arrangements, the achievable spatial density is constrained by the sensor size and the need to avoid mechanical interference between sensors.
In this study, a 20 mm × 20 mm $20\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$\times$20\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$ skin block was used as the basic unit, and all sensors were arranged within this area.
Because Pacinian corpuscles (accelerometers) are larger than Merkel cells (strain gauge sensors), we first defined the placement of the accelerometers and then designed configuration patterns based on their depth within the skin.
Specifically, three configurations (A, B, and C) were constructed by placing the accelerometer at different depths: near the surface (epidermal side), from the deep dermis to the subcutaneous tissue, and in the deeper subcutaneous region.
Strain gauge sensors corresponding to Merkel cells were then distributed while avoiding spatial interference with both the accelerometer and other strain gauge sensors.
Within the 20 mm × 20 mm $20\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$\times$20\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$ skin block, it was determined that up to four strain gauge sensors could be placed per layer without introducing mechanical interference or directional bias, and this constraint was adopted as the basic design principle.
An overview of the configurations is shown in Fig. 1 e.
Here, “shallow” refers to the epidermal side, and “deep” refers to the subcutaneous side.

A: The accelerometer is placed near the surface (without being exposed), and four strain gauge sensors are distributed at deeper locations than the accelerometer.

B: The accelerometer is placed from the deep dermis to the subcutaneous tissue, and eight strain gauge sensors are distributed at shallower locations than the accelerometer.

C: The accelerometer is placed in the deeper subcutaneous region, and eight strain gauge sensors are distributed at shallower locations than the accelerometer.

## 2.2 Mechanical Characterization by Indentation Testing

To evaluate the mechanical properties of the constructed biomimetic skin, indentation tests were performed.
The test samples were fabricated following essentially the same layered construction described in Section 2.1 , except that the dermal papilla structure was omitted to reduce spatial variability in the indentation response.
Mechanical characterization was conducted using a tabletop universal testing machine (MCT-2150, A&D Company, Tokyo, Japan).

A rigid spherical indenter with a radius of R = 2.5 mm R=$2.5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}$ was pressed vertically into the sample surface from a non-contact state at a constant speed of 10.0 mm min − 1 10.0\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{min}}^{-1} .
The indenter was displaced and then returned to the initial position, forming a loading-unloading cycle.
This cycle was repeated ten times, and the force F F and displacement x x were continuously recorded.

The contact point x c x_{c} between the indenter and the sample was determined as the displacement at which the force first exceeded a threshold defined as the mean plus two standard deviations (mean + 2 ​ σ +2\sigma ) of the pre-contact region.
The indentation depth was then defined as δ = x − x c \delta=x-x_{c} .

The Young’s modulus of human skin has been reported over a wide range, typically from 10 kPa 10\text{\,}\mathrm{kPa} to 500 kPa 500\text{\,}\mathrm{kPa} , depending on the measurement method, model, and experimental conditions [ 44 , 45 , 46 , 47 ] .
In some cases, even higher values have been reported [ 48 ] .
Therefore, in this study, we estimate the reduced Young’s modulus E ∗ E^{*} from indentation tests and use it as an approximate indicator to evaluate whether the mechanical softness of the proposed biomimetic skin is comparable to that of human skin.
Since the thickness of skin varies depending on the measurement location and the adhesive properties of the materials differ from those of biological tissue, precise estimation of the intrinsic Young’s modulus is considered difficult.
Accordingly, the purpose of this analysis is limited to an approximate comparison.

In static indentation testing, the reduced Young’s modulus E ∗ E^{*} can be determined from the normal contact stiffness k z k_{z} , which is defined as the slope of the initial portion of the force-displacement curve.
Following previous studies [ 44 , 45 ] , the reduced modulus is given by

The tangent stiffness k z k_{z} was obtained from the derivative of a third-order polynomial fitted to the loading curve after contact:

The contact radius a a and projected contact area A A were geometrically estimated as

However, in this study, a spherical indenter with a radius of 2.5 mm 2.5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} was used, considering the experimental conditions in previous studies [ 45 ] .
Therefore, the condition δ ≪ R \delta\ll R is not strictly satisfied.
To address this, both the Hertzian approximation and the geometric estimation were used to calculate the reduced Young’s modulus E ∗ E^{*} , and the results were compared.

When adhesive effects are significant, the contact mechanics should be described using the Johnson–Kendall–Roberts (JKR) theory [ 49 ] .
However, no significant pull-off force was clearly observed in the present experiments, and therefore adhesive effects were considered to be negligible for the purpose of this analysis.

## 2.3 Two-point Discrimination Threshold Task

To ensure repeatability and reproducibility, we applied indentation stimuli to the skin using HIRO-NX, a dual-arm robot based on NEXTAGE (Kawada Industries Inc., Tokyo, Japan) designed for research use [ 50 ] .
Each arm of HIRO-NX has six degrees of freedom and provides high-precision motion, with a positioning repeatability of less than 30 µ ​ m 30\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} .
The robot is equipped with interchangeable end-effectors, and a six-axis force/torque sensor (IFS-50M31A25-I25, NITTA Corp., Osaka, Japan) was mounted on the wrist.
Appropriate tools were attached depending on the experimental task.
The robot was controlled using the open-source Robot Operating System (ROS) [ 43 ] .

The experimental setup is illustrated in Fig. 2 .
We prepared four types of end-effectors: one for single-point stimulation and three for two-point stimulation with inter-point distances of 5 mm 5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} , 10 mm 10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} , and 15 mm 15\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} .
For each receptor arrangement pattern, the end-effector was aligned with the center of the pattern, and random noise was added to both the rotation angle ( − 180 ° to 180 ° -180\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}180\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} ) and the position ( − 10 mm to 10 mm -10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} ).
The robot then performed repeated motions of pressing vertically onto the surface of the biomimetic skin and returned to its initial position.
Random noise of 0 mm to 3 mm 0\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}3\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} was also applied to the indentation depth, because pressing to a constant depth could allow discrimination based solely on subtle force differences between single- and two-point contacts.
For each condition, 100 indentation trials were performed and sensor data were collected.

To evaluate the performance, the collected sensor data were used in a classification task resembling the two-point discrimination threshold test, where the goal was to distinguish single-touch from multi-touch (two-point) stimuli.
After removing the initial offset values from each sensor signal, waveform peaks were extracted as features.
When no peaks were detected, zero padding was applied.
Using these features, we trained a Random Forest classifier using 200 decision trees.
Classification performance was evaluated using 5-fold stratified cross-validation, repeated three times with different random seeds, and reported as the mean accuracy and standard deviation across the 15 folds.

## 2.4 Small Force Detection Task

Human skin can detect even very slight contacts, whereas conventional force sensors typically used in robotics struggle to achieve this sensitivity.
In this experiment, we quantitatively evaluated the influence of receptor arrangement on the detection of subtle contact stimuli using HIRO-NX.
First, the reference position was defined as the robot height at which a sheet of paper could no longer pass between the end-effector of HIRO-NX and the biomimetic skin, and this height was recorded as the baseline.
For each receptor arrangement pattern, the end-effector was aligned with the center of the pattern, and random noise of − 10 mm to 10 mm -10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} was added to its position.
The robot then repeated 20 cycles of contact with the skin surface and returned to the initial position, during which sensor data were collected.

The collected waveform data were preprocessed in the same manner as in the two-point discrimination experiment, and contact was identified by detecting the peaks.
The number of detected peaks corresponded to the number of successful detections of subtle contacts.
However, because the skin behaves as a continuum, small responses may appear in sensors even when the stimulation point is not directly above them, but is transmitted through adjacent regions.
To improve the precision of the contact localization, it is desirable to distinguish such background responses from genuine small-force contacts.
For this purpose, a threshold was introduced in the peak detection step.
Specifically, during the two-point discrimination experiment, we statistically evaluated the sensor responses of a given receptor arrangement, whereas another arrangement was being pressed.
For example, when evaluating small force detection in Pattern C, the sensor responses of Pattern C during the stimulation of Pattern B were used as the reference baseline.
The mean ( μ \mu ) and standard deviation ( σ \sigma ) of these responses are summarized in Table 1 .
In this study, peaks exceeding μ + 2 ​ σ \mu+2\sigma were regarded as significant contact detections.

## 2.5 Passive Tactile Identification Task under Lateral Shear or Stroking Stimuli

In this experiment, we evaluated how receptor arrangements influence tactile sensing when stroking stimuli were applied to the biomimetic skin described in Section 2.1 .

To ensure reproducibility, we employed the dual-arm mobile robot PR2 [ 51 , 52 ] .
Although preliminary trials were conducted with HIRO-NX, it proved unsuitable for this task owing to its high mechanical stiffness and control gains, which introduced steady-state oscillations that propagated to the sensors.
In contrast, PR2 is equipped with a counterbalance mechanism that offsets the arm weight, has backdrivable and mechanically compliant joints, and operates with relatively low control gains, making it better suited for stroking experiments.
Each arm of PR2 has 7 degrees of freedom, allowing precise manipulation.
In this study, the gripper of one arm was modified to mount test materials with different surface textures, which were then stroked across the biomimetic skin.
The materials used were metal, cork, roughened cork, and cloth.
Each was fabricated in a cylindrical shape with a diameter of approximately 30 mm 30\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} , fixed to the gripper tip to prevent rotation, and gently stroked across the skin.
The roughened cork was prepared by lathe machining, and the cloth was wrapped around a cork cylinder to maintain the same overall diameter.

The experimental setup is shown in Fig. 3 a.
Because it is difficult to precisely define the moment of contact with soft skin, we defined “contact” as the state in which a sheet of paper could no longer pass between the robot gripper and biomimetic skin while the arm was slowly lowered.
The robot memorized the end-effector height at this contact point, and then performed stroking motions with an additional indentation of 3 mm 3\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} .
Although we attempted to ensure precise conditions by using the robot, it was challenging to perfectly align the initial state for each receptor arrangement when performing separate trials.
Therefore, as shown in Fig. 3 b, the stroking path was aligned along the midline across the three receptor arrangement patterns to reduce unintended variation between conditions, enabling the simultaneous comparison of all sensors under identical stimuli.
As depicted in Fig. 3 c, the end effector was first brought into contact and held until the transient effects from the initial impact dissipated, after which it was stroked across the skin surface and lifted away; this sequence was repeated five times.
To account for speed-dependent effects, trials were conducted at three different velocities: 2 cm s − 1 2\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} , 3 cm s − 1 3\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} , and 6 cm s − 1 6\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} .

Sensor data from the accelerometers were processed to extract the frequency-domain features corresponding to frictional interactions with the materials.
After subtracting the gravitational acceleration from each axis ( x , y , z x,y,z ), the lateral magnitude is computed as follows:

RMS (Root Mean Square) : overall signal energy

RMS (Root Mean Square) : overall signal energy

Dominant Frequency : frequency with maximum spectral energy

Spectral Centroid : weighted average of the spectrum

Spectral Bandwidth : spread around the dominant frequency

Zero-Crossing Rate (ZCR) : normalized count of sign changes

Using these features, we trained Random Forest classifiers to discriminate among the four materials.
The performance was evaluated by 5-fold cross-validation.
For each receptor arrangement pattern (A, B, and C), data from five repetitions per material were used.
Classifiers were trained separately for each stroking speed ( 2 cm s − 1 2\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} , 3 cm s − 1 3\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} , 6 cm s − 1 6\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1} ).

2026-10-20.title: RoboValue: A Fine-Grained Sim-and-Real Benchmark for Unified Evaluation of Robotic Value Models
2026-10-20.authors: Shengbang Liu , Zhengye Du , Zhilong Wan , Honghao Su , Chenxiang Xia , Chang Ge , Jinyang Xiao , Nan Wang , Zhipeng Hu , Huining Yuan , Shu'ang Yu , Yue Chen , Tianxing Chen , Chuankang Li , Maoqing Yao , Wenbo Ding , Yu Wang , Guanghui Ren , Chao Yu
2026-10-20.abstract: Robotic value models assess task execution from visual observations and instructions, providing feedback for policy learning and execution monitoring. However, existing evaluations cover only selected aspects of execution understanding, leaving the reliability of value feedback insufficiently tested. We introduce RoboValue, a fine-grained sim-and-real benchmark for unified evaluation of robotic value models. Its framework evaluates four complementary capability dimensions through shared interfaces: task-state understanding, temporal progress monitoring, failure and recovery reasoning, and value consistency. Diagnostic trajectories and instruction variations test whether value judgments accurately reflect task requirements and changes throughout execution. RoboValue-Dataset covers 15 simulation and 20 real-world manipulation tasks, providing expert demonstrations for training and annotated trajectories for fine-grained evaluation. We evaluate representative robotic value models in zero-shot and one-shot settings under standard conditions and separate shifts in robot embodiment and environment. Our results reveal errors in fine-grained instruction grounding, history-dependent progress tracking, and recovery assessment, even in models with strong outcome and forward-progress scores. The same semantic subtask can also receive substantially different value gains across valid execution orders. These findings identify concrete targets for value supervision, while the dataset and public leaderboard support continued assessment of feedback reliability. 2026-10-20.title: EgoRayFormer: Ray-Space Stereo Refinement for Egocentric 3D Human Pose Estimation
2026-10-20.authors: Haozhe Wang , Songyuan Wu , Jihai Xu , Jie Zhao
2026-10-20.abstract:
Head-mounted stereo fisheye cameras provide a compact view of the wearer’s body, but strong distortion, partial
visibility and a short baseline make 3D pose estimation difficult. Existing refinement decoders sample image features
independently in each view, without requiring the samples to correspond to a common 3D hypothesis. We introduce
EgoRayFormer, a causal pose estimator that couples stereo feature sampling and geometric refinement in ray space.
For each joint, the decoder projects shared 3D hypotheses along and around its viewing ray into both images.
A geometric branch then corrects the projected joint locations and intersects the resulting rays; a learned gate
blends this geometric estimate with a learned pose update. This formulation introduces an explicit stereo constraint
while retaining flexibility when the rays provide weak depth constraints.
In local evaluations on the official device-relative test splits, EgoRayFormer achieves three-seed mean MPJPEs of
17.64  mm on UnrealEgo2 and 49.55  mm on UnrealEgo-RW, improving to 47.57  mm with
UnrealEgo2 pre-training. In paired validation ablations, removing the geometric branch increases MPJPE in all three
seeds at both input resolutions. With a common ResNet-18 encoder and input resolution, our system reduces RW test
MPJPE by 9.09  mm relative to the device-relative EgoPoseFormer baseline. A separate protocol analysis
quantifies the difference between device-relative and oracle-root evaluation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Estimating the wearer’s body pose from headset-mounted cameras enables avatar animation and interaction without
external cameras [ 24 , 35 , 28 , 9 ] . A pair of downward-looking
fisheye cameras offers wide coverage in a compact rig [ 37 , 1 , 2 ] , but
the resulting images are difficult to interpret. Limbs appear foreshortened, distal joints occupy few pixels, and body
parts are frequently occluded or outside the field of view. The short stereo baseline adds a geometric difficulty:
for cameras about 12 cm apart, the rays to a joint 1.5 m away meet at an angle of only about five degrees.
Accurate reconstruction therefore requires both useful image evidence and a way to handle weak geometric constraints.

Recent pose decoders refine a coarse 3D estimate by sampling features near its image
projections [ 36 , 16 , 4 ] . This design concentrates computation around
the body, but the sampling offsets are predicted independently for each view. The sampled image locations need not
be projections of a common 3D hypothesis, leaving the relation between the two views implicit in feature fusion.
Direct triangulation provides an explicit relation, yet small localisation errors can produce large depth errors
when the viewing rays are nearly parallel. These observations motivate a refinement step that connects stereo
sampling to 3D geometry while retaining a learned alternative to the geometric estimate.

We propose EgoRayFormer, a causal decoder for stereo fisheye pose estimation. Each refinement layer places shared 3D
hypotheses in a local coordinate frame aligned with the ray from the device to a joint. Projecting each hypothesis
into both cameras couples the locations at which the two feature maps are sampled. From these features, a geometric
branch predicts per-view corrections, computes a differentiable intersection of the corrected rays, and blends the
result with a learned pose update. The complete model combines this refinement with a stereo image encoder and causal
temporal attention, and predicts joint coordinates relative to the device without ground-truth inputs at inference.

Our evaluation distinguishes system performance from evidence about individual components. On the official test
splits, local three-seed evaluations give MPJPEs of 17.64  mm on UnrealEgo2, 49.55  mm on
UnrealEgo-RW with RW-only training, and 47.57  mm with UnrealEgo2 pre-training. With ResNet-18 and matched
input resolution, EgoRayFormer has a 9.09  mm lower RW test MPJPE than our device-relative adaptation of the official
EgoPoseFormer code. This compares complete systems, including their temporal context and training recipes.
More specifically, removing the geometric branch increases validation MPJPE by 0.92  mm at 384 2 384^{2} and
2.34  mm at 256 2 256^{2} , with the same direction in every paired seed. These ablations support the branch as a
whole.

Evaluation coordinates also matter. Device-relative estimation requires the model to recover body position relative
to the headset, whereas root-relative scoring removes global body translation. Some pipelines additionally use the
root to project decoder anchors into the images. We therefore state the inference inputs and scoring coordinates
for each comparison, and measure the complete device/oracle-root protocol gap using one architecture.
Published leaderboard values provide external context, with the unresolved RW split correspondence stated alongside
the comparison ( Sec. 4.2 ). Earlier development use of the public test sets is disclosed in Secs. 4.1 and A .

Our contributions are:

A ray-space refinement decoder that couples stereo sampling through shared 3D hypotheses and combines
corrected-ray intersection with a learned pose update.

A multi-seed evaluation on UnrealEgo2 and UnrealEgo-RW, including comparisons at a common backbone and
resolution, paired ablations of the geometric branch, and analysis of residual errors and gate behaviour.

A paired analysis of device-relative and oracle-root protocols that quantifies their combined effect for
a fixed architecture and clarifies the interpretation of cross-protocol results.

1. A ray-space refinement decoder that couples stereo sampling through shared 3D hypotheses and combines
corrected-ray intersection with a learned pose update.

2. A multi-seed evaluation on UnrealEgo2 and UnrealEgo-RW, including comparisons at a common backbone and
resolution, paired ablations of the geometric branch, and analysis of residual errors and gate behaviour.

3. A paired analysis of device-relative and oracle-root protocols that quantifies their combined effect for
a fixed architecture and clarifies the interpretation of cross-protocol results.

# 2 Related Work

Early systems estimated body pose from helmet- or cap-mounted fisheye
cameras [ 24 , 35 ] , followed by headset-mounted monocular
methods [ 28 , 29 ] , scene-aware models [ 30 ] , and fisheye-specific
representations [ 31 ] . Stereo approaches such as EgoGlass [ 37 ] ,
UnrealEgo [ 1 ] , Ego3DPose [ 11 ] and EgoTAP [ 10 ] lift per-view
2D heatmaps to 3D. Akada et al . [ 2 ] introduced UnrealEgo2 and UnrealEgo-RW and used scene depth
from structure-from-motion to support video-based estimation. Rear cameras [ 3 ] and headset
pose [ 5 ] provide additional observations in other capture settings.

Our decoder builds on the proposal-and-refinement design of EgoPoseFormer [ 36 ] , whose
deformable attention samples features around projected joints. EgoPoseFormer v2 [ 16 ] adds
causal temporal attention, per-joint uncertainty and auto-labelling for a four-camera headset.
TSR-Ego [ 4 ] combines causal mixing of stereo feature maps with temporal, joint and per-view
deformable attention. We instead tie the sampling locations across views to shared 3D hypotheses and use corrected-ray
intersection within the refinement step. This distinction concerns the spatial update; causal attention and the
coarse-to-fine architecture have precedents in these methods.

Learnable triangulation [ 8 ] combines calibrated views through algebraic or volumetric
triangulation. MvP [ 33 ] uses projective attention, while MVGFormer [ 17 ] alternates
learned 2D corrections and confidences with weighted triangulation. In multi-camera detection,
PETR [ 20 ] encodes 3D position and BEVFormer [ 15 ] projects reference points into camera
views. Sparse4D [ 18 ] projects shared 3D keypoints into multiple feature maps, providing a direct
precedent for our shared-hypothesis sampling; RayDN [ 19 ] uses ray-based samples for denoising.
EgoRayFormer adapts shared spatial hypotheses and geometric refinement to a two-camera fisheye rig. The hypotheses are
organised in a ray-local frame, and the geometric estimate is blended with a learned update to accommodate the
weak depth constraints of the short baseline.

FisheyeViT [ 31 ] represents fisheye images using undistorted tangent-plane patches. We adopt
this tokenisation with ray-direction inputs and stereo cross-view blocks inspired by CroCo and
DUSt3R [ 34 , 32 ] , using a DINOv3 backbone [ 26 , 23 ] .
Other camera-aware transformers incorporate geometry through relative positional
encoding [ 22 , 13 ] . We use absolute viewing-ray channels and evaluate the additional encoder
components together against a plain DINOv3 encoder ( Sec. 4.4 ).

The UnrealEgo2 and UnrealEgo-RW benchmarks [ 2 ] evaluate device-relative joint coordinates.
Root-relative scoring, also common in third-person pose estimation [ 7 ] , removes global body
translation. This scoring choice is distinct from supplying a root position to the model. The public EgoPoseFormer
implementation for UnrealEgo uses the ground-truth pelvis as the projection origin; TSR-Ego reports root-relative
results without specifying whether its inference-time root is predicted or ground truth. We keep these distinctions

2026-10-20.title: CAOS-SLAM: Class-Agnostic Object-Aware Real-Time vSLAM for Dynamic Environments
2026-10-20.authors: Gaia Borghi , João Carlos Virgolino Soares , Angelo Bratta , Shahab Heshmati-Alamdari , Claudio Semini
2026-10-20.abstract:
Robust visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM) in dynamic environments faces challenges due to the presence of moving objects that may introduce erroneous observations, corrupt the map reconstruction and overall degrade localization accuracy. Existing vSLAM approaches often rely on predefined semantic classes or costly pixel-wise classification, limiting their robustness or applicability in real-world scenarios. This paper presents CAOS-SLAM, a dynamic vSLAM framework that extends ORB-SLAM3 with a hybrid perception pipeline to detect, track, and filter both semantically known and previously unseen moving objects in real-time. On-demand panoptic segmentation is performed for object discovery, with candidate unknown objects instantiated through depth-based clustering of unclassified regions. Between panoptic updates, persistent object tracks are updated using lightweight detection when available or temporal mask propagation based on world-frame Kalman prediction, depth consistency, and appearance similarity. The estimated object motion is then used to reject dynamic features from the SLAM pipeline. Experimental results on multiple dynamic RGB-D datasets and real-world experiments demonstrate improved localization accuracy over state-of-the-art dynamic vSLAM approaches, achieving up to 59% lower localization error in scenes characterized by unknown dynamic objects and up to 88% lower error in heavily occluded scenes, while achieving a median processing rate of 30 FPS on a laptop. Furthermore, the tracking module provides estimates of object trajectories and velocities, supporting potential future applications in perception, navigation, and motion-planning tasks in dynamic environments.
Code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM) has become a fundamental component for autonomous robots and intelligent systems operating in unknown environments. vSLAM enables robots and autonomous devices to estimate their pose inside an unknown environment, while progressively reconstructing the surroundings only relying on visual data, without external sensors.

Despite significant progress in recent years, vSLAM systems still face notable challenges when deployed in real-world scenarios. The presence of moving objects reduces the availability of reliable static features, which might lead to incorrect data association, localization drift and degraded tracking performance [ 1 ] . Many recent approaches use object detection or instance segmentation models to identify and filter dynamic features [ 2 ] [ 3 ] [ 4 ] . While these methods can achieve real-time or close to real-time performance, they inherently depend on predefined semantic classes. As a consequence, their ability to be generalized into unseen or unfamiliar scenarios is limited, especially when dynamic objects fall outside the categories on which the network was trained [ 5 ] [ 6 ] , [ 7 ] .

Class-agnostic approaches aim to overcome these limitations by detecting motion without relying on semantic labels. These methods often combine deep learning with geometric cues and optical flow. These methods improve generalization to arbitrary dynamic objects, but this robustness comes with a high computational cost, which hinders their applicability in real-time systems [ 8 ] , [ 9 ] , [ 10 ] .

In this work, we address the trade-off between class-agnostic robustness and real-time performance by proposing CAOS-SLAM, a C lass- A gnostic O bject-aware dynamic v S LAM framework (Fig. 1 ). Our approach relies on a panoptic segmentation model that provides object-level masks. To reduce dependency on predefined semantic categories, the framework processes regions that are not assigned to any known panoptic classes, using RGB-D information to instantiate candidate unknown objects.
However, running panoptic segmentation on every frame can introduce a substantial computational overhead, making real-time operation challenging [ 11 ] . Therefore, our approach combines panoptic segmentation with a lightweight temporal mask propagation strategy. This design enables class-agnostic dynamic object detection and tracking while significantly reducing the computational cost associated with panoptic perception, allowing the complete vSLAM system to operate in real time.
The key contributions of the proposed implementation are as follows:

Class-agnostic dynamic reasoning: We introduce a perception framework that combines panoptic segmentation with RGB-D geometric reasoning to detect both known and unknown objects. Unclassified regions are separated into individual object instances through depth-based clustering, enabling dynamic object reasoning beyond predefined semantic classes.

Object-centric temporal propagation: The proposed system decouples object discovery from tracking to avoid running costly panoptic inference at every frame. The system maintains an explicit per-object state and propagates object masks between panoptic observations through Kalman filter prediction combined with depth and appearance consistency, keeping object states updated while preserving real-time operation.

Integrated dynamic object tracking: Unlike previous tracking-based methods, which are limited to predefined semantic categories [ 12 , 13 ] or rely on computationally expensive formulations [ 14 ] , our system tracks both known and unknown objects and estimates their motion in the world frame. It runs in real time on a laptop, providing object-level information that can support other tasks such as navigation and obstacle avoidance.

Extensive Validation: Experiments on multiple dynamic RGB-D datasets and real-world scenarios demonstrated improved localization accuracy and robustness in dynamic and heavily occluded scenes, including up to 59% lower localization error for unknown dynamic objects and up to 88% lower error under severe occlusions, compared to other SOTA methods.

Additionally, the code and the recorded dataset will be released upon acceptance.

2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Literature Review

Traditional visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (vSLAM) systems, such as ORB SLAM3 [ 15 ] , rely on the assumption of static environments. This assumption leads to severe performance degradation in real-world scenarios where moving objects confound data association, cause significant localization drift, and corrupt the 3D map. This issue becomes particularly critical in highly dynamic scenes where the number of reliable static features for pose estimation is severely limited [ 1 , 10 , 16 ] . Consequently, research has focused on identifying, modeling and filtering dynamic entities, to ensure tracking robustness and map reliability [ 1 ] , [ 2 ] , [ 10 ] . Despite significant progress, achieving robust, universal, and real-time dynamic vSLAM remains an open problem.

A prominent direction in the vSLAM field relies on semantic information obtained from deep learning methods to identify and remove dynamic regions. Representative examples include NGD-SLAM [ 2 ] , DRV-SLAM [ 3 ] , SDT-SLAM [ 7 ] , CD-SLAM [ 17 ] and the method proposed by Su et al. [ 5 ] , which combine object detection or instance segmentation with geometric or motion constraints. While these approaches can achieve real-time performance and high accuracy, they are limited by the ability of the network to detect objects. Therefore, they rely on predefined object classes (e.g. humans, chairs, cars) and often fail to handle arbitrary moving objects like robots or manipulated furniture.

To overcome the limitations of semantic priors, a second line of research adopts class-agnostic motion reasoning. PS SLAM [ 16 ] and Panoptic SLAM [ 11 ] utilize Panoptic segmentation models and epipolar geometry to detect and filter features from known and unknown dynamic areas. However, they are highly sensitive to the panoptic model accuracy and incur significant computational overhead.
To enhance generalization, other approaches, such as OSP-SLAM [ 10 ] and RSO-SLAM [ 1 ] , combine optical flow, segmentation, and geometric motion reasoning. However, they typically require computationally demanding perception modules that limit real-time performance on onboard platforms. As a result, a practical trade-off emerges between real-time operation and real-world robustness. Methods that achieve real-time performance often do so by sacrificing universality and relying on lightweight semantic models [ 4 , 7 , 5 ] , whereas more general approaches rely on computationally expensive panoptic segmentation or motion estimation [ 1 , 11 , 10 ] . CAOS-SLAM addresses these limitations by combining class-agnostic object discovery with lightweight temporal tracking, aiming to achieve both the generalization capabilities required for real-world environments and the computational efficiency required for real-time vSLAM.

Efficiency on onboard platforms remains a key challenge for real-world deployment.
Recent work reduces inference cost via temporal mask propagation [ 2 , 10 , 18 ] and by decoupling semantic inference from tracking [ 2 , 19 ] .
NGD-SLAM [ 2 ] tracks keypoints from the latest mask to the current frame with optical flow, reaching 60 FPS on a laptop CPU. NSDM-SLAM [ 19 ] decouples semantic recognition from tracking through a non-blocking buffer. As both works acknowledge, masks propagated from earlier frames can miss newly appearing objects and degrade under fast scene changes. CAOS-SLAM, instead of relying on buffered masks, invokes the panoptic model only when object discovery is required.

Another challenge arises when the scene is highly dynamic. The number of remaining static features can be insufficient for accurate localization. To improve feature matching, DRV-SLAM [ 3 ] adapts the number of extracted features, OSP-SLAM [ 10 ] uses a deep learning network for feature extraction and matching, and PS-SLAM [ 16 ] introduces semantic-aware feature descriptors. Our approach is complementary: by detecting dynamic obstruction as soon as their motion becomes observable, it aims to reduce the number of dynamic artifacts in the map, so that the system can re-localize and subsequently correct drift through loop closure, once the obstruction is gone.

Beyond improving localization, dynamic object tracking provides valuable information for scene understanding and navigation. Rather than treating dynamic entities solely as outliers to be removed [ 14 ] , recent approaches exploit object motion as an additional source of information. DynaSLAM II [ 12 ] proposes a tightly coupled framework in which camera poses improve object state estimations, while object poses provide additional constraints for camera localization. Similarly, DynoSAM [ 14 ] and DOT [ 13 ] jointly estimate camera and object trajectories. Although these approaches still face the real-time versus robustness trade-off discussed above, the object-level information they provide can benefit other robotic tasks such as navigation and obstacle avoidance.

2026-10-20.title: A Probabilistic, Rotation-Preserving Kernel Operator Surrogate for Continuum-Robot Design Spaces
2026-10-20.authors: Branden Frieden , Alan Kuntz , Varun Shankar
2026-10-20.comment: Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
2026-10-20.abstract:
We develop an uncertainty-aware, operator-learning-based surrogate for
tendon-driven continuum robots (TDCRs) that generalizes across robot design
and actuation while predicting the complete equilibrium configuration.
Our central idea is a nonstationary Gaussian-process (GP) kernel whose metric
is learned by a shallow neural network from mechanics-aware design
coordinates. The network learns how similarity changes across design space,
while the resulting kernel defines the design-to-pose operator, its posterior
uncertainty, and a criterion for sequential simulator acquisition. We represent
backbone position and rotational strain with spatial kernels and reconstruct
orientation directly on S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) SO(3) , preserving valid material frames and tendon
geometry. We use ASkotch with Nyström preconditioning for scalable kernel operator
solves and a separate Nyström approximation for posterior covariance.
Experiments show that kernel-coverage acquisition reduces mean trajectory
error by approximately 15 % 15\% relative to IID sampling, while posterior
variance increases for increasingly unsupported designs. Compared with prior
neural-operator TDCR models, the method is 30–50% more accurate using
approximately 5 × 5\times fewer training designs while additionally providing
posterior uncertainty estimates.
2026-10-20.introduction:
A continuum-robot surrogate becomes substantially more useful when it spans robot design as well as actuation, returns the complete equilibrium
shape, and indicates when a query is poorly supported by data. Tendon-driven
continuum robots (TDCRs) are attractive for minimally invasive surgery and
confined-space manipulation because of their compact actuation and large,
smooth deformations [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Geometrically exact Cosserat-rod models capture tendon
loading, backbone mechanics, and routing geometry [ 4 , 5 ] , but repeated
boundary-value solves become costly in planning, control, uncertainty analysis,
and design optimization [ 6 ] . In this work, we
focus on operator-learning-based, uncertainty-aware surrogate models for TDCRs
that take design and actuation parameters as inputs and supply full
backbone/material-frame pose and routed tendon trajectories as outputs, together
with posterior uncertainty estimates; see Figure 1 .

Operator learning has recently been leveraged in several robotics applications.
Examples include DeepONet-type inverse load reconstruction for Cosserat rods [ 7 ] , neural operators for full-shape soft-robot inverse
kinematics [ 8 ] , and design-space neural
operators for TDCR equilibria [ 9 ] .
However, neural operators do not typically come with uncertainty estimates,
requiring reformulation, ensembles, or post-hoc modifications [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] . Gaussian processes (GPs) offer an inherently uncertainty-aware alternative, with growing interesting on GP-based operator-learning methods for PDEs [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . GPs also provide uncertainty-aware models for
continuum-robot pose and strain estimation on S ​ E ​ ( 3 ) SE(3) [ 20 ] , forward and inverse kinematics [ 21 ] , and online probabilistic control [ 22 ] ; more broadly, GP uncertainty supports
data-efficient robot learning [ 23 ] . These
approaches primarily learn state, kinematic, or control maps for a fixed robot.

In this work, we present a probabilistic kernel/GP surrogate model for TDCRs
whose metric is learned by a neural network . We use a small shallow neural network maps mechanics-aware coordinates to local blockwise kernel shapes, which define a positive-definite
nonstationary Matérn covariance kernel [ 24 ] . The
network never predicts the robot pose: it learns how similarity changes across
design space. The resulting kernel simultaneously defines the design-to-pose
operator, its GP uncertainty, and a kernel-coverage criterion for acquiring new
simulator data.

We also build the output representation to respect the mechanics. Spatial kernel
coefficients represent dimensionless backbone position and rotational strain;
we integrate the predicted strain to reconstruct orientation directly on S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) SO(3) , then recover tendon paths analytically from the routing geometry. We
focus on four-tendon TDCRs and enforce the corresponding symmetry in both the
learned metric and prediction. For scalability, we use
ASkotch [ 25 ] with a Nyström preconditioner to solve the kernel
systems associated with the GP mean, and we use an independent Nyström
construction to approximate the posterior covariance. We then propagate both
design-space and spatial uncertainties to Cartesian covariance tubes around the
TDCR.

Our experimental results show that kernel-coverage acquisition reduces mean
trajectory error by approximately 15 % 15\% relative to IID acquisition over the
tested training sizes. We also find that the GP posterior variance increases
systematically as designs move away from the training distribution. The overall
method is 30–50% more accurate, using approximately 5 × 5\times fewer training
designs, than prior neural-operator work for TDCRs [ 9 ] , while also providing posterior
uncertainty estimates.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows.
Section III develops the kernel operator surrogate,
including the rotation-preserving pose representation, mechanics-aware design
coordinates, learned nonstationary kernel metric, sequential acquisition, and
scalable mean and covariance calculations. Section IV evaluates
prediction accuracy, active acquisition, scalable kernel solves, posterior
uncertainty, and Cartesian uncertainty propagation. We conclude with the main
findings and directions for future work.

2026-10-20.title: HAF-VLA: Hierarchical Action Flow Framework for Humanoid Vision-Language-Action Control
2026-10-20.authors: Langzhe Gu , Chengkai Hou , Meng Li , Xinhua Wang , Xinyuan Lv , Shuanghao Bai , Guangrun Li , Jingyang He , Ziluo Ding , Zhiyuan Xu , Ning Ding , Kuan Cheng , Jian Tang , Shanghang Zhang , Zhengping Che
2026-10-20.abstract: Humanoid robots hold great promise as general-purpose agents in human-centered environments, yet adapting generalist vision-language-action (VLA) policies to real-world humanoid loco-manipulation remains challenging. Unlike fixed-base or wheeled manipulators, humanoids must coordinate locomotion, posture, gaze, and dual-arm manipulation over a high-dimensional whole-body action space, where inaccurate base or waist motions can easily induce unstable and aggressive upper-body compensation. We propose HAF-VLA, a hierarchical action-flow framework for humanoid VLA control. Built upon a pretrained flow-matching VLA, HAF-VLA inherits the vision-language prefix encoder and action expert weights, and adapts them to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation with learnable stage embeddings and cross-stage KV-cache conditioning. Instead of generating the full action chunk in a single pass, HAF-VLA progressively denoises a shared whole-body action space: first locomotion and head commands, then waist refinement, and finally full-body manipulation. To preserve structural dependencies across stages, we introduce a cross-stage KV cache conditioning mechanism, enabling subsequent action generation stages to refine and augment their outputs based on the action representations from preceding stages. Experimental results across six real-world tasks demonstrate that our framework significantly enhances the performance of existing models in humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, demonstrating an effective pathway for adapting strong mobile-manipulation VLAs to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Humanoid robots hold the promise of becoming general-purpose agents capable of operating in human-centered environments. Unlike fixed-base or wheeled robots, humanoids must coordinate locomotion, waist motion, gaze, and dual-arm manipulation to navigate large spaces, adjust posture, maintain balance, and physically interact with the environment [ 2 , 37 , 20 , 31 , 12 , 22 , 35 , 13 ] . This whole-body nature makes humanoid loco-manipulation fundamentally different from conventional manipulation: inaccurate base or waist motions can force the upper body to produce compensatory movements, degrading precision, stability, and energy efficiency.

Recent vision-language-action models and world-action models have achieved strong results on fixed-base, dual-arm, and wheeled mobile manipulators [ 4 , 11 , 27 , 16 , 15 , 7 ] . However, most of them are not explicitly designed for the structured action space and unstable bipedal dynamics of humanoids. Directly applying a single-stage action generator to humanoid loco-manipulation may entangle locomotion, posture, and manipulation in an unstructured manner, making the policy prone to unstable base motions or aggressive upper-body compensation [ 12 , 22 , 8 , 38 ] . Therefore, humanoid VLA control requires an action-generation structure that respects the kinematic dependencies among the legs, waist, head, and arms while preserving the semantic reasoning ability of pretrained VLA models.

To this end, we propose HAF-VLA, a hierarchical action-flow framework for humanoid vision-language-action control. Built upon a pretrained flow-matching VLA [ 11 ] , HAF-VLA reuses its vision-language prefix encoder [ 3 ] and action expert weights, and adapts them to humanoid whole-body loco-manipulation through progressive action generation. Instead of synthesizing the full action chunk in a single pass, HAF-VLA first generates locomotion and head commands, then incorporates waist refinement, and finally produces full-body manipulation actions. This design encourages locomotion-related motions to be planned before manipulation, reducing the tendency of the upper body to compensate for inaccurate base or waist movements [ 5 , 14 ] .

We further introduce cross-stage KV-cache [ 21 ] conditioning to propagate structured action information across the hierarchy (see Fig. 1 (b)). After each non-final stage completes flow denoising [ 23 ] , its clean action prediction is re-encoded by the shared action expert to form an action KV cache, which conditions the following stage. In this way, later stages refine and augment their actions based on earlier motion plans, while all stages remain grounded in the same visual-language prefix representation.

We evaluate HAF-VLA on two full-sized humanoid platforms, Tian Gong 3.0 and Tian Gong 2.0, across six real-world loco-manipulation tasks spanning household and industrial scenarios (see Fig. 1 (a)). HAF-VLA consistently improves normalized task scores over imitation-learning, VLA, and world-model baselines (see Fig. 1 (c)), especially on tasks requiring long-distance locomotion, precise body positioning, and coordinated whole-body manipulation. Our contributions are: (i) a hierarchical action-flow formulation for humanoid VLA loco-manipulation over a shared whole-body action space; (ii) a cross-stage KV-cache conditioning mechanism for progressive whole-body action generation; and (iii) real-world validation showing that this structure effectively adapts pretrained mobile-manipulation VLAs to humanoid loco-manipulation.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-language-action models. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) aim to map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions [ 24 , 17 , 40 , 32 ] . Representative works such as RT-2 [ 41 ] and OpenVLA [ 17 ] show that vision-language pretraining can be effectively transferred to robotic manipulation, while π 0 \pi_{0} and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} further move toward continuous generative action modeling with flow matching [ 4 , 11 ] . However, most existing VLAs still focus on tabletop tasks or mobile manipulators, leaving high-dimensional humanoid whole-body action generation underexplored.

Humanoid VLAs. Recent works have begun to extend VLAs to humanoid robots [ 30 , 34 , 6 , 1 ] . GR00T N1.7 [ 27 ] studies general-purpose humanoid action generation from vision-language inputs, while WholeBodyVLA [ 13 ] explores latent VLA learning for large-space humanoid mobile manipulation. Recently, Ψ 0 \Psi_{0} [ 33 ] introduced an open humanoid foundation model pretrained from egocentric human videos. In contrast to methods that rely on latent skills, cross-embodiment transfer, or learning from human videos, our method is directly built upon a pretrained generalist VLA and improves its performance on humanoid by generating structured whole-body actions grounded in the humanoid forward-kinematic chain, sparing the computational cost of training a new model.

Whole-body manipulation. Recent advances in humanoid whole-body control have greatly expanded the motion repertoire of legged humanoids [ 22 , 26 , 19 , 28 ] . With improved reinforcement learning and low-level control techniques, humanoid robots can now perform highly dynamic behaviors. Nevertheless, extending these capabilities to generalizable loco-manipulation remains substantially more challenging. Works such as TWIST2 [ 36 ] and AMO [ 18 ] demonstrate the potential of VR-based teleoperation for whole-body humanoid control and data collection. However, their focus is mainly on teleoperation interfaces and low-level control pipelines, rather than learning a generalizable policy for long-horizon loco-manipulation.

2026-10-20.title: Learning Wheel Motion Uncertainty for Degeneracy-Aware LiDAR-Inertial Odometry on Quadrupedal Wheel-Legged Robots
2026-10-20.authors: Hairuo Wei , Yunfan Ren , Renda Yang , Qiangsheng Huang , Zhongyu Li
2026-10-20.abstract:
Wheel kinematics can support odometry for quadrupedal wheel-legged robots when LiDAR geometry provides weak motion constraints.
However, slip and contact loss make rolling predictions unreliable, and contact state alone cannot determine their reliability across motion directions.
We propose a tightly coupled LiDAR–inertial–kinematic odometry framework that retains analytical rolling predictions and learns per-wheel, direction-dependent process covariances from proprioceptive history.
The estimator maintains moving wheel-center states, allowing the learned uncertainty to regulate the influence of rolling predictions through forward-kinematic corrections.
Degeneracy-aware projection (DAP) complements this mechanism by suppressing LiDAR constraints along geometrically weak directions.
The learned covariance network (CovNet) is trained through a differentiable filter using simulated velocity supervision and deployed on the real robot without fine-tuning.
On the six room sequences with the highest degeneracy ratios in our indoor dataset, the method reduces mean per-sequence position root mean square error (RMSE) by 66.2% relative to FAST-LIO2 and by 31.0% relative to a fixed-covariance variant.
In a severely degenerate corridor run, it achieves an endpoint position error of 0.198 m, compared with 7.531 m for FAST-LIO2.
These results demonstrate robust odometry under challenging geometric and wheel-motion conditions.
We plan to publicly release our code and multimodal dataset.
Project website: https://weihairuo.github.io/wheel-motion-uncertainty/ .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Quadrupedal wheel-legged robots (Fig. 1 ) combine efficient rolling with the ability to traverse uneven terrain [ 1 , 2 ] .
Reliable state estimation is essential for their control, navigation, and mapping.
LiDAR–inertial odometry (LIO) provides accurate motion estimates when the environment contains sufficient geometric features [ 3 , 4 ] .
However, corridors, tunnels, and open areas may provide weak geometric constraints along certain motion directions.
This can make LiDAR registration ill-conditioned and sensitive to noise [ 5 ] .
Joint and wheel encoders provide an additional source of motion information that can support state estimation in these conditions.

Using wheel kinematics to support LIO on quadrupedal wheel-legged robots presents two related challenges.
First, the reliability of each wheel’s rolling prediction varies with its ground interaction and across motion directions.
Conventional wheel odometry commonly assumes a rigid chassis [ 6 ] , while contact-aided legged estimators often assume stationary stance feet [ 7 , 8 ] .
For articulated wheel-legs, forward kinematics (FK) describes each wheel center’s position relative to the body, while a rolling model predicts its motion in the global frame .
Slip, contact loss, and unloaded wheel spin can reduce the reliability of this prediction without invalidating the relative position obtained from FK.
Contact state alone is insufficient to determine reliability: a supported wheel may still slip, with different errors across motion directions.
Second, LiDAR updates must account for direction-dependent geometric weakness while retaining useful measurement information.
Reliable wheel-motion constraints can support estimation along geometrically weak directions, while informative LiDAR measurements can limit drift when rolling predictions become unreliable.
Exploiting this complementarity requires accounting for both wheel-motion uncertainty and the directional weakness of LiDAR constraints.

Existing methods incorporate wheel constraints and adaptive weighting [ 6 , 9 ] , estimate leg-odometry bias [ 10 ] , or introduce wheel-legged kinematic and terrain models [ 1 , 2 ] .
Learning-based approaches estimate contact states, correct kinematic measurements, or learn motion models online [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
Differentiable filtering also enables uncertainty models to be learned from state-estimation objectives [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] .
For a wheel center, nominal motion persists even during ideal rolling, so uncertainty must describe deviations from that motion.
The resulting wheel-motion constraints must be fused with LiDAR information whose reliability varies across pose directions.

We propose a tightly coupled LiDAR–inertial–kinematic odometry framework for quadrupedal wheel-legged robots.
The framework combines analytical rolling predictions with learned wheel-motion uncertainty and degeneracy-aware LiDAR updates.
The main contributions of this work are:

A tightly coupled LiDAR–inertial–kinematic estimator with persistent wheel-center states, reducing mean per-sequence position root mean square error (RMSE) by 66.2% relative to FAST-LIO2 and by 40.4% relative to the model-based NCDM baseline on the six room sequences with the highest degeneracy ratios.

A tightly coupled LiDAR–inertial–kinematic estimator with persistent wheel-center states, reducing mean per-sequence position root mean square error (RMSE) by 66.2% relative to FAST-LIO2 and by 40.4% relative to the model-based NCDM baseline on the six room sequences with the highest degeneracy ratios.

A learning-based approach that estimates per-wheel, direction-dependent rolling-motion uncertainty from proprioceptive history to adaptively weight analytical rolling predictions.

A degeneracy-aware projection (DAP) for LiDAR updates that suppresses direct information along geometrically weak directions while preserving informative constraints.
