# II Related Work

## II-A Kinematics-Aided State Estimation

Robot kinematics provides motion information when environmental features are insufficient for reliable LiDAR registration.
For wheeled robots, LIWO incorporates encoder-derived velocity observations into LiDAR–inertial estimation [ 6 ] , while Kinematic-ICP constrains registration using platform kinematics and adapts the influence of wheel odometry [ 9 ] .
Online neural kinematic models further adapt wheel-motion predictions to changing terrain conditions [ 13 ] .
For articulated robots, VILENS combines leg odometry with visual, inertial, and LiDAR measurements and estimates a velocity bias to reduce kinematic errors [ 10 ] , while a learned leg-kinematics model uses tactile inputs to adapt proprioceptive constraints [ 14 ] .

Wheel-legged estimation must additionally account for rolling motion.
Existing systems introduce kinematic corrections [ 1 ] and terrain constraints [ 2 ] , while contact-anchored odometry propagates contact positions using wheel rolling displacement [ 18 ] .
Zhou et al. combine probabilistic slip modeling, offset wheel-contact geometry, and generalized-momentum-based contact detection in a proprioceptive multimode estimator [ 19 ] .
Our formulation maintains all four moving wheel centers as persistent states and assigns learned process covariances to their analytical rolling predictions.
FK measurements couple these states to the body within the same estimator that incorporates LiDAR information, allowing wheel-motion uncertainty to influence the fused state estimate.

## II-B Contact Modeling and Learned Uncertainty

The usefulness of a kinematic constraint depends on the underlying ground interaction.
Contact-aided extended Kalman filters (EKFs) use stance feet as approximately stationary references and relate them to the body through FK measurements [ 7 ] .
This formulation has been extended to invariant filtering [ 8 ] and factor graphs with preintegrated contact motion or contact forces [ 20 , 21 ] .
Camurri et al. estimate contact probabilities and detect impacts from internal force sensing, using this information to weight individual legs in velocity estimation [ 22 ] .
Learning-based contact predictors determine when a constraint should be used [ 11 ] , while neural measurement models correct the motion information supplied to the estimator [ 12 ] .
For rolling wheels, contact alone does not establish the reliability of the predicted motion: a supported wheel may still slip, with errors that differ across directions.

Differentiable filtering provides a way to learn uncertainty models through their effect on state estimation.
Backprop KF jointly trains an observation network and its predicted observation covariance through Kalman filtering using state-estimation losses [ 15 ] .
Kloss et al. study end-to-end training of differentiable filters, including the learning of process and observation noise models whose covariances vary with the inputs [ 16 ] .
For legged robots, CoCo-InEKF learns directional contact-velocity covariances through a differentiable filter, without contact labels [ 17 ] . CoCo-InEKF learns directional confidence in a zero-mean contact-velocity model.
For wheel-legged robots, however, wheel centers move even during ideal rolling.
Our formulation explicitly models this nominal motion and learns its uncertainty, allowing reliable rolling constraints to support state estimation, with real-world ablation experiments showing a 31.0% reduction in mean per-sequence position RMSE (Table II ).

## II-C Degeneracy-Aware LiDAR Estimation

Reliable wheel constraints can support estimation when LiDAR geometry is weak, but the LiDAR update must also account for that weakness.
Earlier work identifies poorly constrained directions and restricts the corresponding estimation updates [ 23 ] .
X-ICP evaluates how scan-to-map correspondences constrain the principal optimization directions and incorporates the resulting localizability categories into constrained registration [ 24 ] .
Hatleskog and Alexis account for noise in points and surface normals when estimating the probability of degeneracy, then smoothly attenuate updates in unreliable directions [ 25 ] .
Tuna et al. further compare truncated singular value decomposition, inequality constraints, and regularization in field experiments, examining how these choices affect ill-conditioned registration [ 26 ] .
DCReg uses Schur complements to separate rotational and translational constraints when characterizing ill-conditioning [ 5 ] .
Our estimator uses DAP to screen the full pose-information matrix and project the LiDAR Jacobian onto retained directions.
DAP controls direct LiDAR information from weak geometry, while learned wheel-process covariances control uncertainty in the rolling predictions.
These components act through a shared state and covariance, coupling the retained LiDAR information to the IMU–wheel-center prior.

2026-10-20.title: ReInsVLN: Revisiting Historical Evidence for Training-Free Vision-and-Language Navigation
2026-10-20.authors: Siwei Cheng , Hao Wu , Zitong Qi , Xinming Zhang , Haoyu Xi , Peiran Yin , Haozhe Hu , Xudong Wang , Xiaoyu Shen , Wei Zhang
2026-10-20.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) relies on retaining and using relevant observations. Yet growing histories introduce redundancy, and retained information may remain underused. We introduce ReInsBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines history utilization through controlled continuation trials. Its results show that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context. Motivated by this finding, we propose ReInsVLN, a training-free framework supporting memory construction and utilization in frozen navigators. Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression constructs compact visual context through temporal redundancy reduction, coverage-aware protection, and instruction-guided token selection. Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders guide navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls. On R2R Val-Unseen, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 percentage points over the native StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, reaching 64.27% and 64.44%, respectively. Visual compression largely preserves navigation performance while reducing prefill latency and KV cache memory by up to 21.77% and 32.25%, respectively, on matched observation workloads. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the applicability of ReInsVLN to sequential instruction following and ordinal navigation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to follow natural-language instructions using a sequence of visual observations [ 1 , 2 ] . Partial observability makes decisions depend on previously encountered landmarks [ 3 ] . As illustrated in Fig. 1 , following the instruction “Pass the armchair beside the blue cabinet, then stop at the next armchair” requires the navigator to use the previously observed relation between the cabinet and the first armchair to identify the next armchair as the stopping point. Such dependencies make memory essential for retaining information from past observations and using it to guide subsequent actions [ 4 ] .

Effective navigation memory involves two complementary capabilities: memory construction and memory utilization . Here, memory construction selects and organizes past observations into available context, while memory utilization uses that context to guide decisions. Spatial maps offer one way to organize navigation history [ 5 ] . As navigation proceeds, repeated views introduce redundancy into the growing observation history, increasing the cost of processing it [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . This requires retaining useful historical information within limited context and computation budgets, while preserving cues for later decisions. However, retained information does not guarantee effective use, even in long-context language models [ 10 ] . In the example in Fig. 1, the cabinet observation may remain in the navigator’s history without guiding it to stop at the correct armchair. This raises a central question: even when relevant historical information is retained, can the navigator use it effectively?

To examine this question, we introduce ReInsBench , a diagnostic benchmark constructed from selected R2R [ 1 ] navigation episodes. At selected decision points, a frozen navigator continues under different prompts from the same observation history and environment state. The benchmark assesses whether directing the navigator to revisit its existing history improves subsequent navigation, using neutral reminders to control for the effect of generic prompting. In a controlled subset of 198 instances, history review yields 64 successful continuations, compared with 53 for neutral reminders and 40 without an additional prompt. These findings suggest that navigators do not always make effective use of the historical information already available to them.

Building on this diagnosis, we aim to improve memory construction and utilization within existing navigators. A compact visual context must preserve cues whose relevance may emerge only later [ 11 , 12 ] . Once retained, these cues need to inform subsequent decisions at appropriate moments, requiring guidance that encourages their use while limiting interference with otherwise correct navigation.

To this end, we propose ReInsVLN , a training-free framework that combines visual context compression and history-review reminders within the existing context mechanisms of navigators. For memory construction, we adopt a two-stage visual compression strategy consisting of pre-LLM compression and in-LLM compression. The pre-LLM stage reduces temporal redundancy before visual tokens enter the language model, combining causal token reduction with dynamic-token protection to prioritize content poorly covered by previously retained tokens. The in-LLM stage builds a query from the original instruction and expands it with high-scoring visual seeds. It then combines semantic relevance with positional information to select a compact subset of visual tokens, restoring their original order after selection. For memory utilization, short reminders guide the navigator to revisit retained observations in relation to the original instruction. A predefined, forgetting-inspired schedule uses the number of decision calls elapsed since the previous reminder as a temporal prior for determining when to introduce history review. The prompts are inserted at existing decision calls, preserving the native action-execution pipeline.

Experiments on R2R Val-Unseen evaluate ReInsVLN with StreamVLN and InternVLA-N1, representing streaming and non-streaming inference, respectively. With Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression and Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders applied together, ReInsVLN improves success rates by 8.48 and 3.37 points over the corresponding native navigators. These improvements exceed the sum of individual gains on both navigators, suggesting synergy between two components. Visual compression also reduces prefill latency and KV cache usage. Physical deployment is another focus of legged-robot VLN [ 13 ] .

The main contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce ReInsBench to diagnose history utilization through controlled prompting comparisons, showing that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context.

We develop Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression for memory construction in ReInsVLN, combining temporal redundancy reduction with instruction-guided visual token selection.

We introduce Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders to support memory utilization by guiding frozen navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls.

Simulation experiments show navigation gains on both navigators, together with reduced prefill latency and KV cache storage. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the training-free generalization of ReInsVLN to challenging tasks requiring sequential landmark tracking.

1. We introduce ReInsBench to diagnose history utilization through controlled prompting comparisons, showing that history-review reinstruction can recover navigation failures using the existing task context.

2. We develop Coverage- and Instruction-Aware Compression for memory construction in ReInsVLN, combining temporal redundancy reduction with instruction-guided visual token selection.

3. We introduce Forgetting-Inspired History Reminders to support memory utilization by guiding frozen navigators to revisit retained observations according to a predefined schedule, without additional model calls.

4. Simulation experiments show navigation gains on both navigators, together with reduced prefill latency and KV cache storage. Real-world trials on humanoid and quadruped robots further support the training-free generalization of ReInsVLN to challenging tasks requiring sequential landmark tracking.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A History Modeling in VLN

History modeling connects current observations with previously encountered landmarks. Explicit visual-language maps [ 14 ] organize observations spatially, while NaVid incorporates historical observations into action prediction. StreamVLN separates recent interactions from slowly updated visual memory and reuses cached states across decisions. ReInsBench complements these approaches by assessing history utilization through controlled prompting. ReInsVLN builds on existing context mechanisms, combining visual compression and history-review reminders to reduce redundancy and improve history utilization.

## II-B Visual Token Compression

Visual token compression accelerates MLLM inference by shortening visual token sequences, either in a single step or progressively across multiple stages [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . LLaVA-PruMerge [ 18 ] prunes and merges tokens before the LLM. FastV [ 19 ] prunes at a selected LLM layer, while PyramidDrop [ 20 ] and HiDrop [ 21 ] prune progressively across layers. For streaming video, StreamForest [ 22 ] uses hierarchical event-level merging, and ViCoStream [ 23 ] uses chunk-level temporal token dropping. In VLN, STEP-Nav [ 11 ] and history-conditioned pruning [ 12 ] reduce spatial and temporal redundancy. While prior compression work primarily targets inference efficiency, ReInsVLN couples two-stage compression with history-review reminders to improve the utilization of retained visual context.

## II-C Memory Utilization and Reactivation

Memory utilization connects retained information with current decisions. CMMR-VLN [ 24 ] retrieves prior navigation cases as rules, while Memoir [ 25 ] queries observation and behavioral histories using predicted states. MemVR [ 26 ] reinjects visual evidence into intermediate layers under uncertainty, and VisRef [ 27 ] reintroduces selected visual tokens during reasoning. MemoryBank [ 28 ] and DART-VLN [ 29 ] incorporate temporal priors into memory retention and readout, respectively. ReInsVLN provides reactivation at the input level through scheduled history-review prompts, guiding frozen navigators to revisit existing observations without additional retrieval or model calls.

2026-10-20.title: Learning Geometry-Aware Planning Representations for Monocular Flight with Cross-Modal Supervision
2026-10-20.authors: Wencan Feng , Bailing Tian , Yulin Hui , Zhiyu Li , Junjie Lu
2026-10-20.abstract: Existing high-speed navigation systems for micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) commonly rely on depth cameras, stereo vision, or LiDAR to obtain explicit geometric information, while monocular cameras offer a lighter and lower-cost alternative. However, monocular flight remains challenging because RGB images offer no direct metric cues and visual appearance varies considerably across environments. We propose a geometry-aware monocular visual planning framework that predicts trajectories from two image frames, their relative pose, and the MAV state. Without explicitly reconstructing depth, the proposed method complements the downstream planning objective with feature-level geometric supervision by transferring the planning-relevant representation learned by a privileged depth expert to the RGB planner through cross-modal distillation. The framework first trains a depth-based geometric expert, then distills its planning features into a monocular branch using paired RGB-D observations, and finally adapts the planner to the downstream trajectory planning objective. This design encourages the policy to learn planning-relevant geometric features, enabling collision avoidance. We further use a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) simulator to render visual observations for data collection, paired RGB-D supervision, and simulation evaluation. The planner trained in simulation is then deployed in real-world environments without real-world fine-tuning, achieving obstacle avoidance at speeds of up to 6.5 m/s.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Achieving agile autonomous flight in highly cluttered environments remains a long-standing challenge for MAVs. Most existing autonomous navigation systems rely on sensors that provide explicit metric geometry, such as LiDARs and depth cameras, to perceive the surrounding environment, followed by well-established mapping-and-planning pipelines or end-to-end policy networks to generate collision-aware trajectories [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . While these approaches have demonstrated impressive performance, their reliance on dedicated geometric sensors constrains the compactness and design flexibility of miniature aerial platforms. In contrast, monocular RGB planning requires only a lightweight commodity camera, offering greater flexibility under stringent payload and energy budgets.

Biological vision demonstrates that agile flight does not necessarily rely on explicit geometric perception. Small flying animals such as bees and forest-dwelling birds can rapidly navigate through densely cluttered environments using only two-dimensional visual cues, such as object scale changes and scene contours, without explicitly reconstructing the surrounding geometry [ 4 , 5 ] . Likewise, experienced first-person-view (FPV) pilots can execute aggressive maneuvers and traverse narrow gaps using only a monocular video stream [ 6 ] . These observations indicate that monocular images contain sufficient information to support agile autonomous flight, making monocular cameras an attractive sensing modality for MAVs. Compared with LiDARs and depth cameras, monocular cameras are lightweight, inexpensive, easy to integrate, and naturally compatible with wide field-of-view optics such as fisheye lenses. Moreover, they provide rich texture and contextual information that is unavailable to purely geometric sensors.

Despite these advantages, learning agile navigation policies directly from these images remains fundamentally challenging. Most existing navigation methods employ imitation learning or reinforcement learning to train RGB policies directly using downstream task objectives [ 7 , 8 ] , without explicitly constraining their internal representations to preserve planning-relevant geometry. As a result, they often suffer from appearance overfitting and poor cross-scene generalization. Unlike depth sensors, monocular cameras provide no explicit metric distance information, making it difficult to infer the traversable spatial structure required for motion planning. Furthermore, these images are highly sensitive to illumination, textures, and object appearance, forcing the navigation policy to distinguish geometry relevant to obstacle avoidance from appearance variations that are irrelevant to planning. To alleviate these issues, some approaches introduce explicit geometric intermediate representations, such as depth [ 9 , 10 ] or optical flow [ 11 , 12 ] , to extract geometry-aware cues from observations, while others exploit privileged depth supervision or ground-truth geometric information during training to guide policy learning [ 13 , 14 ] . However, explicit geometric intermediate representations incur additional computational overhead and inference latency. Directly trained RGB policies, on the other hand, rely primarily on downstream task supervision, without explicitly encouraging the learned representations to preserve planning-relevant geometric information. Consequently, these representations may remain sensitive to appearance variations and may not reliably capture the geometric structure required for collision avoidance.

To address these limitations, we propose a geometry-aware monocular navigation framework that takes two consecutive RGB images, their relative pose, and the MAV state as input. It should be noted that the primary objective of monocular navigation is not to recover pixel-wise accurate depth, but to learn geometry-aware representations that preserve planning-relevant structural information. Guided by this insight, the framework narrows the geometric gap between a privileged depth expert and a monocular planner by transferring planning-oriented geometric representations through feature-level distillation. During training, the depth expert learns geometry-aware planning features under privileged supervision, while the student network reproduces these structured representations via feature alignment. To further encourage the learned representations to preserve planning-relevant geometry and reduce their dependence on appearance cues, we introduce a lightweight coarse-depth prediction branch with an auxiliary training objective. This auxiliary task provides additional geometric regularization for the distilled representations. Furthermore, we develop a scalable simulation pipeline based on 3DGS, which provides photorealistic images, corresponding geometric supervision, and map-based trajectory cost labels for data generation and training. During deployment, the planner operates solely on two consecutive monocular images and MAV states, without requiring any depth estimation module or additional geometric sensors.
The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We propose a framework that transfers planning-oriented geometric representations from a privileged depth expert to the student planner, aided by a lightweight coarse-depth branch that reinforces geometric structure.

We propose a framework that transfers planning-oriented geometric representations from a privileged depth expert to the student planner, aided by a lightweight coarse-depth branch that reinforces geometric structure.

We develop a monocular planner that plans trajectories from sequential images, relative pose, and MAV states, and performs online evaluation to enable agile, collision-aware flight.

We establish a 3DGS-based data pipeline that provides aligned RGB observations, privileged geometry, vehicle states, and trajectory-cost labels for training and evaluation.

1. We propose a framework that transfers planning-oriented geometric representations from a privileged depth expert to the student planner, aided by a lightweight coarse-depth branch that reinforces geometric structure.

2. We develop a monocular planner that plans trajectories from sequential images, relative pose, and MAV states, and performs online evaluation to enable agile, collision-aware flight.

3. We establish a 3DGS-based data pipeline that provides aligned RGB observations, privileged geometry, vehicle states, and trajectory-cost labels for training and evaluation.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Navigation with Explicit Geometric Perception

Most autonomous navigation systems rely on depth cameras or LiDAR to obtain explicit geometric information. Classical pipelines construct ESDF maps from depth observations and combine path search with trajectory optimization [ 15 , 16 ] , whereas methods based on safe flight corridors (SFCs) optimize trajectories within convex collision-free corridors [ 17 ] . Ren et al. jointly optimized trajectory safety and efficiency using LiDAR, enabling high speed autonomous flight [ 3 ] .

Learning-based planners further reduce latency by directly mapping sensor observations to trajectories or controls. Loquercio et al. used imitation learning to predict planning outputs from depth images and MAV states [ 2 ] . Without expert demonstrations, Lu et al.’s Guidance Learning trains a polynomial-trajectory predictor by back-propagating gradients of the trajectory objective [ 18 , 19 ] . Zhang et al. combined differentiable physics with reinforcement learning to train a GRU policy from depth observations and vehicle states for agile multi-MAV flight [ 20 ] . Xu et al. fused LiDAR range images with temporal point-flow features in an RL policy that directly generates obstacle-avoidance controls [ 21 ] .

## II-B Monocular Vision-based Navigation

Monocular cameras are lightweight and power-efficient, making them suitable for resource-constrained MAVs. Early methods directly mapped RGB images to navigation commands using CNN [ 7 , 8 ] . However, their lack of explicit geometric supervision may limit policy reliability and generalization. Other approaches recover geometric cues as intermediate representations. MonoNav estimates depth and reconstructs local geometry before planning [ 9 ] , whereas Hu et al. use optical flow to represent scene depth and structure for robust and agile navigation [ 11 ] .

Sim-to-real transfer remains another challenge for monocular navigation. CAD2RL combines deep reinforcement learning with domain randomization to transfer policies to real MAVs [ 22 ] . More recently, 3DGS has enabled rapid, high-fidelity reconstruction of real scenes for robotic simulation [ 23 ] . Compared with manually constructed game-engine environments, it provides realistic visual observations with less scene-building effort. Low et al.’s SOUS VIDE uses 3DGS to collect data for end-to-end policies deployed on real MAVs [ 24 ] . Huang et al. further combine 3DGS environments with domain adaptation and randomization to improve real-world generalization [ 13 ] .

2026-10-20.title: Learn the Task, Not the Schedule: Reducing Spurious Cross-Arm Coupling in Bimanual Imitation Learning
2026-10-20.authors: Shuyuan Hu , Deng-Ke Wu , Yifan Jin , Qianhang Luo , Mingchen Ju , Kai Ye , Bo Zhao
2026-10-20.abstract:
A bimanual demonstration specifies both what the robot should do and one particular schedule for when each arm should act.
Standard imitation learning does not distinguish task-required cross-arm constraints from incidental scheduling choices, and may therefore exploit opposite-arm progress as a shortcut cue, creating spurious cross-arm coupling even where relative timing is irrelevant for the current task phase.
We introduce Constraint-preserving Temporal Recombination (CTR), a training-time data intervention that preserves recorded arm-local sensorimotor content while retiming the corresponding segments to realize admissible schedules that preserve task-required cross-arm constraints.
We use CTR to train Diffusion Policy, Action Chunking with Transformers, and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and evaluate them on four simulated and four real-robot tasks.
Across six real-robot bimanual progress-state initializations, CTR raises worst-state success from 56% for the strongest non-CTR schedule mixture to 76%.
With π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} on an Independent task, a 4 s pause transfers 2.56 s of delay to the opposite arm under the Concurrent schedule distribution, but only 0.25 s with CTR.
On real robots, CTR violates task constraints in only 0–4% of trials, versus 36–98% for narrow-schedule baselines.
Code will be released at https://github.com/MINT-SJTU/CTR .
2026-10-20.introduction:
In a bimanual demonstration, the two arms follow one of possibly many admissible schedules. If each arm independently picks an object and the demonstrator does so sequentially, the recorded order is a choice, not a task requirement; likewise, a drawer must be opened before an object is inserted, but not before the object is grasped. Expressive imitation policies such as Diffusion Policy (DP), Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT), and vision-language-action models including π 0 \pi_{0} , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , and OpenVLA ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ; Kim et al., 2025 ) cannot tell these cases apart from the demonstrations alone. When demonstrations cover only a few schedules, one arm’s behavior can come to depend on the other’s progress even where their subtasks are independently schedulable; we call this spurious cross-arm coupling .

The narrow schedule support that creates this ambiguity appears common in existing datasets. Our audit covers four public bimanual datasets: RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCOIN, DexMimicGen, and BiCoord ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025b ; Peng et al., 2026 ) . It finds that 266 of 716 tasks (37.2%) are reschedulable, yet only 3.4% of these exhibit multiple observed admissible schedules ( Appendix 0 ).

This limited coverage motivates learning cross-arm dependence that reflects task constraints rather than the particular schedules demonstrated. We call this selective cross-arm dependence : in independently schedulable phases, delaying one arm should not make the other wait, whereas during insertion, support, or shared-workspace occupancy, the policy must respond to the opposite arm. More demonstrations with the same narrow schedule support cannot resolve this ambiguity ( Section 0 ).

We propose Constraint-preserving Temporal Recombination (CTR) , a training-time data intervention that broadens schedule support without new demonstrations. CTR segments each arm’s recorded stream and retimes the segments into alternative admissible schedules while preserving task-required cross-arm constraints, pairing the same arm-local sensorimotor content with varied opposite-arm progress.

We evaluate CTR with three policy families (DP, ACT, and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ) on four simulated and four real-robot tasks. CTR-trained policies achieve higher default-condition success rates than the same architectures trained with serial schedules in 19 of 24 model–task comparisons, and CTR raises real-robot worst-case progress-state success from 56% to 76%. Pausing one arm for 4 s delays the other arm’s completion by 2.56 s with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} trained on concurrent-start schedules, but by only 0.25 s with CTR. Required coordination is retained: under real-robot constraint interventions, CTR-trained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} violates task constraints in 0% and 4% of trials, versus 98% and 36% for narrow-schedule baselines.

Our contributions are: (1) identifying spurious cross-arm coupling under narrow schedule support and formalizing selective cross-arm dependence as the desired behavior; (2) CTR, which broadens admissible schedule support while preserving arm-local sensorimotor content and task-required cross-arm constraints; and (3) simulated and real-robot evidence across three policy families that CTR reduces spurious coupling without sacrificing required coordination.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Bimanual imitation policies model cross-arm dependence through joint action chunks in ACT ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) or explicit attention and synchronization in InterACT ( Lee et al., 2025 ) .
BUDS structures this dependence through acting and stabilizing roles ( Grannen et al., 2023 ) .
To support independence alongside coordination, the Decoupled Interaction Framework combines arm-specific policies with selective information exchange ( Jiang et al., 2025a ) , while SkillVLA reuses single-arm skills across novel left–right pairings ( Zhai et al., 2026 ) .
These approaches structure dependence at the model or skill level; our focus is the training distribution, where narrow schedule support can make opposite-arm progress predictive even when it is irrelevant to the current arm-local subtask.

This mismatch between predictiveness and task relevance connects schedule-induced coupling to causal confusion in imitation learning ( de Haan et al., 2019 ) .
A related data-level strategy is counterfactual augmentation: CoDA recombines locally factored transitions ( Pitis et al., 2020 ) , and CAIAC exchanges state components estimated to be unaffected by an action ( Armengol Urpí et al., 2024 ) .
RoCoDA brings this principle to visual robot imitation, including bimanual tasks, by recombining state partitions under phase-specific causal structure ( Ameperosa et al., 2025 ) .
Here, the intervention of interest is relative arm timing while the recorded arm-local behavior remains fixed.
Because relative timing can also encode required coordination, this intervention must vary progress pairings without violating task-required cross-arm constraints.

Demonstration generation provides tools for this constrained recombination: MimicGen adapts object-centric segments to new contexts ( Mandlekar et al., 2023 ) , and DexMimicGen adds asynchronous per-arm execution with synchronization and ordering constraints ( Jiang et al., 2025b ) .
TriManPolicy more directly addresses interface-induced waiting by retiming fixed-duration sensorimotor segments under dependency and arm-resource constraints to minimize demonstration makespan ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) .
However, selecting an efficient schedule does not by itself establish robustness to other admissible schedules.
CTR therefore samples alternative schedules for the same recorded arm-local sensorimotor content under annotated task constraints, broadening progress-state support without changing the policy architecture or deployment procedure.
To distinguish selective cross-arm dependence from indiscriminate decoupling, we combine held-out progress tests and paired opposite-arm pauses with task-constraint interventions.

2026-10-20.title: SPAR: Structural Pruning and Action Recovery for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-20.authors: Shenli Zheng , Zhou Fang , Yuan Du , Yijiang Liu , Li Du
2026-10-20.abstract: The limited onboard computing resources of robots make the inference demands of vision-language-action (VLA) models costly to accommodate. Reducing these demands through aggressive compression, however, can degrade manipulation performance beyond what supervised fine-tuning alone recovers. We present SPAR (Structural Pruning and Action Recovery), which simultaneously prunes the hidden and feed-forward intermediate dimensions of the large language model (LLM) backbone through pruning-aware tuning, then applies reinforcement learning (RL) to recover policy performance. Applied to π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , SPAR reduces the language backbone from 2.34B to 0.09B parameters and the full model from 3.37B to 1.12B, removing approximately 96% and 67% of their parameters, respectively. At this compression level, RL raises average success across the four LIBERO suites from 84.55% to 93.45%, an 8.90-percentage-point gain. The compressed policy achieves a 1.98 × \boldsymbol{1.98\times} full-policy inference speedup over the unpruned model. These results identify substantial intermediate-dimension redundancy and show that post-pruning RL can recover manipulation performance in compact policies.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models such as RT-2 [ 1 ] , OpenVLA [ 2 ] , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 3 ] transfer pretrained representations to robotic manipulation, but their inference demands strain limited onboard compute. In π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , the LLM accounts for 2.34B of 3.37B parameters. This motivates a central question: how much language-model capacity do manipulation tasks require, and how can a smaller policy retain useful capabilities?

Efficiency approaches include compact policies such as SmolVLA [ 4 ] and NORA [ 5 ] , preference-based adaptation in NORA-1.5 [ 6 ] , and synthetic pretraining in GraspVLA [ 7 ] . For existing policies, SP-VLA [ 8 ] and DART [ 9 ] reduce tokens, while EfficientVLA [ 10 ] and MoLe-VLA [ 11 ] reduce layer computation. Token reduction alone leaves backbone weights intact. EcoVLA [ 12 ] dynamically selects channels and attention heads; we instead permanently reduce backbone dimensions to produce a smaller dense model.

Permanent compression introduces a second challenge: recovering manipulation capabilities lost when parameters are removed. RLRC [ 13 ] combines structured pruning with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), while SimpleVLA-RL [ 14 ] demonstrates that interaction can improve policies beyond SFT. These results motivate studying how the allocation of a small parameter budget and adaptation during pruning affect subsequent recovery. The hidden dimension couples representations across Transformer blocks, whereas the intermediate dimension controls expansion within feed-forward layers. Their different roles motivate separate retention targets for the two dimensions.

We introduce SPAR (Structural Pruning and Action Recovery), which couples dimension-aware pruning with post-pruning RL to recover task performance ( Fig. 2 ). Building on pruning-aware tuning (PAT) [ 15 ] , SPAR jointly learns masks for the hidden and intermediate dimensions with separate retention targets and a regularized mask-learning objective. Channel selection and supervised adaptation are performed together, followed by physical pruning and fine-tuning of the reduced model. The resulting compact policy provides the initialization for RL, which further improves manipulation performance through interaction.

Our evaluation on LIBERO [ 16 ] and LIBERO-Plus [ 17 ] examines both task success and robustness under compression. Pruning only the intermediate dimension preserves high task success, while additional hidden-dimension pruning at a fixed intermediate-dimension retention target causes larger losses that RL can substantially mitigate. As a representative result, SPAR achieves 93.45% average LIBERO success with a 0.09B language backbone (1.12B total), approximately 4% of the original LLM size ( ). These findings support dimension-aware compression and recovery as complementary tools for compact robotic policies.

Our main contributions are:

A dual-dimension pruning framework that jointly learns masks for the hidden and intermediate dimensions with separate retention targets and a regularized mask-learning objective.

An empirical analysis of dimension sensitivity : pruning only the intermediate dimension preserves high task success, while additional hidden-dimension pruning causes larger performance losses in our evaluated tasks.

An evaluation of recovery and efficiency across compression levels, showing improvements in task success and robustness after RL, together with measured full-policy inference acceleration.

1. A dual-dimension pruning framework that jointly learns masks for the hidden and intermediate dimensions with separate retention targets and a regularized mask-learning objective.

2. An empirical analysis of dimension sensitivity : pruning only the intermediate dimension preserves high task success, while additional hidden-dimension pruning causes larger performance losses in our evaluated tasks.

3. An evaluation of recovery and efficiency across compression levels, showing improvements in task success and robustness after RL, together with measured full-policy inference acceleration.

# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models

VLA models connect pretrained vision-language representations to robotic control. OpenVLA [ 2 ] predicts discretized actions autoregressively, whereas OpenVLA-OFT [ 18 ] uses parallel decoding and action chunking. CogACT [ 19 ] separates action generation into a diffusion expert. The π 0 \pi_{0} family [ 20 ] couples a PaliGemma backbone [ 21 ] with a flow-matching action expert; π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 3 ] adds semantic subtask prediction. TinyVLA [ 22 ] instead combines a compact multimodal backbone with a diffusion decoder.

## II-B Pruning for VLA models

LLM compression includes weight sparsification in SparseGPT [ 23 ] , coupled-structure removal in LLM-Pruner [ 24 ] , and row/column deletion to form smaller dense matrices in SliceGPT [ 25 ] . PAT [ 15 ] jointly performs hidden-dimension pruning and fine-tuning through trainable channel masks and Hybrid Sparsification Modules. For VLA models, DART [ 9 ] and SP-VLA [ 8 ] reduce visual tokens; EfficientVLA [ 10 ] removes low-impact layers, and MoLe-VLA [ 11 ] dynamically skips layers. EcoVLA [ 12 ] adaptively selects channels and attention heads with parallel sparsity updates and custom kernels. Building on PAT, SPAR learns masks for both the hidden and intermediate dimensions with separate retention targets, physically reduces the dense backbone, and applies RL recovery. Our evaluation examines the effects of compression on both manipulation success and robustness.

## II-C Reinforcement learning for VLA models

RL for VLA models includes both offline and online approaches. Offline RL learns from a fixed dataset without additional environment interaction, whereas online RL collects new experience as training proceeds. The RECAP recipe for π 0.6 ∗ \pi_{0.6}^{*} [ 26 ] starts with offline RL pretraining, then alternates robot data collection with offline updates using advantage-conditioned policies. For online VLA training, SimpleVLA-RL [ 14 ] optimizes policies through environment interaction with outcome-based rewards, while RLinf [ 27 ] provides scalable training infrastructure. In the compression setting, RLRC [ 13 ] combines structured pruning, supervised fine-tuning, and RL to recover policy performance.

## II-D Manipulation Benchmarks

LIBERO [ 16 ] evaluates knowledge transfer across language-conditioned manipulation tasks. ManiSkill2 [ 28 ] offers 20 task families spanning stationary and mobile manipulation, single- and dual-arm robots, and rigid and soft objects. Robustness-oriented extensions probe behavior beyond standard task completion: LIBERO-PRO [ 29 ] perturbs manipulated objects, initial states, instructions, and environments to examine sensitivity to memorized task conditions. LIBERO-Plus [ 17 ] evaluates seven perturbation dimensions, including camera viewpoints, robot initial states, and scene appearance. We use LIBERO to evaluate task success and LIBERO-Plus to assess robustness under perturbations after compression.

2026-10-20.title: ALIGN: Aligning Condition Estimation and Expression in Advantage-Conditioned Behavior Cloning
2026-10-20.authors: Zechen Wang , Zhenqi Qiu , Houlong Xiong , Suohang Zhang , Yiyu Ren , Wanting Xu , Hongfei Niu , Chengyang He , Ge Sun , Ran Cheng , Qian Zhu
2026-10-20.abstract:
Human-collected robot manipulation data often mix successful behavior with retries, pauses, recoveries, and failures. A dvantage- C onditioned B ehavior C loning (AC-BC) can exploit such mixed-quality data, but only if the conditioning signal is both accurately constructed from offline trajectories and effectively incorporated into the policy’s action-vector-field prediction.
Existing pipelines can weaken this signal by thresholding estimator-derived advantage scores into noisy conditions, and by routing conditions through prompts that weakly affect the action vector field.
We introduce ALIGN, a condition-aligned AC-BC framework for vision-language-action policies.
ALIGN directly predicts categorical pairwise conditions in the policy-facing label space and injects them into a DiT action expert through AdaRMS modulation fused with flow time.
We evaluate ALIGN on deliberately mixed real-robot datasets for ARX X5 bowl stacking and Franka key hanging, each combining standard demonstrations with retry-heavy trajectories.
ALIGN improves condition fidelity, strengthens conditional vector-field separability, and achieves 90.0% and 56.7% closed-loop success, compared with 56.7% and 33.3% for the strongest AC-BC baseline.
These results indicate that aligning conditions from estimation to action prediction is an effective way to extract robust manipulation policies from data in which success, recovery and error coexist.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Robot manipulation datasets collected from human teleoperation are rarely clean: besides successful execution, they contain pauses, retries, recoveries, and erroneous actions. This heterogeneity is important when adapting vision-language-action (VLA) models, which have emerged as strong robot policy backbones [ 47 , 22 , 37 , 17 , 16 ] , including diffusion- and flow-based variants for multimodal action distributions [ 11 , 3 ] . A dvantage- C onditioned B ehavior C loning (AC-BC) offers a natural way to extract useful behavior from such mixed-quality offline data [ 34 , 30 , 36 ] : it estimates behavior quality, converts it into a policy-facing condition, trains imitation conditioned on that label, and deploys the policy under the desired high-quality condition.
In principle, conditioning can retain useful recovery behavior while learning from both positive- and negative-conditioned examples. Filtering with the same classifier can also retain recovery frames predicted as positive; the distinction is that filtering discards predicted-negative examples.
In practice, its benefit depends on whether the condition is both correctly constructed from data and strongly expressed by the policy.

We argue that existing VLA-based AC-BC pipelines can lose this conditioning signal at both stages. First, the condition is often constructed indirectly: a continuous value, progress, or reward score is evaluated at two frames, differenced, thresholded, and then mapped to a discrete positive/negative label [ 36 , 44 , 9 ] . This indirect conversion is fragile: continuous value/progress estimates are imperfect predictions, differencing can amplify local prediction noise, and thresholding turns near-boundary errors into discrete condition flips. Our temporal-gap supervision likewise represents local task progress, rather than independently annotated action quality or calibrated advantage. We study how this progress-based signal is converted into the condition consumed by AC-BC. The supervision used to define this signal is a separate design axis from estimator parameterization and condition expression. Second, even a correct condition may be weakly expressed. Prompt-based conditioning is convenient for VLA policies, but the condition must pass through the language or vision-language context before reaching the flow-based action expert. If changing the condition barely changes the predicted action vector field, the learned policy has little ability to act differently under different conditions.

We introduce ALIGN, an AC-BC framework that aligns the policy-facing condition from estimation to action prediction. For condition construction, ALIGN replaces post-hoc thresholding of scalar value/progress differences with a direct categorical pairwise estimator, p ϕ ​ ( c ∣ o i , o j ) p_{\phi}(c\mid o_{i},o_{j}) , trained to predict the same discrete condition consumed by the policy.
For condition expression, ALIGN fuses the categorical condition with the flow-time embedding and injects it into the DiT action expert through AdaRMS modulation, giving the condition a direct and repeated influence on vector-field computation rather than relying only on prompt-level conditioning. Figure 1 summarizes this estimation-to-expression pipeline.

We evaluate ALIGN using standard and retry-heavy successful real-robot demonstrations for policy training; failed trajectories are used only for held-out condition evaluation. Our contributions are threefold:

We formulate AC-BC for mixed-quality robot data as two coupled problems: condition construction and condition expression, diagnosed by AC-BC Condition Fidelity (ACF) and Conditional Vector-Field Separability (CVFS).

We propose a direct categorical pairwise condition estimator that predicts the policy-facing AC-BC condition directly, reducing conversion error relative to value/progress thresholding.

We introduce AdaRMS action-expert injection for flow-based VLA policies and validate ALIGN across two real-robot embodiments under controlled standard and retry-heavy training mixtures, showing improved condition fidelity, stronger condition-dependent vector-field separation, and higher closed-loop success.

1. We formulate AC-BC for mixed-quality robot data as two coupled problems: condition construction and condition expression, diagnosed by AC-BC Condition Fidelity (ACF) and Conditional Vector-Field Separability (CVFS).

2. We propose a direct categorical pairwise condition estimator that predicts the policy-facing AC-BC condition directly, reducing conversion error relative to value/progress thresholding.

3. We introduce AdaRMS action-expert injection for flow-based VLA policies and validate ALIGN across two real-robot embodiments under controlled standard and retry-heavy training mixtures, showing improved condition fidelity, stronger condition-dependent vector-field separation, and higher closed-loop success.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-language-action models for robot control. Modern robot policies increasingly use vision-language-action (VLA) backbones that combine perception, language, robot state, and action prediction, spanning embodied multimodal models, scalable transformer policies, cross-embodiment data, open-source generalists, and foundation-model-coordinated visuomotor policies [ 12 , 4 , 47 , 32 , 31 , 22 , 38 , 5 , 2 , 18 , 17 , 16 ] . Diffusion- and flow-based variants further model actions through generative dynamics [ 11 , 26 , 3 , 46 , 20 ] . These backbones improve action modeling but leave open how mixed-quality segments should be selected or conditioned during imitation.

Advantage-conditioned imitation and policy extraction. Offline RL and policy extraction use learned returns, values, rewards, or advantages to bias imitation, including AWR/AWAC, CRR/IQL, and return- or goal-conditioned sequence models [ 34 , 30 , 42 , 23 , 8 , 14 ] . Robot variants learn rewards or progress for data selection, online RL, policy steering, and evaluation [ 41 , 25 , 28 , 27 , 39 , 1 , 40 , 10 , 9 ] ; ReWiND improves policies with language-guided rewards without new demonstrations [ 45 ] , and GR-RL filters progress-positive transitions before VLA specialization [ 24 ] . Other work exploits imperfect or mixed-quality data by self-supervised failure scoring, segment selection, value-guided retrials, or human recovery/correction trajectories [ 43 , 7 , 13 , 21 ] . Closest to our setting, π 0.6 ∗ \pi^{*}_{0.6} converts learned score differences into positive/negative VLA conditions [ 36 ] ; χ 0 \chi_{0} predicts a stage-conditioned pairwise advantage before thresholding it into a binary optimality label [ 44 ] . ARM also uses pairwise supervision, but for advantage reward modeling rather than the local condition consumed by AC-BC [ 29 ] . ALIGN is complementary: instead of treating value, progress, reward, or advantage as a continuous score for filtering, reweighting, or later thresholding, we directly predict the categorical AC-BC condition and study how it enters the action expert.

Conditioning interfaces for generative action policies. Condition estimation is distinct from condition expression. VLA policies can express advantage through prompts or special tokens [ 36 ] , while generative policies provide lower-level conditioning through timestep modulation, feature-wise affine transforms, or conditional vector-field guidance [ 33 , 35 , 19 ] . We compare action-expert condition-injection interfaces using downstream success and CVFS; among the tested mechanisms, AdaRMS gives the strongest vector-field separation and closed-loop performance.

2026-10-20.title: A Human-in-the-Loop Comparison of Proportional Control and Adaptive Gravity Compensation in Elbow EMG-Driven Exoskeletons
2026-10-20.authors: Francesco Pascucci (1), Eldison Dimo (1), Davide Costanzi (1), Mario Sedilesu (1), Andrea Calanca (1) ((1) University of Verona, Italy)
2026-10-20.abstract: Electromyography (EMG)-driven control enables wearable robots to assist users based on their neuromuscular activity. Upper-limb exoskeletons typically rely on proportional myoelectric control (PMC), which amplifies user effort but may compromise stability at high assistance levels. EMG-driven adaptive gravity compensation (AGC) offers a promising alternative, counterbalancing gravitational torques while continuously adapting to neuromuscular activity. However, these approaches have not been systematically compared in a human-in-the-loop setting. This study evaluates five control algorithms: two PMC strategies at different assistance levels, a purely integral AGC ( AGC-PI ), a kinematics- and acceleration-aware model-based (MB) AGC ( AGC-AW ), and a novel MB AGC approach based on Recursive Least Squares ( AGC-RLS ) for online payload estimation. Fourteen healthy participants performed target-reaching tasks using an active elbow exoskeleton under 0 kg \mathrm{k}\mathrm{g} and 2 kg \mathrm{k}\mathrm{g} loading conditions. Performance metrics included muscular activity, movement accuracy, task efficiency, and subjective workload. PMC exhibited a trade-off between physical effort and task performance: low assistance levels required greater physical effort under load, whereas high gains impaired task execution. AGC-PI reduced agonist activity but induced antagonist activation. In contrast, both model-based AGC approaches effectively compensated for external payloads, reducing physical and cognitive demands while improving movement accuracy and completion time.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Upper-limb active exoskeletons have the potential to substantially reduce physical effort, enhance task performance, and support motor function across a broad spectrum of applications, spanning industrial settings, activities of daily living, and clinical rehabilitation [ 1 , 2 ] . Among the available control paradigms, electromyography (EMG)-driven strategies have attracted considerable attention because they establish a direct interface with the user’s neuromuscular activity, enabling intuitive and responsive assistance [ 3 ] . By exploiting EMG signals, these approaches can infer the user’s movement intent before any observable motion occurs, allowing the exoskeleton to proactively support the task [ 4 ] . Among the various EMG-driven control paradigms proposed in the literature, this work focuses on two: proportional myoelectric control (PMC), the most widely adopted strategy in assistive exoskeletons, and EMG-driven adaptive gravity compensation (AGC), an emerging class of assistive controllers.

In the PMC paradigm, the assistive torque is proportional to the muscle activation of the user, typically through a gain-based mapping (that defines the level of assistance) between the processed EMG signals and the actuator torque [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . These approaches provide intuitive assistance that directly amplifies the user’s effort, which explains their widespread adoption in the literature. However, their performance strongly depends on gain tuning, and too high gains may degrade usability and system stability [ 9 ] .

Given that most of the effort in upper-limb motions is spent against gravity, AGC strategies assist the user by generating torque that compensates for the limb’s gravitational effects. Some implementations have been proposed that exploit EMG signals to implicitly or explicitly estimate such gravitational forces [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . AGC approaches have only recently emerged, and they offer a conceptually distinct mechanism of assistance that makes them inherently capable of providing near-complete assistance, a regime that proportional controllers cannot sustain without compromising stability.

Despite the fundamental differences between these two paradigms, no systematic comparison of their relative merits exists. Broader comparative studies in the EMG-driven exoskeleton literature have addressed related but distinct questions: the contrast between EMG-driven and model-based control [ 14 ] , the effect of assistance magnitude on muscle activity in PMC [ 15 ] , and the comparison of PMC with biological torque-based strategies in a hip exoskeleton [ 16 ] . The specific question of which EMG-driven paradigm better serves the user and under what conditions remains open.

This paper addresses this gap by presenting a human-in-the-loop experimental comparison of PMC and AGC strategies implemented on an active elbow exoskeleton. The specific contributions of this work are twofold. First, we propose a novel model-based (MB) AGC strategy based on Recursive Least Squares ( AGC-RLS ) for online adaptation of the gravity-compensating assistive torque. Second, we systematically evaluate this approach against two PMC and two state-of-the-art AGC algorithms using a multidimensional assessment with 14 healthy participants under two loading conditions.

## II-B EMG-Driven Exoskeleton Control

EMG-driven exoskeleton control aims to translate the user’s neuromuscular activity into assistive torque delivered by the device. As shown in Fig. 1 , the control pipeline starts with the acquisition of raw EMG signals from the upper arm. These signals are then processed through filtering, thresholding, and envelope extraction. The resulting activation signals are then typically provided to an EMG-to-torque module, which generates an estimate of the human joint torque τ ^ h \hat{\tau}_{h} [ 17 ] .

Between the estimated torque and the low-level control layer, different transformations can be introduced depending on the chosen assistive strategy. The estimated biological torque τ ^ h \hat{\tau}_{h} can be amplified, reshaped, integrated, or used to adapt internal model parameters. In other words, the mapping between and the commanded assistive torque τ m \tau_{m} is algorithm-dependent and defines the high-level behavior of the exoskeleton. In this work, the comparative analysis focuses on this control block, and the specific control strategies considered are described in the following sections. Finally, the low-level controller is responsible for actuator control. In this paper, we focus on explicit force control, a widely adopted approach in wearable robotics, where the reference assistive torque τ r \tau_{r} is tracked to generate the actuator command τ m \tau_{m} .

2026-10-20.title: RoboMMT: Learning Stable Tracking of Modulated Expressive and Interactive Robot Motion
2026-10-20.authors: Till Hielscher , Kai O. Arras
2026-10-20.abstract: Expressive robot motion can improve naturalness, effectiveness, and perceived likability in human-robot interaction. When deployed on dynamically unstable platforms, however, reactive execution of expressive body motion may bring the robot to its stability limits, especially when expressivity is decoupled from physical control. In this paper, we present RoboMMT (Robot Modulated Motion Tracking), a modular control architecture that couples parameterized expressive motion synthesis, physics-based character control, and reactive adaptation to spatial interaction goals. Our approach trains a reference-conditioned tracking policy across a broad domain of expressivity, enabling it to faithfully realize the commanded motions while maintaining dynamic stability. Goal reactivity is achieved by training lightweight, task-specific interaction policies that modulate the reference generator’s spatial goal-attraction point, with the stabilizing tracking policy kept in the loop. Evaluations on a quadruped and two humanoid robots show that the learned tracker remains stable and accurate across the entire modulation domain, whereas trackers trained without this coverage lose balance, tracking accuracy, or both. We show that layering closed-loop goal adaptation over this foundation enables interactive facing and pointing behaviors, while maintaining stable execution and comparable reference-tracking fidelity. The robot learns to proactively redistribute its weight and take corrective steps. Zero-shot sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated through real-robot experiments on a quadruped under heavy disturbances.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Robots operating in human environments require both verbal and non-verbal channels for social communication, particularly through body language. Beyond executing their primary tasks, these robots must convey social signals to communicate intent or affect. Depending on the context, they need mechanisms to stylize their body language by modulating timing, extent, or motion dynamics in response to how the interaction unfolds [ 29 , 36 , 4 ] . Here, we address the challenge of jointly executing expressive body language while maintaining stability and physical feasibility under complex platform dynamics.

Recent advances in character animation use physics-based control through reinforcement learning to enable robots to reproduce complex, expressive reference motions while accounting for modeled system dynamics [ 25 , 32 ] . This way, behaviors authored for virtual characters can be realized on physical platforms [ 8 , 23 ] .
Other lines of work propose motion representations that make stylization directly and interpretably controllable. Rather than specifying expressivity through authored trajectories, recent kinematic approaches represent expressive characteristics along interpretable dimensions, enabling the design of specific motion styles using Laban features [ 17 ] or Disney’s animation principles [ 10 ] . Such representations can then be embedded into continuous control systems that generate interactive body language automatically from multimodal context inputs [ 11 ] . However, expressive reference generation and physical execution remain largely decoupled [ 3 ] , often rendering online expressivity adjustments physically unfeasible or unstable (see Fig. 1 ).

To bridge this gap, we present an approach that builds on parametrized motion synthesis with physics-based control and reactive interactive behavior. We ground motion expressivity in the Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP) formulation of parametrized animation principles of prior work [ 10 , 11 ] and train a policy to track continuously modulated references while maintaining physical stability. A decoupled interaction loop, driven by interchangeable, lightweight policies, reacts to interaction goals (a person or object in space) by adapting the spatial direction of the expressive reference stream, which is then stabilized by the tracking policy. Specifically, our contributions are:

A method for stable execution of continuously modulated reference motions for social human-robot interaction that trains the tracking policy over the DMP-induced reference domain for robust execution across expressive variations.

An interaction layer that modulates the goal attraction point of the reference generating DMP with lightweight plug-and-play policies to perform spatially directed execution with the stabilizing tracking policy in the loop.

Note that this paper does not raise claims related to the way how expressivity is generated or perceived, for which a user study would be required. Instead, the paper makes the technical contribution of learning to dynamically execute expressive body motion evaluated against the respective task and tracking metrics.

1. A method for stable execution of continuously modulated reference motions for social human-robot interaction that trains the tracking policy over the DMP-induced reference domain for robust execution across expressive variations.

2. An interaction layer that modulates the goal attraction point of the reference generating DMP with lightweight plug-and-play policies to perform spatially directed execution with the stabilizing tracking policy in the loop.

# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Expressive and Interactive Robot Motion

Generating expressive robot motion across humanoid and non-humanoid systems typically relies on manual keyframing, classic animation heuristics, or retargeted motion capture [ 35 , 28 , 29 , 36 , 4 ] . Despite communicating affect and intent effectively, these authoring pipelines remain inherently bottlenecked, where every individual expressive behavior requires dedicated, time-consuming manual specification.

Parameterized motion representations capture expressive variation through a reduced set of variables. Laban Effort features can specify expressive qualities while preserving task motion, and related approaches parameterize kinematic and temporal properties like velocity, spatial extent, and timing [ 16 , 17 , 37 , 38 ] . Beyond parameterizing descriptive traits, representations built on mathematically integrated animation principles allow systems to automatically and interactively modulate expressive motion [ 10 ] . Learning-based methods offer another avenue by extracting latent style spaces directly from motion datasets [ 33 ] . Although these methods vary in their underlying structures, each uses parameterized expressivity to produce a variety of styles. Compared to latent representations, explicit parameterization keeps variables interpretable so designers and high-level controllers can adjust them directly.

Interactive robots must also couple this expressivity to the dynamic state of nearby humans. Social and movement-based platforms typically achieve this by directing attention through gaze or body orientation [ 1 ] , regulating interpersonal distance and spatial layout [ 22 ] , and adapting action timing to human behavior [ 14 ] . These capabilities highlight how responsiveness and behavioral contingency influence the perceived quality of interaction [ 12 , 19 ] . Recent systems build on these insights by explicitly adapting behavior based on human observations, which includes generating interaction-driven control commands [ 7 ] and using context to select and modulate expressive movement parameters [ 11 ] .

However, these interactive and parameter-driven methods predominantly operate at the kinematic level. Rapidly modulating expressive references online provides no guarantees of physical feasibility on dynamic platforms, often inducing balance loss or actuator saturation. Bridging this gap requires decoupling interactive parameter adjustment from low-level physical tracking.

## II-B Physics-Based Character Animation and Robotic Characters

Physics-based character animation translates kinematically authored trajectories into physical execution by learning policies that imitate reference motions under simulated dynamics. Deep reinforcement learning has advanced these capabilities through explicit tracking rewards [ 25 ] , adversarial motion priors [ 27 ] , reusable skill embeddings [ 26 ] , and masked reference completion [ 34 ] . Hierarchical two-layer architectures further decouple high-level reference generation from low-level physical control [ 3 ] , drawing from large-scale motion capture datasets to supply target behaviors [ 21 ] .

While dataset-driven approaches thrive on humanoid platforms that closely resemble human morphology [ 6 , 9 , 32 ] , non-humanoid robotic characters lack comparable motion repositories. Consequently, research on non-humanoid characters emphasizes morphology-independent policy learning, imitation control, and physics-aware retargeting across diverse robot structures [ 25 , 24 ] . On these platforms, carefully authored physical traits and reference trajectories define the character’s expressivity and identity [ 8 , 23 ] , leaving the learned controller to realize these predefined behaviors under real-world dynamics.

More recently, runtime adaptation has been introduced directly into physics-based controllers. For instance, Hopkins et al. [ 13 ] expose continuous style controls for interactive gait design, Alegre et al. [ 2 ] condition tracking controllers on shifting multi-objective preferences at inference, and Kobayashi et al. [ 18 ] inject handcrafted emotion parameters into locomotion policies.

While these developments show that stable physics-based controllers can accommodate behavioral variations beyond a single static motion, current adaptation mechanisms remain bound to uninterpretable latent spaces and scalar preference weights, or narrow locomotion styles. In contrast, our work grounds controller execution in a broad, interpretable DMP parameter space, coupling stable physical tracking with closed-loop goal adaptation for interactive robotic characters.

Animals build cognitive maps of vast environments, use them to perform map-based navigation, and might even be reusing the same circuitry used in spatial reasoning for creating and using maps of arbitrary task-spaces.
In contrast, current embodied AI systems either rely on hand-engineered mapping pipelines, which break in the presence of unmodeled dynamics and are restricted to metric space, or on learned policies that rarely form map-like representations at all.
Developing architectures that could learn to build and use map-like representations as flexibly as animals is, however, difficult because few
embodied AI benchmarks actually require map-based reasoning.
To address this, we present ForagerSim — an interdisciplinary research platform and simulation environment focused on embodied tasks that require map-based reasoning,
with scenarios ranging from mobile-robot search and rescue to animal foraging in both complex mazes and vast, potentially infinite open areas. ForagerSim is highly modular and allows modifying independent axes of difficulty related to perception (abstract 2D sensing to full RGB or LiDAR), scale (room-scale to multi-km scale), topology (open-fields to complex mazes), dynamics (smoke, debris, sensorimotor failures and others) and tasks (from simple 2D coverage to foraging-inspired well-alternation tasks).
We compare reinforcement learning baselines with a simple engineered robotics stack and a human player on 8 example worlds which show how different difficulty axes affect existing methods.
Our results show that, when sensing is simplified to 2D, learned policies can perform multi-object search and well-alternation tasks surprisingly well in simple topologies, but they fall short of human performance in larger or more complex-topology environments where map-based baselines perform well, suggesting that map-based reasoning is the bottleneck in these scenarios.
Code and data are made open source 1 1 1 https://github.com/MrTomzor/foragersim .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Searching for sparse objects (e.g. food) in vast, dynamic environments (deformable and changing), and then returning to known locations (e.g. a nest, a storage, or favorite feeding locations) are critical capabilities for the survival of nearly all animal species.
When performing this task in large environments, animals and humans do not behave purely reactively, but they build highly scalable spatial representations (cognitive maps) ( Tolman, 1948 ; Epstein et al., 2017 ; Geva-Sagiv et al., 2015 ) which enable efficient planning, navigation, and reacting to environment changes.
Bats and other animals are capable of navigating at scales as high as tens of kilometers ( Goldshtein et al., 2024 ; Gurarie et al., 2022 ) .
Dogs trained for search and rescue missions learn to navigate rubble, enter damaged structures, and search systematically over large areas through a curriculum of reinforcement, without being told how to map or plan ( Gerritsen and Haak, 2014 ) , and without human-level language understanding.
Some research even suggests that the cognitive map construction could play a significant role in general task learning in the form of learning reusable schemata that agents can then use for faster learning, efficient decision making, or imagining future trajectories in both physical and abstract spaces ( Aronov et al., 2017 ; Baraduc et al., 2019 ; Epstein et al., 2017 ) .
Importantly, replicating the learnable map-based reasoning observed in animals and humans could enable agents to learn to perform tasks that are currently unsolvable by neither hand-crafted map-based reasoning systems nor by existing end-to-end learning approaches by combining the strengths of both.
The main motivating example, which we also use as inspiration in designing some of the dynamics and topologies in ForagerSim , are search-and-rescue missions in environments that are both large, and highly dynamic (e.g. autonomously finding survivors in a suburb during a wildfire, flood or earthquake), which have not yet been reliably solved by any existing embodied AI approach.

Engineered mobile robotics systems, often called autonomy stacks ( Tranzatto et al., 2022 ; Hudson et al., 2022 ; Petrlík et al., 2025 ) , serve as examples showing that performing localization, mapping and planning at multiple levels of abstraction (e.g. using a global+local planner, and combining both metric and topological maps) can allow robots to search and navigate unknown environments at scales of even up to several kilometers.
However, they are also built on assumptions that break in highly dynamic environments, since every new type of dynamics has to be engineered into the pipeline by hand (e.g. how the mapping and plannning has to be changed, compared to a static environment, in the case of smoke, humans or e.g. actuator or odometry failures).
Even though deep learning is sometimes used in parts of these systems (e.g. for perception or low-level control), the mapping and planning modules, their interactions and their hierarchy levels are hand-designed and not learnable end-to-end.

While deep learning approaches can learn to perform arbitrary tasks in worlds with arbitrary dynamics, for which handcrafting autonomy stacks would be completely infeasible, map-like representations and online planning capabilities are severely limited in existing learning architectures.
Some recent works have investigated the map-building capabilities of commonly used learned memory architectures, and found that map-like representations can emerge, but only in highly specific conditions, ( Wijmans et al., 2023 ; Banino et al., 2018 ) or when a structural prior on spatial transformations is embedded into the architecture ( Yang et al., 2026 ) .
While recent research has shown that the popularly used large language models can sometimes provide reasonable estimates on “where to go to search for a given object”, studies have shown that they are very brittle when tested on long-horizon embodied tasks that require spatial reasoning ( Paglieri et al., 2025 ) .
Some approaches have combined classical autonomy stacks with taking LLM outputs as high-level guidance, which has had success in static environments ( Kim et al., 2026 ) , but this approach still suffers from the core problems of engineered autonomy stacks (inability to learn and brittleness to noise and hard-to-model situations).

Finding learning architectures that could learn to build and utilize maps at the scales and flexibility seen in animals could benefit the robotics community (by removing the need to re-engineer mapping/planning pipelines and heuristics for different morphologies and environments), the reinforcement learning community (by helping with long-term memory and behavior), and the cognitive science community (by providing testable models of how map-like representations may arise in animals).
However, each community evaluates these capabilities on its own tasks, under its own assumptions: robotics on realistic sensing in largely static worlds, reinforcement learning on memory tasks in small abstract environments, and cognitive science on animal experiments that are rarely reproduced in simulation and often only in small box-arenas.
To provide a platform for these communities to collaboratively investigate the problem of learnable map-based reasoning, our paper brings the following contributions:

Environment We introduce ForagerSim, an open-source environment for embodied search and navigation in which perception, scale, topology and dynamics can be varied independently, allowing the construction of tasks that truly require map-like memory and online planning.
To keep it accessible, we design the worlds such that the same scenarios can be addressed in both a fast, low-dimensionality abstract 2D depth+semantics observation mode and a more detailed, 3D mode with RGB/LiDAR sensing.
We replicate scenarios from mobile robot navigation, memory-learning benchmarks and animal experiments, design new environmental topologies and dynamics which challenge existing methods and present an example curriculum learning experiment which smoothly increases topological complexity.
