# 2 Related Work

In this section, we summarize relevant existing benchmarks and simulation environments and discuss their limitations which have motivated the development of ForagerSim .
Table 1 summarizes how ForagerSim differs along the axes most relevant to evaluating map-based reasoning.

The most popular embodied-AI simulation environments, such as Habitat ( Savva et al., 2019 ; Puig et al., 2024 ) and ProcTHOR ( Deitke et al., 2022 ) , allow simulating embodied agents in photorealistic scanned or generated household interiors, but their worlds are limited to the scale of a single building and mostly static.
ExploreBench ( Xu et al., 2022 ) is focused specifically on benchmarking exploration approaches, but its worlds are static and also limited to indoor layouts.
Outdoor and large-scale simulators, such as AirSim ( Shah et al., 2018 ) , UnrealZoo ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) or MetaUrban ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , offer simulation of various robot morphologies in large, photorealistic worlds, including urban scenes with pedestrians.
However, their high rendering cost makes RL training expensive (e.g. UnrealZoo reaches 83 FPS on an RTX 4090).

MemoryMaze Pašukonis et al. (2023) simulates ordered multi-object search tasks in mazes and focuses on RL memory evaluation.
We replicate the same environment topology and scale in memorymaze15x15 and show that for the task of unordered object-search, even the largest maze can easily be solved with memoryless policies.
MemoryGym Pleines et al. (2025) is a newer benchmark focusing on memory on multiple videogame-like scenarios, which can be endless, but are constrained to abstract grid-world scenarios.
POPGym ( Morad et al., 2023 ) contains some grid-world maze-navigation scenarios, but the authors state that wall-following memoryless policies were able to solve these, suggesting that navigation on its own might not be a strong memory benchmark.
Videogame RL wrappers like Crafter ( Hafner, 2022 ) , Craftax ( Matthews et al., 2024 ) , NetHack ( Küttler et al., 2020 ) , and MiniHack ( Samvelyan et al., 2021 ) offer rich open-ended videogame worlds that test long-horizon behavior, but are constrained to highly abstract grid-world scenarios.
Minecraft-based suites like MineRL and MineDojo ( Guss et al., 2019 ; Fan et al., 2022 ) do provide infinite 3D worlds, but they inherit the slowness of Minecraft and the observations and actions are still highly abstract compared to mobile robot embodiments.

Some simulation environments also take inspiration from specific animal capabilities and pose those as learning challenges.
Avalon ( Albrecht et al., 2022 ) , focused on RL generalization, provides procedural 3D videogame-style island worlds with 20 embodied tasks sharing dynamics and action space.
Its scenes range up to 600m in scale, but they contain simple topologies where the reward area can often be seen from the start, and the observation and action dimensionality are relatively high, due to being designed as VR-compatible.
Animal-AI ( Voudouris et al., 2025 ) recreates 900 tasks from cognitive science, such as object permanence, radial-arm-maze tasks, but all within a 40x40 units wide arena, which is not suitable for large-scale navigation.

Compared to the existing environments, ForagerSim is the only one that combines massive scalability (through Minecraft-inspired world generation and streaming), modularity (specifically in being able to independently change axis of difficulty of topology, scale, observations, dynamics and switching between 2D and 3D variants of the same scenario), and cross-disciplinary focus (through offering both a ROS2 and Gym interface and by presenting example environments replicated from across mobile robotics, memory learning benchmarks and animal studies) which are necessary for investigating the problem of learning how to map, plan and navigate at the level of freely foraging animals.

2026-10-20.title: Cartender: Verifiable Language-Conditioned Driving by Learning the Drives Not Taken
2026-10-20.authors: Zhiwen Chen , Benjin Zhu , Yan Xie , Jun Ma
2026-10-20.abstract:
Every driving scene is logged exactly once, yet driving is inherently one-to-many.
The scene decides which behaviors are admissible and the driver’s intent which one to take: vision alone cannot choose
among them, and language alone cannot tell what the scene permits.
But the log keeps only the drive that was taken, and its instruction merely describes it.
Language-conditioned driving policies are reported to follow instructions, yet on such data this cannot be established:
a policy that ignores the instruction and one that obeys it regardless of the scene fit the logs equally well, and neither is distinguishable from one that weighs both.
Trained only on such logs, driving vision–language–action models (VLAs) and world–action models (WAMs) receive no direct supervision on actions that violate their instructions or instructions the scene rules out.
We present Cartender , which learns from the drives not taken.
To construct matched and mismatched instruction–action pairs from real recordings without a simulator, we propose Counterfactual Branching ,
which treats each logged trajectory as one branch among several candidate futures: a vision–language model proposes the others and the instruction that selects each, and instructions the scene cannot support become negative labels.
Cartender then weighs both explicitly: a learned scene–language compatibility regulates language conditioning during trajectory generation, and a reward-trained language residual re-ranks the candidates over a scene-based score.
Branches serve training; instruction following is evaluated by changing instructions under identical recorded inputs, using behavior criteria rather than generated trajectory targets.
On WOD-E2E, the best of four proposals reaches an RFS of 8.642 across 3,603 feasible instruction conditions.
Across all 8,974 admitted proposals, mean RFS is 8.203 versus 7.906 for their matched logged trajectories, and 67% score higher than their logged counterpart.
Relative to matched-only imitation with the same backbone,
Cartender more than doubles the rate of fulfilling both instructions of a same-scene pair (57.00% vs. 23.67%) while RFS rises from 6.32 to 7.10; its gate cuts execution of infeasible instructions from 53.36% to 14.18%.
2026-10-20.introduction:
The same driving situation admits many competent behaviors — overtake the slow truck now or follow it for three seconds first, take the gap at 40 km/h or at 25, return to the right lane the moment it is clear or stay out until the exit — and the scene settles only which are admissible, never which one is preferred ( Liao et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) .
That is settled by an intention the sensors never see.
They record the situation, not the reason one behavior was chosen, and not the behaviors passed over.
Nor can more data recover the rest.
A vehicle occupies one position in space and time and drives one trajectory; the situation never reassembles itself for a second attempt.
Every driving corpus therefore contains single samples from genuinely multi-modal conditional behavior distributions — one sample each, whatever else is recorded alongside it.
The alternatives are not missing from the datasets we happen to have.
They are not collectible as outcomes of that same event.

Their absence is felt twice: once in what can be trained
and, with far less attention, once in what can be checked.
Matched records show the executed behavior, leaving alternative responses unobserved.
Establishing instruction control requires testing what
the policy does under a different instruction
in the same scene.
Matched instruction–trajectory evaluation leaves this response untested.
The instruction-following scores reported on such data are taken to show that the policy reads the instruction.
They do not.
The visual scene may not determine which admissible behavior is preferred, but it can already narrow the space of plausible actions enough for a largely scene-driven policy to fit the recorded trajectory well; an instruction-sensitive policy can fit the same matched pair just as well, while differing only in what happens when the instruction is changed.
Both score well.
Figure 1 makes the ambiguity concrete.
Only an instruction intervention separates them.

Simulation can construct alternative trajectories from a
recorded simulator state.
SimLingo’s Action Dreaming pairs language instructions with alternative trajectories generated from recorded CARLA states through offline, non-reactive simulation ( Renz et al., 2025 ) .
Our construction instead operates on real recordings without a simulator.
Matched-pair evaluation on these recordings retains the ambiguity above.
Whether same-scene supervision helps is not the open question; simulation already indicates that it does.
Two others are.
The first is about data: whether such supervision can be obtained, and trusted, where the situation cannot be replayed.
The second does not wait on the first.
Instruction dependence can already be measured on
released models, and that is where we begin.

Two of the three diagnostics we use to measure instruction dependence need no data beyond what a model was already trained on.
Instructions are first shuffled across scenes. If the action loss does not move, the matched objective is insensitive to instruction identity.
A rise exposes dependence.
At inference, removing the instruction tests whether
its presence changes the predicted trajectory.
Neither diagnostic requires a behavior that was never
driven, so the confound becomes something to measure
rather than something to argue about.
On LMDrive, shuffling increases waypoint L1 loss by 0.011.
Under the evaluated Qwen-Drive interface, instruction
removal shifts predictions by only 0.064 m.
The third holds the scene fixed and changes the instruction,
probing alternative behaviors that a single recorded
event cannot jointly reveal.

We construct same-scene, multi-intent supervision on real driving data, treating its two halves differently.
Declaring an instruction inapplicable to a recorded scene takes a label and no trajectory at all, so scene–instruction applicability is grounded in real observation by construction; supplying the behavior a feasible alternative instruction would have produced takes a trajectory that was never driven, and Sec. 3.1 states how it is branched and on what grounds it is admitted.
We then keep training and measurement apart.
Branched alternatives enter training. Evaluation changes instructions under an identical recorded input, with both requests reviewed for feasibility and predictions assessed by behavior criteria, not by distance to generated teachers.

The feasible half is the hard one: it requires the behavior that a valid alternative instruction would have produced, and we supply it with Counterfactual Branching .
At selected keyframes, a vision–language model proposes route-relative parameters and corresponding instructions; deterministic construction and rule-based admission produce trajectory branches in the planner’s prediction space.
Branch quality is an empirical question, not a design assumption. We evaluate admitted branches against matched logged trajectories using Rater Feedback Score (RFS).
Across the complete set of 3,603 feasible instruction
conditions, the branched set reaches a best-of-four RFS of 8.642.
Across all 8,974 admitted proposals, mean RFS is 8.203, compared with 7.906 for their matched logged trajectories, and 67% of branches individually outperform their logged counterparts.

A demonstration identifies a point; a preference among admissible behaviors is an ordering.
That distinction follows from multimodality: a demonstration says “drive like this,” but does not rank admissible alternatives under an instruction; a reward expresses that ordering.
The supervision supplies the candidates, not the ordering.
Same-scene alternatives make the comparison expressible;
the ordering itself is defined by the frozen key-event
reward in Sec. 3.2 .
Cartender accordingly generates a candidate set, estimates continuous scene–language compatibility to scale language conditioning during generation and ranking, and ranks the candidates with a demonstration-initialized base score plus a reward-trained language residual.
Our main contributions are:

The matched-pair confound, and how to measure it. An instruction-following score on matched
instruction–trajectory pairs does not establish
that the policy’s behavior depends on the instruction.
We expose this ambiguity through instruction removal,
shuffling, and same-scene swapping.
Removal and shuffling, where native action loss is
accessible, need no alternative trajectory targets;
swapping fixes a recorded input and tests two feasible requests
without generated trajectory targets.

Counterfactual Branching. Same-scene, multi-intent supervision built on real
recordings without a simulator, where the logged
trajectory anchors route-relative candidate futures,
each paired with a proposed instruction.
Branches pass rule-based admission before RFS evaluation:
admitted branches average 8.203 against 7.906 for
matched logged trajectories, with 67% individually
scoring higher.
Inapplicable instructions require labels but no
synthesized trajectories.

Cartender. A policy that gates language conditioning through
scene–language compatibility and ranks candidates
with a reward-trained language residual over a
demonstration-initialized base score.
Cartender more than doubles maneuver paired success over matched-only imitation (57.00% vs. 23.67%),
with RFS rising from 6.32 to 7.10. Gating reduces unsupported-request following from 53.36% to 14.18%.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Multi-proposal planners address behavioral multimodality
by predicting several trajectories per scene.
DiffusionDrive ( Liao et al., 2025 ) and
DiffusionDriveV2 ( Zou et al., 2025 ) generate candidates
through truncated diffusion and select among them with a learned
scorer.
The candidate set hedges against missing one answer;
it does not establish which answer the instruction prefers.
We supply what matched demonstrations alone do not—a
same-scene criterion for intention-dependent selection.

LMDrive ( Shao et al., 2024a ) , ORION ( Fu et al., 2025 ) ,
AutoVLA ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and
MindVLA-U1 ( Huang et al., 2026 ) connect language
with trajectory generation through different architectures.
NudgeVAD ( Yang et al., 2026 ) adds language-conditioned
residuals to a frozen planner and examines when navigation
commands make language redundant.
The central issue here is not architecture but what
matched-pair training and evaluation establish.
On matched pairs, the instruction and recorded behavior
co-occur; agreement with that behavior alone does not
establish that the prediction changes when the instruction does.
ICR-Drive ( Hamid et al., 2026 ) tests robustness to
instruction perturbations under matched simulator routes and seeds.
Our question is whether different feasible instructions
select different appropriate behaviors under the same
recorded input.
Our contribution is diagnostic before it is architectural:
we distinguish instruction dependence from agreement with
a matched trajectory, with two tests requiring no new annotation.

LinkVLA ( Wang et al., 2026a ) strengthens language–action
coupling through shared representations, while Drive My
Way ( Wang et al., 2026b ) learns driving preferences.
SimLingo’s Action Dreaming ( Renz et al., 2025 ) constructs
alternatives through offline, non-reactive simulation;
MALT-Drive ( Lu et al., 2026 ) uses rollout-based
counterfactual supervision to align control instructions
with planning.
Our setting requires alternative trajectories for real
recordings without simulator rollouts.
OmniDrive ( Wang et al., 2025 ) supplies counterfactual
descriptions of alternative outcomes; constructing the trajectories
themselves additionally requires checking their validity.
Counterfactual Branching does not sidestep this requirement.
It constructs alternatives from recorded routes, admits
them through rule-based checks, and evaluates their quality
afterward using RFS (Sec. 3.1 );
these checks do not certify full scene feasibility.
Generated teachers serve training, not evaluation targets:
instruction control is assessed by behavior criteria under
fixed recorded inputs.

2026-10-20.title: Robotic Photography System based on Vision-Language-Action Model
2026-10-20.authors: Song-Li Wu , Chubin Zhang , Wenbo Ding , Yansong Tang
2026-10-20.abstract: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Robotic photography is emerging as an important embodied AI application in creative production, event recording, and commercial media, where robots are expected to autonomously execute camera movements according to high-level user instructions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Unlike conventional robotic manipulation [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , whose objective is successful task execution, robotic photography requires balancing two complementary objectives: accurately understanding the semantic intent of the user while producing photographs that satisfy human aesthetic preferences. Achieving this objective demands not only precise camera control, but also reasoning about abstract photographic concepts such as composition, viewpoint, framing, and subject interaction. Developing robots capable of jointly perceiving scenes, interpreting photographic intent, and generating aesthetically pleasing camera behaviors therefore remains a fundamental challenge [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] .

Existing robotic photography systems have explored reference-guided camera control, semantic event photography, and interactive computational photography [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . However, these methods are typically built upon modular pipelines that decouple perception, language understanding, and camera control [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , limiting their ability to reason over abstract photographic intent and adapt to open-ended instructions, unseen subjects, and dynamic shooting environments. Recent Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models address this limitation by unifying perception, reasoning, and action within a single policy [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . Nevertheless, existing VLAs are primarily optimized for task completion rather than photographic quality, lacking both photography-oriented reasoning and explicit optimization toward human aesthetic preferences. Moreover, the scarcity of embodied robotic photography datasets further limits their applicability to autonomous photography.

To address these challenges, we formulate robotic photography as an aesthetic-aware Vision–Language–Action learning problem and propose RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and embodied camera control. Specifically, we introduce PhotoCoT, a photography-oriented reasoning strategy that grounds abstract photographic intent into structured camera operations, including viewpoint selection, framing adjustment, and camera motion planning. To further optimize photographic quality, we propose Aesthetical Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO), which explicitly aligns camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences through preference learning rather than conventional task-success supervision. To facilitate training and evaluation, we further construct OpenPhotography, the first open-ended robotic photography dataset containing language-guided demonstrations together with aesthetic preference pairs.
Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA consistently produces photographs that better align with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively across unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and diverse photographic scenarios.

Our contributions are threefold: we propose RoboPhoto-VLA for aesthetic-aware robotic photography, introduce PhotoCoT and ADPO for structured reasoning and aesthetic alignment, and construct OpenPhotography for real-world evaluation under diverse unseen settings.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Works

Recent Vision–Language Models (VLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in multimodal understanding by combining pretrained vision encoders with large language models, enabling strong performance on visual reasoning, captioning, and question answering tasks [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] . Building upon these advances, Vision–Language–Action (VLA) models integrate perception, language, and robot control into a unified policy, allowing pretrained VLMs to directly predict robot actions for embodied manipulation and long-horizon planning [ 18 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 ] . Representative models such as RT-2-X and OpenVLA demonstrate impressive generalization across robotic manipulation tasks but are primarily designed for task execution rather than photography-oriented reasoning and aesthetic decision-making.
Robotic photography has traditionally focused on camera control, viewpoint selection, framing, and target tracking through rule-based or modular pipelines [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Although recent systems incorporate language understanding and scene perception, they generally lack unified reasoning over visual observations and abstract photographic intent, as well as explicit optimization toward human aesthetic preferences. In contrast, our work formulates robotic photography as an aesthetic-aware Vision–Language–Action problem. Built upon a unified VLA framework, RoboPhoto-VLA introduces photography-oriented reasoning and preference optimization to bridge abstract photographic intent with executable camera actions, enabling aesthetically aligned robotic photography.

2026-10-20.title: AnchorFlow-VIO: Fixed-Template Monocular Visual-Inertial Odometry on LaMAria
2026-10-20.authors: Sudhir Pratap Yadav
2026-10-20.abstract:
We present AnchorFlow-VIO, an open-source Basalt-derived monocular visual-inertial
odometry system, and evaluate a uniform configuration on LaMAria. The system uses
one grayscale camera and one IMU, combining
factory IMU correction, a fixed timing adjustment, windowed initialization and
fixed-template patch tracking. Server evaluation of all 63 test recordings yields
control-point scores of 47.2, 37.1, 24.8, 35.1 and 15.6 for Short, Medium, Long,
Low light and Moving platform. Test pose recalls at 5 m are 84.6%, 69.1%,
53.9% and 62.9% for the four categories reporting dense recall. On ten training
recordings, mean control-point score is 41.38 and all 265,694 image timestamps
receive poses, including 204 filled poses. One training platform recording
diverges and scores zero.
A paired four-record comparison favors fixed over rolling templates on three
recordings, while reversing that ranking on the fourth. Increasing feature
density also yields mixed results. Ten fresh runs at prospectively fixed 30 s
and 120 s offsets expose substantial start sensitivity: a low-light recording
scores 6.14 at the earlier start and 42.00 at the later start. These results
characterize the limits of the frozen system and show why complete output,
feature counts and selected successful runs are insufficient evidence of robust
localization. Source code, frozen configuration and reproducible submission
tools are publicly available; training ablations are reported separately from
the submitted test evaluation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Head-mounted visual-inertial estimation must accommodate rapid viewpoint
changes, poor illumination and scenes in which visible objects move independently
of the observer. LaMAria provides a setting for studying these conditions at city
scale, including low-light and moving-platform challenges [ 4 ] . The present report focuses on a restricted sensor
configuration: the left grayscale camera and a single IMU from the ordinary ASL
recordings. A second camera is neither supplied to the estimator nor used to
generate its initial state or landmarks.

The practical question is how well an existing visual-inertial estimator transfers
to this setting under a uniform configuration. A result on an easy recording
does not determine performance on long walks, dark scenes or platform motion.
Likewise, successful process termination and a pose at every image timestamp do
not establish accurate tracking. Output can remain finite and complete while
the estimated trajectory drifts or diverges.

We study AnchorFlow-VIO, a frozen Basalt-derived monocular visual-inertial
odometry (VIO) configuration. Its main estimator architecture is inherited from prior work [ 7 , 2 ] . Our contribution is an empirical system
characterization: a sensor-isolated implementation, paired template and feature
density comparisons, complete evaluation on ten challenge training recordings,
and fresh-start tests that retain the unfavorable outcomes. A public source
release and server evaluation on all 63 test recordings extend this characterization
beyond the ten training recordings. The benchmark lists the method as AnchorFlow VIO [ 5 ] . We do not introduce
a new estimator formulation or claim that fixed-template tracking is a new
general principle.

Four questions organize the study. First, how does the frozen policy perform
across challenge categories? Second, do template retention and increased feature
density improve the same recordings? Third, how much do results change when
initialization occurs later in an otherwise identical recording? The last
comparison uses matched suffixes of the original trajectories so that different
temporal coverage is not mistaken for a method effect. Fourth, how does the
unchanged configuration perform in the benchmark’s server-side test evaluation?

# 2 Related Work and Scope

Basalt combines visual-inertial odometry with a mapping formulation based on
nonlinear factor recovery [ 7 ] . Square root marginalization
provides a sliding-window formulation that avoids forming normal equations
during marginalization [ 2 ] . We use the Basalt-derived VIO
estimator and its square root configuration; the evaluated candidate does not
include the original global mapping pipeline. IMU preintegration is a standard
way to summarize measurements between visual states; Forster et al. develop
its manifold formulation [ 3 ] . These estimator ideas
are inherited components rather than contributions of this report.

ORB-SLAM3 supports visual, visual-inertial and multiple-map estimation, including
monocular operation [ 1 ] . Our frozen candidate has no
validated loop closure or global relocalization extension. We therefore refer
to it as odometry, even though its output format is intended for a SLAM
benchmark. We do not compare its training scores with other methods’ hidden-test
scores as evidence of relative performance.

LaMAria introduces egocentric recordings with survey-based control-point
evaluation [ 4 ] . This report supplies a focused analysis
of one implementation on ten challenge training recordings and 63 test recordings.
It does not replace
the benchmark’s broader comparison, reproduce every published monocular
baseline, or establish novelty over all prior template-tracking methods.

2026-10-20.title: K-AoI: A Spatio-Temporal Synchronization Metric for Digital Twin-based Teleoperation in Dynamic Network Environments
2026-10-20.authors: Lu Tian , Zhenhui Yuan , Zexin Deng , Wenjuan Zhang
2026-10-20.comment: . Accepted as a short paper at IEEE Smart World Congress (SWC 2026)
2026-10-20.abstract: Synchronization between a digital twin (DT) and its physical robot is critical for effective teleoperation, as mismatches directly degrade operator awareness and task performance. Existing synchronization metrics are predominantly time-based and rarely capture the spatial consequences of delayed information during motion. In this paper, we introduce Kinematic Age of Information (K-AoI), a spatio-temporal metric that weights AoI by instantaneous Cartesian velocity, translating temporal staleness into physically meaningful spatial divergence. We implement and evaluate K-AoI on a DT teleoperation testbed comprising a six-degrees-of-freedom (6-DOF) manipulator, a Unity-based twin, and controlled network impairments using tc netem across seven network conditions. Per-sample analysis shows that K-AoI exhibits rank-correlations with AoI at ρ ≤ 0.65 \rho\leq 0.65 across all networks, dropping to ρ = 0.22 \rho=0.22 under satellite connections. This shows that K-AoI is not a simple transformation of AoI, but instead captures velocity-dependent degradation effects that time-only metrics cannot resolve. We further analyze AoI tail behavior using Ultra-Low AoI (ULAoI) and find that the commonly assumed Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) model is rejected. This reflects the impact of deterministic forwarding and bounded jitter, which violate standard extreme-value assumptions. Overall, K-AoI provides a complementary and physically grounded synchronization metric, linking network delay to task-relevant spatial error in digital-twin teleoperation systems. The dataset and testbed software are publicly available at: https://github.com/luziyaotian/kaoi-testbed .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Robot teleoperation allows human control of physical systems in hazardous or inaccessible environments [ 1 ] . A key challenge lies in the network connection between the human operator and the robot, as delays exceeding approximately 250 ms 250\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} can significantly degrade situational awareness and task performance [ 1 ] . Digital twins (DT) mitigate this by maintaining a synchronized virtual representation, allowing the operator to interact with a local, low-latency virtual robot while control commands are transmitted to the physical robot [ 2 , 3 ] .
However, evaluating the performance of DT-based teleoperation systems remains an open challenge. Subjective workload measures such as NASA-TLX [ 2 ] cannot be derived from system logs and do not generalize well across different operators. Latency reports typically reflect average behavior and miss tail spikes that cause task failure. Age of Information (AoI) [ 4 ] addresses temporal freshness more explicitly, while Ultra-Low AoI (ULAoI) [ 5 ] extends this idea by modeling tail behavior using extreme-value theory.
However, both AoI and ULAoI are purely time-based metrics and ignore physical motion: a 500 ms 500\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{s} delay has negligible impact on a stationary DT, yet produces 250 mm 250\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} of spatial divergence between the robot end-effector and its digital twin at 500 mm / s 500\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{/}\mathrm{s} . Since manipulation performance is fundamentally spatial, and the critical error is the Cartesian distance between the physical robot and its digital counterpart, existing metrics do not capture this combined effect of temporal delay and physical motion.
AoI and its extensions quantify information freshness in the temporal domain. The closest related spatial formulation is Age of Positioning (AoP) [ 6 ] , a mean squared error-based (MSE) metric derived analytically for mobile agents under Random Waypoint mobility and queuing-discipline updates. Our work shares the idea of incorporating motion into a freshness-aware metric, but differs in setting (fixed-based teleoperation versus stochastic mobility), methodology (empirical testbed versus closed-form), and form (linear scale distance versus quadratic MSE). Spatial AoI [ 7 ] also extends AoI spatially, but focuses on vehicular networks rather than robotic manipulation. On the DT side, RoboTwin [ 2 ] , Huang et al. [ 8 ] and ConstrucTwin [ 3 ] are system-level contributions without a motion-aware metric. Kawshan et al. [ 9 ] and the network-aware TeleSim benchmark [ 10 ] report latency mean and task-performance statistics on comparable teleoperation testbeds, but neither analyze the tails nor spatial divergence. Chen et al. [ 11 ] treats reconstruction error as a constraint while compressing transmission (35–44% load reduction), whereas we treat it as the quantity of interest.
Roy et al. [ 12 ] address resource dimensioning analytically through quality of control bounds rather than empirical measurement on a specific testbed.
This paper makes the following contributions:

A spatio-temporal synchronization metric for digital-twin teleoperation. We introduce Kinematic Age of Information (K-AoI), a velocity weighted extension of AoI that converts temporal staleness into a physically meaningful spatial divergence, explicitly capturing when network delay translates into task error during motion.

A reproducible experimental framework for digital twin teleoperation under network degradation , integrating physical robotics, real-time simulation, and controlled network impairment, to enable systematic evaluation of synchronization and communication metrics across different network conditions.

Empirical validation over ( N = 11 N=11 trials) showing that K-AoI captures
velocity degradation effects not shown in AoI. Across all network profiles, the Spearman rank correlations per-sample between AoI and K-AoI remain below ρ = 0.65 \rho=0.65 , decreasing to ρ = 0.22 \rho=0.22 under satellite conditions, indicating clear divergence under high-latency regimes.

2026-10-20.title: Data-Efficient Learning from Demonstration for Humanoid Robots via Feature-Level Perception and Prompt-Based Object Detection
2026-10-20.authors: Keyhan Rayati , AliReza Beigy , Anoosheh Saadati , Pourya Shahverdi , Mehdi Tale Masouleh , Ahmad Kalhor , Wing-Yue Geoffrey Louie
2026-10-20.abstract:
Learning from Demonstration (LfD) allows robots to learn new skills from human examples; however, many vision-based methods require large datasets and resource-intensive end-to-end training.
This paper introduces a data-efficient LfD framework for humanoid robots that learns manipulation skills from compact, task-specific features instead of raw images.
The proposed approach integrates layered visual preprocessing, Kinect-based human joint estimation, prompt-based object detection,
and depth information to extract human motion features and three-dimensional object locations from demonstration videos.
These features are used to train a temporal deep learning model that predicts robot joint-angle trajectories for execution.
The framework is implemented on a NAO humanoid robot, evaluated quantitatively in simulation, and demonstrated on physical hardware.
In simulation, the robot achieves a 78% success rate on a pick-and-place task using only 16 demonstrations, which increases to 86% when trained with 100 demonstrations.
The framework also achieves a 71% success rate on a pushing task using eight demonstrations, highlighting its effectiveness for data-efficient humanoid skill acquisition.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Learning from Demonstration (LfD) offers an effective way for robots to acquire new skills through the observation of human actions, rather than depending on explicitly programmed control policies.
This is especially beneficial for humanoid robots, as creating task-specific controllers for manipulation is labor-intensive and difficult to generalize across different objects,
environments, and users.
Nonetheless, acquiring dependable humanoid manipulation skills from a limited number of demonstrations remains difficult due to perceptual noise,
embodiment differences between humans and robots, and the restricted computational resources available on several humanoid platforms.

LfD has been extensively studied for transferring human skills to robots, from traditional trajectory-based techniques such as Dynamic Movement Primitives
to recent data-driven methods for robot skill learning from demonstrations [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Vision-based robot learning has also shown strong performance in manipulation, from spatial correspondence models such as Transporter Networks [ 4 ] to large-scale visuomotor policies such as RT-1 [ 5 ] .
However, many of these methods still rely on raw visual inputs, large demonstration datasets, or considerable task-specific adjustment [ 4 , 6 , 5 , 7 ] .
For humanoid robots, these challenges become harder because of embodiment differences, restricted joint limits, and the need to translate human motion and task
structure into robot-executable trajectories [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
Recent studies have explored more data-efficient learning from human videos and robot-free demonstrations, including keypoint-based representations, one-shot
transfer, humanoid manipulation from human play videos, whole-body control from monocular videos,
and mobile manipulation from robot-free demonstrations [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] .
Still, learning robust humanoid manipulation skills from only a few task demonstrations remains difficult, especially when the perception and policy learning
stages are trained directly from visual data.
This motivates the feature-level approach used in this work, where prompt-based object detection, depth information, and skeleton-based motion features are
extracted before training the robot trajectory model.

This research introduces a data-efficient LfD framework for humanoid robots that acquires manipulation skills using compact state representations rather than raw images.
The proposed approach extracts task-relevant information from human demonstration videos, including human joint positions, prompt-detected objects,
and depth-based three-dimensional object locations.
Prompt-based object detection localizes task objects without requiring a task-specific detector, while skeleton tracking provides human motion data for estimating robot joint trajectories.
The collected features are then used to train a task-specific temporal model that predicts joint-angle commands for execution on a NAO humanoid robot.

The framework is assessed quantitatively in simulation and demonstrated on real hardware, including upper-body imitation and two manipulation tasks: pick-and-place and object pushing.
In the simulated pick-and-place task, the robot attains a success rate of 78% with 16 demonstrations and 86% with 100 demonstrations.
The framework also attains a 71% success rate in the pushing task with only eight demonstrations.
These results suggest that feature-level perception can facilitate humanoid skill acquisition with limited demonstration resources.

The primary contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A data-efficient LfD framework is provided for humanoid manipulation using compact state representations instead of raw image-based policy learning.

A layered perception pipeline is established to integrate Kinect-based skeleton tracking, prompt-based object detection,
and depth data for extracting task-relevant demonstration features.

A temporal prediction model with explicit step and task-state embeddings is used to condition progress during autoregressive joint-trajectory rollout.

The framework is evaluated on a NAO humanoid robot through quantitative simulation experiments and representative real-world demonstrations, showing upper-body imitation,
pick-and-place, and pushing actions with limited demonstration data.

Supplementary Material: A video demonstration of the proposed framework is available online [Video] .
The code implementation is available online [Code] .

1. A data-efficient LfD framework is provided for humanoid manipulation using compact state representations instead of raw image-based policy learning.

2. A layered perception pipeline is established to integrate Kinect-based skeleton tracking, prompt-based object detection,
and depth data for extracting task-relevant demonstration features.

3. A temporal prediction model with explicit step and task-state embeddings is used to condition progress during autoregressive joint-trajectory rollout.

4. The framework is evaluated on a NAO humanoid robot through quantitative simulation experiments and representative real-world demonstrations, showing upper-body imitation,
pick-and-place, and pushing actions with limited demonstration data.

# II Proposed Framework

## II-A Feature Extraction

The feature vector at each timestep combines human arm configuration, prompt-detected object positions, task state, and progress information.
Human joint localization is obtained from the Kinect Skeleton API, with all joint positions expressed in the Kinect camera coordinate frame.
Building on prior NAO motion-transfer work [ 17 ] , the measured human arm geometry is converted into robot-compatible joint-angle features.
Let 𝐏 shoulder \mathbf{P}_{\text{shoulder}} , 𝐏 elbow \mathbf{P}_{\text{elbow}} , and 𝐏 wrist \mathbf{P}_{\text{wrist}} denote the measured three-dimensional shoulder, elbow, and wrist positions.
Shoulder angles are computed first because they define the local frame used for elbow-angle estimation:

For manipulation tasks, YOLO-World detections provide object locations in image space, which are combined with Kinect depth data to estimate three-dimensional positions of the ball, box, or block.
When an object is temporarily not detected or exits the camera field of view, the last reliable three-dimensional estimate is retained to preserve a continuous state vector.
This design keeps the learning problem low-dimensional while retaining the information needed to adjust motion according to object placement, and it allows object categories to be changed through prompts without collecting new labels for a task-specific detector.
All input and output variables are normalized before training so that object coordinates and joint angles have comparable numerical scales and remain within NAO joint limits during execution.

## II-B Temporal Model

The temporal model predicts robot joint angles from a fixed-length sequence of feature vectors.
As depicted in Fig. 2 , a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layer captures short-term motion dependencies over an input window of 10 timesteps.
Two supplementary embedding layers encode the current execution step and a three-valued grasp/task state representing the manipulation phase.
The LSTM output and embeddings are concatenated and passed through a fully connected output layer with linear activation to predict continuous robot joint angles.

The explicit step embedding provides a progress indicator during autoregressive rollout.
During deployment, the model repeatedly predicts the next joint configuration and incorporates the resulting state into the following input window.
Without such a signal, recurrent models trained on limited datasets may remain near familiar states or cycle through incomplete motions.
The step index provides a clear indication of execution progress, while the LSTM focuses on the relationship among current features, object positions, and joint trajectories.

Variable-length demonstrations are processed at their original temporal resolution rather than being standardized to a fixed duration.
Each network input consists of a fixed window of 10 feature vectors, with the k k -th element sampled at time t − k ​ s t-k\,s for k ∈ { 0 , … , 9 } k\in\{0,\ldots,9\} and step size s s .
Sequences shorter than the specified window are zero-padded at the beginning to support prediction from the initial frames.
During training, step sizes ranging from 5 to 95 frames are used, producing approximately ( L − 1 ) × 10 (L-1)\times 10 windows for a demonstration of length L L , thereby exposing the model to different demonstration speeds.
During deployment, the step size controls execution speed, the step embedding is incremented with each prediction, and a conservative limit of 200 prediction steps is imposed to prevent unbounded rollout.

Model selection involved evaluating 153 configurations with different layer counts, hidden sizes, learning rates,
batch sizes, dropout rates, and optimizers.
Validation loss was used as the primary offline selection criterion because it provides a consistent measure
before robot execution and allows many configurations to be compared efficiently.
However, task-level success is not guaranteed to be perfectly correlated with prediction error, especially in physical robot execution.
Therefore, the selected model is further evaluated through task execution in simulation and representative physical trials.
Training uses the AdamW optimizer, mean squared error loss, early stopping, and learning-rate reduction.
The final training setup is summarized in Table I .

## II-C Human-to-Robot Execution

The learned commands are executed on a NAO humanoid robot.
Because humans and NAO differ in size, reachability, and joint limits, the task setup is configured so that the demonstrated object positions remain within the robot workspace.
Predicted joint commands are constrained to the feasible robot range before execution.
In simulation, object and joint positions are measured relative to a reference plane aligned with the Kinect coordinate system, ensuring that simulated inputs remain compatible with the real-world preprocessing pipeline.
This workspace alignment avoids the need for online replanning while preserving the relative task geometry observed in the demonstrations.
For pick-and-place, a magnet is attached to the robot hand and a small metal component is secured to the ball, allowing the experiment to focus on trajectory learning rather than dexterous grasping.
For pushing, the model predicts the arm motion required to move a block in the specified direction.

2026-10-20.title: Compositional Humanoid Manipulation through Isomorphic Teleoperation and Independent Skill Routing
2026-10-20.authors: Yiming Wang , Peixian Yang , Lifeng Zhuo , Lai Wei , Xinling Du , Kun Song , Weiming Wang , Daolin Ma
2026-10-20.abstract: Humanoid manipulation requires reusable arm skills, yet demonstrating every possible skill combination is impractical. We present Humanoid Semantic Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Policy (HS-MoDP), which composes separately demonstrated arm skills through independent semantic routing over a shared expert pool. This design preserves arm-specific skill control while sharing action-generation parameters across arms. A semantic scheduler integrates the learned policy with an existing locomotion controller through alternating manipulation and repositioning stages, extending the effective workspace and enabling skill reuse across location changes. To acquire demonstrations of whole-body contact manipulation, we develop G1Exo, an isomorphic exoskeleton that provides direct joint-level control of arm configurations. Experiments on a Unitree G1 show stronger skill composition than the baselines. G1Exo enables more reliable contact teleoperation than end-effector VR-IK, and its demonstrations improve contact-skill learning across four policy architectures. For HS-MoDP, switching from VR-IK to G1Exo demonstrations raises full cabinet workflow success from 35% to 65%. All project hardware designs and source code will be released as open source after the review process.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Humanoid manipulation uses dual-arm action, body contact, and mobility to interact with objects across an extended workspace [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Gathering objects with the forearms or holding them against the torso requires control over arm configurations. Reusing separately demonstrated single-arm skills in new dual-arm combinations requires preserving each skill as the other arm’s task changes. We study how to capture the configurations needed for contact manipulation and compose separately demonstrated skills during execution.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models learn robot behaviors from large-scale visual, language, and action data [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Yet demonstrating every combination becomes increasingly costly: m m left-arm and n n right-arm skills admit m ​ n mn candidate pairings in a single stage. As analyzed in SkillVLA [ 7 ] , policies may retain demonstration-specific dependencies between arms in both predicted actions and internal policy representations. An arm’s learned behavior may therefore depend on what the other arm did during demonstration. Successful execution of individual skills does not establish that each skill will be preserved when paired with a different one. We address this composition problem through separate skill conditioning and routing for each arm.

Capturing the configurations needed for body-contact manipulation is a complementary challenge. For a redundant seven-degree-of-freedom arm, an end-effector target does not uniquely determine elbow placement or forearm orientation [ 8 ] . These configurations affect how the arms contact objects and support them against the torso. We develop G1Exo, a wearable exoskeleton kinematically isomorphic to the Unitree G1 arms. Direct joint-level mapping lets operators specify arm configurations, while a physical torso boundary provides a spatial reference for arm–torso interactions.

For skill reuse, we introduce Humanoid Semantic Mixture-of-Experts Diffusion Policy (HS-MoDP). Building on single-arm semantic interfaces and semantic expert routing [ 7 , 9 ] , HS-MoDP conditions two action streams on distinct skill representations and routes them independently through shared experts. Each stream receives its own wrist-camera and proprioceptive inputs alongside shared head-camera observations. This design retains scene context and shares action-generation parameters while limiting direct dependence on the other arm’s local inputs. A frozen VLM schedules skills and coordinates the learned policy with an existing locomotion controller through alternating manipulation and repositioning stages.

Experiments on the Unitree G1 evaluate skill composition, whole-body contact teleoperation, and staged mobile manipulation. With equal demonstration counts, G1Exo improves contact-skill learning across four policies and increases HS-MoDP’s full cabinet workflow success. Our contributions are threefold:

G1Exo, a low-cost wearable isomorphic exoskeleton. Joint-level control and a physical torso boundary support whole-body contact teleoperation and the collection of demonstrations that improve contact-skill learning across policy architectures.

HS-MoDP, a diffusion policy with independent routing and shared experts. Arm-specific skill conditioning and routing support the composition of separately demonstrated skills into unseen dual-arm combinations.

A semantically scheduled system for staged humanoid loco-manipulation. Skill scheduling integrates the learned policy with an existing locomotion controller to support staged manipulation with object-retaining repositioning.

We will release all project hardware designs and source code, including G1Exo and HS-MoDP, as open source after the review process.

1. G1Exo, a low-cost wearable isomorphic exoskeleton. Joint-level control and a physical torso boundary support whole-body contact teleoperation and the collection of demonstrations that improve contact-skill learning across policy architectures.

2. HS-MoDP, a diffusion policy with independent routing and shared experts. Arm-specific skill conditioning and routing support the composition of separately demonstrated skills into unseen dual-arm combinations.

3. A semantically scheduled system for staged humanoid loco-manipulation. Skill scheduling integrates the learned policy with an existing locomotion controller to support staged manipulation with object-retaining repositioning.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Teleoperation and Demonstration Interfaces for Humanoid Manipulation

Teleoperation interfaces determine which aspects of human motion are conveyed to a robot. Physical leader–follower systems provide demonstrations for bimanual and mobile manipulation [ 10 , 11 ] , while human motion tracking and handheld grippers offer alternative collection interfaces [ 1 , 12 ] . For whole-arm contact, demonstrations must also specify configurations relevant to object contact.

Exoskeleton interfaces provide joint-level motion inputs for teleoperation and demonstration collection across embodiments [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . For humanoids, HOMIE integrates isomorphic arm control with body and hand interfaces for loco-manipulation [ 2 ] , while HumanoidExo uses wearable recordings to support whole-body policy learning [ 17 ] . G1Exo focuses on directly specifying arm configurations and their spatial relationship to the torso during whole-body contact manipulation. Its low-cost wearable design combines joint-level arm control with a physical torso boundary, allowing operators to execute contact behaviors and provide corresponding demonstrations.

## II-B Dual-arm Coordination and Compositional Skill Reuse

Dual-arm policies model inter-arm dependence through joint action prediction [ 18 ] , intermediate representation exchange [ 19 , 20 ] , or explicit role assignment [ 21 , 22 ] . Structured latent representations and coordinated versus arm-specific MoE pathways further distinguish shared behavior from individual arm adjustments [ 23 , 24 ] . These mechanisms govern how the arms interact during execution.
Composing separately learned skills additionally requires each arm’s intended behavior to remain independently selectable.

Unimanual policy reuse has been explored through skill management, paired policy architectures, and energy-based coordination [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] . SkillVLA explicitly addresses skill entanglement and unseen left–right skill combinations [ 7 ] . It uses separate semantic instructions and low-level reasoning and action-generation streams for the two arms, with gated cross-arm communication to support cooperative behaviors. This establishes a formulation in which known skills can be invoked separately and recombined during execution. We study this formulation in humanoid joint-space manipulation, including concurrent skill execution in a changing shared workspace and manipulation involving arm–torso contact.

## II-C Semantic Skill Conditioning with Mixture-of-Experts

Sparse MoE policies use selective expert activation to share model capacity across tasks [ 28 , 29 ] . The routing conditions determine how this capacity is organized: MoDE selects denoising experts according to the diffusion noise level [ 30 ] , whereas MoE-ACT conditions routing on task context, visual observations, and proprioceptive states [ 31 ] . Skill-based approaches introduce additional structure, including primitive skill conditioning in diffusion policies and an orthogonal skill basis with sticky routing in SMP [ 32 , 33 ] .

SMoDP connects expert selection to skill semantics through semantic routing, action-chunk consistency, and dual semantic alignment of skill representations and routing behavior [ 9 ] . It evaluates few-shot compositional adaptation with frozen experts on simulation benchmarks and bimanual multitask manipulation on ALOHA. We build on these routing and alignment mechanisms to support independently specified skills for concurrent arm execution.
HS-MoDP gives each arm its own semantic condition and router within a shared diffusion transformer.
In contrast to SkillVLA’s separate single-arm action modules, the two streams access a common expert pool. Arm identity conditions the shared experts, allowing the model to distinguish the G1’s mirrored arms while sharing action-generation parameters.

2026-10-20.title: A GPU-Resident Pipeline for Multi-Robot 3D Inspection with Limited Perception
2026-10-20.authors: Kryštof Pšenička , Stefan Edelkamp
2026-10-20.abstract:
We present a complete, GPU-resident pipeline for multi-robot 3D inspection of
underwater structures. Given a triangle mesh and a fleet of K K robots, each
carrying a short-range, limited field-of-view camera, the pipeline computes
6-DOF trajectories that jointly cover a target fraction of the surface while
minimizing a linearly interpolated makespan/total-cost objective. The joint
problem is NP-hard, so we decompose it into five core stages — candidate
viewpoint generation, visibility computation, set cover, min-max vehicle routing
solved as a mixed integer program (MIP) with lifted Miller–Tucker–Zemlin
subtour elimination, and priority-based multi-agent path finding with
continuous-time inter-robot conflict checking — flanked by mesh loading and
surface sampling as preprocessing and by trajectory smoothing as
postprocessing. Our contributions are: an end-to-end GPU-accelerated
integration of the five stages, with its kernel design documented; a GPU batch
adaptation of Lien’s ε \varepsilon -visibility with four custom CUDA kernels; a β \beta -aware per-vehicle tour upper bound derived from
the interpolated objective, supplementing the Desrochers–Laporte coefficient
lift with forbidden-pair cuts; a 4D space-time extension of Zhou and Zeng’s GPU

2026-10-20.introduction:
Autonomously inspecting the surface of a complex three-dimensional structure
underwater is important across engineering and science: commercial shipping
relies on regular hull inspection for biofouling and corrosion; offshore
wind-farm operators need periodic condition assessment of monopile foundations;
harbor and dam operators inspect submerged walls; and underwater archaeology and
marine biology require dense photographic surveys of wrecks and coral
reefs McMahon et al. (2023) ; Carreno et al. (2020) ; Thompson and Guihen (2019) . These tasks share a
common structure: a fixed surface must be visually covered, and each surface
region has to be seen from within a limited range by a camera with a finite
field of view. Single-robot solutions scale poorly; a fleet of small autonomous
underwater vehicles (AUVs) can cover a complex surface faster and can cover for
each other if one vehicle fails mid-mission.

The underwater setting motivates two design choices. Perception range is short,
so the planner must bring viewpoints close to the surface (our camera far plane
defaults to 6 ​ m 6\,\text{m} ). And because in-mission re-tasking and high-bandwidth
communication are limited, careful pre-mission planning is the dominant
lever for mission success, so we target offline planning.

We address the offline planning layer in isolation, under a deliberately
idealized model of everything around it: a geometric prior exists as a mesh
(from a bathymetric or photogrammetric survey), localization, map registration
and execution are exact, and visibility is a deterministic function of geometry.
Currents, acoustic bandwidth, energy, sensor noise and turbidity are not
modelled — they inform our defaults (short far plane, low cruise speed,
generous margins) but do not enter the
optimization. The evaluation is therefore deterministic simulation, and every
reported quantity is a property of the plan , not of a deployment. These
assumptions make the joint problem separable and let us isolate each stage’s
contribution; Section 6 says which a real mission would
violate first.

We describe 3D-Inspection , a framework that takes a triangle mesh, a
fleet size K K and a coverage threshold, and outputs a collision-free 6-DOF
trajectory per robot whose union of seen surface exceeds the threshold, while
minimizing a user-weighted interpolation of makespan and total cost. The joint
formulation is NP-hard — it combines the 3D watchman route, vehicle routing
and multi-agent path finding — so the framework is a decomposition that
solves each subproblem with strong approximations, leaning on GPU acceleration
to keep end-to-end runtimes in the tens of minutes at | P | ∼ 10 5 |P|\sim 10^{5} .

Most individual stages instantiate established methods; we state explicitly
which parts are new algorithmic work and which are systems integration. Algorithmic:

A GPU batch adaptation of Lien’s ε \varepsilon -visibility Lien (2007) as four custom CUDA kernels over a compacted (viewpoint, point) pair list,
replacing the divergent per-viewpoint radial partitioning of a naive port with
one sort plus two atomic scatter passes (Section 4.6 ), evaluated
against bounding-volume-hierarchy (BVH) raycasting as ground truth.

A min-max vehicle routing MIP combining the lifted Miller–Tucker–Zemlin
subtour elimination of Desrochers and Laporte Desrochers and Laporte (1991) with two
original additions — a β \beta -aware per-vehicle tour upper bound derived from
the interpolated objective, used to tighten arc-filtering cuts, and
forbidden-pair cuts for jointly infeasible arc pairs (Section 4.4 );
both are ablated in Section 5 .

A 4D ( t , x , y , z ) (t,x,y,z) space-time extension of Zhou and Zeng’s GPU
parallel-frontier A* Zhou and Zeng (2015) whose successor filter is a closed-form
continuous-time separation test against earlier robots’ committed motion rather
than a discrete cell reservation (Section 4.5 ), forming the
single-agent core of a priority-based planner after Silver Silver (2005) ;
ablated in Section 5 , where the parallel frontier is worth
a median 38 × 38\times at no measured cost in path quality.

2026-10-20.title: OmniInteract: Towards Unified Whole-Body Interaction Control for Dual Humanoids
2026-10-20.authors: Yinghao Li , Tianyu Zhang , Zhuohao Li , Yi-Lin Wei , Fa-Ting Hong , Qing Zhang , Wei-Shi Zheng
2026-10-20.comment: including appendix, 11 figures. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract: Physical interaction is a key capability for humanoid collaboration, requiring coordinated whole-body motion and precise contact. However, learning diverse dual-humanoid interactions faces two major challenges: (1) human-robot morphological differences disrupt contact interfaces and spatial relationships during retargeting, and (2) jointly learning motor skills and partner coordination makes it difficult to retain control fidelity as interaction diversity grows. In this paper, we propose OmniInteract to address these challenges through surface-aware modeling and scalable residual policy learning. First, we introduce Surface Contact-Aware Retargeting, which leverages dense human-robot surface correspondences to jointly retarget both humanoids, preserving explicit interaction contact interfaces and their near-field geometric context. Second, we propose a Scalable Flow-based Interaction Policy for partner-conditioned residual generation. It factorizes dual-humanoid control into a reusable motor foundation and interaction-specific adaptations: partner-aware experts learn corrections over a frozen whole-body motion prior, while conditional flow matching unifies them in a shared residual action space. This enables scalable skill consolidation while retaining pretrained motor capabilities. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OmniInteract improves retargeting fidelity and dual-humanoid coordination while better retaining interaction performance as skill diversity grows. Real-world deployment further demonstrates successful contact establishment, stable whole-body coordination, and recovery from external perturbations.

2026-10-20.title: A Spiking Ring-Attractor Architecture for Representation and Control of Revolute Robot Joints
2026-10-20.authors: Aung Htet , Alejandro Rodriguez Jimenez , Ruidong Ma , Alessandro Di Nuovo
2026-10-20.abstract: Robotic systems with revolute joints evolve on circular state spaces, yet most control architectures represent these states using Euclidean variables that ignore this underlying geometry. We propose a fully spiking neural control architecture in which ring attractors encode joint states, enforcing representations consistent with the topology of revolute systems.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Neural circuits in biological systems often do not appear to separate representation from control. Internal states are maintained as distributed activity patterns, goals can be encoded within the same substrate, and behavior can emerge through continuous regulation of one activity state toward another. This organization is especially clear in neural systems for orientation and navigation, where heading, goal direction, and steering commands are represented and transformed within population activity [ 7 , 20 , 13 ] . Ring attractors provide a particularly relevant example: in biological head-direction systems, they maintain localized activity bumps on a circular manifold and support angular integration [ 17 , 18 , 10 ] . This circular structure has also made ring attractors useful in computational and robotic models of path integration, grid-cell organization, and bio-inspired navigation [ 11 , 19 , 15 , 2 ] .

Building on this circular population structure, we propose a robotic control
architecture in which ring attractors represent revolute joint states and serve
as dynamical substrates for control. The central idea is to regulate the phase of
a persistent activity bump directly, rather than decoding joint state into an
external Euclidean variable before control. Homeostatic comparison provides a
signed mismatch between goal and state, while opponent gain modulation converts
that mismatch into directed transport of the bump around the ring [ 3 , 16 , 22 ] . Because the neural activity
bump and the physical joint angle both evolve on circular manifolds, this yields
a topology-preserving, fully spiking control primitive for revolute variables.

This perspective also provides a natural geometric and compositional structure.
Phase shifts of a ring-attractor bump correspond to motion on S ​ O ​ ( 2 ) SO(2) , with
infinitesimal displacements described by a Lie-algebraic tangent direction [ 12 , 21 , 9 ] . To interface this distributed representation
with scalar regulatory signals, we derive an NEF-inspired Fourier decoder that
extracts phase from ring activity [ 4 ] . For multi-joint
systems, the same local Fourier features, cos ⁡ q i \cos q_{i} and sin ⁡ q i \sin q_{i} , compose
through known forward kinematics to provide an S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) SO(3) orientation readout.
Thus, individual rings generate controlled S ​ O ​ ( 2 ) SO(2) trajectories, while their
decoded features support robot-level orientation estimates.

Our contributions are: (i) a biologically inspired closed-loop ring-attractor
controller in which a Hammel-style homeostatic comparator drives opponent gain
modulation to transport bump states on an S ​ O ​ ( 2 ) SO(2) -structured manifold; (ii) a
Lie-algebraic transport analysis of the gain-imbalance mechanism; (iii) an
analytic Fourier phase decoder that maps distributed ring activity to scalar
phase estimates compatible with homeostatic comparison; (iv) a forward-kinematic
Fourier decoder that reads out an S ​ O ​ ( 3 ) SO(3) orientation estimate from known
revolute-chain ring states via product Fourier features; and (v) empirical
validation in NEST spiking simulations [ 6 ] and on a Tiago robot [ 14 ] .

The remainder of the paper presents the architecture, derives the S ​ O ​ ( 2 ) SO(2) transport mechanism and Fourier readouts, and evaluates the resulting spiking
controller in NEST and on a Tiago arm. Additional derivations and experimental
details are provided in the appendix.

2026-10-20.title: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
2026-10-20.authors: Yuheng Qiu , Yutian Chen , Carlton Cort , Weison Huang , Shibo Zhao , Pieter Abbeel , Rocky Duan , Koushil Sreenath , C. Karen Liu , Carmelo Sferrazza , Junyi Geng , Sebastian Scherer , Guanya Shi
2026-10-20.abstract:
Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories.
We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision .
Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher.
Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows.
Training on a new platform therefore no longer requires collecting ground-truth trajectories, but only calibrating the IMU and recording data during normal operation.
Across six datasets spanning pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, the same recipe with no velocity or position labels trains models that come within 0.07 0.07 m/s average velocity error of a same-architecture supervised baseline.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Inertial odometry (IO) is self-contained, inexpensive, and remains available when cameras, LiDAR, or GNSS become unreliable or unavailable.
Its main limitation is drift, as double integration accumulates IMU noise and bias into rapidly growing position error.
To reduce this drift, existing methods exploit motion structure obtained from analytical models or trained from labeled data.
Model-based approaches derive motion constraints from platform kinematics or dynamics, such as leg kinematics [ 28 , 26 ] .
Learning-based IO instead learns motion priors from pose- or velocity-labeled trajectories [ 23 , 8 , 27 , 17 , 19 ] .
Whether explicitly through kinematics or implicitly through labeled data, both approaches encode embodiment, so the resulting model is tied to one geometry, sensor mounting, payload, and actuation.
Adapting to a new embodiment thus requires a new analytical model or new labeled trajectories, limiting cross-embodiment generalization.

For learning-based IO, this generalization failure creates a labeling bottleneck.
Ground-truth velocity or pose requires motion capture, RTK, or SLAM, which are costly to deploy and often degrade or become unavailable in complex real-world scenarios.
The burden compounds at deployment because every new embodiment, payload, mounting, or control policy forces re-collecting ground-truth trajectories on the new platform [ 23 , 31 ] .
Meanwhile, robots generate abundant unlabeled IMU data during operation that supervised approaches cannot exploit.
Lifting the label requirement would turn every deployed robot into its own source of training data, enable embodiments where ground-truth is infeasible, and let the model continue learning as mounting, payload, and policy drift from training conditions.
This raises the question:

Can a robot learn its own motion model from IMU data only?

Our thesis is that a myopic integration teacher can train an inertial odometry student that learns the embodiment’s motion model from unlabeled IMU data and becomes more accurate than the teacher.
The teacher integrates accelerometer and gyroscope measurements into rotation, velocity, and position increments over short windows [ 11 ] .
It is myopic because it integrates each window separately, so it carries no memory across windows and no embodiment-specific prior beyond the IMU integration equations, and its increments are noisy.
The student, in contrast, sees a longer IMU context and is trained on thousands of such windows.
Teacher errors vary across windows while the embodiment’s motion repeats, so the student learns the repeated motion patterns, such as gait periodicity or thrust cycles, and averages the noise away.

Grounded on this insight, we introduce a self-supervised method that learns inertial odometry from unlabeled IMU through integration self-supervision .
Integrating the raw IMU over a short window gives the body-frame velocity change between its endpoints.
The network is trained so that its predicted endpoint velocities differ by this change.
Once this signal yields reliable velocity estimates, pose graph distillation (PGD) can further refine the network: one pose graph links the integrated velocity changes of many consecutive windows with the network’s own predictions, and its solution provides sequence-consistent velocity targets for fine-tuning.
Generalizing to a new embodiment therefore requires no new labels and no new analytical model.
Instead of collecting ground truth with mocap, RTK, or instrumented rigs, we only calibrate the IMU and record data during normal operation.
Extra proprioceptive streams such as additional IMUs or joint encoders extend the same losses to a multi-modal student and strengthen the self-supervision.
Across six datasets, self-supervised training approaches the supervised baseline, and its accuracy improves monotonically as more unlabeled data become available.
In summary, our contributions are:

We introduce a self-supervised framework for inertial odometry that learns an embodiment-specific motion model from unlabeled IMU data.

To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to show that training from scratch on unlabeled IMU data alone can approach the performance of a supervised learning-based IO model.

We show that the student exceeds its integration teacher over long horizons, specializes to its embodiment, and improves as unlabeled training data scales.

1. We introduce a self-supervised framework for inertial odometry that learns an embodiment-specific motion model from unlabeled IMU data.

2. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to show that training from scratch on unlabeled IMU data alone can approach the performance of a supervised learning-based IO model.

3. We show that the student exceeds its integration teacher over long horizons, specializes to its embodiment, and improves as unlabeled training data scales.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Learning-Based Inertial and Legged Odometry

Early neural IO systems showed that IMU windows contain motion cues beyond what classical dead reckoning can recover.
IONet [ 8 ] , RIDI [ 27 ] , RoNIN [ 17 ] , TLIO [ 19 ] learn velocity from raw IMU sequences for pedestrians, and later systems extend learned IO to drones and other robots through new representations or dynamics models [ 10 , 29 , 23 ] .
Many of these systems also expose uncertainty for downstream filters and graphs, either through classical IMU integration [ 11 ] , learned velocity covariance [ 19 ] , or learned bias and correction terms [ 4 , 22 ] .
A complementary line keeps a model-based estimator and learns only its corrections, such as noise adaptation inside a Kalman filter [ 2 ] or gyroscope denoising [ 3 ] , while geometric priors such as rotation equivariance [ 7 , 18 ] improve how a learned model generalizes across orientations.
On articulated platforms, classical multi-IMU filters such as MIPO [ 28 ] and DogLegs [ 26 ] fuse body IMU, joint encoders, and additional leg-mounted IMUs to detect contacts and constrain leg kinematics in an EKF, while learning-based proprioceptive odometry systems such as Buchanan et al. [ 5 ] , Legolas [ 25 ] , and AutoOdom [ 20 ] regress velocity from the same multi-modal inputs.
All of these learning-based systems rely on supervised velocity, pose, or simulation labels to fit the embodiment-specific motion prior, whereas our method learns from unlabeled IMU on the target embodiment and reuses the same recipe across body-IMU and proprioceptive inputs.

## II-B Self-Supervision in Inertial Navigation

Prior methods self-supervise the odometry model in two ways.
The first borrows a second sensor.
DeepVIO [ 15 ] trains its IMU branch from stereo geometric constraints, KISS-IMU [ 9 ] supervises the network with LiDAR ICP and pose-graph optimization, and self-supervised visual ego-motion learns from photometric consistency [ 32 ] .
iSLAM [ 13 ] and imperative learning [ 24 ] generalize this to a bilevel structure in which an optimizer over the sensor’s residuals teaches a learned front end through differentiable optimization.
All of these trade the label rig for a camera or LiDAR, so they still require a sensor the target platform may not carry.
The second leverages a prior on the model.
RIO [ 7 ] uses rotation equivariance as an auxiliary signal and EqNIO [ 18 ] builds equivariance into the architecture, but both still fit the motion prior from labels and use the invariance only to reduce how many are needed.
Imperative MPC [ 16 ] instead self-supervises the network through a differentiable model predictive controller, so its supervision rests on a known dynamics model of the platform.
Our method needs neither an additional sensor nor such a prior, because the IMU integrator itself supplies the training target.
