2026-10-20.title: FR-VLA: Implicit Force Reasoning VLA for Contact-Rich Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Jiaju He , Zhiyuan Yang , Ruyang Han , Jiahong Tang , Zhiping Lin , Haiyue Zhu
2026-10-20.abstract:
Integrating force awareness into Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models involves not merely encoding wrench measurements as an additional modality, but determining when and how strongly physical interaction should influence robot action generation.
Existing VLAs that use force typically inject it through a fixed pathway, without explicitly determining when it is relevant to the current action.
This calls for an intermediate force relevance mechanism inside the VLA, in which visual-language context estimates the relevance of physical feedback to the current task before force enters the action pathway.
FR-VLA addresses this gap with a Vision-Language Force-Reasoning Model that uses learnable force query tokens to derive a force admission signal grounded in visual-language context, and uses this signal to modulate an external tokenized force pathway for action generation.
In real-world experiments on five contact-rich tasks across two robotic platforms, FR-VLA achieves the highest mean success rate over six evaluated stages, and trajectory visualizations show that its force admission varies with the interaction phase.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Modern VLAs have become effective generalist policies by grounding robot action generation in visual observations and language instructions through pretrained VLM backbones [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
However, contact-rich manipulation exposes a limitation of this visual-language foundation: interaction states in insertion, assembly, wiping, and pressing are often only partially observable from images, making force feedback essential for precision-oriented tasks [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] .
The importance of force feedback for action generation varies across task phases, depending on the intended interaction and the evolving contact state [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] .
This motivates policies that use visual-language context to determine when and to what extent force feedback should influence action generation.
Consequently, force integration is not merely a problem of sensing or encoding wrench measurements, but one of dynamically grounding physical feedback in visual-language task context [ 13 ] .

Existing force-aware VLA architectures mainly differ in the point at which force is injected, as illustrated in Figure 1 (a).
Injecting low-dimensional wrench signals into the VLM token stream risks diluting force information within high-dimensional visual-language representations [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] .
Relocating force conditioning to the action expert avoids this representational imbalance, but bypasses the VLM state where task progress and interaction phase are inferred [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] .
Both choices therefore provide force exposure rather than force grounding: the policy can react to measured wrench changes, but it is not explicitly supervised to decide when force should affect action generation under a task-dependent contact phase.

We frame force-aware VLA as a modality grounding problem, where grounding denotes estimating the task-conditioned admissibility of physical feedback from the VLA’s visual-language state before measured force is allowed to affect action generation.
Recent advances in multimodal foundation models have shown that heterogeneous inputs can be grounded in pretrained backbones through intermediate interfaces such as latent queries, resamplers, and gated attention [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] .
These interfaces transfer information into VLM representation spaces without requiring raw non-visual signals to be inserted as ordinary input tokens.
For force-aware VLA, such an interface can use visual-language context to assess when physical feedback should influence action generation, taking task progress and contact phase into account.

This perspective motivates separating the estimation of force relevance from the encoding of force measurements.
Such a separation calls for a mechanism that uses the VLA’s visual-language task state to modulate the contribution of measured wrench histories to action generation.
FR-VLA instantiates this mechanism with force query states that infer a force admission signal from visual-language context, while measured wrench histories remain in a separate action-side force pathway.
The resulting admission behavior varies with task progress rather than simply with wrench availability, as illustrated in Figure 1 (b).

Real-world evaluations on two robotic platforms and five contact-rich tasks show improved performance and robustness over vision-only and directly force-conditioned VLA baselines.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
(i) Force-aware VLA is formulated as a modality grounding problem for low-dimensional physical feedback, where force relevance is inferred from visual-language task context rather than assumed from sensor availability.
(ii) FR-VLA introduces a force admission architecture in which visual-language states determine when force can influence action generation, while measured wrench histories are encoded separately for action-side control.
(iii) A detailed analysis of grounded force admission shows that the learned admission behavior follows task phase interaction regimes rather than instantaneous force magnitude.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Force-Aware Policy Learning and Contact Control. Classical contact control provides model-based approaches to compliant manipulation.
Hybrid position/force control assigns position and force objectives to complementary directions in a task-related coordinate frame [ 25 ] .
Impedance control specifies the dynamic relationship between motion and interaction force, shaping the robot’s mechanical response to its environment [ 26 ] .
Force feedback has been studied in both policy learning and contact control [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ] .
ForceMimic combines force-aware demonstration collection with imitation learning of force–motion commands and hybrid force-position control [ 32 ] .
Force Policy separates vision-guided global behavior from a local force feedback policy that estimates an interaction frame for hybrid force-position control [ 21 ] .
Learning variable impedance provides another approach to adapting robot behavior under contact uncertainty [ 33 , 34 ] .
Beyond control design, effective multimodal learning requires preventing policies from neglecting force feedback.
FACTR addresses this issue through a curriculum that progressively reduces visual corruption, encouraging the policy to use force information rather than overfit to vision [ 35 ] .
CRAFT similarly addresses modality imbalance in VLAs, using a variational information bottleneck to regulate visual-language representations during curriculum fine-tuning [ 36 ] .
FR-VLA addresses force utilization through an explicit architectural separation between context-dependent force admission and wrench history representation.

Force-Aware VLAs and Contact-Dependent Fusion. Recent approaches incorporate physical feedback into VLAs through different interfaces [ 16 , 20 , 37 , 38 ] .
ForceVLA introduces a force-aware mixture of experts for action generation, while ForceVLA2 combines force-based prompts in the VLM with cross-scale fusion in the action expert for hybrid force-position control [ 18 , 14 ] .
Other approaches exploit physical information during training while reducing deployment-time sensing requirements: FD-VLA distills force information into latent tokens, and HapticVLA transfers tactile-aware behavior to a student that operates without inference-time tactile sensing [ 15 , 39 ] .
Prediction-based designs anticipate future interaction: FoAR uses future contact prediction to guide visual–force fusion and dynamically adjust force use across contact and non-contact phases [ 10 ] , and 3D world model policies forecast future scene states to guide action generation [ 40 ] .
In FR-VLA, force query states infer interaction phases from visual-language context, and the resulting admission signal biases action-side attention to a separately represented wrench history.
This phase-supervised interface connects task context to force utilization while keeping measured wrench inputs in a dedicated action-side pathway.

Cross-Modal Interfaces and Grounding. Latent queries and gated interfaces offer useful building blocks for connecting heterogeneous modalities.
Perceiver IO uses latent arrays to process structured inputs, Flamingo introduces gated cross-attention between visual features and a language model, and BLIP-2 uses a query-based interface between frozen visual and language models [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] .
FR-VLA adopts a task-specific query interface: its force query states receive motion phase supervision to ground force admission in visual-language context.
Measured wrench histories remain outside the VLM token stream and condition the action model through a separate force pathway.
This design distinguishes the inference of force relevance from the representation of measured physical feedback.

2026-10-20.authors: Mohsen Reda Mahmoud Moursi , Ahmed Stohy
2026-10-20.abstract: This article presents an analytical-DES benchmark for intra-aisle robotic picking in automated warehousing. The investigated cycle combines horizontal shuttle travel, tote handling and item picking at storage locations. Simulation results are compared with the analytical formulation of Lerher et al. under the same rack geometry, shuttle-motion, handling and picking conditions, and the same definitions of cycle time and derived item throughput. Reproducing the published analytical tables requires the distance interpretation dES = 1.5 m and dTB = 0 m. The analytical-DES benchmark comprises 180 scenarios formed from three rack lengths, two paired motion profiles and n = 1 to 30 visited picking locations, with ten simulation replications per scenario. The six n = 1 cases are reported separately because no travel-between component is present. Across the remaining 174 scenarios, the mean absolute relative cycle-time discrepancy is 0.8655%, the median is 0.6758%, and the maximum is 7.0370%. The mean absolute error is 2.411 s and the RMSE is 2.744 s. The simulated scenario-mean cycle time is below the analytical value in all 174 principal scenarios. The results therefore show close numerical correspondence under the tested conditions, but not exact agreement, formal statistical equivalence, or validation against an operating warehouse.

2026-10-20.title: SkateNav: Learning Energy-Efficient Navigation through Adaptive Skating on Passive-Wheel Quadrupedal Robots
2026-10-20.authors: Jeil Jeong , Taeyun Kim , Sangjin Kim , Jinyoung Choi , Sung-Eui Yoon
2026-10-20.abstract:
Passive-wheel quadrupedal robots offer energy-efficient locomotion through leg-driven propulsion and momentum-driven gliding.
However, navigation requires coordinating steering with intermittent propulsion and adapting push–glide timing to task demands.
Velocity-tracking objectives may suppress the speed variations inherent in skating, discouraging efficient gliding.
To address these challenges, we propose SkateNav, a unified skating-navigation framework based on reinforcement learning.
A time-budgeted goal-reaching objective allows the policy to jointly learn steering, propulsion, and their temporal allocation.
An adaptive skating cycle structures gliding, pushing, and recovery, while frequency modulation at every control step adjusts phase durations to navigation demands.
Simulation experiments demonstrate higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than the evaluated planner–controller baselines, with ablations confirming the contributions of cycle structure and frequency adaptation.
Real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot transfer from simulation to a passive-wheel Mini Cheetah across cluttered indoor spaces, slopes, and paved outdoor surfaces.
Supplementary videos are available on the project page .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Quadrupedal robots can adapt their footholds and posture to traverse rough and discontinuous terrain [ 26 , 1 , 7 ] .
However, they generally have lower energy efficiency than wheeled platforms on flat terrain, partly due to energy loss during foot–ground impacts [ 32 ] .
To address this, wheeled-legged robots have been proposed to combine the terrain adaptability of legs with the energy efficiency of wheels.
These systems can be classified into active-wheel configurations with dedicated wheel actuators for propulsion and braking [ 3 , 23 ] and passive-wheel configurations without additional wheel actuators [ 5 ] .
Passive-wheel systems use leg-driven pushes to build momentum and exploit low rolling resistance for energy-efficient gliding, as in human skating [ 8 ] .

Model-based controllers realize skating by coordinating leg motion and contact forces under nonholonomic rolling constraints [ 2 , 6 ] .
Recent reinforcement learning (RL) approaches improve speed and robustness but primarily track prescribed velocity commands [ 13 , 35 ] .
Leg-driven pushes provide propulsion and steering at an energy cost, whereas gliding sustains motion with lower energy use but offers limited control over propulsion and steering.
Energy-efficient navigation therefore requires deciding when to push and how long to glide to balance timely goal arrival and energy use.
However, velocity-tracking objectives may penalize the speed variations inherent in push–glide motion, discouraging sustained gliding and limiting the allocation of pushing and gliding according to navigation demands.
Thus, a planner and controller interfaced through velocity commands may not fully accommodate such push–glide timing.

A goal-reaching objective specifies a destination and time budget [ 29 ] , allowing the velocity profile to vary.
This flexibility alone, however, does not ensure that efficient push–glide behavior emerges.
Predefined skating cycles provide motion structure [ 2 ] , but fixed contact timings limit adaptation to navigation demands.
The challenge is therefore to preserve the skating structure while adapting when to push and how long to glide for energy-efficient navigation.

To address this, we propose SkateNav, a unified skating-navigation policy for energy-efficient local navigation of passive-wheel quadrupedal robots (Fig. 1 ).
Given waypoints, remaining time, and terrain and robot observations, the policy jointly determines steering, propulsion, and skating-cycle progression.
The cycle organizes skating motion into gliding, pushing, and leg recovery in the phase domain, while the policy modulates its frequency at every control step to adapt phase durations to navigation demands.

The main contributions of this work are:

We formulate passive-wheel local navigation as a time-budgeted goal-reaching problem in which steering, propulsion, and push–glide timing are learned jointly.

We introduce an adaptive skating cycle representation that preserves leg coordination while exposing phase progression as a navigation-conditioned policy action.

We demonstrate higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than the evaluated planner–controller baselines, conduct component ablations, and validate real-world navigation across indoor and outdoor environments.

1. We formulate passive-wheel local navigation as a time-budgeted goal-reaching problem in which steering, propulsion, and push–glide timing are learned jointly.

2. We introduce an adaptive skating cycle representation that preserves leg coordination while exposing phase progression as a navigation-conditioned policy action.

3. We demonstrate higher average success rates and lower cost of transport than the evaluated planner–controller baselines, conduct component ablations, and validate real-world navigation across indoor and outdoor environments.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Passive-Wheel Legged Robot Locomotion

Passive-wheel legged robots achieve energy efficiency by generating propulsion through leg-driven ground pushes and gliding on the resulting momentum [ 9 , 5 ] .
Prior studies have explored control strategies for passive-wheel skating behavior [ 15 , 19 , 12 ] .
Model-based controllers coordinate body motion and contact forces under nonholonomic constraints to realize designed skating gaits [ 2 , 6 ] .
Recently, RL approaches have improved skating speed and robustness by leveraging contact modeling, constraint-aware rewards and hardware-policy co-design [ 25 , 13 , 35 ] .
While prior studies focus on realizing robust skating motion, they do not address how skating behavior should adapt to navigation demands.
Passive-wheel navigation requires steering to be coordinated with intermittent leg-generated propulsion and retained rolling momentum.
Moreover, energy-efficient gliding must be balanced with sufficient pushing for timely task completion.
To this end, our SkateNav framework learns a unified skating-navigation policy that jointly coordinates steering and propulsion under a goal-reaching objective while determining the durations of pushing and gliding as part of the navigation decision.

## 2.2 Gait Encoding for Skating Motion

In RL-based legged locomotion, gait patterns have been discovered without explicit structure [ 17 ] or under only implicit guidance penalizing excessive swing times [ 30 , 18 ] .
To achieve diverse and natural gaits, however, preferred patterns have been structured through phase-based encodings such as central pattern generators [ 22 , 26 ] .
For passive-wheel systems, such structure can help separate propulsion from gliding, as learned policies tend to maintain wheel–ground contact without clearly distinguishing these phases [ 35 ] .
Accordingly, prior work has encoded human-inspired skating gaits as time-phased push–glide cycles, in which the legs alternate with a phase offset [ 2 ] .
However, these cycles use predefined contact timings, making it difficult to accommodate varying navigation demands, from repeated pushes for acceleration or rapid steering for obstacle avoidance to prolonged gliding when momentum suffices.
We therefore let the policy modulate the cycle frequency online, adapting the durations of pushing and gliding according to task requirements.

## 2.3 Goal-Conditioned Local Navigation

Recent RL approaches train a single goal-conditioned policy that directly maps a local waypoint and sensory observations to joint-level actions [ 39 , 7 , 38 ] .
A goal-reaching objective defined by a time budget rather than instantaneous velocity commands allows policies to discover embodiment–specific behaviors such as terrain-negotiating gaits [ 29 ] or high-speed obstacle avoidance [ 16 ] .
Existing learning-based skating controllers have primarily been trained to track prescribed velocity commands [ 25 , 13 , 35 ] .
For passive-wheel systems, such objectives may suppress the speed variations inherent in the push–glide cycle and discourage energy-efficient gliding.
Accordingly, SkateNav adopts a goal-conditioned formulation, providing temporal flexibility for the policy to shape its motion according to passive-wheel dynamics and task demands rather than prescribed instantaneous velocities.

2026-10-20.title: PaceVLA: Adaptive Temporal Action Quantization in Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-20.authors: Hojin Jeon , Jimin Lee , Taekwan Kim , Nayoung Oh , Taeyoung Kim , Myungkyu Koo , Jinmo Koo , Joonwoo Ahn , Jinwoo Shin
2026-10-20.abstract:
Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment.
Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient.
A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed–accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions.
To address this, we propose PaceVLA , a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: (1) mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and (2) a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step.
Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation. The project page is available.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Pertsch et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ) have emerged as a promising framework for generalist robot policies, achieving strong performance through imitation learning from diverse robot demonstrations ( Walke et al., 2023 ; O’Neill et al., 2024 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) , many of which are collected through human teleoperation ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) .
However, teleoperated demonstrations often exhibit conservative behavior: human-in-the-loop control is typically performed through limited-rate interfaces, and human operators adopt cautious motions to avoid failures during data collection ( Mandlekar et al., 2018 ; Mandlekar et al., 2021 ) .
Since imitation learning trains policies to reproduce the demonstrated trajectories, VLAs inherit these patterns and execute tasks through many slow action steps even in phases where faster motion is physically feasible.

Recent works have explored accelerating robot policies beyond demonstration speed, addressing two complementary questions: where to accelerate and how coarsely to execute actions.
DemoSpeedup ( Guo et al., 2025 ) segments per-frame action entropy with a proxy policy and trains a policy on the resulting accelerated trajectories.
SAIL ( Arachchige et al., 2025 ) combines high-fidelity tracking with switching between preset slow and fast speeds based on motion complexity and gripper events.
A particularly simple mechanism is temporal action quantization ( Figure AI, 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) , which merges consecutive actions into coarser ones.
It fits naturally with chunk-based VLAs since each predicted action chunk can be executed at a chosen granularity.

Despite their promise, these approaches have two limitations.
First, the acceleration decision is either fixed into the training data, using the action entropy of a fine-tuned proxy policy as an implicit indicator ( Guo et al., 2025 ) ,
or applied at execution time to the output of a policy trained at demonstration speed, switching between preset speeds according to kinematic cues ( Arachchige et al., 2025 ) .
Both signals are statistics of the actions, yet how much precision a phase demands is determined by the robot’s interaction with the scene rather than by the motion itself.
Second, existing temporal action quantization applies a fixed granularity across the entire trajectory, inducing a speed–accuracy trade-off: coarse actions suffice during free-space motion but discard trajectory details required in precision-critical phases such as grasping and contact-rich interaction.
Moreover, granularity is closely coupled with the prediction horizon: phases that tolerate coarse execution can commit to longer predictions, whereas precision-critical phases benefit from shorter horizons with more frequent re-planning.
We argue that both the temporal granularity and the prediction horizon of action execution should be treated as a policy decision, adapted to the precision each phase requires.

To this end, we propose PaceVLA , a unified framework for adaptive temporal action execution in VLAs. PaceVLA equips a shared action expert with mode-specific action decoders that support different temporal granularities and prediction horizons. At each inference step, a quantization judge and a router jointly select an execution mode from the visual and language context.
Each execution mode is defined by a temporal action quantization level and a prediction horizon, allowing the policy to choose both the granularity of its commands and the temporal extent of its action predictions.
To validate the effectiveness of PaceVLA , we conduct extensive experiments across Robocasa-Kitchen ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) , LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , and DexJoCo ( Wang et al., 2026 ) simulated robotic benchmarks and six real-world manipulation tasks including long-horizon, dexterous tasks covered on three robot platforms: Franka Research arm with gripper, OpenArm robot arm with two 6-DoF dexterous hands, and humanoid ALLEX robot with two 15-DoF dexterous hands.
Compared with the baselines, PaceVLA achieves up to 1.8 × \times faster than the base VLA, and 1.75 × \times throughput on the conveyor package-handling task with the humanoid ALLEX, while maintaining task success rates.

Our contributions are:

We highlight the tendency of VLA policies to inherit fine-grained execution patterns from teleoperated demonstrations as a key source of temporal inefficiency.

We propose PaceVLA , a lightweight architecture that models execution modes with different temporal quantization levels and action horizons using mode-specific action decoders, a quantization judge and a context-conditioned router.

We demonstrate consistent gains on simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks, achieving a stronger balance between task success and execution efficiency than the base VLA and fixed temporal quantization baselines.

1. We highlight the tendency of VLA policies to inherit fine-grained execution patterns from teleoperated demonstrations as a key source of temporal inefficiency.

2. We propose PaceVLA , a lightweight architecture that models execution modes with different temporal quantization levels and action horizons using mode-specific action decoders, a quantization judge and a context-conditioned router.

3. We demonstrate consistent gains on simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks, achieving a stronger balance between task success and execution efficiency than the base VLA and fixed temporal quantization baselines.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs). VLAs have recently shown great promise in robotic policy learning by leveraging large-scale robot datasets.
One line of VLA models ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Pertsch et al., 2025 ; Driess et al., 2023 ) discretizes the continuous action space and predicts actions as tokens, showing that pre-trained VLMs ( Beyer et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Bai et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) can be effectively adapted to low-level action prediction.
In contrast, a growing body of studies ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ) attaches action experts that generate continuous action chunks via diffusion or flow-matching, enabling more accurate predictions.
For example, GR00T N1.5 ( Bjorck et al., 2025 ) and RLDX-1 ( Kim et al., 2026 ) condition a flow-matching head on VLM features to produce action chunks.
In this work, we build on a flow-matching action expert for action generation.
While most diffusion-based VLAs predict action chunks at a single, fixed temporal granularity set by the data collection frequency, this single granularity is not equally suited to all phases of a task.
Motivated by this observation, we explore whether jointly learning actions at multiple temporal granularities and adapting the action granularity to the current context can lead to faster and more accurate task execution.

Faster-than-Demonstration Execution. The execution speed of imitation-learned policies is bounded by the pace of their demonstrations, and several lines of work have aimed to exceed it.
Reinforcement-learning-based fine-tuning adjusts the policy using task-level rewards to encourage faster and more decisive behaviors ( Yuan et al., 2025 ) , but tends to push the policy toward uniformly faster execution.
Another direction modifies the temporal structure of actions, as explored in DemoSpeedup ( Guo et al., 2025 ) and SAIL ( Arachchige et al., 2025 ) .
While these approaches improve execution speed, they determine the degree of acceleration either at implicit action entropy signals or through kinematic cues for switching between preset speeds, both derived from action statistics, rather than letting the policy itself decide how much to accelerate from the scene it perceives at inference time.

Router-Based Expert Selection. Conditional computation employs a lightweight router that selects which sub-network to apply to each input, and has been widely adopted to scale capacity without proportional cost.
In most designs the candidates are structurally identical and differ only in learned weights, whether FFN experts ( Fedus et al., 2022 ) or attention heads ( Jin et al., 2024 ) , so a routing decision carries no predefined meaning.
Within VLAs, MoLe-VLA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) routes over backbone layers to reduce the cost of each forward pass, leaving the action output unchanged.
Mixture of Horizons ( Jing et al., 2025 ) is the closest to our setting, as it constructs action heads at several chunk lengths, but it fuses their outputs through a gate, so each action is still emitted at a single fixed temporal granularity.
None of these, however, treat the temporal granularity of the action as the routing target, where a router selects one decoder per state from a set of decoders that differ in temporal resolution and horizon.

2026-10-20.title: Policy Search in Code Space for Multi-Agent Pathfinding
2026-10-20.authors: Matthias Eder , Pantelis Emmanouil , Vivek Farias , Fabian Fischer , Adam Jozefiak , Tianyi Peng , Thomas Ulz , Raphael Watschinger , Fangyu Wu , Andrew Zheng
2026-10-20.abstract:
Developing coordination policies for complex multi-agent systems relies on either labor-intensive algorithm design or opaque task-specific reinforcement learning. With recent advances in autonomous coding agents, we show that policy search directly in code space offers a compelling third path that combines automated optimization with explicit interpretability.
We investigate a human-directed workflow in which coding agents iteratively propose, implement, evaluate, diagnose, and eventually refine algorithms guided by simulation feedback and explicit correctness verification.
We conducted two case studies and found that this workflow robustly outperformed any manually engineered solutions.
On a challenging map in the 2024 League of Robot Runners competition, a two-day search discovered a policy that exceeds the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by 35.0% on the densest instance and generalizes to unseen map instances.
In simulated real-world warehouses with irregular lanes, continuous robot geometry, and asynchronous motion, a week-long search discovered an entirely new class of multi-agent pathfinding algorithm that outperforms a calibrated proprietary solution in throughput by 58.9%.
Under stated assumptions, we further prove that the new algorithm is collision-free and completes, in finite time, every accepted goal that is not withdrawn or replaced.
Together, the studies show that policy search in code space powered by state-of-the-art coding agents offers a highly competitive path to building real engineering solutions that are both effective and analytically tractable.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Multi-agent coordination underlies warehouse fulfillment, factory automation, and parcel sorting.
In lifelong multi-agent pathfinding (LMAPF), tasks arrive continuously, requiring a fleet of robots to coordinate both task allocation and collision-free navigation through a shared spatial network ( Wurman et al., 2008 ; Ma et al., 2017 ; Li et al., 2021b ) .
The operational objective is to maximize system throughput subject to collision avoidance and strict real-time compute budgets.
Because uncoordinated routing decisions cause severe congestion and deadlocks, effective warehouse operation typically requires sophisticated joint optimization of task assignment and trajectory coordination across the fleet.

Existing methods generally fall into two paradigms.
First, the standard approach relies on human experts to engineer sophisticated solvers, dispatch rules, and traffic guidance heuristics ( Okumura et al., 2022 ; Jiang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) .
Although effective, manual engineering is bottlenecked by human engineering throughput and cannot scale algorithm discovery with available compute.
Second, learning-based methods attempt to bypass this manual effort by training neural policies directly through simulated interaction ( Damani et al., 2021 ; Skrynnik et al., 2024 ; Andreychuk et al., 2025 ) .
However, neural policies often lack formal safety guarantees, remain difficult to inspect and verify, and resist modular modification when operational constraints shift.

We study a third approach: policy search in code space (PSCS), driven by coding agents.
In this paradigm, human designers specify the system objective, physical constraints, and scaffolding interfaces, while coding agents iteratively refine the implementation of the planner and scheduler directly in source code, which we refer to as code space .
Guided by simulation benchmarks, unit tests, and execution traces, the agent discovers procedural algorithms that are computationally efficient, interpretable, and maintainable.
Unlike manual design, the search scales directly with compute; unlike black-box learning, the resulting policy remains fully transparent and verifiable.

Automated code generation has demonstrated promise in discovering novel mathematical algorithms and discrete heuristics ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ; Novikov et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) .
However, existing studies focus primarily on idealized theoretical benchmarks or stylized combinatorial problems.
It remains an open question whether PSCS can scale to demanding cyber-physical systems such as LMAPF, where task allocation, spatial planning, and low-latency runtime engineering must interact robustly under realistic constraints.
Specifically, we investigate whether coding agents can navigate these coupled requirements across both standardized benchmarks and complex industrial environments.

We evaluate PSCS across two distinct domains.
The first is the 2024 League of Robot Runners (LoRR) benchmark ( Chan et al., 2024 ) , a synchronous grid competition environment operating with 100 100 to 800 800 robots.
In this domain, PSCS systematically refines existing baselines to discover layout-specific routing heuristics, outperforming the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by up to 35.0% in mean throughput (Figure 1a ).
The second is a high-fidelity simulation of an operational warehouse from KNAPP characterized by irregular lanes, continuous vehicle geometry, and asynchronous execution.
In a challenging production map, our synthesized algorithm outperforms an optimized proprietary baseline by 58.9% (Figure 1b ) while preserving provable progress certificates against deadlock under stated assumptions.

The contributions of this work are as follows:

We demonstrate the feasibility and effectiveness of policy search in code space (PSCS) for automated, nontrivial combinatorial algorithm design in LMAPF.

On the LoRR 2024 benchmark, we show that PSCS effectively refines established planners to discover map-specific heuristics, outperforming the stronger locally reproduced competition entry by up to 35.0% in mean throughput.

In high-fidelity industrial warehouse environments, we show that PSCS discovers an entirely new class of algorithms that outperforms an optimized proprietary baseline by 58.9% while maintaining provable progress certification under stated assumptions.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

This work sits at the intersection of multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) and automated program synthesis.
Rather than hand-crafting domain heuristics or optimizing parametric weights, we search for coordination policies directly in code space.

MAPF seeks collision-free trajectories for a team of agents ( Stern et al., 2019 ) .
In lifelong MAPF (LMAPF), agents continuously receive new tasks upon completing previous assignments ( Ma et al., 2017 ; Li et al., 2021b ) .
Because optimal solvers such as conflict-based search ( Sharon et al., 2015 ) do not scale to hundreds of agents, large-scale deployments rely on fast suboptimal planners that human experts design and tune for specific topologies.
Representative rule-based methods include PIBT ( Okumura et al., 2022 ) for one-step priority inheritance, Causal-PIBT ( Okumura et al., 2021 ) for asynchronous execution, and WPPL ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) , which combines windowed PIBT with large neighborhood search ( Li et al., 2021a ; Li et al., 2022 ) and traffic guidance graphs.
Although guidance graph optimization ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) automates edge-cost tuning over these graphs, the underlying planning algorithms remain fixed.
Alternatively, learning-based formulations train neural policies via reinforcement or imitation learning ( Sartoretti et al., 2019 ; Damani et al., 2021 ; Skrynnik et al., 2024 ; Andreychuk et al., 2025 ) , with recent neural planners and schedulers outperforming earlier benchmark baselines ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Gaber et al., 2026 ) .
Large language models (LLMs) have also been explored as direct online planners; however, prompting LLMs to emit next-step moves sequentially struggles to scale beyond small stylized instances ( Chen et al., 2025 ) .

Policy search in code space builds upon a broader lineage of program synthesis and algorithmic discovery.
Early programmatic reinforcement learning formulated policies as interpretable programs, though restricted to small, domain-specific languages ( Verma et al., 2018 ; Trivedi et al., 2021 ) .
Modern LLMs lift these grammar constraints, enabling coding agents to manipulate general-purpose programming languages such as C++ and Python directly.
Recent frameworks leverage this capability to evolve individual functions or isolated files for discrete algorithms and combinatorial optimization heuristics ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ; Novikov et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2024 ) .
Complementary lines of work optimize prompt graphs and textual variables through verbal feedback and execution traces ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2025 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) .
More recently, automated loops have advanced to whole programs and repositories, in SAT solving, model training, and optimization contests ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Karpathy, 2026 ; Imajuku et al., 2025 ) , as well as dispatch and charging policies for automated guided vehicles without spatial path planning ( Li & Li, 2026 ) .

Our study differs from existing literature in the following aspects. 1 ) Whereas existing automated MAPF methods predominantly tune heuristic parameters or train parametric neural weights, our work searches over planner and scheduler implementations directly in code space. 2 ) Furthermore, while prior program synthesis frameworks rely on sophisticated evolutionary harnesses for stylized benchmarks, we demonstrate that state-of-the-art coding agents discover effective algorithms for demanding LMAPF problems without rigid search harnesses.

2026-10-20.title: Vision-Language-Delta-Action: Learning Compact Deltas as Actionable Transition Interfaces for Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Lingsen Zhang , Wei Li , Jie He , Henghua Zhang , Kai Mo , Shiyong Li , Yanpeng Wang , Rui Shao
2026-10-20.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

2026-10-20.introduction:
Similar to human actions, robotic manipulation is a process of controlled physical state transformation [ 56 , 49 ] .
As shown in Fig. 1 (top), conditioned on visual observations, a robot must not only recognize the current scene and interpret the task-relevant physical context around it [ 27 , 23 ] , but also determine which part of the scene should change and how such change can be realized through continuous action execution [ 43 , 1 ] .
This requirement fundamentally distinguishes robotic manipulation from generic vision-language understanding, as the critical decision variable is not the complete visual state itself, but the task-relevant transition that drives the current state toward the desired physical outcome.

However, existing VLA and WAM paradigms share a common limitation in lacking a dedicated, action-grounded representation of task-relevant physical transitions. 1) Most VLA models still follow an observation-to-action formulation that entangles task-relevant object identification [ 26 , 4 , 53 , 61 ] , desired physical state-change inference, and executable action-chunk generation within a single policy.
Without dedicated modeling of task-relevant state changes, the policy must implicitly infer the intended physical transition from action supervision alone, leaving a substantial representational gap between semantic understanding and action execution.

A straightforward way to bridge semantic understanding and action execution is future modeling, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (a) and (b). 2) WAMs predict future observations [ 59 , 7 , 54 ] , visual latents [ 44 , 39 ] , or action-conditioned dynamics [ 2 , 25 ] to provide temporal cues beyond the current observation.
However, they typically represent the future as another complete state, causing task-relevant transition cues to remain entangled with static scene content and action-irrelevant variations. Moreover, future prediction is often used only as an auxiliary objective, without providing a structured intermediate variable that can directly guide action generation.
Robotic manipulation instead requires a compact transition variable that captures task-relevant manipulation-centric changes, remains consistent with the overall direction of future evolution, and is directly grounded in executable actions.

Taken together, these limitations motivate a transition interface that is selective, predictive, and actionable. It should isolate task-relevant manipulation-centric changes, remain consistent with future evolution, and be directly consumable by the action generator. To this end, we propose Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA) , a new paradigm that models actionable transitions through a low-dimensional Delta interface rather than predicting the complete future state.

Specifically, VLDA instantiates the transition interface as a compact low-dimensional Delta that captures the task-relevant transition implied by the task. To make Delta both selective and predictive, VLDA introduces a unified learning objective with two complementary constraints. 1) Local Transition Filter (LT-Filter) distills sparse, manipulation-centric transition evidence from dense current-to-future visual differences, suppressing static scene content and action-irrelevant variations. 2) Global Transition Anchor (GT-Anchor) regularizes Delta with a coarse summary of future evolution, preventing overly local transition modeling and preserving the global direction of state change.
Together, these constraints reconcile local transition selectivity with global predictive consistency, yielding a compact and future-grounded representation of task-relevant physical change.
To make Delta directly actionable, VLDA further introduces 3) Delta-Driven Action Refinement (DDAR) , which grounds Delta in the action manifold through Delta-action alignment and injects it into the action flow as a structured transition seed.
The action expert then refines this transition-informed seed into executable action chunks conditioned on the predicted transition.
Rather than treating future prediction as auxiliary supervision, VLDA therefore establishes a closed understanding-transition-execution loop , where vision-language representations interpret the task context, Delta specifies the required state transition, and DDAR realizes that transition through continuous action generation.

We evaluate VLDA on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks and challenging long-horizon tasks. Experimental results show that VLDA improves long-horizon consistency, robustness under distribution shifts, and generalization to complex manipulation scenarios. These results demonstrate that modeling actionable Delta provides a more effective alternative to both direct observation-to-action learning and full future-state prediction.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA) , a new robotic manipulation paradigm that replaces complete future-state prediction with a compact Delta serving as an actionable transition interface.

We design a unified Delta learning objective with Local Transition Filter and Global Transition Anchor , enabling Delta to capture sparse task-relevant changes while remaining consistent with future transition trends.

We develop Delta-Driven Action Refinement , which aligns Delta with the action manifold and uses it as a structured seed for action denoising, forming an explicit understanding-transition-execution loop.

1. We introduce Vision-Language-Delta-Action (VLDA) , a new robotic manipulation paradigm that replaces complete future-state prediction with a compact Delta serving as an actionable transition interface.

2. We design a unified Delta learning objective with Local Transition Filter and Global Transition Anchor , enabling Delta to capture sparse task-relevant changes while remaining consistent with future transition trends.

3. We develop Delta-Driven Action Refinement , which aligns Delta with the action manifold and uses it as a structured seed for action denoising, forming an explicit understanding-transition-execution loop.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2  Related Work

Existing VLA models primarily employ action-token prediction, implemented either autoregressively or in parallel [ 5 , 26 , 27 , 20 , 41 , 32 ] , and continuous action experts based on diffusion or flow matching [ 11 , 4 , 23 , 51 , 33 , 17 , 34 ] .
Despite different action decoders, both paradigms directly supervise actions from observations, requiring a single policy to jointly resolve task grounding, intended physical change, and motor realization. This creates a substantial gap between high-level semantic observations and low-level executable actions. VLDA bridges this gap with a compact Delta that explicitly mediates what should change and how that change is executed.

Recent WAMs couple future modeling with robot control through cascaded future-to-action generation [ 47 , 30 , 62 ] , joint world-action prediction [ 16 , 7 , 54 , 63 ] , and predictive latent dynamics [ 18 , 21 , 40 ] .
In these formulations, future prediction typically serves as an upstream context, a jointly decoded target, or a regularizer for action learning, with its contribution to control determined by architecture-specific fusion mechanisms.
VLDA instead reparameterizes the prediction-control connection through a compact Delta, whose control role is explicitly defined by transition learning and Delta-driven action refinement.

Discrete approaches tokenize visually inferred motion patterns for scalable VLA pretraining [ 52 , 6 , 9 ] , while continuous formulations learn smooth latent control variables that can be mapped to embodiment-specific actions with limited supervision [ 35 , 45 ] . CLAP [ 57 ] and LARA [ 37 ] further improve physical grounding by aligning visually inferred representations with robot actions or proprioceptive dynamics. However, these representations mainly serve as pseudo-action labels, pretraining targets, or shared control spaces. They do not explicitly isolate task-relevant physical changes under complementary local and global constraints, ground such changes in the action manifold, and use them to directly guide action refinement.

2026-10-20.title: AeroIntent: A Synchronized Multimodal Benchmark for UAV Mission Intent Recognition
2026-10-20.authors: Yutong Chen , Jingxin Mao , Zhiwei Wei , Bing Li , Jianzhong Ni , Rongqing Zhang
2026-10-20.abstract: Reliable recognition of mission-level UAV intent from multimodal observations is essential for low-altitude airspace surveillance and security. Existing multimodal UAV datasets primarily support detection, tracking, and localization, leaving limited support for evaluating mission-intent recognition across held-out trajectory programs and incomplete radar histories. We introduce AeroIntent, a simulation-based benchmark comprising 990 synchronized multimodal sequences generated by 22 trajectory programs across five mission intents. The benchmark provides radar, RGB, infrared, and depth observations, together with program-disjoint, radar-gap, and observation-prefix evaluation protocols. Building on this benchmark, we propose AeroMIR , a structured Multimodal Intent Reasoner that integrates radar trajectories, derived behavioral features, selected visual evidence, and task knowledge for candidate-based UAV intent recognition. Under a strict program-disjoint protocol evaluating unseen tactical realizations, AeroMIR achieves a mean accuracy of 71.56% and a mean Macro-F1 of 69.84% across three seeds, outperforming the strongest trajectory-only baseline by 7.79 Macro-F1 points and a conventional radar–RGB late-fusion baseline by 19.32 points. AeroMIR also demonstrates strong performance under controlled radar gaps and early intent recognition settings. AeroIntent and AeroMIR provide a reproducible foundation for multimodal UAV intent recognition. The benchmark is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AeroIntent .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Recognizing UAV intent is important for low-altitude airspace surveillance and security. Beyond detecting and tracking an aircraft, mission-intent recognition identifies the purpose of its observed behavior. Distinguishing transit, reconnaissance, probing, strike, and escape helps to interpret an encounter as it develops. In practice, intent must often be inferred before a complete trajectory is available, motivating evaluation from partial observation histories.

Conventional approaches predominantly rely on temporal deep learning models operating on numerical radar trajectories. Temporal networks [ 1 , 2 ] , radar-specific representations [ 3 ] , and behavior-to-language models [ 4 ] have demonstrated the value of motion patterns for intent recognition. However, as illustrated in Fig. 1 , when intermittent radar returns result in incomplete motion histories, these radar-only methods struggle to obtain sufficient behavioral evidence, reducing recognition accuracy. Moreover, the same mission intent can be expressed through different motion patterns and geometric configurations, which we refer to as tactical realizations . The generalization of existing trajectory-based methods to unseen tactical realizations under incomplete radar observations remains insufficiently characterized. Visual observations provide scene and appearance cues that complement incomplete radar histories, while radar-derived behavioral descriptors make motion relations explicit. Combining these representations motivates a structured multimodal approach, whose generalization to unseen tactical realizations can be assessed using held-out trajectory programs.

Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer a new avenue for integrating heterogeneous perceptual evidence with task semantics. JTD-UAV [ 5 ] combines thermal UAV tracking with language-based behavior and intent description, without incorporating radar observations. Lei et al. [ 6 ] further propose a framework connecting multimodal perception with intent reasoning, although its effectiveness has yet to be systematically evaluated. These studies suggest that MLLMs have the potential to integrate heterogeneous perceptual information with task semantics.

Nevertheless, existing research lacks a systematic benchmark and a unified evaluation protocol for multimodal intent recognition, particularly under unseen tactical realizations and incomplete radar observations. Existing benchmarks, including Anti-UAV [ 7 ] , MMAUD [ 8 ] , and LAMBDA [ 9 ] , provide multimodal data for UAV tracking, localization, and low-altitude sensing and communication, but do not support mission-intent recognition with annotated intent labels.

To address this gap, we introduce AeroIntent , a simulation-based benchmark comprising 990 synchronized multimodal sequences, five mission intents, 22 trajectory-generation programs, three simulated environments, and 15 UAV–payload configurations. The dataset records radar, RGB, infrared, depth, and UAV state data. To evaluate generalization to unseen tactical realizations, the benchmark adopts a program-disjoint protocol: the test set excludes all scene–configuration instances associated with trajectory programs used in training or validation. We also introduce controlled radar-gap and early intent recognition protocols to examine model performance under missing measurements and progressively accumulating observational evidence. We further propose AeroMIR , a structured multimodal intent reasoner that integrates radar trajectories, derived behavioral features, selected visual evidence, and prior task knowledge for candidate-based UAV intent recognition. Under the program-disjoint protocol across three seeds, AeroMIR achieves a mean Macro-F1 of 69.84%, outperforming the strongest trajectory-only baseline by 7.79 percentage points and the radar–RGB late-fusion baseline by 19.32 percentage points. With a radar gap covering 40% of the recording duration,
AeroMIR exceeds the strongest baseline by 6.30 Macro-F1
percentage points. In a separate observation-prefix
evaluation at P75, the margin is 9.88 points.

The main contributions of our work are:

We introduce AeroIntent , a synchronized multimodal benchmark for UAV intent recognition with trajectory-generation metadata and a program-disjoint protocol, enabling systematic evaluation under unseen tactical realizations and incomplete radar observations.

We propose AeroMIR , a structured multimodal intent reasoner that integrates radar trajectories, behavioral features, visual evidence, and task knowledge through candidate-based fine-tuning.

Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of AeroMIR under unseen tactical realizations, controlled radar gaps, and early intent recognition, outperforming competitive baselines and highlighting the value of multimodal and behavior-aware intent recognition.

1. We introduce AeroIntent , a synchronized multimodal benchmark for UAV intent recognition with trajectory-generation metadata and a program-disjoint protocol, enabling systematic evaluation under unseen tactical realizations and incomplete radar observations.

2. We propose AeroMIR , a structured multimodal intent reasoner that integrates radar trajectories, behavioral features, visual evidence, and task knowledge through candidate-based fine-tuning.

3. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of AeroMIR under unseen tactical realizations, controlled radar gaps, and early intent recognition, outperforming competitive baselines and highlighting the value of multimodal and behavior-aware intent recognition.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A UAV Intent Recognition

Motion-based intent recognition includes LSTM prediction with an entropy decision tree [ 10 ] , radar trajectory-frequency classification [ 3 ] , BiGRU-attention [ 11 ] , attention–TCN–BiGRU [ 1 ] , and hierarchical LSTM with data enhancement [ 12 ] . Formation-level STFN combines formation geometry and swarm-centroid trajectories [ 13 ] . Li et al. translate flight attributes into language [ 4 ] , while Zheng et al. use looming cues for early non-cooperative encounter recognition [ 14 ] . GenRec studies recognition from partial video observations [ 15 ] ; AeroIntent instead evaluates multimodal mission-intent recognition on held-out UAV trajectory programs.

## II-B Multimodal Perception and Incomplete Observations

Multimodal learning studies complementary representations, alignment, and fusion [ 16 ] . Anti-UAV supports RGB–thermal tracking [ 7 ] ; MMAUD provides camera, radar, LiDAR, and audio data for detection and localization [ 8 ] ; LAMBDA combines visual, motion, LiDAR, radar, and wireless observations [ 9 ] . These resources do not provide a unified labeled mission-intent evaluation with held-out trajectory programs.

In driving-scene 3D perception, CenterFusion associates radar measurements with image detections [ 17 ] , and CRN fuses camera–radar features [ 18 ] . SMIL addresses severely missing modalities [ 19 ] , while Lee et al. learn missing-modality-aware prompts for visual recognition [ 20 ] . Our radar-gap protocol instead removes contiguous intervals within radar histories while retaining clean RGB evidence.

## II-C Multimodal and Time-Series Language Models

BLIP-2 bridges frozen pretrained image encoders and language models [ 21 ] ; LLaVA develops visual instruction tuning [ 22 ] ; PaLM-E incorporates sensory inputs into embodied language modeling [ 23 ] . For UAV understanding, JTD-UAV combines thermal tracking and language description [ 5 ] , while Lei et al. organize perception summaries and task knowledge for intent reasoning [ 6 ] . AeroIntent provides complementary labeled evaluations of generalization and incomplete observations.

For temporal data, LLMTIME encodes numerical sequences as text [ 24 ] , and Time-LLM reprograms time-series patches for a frozen language model [ 25 ] . These forecasting studies motivate careful numerical interfaces. AeroMIR combines radar states, deterministic behavioral descriptors, visual evidence, and task knowledge for candidate-based intent recognition.

2026-10-20.title: OV-PEAR: Observation-Verified Pose-Scale Estimation and Reconstruction for Unknown Industrial Manipulation Objects
2026-10-20.authors: Guoqin Tang , Qingxuan Jia , Yichen Tan , Zihang Lv , Ruiquan Wang , Zeyuan Huang , Gang Chen
2026-10-20.abstract: Fine industrial robotic manipulation requires 6D pose, scale, and an operation-ready 3D model. Existing industrial pose estimation relies on CAD models, object-specific training data, or stable workcells, limiting use with unseen objects; zero-shot methods suffer from single-view occlusion, generative bias, and scale uncertainty. We present OV-PEAR, an observation-verified framework for 3D reconstruction and pose-scale estimation of unknown industrial objects. Its three-stage object-centric pipeline: (1) segments RGB-D instances and generates object-level 3D hypotheses; (2) anchors them to the robot frame via appearance-aware view retrieval, explicit scale search, and visibility-sensitive registration; (3) back-projects multi-view RGB-D evidence into the object-canonical frame to verify voxel occupancy, suppress hallucinations, and produce reusable trusted object models. On BOP-Industrial, OV-PEAR achieves 0.657 average AR and improves pose and voxel-level geometric consistency in real scenes; real-robot connector assembly reaches 99.67% grasp and 84.00% assembly success. The model library and pose-scale log enable short-term object-level state maintenance at 0.02 ms/frame.

2026-10-20.title: Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions
2026-10-20.authors: Kallol Saha , Yining Hong , Amber Li , Yejin Choi , Maxim Likhachev , David Held
2026-10-20.comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026 (Oral). Project page: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract:
Despite recent advances in policy learning, long-horizon manipulation remains difficult because learned policies must avoid compounding errors while preserving future feasibility. While search-based planning can explicitly reason over such future consequences, it quickly becomes expensive in high-dimensional continuous action spaces.
This raises a central question: how can long-horizon reasoning from search be transferred into policies in continuous action spaces ? To this end, we propose DISCO : Di stilled Tree S earch over Co ntinuous Actions. DISCO uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation to generate long-horizon plans. During search, a learned policy proposes continuous actions, while a learned value function scores actions by their expected progress toward task completion. Using GPU-parallelized simulation, DISCO periodically distills MCTS-generated plans into the policy-value model, improving the action proposals and value estimates used in subsequent searches. Finally, the learned policy-value model can be directly deployed without the need for simulator-based search at test time. Across simulated and real-world rearrangement tasks, DISCO outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Robot learning has advanced rapidly in recent years, enabling neural network policies to acquire complex behaviors across a wide range of tasks in robot manipulation [ 17 , 35 , 70 , 18 , 48 , 96 , 33 ] .
Despite their strong performance on short-horizon behaviors, these methods still struggle with long-horizon manipulation tasks such as multi-object rearrangement [ 81 , 63 , 28 , 88 , 36 , 44 , 90 ] . Such tasks require reasoning over many sequential decisions, where each action must be locally feasible while preserving future task feasibility. This makes behavior-cloned policies brittle: errors compound over long sequences [ 77 , 62 ] , and short-horizon supervision does not capture how early actions affect later success [ 58 , 23 , 31 ] . For example, shelf packing requires fine-grained pick-and-place actions that are feasible and preserve space for later objects (Figure Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions ).
Meanwhile, search-based planning [ 66 , 65 , 67 , 69 , 94 ] provides a natural mechanism for reasoning over future consequences of an action, by evaluating whether it leads to successful downstream configurations. Building on this, the integration of learning with tree search has been powerful in solving long-horizon decision-making problems like Go, chess, and Atari. Most notably, AlphaGo [ 71 , 72 , 68 , 1 ] combines Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) [ 42 , 4 ] with learned policy and value networks to achieve strong sequential reasoning capabilities. In these systems, search explores the future consequences of actions, while learned policies and value functions guide exploration toward promising regions of the decision space.
However, these domains are highly structured, with discrete actions and exact transition dynamics. In contrast, robots see noisy, partially-occluded observations such as point clouds and operate in continuous action spaces. As a result, naively applying tree search quickly becomes computationally expensive.
This raises a question: how can the long-horizon reasoning of search be transferred into learned policies for robot manipulation in continuous state-action spaces?

In this work, we take a step toward bridging this gap with DISCO , a framework for DI stilled tree S earch over CO ntinuous actions. DISCO combines a learned manipulation policy with MCTS using progressive widening to efficiently search over continuous action spaces [ 6 , 9 , 61 ] . The policy proposes continuous grasp-and-place actions conditioned on point clouds, while a learned value function estimates long-term task completion to guide search towards promising regions. To efficiently explore the space of feasible long-horizon plans, we leverage GPU-parallelized simulation for batched node expansion and rollout evaluation [ 24 , 69 ] . Similar to AlphaGo, DISCO distills MCTS-generated plans back into both the policy and the value function, allowing search to progressively discover long-horizon plans. The distillation process also enables DISCO to directly execute long-horizon behaviors
during execution (Figure Long-Horizon Multi-Object Rearrangement via Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions ). Search and simulation are used only during training: DISCO trains one shared policy-value model per task on randomized simulated instances, and at test time this model acts directly from point clouds on unseen instances, without search or a simulator. In this way, DISCO incorporates long-horizon reasoning capabilities into manipulation policies through iterative search-based self-improvement.
We evaluate DISCO on several challenging multi-object rearrangement tasks in simulation and in the real world. We observe that DISCO achieves stronger long-horizon success than behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, sampling-based optimization, and alternative search-based planners. We also show that DISCO benefits from both policy-guided expansion and progressive widening, scales with task complexity, and transfers to real-world manipulation tasks. Our main contributions are: (1) We show that long-horizon behavior can be bootstrapped purely from short-horizon data (e.g., single-object pick-and-place) by using MCTS with progressive widening to search over continuous state-action spaces. This removes the need for expensive long-horizon demonstrations. (2) We show that DISCO self-improves both the policy and the value function through iterative distillation rounds, enabling search to progressively generate more long-horizon plans for supervision. (3) We show that the distilled point-cloud-conditioned policy-value model executes long-horizon tasks by direct rollout, without search or a simulator at test time, scales better than baselines as the number of objects increases, and transfers to held-out simulation tasks and a real robot.
2026-10-20.related_work: Combined Learning and Planning. Recent Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) methods [ 15 , 16 , 69 ] incorporate learning for continuous samplers [ 89 , 74 , 8 , 41 ] , symbolic abstractions and operators [ 76 , 74 , 75 , 10 , 47 ] , skill and parameter models [ 50 , 45 ] , and search heuristics [ 40 , 93 , 37 , 94 ] . These methods rely on symbolic representations, whereas DISCO operates directly on point-cloud observations and predicts continuous actions. Skill-chaining methods [ 43 , 46 , 53 , 52 , 91 , 32 ] compose temporally extended skills or options [ 86 , 2 ] for long-horizon planning. Rather than learning a skill graph or composing separate skill models, DISCO distills plans into a policy-value model. World-model-based planning methods learn transition models for imagined rollouts or model-predictive control [ 19 , 95 , 21 , 20 , 22 , 49 , 38 ] . In contrast, DISCO does not learn a transition model, and uses physics simulation only during training to generate long-horizon supervision. Other approaches plan from point clouds using object-centric transformations [ 63 ] , relational abstractions [ 28 , 29 , 55 ] , or neural object descriptors [ 78 , 7 ] . DISCO instead learns a closed-loop policy-value model and executes without explicit tree search at inference. Plan Distillation and Policy Learning. Prior work has distilled planning pipelines into neural policies, including TAMP imitation [ 12 ] and neural motion-planner distillation [ 5 , 64 , 13 , 92 ] . Related learning-to-search methods [ 58 , 31 ] train policies to reduce compounding errors from imitation learning [ 62 ] . In contrast, DISCO iterates between planning and learning: generated long-horizon plans update the policy-value model, which then guides subsequent plan generation. Recent 3D visuomotor policies map point clouds [ 17 , 35 , 96 , 33 ] , voxel grids [ 70 ] , or multi-view features [ 18 , 48 , 11 ] directly to robot actions, but are typically trained from fixed-horizon demonstrations. DISCO instead self-generates long-horizon plans to train a closed-loop model for execution. Monte-Carlo Tree Search. For continuous high dimensional action spaces, prior work extends MCTS using progressive widening [ 6 , 9 , 61 ] , learned action sampling [ 39 ] , policy priors [ 56 , 30 ] , state abstraction [ 79 ] , or prioritized branching [ 51 , 73 , 83 ] . In robotics, MCTS has been used for nonprehensile rearrangement [ 80 ] , clutter retrieval [ 26 , 25 ] , batched long-horizon planning [ 24 ] , contact planning [ 97 ] , confined-space rearrangement and occluded-object grasping [ 59 , 34 ] , multi-goal task planning [ 57 ] , and world-model-based planning [ 38 , 27 ] . AlphaGo-style systems further show that MCTS can be coupled with policy-value learning in a self-improving loop [ 71 , 72 , 68 , 1 ] , and dual policy iteration [ 82 ] alternates between a planning policy and a learned reactive policy. Neural Tree Expansion [ 60 ] guides MCTS with learned policy-value models for continuous multi-robot planning, but runs MCTS online at test time, whereas DISCO runs MCTS only during training. DISCO extends progressive-widening MCTS over continuous actions into robot manipulation problems, using a point-cloud conditioned policy-value model that is iteratively improved during search.

2026-10-20.title: TrajWAM: An Efficient Trajectory-Guided World Action Model for Dynamic Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Haohan Geng , Sha Zhang , Weishuo Sun , Guanting Ye , Wenhao Yu , Yuang Xie , Qicheng Zeng , Peng Ye , Jiajun Deng , Jianmin Ji
2026-10-20.abstract:
Dynamic object manipulation requires robots to anticipate target motion while replanning fast enough to avoid executing outdated actions.
Existing approaches either rely on fast reactive control without an explicit future target state or encode anticipated motion only implicitly.
World Action Models (WAMs) offer a promising alternative by coupling future visual prediction with action generation, but scene-level video objectives may underrepresent target dynamics that are critical for manipulation, while iterative video-action denoising introduces substantial latency.
We present TrajWAM , a trajectory-guided world action model for efficient dynamic robotic manipulation.
Our key insight is to explicitly ground future visual imagination in predicted target-object motion and use the resulting future representation to condition action generation, while preserving this anticipation pathway after acceleration.
Given a short history of object masks, a history-conditioned motion predictor forecasts future masks encoding the target object’s trajectory.
A lightweight Trajectory ControlNet then steers a pretrained video model toward trajectory-consistent futures. The resulting future representation conditions an action expert to predict executable action chunks.
To enable one-step inference without breaking this interface, we introduce a decoupled distillation scheme that combines distribution matching for the video backbone, Trajectory ControlNet realignment, and action rollout distillation to support accurate one-step action prediction conditioned on the compressed future representation.
Comprehensive evaluations in simulation and the real world show that TrajWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance on dynamic object manipulation tasks while enabling efficient one-step video-action inference.
