2026-10-20.introduction:
Dynamic object manipulation is essential for robots operating in human environments, factories, and warehouses, where task-relevant objects may continue moving while the robot perceives and acts [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Unlike static manipulation, in which the target state is approximately fixed between observation and execution, dynamic manipulation couples perception, prediction, and control in a continuously changing scene. An action that is appropriate for the current observation may therefore become outdated before execution, and even a small delay may lead to a missed grasp or inaccurate contact. Successful dynamic manipulation consequently requires both anticipation of the target object’s motion and sufficiently fast closed-loop replanning.

World Action Models (WAMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to vision-language-action policies by coupling future visual prediction with action generation [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
By modeling how observations evolve under interaction, WAMs provide an additional physical prior for control and are particularly appealing for dynamic manipulation.
However, as illustrated in Fig. 1 ,
existing WAMs predict scene evolution at the full-frame level, where robot-induced changes can dominate the imagined future.
In dynamic manipulation, task success may instead depend critically on target motion that evolves independently of the robot’s actions.
A scene-level forecast entangles robot motion, background dynamics, and target-object motion, making the task-relevant trajectory only indirectly represented and difficult to control explicitly during generation.
Extending WAMs to dynamic object manipulation thus calls for an object-centric future representation that specifies the anticipated spatial trajectory of the target while remaining coupled to action prediction.

Moreover, most existing WAMs synthesize future videos and actions through iterative denoising, introducing latency that can make the resulting prediction stale before execution. Recent methods reduce this cost either by skipping future imagination during inference [ 7 , 8 ] or by compressing the denoising process [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . However, the former sacrifices an explicit predictive pathway for anticipating target motion, while the latter leaves open whether a spatially explicit motion condition can remain effective after aggressive denoising compression.

To address these challenges, we propose TrajWAM , a trajectory-guided world action model for efficient dynamic robotic manipulation.
Our key insight is to explicitly incorporate predicted target-object motion into future visual imagination and propagate its influence to action generation through the resulting video representation.
Starting from a short observation history, TrajWAM predicts how the task-relevant object will evolve and represents this motion as a sequence of future object masks. These predicted masks provide an explicit spatial guide for future generation, steering the world model toward futures that are consistent with the anticipated target motion.
The resulting imagined future then conditions action prediction, allowing the robot to act not only on what is currently observed, but also on where the target is expected to be.

The remaining challenge is to make this anticipation pathway fast enough for dynamic control.
Simply bypassing future imagination would remove the mechanism through which predicted target motion influences the action, while naively compressing the generative process can degrade both trajectory controllability and downstream action prediction.
We therefore introduce a decoupled one-step distillation strategy that accelerates the video and action generation processes according to their different requirements.
The video pathway is distilled while explicitly preserving its response to trajectory guidance, whereas the action pathway is distilled to retain accurate predictions under the compressed future representation.
In this way, TrajWAM substantially reduces inference latency without discarding the trajectory-guided future imagination that enables anticipatory control.

We evaluate TrajWAM on dynamic manipulation tasks in both simulated and real-world settings, covering diverse object categories, motion patterns, and task types. On DOMINO, as shown in Fig. 1 (b), TrajWAM achieves state-of-the-art performance with a success rate of 43.54%, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 14.24 percentage points at an inference latency of 108.5  ms.
In real-world experiments, TrajWAM achieves success rates of 77.9% on conveyor-belt grasping and 70.4% on rotating-disc grasping, consistently outperforming the evaluated baselines.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce TrajWAM, a trajectory-guided world action model that explicitly incorporates predicted target-object motion into future visual imagination and propagates this anticipation to downstream action prediction.

We introduce TrajWAM, a trajectory-guided world action model that explicitly incorporates predicted target-object motion into future visual imagination and propagates this anticipation to downstream action prediction.

We develop a decoupled one-step distillation strategy that accelerates video and action generation while preserving trajectory controllability and accurate future-conditioned action prediction.

Extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots establish state-of-the-art dynamic manipulation performance while demonstrating efficient one-step inference and the effectiveness of trajectory-guided anticipation.

1. We introduce TrajWAM, a trajectory-guided world action model that explicitly incorporates predicted target-object motion into future visual imagination and propagates this anticipation to downstream action prediction.

2. We develop a decoupled one-step distillation strategy that accelerates video and action generation while preserving trajectory controllability and accurate future-conditioned action prediction.

3. Extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots establish state-of-the-art dynamic manipulation performance while demonstrating efficient one-step inference and the effectiveness of trajectory-guided anticipation.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Vision-language-action models have made substantial progress in robot manipulation by directly mapping visual observations and language instructions to actions [ 12 , 13 ] . World-action models (WAMs) extend this paradigm by jointly modeling future observations and executable actions, using visual dynamics prediction as an additional physical prior for control. Recent WAMs have studied different ways to balance future imagination and action execution. Fast-WAM [ 7 ] shows that explicit future generation can be skipped at inference, while AHA-WAM [ 11 ] and HarmoWAM [ 14 ] further improve the temporal coordination between world prediction and action generation. Dynamic manipulation requires anticipating the motion of objects that move independently of the robot. DOMINO [ 15 ] exposes the resulting performance degradation, while DynamicVLA [ 16 ] and PUMA [ 15 ] address it through low-latency inference and implicit object-motion prediction, respectively. DynamicWAM [ 17 ] incorporates recent motion into WAMs through dual-path flow conditioning, whereas TrajWAM predicts future target-object mask trajectories to guide future imagination for action prediction.

Trajectory-controllable video generation aims to synthesize videos that follow explicit spatial motion conditions, complementing text- or image-conditioned generation where object motion is often under-specified. Existing methods use point tracks or trajectories for fine-grained motion control [ 18 ] , bounding boxes or tracklets to guide object locations [ 19 ] and interactions [ 20 ] , and 3D or depth-aware trajectories to reduce ambiguity in object motion [ 21 ] . More recently, MagicMotion [ 22 ] proposes dense-to-sparse trajectory guidance with masks, boxes, and sparse boxes, improving trajectory adherence and object consistency. We build on this idea of explicit motion conditioning, but use it as a future-imagination mechanism inside WAMs: future object masks are predicted from observation history and injected into the video branch to support downstream dynamic manipulation.

Dynamic manipulation requires low-latency inference, since the policy must continuously update actions while objects move. This is challenging for diffusion-based WAMs, where both future imagination and action generation rely on iterative denoising. Diffusion distillation provides a common way to reduce sampling steps [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] , and has been extended to efficient video generation [ 26 , 27 ] and trajectory-controllable generation [ 28 ] . Recent WAMs also explore this direction: Flash-WAM [ 10 ] proposes modality-aware step distillation for joint video-action diffusion, while AHA-WAM-Flash [ 11 ] applies ODE distillation to compress its action sampler from multi-step denoising to few-step inference. While these works primarily improve the efficiency of existing WAM inference pipelines, preserving trajectory controllability and action accuracy under compression remains underexplored.

2026-10-20.title: Learning from Fleet Experience: A Collective Learning Paradigm for Robots
2026-10-20.authors: Chao Yu , Shu'ang Yu , Hao Lin , Hongzhi Zang , Yuxiang Yan , Chenxi Jiang , Zhen Guo , Chuankang Li , Yihao Chen , Xin Xu , Xu Fu , Jiakai Zhou , Liangzhi Shi , Hongyi Ren , Yiwei Liu , Jing Wu , Yuanqing Wang , Chen Wu , Bo Dai , Chunyu Yang , Hongliang Huang , Shuoyu Yue , Weiqi Yin , Yinuo Chen , Ruihua Chen , Chunyang Zhu , Han Xiao , Yanghao Li , Ruipu Wu , Zhikai Cai , Xiu Chen , Xu Tan , Yuchen Yan , Jialin Zhang , Wen Zeng , Yiming Zhou , Zixiao Huang , Guanghui Ren , Quanlu Zhang , Boxun Li , Maoqing Yao , Yu Wang
2026-10-20.abstract: Experience generated during deployment offers an opportunity for robots to improve policy reliability through learning from their own executions. However, learning through human corrections requires teleoperators to monitor execution and intervene when policies fail, a demand that is difficult to meet as robot fleets grow. We introduce collective experience learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which deployed robots share their execution experience to improve a common policy. We realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT), which uses failure contexts from robot executions to retrieve relevant trajectory segments from the fleet’s shared successful experience and uses their actions as supervision for policy updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates experience collection, policy optimization and policy distribution despite local interruptions within the robot fleet. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and FERT generally achieves higher success rates across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots increases success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support collective experience as a practical basis for scalable robot learning and a path towards improving policy reliability during deployment without collecting additional expert corrective actions.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Execution during deployment generates experience that robots can use to improve policy reliability. Robot foundation models provide initial capabilities by translating visual and language understanding into physical action [ 4 , 44 , 20 , 11 , 3 ] , but these initial capabilities do not automatically yield reliable execution [ 31 , 19 , 5 ] . Variations in object properties, contact conditions and individual robots expose gaps in these capabilities, particularly when errors accumulate over multi-stage tasks [ 21 , 43 ] . At the same time, robots operating in the real world generate experience that can support further policy improvement [ 6 , 1 ] . As deployment expands to larger fleets, parallel execution provides a growing source of physical experience [ 22 , 16 , 17 , 32 , 36 ] . The question is how to turn this growing experience into more reliable task execution during deployment.

A central constraint is the human effort required to supply corrective actions during deployment. Expert demonstrations and corrective interventions have proved useful for improving policies during real-world execution [ 34 , 18 , 25 , 24 , 1 , 13 ] . Recent fleet-learning systems combine parallel collection with human supervision to connect robot execution and policy updates [ 14 , 32 , 36 ] . When learning depends on new expert actions, teleoperators must remain available to monitor execution, recognize failures and take control to provide appropriate corrections. As the deployed fleet grows, the capacity to supply this action supervision is difficult to scale alongside robot interaction [ 14 , 13 ] . This motivates a learning process in which deployed robots improve from their own experience without relying on continued collection of expert demonstrations or corrective actions .

We introduce \onethreeblue Collective Experience Learning (CEL), a learning paradigm in which robots contribute experience generated during deployment to improve a shared policy. Experience from multiple robots is pooled for learning, and the updated policy guides subsequent fleet execution and generates further experience. This closes the loop between distributed robot execution and shared policy improvement, allowing experience contributed by individual robots to support learning across the fleet.

Turning collective experience into policy improvement requires selecting experience relevant to the policy’s current difficulties. Successful trajectories differ in their relevance, so collecting more successes alone does not determine which behaviours to emphasize during an update. We develop Failure-guided Experience Retrieval fine-Tuning (FERT) as an algorithmic realization of CEL. FERT stores successful fleet trajectories in a collective experience buffer and uses contexts from failed executions to retrieve relevant successful segments. Retrieval increases the sampling priority of these segments, whose recorded actions provide supervision for policy updates. Failures therefore guide experience selection, while successful executions supply the action targets. Following expert-supervised initialization, FERT draws its action supervision from robot-generated experience without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. In our implementation, humans label episode outcomes and reset environments, while robots supply the actions used for subsequent learning.

Sustaining this learning loop across a robot fleet requires coordinating processes that operate at different rates and remain subject to local interruptions. Robots may pause for environment resets, maintenance or recovery, while experience collection, policy inference and optimization proceed on different schedules [ 32 , 36 ] . We develop a Fault-tolerant Asynchronous Training System (FATS) as the system realization of CEL. FATS coordinates robot and computing resources and decouples execution from policy optimization. Its data plane, SwarmLink, pools cloud inference and assembles streamed trajectory fields for training. Its control plane, HotSwarm, restarts failed robot workers in place while available robots continue collecting experience. Whereas FERT determines how collective experience improves the shared policy, FATS supports the distributed process through which that experience is generated, incorporated into learning and used in subsequent execution.

We evaluate this realization of CEL across five real-world manipulation tasks involving deformable objects, precise alignment, tool use and multi-stage execution. For each task, policies are evaluated over 120 trials, split equally between two physical robots excluded from training data collection. This tests whether experience contributed by the training fleet benefits other robot instances of the same platform. At the largest evaluated fleet size for each task, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2% . In fleet-size experiments with collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience, and FERT success rates generally increase across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with \onethreeblue 96 robots increases success from 79.2% at the start of FERT to 98.3%. In a 16-robot experiment on the same task, removing failure-guided retrieval reduces success from 86.7% to 64.2%, supporting the contribution of targeted experience selection. System measurements further characterize local interruptions, recovery and communication overhead during fleet operation, providing operational evidence for the asynchronous collection and learning process supported by FATS.

These results show that experience generated during deployment can support further policy improvement. By pooling experience from multiple robots to update a shared policy, CEL connects individual executions to learning across the fleet. This offers a path towards improving robot reliability through collective operational experience, without requiring a corresponding expansion of expert action supervision.

2026-10-20.title: Enhancing Lunar PNT Performance Through Surface Station Enabled Radiometric Observables
2026-10-20.authors: Toshiki Tanaka , Satoshi Ikari
2026-10-20.abstract: Future lunar surface missions will require reliable and accurate positioning, particularly for autonomous rover operations. Although dedicated lunar navigation satellite systems are being developed, their vertical positioning performance can be limited by satellite availability and observation geometry, especially during early deployment phases. In this context, this study investigated a radiometric navigation architecture in which a surface station (SS) complements lunar navigation satellites by providing satellite observations for differential processing and an additional surface-to-surface ranging measurement to improve the vertical positioning performance of lunar surface users. The SS receives pseudorange and Doppler signals from the navigation satellites, which are used by the user to form double-differenced measurements that reduce clock and common-mode ephemeris errors and enable positioning of the rover relative to the SS. In addition, dual one-way ranging (DOWR) is performed between the SS and rover. The user (rover) then integrates the position solution obtained from these radiometric measurements with dead-reckoning information from a rover navigation sensor. Numerical Monte Carlo simulations were performed using five lunar navigation satellites representing NASA’s LCRNS constellation and a rover trajectory around Connecting Ridge near the lunar south pole. The results showed that introducing the SS improved both horizontal and vertical relative positioning performance, and that SS–rover ranging provided an additional improvement. In the simulated representative case, the mean 99.7% vertical positioning error was reduced from 29.9 m without the SS to 5.5 m when the SS was used for double-differenced pseudorange and Doppler processing, and further reduced to 4.8 m when SS–rover DOWR was additionally included. The simulations also showed that an uncorrected DOWR hardware bias could significantly degrade positioning performance, whereas the proposed bias-estimation process reduced the final DOWR-bias estimation error to 0.058 ± 0.057 0.058\pm 0.057 m. The results further revealed that the benefit of SS–rover ranging depended on the observation geometry. Overall, the results quantitatively demonstrated the potential of a lunar SS to play an additional role beyond communication, differential corrections, and satellite orbit determination: directly improving the vertical relative positioning of lunar surface users through an additional radiometric ranging measurement.
2026-10-20.introduction:
As lunar exploration enters a new phase of sustained and increasingly
complex surface activities, the demand for reliable navigation
capabilities on the lunar surface is rapidly growing. In particular,
autonomous navigation has been identified as an important capability
for future lunar surface missions [ 1 ] .

Several international efforts are currently developing dedicated
lunar communication and navigation infrastructures, including NASA’s
Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems (LCRNS), ESA’s
Moonlight programme, and JAXA’s Lunar Navigation Satellite System
(LNSS), with the broader goal of providing interoperable positioning,
navigation, timing, and communication (PNT+C) services around the Moon [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Such architectures are expected to
eventually provide Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-like
services to a broad range of lunar surface users. However, deployment
of a sufficiently large lunar constellation requires substantial
infrastructure investment and can take many years, while the number of
available orbiters and the resulting navigation geometry may remain
limited during the early deployment phase [ 6 ] .

As a means of improving navigation system performance, a surface
station (SS) with a known location can complement the orbital
infrastructure by providing additional navigation functions to users
on the lunar surface and in the vicinity of the Moon. In previous
studies, SS have primarily been considered for two purposes. First,
measurements obtained at known SS locations can be used to generate
differential corrections and mitigate common ranging error sources [ 1 , 7 , 8 , 6 ] . Second, SS-originated ranging
can support orbit determination of lunar navigation satellites [ 7 , 9 ] .

The potential role of SS, however, is not limited to these
applications. This study investigates a third use of SS: providing
additional ranging signals to improve user positioning accuracy,
particularly in the vertical direction (the local Up direction in the
topocentric coordinate frame).

Current lunar navigation satellite constellation designs primarily
focus on horizontal user positioning performance, while explicit
requirements for vertical positioning accuracy have not been clearly
established [ 10 , 4 ] . Therefore,
ranging signals from these lunar navigation satellites could result
in relatively weak observability in the vertical direction. To this
end, a SS-originated ranging measurement provides a different
line-of-sight geometry, improving measurement diversity and thereby
the vertical positioning accuracy of the rover.

The use of surface-to-surface ranging for positioning is not new.
Terrestrial applications of surface-to-surface ranging have been
extensively investigated using technologies including ultra-wideband
(UWB), for purposes such as cooperative positioning [ 11 ] . Similar concepts have also been investigated
for lunar surface navigation [ 12 , 13 ] , including the CADRE flight
mission [ 14 ] . However, previous lunar studies
have mainly focused on horizontal positioning or general relative
localization. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first
study to specifically evaluate the vertical positioning benefit of
SS-originated ranging for lunar surface users.

Alternatively, the vertical position can be constrained using a lunar
digital elevation model (DEM). A lunar DEM represents the lunar surface
topography and provides terrain elevation information. Existing lunar
DEMs are constructed from satellite remote-sensing observations rather
than in-situ measurements on the lunar surface. Using such DEM
information, DEM-based altitude constraints have previously been
incorporated into lunar rover navigation and positioning algorithms [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] .

In these methods, the achievable vertical positioning accuracy depends directly on the accuracy of the lunar DEM. For example, SLDEM2015, which covers latitudes within ± 60 ∘ \pm 60^{\circ} , has a typical vertical accuracy of approximately 3–4 m [ 18 ] . Higher-resolution and more accurate DEMs have been developed for selected regions, particularly near the lunar poles, such as NASA PGDA’s High-Resolution LOLA Topography for Lunar South Pole Sites product [ 19 ] , while Bertone et al. [ 20 ] showed that the effective resolution of LOLA-based polar DEMs varies with observation density, leaving some terrain features unresolved between LOLA tracks. However, such high-resolution and high-accuracy DEMs are available only for selected regions of the lunar surface. Furthermore, existing lunar DEM accuracy assessments have primarily relied on internal consistency or cross-comparison among remotely sensed datasets, rather than direct comparison with ground-truth elevation measurements on the lunar surface. This limitation further motivates the development of a vertical positioning method that does not rely on a lunar DEM.

Therefore, this study evaluates a radiometric navigation architecture
that does not rely on a DEM-derived altitude constraint, with the goal
of achieving high vertical positioning accuracy. The proposed
architecture consists of lunar navigation satellites, a SS, and a
surface user. The SS receives radiometric signals from the
navigation satellites and uses these measurements to generate
differential corrections for the user. In addition, the SS provides a
direct radiometric measurement to the user through dual one-way ranging
(DOWR). The user (rover) then combines the satellite-based measurements, the
differential information provided by the SS, the SS–rover DOWR
measurement, and its navigation-sensor measurements through filter-based
estimation.

Based on this architecture, this study investigates the error sources
inherent in the proposed navigation scheme, develops methods to mitigate
or estimate these errors, and evaluates the resulting benefits and
limitations of the architecture through numerical simulations.
The simulations used five lunar navigation satellites based on the
latest available LCRNS orbital configuration [ 21 ] . The SS location and rover trajectory were defined
around Connecting Ridge, one of the candidate regions for Artemis lunar
south-pole exploration [ 22 ] .

In summary, the main contributions of this paper are as follows:

Architecture design and error mitigation strategy development: A SS-enabled navigation architecture is proposed, and key error sources
and their mitigation methods are identified and investigated.

Performance benchmarking: Numerical simulations evaluate the vertical positioning performance,
limitations, and applicability of the proposed architecture.

1. Architecture design and error mitigation strategy development: A SS-enabled navigation architecture is proposed, and key error sources
and their mitigation methods are identified and investigated.

2. Performance benchmarking: Numerical simulations evaluate the vertical positioning performance,
limitations, and applicability of the proposed architecture.

# 2 System Architecture

The proposed navigation architecture uses radiometric ranging signals
from a LCRNS satellite constellation together with signals from a SS
installed at a known location on the lunar surface. The SS–rover
ranging signal is assumed to be available only when LOS between the SS
and rover is maintained, considering possible terrain blockage. The
radiometric architecture is illustrated in Fig. 1 .

The rover is also assumed to use an inertial navigation system (INS),
and therefore the required navigation accuracy does not need to be
achieved by radiometric ranging alone. Instead, radiometric measurements
and INS measurements are integrated through sensor fusion. The two
measurement sources are complementary because they have different error
characteristics. In particular, when satellite geometry is unfavorable
and radiometric positioning performance degrades, the INS can be used
to propagate the rover state until reliable radiometric measurements
become available again. Similar integration of radiometric measurements
and onboard navigation sensors has been considered in previous lunar
rover navigation studies [ 15 , 17 ] .

The types of radiometric measurements used in the proposed architecture
are selected considering several representative challenges associated
with lunar navigation. The following issues describe these challenges
and how they are addressed in the proposed architecture.

Issue 1: Integration of Pseudorange and Doppler Measurements

Current lunar navigation satellite systems are designed to provide
pseudorange measurements as a primary ranging observable for user
positioning. In addition to pseudorange measurements, Doppler
measurements from the lunar navigation satellites are assumed to be
available at both the SS and rover in this study. Doppler provides
independent range-rate information and therefore increases the available
measurement information.

Issue 2: Satellite clock, satellite ephemeris, and lunar ephemeris errors

Satellite clock and ephemeris errors are important error sources in
satellite-based navigation. In terrestrial GNSS, these parameters can
be estimated and updated with high accuracy using frequent observations
from a large network of ground stations. For lunar navigation systems,
however, the long Earth–Moon distance and the limited number of ground
stations available for lunar missions may result in larger uncertainties
in these parameters. The proposed architecture therefore assumes that
satellite clock and ephemeris errors cannot always be neglected.

To reduce their impact, the proposed architecture uses double difference
(DD) measurements between the SS and rover. DD is an established
differential positioning technique that combines measurements from two
receivers and two satellites to eliminate satellite and receiver clock
errors and mitigate common-mode components of satellite ephemeris
errors, enabling accurate positioning of the rover relative to the SS [ 23 ] . The effectiveness of differential positioning
in reducing common-mode errors depends on the SS–rover baseline and
measurement geometry. In general, stronger common-mode error cancellation
can be expected when the two receivers are sufficiently close relative
to the satellite range. In this study, the SS–rover baseline ranged
up to approximately 6 km.

In addition, other common errors associated with the lunar reference
frame and ephemerides can also be reduced by relative positioning.

Issue 3: SS clock error and time transfer

The clock error of the SS is another potential error source. If a
conventional one-way pseudorange measurement is used between the SS and
rover, the relative clock offset directly appears in the ranging
measurement. To reduce this dependency, DOWR is used for the SS–rover
link. By combining one-way measurements in both directions, DOWR
removes the dominant relative clock offset between the SS and rover [ 23 ] . A similar approach is two-way ranging, which
also does not require precise clock synchronization between the SS and
rover and could alternatively be adopted in place of DOWR.

Issue 4: DOWR hardware bias

Although DOWR reduces the effect of the relative clock offset between
the SS and rover, the measurement can contain hardware-dependent biases
caused by signal delays in the transmitting and receiving hardware [ 23 ] . Internal loopback measurements can determine
the combined transmit (TX) and receive (RX) delays at each node, but
cannot separately determine the individual TX and RX delays. Therefore,
a residual bias can remain in the DOWR measurement.

In this study, the residual DOWR hardware bias is estimated and removed
through filtering. The observability and convergence of the DOWR bias
estimation depend on the available measurement geometry and rover motion
and were therefore evaluated through numerical simulations.

Issue 5: SS position error

An error in the assumed SS position affects absolute rover positioning.
In the proposed architecture, however, the rover position is estimated
relative to the SS, and therefore the absolute SS position error does
not directly affect the SS-relative rover position.

2026-10-20.title: SWAP: Test-Time Steerable Humanoid Whole-Body Collision Avoidance
2026-10-20.authors: Zeji Yi , Guanqi He , Xiaofeng Guo , Guannan Qu , Pieter Abbeel , Yan Duan , Karen Liu , Guanya Shi
2026-10-20.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in human-centric environments must coordinate the entire body to traverse tight, cluttered spaces while maintaining balance. Existing methods often struggle to jointly consider dynamic stability and collision avoidance from high-dimensional perceptual inputs. Moreover, for humanoids, safe behavior is inherently multimodal: the same obstacle may admit multiple valid traversals, which is difficult to represent with a single deterministic policy. To address these challenges, we propose SWAP ( Steerable Whole-body Avoidance Policy ), a hierarchical framework that separates collision-aware decision making from stabilization. A high-level, perception-conditioned diffusion policy generates multimodal, collision-aware motion proposals, while a low-level whole-body RL controller tracks these proposals and maintains dynamic balance. To efficiently train the high-level policy, we obtain scalable supervision via hindsight labeling: we roll out the low-level policy under randomized commands, place obstacles only in the space that each executed motion did not sweep, so the motion is collision-free by construction, and re-render the perception the robot would have seen. At deployment, Monte Carlo sampling with simple cost signals steers the diffusion model toward safe, task-aligned behaviors without heavy reward tuning.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Humanoid robots possess the kinematic flexibility to navigate cluttered, human-centric environments in ways that simpler platforms cannot: ducking under obstacles, twisting through narrow gaps, and sidestepping around barriers while maintaining balance. Exploiting this flexibility requires whole-body coordination —orchestrating not just footsteps, but whole-body posture in concert ( Radosavovic et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ) . This capability represents both the defining advantage of the humanoid form factor and its central control challenge.

Yet, achieving reliable whole-body obstacle avoidance remains fundamentally difficult precisely because of the high degree-of-freedom, inherently unstable nature of humanoid robots. A successful policy must simultaneously satisfy dynamic feasibility, control stability, and collision avoidance—a combination that existing methods struggle to achieve. Reinforcement learning struggles with the multimodality of avoidance: many valid traversals exist, but reward-driven optimization collapses to a narrow mode. Shaped, multi-term objectives introduce spurious local minima and reward-sensitive behavior as shown in both humanoid and other legged robots ( Wang et al., 2025b ; He et al., 2024 ) . Model-based planners face analogous issues—whole-body planning with hand-crafted costs is nonconvex and initialization-sensitive, often yielding stiff, conservative motions that underutilize the humanoid’s flexibility ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Zucker et al., 2013 ) . Behavior cloning can learn natural motions from demonstrations but requires large-scale data; teleoperation on humanoids is difficult and does not scale. In manipulation, imitation-based generative policies can represent multimodal manipulation while achieving collision avoidance, but still depend on demonstration coverage ( Li et al., 2025 ; Jung et al., 2025 ; Ze et al., 2024 ; Chi et al., 2023 ) .
Moreover, policies trained under any of these paradigms cannot easily adapt to changing objectives
at deployment—any shift in user preference (e.g., prioritizing certain gestures) typically demands retraining.

In this work, we propose SWAP ( Steerable Whole-body Avoidance Policy ), a hierarchical framework that decouples high-level collision-aware decision making from low-level locomotion control. This separation is key to resolving the stability and collision avoidance dilemma that plagues joint optimization: the low-level RL controller focuses solely on stable trajectory tracking, while the high-level planner handles collision-aware motion generation. For the high-level policy, inspired by diffusion-based whole-body motion synthesis ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2025 ) ,
we adopt a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) conditioned on LiDAR observations and trained on trajectories derived from the LAFAN1 human motion dataset ( Harvey et al., 2020 ) . This motion prior helps the planner preserve diverse, human-like whole-body behavior.

To obtain collision labels without teleoperation, we use a hindsight labeling ( Andrychowicz et al., 2017 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) pipeline in simulation. We roll out the low-level controller under randomized commands, then run geometric collision checking along the executed motion by testing the robot’s swept volume against the environment, producing collision-free labels for each trajectory. This yields scalable collision-aware supervision while avoiding reward shaping: collision enters only as a label on motion-prior trajectories, which helps retain multimodality and naturalness while learning to avoid obstacles. This self-supervised pipeline provides a more scalable way of collecting data and bypasses the need for teleoperation. At deployment, we further steer the diffusion sampling process using Monte Carlo sampling with lightweight cost signals.
Together, these components transform avoidance from a fixed reactive mapping into a flexible, steerable generative task, enabling zero-shot adaptation to new objectives without retraining.

The key capability of SWAP is not any single motion primitive, such as ducking or sidestepping, but the ability to produce collision-aware whole-body proposals that remain steerable at deployment . A user can plug in analytical objectives such as speed, heading, height, or posture, or use a learned collision-aware Q-function, and the same trained diffusion prior can adapt by selecting among its sampled trajectory modes. This distinguishes SWAP from approaches that require a new reward, curriculum, or demonstration set whenever the deployment objective changes.

Our main contributions are three-fold:

A hierarchical framework combining a perception-conditioned DiT with an RL-based controller for whole-body obstacle avoidance, validated on the Unitree G1 in simulation and real-world deployment.

A hindsight labeling pipeline that uses synthetic environments to generate collision-aware supervision for the high-level diffusion policy at scale, without teleoperation.

A lightweight test-time steering mechanism that adapts to new objectives without retraining, improving targeted metrics by 34% on average.

We validate SWAP extensively in simulation and on a Unitree G1 humanoid equipped with LiDAR sensors in the real world. Our experiments demonstrate reliable avoidance of both static and dynamic obstacles, with the robot exhibiting diverse whole-body maneuvers including ducking, sidestepping, and twisting. Together, these results establish a practical framework for humanoid whole-body collision avoidance that integrates naturally with downstream navigation stacks.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Learning-Based Humanoid Locomotion

Humanoid locomotion has seen significant progress through reinforcement learning (RL), moving from basic bipedal balance ( Radosavovic et al., 2024 ) to perceptive locomotion in rough terrains ( Zhuang et al., 2024 ) .
Recent hierarchical approaches, such as HWC-Loco ( Lin et al., 2025 ) , decompose the problem into high-level planning and low-level control to achieve robust gait. Similarly, HumanPlus ( Fu et al., 2024 ) demonstrates the effectiveness of shadowing and imitation learning for whole-body coordination.
Generative motion priors, such as NaturalGMP ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) , further enhance motion naturalness without hand-crafted style rewards. While these research efforts provide a solid foundation for mobility, the integration of these motor skills into active collision avoidance in complex, cluttered environments remains a central challenge.

## 2.2 Diffusion Models for Motion Planning

Diffusion models have emerged as powerful generative priors for robot policy learning. In manipulation, diffusion policies have shown strong performance ( Chi et al., 2023 ; Ze et al., 2024 ) , including on humanoid robots ( Ze et al., 2025 ) . For navigation, NavDP ( Cai et al., 2026 ) combines a diffusion policy with privileged information guidance and a safety critic, achieving successful sim-to-real navigation transfer.

For humanoid control specifically, recent works leverage diffusion as a motion prior.
DreamControl ( Kalaria et al., 2026 ) uses a diffusion prior over human motions to help an RL policy solve long-horizon humanoid tasks. Most relevant to our work, BeyondMimic ( Liao et al., 2025 ) demonstrates that guided diffusion can achieve zero-shot task adaptation, including obstacle avoidance, by applying cost-guided sampling to a diffusion controller. While these frameworks excel at generating feasible behaviors, steering them toward task-specific safety in cluttered environments often requires expert data or costly online optimization; this motivates our hindsight collision labeling as an efficient supervision signal for systematic whole-body obstacle avoidance.

## 2.3 Safe Navigation for Legged Robots

Ensuring safety in humanoid navigation remains challenging, as it requires satisfying dynamic feasibility, control stability, and collision avoidance simultaneously. Control barrier functions (CBFs) ( Ames et al., 2019 ) provide formal safety guarantees but can be conservative. Wang et al. (2025b) formulate humanoid locomotion as a constrained MDP with CBF costs, achieving safe and comfortable walking in crowds with the perception module of Omni-Perception ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . However, such constraint-based approaches often require careful tuning and may not generalize across diverse environments.

To address these limitations, reactive approaches like HumanoidPF ( Xue et al., 2026 ) encode humanoid-obstacle relationships into an artificial potential field to guide RL policies. While effective for narrow passage traversal, such methods typically rely on explicit geometric mappings and require intensive reward engineering to balance stability with safety. Other learning-based approaches to safety include training with collision penalties, using safety critics as seen in NavDP ( Cai et al., 2026 ) , or employing curriculum learning. For example, Kim et al. (2024) propose ARMOR, which uses an inverse hindsight strategy by synthetically placing obstacles around known collision-free human motions to guarantee safe demonstrations.

In contrast, our approach introduces a physically grounded hindsight labeling strategy derived from the robot’s own swept volume. This enables the policy to internalize diverse, multimodal avoidance maneuvers consistent with its kinematic limits, eliminating the need for manual reward shaping or external expert demonstrations.

Positioning. Prior systems provide important pieces of the humanoid avoidance stack, but none combines whole-body obstacle avoidance with plug-and-play test-time objectives. Motion-imitation and generative locomotion methods provide natural behavior priors but do not directly solve perception-conditioned collision avoidance. ARMOR ( Kim et al., 2024 ) and HumanoidPF ( Xue et al., 2026 ) target perception-driven avoidance, but their deployment behavior is tied to the trained objective or hand-designed potential field. Model-based planners such as SPARK ( Sun et al., 2025 ) can optimize explicit costs, but scaling them to real-time whole-body humanoid motion with learned perception remains difficult. SWAP instead learns a multimodal diffusion prior over feasible whole-body commands and adapts online by scoring sampled trajectories, preserving the hierarchy while avoiding task-specific retraining.

2026-10-20.title: Validation of Human Motor Development Scales with Humanoid Robots
2026-10-20.authors: Fanxing Meng , Jing Xiao
2026-10-20.comment: . Submitted to ICRA 2027. Video available at this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract: We investigate how humanoid robots can learn a series of motor skills defined by human infant motor development scales, and we evaluate which scales are comprehensive enough to serve as self-contained guides for developing gross motor skills up to standing and walking. We represent each motor development scale as a developmental graph that guides the training of a humanoid robot. We then apply this graph within a reinforcement learning framework so that the robot learns skills following the natural phases of human motor development described by the scale. Our work demonstrates that graphs derived from three out of four popular pediatric motor scales can successfully guide humanoid robots to develop these skills. The fourth scale misses some intermediate milestones that the other scales have, which causes some failures. After adding a missing milestone in its graph, it also enables the robot to develop those skills successfully. Video available at https://youtu.be/SR3LUVhohV4 .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Human infants acquire motor skills in a predictable order: rolling precedes sitting, kneeling precedes crawling, and standing precedes walking. Developmental scientists have captured this progression in standardized motor scales that list milestones and the typical order in which they appear. These scales are used clinically to detect delays in infant development, but they also reflect something deeper: a structured curriculum in which simpler skills provide the physical and coordinative prerequisites for more complex ones.

For humanoid robots, standing up and walking from an arbitrary fallen state remains difficult. Most learning-based approaches either imitate reference trajectories, which must be captured, cleaned, and retargeted for each skill, or require carefully designed reward functions and regularization terms with hand-tuned coefficients. An alternative is to utilize the curriculum that developmental science has already discovered. Our hypothesis is that if a developmental scale correctly orders human motor learning, it should also guide humanoid robot motor learning, provided the robot’s body is sufficiently human-like.

This paper tests that hypothesis. We take four widely used pediatric scales: the Alberta Infant Motor Scale (AIMS) [ 1 ] , the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development (BSID) [ 2 ] , the Gross Motor Function Measure (GMFM) [ 3 ] , and the Peabody Developmental Motor Scales (PDMS) [ 4 ] . We translate each into a developmental graph that directly encodes the milestone sequence and prerequisite structure described in the scale.

We evaluate the four graphs on a simulated 21-DoF humanoid robot in Isaac Lab [ 5 ] . Three of the four scales produce a consistent developmental progression from supine lying to standing and walking under all four tested training settings. The fourth, PDMS, fails under certain training settings, and notably, it does not include the kneeling-to-standing progression that the other scales use as a bridge to an upright posture. These results validate the idea that human developmental scales can serve as self-contained, science-based curricula for humanoid skill acquisition, and they highlight which milestone sequences matter for standing and walking.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Developmental Scales

AIMS is a norm-referenced observational assessment of infant gross motor development from birth to independent walking [ 1 ] . It evaluates four positions: supine, prone, sitting, and standing, as well as the transitions between them. AIMS is designed to detect motor delay by comparing an infant’s observed skills to age norms.

BSID is a broad assessment of cognitive, language, and motor development in young children [ 2 ] . The motor scale includes items from prone control and sitting through crawling, standing, and walking. BSID’s progression is similar to that of AIMS but with fewer intermediate milestones, making it a test of whether a sparser developmental graph can still guide a robot to walking.

GMFM was developed to evaluate changes in gross motor function in children with cerebral palsy [ 3 ] . It organizes skills into five dimensions: lying and rolling, sitting, crawling and kneeling, standing, and walking/running/jumping. Because GMFM was built to track functional improvement, its milestones are explicitly ordered by difficulty and prerequisite. This makes it particularly natural to translate into a robot curriculum.

PDMS assesses gross and fine motor skills in children from birth to five years [ 4 ] . Its gross-motor subtest includes reflexes, stationary skills, locomotion, and object manipulation. Unlike AIMS, BSID, and GMFM, the PDMS gross-motor pathway contains only one upright transition (sitting to standing) without the intermediate half-kneeling or high-kneeling milestones that appear in the other scales.

## II-B Developmental Robotics

Developmental robotics uses robots to model cognitive and motor development [ 6 ] . The field focuses on autonomous, open-ended learning [ 7 ] . It draws on principles such as embodiment (how the body shapes learning) [ 8 ] , intrinsic motivation [ 9 ] , and the shift from egocentric (self-centered) to object-centric views [ 10 ] . A key concept is Piaget’s theory of developmental stages, in which new abilities are built on mastered ones [ 11 ] . This implies that the sequence of learning is just as important as the skills themselves. While studies have applied these principles to simpler robots, it remains difficult to create a framework that lets a complex humanoid robot progress through a full trajectory from helplessness to functional behavior.

## II-C Curriculum Learning

Curriculum learning structures training from easy to hard to improve efficiency [ 12 ] . In robotics, this takes various forms. Some methods hide difficult goals initially [ 13 ] or generate intermediate goals [ 14 ] . Others break the learning process into stages [ 15 ] or sequence discrete subtasks [ 16 , 17 ] . A third category changes the environment, such as starting the agent in states progressively farther from the goal [ 18 , 19 ] or slowly increasing terrain difficulty [ 20 ] . The main goal of these techniques is usually to speed up convergence for a specific, single task.

2026-10-20.title: ReDOA: Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment for Image-Based Manipulation Policy Learning
2026-10-20.authors: Kotaro Kajitsuka , Masaki Murooka , Fumio Kanehiro
2026-10-20.abstract:
Data-driven learning for general-purpose robotic manipulation presents a fundamental trade-off between data-collection cost and adaptability to real-world environments.
Imitation learning (IL) requires costly human demonstrations, whereas simulation-based learning is vulnerable to sim-to-real gaps in dynamics and sensor observations.
We propose ReDOA (Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment), a framework that decouples control learning from perception learning to learn image-based policies in the real world.
A state-based teacher policy trained in simulation is executed on a real robot, and its control knowledge is distilled into an image-based student policy using the collected trajectories.
Observation Alignment resolves observation mismatches between data collection and deployment.
This framework collects successful, efficiently executed trajectories paired with real-world visual observations, without requiring demonstrations from human experts.
In real-robot experiments on three non-prehensile manipulation tasks, including bimanual manipulation, our method achieves better overall performance when jointly considering task success and execution efficiency than both IL based on human demonstrations and policy distillation in simulation.
https://isri-aist.github.io/redoa-project-page/
2026-10-20.introduction:
Although demand for automating manipulation tasks in unstructured environments, such as homes and industrial workplaces, continues to grow, successful real-world deployments remain limited.
Data-driven learning has therefore attracted considerable attention as a promising solution.
However, learning both robust control under complex dynamics and reliable perception across diverse real-world environments remains challenging while keeping the costs of collecting demonstrations and setting up environments low.

Existing data-driven approaches face an inherent difficulty in balancing data collection cost and real-world adaptability.
Imitation learning (IL) based on human demonstrations can naturally adapt to real-world visual observations and contact dynamics, but teaching complex dual-arm manipulation through teleoperation requires operator skill and teleoperation interface setup.
Moreover, because vision-based IL is sensitive even to minor appearance variations such as lighting or background shifts, adapting to new environments requires collecting demonstrations again, repeatedly imposing substantial labor and time on human demonstrators.
In contrast, simulation-based methods (sim-to-real approaches) enable training on large datasets at low cost, but gaps in dynamics and sensor observations tend to degrade real-world performance.

However, recent work has shown that separating control learning in simulation from perception learning in the real world can bypass the sim-to-real gap in observations.
For example, PTLD [ 1 ] uses real-world policy distillation to bypass the sim-to-real gap of tactile sensors.

We propose ReDOA (Real-World Distillation via Observation Alignment), which applies distillation across observation spaces in the real world to image-based manipulation policy learning.
Figure 1 illustrates the concept of our method.
The pipeline proceeds as follows.
First, we roll out the teacher policy while estimating the object state using temporarily installed trackers, collecting demonstrations for distillation.
The trackers appear in the collected images; using these images directly to train the student policy creates an observation mismatch when the trackers are removed at deployment.
We therefore perform Observation Alignment to resolve this mismatch and train the student policy using the aligned observations and collected actions.
These stages form a sim-to-real-to-real pipeline.

The framework reduces the burden of human demonstration and bypasses the visual sim-to-real gap by learning perception from images collected in the real world.

We evaluate the proposed method on three non-prehensile manipulation tasks using a real robot.
Non-prehensile manipulation requires continuous visual perception to maintain precise robot–object–environment contact, making it a suitable benchmark.

Prior sim-to-real studies have attempted to limit the performance degradation of vision-based policies by using visual domain randomization [ 2 ] , green-screening, or texture projection [ 3 ] .
However, these methods suffer from training instability caused by randomization [ 4 ] and require substantial effort to set up the environment.
Our method uses images collected in the real environment to train the student policy, eliminating the need to render its training images in simulation.
Observation Alignment then mitigates the appearance mismatch caused by trackers introduced for real-world data collection.

Unlike conventional IL based on human demonstrations, our method collects data using a consistent policy without relying on human experts or being affected by human fatigue or individual operating habits.
Because the state-based teacher does not depend on visual appearance, it can also autonomously collect new real-world demonstrations without retraining when lighting or backgrounds change.

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

A real-world distillation framework for bypassing the visual sim-to-real gap through Observation Alignment that resolves observation mismatches between demonstration collection and deployment.

Automated generation of high-quality demonstration data without expert teleoperation, reducing human labor costs.

Real-world validation on three non-prehensile tasks, demonstrating the simultaneous achievement of high success rates and high motion efficiency.

1. A real-world distillation framework for bypassing the visual sim-to-real gap through Observation Alignment that resolves observation mismatches between demonstration collection and deployment.

2. Automated generation of high-quality demonstration data without expert teleoperation, reducing human labor costs.

3. Real-world validation on three non-prehensile tasks, demonstrating the simultaneous achievement of high success rates and high motion efficiency.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Challenges in IL and Demonstration Data Collection

Recent advances in IL, including ACT [ 5 ] and Diffusion Policy [ 6 ] , have led to significant success in approaches that generate robot actions directly from visual observations.
However, the performance of these data-driven methods depends strongly on the quality and quantity of demonstration data collected from human experts [ 7 , 8 ] .

In particular, the non-prehensile manipulation tasks considered in this study require controlling continuous contact dynamics among the object, the environment, and the robot [ 9 ] .
Prior work has proposed RL-based approaches focused primarily on control, including maintaining contact modes during whole-arm manipulation [ 10 ] , integrating tactile sensors into the end effectors of a dual-arm robot [ 11 ] , and combining optimization-based demonstration generation with RL [ 12 ] .
These studies show that non-prehensile manipulation requires continuous state observation and sequential action correction to handle delicate physical interactions.
Consequently, collecting a large-scale, high-quality, and consistent real-world dataset for IL through teleoperation is costly.

To address the cost of collecting human demonstrations, RLDG uses reinforcement learning directly on real robots to collect demonstrations containing real-world RGB images and fine-tunes a generalist model on these data [ 13 ] .
By autonomously generating high-quality trajectories through reward maximization, this approach has been shown to outperform fine-tuning on human demonstrations.

In contrast, this study focuses on training task-specific image-based policies from scratch.

## II-B Policy Distillation across Observation Spaces

Deploying a state-based policy in the real world requires continuously providing the policy with task-relevant state information, such as object poses.
Such state information can be obtained using planar fiducial markers attached to objects [ 14 ] or marker-based motion capture [ 15 ] .
However, in settings where many objects of the same type are handled in sequence, attaching markers to each object in advance is impractical.

Image-based policies avoid explicit object-state measurement [ 16 , 17 ] .
However, end-to-end policy learning from high-dimensional visual observations requires learning of visual representations and control simultaneously, which tends to reduce sample efficiency and training stability.
In addition, repeatedly rendering visual observations in simulation also increases computational resource requirements and training time.

Policy distillation across observation spaces is used to address these sample-efficiency and computational-cost issues.
A teacher policy is first trained in simulation using privileged observations, and its control knowledge is then distilled, also in simulation, into a student policy that uses observations available at deployment, such as RGB images [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] , depth images [ 21 ] , or point clouds [ 22 , 23 ] .

PTLD [ 1 ] also performs policy distillation in the real world.
It bypasses the sim-to-real gap of tactile sensors by using real-world data to learn to estimate latent representations based on privileged information from tactile and proprioceptive observations.

Our method likewise performs distillation in the real world, using Observation Alignment to resolve the image-observation mismatch caused by the presence of trackers during data collection and their absence at deployment, thereby enabling real-world distillation into an image-based policy.

## II-C Visual Sim-to-Real Gap

In sim-to-real transfer, the visual gap associated with RGB images is a serious problem and degrades real-robot deployment performance [ 24 , 25 ] .
Real-to-sim-to-real methods such as Re 3 Sim [ 26 ] reduce the visual sim-to-real gap by reconstructing real-world 3D geometry and appearance in photorealistic simulation environments.
Whereas their training data are generated entirely in simulation, our method executes the teacher policy on a real robot to generate demonstrations that directly reflect real-world visual observations and contact dynamics.
Moreover, Re 3 Sim considers only rigid objects, and its applicability to articulated-object manipulation, as studied here, remains unverified.

By training the student policy using real-world images, our method eliminates the need to transfer from simulated images to real images.
Observation Alignment further mitigates the observation mismatch caused by tracker artifacts in the real data.

2026-10-20.title: ScaleNav: Scalable Internet Video Pretraining for Language-Conditioned Local Navigation
2026-10-20.authors: Yihui Yang , Yuanhong Yu , Jiawei Wang , Zhongrui Yu , Jia Shi , Kun Zhan , Ruizhen Hu , Xiaowei Zhou , Yu Liu , Sida Peng
2026-10-20.abstract: We study language-conditioned local navigation, where a robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial observation and stop at the described location. End-to-end navigation policies require diverse training data to generalize across scenes, yet real-robot data is costly to collect and simulated data leaves a sim-to-real gap. Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of real-world navigation experience. Our key insight is to learn goal-directed visual dynamics from Internet egocentric videos, and use these dynamics to support robot action generation. To this end, we propose ScaleNav, a unified world-action framework with three-stage training. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on these videos to learn how observations evolve as the camera approaches instructed targets across diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks. Joint fine-tuning subsequently optimizes all trainable components together for navigation. ScaleNav achieves success rates of 86.5% on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on our HabitatGS-LN benchmark, outperforming the evaluated baselines on both benchmarks. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot, with results supporting the model’s ability to generalize to real-world navigation. Code and videos are available at https://zju3dv.github.io/ScaleNav/ .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Navigating to visible targets according to natural-language instructions is an important capability for robots. For example, a person may ask a robot to walk to the desk by the window and stop there. Similar instructions also arise in long-horizon systems, where a high-level planner, such as an agent based on a large language model (LLM), decomposes a task into a sequence of short-range goals involving visible objects or regions ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Rajvanshi et al., 2024 ; Ding et al., 2025 ) . We study this language-conditioned local navigation setting: the robot must navigate to a text-specified target visible in its initial field of view and stop at the described location.

One possible solution is to connect a grounding module to an existing navigation method ( Shah et al., 2023a ; Huang et al., 2023 ; Cai et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Long et al., 2025 ; Cerdio et al., 2026 ) , but errors in target grounding and spatial-goal conversion can lead to navigation errors. End-to-end policies provide an alternative by mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to actions ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Hirose et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . To generalize across real-world scenes, these policies require diverse training data ( Shah et al., 2023b ; Shah et al., 2023c ; Sridhar et al., 2024 ) . However, real-robot action data is costly to collect across diverse environments ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Cai et al., 2025 ) , whereas simulated action data still leaves a sim-to-real gap ( Cai et al., 2025 ; Xia et al., 2026 ) .

Internet egocentric videos offer a scalable source of visual experience covering diverse real-world scenes and human navigation behavior. However, they lack corresponding robot action labels. Some methods attempt to leverage these videos by extracting intermediate motion-related supervision, such as estimated trajectories and geometric targets ( Cheng et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Hirose et al., 2025 ; Seneviratne et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) , or latent actions inferred from visual transitions ( Bu et al., 2025 ) . Errors or biases introduced during this extraction can propagate through the resulting supervision into subsequent policy learning.

To effectively learn navigation priors from these videos and translate them into executable actions, we propose ScaleNav, a framework for language-conditioned local navigation that combines a unified world-action model (WAM) with a three-stage training procedure. As illustrated in Figure 2 , the model uses a shared Diffusion Transformer (DiT) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) to jointly predict future observations and action chunks. We first perform instruction-conditioned video pretraining on Internet egocentric videos to learn navigation priors from human navigation behavior in diverse real-world scenes. Action alignment then uses action-labeled simulated data to train the model to predict executable action chunks while keeping part of the model frozen. Finally, joint fine-tuning optimizes all trainable components together for video and action prediction in navigation. During navigation, the model predicts an action chunk from the instruction and visual observations, executes actions from the chunk, and repeats this process with updated observations until it reaches the target and stops.

For evaluation, we construct HabitatGS-LN, a benchmark for navigation to specific objects described in natural-language instructions. We also evaluate ScaleNav on a single-view adaptation of Short-Horizon OVON ( Gong et al., 2026 ) . ScaleNav achieves success rates (SR) of 86.5% on Short-Horizon OVON and 94.9% on HabitatGS-LN, outperforming the compared methods on both benchmarks. With identical action-labeled simulated data, incorporating Internet egocentric videos improves success by 5.3 and 4.5 percentage points on the two benchmarks, respectively. We further deploy and evaluate ScaleNav on a real quadruped robot in three indoor environments. ScaleNav achieves 83.3% overall SR and outperforms the evaluated baselines in all three environments.

Our contributions are as follows:

We propose ScaleNav, a framework for language-conditioned local navigation that transfers navigation priors learned from diverse Internet egocentric videos through video pretraining into executable action chunks via action alignment.

Experiments show that ScaleNav outperforms the compared methods in both navigation success rate and path efficiency on the two simulation benchmarks. Real-robot experiments further support ScaleNav’s ability to generalize to real-world navigation.

1. We propose ScaleNav, a framework for language-conditioned local navigation that transfers navigation priors learned from diverse Internet egocentric videos through video pretraining into executable action chunks via action alignment.

2. Experiments show that ScaleNav outperforms the compared methods in both navigation success rate and path efficiency on the two simulation benchmarks. Real-robot experiments further support ScaleNav’s ability to generalize to real-world navigation.

# 2 Related Work

Language-conditioned navigation connects language understanding with visual perception, planning, and action generation.
Modular approaches combine pretrained foundation models with explicit maps, candidate waypoints, or planning components ( Shah et al., 2023a ; Huang et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Long et al., 2025 ; Cerdio et al., 2026 ) .
Learned vision-language-action policies adapt pretrained vision-language backbones to predict navigation actions from instructions and visual observations ( Zhang et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Wei et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Zhu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) .
Within this direction, dual-system architectures connect high-level semantic reasoning to low-level action generation ( Wei et al., 2026 ; Gong et al., 2026 ) .
Within language-conditioned navigation, local navigation focuses on reaching a language-specified destination without a prescribed route.
Methods for this setting learn language-conditioned goal-reaching policies ( Hirose et al., 2025 ; Glossop et al., 2026 ; Mei et al., 2026 ) or address local target grounding under occlusion ( Gao et al., 2026 ) .
We focus on this local navigation setting.

Using video prediction for robot control requires linking visual predictions to executable actions ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) .
One approach generates visual plans and recovers actions through inverse dynamics or geometric estimation ( Du et al., 2023 ; Ko et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ) .
Related approaches condition their action decoders on predictive visual features or latents ( Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) .
Another line of work jointly models future observations and actions within a unified architecture ( Guo et al., 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ; Cen et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Dong et al., 2026 ; Azuma et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) .
Following DreamZero, we adopt this joint video-action architecture for navigation.

Prior work in robot manipulation learns from action-free human videos through video pretraining ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Cheang et al., 2024 ) or video-only cross-embodiment transfer ( Ye et al., 2026 ) .
In navigation, existing approaches leverage these videos mainly in two ways.
One line of work uses Internet videos to train navigation policies through intermediate motion-related supervision or latent-action representations.
Geometry-based methods derive trajectory or geometric prediction targets from estimated camera motion or reconstructed scenes ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ; Mei et al., 2026 ; Han et al., 2025 ; Seneviratne et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) .
Other methods obtain action annotations or teacher supervision from learned models ( Lin et al., 2023 ; Hirose et al., 2025 ) .
Related video-based methods infer latent actions from visual transitions for policy pretraining ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Bu et al., 2025 ) .
Errors or biases in these derived targets and representations can propagate into subsequent policy learning.

Another line of work uses Internet videos to learn world models for navigation planning.
NWM learns a navigation world model from unlabeled videos without proxy motion targets ( Bar et al., 2025 ) . Garrido et al. (2026) learn a latent-action world model from Internet videos and adapt it to navigation by mapping robot actions to latent actions.
These models evaluate candidate trajectories determined by a separate search procedure or policy.
Better predictions therefore do not necessarily yield better navigation decisions when suitable candidates are missing.
Our framework learns navigation priors from Internet egocentric videos and directly predicts executable action chunks, without constructing proxy motion targets for these videos or relying on an external planner at inference.

2026-10-20.title: Vehicle-State-Aware Confidence Estimation for Direct Wind Sensing on a Multirotor
2026-10-20.authors: Sri Arjun Senthil Kumar , April Zi Qian Chan , Chen-Hua Yeow
2026-10-20.abstract:
Direct wind sensing from a multi-rotor UAV enables localized atmospheric measurements, but the reliability of the anemometer depends on vehicle motion. This work presents a vehicle-state-aware confidence method that uses horizontal and vertical vehicle speed to quantify the acquisition of each wind observation. The resulting confidence score is used to adapt measurement influence to a two-dimensional vector estimator. Experiments were conducted during horizontal translation, vertical motion, and held-out autonomous waypoint flight. The proposed two-feature formulation achieved an ROC–AUC of 0.995, with 98.84% of translation
observations identified as unreliable. The confidence-aware adaptation reduced median estimator gain during translation from 0.207 to 0.064 while retaining median gain of 0.151 during hover. The results show that vehicle state provides useful proprioceptive context for regulating the influence of direct airborne wind observations.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicles provide flexible platforms for localized atmospheric observation as they can hover at required locations and perform vertical hovers and traverse short trajectories in the atmospheric boundary layer [ 1 , 2 ] . Multirotor platforms are suitable for in-situ wind, sensing as a lightweight sonic anemometer can be carried to locations difficult to instrument using fixed towers [ 3 , 4 ] .

Direct airborne wind sensing introduces a coupling between environmental observation and the motion of the sensing platform, as the anemometer is exposed not only to atmospheric flow but also to changes in relative airflow associated with vehicle translation and the local aerodynamic environment generated by the propulsion system. Sensor elevation can reduce these effects but does not eliminate them [ 3 , 5 , 4 ] . Additionally, the calibration of the anemometer alone does not imply that every airborne wind observation is under favorable sensing conditions.

The vehicle motion itself provides information about the acquisition condition. Previous work has used attitude, internal measurements, motor information and learned dynamic models to estimate wind without a dedicated sensor [ 6 , 7 , 2 , 8 , 9 ] . These approaches show the relationship between wind and multirotor dynamics. However, vehicle state is primarily used for reconstructing wind fields.

This work takes the approach where rather than estimating ambient wind directly from vehicle dynamics, we use the instantaneous vehicle state to quantify vehicle conditions associated with direct onboard wind observation. Horizontal and absolute vertical speeds are compared with an empirically determined stable hover reference to obtain a continuous wind observation confidence score. The score is used to adapt the measurement covariance of a navigation-frame wind-vector estimator, reducing the influence of observations obtained during strong departure from stable sensing while preserving measurement streams.

The contributions of this work are:

A proprioceptive confidence model that uses multirotor motion state to assign sample-level confidence to direct wind observations, enabling motion-aware adaptation of measurement uncertainty in downstream state estimation without discarding observations or requiring a vehicle dynamic model.

A confidence-aware vector wind estimator that propagates
calibrated wind-speed and direction uncertainty into a
sample-dependent measurement covariance and continuously adapts
measurement influence using the vehicle-state confidence score.

Experimental validation across development, independent vertical-motion, and held-out autonomous waypoint flights, including feature ablation and estimator sensitivity analyses, demonstrates that the frozen confidence models transfer across distinct flight regimes and selectively reduce the influence of wind observation acquired under motion-disturbed sensing conditions.
