2026-10-20.title: AQUAACT: A Joystick-Level Underwater Teleoperation Dataset and Closed-Loop Benchmark
2026-10-20.authors: Zhenqi Wu , Trung Tien Dong , Aditya Penumarti , Mohamed A. Fouad , Menna A. Fouad , Mingyang Mao , Jane Jaejeong Shin , Xiaomin Lin
2026-10-20.abstract:
Underwater robots support a growing range of work, from inspecting offshore structures and
pipelines to surveying reefs and accompanying divers. Most of these tasks, however, are
still flown by hand by a pilot, which raises the question of whether they can be carried out
autonomously instead. On land,
vision-language-action (VLA) models already let robots carry out tasks autonomously from language instructions, which makes them a natural candidate for taking
the pilot’s place. Underwater, however, there is little data to
train such models. We take inspiration from how these tasks are flown today: the pilot watches the camera image
and steers with a joystick, whose commands the flight controller turns into motion. We
therefore record the pilots and introduce AquaAct , to our knowledge the first publicly
available language-annotated underwater dataset pairing camera images with human joystick
commands. It comprises 2.0 hours of real-world and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations,
both flown by human pilots, together with the vehicle’s inertial measurements. Experiments with AquaAct show that its simulated demonstrations transfer to real data and
greatly reduce the real demonstrations a policy needs. A closed-loop benchmark of seven policies in simulation, from imitation-learning baselines
to VLA models, each trained with its default recipe, shows that these tasks remain far from
solved: no policy completes more than a fifth of the episodes. Pretraining on land data gives
large VLA models no advantage over small policies trained from scratch, a gap that
land-trained models have yet to close underwater.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Underwater inspection, monitoring, and surveying are essential for
maintaining marine infrastructure and studying ocean environments:
subsea pipelines, offshore wind foundations, and aquaculture facilities
require regular inspections, while reef monitoring, shipwreck
exploration, and diver assistance demand operations in diverse and
often challenging environments [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
These environments often exceed the depth, bottom time, and risk
that human divers can safely accept [ 7 ] , so underwater
robots increasingly take over this work [ 8 ] .
However, most of these operations still rely on remotely operated
vehicles (ROVs) flown by human pilots through onboard camera feedback,
so pilot workload limits the scale and duration of these
missions [ 2 , 9 , 10 ] .

Reducing this dependence on human pilots requires autonomous systems
that interpret underwater scenes, follow high-level instructions, and
act accordingly.
Conventional underwater autonomy builds a perception–planning–control
pipeline for each task and sensor
setup [ 11 , 12 , 3 ] , which must be
adapted for every new environment or task [ 13 ] .
Vision-language-action (VLA) models offer an alternative: they learn to
predict robot actions from visual observations and language
instructions [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] and,
trained on large demonstration datasets such as
Open X-Embodiment [ 21 ] and BridgeData V2 [ 22 ] , have
shown that skills transfer across tasks and
robots [ 16 , 23 ] .

Despite these advances, underwater robotics lacks comparable
demonstration data for training general-purpose policies.
Collecting real underwater demonstrations requires deploying a vehicle
and a skilled pilot, making large-scale data acquisition costly and
difficult.
For an underwater vehicle, the natural action for such data is the
pilot’s joystick command.
It is what the pilot actually issues in response to the onboard
camera view.
It also leaves stabilization to the vehicle’s flight controller,
which holds attitude and depth in a control loop far faster than a
policy can run.
The policy then only decides where the vehicle should go, much as
VLA models on land output end-effector targets and leave joint
control to the robot’s own controllers.
Existing underwater learning datasets provide only parts of this.
The closest vehicle-level effort relies entirely on simulation,
with demonstrations generated by scripted experts and actions given
as thruster commands [ 24 ] .
Real-world imitation learning with recorded operator commands has
primarily focused on manipulation tasks in controlled pools or
tanks [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] , while underwater
navigation datasets have relied on retrospectively annotated actions
rather than the actual commands issued by human
pilots [ 28 , 29 ] .
Consequently, to our knowledge, no publicly available
language-annotated dataset provides synchronized onboard observations
and pilot-issued joystick commands for learning real-world underwater
vehicle action.

We therefore collect such data by recording the pilots themselves,
on the real vehicle and in simulation.
Recording the onboard camera view together with the pilot’s joystick
commands yields paired observations and actions directly, without
manual action labeling, and we annotate each task with a language
instruction that states its goal, such as “Scan the deck from left
to right” or “Follow the pipeline”.
Because the control chain, from the joystick through the
ground-control software to the flight-controller firmware, can be
reproduced in simulation, pilots can record further demonstrations
there, at sites a real vehicle reaches only rarely.

Building on this approach, we introduce AquaAct , comprising
2.0 hours of real-world underwater demonstrations
(Fig. 1 ) and 17.9 hours of simulated
demonstrations (Fig. 2 ), with the simulator
calibrated against real-world runs.
This combination allows us to investigate whether pretraining
on underwater demonstrations collected from our simulation pipeline
improves learning from limited real-world data.
We further evaluate how existing general-purpose robot
policies perform when learning to control underwater vehicles
through joystick commands: we train seven policies, from
imitation-learning baselines to VLA models, on the simulated part
with their default recipes and run each for 50 closed-loop episodes
in the same simulation pipeline, where a program scores the success
and completion of every episode from the ground-truth state and a
human reviewer checks each score.
Our contributions are:

Underwater Dataset: We introduce AquaAct , a language-annotated dataset
of real and simulated ROV demonstrations with synchronized
visual, inertial, and joystick data (Sec. IV ).

Underwater Dataset: We introduce AquaAct , a language-annotated dataset
of real and simulated ROV demonstrations with synchronized
visual, inertial, and joystick data (Sec. IV ).

Simulation Data Collection: We develop a real-world-calibrated, firmware-in-the-loop
simulation pipeline for collecting human demonstrations through
the same control chain as the real ROV
(Sec. III-B , III-C ).

Sim-to-Real Evaluation: We show that pretraining using data from our simulation pipeline reduces
real-world data requirements for policy learning
(Sec. V ).

Policy Benchmark: We benchmark seven policies, from imitation-learning baselines
to VLA models, in closed-loop simulation and analyze where they
fail, revealing a clear gap in transferring land-trained models
underwater (Sec. VI ).

1. Underwater Dataset: We introduce AquaAct , a language-annotated dataset
of real and simulated ROV demonstrations with synchronized
visual, inertial, and joystick data (Sec. IV ).

2. Simulation Data Collection: We develop a real-world-calibrated, firmware-in-the-loop
simulation pipeline for collecting human demonstrations through
the same control chain as the real ROV
(Sec. III-B , III-C ).

3. Sim-to-Real Evaluation: We show that pretraining using data from our simulation pipeline reduces
real-world data requirements for policy learning
(Sec. V ).

4. Policy Benchmark: We benchmark seven policies, from imitation-learning baselines
to VLA models, in closed-loop simulation and analyze where they
fail, revealing a clear gap in transferring land-trained models
underwater (Sec. VI ).

# II Related Work

## II-A Classical Underwater Autonomy

Autonomous underwater inspection has traditionally been built as a modular
perception–planning–control pipeline engineered around one task, such as ship-hull
inspection [ 11 ] , subsea cable tracking [ 30 ] ,
net-pen inspection [ 3 ] and intervention [ 12 ] . Learning has
entered these stacks mainly as better components, such as detectors or
controllers [ 31 ] . These systems are reliable within
their design envelope, but each new task or site calls for new modules and new
tuning [ 13 ] .

## II-B Learning from Demonstrations and VLA Models

Learning from demonstrations removes the need to engineer a pipeline for each task: a policy
maps observations to actions directly, and a new task calls for new data rather than new
modules. Imitation-learning policies such as action-chunking transformers (ACT) [ 32 ] and diffusion policies [ 33 ] map images and proprioception to short action
sequences and learn fine-grained skills from a modest number of demonstrations, but each is
typically trained for a narrow task family. Generality has come from data: large corpora such
as BridgeData V2 [ 22 ] and Open X-Embodiment [ 21 ] pool demonstrations across
tasks, scenes and robots, and VLA models build on them by attaching an action output to a
pretrained vision-language backbone, so that one model follows language instructions across
tasks. RT-2 [ 14 ] emits actions as tokens, OpenVLA [ 15 ] and Octo [ 16 ] are open, fine-tunable generalist policies, π 0 \pi_{0} [ 17 ] and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 18 ] add a flow-matching action expert, GR00T N1 [ 19 ] targets humanoids,
SmolVLA [ 20 ] shows that a compact model can be competitive, and
MemoryVLA [ 34 ] adds a memory of past observations. Vision-language navigation
models [ 35 , 36 , 37 ] also follow instructions through space, but they output
waypoints or motion primitives for a lower layer to execute rather than the continuous
commands a pilot issues. All of these models, however, are trained on terrestrial data; none
of their corpora contains underwater demonstrations or uses an operator’s joystick as the
action space.

## II-C Underwater Robot Learning and Simulation

Underwater, learning from demonstrations is still small in scale. AquaBot [ 25 ] records a pilot’s gamepad commands with video for about a thousand manipulation
demonstrations in a pool, without language, and imitation learning for underwater arms has
likewise been shown in pools and tanks [ 26 , 27 ] , including a VLA evaluated
on real underwater manipulation [ 27 ] . For navigation, real-world learning has used
camera footage whose actions were labeled afterwards [ 28 , 29 ] , and
Khanmeh et al. [ 38 ] released BlueROV2 pilot inputs without camera
images. Simulation is the standard way to scale beyond this. MarineGym [ 39 ] adds
hydrodynamics to GPU physics for reinforcement learning, and USIM [ 24 ] , the closest
vehicle-level effort toward underwater VLA, generates 20 navigation and manipulation tasks in
simulation with hand-crafted experts that use ground-truth state and fine-tunes U0 from
GR00T N1.5 to map images, language and sensor readings to per-thruster commands and arm joint
angles, without real-world deployment. Thus real-world work records a human operator’s
commands only for manipulation in pools or tanks; no existing dataset pairs open-water
observations with pilot commands for vehicle-level tasks, in reality or in simulation.

Filling this gap in simulation, where demonstrations are cheap, adds a further requirement:
simulated demonstrations help if the simulated vehicle moves like the real
one, which depends on the hydrodynamic model [ 40 ] and on the controller in the loop,
and looks like it, which depends on how water attenuates and scatters
light [ 41 , 42 ] .
Taken together, these lines of work point to four needs that guide our collection pipeline
and dataset: (i) real underwater observations paired with the joystick commands a human pilot
actually sent; (ii) simulated demonstrations recorded through the same control chain, from
the pilot’s joystick through the ground-control software to the flight-controller firmware;
(iii) a simulator whose dynamics and appearance are calibrated against the real vehicle; and
(iv) an evaluation of how current policies, developed for other action spaces, learn from the
pilot’s commands.
Table I summarizes how AquaAct differs from the closest datasets.

2026-10-20.title: CusADi2: Latency-Optimized Batch Computation of Robot Kinematics, Jacobians, and Hessians on the GPU
2026-10-20.authors: John Viljoen , Lasse Peters , Masayoshi Tomizuka , Negar Mehr
2026-10-20.comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). Code: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract:
Trajectory optimization methods, from sampling-based zero-order to gradient-based first- and second-order approaches, require many evaluations of dynamical system functions , i.e., functions derived from a robot’s dynamical model, such as forward kinematics and their Jacobians and Hessians.
These evaluations are largely independent, e.g., across sampled trajectories or time steps, and can thus be evaluated in parallel as a batch .
When used to make decisions online , these methods require low latency , i.e., each batch must complete in as little wall-clock time as possible.
Existing frameworks utilize modern GPU hardware primarily to parallelize across batch instances, thereby optimizing throughput but not latency .
We present CusADi2, a software library that reduces the batch evaluation latency by additionally parallelizing computation within each batch instance.
We benchmark forward kinematics, Jacobians, and Hessians for all 67 robots in the MuJoCo Menagerie, including arms, hands, quadrupeds, humanoids, and biomechanical models, against MuJoCo XLA, MuJoCo Warp, frax, CusADi, and CasADi.
CusADi2 achieves lower latency than all baselines at batch sizes of 64 to 4096, while matching them at larger batch sizes.
We also demonstrate the performance advantage of CusADi2 in a sampling-based control application.
All code is open-source at: https://github.com/johnviljoen/cusadi2 .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Modern robotics algorithms often make decisions by repeatedly evaluating dynamical system functions , i.e., functions derived from a robot’s dynamical model, such as forward kinematics and their Jacobians and Hessians [ 1 , 2 ] .
In some cases, this dependence on a model is explicit.
For example, model-based online planning techniques, whether zero-order (sampling-based) [ 3 , 4 ] or first- and second-order (gradient-based) [ 5 ] , all repeatedly evaluate a model to predict the effect of their actions on the environment [ 1 ] .
In other cases, the dependence on a model may be implicit .
For example, model-free techniques such as Reinforcement Learning (RL) usually rely on a simulator to generate sufficient training data [ 2 ] .
Approaches that evaluate the model offline , such as RL, require high throughput.
Therefore, modern GPU tools [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] have been optimized for this criterion.
However, techniques that evaluate the model online require a different criterion, namely low latency , which remains a secondary concern for these tools.
Sampling-based methods evaluate batches of hundreds of rollouts for every control action, and gradient-based methods evaluate Jacobians and Hessians along the trajectory at every iteration.
In both cases, the latency of these evaluations directly limits the achievable control rate.
These online methods thus directly benefit from low-latency evaluation of dynamical system functions.

In this paper, we fill this gap by introducing CusADi2, a software library for low-latency batched evaluation of dynamical system functions on the GPU.
To be broadly applicable in online planning, CusADi2 supports not only forward kinematics but also Jacobians and Hessians.
It exploits the structure of each function’s computational graph to parallelize its evaluation.
Two further optimizations reuse one schedule across trajectory stages and group same-type operations, which GPUs execute more efficiently.
It thus achieves lower latency than prior methods such as MuJoCo Warp [ 7 ] , MuJoCo XLA [ 6 ] , and CusADi [ 9 ] .
For 256 forward kinematics evaluations, existing GPU frameworks need at least 100 μ \mu s on nearly every MuJoCo Menagerie [ 10 ] robot, whereas CusADi2 needs under 40 μ \mu s on common platforms ( CusADi2: Latency-Optimized Batch Computation of Robot Kinematics, Jacobians, and Hessians on the GPU ).
Across all 67 robots, from dexterous hands to humanoids, this advantage is largest for batches of 64 to 4096, with no throughput loss beyond.
Finally, we demonstrate a 50 Hz 50\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} safe sampling-based planner for a Franka Panda arm, with a Higher-Order Control Barrier Function (HOCBF) [ 11 ] safety filter per sampled trajectory.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Works

GPU tools for evaluating dynamical system functions have so far been designed for throughput, as required by RL.
Below, we review these tools along three axes, namely batched simulation, per-instance latency, and derivative sparsity.

Batched GPU Simulation. Modern batched GPU simulators [ 8 , 12 , 6 , 7 , 13 , 14 , 9 ] parallelize simulation across thousands of independent instances to generate data at high throughput.
These tools were originally designed for RL, where more environment interactions directly accelerate training [ 2 ] .
However, batched simulation is increasingly used beyond RL, often targeting online deployment [ 3 , 15 ] .
Such online applications require low-latency batched evaluation, which is of secondary importance to existing GPU simulators but the primary focus of this paper.

Latency. Reducing the latency of a batched evaluation requires accelerating each instance, not only parallelizing across instances.
Existing frameworks take one of two approaches to this per-instance parallelism.
Some frameworks [ 6 , 12 , 14 ] rely on the OpenXLA compiler [ 16 ] from the JAX ecosystem [ 17 ] , whose heuristics are designed for machine learning workloads dominated by large tensor operations, rather than fine-grained scalar operations that make up dynamical system functions.
Hence, they accelerate each instance only to a small degree.
Other frameworks [ 8 , 13 , 7 , 15 ] instead require the user to supply a function that is already parallelized per instance, leaving this burden to the practitioner.
In this paper, we introduce a method that automatically parallelizes per-instance computations.

Sparsity. A further limitation of existing batched evaluation frameworks is that they treat the highly sparse Jacobians and Hessians as dense . [ 18 ] addresses this with sparse automatic differentiation, but is designed for Jacobians and is inefficient for Hessians.
Other works [ 19 , 20 , 9 ] use symbolic differentiation to obtain sparse Jacobians and Hessians, but either their compilation time grows prohibitively with expression size, or they apply no latency reduction techniques [ 9 ] .
Our method inherits the fast sparse symbolic differentiation pipeline of CasADi [ 21 ] and combines it with latency reduction techniques.

2026-10-20.title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
2026-10-20.authors: Yong Wang , Kecheng Zheng , Xing Zhu , Chao Xu , Yujun Shen , Shengze Cai
2026-10-20.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-20.abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/ .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Bimanual dexterous manipulation, the coordinated control of two multi-fingered hands acting on a shared workspace, is widely regarded as a prerequisite for general-purpose household and industrial robots. The past two years have brought this capability within reach: VLA models [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] now absorb large-scale demonstrations and generalize across scenes, objects, and instructions. What has not kept pace is our ability to measure where such policies actually fail. As training corpora grow, average success on narrow pick-and-place suites saturates, and the discriminating power of a benchmark shifts away from task coverage toward capability edges : remembering scene state, sustaining long horizons, obeying instructions that change mid-episode, learning from few demonstrations, and degrading gracefully under visual and geometric shift. A 58-DoF bimanual dexterous system amplifies every one of these edges relative to the 7-DoF gripper platforms that dominate current evaluation. Its action space is high-dimensional and redundant, its success hinges on contact-rich finger coordination, and its failure modes are invisible to a binary success rate.

Existing manipulation benchmarks leave this gap open in three distinct ways. First, the widely used suites, among them Meta-World [ 6 ] , RLBench [ 7 ] , LIBERO [ 8 ] , CALVIN [ 9 ] , RoboCasa [ 10 ] , and ManiSkill [ 11 ] , are built around single arms terminated by parallel-jaw grippers, so the entire dexterity dimension is abstracted away. Second, dexterous-hand benchmarks such as Bi-DexHands [ 12 ] and DexMV [ 13 ] target reinforcement learning from scratch on small task sets, without language grounding, large-scale demonstrations, or automated compositional scoring. Third, even recent large-scale efforts, such as RoboTwin [ 14 , 15 ] and RoboDojo [ 16 ] , evaluate bimanual gripper platforms and report largely binary success, while the community has converged on the need for capability-targeted diagnosis of memory, long-horizon competence, and instruction fidelity that binary scores cannot provide. In short, the field lacks a benchmark that simultaneously offers bimanual dexterous hands, a capability-organized task suite with progress-based predicate scoring, matched In-Domain and Out-of-Domain evaluation, and a large teleoperated demonstration dataset released alongside the benchmark.

To address this gap, we introduce BiDex-100, a MuJoCo benchmark of 106 bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks spanning five capability axes. BiDex-100 is built on a simple premise: as average task success improves, evaluation should reveal not only whether a policy succeeds, but also what it can do reliably and where it fails. Our contributions are:

A capability-based benchmark for bimanual dexterity. The 106 tasks measure Generalization, Instruction-Following, Limited Demonstrations, Long Horizon, and Memory. These axes expose distinct limitations of VLA policies. Results therefore form a capability profile rather than a single aggregate score.

A capability-based benchmark for bimanual dexterity. The 106 tasks measure Generalization, Instruction-Following, Limited Demonstrations, Long Horizon, and Memory. These axes expose distinct limitations of VLA policies. Results therefore form a capability profile rather than a single aggregate score.

Matched In-Domain (ID) and Out-of-Domain (OOD) evaluation. Each task has a reproducible OOD counterpart with controlled changes to appearance, scene layout, distractors, object scale, and left-right configuration. This design makes in-domain performance and robustness directly comparable.

A large-scale dataset and reference study. We provide 8,080 success-validated teleoperation episodes, covering 6.25M frames of data across the 106 released tasks. We also evaluate 7 recent VLA models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

The field’s standard suites measure gripper-based manipulation. Meta-World [ 6 ] and RLBench [ 7 ] offer 50–100 tasks for meta-RL and few-shot learning. LIBERO [ 8 ] studies lifelong transfer across 130 tasks. CALVIN [ 9 ] targets language-conditioned long-horizon chains. RoboCasa [ 10 ] and BEHAVIOR-1K [ 17 ] scale scene and activity diversity. ManiSkill2 [ 11 ] and VLABench [ 18 ] emphasize generalizable skills and language grounding. SimplerEnv [ 19 ] aligns simulation with real-world policy rankings. All of these terminate the arm in a parallel-jaw gripper and score success binarily. RoboTwin [ 14 ] and RoboTwin 2.0 [ 15 ] move to bimanual grippers with generative digital twins and strong domain randomization, and RoboDojo [ 16 ] organizes 60 gripper tasks along capability dimensions with a unified sim-and-real protocol, but neither exercises multi-fingered dexterity, and their scoring remains predominantly binary. DexJoCo [ 20 ] is a bimanual dexterous benchmark with teleoperated demonstrations and matched ID/OOD variants, but only 11 tasks, binary scoring. BiDex-100 extends the design to 106 capability-organized tasks with progress-based predicate scoring. BiDex-100 occupies the vacant corner of this design space (Table I ): bimanual 22-DoF dexterous hands, five capability axes, progress-based predicate scoring, and matched ID/OOD evaluation.

Dexterous-hand benchmarks historically trade breadth for fidelity: early Shadow-Hand suites [ 21 ] cover a handful of canonical tasks; Bi-DexHands [ 12 ] provides RL environments for two Shadow hands without demonstrations or language; DexMV [ 13 ] retargets human videos but offers no standardized compositional scoring. Demonstrations for such systems depend on teleoperation: DexPilot [ 22 ] and AnyTeleop [ 23 ] retarget visual hand tracking, TeleMoMa [ 24 ] composes input modalities, Open-TeleVision [ 25 ] streams immersive head-mounted video, and FACTR [ 26 ] adds low-cost force-aware exoskeleton. BiDex-100 adopts the last two modalities and unifies them through a single optimization-based retargeting stack (Section IV-A ).

VLAs fine-tune web-scale vision-language backbones into action policies [ 1 , 2 , 27 ] , with recent designs adding flow-matching or diffusion action experts for high-frequency dexterous control [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Their published evaluations concentrate on gripper embodiments, and cross-model comparisons are complicated by per-paper protocols, action spaces, and data mixtures. BiDex-100 supplies the missing controlled substrate for this model class on dexterous bimanual tasks: a fixed 58-DoF joint-space interface, a shared demonstration corpus, and a stratified, automated scoring protocol, which we use to benchmark seven contemporary VLAs.

2026-10-20.title: Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees: Amortizing Foundation-Model Reasoning into Deterministic Control for Autonomous Drones
2026-10-20.authors: Behnam Moradi
2026-10-20.abstract: Classical robot control architectures, Finite State Machines (FSMs) and Behavior Trees (BTs), are deterministic, inspectable, and fast, but fixed at design time: they fail on the long tail of situations their designers did not anticipate. Foundation models can synthesize new control logic at runtime, at the price of latency, cost, and non-determinism that are hard to accept in safety-critical aerial systems. Existing LLM-driven approaches keep the model permanently in the loop and discard what it produces after each use. We propose Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees (SCBT), in which the foundation model is a compiler rather than a runtime . When a node of a vehicle’s BT fails, an LLM proposes a minimal subtree patch in a constrained, mission-agnostic grammar; CMA-ES tunes the patch’s continuous parameters in simulation; a contextual bandit decides whether a stored patch or a new LLM call is worth paying for; and a three-stage admission pipeline (static check, invariant monitors over randomized replays, and an empirical margin over the unpatched tree) admits only patches that demonstrably recover. Admitted patches are stored in a fleet library indexed by failure context and, once the LLM call rate has decayed, crystallized into a conventional deterministic BT that no human wrote. We implement SCBT on Microsoft Project AirSim with a schema-constrained LLM pipeline (Google ADK, Gemini 3.1 Pro) and a lockstep simulator. Over three seeds of a 20-episode learning phase with injected wind-gust and battery failures, SCBT used 11 ± 1.4 11\pm 1.4 LLM calls against 26 for whole-tree regeneration and 22 for patching without a library, with 0.33 calls per episode in the second half. The crystallized trees, with 28 and 33 nodes and two patches each, reached 97 ± 2 % 97\pm 2\% mission success on the curriculum with no learning component running, against 12% for the unpatched base tree and 98% for a hand-coded expert tree; re-ticked offline against recorded observations they reproduce their online decision traces exactly. Two negative results are reported: replay admission as parameterized rejected useful wind recoveries because it attributed wind-induced geofence excursions to the patch, and the static-only ablation generalized better to held-out failures as a consequence.
2026-10-20.introduction:
For half a century robot behavior has been specified explicitly, first as FSMs and, over the last decade, as BTs [ 1 , 2 ] . These architectures are attractive precisely because they are closed : every branch can be inspected, every transition is deterministic, and the controller runs at a fixed rate on embedded hardware. The same closedness is their limitation. A BT cannot execute a branch that was never written, and in open environments the set of situations that require a branch is effectively unbounded. We call this design-time rigidity .

Foundation models offer an apparent escape: LLMs write robot programs from natural-language goals [ 9 ] , generate BT XML on demand [ 15 , 16 ] , ground plans in perceptual affordances [ 10 , 12 ] , and coordinate heterogeneous teams [ 26 , 27 ] . But these systems share a structural assumption: the model stays in the control loop for the lifetime of the system, and what it produces is discarded after use. For aerial robots this has three consequences. Latency : in our implementation a single structured proposal from a frontier model takes 31–105 s (two schema-constrained calls); a vehicle in a wind gust cannot wait for it. Cost : operating cost grows with activity. Non-determinism : two flights under identical conditions may execute different logic, which defeats the certification argument that makes BTs acceptable in the first place.

The two camps are usually framed as a trade-off between adaptability and determinism. We argue the trade-off is an artifact of when the foundation model is invoked. If the model is called only when the existing control structure fails, if what it produces is verified and retained , and if a learned policy stops calling it once stored structure suffices, then adaptability is paid for once, during a learning phase, and the deployed system is an ordinary deterministic BT.

SCBT assigns each mechanism to the job it is suited for:

The LLM proposes structure : given a failed node and its context, it emits one minimal, local, mission-agnostic patch in a constrained grammar. Structure synthesis is discrete, symbolic, and rare.

CMA-ES tunes parameters : each patch declares its uncertain numeric ports as tunables with bounds; these are optimized against simulated replays before admission.

A contextual bandit selects : among stored patches that match the failure context and the option of a new LLM call, with the call’s cost in the reward.

A three-stage admission pipeline gates library entry: static check against the grammar and the vehicle’s capability manifest; invariant monitors over randomized replays; and an empirical success margin over the tree as it currently stands.

A deterministic BT executes : the vehicle controller is always a plain BT ticked in lockstep with the simulator. No neural component is in the tick path.

The SCBT framework: failure interception, a mission-agnostic patch grammar with anchor-port references, a context-indexed fleet library, bandit-based selection with an explicit LLM-call arm, and replay-based admission with CMA-ES tuning (Sec. IV ).

An evaluation against hand-coded, regenerate-on-failure, and five ablated baselines over a frozen phase in which all learning is disabled, with an exact decision-determinism test, and an analysis of what the admission pipeline caught and what it wrongly rejected (Secs. VI , VII ).

2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Classical Control Architectures

FSMs require transitions from every state to handle global events, so transition count grows quadratically with state count [ 1 ] . BTs [ 3 , 4 ] standardize the node interface to a ternary status and decouple nodes; the survey by Iovino et al. [ 2 ] documents the gains in modularity and reactivity and the persistent limitation that BT structure is fixed at design time. Learned BTs via genetic programming [ 5 , 6 ] or learned leaf policies [ 7 ] learn from reward alone and are sample-hungry when the needed structural change is semantically obvious.

## II-B Foundation Models for Control Synthesis

Code as Policies [ 9 ] prompts an LLM with a robot API to write programs; SayCan [ 10 ] and Inner Monologue [ 11 ] ground plans in affordances and feedback; VoxPoser [ 12 ] composes LLM reasoning and VLM grounding into value maps; VLA models [ 13 , 14 ] map pixels to actions. Closest to us are BTGenBot [ 15 ] , which fine-tunes small LLMs to emit BehaviorTree.CPP XML and validates it syntactically and in simulation, and LLM-BT [ 16 ] . These regenerate structure on demand and do not retain, verify against an empirical margin, or learn when to stop calling the model. Surveys [ 17 , 18 ] discuss the latency, cost, and hallucination risks that motivate our design.

## II-C Combining LLMs with Learning

Eureka [ 19 ] has an LLM write reward functions that RL optimizes; RL-GPT [ 20 ] lets an LLM decide what to code and what to learn; Voyager [ 21 ] keeps a growing library of LLM-written skills retrieved by embedding. SCBT shares the library with Voyager and the LLM/optimizer division of labor with Eureka, but the stored artifacts are BT subtrees, admission is gated by simulated invariants and an empirical margin, and the stated end state is a system with no model running.

## II-D Multi-Robot Coordination and Verification

Classical MRTA [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] requires pre-defined tasks with comparable costs. LLM coordination [ 26 , 27 ] describes robots by textual capability profiles; we adopt that idea as a capability manifest that gates which leaves a patch may use and declares substitutions across vehicle classes. Prior verification of generated control checks syntax and simulated execution [ 15 ] ; we add invariant monitors, a landing-reserve constraint, and a required margin over the unpatched tree.

2026-10-20.title: Intent-Informed Model Predictive Control for Shared Autonomy in Remote Manipulation Tasks
2026-10-20.authors: Lorena Maria Genua , Camilla Tabasso , Mya Schroder , Joshua Migdal , Tye Brady , Taskin Padir
2026-10-20.abstract:
Shared autonomy is a control paradigm that combines human cognitive abilities with robot precision to enable effective remote manipulation in complex environments.
A key challenge is how to adapt the level of autonomy using information extracted from the human, task, and/or environment.
In this paper, we propose a novel arbitration strategy that dynamically adjusts the level of autonomy in the system using the entropy of a belief distribution derived from a multimodal intent inference.
Human intent is modeled with a Dynamic Bayesian Network (DBN), which updates beliefs over goals given real-time operator gaze data and robot arm motion during teleoperation.
We then formulate the blending of human input and autonomous control as a Model Predictive Control (MPC) problem, where the system’s autonomous behavior is guided by the belief distribution.
This approach enables continuous, gradual transitions across the full spectrum of autonomy levels, from direct teleoperation to full autonomy.
To validate our approach, we conducted experiments to compare the performance of our proposed algorithm against two MPC-based shared autonomy methods.
Compared to the baselines, our approach achieved reductions of at least 61% in object retrieval time, 44% in trajectory length, and 60% in human control input.
Participants reported high perceived control, predictability, intent recognition, and responsiveness, along with low workload.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Teleoperation has been effective for controlling robots in remote and hazardous environments.
However, the full control of robot manipulators poses several challenges due to the reduced dexterity in precise manipulation, limited situational awareness from camera views, and communication delays [ 1 , 2 ] .
Recent advances in teleoperation systems, such as those developed by teams participating in the ANA Avatar XPRIZE [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] , have addressed these issues by integrating virtual reality interfaces with multisensory feedback to enable high-dexterity manipulation in remote environments.
While these systems enhance operator embodiment, the human operator is responsible for continuous low-level control and decision-making during task execution.
As a result, prolonged operation leads to increased operator fatigue and degraded performance [ 6 ] .
Conversely, fully autonomous robots fall short in complex and ambiguous situations found in unpredictable and unstructured environments, often necessitating human intervention [ 7 ] .
Shared autonomy enables the collaborative control between human operators and autonomous systems [ 8 ] , therefore leveraging human cognitive abilities for high-level decision-making and robotic precision for low-level control.

Two key aspects of shared autonomy are: arbitration, which is who to allocate control authority based on different contextual factors, and policy blending, how to combine human input with autonomous actions.
Existing related work has explored various arbitration strategies for shared-autonomy based on performance metrics and user-centric approaches [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] .
However, how to smoothly adjust the autonomy levels by leveraging the information extracted from the human still remains an open research question [ 17 ] .
The existing works do not fully leverage real-time human intent inference from multimodal inputs to inform the arbitration process. In this work, we propose an Intent-Informed Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework for adaptive shared autonomy in remote manipulation tasks.
Our approach combines human intent inference using a Dynamic Bayesian Network with MPC to dynamically adjust the level of autonomy based on the confidence in the inferred operator intent. Our main contributions are the following:

1) We introduce a novel arbitration strategy that uses the entropy of belief distributions as a measure of intent inference uncertainty. This allows a gradual and continuous autonomy-level adaptation, shifting control authority between direct teleoperation and full autonomy.

2) We formulate the policy blending problem as a Model Predictive Control (MPC) problem , where the probabilities from the intent inference guide the autonomous control.

3) We conducted experimental studies with 20 participants and compared our approach with two existing MPC formulations for shared-autonomy.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related work

## II-A Arbitration strategies

Arbitration determines how the control authority is allocated between a human operator and an autonomous agent.
Early approaches used a discrete switching between manual and autonomous control modes, often triggered by intent confidence [ 11 , 18 ] .
Such methods typically result in abrupt transitions, which can be disorienting for users and may fail to optimize task performance.
More recent work has explored continuous arbitration strategies, which allow smooth adjustments across the spectrum of autonomy levels.
Various methods for adjusting arbitration weights have been proposed, focusing on different performance metrics.
For instance, Xing et al. [ 12 ] developed a fuzzy logic-based arbitration which modulates control weights according to interaction force, human-robot velocity, and proximity to obstacles.
Balachandran et al. [ 15 ] apply Bayesian filtering to estimate manipulation performance and allocate control accordingly.
However, because these methods do not incorporate intent inference, they may lead to conflicts between human intentions and the actions of the autonomous controller.
Other works have addressed this by relying on human control input and distance to targets [ 10 , 19 ] .
These approaches struggle in cluttered environments and are challenging for novice teleoperation users, who tend to exhibit jerkier manipulation control and experience sharp declines in performance as task complexity increases [ 20 ] .
User-centric approaches, conversely, adjust the level of autonomy based on user expertise and training experience [ 13 , 16 ] , or models of bilateral trust between humans and robots [ 9 ] . The challenge of accurately anticipating human intentions through multimodal information integration, and use it to adapt the level of autonomy, still remains an open research question [ 17 ] .
Existing approaches have overlooked the potential of biological signals for intent inference.
Human gaze, in particular, provides valuable insight into task-relevant attention and intended actions [ 21 ] , yet it has not been leveraged for arbitration strategies.
In this work, we propose an intent inference method that incorporates multimodal inputs, e.g. gaze tracking and motion direction.
We then use the entropy of the beliefs, a measure of uncertainty in the system, as an arbitration strategy to adjust the level of autonomy.

## II-B Model Predictive Control for Shared Autonomy

Model Predictive Control (MPC) is an optimal control technique that uses a model of the system to predict the future behavior, then optimizes the control inputs to minimize a desired cost function.
In the context of shared autonomy, the application of MPC remains mostly limited to trajectory correction and obstacle avoidance.
Several works have used MPC to satisfy system constraints and prevent collisions with static and dynamic obstacles while following human input [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] .
More recently, two works have explored MPC as a blending strategy, which we use as comparison methods in this paper.
Lima et al. [ 19 ] provide continuous assistance towards multiple targets using distance-based weighting in their cost function to switch between autonomous motion and user input.
While this approach blends user input with robot autonomy, it has two main limitations.
First, it does not provide a gradual transition between autonomy levels, resulting in abrupt changes in control.
Second, because it relies on distance to targets, it faces challenges in cluttered environments where objects are in close proximity. Jabbour et al. [ 18 ] use distance to the target as a weight to distribute the control authority.
This method however, requires a predefined goal location.
We include this work for comparison as it combines a common shared autonomy strategy (proximity-based assistance) with MPC formulation.
While common in shared autonomy, distance-based thresholds methods do not provide a continuous blending and require predetermined goals.
Our work extends the use of MPC in shared autonomy by introducing two novelties.
First, we employ MPC as a continuous blending strategy, enabling a gradual transition in control authority from full teleoperation to full autonomy.
Second, we incorporate the entropy of intent inference beliefs as a weight to dynamically adjust the level of autonomy in the system.
Additionally, our formulation includes both position and orientation tracking, unlike the previous two approaches which focus solely on position.

2026-10-20.title: SurGPT: A Multi-Task Foundation Model for Robotic Surgical Skills Assessment and Gesture Recognition
2026-10-20.authors: Parham M. Kebria , Saeid Nahavandi , Mehrdad Saif , Fernando Bello
2026-10-20.abstract: The assessment of surgical skills in robotic surgery training has traditionally relied on subjective evaluations by human experts, creating bottlenecks in surgical education and limiting scalability. We present a novel foundation model that automatically analyzes robotic surgical videos to provide comprehensive skill assessment and gesture understanding. Combining a visual encoder with a transformer architecture, the model performs three key tasks simultaneously: 1) surgical task classification (knot tying, needle passing, suturing), 2) skill level assessment on a standardized scale, and 3) natural language generation of surgical gesture descriptions. The model processes video sequences from the da Vinci surgical robot and generates human-readable text descriptions of surgical actions, similar to how language models generate text from prompts, using a multi-task learning framework with adaptive uncertainty weighting to optimize performance across all objectives. Our transformer-based architecture incorporates positional encoding for temporal understanding and attention mechanisms for spatial-temporal feature integration. Evaluated on the da Vinci Skills Simulator dataset, the proposed framework demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in surgical task recognition and provides interpretable skill assessments that correlate with expert evaluations, with the model’s ability to generate natural language descriptions of surgical gestures opening new possibilities for automated surgical education, real-time feedback systems, and objective skill assessment in surgical training and certification programs.
2026-10-20.introduction:
The emergence of robotic systems in clinical and healthcare practices makes them a critical element in a variety of medical procedures [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Therefore, surgeons and clinicians need to learn, adapt, and practice the new technology. Employing all their skills, knowledge, and experience in this new schema of practice becomes a challenge, considering their limited time for training. This phenomenon requires a methodology to properly evaluate surgical skills in robotic practices [ 4 ] . Surgical skill assessment in robotic surgery training has traditionally relied on subjective evaluations by human experts, creating bottlenecks in education and restricting scalability [ 5 ] . However, such expert-driven evaluations are time-intensive, costly, and inherently inconsistent, as they are susceptible to variability and human bias [ 6 , 7 ] .

Recent advances in deep learning have significantly expanded the scope of surgical scene understanding, shifting from handcrafted features and task-specific models toward end-to-end learning frameworks. In particular, transformer-based architectures have emerged as a powerful paradigm for modeling long-range temporal dependencies and complex spatiotemporal interactions in surgical videos [ 8 ] . By leveraging self-attention mechanisms, transformers can capture both local motion patterns and global procedural context, enabling a more holistic understanding of surgical scenes compared to traditional sequential models.

The foundation model paradigm enables transfer learning across different surgical procedures and institutions, potentially revolutionizing surgical education through scalable, objective, and consistent skill evaluation [ 9 ] . Toward this paradigm, a wide range of techniques have been investigated to utilize expert human demonstrations to provide data-driven models with the vast amount of knowledge and context of the target procedures [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Surgical scene understanding introduces advanced machine learning and deep learning techniques used in image processing in the context of surgical procedures. This includes instrument detection, instrument-tissue segmentation, instrument tracking, instrument pose estimation, and tissue classification, to name a few [ 13 ] . Foundation models have shown promising performance in precision and effectiveness in the analysis of medical images and anatomical information [ 14 ] .

Despite these advances, there are still drawbacks and challenges in the deployment of foundation models in clinical applications that have not yet been investigated. Being large in size with the corresponding large number of parameters, foundation models are extremely data-thirsty. However, the privacy of healthcare data is a major concern, which limits the accessibility of large enough medical datasets for training such models [ 15 ] . On the other hand, the lack of interpretability and explainability in these deep models poses significant challenges to their adoption in clinically critical applications [ 16 ] . Still, foundation models provide novel benefits in the field, such as integrating multi-modal data to obtain more comprehensive diagnosis decisions [ 17 ] . Specifically, extracting diagnostic information from clinical videos is one of the areas where foundation models demonstrate unmatched benefits [ 18 ] .

Moreover, surgical videos are characterized by high variability due to differences in anatomy, surgeon style, viewpoint, and occlusions, while annotated datasets remain limited and costly to obtain. Specifically, for clinical adoption, surgical scene understanding systems must provide interpretable and reliable outputs that align with expert reasoning. Transformer-based foundation models, particularly when coupled with interpretable outputs such as natural language descriptions, represent a promising direction for addressing these challenges and advancing automated, scalable, and clinically meaningful surgical intelligence systems. Existing surgical AI methods are often designed for single tasks, which limits transfer across related clinical objectives. They also provide limited interpretability and rarely use uncertainty as an adaptive learning signal, reducing trust and robustness.

Motivated by prior limitations, we propose a unified multi-task foundation model for robotic surgical video analysis that jointly performs gesture recognition and real-time skill assessment, combining a visual encoder and transformer for shared spatiotemporal reasoning, improved interpretability, and adaptive uncertainty weighting for better generalization and reliability. Objective surgical skill assessment: The model provides a standardized and scalable evaluation of surgical skill levels, producing objective proficiency scores that correlate strongly with expert assessments.

Interpretable gesture understanding via natural language generation: We introduce a novel capability for generating human-readable textual descriptions of fine-grained surgical gestures from video data, improving interpretability and supporting automated feedback and educational applications.

The model processes video sequences captured from the da Vinci surgical robot and produces human-readable textual explanations of surgical actions, analogous to prompt-driven language generation in large language models. A multi-task learning strategy with adaptive uncertainty weighting is employed to balance and optimize performance across all objectives. The transformer architecture incorporates positional encoding to capture temporal dynamics and attention mechanisms for effective spatiotemporal feature integration. Extensive evaluation on the da Vinci Skills dataset [ 19 , 20 ] demonstrates that the model achieves state-of-the-art performance in surgical task recognition, while providing interpretable skill assessments that closely correlate with expert evaluations. Moreover, its ability to generate natural language descriptions of surgical gestures introduces new opportunities for automated surgical education, real-time feedback, and objective skill assessment in robotic surgery training and certification programs.

Surgical scene understanding aims to computationally interpret the visual and temporal context of surgical procedures by recognizing tools, actions, phases, and skill-related patterns from intraoperative data. In robot-assisted and minimally invasive surgery, this problem is primarily addressed through the analysis of surgical videos and kinematic signals to enable context-aware assistance, objective skill assessment, and intelligent feedback systems [ 4 ] .

Surgical motion can be viewed as being similar to human language because it is made up of small, meaningful actions that occur in a structured sequence. These actions follow implicit rules and constraints, just as words and sentences do in language. As a result, methods originally developed for modeling human language and speech can also be applied to the analysis of surgical motion.

At Johns Hopkins University, the Language of Surgery project studies surgical activity as a form of complex and dexterous human motion. The project aims to build curated surgical motion datasets, establish protocols for secure data storage and sharing, and develop computational models to analyze surgical activity. These models are then used to support surgical training, objective skill assessment, and research on human–machine collaboration in surgery.

Surgical activity data include multiple sources of information, such as surgical tool kinematics, endoscopic video, system event logs, and additional signals such as surgeon posture, speech, and manual annotations. Together, these data provide a comprehensive representation of surgical behavior that supports systematic analysis and learning.

A central challenge in surgical scene understanding is the lack of standardized, fine-grained annotations that capture both the temporal structure and skill-related aspects of surgical activity. The JIGSAWS (JHU–ISI Gesture and Skill Assessment Working Set [ 20 ] ) dataset was introduced to address this gap and has since become a foundational benchmark for modeling and evaluating surgical scene understanding in robot-assisted surgery.

JIGSAWS consists of synchronized video and kinematic recordings collected from the da Vinci surgical system during the execution of three fundamental robotic surgery tasks: knot tying, needle passing, and suturing (Fig. 1 ). These tasks represent core psychomotor skills essential in robotic surgery and are commonly incorporated into surgical training curricula. The dataset comprises multiple trials conducted by surgeons with varying levels of expertise, categorized as novice, intermediate, and expert, to facilitate a systematic analysis of both task execution and surgical skill proficiency.

A defining characteristic of JIGSAWS is its fine-grained temporal annotation of surgical gestures, referred to as surgemes. Each trial is segmented into a sequence of elementary gestures that capture meaningful units of surgical motion and interaction. The gesture taxonomy includes eleven standardized classes, denoted as G1–G11, which describe recurrent actions across tasks:

G1: Reach for needle with right hand

G2: Position needle

G3: Push needle through tissue

G4: Transfer needle from right to left hand

G5: Move to center with needle in left hand

G6: Pull suture with left hand

G7: Pull suture with right hand

G8: Orient needle

G9: Use right hand to help tighten suture

G10: Use left hand to help tighten suture

G11: Drop suture at end of task

This gesture-level decomposition provides a structured representation of surgical activity, enabling models to learn the temporal organization and hierarchical composition of surgical motion. In addition to gesture annotations, JIGSAWS provides standardized skill scores based on expert evaluations, supporting objective assessment of surgical proficiency and correlation analysis between automated predictions and human judgment.

Despite its impact, JIGSAWS exposes several open challenges in surgical scene understanding. The dataset is relatively small by modern deep learning standards, and its annotations focus primarily on discrete gesture labels and numeric skill scores, without explicit semantic descriptions of surgical intent or context. Moreover, many existing methods treat gesture recognition, task classification, and skill assessment as separate problems, resulting in fragmented pipelines that fail to capture global procedural structure and limit interpretability.

In JIGSAWS, surgical skill is quantified using expert-derived global rating scores, not gesture-level labels. These scores are provided per trial and are commonly used as ground truth for skill assessment and regression/classification tasks. Each surgical trial is evaluated by expert surgeons using a standardized Global Rating Scale (GRS) adapted for robotic surgery [ 19 ] . The GRS consists of the following six skill metrics:

Depth Perception : Ability to judge spatial relationships and accurately manipulate tools in 3D space.

Bimanual Dexterity : Effective and coordinated use of both hands during task execution.

Efficiency : Economy of motion and avoidance of unnecessary or redundant movements.

Force Sensitivity : Appropriate application of force to tissue and instruments.

Robotic Control : Smoothness and precision of tool manipulation using the robotic interface.

Overall Skill : Holistic assessment of surgical proficiency.

Strong correlation metrics (Pearson: 0.833, Spearman: 0.904) demonstrate reliable skill level prediction, with the model achieving 91.7% classification accuracy and low regression errors (MAE: 0.314, RMSE: 0.840). High BLEU-4 (0.847) and ROUGE-1 (0.962) scores indicate the generation of high-quality, relevant surgical scene descriptions with good semantic and syntactic alignment to ground truth annotations. The overall score of 92.1% reflects the balanced performance across all tasks, validating the multi-task learning approach for comprehensive surgical scene understanding. Figure 3 demonstrates a sample test scenario of the multi-task model.

This work presented a comprehensive transformer-based foundation model for surgical scene understanding that successfully integrates task classification, skill assessment, and natural language description in a unified multi-task framework, achieving strong performance across all evaluation metrics with an overall score of 92.1%, perfect task classification accuracy, reliable skill assessment with high correlation coefficients, and high-quality text generation. The framework’s primary limitations include its scope, being limited to three basic surgical tasks on a single robotic platform, which limits generalizability to diverse surgical procedures and environments. Future work should focus on expanding the framework to more complex procedures across multiple surgical platforms while incorporating uncertainty-aware methods to improve trustworthiness and clinical applicability.

2026-10-20.title: Learning When to Adapt: Reactivity-Conditioned Residual Adaptation under Human-Robot Distribution Shift
2026-10-20.authors: Immanuel R. Santjoko , Benedictus C. G. Cinun , Jing Chen , Bin Hu
2026-10-20.abstract:
Pedestrians differ in whether they respond to a robot, yet many RL policies assume all are non-reactive to prioritize safety.
Policies trained without conditioning on local pedestrians’ reactivity may therefore be unnecessarily conservative or rely on cooperation that does not occur.
We propose RCRA , an online adaptation framework that modulates a learned residual around a frozen conservative navigation policy according to estimated pedestrian reactivity.
A Transformer-based estimator infers latent pedestrian reactivity from motion histories and robot context, providing a more accurate signal for navigation adaptation and improving scenario-averaged simulation accuracy by 12.62 12.62 percentage points over the Bayesian baseline, which assumes known pedestrian goals.
These estimates are spatially aggregated into an adaptation scale that gates LoRA modules, enabling cooperative behavior near reactive pedestrians and conservative behavior near non-reactive pedestrians.
Among baselines achieving SR above 90 % 90\% in every scenario, RCRA reduces scenario-averaged path length by 16.7 % 16.7\% relative to the conservative backbone and by 7.3 % 7.3\% relative to randomized-training baselines.
It improves mean SR by 14.88 14.88 percentage points over the reactive-trained policy.
Website is available at https://nail-uh.github.io/rcra-website.github.io/ .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Pedestrians respond heterogeneously to mobile robots: some adjust their motion in response to the robot, while others continue along their nominal paths.
We study human–robot interaction distribution shift : pedestrian responses to the robot can differ between training and deployment and vary across individuals, locations, and time.
Policies trained under non-reactive pedestrian assumptions tend to preserve safety, but they can remain overly conservative when pedestrians actually make space.
Conversely, policies adapted to fully cooperative pedestrians can move efficiently but may collide when deployed around pedestrians who do not yield.
Uncertainty-based navigation methods can respond to prediction mismatch by increasing safety margins [ 37 , 38 ] .
However, in interaction-sensitive crowds, not all prediction errors indicate danger: a pedestrian who yields may deviate from a non-reactive forecast in a way that creates more free space for the robot.
Increasing margins alone can therefore overlook opportunities created by robot-directed responses. This motivates estimating how pedestrians respond to the robot and using that estimate to adjust navigation behavior.

We investigate whether explicit estimates of pedestrian reactivity provide a useful signal for modulating a pretrained navigation policy as local interaction conditions change.
We propose reactivity-conditioned residual adaptation ( RCRA ), which couples two components: a learned estimator of latent robot-directed reactivity and a policy residual modulated by those estimates. The estimator uses human motion history and robot context to infer which pedestrians are likely to respond. Spatial aggregation converts these estimates into a continuous scale that modulates a residual learned from reactive crowds around a frozen conservative policy. This lets the robot adjust to local interactions without online gradient updates or a supplied scenario label.
Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce RCRA for human–robot interaction distribution shift, using estimated pedestrian responses to modulate an interaction-specific residual around a frozen conservative navigation policy. Second, we learn per-pedestrian reactivity from partial observation histories, refine the estimator with DAgger, and use it for policy modulation through spatial relevance weights. Finally, we evaluate the empirical safety–efficiency trade-off across five homogeneous, heterogeneous, and time-varying response regimes, and separately validate residual adaptation in controlled robot trials with prescribed reactivity labels.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Classical crowd-navigation methods use structured motion and collision-avoidance models [ 11 , 9 , 35 ] , while cooperative planners account for human responses to robot motion [ 33 , 34 ] .
Learning-based methods represent crowd interactions through reinforcement learning and attention [ 6 , 7 , 5 , 19 ] , with trajectory prediction supporting anticipatory navigation [ 18 ] .
Uncertainty-aware methods incorporate safety costs and adaptive prediction bounds [ 38 , 15 ] , although standard conformal guarantees require assumptions such as exchangeability [ 3 ] .
Prediction mismatch alone does not distinguish hazardous motion from yielding that creates free space, motivating explicit estimation of pedestrian responses to the robot.

Training across varied pedestrian-response conditions can improve robustness [ 30 ] , but does not explicitly condition online adaptation on estimated robot-directed reactivity.
BDDS uses Bayesian inference to estimate human responses [ 12 ] , but its behavioral cost model requires pedestrian goals, which may be unknown or change during deployment.
Policy adaptation also includes domain randomization, meta-learning, and imitation-learning correction [ 32 , 8 , 25 ] .
Parameter-efficient methods adapt pretrained networks while freezing most parameters [ 13 , 14 , 20 ] .
Context-dependent adapter selection and scaling further enable dynamic modulation of pretrained models [ 29 ] .
We combine goal-free reactivity estimation with online modulation of a learned LoRA residual around a frozen conservative policy, adjusting navigation to local responses without online gradient updates.

2026-10-20.title: T(R,O) Grasp++: Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasping in Cluttered Environments at Scale
2026-10-20.authors: Xin Fei , Zhixuan Xu , Huaicong Fang , Fangjun Chen , Zhaoyu Mu , Rui Yang , Zhexi Luo , Lin Shao
2026-10-20.abstract: Dexterous grasping in cluttered scenes remains a central challenge in robotic manipulation, as it requires high-dimensional hand coordination under complex object-environment constraints. To address this problem, we introduce one of the largest simulation benchmarks to date, comprising around 0.5B grasp annotations across eight dexterous hands and approximately 50K objects. Furthermore, we propose 𝒯 ⁡ ( R , O ) \mathcal{T}(R,O) Grasp++, a scalable diffusion-based framework for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp synthesis in cluttered environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving an average success rate of 88% across eight dexterous embodiments. Meanwhile, our pipeline achieves only 0.3s inference latency while improving inference sample efficiency by over 10 times.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

## 2.1 Dexterous Grasping Dataset

Creating large-scale datasets for dexterous grasping is challenging due to the high-dimensional hand action space and complex hand-object contacts. One line of work constructs such datasets through optimization-based synthesis, where grasp poses are directly optimized with force-closure, contact, penetration, and stability objectives [ 37 , 39 , 30 , 32 ] . Another line of work trains grasping policies in simulation and rolls out on large object sets, collecting successful executions as grasp annotations [ 36 , 3 , 5 ] . In our work, we train reinforcement learning policies for each dexterous hand and use successful rollouts to annotate 444 million grasps across large-scale object datasets. As shown in Tab. 1 , our dataset covers 53,675 objects and 8 dexterous hands, while additionally providing per-grasp difficulty scores and a mount link to approximate real-world hand-arm deployment.

## 2.2 Learning-based Dexterous Grasping Synthesis

Learning-based frameworks for dexterous grasping synthesis can be categorized into single-object and scene-aware approaches. Single-object methods typically predict or optimize grasp poses for an isolated target object without modeling environment constraints [ 39 , 31 , 10 , 28 , 23 , 34 , 17 , 15 , 1 , 12 ] . While these methods achieve promising results in single-object settings, their inference sample efficiency drops substantially when applied to real-world cluttered environments, as many predicted grasps suffer from severe collisions with surrounding objects or environment.

In comparison, scene-aware methods further incorporate environment constraints into grasping synthesis [ 37 , 39 , 16 , 9 , 5 , 6 , 29 , 2 ] . Despite their progress, existing methods still face limitations in both task setting and grasp representation. In terms of task setting, existing methods generate grasp proposals over the entire scene and then rely on collision checking, grasp scoring, or feasibility filtering to select executable grasps [ 37 , 39 , 16 , 9 , 19 , 7 ] . While suitable for open-world scene grasping, this setting suffers from poor sample efficiency in target-object grasping, as many generated proposals correspond to irrelevant objects or collide with the surrounding environment. As for grasp representation, prior methods either directly predict hand-specific joint values [ 37 , 9 , 6 ] , which limits cross-embodiment generalization, or rely on object-centric predictions that require additional slow optimization to recover executable joint configurations [ 39 , 38 ] . To overcome these limitations, we propose 𝒯 ⁡ ( R , O ) \mathcal{T}(R,O) Graph++ as a unified grasp representation across embodiments, enabling direct grasp prediction on the target object in cluttered environments within a unified framework.

2026-10-20.title: AeroDASH: Asynchronous Vision-Language-Action Control for Continuous UAV Flight
2026-10-20.authors: Zhe Liu , Yuxuan Zheng , Jinzhe Qin , Ziqi Gao , Boyu Zhou
2026-10-20.abstract:
Onboard inference latency creates a mismatch between the trajectories predicted
by vision–language–action (VLA) policies and the ongoing motion of unmanned
aerial vehicles (UAVs).
We present AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous
language-conditioned flight. A B-spline policy is initialized through supervised
fine-tuning on expert demonstrations, providing continuous trajectory references
in position and yaw. During execution, trajectory fusion removes the expired
prediction prefix and connects the remaining segment to the active reference
with derivative continuity while limiting trajectory deformation.
To account for deviations induced by asynchronous execution,
execution-aware group relative policy optimization (GRPO) further adapts the policy
using trajectory-level rewards. On the UAV-Flow test set, AeroDASH achieves a
success rate of 76.56%, exceeding OpenVLA-UAV and AeroDASH w/o GRPO by 38.1 and
20.1 percentage points, respectively. Execution experiments show that AeroDASH
sustains motion during inference and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed
fluctuations relative to asynchronous tracking of waypoint sequences.
We further demonstrate language-conditioned flight with onboard inference and
asynchronous trajectory execution. The code will be released upon acceptance.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Language-conditioned flight requires an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to ground natural language instructions in visual observations and translate them into continuous three-dimensional motion. Vision–language–action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for this task, learning to map visual observations and language commands directly to robot actions. However, continuous UAV flight imposes a stringent execution requirement that goes beyond discrete action prediction: the flight controller needs a temporally smooth reference between successive policy updates, with high-order derivative continuity across all degrees of freedom in the vehicle’s flat-output space.

Current VLA approaches for UAVs predict discrete waypoints or pose targets, leaving the system without a continuous reference between updates. Onboard inference latency further exacerbates this gap: during VLA inference, the UAV continues to move, so each delayed prediction is conditioned on a stale observation and arrives after part of its intended horizon has elapsed. Existing asynchronous execution strategies address this mismatch at the position level only, without enforcing the high-order derivative continuity that UAV flight controllers require across the flat-output space. Abrupt transitions in these derivatives produce large jerks that can destabilize the vehicle. A second gap lies in the mismatch between open-loop training and closed-loop execution. Supervised fine-tuning trains the policy to match individual predictions to expert demonstrations but does not directly evaluate the complete trajectory produced by asynchronous execution.

To overcome these challenges, we present AeroDASH (Fig. 1 ), an asynchronous VLA framework for UAVs that sustains continuous language-conditioned flight under onboard inference latency. To address the first gap, the VLA policy predicts control points that define a cubic B-spline over the quadrotor’s four-dimensional flat-output space, providing an analytically differentiable reference throughout each inference interval. When a delayed proposal arrives, the portion preceding the scheduled switch time is removed and the remaining segment is refitted to enforce high-order derivative continuity with the active reference. The fusion formulation enforces C 2 C^{2} continuity of the trajectory reference at switching boundaries while penalizing deviations from the retained prediction. To address the second gap, we introduce execution-aware post-training with group relative policy optimization (GRPO). We optimize the policy using trajectory-level rewards that measure agreement between the complete trajectories produced by asynchronous execution and expert demonstrations.

We design an asynchronous B-spline fusion mechanism that aligns delayed predictions with execution time and enforces C 2 C^{2} continuity at switching boundaries while limiting trajectory deformation.

We introduce GRPO post-training with trajectory-level rewards computed from asynchronously executed trajectories to improve agreement with expert demonstrations.

2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action for Drones

General-purpose VLA frameworks learn language-conditioned robot actions from
diverse embodied demonstrations [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . For UAVs, existing work spans long-horizon
language-guided navigation and fine-grained flight control.
AerialVLN [ 5 ] studies navigation toward a distant goal,
whereas UAV-Flow Colosseo [ 6 ] pairs individual flight
instructions with pilot demonstrations and trains VLA policies to predict
UAV poses. Its Flying-on-a-Word tasks require the flight path to follow the
spatial relationships specified by the instruction, making the executed path
relevant in addition to the final position.

Reinforcement learning extends VLA training beyond demonstration imitation.
SimpleVLA-RL [ 7 ] applies outcome-driven reinforcement
learning to OpenVLA-OFT, using online trajectory sampling and exploration to
improve manipulation performance and generalization. Its formulation provides
feedback on the consequences of sequential actions, rather than supervising
each prediction solely against demonstrated actions. In aerial navigation,
EG-GRPO [ 8 ] augments online rollouts with expert data to guide
exploration and improve alignment with fine-grained instructions.

These studies establish reinforcement learning as a means of improving
instruction-conditioned behavior, while AeroDASH focuses on the effect of
asynchronous execution on the resulting flight trajectory. The policy predicts
B-spline control points and receives GRPO updates from closed-loop trajectory
returns. This training objective evaluates successive predictions through
their execution outcomes, complementing the temporal alignment and trajectory
fusion discussed next.

## II-B Asynchronous Trajectory Execution

Optimization-based trajectory generation provides a foundation for continuous
UAV flight. Minimum-snap methods [ 9 ] penalize
high-order derivatives of polynomial trajectories to generate smooth motion
through prescribed waypoints. Richter et al. [ 10 ] develop an efficient formulation for jointly optimizing polynomial segments
and allocating their durations. MINCO [ 11 ] further supports
efficient trajectory optimization under geometric and dynamic constraints.
These methods optimize flight trajectories from planning objectives and
constraints; AeroDASH instead uses optimization to correct a trajectory
predicted by a language-conditioned policy while limiting changes to its shape.

Receding-horizon planners update trajectories as the flight state evolves.
B-spline-based systems exploit local support and analytic derivatives for
online kinodynamic replanning [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] , while FASTER [ 16 ] maintains a committed trajectory during successive planning cycles. These
mechanisms allow flight to continue during planning. For a VLA, however, a
prediction is conditioned on an earlier visual observation and may arrive
after part of its intended execution interval has elapsed. Maintaining an
executable trajectory during inference therefore does not by itself resolve
how the delayed prediction should be aligned and connected to it.

RTC and REMAC address asynchronous execution through action generation.
RTC [ 17 ] guides new predictions using overlapping actions,
whereas REMAC [ 18 ] learns delay-aware corrections and preserves
the executed prefix during sampling. Both promote consistency between
successive predictions, but neither explicitly imposes velocity and
acceleration matching at the switching boundary.

AeroDASH aligns delayed B-spline predictions with execution time and refits
the remaining curve to match the current reference’s position, velocity,
and acceleration while limiting deformation. GRPO post-training further
adapts the policy to asynchronous execution using closed-loop trajectory returns.
