2026-10-20.title: Energy-Score Stabilized Attentive Mixture-Density Policy: A Lightweight Approach to Multimodal Robot Motion
2026-10-20.authors: Sachiya Fujita , Hideyuki Ichiwara , Shigeki Sugano , Tetsuya Ogata
2026-10-20.abstract:
For practical
motion generation, it is essential to handle multimodality—multiple actions can be correct for the same observation—while maintaining low inference cost and strong generalization from limited demonstrations. We introduce an attentive mixture-density policy trained with the Energy Score that represents future visuomotor trajectories as explicit probability distributions with a single forward pass. Concretely, we output Gaussian mixture parameters for joint commands (and optionally attention points) and optimize them with the Energy Score
(computed as a sum of 1D CRPS under a diagonal covariance assumption)
instead of the negative log-likelihood (NLL) to avoid MDN singularities and gradient-scale instabilities. Our architecture couples explicit spatial attention with mixture-density outputs, enabling robust multimodal behavior selection under visual noise and small-data regimes. On an 8-DOF manipulator, the method generates distinct avoidance trajectories and stabilizes learning in obstacle avoidance. Moreover, in a randomized moving-object grasping task, where spatiotemporal multimodality and fast timing decisions are required, the proposed model outperforms Diffusion Policy by 15–25%
under several unseen conditions, demonstrating superior generalization and real-time feasibility.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Recent advances in imitation learning (IL) have pushed robot skill acquisition beyond laboratory benchmarks toward deployment on real robots. A key missing capability, however, is robust manipulation of randomly moving targets in real time—tasks that require continuous tracking, rapid timing decisions, and safe execution under strict onboard compute budgets.
Such capabilities are increasingly relevant for high-value applications in dynamic settings, including automated capture/restraint of laboratory animals, handling of moving specimens, and time-critical retrieval tasks, where environment dynamics and safety constraints make repeated re-planning or cloud computation impractical.

To enable these applications, IL methods must satisfy three requirements simultaneously: (i) low inference cost for resource-constrained robots, (ii) high generalization performance with limited demonstrations, and (iii) explicit handling of task multimodality, where multiple correct actions exist
per state. Multimodality arises both spatially (e.g., choosing left vs. right paths around an obstacle) and temporally (e.g., selecting grasp timing for periodic or irregular target motion). However, existing approaches often satisfy at most two
requirements. Deterministic regressors such as the Spatial Attention Point Network (SARNN) [ 1 ] achieve excellent data efficiency and lightweight inference but suffer from mode averaging in multimodal tasks [ 13 ] . Conversely, expressive probabilistic models such as diffusion-based policies [ 2 ] capture multimodality but require iterative sampling and substantially larger datasets, which can be prohibitive for real-time onboard control.

We propose an energy-score stabilized attentive mixture-density policy that enables real-time multimodal motion generation and long-horizon tracking from small datasets. Our method outputs Gaussian mixture parameters for future joint trajectories (and optionally attention points), allowing multiple candidate behaviors to be represented explicitly as a probability distribution.
Crucially, we replace Negative Log-Likelihood with the Energy Score
(implemented as a sum of independent CRPS terms for computational efficiency) [ 4 ] ,
evaluating
the distance between the predicted distribution and ground truth without variance-collapse singularities, thereby stabilizing MDN training in multimodal settings.
While our implementation leverages SARNN’s spatial attention mechanism for robust perception, the central contribution is a general and practical recipe: combining attentive state abstraction with energy-score–trained mixture-density
outputs for stable, low-cost multimodal control.

To validate the method, we conduct two real-robot experiments with an 8-DOF manipulator: obstacle avoidance (spatial multimodality) and grasping a randomly moving object (spatiotemporal multimodality). The latter demonstrates that our policy can track and intercept unpredictable target motion under unseen patterns and speed changes—an ability directly aligned with real-world dynamic manipulation demands.

The primary contributions are:

Energy-score stabilized Attentive MDN Policy: A lightweight policy framework that couples spatial attention with explicit mixture-density outputs for multimodal action generation.

Stable Multimodal Learning: Energy Score training that avoids MDN singularities and improves convergence when multimodal distributions and auxiliary reconstruction losses coexist.

Real-robot Dynamic Tracking: A randomized moving-object grasping benchmark on hardware, showing strong generalization under unseen trajectories and speeds with onboard real-time inference.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Robot behavior generation is broadly categorized into deterministic and probabilistic models. A representative deterministic model,
SARNN [ 1 ] , estimates spatial coordinates (attention points)
for the task
from input images and learns temporal variations alongside joint angles using a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). This approach enables efficient behavior learning by focusing on visually significant regions and exhibits high generalization performance against changes in object positions. Furthermore, the use of an RNN for the temporal model offers the advantages of extremely low inference costs and high generalization with limited data. However, deterministic regression suffers from an inherent ”averaging problem” when handling multimodal data where trajectories branch.
This
stems from
the L 2 L_{2} loss (MSE),
which converges to the conditional expectation E ⁡ [ y | x ] E[y|x] , potentially generating physically inappropriate actions
, like
moving straight toward an obstacle
at a bifurcation point.

Generative
models that treat output actions as probability distributions have been extensively studied. Urain et al. [ 5 ] categorized methods for representing multimodality into five groups and compared their characteristics: (1) Diffusion, (2) Sampling, (3) Energy-based, (4) Categorical, and (5) Mixture Density Models.

(1)
Diffusion models reconstruct distributions via iterative denoising
to offer
expressive, non-parametric multimodal modeling. Diffusion Policy [ 2 ] succeeds on complex tasks (e.g., Push-T), but iterative inference
is costly for
real-time dynamics; despite acceleration [ 6 , 7 ] ,
few-shot generalization is limited for
unseen speeds or placements.

(2) Sampling-based methods model complex distributions using latent variables. ACT [ 8 ] employs a CVAE to capture stochasticity and operator variability
, enabling high-precision manipulation (e.g., opening Ziploc bags). However, its continuous Gaussian latent space can blur discrete modes (e.g., left vs. right avoidance), often producing unnatural intermediate actions. Similarly, ActionFlow [ 9 ] applies Flow Matching [ 10 ] to joint-angle generation; however, due to FM’s strong linear constraint, it is prone to overfitting in low-data regimes, leading to degraded generalization [ 11 ] .

(3) Energy-Based Models (EBMs) [ 12 ] learn a function E θ ​ ( a , s ) E_{\theta}(a,s) assigning
a scalar
(energy) to a state s s and action a a . A representative application in imitation learning is Implicit Behavioral Cloning (IBC) [ 13 ] . While EBMs
allow
highly flexible distribution representation,
iterative optimization during inference
to find
action a a that minimizes energy results in
extremely
high computational load, becoming a bottleneck in real-time robot control.

(4) Categorical models (e.g., Behavior Transformer (BeT) [ 14 ] ) treat multimodal action selection as a classification problem over discrete indices. However, their expressive power depends on
the number of clusters, constraining flexible interpolation capabilities against environmental changes.

In contrast, (5) Mixture Density Models (MDNs) parameterize the output density as a Gaussian mixture (e.g., the behavior generation policy BC-RNN [ 15 ] with a GMM output layer [ 3 ] ), enabling low-cost one-pass inference. Compared to non-parametric diffusion models and discretized categorical approaches, MDNs provide a strong mixture-of-Gaussians inductive bias that is data-efficient and relatively hyperparameter-tolerant, since redundant components’ weights often shrink during training.

However, conventional BC-RNN structures directly input high-dimensional features processed by a CNN into the RNN without explicitly extracting object positions. Consequently, in small-data regimes, they are
vulnerable to visual noise (e.g., background changes, object misalignments)
leading to challenges in generalization. In contrast, SARNN [ 1 ] explicitly extracts ”spatial coordinates to be focused on” as attention points through its spatial attention mechanism, making it robust against environmental changes even with limited data. Therefore, integrating SARNN’s spatial recognition capabilities with the multimodal representation of MDNs is a rational approach to achieving advanced generalization with small datasets.

Nevertheless, while MDNs are structurally superior for representing multimodal action distributions, they face challenges in learning stability when using the Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss.
NLL is prone to numerical divergence (singularity problem) via variance minimization and causes scale and gradient mismatches with zero-bounded losses like MSE, complicating multimodal learning.
To address such instability, proper scoring rules—notably CRPS and its multivariate extension, the Energy Score (ES)—have been studied as objectives for probabilistic learning in other domains, including weather/forecasting (CRPS-based training) [ 16 ] and autonomous-driving trajectory distribution evaluation [ 17 ] .
In robotics, there also exist works that incorporate energy-score-based objectives or energy-based formulations for multimodal behavior learning [ 18 , 19 ] . However, to the best of our knowledge , prior robot motion-generation studies have not introduced ES/CRPS as a proper scoring-rule loss specifically to stabilize MDN (Gaussian-mixture) policies under multimodal sensory inputs .
Motivated by this gap, our research inherits the environmental robustness of SARNN’s spatial attention mechanism while introducing the Energy Score (ES), a multivariate generalization of CRPS [ 4 ] , as a loss function to stabilize MDN training. In our implementation, we assume diagonal-independent covariances, so ES can be optimized as a sum of closed-form one-dimensional Gaussian CRPS terms (and their mixture extension) [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . This design stabilizes variance convergence and fundamentally avoids the singularity problem. Furthermore, because it is based on the expectation of distances, it possesses high mathematical affinity with MSE, enabling stable convergence and high generalization in multimodal visuomotor policy learning that combines spatial attention with mixture density models.

2026-10-20.title: TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models
2026-10-20.authors: Yuxiang Lu , Yantong Liu , Jinghua Hou , Xueli Sun , Ruihua Han , Zhe Liu , Hengshuang Zhao
2026-10-20.abstract:
Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with
strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in
generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining
requires substantial robot data and computation. To transfer these
capabilities from pretrained EFMs to policies without action pretraining,
we introduce TILDE ( T eacher- I n-the- L oop D istillation from E FMs), which synergizes on-policy
distillation at student-induced states with learning from teacher-executed
recovery trajectories. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data
aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task
progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience
without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates
recovery-trajectory collection by more than 2 × 2\times compared with the
human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy
teacher supervision, and teacher’s corrective behavior, TILDE improves
task performance by up to 4.1 × 4.1\times over behavior cloning across three
real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs), including Vision-Language-Action (VLA)
models ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Shao et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2024 ; Sapkota et al., 2025 ) ,
have demonstrated remarkable manipulation capabilities and generalization. However,
these capabilities often rely on action pretraining on large-scale robot
datasets ( Bu et al., 2025 ; Padalkar et al., 2024 ; Walke et al., 2023 ; Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) , making it costly to
endow new policy architectures, particularly efficient models, with
comparable capabilities ( Yu et al., 2025 ; Guan et al., 2025 ) . Reproducing
foundation-scale pretraining requires access to sufficiently diverse, high-quality
robot data and substantial computational resources, which is prohibitively
expensive in many research and deployment settings.

Policies without large-scale action pretraining ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Community, 2026 ) can still achieve competitive performance on standard simulation benchmarks such
as LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Object ( Liu et al., 2023 ) . However, our pilot study
suggests that this apparent parity does not consistently extend to more
challenging settings. As shown in Figure 1 , substantially larger
gaps emerge on long-horizon tasks in LIBERO-10, under visual and robot-initial-state
perturbations ( Fei et al., 2025 ) , and in real-world tasks. These
observations are consistent with action pretraining providing benefits
beyond nominal action prediction, particularly improved closed-loop robustness
under challenging and out-of-distribution conditions. This motivates a
natural question: Can such capabilities be transferred from a
pretrained EFM to a student policy without repeating expensive action
pretraining?

Policy distillation offers an intuitive route by transferring teacher knowledge
in a task-specific domain ( Rusu et al., 2015 ; Dong et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) .
However, for closed-loop policies, effective distillation depends not only on what actions are supervised, but also on where supervision is
provided. When distillation is restricted to a fixed demonstration dataset ( Figure 1 (a)),
supervision remains concentrated on the nominal distribution. During closed-loop
deployment, compounding student errors and environmental stochasticity can drive
the policy into out-of-distribution states. This distribution mismatch
between training and inference leaves the student insufficiently prepared to
handle execution deviations ( Yan et al., 2026 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) .

Interactive imitation learning mitigates this mismatch by querying expert supervision
at states induced by the learner ( Ross et al., 2011 ) . In On-Policy Distillation (OPD) ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2023 ) ,
the student interacts with the environment while the teacher provides action
targets at student-visited states ( Figure 1 (b)). This expands supervision
to student-induced rollout states, but the queried teacher actions are not
executed ( Zhong et al., 2026 ; Wan et al., 2026 ) . Consequently, OPD does not
observe the subsequent states that would arise following the teacher’s correction.
Human-in-the-loop approaches such as HG-DAgger ( Kelly et al., 2019 ) ( Figure 1 (c))
can collect recovery trajectories but require continuous human monitoring
and teleoperated takeover ( Murray et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) ,
severely limiting data scalability.

To address these limitations, we introduce TILDE ( T eacher- I n-the- L oop D istillation from E FMs), a policy distillation framework
that transfers teacher knowledge over three complementary data distributions:
human demonstration, student-induced rollouts, and recovery trajectories ( Figure 1 (d)).
Central to TILDE is AutoDAgger, an autonomous teacher-in-the-loop data
aggregation pipeline. An off-the-shelf robotic reward model monitors student
execution, while the execution manager uses its feedback to trigger
intervention, after which the EFM teacher directly takes control and executes
a recovery trajectory toward task completion. Automated progress monitoring
removes the need for expensive human oversight, while teacher policy takeover
avoids the reaction and teleoperation overhead of human intervention,
substantially enhancing recovery-data collection throughput.

Given the aggregated data, TILDE applies supervision according to the sample
source. Offline demonstrations and teacher recovery trajectories provide
both behavior-cloning targets from executed actions and teacher distillation
targets, while student rollout states use on-policy teacher supervision only.
Importantly, all distillation is performed directly in the common action space
and requires no alignment of internal representations, allowing the
framework to accommodate heterogeneous teacher and student architectures.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate policy distillation from a distributional perspective
and propose the TILDE framework, which jointly transfers teacher
knowledge over offline demonstrations, student-induced rollouts, and
teacher-generated recovery experience.

We introduce AutoDAgger, an autonomous teacher-in-the-loop data
aggregation pipeline that expands the training distribution through
automatic task monitoring and teacher takeover, enabling efficient recovery-data
collection while bypassing expensive human involvement.

Extensive experiments on real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate
that TILDE improves student performance by up to 4.1 × 4.1\times over behavior
cloning, consistently outperforms offline and on-policy distillation,
and enables effective cross-architecture capability transfer.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Recent advances in large-scale robot learning have given rise to Embodied Foundation
Models (EFMs) that integrate visual perception, language understanding, and low-level
control, showing impressive performance across a broad spectrum of dexterous
tasks and improved generalization to diverse environments ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Shao et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2024b ) .
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models directly map multimodal observations and
language instructions to robot actions ( Intelligence et al., 2025a ; Intelligence et al., 2026 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Fan et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) .
An emerging alternative is the World Action Model (WAM), which jointly models
future world states and robot actions, rather than relying solely on
reactive observation-to-action prediction ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026b ) .
Despite their strong capabilities, training such foundation models from scratch
requires substantial data and computational resources. Our work instead
studies how the capabilities of a pretrained EFM can be transferred to a
student policy without repeating foundation-scale pretraining.

Knowledge Distillation (KD) transfers predictions or representations from a
teacher to a smaller student and is widely used for model compression and
capability transfer ( Hinton et al., 2015 ; Buciluǎ et al., 2006 ) . Policy
distillation extends this paradigm to robot learning ( Rusu et al., 2015 ; Torne et al., 2024 ; Dong et al., 2025 ; Shao et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) ,
with recent advances leveraging foundation models as teachers ( Jülg et al., 2025 ) .
Existing methods perform distillation through model-level alignment ( Jeon et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) or teacher-generated data and supervision ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2024a ) .
On-Policy Distillation (OPD) further queries teacher supervision on student-induced
states rather than relying solely on a fixed offline dataset ( Agarwal et al., 2024 ; Agarwal et al., 2023 ) ,
providing corrective signals where the student tends to encounter uncertainty
or make mistakes ( Zhong et al., 2026 ; Wan et al., 2026 ) . Our method extends
OPD by executing teacher takeover after intervention, thereby collecting the
subsequent recovery trajectory and providing direct supervision for
returning from off-nominal states to successful task execution.

Imitation learning suffers from distribution shift when the learned policy
encounters states absent from expert demonstrations. Interactive imitation learning
mitigates this issue by querying an expert on learner-induced states and iteratively
aggregating the resulting supervision ( Ross et al., 2011 ) . Subsequent methods reduce
expert queries using predicted novice–expert discrepancy ( Hoque et al., 2021b ) ,
policy uncertainty ( Menda et al., 2019 ; Kelly et al., 2019 ; Zurbrügg et al., 2026 ) ,
or estimates of state novelty and task risk ( Cronrath et al., 2018 ; Hoque et al., 2021a ) .
However, these approaches generally depend on policy-specific techniques or continuous
human oversight, and still request human teleoperation for corrective
takeover on physical robots ( Murray et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . In
contrast, we propose a novel data aggregation framework that automatically detects
intervention needs and executes corrective actions, substantially reducing
the human-effort bottleneck in interactive data collection.

2026-10-20.title: Vision as Proprioception: Estimating Humanoid Robot Pose from Video
2026-10-20.authors: Jiaxi Jiang , Matthias Heyrman , René Zurbrügg , Marco Hutter , Christian Holz
2026-10-20.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-20.abstract:
Estimating a humanoid robot’s internal state from video has a wide range of real-world applications but remains unexplored. During interactions with a robot, its onboard state information may be unavailable due to privacy, ownership, or communication constraints.
Meanwhile, online and AI-generated robot videos provide rich sources of data but typically lack corresponding joint configurations, limiting their direct use in robot learning.
To address these issues, we present HumanoidPose, a new framework that treats vision as proprioception to recover full-body joint configurations in world space from video alone.
Specifically, we combine pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics in a unified model that predicts each embodiment’s joint configurations.
We retarget human motions to sixteen different humanoid embodiments, enabling scalable learning entirely from synthetic data.
To improve real-world generalization, we further leverage unlabeled online videos through self-training to develop a 2D robot-pose detector.
In our evaluation, HumanoidPose improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over the evaluated baselines and reduces joint-angle error by 18 18 – 32 % 32\% relative to the best-performing baseline on each of the three real humanoid platforms.
We further show improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments.
HumanoidPose enables visual understanding of other robots during interaction and extraction of robot motion from online and generated videos.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Understanding and interacting with humanoid robots requires interpreting how their bodies move. People and other robots may need to anticipate a reaching arm, recognize an action, or coordinate with the robot. Although onboard sensors measure the robot’s configuration, privacy, ownership, or communication constraints may prevent access to these measurements, making vision the primary means for an external observer to recover it. The same need extends to learning from video: online robot videos capture motion in varied environments without accompanying joint-state logs, while AI-generated videos provide candidate motion demonstrations with no physical robot or encoder measurements at all. Together with real-robot recordings and synthetic videos, these sources motivate recovering articulated robot motion directly from visual observations (Fig. ). Expressing this motion in the robot’s joint coordinates makes it available for analysis, prediction, and learning.

We study visual proprioception for humanoid robots: recovering full-body joint configurations in world space from ordinary video without access to onboard state. This setting introduces several challenges. Humanoids differ in body proportions, joint layouts, and mechanical limits, requiring an estimator that can accommodate different kinematic structures and output spaces. Occlusion and monocular depth ambiguity make articulation underdetermined from appearance alone, calling for learned priors that generalize across embodiments, motions, and visual conditions. Recovering world-space trajectories further requires separating robot motion from camera motion.

Learning these priors requires large-scale data pairing images with robot configurations
across motions, embodiments, and environments. Such data are difficult to obtain:
collecting encoder-synchronized footage across many platforms is costly.
Existing robot pose estimators address
articulated manipulators [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , but humanoid motion recovery
requires full-body estimation across robot designs and appearances.
Human mesh recovery offers a way to reuse priors learned from extensive human
imagery [ 4 , 5 ] : estimate a human pose and retarget it to the
robot [ 6 ] . However, human articulation differs from robot articulation,
and retargeting can amplify prediction errors. We instead transfer pretrained human-pose
features to directly predict robot joint poses.

We present HumanoidPose , a framework for recovering full-body robot pose
and world-space motion from video. Its key design is a shared decoder that combines
frozen human-pretrained image features with queries derived from robot kinematics to
predict joint configurations and root pose across embodiments. We combine the
predicted root pose with estimated camera motion to recover world-space trajectories.
Queries follow each robot’s joint layout, allowing a shared decoder and prediction head.

Our synthetic pipeline retargets motions from the Archive of Motion Capture as
Surface Shapes (AMASS) [ 7 ] to sixteen humanoids using General Motion
Retargeting (GMR) [ 6 ] and renders paired images and robot states under varied
conditions. These data supervise the pose decoder and initialize a YOLO11-based detector
for robot boxes and 2D keypoints, and unlabeled online videos further adapt this detector. Across three real platforms,
the unified model improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over the
evaluated baselines.

Our contributions are:

We formulate visual proprioception for humanoid robots, the problem of recovering full-body joint configurations and world-space motion from video without access to onboard state.

We introduce a unified, kinematically conditioned model for 3D robot pose estimation that predicts joint configurations and root pose across humanoid embodiments without robot-specific prediction heads.

We generate 128,000 128{,}000 synthetic images across sixteen humanoids with paired 2D and 3D labels to train the 3D pose model and a 2D detector, further adapting the detector through self-training on online videos.

We evaluate HumanoidPose on three real humanoid platforms, demonstrating improved joint-angle and joint-position accuracy, improved root translation on G1, and transfer and adaptation to unseen embodiments.

1. We formulate visual proprioception for humanoid robots, the problem of recovering full-body joint configurations and world-space motion from video without access to onboard state.

2. We introduce a unified, kinematically conditioned model for 3D robot pose estimation that predicts joint configurations and root pose across humanoid embodiments without robot-specific prediction heads.

3. We generate 128,000 128{,}000 synthetic images across sixteen humanoids with paired 2D and 3D labels to train the 3D pose model and a 2D detector, further adapting the detector through self-training on online videos.

4. We evaluate HumanoidPose on three real humanoid platforms, demonstrating improved joint-angle and joint-position accuracy, improved root translation on G1, and transfer and adaptation to unseen embodiments.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Robot Pose Estimation. Camera-to-robot calibration methods such as
DREAM and PoseFusion combine image keypoints with known 3D robot keypoint locations to
estimate the camera transform [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Recovering unknown joint
states additionally requires estimating articulation, addressed through rendering-based
refinement in RoboPose and GISR [ 1 , 11 , 12 ] , geometric lifting [ 13 , 14 ] ,
and feed-forward regression in HoRoPose [ 2 ] . More recent methods such as
RoboPEPP and RoboTAG learn visual representations that reflect robot articulation [ 3 , 15 , 16 ] .
For humanoids, Amini et al. and Heo et
al. [ 17 , 18 ] estimate 2D image keypoints across robot platforms, without
recovering full 3D articulation or actuated joint configurations. In contrast, HumanoidPose
estimates full-body 3D humanoid robot poses in robot coordinates across embodiments.

Human Pose and Motion Estimation. Parametric body models and image
fitting [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] underpin learned body recovery [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] , while
kinematic formulations connect joint positions and body rotations [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] .
SAM 3D Body [ 28 ] supports keypoint and mask prompts for single-image body
recovery. Video methods progress from temporal motion priors [ 29 ] to global motion
reconstruction [ 30 , 31 ] . WHAM and TRAM [ 32 , 33 ] explicitly account for
camera motion, while GVHMR [ 34 ] uses gravity-view coordinates.
PromptHMR [ 5 ] incorporates spatial and semantic prompts into full-image
SMPL-X recovery and extends to temporally coherent reconstruction from video.
Complementary approaches combine egocentric tracking and exocentric observations
for full-body motion capture [ 35 ] .
However, humanoid morphology, joint limits and actuated coordinates make human-body
representations indirect for robot-state recovery. HumanoidPose directly estimates
robot joint coordinates and world-space motion from video.

Synthetic Data and Sim-to-Real Transfer. Synthetic human data [ 36 ] and
domain randomization [ 37 ] establish rendering as a source of visual supervision.
Motion archives [ 7 ] and increasingly realistic datasets [ 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 , 42 ] broaden coverage of appearance, motion, and scenes, while procedural
tools [ 43 ] automate rendering and annotation. Rendered robot images and adaptation
techniques also support transfer to real robot observations [ 8 , 1 , 9 , 18 ] .
Motion retargeting [ 44 ] further connects human motion resources to new embodiments,
supporting humanoid control and imitation [ 45 , 46 , 47 , 48 ] . Recent pipelines
such as UH-1 and GMR retarget human motion capture and internet videos into humanoid robot references [ 49 , 6 ] ,
showing that human motion priors can provide scalable supervision for humanoid behaviors.
We combine retargeted motions with robot-specific rendering to pair images with the exact joint
configurations used to generate them. This directly supervises actuated coordinates, enabling
our decoder to train entirely on synthetic images and transfer to real robot videos.

2026-10-20.title: The Bitter Lesson Comes to Robotics
2026-10-20.authors: Christopher Leet , Achyutha Menon , Sravanthi Machcha , Sven Koenig , Tzu Kit Chan , Jay Chooi
2026-10-20.comment: Submitted to the Workshop on The Action Gap (TAG) at CoRL 2026
2026-10-20.abstract: General purpose multimodal language models (LMs) are increasingly capable of directly controlling robotic arms (e.g., by commanding end effector poses) to manipulate their environment. Tracking the development of these capabilities is important for understanding their potential benefits, such as improving industrial automation, and risks, such as enabling malicious users to produce dangerous chemical or biological agents. To this end, we investigate the ability of frontier multimodal LMs to directly control physical robotic arms. We evaluate seven models at multiple reasoning-effort settings on six manipulation tasks taken from the RoboDojo benchmark. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison of a broad range of frontier LMs across a common suite of manipulation tasks on physical hardware. We find that current frontier models can directly control real robotic arms to perform a variety of manipulation tasks but are not yet precise or efficient enough to complete them within a practical action budget. However, these capabilities are improving rapidly: performance increases on our benchmark between July and September 2026 (inclusive) correspond to a performance doubling time of 44.5 days, while the best recorded execution rate increased by a factor of 4.4 and the lowest recorded execution cost fell by a factor of 6.2. These trends raise the possibility that the Bitter Lesson is coming to robotics; the capabilities of embodied general purpose LMs may one day be comparable to those of more specialized models.
2026-10-20.introduction:
General purpose multimodal language models (LMs) are increasingly capable of manipulating physical environments by directly controlling robotic arms. For example, Zhang et al. [ 13 ] demonstrate that GPT-6 Astra can grasp a variety of objects by specifying successive end-effector targets, that is, positions, orientations, and openings for the robot’s grippers. Tracking the growth of these capabilities is important for understanding their potential benefits and risks.

To date, however, evaluations of LM manipulation capabilities on physical hardware have either focused on a small number of models or compared multiple models on only one or two manipulation tasks. Systematic comparisons of multiple models on multiple tasks run in the real world remain scarce. Simulation, however, may not fully capture physical effects such as calibration drift, camera parallax, and arm sag, which can substantially affect model performance. Moreover, evaluating a range of models on the same tasks and hardware is essential for tracking capability improvements.

We address this gap by evaluating seven frontier LMs’ performance, inference costs, and execution rate on six manipulation tasks from the RoboDojo benchmark using a real I2RT YAM bimanual robot [ 5 ] . We capture partial progress by dividing each task into a series of subtasks and scoring models based on the subtasks that they completed. Subtasks provide a more granular measure of performance than task success and allow us to identify specific manipulations that models struggle to complete. We measure inference cost and execution rate in terms of average cost per subtask and average subtasks completed per hour. These metrics allow us to draw conclusions about model efficiency from partially completed tasks.

We find that frontier models can directly control robotic arms to perform a variety of physical manipulation tasks, but are currently not precise or efficient enough to complete them reliably within a practical action budget. We also find, however, that performance is improving rapidly. Performance increases on our benchmark from July through September 2026 correspond to a performance doubling time of 44.5 days. Moreover, the best recorded subtask completion rate increased by 4.4 × 4.4\times and the lowest recorded inference costs per subtask decreased by 6.2 × 6.2\times over that period. This suggests that, in the near future, the performance, cost and execution time achieved by general purpose multimodal LMs may be comparable to those of specialized robotic systems: The Bitter Lesson [ 11 ] may be coming to robotics.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Evaluating the Manipulation Capabilities of Embodied General-Purpose LMs. Several recent studies evaluate whether frontier multimodal LMs can directly control robotic hardware. Zhang et al. [ 13 ] study whether GPT-6 Astra, GPT-5.5 Sol, and DeepSeek-Flash can control bimanual robots via end-effector pose commands. They evaluate these models on all 42 tasks in the RoboDojo [ 2 ] benchmark in simulation and find that Astra outperforms all 40 published robot policy entries. They also test Astra on real robotic arms but halt the experiments after 33 recorded trials because Astra repeatedly commanded unsafe actions, leading to hardware damage.

Jia et al. [ 6 ] evaluate GPT-6 Astra on eight task configurations of five manipulation tasks, including assembly, targeted throwing, and towel folding, using physical I2RT YAM [ 5 ] robotic arms. They allow Astra both to command joint-space or Cartesian end-effector targets directly and to write and execute Python programs that compute and submit motion commands. They find that Astra achieves success rates of at least 80% in seven of eight task configurations, although execution is expensive and slow (tens of minutes and dollars). They additionally compare Astra with five other models on a two-pair assembly task and find that it achieves a 100% success rate (along with GPT-5.6 and Opus 5) and achieves the shortest mean completion time (only counting successful trials). On a block construction task, Astra achieves a higher success rate than GPT-5.6 Sol.

Berman et al. [ 1 ] evaluate 12 models’ performance in manipulation (e.g., moving objects), locomotion (e.g., balancing a Unitree Go2 quadruped [ 12 ] ), and classical control (e.g., pendulum balancing) in simulation. Their manipulation experiments use 40 tasks from the LIBERO [ 10 ] benchmark and a seven-DoF Franka Panda [ 4 ] arm. They also perform exploratory experiments using a real Unitree Go2 quadruped, primarily centered on navigation. They study both direct control (where their models issue low-level actions) and indirect control (where their models code, train, and direct policies). They find that direct control is improving but remains unreliable compared to indirect control.

While these studies demonstrate that general-purpose LMs can control robots, systematic comparisons of their ability to perform manipulation tasks on physical hardware remain limited. Such evaluations are important because physical robots often have imperfections such as sag, calibration drift, and positioning scatter, which may not be accurately captured in simulation. In this paper, we evaluate the ability of frontier LMs to directly control physical robotic arms. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison of a broad range of frontier LMs across a common suite of manipulation tasks on physical hardware. We evaluate seven models in twelve configurations on six tasks from RoboDojo. We use the same embodiment and experimental interfaces for each evaluation, allowing us to compare performance, execution time, and cost under shared experimental conditions.

Tracking the Capabilities of LMs. Our analysis of progress over time is inspired by prior work tracking capability improvements. Kwa et al. [ 8 ] track how the length of the software tasks that LM agents can complete at a given success rate increases over time. They use the time required for human experts to complete each task to define its length. We track how manipulation capabilities are increasing over time. We measure progress as performance on a set of physical tasks.

Performance alone does not determine an agent’s practical usefulness. Kapoor et al. [ 7 ] argue that agent evaluations should also measure cost since this often affects which systems are preferable. We apply this perspective to robotic control by evaluating performance, cost, and wall-clock time, allowing us to characterize the tradeoffs between these three dimensions.

2026-10-20.title: GOFusion: Real-Time Gaussian-Occupancy Submap Fusion for Fisher-Informed Autonomous Robot Navigation
2026-10-20.authors: Boxin Bu , Simon Boche , Haoming Zhang , Jaehyung Jung , Jiaxin Wei , Hannah Schieber , Daniel Roth , Angela P. Schoellig , Stefan Leutenegger
2026-10-20.abstract: In this letter, we present GOFusion , a real-time visual mapping system for autonomous robot navigation that anchors Gaussian primitives to local occupancy maps, providing both spatial awareness for path planning and high-fidelity appearance that enables information-driven robot navigation. GOFusion builds 3D Gaussian maps from pose estimates and local occupancy maps obtained via visual-inertial slam ( slam ) and enables pose corrections to maintain both geometric and visual consistency. Furthermore, it restricts the 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization to active submaps to bound GPU memory usage. Building on the appearance-rich Gaussian map, we introduce a rasterizer-integrated Fisher approximation that quantifies per-primitive sensitivity online, serving as an information-driven heuristic for Gaussian pruning and next-best-view planning. We evaluate GOFusion on public datasets and in real-world drone flights. It not only outperforms several baselines in mapping quality, but also achieves real-time, high-fidelity and uncertainty-aware mapping at scale. Finally, we demonstrate fully autonomous drone exploration for Gaussian map refinement using the proposed Fisher-informed heuristic. Code is available at https://github.com/Bennnoo/GOFusion . We provide a supplementary video demonstration at https://youtu.be/pLQKbxQvb6I .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Autonomous robots need maps that support safe motion, reliable localization, and visual understanding in unknown environments. Occupancy maps [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] distinguish between free, occupied, and unknown space so that planners can check collisions, extract frontiers [ 4 ] , and generate paths in large environments [ 5 ] .
Such maps, however, encode geometry alone and discard appearance, whereas advanced tasks such as inspection and human-robot interaction require detailed scene appearance.

Radiance field map representations address this limitation, either by implicitly encoding the scene in a neural network [ 6 ] or by explicitly optimizing Gaussian primitives via 3dgs ( 3dgs ) [ 7 ] . While the former relies on dense per-ray sampling of an implicit field and therefore remains costly to train and query, 3dgs supports efficient rendering via rasterization of an explicit set of primitives and is therefore better suited to online mapping. However, vanilla 3dgs maps describe only observed surfaces and do not distinguish free space from potentially occupied space, which is unsafe for robot navigation.

In principle, combining occupancy and Gaussian maps yields a complementary hybrid representation, in which an occupancy layer supports free-space reasoning, completeness assessment, and planning, while a Gaussian layer provides high-fidelity appearance. However, existing systems realize only half of this potential. GSFusion [ 9 ] and GPS-SLAM [ 10 ] exploit this coupling in one direction, predominantly using the geometric map to improve the reconstruction quality and efficiency rather than to support robot localization and navigation. Therefore, a hybrid representation that directly supports navigation remains an open challenge.

To address this challenge, we propose GOFusion , a real-time hybrid Gaussian-and-occupancy mapping system for autonomous robot navigation. GOFusion is built directly on a real-time visual-inertial slam system, OKVIS2-X [ 11 ] , and inherits its state estimates and occupancy submaps. However, unlike previous reconstruction-oriented methods, we close the loop between the two map layers. While the occupancy submaps anchor and initialize the Gaussians, photometric optimization of 3dgs , in turn, refines the camera poses, thereby reducing pose jitter and improving map consistency. Our submap-local design keeps online optimization scalable, since trainable states are maintained only for active submaps. Beyond geometry and appearance, we further accumulate Fisher information from the Gaussian primitives to identify poorly-constrained map regions, providing an information-theoretic heuristic for trajectory planning that enables the robot to actively complete its own map. Fig. 1 presents the performance of our method compared to various baselines.

To our knowledge, GOFusion is the first hybrid Gaussian-occupancy mapping system that supports real-time 3D navigation outdoors from cameras and an IMU alone. The contributions of this paper are:

A submap-based 3D Gaussian representation for large-scale high-fidelity mapping that supports appearance-dependent tasks such as inspection and teleoperation alongside navigation, where slam pose-graph updates, including loop closures, also directly update both the occupancy and Gaussian layers.

A submap-based 3D Gaussian representation for large-scale high-fidelity mapping that supports appearance-dependent tasks such as inspection and teleoperation alongside navigation, where slam pose-graph updates, including loop closures, also directly update both the occupancy and Gaussian layers.

A rasterizer-integrated online Fisher approximation that maintains a diagonal, accumulated Fisher information over all Gaussians at negligible cost. Serving as an information heuristic for robot exploration, it highlights another key methodological advantage of Gaussian mapping in robotics.

A real-time navigation framework that integrates visual-inertial SLAM with our hybrid map, deployable either fully onboard or split across onboard and offboard compute for resource-limited platforms.

Real-world UAV experiments demonstrate GOFusion ’s online capabilities and how Fisher information can be used in Gaussian pruning and next-best-view selection.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Volumetric Mapping for Robot Navigation

Volumetric representations have dominated robot mapping for decades. Occupancy maps [ 1 ] explicitly distinguish free, occupied, and unknown space, supporting collision checking, frontier extraction [ 4 ] , and navigation under partial observation [ 12 ] . tsdf ( tsdf )- and sdf ( sdf )-based systems such as [ 13 , 14 ] instead target continuous surface reconstruction. They encode distance to the nearest observed surface, so unobserved volume is not separated from free space by the representation itself and must be handled by convention. Octree frameworks such as [ 3 ] improve scalability through hierarchical subdivision. These methods scale in space but not in time, since a globally parameterized map must be re-optimized whenever loop closure revises past poses.

Submap-based SLAM resolves this issue by integrating measurements into local maps, whose poses are frequently updated during graph optimization, improving global map consistency across all maps. This concept lends itself to exploration in large environments, where local submaps enable efficient updates while still supporting global planning [ 5 ] .
OKVIS2-X [ 11 ] follows this direction for multi-sensor state estimation with occupancy submapping and submap alignment. Because pose corrections act at the submap level, the occupancy map remains directly available for planning throughout.

These advantages, however, concern geometry alone. As occupancy quantifies uncertainty about space, not appearance, a surface can be reliable for collision avoidance yet unusable for inspection or human-robot collaboration.

## II-B Gaussian Mapping for Robot Navigation

A more recent line of work in mapping replaces volumetric structures with explicit, addable, prunable, and rigidly transformable Gaussian primitives. Moreover, they are also differentiable under a fast rasterizer. Supervision is derived directly from image intensities, so every pixel contributes a residual [ 7 ] . Dense visual SLAM systems exploit this to jointly optimize camera poses and Gaussian primitives [ 15 , 16 ] , or to embed Gaussians in online pipelines through selective primitive updates, conventional frontends, and RGB-D alignment [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . Others pair Gaussian maps with dedicated planners or semantic objectives for closed-loop navigation [ 20 , 21 ] . Hybrid systems go one step further: previous work [ 9 , 10 ] use tsdf geometry to guide Gaussian insertion and suppress redundant primitives, although the geometry serves reconstruction rather than a trajectory planner.

At the robot scale, Gaussian SLAM faces two further obstacles. A single global Gaussian map carries optimizer states, gradients, and rendering buffers that grow with scene size, and, once built, cannot easily adopt pose corrections. LoopSplat [ 22 ] addresses the second by organizing Gaussians into submaps that loop closure can rigidly transform, while DiskChunGS [ 23 ] addresses the first with disk-backed chunking. Neither, however, maintains an occupancy representation for downstream robotic tasks.

## II-C Uncertainty-Aware Mapping for Robot Navigation

Mapping to support real-world robot navigation, however, requires more than geometry and appearance, since the robot must also decide where to go next. Frontier-based exploration [ 4 , 5 ] exposes unknown regions, but is blind to observed regions where the appearance model remains poorly constrained. Neural and Gaussian methods therefore study uncertainty-aware view selection, using Fisher information [ 24 ] or related visibility and information-gain signals [ 25 , 26 ] to improve reconstruction quality. A second line keeps uncertainty inside the estimator, reweighting tracking, registration, and loop constraints [ 27 ] .

Closest to our setting, μ \mu SLAM [ 28 ] maintains a per-primitive confidence and plans on an occupancy grid projected from its Gaussian field. Its uncertainty never enters the planner, and the projected grid supports no planning beyond the ground plane.
None of these systems, however, couples map uncertainty with the free-space reasoning required for real-time robot exploration. This motivates GOFusion ’s unified hybrid map representation that keeps Gaussian optimization local to the active submap while exposing a per-primitive uncertainty for downstream decisions.

2026-10-20.title: AI-Enhanced Radiation Classification in ROS
2026-10-20.authors: Youngseo Lee , Cesar Alan Contreras , Tianshu Ruan , Manolis Chiou , Rustam Stolkin
2026-10-20.abstract: This study presents the development of two Robot Operating System (ROS) nodes with a primary focus on differentiating seven radioactive isotopes. The first node, referred to as the model training node, uses a Gradient Boosting classifier to identify and classify these isotopes. The classifier achieved a reported overall accuracy of 95% on the held-out test dataset. The second node, known as the prediction node, provides classification results when users input data in CSV format. For the practical demonstration, the C12137 radiation detector module was mounted on the Jackal UGV, and an operator approached different radiation sources to collect data. To support future dataset expansion, we also developed a method for converting gamma-spectrum graph images into CSV files. In a separate robotic evaluation across three source locations, 30 of 42 trials were correctly classified (71.43%). Am-241, Co-60, Cs-137, Na-22, and Ti-44 were correctly classified in all six trials each, whereas Ba-133 and Eu-152 were incorrectly classified in all six trials each. These results show lower accuracy in robotic trials than in the held-out test set.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Detecting and classifying radioactive isotopes is important in nuclear decommissioning and robotics because isotope identification can inform source handling and operational decisions. Although recent work has demonstrated that training spectra can be generated by combining simulated isotope spectra with measured background spectra, developing labeled datasets that represent a broader range of isotopes and environmental conditions remains challenging [ 1 ] .

In this study, we use a self-collected dataset comprising measured spectra from seven radioactive isotopes to investigate isotope classification in a robotic radiation-detection setting. We developed two Robot Operating System (ROS) nodes: a model-training node using a Gradient Boosting classifier and a prediction node that processes spectrum data in CSV format and provides isotope classifications. We also developed a method for converting gamma-spectrum graph images into CSV files to support the incorporation of additional spectral data in future work.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews previous research and provides context for our study. In Section III , we describe data collection, machine-learning methods, ROS-node development, gamma-spectrum graph-image conversion, and robotic testing. Section IV presents the classifier comparison and robotic-evaluation results. Finally, Section V summarizes our findings and suggests directions for future work.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Literature Review

## II-A Synthetic Datasets and Radiation Analysis

In the domain of machine learning model training, the creation of accurate synthetic datasets is crucial. A. C. Jones et al. [ 4 ] evaluated spectroscopic anomaly-detection and isotope-identification algorithms using a synthetic urban search dataset. Similarly, L. Lee-Brewin et al. [ 1 ] generated training spectra by combining simulated isotope spectra with measured background spectra from the SIGMA dataset. They evaluated their model using both simulated spectra and real spectra from SIGMA. Together, these studies illustrate the use of synthetic gamma-ray data in isotope-identification research.

## II-B Data Conversion Techniques Relevant to Nuclear Applications

Recent work on extracting information from figures and documents has produced methods that may be relevant to gamma-spectrum digitization. Research by Gemelli et al. [ 5 ] , which applies graph neural networks to table extraction from PDF documents, shows progress in transforming document content into more accessible formats, enhancing data analysis and application usability. The application of the metaDigitise R package for extracting descriptive statistics from images of common plot types is another noteworthy development, contributing to improved data analysis [ 6 ] . An OpenCV-based computer-vision system for character extraction from images provides another example of visual information extraction [ 7 ] . Additionally, GFTE addresses financial-table extraction from digital files, offering a related example of structured data extraction [ 8 ] . The method developed by Hamlin for extracting data points from vector graphics to analyze electrical-resistance data is also relevant to graph digitization [ 9 ] . Together, these studies illustrate a range of approaches to extracting and digitizing information from figures and documents, providing relevant context for the gamma-spectrum graph-image conversion method investigated in this study.

## II-C Artificial Intelligence in Isotope Identification

Machine learning methods have been applied to radioactive-isotope identification. J. Stinnett’s research [ 10 ] developed a peak-based Bayesian classifier for automated isotope identification using low-resolution gamma-ray spectra. In a related nuclear application, Braden Burt et al. [ 11 ] applied machine learning and deep learning methods to magnetic-field sensor data to classify the High Flux Isotope Reactor’s ON/OFF operational status; the DNN achieved 95.70% balanced accuracy for cycle 488.

Complementing these developments, studies have stressed the capabilities of artificial neural networks in isotope identification. M. Park et al. [ 12 ] introduced a deep learning-based radionuclide identification algorithm, while L. Lee-Brewin et al. [ 13 ] developed a convolutional neural network for multi-isotope detection. M. J. Neuer and C. Henke [ 14 ] proposed an autoencoder-based method for identifying marker isotopes in special nuclear materials. However, developing large and representative gamma-ray spectral datasets remains challenging for isotope identification [ 10 , 13 ] . Our study contributes a dataset comprising spectra from seven isotopes and a method for converting gamma-spectrum graph images into CSV files, which may support future dataset expansion.

## II-D Advancements in ROS for Nuclear Applications

Integrating advanced technologies with the ROS supports practical mobile-robot applications. H. Ahmad et al.’s research [ 15 ] shows the use of ROS for environment modeling and mobile-robot position estimation under uncertain conditions. Separately, Ye et al. [ 16 ] developed a neural network combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to generate robot actions based on current and historical scenes and robot movements.This historical context enables the network to use past observations when selecting actions to obtain a better view of an object for detection.

The convergence of machine learning, neural networks, data conversion techniques, and ROS integration may create opportunities for further research on radioactive isotope differentiation in nuclear decommissioning and safety. Future studies could investigate potential applications in other areas requiring precise identification and handling of hazardous materials, such as healthcare and the chemical industry.

2026-10-20.title: Structure over Reasoning: Unified Zero-Shot Navigation with a Small Vision-Language Model
2026-10-20.authors: Zeqi Li , Xunyi Zhao , Zerui Li , Sihao Lin , Qi Wu , ShiJie Li
2026-10-20.abstract: Vision-language navigation is moving into photorealistic, physically simulated scenes, where the leading zero-shot agents put a vision-language model in the control loop to choose every move and stop. Robots favour small models, whose abilities are uneven: Qwen3-VL-4B can judge whether a single view looks like the goal, but its route reasoning is at chance, its distance estimates nearly constant, its stop votes unreliable. Our agent therefore asks it two perceptual questions per step, which direction looks like the goal and whether the view justifies stopping, plus one gated frontier query on route-bearing instructions, and treats the answers as evidence, not actions: a route-blind semantic field over a bird’s-eye map accumulates the directional scores through a tempered update, a skeleton graph supplies frontiers and geodesic distances, and a two-stage terminator turns stop votes into termini through a trail-consistency gate and a budget-forced return. With every baseline re-run in one installation at one budget, the agent exceeds all four zero-shot baselines of the VLNVerse subset in mean success on both granularities, though the paired interval against the strongest coarse-grained baseline includes zero. Termination is the dominant lever in ablation, thirteen attempts to give the model more of the navigation establish no reliable gain, and the agent runs on a Unitree Go2 quadruped with off-board inference. Code, per-episode logs and a robot video will be released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/structure-over-reasoning-PAGE .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Vision-language navigation asks an agent to follow a natural-language instruction to a goal it has never seen. The field is moving from panoramic graphs into photorealistic, physically simulated scenes such as VLNVerse [ 1 ] , where the leading zero-shot agents place a vision-language model in the control loop and let it decide each move and each stop from panorama, history and full instruction [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . The recipe needs no training, but it assumes a model large enough to reason about a whole route from a few images and to judge, from a single view, whether the goal has been reached.

A robot cannot always afford one: a cloud model adds latency and recurring cost, an onboard one must fit limited memory and compute. Qwen3-VL-4B [ 6 ] occupies 8.3 GB and answers a step of our agent in 1.51 seconds on an RTX 5090, against 3.10 seconds when asked to reason at length. A smaller model does not make every part of navigation slightly worse; some parts fail while others hold. Shown one view and the goal phrase, the 4B model can usually tell whether that direction looks like the goal; across the variants we tried, its route reasoning over candidate directions stays at chance, its distance estimates are nearly constant, its grounding finds the right category but not the instance the instruction names, and its fine-grained stop votes fall within three metres of the goal less than a third of the time. A small-model navigator should use what stays reliable and move the rest into structure the model only feeds.

Our agent asks two narrow perceptual questions, which of twelve directions looks like the goal and whether the view justifies stopping, and treats the answers as evidence and proposals, not actions. A bird’s-eye occupancy map built from depth supports a skeleton graph whose frontier nodes are the only sub-goals the agent adopts, the moves being chosen among the benchmark’s waypoint candidates, and a route-blind semantic field over the same map accumulates the directional scores with a tempered update, so that the field, not the model, remembers where the goal probably is. When a fine-grained instruction carries route clauses the model may also propose a frontier through a chain-of-thought query [ 7 ] , gated and coupled conservatively; on coarse-grained instructions, which name only the destination, or without a usable proposal, the field drives alone. A stop vote is likewise checked against the trail’s evidence rather than executed, and an episode nearing its budget without an accepted vote walks back to the best position seen. One policy with a single granularity-specific parameter serves both.

Among the components removed in our ablations, termination produces the largest drop in success. On fine-grained instructions an agent that never stops and walks the full forty-step budget of our ablations passes within three metres of the goal in 77.42% of episodes but succeeds in 20.97%; the full terminator raises this to 42.11% in about half the steps. Reaching is not solved either, since even that agent stays beyond three metres in more than a fifth of episodes, but the gap shows that nearing a good position and ending there are separate problems. The ablations agree elsewhere: the field and the route channel contribute nearly additively, and the terminator is the largest single lever. Thirteen attempts to hand responsibility back to the model, from longer route reasoning and sub-goal decomposition to grounding-based final approach and model-selected return positions, establish no reliable gain, and two lose beyond the run-to-run spread. Throughout, the model supplies local evidence and structure mediates it.

The contributions are fourfold. First, a decomposition of zero-shot navigation around a small vision-language model into a route-blind semantic field, a skeleton graph and a gated route channel, with the field update, the coupling and the action utility in closed form and one policy for both granularities. Second, a two-stage terminator with a trail-consistency gate and a budget-forced return proved affordable under the benchmark’s displacement protocol, with an ablation that quantifies each stage. Third, on the official VLNVerse subset, with every zero-shot baseline re-run in one installation at the same thirty-step budget, the agent exceeds the strongest baseline in mean success by 9.1 points on fine-grained instructions, with lower navigation error and higher path efficiency, and by 6.2 on coarse-grained ones, all three-run means, and runs on a Unitree Go2 quadruped. Fourth, ablations and thirteen attempts to give the model more of the navigation, mapping what this model and prompt family support reliably and what still needs explicit structure.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Vision-language navigation. The task was introduced on panoramic graphs of real buildings [ 8 ] and extended to finer-grained instructions [ 9 ] , object-centric goals [ 10 ] and continuous environments [ 11 ] , where trained agents pair a waypoint predictor with a learned policy [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] or train a vision-language-action model end to end [ 15 , 16 ] . VLNVerse [ 1 ] moves the task into a physics-based simulator with real-scale scenes and two instruction granularities; we adopt its official evaluation subset and protocol without change.

Zero-shot navigation with language models. A line of work replaces the trained policy by a language model that reads a textual description of the panorama and the history and chooses among candidate directions [ 2 , 4 , 17 ] , with a map-like textual memory in MapGPT [ 3 ] , open-source models in continuous environments in Open-Nav [ 5 ] and sub-task decomposition in InstructNav [ 18 ] . For object-goal search, language models score frontiers [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] and vision-language embeddings build value maps over the explored area [ 22 ] ; VoroNav reasons over a reduced Voronoi graph with captions of far-sighted views [ 23 ] , which our skeleton graph and frontier captions resemble. Two things separate our agent from this family: the model never chooses a waypoint, since it scores sectors and proposes frontiers while a belief over the map decides where to go, and it never decides to stop on its own, since its vote is verified against the trail; Section IV-D shows that with a 4B model both restrictions are what make the agent work.

Semantic maps and stopping. Occupancy grids [ 24 , 25 ] , frontier-based exploration [ 26 ] and semantic exploration policies [ 27 ] are the classical basis of our map, and open-vocabulary maps [ 28 ] show that language-conditioned scores can be written into spatial memory; our field differs in being a probability distribution over reachable cells, updated by tempered exponential evidence accumulation and blind to the route. When to stop is a known weakness of VLN agents, addressed by progress monitors [ 29 ] and backtracking [ 30 ] on the panoramic graph; the VLNVerse baselines execute the model’s stop directly [ 1 ] . We keep the vote as a proposal, add two cheap verifications and quantify each.
