2026-10-20.title: Compile Once, Run Cheap: Frozen, Portable Skills for Embodied Agents, and What Recursive Self-Improvement Adds
2026-10-20.authors: Jingwen Bai , Guochao Bai , Canbo Zhang , Shuangqi Li , Minchao Hu , Weichun Huang , Shuang Liu
2026-10-20.comment: . Code and data: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract: Language models acquired agents, harnesses and reusable skills only after data-rich pretraining had produced a strong base model. Embodied intelligence has no comparable corpus, so current routes to new manipulation capability either collect demonstrations for every task or keep a frontier model in the control loop for every episode. We study a third route: a strong general model acts only as an offline author that writes, executes, diagnoses and repairs a manipulation skill in simulation until it passes a qualification exam on layouts drawn only after freezing; the frozen skill is then executed by code alone or by an inexpensive caller that reads nothing but its description, whereas concurrent self-evolving systems still run a frontier model in every episode at execution time. We call this skill-level recursive self-improvement Skill-RSI and specify a compile protocol, with an isolated and audited author, hidden validation layouts that are never fed back, no-feedback and inherit-only control lineages and a tamper-evident ledger, and a reuse protocol that runs the identical frozen files with executors from another model family. On 7 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with cluttered tables, 4 tasks were compiled into 7 frozen skills by Claude Code; 5 of the 7 came from a first draft that already met the targets and needed only qualification, at $4.29–8.22 of author cost each ($55 per frozen skill once the 13 campaigns that did not compile are counted). The other three tasks did not compile in 18 campaigns, including five with GPT-6 and a pre-registered experiment with 150 development layouts: on the hardest task every campaign scored 78–95 of 100 but had 3–16 safety aborts, so the pre-registered gate of 95% success with zero aborts was not met, and a 100-episode exam bounds an abort rate only to 3.6%. On hidden layouts, a repair session that inherits the previous version and its evidence delivered a better version than a from-scratch rewrite in 8 of 8 controlled campaigns (sign test p = 0.004 p=0.004 ; the selection-matched best-of- k k comparison is 5–3), and an inherit-only lineage, which revises the previous version with its own practice runs but without the runtime’s development-layout feedback, shows that most of that gap comes from inheriting the previous version, with the development feedback adding a little more (3 of 3 campaigns in the same direction, p = 0.125 p=0.125 ). Six write-once campaigns found no detectable first-draft difference from practice, within a design that cannot exclude effects below about 14 points. The frozen skills measured for reuse retained 148/150 successes on new layouts with no model and 147/150 with a DeepSeek-flash caller at $0.00028–0.00054 of model cost per episode; no direct-control baseline was run, so no break-even is reported.
2026-10-20.introduction:
The capabilities that make language models useful as agents were built in a fixed order. Web-scale pretraining produced a strong base model first; agent loops, tool harnesses, reusable skills and protocols for calling them came afterwards, on top of that model. Embodied intelligence is trying to repeat the first step and has no corpus with which to do it. Robot foundation policies consolidate demonstrations, but each new task still asks for new demonstrations or post-training [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . A second route places a frontier multimodal model inside a structured harness and lets it reason per episode; it solves tasks zero-shot but keeps the expensive model in the loop for every execution [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] . A third route lets a frozen model evolve skills, critics or code through execution and revision [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] .

The third route produces a loop; it does not yet say what kind of object the loop produces or how its claims should be tested. Prior and concurrent systems have begun to evaluate frozen experience on scenes the loop did not see [ 14 , 15 ] , but at execution time each episode still runs a frontier model, at a few dollars per episode where the cost is reported [ 14 ] , and neither of these systems separates learning from feedback from selection among attempts with a control. Three questions follow. First, can the product of the loop run without the model that wrote it, and with what loss when a cheaper model from another family calls it? Second, how much of the improvement across rounds is learning from feedback, how much is inheriting a previous version, and how much is trying several times and keeping the best? Third, what does the skill cost, counted as the full ledger of authoring, failed candidates, simulation and deployment, so that the claim that a skill is cheap has a denominator?

We take the position that the order of the language-model history can be inverted for robots: skills can come before the strong embodied base model, be compiled by a strong general model that already exists, and let robots start working, and generating structured data, in specific scenes now. This is a hypothesis, not a result. Its necessary precondition is empirical: a skill must be compiled cheaply enough, qualify on unseen layouts, run without the author, and cost little per episode. This paper tests that precondition.

Skill-RSI separates authoring from execution ( Figure 1 ). In Protocol A a strong model, whose weights never change, acts as an offline author: it drafts a skill package from a task card, runs it on fixed development layouts, reads the execution evidence, and revises, until the package meets a target on those layouts and on hidden validation layouts whose results it never sees. A qualification exam on layouts drawn only after freezing decides whether the package becomes a FrozenSkill , an immutable bundle of a skill description, restricted-Python skill code, a perception module and a manifest with hashes, seeds, environment fingerprint and compile cost. In Protocol B the same bundle is executed by a code-only runner and by a caller from another model family that reads only the skill description, on layouts disjoint from every compile-time seed. We ask:

How many repair rounds and how much author cost does it take to compile a task to a 95 % 95\% qualification bar with zero unsafe motions, and what stops the tasks that do not compile?

How many repair rounds and how much author cost does it take to compile a task to a 95 % 95\% qualification bar with zero unsafe motions, and what stops the tasks that do not compile?

Is the improvement across rounds learning from feedback, or selection among independent attempts; within a repair round, how much comes from inheriting the previous version and how much from reading its execution evidence; and does the author’s own testing within a session contribute?

When the frozen skill is executed by code alone or by a low-cost caller from another model family, how much success is retained?

What does a frozen skill cost per episode, with compilation amortized over deployments?

Our contributions are: (i) an author–executor separation in which the unit of adaptation is a verified, portable FrozenSkill that executes with no model at all or with a cheap caller from another family, with two protocols that operationalize compile-once-run-cheap; (ii) a credible measurement of what self-improvement contributes: an isolated and audited author, hidden validation layouts, exam layouts drawn after freezing and run to completion, no-feedback and inherit-only control lineages re-run on hidden layouts under a pre-registered design, and a per-decision cost ledger that includes every failed campaign; and (iii) measurements on RoboTwin 2.0 with two author products that answer Q1–Q4, including three findings we did not anticipate: the frozen skills came mostly from first drafts, so the protocol’s measured contribution on the tasks that compiled is qualification and freezing; the gate binds on rare safety aborts rather than on task completion, and more development layouts did not change that; and most of the per-round advantage of repair over rewriting comes from inheriting the previous version rather than from the runtime’s development-layout feedback on it, while in-session self-testing shows no detectable effect on first drafts. We use the name Skill-RSI because the author recursively refines a persistent external skill from that skill’s own execution evidence; Section 3.3 states precisely what is and is not claimed under that name.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Improvement in weight space

OpenVLA and later generalist policies map vision and language to actions through learned parameters [ 1 ] ; π 0.7 \pi_{0.7} extends this view with steerable, context-conditioned behavior [ 2 ] . Self-improvement in this family updates the policy from experience: RoboCat and self-improving embodied foundation models practice autonomously [ 16 , 17 ] ; SOAR lets foundation models propose and judge practice [ 18 ] ; PLD probes a VLA’s failure regions with residual RL and distills recovery data back [ 19 ] ; RISE trains on imagined rollouts from a compositional world model [ 20 ] ; RECAP turns deployment experience into advantage-conditioned updates of π 0.6 ∗ \pi^{*}_{0.6} [ 3 ] ; ENPIRE lets coding agents rewrite the training code itself on real hardware [ 21 ] . World-action models couple prediction and action for contact-rich control [ 22 , 23 ] . These routes need demonstrations, on-robot experience or training compute for every task. Skill-RSI holds all weights fixed and evolves an external artifact; the comparison is weight-space adaptation versus artifact-space adaptation, not learning versus no learning.

## 2.2 Frozen models in harnesses

Code as Policies, Inner Monologue, VoxPoser and ReKep showed that language models can write executable control programs and use feedback [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] ; REFLECT summarizes experience for failure explanation [ 28 ] . Recent harnesses put frozen models or policies behind structured observation–action interfaces: Show-Harness exposes discrete semantic actions to a VLM [ 4 ] , Harness VLA orchestrates frozen VLA primitives with memory [ 29 ] , Guava and hierarchical VLA agents study which harness components matter [ 30 , 31 ] , AgentSpec studies scaffold composition [ 32 ] , and EmbodiedSkills wraps VLA agents in skills defined as executable contracts with pre- and post-checks [ 33 ] . FAEA applies a software-engineering agent to manipulation without demonstrations [ 5 ] , RoboDawn transfers VLM competence to RoboTwin 2.0 control zero-shot [ 6 ] , and RoboICL adapts a frontier model to bimanual tasks from a few in-context demonstrations [ 7 ] . The clearest statement of the per-episode route is the early evaluation of GPT-6 Astra as a policy: given RGB views, robot state and a task recipe, with no depth and no privileged pose, the model chooses end-effector targets turn by turn and reaches 22.5% success over 2,100 trials on the 42 RoboDojo tasks, far ahead of two other language models used the same way [ 34 ] . In all of these the model reasons during execution. Our runtime design follows theirs; our question is whether the reasoning can be done once, offline, and its result handed to something cheaper.

## 2.3 Self-evolving skills

Voyager grew a code skill library in an open-ended digital world [ 35 ] . Embodied systems now close the execute–diagnose–revise loop around frozen models ( Table 1 ). RoboRSI coordinates Manager, Planner, Engineer and Reviewer agents over a skill tree and consolidates stable tool-call chains into code [ 8 ] ; Zetta evolves runtime critics and recovery skills around a frozen policy [ 9 ] ; SHAPER evolves skills and context-code harnesses with one frozen model as planner and optimizer [ 10 ] ; ASPIRE refines code-as-policy programs into a library [ 11 ] ; Playful Agentic Robot Learning acquires skills through self-proposed play [ 12 ] ; EmbodiSkill adds skill-aware reflection [ 36 ] ; VASO targets formally verifiable skills [ 37 ] ; visual verification steers policies at inference time [ 38 ] ; Practice trains a skill learner that maintains a library for frozen executors [ 13 ] ; ELITE accumulates procedural strategies for a frozen VLM and retrieves them by procedural similarity [ 39 ] . SkillSmith and SkCC compile software-agent skills into typed runtime interfaces [ 40 , 41 ] . Two concurrent systems are closest to ours. EmbodiedEvo lets a coding agent evolve reusable Skills and Lessons on one playground scene of each RoboDojo task, freezes them, and evaluates on new scenes, raising a matched-test success rate from 8.50% to 30.17% and transferring the experience to two other models (+8.86 and +5.50 points); at test time a GPT-6 Astra agent still reasons in every episode with that experience as context, with up to 100 accepted code executions per episode (29.0 on average with Skills and Lessons), at a mean model-API cost of $5.73 per test episode, excluding the playground learning phase [ 14 ] . EmbodiedRSI is an agentic harness that adapts around the robot model: it co-evolves code and skills, holds competing hypotheses in a graph, chooses the physical experiments that discriminate between them, and reports 77.0% on RoboCasa365, 86.8% on LIBERO-Pro and 71.3% on a real robot [ 15 ] . Both evaluate frozen experience beyond the scenes it was learned on; neither measures execution without a large model, and neither includes a control that separates learning from selection. Our difference from them is in those two measurements, not in the loop. The repair loop itself has antecedents outside robotics: Reflexion and Self-Refine revise an answer from verbal feedback [ 42 , 43 ] , Eureka refines reward code from execution statistics in robot simulation and compares against sampling more candidates [ 44 ] , and two audits found that self-repair of code pays only when external execution feedback is strong and that models do not improve their own reasoning without it [ 45 , 46 ] ; our write-once and inherit-only results ( Sections 7.3 and 7.4 ) replicate that pattern in the embodied setting. Skill-RSI could wrap any of these systems as its author. Its requirements are on the output and the evidence: an immutable package with a manifest, a gate between discovery and release, execution of the identical package by an executor from another model family, and a control that separates learning from selection.

## 2.4 Recursive self-improvement as a term

The term goes back to Good’s ultraintelligent machine [ 48 ] and Schmidhuber’s Gödel machine, which rewrites its own code under proof [ 49 ] ; STOP and the Darwin Gödel Machine brought it to frozen language models that improve an external scaffold or agent code against held-out tasks [ 50 , 51 ] . Duan et al. order recursive self-improvement into five levels, from executing improvements to improving the improvement process itself, and name embodied intelligence as an application [ 52 ] . Surveys of self-evolving embodied AI and post-deployment humanoid self-improvement describe memory, task, environment, embodiment and model self-evolution with a slow outer loop [ 53 , 54 ] . In software agents the term is now used for loops that improve an external artifact while the model stays frozen: RRSI regularizes recursive improvement of prompts, control flow, tools and memory so that reusable mechanisms win over benchmark-specific ones [ 55 ] ; AIDE 2 lets an outer agent rewrite the harness of an inner research agent and keeps changes that survive held-out benchmarks [ 56 ] ; MetaSkill-Evolve evolves task skills on a fast loop and a meta-skill on a slow one [ 57 ] ; RSIAgent builds environment memory by exploration without parameter updates [ 58 ] . In embodied systems the term is now used concurrently by several groups: EmbodiedRSI for hypothesis-guided co-evolution of code and skills in a harness around the robot model [ 15 ] , and PhysicalRSI, a preview release without a paper, for a propose–evaluate–select–inherit loop over a harness, skills and memory [ 47 ] . Our loop uses the term in the artifact-level sense, sits at the first three of Duan et al.’s levels, does not claim the fifth, and calls a gain self-improvement only where a control lineage shows what the gain is relative to; Section 3.3 makes the boundary explicit.

## 2.5 Hidden physical properties and touch

Text corpora contain almost no quantitative tactile knowledge, and touch data are scarce; Sparsh learns touch representations from tactile sensors [ 59 ] , TacGen synthesizes tactile latents from RGB to mitigate the scarcity [ 60 ] , and DeliGrasp asks an LLM to infer mass, friction and compliance from object semantics to set grasp forces [ 61 ] . These works complete the missing modality. Our route is complementary: a skill can encode a strategy that avoids needing the modality, such as supporting a fragile object from below rather than estimating a safe grip force; Section 8 discusses where that substitution stops working.

## 2.6 Evaluation validity

LIBERO measures lifelong transfer [ 62 ] ; LIBERO-PRO and LIBERO-Plus expose memorization and decompose robustness into perturbation dimensions [ 63 , 64 ] ; RoboTwin 2.0 provides domain-randomized bimanual tasks and a public expert generator [ 65 ] ; VLABench, ESI-Bench and BEHAVIOR-1K extend scope [ 66 , 67 , 68 ] . Recent audits find shortcuts, repeated test exposure and low trial counts behind reported progress [ 69 ] , and cost-controlled evaluation of agents asks that accuracy be reported with the dollars spent to reach it [ 70 ] . These concerns apply with particular force to self-evolving systems, whose tasks are also their discovery set, and to agentic authors with shell access, which, we found, read other campaigns’ work when nothing stops them ( Section 4 ). We respond with author isolation and session audits, hidden validation layouts, exams drawn after freezing, run-to-completion exams, seeds disjoint across protocols, and a full ledger of failed candidates.

2026-10-20.title: Localization and Neural Splatting on the Edge: An FPGA Scene Memory for Robots
2026-10-20.authors: Que Haohua , Mingkai Liu , Handong Yao
2026-10-20.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-20.abstract:
Resource-constrained robots and autonomous vehicles need scene memories that
localize a camera and render nearby views without a desktop GPU. Scene-coordinate
regression (SCR) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) fit because they avoid an SfM
stage, but ACEsplat-style pipelines are GPU-centered, and moving them to an edge
FPGA is hard because SCR is pose-sensitive and 3DGS rendering is irregular and
capacity-sensitive. We present LENS, an edge scene-memory acceleration system on
the AMD KR260 that brings an ACEsplat-style workload to a low-power FPGA/ARM
platform. Rather than proposing a new scene model, LENS co-designs the two
dominant kernels with the board data path: an INT16 SCR accelerator that
preserves pose accuracy, and a bit-exact fixed-point ordered 3DGS renderer that rewrites
alpha transmittance as a log-sum-exp recurrence and removes provably useless
streamed Gaussians. All LENS latency, power, and quality results are board-measured.
The SCR engine preserves DSAC* localization accuracy at
25.42 ms, the on-board renderer reaches 34.11 dB on Cambridge against ACEsplat’s
33.20, novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K reaches 27.84 dB against 26.11, and
all ten Wayspots scenes reach the ACEsplat rendering target. LENS wins performance
per watt over a Jetson Orin NX on every deployment task, by 1.9x to 5.7x at about a
quarter of the power, and is faster in absolute latency on localization and
Wayspots rendering. On-device training reaches ACEsplat-level quality but not the
GPU’s time or energy, marking the remaining boundary for a future training
accelerator.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Edge autonomy is increasingly limited by what a system can remember under its
own power and thermal budget. A mobile robot revisiting a building, or an
autonomous vehicle returning to a mapped route, needs more than a single pose
estimate. It needs a scene memory that can answer two questions locally: where
is the camera in this place, and what would the scene look like from a nearby
view? Visual localization has been studied through direct pose regression,
prioritized 2-D/3-D search, dense matching, hierarchical retrieval and matching,
and SfM-backed maps [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
Today, however,
localization plus rendering is usually built around GPU-backed reconstruction
and neural scene optimization. Such systems are powerful, but they are difficult
to carry into small platforms that must localize, render, and reason while
sharing watts with sensing, planning, and control.

SfM-free neural scene pipelines offer a promising alternative. Scene-coordinate
regression (SCR) predicts dense 3-D coordinates from image pixels [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
ACE makes this per-scene relocalization practical within minutes [ 11 ] . On the rendering side, neural radiance fields [ 12 , 13 ] and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) [ 14 ] have made view synthesis a useful scene-memory interface,
and recent Gaussian SLAM systems use explicit Gaussians for tracking and mapping [ 15 , 16 ] . Autonomous-driving scene
models have also adopted Gaussians for surround-view dynamic reconstruction and
urban scene understanding [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] . ACEsplat
combines SCR and 3DGS into a pipeline for localization, reconstruction, and
novel-view synthesis without an offline SfM stage [ 20 ] . The
algorithmic story is attractive for autonomy: the same scene representation can
support both relocalization and visual prediction.

The deployment story is harder. General FPGA DNN frameworks show that
quantized neural inference can be efficient on reconfigurable logic [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] ,
and recent neural-rendering accelerators target NeRF and 3DGS kernels [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] .
LENS targets a different composition of constraints. SCR is a dense CNN, but its
output is geometry, not a class score; small coordinate errors can become large
pose errors, so the convenient INT8 path used by many embedded neural
accelerators is not automatically safe. The 3DGS renderer has the opposite
structure: it is irregular, view-dependent, and dominated by sorted per-pixel
Gaussian contributions. A small tile capacity makes the renderer fast but inaccurate;
a faithful renderer must carry long Gaussian tails through a low-power memory
system. For edge autonomy, success is therefore a system property: pose accuracy,
render quality, latency, power, and board data movement must hold together. The
question is not simply whether ACEsplat can run on an FPGA, but which parts of a
neural scene-memory pipeline can be made accurate, which parts can be made fast,
and which limits remain visible only on the board.

We answer this question with LENS (Localization and Embedded Neural Splatting),
an embedded-FPGA scene-memory system for resource-constrained edge autonomy.
LENS runs on an AMD Kria KR260, a ∼ 5 {\sim}5 W-class Zynq UltraScale+ platform [ 28 ] , and compares against a Jetson Orin NX edge GPU. It keeps SCR
accuracy-first through INT16 custom logic and moves 3DGS rendering into a bit-exact
fixed-point log-sum-exp datapath. This paper makes a hardware-system claim: an
SfM-free localization and rendering pipeline can serve as an edge scene memory
only when arithmetic, representation, and board-level data movement are
co-designed.
Our contribution is threefold:

A board-measured edge scene-memory system. We map SCR
relocalization and 3D Gaussian rendering to a KR260-class FPGA/ARM system
and report accuracy, latency, and power with explicit board/GPU/emulator
provenance.

An accuracy-gated SCR accelerator. We show that INT16 custom
logic, low-rank encoder decomposition, and DSP double-pumping can preserve
DSAC* pose accuracy while reaching 25.42 ms on board.

A bit-exact fixed-point LSE 3DGS render datapath. We replace the
loop-carried alpha update with a fixed-point log-transmittance add, add a
provably bit-exact stream truncation that removes 24 to 60 percent of
streamed Gaussians, and reach ACEsplat-level reconstruction, novel-view
synthesis, and Wayspots rendering on board at a performance-per-watt
advantage over a Jetson Orin NX.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Visual localization and scene coordinates. Visual relocalization spans direct pose regression, structure-based 2-D/3-D
matching, visual odometry/SLAM, and SfM-backed maps [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 6 , 34 ] .
These methods differ in how much geometry is stored explicitly and how much
query-time matching is required. Scene-coordinate methods predict dense
correspondences and solve pose with robust geometry, from regression forests and
DSAC/DSAC++ to DSAC* and ACE [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] .
LENS keeps this relocalization model and studies the hardware mapping when pose
accuracy, not classification accuracy, is the acceptance criterion.

Neural scene representations. Neural scene representations have moved from NeRF-style implicit fields to
factorized, baked, voxel, and hash-grid variants [ 12 , 13 , 35 , 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 ] and to explicit 3D Gaussian splatting [ 14 ] . Recent Gaussian SLAM and
driving-scene systems use Gaussians for tracking, mapping, and urban scene
memory [ 42 , 43 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] .
ACEsplat is closest to our workload because it couples ACE-style SCR with 3DGS
reconstruction and NVS [ 20 ] , while MACE accelerates coordinate
encoding [ 44 ] . LENS is complementary: it keeps the scene model but moves
its relocalization and rendering bottlenecks onto an embedded FPGA, where the
limits come from arithmetic width, sorted Gaussian streams, and board data
movement rather than from the scene representation itself.

Embedded acceleration for scene memory. FPGA DNN accelerators exploit quantization and streaming dataflow [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] ,
and neural-rendering accelerators target NeRF or 3DGS kernels [ 25 , 26 , 27 , 45 , 46 , 47 , 48 ] .
Most accelerate a single render or train kernel, often as ASICs, while a deployed
scene memory must preserve pose accuracy, render quality, latency, and power on
the same board. LENS therefore reports a board-measured localization and
Gaussian-rendering path on a commodity FPGA/ARM platform, exposing both the
regular SCR arithmetic wins and the irregular Gaussian capacity limits.

2026-10-20.title: Learning Waypoints and Passage Events for Decentralized Multi-Quadrotor Trajectory Planning
2026-10-20.authors: Yunhan Shi , Jia Deng , Zehao Jia , Lin Cheng , Shengping Gong
2026-10-20.abstract: Multi-quadrotor passage planning requires coordinated spatial routes and passage times under vehicle dynamics and actuation constraints. Optimizing these decisions jointly couples temporal allocation, nonlinear motion, and inter-vehicle interactions, creating a computational challenge for local trajectory generation. We propose a learning–optimization framework that predicts spatial waypoints and ordered passage events for independently solved quadrotor planners. A common physical time grid aligns the vehicles, with intermediate events fixed by the networks and terminal progress optimized locally to permit different completion metrics. Differentiable sequential convex programming incorporates rigid-body dynamics and rotor-thrust bounds, allowing collision and completion gradients to train both networks through the generated trajectories. In a two-quadrotor evaluation across 24 layouts, the adapted policy passes physical feasibility and sampled separation checks in all five held-out layouts. Their mean completion metric decreases by 1.52% relative to the inherited policy. The median forward time is 21.01 ms on the held-out exchange layout with matching numerical trajectory references. These results demonstrate that learned spatial and event parameters can coordinate independent rigid-body planners while preserving local vehicle constraints in the evaluated scenarios.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Multi-quadrotor passage planning concerns the coordinated motion of several vehicles through prescribed gates toward individual targets. Such tasks arise in swarm racing and navigation through cluttered environments, where vehicles share limited passage space [ 1 , 2 ] . Successful traversal requires each trajectory to satisfy vehicle dynamics and each pair of vehicles to maintain suitable separation. Spatial route selection and passage timing therefore form a common planning problem for coordinated flight.

The central computational difficulty is the coupling between passage timing, vehicle motion, and inter-vehicle separation. Changing an arrival time changes where a vehicle meets its neighbors, and generating the corresponding motion requires satisfying nonlinear attitude and actuation constraints. Solving these decisions jointly introduces temporal variables and interaction constraints into the trajectory optimization. This coupling motivates three complementary approaches: direct optimization, learned motion generation, and hybrid learning–optimization planning.

Optimization-based methods provide explicit representations of trajectory objectives and physical constraints. Minimum-snap and MINCO formulations exploit polynomial structure for efficient trajectory generation [ 3 , 4 ] , while complementary progress constraints (CPC) optimize ordered waypoint completion together with motion [ 5 , 1 ] . Decentralized planners such as MADER and Robust MADER incorporate shared trajectory information into local collision handling [ 6 , 7 ] . The resulting formulations make passage allocation and inter-vehicle coupling explicit, identifying the decisions that a learned planner can help organize.

Learning-based methods offer a direct mapping from observations to motion decisions. Sensor-to-trajectory policies have been trained through privileged imitation learning for high-speed flight [ 8 ] , and differentiable simulation has supplied analytical gradients for quadrotor control from states and visual features [ 9 ] . Their training objectives encode desired behavior in network parameters and support rapid inference. For constrained multi-vehicle passage, this motivates learning spatial and temporal decisions together with a physical trajectory-generation model.

Hybrid learning–optimization methods provide a mechanism for coupling neural predictions to constrained planning. AllocNet predicts segment durations for a differentiable trajectory quadratic program [ 10 ] , Jiang et al. jointly learn waypoints and time allocations [ 11 ] , and Marino et al. combine learned multi-UAV trajectory parameters with a differentiable correction layer [ 12 ] . These approaches show how optimization gradients can shape planning parameters during training. Inspired by these approaches, we learn spatial and event parameters to coordinate independently solved rigid-body trajectories on a shared time grid.

This design involves three linked challenges. First, pairwise separation must be evaluated at common physical times even when the vehicles complete their routes at different times. Second, the trajectory layer must incorporate nonlinear rigid-body motion and rotor-level limits while retaining usable derivatives for network training. Third, independent local solves need spatial and temporal decisions that respond to neighboring vehicles. A suitable hierarchy must therefore connect synchronized event allocation, constrained local motion, and inter-vehicle learning within one training objective.

We propose a learning–optimization framework that connects these three requirements through spatial waypoints and passage events. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , shared networks use the vehicle state, known gate locations, and current relative neighbor positions to predict waypoint centers and ordered intermediate events. Independent differentiable CPC-based planners then generate trajectories on a common physical grid, and the outer objective evaluates collision and completion costs across the resulting trajectories. This hierarchy makes learned event allocation the connection between multi-vehicle coordination and local physical planning.

The framework has three main technical contributions:

A shared-grid event representation organizes spatial targets and passage timing for independent local planners. Continuous intermediate timestamps parameterize interpolated passage constraints, and the final CPC progress distribution remains a local decision variable. This construction supports common-time interaction evaluation together with vehicle-specific completion metrics.

A differentiable sequential convex programming (SCP) trajectory layer incorporates rigid-body dynamics and individual rotor-thrust limits. Local approximations of the dynamics and terminal progress yield convex conic subproblems whose parameterization satisfies disciplined parametrized programming. The layer provides a constrained trajectory map through which waypoint and event predictions can be trained.

An outer coordination objective adapts both networks through independently generated trajectories. Collision penalties act on synchronized vehicle positions, and the completion term links the learned parameters to local progress. This objective makes inter-vehicle behavior part of parameter learning while keeping the trajectory solves independent.

The numerical evaluation examines coordination, physical feasibility, and computation within a two-vehicle setting. Gate-perturbation and goal-exchange layouts test spatial and temporal adaptation, a frozen-policy experiment examines thrust-difference regularization, and selected finite differences check the network derivatives. Warm-reference forward timings characterize the solver’s computational cost. Together, these experiments assess the framework through trajectory behavior, local constraint satisfaction, and measured planning cost.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Waypoint Timing and Trajectory Optimization

Polynomial minimum-snap trajectories provide an efficient representation for quadrotor flight through waypoint sequences [ 3 ] . MINCO provides a compact polynomial representation with efficient spatial–temporal deformation and supports geometrical and dynamic constraints through trajectory optimization [ 4 ] . CPC models ordered completion through continuous progress variables and jointly optimizes passage allocation and vehicle motion [ 5 ] . Shen et al. extend this principle to a swarm racing task [ 1 ] . Our formulation retains complementary progress only for the final event and uses learned continuous timestamps for intermediate events, which restrict the feasible trajectories to those compatible with the assigned passage times.

## II-B Decentralized Multi-Vehicle Planning

MADER generates trajectories asynchronously using enclosing polyhedra, optimized separating planes, and collision checks against other agents’ committed trajectories [ 6 ] . Robust MADER extends trajectory sharing with delay checks and a two-step publication scheme to accommodate communication delays in dynamic environments [ 7 ] . EGO-Swarm combines gradient-based local planning, collision-risk penalties, and lightweight topological trajectory generation for decentralized navigation in cluttered environments [ 2 ] . These methods make exchanged trajectory information part of decentralized collision handling. In our formulation, current relative neighbor positions condition the shared networks, and synchronized local trajectories enter the outer collision objective during training.

## II-C Learning with Differentiable Planners

Differentiable MPC learns controller costs and dynamics by differentiating the KKT conditions of a convex approximation at a controller fixed point [ 13 ] . AllocNet predicts segment durations and differentiates through the fixed-duration trajectory QP [ 10 ] . Jiang et al. combine depth-based waypoint prediction, time allocation, and differentiable minimum-snap optimization [ 11 ] . Marino et al. predict MINVO control points and a learned collision constraint from point clouds and communicated features, then use an OptNet-based QP layer during imitation learning [ 12 , 14 ] . These works establish the broader learning–optimization architecture. Our focus is the event representation and the separation of outer inter-agent collision learning from local rotor-level planning.

For interacting aerial systems, learned model predictive games project neural reference strategies into dynamically feasible trajectories and train with game objectives [ 15 ] . DiffCoord differentiates a distributed ADMM–DDP pipeline to learn problem and solver parameters for cooperative trajectories [ 16 ] . Our local optimizers interact through shared observations and the outer training objective. This choice reduces explicit coupling in each local solve, while leaving collision avoidance dependent on the learned policy and numerical validation.

Learning also connects visual observations to aerial motion. Loquercio et al. train a sensor-to-trajectory policy through privileged imitation learning in simulation for high-speed flight [ 8 ] . Heeg et al. train quadrotor control policies using analytical gradients through differentiable dynamics and learned visual-state representations [ 9 ] . These studies provide context for trajectory-level learning and dynamics-based policy gradients. The present formulation learns spatial and event parameters from state observations through differentiable local optimization.

2026-10-20.title: Scalable, Intuitive, Mixed Reality-Based Semi-Autonomous Robotic Telemanipulation for the Execution of a Fine-Grained Bimanual Task
2026-10-20.authors: Shifei Duan , Zhe Wang , Francesco De Pace , Minas Liarokapis
2026-10-20.comment: . Accepted to IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS) 2026
2026-10-20.abstract: Nowadays, robotic telemanipulation enables humans to control robots so as to execute tasks in a manner similar to how they perform them, and serves as an essential approach for collecting on-robot data for robot learning by human demonstrations. The quality of collected demonstrations directly impacts the performance of the learned policy. However, existing telemanipulation systems rely heavily on human operation, particularly for large-scale data collection. Collecting dozens or hundreds of demonstrations is a demanding process, as operators tend to fatigue quickly, especially during the execution of dexterous tasks that require sustained concentration. Recently, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation has emerged as a promising direction that reduces operator workload while preserving human-in-the-loop control for task execution. We therefore introduce a scalable, intuitive, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation system that leverages a mixed reality (MR) headset for on-robot data collection. The system autonomously executes the majority of the task trajectories and only requires the operator to make fine adjustments at key stages. We validate the effectiveness of our system by collecting data and training imitation learning policies on the execution of a high-precision, fine-grained bimanual peg-in-hole task. With lower data collection effort, our system obtains high-quality demonstrations that can be used to train fully autonomous task execution policies.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Recent years have witnessed significant progress in learning-based robotic manipulation, where the availability of large-scale real-robot datasets has significantly boosted robot deployment across a wide range of applications, from daily tasks to industrial scenarios [ 1 ] . Among the various methods for collecting data, telemanipulation has proven particularly valuable for imitation learning, providing high-quality demonstrations characterized by natural and smooth trajectories that are essential for policy generalization [ 2 ] . Various telemanipulation systems have been investigated, including virtual reality (VR) devices [ 3 ] , cameras [ 4 ] , and wearable gloves [ 5 ] . VR devices in particular have been widely adopted, offering immersive three-dimensional workspace representations that enhance spatial awareness and task execution accuracy [ 6 , 7 ] . More recently, the emergence of advanced Mixed Reality (MR) platforms, particularly the Apple Vision Pro, has renewed interest in telemanipulation research, as its high-resolution displays, rich sensor suite, and onboard processing capabilities open new avenues for immersive robotic operation [ 8 , 9 ] .

Despite its advantages, telemanipulation presents notable challenges, particularly for the execution of fine-grained manipulation tasks that require subtle adjustments that are difficult for operators to perceive and execute accurately. Furthermore, large-scale data collection requires operators to repeat the same task numerous times so as to acquire sufficient demonstrations, making it increasingly difficult to maintain concentration throughout the entire process.
Fully autonomous systems, although effective for repetitive tasks in structured environments, often struggle in unstructured or unfamiliar scenarios demanding high dexterity. While vision-based autonomous systems have made considerable progress in addressing these challenges, ensuring reliable execution without any human supervision remains difficult, as even minor errors can lead to task failure.

To address these complementary limitations, semi-autonomous systems have emerged as a promising approach [ 10 , 11 ] , in which human-in-the-loop control allows operators to leverage their natural perception and decision-making capabilities to detect and correct errors in real time, while the robot autonomously handles the remaining execution [ 12 , 13 ] . Although prior work has demonstrated the feasibility of such systems, their application to fine-grained bimanual tasks remains an open challenge. Specifically, bimanual tasks offer much lower error tolerance, as any misalignment in one arm is often accumulated by the required synchronization with the other, leading to rapid task failure.

Therefore, this paper introduces a Mixed Reality-based semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation system designed for fine-grained manipulation tasks. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , by capturing the user’s hand gestures and movements through the Apple Vision Pro (AVP), our system translates them into precise robotic control commands in real time. The proposed system addresses existing limitations by integrating human-in-the-loop control with autonomous robotic execution, reducing operator workload while enabling efficient collection of large-scale high-accuracy demonstrations. The collected demonstrations are used to train an Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) policy, validating the quality of the collected data and demonstrating the scalability of the proposed pipeline.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related work

Telemanipulation. Recent advances in learning-based robotic manipulation have driven increasing demand for large-scale data collection, leading to the development of diverse telemanipulation systems. Among these, virtual reality-based interfaces have gained particular attention for enabling immersive and intuitive remote control of robotic manipulators. Various VR-based telemanipulation systems have been studied for collecting human demonstrations for robot learning [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 2 ] . Building on this, mixed reality-based telemanipulation further enhances the operator experience by overlaying virtual information onto the real environment, enabling more intuitive control and richer situational awareness [ 17 ] . Several studies have leveraged the AVP headset for dexterous telemanipulation, achieving improved data collection efficiency by utilizing its high-quality display and built-in hand-tracking capabilities [ 9 , 8 ] . Moreover, the AVP has been shown to outperform traditional VR headsets and other teleoperation interfaces in terms of usability and operator performance [ 18 ] . Nevertheless, these systems often require considerable telemanipulation experience from the operator, and the tasks demonstrated tend to be relatively simple, failing to meet the precision requirements of industrial applications. In order to solve more complex tasks while maintaining usability, semi-autonomous telemanipulation has emerged as a direction. Previous work has demonstrated its effectiveness in complex assembly tasks, with standardized user studies including the System Usability Scale (SUS) and NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX) showing that semi-autonomous telemanipulation offers notable improvements over pure telemanipulation in terms of physical demand, mental workload, and overall user experience [ 12 , 13 ] . Consequently, rather than pursuing dexterous hand-based systems focused on daily tasks, our work targets industrial scenarios where parallel grippers are sufficient for most operations [ 19 ] . Compared to dexterous hands, parallel grippers reduce the degrees of freedom involved, minimizing accumulated errors and yielding simpler and more predictable grasping behavior.

Data Collection. Collecting real-robot demonstrations has been shown to be more effective than simulation-based approaches [ 20 , 1 , 21 , 22 ] , primarily due to the large sim-to-real gap arising from complex physical contacts between the robot end-effector (EE) and objects. A classic approach involves exoskeleton devices or mirroring arms for joint-space mapping [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] , where the follower arm directly replicates the motion of the leader arm, enabling precise control for tasks such as battery insertion and velcro fastening [ 23 ] . However, these systems rely entirely on manual operation, requiring operators to control every stage of the task, which leads to fatigue and limits the scalability of data collection, motivating the requirement for more efficient and accessible data collection approaches.

Imitation Learning. Imitation learning enables robots to learn manipulation skills directly from expert demonstrations. Early approaches based on behavioral cloning cast imitation as supervised learning from observations to actions [ 27 ] , with subsequent works improving upon this by incorporating temporal history through various architectures, adopting alternative training objectives, and introducing regularization techniques [ 28 , 29 ] . Among recent advances, ACT [ 23 ] proposes to predict sequences of actions rather than single-step outputs, reducing the effect of compounding errors and enabling more stable execution of fine-grained manipulation tasks. Diffusion Policy [ 30 ] takes a generative approach by modeling the action distribution as a diffusion process, which effectively captures multimodal behavior and produces smooth, consistent trajectories. Building upon these foundations, subsequent works have achieved notable progress across a wide range of robotic manipulation tasks, further validating the effectiveness of these frameworks [ 31 , 32 ] .

2026-10-20.title: Dream What I Can: Sparse Visual Planning for Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Chongkai Gao , Wenlong Huang , Haonan Chen , Lin Shao , Yilun Du , Jiajun Wu , Ruohan Zhang , Li Fei-Fei
2026-10-20.abstract:
Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce DreamCan , a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual planning : a high-level planner adapted from a pre-trained video model and a low-level visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the high-level planner generates sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility . From offline, action-free robot videos, we estimate these quantities and use dynamic programming to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced alternatives, and the full system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners, reaching high planning success rates on Language-Table tasks and 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long with a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. Additional suboptimal videos and test-time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations.
More results are on https://dreamcan.github.io/ .
2026-10-20.introduction:
The promise of video models for robotics lies not merely in predicting how the world may evolve under interaction, but in revealing intermediate outcomes through which a task can be accomplished.
For manipulation, this knowledge extends beyond the task semantics readily expressed in language: visual predictions can depict contact, fine adjustment, and detailed configurations connecting a scene to a desired outcome. Video therefore offers an expressive medium for planning interactions whose geometric and physical details are cumbersome to specify in words.

Yet a plausible visual future is not necessarily one a robot can realize.
We argue that a visual plan should specify intermediate outcomes that support execution, rather than every intermediate frame. A goal image prediction may leave too much for the controller to solve, while a dense trajectory prescribes overly constrained motions that can be hard to realize by the controller. We thus propose sparse visual planning : learning to predict a sequence of subgoal images that both (i) makes meaningful progress towards achieving the task and (ii) remains executable by a low-level subgoal-conditioned policy.

We formalize these principles through reachability , which estimates how readily one visual state can be attained from another, and task utility , which measures progress toward the instruction. Under a fixed subgoal budget, a good subgoal sequence plan should reward terminal utility and penalize difficult transitions. Utility directs the plan toward task completion; reachability determines its intermediate steps. This formulation echoes SayCan’s decomposition into task relevance and robotic affordance [ 1 ] , but does not require a predefined vocabulary of language-labeled skills. Instead, intermediate objectives can be discovered from video datasets, allowing them to reflect visual configurations useful for execution rather than language-based task decompositions.

We term our approach DreamCan , a sparse visual planner that generates policy-aware sequences of visual subgoals. Given a dataset of robot manipulation videos, we first learn two complementary value functions from the action-free data: a reachability value , estimating whether one visual state can be reliably reached from another, and a task utility value , measuring progress toward task completion. We instantiate reachability with goal-conditioned offline RL [ 2 , 3 ] under sparse rewards, and estimate utility using a task-progress model [ 4 ] or a VLM. We then jointly use these two values to automatically annotate each video with a sequence of visual subgoals that balances local reachability with global task progress. The resulting subgoal sequences are used to fine-tune a pretrained video generation model, WAN-2.2 [ 5 ] , to predict sparse visual subgoals from the current observation and language instruction, serving as the planning output of our model. These predicted subgoals can be subsequently executed by a goal-conditioned low-level policy.

Through extensive experiments, we show that DreamCan consistently outperforms alternative planning representations, including language plans, dense video predictions, and uniformly sampled visual subgoals. On three challenging Language-Table tasks [ 6 ] , DreamCan achieves substantially higher planning success rates than the prior state-of-the-art method [ 7 ] . On LIBERO-Long [ 8 ] , our hierarchical system achieves a 91.2% success rate with only a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. We further show that DreamCan benefits from scaling suboptimal action-free video data on RoboMimic-MH Square [ 9 ] , without additional policy training, as well as from increased test-time compute on Language Table [ 6 ] . The sparse planning representation also naturally supports language-guided steering at test time, enabling users to specify preferred plans. Finally, on a suite of challenging real-world tasks, our system demonstrates effective manipulation under contact-rich interactions, long horizons, and combinatorial generalization using a bimanual robot platform, while maintaining fast closed-loop replanning at 1.03s per planning step on an RTX 5090 GPU.

Our contributions are: (i) We propose DreamCan, a sparse visual planner for robot manipulation that learns from action-free video datasets using automatically discovered subgoals that balance reachability and task utility; (ii) We integrate DreamCan with a goal-conditioned policy to form a closed-loop hierarchical manipulation system, and demonstrate strong performance across simulated benchmarks and real-world contact-rich tasks; and (iii) We show that the proposed sparse planning framework scales effectively with both suboptimal video data and test-time compute, while supporting language-guided plan steering at inference time.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Keystate Planning for Robot Manipulation Tasks

Sparse temporal abstractions have long been used to reduce the redundancy of dense robot trajectories. Keystates can be obtained from manual annotations [ 10 , 11 ] , embodiment-specific signals such as actions, proprioception, gripper states, and unsupervised objectives based on temporal structure, reconstruction, or information-theoretic criteria [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . However, these approaches either scale poorly or rely on signals unavailable in video-only data. VLMs can instead identify semantically salient task stages [ 15 ] , but semantic salience does not guarantee executability. Several works directly use visual subgoals for planning and control. KeyIn [ 14 ] discovers keyframes through prediction and reconstruction, SuSIE [ 16 ] generates subgoal images through a pretrained image generator, and LBP [ 17 ] predicts latent subgoal sequences using fixed temporal supervision. In contrast, we construct sparse visual subgoals by balancing task utility and reachability , favoring states that are both reachable and useful.

## II-B World Models for Robot Manipulation Tasks

World models support robot control by predicting future dynamics. Latent models such as Dreamer [ 18 ] and TD-MPC [ 19 ] enable policy optimization or model-predictive control, while visual models such as UniPi [ 20 ] , UniSim [ 21 ] , and other works [ 22 , 23 ] predict future observations for action generation or interaction. More recent world-action models jointly model visual futures and actions [ 24 , 25 ] , with Fast-WAM [ 26 ] improving inference efficiency. Our work instead focuses on the temporal granularity of explicit visual planning. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, we generate sparse subgoal images supervised by reachability and task utility . This reduces prediction overhead, enables test-time search, and enables learning from suboptimal datasets. We further decouple the planner and policy, allowing them to communicate solely through subgoal images without sharing gradients or features. This modular design enables either component to be independently replaced or upgraded.

2026-10-20.title: Anticipatory Gait Switching for Quadrupeds via Look-Ahead MDP Planning
2026-10-20.authors: Kelvin Aladum , Justin Peel , Nisar Ahmed
2026-10-20.abstract:
Quadruped robots often switch gaits to traverse mixed terrain safely. Many practical supervisors enforce hardware constraints (e.g., dwell or guard intervals) using a transition handler. However, the switch decision itself is often driven by near-field thresholds, which can delay commitment when rough terrain is only detected shortly before contact in the local height map.
We propose a lightweight height-map-only gait supervisor that unifies look-ahead and locomotion constraints in a single decision policy. A robot-centered height map is partitioned into near-, mid-, and far-field bands, each discretized into a terrain class, and band evolution is modeled as a Markov process. Gait selection is cast as a look-ahead Markov Decision Process whose transition model and cost explicitly encode platform-specific switching constraints.
Indoor and outdoor experiments on a Unitree Go2 platform show reduced late switching, lower time spent using ineffective gaits on rough terrain, and improved roll stability compared to tuned reactive baselines. Overall, the MDP formulation yields anticipative constraint-aware gait switching that improves robustness without course-specific retuning.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work and Problem Statement

## II-A Problem Statement

We study high-level gait switching for a quadruped using a robot-centered, short-horizon 2.5D LiDAR height map observed online in previously unseen environments. The robot may support multiple locomotion modes with direction-dependent transition requirements; in this work, we focus on switching between a fast trot ( T T ) and a cautious climb ( C C ) to isolate the decision problem under real transition constraints. At discrete decision times t = 0 , 1 , 2 , … t=0,1,2,\dots with period Δ ​ t \Delta t , the supervisor must choose whether to remain in the current gait or initiate a switch.

On real hardware, gait transitions can be asymmetric and delayed by controller logic and safety checks. In particular, the T → C T\rightarrow C transition may require stopping and dwelling before the new gait reliably engages. The objective is to compute a switching strategy that anticipates rough terrain early enough to complete this transition cost, while avoiding unnecessary switching on smooth ground despite noisy height maps and short look-ahead.

2026-10-20.title: DiPLO: Self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Shafeef Omar , Sebastian Sanokowski , Elham Daneshmand , Dian Yu , Daniel Cremers , Cordelia Schmid , Majid Khadiv
2026-10-20.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation is particularly challenging because it requires coordinating locomotion, balance, and object interaction, making it difficult to learn from limited demonstrations or from scratch through Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce DiPLO (self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation), a framework that combines a self-distilled diffusion planner with a low-level whole-body tracking policy. Our planner is pretrained via supervised learning on motions derived from human-to-humanoid retargeting, while the tracker is trained via RL to execute them. DiPLO centers around two complementary post-training stages. First, we introduce Self-Distillation Diffusion Policy Optimisation (SD:DPO) to remove the planner’s dependence on strong task conditioning, which we identify as a crucial ingredient for effective pretraining, as downstream fine-tuning does not recover comparable performance when it is omitted.. We then fine-tune this distilled model with Diffusion-Augmented Proximal Policy Optimization (DA:PPO), a maximum-entropy RL method for diffusion models, to improve task success and align generated plans with the frozen tracker’s execution capabilities. Together, these stages enable motion generation through state-history and goal conditioning alone, enabling ∼ 99 % \sim 99\% task success in pick-carry-place tasks, compared to just 45 % 45\% for the pretrained model. The resulting planner also generates motions for unseen object goals, with further evaluations on kicking and pushing/pulling tasks. Finally, we deploy our pipeline on the hardware, using our DA:PPO planner-tracker on a Unitree G1, achieving repeated successful executions without any real-world fine-tuning. Video: https://youtu.be/rDrdnYQUYoM
2026-10-20.introduction:
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating locomotion, balance, and object interaction. Human motion data provides useful supervision for learning these behaviors, but collecting large datasets is costly [ 1 , 2 ] . Our goal is to learn from a small dataset of retargeted motions while keeping task specification simple: the user provides the desired object position and orientation, and the robot determines how to reach it. This requires a planner that can generate trackable motions for different object goals, including goals beyond those represented in the demonstrated behaviours.

We introduce DiPLO (self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation), which combines a diffusion motion planner with an RL-trained tracker. Starting from 29 retargeted robot–object motion sequences from an existing dataset [ 3 ] (which amounts to just 2.7 2.7 mins of data), we use trajectory optimization [ 4 ] and augmentation to generate dynamically feasible training motions for both components. During execution, the diffusion planner generates motion chunks and replans from the measured state as the tracker executes them.
Such a pretrained planner still relies strongly on kinematic reference conditioning, which limits its ability to generate motions to new goals.
To remove this dependence after pretraining, we propose Self-Distillation Diffusion Policy Optimization (SD:DPO). SD:DPO transfers guidance from a reference-conditioned teacher to a student conditioned only on state history and the object goal. The student learns to match the teacher’s denoising predictions at states encountered during environment rollouts with the tracker. These rollouts expose the student to the consequences of planning and tracking errors, extending its supervision beyond the contexts represented in the training data. SD:DPO thereby enables high survival without requiring a kinematic reference at deployment.

Trackable motions alone, however, do not ensure that the object reaches its goal. We therefore follow self-distillation with planner fine-tuning using DA:PPO [ 5 ] , a maximum-entropy RL method for diffusion models. With the tracker fixed, DA:PPO improves task completion through closed-loop interaction while encouraging diversity in generated plans. SD:DPO and DA:PPO thus address complementary requirements: removing dependence on reference conditioning and improving task success.
Our main contributions are:

We introduce DiPLO, a framework that combines a self-distilled diffusion-based planner for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly generates whole-body and object motion for execution by a single generalist RL tracking policy.

We propose SD:DPO, which distills a reference-conditioned diffusion planner into a goal-conditioned planner, removing the need for kinematic reference conditioning at deployment. We further apply DA:PPO fine-tuning through closed-loop interaction with a fixed genralist tracker, improving object-goal completion while maintaining diverse, trackable plans.

We provide extensive ablations across a diverse set of loco-manipulation tasks, demonstrating the effectiveness of DiPLO and its components compared with state-of-the-art baselines, together with zero-shot transfer to a real humanoid robot.

2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Retargeted motions provide supervision for learning whole-body tracking policies [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] , but kinematic retargeting [ 9 , 3 ] alone does not ensure physically feasible robot–object interaction. DynaRetarget [ 4 ] addresses this limitation through sampling-based trajectory optimization (SBTO), which refines a kinematic reference into a dynamically feasible motion. To scale demonstrations beyond those recorded, HumanoidMimicGen [ 10 ] augments loco-manipulation data by adapting object-centric skill segments of a source demonstration to new object poses. However, it plans kinematically and decouples locomotion from stationary manipulation, so dynamic feasibility is not enforced during generation. In contrast, we repurpose SBTO, originally proposed to refine individual demonstrations, for data augmentation: starting from perturbed initial conditions, we exploit the stochasticity of the sampling-based optimizer to synthesize locally diverse, dynamically feasible robot–object motions in which locomotion and manipulation remain coupled.

Diffusion Policy [ 11 ] models multimodal action sequences for robotic manipulation. In humanoid locomotion, however, maintaining balance while accomplishing the task motivates delegating execution to a low-level controller [ 12 ] . PDP [ 13 ] learns action generation from expert policies, while BeyondMimic [ 14 ] uses guided state–action diffusion to generate goal-directed behaviors. An alternative is to separate motion generation from execution: [ 15 ] combine a diffusion motion generator with a tracking policy for terrain locomotion.
Recent works have shown the success of this separation in loco-manipulation settings [ 16 , 17 ] .
REFINE-DP [ 16 ] is closest to our approach in combining diffusion planning with RL fine-tuning for humanoid loco-manipulation. Its planner generates motion commands for separate upper- and lower-body controllers. DiPLO instead jointly plans whole-body and object motion for a single generalist tracking policy.
Our post-training procedure also differs. We first use SD:DPO to remove the dependence on kinematic reference conditioning introduced during pretraining on retargeted motions. We then apply maximum-entropy fine-tuning with DA:PPO while keeping the tracker fixed. Finally, our generalization evaluation examines whether the same trained planner can reach different requested object positions and orientations that are absent from the retargeted dataset.

Our planner also treats rotational features through diffusion on SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) . Such processes have been developed for rotational alignment [ 18 , 19 ] , while DiffDock [ 20 ] combines diffusion over translational, rotational, and torsional degrees of freedom. We apply this geometric formulation to humanoid–object motion, evaluate its effect on closed-loop survival, and retain it during planner post-training.

Teacher–student distillation allows policies to benefit from information unavailable at deployment [ 21 ] . Following such a recipe, OmniH2O [ 8 ] distills a controller with privileged observations into a policy using deployable observations and sparse motion commands. Our objective concerns the high-level task specification: removing the diffusion planner’s dependence on strong task conditioning (kinematic reference trajectory).

The closest methodological precedent is Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) [ 22 ] , which uses a language model conditioned on additional feedback as a self-teacher and distills its next-token predictions into a student. Inspired by SDPO, we propose SD:DPO for diffusion motion planning. A teacher with access to privileged task-prior conditioning supervises the student’s denoising predictions on states encountered during closed-loop environment rollouts with the tracker, enabling reward-free credit assignment through denoising-step matching. This distills the guidance provided by the privileged task prior into a planner conditioned only on the robot’s state history and object goal, allowing the task prior to be removed at deployment. We evaluate both the resulting improvement in survival and the ability of the distilled planner to generate motions for object goals absent from the retargeted dataset.

Diffusion-Policy Policy Optimization (DPPO) [ 23 ] enables reinforcement learning for diffusion policies by treating denoising transitions as decisions with tractable likelihoods and applying PPO to the resulting augmented process. REFINE-DP [ 16 ] applies diffusion-policy fine-tuning to humanoid loco-manipulation, considering both a fixed controller and alternating updates of the planner and controllers. However, DPPO promotes exploration by truncating the denoising process during training, which can lead to jittery motions. Such behavior is particularly undesirable for real-world humanoid control, where smooth and dynamically consistent motions are essential.

Diffusion-Augmented MDPs [ 5 ] instead provide a maximum-entropy formulation in which ratios of reverse and forward transition densities yield tractable entropy regularization at each denoising step. We use their PPO instantiation, DA:PPO, to fine-tune the planner after SD:DPO. Our setting combines Euclidean and SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) diffusion and evaluates generated motions through a frozen generalist tracker. DA:PPO optimizes task completion after kinematic reference conditioning has been removed, while entropy regularization encourages diversity in the generated plans. We separately evaluate tracker adaptation to distinguish improvements due to planner fine-tuning from those obtained by adapting the tracker.

2026-10-20.title: Escape Without a Recipe: Maneuver-Agnostic Mars Rover Recovery from Granular Entrapment
2026-10-20.authors: Meraj Hossain Promit , Chandak Chakma , Md Jubair Ahmed Sourov , Sejuti Rahman
2026-10-20.abstract: Wheeled planetary rovers immobilised in loose regolith have no principled recovery controller: scripted maneuvers are terrain-specific, and naive driving deepens entrapment. We introduce a recurrent policy that learns to escape without a predefined maneuver. The framework rests on a verified trap: in a continuum material point method (MPM) simulator we identify a configuration at sinkage-to-radius ratio z / r = 2.0 z/r=2.0 where the strongest of ten scripted controllers succeeds in only 7 / 32 7/32 trials, yet the regolith retains traction and continues to shear, confirming granular entrapment rather than a numerical artifact. A frozen entrapment detector, trained on 81,771 windows spanning three materials and six sinkage levels, supplies a three-state belief to the policy observation. A separate simulator mobility latch gates training rewards. Across five training seeds, mean-action evaluation achieves 62.5 % 62.5\% escape (range 28.1 28.1 – 81.3 % 81.3\% ; 32 trials per seed) versus 7 / 32 7/32 for the strongest scripted controller and 0 / 32 0/32 for action noise. A numerical audit identifies a coupling-buffer fault that silently discarded 9.7 % 9.7\% of contact nodes at 16 parallel environments. Results establish recovery in the tested simulation regime; physical transfer remains unverified.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Spirit’s immobilization at Troy illustrates the difficulty of recovery after wheel burial [ 1 ] . Scripted approaches prescribe push-pull locomotion [ 2 ] or material-remodeling gaits [ 3 ] ; optimization adapts their parameters [ 4 ] . Reinforcement learning (RL) can instead discover commands directly. Prior learned extrication [ 5 ] and deformable-terrain locomotion [ 6 , 7 ] motivate combining continuous recovery control with numerical checks of wheel–soil coupling.

Our framework (Figs. – 2 ) learns recovery without demonstrations or prescribed maneuvers. We evaluate five training seeds against ten scripted controllers and audit numerical coupling.

2026-10-20.title: SARAM: Sparse Adapter Allocation with Reuse and Merging for Lifelong Robot Learning
2026-10-20.authors: SeongJun Jeong , Chungwoo Lee , Gi-Cheon Kang , Byoung-Tak Zhang
2026-10-20.abstract:
Lifelong robot learning requires acquiring new tasks sequentially without forgetting earlier ones.
With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, adapter-based methods effectively mitigate this challenge.
However, their task-specific adapters and selection modules accumulate with the task stream, creating a scalability challenge in on-disk storage and deployment cost under fixed onboard resource budgets.
We propose SARAM , a lifelong learning framework that limits storage growth while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the task stream length.
For each new task, SARAM reuses frozen adapters from previous tasks and introduces new adapters only at sparsely selected layers, with a duplication penalty encouraging them to capture information not already represented by the adapter library.
At deployment, a compact signature derived from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone, leaving only the backbone in the control loop.
Across four LIBERO suites, SARAM matches or exceeds adapter-based baselines while adding up to 4.5 × 4.5\times less on-disk state per task.
GPU memory usage and control frequency remain comparable to those of the backbone as the task stream grows.
Experiments on a real UR5 arm with a different backbone further demonstrate retention throughout a sequential task stream.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Robots deployed in real environments need to learn new tasks continually [ 1 ] , yet onboard hardware imposes fixed budgets on storage, memory, and compute.
Learning tasks sequentially causes catastrophic forgetting [ 2 , 3 ] , where acquiring a new task degrades performance on previously learned ones.
Existing approaches address this through replay, regularization, or architectural isolation, which require storing past demonstrations, provide weaker protection against forgetting, or leave progressively less free capacity for new tasks, respectively [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] , recent methods [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] increasingly adopt lightweight adapters such as LoRA [ 14 ] .
The backbone remains frozen, while each task learns its own adapters, which are then frozen so that later training cannot overwrite them.
By freezing the backbone and task-specific adapters, these methods effectively preserve previously learned tasks.

However, task-specific adapters must be selected at deployment, and the oracle task ID is typically unavailable.
Instead, the robot receives the current observation and language instruction, from which the appropriate task-specific adapter must be identified.
Recent methods [ 12 , 13 ] dynamically select task-specific adapters from the current input during execution.
By design, the adapters and selection modules therefore remain active in the control loop, increasing GPU memory and per-step computation as tasks accumulate.

As illustrated in Fig. 1 , this accumulation appears along two axes.
During training, task-specific adapters, selection modules, and associated state accumulate on disk as new tasks are learned.
At deployment, the adapters and selection modules must remain available on the GPU and are used throughout the control loop.
Both axes therefore grow with the task stream, conflicting with the fixed resource budgets of onboard robot hardware. Can a VLA policy learn new tasks continually while keeping its deployment cost independent of the task stream and limiting task-dependent storage growth?

To address this, we propose SARAM , a lifelong robot learning method that addresses the two axes at their respective stages: storage as tasks accumulate, and deployment cost at execution.
During learning, each new task first reuses a linear combination of frozen LoRA adapters from previous tasks, then adds new adapters only at layers selected under a sparsity penalty.
A duplication penalty discourages the new adapters from reproducing what the reused library already expresses.
The newly allocated adapters and combination coefficients are frozen after training, so later tasks cannot overwrite previously learned parameters. Because every per-task update stays linear in the weights, it can later be folded into the backbone rather than evaluated as a separate module.

SARAM then removes task selection from the control loop.
After each task is learned, the demonstrations are passed through the adapter-free backbone and its layer-wise activation statistics are summarized into a compact task signature.
These frozen-backbone statistics provide task-dependent signatures without requiring a learned selection module.
At deployment, the initial observation and instruction are summarized in the same way, matched against the stored signatures, and the selected update is merged into the backbone before execution.
The episode therefore runs on a single backbone, with no task-specific adapter or selection module inside the control loop, keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost at the backbone’s level regardless of the number of learned tasks.

We evaluate SARAM on four LIBERO suites against adapter-based methods [ 13 , 12 ] and standard continual learning baselines. SARAM attains the highest final success rate and AUC on all four suites while requiring up to 4.5 × 4.5\times less on-disk state per task than adapter-based baselines.
At deployment, SARAM remains at the backbone’s level in both GPU memory and control frequency: after ten tasks it runs at 15.2 Hz with 748 MB of GPU memory, identical to the backbone alone.
By contrast, CLARE and DMPEL grow to 922 MB and 829 MB of GPU memory and slow to 10.1 Hz and 5.0 Hz after ten tasks, respectively.
On a seven-task real-robot stream with a different VLA backbone, SARAM ends the stream at the same success rate it reached when each task was learned, showing that the method transfers to a physical robot and a different backbone architecture.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

We propose SARAM , an adapter-based lifelong robot learning method that limits per-task storage through adapter reuse, sparse allocation, and compact task signatures in place of learned selection modules.

At deployment, task signatures move selection outside the control loop, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone to keep GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the number of learned tasks.

On four LIBERO suites, SARAM attains the highest final success rate and AUC while requiring up to 4.5 × 4.5\times less on-disk state per task, and real-robot experiments with a different VLA backbone demonstrate applicability beyond simulation.

2. At deployment, task signatures move selection outside the control loop, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone to keep GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the number of learned tasks.
