# II RELATED WORK

Lifelong Robot Learning. Lifelong robot learning [ 15 , 1 ] studies how robots can learn new tasks sequentially while retaining those learned before.
A central challenge, shared with continual learning in general [ 3 ] , is catastrophic forgetting [ 6 ] , where learning new tasks degrades performance on earlier ones.
Existing approaches address this problem through replay, regularization, or architectural isolation.
Replay methods retain past demonstrations for later training [ 4 ] , which incurs storage overhead and can be undesirable when past demonstrations cannot be retained.
Regularization methods such as EWC [ 6 ] avoid storing past data but often provide weaker protection against forgetting.
Architectural-isolation methods such as PackNet [ 7 ] protect previous tasks by reserving separate capacity, but the available capacity becomes increasingly constrained as more tasks are learned.
In robot manipulation, LIBERO [ 1 ] provides a standard benchmark for evaluating sequential task learning and retention.

Adapter-Based Lifelong Robot Learning. With the emergence of large pretrained VLA policies [ 9 , 8 , 16 , 17 , 10 ] , recent work has increasingly adopted lightweight adapters for task-specific adaptation while keeping the backbone frozen [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
After each task is learned, its adapter is frozen, preventing later training from overwriting previously learned task parameters.
This provides strong retention, but requires maintaining additional task-specific parameters as the task stream grows.
When the oracle task ID is unavailable, CLARE [ 12 ] and DMPEL [ 13 ] dynamically select or combine task-specific modules from the current input using learned discriminators and a router, respectively.
These input-dependent mechanisms remain active during control, causing task-specific storage and deployment cost to grow with the task stream.

Resource-Efficient Continual Learning. Recent work beyond robotics has explored reducing the parameter growth of adapter-based continual learning.
Some approaches compress task-specific adapters into a shared low-rank representation or merge multiple task updates into a shared model [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] .
These methods reduce parameter growth, but typically update shared parameters that also represent previously learned tasks.
Their evaluation settings typically do not consider task selection from observations and instructions at deployment.
In contrast, SARAM keeps previously learned task parameters frozen, reuses past adapters through combination coefficients, and adds new adapters only at layers retained by sparse allocation.
It further replaces learned selection modules with task signatures and merges the corresponding task update into the VLA backbone before execution, so only the backbone runs during control.

2026-10-20.title: When Better Policies Leave Harder Failures: Coverage Shift in VLM Success Monitoring
2026-10-20.authors: Isabel Guan , Dingyuan Zhang , Shipeng Lyu , I-Ming Chen
2026-10-20.abstract: Can a better robot policy become harder to monitor? We study a fixed vision-language model (VLM) that judges success while a policy improves. In a controlled 20-seed tray-placement experiment, training selects only simulator-verified successes. Success rises from 66.8% to 97.0%, and accepted hover failures fall from 5.0% to 0.9% of executions. Yet the judge accepts 50.0% of remaining hovers, versus 31.1% under untrained sampling. These residual failures more often lie below the tray rim, which can conceal the gap beneath a grasped cube. A separate boundary probe accepts 148/160 below-rim hovers and 0/160 above-rim hovers. We call this change in conditional monitoring sensitivity coverage shift : learning changes which failures reach a fixed judge. A broader diagnosis covers nine judges and 1,392 stimuli. Judge-filtered experiments across eight settings further show heterogeneous effects of state-dependent acceptance. The results distinguish task improvement from failure detectability and motivate reporting absolute misses, conditional misses, and audit coverage together.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Robot learning systems increasingly ask vision-language models (VLMs) whether an attempt succeeded. A verdict can select experience for further training, provide a reward, or alert an operator to failure [ 5 , 25 , 10 ] . These uses share a requirement: the judge must recognize the failures produced by the policy it serves. Evaluating it on a fixed set of outcomes measures this ability only for the states in that set. As the policy learns, the failures requiring detection may change.

The change can occur while task performance improves sharply. Consider placing a cube in a tray. A cube still grasped above the tray is an obvious failure when its bottom is above the rim. Lowering it below the rim can hide the gap from a low frontal camera, even though it remains grasped and off the floor. If learning removes many high hovers but leaves low hovers, a fixed judge faces fewer failures overall and a more difficult mixture of failures. Both facts matter: the system makes fewer undetected errors per attempt, while its monitor detects a smaller fraction of the errors that remain.

Our principal experiment establishes this distinction without using the judge to train the policy. A truth-filtered arm selects only simulator-confirmed successes. Compared with untrained sampling, it raises success from 66.8% to 97.0% and reduces hover incidence from 15.9% to 1.8%. Yet the judge’s acceptance conditional on a hover rises from 31.1% to 50.0%, a paired difference of 18.9 percentage points across 20 seeds. The share of hovers below the rim rises from 31.3% to 52.6%. The mechanism overview in Fig. 2 separates the training path, the changed failure geometry, and the two monitoring denominators.

We use coverage shift to describe this change in the failure states on which a fixed judge is evaluated. The term identifies a distributional mechanism, not a new learning algorithm. It does not imply that the judge deteriorates on the same images. It also does not require a policy to exploit the judge: simulator truth supplies every training decision in the central comparison. The policy family nevertheless matters. Our controller shares height parameters between released and unreleased actions, and its refitting procedure imposes smoothing and probability constraints. These implementation choices provide a plausible route from successful training to low residual hovers, which our experiments localize but do not fully isolate.

We organize the evidence around three questions. What physical and visual coverage does a static diagnosis provide? How does learning change conditional monitoring sensitivity when truth supplies the labels? When a judge does select training samples, does the assignment of its errors to individual states affect subsequent failures? The last question uses a separate permutation intervention across eight judge–task–view settings. Its results concern the learning signal and cannot be added to the monitoring comparison as an effect decomposition.

The contributions are an empirical counterexample to treating task improvement as preserved monitoring sensitivity, a boundary-based account supported by executed states, and controls that distinguish refitting, truth selection, and state-dependent judge selection. The broader nine-judge diagnosis and eight-setting experiments also expose limits: static prediction and a proposed repair criterion fail their prespecified tests, and several permutation contrasts remain unresolved. Our recommendation is therefore specific: evaluate the failures the policy visits, retain probes near physical success boundaries, and report conditional misses alongside their absolute frequency.

# 2 Related Work

SuccessVQA studies task-success detection through visual questions [ 5 ] , and Luo examines sensitivity to visual distribution shift [ 12 ] . VLM-RMs and RoboCLIP derive rewards from pretrained vision–language representations [ 20 , 21 ] . RoboReward broadens robotic reward modeling with negative examples [ 10 ] . REFLECT uses multisensory summaries to explain failures [ 11 ] ; AHA trains failure detection and explanation [ 6 ] ; FailBench studies natural manipulation failures and visual evidence [ 15 ] . Our diagnosis holds an executed physical state fixed across views, then asks how learning changes the states that a monitor must judge.

SOAR autonomously collects and evaluates robot experience [ 25 ] , while RoboCat trains on additional self-generated data [ 3 ] . We isolate the selection step through a small controller distribution. Selection followed by distribution fitting is classical in the cross-entropy method [ 4 ] . Erroneous pseudo-labels can reinforce errors [ 1 ] ; our truth-filtered comparison instead supplies correct labels and measures changes in a separate monitor. This also relates to performative prediction [ 17 ] : decisions can change an evaluated distribution, including when the evaluator does not direct those decisions.

Goodhart-style failures and reward overoptimization concern a proxy’s relationship to its target under selection [ 14 , 8 , 24 , 9 ] . Imperfect verifiers limit resampling [ 22 ] , and verifier error structure affects arithmetic reinforcement learning and language-model cascades [ 7 , 19 ] . CriticHack is the closest robotic comparison: it studies visual reward optimization, diffusion-policy fine-tuning, an exponential-tilt account, and a frozen verifier intervention [ 13 ] . Its results include rising wrong-object failures alongside rising success. Our central observation instead combines decreasing absolute accepted failures with increasing conditional acceptance under truth-based training. The subsequent permutation study concerns threshold filtering and parametric refitting. CriticHack was available during the later interpretation and audit; the supplement preserves chronology and evidence scope without claiming independent conceptual priority.

2026-10-20.title: Learning Structured Locomotion References for Optimization-Based Whole-Body Control
2026-10-20.authors: Ömer Tarık Banuş , Uluç Saranlı , M. Mert Ankaralı
2026-10-20.abstract:
Quadruped locomotion requires coordinating body motion, contact forces,
foothold placement, and gait timing. We present a hierarchical controller in
which reinforcement learning adapts these structured locomotion references
while a gait scheduler, reactive footstep planner, and whole-body impulse
controller retain responsibility for high-frequency execution. The model-based
backbone can sustain a nominal trot independently, allowing the policy to focus
on when and how to modify an already functional locomotion controller. We train the
complete hierarchy in a vectorized controller-in-the-loop environment using a
six-direction disturbance curriculum. Under a common simulator and evaluation
protocol, the proposed controller achieves 77.29% mean survival across the
tested disturbance grid, compared with 50.35% for the model-based reference
controller. Training-time channel ablations identify adaptive foothold placement
as the largest marginal contributor to grid survival and reveal
direction-dependent effects of gait-rate adaptation. Together, these results
demonstrate the viability of the proposed hierarchical controller architecture
for integrating learned adaptation with optimization-based whole-body control
through structured locomotion references.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Quadruped locomotion is a hybrid control problem that couples continuous
floating-base dynamics with discrete changes in unilateral contact [ 1 ] . The
controller must coordinate body motion, ground-reaction forces, foothold
placement, and contact timing while respecting friction and actuator limits.
During a disturbance, several of these quantities may need to change
simultaneously and within a short time.

Model-based locomotion controllers address this complexity by separating gait
scheduling, footstep planning, force generation, whole-body control, and
joint-level feedback [ 2 , 3 ] .
Template-based controllers likewise organize locomotion through
low-dimensional gait variables [ 4 ] . Convex model
predictive control (MPC), for example, plans ground-reaction forces (GRFs)
using a reduced-order model [ 5 ] . Kim et al. ’s
whole-body impulse control (WBIC) is a specific optimization-based whole-body
control (WBC) formulation that converts force and motion references into
dynamically consistent joint commands at high frequency [ 6 ] . Related whole-body optimization methods reason more
directly about contact and full-body dynamics [ 7 ] . These intermediate references provide a useful
abstraction boundary: higher layers select behaviorally meaningful quantities,
while lower layers resolve full-body dynamics and joint commands. This
structure provides reliable and physically interpretable execution, but its
adaptability depends on how the references are generated. Contact sequences
and gait cadence are often
prescribed, while footholds are commonly selected using engineered rules such
as Raibert-style heuristics [ 8 ] . Extending the resulting
behavior can therefore require additional modeling, planning, and manual
tuning. More general motion-optimization methods expose footholds and contact
timing as decision variables, but still require an explicit model and objective [ 9 , 10 ] .

Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a complementary way to adapt these
decisions through interaction. Learned policies have demonstrated agile
locomotion and robust terrain traversal in simulation and on hardware [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
Here, we use joint-space RL to denote policies that output
joint-position targets or residuals tracked by joint-level feedback, as in [ 14 ] . Such a policy must implicitly learn how joint
commands produce coordinated body and foot motion. Training requires
substantial experience, and the policy outputs do not by themselves enforce
dynamic or contact feasibility.
Task-space and hybrid approaches instead use learning to command physically
meaningful variables while retaining a model-based execution layer [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] . Related approaches augment MPC or WBC using learned
corrections, optimal-control guidance, model-error compensation, or constrained
execution layers [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] .

We follow this principle with a quadruped locomotion stack comprising a
continuous gait scheduler, Raibert-style footstep planning, WBIC, and
joint-level feedback, as shown in Fig. 1 . The model-based
backbone can sustain a nominal trot from fixed motion and force references
without learned modifications. RL replaces MPC as the adaptive reference
generator rather than replacing the low-level controller. Through a
25-dimensional structured action, the policy modifies commanded body motion,
desired stance forces, foothold placement, body height, and gait progression.
The policy can therefore coordinate balance, stepping, and cadence, while the
model-based layers remain responsible for high-frequency execution.

The contribution is not the integration of RL with whole-body control alone.
Instead, we give one policy broad supervisory authority over several coupled
levels of an already functional locomotion controller. This allows learning to
focus on adapting nominal locomotion rather than rediscovering joint
coordination from scratch.

Our contributions are a hierarchical controller architecture that exposes
body motion, contact forces, foothold placement, body height, and continuous
gait timing to one learned supervisor; a vectorized MuJoCo–EnvPool environment
for training the complete controller–simulator loop; and an empirical
characterization through disturbance-survival evaluation and training-time
action-channel ablations. We evaluate the resulting configured system
under the same simulator and protocol as MPC+WBIC [ 6 ] and joint-space RL [ 14 ] . The
disturbance experiments test the resulting architecture under large
perturbations; they are not intended to establish the structured interface as
a universally optimal action representation.

2026-10-20.title: EndoVLA-OOV: Language-Conditioned Out-of-View Target Acquisition in Robotic Endoscopy
2026-10-20.authors: Chi Kit Ng , Yidong Zhang , Tianchun Wu , Zhiqing Tang , Hanlin Zhao , Siu Hing Lui , Tao Yang , Jingsong Lin , Huxin Gao , Yeung Trevor , Raymond Tang , Hongliang Ren
2026-10-20.abstract: The scan-then-revisit workflow of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy requires bringing a previously observed suspicious region back into view for closer inspection. Acquiring such targets requires translating anatomical and appearance descriptions into camera motions from partial observations of a confined, deformable environment. We present EndoVLA-OOV, a language-conditioned vision-language-action policy for out-of-view target acquisition in robotic endoscopy. The policy adapts a pretrained backbone to continuous two-degree-of-freedom distal bending commands and combines initial, intermediate, and current images to guide search. To support policy learning, we provide a VLA dataset containing 1,050 episodes across six tasks and approximately 262k observation–action pairs. Physical evaluation spans wet-lens and low-light conditions, two unseen stomach phantoms, and cross-embodiment transfer to an unseen ex-vivo environment. In the cross-embodiment evaluation, the full-data policy achieves 93.3% target acquisition success (28/30). In a controlled training-data comparison, expanding the corpus from 312 to 1,050 episodes increases acquisition success from 40.0% to 90.0% under the same model, training, and test configuration. Instruction and observation interventions further support the use of language and temporal context in the evaluated acquisition tasks. These results support language-guided endoscopic revisitation across the evaluated environments and robot embodiments and demonstrate the benefit of expanded task-specific demonstrations.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy combines systematic mucosal inspection with focused examination of suspicious regions. Screening protocols organize stomach coverage into anatomical stations and recorded views, providing a spatial framework for inspection and subsequent review [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Quality standards emphasize careful examination and photographic documentation [ 4 , 5 ] , and a study of systematic image acquisition reported an association between more gastroscopy images and detection of clinically significant gastric lesions [ 6 ] . These practices motivate robotic assistance that links a region of interest to the camera motion needed to inspect it. After an initial scan, an operator can specify an anatomical station and target appearance, and ask the robot to bring that target back into view for closer examination.

This scan-then-revisit workflow creates a specific control problem: language-conditioned acquisition of an initially out-of-view (OOV) target (Fig. 1 ). The instruction supplies a semantic goal, while the current image shows only a local portion of the stomach. Bending changes the visible folds, distances and illumination, and successive views reveal different parts of the target’s surroundings. Successful acquisition therefore involves choosing camera motions from partial observations until the requested target becomes visible. Once acquired, the target supports image-space feedback for centering.

Flexible endoscope operation combines insertion, axial shaft rotation and two distal bending degrees of freedom (DoFs). Robotic assistance has introduced motorized steering, lumen centralization and feedback control to support camera positioning [ 7 , 8 ] . Visual servoing provides a general framework for converting visible feature errors into corrective motion [ 9 ] . OOV acquisition extends the observation requirements of this interface: the policy uses the requested region, target appearance and previous observations to guide motion toward a target that becomes visible later in the trajectory. In this work, autonomous commands act on the two distal bending DoFs, while insertion and shaft rotation remain fixed throughout autonomous model trials. This defines a bounded action interface for studying acquisition in stomach phantoms and ex-vivo organs.

Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect semantic requests to robot commands. RT-1 learns language-conditioned actions from robot demonstrations [ 10 ] ; RT-2 transfers web-scale visual-language knowledge into control [ 11 ] ; and OpenVLA demonstrates adaptation and generalization across downstream tasks [ 12 ] . Cross-robot datasets and generalist policies extend this shared experience across tasks and embodiments [ 13 , 14 ] . These pretrained representations provide visual and semantic priors beyond the available endoscopic demonstrations. This is relevant to low-light views with reduced contrast and wet-lens views with droplets and reflections, where target appearance shifts from the high-light, dry training condition. Broad pretraining therefore motivates our choice of a VLA backbone for language-guided OOV acquisition under appearance change. The physical evaluation measures transfer across appearance, organ geometry and robot hardware.

To support embodied learning in this setting, we provide a VLA dataset containing 1,050 episodes across six tasks and approximately 262k pairs.

EndoVLA-OOV adapts the pretrained π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} action-chunk backbone [ 15 ] through low-rank updates [ 16 ] and a continuous two-component action head. Its visual input combines an initial global view, an intermediate observation and the current frame. Action chunks represent a sequence of future bending commands, following a widely used approach to visuomotor sequence prediction [ 17 , 18 ] . Together, the task interface, temporal observations and adaptation procedure form a domain-specific recipe for instruction-conditioned endoscopic acquisition.

We study transfer using two robotic embodiments: R1 denotes the 6 mm platform used for demonstration collection and baseline evaluation, and R2 denotes the 3.9 mm platform used for cross-embodiment evaluation. Experiments on R1 examine acquisition and composite finding-and-tracking (FT) under lighting and wetness changes and across two unseen phantoms and ex-vivo tissue. Experiments on R2 examine acquisition in an unseen ex-vivo environment and the effect of expanding the training corpus. Competing-target instructions and contextual-view interventions assess how language and temporal images guide the policy’s search.

The transition from target acquisition to centering also motivates a clear account of feedback timing. A model that processes an input every T infer T_{\rm infer} seconds has perception rate A = 1 / T infer A=1/T_{\rm infer} . A chunk of H H actions gives a theoretical maximum chunk-equivalent control rate B = A ​ H B=AH when all actions are consumed between successive processed observations; the chunk shares one input. Our common 300-input benchmark reports both quantities. This distinction connects action generation to the fresh-observation updates needed for precise centering and informs a future architecture that combines VLA acquisition with a low-latency visual controller. The Supplementary Information provides full data distributions, robot and annotation details, exact prompts, offline diagnostics and supplementary camera-control experiments.

The contributions of this work are:

An embodied endoscopic dataset: We provide a VLA dataset linking language, endoscopic observations and recorded robot states to continuous two-DoF bending actions. Its 1,050 episodes span six tasks and approximately 262k pairs, covering both target tracking and OOV acquisition. This resource provides a shared data and control basis for developing and evaluating instruction-conditioned endoscopic policies.

Temporal-context VLA control for OOV acquisition: We introduce EndoVLA-OOV, which translates anatomical and appearance descriptions into continuous distal steering by conditioning a pretrained action-chunk policy on initial, intermediate and current views. Physical instruction and observation interventions support target selection through language and the use of contextual images during search. This formulation extends language-conditioned endoscopic assistance to targets beyond the current field of view.

Transferable acquisition across endoscopic embodiments: We demonstrate that a VLA policy adapted on R1 acquires language-specified targets on R2 in an unseen ex-vivo environment. Target acquisition reaches 93.3% on R2, and a controlled training-data comparison raises acquisition from 40.0% to 90.0% with corpus expansion. These findings support reuse of the acquisition policy across the evaluated endoscopic platforms and identify demonstration coverage as a practical means of improving transfer.

# II Related Work

## II-A Robotic Endoscopy and Target Acquisition

Robotic endoscopy supports camera positioning and instrument manipulation within a confined anatomical workspace. Endoluminal platforms provide coordinated actuation for interventions such as endoscopic submucosal dissection [ 19 , 20 ] , while steering systems use motorized bending and image feedback to regulate the viewing direction [ 7 , 8 ] . Visual servoing expresses a camera-positioning objective through measured feature errors and their relationship to motion [ 9 ] . These approaches connect an observable image-space goal to corrective commands, making them relevant to lumen centralization and the centering of visible targets. For endoscopic revisitation, acquiring a requested target supplies the visual reference needed for this local feedback stage and links anatomical inspection to focused camera control.

Language-conditioned endoscopic policies extend this interface by allowing an operator to specify the feature to follow. EndoVLA [ 21 ] combines a vision-language backbone with supervised and reinforcement fine-tuning for tracking tasks, predicting discrete directional or stop commands from the current image and prompt. This work establishes a direct connection between semantic target descriptions and endoscopic motion. EndoVLA-OOV addresses the preceding acquisition stage: the requested target begins outside the field of view, and the policy steers through successive observations until it becomes visible. Continuous bending actions and temporal visual context support this formulation. Table I summarizes the task, action, data and evaluation scope of the two approaches, positioning language-guided acquisition within the broader endoscopic control workflow.

## II-B Language-Conditioned Control and Visual Context

Language-conditioned control links semantic descriptions to spatially meaningful robot behavior. SayCan combines language-derived task proposals with robotic affordance estimates [ 22 ] ; CLIPort couples semantic representations with spatial action prediction [ 23 ] ; and VIMA uses multimodal prompts to specify manipulation tasks [ 24 ] . PerAct represents language-conditioned actions in a voxel-based spatial representation [ 25 ] , while VoxPoser composes language-driven three-dimensional value maps [ 26 ] . Together, these methods connect what an instruction requests to where and how the robot acts through complementary representations of task intent, geometry and action. In endoscopy, anatomical-region and appearance descriptions similarly specify a target for camera motion. This connection motivates treating the instruction as part of the control problem, with acquisition measured for the requested target.

Semantic navigation extends language-conditioned behavior to goals encountered after a sequence of observations. LM-Nav grounds instruction landmarks through pretrained language, image-language and navigation models [ 27 ] . VLFM combines observed geometry with a language-grounded value map to select exploration frontiers [ 28 ] . These approaches make observations gathered along a route useful for deciding where to search next. We draw on this relationship between semantic goals and accumulated visual evidence when formulating endoscopic OOV acquisition. Distal bending reveals different folds and surfaces, so the current image represents one part of the scene traversed during search. Temporal visual context offers a way to relate that local view to the preceding trajectory while preserving the requested target as the search objective.

## II-C Pretrained VLA Policies and Cross-Embodiment Transfer

Pretrained robot policies share representations across tasks and adapt them to a deployment interface. RT-1 learns language-conditioned control from robot demonstrations [ 10 ] , while CLIP and PaLM-E establish complementary connections between visual observations, language and embodied inputs [ 29 , 30 ] . RT-2 incorporates robot actions into vision-language training to transfer semantic knowledge to control [ 11 ] , and OpenVLA provides an open pretrained policy with downstream adaptation [ 12 ] . The π 0 \pi_{0} family couples a vision-language backbone with continuous action generation, with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} emphasizing generalization through heterogeneous training [ 18 , 15 ] . Low-rank adaptation provides an efficient parameter-update mechanism for such specialization [ 16 ] . These studies motivate adapting shared visual-language representations to endoscopic imagery and a compact distal-bending action space.

Training diversity and embodiment coverage determine the experience available to a shared policy. BridgeData V2 and DROID broaden manipulation demonstrations across tasks and collection settings [ 31 , 32 ] ; Open X-Embodiment aggregates experience across robots [ 13 ] ; and Octo studies generalist pretraining followed by adaptation to downstream observation and action spaces [ 14 ] . These resources connect transferable policy learning with variation in both visual conditions and robot interfaces. Endoscopic deployment introduces corresponding changes in tissue appearance, camera geometry and the response of the bending mechanism. This motivates an embodied dataset that links instructions and observations to recorded controls, together with evaluation of acquisition across environments and robotic platforms.

Continuous control also requires organizing predicted actions over time. Diffusion Policy generates action sequences using iterative denoising [ 33 ] , ACT combines action chunks with temporal ensembling [ 17 ] , and flow matching supplies the generative formulation used by flow-based VLA action experts [ 34 , 18 , 15 ] . Real-time chunking further addresses how prediction overlaps with execution under inference delay [ 35 ] . These developments connect temporally coherent commands with the scheduling of observation updates. For endoscopic acquisition and subsequent centering, that relationship motivates reporting input-processing rate separately from generated-action throughput, linking the policy’s sequence output to the feedback information available during control.

2026-10-20.title: Relational Spatial Alignment for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-20.authors: Chaoran Zhu , Hengyi Wang , Chenglin Cui , Yazhe Wan , Taein Kwon , Changjae Oh
2026-10-20.abstract:
Spatial understanding is essential for robots to perceive their surrounding environments and execute actions. Existing approaches typically encode 3D awareness into vision-language-action (VLA) models by directly aligning their representations with pre-trained 3D foundation models. However, we observe that such direct geometric feature alignment essentially exploits 3D foundation priors as a form of low-rank regularization in the feature space, resulting in severe rank collapse of the pre-trained VLA representations. In contrast, we shift the focus from enforcing point-wise equality to aligning pair-wise relationships. We propose a representation-alignment method that enables the injection of 3D spatial awareness without compromising the model’s original expressivity.
Extensive experiments on public benchmarks, our new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation scenarios demonstrate that our approach effectively incorporates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning, achieving robust performance and enhanced spatial awareness across diverse manipulation tasks.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Spatial understanding is fundamental to robotic manipulation, enabling robots to interpret their environment from multi-view RGB observations, estimate distances, localize objects, and infer 3D structure either explicitly or implicitly. Traditional approaches [ 34 , 47 ] typically follow a reconstruction-before-action paradigm, in which an explicit 3D scene is first reconstructed and then used for downstream tasks such as path planning and control [ 15 , 36 ] .

Inspired by the success of end-to-end learning in natural language processing [ 2 ] and autonomous driving [ 18 , 5 ] , recent attention has shifted toward Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, a unified end-to-end learning framework for embodied AI. To incorporate spatial awareness, some prior methods [ 42 , 58 , 19 , 26 ] follow the reconstruction-before-action paradigm by leveraging explicit spatial representations, such as depth maps or point clouds, as additional inputs to VLA models. However, such approaches often depend on pre-scanned environments or high-quality sensor observations, both of which can be unreliable in real-world scenarios due to sensor noise, reflective surfaces, and occlusions. Consequently, such methods remain limited in constrained environments and struggle to generalize to open-world problems.

To avoid reliance on explicit 3D representations, recent works [ 27 , 45 ] shift the focus to encode implicit 3D geometric structure within the latent space. Building on recent advances in 3D foundation models [ 51 , 48 , 50 ] , this approach transfers geometric knowledge into VLAs through feature-level distillation. While these approaches bypass the need for explicit 3D representations, the underlying mechanism of this latent geometric transfer remains underexplored. More importantly, it raises a fundamental question: Does injecting spatial awareness into the VLA with direct feature alignment compromise its original semantic-level representational capabilities?

In this work, we systematically investigate the direct feature alignment between 3D foundation models and 2D VLA models. Our analysis suggests that direct spatial alignment does not necessarily lead to genuine 3D understanding. Instead, it primarily behaves as a form of low-rank regularization. Specifically, we observe a substantial collapse in the numerical rank of the VLA feature space after alignment (Fig. 1 (b); see Sec. 3.1 ), indicating a significant loss of representation capacity. Consequently, experiments across diverse benchmarks show that models trained with direct spatial alignment suffer from degraded generalization performance.

To overcome these limitations, we propose a new paradigm of relational spatial alignment that aims to distill 3D awareness into 2D VLAs while preserving their expressivity. Motivated by the observation that 3D foundation models encode spatial structures through cosine similarity (i.e., the attention maps) between corresponding features, we argue that effective spatial understanding can be achieved by aligning pair-wise relationships rather than enforcing point-wise equality . By supervising relative similarities instead of absolute feature directions and norms, our method allows the 2D VLA representations to maintain their native feature coordinate system, with 3D knowledge being encoded in its feature similarity. (Fig. 1 (a)). Theoretically, we demonstrate that this relational alignment objective is inherently rotation-invariant : The optimization objective remains strictly unchanged under arbitrary orthogonal transformations within the latent feature space, which is crucial for preventing the feature collapse. To practically instantiate this paradigm, we introduce RIGID: Rotation-Invariant Geometry Distillation , which implements the relation alignment paradigm and formulates the geometry knowledge transfer as an Optimal Transport problem over spatial attention distributions. Compared to direct feature supervision, RIGID improves spatial awareness while maintaining the numerical rank of the learned representations, effectively preventing capacity collapse. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that RIGID achieves state-of-the-art performance, exhibiting better robustness and open-world generalization than direct feature alignment.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Explicit 3D representations in VLA models. Recent advancements seek to enhance the spatial grounding of vision-language-action (VLA) models by directly incorporating geometric information. One main stream of methods embeds raw 3D observations, such as depth maps or point clouds, directly into the input space. Frameworks including 3D-VLA [ 58 ] , 3DS-VLA [ 29 ] , PointVLA [ 26 ] , 3D-CAVLA [ 3 ] , GeoVLA [ 46 ] , FALCON [ 56 ] , and BridgeVLA [ 28 ] align these 3D inputs with 2D backbone or action experts to unify perception and manipulation, while 4D-VLA [ 54 ] extends this by stacking multiple depth maps for temporal context. Another paradigm utilizes auxiliary explicit 3D cues instead of raw sensory data. For instance, SpatialVLA [ 41 ] applies Egocentric 3D Position Encoding, and TraceVLA [ 59 ] leverages visual traces. Furthermore, approaches like ReconVLA [ 43 ] , DreamVLA [ 55 ] , and GuidedVLA [ 21 ] enforce 3D representation learning by employing explicit 3D feature reconstruction as an auxiliary supervision signal. Although these models provide precision in handling height variations and object posing, they suffer from substantial data dependencies, as they often require high-fidelity 3D annotations or depth estimations that are frequently noisy in real-world environments.

Implicit 3D representations in VLA models. Recent advances in 3D reconstruction have enabled the end-to-end learning of multi-view geometry [ 51 , 25 , 48 , 50 , 52 , 49 , 30 ] . These methods typically employ transformer-based architectures to infer geometric properties such as point maps, depth, and camera parameters from multi-view images. To circumvent the dependency on physical 3D sensors or explicit annotations, recent vision-language-action (VLA) models leverage these learned geometric cues for implicit spatial grounding. Methods such as Evo-0 [ 31 , 32 ] and GeoAware-VLA [ 1 ] directly integrate geometric features generated by 3D foundation models into the VLA backbone. Conversely, techniques including Spatial Forcing [ 27 ] , ROCKET [ 45 ] , and GLaD [ 13 ] leverage feature distillation. They align the intermediate latent states of the VLA with the geometric embeddings of a frozen teacher model (e.g., VGGT) to acquire spatial awareness. However, this feature integration or direct alignment across different modalities can potentially compromise the 2D image-derived representations acquired during large-scale pre-training, such as semantic understanding and general reasoning abilities, thereby degrading the overall robustness of the model.

Relational knowledge distillation. Relational Knowledge Distillation (RKD) [ 39 ] is built upon the knowledge distillation (KD) [ 14 ] , which focuses on transferring knowledge from the teacher model by distilling the in-batch structure. While traditional RKD methods primarily focus on single-modality and inter-instance associations, our approach targets the latent feature alignment between VLA models and 3D foundation models in spatial through multi-view inputs.

2026-10-20.title: Action-Aligned Latent Planning for Versatile Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Yutang Lin , Guanya Shi , C. Karen Liu
2026-10-20.abstract:
Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed.
This makes the representation between high-level planning and whole-body control critical: kinematic or contact targets provide compact abstractions but do not directly encode interaction-specific control responses, while directly predicting low-level actions requires the planner to model high-frequency closed-loop feedback.
We propose Fiber , a framework that uses the executable latent space of a frozen bfm ( bfm ) as a shared planning representation for heterogeneous interaction skills.
Our lpp ( lpp ) maps independently acquired task-specific policies into this representation by identifying latent commands whose induced actions match their local control responses, enabling lower-rate planning while retaining the BFM’s high-frequency state feedback.
After projection, we aggregate closed-loop latent rollouts from all skills and
train a single perceptive flow planner entirely offline.
We further introduce AH-BFM , an adaptive-horizon bfm trained with
multi- γ \gamma fb ( fb ) learning to support both precise control
and temporally extended whole-body behavior.
We evaluate Fiber on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping in
simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid.
Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, Fiber achieves 42.0 % 42.0\% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay ( 11.6 % 11.6\% )
and substantially outperforming kinematic planning ( 3.5 % 3.5\% ).
Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill
chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.
Project website: https://fiberaa.github.io/.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires both deciding what interaction to
perform from visual and semantic context and determining how to realize
it through balance, contact, and coordinated whole-body control.
Recent work has achieved strong task-specific interaction skills, including
object manipulation, articulated-object interaction, and object
transport [ 1 , 2 ] , often using task-specific
objectives, observations, and training procedures.
Scaling these successes to a versatile policy requires unifying diverse
task-level decisions without losing the physical responses that make each
skill succeed.

A common strategy separates task-level decision making from whole-body control.
A high-level policy predicts structured targets such as body motion,
end-effector poses, or contacts, while a low-level controller realizes them on
the robot.
However, the same target may require different actions under different contacts,
object states, or disturbances, so such representations do not directly capture
the state-dependent control responses required for interaction.
Predicting low-level actions avoids this abstraction, but offline learning then
requires broad coverage of closed-loop corrective responses, which is difficult
for contact-rich interaction.
This exposes a central challenge for humanoid planning: how can we abstract low-level control complexity without abstracting away the physical responses that make interaction succeed?

A learned behavioral representation offers a way to resolve this tension.
We build on a bfm that exposes an executable behavioral latent space.
Given the current robot state and a latent command, bfm produces low-level actions at high frequency.
A latent therefore indexes a state-dependent control policy rather than merely a desired motion, allowing high-level planning to operate over compact behavioral commands while the bfm retains high-frequency closed-loop physical feedback.

Using such an interface for versatile loco-manipulation still requires acquiring the interaction capabilities that the planner should invoke.
One approach is to collect demonstrations for the desired interactions through a common data-acquisition pipeline [ 3 , 4 ] , but obtaining broad coverage of contact-rich and corrective behavior is expensive.
Another approach is to first train task-specific interaction policies and distill them into a generalist.
On-policy multi-expert distillation can improve closed-loop coverage by querying these policies at states visited by the generalist, but requires all policies and their environments to remain available during integration.
We instead consider a decoupled setting: each interaction policy can be acquired independently, and only afterward incorporated into the shared behavioral interface.

Under this decoupled setting, different interaction policies need not share
their observations, objectives, or task representations.
They nevertheless share one quantity that directly describes their physical
realization: the actions applied to the robot.
A latent command from the frozen bfm is grounded in the same quantity,
because it also produces robot actions conditioned on the current robot state.
This common action space provides a direct way to relate an independently
acquired interaction policy to the bfm latent representation.

Based on this insight, we propose Fiber , which represents independently
acquired interaction policies, or experts, in the executable latent space of a frozen bfm .
At the core of Fiber is lpp , which identifies latent commands by matching
the actions induced by the bfm to an expert’s local state-dependent control
responses.
The resulting projected policy executes through the frozen bfm , preserving
high-frequency state feedback while expressing heterogeneous interaction skills
through a common lower-rate representation.

Because each expert is projected independently, the experts need not share an
acquisition procedure or remain jointly available during subsequent training.
After projection, we roll out the projected policies and collect their latent
commands together with the perceptive and proprioceptive observations available
to the final policy.
These closed-loop latent rollouts are aggregated across skills to train a single
perceptive planner entirely offline.
At deployment, the planner predicts future latent commands from onboard
observations and a high-level steering condition, while the frozen bfm provides the state-dependent whole-body responses required to execute them.

Finally, projection and planning impose different temporal requirements on the latent representation.
Matching an expert’s control response favors precise short-horizon
behavior, whereas lower-rate planning benefits from stable commands that preserve behavior over longer horizons.
We therefore introduce AH-BFM , an adaptive-horizon bfm trained with
multi- γ \gamma fb learning to support both control fidelity
and temporally extended behavioral structure.

We evaluate Fiber on three heterogeneous interaction tasks—box pickup, door
opening, and object grasping-in simulation and on a real Unitree G1.
In simulation, lpp largely preserves expert performance on box pickup and
door opening near the interaction regime.
The unified perceptive planner achieves 42.0 % 42.0\% mean success, compared with 11.6 % 11.6\% for fixed projected latent replay and 3.5 % 3.5\% for kinematic planning.
Real-world experiments further demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer,
interaction chaining, and waypoint-conditioned steering through the same
planner.

Our contributions are threefold:

A shared executable representation for humanoid interaction
planning. We use the latent space of a frozen bfm as a behavioral interface that
supports lower-rate high-level planning while retaining state-dependent
interaction realization responses.

Action-aligned latent policy projection. We introduce lpp , which maps independently acquired interaction
experts into the shared bfm representation by aligning their local
control responses in robot action space, decoupling skill acquisition from
subsequent integration.

Adaptive-horizon BFM and SF-guided behavior reuse. We introduce multi- γ \gamma fb learning and AH-BFM that balance precise control with temporally extended behavioral structure, together with sf ( sf )-guided interaction-preserving behaviors reuse.

1. A shared executable representation for humanoid interaction
planning. We use the latent space of a frozen bfm as a behavioral interface that
supports lower-rate high-level planning while retaining state-dependent
interaction realization responses.

2. Action-aligned latent policy projection. We introduce lpp , which maps independently acquired interaction
experts into the shared bfm representation by aligning their local
control responses in robot action space, decoupling skill acquisition from
subsequent integration.

3. Adaptive-horizon BFM and SF-guided behavior reuse. We introduce multi- γ \gamma fb learning and AH-BFM that balance precise control with temporally extended behavioral structure, together with sf ( sf )-guided interaction-preserving behaviors reuse.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Humanoid Controller and Behavioral Foundation Models

Humanoid control has increasingly moved from skill-specific policies toward shared controllers that support broad motor repertoires through a common conditioning interface.
Motion-conditioned approaches unify locomotion and whole-body behaviors through dense or sparse motion specifications [ 5 , 6 ] ,
while recent systems extend unified control toward language-conditioned behaviors and humanoid loco-manipulation [ 7 , 8 ] .
These works demonstrate that diverse behaviors can be consolidated within a single controller, but the supported behaviors are typically acquired through the controller’s predefined training and conditioning interface.
Our work instead considers a complementary setting: integrating interaction behaviors acquired independently of this interface into an already-trained controller.

bfm s expose a learned behavioral latent space as such a shared control interface.
BFM-Zero [ 9 ] uses fb to learn a promptable humanoid behavioral space, while subsequent behavioral inference methods show that expert behaviors can be recovered by optimizing within a frozen fb latent space [ 10 ] .
These results establish latent inference as an effective mechanism for behavior reproduction.
We build on this capability but study its use as an interface for interaction representation, where the latent sequence must capture temporally varying local control responses rather than only recover a stationary behavior or desired state trajectory.
This setting further exposes a trade-off in conventional fb learning: the successor horizon favorable for precise local tracking differs from that required to preserve long-term behavior.
Our adaptive-horizon bfm is designed to retain both properties within the same behavioral space.

## II-B Humanoid Loco-Manipulation and Representation

Humanoid loco-manipulation requires specifying not only the desired motion of the robot, but also how it should respond to physical interaction with objects and the environment.
A broad family of methods makes interaction explicit through structured task representations, including contact sequences, end-effector constraints, task-motion objectives, distance fields, and interaction-preserving references [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] .
Such representations provide effective and often interpretable interfaces for learning diverse skills.
However, they specify interaction through variables chosen in advance; the resulting task description does not directly encode the state-dependent control response induced by contact and environment dynamics.

Alternatively, interaction responses can be learned directly through task-specific rl ( rl ) or demonstrations [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] .
Teleoperation and human-video-based pipelines further broaden the sources from which such behaviors can be acquired [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 ] .
These approaches can capture interaction-specific control responses through rl , but the acquired behavior generally remains tied to the specialist policy or downstream training process.
In contrast, we decouple interaction acquisition from execution: demonstrated state-action responses are projected into the native latent interface of a frozen behavioral foundation controller, allowing independently acquired interactions to share a common executable substrate.

2026-10-20.title: Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding for 3D Manipulation Policies under Depth Corruption
2026-10-20.authors: Zhiyuan Yang , Jiaju He , Ruiteng Zhao , Anqi Cheng , Haiyue Zhu , Kezhi Mao
2026-10-20.abstract:
3D manipulation policies derive actions from explicit scene geometry rather than color images alone, enabling them to reason over metric distances, object relations, and robot-scene reachability.
This geometric interface is also a vulnerability: commodity RGB-D sensors return missing measurements, boundary artifacts, and plausible but wrong surfaces around transparent, reflective, thin, or textureless objects.
We study this failure under realistic depth corruption and observe a sharp depth-noise cliff across modern 3D policies, even when they are trained with matched noisy depth.
This residual gap motivates a spatial-encoding approach: corrupted depth becomes entangled with the token coordinates and geometry features consumed by the action expert.
We propose Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding ( NISE ), a 3D policy architecture that learns trustworthy geometry features even facing imperfect depth. NISE uses Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision to shape shared policy features with calibrated multi-view depth, and Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention to carry position uncertainty into deployed attention rather than treating every lifted token as exact.
Across simulated benchmarks with sensor-realistic corruption and real-robot tasks involving transparent and reflective materials, NISE improves depth-noise robustness while preserving clean-depth performance, supporting 3D policies designed for commodity RGB-D deployment rather than clean-depth benchmarks alone.
2026-10-20.introduction:
3D manipulation policies derive actions from explicit scene geometry rather than color images alone, whether by processing point clouds [ 4 , 5 ] , encoding voxel grids [ 2 ] , reasoning over virtual views [ 6 , 7 ] , or pairing visual tokens with 3D coordinates [ 8 ] .
The appeal comes from the metric nature of manipulation, where contact, clearance, and reachability depend on detecting distances between the robot and the scene.
Depth gives policies direct access to these relationships, turning image observations into spatial representations that can guide action.
This reliance creates a fragile premise: the depth measurements must be reliable enough to support trustworthy geometry.
Commodity RGB-D sensors routinely violate this premise through missing depth measurements, boundary artifacts, and plausible but incorrect surfaces, especially around transparent, reflective, thin, or textureless objects.
This motivates our central question: how severely does realistic depth corruption degrade current 3D policies, and how can 3D policies learn spatial representations that remain reliable under such noise?

We study this question by introducing realistic depth corruption into modern 3D policies.
The failure is sharper than ordinary robustness degradation.
Clean-trained policies deteriorate rapidly as depth corruption increases.
Even after training on matched noisy depth, substantial degradation remains (Fig. 1 ).
This suggests that the problem is not simply a missing training augmentation.
These policies construct spatial representations from corrupted depth measurements, so residual depth errors become entangled with the features passed to the action generator.
The key step is therefore to prevent depth corruption from being inherited by the spatial encoding.

Prior work on depth-noise robustness has mostly intervened upstream of the policy, repairing the depth signal before it is consumed by the policy [ 9 , 10 ] .
These directions are valuable, but they remain observation-side repairs.
Even with improved geometric representations, residual errors in depth-derived coordinates can continue to perturb positional attention and the action features it produces.
The missing piece is therefore the spatial encoding itself: after depth is sensed, or repaired, the policy still needs a learned ability to form trustworthy geometry features for action prediction.

To address this gap, we propose Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding ( NISE ) for 3D manipulation policies.
Rather than treating depth corruption as an input-repair problem, NISE shifts the robustness target to the spatial representation consumed by the action policy.
It introduces two complementary mechanisms.
Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision (GCVSS) trains the policy encoder with a cross-view geometry head that uses multi-view depth to encourage view-consistent spatial features.
Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention (GM3A) modifies 3D positional attention with a learned dampening surface, so unreliable coordinate bands have less influence on action-relevant spatial features.

Our contributions are three-fold:

We identify and analyze a depth-noise cliff in 3D manipulation policies, showing that realistic depth corruption can cause sharp performance collapse across visual backbones and action-generation mechanisms, while matched noisy-depth training only partially recovers the loss.

We propose NISE , a 3D policy architecture that learns noise-invariant spatial encodings through Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision and Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention, rather than repairing the depth observation.

We evaluate NISE on simulated benchmarks with realistic depth corruption and real-world manipulation tasks involving challenging depth-sensing materials, demonstrating that 3D policies can be designed for sensor-realistic deployment.

1. We identify and analyze a depth-noise cliff in 3D manipulation policies, showing that realistic depth corruption can cause sharp performance collapse across visual backbones and action-generation mechanisms, while matched noisy-depth training only partially recovers the loss.

2. We propose NISE , a 3D policy architecture that learns noise-invariant spatial encodings through Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision and Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention, rather than repairing the depth observation.

3. We evaluate NISE on simulated benchmarks with realistic depth corruption and real-world manipulation tasks involving challenging depth-sensing materials, demonstrating that 3D policies can be designed for sensor-realistic deployment.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

3D Manipulation Policies. Explicit 3D representations support both point-cloud recognition and robotic manipulation [ 2 , 4 , 6 , 11 ] .
Point-cloud policies use explicit 3D geometry to condition action generation [ 4 , 5 , 12 ] ; virtual-view policies such as RVT-2 [ 6 ] and SAM2Act [ 7 ] render RGB-D observations into canonical views; and depth-lifted-token policies such as 3D Diffuser Actor (3DDA) [ 8 ] and 3D FlowMatch Actor [ 13 ] pair visual features with 3D coordinates before action prediction.
These methods differ in action heads and backbones, but they share a useful interface: depth is converted into spatial tokens that the policy can attend to, sample, or aggregate.
Auxiliary reconstruction and distillation objectives provide additional supervision for learning geometric and physical representations [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] .

A parallel trend strengthens this interface with larger geometric backbones.
R3DP [ 17 ] , VGGT-DP [ 18 ] , and GP3 [ 19 ] draw 3D features from frozen geometry transformers, while Spatial Forcing [ 20 ] distills VGGT features into a separate action stream.
PromptDA-style depth fusion [ 21 ] and 3D rotary position embeddings [ 8 , 13 ] further make metric scene structure available to downstream attention.
Robo3R [ 22 ] reconstructs metric scene geometry from RGB images and robot states for downstream manipulation.
The gap is that these policies usually treat the lifted coordinates as reliable once they enter the model.
Our work asks how the spatial encoder should behave when the depth that constructs those coordinates is uncertain.

Depth Noise and Robustness in Robotic Manipulation. Depth robustness is often approached before the policy reasons over the scene.
Classical filters and learned depth completion or estimation methods aim to recover a cleaner depth image [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] .
Manipulation-specific systems such as CDM [ 9 ] and D3RoMa [ 10 ] follow the same observation-side logic: improve the depth signal before it is consumed by the policy.
This direction is valuable, but its objective is still depth repair rather than learning how the policy should encode imperfect geometry.

Recent work also addresses noisy geometry through the policy’s internal representations.
SpatialActor [ 26 ] separates semantic and geometric representations and fuses measured-depth features with pretrained depth-expert features.
EquiForm [ 27 ] combines geometric denoising with contrastive equivariant representation learning, while PEAfowl [ 28 ] uses depth-distribution lifting, cross-view aggregation, and training-only depth distillation.
These approaches advance robustness through geometric priors, denoising, and depth-aware representation learning.
Our focus is how residual depth errors affect both learned geometric features and the positional interactions between them.
Improving the features alone does not ensure that depth-derived coordinates are reliable for 3D attention. NISE addresses these coupled effects by learning geometric consistency directly from noisy camera views and adapting the frequency components of 3D rotary attention to coordinate uncertainty.

2026-10-20.title: Solving a Giant Rubik's Cube with a Quadruped Robot
2026-10-20.authors: Lukas Amiet , Gabriel Sánchez-Blanco Repgen , Mayank Mittal , Victor Klemm , Andrei Cramariuc , Marco Hutter , Cesar Cadena
2026-10-20.comment: L. Amiet and G. Sánchez-Blanco Repgen contributed equally. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract:
Pedipulating a freestanding articulated object requires controlling its pose and internal configuration while maintaining balance. We demonstrate this capability by autonomously solving a giant Rubik’s Cube with a quadruped using only its feet. The task demands repeated precise interactions, since unintended layer motion can invalidate subsequent operations. We develop an onboard RGB-D perception pipeline that estimates the cube’s metric pose and its full color state from partial views acquired through locomotion and flipping. A planner converts the computed solve into robot-executable skill sequences. Learned whole-body skills reorient the cube while preserving its layer configuration and turn its layers with one foot pinning the cube as the other pushes. We train these skills using reinforcement learning with privileged observations and distill them into policies that map onboard depth and proprioception to joint targets. The deployed policies tolerate variations in relative robot–cube placement and recover from external disturbances. The system completes three autonomous hardware solves, each about 30 steps over 8-9 minutes.
These results show that combining onboard perception with coordinated pedipulation enables a quadruped to complete extended multi-step physical tasks.
Additional material can be found at: https://leggedrobotics.github.io/rubik-skills/
2026-10-20.introduction:
Pedipulation extends a legged robot’s capability to interact with its environment without an additional arm. Prior works have demonstrated button pressing [ 1 , 2 ] , ball dribbling [ 3 ] , and door opening [ 4 ] .
Freestanding articulated objects introduce an additional challenge: the robot must establish stabilizing contacts while controlling both the object’s pose and its internal configuration. This raises the question of whether coordinated pedipulation can support extended sequences of precise transformations on such objects.

We investigate this question by autonomously solving a giant Rubik’s Cube (hereafter, the cube) with a quadrupedal platform. The task requires reorienting the whole cube while preserving its layer configuration, and turning layers while stabilizing the cube. During a layer turn, one foot needs to pin the bottom layer while the other rotates the upper layers. Unintended layer motion can corrupt the planned cube state, making complete solves a demanding test of precise, repeatable pedipulation.

Our proposed system ( Fig. 1 ) separates cube state estimation from skill execution. Onboard RGB-D observations collected between interactions provide the cube’s pose and color state needed for solution planning and robot repositioning. During interactions, the pedipulation policies use onboard depth and proprioception for local feedback control. We train skill-specific teacher policies with privileged observations using reinforcement learning and distill them into perceptive student policies that command joint position targets.

Our contributions are:

An onboard RGB-D perception pipeline that recovers the metric pose and full color state of a freestanding cube from multiple partial views, without a fixed camera rig or assumptions on the exact cube motions.

# II RELATED WORK

Cube perception. Existing Rubik’s Cube perception methods differ in the state they recover and the observation setup they require. Kasprzak et al. [ 5 ] estimate pose and recognize up to three visible faces from a single image. Their color segmentation requires lighting calibration, and the method does not fuse observations into a complete color state. Ďurovský [ 6 ] addresses robustness to occlusion and varying illumination in 2D cube-state detection. Chalise et al. [ 7 ] reconstruct the complete color state using a mechanical rig that presents successive faces to the camera. OpenAI [ 8 ] estimates cube pose and layer angles from three external cameras for in-hand control, starting from a known puzzle configuration rather than reconstructing an unknown color state. In contrast, our setting requires both metric pose and complete color-state estimation for a freestanding cube observed from changing onboard viewpoints. We reconstruct these quantities from partial RGB-D views acquired through locomotion and flipping, without a fixed scanning rig or assumptions of exact cube motion between observations.

Pedipulation. Prior works have explored both task-specific joint-space policies [ 3 ] and hierarchical control through foot-level commands. Hierarchical approaches use a whole-body controller to maintain balance while tracking foot positions [ 2 , 9 ] or parameterized trajectories [ 1 , 4 ] . These single-foot commands support task execution through teleoperation [ 2 ] , behavior trees [ 1 ] , trajectory planners [ 10 ] , and learned visual policies [ 4 ] .
Perceptive feedback enters these architectures at different levels. DribbleBot [ 3 ] conditions its joint-space policy on ball-position estimates from a separate onboard perception module. Stolle et al. [ 9 ] incorporate a height scan into the foot-tracking policy for obstacle avoidance. In related work with an arm-equipped quadruped, Liu et al. [ 11 ] use segmented depth to generate gripper and base commands for a pre-trained low-level controller.

These works do not address the combined demands of repeated manipulation of a freestanding articulated object. Reorienting the cube must preserve its internal layer configuration, whereas turning its layers requires coordinated contacts that stabilize the cube while actuating the passive joints. These demands extend beyond single-foot target tracking: the robot must coordinate multiple contacts, maintain balance, and leave the cube’s state intact.

2026-10-20.title: RoMo-GS: Efficient Online 3D Gaussian Splatting for Robot Mapping via Exposure-Integrated Motion Blur
2026-10-20.authors: Sangwoo Jung , Di Deng , Jiahui Fu , Laura Herlant , Ayoung Kim , Yafei Hu
2026-10-20.abstract: Online 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is emerging as a practical way to build a representation for robotics applications. However, deploying it on real-world platforms exposes multiple challenges. Rapid maneuvers of a robot induce motion-blurred images, which corrupt the reconstructed geometry and cause camera pose drift. Furthermore, the number of Gaussians grows without bound during continuous online mapping. In this study, we present RoMo-GS , an online 3DGS system designed to address these challenges. Instead of averaging N N discrete sub-frames as in prior motion blur-aware 3DGS, we analytically integrate each projected Gaussian over the exposure interval, yielding an 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathcal{O}(1) complexity per Gaussian. Building on this, we bound the Gaussians’ growth with a Hessian-based pruning score, while jointly refining pose, velocity, and Gaussians with Adam and an online LM step over the Gaussians. On multiple public datasets and a self-collected dataset, RoMo-GS matches or exceeds offline deblurring 3DGS methods in rendering quality while running 15–150 × \times faster, and operates online at competitive quality with about 20% fewer Gaussians than the online 3DGS baseline.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Online dense 3D reconstruction is essential for robotics, enabling downstream tasks such as autonomous navigation and reliable interactions. While implicit representations such as NeRF ( NeRF ) [ 19 ] have advanced novel-view synthesis, their slow rendering ( ∼ \sim 0.03 FPS) limits their online use on real-world robots. 3DGS ( 3DGS ) [ 12 ] addresses this by replacing the implicit field with explicit Gaussian primitives and a differentiable rasterizer, achieving real-time rendering ( ∼ \sim 100 FPS). Moving the rasterizer from controlled benchmarks onto actual robots, however, exposes the Gaussians to less controlled conditions. Rapid maneuvers and mechanical impacts induce motion blur in the input frames, corrupting the reconstructed geometry and causing trajectory drift, while the Gaussians grow unbounded along the trajectory until memory exhaustion.

As 3DGS migrates to real-world robotic systems, contact impacts, vibration, and rapid maneuvers produce motion-blurred frames that corrupt the reconstructed geometry. Prior motion blur-aware 3DGS methods [ 35 , 25 , 15 ] mitigate this numerically, approximating the exposure integral by averaging N N discrete subframes and incurring an N × N\times training-cost overhead that is incompatible with online operation. We eliminate this trade-off by analytically evaluating the exposure-time integral of each projected Gaussian under a linear motion model, yielding 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathcal{O}(1) complexity per Gaussian.

Beyond rendering, an online 3DGS system on a real-world robot faces remaining challenges. As the robot continuously explores the environment, new Gaussians are spawned with each incoming frame. Without a principled mechanism to prune the redundant or uninformative Gaussians, the number of Gaussians grows without bound and exhausts the robot’s memory budget. Naive pruning, on the other hand, degrades overall reconstruction quality. Furthermore, during rapid maneuvers, pose tracking may become unstable, introducing pose drift and corrupting structural integrity.

To address these constraints, we propose RoMo-GS , an online 3DGS pipeline designed for real-world robot deployment. To handle motion blur without multi-sampling, we analytically evaluate intra-exposure camera motion. To bound memory, we introduce an online Gaussian pruning score based on the opacity-axis diagonal of the Gauss-Newton Hessian. Finally, to resolve pose drift by tightening the tracking and mapping, we run a joint Adam loop over camera states and Gaussian parameters, followed by an online LM ( LM ) step on the Gaussians. We evaluate RoMo-GS on multiple public datasets containing real-world and synthetic blurry scenes, as well as a custom multi-platform dataset. In summary, our contributions are as follows.

Exposure-Integrated Motion Blur. We evaluate the exposure-time integral of each projected Gaussian’s motion in terms of the ERF ( ERF ), replacing the discrete numerical approximations of prior approaches with our analytically evaluated formulation.

Single-Sample Blur Rasterization. We integrate the proposed motion-blur model into the CUDA rasterizer to render motion-blurred frames in a single pass with 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathcal{O}(1) complexity per Gaussian, removing the N × N\!\times rasterization overhead of multi-sample averaging approaches.

Online Optimization and Density Control. We jointly optimize pose, velocity, and Gaussians with Adam, followed by an online LM step on the Gaussians, and bound the map size with a Hessian-based pruning score that retains ∼ \sim 20% fewer Gaussians at comparable quality.

1. Exposure-Integrated Motion Blur. We evaluate the exposure-time integral of each projected Gaussian’s motion in terms of the ERF ( ERF ), replacing the discrete numerical approximations of prior approaches with our analytically evaluated formulation.

2. Single-Sample Blur Rasterization. We integrate the proposed motion-blur model into the CUDA rasterizer to render motion-blurred frames in a single pass with 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 ) \mathcal{O}(1) complexity per Gaussian, removing the N × N\!\times rasterization overhead of multi-sample averaging approaches.

3. Online Optimization and Density Control. We jointly optimize pose, velocity, and Gaussians with Adam, followed by an online LM step on the Gaussians, and bound the map size with a Hessian-based pruning score that retains ∼ \sim 20% fewer Gaussians at comparable quality.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Online Differentiable Rendering for Robotics

Driven by modern GPUs, neural rendering has emerged as essential for 3D reconstruction. NeRF [ 19 ] produces high-quality novel views via ray-tracing through an implicit MLP ( MLP ), and subsequent works accelerate its training and rendering [ 3 , 5 , 6 , 32 ] . 3DGS [ 12 ] achieves real-time rendering through an explicit representation and differentiable Gaussian rasterization.

Leveraging the speed of 3DGS , recent work has extended to online reconstruction. With RGB-D input, MonoGS [ 18 ] and SplaTAM [ 11 ] couple 3DGS with pose tracking; RTG-SLAM [ 22 ] accelerates optimization through a compact representation. GS-ICP SLAM [ 7 ] fuses GICP ( GICP ) to enhance tracking speed and mapping quality, and Photo-SLAM [ 10 ] adopts Gaussian-Pyramid learning to accelerate optimization. With RGB input, HI-SLAM2 [ 34 ] integrates learning-based dense SLAM ( SLAM ) for improved geometry, and MODP [ 30 ] presents hierarchical Gaussian management and global consistency optimization.

Still, deploying these systems on real robots breaks the assumption of high-quality inputs: vibration, contact impacts, and rapid maneuvers produce motion-blurred frames that degrade the reconstruction and drive pose drift, while unbounded Gaussian growth during online mapping inflates memory.

## 2.2 Deblurring Neural Rendering

Prior works have explored deblurring strategies within the neural rendering framework to mitigate motion blur. Early approaches, such as Deblur-NeRF [ 17 ] , adopt 2D blind-deblurring with a learned blur kernel. Deblurring 3DGS [ 13 ] and BAGS [ 21 ] extend the kernel-based formulation with MLP - and CNN ( CNN )-based kernels. Unblur-SLAM [ 33 ] combines a feed-forward deblurring network with multi-view kernel learning. Still, kernel-based approaches treat blur as an image-space artifact and lack a physical interpretation of the camera’s kinematics.

To preserve geometric consistency, methods such as DP-NeRF [ 14 ] model intra-exposure camera motion as a rigid-body trajectory. Building on this, BAD-NeRF [ 29 ] and BAD-Gaussians [ 35 ] model camera trajectories by interpolating with spline-based methods. GSOM ( GSOM ) [ 25 ] derives a pixel-velocity motion blur model under a screen-space approximation, while CoMoGaussian [ 15 ] extends kinematic deblurring to continuous motion by leveraging neural ODEs ( ODEs ). These kinematic motion-based approaches simulate blur by rendering and averaging N N sub-frames along the trajectory and scale the training cost as 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ) \mathcal{O}(N) , prohibitive for online robot deployment. Instead, we leverage the explicit representation of 3DGS to analytically compute motion blur in a single rasterization pass.

## 2.3 Recent Advances in Enhancing 3DGS

To achieve fast convergence and compact scene representation in 3DGS , recent work has refined optimization and pruning. 3DGS-LM [ 9 ] appends second-order LM steps after the Adam loop to accelerate convergence, while Speedy-Splat [ 8 ] and FastGS [ 23 ] compact the Gaussians via offline score-based pruning and tighten per-Gaussian pixel coverage. Although effective offline, they rely on access to the converged scene or a full backward pass over all training views, so directly applying them to online 3DGS introduces additional compute overhead and degrades render quality.

A complementary line of work [ 16 , 27 ] explored feed-forward Gaussian reconstruction, leveraging recent 3D vision foundation models [ 16 , 28 ] . They exploit robust depth priors to suppress the floater artifacts that plague optimization-based pipelines. Still, their fixed Gaussian count removes the adaptive density control, which limits capturing high-frequency textures. We adopt the score-based pruning and the depth-prior bootstrapping, reformulating both to operate within an online system.
