2026-10-20.title: Refuse the Harm, Complete the Task via Graph-of-Rules Planning for LLM-Enabled Robots
2026-10-20.authors: Ali Taheri , Alireza Taban , Qizhou Wang , Wanhua Li
2026-10-20.abstract:
Large Language Models (LLMs)
are increasingly used in embodied AI for robotic manipulation and planning, but their deployment in physical systems exposes vulnerabilities such as jailbreak attacks that can induce unsafe behavior. Existing inference-time defenses are mainly evaluated on short instructions containing a single hazard, whereas realistic tasks may interleave safe and unsafe sub-tasks, conceal hazardous steps, or combine individually safe actions into unsafe outcomes. Such compound instructions make it harder for a single safety decision to distinguish hazardous sub-tasks from legitimate ones, increasing the risk of either overlooking the hazard or rejecting the entire instruction.
Thus, we introduce safe task completion , a task that requires an LLM-enabled robot to refuse the harmful part of an instruction while completing its legitimate part.
To address this problem, we propose RuleGraph, a multi-agent Graph-of-Rules planning framework that distributes safety enforcement across multiple reasoning and verification stages.
Five cooperating agents are used to ground general safety principles into world-specific rules, assess the instruction’s sub-tasks in context, and derive a safe goal from the legitimate ones.
Planning toward this goal is then organized as a graph of rule-specific nodes, where higher-level nodes inherit the union of their parents’ rules, and candidate plans are progressively verified and aggregated until a single plan satisfies every relevant rule.
In this way, RuleGraph reduces reliance on a single centralized safety decision. We evaluate RuleGraph on pure-attack and compound instructions across two benchmarks in two different environments using Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). RuleGraph reduces ASR to 0% on both benchmarks while achieving the highest TSR among all methods, reaching 98.57% on the RoboGuard benchmark and 84.54% on our long-horizon compound instructions.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly in recent years and have demonstrated strong reasoning capabilities, such as interpreting driving scenes and justifying decisions step by step in autonomous vehicles ( Nie et al., 2025 ; Sima et al., 2025 ) , or autonomously designing and executing scientific research ( Boiko et al., 2023 ; Wuwu et al., 2025 ) . These capabilities have also been largely used for robotic task planning and decision-making ( Li et al., 2026 ; Driess et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2023b ) .
As LLMs are increasingly used to translate natural-language instructions into robot behavior ( Ahn et al., 2022 ; Liang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2023a ; Rana et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2023 ) , their vulnerabilities can lead to physical safety risks.

BadRobot ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and RoboPAIR ( Robey et al., 2025 ) show that jailbreak attacks can induce harmful actions in LLM-controlled robots. Unlike a chatbot’s harmful text, these are actions executed in the world and can be difficult to reverse. In response, inference-time defenses aim to verify robot behavior before execution. RoboGuard ( Ravichandran et al., 2026 ) grounds safety rules into world-specific Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) constraints for formal verification, while SafePlan ( Obi et al., 2025 ) uses a multi-stage pipeline to screen instructions and verify generated plans. Other approaches address complementary risks, for example, VLSA ( Hu et al., 2025 ) targets physical collision avoidance through control barrier functions.

However, current inference-time defenses are evaluated on short attack instructions that target one hazardous behavior, and they often concentrate safety verification in a single stage. Such single-stage verification becomes unreliable when a hazardous step is hidden among many legitimate steps of a long-horizon instruction. The reason could be that LLMs become less reliable as a task grows longer and more complex, especially when they must reason about the whole task at once ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Besta et al., 2024 ) .
Moreover, some existing defenses rely on formal safety specifications written in LTL. When such a specification is produced by an LLM in a single unverified pass, it may not reflect the scene properly, and our experiments show that on long-horizon compound tasks the resulting constraints can be incomplete or incorrect.
As a result, a defense that judges the instruction as a whole may either overlook the hidden unsafe sub-task or reject the instruction and discard its legitimate parts. For example, in Figure 1 (right), RoboGuard accepts the hazardous sub-task of leaving the oven on with its door open, whereas SafePlan refuses the instruction altogether, including the harmless request to put the oven mitt on the counter. We therefore argue that, instead of simply accepting or rejecting an instruction, an LLM-enabled robot should refuse its harmful sub-tasks while completing its legitimate ones, a problem we refer to as safe task completion.

To address this limitation, we propose
Graph-of-Rules Planning, termed RuleGraph.
RuleGraph decomposes the problem into smaller sub-problems that an LLM can solve more reliably. This distributes safety enforcement across multiple reasoning and verification stages. RuleGraph grounds general safety principles in the symbolic world and robot skills, then instantiates an independent planning node for each relevant rule. Each node generates, verifies, and refines a candidate plan against its assigned rule, after which the resulting plans are progressively combined through hierarchical aggregation until a single plan satisfies all relevant rules. This distribution gives subsequent stages additional opportunities to detect, refine, or reject unsafe behavior when an earlier component fails.
While the rules define what a plan must avoid, a safe goal defines what it must achieve. RuleGraph splits the instruction into sub-tasks, judges each one in the context of the full instruction, and derives this goal from the legitimate ones. Every node plans toward this same goal.
As a result, for an instruction containing at least one legitimate sub-task, RuleGraph neutralizes the unsafe behavior while still accomplishing the safe goal, rather than merely recognizing the attack. This addresses the loss of usefulness that can result from overly conservative safety mechanisms ( Yuan et al., 2025 ; Ding et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Yoon et al., 2025 ) .

This paper makes three contributions.

To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to address safe task completion in embodied safety, moving beyond accepting or rejecting an instruction as a whole.

We propose a Graph-of-Rules planning method, which assigns each relevant safety rule to a dedicated node of a graph and progressively merges the resulting per-rule plans into a single plan that satisfies every rule.

We evaluate RuleGraph on the RoboGuard benchmark and on Compound, our set of 97 long-horizon compound instructions. It achieves 0% Attack Success Rate (ASR) on both, with a Task Success Rate (TSR) of 98.57% and 84.54%, respectively.

1. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to address safe task completion in embodied safety, moving beyond accepting or rejecting an instruction as a whole.

2. We propose a Graph-of-Rules planning method, which assigns each relevant safety rule to a dedicated node of a graph and progressively merges the resulting per-rule plans into a single plan that satisfies every rule.

3. We evaluate RuleGraph on the RoboGuard benchmark and on Compound, our set of 97 long-horizon compound instructions. It achieves 0% Attack Success Rate (ASR) on both, with a Task Success Rate (TSR) of 98.57% and 84.54%, respectively.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Jailbreaking attacks target an LLM-controlled robot after it is deployed. A crafted instruction makes the robot carry out a harmful decision, even though the underlying model was never changed. BadRobot ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) shows three ways to do this, including a Contextual Jailbreak that wraps the malicious request in a jailbreak prompt reassigning the robot’s role, a Safety Misalignment attack that exploits the gap between what the robot says and what it does, and a Conceptual Deception that rephrases a harmful request so it sounds ordinary. RoboPAIR ( Robey et al., 2025 ) automates the attack instead of hand-crafting it, rewriting a prompt over several rounds until it succeeds across white-box, gray-box, and black-box access. In another study ( Jones et al., 2025 ) , rather than crafting a semantically harmful prompt, the authors adapt the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) attack ( Zou et al., 2023 ) , which uses gradients through the model to greedily search for an adversarial suffix of tokens, and apply it to a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model’s action-prediction loss instead of a chatbot’s text loss. The resulting suffix drives the VLA’s discretized action output to an attacker-chosen target, without the prompt needing to reference harm at all.

Safety guardrails check a robot’s plan against safety conditions before it executes, without changing the underlying model. RoboGuard ( Ravichandran et al., 2026 ) uses one LLM call to turn a set of safety rules into LTL for the current scene, then checks the plan against that logic via an automaton.
SafePlan ( Obi et al., 2025 ) uses a four-step pipeline, where it first screens the prompt for safety, then generates invariants, preconditions, and postconditions, then generates the plan, and finally verifies the plan against them.
VLSA ( Hu et al., 2025 ) instead addresses physical safety, using control barrier functions (CBFs) to stop a VLA model from colliding with objects. They model both the obstacle and the end-effector as ellipsoids so a CBF-based quadratic program can correct the VLA’s nominal action only when a collision is imminent. Another study ( Feng et al., 2025 ) takes natural language safety instructions for a navigation robot, parses them into structured spatial and kinematic constraints, and enforces them with a sampling-based Model Predictive Control (MPC) filter which scores, and then overrides, the robot’s planned motion, keeping it as close as possible to the original path while maintaining a positive safety margin. In both approaches, safety correction operates at the current control-action level, where an optimization-based filter modifies the nominal action at the current timestep rather than reasoning over and revising an entire multi-step plan. HazardArena ( Chen et al., 2026 ) adds a lightweight Safety Option Layer that runs at inference time to block unsafe actions in a VLA policy, without retraining it.

2026-10-20.title: LIBERO-Pro2.0: A Benchmark for Evaluating the Robustness of Embodied Foundation Models
2026-10-20.authors: Xueyang Zhou , Yangming Xu , Qianjiang Li , Guiyao Tie , Junhao Wu , Ziheng Huang , Guowen Zhang , Zhijie Yuan , Di Wu , Duanfeng Chu , Pan Zhou , Lichao Sun , Yongchao Chen
2026-10-20.abstract: LIBERO has emerged as a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating robotic manipulation policies. However, strong performance on LIBERO does not necessarily indicate robust embodied capabilities, as models may exploit benchmark-specific regularities rather than generalize to diverse operating conditions. In this work, we introduce LIBERO-Pro2.0 , a comprehensive benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of embodied foundation models under distribution shifts. LIBERO-Pro2.0 encompasses 22 static perturbations and 20 runtime interventions across six dimensions: Condition, Environment, Observation, Execution, Robot State Configuration, and Language, yielding 1,648 validated shifted task instances . To support robustness-oriented learning, we further collect 39,390 training trajectories through model-generated and human demonstrations. All shifted task instances undergo six rounds of iterative human review and correction to ensure physical plausibility and task validity. We evaluate 17 representative robot policies spanning vision-language-action models, world-action models, and robustness-oriented policies. Our results reveal substantial robustness gaps across all evaluated paradigms: under runtime distribution shifts, the evaluated models exhibit an average performance drop of 26.5 percentage points , with individual drops reaching 32.5 points . These findings highlight the gap between nominal benchmark performance and robustness under distribution shifts, underscoring the need for systematic robustness evaluation of embodied foundation models.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Reliable evaluation is essential for measuring progress in embodied intelligence ( Yu et al., 2020 ; James et al., 2020 ; Mees et al., 2022 ; Gu et al., 2023 ; Mu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . LIBERO has emerged as a de facto standard for tabletop manipulation ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , with increasingly many systems approaching saturated performance under its standard protocol ( Kim et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025 ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Fang et al., 2026 ) . Yet a fundamental question remains: do these high success rates reflect generalizable embodied capabilities, or merely strong performance within a familiar training–evaluation distribution?

To examine this question, we revisit high-performing systems on LIBERO and observe three striking failure patterns under simple task variations: (1) when the target object is replaced or even removed, models still execute the original grasping behavior; (2) when the task instruction is replaced with meaningless tokens, models continue to produce nearly identical action trajectories; and (3) when the target object is moved away from its familiar position, models still move toward the location commonly seen during training. These qualitative observations motivate a systematic evaluation of sensitivity to task-relevant visual, linguistic, and spatial changes, but do not by themselves establish memorization as the underlying failure mechanism.

These failures expose a broader limitation of current evaluation protocols. Standard benchmarks largely test whether a policy can reproduce successful behavior under conditions close to those seen during training ( Yu et al., 2020 ; James et al., 2020 ; Mees et al., 2022 ; Gu et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) , while deployment requires the same system to remain effective when the scene changes before execution, when unexpected events occur during interaction ( Li et al., 2024 ; Fei et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and when an initial action fails. Consequently, nominal task success alone does not characterize robustness when operating conditions change. A meaningful evaluation protocol should therefore separate training from evaluation distributions and explicitly test both generalization to static shifts and adaptation to runtime interventions.

To this end, we introduce LIBERO-Pro2.0, a large-scale robustness benchmark for embodied foundation models under static distribution shifts and runtime interventions. LIBERO-Pro2.0 defines 42 perturbation types (22 static and 20 runtime), yielding 1,648 perturbed task variants . These perturbations span scene and object configurations, visual observations, camera settings, robot states, among others. We reserve 8 comprehensively perturbed tasks for evaluation and release the remaining perturbations for training, collecting 39,390 training trajectories . Each perturbed task undergoes six rounds of human verification to ensure validity and reproducibility. We evaluate 17 representative policies spanning vision-language-action models, world-action models, and robustness-oriented policies. Results reveal substantial robustness degradation under both static and runtime distribution shifts, with runtime shifts causing an average performance drop of 26.5 percentage points . Moreover, robustness varies substantially across perturbation types. High nominal success does not guarantee small robustness losses or preservation of policy rankings under distribution shifts. Our main contributions are threefold:

We introduce LIBERO-Pro2.0 , a large-scale robustness benchmark for embodied foundation models, extending LIBERO beyond nominal task success to systematically evaluate robustness under both static distribution shifts and runtime interventions.

We develop a comprehensive perturbation suite with 42 perturbation types , yielding 1,648 perturbed task variants and 39,390 training trajectories across diverse environments, observations, instructions, robot states, and execution conditions, with rigorous human verification.

We conduct a large-scale evaluation of 17 representative policies across different model paradigms, revealing substantial robustness degradation under both static and runtime shifts and showing that nominal LIBERO performance does not consistently reflect robustness.

1. We introduce LIBERO-Pro2.0 , a large-scale robustness benchmark for embodied foundation models, extending LIBERO beyond nominal task success to systematically evaluate robustness under both static distribution shifts and runtime interventions.

2. We develop a comprehensive perturbation suite with 42 perturbation types , yielding 1,648 perturbed task variants and 39,390 training trajectories across diverse environments, observations, instructions, robot states, and execution conditions, with rigorous human verification.

3. We conduct a large-scale evaluation of 17 representative policies across different model paradigms, revealing substantial robustness degradation under both static and runtime shifts and showing that nominal LIBERO performance does not consistently reflect robustness.

2026-10-20.title: LIBERO-Dynamic: Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation in Dynamic Environments
2026-10-20.authors: Shaojie Ren , Jingwen Sun , Zezhi Liu , Hongjin Chen , Xin Jin , Wei Zou , Zhibo Chen
2026-10-20.abstract: Most simulation benchmarks for robotic manipulation keep target objects static and treat policy inference as instantaneous. These assumptions simplify repeatable evaluation, but they hide how a moving target evolves during computation and how stale an observation may be when its predicted action is executed. We introduce LIBERO -Dynamic, a controlled dynamic extension of all 40 LIBERO tasks. It drives objects through contact friction along three trajectory families and three speed tiers, while continuously advancing the physical world according to calibrated, model-specific inference latency. The same motion mechanism also supports training: we replay verified static demonstrations and compensate robot actions online using the target’s displacement relative to the reference, producing 9,000 quality-filtered dynamic trajectories. We evaluate six pretrained policies on a shared set of 1,800 dynamic conditions per configuration, compare execution strategies and action horizons with the checkpoint fixed, and fine-tune three architectures using dynamic and mixed data. The experiments show that faster motion degrades every evaluated policy, but not uniformly; execution timing and horizon can change the behavior of the same policy; and, in the measured sweep, asynchronous replanning benefits from frequent feedback only after the action queue can be sustained without underflow. Dynamic demonstrations improve each evaluated architecture under at least one training recipe, while the magnitude of improvement varies with temporal conditioning, data composition, and training budget. In a small-scale physical study using policies trained on real-robot dynamic demonstrations, we observe execution-strategy differences consistent with those found in simulation, with task-dependent effects, providing complementary evidence for the corresponding benchmark findings. By making object motion, inference latency, and action execution explicit and controllable within a broad task suite, LIBERO -Dynamic provides a reproducible platform for evaluating and improving robot policies for moving-target manipulation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
General-purpose robot policies—including vision-language-action (VLA) models and policies built on video or world models—have advanced rapidly with growing data scale, architectural innovation, and improved post-training techniques ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) .
Reliable comparison increasingly depends on benchmarks that evaluate not only task completion, but also behavior under deployment-relevant conditions.

Real-robot platforms such as RoboArena ( Atreya et al., 2025 ) , RoboChallenge ( Yakefu et al., 2025 ) , and RoboDojo ( Chen et al., 2026a ) provide direct evidence under physical deployment, whereas simulation benchmarks such as LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) , RLBench ( James et al., 2020 ) , and RoboTwin ( Mu et al., 2024 ) enable repeatable evaluation across broad task collections. Recent extensions including LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) , LIBERO-PRO ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) , and LIBERO-X ( Wang et al., 2026 ) further examine robustness and generalization under controlled variations.

Dynamic manipulation adds a critical temporal dimension. In common step-based simulation evaluations, policy inference is typically treated as instantaneous, or the physical world does not continue to advance during inference, leaving observations and actions ideally aligned in time. In a static scene, waiting for inference does not change the state of the target object; when the object continues to move, however, the observation underlying a returned action may already be stale. DOMINO ( Fang et al., 2026 ) studies moving-object interaction, while DOM ( Xie et al., 2026 ) and ReflexBench ( Chen et al., 2026b ) also account for inference latency and compare execution mechanisms. These advances motivate a complementary question: how do object motion, execution timing, and training choices affect policy performance when the underlying manipulation tasks are held consistent?

To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO -Dynamic, a dynamic manipulation benchmark that combines controlled object motion with model-specific inference latency in a unified simulation loop; its overall framework is shown in Figure 2 .
Across LIBERO ’s 40 tasks, LIBERO -Dynamic introduces three trajectory families and three motion-speed tiers, using a friction-driven invisible contact platform to preserve contact interactions among the robot, target, and surrounding objects.
The physical world continues to evolve during policy inference, and the benchmark advances simulation according to pre-calibrated model latency so that observation–action staleness can be evaluated explicitly. With the checkpoint fixed, we conduct controlled comparisons of synchronous execution, the LeRobot asynchronous queue ( Cadene et al., 2026 ) , and Real-Time Chunking (RTC) ( Black et al., 2025a ) , while treating VLASH ( Tang et al., 2025 ) , which uses a separate checkpoint, as a future-state-aware system reference.

Under a unified protocol, we evaluate diverse robot policies and compare dynamic manipulation performance across execution mechanisms and action horizons.
We further conduct controlled fine-tuning experiments on three model families using dynamic demonstrations and mixed static–dynamic data, examining how gains from dynamic data vary with the form of temporal conditioning.
A compact real-robot study, using policies trained on physical dynamic demonstrations in a DROID-style setup ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) , provides supplementary evidence for the execution-timing observations under physical sensing and actuation.

In summary, this work makes the following contributions:

We introduce LIBERO -Dynamic, a dynamic robotic manipulation benchmark that combines controlled object motion with model-specific inference latency. It defines a controlled spatiotemporal evaluation space through motion pattern, speed, trajectory phase, and perception–action delay for comparing dynamic responsiveness across robot policies.

We introduce a method for converting successful static demonstrations into dynamic ones: invisible conveyors drive objects through contact friction, while static manipulation references are adapted to changing target states through online motion compensation. Using this method, we construct a dataset of 9,000 dynamic trajectories spanning multiple motion patterns, speeds, spatial trajectories, and motion phases.

We evaluate representative models and execution strategies under a unified protocol and use controlled fine-tuning to analyze the relationship among dynamic data, temporal conditioning, and execution. Dynamic data improves several evaluated policies, while the gains vary with the form of temporal conditioning, providing empirical evidence for model training and execution design in dynamic manipulation.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

General-purpose robot policies span autoregressive action-token prediction, continuous action generation, and video- or world-model-based control, represented by RT-2 and OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT and the π \pi family, and VLA-JEPA and Fast-WAM, respectively ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Black et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) .
Recent methods for dynamic settings further incorporate observation history, future-state prediction, or continuous inference–execution coordination into policy design ( Fang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Xie et al., 2026 ) .
Because these systems also differ in training data and execution protocol, direct comparison across reported results is difficult.
We evaluate representative policy families under a common task distribution and timing protocol, and study how temporal conditioning interacts with dynamic-data fine-tuning.

LIBERO, RLBench, and RoboTwin support reproducible multi-task manipulation evaluation, while LIBERO-Plus, LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-X, VLA-Arena, and LIBERO-Safety extend this setting toward robustness, generalization, or safety under controlled variations ( Liu et al., 2023 ; James et al., 2020 ; Mu et al., 2024 ; Fei et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Cui et al., 2026 ) .
More recent benchmarks study within-rollout dynamics: DOMINO provides 35 tasks with hierarchical motion complexity and large-scale dynamic demonstrations; DynamicVLA introduces DOM for dynamic interaction, perception, and generalization in simulation; and ReflexBench couples six reaction-critical tasks with configurable latency under synchronous and asynchronous execution ( Fang et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ) . Table 1 summarizes the benchmark properties most directly related to our scope.

These benchmarks address complementary gaps. DOMINO studies motion complexity and static–dynamic co-training; DOM evaluates dynamic interaction, perception, and generalization, and analyzes continuous inference and latency-aware action streaming. ReflexBench compares synchronous and asynchronous execution under configurable latency. LIBERO -Dynamic retains the goals of all 40 LIBERO tasks and applies matched trajectory and speed controls with pre-calibrated model latency. This setting supports action-horizon sweeps and queue-underflow analysis, together with comparisons of dynamic-only and mixed fine-tuning across policy structures. Its emphasis is on how motion, execution timing, and training choices affect performance within a shared task distribution.

Action chunking trades feedback frequency for temporal consistency: long execution horizons reduce policy queries, whereas short horizons refresh observations more often but can exhaust the action queue under non-negligible inference latency.
LeRobot implements a producer–consumer asynchronous queue that overlaps action prediction and execution ( Cadene et al., 2026 ) .
RTC conditions generation on committed actions through inference-time inpainting, while training-time RTC learns prefix-conditioned continuation during training to avoid the additional guidance pass ( Black et al., 2025a ; Black et al., 2025b ) .
A2C2 adds a lightweight per-step correction head driven by the latest observation, and VLASH aligns prediction with execution by rolling the robot state forward over the expected delay ( Sendai et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2025 ) .
FASTER reduces time to first action through horizon-aware flow-sampling schedules ( Lu et al., 2026 ) .
Together, these works address latency and action-chunk continuity at the levels of execution, training, online correction, and sampling.

2026-10-20.title: Retrieval-triggered Action Projection Adjustment for Frozen VLA Policies: An Empirical Study and Failure Analysis
2026-10-20.authors: Jinming Wang , Ruiheng Zhang , Yong Wang , Zipan Xiong , Keyuan Luo
2026-10-20.abstract: Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies cannot incorporate previously encountered failures without updating the underlying model. We present retrieval-triggered projection correction (RTPC), an auditable external-memory wrapper for frozen OpenVLA policies that retrieves stress-collected local-depth records and applies translation-only projection correction while keeping rotation and gripper commands unchanged. RTPC is evaluated on CALVIN single-task manipulation using primary and independent replication cohorts. In the primary evaluation, RTPC reduced a depth-based near-collision or stall proxy event rate without changing task-success count. However, this reduction was not reproduced in the independent replication, and retrieved correction directions were not distinguishable from random same-family directions. Analysis identifies endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the lack of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline as limitations for attributing effects to retrieval-based correction. These findings do not establish physical safety improvement or memory-specific benefits, but provide an empirical evaluation and failure analysis of retrieval-conditioned intervention for frozen VLA policies.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions to robot actions by transferring large-scale visual and linguistic knowledge to robotic control Driess et al. (2023) ; Li et al. (2024) ; Zitkovich et al. (2023) . OpenVLA offers an open pretrained policy, while CALVIN provides language-conditioned manipulation tasks with a standardized policy interface Kim et al. (2025) ; Mees et al. (2022a) . A frozen policy does not retain information about prior adverse observations. Prior autonomous systems have explored persistent external information storage to support reliability-oriented decision processes Li et al. (2023) . An external memory therefore provides an inspectable alternative to policy retraining or architectural modification. We ask whether a simple external correction can produce a reproducible
and interpretable effect. RTPC mines stress episodes using gripper-depth,
translational-motion, and low tool-center-point (TCP) progress cues to
store local-depth descriptors and correction directions. During
evaluation, same-family retrieval gates a one-step projection correction
around frozen OpenVLA. The endpoint is a depth-proximity or stall proxy,
not physical contact or a certified safety condition. Across eight
single tasks, a 112-state primary batch and an independent 40-state
replication batch test proxy change, task success, replication, and
retrieved-versus-random directions.
This paper makes the following contributions:

We present RTPC, an auditable external-memory wrapper that
retrieves stress-collected local-depth records and applies
translation-only projection correction to actions proposed by a
frozen OpenVLA policy.

We show that the primary proxy effect did not replicate,
task success did not improve, and retrieved directions were not
statistically distinguishable from random same-family directions.

We identify endpoint coupling as a barrier to physical-safety
interpretation, and batch sensitivity and the absence of a
trigger-matched, memory-free baseline as barriers to memory-specific
attribution.

2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Multimodal transformers and cross-modal attention have been applied to pedestrian crossing-intention prediction in safety-critical urban settings, while diffusion-based visuomotor controllers have demonstrated strong manipulation performance Chi et al. (2023) ; Li and Müller (2025a) ; Li and Müller (2025b) ; Li et al. (2025) . OpenVLA is an open 7B-parameter vision-language-action model that supports parameter-efficient adaptation Ghosh et al. (2024) ; Kim et al. (2025) ; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration et al. (2024) . Recent VLA memory systems have investigated recurrent history representations, experience retrieval, and agent-level reuse of previous interactions Cherepanov et al. (2026) ; Li et al. (2026) ; Qu et al. (2026) ; Shah et al. (2026) ; Wu et al. (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026) . These approaches incorporate prior experience through learned representations, retrieved context, or agent-level memory mechanisms, following the broader idea of retrieval-augmented reasoning Borgeaud et al. (2022) ; Lewis et al. (2020) . In contrast, RTPC maintains a frozen external correction memory and applies a deterministic one-step modification to the translational action without updating the underlying policy.

Shielding, control barrier functions, and recovery policies constrain or replace potentially unsafe actions using specified dynamics, formal constraints, or learned risk estimates Alshiekh et al. (2018) ; Ames et al. (2019) ; Dawson et al. (2023) ; Thananjeyan et al. (2021) . SafeVLA instead modifies a VLA policy through constrained learning and explicit safety costs Zhang et al. (2025) . RTPC differs from these methods because it applies retrieval-conditioned projection correction around a frozen policy. It does not optimize a safety objective, use a contact-grounded endpoint, or provide an invariance guarantee. The measured proxy events should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of formal or physical safety.

2026-10-20.title: SocialCoAct: Enabling and Benchmarking Egocentric Social Co-Action for VLM-Based Humanoid Robots
2026-10-20.authors: Jiancong Ma , Kun Li , Jin Jiang , Shengcai Liao
2026-10-20.abstract: Enabling humanoid robots to participate effectively in social interactions is important for their integration into human-centered environments. Existing methods, however, typically map pre-generated speech directly to continuous motion trajectories but have limited awareness of complex social environments and lack explicit high-level semantic action planning. We introduce SocialCoAct, a unified agent-centered framework for VLM-based egocentric social co-action. We formulate egocentric social co-action as an end-to-end agent task and develop SocialCoAct-Agent, which transforms egocentric observations and dialogue history into verbal responses and atomic action sequences, aligns each action with its corresponding utterance span, and executes the resulting behaviors in MuJoCo and on a physical humanoid robot. To evaluate the VLM capabilities required by this task, we construct SocialCoAct-Bench from continuous egocentric recordings of natural multi-party interactions. The benchmark comprises 423 human-verified multiple-choice questions across three subtasks: Long Episode Understanding (LEU), Speaker Intention Understanding (SIU), and Coordinated Action Planning (CAP). Across a diverse set of closed-source and open-weight VLMs, including general and egocentric models, the highest overall accuracy is 77.54%, while accuracy on the hard subset reaches only 46.51%. Extended reasoning improves Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B by 19.62 and 17.02 percentage points, respectively, but reduces inference throughput by 53.6 × \times and 20.2 × \times . Visual-input ablations further show that the benefits of visual context vary across models. SocialCoAct provides a foundation for developing and evaluating VLM-based humanoid agents that coordinate context-aware speech and action in complex social interactions. The codebase and benchmark will be made publicly available upon publication.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Humanoid robots are increasingly expected to participate in everyday social interactions. An ideal humanoid robot should be able to visually comprehend complex social scenes and ongoing activities, infer the intentions conveyed through human language, and respond naturally through coordinated verbal and bodily behaviors [ 1 , 2 ] . Such responses should not only be semantically appropriate but also align with the interaction context, timing, and intended addressee, thereby resembling the integrated way in which humans communicate through speech and action [ 3 , 4 ] .

Recent systems can generate synchronized co-speech gestures for physical robots, while a few can jointly produce verbal and embodied responses [ 5 ] . However, their gestures are typically conditioned on pre-generated text or speech rather than grounded in an online visual understanding of evolving social interactions [ 6 ] . They may also inherit idiosyncratic styles from individual demonstrators without explicitly modeling semantic alignment. Consequently, existing evaluations do not jointly assess whether verbal and bodily responses are appropriate given scene dynamics, conversational history, speaker intention, ongoing activities, and addressee relations in multi-party interactions.

Evaluating this capability poses a parallel challenge. Social appropriateness cannot be judged from an isolated frame or utterance; it depends on conversational history, speaker intention, turn-taking dynamics, addressee relations, and the norms of the ongoing activity. Moreover, because humans communicate through coordinated speech and bodily behavior, an evaluation must consider not only the appropriateness of each modality but also their semantic alignment [ 6 ] . Existing evaluations of robotic social intelligence, however, primarily focus on human–robot interaction or the recognition and correction of observed social behaviors [ 7 ] . Although these tasks assess the perception of social cues and inappropriate behavior, they rarely examine whether a humanoid agent can actively generate a contextually appropriate verbal response together with semantically aligned bodily actions.

To address this gap, we introduce SocialCoAct ( Social Co ordinated Act ion), a unified VLM-based framework for egocentric social co-action in humanoid robots. The framework includes SocialCoAct-Agent , which reasons about the ongoing interaction and the current speaker’s intent from egocentric observations and dialogue history, generates a verbal response together with an ordered sequence of atomic actions, aligns each action with its corresponding utterance span, and executes the resulting co-speech behavior in MuJoCo and on a physical humanoid robot. To evaluate whether current VLMs can support this task, we construct SocialCoAct-Bench from continuous first-person recordings of diverse, natural multi-party interactions.
As shown in Fig. 1 , SocialCoAct-Bench evaluates the VLM capabilities required by this agent task at two complementary temporal levels through three subtasks. At the long-context level, Long Episode Understanding (LEU) assesses the model’s understanding of the overall activity and interaction context across an egocentric episode. At the short-turn level, Speaker Intention Understanding (SIU) evaluates the interpretation of the current speaker’s intention, while Coordinated Action Planning (CAP) assesses whether and how the agent should produce an ordered plan of predefined atomic actions aligned with spans in a given verbal reply.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We develop SocialCoAct-Agent , an agent capable of transforming egocentric observations and dialogue history into verbal responses and utterance-aligned atomic actions executable in MuJoCo and on a physical humanoid robot.

To evaluate the capabilities required by this agent, we introduce SocialCoAct-Bench , an egocentric benchmark of 423 human-verified questions organized into three progressive tasks: LEU for long-context understanding, SIU for speaker-intention understanding, and CAP for planning atomic actions aligned with a given verbal reply in complex multi-party interactions.

We benchmark a diverse set of closed-source and open-weight VLMs, including general and egocentric models, and characterize their capability boundaries across tasks and difficulty levels. Our reasoning ablations demonstrate substantial trade-offs between accuracy and efficiency, while our modality ablations show that the benefits of visual context vary across models.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Embodied Social Response Generation

Existing research on embodied social response generation spans facial reaction
generation, gesture synthesis, and multimodal conversational behavior.
Responsive Listening Head Generation introduces a benchmark and baseline for
synthesizing listener head movements and facial expressions from a speaker’s
audiovisual behavior, while REACT defines online and offline settings for
generating diverse and appropriate facial reactions in dyadic
conversations [ 8 , 9 ] . More recent systems capture richer interaction
dynamics. PolySLGen generates speaking and listening reactions for a target
participant based on the speech and motion history of polyadic
interactions [ 10 ] , whereas ProAct combines long-horizon social reasoning
with streaming nonverbal behavior to enable proactive embodied
interaction [ 11 ] .

Collectively, these studies have advanced response-generation benchmarks,
generative architectures, and integrated interactive systems. However, their
evaluations are generally not designed to isolate the upstream decision-making
capabilities required of VLMs, including long-horizon contextual understanding,
speaker-intent inference, and the construction of language-aligned action plans
for humanoid robots.

## II-B Multimodal Social and Egocentric Benchmarks

Existing benchmarks evaluate different aspects of social intelligence. Social-IQ and Social Genome assess multimodal reasoning about social situations, whereas SIV-Bench further evaluates social scene understanding, latent-state reasoning, and interaction dynamics prediction. SocialGesture focuses on gesture recognition, temporal localization, and vision-language reasoning in multi-person interactions [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] . EasyCom, EgoCom, and Ego4D provide first-person recordings of natural communication, whereas JRDB-Social captures individual behaviors and group dynamics from the perspective of a mobile robot [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] .

Recent benchmarks have increasingly emphasized interactive decision-making. HoloAssist evaluates mistake detection and intervention-type prediction in egocentric task assistance, whereas OmniMMI benchmarks proactive reasoning and turn-taking in streaming multimodal contexts [ 20 , 21 ] . In embodied human–robot interaction (HRI), SHREC evaluates social errors, competencies, interaction flow, and corrective actions using videos of real-world human–robot interactions, whereas ERR@HRI 2.0 focuses on multimodal failure detection in dyadic human–robot conversations [ 7 , 22 ] .

Nevertheless, these benchmarks largely evaluate social perception, reasoning, error diagnosis, and response generation in isolation. They do not jointly assess the VLM capabilities needed to understand an evolving multi-party interaction and plan bodily actions that are semantically aligned with a given verbal response.

2026-10-20.title: ContactBench 1.0: A Benchmark for Everyday Contact-Rich Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Jingyi Xiang , Yixuan Wang , Jeannette Bohg , Wenzhen Yuan
2026-10-20.abstract:
Contact-rich manipulation is essential to everyday activities, yet evaluating robots’ ability to perform these activities remains challenging because of their diverse contact behaviors and the difficulty of reproducing tasks across laboratories. Drawing on observations of everyday human manipulation, we identify eight recurring skill categories that provide a practical framework for studying these capabilities. We introduce ContactBench 1.0, an extensible benchmark that instantiates these skills through 36 reference tasks and more than 40 object assets. The assets capture task-relevant geometry and contact behavior, support reproducible fabrication using consumer-grade 3D printers, and are paired with simulation models with tunable resistance loads. Controlled task variations enable evaluation of policy generalization. We evaluate recent vision-based and vision-tactile policy learning methods on six benchmark tasks. The results reveal that the evaluated vision-only policies struggle to perceive or react to contact events, while the evaluated visual-tactile policies do not meaningfully improve performance. By providing shared tasks and physical and simulated assets, ContactBench 1.0 establishes a foundation for reproducible evaluation of contact-rich manipulation research.
The benchmark is open-sourced at https://jingyi-xiang.github.io/contactbench .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Achieving human-level generality in robotic manipulation remains a long-standing goal of the robotics community. Recent progress in robot learning has produced increasingly capable systems, supported by large-scale demonstrations, expressive policy architectures, and broad task suites. Much of this progress has been demonstrated on tasks in which visually observable properties, such as object identity, appearance, and pose, provide strong guidance for action. Everyday manipulation, however, also requires robots to regulate forces, exploit environmental constraints, and respond to changes in contact. In these tasks, contact is the mechanism through which the robot accomplishes its goal. Developing robots that can effectively exploit contact is therefore essential to general-purpose manipulation.

This raises a core question: “What constitutes success in contact-rich manipulation?” Although contact-rich manipulation has been widely studied, many existing works focus on insertion and peg-in-hole tasks [ 23 , 9 , 21 , 17 , 20 , 8 ] or tasks that require sustained force against a surface, such as wiping and peeling [ 42 , 27 , 15 ] . Everyday human activities, however, involve a much broader range of contact modes, such as grasping challenging objects with various environmental constraints, leveraging extrinsic contact for accurate manipulation, and manipulating articulated object based on force feedback. Progress toward general-purpose manipulation therefore requires systematic, reproducible evaluation across a diverse set of tasks that cover this breadth of contact interaction.

We sought answers to this question by observing everyday human manipulation. These observations suggest that, despite differences in objects’ appearances and functions, most manipulation sequences involving contact can be broadly described in terms of eight skills that remain underrepresented in current robotics research: grasping thin or small objects, grasping multiple objects, grasping from clutter, placing under environmental constraints, in-hand repositioning, extrinsic contact control, articulated object manipulation, and insertion and alignment. Many complex manipulation tasks can be understood as combinations of these skills. We therefore believe that mastering these skills is essential for robots to perform a broad range of contact-rich manipulation tasks.

To support the community’s efforts to develop these capabilities, we introduce ContactBench 1.0, an extensible benchmark that instantiates these skill categories through 36 reference tasks and more than 40 standardized object assets. The assets are designed to capture the functional contact interactions of everyday objects through their geometry and mechanical response. Each asset can be fabricated using 3D printing and is designed for reproducible fabrication on consumer-grade printers while preserving task-relevant contact behavior. Controlled variations in object geometry and internal mechanics support evaluation of policy generalization. Corresponding simulation models provide tunable resistance loads for studying related contact interactions in simulation. By providing shared task definitions and standardized physical and simulated assets, ContactBench 1.0 establishes common experimental ground for comparing methods across laboratories and supporting cumulative progress.

We demonstrate the utility of ContactBench 1.0 by evaluating recent vision-based policy learning methods (Diffusion Policy [ 6 ] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 18 ] ) and their tactile-augmented versions (Reactive Diffusion Policy [ 42 ] , Foundation Tactile Policy [ 45 ] ) on six tasks from our benchmark. The results reveal mixed performance across the evaluated methods. Vision-only policies struggle with the precision required by these tasks and with perceiving and reacting to contact-dependent information that is difficult to infer from images. The evaluated visual-tactile policies do not meaningfully improve performance. Our analysis suggests that limited sensor coverage and difficulties in translating tactile observations into appropriate actions are the potential bottlenecks. These findings highlight challenges that extend beyond access to tactile sensing alone.

We open-source ContactBench 1.0 at https://jingyi-xiang.github.io/contactbench . The initial release focuses on rigid and articulated objects; deformable objects and objects with more challenging surface properties remain beyond its current scope, but will be a potential future extension direction. We envision ContactBench 1.0 as a growing community resource that can incorporate additional tasks, assets, and skill categories over time. By providing shared infrastructure and a systematic account of contact-rich skills, we aim to make physical interaction a measurable dimension of general-purpose robotic manipulation.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Simulation Benchmarks for Manipulation

Simulation benchmarks support reproducible comparisons across tasks and learning methods. RLBench [ 19 ] , Meta-World [ 44 ] , and robosuite [ 49 ] provide standardized task suites, ManiSkill2 [ 14 ] adds wide object variation, and ManiSkill3 [ 36 ] parallelizes simulation and rendering on the GPU. CALVIN [ 30 ] and LIBERO [ 26 ] extend evaluation to long-horizon language-conditioned tasks and lifelong learning. Other environments focus on particular interactions. UniDoorManip [ 24 ] simulates doors with diverse geometries and mechanisms, and several platforms address touch: Taxim [ 34 ] renders vision-based tactile images, Tactile Gym 2.0 [ 25 ] compares optical tactile sensors through sim-to-real reinforcement learning, and the Robot Tactile Olympiad [ 31 ] benchmarks tactile reinforcement learning on four dexterous hands. None of these environments, however, pairs its tasks with physical assets whose contact behaviors can be varied. Our simulation suite mirrors each printable mechanism in the benchmark and exposes that contact behavior as an explicit tunable parameter.

## II-B Reproducible Physical Assets and Benchmarks

Physical benchmarks pursue reproducibility in two main ways. Some standardize the hardware: YCB [ 3 ] provides everyday objects with geometric models, NIST task boards [ 22 ] define small-parts assembly tasks and protocols, and ManipulationNet [ 5 ] supports distributed real-world evaluation with standardized hardware kits. Others release printable designs that any lab can fabricate: FurnitureBench [ 16 ] pairs printable furniture with demonstrations and a simulator for long-horizon assembly, Fabrica [ 38 ] benchmarks dual-arm multi-part assembly, and FMB [ 29 ] evaluates grasping, repositioning, and insertion, finding that force/torque input substantially improves insertion. Recent work also varies task conditions in a controlled way. MatchMaker [ 41 ] generates mating parts with user-specified clearances, and Peg-in-Bench [ 8 ] varies peg geometry, insertion tolerance, spatial layout, and assembly structure. BusyBox [ 12 ] instead varies appearance, rearranging modules of buttons, switches, sliders, and other controls while preserving their affordances. Most of these tasks involve assembly or insertion, and the forces they require are either fixed by the asset or set by part clearance. Our benchmark spans a broader range of everyday contact-rich skills, and its printed compliant springs set the required force independently of fit and appearance.

2026-10-20.title: GazeAct: A Human-Gaze-Annotated Manipulation Dataset for Attention-Regularized Policies
2026-10-20.authors: Anupam Pani , Wang Yuan , Qifan Wang , Yanchao Yang
2026-10-20.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies must ground language instructions in
the right objects, contact points, and target locations for reliable manipulation.
Human gaze provides a natural signal for this grounding, but existing robot
datasets rarely pair real human gaze with the multi-camera observations used by
modern policies. We introduce GazeAct, a gaze-equipped real-robot
manipulation dataset and training framework for multi-view VLA policies.
Using screen-based teleoperation, we record gaze directly on the robot camera
feed viewed by the operator, yielding 12,000 12{,}000 demonstrations across 40 40 tasks and five domains with 300 ​ Hz 300\,\mathrm{Hz} gaze synchronized with images,
proprioception, and actions. We transfer gaze from the operator-selected view
to the remaining synchronized cameras, producing spatially consistent targets
across the policy’s visual inputs. We then use these gaze-derived targets to
regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training while keeping
inference gaze-free. Across 18 18 real-world tasks, our method improves average
success from 48.1 % 48.1\% to 58.6 % 58.6\% , with gains up to 25 25 percentage points.
Ablations show that gaze works best as soft supervision and that real human
gaze provides stronger attention targets than generic attention-shaping priors.
The gains transfer to LIBERO-Spatial ( 57.9 % 57.9\% to 69.6 % 69.6\% ) and different VLA
backbones.These results show that gaze collected in the robot observation space can provide
effective training-time targets for improving visual grounding in VLA
manipulation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
VLA models have become a promising paradigm for
language-conditioned robotic manipulation, mapping visual observations, language
instructions, and proprioception to continuous actions [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Despite large-scale
pretraining, a basic difficulty remains: knowing where to look. Many
manipulation failures arise not from misunderstanding the language instruction
alone, but from failing to attend to small, transient, and ambiguous visual
regions such as the object, grasp region, contact point, handle, button, or
target location. Standard VLA policies must infer these regions indirectly from
action supervision.

Human gaze provides a natural signal for this missing visual grounding. During
manipulation, demonstrators often look at task-relevant objects
and target regions before or while acting. Gaze can therefore provide a compact
trace of the visual evidence used to support action decisions. However, the
primary obstacle is not the idea of using gaze, but the lack of robot learning
data in which gaze is aligned with the observations consumed by modern policies.
Large robot manipulation datasets typically contain images, proprioception, and
actions, but no human gaze. Conversely, existing gaze-equipped manipulation
datasets usually record gaze in a single egocentric, head-mounted, or displayed
view, which does not directly provide supervision over the multi-view robot
observations used by current VLA policies.

We introduce GazeAct, a gaze-annotated manipulation dataset and acquisition
pipeline designed to close this alignment gap. Our key idea is to record gaze
directly on the robot camera stream used by the teleoperator, so each gaze point
is obtained in robot-image coordinates and tied to the visual evidence used for
action selection. We implement this with a screen-based ALOHA teleoperation
system in which a Tobii Pro Spectrum eye tracker records gaze on the active
robot camera view while the robot logs multi-view images, proprioception, and
actions. Hardware triggers and synchronized clocks align gaze and robot streams
in time, while active-view logging records which camera the operator observed at
each moment. Because only one view is displayed at a time but VLA policies
consume multi-view observations, we transfer gaze to the remaining synchronized
camera views, producing spatially consistent gaze targets for all visual inputs
used by the policy.

The resulting dataset contains 12,000 12{,}000 demonstrations across 40 40 manipulation tasks in five domains, with synchronized gaze, multi-view RGB
observations, proprioception, and actions. To turn this gaze into a learning
signal, we convert synchronized and cross-view-aligned gaze into patch-level
distributions over the policy’s visual tokens. We then use these gaze-derived distributions as targets for attention
regularization, encouraging the policy’s language-conditioned visual attention
to align with human-fixated regions during training., without changing the policy architecture or
inference-time inputs.

Real human gaze therefore acts as an auxiliary supervision signal: it guides visual grounding during
training, but is removed at deployment. We evaluate this supervision signal through
expanded real-world rollouts, robustness trials, gaze-source and
regularization-strength ablations, transfer across VLA backbones, and simulation
transfer. Across these settings, real robot-view gaze improves policy learning
most strongly when manipulation depends on grounding small objects, contact
points, or target regions.

Our contributions are threefold. First , we introduce GazeAct, a
gaze-annotated manipulation dataset in which human gaze is grounded in the
robot’s own observations and made available across synchronized camera views. Second , we develop a screen-based, hardware-synchronized data-collection
and cross-view alignment pipeline for pairing high-frequency human gaze with
multi-view robot demonstrations. Third , we show that gaze-derived targets provide an effective training-time
signal for regularizing visual attention in modern VLA policies,
improving visual grounding and manipulation success while preserving the
standard gaze-free deployment interface.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Manipulation Datasets with and without Gaze. Large-scale teleoperation datasets have driven the recent generation of VLA models.
RT-1 [ 4 ] ,
BridgeData V2 [ 5 ] and DROID [ 6 ] provide hundreds of thousands of demonstrations across diverse robots and scenes, but record only what the operator did,
not where they looked.
A smaller body of work adds human gaze.
HARMONIC [ 7 ] captures gaze
with head-mounted glasses in a single assistive-eating task, but projects it onto the operator’s egocentric view rather than the robot’s cameras.
DAA [ 8 ] and
GazeBot [ 9 ] record real gaze on the robot’s stereo feed through an HMD (Head-mounted display) at large scale, but the HMD shows a single stereo composite, so gaze covers only one view and trajectories last a few seconds,
capturing brief reaches rather than complete manipulations. In contrast, GazeAct records
screen-based gaze directly on the robot camera feed used for teleoperation,
synchronizes it with robot observations and actions, and transfers it across
camera views so that gaze can supervise the multi-view inputs used by VLA
policies.

Gaze as a Learning Signal. Human gaze has been used in robot learning and visuomotor learning in several
ways. One line of work uses gaze as an offline cue for segmenting demonstrations;
for example, Takizawa et
al. [ 10 ] use fixation
transitions to decompose long-horizon demonstrations into sub-tasks. A second
line modifies the perceptual input pipeline, using gaze or predicted gaze to crop,
zoom, or foveate observations [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
These approaches can improve perception, but often change the input interface or
require gaze-like predictions at deployment. A third line, closer to our work,
uses gaze only during training to guide internal attention. Prior work has shown
that aligning model saliency or attention with human gaze can improve imitation
learning and visual recognition while keeping inference gaze-free [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] .
In vision-language models, Voila-A [ 23 ] uses gaze heatmaps to modulate attention, while gaze-regularized
models [ 24 ] align attention with ground-truth gaze during training.
GazeAct brings this training-time gaze supervision paradigm to real
teleoperated VLA manipulation, using synchronized robot-view gaze, cross-view
alignment, and gaze-free deployment.

Vision-Language-Action Models and Attention. Our method builds on transformer-based VLA policies, including π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 2 ] ,
RT-1 [ 4 ] ,
OpenVLA [ 3 ] ,
RoboMamba [ 25 ] ,
Octo [ 26 ] , and
SAM2Act [ 27 ] .
These models map
visual observations and language instructions to robot actions through internal
vision-language representations, often including attention over visual tokens.
GazeAct uses this attention interface as the point of supervision: real
human gaze is converted into patch-level gaze distributions and used to
regularize language-conditioned visual attention during training. Because the
regularizer acts on the policy’s internal attention rather than changing the
input stream or action head, it can be applied to different VLA backbones while
preserving the standard inference interface.

2026-10-20.title: Touch Where It Matters: Learning Local Tactile Policies for Fine-Grained Gripper Control
2026-10-20.authors: Mingyuan Ba , Yanan Zhou , James Zhao , Weiming Zhi
2026-10-20.abstract:
Visual imitation policies can organise task motion, yet contact-rich object
use demands gripper adjustments beyond coarse opening and closing. We study
fine-grained gripper control as a local feedback problem within ongoing
task execution. Our approach assigns tactile feedback a dedicated control
role during contact-rich task stages. We introduce ContactPolicy, a learned
local controller that takes over the gripper while a visual base policy
continues to control the arm. ContactPolicy combines tactile and force
histories with current robot state to jointly predict gripper increments and
their modulation, updating the gripper target from each new observation. An
Intent policy manages control handover between the visual base policy and ContactPolicy.
Real-world experiments on container opening, object handling, and tool
operation show improved task success over both the Visuomotor Policy and
Tactile–Force Policy baselines. Execution analysis illustrates how the gripper
adjusts contact within an ongoing task, including periods of target
retention and fine-grained changes as interaction conditions evolve.
Arm-state ablations and failure analysis further examine how execution
context supports local regulation. These results support task-local tactile
policies for fine-grained gripper control within visual manipulation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Visual imitation learning has enabled robots to acquire increasingly
complex manipulation skills from demonstrations. Visual imitation policies
learn coordinated action sequences from visual observations and robot
state [ 1 ] , while Mobile ALOHA and UMI extend
data collection to bimanual, mobile, and in-the-wild
settings [ 2 , 3 ] . Localisation feedback can improve
mobile execution by tracking map-frame base-pose targets, as in
MAVP [ 4 ] . Alongside reliable task motion, success also
depends on how the gripper interacts with the object during contact.

In the visual-policy executions we study, gripper behaviour is often
dominated by coarse opening and closing. Such commands can acquire and
release objects, but provide limited control over their use. A loaded
dropper must be held during transport and squeezed to dispense; a blower
must be compressed while the arm positions its outlet; and nested cups
must remain securely grasped as the arm separates them. Here, the gripper
actively performs the operation. Even when arm motion is appropriate,
small errors in gripper adjustment can determine whether the task succeeds.
Visual runtime monitors such as PATCH detect persistent local scene
disturbances and trigger intervention [ 5 ] . Object use
also requires feedback that regulates the ongoing gripper–object interaction.

These tasks expose a local control problem within visual manipulation: when should the gripper change its target, by how much, and when
should it hold that target? Touch is well suited to these decisions
because it senses the contact interface where gripper actions take
effect. Visual–tactile datasets and tactile skill learning demonstrate
the value of this complementary
information [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
Contact history reveals how an interaction evolves, while robot state
provides the context needed to coordinate adjustments with arm motion.

We therefore study task-local fine-grained gripper control (Fig. 1 ): tactile feedback regulates the gripper during
contact-rich stages while the visual base policy continues to advance the arm.
The relevant feedback is concentrated at the fingertips and is most useful
during object use. Assigning it to this stage lets the gripper respond to
changing contact without requiring the visual base policy to resolve every small
adjustment.
Recent reactive, force-aware, and modular policies explore complementary
ways to incorporate contact feedback [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] ,
and RETAF separates arm prediction from gripper force
regulation [ 16 ] . Our focus is learning gripper position
updates together with the decision to apply or withhold each update.
Locality specifies both the controlled component and the stage in which
contact feedback assumes control.

We introduce ContactPolicy to implement this division of control. It
encodes tactile and force histories, combines them with current arm and
gripper states, and jointly predicts gripper increments and their
modulation. The controller applies the first modulated increment to the
commanded target, then replans from the next observation. An Intent
policy manages handover between the visual base policy and ContactPolicy,
allowing local contact regulation within ongoing task execution.

Real-robot experiments improve task success over the Visuomotor Policy
and Tactile–Force Policy baselines. Execution analyses highlight how local
contact adjustment coordinates gripper operation with arm motion.

Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate task-local fine-grained gripper control for
contact-rich manipulation: the arm advances the task while the gripper
uses local feedback to adjust contact beyond coarse opening and closing.

We introduce ContactPolicy, a learned local tactile controller
that combines contact histories and current robot state to predict and
modulate gripper increments. Control handover integrates its iterative
target updates into visual task execution.

We evaluate ContactPolicy on real-world contact-rich
tasks, demonstrating improved success over the visual base policy.
Input ablations and execution failure analysis examine how robot state
supports local tactile regulation and coordination with task motion.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Visual imitation and generalist policies. ACT and Diffusion Policy learn action sequences from
demonstrations [ 17 , 1 ] ; Mobile ALOHA and UMI
extend demonstration collection to mobile and in-the-wild
settings [ 2 , 3 ] . Learned hand skills can assist
dexterous demonstration collection [ 18 ] .
Open X-Embodiment and DROID expand
robot experience [ 19 , 20 ] , while Octo and OpenVLA
learn generalist policies across tasks and
environments [ 21 , 22 ] .
Demonstration timing also affects learned coordination: retimed segments
support synchronous multi-arm policy learning [ 23 ] .
Our focus is the contact adjustment required within visual task execution.

Tactile representations and multimodal learning. UniTouch aligns touch with other modalities [ 24 ] .
Sparsh, T3, and UniT learn reusable contact features across tasks,
sensors, or objects [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] .
AnyTouch and AnyTouch 2 model static and dynamic tactile information
across sensors [ 28 , 29 ] , while Tactile
Beyond Pixels combines complementary touch
channels [ 30 ] . These advances support
contact perception and downstream manipulation. A reusable representation
must still be mapped to task-appropriate actions during closed-loop
execution. We study the control
role of contact feedback, using its history and current robot state
to predict and modulate local gripper increments from updated contact observations.

Reactive tactile and force-aware control. RDP and FoAR couple visual task execution with reactive contact
feedback [ 11 , 12 ] . TacDiffusion and FARM learn
force-aware actions [ 31 , 13 ] , while RETAF
decouples arm prediction and gripper force regulation [ 16 ] .
TouchGuide guides action sampling with a tactile model, while Policy
Consensus combines modality-specific experts through learned
routing [ 14 , 15 ] .
At the team level, CoRE routes collaboration-role experts within a shared
policy for decentralized multi-robot manipulation [ 32 ] .
ContactPolicy focuses on task-local gripper position updates: contact
history and execution state condition increments and demonstrated-action
modulation, with Intent managing control handover. Ablations assess
execution context for local regulation within the ongoing visual task execution.
Each update responds to the evolving contact.

2026-10-20.title: Tension Tells the Tail: Cable-Obstacle Interaction Sensing for Tethered Mobile Robot Navigation
2026-10-20.authors: Ryuki Shimada , Koki Suzuki , Genya Ishigami
2026-10-20.comment: . Accepted to 2026 IEEE International Symposium on Safety, Security, and Rescue Robotics (SSRR)
2026-10-20.abstract: Tethered mobile robots can sustain long-duration operation through continuous power supply and stable communication via their cables. However, cable–environment interaction causes unintended obstacle displacement, cable snagging or entanglement, and even cable damage, leading to mission failure. To assess the risk of individual cable–obstacle contacts, this study investigates cable tension as a sensing modality for estimating whether a contacted obstacle is movable or non-movable. We conducted experiments with a tethered mobile robot and collected tension data while varying robot velocity, contact angle between the obstacle and cable, obstacle mass, and obstacle side-surface material. The results show that obstacle movability is characterized by the initial tension rise and, more importantly, by whether the tension relaxes or remains high after its peak. Based on these observations, we select six features from the tension profiles and train a logistic-regression classifier using 117 labeled trials. The proposed method distinguishes movable and non-movable cases with a balanced accuracy of 95.5% after 30 cm of post-contact travel. These results demonstrate the potential of cable tension for risk assessment of cable–obstacle interactions and provide a step toward online, cable-aware autonomous navigation.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Tethered mobile robots are essential platforms for extended operation in hazardous environments. By maintaining a physical connection to a remote base station via cable, the robots receive a continuous power supply and stable communication in environments where wireless transmission is unreliable or impossible, for example, in post-disaster nuclear buildings [ 1 ] and subterranean spaces [ 2 ] . The cable itself also serves as a physical lifeline, preventing the robot from falling off steep terrain and providing emergency recovery through cable retrieval. These advantages enable tethered robots to operate safely in diverse and challenging field environments.

However, when a tethered robot navigates in confined or unstructured environments, its cable inevitably comes into contact with obstacles (Fig. 1 ), and these interactions can threaten mission completion. Such contacts may cause unintended environmental changes, cable entanglement, cable damage, and ultimately robot immobilization. A notable example occurred during the post-accident investigation of the interior of the Fukushima nuclear power plant in 2011, when the communication cable of the tethered robot Quince 1 became snagged on piping, leading to cable damage and irreversible robot loss [ 3 ] . As this case exemplifies, cable–obstacle contact can, in the worst case, render the robot completely disabled and unable to complete its mission.

To address this problem, one research direction has focused on path and motion planning methods that tackle the problem of reduced moving area caused by cable–obstacle interactions under finite cable length. Following the first work on path planning under limited cable length [ 4 ] , subsequent research [ 5 ] introduced the mathematical concept of homotopy—which distinguishes paths by whether they traverse the left or right of each obstacle—and formalized it mathematically [ 6 ] . They have been extended to coverage planning [ 7 ] , online exploration [ 8 ] , and motion planning for steep terrain [ 9 ] . These approaches, however, share two limitations: they assume obstacles are immovable, and they are indifferent to cable–obstacle contact. More recent work has explicitly addressed cable–obstacle contact avoidance [ 10 , 11 ] ; however, these approaches remain conservative, i.e., avoiding all cable–obstacle interactions. They lack assessment of individual obstacles to determine which contacts are actually dangerous and should be definitely avoided.

In parallel, another research direction has focused on the active exploitation of cable–obstacle interactions to extend robot capabilities. A tethered robotic system called TReX [ 12 ] can wrap the cable around natural or artificial objects, enabling traversal of near-vertical slopes. This system also realizes cable-aware SLAM [ 13 ] by recording contact positions between the cable and pole-like obstacles. Additional work [ 14 ] has leveraged the Capstan effect, in which wrapping a cable around an object exponentially amplifies holding force, as illustrated in Fig. 2 . When a large robot equipped with a cable drum becomes immobilized, a small robot at the cable end can wrap the cable around a nearby object such as a tree. The resulting Capstan effect amplifies the holding force, allowing the large robot to achieve self-recovery by reeling the cable. While these approaches successfully extend robot mobility and manipulation capabilities, they lack evaluation to determine which obstacles the robot should contact or wrap the cable around.

In this work, we investigate the use of cable tension as a sensing modality for estimating obstacle movability in tethered mobile robot systems. This tension-based sensing approach is particularly valuable in low-visibility environments, where obstacles may be hidden by smoke, darkness, or other objects, because it enables obstacle movability estimation from tension signals alone. We acquire tension data through controlled experiments and develop a machine learning-based classifier that determines whether contacted obstacles are movable or non-movable by analyzing time- and frequency-domain characteristics of the tension signals.

This foundational method addresses a critical gap common to both avoidance and exploitation of cable–obstacle interactions, thereby supporting the real-world deployments of these strategies. Specifically, we contribute:

An experimental characterization of cable–obstacle interaction behaviors that identifies the dominant cable–obstacle interaction behaviors and analyzes the influence of robot velocity, contact geometry, and obstacle surface properties on the resulting tension signals.

An experimental characterization of cable–obstacle interaction behaviors that identifies the dominant cable–obstacle interaction behaviors and analyzes the influence of robot velocity, contact geometry, and obstacle surface properties on the resulting tension signals.

A tension-based obstacle movability estimation method that classifies movable and non-movable interaction behaviors from tension features within 0.30 m after contact.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Problem Statement

In this paper, we define the problem as estimating obstacle movability from tension signals measured during cable–obstacle contact (Fig. 1 ). When the cable makes contact with an obstacle, the force sensor mounted at the rear of the robot records the resulting tension profile. This response depends on obstacle properties (mass, shape, ground contact friction, side-surface friction) and interaction parameters (robot velocity, contact geometry). We argue that the robot can distinguish whether the obstacle is displaced or remains in place based on tension signatures measured within a short moving distance after contact.

Here we define two categories of obstacles according to how they behave during cable–obstacle interaction:

Movable obstacle: An obstacle whose position changes as a result of cable–obstacle interaction.

Non-movable obstacle: An obstacle whose position does not change as a result of cable–obstacle interaction. This category also includes obstacles that only rotate in place during cable contact. As a first step toward assessing cable–obstacle interactions, we focus on changes in obstacle position; other effects such as cable snagging are discussed in Section V-E .

The input and output of the system are defined as follows:

Input: Tension signal after contact detection, over a time window scaled to robot velocity.

Output: Binary class (movable or non-movable) with a predicted probability.

Controlled robot motion: During each interaction, we command the robot to move straight at constant velocity.

Single-obstacle interaction: Each cable–obstacle interaction involves a single obstacle.
