2026-10-20.title: Rollbot 2: Agile Locomotion by a Single-Actuator Spherical Robot
2026-10-20.authors: Jingxian Wang* , Chen Yu* , Sam Kriegman , Michael Rubenstein
2026-10-20.abstract: Reducing actuator count simplifies robot hardware but also removes independent inputs for maneuvering. The original Rollbot steered by modulating a quasi-stable helical orbit, but moved slowly and relied on external motion capture. Rollbot 2 preserves the single-actuator design while its redesigned mass distribution enables near-straight rolling and more direct travel toward commanded paths and beacon targets. Onboard inertial and ultra-wideband sensing support learned steering, beacon seeking, and waypoint following through one motor-velocity command. Rollbot 2 autonomously approaches UWB beacons without motion capture and completes a 468 m manually commanded indoor route at 0.87 m/s. On the shared 4.8 m “N” waypoint benchmark, all 16 trials complete the path with a mean traversal time of 10.8 s and mean time-averaged deviation of 7 cm. Its fastest traversal takes 8.0 s, over 70 times faster than the original Rollbot’s 564 s run despite minor protocol differences. These results show how mechanical redesign, onboard sensing, and learning-based control improve the agility and autonomy of a single-actuator spherical robot.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Underactuated robots have fewer independent control inputs than mechanical degrees of freedom, offering potential savings in mass, volume, power, material, and hardware complexity [ 1 ] . These advantages have motivated extensive work on inverted pendulums [ 2 , 3 ] , robotic hands [ 4 , 5 ] , and underactuated fingers and wrists [ 6 , 7 ] . Extreme underactuation is challenging in mobile robots because planar maneuvering normally requires independent control of propulsion and steering. Single-actuator locomotion has nevertheless been demonstrated using one-way bearings [ 8 ] , passive wheels [ 9 ] , and carefully timed dynamic motion in jumping [ 8 ] , wheeled [ 9 ] , walking [ 10 , 11 ] , and flying robots [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . These examples show that reducing actuator count need not eliminate mobility, but shifts the burden of generating useful behavior to the mechanism, passive dynamics, and controller.

Spherical robots are a compelling platform for studying this tradeoff. Their shells protect the internal mechanisms and electronics, allow rolling without exposed wheels or legs, and are attractive for operation in environments where robustness is important. Conventional spherical robots use barycentric mechanisms, control-moment gyroscopes, or deformable shells to control their motion [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . These mechanisms generally use multiple actuators or multiple independently controlled internal degrees of freedom to generate propulsion and steering. Although models have considered rolling balls driven by internal point masses [ 21 ] , obtaining fast, controlled two-dimensional motion from one physical actuator remains difficult because the same input must propel the robot, regulate its rolling state, and redirect its trajectory.

The original Rollbot demonstrated controlled planar locomotion with a single internal motor [ 22 ] . It used a rotating pendulum and operated near a quasi-stable circular trajectory. Slowly accelerating and decelerating the pendulum varied trajectory curvature and guided the robot between waypoints. This proof-of-concept design established controllability but had limited speed and relied on OptiTrack for global position and orientation feedback. In work developed at about the same time, ROCK demonstrated reinforcement-learning-based steering of a one-degree-of-freedom internal-pendulum robot with an uneven shell [ 23 ] . Its nonspherical contact surface provides steering authority, and the robot operates in an OptiTrack motion-capture environment. These studies motivate fast locomotion with a spherical shell and onboard sensing.

This paper presents Rollbot 2 as a performance-oriented redesign of the original Rollbot. The goal is not only to demonstrate controllability with one actuator, but to bring the speed and maneuverability of a mechanically minimal robot closer to those of conventional spherical robots. First, we redesign the mass distribution so that approximately constant pendulum rotation produces continuous straight-line rolling instead of a quasi-stable helical trajectory. Transient modulation of the same motor command then generates responsive steering. Second, we integrate an inertial measurement unit (IMU) and ultra-wideband (UWB) ranging module for onboard motion estimation and target-relative navigation. Third, we use reinforcement learning to exploit dynamic motions that were deliberately suppressed by the original quasi-stable controller.

We study three complementary tasks: commanded rolling and steering, onboard beacon seeking, and waypoint following. Together, they examine how mechanical redesign, onboard sensing, and learning-based control extend the capabilities of a single-actuator spherical robot.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II System Overview

Rollbot 2 preserves the core single-actuator architecture [ 22 ] : an internal motor drives a pendulum-like mass to produce shell motion. The redesigned mass distribution favors continuous straight rolling, while transient motor-speed changes generate steering (Fig. 3 ).

The onboard system is also redesigned. Rollbot 2 integrates an IMU for local motion estimation and a UWB ranging module for distance measurements to external beacons. Commanded steering and beacon seeking use these sensors without OptiTrack feedback, while the waypoint benchmark retains external localization. The IMU and UWB range history allow the robot to estimate relative beacon position and approach the beacon using onboard computation and sensing.

The control architecture combines a learned policy with the motor’s native velocity controller. At 50 Hz, the policy maps a short observation history and a task specification to one motor target velocity. The firmware clips this output to ± 20 \pm 20\, rad/s at the geared output and sends velocity commands to the motor controller at 200 Hz. Separate policies share this interface for commanded steering, beacon seeking, and waypoint following. The policies exploit transient and oscillatory motions that were intentionally excluded from the original Rollbot’s quasi-stable controller.

2026-10-20.title: Switch-Time-Aware Hybrid Model Predictive Control Using the Hybrid Minimum Principle
2026-10-20.authors: Valentin Gaucher , Wenlong Zhang
2026-10-20.abstract: This article presents a time-aware hybrid model predictive control (MPC) framework that simultaneously optimizes the objective with respect to both continuous control inputs and event switching times. Rather than relying on a fixed time grid, the switching instant is lifted into the decision vector and treated as an explicit optimization variable. The resulting transcription is a smooth nonlinear program whose Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions are consistent with the Hybrid Minimum Principle (HMP) event-time stationarity condition, so first-order hybrid sensitivities are recovered implicitly through the KKT system rather than by evaluating saltation matrices. Each MPC step solves a single sparse Quadratic Program (QP), jointly optimizing control inputs and impact timing in real time. On a bouncing mass landing on an oscillating platform, the method attaches in half the time of fixed-grid saltation MPC, reduces cumulative control effort by 30%, and removes the post-impact rebounds, at a 15% increase in per-cycle solve time. It matches the cumulative effort of offline time-aware solvers to within 4% while running at 2.4 ms per cycle against 281 ms for a complementarity-based formulation of the same problem, of which a 10.6 × \times reduction is attributable to the transcription alone at a fixed solver.
2026-10-20.introduction:
In this paper, we address Model Predictive Control (MPC) for hybrid systems subject to state-dependent, instantaneous resets within the prediction horizon. In these systems, the event time is a critical decision variable coupled with the continuous states and inputs [ 1 ] . A primary challenge in real-time execution is handling state-dependent resets. Standard fixed-step Jacobians neglect the sensitivity of the state trajectory to the exact switching time, yielding suboptimal mode-switching decisions [ 2 , 3 ] . The proposed approach in this paper converts the implicit dependence of switching time on the state trajectory into an explicit optimization variable, allowing standard nonlinear programming (NLP) solvers to handle hybrid sensitivity information without differentiating through discontinuities.

While rigorous frameworks address this complexity, they are often computationally demanding for real-time applications. Mixed-Integer QP (MIQP) [ 4 , 5 ] uses binary variables to optimize timings, Mathematical Programs with Complementarity Constraints (MPCC) [ 6 ] optimize across transitions, and move finite-element meshes [ 7 ] precisely align switching surfaces. Despite robust embedded solvers for these formulations [ 5 ] , they rely on combinatorial searches or large-scale formulations that can be prohibitive in real time, while standard real-time MPC instead fixes the switching time or ignores first-order timing sensitivities. This gap calls for a formulation that achieves the timing precision of MPCC or variable-step methods while preserving the speed of fixed-step Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) solvers.

Related Work. The theoretical conditions for optimality in hybrid systems are well-established. Sussmann [ 8 ] and Caines [ 9 ] extended the Pontryagin Maximum Principle to hybrid systems, deriving conditions that optimize both continuous controls and discrete switching times. Dmitruk and Kaganovich [ 10 ] unified these under the Hybrid Minimum Principle (HMP). While mathematically powerful, the HMP is traditionally a continuous-time, open-loop theory. Enforcing these optimal conditions inside a discrete-time, receding-horizon feedback loop remains challenging.

Numerical transcriptions bridge the gap between continuous theory and discrete solvers. Ross and Fahroo [ 11 ] demonstrated that for smooth systems, KKT stationarity conditions and their multipliers in pseudospectral methods converge to Pontryagin costates. Indirect methods, such as the recent work by Hu et al. [ 12 ] , solve HMP conditions directly via successive approximation, but are designed for open-loop trajectory generation rather than closed-loop control.

To incorporate switching effects into gradient-based controllers, one must differentiate through the discrete transition. This is achieved via the saltation matrix, which corrects the sensitivity analysis across a transversal guard. Formalized by Aizerman et al. [ 13 ] and further developed in foundational works [ 14 , 15 ] , Kong et al. [ 2 ] recently showed the practical utility of these matrices for robotics. However, standard discrete-time implementations typically treat the switching time as a passive consequence of the forward rollout, rather than an active decision variable.

Contributions. This paper presents HMP-MPC, a framework that incorporates Hybrid Minimum Principle (HMP) consistency within an SQP-based Real-Time Iteration (RTI) scheme. The idea is lifting the switching instant as an explicit decision variable, transforming the nonsmooth dependence of the dynamics on event timing into a smooth NLP with algebraic constraints. This enables standard gradient-based solvers to optimize impact timing directly. The contributions are: (i) Lifting the switching time as an intra-step decision variable, localizing temporal adjustments to each event interval while preserving the 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ) \mathcal{O}(N) sparse block-tridiagonal structure. (ii) A smooth NLP transcription of hybrid transitions using algebraic equality constraints, yielding a C 1 C^{1} representation suitable for SQP-based optimization. (iii) Implicit recovery of first-order hybrid sensitivities through the KKT system, yielding conditions consistent with the HMP time-stationarity relation.

2026-10-20.title: CLARO: Clutter Aware Robot Orchestrator for Open-Vocabulary Grasping using VLM Agents
2026-10-20.authors: Sungsu Kim , Vineet Bhat , Prashanth Krishnamurthy , Ramesh Karri , Farshad Khorrami
2026-10-20.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-20.abstract:
Robots that follow natural-language instructions unlock a wide range of
autonomous applications in households, warehouses, and labs. Real-world
environments are diverse and often heavily cluttered, requiring robots to plan over multiple steps, act, and replan as they work toward a goal.
We present CLARO ( CL utter- A ware R obot O rchestrator), a VLM agent that orchestrates a set of perception and
manipulation skills: open-vocabulary object detection, segmentation, 6 6 -DoF grasping,
and non-prehensile pushing to locate and retrieve a language-specified target in clutter. CLARO maintains a memory of its past actions to support long-horizon execution, and emits manipulation
targets (grasp poses/3D waypoints) allowing transfer across robot arms without task-specific training. We evaluate CLARO against a range of methods
on a dynamic simulation environment and standard image-based benchmarks, demonstrating
strong generalization across object classes, lighting, and clutter levels. CLARO attains an average success rate of 89.1 % 89.1\% , a relative
improvement of over 16 % 16\% on the strongest competing method in high cluttered scenes. We further analyze performance along grounding and grasping axes to
characterize where each method succeeds and fails. Finally, we deploy CLARO on a
robot arm across diverse cluttered scenes, achieving a success rate of 88.8 % 88.8\% , and demonstrating strong sim2real generalizability.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Grasping objects specified by natural-language is a
long-standing goal of robotics and embodied AI [ 8 ] .
An instruction like “hand me the small screwdriver behind the mug” requires
grounding an open-vocabulary referred object and reasoning about its spatial
position in the scene. Vision Language Models (VLMs) have brought this
goal within reach: by jointly reasoning over images and language, they form a
perception backbone that grounds free-form text instructions to the robot’s visual
observations [ 7 , 28 ] . VLMs have been adapted for Language-Driven Robot Manipulation (LDRM) in tasks such as pick-and-place and articulated-object
manipulation [ 2 , 22 ] .

Recent works use two frameworks for LDRM. Referring Grasp Synthesis (RGS) methods finetune VLMs to predict grasp poses
directly from an image and a task
instruction, which are then executed by a controller [ 29 , 2 , 23 ] . These methods are trained on large datasets comprising static RGB-D scenes in which the target is assumed to be visible and graspable from the camera view. This assumption breaks down in dynamic environments when objects are occluded and the robot must intelligently search through multiple manipulation steps. The second framework uses end-to-end Vision Language Action
(VLA) models that learn a mapping from pixels and language to motor actions, and are deployed closed-loop in both simulation and real
hardware [ 22 , 14 , 9 ] . VLAs enable fine-grained robot control and adaptability to a wide range of embodiments but are often evaluated in-distribution: on objects, scenes, and instructions close to the training data. VLAs report poor performance on unseen and open-vocabulary objects, making them unsuitable for deployment in novel environments [ 1 , 32 ] .
Neither framework suffices: RGS cannot search through clutter, and VLAs do not
generalize beyond their training distribution, yet retrieving a target in
practice requires both. Real environments such as homes, labs, and warehouses
are noisy and cluttered, with targets frequently occluded, so a robust system
must actively declutter the scene through a multi-step, closed-loop process of
planning, grounding, and execution, all while remaining open-vocabulary and
deployable without retraining.

Grounding novel objects and decluttering over multiple steps requires a
system that perceives, plans, and acts in a closed loop. Tool-calling VLM agents, which show strong spatial reasoning beyond conventional
VLMs, are naturally suited to this:
rather than learning a monolithic policy, they invoke skills, observe outcomes, and re-plan [ 5 , 26 ] .
A VLM agent in robotics can use a set of skill APIs within a closed loop safety-bounded rulebook, to invoke perception and manipulation functions, observe the environment, and re-plan [ 11 ] . Such methods are suitable for clutter manipulation precisely because robot environments are dynamic, the
scene changes after every action, demanding iterative grounding, occlusion reasoning, and re-planning ( Fig. 1 ).

We present CLARO ( CL utter- A ware R obot O rchestrator), a VLM agent that turns a set of perception and
manipulation skills into a general-purpose, open-vocabulary object
grasper. Given a cluttered workspace and a language-specified target, CLARO generates planning traces, reasons about occlusions, and executes motion that actively declutters the scene while searching for the target. Once
the object is sufficiently exposed, it executes a feasible grasp to retrieve it. CLARO requires no environment-specific finetuning and is the only system to combine open-vocabulary grounding, closed-loop planning, long-term memory, 6 6 -DoF grasping, and non-prehensile decluttering ( Tab. 1 ).

The main contributions of this work are:

We develop CLARO ( Fig. 2 ), a VLM agent that plans, declutters, and grasps open-vocabulary objects in tightly cluttered
workspaces using a robotic arm, and transfers across robot arms and environments without
retraining.

We benchmark CLARO against open-vocabulary and trained VLM baselines, across a simulation environment spanning diverse objects, lighting conditions, occlusion levels, and standard image-based RGS benchmarks. CLARO consistently outperforms all methods, with a relative improvement of 16 % 16\% in high-clutter success rate over the strongest baseline.

We deploy CLARO on a robotic arm across 80 trials covering 40 objects in two clutter levels, achieving an average success rate of 88.8%.

# 2 Related Work

These methods leverage the joint vision-language embedding space of VLMs to predict a grasp pose directly from an RGB-D image and referring instruction by training on largescale RGB-D object pose and grasping datasets.
CROG used CLIP encoders and a lightweight decoder to train on the OCID-VLG dataset for 4 4 -DoF grasp pose estimation [ 30 ] .
MapleGrasp introduced mask-guided feature pooling to focus grasp prediction on the referred region while contributing the RefGraspNet 6 6 -DoF grasping dataset [ 2 ] . UnoGrasp finetuned a VLM for multi-step obstruction reasoning over cluttered scenes through an occlusion pointing task [ 13 ] . Some methods incorporate chain-of-thought reasoning or attribute and spatial grounding to predict grasps from flexible language instructions [ 34 , 6 , 33 ] . While trained RGS models report strong
results on in-domain objects, their performance degrades on out-of-domain objects as models finetuned on a fixed closed-vocabulary datasets lose priors about the open-world objects [ 2 ] . RGS models are evaluated on static images (where the target is assumed visible and graspable in the scene) rather than in dynamic environments.

VLAs map RGB observations and language to motor actions, trained
on large-scale simulation and tele-operation corpora to provide fine-grained,
closed-loop control [ 15 , 22 ] . They excel at contact-rich, articulated and pick-and-place tasks [ 9 ] , but are typically evaluated
in-distribution (objects, scenes, and task variations close to their
training data) and in low-clutter settings [ 1 ] . Current VLAs struggle with limited generalization to
unseen tasks [ 32 ] making them unsuitable for the open-vocabulary grasping problem studied in this paper.

These methods target the limitations of the previous two by pairing a strong open-vocabulary perception module (usually untrained to avoid dataset-specific bias) that grounds the language in 2D bounding boxes or masks with a separate extensively trained grasping module able to handle diverse
geometries. OWG combines a VLM with
segmentation and grasp synthesis, grounding the target via visual prompting and
ranking candidate grasps, while removing obstacles when the target is
blocked [ 29 ] . ThinkGrasp prompts a VLM to identify the
goal object or the next object likely to reveal it and to suggest grasp locations, which it executes with a segmentation and grasping
network [ 23 ] . GraspMAS uses compositional python program
synthesis, generating executable code that chains vision tools to ground the
referring expression followed by grasping [ 20 ] . RoboDexVLM [ 17 ] plans a sequence of atomic skills with a VLM, verifies each
execution through depth and fingertip feedback, and re-invokes the planner,
conditioned on earlier episodes, when a skill fails; it
executes with a dexterous hand, and always acts on the target rather than
clearing occluders first. We adapt it to our parallel-jaw setting for comparison
(Supp. Sec. 3.1). Other methods add occlusion-aware 3D
detection with active viewpoint planning [ 25 ] or retrieve past episodes
to guide planning [ 16 ] . CLARO falls in this family: it is a
training-free, closed-loop VLM agent, that incorporates
long-horizon memory and non-prehensile push primitive allowing the robot to
operate in cluttered scenes to find and grasp the target object.

Concurrent work extends the agentic framework beyond grasping, such as articulated-object manipulation that requires a broader skill
vocabulary. VoLo [ 4 ] treats a VLA model as an interruptible tool,
monitoring its rollout and halting or redirecting it when a subgoal stalls, while
Maestro [ 24 ] composes perception, geometry, and control modules by
writing and revising executable code, repositioning a wrist camera to obtain the
views needed. In both, the target is always visible and reachable. VLMgineer [ 12 ] applies
the same priors offline, placing the model inside an evolutionary search that
co-designs an end-effector and the open-loop trajectory wielding it; its tools are
hardware synthesised for a target action rather than modules invoked over a long
horizon. Articulated manipulation is outside the scope of this work, but the toolshed is the natural place to
extend it: skills such as rotate_handle or grasp_and_pull would be exposed to CLARO exactly as grasp and push are,
leaving the memory and replanning loop unchanged.

2026-10-20.title: ChairNav: Cross-Embodiment Pre-training and Personalization for Long-Horizon Wheelchair Navigation
2026-10-20.authors: Junhua Huang , Zhizheng Liu , Honglin He , Xiang Zhang , Bolei Zhou
2026-10-20.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-20.abstract:
Developing autonomous electric wheelchairs capable of long-horizon sidewalk navigation is critical for accessible personal mobility, yet existing approaches either focus on indoor map-based navigation or rely on expensive, complex sensor stacks to achieve full autonomy.
In this work, we propose to tackle outdoor sidewalk navigation by leveraging visual navigation foundation models and large-scale navigation datasets, which offer strong generalization using lightweight hardware.
To this end, we present ChairNav, a novel framework that adapts a general visual navigation model into a personalized electric wheelchair navigation system using a three-stage data pyramid.
To address the scarcity of in-domain data, ChairNav first pre-trains on large-scale cross-embodiment datasets transformed into the wheelchair domain, followed by mid-training on a small number of wheelchair demonstrations to eliminate remaining domain gaps. Finally, a post-training stage refines the deployed model from user interventions to personalize its behavior.
We deploy ChairNav on a commercial electric wheelchair equipped with an RGB-D camera and an onboard NVIDIA Jetson compute module. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of each stage in our data pyramid: pre-training reduces lateral ADE by 18 % 18\% , and post-training increases the mean distance between user interventions from 29.2 ​ m 29.2\text{ m} to 57.4 ​ m 57.4\text{ m} . Further evaluation on kilometer-scale urban sidewalk routes shows that our system operates autonomously for 93.4 % 93.4\% of total driving time, demonstrating its potential for everyday accessible mobility. Demo video and more details are at https://vail.cs.ucla.edu/ChairNav/ .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Electric wheelchairs (EWs) provide essential mobility assistance to individuals with physical impairments. Safely operating an EW requires constant human attention and maneuvering skills for tasks such as obstacle avoidance and reactive navigation on cluttered sidewalks, posing significant challenges for users with visual, motor, or cognitive impairments. Therefore, developing autonomous EW systems that navigate challenging sidewalk conditions and reduce the burden of manual control is critical to accessible mobility.

Extensive research on autonomous EWs has focused on shared-control systems that mitigate safety risks while providing driving assistance [ 1 , 2 ] . However, these systems still require active, continuous control inputs from the user.
Although a few studies [ 3 , 4 ] have tackled autonomous EW driving, they predominantly rely on traditional modular pipelines equipped with laborious and expensive sensor stacks, which often suffer from integration complexity and error accumulation across modules.
Conversely, recent advances in end-to-end visual navigation foundation models [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] and large-scale visual navigation datasets [ 7 , 9 ] offer a promising alternative with a lightweight sensor stack and strong generalization ability. Nevertheless, directly deploying these models on EWs or fine-tuning them with existing datasets yields suboptimal performance due to significant gaps in sensor placement, platform dynamics, and physical constraints.
Meanwhile, collecting EW demonstrations for imitation learning (IL) is also prohibitively expensive, posing challenges to training the EW navigation model.

Furthermore, since EWs are personal mobility devices, their autonomous operation must align with individual users’ preferences, such as maintaining a specific distance from the sidewalk curbs, adjusting comfortable driving speeds, or navigating a neighborhood that differs significantly from the data used to train the models. Yet current paradigms rely on fixed models after deployment, failing to continuously adapt to user feedback and improve the user experience during real-world operation.

In this work, we present ChairNav, a novel learning framework that adapts visual navigation foundation models for autonomous EW navigation. To bridge the domain gap of existing models and datasets, we introduce a data transformation technique that aligns cross-embodiment observations and dynamics with the target EW domain via viewpoint reprojection and trajectory re-fitting. This enables us to leverage existing large-scale visual navigation datasets to effectively train visual navigation foundation models. In addition, to accommodate individual driving styles, we develop an efficient preference learning strategy that handles delays in user takeovers and refines the model through deployment-time user feedback.
Consequently, our framework forms a data pyramid to train the models from three complementary stages:
1) Pre-training on 170 hours of transformed cross-embodiment data, 2) Mid-training on 3.19 hours of high-quality wheelchair demonstrations to bridge the embodiment gap, and 3) Post-training using 0.48 hours of human preference feedback to align the user’s habits and expectations.

Our system is built upon a commercial EW with an RGB-D camera to provide observations and an NVIDIA Jetson computer with a CAN-bus interposer that lets the low-level control system receive control commands from both the model and the user for preference learning (Fig. ). Extensive experiments demonstrate that the pre-training stage is crucial for achieving robust navigation: compared to fine-tuning the base model with only the wheelchair demonstrations, it reduces lateral ADE from 0.082 m to 0.067 m. Concurrently, the post-training stage continuously aligns the system with user preference, increasing the average distance between user interventions from 29.2 m to 57.4 m.
In addition, indoor evaluations of autonomous EWs are short-horizon, with reported routes typically under 50 m [ 10 ] .
Instead, we evaluate on kilometer-scale drives on real-world urban sidewalks, and the results show that our final system operates autonomously for 93.4% of the total driving time in urban public spaces, underscoring its strong potential to improve the user’s everyday mobility.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:
1) ChairNav, a data-pyramid learning framework that adapts visual navigation foundation models for autonomous long-horizon sidewalk navigation.
2) A data transformation method that aligns cross-embodiment data with the target EW domain to address the lack of in-domain data. Compared to fine-tuning the base model on only the wheelchair data, the transformed data reduces lateral ADE by 18%.
3) An efficient preference learning method for post-training the model during real-world deployment. Post-training on only 0.48 h of user takeovers raises the distance between interventions by 97%.

# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Autonomous wheelchair navigation

Prior work on autonomous wheelchairs has predominantly adopted shared-control paradigms that keep the user in the loop [ 11 , 12 ] , either by filtering continuous joystick commands [ 13 ] or predicting user intent and intervening when necessary [ 2 ] . Systems that achieve autonomous and kilometer-scale navigation typically rely on modular pipelines and environment-specific information prepared in advance, such as large-scale landmark maps for over 12 12 km of outdoor navigation [ 3 ] , prior 3D maps for 8.8 8.8 km of Tokyo sidewalks [ 14 ] , GPS/RTK-GNSS waypoints for routes of about 1 km [ 15 , 16 ] , or routes obtained from commercial map services [ 4 ] . Other evaluations are largely restricted to short or controlled settings, including doorway traversal [ 10 ] , a 100 100 m hospital route [ 17 ] , imitation-learned person following [ 18 ] , and approximately 100 100 m of visual servoing along tactile paving [ 19 ] ; indeed, a survey of 132 132 robotic wheelchairs found only five designed for both indoor and outdoor operation [ 12 ] . In contrast, our approach learns an end-to-end visual wheelchair navigation model that requires neither continuous user control nor a prior map, survey pass, or pre-specified waypoint route, and we evaluate it over 1.61 1.61 km of public urban sidewalks using only a forward-facing camera, with closed-loop results reported in Table III .

## II-B Visual navigation foundation models and datasets

Recent work learns generalizable visual navigation foundation models from large-scale heterogeneous data spanning robots, environments, and embodiments. GNM combines eight datasets from six robot platforms [ 5 ] , ViNT scales this paradigm to hundreds of hours of navigation experience [ 6 ] , and NoMaD unifies goal-directed navigation and exploration within a diffusion policy [ 20 ] . Navigation data have been collected through teleoperation [ 21 ] , autonomous robot operation [ 22 ] , and human-carried sensors [ 23 ] , while recent efforts further scale to 2,000 2{,}000 h of web-sourced walking videos [ 7 ] , crowdsourced teleoperation relabeled by a model-based expert [ 24 ] , and 4,565 4{,}565 h of teleoperation across 35 35 countries [ 9 ] . For sidewalk navigation, MIMIC [ 8 ] and FlowPilot [ 25 ] leverage teleoperated robot fleets, while recent models have demonstrated up to 125 125 km of map-free navigation [ 9 ] and further improvement through reinforcement-learning post-training [ 26 , 27 ] .
Instead, our work focuses on adapting these models to autonomous wheelchairs, which present a substantial domain gap and limited in-domain data. Additionally, we aim to align the model with individual user preferences to enable effective personalization.

2026-10-20.title: Weakly Supervised Discovery of Motion Styles for Compositional Robot Control
2026-10-20.authors: Heedo Woo , Antonio Marino , Eduardo Sebastián , Amanda Prorok
2026-10-20.abstract:
When a robot possesses more degrees of freedom than a task requires, multiple trajectories can achieve the same objective using distinct motion styles. Compositional robot control aims to preserve a selected style while simultaneously executing an independent task command, effectively balancing these potentially competing objectives.
In this paper, we present CODES, a framework for compositional robot control that discovers a coherent style repertoire from diverse recordings and composes it with independent commands. First, motion retargeting maps the recordings to motions executable by the target robot; next, weakly supervised consensus encoding and density-based clustering identify styles within and across recordings without a prescribed count; finally, reinforcement learning trains a policy to compose the discovered styles with independent commands.
We evaluate CODES on a Unitree Go2 quadruped across two simulators and physical hardware. Compared to baselines, CODES significantly improves kinematic coherence. Furthermore, our controller successfully tracks velocity commands that generalize beyond the support of the recorded data, exhibiting robust and distinguishable style characteristics during both cross-simulator and real-world hardware deployments.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Robot motion control is commonly formulated in terms of task objectives, such as target velocities, poses, or trajectories. However, a given objective typically admits many executions that differ in motion characteristics, including posture, contact patterns, and coordination. These characteristics, referred to here as motion styles , influence aspects such as clearance, interaction with the environment, and predictability [ 1 , 2 ] . This freedom is particularly relevant when a robotic system has more degrees of freedom than those that the task constrains. The task command alone does not select these characteristics. A compositional robot controller therefore accepts a style reference and a task command as independently selectable inputs, so that the requested execution can change without changing the task objective.

To compose motion styles and task commands, some representation of the styles is needed. Motion style characteristics can be specified explicitly through coupled oscillators, such as in AllGaits [ 2 ] , or parameterized via posture commands, such as in Walk These Ways [ 1 ] , allowing selection within predefined families of styles. As an alternative to manual parameterizations, motion recordings offer more flexibility for learning motion structure [ 3 , 4 ] , but entangle embodiments, regimes, and constraints. In computational ethology, B-SOiD [ 5 ] , VAME [ 6 ] , and Keypoint-MoSeq [ 7 ] identify recurring patterns from pose sequences without predefined taxonomies. A single recording may contain several styles, and similar styles may recur across recordings. Segmentation alone does not identify the characteristics that should persist as task commands change.

On the control side, reference-based reinforcement learning uses demonstrations through explicit tracking (DeepMimic [ 8 ] ) or learned adversarial motion rewards (AMP [ 9 ] ). Multi-behavior controllers select among motions using separate adversarial motion priors (Multi-AMP [ 10 ] ), continuous embeddings [ 11 , 12 ] , or discrete codes [ 13 , 14 ] . Coarse annotations can nevertheless group distinct execution patterns under one label; diverse execution therefore does not ensure a distinguishable, coherent style representation.

Consequently, neither raw recording boundaries nor existing annotations alone define an adequate repertoire. For successful compositional control, styles extracted from data must be coherent and independently selectable from task commands. This separation parallels Walk Like Dogs [ 15 ] , which pairs locomotion modes independently with steering commands. Kinematic coherence requires windows in the same style group to share motion characteristics (e.g., posture, joint-velocity patterns, and periodicity), with windows from different groups remaining distinguishable. The controller must exhibit both command and style fidelity , following the task command while preserving the selected style’s motion characteristics.

These considerations motivate CODES (Composition Of Discovered Expressive Styles), which identifies motion styles from recordings and trains a policy to execute them under independently specified task commands (Sec. II ). Recordings are first expressed on the target robot, providing executable motion examples from which candidate styles are identified by a weakly supervised discovery method; these styles are then exposed to the policy as a separate control input (Sec. III ). We evaluate the framework in a quadruped case study on the Unitree Go2 (Sec. IV ). Ablations and comparisons with alternative decomposition methods show a compact repertoire with higher kinematic coherence than the no-coarse-guidance and VQ-VAE baselines (Sec. V ). We further assess the robot motion controller in two simulators and real hardware deployments, showing that the resulting policy achieves command and style fidelity across a broad range of motions.

2026-10-20.title: REAP: Learning General Rearrangement Heuristics from Motion-Planner Feedback
2026-10-20.authors: Daniel Swoboda , Hector Geffner
2026-10-20.abstract:
Robotic rearrangement tasks require planning sequences of actions that
fulfill high-level specifications while also being geometrically feasible.
Symbolic abstractions make the combinatorial structure of rearrangement
tasks tractable, but they usually do not fully capture the geometric
constraints that determine which actions a robot can actually realize.
These constraints are hard to express in the symbolic model.
We propose REAP (Rearrangement with Elicited Action Preconditions), a framework in which a
relational graph neural network heuristic is learned over a simple
symbolic abstraction. A motion planner serves as a supervisor that elicits
the hidden geometric preconditions of the problem during training.
Deployed with greedy best-first search, the learned heuristic generalizes
out-of-distribution along object count, plan length, and object arrangement, and can be trained jointly on several domains.
Compared to classical heuristic search and learning-based baselines, REAP solves
more problems, requires roughly an order of magnitude fewer motion-planner queries
than comparable methods, and the action it ranks first is geometrically feasible in 94% of
sampled states, against 22% for a random choice.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Robots performing tasks in cluttered environments like clearing a table,
retrieving an occluded target, or constructing an object from parts must
select what to do symbolically and how to realize each step
as a collision-free motion. These tasks are examples of combined
task and motion planning (TAMP) [ 1 , 2 ] ,
where a symbolic plan reaching the given goal is sought and every action
of that plan must be geometrically feasible. The simplest approach
incrementally searches for plans while checking the feasibility of each
candidate with a motion planner. This, however, is too inefficient as
the geometric constraints play only a passive role in the
search [ 3 , 4 ] . Other
approaches make the geometric constraints explicit in the planning
formulation, but modeling such constraints and solving the resulting
joint problem is similarly
hard [ 5 , 6 ] . A third line of work
aims to amend the heuristics used to guide the
search to take into account both the goals and the geometric
constraints. The resulting search is more informed, and the challenge
is the formulation and computation of such hybrid
heuristics [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .

In this work, we propose a novel approach for addressing robot rearrangement tasks
based on heuristic estimators leveraging recent progress on generalized planning,
where policies are learned for solving large collections of classical planning problems [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
Some of these methods learn these policies in terms of parametric value functions Q θ ​ ( s , a ) Q_{\theta}(s,a) represented in relational graph neural networks (R-GNN) and trained without supervision using reinforcement learning [ 15 , 16 ] . As in goal-conditioned RL [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] ,
the atoms in s s represent both the current state and the goal of the instance.

Generalized symbolic planning policies are particularly relevant in this setting in two ways.
On the one hand, a single policy generalizes across instances varying in object count, initial
state, and goal by acting greedily on the learned Q Q -value function.
On the other, the policy can be learned model-free : it does not need to know the action
preconditions and effects a priori.
The training loop only requires a simulator that, for each state s s , exposes the applicable
action set A ⁡ ( s ) A(s) , the successor s ′ = f ⁡ ( a , s ) s^{\prime}=f(a,s) , an action cost c ⁡ ( a , s ) c(a,s) , and a goal check. 1 1 1 Even a
uniform-random policy needs these signals: knowing which actions are applicable, advancing the state, and detecting the goal is the minimum any policy needs to act. What distinguishes TAMP from classical planning, given a suitable symbolic abstraction,
is that not every symbolically applicable action is geometrically executable .
Alongside A ⁡ ( s ) A(s) there is a hidden function X ⁡ ( s ) ⊆ A ⁡ ( s ) X(s)\subseteq A(s) encoding the set of feasible actions, decidable by the motion planner provided s s encodes a suitable
abstraction of the geometry. We illustrate this in Figure 1 on one
of our rearrangement tasks where typically ∼ \sim 80% of the symbolically applicable actions are not
executable.
Making the symbolic policy aware of this hidden function is a minor modification to the
RL algorithm: selected actions a ∈ A ⁡ ( s ) a\in A(s) found not to be executable in s s , i.e., a ∈ A ⁡ ( s ) ∖ X ⁡ ( s ) a\in A(s)\setminus X(s) , are penalized in the state s s . The learned Q Q -values
then reflect both the number of steps to the goal and the feasibility of the actions.

In order to have a complete TAMP planner, REAP (Rearrangement with Elicited Action Preconditions) uses the learned Q Q -values not to push greedily for the goal, but to guide a
greedy best-first search [ 20 , 21 ] , over a coarse
abstraction of the geometry, that uses grid-based adjacency relations and occupancy.
The learned heuristic solves more problems than baselines, generalizes out-of-distribution
along object count, plan length, and arrangement, and requires an
order of magnitude fewer motion-planner queries at run time than classical
heuristic search and learning-based baselines. Removing the motion-planner feedback
collapses the framework to symbolic search, like our BrFS and h FF h_{\text{FF}} baselines, but guided by the learned Q θ ​ ( s , a ) Q_{\theta}(s,a) values. We
demonstrate this approach across five rearrangement environments with
distinct hidden-precondition structures, using the same architecture and training loop
across all of them.

We contribute REAP, a TAMP framework that (i) trains a generalized TAMP planning heuristic with
motion-planner verdicts as the RL signal, (ii) requires an order of magnitude
fewer motion-planner queries at deployment, (iii) scales without retraining to
OOD instances, and (iv) shows that the same approach applies across different robotic rearrangement
environments.

# 2 Related Work

Integrating planning, learning, and execution is a long-standing problem in robotics,
where a symbolic plan is only useful insofar as it grounds out in physically executable
motion. Prior work approaches this from several directions, which we group below.
Related work on generalized planning was discussed in the introduction.

Classical task-and-motion planning couples symbolic search with parameter
sampling and feasibility checks in an integrated search loop [ 3 , 1 , 2 ] .
Various works attempt to replace parts of this stack with learned components.
The closest to ours is Khodeir et al. [9] , a GNN heuristic guiding
search in a stream-based TAMP planner [ 1 ] .
They use offline learning from past execution traces to prioritize the sampling
of numerical parameters for the planners (modeled as streams).
Another predecessor of our work is Wells et al. [7] . They learn an SVM-based
binary feasibility classifier from offline trajectories with motion planner feedback, and use it
to prune candidate task plans before invoking the motion planner.
Other supervised approaches predict action feasibility from visual observations [ 8 ] ,
or use diffusion models as learned samplers for the continuous parameters of a TAMP solver [ 22 ] . Yang et al. [10] move from single-action feasibility classifiers to predicting feasibility for an
entire candidate plan skeleton. Curtis et al. [23] use
LLMs to generate continuous CSPs from the task description to constrain the search space.
Closest to REAP is Kim and Shimanuki [24] , who also learn a relational value function with a GNN to guide
a TAMP planner. Their approach (SAHS) differs in where geometric feasibility enters.
SAHS encodes it in the state representation, through crafted predicates defined over swept
volumes that require inverse kinematics and motion planning to evaluate. We
learn a heuristic to guide the planning directly, leaving feasibility out of the symbolic
representation entirely and learning to avoid infeasible actions during training.
Their target Q Q -values are derived from successful plans produced by an oracle planner and scale
with the number of remaining steps, so their training data contains no dead-ends and no
infeasible actions. REAP’s training data contains both. Silver et al. [25] (PLOI) rank object
importance from demonstrations in order to plan on a problem with a reduced number of objects, which is
efficient when few objects matter but degrades when most objects are genuine occluders. Cieślar et al. [26] predict the refinability of a given plan skeleton to guide
continuous parameter search. We assume no such skeleton, but instead learn a policy that
guides the planning. Furthermore, we are agnostic to the controller, assuming we only need
to select a high-level action, and not how to realize it. Chitnis et al. [27] learn symbolic operators from demonstrations
for both high-level planning and low-level sampling, whereas we learn action values
over pre-defined operators without direct access to low-level information.

REAP’s evaluations adapt environments from prior rearrangement
benchmarks: confined-shelf rearrangement [ 28 ] ,
multi-layer shelf retrieval [ 29 ] , and multi-level
stacking [ 30 ] . Adjacent work on non-prehensile
manipulation among movable obstacles [ 31 ] shares our
cluttered, geometrically constrained setting. REAP focuses on
prehensile actions.

SPOT [ 32 ] plans without symbolic discretization, running
A* directly over a sequence of transformations of point-cloud scenes. Shah et al. [33] learn
relational predicates and PDDL-style operators from unsegmented motion
demonstrations, then plan symbolically on instances with longer
horizons and far more objects than demonstrated.
Further afield, Dhakal et al. [34] learn to weight multiple
candidate plans, based on the incurred costs of future tasks in the same environment. Jung et al. [35] distill a motion-planning algorithm into a reactive
policy via imitation, eliminating search at deployment. End-to-end
visuomotor policies [ 36 ] produce motion trajectories directly
without an explicit planning step.

2026-10-20.title: ESCAPE: Egocentric Sensing for Collision Avoidance and Policy Execution
2026-10-20.authors: Weiqing Shen , Wenhao Huang , Baokang Zhang , Shuo Shang , Yanmiao Hu , Haojun Li , Yifan Han , Wenzhao Lian
2026-10-20.abstract: Motion planning in unstructured environments is a bottleneck for robot deployment. Current visuomotor policies predominantly rely on external cameras, introducing perceptual blind spots and fragility due to occlusions, clutter, and calibration constraints. To overcome these limitations, we propose ESCAPE, an online egocentric sensing framework for collision-free trajectory generation. ESCAPE aggregates sparse measurements from distributed depth sensors, converting them into a structured, obstacle-aware point cloud representation. Our policy leverages a flow matching-based generative framework, and trains on a high-quality dataset comprising over 100K safety-critical trajectories. With joint optimization of goal-reaching and collision objectives, it produces safe trajectories directly from these egocentric inputs. Crucially, ESCAPE is trained entirely in simulation and transfers zero-shot to physical hardware without any real-world fine-tuning. Extensive simulation and real-world evaluations demonstrate that ESCAPE achieves stable motion planning using only egocentric perception, outperforming external-view and voxelized-planning baselines across both simulation and real-world evaluations. Our website: escape-policy.github.io/ .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Autonomous systems operating in the wild, such as self-driving vehicles, rely fundamentally on onboard, egocentric perception to navigate in complex environments. By coupling the perceptual frames directly to the agent’s motion, these systems maintain situational awareness independent of pre-installed external infrastructure.
In contrast, many robot motion-generation systems still rely on third-person cameras or globally reconstructed point clouds, which can be fragile in cluttered manipulation settings due to self-occlusion, scene occlusion, camera displacement, and careful placement or calibration requirements.

To bypass these limitations, modern paradigms have shifted away from classical motion planning methods [ 18 , 8 , 10 , 25 ] – which generate reliable trajectories but require accurate environment geometric models –
and moved towards learning based motion policies. These learning-based policies distill expert planning experience into perception-conditioned action generation.
Recent end-to-end motion planning methods have widely adopted point clouds to improve geometric generalization in cluttered environments [ 5 , 6 , 2 , 31 ] .
However, these methods still predominantly depend on external-view observations or global point-cloud reconstructions, which can be difficult to maintain in real-world workspaces with occlusions and changing camera configurations.

Egocentric sensing offers a promising direction by mounting sensors directly on the robot body. Moving with the robot, they capture near-field geometry and reduce reliance on fixed external cameras. While recent work like ARMOR [ 12 ] demonstrates the potential of body-mounted ToF sensors for collision avoidance, cluttered manipulator reaching remains challenging due to the local, motion-dependent, and highly sparse nature of these observations.

To address this gap, we propose ESCAPE, an online egocentric motion-generation framework for collision-free reaching in cluttered and partially observed environments. ESCAPE deploys distributed body-mounted depth sensors and generates safe motion trajectories from egocentric sensory inputs, robot state, and goal information.
To handle sparse near-field observations, we temporally aggregate multi-joint ToF measurements and convert them into an obstacle-avoidance-aware point-cloud representation.
We then use a flow matching-based generative policy, trained from collision-free expert trajectories generated by cuRobo [ 26 ] , and jointly optimize goal-reaching and collision objectives to guide safe trajectory generation.
For controlled comparison with prior work, our simulation pipeline uses scene categories adapted from DRP [ 31 ] ; training on broader environment distributions is left for future work.
Importantly, once the policy is trained in simulation,
the same robot-mounted egocentric sensing setup can be deployed in the real world without external camera placement, multi-camera calibration, or scene-dependent view adjustment.
As validated in our experiments, ESCAPE is deployed zero-shot onto a real Franka robot, demonstrating a plug-and-play sim-to-real path for collision-aware manipulation.

Our core contributions are:

We present an online egocentric motion-generation framework that uses robot-mounted near-field depth sensing to generate safe, goal-directed trajectories in cluttered environments.

We design a temporal aggregation representation to convert sparse distributed ToF measurements into a structured, obstacle-aware point cloud for collision-aware policy learning.

We build a simulation-only training pipeline with obstacle-proximal expert demonstrations and synchronized egocentric observations, producing over 100K safety-critical trajectories.

We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real deployment on a real Franka robot, showing that egocentric sensing avoids careful external-camera placement, calibration, and view adjustment.

Extensive evaluations in cluttered environments show that ESCAPE outperforms external-view and voxelized-planning baselines using only egocentric perception, achieving robust zero-shot deployment on a real robot.

1. We present an online egocentric motion-generation framework that uses robot-mounted near-field depth sensing to generate safe, goal-directed trajectories in cluttered environments.

2. We design a temporal aggregation representation to convert sparse distributed ToF measurements into a structured, obstacle-aware point cloud for collision-aware policy learning.

3. We build a simulation-only training pipeline with obstacle-proximal expert demonstrations and synchronized egocentric observations, producing over 100K safety-critical trajectories.

4. We demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real deployment on a real Franka robot, showing that egocentric sensing avoids careful external-camera placement, calibration, and view adjustment.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Classical Motion Planning

Classical motion planning generates collision-free trajectories by searching or optimizing over the robot configuration space. Graph-search methods such as A* and its variants [ 8 , 17 , 16 , 13 ] provide strong search guarantees under appropriate assumptions, while sampling-based planners such as RRT, PRM, and their extensions [ 15 , 11 , 10 , 25 ] improve scalability in high-dimensional continuous spaces. Trajectory optimization methods further refine paths by minimizing smoothness, goal, and collision costs [ 35 , 4 , 23 , 26 ] . Control Barrier Function-based methods provide another line of safety-aware planning and control [ 24 , 27 , 32 ] . Despite strong performance with accurate geometric models, these approaches typically depend on explicit environment representations and collision queries, making them less suitable for unknown, cluttered, or severely occluded real-world scenes.

## 2.2 Learning-based Motion Planning

Learning-based motion planners aim to improve generalization and responsiveness by distilling planning experience into neural policies. Early methods use learned modules to bias sampling, generate roadmaps, or guide classical planners [ 20 , 14 , 33 , 1 , 9 , 19 ] . More recent closed-loop visuomotor policies directly map partial point-cloud observations and robot states to actions. M π \pi Nets [ 5 ] and M π \pi Former [ 6 ] demonstrate online neural motion generation from point-cloud inputs, while NeuralMP [ 2 ] improves generalization through large-scale training and test-time optimization. DRP [ 31 ] further enhances reactive manipulator planning in dynamic environments by combining a pretrained motion policy with local reactive modules. However, these methods still primarily rely on external cameras or global point-cloud observations. In cluttered workspaces, such observations can be degraded by self-occlusion, scene occlusion, and camera-placement constraints, motivating alternative sensing strategies that are directly coupled to robot motion.

## 2.3 Egocentric Perception

Egocentric perception places sensors on the robot body or near the end effector, providing local observations that move with the robot. This paradigm has been explored in visual manipulation through whole-body vision, active egocentric cameras, and in-hand view reasoning [ 29 , 3 , 34 ] . For collision avoidance, proximity skins and distributed depth sensors provide near-field measurements without requiring a complete scene model [ 28 , 7 , 22 ] . ARMOR [ 12 ] recently integrates multiple ToF sensors on humanoid arms and demonstrates the value of body-centric perception for collision avoidance and motion planning. However, achieving robust performance using purely body-mounted perception on real physical robots remains a significant challenge, and existing methods, including ARMOR, have yet to demonstrate stable and highly effective results in complex, real-world cluttered environments.

2026-10-20.title: UMI-WM: Interactive World Modeling for Bimanual Manipulation from Wrist Cameras
2026-10-20.authors: Jingxiang Guo , Haoyu Zhao , Xidong Zhang , Yuhang Zheng , Hao Wu , Chen Gao , Jianshu Zhou , Shuicheng Yan , Weihao Yuan
2026-10-20.abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) pairs wrist-camera videos with camera trajectories and gripper openings, providing scalable, robot-free data for learning how bimanual actions change a shared scene. Existing interactive world models, however, typically rely on text or single-camera control and struggle to follow each arm’s actions while maintaining consistency between the two wrist views. We introduce UMI-WM, an action-conditioned bimanual world model that jointly generates both wrist views from observation history, per-arm relative camera poses, and gripper widths, with cross-view consistency, action following, and visual fidelity. UMI-WM injects each arm’s actions into its own wrist stream, while sparse hub tokens exchange scene information between the two streams. Camera-aware geometry conditioning and camera-guided noise further support per-view motion control and cross-view geometric exchange. We adapt the model for block-causal generation and distill the 30-step Teacher into a Student with four denoising steps. We train UMI-WM on self-collected open-world and in-studio UMI recordings combined with public manipulation data. To evaluate action following, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) to recover relative camera poses and gripper widths from generated videos, and introduce Bimanual Action Fidelity (BAF) to measure how closely these recovered actions match the conditioning actions. UMI-WM achieves the best results on all five reference-video fidelity metrics and the best or competitive performance on VBench and WorldArena. The Teacher and Student outperform all compared baselines in action following, while the four-step Student generates paired wrist videos 6.9 × 6.9\times faster than the Teacher.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Recent interactive world models, including HY-WorldPlay ( Sun et al., 2026 ) , LingBot-World ( Robbyant Team et al., 2026 ) , Wonder ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and Matrix-Game 3.5 ( Qian et al., 2026 ) , generate videos conditioned on camera poses, allowing users to control viewpoint motion through a scene. Extending this capability to bimanual manipulation requires modeling not only the motion of two independently controlled viewpoints but also how each end-effector’s actions affect the shared environment. The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) ( Chi et al., 2024 ) provides a natural interface for this extension. Its handheld grippers collect wrist-camera videos, relative end-effector trajectories, and gripper widths without requiring a robot. Because each wrist camera is rigidly mounted to its gripper, the relative camera poses constitute the end-effector pose component of the action, while a single additional dimension specifies the gripper opening. Together, these controls provide a compact bimanual action representationfor jointly predicting both future wrist-camera views.

Extending interactive world models to bimanual manipulation raises three consistency requirements. First, cross-view consistency: the two independently controlled wrist views must show the same shared scene, so that changes caused by either hand appear in both. Second, spatial consistency within each view: the persistent gripper foreground must stay stable while the scene moves, whereas existing models let it drift. Third, action consistency: the generated viewpoint motion and gripper opening must follow the commanded per-arm camera pose and width, including small pose changes.

To address these challenges, we introduce UMI-WM , an interactive world model that jointly predicts both wrist videos conditioned on bimanual actions (Fig. 1 ). UMI-WM injects each arm’s actions into its own wrist stream, exchanges shared-scene context between the two streams through hub tokens, and adds camera-aware geometry conditioning, so that each wrist’s motion and the scene changes caused by either hand are modeled together; causal generation and distilling the 30-step Teacher into a four-step Student keep the rollout efficient. Training uses a unified data processing pipeline that integrates self-collected UMI demonstrations with public robot data through a shared camera-centric action representation. Finally, an inverse dynamics model (IDM) recovers relative camera poses and gripper widths from generated videos, and Bimanual Action Fidelity (BAF) measures how closely these recovered actions agree with the conditioning actions.

Our contributions are then summarized as follows:

UMI-WM. We develop an interactive world model that jointly generates both wrist-camera views conditioned on per-arm camera poses and gripper widths, combining cross-view interaction and camera-aware conditioning with few-step causal generation.

Data pipeline and action-level evaluation. We construct a three-tier data pyramid of public robot data, in-the-wild UMI recordings, and in-studio UMI recordings with a unified processing pipeline, and develop an IDM that recovers relative camera poses and gripper widths from video to compute Bimanual Action Fidelity (BAF).

Results. On 320 held-out UMI episodes, UMI-WM leads all five reference-video fidelity metrics and is best or competitive on VBench and WorldArena. The Teacher and Student reach BAF scores of 76.36 and 71.55, respectively, outperforming all compared baselines, while the four-step Student achieves a 6.9 × 6.9\times speedup over the 30-step Teacher.

1. UMI-WM. We develop an interactive world model that jointly generates both wrist-camera views conditioned on per-arm camera poses and gripper widths, combining cross-view interaction and camera-aware conditioning with few-step causal generation.

2. Data pipeline and action-level evaluation. We construct a three-tier data pyramid of public robot data, in-the-wild UMI recordings, and in-studio UMI recordings with a unified processing pipeline, and develop an IDM that recovers relative camera poses and gripper widths from video to compute Bimanual Action Fidelity (BAF).

3. Results. On 320 held-out UMI episodes, UMI-WM leads all five reference-video fidelity metrics and is best or competitive on VBench and WorldArena. The Teacher and Student reach BAF scores of 76.36 and 71.55, respectively, outperforming all compared baselines, while the four-step Student achieves a 6.9 × 6.9\times speedup over the 30-step Teacher.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 UMI Gripper and UMI Datasets

UMI ( Chi et al., 2024 ) pairs wrist-camera videos, SLAM-reconstructed camera trajectories, and gripper widths for portable demonstration collection. Variants include FastUMI ( Zhaxizhuoma et al., 2025 ) , which simplifies hardware integration and pose tracking; DexUMI ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , which supports dexterous hands through a wearable exoskeleton; and MV-UMI ( Rayyan et al., 2025 ) , which adds third-person observations for broader scene context. Public datasets such as FastUMI-100K ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , RealOmni-Open ( GenRobot, 2026 ) , and Daimon-Infinity ( Daimon Robotics, 2026 ) broaden the coverage of manipulation tasks and sensing modalities. We combine public manipulation data with self-collected UMI recordings to learn a bimanual world model conditioned on relative wrist-camera poses and gripper widths.

## 2.2 Camera-Controlled Interactive World Models

Camera-controlled world models generate observations along camera trajectories. CameraCtrl ( He et al., 2025a ) , CamI2V ( Zheng et al., 2024 ) , and ReCamMaster ( Bai et al., 2025a ) introduce camera-pose conditioning into video generation, while HY-WorldPlay ( Sun et al., 2026 ) and LingBot-World ( Robbyant Team et al., 2026 ) support interactive exploration with persistent scene context. Extending this setting to multiple viewpoints requires modeling how independently controlled views evolve within a shared environment, as explored by SynCamMaster ( Bai et al., 2025b ) , Gamma-World ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , and Khora ( Zhao et al., 2026d ) . UMI-WM extends camera control to bimanual manipulation, where gripper actions change both wrist views and their shared scene.

## 2.3 World Models for Robotic Manipulation

World models as planners. World models generate visual plans and then translate them into robot actions. UniPi ( Du et al., 2023 ) , RoboDreamer ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) , and GE-Act 2.0 ( AgiBot Research Team et al., 2026 ) couple visual planners with IDMs to recover actions. Large Video Planner ( Chen et al., 2025a ) similarly extracts actions from visual plans, while Goal-VLA ( Chen et al., 2025b ) derives target object poses from generated goal images. UMI-WM also uses an IDM to recover actions from video and defines BAF by comparing them with the conditioning actions.

World models as simulators. Genie Envisioner ( Liao et al., 2026 ) , GE-Sim 2.0 ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) , Interactive World Simulator ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , and Ctrl-World ( Guo et al., 2026 ) generate visual responses to robot actions for policy evaluation, while RynnWorld-Teleop ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) enables teleoperation within a generative world model. UMI-WM serves as an interactive simulator for bimanual manipulation, generating wrist-camera videos conditioned on per-arm relative camera poses and gripper widths. Appendix D reviews further related work.

2026-10-20.title: MicroSplat: Towards Automating 3D Small-Scale Reconstruction
2026-10-20.authors: Roman Mineyev , Robert Azarcon , Suvrat Jain , Chuizheng Kong , Shreyas Kousik
2026-10-20.abstract:
Reconstructing sub-millimeter detail of small objects underpins tasks such as circuit-board defect detection, specimen digitization, and archiving.
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) makes photorealistic reconstruction possible from posed images alone, but macro optics violate two conditions it depends on.
The field of view (FOV) and the depth of field (DoF) shrink to millimeters, so viewpoint error can take a sample out of frame, and only a thin focal plane is sharp in frame.
Existing automated macro-capture rigs handle the shallow DoF with per-view focus stacking, but typically rely on classical photogrammetry and offline, human-in-the-loop processing.
We present MicroSplat, which generates a 3DGS using a low-cost consumer microscope on a manipulator arm.
After a single up-front object-localization step, the system runs unattended.
It performs calibration,
plans collision-free viewpoints, captures and fuses a focal stack at each viewpoint, segments the object across all views, and optimizes a 3DGS model warm-started with the arm’s own poses.
We further compare against blur-aware 3DGS methods, which infer sharp scenes from defocused images, and find that measuring sharpness with a controlled focal sweep outperforms inferring it. We provide real and synthetic datasets (including robot and camera parameters) and the fitted 3DGS reconstructions.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Centimeter-scale objects resolved at sub-millimeter detail are the working domain of a range of inspection and digitization tasks: defect detection on printed circuit boards (PCBs) and solder joints, the digitization of insects and biological specimens,
and the archiving of coins and other small artifacts [ 9 , 31 , 20 , 30 ] .
3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [ 15 ] makes photorealistic reconstruction possible from posed RGB images alone, but macro optics break two of its working assumptions at once.
The field of view and the depth of field (DoF) both shrink to millimeters, so viewpoint error decides whether the sample is in frame at all; and within a single exposure only a thin focal plane is sharp, so recovering sharp detail requires an explicit strategy.
Two families exist: focus stacking, which recovers sharpness before reconstruction by combining multiple images per viewpoint, and blur-aware methods, which recover a sharp scene from defocused images during the reconstruction phase.
Systems that automate macro capture, such as the Orbitoscope [ 35 ] , already handle the shallow DoF with per-view focus stacking, positioning their sample by hand at a fixed orbit center. What they do not produce is a Gaussian Splat; these systems reconstruct with classical photogrammetry and rely on offline, human-in-the-loop processing.
The manual efforts that do create a Gaussian Splat require labor-intensive hand-masking of hundreds of images to suppress floater artifacts (spurious semi-transparent Gaussians) induced by blurred backgrounds [ 1 ] .

MicroSplat 1 1 1 Project page (includes interactive viewer): https://microsplat.github.io/ . Code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Microscopic-3D-Reconstruction-FA3D pairs a robotic manipulator arm (KUKA iiwa14 R820) with a low-cost consumer microscope as its end-effector ( Fig. 1 ).
We leverage the arm’s ± 0.1 mm \pm 0.1\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} repeatability to enable microscope calibration and precise microscope placement for focus stacking.
Our use of a low-cost microscope introduced noise in both our images and poses. We developed several engineering solutions such as a human-in-the-loop object-centering pipeline, SfM initialization with robot pose and camera intrinsics, and Gaussian-fit-based window selection for focus stacking to make our pipeline robust to this noise.

To summarize, we make three main contributions:

An autonomous capture-to-reconstruction pipeline , in which, after calibration and object-centering, the system captures data and generates a 3DGS model of a small object.
We also extensively evaluate the impact of key engineering choices in our pipeline (object centering and robot pose SfM initialization) through ablations and comparison to baselines.

An autonomous capture-to-reconstruction pipeline , in which, after calibration and object-centering, the system captures data and generates a 3DGS model of a small object.
We also extensively evaluate the impact of key engineering choices in our pipeline (object centering and robot pose SfM initialization) through ablations and comparison to baselines.

A comparison against blur-aware 3DGS methods , in which we benchmark our focus-stacking approach on synthetic data using ground-truth in-focus renderings, and show that when a controlled robotic focal sweep captures sharp detail from every viewpoint, measuring sharpness directly outperforms inferring it from defocused images during reconstruction.

A reconstruction dataset of eight real objects and eight synthetic objects, spanning a wide range of attributes. The dataset contains information on scans, 3DGS reconstructions, initial robot arm poses and camera intrinsics. For each synthetic object we additionally release the Blender scene and object mesh, along with both the shallow-DoF focal stacks and the corresponding fully in-focus renderings, which serve as ground truth. 2 2 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/splatmicro/microsplat , released under CC BY 4.0.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section II covers related work, Section III details our method’s hardware, calibration, planning,
and reconstruction stack, and Section IV presents experimental results.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Automated Capture Rigs

3D reconstruction is an essential tool used across a wide range of domains such as film, video games, virtual and augmented reality, medical imaging, and robotics.
Neural rendering has emerged as a powerful approach to this problem, with Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) [ 21 ] and 3DGS [ 15 ] being commonly adopted over classical photogrammetry for their ability to produce photorealistic novel-view synthesis from posed images alone.

With so many applications relying on 3D reconstruction, much work has focused on automating the data collection process.
For example, the Google Scanned Objects dataset demonstrated a custom enclosure with structured light and machine vision cameras capable of generating high-fidelity 3D models for over 1,000 household items for the downstream task of robot learning [ 5 ] .

More recently, automated pipelines have moved toward reconstructing objects directly with 3DGS from RGB images alone, without the depth or structured-light hardware these earlier systems require [ 24 , 28 , 13 , 22 ] .
For example, Omni-Scan [ 24 ] used a bi-manual robot to rotate a grasped object in front of a fixed RGB camera, merging two scans into a 3DGS model.
To isolate the object from the gripper and background, it prompts SAM 2 [ 25 ] with foreground cues and scores the resulting candidate masks.
We similarly use SAM 2 for object mask generation in MicroSplat.

## II-B Small-Scale Reconstruction

Beyond standard objects, there is great interest in applying 3D reconstruction to resolve sub-millimeter detail as well.
In electronics and semiconductor manufacturing, high-fidelity reconstructions of PCBs, microcontrollers, and solder joints enable automated defect detection and quality control [ 9 , 31 ] .
Similar techniques are used to digitize insects and biological specimens in entomology, to archive coins, engravings, and other small artifacts in cultural heritage, and to characterize surface morphology in materials science [ 20 , 10 , 30 , 16 ] .

## II-C Small-Scale Capture and Sharpness Recovery

Hobbyists such as Danny Bittel have shown that Gaussian Splatting of small objects is possible with manual macro photography [ 1 ] , using focus stacking [ 33 ] to overcome shallow DOF: a series of images are captured from a single viewpoint while the camera steps along the optical axis, and the resulting slices are fused into one all-in-focus composite.

Manually producing such a capture, however, faces two bottlenecks.
First, at macro working distances, both FOV and DOF are small, so precise viewpoint control is essential.
Second, masks are necessary since blurred backgrounds lack geometric cues, causing background-colored floater artifacts that forced Bittel to hand-mask hundreds of images.

Several works do automate this capture process for small samples via focus stacking [ 10 , 6 , 35 ] .
Closest to this work, Orbitoscope [ 35 ] uses a custom six-axis gantry with a dedicated stacking axis for per-view focal stacks.
Its viewpoints are fixed and the sample is manually positioned at the orbit center with intersecting laser pointer.
We take the complementary approach of leaving the sample untouched and adjusting the viewpoints (i.e., the robot’s motion) to the estimated sample center.

All of these autonomous systems for small-scale objects, however, reconstruct with classical photogrammetry rather than Gaussian Splatting.
To our knowledge, MicroSplat is the first fully autonomous pipeline for small-scale objects that goes from robotic data collection to a 3DGS model without human intervention after setup.

An alternative to capture-time focus stacking is to recover sharpness during reconstruction: Deblurring 3DGS [ 17 ] and its successors [ 23 , 18 ] jointly estimate a blur model and a sharp scene from defocused images. However, with a robot arm we can capture in-focus detail directly from every viewpoint rather than inferring it. We compare these methods in Section IV-E .
