2026-10-20.title: InJePA: Intention-First Latent Planning with Coupled JEPA World Models for Visual Navigation
2026-10-20.authors: Siming Zhou , Bowen Ma , Ruiran Du , Pengcheng Zheng , Sheng Zheng , Dongshen Han , Zhijie Li , Wei Dong , Fan Mo , Chaoning Zhang
2026-10-20.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-20.comment: . Includes appendices. Code is available at this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract:
Visual navigation requires goal directed planning informed by predictions of environment dynamics.
Representative navigation world model methods propose complete action candidates before predicting consequences for selection or search updates.
For each candidate, predictions primarily evaluate proposed actions rather than guide its stepwise construction.
To this end, we propose InJepa, an intention first planning paradigm centered on latent states.
A goal conditioned JEPA proposes latent intentions, and an action conditioned JEPA continually predicts future latent states.
Both operate in a shared latent space to align their predictive representations.
Within each candidate, predicted consequences feed into the next intention proposal and action inference, forming a closed loop of intention, action, and consequence.
This extends the world model’s role beyond evaluation to leading candidate construction through latent intentions.
We evaluate InJepa through closed loop image goal navigation in Habitat MP3D.
The results show effective multistep navigation through intention guided action generation and consequence feedback.
Experiments across encoders further support applicability across visual representations.
These findings support latent intentions as the central planning object and show that world models can directly guide plan construction through coordinated reasoning about intentions and consequences.
Code is available at https://github.com/zhuxun132/InJepa .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Visual navigation is fundamental to autonomous robotics and embodied intelligence.
Agents must use visual observations to reach goals through continued interaction with the environment ( Chaplot et al., 2020 ; Zeng et al., 2023 ; Ko et al., 2024 ) .
In image goal navigation, reaching the goal from the current observation requires a sequence of state transitions.
Each action affects both the distance to the goal and the state for subsequent decisions.
Navigation must therefore connect visual goals with sequential decisions, accounting for both goal proximity and action consequences ( Ma et al., 2022 ) .
Reasoning about future state changes provides an important basis for coherent multistep planning and goal directed navigation ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) .

Existing learned navigation methods typically generate actions through goal conditioned policies and use world model predictions to support planning.
These policies directly output action sequences from observation histories and goal images ( Shah et al., 2023 ; Sridhar et al., 2024 ) .
World models predict future observations, latent states, or compatibility between consequences and goals ( Hafner et al., 2019a ; Hafner et al., 2020 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ) to support candidate comparison ( Chua et al., 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2019b ; Wang & Gao, 2026 ; Hansen et al., 2024 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) .
In representative candidate search methods, a policy or optimizer first proposes complete action sequences.
The world model then predicts their consequences to select candidates or update the search distribution ( Zhang et al., 2026c ; Chahe & Zhou, 2026 ; Bar et al., 2025 ) .
Predictive modeling ( Zheng et al., 2026a ) has expanded from image generation to latent space ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ; Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ; Kuhn et al., 2026 ; Maes et al., 2026 ) .
These methods evaluate candidate consequences before execution using different representations and computational forms to compare predicted outcomes with the goal.

However, this action first construction order limits the world model’s role in forming each candidate.
Desired state changes toward the goal can only be determined indirectly through action candidates.
Although consequence evaluation can guide subsequent search, the current candidate’s actions are fixed before prediction.
Predictions primarily evaluate proposed behaviors and do not participate in the stepwise generation of subsequent actions within that candidate.
We therefore reconsider the starting point of planning: can world models lead the stepwise construction of navigation plans by proposing desired changes and jointly reasoning about intentions and consequences?

To address this issue, we propose InJepa, an intention first planning architecture.
We define an intention as a candidate desired latent state conditioned on the goal and couple intention proposals with consequence prediction in a shared latent space.
At each step, Proposal JEPA proposes an intention from the current state and goal.
The action model translates the difference between the intention and the current state into an action ( Sun et al., 2026 ) .
Forward JEPA then predicts the successor state under that action.
The predicted state becomes the common basis for subsequent intention generation and action inference within the same candidate.
As shown in Figure 1 , the world model directly leads stepwise plan construction while retaining candidate evaluation.
Closed loop experiments in unseen MP3D scenes and evaluations with three visual encoders support the architecture’s navigation effectiveness and applicability across representations.
Controlled mechanism comparisons further examine the roles of intention proposals and consequence feedback.

To conclude, the main contributions of this paper are as follows:

To the best of our knowledge, we propose the first intention first planning paradigm for world models in visual navigation.
We shift the primary planning object from action sequences to goal conditioned latent intentions.
World models thus lead stepwise plan construction through the generation and realization of desired state changes.

We introduce InJepa, a dual JEPA architecture for joint reasoning over intentions and consequences in a shared latent space.
Within each candidate, predicted successor states guide both subsequent intention generation and action inference, so plans are progressively constructed in response to the predicted consequences of earlier actions.

We validate effective closed loop navigation in unseen MP3D scenes and applicability across three visual encoders.
Through controlled mechanism comparisons and ablation studies, we further examine how intention proposals, consequence feedback, and training supervision contribute to effective navigation.

1. To the best of our knowledge, we propose the first intention first planning paradigm for world models in visual navigation.
We shift the primary planning object from action sequences to goal conditioned latent intentions.
World models thus lead stepwise plan construction through the generation and realization of desired state changes.

2. We introduce InJepa, a dual JEPA architecture for joint reasoning over intentions and consequences in a shared latent space.
Within each candidate, predicted successor states guide both subsequent intention generation and action inference, so plans are progressively constructed in response to the predicted consequences of earlier actions.

3. We validate effective closed loop navigation in unseen MP3D scenes and applicability across three visual encoders.
Through controlled mechanism comparisons and ablation studies, we further examine how intention proposals, consequence feedback, and training supervision contribute to effective navigation.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Navigation World Models

Navigation world models mainly use two forms of prediction.
One generates future images or videos and evaluates candidates by comparing predicted observations with the goal.
NWM predicts videos conditioned on actions ( Bar et al., 2025 ) .
Subsequent work improves generation consistency and rollout efficiency ( Yan et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) .
It also explores joint or alternating generation of visual sequences and actions ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Dong1 et al., 2026 ) .
The other predicts and evaluates consequences in latent space.
RAE-NWM, PiJEPA, and ReL-NWM use feature predictions to guide action search ( Zhang et al., 2026c ; Chahe & Zhou, 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) .
LWM learns compatibility between consequences and goals for candidate selection and policy learning ( Wang & Gao, 2026 ) .
Related work jointly models latent prediction and action generation ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , or uses compact representations to reduce rollout cost ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2022 ; Zheng et al., 2026b ) .
Across both forms, action candidate methods plan directly over action sequences, determining desired changes indirectly through consequence evaluation or action optimization.

## 2.2 Planning in State Space and Action Realization

Guidance by anticipated effects and coordination between forward and inverse models provide cognitive and control foundations for planning in state space ( Kunde et al., 2002 ; Wolpert & Kawato, 1998 ) .
One class decomposes tasks using latent landmarks or visual subgoals for execution by lower level policies ( Shah et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Moghaddam et al., 2021 ; Nair & Finn, 2019 ; Bell et al., 2024 ) .
FF-JEPA predicts latent subgoals and uses CEM to search for actions to realize them ( Masip et al., 2026 ) .
HWM generates subgoals through high level macro actions, then optimizes low level actions ( Zhang et al., 2026d ) .
Another class learns mappings from plans to actions ( Lynch et al., 2020 ; Thomas et al., 2023 ; Ajay et al., 2022 ; Li, 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ) .
LDP decodes latent state trajectories into actions through inverse dynamics ( Xie et al., 2025 ) .
NavDreamer converts video plans into navigation waypoints ( Huang et al., 2026 ) .
INTACT infers actions from the difference between the goal and current states.
It uses predicted consequences to update the state reference for the next action inference step ( Sun et al., 2026 ) .
These approaches establish state planning and predictive feedback ( Du et al., 2024 ) , but separate subgoal execution, trajectory decoding, or high level proposal search from the coupled process studied here.
Our focus is the dependency within each candidate: a desired latent state determines an action, whose predicted consequence conditions both the next local intention and its action realization.

2026-10-20.title: Language-Forcing: Advancing Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Semantic Alignment of Whole-Body World Action Models
2026-10-20.authors: Yanjun Li , Jiarui Ye , Weiyu Guo , Zixiao He , Kangjie Ye , Dihan Wang , Yishuo Cheng , Zishang Xiang , Mingju Gao , Hao Tang
2026-10-20.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict robot actions and future observations. However, their visual prediction objectives do not explicitly distinguish task-relevant transitions from incidental scene changes. For whole-body policies, this distinction matters because task progress depends on coordinated changes in body pose, contact, and object state. We introduce Language-Forcing , a training strategy that uses language to emphasize task-relevant changes in the future-visual representations of a whole-body WAM. Given paired current and ground-truth short-horizon future frames, a frozen vision-language model assesses task progress and predicts plausible subsequent state changes. We encode these descriptions with a frozen text encoder and align their embeddings with intermediate, action-conditioned future-visual features, complementing the original visual and action prediction objectives. All auxiliary components are used only during training, introducing no additional inference overhead. On HumanoidArena, Language-Forcing achieves an average success rate of 79.17 % 79.17\% , exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 9.46 percentage points and the same WAM without language alignment by 10.77 10.77 percentage points. Across five real-world tasks, language alignment raises average success from 53.33 % 53.33\% to 71.33 % 71.33\% over the same WAM baseline.
2026-10-20.introduction:
World models learn predictive state representations for control ( Finn and Levine, 2017 ; Hafner et al., 2019 ) , and recent video-based policies and WAM-style formulations increasingly couple action generation with future state prediction ( Du et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . In parallel, vision-language-action models improve instruction following and generalization, with growing coverage of whole-body humanoid interaction ( Brohan et al., 2023a ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) . Despite this progress, whole-body action selection depends on coupled robot–object states: contact enables manipulation and stance adjustments enable reaching ( Sentis and Khatib, 2006 ) . Predictive representations must therefore emphasize the state changes that actually advance the task.

Visual prediction offers dense supervision but can overemphasize large, task-irrelevant changes (e.g., viewpoint shifts) while underweighting subtle but action-critical events (e.g., first contact with a handle). The resulting representation may therefore be misaligned with what the policy needs to decide the next action. Since the task instruction specifies the goal rather than per-transition progress, additional guidance is needed to focus predictive features on task advancement; closed-loop results also suggest visual fidelity alone is not sufficient ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) .

Language can make this distinction explicit: grasping a handle
identifies task progress, while predicting that the door will open
describes a possible subsequent outcome.
The task instruction remains the same across these stages, whereas
the desired language target changes with the observed transition.
Prior work uses language to learn robot representations and rewards ( Karamcheti et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2023 ) or introduces spatial knowledge into policies ( Qu et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) .
Spatial Forcing aligns visual features with pretrained geometric
representations ( Li et al., 2026a ) ,
while WorldScape Policy 2.0 supervises WAM planning representations
with event descriptions ( Su et al., 2026 ) .
We focus on the action-conditioned future-visual representation.
These features are learned jointly with action generation and
conditioned on the action trajectory, making them a natural point
for relating predicted physical changes to their task-level meaning.
Our insight is that assessments of task progress and predictions
of subsequent states can guide these features toward changes
relevant to action generation.
Visual and language supervision are complementary: one captures
scene dynamics, while the other relates them to task progress
and likely next steps.

We introduce Language-Forcing , a training strategy for whole-body WAMs.
A frozen vision-language model receives the task context and paired
current and future observations, assesses task progress, and describes
a plausible continuation beyond the observed endpoint.
A frozen UMT5 encoder ( Chung et al., 2023 ) encodes its response for alignment with intermediate future-visual
features conditioned on the scene, robot state, and action trajectory.
This supervision complements the original visual and action objectives.
All auxiliary components are used only during training, leaving the
deployed action-generation path unchanged without additional
inference computation.

On HumanoidArena ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , Language-Forcing achieves 79.17 % 79.17\% average success across seven tasks,
exceeding the strongest competing policy by 9.46 9.46 percentage points.
Matched WAM comparisons and five real-world tasks further
demonstrate its effectiveness.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce Language Forcing, which uses a VLM’s assessments
of task progress and predictions of future states to supervise
the intermediate visual features used by a WAM to predict
future observations.

We incorporate Language Forcing into a whole-body humanoid
WAM for modeling whole-body actions, without additional computational overhead at test time.

We achieve state-of-the-art performance on HumanoidArena
and demonstrate the effectiveness of Language Forcing through
a matched comparison with the same WAM trained without
language supervision.

1. We introduce Language Forcing, which uses a VLM’s assessments
of task progress and predictions of future states to supervise
the intermediate visual features used by a WAM to predict
future observations.

2. We incorporate Language Forcing into a whole-body humanoid
WAM for modeling whole-body actions, without additional computational overhead at test time.

3. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on HumanoidArena
and demonstrate the effectiveness of Language Forcing through
a matched comparison with the same WAM trained without
language supervision.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Generalist robot policies learn instruction-conditioned actions across tasks and embodiments, drawing on large-scale demonstrations and pretrained vision-language representations ( Brohan et al., 2023b ; Driess et al., 2023 ; Brohan et al., 2023a ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024 ) .
Diffusion and flow-based policies support continuous action generation ( Chi et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) , while related work studies data diversity, few-shot adaptation, cross-embodiment learning, and instruction tuning ( Lin et al., 2025 ; Vosylius and Johns, 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026 ) .
Predictive visuomotor methods use future videos or visual features for planning and action learning ( Du et al., 2023 ; Tian et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) .
World-action models further couple future prediction with action generation ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Bi et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026b ) , alongside efforts to evaluate world models through closed-loop control ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) .
Recent approaches investigate action-centered architectures and efficient predictive representations ( Ye et al., 2026a ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026 ) , while MotionWAM and ω \omega -0 extend predictive learning to humanoid whole-body actions ( Zheng et al., 2026a ; Li et al., 2026e ) .

Humanoid policies have progressed from whole-body motion tracking ( He et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2026b ) toward promptable and language-guided control for coordinated movement and task execution ( Li et al., 2026c ; Li et al., 2026d ) .
GR00T N1 and WholeBodyVLA extend this direction to generalist humanoid policies and loco-manipulation ( NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) .
RobotArena ∞ \infty and HumanoidArena provide large-scale policy evaluation and egocentric tasks requiring coordination of the legs, torso, arms, and hands, respectively ( Jangir et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) .

Visual pretraining and language supervision provide transferable representations for robot learning ( Xiao et al., 2022 ; Nair et al., 2022 ; Karamcheti et al., 2023 ; Ma et al., 2023 ) .
Spatially informed policies further incorporate explicit spatial encodings, 3D feature alignment, or pretrained spatial features ( Qu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) .
Being-H0.7 transfers future-informed representations into a deployable policy ( Luo et al., 2026a ) , while WorldScape Policy 2.0 supervises planning representations with event captions ( Su et al., 2026 ) .
Language-Forcing aligns action-conditioned future-visual features with language representations describing observed short-horizon state transitions, using this auxiliary supervision only during training.

2026-10-20.title: When to Make a Decision: Task-Sufficient Active Perception for Mobile Manipulator Robots
2026-10-20.authors: Mariana da Silva Barros , Matthias Kerzel , Cornelius Weber , Stefan Wermter
2026-10-20.abstract: A robotic agent operating in an unknown environment must gather sufficient task-relevant information before acting. However, determining when the available information is sufficient remains a challenge. We propose a conceptual hybrid neuro-symbolic framework for task-sufficient active perception in unknown environments. After interpreting a requested task, the agent generates an initial plan and iteratively reevaluates it as new information becomes available. At each iteration, it can acquire a more informative viewpoint, inspect or manipulate candidate objects, ask the user for clarification, or perform the task. Neural perception modules update an object-centric belief state, while a symbolic decision layer determines whether the remaining uncertainty justifies further information gathering. The framework will be implemented on a mobile manipulator comprising a humanoid torso and a mobile base, with complementary evaluation in simulation. The proposed approach aims to enable robots to determine not only how to gather additional information, but also when further perception is no longer necessary.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Advances in robotics and artificial intelligence are enabling robots to perform an increasingly broad range of assistive tasks. However, when placed in an unknown and dynamic environment before performing a task, the robotic agent must perceive and gather sufficient information about the surroundings, which is often challenging for robots to do [ 11 ] .

Consider a robot operating in a previously unseen environment and receiving a task such as "collect all the mugs in the room". The example is illustrated in Figure 1 . The robot has sensors to collect information about its surroundings, but in its current position, it can only observe part of the environment. After making an initial plan based on the current situation, at each iteration, the robot can explore the environment, inspect or manipulate objects, or ask the user for clarification. Only when the robot has sufficient relevant knowledge can it perform the requested task.

Depending on different factors such as the environment, the required task, user preferences, or how much information the robot has already gathered, there may be several choices for each situation. In the above mug scenario, the robot can see two mugs on the table, but some viewpoints are obstructed by the vase from its current position. Therefore, it could explore further the surroundings or seek a better point of view (on the other side of the table). Another option would be to open the closet and see if there are mugs inside. Once it finds a mug in the room, it can either explore to see if there are other mugs, pick it up and deliver it to the user, or ask the user if there are more mugs present in the room. If it acts too soon, it may miss unseen objects and cause the task to fail. However, if the robot explores for too long, it may only get redundant or unnecessary information and waste time.

This scenario motivates the need for a framework that focuses on the task-relevant view of active perception. The main goal is for the robotic agent to acquire enough task-relevant knowledge to act safely and effectively. Or, in other words, for a robot to determine when its current knowledge is sufficient for task execution in an unknown environment. If the robot still does not have enough information to perform the task, it must move its base, head position, or hand position to collect more necessary data. Therefore, this work proposes investigating how a mobile robot with a manipulator can determine when its current knowledge is relevant and sufficient for task execution in an unknown environment. The conceptual work proposed includes modules that will perform task interpretation and planning, active perception, object inspection, and interaction with the user.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

In recent years, various approaches have been developed in different areas related to the execution of robot tasks, including perception, object detection, navigation, and task planning. In real-world environments, where object occlusion is particularly common (due to the environment itself or other objects), static perception is not sufficient for the robot to observe the environment completely. Therefore, in such scenarios, it is essential for robotic agents to perform active perception, where a robot actively moves its body and sensors to acquire relevant knowledge from the environment [ 1 ] . This ability allows the robotic agent to determine what it wants to perceive and a way to achieve this [ 2 ] .

Scene understanding is crucial for task execution in different situations, especially in unknown and dynamic environments. For robotic agents, it is vital to ensure robustness in grasping movements in cluttered scenes [ 8 ] . Active vision can also support navigation by directing the robot toward viewpoints expected to improve localization accuracy [ 3 ] . For mobile manipulation, active-perceptive methods can jointly optimize viewpoint selection, base motion, and grasp feasibility [ 8 ] .

Recent advances in computer vision and machine learning have enabled different approaches in active perception. A perception model [ 11 ] is proposed that improves the estimation of information gain using perceptual factors to quantify the aggregated influence of the environment on candidate viewpoints. However, this work uses only a mobile robot, not including manipulation or interaction with objects or the environment. Jauhri et al. [ 8 ] propose an active perception pipeline for mobile manipulators that balances exploration (maximizing visual information gain) and exploitation of task-specific information (such as grasp executability for mobile grasping). However, the robot can get stuck in deadlocks while trying to switch targets, leading to oscillating motions. Another limitation is the limited observability in occluded scenes, making the information gain computation difficult. Another approach consists of an active vision-based path planning method that, in addition to robust path planning and obstacle avoidance, guides the robot to areas with the most robust visual features to further refine the localization error [ 3 ] . However, this approach generates paths that are longer than necessary and is also constrained by an empirically selected static threshold used to assess the probability of tracking failure in localization.

Despite the various approaches that implement perception for mobile robots, they often separate planning, perception, exploration, and interaction into distinct modules, which are not motivated by the relevance and sufficiency of the underlying knowledge. As a result, either the robot may gather irrelevant information (not necessary for the task) or may fail to gather sufficient data or correctly interpret the task. In addition, there is a gap in the efficient use of all the robot’s capabilities (motion, manipulation, and human interaction) to support task execution.

2026-10-20.title: MoDex: Towards Universal Multi-Object Dexterous Grasping
2026-10-20.authors: Jing Xiong , Jiale Xie , Haoqi Yuan , Chaoyi Xu , Zongqing Lu
2026-10-20.comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026. Code: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract:
Multi-object grasping is a fundamental yet challenging problem, constrained by data collection costs, varying spatial layouts, and the need for broad generalization. To address these challenges, we propose MoDex, a data-efficient framework that provides the first unified solution for universal multi-object dexterous grasping across diverse spatial layouts. MoDex accomplishes this by formulating the task as a single-step decision problem of learning residual corrections to a reference trajectory, and introducing a spatially adaptive dual-strategy that performs single-shot grasping for proximal objects and sequential interaction for separated objects. Extensive evaluations show that MoDex significantly outperforms baselines in proximal configurations, achieving 61.24% success on unseen objects, and achieves high success rates in separated layouts. Further experiments demonstrate its generalization across robot embodiments, scalability and zero-shot sim-to-real deployment through a vision-based policy trained solely on simulation data.
Code and pretrained models are available at https://github.com/Aurora-Xiong/MoDex .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Multi-object grasping is a fundamental yet challenging problem in dexterous manipulation [ 1 , 11 , 36 , 41 , 42 ] . The intrinsic complexity of this task arises from three challenges: data efficiency , where diverse object combinations and layouts make large-scale data collection or grasp generation costly; spatial adaptivity , where proximal layouts may allow single-shot grasping while separated layouts require sequential interaction; out-of-distribution robustness , where the policy must transfer across object geometries, placements, embodiments, and real-world visual observations. An effective framework must therefore make sample-efficient use of limited supervision, adapt to varying spatial layouts, and generalize broadly.

Existing multi-object approaches typically rely on explicit grasp synthesis. MultiGrasp [ 17 ] uses optimization or diffusion models to generate whole-hand grasps, while SeqGrasp [ 22 ] synthesizes stable sequential grasps using partial hand degrees of freedom. SeqMultiGrasp [ 12 ] also studies sequential multi-object grasp synthesis. These generation-based approaches rely on explicit grasp synthesis, introducing additional computation as object combinations and layouts scale. Meanwhile, recent single-object dexterous grasping methods, such as UniDexGrasp++ [ 37 ] , ResDex [ 15 ] , and DemoGrasp [ 43 ] , have made progress in generalizing across diverse objects, but they are not directly applicable to multi-object interactions. Consequently, prior methods address only subsets of the three challenges, leaving the full problem unresolved.

We propose MoDex , a data-efficient framework for universal multi-object dexterous grasping. Our core insight is that a single reference trajectory already encodes rich interaction priors, allowing diverse object instances to be handled by learning compact residual corrections rather than a full action sequence. This reduces the long-horizon problem to a single-step Markov Decision Process. We further observe that the optimal strategy is layout-dependent: proximal objects favor efficient single-shot enclosure, whereas separated objects require sequential interaction. Accordingly, we introduce a spatially adaptive dual-strategy mechanism that handles both regimes under the same residual formulation. Finally, we train a vision-based policy solely from randomized simulation rollouts, enabling zero-shot real-world deployment.

Experiments show that MoDex substantially outperforms baselines in dual-object proximal layouts, achieving 78.73% success on seen object pairs and 61.24% on unseen objects, which further improve to 80.74% and 63.69% with distillation. In separated layouts, MoDex reaches 92.76% success on seen object pairs and 39.85% on unseen objects. We also validate its effectiveness across different robot embodiments and a larger object set. In real-world tests, our vision-based policy achieves a 55% success rate on 20 unseen objects in proximal layouts and 45.5% in separated layouts, without using any real-world training data.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we show that multi-object dexterous grasping can be learned data-efficiently by adapting a single demonstration through a single-step residual policy. Second, we offer a unified solution to diverse object layouts, seamlessly integrating single-shot and multi-stage strategies within one spatially adaptive framework. Third, our method generalizes across unseen geometries, layouts, embodiments, and achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer by a vision-based policy trained exclusively on simulation data.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Multi-object Grasping. Multi-object grasping aims to enclose and stabilize multiple objects in one hand, introducing spatial competition and force constraints beyond single-object grasping [ 1 , 11 , 36 , 41 , 42 ] . Recent works address this via grasp generation: MultiGrasp [ 17 ] identifies hand configurations through differentiable force closure optimization [ 21 ] or diffusion models [ 13 ] , then executes the grasp with a goal-conditioned RL policy; SeqGrasp [ 22 ] partitions the hand’s degrees of freedom for sequential synthesis. SeqMultiGrasp [ 12 ] likewise addresses sequential multi-object grasping through grasp synthesis and generation. In contrast, we bypass expensive optimization and learn a universal policy via demonstration-guided RL. Our spatially adaptive dual-strategy mechanism further enables the first unified framework handling both proximal and separated layouts.

Reinforcement Learning for Dexterous Manipulation. Deep RL enables high-dimensional continuous control through environment interaction [ 24 , 19 , 33 , 10 ] . To master dexterous contact dynamics, recent methods structure learning for scalability and sample efficiency. To scale across thousands of objects, UniDexGrasp [ 40 ] pioneered task decoupling and geometry-aware curriculum distillation, while UniDexGrasp++ [ 37 ] later advanced this approach with iterative specialist–generalist training. Residual learning frameworks [ 15 , 35 , 14 ] improve sample efficiency by learning corrections on top of pre-trained policies or priors. DemoGrasp [ 43 ] adapts an expert demonstration as a single-step MDP, yielding a universal grasping policy. However, these learning frameworks are designed for single-object manipulation. Inspired by their success, we learn residual corrections to one demonstration through single-step reinforcement learning.

Imitation Learning for Dexterous Manipulation. Imitation learning [ 2 , 16 , 27 ] avoids complex reward design by learning from expert trajectories. Foundational behavioral cloning [ 28 ] and inverse RL [ 26 , 47 ] struggle to scale to dexterous hands due to data scarcity and high-DoF control. Recent works bridge this gap by collecting large-scale human demonstrations: DexMV [ 30 ] and AnyTeleop [ 31 ] use visual retargeting and teleoperation. Diffusion policies [ 8 , 44 ] are employed to model the intricate, high-DoF action spaces [ 39 , 34 , 18 ] . However, massive data collection remains expensive. In contrast, our method distills necessary control priors from only a single demonstration, removing the need for exhaustive data and complex morphological mapping.

2026-10-20.title: ContactKernels: Adaptive Proposals using Geometry-COnditioned Wrenches for Contact-Rich Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Aditya Kamireddypalli , Matías Mattamala , João Moura , Sethu Vijayakumar , Steve Tonneau , Subramanian Ramamoorthy
2026-10-20.abstract:
Contact-rich insertion requires precise geometric alignment despite uncertainty in perception, geometry, and control.
When this uncertainty causes unintended contact, the resulting contact provides local information that can guide corrective motion.
Sampling-based Model Predictive Control (SMPC) is well suited to this setting because it optimizes through forward simulation without requiring gradients through contact dynamics.
However, standard SMPC methods typically use generic proposal distributions that do not exploit observed contact to determine where to search next.
We introduce ContactKernels , a contact-adaptive proposal kernel that uses geometry-conditioned wrench measurements to estimate contact location and local contact geometry.
The estimated contact state directly adapts the proposal distribution: contact location biases the search toward corrective motions, while the contact normal shapes the sampling covariance.
We evaluate ContactKernels with Predictive Sampling (PS) and Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control across multiple insertion geometries in simulation and on a real robot.
In simulation, ContactKernels improves mean insertion success by over 50 % 50\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} points across both controllers.
On the real robot, it increases insertion success from 53.3 % 53.3\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} to 90.0 % 90.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} and reduces mean time to insertion by 33 % 33\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} .
These results show that contact information can improve sampling-based control not only as feedback, but also by directly determining where the controller searches.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Insertion is a fundamental manipulation task in which small uncertainties in geometry, perception, or control can lead to unexpected contact [ 11 ] .
Successful insertion requires precise alignment between the manipulated object and its environment.
Tight geometric tolerances make this alignment difficult in the presence of uncertainty in perception, local geometry, and control execution [ 18 ] .
This uncertainty can cause unintended contact and prevent insertion.

Contact, however, is not only a constraint.
It also provides information about the local geometric mismatch.
In particular, sensed contact can provide information about where the manipulated object contacts its environment.
Humans use this information to guide corrective motion.
When inserting a key, for example, we often “wiggle” the key after contact to search for a initial point of a potential feasible insertion path.
A robot can similarly use sensed contact location to determine where to explore next.

This has motivated the development of controllers that can use contact information to adapt its motion online [ 15 , 14 ] .
Learning-based methods can react to contact, but acquire the contact-to-action mapping from prior experience [ 19 , 20 ] .
Trajectory optimization can instead reason explicitly about contact at test time, but it requires an optimization formulation that handles nonlinear and nonsmooth contact dynamics [ 28 ] .
We seek an alternative that can use contact to adapt its search online without requiring a learned contact-to-action mapping or gradients through contact dynamics.

Sampling-based Model Predictive Control (SMPC) provides this capability.
SMPC searches for control trajectories through forward simulation and does not require gradients through contact dynamics.
However, standard SMPC methods typically sample controls from generic proposal distributions.
After contact, these proposals might continue to sample motions that are inconsistent with the observed contact state, because contact information has not been used in the sampling process.

We address this gap with ContactKernels , a contact-adaptive proposal kernel for sampling-based MPC. ContactKernels uses geometry-conditioned wrench measurements to estimate the contact location and local contact geometry.
The estimated contact location biases the proposal toward corrective motions, while the contact normal shapes the sampling covariance.
Contact confidence scales the strength of this adaptation, directly determining where the controller should search after unintended contact.

The contributions of this work are threefold:

We formulate contact-rich insertion using sampling-based Model Predictive Control (SMPC) and implement the controller with both Predictive Sampling (PS) and Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control.

We introduce ContactKernels , an adaptive proposal kernel that uses estimated contact location and local contact geometry to guide where the controller samples. In simulation, ContactKernels increases mean insertion success from 15.8 % 15.8\% to 66.7 % 66.7\% with PS and from 13.5 % 13.5\% to 65.6 % 65.6\% with MPPI.

We validate the approach across multiple insertion geometries in simulation and on a real robot. On the robot, MPPI with ContactKernels increases insertion success from 53.3 % 53.3\% to 90.0 % 90.0\% and reduces the mean time to insertion by 33 % 33\% .
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Contact-rich Insertion Strategies

Contact-rich insertion requires the robot to adapt when uncertainty causes unintended contact [ 11 ] .
Existing methods use model-based or learning-based strategies.

Model-based methods explicitly represent contact between the robot and its environment.
Classical methods use geometric and contact models to define corrective or compliant motions based on contact mode detection [ 35 , 29 , 33 ] .

Alternately, Trajectory Optimization (TO) directly estimates parameters of a trajectory subject to dynamics and kinematics constraints.
At suitable high frequencies, TO utilised in a receding horizon MPC loop generates trajectories that potentially adapt to unintended contact.
While successfully applied to contact-rich pushing tasks [ 1 , 34 ] , and tool manipulation [ 28 , 27 ] TO has seen limited application to the problem of contact-rich insertion.
Optimization-based methods must handle nonlinear and nonsmooth contact dynamics, exacerbated by changing contact modes for the insertion model.
Recent contact-implicit methods include smooth approximations to contact dynamics within an optimal control problem [ 4 ] .
These methods can reason about contact at deployment time.
Contact-rich trajectory optimization typically requires additional modeling machinery—such as complementarity relaxation, smoothing, or specialized differentiable simulation—to obtain informative gradients across changing contact modes.
ContactKernels instead avoids this requirement by performing zero-order optimization directly over simulated interactions and using realized contact to adapt the sampling distribution.

To circumvent the limitations of model specification, learning-based methods learn contact-dependent behaviours from data.
Learning-from-Demonstration (LfD) learns insertion strategies from expert demonstrations [ 10 , 8 ] .
Reinforcement learning instead learns through interaction in simulation or the real world [ 16 , 6 , 23 , 30 ] .
Demonstrations can also bootstrap reinforcement learning and improve sample efficiency [ 3 , 16 , 26 , 19 ] .
Recent methods use human corrective feedback to further improve exploration [ 20 ] .
These methods can react to contact online.
However, the contact-to-action mapping is learned from prior experience.
Generalisation to unseen contact conditions therefore depends on the learned policy.
When this fails, adaptation requires further interaction, expert demonstrations, or policy fine-tuning.

Model-based and learning-based approaches thus provide complementary mechanisms for contact adaptation. Model-based methods explicitly reason about contact, but require an appropriate interaction model and control or optimization formulation. Learning-based methods can represent complex contact-dependent behaviours, but acquire the adaptation mechanism from prior experience.

Our approach instead estimates contact location and local contact geometry during execution.
We use this information within a zero-order optimization framework, where the estimated contact state directly changes where the controller searches for subsequent motions.
This enables test-time contact adaptation without additional policy training or differentiation through contact dynamics.

## II-B Sampling-based MPC for Contact-rich Manipulation

Sampling-based model predictive control (SMPC) performs online trajectory optimization by evaluating sampled control sequences through forward simulation [ 31 , 36 ] .
Rather than relying on gradients of the system dynamics, these methods optimize control by comparing the predicted performance of candidate trajectories [ 12 ] .
This makes them particularly attractive for contact-rich manipulation, where dynamics is nonlinear, hybrid, and difficult to differentiate due to intermittent contact, friction, and mode transitions.
When paired with modern parallelised simulation tools [ 32 ] , SMPC becomes a powerful paradigm for contact-rich robot control [ 9 , 25 ] .

Recent work has demonstrated this effectively for pushing and dextrous manipulation by including GPU-parallel physics rollouts inside the MPC loop [ 25 ] .
However, the literature for applying SMPC to the peg insertion task remains limited.
MPQ( λ \lambda ) [ 2 ] and CaPTURe [ 22 ] tackle transition model bias that arises from chosen approximation strategies, and uncertainty associated with changing contact modes in peg insertion setups respectively.
Both incorporate partially learned dynamics as an offline step, and do not evaluate on a real robot.
This leaves real-world peg insertion using parallel sampling simulation-based MPC largely unexplored.

However, applying SMPC to insertion does not by itself exploit the contact information acquired during execution.
Standard SMPC methods typically sample controls from generic proposal distributions [ 7 , 25 ] .
These distributions do not use the observed contact state to determine where to explore next.
This can lead to inefficient exploration after unintended contact.
ContactKernels addresses this gap by conditioning the proposal distribution on the estimated contact location and local geometry.
Contact therefore directly guides where the controller searches for subsequent motions.

## II-C Closing the Loop on Contact State

Integrating contact state information can improve adaptation during contact-rich insertion [ 15 , 24 , 14 ] .
Learning-based methods can incorporate tactile observations directly into a feedback policy [ 15 ] .
These methods can learn complex contact-dependent behaviours from high-dimensional sensory inputs.
However, the contact-to-action mapping is acquired during training.
The resulting adaptation therefore depends on the contact behaviours represented by the learned policy.

An alternative is to explicitly estimate a task-relevant contact state before selecting an action.
Kim and Rodriguez [ 14 ] estimate the extrinsic contact line between a grasped object and its environment.
An active tactile controller regulates the contact mode to improve this estimate.
The estimated contact line is then provided to an object-agnostic insertion policy trained in simulation.
This structured representation enables the policy to generalize across different object and hole geometries.

These approaches demonstrate the benefit of closing the loop on contact state.
However, the estimated contact state is still mapped to actions through a learned policy.
We instead use contact state to adapt the search process of an online optimizer.
ContactKernels estimates contact location and local contact geometry from measured wrenches.
This information directly shapes the proposal distribution of the SMPC controller.
Contact therefore determines where the controller searches for subsequent motions, without requiring the contact-to-action mapping itself to be learned.

2026-10-20.title: EvoAD: Self-Evolving Autonomous Driving via Latent World-Model Guided Post-hoc Reflection
2026-10-20.authors: Junjie Yang , Qiming Zhang , Yuyan Li , Shuqi Shen , Yusong Huang , Yanggang Sheng , Wenpeng Xu , Ziyi Shi , Tianshun Li , Yijie Chen , Yujia Wang , Jun Ma , Xinhu Zheng , Hongliang Lu , Hai Yang
2026-10-20.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have achieved rapid progress by learning unified policies that map sensor observations directly to driving trajectories. However, once deployed, these systems typically remain frozen: they may repeat similar decisions in similar scenes, and failures can only be addressed through costly data collection and retraining. This sharply contrasts with human drivers, who improve lifelong through experience, memory, and reflection. In this work, we ask whether autonomous driving systems can achieve similar post-deployment self-evolution to human drivers. We propose EvoAD, a self-evolving autonomous driving framework via latent world-model guided post-hoc reflection. EvoAD stores driving experiences in a bird’s-eye-view feature memory pool, retrieves scene-relevant precedents according to geometric and semantic similarity, and uses a latent world model to evaluate the future consequences of candidate trajectories in a compact planning-oriented space. Instead of treating memory as external textual contexts or using world models only for pre-action simulation, EvoAD transforms executed driving outcomes into reusable improvement signals for future decisions. This enables the system to diagnose how prior trajectories could have been improved and to refine behavior in similar future scenarios without retraining the base driving policy. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 show consistent improvements across reflection rounds and state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the potential of world models as reflective mechanisms for post-deployment self-evolution in autonomous driving.
2026-10-20.introduction:
End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving (AD) has advanced rapidly as a unified data-driven paradigm, where a single neural policy is trained on large-scale driving data to map raw sensor observations directly to driving trajectories ( Hu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ) .
Yet after training, these systems are typically deployed as frozen models: given the same scene, they are likely to repeat the same decision, and any failure observed after deployment can only be corrected through another costly cycle of data collection, labeling, and retraining ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Caesar et al., 2021 ) . In stark contrast, human drivers exhibit a fundamentally different form of competence. Even after obtaining a license, they continue to improve lifelong: they remember previously encountered situations, mentally revisit decisions that felt unsafe or suboptimal, and adjust their future behavior when similar scenarios arise ( Groeger, 2013 ; Fuller, 2005 ) . This contrast exposes a central limitation of current E2E AD systems: driving competence is never achieved once and for all; it continually evolves through experience, memory, and reflection.

A growing line of work has sought to recover this missing adaptability by moving self-improvement into the test-time loop, including online or test-time fine-tuning ( Wang et al., 2020 ; Hanselmann et al., 2022 ) , knowledge- and retrieval-augmented driving ( Yuan et al., 2024b ; Wen et al., 2023 ) , and score-based candidate re-ranking ( Li et al., 2024b ; Li et al., 2025c ) . However, retrieval and memory in these methods are typically used as external context, such as textual knowledge, high-level experience, or demonstration priors. They rarely provide feedback grounded in the actual consequences of the trajectory just produced by the planner. More recently, world models promise to bridge this gap by creating an imaginative space for action evaluation, where each candidate trajectory can be rolled forward into its possible visual or latent consequences ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Gao et al., 2023 ; Lu et al., 2024 ) . Consequently, many AD approaches have incorporated world models as forward simulators, using them to imagine future outcomes before selecting an action, such as World4Drive ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , and Drive-WM ( Wang et al., 2024b ) . In these systems, world models behave like a forward-looking advisor: they imagine possible futures to guide action selection before the vehicle acts. This dominant use of world models, however, obscures a broader question about their role in AD: can their imaginative capacity support human-like self-evolution through post-hoc reflection?

In this study, we propose EvoAD , a self-evolving AD framework based on latent world-model guided post-hoc reflection. As shown in Fig. 1 , rather than treating a trained E2E model as a fixed policy, EvoAD converts past driving experiences into reusable improvement signals for future decision-making.
First, we introduce bird’s-eye-view (BEV) feature-based memory to store reflected driving experiences, including scene representations, trajectories, future latents, and evaluation feedback. Compared with text-only memory or high-level action descriptions, BEV-level memory better preserves the geometric layout and spatial relations of the driving scene, making retrieval more aligned with the structure of AD decisions.
Second, we use a latent world model to imagine the future consequences of candidate trajectories in a compact planning-oriented latent space, which enables safer or more efficient trajectory evaluation without expensive pixel-level future reconstruction.
Third, EvoAD performs outcome-aware post-hoc reflection based on trajectory evaluation feedback, so the reflection is not merely past-action evidence, but a targeted improvement based on the previous weakness. In doing so, EvoAD enables a trained base model to accumulate experience, retrieve relevant prior reflections, and refine future behavior without retraining.

In summary, our contributions are threefold: 1) We propose a self-evolving AD framework based on post-hoc reflection, enabling AD systems to improve after deployment without retraining the base model; 2) We redefine the role of the world model as a post-hoc reflective evaluator, which explores better alternatives in a latent imaginative space; and 3) We introduce BEV-feature-based memory and retrieval, which stores scenario-level driving experiences and retrieves relevant ones to support future decision refinement. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 show that EvoAD improves WoTE from 88.3 to 93.4 PDMS and from 84.2 to 91.5 EPDMS, respectively, achieving state-of-the-art performance on both benchmarks.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Post-hoc Reflection and Retrieval Memory for Autonomous Driving

Recent vision-language and multimodal driving models increasingly use reasoning, explanation, retrieval, and memory to support driving decisions. Existing studies have explored scene-graph-based explanations for auditable decision making ( Belmecheri et al., 2024 ) , retrieval-augmented expert demonstrations for control and explanation ( Yuan et al., 2024b ) , reward-aligned reasoning for trajectory or meta-action prediction ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and diagnostic analyses of the reasoning-planning disconnect in driving vision-language models. In parallel, retrieval and memory have been introduced to incorporate traffic regulations, expert trajectories, commonsense knowledge, and past experience into driving systems ( Cai et al., 2026 ; Fu et al., 2025 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) . Yet prior methods mainly use post-hoc reasoning for explanation or retrieval as auxiliary knowledge, external demonstrations, or planner priors, lacking a closed-loop mechanism that reflects on the model’s own driving outcomes and turns them into reusable improvement signals. EvoAD fills this gap by using latent world-model feedback to evaluate its own trajectory consequences, store reflected experiences in BEV-feature memory, and retrieve relevant experiences to refine future decisions.

## 2.2 Latent World Modeling in Autonomous Driving

World models provide a natural substrate for deliberative AD by simulating possible future scene evolutions before action execution. Early driving world models such as Drive-WM couple multiview future visual forecasting with planning by rolling out candidate futures and selecting actions according to predicted outcomes ( Wang et al., 2024b ) . Recent methods increasingly move from pixel-level generation to planning-oriented latent representations: LAW predicts future scene features as self-supervision for E2E driving ( Li et al., 2024a ) ; World4Drive learns intention-aware physical latent dynamics for multimodal trajectory selection and closed-loop performance ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) ; WorldRFT fine-tunes latent world models with reinforcement signals to better align them with planning objectives ( Yang et al., 2026 ) ; and DriveWorld-VLA unifies vision-language-action planning and latent-space world modeling within a shared latent state ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . These studies establish latent world models as planning-aware future simulators. EvoAD builds on this trend but uses the latent world model differently: instead of merely predicting future states or selecting actions, it uses latent future feedback for post-hoc reflection and iterative self-evolution of the driving policy.

2026-10-20.title: From Likelihood to Utility: Quality-Axis Diffusion for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
2026-10-20.authors: Junjie Yang , Ziyi Shi , Shuqi Shen , Xinhu Zheng , Hongliang Lu , Hai Yang
2026-10-20.abstract:
Diffusion models have become a dominant paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving, yet existing planners organize trajectory generation along the Gaussian-noise axis, treating driving utility only as an auxiliary guidance or selection signal. We instead formulate diffusion along a driving-quality axis. We propose QualiDrive, which constructs scene-specific quality ladders by ranking observed trajectories according to measured driving utility and learns to reverse this ordered degradation through
ordered low-to-high-quality refinement. Each reverse step is conditioned on the scene, ego state, current trajectory, and target quality level, progressively refining trajectories toward higher driving quality. On NAVSIM, QualiDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on v1 and a state-of-the-art 92.74 EPDMS on v2. QualiDrive improves Oracle EPDMS only modestly over endpoint-only quality supervision (98.52 to 98.57), but substantially increases the fractions of candidates above 0.95 and 0.98 EPDMS from
12.94%/9.71% to 21.53%/15.93%, raising selected EPDMS from 92.63 to
92.74. These results suggest that diffusion is not merely a process of denoising, but one of progressive quality-ordered refinement.
2026-10-20.introduction:
End-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has emerged as a promising paradigm for directly mapping sensor observations to future trajectories [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] .
Leveraging large-scale human driving demonstrations, existing E2E systems primarily learn to generate trajectories with high likelihood under the human demonstration distribution [ 6 , 7 ] .
However, high likelihood does not necessarily imply high driving utility, as human driving demonstrations are not necessarily optimal, and high-utility driving must simultaneously account for multiple objectives, such as safety, progress, and comfort [ 8 , 9 ] .

Recently, diffusion models have been increasingly adopted for trajectory planning due to their ability to generate diverse candidates [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Conventional diffusion-based planners are organized along a Gaussian noise axis: their denoisers are trained to recover clean human demonstrations from Gaussian-corrupted trajectories, learning to eliminate synthetic perturbations. Yet diversity alone provides no guarantee of higher utility, and additional denoising steps may not translate into better plans [ 13 , 14 ] . This reveals a fundamental mismatch between the generative process and the planning objective: conventional diffusion progresses toward likely demonstrations, whereas planning ultimately seeks high-quality trajectories.

Prior work has sought to improve diffusion-based planning from both the generation and selection sides. Generation-oriented methods introduce reinforcement learning or safety guidance to steer diffusion toward higher-quality trajectories [ 15 , 11 ] , while selection-oriented methods enhance candidate ranking through progressive scoring or multi-teacher distillation [ 16 , 17 ] . Despite using driving utility for guidance or selection, diffusion remains organized along the noise axis, with driving utility serving only as an auxiliary signal. Consequently, the generated candidate pool may still contain many low-quality trajectories, placing a heavy burden on downstream selection. This motivates a more fundamental question: can driving utility itself serve as the semantic coordinate of trajectory diffusion?

In this study, we propose QualiDrive, a quality-axis diffusion framework for E2E trajectory generation.
As illustrated in Figure 1 , we organize the diffusion process by ordered quality levels rather than Gaussian-noise levels, transforming reverse diffusion from trajectory reconstruction into progressive quality refinement.
Specifically, the forward process constructs a sequence of quality-degradation transitions from a high-scoring target trajectory toward a low-scoring anchor, while the reverse process learns to progressively move trajectories toward higher driving scores conditioned on their current quality levels.
By supervising these ordered transitions with explicit quality scores, each reverse step is directly associated with measurable utility improvement.
Consequently, driving quality is embedded into the trajectory generation, guiding diffusion toward higher-quality trajectories rather than higher likelihood under the demonstration distribution.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce quality-axis diffusion, which replaces Gaussian noise with driving quality as the diffusion coordinate, shifting generation from demonstration recovery to utility improvement.

We propose QualiDrive, a framework that combines quality-conditioned trajectory refinement with multi-objective scoring for progressive generation and final selection.

We achieve state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM v1 and v2, reaching 92.74 EPDMS on v2—2.34 points above the previous best, while substantially increasing the density of high-quality trajectory candidates.

1. We introduce quality-axis diffusion, which replaces Gaussian noise with driving quality as the diffusion coordinate, shifting generation from demonstration recovery to utility improvement.

2. We propose QualiDrive, a framework that combines quality-conditioned trajectory refinement with multi-objective scoring for progressive generation and final selection.

3. We achieve state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM v1 and v2, reaching 92.74 EPDMS on v2—2.34 points above the previous best, while substantially increasing the density of high-quality trajectory candidates.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 End-to-End Trajectory Generation

End-to-end autonomous driving directly maps sensor observations to future
trajectories within a unified learnable system. Early planning-oriented
frameworks predict trajectories from structured scene representations or
planning queries [ 3 , 4 , 18 , 19 ] . More recent proposal-based
planners construct multiple candidates from learned queries, anchors, or
factorized vocabularies, then select a final plan using scene-conditioned
scores [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] . Hydra-MDP
distills human and rule-based teachers, while CLOVER learns evaluator
sub-scores for proposal ranking [ 24 , 22 ] . Online
trajectory evaluation and register-token scene compression further strengthen
candidate scoring [ 25 , 26 ] . These methods improve
coverage and selection, but generation remains bounded by learned proposal
sets or discrete trajectory vocabularies, motivating flexible generative
models.

## 2.2 Diffusion-Based Trajectory Generation

Diffusion provides a flexible way to model multimodal trajectory
distributions through iterative generation [ 27 ] .
In end-to-end driving, DiffusionDrive combines multimodal trajectory anchors
with a truncated diffusion schedule for efficient and diverse
generation [ 10 ] , while DiffRefiner uses diffusion to
refine coarse proposals toward stronger scene compliance [ 28 ] . Subsequent work enhances diffusion planning with
additional optimization signals. Diffusion Planner uses classifier guidance
to incorporate safety constraints, goals, and driving styles [ 29 , 11 ] ; SafeDiffuser imposes
safety constraints during the reverse process [ 30 ] ;
and Diffusion-ES combines a diffusion prior with gradient-free evolutionary
search for black-box rewards [ 31 ] . DiffusionDriveV2
uses reinforcement learning to suppress low-quality modes and explore beyond
demonstrations [ 15 ] , while Gen-Drive improves
generation with a learned reward model and reinforcement-learning
fine-tuning [ 32 ] . Despite their different mechanisms,
these approaches retain diffusion time or noise level as the generative
coordinate and introduce driving quality through guidance, constraints,
search, or reward optimization. Cold Diffusion shows that diffusion need not
be tied to Gaussian corruption, as paired degradation and restoration
operators can define a generative process [ 33 ] . Building on
this view, QualiDrive uses measured driving quality as the diffusion
coordinate, directly learning lower-to-higher-quality trajectory refinement.
