2026-10-20.title: PrismPlan: A Shared GPU Substrate for Motion Planning Across Paradigms
2026-10-20.authors: Hong Wu , ChaoXuan Liu , ShuJie Wang
2026-10-20.abstract:
GPU acceleration has made motion planning one to two orders of magnitude
faster ( Pan and Manocha, 2012 ) , but it has not made the three
paradigms—sampling, search, and optimization—comparable to one another:
every GPU-accelerated planner is built around a single paradigm, so comparing
across libraries also compares their collision checkers. All three, however,
bottleneck on the same GPU primitive: batched collision detection and the batched forward
kinematics beneath it. PrismPlan builds that primitive once, as a shared
substrate of per-sphere collision–kinematics device code that every planner
consumes. Because they all execute the same device code, the backend is held
fixed by construction and the paradigms can be compared head-to-head. We run six
planners over 1800 MotionBenchMaker problems on three robots (7–14 DoF, one a
dual-arm whole-body composite) at an equal 2 s budget. On the 7-DoF Panda,
sampling (pRRTC) is the most reliable paradigm at 98%, while parallel search
(wPA ∗ SE) follows within four points at a 3 – 4 × 3\text{--}4\times lower median
latency, and the local optimizers trail well behind when made to solve from
scratch. On the 14-DoF dual-arm composite, sampling still solves about 90% of
feasible problems, while no search or optimization planner clears a third of
them. Our open-source code is available at https://github.com/XiaoyubotMotionTeam/PrismPlan .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Sampling, search, and optimization each win on some motion-planning problems and
lose on others ( Fishman et al., 2022 ) , and a practitioner with a GPU has no principled way to choose
between them: every GPU-accelerated planner is built around a single paradigm, so
any comparison across them compares collision checkers, sphere models, and
floating-point paths as much as it compares algorithms. This paper removes that
confound. We observe that all three paradigms bottleneck on one GPU
primitive—batched collision detection and the batched forward kinematics
beneath it—so we build that primitive once as a shared substrate and let each
paradigm consume it through a thin reduction. Six planners spanning the three
paradigms then run on bit-identical device code, which turns “which paradigm,
when” from a matter of opinion into a controlled measurement. That measurement,
over 1800 MotionBenchMaker problems on three robots at an equal budget, says that
configuration-space dimension —not clutter—is what separates the
paradigms, and that by 14 DoF the ordering has inverted relative to what today’s
GPU tooling would lead one to expect. The rest of this section sets out why the
question is worth asking, what stands in the way, and how the system answers it.

Motion planning remains a central bottleneck for robotic manipulation, and two
trends have sharpened the need for throughput rather than single-query latency
alone. First, learning-based methods (imitation, reinforcement learning, and data
generation for foundation models) consume planned trajectories by the thousands,
and the planner rather than the learner is often the rate-limiting step. Second,
reactive, contact-rich applications must replan many candidate motions
concurrently. Both regimes favor a planner that solves a batch of B B problems at
once and amortizes fixed costs across the batch, which maps naturally onto the
GPU’s data-parallel execution model. Our substrate is batch-parallel within a
solve, but the API we ship is single-problem, so we report
intra-solve scaling (§ 6.2 ) and leave a concurrent
batch-of- B B entry point to future work (§ 3.4 ). The contribution
we make is orthogonal to raw throughput: it is the controlled measurement
described above, not a new speed record.

GPU-accelerated planning has responded to this need. cuRobo ( Sundaralingam et al., 2023 ) and its whole-body successor ( Sundaralingam et al., 2026 ) demonstrate that
parallelized collision-free trajectory generation can be one to two orders of
magnitude faster than CPU baselines, and parallel sampling-based planners such
as pRRTC ( Huang et al., 2025 ) (itself built on the vectorized collision checking
of VAMP ( Thomason et al., 2024 ) ) show comparable gains for
RRT-Connect ( Kuffner and LaValle, 2000 ) . These systems are single-paradigm artifacts
by design. A practitioner ought to be able to pick
the planner a scenario calls for, and to compare candidates on one backend;
committing to a single paradigm forecloses both. Three gaps follow.

Production GPU libraries are optimization-centric. Their internals may contain
geometric or graph-search components, but those act as seeding subroutines inside
the optimizer; they are not sampling-based
(RRT/PRM) ( LaValle, 2006 ; LaValle, 1998 ; Kavraki et al., 1996 ) or search-based
(motion-primitive lattice A ∗ /MHA ∗ /ARA ∗ ) ( Hart et al., 1968 ; Aine et al., 2014 ; Likhachev et al., 2003 ) planners that a user can invoke on their own and compare against one another. No
GPU tool today answers the question of which paradigm to use for a given problem
class.

Comparing planners across libraries conflates the algorithm with its collision and
kinematics implementation ( Pan et al., 2012 ) : differences in sphere models, ESDF
conventions, early-exit heuristics, and floating-point paths can dominate the
metrics under study. A trustworthy comparison of paradigms requires that the
collision predicate and forward kinematics be bit-identical across all planners.
No existing multi-paradigm platform provides that property, since the one
multi-paradigm framework in wide use, MoveIt ( Chitta et al., 2012 ) , is a CPU
orchestrator whose plugins each carry their own collision representation.

On whole-body composite systems, meaning dual-arm and humanoid platforms modeled
as a single high-DoF kinematic tree with self-collision, the only GPU-native
option is trajectory optimization ( Sundaralingam et al., 2026 ) . Whether sampling or
search remains viable and competitive at these dimensionalities, on the same
backend, is unknown.

These three gaps share a root cause. Although sampling, search, and optimization
differ in how they explore configuration space, their GPU cost is dominated by the
same primitive: batched collision detection together with the batched forward
kinematics it depends on. Sampling spends its budget validating candidate edges,
search evaluates batches of successor edges, and optimization queries costs and
gradients along a trajectory. Each of these is a batched query against a
robot-vs-scene collision–kinematics primitive, which suggests reducing planning
across paradigms to one shared GPU substrate instead of accelerating each paradigm
in isolation.

We realize this reduction as a system. A common substrate provides per-sphere
forward kinematics and sphere-vs-scene geometry, tested against oriented bounding
boxes and an in-house Euclidean signed distance field, zero-copy from the same GPU
tensors the perception and optimization stack already holds. Each paradigm then
applies its own thin reduction on top of that substrate: a boolean
any-collision test for sampling and search, a minimum-clearance reduction for
anytime-optimal sampling, and a summed hinge penalty for optimization, which
supplies the differentiable signal a boolean cannot. The boolean collision
predicate and the forward kinematics are literally the same device code for every
planner, so a cross-paradigm benchmark holds the backend fixed by construction.

We do not claim to invent the algorithms we host: pRRTC ( Huang et al., 2025 ) and its
VAMP-derived collision checking ( Thomason et al., 2024 ) , STOMP ( Kalakrishnan et al., 2011 ) ,
multi-heuristic search ( Aine et al., 2014 ) , and the BIT ∗ /EIT ∗ family ( Gammell et al., 2015 ; Strub and Gammell, 2022 ) all have prior origins. Nor is a
multi-paradigm framework itself new; MoveIt established that a decade ago. Our
novelty lies one layer below the framework, in the shared GPU primitive substrate
that otherwise dissimilar algorithm families consume through different call
patterns, the reduction design that makes such sharing possible, and the
comparison it enables.

Our three contributions answer the three gaps in order.

A unifying reduction and a shared GPU substrate. We identify
batched collision–kinematics as the common GPU bottleneck of all three
paradigms and give a substrate-plus-reduction design that maps sampling to
batched edge validation, search to batched successor/edge evaluation, and
optimization to batched cost/gradient queries, all over one set of per-sphere
primitives. The substrate is agnostic to the planner built on top of it: a new
algorithm need only express its queries as one of these batched reductions, so
the three paradigms we instantiate here are an initial population of the
substrate and not a closed set.

Runtime-arbitrary robots and a uniform result contract. We lift the compile-time fixed-robot restriction of upstream GPU planners to
runtime-specified kinematics, and expose every planner behind one problem
interface that returns a common result struct with wall-clock solve time. The
uniform interface is what makes the cross-paradigm comparison, and the empirical
conclusions we draw from it, possible. Only wall-clock time is exposed
uniformly; a per-planner kernel/copy breakdown is not yet instrumented
(§ 5 ).

A shared substrate that carries whole-body composites. The
substrate is parameterized only by the robot’s sphere set and allowed-collision
matrix, so composite high-DoF systems require no paradigm-specific machinery
(§ 4.5 ). We evaluate this claim rather than assert it: all six
planners run unmodified on a 14-DoF dual-arm Baxter composite, with both arms
fused into one kinematic tree and an inter-arm self-collision specification, as
well as on 7-DoF and 8-DoF single arms (§ 6.4 ). The
composite is also where the paradigms separate most sharply.

We call the resulting system PrismPlan : as a prism refracts one beam into
its component colors, it refracts a single batched collision–kinematics substrate
into a spectrum of planning paradigms, three of them in this release. The name also
reads P arallel R obot-motion I n a S hared M anifold .
Figure 1 summarizes the system: one batched
collision–kinematics substrate, consumed zero-copy by three paradigm-specific
reductions behind a single problem interface.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

We position PrismPlan against four bodies of work: multi-paradigm planning
frameworks, the specific algorithms and collision engines we build upon, CPU
planning libraries, and GPU-accelerated planners. In each case the distinction
that matters is not whether multiple paradigms coexist, but what they share
underneath.

MoveIt ( Chitta et al., 2012 ) is the canonical multi-paradigm planning framework:
through its plugin system it unifies sampling-based planning via
OMPL ( Şucan et al., 2012 ) , optimization via CHOMP ( Ratliff et al., 2009 ) and
STOMP ( Kalakrishnan et al., 2011 ) , industrial motion via Pilz, and historically
search-based planning via SBPL. A unified multi-paradigm framework is not,
by itself, a contribution, and the distinction we draw is architectural.
MoveIt is a CPU orchestrator: each plugin owns its collision representation and
world model, so the planners share neither a common GPU data structure nor a
bit-identical collision predicate. MoveIt can route a query to different
paradigms, but it can neither accelerate them on a common GPU backend nor support
a controlled comparison in which the collision and kinematics implementation is
held fixed. PrismPlan differs here: all three paradigms consume one GPU substrate,
zero-copy, which is what delivers GPU acceleration and bit-identical comparison
at once. This is the difference between a framework and a shared
primitive .

We credit our upstream sources explicitly and claim no part of their invention.
pRRTC ( Huang et al., 2025 ) contributes GPU-parallel RRT-Connect and, following the
SIMD/SIMT vectorized collision checking of VAMP ( Thomason et al., 2024 ) , the
edge-validation kernels we reuse. Trajectory optimization draws on
STOMP ( Kalakrishnan et al., 2011 ) , CHOMP ( Ratliff et al., 2009 ) , and Gaussian-process motion
planning ( Mukadam et al., 2018 ) ; our search module
implements multi-heuristic A ∗ ( Aine et al., 2014 ) and weighted Parallel
A ∗ for Slow Expansions (wPA ∗ SE) ( Phillips et al., 2014 ; Pohl, 1970 ) ; and our anytime-optimal
sampler is informed by the BIT ∗ /EIT ∗ family ( Karaman and Frazzoli, 2011 ; Gammell et al., 2015 ; Strub and Gammell, 2022 ) . Our contribution is the unification of
these paradigms over a shared GPU primitive substrate, their generalization to
runtime-specified robots, and the cross-paradigm benchmark this makes possible.

Mature CPU libraries are typically organized around a single paradigm: OMPL for
sampling ( Şucan et al., 2012 ) , search-based libraries such as SRMP ( Mishani et al., 2025 ) for lattice/heuristic search, and TrajOpt ( Schulman et al., 2014 ) /CHOMP ( Ratliff et al., 2009 ) for
optimization. They provide neither GPU batching nor a common backend across
paradigms, and so address a different regime, single-query latency, from the
high-throughput batched setting we target.

cuRobo ( Sundaralingam et al., 2023 ) and cuRobo v2 ( Sundaralingam et al., 2026 ) are the closest
GPU systems. They pair a highly engineered shared GPU backend (collision,
kinematics, and GPU-native perception) with trajectory optimization, and cuRobo
v2 extends this to whole-body dual-arm and humanoid systems. That backend,
however, feeds a single paradigm: geometric and graph components exist only as
seeding subroutines within the optimizer, not as independently invocable planners
that can be compared with one another. PrismPlan feeds one backend to three
paradigms that remain first-class and comparable, and it demonstrates sampling and
search, not only optimization, on whole-body systems. What separates us from
cuRobo v2 is therefore the three comparable paradigms, including on whole-body
systems, and not multi-arm support, which cuRobo v2 already provides.

Conflict-based methods such as CBS ( Sharon et al., 2015 ) and its bounded-suboptimal
variants address multi-agent coordination on the CPU. We treat multi-arm setups as
whole-body composite systems, that is, as a single high-DoF kinematic tree
with self-collision, rather than as coordinated agents; multi-agent coordination
is left to future work.

MoveIt offers a framework but no shared GPU primitive; cuRobo offers a shared GPU
backend but serves optimization alone. To our knowledge no prior work reduces all
three planning paradigms to a single GPU primitive substrate and uses it to
benchmark them fairly, which is the gap PrismPlan fills.

2026-10-20.title: Learning Whole-Body Kinetic Coordination for Wheeled-Quadruped Long-Range Throwing
2026-10-20.authors: Qinglian Wu , Yidian Hu , Weiqi Fan , Yutian Zhang , Siyuan Ma , Jiaqi Zhai , Wei Dong , Li Xu
2026-10-20.abstract: Long-range throwing on unstructured terrain is a key capability for mobile robots in delivery and retrieval tasks, but it requires high release velocity, coordinated whole-body motion, and robustness to terrain-induced disturbances. We present a whole-body kinetic-coordination framework for a wheeled-quadruped manipulator that combines kinetic-chain arm modeling with SQP-based trajectory optimization and a reference-guided reinforcement learning policy for coordinated base motion. The manipulator is first reduced to a kinetic-chain model and optimized under kinematic and dynamic constraints to produce a high-speed throwing reference. On a stationary base, the optimized arm trajectory reaches a release speed of 12.75 m/s and a throwing distance of 16.68 m. When whole-body coordination is enabled, the system further increases the release speed to 16.64 m/s and the throwing distance to 28.25 m. We then integrate the mobility of the wheeled-quadruped platform and validate the complete policy through hardware experiments on flat ground, grass, slopes, and rough roads. The results show that kinetic-chain optimization and whole-body coordination together enable robust long-range throwing across diverse unstructured terrains.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Mobile robots with manipulators are increasingly used for outdoor delivery, inspection, and intervention tasks, where targets often lie beyond the immediate manipulation workspace. Throwing offers an efficient way to extend the reachable range, but many practical scenarios require the robot to release the payload from a moving platform rather than a stationary base. This run-and-throw setting turns throwing from an arm-centric skill into a whole-body mobile manipulation problem.

Executing high-speed throwing on unstructured terrain creates a tightly coupled whole-body control problem. The arm motion required for release velocity generates large self-induced reaction forces on the floating base, while uneven terrain continuously changes support conditions and body posture. The controller must therefore coordinate base motion and manipulator acceleration in a single dynamic process, rather than treating locomotion stabilization and throwing execution as separate modules.

Beyond stability, long-range throwing requires efficient kinetic energy transfer from proximal joints to the distal end-effector. Inspired by the human kinetic chain, which amplifies release velocity via proximal-to-distal motion propagation, the robot must preserve this inertial coupling despite base disturbances. This motivates a unified framework combining terrain-robust whole-body stabilization with kinetic-chain-guided arm motion.

Prior work has studied terrain-robust locomotion, whole-body loco-manipulation, and robotic throwing from complementary perspectives. Learning-based locomotion controllers have enabled legged robots to traverse irregular terrains through large-scale reinforcement learning with simulated-response and implicit-terrain modeling [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , but these methods mainly address base mobility and do not consider coordination with a mounted manipulator. Whole-body control enables legged and wheeled-legged robots to coordinate locomotion with manipulation [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , yet these methods typically focus on general manipulation or tracking tasks rather than highly dynamic motions on unstructured outdoor terrains. Robotic throwing has been explored through kinetic-chain modeling [ 7 ] and learning-based planning [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] , but most approaches are designed for fixed or slow-moving bases and do not address whole-body dynamic coordination. More recently, studies have begun integrating throwing with legged systems [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] , showing that base motion can improve throwing performance. Nevertheless, long-range throwing on unstructured terrain remains largely unexplored. In this setting, rapid arm acceleration can severely disturb a floating base, requiring coordinated kinetic-chain energy transfer with robust whole-body stabilization.

In this work, we address terrain-robust long-range throwing with a reference-guided whole-body reinforcement learning framework. We first optimize a high-speed arm reference trajectory with SQP on an approximate kinetic-chain model, then train a whole-body policy to track this reference while coordinating the manipulator and wheeled-quadruped base. The resulting formulation balances proximal-to-distal energy transfer with traction and whole-body stability. Experiments show that the unified policy enables consistent long-range throwing across diverse unstructured terrains.

We summarize our contributions as follows:

A whole-body RL framework that coordinates the wheeled-quadruped base and manipulator under terrain disturbances and arm-induced reaction forces.

A kinetic-chain-based trajectory optimization method that increases release velocity through proximal-to-distal energy transfer under manipulator constraints.

Extensive hardware and simulation validation of the proposed method on flat ground, rough roads, slopes, and grass, demonstrating robust run-and-throw behavior.

1. A whole-body RL framework that coordinates the wheeled-quadruped base and manipulator under terrain disturbances and arm-induced reaction forces.

2. A kinetic-chain-based trajectory optimization method that increases release velocity through proximal-to-distal energy transfer under manipulator constraints.

3. Extensive hardware and simulation validation of the proposed method on flat ground, rough roads, slopes, and grass, demonstrating robust run-and-throw behavior.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Whole-body loco-manipulation has progressed from decoupled locomotion-manipulation pipelines to unified policies that coordinate the robot body and arm. Early methods combined a learned locomotion policy with model-based manipulation, allowing the base controller to compensate for arm-induced disturbances but still relying on a decoupled control structure [ 4 ] , while later work learned unified policies that integrate locomotion and manipulation within a single control framework [ 5 ] . Whole-body task-space tracking has also been improved through a reward-fusion module that enables precise 6D end-effector pose tracking [ 6 ] . Recent coordinated policies have achieved dynamic skills such as badminton playing and accurate prehensile throwing with legged manipulators [ 13 , 14 ] . In contrast, this work focuses on terrain-robust long-range throwing, where the robot must coordinate whole-body stability on unstructured terrain with explicit kinetic-chain energy transfer for high-speed release.

a) Unified Whole-Body Control: Whole-body control has been increasingly studied as an alternative to modular locomotion-manipulation pipelines. Fu et al. [ 5 ] showed that a unified reinforcement learning policy can coordinate the legs and arm more effectively than decoupled controllers, highlighting the promise of unified control for mobile manipulation. However, existing methods have largely focused on relatively moderate manipulation motions and do not explicitly address complex terrain conditions, leaving the manipulator’s full dynamic potential underexploited. Our work builds on this unified-policy perspective and targets terrain-robust long-range throwing by coordinating whole-body stability with kinetic-chain-driven high-speed release under terrain disturbances.

b) Kinetic-Chain-Based Throwing: Kinetic-chain modeling has been used to generate high-speed throwing motions by exploiting proximal-to-distal energy transfer. Senoo et al. [ 7 ] derived approximate swing dynamics and decomposed the throwing motion into basis functions, showing that inertial coupling can amplify distal joint velocity for fast release. However, their formulation was developed for a fixed-base manipulator. Here, we extend this principle to a wheeled-quadruped platform, where whole-body coordination enables the arm to exploit a moving base and thereby expand its effective throwing capability under real joint constraints.

2026-10-20.title: AutoPruner: Agentic Depth Pruning for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-20.authors: Tao Lin , Yikeng Chen , Qiwei Liang , Zinan Xie , Zhengtu Liang , Renjing Xu
2026-10-20.abstract:
Layer pruning reduces the size and inference cost of vision-language-action
(VLA) models, but selecting a deployable configuration requires deciding both
which layers to remove and how to recover task performance. These decisions
depend on the model and task, and a failed trial can reflect either the
deletion set or insufficient recovery. We present AutoPruner, an agent-driven
framework that jointly searches pruning structures and recovery recipes
through closed-loop experimentation. Offline layer interventions measure
changes in action output to provide functional evidence. An LLM agent combines
this evidence with evaluation history and retained diagnoses to propose
deletion sets and recovery recipes within a search budget. Each proposal is
executed and evaluated on the target tasks, and the resulting feedback guides
the next experiment. Across OpenVLA-OFT, StarVLA, and FastWAM on four LIBERO
suites, AutoPruner removes 16.7–87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining
task success above 90%, with measured inference speedups of up to
2.50 × \times . Further analysis shows that functional probes identify action-sensitive layers despite high representation similarity, and that recovery can make previously failing structures viable.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models rely on billion-parameter
backbones whose memory and computation requirements constrain robot
deployment [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Runtime techniques including token
skipping and computation caching can reduce inference cost without
shrinking the stored model [ 4 , 5 ] . Layer pruning instead removes transformer
blocks, reducing model size and backbone computation [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . The challenge is
finding a deletion set and recovery recipe that preserve task success
on the deployment.

Structure and recovery are coupled. A deletion set that initially disrupts
behavior may become viable after recovery. In our experiments, two deletion
sets exhibit a reversal in observed task performance after the same recovery
procedure. Immediate pruning damage alone therefore cannot determine the
preferred deployment configuration. Feasible structures also vary across
models and tasks: some tolerate long contiguous deletions, while others
require preserving sensitive internal layers. These observations motivate
joint selection of deletion sets and recovery recipes for each deployment.
Single-layer measurements guide this selection, while task evaluations
reveal the combined effect of deleting multiple layers and recovering the policy.

Each trial may require recovery training and hundreds of closed-loop
rollouts. When performance falls short, the next decision is whether to
revise the deletion set or try another recovery recipe. Failure alone cannot
distinguish an unsuitable structure from insufficient recovery; previous
trials provide context for choosing the next step. As
Figure (a) illustrates, manual pruning requires repeated human
intervention to interpret results and rerun experiments. We therefore treat pruning as an iterative experimental process in which previous trials determine the next structure–recovery configuration to evaluate.

We introduce AutoPruner , an agentic framework that jointly searches
deletion sets and recovery recipes for a target deployment, as shown in
Figure (b). Layer interventions measure changes in action
output, providing functional evidence for initial proposals. AutoPruner uses
an LLM agent to integrate functional measurements, trial history, and
diagnoses, jointly revising deletion sets and recovery recipes through
closed-loop task feedback within a search budget. Model-specific tools
execute proposals, and closed-loop evaluation identifies configurations
meeting the target success threshold. The user selects a passing
configuration for export as a physically pruned checkpoint with its
evaluation records.

We evaluate pruning and recovery on OpenVLA-OFT [ 9 ] , StarVLA [ 3 ] , and FastWAM [ 10 ] .
On OpenVLA-OFT Object, the pruned policy retains four of 32 backbone
layers with 92.6% success, reducing parameters from 7.71B to 2.05B and
latency from 102 to 41 ms. Further analyses examine functional layer evidence
and recovery-dependent pruning depth, while a logged OpenVLA-OFT search
demonstrates proposal revision using task feedback.

Our contributions are threefold:

We formulate deployment-specific VLA depth pruning as a
sequential decision problem over layer removal and recovery,
guided by closed-loop task performance under a search budget.

We develop AutoPruner, an agentic framework that integrates
functional measurements, retained diagnoses, and tool execution
to revise deletion sets and recovery recipes through experimental feedback.

We evaluate pruning and recovery across three heterogeneous VLA systems
on four LIBERO suites, removing 16.7–87.5% of backbone layers
with inference speedups of 1.11–2.50 × \times while maintaining
measured task success above 90% across all twelve deployments.

1. We formulate deployment-specific VLA depth pruning as a
sequential decision problem over layer removal and recovery,
guided by closed-loop task performance under a search budget.

2. We develop AutoPruner, an agentic framework that integrates
functional measurements, retained diagnoses, and tool execution
to revise deletion sets and recovery recipes through experimental feedback.

3. We evaluate pruning and recovery across three heterogeneous VLA systems
on four LIBERO suites, removing 16.7–87.5% of backbone layers
with inference speedups of 1.11–2.50 × \times while maintaining
measured task success above 90% across all twelve deployments.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Agentic Model Optimization

ReAct grounds language-model decisions in tool feedback [ 11 ] ,
and Reflexion retains textual reflections on task feedback to guide later
attempts [ 12 ] . This pattern has been extended to
score-guided optimization, code search, automated experimentation, and full
machine-learning
pipelines [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] .
Agentic methods have also been applied to compression. ProfilingAgent reasons
over static cost metrics and runtime profiles to plan layer-wise structured
pruning and post-training quantization [ 18 ] .
Agent-guided pruning selects layers from weight-activation and gradient
sensitivity profiles, using self-reflection and checkpoint rollback across
iterations [ 19 ] . These systems score a fixed
compression operator against static accuracy or perplexity proxies.
AutoPruner instead jointly selects deletion sets and recovery recipes using
functional measurements and closed-loop task success.

## II-B Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models

Compact VLAs such as TinyVLA and SmolVLA reduce model size or
action-generation costs [ 20 , 21 ] , while
OpenVLA-OFT and FAST improve action decoding or
representation [ 9 , 22 ] . Quantization reduces
inference memory [ 1 ] , and SQAP-VLA combines it with
visual-token pruning [ 23 ] . LightVLA and VLA-Pruner prune
visual tokens [ 4 , 24 ] , and VLA-Cache reuses
token features across control steps [ 5 ] . DeeR-VLA uses
early exits [ 25 ] , while MoLe-VLA and DySL-VLA dynamically
skip layers [ 26 , 27 ] , retaining backbone layers
in the model. EfficientVLA prunes layers in a training-free manner from input–output
hidden-state similarity and reuses diffusion-head
features [ 7 ] .

Removed capacity is typically restored by retraining a small set of
parameters or by distilling from the dense
model [ 28 , 29 , 30 ] ,
as in LLM-Pruner, which pairs structural pruning with low-rank
adaptation [ 31 ] . GLUESTICK recovers pruned VLA policies
through training-free weight-space correction [ 32 ] .
These methods apply recovery after the deletion set is fixed. AutoPruner
incorporates recovery into the search, evaluating deletion sets together with
recovery recipes on the target tasks.

AutoPruner proposes deletions from the action changes caused by individual
layer bypasses, and exports policies meeting the deployment success threshold
with the selected layers physically removed.

2026-10-20.title: Adaptive Rejection of Unknown Hybrid Sinusoidal Disturbances with Application to Humanoid Walking under Unknown Ground Motion
2026-10-20.authors: I-Chia Chang , Jacob Stewart , Petros A. Ioannou , Yan Gu
2026-10-20.abstract:
Legged robot control is not yet practical in non-inertial environments, where the ground and surroundings accelerate in the inertial Earth frame, mainly because of the unknown, time-varying, persistent perturbations caused by environmental motion, compounded by the associated hybrid robotic dynamics.
We formulate the problem of robot walking control as unknown-disturbance rejection for hybrid linear systems subject to hybrid sinusoidal disturbances (i.e., a linear combination of sinusoidal components with instantaneous phase jumps at discrete events).
First, necessary and sufficient conditions for solvability of the disturbance rejection problem are derived and used to characterize the control input that rejects the disturbances.
Second, with the Youla-Kucera parametrization, an output feedback controller capable of rejecting the disturbance is introduced.
Third, an adaptive law is proposed to estimate the controller parameters that reject the disturbance in the practical case where the disturbance and its parameters are unknown.
Experiments on bipedal walking during ground motion demonstrate substantially improved body-position tracking accuracy, with an average improvement of over 60 % 60\% in simulations and up to 47 % 47\% in real-world experiments.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Legged locomotion in non-inertial environments, where the ground accelerates relative to an inertial Earth frame, remains an open challenge as the ground motion induces unknown, time-varying, persistent perturbations to the complex robot dynamics [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Legged robot dynamics associated with locomotion can be modeled as a hybrid, nonlinear dynamical system, with the shifts in the support-foot position and the body velocity, upon a foot landing, formulated as discrete jumps [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
Additionally, surface motion acts as an unknown, time-varying exogenous disturbance applied to the robot’s supporting leg that continuously perturbs the system, rendering legged locomotion in non-inertial environments an unknown, time-varying disturbance rejection problem for hybrid dynamical systems.

By explicitly including non-inertial environments during control policy training, data-driven methods have enabled quadruped skateboarding [ 7 , 8 ] and balancing on diverse moving platforms [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] .
However, data-driven methods typically cannot provide theoretical performance guarantees, and the tasks considered primarily focus on quadrupedal locomotion, which is inherently more stable than bipedal locomotion.
Prior feedback and predictive control literature typically utilizes reduced-order models to ensure real-time computation and simplify the challenge by assuming full ground-motion knowledge [ 12 , 3 ] , treating environment dynamics as simple bounded input perturbations [ 13 ] , or transforming the hybrid error dynamics to a discrete or continuous error system [ 14 , 3 ] .
In this paper, we directly handle the hybrid disturbance rejection problem with linear reduced-order models assuming the disturbance is the sum of sinusoids with unknown frequencies, amplitudes, and phases, which is an effective model for platform motion such as ship or wave-induced motion [ 1 ] .

Although the controller design for hybrid dynamical systems has been widely studied, e.g., output regulation [ 15 ] , output feedback stabilization [ 16 ] , and optimal tracking [ 17 ] , the output feedback control design for hybrid linear systems with unknown and unmatched sinusoidal disturbances for both continuous and discrete phases remains open.
For example, [ 18 , 19 ] study the ℒ 2 \mathcal{L}_{2} -gain from the disturbance with unknown structure to the output of a hybrid linear system. [ 20 ] proposes a model reference adaptive controller for nonlinear, time-varying, hybrid systems affected by matched and parametric uncertainties. [ 21 ] suppresses the disturbance for switched systems using a disturbance observer and state feedback.
In contrast, this paper aims to achieve unknown disturbance rejection with only output feedback through Youla-Kucera (YK) parameterization [ 22 , 23 ] .

The YK parameterization [ 22 , 23 ] describes the family of all stabilizing controllers for a linear time-invariant system in terms of a stable linear operator whose parameters may vary without destabilizing the closed-loop system.
The capability to ensure closed-loop stability is critical when designing an adaptive controller as the time variation of controller parameters is inevitable during adaptation.
Robust adaptive controllers exploit the ability to vary the parameters by using the swapping lemma [ 24 , 25 ] to generate a linear estimation equation whose optimal parameters result in a controller that makes the output zero [ 26 , 25 , 24 ] .
Combined, the YK structure and the swapping lemma offer a systematic framework for designing robust adaptive controllers for linear systems with guaranteed stability and robustness to noise, model uncertainty, and time-varying parameters [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 14 , 34 ] .
However, extending the observer-compensator structure of the YK parameterization to a hybrid linear system is not straightforward as the jump dynamics consistently inject time-varying transition effects into the system.

In this paper, motivated by bipedal locomotion in non-inertial environments, we analytically study disturbance rejection for hybrid linear dynamical systems subject to hybrid sinusoidal disturbances.
Our prior work [ 14 ] addressed the same locomotion control problem by assuming zero swing foot tracking error to transform the hybrid error system into a continuous one, enabling the use of continuous-system adaptive controllers but validated only in simulation on a five-link robot in MATLAB.
Here, we instead develop an adaptive controller directly for the hybrid linear system and integrate it into a proposed hierarchical control framework.
The new contributions of this work are:

We derive Hybrid Regulator Equations that give necessary and sufficient solvability conditions for the disturbance rejection problem in a class of hybrid linear systems. Their solutions are constant matrices, which makes them more tractable than the equations in [ 15 ] , whose solutions are time-varying matrices.

We develop an adaptive output feedback controller for hybrid linear systems with unknown and unmatched hybrid sinusoidal disturbances. This is enabled by (i) extending the observer-compensator structure of the YK parameterization to hybrid linear systems by canceling the time-varying transition effect using the hybrid structure (see Theorem 2 ), and (ii) deriving the Hybrid Swapping Lemma , which extends the continuous and discrete Swapping Lemma [ 24 , 25 ] to hybrid cases and yields a linear parameter estimation equation to estimate the compensator parameters that reject the disturbance without the knowledge of the disturbance state and characteristics.

The proposed hybrid adaptive controller is integrated into a hierarchical control framework for bipedal locomotion in non-inertial environments. The whole framework is validated in a high-fidelity MuJoCo simulator and a real-world experiment using a Digit robot walking on a platform with unknown and multi-directional motion. We show that the center-of-mass (CoM) tracking error is reduced by an average of 60 % 60\% in simulations and up to 47 % 47\% in hardware experiments, confirming the disturbance rejection capability of the proposed controller under complex and real-world uncertainties.

This paper is organized as follows.
We first focus on the abstracted disturbance rejection problem for hybrid linear systems; Section II – III presents preliminaries and problem formulation and Sections IV – VI propose an adaptive output feedback controller to resolve the abstracted problem.
Then, Section VII – IX applies the resulting adaptive controller to a bipedal robot walking on a moving platform and validate it in simulations and hardware experiments.
Section X provides discussions and Section XI concludes the work.

2026-10-20.title: A Heterogeneous UAV UGV Methodology for Aerial Tracking of Mini Autonomous Cars
2026-10-20.authors: Santiago Fernandez , Angel da Silva , Hiago Sodre , Pablo Moraes , Bruna Gutterres , Ricardo B. Grando
2026-10-20.comment: This paper was accepted at the Latin American Robotics Symposium LARS 2026
2026-10-20.abstract: Aerial tracking of autonomous ground vehicles can provide useful situational awareness in environments where fixed external perception infrastructure is unavailable. However, visual-only tracking from an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is limited by camera field of view, viewpoint changes, occlusions, and temporary loss of target visibility. This paper presents a heterogeneous UAV–UGV methodology for aerial tracking of small-scale autonomous ground vehicles in simulation. The system is implemented in ROS 2 and Gazebo Sim using a Tello-like UAV equipped with a front-facing RGB camera and multiple LIMO-like unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs). Three approaches are evaluated: a training-free color-marker baseline, a YOLO-based visual baseline, and a proposed UAV–UGV fusion method. The proposed method uses the same visual detector as the YOLO baseline, but combines visual detections with UGV state information to maintain the target estimate during visual gaps. The methods are evaluated across four scenarios: single-car tracking, crossing trajectories, occlusion, and UAV-assisted awareness. Results over 600 simulation runs show that the proposed fusion method achieves nearly continuous track coverage across all scenarios while reducing localization error relative to the YOLO baseline. Compared with the visual-only YOLO approach, the fusion method reduces RMSE by 37.3%, 64.2%, 62.6%, and 61.8% in the four evaluated scenarios, respectively. The method also enables conflict-awareness lead times of 10.20 s in the crossing scenario and 9.07 s in the UAV-assisted awareness scenario. These results indicate that heterogeneous UAV–UGV fusion can improve aerial tracking continuity and robustness when visual observations are intermittent.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Heterogeneous robotic teams combine platforms with complementary sensing, mobility, and computational capabilities. In air–ground systems, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) provide an elevated viewpoint and wide-area perception, while unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) offer stable ground-level motion, longer operational persistence, and direct interaction with the environment. This complementarity has motivated increasing interest in UAV–UGV cooperation for inspection, mapping, monitoring, search-and-rescue, and collaborative autonomy [ 8 , 3 ] .

Aerial tracking of autonomous ground vehicles can be particularly useful in environments where fixed external perception infrastructure is unavailable. This aerial perspective allows the UAV to simultaneously monitor multiple vehicles, detect potentially hazardous situations, and provide complementary information for trajectory coordination. This capability can support fleet monitoring, collision prevention, large-area inspection, and assistance to ground vehicles whose perception is limited by obstacles, short-range sensors, or unfavorable environmental conditions.

Despite these advantages, purely visual tracking is limited by the camera field of view, viewpoint changes, partial occlusions, and target appearance variations. These limitations become more critical in multi-robot scenarios where ground vehicles may cross paths, become partially occluded, or enter shared areas where early conflict awareness is required.

Real-time object detection has become a standard component of robotic perception systems. The YOLO (You Only Look Once) family is widely adopted because it combines accurate object localization with real-time inference [ 4 ] . Recent implementations such as YOLOv8 provide practical training and deployment pipelines for robotic applications [ 2 ] . However, continuous target awareness cannot be achieved through visual detection alone. Visual observations become unavailable when the tracked UGV leaves the camera field of view or becomes temporarily occluded. Under these conditions, a UAV relying only on visual perception loses the target despite the detector providing accurate observations whenever the vehicle is visible.

This paper proposes a heterogeneous UAV–UGV methodology for simulated aerial tracking of small-scale autonomous ground vehicles. The system employs a mini UAV with a front-facing RGB camera to observe UGVs in a ROS 2 and Gazebo Sim environment. Three tracking approaches are evaluated. The first is a training-free color baseline. The second is a visual baseline based on YOLO. The third is the proposed heterogeneous UAV–UGV approach that integrates visual perception with information shared by the ground vehicle. This comparison isolates the contribution of heterogeneous cooperation to aerial target tracking.Figure 1 summarizes the proposed heterogeneous UAV–UGV tracking methodology. The simulated environment provides two complementary information streams. The first is the UAV front RGB image. The second is the UGV state information. The RGB stream is processed by both visual baselines. The proposed method combines visual detections with UGV state information to estimate the target position when visual observations become unavailable. This design isolates the effect of heterogeneous information on tracking continuity.

The main contributions of this work are:

A ROS 2/Gazebo Sim methodology for heterogeneous UAV–UGV aerial tracking of small-scale autonomous ground vehicles.

A comparison between a color-based visual baseline, a YOLO visual baseline, and a UAV–UGV fusion approach.

An evaluation across four scenarios: single-car tracking, crossing trajectories, occlusion, and UAV-assisted awareness.

Experimental evidence that the proposed fusion method increases track coverage to nearly 100% while reducing localization error across all evaluated scenarios.

1. A ROS 2/Gazebo Sim methodology for heterogeneous UAV–UGV aerial tracking of small-scale autonomous ground vehicles.

2. A comparison between a color-based visual baseline, a YOLO visual baseline, and a UAV–UGV fusion approach.

3. An evaluation across four scenarios: single-car tracking, crossing trajectories, occlusion, and UAV-assisted awareness.

4. Experimental evidence that the proposed fusion method increases track coverage to nearly 100% while reducing localization error across all evaluated scenarios.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A UAV Target Tracking

UAV target tracking has been studied as both an active and passive perception problem. In active tracking, the UAV adjusts its motion to maintain the target within its field of view, while passive tracking focuses on estimating information about the target from the available observations. State-estimation and fusion strategies, such as Kalman filtering, particle filtering, and learning-based tracking, are commonly used to improve robustness under noisy or intermittent observations [ 6 ] .

Vision-based UAV tracking systems often combine object detection with temporal filtering. Barisic et al. presented a vision-based system for real-time detection and following of UAVs using YOLO and a Kalman filter, showing that combining visual detections with dynamic estimation improves tracking stability [ 1 ] . These works support the idea that visual detections are useful but should be complemented with temporal state estimation.

## II-B YOLO-Based Robotic Perception

YOLO is a family of single-stage detectors capable of estimating object locations and classes within a single inference step [ 4 ] . Its balance between detection accuracy and processing speed makes it particularly suitable for robotic applications requiring real-time visual perception. YOLOv8 is distributed through the Ultralytics framework, which provides pretrained models, training utilities, and deployment tools [ 2 ] . Recent work has analyzed YOLOv8 and reported its practical advantages for real-time object detection, including its anchor-free design and efficient training pipeline [ 7 ] .

In UAV applications, YOLO-based detectors have been used for flying-object detection, small-object recognition, and lightweight onboard perception. Reis et al. evaluated YOLOv8 for real-time flying-object detection and emphasized challenges related to small target size, motion, occlusion, and cluttered backgrounds [ 5 ] . These challenges are also present in UAV–UGV tracking, where temporary occlusions or field-of-view limitations may interrupt visual observations of the target.

## II-C Heterogeneous UAV–UGV Cooperation

Heterogeneous UAV–UGV systems have been studied for cooperative localization, mapping, planning, and semantic collaboration. Recent surveys describe air–ground heterogeneous systems as a promising robotic paradigm because UAVs and UGVs provide complementary capabilities in perception, mobility, and mission execution [ 8 ] . Other works have explored air–ground cooperation for semantic mapping and navigation, where aerial perception provides information that improves ground-robot decision-making [ 3 ] .

However, it remains important to evaluate under controlled conditions to what extent shared UGV state information can preserve aerial tracking continuity during temporary visual loss.

The present work follows this research direction but focuses specifically on aerial tracking of small-scale autonomous ground vehicles. Unlike a purely visual method, the proposed approach uses the same visual detector as the YOLO baseline and combines visual detections with UGV state information, including position, orientation, and velocity, to maintain continuous tracking during temporary visual loss. This design isolates the contribution of heterogeneous fusion from the contribution of the learned detector.

2026-10-20.title: Stress-Query and Temporal Reliability of Vision-Language Models as copilots in Autonomous UAV Navigation
2026-10-20.authors: Hiago Sodre , Sebastian Barcelona , Vincent Sandin , Pablo Moraes , Andre S. Kelbouscas , Ricardo B. Grando
2026-10-20.comment: Paper accepted at the Latin American Robotics Symposium LARS 2026
2026-10-20.abstract: Integrating Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into autonomous UAV navigation enables high-level semantic reasoning but introduces critical temporal bottlenecks that can destabilize flight control. This paper presents a systematic benchmark that evaluates the operational trade-offs among model scale, hardware constraints, and flight reliability. By subjecting the system to extensive stress tests on both a high-performance workstation and a constrained integrated-graphics laptop, we isolate the kinetic impact of inference latency against reasoning accuracy. Our findings reveal a performance dichotomy: lightweight models struggle with structural hallucinations that break deterministic state machines, while heavyweight models induce trajectory overcorrections due to inference lag. We demonstrate that a mid-weight architecture strikes the optimal balance, successfully rehabilitating navigation in degraded environments without compromising real-time stability across different hardware profiles. A video of the tests is available at: https://youtu.be/vHtjc7HarJ0
2026-10-20.introduction:
Traditional autonomous navigation tasks in Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) have relied on conventional perception pipelines that utilize rigid computer vision architectures and sensor fusion. While these geometric systems are highly reactive, their performance degrades significantly in uncertain environments, such as when navigation markers are severely damaged or visual cues are ambiguous. In contrast, the rapid development of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) represents a paradigm shift [ 5 ] . By incorporating multimodal semantic reasoning into the perception process, UAVs can interpret high-level contextual information in complex scenarios. This approach bridges the gap between rigid pixel-level processing and contextual scene understanding, enabling UAVs to conduct a more intelligent secondary assessment of their surroundings.

However, the transition of VLMs from cloud-based APIs to real-time embedded robotic control presents profound operational challenges. The main obstacle is the bottleneck between model scale and inference time limits. Models with many parameters exhibit robust reasoning but impose inference latencies that often exceed several seconds on edge hardware, decoupling the control loop and causing severe deviations in the physical trajectory. On the other hand, lightweight edge-optimized models minimize latency but often suffer from structural distortions, failing to maintain the rigorous formatting schemes, such as JSON outputs, required by classical deterministic controllers. While previous research has explored end-to-end visuomotor policies [ 5 ] or reinforcement learning [ 4 ] , there is a critical gap in the empirical understanding of the exact time limits and trade-offs that dictate when a VLM mathematically breaks an autonomous control loop.

The evaluations are executed within a high-fidelity Software-In-The-Loop (SITL) Gazebo simulation, subjecting multiple visual architectures to incremental stress tests under both structured and severely degraded environments, as shown in the proposed diagram in Figure 1 .

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

A comprehensive quantitative benchmark that evaluates the real-time operational limits of varying VLM parameter scales (from 1.8B to 11B) in closed-loop UAV navigation systems natively available at https://github.com/hiagojacobs/UAV_Sim_VLM/tree/stress .

The conceptualization and empirical measurement of the Temporal Reliability Boundary , demonstrating how excessive hardware-induced latency directly correlates with physical trajectory overcorrections in real-time edge robotics.

A systematic stress-testing protocol that varies asynchronous query intervals to isolate the critical trade-off between semantic reasoning capabilities and structural output hallucination rates in degraded environments.

The identification of an operational ”Sweet Spot” in mid-weight VLM architectures, establishing a blueprint for maximizing visual navigational recovery without compromising the strict timing requirements of deterministic FSM controllers.

1. A comprehensive quantitative benchmark that evaluates the real-time operational limits of varying VLM parameter scales (from 1.8B to 11B) in closed-loop UAV navigation systems natively available at https://github.com/hiagojacobs/UAV_Sim_VLM/tree/stress .

2. The conceptualization and empirical measurement of the Temporal Reliability Boundary , demonstrating how excessive hardware-induced latency directly correlates with physical trajectory overcorrections in real-time edge robotics.

3. A systematic stress-testing protocol that varies asynchronous query intervals to isolate the critical trade-off between semantic reasoning capabilities and structural output hallucination rates in degraded environments.

4. The identification of an operational ”Sweet Spot” in mid-weight VLM architectures, establishing a blueprint for maximizing visual navigational recovery without compromising the strict timing requirements of deterministic FSM controllers.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Works

Reliable navigation in complex aerial missions requires the capacity to perceive, interpret, and respond to environmental information in real time. Traditional unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) systems address this challenge using computer vision, sensor fusion, and deterministic control strategies, which provide robust performance in structured environments. However, their effectiveness declines significantly when visual cues are ambiguous, partially occluded, or degraded. These conditions reveal the inherent limitations of purely geometric perception methods, which restrict their ability to support advanced decision-making or navigational recovery [ 1 ] .

Recent advances in multimodal learning have introduced Vision-Language Models (VLMs) as a paradigm for incorporating abstract semantic reasoning into robotic perception systems. Models such as CLIP [ 8 ] , BLIP-2 [ 6 ] , and LLaVA demonstrate strong capabilities in visual understanding and zero-shot reasoning by integrating advanced visual encoders with large language models [ 10 ] . Although these architectures have shown promising results on static, open-ended tasks, their application to dynamic, real-time autonomous systems is limited by significant inference latency and the lack of mathematical guarantees.

To achieve both flexibility and deterministic safety in robotics, hybrid architectures that combine learning-based components with classical control systems have been extensively investigated. Previous research on visuomotor policies [ 5 ] and reinforcement learning [ 4 ] has demonstrated the effectiveness of data-driven approaches for sequential decision-making. Nevertheless, these methods generally function within narrowly defined action spaces and do not address the challenge of integrating large, free-form generative models into safety-critical, asynchronous control loops. Asynchronous control loops.

2026-10-20.title: Adaptive Question Generation for Ambiguous Robot Instructions Based on Information Gain and Human Cognitive Characteristics
2026-10-20.authors: Ryo Terashima , Yuga Yano , Hakaru Tamukoh
2026-10-20.comment: accepted as a conference paper for 2026 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026)
2026-10-20.abstract:
In this study, we propose an adaptive question generation mechanism that addresses uncertainty arising from ambiguous instructions.
Natural-language instructions for service robots often contain ambiguities.
In scenes with multiple similar objects, the robot must identify the target object by asking questions.
However, existing question generation methods focus on probabilistic discrimination efficiency and do not sufficiently account for user ease of response.
Asking questions without considering the user’s ease of response may cause incorrect or uncertain answers.
Such incorrect or uncertain answers lead to additional clarification turns and degraded dialogue efficiency.
The proposed mechanism integrates probabilistic discrimination efficiency and human cognitive characteristics to generate questions that users can intuitively and easily answer.
First, the proposed mechanism extracts visual attributes of candidate objects using a vision-language model (VLM).
Next, the proposed mechanism computes the information gain (IG) of each attribute and selects the visual attribute (e.g., color, shape) that most reduces uncertainty in the candidate set.
When multiple attributes have the same IG, the proposed mechanism applies a visual attribute filter based on cognitive characteristics to select the visual attribute that users can most intuitively perceive.
The proposed mechanism then prompts the VLM with the selected attribute and the corresponding attribute values of each candidate object to generate a concise natural-language question.
This process is repeated until the target object is uniquely identified.
The proposed mechanism achieved a target identification success rate of 88.5% in the evaluation using a dataset of 120 scenes.
Furthermore, the proposed mechanism received high ratings in subjective evaluations of response ease.
2026-10-20.introduction:
In recent years, the demand for service robots that coexist with humans in homes and commercial facilities has grown, driven by the declining birthrate, aging population, and shrinking workforce [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
Furthermore, robots require the ability to understand natural language instructions from users and handle various situations [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
However, natural language instructions from users often involve ambiguity, as target objects are not always specified [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
For example, an instruction such as “bring me a drink” specifies only the target object’s category.
Therefore, when multiple drinks exist in the environment, the robot cannot identify the target.
To select appropriate actions, the robot must obtain additional information from the user and resolve the ambiguity.

Ren et al. proposed KnowNo to address uncertainties arising from such ambiguous instructions and situations [ 14 ] .
KnowNo quantifies the uncertainty before task execution and asks the user for clarification when ambiguity exists.
This approach focuses on determining when to ask questions to resolve ambiguity.
However, KnowNo does not address how to generate questions that users can easily answer.

Regarding question content, an approach that generates questions based on the probabilistic discrimination efficiency of candidate objects has been proposed [ 15 ] .
This study demonstrates the effectiveness of selecting visual attributes that efficiently partition the candidate object set.
However, attributes with high discrimination efficiency are not always easy for users to answer.
Even among attributes with the same discriminability, when users cannot intuitively recall those attributes, response errors and ambiguities may occur.
Response errors and ambiguities can lead to additional clarifications and increased user dialogue.
Human cognitive characteristics form the background of this issue.
When humans recognize and memorize objects, they do not recall all visual attributes equally.
There is a human tendency to recall visually salient features such as color and shape [ 16 ] .
Therefore, selecting attributes for questions requires consideration not only of probabilistic discrimination efficiency but also of user cognitive characteristics.
However, an approach that integrates probabilistic discrimination efficiency and human cognitive characteristics has not been explored.
Based on the above, this study establishes the following hypothesis. Hypothesis : “Integrating probabilistic discrimination efficiency and human cognitive characteristics enables the generation of questions that achieve high discrimination efficiency and are easy for users to answer.”

Based on this hypothesis, we propose an adaptive question generation mechanism that integrates information gain (IG) and cognitive characteristics.
Fig. 1 shows a comparative scenario in which a robot receives an ambiguous instruction.
Without the proposed mechanism, the robot generates a question that is unclear, making it difficult for the user to answer.
With the proposed mechanism, the robot generates a concise question focused on a single visual attribute with high discrimination efficiency, enabling the user to answer intuitively.

In this study, we conducted large-scale user experiments using crowdsourcing to quantitatively verify the discrimination efficiency and ease of response of the proposed mechanism.
In this study, we collect an original dataset of 120 scenes collected on a university campus.
The experimental results show that the proposed mechanism achieves a high target identification success rate and high ease of response for users.

The main contributions of this study are the following two points.

Proposal of an adaptive question generation mechanism that integrates information gain and cognitive characteristics

Proposal of an adaptive question generation mechanism that integrates information gain and cognitive characteristics

Quantitative demonstration that human cognitive characteristics are effective for intuitive question generation.

1. Proposal of an adaptive question generation mechanism that integrates information gain and cognitive characteristics

2. Quantitative demonstration that human cognitive characteristics are effective for intuitive question generation.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II RELATED WORKS

## II-A Handling ambiguous instructions

Ren et al. proposed KnowNo as a method for handling ambiguous natural language instructions [ 14 ] .
KnowNo takes user instructions and object recognition results from the environment as input, and generates multiple action candidates using a large language model (LLM) [ 17 ] .
Then, KnowNo applies Conformal Prediction (CP) based on the likelihood of each candidate.
CP is a statistical method that constructs a prediction set that contains the correct answer with a given confidence level.
When the prediction set contains a single candidate, the robot proceeds with the execution action.
When multiple candidates remain, the robot asks the user for help to avoid taking an incorrect action.
In this way, KnowNo interacts with the user only when necessary and addresses ambiguous situations.
KnowNo achieves a high task success rate in both simulated and real environments.
However, KnowNo assumes that the user will always provide a correct answer to each question.
Therefore, KnowNo does not address how to generate questions that are easy for users to answer.

## II-B Question strategy design in dialogue

As question strategies for ambiguous instructions, methods that minimize the entropy of the candidate set and approaches that maximize IG have been proposed [ 15 , 18 ] .
For example, Deits et al. demonstrated that selected questions with high discrimination efficiency based on entropy minimization can quantitatively reduce uncertainty with each dialogue turn [ 18 ] .
Furthermore, Yang et al. proposed a method that progressively resolves ambiguity using visual attributes such as object color [ 15 ] .
Yang et al. achieved a target identification accuracy of 91% in real-world experiments, confirming that attribute-based questions are effective for object identification.

These studies demonstrate the effectiveness of question selection based on probabilistic efficiency.
However, an attribute that efficiently partitions the candidate set is not necessarily easy for users to answer.
This gap between discrimination efficiency and user ease of response has not been sufficiently explored.
In this study, we investigate whether considering users’ ease of response when selecting questions leads to more effective ambiguity resolution.

## II-C Question design based on human cognitive characteristics

When humans recognize and memorize objects, they do not memorize all visual attributes equally.
Visually salient features such as color and shape tend to be more memorable and preferentially recalled [ 16 ] .
Based on these findings, SalBench [ 19 ] defines visual attributes that humans can intuitively perceive.
These findings indicate that selecting attributes for questions requires not only discrimination efficiency but also a cognitive perspective on whether users can intuitively recall and answer them easily.

However, existing studies have not sufficiently explored an approach that defines attributes suitable for questions based on human cognitive characteristics and incorporates them into question design.
Focusing on this point, we propose a framework that integrates cognitive characteristics into question design.

2026-10-20.title: Context-Aware RGB-Thermal-Radar Obstacle Perception for Resource-Constrained ASVs
2026-10-20.authors: Pranav Kedia , Edwin Redhead , Heiko Hamann
2026-10-20.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-20.abstract:
Reliable obstacle perception is challenging for small autonomous surface vessels (ASVs): reflections and glare confound visible-light cameras, vessel motion shifts the apparent waterline, and darkness removes the dominant sensing modality altogether. Rather than treating multimodal fusion as a static accuracy gain, we propose a context-aware architecture that combines RGB and
long-wave infrared (LWIR) imagery, frequency-modulated continuous-wave
(FMCW) mmWave radar, and inertial context.
A bearing-sector interface
provides the navigation controller with calibrated obstacle probabilities,
radar ranges, and sensor status.
It also distinguishes sensor dropout from a valid observation with no detected obstacle.
Using new multimodal lake recordings, we deployed the pipeline in a 24-leg closed-loop pilot under uncontrolled
lake conditions (16 day, 4 dusk, and 4 night; 351 m 351\text{\,}\mathrm{m} ), including
night legs in which RGB was unusable and the vessel drove on LWIR and radar evidence alone.
On eight held-out low-light recordings, the calibrated fusion model achieved average precision (AP) 0.869 and expected calibration error 0.108, compared with AP 0.673 for rule-based fusion, 0.620 for gated fusion, and 0.903 for RGB alone. Our results expose a central tradeoff:
RGB ranks best when usable, whereas fusion preserves a navigation input when RGB fails.
This work is a step toward perception that remains usable and degrades predictably across multi-day ASV missions.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Small ASVs are attractive for environmental monitoring and long-duration observation (e.g., for several days and nights) because they can operate in water with low logistical cost. On inland water bodies, however, their safety and autonomy depend on detecting obstacles that range from boats and fixed structures to swimmers, animals, buoys, and partly submerged debris. This is a difficult visual domain. Sun glitter and wakes can resemble physical obstacles, and the horizon moves with roll and pitch [ 1 ] . At night, the visible-light channel that many perception systems on small ASVs rely on may cease to be useful. The challenge is to interpret changing sensor evidence while preserving the information needed for robot decisions. Long-duration field autonomy requires sustaining task performance without exhausting energy, and on an ASV that budget must cover both perception (sensors and computation) and propulsion [ 2 ] .

Autonomous wind-powered surface vessels (ASWVs) [ 3 ] can reduce electrical propulsion demand, while sensing, computation, communication, and control continue to draw battery power. Perception must therefore deliver timely, decision-relevant obstacle information across day and night, from sensors whose reliability and availability vary, and within the energy and compute budget of a small vessel. No single compact sensor resolves all of these challenges. RGB imagery provides texture and semantic class information in daylight, but is sensitive to illumination. Long-wave infrared (LWIR) imaging retains contrast for warm objects in darkness, but has lower resolution and weak contrast for thermally uniform structures. FMCW mmWave radar provides range and radial velocity independently of visible illumination, but sparse returns and target-dependent reflectivity complicate interpretation. Inertial measurements provide no obstacle evidence, but they describe the viewing geometry and platform motion under which the other sensors observed the scene. A measurement’s value therefore depends on its acquisition conditions: illumination, roll and pitch, and sensor availability (dropouts, field-of-view gaps, unresolvable sectors). We study whether explicitly representing these conditions, rather than uniformly fusing sensor outputs, yields better-calibrated and more robust obstacle estimates on an ASV.

Existing maritime work has made substantial progress in camera-based water-obstacle segmentation [ 4 ] and in radar–camera datasets and fusion [ 5 ] . Researchers have also fused electro-optical and infrared cameras for maritime tracking [ 6 ] . These systems show the value of multiple modalities, but a resource-constrained ASV also needs low-energy, bandwidth-efficient, navigation-specific output, explicit sensor-health handling, and evidence that the full perception-to-control chain survives severe condition changes. This paper connects session-disjoint perception evaluation to embedded runtime measurements and a closed-loop lake pilot, distinguishing offline model performance from the evidence available during robot decisions. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of in-field closed-loop obstacle avoidance in the marine robotics domain using joint RGB, LWIR thermal, and FMCW mmWave radar fusion with inertial context.

Our key contributions are:
(1) A context-conditioned RGB–LWIR–FMCW mmWave radar perception method with inertial context and a compact sector interface to navigation.
(2) A session-disjoint evaluation, isolating the effects of geometric compensation, contextual inference, probability calibration, and sensor degradation, and showing that at true night every learned or pseudo-labeled path must be gated on RGB luminance.
(3) An embedded lake pilot (Fig. 1 ) relating the available obstacle evidence, processing configuration, and control policy to 24 driven legs across daylight, dusk, and night.

Extending small-ASV autonomy beyond daylight requires obstacle estimates that remain trustworthy as sensors degrade and drop out, and we show that this can be achieved on a single low-power embedded board.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Classical maritime detection estimates the water edge and separates obstacles from navigable water [ 1 ] . Deep segmentation improved robustness to reflections and wakes (WaSR) with inertial cues [ 7 ] , eWaSR for embedded compute [ 4 ] , and LaRS extends evaluation to diverse lake, river, and sea scenes [ 1 ] .
We use an embedded segmentation model distilled from these models to provide visual cues, relying on complementary sensors when segmentation degrades in darkness.

Multimodal sensing on ASVs is well motivated but rarely carried through to inference and control. WaterScenes provides a benchmark demonstrating that radar and camera provide complementary information for detection, free-space segmentation, and waterline estimation on ASVs [ 5 ] , and electro-optical/infrared track fusion has been applied to maritime targets [ 6 ] . RGB, LWIR, mmWave radar, and inertial recordings exist for indoor and outdoor ground robots [ 8 , 9 ] , and HydraFusion studies context-dependent sensor selection for road vehicles [ 10 ] . These studies leave open how joint RGB, LWIR, and FMCW mmWave radar evidence supports marine robot navigation when illumination, viewing geometry, and onboard resources change. Our study examines context-adaptive obstacle estimates and their use for control under the resource and viewing-geometry constraints of a small ASV.

Creating ground truth for maritime scenes is labor-intensive: classes are diverse, instances are rare, and existing detectors recognize only a limited set of classes. Open-vocabulary detectors such as Grounding DINO [ 11 ] and concept-prompted segmentation in SAM 3 [ 12 ] make it practical to generate candidate annotations from text prompts, reducing the need for maritime class-specific detectors.
We use these annotations as teachers whose proposals we audit, and quantify recall and precision against that audit rather than treating them as truth.

Perception benchmarks alone do not reveal whether errors occur at safety-critical ranges or whether an embedded system reacts quickly enough for control. Radar has been used directly in ASV obstacle-avoidance systems [ 13 ] , but radar-only control sacrifices the semantic and navigable water information available from cameras. We therefore evaluate both obstacle perception and its effectiveness in closed-loop behavior.

2026-10-20.title: DUET: Decoupled Upper- and Lower-Body Execution for Task-Agnostic Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
2026-10-20.authors: Kapalik Khanal , Biswash Khatiwada , Stephen Afrifa , Fan Wu , Ramesh Bahadur Bist
2026-10-20.abstract: Changing a humanoid robot's manipulation policy should not require retraining the controller that maintains the robot's balance. This study introduces DUET, a decoupled execution framework that enables locomotion and manipulation controllers to operate simultaneously by combining their commands only at the robot interface. A reinforcement-learning locomotion policy controls the 12 leg joints and a waist yaw joint, tracking planar velocity, turning rate, and pelvis height from deep crouching to upright standing on a 23-degree-of-freedom Unitree G1. The 10 arm joints are excluded from the action space, while their positions and velocities are included only as observations, so that any compatible manipulation policy that generates arm-joint targets can control the upper body, and the locomotion policy keeps the lower body stable without requiring shared training or direct coordination. This study demonstrates the modular approach on hardware by pairing the same locomotion checkpoint with two different vision-language-action models, GR00T N1.7 and pi0.5. In simulation evaluation, the locomotion controller kept the robot's lower body stable with no falls while tracking the commanded planar velocity, yaw rate, and pelvis height with errors of 0.186 m/s, 0.142 rad/s, and 0.016 m, respectively. Ablation studies identify the upper-body pose curriculum as the dominant component, and removing this training step reduces episode survival from 20.0 to 7.4 seconds and increases the fall rate to 6.06 per environment minute. Robustness tests show no falls under pushes of up to 1.0 m/s within the trained payload range, and no falls at twice the payload limit for pushes below 0.7 m/s. These results show that a manipulation policy can be exchanged without retraining, restarting, or otherwise touching the layer that keeps the robot upright.
