2026-10-20.title: Ropedia W0: Scaling Loco-Manipulation World Models across Embodiments with Human Experience
2026-10-20.authors: Tianqi Liu , Hanfei Zhao , Qifeng Liang , Hui En Pang , Jiarui Xu , Sayang Mu , Penghao Qiu , YingSheng Zhang , Jun Wang , Ziang Cao , Mingze Sun , Yukang Cao , Fangzhou Hong , Zhaoxi Chen , Ziwei Liu
2026-10-20.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-20.comment: Project page: this https URL ; Code: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract: World models enable embodied agents to anticipate action consequences, yet jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation across diverse embodiments remains challenging due to heterogeneous action spaces and limited multimodal supervision. We present Ropedia W0 , the first egocentric loco-manipulation world foundation model spanning humans and robots with diverse embodiments. We curate Xp-Data , comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data with unified multimodal annotations and systematic quality control. A unified kinematic representation encodes locomotion through camera poses and manipulation through projected skeletons, with robot skeletons combining embodiment-specific forward kinematics with extensive manual keypoint annotation and correction. We also introduce Xp-Teleop , a long-horizon loco-manipulation benchmark based on high-quality dexterous humanoid teleoperation data. Evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, Ψ 0 \Psi_{0} , ω \omega -HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot) and on held-out human egocentric video, from zero-shot inference to few-shot and full-data post-training. Scaling human pre-training data improves performance on both human and robot evaluations. After distillation, our model supports real-time, minute-long rollouts, enabling live VR interaction. Applications in policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world–action modeling further demonstrate the model’s utility for embodied decision-making.
2026-10-20.introduction:
World models predict how environments evolve in response to actions [ 42 , 14 ] and support decision-making by imagining future outcomes [ 43 ] , giving them considerable potential in embodied intelligence. However, most existing models [ 119 , 122 , 4 ] focus on fixed-base, gripper-based manipulation, leaving locomotion-induced viewpoint changes and dexterous hand–object interactions largely underexplored. Moreover, generalizing across embodiments poses a further challenge. DreamDojo [ 34 ] replaces latent-action conditioning with robot-specific actions during post-training, and Cosmos3 [ 1 ] relies on domain-specific action projections despite a shared backbone; both therefore require a dedicated control interface or additional adaptation for each new embodiment. Therefore, jointly modeling locomotion and manipulation while seamlessly generalizing across diverse embodiments remains an open problem.

Learning a generalizable world model hinges on large-scale, high-quality egocentric video paired with rich multimodal annotations, such as camera trajectories, hand motion, and task descriptions. While robot demonstrations across diverse tasks and embodiments remain expensive to collect, egocentric human video offers an abundant and complementary source of experience on how humans navigate and interact with their surroundings. However, existing public egocentric datasets [ 39 , 40 , 46 , 113 , 27 , 2 , 78 ] frequently suffer from incomplete or unreliable annotations. Specifically, many lack metric camera trajectories, provide noisy or missing hand poses, and adopt heterogeneous formats that hinder joint training. Furthermore, the scale of these datasets remains limited, falling short of the data required to train a generalizable world model.

To address these challenges, we present Ropedia W0 , a unified egocentric world model that scales learning from human and robot videos for cross-embodiment loco-manipulation. We curate Xp-Data , comprising 10k hours of egocentric human data and 3k hours of robot data, with unified geometric, kinematic, and semantic annotations produced through automated processing, manual robot-keypoint annotation, and quality checks. To connect human motion and robot actions, we introduce a shared explicit kinematic representation that combines metric camera poses for locomotion-induced viewpoint changes with projected skeletons for manipulation. The skeletons combine human pose annotations with robot forward kinematics (FK) and manually annotated or corrected robot keypoints, preserving embodiment-specific structure in an image-aligned format. This conditioning interface remains consistent across human pre-training, human–robot mid-training, and optional post-training. We further introduce Xp-Teleop , a humanoid teleoperation benchmark for evaluating long-horizon prediction during locomotion and dexterous manipulation.

We evaluate Ropedia W0 on five cross-embodiment benchmarks (DreamDojo, Ψ 0 \Psi_{0} , ω \omega -HOME, Xp-Teleop, and AgiBot), alongside held-out human egocentric video. Results demonstrate strong predictive performance across embodiments and post-training budgets, including zero-shot transfer and data-efficient adaptation. Scaling analyses show that increasing the amount of human pre-training data improves both prediction on human videos and transfer to robots. Ablations establish the complementary roles of camera and skeleton conditioning, while distillation enables real-time, minute-long rollouts and live VR interaction across embodiments. Downstream experiments further demonstrate accurate policy ranking, improved trajectory planning, and more robust action learning in simulation and on real robots.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce Ropedia W0 , which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first unified egocentric world model for cross-embodiment loco-manipulation. A shared explicit kinematic representation of camera poses and projected skeletons enables scalable learning from human and robot videos.

We design a human-in-the-loop pipeline that unifies collection, annotation, and quality checks, including extensive manual robot-keypoint annotation and correction of inaccurate FK projections. Consequently, we build Xp-Data , comprising over 10k hours of human data and 3k hours of robot data in a shared schema.

Extensive experiments show that Ropedia W0 achieves state-of-the-art cross-embodiment prediction, including on our long-horizon loco-manipulation Xp-Teleop benchmark. We further show that Ropedia W0’s performance scales with human data and demonstrate applications in real-time interaction, policy evaluation, model-based planning, and world–action modeling.

2. We design a human-in-the-loop pipeline that unifies collection, annotation, and quality checks, including extensive manual robot-keypoint annotation and correction of inaccurate FK projections. Consequently, we build Xp-Data , comprising over 10k hours of human data and 3k hours of robot data in a shared schema.

3. Extensive experiments show that Ropedia W0 achieves state-of-the-art cross-embodiment prediction, including on our long-horizon loco-manipulation Xp-Teleop benchmark. 2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Robotic video world models. Early world models learned compact latent dynamics for control [ 42 , 43 ] ; large video generators yield interactive worlds [ 14 , 88 , 89 , 75 , 24 , 74 ] and ego-motion-controlled driving simulators [ 47 , 98 , 35 ] .
Distillation and self-rollout training convert video generators into causal few-step models [ 130 , 50 , 26 , 72 ] , augmented with long-horizon memory [ 45 , 100 ] . Robotic world models learn video dynamics from robot trajectories [ 124 , 142 , 55 , 67 , 41 , 139 , 122 , 44 ] , often adapting a video foundation model [ 3 , 108 ] .
Numerical action tokens require embodiment-specific encoding [ 111 , 41 ] ; latent actions inferred from video [ 14 , 128 , 36 , 38 , 34 ] make unlabeled footage usable, but may entangle actions with other visual changes [ 133 ] ; spatially aligned renderings provide explicit geometric conditioning [ 55 , 122 , 126 , 115 , 119 ] .
Cross-embodiment models use embodiment-specific action heads, projections, or adaptation [ 111 , 34 , 1 ] , a single rendered interface [ 115 , 119 ] , or factorized human-to-robot recomposition [ 22 ] . The last, AnyWorld [ 22 ] , recomposes human interactions into robot experiences but conditions on source human skeletons rather than target-robot kinematics and is evaluated mainly on manipulation, leaving sustained loco-manipulation untested.
Ego-motion is also studied in navigation and driving [ 8 , 47 ] and in egocentric predictors conditioned on or jointly modeling full-body pose [ 7 , 87 , 121 ] .
Ropedia W0 uses an explicit kinematic interface to unify loco-manipulation across humans, gripper robots, and dexterous humanoids.

Human and robot datasets. Large egocentric human collections cover daily and skilled activity [ 39 , 27 , 40 ] ; pose-annotated collections add body or hand pose [ 82 , 78 , 46 , 92 ] , and portable rigs bring hand pose into everyday scenes [ 109 , 76 ] .
Aggregated and in-the-wild demonstrations [ 86 , 58 , 107 , 30 , 118 ] and large teleoperation sets [ 15 ] provide robot actions, calibrated views and task captions in varying combinations, with substantial coverage of tabletop arm and gripper manipulation; humanoid sets include locomotion or dexterous hands [ 138 , 101 , 94 , 117 , 65 ] .
Evaluation data include held-out robot video clips [ 142 , 34 , 119 ] , multimodal world-model benchmarks [ 1 ] , and benchmarks measuring visual quality, physical consistency or embodied utility [ 132 , 84 ] .
Xp-Data unifies annotations for public human and robot data and self-collected egocentric video; Xp-Teleop benchmarks long-horizon dexterous humanoid loco-manipulation with robot-native kinematics.

Policy evaluation, planning, and learning. Policy evaluation extends real-to-sim protocols [ 62 ] to video world models through recorded-action rollouts [ 142 , 64 , 119 ] or closed-loop policy interaction [ 95 , 41 , 103 , 102 ] .
For planning, world models score or refine action proposals using predicted outcomes [ 93 , 28 , 53 , 34 ] , in pixel or learned latent spaces [ 140 , 5 ] , and support reinforcement fine-tuning and synthetic data generation [ 143 , 56 , 61 , 120 , 54 ] .
Vision-language-action models map observations and language to actions using pretrained vision-language models [ 13 , 59 , 12 , 52 , 11 ] , increasingly trained with human video [ 128 , 16 , 15 , 123 , 80 , 57 , 117 ] , whereas world–action models couple future video or latent-state prediction with action learning [ 21 , 141 , 48 , 111 , 67 , 127 , 1 , 9 , 81 , 65 , 112 , 131 ] .
Ropedia W0 supports these applications in Sec. 6 ; for world–action modeling, we transfer its pretrained video backbone to initialize such a model rather than adding a dedicated action head.

2026-10-20.title: PICA-WAM: Visual Perturbation Invariance via Cross-Appearance Self-Alignment in World Action Models
2026-10-20.authors: Yude Zou , Yifei Yao , Guanbo Jiao , Jianming Ma , Guanjie Zheng , Xing Gao
2026-10-20.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-20.abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future video and generate actions, yet remain sensitive to task-irrelevant visual perturbations, i.e. , changes in visual appearance that should not affect robot behavior. We identify a gap in conventional WAM training: video prediction encourages representations to preserve appearance information, while action generation does not explicitly enforce invariance to task-irrelevant appearance.
Data augmentation exposes WAMs to such perturbations but does not require perturbed and nominal observations to produce consistent action representations, and alignment with external pretrained features does not guarantee the desired invariance.
To address this gap, we propose PICA-WAM, a self-supervised training framework that casts perturbation invariance as an auxiliary cross-appearance self-alignment task for WAMs.
An exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher processes the nominal observation to provide a deeper-layer target, while the online WAM processes a perturbed observation and aligns its shallower-layer action representation to this target through a lightweight projection head.
Across four strong WAMs evaluated on RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO-Plus, EBench, and a real robot, PICA-WAM consistently improves robustness under visual perturbations, preserves nominal performance in simulation, and raises the real robot success rate. PICA-WAM further reduces the sensitivity of video features to task-irrelevant appearance and its propagation into actions, as shown by paired layer-wise diagnostics. Code: https://github.com/YudeZou/PICA-WAM-release .
2026-10-20.introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) build robot policies on top of pretrained video generators, coupling predictions of how a scene will evolve with the actions that drive it ( Yuan et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026b ; Ye et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Cai et al., 2026b ) . Video–action co-training transfers the dynamics prior of large-scale video pretraining into control, and WAMs now approach saturation on standard manipulation benchmarks such as LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023 ) and RoboTwin ( Mu et al., 2024 ; Mu et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) . Yet these models remain brittle when observations depart from the training distribution ( Hong et al., 2026 ) . On LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) and RoboTwin 2.0 Clean-to-Random ( Yuan et al., 2026a ) , shifts in appearance, viewpoint, sensing, and scene configuration can substantially reduce success. The task goal remains the same, but the policy must act under unfamiliar observations and starting conditions.

We view this brittleness as a gap in the training objectives of WAMs. The video prediction objective requires faithful reconstruction of appearance details such as lighting and texture, while reliable control calls for consistent actions when the same underlying task state is observed under different task-irrelevant appearance variations, and joint video–action training does not explicitly enforce this consistency. As the action expert reads video-stream representations, task-irrelevant appearance variation leaks into the action pathway.

Existing approaches address this gap only partially. (i) Data augmentation ( Tobin et al., 2017 ; Kostrikov et al., 2020 ) exposes the model to perturbed observations but never requires their representations to agree with those of their nominal counterparts. The resulting invariance is incidental rather than enforced: in our layer-wise analysis, augmentation lowers appearance sensitivity in intermediate video layers, but sensitivity rises above the unaugmented baseline in layers 21–25 (Figure 3 , left). (ii) External representation alignment regularizes WAM features toward priors from outside the model, such as semantic vision encoders ( Qiu et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ) , 3D trajectory fields ( Yang et al., 2026b ) , 4D tracking features ( Miao et al., 2026 ) , or rendered Gaussian fields ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . These priors provide semantic and geometric guidance, but alignment to an external teacher does not keep the representations of the same underlying task state consistent under visual perturbations. This leaves a need for explicit cross-appearance supervision. (iii) Self-alignment constructs representation targets from the generative model itself, without an external encoder. In image and video generation, Jiang et al. (2025a) and Chefer et al. (2026) align shallower, noisier features to deeper, cleaner features of an exponential-moving-average (EMA) teacher of the model ( Tarvainen and Valpola, 2017 ; Grill et al., 2020 ) , matching the gains of alignment to external encoders ( Yu et al., 2024 ) .
These methods align differently noised versions of the same sample, without matching nominal and perturbed observations of the same underlying task state. Self-alignment also remains underexplored in WAMs, where joint video–action prediction raises the question of whether to align the video stream, the action stream, or both.

To this end, we propose PICA-WAM , a self-supervised training framework that promotes visual P erturbation I nvariance via an auxiliary C ross- A ppearance self-alignment task in WAM s. An EMA teacher of the WAM reads the nominal observation at a lower noise level and provides a deeper-layer target. The online WAM reads a perturbed observation of the same underlying task state and aligns its shallower-layer action representation to this target through a lightweight projection head (Figure 2 ). Each pair thus spans three gaps. The appearance gap supplies the invariance signal. The noise-level and layer gaps, which Jiang et al. (2025a) identified as key ingredients of self-alignment, make the target stronger than the student it supervises. We apply the objective to the action stream, which directly encourages consistency in the representation used for control while leaving the video prediction objective unchanged. In our ablations, this choice outperforms aligning the video stream or both streams. The teacher and the head are discarded after training, so PICA-WAM adds no parameters and no computation at inference and applies to any WAM with a layered backbone.

We evaluate PICA-WAM on four strong WAM backbones across simulation and real-world settings: Fast-WAM ( Yuan et al., 2026b ) on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean-to-Random and LIBERO-Plus, LingBot-VA ( Li et al., 2026b ) on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean-to-Random, InternW0- Δ \Delta ( Miao et al., 2026 ) on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean-to-Random and LIBERO-Plus, and OpenWAM- α \alpha ( Wang et al., 2026b ) on EBench ( Gao et al., 2026 ) and a real robot. PICA-WAM consistently improves robustness over the corresponding baselines and achieves the best results among the compared methods on all three simulation benchmarks: built on InternW0- Δ \Delta , it reaches 74.7% on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean-to-Random and 93.3% on LIBERO-Plus, and built on OpenWAM- α \alpha , it reaches 61.4% on EBench. Even without embodied pretraining, it brings Fast-WAM to success rates comparable to those of models with large-scale embodied pretraining. Paired analyses further show that it reduces both the appearance sensitivity of video features and its propagation into actions, including under perturbation families unseen during training.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

We propose PICA-WAM , a self-supervised training framework for WAMs in which the action representation from a perturbed observation is aligned to a cleaner, deeper target computed from the nominal observation by an EMA teacher of the model, and that needs no external encoder, no additional data, and no inference-time computation.

We design a paired diagnostic protocol that traces a visual perturbation from layer-wise features to executed actions, and show that augmentation alone leaves late video layers appearance-sensitive and lets this sensitivity reach the action, whereas PICA-WAM reduces both.

We demonstrate consistent robustness gains on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean-to-Random, LIBERO-Plus, EBench, and real-world manipulation under visual perturbation across four strong WAMs with and without embodied pretraining, while preserving in-distribution performance.

We propose PICA-WAM , a self-supervised training framework for WAMs in which the action representation from a perturbed observation is aligned to a cleaner, deeper target computed from the nominal observation by an EMA teacher of the model, and that needs no external encoder, no additional data, and no inference-time computation.

2. We design a paired diagnostic protocol that traces a visual perturbation from layer-wise features to executed actions, and show that augmentation alone leaves late video layers appearance-sensitive and lets this sensitivity reach the action, whereas PICA-WAM reduces both.

3. We demonstrate consistent robustness gains on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean-to-Random, LIBERO-Plus, EBench, and real-world manipulation under visual perturbation across four strong WAMs with and without embodied pretraining, while preserving in-distribution performance.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Early work synthesizes future frames and infers actions from them ( Du et al., 2023 ) , or conditions a policy on video pretraining and predictive representations ( Wu et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2024 ) . Later models jointly denoise video and actions ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Liao et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) , and current WAMs scale this recipe with stronger video backbones, action experts, and embodied pretraining ( Yuan et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2026b ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Ye et al., 2026b ; Cai et al., 2026b ; Miao et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ; Guo et al., 2026 ) .
Yet WAMs remain brittle under visual perturbations ( Fei et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026a ) , and their predicted futures can hallucinate training-domain content ( Wang et al., 2026a ) .
Remedies include inference-time activation steering ( Hong et al., 2026 ) and training-time priors from outside the model: semantic features from pretrained encoders such as DINOv3 and V-JEPA or from text ( Qiu et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Feng et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ) , geometric supervision such as 3D trajectory fields, 4D tracking features, and Gaussian fields ( Ma et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Miao et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and distractor-invariant object slots ( Liu et al., 2026b ) . Data augmentation and domain randomization ( Tobin et al., 2017 ; Kostrikov et al., 2020 ) expose a policy to appearance variation but supervise each observation independently. Self-Guided WAM ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) uses an EMA teacher, but to supervise future dynamics rather than cross-appearance agreement.
None of these methods constrains WAM representations across task-irrelevant appearance variations of the same underlying task state. PICA-WAM instead casts perturbation invariance as a cross-appearance self-alignment task, without any external encoder.

REPA ( Yu et al., 2024 ) aligns intermediate diffusion-transformer features with a pretrained visual encoder to accelerate training and improve generation, and follow-up work extends it to end-to-end VAE tuning ( Leng et al., 2025 ) and video generation ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) . Several of the semantic WAM methods above follow the same recipe. Such targets inherit the properties of the external encoder: frozen pretrained encoders, including DINO- and SigLIP-style ones, are strongly appearance-coupled, and the action information decodable from their features collapses under noise and blur ( Yeom et al., 2026 ) .
Self-alignment instead constructs targets within the model. SRA ( Jiang et al., 2025a ) aligns shallower-layer features of a student at a higher noise level with deeper-layer features of an EMA teacher at a lower noise level. Self-Flow ( Chefer et al., 2026 ) noises the student’s tokens at heterogeneous levels while the teacher observes the cleaner input, scaling self-alignment to image, video, and audio generation. These approaches train a student to agree with a slowly updated teacher on a different view of the same input, but their views differ in noise level or network depth, not in task-irrelevant appearance, so the agreement does not encode appearance invariance. PICA-WAM makes task-irrelevant appearance the difference between the two views: the teacher reads the nominal observation and the student a perturbed observation of the same underlying task state.

2026-10-20.title: Simulation Priors for Rapid Adaptation in Model-Based RL for Autonomous Racing
2026-10-20.authors: Adrian Remonda , Jiajun Xi , Nicklas Hansen , Marcus Greiff , Thomas Lew , John Talbot , John Subosits , Xiaolong Wang
2026-10-20.subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-20.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables learning high-performance control policies, but its reliance on extensive interaction limits deployment on physical systems where data collection is costly, and failures are unsafe. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online model-based RL framework that uses structured simulation priors for rapid adaptation. PIA pretrains a world model on heterogeneous low- and high-fidelity simulated trajectories, then adapts it with limited target-domain interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning. Rather than requiring an accurate simulator for policy transfer, PIA treats simulated trajectories as biased priors whose residual mismatch is corrected during online adaptation. We evaluate PIA in autonomous racing using high-fidelity simulation and on a real full-size autonomous race car. In simulation, PIA adapts faster across track and surface shifts than strong baselines, achieving lower lap times and fewer failures. On hardware, PIA achieves reliable few-shot adaptation with less than one hour of on-vehicle interaction.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as an effective data-driven framework for learning high-performance control policies, but its strongest successes often rely on large quantities of interaction data [ 1 , 2 ] . For example, [ 3 ] demonstrated that an RL policy can outrun the world’s best human drivers in Gran Turismo, but only after 45,000 45{,}000 hours of online interaction. This data requirement limits RL in settings where interaction is costly, failures are unsafe, or tasks change over time, such as robotics and real-world driving [ 4 ] .

As a result, RL practitioners often face a tradeoff between dataset diversity and interaction budget. Offline RL is attractive due to its reliance on existing data, but may lead to (unsafe) extrapolation errors when the policy encounters out-of-distribution states [ 5 , 6 ] . Such errors can be corrected with additional data collected by online RL [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] , but that too can be unsafe. In domains such as high-speed racing, where mistakes can be costly, this tradeoff often produces one of two undesirable outcomes: systems that require thousands of laps to achieve stable performance, which is unrealistic for real-world racing, or controllers that rely on highly accurate physics models, which limit flexibility and may potentially lead to suboptimal policies.
The challenge is to exploit structured but imperfect prior data while adapting to new geometries or dynamics under strict interaction budgets.

Prior work, such as Dyna-Q [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] , has shown that synthetic rollouts can significantly improve sample efficiency in model-based RL (MBRL) relative to model-free RL methods such as SAC [ 14 ] . However, when rollouts are generated from learned dynamics, compounding prediction error can make long trajectories unreliable, which in practice restricts their usefulness to short rollouts. As a result, many MBRL methods rely on frequent replanning or conservative objectives to remain reliable. High-fidelity simulators used in control and robotics, such as MuJoCo [ 15 ] and NVIDIA Isaac Gym [ 16 ] , provide a complementary source of synthetic experience: they can cheaply generate structured long-horizon trajectories, but depending on the simulator fidelity, may limit transfer to the target system. This motivates viewing data augmentation not simply as adding more data, but as simulation priors : structured data generators that complement learned world models rather than replacing them.

In this work, we study how heterogeneous simulated trajectories can initialize modern MBRL when they do not exactly match deployment. We introduce Prior-Informed Adaptation (PIA), an offline-to-online MBRL framework that pretrains a world model on structured simulator data and then adapts using limited target-domain interaction. As shown in Figure , a mixed replay retains broad prior coverage while updating the model with newly collected target data, and uncertainty-regularized planning discourages predictions associated with high epistemic uncertainty. Simulation is therefore used as an imperfect data prior rather than as an environment from which a policy transfers directly. This avoids the need for an exact simulator or a domain-randomized distribution [ 17 ] that fully covers the target domain.

We evaluate PIA in an autonomous racing task, where track geometry is typically available before deployment and can be simulated, while the vehicle dynamics remain difficult to reproduce accurately due to effects such as actuator latency, sensing/estimation mismatch, engine dynamics, changing weather, and tire variation. The Assetto Corsa racing simulator (ACGym) [ 18 ] , shown in Figure 3 , provides a controlled high-fidelity proxy for real-world racing, allowing us to study rapid adaptation across unseen tracks and surface changes before hardware deployment. We then deploy the same offline-to-online pipeline on a full-size autonomous race car, where simulated trajectories are combined with a small amount of limited real hardware interaction to anchor the learned world model (see Figure 2 ).
Extensive evaluations show that our proposed PIA method requires significantly fewer trials than other MBRL methods.
Our main contributions are:

A simulation-prior regime for offline-to-online MBRL :
PIA uses heterogeneous trajectories as an imperfect offline initialization, then updates the learned world model with limited target-domain interaction rather than requiring direct policy transfer from an accurate simulator.

Adaptation rate and robustness in simulation :
We conduct experiments in ACGym demonstrating that PIA improves adaptation rate, with lower lap times and fewer failures than offline-only and offline-to-online baselines.

Full-size autonomous racing deployment :
To our knowledge, we provide the first demonstration of offline-to-online adaptation of a simulation-pretrained world model on a full-size autonomous race car, using less than one hour of real-car interaction.

Reproducible benchmark :
We release code and datasets covering 15 tracks and multiple surface conditions, including more than 740 hours of Assetto Corsa driving data and low-fidelity simulated rollouts, enabling future research on few-shot and sim-to-real adaptation.

Overall, our results show that structured simulated trajectories can substantially reduce the amount of target-domain interaction required for online adaptation.

1. A simulation-prior regime for offline-to-online MBRL :
PIA uses heterogeneous trajectories as an imperfect offline initialization, then updates the learned world model with limited target-domain interaction rather than requiring direct policy transfer from an accurate simulator.

2. Adaptation rate and robustness in simulation :
We conduct experiments in ACGym demonstrating that PIA improves adaptation rate, with lower lap times and fewer failures than offline-only and offline-to-online baselines.

3. Full-size autonomous racing deployment :
To our knowledge, we provide the first demonstration of offline-to-online adaptation of a simulation-pretrained world model on a full-size autonomous race car, using less than one hour of real-car interaction.

4. Reproducible benchmark :
We release code and datasets covering 15 tracks and multiple surface conditions, including more than 740 hours of Assetto Corsa driving data and low-fidelity simulated rollouts, enabling future research on few-shot and sim-to-real adaptation.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Model-Based Augmentation. Since Dyna-Q [ 11 ] , synthetic rollouts from learned dynamics have been widely explored (e.g., MBPO [ 12 ] , MOPO [ 13 ] , Dreamer [ 19 ] , and TD-MPC2 [ 20 ] ), and have shown that model-based rollouts can significantly improve sample efficiency. However, learned rollouts are prone to compounding error, so they are typically kept short to remain reliable. Physics-informed models such as PhIHP [ 21 ] mitigate this by combining analytic priors with residual corrections, but are still constrained to short rollouts. AnyCar [ 22 ] explores the use of transformers for world model generation and zero-shot deployment. While impressive, learned-model approaches remain tied to model fidelity when used for direct transfer.

Offline RL and Adaptation. Offline RL methods such as CQL and IQL [ 23 , 5 , 6 ] mitigate extrapolation error through conservative or implicit constraints on value learning, but this can limit generalization. H2O [ 24 ] combines a fixed offline real-world dataset with online rollouts from a simulator using dynamics-aware value regularization and corrected Bellman updates. PIA considers the complementary direction: it pretrains from fixed simulator trajectories and adapts through limited online interaction with the target environment. [ 7 , 10 , 9 ] .
FOWM [ 8 ] pretrains a world model offline on target-domain data and finetunes it with limited online interaction using uncertainty-regularized planning.
To mitigate distribution shift when learning, FOWM augments TD-MPC with a V-AWR objective that biases learning toward actions supported by the offline data. PIA follows the same offline-to-online template, but targets a different transfer setting: its offline initialization is constructed from heterogeneous simulation priors. Rather than using the V-AWR offline objective, PIA retains the TD-MPC2 training objective and conditions the model on task context to distinguish heterogeneous dynamics. Thus, the central problem is not only offline-to-online fine-tuning under task or policy shift, but cross-domain correction of the simulator’s bias with limited target-domain interaction.

Sim-to-real Adaptation. Domain randomization trains policies over randomized simulator dynamics to improve transfer under simulator mismatch [ 17 ] .
Rapid motor adaptation instead trains a base policy and adaptation module in simulation, enabling fast online adaptation to unseen deployment conditions [ 25 ] .
These methods are most effective when the simulated variation covers the relevant target-domain variation.
More broadly, sim-to-real systems may incorporate real data for system identification, residual modeling, or validation; Kaufmann et al. [ 26 ] improve drone racing by augmenting simulation with data-driven residual perception and dynamics models identified from real-world experience.
PIA is complementary: simulated trajectories are treated as biased replay priors rather than as the final training environment, and their residual mismatch is corrected with target-domain interaction during offline-to-online MBRL.

Autonomous Racing. Model Predictive Control (MPC) delivers strong performance on full-size autonomous race cars but requires carefully engineered models [ 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 4 ] . At the limits of handling, however, small residual mismatches in tire grip or actuator response can cause failures, motivating controllers that can update from physical interaction [ 31 ] . RL systems have achieved strong autonomous-racing results in simulation with large interaction budgets, including GT Sophy in Gran Turismo [ 3 , 32 ] , Formula RL [ 33 ] , and AssettoCorsaGym [ 18 ] , but these works do not address few-shot physical adaptation on a full-size race car. Closest to our hardware setting, Djeumou et al. [ 34 ] train RL policies in a neural-SDE vehicle model learned from real driving data and deploy them zero-shot for a drifting task. PIA instead adapts a simulation-pretrained world model using limited physical interaction.
To our knowledge, none of the cited literature has demonstrated this offline-to-online adaptation regime on a full-size autonomous race car.

2026-10-20.title: Foundation Model Driven Optical Flow
2026-10-20.authors: Praroop Chanda , Suryansh Kumar
2026-10-20.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-20.comment: 19-pages, 5 figures, 16 tables. Accepted for publication at 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: RoCo-Spring: The Robust Correspondence Challenge
2026-10-20.abstract:
We investigate how frozen pretrained visual and depth representations support dense optical flow when coupled with a supervised matching network. Building on TTSFlow, this paper studies Dense Prediction Transformer (DPT) feature decoding and one coarse-to-fine refinement stage. Our method fuses features from frozen DINOv2 and Depth Anything V2 models and estimates optical flow through a trainable transformer-based matching pipeline. After optical-flow training on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings3D, it achieves 2.37 endpoint error (EPE) on the Sintel training split, Final pass, compared with 2.52 for the FlowSeek (T) configuration reported here.
Our RoCo-Spring 2026 entry, RoCo-29 ⋅ \cdot VSAI , obtains a robustness-balanced score of 1.1038, Spring EPE of 1.411, and RobustSpring proxy EPE of 4.739,
with a lower balanced score than seven of the twelve listed reference baselines. These results characterize the complete pipeline, which reuses frozen foundation backbones and performs one refinement stage.
Code is available at: https://github.com/Visual-and-Spatial-AI-Lab/FFlow
2026-10-20.introduction:
Dense optical flow lies at the core of visual perception [ 43 ] . It estimates a motion vector for every pixel between consecutive frames. It enables a wide range of applications, including video understanding [ 8 ] , saliency detection [ 21 ] , action recognition [ 62 , 33 , 45 ] , dense 3D reconstruction [ 25 , 19 , 36 ] , and motion modeling [ 11 ] . Over the past decade, deep learning-based approaches have dramatically improved the accuracy of optical flow [ 4 , 5 , 9 , 12 , 20 , 24 , 39 , 40 , 42 , 44 , 46 , 47 , 52 , 53 , 55 , 63 , 61 ] . Notable methods such as RAFT [ 47 ] and its variants [ 51 , 12 , 34 ] combine learned representations with repeated flow updates. This motivates studying how pretrained representations can be used within an alternative matching pipeline.

In parallel, vision foundation models have reshaped the field of computer vision [ 31 , 2 , 17 , 35 , 7 ] . Models trained once on internet-scale imaging data now transfer effectively across computer vision tasks such as object detection [ 64 ] , segmentation [ 60 ] , depth estimation [ 57 , 58 ] , and geometric reasoning [ 22 ] . Rather than retraining specialized architectures for each problem, we increasingly reuse pretrained representations as general-purpose visual priors. These developments motivate reusing pretrained representations while learning the modules needed for optical-flow estimation.

Pretrained representations have also been investigated for optical flow, including cross-view pretraining in CroCo v2 [ 53 ] , depth-informed estimation in FlowSeek [ 34 ] , and pretrained input encoders in WAFT [ 50 ] . Our question is how to combine frozen visual and depth representations within a dense optical-flow pipeline. We evaluate that pipeline on cross-dataset optical-flow benchmarks and the RoCo-Spring corruption benchmark. Appendix C discusses these approaches and the related video-based reconstruction setting of D4RT [ 59 ] .

This paper extends our TTSFlow framework [ 3 ] , retaining its combination of frozen DINOv2 and Depth Anything V2 features before matching. The changes studied here are DPT-based decoding of intermediate DINOv2 features, one higher-resolution refinement stage, and evaluation of a Spring-adapted model on RoCo-Spring. The matching transformer, correlation-to-flow formulation, feature-based propagation, coarse-to-fine refinement, and convex upsampling follow GMFlow [ 55 ] . These are inherited components, not new matching operators. The downstream transformer, projection and fusion layers, propagation projections, and upsampling predictor are learned from optical-flow supervision. Experiment (Table 5 ) compares DPT configurations at a fixed refinement count. The historical TTSFlow fusion ablation is explicitly identified in the experiments (Table 4 ). Our experimental results evaluate this combined system rather than isolating what frozen foundation features can achieve alone.

2026-10-20.title: VaDar: Implicit Goal Conditioning via Value Disaggregation
2026-10-20.authors: Shashwat Saxena , Mehul Goel , Sreyas Venkataraman , Sarvesh Patil , Max Simchowitz
2026-10-20.abstract:
Long-horizon tasks are important for modern AI and robotics, yet pose a challenge for reinforcement learning. Historically, a popular approach has been to decompose a task into subgoals, and learn a subgoal-conditioned policy to execute each subtask in sequence.
We introduce an alternative called Value Disaggregation ( VaDar ), which trains a single subgoal-independent policy to maximize a linear combination of per-subgoal critic values. Because subgoal information is needed only at training-time , VaDar removes the need for possibly costly or cumbersome subgoal-selection during policy deployment. Moreover, through careful experiments, we show that VaDar (1) is always competitive with, and frequently outperforms , natural baselines like goal-conditioning and (2) succeeds on tasks with non-sequential goal structure and multiple optimization objectives. In particular, VaDar is the first algorithm to solve challenging, long-horizon tasks in the Robocasa365 suite, even when starting from a policy pretrained from behavior cloning with near-zero initial task success. Taken together, VaDar ’s successes suggest that subgoal information benefits actor-critic reinforcement learning by enhancing the efficacy of critic learning , whereas policy goal-conditioning is often unnecessary.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Learning to complete long-horizon, multi-step tasks is a fundamental challenge across a number of core AI domains, from robotics ( Gupta et al., 2019 ) , to language modeling ( Wei et al., 2022 ) , to chemical reaction design ( Liu et al., 2023b ) . A popular approach, often referred to as hierarchical goal conditioning ( HGC ) in reinforcement learning literature, decomposes these complex, long-horizon tasks into a set of subgoals, each of which can be executed in sequence by a dedicated learned, goal-conditioned policy ( Gupta et al., 2019 ; Nasiriany et al., 2019 ; Levy et al., 2019 ; Nachum et al., 2018 ) . However, attempting to learn per-sub-task policies introduces a new set of challenges. Myopic completion of a given sub-task might compromise performance on future sub-tasks. Moreover, explicit decompositions often require sub-tasks to be sequential in nature, and necessitate a dedicated sub-task planner to decide the current subtask to be attempted during policy deployment.

In this paper, we propose an alternative to HGC that we call Value-Disaggregation ( VaDar ), a framework for sample-efficient reinforcement learning on long-horizon multi-step tasks. We focus on continuous control robotic manipulation tasks that can be decomposed into sub-tasks g 1 , … , g | G | g^{1},\dots,g^{|G|} . These subgoal evaluations are rapidly becoming highly reliable with today’s VLMs ( Du et al., 2023 ) .
While HGC learns policies π ⁡ ( s , g ) \pi(s,g) that take sub-goals g g as explicit input, VaDar instead learns a sub-goal agnostic policy π ⁡ ( s ) \pi(s) , with a critic that estimates the values of all sub-tasks simultaneously. The policy is then trained to maximize a linear combination of critic values, optimizing for an aggregate performance on current-sub-goals as well as future tasks. We stress that VaDar is a generic algorithmic template, being compatible with any preferred choice of critic learning algorithm or policy extraction method; we depict VaDar in Figure 1 .

VaDar removes the need for subgoal-evaluation at inference by design . Thus, compute-intensive VLM calls used to delineate subgoals, need only be made at training time , and not during policy rollouts. Moreover, VaDar is flexible across both task structure and reward constraints, enabling activations both to safety-constrained reinforcement learning ( Section K.1 ), and to non-sequential task orders which could admit a directed acyclic graph (DAG) structure. ( Appendix G ).

Across a variety of benchmarks for continuous control and policy extraction methods, we find that VaDar , (1) Consistently outperforms HGC ( Section 4 ), hindsight experience replay (HER) ( Andrychowicz et al., 2018 ) , and dense preference-based rewards ( Brown et al., 2019 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) ; (2) Enables the first non-VLA BC-to-online RL method to converge on the evaluated long-horizon Robocasa365 tasks ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) under fixed initial-state conditions; (3) Enables multi-objective reinforcement learning by incorporating safety constraints ( Section K.1 ), and enables test-time steering ( Section 6.3 ) by combining critic learning with best-of- N N sampling ( Li et al., 2026 ) ; and (4) Works seamlessly with VLM supervision ( Appendix I ) and reaches convergence when goals are specified by reasoning Vision-Language Models (VLMs). This allows sample efficient robot learning from high-dimensional visual observations.

To understand these gains, our ablations examine dense subgoal supervision and future-aware policy extraction ( Section 6.2 ). We find that future-aware policy extraction reduces myopic behavior, while intermediate subgoal supervision improves learning even when policy extraction uses only final-subgoal values. This suggests that subgoals can support long-horizon RL through critic learning without explicit policy goal conditioning.
Taken together, our findings invert the traditional perspectives on overcoming the challenges of long horizon, valued-based reinforcement learning. In short, we find: Rather than myopically conditioning policies via decomposed long-horizon sub-goals, predicting temporally rich subgoal successes can provide critics with dense supervision to enhance the accuracy of long-reaching measurements of full-task success.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Long-horizon reinforcement learning via temporal abstraction. Long-horizon reinforcement learning is commonly addressed by introducing temporal abstraction: instead of reasoning over primitive actions, the agent reasons over extended behaviors, skills, or subgoals. Classical formulations include the options framework, where temporally extended actions are specified by initiation sets, intra-option policies, and termination conditions ( Sutton et al., 1999 ; Bacon et al., 2016 ) ; hierarchical abstract machines ( Parr and Russell, 1997 ) ; feudal reinforcement learning ( Dayan and Hinton, 1992 ; Vezhnevets et al., 2017 ) ; and MAXQ value decomposition ( Dietterich, 1999 ) . Subsequent work studies how such skills and hierarchies can be discovered from data ( Fox et al., 2017 ; Evans and Şimşek, 2024 ; Cannon and Simsek, 2025 ; Peng et al., 2022 ) . While these methods differ in how subtasks are specified or learned, they use subgoal structure to organize policy execution: the learned policy must either act through a prescribed hierarchy of subtasks ( Dietterich, 1999 ; Parr and Russell, 1997 ) or utilize temporally extended controllers ( Bacon et al., 2016 ; Fox et al., 2017 ) . In contrast, VaDar assumes that subgoals are part of the MDP design, but does not learn or execute a hierarchy over them; subgoals are used only to construct training-time value targets for a single flat policy.

Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning. Goal conditioned RL provide a natural design for conditioning on desired outcomes/sub-goals.
Instead of learning a separate controller for each task, goal-conditioned methods learn policies or value functions indexed by a goal, enabling transfer across related goal-reaching problems.
Classical dynamic-goal learning first studied transfer across changing goal-reaching tasks ( Kaelbling, 1993 ) .
This idea was later extended through universal value function approximators, which learn goal-indexed value functions with function approximation ( Schaul et al., 2015 ) , and hindsight relabeling, which reuses failed rollouts as successful examples for alternative achieved goals ( Andrychowicz et al., 2018 ) .
However, conditioning a flat policy on the final task goal does not by itself resolve long-horizon credit assignment.
For this reason, hierarchical goal-conditioned RL (HGC) uses goal conditioning as a local control primitive: a high-level policy, planner, or task specification provides intermediate subgoals, and a low-level goal-conditioned policy learns to reach them ( Nachum et al., 2018 ; Levy et al., 2019 ; Gupta et al., 2020 ; Nair et al., 2018 ) .
This reduces the effective horizon, but introduce additional dependencies: they often assume a sequential subgoal structure, treat only one subgoal as active at a time, and require the deployed policy to be supplied with the correct current goal.
These issues are costly and difficult when subgoal progress and completion must be evaluated by expert rules or large vision-language models during inference. VaDar avoids this test-time dependency by learning a subgoal-agnostic policy; goal information enters only through the critic during training.

Value decomposition and reward-factorized critics. MAXQ decomposes the value of a hierarchical policy into child-task values and completion functions, reflecting the procedural structure of a subroutine hierarchy ( Dietterich, 1999 ) . Successor representations and successor features instead factor value prediction into predictive components and reward-dependent weights ( Dayan, 1993 ; Barreto et al., 2017 ) . VaDar follows this latter spirit of reward-factorized value estimation, but uses subgoal-completion signals to learn a vector-valued critic in an offline-to-online actor-critic pipeline. Closer to robotics, task-and-motion planning (TAMP) couples high-level symbolic task planners with low-level continuous motion planners over a fixed subtask vocabulary ( Kaelbling and Lozano-Pérez, 2011 ; Garrett et al., 2021 ) . VaDar shares the assumption that the task admits a subgoal-level decomposition, but does not plan over symbolic actions or commit to a fixed sequencing at execution time: the decomposition enters only through the critic, and the deployed policy is a single flat, subgoal-agnostic controller.

Representation learning for value-based RL. Recent work has shown that auxiliary prediction objectives can improve value learning by shaping the
representations used by the critic. MR.Q ( Fujimoto et al., 2025 ) learns state and state-action
representations that predict rewards, termination, and future latent states, using model-based objectives
to improve a model-free actor–critic without planning through the learned dynamics.
DR.Q ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) builds on this approach by encouraging the learned representations to
retain information about future states through a mutual-information objective, together with a
recency-aware replay scheme. VaDar is complementary to these approaches: rather than introducing
an auxiliary dynamics or representation-learning objective, it obtains additional supervision directly
from the RL problem by fitting subgoal value functions at multiple temporal resolutions . Thus, the
shared critic representation is trained simultaneously by intermediate and long-horizon TD targets,
which we find can improve final-task value estimation even when the intermediate values are not used
for policy extraction.

2026-10-20.title: PhantomTac: Hijacking Robotic Tactile Systems with Deploy-and-forget Tags
2026-10-20.authors: Binbin Zhang , Yifeng Zhang , Xiaomeng Chen , Dongyao Chen
2026-10-20.comment: Accepted at ACM CCS 2026. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract:
Tactile perception is crucial for precise robotic manipulation, providing an important foundation for dexterous, closed-loop force control.
Among various tactile sensing techniques, magnetic tactile sensors stand out thanks to their fine-grained, three-dimensional force perception capability and strong robustness against visual occlusion.
In this study, we discover a physical loophole called PhantomTac in magnetic tactile sensors.
The attacker can alter the magnetic field, thus spoofing the force interpreted by magnetic tactile sensors.
The attacker can stealthily deploy such an attack by simply attaching a thin (the thickness is around 0.5 mm), battery-free magnetic tag to the surface of an object.
Hence, the attack tag can be easily concealed by a barcode sticker.
Such an attack scheme is “deploy-and-forget” — the attacker can deploy the tag and leave.
When a robotic hand is picking up an object, it may severely damage the object.
Specifically, spoofing the normal force can crush the object, whereas spoofing the shear force can lead to a loose grip, thus dropping the object.
Compared with directly sabotaging the robotic hand, PhantomTac is much more concealed as the attacker does not need access to the device.
We performed extensive reverse-engineering efforts to characterize the sensing mechanism of commercial-off-the-shelf tactile sensors and proposed a practical tag design.
End-to-end evaluations conducted on real robots and robotic arms demonstrate that our attack can bypass existing anti-interference mechanisms and effectively hijack their closed-loop control processes, achieving an attack success rate exceeding 95% when the grasping-position offset is bounded within 8 mm.
Finally, based on the limitations of existing anti-magnetic interference mechanisms, we propose a multimodal-consistency defense mechanism to mitigate such physical-layer security threats.
2026-10-20.introduction:
As embodied AI systems are deployed in increasingly complex physical environments, robotic manipulation has become critically dependent on multimodal sensing ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) .
Among predominant perceptual modalities, e.g., vision and audition, tactile perception is fast emerging as an indispensable sensing ability for contact-rich manipulation ( Meribout et al., 2024 ; Bhirangi et al., 2025 ) .
Tactile perception provides fine-grained measurements of contact states and force distributions that neither vision nor proprioception can fully replicate ( Andrussow et al., 2023 ; Mao et al., 2024 ) .
Specifically, visual perception is susceptible to environmental interference such as lighting variations and occlusion, making it difficult to perceive contact states within visual blind spots; proprioception mainly reflects the robot’s internal motion state and therefore cannot acquire fine-grained interaction data at the contact interface ( Luo et al., 2024 ) .

In contrast, tactile perception demonstrates unique advantages in sensing granularity, real-time performance, and environmental resilience.
Tactile sensors can directly acquire the precise force feedback at the physical contact points.
This core feature allows robots to accurately characterize key parameters ( Li et al., 2020 ) , such as weight ( Silva et al., 2019 ) , stiffness ( Yuan et al., 2017b ) , and friction coefficient ( Khamis et al., 2021 ) .
In the system scope, tactile sensing enables closed-loop force control systems, thus adjusting the robot’s fine-grained manipulation in real time.
It also prevents manipulation failures caused by perceptual deficits, thereby ensuring the safety and precision of human-robot collaboration.
This capability can be the cornerstone for several crucial real-world tasks.
For example, when a robotic gripper closes on an object, understanding subtle variations in the normal force helps apply an appropriate force, thereby enabling a firm grip without crushing the object.
When a robotic hand is holding a fragile object while moving, sensing the shear force in real-time can prevent the gripper from dropping or damaging the object.

To achieve tactile sensing, there are the following key approaches: optical, capacitive, resistive, and magnetic.
Specifically, vision-based tactile sensors are commonly composed of light sensors and an elastomer ( GelSight, 2026a ) .
An applied force can incur deformation in the elastomer.
Then, the light sensor can interpret the deformation, thus characterizing the force.
However, this approach is undermined by the cost of frame rate, image processing overhead, and packaging volume.
For example, the GelSight Mini is listed at USD 510 and integrates an 8MP camera with a nominal frame rate of 25 FPS, while its package size is approximately 32 mm by 31 mm by 28 mm ( GelSight, 2026c ; GelSight, 2026b ) .
Capacitive tactile sensors ( SingleTact, 2026b ) perform measurements via capacitance changes caused by force to decode tactile information.
However, this approach is susceptible to parasitic capacitance, noise, humidity, and temperature variations.
Piezoresistive tactile sensors ( Tekscan, 2026 ) utilize resistance changes caused by force to decode tactile information.
Although being a low-cost option, this line of approaches is prone to hysteresis, drift, and insufficient long-term stability.

As we will elaborate in Sec. 2 , magnetic tactile sensors are fast emerging as an approach that can achieve both multi-dimensional force sensing and low cost.
For example, magnetic tactile sensors can be composed of an underlying array of magnetometers and a magnetic elastomer.
As the magnetic field drops with distance cubed, subtle deformation of the elastomer can be captured by the sensor.
Compared to other tactile solutions, magnetic tactile sensing possesses significant advantages: rich three-dimensional force sensing, compact form factor, low cost, and resilience against light conditions.

In this paper, we discover a fundamental physical vulnerability in magnetic tactile sensors.
That is, one can alter the environment’s magnetic field, thus injecting erroneous force into magnetic tactile sensors.
As shown in Sec. 2.3.1 and Sec. 6.5 , this underlying vulnerability is present across multiple evaluated magnetic tactile sensor models.
Exploiting this vulnerability, we propose PhantomTac (as shown in Fig. 6 ), the first stealthy physical adversarial attack targeting magnetic tactile sensors using passive magnetic tags.

To achieve a fine-grained, stealthy attack on magnetic tactile sensors, it is crucial to answer the following key challenges:
(1) How to characterize commercial-off-the-shelf (COTS) magnetic tactile sensors?
(2) How can the attack effectively alter/modulate the environment’s magnetic field while staying stealthy?
(3) How to affect the closed-loop force control, thus achieving severe damage to real-world objects?

Addressing the first challenge is essential for achieving an in-depth understanding of the magnetic tactile sensor’s mechanism.
Specifically, magnetometers interpret the magnetic field as a three-dimensional field strength, i.e., B x , B y B_{x},B_{y} , and B z B_{z} .

Therefore, we conducted extensive reverse engineering research on representative COTS magnetic tactile sensors, e.g., PX6AX-GEN3-MC-M2020-Elite ( PaXini, 2026 ) .
Specifically, we collected sensor response data from magnetic tactile sensors under the intervention of external magnetic sources, utilized this dataset to construct a fitting model based on the Radial Basis Function (RBF), and used this model to characterize the response characteristics of magnetic tactile sensors to external magnetic sources.

To address the second challenge, we employ micro-passive permanent magnets (with a thickness of 0.5 mm) as the attack source.
This endows PhantomTac with extremely high stealth characteristics: it requires no external power supply, generates no monitorable thermal signals or acoustic signatures, and causes almost no changes to the visual appearance of the target object. Furthermore, since the magnetic field itself can penetrate non-ferromagnetic materials without attenuation, this attack is completely independent of line-of-sight conditions, allowing the attack tag to be well hidden under normal labels on the object’s surface. Based on this, we can achieve the injection of forged normal or shear force signals through carefully designed attack tags while staying stealthy.

To address the third challenge, we characterize the target magnetic tactile sensor model’s responses to external magnetic sources.
This one-time-effort allows the attacker to customize the attack tag using the aforementioned passive magnetic tag design framework for deterministic force injection.
Once deployed, when a humanoid robot or robotic arm performs a touching or grasping task, the attack tag prompts the sensor to generate erroneous raw force signals and feed them back into the closed-loop control system. PhantomTac also shows high robustness in repetitive experiments. For example, PhantomTac maintains an attack success rate above 95% for grasping-position offsets within 8 mm in our experiments.
This signal injection causes the system to make erroneous judgments at the decision-making level, such as erroneously increasing or decreasing the contact force, ultimately leading to object damage or operational failure in the real world.
We demonstrated these end-to-end attacks in the online artifact.

In PhantomTac , we make the following contributions:

We discover and formally characterize an underlying hardware vulnerability in magnetic tactile sensors, namely the physical inseparability of internal and external magnetic flux, proving that current anti-interference mechanisms possess fundamental flaws when facing static adversarial magnetic fields.

We propose PhantomTac , a passive and highly stealthy tactile perception attack framework. By utilizing reverse engineering, we design the passive magnetic tag that is as thin as a piece of paper.

Based on the limitations of existing anti-magnetic interference mechanisms, we propose a novel defense mechanism to effectively mitigate such physical-layer security threats.

1. We discover and formally characterize an underlying hardware vulnerability in magnetic tactile sensors, namely the physical inseparability of internal and external magnetic flux, proving that current anti-interference mechanisms possess fundamental flaws when facing static adversarial magnetic fields.

2. We propose PhantomTac , a passive and highly stealthy tactile perception attack framework. By utilizing reverse engineering, we design the passive magnetic tag that is as thin as a piece of paper.

3. Based on the limitations of existing anti-magnetic interference mechanisms, we propose a novel defense mechanism to effectively mitigate such physical-layer security threats.

# 2. Background

## 2.1. Primer on Magnetic Tactile Sensing

The rapid advancement of embodied intelligence, robotic manipulation, and dexterous grasping has underscored the critical importance of tactile perception.
Compared with visual sensing, tactile feedback directly captures fine-grained contact states, force variations, and slip — information essential for fine manipulation, closed-loop control, and operation in harsh environments (e.g., visual blind spots).
Among emerging sensing modalities, magnetic tactile sensors have gained significant traction due to their high sensitivity, multidimensional force perception, and flexibility in integration.
In academia, the number of related research efforts has exhibited a rapid growth trend in recent years ( Man et al., 2024 ; Bhirangi et al., 2025 ; Pattabiraman et al., 2025 ; Hu et al., 2024 ; Yan et al., 2021a ) .
The industrial sector has also been heavily advancing magnetic tactile sensors since 2021.
Specifically, PaXini introduced various models (e.g., fingertip, palm, and finger pad) of magnetic tactile sensors in 2021 ( PaXini Tech, 2026b ) .
Another leading manufacturer, XELA ( XELA Robotics, 2026a ) , presented uSkin in 2021.
Meta has open-sourced ReSkin ( Bhirangi et al., 2021 ) in 2021.
Major semiconductor manufacturer, e.g., Melexis, introduced magnetic tactile sensors (Tactaxis) for a dexterous robotics system in 2022 ( Signor et al., 2022 ) .
In the following, we first describe the components of a magnetic tactile sensor. Then, we elaborate on its advantages.

The fundamental working principle of magnetic tactile sensors is to convert mechanical forces
into measurable magnetic field variations.
As illustrated in Fig. 1 (a), the sensor typically consists of a flexible elastomer layer, an embedded magnet, and an underlying sensor array composed of several magnetometers, e.g., Hall-effect sensors ( Tomo et al., 2016 ) or magnetoresistive sensors ( Oh et al., 2017 ) .
When an external pressure is applied to the elastomer, the elastic structure undergoes compressive, bending, or shear deformation, which alters the relative position, distance, or pose between the magnet and the magnetic sensing units.
As the magnetic field follows an inverse-cube law with the distance:

To better demonstrate the principles and structure of the magnetic tactile sensor, we disassembled a magnetic tactile sensor (PaXini PX6AX-GEN3-MC-M2020-Elite) to reveal the inside view, i.e., Fig. 1 (b).

## 2.2. Advantages of Magnetic Tactile Sensors

Fine-grained force sensing. Magnetic tactile sensors typically achieve perception by embedding magnets or magnetic materials within a flexible elastomer, e.g., silicone.
When external contact induces deformation in the elastomer, the position and/or orientation of the magnet changes accordingly, thereby altering the local magnetic field distribution. Magnetic field sensors exhibit high sensitivity to such variations.
Consequently, even miniaturized displacements or slight contact forces can be effectively converted into measurable electrical signals, thereby enabling highly granular micro-force detection.
For example, a single sensing point of the XELA uSkin sensor achieves a resolution of 0.1 gf, approximately equivalent to 0.98 mN ( XELA Robotics, 2026b ) .

Multi-dimensional force decoupling. The magnetic field can be characterized as a 1 × 3 1\times 3 vector in three dimensions, i.e., x, y, and z.
When forces are applied in different directions, they induce displacement or rotation of the magnet in distinct directions, thus leading to corresponding variations in the magnetic field.
For example, normal forces predominantly manifest as magnetic field variations in the vertical direction to the magnetometer array.
In contrast, shear forces are more readily reflected as magnetic field deviations in the horizontal plane of the magnetometer array.
For example, the IPTU GEN3 series from PaXini ( PaXini, 2026 ) can interpret three-dimensional forces.

Low cost & overheads. The magnetometer array of magnetic tactile sensors is commonly comprised of 8-16 magnetometers — tiny, chip-level sensors with an edge length of around 2 mm.
For each frame of the magnetic tactile data stream, the data is a 3 × N ​ u ​ m 3\times Num matrix of single-precision (32-bit) floating-point numbers, thus minimizing the overhead in the peripheral readout.
These features lead to a compact form factor and low prices of magnetic tactile sensors.
For example, the price of the GelSight Mini (optical solution) is $510 ( GelSight, 2026c ) , whereas the base kit of the SingleTact (capacitive solution) is around $81 ( SingleTact, 2026a ) .
In contrast, the PaXini PX-6AX GEN3 (magnetic solution) is around $29 per unit ( PaXini Tech, 2026c ) .
Thanks to the compact form factor, magnetic tactile sensors can also be integrated for various scenarios.
For example, both PaXini ( PaXini Tech, 2026b ) and XELA ( XELA Robotics, 2026a ) offer magnetic tactile sensor solutions tailored for various locations, e.g., fingertips, finger pads, and palms.

Robust static & dynamic sensing. Regarding static perception, magnetic tactile sensors are typically capable of directly measuring absolute magnetic fields or differential magnetic field signals. Therefore, they are more adept at stably characterizing the force state under continuous contact conditions. Regarding dynamic perception, their advantages primarily stem from the high sampling frequency of the underlying magnetic field chips, as well as the high sensitivity of the magnetic field to the displacement and rotation of the magnet. Taking the public data of the PaXini PX-6AX GEN3 as an example, its sampling frequency reaches up to 1,000,000 Hz, with a maximum output frequency of 1000 Hz ( PaXini Tech, 2026a ) . The 2023 paper by the Melexis team ( Le Signor et al., 2023 ) also indicates that magnetic tactile sensors possess high-speed three-dimensional perception capabilities, demonstrating their potential for slip detection applications in industrial grippers.

In Table 1 , we characterized the key features of optical, capacitive, resistive, and magnetic tactile sensors.
However, to build practical systems based on these key features, it is also essential to mitigate the impact of common interferences, e.g., the magnetic field incurred by the Earth and everyday electronics.
In the following, we will elaborate on existing efforts to overcome interference and highlight their limitations.

## 2.3. Existing Methods for Mitigating Magnetic Interferences

In a magnetic tactile sensor, the magnetic field sensed by a magnetometer, i.e., 𝐁 \mathbf{B} can be denoted as the following formula:

For a single magnetometer, it is infeasible to differentiate 𝐁 𝐞𝐦 \mathbf{B_{em}} from other components.
To overcome this challenge, Le Signor et al. ( Signor et al., 2022 ) proposed a gradiometric design that uses multiple closely aligned magnetometers within a single compact IC package (about 2 mm span).
Now, based on Eq. 2 , we can denote sensor i i ’s measurement of the magnetic field as:

Although the aforementioned approach can effectively remove 𝐁 𝐄 + 𝐁 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐬 \mathbf{B_{E}}+\mathbf{B_{others}} , there is a major loophole:
If the interfering magnetic field is not uniformly distributed across the magnetometers, the subtraction approach would fail.
Then we ask a question: Is it possible to produce such a magnet in the real world?
The most intuitive interfering source is a small, strong magnet placed close to the underlying sensor array. Due to the short distance, its magnetic field varies across adjacent magnetometers instead of appearing as a uniformly distributed interference.
Therefore, subtraction cannot fully cancel this external magnetic field.
The remaining differential signal may therefore be interpreted as a change in the embedded magnet’s field and converted by the tactile sensor into an erroneous force reading.

To verify this, we selected up-to-date COTS magnetic tactile sensor models, i.e., PaXini PX6AX-GEN3-MC-M2020-Elite and XELA’s uSPa 46 (as shown in Fig. 3 ), to perform a real-world study.
For the interfering magnetic field, we select representative electronic devices (e.g., earbuds and speakers) and a small passive magnet.
Here, we use electronic devices to verify if the tactile sensors are competent for overcoming common interferences.
We picked the passive magnet for verifying the aforementioned loophole.

We designed a comparative experiment (as shown in Fig. 2 ) that evaluated sensor behavior under two categories of external magnetic input.
Specifically, we categorized the test sources into two classes: ambient magnetic field sources and localized concentrated magnetic objects.
The ambient stray magnetic field sources encompass the natural background magnetic field and several everyday electronic devices (e.g., smart bands, Bluetooth earphones, and Bluetooth speakers); whereas localized concentrated magnetic objects (e.g., small strong magnets) are utilized to simulate external magnetic disturbances with higher spatial locality and more pronounced magnetic field gradients.

In this experiment, we maintained the installation configuration and relative testing posture of the magnetic tactile sensors consistent, exclusively varying the category of the external magnetic source (as shown in Fig. 2 (b)—(e)).
We first employed the MLX90393 ( Melexis, 2025 ) to record the magnetic field of each object (as shown in Fig. 2 (a)).
This step is for verifying whether the object’s magnetic field strength is sufficient.
Next, we recorded the sensor outputs by putting the object close to the magnetic tactile sensor (as shown in Fig. 2 (b)—(e)).
This step is for verifying whether the object’s magnetic field can interfere with the tactile sensor.
The distance is fixed to be 10 mm.

As shown in Fig. 4 , all objects demonstrate strong magnetic field strength. Note that the earbuds’ magnetic field is even stronger than the passive magnet.
However, Fig. 5 demonstrated that for the PaXini sensor, electronic devices do not have a sustained effect on the tactile sensor.
Here, the force values in the figure represent the vector sum of F x F_{x} , F y F_{y} , and F z F_{z} .
This experiment revealed two key findings:
(1) The small passive magnet produces erroneous readings on both major tactile sensors.
(2) The PaXini model achieves better resilience against an interfering magnetic field compared with XELA’s model. (That is, under magnetic interference from common electronic devices, the abnormal output of XELA is 5.8–7.7 times that of PaXini, and the abnormal output of XELA persists continuously.)

This experiment demonstrates that a small passive magnet without sensor-specific customization can effectively interfere with multiple COTS magnetic tactile sensor models, indicating that the underlying vulnerability is not limited to a single sensor model.
Next, we ask: Is it possible to formulate a practical attack for these tactile systems?

2026-10-20.title: CondenseVLA: Learnable History Condensation for Efficient Multi-Frame VLA
2026-10-20.authors: Feiyang Hong , Yujie Wei , Bo Zhao , Xiu Su , Hongxun Yao , Shuo Yang
2026-10-20.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-20.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. including supplementary material and the NeurIPS paper checklist. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract:
Robot manipulation often depends on short-term cues—such as brief contacts, temporary occlusions, and intermediate object states—that are ambiguous in a single frame and can only be resolved by integrating observations over time. However, injecting historical information solely by enlarging the history window is computationally costly and frequently yields limited gains due to substantial redundancy and task-agnostic, inflexible sampling of observations.
We propose CondenseVLA, a multi-frame VLA policy with a learnable decoder-side history condensation module for using short-term visual context in action decoding. Given a sequence of cached per-frame features from the VLM backbone, CondenseVLA distills observation history into a fixed set of slot tokens using learnable queries and multi-head cross-attention. Simple auxiliary regularization penalizes overlap among slot attention maps and decorrelates slot embeddings, encouraging complementary attention and reducing slot redundancy.
Across the evaluated tasks, CondenseVLA improves Simpler-WidowX success from 58.7% to 69.8% (+11.1 percentage points), achieves 97.2% on LIBERO, and reaches 52.8% on real-world tasks. It achieves 21.6% success on memory-dependent RMBench tasks. These results support selective condensation of bounded recent visual evidence for action decoding, while harder multi-observation tasks expose the limits of a finite history window.
