2026-10-20.title: Finite-Time Capture by a Dubins Pursuer Against Unknown Evader Strategies
2026-10-20.authors: Dinesh Patra , Bhargav Jha , Ashish R. Hota
2026-10-20.abstract: We consider a planar pursuit-evasion problem in which a Dubins pursuer seeks to capture a slower first-order point-mass evader that can change its heading instantaneously. First, we propose a turn-rate feedback law with a single tunable gain and derive an explicit admissible gain interval that guarantees finite-time capture against any admissible evader strategy while satisfying the turn-rate constraint. Next, we obtain an explicit capture-time bound and characterize the turning authority required for the gain interval to be non-empty. Finally, we show that the dependence on the evader’s speed bound can be removed by deriving a speed ceiling, computable solely from the pursuer’s parameters, below which the guarantees hold at the maximum allowable gain. Numerical simulations illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach.
2026-10-20.introduction:
F ixed-wing aircraft, wheeled robots, and other vehicles that move at a nearly constant speed and steer through a bounded turn rate are routinely tasked with capturing a moving target, in applications ranging from aerial combat [ 42 , 33 , 34 , 35 ] and surveillance [ 17 , 20 ] to target tracking [ 49 ] and formation control [ 6 , 19 , 38 , 48 ] ; see [ 36 ] for an overview of the underlying guidance problems. When the target is an adversarial evader, a practical guidance law for such a pursuer must meet three requirements. First, it must guarantee capture against every evader strategy while using only quantities available to the pursuer. Second, its turn-rate command must never exceed the actuator limit. Third, the command should vary continuously in time rather than switch between extreme values. This paper presents a feedback law that meets all three.

Much of the existing theory treats simpler settings. Pursuit games between holonomic players with simple motion, who can change their direction of motion instantaneously, are well developed [ 13 ] .
Open-loop capture strategies are known for one-on-one [ 13 , Chapter 6] , multiplayer [ 25 ] , and obstacle-cluttered [ 23 ] engagements.
The singular surfaces that arise in these solutions are examined in [ 10 ] , which proposes a Lyapunov-based feedback strategy that guarantees capture within an ε \varepsilon -neighborhood of the initial Apollonius circle [ 13 , Chapter 6] .

Cars, robots, and aircraft, however, cannot turn instantaneously. A constant-speed unicycle with zero minimum turn radius captures this nonholonomic constraint alone, and the Markov–Dubins model [ 12 , 16 , 37 ] adds a bounded turn rate, which makes the minimum turn radius a central parameter. For both models, time-optimal open-loop interception has been characterized only when the target is stationary [ 7 ] or follows a trajectory known in advance [ 40 , 22 , 47 ] , and the resulting solutions are not available in closed form.

Closed-form guidance laws are straightforward to implement, but their guarantees rely on benign target motion. Linearized proportional navigation [ 45 , 14 ] , impact-angle-constrained guidance [ 31 , 29 ] , Lyapunov-based steering in polar coordinates [ 1 ] , and trajectory-shaping guidance for path following [ 30 ] are all analyzed for stationary or non-maneuvering targets. For a constant-speed unicycle, the bearing-proportional turn-rate law of [ 11 ] ensures only that the pursuer either captures the target or settles into a bounded tracking motion. None of these laws, therefore, meets the first requirement.

The homicidal chauffeur game (HCG) [ 13 , 21 , 24 ] addresses the adversarial setting directly, where a faster pursuer with bounded curvature seeks to capture a slower evader that can change its heading instantaneously. Its solution is intricate because the type and arrangement of singular surfaces, and hence the structure of the optimal strategies, change considerably across parameter regimes [ 21 ] . The game has been extended to bounded controls for both players, both under kinematics linearized about the collision triangle [ 35 ] and in three dimensions [ 34 ] ; to cooperative and reach–avoid variants [ 5 , 43 , 44 ] ; and to persistent tracking [ 46 ] , where the objective is to keep the target within a sensing region rather than to capture it, and the target must start inside a computed viability set.

The HCG pursuer, however, violates the third requirement and, because its strategy depends on the evader’s speed, partly the first.
Under the optimal HCG strategy, the pursuer turns at the maximum rate until its heading is aligned with the line of sight (LOS) and then switches abruptly to straight-line motion.
The command is therefore saturated throughout the turn and discontinuous at the switch, where measurement noise may cause chattering, thereby accelerating actuator deterioration.
Bounded-curvature-rate maneuvers that avoid such switching have been constructed [ 2 , 28 , 32 ] , but only for stationary targets or targets with known trajectories. In addition, HCG winning conditions and strategies are expressed in terms of the pursuer–evader speed ratio, so the evader’s maximum speed must either be known or be estimated online. In an HCG where the evader may switch once from a lower to a higher speed, [ 18 ] shows that a pursuer estimating this speed from the evader’s observed motion plays suboptimally and that from certain initial configurations the evader can prolong capture by initially moving slowly and later revealing its higher speed; moreover, a conservative estimate close to the pursuer’s own speed does not benefit the pursuer.

A different route was taken in [ 15 , 39 ] , where finite-time directional capture is established using input-to-state stability-based feedback designs. These designs use the evader’s heading and speed and allow the pursuer to vary its forward speed, while [ 39 ] additionally requires a known bound on the evader’s turning rate.

Consequently, existing methods either assume known target maneuvers, require information that is unavailable to the pursuer, such as the evader’s heading or maximum speed, or yield saturated, discontinuous turn-rate commands.
Thus, to the best of our knowledge, the existing literature does not provide a closed-form feedback law for a Dubins pursuer that guarantees finite-time capture of a simple-motion evader with a continuous, turn-rate-feasible command without relying on the evader’s strategy in its design.

In view of the above limitations, this paper proposes a turn-rate feedback law with a single gain that uses only the range to the evader and the pursuer’s heading error relative to the LOS. Its contributions are as follows.

An explicit interval of gains is derived for which, against every admissible evader strategy, capture occurs in finite time and the turn-rate command remains continuous in time and within its limit. Furthermore, an explicit upper bound on the capture time is obtained.

The turning authority the pursuer needs for this interval to be non-empty is characterized in terms of its speed, its capture radius, and the evader’s speed bound.

A speed ceiling μ ⋆ \mu^{\star} , computable from the pursuer’s parameters alone, is derived such that the largest admissible gain guarantees capture and turn-rate feasibility against every evader slower than μ ⋆ \mu^{\star} . The gain can therefore be designed without knowing or estimating the evader’s speed.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the kinematics, the information available to the pursuer, and the problem statement. Section 3 presents the proposed law and the main results, Section 4 reports numerical results, and Section 5 concludes the paper.

2026-10-20.title: Scene-Adaptive VLA: Efficient Autonomous Driving via Dynamic Layer Routing
2026-10-20.authors: Yujia Yang , Quan Yuan , Jiawei Fan , Yang Li , Tiange Fu , Xiaoyuan Fu , Guiyang Luo , Jinglin Li
2026-10-20.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-20.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. However, the massive parameter scale of VLAs strains onboard computational resources during real-time inference. This directly increases energy consumption and limits vehicle battery range, making it critical to minimize computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability. Current research on efficient VLA-based driving focuses on sequential adaptation ( e.g. , Chain-of-Thought and token adjustment), leaving structural adaptation underexplored despite parameter redundancy across dynamic driving scenes. To address this gap, we propose Scene-Adaptive VLA, an efficient framework leveraging dynamic layer routing to adjust active parameters based on real-time scenes. Inspired by the temporal continuity of scenes and model predictive uncertainty, our approach characterizes model-perceived scene complexity via frame-level temporal scene variations and decision deviations. To uncover latent scene-to-parameter correspondences, we encode this characterization into scene-aware tokens, alongside two specialized queries. A budget-conditioned layer routing mechanism evaluates these refined queries to allocate a budget that determines the active parameter ratio and subsequently selects appropriate layer combinations. The entire framework is optimized end-to-end. Extensive evaluations on the Bench2Drive benchmark show that when adapted to a state-of-the-art VLA model, our approach significantly reduces inference-time computational overhead by 53.5% with negligible degradation in driving and language capabilities. Code is available at https:github.com/yang-luvu/Scene-Adaptive-VLA .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Built on Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a dominant paradigm in autonomous driving, unifying visual perception, linguistic reasoning, and action prediction within a cohesive framework [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
However, the massive parameter scale of VLA models creates severe onboard computational resource pressure for real-time inference, directly increasing energy consumption and reducing vehicle battery range.
Consequently, minimizing computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability has become a paramount objective in VLA-based autonomous driving research [ 5 , 6 ] .

Currently, efforts to improve inference efficiency in VLMs can be broadly categorized into two directions: sequential adaptation , which dynamically adjusts the number of input or output tokens based on the task [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] , and structural adaptation , which selectively activates model parameters during inference to adapt to the task [ 11 ] .
In the domain of VLA-based autonomous driving, existing efficient inference strategies predominantly focus on sequential adaptation, such as adjusting the length of Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning [ 5 ] or modulating input token counts based on the scene [ 6 ] . Conversely, structural adaptation remains largely underexplored.

As illustrated in Fig. 1 (a), the ratio of parameters required for successful driving varies significantly across scenes of varying complexity. Structural adaptation thus holds substantial potential to enable dynamic, task-aware adjustment of active parameters, thereby facilitating efficient autonomous driving.
Furthermore, varying the active parameter ratio and combination yields distinctly different performance within identical scenes as shown in Fig. 1 (b) and (c). Therefore, we aim to design a VLA framework that dynamically determines the optimal parameter ratio and combination for each driving frame. However, establishing this scene-to-parameter mapping is non-trivial due to the considerable diversity of driving scenes and the abstract nature of model capabilities. Specifically, determining the scene-to-parameter ratio is challenging because perceiving scene complexity and translating it into a measure of required model capacity is a highly implicit process. Furthermore, optimizing the scene-to-parameter combination is complex. Accurately selecting optimal active parameters for a specific driving scene is complicated by the entangled black-box nature of neural networks and the high variance of driving scenarios.

To address these challenges, we propose Scene-Adaptive VLA, an efficient VLA-based autonomous driving framework leveraging dynamic layer routing. Inspired by the temporal continuity of driving scenes and model predictive uncertainty theory [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , Scene-Adaptive VLA characterizes model-perceived scene complexity via frame-level temporal scene variations and decision deviations.
To uncover latent scene-to-parameter correspondences, we formulate scene-aware tokens that encode the aforementioned scene characterization, alongside two specialized queries: a budget token for determining parameter ratios and a routing token for selecting layer combinations. After processing these tokens through shallow layers of the Large Language Model (LLM) to capture their complex interdependencies, we introduce a budget-conditioned layer routing mechanism. This mechanism evaluates the refined queries to first determine the active parameter ratio and subsequently route inputs to the optimal layer combinations. Finally, the entire framework is optimized via two-stage fine-tuning supervised by both driving performance and resource consumption, effectively establishing an efficient scene-to-parameter mapping. Theoretically, our framework can be integrated into prevailing VLA architectures that employ dense backbones. To validate its effectiveness under hardware constraints, we adapt our framework to SimLingo [ 3 ] , which achieves optimal performance with minimal parameter scale in VLA-based driving models. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

1. A novel formulation for the characterization of model-perceived scene complexity. Leveraging temporal continuity of driving scenes and model predictive uncertainty theory, it effectively characterizes scene complexity via temporal frame-level driving scene variations and decision deviations, encoding them into scene-aware tokens.

2. A lightweight, budget-conditioned routing mechanism for efficient dynamic parameter activation. Utilizing two queries alongside the extracted scene-aware tokens and the LLM’s shallow layers, this mechanism dynamically allocates a real-time inference budget to determine the active parameter ratio and selects the optimal parameter combination via layer routing, all optimized end-to-end.

3. Exceptional closed-loop performance on the Bench2Drive benchmark. When adapted to the state-of-the-art (SOTA) VLA-based driving model, our framework achieves a 53.5% reduction in inference-time computational overhead with negligible degradation in driving proficiency and language capabilities, as demonstrated by extensive evaluations on the Bench2Drive benchmark and language tasks.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

VLA-based End-to-end Autonomous Driving. End-to-end autonomous driving has witnessed rapid advancements in recent years. These frameworks integrate perception and planning within unified architectures to enhance driving efficacy [ 15 , 16 ] . To address complex long-tail scenarios, recent approaches integrate VLMs either for language-centric scenario understanding [ 17 , 2 ] or for guiding downstream driving models [ 18 , 19 ] . However, these decoupled paradigms lack direct end-to-end optimization grounded in continuous actions. Consequently, VLA architectures have emerged to directly couple VLMs with action generation. While Drivegpt4-v2 [ 1 ] maps multimodal inputs to control signals and EMMA [ 20 ] unifies tasks via plain text representations, a critical modality gap remains. To bridge this gap between semantic reasoning and numerical control, ORION [ 4 ] incorporates a generative planner alongside a query-based temporal module, enabling unified optimization for scenario reasoning and trajectory prediction. Concurrently, SimLingo [ 3 ] enforces strict language-action alignment via an auxiliary task trained on synthetic instruction-action pairs, yielding superior performance in closed-loop evaluation.

Efficient VLA-based Model Inference in Autonomous Driving. Despite their formidable capabilities, the immense parameter scale of VLA models imposes a prohibitive computational burden on vehicular hardware. To address this, recent studies have explored efficient inference strategies. For instance, AutoVLA [ 5 ] reduces reasoning overhead by introducing a fast-and-slow thinking mechanism that dynamically adjusts CoT lengths via Group Relative Policy Optimization [ 21 ] (GRPO). Similarly, DriveMoE [ 6 ] alleviates the cost of long vision sequences by employing a Mixture-of-Experts architecture with on-demand vision token filtering. While effective, these methods largely overlook active parameter redundancy during inference.

Structural Adaptation in VLMs. Structural adaptation optimizes the performance-efficiency trade-off by dynamically allocating active parameters based on task demands. For Vision Transformers and LLMs, this is typically achieved by selectively dropping computational modules or employing adaptive early-exit mechanisms [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Extending these paradigms to VLMs, AdaLLaVA [ 11 ] introduces a framework that selectively disables entire Transformer layers using binary switches under an inference latency constraint. For structural adaptation in VLA-based autonomous driving, it is essential to determine the optimal parameter activation ratio and enable flexible parameter combinations conditioned on driving scenes. Thus, we adopt a similar paradigm to achieve active-ratio-aware layer selection for VLA models.

2026-10-20.title: CARVS: A Congestion-Aware Algorithm for Online Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery in Human-Collaborative Warehouses
2026-10-20.authors: Chaoran Li , Zeyuan Zhao , Shao Zhang
2026-10-20.abstract: Intelligent warehouse systems have transformed logistics by integrating robots with minimal infrastructure changes, boosting efficiency and optimizing workflows compared to traditional human-only operations. However, human-robot collaboration introduces new challenges, particularly due to human uncertainty, which leads to dynamic interactions and unpredictable behavior. To address these complexities, this paper presents the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery with Human Collaboration (MAPDwHC) problem, an extension of the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery (MAPD) problem that incorporates human unpredictability. This problem adds key constraints, such as dynamic obstacles caused by robots temporarily blocking paths when interacting with humans, and the need for real-time responsiveness . We formalize the MAPDwHC problem with additional constraints and properties. Based on this problem setting, we propose the CARVS algorithm, which improves task assignment and path planning by integrating task swapping, validation checks, and random initialization. CARVS reduces congestion, enhances adaptability to human-robot interactions, and ensures real-time responsiveness. Simulation results show that CARVS significantly reduces timeouts of path planning in large-scale scenarios where traditional MAPD algorithms fail, improving both efficiency and scalability.
2026-10-20.introduction:
The rise of automation in logistics, particularly in warehouse management, has driven the development of advanced multi-agent systems ( Kou et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2018 ) .
These systems are crucial for enhancing efficiency and managing the complexity of automated warehouses ( Duinkerken and Lodewijks, 2015 ) .
In particular, Multi-Agent Path Finding (MAPF) ( Stern et al., 2019 ) plays a key role in coordinating robot movements to prevent conflicts and optimize path efficiency ( Ma et al., 2016 ) .
While significant progress has been made in MAPF research ( Li et al., 2021a ; Shen et al., 2023 ) , the integration of task assignment within this framework remains underexplored.
To address this, Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD) algorithms ( Ma et al., 2017 ) were developed, combining task assignment and pathfinding to enhance system adaptability and throughput.
Since MAPF is NP-hard ( Ma et al., 2016 ) and MAPD generalizes MAPF, MAPD is also NP-hard, complicating system-wide optimization. To reduce computational complexity, traditional approaches often separate task assignment from path planning ( Chen et al., 2021 ) .
While A*-based algorithms ( Hart et al., 1968 ; Gong et al., 2023 ) optimize task assignment by minimizing travel time, they frequently overlook warehouse congestion, agent status, and environmental constraints, resulting in poor real-time adaptability and delayed responses to dynamic changes.

Despite these advancements, MAPD assumes an environment free of human workers, limiting its real-world applicability.
Modern intelligent warehouse systems ( Gong et al., 2023 ) have transformed logistics by integrating Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs) ( Loganathan and Ahmad, 2023 ) without requiring major infrastructure changes.
Full warehouse automation requires standardized shelving and uniform packaging, which is prohibitively expensive for most existing facilities.
While AMRs handle routine transport tasks, human workers perform critical operations such as picking and packing, which require dexterity to handle items of varying sizes.
During these operations, robots must remain stationary while interacting with humans, temporarily forming dynamic obstacles (see Figure 1 ).
Warehouse aisles are typically narrow to maximize storage capacity, so a stationary agent during interaction can block paths for other agents, rendering some MAPF instances unsolvable.
Unlike robots, humans do not strictly follow predefined schedules, resulting in unpredictable behavior that affects task allocation and path planning.
Consequently, algorithms need real-time responsiveness to respond dynamically to these changing conditions.
These constraints significantly heighten the problem’s challenge and necessitate adaptive algorithms capable of reacting to real-time changes.

Existing MAPD algorithms are insufficient for addressing these challenges, as they assume static environments without human involvement.
Adding human collaboration imposes time-coupled constraints that break standard MAPD solvers, reducing task completion to less than 10% of each solver’s own peak in some scenarios (see Section 5 ).
Traditional MAPD algorithms ( Ma et al., 2017 ; Liu et al., 2019 ) fail to account for human movement and dynamic constraints.
Addressing these limitations requires a novel approach that integrates real-time adaptability with congestion-aware planning to ensure effective coordination between AMRs and human workers.

To bridge this gap, we formalize the Multi-Agent Pickup-and-Delivery with Human Collaboration (MAPDwHC) problem, incorporating additional constraints such as dynamic obstacles and real-time adaptability .
We introduce CARVS ( C ongestion- A ware R andom-initialization, V alidation, and S wapping), a new algorithm designed to enhance task assignment and path planning in human-robot collaborative environments.
CARVS extends a baseline greedy assignment with three key improvements: random initialization, validation checks, and task swapping.
These enhancements mitigate congestion, adapt to human unpredictability, and improve real-time responsiveness.
Our theoretical analysis establishes the solvability of MAPDwHC, and extensive simulations demonstrate that CARVS significantly outperforms existing methods in terms of completed tasks.
This work advances the field of multi-agent systems and paves the way for optimizing human-robot collaboration in real-world logistics applications.

Our contributions are as follows:

We formalize the MAPDwHC problem and demonstrate that incorporating human collaboration heightens its computational difficulty relative to the traditional MAPD problem.

We introduce CARVS , an algorithm that integrates random initialization, validation checks, and task swapping to mitigate congestion, adapt to human-robot interactions, and maintain real-time responsiveness.

Through extensive simulations, we show that CARVS outperforms existing methods in terms of completed tasks, underscoring its practical potential in human-robot collaborative warehouse systems.

1. We formalize the MAPDwHC problem and demonstrate that incorporating human collaboration heightens its computational difficulty relative to the traditional MAPD problem.

2. We introduce CARVS , an algorithm that integrates random initialization, validation checks, and task swapping to mitigate congestion, adapt to human-robot interactions, and maintain real-time responsiveness.

3. Through extensive simulations, we show that CARVS outperforms existing methods in terms of completed tasks, underscoring its practical potential in human-robot collaborative warehouse systems.

# 2. Related Works

## 2.1. Multi-Agent Path Finding

In Multi-Agent Pathfinding (MAPF), algorithms are broadly classified into optimal and suboptimal categories.
Optimal algorithms like CBS ( Sharon et al., 2012a ) and MA-CBS ( Sharon et al., 2012b ) aim to minimize the total cost but are computationally expensive, making them impractical for real-time applications with many agents.
As a result, suboptimal algorithms have become the focus of MAPF research, prioritizing runtime efficiency over strict optimality.

Suboptimal algorithms are typically divided into complete and incomplete methods.
Incomplete approaches, such as Rolling-Horizon Collision Resolution (RHCR) ( Li et al., 2021d ) , simplify planning by resolving conflicts within limited timeframes but can suffer from deadlocks in constrained environments due to their non-exhaustive search.
On the other hand, complete suboptimal algorithms like LaCAM ( Okumura, 2022 ) and LaCAM* ( Okumura, 2023 ) use dual-level search techniques that guarantee finding a feasible solution or proving its non-existence, though they can result in significant computational delays, particularly in complex scenarios like those encountered in MAPDwHC.

Recent studies ( Lau and Sengupta, 2022 ; Damani et al., 2021 ) have applied multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) ( Wang et al., 2023 ) to MAPF problems, but these methods often struggle to meet the runtime requirements necessary for real-time human-robot collaboration in the MAPDwHC problem.
While MARL can improve adaptability and decision-making, it still faces challenges in balancing computational demands with the need for real-time solutions.

## 2.2. Task Assignment

Task assignment is often overlooked in traditional Multi-Agent Pathfinding (MAPF), resulting in inefficiencies as agents may be assigned suboptimal tasks that are difficult to coordinate.
To address this, several studies have integrated task assignment with path planning.
Nguyen et al. ( Nguyen et al., 2017 ) propose a generalized Combined Target Assignment and Path Finding (TAPF) model using Answer Set Programming, which handles scenarios with unequal numbers of agents and tasks, and incorporates complex requirements such as deadlines.

Honig et al. ( Hönig et al., 2018 ) introduce Conflict-Based Search with Optimal Task Assignment (CBS-TA), integrating task assignment directly into pathfinding to optimize both simultaneously.
However, these integrated approaches often struggle with scalability in large or complex environments.
Okumura et al. ( Okumura and Défago, 2022 ) address the unlabeled variant of MAPF, where any agent may be sent to any target.
Their algorithm TSWAP swaps targets between agents and uses a cached distance table to keep the planning cost of each time step low even at large agent counts.
All targets are given at the start rather than arriving over time.
While MAPD addresses dynamic environments with real-time task arrivals, TAPF is typically designed for static settings.

Ma et al. ( Ma et al., 2017 ) extend the Lifelong MAPF framework to Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MAPD), proposing algorithms like Token Passing (TP) and Token Passing with Task Swaps (TPTS) to improve flexibility and efficiency.
Building on this, Liu et al. ( Liu et al., 2019 ) develop MAPD strategies by framing task allocation as a Traveling Salesman Problem for each agent, while integrating deadlock avoidance mechanisms.

In a recent work, Xu et al. ( Xu et al., 2022 ) introduce algorithms for the Multi-Goal Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery (MG-MAPD) problem, extending MAPD to handle tasks with multiple goal locations.
While their algorithms, LNS-PBS and LNS-wPBS, show significant scalability and efficiency improvements, particularly in large-scale settings, they focus primarily on offline environments and assume that tasks are known in advance.
In contrast, our work deals with real-time task arrivals and dynamic human-robot collaboration, which introduces additional complexities and requires more adaptive solutions.

Despite these advancements, challenges remain in managing dynamically increasing tasks and ensuring scalability in complex environments.
For instance, Chen et al. ( Chen et al., 2021 ) present a unified approach combining task assignment and MAPF but may encounter efficiency issues in larger-scale settings.
Additionally, Krnjaic et al. ( Krnjaic et al., 2022 ) apply Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning to similar problems, though their methods do not address potential collisions, limiting their applicability in real-world scenarios.
Lodigiani et al. ( Lodigiani et al., 2023 ) study a related problem, MAPD with delays (MAPD-d), where agents may experience unexpected delays during execution. They propose k k -TP and p p -TP, two Token Passing variants offering deterministic and probabilistic robustness guarantees respectively, where k k bounds the delay an agent may absorb without triggering a replan. Their approach trades efficiency for robustness but does not support real-time replanning upon state changes.

2026-10-20.title: MOMO: Human Motion from Moving Sounds
2026-10-20.authors: Deli Cai , Shuyang Xu , Zhiyang Dou , Zitong Lan , Mingmin Zhao , Changxing Ding , Taku Komura
2026-10-20.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Graphics (cs.GR); Robotics (cs.RO); Sound (cs.SD)
2026-10-20.abstract:
Human responses to sound depend not only on its semantic content, but also on the evolving spatial relationship between source and listener, conveyed through spatial audio and its temporal dynamics. Modeling human reactions to such dynamic spatial audio is important for character animation, human behavior analysis, and robotics. As of yet, existing audio-driven motion generation methods primarily focus on non-spatial or static acoustic conditions, leaving this important problem largely underexplored. To bridge this gap, we formulate the novel task of dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation and introduce two motion-captured datasets. We introduce the Dy namic S patial A udio and M otion dataset (DySAM) as the first dataset and benchmark for this task, providing synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motions, and moving sound source trajectories. Given the importance of dynamic spatial cues of sound sources, we further provide the Dy namic S patial A udio L ocalization dataset (DySAL), an auxiliary binaural localization dataset that pairs diverse acoustic events with head poses and moving source trajectories to support spatial audio perception.
For benchmarking, we propose MOMO for human Mo tion generation from Mo ving Sounds, a diffusion-based framework guided by three coupled principles: localization, understanding, and generation.
MOMO performs localization by estimating head-centric spatial direction cues of the moving source directly from raw binaural audio, avoiding reliance on ground-truth source coordinates. It performs understanding by extracting frame-wise audio-content representations, and performs generation by conditioning motion diffusion on both semantic features and dynamic spatial cues. Moreover, MOMO incorporates frame-wise motion correction during denoising, enabling temporally adaptive motion synthesis under evolving audio-spatial cues.
Experiments show that MOMO outperforms existing baselines in motion fidelity, audio-motion alignment, and physical plausibility, demonstrating the potential of dynamic spatial audio for embodied motion generation.

2026-10-20.introduction:
Human responses to sound arise from integrating semantic meaning with spatial audio cues and the temporal dynamics of sound sources . A barking dog approaching from behind may elicit avoidance, whereas a speeding car approaching may prompt reorientation. Crucially, the same sound can evoke different actions depending on its source’s location and motion relative to the listener. Modeling this perception–action coupling supports context-aware virtual humans and embodied agents in character animation, virtual reality, human–computer interaction, and embodied intelligence.

Existing human motion datasets and methods have mainly focused on conditions such as action labels ( Guo et al., 2020 ) , text descriptions ( Guo et al., 2022 ) , music ( Zhuang et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Tseng et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) , and speech ( Ao et al., 2022 ; Ao et al., 2023 ; Alexanderson et al., 2023 ) . Recently, to the best of our knowledge, MOSPA ( Xu et al., 2025 ) introduced the first spatial-audio-driven human motion dataset, SAM, along with a corresponding motion generation method, showing that spatial audio cues are crucial for generating realistic human motions. However, the SAM dataset mainly focuses on a static sound source, where the sound source position remains fixed within each sequence. Moreover, MOSPA requires the ground-truth absolute position of the sound source as a condition for motion generation, which is difficult to obtain in real-world scenarios and limits its applicability to embodied agents. Therefore, dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, which models human motion responses to time-varying spatial audio from moving sound sources, remains largely underexplored, especially in practical settings without access to ground-truth sound source positions.

To address this gap, we introduce DySAM, a dataset for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation. DySAM contains synchronized binaural audio, 3D human motion, and dynamic sound source trajectories captured in an indoor environment. Human motion and sound source trajectories are recorded using a Vicon motion capture system ( Vicon, 2026 ) , while binaural audio is captured by high-sensitivity microphones near the actors’ ears, approximating the audio perceived by the actors. The main dataset contains 2,336 ten-second audio-motion sequences, totaling 23,360 seconds (approximately 6.5 hours), with motion at 30 FPS and audio at 48 kHz. It covers 42 audio types and 109 unique audio sources, including human sounds, animal sounds, vehicles, and environmental sounds, with 8 subjects and a binary genre label indicating sensitive or insensitive reactions. In addition, we provide DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset of 11,730 seconds, pairing binaural audio of diverse acoustic events with listener head 6DoF poses and frame-wise moving sound source annotations to support dynamic spatial audio perception.

Motivated by the fact that human reactions to spatial sound depend on both where the sound comes from and what the sound is, we formulate spatial-audio-driven motion generation around three coupled functional components: localization , understanding , and generation . Guided by this design principle, we propose MOMO, a diffusion-based framework for generating human motion conditioned on dynamic spatial audio. For localization, MOMO estimates frame-wise head-centric spatial cues of sound source from raw binaural audio using a sound source localization network, eliminating the reliance on privileged ground-truth source coordinates. For understanding, a pretrained CLAP audio encoder ( Wu et al., 2023 ) encodes the binaural audio to obtain frame-wise audio-content features. For generation, MOMO employs a diffusion-based motion generator conditioned on the predicted spatial cues, CLAP audio features, and genre label.
Since human motion needs to continuously adapt to the evolving spatial cues of the sound source, while self-attention only provides implicit interactions between motion tokens and condition tokens, we further introduce a Frame-wise Motion Correction module in the Transformer denoiser to explicitly refine motion tokens with frame-wise conditions, along with a Correction Strength Predictor that adaptively controls the correction magnitude for each frame.

By using head-centric DoA estimated directly from binaural audio, MOMO provides a more practical formulation for spatial-audio-driven motion generation in embodied robot settings. Compared with MOSPA ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , which relies on ground-truth global sound source coordinates, our egocentric formulation avoids privileged source-location annotations and better reflects how embodied agents infer dynamic sound direction from their own auditory observations. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments show that MOMO outperforms existing baselines, producing more realistic motions that respond to dynamic spatial-audio cues.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce two datasets: DySAM, to the best of our knowledge the first dataset for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, and DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset collected in indoor reverberant environments.

We propose MOMO, a practical framework for generating human motion from binaural audio without requiring ground-truth source coordinates. It integrates sound source localization, CLAP-based audio content encoding, and diffusion-based motion generation to model human responses to moving sound sources.

Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments show that MOMO generates natural, plausible, and spatially consistent human motion, better aligning with real motion and outperforming existing baselines.

1. We introduce two datasets: DySAM, to the best of our knowledge the first dataset for dynamic spatial-audio-driven human motion generation, and DySAL, an auxiliary sound source localization dataset collected in indoor reverberant environments.

2. We propose MOMO, a practical framework for generating human motion from binaural audio without requiring ground-truth source coordinates. It integrates sound source localization, CLAP-based audio content encoding, and diffusion-based motion generation to model human responses to moving sound sources.

3. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments show that MOMO generates natural, plausible, and spatially consistent human motion, better aligning with real motion and outperforming existing baselines.

# 2 Related Work

Conditional human motion generation has been extensively studied under various conditions, such as action labels ( Guo et al., 2020 ) , textual descriptions ( Guo et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ; Dabral et al., 2023 ) , trajectories ( Cai et al., 2026 ) , and motion language models that treat human motion as a foreign language ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) . These methods generate diverse and natural motions from semantic conditions, but they generally do not consider audio, let alone its spatial attributes. In contrast, our work focuses on audio-driven conditions with explicit spatial information.

Audio-driven human motion generation has been studied mainly in two directions. The first is music-driven dance generation ( Tang et al., 2018 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2022 ; Li et al., 2023 ; Siyao et al., 2022 ; Tseng et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Luo et al., 2024 ) , which generates choreography that matches the rhythm and style of the music. The second is speech-driven gesture synthesis ( Ginosar et al., 2019 ; Yoon et al., 2020 ; Ao et al., 2022 ; Ao et al., 2023 ; Alexanderson et al., 2023 ) , which generates co-speech gestures from speech content and prosody. Most of these methods use monaural or stereo audio and ignore the spatial attributes of the sound source. MOSPA ( Xu et al., 2025 ) is the first to study spatial-audio-driven human motion generation with binaural audio, but it assumes a static sound source position. Different from MOSPA, we consider dynamic spatial audio, where the source moves over time, and the DoA changes accordingly.

Estimating the direction of a sound source from binaural signals is a classic problem in acoustic scene analysis, for instance using binaural cues combined with deep learning ( García-Barrios et al., 2022 ; Min et al., 2025 ) .
Recent works also model room acoustics and room impulse responses to support sound source localization in complex indoor scenes ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Luo et al., 2022 ; Ratnarajah et al., 2022 ; Um et al., 2025 ; Lan et al., 2024 ; Lan et al., 2026 ) .
In this paper, we adopt a sound source localization network to predict the head-centric DoA from binaural audio, which serves as the spatial condition for motion generation. This makes our framework practical in real-world scenarios where ground-truth source coordinates are unavailable.

2026-10-20.title: CROPS: Cosserat-Rod-Based Co-Design of Soft Slender Programmable Material Systems for Biomedical Applications
2026-10-20.authors: Aaditya Chandrasekhar , Dex Doksoo Lee , Hyunwoo Kwon , Shicheng Li , Wei Chen
2026-10-20.subjects: Computational Engineering, Finance, and Science (cs.CE) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-20.comment: Submitted to Finite Elements in Analysis and Design
2026-10-20.abstract: Slender structures made of stimuli-responsive materials represent an emerging class of programmable material systems, with applications in soft robotics, minimally invasive surgery, wearable electronics, and deployable structures. In biomedical applications, the on-demand design of slender structures, encompassing both their material layout and actuation, is essential to harnessing their large deformation and multiphysics actuation to meet patient-specific design requirements. However, owing to geometric and material nonlinearities, their structure-actuation-response relationship is highly nonintuitive and computationally demanding. This often makes trial-and-error and conventional design approaches challenging for addressing patient-specific needs. To this end, we present a Cosserat-rod-based design optimization framework for the autonomous design of programmable slender structures. Leveraging the Cosserat rod representation, the end-to-end differentiable framework is demonstrated on two case studies: (i) design of swellable stents that morph to the shape of carotid vessels; (ii) co-design of the remnant magnetization and the applied field of magnetically-active catheters to reduce the force exerted on the patient-specific vessel wall during insertion. Both self-contact and external contact with surrounding structures are accounted for. We consider two actuation mechanism, namely the swelling of gel-elastomer composites and the magnetic actuation of hard-magnetic composites. The proposed framework presents an autonomous design platform of soft slender material systems that support large deformations and multiphysics actuation toward personalized biomedical design.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Programmable material systems (PMS) form a class of material systems that can adapt their shapes or properties in response to external stimuli, enabling dynamic changes in shape, motion, properties, or functions mediated by the stimuli.
PMS have been developed for a range of functions, including mechanical actuation and locomotion [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] , tuning of mechanical properties [ 5 , 6 ] , and shape programming and reconfiguration [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Across these applications, functional behavior often emerges from nonlinear coupling among spatial material distribution, geometry, and actuation. Optimizing these variables independently or fixing some a priori may overlook design combinations that achieve better mechanical performance, motivating their co-design [ 10 ] . Co-design can therefore expand the range of achievable responses while better satisfying geometric and functional requirements; however, exploring this coupled design space remains computationally demanding because it requires repeated evaluations of nonlinear mechanical responses throughout design optimization.

For PMS composed of active slender structures, Cosserat rod theory [ 11 ] offers a promising approach to reducing the computational burden of co-design.
Slender structures serve as versatile building blocks for PMS, enabling complex three-dimensional shape changes in applications ranging from shape-morphing lattice structures [ 12 , 7 ] to steerable soft continuum robots [ 4 , 13 ] . In conducting the analysis and design of such structures, Cosserat rod theory represents slender structures using centerline positions and cross-sectional orientations along their length [ 11 ] . Such formulations have been applied to modeling large deformations [ 14 , 11 ] , swelling-driven shape changes [ 15 ] , and interactions involving contact and friction [ 16 , 17 ] . Cosserat rod-based models can reduce the computational cost of repeated design evaluations involving nonlinear finite element analyses, complex boundary conditions, and demanding functional requirements across states, making iterative material–geometry–actuation co-design more tractable than the standard three-dimensional finite element methods developed for general purposes.

A computationally efficient co-design framework holds significant promise for biomedical devices such as catheters and stents. Their designs must accommodate patient-specific anatomical constraints while satisfying coupled mechanical, fluidic, and other functional requirements, subject to stringent safety and regulatory standards. As such, existing biomedical design approaches have explored different subsets of this coupled design space, with many focusing on programming mechanical performances. For stents, gradient-based optimization has been used to tailor mechanical stiffness and flexibility through strut dimensions, junction positions, and periodic unit-cell topology [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] . For magnetically actuated catheters, evolutionary optimization has been utilized to tailor axial magnetic-particle distributions under prescribed geometry and actuation conditions [ 13 ] . More integrated approaches have explored sequential optimization of catheter geometry and material distribution [ 21 ] , as well as joint optimization of magnetization profiles and applied magnetic fields [ 22 , 23 ] . Despite these advances, existing catheter co-design approaches remain limited to coarse axial segments or discrete material choices, rather than continuous three-dimensional vector profiles and cross-sectional layouts under contact. Gradient-free optimization often suffers from slow convergence and weak scalability as the number of design variables in the joint design space increases.

Addressing these limitations requires both spatially resolved material parameterizations and optimization methods that remain tractable as the number of design variables grows. Topology optimization has enabled the design of spatially heterogeneous material distributions in hard-magnetic soft materials [ 24 ] , reprogrammable magneto-mechanical structures [ 6 ] , and multi-material gel–elastomer systems [ 25 ] . Differentiable simulation further enables sensitivity-based optimization of coupled material and actuation variables, as demonstrated in magnetic soft robots undergoing large deformation and contact using the material point method [ 1 ] . For slender structures, gradient based approaches have been utilized to optimize centerline shapes and parameters within prescribed cross-sectional architectures using rod models with linear elastic sectional laws [ 26 , 27 ] . However, extending these approaches to locally parameterized material distributions along the rod and across its cross-section requires design sensitivities that account for nonlinear coupling among material response, actuation, and deformation. Cross sectional homogenization of heterogeneous material responses incorporates local material behavior into the reduced rod model without independently resolving the three-dimensional displacement field. By differentiating through this homogenization and the nonlinear Cosserat rod solution, including contact, we demonstrate that our framework can support spatially resolved material–actuation co-design while accounting for nonlinear deformation and contact.

Building upon our previous work on differentiable multi-material topology optimization [ 25 ] , we develop CROPS, a differentiable C osserat r od-based o ptimization framework for p rogrammable s lender material systems.

The main contributions are threefold:

Differentiable Multiphysics Rod Formulation :
We develop a differentiable Cosserat rod formulation that incorporates fiber-resolved cross-sectional integration to model heterogeneous material responses under swelling and magnetic actuation. The framework further incorporates regularized contact mechanics and implicit differentiation to compute sensitivities of deformation and contact forces with respect to material and actuation variables.

Differentiable Multiphysics Rod Formulation :
We develop a differentiable Cosserat rod formulation that incorporates fiber-resolved cross-sectional integration to model heterogeneous material responses under swelling and magnetic actuation. The framework further incorporates regularized contact mechanics and implicit differentiation to compute sensitivities of deformation and contact forces with respect to material and actuation variables.

Spatial Material–Actuation Co-Design : We establish a gradient-based optimization framework that accommodates continuous-valued material distributions along the rod axis and across its cross-section, enabling joint optimization of spatial material properties, magnetization profiles, and applied actuation.

Demonstrations for Patient-Specific Biomedical Design : We demonstrate the framework through the inverse design of gel-elastomer stents to achieve prescribed deployed geometries and co-design of magnetically actuated catheters to minimize wall-contact forces given patient-specific insertion trajectories.

# 2 Method

## 2.1 Overview

In this study, we consider the design optimization of programmable slender structures, in which the material distribution within the structure is optimized to obtain prescribed responses under actuation. We adopt a geometrically exact Cosserat rod [ 28 , 11 ] to represent the slender structure. In addition to resolving the deformation through the centerline, we retain a material description over the cross-section. In particular, we consider two forms of actuation ( Figure 2 ). The first form of actuation is a gel-elastomer composite in which an active gel swells upon exposure to a solvent while a passive elastomer resists and redirects the deformation. The other one is a hard-magnetic composite in which particles carrying a remnant magnetization embedded in a soft matrix develop moments under an applied magnetic field. In both cases, the spatial distribution of material encodes the mapping from stimulus to deformation.

We begin by assuming an unstressed reference configuration of the centerline with prescribed arc length and specified cross-sectional orientations along the curve. Furthermore, we assume a prescribed set of candidate material phases and their properties, for instance the gel and elastomer phases of the swelling system. Additionally, we assume prescribed fixtures, forces, and moments. We also assume prescribed environmental conditions: (i) for swelling, these include the chemical potential, temperature, and molar volume of the solvent bath; (ii) for magnetic actuation, these include the bounds on the magnitudes of the remnant magnetization and the applied magnetic field. Where relevant, the geometry of confining surroundings and obstacles is also prescribed. Our design goal is to compute the material distribution, and where relevant the applied magnetic field, for which the actuated structure attains a prescribed target shape or mechanical output, while imposing the design constraints.

2026-10-20.title: HAVANA: A Hierarchical Video-Action Model for Vision-Language Navigation
2026-10-20.authors: Dongzhihan Wang , Yi Du , Chen Wang , Xiuxian Li , Liang Xu
2026-10-20.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-20.abstract: Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires long-horizon instruction-consistent planning and short-horizon local planning in current geometry. Video-action models (VAMs) offer a promising way to learn predictive representations for navigation. However, existing VAMs jointly predict visual futures and local trajectories in a single process, even though they operate at different paces: future prediction remains stable across multiple updates while local trajectories must react to fresh observations. To bridge this gap, we introduce HAVANA , a dual-system VAM that decouples predictive reasoning from reactive local planning. A slow system produces a compact language-conditioned latent plan from observation history, while a fast system combines the latest plan with the current observation to generate local trajectories. Their asynchronous execution enables rapid adaptation without repeated future prediction, and no future video is generated during inference. Experiments on OmniNavBench demonstrate state-of-the-art navigation performance over prior baselines, while real-world deployments further show robust generalization to unseen environments across different robot embodiments. Our code and checkpoints will be available at 1 1 1 https://github.com/Anastasiawd/HAVANA .
2026-10-20.introduction:
Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow natural-language instructions through sequential interaction with its environment [ 2 ] . Recent approaches [ 46 , 9 , 39 ] directly predict actions or local navigation goals from instructions and observation histories. This leaves future route consistency implicit: when the next instruction-relevant landmark is not yet visible, a locally plausible action does not guarantee reaching the scene expected by the instruction. Learning to predict future semantics provides an additional supervision for this correspondence and has been shown to improve navigation on longer routes [ 18 ] .

Video-based World-Action Models (WAMs), also referred to as Video-Action Models (VAMs) [ 25 , 44 , 38 ] , introduce predictive capability by learning future visual states together with actions. For VLN, however, long-horizon instruction-consistent planning and short-horizon local path planning require different information at different rates. To follow instructions beyond the current field of view, long-horizon planning requires semantic reasoning about future observations and route progression, whereas local trajectory generation needs to continuously adapt to latest observed geometry to avoid obstacles. This conflict leaves open how those representations should be organized for navigation across different temporal scales.

Existing fast-and-slow VLN frameworks [ 40 , 48 ] demonstrate the benefits of separating reasoning from execution. They typically condition a trajectory policy on latent goals and current observations, with its planning interface learned through pixel-goal grounding and trajectory supervision. We instead investigate how future visual prediction can ground a reusable planning interface in anticipated route progression. Such instruction-conditioned guidance can remain useful across multiple trajectory updates, while each local trajectory prediction must account for newly observed geometry. We therefore ask: how can low-frequency future visual prediction guide high-frequency trajectory generation from fresh observations?

We introduce HAVANA ( H ier A rchical V ideo- A ction Model for NA vigation), a dual-system framework that reuses predictive latent plans for local trajectory prediction. The slow system uses a pretrained Vision-Language Model (VLM) to encode observation history and language instructions into planning states. Joint future-video and long-horizon waypoint supervision grounds these states in visual evolution and intended motion. The lightweight fast system combines the latest latent plan with the current RGB-D observation to generate short-horizon trajectories, which a tracking controller converts into velocity commands. Both systems run asynchronously, allowing the fast policy to incorporate new observations between planning updates while reusing latent route guidance, without video generation.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We propose HAVANA, a dual-system VAM for VLN that decouples low-frequency predictive reasoning from high-frequency reactive trajectory prediction.

We propose HAVANA, a dual-system VAM for VLN that decouples low-frequency predictive reasoning from high-frequency reactive trajectory prediction.

We learn plan representations through joint future-video and waypoint supervision, augmented with an instruction-ranking objective that encourages instruction-consistent predictions over conflicting alternatives.

We transfer trajectory prediction priors learned from language-free expert data to language-conditioned navigation through predictive latent plans, enabling local trajectory prediction without video generation.

1. We propose HAVANA, a dual-system VAM for VLN that decouples low-frequency predictive reasoning from high-frequency reactive trajectory prediction.

2. We learn plan representations through joint future-video and waypoint supervision, augmented with an instruction-ranking objective that encourages instruction-consistent predictions over conflicting alternatives.

3. We transfer trajectory prediction priors learned from language-free expert data to language-conditioned navigation through predictive latent plans, enabling local trajectory prediction without video generation.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Video-Action Models for VLN

Explicit Video-to-Action Models. Video-based planning uses generated visual futures as intermediate plans for action execution. UniPi [ 10 ] formulates control as text-conditioned video generation followed by inverse dynamics. ImagiNav [ 7 ] extends this paradigm to navigation through subgoal-conditioned egocentric videos, while NavDreamer [ 15 ] selects imagined visual plans and reconstructs executable 3D waypoints. These approaches provide explicit visual foresight, but action recovery depends on the geometric consistency of generated videos. Iterative video generation also increases the cost of replanning from new observations, complicating high-frequency closed-loop control.

Latent World-Action Models. World-action models (WAMs) integrate predictive visual representations with action learning. DreamZero [ 43 ] and AstraNav-World [ 13 ] jointly model future visuals and actions, while WAM-Nav [ 42 ] uses asymmetric joint diffusion for long-horizon actions and short-horizon visual foresight. WorldVLN [ 47 ] decodes predicted latent world transitions into waypoints, and SparseVideoNav [ 45 ] reduces inference cost through sparse future prediction. Other approaches retain predictive supervision while avoiding explicit future-video generation at inference: Fast-WAM [ 44 ] uses video co-training to improve direct action prediction, whereas ForeWAM [ 14 ] exposes latent future context to an action decoder. AHA-WAM [ 4 ] separates low-frequency world planning from high-frequency action execution for robotic manipulation. These advances establish predictive representations as useful control signals. For VLN, a key design question is how instruction-conditioned visual and motion foresight can provide reusable route guidance across successive reactive control updates.

## 2.2 Hierarchical VLN Frameworks

Inspired by fast-and-slow dual-process theory [ 16 ] , hierarchical navigation frameworks separate deliberative reasoning from reactive execution. At the reactive level, ViNT [ 28 ] learns transferable visual navigation representations, NoMaD [ 29 ] employs diffusion policies for local trajectory generation, and FlowNav [ 11 ] uses flow matching [ 20 ] . DualVLN [ 40 ] combines a slow VLM planner producing pixel goals and latent planning features with a fast diffusion policy [ 5 ] for asynchronous navigation. FSD-VLN [ 48 ] extends this separation to aerial navigation, while NavForesee [ 21 ] combines hierarchical language planning with short- and long-horizon visual prediction. In VLN, route planning must preserve instruction intent over a longer horizon, whereas local control must adapt to current observation. HAVANA connects these roles through language-conditioned predictive latent plans learned with future video and waypoint supervision. A separately trained reactive policy reuses these plans alongside real-time RGB-D observations, enabling asynchronous control without video generation.

2026-10-20.title: IMPULSE: Push First, Then Predict in V-JEPA 2 Feature Space
2026-10-20.authors: Tingan Jin
2026-10-20.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-20.abstract: Latent world models such as V-JEPA 2 forecast in the feature space of a video encoder, but one look at an object does not reveal how hard it is to rotate, how much it bounces or how much it slides. People find out by trying: a few pokes reveal how an object responds. IMPULSE, named after the impulse response it infers, gives a predictor in frozen V-JEPA 2 feature space the same ability. A Bayesian contact memory summarizes three short calibration pushes, a predicted object pose carries it into the predictor, and a lightweight random-Fourier pose head lets the predictor use the pose. On 512 fresh objects, in a pre-specified held-out confirmation with models sealed before the data existed, the memory lowers the 1-second feature-forecast error by 11.6–12.8% relative to the same predictor without experience, for all 8 training seeds, with a 95% seed-and-object interval excluding zero. The gain also holds for 128 objects with out-of-range physics (11.7–14.0%), and the full extension beats a plain predictor by 15.5–16.6%. An information-ladder argument, exact for ideal predictors, shows that physics reaches the features only through motion, so we measure how much the pathway lets pose help. On fresh objects, the Fourier head roughly triples the gain of a perfect memory over plain pose tokens (2.8–3.2 × \times ). Raw push measurements fed through the same pathway give a similar gain, so the Bayesian summary is not required; it condenses the trials into eight interpretable numbers. The gain is absent at contact onset and grows afterwards.
2026-10-20.introduction:
World models predict what will happen next and are a basic building block for planning agents [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn representations by predicting the embeddings of masked or future content instead of reconstructing pixels [ 4 , 5 ] . V-JEPA 2 couples a large self-supervised video encoder with an action-conditioned predictor trained on its frozen features and uses it for robot planning [ 6 ] , and its predecessor V-JEPA captures surprisingly much intuitive physics [ 7 ] .

Some physical properties, however, cannot be seen. Two T-shaped blocks that look identical may differ in how their mass is distributed, how elastic they are and how much friction they meet. Pushed the same way, they move differently (Fig. 1 ), and no amount of staring at a single frame tells them apart. People solve physical problems by rapid trial and error [ 8 ] , and robots resolve such ambiguity by interacting: a few exploratory pokes reveal how an object responds [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Physical parameters inferred from video or interaction improve physical predictions [ 12 , 13 ] and let control policies adapt to new dynamics [ 14 , 15 ] , and an embedding of a few earlier push videos of a novel object improves pixel-space video prediction [ 16 ] . Recent work asks which physical quantities latent world models encode [ 17 ] , supplies true physical parameters to a JEPA predictor [ 18 ] , or adapts a latent world model at test time [ 19 ] . To our knowledge, how much a few active trials before the query improve a predictor whose targets are frozen, pretrained video features, and what limits that gain, has not been measured.

We study this question in a controlled pushing task with hidden inertia, restitution and friction. Our method, IMPULSE, pushes first and predicts second (Fig. 2 ). Before a forecast, the agent performs three short calibration pushes. A Bayesian contact memory summarizes in eight numbers how the object responds to an impulse. We compare a predictor in frozen V-JEPA 2 feature space with and without this memory, with the same architecture, data and training, and evaluate on fresh objects under a protocol fixed in advance.

With a standard pose-token pathway the gain is small: on fresh objects, even a perfect memory, holding the true physical parameters, improves the forecast by only 6.9–7.8%. The bottleneck is not the memory. Physics changes the future features only by changing where the object is, so for an ideal predictor physical knowledge can help a feature forecast at most as much as knowing the future pose . We make this precise as an information ladder (Section III-E ) and measure every rung through the same pathway. A pose-only regressor shows that the features are highly pose-predictable, yet the pose-token predictor uses little of it. A lightweight random-Fourier pose head raises the gain of a perfect memory 2.8–3.2 × \times and that of the real memory 2.4–4.1 × \times . Finally, a same-information control feeds the raw push measurements through the same pathway and finds a similar gain, with no clear difference from the memory. What matters is that the predictor gets to try, and that the pathway lets the result reach the features.

Our contributions are:

A push-first, predict-second world model. IMPULSE extends a predictor in frozen V-JEPA 2 feature space with a contact-experience memory and a pose pathway. In a pre-specified held-out confirmation on 512 fresh objects, they cut 1-s feature-forecast error by 11.6–12.8% for all 8 training seeds. The gain holds for out-of-range physics and for frictionless objects, and the full extension beats a plain predictor by 15.5–16.6%. A same-information control shows that the gain does not require the Bayesian form of the summary.

An information ladder. A simple proposition orders the errors of predictors that know nothing, a memory, the true physical parameters, or the true future pose. The ladder turns “does the memory help?” into two measurable questions: how much the pathway lets pose help, and what share of that the memory captures.

The pathway is the lever. On fresh objects, a random-Fourier pose head multiplies the absolute gain of a perfect memory by 2.8–3.2, with 95% bootstrap intervals that stay above 2.3, and that of the real memory by 2.4–4.1. The improvement is absent at contact onset and grows afterwards.

2026-10-20.related_work:
# II Related Work

Latent world models. Recurrent and imagination-based world models learn compact dynamics for control [ 1 , 2 ] . JEPAs predict masked or future content in the representation space of an encoder [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . V-JEPA 2 adds an action-conditioned predictor (V-JEPA 2-AC) on top of a frozen video encoder [ 6 ] , and DINO-WM plans with a world model over frozen DINOv2 features, including on Push-T [ 20 ] . These models predict from what they see. Contextual world models condition dynamics on environment parameters [ 21 ] ; Semigroup-JEPA gives a JEPA predictor the true physical parameter [ 18 ] , and AdaJEPA adapts a latent world model at test time from observed transitions [ 19 ] . PokeWorld asks which hidden quantities (mass, drag, contact stiffness) the latent states of action-conditioned world models encode when visually identical objects are pushed [ 17 ] . We instead infer the parameters from a few trials before the forecast, feed them to a predictor in a frozen video-encoder feature space, and measure what limits the gain.

Physical properties from video and interaction. Physics engines combined with learning infer mass and friction from videos [ 12 , 22 ] . Interaction networks learn object dynamics [ 23 ] , and benchmarks probe physical prediction from vision [ 24 , 25 ] . ComPhy [ 26 ] and Physion++ [ 27 ] require inferring hidden properties such as mass, friction or elasticity from how objects interact. Features of video foundation models, V-JEPA 2 among them, encode dynamic properties such as elasticity and friction when the motion is observed [ 28 ] . PIN-WM identifies friction and restitution from a few interactions with a differentiable physics simulator [ 13 ] . We infer the properties from a few active trials before the forecast, and our predictor has no simulator: it forecasts encoder features. Interactive perception argues that acting reveals what passive perception cannot [ 9 ] . DensePhysNet [ 11 ] learns physical representations from active interactions, and environment-probing policies [ 10 ] explicitly probe before acting. Planar pushing is a classical testbed for such questions [ 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 ] , and Push-T is a standard visuomotor benchmark [ 33 , 34 ] .

Adaptation and system identification. Hidden-parameter MDPs formalize dynamics that differ by a few latent parameters [ 35 ] . Policies conditioned on identified or latent physical parameters adapt to new dynamics [ 14 , 15 ] , learned dynamics models can be adapted online from recent experience [ 36 ] , and SimDist keeps a simulation-pretrained encoder fixed while adapting only its latent dynamics to real-world data [ 37 ] . Neural processes and set encoders summarize a context set into a conditioning vector [ 38 , 39 ] . Closest to our work, experience-embedded visual foresight encodes five earlier push videos of a novel object into such a vector and conditions a pixel-space video predictor on it, evaluated on real pushes of unseen objects [ 16 , 40 ] . Our memory plays the same role, but its targets are frozen video-encoder features, its gain is confirmed on held-out objects under a protocol fixed in advance, and we show that the pathway from memory to those features decides the gain.

Fourier features. Random Fourier features approximate shift-invariant kernels with a linear readout [ 41 ] , and Fourier input mappings let networks fit high-frequency functions of low-dimensional coordinates [ 42 ] . We use them to map object pose to its appearance in V-JEPA 2 feature space.

2026-10-20.title: Fast Construction of Inner Sphere Trees Using Machine Learning
2026-10-20.authors: Jianneng Huang , Wenjia Rao
2026-10-20.abstract: Collision detection for complex non-convex objects is a bottleneck in physics simulation, virtual reality, and robotics. Inner sphere trees (ISTs) answer proximity and penetration queries efficiently, but their greedy leaf-sphere construction is sequential and computationally expensive, which limits both large-scale preprocessing and runtime use. In this work, we present ML-IST, a machine-learning-based method that reformulates leaf-sphere generation as a single-shot set-prediction problem: a network predicts a fixed set of inscribed sphere candidates from multichannel voxel geometry, differentiable coverage feedback corrects the coarse prediction and fills residual gaps at finer scales, and a lightweight geometric projection enforces validity. Averaged over the test set, a single-GPU implementation of ML-IST reduces mean leaf-generation time by a factor of 2.0 2.0 – 2.6 2.6 over single-core CPU construction across target capacities of 64–512 spheres, and qualitative results on complex models show multiscale sphere distributions that follow principal volumes and slender features. We further integrate ML-IST into the Jolt Physics and Bullet engines; in an alpha-puzzle benchmark it reaches 55.89 FPS, the highest among the compared representations (conventional IST, GImpact, and convex decomposition). These results support learned leaf generation as a practical component for fast, runtime construction of detailed collision representations.
2026-10-20.introduction:
Collision detection is essential to realism and responsiveness in virtual reality, physics simulation, robotic path planning, and medical interaction. For objects with complex non-convex features, such as holes, recesses, and thin structures, an effective collision representation must support efficient queries while accurately describing the occupied interior. Many acceleration structures have been developed for this purpose, including convex-body distance tests [ 1 ] , convex-hull constructions [ 2 ] , and exterior bounding-volume hierarchies [ 3 , 4 ] . Sphere hierarchies approximate a model with nested spheres and have long been used for time-critical collision detection and medial-axis approximation [ 5 , 6 ] . Among them, the inner sphere tree (IST) [ 7 ] places non-overlapping inscribed spheres inside the object and organizes them hierarchically, approximating the occupied volume compactly and supporting proximity and penetration queries.

Although ISTs are efficient at query time, their construction remains expensive. Conventional leaf generation uses a greedy iterative strategy over a signed distance field (SDF) [ 8 ] , which encodes boundary clearance and inside–outside information and is widely used in collision-related computation [ 9 ] : the largest admissible inner sphere is repeatedly located in voxel space, and the residual feasible region is updated after every placement. The procedure is therefore inherently sequential and cannot fully exploit the parallelism of modern GPUs; construction time grows with voxel resolution, geometric complexity, and the target number of leaf spheres. Prior IST research has emphasized hierarchical organization, query performance, and penetration-depth estimation, whereas the cost of generating the leaf spheres has received less attention. Reducing this cost would benefit both large-scale preprocessing and rapid, runtime construction of collision representations.

Recent progress in deep learning has produced data-driven representations of three-dimensional geometry [ 10 , 11 ] and neural implicit models such as DeepSDF and Occupancy Networks, which learn continuous geometric fields from spatial coordinates [ 12 , 13 ] . For collision-related computation, Zesch et al. predict signed distances for deformable objects from a deformation code and a query point [ 14 ] , and neural builders have been used to accelerate the construction of spatial subdivisions such as k-d trees and BVHs [ 15 ] . These methods demonstrate that search- or optimization-intensive geometric procedures can be transferred to offline training and approximated by a forward pass at runtime. They primarily predict query-level quantities, such as an SDF value, an occupancy probability, or a collision state, or they target exterior spatial subdivision for traversal optimization. ML-IST instead predicts an explicit, reusable set of interior spheres from multichannel voxel geometry, providing the leaves for a conventional IST hierarchy.

To this end, we propose ML-IST (machine-learning-based inner sphere tree generation), which reformulates leaf-sphere construction as the prediction of a fixed-capacity candidate set. Given a normalized 3D model, a multistage network predicts candidate centers, radii, and objectness scores from a multichannel voxel representation: it first establishes coarse coverage with large base spheres and then corrects them and fills residual gaps at finer scales through differentiable coverage feedback, after which a lightweight geometric projection enforces validity. Inference requires a single network forward pass. The contribution of this work is threefold. First, it formulates IST leaf generation as fixed-capacity sphere-set prediction. Second, it combines coarse prediction with differentiable coverage feedback and bounded multiscale refinement. Third, it evaluates generation time against the conventional greedy builder and demonstrates the predicted proxy in rigid-body and physics-engine benchmarks, including runtime construction inside Jolt Physics and Bullet.

The scope of this work is the leaf-sphere generation stage, which is the dominant construction cost in a conventional IST, rather than the replacement of the complete IST framework. The predicted spheres can still be organized into a conventional hierarchy and used by existing collision-query procedures, so ML-IST is a hybrid approach that moves much of the geometric search from online construction to offline training. This design supports both offline batch preprocessing and the runtime construction of detailed collision representations for objects that appear only after a physics engine has started; Section 5 evaluates the latter setting.
