## 2.3 Geometric Training Objective

Training uses reference sphere sets generated by the conventional SDF-based greedy IST algorithm together with voxel-geometric constraints. The final set receives the main supervision, while the base set receives auxiliary supervision emphasizing large-scale coverage. Gap filling, base-sphere preservation, feedback-map supervision, and correction regularization are gradually introduced during refinement. The terms are combined with configurable weights and serve the following purposes.

Coverage and geometric validity. Interior samples encourage volume coverage, exterior samples penalize coverage outside the object, and additional weight is assigned to high-clearance regions and poorly covered samples. Coverage supervision first limits radii using the local distance field, then softly gates activation according to objectness, interior occupancy, and viable radius. Separate validity penalties discourage exterior centers and predicted radii exceeding a conservative fraction of local clearance.

Reference-set supervision. Sphere sets are unordered [ 19 ] , so supervision uses bidirectional nearest geometric matching [ 20 ] . The matching cost combines squared Euclidean center distance and squared radius difference, both normalized by grid resolution, with a weight of 2 on the radius term. Larger reference spheres receive higher weights, predicted spheres are weighted by objectness, and candidates matched to references receive positive objectness supervision. Additional large-sphere supervision helps preserve the principal interior structure.

Overlap control and sphere utilization. Pairwise constraints emphasize severe penetration and excessive nearest-neighbor overlap. Local tangency constraints and reference-derived contact supervision encourage compact arrangements of neighboring spheres. A soft active-count constraint sets a target based on the reference count and candidate capacity, reducing both insufficient viable activation and excessive activation. Radius-utilization constraints encourage viable spheres to use the available local clearance.

Preservation and residual gap filling. Preservation constraints discourage excessive shrinking, suppression, and displacement of useful base spheres, and penalize final coverage falling below Stage 1 coverage. Residual supervision emphasizes uncovered interior regions and directs additional centers and coverage toward them. A separate radius-utilization constraint helps medium spheres fill larger gaps. Feedback-map supervision promotes base coverage, and correction regularization limits adjustment magnitude.

Optimization schedule. The model is optimized with AdamW. The default learning-rate schedule uses warmup followed by cosine decay, with gradient clipping to stabilize updates. Early in training, gradients are detached from feedback maps and base predictions passed to the refiner; later, gradient propagation is restored for joint training. Refinement supervision is introduced gradually, soft-coverage temperatures decrease, and geometric and packing weights are adjusted over training so that the network first establishes principal coverage and then strengthens local refinement.

If no candidate passes this filtering, the implementation falls back to the highest-scoring candidates before applying radius projection and the minimum-radius check.

2026-10-20.title: EgoVine: Post-Training with Branching Experience Compiled from Real-World Videos
2026-10-20.authors: Qinchuan Cheng , Bowen Lyu , Zhantao Gong , Angela Yao , Cheston Tan , Shijie Li
2026-10-20.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-20.abstract: Real-world egocentric videos capture multi-step household procedures, but their recorded trajectories leave alternative actions and recovery from the learner’s own mistakes largely unexplored. We introduce EgoVine, a post-training framework that turns a fixed demonstration set into interactive experience for long-horizon planning. EgoVine operates in executable symbolic environments compiled from real-world video annotations, where an agent must coordinate object manipulations under partial observation and account for delayed consequences. Restoring a decision state allows the learner to explore alternative actions and compare their eventual outcomes. Union jointly trains action generation and consequence prediction in one model, using the same executions to supervise candidate comparison and recovery. Verified repairs add recovery targets from failed attempts, while comparisons among sampled continuations guide policy updates. The updated planner then returns to the environments, with its own decisions and mistakes shaping the next round of experience. On a shared benchmark, EgoVine-1.5B achieves 81.8% success on Main planning tasks and 66.7% on longer task compositions, outperforming all evaluated Flash LLM baselines on both. EgoVine connects real demonstrations to an iterative learning process that trains compact planners on choices and futures beyond the recorded trajectories.
2026-10-20.introduction:
A demonstration shows one way to complete a task. It rarely shows what would have happened after a different action, how to recover from a learner’s mistake, or when a seemingly unhelpful step becomes necessary later. To retrieve an object and leave its cabinet closed, for example, an agent may first have to open the cabinet, temporarily violating a condition of the final goal. A learner also reaches states absent from the recording, where several actions may be executable but lead to different futures. Learning requires experience of those choices and their continuations.

Egocentric videos capture rich object interactions and everyday procedures ( Perrett et al., 2025 ) . Their value for planning extends to the objects, state changes, and action requirements that govern other possible procedures. Ego2World ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) compiles these annotations into executable symbolic worlds for planning under partial observation. EgoVine turns these worlds into a source of post-training experience: the learner can revisit a decision, try alternatives under the grounded rules, and follow their consequences beyond the recorded trajectory.

We study how environments compiled from a fixed set of real demonstrations can turn passive trajectory supervision into interactive learning . Execution supplies action–consequence targets; restoration makes alternatives comparable from a common decision. Their continuations reveal useful detours, failures, and repairs. These experiences support both supervised learning and policy optimization. As the actor changes, its state visits expose further gaps in the experience available for learning.

EgoVine organizes experience around decisions, their executable alternatives, and what follows each choice. A shared context makes alternatives comparable; a verified suffix can supply a future from a new starting point. This connects three contributions:

Expanding experience beyond demonstrated paths. We construct executable alternatives, failures, and repair continuations from demonstrated and policy-visited states.

Learning aligned lessons from each execution. Union connects action, consequence, candidate-selection, and bounded-rejoin targets for one planner. Each execution provides corresponding targets for action choice, consequences, and continuation, with the checked outcome determining its supervision.

Continuing learning through controlled interaction. BunchFusion organizes restored-state comparisons and compatible reuse; supervision and relative policy updates learn from the resulting branches. The updated actor’s state visits then determine which alternatives and repairs to collect next.

Our experiments follow this process from available supervision to learning and task performance. Recovery-expanded supervision produces the largest observed training-stage improvement. The compact planners lead complementary benchmark panels; paired traces reveal differences in subgoal choice and prerequisite handling, and fixed-workload measurements quantify compatible reuse.

1. Expanding experience beyond demonstrated paths. We construct executable alternatives, failures, and repair continuations from demonstrated and policy-visited states.

2. Learning aligned lessons from each execution. Union connects action, consequence, candidate-selection, and bounded-rejoin targets for one planner. Each execution provides corresponding targets for action choice, consequences, and continuation, with the checked outcome determining its supervision.

3. Continuing learning through controlled interaction. BunchFusion organizes restored-state comparisons and compatible reuse; supervision and relative policy updates learn from the resulting branches. The updated actor’s state visits then determine which alternatives and repairs to collect next.
2026-10-20.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

UniSim learns a visual simulator from diverse static datasets and uses simulated interaction to train policies ( Yang et al., 2023 ) . Ctrl-World develops a controllable video world model for manipulation, using successful imagined trajectories for fine-tuning ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . RoboCasa365 expands household task and scene coverage ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) , while MagicSim unifies world construction, embodied execution, and trajectory generation in a shared runtime ( Lu et al., 2026 ) . Ego2World compiles egocentric annotations into symbolic worlds for belief-state planning ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . EgoVine studies the learning opportunities within a fixed set of these worlds. Restorable states and explicit rules let the learner explore unrecorded decisions, check their consequences, and connect new branches to verified continuations. The research focus is how this experience becomes training supervision and policy credit.

Seeing-to-Experiencing (S2E) combines video pretraining with reinforcement learning in simulation to acquire reactive navigation while retaining pretrained knowledge ( He et al., 2025 ) . EgoVine addresses discrete, object-centered procedures in worlds compiled from the source demonstrations: interaction exposes alternative action sequences and repairs, which supply both supervised targets and policy outcomes. VAGEN learns explicit state estimation and transition reasoning for partially observed visual-agent tasks ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Union aligns the chosen action, observed effects, candidate preferences, and bounded-rejoin labels around one executed decision. A failed attempt can teach applicability while a checked repair teaches how to continue. The planner learns these correspondences from textual observations and execution feedback.

VinePPO estimates credit in mathematical reasoning using Monte Carlo continuations from intermediate prefixes ( Kazemnejad et al., 2025 ) . TreeRL branches at uncertain reasoning steps in mathematics and code ( Hou et al., 2025 ) ; Tree-GRPO combines shared-prefix sampling with intra-tree and inter-tree advantages for multi-turn question answering ( Ji et al., 2026 ) . GiGPO groups recurring states for finer credit in ALFWorld, WebShop, and search-augmented question answering ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . In EgoVine, intermediate choices change an executable world. Restoring the decision context supports relative policy credit, and executing its alternatives also supplies applicability, effects, selection targets, and checked continuations. Branch comparison thus serves the broader process of expanding and learning from experience across policy-visited states.

ReAct uses interaction to revise reasoning and plans ( Yao et al., 2023 ) . AgentRefine constructs feedback-driven correction examples in synthetic environments ( Fu et al., 2025 ) ; SCoRe learns self-correction from the model’s own traces in mathematics and coding ( Kumar et al., 2025 ) . Process supervision labels reasoning steps, while STaR trains on rationales yielding correct answers ( Lightman et al., 2024 ; Zelikman et al., 2022 ) . DAgger gathers expert actions at learner-visited states to address policy-induced distribution shift ( Ross et al., 2011 ) . EgoVine obtains targets at such states through execution and bounded continuation search. Several valid futures can supply supervision, including a connector to an existing suffix or a new completion. Recovery concerns changes in the world, and each attempt also supplies consequence and selection targets.

2026-10-20.title: Transmission Error Compensation for Industrial Robots Using Fourier Series
2026-10-20.authors: Christian J. E. Bauer , Simon Nowinski , Valentin Kamm , Lukas Steinle , Armin Lechler , Alexander Verl
2026-10-20.subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Signal Processing (eess.SP)
2026-10-20.comment: . Accepted for publication in Annals of Scientific Society for Assembly, Handling and Industrial Robots, 2026. Dataset available on this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract:
Due to their low accuracy, industrial robots commonly require online teaching after the offline development of a robot program in simulation.
The accuracy is limited by compliance and transmission errors in the robot joints.
Transmission errors are defined as errors between the load-side angles of the gearboxes and the motor encoder angles.
An approach to identify the transmission errors based on laser tracker measurements is presented.
The developed velocity-dependent Fourier series model is integrated in a virtual commissioning software as a co-simulated functional mock-up unit.
Additionally, it is used to compensate the transmission errors by correcting the setpoint from the computerized numerical control (CNC).
The model identification and the compensation are experimentally evaluated with a Stäubli TX2-40 industrial robot.
The model has a mean absolute error of 0.114 mrad, and the compensation improves the accuracy by 83.26 % for axis 2 and 49.21 % for axis 3.
2026-10-20.introduction:
The programming of industrial robots (IR) currently heavily relies on online teaching, where only repeatability is relevant.
Although the usage of digital twins for offline programming is common, the online adaptation of previously offline prepared robot programs is still necessary due to insufficient accuracy of standard IRs.
For example, a mean error of 0.968 mm 0.968\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} and a maximum error of 2.158 mm 2.158\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} were reported for an ABB IRB 1600 with a reach of 1.45 m 1.45\text{\,}\mathrm{m} Nubiola and Bonev (2013) , while a mean error of 4.257 mm 4.257\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} and a maximum error of 5.751 mm 5.751\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} were measured for a KUKA KR210-2 with a reach of 2.7 m 2.7\text{\,}\mathrm{m} Dzubba et al. (2025) .
Since the models for the inaccuracy of standard IRs are usually not available, these inaccuracies are neither considered in digital twins, nor compensated in the robot control.
This increases overall commissioning time, and therefore, commissioning cost.
Due to this limited accuracy and the restricted offline programming capabilities, IRs are mainly used for handling applications, which do not require frequent changes in the robot program.
In contrast, manufacturing tasks require high accuracy and the ability for flexible reprogramming.
Therefore, robot models with high accuracy are needed to enable the direct use of offline developed robot programs.
Furthermore, they are required to increase the accuracy of an IR to a suitable level for manufacturing processes with low to medium accuracy demands.
The path errors of IRs mainly originate from the robot joints consisting of permanent-magnet synchronous motors (PMSM) and gearboxes Olabi et al. (2012) .
Within these drive trains, the angular position error is caused by gearbox compliance, kinematic transmission errors (TEs), and motor torque ripples Renders et al. (1991) .
The errors of individual joints are accumulated along the serial kinematic chain and amplified by the length of the arm to the tool center point (TCP).
TEs cannot be compensated for by the position controller because encoders in standard IRs are mounted at the motor shaft.
A TE model for cycloidal drives considering load-, velocity-, and temperature-dependency was previously presented by the authors Bauer et al. (2025a) .
This paper aims at presenting a first approach to identify TEs for standard IRs using a laser tracker, transferring the modeling method, and showing the potential of improving digital twins by more accurate, dynamic robot joint models.
Deviations of the kinematic robot description are not considered here.

TEs are defined as errors between motor and load-side angles of the gearbox.
These errors are angle-dependent and periodic Blanche and Yang (1989) .
TEs are caused by manufacturing and assembly tolerances.
In previous works, TEs were mainly modeled using angle-dependent Fourier series. Ghorbel et al. additionally considered the load-torque and velocity dependency Ghorbel et al. (2001) .
Furthermore, a lubricant temperature dependency was described, which can be explained by changes in the viscous friction Qiu and Xue (2021) .
In literature, many works cover the modeling of TEs in strain wave gears Iwasaki et al. (2009) ; Han et al. (2008) ; Iwasaki and Nakamura (2014) , while there is less research covering TEs in cycloidal drives (CDs) Zhang et al. (2011) .
Disturbance observers for strain wave gears Iwasaki et al. (2009) and for CDs Kawahara et al. (2013) based on purely angle-dependent Fourier series have been shown. Bilancia et al. reported the velocity and temperature dependency of TEs also for CDs Bilancia et al. (2022) .
In Bilancia et al. (2025) , Bilancia et al. modeled and compensated the influence of load-, velocity-, and temperature-dependency using machine learning models with the load-side angle as an input. Bauer et al. use a load-, velocity-, and temperature-dependent Fourier series with the motor angle as an input to model TEs in CDs Bauer et al. (2025a) . Han et al. applied an acceleration sensor with a peak filter to suppress vibrations due to TEs in an industrial robot Han et al. (2008) , while Iwasaki et al. corrected the torque setpoint with an adaptive notch filter Iwasaki and Nakamura (2014) .
Moreover, there are several approaches based on load-side encoders, incorporating H-infinity control, unscented Kalman filters Mesmer et al. (2020) , and gain scheduling Mesmer et al. (2022) . Olabi et al. analyzed the TEs of a Stäubli RX 170 BH based on laser tracker measurements of the load-side angles.
The authors identified the stiffness of the joints by attaching constant weights and measuring the deformation.
The TEs of axis 2 2 were compensated by adapting the motor angle setpoint using a lookup table Olabi et al. (2012) . Vakilinejad et al. analyzed the TEs of the first three joints of a Stäubli TX90 under the assumption that the first three joints contribute most to the TCP error due to their larger lever arm and higher gear ratios.
The authors model the influence of gravity load and runout error as third-order polynomial and the periodic TEs as angle-dependent sinus series with seven harmonics Vakilinejad et al. (2019) .

First, this paper aims at presenting a method to identify the velocity-dependent TEs from laser tracker and motor encoder measurements.
The laser tracker measurements are captured in the Cartesian laser tracker coordinate frame and have to be transformed to load-side angles.
A Stäubli TX2-40 ( Fig. 1 (a)) with a reach of 0.515 m 0.515\text{\,}\mathrm{m} and a load capacity of 2 kg 2\text{\,}\mathrm{kg} is used for experiments (2025) .
Second, the integration of accurate TE models in the digital twin of robot cells is demonstrated.
ISG-virtuos is used as deterministic real-time simulation tool. Here, the TE models are integrated as co-simulated functional mock-up units (FMUs) with a non-real-time solver.
During the virtual commissioning, the simulated robot considering the TEs is shown as a shadow model over the purely kinematic simulation, highlighting the differences in modeling complexity ( Fig. 1 (b)).
Third, the derived models are integrated as feedforward control to compensate the TEs. This proposes an alternative to the consideration of TEs during offline programming.
The compensation is implemented as a feedforward control in TwinCAT 3.
It corrects the angle setpoint from the computerized numerical control (CNC) in the programmable logic controller (PLC) and sends the corrected setpoint via EtherCAT and the uniVAL interface to the robot.
The TEs were only identified for the first three axes of the robot, since it is assumed that they contribute most to the TCP error due to a larger lever arm Vakilinejad et al. (2019) .
Furthermore, only TEs including compliance were identified and compensated within this contribution.
To increase the overall accuracy at the TCP, the additional identification of deviations from the kinematic description provided by the manufacturer is necessary.

2026-10-20.title: Lubricant Temperature Observer for Gearboxes in Industrial Robots
2026-10-20.authors: Christian J. E. Bauer , Markus Neher , Valentin Kamm , Lukas Steinle , Armin Lechler , Alexander Verl
2026-10-20.subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) ; Robotics (cs.RO); Signal Processing (eess.SP)
2026-10-20.comment: . Dataset available on this https URL
2026-10-20.abstract: The position and path accuracy of industrial robots is strongly affected by temperature. In particular, temperature-dependent friction and altered hysteresis and transmission errors in the gearboxes are the main causes of these deviations. Since standard industrial robots lack temperature sensors, it is proposed to estimate the gearbox lubricant temperature using observer structures. It is planned to apply the proposed lubricant temperature observer to provide the input for temperature-dependent error compensation for gearboxes in industrial robots. First, a two-state heat transfer model describing the heat transfer from the lubricant through the gearbox housing to the environment is described and identified. It is integrated into a Luenberger observer and a Kalman filter with a correction of the lubricant temperature estimation based on measurements from a housing temperature sensor. Temperature measurements were performed in an experimental setup with a cycloidal gear filled with grease, which is common for industrial robots. Due to its changing viscosity and changing thermal conductivity at different shear rates, it shows a less uniform thermal behavior than gear-oil. For the validation measurements, the developed observers showed a mean absolute error of 1.3 K.
2026-10-20.introduction:
The position accuracy of industrial robots is significantly affected by thermal changes.
For a standard industrial robot such as the ABB IRB 2400, position errors of 0.441 mm 0.441\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} due to temperature changes can be measured at the tool center point [ 1 ] . Heisel et al. showed the influence of temperature on the position accuracy for SCARA, tripod, and six-axis kinematics.
For a single robot joint an angular error of 0.0006 ° / K 0.0006\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree}\text{/}\mathrm{K} was measured [ 2 ] .
The drives are the main source of heat in industrial robots [ 3 ] due to the thermal power generated by friction.
In previous works, a compensation approach was introduced, accounting for temperature-dependent hysteresis and friction [ 4 ] .
Since a temperature difference of 50 K 50\text{\,}\mathrm{K} results in a change of 40 % 40\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} to 60 % 60\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} in the friction parameters [ 5 ] , a temperature-dependent friction model is required.
In [ 6 ] , the authors proposed a state-dependent transmission error compensation to further improve position accuracy.
Both approaches currently depend on sensors to measure the temperature of the gearbox lubricant.
Standard industrial robots are not equipped with gearbox temperature sensors [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] .
Therefore, an observer approach to estimate the gearbox lubricant temperature was developed and validated in this work.
Temperature measurements were carried out with an experimental setup incorporating a single robot joint ( Fig. 1 ).

Current approaches to gear temperature estimation originate from research in temperature-dependent friction modeling.
Since friction is assumed to be temperature-dependent on the one hand, and friction is considered to be the main thermal input to the gearboxes on the other hand, the two fields are closely related. Bittencourt et al. extended a friction model for robot joints to include load- and temperature-dependent effects.
Robot gearboxes filled with oil were used in experiments to ensure a uniform temperature measurement by the lubricant temperature sensor.
An exponential description of the thermal effects on viscous friction was applied in [ 7 , 8 , 12 ] , which is related to the Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann equation [ 13 ] .
In [ 14 ] , the approach was extended to detect the wear of the modeled gear based on a deviation of the friction from the corresponding model. Márton et al. applied a friction model that describes the thermal influence via an internal, non-measurable state [ 5 ] .
This approach with a state corresponding to the liquefying of the lubricant under the influence of shear was introduced by Batista and Carlson [ 15 , 16 ] .
The model was integrated with a viscous friction observer for robot gearboxes to detect changes in the lubricant consistency and wear and it was validated in simulation.
While the influence of temperature on viscous friction is assumed to show exponential behavior, the influence of thermal effects on the viscosity was modeled linearly [ 17 ] .
In [ 9 ] , the authors introduced a model based on the energy balance that describes the heat transfer from the lubricant over the gearbox housing to the environment.
It was integrated into a Kalman filter with the environment temperature and the product of velocity and friction torque as inputs to estimate the lubricant temperature.
This temperature estimation was used to detect faults based on changes in the friction parameters.
Tests were performed using a gear pair with a reduction ratio of 3 3 and standard gear oil in the gearbox.
Temperatures in between approximately 22 °C 22\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} and 32 °C 32\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} were considered.
A similar two-state heat transfer model was used by Legnani et al. [ 18 ] and Pagani et al. [ 19 ] without an observer structure. Carlson et al. suggested a simpler model with a single state that considers only environment and gearbox temperature.
In their contribution, the approach was evaluated experimentally on two industrial robots.
The grease in the gearboxes was replaced by oil [ 10 ] .
A similar model was used by Simoni et al. to provide the input temperature to a third-order polynomial friction model.
The model was experimentally validated in an industrial robot with different gearboxes filled with oil and grease [ 20 ] . Legnani et al. used the same robot to validate an alternative gearbox temperature model incorporating the duty cycle of the joint drive [ 21 ] . Simoni et al. extended their approach to include the Stribeck effect [ 22 ] and evaluated it in a polishing task [ 23 ] .
The single-state heat transfer model was embedded in an observer to estimate the initial gearbox temperature.
It showed a convergence time of a few minutes [ 23 ] .
Increasing the observer gain led to an convergence in less than a second at cost of an oscillating and noisy estimation [ 24 ] . Shimada described a single-state model based on Newton’s law of cooling for a lead-screw drive.
The model incorporates a disturbance observer to estimate the friction force as input [ 25 ] Nevmerzhitskiy et al. estimated the gearbox temperature based on measurements from the motor temperature sensor in a KUKA KR10 and a correction term derived from a friction estimation during specific periodic trajectories [ 26 ] . Pagani et al. extended the two-state heat transfer model with an additional input for the thermal power from the motor and a third state for an optional temperature sensor placed nearby on the robot structure [ 27 ] .
A detailed analytical model of thermal lubrication characteristics for a cycloidal drive was proposed by Han et al. for simulations [ 28 ] . Paschold et al. derived an analytical thermal model of oil-lubricated gearboxes with multiple states based on the thermal network method [ 29 , 30 ] .

In this paper, a lubricant temperature observer for robot gearboxes based on the two-state heat transfer model proposed by Márton et al. in [ 9 ] was developed.
In the state of the art, this approach was only elaborated for a small gearbox and comparably low temperatures, while the thermal behavior of industrial-scale gearboxes has not been addressed.
In this contribution, the thermal properties of a cycloidal drive with an 185 185 : 1 1 reduction ratio were investigated and modeled.
The experimental setup used for the temperature measurements represents a base joint in a standard industrial robot for heavy payloads.
A lubricant temperature range in between approximately 20 °C 20\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} and 50 °C 50\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} was investigated. As common for the joints of many industrial robots, it is lubricated with grease instead of gear oil.
Since grease shows a reduced circulation within the gearbox, it has reduced heat dissipation properties compared to oil [ 31 ] .
Grease is pasty at room temperature and with increasing temperature it decreases its viscosity.
Unlike oil, grease is a non-Newtonian fluid and shows a decreasing viscosity with increasing shear strain [ 13 ] .
While in [ 9 ] an oil-lubricated gearbox was considered, the suitability of a two-state heat-transfer model for grease-lubricated gearboxes was not investigated yet.
The specific properties of grease are taken into account in the present work. In this work, the accuracy of the model without an observer structure was compared to a Luenberger observer (not covered in [ 9 ] ) and a Kalman filter using the measured housing temperature for correction.
In addition to the analysis in [ 9 ] , the reliability of the temperature observer was tested by evaluating the transient behavior after an initialization with an incorrect initial lubricant temperature estimate.
The lubricant temperature observer is the basis for a potential sensorless application of the friction model and the joint hysteresis compensation in [ 4 ] as well as the state-dependent transmission error model in [ 6 ] .
Standard industrial robots are not equipped with gearbox lubricant temperature sensors.
However, housing temperature sensors, which are easy and cost-effective to integrate, can be used as a basis to estimate the lubricant temperature.
If the robot has been idle for several hours and all mechanical components have cooled down to the known environmental temperature, the approach works even without housing temperature sensors [ 28 ] .

2026-10-21.title: Learning Adaptable Dexterous Skills via Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking
2026-10-21.authors: Yuxuan Kuang , Jiashun Wang , Yixuan Sun , Yufei Ye , Sungjae Park , Umar Iqbal , Katerina Fragkiadaki , Shubham Tulsiani
2026-10-21.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-21.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract:
Dexterous multi-finger hands hold promise to unlock diverse skills like functional grasps, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic handover that the human-designed world assumes, yet existing learning recipes force a trade-off. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning generalizes to arbitrary object poses but, lacking any human prior, converges to unnatural and unreliable finger strategies; motion tracking reproduces human-like behavior from a single clip but cannot deviate from it. We present AdaDex , a goal-conditioned RL framework that turns a single hand-object trajectory of a few seconds—from mocap data or HOI reconstruction from in-the-wild RGB(D) video—into an adaptable dexterous skill. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking : a shared policy is trained on two populations of massively parallel environments: motion tracking environments trained with dense motion tracking objective, which instill the human prior from human motion; and generalization environments with noised initial states and goals and a sparse object-success reward, which force the skill to work far off the reference. From seconds of human motion per skill, the resulting policies can learn diverse adaptable dexterous skills, such as functional grasping, object reposing, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Our method outperforms baselines in terms of generalization and functionality, and we demonstrate transfer across simulators and to the real world.
Project page: https://yuxuank.com/AdaDex .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Our built environment is designed around the human hand: tools, handles, lids, and switches all presuppose a multi-fingered end-effector.
Many of the skills this design affords, including functional tool use, in-hand reorientation, and dynamic behaviors such as throwing and catching, remain difficult for parallel-jaw grippers, which makes dexterous hands a natural embodiment for general-purpose manipulation.
Despite this promise, learning dexterous skills is challenging.
A multi-fingered hand must act in a high-dimensional continuous action space with 20+ degrees of freedom, and each skill must regulate contact forces, friction, and gravity across many simultaneous and often intermittent contacts under fast dynamics.

Two paradigms currently dominate learning-based dexterous manipulation, and they fail in complementary ways. Consider picking up a hammer lying on a table and striking a nail. Goal-reaching reinforcement learning ( Kuang et al., 2026 ; Kedia et al., 2026 ) trains a single policy to move an object from any initial pose to any target pose, achieving broad coverage. Given target hammer poses, such a policy can bring the hammer to the nail. However, an object-centric reward specifies only where the object should end up, not how to get it there. Without explicit shaping, the policy could seize the hammer by its head or pinch it mid-shaft. These grasps might satisfy the goal but are not functional for hammering.
Additionally, behaviors that require finger gaiting or regrasping, such as reorienting the hammer in hand from a lying-flat pickup to a striking grip with functional thumb bracing, are rarely discovered at all. As a result, the intricate motion the task demands remain largely out of reach. Motion tracking ( Li et al., 2025 ; Mandi et al., 2025 ) , in contrast, imitates a hand-object trajectory under dense supervision and thereby inherits the demonstrator’s functional grasp, in-hand regrasp, and swing. The resulting policy, however, is bound to the reference. If the nail sits at a different location or angle, the policy has no mechanism to adapt, and it typically requires the dense reference as input at inference time. In short, tracking supplies the human prior and goal reaching supplies generalization, but neither alone yields a skill that is both human-like and adaptable.

To that end, we present AdaDex , which treats the two paradigms as complements rather than alternatives. At the core of AdaDex is Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking , built on the observation that motion tracking and goal reaching are the same goal-conditioned problem: both ask a policy π θ ​ ( a ∣ s , g ) \pi_{\theta}(a\mid s,g) to bring the object and wrist to a target pose g g , and differ only in where g g comes from and how progress is rewarded. We therefore train one policy across two kinds of massively parallel environments: Tracking Environments (TrackEnv) initialize along a human hand-object reference τ ^ \hat{\tau} , take goals from τ ^ \hat{\tau} , and apply a dense tracking reward on object, wrist, fingers, and contacts, teaching the policy how a human grasps, gaits, and releases. Generalization Environments (GenEnv) perturb the initialization with large noise, offset the goal by a random SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) transformation that can be far from any frame of τ ^ \hat{\tau} , and reward only sparse object success plus wrist guidance, with no finger terms. The two are mutually reinforcing. TrackEnv supplies the prior and the exploration: skills that sparse reward almost never discovers, such as throwing an object and catching it mid-flight, are learned under dense tracking and, because g g is the only channel of task information, become directly addressable by novel goals. GenEnv supplies the generalization: it forces success from off-reference states toward off-reference goals so the skill can be adaptable to new scenarios and does not collapse into replaying one clip, while leaving the finger strategy to the human prior. Neither suffices alone; together they yield a skill that is both functional and adaptable. The recipe needs no discriminator, phase variable, or distillation stage, and the dense reference is not required at test time: at deployment the policy consumes only proprioception, object pose, object shape, and a goal pose, so it can be driven by any goal source, such as VLM Agent planner’s output waypoints.

We evaluate AdaDex on functional grasping of diverse tools and household objects, in-hand reorientation requiring finger gaiting and contact switching, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch. Every skill is learned from a single human motion trajectory of a few seconds. The learned policies preserve the grasp type, in-hand manipulation, and dynamic behaviors from human motion, while generalizing to unseen trajectories and randomized object goals far from the reference, and achieve various downstream tasks with VLM Agents under multiple embodiments. Additionally, we demonstrate that our recipe can be embedded in between real-to-sim and sim-to-real, where a few seconds of human motion from in-the-wild RGB(D) videos is converted into a simulation-ready hand-object reference via our advanced HOI reconstruction pipeline. And then the reference is broadened into an adaptable skill in simulation as described above, and the resulting simulation rollout is transferred to a real arm-hand robotic system with real-time dynamics. In summary, our contributions are:

Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking. A goal-conditioned RL formulation in which dense reference tracking and sparse goal reaching are trained as parallel environment types under a single shared actor, so that the human prior from tracking and the coverage from goal reaching reinforce one another. The formulation requires no dense reference input at inference.

Hybrid Dexterous Mimicking. A goal-conditioned RL formulation in which dense reference tracking and sparse goal reaching are trained as parallel environment types under a single shared actor, so that the human prior from tracking and the coverage from goal reaching reinforce one another. The formulation requires no dense reference input at inference.

Adaptable dexterous skills. Human-like functional grasping, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch, each learned from seconds of human motion and generalized to novel states and goals. The resulting adaptable skills can achieve various downstream tasks under diverse embodiments with VLM Agent planners.

Learning from real-to-sim HOI motions. A reconstruction pipeline that converts a clip of in-the-wild human video into a simulation-ready hand-object reference, outperforming existing HOI reconstruction baselines. This pipeline allows us to learn adaptable dexterous skills from human data and transfer their simulation rollouts across simulators and to the real world.

The formulation requires no dense reference input at inference.

2. Adaptable dexterous skills. Human-like functional grasping, in-hand reorientation with finger gaiting, and dynamic behaviors like throw-and-catch, each learned from seconds of human motion and generalized to novel states and goals. # 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Dexterous Skill Learning

Endowing robots with human-level, generalizable dexterity is a long-standing goal toward generalist agents that operate across diverse real-world scenarios. A large body of prior work formulates dexterous manipulation as contact-based optimization ( Liu et al., 2020 ; Liu et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Yin and Abbeel, 2025 ) , synthesizing static grasps and planning motions. These approaches are largely confined to grasping and, lacking closed-loop feedback, remain brittle under disturbances. An alternative line of work collects teleoperated demonstrations for behavior cloning ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Wen et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025a ) . The resulting policies are bound to the distribution of in-domain demonstrations and generalize poorly; moreover, existing teleoperation interfaces (e.g., gloves and exoskeletons) struggle to capture behaviors that demand high dexterity or dynamic motion.
More recently, reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising route to generalizable dexterity. Task-specific methods have been developed for dexterous grasping ( Wan et al., 2023 ; Lum et al., 2024 ; Singh et al., 2025 ) and in-hand reorientation ( Qi et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2025b ) , while two more general paradigms have gained traction: motion tracking ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2025 ; Mandi et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025b ; Liang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) and generalized goal reaching ( Kuang et al., 2026 ; Kedia et al., 2026 ) . Each paradigm exhibits a complementary limitation: motion tracking faithfully reproduces a reference but cannot generalize beyond it, whereas goal reaching handles arbitrary goals but yields motions that lack human-like functionality. Our method unifies the two so that they reinforce each other, learning adaptable dexterous skills that span functional grasping, in-hand manipulation, and dynamic behaviors from only seconds of human motion.

## 2.2 Robot Learning from Human Motion

Human data constitutes the most scalable source of supervision for robot learning, and human motion in particular has been widely exploited ( Wu et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2023 ) . Motion tracking has become the dominant recipe for humanoid control and loco-manipulation ( Liao et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ) , and the same idea has been extended to dexterous manipulation ( Liu et al., 2025a ; Xu et al., 2025b ; Lum et al., 2025 ; Liang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . These methods, however, typically offer limited generalization and require a dense reference trajectory as the goal at inference time.
We are inspired by recent work on hybrid imitation learning, including HIL ( Wang et al., 2026b ) and GfR ( Wang et al., 2026c ) , which relax this requirement, enabling humanoid parkour from sparse goals while still generalizing beyond the reference. Building on this insight, our method couples motion tracking with goal reaching RL to learn dexterous skills that are simultaneously human-like and generalizable from seconds of human motion.

2026-10-21.title: UniWALM: Unified World Action Language Model for Embodied Robot Control
2026-10-21.authors: Rahul Sajnani , Diego Romeres , Mingyuan Zhang , Kai Gao , Carl Qi , Baichuan Huang , Srinath Sridhar , Dylan Randle , Lillian J. Ratliff , Jose Barreiros , Manikantan Nambi , Jeroen Vanbaar
2026-10-21.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-21.comment: Preprint
2026-10-21.abstract:
Motivated by the human ability to integrate experience across language, perception, and action, we introduce UniWALM, a unified world-action-language model that learns video, action, and language in a single shared representation, where each modality is both a conditioning signal and a supervision target.
We ask: can jointly generating language enrich this shared representation, improving manipulation and supporting memory-dependent behavior? Unlike prior approaches that attach a reasoning or vision-language model to a video-action backbone and run them as distinct stages, UniWALM unifies all three modalities inside a single mixture-of-transformers backbone whose per-modality diffusion heads co-denoise synchronously, decoding subtask and textual memory in the same pass as action with no separate planning stage; the generated language is re-consumed on the next step, closing a language-as-memory loop without an external planner or memory bank.
To keep the action stream reliable under this richer objective, we further introduce Flow Matching with Correction (FMC), a training objective that teaches recovery from perturbed action trajectories at no inference-time cost.
UniWALM consistently improves over same-backbone baselines (e.g., FastWAM [ 52 ] ) on compositional pick-and-place (MolmoSpaces) and across the memory-dependent subset of RMBench [ 10 ] , where it reaches 34.5% without any pretrained language or reasoning model and exceeds Mem-0’s keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using only a single anchor frame.
On a real-world Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% to 61.1% , while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance ( ≤ 33.3 % \leq 33.3\% ).
2026-10-21.introduction:
Humans integrate perception, language, and action in an any-to-any manner: regions like the posterior parietal and premotor cortex continuously fuse afferent inputs with efferent motor copies [ 2 ] , and cognitive representations are inherently shaped by what an agent can do in the world [ 19 , 12 ] . For embodied agents, language, video, and action are three complementary views of a single interaction; a unified representation should let each one inform the others: language guiding physical prediction, visual dynamics grounding action, and action anchoring predictions in embodied behavior. Multimodal models have operationalized this framing for vision and text [ 31 , 47 , 55 ] but largely omit action and motor control.

The same substrate that integrates these modalities also remembers : the hippocampus, which the brain uses to recall past experience, is also recruited to imagine the future and locate the self in time [ 17 , 53 ] . We routinely enlist language itself as working memory (counting out loud, repeating a phone number, silently rehearsing a passage while reading to retain it) to track state through long-horizon, memory-dependent tasks. A truly unified representation should therefore not only let modalities inform one another but also let generated language serve as the working memory that threads behavior across step boundaries. Concretely, because language is co-denoised with action in one representation, the generated string serves as a learned, in-loop plan (next subtask) and textual memory (what has been done so far), while an anchor-frame visual memory preserves scene context across occlusion; re-consumed on the next step, these close a memory loop with no external planner, VLM, or retrieval buffer.

Recent robotic foundation models connect video, language, and action, but typically along only a subset of these directions. Vision-language-action models [ 36 , 26 ] consume language as fixed conditioning but do not generate it. Chain-of-thought VLAs [ 21 , 6 , 54 , 3 , 56 ] generate intermediate language within a control step, but autoregressively, so action must wait for token decoding, and the generated string is not re-consumed across steps. World-action models (DreamZero [ 51 ] , FastWAM [ 52 ] ) co-model video and action but drop language entirely. Memory-augmented systems [ 42 , 35 , 10 ] attach retrieval buffers or an external planner to a pretrained backbone; π 0.7 \pi_{0.7} [ 35 ] supplies language from a high-level semantic policy while a separate world model generates subgoal images that condition a VLA ( Fig. 1 (f)). On memory-dependent evaluations like RMBench [ 10 ] ’s M ⁡ ( n ) M(n) subset, where decisions require n n task-relevant past observations, policies that condition only on the current frame and prompt collapse.

A natural response is to compose a pretrained vision-language model with a video-action backbone and supply reasoning via auxiliary conditioning or an additional loss ( Fig. 1 (f)). This family (hybrid planner + VLA systems [ 35 ] , concurrent compositional WALMs) is more accurately described as WAM + VLM features : it typically uses two vision backbones optimized for different objectives and only loosely coupled, treats language as an external hidden state rather than a generation target, and bolts memory on as a separate retrieval module. UniWALM ( Fig. 1 (g)) uses a single video backbone jointly optimized for all three modalities , with video, action, and language as first-class diffusion heads co-denoised in one pass; the generated language is re-consumed next step, closing a language-as-memory loop with no external planner, VLM, or memory bank. Where prior world-action models supervise the backbone with frame-level predictive structure (future video), UniWALM adds a task-level predictive stream (future subtask and task state as language), a second, longer-horizon supervision signal that frame prediction alone cannot cheaply express.

In this work we study two questions: (i) does jointly generating language enrich the shared representation of a video-action model and improve manipulation? ( Fig. 1 (g)) and (ii) can a policy use its own generated language, re-consumed across steps, as working memory on memory-dependent tasks? ( Fig. 2 )

We introduce UniWALM, a multimodal world-model architecture that takes a step toward any-to-any modeling across language, video, and actions, where each modality serves as both a conditioning signal and a supervision target. Specifically:

World-Action-Language Model (WALM): We introduce WALM, a unified World Action Language Model implemented as a mixture of transformers that takes video, language, and actions as input and generates all three as output. The language stream emits a subtask and textual memory in the same denoising pass as action, and re-consumes them as prompt on the next control step, closing a language-as-memory loop. UniWALM’s language and action experts are trained from scratch on a video-only backbone: no pretrained language or reasoning model is used .

World-Action-Language Model (WALM): We introduce WALM, a unified World Action Language Model implemented as a mixture of transformers that takes video, language, and actions as input and generates all three as output. The language stream emits a subtask and textual memory in the same denoising pass as action, and re-consumes them as prompt on the next control step, closing a language-as-memory loop. UniWALM’s language and action experts are trained from scratch on a video-only backbone: no pretrained language or reasoning model is used .

Flow Matching with Correction (FMC). We introduce FMC to improve the reliability of generated actions. During training, FMC perturbs action trajectories and supervises a corrective velocity that returns the perturbed denoising path toward the clean trajectory. This trains recovery from action-space perturbations without adding model capacity or sampling steps at inference.

Evaluation in simulation and real-world manipulation. UniWALM achieves the highest success on all three MolmoSpaces [ 24 ] compositional pick-and-place variants, improving over the same-backbone FastWAM baseline by +14.8% on average ( Tab. 1 ). On RMBench’s memory-dependent M(n) subset, UniWALM reaches 34.5% without pretrained language or reasoning model, improving over same-backbone FastWAM (13.3%) by +21.2 points and above Mem-0’s keyframe-equipped setup (28.5%) using a single anchor frame instead of per-task privileged keyframes ( Tab. 3 ). On a real-world bimanual Find-the-Item task, generating textual memory lifts success from 11.1% (FastWAM, same video backbone, no language) to 61.1% , while state-of-the-art VLAs stay at or below chance ( ≤ 33.3 % \leq 33.3\% ) ( Tab. 2 ).

Together, these results motivate further investigation of any-to-any world modeling as a foundation for generalist embodied agents.

2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Generalist robot policies [ 36 , 5 , 14 , 33 , 46 , 6 , 34 , 44 ] improve over single-task models [ 11 , 57 ] by initializing from vision-language backbones [ 49 , 13 , 9 , 39 , 8 , 32 ] and training for action. These policies map observations to actions but do not model world dynamics or reason over long-horizon subtasks.

A recent line of works [ 52 , 51 , 23 , 4 , 16 , 30 , 27 ] adds a video-prediction objective, jointly modeling world dynamics and action. FastWAM [ 52 ] , closest to our work, couples a pretrained Wan2.2 [ 45 ] video DiT with a parallel action DiT through unified attention. These models treat language purely as a conditioning input, never as a generation target and provide no mechanism for subtask reasoning or memory.

Long-horizon and memory-dependent tasks have motivated explicit reasoning and memory [ 10 , 38 ] , and hybrid systems [ 35 , 43 , 7 , 25 , 48 ] that combine a high-level VLM planner, a low-level policy, and a video model to imagine action effects. Because these components are trained separately on heterogeneous data, they lack a shared representation and execute planning and control asynchronously.

Any-to-any modeling originates in multimodal LLMs [ 55 , 47 ] which omit generating actions, and vision works like 4M [ 31 ] , which unify many modalities via masked token modeling but target perception rather than control and do not reason. Concurrent work [ 48 ] additionally generates actions, DINO features, semantics, and video, but cannot reason or preserve memory during manipulation. Concurrent omnimodal models such as Cosmos 3 [ 1 ] extend any-to-any modeling to action within a single framework, but decode text autoregressively in one tower and continuous modalities by diffusion in another, running reasoning and generation as separate stages in a 64B model. UniWALM instead generates language, video, and action entirely by diffusion in one shared representation , denoising language and action synchronously so that reasoning and control co-refine in a single unified model.

An extended discussion contrasting UniWALM with CoT / inner-monologue policies, multi-scale memory VLAs, and recent unified models is deferred to Appendix A .

2026-10-21.title: Industrial ReMEmbR: Scaling Spatiotemporal Memory to Robot Fleets
2026-10-21.authors: Jad Yammine , Malek Wahidi , Abrar Anwar , Yan Chang , Mihir Acharya , Anthony Rizk
2026-10-21.abstract: Warehouse robot fleets continuously observe operational conditions, but preserving these observations as reusable semantic memory incurs substantial computation, communication, and storage costs. For example, explaining recurring aisle blockages can require reviewing video from multiple robots across several shifts. We present Industrial ReMEmbR , a shared spatiotemporal memory system that extends NVIDIA ReMEmbR to robot fleets and reduces server-side computation by generating scene descriptions only on demand. On each robot, an NVIDIA Jetson encodes video clips into retrieval embeddings with Cosmos-Embed1, vision tokens with Cosmos3-Edge, and reconstruction latents with the Wan2.2 VAE, without uploading raw camera frames. The encoding models are re-used to detect people in image patches, zeroing them out to support PII abstraction for GDPR-compliant deployments. We split Cosmos3-Edge at its vision–language boundary, placing the vision encoder on the robot and the language decoder on an on-premises server. A Nemotron agent retrieves memories by content, position, and time and queries the decoder using cached vision tokens. This design eliminates caption generation at write time, while cached-token decoding reproduces the unsplit model’s output in all 450 tested decodes. On the NaVQA benchmark, the updated model stack achieves comparable retrieval recall while reducing unparsable answers from 4.5% to 1.9% with an agent half the parameter size. We further demonstrate a live semantic traffic map that classifies aisle conditions directly from retrieval embeddings. Across 914 simulated warehouse frames, this method exceeds the best caption-based alternative by 6.0 percentage points. By decoupling memory encoding from description, Industrial ReMEmbR transforms a fleet’s collective experience into an extensible foundation for spatial and temporal reasoning, including faithful scene reconstruction, context-guided elaboration, and semantic mapping of dynamic warehouse conditions as they unfold.
2026-10-21.introduction:
An embodied memory lets a robot recall what it has seen, where, and when, long after the moment has passed. NVIDIA’s ReMEmbR ( Anwar et al., 2025 ) , a spatiotemporal memory system designed for long-horizon visual question answering for robot navigation, showed that a single robot can build such a memory from its own camera stream. On a warehouse floor, however, that robot is only one of many. A fleet management system, or fleet manager, continuously tracks dozens of autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) and other integrated devices in a modern warehouse, assigning them orders and planning their routes over VDA5050, the standard interface between mobile robots and fleet management systems. Obstacles outside the tracking system are left to each robot’s intelligent navigation system to recognize and avoid. What a passing robot sees is rarely kept, because continuously uploading and storing raw video from every robot is expensive, so the rich semantic context of each scene never reaches the rest of the fleet.

To illustrate, consider the case of a fleet management system that keeps routing AMRs through an aisle partially blocked by a clutter of untracked obstacles. Each robot independently maneuvers around the clutter, losing time before carrying on with its scheduled tasks. A few days later, a human operator reviewing the daily logs notices that task completion times slipped that day, but has no record of the scene from which to trace its root cause. Neither the fleet manager nor the operator has the semantic context that could have prevented the congestion, by adaptively routing later robots away from the aisle, or its recurrence, by revealing what caused it.

Closing this contextual blind spot requires scaling embodied memory from a single robot to the entire fleet, with every connected robot acting as a live reporter from the warehouse floor that continuously contributes its observations, tagged with location and time, to a shared fleet memory. In the scenario above, the first robot to encounter the clutter would report it on a live semantic map, letting the fleet manager route subsequent robots around the blocked aisle. Days later, the operator could ask the fleet’s shared semantic memory what caused the reroutes and receive an answer grounded in direct visual observation: when and where the clutter appeared, and what it consisted of. The same record can supply the world state of a centralized planner such as RobotFleet ( Gupta et al., 2025 ) , which schedules heterogeneous robots from declarative statements about the site and replans when a robot reports a discovery.

To this end, we build on ReMEmbR, which captions each short video clip, stores the caption along with the robot’s time and location and a corresponding caption embedding, and lets an agentic model perform semantic retrieval over the vector database to answer arbitrary questions. Scaling this design from one robot to a fleet breaks three of its assumptions, and each break motivates one principle of our design. First, ReMEmbR generates a caption for every clip as it is written, so its cost grows with every robot added and every hour it operates, and continuously uploading raw video from every robot is costly to begin with. We therefore encode once , compressing each clip on the robot’s own edge compute into compact representations that every later step reuses. Second, ReMEmbR answers occasional questions, whereas the fleet manager also needs a continuously updated view of the site. We therefore interpret continuously , reading that state directly from each memory as it arrives, without generating any text. Third, the questions a memory must answer are not known when it is first encoded. We therefore elaborate on demand , deferring any description of a scene until a question about it arrives. In the blocked aisle example, the clutter is encoded once by the first robot that passes it, flagged on the live map as soon as its memory arrives, and described in detail only when the operator asks about it days later.

We present Industrial ReMEmbR (Fig. 1 ), a shared memory system built around these three principles. It encodes clips on edge compute across the fleet, continuously aggregates and interprets them on server compute for live semantic mapping, and elaborates on any of them on demand. Each robot’s onboard Jetson edge-compute device runs iw.encode , the edge component for efficient multi-purpose encoding. This deployed service continuously generates video-text embedding vectors for memory retrieval derived from Cosmos-Embed1 ( NVIDIA, 2025 ) , vision tokens for optional scene description derived from the detached vision encoder of Cosmos3-Edge ( NVIDIA, 2026a ) , and compressed latent frames for optional scene inspection generated by the Wan2.2 VAE ( Team Wan, 2025b ; Team Wan, 2025a ) encoder. Only the aforementioned multi-purpose scene representations, robot pose and memory timestamp are uploaded into a shared fleet memory, whose vector index is accelerated with NVIDIA cuVS ( RAPIDS Team, 2024 ) .

To reduce server-side computation, we generate scene descriptions and answers on demand for memories retrieved by the agent, rather than captioning every encoded clip.
We enable this by splitting Cosmos3-Edge at its vision–language boundary, where its server-side language decoder answers questions from cached vision tokens without accessing or re-encoding the original clips.
We deploy a Nemotron-3-Nano-4B ( NVIDIA, 2026b ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ) agent through an NVIDIA NIM inference microservice to retrieve memories by content, position, and time, and optionally query the decoder with a text prompt and the retrieved vision tokens.
Operators can also reconstruct scenes from stored latent frames for visual inspection.
On NaVQA, Upgraded ReMEmbR , our version of ReMEmbR updated with the NVIDIA models and a video-based index, achieves comparable retrieval recall while reducing unparseable answers from 4.5% to 1.9% with an agent half the parameter size.

We demonstrate the system through a live semantic traffic map that communicates observed aisle conditions to the fleet manager.
We classify each robot’s latest observation by comparing its retrieval embedding with paired text prompts describing occupied and clear aisles.
A map service periodically queries the agent for these classifications and updates predefined semantic zones using robot poses already reported to the fleet manager over VDA5050.
In a simulated warehouse, this approach achieves 71.3% balanced accuracy, exceeding the best caption-based alternative evaluated with the same models by 6.0 percentage points.
We deploy each model as a modular service to support future extensions for station-readiness checks, landmark-based navigation guidance for deployed policy models, and curation of diverse preprocessed training data (Section 7 ).

Our contributions are:

Video-native agentic memory. We rebuild ReMEmbR on an efficient NVIDIA model stack and move its index key from the caption to the video itself. Retrieval is no longer bottlenecked by what a captioner chose to mention, and a smaller, tool-calling agent returns more reliable structured answers (Section 3 ).

Encode once, distributed across the fleet. Every robot acts as a distributed sensor, and a modular set of parallel encoder services on its Jetson turns each clip, in a single pass, into multi-purpose representations for memory retrieval, description and reconstruction. Per-clip compute is offloaded to the edge and scales out with the fleet, and raw camera frames never leave the robot (Section 4.1 ).

Disaggregated vision-language inference for describe-on-demand. Cosmos3-Edge is split at its vision–language boundary, with the vision encoder on the robot and the language decoder on the server. Cached vision tokens are encoded once and queried many times, so description cost scales with the questions asked rather than with the video recorded (Sections 4.2 and 4.3 ).

A zero-shot, multi-purpose live semantic map. The retrieval embedding the robot already computes doubles as a training-free semantic classifier, in this case reused for traffic classification, interpreted continuously and fed to the fleet manager over its existing VDA5050 interface. An agent sits between the map and the memory as a natural-language interface, so a new site-level insight requires only a new question, with no new model to train (Section 5 ).

A modular, scale-out service architecture. Encoders, a GPU-accelerated vector index, a tiered object store, NIM-served agents and on-demand decoders run as independent, versioned services that can each be scaled or upgraded in isolation. We profile the edge encoders on Jetson and model how server compute, bandwidth and storage scale from a single robot to a full fleet (Sections 4.3 and 6.3 ).

2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Preliminaries

Industrial ReMEmbR builds on three main lines of research: large language model (LLM) agents that support versatile tool use, retrieval-augmented generation from semantic embeddings, and the ReMEmbR system, which combines the two to encode and query a robot’s memories over long horizons.

Agents. In this context, an agent is an LLM that runs in an interactive loop with access to predefined tools. At each step in the loop, the model reads the task and its own running history, and then either calls any of the available tools or provides its final answer. ReAct ( Yao et al., 2023 ) features the model writing out its intermediate reasoning between tool calls, so that the result of one call guides the next. Practically, every tool call must be well-formatted to allow for deterministic parsing and automated execution. The loop also needs a limit on the allowed number of steps, so that it always ends with a concrete answer. Industrial ReMEmbR follows this loop, and adds a tool that lets the agent ask a vision–language decoder its own question about any memory it retrieves.

Retrieval-augmented generation. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ( Lewis et al., 2020 ) allows a model to derive answers from a corpus even if it is too large to directly fit in context. The corpus is chunked and indexed in advance, and for each question the k k most relevant chunks are retrieved and incorporated in the model’s context window. Retrieval is usually done with a bi-encoder , which embeds queries and documents separately so that search involves a fast vector comparison ( Karpukhin et al., 2020 ) . The trade-off is that every document vector is computed before any query is known. A cross-encoder , by contrast, reads a query and a document together, which tends to be more accurate but often too slow to apply to a whole corpus, so it normally only re-ranks a shortlist already retrieved ( Nogueira and Cho, 2019 ) by the bi-encoder. Agentic RAG ( Singh et al., 2025 ) exposes retrieval as a tool for the agent. The agent writes its own retrieval queries, retries upon search misses, and decides when it has sufficient evidence to return with a contextually grounded response. Industrial ReMEmbR uses agentic RAG over video instead of text, with a video–text bi-encoder as the index and a decoder that reads the question and the retrieved memory together.

ReMEmbR. ReMEmbR ( Anwar et al., 2025 ) lets a user ask a mobile robot where something is, when something happened, or what it saw over hours of operation, and returns answers the robot can act on, such as an ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) position to navigate toward. Because a question rarely needs the whole history H H , ReMEmbR answers from a small retrieved subset R ⊆ H R\subseteq H , approximating p ⁡ ( A ∣ H , Q ) p(A\mid H,Q) with p ⁡ ( A ∣ R , Q ) p(A\mid R,Q) for a question Q Q and answer A A .

It works in two phases. In the memory-building phase, VILA ( Lin et al., 2024 ) captions each 3 s video segment, MxBai ( Lee et al., 2024 ) embeds the caption, and Milvus ( Wang et al., 2021 ) stores the embedding with the segment’s mean position and time. 1 1 1 Position and orientation are stored in separate columns. In the querying phase, an LLM agent searches this memory by text, position or time for up to three rounds, and then returns a structured JSON answer that holds text, a yes/no value, a time, a duration or a goal position. The accompanying NaVQA benchmark contains 210 questions over seven CODa sequences ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) of 15 to 30 minutes each. A position answer counts as correct within 15 m, and a time answer within 2 min.

The memory is built before any question is asked, so it has to be general enough to serve whichever question comes later. However, ReMEmbR captions every clip when it is recorded. The memory can answer only what the captioner chose to mention, and generating a caption for every clip is the main cost of writing a memory.

Upgraded ReMEmbR keeps its pipeline and updates its models (Section 3 ). Industrial ReMEmbR keeps the two-phase design but stores no caption, and describes a memory only once a question asks about it (Section 4 ).

2026-10-21.title: Physical Canvas: A Vision Tactile World Model For Robot Policy Evaluation And Learning
2026-10-21.authors: Zebin Xing , Yuhang Zheng , Yupeng Zheng , Yichen Zhang , Zichen Li , Shangqing Zhou , Yujie Zang , Yuchen Liu , Zhongpu Xia , Haoran Li , Qichao Zhang
2026-10-21.abstract: Evaluating and post-training robot policies through physical interaction is costly and difficult to scale, motivating action-conditioned world models as interactive simulators. However, visually plausible predictions can misrepresent contact dynamics, providing unreliable feedback for policy evaluation and learning. We introduce PhysCanvas , a state-consistent visuo-tactile world model for contact-rich robot manipulation. PhysCanvas unifies multi-view RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, task state, and actions within a unified vision space. All modalities share a video VAE and pretrained generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse visual and temporal priors. Motion images derived through forward kinematics and camera projection provide spatially aligned action conditioning, while an initial RGB anchor and updated reference observations guide sequential generation. Our consistency-aware post-training uses the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model to supervise scene preservation, visual–tactile compatibility, and agreement with real task outcomes. The resulting world model supports closed-loop policy rollouts for evaluation and provides imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, when policies are rolled out in the world model, State Reward Model supervision increases the arithmetic mean of task-wise Pearson correlations between world-model and real-world success rates from 0.602 0.602 to 0.885 0.885 . Policy post-training in the reward-guided world model further increases π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ’s mean real-world success rate from a 59.1 % 59.1\% SFT baseline to 70.8 % 70.8\% . These results demonstrate the value of unified multimodal modeling and consistency-aware post-training for robot policy evaluation and learning. Project page: https://zebinx.github.io/PhysCanvas_HomePage/ .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Robot world models predict how environments evolve in response to actions, offering low-cost, reproducible interactions for policy evaluation and learning ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Contact-rich manipulation requires both visual observations of scene dynamics and tactile feedback about contact changes ( Yuan et al., 2017 ; Lambeta et al., 2020 ; Lee et al., 2020 ; Guzey et al., 2024 ) . A world model that captures these complementary signals and their associated task outcomes could reduce the need for repeated physical trials.

Recent action-conditioned video models combine pretrained generative priors with action representations to support interactive prediction, policy evaluation, and learning in imagination ( Wu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) . Existing visuo-tactile models, however, typically require a dedicated tactile encoder and a custom interface for injecting tactile features into a general backbone ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . Adapting to new tactile data or sensor configurations may therefore require retraining, limiting generality and complicating the pipeline. Meanwhile, token-wise reconstruction supervision emphasizes local fidelity and can miss high-level semantics such as task success. Reliable rollouts thus require visual observations, tactile feedback, and predicted task outcomes to describe the consequences of the same action; inconsistencies can mislead policy optimization ( Yang et al., 2026b ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . For example, after an object slips, predicting stable tactile contact or eventual success is semantically inconsistent despite visually plausible frames. The challenge is to build a reusable multimodal model while preserving scene, cross-modal, and task-outcome consistency for policy evaluation and learning.

We investigate two questions: (1) Can a simple, general mechanism encode heterogeneous modalities in a shared space? (2) Can high-level semantics be injected into the world model without additional networks?

To address this challenge, we introduce PhysCanvas , a world model with state consistency for visual and tactile prediction, robot policy evaluation, and learning. PhysCanvas places multiple modalities in a shared generative space and uses consistency supervision during post training to preserve the interaction dynamics and task outcomes induced by actions, providing interactive, coherent observations.

Specifically, PhysCanvas places multiview RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, and task state on a unified canvas predicted by a shared video VAE and generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse pretrained visual and temporal priors ( Wan Team et al., 2025 ) . Actions are encoded as spatially aligned motion images through forward kinematics and camera projection ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , while an initial RGB anchor and updated references guide sequential generation. During post training, the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model enforce scene preservation, visual and tactile compatibility, and agreement with real outcomes, including both success and failure. The resulting model supports evaluation in a closed loop and supplies imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) .

We evaluate PhysCanvas on four real-world manipulation tasks: test-tube placement, bottle-cap unscrewing, block relocation, and Rubik’s Cube manipulation (Figure 2 ). When policies are rolled out in the world model, post-training improves the Pearson correlation between their world-model and real-world success rates on every task, increasing the arithmetic mean of task-wise correlations from 0.602 0.602 to 0.885 0.885 . Each task includes nine evaluation batches spanning ACT, FM, and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Lipman et al., 2023 ; Black et al., 2025 ) ; the batches are evaluated at different times, and each task receives equal weight in the summary. Policy optimization through reward-guided imagined interactions further improves the mean real-world success rate of π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} by 11.7 11.7 percentage points over SFT, from 59.1 % 59.1\% to 70.8 % 70.8\% across the four tasks. These results demonstrate utility for reliable evaluation and policy improvement.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) a unified canvas space that jointly models vision, touch, task state, and actions using a shared video generation framework; (2) consistency-aware post-training that constrains generated interactions through scene, modality, and task-state supervision; and (3) a framework for policy evaluation and learning in imagination, evaluated on real robots.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Action-Conditioned World Models for Robotics

Action-conditioned video models have advanced robot planning and interactive prediction ( Finn and Levine, 2017 ; Yang et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2023 ; Micheli et al., 2023 ; Bruce et al., 2024 ) . Pretrained video priors ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Blattmann et al., 2023 ; Wan Team et al., 2025 ) and embodied action conditioning ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2026 ) improve controllability, while unified architectures connect video prediction with policy modeling ( Bi et al., 2026 ; Kim et al., 2026 ) . Extending these visual simulators to contact-rich manipulation also requires predicting the tactile observations on which policies act.

Imagined rollouts also support policy evaluation and learning ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ; Hansen et al., 2024 ; Hafner et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) , making reliable action consequences and task outcomes essential. Recent work studies long horizon consistency and simulator validity ( GigaWorld Team et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026b ) , or improves generation through reward based optimization ( Bardhan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . PhysCanvas brings these requirements to joint visual and tactile prediction through scene and task state consistency supervision, and evaluates generated rollouts against real policy outcomes.

## 2.2 Visuo-Tactile World Modeling

Touch exposes contact, deformation, and slip that can be ambiguous in RGB, motivating joint visual and tactile prediction ( Yuan et al., 2017 ; Lambeta et al., 2020 ; Lee et al., 2020 ; Guzey et al., 2024 ) . OmniVTA ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) combines two stream dynamics with contact aware action generation; FeelWorld ( Ma et al., 2026 ) predicts contact and slip states through contact gated attention. DexTouch-WM ( Qin et al., 2026 ) couples video and tactile experts, whereas DexTacWAM ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) integrates tactile latents specific to each finger into video diffusion. TACO ( Liu et al., 2026 ) uses generated visual and tactile corrections for policy post training. Rather than add a separate tactile predictor, PhysCanvas renders tactile appearance and marker displacement as regions of the same visual canvas as RGB and task status. The shared visual VAE and video denoiser then model aligned sensory futures, with explicit supervision of visual and tactile agreement.
