2026-10-21.title: AgenticRoboRL: Bringing Coding-Agent Post-Training to Agentic Robotics
2026-10-21.authors: Xinxin Liu , Bingxin Xu , Wenrui Bao , Ming Li , Wentao Bao , Chen Chen , Yuzhang Shang
2026-10-21.abstract: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners’ own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce AgenticRoboRL , a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Agentic robotics systems can perform complex manipulation tasks by combining a planner with a robot harness. The planner invokes VLA skills ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) or generates control code ( Liang et al., 2023 ; Fu et al., 2026 ) , observes the execution results, and decides what to do next over multiple rounds of interaction. Recent work has improved performance by refining robot harnesses and storing experience from task exploration in external memory ( Zhang et al., 2026c ; Xu et al., 2026b ) , with coding agents such as Codex and Claude Code ( OpenAI, 2025 ; Anthropic, 2025 ) serving as planners. However, these approaches primarily leverage existing planner capabilities and strengthen the support available to the planner. We explore a complementary direction: enhancing planners’ own capabilities to improve the performance of agentic robotics systems.

For coding agents, enhancing the model’s own capabilities through post-training, including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, has proven highly effective ( Pan et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Cao et al., 2025 ) . These advances raise a natural question: Can the post-training methods used for coding agents also improve the performance of agentic robotics systems?

Applying these methods to robot planners is complicated by the fact that robot harnesses differ in how they carry out a planner’s response. In some harnesses the planner calls learned VLA skills, and a VLA policy executes each call. In others the planner writes control code over perception and control APIs, and a motion controller executes it. Harnesses also differ in what feedback they return to the planner and in how they decide whether the task has succeeded. Training planners across harnesses therefore requires a single pipeline that supports these different execution mechanisms.

To realize such a pipeline, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses (Figure 1 ). The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL). SFT trains the planner on successful demonstrations, providing a starting point for RL. During RL, we train on recorded planner requests and responses, while harness-specific adapters associate these interactions with episode outcomes. This allows the same RL pipeline to support VLA skill invocation and control-code generation without changing their execution interfaces. In both stages, only the planner is optimized, while the underlying execution components remain fixed (Figure 2 ).

We evaluate the pipeline across these two execution mechanisms using a 9B planner. With RPent ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) , a harness that invokes VLA skills, SFT improves success on LIBERO-PRO from 18.1% to 65.1%, and RL further raises it to 71.0%, without external memory. The same checkpoint achieves 72.2% on LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025a ) without additional training, compared with 19.2% for the original model. With the CaP-X harness ( Fu et al., 2026 ) , post-training improves success from 2.7% to 28.5%. These results establish post-training as an effective approach for improving agentic robotics systems.

Our contributions are threefold:

To our knowledge, AgenticRoboRL is the first general post-training framework to agentic robotics systems.

AgenticRoboRL first fine-tunes the planner on successful demonstrations and then refines it with RL, updating only the planner while keeping execution components fixed. Lightweight harness-specific adapters link each recorded planner call to its episode outcome, so the harnesses do not need a shared low-level action representation.

Strong empirical results and an open release. With AgenticRoboRL , a 9B planner improves from 18.1% to 71.0% on LIBERO-PRO without external memory. This nearly matches Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory (72.1%) ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) . With the CaP-X harness, it improves from 2.7% to 28.5%. We will release the AgenticRoboRL framework and trained planner checkpoints.

1. To our knowledge, AgenticRoboRL is the first general post-training framework to agentic robotics systems.

2. AgenticRoboRL first fine-tunes the planner on successful demonstrations and then refines it with RL, updating only the planner while keeping execution components fixed. Lightweight harness-specific adapters link each recorded planner call to its episode outcome, so the harnesses do not need a shared low-level action representation.

3. Strong empirical results and an open release. With AgenticRoboRL , a 9B planner improves from 18.1% to 71.0% on LIBERO-PRO without external memory. This nearly matches Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory (72.1%) ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) . With the CaP-X harness, it improves from 2.7% to 28.5%. We will release the AgenticRoboRL framework and trained planner checkpoints.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Language models can guide robot behavior by selecting learned skills or generating programs over perception and control APIs ( Ahn et al., 2022 ; Liang et al., 2023 ; Singh et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2023 ; Mu et al., 2024 ) . In this organization, the planner chooses how to use the available capabilities, while the harness executes its decisions and returns observations. Execution feedback and reusable skill libraries support interaction over multiple turns ( Huang et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . Hierarchical systems place a language-level reasoning model above a learned low-level policy ( Belkhale et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) . Recent harnesses expose these capabilities to coding agents: Harness VLA combines a frozen VLA with analytic primitives and task memory ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) , while CaP-X provides interfaces for generating executable control code ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . General-purpose coding agents have also been applied to manipulation without robot-specific training ( Kumar, 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026b ) . Other systems improve perception, memory, safety, or skill libraries around the planner ( Li et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026b ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Kagaya et al., 2025 ; Woods and Seifi, 2026 ) . A concurrent training-free approach, RV-ICL, provides on-demand access to a hierarchy of demonstration-video keyframes and clips ( Bao et al., 2026 ) . AgenticRoboRL instead improves the planner through SFT and multi-turn RL while reusing the harness’s execution components.

RL has been used to improve language and vision-language planners in embodied environments ( Fei et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Jia et al., 2026a ) . CaP-RL applies RL to a code model that generates a complete control program in a single turn ( Fu et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, AgenticRoboRL trains planners that interact with the harness over multiple turns, and it applies to harnesses based on VLA skills as well as to harnesses based on control code. Closer to our supervised stage, Robo-Harness K1 and World Action Agent train 9B students on teacher trajectories collected within their respective harnesses ( Li et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ) . These methods use supervised training to transfer the capabilities of stronger agents. REAL combines SFT with online RL for mobile manipulation, using a rule-based planner for supervision and a shaped reward ( Mi et al., 2026 ) . AgenticRoboRL instead uses teacher-agent trajectories followed by multi-turn RL with task success as the sole reward. It adapts teacher supervision when the teacher and student have different prompts, tools, or access to memory.

Coding-agent training commonly combines supervision from successful teacher trajectories ( Pan et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Jain et al., 2025 ) with multi-turn RL on verifiable outcomes ( Cao et al., 2025 ) . Related approaches extend to search and computer-use agents ( Jin et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2026 ) . Frameworks including Agent Lightning and LEGO-RL separate agent execution from model optimization and construct training data from recorded interactions ( Luo et al., 2025 ; He et al., 2026 ; Du et al., 2026 ) . AgenticRoboRL builds on this approach for robot harnesses: a proxy records planner calls, and harness-specific adapters associate them with episode outcomes. This interface accommodates different execution mechanisms without requiring a common low-level action representation.

2026-10-21.title: SceneRig: An Agentic System for Simulation-Ready 3D Scene Reconstruction from Single Images
2026-10-21.authors: Rundong Luo , Yunong Liu , Di Cao , Matthew Tancik , Shyamal Buch , Colton Stearns , Wenqi Xian
2026-10-21.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-21.comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026 Agentic Robotics Workshop. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract:
Simulation is a powerful tool for robotics, but building diverse, simulation-ready scenes at scale remains difficult. Reconstructing scenes from single images is a promising alternative, but visual similarity alone is insufficient: objects must also be recovered, accurately placed, and physically grounded. Existing methods that rely on post-hoc physics settling often misplace objects, producing scenes that look correct but behave poorly under manipulation.
We present SceneRig , an agentic system that turns a single image into an editable, simulation-ready scene. SceneRig combines geometric, visual, and physical tools to reconstruct a faithful 3D scene. An agent then performs edit-and-validate loops inside a physics simulator to achieve physical stability.
Across diverse inputs, SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D placement while keeping the reconstructed scenes physically stable. Furthermore, SceneRig is effective for downstream robotics: its scenes predict real-robot policy outcomes more accurately than the baseline method and more reliably support replay of recorded manipulations without trajectory adaptation.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Evaluating the quality and robustness of action policies remains a fundamental bottleneck in robotics.
While physical execution is the gold standard, on-robot evaluations are notoriously difficult to scale: they demand expensive hardware, human supervision, and repeated trials across tasks and conditions [ li2024simpler ] .
Consequently, simulation is a powerful alternative that enables large-scale policy evaluation [ yang2026robolab ] .
However, scaling these environments remains difficult, as constructing realistic scenes requires substantial manual effort [ jain2025polaris ] .

Recent advances in agentic reconstruction and 3D generation have made real-to-sim scene reconstruction a promising route to scaling simulation environments [ viga2026 , chen2026sam3d , simfoundry2026 ] .
In fact, real-to-sim digital twins go beyond mere scaling: they capture the objects and arrangements of physical workspaces and let anyone turn a single photo into a simulation environment for policy evaluation.
Yet, despite recent progress in real-to-sim, balancing high-quality 3D reconstruction with faithful, robot-ready simulation physics remains challenging [ ma2026rest3d , chen2026agentic ] .
Even when a reconstruction is physically settled, objects can move away from their observed positions, producing a stable scene that no longer matches the robot’s workspace.
To bridge this gap, we propose SceneRig , an agentic system for simulation-ready 3D scene reconstruction from a single image. SceneRig addresses this problem by coupling image-guided pose refinement with physical validation for faithful trajectory replay and policy evaluation.

Making this coupling effective requires the agent to inspect the effects of physical simulation and use that feedback to guide further corrections.
Even GPT-6 Astra struggles to achieve accurate, physically stable object placement through VIGA or a general-purpose coding agent when the reconstructed scenes are evaluated after physical settling (Table 4 ). SceneRig ’s core contribution is therefore a harness that connects the agent’s visual reasoning with geometric and physical tools for accurate, stable scene reconstruction. The agent uses the updated scene and feedback from the edit to decide what to investigate or correct next.

More concretely, SceneRig uses a flexible, modular harness with four stages.
First, SceneRig builds a relational scene graph , identifying objects and their support relationships.
Next, scene object creation uses 2D and 3D vision
models to estimate metric geometry and reconstruct object meshes. We then assign physical properties and initialize object placement through geometric alignment and support-ordered settling.
Third, specialized agents construct the surrounding geometry, materials, and lighting, with
strict rule-based verification gates for geometry and visual verification of all three.
Finally, and most importantly, SceneRig executes a physical edit-and-validate loop .
The agent selects which object to adjust and whether to change its position, scale, or orientation; geometric and physical tools search for an adjustment and test its effects in simulation.
Although the current implementation leverages specific state-of-the-art models, SceneRig is designed to incorporate future foundation models.

We evaluate SceneRig on diverse images, spanning synthetic renderings, real robot workspaces, AI-generated images, and in-the-wild smartphone captures.
We demonstrate that SceneRig improves instance segmentation, object-centric appearance, and 3D object placement over existing methods, with all evaluated scenes passing physical stability checks (Tables 1 , 2 ).
Beyond geometric reconstruction, we show that SceneRig yields robot-ready environments (Figure 1 ), supporting both real-to-sim policy evaluation and open-loop trajectory replay.
In summary, our contributions are:

We introduce SceneRig , an agentic system that reconstructs simulation-ready digital twins from a single image, prioritizing physical grounding in addition to visual similarity.

We build a modular harness that equips agents with geometric and physical tools.
Through iterative edit-and-validate loops, SceneRig directly incorporates physics into pose refinement.

SceneRig improves reconstruction quality and robotics performance over single-image real-to-sim systems. Compared with the baseline, it increases open-loop trajectory replay success from 36% to 80% and episode-level agreement with real-world policy result from 54% to 69%.

1. We introduce SceneRig , an agentic system that reconstructs simulation-ready digital twins from a single image, prioritizing physical grounding in addition to visual similarity.

2. We build a modular harness that equips agents with geometric and physical tools.
Through iterative edit-and-validate loops, SceneRig directly incorporates physics into pose refinement.

3. SceneRig improves reconstruction quality and robotics performance over single-image real-to-sim systems. Compared with the baseline, it increases open-loop trajectory replay success from 36% to 80% and episode-level agreement with real-world policy result from 54% to 69%.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Single-Image Scene Reconstruction. Object-centric reconstruction recovers individual objects and their spatial arrangement. Supervised methods predict geometry or retrieve assets: Total3D [ nie2020total3d ] predicts indoor layout and meshes, while ROCA [ gumerli2022roca ] retrieves and aligns CAD models. Without object annotations, uORF [ yu2022uorf ] and uOCF [ luo2024uocf ] learn compositional neural fields from multi-view images to separate objects and backgrounds. For explicit meshes, generative methods reconstruct instances separately and align them [ dogaru2025gen3dsr , zhou2024dpa , han2025reparo , zhao2025depr ] , while MIDI [ huang2025midi ] jointly generates multiple objects. CAST [ yao2025cast ] combines occlusion-completed object generation with pose refinement using scene relations and signed-distance constraints. SAM3D [ chen2026sam3d ] predicts object geometry, texture, and camera-relative layout. However, visual fidelity alone does not ensure physical stability or readiness for simulation.

Agentic 3D Scene Creation. VLM agents construct 3D scenes through tool use and iterative feedback [ hu2024scenecraft , huang2024blenderalchemy ] . To ground generation and editing in scene structure, liu2025agentic3d maintain labeled point clouds and scene relations. SceneWeaver [ yang2025sceneweaver ] adaptively selects synthesis and editing tools, while Scenethesis [ ling2025scenethesis ] combines language-based planning with generated-image guidance and geometric constraints. Beyond planning and tool selection, SAGE [ xia2026sage ] and SceneSmith [ pfaff2026scenesmith ] use editor-critic loops for indoor scene generation.
For precise placement, agents also use numerical solvers [ yang2024holodeck , sun2025layoutvlm , wang2026physcensis ] .

Agentic workflows also support reconstruction from visual references. VIGA [ viga2026 ] reconstructs 3D scenes with a generator–verifier loop, while SEIG [ seig2026 ] extends this approach to refine geometry, materials, and lighting sequentially. SceneConductor [ kim2026sceneconductor ] initializes layouts, builds environments from point maps, and delegates local corrections to specialist agents. For evaluation, BlenderGym [ gu2025blendergym ] benchmarks graphics editing, while IR3D-Bench [ liu2025ir3dbench ] evaluates scene understanding through agentic inverse rendering. In contrast, SceneRig ’s agent corrects objects using geometry- and physics-grounded tools.

Physically Grounded Real-to-Sim. Real-to-sim aims at building interactive environments for robot learning and evaluation. RialTo [ torne2024rialto ] , Re3Sim [ han2025re3sim ] , and HoloScene [ xia2025holoscene ] recover interactive assets from video or scans. Agentic Real2Sim [ chen2026agentic ] turns a recorded robot–object interaction into a simulatable twin. Our closest baseline, SimFoundry [ simfoundry2026 ] , reconstructs editable digital twins from video and generates digital cousins for real-to-sim policy evaluation and sim-to-real policy training. For data generation without dynamics simulation, Real2Render2Real [ yu2025real2render2real ] renders robot training images from scans.

Concurrent single-image methods use several correction strategies. TableVerse [ tableverse2026 ] resolves collisions through geometric translations before settling; ϕ \phi -Scene [ li2026phiscene ] optimizes clearance and settles objects in support order. REST3D [ ma2026rest3d ] optimizes poses with cross-entropy optimization, while RoboSnap [ zhang2026robosnap ] alternates signed-distance optimization with settling. SimuScene [ lee2026simuscene ] uses simulated displacement to trigger shape stretching or regeneration. In SceneRig , an agent identifies misplaced objects and calls geometry- and physics-grounded tools to correct them. These tools search for pose adjustments and test edits in simulation, returning feedback to guide further inspection and correction.

Simulation for Policy Evaluation. kadian2020sim2real tune simulation to improve sim–real correlation. SIMPLER [ li2024simpler ] calibrates controllers from trajectories and matches backgrounds and textures. PolaRiS [ jain2025polaris ] combines Gaussian splatting with policy co-training on real and simulated data; REALM [ sedlacek2026realm ] calibrates robot dynamics through replay and tests visual, semantic, and behavioral generalization. Following these, we assess our system through real-sim policy rollout agreement, task success-rate correlation, and open-loop trajectory replay.

2026-10-21.title: MAPLE: Mondrian-Anchored Prior for Learning-free Indoor Exploration
2026-10-21.authors: Kelvin Aladum , Nisar Ahmed
2026-10-21.abstract: Robots exploring unknown indoor environments must decide where to move while much of the environment remains unseen. Predicting the occupancy of unseen space beyond the current sensor range can improve these decisions, but recent approaches commonly rely on learned models that require offline training and repeated inference during exploration. We introduce the Mondrian-Anchored Prior for Learning-free Indoor Exploration (MAPLE), a training-free predictive approach that adapts the Mondrian process into an online generative prior conditioned on observed geometric cues in the current partial map. MAPLE generates multiple plausible map hypotheses and evaluates visibility separately within each to estimate frontier gain, preserving differences in predicted visibility across hypotheses. Across KTH floor-plans and real-SLAM environments at multiple sensor ranges, MAPLE consistently improves over non-predictive exploration and remains competitive with learned predictive approaches. Its lightweight procedural construction enables predictive exploration with limited computational resources. Experimental results further show that more accurate map prediction does not necessarily produce better exploration, highlighting the importance of how predictions are represented and used in exploration decisions.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Autonomous exploration is a key capability for robots operating in unknown or dangerous environments, with applications in search and rescue, emergency response, and infrastructure inspection [ 1 , 2 ] . In these settings, robots must repeatedly decide where to move while much of the environment remains unseen. Frontier-based exploration makes this decision by identifying frontiers at the boundary between observed free space and unknown space [ 3 ] . Connected frontier regions are represented by frontier candidates that serve as possible exploration goals, and selecting among them directly affects exploration efficiency.

Classical frontier methods select frontiers using measures such as travel cost, expected coverage, or information gain [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . These measures are typically computed from the current partial occupancy map, so they provide little information about occupancy beyond the sensor range, even though that occupancy can strongly affect how much new space a frontier will reveal. Predictive exploration addresses this limitation by estimating the occupancy of unseen space before frontier selection [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
Most recent predictive approaches rely on learned models [ 8 , 10 , 11 ] . These methods can produce useful occupancy predictions but require offline training and repeated inference during exploration. Their computational demands can be restrictive for robots with limited compute and power, and performance may degrade when the operating environment differs from the training data. This tradeoff is particularly relevant at short sensor ranges, where frontier selection depends more heavily on occupancy beyond the current sensor range [ 14 ] . These considerations motivate a lightweight alternative that can generate predictions directly from the partial map during exploration.

We introduce the M ondrian- A nchored P rior for L earning-free Indoor E xploration (MAPLE), a training-free predictive approach for two-dimensional occupancy-grid exploration. MAPLE builds on the Mondrian process [ 15 ] , which recursively partitions a rectangular region using axis-aligned cuts, and guides this process using geometric cues from the current partial map. Repeated sampling produces multiple plausible map completions of the unseen space, each treated as a map hypothesis.
Different map hypotheses can imply different visibility from the same frontier candidate. MAPLE therefore evaluates each hypothesis separately and averages the resulting coverage gains before accounting for travel cost. Fig. 1 illustrates how differing predicted walls can change visibility for the same candidate.

We evaluate MAPLE on ten KTH floor plans and ten real-SLAM maps at sensor ranges of 5, 10, and 20 m. The experiments examine end-to-end exploration, map-prediction quality, frontier-decision quality, and computational cost. Controlled ablations also test the effects of the map-prediction method, gain estimator, conditioning on observed geometry, and the number of hypotheses.

Our contributions are as follows:

We introduce MAPLE, a lightweight training-free generative prior that adapts the Mondrian process to generate multiple plausible map hypotheses from geometric cues in the current partial map.

We formulate a hypothesis-wise frontier-gain estimator that evaluates visibility separately within each map hypothesis before averaging the resulting gains.

We provide a controlled comparison of learned, training-free, and non-predictive exploration under shared sensing, frontier candidates, and travel cost, separating prediction, decision, exploration, and computational performance.

2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

Frontier and Information-Theoretic Exploration: Classical frontier-based exploration methods provide established ways to prioritize frontiers but typically only reason from the current partial map. Early work prioritizes nearby frontiers, while later work balances expected visible area against travel cost [ 3 , 4 ] . Information-theoretic approaches instead score actions by expected information gain or mutual information [ 5 , 6 ] . Receding-horizon planners and hierarchical planners extend these methods to much larger and three-dimensional environments [ 16 , 17 ] . MAPLE retains this frontier-selection framework but uses multiple map completions to represent unseen occupancy beyond the current partial map.

Learned Prediction of Unseen Space: Predictive exploration addresses this limitation by estimating occupancy beyond the current sensor range. Earlier work used previously mapped environments to reason about unseen space [ 18 ] . Learned approaches later completed or anticipated unseen occupancy for exploration and navigation [ 7 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . UPEN uses an ensemble of occupancy predictors to guide exploration toward uncertain regions [ 8 ] . Ericson and Jensfelt predict unseen walls as line segments [ 9 ] . MapEx combines LaMa map completion with prediction uncertainty, and SEER learns to predict information gain for aerial exploration [ 10 , 22 , 23 ] . More recent methods use conditional consistency or diffusion models for unseen occupancy, including 4CNet and SceneSense [ 11 , 24 ] . Achey et al. further integrate generative occupancy synthesis into real-world exploration [ 25 ] . These methods demonstrate the value of predicting unseen occupancy but rely on learned models and repeated inference. In contrast, MAPLE generates map completions online without offline training.

Structural and Training-Free Priors: Indoor spaces contain geometric regularities that can support reasoning about unseen space. Aydemir et al. showed from over 38,000 rooms that room geometry and connectivity exhibit useful regularities [ 26 ] . Luperto et al. used prior floor plans to facilitate exploration and later predicted the remaining geometry of partially observed rooms from the current occupancy map [ 2 , 27 ] . Related work on building and floor plan generation has used procedural modeling, stochastic layout synthesis, and learned generative models [ 28 , 29 , 30 ] . These methods primarily target layout generation or rely on prior maps. MAPLE instead uses a Mondrian-based generative process [ 15 ] conditioned on the current partial map to sample plausible map completions online.

Multi-hypothesis Beliefs and Exploration Decisions: When multiple map hypotheses are available, they must be combined or evaluated to guide exploration. Prior work has addressed this mainly in the context of SLAM uncertainty. Stachniss et al. evaluate exploration actions over map and pose hypotheses represented by a Rao-Blackwellized particle filter [ 31 ] . Wang and Englot combine utilities across hypotheses induced by ambiguous data association [ 32 ] . Recent learned approaches also summarize their ensembles before planning. UPEN converts ensemble disagreement into a per-cell uncertainty map [ 8 ] . MapEx computes frontier scores from the ensemble mean and pixel-wise variance [ 10 ] . CogniPlan plans with multiple layouts produced by a conditional generative model and couples them to a learned graph-based planner [ 33 ] . Ericson et al. show that planner behavior can strongly affect the benefit obtained from map prediction [ 14 ] . More broadly, planning-aware evaluation has shown that prediction accuracy can be poorly aligned with downstream decision quality [ 34 ] . Recent exploration work finds that improved information-gain estimates do not necessarily improve exploration efficiency [ 35 ] . MAPLE isolates this issue within a common frontier-selection framework by preserving individual map hypotheses during visibility evaluation and testing how this choice affects exploration.

2026-10-21.title: VLM-Guided Contact Retargeting and Generative Partner Modeling for Humanoid-Human Interaction
2026-10-21.authors: Yuto Shibata , Kotaro Amaya , Kashu Yamazaki , Lalit Jayanti , Yoshimitsu Aoki , Mariko Isogawa , Katerina Fragkiadaki
2026-10-21.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-21.comment: CoRL2026, project page: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract: Humanoid–human interaction requires robots to operate under severe partial observability: during close physical contact, the human partner is occluded, truncated, or outside the robot’s field of view, causing pose estimation to fail and often necessitating external tracking or privileged human state. At the same time, heavy mutual occlusions introduce errors into the human–human motion-capture data used for learning. We present REACT, a framework for learning deployable humanoid–human interaction policies from human–human demonstrations. REACT treats semantic contact structure as the key supervisory signal connecting demonstration processing, interaction learning, and onboard control. First, a VLM-guided contact modeling and retargeting pipeline identifies semantically meaningful contacts and transfers them onto humanoid–human geometry while preserving interaction structure. Using these annotations, privileged interaction policies learn physically grounded behaviors through interaction-aware contact rewards and are then distilled into deployable egocentric depth policies trained entirely from onboard sensing using photorealistic human depth rendering. To address severe partial observability, we introduce generative partner-state modeling objectives that predict partner motion from occluded egocentric views. We evaluate REACT in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid across five contact-rich interactions. Semantic contact modeling substantially improves preservation of demonstrated interactions, while generative partner-state modeling improves contact recall on four of five interactions, most under heavy occlusion. On real hardware, REACT performs all five interactions using onboard sensing alone.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Humanoid hardware and learning-based control have advanced rapidly in recent years, bringing the deployment of humanoid robots in homes, workplaces, and care settings increasingly within reach. Realizing this vision, however, requires robots capable of sustained, reactive physical interaction with humans using only onboard sensing. Unlike existing humanoid controllers, which primarily focus on isolated motion tracking or interaction with static scenes and objects [ 14 , 21 , 3 ] , humanoid–human interaction (HHI) requires continuous perception, prediction, and physical coordination with a human partner whose motion evolves under independent intent and frequent contact.

A central challenge in HHI is that close-contact interaction fundamentally operates under severe partial observability. During interaction, the human partner is frequently self-occluded, truncated, or partially outside the robot’s field of view, causing off-the-shelf human pose-estimation systems to fail precisely when accurate perception matters most. As a result, many existing approaches rely on external tracking systems, motion-capture instrumentation, or privileged access to human state during deployment, limiting robustness and real-world deployability. The problem begins even earlier in the learning pipeline: heavy mutual occlusions also corrupt the underlying human–human motion-capture data itself, introducing reconstruction artifacts and inconsistent contact geometry that propagate through downstream retargeting [ 2 , 46 ] and policy-learning pipelines.

We argue that deployable humanoid–human interaction fundamentally requires recovering the interaction state from incomplete observations, and that semantic contact structure provides the key supervisory signal connecting noisy demonstrations, physics-based learning, and onboard control. While motion trajectories may vary substantially across embodiments, interactions are often defined by a much more stable structure: who touches whom, where, and when. We therefore propose to represent interactions through semantic contacts and train policies to infer latent partner state under severe partial observability.

To this end, we introduce REACT ( R eactive E gocentric A gent for C ontact-rich Humanoid-Human In T eraction), a framework for learning deployable humanoid–human interaction policies from large-scale human–human motion-capture data (Figure 1 ). REACT first runs a VLM-guided semantic contact pipeline that retargets the demonstrated interaction contacts onto humanoid–human geometry while preserving interaction structure across the embodiment gap. These semantic contacts then supervise a privileged interaction teacher through interaction-aware contact rewards, anchoring the policy in physics. The teacher is distilled into an egocentric depth student trained entirely on onboard sensing via photorealistic in-simulator SMPL-X rendering of dynamic human partners. To address severe partial observability, the student is further trained with a generative partner-state prediction objective that infers past, present, and future partner motion from egocentric observations.

We evaluate REACT on a large corpus of close-contact human–human interactions in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Our experiments show that semantic contact modeling substantially improves preservation of demonstrated interaction structure compared to existing retargeting approaches, and its contact annotations improve downstream interaction learning. We further show that generative partner-state prediction improves contact recall on four of five interactions, most where the partner is hardest to see, enabling depth-based policies to recover most of the contact recall of privileged interaction teachers ( 75 % 75\% at a 30 30\, cm tolerance). On real hardware, REACT successfully executes diverse contact-rich interactions, including high-fives, hugs, handshakes, link-arms, and pats on the back, using onboard sensing alone.

In summary, our contributions are
(1) A semantic contact modeling and retargeting framework that transfers human–human demonstrations to humanoid–human interactions while preserving interaction structure across embodiments,
(2) An interaction-learning framework that uses semantic contacts as supervision for physics-based humanoid–human behavior learning,
(3) Generative partner-state prediction objectives that enable latent interaction-state inference under severe partial observability from egocentric observations, and
(4) extensive simulation ablations and real-world deployment on a Unitree G1 across diverse contact-rich humanoid–human interactions.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Recent work has achieved impressive progress in humanoid teleoperation and motion tracking through imitation learning, teacher–student distillation, and large-scale behavioral modeling [ 14 , 16 , 21 , 13 , 5 , 49 , 31 , 48 , 25 ] . A growing body of work further extends humanoid control toward object and scene interaction through manipulation and loco-manipulation, physics-based human–object interaction, scene-conditioned motion generation, and visual sim-to-real learning [ 50 , 42 , 36 , 23 , 44 , 40 , 47 , 15 , 45 , 22 , 1 ] . However, these methods either treat the humanoid in isolation or restrict interaction to static scenes and inanimate objects, whereas REACT targets closed-loop humanoid–human interaction with a dynamically moving human partner.

Human–human interaction synthesis has advanced rapidly through diffusion-based and generative motion models.
Recent methods such as InterMask [ 19 ] , PINO [ 35 ] , UMO [ 9 ] , and MAGNet [ 32 ] further improve motion diversity, long-horizon interaction synthesis, and flexible multi-agent conditioning. However, these approaches primarily operate in kinematic space and therefore lack physical grounding and closed-loop interaction control. More recent physics-based interaction methods couple diffusion-based motion generation with physics-based tracking [ 20 , 39 ] or forward-dynamics-guided imitation [ 27 ] , but they generate the reference interaction offline [ 39 ] or observe the partner fully, either in simulation [ 27 ] or through an unoccluded third-person capture [ 20 ] , rather than through deployable onboard sensing.

Motion retargeting offers a promising avenue for transferring large-scale human interaction data to humanoid robots. Optimization-based methods, ranging from inverse kinematics to trajectory optimization [ 7 , 11 , 2 ] , adapt the source motion to the humanoid’s kinematics frame by frame or over the whole trajectory, while learning-based retargeting [ 8 ] improves stylistic consistency and motion realism. However, because their objectives are defined on each body separately, they carry no notion of which body parts are meant to touch the partner, so contacts present in the source interaction are easily lost once the motion is transferred to a different embodiment. Graphics-oriented approaches have explored geometry-aware and contact-aware retargeting objectives [ 6 , 18 ] , while recent interaction-preserving methods [ 46 ] emphasize maintaining relational geometry for downstream policy learning. Beyond Mimicry [ 17 ] retargets human–human interactions to a humanoid by preserving pairwise keypoint distances between the two agents, without reasoning about which of them correspond to physical contact. In contrast, REACT introduces semantic contact-aware retargeting that explicitly preserves interaction contacts and relational geometry while suppressing interpenetration between the humanoid and its partner.

Closer to our setting, recent work has approached human–robot interaction by learning from human–human–object demonstrations [ 4 ] , forecasting social motion to generate robot behavior [ 33 ] , and adding compliance to whole-body control for physical contact with people [ 29 ] .
However, these systems depend on robot-side teleoperation data [ 4 ] , external motion capture [ 29 ] , or a separate human-pose estimator [ 17 , 20 ] , which becomes unreliable at the close range where physical contact occurs.
Privileged-to-perceptual distillation has produced visual humanoid policies [ 15 , 45 , 47 ] , but only for interaction with objects and scenes rather than a moving human partner. In contrast, REACT maps egocentric depth to actions end-to-end and explicitly trains policies to infer hidden
partner motion under occlusion through generative
partner-state modeling.

2026-10-21.title: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model
2026-10-21.authors: Qiayuan Liao , Yiyang Shao , Junfeng Long , Kevin Zakka , Roberto Horowitz , Pieter Abbeel , Koushil Sreenath
2026-10-21.comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026 (Oral). Project website: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.

2026-10-21.title: Fast Motion Retargeting Pipeline for Scalable Humanoid Robot Learning
2026-10-21.authors: Daniel Marew , Sangjun Park , Nisal Perera , Donghyun Kim
2026-10-21.abstract: While large-scale human motion capture datasets provide a rich source of demonstrations for humanoid robot learning, retargeting the diverse motions to different humanoid robots remains a nontrivial challenge. Existing kinodynamic trajectory optimization pipelines are computationally expensive and often require manual adjustments per motion. We present FRDV ( F ast R etargeting with D ynamics V alidation), a scalable framework consisting of rapid constrained kinematic retargeting and an additional dynamics validation pipeline. Its kinematic stage integrates a custom Sequential Quadratic Programming solver, Real-Time Iteration, and parallel chunk-based processing, achieving up to 9,156 frames per second — approximately up to 𝟏𝟑𝟔 × \mathbf{136\times} faster than GMR and ProtoMotions — while robot-specific constraints are incorporated into the optimization to reduce common retargeting artifacts, such as ground penetration and self-collision. For motions requiring additional verification, a contact implicit iLQR controller is utilized to test the retargeted reference under full rigid body dynamics. This dynamics-based validation identifies dynamically infeasible motions and refines contact-related artifacts such as foot floating and foot skating. We evaluate retargeting quality by training motion tracking reinforcement learning policies using several state-of-the-art pipelines and comparing their tracking fidelity and success rates. Furthermore, sim-to-real transfer is demonstrated on a Unitree G1 humanoid. Videos and code are available at: https://daroslab.github.io/frdv/ .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Large-scale human motion capture (MoCap) datasets are increasingly used to train humanoid robots to reproduce diverse locomotion, manipulation, and whole-body behaviors [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] . Datasets such as AMASS [ 6 ] , LAFAN1 [ 7 ] , OMOMO [ 8 ] , and BONES-SEED [ 9 ] collectively contain hundreds of thousands of human motion sequences. However, these motions are hard to directly use for humanoid learning due to differences in morphology, joint structure, and hardware limitations. A common approach is to adapt human motion data to the morphology and kinematic constraints of a target robot through motion retargeting [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] .

Despite its widespread use, existing retargeting pipelines face two major challenges when applied to large-scale datasets. The first is computational efficiency . For example, our runtime evaluation shows that existing retargeting methods, such as ProtoMotions [ 13 ] , require more than 40 hours to process the AMASS dataset (see Table II ), which contains approximately 11,000 motion sequences spanning over 40 hours of motion data from more than 300 subjects [ 6 ] . The second challenge is retargeting quality . Differences in body proportions, joint limits, and kinematic structures between humans and humanoid robots can introduce artifacts such as foot sliding, ground penetration, and self-collisions. These artifacts can reduce the robustness of downstream reinforcement learning (RL)-based motion-tracking policies and, for challenging motions, may even prevent successful policy learning [ 12 ] .

To address these challenges, we introduce FRDV ( F ast R etargeting with D ynamics V alidation), which combines high-speed kinematic retargeting with optional dynamics validation. Its kinematic stage uses a specialized Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) solver, Real-Time Iteration (RTI), and chunk-based parallelism, achieving up to 9,156 FPS—approximately 136 × 136\times and 191 × 191\times the throughput of ProtoMotions [ 14 ] and GMR [ 12 ] , respectively—while enforcing robot-specific constraints to reduce ground penetration and self-collision. For motions requiring further verification, contact-implicit iLQR [ 15 ] tracks the resulting references under MuJoCo dynamics and actuator limits to assess trackability and refine residual contact artifacts before RL training.

We evaluate downstream trackability beyond kinematic similarity by training motion-tracking RL policies on LAFAN1 references generated by FRDV, GMR [ 12 ] , and ProtoMotions [ 14 ] and comparing tracking fidelity and success rates across diverse motion categories. We also evaluate sim-to-real transfer by deploying the trained policy on Unitree G1 to execute FRDV-retargeted motions. In summary, the main contributions of this work are:

A fast motion retargeting pipeline based on a custom SQP solver, RTI, and parallel chunk-based processing, achieving up to 9,156 frames per second on average while enforcing robot-specific constraints to prevent self-collision and ground penetration.

A contact-implicit iLQR stage for dynamics validation and refinement under full rigid-body dynamics and actuator bounds.

A comprehensive evaluation using motion-tracking reinforcement learning, including comparisons with existing retargeting pipelines and a zero-shot hardware demonstration on the Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Kinematic Retargeting

Kinematic motion retargeting maps human motion capture data to robot configurations subject to the target robot’s kinematic constraints. Pipelines such as GMR [ 12 ] and OmniRetarget [ 18 ] perform frame-by-frame optimization, whereas PHC [ 17 ] optimizes an entire motion clip at once. ProtoMotions [ 14 ] jointly retargets consecutive frames using PyRoki. Nevertheless, these methods achieve only tens of frames per second, as summarized in Table I . The practical impact of this limitation is evident in systems such as SONIC [ 1 ] , which retargets more than 100 million frames, corresponding to approximately 700 hours of human motion, to construct robot space training data. At this scale, retargeting throughput directly affects both preprocessing cost and iteration speed. In contrast, our work treats retargeting throughput as a primary objective while maintaining compatibility with downstream motion-tracking policy training.

## II-B Numerical Optimization for Inverse Kinematics

The inverse kinematics problem can be formulated as a constrained nonlinear least squares problem. General-purpose nonlinear programming solvers such as IPOPT [ 19 ] and SNOPT [ 20 ] can solve such problems robustly, but their generality can introduce computational overhead in large-scale, frame-wise retargeting. Existing pipelines use different numerical formulations. GMR [ 12 ] uses the Mink differential inverse kinematics framework [ 21 ] , which formulates each
differential IK step as a quadratic program. PyRoki [ 22 ] uses a Levenberg–Marquardt optimizer and supports hard constraints through an augmented Lagrangian formulation. ProtoMotions [ 14 ] uses PyRoki in its motion retargeting workflow.

Our method instead utilizes an SQP solver specialized for explicit constraint handling, achieving high-throughput retargeting. At each iteration, the nonlinear constraints are linearized, and the Hessian is approximated by the Gauss–Newton matrix. Because the objective is a weighted sum of squared residuals with nonnegative weights, this approximation is positive semidefinite, yielding a convex QP that can be solved efficiently using OSQP [ 23 ] . Furthermore, the Real-Time Iteration (RTI) scheme [ 24 ] , originally developed for nonlinear model predictive control, reduces the per-frame cost to a single SQP step by exploiting temporal continuity as a warm start. Our solver combines these ideas and specializes them for the motion retargeting setting.

## II-C Dynamics Verification and Contact-Implicit Control.

Assessing and improving the dynamic consistency of retargeted motions
requires considerations about full-body dynamics and contact. Methods based on explicit contact mode sequences generally require the mode schedule
to be prescribed, whereas contact implicit trajectory optimization methods optimize the motion and contact behavior jointly without requiring a predefined contact sequence [ 25 , 26 ] . More recently, sampling-based dynamics refinement methods such as SPIDER [ 16 ] and DynaRetarget [ 27 ] have been proposed to transform or refine kinematic demonstrations into dynamically consistent robot trajectories. In this paper, we use a gradient based, contact implicit optimal control approach [ 26 , 15 ] , in which contact is embedded directly in the dynamics model and differentiated through, allowing contact transitions to emerge during optimization. We build upon and modify the MuJoCo MPC framework [ 15 ] to track IK retargeted reference motions under MuJoCo’s full rigid body dynamics and contact model. Actuator limits are enforced during optimization, ensuring that the simulated trajectories remain within the torque bounds while reducing contact related artifacts such as foot floating and foot skating. References that do not yield a valid optimized rollout are excluded from the dataset used to train downstream motion tracking policies.

2026-10-21.title: MARE: An Open-Source Lunar Rover Simulator with Shadow Ground Truth for Perception and Autonomy
2026-10-21.authors: Raúl Castilla-Arquillo , Miguel Olivares-Mendez
2026-10-21.comment: . Code: this https URL . Video: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract: Lunar surface exploration increasingly relies on autonomous rovers that must perceive and traverse unstructured terrain under extreme illumination conditions. Near the lunar poles, low sun elevations produce long, high-contrast shadows that challenge stereo vision, terrain segmentation, and localization. Developing perception and navigation algorithms for these conditions requires large amounts of sensor data with accurate ground truth, which field campaigns and analog facilities can only provide at high cost and with limited variety. This paper presents MARE (Modular Autonomy and Rendering Environment), an open-source simulation suite for lunar rover perception and autonomy built on Unreal Engine 5 and ROS 2. MARE consists of three integrated components. Terrain Studio generates cratered and rocky lunar Digital Elevation Maps (DEMs) to build simulation scenes. A dedicated Unreal Engine project hosts two physics-based rovers with plugins for stereo, lidar, event, and Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) cameras, streaming time-stamped sensor data and pixel-accurate ground truth. Lastly, a Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) stack provides web-based mission control. Validation shows a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.79 between predicted and rendered shadows at low sun elevations, and stereo depth analysis verifies decreased pixel coverage in shadowed regions relative to sunlit terrain.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Planetary rovers depend on their Guidance, Navigation, and Control system to traverse complex terrain autonomously, since communication delays limit direct human control. On the Moon, extreme illumination conditions complicate this task: near the poles, the sun remains only a few degrees above the horizon, casting long, high-contrast shadows that continuously alter the terrain’s appearance over time [ 1 , 2 ] . Developing and validating perception and navigation algorithms for these environments requires large volumes of sensor data paired with accurate ground truth, including object labels, shadow masks, depth maps, and the rover pose.

While field campaigns at analog sites and laboratories produce realistic datasets, they are costly and provide little control over terrain geometry and illumination. Simulation bridges this gap by generating labeled data within strictly controlled, repeatable environments. Building on the success of terrestrial game-engine simulators like CARLA [ 3 ] and AirSim [ 4 ] , recent work has adapted high-fidelity rendering for planetary contexts. Allan et al. [ 5 ] developed a Gazebo simulator utilizing physically based rendering and fractal terrain for polar rovers. OmniLRS [ 6 ] leverages NVIDIA Isaac Sim to offer ray-traced lunar rendering, terrain deformation, and mission integration. Similarly, Space Robotics Bench [ 7 ] applies procedural generation and domain randomization in parallel environments for zero-shot sim-to-real learning. Other notable platforms include LunarSim [ 8 ] , which pairs Unity’s visuals with ROS 2 for computer vision evaluation, and MarsSim [ 9 ] , which links multiscale Martian landscapes with a Gazebo wheel-soil terramechanics plugin.

Despite these advances, planetary simulation tools remain fragmented. A recent survey [ 10 ] noted that only eight of fifteen reviewed simulators are publicly available, limiting reproducibility in the community. Current systems typically isolate specific domains like rendering, policy learning, or vehicle dynamics, rather than providing a unified pipeline from terrain creation to closed-loop autonomy with pixel-accurate labeling. Bridging this gap requires complete stack consistency: the same terrain model used to build the scene must also generate the ground truth and serve as the rover’s planning map, ensuring labels, maps, and sensors all operate within the same world.

Within this ground truth, shadows and wheel tracks deserve particular attention. Because the Moon lacks an atmosphere, shadowed regions remain almost completely dark; a shadow can conceal a rock or crater, eliminate the surface texture needed for stereo matching, or be mistaken for an obstacle. Consequently, rock and crater detection depends strongly on illumination [ 11 ] . At low sun elevations, the rover’s own shadow also extends far ahead of or behind the vehicle, occupying a large portion of the navigation camera images. Because this shadow moves with the rover, it undermines the static-scene assumption of visual odometry and compromises terrain segmentation. Similarly, the wheel tracks the rover leaves alter the appearance of the traversed surface. Perception algorithms operating under these conditions must therefore be trained and evaluated with labels that distinguish sunlit from shadowed terrain, the rover’s self-shadow from static terrain shadows, and wheel tracks from the undisturbed surface, which existing planetary simulators rarely provide.

These illumination extremes also motivate sensing modalities beyond conventional cameras and lidar. Emerging sensors, such as event cameras and Single-Photon Avalanche Diode cameras, are of growing interest for lunar perception under low- and high-contrast lighting [ 2 ] . However, they remain largely absent from existing planetary simulators: none of the surveyed platforms supports event cameras, and only one provides limited Single-Photon Avalanche Diode support [ 10 ] .

To address these gaps, we present MARE (Modular Autonomy and Rendering Environment), an open-source simulation suite for lunar rover perception and autonomy built on Unreal Engine 5 and ROS 2. Figure 1 shows its end-to-end pipeline. Terrain Studio generates procedural or real lunar terrain with craters and rock fields and builds the scene in Unreal Engine. Two physics-based rovers carry reusable sensor plugins, including stereo, lidar, event, and Single-Photon Avalanche Diode cameras, synchronized by a shared simulation clock. A ground-truth module produces pixel-accurate object and shadow masks for craters, crater rims, rocks, wheel tracks, and the rover’s own shadow. Finally, a containerized Guidance, Navigation, and Control stack drives the rover autonomously, supervised from a web-based mission control. We validate the suite in two ways: by comparing shadows predicted from the terrain model with those rendered by the engine on three terrains, and by evaluating stereo depth separately on sunlit and shadowed terrain using the ground-truth masks. The source code is publicly available on GitHub 1 1 1 https://github.com/raulcastar/MARE-Lunar-Simulator , together with a video overview 2 2 2 https://youtu.be/EI4HgbMFbBE .

# II System Overview

MARE runs on a single workstation and consists of three components, each released as an open-source repository. As shown in Figure 2 , Terrain Studio and the Unreal Engine editor run on Windows, while the Guidance, Navigation, and Control stack runs under WSL2 as one Docker container per ROS 2 [ 12 ] node. This section outlines each component and how they communicate.

MARE is built on Unreal Engine 5. The engine combines real-time global illumination and virtual shadow maps, which reproduce the long, sharp shadows of a low sun, with landscape tools that scale to kilometer-sized terrains. It also runs on consumer-grade graphics hardware, such as the laptop used in this work, supports virtual reality headsets natively for immersive scene inspection, and has a large user community. Unreal Engine provides no robotics interfaces, so we implement ROS 2 communication, sensor models, and time synchronization as reusable plugins, described in Section IV .

Terrain Studio (scene generation): Generates the scene in four steps: terrain, rock fields and corridors, ground-truth configuration, and sun. Using Python remote execution, it builds the simulation level in the open Unreal Engine editor with a single action. It also exports terrain elevation and soil maps, which the Guidance, Navigation, and Control stack uses for path planning. The implementation is available on GitHub 3 3 3 https://github.com/raulcastar/Unreal-Moon-Terrain-Generation .

Unreal Engine project (simulation and rendering): Contains the simulation level, sensor plugins, physics-based rovers, and the editor Python scripts Terrain Studio uses to build the level. During simulation, each sensor plugin renders its own captures and streams them over TCP to a dedicated ROS 2 node. The rover exchanges wheel commands and pose telemetry with the GNC stack.

GNC stack (autonomy and operations): Comprises perception, path-planning, and rover nodes. Together they turn sensor streams into depth and local maps, plan routes on the planner maps, and command the rover. A web-based mission control supervises the operation. The implementation is available on GitHub 4 4 4 https://github.com/raulcastar/GNC-Moon-Simulator .

All sensor data is time-stamped with the Unreal Engine simulation time, which the UnrealSimClock plugin also provides to the ROS 2 nodes as their clock. As a result, the autonomy stack stays consistent with the simulation even when rendering slows down, or the simulation is paused, and recorded data replays with the timestamps observed at capture.

2026-10-21.title: GPT-6-Astra Understands Touch and Outperform Vision--Tactile--Language--Action Models
2026-10-21.authors: Ziyong Wang , Yupei Lin , Runxuan Huang , Liang Lin , Dongyu Zhang , Guangrun Wang
2026-10-21.comment: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract:
General-purpose multimodal models have shown promise as direct robot action policies, yet whether they grasp the physics underlying real-world interactions and can apply that understanding to guide action remains underexplored. We investigate this question using contact-rich manipulation as a representative testbed, examining tactile understanding as a concrete instance of this broader capability.
Contact-rich manipulation requires interpreting tactile feedback and adjusting actions after obstruction. Existing learned tactile policies acquire these capabilities through specialized pretraining and per-task optimization, with substantial data and training costs. We present GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, which summarizes expert demonstrations into task guidance and tactile references for contact assessment and corrective action. GPT-6-Astra combines this context with multimodal observations and interaction history to generate control commands and adjust actions through contact feedback. Without additional robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning, our method achieves 93.8% mean success across five UniVTAC tasks. Overall performance is comparable to state-of-the-art policies, with higher success on selected tasks. On Insert Hole, tactile feedback improves success from 31% to 99%. Execution analysis further demonstrates contact-guided probing and correction, supporting manipulation progress through explicit expert experience and online feedback.
2026-10-21.introduction:
The role of general-purpose large models in robotics is expanding
from task planning and skill selection ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) and control program generation ( Liang et al., 2023 ) to direct action decisions. Recent evaluations of GPT-6-Astra
show that a general-purpose multimodal model can generate
numerical robot actions from observations, task instructions,
and execution history, using feedback to determine subsequent
behavior ( Team et al., 2026a ) .
These studies progressively connect general knowledge to robot action,
raising a fundamental question: do general-purpose multimodal models
grasp the physics underlying real-world interactions, and can they
apply that understanding to guide their actions? Exploring this
question requires examining how models reason the physical
consequences of their actions and use interaction feedback to adjust
subsequent behavior ( Huang et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2023 ) .

Tactile understanding provides a representative test case for a model’s grasp of physics, because interpreting tactile feedback involves making sense of physical phenomena such as contact, deformation, and constrained motion. We therefore choose contact-rich tasks such as insertion and alignment as our experimental setting ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Bi et al., 2026 ) . Even after identifying a target and reaching the contact location, a robot can be obstructed by local pose errors and hidden geometric constraints ( Huang et al., 2024 ; Xue et al., 2025 ) . External vision provides scene layout and visible object motion, but offers limited access to deformation and motion constraints at the contact interface ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Higuera et al., 2026 ) . In this setting, tactile feedback allows us to examine whether models can connect the observed physical effects to their own actions and use that understanding to guide subsequent control.

Existing research has developed learned policies that integrate
touch into contact-rich manipulation. Representative approaches
include ACT with the UniVTAC encoder ( Chen et al., 2026 ) ,
the tactile-predictive 𝒩 0 \mathcal{N}_{0} -VTLA ( Team et al., 2026c ) , and the tactile-native world-action model 𝒩 0 \mathcal{N}_{0} -TWAM ( Team et al., 2026b ) . These approaches
acquire contact representations and manipulation capabilities
through representation learning, pretraining, and downstream
policy optimization. Their use of expert experience therefore
involves training dedicated representations or updating policy
parameters for downstream tasks. This motivates exploring an
alternative: making expert manipulation experience directly
available to a general-purpose model as task guidance,
without an additional task-specific policy training stage.

To investigate this question without additional specialized pretraining
or per-task policy fine-tuning, we introduce GPT-as-Tactile-Policy,
which summarizes expert manipulation experience into task guidance
that a general-purpose model can use directly. As shown in Fig. 1 A, the model
combines this experience with current visual and tactile observations
and interaction history to directly generate robot actions, revising
subsequent attempts based on contact changes. Expert experience provides
principles for probing and correction, while real-time tactile feedback
helps the model determine how to apply them to the current interaction.
This process requires no policy parameter updates;
Tab. 1 compares its training
requirements with those of existing methods.

Fig. 1 B and Fig. 2 illustrate how tactile feedback changes the policy’s response to obstruction. Without tactile feedback, the policy repeatedly presses downward, retracts, and retries, but its orientation and lateral adjustments remain limited, leaving insertion incomplete. With tactile feedback, the policy actively explores alternative insertion directions and progressively adjusts the tube orientation and lateral position until insertion succeeds. This contrast illustrates how tactile feedback helps identify ineffective attempts, guide local correction, and restore manipulation progress. Across five contact-rich UniVTAC tasks, our method achieves overall performance comparable to extensively pretrained state-of-the-art methods and higher success rates on selected tasks, without additional robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning, as shown in Fig. 1 C. Our main contributions are:

Direct visuo-tactile control. We introduce GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, enabling a fixed-parameter
general-purpose multimodal model to translate tactile feedback into
effective action adjustments. By relating contact changes to preceding
motions, the model revises its approach and pose to improve alignment
and make progress after obstruction.

Direct visuo-tactile control. We introduce GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, enabling a fixed-parameter
general-purpose multimodal model to translate tactile feedback into
effective action adjustments. By relating contact changes to preceding
motions, the model revises its approach and pose to improve alignment
and make progress after obstruction.

Experience-guided tactile reasoning. We summarize expert manipulation experience into fixed task guidance
covering contact cues, probing, and corrective strategies. Together
with representative tactile references, this guidance helps the model
apply prior experience to current interactions.

SOTA-level performance without policy fine-tuning. Across five UniVTAC tasks, evaluated over 100 seeds per task
following the benchmark protocol, our method achieves overall
performance comparable to extensively pretrained state-of-the-art
methods and higher success rates on selected tasks, without additional
robotics-specific pretraining or per-task policy fine-tuning.
Execution analyses further demonstrate how the model uses tactile
feedback to select probing directions, correct its pose, and make
progress after obstruction.

1. Direct visuo-tactile control. We introduce GPT-as-Tactile-Policy, enabling a fixed-parameter
general-purpose multimodal model to translate tactile feedback into
effective action adjustments. By relating contact changes to preceding

and make progress after obstruction.

2. Experience-guided tactile reasoning. We summarize expert manipulation experience into fixed task guidance
covering contact cues, probing, and corrective strategies. Together

3. SOTA-level performance without policy fine-tuning. Across five UniVTAC tasks, evaluated over 100 seeds per task

2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Language Models as Robot Policies

Language models have been used to translate pretrained task knowledge
into robot behavior through skill selection, program generation, and
motion planning. SayCan Brohan et al. (2023) combines language-model
estimates of task relevance with value-function estimates of skill
feasibility to select skill sequences for long-horizon manipulation.
Code as Policies Liang et al. (2023) generates policy
programs that process perception outputs and parameterize control
primitives, using program logic to express motion parameters,
conditional behavior, and feedback loops.
Instruct2Act Huang et al. (2023a) maps multimodal instructions
to Python policy programs that invoke perception, planning, and
action interfaces.
RoboScript Chen et al. (2024) emphasizes the deployability of
generated programs by integrating perception, motion planning, and
control through a unified interface for simulation and real robots.
VoxPoser Huang et al. (2023b) grounds language-inferred affordances
and constraints in visual observations through composable 3D value
maps, which support closed-loop trajectory generation through
model-based planning.
These approaches connect language-model knowledge to robot execution
through different intermediate representations.

Execution feedback further enables language models to revise their
decisions based on observed outcomes.
Inner Monologue Huang et al. (2022) incorporates success
detection, scene descriptions, and human interaction as language
feedback to update task plans during execution.
REFLECT Liu et al. (2023) constructs hierarchical summaries of
robot experiences from multisensory observations, uses a language
model to explain failures, and provides these explanations to a
language-based planner for corrective planning.
These studies incorporate the consequences of previous actions
into subsequent decisions.

Another line of work investigates language models that generate
explicit action parameters.
Natural Language as Policies Mikami et al. (2024) reasons
over textual descriptions of tasks and scene objects to generate
coordinate-level parameters for pick-and-place or sweeping actions,
reducing reliance on intermediate policy code.
GPT-as-Policy Team et al. (2026a) systematically evaluates
GPT-6-Astra as an embodied policy across multiple domains, examining
numerical action generation, cooperation with learned policies,
and feedback-driven adaptation.
Following this direct action-decision paradigm, We study this direct-policy paradigm in contact-rich manipulation,
focusing on how a general-purpose multimodal model uses
visual–tactile feedback to interpret contact and select subsequent
actions.

## 2.2 Visuo-Tactile Manipulation Policies

Visuo-tactile manipulation combines scene observations with local
contact feedback to support fine-grained perception and control.
VITaL Pretraining George et al. (2025) investigates visuo-tactile
pretraining for imitation learning, showing benefits for both
policies that use touch during execution and policies deployed
without tactile input.
3D-ViTac Huang et al. (2024) integrates visual and tactile
observations into a unified 3D representation that preserves their
spatial structure and relationships, and combines this representation
with diffusion policies for fine-grained manipulation.
Reactive Diffusion Policy Xue et al. (2025) introduces
a slow-fast hierarchy that combines latent action-chunk generation
with high-frequency tactile feedback control, allowing the policy
to respond to contact changes during chunk execution.
These studies investigate how tactile information supports skill
learning and execution through representation learning and
feedback-aware control architectures.

Recent work further integrates tactile sensing with the task
knowledge of vision-language-action (VLA) models.
VLA-Touch Bi et al. (2026) keeps the base VLA fixed while using
a pretrained tactile-language model to provide semantic feedback
for high-level planning and a diffusion-based controller to refine
actions using tactile signals.
Tactile-VLA Huang et al. (2025) combines tactile sensing with
hybrid position-force control to connect vision-language knowledge
to physical interaction; its CoT variant further explores
tactile-feedback-driven failure analysis and strategy adaptation.
OmniVTLA Cheng et al. (2026) addresses heterogeneous tactile
inputs through a dual-path tactile encoder and semantically
aligned representations. N 0 N_{0} -VTLA Team et al. (2026c) further explores large-scale
visuo-tactile pretraining, a predictive latent tactile pathway,
and offline policy improvement from stored deployment data.
Together, these approaches incorporate touch into semantic
understanding, policy adaptation, and action generation at
different decision levels.

Another line of work uses predictions of physical interactions
to support manipulation.
Visuo-Tactile World Models Higuera et al. (2026) incorporate touch into action-conditioned world models to improve
the physical consistency of imagined futures and support robot
planning.
Tactile-WAM Wu et al. (2026) introduces asymmetric attention
that isolates the visual prediction pathway from tactile tokens
while preserving tactile access for action generation.
VT-WAM Tian et al. (2026) jointly learns future visual,
tactile-deformation, and action prediction, and uses training-time
contact-gated attention guidance to strengthen the use of tactile
evidence in action generation. N 0 N_{0} -TWAM Team et al. (2026b) further combines large-scale
visuo-tactile joint training, a unified force-based tactile
representation, and contact-event-based task staging to support
multi-stage manipulation.
These studies extend the role of touch from observing the current
contact state to anticipating how contact evolves under robot
actions.

Our work studies a complementary setting in which a
general-purpose multimodal model serves as a direct action
policy with its parameters fixed.
Task knowledge is supplied through in-context guidance, and
the model combines this guidance with visual–tactile
observations and execution history to select subsequent actions.
Our focus is on how the model interprets contact feedback and
uses it to make online action decisions, complementing research
on learned visuo-tactile representations, control architectures,
and predictive models.
