2026-10-21.title: Safe Multi-Robot Collaboration With Uniform Exclusion Using Trust
2026-10-21.authors: Thomas Kaminsky , Áron Vékássy , Hammad Izhar , Angelia Nedić , Stephanie Gil
2026-10-21.comment: (30 main text + 14 supplementary); 10 figures, 6 tables
2026-10-21.abstract:
Robot swarms coordinate through directed, time-varying local communication links, some of which may be compromised to allow the transmission of arbitrary malicious data.
We provide an algorithm that acts as a wrapper around robot communication—when a robot seeks to update its state using data from some incoming links, our wrapper provides a subset of trusted links whose data can be safely incorporated. It selects these links by testing a stream of trust values —data collected from an anomaly detector on each robot—using Safe Anytime-Valid Inference. We require only that the detector be better than chance.
This wrapper ensures safe and performant autonomy by providing two powerful statistical guarantees: it uniformly excludes all compromised links for all time with high user-chosen probability, but nevertheless quickly learns to trust legitimate links. Both guarantees are vital to secure generic tasks, but no previous work provides them simultaneously without restrictive assumptions on connectivity structure or the number of compromised links that are not guaranteed in practice.
We study our Safe Wrapper’s performance in hardware for two contrasting tasks—neural implicit mapping and heading consensus—deploying on 3 LoCoBots and 8 GoPiGos, respectively. We provide simulations using trust values sampled from hardware to validate that our approach scales well to swarms of hundreds of robots.
2026-10-21.introduction:
We associate the set of robots (and Sybil entities) in a swarm with vertices of a graph. We model communication among robots as a time-varying directed graph, where a directed edge indicates that a robot can send a message to another robot at the given time. From the point of view of a receiving robot, we call the sender of a compromised link a malicious neighbor , and the sender of a legitimate link a legitimate neighbor .

Following a class of previous works which use stochastic observations of trust (trust values) derived from physical sensors on robotic platforms [ 17 , 18 ] , we assume that each robot can leverage local sensor information to estimate whether its incoming links are compromised. In the case of a Sybil attack, such trust values can be derived from the channel state information of the wireless communication [ 15 ] , and for injection attacks by looking at the transmission rates on the communication link [ 2 ] . We provide more details in Sections 3.2.5 and 3.1.2 .

In this section, we will describe the capabilities of our framework through hardware experiments. In Supplementary Section 3.6 , we also theoretically ground our empirical observations by providing proofs of safety and performance under mild assumptions, and provide a list of distributed algorithms that can be secured using our approach in Table S1 .

Five legitimate robots try to agree on a common heading direction, with 3 malicious robots spoofing 2 additional malicious identities each, making the total number of malicious agents in the network 9. This resulted in legitimate agents having more compromised links than legitimate ones in nearly all timesteps of the consensus algorithm ( Figure S2 ).
We test whether the swarm reaches safe consensus , meaning that its final heading direction is inside the convex hull of the initial headings of the legitimate robots. Because of the frequent malicious majority, existing intrinsic approaches cannot be guaranteed to reach a safe consensus in our setting. The consensus algorithm and online computation of trust values were run completely locally on the swarm. For more details see Section 3.2 .

In Figure 3 we compare our approach to an unsecured run and a baseline algorithm [ 18 ] that uses trust values, but does not guarantee time-uniform exclusion of malicious agents from communication. We ran 18 separate runs of consensus using our approach and 17 using the baseline. We also collected all of the trust value sequences and evaluated the other approach with them, so both methods were compared on the same set of 35 sequences. Our wrapper uniformly excluded compromised links in 100% of the trials and reached safe consensus, with all legitimate links being identified after an average of 40.3 samples per link at significance level γ = 0.05 \gamma=0.05 ( Table 1 ). The reference baseline eventually learned to exclude the compromised links. However, an average of 70.3 malicious messages were included in legitimate updates before exclusion, causing the legitimate swarm to converge to a heading outside the convex hull in all trials ( Figure 4 ). We report the histogram of aggregated trust observations collected over all malicious and legitimate links in Figure 5 .

To test the generality of our safe wrapper, we ran additional experiments with a team of 3 robots learning a neural implicit reconstruction of their environment using UDON [ 24 ] .
In this algorithm, the swarm tries to jointly learn a neural network representation of the environment by iteratively exchanging networks trained on local RGB-D datasets collected online. In our setup, a malicious robot attempts to overwrite messages sent along one robot’s outgoing links by injecting a network trained on an adversarially altered environment, overwriting each message with high probability ( p = 0.9 p=0.9 ). Since these learned representations are non-interpretable, this message is difficult to distinguish from legitimate network updates. Details of the method, attack, and trust values are provided in Section 3.3 .

Without our wrapper, the legitimate robots’ mesh reconstruction includes the malicious model’s fictitiously added and removed objects ( Figure 1 ) as well as adversarial replacements ( Figure S1 ). Quantitatively, the attacked model converges almost exactly to the malicious model, with a weight-space distance of d θ mal = 0.028 d_{\theta}^{\text{mal}}=0.028 (versus 0.912 0.912 for the nominal model, where no attack occurs). Using our safe wrapper, the learned model uniformly excludes malicious messages. Though it has a weight-space distance of d θ nom = 0.508 d_{\theta}^{\text{nom}}=0.508 to the nominal model since both reach different local minima, the reconstructed maps are close, with a Chamfer distance of only 2.30 2.30 cm. Visually, we see that the reconstructed meshes have no hallucinations ( Figures 1 and S1 ).

We seek to examine how our wrapper scales to large robot swarms that are difficult to evaluate in hardware due to time, battery, and space constraints. To do so, we collect trust values along all links for the distributed consensus hardware experiments, yielding a large dataset of empirical trust values ( Figure 5 ). Sampling trust values directly from these empirical distributions for all simulated links, we evaluate detection performance on swarms of up to 500 robots. Details are provided in Section 3.4.1 .

We consider two important times: when perfect classification is achieved, meaning that all links are correctly identified for all subsequent timesteps, and when strong connectivity is achieved, meaning that the legitimate robots can all communicate on a strongly connected subgraph. Results are reported in Table 2 .
We find that the number of malicious robots has almost no impact on these times, since they are already uniformly excluded with high probability.
Even when M = L = 500 M=L=500 , and thus 250,000 links are compromised, we do not observe a single false positive in these experiments.
More legitimate robots yield slower perfect classification times since more tests must all pass, but this delay grows very slowly. For example, even though 187,250 187{,}250 new links are added between the L = 250 L=250 and L = 500 L=500 cases, fewer than 10 more samples are required on average to achieve perfect classification. Moreover, we see that the time to learn a trusted subgraph actually decreases with L , L, since there exist more simultaneous paths available to trust. Additional simulations are provided in the Supplementary Materials with trust values collected from sparse deterministic graph links ( Table S3 ) and sparse random graph links ( Table S4 ).

In hardware experiments, no compromised links were trusted under our safe wrapper.
However, an understanding of the per-compromised-link false positive rate is useful for understanding how the false-trust rate increases with larger swarms.
Thus, we consider the false positive rate for one malicious link, under varying levels of detector quality ( Figure 6 ). We see that even with a trivial detector that performs entirely at chance (trust values drawn from Bernoulli ​ ( 0.5 ) \text{Bernoulli}(0.5) ), the false positive rate remains below half of the significance level, and often far below it. When the detector has reasonable quality, no false positives are recorded. Our trust values for the consensus case are closest to the ( p = 0.25 , γ = 0.05 ) (p=0.25,\gamma=0.05) case; we see here that no false positives are recorded across 5,000 trials.

# 2 Discussion

## Challenges

Securing our algorithm requires that the anomaly detector be better than chance , in the sense that the expected output of the detector is greater than 0.5 0.5 for legitimate links, and less than 0.5 0.5 for compromised links. One important class of detectors that fails this criterion is manipulable anomaly detectors, whose outputs can be manipulated by adversaries to take abnormal values. For example, adversarial patches can be generated to minimize the probability of being detected by pre-trained anomaly detectors [ 26 ] . Such a detector could be manipulated to output trust values above 0.5 0.5 for compromised links, causing them to be falsely trusted.

There has been much discussion on which data are effective for avoiding manipulable trust values. We follow the Cyberphysical Trust framework [ 17 ] , which emphasizes cyberphysical features based in the physical world as the source of detectability. In analogy to cryptography, which enforces security by computational hardness , cyberphysical trust enforces security by physical hardness , recording sensor data that result from complex interactions in the physical world.

Our attack model assumes that the set of compromised links is fixed throughout time. It remains a challenge to exclude malicious data when attacks can start or stop at different times, causing the trust value distributions of those links to dynamically change. This is especially challenging because the asymptotic power of the test relies centrally on uniform separability of trust values over time ( Assumption 3.5 ). As such, new methodologies must be developed to effectively accommodate dynamic attackers and mitigate their influence.

We note that this approach ensures that no legitimate robots incorporate malicious data and that eventually legitimate robots learn to incorporate information along legitimate links. Another important problem that we do not address is the problem of data leakage . At times, it is undesirable to allow malicious actors to receive any unencrypted legitimate data. These problems are typically handled using cryptographic techniques—encryption in the case of link-level attacks, and secure distributed computation protocols for node-level attacks.

2026-10-21.title: Perceives but Doesn't Brake: A Perception-Action Binding Gap in Reasoning Driving VLAs
2026-10-21.authors: Matteo Cercola , Katie Z Luo , Simone Formentin , Marco Pavone
2026-10-21.abstract: Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. We characterize this failure as a perception–action binding gap : hazard information is available inside the model but exerts insufficient control over trajectory generation. Using matched simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, we show that in-path hazards are actually encoded in the visual representation, but longitudinal plans are dominated by ego-speed history and respond only weakly to hazard proximity or the model’s own reasoning trace. Further analysis shows that the trajectory generator is capable of braking but sometimes fails to do so due to the perception-action binding gap. Without retraining or modifying any weights, we inject a hazard-conditioned energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, restoring the missing coupling at generation time. With exact obstacle geometry, guidance cuts footprint intrusion from 58.1% to 14.5% and recovers safe braking whenever sufficient stopping distance remains, eliminating collisions entirely in our braking-relevant closed-loop battery. It also reverses the diagnosed dependence of the plan, from tracking ego speed to responding to obstacle range. These results separate hazard perception from hazard control in driving VLAs, show that unsafe behavior can arise even when the model has both the evidence and the ability to act on it, and propose a simple fix for bridging this binding gap.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Reasoning-augmented vision–language–action (VLA) models are increasingly
designed to do more than map observations directly to actions: they perceive
the scene, produce an explicit reasoning trace, and then generate a driving
trajectory. This architecture suggests a natural safety premise: if the model
correctly identifies a hazard and reasons that the vehicle should respond, that
evidence should influence the resulting action.
However, on simulated scenes containing a stationary obstacle in the ego
lane, a state-of-the-art
reasoning VLA [ 1 ] generates trajectories that enter the
obstacle footprint on 58.1% of samples, and its selected actions collide
with a reconstructed version of that obstacle in most closed-loop rollouts, even though a comfortable stop was still possible. Crucially, the failure does
not arise because the hazard is absent from the model. The obstacle is
recoverable from the visual representation and is often explicitly
identified in the model’s own reasoning, yet neither source of evidence
exerts sufficient influence on the generated longitudinal plan. Instead,
the plan remains strongly governed by the supplied ego-speed history. We
call this dissociation between accessible hazard evidence and its influence
on action a perception–action binding gap ( Figure 1 ); here perceives means recoverable from the model’s representation
(formalized as availability , Section IV ), not awareness.

This distinction matters because an unsafe action can have at least three
different causes. First, the relevant hazard may not be represented at all
( availability ). Second, the trajectory generator may be incapable of
producing an appropriate response even when the hazard is known
( action-side sufficiency ). Third, the evidence may be available and a
safe action may be expressible, but the evidence may have insufficient action authority : changing the hazard does not sufficiently change the
generated plan. These cases imply different remedies, yet standard driving
metrics typically conflate them.

We disentangle them with matched simulated interventions that vary
visual hazard content, obstacle range, ego-speed history, and textual reasoning
while holding competing inputs fixed. Hazard information is available
throughout, yet longitudinal behavior is far more sensitive to ego history than
to the hazard itself, under closed-loop control in AlpaSim/NuRec [ 2 ] as well as
open-loop scoring.

Next, we ask whether the missing coupling can be restored without retraining the
policy. We inject a differentiable hazard energy into the frozen
flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, steering trajectory generation during
flow integration while leaving all model parameters unchanged. Supplied exact
obstacle geometry, this reduces footprint intrusion from
58.1% to 14.5% and changes the governing dependence of the generated plan:
trajectory reach becomes primarily responsive to obstacle range rather than ego
speed. Controlled CARLA sweeps further show that the remaining failures are
those in which insufficient stopping distance remains.

Finally, we ask how far this intervention can be driven by signals
already present in the frozen model, rather than by privileged geometry.
Lightweight readouts of the visual cache estimate both when an in-path
hazard is present and where it lies. The key is to preserve the spatial
structure needed for that estimate: on sites held out in both geometry
and appearance, a spatially aware readout reduces footprint intrusion
from 65.0% to 11.7%, approaching the
6.0% obtained with exact geometry, with no measured
reach loss on matched clear scenes. Thus, much of the safety constraint
needed to restore perception-action binding is already recoverable from the model’s own
representation.
Autonomous binding is therefore feasible within
the evaluated visual domain, while robust semantic triggering under
domain shift remains open.

Our contributions are threefold. First, our primary contribution is to identify and causally diagnose a perception–action binding gap in a reasoning driving VLA. Across logged driving, matched counterfactuals, and closed-loop replay, we
separate hazard availability from action authority and show that
longitudinal planning is dominated by ego-speed history; to our knowledge,
this is the first causal, rather than correlational, separation of hazard
availability from action authority in a reasoning driving VLA. Second,
we show that the missing coupling can be enforced at inference time without
retraining. A differentiable hazard-conditioned energy steers the frozen
flow-matching sampler toward safe braking and, when supplied an accurate
constraint, shifts the plan’s dependence from ego speed toward obstacle
range, demonstrating action-side sufficiency. Third, we show why standard logged evaluation can miss such a
failure. Because a binding gap is a failure of hazard-conditioned action response rather
than average prediction quality, standard logged evaluation can miss it:
safety-critical states in which a moving ego must brake for a stationary
in-path obstacle are rare because human drivers typically avoid them.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Ego-State Shortcuts and Driving Evaluation

Prior work shows that open-loop driving benchmarks can be solved surprisingly well from ego dynamics alone [ 3 ] , and that planners remain nearly unchanged under severe visual corruption while responding strongly to ego-velocity perturbations [ 4 ] . These findings establish an ego-state shortcut but do not distinguish whether visual evidence is absent from the representation or present yet uncoupled from action.

## II-B Reasoning and Video–Action Driving Models

Recent driving policies increasingly couple visual observations, language or
reasoning, and action generation. Alpamayo-1.5 combines chain-of-causation
reasoning with a flow-matching trajectory expert [ 1 ] ;
Senna predicts language-level driving decisions [ 5 ] ;
LMDrive combines language, perception, navigation, and explicit ego
state [ 6 ] ; and VaVAM is a language-free video–action
policy without explicit ego-state input [ 7 ] .

## II-C Reasoning–Action Faithfulness

Prior work shows that stated reasoning and executed behavior can disagree,
including within the same model family [ 8 ] , and that
embodied reasoning faithfulness can be improved with learned
critics [ 9 ] . These studies show language and action can
diverge, but do not separate hazard availability from whether it exerts
causal authority over the trajectory.

## II-D Inference-Time Guidance for Generative Policies

Gradient guidance can steer pretrained diffusion and flow samplers during
generation without retraining [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] ;
runtime reasoning–action alignment has also used sample-and-rerank
schemes [ 13 ] . We use guidance as a diagnostic intervention rather than proposing a new
control mechanism: by granting a safety constraint direct authority during sampling, we test whether the frozen generator can produce a response that its native conditioning fails to elicit.

2026-10-21.title: Reasoning as a Distribution: Generative Plan Latents for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-21.authors: Matteo Cercola , Katie Z Luo , Milan Ganai , John Alora , Simone Formentin , Marco Pavone
2026-10-21.abstract: Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies increasingly reason before acting, but existing reasoning models compress this intermediate decision into a single representation. When several plans are valid, this commitment hides alternatives that could otherwise be selected or revised. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (GPL), which represents the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over plans, such as which object, grasp, or route to use. This makes the reasoning state addressable : without retraining the VLA, plans can be sampled ( coverage ), selected on request ( steering ), and reweighted by deployment outcomes ( outcome adaptation ). We test all three on SimplerEnv manipulation with π 0 \pi_{0} , and extend the analysis to RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a maze domain. Steering the plan raises the fraction of executions that follow the request from 0.48 to 0.94, while the same guidance on the native action distribution shows no reliable gain. Finally, we show that an explicit plan is most useful when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies increasingly place a reasoning stage
between perception and action ( Zawalski et al., 2024 ; Hao et al., 2024 ; Bai et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026b ; Huang et al., 2026a ) , and this intermediate state empirically
improves policy success rate. This intermediate state is attractive because it can separate what the robot decides to do from the motor trajectory that realizes that decision. Yet existing reasoning models represent this state as one vector per observation. This raises the question: should a model expose one committed decision per observation, or
a distribution over valid ones?

The distinction matters whenever the observation leaves more than one decision valid. Consider a robot facing two identical cubes, with an instruction that names neither: nothing favors one target over the other. The same ambiguity is pervasive in everyday tasks: whether to pick up a can or push it aside, how to grasp a mug, or which route to take. A reasoning state that must produce a single decision necessarily collapses these alternatives. Averaging them may yield an invalid plan between the cubes; choosing one avoids this failure but still hides the equally valid alternative. The missing property is therefore not simply validity, but a representation that preserves the alternatives so they remain accessible at inference time, allowing preferences or outcomes to dynamically select the most viable strategy at deployment without retraining ( Figure 1 ). We call a reasoning state addressable when, at inference time, the policy can be: sampled to obtain distinct valid decisions ( coverage ), conditioned to select among them a single decision ( steering ), and reweighted by outcome to adapt the decision in closed-loop ( outcome adaptation ).
The limitation of prior
designs is therefore a lack of addressability.
This is not the usual action-multimodality problem: robot learning has
already developed generative action models precisely to avoid averaging
incompatible motor trajectories ( Section 2 ).
The unresolved question is whether the upstream decision should itself also be represented as a distribution.

We introduce the Generative Plan Latent ( gpl ), which replaces a
deterministic plan readout with a conditional distribution p θ ​ ( z ∣ c ) p_{\theta}(z\mid c) of plans z z given a VLA representation c c . This distribution can be sampled, steered toward a requested mode, and reweighted from
deployment experience, all without retraining the underlying VLA. We show that the plan provides a substantially stronger handle than the action distribution for expressing an external preference. Under matched executors, selecting a requested plan increases the fraction of executions that follow it from 0.48 to 0.94, whereas applying the same inference-time intervention to π 0 \pi_{0} ’s native action distribution yields no reliable improvement. Because these alternatives remain explicit, deployment outcomes can also change which plans are preferred without updating the plan generator or VLA. This benefit is conditional: an explicit plan can influence behavior only when it carries decision information that the executor cannot already recover from the observation. We call this the redundancy principle . In a controlled test, changing only the demonstrations to reduce this redundancy increases the plan-selection effect from +0.19 to +0.65. Finally, these capabilities do not depend on hand-designed plan coordinates: they persist when the plan representation is learned directly from demonstrated behavior.

Our contributions are:

We identify the decision bottleneck as a distinct locus for multimodality in VLAs and define addressability , the capacity to preserve alternative decisions so they can be sampled, selected, and revised. Matched plan- and action-level interventions show that the decision bottleneck provides the stronger handle for controlling behavior.

We introduce gpl , a distribution over task-level plans,
instantiated by a rectified-flow head and integrated into π 0 \pi_{0} with
frozen base weights and a small adaptation.

We propose the redundancy principle : an explicit plan should affect behavior only when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.

# 2 Related Work

Recent VLAs increasingly insert an intermediate reasoning stage between
perception and action. Embodied Chain-of-Thought (ECoT) ( Zawalski et al., 2024 ) makes this reasoning
explicit in language, grounded in robot-relevant quantities such as subtasks,
objects, and motion; other approaches move this computation into continuous
hidden states ( Huang et al., 2026b ; Huang et al., 2026a ; Bai et al., 2026 ; Tur et al., 2026 ) . CoT-VLA ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) instead samples visual subgoals as
sequences of future frames, yielding a visual chain-of-thought in pixel space
rather than a compact plan representation. Despite these different representations, continuous action-domain reasoners typically expose a single intermediate state per observation ( Table 2 ), rather than an explicit distribution over alternative
decisions.

Continuous reasoning was first studied in the language domain: Coconut ( Hao et al., 2024 ) feeds hidden states back into the model as continuous
thoughts, while generative approaches place a distribution over the reasoning
state ( Ye et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Kang et al., 2026 ; Tu et al., 2026 ) .
STAR-LDM ( Lovelace et al., 2025 ) similarly samples a latent reasoning state
that is injected as soft tokens before generation. These works establish
continuous and stochastic reasoning for text.

Sampling latent plans to condition low-level control is well established in
robot learning ( Lynch et al., 2019 ; Lynch & Sermanet, 2021 ; Mees et al., 2022 ) .
Higher-level policies can search these spaces ( Rosete-Beas et al., 2022 ) , while LDCQ ( Venkatraman et al., 2024 ) learns a multimodal distribution over latent
skills and selects among them with a value function.
Trajectory-level generative planners ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Ajay et al., 2023 ) combine sampling with test-time
guidance, while SuSIE ( Black et al., 2024b ) and UniPi ( Du et al., 2023 ) generate visual subgoals for downstream control.

Generative action models ( Florence et al., 2022 ; Lee et al., 2024 ; Chi et al., 2025 ) and flow-based
VLAs ( Black et al., 2024a ) already represent multimodal motor behavior.
Flow-reversal and noise-space methods ( Wagenmaker et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) steer these
action distributions, while verifier-based selection ( Kwok et al., 2025 ) , rejection-based post-training ( Tan et al., 2025 ) , reinforcement-learning-style updates ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) , and failure- or energy-guided action
generation ( Zheng et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ) use feedback to improve
behavior.

Together, these lines of work provide intermediate reasoning states,
generative latent plans, and multimodal action distributions, but leave open
where multimodality should reside in a reasoning-augmented VLA.

2026-10-21.title: From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation
2026-10-21.authors: Xiaoxu Xu , Hao Li , Hongtao Zhang , Yili Tang , Jiafei Cao , Junhao Cai , Haoxiang Ma , Weixin Li , Weinan Zhang
2026-10-21.abstract: Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Anticipating how the physical world will evolve ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Assran et al., 2023 ) under interaction is becoming increasingly important for vision-language-action (VLA) models ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) and world action models (WAM) ( Li et al., 2026b ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . Such predictive capability allows an agent to reason about the consequences of interaction, rather than mapping only its current observation to an immediate action. Yet effective manipulation requires more than temporal foresight alone: it also depends on a precise understanding of how the scene is spatially organized. Geometry specifies object layouts, spatial relationships, and robot-scene configurations, while dynamics describe how these structures evolve as an interaction unfolds. For action generation, these two aspects play distinct but complementary roles: geometry provides the spatial structure within which actions are executed, while its evolution provides cues about how the scene may change over time. This naturally raises a central question: how should geometric structure and its predicted evolution be represented so that they can more effectively support action generation?

Recent efforts to incorporate geometry into predictive policy learning follow two directions. As shown in Fig. 1 , input-centric approaches ( Sun et al., 2025 ; Qu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026c ; Zhang et al., 2025b ) augment observations with depth, point clouds, 3D coordinates, or pretrained geometric features. These methods improve spatial grounding, but use geometry as additional context for describing the currently observed scene and may rely on sensing or geometry-estimation pipelines. Prediction-centric approaches ( Yang et al., 2026a ; He et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Li et al., 2025c ; Su et al., 2026 ) instead supervise models with future RGB-D observations, future geometric states, or other world-prediction targets, explicitly exposing the policy to future scene structure. However, such targets are represented as dense observations or holistic latent states, requiring the learned representation to retain geometric information whose relevance to control may vary substantially. More broadly, these approaches primarily organize geometry to represent the scene and its evolution. They leave less explicit how action-relevant information should be distinguished from geometry needed for a coherent world representation. This creates a gap between predictive geometric modeling and action-oriented motor representation learning.

A natural way to bridge this gap is to recognize that predictive geometry and action generation place different preferences on learned representations. Predictive geometric modeling benefits from preserving a sufficiently complete and coherent account of scene structure. Action generation, in contrast, benefits from emphasizing geometric variations that are informative for motor commands while reducing the influence of static or action-irrelevant scene content. Rather than forcing these roles to be served in exactly the same representation, we introduce two complementary representations with distinct but related purposes: a predictive geometric representation that provides a compact and structured description of scene geometry and its evolution, and a motor representation that emphasizes action-aware information from geometric transitions. The former provides structured predictive context, while the latter focuses this predictive information toward control.

Building on this observation, we propose the two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations (CPR) from large-scale heterogeneous interaction videos ( Collaboration, 2023 ; Jin et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Goyal et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2025a ) and transfers them to downstream policies. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , our framework first constructs a predictive geometric representation from dense geometric features and then extracts action-aware information from the temporal evolution of scene geometry across video clips, providing complementary guidance for downstream action generation. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 2 , during representation pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model ( Wang et al., 2025 ) extracts dense geometric features from multi-view video observations, which are progressively compressed by a hierarchical query-based encoder into compact temporal states. Geometry reconstruction, masked representation prediction, and geometric transition prediction encourage the predictive geometric representation to preserve scene structure while capturing its evolution over time. We then apply action supervision to transitions between consecutive predictive geometric states, yielding a motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant geometric transitions. The predictive geometric representation therefore captures structured information about the evolving scene, while the motor representation focuses on transitions that are more directly informative for action. During post-training, as shown in Fig. 3 , these two representations are transferred through role-specific supervision pathways. Dedicated geometry queries are trained to infer the predictive geometric representation from current-time inputs, while intermediate features along the action-generation pathway are aligned with the motor representation. Importantly, future observations and the pretrained representation model are used only to construct privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. We evaluate CPR on both multiple VLA architectures and WAM across diverse simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements across different robot embodiments and action-generation paradigms. Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We identify complementary roles for predictive geometric and motor representations in predictive policy learning: predictive geometric modeling benefits from preserving structured scene geometry, while action generation benefits from emphasizing control-relevant geometric transitions.

We develop a two-stage framework that learns and transfers these complementary predictive representations. Hierarchical geometric tokenization and predictive objectives learn geometric states, while action supervision extracts action-aware information from their transitions; the two representations are transferred through geometry-query and motor-alignment pathways.

Extensive experiments across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent improvements across policy architectures and robot embodiments. CPR yields a 10.4% absolute gain on the WidowX evaluation and improves future-world and action prediction in WAM.

# 2 Related Work

Predictive modeling provides VLA models and WAMs with foresight beyond the current observation. Existing approaches introduce future information either through observation prediction or compact predictive representations. Observation-level methods predict future RGB observations, videos, or world states to support action generation ( Zhang et al., 2025a ; Lv et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ; Agarwal et al., 2026 ) , while latent-space approaches compress future information into compact conditions or visuomotor representations ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Su et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . Recent methods ( Lee et al., 2026b ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2025b ; Chen et al., 2025b ; Yang et al., 2025b ; Ding and Wang, 2026 ) , also explore structured predictive signals such as dynamic, spatial, or semantic information to connect VLMs or world modeling with control. However, existing methods vary in how geometric structure and action-relevant temporal transitions are organized. Our work focuses specifically on predictive geometry: we learn a structured representation that preserves scene geometry and its evolution, and derive a complementary motor representation from geometric transitions.

Geometric information has been increasingly incorporated into robotic policies to improve spatial grounding. Input-centric approaches ( Qu et al., 2025 ; Sun et al., 2025 ; Bhat et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Yang et al., 2026b ) augment current observations with depth, point clouds, 2D or 3D coordinates, or spatial features, providing direct access to the geometry of the observed scene. More recent prediction-centric approaches ( Li et al., 2025c ; He et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Su et al., 2026 ) instead use geometric or spatiotemporal prediction as auxiliary supervision, including depth prediction, robot trajectories, and 3D motion representations. These approaches demonstrate the value of geometry for predictive policy learning, but geometric structure and action relevance may favor different types of information: preserving scene geometry requires broad structural fidelity, whereas action generation benefits from transitions that are informative for motor behavior. Our work addresses this distinction by learning complementary predictive geometric and motor representations, and transferring them separately to downstream policies through dedicated interfaces.

2026-10-21.title: Design and implementation of thermal control strategy for micro-size lunar exploration rover hakuto
2026-10-21.authors: Toshiki Tanaka , Takuto Oikawa , Keeni Shruti , Teruhito Iida , Kazuya Yoshida , John Walker
2026-10-21.comment: 69th International Astronautical Congress (IAC), Bremen, Germany, 1-5 October 2018
2026-10-21.abstract: The research focuses on the thermal interface design of the HAKUTO Rover Flight Model (FM) and its evaluation using the final thermal vacuum experiment. Initially, an analytical thermal model was developed, dividing the rover into six distinct radiating surfaces. The surface temperature of the rover was then determined based on its orientation relative to the solar radiative flux, as well as other thermal factors such as lunar radiation, solar albedo, and conduction from the lunar regolith. By considering the impact of these heat sources, suitable mounting locations for the avionics and the angle of the solar panels were determined to optimize the rover's thermal performance and power generation while ensuring the rover's mass remained under 4 kg. After the preliminary thermal analysis, numerical computational simulations were conducted to further elaborate on the thermal response of the final HAKUTO Rover FM design, which was then verified through a thermal balance test in a vacuum environment.

2026-10-21.title: De-Diffusing WAMs: Action-Sufficient Direct Prediction for Robot Control
2026-10-21.authors: Shaoyi Zheng , Zhongtao Jiang , Yue Peng , Wenbo Lu , Shunchi Zhang , Xi Wang , Shengji Wan
2026-10-21.abstract:
Cascade world-action models (WAMs) use predicted visual futures to condition robot actions, but inherit costly iterative inference from diffusion-pretrained experts.
We ask what a single-step predicted future must preserve to support accurate single-step action prediction.
In the evaluated WAM, resampling video noise has little effect on downstream actions, yet naively truncating both streams to one step substantially reduces task success.
Video-space supervision only partially closes this gap, and a local sensitivity analysis shows that vision prediction errors have highly unequal consequences for action accuracy.
These findings motivate DirectWAM , which converts pretrained video and action experts into single-step predictors without stochastic sampling through action-sufficient distillation , while retaining the explicit future-to-action cascade.
After learning a one-step action model, we train the future predictor by decoding actions from its own predicted futures and backpropagating demonstration action error through the expert, with an optional future-latent reconstruction loss.
The resulting objective evaluates the student-generated future through its downstream control consequences rather than relying on representation matching alone.
DirectWAM achieves 97.1% average success across four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same one-evaluation-per-stream budget.
This advantage has also extended to three real-world tasks that we designed.
Compared with the full iterative teacher, it reduces inference latency by 28.0 × 28.0\times .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Cascade world-action models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video models to predict visual futures, which then condition an inverse dynamics model (IDM) for action generation.
Unlike standalone video generation, the predicted future is not the final output but an intermediate representation for robot control.
This causal future-to-action relationship allows a robot policy to utilize world prior from video while retaining futures that can be decoded for inspection.
However, diffusion-based video and action experts realize this computation through repeated denoising, introducing a substantial inference cost.
We study how to retain the pretrained experts and explicit future-to-action interface while replacing their iterative inference procedure with direct prediction.

Recent acceleration methods either modify the future-to-action interface or compress its computation.
Fast-WAM retains video co-training but removes explicit future prediction at deployment Yuan et al. (2026) ; Motus supports action-only inference alongside other joint and conditional modeling modes Bi et al. (2026) .
Among methods that retain the cascade, Flash-WAM Akbari et al. (2026) uses modality-aware consistency distillation to achieve one-step inference in both the video and action streams.
DIDO Lyu et al. (2026) concentrates supervision on control-relevant visual regions to learn single-step future prediction, while retaining iterative action generation.
These advances establish that cascade inference can be accelerated.
However, a more basic question is largely overlooked in WAM acceleration: what must a single-step future preserve to support accurate downstream action prediction?
As the future serves only as an intermediate representation, the reconstruction objective of video diffusion may not naturally align with the control objective of the downstream IDM.

We first disentangle the roles of stochastic sampling and iterative refinement, using LingBot-VA as our experimental instantiation.
Varying only the video noise produces limited changes in downstream actions, and fixing it throughout an episode barely affects closed-loop success.
Stochasticity can therefore be removed, yielding a deterministic future predictor that nonetheless still relies on the teacher’s multi-step computation.
Removing this iteration is non-trivial: naively reducing the steps degrades control, and learning a one-step predictor with video-space supervision recovers only part of the gap.
Therefore, these results motivate learning the direct future predictor through the action model that consumes its predictions, rather than relying on video-space supervision alone.

To understand how the remaining prediction errors affect control, we selectively correct components of the future-representation error under a frozen action expert.
Correcting only a small, locally action-sensitive component recovers a disproportionate share of the achievable offline action-error reduction.
The complementary component still contributes, but the imbalance shows that representation-error magnitude is a poor proxy for downstream importance.
This motivates action sufficiency as the learning principle for single-step prediction: the predicted future should be optimized according to the action decoded from it, rather than through representation matching alone.

We implement this principle in DirectWAM through action-sufficient distillation .
Starting from diffusion-pretrained video and action experts, we first train a single-step action expert with the video expert fixed.
We then train the single-step future predictor end-to-end through this action expert: actions are decoded from the student’s own predicted futures, and the demonstration action error is backpropagated into the future predictor.
An optional future-latent reconstruction loss anchors predictions to the demonstrated future.
Because both objectives supervise final predictions rather than intermediate denoising states, the pretrained experts are converted into a direct cascade without the student having to reproduce the teacher’s denoising trajectory.

In experiments, DirectWAM achieves 97.1% average success on LIBERO and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming cascade baselines at the same compute budget and substantially narrowing the single-step control gap. These gains further carry over to three real-world manipulation tasks.
Inference latency decreases from 5042 ms for the full iterative teacher to 180 ms for DirectWAM, a 28.0 × 28.0\times speedup.
Together, these results demonstrate a practical route to retaining explicit future prediction while replacing iterative diffusion inference with direct computation trained for downstream control. Our contributions are threefold:

Separating stochastic sampling from iterative refinement. We characterize their distinct roles in the evaluated cascade WAM: video-noise resampling has limited downstream effects, whereas naively truncating both streams to one step causes control drops.

Action sufficiency as a learning criterion. We show that the magnitude of future-prediction error is a poor proxy for its effect on action accuracy, motivating a training objective that supervises the student-generated future through the actions it induces online.

A deterministic single-step future-to-action cascade. We introduce DirectWAM , a one-step de-diffused cascade WAM that preserves explicit future prediction while achieving strong control performance both in simulation and in the real world.

# 2 Related Work

Video-based control uses predicted observations as an intermediate representation for action generation ( Du et al., 2023 ) .
Recent World-Action Models (WAMs) more tightly integrate visual dynamics and action prediction: LingBot-VA through autoregressive video–action modeling Li et al. (2026) , DreamZero with a video-pretrained backbone Ye et al. (2026) , and Motus within a multi-expert architecture Bi et al. (2026) .
Building on the cascade WAM interface, we investigate how to learn direct future prediction according to its action consequences, rather than assuming that control requires fully refined video.

Consistency models and distribution matching distillation provide general
routes to reducing diffusion sampling steps Song et al. (2023) ; Yin et al. (2024) .
A distinct architectural approach, Fast-WAM, retains video co-training but
removes explicit future prediction at deployment Yuan et al. (2026) .
We instead focus on acceleration that preserves the future-to-action cascade.
Flash-WAM addresses the different noise regimes of video and action streams
by assigning modality-specific consistency functions, enabling single-step
inference in both streams Akbari et al. (2026) .
DIDO combines distribution matching with interaction-centric representation
guidance for one-step video prediction, using explicit interaction
representations together with visual feature alignment to preserve
manipulation-relevant information Lyu et al. (2026) .
These methods demonstrate that efficient cascade WAM prediction requires
more than applying a generic sampling shortcut.
DirectWAM pursues the same goal of retaining useful future prediction, but
defines its learning criterion through the existing action model.

Predictive accuracy need not align with downstream decision quality, as studied through objective mismatch Lambert et al. (2020) , value-aware model learning Farahmand et al. (2017) , and value equivalence Grimm et al. (2020) . Recent WAMs address related representation challenges through geometric or semantic supervision: MECo-WAM Zhang et al. (2026) transfers action-relevant 4D geometric priors from a frozen VGGT Wang et al. (2025) , while Robust-WAM augments video-generation-based policies with future-semantic alignment Yan et al. (2026) . GigaWorld-Policy-0.5 Team et al. (2026) strengthens action–dynamics coupling through action-conditioned future modeling while allowing action-only inference. Our work shares the broader goal of learning predictive information useful for control, but focuses on how a predicted future should be learned when it must condition a single-step action predictor. Specifically, DirectWAM converts diffusion-pretrained experts into a deterministic single-step cascade while retaining their future-representation interface. Rather than introducing a new semantic or geometric target space, it trains the future predictor through demonstration-action error decoded from its own predictions by a learned direct action model, with optional future-latent anchoring. This places the learning criterion at the interface between the student-generated future and its action consumer, while preserving explicit future conditioning with one evaluation per stream.

2026-10-21.title: FIT-MAC: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Robust Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-21.authors: Jiatong Li , Jisheng Dang , Qiangqiang Ma , Bimei Wang , Jingwen Zhao , Wenjun Ma , Juncheng Li , Hong Peng , Bin Hu
2026-10-21.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, their reliability can degrade substantially when task conditions deviate from the nominal setting. Perturbations in object positions and task instructions may lead to complete task failure. Existing VLA policies generally lack an explicit runtime mechanism for distinguishing these failure modes and selecting an appropriate recovery strategy.
To systematically mitigate this issue, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time.
FIT-MAC augments a VLA policy with an inference-time control layer. First, the Planner Agent parses the language instruction into a structured task specification that captures the manipulation goal and spatial constraints, and the Grounder Agent resolves each instruction-level reference to a visual target. Next, the Verifier Agent tracks phase-specific execution progress, distinguishes target-binding errors from local execution failures, and determines whether intervention is warranted. The Correction Agent then routes permitted interventions to target rebinding or bounded grasping or placement recovery, depending on the failure type. When no intervention is required, the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator.
Extensive experiments on LIBERO-PRO demonstrate that FIT-MAC improves robustness across multiple VLA backbones, consistently increasing success rates and achieving state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations. 2026-10-21.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding to generate actions for robotic manipulation. OpenVLA provides an open-source foundation for generalist robot control ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , while π 0 \pi_{0} uses flow matching to generate continuous actions ( Black et al., 2024 ) . Its successor, π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} , further improves open-world generalization through heterogeneous co-training ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . Recent models pursue complementary directions, NORA reduces the computational cost of generalist VLA policies ( Hung et al., 2025 ) , while X-VLA targets scalable cross-embodiment transfer ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . MolmoAct incorporates structured spatial reasoning between perception and low-level control ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . Other methods improve predictive modeling and long-horizon execution through world-knowledge modeling, future-goal prediction, and phase-aware policies ( Zhang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Fan et al., 2025 ) . Collectively, these advances highlight the potential of VLA models for generalist robot control.

However, strong benchmark performance does not necessarily translate into reliable execution under distribution shift. AGNOSTOS reports limited zero-shot generalization across tasks, while SAFE identifies frequent failures on novel tasks, underscoring the need for runtime failure detection ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2026 ) . Broader evaluations show substantial sensitivity to perturbations in actions, instructions, observations, and environments ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) . VLATest documents similar robustness gaps under variations in clutter, lighting, viewpoints, and instructions, as well as in the presence of unseen objects ( Wang et al., 2025b ) . Adversarial evaluations further expose vulnerabilities to digital and physical perturbations ( Wang et al., 2025a ) . Together, these findings highlight the challenges of robust VLA execution.

Addressing these challenges requires both reliable temporal visual evidence and
effective runtime recovery. Reasoning-based video segmentation improves
language-conditioned grounding by decoupling textual semantics from dynamic
visual representations ( Dang et al., 2026a ) . At the control level, RACER
combines a VLM supervisor with an actor trained on automatically generated
recovery trajectories ( Dai et al., 2025 ) . Sparse spatio-temporal propagation
strengthens object correspondence across frames ( Dang et al., 2026b ) , while
COME-robot uses execution feedback for closed-loop failure diagnosis and
recovery ( Zhi et al., 2025 ) . Frame-relation mining reduces redundant memory
and mitigates error accumulation ( Dang et al., 2023 ) , whereas TCoT
integrates hierarchical reasoning with global–local recovery ( Li et al., 2026 ) . Parallel temporal–spatial memory further captures
complementary motion and contextual cues ( Dang et al., 2024 ) .

We study a complementary runtime decision problem of distinguishing incorrect target binding from local execution failure and selectively applying the appropriate recovery mechanism. The pretrained VLA remains the default action generator.
As illustrated in Figure 1 , we aim to improve the robustness of pretrained VLA policies through runtime recovery without modifying the underlying policy. Our key observation is that perturbations induce distinct failure types. Target failures arise when incorrect grounding of the language-specified target object or reference relation directs the policy toward the wrong object instance before grasping. Execution failures occur when the target is correctly identified, but local control becomes unstable during grasping, transport, or placement. These failures manifest as empty grasps, failed lifts, unstable releases, or stalled execution. Distinguishing between these failure types allows an external controller to select targeted recovery mechanisms rather than apply generic retries.

Building on this observation, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time. Specialized agents coordinate task parsing, visual grounding, execution monitoring, and recovery through a shared execution state. FIT-MAC retains the pretrained VLA as the default action generator and intervenes only when task progress, target visibility, or grasping and placement signals indicate failure. It distinguishes incorrect target binding from local execution failure and routes them to target rebinding or bounded local recovery, respectively. This design enables selective, interpretable correction while limiting disruption to nominal execution and leaving the pretrained policy unchanged.

Experiments on LIBERO-Object and LIBERO-Spatial show that FIT-MAC consistently improves the robustness of OpenVLA, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} across diverse perturbations. The largest gains occur under position, task, and environment perturbations, where successful execution often requires target rebinding and stage-wise recovery. FIT-MAC also maintains high success rates under object and semantic perturbations, demonstrating its effectiveness across perturbation types. Our contributions are as follows:

We propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework that improves the robustness of VLA policies at inference time. Specialized agents coordinate monitoring, diagnosis, routing, and correction through a shared execution state, while the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator.

Specialized agents coordinate monitoring, diagnosis, routing, and correction through a shared execution state, while the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator.

We introduce a runtime verification and correction mechanism that assesses target grounding and execution progress to determine when to intervene. It distinguishes target-binding errors from local execution failures and addresses them through target rebinding and bounded local recovery, respectively.

FIT-MAC achieves state-of-the-art success rates across LIBERO-PRO perturbation settings and consistently improves the robustness of OpenVLA, π 0 \pi_{0} , and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} . Ablation studies further demonstrate the contribution of each component.

2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 RELATED WORK

Generalist VLA models learn language-conditioned visuomotor policies from heterogeneous robotic data. OpenVLA provides an open-source autoregressive foundation model ( Kim et al., 2024 ) . π 0 \pi_{0} uses flow matching for continuous action generation, while π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} improves open-world generalization through heterogeneous co-training ( Black et al., 2024 ; Intelligence et al., 2025 ) . NORA improves inference efficiency, X-VLA supports cross-embodiment transfer through soft prompts, and MolmoAct integrates depth-aware perception, spatial reasoning, and action prediction ( Hung et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2025 ) .
Recent approaches address long-horizon manipulation through hierarchical reasoning, memory, future-state prediction, and spatial representations. AtomVLA decomposes demonstrations into atomic subtasks and scores action chunks using a latent world model ( Sun et al., 2026 ) . LaMP incorporates a 3D scene-flow prior, R3DP introduces a real-time 3D-aware policy, and RoboTALES uses task-aligned simulated futures to guide policy learning ( Wang et al., 2026b ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Gani et al., 2026 ) . These methods modify the policy architecture, representation, or training procedure.

Benchmarks such as LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-X, VLATest, adversarial VLA benchmarks, and LIBERO-RECOVER assess VLA robustness to changes in objects, positions, language, observations, and environments ( Zhou et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2026a ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2025a ; Liu et al., 2026a ) . Existing methods improve robustness through perturbation-based training, post-training, uncertainty-aware action refinement, or latent world-model scoring ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2025a ; Islam et al., 2026 ; Sun et al., 2026 ) . VLS instead uses a vision-language model to steer a pretrained policy at inference time ( Liu et al., 2026b ) .

Runtime recovery methods monitor execution and intervene when failures occur. SAFE, RecoveryChaining, RACER, COME-robot, and TCoT explore failure detection, recovery to resumable states, VLM supervision, execution tracing, and hierarchical recovery ( Gu et al., 2026 ; Vats et al., 2025 ; Dai et al., 2025 ; Zhi et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . GTA-VLA uses interactive visual guidance, including points, boxes, and traces, to steer VLA execution under spatial and visual ambiguity ( Ling et al., 2026 ) . Code-based and agentic systems extend runtime recovery through execution feedback, visual verification, skill synthesis, and modular coordination ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ; Garrabé et al., 2025 ; Singh et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Yoon et al., 2026 ) .

Our method explicitly distinguishes target failures from execution failures and addresses them through target rebinding with closed-loop correction and bounded local grasping and placement control, respectively. The pretrained VLA remains the default action generator, and intervention is triggered only by runtime evidence of failure.

2026-10-21.title: Temporal Difference Learning of Probabilistic Reach-Avoid Value Functions
2026-10-21.authors: Elias Fontanari , Pietro Noah Crestaz , Matteo Saveriano , Andrea Del Prete
2026-10-21.comment: Submitted to ICRA 2027
2026-10-21.abstract: Reach-avoid sets, defining the states from which a task can be completed while avoiding unsafe regions, are fundamental tools for deploying robots in environments subject to disturbances and uncertainty, as well as for runtime task-feasibility monitoring, allowing prediction of whether a state is safe and will lead to successful task completion. Classical Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability (HJR) and its recent neural extensions (e.g., Lipschitz Continuous Reachability Learning, DeepReach) treat disturbances adversarially, computing the reach-avoid set under worst-case disturbances from a bounded set. This guarantees safety but can yield overly conservative sets when disturbances are stochastic rather than adversarial, and additionally requires the disturbance set to be known or specified in advance.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Autonomous robotic systems are increasingly deployed to perform complex tasks in environments subjected to different sources of noise and uncertainty. Determining, from a given state, whether a task of interest can be completed while satisfying critical safety constraints can often be framed in terms of the Reach-Avoid set : the set of states from which the system can reach a target region while avoiding an unsafe one. Avoid and Reach-Avoid sets are essential in runtime safety monitoring, as done in model predictive shielding [ 1 ] . Reach-avoid sets are also a useful tool for computing Control Invariant Sets (CIS) [ 2 ] : if the target set used to compute a reach-avoid set is itself control invariant, the resulting reach-avoid set is also control invariant, and typically larger. CISs are essential tools in safe control methods such as Model Predictive Control (MPC) [ 3 ] , since constraining the terminal state of the associated optimal control problem to lie in a CIS ensures recursive feasibility and constraint satisfaction.
Therefore, the accurate computation of reach-avoid sets is extremely useful for deploying robots in safety-critical settings.

Existing approaches to computing reach-avoid sets are predominantly grounded in Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability (HJR) [ 4 ] , which treats disturbances as an adversary selecting the worst-case action from a bounded set.
This comes with two main drawbacks: i) these methods cannot be applied to disturbances with unbounded support, such as a Gaussian distribution, and ii) when the disturbance is random they tend to be extremely conservative.
Classic HJR methods rely on grid-based dynamic programming over the state space, which scales exponentially with the system’s dimensionality, rendering them intractable for high-dimensional systems.

For this reason, the computation of reach-avoid sets has been addressed mainly by two lines of work, alleviating the curse of dimensionality: physics-informed neural networks such as DeepReach [ 5 ] , and reinforcement learning [ 6 , 7 ] .
DeepReach learns the reach-avoid set through a curriculum learning procedure that enforces the conditions of the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs partial differential equation (PDE).
RL-based methods, instead, learn a critic that encodes the safe set, replacing the PDE-based Hamilton-Jacobi formulation with a Bellman recursion that can be solved via RL algorithms.
However, in the adversarial setting the disturbance policy must be learned jointly with the control policy, turning training into a min-max optimization problem that is notoriously unstable and slow to converge.
In addition, the theoretical guarantees typically rely on regularity assumptions on the dynamics, most commonly Lipschitz continuity, which may not hold for hybrid or contact-rich systems.
DeepReach has been tested on large nonlinear systems such as quadrotors, but, unlike RL methods, it cannot be applied to non-differentiable dynamical systems, such as legged robots or black-box systems, since the dynamics is needed in the computation of the Hamiltonian.

A separate line of work, stochastic reachability analysis [ 8 ] , [ 9 ] , addresses reach-avoid problems directly as probabilities of success under a stochastic disturbance model, formulated via dynamic programming over the system’s transition kernel in a measure-theoretic setting.
While closer in spirit to our probabilistic formulation, these approaches rely on the numerical solution of the associated Bellman recursion over a gridded or otherwise explicitly represented state space, which precludes their use with the high-dimensional, black-box dynamics typical of robotic simulators.

In another line of work [ 10 ] the authors used actor-critic RL to learn a safe policy, where the critic expresses a pseudo-probability of future failure.
However, several aspects of this formulation limit its use as a set-computation method.
First, the critic addresses only the avoid component: it estimates the probability of failure with no notion of task completion and cannot distinguish states from which the task is achievable from states that are merely never-failing.
Second, the critic is defined with respect to the policy induced by the critic itself, a self-referential construction that the authors report to be excessively pessimistic early in training and that requires implementation-level corrections, namely computing Bellman targets under the unconstrained policy and maintaining a separate near-on-policy replay buffer.

Another method capable of computing reach-avoid sets, specifically used to compute CISs, is Viability Boundary Optimal Control (VBOC) [ 11 ] , which avoids resorting to HJR by directly identifying states on the boundary of the reach-avoid set and training a neural network to represent it. The target set corresponds to the system’s equilibria, while the avoid set represents collisions with the environment or joint limit violations. By directly learning the boundary of the reach-avoid set, VBOC achieves higher data efficiency compared to HJR, but its main drawbacks are that it does not account for disturbances and can only handle fully-actuated systems.

We introduce PVF ( P robabilistic Reach-Avoid V alue F unctions), addressing the typical drawbacks of HJR methods in settings where there is no adversary, but simply non-adversarial stochastic noise, as is often the case in robotics scenarios, wind disturbances acting on an aerial vehicle being a representative example.
By learning a value function that expresses, for each state, the probability of reaching the target set without ever entering the failure set, we are able to assess safe target reaching in a graded fashion: states that succeed under most disturbance realizations, and fail only under a highly unfavourable sequence of disturbances, are distinguished from states that fail under typical conditions.

Crucially, the entire procedure treats the system as a black box: it requires only the ability to sample transitions from the environment, with no access to an analytical model, no differentiability of the dynamics, and no knowledge of the disturbance distribution.
This makes the approach directly applicable to contact-rich and hybrid systems, such as legged robots, for which a closed-form model is either unavailable or non-differentiable, and where PDE-based methods cannot be applied. Fig. 1 provides an overview of the proposed method.

Additionally, our value function provides interpretable probabilities, as opposed to those computed by HJR methods, which provide either the worst-case constraint violation the trajectory will incur, or the value of the target-set membership function at the time the target is reached.

Summarizing, the contributions are the following: (i) a novel self-supervised method for computing probabilistic reach-avoid sets under stochastic disturbances with potentially unbounded support, without assuming worst-case behavior; (ii) a comparison against HJR-based baselines on systems of increasing complexity, up to a Hopper locomotion task, showing that the resulting sets are more interpretable, less conservative and more accurate under non-adversarial disturbances.

2026-10-21.title: PACT-VLA: Speculative Action-Chunk Verification with Pre-Commit Observations
2026-10-21.authors: Yixiang Zhu , Ruilong Wu , Yonghao Chen , Jiaxiang Zou , Yusong Hu , Xinyu Chen
2026-10-21.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are commonly deployed with asynchronous inference in real-world settings, where the next action chunk is generated while the robot is still executing the previous one. By the time the new chunk is committed, the robot and scene have changed, so the chunk is conditioned on a stale observation and task success drops sharply as this inference delay grows. Generating multiple candidate chunks could let newer observations inform the final choice, but existing multi-candidate methods either rank candidates
with the stale inference-start observation or repeatedly switch between
candidates during execution, which can make the executed action sequence
discontinuous. Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as decision time. While
candidate generation is still underway, candidate selection can reuse the VLA
itself to choose the complete action chunk that best fits a later observation. We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework that generates candidates from the inference-start observation and selects one using this pre-commit observation. Its scoring function, FlowRes, measures the residual between each candidate’s implied flow direction and the velocity predicted by the frozen policy under the pre-commit observation, requiring no separate verifier. A pipelined implementation overlaps observation processing with candidate generation and batches scoring, so selection adds no control-step delay on the evaluated hardware. At a four-step delay, PACT-VLA improves average success by 15.0 percentage points over RTC on Kinetix and by 5.2 points over single-candidate asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO, and it further improves existing delay-robust methods. On three real-robot tasks, it raises average success from 60% to 82% over naive asynchronous execution with the same frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} checkpoint.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Wen et al., 2024 ) increasingly predict action chunks rather than individual actions ( Li et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Black et al., 2024 ; Team et al., 2024 ) , allowing several control steps to be executed from a single policy inference and preserving temporal coherence across consecutive actions ( Black et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025 ) . However, action-chunk generation is not instantaneous. While inference is running, the robot continues to act and the surrounding scene may change. Consequently, by the time a newly generated chunk is ready for execution, the observation from which it was generated may already be stale, and the chunk may no longer fit the scene ( Black et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Agouzoul, 2026 ) .
The challenge is that action generation begins before later changes are observed.

Existing approaches address this challenge in different ways. Future-state methods use information available at inference start to
anticipate the conditions under which the next action chunk will be executed ( Tang et al., 2025 ) .
However, these methods determine the next action chunk before changes during
the current inference interval are observed, so the conditions at execution
may differ from what was anticipated. A natural alternative is to postpone
this decision by keeping multiple candidate action chunks available until more
information about the upcoming execution conditions becomes available. However, some test-time
sampling methods still rank these candidates using the inference-start
observation ( Kwok et al., 2025 ; Jang et al., 2026 ) , so the final choice
remains fixed before later changes are observed.

DreamChunk ( Chen et al., 2026 ) goes further by using a learned world model to predict a trajectory for each
candidate. As new observations arrive during execution, it compares them with
these predicted trajectories and repeatedly reselects which candidate to
follow.
This allows the choice to respond to newly observed changes, but keeping the
decision open during execution can cause repeated candidate switching, making
the executed action sequence discontinuous, which can hurt task performance. However, sensing
continues while the next chunk is being generated, so an observation arriving
during inference can already be available before commitment. This leaves open
whether such an observation can be used to finalize one complete action chunk
before commitment, without switching between candidates during execution.

Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as decision time. While
candidate generation is still underway, candidate selection can reuse the VLA
itself to choose the complete action chunk that best fits a later observation.
We propose PACT-VLA, which realizes this principle by generating a fixed
candidate pool from the inference-start observation and selecting one candidate
using a pre-commit observation received shortly before execution. To choose among the candidates, PACT-VLA uses the original
flow-based VLA policy ( Lipman et al., 2022 ; Black et al., 2024 ) to evaluate each
candidate under the pre-commit observation. We introduce FlowRes, which
measures the mismatch between the flow direction implied by each candidate
and the direction predicted by the frozen policy under this observation.
The candidate with the lowest FlowRes score is selected, and the controller
executes actions from the selected chunk until the next planned chunk switch.

Using a pre-commit observation leaves only a short interval for candidate selection before the planned chunk switch. PACT-VLA therefore processes the pre-commit observation while candidate generation is still running and scores all candidates in a single batch. On the evaluated hardware, the full generation-and-selection cycle remains in the same control-step delay bucket as single-candidate generation. Experiments on Kinetix, LIBERO, and three real-robot tasks demonstrate the benefit of this design. At a four-step delay, PACT-VLA improves average success by 15.0 percentage points over RTC on Kinetix and by 5.2 points over single-candidate asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO. Across the three real-robot tasks, average success increases from 60% to 82% using the same frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} checkpoint.

Our contributions are as follows.

We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework for action selection
under inference delay. PACT-VLA uses observations arriving during inference
to select one complete action chunk before commitment, reducing the
prediction–execution mismatch.

We introduce FlowRes, a candidate-verification method that reuses the
frozen VLA to rank candidates under the pre-commit observation, without
additional training or a separate verifier.

We design a pipelined implementation that overlaps pre-commit observation processing with candidate generation and batches candidate verification.

Experiments on Kinetix, LIBERO, and real robots show gains across multiple flow-based VLA policies and further improvements when combined with existing delay-robust methods.

1. We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework for action selection
under inference delay. PACT-VLA uses observations arriving during inference
to select one complete action chunk before commitment, reducing the
prediction–execution mismatch.

2. We introduce FlowRes, a candidate-verification method that reuses the
frozen VLA to rank candidates under the pre-commit observation, without
additional training or a separate verifier.

3. We design a pipelined implementation that overlaps pre-commit observation processing with candidate generation and batches candidate verification.

4. Experiments on Kinetix, LIBERO, and real robots show gains across multiple flow-based VLA policies and further improvements when combined with existing delay-robust methods.

## 2.1 Flow-Based Action-Chunk Generation under Inference Delay
