## 2.2 Action Generation and Selection under Inference Delay

Existing methods address the prediction–execution mismatch in different ways.
One approach is to predict what the robot will be like when the next chunk is
executed. VLASH ( Tang et al., 2025 ) predicts the robot state at the expected
execution time and generates the next action chunk based on that prediction.
However, the robot may continue to change during inference, so its state at
execution may differ from the prediction.

A different approach is to keep multiple candidate action chunks available
instead of fixing one chunk immediately. Some test-time sampling methods
generate multiple candidates but rank them using the inference-start
observation o t o_{t} , as shown in Figure 1 (a) ( Kwok et al., 2025 ; Jang et al., 2026 ) . Later observations therefore
cannot change which candidate is selected.
DreamChunk ( Chen et al., 2026 ) goes further by using a learned world model
to predict a trajectory for each candidate. As new observations arrive during
execution, it compares them with the predicted trajectories and repeatedly
reselects which candidate to follow, as shown in
Figure 1 (b). This allows the choice to respond to
newly observed changes, but keeping the decision open during execution can
cause repeated candidate switching, making the executed action sequence
discontinuous, which can hurt task performance.
Sensing, however, continues while the next chunk is being generated, so a
later observation can already be available before commitment.
This leaves
open whether the inference interval itself can be used to complete the choice
of one complete action chunk before commitment.

## 2.3 Our Insight

Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as a decision-making window. While candidate generation is still ongoing, the selection process can already leverage a later observation, and the VLA itself can determine which complete action chunk best fits that observation before commitment.
PACT-VLA builds on this idea by generating a fixed candidate pool from the
inference-start observation and completing selection with a pre-commit
observation. Section 3 describes how FlowRes reuses the frozen
VLA to evaluate the candidates and how pipelined execution completes the
selection before the planned chunk switch.

2026-10-21.title: Knowing When to Stop Thinking: A Dissection of Expected Free Energy as a Test-Time Compute Controller for Latent World-Model Planning
2026-10-21.authors: Tong Zhang , Zhiyuan Shi , Yun Peng , Tao Xie
2026-10-21.abstract: A planner using a learned world model can improve its predicted outcome while choosing a worse action. We study when expected free energy (EFE) can help decide how much computation to spend on a plan. An EFE-inspired objective combines goal distance with disagreement among stochastic predictions. We test candidate scoring, stopping, and online predictor updates separately. Stopping when elite cost stalls reduces refinement on tasks whose success plateaus with depth, with mean success close to fixed-depth references. At the larger tested weights, rewarding disagreement lowers success with a frozen model. Penalizing it helps at some task and weight settings but harms others. When training data omit a region needed to reach the goal, online updates recover part of the resulting loss. The tested cost-stall rule can fail when further optimization exploits model errors, because predicted cost keeps falling after task success peaks. Cost progress can guide computation on a plateau, but protecting performance after a peak requires information about the consequences of the chosen actions.
2026-10-21.introduction:
A robot planning from images can improve its next action by repeatedly imagining and comparing possible futures. Each refinement step costs computation. Stopping too early may leave a useful action undiscovered. Continuing too long can favor an action that exploits errors in the learned dynamics. The planner must decide whether further optimization will improve the action it executes.

Test-time computation has improved iterative reasoning and model-based control. Recurrent language models refine internal representations before producing an answer ( Geiping et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025 ) . World-model agents predict future states to evaluate candidate actions ( Hafner et al., 2023 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) . A larger optimization budget gives the planner more opportunities to improve a plan. Its objective, however, remains a prediction of task performance. A fixed budget cannot respond to differences between instances, and convergence of the objective does not establish that the predicted consequences are correct.

Expected free energy (EFE) connects goal achievement and information seeking ( Friston, 2010 ; Parr et al., 2022 ) . Its pragmatic component favors preferred outcomes, and its epistemic component values information. These components suggest ways to control planning. Goal progress may indicate when refinement has stalled. Prediction uncertainty may change which plan the agent selects. New observations may improve the model before the next decision. Disagreement-based exploration methods collect information during learning ( Sekar et al., 2020 ) , whereas uncertainty penalties discourage plans that rely on unreliable predictions ( Yu et al., 2020 ) . Whether disagreement helps immediate task execution with a frozen predictor remains unclear. Internal progress may also fail to reveal when more planning becomes harmful.

We test these decisions with a compact latent world model and a sampling planner. In Figure 1 , candidate trajectories provide goal cost and disagreement among stochastic predictions. We vary the disagreement weight and stopping statistic with the model frozen. We then test stopping in additional planner families and remove training data from a required region to study online learning. These comparisons separate the effects of reducing refinement, changing action selection, and updating the predictor.

Cost-stall rules reduce refinement on tasks whose success plateaus with depth, with mean success close to fixed-depth references. A best-elite baseline is competitive and often stops earlier. On tasks whose success declines after a peak, falling cost sustains harmful refinement. Rewarding disagreement reduces frozen-model planning success, whereas penalties help at selected task and weight settings. Online updates improve success when the agent must enter a region missing from its training data.

Our experiments address the stopping decision and the uses of prediction uncertainty.

We separate candidate scoring, stopping, and online adaptation in a common world-model planning protocol.

We measure when cost-stall controllers reduce planning effort and when model exploitation defeats the tested stopping signals.

We measure the task-dependent effects of disagreement penalties and test online learning by removing training data from a required region.

1. We separate candidate scoring, stopping, and online adaptation in a common world-model planning protocol.

2. We measure when cost-stall controllers reduce planning effort and when model exploitation defeats the tested stopping signals.

3. We measure the task-dependent effects of disagreement penalties and test online learning by removing training data from a required region.

# 2 Related Work

Active inference formulates perception and action through free-energy objectives ( Friston, 2010 ; Parr et al., 2022 ) . Deep implementations combine learned representations with approximate inference ( Ueltzhöffer, 2018 ; Fountas et al., 2020 ; Mazzaglia et al., 2021 ; Mazzaglia et al., 2022 ) . The information-seeking term requires assumptions beyond free-energy minimization ( Millidge et al., 2021 ) , and Bellman-optimality results hold under specified conditions ( Da Costa et al., 2023 ) . We use this framework to motivate a cost combining goal distance and stochastic prediction disagreement. Disagreement provides an uncertainty proxy. It is not a calibrated estimate of information gain.

Learned latent dynamics support planning from images ( Hafner et al., 2019 ; Hansen et al., 2022 ; Assran et al., 2025 ) . We build on LeWM, a compact joint-embedding predictive architecture that predicts future image representations ( Maes et al., 2026 ) . Dreamer improves policies through imagined returns ( Hafner et al., 2023 ) , whereas Plan2Explore uses disagreement to gather experience during learning ( Sekar et al., 2020 ) . Our frozen-model experiments test disagreement for immediate goal-directed execution. The adaptation experiment tests what changes when observed transitions update the predictor.

Adaptive computation allocates different amounts of work to different inputs ( Graves, 2016 ) . Recurrent and recursive reasoning apply this idea to internal model computation ( Geiping et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Jolicoeur-Martineau, 2025 ) . We study stopping inside sampling-based model predictive control and compare statistics from the same optimization process. Pessimistic offline reinforcement learning addresses unreliable estimates through model uncertainty penalties in MOPO ( Yu et al., 2020 ) and conservative value estimates in CQL ( Kumar et al., 2020 ) . We compare a disagreement penalty with a disagreement reward. The coverage experiment then tests a setting where the goal requires entering a region absent from training, so avoiding uncertain dynamics cannot solve the task.

2026-10-21.title: LocoPilot: Single-Operator Bilateral Teleoperation for Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning
2026-10-21.authors: Antonio Langella , Giovanni Minelli , Giovanni B. Dessy , Lorenzo Amatucci , Giulio Turrisi , Victor Barasuol , Claudio Semini
2026-10-21.abstract:
Learning loco-manipulation policies requires demonstrations that
capture coordinated base and arm motion on the target embodiment.
Robot-free interfaces allow demonstrations to be collected
independently of the target robot, increasing flexibility but
without directly capturing platform-specific commands, proprioception, and
body-mounted observations. On-robot teleoperation allows to capture these signals directly, but requires an interface capable of commanding the complete system concurrently.
This paper presents LocoPilot, a single-operator bilateral teleoperation and
data-collection framework implemented on a 12-DoF Unitree Go2
quadruped equipped with a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator, an Intel
RealSense D435 wrist camera, and an Intel RealSense D405 head
camera. A second 6-DoF Piper L arm, used as the leader and two
handheld controllers provide simultaneous control of the base,
body posture, manipulator, and gripper. The follower arm interaction forces are estimated without a
dedicated force/torque sensor and rendered to the operator through a
passivity-constrained haptic channel. A ROS 2 pipeline records
synchronized multimodal observations together with a unified
11D action shared by teleoperation and
policy deployment. Compared to prior work, LocoPilot uniquely unifies robot-in-the-loop legged data collection,
force feedback without motion-capture instrumentation, and the
same action interface at deployment. We evaluate the interface across multiple
loco-manipulation tasks and validate the complete
collection-to-deployment pipeline by fine-tuning MolmoAct2 [ 1 ] on
pick-and-place demonstrations and deploying on
the physical robot without action retargeting or additional inverse
kinematics.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Robots capable of both locomotion and manipulation extend physical interaction beyond the workspace of fixed-base manipulators. Arm-equipped quadruped robots are particularly suited to unstructured environments, where they combine legged mobility with physical interaction capabilities. Prior work has explored legged loco-manipulation through model-based whole-body control [ 2 ] , or learned
coordination of locomotion and manipulation [ 3 , 4 ] .
More recently, generalist Visual Language Action (VLA) models have gained increasing attention
for learning manipulation behaviors from multimodal demonstrations,
leveraging large-scale visual and language representations [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . For loco-manipulation, however, such
demonstrations must capture both base and arm actions on the target
embodiment. Ideally, the collection interface should therefore
minimize the collection–deployment gap while preserving direct
operator authority over all task-relevant commands.

Existing systems trade off these requirements in different ways:

Teleoperation systems place a human directly in the control loop of the physical robot, combining the operator task understanding with the constraints of the target embodiment. Leader-follower interfaces with direct joint correspondence provide intuitive control of fixed-base manipulators [ 9 , 10 ] , while mounting the same kind of interface on a wheeled base extends the concept to mobile manipulation, recording base motion alongside bimanual manipulation [ 11 ] . XR-based systems provide more general cross-embodiment interfaces [ 12 , 13 ] , and DROID demonstrates the use of teleoperation for standardized large-scale data collection [ 14 ] .
Immersive interfaces additionally stream the robot’s own onboard imagery to the operator [ 12 ] , allowing real-time inspection of the visual inputs that will directly condition the downstream policy.
For arm-equipped quadrupeds, previous systems have used wearable motion capture, joysticks, haptic devices, or hand gestures [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] . Collecting directly on the target robot reduces observation and action mismatch, but simultaneously commanding all task-relevant DoFs becomes increasingly difficult for a single operator.

Robot-free interfaces make the opposite trade-off. The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) [ 19 ] records demonstrations using a sensorized handheld gripper, allowing the operator to demonstrate manipulation without the kinematic constraints of the target robot. This improves collection flexibility, but omits embodiment-specific signals such as base
commands, proprioception, and body-mounted observations. Deployment therefore requires an additional mapping from demonstrated
end-effector motion to the target embodiment, as in UMI on Legs [ 20 ] .

This work aims to combine the collection-deployment consistency
of on-robot teleoperation with the flexibility of learning-based
interfaces for arm-equipped quadrupeds. As illustrated in
Fig. , both the human operator and the
learned policy act through the same loco-manipulation interface,
while the resulting demonstrations are collected directly on the
target platform. Achieving this requires addressing two main
challenges.

The first challenge is enabling a single operator to command the
entire loco-manipulation action concurrently. Reaching and grasping
may require the robot to translate, rotate, or change body posture
while the arm is moving, so sequential base and manipulator control
produces segmented demonstrations rather than the smooth continuous
coordination desired from the final policy. Existing systems address
this through multiple operators, wearable instrumentation, or
partial autonomy, introducing additional coordination or removing
task decisions from the demonstrator.

To retain these decisions under single-operator control, we propose a bimanual interface design where a handheld controller is mounted on the end-effector handle of the leader arm. The dominant hand articulates the manipulator while
operating the mounted controller, and the non-dominant hand provides
the remaining base commands through a second controller. Together,
the two interfaces provide concurrent control of planar base
velocity, yaw rate, body pitch, arm configuration, and gripper
aperture. Interaction forces at the follower are additionally
estimated online and rendered through the leader arm, providing
contact feedback without a dedicated force/torque sensor.

The second challenge is maintaining consistency between collection
and deployment. On a legged manipulator, high-level commands are
executed through a locomotion and manipulation stack whose behavior
also shapes the recorded motion. Replacing this stack at deployment
can therefore shift the distribution of observations and executed
motions away from the demonstrated one, even when the high-level
action representation is unchanged.
We avoid this by using the same 11-dimensional loco-manipulation
action in both regimes and by keeping the same downstream execution
modules: the locomotion policy and leg controller, the arm controller,
and the gripper interface.
During collection, the action is generated by the
operator, whereas at deployment it is generated by the learned
policy; the locomotion policy, arm controller, and gripper interface
remain unchanged.
Table I compares LocoPilot with the closest prior
systems in terms of the teleoperation and data-collection properties
discussed above.
The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows:

A single-operator bilateral teleoperation interface for
arm-equipped quadrupeds, combining concurrent base, body, arm,
and gripper control with sensorless force reflection and an
operator-side passivity layer.

A unified 11-dimensional action interface shared between
teleoperation and learned-policy deployment, with the same
locomotion and manipulation controllers used in both regimes.

A synchronized learning-oriented data pipeline recording
multi-camera RGB-D observations, robot state, odometry, and
commanded actions, validated through multiple teleoperation
tasks and real-robot deployment of a fine-tuned MolmoAct2 policy.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows:
Section II presents the hardware and
software architecture. Section III the
teleoperation mapping and unified command.
Section IV reports the teleoperation
experiments and validates the collected demonstrations through
real-robot deployment. Section VI draws the final conclusions.

arm-equipped quadrupeds, combining concurrent base, body, arm,
and gripper control with sensorless force reflection and an
operator-side passivity layer.

2. A unified 11-dimensional action interface shared between

locomotion and manipulation controllers used in both regimes.

# II System Overview

## II-A Hardware

Figure shows both the teleoperation setup and the system being controlled.
In particular, the follower platform, shown on the right, consists of a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator and parallel gripper.
Two RGB-D cameras provide complementary observations: an Intel RealSense D435 mounted near the gripper captures close-range manipulation, while an Intel RealSense D405 mounted on the quadruped head, thanks to its larger field of view, observes the wider workspace in front of the robot.
This platform is the same during both demonstration collection and autonomous deployment.

The leader station, on the left of Fig. 2 , is used only during data collection.
It is built around a second Piper L arm serving as a leader device.
A custom handle at the end-effector improves ergonomics and holds one of two Nintendo Joy-Con controllers [ 21 ] .
The operator grips this handle with the dominant hand and articulates the leader arm. With the thumb of the same hand, the operator reaches the controller’s analog stick and buttons, which respectively control the quadruped robot pitch and yaw rate and the episode markers, while the index finger controls the gripper through the trigger button.
With the non-dominant hand the operator holds the second controller, which commands the base velocity.
The configuration shown in Fig. 2 assumes a right-handed operator: for left-handed operation, a specular handle can be employed while swapping the controller assignment without changing the teleoperation scheme.

To ensure visual consistency, the operator drives the robot using the exact onboard camera streams recorded for downstream policy training, displayed in real time at the leader station. This visual alignment ensures the demonstrator and the policy share the exact same perspective.At the same time, placing all commands under a single operator makes it easy to execute base and arm movements concurrently instead of sequentially; for instance, the operator can steer and turn the quadruped while reaching toward an out-of-reach object in a single coordinated motion.

## II-B Software Architecture

On the software side, the framework is composed of interconnected, distributed modules running on the quadruped’s onboard computer and an operator workstation, as shown in Fig. 3 .
In particular, the quadruped’s onboard computer runs: the reinforcement-learning base policy of [ 22 ] , which converts base-velocity and body-pitch references into joint position targets for a low-level PD controller; the MUSE state estimator [ 23 ] , which provides the state estimates used as input by the policy; the arm control stack; and the camera nodes, which publish the two RGB-D streams.

As a direct consequence of unifying the action and observation interfaces, the same software modules run on the robot both for data collection and for autonomous deployment.
What changes between the two modes is the operator side.
During demonstration collection the workstation runs: the leader arm control stack; the teleoperation module described in Sec. III-A that couples leader and follower and renders contact back to the operator; and the recording module that assembles episodes from the observation, state, and command streams.
During autonomous deployment a single policy-inference node replaces all three, receiving the same observations and emitting the same commands the teleoperation loop previously produced.
The switch between the operator and the policy therefore falls at one interface, and everything after it is unaffected by which of the two is in control.

Having defined explicit software interfaces that decouple the teleoperation and autonomous deployment stack from the underlying robot hardware, each hardware-dependent subsystem can be replaced independently, provided that it preserves the corresponding input-output contract.
In particular, the locomotion subsystem, including the base, leg controller, reinforcement-learning policy, and state estimator, can be replaced by any implementation that accepts commanded planar velocity and absolute body pitch and exposes the leg states and base-velocity estimate required by the higher-level stack.
Likewise, the manipulation subsystem can be replaced by any arm and
controller implementation that supports joint-space impedance control
and exposes joint position, velocity, and torque feedback.
All components above these interfaces, including the teleoperation logic, action representation, and data-collection pipeline, remain unchanged.

This interface-based organization therefore reduces the engineering effort required to port the framework to a different platform and makes the overall architecture modular at both the software and hardware levels.
The present implementation uses ROS 2 Jazzy with Cyclone DDS.
Section III details the central elements of the software stack, i.e., the teleoperation and data collection modules.

2026-10-21.title: Learning Tactile-Aware Hand Representations from Human Hand-Object Interaction Data
2026-10-21.authors: Yeonguk Yu , Jaehong Kim , Byungok Han
2026-10-21.abstract: Tactile representation learning for dexterous manipulation often requires substantial robot-side data collection, limiting its scalability across different hands and sensors. We explore whether large-scale human hand-object interaction (HOI) data can provide a useful prior for robotic tactile learning. To this end, we propose HuTact , a framework that pretrains tactile-aware hand representations from human HOI data without requiring real tactile signals during pretraining. HuTact transfers the interaction structure learned from human hand motions to robotic tactile observations and can be further adapted with a small amount of unlabeled robot interaction data. We evaluate HuTact on tactile perception and manipulation tasks, including grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning. Across these tasks, human HOI pretraining improves data efficiency and provides a strong initialization for downstream learning. Notably, with HOI pretraining followed by midtraining on unlabeled robot play data, HuTact achieves 88.26% Macro-F1 on grasp prediction using only 25% of the labeled downstream data, comparable to training from scratch on the full labeled dataset (88.23%). These results suggest that human interaction data can serve as a scalable complementary source for robotic tactile representation learning.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Tactile sensing enables humans to perceive and interact with the physical world, providing direct information about contact, force, texture, and motion that is difficult to obtain through vision alone [ 1 ] .
Inspired by this remarkable human capability, tactile sensing has emerged as a critical modality for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to perceive subtle contact interactions, infer local physical properties, and regulate contact forces during complex manipulation tasks that demand precise and adaptive physical interaction [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] .

Accordingly, a wide range of tactile sensors have been developed to capture rich information arising from physical contact, including vision-based sensors (e.g., GelSight [ 2 ] , DIGIT [ 5 ] ) and magnetic-based sensors (e.g., AnySkin [ 4 ] , ReSkin [ 6 ] ).
Beyond advances in tactile sensing hardware, the growing availability of large-scale tactile interaction data has further motivated learning-based approaches to extract generalizable representations from raw tactile observations [ 7 ] . In particular, recent works have explored self-supervised pretraining using large-scale tactile interaction data collected with respective tactile sensors, learning representations that can be transferred to downstream manipulation tasks [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] .

Learning generalizable tactile representations can reduce the amount of task-specific data required for downstream tasks. For vision-based tactile sensing, Feng et al. propose AnyTouch [ 12 ] , which learns transferable representations from a sensor-aligned dataset collected across multiple visuo-tactile sensors. For non-vision-based tactile sensing, Sharma et al. [ 8 ] apply DINO-based self-distillation to masked tactile sequences collected from a dexterous hand, while Guzey et al. [ 9 ] pretrain tactile representations using task-agnostic robotic play data. However, existing approaches for non-vision-based tactile sensors still largely require real tactile interaction data collected directly with the target robotic hand and sensing hardware. As a result, adapting representation learning to a new robotic platform or tactile sensor requires additional data collection, introducing substantial time and cost for pretraining.

As an alternative, human hand-object interaction (HOI) data provide a promising source of pretraining supervision, where they contain large-scale and diverse interactions across objects, hand configurations, and manipulation behaviors [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . These datasets are particularly attractive for learning transferable hand representations because they provide (1) interaction patterns that can be shared across different hand embodiments, (2) large-scale interaction data that would be costly to collect on robotic platforms, and (3) an opportunity to reduce embodiment-specific data collection when adapting to a new robotic hand. Many of these datasets also provide temporally aligned 3D reconstructions of human hands and manipulated objects, allowing fingertip configurations and their evolution during interaction to be recovered without collecting data on a robotic platform. Although HOI datasets do not contain real tactile signals, their hand–object trajectories encode spatial and temporal structure associated with physical interaction. We hypothesize that this structure can serve as a transferable prior for robotic tactile representation learning and reduce the amount of robot-side tactile data required for adaptation.

In this work, our research question is: Can human hand-object interaction (HOI) data provide a transferable prior for robotic tactile representation learning? To answer this question, we propose HuTact , a framework for learning tactile-aware robot hand representations from human HOI data.
Rather than attempting to reconstruct real tactile signals from human data, HuTact learns the spatial and temporal structure of hand interactions from wrist-local fingertip trajectories.
To bridge human HOI pretraining and robotic tactile sensing, we separately tokenize fingertip coordinates and tactile observations, allowing the coordinate representation and shared Transformer backbone learned from HOI data to be retained while adapting the sensor-specific tactile input embedding. We further incorporate geometry-derived pseudo-contact signals as an auxiliary cue, encouraging the model to capture the relationship between fingertip coordinates and their corresponding tactile-like signals. This framework enables large-scale human interaction data to provide a transferable initialization for tactile-aware robot learning while reducing the amount of robot-side tactile data required for adaptation.

To validate the effectiveness and transferability of HuTact, we evaluate it on tactile-sensitive downstream tasks, including grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and policy learning on tactile-sensitive tasks, and analyze the factors that enable transfer from human HOI data to robotic tactile sensing. In summary, our contributions are as follows:

We propose HuTact, a framework that uses large-scale human hand-object interaction data to pretrain tactile-aware robot hand representations without requiring real tactile signals during the initial pretraining stage.

We show that representations learned from HOI data transfer to robotic tactile perception and manipulation, improving grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning.

We provide systematic analyses of the transfer mechanism through architectural ablations and data-efficiency experiments, studying the roles of temporal modeling, token separation, pseudo-contact cues, and robot-side midtraining. Our results show that HOI pretraining can substantially reduce the amount of task-specific robotic tactile data required for downstream adaptation.

1. We propose HuTact, a framework that uses large-scale human hand-object interaction data to pretrain tactile-aware robot hand representations without requiring real tactile signals during the initial pretraining stage.

2. We show that representations learned from HOI data transfer to robotic tactile perception and manipulation, improving grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning.

3. We provide systematic analyses of the transfer mechanism through architectural ablations and data-efficiency experiments, studying the roles of temporal modeling, token separation, pseudo-contact cues, and robot-side midtraining. Our results show that HOI pretraining can substantially reduce the amount of task-specific robotic tactile data required for downstream adaptation.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

Tactile Sensing: Tactile sensors for robotic manipulation broadly include vision-based and non-optical sensing modalities. Vision-based sensors [ 2 , 5 ] capture fine-grained contact geometry and have been applied to object identification [ 17 ] , geometry sensing [ 18 , 3 ] , pose estimation [ 19 , 20 ] , and policy learning [ 21 , 22 ] . However, their optical components can result in a relatively large form factor, making integration across multiple fingers challenging. Non-optical sensors instead use compact magnetic [ 4 , 23 ] or capacitive sensing elements [ 24 ] to enable distributed tactile sensing. In this work, we use the BrainCo Revo 2 hand [ 25 ] , which is equipped with fingertip capacitive sensors that measure normal force, tangential force, tangential-force direction, and proximity.

Tactile Representation Learning: Recent work has explored transferable tactile representations through large-scale self-supervised pretraining. For vision-based tactile sensors, objectives developed for visual representation learning [ 26 , 27 , 28 ] have been adapted to tactile observations [ 29 , 10 , 12 , 11 ] . For skin-like tactile sensors, Sharma et al. [ 8 ] apply self-distillation to masked tactile sequences from a dexterous hand, while Guzey et al. [ 9 ] pretrain tactile representations using task-agnostic robotic play data. While these approaches demonstrate the benefits of tactile pretraining, they generally require interaction data collected with the target robot and tactile sensor. In contrast, HuTact initializes tactile-aware representations from human hand–object interaction data without real tactile signals. We pretrain on the spatial and temporal structure of wrist-local fingertip interactions, augmented with geometry-derived pseudo-contact cues, and subsequently adapt the representation to the target robotic tactile sensor.

Robot Learning from Human Data: Human interaction data have been increasingly used to reduce robot-specific supervision for manipulation learning [ 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 , 34 ] , by extracting hand poses, object motions, and interaction trajectories from large-scale demonstrations. HOI data have also been applied directly to dexterous manipulation: Zhao et al. [ 35 ] retarget human hand-object interactions to dexterous robot hands and learn a residual policy for embodiment mismatch, while Zeng et al. [ 36 ] use HOI data for vision-language-action learning. Large-scale datasets such as OakInk2 [ 16 ] , TACO [ 37 ] , ARCTIC [ 38 ] , and HOT3D [ 39 ] provide scalable supervision for learning hand–object interaction structure. HuTact differs in objective: rather than transferring human motion directly to a robot policy, we use HOI data to pretrain a tactile-aware hand representation that is subsequently adapted to real robotic tactile sensing. To our knowledge, prior work has not systematically studied large-scale HOI data as a pretraining source for robotic tactile representation learning.

2026-10-21.title: EventSync: Event-Driven Memory Updates for History-Dependent Manipulation
2026-10-21.authors: Jingjiao Zhao , Dong Jing , Mingyu Cao , Ruochuan Shi , Xiansheng Chen , Pengwei Wang , Zhiwu Lu
2026-10-21.abstract:
History-dependent robotic manipulation requires task context and interaction history, as the current observation alone is insufficient to determine the next action.
Hierarchical frameworks use task memory for high-level subgoal reasoning and low-level policies for execution.
However, memory updates require accurate completion assessment: similar observations may correspond to different execution phases, and prematurely recording completion can mislead subsequent subgoal reasoning.
We present EventSync , a hierarchical framework that coordinates task reasoning and action execution through event-driven memory updates.
A vision-language model generates subgoals from task plans and interaction history, while a vision-language-action model executes them.
A lightweight Event Monitor combines visual observations with end-effector trajectories to determine whether the current subgoal is complete.
The framework records the current subgoal in its completed-subgoal history and triggers subsequent reasoning only after obtaining completion evidence.
With visual history in the executor, EventSync achieves 64.5% overall success on RoboMME, exceeding the best baseline reported in the benchmark by 20.0 percentage points.
Further analysis shows that this update mechanism helps build a reliable completed-subgoal history.
Experiments on four real-robot tasks with different memory requirements validate the framework’s effectiveness in real-world robotic manipulation.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Real-world robotic manipulation often requires decisions based on previous interactions.
In assembly, tidying, and everyday service tasks, earlier requirements and interaction outcomes can determine what the robot should do next [ 19 ] .
History may also be needed to interpret the current phase of an ongoing operation.
Such tasks are non-Markovian with respect to instantaneous observations: robots must retain task context and interpret execution history to select subsequent goals and actions [ 18 , 31 , 11 , 9 ] .

Prior work introduces memory into vision-language-action (VLA) models to use historical information [ 23 , 31 , 39 , 38 ] , while other approaches assign task memory to a high-level reasoner that guides action execution through subgoals [ 36 , 7 ] .
We argue that hierarchical frameworks are well suited to history-dependent manipulation.
The limited performance of hierarchical methods reported in existing evaluations [ 9 ] motivates us to revisit memory updates within this framework.
As illustrated in Fig. 1 , an instruction issued by the high-level reasoner does not imply that the corresponding operation has been completed, and similar current poses may correspond to different execution phases.
If an unfinished operation is recorded as completed, subsequent reasoning may rely on an incorrect estimate of task progress and advance to the next subgoal prematurely.
For task-memory updates, completion judgments must be accurate enough to avoid premature goal transitions and timely enough to keep subsequent reasoning and actions aligned with execution progress.

We propose EventSync , a hierarchical framework that coordinates task reasoning and action execution through event-driven memory updates.
A Memory Reasoner built on a vision-language model (VLM) obtains a task plan and combines it with interaction history to generate subgoals, which a VLA-based Action Executor executes.
EventSync maintains an event state for the current operation, and a lightweight Event Monitor with 87.39M total parameters estimates completion from visual observations and end-effector trajectories.
The framework adds the current subgoal to the completed-subgoal history and triggers high-level reasoning for the next subgoal only after obtaining completion evidence.

With visual history in the executor, EventSync achieves a 64.5% overall success rate on RoboMME, exceeding FrameSamp+Modul, the best baseline reported in the benchmark, by 20.0 percentage points [ 9 ] .
Our variant without visual history in the executor achieves 94.0% on SwingXtimes, compared with the 7.3% reported for the hierarchical framework GroundSG + QwenVL [ 9 ] .
Analysis of execution records further shows that updates guided by completion evidence help reduce premature progression and build a reliable completed-subgoal history.
Experiments on four real-robot tasks further demonstrate the effectiveness of combining task-memory reasoning with event-driven memory updates.

Our contributions are as follows:

A hierarchical memory framework for history-dependent manipulation. We introduce EventSync, in which a high-level reasoner manages task memory and generates subgoals, a low-level policy executes actions, and an independent lightweight monitor provides completion feedback.

Event-driven task-memory updates. We design a lightweight Event Monitor that combines visual observations with end-effector trajectories to assess operation completion, using the resulting evidence to trigger updates to the completed-subgoal history and subsequent high-level reasoning.

Empirical evaluation in simulation and on real robots. We evaluate EventSync on the RoboMME simulation benchmark and real-robot tasks to assess its effectiveness in history-dependent manipulation, with comparisons and ablations examining the role of event-driven memory updates.

1. A hierarchical memory framework for history-dependent manipulation. We introduce EventSync, in which a high-level reasoner manages task memory and generates subgoals, a low-level policy executes actions, and an independent lightweight monitor provides completion feedback.

2. Event-driven task-memory updates. We design a lightweight Event Monitor that combines visual observations with end-effector trajectories to assess operation completion, using the resulting evidence to trigger updates to the completed-subgoal history and subsequent high-level reasoning.

3. Empirical evaluation in simulation and on real robots. We evaluate EventSync on the RoboMME simulation benchmark and real-robot tasks to assess its effectiveness in history-dependent manipulation, with comparisons and ablations examining the role of event-driven memory updates.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Memory for Robotic Manipulation

Research on robot memory studies how to retain task-relevant history for subsequent decisions.
Existing methods preserve interaction history through recurrent states [ 23 ] , spatial memory [ 11 ] , and historical feature aggregation and retrieval [ 21 , 31 ] .
Compressed context [ 17 , 38 ] , motion trajectories overlaid on images [ 40 ] , and visual evidence selected by event predictions [ 39 ] further provide temporal information for action prediction.
MemER [ 36 ] retrieves historical keyframes for subgoal generation and runs reasoning asynchronously with control.
RoboMME [ 9 ] systematically evaluates how memory representations and their integration with action policies affect history-dependent manipulation.

## II-B Vision-Language Reasoning and Closed-Loop Control

Language-conditioned manipulation policies combine semantic and spatial representations to map instructions to actions [ 33 , 34 ] .
Generalist robot policies and VLA models, including RT-1 [ 6 ] , RT-2 [ 5 ] , OpenVLA [ 20 ] , Octo [ 12 ] , RDT-1B [ 26 ] , and the π \pi family [ 4 , 30 ] , support action generation from visual observations and language instructions.
High-level reasoning further organizes low-level execution through environment-grounded task planning [ 1 , 10 ] , language-based action abstractions [ 3 , 32 ] , or predicted trajectories [ 24 ] .
Programmatic control [ 25 ] and 3D value maps [ 15 ] also provide interfaces between language requirements and robot control.

Execution feedback allows subsequent decisions to adapt to actual observations.
Prior work supports replanning and execution recovery through success detection and scene feedback [ 16 ] , precondition checking [ 35 ] , constraint monitoring [ 13 ] , and failure explanation [ 27 ] .
Recently, τ 0 \tau_{0} -VLA [ 7 ] has combined world-model-guided subtask search with a high-level model that jointly updates execution memory and generates subgoals.
EventSync separates completion monitoring from high-level goal reasoning.
A lightweight Event Monitor combines visual observations and end-effector trajectories to provide completion evidence, which governs additions to the completed-subgoal history and triggers subsequent high-level reasoning.

2026-10-21.title: What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns: A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation for Teleoperated Demonstration
2026-10-21.authors: Amane Yamaguchi , Shohei Kamiguchi , Masashi Hamaya , Shigeo Yoshida , Takuji Narumi , Mai Nishimura
2026-10-21.abstract:
Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts’ in number and inter-trial consistency.
Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them, has not been examined.
We study this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders a multi-fingered robot hand as sparse keypoints at its fingertips and joints, the same keypoints a policy can observe.
In a simulated mug-in-box task, 18 novices and 4 experts collected 2,200 trials under three renderings: the real shape of the hand, all keypoints emphasized, or the thumb and index finger alone emphasized.
The novices shown the thumb and index finger emphasized collected 441 successful demonstrations from 600 trials, against 320 for those shown the real shape.
We then trained diffusion policies on these demonstrations, replacing the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state they observe with the hand keypoints and two object keypoints.
Within 400 steps these demonstrations went from the weakest of the three novice conditions under the point-cloud policy (46.3%) to the strongest under the keypoint policy (57.3%), a gain of + 11.0 +11.0 percentage points in all five seeds.
Those collected with all keypoints emphasized changed by at most + 0.7 +0.7 percentage points, and in no more than three seeds.
The value of a demonstration therefore depends on the rendering shown during collection and on what the policy observes together.
A shared representation can pay off on both sides, in the number of successful demonstrations and in the success rate of the policy trained on them.
Project page: https://omron-sinicx.github.io/point-hand/ .
2026-10-21.introduction:
In imitation learning for multi-fingered robot hands, the quality of the demonstrations collected by novice operators limits the performance of the policy.
As policies and datasets scale up [ 1 , 2 ] , imitation learning is expected to rely increasingly on novices who have no knowledge of policy learning or robot kinematics.
Multi-fingered hands make this especially visible: teleoperation constrains observation and action more than one’s own body [ 3 ] , and the number of possible postures is vast, so consistent control takes practice.

What makes a demonstration good is inter-trial consistency, and it has to hold with respect to what the policy observes rather than to the operator alone.
Sakr et al. define the quality of demonstration data by how repeatably the operator performs the same task [ 4 ] , and a policy can only learn from repetitions it can tell apart in its own observation [ 5 ] .
Operators act on what they are shown, so the rendering of the robot decides which cues they rely on.
When those cues are absent from the policy’s observation, demonstrations that were consistent for the operator can look inconsistent to the policy, an effect related to the imitation gap [ 6 ] .
How the rendering shown to the operator affects the demonstrations and the policies trained on them has nevertheless not been examined.

This paper investigates this question with PointHand , a teleoperation interface that renders the robot hand to the operator as sparse keypoints at the fingertips and at the joints that bend each finger (Fig. What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns: A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation for Teleoperated Demonstration ), a keypoint hand visual representation.
Unlike the real shape, which occupies much of the view, the keypoints remove occlusion and limit the operator’s cues to these parts, so we expect the task to become easier and the number and inter-trial consistency of demonstrations to increase.
We compare three renderings of the hand: its real shape ( Baseline ), all 11 keypoints emphasized ( KP-Standard ), and only the five keypoints on the thumb and index finger emphasized ( KP-Salient ).
In a user study, each novice collected demonstrations under one of the three renderings, and the experts under the real shape as a reference.
We train the same diffusion policy under two observation representations and compare them.
DP3 [ 7 ] observes the dense scene point cloud with the proprioceptive state. DP-KP replaces both with a sparse set of 13 points, the same hand keypoints and two object keypoints on the symmetry axis of the object.

We ask three questions.
RQ1: does the keypoint hand visual representation bring the number and inter-trial consistency of novice demonstrations closer to the expert level?
RQ2: how does the collection condition change the performance of policies trained on these demonstrations?
RQ3: does the effect of switching the policy’s observation from the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state to the hand and object keypoints depend on how the demonstrations were collected?
Our contributions are as follows.

We built PointHand, a teleoperation interface that varies the hand rendering shown to the operator while giving the same keypoints to the policy.

We show that emphasizing only the thumb and index finger yielded the most successful novice demonstrations, 441 of 600 trials against 320 for the real shape, and the most consistent on four of the five kinematic metrics (Study 1).

We find that in the fraction of episodes that place the mug within 400 steps, these demonstrations were the weakest of the novice conditions under DP3 and the strongest under DP-KP, so the rendering at collection and what the policy observes are worth choosing together (Study 2).

1. We built PointHand, a teleoperation interface that varies the hand rendering shown to the operator while giving the same keypoints to the policy.

2. We show that emphasizing only the thumb and index finger yielded the most successful novice demonstrations, 441 of 600 trials against 320 for the real shape, and the most consistent on four of the five kinematic metrics (Study 1).

3. We find that in the fraction of episodes that place the mug within 400 steps, these demonstrations were the weakest of the novice conditions under DP3 and the strongest under DP-KP, so the rendering at collection and what the policy observes are worth choosing together (Study 2).
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

One approach to obtain better demonstrations is to make the robot easier for the operator to control.
Retargeting maps human hand motion to the robot so that the input stays accurate [ 8 , 9 ] .
Other methods adjust the camera viewpoint [ 10 ] .
Diminished reality, surveyed by Mori et al. [ 11 ] , removes the robot from the view so that the operator can see the workspace behind it.

The other approach leaves the operator alone and works on the data after collection.
Data curation discards low-quality demonstrations to improve policy performance [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
Keypoint annotation reduces the dimensions the policy must learn [ 15 , 16 ] .
Curation, however, increases the collection time per retained demonstration, and keypoints require defining what matters for the robot and the object.
The first approach improves control without asking what that does to the data.
The second improves the data without touching how it was produced.
Neither treats the operator’s view of the robot as something that shapes the demonstrations and, through them, the policy.

Closest to this question is work that aligns what the operator sees with what the policy observes.
Open-TeleVision [ 17 ] streams the policy’s camera images to the operator.
Other methods re-render the robot in collected data to match the policy’s input [ 18 , 19 ] .
Both show that alignment helps, but they align a stream or data that already exists.
The rendering is never designed at collection time for what it will do to the demonstrations.

Designing that rendering raises the question of how far the robot’s appearance has to be retained.
Humans read biological motion from a few moving points [ 20 ] .
Studies of VR avatar embodiment report that the sense of embodiment depends on more than visual fidelity [ 21 ] .
Operators have even embodied a swarm of discrete robots and acted through it [ 22 ] .
A hand reduced to keypoints at the fingertips and joints may therefore remain controllable.

2026-10-21.title: High-Precision RCM Motion for Ophthalmic Robotics via Hierarchical QP Control and Authority-Guided Recovery Planning
2026-10-21.authors: Huanyu Tian , Adriana Namour , Lingyun Zeng , Zicong Wu , Sebastien Ourselin , Lyndon da Cruz , Christos Bergeles
2026-10-21.abstract:
General-purpose manipulators can position ophthalmic instruments under a software Remote Centre of Motion (RCM). However, at some reachable configurations that are nonsingular for the tip task alone, the RCM and tip-tracking objectives conflict and the servo oscillates.
We formalise this failure as a constraint-induced task singularity: the RCM-projected tip Jacobian loses rank while the unprojected tip Jacobian stays well conditioned. Thus, the effective tip authority collapses although the target remains reachable.
We present a high-precision RCM servo architecture with built-in singularity recovery: for each commanded target, an authority-guided planner selects a well-conditioned arm configuration that reaches it and plans an RCM-consistent route, executed by a fixed hierarchical-QP controller.
On a 200-scenario kinematic benchmark, the complete nominal-and-recovery protocol reaches 128/128 near-singular targets and 71/72 near-joint-limit targets (100% and 99%, respectively), with the software-RCM residual below 0.142 mm.
On a physical 6-DOF arm it executes across four RCM entry points, with a worst-case kinematically reconstructed RCM residual of 178 μ ​ m \mu m and a median tip-regulation error of 32 μ ​ m \mu m , within the 200 μ ​ m \mu m control requirement adopted for the ophthalmic task.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Robot-assisted vitreoretinal surgery is a keyhole task: a slender instrument is steered inside the eye while its shaft pivots about a fixed scleral entry, the Remote Centre of Motion (RCM) [ 1 ] .
In vitreoretinal surgery, both the robot tip error and the RCM residual must be held to maximum 200 µ ​ m 200\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} , against retinal structures only a few hundred micrometres thick, leaving little margin to trade between the two objectives [ 2 , 3 ] .
Purpose-built platforms realise the RCM through a mechanical linkage [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] , which may also be adaptable [ 9 , 10 ] . A general-purpose manipulator, e.g. such as that used in [ 11 ] , however, enforces it through software and control, and the constraint becomes coupled with tip tracking and competes for the same joint velocities.

At certain reachable configurations that are nonsingular for the unconstrained tip-position task, this coupling becomes a constraint-induced task singularity : the joint motion that advances the tip is the same motion that sweeps the shaft laterally through the sclera, i.e. the tip-progress gradient aligns with the RCM constraint directions. In such a case, no RCM-consistent joint velocity produces the required first-order tip progress (Fig. 1 ).
Partial alignment can be accommodated within the residual null space by a prioritised controller [ 12 , 13 ] . As the alignment approaches completion, however, the available first-order tip authority vanishes.
A loose RCM tolerance may absorb the conflict through temporary constraint violation, whereas the tight ophthalmic tolerance leads to oscillatory tip motion or loss of tip progress toward the target (Sec. II-B ).

In prior work, programmable RCM enforcement is realised with task-priority (hierarchical) control and solved by hierarchical quadratic programming (HQP). The RCM residual is imposed as the high-priority level, and tip tracking is resolved on the remaining subspace. The constraint is written as an equality in the hierarchy or as an inequality in a positional- or velocity-level QP [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] . The residual null space is used for a redundancy resolution, typically toward a manipulability/conditioning measure [ 19 , 18 ] .
Because this resolution is local and provides no path-level lookahead, it cannot route around a singularity lying on the nominal path. The underlying projected-Jacobian rank loss is known in task-priority control as an algorithmic singularity [ 20 ] .

Two gaps therefore remain. First, software-RCM work reports RCM and tip accuracy, but rarely analyses the closed-loop oscillation produced by constrained-induced task singularity under a strict tolerance. Second, redundancy-resolution studies typically involve more redundant degrees of freedom and looser task tolerances, so the constrained null space retains enough dimensions, and the solver enough slack, to absorb the conflict, which then never appears as a task singularity.

We study a representative challenging case: a 6 6 -DOF arm performing 3D point positioning under a high-priority RCM constraint with bounded slack, where a single redundant degree of freedom (roll about the shaft) leaves little room to reconcile the RCM and tip objectives once joint limits are active.
The contributions of this work are:

A bounded-slack HQP controller that enforces the RCM while servoing the tip.

An authority-guided recovery planner, built on our characterisation of the constraint-induced task singularity, that acts only on the reference the controller tracks.

2026-10-21.title: Enumeration-Guided Training of Neural Hamilton-Jacobi Safety Certificates
2026-10-21.authors: Mihaela-Larisa Clement , Tosca Pierro , Ezio Bartocci , Luca Marzari
2026-10-21.abstract: Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis offers formal safety guarantees for control systems, but training accurate neural certificates remains difficult, particularly when unsafe regions are hard to characterize. We propose a verification-guided training framework that addresses this by using probabilistic enumeration of safety constraints to detect forward-invariance violations, i.e., states where the learned certificate incorrectly classifies unsafe behavior. This produces a compact, targeted set of counterexamples that more precisely captures the failure boundary than inputs generated by standard adversarial attack methods. Crucially, using this representation to fine-tune a pretrained HJ value function yields larger certified regions and reduces certification time across all tested benchmarks. We further introduce a shielding mechanism based on the refined certificates to enforce safety constraints at deployment time. We evaluate the proposed safety filter in a realistic, physics-based Isaac Sim environment and through real-world autonomous racing experiments, achieving zero safety constraint violations compared to a nominal controller and a backup policy based on Linear Quadratic Regulation (LQR). These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed shielding mechanism in ensuring safe operation under high-speed, safety-critical conditions.
2026-10-21.introduction:
For control systems interacting with the physical world, safety is a primary concern in controller design, as controllers must satisfy safety constraints at all time steps over an infinite horizon. Consider, for example, a robot locomotion task where safety requires maintaining a positive clearance from surrounding obstacles at all times. Two distinct challenges arise in such settings. The first is identifying the set of states from which long-term constraint satisfaction is guaranteed, the so-called feasible region , since the deployment of a controller should be restricted to this set. The second is actively enforcing safety at runtime, as even when a controller is initialized within the feasible region, it may issue actions that push the system toward constraint violations, and an explicit safety mechanism is required to intercept and correct such actions before they are executed. Addressing both challenges simultaneously is essential for deploying safety-critical controllers in realistic environments.

A widely adopted approach to enforce safety constraints is based on Model Predictive Control (MPC) [ 1 ] . Nominal MPC incorporates state and input constraints directly into a finite-horizon optimal control problem solved repeatedly online. Under suitable assumptions, nominal MPC can exhibit a degree of robustness; however, when hard state constraints are present, these safety margins can become very small. To account for bounded disturbances and model uncertainty, robust MPC variants such as tube-based methods [ 2 , 3 ] confine the system trajectory to a tube around the nominal trajectory, ensuring constraint satisfaction through tightening of the nominal problem. Nonetheless, constraint tightening can introduce conservatism that degrades performance in demanding tasks, and the finite planning horizon limits the scope of safety guarantees that can be provided.

A more principled framework for characterizing safety over an infinite horizon is Hamilton–Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis [ 4 ] , which offers a formal setting for computing feasible regions of control systems subject to safety constraints. HJ reachability defines the feasible region as the zero-sublevel set of a value function V ⁡ ( x ) V(x) , representing the worst-case constraint violation along an optimally controlled trajectory originating from state x x . Compared with MPC-based approaches, HJ reachability provides direct global safety guarantees rather than relying on finite-horizon optimization and repeated replanning. This makes V V a natural candidate not only for certifying the feasible region, but also for constructing a runtime safety filter, namely a shield , that corrects unsafe control actions by substituting a verified backup policy whenever a nominal controller would violate the safe set boundary. However, this increased rigor comes at a high computational cost, as the underlying HJ partial differential equations suffer from the well-known curse of dimensionality, making exact solutions intractable for high-dimensional systems.

To address this limitation, several recent works have proposed neural HJ certificates, leveraging function approximation to scale reachability analysis to more complex systems [ 5 , 6 ] . Nevertheless, learned certificates do not inherently guarantee that the resulting zero-sublevel set defines a sound feasible region and therefore require formal verification to confirm that safety guarantees are preserved. This limitation motivated the approach of Yang. et al. [ 7 ] , which integrates neural value function learning within a training loop guided by adversarial search and formal verification. While this approach improves scalability and enables learning of provably safe certificates, it faces three critical challenges that we aim to address in this work.
First, the adversarial procedure is empirical and relies on sparse, locally generated counterexamples as gradient-based attacks explore only a narrow neighborhood of the current iterate and may therefore miss failures located in other regions of the state space. As a result, the search may report no violation even when unsafe states remain in the fine-tuned certificate, not because these states are genuinely safe, but because the search did not reach them. This false negative prematurely triggers the formal verifier, which, being NP-hard [ 8 ] , can incur substantial computational cost. The verifier then identifies the violation that the adversarial search missed, generates additional counterexamples, and initiates another fine-tuning cycle. This process can repeat over many iterations, leading to significant verification overhead before convergence. The inefficiency becomes particularly acute in high-dimensional systems, where the local coverage of adversarial search can be small relative to the global extent of the failure set. Second, even after a verified certificate has been obtained, the question of how to exploit it as a practical runtime safety filter for a learned controller operating in a complex environment remains unaddressed: translating the certified feasible region into an effective shielding mechanism requires additional design choices that the learning procedure alone does not resolve.

This paper addresses both limitations by introducing a novel enumeration-guided training strategy depicted in Fig. 1 . At the core of our approach is the enumeration of compact unsafe regions, which replaces purely local counterexample search with a more structured exploration of the state space based on preimages of the unsafe set in deep neural networks [ 9 , 10 ] . The underlying intuition is that isolated local violations provide only limited information about the geometry of the failure set, whereas counterexamples drawn from a globally organized, spatially distributed exploration better characterize its shape and extent, offering a richer training signal to the learning algorithm. Crucially, our enumeration-guided training is not a substitute for formal verification; it improves the quality, diversity, and coverage of the counterexample set during training, while verification retains its role as the provable safety certification. In addition to this new training strategy, and building on the least-restrictive safety framework of Fisac et al. [ 11 ] , we introduce a shielding mechanism that leverages the refined neural HJ certificate to enforce safety at deployment time. The proposed shield acts as a safety filter between a nominal controller and the plant: at each time step, it checks whether the intended action preserves forward invariance of the certified safe set and, if necessary, overrides it with a safe recovery action provided by a backup policy based on Linear Quadratic Regulation (LQR) [ 12 ] . Unlike existing HJ-based safety filters, which typically rely on grid-based value functions or learned approximations without formal safety guarantees, our approach introduces a formally verified neural HJ certificate that, by construction, ensures forward invariance of the certified safe set under the verified system dynamics. This enables the deployment of formally certified safety filters in complex systems where closed-form safety certificates are unavailable.

Our empirical evaluation spans four safe-control verification benchmarks from [ 7 ] , covering systems with both linear and nonlinear dynamics, as well as a new obstacle-avoidance benchmark based on the RoboRacer platform (formerly F1TENTH) [ 13 ] . Enumeration-guided training yields faster convergence times and, in general, larger certified regions across all benchmarks, with the largest gains on higher-dimensional and more complex tasks. The verified RoboRacer certificate is first evaluated in a realistic, physics-based Isaac Sim environment to assess its robustness against different track geometries, corridors, and heading disturbances. We further validate its effectiveness under real-world conditions by deploying it on a physical RoboRacer platform on an unseen real racing circuit. This deployment confirms the effectiveness of the proposed solution for complex safety-critical tasks.

2026-10-21.title: Frontier LLMs Enter the World of Robotics: A Cross-Model Evaluation on RoboColiseum
2026-10-21.authors: Da Huang , Jichao Wang , Junhui Wu , Tong Ran , Linting Guo , Siying Zhang , Chuang Men , Sukai Wang , Yue Zhou , Maoqing Yao , Mo Wu
2026-10-21.abstract: Recent studies have explored the potential of multimodal large language models for robot control, yet the models’ embodied capabilities remain insufficiently characterized across models, tasks, and execution settings. We conduct a multidimensional comparative evaluation on RoboColiseum across four tracks: Instruction Following, Spatial Reasoning, General Manipulation, and Robustness. We implement Agent2Act, a control harness that integrates GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon into the evaluation environment through shared observation, action execution, and feedback interfaces. Under common task settings and scoring criteria, all four models exhibit a consistent capability profile: high instruction-following scores, with three approaching perfect performance; strong spatial reasoning; and general manipulation scores below those of the other three tracks. Within the evaluated configurations, Astra leads instruction following and robustness, while Opus leads spatial reasoning, general manipulation, and overall performance. These results reveal complementary strengths across models and a persistent gap between task understanding and reliable physical execution. Component comparisons on selected tasks further show that harness design affects task success, planning cost, and execution time. Additionally, case studies with Astra examine whole-body coordination, manipulation across robot embodiments, precision manipulation, dexterous-hand manipulation, and real-robot tasks, providing further insight into the model’s capabilities and limitations across embodied tasks.
2026-10-21.introduction:
The release of GPT-6 Astra [ 1 ] raises a practical question: what can a
multimodal large language model achieve when it directly controls a robot?
A growing body of work explores how large language models (LLMs) can use
observations to control robots.

In simulation, W. Zhang et al. evaluate LLMs as manipulation policies and
identify a gap between semantic task understanding and precise physical
control [ 2 ] . GPT-as-Policy compares Astra-generated
end-effector actions with a hybrid controller in which Astra reviews and
corrects π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} action proposals [ 3 ] . Galbot’s study
examines direct and hybrid control across simulated manipulation and other
embodied domains, distinguishing model-generated commands from actions
provided by learned policies or whole-body controllers [ 4 ] . Y. Yao et al. evaluate tabletop and mobile
manipulation in Ebench, where Astra generates end-effector waypoints,
gripper targets, and base targets through a fixed execution interface [ 5 ] .

On real hardware, RoboCurve compares Astra with a VLA policy on bimanual
tabletop tasks using YAM robot arms. Astra issues absolute end-effector
poses through action tools [ 6 ] . RoboICL evaluates
both simulated tasks and three real-robot tasks on a Franka Research 3
arm. Its frozen Astra model uses demonstrations and interaction memory
to generate numerical action chunks through a fixed tool schema [ 7 ] .

These studies provide initial evidence of LLM-driven robot control across
different tasks and control configurations. Building on this work, we
compare four frontier multimodal large language models across
RoboColiseum’s four tracks, using shared sensing and execution interfaces
to examine their strengths and limitations.

Our evaluation covers GPT-6 Astra [ 1 ] , GPT-6.1
Sol [ 8 ] , Claude Opus 5.5 [ 9 ] , and
Gemini 4 Argon [ 10 ] . To integrate these models into
RoboColiseum, we implement Agent2Act, a harness that provides a unified
interface for interaction with robotic environments and action execution.
RoboColiseum’s consistent task settings and scoring criteria allow us to
systematically examine the models’ relative strengths, weaknesses, and
capability boundaries in embodied tasks.

RoboColiseum is a multidimensional benchmark for embodied model
capabilities. It supports vision-language-action (VLA) models, world/action
models (WAM), and agent-based systems. Its four tracks assess complementary
dimensions of embodied performance:

Instruction Following: evaluates instruction understanding
across ten dimensions, including color, size, quantity, semantics, and
logical conditions.

Spatial Reasoning: evaluates understanding of spatial

# II Agent2Act Harness

## II-A Framework Workflow

Agent2Act connects a multimodal large language model (LLM) to a
robot through a closed loop of observation, decision, execution,
and feedback (Figure 1 ). In our
experiments, the model interprets the task and scene, selects the
next manipulation objective, and specifies motion targets and
gripper actions. Agent2Act provides the model with sensing,
execution, and feedback interfaces and translates its decisions
into physical interactions in the simulator.

At each turn, the model receives current visual observations,
robot state, and a concise history of previous decisions and their
observed effects. It uses this information to advance the task,
assess earlier actions, and revise its plan. Direct control therefore
means that the LLM determines which action to attempt, while the
execution layer converts that decision into robot commands.

## II-B Model Input Modules

Table II summarizes the contents and
roles of the model input modules. The same Agent2Act harness
constructs these inputs for all four models.

Authored guidance is an optional framework capability separate from
the original benchmark instruction. It is not supplied in the reported
benchmark evaluation: all tasks in all four tracks use the original
benchmark instructions without supplementary task prompts.
General robot control instructions remain part of the shared interface.

The LLM decides when to query depth based on the current
observation. In simulation, the tool returns depth observations
with simulated noise rather than ground-truth values. These
read-only queries do not execute robot actions.

## II-C Action Validation, Execution, and Feedback

The LLM expresses each decision as a manipulation objective,
candidate motion targets, gripper commands, and an expected
observable outcome. Motion targets use a common robot reference
frame, and Agent2Act converts them into executable robot commands.

Agent2Act checks candidates for kinematic feasibility and
compliance with the action interface, then executes the
highest-ranked admissible candidate. If no candidate passes
these checks, it returns the rejection reasons to the model
for revision. Actions execute over a bounded horizon before
a new observation returns control to the model, allowing
subsequent decisions to respond to the actual robot and scene state.

The next observation closes the loop with visual evidence and
the measured robot response. The LLM compares this feedback
with the intended outcome to decide whether to continue,
correct its action, or declare completion. Agent2Act records
model-proposed actions, issued commands, and observed execution
outcomes separately: generating an executable command does not
establish that the robot has completed the operation.

## II-D Benchmark Integration

RoboColiseum supplies the scenes, robots, task instructions,
action budgets, and scoring rules. Agent2Act connects the model
to this environment while preserving the original task definitions
and evaluation protocol. Section II-B details the
model inputs used in the reported experiments. The benchmark’s
native evaluation determines final task outcomes, independently
of the model’s completion judgment.
