2026-10-21.authors: Haocheng Wang , Youquan Liu , Weiyu Guo , Aokai Zhang , Donghang Wu , Hongyu Liu , Sha Zhang , Weidong Yang , Ben Fei
2026-10-21.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks. We introduce RoboCasa-Shift , a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields Δ ​ SR = 0 \Delta\mathrm{SR}=0 despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera L 2 L_{2} and Gaussian blur L 1 L_{1} both yield Δ ​ SR = 0.188 \Delta\mathrm{SR}=0.188 , yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0% and 36.4%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi-dimensional property of execution rather than a single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression.
The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an increasingly important paradigm for robotic manipulation by integrating visual observations, language instructions, and robot actions within unified policy frameworks [ 1 , 2 ] . Despite their growing capabilities, maintaining reliable behavior under distribution shifts remains a key challenge for deployment, as robots may encounter variations in observations, environments, and physical states that differ from those seen during training.
Systematically evaluating VLA robustness under such distribution shifts is important for understanding the reliability of these models in robotic applications.

Recent robustness benchmarks have expanded the evaluation of VLA policies beyond nominal task settings through diverse controlled distribution shifts and increasingly systematic evaluation protocols [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] .
Despite this broader coverage, robustness is still commonly summarized at the task or evaluation-condition level through aggregate metrics such as success rate. Such summaries do not reveal how individual executions change under a distribution shift or where failures emerge within long-horizon task execution, leaving a need for more diagnostic evaluation at the execution level.

Such diagnosis requires controlling episode-level variation for meaningful comparison, since clean and shifted evaluations with different task instances or initial conditions may confound episode difficulty with the target distribution shift.
We therefore compare each perturbed execution with a corresponding clean execution under the same underlying task conditions, changing only the target perturbation. This counterfactual pairing provides a controlled basis for identifying episode-level outcome changes associated with the evaluated shift.

Even under such controlled comparisons, a binary task outcome provides only a coarse description of failure in long-horizon manipulation. These tasks unfold through a sequence of semantically meaningful subgoals [ 6 , 7 ] , so two failed executions may terminate after very different amounts of task progress.
Stage-aware evaluation can therefore complement final success or failure by tracking semantic progress and identifying the first incomplete subgoal, providing a clearer view of where robustness failures emerge during execution.

We introduce RoboCasa-Shift, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 [ 3 ] for evaluating VLA policies under controlled distribution shifts in long-horizon household manipulation, as illustrated in Figure 1 .
The benchmark defines controlled single-factor shifts at multiple frozen severity levels and a matched clean-perturbed protocol for episode-level counterfactual comparison.
It further incorporates simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics to track semantic execution progress and localize where failures emerge during long-horizon task execution. RoboCasa-Shift characterizes robustness from complementary perspectives, including end-to-end task outcomes, episode-level outcome changes, and stage-aware execution behavior.

Our evaluation reveals that robustness responses vary across perturbation factors and tasks, and that increasing calibrated severity does not always lead to monotonic degradation in end-to-end performance.
Aggregate success rates can also mask considerable episode-level outcome changes, while similar end-to-end degradation can correspond to failures emerging at different semantic depths of task execution.
Stage-aware analysis further shows that perturbation severity can alter the semantic depth reached by failed executions, with stronger shifts in some conditions associated with earlier incomplete milestones.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We develop RoboCasa-Shift , a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 for long-horizon household
manipulation. The benchmark defines controlled single-factor distribution shifts at multiple frozen severity levels under an
episode-level clean-perturbed counterfactual protocol, enabling robustness changes to be examined under matched task conditions.

We develop RoboCasa-Shift , a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 for long-horizon household
manipulation. The benchmark defines controlled single-factor distribution shifts at multiple frozen severity levels under an
episode-level clean-perturbed counterfactual protocol, enabling robustness changes to be examined under matched task conditions.

We introduce a simulator-grounded stage-aware robustness diagnostic that complements final task success with semantic execution information. Long-horizon tasks are represented through ordered semantic
subgoals evaluated by simulator-state predicates, allowing execution progress and the first incomplete subgoal to be tracked for failure localization.

We conduct a controlled robustness study on four clean-qualified long-horizon RoboCasa tasks across four perturbation factors and three severity levels, jointly analyzing end-to-end task outcomes, counterfactual episode-level changes, and stage-aware execution depth. The analysis reveals
robustness behaviors not captured by aggregate success alone, including heterogeneous severity responses and differences in
the semantic depth reached by failed executions.

# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Language-Action Models for Robot Manipulation

VLA models have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding,
and action prediction within a unified policy framework [ 1 , 2 ] .
Building on large-scale and heterogeneous robot datasets, subsequent works have
further developed generalist policies that can operate across diverse tasks, robot embodiments, and observation or action spaces [ 8 , 9 ] .
Recent studies have continued to extend VLA models toward more complex sequential manipulation by improving temporal reasoning and visual grounding during task execution [ 10 , 11 ] .
As VLA policies expand to diverse and complex manipulation settings, evaluating their reliability under distribution shifts becomes increasingly important.

## II-B Robustness and Generalization Benchmarks for Robot Manipulation

Existing robot manipulation benchmarks have increasingly emphasized generalization beyond the training distribution by evaluating policies across diverse tasks, environments, and controlled variations [ 12 , 13 ] .
More recent benchmarks have substantially expanded this direction by evaluating generalist robot policies under increasingly diverse and systematically controlled distribution shifts [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] .
These benchmarks support systematic analysis across perturbation factors, difficulty levels, and task variations, providing broad measurements of policy robustness and generalization. However, such analyses predominantly characterize performance
at the task or evaluation-condition level, providing limited information about how distribution shifts affect the semantic execution process within a long-horizon task. RoboCasa-Shift complements these efforts through controlled distribution-shift evaluation, episode-level counterfactual comparison, and semantic subgoal-aware diagnosis of robustness degradation in long-horizon execution.

## II-C Long-Horizon and Compositional Manipulation Evaluation

Recent progress in robot manipulation evaluation has extended benchmark tasks from short-horizon skills to long-horizon and multi-stage executions that require policies to coordinate multiple interactions over time [ 14 , 15 , 16 ] .
Beyond increasing task horizon, several benchmarks further expose the temporal or subtask structure of manipulation tasks to evaluate capabilities such as planning, sequential reasoning, and memory-dependent execution [ 7 , 6 ] .
Despite these advances, such task structure is primarily used to characterize long-horizon manipulation capabilities themselves, while its role as a diagnostic unit for robustness under controlled distribution shifts remains less explored. RoboCasa-Shift builds on this structured view of long-horizon execution by using semantic subgoals to track execution progress and characterize the
semantic depth under distribution shifts.

2026-10-21.title: Agentic discovery of interpretable car-following laws from multi-source trajectory data
2026-10-21.authors: Jiamei Xu , Jie Sun , Keshuang Tang , Jian Sun
2026-10-21.abstract: Car-following (CF) models is a fundamental component of microscopic traffic simulation and underpin the analysis of collective traffic dynamics, while its modeling becomes more challenging due to diverse human driving behaviors and the increasing presence of automated vehicle. Analytical CF models offer interpretable representations of longitudinal vehicle interactions, but their prescribed functional structures may limit the representation of heterogeneous driving behavior. This study proposes an agent-centered, physics-aware framework for the empirical discovery of CF laws from multi-source trajectory data. The framework iteratively combines agent-guided hypothesis generation, informed by traffic flow knowledge and state-dependent reconstruction errors, with evolutionary symbolic search and physics-aware multi-objective evaluation. Using NGSIM US-101, highD, and exiD, the framework discovers the Adaptive Equilibrium Response Model (AERM), which couples state-dependent relative-speed response with spacing-dependent equilibrium-speed restoration. AERM admits analytical equilibrium speed–spacing and flow–density relationships; its stability conditions are derived for the zero-delay formulation, and platoon simulations examine disturbance propagation. Evaluated against seven classical CF models on Shanghai naturalistic driving data, NGSIM I-80, and Waymo trajectories, AERM attains the lowest spacing and speed reconstruction errors under trajectory-specific calibration, reducing spacing RMSE by 9.11%, 7.59%, and 21.73% relative to the strongest baselines, and remains competitive under dataset-level shared parameters. These results demonstrate the fitting flexibility and analytical tractability of the discovered CF law, providing an interpretable basis for microscopic traffic simulation.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Car-following (CF) models describe how a follower vehicle adjusts its longitudinal motion in response to its leader and the prevailing traffic state. They constitute the fundamental component of microscopic traffic simulation and underpin the analysis of collective traffic dynamics ( Brackstone and McDonald, 1999 ; Treiber et al., 2000 ; Jiang et al., 2001 ) . Their importance rests on a simple observation that the local acceleration response of a vehicle governs not only its own trajectory but also the formation and propagation of traffic disturbances, so that errors in the assumed longitudinal interaction can amplify into large-scale congestion patterns. An accurate yet tractable CF law is therefore a prerequisite for reproducing and explaining realistic traffic behavior. This raises a twofold requirement for such laws, as they must capture nonlinear, condition-dependent vehicle interactions with sufficient accuracy, and they must retain enough analytical structure that their traffic flow implications (e.g., equilibrium states, fundamental diagrams, and stability) can be derived and interpreted.

Classical CF modeling has produced a family of interpretable equations built on distinct behavioral hypotheses: stimulus–response relations ( Gazis et al., 1961 ) , safety-based speed constraints ( Gipps, 1981 ) , relaxation toward a spacing-dependent desired speed ( Bando et al., 1995 ) , relative-speed feedback ( Jiang et al., 2001 ) , and free-flow and desired-spacing interactions ( Treiber et al., 2000 ) . These formulations connect microscopic behavior to traffic flow theory, but they are developed in a structure-first fashion that the functional form is fixed by behavioral assumptions, and trajectory data are used only to calibrate its parameters ( Kesting and Treiber, 2008 ) . Extensions with heterogeneous parameters or added behavioral terms improve flexibility, yet they remain confined to the analytical skeleton that was assumed in the first place ( Ossen and Hoogendoorn, 2011 ; Saifuzzaman and Zheng, 2014 ) . With increasingly heterogeneous traffic, the natural question is whether the governing functional relationship itself (not just its parameters) can be determined from observed behavior.

High-resolution trajectory data and machine learning have made this question tractable. Nonparametric and neural CF models approximate complex responses without committing to a prescribed equation ( Papathanasopoulou and Antoniou, 2015 ; Huang et al., 2018 ) , although an implicit predictor is less convenient for extracting an explicit mechanism or deriving equilibrium and stability conditions, and dedicated methods are required to analyze its dynamics ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) . Symbolic regression offers a complementary route by searching for compact, inspectable expressions. Within traffic research, SciNet-CFM discovers tractable CF relations through neural-symbolic regression ( Li et al., 2025 ) ; SR-LLM combines LLM-assisted knowledge retrieval with incremental symbolic regression ( Guo et al., 2025b ) ; deep symbolic regression with variable-selection regularization has been applied to identify CF dynamics from trajectories ( Angah et al., 2024 ) ; and NOVA investigates structural recurrence and residual-guided refinement at scale ( Abassi et al., 2026 ) . Together these studies establish that empirical CF-law discovery is feasible, and they sharpen the question of how discovery can remain accurate and physically meaningful across heterogeneous observations.

More importantly, what existing methods leave under-specified is not the search itself but the loop that surrounds it. First, although these methods perform residual analysis and iterative feedback, they rarely convert persistent, state-dependent reconstruction errors (which are concentrated in specific driving regimes) into concrete, testable structural modifications, and they seldom verify such modifications across heterogeneous trajectory sources. Second, when the functional form emerges from open-ended search, physical admissibility and behavioral interpretability are usually imposed as post-hoc filters rather than treated as explicit objectives in model selection. Third, a discovered law is only as useful as the theory it supports, where its analytical consequences, such as equilibrium relations, fundamental diagrams, and stability regimes, must remain derivable. These gaps motivate a discovery framework that couples structural hypothesis generation, cross-source verification, and physics-aware selection into one evidence-driven process.

To fill the gap, we propose an agentic CF law discovering framework, which couples an agent-guided hypothesis generator, which draws on traffic flow knowledge and on diagnosed state-dependent reconstruction errors, with evolutionary symbolic search, and it ranks candidates under a physics-aware, multi-objective scheme in which physical admissibility and interpretability enter explicitly. Applying the framework to NGSIM US-101, highD, and exiD yields an explicit CF law—the Adaptive Equilibrium Response Model (AERM)—that pairs state-dependent relative-speed response with spacing-dependent equilibrium-speed restoration, and whose structure admits closed-form equilibrium and fundamental-diagram relations as well as local and string stability conditions. We evaluate AERM against seven established CF models on Shanghai naturalistic driving data, NGSIM I-80, and Waymo trajectories under both dataset-level and trajectory-specific calibration, and we examine its dynamical behavior through equilibrium, stability, and platoon analyses.
The main contributions are summarized as follows:

An evidence-driven structural-evolution framework. We develop an iterative loop in which an agent translates persistent, state-dependent reconstruction errors into testable structural hypotheses, evolutionary search explores the resulting candidates, and physics-aware multi-objective evaluation selects and refines them, with candidate laws verified across heterogeneous trajectory sources without prescribing the final equation in advance.

An evidence-driven structural-evolution framework. We develop an iterative loop in which an agent translates persistent, state-dependent reconstruction errors into testable structural hypotheses, evolutionary search explores the resulting candidates, and physics-aware multi-objective evaluation selects and refines them, with candidate laws verified across heterogeneous trajectory sources without prescribing the final equation in advance.

An interpretable empirical CF law. The framework identifies AERM, an explicit acceleration law with state-dependent relative-speed sensitivity and nonlinear equilibrium-speed restoration, whose analytical structure permits the derivation of steady-state relationships, the associated fundamental diagram, and traffic flow stability.

Behavioral and dynamical evaluation. We assess the discovered law against seven classical CF models using real-world trajectory reconstruction under both common- and trajectory-specific parameter calibration, complemented by equilibrium analysis, stability analysis, and platoon simulations of its dynamical properties.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Analytical Car-Following Models

Classical analytical car-following (CF) models describe longitudinal vehicle interactions through explicit mathematical relationships derived from behavioral assumptions and traffic flow theory. Representative models include the GHR stimulus–response family ( Gazis et al., 1961 ) , the safety-based Gipps model ( Gipps, 1981 ) , Newell’s trajectory-translation model ( Newell, 2002 ) , the Optimal Velocity Model (OVM) ( Bando et al., 1995 ) , the Full Velocity Difference Model (FVDM) ( Jiang et al., 2001 ) , and the Intelligent Driver Model (IDM) ( Treiber et al., 2000 ) . These models describe different aspects of vehicle interactions, including relative-speed responses, desired-speed adaptation, and safe-spacing behavior. Their explicit mathematical structures also provide a foundation for equilibrium and stability analysis.

Considerable research has focused on improving analytical CF models through parameter calibration and structural extensions. Trajectory-based optimization enables model parameters to be estimated from empirical observations ( Kesting and Treiber, 2008 ) . However, the underlying behavioral relationships are generally specified before calibration, and their subsequent refinement often depends on manually adjusting or extending the prescribed functions. Consequently, the range of driving responses represented by a model remains closely related to its assumed mathematical structure. This motivates the development of methods that can explore alternative functional relationships directly from observed driving behavior, while preserving the interpretability and analytical tractability of classical CF models.

## 2.2 Data-Driven and Symbolic Discovery of Car-Following Models

Data-driven approaches have expanded the ability to represent complex and nonlinear CF behavior. For instance, Papathanasopoulou and Antoniou (2015) employed locally weighted regression to estimate driving responses, while Huang et al. (2018) introduced long short-term memory networks to capture asymmetric driving behavior and temporal dependencies. Although these approaches provide flexible representations of vehicle interactions, their learned relationships generally lack explicit analytical forms, making it difficult to directly interpret the underlying behavioral mechanisms and derive traffic flow properties. Additional theoretical methods are therefore required to analyze their dynamical behavior, as demonstrated by the string stability analysis of neural-network-based CF models developed by Zhang et al. (2024) .

Symbolic regression provides an alternative by discovering explicit mathematical relationships from observed data. General scientific discovery methods, such as sparse identification of nonlinear dynamical systems ( Brunton et al., 2016 ) , have demonstrated the feasibility of recovering governing equations through data-driven structural identification. In CF modeling, Li et al. (2025) combined neural networks with symbolic regression to discover interpretable driving relationships and examined their theoretical and numerical properties. More recently, Abassi et al. (2026) investigated automated symbolic discovery and evaluated the recurrence of mathematical structures across experimental settings, including residual-guided structural refinement. These studies demonstrate the potential of symbolic regression to recover interpretable CF laws that support subsequent traffic-dynamic analysis.

## 2.3 LLM-Assisted and Agentic Scientific Discovery

Recent developments in large language models (LLMs) have introduced new approaches to scientific equation discovery. Early studies mainly exploited the scientific knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs to guide symbolic search. For example, Shojaee et al. (2025) combined language-model-generated scientific priors with evolutionary search, while Grayeli et al. (2024) employed LLMs to extract reusable concepts from high-performing equations and guide subsequent exploration. In CF modeling, Guo et al. (2025b) integrated retrieval-augmented scientific knowledge with reinforcement-learning-based symbolic regression, enabling the discovery of interpretable equations informed by established traffic models. These approaches demonstrate the benefits of incorporating domain knowledge and accumulated search experience into mathematical structure discovery.

Recent studies have further extended the role of LLMs toward autonomous scientific reasoning and model refinement. In transportation, Guo et al. (2025a) developed a research agent that integrates knowledge retrieval, model formulation, performance evaluation, and iterative improvement of established traffic models. Xia et al. (2026) introduced an agentic framework capable of analyzing data, conducting computational experiments, and revising equations based on experimental feedback. Similarly, Yang et al. (2026) employed physics-guided reasoning to infer intermediate physical properties and use them to configure symbolic regression. These studies demonstrate the growing potential of scientific agents to participate in the complete process of hypothesis generation, evaluation, and refinement.

Table 1 summarizes representative approaches
to car-following modeling and empirical equation discovery.

2026-10-21.title: Multi-View Latent Action Pretraining for Cross-Embodiment Robot Learning from Videos
2026-10-21.authors: Oliver Hausdörfer , Felix Minzenmay , Mani Majd , Maximilian P. Christof , Shiyuan Zhang , Angela P. Schoellig
2026-10-21.comment: Website: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract: Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by + 13.5 % +13.5\% compared to + 6.2 % +6.2\% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by + 20 % +20\% over action-only policies in 850 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Qualitative results are in the suppl. video. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/ .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Data availability remains a limiting factor for learning robot policies. Recent works propose leveraging action-free video data that contains semantically rich information, which can aid robots in long-term task planning. One
approach infers latent actions from videos using an inverse dynamics model
(IDM), and conditions a downstream policy on
those latents [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . The latent actions are an abstract representation describing the transition dynamics in the video. Downstream policy success highly depends on how well the latent actions predict real robot actions. A number of approaches have been proposed to improve this transferability, including grounding latent actions in real robot actions or states [ 4 , 5 ] and visual pre-processing approaches [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . However, we show that existing single-view approaches cannot sufficiently recover the full 6D poses that define robot actions. Single views capture actions only ambiguously: out-of-plane motion is underdetermined and parts of the scene may be occluded.

We therefore propose a Latent Action Model (LAM) that ingests synchronized multi-camera

We demonstrate that this spatial awareness leads to better recoverability of 6D robot actions compared to single-view approaches. Crucially, multiple views are only required during LAM pretraining to improve latent action quality, but not during the policy learning stage where only a single external camera and wrist view are used.

A key advantage of learning from video is the ability to leverage cross-embodiment demonstrations, with the ultimate goal of learning from human demonstrations. Most existing works use only videos from the target robot embodiment, or leverage large-scale public datasets that confound different embodiments, tasks, and visual diversity [ 3 , 4 , 8 ] , making performance attribution to cross-embodiment transfer difficult. We specifically evaluate our policy under cross-embodiment demonstrations, where task-specific demonstrations come from other robots in simulation or humans on hardware. We then add a small number of demonstrations on the target embodiment and investigate performance as we scale. We find that a single cross-embodiment video source already enables transfer learning both in simulation and on hardware. Adding a second viewpoint consistently outperforms adding cross-embodiments, establishing multiple viewpoints as an affordable lever for policy performance.

The sequential design provides a strong inductive prior, enabling the action expert to effectively leverage the latent plan. We show that a single cross-embodiment already enables skill transfer, and that videos from a second viewpoint outperform adding embodiments.

On hardware, dual-view pretraining improves policy success rate by + 20 % +20\% , and we demonstrate skill transfer from human-only demonstrations for novel tasks.

# II Related Work

Latent Action Pretraining. Inverse-dynamics models (IDMs) for latent action learning started with LAPO [ 1 ] and Genie [ 2 ] . The LAPO design of coupling an IDM and FDM (forward dynamics model) forms the template of modern LAM approaches. LAPA [ 3 ] adopted this for robotics by finetuning a VLM on latent actions, and subsequently adding a small MLP head to predict actions. villa-X [ 4 ] uses robots’ proprioceptive states and CLAM [ 5 ] and LAOM [ 6 ] robot actions during IDM training for physical grounding of the latent actions. However, these methods ground latent actions solely in robot data from the target platform and leave human videos entirely ungrounded.
LAOF [ 7 ] introduces optical flow as an intermediate representation to learn latent actions from videos, and UniVLA [ 8 ] proposes using DINO features instead of pixels. Those methods still rely on video pre-processing from a single viewpoint, whereas we propose using multiple viewpoints to improve action recoverability.

Multi-View Learning. Most robot policies operate on a single external viewpoint [ 12 , 13 ] , although recent work shows that 3D spatial perception yields stronger manipulation capabilities [ 14 , 15 ] . One approach injects explicit geometric reconstructions using point clouds [ 14 ] , depth maps [ 16 ] , or voxels. These approaches rely on auxiliary depth sensors or complex reconstruction pipelines that introduce noise. Geometric structure can be learned implicitly using multi-view supervision: RoboUniView [ 16 ] pretrains a unified view representation from multi-view images, 3D-MVP [ 15 ] pretrains the visual encoder via masked autoencoding over multi-view RGB-D renderings, and CLAMP [ 17 ] learns visual representations through a contrastive objective. MV-MWM [ 18 ] and ReViWo [ 19 ] train multi-view encoder-decoders to build viewpoint-robust world models. Concurrent work MVP-LAM [ 20 ] proposes latent action alignment between multiple viewpoints.

As latent action models aim to encode robot actions in 3D space, they stand to benefit substantially from 3D-aware pretraining. We propose to leverage multi-view pretraining of LAPA-style models to improve latent action learning.

Cross-Embodiment Learning. Videos are a natural source for cross-embodiment learning. Demonstrations from different robots can be architecturally absorbed through per-embodiment
input tokenizers [ 13 ] ,
separate action heads [ 12 ] ,
or embodiment identity tokens [ 21 ] around a shared trunk. The visual gap can be closed directly by editing pixels through inpainting at test time [ 22 ] or train time [ 23 ] . The same method can bridge the human–robot gap by rendering a robot at
the estimated hand pose [ 24 ] . These methods make the mechanism of transfer interpretable, but depend on URDFs, renderers, or hand-pose estimators. XSkill [ 25 ] discovers
embodiment-agnostic skills from unlabeled videos. UniAct [ 26 ] decodes a vector-quantized codebook of universal
behaviors, and [ 27 ] contrastively aligns end-effector actions across hands and grippers.

LAMs can achieve embodiment transfer from video alone without explicit reconstruction. The transfer question, however, remains confounded. Work that leverages aggregated datasets [ 4 ] such as OXE [ 28 ] varies embodiment, task, scene, and visual diversity all at once. Those settings make it difficult to quantify cross-embodiment skill transfer. We adopt a controlled
protocol in which task-specific video demonstrations stem from other robots in simulation and from human demonstrations on hardware.

2026-10-21.title: AWLS: Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering for One-Step Generative Robotic Manipulation Policies
2026-10-21.authors: Jiahong Tang , Jiaju He , Zhiyuan Yang , Ruyang Han , Haiyue Zhu
2026-10-21.comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026
2026-10-21.abstract:
Human-collected real-world robotic manipulation demonstrations often contain
mixed-quality trajectories, including hesitant, indirect, or inefficient
action segments.
While diffusion- and flow-based policies can model such multimodal data,
standard behavior cloning (BC) assigns equal likelihood to all demonstrated
actions and may therefore reproduce suboptimal modes.
Offline RL value estimates offer a natural signal for biasing policies
toward higher-value behavioral modes, but directly fine-tuning the
generative policy or using critic gradients for policy steering can amplify
critic errors and induce prior drift.
We propose Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering (AWLS), an offline
post-training method for improving frozen one-step generative manipulation
policies without updating their decoders.
AWLS learns a residual noise shaper, an observation-conditioned residual
correction to the policy’s latent noise, and trains it with an
advantage-weighted action reconstruction objective.
The advantages are detached, scale-normalized, and used only as supervised
weights on demonstrated actions, avoiding critic-gradient policy updates
while preserving fast single-step inference.
We further introduce a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity criterion for
selecting pretrained checkpoints that remain responsive to latent-noise
perturbations.
Experiments on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks with
clean and mixed-quality demonstrations show that AWLS improves over the
frozen base policy while limiting drift from the pretrained behavior prior.
Project page: https://awls-corl2026.github.io/ .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Generative policies based on diffusion and flow
matching [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] have become a
standard approach to imitation learning for robotic manipulation.
They are typically trained by behavior cloning (BC), which fits the policy to
human-collected demonstrations and therefore inherits their quality.
Yet even successful demonstrations are rarely uniformly optimal.
Some trajectories are smooth and efficient, while others are hesitant,
indirect, or unnecessarily long [ 4 , 5 ] .
Standard BC does not distinguish between these quality levels, so it
reproduces hesitant behavior as faithfully as efficient behavior
(Figure 1 , left).
Can a policy trained on such data instead be steered toward the better
behavior in those demonstrations?

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) offers an answer: value estimates learned
from the same demonstrations can identify higher-advantage demonstrated
actions in their respective contexts.
The question then becomes how to inject this signal into a pretrained
generative policy.
Guiding the sampling process with the value
signal [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] keeps the
critic in the loop at inference time, and fine-tuning the decoder with value
gradients can amplify offline critic errors while eroding the pretrained
prior [ 9 , 10 ] .
This makes frozen-decoder latent steering an appealing interface: the
pretrained decoder is kept fixed, and improvement is attempted by reshaping
the latent noise.
Yet this interface exposes two hidden failure modes.
First, critic-gradient (Q-maximization) steering in latent
space [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] can still chase extrapolated value artifacts rather than demonstrated
high-value behavior (Figure 1 , middle).
Second, latent steering is only effective if the frozen decoder remains
sensitive to its latent noise, a property that behavior cloning may weaken
during training.

We propose Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering (AWLS) to mitigate both failure
modes simultaneously.
AWLS post-trains the policy with the pretrained decoder frozen, learning only
a residual noise shaper that applies observation-conditioned corrections to
the latent-noise input.
These corrections are initialized near zero to bias post-training toward the
original latent prior.
Critically, the offline critic never provides a gradient to the policy:
advantages estimated via implicit Q-learning (IQL) [ 15 ] are detached and enter
training only as scalar weights on demonstrated
actions [ 16 ] (Figure 1 , right)—critic errors
may change which demonstrated actions are emphasized without directly
providing gradients toward potentially unsupported actions.
Two additional mechanisms help make this interface practical across tasks:
scale-normalized advantage weighting bounds weight concentration
independently of reward magnitude, and a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity
diagnostic selects frozen checkpoints that remain responsive to latent-noise
perturbations.

Our contributions are: (i) we identify two reliability issues in frozen latent steering
for one-step generative manipulation policies, critic-gradient failure
modes and decoder-sensitivity degradation, and address them with detached
advantage weights and decoder-sensitivity checkpointing; (ii) we propose AWLS, a residual noise shaper trained by
advantage-weighted reconstruction with scale-normalized weights while
keeping the decoder frozen; (iii) we evaluate AWLS on simulation benchmarks, controlled
mixed-quality demonstrations, and real-world robot tasks.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Diffusion and flow policies learn expressive action distributions for
manipulation [ 17 , 18 ] , using RGB and depth
perception [ 1 , 2 , 19 ] to condition
action generation.
Few- and one-step variants reduce sampling cost for fast closed-loop
control [ 20 , 21 ] .
Building on these policy classes, offline RL uses learned value functions to
guide policy training and action
selection [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] .
Pretrained policies can also be adapted through offline-to-online RL,
policy-gradient updates, or generative-model
optimization [ 10 , 25 , 9 , 26 , 27 , 28 ] .
In offline settings, value-gradient updates can exploit critic extrapolation
errors and move the policy away from its behavior-cloning
prior [ 29 ] .
Behavior-cloning regularization can reduce this drift, but the policy update
still depends on critic gradients.

A complementary line keeps the pretrained decoder fixed.
Inference-time guidance steers multi-step denoising with value functions,
return conditioning, or dynamics guidance [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 30 ] , but needs an iterative
sampler that one-step generators do not expose.
Noise-space steering instead adapts the latent noise of a frozen decoder
through critic gradients, rollout search, or external
feedback [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] ; critic-gradient variants still depend on the learned
value landscape, and search- and feedback-based variants need additional
evaluation signals.
Latent-action offline RL [ 31 , 32 ] trains a
VAE-style latent policy with value gradients or advantage weights, and
learned noise priors [ 33 ] guide an iterative diffusion sampler.
AWLS differs from all of these in how it uses the latent interface.
Following advantage-weighted imitation [ 16 , 34 , 35 ] , offline advantages
estimated with IQL [ 15 ] serve only as detached weights for
supervised reconstruction of demonstrated actions.
AWLS therefore trains no new generative model, keeps single-step inference,
and needs neither value gradients nor critic-defined targets.

2026-10-21.title: Prescribed Performance Guided Safe Reinforcement Learning for Roundabout Navigation of Autonomous Vehicles
2026-10-21.authors: Wenhan Li , Yangrui Zhang , Hang Zhou , Peiran Liu , Yiding Ji
2026-10-21.abstract: Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) face significant challenges in roundabout navigation due to dense traffic interactions and unpredictable agent behaviors, necessitating high levels of adaptability and safety. While the combination of Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Model Predictive Control (MPC) offers a promising approach, existing frameworks suffer from a structural mismatch where pointwise RL decisions fail to align with MPC’s trajectory level optimization, and often lack rigorous safety guarantees. This work proposes RLTrajGen-PPMPC-CBF, a hierarchical framework for safe, smooth and comfort roundabout navigation, which regulates the coupling between RL-based planning and MPC-based control. We employ Prescribed Performance Constraints (PPC) to enforce a gradual, stable convergence between reference trajectories and control outputs, ensuring MPC tracking performance remains consistent with intended behavior from RL. Additionally, a Control Barrier Function (CBF) layer provides real-time safety corrections that are fed back into the RL process. Simulation results in the MetaDrive environment demonstrate that our method achieves a 6.25% increase in average success rate and a 65.87% reduction in Motion Sickness Dose Value (MSDV) compared to the optimal baseline, meanwhile accelerating training convergence.
2026-10-21.introduction:
The advancement of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) has accelerated the deployment of Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs), enabling them to navigate diverse urban environments [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Significant progress has been achieved in standard driving tasks, including lane keeping [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] , lane changing [ 8 , 9 ] , and adaptive cruise control [ 10 , 11 ] . However, roundabouts remain particularly challenging due to dense vehicle interactions and rapidly changing traffic conditions, where planning or control failures may compromise both safety and ride comfort [ 5 , 12 ] .

Current autonomous driving approaches mainly fall into learning-based and model-based methods. Reinforcement Learning (RL) has demonstrated strong capability in high-dimensional perception and decision-making [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . However, its model-free nature makes it difficult to explicitly incorporate vehicle dynamics and safety constraints [ 17 , 18 ] . In contrast, Model Predictive Control (MPC) explicitly considers system dynamics and constraints, while Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) have been widely integrated into MPC to provide formal safety guarantees [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] . Nevertheless, model-based approaches generally exhibit limited adaptability in highly dynamic environments.

To combine the adaptability of RL with the capability to enforce safety and other constraints of MPC, hybrid RL-MPC frameworks have recently attracted increasing attention [ 23 , 24 , 25 , 26 ] . Oliveira et al. [ 25 ] employed RL to determine discrete decision variables to accelerate MPC optimization, while Lubars et al. [ 26 ] combined DDPG with MPC, where MPC served as a safety backup for potentially unsafe RL actions. Zhang et al. [ 8 ] further incorporated a CBF safety filter into an RL-MPC framework (Fig. 1 (b)). Nevertheless, these methods still suffer from a structural mismatch: RL produces pointwise decisions whereas MPC optimizes trajectories, limiting MPC’s ability to accurately realize the planning intent and resulting in less smooth trajectories in complex driving scenarios.
Zhang et al. [ 8 ] introduced a CBFG-PPO framework (Fig. 1 (b)), where RL provides target states for MPC, and CBF filters unsafe actions and feeds corrections back to RL.
Nevertheless, RL produces pointwise decisions while MPC optimizes over trajectories in this framework, which results in structural mismatch and limits MPC’s ability to accurately realize RL intent, producing less smooth trajectories for CAVs in complex environments.

To address the mentioned issues, we propose a novel RLTrajGen-PPMPC-CBF framework, as illustrated in Fig. 1 (c), and validate its effectiveness in a roundabout scenario. The proposed framework consists of three key components: an RL-based Trajectory Generator (RLTrajGen) that facilitates high-level decision making by producing reference trajectories, a prescribed performance MPC (PPMPC) that dynamically adjusts trajectory tracking within a predefined performance envelope, and a CBF-based safety filter that corrects unsafe behaviors. Specifically, we first introduce a trajectory generator that transforms the pointwise outputs of RL into reference trajectories for MPC tracking. In addition, we incorporate a prescribed performance constraint (PPC) mechanism to progressively reduce the tracking error, enabling MPC to more accurately follow the trajectories generated by RL. This design improves the consistency between planning and control, facilitating more stable policy learning and enhanced navigation performance. The main contributions of this work are summarized below:

We design a trajectory generation mechanism that converts single-step outputs from RL into trajectories with adaptive parameters for MPC tracking, thereby effectively resolving the structural mismatch between RL and MPC and significantly accelerating the convergence of training.

We design a trajectory generation mechanism that converts single-step outputs from RL into trajectories with adaptive parameters for MPC tracking, thereby effectively resolving the structural mismatch between RL and MPC and significantly accelerating the convergence of training.

We utilize PPC to regulate the coupling between RL-based planning and MPC-based control, which is the first one in RL-MPC hierarchical framework to our best knowledge. Our method facilitates the progressive reduction of trajectory tracking errors between the planning and control layers, thus balancing the adaptability to complex scenarios and the safety for autonomous systems, and improving ride comfort by producing smoother trajectories.

The remaining sections are organized as follows. Section II introduces the dynamic model of CAVs, prescribed performance constraints, control barrier functions, and formulates the safe navigation problem. Section III presents the RLTrajGen-PPMPC-CBF framework. Section IV includes simulation results and compares our approach with baselines. Section V concludes the paper and outlines future directions.

2026-10-21.title: Adaptive Traversal Tubes for Posture-Aware Navigation of Bipedal Humanoids
2026-10-21.authors: Zijian Ge
2026-10-21.abstract:
Bipedal humanoids can change their effective footprint by adjusting body yaw, enabling both narrow-passage traversal and socially aware yielding.
This paper presents a posture-aware navigation framework centered on Adaptive Traversal Tubes (ATT), Interval Velocity–Heading (IVH) control, and a sidestep-enhanced AMP locomotion prior.
ATT represents a behavior-feasible corridor width field along a reference path, unifying geometric clearance and social comfort into a continuous signal.
IVH maps this width to a continuous frontal-to-sidestep posture schedule and omnidirectional velocity commands.
A velocity-conditioned AMP policy, trained with GVHMR-retargeted frontal/sidestep motions and coupled ( v x , v y ) (v_{x},v_{y}) tracking rewards, is designed to improve transition stability over a generic locomotion controller while remaining interchangeable with the default onboard policy.
This preprint presents the full method; a planned evaluation protocol on a Unitree G1 is outlined, with quantitative results to follow.
Demo videos of MuJoCo simulation and real-robot deployment are available at: https://github.com/lborogzj997/Humanoid-Navigation-in-Crowds-and-Narrow-Spaces .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Indoor service settings—offices, hospitals, apartments, and retail floors—are built around the human body:
doorways, corridors, and furniture clearances are often only marginally wider than a person’s shoulders, while the same spaces are shared with pedestrians who expect socially acceptable distances and yielding [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
Bipedal humanoids are uniquely well matched to this ecology.
Unlike wheeled platforms, whose chassis footprint is essentially fixed in the horizontal plane, a humanoid can reshape its effective passage width by changing body yaw and locomotion style—walking face-forward in open space, then rotating into a lateral (sidestep) posture when the corridor tightens [ 4 , 5 ] .
The same posture change also supports socially polite yielding: by presenting a thinner frontal profile and shifting sideways, the robot can open a lane for a person without abandoning the intended route.
This combination of geometric squeeze-through and socially aware lateral yielding is difficult to realize with classical wheeled navigation stacks, which typically inflate a disk or polygon footprint and either declare a passage infeasible or merely slow down [ 6 ] .

Realizing that potential, however, exposes several general challenges that cut across applications.
First, posture-dependent footprint ambiguity : the clearance that matters is not raw wall-to-wall distance, but whether the robot’s current (and scheduled) body orientation makes the passage behaviorally feasible.
A frontal shoulder width that is safe in a hallway may be too large for a door, while the same door may be passable in a sidestep posture; treating the robot as a fixed disk therefore both over-rejects and under-explains failures [ 4 , 7 ] .
Second, unified geometric and social constraints : in human environments, free space is further compressed by comfort and proxemic expectations [ 1 , 2 ] .
Prior social-navigation work—including our own congestion-aware and spatial–temporal routing methods for mobile robots [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] —has largely addressed crowd-aware path selection and speed adaptation for platforms with essentially fixed footprints.
For bipeds, social compression should instead trigger the same continuous posture response as a physical bottleneck: earlier sidestepping and lateral yielding, not only detours or slowdowns.
Third, navigation-layer posture scheduling under locomotion interfaces : modern humanoids often expose omnidirectional velocity commands to a learned or commercial locomotion policy.
Contact-level footstep and whole-body planners can traverse tight spaces [ 7 , 5 ] , but their computational focus is on footholds and balance rather than on an explicit, tunable mapping from corridor or social width to body yaw.
Conversely, wheeled stacks such as Nav2 [ 6 ] provide mature map-based planning yet lack a first-class notion of frontal-to-sidestep posture.
The general concern is therefore not merely find a collision-free path, but schedule posture and omnidirectional velocity so that the path remains behavior-feasible as clearance and social comfort vary along it.

This paper argues that posture should be elevated to the navigation layer through a shared width signal (Fig. 1 ).
We introduce Adaptive Traversal Tubes (ATT): a path-parameterized width field that represents an effective passage width along a reference path for frontal walking decisions, rather than the raw gap between walls.
Far from obstacles this width saturates at a nominal upper bound w nom w_{\mathrm{nom}} ; it shrinks when geometric clearance or social comfort tightens, thereby unifying static squeeze-through and dynamic yielding in one continuous scalar signal.
We then introduce Interval Velocity–Heading (IVH) tracking, which maps the tube width to a continuous frontal-to-sidestep posture schedule and the corresponding omnidirectional velocity and heading commands for bipedal locomotion.
To execute these commands stably, we further train a sidestep-enhanced AMP locomotion prior from custom human videos (GVHMR capture and GMR retargeting), with task rewards that explicitly couple frontal and lateral velocity tracking during yaw transitions.
ATT and IVH remain compatible with a generic onboard controller; the enhanced prior mainly improves transition smoothness and lateral tracking when IVH requests nonzero ( v x , v y ) (v_{x},v_{y}) jointly.

ATT: a behavior-feasible traversal tube along a reference path that unifies static geometric clearance and dynamic social compression into one posture-relevant width field.

ATT: a behavior-feasible traversal tube along a reference path that unifies static geometric clearance and dynamic social compression into one posture-relevant width field.

IVH: a continuous frontal–sidestep posture schedule driven by the tube width, producing omnidirectional velocity and heading commands for bipedal locomotion.

Sidestep-enhanced AMP prior: a velocity-conditioned locomotion policy trained with frontal/sidestep reference motions and coupled ( v x , v y ) (v_{x},v_{y}) tracking objectives, intended to improve stability of frontal–sidestep transitions relative to a generic locomotion controller while remaining drop-in interchangeable with it.

Evaluation protocol: a planned simulation and real-robot comparison on a Unitree G1 against a frontal-only navigation baseline, to be reported in an updated version of this preprint.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

We organize prior work on bipedal humanoid navigation into three strands: contact-level footstep and whole-body control, learning-based locomotion and tightly coupled navigation policies, and geometry-/social-aware mid-level navigation.
Across these strands, a recurring gap is an explicit, lightweight interface that schedules frontal-to-sidestep posture from a shared geometric–social width signal while remaining compatible with an existing stable locomotion stack.

Classical humanoid navigation plans discrete footholds (or contact sequences) and tracks them with walking-pattern generation, whole-body control (WBC), or model predictive control (MPC), while regulating CoM/ZMP or related balance quantities [ 7 , 11 ] .
This line of work is particularly strong when contact timing, rough terrain, and balance certificates dominate, and it has long recognized that humanoids can alter locomotion style to pass narrow spaces [ 4 , 5 ] .
Subsequent work further develops real-time pattern generation with nonlinear MPC and obstacle avoidance [ 12 ] , as well as efficient contact-surface selection via sparse optimization for online footstep planning [ 13 ] .
Recent formulations continue to push whole-body feasibility in footstep MPC [ 11 , 14 ] .
Their computational focus, however, remains on where to step and how to stay balanced .
Body yaw as a continuous navigational degree of freedom—used to reshape the effective frontal footprint for squeeze-through or yielding—is typically not exposed as a tunable navigation-layer schedule; when sidestepping appears, it is often a byproduct of contact optimization rather than an explicit posture policy.
For indoor corridor and social settings where a reliable velocity-conditioned locomotion controller already exists, solving contact-level WBC/MPC online can also be heavier than necessary for the posture-scheduling decision we target.

Reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially advanced bipedal locomotion, from motion-prior stylization [ 15 ] and adaptive CPG-style bipedal controllers [ 16 ] to real-world humanoid walking policies [ 17 ] .
Building on such controllers, recent work couples navigation more tightly with learning: emotion-aware social navigation for bipeds [ 18 ] , end-to-end LiDAR-to-motor safe/comfortable policies [ 19 ] , physics-guided narrow-path traversal [ 20 ] , and navigation priors learned from human walking data [ 21 ] .
These methods can discover agile behaviors with limited hand-designed structure, but they typically entail costly training, careful reward or constraint design, and nontrivial sim-to-real transfer when perception, posture transitions, and balance are learned jointly.
Retargeting to a new map stack, planner, or locomotion backend often requires substantial retraining rather than local parameter retuning.
We keep ATT+IVH modular with respect to the locomotion backend, and additionally train a sidestep-enhanced AMP prior (Section III-D ) that better matches IVH’s coupled ( v x , v y ) (v_{x},v_{y}) and yaw-transition commands than a generic walking controller.

A complementary trend keeps learned (or model-based) locomotion in the inner loop and adds mid-level planners or safety filters for cluttered scenes: hierarchical task-and-motion planning for safe bipedal navigation under partial observability [ 22 ] , Koopman-lifted MPC for narrow passages [ 23 ] , geometry-aware CBF–MPC safety filters that can reorient a humanoid through tight gaps [ 24 ] , and related CBF safety layers on learned humanoid controllers [ 25 ] .
For human-shared spaces, social bipedal navigation has begun to incorporate proxemics and pedestrian prediction into footstep MPC [ 26 ] , while wheeled social planners increasingly inject context or language-model cues into navigation costs [ 27 , 28 ] .
Classical wheeled stacks and social-navigation surveys, however, largely assume a fixed footprint and solve crowding by detours, inflation, or slowing down [ 6 , 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
These approaches are closest in spirit to our setting, yet most still either optimize contact sequences under social costs, or filter velocities for collision safety, without an explicit behavior-feasible width field that unifies geometric squeeze-through and social comfort into one continuous posture schedule.

Relative to footstep–WBC/MPC pipelines, ATT+IVH do not aim to replace contact-level optimality; they provide a lighter navigation interface that schedules frontal–sidestep posture from tube width and leaves balance to the locomotion layer.
Relative to end-to-end or tightly coupled RL navigation, we trade joint training flexibility for modularity: the same ATT/IVH block can sit atop different velocity-conditioned locomotion controllers with limited retuning, and the width field remains visualizable and parameter-interpretable.
Relative to geometry-aware safety filters and social footstep MPC, we emphasize a shared path-parameterized width signal for both geometric and social compression, mapped by IVH into omnidirectional velocity–heading commands.
In short, whenever a bipedal platform already offers stable omnidirectional locomotion, ATT+IVH add posture-aware passage and yielding without requiring a full contact planner or a navigation policy retrained from scratch.

2026-10-21.title: CovNav: Conformal Prediction-Guided Adaptive Inference for Object Goal Navigation
2026-10-21.authors: Pengying Wu , Zhejia Wen , Kang Ding , Kangjie Zhou , Chunxuan Jiao , Wei Pan , Xiangli Nie , Chang Liu
2026-10-21.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-21.abstract: In object goal navigation (ObjectNav), an embodied agent must find a target object (e.g., “find a bed”) in a previously unseen environment, relying on spatial commonsense such as object co-occurrence. Large Language Models (LLMs) encode this commonsense, but deploying them on robots exposes a trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency: cloud-based models incur latency and privacy risks, whereas small on-device LLMs are fast but prone to hallucinated spatial judgments. Hybrid reasoning LLMs offer both a fast non-thinking mode and a slow thinking mode, which raises a key question for embodied agents: when is slow thinking worth its cost? We propose CovNav , a training-free framework that answers this question with Conformal Prediction (CP), turning dual-process (System 1 / System 2) inference into an uncertainty-aware decision. Much like recent decision models such as Jev, CovNav casts each spatial query as a structured binary decision rather than free-form generation: a local LLM in fast mode judges whether the target is likely near an observed object, CP converts its token probabilities into a prediction set, and only ambiguous queries are escalated to slow chain-of-thought reasoning. The object-pair formulation keeps calibration tractable and supports open-set objects through off-the-shelf detectors. Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show that CovNav surpasses the strongest zero-shot baseline by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points in success rate on HM3D v1 and v2, while invoking slow reasoning for only 12.4% of queries and retaining most of the gain of always-on thinking at a fraction of its latency. Real-robot experiments on a TurtleBot 4 further validate the approach. CovNav shows how calibrated uncertainty can decide when an embodied agent should think slowly, offering a principled form of adaptive test-time reasoning for LLM-based robots.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Recent advances in large foundation models have achieved remarkable success across language understanding, visual reasoning, and knowledge-intensive tasks. A pivotal next step for artificial intelligence is to ground these capabilities in the physical world, building embodied agents that can perceive, reason, and act within complex, unstructured environments [ 1 ] . Among the core competencies required for such agents, the ability to autonomously navigate to semantically specified targets is both fundamental and practically significant, underpinning applications from domestic assistance to search and rescue.

Object goal navigation (ObjectNav) serves as a representative testbed for this capability. Given a semantic target (e.g., “find a bed”), an agent must explore and navigate through a previously unseen environment without any prior map [ 2 , 3 ] . A key enabler for efficient exploration is commonsense spatial knowledge, that is, the understanding that functionally related objects tend to co-locate within the same room (e.g., beds and nightstands in bedrooms, sofas and televisions in living rooms). Large Language Models (LLMs), which encode vast commonsense knowledge from pre-training, have recently emerged as a powerful tool for providing such spatial priors without task-specific training [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , motivating a growing body of work on LLM-based object goal navigation.

Existing LLM-based navigation approaches face significant deployment challenges. First, many state-of-the-art methods rely on cloud-based APIs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) [ 5 , 7 ] , which introduces network latency, raises privacy concerns, and limits deployment in offline or network-constrained scenarios. Second, directly deploying smaller open-source LLMs on resource-constrained robot platforms often leads to performance degradation, manifesting as hallucination and unreliable spatial judgments when processing complex relationships. Third, existing approaches lack adaptive mechanisms to dynamically adjust inference depth based on problem difficulty, resulting in either consistently invoking large models (incurring high computational costs) or relying exclusively on small models (sacrificing accuracy). This raises a critical question: How can we achieve both efficient and accurate spatial reasoning on resource-constrained robotic platforms?

To address this challenge, we propose an adaptive inference framework that dynamically adjusts inference depth based on problem difficulty, utilizing LLM prediction uncertainty as a core metric. A key insight driving our work is that not all spatial reasoning problems require deep deliberation, as illustrated in Figure 1 . For instance, judging the spatial proximity between a television and a sofa is straightforward, given their typical co-occurrence in living rooms. However, determining the relationship between a sofa and a bed requires cross-room reasoning to recognize they belong to distinct functional spaces. Crucially, the output confidence produced by small LLMs, specifically the logits generated during deployment, serves as an effective indicator of problem difficulty, reflecting how well the input aligns with the training corpus. We leverage Conformal Prediction (CP) [ 8 ] , a statistically rigorous uncertainty quantification framework, to assess this confidence without requiring additional model training. CP constructs prediction sets based on model outputs: when the model is highly confident, the prediction set contains a single answer, indicating that the fast direct inference mode is sufficient. Conversely, when uncertain, the prediction set contains multiple possible answers, indicating the model’s inability to identify a unique solution, which triggers a slow deliberative reasoning mode. This mechanism mirrors human cognitive processing: System 1 thinking (fast, intuitive) handles routine decisions, while System 2 thinking (slow, analytical) engages for complex problems [ 9 ] .

This perspective also connects CovNav to two recent trends in LLM reasoning. First, hybrid reasoning models such as Qwen3 [ 10 ] expose both a fast non-thinking mode and a slow thinking mode, and recent work trains such models with reinforcement learning to decide when to think [ 11 , 12 ] ; CovNav makes this decision without any training, using a statistically calibrated criterion. Second, decision models such as Jev [ 13 , 14 ] answer queries with structured choices, binary judgments, or scores instead of free-form text, trading open-ended generation for speed and reliability. CovNav’s fast mode follows the same principle by casting each spatial query as a binary object-pair decision with a confidence score, and adds a CP gate that escalates to System 2 reasoning only when this System 1 decision is uncertain.

Building on this insight, we design a CP-guided navigation framework (CovNav) where the robot constructs an object-wise semantic map using off-the-shelf detection models. For each newly observed object, it queries the LLM to assess spatial relationships with the target object. CP analyzes the response confidence to determine whether the fast direct inference mode can reliably answer the question. If confidence is sufficient, the system directly utilizes the response; otherwise, it activates the slow deliberative reasoning mode for more thorough analysis. The resulting semantic value map, weighted by these assessments, guides the robot toward high-potential exploration regions. Two key design choices facilitate this framework: (1) formulating queries as object-pair relationships rather than open-ended visual question answering makes the problem space more tractable for CP calibration, and (2) leveraging open-source detection models enables open-set semantic understanding without task-specific training.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We propose a novel fast-slow inference paradigm for robotic navigation that adaptively switches between fast direct inference and slow deliberative reasoning based on LLM response uncertainty, effectively achieving a balance between computational efficiency and decision accuracy on resource-constrained platforms.

We propose a novel fast-slow inference paradigm for robotic navigation that adaptively switches between fast direct inference and slow deliberative reasoning based on LLM response uncertainty, effectively achieving a balance between computational efficiency and decision accuracy on resource-constrained platforms.

We introduce the first use of Conformal Prediction to gate between the fast and slow reasoning modes of an LLM for object navigation, providing a theoretically grounded and training-free switching mechanism. We further design an object-pair-based query formulation that makes CP calibration tractable while enabling open-set semantic understanding through off-the-shelf vision models.

We validate our approach through extensive simulated and real-world robot experiments, demonstrating significant improvements in both navigation efficiency and success rate compared to existing methods.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work in zero-shot object navigation, LLM-based navigation and uncertainty quantification in Embodied AI. Section III provides the problem formulation and details our proposed methodology, specifically the object-based semantic mapping and the CP-guided fast-slow switching mechanism. Section IV presents extensive experimental results, including simulation comparisons and ablation studies. Section V details real-world validations, demonstrating the effectiveness and efficiency of our approach in physical environments. Section VI concludes the paper and discusses future directions.

# II Related Work

## II-A Zero-Shot Object Goal Navigation

Object goal navigation (ObjectNav) requires an agent to navigate to instances of specific object categories in unknown environments, combining visual perception, semantic understanding, and spatial reasoning [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . It is closely related to other embodied navigation tasks, such as image-goal navigation [ 18 ] and multi-agent cooperative navigation [ 19 ] . End-to-end approaches learn navigation policies directly from observations via reinforcement learning [ 20 ] , but tend to generalize poorly to unseen environments compared with modular pipelines [ 2 ] . The Object Memory Transformer (OMT) [ 3 ] introduced long-term semantic memory to improve navigation efficiency, while Goal-Oriented Semantic Exploration [ 2 ] pioneered episodic semantic maps with efficient exploration strategies.
Recent modular approaches decompose navigation into separate components. The SEEK framework [ 17 ] combines spatial configurations with commonsense knowledge about object relationships. Liu et al. [ 21 ] explore implicit scene memory for target-directed navigation by storing historical observations in a NeRF-based memory and retrieving target-relevant cues through dual-space attention with uncertainty masking. Heterogeneous Scene Representation (HSR) [ 22 ] models human-robot-object interactions using graph attention networks, while Commonsense-Aware Object Value Graph (OVG-Nav) [ 23 ] incorporates topological structures leveraging visual observations and commonsense priors. Multi-View Visual Transformer (MVVT) [ 24 ] expands input perspectives to capture richer spatial context relationships for navigation.

Zero-shot object navigation (ZSON) enables agents to locate objects without explicit training on specific categories or environments [ 25 ] , [ 26 ] . ZSON [ 27 ] established the foundational approach by training on image-goal navigation and projecting language queries into multimodal semantic embedding spaces. The Target-Directed Attention Network (TDANet) [ 26 ] advanced zero-shot capabilities through attention mechanisms learning spatial and semantic relationships using Siamese architecture designs.
Training-free approaches have emerged with Exploration with Soft Commonsense constraints (ESC) [ 4 ] , which transfers commonsense knowledge from pre-trained models using prompt-based grounding and spatial reasoning. TriHelper [ 28 ] addresses specific challenges including collision avoidance and exploration efficiency through specialized helper modules.
Foundation model integration has enabled sophisticated zero-shot approaches. SemNav [ 29 ] integrates Vision Foundation Models with model-based planners for long-horizon decision making through frontier exploration, achieving promising performance in ZSON.

## II-B LLM-Based Visual Navigation

Large Language Models have revolutionized zero-shot navigation by providing reasoning capabilities and semantic understanding for interpreting natural language instructions [ 5 , 25 ] . OpenFMNav [ 25 ] pioneered LLM integration with vision-language models for open-set navigation, using LLMs to extract object proposals and VLMs to build Versatile Semantic Score Maps (VSSM) for exploration.
Beyond navigation, multi-agent LLM frameworks such as MALMM [ 30 ] distribute high-level planning and low-level control across specialized LLM agents with a supervisor for zero-shot robotic manipulation. Cognitive Planning frameworks [ 31 ] integrate LLMs with Large Vision-Language Models for efficient exploration strategies using 3D modular scene representations. LIM2N [ 32 ] enables multimodal input processing where language and hand-drawn inputs serve as navigation constraints.
Advanced reasoning approaches include Tree-of-Thought methods in VLTNet [ 6 ] for navigation frontier selection with multi-path reasoning and backtracking capabilities. Chain-of-Thought integration in CL-CoTNav [ 7 ] provides closed-loop hierarchical reasoning with structured feedback in decision-making. World model integration in WMNav [ 33 ] predicts outcomes and builds memories using Curiosity Value Maps for dynamic policy configuration. NavGPT [ 34 ] demonstrated early purely LLM-based navigation through zero-shot sequential action prediction with explicit high-level planning capabilities. Beyond navigation, hybrid reasoning models such as Qwen3 [ 10 ] can switch between thinking and non-thinking modes, and recent methods learn when to invoke deliberate reasoning through reinforcement learning [ 11 , 12 ] .

## II-C Uncertainty Quantification in Embodied AI

Uncertainty quantification is essential for safe and reliable robot decision-making. Classical approaches such as MC-Dropout [ 35 ] and Deep Ensembles [ 36 ] estimate epistemic uncertainty by performing multiple stochastic forward passes or training several independent networks, respectively. While effective in controlled settings, these methods incur substantial computational overhead, making them impractical for real-time robotic deployments on resource-constrained platforms.

Conformal Prediction (CP) [ 8 ] has recently gained traction as a lightweight, distribution-free alternative that provides rigorous statistical coverage guarantees without retraining. In robotics, CP has been applied to safe motion planning among dynamic agents [ 37 , 38 ] , where prediction sets over future trajectories enable conservative yet efficient collision avoidance. Ren et al. [ 39 ] introduced KnowNo, which applies CP to LLM planners so that a robot asks for help when the prediction set contains multiple options, and later used CP for embodied question answering [ 40 ] , where prediction set sizes decide when additional exploration is needed.

In the context of LLMs, quantifying output uncertainty remains an open challenge. Kadavath et al. [ 41 ] showed that large language models are reasonably well calibrated on multiple-choice questions and can estimate the probability that their own answers are correct, though such self-evaluation lacks formal statistical guarantees. Kumar et al. [ 42 ] applied CP to LLM outputs in multiple-choice question answering, showing that conformal prediction sets achieve the target coverage and that their uncertainty estimates closely track prediction accuracy. However, existing work has not explored CP-based uncertainty quantification for LLM-guided robotic navigation. Our work addresses this gap by using CP to dynamically gate between fast direct inference and slow deliberative reasoning, thus providing the first principled mechanism for adaptive LLM inference in embodied navigation tasks.
