2026-10-21.title: PLaCA: Learning Patch-Level Future Latent Change for Action Generation
2026-10-21.authors: Zhan Yi , Yuchen Wang , Chao Li , Lei Hong , Boyuan Yang
2026-10-21.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-21.abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot
actions from visual observations and language
instructions, but effective manipulation also
requires anticipating how the environment will
change. Existing world-action models explore future
image prediction and latent dynamics modeling.
However, generating complete future images can be
computationally expensive, while highly compressed
latent representations may obscure local changes.
To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA,
a world-to-action framework built around future
latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially
structured patch-level future latent change from
the current multimodal input, preserving local
information about expected environmental changes.
We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision
to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes
and a future-to-action interface that explicitly
incorporates predicted future latent change into
action generation.
Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves
a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only
baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA
improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to
3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating
only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second
training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of
future latent change modeling for downstream robotic
manipulation.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically generate robot
actions from current visual observations and language
instructions [ 7 , 15 , 30 ] . However, in manipulation tasks such as grasping,
pushing, and placing, effective action generation requires
more than understanding the current environment. A policy
must also consider how its actions may change object positions,
contact relations, and local environmental states. To
incorporate such future information, recent studies have
explored integrating world modeling with VLA policies,
motivating the development of world-action modeling (WAM) [ 10 , 40 ] .

Existing approaches represent future information in different
ways. Some predict future images or videos [ 8 , 55 ] ,
while others model future states or temporal dynamics in latent
space [ 16 , 2 ] .
Recent studies have further explored compact latent motion
representations [ 29 , 46 , 47 ] .
Latent-space modeling has become a widely adopted approach
in world modeling and robot learning [ 16 , 2 , 46 ] .
While pixel-level future prediction provides rich visual
details, generating complete future images often involves
reconstructing substantial redundant visual content,
leading to additional computational costs [ 44 , 46 ] .
In contrast, latent-space modeling avoids explicit pixel-level
reconstruction, yet choosing an appropriate future representation
for robotic manipulation remains an important question.
For action generation, it may not be necessary to recover
the complete future state or all intermediate dynamics.
Instead, a policy may benefit from information about
how the environment is expected to change.

Recent work has shown that differences between latent states
can capture information related to robot motion. StaMo [ 29 ] learns
highly compressed latent state representations and uses
the latent displacement between states to represent robot
motion. It also explores latent motion prediction for world
modeling. However, latent representations differ
in how they preserve spatial information. As illustrated in
Fig. 1 (a), when a robot places an object into
a box, the changes are mainly concentrated around the robot
arm and the object, while much of the background remains
unchanged. Highly compressed state representations can encode
such changes, but they do not explicitly preserve the
correspondence between spatial locations and their latent
changes. In contrast, retaining the patch-level spatial
structure allows future changes at different image locations
to be represented separately, as shown in
Fig. 1 (b). Moreover, the magnitude of future
change can vary considerably across patches, while uniform
patch supervision does not specifically emphasize regions
undergoing larger changes. This motivates our first research
question: How can we preserve the spatial structure
of future latent change and learn local changes more
effectively by accounting for their different magnitudes?

Another important question is how future modeling can be effectively coupled with action generation. Prior work has explored different approaches, including jointly learning future prediction and action policies within shared architectures [ 40 , 46 ] , using predicted future images or video plans to guide downstream control [ 52 , 14 ] , and leveraging learned latent or interaction dynamics for action inference [ 37 , 41 ] . These studies provide different ways of using future information to inform robotic behavior. For the spatially structured future latent change considered in this work, the predicted representation preserves local information about expected environmental changes across image regions. This motivates investigating how such spatially organized predictions can be incorporated into action representations to support action generation. We therefore pose our second research question: How can predicted future latent change be effectively used to support action generation?

To address these questions, we propose PLaCA ,
a world-to-action framework built around future latent change . PLaCA directly predicts
spatially structured patch-level future latent change
from the current multimodal input and employs patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize
regions with larger changes. We further introduce a future-to-action interface that incorporates the
predicted future latent change into the action representation,
allowing it to directly contribute to full action-chunk
generation.

We evaluate PLaCA on LIBERO-Long, achieving a 79.0% task success rate. Ablation studies demonstrate that preserving fine-grained spatial structure, employing change-aware supervision, and incorporating predicted future latent change into action generation through the future-to-action interface contribute to improved downstream manipulation success rates.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We investigate patch-level future latent change
modeling , which directly predicts future latent change
from the current multimodal input while preserving its
spatial structure, providing local future information
for action generation.

We propose patch-level change-aware supervision ,
which adjusts the supervision weights according to the
magnitude of ground-truth future latent change.
Ablation results show that this approach improves
closed-loop manipulation performance compared with
uniform patch supervision.

We design an explicit future-to-action interface that incorporates the final predicted future latent
change into the action representation, allowing future
information to directly contribute to full action-chunk
generation.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 World-Action Modeling

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models unify visual observations, language
instructions, and robot actions within end-to-end policies, extending
large-scale vision-language models toward general-purpose robotic
control [ 57 , 25 , 6 , 7 , 12 , 15 , 30 ] . While conventional VLAs
primarily focus on predicting continuous actions or action sequences from
current multimodal observations [ 22 , 5 , 38 , 43 , 42 ] , recent studies have increasingly incorporated
future modeling, enabling policies to reason not only about what to do but also about what may happen after an action is
executed [ 10 , 56 , 52 , 14 ] . This trend has gradually extended
VLA research from direct observation-to-action mapping toward joint modeling of
environmental dynamics and robot behavior.

One line of work models future environmental changes through
image or video prediction [ 44 ] , while other
approaches jointly learn future modeling and action
generation [ 10 , 56 ] .
WorldAgen performs future-state prediction and action prediction
within a unified Transformer, allowing world modeling and policy
learning to share internal representations [ 40 ] .
CoT-VLA uses predicted future images as intermediate visual guidance
for subsequent action generation [ 52 ] . DynBridge learns interaction dynamics that connect future
interaction modeling with robot control [ 41 ] , while Motus further
integrates latent action modeling, world modeling, and action generation into a
unified framework, using shared latent representations to characterize the
relationship between robot behavior and environmental changes [ 4 ] .
DreamVLA combines dynamic-region-guided future information with spatial and
semantic cues for action generation [ 51 ] , while Mantis
learns latent visual foresight with a separate prediction
head [ 48 ] . Collectively, these studies reflect a growing trend
in which future modeling is increasingly coupled with action generation through
shared or explicitly connected representations. We focus on directly predicting
spatially structured future latent change and incorporating its predicted tokens
into the action representation through gated cross-attention.

## 2.2 Latent Dynamics

Future image and video prediction provides a detailed
description of environmental changes, but generating full
future frames can be computationally expensive [ 55 , 8 ] . Recent
studies have therefore explored latent state, latent motion,
and latent action representations for future modeling and
robot control [ 9 ] [ 49 , 3 , 2 , 16 ] .

One line of work focuses on representing dynamics in
latent space. CoWVLA separates structural and motion
information and learns a continuous latent motion chain
to represent temporal evolution [ 46 ] . CoMo learns
continuous latent motion by combining temporal differences
with contrastive learning [ 47 ] . StaMo takes
a different approach by learning highly compressed latent
state representations from individual observations. It
shows that differences between these states contain robot
motion information and can support action decoding.
StaMo further uses state and motion representations as
prediction targets for VLA world modeling and explores
latent-motion co-training [ 29 ] . These studies
explore different ways to capture temporal changes in
latent space, including continuous motion representations
and differences between compact latent states.

Another line of work investigates how latent dynamics
can support action generation. VideoWorld learns discrete
latent codes that represent future visual changes and
uses the predicted codes together with visual information
for inverse dynamics-based action decoding [ 37 ] .
Latent Bridge instead predicts continuous feature changes
to update latent representations, allowing the policy to
reduce repeated VLM computation during action
generation [ 31 ] . These approaches illustrate
different ways of using learned latent dynamics to
support action generation.

Our work focuses on learning spatially structured
future latent change and using the predicted
representation for action generation.

u\leq 1 , and escape is possible from every state for ν > 1 
u>1 . For the slower or equally fast evader, sin ⁡ α < ν ≤ 1 \sin\alpha<
u\leq 1 , we construct the solution with Isaacs’ characteristics and verify it in feedback form, using a Filippov pursuer relay and a one-sided evader branch. The finite escape time is the first root of one scalar equation, and the holding region is bounded by the nonusable parts of the rays and a barrier that closes with a convex corner on the front axis. Sample-and-hold counter-controls show that this escape time is the value of the game in nonanticipative strategies at every state except the corner. 2026-10-21.introduction:
A directional sensor attached to a moving vehicle observes only part of the plane. Escaping surveillance therefore requires leaving its field of view, rather than outrunning the observer. We study minimum-time escape from an unbounded forward cone of half-angle 0 < α < π / 2 0<\alpha<\pi/2 , with an omnidirectional evader and a Reeds–Shepp pursuer that can drive forward or in reverse but cannot rotate in place ( Reeds and Shepp, 1990 ) . The evader minimizes the exit time and the pursuer maximizes it.

The closest forward-only model is the conic surveillance–evasion game of Lewin and Olsder (1979) . Reverse motion changes its geometry: backing away reduces the evader’s bearing without turning and can preserve observation indefinitely.

Our analysis uses Isaacs’ characteristics and singular surfaces ( Isaacs, 1965 ; Lewin, 1994 ) . Related surveillance games include circular detection regions ( Dobbie, 1966 ; Lewin and Breakwell, 1975 ) , an isotropic rocket ( Lewin and Olsder, 1989 ) , two identical cars ( Greenfeld, 1987 ; Ruiz, 2026 ) , an agile pursuer ( Braun et al., 2025 ) , and a fixed-course target ( Weintraub et al., 2023 ) . Differential-drive capture and surveillance games are developed in several works ( Ruiz et al., 2013 ; Ruiz and Murrieta-Cid, 2016 ; Ruiz, 2022 ; Saavedra and Ruiz, 2024 ) , including escape from a conic field of view ( Ruiz, 2023 ) . Their velocity set is a diamond, allowing rotation in place; the Reeds–Shepp set is a bow tie, allowing full speed and full turn rate simultaneously. 2026-10-21.title: A Head Camera Is (Almost) All You Need: An Electronics-Free UMI Glove Labelled and Observed by One Moving Camera
2026-10-21.authors: Yosub Shin , Yuan Liu , Igor Molybog
2026-10-21.abstract: Handheld demonstration devices decouple data collection from the robot, but conventional designs burden the hand with a wrist camera, cables and a pose tracker (SLAM, an IMU, a VR controller, or a fixed external camera that the collector’s body occludes), and burden the pipeline with as many data streams to timestamp, synchronise and cross-calibrate. We show that a single egocentric camera ($122) worn on the collector’s head replaces both the camera and the tracker, and the streams with one. It reads printed fiducials on an electronics-free glove ($22) against paper tiles taped around the workspace, giving the 6-DoF gripper pose and the jaw width from the same frames the policy will see; at deployment the same camera rides a low-cost ($120) arm beside the robot that mimics the collector’s head from the robot’s joint state. Against the robot’s encoders the labels are accurate to 6.5 mm 6.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} and 1.6 ° 1.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} median with 93 93\text{\,} – 100 % 100\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} frame coverage, and a policy trained on them instead of encoders pays 3 % 3\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} in validation loss. Adding 194 glove demonstrations to 48 teleoperated episodes lifts rollout success from 10/25 to 17/25, level with 172 teleoperated episodes alone (18/25), and the full co-trained head-camera policy succeeds in 20/25 against 15/25 for the wrist-camera recipe, whose policies drop the object when the goal leaves their view, and 12/25 for a fixed camera.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Teleoperation occupies a robot and an operator for every demonstration. Handheld devices decouple collection from the robot: with ours a collector records 2.0–3.1 demonstrations per minute against 1.6 by teleoperation on the same task (§ 2 ), in parallel and without robot time, with a $22 printed glove, a $122 wearable camera and four paper tiles. The glove is purely mechanical, a replica of the robot’s gripper carrying fiducials and nothing else, and the one head-worn camera is at once the policy’s observation and the source of the gripper’s pose and jaw width, so there is no second sensor stream to synchronise or calibrate against.

Every UMI-style device answers two questions: what does the policy see , and how is the gripper tracked ? The conventional answer puts both on the wrist. SLAM on the wrist camera [ 7 , 4 ] needs a mapping pass and textured scenes and loses track under occlusion or fast motion; a visual-inertial sensor adds a second device [ 26 ] ; a VR controller adds weight ( 119 g 119\text{\,}\mathrm{g} of YUBI’s 319 g 319\text{\,}\mathrm{g} [ 16 , 23 ] ) and external tracking infrastructure [ 2 , 5 ] ; a fixed overhead camera [ 20 ] avoids drift but ties collection to a mount and loses the hand behind the body in 8 8\text{\,} – 22 % 22\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of frames (§ 2 ). Each tracker is a second stream beside the camera, with its own clock and calibration to reconcile, and the wrist camera itself adds cable and weight while its view is tied to the hand: even through UMI’s 155 ° 155\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} fisheye the frame holds what the jaws face, so a drop-off bin leaves it once the hand lifts or turns [ 11 ] .

We answer both with one head-worn camera, addressing two challenges this workshop names [ 1 ] : tracking without SLAM and the human-to-robot viewpoint gap. Gaze precedes the hand [ 14 ] , so the head keeps the gripper at arm’s length, unoccluded by the torso, with the workspace around it. From that vantage an 11-face fiducial ball gives the pose, tags on the jaws the opening, and four AprilTag tiles [ 17 ] the world frame. At deployment the camera rides a small printed servo arm beside the robot that imitates head motion from the robot’s joint state, identically in teleoperation and rollouts, so glove, teleoperated and rollout data share one viewpoint. EgoMimic [ 13 ] co-trains on egocentric human video with the hand pose estimated from the video; our collector holds a replica of the robot’s gripper, so contact and jaw width are the robot’s. Active-vision teleoperation [ 8 , 6 ] steers a robot camera from a VR headset; our positioner needs neither operator nor headset.

# 2 System

The glove is an unpowered printed replica of the YAM gripper [ 12 ] from Shin [20] , stock fingers on a rack-and-pinion, with an 11-face 15 mm 15\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} ArUco dodecahedron [ 10 , 24 ] on the back of the hand. Fingertip tags facing a wrist camera [ 7 ] are edge-on from the head, so each jaw carries a printed wedge, the tail , with 12 mm 12\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} AprilTags on five faces beside a fixed tag on the gripper back: one face is always visible, and the tail-to-back distance along the jaw axis gives the width. Parts cost $22. The collector wears an Arducam B0587 4K camera ($122) on a $10 GoPro head strap ( 103 g 103\text{\,}\mathrm{g} worn), recording at 15 Hz 15\text{\,}\mathrm{H}\mathrm{z} with a short exposure, aimed once per session so the frame centre coincides with the collector’s own (App. A ). Four 60 mm 60\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} AprilTag tiles define the workspace frame, placed where the gaze lands during grasping so that two stay in view, with no other tag in the scene. Continuous recording with keypress episode boundaries gives 2.0–3.1 pick-and-place demonstrations per minute (median 6 6\text{\,} – 8 s 8\text{\,}\mathrm{s} ) against 1.6 by teleoperation on the same arm (median 14 s 14\text{\,}\mathrm{s} ).

Each frame yields (i) the camera pose from the tiles, (ii) the gripper pose in the camera frame from PnP over the visible ball faces, and (iii) the jaw width from the tails by a per-unit linear map ( 0.9 0.9\text{\,} – 3.8 mm 3.8\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} holdout RMS on calipered spacers). Composing (i) and (ii) gives the tool pose in the tile frame; a one-time link to the robot base, fitted with the ball mounted on the YAM (App. A ), turns it into joint-space actions comparable to teleoperation. Two mechanisms keep the camera localised under head motion: the tile layout is refit from the multi-tile frames of the footage itself (four-tile reprojection 3.4 px 3.4\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} to 0.5 px 0.5\text{\,}\mathrm{p}\mathrm{x} RMS), and frames with a single tile are chained to the previous accepted pose under velocity bounds rather than discarded. Dropouts over 0.3 s 0.3\text{\,}\mathrm{s} split an episode and segments under 1 s 1\text{\,}\mathrm{s} are dropped: 0.7 0.7\text{\,} – 7.4 % 7.4\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of frames are cut per session, 200 segments from 198 demonstrations. A fixed external camera on the same demonstrations loses 8 8\text{\,} – 22 % 22\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} to body occlusion and fragments them into 259 segments.

A six-joint SO-101 follower arm [ 21 ] (six Feetech STS3215 servos, $122 in parts) stands beside the YAM and carries the same camera on a GoPro-pattern mount in place of its gripper (Fig. 1 c). Its kinematics are fitted once from 60 tile-verified poses ( 7 mm 7\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} / 0.7 ° 0.7\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} residual). At each session start it parks at the collector’s median head pose and registers against the tiles; thereafter it tracks the gripper from the YAM’s joint encoders alone, transparent to the policy: a fixed-gain controller holds the gripper’s bearing and a ridge-regression residual fitted on about 100 glove episodes reproduces head motion relative to the hand ( 46 mm 46\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} / 5.4 ° 5.4\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} median head-pose error on held-out episodes against 87 mm 87\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} / 7.0 ° 7.0\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} for a static camera; App. A ). The camera follows the gripper with 0.4 s 0.4\text{\,}\mathrm{s} lag and 16 mm 16\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\mathrm{m} median tile-referenced error, and frames it where the collector did (normalised gripper centroid 0.37/0.62 against 0.38/0.60).

Teleoperation under the positioner gave 178 episodes (38.6k frames; 6 held out for validation); four glove sessions gave 198 demonstrations, 200 segments (50.0k frames; 6 held out). All policies are ACT [ 25 ] in LeRobot [ 3 ] , 50k steps, joint-space actions, best checkpoint by validation loss on the held-out teleoperated episodes. Following Shin [20] , glove timelines are resampled to teleoperation pace and widths mapped into the gripper command space, with the closed state anchored to the teleoperators’ minimum commanded squeeze (0.22 of stroke rather than the 0.25 median): the head-view policies released no block during the carry in 120 rollouts.

2026-10-21.title: JARVIS: From Visual Manuals to Autonomous Robotic Assembly
2026-10-21.authors: Fan Ding , Fucai Ke , Kevin Yuchen Ma , Xuewen Luo , Wenyu Liang , Vishnu Monn Baskaran , Hamid Rezatofighi , Yan Wu
2026-10-21.abstract: Visual manuals communicate procedural knowledge through stepwise diagrams, but translating these instructions into reliable long-horizon robotic execution remains challenging. We introduce JARVIS, a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous visual-manual-guided execution without additional language instructions. JARVIS comprises 236,679 236{,}679 LEGO assembly tasks across 8,987 8{,}987 scenes, with a carefully curated JARVIS-v1 suite of 50 50 tasks for interactive robotic evaluation. Tasks span varying initial structural complexities and assembly horizons, requiring agents to interpret manuals, ground actions in an evolving workspace, and execute the intended procedure. A structure-aware evaluation protocol captures geometric accuracy, structural relations, construction order, partial progress, and completion. We further introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that composes robot primitives into executable programs and uses execution feedback for verification and recovery, without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates. Across nine multimodal and reasoning models, task-oriented primitives increase the average assembly score. Performance nevertheless declines sharply with assembly horizon, and execution errors remain difficult to correct. Prior-task experience improves initial performance, while repeated reflection provides inconsistent benefits, highlighting persistent limitations in connecting visual procedural reasoning with reliable physical execution.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Across many everyday activities, people learn how to build, assemble, and operate things by following visual manuals. These manuals organize tasks into standardized step-by-step diagrams, providing a compact and transferable representation of procedural knowledge that conveys both the desired outcome and the process required to achieve it [ 31 ] . Following such manuals requires humans to interpret the visual instructions, align each illustrated step with the current physical state, and translate the inferred procedure into concrete actions. This ability goes beyond visual recognition alone, requiring visual reasoning to be tightly coupled with sequential decision-making and physical execution [ 32 ] . As multimodal models increasingly move beyond passive perception toward embodied interaction [ 16 , 12 , 17 ] , a fundamental question is whether machines can interpret procedural knowledge from visual manuals and autonomously translate it into action.

Recent studies have taken initial steps toward this capability, particularly in manual-guided robotic assembly [ 31 , 39 , 9 , 15 ] . Existing approaches have primarily developed task-specific solutions for extracting assembly structures, predicting part poses, and generating assembly plans [ 31 , 28 , 18 , 32 , 36 , 22 ] .
Many therefore stop before physical execution; when execution is included, it is often realised through predefined or manually engineered control pipelines. As a result, they do not directly evaluate whether a model can autonomously close the loop from visual manual understanding to physical construction. Benchmarking this capability further requires end-to-end execution tasks and metrics that capture partial progress and structural correctness beyond binary task success [ 11 , 33 ] . Consequently, it remains unclear how well current multimodal models can use a visual manual as the task specification and autonomously carry out a complete procedure over multiple steps.

To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce JARVIS, a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous visual-manual-guided execution. We construct a large-scale task collection comprising 236,679 236{,}679 assembly tasks across 8,987 8{,}987 LEGO scenes, spanning diverse initial structures and assembly horizons. From this collection, we curate JARVIS-v1, a suite of 50 50 tasks across three difficulty levels for interactive robotic evaluation. As shown in Fig. 1 , an agent receives a visual assembly manual and workspace observations, infers the intended procedure, and executes it while adapting to the evolving physical state. Each manipulation affects subsequent steps, requiring coherent planning and execution throughout assembly. We further introduce a structure-aware evaluation protocol that measures relative geometry, structural relations, and completion, capturing partial progress and accumulated errors beyond binary task success.

Turning manual understanding into physical execution poses a separate practical challenge. Learned control policies typically require task-specific robot action supervision, as low-level trajectories are tied to the robot’s kinematics and control interface. Collecting dedicated demonstrations or trajectories for each new construction task is therefore costly. We introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that bridges manual-derived reasoning and physical execution without task-specific action trajectories. Equipped with a compact library of verified robot primitives, the agent grounds the manual, composes executable behaviours, and uses execution reflection for verification, recovery, and replanning.

Using JARVIS, we evaluate 9 multimodal and reasoning models on manual-guided assembly tasks spanning different structural complexities and assembly horizons. Task-oriented robot skills raise the average assembly score from 7.88 7.88 to 14.71 14.71 without task-specific action trajectories, demonstrating the value of tool-grounded execution. Nevertheless, performance declines sharply with assembly horizon, and improvements in intermediate grounding do not reliably translate into successful assembly. Prior-task experience improves first-round performance, whereas repeated reflection and recovery from execution errors remain unreliable. These findings expose the difficulty of connecting procedural reasoning, physical execution, and reflection-based correction in long-horizon assembly.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate autonomous visual-manual-guided execution for long-horizon robotic assembly and introduce JARVIS, comprising 236,679 236{,}679 tasks across 8,987 8{,}987 scenes, with a curated JARVIS-v1 suite for interactive evaluation. A structure-aware protocol measures geometric and relational correctness, partial progress, and completion.

We introduce JARVIS-agentic , a tool-grounded embodied agent that translates visual assembly instructions into executable programs through reusable robot primitives. The framework integrates planning, execution verification, and recovery without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates.

We evaluate nine multimodal and reasoning models , revealing persistent difficulties in translating manual understanding into reliable long-horizon execution. Our analysis shows that task-oriented tools and prior-task experience improve performance, while online reflection provides inconsistent benefits and error recovery remains limited.

A structure-aware protocol measures geometric and relational correctness, partial progress, and completion.

2. We introduce JARVIS-agentic , a tool-grounded embodied agent that translates visual assembly instructions into executable programs through reusable robot primitives. The framework integrates planning, execution verification, and recovery without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates.

Our analysis shows that task-oriented tools and prior-task experience improve performance, while online reflection provides inconsistent benefits and error recovery remains limited.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related work

Visual assembly planning focuses on recovering structural and procedural representations from images. MEPNet predicts stepwise component poses from LEGO manuals [ 32 ] , while Manual-PA estimates assembly order and part poses from instruction diagrams [ 39 ] . Neural Assembler infers component graphs and assembly sequences from multiple views of a completed structure [ 37 ] , and AssemLM predicts assembly poses from manuals, point clouds, and language [ 14 ] . Related generative methods produce buildable structures from text [ 27 ] or represent brick sequences through connectivity [ 20 ] . These tasks assess whether a model can infer a valid assembly representation. Autonomous execution additionally requires grounding that representation in a changing workspace and maintaining its validity through physical interaction.

Several systems connect assembly representations to robot control. Manual2Skill uses assembly graphs, learned pose estimation, and motion planning for furniture assembly [ 31 ] , and Manual2Skill++ incorporates explicit connector constraints [ 30 ] . BrickCraft derives assembly sequences and situated manuals from digital designs to guide learned visuomotor skills [ 38 ] . ManualVLA generates intermediate manuals from goal states to condition action execution [ 10 ] . These systems demonstrate assembly under their respective representations and control designs. A distinct evaluation question is how reliably general-purpose multimodal agents can interpret a supplied visual manual, determine executable actions, and respond to deviations during construction. JARVIS formulates this capability as a method-agnostic benchmark.

AssemblyBench evaluates assembly order and physically plausible part trajectories [ 22 ] , while WorkBenchMark evaluates robotic construction of target LEGO Duplo structures [ 24 ] . CaP-X studies coding agents under different tool abstractions and feedback settings [ 6 ] , and ENPIRE investigates policy improvement through repeated physical trials [ 34 ] . The central question in JARVIS is whether visual procedural understanding survives execution: can an agent preserve the intended structure as actions accumulate, and recover when the observed state departs from the manual? Our structure-aware evaluation measures partial assembly quality, while controlled experiments examine the effects of horizon, initial complexity, and execution feedback.

2026-10-21.title: EchoNav: Evidential BEV Completion from Historical Observations for Visual Navigation
2026-10-21.authors: Diwen Liu , Yiyang Shao , Borui Wang , Chi Zhang , Yunhui Liu
2026-10-21.abstract: Visual navigation in cluttered environments requires robots to recover previously observed structure and infer obstacles and free space that remain occluded. We present a framework that combines temporal aggregation and occupancy completion in an evidential bird’s-eye-view (BEV) representation predicted from short RGB sequences. A decoder adapts frozen VGGT-Omega features and combines historical residual proposals using cellwise weights and a learned no-update option. The BEV predictor produces a local map in the latest ego frame without depth or camera-pose inputs or explicit geometric warping. The evidential model treats observed free space separately and predicts occupancy with associated confidence across the remaining supported region. We train the predictor on simulated RGB sequences paired with complete and visibility-masked occupancy annotations. Our experiments evaluate navigation in simulation and on a wheeled robot, with additional demonstrations on quadruped and humanoid robots. In simulated sequential two-goal navigation, our system achieves 89.6% success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 32.5 percentage points. Across 60 wheeled-robot trials in 20 scenes, it achieves 73.3% success, compared with 33.3% for the strongest evaluated baseline.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Mobile robots navigating cluttered environments must make spatial decisions from incomplete visual observations (Fig. ). Each camera view reveals only part of the surrounding layout. Relying only on the latest view can cause a robot to revisit unproductive routes or become trapped in local minima and fail to reach its goal. Observations retained within the RGB window provide evidence about nearby regions that are no longer visible in the current image. The more complete map gives the planner additional local context to choose more efficient paths. Yet some obstacles and free space remain hidden behind furniture and walls throughout this process. Predicting these hidden regions can inform planning, but the robot must account for the uncertainty of those predictions. The challenge is therefore to build a local BEV map that retains useful information across time, distinguishes observed space from inferred structure, and indicates how reliable its predictions are.

Learned occupancy anticipation has demonstrated that visual context can help predict unseen structure [ 1 ] . In autonomous driving, occupancy completion has shown strong results in scene understanding by predicting occupancy in both visible and occluded regions [ 2 , 3 ] . For mobile robots, anticipating obstacles and free space beyond current observations can similarly provide a more complete map for planning, supporting exploration and navigation before those regions are directly observed [ 1 , 4 ] .

BEV occupancy maps place obstacles, free space, and candidate paths in a common top-down frame. This representation makes the basis of motion decisions transparent. The map describes the environment, while the planner and controller handle robot footprints, clearance margins, and motion constraints. This separation leaves the choice of planning algorithm open to the task and robot platform.

To address these challenges, we propose an RGB-based framework for temporal BEV mapping and occupancy completion. It combines evidence from earlier observations with predictions of persistently hidden obstacles and free space, producing occupancy and reliability estimates for local planning. The BEV predictor requires neither depth nor camera-pose inputs and uses no explicit geometric warping.

The main contributions are:

Spatially selective temporal BEV fusion. We propose a framework that integrates RGB histories into an ego-centric occupancy BEV. Historical residual proposals from a shared decoder are weighted independently at each map location. The fusion includes a learned no-update option that allows the anchor representation to be retained.

Observation-aware evidential occupancy completion. We develop an occupancy-learning formulation that distinguishes observed free space from inferred occupancy and predicts spatial support and confidence for planning. Visibility-aware supervision supports completion of occluded obstacles and free space while regularizing evidence assigned to incorrect predictions.

Navigation integration and physical validation. We integrate predicted occupancy and reliability with established local motion planners. Experiments show higher navigation success rates than the evaluated baselines in simulation and wheeled-robot trials. Additional quadruped and humanoid demonstrations illustrate deployment on other embodiments.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Visual Navigation and Map-Based Planning

Goal-conditioned policies learn visual navigation through diverse robot experience and action diffusion [ 5 , 6 ] , while geometric supervision [ 7 , 8 ] and multimodal goals [ 9 ] extend their capabilities. Despite demonstrated cross-embodiment transfer, their behavior can remain sensitive to robot size, motion capabilities, and camera configurations represented in training [ 5 , 7 ] .

Explicit traversability methods connect visual predictions to local planning. GeNIE [ 10 ] projects single-frame traversability into a BEV cost map and identifies the absence of a maintained local map as a source of local-minimum failures.

In autonomous driving, camera-based BEV methods provide spatial representations for downstream perception and planning. Lift-Splat-Shoot [ 11 ] and BEVFormer [ 12 ] combine RGB features from multiple cameras in a common BEV representation. These maps provide a spatial basis for navigation. More recent methods such as ViGT [ 13 ] learn to combine surround-view RGB images without requiring camera calibration. The wider view helps planners identify obstacles and choose clear routes.

These designs motivate our learned spatial queries. Our system supplies occupancy and reliability to motion planners. The robot footprint and traversal costs can be adjusted at planning time without changing the learned BEV predictor.

## II-B Occupancy Prediction and Anticipation

Occupancy anticipation addresses a further requirement for indoor navigation: inferring obstacles and free space hidden by furniture and walls. Map-based completion methods extend partially observed top-down layouts after map construction [ 4 , 14 ] , whereas geometry-guided semantic scene completion methods predict volumetric geometry and semantic categories from RGB using supplied camera geometry and, in some designs, internally predicted depth [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . Navigation-oriented methods further couple hidden-space prediction with confidence for exploration and navigation, including RGB or RGB-D occupancy anticipation in OccAnt [ 1 ] and RGB-D semantic completion in SSCNav [ 18 ] .

We focus on local occupied/free completion in persistently unobserved regions, distinguishing observed free space from inferred occupancy and estimating confidence in the completed map. This distinction allows the map to represent both the inferred spatial layout and the reliability of its predictions.

## II-C Temporal Visual Geometry and Spatial Memory

Temporal integration complements occupancy completion by retaining spatial evidence across successive observations. Dense mapping has long pursued this objective through active ranging, as in LiDAR-inertial systems such as FAST-LIO2 [ 19 ] . Cameras offer rich visual information without a dedicated range sensor, but recovering structure and motion from images depends on reliable correspondence and alignment. Weak texture, motion blur, and rapid viewpoint changes can challenge this estimation process [ 20 , 21 ] . Learned visual SLAM improves robustness by combining learned correspondence with geometric optimization, as in DROID-SLAM [ 21 ] ; feed-forward models such as VGGT [ 22 ] and VGGT-Omega [ 23 ] further learn geometry across multiple images.

However, accurate surface reconstruction alone does not establish the free-space coverage required for navigation. BEVFormer [ 12 ] aligns historical BEV features using ego-motion; SSCNav [ 18 ] registers observations using camera poses; GeoUP [ 24 ] conditions visual features on camera intrinsics and camera-to-reference poses. Errors in this information can misalign historical features or maps, creating false obstacles or distorting passage clearance. Such errors are especially consequential when motion degrades image quality or alignment.

Our work adopts the idea of learning spatial relationships across views to selectively integrate RGB history into a local BEV anchored to the latest ego frame, retaining evidence of previously observed structure. The BEV predictor decodes this history without depth or camera-pose inputs or explicit geometric warping.

2026-10-21.title: Embodied Task Agents Can Perform Fine Manipulation through Tactile In-Context Learning
2026-10-21.authors: Yubang Wang , Zezheng Huai , Yifei Zhang , Jinhao Wu , Yitong Chen , Haozhe Zhang , Sixian Li , Jingjing Gong , Zhenyang Lin , Ziyang Chen , Xipeng Qiu
2026-10-21.comment: . Project page: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract: Can embodied task agents use tactile experience to perform fine manipulation without task-specific model training? We investigate this capability through Tactile-ETA, a system that incorporates tactile experience into an embodied task agent through in-context learning. Successful expert demonstrations show how contact changes during manipulation. We pair each recorded robot movement with its camera views and bilateral tactile observations. We keep tactile observations at the start and end of each movement and add two neighboring time points when the tactile images change markedly in between. The agent combines these demonstrations with current vision, tactile observations, and proprioception to select actions through general-purpose robot tools, without updating model parameters. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, adding tactile observations to the same two expert demonstrations increases average success from 15.75% to 24.00%, with current sensing and execution interfaces held fixed. Further experiments show that performance depends on the sensory content and representation of demonstrations, while comparing agent models on Lift Bottle reveals substantial differences under the same system configuration. On the real-robot tasks, demonstrations with aligned visual and tactile observations increase the task success rate from 0% to 60%. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using tactile experience in context for fine manipulation and suggest a path toward extending embodied task agents to additional sensory inputs.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Embodied task agents such as ETA ( Chen et al., 2026d ) ,
Show-Harness ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , and
RoboDawn ( Guo et al., 2026 ) demonstrate that general-purpose models can execute robot tasks through
observations, reasoning, and robot commands.
However, fine manipulation remains challenging.
Recent real-robot evaluation also shows a substantial performance
gap between pick-and-place tasks and fine insertion tasks ( Menon et al., 2026 ) .
Such manipulation requires adjusting actions to contact conditions,
which can be difficult to infer reliably from vision alone.
Tactile feedback provides complementary information for these adjustments ( Bi et al., 2025 ) .
In-context learning further allows demonstrations to provide task guidance
at deployment without additional parameter updates ( Palo and
Johns, 2024b ; Yin et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) .
This creates an opportunity to extend the sensory information these agents
can use: can embodied task agents similarly use tactile experience
in context to perform fine manipulation that requires contact-sensitive
adjustments? We investigate this question through Tactile-ETA (Figure 1 ), which incorporates expert tactile experience
into an embodied task agent that acts through general-purpose robot tools,
without task-specific fine-tuning.

Current tactile
observations describe ongoing contact, whereas expert demonstrations can
provide a reference for how contact evolves during movement. For example,
during rotation or insertion, a demonstration can show how an expert
continues moving, adjusts its pose, or changes manipulation stages around
a contact transition. Visual–motion records capture what the expert did, but not how contact evolved during the demonstrated actions. We organize expert demonstrations so that the agent can see each movement
together with the visual and tactile changes that accompany it.

Tactile-ETA divides successful expert demonstrations into action-aligned
interaction segments, each containing robot motion, before-and-after
camera observations, and bilateral tactile sequences from the same interval.

Full tactile sequences can contain many observations within one movement,
while the endpoints alone can miss changes during contact. We therefore
retain tactile observations at motion boundaries and, when a change
threshold is met, add an adjacent pair spanning the selected change.
Complete demonstrations are provided in interaction order as references
for execution. The agent combines them with current visual and tactile observations, proprioception, and
execution feedback to select motion and
gripper commands. Model parameters remain unchanged: task guidance is
provided through context, while general-purpose tools and the underlying
controller execute the selected actions.

We evaluate the system on four UniVTAC simulation tasks ( Chen et al., 2026a ) , with 100 trials per task
and condition. Adding tactile observations to the same two visual–motion
demonstrations increases average success from 15.75% to 24.00%, with current
sensing and execution interfaces held fixed. Content ablations reveal
task-dependent contributions from demonstration vision and tactile
observations, while representation ablations show that retaining more
tactile frames does not automatically improve performance. A comparison of agent models
on Lift Bottle also reveals substantial differences under the
same system configuration. Execution statistics and cases illustrate
behavioral differences in contact-guided corrections and stage transitions.
On two real-robot tasks, a single multimodal demonstration enables three
successful trials out of five per task, compared with zero without demonstrations.
Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of using tactile
experience in context for embodied task agents and suggest a path toward
extending them to additional sensory inputs.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce Tactile-ETA, a system that incorporates expert tactile
experience into embodied task agents through context for fine manipulation,
without task-specific parameter updates.

We construct action-aligned visual–motion–tactile demonstrations
that compactly retain motion boundaries and intermediate contact changes.

We show that tactile demonstration experience can improve
manipulation performance, with outcomes depending on context organization
and the underlying agent model. Execution records illustrate associated
differences in contact adjustment and stage transitions.

1. We introduce Tactile-ETA, a system that incorporates expert tactile
experience into embodied task agents through context for fine manipulation,
without task-specific parameter updates.

2. We construct action-aligned visual–motion–tactile demonstrations
that compactly retain motion boundaries and intermediate contact changes.

3. We show that tactile demonstration experience can improve
manipulation performance, with outcomes depending on context organization
and the underlying agent model. Execution records illustrate associated
differences in contact adjustment and stage transitions.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Language and vision-language models connect task reasoning to robot execution through skill selection, environmental feedback, and program generation ( Ahn et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2022 ; Liang et al., 2023 ) . Visual grounding translates model outputs into spatial targets, objectives, or constraints for robot execution ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2024 ; Nasiriany et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024a ) . Recent work studies general-purpose models operating through robot interfaces ( Fu et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026d ; Chen et al., 2026c ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Su et al., 2026 ) . Related systems improve robot programs, skills, or policies through agent-driven iteration ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Lu et al., 2026 ; Xiao et al., 2026 ) . We build on OpenETA’s tool-based execution ( Chen et al., 2026d ) , in which the agent selects motion and gripper commands and receives observations and feedback after execution.

Demonstration-guided robot learning ( Argall et al., 2009 ) includes methods that use examples at deployment without further parameter updates ( Jiang et al., 2023 ; Palo and
Johns, 2024a ; Heppert et al., 2024 ) . Some methods train policies to predict actions conditioned on demonstration trajectories ( Fu et al., 2024 ; Vosylius and Johns, 2025 ) . For frozen general-purpose models, demonstration context can encode visual keypoints and end-effector trajectories as tokens ( Palo and
Johns, 2024b ) , or initial object poses and keyframe actions as text ( Yin et al., 2025 ) . More closely related to our setting, visual demonstrations and action references are combined with online observations and execution feedback for closed-loop manipulation ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) . Interface-aligned demonstrations further illustrate motion-command effects and task strategies ( Guo et al., 2026 ) .

Tactile learning supports physical perception and action generation ( Guzey et al., 2023 ) . Existing work learns transferable tactile representations ( Higuera et al., 2025 ) , connects tactile observations to language-based reasoning ( Yu et al., 2024 ; Yu et al., 2025 ) , and learns sequential visuotactile representations for manipulation ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . Policy learning incorporates tactile information through model training ( Hao et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) , with generalist tactile policies extending across sensors ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) . Semantic tactile feedback can also support planning alongside a learned controller for action refinement ( Bi et al., 2025 ) . Particularly relevant, visual, tactile, and force–torque demonstrations have been used to infer skill sequences and refine their transition conditions, producing a reference plan for subsequent execution and replanning ( Chen et al., 2025 ) . Our approach retains expert motions and aligned visual and bilateral tactile observations as demonstration context for successive tool-based decisions. We study how this contact experience can guide an embodied task agent, including controlled comparisons that vary demonstrated tactile information while holding current sensing and execution interfaces fixed.

2026-10-21.title: Sensitivity-Orthogonal Residual Learning for Adaptive Sideslip and Cornering Stiffness Estimation
2026-10-21.authors: Kyoungtae Ji , Dongyeol Won , Kyoungseok Han
2026-10-21.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-21.comment: . Submitted to Vehicle System Dynamics
2026-10-21.abstract:
Online adaptation of the cornering stiffness keeps a model-based sideslip estimator
valid as tires change, but competes with learned model correction for the same
filter innovation. A corrector with enough parameters can absorb the innovation pattern
that a stiffness change produces, and adaptation is suppressed while the fit
improves. We propagate the stiffness sensitivities of the predicted measurements through
the vehicle states and construct a corrector orthogonal to them. A null-space parameterization enforces the constraint without a penalty
coefficient and preserves the static least-squares stiffness estimate on each
identification segment. In full-vehicle simulation, the stiffness response of the
unconstrained corrector declines as its parameter count grows, whereas the orthogonal
corrector responds at least as fully as the uncorrected filter at all sizes and lowers
sideslip error by 12.7 % 12.7\% to 22.0 % 22.0\% . In a simulated drive with a stiffness step, the
orthogonal corrector adapts as quickly as the uncorrected filter and lowers sideslip
error during and after the transient. On public real-vehicle data, the 430-parameter
unconstrained corrector loses most of its response to deliberate offsets of the filter’s
nominal stiffness, whereas the orthogonal corrector of the same size retains most of it, with a sideslip
error slightly above the uncorrected filter’s.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Vehicle sideslip angle is a key input to stability control, yet it is not measured in
production vehicles [ 1 ] , and the axle cornering stiffnesses that govern its dynamics drift
in service with tire wear, inflation pressure, load, and temperature [ 2 ] . Joint estimation
addresses both problems at once. A model-based filter estimates the sideslip angle
while adapting the stiffness parameters online from the yaw rate and lateral
acceleration. The adapted stiffness has diagnostic value of its own and keeps the
sideslip estimate consistent as the tires change. Holding it constant instead exposes the sideslip
estimate to stiffness mismatch, which raised the error by an order of magnitude in a
simulation study [ 3 ] .

The single-track model at the core of such filters is kept simple to limit computation and
the number of parameters to be identified, and its discrepancy from the real vehicle is
systematic rather than random [ 4 ] . Methods that combine learned
components with physics-based filters have been proposed to account for this discrepancy [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . These
augmentations reproduce the measurements more closely than the physical model alone. In
the vehicle state estimator closest to ours [ 8 ] , the network
is trained with the stiffnesses fixed at offline-identified values. Its sideslip
estimation error increased when both axle cornering stiffnesses in the model were
increased by 10 % 10\% .

As Figure 1 illustrates, a mismatch between the measured and the predicted
output can be explained either by a change of the cornering stiffness or by a learned map
of the measured signals, and both explanations reproduce the measurement. A corrector, a learned term added to the model prediction,
absorbs whatever it can predict from its inputs. This includes the component that a
stiffness deviation produces, so the adaptation is suppressed while the fit to the
measurements still improves. This is the confounding between physical parameters and model discrepancy that
is well known in static Bayesian calibration [ 9 , 10 ] . In a sequential filter it appears
as a reduced response of the adapted stiffness to a real stiffness change. The more
parameters the corrector has, the less the filter responds to a real change. The
corrected filter still fits the identification data despite this reduced response, and
the adapted stiffness is rarely compared with an independent reference. Without such a
reference, the adapted values alone do not show whether the response to a stiffness
change is preserved.

The method proposed here constrains the corrector so that its output contains no
component of the form that a stiffness change produces, that is, so that it is orthogonal
to the sensitivities of the predicted outputs to the stiffness. The constraint is enforced
through the parameterization of the corrector. This paper makes three contributions.

We show that the parameter–discrepancy confounding known from static Bayesian
calibration appears in joint sideslip and cornering stiffness estimation as a reduced
response of the adapted stiffness to a real stiffness change.

We introduce a residual corrector whose output is orthogonal by construction to
the stiffness sensitivities of the predicted outputs along the state trajectory. The
constraint is built into a null-space parameterization and needs no penalty coefficient.
We show in closed form that the correction leaves the static least-squares stiffness
estimate unchanged.

We evaluate stiffness response, axle separation, and transient adaptation together
with sideslip accuracy in full-vehicle simulation. Real-vehicle data with an optical
sideslip reference further test the response to offsets of the nominal stiffness.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related work

## 2.1 Joint sideslip and stiffness estimation

Cornering stiffness varies in service, and joint state–parameter filters estimate it
online by including the axle stiffnesses in the state vector as random-walk states driven
by production sensors [ 11 , 12 , 3 , 13 , 4 , 14 ] ,
or by estimating them as an adapted noise statistic [ 15 ] .
Two observations from this literature matter here. First, the
stiffnesses are unobservable in straight driving and only weakly excited at small slip
angles, so the estimates drift unless the adaptation is scheduled by excitation [ 12 , 16 , 13 ] or gated on
observability [ 15 ] . A batch least-squares fit over a long
window avoids much of the issue [ 17 ] . Second, the adapted stiffness is
rarely compared with
an independent reference. The references used are bench tests [ 15 ] , offline identification on the same vehicle [ 11 ] , simulation truth [ 3 ] , or supplier
values [ 14 ] . Where the adapted value is discussed, it
is understood to absorb what the vehicle model omits. The stiffness state is allowed to
track nonlinear and friction-dependent behavior [ 13 ] and is noted
to compensate approximations of the suspension kinematics [ 4 ] .
None of these adaptive-stiffness estimators is combined with a learned correction term.

## 2.2 Learning-augmented filtering

Augmented physics-based models place a learned component inside a Bayesian filter and
train it jointly with the state estimate [ 5 ] . Constraining the
magnitude of the learned contribution has been proposed to preserve the meaning of the
estimated states [ 18 ] . Such bounds limit the size of the correction,
whereas the constraint proposed here governs whether the correction resembles a
parameter change. In vehicle state estimation, learned tire models
have been placed inside Kalman filters in place of the stochastic stiffness state, as
offline-trained networks [ 13 ] or Gaussian processes [ 19 ] . The architecture closest to ours is a network that
supplies a sideslip pseudo-measurement to a single-track filter and is trained through
it [ 8 ] . The stiffnesses stay at their offline values during
training and operation, and the reported accuracy of the hybrid remains sensitive to a ± 10 % \pm 10\% stiffness mismatch. Another design instead lets a network generate
time-varying stiffness scaling factors for a bicycle model [ 20 ] . The
stiffness is then determined entirely by the learned component and, as noted in that
work, cannot be compared with any reference measurement. These designs do not combine a separate
innovation-driven stiffness adaptation with an additive learned corrector.

## 2.3 Orthogonal discrepancy and decorrelation

In static Bayesian calibration, an unconstrained discrepancy term absorbs the
parameter’s effect and the calibrated parameter loses its physical meaning [ 9 , 10 ] . Discrepancy priors orthogonal
to the parameter gradients reduce this confounding between the physical parameters and
the discrepancy term [ 21 ] . Soft penalties serve the same purpose
in learning-based modeling. They decorrelate a learned residual from the outputs of the
physics terms [ 22 ] or from the parameter Jacobians of the physical
model, as applied to vehicle dynamics in [ 23 ] . The choice of such a regularizer determines which physical
parameters are inferred [ 6 ] , and mechanistic–neural
non-identifiability can be diagnosed from joint output sensitivities [ 7 ] . These penalties act on the training loss only. A method for
input–output modeling projects the learned component onto the complement of the
physical regressors’ column space by construction, using measured regressors offline [ 24 ] . This construction also has a kernel-form counterpart [ 25 ] . Neither involves a filter or online parameter adaptation. The present
corrector differs in two respects. It is orthogonal to sensitivities propagated through
unmeasured states, not to measured regressors. It also acts on the innovation that drives
online adaptation in the filter, and on the data used for identification it leaves the
part of that innovation aligned with the sensitivities unchanged.

2026-10-21.title: Velocity Optimization via Thermal Imaging Enhances Autonomous Tumor Resection
2026-10-21.authors: Naveed D. Riaziat , Jiawei Ge , Ethan Kilmer , Michael W. Mikula , Paul Maria Scheikl , Michael Kam , Leila J. Mady , Axel Krieger , Jeremy D. Brown
2026-10-21.comment: submitted to IEEE Access
2026-10-21.abstract:
Objective : To demonstrate and evaluate THERMO, a thermal-velocity optimization algorithm for autonomous electrosurgery, in ex vivo porcine tissue using the UR10e-based ASTR system. Methods : Thermography for Electrosurgical Rate Modulation via Optimization (ThERMO) , a closed-loop algorithm that uses real-time thermal imaging data to minimize thermal injury while ensuring accurate cut margins, was tested on ex vivo porcine tissue. Histological analysis was performed to detect thermal injury extent at a cellular level, and 3D photogrammetric measurement was used to verify margin accuracy. ThERMO ’s performance was compared against two previously used fixed velocity methods.
Results: ThERMO outperformed both fixed velocity comparison methods without requiring data-driven training or iterative tuning, reducing thermal injury by up to 52%, improving cut accuracy by up to 59%, and maintaining task completion speed. Conclusions : Closed-loop thermal feedback via ThERMO improves autonomous robotic electrosurgery by simultaneously reducing thermal injury and improving margin accuracy, reinforcing its value over fixed velocity approaches for tumor resection applications. Significance : This work advances autonomous robotic tumor resection by demonstrating that real-time closed-loop thermal feedback control can substantially reduce collateral tissue damage and improve surgical margin accuracy.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Oral cavity cancer (OCC) is cancer of the mouth, tongue, lips, and cheeks. Approximately 377,000 new OCC cases are diagnosed each year globally, leading to 178,000 deaths. Tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and human papillomavirus (HPV) are risk factors for developing OCC . Over 90% of OCC cases are squamous cell carcinoma, or cancer of the cells that line the outer layer of the tongue, cheeks, gums, and throat [ 1 ] . For treatment of pre-metastatic oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) , surgical intervention is often the most effective treatment [ 2 ] .

The standard surgical approach is the partial glossectomy procedure, where the portion of the tongue consisting of the OSCC tumor is removed. Cancer recurrence rates are minimized if the surgical margins (the region between the tumor and the cut boundary) reach 5 mm 5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} [ 3 ] . The term negative margin indicates that no cancer cells were found in the margin, while positive margin indicates the opposite. Though positive margins increase recurrence risk, excess negative margins indicate excess healthy tissue removal and worsen post-operative recovery and quality of life [ 4 , 5 ] . Therefore, it is critical to ensure accurate surgical margins during tumor resection.

Electrosurgery is a common technique for removing tumor tissue, wherein a surgical tool conducts electricity to generate heat in tissue, thereby causing it to denature. The heat-induced tissue denaturation reduces mechanical cutting effort while controlling bleeding. Monopolar electrosurgery directly heats the tissue by passing current from the tool tip through the body to an alternate-site grounding pad. Excess application of electrosurgery, however, may cause trauma to the lingual nerve in the tongue and permanently impair tongue sensory function. Insufficient application, by contrast, reduces cut accuracy by causing tissue snagging, which negatively impacts surgical margins and outcomes. As such, electrosurgery requires surgeons to diligently monitor tissue conditions to prevent adverse outcomes.

Monitoring and safely controlling electrosurgery becomes increasingly difficult in the tight constraints of the oral cavity. Consequently, robotics has provided advances in ergonomics and visualization during oral surgeries [ 6 , 7 ] . Systems like the da Vinci Single Port (Intuitive Surgical Inc., Sunnyvale, California, USA) have made trans-oral robotic surgery (TORS) possible by reducing tool size while maintaining high-quality stereoscopic vision. The application of robotics to head and neck surgery offers the possibility of procedural enhancements with sensing, feedback, and automation.

Though current commercial soft tissue surgical robots have little to no autonomous capability, increased electrosurgical autonomy could greatly reduce surgeon workload and improve surgical outcomes [ 8 ] . In the few early demonstrations of autonomous tumor resection has been an active research field, a discrepancy exists between the surgeon’s technique and the robot’s. While experienced surgeons adjust their cutting speed based on visual feedback of cut accuracy and thermal injury, current autonomous electrosurgical robots do not.

Autonomous surgical debridement of bone tissue was first demonstrated in human cadavers by Sefati et al. [ 9 ] . They used a hybrid continuum robot on a UR10 robot to perform osteolytic debridement in the pelvis using a surgeon-approved preoperative plan. Autonomous cutting of hard tissue like bone does not face many of the challenges of cutting soft tissue. Autonomous surgical cutting has typically run in an open-loop fashion, using a velocity predetermined via trial-and-error tuning or simulation. Studies have shown that autonomous robotic electrosurgery of this form causes more cellular injury than manual electrosurgery, indicating that the fine adjustments surgeons make during surgery have a substantial impact on excess heat injury [ 10 ] . In past demonstrations of autonomous tumor resection, researchers have prioritized cutting accuracy over thermal injury and manually selected low cutting speeds. For instance, Opfermann et al. first demonstrated a visual servoing approach for electrosurgical cutting on the Smart Tissue Autonomous Robot (STAR) [ 11 , 12 ] . Saeidi et al. similarly showed that STAR could perform tissue-cutting tasks using a predetermined cut speed [ 13 ] . Ge et al. introduced the Autonomous System for Tumor Resection (ASTR) system for fully autonomous tumor resection and demonstrated successful cutting at 2 mm / s 2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}\text{/}\mathrm{s} [ 14 ] . Ge et al. later proposed that for faster velocities that excessively deform tissue, simulation-based trajectory augmentation could reduce spatial error [ 15 ] . However, soft tissue simulation is both challenging and not patient-specific, potentially limiting robustness, optimality, and safety without additional feedback mechanisms.

Closed-loop sensing has shown promise in optimizing electrosurgical performance. Since thermal injury is largely invisible to the naked eye until permanent damage has been done, researchers have used thermal imaging to measure electrosurgical thermal spread [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] . Recent works have developed miniaturized endoscopic thermal cameras as well, which are compatible with the laparoscopic surgery workflow [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] . Bao and Mazumder showed that thermal imaging can control the denaturation zone using a novel computer-controllable electrosurgical unit (ESU) [ 22 ] . Surgeons, however, typically employ a fixed power level, and most ESUs are not capable of real-time power modulation. El-Kebir et al. instead used thermal sensing to train a data-driven non-linear autoregressive exogenous input (NLARX) model to determine when a static surgical tool should move to the next waypoint [ 23 ] . It is still unclear, however, if these data-driven models generalize from laboratory settings to the complex surgical environment. Some researchers instead have developed methods to estimate soft tissue parameters online, including by use of thermography, Bayesian and Gaussian Estimation, and finite element models [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 , 28 ] .

While these prior works have demonstrated the potential benefits of thermal injury measurement and control, electrosurgery is more appropriately solved as an optimal control problem with competing goals of limiting thermal injury and maximizing cut accuracy, which is significantly impacted by tissue deformation. In an attempt to maximize accuracy, Shademan et al. used near-infrared fluorescent markers to track tissue deformation during autonomous porcine intestinal anastomosis [ 12 ] . Kam et al. showed promising results controlling electrosurgical cut velocity with tracker-based tissue deformation feedback [ 29 ] . Similarly, Ferrari et al. used deformation modeling and feedback to track and therefore more accurately target tumor biopsy sites [ 30 ] . Giannarou et al. utilized microscopy images during retinal surgery to estimate tissue deformation and tool forces [ 31 ] . Despite these advancements, the combination of deflection and thermal injury feedback has yet to be demonstrated. Without considering both deflection and thermal injury, the above approaches to autonomous electrosurgical control cannot achieve optimality, especially in the highly muscular and therefore tough tissue found in the tongue.

Our previous work demonstrated optimal autonomous electrosurgical cutting speed in tissue phantoms using a thermal-feedback algorithm, Thermography for Electrosurgical Rate Modulation via Optimization (ThERMO) . ThERMO improved resistance to disturbances, reduced thermal injury, and minimized tool deflection without the need for simulation or model training [ 32 ] . ThERMO prevented the need for trial-and-error speed selection by using online tissue parameter identification. However, up to this point, autonomous cutting under visual thermal feedback has not yet been demonstrated for 3D cutting in biological tissues with a multi-DoF robotic system. Testing in ex vivo tissue is a critical step towards eventual cadaveric and in vivo studies. Likewise, the connection between thermal feedback and cell death and the relationship between tool deflection and margin accuracy have not been validated through histological analysis or post-hoc margin measurement. Validating these outcomes is critical for the eventual clinical translation of autonomous thermal-feedback electrosurgical technologies.

Here, we evaluate adaptive velocity control using ThERMO on the Autonomous System for Tumor Resection (ASTR) system, an autonomous robotic surgery platform with an electrosurgical tool and RGB-D camera (see Fig. 1 ) [ 14 ] . Our contributions are threefold. First, we validate ThERMO ’s effectiveness in improving margin accuracy while minimizing thermal spread in an ex vivo porcine tissue model. Second, we present histological analysis quantifying thermal injury in relation to cutting accuracy during a simulated electrosurgical tumor resection. Third, we provide a comparative study measuring thermal injury and cut accuracy against fixed-speed robotic methods, highlighting the benefits of thermal feedback in surgical performance. These results underscore the promise of intelligent electrosurgical automation for improving tumor resection outcomes in future surgeries.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Methods and Materials

## 2.1 Current Clinical Resection Technique

Most OSCC occurs on the tongue, where the mortality rate is also the highest [ 33 ] . OSCC tumors are typically 2 cm to 4 cm 2\text{\,}\mathrm{cm}4\text{\,}\mathrm{cm} in diameter and the depth of invasion is typically ≤ \leq 10 mm 10\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} when surgical intervention is most effective [ 33 ] . A common surgical technique for tumor resection is called a “partial glossectomy”, where a portion of the tongue containing the tumor is removed.

In cases where the cancerous tissue is small and near the tip of the tongue, access to the tumor may be obtained trans-orally. For larger tumors near the base of the tongue which cannot be accessed easily, a trans-cervical pull-through or mandibulotomy may be performed to create additional space to operate. Robotic approaches often have better small-space dexterity and access and thus can avoid additional access procedures. With access gained and the tongue prepared, the tongue is sutured at its tip to pull it from the oral cavity and provide tension on the tissue. Then, the tumor outline is marked and the cutting boundary is defined 5 mm 5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} from this edge [ 34 ] . This space between the tumor and the cut defines the resection margin, and is critical to ensuring no cancerous cells are left behind. Then, with the goal of precisely maintaining this margin to prevent excess tissue damage or leftover cancerous tissue, the surgeon will use an electrosurgical tool to cut around this defined periphery, eventually approaching from the underside of the tumor to complete the resection. The removed samples will be sent to pathology for margin confirmation; if the margins are positive (there is no healthy tissue around the tumor), the surgeon will remove additional tissue until there are negative margins. The studies presented here will focus on the first peripheral cut step of the above, as they are most critical in determining surgical margins.

## 2.2 Autonomous System for Tumor Resection

The Autonomous System for Tumor Resection (ASTR) system, shown in Fig. 1 , is a software and hardware system consisting of a monopolar electrosurgical tool and Zivid 2+ structured-light RGB-D camera (Zivid, Oslo, Norway) mounted to a UR10e robot [ 14 ] . The UR10e arm is controlled using the Open Robot Control Software Kinematics and Dynamics Library and ROS 2 on Ubuntu 22.04. Trajectory generation is computed using the Reflexxes Motion Library.

The Zivid 2+ is used to measure the tissue surface with 55 µ ​ m 55\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} accuracy for trajectory planning. The tool and grounding pad are connected to the ESU , which is the source of electrosurgical energy. The tool is the electrical anode, and the grounding pad, typically attached to the patient’s back, serves to close the current loop. The ESU generates high-frequency current with selectable wattage and waveform shapes. Different waveforms allow for different effects, such as coagulation and fulguration. Typical wattage varies between 20 W to 50 W 20\text{\,}\mathrm{W}50\text{\,}\mathrm{W} . For these experiments, the ESU is set to 35 W 35\text{\,}\mathrm{W} and cut mode as advised by an expert head-and-neck surgeon.

## 2.3 ThERMO

ThERMO is an online parameter estimation and optimization framework that uses thermal imaging to determine the optimal electrosurgical cutting velocity via a prototypical thermal and mechanical model of the tissue with unknown parameters. Here, a brief overview is provided; for a more detailed discussion, please refer to our previous work. [ 32 ] . In the preceding work, we developed the thermal sensing system, adaptive parameter identification, and optimization techniques underlying the thermo device. Results were demonstrated in 2D hydrogel phantoms, showcasing the potential of extending the work to 3D cuts in biological tissue. The iteration of ThERMO used in this article is minimally modified from the previous work, with only necessary adjustments for the new robot’s kinematic constraints. This should further demonstrate that manual tuning is not required to achieve satisfactory performance with the thermo device.

A model is developed to predict the thermal injury extent by extracting the width of the denaturation isotherm. The denaturation isotherm is defined at 60 °C 60\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} [ 35 ] . The electrosurgical cut is modeled as a 2D moving heat source problem, since the cuts are shallow and the curvature is low. The thermal model from the 2D heat equation is thus

Lu et al. developed a model to predict isotherm widths [ 36 ] from a quasistatic approximation of the 2D heat equation [ 37 ] . The selected isotherm temperature T c T_{c} is the denaturation temperature referenced above at 60 °C 60\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} . The asymptotic isotherm width w w with correcting factor f ⁡ ( T c ∗ ) f(T^{*}_{c}) is given as a function of the control velocity u u :

Cutting force contributes to reduced cut accuracy due to tissue snagging and deformation. Due to Hooke’s law, tool deformation can be used as a proxy for directly measuring force. The cutting force as a function of velocity, adjusted to match empirical observations, is:
