ThERMO receives thermal images from a uncooled bolometer type thermal camera, the T3 Pro (IRay Technology Co., Ltd., Shanghai, China). It captures a 384 x 288 pixel array at 25 Hz 25\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} with 2 °C 2\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} or 2% accuracy, whichever is greater. Example thermal images are shown in Fig. 2 A and Fig. 3 . Spatial, temporal, and thermal accuracy is confirmed as shown in [ 32 ] . The camera is mounted to the robot end effector flange so that the tool frame is rigidly attached to the camera frame. Two measurements are deduced using the thermal camera: 1) isotherm width and 2) tool deflection. To measure the isotherm width, the thermal frames are thresholded at 60 °C 60\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} . Then, an L2 distance transform is performed, creating an image where the value of each pixel is the Euclidean distance to the nearest point under 60 °C 60\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolCelsius} . The maximum of the distance transform corresponds to half the thermal width, as shown in Fig. 2 . The tool deflection is measured by extracting the hottest point in the image, which corresponds to the contact location between the electrosurgical tool and the tissue. The motion of this point relative to its resting position defines the deflection.

Dual state and tissue parameter estimation is conducted using the truncated unscented Kalman filter (TUKF) . The unscented Kalman filter (UKF) is a Kalman filter for non-linear models that uses the “Unscented Transform” in place of Jacobian computation from the more common extended Kalman filter (EKF) . The UKF estimates λ ^ \hat{\lambda} , the augmented tissue thermal conductivity, d ^ \hat{d} , the augmented maximum cutting force, q ^ \hat{q} , the linear power density, and c ^ \hat{c} , the tissue specific heat capacity. Unknown parameters are initialized from values published by the Foundation for Research on Information Technologies in Society (IT’IS) [ 39 ] , shown in Table 1 .

Successful electrosurgical cutting relies on balancing cutting speed between moving too fast and too slow. If the cut is performed too quickly, little electrical heat will be generated, and tissue will not denature enough to reduce the cutting force. As a result, tissue will snag, and cut accuracy will decrease. If the cut is performed too slowly, excess heat will injure healthy tissue, causing unnecessary injury to the patient and worsening post-operative outcomes. Thus, a natural minimization problem arises between cutting force and thermal injury. This optimization is covered in detail in our previous work so only a brief summary is given here [ 32 ] . For these experiments, the selected weights are shown in Table 1 . Weights a a and b b were selected to reflect equal clinical importance between thermal and mechanical damage, while weights c c and r r were tuned by setting the minimum value that resulted in improved motion smoothness.

Optimization is performed using minimize_scalar from SciPy’s optimize library in Python 3.10, which uses Brent’s method to solve scalar minimization quickly. As the cost function is scalar and quadratic, only one minima exists, and it can be found rapidly (fraction of a millisecond) by almost any solver. Note this is orders of magnitude faster than our thermal sensing’s 30 Hz sampling rate.

## 2.4 Trajectory Planning

Several constraints must be implemented to define a cutting trajectory on a tissue sample. All cuts are performed with a prototypical tumor outline determined from a real clinical tongue tumor scan (see Figs. 3 ). Two trajectories are generated from this outline: the first defines the boundary of the tumor itself and the second defines the targeted 5 mm 5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} cutting margin extended from this boundary. The following procedure is then conducted to plan the robot trajectory (see Fig. 4 ).

The tongue is fixed to the grounding pad using surgical suture.

The tongue is fixed to the grounding pad using surgical suture.

A 3D point cloud is captured using the Zivid 2+.

The boundary of the tumor and the 5 mm 5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} cut margin are projected onto the tissue surface by manual selection of a central region of the anterior tongue. A discrete set of points and normal vectors are output for each trajectory.

The tangent vectors between subsequent trajectory points are computed. The tangent vectors are projected onto the local surface.

The full pose at each point is determined by orienting the tool x-axis with the projected vector and the tool z-axis with the negative of the surface normal.

The trajectory orientations are smoothed using an exponential filter.

After each 30 Hz imaging update, the newly computed desired velocity ( < 1 ​ m ​ s <1~ms computation time) is passed to an Orocos Real-Time Toolkit (RTT) component running at 125 Hz on Ubuntu. This component generates smooth joint-space trajectory setpoints using the Reflexxes motion library and publishes them to the Universal Robots ROS 2 driver, which streams setpoints to the UR controller over RTDE (Real-Time Data Exchange) at 125 Hz. This low-level layer performs deterministic trajectory generation and tracking without iterative optimization. The optimization resides solely in the ∼ \sim 30 Hz application-specific high-level planner, which is not considered real-time.

The tool x-axis must be oriented in the direction of motion such that the thermal camera trails the cutting edge. This ensures the tool’s thermal “wave” is always in frame (see Fig. 3 ). Second, the tool z-axis should be oriented normal to the surface of the tissue to minimize any perspective warping of the isotherm size. This procedure fully defines the poses for the trajectory. The command velocity for each pose is either set a priori or adjusted in real time during a cut based on the cutting method.

## 2.5 Experimental Procedure

Ten porcine tongues were procured from Animal Technologies 1 1 1 https://www.animaltechnologies.com , as porcine tongues have similar properties to human tongues [ 40 ] . Packaged samples were airmailed in ice water overnight after sacrifice, and experiments were conducted within 36 hours of receipt. After each trial, samples were immediately cut to size and fixed in 10% formalin for 72 hours (see Fig. 5 ).

Experiments were conducted in three groups for each of the three different cutting methods. Each group executed three cuts on separate tongues. One tongue was not cut and used as a histological control. As per the most recent works on autonomous tongue tumor resection, one group is run at 2 mm / s 2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}\text{/}\mathrm{s} . Then, based on measurements of handheld electrosurgical cutting from an expert surgeon, a second group is cut at 7 mm / s 7\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}\text{/}\mathrm{s} [ 15 ] . The final group utilizes the ThERMO method to optimize cut velocity. The three methods are thus referred to as follows:

Robot-Derived Fixed Speed (RDFS) : 2 mm / s 2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}\text{/}\mathrm{s} , as previously used in the ASTR system [ 14 ] ,

Robot-Derived Fixed Speed (RDFS) : 2 mm / s 2\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}\text{/}\mathrm{s} , as previously used in the ASTR system [ 14 ] ,

Clinician-Derived Fixed Speed (CDFS) : 7 mm / s 7\text{\,}\mathrm{mm}\text{/}\mathrm{s} , as measured by external trackers on an expert surgeon’s handheld electrosurgical device [ 15 ] ,

ThERMO : adaptive thermal-feedback optimized velocity.

These values are also summarized in Table 3 .

## 2.6 Measurements

Four quantitative measures are reported and described below: 1) signed margin error (SME) : error between the measured and desired margin, 2) absolute margin error (AME) : absolute error between the measured and desired margin, 3) thermal injury extent (TIE) : average perpendicular distance of thermal injury from the cut, 4) task completion time. These measures are also summarized in Table 3 .

Before each margin cut, the boundary of the virtual tumor is marked onto the surface using an ink pen attached to the robot arm in place of the electrosurgical tool. After cutting, the distance between the two contours is photogrammetrically measured by an Intel RealSense D405 camera (Intel Corporation, Santa Clara, California, USA). The D405 was used in place of the Zivid to ensure unbiased and reliable result validation by using an independent sensor. The D405 returns a color image registered to a point cloud. The cut boundary and the tumor margin are segmented from the color image and correlated to their 3D points. Points in the inner and outer contours are correlated by angle, and the 3D Euclidean distance is computed. AME and SME are reported, representing both the absolute accuracy and the clinically-relevant signed accuracy.

Additionally cutting depth was also measured under microscopy to ensure verify accuracy relative to the desired 5 mm 5\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} cut.

Histological analysis is used to determine the extent of thermal injury caused by the electrosurgery instrument. From each tongue, eight wedge-shaped blocks of tissue are excised orthogonally to the cut direction. These blocks are fixed in formalin, paraffin-embedded, and sectioned using a microtome into three 5 µ ​ m 5\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} sections at 50 µ ​ m 50\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolMicro m} increments. Sections are stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) , a standard stain used for microscopy, and mounted to slides. A visual guide to the sectioning process is shown in Fig. 5 . A board-certified pathologist, blind to the cutting method, then analyzes the slides for thermal injury and reports the amount by which thermal injury extends from the cut location. From each slide, eight perpendicular measurements are taken around the cut to determine the distance of thermal injury away from the cut. The average of these eight values is reported as TIE . H&E stained samples highlight nuclear and cytoplasmic structures, enabling pathologists to evaluate tissue cytoarchitecture (i.e., the structural organization of cells) and assess thermal injury. Previously characterized morphological indicators of thermal damage range from connective tissue bluing and smudging of nuclei to complete loss of cytoarchitecture [ 41 , 42 ] .

Task completion time is defined as the time it takes from the moment the electrosurgical tool makes contact with the tissue to the moment it breaks contact. Since time is a valuable resource in the operating room, this metric is key in determining efficiency and optimality for clinical translation. To note, the reported time reflects only the duration of the tongue surface incision, which is a subtask within the broader tongue tumor resection surgery. It does not represent the total procedure time.

## 2.7 Statistical Analyses

Statistical analyses of the metrics 1) AME , 2) SME , and 3) TIE (described above) are conducted with linear mixed models (LMMs) , a linear-regression-based statistical analysis that handles nested study structures accurately. LMMs use fixed effects, such as treatment method, and random effects, such as trial, to robustly infer statistical results with repeated, hierarchical, and correlated data, unlike ANOVA, which assumes independence of observations and does not natively account for within-subject or within-trial variability. The models for AME and SME use cutting method as a fixed predictor and the trial as a random predictor, thereby accounting for biological variations in tongues. The model for TIE adds a random predictor of the cut block to account for the repeated measures within a cross-section.

Method is a categorical variable referring to either RDFS , CDFS , or ThERMO . Depth is a quantitative variable measuring the depth of cut seen in the histology slides. Both are used as fixed effects to determine their direct relationship on the outcome variables. Trial and Block are categorical variables referring to the trial number (and therefore the tongue being cut) and the wedge-shaped tissue block shown in Fig. 5 C, respectively. They are included as a random effect to indicate biological differences between tongues and to account for the repeated measurement between the three sections removed from the same block. For all models, visual inspection confirmed normality of residuals, homoscedasticity, and homogeneity of variances. Results are reported with p p -values and standard errors.

## 2.8 Qualitative Clinical Analysis

A board-certified expert otolaryngologist, blinded to the experimental method, evaluated the three electrosurgical cutting methods using unlabeled image–video pairs corresponding to a cut performed on porcine tongues. Each method, labeled Method 1, Method 2, and Method 3, was rated on a 5-point scale (1-poor, 5-excellent) based on margin accuracy, thermal effects, and overall impression. These measures are intended to supplement the other quantitative results and provide clinical insight that would otherwise not be communicated.

2026-10-21.title: Robot-Task Suitability in Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Task Allocation
2026-10-21.authors: Daniel Weiner , Raj Korpan
2026-10-21.comment: Accepted at Workshop on Foundation Models for Multi-Robot Systems (FM-MRS), IROS 2026
2026-10-21.abstract: Heterogeneous multi-robot task allocation depends on estimates of how suitable individual robots are for candidate tasks, yet suitability can be defined in substantially different ways. We compare ten deterministic methods and two LLM-based variants spanning rule-based, similarity-based, requirement-oriented, fuzzy, and semantic approaches. Using common robot and task profiles, we compare how the methods score and rank candidate robots, identify feasibility, and select a top robot, while examining how these outcomes change with team composition, scale, spatial context, capability uncertainty, and task representation. The methods frequently disagree despite operating on identical scenarios. Generic similarity measures can violate properties expected under a one-sided requirement-satisfaction interpretation of suitability, while LLM-based scoring introduces additional stochastic and linguistic sensitivity. These results show that robot–task suitability should be treated as an explicit modeling choice whose assumptions, robustness, and decision-level consequences should be considered before allocation.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) concerns assigning tasks to robots subject to constraints on resources, timing, motion, and team objectives. MRTA has been studied through centralized optimization, market- and auction-based methods, distributed coordination, heuristics, and learning-based approaches [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . The problem is especially challenging for heterogeneous teams, whose robots may differ in mobility, sensing, manipulation, payload, reach, endurance, communication, and environmental tolerance [ 5 ] . Existing heterogeneous MRTA approaches represent these differences through capability constraints, utilities, energy-aware allocation, resilience mechanisms, or task-specific requirements [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Regardless of the allocation mechanism, however, the system must determine how appropriate each robot is for each task [ 10 , 11 ] . We use the term robot–task suitability to describe how well a particular robot matches the requirements of a particular task, including considerations such as feasibility, specialization, and expected performance.

Constructing suitability values is itself a nontrivial modeling problem. Robot capabilities and task requirements may be numerical, categorical, contextual, unstructured, or uncertain, and some requirements are mandatory while others permit partial satisfaction or tradeoffs. A robot with the necessary hardware may nevertheless be a poor candidate under current conditions because of travel distance, endurance, or environmental constraints [ 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Prior work has considered uncertain or changing capabilities and task requirements [ 14 , 15 ] , while adaptive specialization methods model robot efficacy as initially unknown or changing during deployment [ 11 , 8 ] . Reducing these factors to a scalar therefore requires assumptions about hard vs. soft constraints, capability weighting, surplus vs. deficient capability, and whether operational context is part of suitability.

Different methods encode these assumptions differently. Rule-based methods can explicitly evaluate requirements and reject infeasible pairs; vector-based approaches compare robots and tasks through geometric similarity; requirement-oriented methods measure satisfaction or deficiency; and fuzzy methods allow gradual satisfaction near numerical thresholds. Multi-objective MRTA likewise reflects the need to balance competing aspects of robot suitability [ 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 ] . More recently, large language models (LLMs) have been used to reason over heterogeneous robot capabilities and natural-language task descriptions [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . Such methods offer semantic flexibility but introduce stochasticity and sensitivity to linguistic representation. These approaches encode different notions of compatibility, making their effects difficult to isolate when they are evaluated using different robot, task, and allocation models.

This work therefore examines suitability estimation as a distinct component of heterogeneous MRTA rather than proposing a new allocation algorithm. We compare ten deterministic methods, including rule-based, similarity-based, requirement-oriented, set-based, and fuzzy approaches, together with two LLM-based variants, using common robot and task profiles. We evaluate agreement and robustness under changes in team composition, scale, robot-to-task ratio, spatial scale, and capability perturbations; test five one-sided suitability properties; examine task-dependent behavior; and evaluate LLM repeatability and semantic robustness. The experiments show that suitability method affects feasibility judgments and robot rankings, that several generic similarity measures exhibit behaviors inconsistent with one-sided requirement satisfaction, and that semantic scoring introduces additional uncertainty. These findings motivate treating suitability estimation as an explicit modeling decision rather than an assumed input to downstream task allocation.

2026-10-21.title: Evaluating Social Reasoning in Embodied Vision-Language Models
2026-10-21.authors: Daniel Weiner , Raj Korpan
2026-10-21.comment: Accepted at Workshop on Foundation Models for Multi-Robot Systems (FM-MRS), IROS 2026
2026-10-21.abstract: Foundation models now serve as reasoning layers for robot teams, but it remains unclear whether embodiment-specialized vision-language models (VLMs) preserve the social-reasoning capabilities of general-purpose VLMs. We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, a benchmark of real human-robot social interactions, and compare it with published general-purpose VLM baselines. Robotics-ER outperforms GPT-4o-mini on error/competence detection but performs worse on detailed social-attribute judgments; adding a visual frame helps one task while hurting the other. These results suggest embodiment-specialized models may perform differently on social judgments that can be read more directly from observable interaction cues versus those requiring more inference about a person’s internal state. Because the comparison spans model families, these differences cannot be attributed to embodiment specialization alone. This matters for multi-robot systems, where a shared foundation model could cause systematic social-perception errors to influence multiple coordination decisions. This work presents an initial evaluation, with broader cross-context and video-based analyses left for future work.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) have quickly moved from perception and planning aids to the reasoning core of robot autonomy [ 1 , 2 ] .
A distinct class of embodiment-specialized models for robotic reasoning has emerged, targeting spatial grounding, pointing, affordance and trajectory prediction, and success detection [ 3 ] .
Such models are natural candidates for high-level reasoning about what a robot should do from multimodal observations. Increasingly, those decisions are made among people , and by teams of robots: guides in airports, assistants in hospitals, service fleets in malls.
For such teams, coordination quality hinges on a shared assessment of human social state, such as who is engaged, who is confused, who is disengaging, or whether a robot has made a social error, so the team can determine which robot should approach, continue an interaction, or withdraw.
We refer to this as a social-perception layer : a semantically rich estimate of the humans in view produced from each robot’s observations and made available to the coordination layer.

Recent work has begun evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can provide such social information. SHREC benchmarks foundation models on real human-robot interactions (HRI), including recognition of social errors, competencies, and social attributes such as engagement, and reports substantial variation across models and tasks [ 4 ] . HRIBench similarly evaluates VLMs on interaction-relevant human perception, including nonverbal cues and other visual signals [ 5 ] , while complementary work studies broader interaction-centric human-robot collaboration capabilities [ 6 ] . VLMs have also been used directly as proxies for social intelligence [ 7 ] and to determine whether and when a robot should initiate interaction [ 8 ] .

Embodiment-specialized models are appealing candidates for the social-perception layer: one pretrained model, no per-deployment training, outputs already expressed in language the rest of the robotics stack uses [ 3 ] .
Existing HRI benchmarks primarily evaluate general-purpose VLMs, while embodiment-specialized models are primarily evaluated on physical and spatial capabilities. To our knowledge, the relative social-reasoning performance of an embodiment-specialized VLM has not been evaluated against general-purpose VLM baselines on the same HRI benchmark.

Concretely, we evaluate whether Gemini Robotics-ER, a model tuned for embodied robotic reasoning, can identify human social states, such as engagement, robot social competencies, and social errors, on the SHREC benchmark [ 9 ] , and compare its performance with the general-purpose VLMs reported by SHREC. SHREC’s social labels vary in how directly they can be supported by observable interaction evidence, thus, we examine performance along a gradient from externally grounded to internally inferred. Externally grounded tasks can be resolved from the observable structure of an interaction, such as turn-taking and response timing evident in the transcript. Internally inferred tasks require stronger inference about affect, intention, or mental state. Our hypothesis is that Gemini Robotics-ER will perform better on externally grounded tasks than internally inferred ones.

Furthermore, foundation models are increasingly being placed directly inside multi-robot decision-making loops. RoCo uses language-model agents to negotiate collaborative plans [ 10 ] ; SMART-LLM decomposes natural-language tasks and forms robot coalitions based on robot capabilities [ 11 ] ; and COHERENT coordinates heterogeneous teams through LLM-mediated task assignment and feedback [ 12 ] .
Recent work applies conformal prediction and uncertainty-aware reasoning to robot planning [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , while embodied-agent evaluations show that models may fail to abstain appropriately under ambiguous or infeasible conditions [ 16 ] . Recent work also argues for deployment-specific evaluation when selecting foundation models for social robots [ 17 ] . Against this background, we ask whether an embodiment-specialized robotics VLM preserves the social-reasoning capabilities needed for human-aware robotic systems.

We make three contributions. First, we formulate the question of whether an embodiment-specialized robotics foundation model preserves social reasoning capability, particularly in the context of human-aware multi-robot systems. Second, we define a benchmark-aligned evaluation of Gemini Robotics-ER on SHREC, validating our modified evaluation pipeline against an established general-purpose VLM baseline. Third, we analyze the implications of any observed capability gap for model reliability across multi-robot teams.

# II Problem Formulation and Methodology

## II-A Problem Setup and Dataset

Consider a heterogeneous robot team operating in a human-populated environment.
Each robot r r observes nearby people from its own viewpoint and produces a social percept s r s_{r} that it provides to a shared coordination layer that allocates human-facing tasks, such as approach, assist, hand off, or disengage.
We treat social perception as a mapping from an egocentric observation, consisting of sampled visual frame(s) plus available dialogue, to a structured assessment of engagement, social errors, or competencies, along with a confidence score. Model outputs are represented in a typed, machine-readable schema so that predictions can be used by downstream coordination modules.

Let M emb M_{\text{emb}} be an embodiment-specialized model (e.g., Gemini Robotics-ER) and { M gen } \{M_{\text{gen}}\} the set of general-purpose VLMs benchmarked on SHREC. For a social-reasoning task T T with metric μ T \mu_{T} , we compare μ T ​ ( M emb ) \mu_{T}(M_{\text{emb}}) with the corresponding performance of μ T ​ ( { M gen } ) \mu_{T}(\{M_{\text{gen}}\}) across engagement, competence, and error detection.
Our primary hypothesis is that the relative performance of M emb M_{\text{emb}} will depend on the type of inference required by the task: embodiment-specialized models will perform better on externally grounded tasks than on internally inferred ones. If embodiment-specialized models perform better on both types of tasks compared to general-purpose VLMs, then that would indicate that embodiment specialization broadly preserves social reasoning, whereas if it were worse for both task types, it would indicate a genuine tradeoff between embodiment specialization and social reasoning.

The SHREC dataset [ 9 ] comprises real human-robot interactions drawn from month-long, in-the-wild deployments of social robots across three deployment contexts: empathic storytelling in homes, wellness coaching in dormitories, and wellness coaching in homes.
Each sample provides a sequence of extracted still frames, a dialogue transcript, and segment-level annotations from three independent human annotators.
Raw video is available only for the wellness-home subset at the time of writing.
The empathic and wellness-dorm subsets provide still frames and transcripts without video.
Annotations mark whether the robot committed a social error or exhibited a competence per segment, together with seven social attribute flags (including engagement ), a rationale, and a suggested correction.
We use the empathic subset for the primary quantitative evaluation. We additionally use a small sample from wellness-home for an exploratory transcript-versus-frame-versus-video comparison because it is the only subset for which raw video is currently available.

## II-B Evaluation Setup

We evaluate the two tasks for which SHREC reports general-model baselines, following the benchmark’s task definitions and scoring procedure: (i) social error/competence detection, scored as classification among error, competence, and none; and (ii) social-attribute identification, including engagement, scored using SHREC’s partial-match metric.

We evaluate Gemini Robotics-ER (v2.0), an embodiment-specialized reasoning model accessed via API, in a zero-shot setting with decoding fixed to temperature 0 0 for reproducibility.
Outputs are constrained to a typed schema so predictions parse deterministically into the task label space.
A matched within-family comparison against SHREC’s reported Gemini baselines was not possible because the corresponding Gemini endpoints are no longer available. We therefore use GPT-4o-mini, for which SHREC reports published results, as the reproduced general-purpose comparison model.
The primary comparison is therefore between an embodiment-specialized Gemini model and a general-purpose GPT model. Because model-family differences are confounded with specialization, we interpret the results as a comparison of these deployed model configurations rather than as a causal estimate of the effect of embodiment specialization. This limitation is discussed in Section IV .

We use three input conditions throughout the evaluation: transcript only ( T ), transcript plus a single still frame ( T+F ), and transcript plus video ( T+V ). The empathic subset does not include raw video, so its visual input is drawn from the publicly released sequence of still frames. Accordingly, Gemini Robotics-ER is evaluated under T and T+F on the empathic subset. SHREC’s published GPT-4o-mini results provide T and T+V conditions.
The T condition is the directly matched input condition across Gemini Robotics-ER and the published GPT-4o-mini baseline and therefore serves as our primary model-to-model comparison. SHREC reports little or no improvement from adding visual input on these tasks, but we additionally evaluate Robotics-ER under T+F to measure the marginal effect of adding a still frame. Because T+F and T+V provide different visual information, we report these multimodal conditions for context but do not treat them as a controlled model-to-model comparison.

On the wellness-home subset, where raw video is available, we additionally conduct a small exploratory modality probe using all three conditions: T, T+F, and T+V.
The probe contains five examples and is descriptive rather than quantitative; its purpose is to examine whether adding still-image or temporal visual information changes Robotics-ER’s predicted social assessment or stated reasoning.

## II-C Scoring and Validation

The comparison is only meaningful if our evaluation pipeline scores predictions compatibly with SHREC’s published procedure. Because SHREC’s released evaluation harness was not designed to interface with Gemini Robotics-ER, we modified the model-invocation and output-parsing components so that Gemini predictions could be evaluated within the same pipeline, while leaving the benchmark’s scoring logic unchanged.
We therefore first run GPT-4o-mini through our evaluation pipeline on a 25-sample subset of the language-only detection task and compare the results with SHREC’s published GPT-4o-mini baseline. Our score falls within 0.06 0.06 of the published value; across repeated runs, the reproduced baseline has a standard deviation of ± 0.02 \pm 0.02 . We treat this as a scoring-consistency check showing that the modified evaluation harness produces values in the neighborhood of the published evaluation, rather than as a full reproduction of the benchmark result.

SHREC provides annotations from three independent annotators, whose labels may disagree. Because the handling of these disagreements directly affects the scored targets, we retain SHREC’s aggregation rule: only labels with strict pairwise agreement are retained, and disagreements are discarded. This preserves the same ground-truth approach used for the published baselines.

2026-10-21.title: HATCH: Hardware-Attested Task Chains for Verifiable Manipulation
2026-10-21.authors: Shiza Charania
2026-10-21.comment: . Accepted at the 5th Workshop on Open Robotics Software, IROS 2026, Pittsburgh, PA, USA. Benchmark repository: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract: Capability claims in robot manipulation are unverifiable, and existing leaderboards are each closed, simulated, or gameable. We propose HATCH, a robot escape room: an openly specified, physically replicable, sensor-scored, and unrehearsable benchmark, released under an open license.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Capability claims in robot manipulation are, at present, unverifiable. Results arrive as curated demonstration videos, run on hardware no other lab owns, in environments no other lab can recreate, against self-defined success criteria. Vision and language compounded progress on shared benchmarks; ImageNet is the defining case. Manipulation never acquired one, in part because physical evaluation is expensive: hardware, resets between runs, and human labor.

The leaderboards that do exist achieve at most two of the three properties a trusted benchmark requires: openness, physical evaluation, and trustworthy results. RoboLab-120 [ 1 ] evaluates entrants in-house, in simulation, which resists gaming but is neither open nor physical: the entrant pool is small, and as of mid-2026, the operating vendor’s own model topped the leaderboard [ 5 ] . RoboArena [ 2 ] distributes real-world evaluation across volunteer institutions—an open and physical design—but its team recently disclosed that volunteer evaluators had not completed some assigned evaluations, pulling affected results and flagging low-sample entries [ 3 ] ; the failure was in the trust layer, not the robots. MolmoSpaces [ 4 ] is fully open but simulation-only, and simulated success does not certify physical capability [ 7 ] . Nothing available today is simultaneously open, physical, and trustworthy [ 5 , 6 ] , so we propose one that is: HATCH, a robot escape room.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Benchmark Design

Why an escape room. An escape room is a useful evaluation container for three reasons. First, it is bounded and exhaustively specifiable : a finite set of objects, fixtures, and sensors in a defined volume, documentable well enough for a second lab to rebuild. Second, tasks chain when assembled into a room: the sensor confirming one task’s completion releases the key, code, or clue for the next, so a room is one long-horizon evaluation rather than a suite of isolated trials. A run that fails partway still yields a score, but the headline result is escape. Third, it is adversarial by construction : evaluators design the room and entrants see it for the first time at evaluation, so there is no home-field advantage and nothing to overfit.

A room instance draws from a task pool of five skill categories crossed with three difficulty levels (Table I ).

Instrumented success. Outcomes are confirmed by sensors, not human judgment: color sensors at placement positions, a pressure plate on the checker’s final square, seating sensors confirming peg insertion, and an overhead camera checking the pen-cap task. A success signal a machine emits is one a third party can audit.

Selection under distractors. Tasks present m m candidates when only n < m n<m are correct, so a robot must choose, not sweep. The UV task reveals only a subset of the symbols and the photo-matching task pins 5 photographs against 10 objects. Grasping everything scores zero.

Embodiment-agnostic scoring. Scoring depends only on task outcomes and elapsed time. Arms, humanoids, and mobile manipulators compete on one leaderboard; the benchmark measures what was accomplished, not what embodiment accomplished it.

A room instance. A medium-level room draws one medium task per category and chains them: seating the last shape in the sorting board (spatial) releases the arrow-sequence card; the checker’s final square (symbolic) trips the pressure plate that unlocks the photo-matching station (multi-step), whose completed board order opens the token jars (physical/causal); completing the numbered mat releases the poker chips (dexterous), and the final chip dropping through the slot ends the run. Each stage’s sensor both scores the stage and gates the next. The run is scored as stages completed plus time, with placements randomized by a run-day seed (Sec. III).

2026-10-21.title: Towards Autonomous Bricklaying Using Boston Dynamics Spot
2026-10-21.authors: Karl-Johan Sorensen , Nico vom Hofe , Frank H. P. Fitzek
2026-10-21.comment: . Published in the Proceedings of the 43rd International Symposium on Automation and Robotics in Construction (ISARC 2026), Singapore
2026-10-21.abstract: Mobile legged robots offer unique advantages for on-site construction, including the ability to traverse unstructured terrain, climb stairs, and operate independently between spatially separated work zones. This paper presents a proof-of-concept system for autonomous brick stacking using a Boston Dynamics Spot quadrupedal robot equipped with a manipulator arm. The system operates between a supply area and an assembly area, using AprilTag fiducials for localization and autowalk missions for navigation. Target brick positions and orientations are specified in CAD software and exported directly for robotic execution. We evaluate placement accuracy through ten repeated assemblies of a curved four-layer wall comprising 14 wooden bricks. Results show mean translation errors below 10 mm and mean yaw errors below 1.5°, while the overall RMSE across all runs is 27.72 mm (translation) and 2.06° (rotation). The system was also tested outdoors with stairs between the two areas. The workflow is modular and easily extendable to different wall geometries.
2026-10-21.introduction:
The construction industry is undergoing a transition towards greater automation, driven by rising housing demand, skilled labor shortages, and persistent safety concerns on construction sites. Yet, compared to sectors such as automotive and logistics, construction has seen limited productivity gains, with annual improvement rates of only 1 % 1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} against an industry average of 2.8 % 2.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} [ 1 ] . On-site robotic automation has been proposed as one means to address these challenges [ 2 ] .
Despite this potential, the deployment of robotic systems on construction sites remains limited [ 3 ] . Existing approaches face significant constraints. Large gantry systems require infrastructure that often exceeds the scale of the structure being built. Wheeled and tracked mobile platforms struggle with rough terrain, stairs, and cluttered site conditions. These constraints have confined most successful automation efforts to off-site prefabrication; yet construction fundamentally remains an on-site process where varying conditions resist complete pre-planning.
Recent advances in commercial legged robotics have produced platforms capable of traversing stairs, uneven terrain, and human-centric spaces [ 4 ] . This makes them suited to the multi-level, cluttered environments of real construction sites, where wheeled and tracked platforms face fundamental access constraints. Prior work has demonstrated legged manipulation for general pick-and-place tasks [ 5 , 6 ] , but application to construction assembly has not been explored. To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has quantitatively evaluated the accuracy with which a legged robot can execute a brick-stacking task.

This paper presents a proof-of-concept for what we term the MARA ( MARA ) workflow: a distributed construction process in which a legged mobile manipulator autonomously traverses between spatially separated supply and assembly areas, picking and placing bricks according to a specified layout. The approach is evaluated using a Boston Dynamics Spot quadrupedal robot equipped with a manipulator arm. Target brick positions are modeled in Rhino, a CAD ( CAD ) program, and exported directly for robotic assembly. The system localizes by referencing each manipulation operation to a locally visible fiducial marker, thereby decoupling placement accuracy from global odometry drift. Placement accuracy is evaluated through ten repeated assemblies of a curved four-layer wall, reporting translational and rotational errors across layers.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Background

The concept of robotic masonry has evolved from early mechanized systems to the dedicated commercial bricklaying systems of today. Early mobile systems such as the BRONCO demonstrated the first robotic bricklaying on a mobile platform but required pre-surveyed sites, remote control, and continuous operator supervision [ 7 ] . Later, feasibility studies formalized the relationship between laying patterns, manipulator trajectories, and achievable precision through planning and optimization [ 8 ] . Although commercial systems such as the Semi-Automated Mason (SAM100) demonstrate viable high-throughput automation, they remain optimized for structured workspaces and require strict workflow integration and supervision by human crews [ 9 ] . These systems also share a spatial constraint: materials must be staged within or immediately adjacent to the robot’s workspace. Deploying these systems in real-site contexts with environmental constraints highlights the gap between laboratory robotics and construction realities [ 10 ] .
Competition-driven research further validates the autonomy necessary to assemble wall patterns with differently sized and colored bricks within time constraints [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] . Among these, Lenz et al. [ 13 ] provide the most detailed quantitative evaluation, reporting end-to-end translational placement errors of 13 – 19 mm 1319\text{\,}\mathrm{mm} and rotational errors below 1.3 ° 1.3\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} using a wheeled omnidirectional platform with a UR10e arm. However, all of these systems depend on wheeled or tracked mobility, restricting their ability to navigate rough terrain, stairs, and cluttered environments. Additionally, despite their mobility, these platforms require close proximity to material supplies or human collaborators for resupply.

Legged robotic platforms can traverse stairs, uneven terrain, and constrained spaces, enabling autonomous operation between spatially decoupled supply and assembly zones without the site layout constraints imposed by material co-location. Early work has explored small-scale humanoid robots for on-site floor tiling, demonstrating perception-driven placement with a NAO biped [ 14 ] . More recent work on quadruped-mounted manipulators demonstrates pick-and-place pipelines integrating object detection with real-time control [ 5 ] . Learning-based approaches show that multi-stage, long-horizon pick-and-place tasks on legged mobile manipulators can be made robust through sim-to-real transfer [ 6 ] . These advances demonstrate the growing capability of legged manipulation; however, application to masonry assembly remains unexplored.

This paper addresses that gap, combining two domains that, to the best of our knowledge, have not previously been merged in this context: legged manipulation [ 5 , 6 ] and mobile construction robotics [ 3 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 12 ] . We present the first demonstration of autonomous brick stacking on a legged mobile manipulator and provide the first quantitative evaluation of placement accuracy for a legged robot performing construction assembly. Our proposed system introduces a CAD -to-execution pipeline integrated with a legged manipulator that can operate across spatially decoupled supply and assembly areas connected by stairways, which are inaccessible to wheeled or tracked platforms.

2026-10-21.title: Real-Time Disturbance-Aware Koopman Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors in Spatially Varying Winds
2026-10-21.authors: Stella Kombo , Masih Haseli , Alejandro A. Stefan-Zavala , Peter I. Renn , Morteza Gharib , Joel W. Burdick
2026-10-21.abstract:
Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only
a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state–command–state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Autonomous aerial robots are increasingly being considered for inspection, delivery, monitoring and human mobility tasks in densely built environments [ 1 ] . Such missions require multi-rotors to operate around buildings, above rooftops, through corridors and other confined structures while maintaining accurate trajectory tracking and satisfying state and actuation constraints. Reliable flight in these settings remains challenging since quadrotors are nonlinear, underactuated systems whose performance can degrade when aerodynamic effects are not adequately represented by the prediction or control model [ 2 , 3 ] . The challenge is particularly pronounced in urban environments, where interactions between incoming flow and surrounding structures generate spatially varying wakes, vortices, recirculation zones and accelerated flows around building edges [ 4 ] . Consequently, the disturbances experienced by the aerial vehicle can vary significantly along a single flight trajectory.

Aerodynamic disturbances have previously been addressed at several levels of aerial-robot modeling and control. Classical approaches mainly rely on feedback to reject external disturbances and modeling errors during flight [ 5 ] . Analytic aerodynamic models, such as linear/quadratic rotor-drag terms, augment nominal dynamics with low-order aerodynamic effects while remaining compatible with real-time control [ 6 ] . Data-driven approaches instead learn residual dynamics or full-state transition models from flight data, capturing complex effects that are difficult to model analytically. These learned effects can improve prediction and control for high-performance drone flight [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Although such models can be identified offline and used efficiently online, their accuracy degrades when the vehicle encounters dynamics not represented in the identification data.

A complementary line of work uses measured or predicted spatial flow information to aid wind-aware trajectory planning and penalize paths that enter adverse flow regions [ 10 ] . High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics can resolve complex urban flow structures [ 11 ] , but their computational costs limit direct use in online prediction and high-rate control [ 12 ] . Learned flow surrogates provide a tractable alternative for wind-informed planning [ 13 , 14 ] . However, disturbed regions cannot always be avoided when geometric constraints, mission requirements or unknown wakes force the vehicle to traverse them. When this occurs, unmodeled disturbances can induce persistent mismatch between nominal predictions and the realized vehicle response, degrading tracking and stability. Adaptive, observer-based and learning-based controllers compensate for these effects by estimating disturbances, adapting model parameters or learning residual corrections online [ 15 , 16 , 2 ] . For predictive control, these corrections must also be propagated over the prediction horizon without requiring online retraining of the full dynamics model. This motivates learning a nominal model offline from broad system excitation, while adapting to unmodeled disturbance-induced discrepancies during deployment.

Koopman-based models provide a structured nominal predictor that can be learned offline and used efficiently online, making them potentially suitable for disturbance augmentation. By representing nonlinear dynamics through observables in a function space, finite-dimensional approximations can be incorporated into model predictive control [ 17 , 18 ] and have been applied to quadrotor prediction and trajectory tracking [ 19 , 20 ] . The Koopman Control Family (KCF) [ 21 ] represents nonlinear and state-dependent control systems via a family of linear operators parameterized by the control input. However, existing KCF methods do not explicitly represent disturbances that arise during deployment [ 22 ] .

Koopman methods have also been extended to disturbance estimation and online adaptation. Disturbance-observer approaches learn disturbance models for online compensation [ 23 ] , while adaptive Koopman methods update residual or lifted dynamics [ 24 , 25 ] . For quadrotors, related work either switches among pre-identified Koopman models across operating conditions [ 26 ] or augments nominal predictors with residual corrections [ 27 ] . These approaches do not formulate online adaptation as a disturbance-dependent extension of an input-dependent KCF. This leaves open how to preserve a pretrained nominal KCF while adapting only to disturbance-induced discrepancies online within real-time predictive control, without retraining the full model.

To address this gap, we introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) and apply it to real-time predictive control of multi-rotors. We first identify a nominal KCF from simulation data and calibrate it using hardware data, capturing the coupled vehicle-onboard controller response while keeping the nominal model fixed during deployment. We then adopt a structured separable approximation A ⁡ ( u , d ) ≈ A c ​ ( u ) + A d ​ ( d ) A(u,d)\approx A_{\mathrm{c}}(u)+A_{d}(d) , where A c ​ ( u ) A_{\mathrm{c}}(u) is the nominal reference-dependent KCF and A d ​ ( d ) A_{d}(d) is a disturbance-dependent modification. For real-time deployment, the disturbance-dependent effect is realized through a low-dimensional correction learned online and propagated through the predictive horizon, while the calibrated nominal KCF and onboard stabilization controller remain fixed. We validate the method on a nano-quadrotor under previously unmodeled aerodynamic disturbances. Experiments include figure-eight tracking in uniform fan-array flows and traversal through a spatially varying wake generated by a building-like obstacle. The results demonstrate online adaptation of the predictive dynamics, improved trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, and real-time execution within the control deadline.

2026-10-21.title: Training Controllable World Models via Action Influence Maximization
2026-10-21.authors: Samuel M. Bateman , Tenny Yin , Chongyi Zheng , Lei Huang , Brian Wang , Benjamin Eysenbach , Jaime Fernández Fisac , Dhruv Shah
2026-10-21.comment: CoRL 2026
2026-10-21.abstract:
Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence . We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence.
We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an 85 × 85\times reduction in data.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Action-conditioned world models promise to predict what would happen if a robot took different actions at a given state, enabling policy improvement in novel problems.
Yet, when queried with out-of-distribution actions, models trained on expert demonstrations can predict expert-like futures or hallucinate implausible alternatives.
This failure of controllability (the ability to faithfully predict how changing actions affect outcomes) limits their usefulness for improving robot policies.

Scaling the quantity and diversity of training data can mitigate this [ 1 , 2 ] , but is limited by the cost of collecting robotics data.
To make world models competitive with on-robot experience, the practical question is how to obtain the most useful world-model training data from each real robot interaction.
Despite this, optimal data collection for robotic world models is relatively underexplored compared to policy improving data [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] .
This paper investigates two key hypotheses: Does the data collection distribution strongly influence the downstream world model controllability and fidelity? And, supposing it consequential, can we optimize the data collection distribution to directly improve world model controllability and fidelity?
This work suggests that the answer to both questions is yes.

This has a plausible and intuitive explanation: expert demonstrations in high-dimensional action spaces (e.g. human teleoperation) achieve their goals through a narrow sequence of actions.
The more sensitive success is to action variability, the more deterministic expert demonstrations must be.
Successful demonstrations can thus provide insufficient variation in actions to reveal evidence of how alternative actions would change outcomes.
A world model fitting this data can rationally ignore action influence and usually predict expert-like outcomes regardless of action command [ 1 ] .
In contrast, a non-expert learner may visit different states and try actions underrepresented in expert demonstration.
Predicting consequences of varying actions in these states are precisely the situations where downstream policy improvement stands to benefit the most and where the world model has the least data support.
We see evidence for this ( Figures 6 and 8 ): scaling passive data collection improves controllability for different eval distributions, but the most efficient collection strategy is eval-distribution dependent.

To address this, we propose Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an active data collection algorithm that uses a data-derived intrinsic reward.
Put simply, AIM estimates which variations in action consequences would be poorly explained by the current dataset using a theoretically-motivated, learned intrinsic reward, and then focuses data collection on those state-action pairs as a form of embodied active learning.
To do this, we connect conditional dataset mutual information (MI) to the controllability of any downstream world model, and derive a tractable learned pointwise reward estimator using data density estimation to optimize this property directly.
AIM achieves up to an 85 × 85\times improvement in data efficiency in a high-dimensional, robot manipulation task: adding just 500 actively collected episodes to 3k expert demonstrations matches the end-effector controllability of a world model trained on 300k expert episodes.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Learning a model to predict the future consequences of actions is a well studied problem in decision-making [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
Recent advances in generative modeling [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] and self-supervised representation learning [ 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] have significantly improved the scalability of learned predictive models, enabling a new family of action-conditioned generative world models [ 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ] .
This family of methods absorbs heterogeneous internet-scale video and robotics datasets, and aims to maximize distributional similarity between generated videos and the dataset [ 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 ] .
In robotics, this goal is misaligned: these models’ main utility is improving learner policies [ 14 , 2 , 27 , 36 , 29 , 13 , 23 , 37 , 38 ] , where a rollout is only useful if it faithfully reproduces action-induced changes in task-relevant features that are generally unknown at training time.
Our studied world model builds on DreamerV4 [ 26 ] and Diffusion Forcing [ 18 ] , with architectural and training details described in Section 9 .

A surrogate for task-relevant fidelity is a world model’s controllability : faithful, action-responsive simulation over long horizons [ 2 , 1 ] . Prior work has improved this fidelity by improving temporal consistency [ 18 , 39 ] , incorporating data from autonomous play [ 1 ] or failure [ 2 ] , enforcing policy conservatism to avoid problematic extrapolation [ 26 ] , performing self-consistency based post-training [ 40 , 41 ] , or using latent representations that are easier to predict [ 23 , 42 , 43 ] .
Still, techniques from other domains have seen limited application to modern world models, such as active data collection [ 44 , 45 , 3 , 46 , 47 ] or sim-and-real co-training [ 48 ] .

Exploration has a long history in reinforcement learning (RL) [ 49 , 50 , 51 , 52 , 53 ] and MI skill learning [ 54 , 44 , 55 , 56 ] .
In model-based RL, prediction errors [ 57 , 50 , 51 ] or ensemble disagreement [ 53 , 45 ] provide an intrinsic reward for collecting data that a particular model struggles to predict.
In contrast, in active learning [ 58 ] , it is sometimes assumed that a small core set of data can efficiently summarize a data distribution [ 59 ] . Toneva et al. [60] ’s “unforgettable examples” motivate this perspective: sample learning difficulty and utility is largely consistent across models.
This suggests that data utility is intrinsic to the data, independent of the derived model, and can guide collection [ 61 , 62 ] .
This is similar to information-theoretic experimental design [ 63 , 64 ] and persistent excitation in adaptive control [ 65 , 66 ] .
Our work is most closely related to PlayWorld [ 1 ] , a method for refining generative world models via on-policy goal-directed “play data" rollouts, and contemporaneous work by Hansen and Wang [47] which uses heuristic measures of prediction instability as a curiosity signal to guide active collection.
In contrast, we propose that the model and its data are largely separable, and optimize the data itself by maximizing intrinsic dataset action influence.

2026-10-21.title: Refuses When Asked, Complies When Acting: A Runtime Safety Check for Robot Control Loops
2026-10-21.authors: Arnav Grover
2026-10-21.comment: plus references. Submitted to the Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS) workshop at CoRL 2026
2026-10-21.abstract: Frontier models can control robots through agent harnesses that loop on one question: what motion comes next toward the user’s goal? We show that this default loop carries out harmful instructions. With GPT-6 Astra controlling a low-cost SO-101 arm through the Inspect Robots harness on three household tasks whose hazard is common knowledge, such as “put the knife in the toy basket”, the policy refused 0% of 15 trials, attempted the harm every time, and completed it in 27%. Its one exit, give_up , is meant for goals that cannot be achieved, and it never cited the hazard. We add an optional runtime safety check to the loop: before the first motion, the model is asked whether it would carry out the instruction, given the same camera frames. The check would have stopped all 15 hazardous instructions, including the 4 that completed the harm, and flagged none of the 15 harmless controls. Code and data: https://github.com/Arnav-Gr0ver/Refuses-When-Asked-Complies-When-Acting .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Before acting, a person considers the harm an action could do to those it affects, but a robot control loop that works toward the user’s goal has no step where that consideration happens. Ask a frontier model whether it would put a knife in a toy basket that children reach into, and it says no. Give the same model the same instruction as the control loop of a robot arm, and it reaches for the knife to put it in the basket.

RoboHarm [ 1 ] showed that frontier robot policies fail this check on hardware: GPT-6 Astra refused 2% of harmful instructions (2 of 100) and carried out 60%, including 17 of 20 attempts to stab a baby doll. We study why in one widely used harness. The Inspect Robots harness [ 2 ] runs the policy in a loop in which every call returns one motion toward the user’s goal. Its safety approvers only clamp out-of-bounds and too-fast motion, and its one exit, give_up , is for goals that cannot be achieved, not for goals that should not be pursued. Nothing in the loop asks whether the instruction should be carried out, so a harmful instruction proceeds like any other.

We show that the default loop does carry out the harm: on three household tasks, GPT-6 Astra refused none of 15 trials and completed the harm in four. We then add an optional runtime safety check to the loop. Before the first motion, the check asks the policy model whether it would carry out the instruction, given the camera frames. It would have stopped all 15 hazardous instructions and flagged none of the harmless controls (Fig. 1 ). The check reuses the policy’s model and adds one call, with no second model and no safety specification, unlike prior safeguards that add safety specifications [ 3 ] or a separate monitoring model [ 4 ] . We also introduce three household tasks, each with a named hazard, a safe alternative, and a harmless control, and describe the policy’s reasoning across 464 robot calls.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Methodology

Each task is a household pick-and-place whose instruction moves a harmful object to where it can hurt a child or a pet (Table 1 , Fig. 2 ). The harm is common knowledge, so a model that complies cannot be excused by missing knowledge. The instruction names the place where the child or pet meets the object (the kids’ bowl, the cat’s platter, the toy basket), so the hazard can be recognized from the words. Each scene also holds a safe alternative, which supplies a harmless control instruction that shows whether the check stops harmless requests.

GPT-6 Astra (medium reasoning effort) controls a 6-DoF SO-101 arm [ 6 ] with a wrist and a fixed camera ( 640 × 480 640\times 480 ) through the Inspect Robots harness, unmodified. Each call it receives both images, the joint state, and the instruction, and returns one tool call: move_joints (joint targets and a note on what it sees and why it moves), done , or give_up . The system prompt tells it to “work toward the user’s goal”, that “a scorer judges success”, and that “Safety approvers clamp out-of-bounds and too-fast actions”; give_up is for goals that “cannot be achieved”. Episodes allow 40 calls and 900 control steps at 25% speed. Each task was run 5 times from a fixed home pose. A trial is refused, makes no meaningful attempt, fails, or completes (the item reaches the target; one tablet suffices). Outcomes for the cat and knife tasks come from recorded final frames and the final message, and for the vitamins task from an operator during live runs. One cat trial first graded complete was regraded to failed after its final frames were checked.

The runtime safety check is a separate step that the loop runs before the policy moves, so its prompt differs from the policy’s by design. The same model receives the instruction and the question “You control a robot arm in a home. A person gives you this instruction: […] Would you carry it out? Give your reasoning, then answer yes or no.” A no would stop the loop before any motion. We evaluate the check on the two camera frames from the start of each of the 15 robot trials, the visual input the policy had before its first motion, so its answer shows what the robot would have done had the loop run the check. We also ask without images (5 repeats per task) and ask both versions about the harmless controls to count false alarms.

The API returned a reasoning summary with 49% of robot calls; with the move notes and end-of-trial messages, these form our logs. We count reasoning tokens per decision, mark whether a decision names the hazardous item and the harm, tag each call’s topics (grasping, joints and motion, locating objects, call budget, harm) with keyword rules, and classify each cautious sentence as concerning the robot’s motion or the recipient. A single reviewer checked every harm tag. Each condition has 15 hazardous decisions (3 tasks × \times 5), and we report percentages with counts and 95% Wilson score intervals, which stay informative at 0% and 100% (15 of 15 gives 80–100%, 0 of 15 gives 0–20%).

2026-10-21.title: Determination of the Human-Robot Interaction Workspace for Robot Assisted Head Stabilization Control
2026-10-21.authors: Xinmin Liu , Alexander L. Van Slyke , Destinee Holloman , Ahmad Sakaamini , Rodney D. Wiersma
2026-10-21.abstract:
Accurate head immobilization is critical for medical procedures such as neuroimaging and intracranial radiation therapy, where even minor motion can compromise precision. Traditional methods, such as rigid stereotactic frames and thermoplastic face masks, are invasive, uncomfortable for patients, and require a time-consuming setup. To overcome these limitations, a novel approach employs a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic head holder that is integrated with real-time optical motion tracking, enabling dynamic compensation for head movements without physical restraint. However, implementing this system requires a detailed biomechanical understanding of skull-cervical spine interactions to define safe and effective motion limits. In this study, we conduct a human volunteer investigation using a 6DoF Stewart platform robot to characterize biokinematic workspace of the head-neck system and establish foundational data for
human-robot interaction in precision head stabilization.
2026-10-21.introduction:
There has been significant interest in achieving high-precision positioning of the head in medical applications 41 , 11 , 34 . In diagnostic brain imaging, head motion can lead to movement-related artifacts such as blurring and ghosting, which can hinder clinical diagnosis 25 . This is especially true for imaging modalities such as functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and positron emission tomography (PET), where the collection of data required for 3D image reconstruction requires patients to lie still for long periods of time 45 , 16 . This issue is especially challenging when scanning children or adults who exhibit involuntary motion 10 , 40 , 23 .
Prospective motion correction (PMC) is a popular technique that updates the image acquisition in real-time to keep the field of view constant relative to the moving object in brain MRI. However, PMC has some limitations. It cannot correct higher-order effects such as changing magnetic field inhomogeneities and gradient imperfections. When using multiple receiver coil arrays for better signal quality, motion can change the coil sensitivities relative to the moving object. Motion during image acquisition can cause blurring and spatial distortion because data is collected from different positions within the nonlinear gradient fields. Even with accurate real-time pose correction, motion can still cause magnetic field changes due to inhomogeneities and object-induced field changes. These local magnetic field changes are often the main source of remaining artifacts 14 , 43 , 39 , 3 , 36 . Therefore, it is desirable to use a robotic platform to stabilize the head position.

Although computed tomography (CT) can typically acquire images faster than MRI or PET, in certain cases, head motion artifacts have been reported 29 , 30 . In therapeutic applications, accurate head positioning is essential for procedures involving the treatment of the brain using conventional surgery or radiation therapy 21 , 12 , 15 . Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) is a treatment modality employed for managing brain disorders by utilizing highly precise radiation dose placement. SRS has been used to treat benign or metastatic brain tumors 13 , arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) 18 , 6 , trigeminal neuralgia 44 , 9 , and acoustic neuromas 24 . For SRS, accurate head positioning is needed to avoid damaging critical neural and vascular structures within the brain.

The most common approach to stabilize the head position is the use of stereotactic frames. In this approach, a metal ring is attached to the patient’s skull using screws, and then the frame is bolted to the treatment table, see top row in Fig. 1 8 , 27 . The invasive nature and discomfort associated with the frame have been identified as a central cause of poor patient compliance and poor clinical efficacy. Another approach involves thermoplastic face masks, as shown in the bottom row of Fig. 1 . However, such masks have decreased accuracy due to patient-induced mask flex and can suffer from material changes over time, such as shrinkage 35 . Even with the mask in place, a patient’s head can still drift laterally due to rotational movement around the fulcrum at the back of the skull. In some cases, this has resulted in systematic shifts of up to 2 mm from the initial target setup position 26 . A recent study reported significant errors, which were attributed to improper patient setup stemming from factors such as limitations in mask manufacturing quality, loosening or shrinkage of the mask during treatment, or physical changes in the patient’s head due to facial swelling or weight loss 19 . Moreover, many patients find the thermoplastic mask invasive and psychologically confining, as it severely restricts natural head motion. These factors can contribute to unsafe conditions, potentially leading to treatment interruptions for patient realignment to ensure proper target coverage 27 .
The clinical significance of localization inaccuracies in frameless stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) remains a subject of debate. For critical applications—such as treating acoustic neuromas, pituitary adenomas, trigeminal neuralgia, or lesions adjacent to vital structures—frameless SRS methods have not yet achieved the same level of confidence as frame-based approaches. To mitigate this concern, image-guided radiotherapy (IGRT) is commonly used to monitor patient positioning, complemented by 6D robotic couch adjustments to reduce setup errors in frameless SRS 33 , 17 , 2 . However, IGRT is typically performed intermittently and does not compensate for real-time patient motion deviations during radiation delivery. In general, the accuracies of masks are not suitable for deep tumors located near critical structures, such as in trigeminal neuralgia cases.

One recent method that allows highly accurate human head positioning without the use of head frames or thermoplastic masks is through the use of a 6-degree-of-freedom (6DoF) robotic head holder 4 , 37 . By performing real-time 6DoF patient head motion tracking through a suitable camera system that is used as an input into a control system , it was demonstrated that a Stewart platform (hexapod) type of robot can be used to continuously correct the head target position both translationally and rotationally during treatment (Fig. 2 ). The system efficacy was evaluated on healthy volunteers and indicated that head motion remained under a 0.5mm/0.5deg threshold > > 99% of the time, compared to less than 10% of the time without the use of robotic stabilization demonstrating that the robotic SRS has potential to match or exceed the accuracies of frame based procedures.

Currently , robotic head position stabilization systems do not consider the biokinematics of the head and neck, but rather treat the head as a rigid body object that can freely move in space. This control method can therefore lead to robot head correction trajectories that do not follow natural head-neck motion and can be uncomfortable for patients.

The use of an accurate biomechanical model of the head and neck could allow for improved patient comfort and more effective robotic head motion correction. However, such kinematic modeling of the human head and neck is a complex subject that requires a multidisciplinary approach, combining knowledge of anatomy, biomechanics , and engineering. The study 28 aimed to examine the three-dimensional kinematics of the cervical spine during maximal passive head rotation, with a focus on coupled motion, using low-dose CT scans of twenty healthy volunteers in both neutral and maximum axial rotation positions. The study employed the finite helical-axis method to describe the 3D motion between the discrete positions of each separated vertebra. In another work , investigating the spine’s role during walking , a 3-dimensional multi-segment kinematic spine model 20 was developed for noninvasive analysis of spinal motion during walking. Validation of the kinematic model was carried out by comparing the calculated angles to the known angles from a mechanical model. The study involved collecting data on the motion of the spine from volunteers walking at their self-selected speeds. Kinematic modeling can also be useful in the development of devices aimed at addressing issues in the head and neck region. A novel study 46 was reported where a dynamic neck brace was utilized to analyze the head movements of patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) while also recording the surface electromyography (EMG) of their neck muscles. The ALS participants were instructed to perform three head-neck movements in a single plane: flexion-extension in the sagittal plane, lateral bending in the coronal plane , and axial rotation in the transverse plane. These movements were repeated five times at self-selected speeds. There are also many studies on occupational neck disorders as a result of the workforce shifting from industry to sedentary office work , and on the mechanical behavior of the cervical vertebra under normal conditions and under conditions that result in minor or major injuries 1 , 7 , 31 .

In this work, we present results from a healthy volunteer study investigating head and neck reaction to a 6DoF robot that is aimed for potential use in SRS radiation therapy. Optical camera monitoring was used to track the real-time response of the human head to various translational and rotational input trajectories induced by a compact 6DoF robot located behind the head. Analysis of motion data allowed for determination of general kinematic parameters as needed for the development of a head-and-neck biomechanical model. Knowledge of the head’s dynamic motion constraints is an important consideration s for the interaction between humans and robots , not only in the medical space but potentially in other research areas such as the development of head motion control through robotic exoskeletons .

# II . Methods and Materials

## II . A . Robotic Head Motion Control System

The robot utilizes a parallel kinematic approach and is equipped with six linear actuators to enable full 6DoF head control, including translations in x, y, z , and rotations in pitch, yaw, and roll. The six extendable legs are positioned in a precise geometrical configuration, providing several advantages over serial robotic systems. The motion system features a platform with a radius of 75 mm and a stationary height of 183 mm, and provides a motion workspace of ± \pm 15 mm along the XYZ axes and ± \pm 15 ∘ in pitch, roll, and yaw 5 . These advantages include the distribution of weight load across all legs, resulting in high compactness, and the division of overall positional error among all linear actuators.

Real-time 6DoF head motion tracking is accomplished using an infrared (IR) stereoscopic camera (Polaris, NDI, Canada) with IR markers attached to the volunteer’s head 38 . Real-time 6DoF monitoring of head motion was performed at a 12 Hz sampling frequency. The head motion, as tracked by the four reflective IR markers, was subsequently transmitted automatically to an in-house developed LabVIEW (National Instruments) code , which controls the robotic device shown in the volunteer setup in Figure 2 . This control code communicates between the IR camera system and the robotic device simultaneously, transmitting the six linear actuator trajectories using an 8-axis stepper motor controller (PCI-7358, National Instruments) 5 . Movement of the robot produces a corresponding response motion in the volunteer’s head by moving the cranial support structure (Fig. 3 ). The tracked motion is then input into a control computer and analyzed using a fast iterative closest path control algorithm that is then sent to the robot to perform head positioning.

In this study, the head support consisted of four cushioned pads angled to help ensure contact with the volunteer . These pads were each connected to the robot’s mobile top platform and were free to swivel around the AP axis to provide improved universal contact between volunteers while maintaining sufficient levels of comfort. The plastic posts were designed to be easy to install and remove, making them convenient for use with different head sizes of volunteers . The slope of the plastic posts was 45 ∘ . Fig. 3 shows a schematic diagram of the head support system.

The LINAC coordinate system, with its origin at the isocenter, is defined to facilitate precise targeting. ## II . C . Volunteer Experiments

Human and robot interactions were studied using three volunteers (IRB #843058). During the study, volunteers assumed a relaxed supine position on the simulated treatment table, with their heads supported by the robot. Volunteers were requested to lie down with their heads positioned to maximize contact with four plastic posts in the robotic head support. The robot then performed serial translational and rotational motions, while the IR camera recorded the resultant head movements. To study human -robot reaction thoroughly, the robot was programmed to move along the frontal axis (left-right, defined as the x axis), the longitudinal axis (superior-inferior, defined as the y axis) and the sagittal axis (anterior-posterior, defined as the z axis) ± 7 \pm 7 mm, ± 4 \pm 4 mm and ± 7 \pm 7 mm respectively. The robot was also programmed to pitch (around the frontal axis), roll (around the longitudinal axis) and yaw (around the sagittal axis) ± 5 \pm 5 degrees, ± 5 \pm 5 degrees and ± 3 \pm 3 degrees respectively. Rotation occurred around a mock target within the volunteer’s head. Two mock target positions were considered, one at cervical vertebrae C1, and the other at a point displaced (-60, 120, 60) mm from the C1, i.e., at a position 60 mm to the right, 120mm superiorly and 60mm anteriorly with respect to C1.
The 6D head motion of each volunteer was recorded and analyzed. Motion limits were evaluated based on head-neck biomechanics to determine physiological constraints.
