2026-10-21.title: Design and Control of a Multimodal Legged-Aerial Robot Through Separate Control Contraction Metrics
2026-10-21.authors: Kaushik Venkatesh Krishnamurthy , Eric Sihite , Alireza Ramezani , Morteza Gharib
2026-10-21.comment: Presented at 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems, Pittsburgh PA
2026-10-21.abstract: The integration of dynamic legged locomotion and aerial mobility offers versatility that is deterred by challenges in payload distribution, actuation, and the contrasting requirements of both domains. In this paper, we present the design and operation of a multimodal quadrupedal aerial-legged robot. The presence of legged aerial systems also allows for thruster-assisted legged locomotion, which we make possible with a unified control framework using Control Contraction Metrics (CCM). We search for separate domain-specific contraction metrics for walking and flight independently offline and unify them using an online energy-based Control Lyapunov Function Quadratic Program (CLF QP). This enables optimal, cross-domain control allocation, which we show using simulations. We also show experimental results that validate the mechanical viability of our hardware and the paradigm of thruster-assisted trotting. The stability of said experiments motivates the deployment of the control framework for multimodal operations.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Robotic biomimicry of birds’ dynamic bipedal and flight locomotion can be a significant ordeal. The prohibitive design restrictions, such as a tight power budget, limited payload, complex multi-modal actuation and perception, an excessive number of active and passive joints involved in each mode, sophisticated control, and environment-specific models, just to name a few, have alienated these concepts. It is worth noting that, as multi-modality has secured birds’ (and other species) survival in complex environments, similar manifestations in mobile robots [ 7 ] can be rewarding and important.

In this work, we will report our legged-aerial quadrupedal robot’s first multi-modal operations, including thruster assisted dynamic trotting and hovering. Our long-term objective has remained to integrate dynamic legged locomotion and aerial mobility in a single platform. Our robot design primarily focused on mass allocation to minimize the total cost of transport, which consequently yields smaller actuation bulk in the system, and component selection for the flight unit was systematically made to achieve successful lift-off while not too much negatively affecting dynamic legged mobility.

Standard control theory have struggle with dynamic, changing trajectory tracking. A contraction metric is a Riemannian metric, with respect to which the distance between any two solutions of a differential equation is decreasing. Unlike a Lyapunov function, which measure the decreasing generalized distance between a point and an attractor such as an equilibrium, contraction does not require any knowledge about the position of the attractor. Simply, contraction ensures incremental stability between two trajectories, instead of the stability of an equilibrium point.
Control Contraction Metrics (CCM) ensures that small displacements in directions orthogonal to the span of the control inputs must be contracting.
The existence of a CCM can be formulated as a convex problem as specified in previous works [ 8 , 18 ] . To overcome the computational bottleneck of global stability analysis for this coupled hybrid system, we propose a unified control framework inspired by CCMs.

We outline this work’s contributions as follows:

The design and operation of a multimodal legged-aerial robot.

A proposed control framework using contraction theory to create separate metrics for walking and flight, which are then unified online using an energy-based control Lyapunov function quadratic programming (CLF-QP).

Experimental results on hardware, with a decoupled heuristic control policy to demonstrate the capabilities of thruster-assisted trotting and flying. These experiments seek to prove that the physical paradigm of combining thrusters with legs is robust.

2. A proposed control framework using contraction theory to create separate metrics for walking and flight, which are then unified online using an energy-based control Lyapunov function quadratic programming (CLF-QP).

3. Experimental results on hardware, with a decoupled heuristic control policy to demonstrate the capabilities of thruster-assisted trotting and flying. These experiments seek to prove that the physical paradigm of combining thrusters with legs is robust.

# II Related Work

Multi-modality in a robot expands the robot’s capability in performing tasks that a single mode can’t do, such as a ground-aerial robot that can use ground locomotion to traverse a relatively flat terrain efficiently and fly over an obstacle when the ground locomotion is unable to drive through it. Therefore, the robot’s range and reach can be expanded greatly by utilizing both locomotion modes, and they can augment each other if the design allows it.

There are various robot designs related to ground-aerial robots, such as, a bipedal robot with quadrotor propulsion attached to its torso [ 3 ] , a transforming quadruped that can switch between legged and aerial modes [ 23 ] , thruster-assisted hopping robot [ 2 ] , a quadrotor with active wheels underneath [ 1 , 11 ] , a quadrotor encased in a rolling cage where the thrusters can drive the cage to perform ground locomotion [ 20 ] , ornithopters with wheels for ground locomotion [ 12 ] , and a transforming robot that can reorient its appendages to transition between a UGV and UAS modes [ 16 ] . Thrusters can be used to augment ground locomotion capabilities to assist in stabilization by using them to satisfy ground contact constraints [ 15 , 24 ] , can also assist in jumping [ 17 , 5 ] and in steep slopes [ 13 , 6 , 4 ] where is not normally possible using just legged locomotion. We aim to use CCM as a control framework to create metrics for walking and flight to be used in our legged-aerial multi-modal robot.

There have been many works that use Control Contraction Metrics (CCM) for either Robust or Adaptive Control [ 8 , 9 , 18 , 25 , 21 , 22 ] . Manchester and Slotine [ 8 ] introduced the idea of Control contraction metrics for a nonlinear system for universal exponential stabilizability. The control contraction metric can then be used for real-time optimization which involves finding a geodesic to the desired state from the current state and finding the control input. This problem is simpler than executing model predictive control. This work then extended to obtain Robust CCMs by using a metric to synthesis a nonlinear state feedback H ​ ∞ H\infty controller [ 9 ] . This powerful tool for trajectory, while setting the foundation of our research, assumes exact model knowledge.

To solve control problems at the scale of multicopters and drones, one requires careful structuring of the CCM metric and the polynomial optimization problem to bypass the computational complexity of synthesis. Singh et al. [ 18 ] extended this CCM synthesis with robust feedback control on multicopters and implemented this with experimental results on hardware. This was achieved using exploiting the structure of the problem and Sum of Squares Programming to obtain a metric for a high-dimensional dynamical system. Sun et al. [ 19 ] were able to obtain a tracking controller for different dynamical systems using contraction metrics that were learned using a Neural Network, with controller execution much faster than MPC. Exploring data-driven approaches, Tsukamoto et al. [ 22 ] introduced Neural Contraction Metrics (NCMs) by training LSTM networks to globally approximate these metrics. The NCM approach derives provably stable, dual estimation and control policies that are strictly optimized for disturbance attenuation.
Shiromoto et al. [ 14 ] proposed decentralized control for large networks using contraction theory by forcing a sum-separable global metric, which guarantees stabilization around a target trajectory. Their results demonstrate that utilizing separable structures to break complex global metrics into solvable localized pieces is highly effective. While CCMs have been used to control aerial robots and other simpler systems such as inverted pendulums [ 10 ] , we also propose a way to extend this to legged robots.

2026-10-21.title: RadGeoLoc: Radar Geolocalization via Particle Filtering
2026-10-21.authors: Shaunak Kolhe , Peng Jiang , Kasi Viswanath , Srikanth Saripalli
2026-10-21.comment: Submitted to ICRA 2027
2026-10-21.abstract: In real-time autonomous field applications, GNSS is often unreliable and inaccurate. A possible solution is localizing against a prebuilt map like a satellite image, as it is georeferenced and already surveyed. In this work, we localize a spinning radar measurement against overhead RGB imagery with a learned observation model. We use a radar representation pretrained by masked reconstruction and align it to features from a satellite image. A particle filter propagated by radar odometry proposes candidate poses, and our observation model provides a likelihood over these poses. We evaluate our method over 31 distinct routes, over 8 datasets spanning both urban and offroad conditions using only ground radar and a coarse local prior. We also examine the robustness over changing weather using repeated traversals over the same route over 13 months, in both urban and offroad conditions.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Reliable robot localization in operating environments is essential for their effective operation. In GPS-denied environments, this proves to be difficult. A common remedy to this problem is to localize against a prior map, often built by a previous field deployment. This approach limits localization to pre-mapped areas, and is vulnerable to scene changes over time. Additionally, if such a prebuilt map is to be built at runtime [ 1 ] , [ 2 ] , these methods scale poorly with the size of the environment. Satellite and aerial orthophotos instead provide a useful map, since they are georeferenced, widely available, and globally consistent.

Localizing against a satellite image introduces its own set of challenges. For instance, with cameras, the gap between a top-down orthophoto and the forward camera measurement must be bridged by a view transform, termed as crossview localization [ 3 ] . While this gap is reduced significantly with other sensors that measure radially, such as LiDAR [ 4 ] , there is also the temporal gap from the time of capture of the satellite image. What both sensors also lack is robustness to weather, which can be bridged by using Radio Detection and Ranging (radar). Radar sensors prove to be suitable for detection in these scenarios and yield geometric features over a longer range due to their longer wavelength [ 5 ] .

Spinning radar [ 6 ] presents a practical alternative to the geolocalization problem. A radar measurement is already metric and in BEV form. Existing methods that localize radar against a public map build an explicit intermediate representation first, and then solve for a geometric alignment against it using OpenStreetMap routes and semantic layers [ 7 ] , or points extracted from overhead imagery and registered against radar-derived points [ 8 ] , [ 9 ] , [ 10 ] , [ 11 ] . Each of these commits to a class label or a fixed structural representation derived from the satellite images. However, performance of such methods in unstructured environments is not explored.

In this work, we instead pose a learned, shared representation for this task. A radar encoder pretrained by masked reconstruction is aligned by a contrastive objective to features of the satellite image on a shared metric grid, and the model is then asked the question: given a candidate pose, how compatible are the two representations? We use this to score pose hypotheses derived from a particle filter. We achieve a median per-frame ATE of 2.9m and 5.17m on urban and offroad routes respectively.

Our main contributions are:

An observation model for particle filtering which computes pose likelihoods by matching learned features from a radar image and a satellite image, by explicitly learning scene structure from radar.

An exhaustive evaluation, to the best of our knowledge, of over 8 of 10 published datasets 1 1 1 We exclude the BoreasRT [ 12 ] and MOANA [ 13 ] datasets, since BoreasRT provides only Doppler radar and MOANA provides marine scenarios showing very sparse returns spanning over 31 distinct routes in both urban and offroad scenarios.

An analysis of what radar reconstruction pretraining contributes, by ablating the pretrained weights.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Radar and Cross-View Geolocalisation

The crossview geolocalization problem is well explored, primarily in computer vision. Klammer et al. [ 3 ] take a coarse to fine matching approach using learnt representations with a factor graph. Nash et al. [ 14 ] use a modified census transform over panoramic stereo images against satellite images on the Perseverance rover to achieve sub meter global localization. Lee et al. [ 15 ] use DINOv3 [ 16 ] and the BEV projection coupled with a particle filter to achieve less than 8m of absolute trajectory error.

Spinning radar became viable for motion estimation once the returns could be reduced to stable landmarks [ 17 ] . Feature-based pipelines extract keypoints from the polar scan and register consecutive sweeps [ 17 , 18 ] , and radar SLAM adds loop closure over those estimates [ 19 ] . For radar sensors supplying doppler information, Le Gentil et al. [ 20 ] and [ 21 ] use doppler measurements and a direct registration method to yield sub meter accuracy in relative pose estimation.
Within radar geolocalization, RSL-Net [ 8 ] align a live radar scan to satellite imagery by scoring rotated scans to estimate orientation, synthesizing a radar view, and recovering translation by cross-correlation. Its self-supervised follow-up [ 9 ] retains this basic pipeline while removing supervision. This is further developed into [ 10 ] overhead-image localization to radar and LiDAR through a learned point-based occupancy representation generated by ray tracing from the image center. This approach, coupled with OpenStreetMaps is exploited by Abdullai et al. [ 11 ] , and achieves less than 2m of ATE on the Boreas dataset [ 22 ] , and also shows demonstrations on an unmanned surface vehicle. Considering an alternative public map, Hong et al. [ 7 ] use OpenStreetMaps to exploit road segments and lane information to localize ground radar.

While these methods show promising results in urban scenarios, they are not explored in unstructured environments, where prior information like OpenStreetMaps may not exist. Additionally, some of these approaches [ 10 , 8 ] also focus on single-frame evaluation, which does not show localization performance over a complete traversal. In II-B we explore how literature learns image representations.

## II-B Learning image representations

We focus on self-supervised image representation learning in particular, since these provide a task-agnostic feature representation, which can be fine-tuned.
Learning image representations without labels has converged on a few objectives. Masked image modeling reconstructs deliberately hidden pixels. MAE [ 23 ] masks a large fraction of patches and
rebuilds them from the rest, SimMIM [ 24 ] shows the same
idea needing only a minimal decoder, and PixMIM [ 25 ] observes that a raw-pixel target spends capacity on high-frequency detail
and replaces it with a low-pass version of the input. Joint-embedding
methods drop reconstruction entirely and relate two views of one input in
feature space. VICReg [ 26 ] keeps the embeddings of
different views close while variance and covariance terms prevent
collapse, and I-JEPA [ 27 ] predicts the
representations of target blocks from a context block in latent space.
Contrastive methods, learning by separating a positive
from sampled negatives [ 28 ] also demonstrate comparable results.

2026-10-21.title: What Would Removing This Corruption Change? Failure Attribution for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-21.authors: Carson Sobolewski , Anjali Parashar , Fei Chen , Yingke Li , Chuchu Fan
2026-10-21.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are sensitive to visual corruptions, but knowing that a corruption is typically harmful does not establish whether removing it would benefit the current episode. Furthermore, when several corruptions co-occur, deciding what to correct requires understanding which ones contribute to failure risk and how much their removal would help. We define this problem as failure attribution . Detecting corruption presence alone cannot answer this question, as corruptions can be present but relatively harmless, while directly measuring removal benefits requires costly paired policy rollouts with and without the corruption present. To address this, we introduce a factorized risk model that learns separate representations of the scene and corruptions, allowing us to estimate removal benefits through latent intervention from the current image and task instruction, without paired clean images or additional counterfactual rollouts. We evaluate our approach on OpenVLA and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} in simulation and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -DROID on a Franka robot. Our method outperforms monolithic and vision-language-model (VLM) baselines, including achieving approximately 3x lower attribution error than frontier VLMs. We also demonstrate our method adapts to execution context and corruption intensity, and can be used for online failure monitoring on hardware.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] have emerged as generalist robotic policies capable of performing manipulation tasks directly from images and natural language instructions. However, their reliance on visual input makes them sensitive to visual corruptions [ 4 ] . For example, viewpoint changes and sensor noise have considerable impact on OpenVLA’s performance, reducing success rate from 76.5% to 1.1% and 19.3%, respectively [ 4 ] . These effects motivate knowing how each corruption influences a policy during execution. A straightforward approach is to estimate average failure rates for each corruption combination based on historical data. However, these averages assign the same prediction to episodes with the same corruption combination, regardless of corruption intensity or the current scene context. Knowing that a corruption is harmful on average therefore does not establish whether removing it would reduce failure risk in the current episode.

When several corruptions co-occur, this problem is compounded: we need to determine which corruptions contribute to the current failure risk and which would offer the greatest benefit if removed. We call this failure attribution : quantifying each corruption’s contribution by asking, “How much would failure risk decrease if this corruption were removed?” Answering this question can guide whether and how to correct an execution failure.

However, failure attribution presents two challenges.
First, corruption presence alone does not establish its effect on performance. A corruption may be clearly visible yet have little impact on a particular policy, so detecting it does not indicate whether correcting it would help.
Prior works address neighboring problems, including improving robustness through corruption-inclusive training [ 4 , 5 ] or input restoration [ 6 ] , and predicting failure through online monitoring [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] . However, these approaches do not directly answer the attribution question of how much removing each corruption would reduce failure risk.

Second, directly measuring this removal benefit requires intervention: executing the policy repeatedly with and without each corruption from the same underlying state. Because a corruption’s effect depends on which others remain present, exhaustively characterizing these interactions requires covering a large majority of combinations, rather than just single corruptions. Such comparisons are expensive in simulation and difficult to reproduce during deployment, where repeated failed executions can also put hardware at risk. We therefore seek to estimate removal effects from the available observation, without executing these counterfactual rollouts.

To address these challenges, we introduce a factorized risk model that estimates each corruption’s contribution to failure risk from the current image and task instruction alone.
The model learns separate latent representations of the scene and corruptions. By intervening on the corruption latent while holding the scene latent fixed, it estimates how failure risk would change if a corruption were removed ( Figure 3 ), without modifying the physical scene or rerunning the policy.

We evaluate the model on OpenVLA and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} in simulation and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -DROID on hardware. Our experiments validate that our approach accurately estimates per-corruption attributions, captures interactions between co-occurring corruptions, and learns sensitivity to scene context and corruption intensity. Under co-occurring corruptions, it achieves approximately 3x lower attribution error than frontier VLMs. Hardware experiments demonstrate our approach can be used for online monitoring ( ) as corruptions change during an episode. In summary, we:

Formulate failure attribution for VLA models as estimating the reduction in failure risk from removing individual visual corruptions.

Introduce a factorized risk model that estimates these removal effects through latent interventions, using only the current image and task instruction.

Evaluate the method on OpenVLA and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} in simulation and π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} -DROID on hardware, demonstrating attribution under co-occurring corruptions, sensitivity to execution context and corruption intensity, and online failure monitoring.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

Prior works evaluate VLA robustness to visual and environmental disturbances through benchmarks such as LIBERO-Plus [ 4 ] and The Colosseum [ 11 ] , as well as adversarial attacks [ 12 ] . Other approaches improve robustness through corruption-aware training [ 4 , 5 ] or input restoration [ 6 ] . These works characterize or mitigate aggregate sensitivity, but do not attribute an observed failure to the responsible corruption, which is the gap this work addresses.

Online failure monitors use internal policy representations [ 7 , 8 ] , action consistency [ 9 ] , failure-free training [ 10 ] , out-of-distribution detection [ 13 ] , or conformal prediction [ 14 ] . VLM-based methods provide post-hoc failure explanations [ 15 , 16 ] , while image-region attribution links reliance on nuisance features to poor performance [ 17 ] . These approaches predict whether failure is likely or identify generic visual cues, but do not quantify the counterfactual effect of removing a specific corruption. Our factorized latent model estimates this effect without paired counterfactual trajectories.

2026-10-21.title: On Maximum Clique and Maximum Consensus Formulations in Point Cloud Registration
2026-10-21.authors: Abolfazl Babanazari , Kaveh Fathian
2026-10-21.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-21.comment: . Interactive examples and Lean proof verification: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract:
Maximum clique and maximum consensus are widely used formulations for robust point cloud registration in robotics.
Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many matches as possible, while maximum clique selects matches through pairwise distance tests.
Maximum clique is often used as a substitute for or an approximation to maximum consensus, with empirical evidence suggesting a close relationship.
However, how closely the two formulations agree is not fully understood.
We study this relationship theoretically.
We show that a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than the maximum consensus set at any fixed positive tolerance, and derive geometric conditions that bound this error.
When rotation is fixed, we derive sharp error bounds and tests that exactly characterize maximum consensus for the translation subproblem.
Finally, we study group- k k consistency, which tests groups of k k matches, and determine the smallest group sizes that guarantee alignment error bounds independent of point cloud scale and geometry.
These are d + 1 d+1 for rotations and translations and d + 2 d+2 when reflections are allowed, in dimensions d ≥ 2 d\geq 2 .
Interactive examples and proof verification using the Lean theorem prover are available at https://ariarobotics.github.io/mc-vs-mc-registration/ .
2026-10-21.introduction:
To build a map or localize within one, a robot needs to align 3D environment scans taken from different viewpoints [ 3 , 4 ] .
Point cloud registration estimates the alignment between the scans when they are represented as point clouds.
When no initial alignment is available, registration pipelines begin by matching local features across the scans, providing a set of tentative correspondences [ 1 ] .
Repeated structures and limited overlap can make many of these matches incorrect, so registration must identify reliable matches for an alignment.

Maximum consensus and maximum clique are two widely used formulations for selecting reliable matches. Maximum consensus seeks one transformation that aligns as many correspondences as possible within a prescribed tolerance. Maximum clique selects a largest set that passes all pairwise distance tests, without estimating a transformation.
The two are closely related, and maximum clique is often used as a substitute for maximum consensus, but how far their solutions can differ is not fully understood.

At matched tolerances, maximum clique is a relaxation of maximum consensus.
Any set that one transformation aligns within the point tolerance passes every pairwise test and therefore forms a clique, so maximum clique size gives an upper bound on maximum consensus.
The converse does not hold in general [ 5 , 6 ] .
This upper bound alone does not tell us the clique’s alignment error or how many of its matches can be aligned within the prescribed tolerance.
Fig. 1 shows an example in practice, where a maximum clique and a maximum consensus set of similar sizes have few matches in common and produce very different registration results.

Testing larger groups offers a way to narrow this gap by detecting inconsistencies that pairwise tests miss.
In group- k k consistency , every group of up to k k matches must admit an alignment within the prescribed tolerance, although different groups may use different transformations [ 7 ] .
Fig. 2 compares these three selection approaches on a small example.

In this paper, we study the theoretical relationship between these three formulations, independently of a specific registration pipeline.
We begin with the simpler problem of known rotation, where pairwise tests bound the translation error and testing larger groups gives an exact characterization of maximum consensus.
When rotation must also be estimated, we show a maximum clique can have arbitrarily large alignment error and be arbitrarily larger than a maximum consensus set. We derive bounds that explain how this error depends on point cloud geometry.
We then show how group- k k tests give alignment error guarantees without assumptions on point cloud scale or geometry, and determine the smallest group sizes needed.
In summary, the contributions of this paper are as follows:

We show that maximum clique and maximum consensus methods for point cloud registration can give different results in general.
In particular, for certain point clouds, maximum clique can produce matches that cannot be obtained through maximum consensus, regardless of the chosen tolerance.

When the rotation that aligns two point clouds is fixed, we provide sharp lower and upper bounds on the maximum consensus solution size in terms of the maximum clique size.
In particular, in a d d -dimensional space, we show that maximum clique using group- ( d + 1 ) (d+1) consistency is equivalent to maximum consensus.

In the general case with unknown rotation, we show that d + 1 d+1 is the smallest group size for which maximum clique using group consistency can provide lower and upper bounds on the maximum consensus solution size.
When reflections are allowed, the smallest such group size is d + 2 d+2 .

In particular, for certain point clouds, maximum clique can produce matches that cannot be obtained through maximum consensus, regardless of the chosen tolerance.

2. When the rotation that aligns two point clouds is fixed, we provide sharp lower and upper bounds on the maximum consensus solution size in terms of the maximum clique size.
In particular, in a d d -dimensional space, we show that maximum clique using group- ( d + 1 ) (d+1) consistency is equivalent to maximum consensus.

2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

Maximum consensus methods jointly estimate a transformation and select the correspondences that it fits within a tolerance.
Random sampling can approximate maximum consensus by fitting small subsets and counting their inliers [ 8 ] .
Deterministic methods use branch-and-bound search to solve the maximum consensus problem [ 9 ] or subproblems based on other robust losses [ 10 ] .
Geometric pruning methods can reduce this search by removing correspondences while preserving the maximum consensus solution [ 11 ] .

Clique-based outlier rejection offers practical runtimes and robustness to extreme outlier rates, with reported registration results including cases where over 99 % 99\% of matches are incorrect [ 12 , 13 ] .
Approaches include exact maximum clique search [ 12 ] , approximations using large maximal cliques [ 13 ] , and evaluating multiple candidate cliques before selecting an alignment [ 5 , 6 ] .
Graph structure and effective pruning can make maximum clique search practical despite its worst-case complexity [ 14 , 12 ] .
Clique selection can precede robust fitting [ 3 , 15 ] or maximum consensus in separate rotation, translation, and scale subproblems [ 16 ] .

Extensions of pairwise consistency use triangles [ 17 ] or shared neighbors [ 18 ] to reject matches that pass individual pairwise tests.
Group- k k consistency generalizes compatibility checks to k k measurements and formulates selection as maximum clique in a hypergraph [ 7 ] .
These tests capture relations among larger groups that pairwise checks can miss.

Beyond point cloud registration, consistency-based selection is used in inter-robot loop-closure selection [ 4 ] , rotation averaging [ 15 ] , and object-based localization [ 19 ] .
These applications share the question of whether locally compatible measurements support one common estimate.
A related geometric question arises in global graph rigidity, which asks when edge lengths uniquely determine a point configuration up to rigid motion [ 20 ] .

This work studies the theoretical relationship between maximum consensus, maximum clique, and group- k k consistency in point cloud registration.
We use results from classical geometry [ 21 ] , near-isometry theory [ 22 , 23 ] , and Procrustes analysis [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] to establish when consistency tests guarantee a bound on alignment error and when they can fail.

2026-10-21.title: XoNav: An Exoskeleton as a Personalized Haptic Interface for Assisted Navigation
2026-10-21.authors: Debadrata Sarkar , Soumen Sen , Aman Arora
2026-10-21.comment: A supplementary video illustrating the XoNav hardware, haptic cues, Wizard-of-Oz trials and autonomous navigation is available at this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract: Walking without vision requires timely, unambiguous guidance, yet many wearable aids encode directions as audio or vibrotactile signals that users must translate into movement. We present XoNav, a four-actuator hip exoskeleton that renders guidance cue directly at the hip joint. It renders Advance cue and two-level Braking cues through sagittal-plane actuators and two-level Steering cues through frontal-plane actuators. A bilateral LSTM-based gait-state classifier uses two thigh-mounted IMUs to identify gait states, enabling haptic cues to be delivered in coordination with the wearer’s gait while suppressing them during standing. The classifier generalized to unseen users with recalls of 95.2–97.9%, with mean detection delays of 38.6 and 63.1 ms for stance-to-swing and swing-to-stance transitions respectively. Constrained human-in-the-loop Bayesian optimization personalized Braking for minimum resistance and Steering for maximum comfort while ensuring detectability and safety. All participants reliably distinguished between grades of their personalized cues and the firmest Braking cue remained below 53% of the safety limit. In blindfolded Wizard-of-Oz navigation trials along three paths, the participants kept 98.8% of the walked distance within a 0.75 m wide passage, with a 4.9% increase in mean progression speed per trial. A body-worn camera, RTAB-Map and Nav2 further enabled a feasibility study of autonomous navigation and detours around previously unmapped obstacles.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Navigating without vision requires guidance about both direction and movement. Canes, guide dogs and electronic aids serve people with visual impairment, while comparable needs arise when sight is obscured or occupied, such as for firefighters in smoke [ 1 ] or industrial workers engaged in visually demanding tasks. A wearable RGB-D, audio and vibrotactile system improved navigation for blind and low-vision users [ 2 ] , and bone conduction preserves awareness of environmental sounds [ 3 ] . Personalized smartphone audio has also guided blind users outdoors with performance comparable to a human guide [ 4 ] . Robotic canes [ 5 ] and quadruped guides [ 6 ] provide physical guidance but occupy a hand and act from outside the body.

Body-worn haptic interfaces offer hands-free guidance, although a survey found that many walking aids still depend on Wizard-of-Oz operators and are not ready for daily use [ 7 ] . Vibrotactile belts reduce collisions during training [ 8 ] , instrumented walker handles can improve confidence [ 9 ] , and textile interfaces distribute haptic feedback across the body [ 10 , 11 ] . Vibrotactile directions nevertheless require interpretation as locomotor actions, while audio competes with ambient cues. Kinesthetic interfaces instead communicate movement through force, as demonstrated by the resistance and pulling rendered by the Kinethreads exosuit [ 12 ] .

Lower-limb exoskeletons can convey guidance at the joints responsible for walking. Recent works include multi-activity [ 13 ] as well as task-agnostic [ 14 ] joint-moment assistance, data-driven community ambulation [ 15 ] and online personalization [ 16 ] , frontal-plane control of step width and balance [ 17 , 18 ] , and improved haptic transparency [ 19 ] . Variability in individual responses have motivated human-in-the-loop optimization (HILO) [ 20 , 21 ] , including Bayesian optimization [ 22 ] and preference-based methods [ 23 , 24 ] . Adding vibrotactile signals to exoskeleton torques can modulate walking speed but may increase cognitive load [ 25 ] .

Closest to our work, Carrasquillo et al. [ 26 ] used artificial potential fields to modulate lower-limb exoskeleton impedance for obstacle avoidance. In virtual reality with occluded vision, this increased clearance and reduced collisions, demonstrating the potential of exoskeleton force feedback for human navigation. However, four gaps remain for real-world wayfinding. First, directional cueing through the hip’s frontal-plane degrees of freedom, which govern mediolateral foot placement and heading, remains unexplored. Second, guidance has not been phase-locked to gait events, potentially displacing an unloaded swing limb and overriding, rather than informing, motor intent. Third, navigation cues have used fixed parameters despite individual differences in perception and comfort, while HILO has not been formulated to jointly satisfy detectability, safety and comfort. Finally, reliance on external tracking leaves untested whether egocentric localization from a body-worn camera, despite gait-induced sway, can couple a navigation stack [ 27 ] with a human walker.

Here, we present XoNav, a hip exoskeleton serving as a personalized haptic interface for assisted navigation (Fig. 1 ). XoNav renders Advance and two-level Braking cues in the sagittal plane and two-level Steering cues in the frontal plane. Each cue is gait-informed, being released at its gait event and withheld while the wearer stands, so that the exoskeleton guides the movements the wearer initiates and never overrides them. The graded cues are personalized for reliable detection at the lowest intensity, within safety limits and in the profile the wearer finds most comfortable. The main contributions are: (i) a four-actuator hip exoskeleton realizing gait-informed haptic navigation cues, timed by a classifier that uses only two thigh IMUs and generalizes to unseen users; (ii) a constrained HILO framework that balances detectability, safety and comfort through a detection constraint, an analytic safety screen and duel-based comfort scoring; (iii) a blindfolded Wizard-of-Oz navigation study, using motion capture and user ratings to evaluate haptic guidance independently of robotic perception and planning errors; (iv) an autonomous navigation feasibility study integrating a body-worn camera with a ROS 2 navigation stack, demonstrating guidance and detours around unmapped obstacles. Our results show that wearers navigate reliably with personalized cues of minimal intensity, a step towards exoskeletons that guide human locomotion rather than driving it.

A Jetson Orin Nano (NVIDIA, USA) running ROS 2 Humble performs gait inference, cue generation and navigation. 2026-10-21.title: EmbodyHOI: Embodiment-Aware Generation of Hand-Object Interactions for Humanoid Dexterous Manipulation
2026-10-21.authors: Chaitanya Chawla , Kartik Sharma , Ananya Bal , Laszlo A. Jeni , Guanya Shi
2026-10-21.abstract:
Humanoid dexterous manipulation needs reference motions that are both semantically rich and
kinematically feasible for the target robot.
Text-conditioned hand–object interaction (HOI) generators supply diverse, language-specified
demonstrations, but they synthesize motion in human (MANO) space.
The embodiment gap is therefore deferred to post-hoc retargeting, where trajectories deployed on the robot can fail to maintain contact with objects and also degrade policy learning.
Our key idea is that robot reachability should constrain the interaction trajectories while they are being
generated .
We present EmbodyHOI , which runs a differentiable inverse-kinematics (IK) solver for a specific humanoid embodiment inside the
sampling loop of a frozen flow-matching HOI trajectory generator. We feed back gradients from the embodiment-aware IK solver into the HOI sampler and jointly optimize the position of the humanoid with respect to the object.
Because guidance acts only at inference, one HOI trajectory generator trained on human hand poses transfers across humanoid embodiments without
retraining.
On ARCTIC trajectories with two contrasting humanoids (Unitree G1 and H1-2), our proposed guidance-based method cuts the retargeted
wrist error from 8.9 cm to 0.6 cm while leaving text-to-HOI generation quality intact, and
raises task success from 68% to 79% on 50 random G1 tasks
and from 62% to 76% on a four-task H1-2 suite.
Critically, cheaper alternatives for bridging the embodiment gap fail to beat EmbodyHOI. Post-hoc wrist refinement and
compute-matched best-of- N N selection both reach lower IK energy than our guidance yet
train worse policies. For simulation results, see our website: https://embodyhoi.github.io/
2026-10-21.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands remains difficult for humanoids that can reliably walk and loco-manipulate [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] .
A robot must coordinate reaching, finger contact, and whole-arm motion under embodiment-specific kinematic constraints to execute trajectories that actually manipulate objects.
A human trajectory when kinematically retargeted to a humanoid is often not executable, due to differences in finger morphology, joint limits, and wrist reachability.

We study how to generate human interactions which can easily close the above gap. Given a language prompt and an
articulated object, we produce bimanual hand–object trajectories specific to a humanoid, which are easily executable by the robot.

A natural route to this goal of end-to-end policies is generate-then-track, but today’s Hand-Object Interaction (HOI) generators have no notion of the robot that will execute their output. In this route, a generator proposes diverse task-conditioned reference motions and a physics-based RL policy learns to track them under contact and actuation limits [ 5 ] .

Hand-centric HOI generators are the natural source of dexterous references as they model finger-object contact, but they generate in MANO [ 6 ] space with no term that couples the wrist to a robot’s kinematic chain. This mismatch only surfaces during retargeting, after the finger and object motions are committed, and the tracking policy inherits wrist targets that the arm cannot reach. Previous works resolve this on either side of generation. Training the motion prior in robot space [ 7 ] yields one generator per robot, which rules out cross-embodiment reuse. Whereas repairing a generated human motion [ 8 , 9 ] only makes delta modifications, and cannot always rectify retargeted wrist trajectories unreachable for the robot. Tracking systems such as DexMachina [ 10 ] and ManipTrans [ 11 ] sidestep the question by commanding a floating wrist with no arm.

We take a different approach: keep a frozen MANO HOI generator as a reusable motion prior and make its samples embodiment-aware during generation (Fig. ).
We build on MAD-HOI [ 12 ] , a text-conditioned HOI generator that fills object and hand tokens over a sequence of unmasking steps, integrating a flow-matching ODE for the unmasked tokens at each step. Inside every ODE step, we decode the current wrist trajectories, solve a differentiable IK problem on the target humanoid, and add a gradient of the IK residual ( IK energy ) to the learned velocity field, in a manner of classifier guidance. A wrist correction made in one unmasking step conditions the finger and object tokens generated in later ones, so the interaction re-forms around the corrected wrist instead of being patched afterward.

A full humanoid raises another problem that floating hands and fixed-base arms do not, where the robot stands. The base placement decides whether both arms stay reachable over the whole interaction, and a fixed-base IK cannot differentiate between a feasible interaction performed from the wrong standing position from an infeasible one. We therefore solve for the base translation together with the arm joints, and re-solve it at every unmasking step so that the base follows the partially generated motion. Finally, we retarget the guided motions and train a PPO tracking policy with separate imitation rewards for arm and hand, as they differ in error scale and contact requirements.

IK energy is a diagnostic, not a quantity to minimize on its own.
Guidance costs 32 × 32\times a native sample (5 s to 160 s on an A100), paid once per reference, so we compare it with alternatives that lower the energy after generation at the same or lower cost.
Post-hoc IK refinement of a finished sample reaches the lowest energy of any method, and compute-matched best-of- N N selection also beats guidance on energy, yet both train worse policies (Table I ).
Refinement moves the wrists after the fingers and object are fixed, and selection returns a different interaction instead of correcting the requested one.
Reachability has to be imposed while the interaction is still being generated.

Our contributions are as follows.

Training-free IK guidance for a frozen HOI generator. A differentiable IK solve on the target humanoid runs inside every ODE step of the sampler, and its gradient steers the hand tokens.
One objective with one set of weights serves the Unitree G1 and H1-2, and it also lowers the IK energy of a second generator, Text2HOI [ 13 ] , without modification.

Base placement inside guidance. Solving for the base removes near-singular G1 arm configurations (2.6% to 0.2% of test samples) even when applied once to a finished sample, and re-solving it at every unmasking step accounts for 2.8 of the 5.7 success-rate points that guidance adds over post-hoc base optimization on the four-task G1 suite (Table III ).

Lower IK energy after generation does not give better references. Post-hoc refinement and compute-matched best-of-32 selection reach lower energy than guidance (0.35 and 1.21 vs. 1.81), yet their policies succeed less often (32.8% and 74.0% vs. 79.7%, Table I ).

Downstream gains on two humanoids. Policies trained on guided references with decoupled hand and arm reward streams, raise success from 68% to 79% on 50 randomly drawn ARCTIC tasks on the G1 and from 62% to 76% on a four-task H1-2 suite.
We will release the guidance code, the generated references and the trained policies.

2026-10-21.related_work:
# II Related Work

EmbodyHOI draws on three lines of work, and none of them adapts the reference motion to a humanoid’s arm chain while the interaction is being generated.

Human-space HOI generation and test-time guidance.

Text-to-motion models generate full-body SMPL [ 14 ] motion with pose-space diffusion [ 15 , 16 ] or masked-token generation [ 17 ] .
Full-body HOI methods [ 18 , 19 ] model contact only coarsely at the body surface.
Hand-centric methods parameterized by MANO [ 6 ] model fine-grained finger–object contact on datasets such as ARCTIC [ 20 ] , GRAB [ 21 ] , and OakInk [ 22 ] , from grasp synthesis and interaction denoising [ 21 , 23 ] to language-conditioned sequence generation [ 13 , 24 , 25 , 26 , 12 ] .
Test-time guidance steers such generators toward keyframes, trajectories, and contacts, but always toward targets specified in human space [ 27 , 28 ] .
Our guidance has the same form but no human-space target: it scores the decoded wrist against a robot’s kinematic chain, so its optimum moves when the robot or its base changes.

Retargeting and RL from human demonstrations. Human-to-robot retargeting typically optimizes joint angles against keypoint and end-effector errors [ 29 , 30 ] , and it underpins teleoperation [ 30 , 31 ] and robot-space datasets [ 7 ] .
Dexterous-hand retargeting [ 32 , 33 , 34 ] is a standard preprocessing step for RL from human demonstrations.
ManipTrans [ 11 ] pretrains a hand-trajectory imitator and then fine-tunes a residual policy.
DexMachina [ 10 ] uses retargeted joints and contacts as auxiliary rewards under a decaying virtual-object curriculum.
DexMan [ 35 ] extends this recipe to RGB video, and HERMES [ 36 ] unifies heterogeneous motion sources for mobile bimanual manipulation.
In all of them the reference is fixed before the robot is considered.
ManipTrans and DexMachina command a floating 6-DoF wrist with no arm chain, and DexMan drives a G1 arm through IK but keeps the robot at the origin, so neither arm reachability nor base placement is ever optimized.
We reuse their object-side recipe (Sec. III-C ) and make the reference itself the variable.

Generative priors for policy learning. Example-guided RL [ 37 , 38 ] extends to HOI imitation [ 39 , 40 ] and to tracking-as-reward execution [ 41 , 5 ] .
The two works closest to ours resolve the embodiment mismatch after the motion exists.
Chen et al. [ 9 ] guide an RL finger controller with a generative prior that emits only wrists, fixed before the robot is considered, and DemoDiffusion [ 8 ] denoises a retargeted human trajectory with a robot diffusion policy that stays close to that trajectory and so inherits its reachability.
DreamControl-v2 [ 7 ] avoids retargeting by training in robot space, and fine-tuning a human-space generator on reachable data would likewise remove our inference cost; both need robot-feasible data for every embodiment, which a method like ours would have to produce, and yield one generator per robot.
However, none of them keeps one frozen human-space generator: we resolve reachability inside its sampling loop and handle base placement for a full humanoid arm chain.

2026-10-21.title: Which Depth Estimator for Jetson AGX Orin? A 2026 Benchmark of Monocular and Stereo Methods
2026-10-21.authors: Leaf Jiang
2026-10-21.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-21.comment: . Code and per-scene results: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract:
The Jetson AGX Orin is a common computer for robots and vehicles, yet measured accuracy, speed and
energy of current depth estimators on it are hard to find. We benchmark nine model families as of
October 2026: the monocular Depth Anything V2 and 3, Depth Pro, MoGe-2, Metric3D v2 and UniDepth V2,
and the stereo methods libSGM, NVIDIA ESS and Fast-FoundationStereo. Every method runs on the Orin as a
TensorRT FP16 engine or native CUDA code at up to three input sizes, up to the full 5.7 MP, and is
scored for metric accuracy against Middlebury 2014 ground truth (non-occluded pixels of the 10 scenes
whose disparity stays below 256 px), GPU time, energy and licence. Stereo is far more accurate. At
30 fps, NVIDIA’s ESS reaches 0.70% AbsRel in 8.6 ms and libSGM 0.73% in 25 ms; with more compute,
Fast-FoundationStereo reaches 0.33%. The best monocular models reach 12% with the true focal length
(Depth Anything 3 Metric-L in 33 ms, Depth Pro in 803 ms), and 3.8–4.0% only with an oracle per-image
scale (MoGe-2-L, UniDepth V2-B, Metric3D v2-L). Stereo error falls as the input resolution grows; no
monocular model improves, and the metric scale of most drifts away from the truth outside their training
resolution. At depth discontinuities, which AbsRel barely registers, the monocular models scatter
17–46% of the edge points between foreground and background, learned stereo 2–9% and libSGM at full
resolution 1%. We give recommendations per frame-rate budget and release all code, per-scene results
and engine build scripts.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Dense metric depth is a core input for driving, robotics and industrial automation, and the NVIDIA
Jetson AGX Orin is one of the most common computers on which it runs. Two families of camera-based
methods compete for it. Monocular depth networks such as Depth Anything
V2 [ 1 ] and 3 [ 2 ] , Depth Pro [ 3 ] ,
MoGe-2 [ 4 ] , Metric3D v2 [ 5 ] and UniDepth
V2 [ 6 ] infer metric depth from a single image with large vision
transformers. Stereo methods triangulate depth from two calibrated cameras, with classical
matching such as semi-global matching (SGM) [ 7 ] or with learned matchers such as
NVIDIA’s ESS [ 8 ] and Fast-FoundationStereo [ 9 ] .

Choosing among them for an Orin is hard. Papers report accuracy on desktop GPUs, at the networks’
training resolution and often after aligning the prediction to the ground truth; embedded timings, if
any, come from different devices, precisions and input sizes; and licences differ from permissive to
non-commercial. This paper is a practical benchmark for that choice. We run every method on the same
Jetson AGX Orin 64GB as a TensorRT FP16 engine (accuracy from FP32 where FP16 is unreliable) or as native
CUDA code, at up to three input sizes from its native or smallest input to the full 5.7 MP, and score
every output against the same full-resolution Middlebury 2014 ground truth [ 10 ] on the 10 scenes whose disparity stays within the 256-level range of the semi-global matcher. We report
metric accuracy, GPU time, energy and licence, and derive recommendations per frame-rate budget.

(i) Measured metric accuracy, GPU time and energy on Jetson AGX Orin for nine current monocular and
stereo model families, each at up to three input sizes ( table 7 ).
(ii) Recommendations: the most accurate stereo and monocular configuration for each frame-rate budget,
with licences ( section 5 ).
(iii) A resolution-scaling study: stereo error falls with resolution, monocular error does not, because
the monocular metric scale drifts outside the training resolution and the shape does not improve
( section 6.1 ).
(iv) An analysis of depth discontinuities, where AbsRel is blind to the “flying” points that the
networks produce and a classical matcher can be the better choice ( section 6.3 ).
(v) All code, per-scene results, engine build scripts and this paper’s source, released at https://github.com/nodarhub/orin-depth-benchmark .
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related work

MiDaS [ 11 ] and DPT [ 12 ] established zero-shot relative depth by
mixing datasets. Depth Anything [ 13 , 1 ] scales this with DINOv2
features [ 14 ] and pseudo-labelled data, with metric variants fine-tuned on
Hypersim [ 15 ] (indoor) and Virtual KITTI (outdoor). Depth Anything
3 [ 2 ] predicts depth and camera rays from any number of views with a plain DINOv2
transformer; its monocular metric model predicts depth relative to the focal length. Depth
Pro [ 3 ] predicts metric depth and focal length from a multi-scale ViT at 1536 2 1536^{2} . MoGe-2 [ 4 ] predicts an affine-invariant point map, from which it recovers the
focal length and shift, plus a global metric scale from the class token. Metric3D
v2 [ 5 ] predicts depth in a canonical camera space with a fixed focal length and
rescales it with the true one; UniDepth V2 [ 6 ] predicts a camera
representation together with depth and can take the true intrinsics as input. Tile-based methods such as
PatchFusion [ 16 ] and PatchRefiner [ 17 ] target high-resolution
monocular metric depth by processing overlapping crops and fusing them with a global estimate.

SGM [ 7 ] remains the workhorse of embedded stereo, with open-source GPU
implementations such as libSGM [ 18 ] . Learned matchers such as
RAFT-Stereo [ 19 ] and FoundationStereo [ 20 ] are far more
accurate but expensive. Fast-FoundationStereo [ 9 ] distils
FoundationStereo into a real-time model. NVIDIA’s ESS [ 8 ] , distributed with Isaac ROS,
is a compact learned stereo network designed for robots on Jetson. Embedded GPUs also ship dedicated
stereo hardware: the Orin’s optical flow accelerator (OFA) computes SGM-style disparity, exposed
through NVIDIA VPI; we do not evaluate it.

Pseudo-LiDAR [ 21 ] showed that image-based depth representation matters for
3D detection, with stereo far ahead of monocular. Depth networks are also known to smooth across
depth discontinuities and produce “flying pixels” between foreground and background. We are not aware
of a study that compares how the metric accuracy of current monocular foundation models and of stereo
changes with input resolution, or that compares them under a common embedded compute budget.

2026-10-21.title: Learning to Be Different: Component Specialization for Compositional Diffusion Policies
2026-10-21.authors: Alec Laprevotte , Haonan Chen , Xiaoshen Han , Yilun Du
2026-10-21.abstract: Diffusion policies with linearly composed scores have emerged as a promising approach to multitask robotic learning by combining separate factors to enable modular, task-wise adaptation, compositional generalization, and interpretable functional decomposition. However, current training objectives do not encourage factor specialization, often resulting in uninterpretable denoisers whose composed prediction is an average over identical copies, undermining their architectural premise. To address this, we propose a drop-in score-decorrelation auxiliary loss, motivated by projective composition theory. Our approach encourages specialization by penalizing overlap directly between component noise predictions, with little architectural change or computational overhead. We demonstrate across multiple benchmarks that our decorrelation loss consistently reduces measurable double-counting between components, improves task decomposition, and produces behaviorally meaningful specialization without compromising multitask performance. Website: https://al3cl1.github.io/robotics-score-decorrelation .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Offline imitation learning has become one of the dominant paradigms to replicate complex robotic manipulation skills [ 12 , 36 , 29 ] . However, as the diversity of tasks scales, their action distributions become highly multimodal. Monolithic policies model these behaviors jointly, merging them together and complicating both specialized skill interpretation and recombination across tasks [ 56 , 29 , 10 ] .

To address these limitations, a growing line of work instead breaks down larger monolithic policies into smaller, composable generative models for better interpretability and test-time generalization [ 16 ] . Particularly, many robotics models sum multiple diffusion components via linear score combination, breaking down complex action distributions into simpler, specialized factors that are aggregated at inference time [ 47 , 42 , 48 , 9 , 31 , 25 ] . While these methods provide architectural factorization, their training objective supervises only the composed sum of component scores, leaving the decomposition itself weakly constrained. As a result, components often collapse into overlapping predictors [ 31 , 48 ] , undermining the modular adaptation, compositional generalization, and interpretability that motivated factorization in the first place.

We propose an auxiliary loss that directly encourages the components of a compositional diffusion policy to specialize. During training, it penalizes overlap between the noise predictions of each pair of components, pushing them toward distinct contributions to the composed score. The loss is a drop-in addition to the standard denoising objective: it requires no change to the component networks and is discarded at inference. Our approach is motivated by recent theory on projective composition of diffusion models [ 5 ] , in which Factorized Conditionals, a sufficient condition for projective composition, imply orthogonality between background-relative score deltas. Because compositional policies rarely include an explicit background model, we use output decorrelation as a practical proxy for this structure. Unlike orthogonality regularizers for mixture-of-experts models, which act on hidden activations [ 20 , 22 ] , our loss acts directly on the score outputs, where overlap between components has a direct generative meaning.

We validate our approach on Factorized Diffusion Policy (FDP) [ 31 ] across RLBench [ 27 ] , RoboCasa [ 35 ] , and LIBERO [ 30 ] , and further demonstrate its benefits on a real-world cup-flipping task. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We introduce a training-time decorrelation loss that encourages specialization among the components of compositional diffusion policies, motivated by projective composition theory. (2) We show that it consistently reduces redundancy between components across factor counts and outperforms alternative decorrelation objectives, while maintaining or improving task success, especially on diverse and multi-step tasks. (3) We show that the resulting components specialize to behaviorally meaningful parts of the action space, such as the mobile base and the gripper, without supervision over the action space.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Compositional Diffusion Policies in Robotics: Diffusion models have driven major progress in image and video generation [ 24 , 43 ] , and have been rapidly adopted in robotics as flexible policy representations. Diffusion Policy [ 12 ] models a visuomotor policy as a conditional denoising process over action chunks and has since been extended with richer input representations [ 54 , 46 ] , score-based goal conditioning [ 41 ] , and trajectory-level planning [ 28 , 1 , 8 ] . More recently, scaling these policies to multitask regimes has motivated architectures designed around reuse and specialization of sub-modules to better aid in generalization. One line of work introduces a mixture-of-experts (MoE) structure with sparse routing over noise levels or skills [ 48 , 42 , 25 , 21 ] . However, these approaches inherit well-documented pathologies of MoE training: an auxiliary load-balancing loss, usually meant to prevent expert collapse, also drives overlapping gradient flow across experts, homogenizing their representations and suppressing specialization [ 20 , 14 , 18 ] , while sparse routing introduces training instability and load imbalance [ 18 ] , and hard expert selection makes individual experts difficult to reuse across different, unseen tasks. In response, a complementary line of models addresses these limitations by composing diffusion policies via linear score combination [ 32 , 15 ] . Components can be separately trained and aggregated at inference [ 47 , 7 , 6 ] , or jointly trained with learned routers (or uniform weights) over per-component noise predictions [ 31 , 9 ] . Trajectory-level compositional diffusion follows a similar template, summing per constraint or per-skill scores to recombine behaviors at planning time [ 34 , 52 , 45 , 2 ] .

However, a common pattern across this latter lineage is that compositionality is enforced architecturally, but only weakly enforced functionally. The composed score is supervised end-to-end, so the decomposition itself is weakly identified: components can collapse to redundant predictors of the same conditional, which limits the generalization that composition is meant to provide. Our work addresses this gap by regularizing component outputs during training, motivated by Bradley et al. [5] , whose Factorized Conditionals, a sufficient condition for projective composition, imply orthogonal background-relative score deltas.

Expert Specialization and Decorrelation: Decorrelation and orthogonality losses are well studied across several model families, each operating on a different representational substrate. Self-supervised learning penalizes the cross-correlation of hidden activations to prevent feature collapse [ 53 , 4 , 13 ] , while classical disentanglement penalizes statistical dependence among latent codes [ 23 , 11 , 17 ] . In MoE models, orthogonality is often applied to intermediate FFN outputs of co-activated experts, router weights, or learned routing distributions [ 37 , 50 , 14 , 44 ] . Parameter-level approaches enforce orthogonality between LoRA residuals or task vectors [ 26 , 40 , 38 ] . In diffusion specifically, prior work enforces or analyzes near-orthogonal concept embeddings or representation subspaces [ 49 , 19 ] . In robotics, classical compositional policies multiply or blend primitives without enforcing decorrelation [ 39 , 51 ] , while, outside robotics, multi-branch architectures orthogonalize at the feature level for adversarial robustness [ 55 ] . Across these techniques, the decorrelation signal acts on hidden features, router weights, parameter residuals, concept embeddings, or latent codes rather than directly on the generative output. Our loss instead operates on the raw noise-prediction outputs of separately parameterized components combined through linear score composition.

2026-10-21.title: Visual Task Modeling and Automated Planning for Humanoid Robots in Education of Individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder
2026-10-21.authors: Lada Kudláčková
2026-10-21.comment: presented at conference AICCONF 2026 in Prague, Czech Republic
2026-10-21.abstract: In robot-assisted education, a robot must understand how to complete a task in order to effectively guide a student through it. We present a novel method that enables a semi-autonomous, camera-equipped robot to recognise the task goal and plan actions to achieve it. Our work focuses on Shoebox Tasks, an activity commonly used in the education of individuals with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD). These tasks are designed so that the goal can be inferred directly from their visual structure. We have developed a solver that uses a vision-based Large Language Model to convert photos of a Shoebox Task into a Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) representation and generate action plans for solving it. We have also implemented a robotic interface that enables a Nao robot to autonomously execute various Shoebox Tasks and assist a student by suggesting next steps or signalling detected failures through action demonstrations, voice commands, or gestures. With an adapted robotic interface, the solver can be integrated into a variety of educational robots. No programming expertise is required from teachers, and the solver operates exclusively on captured images as input. Research in special educational needs indicates that students with ASD can benefit substantially from robot-assisted teaching, and our system aims to strengthen these learning opportunities while also fostering interest in robotics among individuals with ASD.

Photos can be captured via a PC-connected camera or uploaded from a mobile phone through a web interface. Both task analysis and plan generation are executed directly by the VLM, which outputs a single PDDL problem file containing the action plan as a comment. # II Method

## II-A System overview

Our system operates as a perception–analysis–action loop (Fig. 2 ) implemented in Python and driven by a Vision–Language Model (VLM). Starting from an image of the initial Shoebox Task configuration and a general PDDL domain file, the system analyzes the visual structure and generates a corresponding PDDL problem instance under the given domain together with an action plan. After one or more actions are performed, a new image is captured and provided to the system together with the previously generated PDDL file and the earlier image. The VLM infers which actions have been executed between states, removes them from the remaining plan, and updates the PDDL problem description accordingly. This loop continues until the task is completed or an invalid state is detected. Actions may be executed autonomously by a robot, or performed by a student, with the robot providing guidance, error alerts, or corrective feedback.

## II-B Vision–Language Analysis

For the initial state, before any action is performed, the VLM is given:

an image of the start configuration,

a general PDDL domain file,

an example PDDL problem file,

a prompt containing analysis rules.

The VLM (ChatGPT-5) is instructed to detect objects in the image, identify which objects are movable and which are static containers, and infer the intended distribution of objects given the visual structure of the task. The PDDL domain and the example problem file are designed to be general and applicable across a variety of Shoebox Tasks. The domain file defines three object types: items , initial_container , and targets . All movable items begin stacked inside a single initial container, placed side by side to avoid occlusion. All other static objects are considered targets, and the task is to determine how items should be distributed among them. Detected objects are assigned types and deterministic names based on their visual features and numbered by their position in the image. Objects that share the same visual appearance are grouped and named using a descriptive label and an index (e.g. blue_ball_3). Unique objects receive unique descriptive identifiers. Clear naming is essential for correctly tracking objects across state updates. The VLM produces a complete PDDL problem instance and an associated action plan consisting of an unordered set of valid actions. After one or more actions have been executed, a new image is captured and the VLM is given:

the latest PDDL problem file,

the image of the latest (captured) configuration,

the image of the current configuration.

The VLM, following the strict naming rules, re-identifies all objects, verifies whether the new state is valid, and determines which planned actions were executed. These actions are removed from the remaining plan and the corresponding predicates in the PDDL problem file are updated. Once the plan is empty, the goal state has been reached. If the new state is invalid (e.g., an object disappears or is corrupted), the system reports a failure.

## II-C PDDL Problem Generation

The PDDL domain defines three object types: item, init_container, and target.

The predicates are as follows:

(in_container ?x – item),

(in_target ?x – item ?y – target),

(free ?x – target).

Two Pick&Place actions are defined:

move_to_target, which transfers an item from the initial container to its designated target.

move_to_container, which returns a misplaced item from a target back to the container.

The generated PDDL problem file contains the object list, initial state, and goal specification, followed by a comment section containing explanatory notes and the action plan. Object names follow the deterministic naming scheme, and the goal section specifies which item should be placed in which target. Generated PDDL files are validated against the domain. When visual analysis is correct, the files are usually syntactically valid. However, VLMs occasionally produce false-positive refusals (e.g., “I’m sorry, I can’t assist with that”), which leads to PDDL validation failure. In such cases, the request is simply repeated.

## II-D Robotic Interface

We implemented a simple robotic interface for a Nao v5 humanoid robot to demonstrate how the solver can be used in robot-assisted education. Each suggested PDDL action is mapped to either a robot-executed manipulation or a robot-guided instruction, depending on the educational mode. In manipulation mode, we restrict tasks to those involving objects that are easy for the robot to grasp (e.g. balls, cubes). To simplify manipulation and avoid solving complex inverse kinematics, items are placed at predefined positions within the initial container. In this mode, the robot performs only forward actions (moving items to targets), and recovery actions are not executed. After each step, a new image is captured. Tasks requiring fine manipulation, such as using coins, are executed in voice-guidance mode, where the robot issues simple verbal instructions and gestures. Since the student may follow, ignore, or perform multiple actions at once, a new photo is captured on request to re-evaluate the state. In this prototype implementation, the Nao’s onboard camera is not used. Instead, images are captured by a mobile phone or a PC-connected camera and uploaded through a web interface. This design allows the user (e.g., a teacher) to maintain strict control over the experimental process. The image capture frequency is configurable and depends on the educational context. For example, when the robot demonstrates the task by executing the solution autonomously, a single initial image
is sufficient to compute the full action plan, which is then executed sequentially. However, to verify correct execution (e.g., detecting dropped items), images may be captured after each action. When the student performs the task manually, images must be captured after each action (or at fixed time intervals) if the robot is expected to detect and alert incorrect actions. Alternatively, if the robot
provides assistance only upon student request, images may be captured after multiple actions.

2026-10-21.title: Towards Interaction State Recognition in Sensorized Gecko-Inspired Adhesive Interfaces for Orbital Servicing
2026-10-21.authors: Eduart Abdullahu , Francesco Grella , Carol Martinez
2026-10-21.abstract: Reliable contact establishment remains a critical challenge for autonomous on-orbit servicing (OOS), particularly when interacting with non-cooperative targets. Gecko-inspired dry adhesives provide a lightweight, passive, and residue-free solution for robotic capture in space, yet current systems operate in open loop, without the ability to estimate their own contact or adhesion state during interaction. This paper presents a real-time interaction-awareness framework that enables sensorized gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces to estimate their contact state throughout the adhesion lifecycle using embedded capacitive sensing. Five discrete interaction states (idle, proximity, contact, engaged, and disengaged) are classified using experimentally collected and augmented sensor data, enabling a comparative evaluation of six lightweight machine learning models suitable for embedded deployment. Among the evaluated models, Random Forest achieved the highest offline classification accuracy of 95.65%. For online deployment, combining Random Forest with a rule-based state machine improved accuracy from 78.02% to 93.14%, achieving a macro F1-score of 0.9343 while maintaining a 53 ms inference cycle. These results demonstrate that incorporating physics-consistent state constraints significantly improves robustness during real-time inference, representing a step toward interaction-aware capture in future autonomous orbital servicing missions.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Since the launch of Sputnik-1, Earth orbits have become increasingly congested [ 1 ] . The planned deployment of megaconstellations is expected to intensify this congestion and increase the risk of collisions and debris generation [ 2 ] . Addressing this challenge and ensuring long-term orbital sustainability require advanced debris-removal and on-orbit servicing (OOS) systems capable of establishing safe and reliable initial contact with non-cooperative targets.

Gecko-inspired dry adhesives offer a promising solution for first contact with space structures. Unlike conventional mechanisms, they require no suction or mechanical interlocking, can attach and detach from unprepared surfaces without leaving residue, and can operate in vacuum environments [ 1 ] with demonstrated performance under space-relevant thermal conditions [ 3 ] . Inspired by the hierarchical setae structure of gecko feet, these materials rely on van der Waals interactions, enabling adhesion without chemical bonding, contamination, or consumable materials. In particular, wedge-type architectures require only low normal preload combined with controlled shear displacement, minimising reaction forces during contact and making them well-suited for repeated attachment cycles when interacting with free-floating targets.

Despite successful space demonstrations [ 4 ] [ 5 ] , reliable use of gecko adhesives remains challenging because of sensitivity to contact trajectory, misalignment, and variability in applied normal and shear loads [ 6 ] . Most systems are open-loop and lack awareness of contact state, thereby limiting autonomy and making recovery from partial engagement or premature release difficult. Moving from passive interfaces toward intelligent adhesive systems, therefore, requires real-time interpretation of the contact interface during interaction.

Integrating sensing into gecko-inspired adhesives can address this gap. Capacitive sensing with embedded flexible electrodes enables mechanically transparent measurement without affecting adhesion [ 7 ] . However, the resulting signals are complex and capture multiple overlapping interaction phenomena (proximity effects, initial contact, conformational engagement, and shear loading), requiring data-driven methods to extract meaningful information.

This paper presents an initial step toward intelligent gecko-inspired interfaces by enabling real-time interaction-state estimation in sensorized adhesives. As shown in Fig. 1 , such awareness of the interaction can provide feedback on the state of the adhesive interface during capture, supporting higher-level decision-making in future autonomous OOS missions. Using a wedge-shaped gecko-inspired adhesive equipped with an embedded interdigitated capacitive sensor developed by the Stanford Biomimetics and Dexterous Manipulation Lab (BDML) [ 6 ] [ 3 ] , we collect experimental data throughout the adhesion lifecycle, including approach, contact, engagement, and release. We apply signal processing and feature extraction methods to characterize the evolving adhesive interaction, then evaluate six lightweight machine learning models for real-time contact-state classification. To improve robustness during dynamic operation, classifier predictions are combined with a state machine that enforces physically consistent interaction transitions.

The main contribution of this work is a real-time interaction-state recognition framework for sensorized gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces, combining lightweight machine learning with physics-informed state-transition constraints for robust online deployment. Experimental validation demonstrates that incorporating these constraints improves online inference robustness, increasing classification accuracy from 78.02% to 93.14% during real-time operation, enabling reliable recognition of the adhesive interaction throughout the contact lifecycle.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work enabling real-time interaction awareness in sensorized gecko-inspired adhesive interfaces for autonomous space robotic applications, moving adhesive-based capture systems from passive mechanisms toward interaction-aware autonomous operation.
