# II Related Work

Gecko-inspired dry adhesives have emerged as a promising technology for robotic capture and manipulation in space due to their lightweight, passive, and reusable adhesion mechanism. Early work on ON-OFF adhesive grippers demonstrated the feasibility of reversible, residue-free attachment for orbital applications [ 8 ] . Subsequent developments have focused on improving the reliability and controllability of adhesive contact [ 5 ] . A major milestone was the demonstration of gecko-inspired adhesives on the International Space Station using NASA’s Astrobee platform, which validated their performance in true microgravity and highlighted operational challenges, including alignment sensitivity, impact rebound, incomplete contact formation, and variability in normal and shear loading [ 6 ] . Related efforts, such as mushroom-type gecko inspired docking mechanisms [ 9 ] , compliant debris capture systems [ 10 ] , and commercial technologies such as Kall Morris Inc.’s REACCH platform [ 11 ] , further demonstrate the potential of adhesive-based capture and docking systems for orbital applications.

To improve the reliability and controllability of adhesive interaction, recent research has increasingly focused on integrating sensing directly into adhesive interfaces. In [ 12 ] , a thin-film pressure sensor enabled the detection of adhesion, slip, and detachment states, while piezoelectric sensing based on Lamb wave attenuation has been used to correlate contact area with adhesion behavior [ 13 ] . Capacitive sensing with interdigitated electrodes enables estimation of contact and adhesion state through changes in electric field distribution [ 7 ] . More recent designs incorporate compliant adhesives with embedded electrodes for simultaneous contact detection and mechanical adaptability [ 14 ] , as well as resistive-capacitive electrode arrays that detect adhesion and deformation, particularly on rough surfaces [ 15 ] . Vision-based tactile sensing has also been explored, using internal imaging to infer contact distribution and shear forces beneath the adhesive layer [ 16 ] . Together, these works demonstrate that adhesive interfaces can be instrumented using a variety of sensing modalities while preserving their mechanical functionality.

However, existing work primarily focuses on sensing and signal acquisition, with limited attention devoted to interpreting these measurements as high-level interaction states that can directly support autonomous robotic decision-making. In particular, real-time inference of the complete contact progression, from approach and initial contact to adhesive engagement and release, remains largely unexplored for space robotic applications. This work addresses this gap by investigating the feasibility of a real-time interaction-state recognition framework capable of translating continuous sensor measurements into discrete, physically meaningful states during online operation.

2026-10-21.title: ACE-Brain-0.6: Scaling Spatial Grounding for Physical Foundation Models
2026-10-21.authors: Yinhe Wang , Tao Tao , Zexin He , Shuang Luo , Wei Mao , Yao Mu , Feng Pan , Hanming Deng , Lewei Lu , Zhi Hou , Xingang Pan , Dahua Lin , Dacheng Tao , Xiaogang Wang
2026-10-21.abstract:
General-purpose multimodal models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, demonstrate broad capabilities in embodied manipulation.
Our analysis indicates that this generality is accompanied by strong spatial perception, as Astra can determine where to interact with task-relevant entities amid visual distractors.
Because spatial perception connects high-level reasoning to the physical scene, we investigate scaling visual grounding to strengthen the perceptual foundation of general embodied operation.
We develop a unified data pipeline that combines robot manipulation recordings with complementary visual data from diverse sources.
After automatically annotating the robot recordings, the pipeline converts the collected data into verifiable grounding supervision.
Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on approximately 1.5 million samples produced by this pipeline yields ACE-Brain-0.6.
The model outperforms GPT-6 Astra on four of seven public grounding benchmarks, with an overall average score of 75.41 compared with Astra’s 73.68.
Under a fixed Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuning setup, aggregate grounding performance improves steadily as successive data releases expand the training collection to cover a broader range of grounding scenarios.
These results show that scaling verifiable grounding supervision from diverse sources can strengthen the spatial perception of an open 9B model for general embodied operation.
2026-10-21.introduction:
General-purpose reasoning models are beginning to generalize across diverse embodied settings.
GPT-6 Astra [ 1 ] , in particular, demonstrates strong performance in embodied manipulation.
A closer examination of its behavior shows that this embodied competence is accompanied by strong spatial perception.
It can localize task-relevant interaction targets in cluttered scenes despite the presence of visually similar distractors.

This observation highlights the role of spatial perception in translating high-level reasoning into physical action.
Grounding provides this connection by linking natural-language descriptions to their visual referents in an image [ 2 , 3 ] .
Reliable grounding requires precise localization of all image regions that satisfy a description, with explicit recognition when no match exists [ 4 ] .
In embodied environments, clutter and occlusion make this correspondence particularly difficult to establish [ 5 ] .
A grounding error can therefore misdirect an agent’s actions even when its high-level reasoning is sound.

We therefore examine Astra’s spatial grounding capabilities in greater detail.
Our analysis in Section 3 illustrates its ability to handle diverse grounding queries, while also revealing localization errors in tasks with precise spatial requirements.
Using Astra as a reference, we ask whether an open 9B-parameter vision-language model can match or surpass Astra’s grounding performance by expanding the scale and coverage of grounding supervision, with the model architecture and training recipe held fixed.

To investigate this question, we develop a unified pipeline for constructing grounding supervision from existing open datasets.
The pipeline combines robot manipulation recordings from more than thirty dataset families with complementary visual data to broaden task coverage.
We automatically annotate the robot recordings to supply the object-level labels they generally lack.
All sources are then converted into question–answer supervision that is verifiable against the supporting annotations, with controls to reduce shortcuts between question wording and answer format.
This pipeline yields approximately 1.5 million training samples, which we use to fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B [ 6 ] for a single epoch, producing ACE-Brain-0.6.
Figure 1 provides an overview of our approach.

We evaluate ACE-Brain-0.6 on seven public grounding benchmarks.
The model outperforms the Qwen3.5-9B baseline on six benchmarks and remains behind on PixMo-Count.
It exceeds GPT-6 Astra on four benchmarks and achieves a slightly higher seven-benchmark average (75.41 versus 73.68), while remaining behind on PixMo-Count, RefSpatial, and PointArena.
These results suggest that a 9B open model trained with diverse, verifiable grounding supervision can match Astra’s aggregate performance on the evaluated benchmarks.

We further examine data scaling by fine-tuning from the same base checkpoint with a fixed training recipe for each data release.
Across releases that expand both sample count and supervision coverage, the seven-benchmark average increases approximately linearly with the logarithm of sample count over the evaluated range, slightly exceeding Astra’s average at about 1.5 million samples.
In a control experiment, adding samples only from existing sources improves this average by less than one point, suggesting that broader supervision coverage contributes to the observed gains.

Our contributions are threefold:

A data pipeline for grounding. We collect large-scale open-source robot, egocentric, object-centric, and spatial data, automatically annotate robot recordings, and convert these sources into verifiable question–answer supervision for target identification, complete instance coverage, and precise localization.

An empirical study of grounding-data scaling. Through a controlled series of training runs, we show that grounding performance improves steadily with data scale and that expanding the coverage of supervision contributes substantially more than increasing the volume of existing sources.

ACE-Brain-0.6. By scaling verifiable grounding data to approximately 1.5 million samples, we train a 9B model that exceeds GPT-6 Astra on four of seven grounding benchmarks and achieves a higher overall average.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Visual Grounding and Embodied Spatial Understanding

Visual grounding links language descriptions to image locations. Detector-based methods such as GLIP and Grounding DINO align visual and language features for phrase grounding and open-set localization [ 7 , 8 ] . Generative approaches represent spatial outputs as token sequences, from coordinate and class prediction in Pix2Seq [ 9 ] to multi-task visual prediction in Florence-2 [ 10 ] and detection, referring, and pointing in Rex-Omni [ 11 ] . Grounding also supports broader embodied understanding: PaLM-E integrates sensor inputs into language modeling [ 12 ] , Gemini Robotics-ER develops spatial understanding and embodied reasoning [ 13 ] , and RynnBrain and Embodied-R1.5 combine localization with embodied understanding and reasoning [ 14 , 15 ] . These works connect spatial prediction with increasingly broad model capabilities. We focus on grounding itself, keeping the base vision-language model and training recipe fixed to examine the effect of training data.

## 2.2 Grounding Data and Supervision

Grounding supervision comes from human annotation, automatic labeling, and geometric derivation. Molmo-and-PixMo collects language-conditioned point annotations, including complete instance sets and absent-target examples [ 16 ] . GrIT pairs caption phrases with predicted image regions [ 17 ] . SpatialVLM constructs spatial question–answer data using segmentation, depth, and object descriptions [ 18 ] , while RoboPoint derives instruction-point supervision from simulated scene geometry [ 19 ] . We build on these approaches by combining robot recordings, egocentric interactions, dense object and part annotations, and 3D scenes. Our pipeline automatically annotates robot recordings and converts these heterogeneous sources into a common question–answer format. Answers remain linked to supporting annotations, with checks for instance completeness, spatial constraints, and target absence. This training collection allows us to study how supervision scale and composition affect grounding performance.

2026-10-21.title: Embodied Playground: A Long-Horizon Agentic Robotics Benchmark for Physical, Strategic, and Spatial Reasoning
2026-10-21.authors: Feng Chen , Pei Zhou , Lixuan He , Yunchao Yao , Li Sun , Shenghua Gao , Mingyu Ding , Kaifeng Zhang , Kaichen Zhou , Yi Ma
2026-10-21.abstract:
Foundation models offer a promising basis for robotic agents, but long-horizon tasks require them to sustain coherent reasoning and reliable physical execution across interdependent stages. We introduce Embodied Playground , a benchmark for evaluating how foundation-model agents coordinate physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning throughout such tasks. Agents must track task progress, satisfy intermediate constraints, and revise their plans using execution feedback as earlier actions shape subsequent decisions. The playground comprises 410 task environments spanning basic manipulation, sequential puzzles, and multi-stage household activities, with variations in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. We curate EP-100 , a representative selection of 100 tasks across five suites and 16 task types, together with the EP-Easy and EP-Hard difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection. A shared protocol specifies observation and tool access, resource budgets, repeated trials, and independent checks of goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity. Embodied Playground provides a unified framework for studying whether foundation-model agents can sustain effective reasoning and action over extended task horizons.
The project website is available at Embodied Playground Website .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Foundation models have shown promising capabilities in robotic tasks, supported by their ability to interpret visual observations, reason about spatial relationships and physical interactions, and formulate strategies. [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] Existing robotics benchmarks largely emphasize the performance and generalization of control policies. [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] This leaves a complementary question: can a foundation-model agent sustain these capabilities over long-horizon robotic tasks, where actions must establish the conditions for later stages and execution errors can affect subsequent decisions? Addressing this question requires evaluating how an agent tracks task progress, satisfies intermediate constraints, and adapts its plan throughout physical execution.

We introduce Embodied Playground , a benchmark for studying long-horizon robotic problem solving by foundation-model agents. Tasks couple physical, strategic, and spatial reasoning across dependent stages: an agent must determine what to do next, execute it through the robot interface, and use the resulting observations to update its understanding of the remaining task. Earlier actions can change object configurations, consume resources, or constrain later choices, making sustained coordination between planning and execution central to successful completion. Given a task description, permitted observations, and a specified set of tools, the agent must ground its decisions in the observed scene and revise its plan using execution feedback. Success requires achieving the final goal while respecting task rules and physical constraints throughout the episode.

Embodied Playground comprises 410 robotic task environments, ranging from basic object manipulation to long-horizon planning and dexterous coordination. These tasks vary in planning depth, geometric constraints, and physical execution demands. Tower of Hanoi requires executing legal move sequences while preserving valid intermediate configurations; cube puzzles require keeping track of puzzle states and object orientations through successive physical turns; and Kongming locks couple assembly or disassembly order with geometric feasibility and contact-rich manipulation. Multi-stage household tasks combine ordered interactions with object-placement and final-scene requirements. Launcher tasks connect trajectory prediction and causal effects with finite ammunition and, in selected scenes, target-order constraints. Shorter manipulation, precision, and dynamics tasks complement these extended sequences by probing constituent capabilities across multiple robot embodiments.

To facilitate evaluation, we curate EP-100 , a representative selection of 100 tasks organized into five subsets: Launch , Tower , Lock , Cube , and Home . Together, these subsets cover 16 task types and provide focused evaluations alongside the full playground. EP-100 is divided into EP-Easy and EP-Hard by ranking the tasks of each type according to their workload, and EP-20 offers a compact selection that spans both splits. All tasks follow a common interaction interface and evaluation protocol, with specified observation and tool access, execution budgets, repeated trials, and task-specific physical success criteria.

Our contributions are threefold:

An agent-centered perspective on long-horizon robotic problem solving. We evaluate a foundation-model agent’s ability to sustain coordinated perception, reasoning, tool use, and action across interdependent task stages, using execution feedback to track progress, revise plans, and satisfy task constraints throughout an episode.

A diverse playground spanning task horizons and execution demands. We introduce 410 robotic task environments spanning basic manipulation and multi-stage problem solving, with variations in planning depth, geometry, and physical execution requirements. EP-100 provides a representative selection across five suites and 16 task types, complemented by two difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection.

An episode-level protocol for evaluating completion and validity. We specify observation and tool-access levels, resource budgets, and repeated-trial conditions, with independent checks of final goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity over the executed trajectory.

1. An agent-centered perspective on long-horizon robotic problem solving. We evaluate a foundation-model agent’s ability to sustain coordinated perception, reasoning, tool use, and action across interdependent task stages, using execution feedback to track progress, revise plans, and satisfy task constraints throughout an episode.

2. A diverse playground spanning task horizons and execution demands. We introduce 410 robotic task environments spanning basic manipulation and multi-stage problem solving, with variations in planning depth, geometry, and physical execution requirements. EP-100 provides a representative selection across five suites and 16 task types, complemented by two difficulty splits and the compact EP-20 selection.

3. An episode-level protocol for evaluating completion and validity. We specify observation and tool-access levels, resource budgets, and repeated-trial conditions, with independent checks of final goal completion, task-rule compliance, and physical validity over the executed trajectory.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Foundation-model agents and harnesses for Robotics.

Early systems such as SayCan, Code as Policies, and ProgPrompt connected language-model reasoning
to robot action through skill selection or executable
programs [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] .
Inner Monologue and subsequent systems such as REFLECT and Statler used execution feedback,
failure explanations, or maintained world-state estimates to inform later
actions [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
Spatial grounding developed through representations such as scene graphs, value maps, and
keypoint constraints [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] .
Systems developed in 2024–2025, such as RoboScript, ROS-LLM, and RAI, connected model-generated
decisions to robot software and execution services [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] .
Hi Robot, Agentic Robot, and Code-as-Monitor illustrate related directions in hierarchical action
selection, execution coordination, and failure monitoring [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] .
The interface between reasoning and execution has become an explicit design focus, exemplified by
Robot Context Protocol and later visual, semantic, and native-software interfaces in VIA,
Show-Harness, and OpenRUA [ 24 , 25 , 26 , 27 ] .
Recent tool-based harnesses also examine perception support, context management, and outcome
verification [ 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 , 33 ] .
Alongside these interface designs, systems such as RoboHarness, RATs, ASPIRE, and CarryOn use memory
or reusable skills to adapt across interactions [ 34 , 35 , 36 , 37 ] .
We offer a common basis for assessing these diverse agent designs through their physical outcomes. Its protocol makes differences in assistance and resource use explicit, supporting fair comparisons of task completion, consistency, and efficiency.

## 2.2 Simulation infrastructure and robotic policy benchmarks.

Simulation platforms and task benchmarks serve complementary roles in robotic policy evaluation.
Early simulators such as Gazebo and MuJoCo, followed by platforms such as PyBullet, SAPIEN, and
Isaac Gym, established infrastructure for robotic
experiments [ 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 , 42 ] .
Building on simulator backends, frameworks such as robosuite and ORBIT package environments and
robot-learning workflows, with more recent examples including Isaac Lab, MuJoCo Playground, and
ManiSkill3 [ 43 , 44 , 45 , 46 , 47 ] .
Task benchmarks specify the learning problems and evaluation protocols.
Early benchmarks such as Meta-World examine multi-task and meta-reinforcement learning, while
RLBench provides manipulation tasks with demonstrations [ 48 , 49 ] .
Subsequent suites study generalizable manipulation, language-conditioned action sequences, and
lifelong transfer, as illustrated by ManiSkill, CALVIN, ManiSkill2, and
LIBERO [ 50 , 51 , 52 , 53 ] .
Household activities and longer manipulation tasks feature in benchmarks such as BEHAVIOR-1K,
RoboCasa, VLABench, and RoboCasa365 [ 54 , 55 , 56 , 57 ] .
Recent evaluation also examines robustness to variation, for example in Colosseum, RoboTwin 2.0,
LIBERO-Plus, RoboLab, and Colosseum V2 [ 58 , 59 , 60 , 61 , 62 ] .
SIMPLER and RoboDojo connect policy evaluation in simulation with real-robot
performance [ 63 , 64 ] .
Embodied Playground adopts this foundation and organizes its evaluation around a foundation-model agent’s problem-solving episode. Its combination of abstract challenges and household tasks makes reasoning demands central to evaluation while preserving the need for successful physical execution.

## 2.3 Embodied-agent benchmarks.

Embodied-agent benchmarks examine reasoning through task performance under specified observation
and action interfaces.
Earlier examples examined physical puzzles in PHYRE and language-guided robot planning in
LoHoRavens and RoboEval [ 65 , 66 , 67 ] .
Benchmarks such as LoTa-Bench and Embodied Agent Interface subsequently evaluated task planning and
its component capabilities [ 68 , 69 ] .
In 2025, EmbodiedEval and EmbodiedBench evaluated multimodal agents in simulated tasks, while PARTNR
examined collaborative household planning [ 70 , 71 , 72 ] .
Physical reasoning benchmarks such as PhyBlock and DeepPHY, followed by COIN and KinDER, probe
assembly planning, physical prediction, causal interaction, and kinematic or dynamic
constraints [ 73 , 74 , 75 , 76 ] .
Recent benchmarks examine the interaction interface itself: CaP-X and Embodied Skill Bench vary
control abstractions and supplied capabilities, while VABench studies active perception and metric
control [ 77 , 78 , 79 ] .
CodeActionBench and LIBERO-Agent evaluate direct robot interaction, while Embodied Agent Arena
connects component capabilities to task completion [ 80 , 81 , 82 ] .
Longer execution and broader task coverage feature in benchmarks such as EmbodiedSWE and
RobotWorld [ 83 , 84 ] .
LADDER varies the number of subgoals within the same environment [ 85 ] .
SCOPER studies recovery under controlled skill failures, while SEAR isolates the contribution of
retained experience under controlled interaction budgets [ 86 , 87 ] .
Physical-robot evaluations also appear in Words to World and the AA-Robotics research
preview [ 88 , 89 ] .
Our structured task coverage supports interpretable comparisons across reasoning demands and robot embodiments. It allows performance to be examined as task demands increase, helping identify strengths and limitations that a single aggregate score may obscure.

2026-10-21.title: Replan for Error Recovery: Training Embodied VLMs through Verifiable Interaction with Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO
2026-10-21.authors: Zhuoran Wang , Keqing Fan , Yang Li , Jinbo Su , Ke Wang , Sijia Luo , Yuanzheng Tan , Junken Peng , Jing Zhang
2026-10-21.abstract:
Embodied VLMs can execute increasingly complex manipulation tasks, yet execution errors can leave the environment in states that require replanning for recovery.
Existing recovery methods either rely on inference-time mechanisms with fixed policies or learn from failure examples and reference corrections rather than verified action outcomes.
To enable recovery learning through verifiable interaction, we introduce the Embodied Replanning for Recovery Environment (ERR-Env), which provides feedback on task progress and execution errors.
We further construct ERR-Bench, a benchmark with held-out tasks spanning nominal, intermediate, and error states for evaluating recovery capability and execution reliability.
We then propose Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO (AGT-GSPO), an online reinforcement learning method combining turn-level rewards for task progress and error states with action-grouped advantage estimation, and use it to train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM.
Evaluation on ERR-Bench reveals a mismatch between task progress and execution reliability across diverse VLMs. AGT-GSPO improves ERR-VLM by 10.25 percentage points in Strict Success Rate for error-free completion and 22.95 percentage points in Recovery Rate, while ablations and zero-shot transfer further validate the effectiveness of our method.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as high-level
decision makers for embodied agents, enabling multi-step manipulation through visual observations, language goals, and semantic action interfaces ( Driess et al., 2023 ; Tan et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) .
During execution, errors, limited visibility, or unexpected scene conditions can leave the task in a state for which the original plan is no longer appropriate.
Reliable task completion therefore requires the model to recognize these deviations and replan from the resulting state to recover and continue execution.

To support recovery from execution errors, inference-time approaches equip VLMs with prompting strategies, external monitors, or specialized mechanisms to detect errors and trigger replanning ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Ahmad et al., 2025 ) .
But with the policy fixed, recovery is limited to existing model capabilities.
Recovery-oriented post-training instead uses error cases and reference corrections to improve error recognition and corrective action selection ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Pacaud et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) .
However, reference-based supervision does not optimize the policy against verified outcomes of recovery actions, leaving a gap between imitating corrections and resolving execution errors.
This motivates training through environment interaction, where action outcomes are verified for error correction and task progress to improve recovery decisions.

In this paper, we aim to train embodied VLMs to recover from execution errors through verifiable interaction and evaluate their recovery capability and execution reliability. Interaction-based recovery learning requires explicit feedback on errors and task progress, which existing embodied benchmarks typically lack ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) .
To address this gap, we develop the E mbodied R eplanning for R ecovery Environment (ERR-Env), an executable and verifiable interaction environment built on RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025c ) .
ERR-Env uses task-specific checkers to verify task progress, completion, execution errors, and visibility, supporting recovery-oriented data generation, online reinforcement learning, and evaluation.
To assess recovery capability and execution reliability beyond task progress alone, we construct ERR-Bench based on ERR-Env, a controlled benchmark with held-out tasks spanning nominal, intermediate, and error states.

To learn recovery from verifiable interaction in ERR-Env, verified action outcomes need to be translated into signals that reinforce effective corrections and discourage error-inducing actions.
However, a trajectory-level signal cannot assign distinct feedback to error-inducing and corrective actions.
Therefore, we propose Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO (AGT-GSPO), an online reinforcement learning method that uses turn-level rewards capturing task progress and error states after each executed action.
AGT-GSPO further estimates advantages within action groups, avoiding comparisons across action types.
Using AGT-GSPO, we train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM that learns to recognize execution errors and select corrective actions through replanning.

Evaluation of diverse VLMs on ERR-Bench shows that high task progress does not guarantee reliable execution. Against this backdrop, training ERR-VLM with AGT-GSPO improves both task completion and recovery, raising Strict Success Rate for error-free task completion by 10.25 percentage points and Recovery Rate by 22.95 percentage points over its supervised initialization. Ablations and zero-shot transfer to external simulators and a physical robot further validate our approach.

In summary, our principal contributions comprise:

We introduce ERR-Env, an executable and verifiable interaction environment with feedback on task progress and execution errors, supporting recovery data generation, online RL, and evaluation. We further construct ERR-Bench to evaluate recovery capability and execution reliability.

We propose AGT-GSPO, an online RL method that learns from verifiable interaction by combining turn-level rewards for task progress and error states with action-grouped advantage estimation. Using AGT-GSPO, we train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM for error recovery.

Evaluation on ERR-Bench across diverse VLMs reveals a clear mismatch between task progress and reliable execution, while ERR-VLM, trained with AGT-GSPO, substantially improves both recovery capability and execution reliability.

1. We introduce ERR-Env, an executable and verifiable interaction environment with feedback on task progress and execution errors, supporting recovery data generation, online RL, and evaluation. We further construct ERR-Bench to evaluate recovery capability and execution reliability.

2. We propose AGT-GSPO, an online RL method that learns from verifiable interaction by combining turn-level rewards for task progress and error states with action-grouped advantage estimation. Using AGT-GSPO, we train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM for error recovery.

3. Evaluation on ERR-Bench across diverse VLMs reveals a clear mismatch between task progress and reliable execution, while ERR-VLM, trained with AGT-GSPO, substantially improves both recovery capability and execution reliability.

# 2 Related Work

Interaction Environments and Benchmarks. Existing embodied environments and benchmarks support long-horizon interaction and evaluation ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ; Padmakumar et al., 2022 ; Srivastava et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2025c ) , but largely focus on task completion and general capabilities rather than explicit verification of execution errors and recovery progress. Failure-aware benchmarks further evaluate error detection and correction ( Song et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026a ) , yet lack verifiable interaction feedback for recovery learning and controlled evaluation. In contrast, ERR-Env provides explicit error and progress feedback for recovery learning, while ERR-Bench evaluates recovery capability and execution reliability under controlled error states.

Error Recognition and Recovery. Inference-time methods use prompting, external monitors, or dedicated mechanisms to detect errors and trigger replanning ( Chen et al., 2025b ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Ahmad et al., 2025 ) , but leave the policy fixed, limiting recovery to existing model capabilities. Training-based methods improve error awareness through error detection, reasoning, and verification ( Duan et al., 2025 ; Pacaud et al., 2026 ) , but do not directly optimize corrective actions. More recent work supervises error correction and recovery planning ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) , but mainly relies on constructed error cases and reference corrections rather than verified action outcomes. We instead learn recovery through executable interaction with error and progress feedback.

Online RL for Multi-turn Interaction. For general LLM agents, GRPO and GSPO use group-relative objectives for policy optimization ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) , while GiGPO extends this paradigm to multi-turn interaction with finer-grained credit assignment at both the episode and interaction-step levels ( Feng et al., 2025 ) . In embodied settings, prior work applies offline GRPO without environment interaction ( Wu et al., 2025 ) , while online methods learn from grouped trajectories with completion-level rewards ( Fei et al., 2025 ) , lacking fine-grained turn-level information. VAGEN and ERA further introduce online turn-level rewards with GAE-based credit assignment ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Chen et al., 2025a ) , but rely on value-function estimation. In contrast, we combine verifiable turn-level error and progress feedback with group-relative advantage estimation within action groups for critic-free recovery optimization.

2026-10-21.title: DexGraspFlow: Topology-Aware SE(3) Flow Matching for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasp Generation
2026-10-21.authors: Bin Zhou , Boyu Ma , Xinyu Zhou , Jiahua Dong , Chuhao Zhou , Yizhou Liu , Hao Wan , Jianfei Yang
2026-10-21.abstract: Differences in hand geometry, joint parameterization, and kinematic topology pose challenges for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation. However, spatial relations among links alone are insufficient to fully capture the hand’s kinematic topology. We propose DexGraspFlow, a conditional link-level SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) flow-matching framework integrating geometric relations and kinematic topology. The framework encodes local object geometry, link geometry, and current poses. A dual-stream DiT models link–link coordination and link–object interaction, while attention biases derived from kinematic-tree distances provide explicit structural information for modeling evolving geometric interactions. The model jointly learns translational and rotational velocity fields, integrates them to generate link poses, and recovers joint configurations through inverse kinematics. Additionally, inference-time palm-orientation guidance enables controllable grasp generation without retraining. Across three robotic hands and 30 object–hand pairs, DexGraspFlow achieves a 95.33% average simulation success rate, with an average generation latency, including inverse kinematics, approximately 49% lower than that of a state-of-the-art baseline. Further experiments demonstrate zero-shot adaptability to seven finger-removal variants and palm-orientation control. A model trained on demonstrations for the deployed hand achieves a 91% success rate over 100 real-robot grasping trials, supporting the framework’s applicability to physical grasp execution.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Dexterous hands are robotic end-effectors that interact directly with the physical world, performing the last centimeter of robotic manipulation. Through coordinated finger motions, they enable versatile grasping and precise manipulation, supporting the practical deployment of embodied intelligence ( Dong et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Reliable dexterous grasping requires jointly accounting for object geometry, hand–object interactions, and kinematic constraints ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . Differences in link geometry and kinematic topology across hands further complicate cross-embodiment grasp generation. Embodiment-specific joint representations differ in dimensionality and physical meaning, making it difficult to learn a unified model directly from grasp demonstrations collected across different hands ( Li et al., 2023 ) . Training a separate model for each hand also increases training and deployment costs. These challenges motivate cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation methods that share grasping knowledge while accommodating differences in hand morphology and kinematics, facilitating the reuse of grasping capabilities across robotic platforms.

Existing approaches address cross-embodiment grasp synthesis through optimization or shared interaction representations. Optimization-based methods require computationally intensive iterative search for each grasp instance ( Liu et al., 2021 ) , while contact- and distance-based formulations necessitate auxiliary matching or complex reconstruction to recover executable configurations ( Li et al., 2023 ; Wei et al., 2025 ) . Recently, 𝒯 ⁡ ( ℛ , 𝒪 ) \mathcal{T}(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O}) Grasp (TRO-Grasp) introduced a transformation-graph diffusion model via object-centric link poses and relative spatial relations without requiring a shared joint parameterization ( Fei et al., 2026 ) . However, relying solely on continuous spatial relations ignores kinematic topology: spatially adjacent links across diverse hands may belong to distant topological branches with fundamentally different kinematic meanings. GraspGraphNet ( Lee et al., 2026 ) incorporates kinematic structure through local message passing, but propagating information between distant links along the kinematic tree requires multiple graph hops. Beyond unconditioned synthesis, practical deployment also requires efficient control over grasp approach orientations while maintaining grasp stability across different hand embodiments.

To this end, we propose DexGraspFlow, a cross-embodiment dexterous grasp synthesis framework that unifies continuous SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) flow matching with URDF-derived kinematic topology (Fig. 1 ). To resolve structural ambiguities across heterogeneous hands, DexGraspFlow augments dynamic link states and spatial relations with kinematic-tree shortest-path distances, providing complementary geometric and structural information that explicitly separates spatial arrangement from kinematic connectivity. Grasp synthesis is formulated as link-level flow matching with separate translational reference paths in ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} and geodesic rotational reference paths on SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Chen and Lipman, 2024 ) . This formulation preserves valid link orientations and supports inference-time palm-orientation guidance through tangent-space velocity corrections without retraining. A geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) predicts these coupled velocity fields, followed by batched inverse kinematics ( Kim et al., 2025 ) to recover executable joint configurations.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work on cross-embodiment grasp representations and geometric generative models. Section 3 presents the grasp representation and geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT architecture of DexGraspFlow. Section 4 evaluates DexGraspFlow through grasp generation on unseen objects, zero-shot generation on finger-removal variants, and palm-orientation-conditioned generation, along with ablation studies and real-robot experiments. Section 5 concludes the study and discusses the limitations of the proposed framework and directions for future research.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We address the core discrepancy that geometric spatial relations do not reflect kinematic topological connectivity across diverse embodiments, proposing a topology-aware link representation that couples dynamic spatial interactions with kinematic-tree distances to preserve structural coordination under hand topology changes.

We formulate grasp synthesis via link-level SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) flow matching that couples Euclidean translation with Riemannian rotation on SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) , and design a geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT, demonstrating superior grasp success with substantially reduced generation latency compared to diffusion baselines in our empirical evaluations.

We propose a training-free directional grasp guidance formulation. By injecting geodesic velocity corrections directly into the tangent space of the continuous flow during inference, DexGraspFlow achieves high-precision, user-specified palm-orientation steering without requiring conditional retraining or auxiliary classifiers.

We conduct extensive empirical evaluations across multi-embodiment simulations, zero-shot generalization to seven finger-removal variants, and 100 real-robot physical trials (91% success rate), demonstrating the superior adaptability and physical viability of DexGraspFlow.

2. We formulate grasp synthesis via link-level SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) flow matching that couples Euclidean translation with Riemannian rotation on SO ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SO}(3) , and design a geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT, demonstrating superior grasp success with substantially reduced generation latency compared to diffusion baselines in our empirical evaluations.

3. We propose a training-free directional grasp guidance formulation. By injecting geodesic velocity corrections directly into the tangent space of the continuous flow during inference, DexGraspFlow achieves high-precision, user-specified palm-orientation steering without requiring conditional retraining or auxiliary classifiers.

4. We conduct extensive empirical evaluations across multi-embodiment simulations, zero-shot generalization to seven finger-removal variants, and 100 real-robot physical trials (91% success rate), demonstrating the superior adaptability and physical viability of DexGraspFlow.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related work

## 2.1 Cross-embodiment grasp representations

GraspIt! ( Miller and Allen, 2004 ) supports optimization-based grasp planning, while DFC ( Liu et al., 2021 ) and DexGraspNet ( Wang et al., 2023 ) employ iterative optimization for grasp synthesis and dataset construction, incurring per-instance computational costs. FFHNet ( Mayer et al., 2022 ) and UniDexGrasp ( Xu et al., 2023 ) represent grasp configurations through global hand poses and joint coordinates, while UniDexGrasp++ ( Wan et al., 2023 ) learns grasping policies for a hand-specific state and action space. However, differences in joint dimensionality and semantics complicate sharing these configurations across embodiments, motivating hand–object interaction representations that do not require a common joint parameterization.

GenDexGrasp ( Li et al., 2023 ) uses hand-agnostic contact maps and recovers hand configurations through contact matching and optimization. 𝒟 ⁡ ( ℛ , 𝒪 ) \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{R},\mathcal{O}) Grasp (DRO-Grasp) ( Wei et al., 2025 ) predicts robot–object point-to-point distances using a configuration-invariant pretrained hand encoder, followed by link-pose reconstruction and joint-configuration recovery. Its dense pairwise representation incurs memory overhead, while encoder pretraining adds a separate training stage. TRO-Grasp ( Fei et al., 2026 ) models hands via relative spatial transformations on fully connected link–object and link–link edges. However, spatial link proximity alone is insufficient across diverse embodiments, as spatially adjacent links can belong to disparate topological branches that convey fundamentally different kinematic semantics. Alternatively, GraspGraphNet ( Lee et al., 2026 ) encodes articulated hand states using a kinematic-tree MPNN and incorporates object information through cross-attention and dynamic interaction edges. Within its kinematic-tree encoder, information exchange between distant links relies on successive local message-passing steps. DexGraspFlow instead uses link–link self-attention to directly model interactions between all valid link pairs, with kinematic-tree distance biases providing structural information alongside state-dependent geometric relations. This design combines direct long-range link interaction with explicit kinematic proximity encoding.

## 2.2 Geometric generative models

Generative grasp synthesis has been explored through adversarial and diffusion models ( Feng et al., 2024 ; Weng et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) , drawing on broader denoising and score-based formulations ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ) . Flow-based approaches learn continuous transport dynamics in Euclidean and non-Euclidean spaces ( Lipman et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2023 ; Chen and Lipman, 2024 ) . Complementary advances in equivariant geometric modeling ( Fuchs et al., 2020 ; Satorras et al., 2021 ) , diffusion-based grasp and motion optimization ( Urain et al., 2023 ) , and Transformer generative architectures ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) provide foundations for geometry-aware generation.

For cross-embodiment grasping, these formulations differ in their conditioning requirements and the computational path to executable grasps. DRO-Grasp ( Wei et al., 2025 ) combines CVAE latent variables with features of an initial hand configuration and the object to predict grasp distances. Although latent sampling enables diversity, generation remains conditioned on the initial hand state and requires subsequent pose reconstruction. TRO-Grasp ( Fei et al., 2026 ) instead samples link poses from noise through graph diffusion in Lie-algebra coordinates. Its denoiser processes node and edge features through multiple graph layers, with repeated evaluations accumulating sampling costs. DexGraspFlow adopts link-level SE ⁡ ( 3 ) \mathrm{SE}(3) flow matching, jointly learning translational and rotational velocities from Euclidean and geodesic reference paths, respectively. Geometric interactions and kinematic topology condition the velocity field within a unified formulation supporting both unconditioned and condition-guided grasp generation. Our experiments demonstrate lower generation latency than DRO-Grasp and TRO-Grasp while maintaining competitive grasp success.

2026-10-21.title: Joints, Camera, Action! Co-Generating 3D Motion and Video for Arbitrary Rigs
2026-10-21.authors: Noam Rotstein , Yoad Tewel , Chen Tessler , Haggai Maron , Gal Chechik , Or Litany , Yoni Kasten , Yuval Atzmon
2026-10-21.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Graphics (cs.GR); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-21.abstract:
Video generation models can now depict remarkably realistic motion.
Yet it is unclear how to use this motion beyond pixels: to animate a specific 3D asset and replay the animation in its 3D scene.
For instance, a video model can show a monkey jumping over a crossbar, but it cannot return that jump as replayable 3D motion placed in the 3D scene.
Here we present a model that directly co-generates the video and 3D motion for any supplied rig, along with a camera that registers this motion to the scene. Prior video–motion models either handle only human skeletons, often adding billions of parameters, or triangulate 3D motion from generated 2D pose maps. We instead keep 3D motion in a separate model that supports arbitrary skeletons, and connect it to a pretrained video model through a small set of cross-attention layers. This separation lets the motion model first learn how skeletons move from motion-only data, which is easier to obtain and augment than paired video. Additionally, our model learns to locate each joint in the video frames, which lets us recover the camera and place the 3D motion in the scene. To train across many skeletons, we use a generative video editor to place animated 3D assets in scenes suited to their actions, curating the edits so their known motion remains valid. Together with human and robot video, this yields nearly 200K training pairs. Our evaluations demonstrate that our model animates diverse rigs from text more faithfully than video-first pipelines, and its motion responds to the surrounding scene. It also turns video into rig motion, rig motion into video, and enables keyframe-based control of the 3D motion.
Videos and additional results are available on our project page .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Video generation models capture complex real-world dynamics, making them promising world models for animation, robotics, and synthetic data generation. Yet they produce only pixels, so their motion cannot directly drive a 3D asset or robot. Imagine placing a monkey asset in front of a crossbar in a 3D scene, asking a video model to make it jump over, and replaying the resulting jump on the monkey’s rig inside that scene. Current video models deliver only the first step: a convincing video of the jump, with no 3D motion for the rig and no way to place that motion in the scene.

Replaying a generated motion on an arbitrary rig in a 3D scene requires two things: 3D motion that matches the video and a camera transformation that registers that motion to the generated scene. One natural approach is to recover the motion from a generated video post hoc ( Sabathier et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2025 ) , but lifting motion from pixels may introduce errors that can make the animation drift from the video. Alternatively, generating video and motion together aims to avoid this post-hoc step, yet no joint model animates an arbitrary rig directly in 3D, and none registers its motion to the scene it generates. Existing ones either handle only human skeletons ( Pang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) , or triangulate 3D motion from 2D pose maps learned from multi-view videos ( Huang et al., 2025 ) .

In this work, we present Joints, Camera, Action! ( JCA ), a model that co-generates a video, motion for any supplied 3D rig, and a camera that places the 3D motion in the generated scene. To support arbitrary rigs, a dedicated motion model treats a rig skeleton as a graph, with joints as nodes and bones as edges. We pretrain it on motion alone, including motions retargeted to randomized skeletons. We then connect it to a pretrained video model through a few cross-attention layers, keeping the added parameters small. Zero-initializing these layers preserves the behavior of both pretrained models at the start of coupled training.

Through these layers, video and motion shape each other’s generation throughout denoising; two components strengthen this interaction and place the motion in the scene. First, we introduce a novel bridge guidance mechanism. At inference, we contrast predictions made with the connections enabled and disabled, then amplify the change caused by their interaction. Co-generating the motion with the video, however, does not determine where that motion lies in the depicted scene. Second, to solve this registration problem, we introduce learned localization of the rig’s joints: the model predicts where every generated 3D joint appears in the image. These 2D locations and the generated 3D positions provide correspondences from which we fit a camera that registers the motion to the generated scene.

Training the model poses a challenge: no corpus pairs natural video with 3D motion across many rigs. We start from human video, which offers rich motion and rich backgrounds, but only a single skeleton. To cover many rigs, we turn to animated 3D assets ( Deitke et al., 2023b ; Deitke et al., 2023a ) , which offer diverse rigs and precise labels, but simple actions and plain renders. Rather than build a 3D scene for every asset, a generative video editor ( Liu et al., 2026 ) places our animated-asset renders in scenes suited to their actions. Editing may move the subject or camera, invalidating 3D labels; we verify results and regenerate failures. Together, the two sources combine the rich motion and scenes of human video with the rig diversity of assets. With additional robot video, our corpus reaches 200K video–motion pairs in total.

We evaluate the model on text-driven animation of diverse rigs and demonstrate motion that responds to the surrounding scene ( fig. 1 ). The same model can recover motion for a supplied rig from video or generate video from prescribed rig motion. From a few reference image keyframes, it generates a complete 3D rig trajectory and matching video, providing image-based control over 3D motion.

Our contributions are: (1) JCA , the first model to directly co-generate video and 3D joint motion for arbitrary rigs, with motion that responds to the surrounding scene and can be controlled by image keyframes; the same model also generates either modality from the other; (2) a parameter-efficient architecture that represents arbitrary rigs as graphs, with bridge guidance amplifying video–motion agreement; (3) learned scene registration that recovers the camera needed to replay generated 3D motion in the scene; and (4) a data pipeline that places labeled asset animations in scenes suited to their actions and, together with human and robot video, yields 200K video–motion pairs spanning diverse rigs.

# 2 Related Work

Joint Video and Motion Generation. Video generators capture rich appearance and motion and have shown promise across diverse tasks ( Rotstein et al., 2025 ; Wiedemer et al., 2025 ; Atzmon et al., 2025 ) .
However, they output pixels rather than the underlying 3D motion.
UniMo ( Pang et al., 2025 ) , EchoMotion ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and CoMoVi ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) jointly model video and human motion; SViMo ( Dang et al., 2025 ) and VAG ( Lang et al., 2026 ) cover hand–object interactions and robot actions.
UniMo uses a shared autoregressive backbone, whereas EchoMotion and CoMoVi introduce billion-scale motion branches derived from video backbones.
EchoMotion’s joint attention assigns motion tokens spatial offsets relative to the video grid.
AnimaX ( Huang et al., 2025 ) handles arbitrary skeletons by generating RGB and 2D pose maps from four fixed views, then recovers 3D motion through triangulation and inverse kinematics. This indirect route also limits training to multi-view videos, which rich scenes rarely have.
We couple separately pretrained video and text-to-rig-motion networks through cross-attention, avoiding joint self-attention and spatial offsets.
Our model directly generates video and 3D joint parameters for a supplied rig, without mesh input or multi-view triangulation, optionally conditioned on a first image.

Animating Diverse Skeletons and Meshes. AnyTop ( Gat et al., 2025 ) learns a shared motion prior across diverse skeletons; RigMo ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) learns rigs and motion from deforming meshes without predefined skeletons. AnimateAnyMesh ( Wu et al., 2025 ) maps mesh and text to vertex trajectories.
Video priors inform ViPS’s feed-forward pose sampling ( Chen et al., 2026 ) and per-instance animation optimization by AKD ( Li et al., 2025 ) , Puppeteer ( Song et al., 2025 ) , and skeleton-free CHORD ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) ; AKD reports about 25 hours per asset. AnimaSpark ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) avoids such optimization through video generation, tracking, and planar lifting. ActionMesh ( Sabathier et al., 2026 ) and STAC ( Samuel et al., 2026 ) output mesh deformations and Bekor et al. (2025) transfers motion across object categories without a rig by distilling video diffusion priors into dynamic Gaussians.
Our model jointly generates motion and video through coupled denoising, without tracking or fitting the motion to video.

Conditional Generation and Guidance. Structural and motion cues can guide visual generation:
ControlNet ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) conditions image synthesis on structural input signals, Lay-A-Scene ( Rahamim et al., 2024 ) on 3D objects, MeshToken ( Liang et al., 2026 ) conditions video on 3D human mesh motion, LooseControlVideo ( Bhat et al., 2026 ) uses coarse oriented 3D boxes, and training-free Time-to-Move ( Singer et al., 2026 ) uses crude reference animations under a dual-clock denoising schedule.
Motion inpainting and constrained generation ( Tessler et al., 2024 ; Rempe et al., 2026 ) complete partial motion specifications.
EchoMotion ( Yang et al., 2026 ) supports video-to-motion and motion-to-video generation for humans.
Our training combines joint denoising with conditioning on a noise-free modality, enabling both conditional directions for arbitrary rigs through our specialized rig encoder and denoiser.
To improve generation at inference, latent optimization corrects spatial relations ( Yiflach et al., 2026 ) , VideoJAM ( Chefer et al., 2025 ) contrasts predictions with and without the jointly generated optical-flow input, and Spatiotemporal Skip Guidance ( Hyung et al., 2025 ) contrasts predictions with and without selected spatiotemporal layers.
Our bridge guidance strengthens video–motion consistency by contrasting predictions with video–motion cross-attention enabled and disabled.

Motion Recovery. While human-specific methods recover body ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2024 ) and hand motion ( Yu et al., 2025b ) from video, MoCapAnything V2 ( Gong et al., 2026 ) and TopoCap ( Pu et al., 2026 ) support arbitrary skeletons without per-instance optimization.
Our model also supports this video-to-motion task within its joint generative framework.

Training Data Pipeline. Joint video–motion methods ( Pang et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) train on human videos paired with estimated motion, using a fixed skeletal representation.
VideoMDM ( Mann et al., 2026 ) avoids 3D annotation through 2D projection supervision, but also assumes a fixed skeleton.
Animated asset datasets such as AnimaX’s ( Huang et al., 2025 ) provide motion for diverse skeletons, but their renders have a white background.
Generative models have enabled the construction of training pairs for image and video editing ( Wasserman et al., 2025 ; Yu et al., 2025a ) , and video editors can change a video’s scene while preserving its structure ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Tewel et al., 2026 ) . We use Bernini to place rendered animations of diverse rigs in suitable scenes while retaining their known 3D motion as supervision.

2026-10-21.title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators
2026-10-21.authors: Michael Chen , Hong Chul Nam , Xi Deng , Anima Anandkumar
2026-10-21.abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN) , a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt) , to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95–100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D ( λ = 4 \lambda=4 ), PUN achieves 10.7–60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29–32.15 × \times faster.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Planning ( Latombe, 1991 ) is one of the most fundamental problems in robotics. Given a robot’s configuration space ( LaValle, 2006 ) , planning computes a path from the current configuration to a goal that is optimal under a given cost function. Real robots do not execute a commanded motion exactly ( Thrun, 2002 ) . These errors accumulate along a motion, so a route planned with a few centimetres of clearance can be executed into a wall. Sampling-based planners such as PRM ( Kavraki et al., 1996 ) and RRT ( LaValle and Kuffner, 2001 ) , and graph search such as A ⋆ ( Hart et al., 1968 ) , plan for a nominal system that executes commands exactly and leave the noise to a tracking controller. Sampling-based methods such as MPPI ( Williams et al., 2017a ) and PI 2 -CMA ( Stulp and Sigaud, 2012 ) optimize control sequences or policy parameters using sampled trajectory costs. Optimal feedback under execution noise can be derived from a value function, which gives the minimum expected cost of reaching the goal from each configuration and satisfies the nonlinear Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation ( Fleming and Soner, 2006 ) . Solving this equation on a grid scales exponentially with the dimension of the configuration space ( Bellman, 1957 ; Han et al., 2018 ) .

While the problem can be converted into a linear screened Poisson equation ( Theodorou et al., 2010 ) under control–noise matching (Assumption 1 ), a central difficulty in Poisson-based planning is specifying boundary conditions that produce a reliable value field across varying geometries.

Conventional mesh-based numerical methods can solve the screened Poisson equation efficiently in two and three dimensions. However, a robot with d d degrees of freedom (DoF) induces a d d -dimensional configuration space, making volumetric discretizations and numerical PDE solution increasingly expensive. Planning must also accommodate complex and previously unseen obstacle geometries, for which constructing a new mesh and solving the PDE from scratch can be costly. Mesh-free Monte Carlo methods ( Muller, 1956 ; Sawhney and Crane, 2020 ; Sawhney et al., 2023 ; Jambon et al., 2026 ) support PDE solution on complex geometries, motivating their use for planning in higher-dimensional configuration spaces.

Among these, Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) ( Muller, 1956 ) estimates the solution at a point by jumping repeatedly to a uniformly sampled point on the largest ball fitting in free space, until it reaches a boundary of known value, which requires every reachable boundary to be Dirichlet. Walk-on-Stars (WoSt) ( Sawhney et al., 2023 ) accommodates reflecting obstacles by replacing that ball with a star-shaped region that may contain part of the obstacle boundary, keeping every boundary point visible from the center so that one ray continues the walk instead of branching at each contact. The screened kernels for Walk-on-Stars have been derived only in two and three dimensions ( Sawhney et al., 2023 ) . Moreover, directly planning with Monte Carlo estimates is unreliable: trajectories depend on local value gradients, and even modest estimator noise can corrupt or reverse the estimated direction, leading to planning failure.

Neural operators ( Kovachki et al., 2023 ) can amortize expensive PDE solves by learning mappings from input geometries directly to solution fields. Moreover, prior work has shown that fully converged labels are unnecessary when training from Monte Carlo simulations: neural operators can recover accurate predictions from noisy, partially converged estimates ( Viswanath et al., 2026 ) . This enables training of neural operators with inexpensive Monte Carlo supervision while providing fast, smooth value-field predictions at inference time.

We propose P lanning U nder N oise (PUN), shown in Fig. 2 , an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to value fields that account for control noise. Boundary conditions can be understood through a heat analogy. With unit desirability at the goal and zero desirability on obstacle boundaries, the goal acts like a hot source, while the obstacle walls act like cold sinks. The zero-Dirichlet condition fixes the field to zero along each obstacle surface, making the entire obstacle boundary a heat sink. In a long or narrow passage, heat spreading from the goal therefore leaks into the walls along the route. The farther the goal’s influence must travel, the more it is attenuated, leaving a weak signal in distant parts of free space that discretization, sampling, or learning errors can obscure. Narrow passages make this particularly pronounced because the absorbing walls remain close on both sides. This attenuation is visible in Fig. 1 (c), where the weak goal signal provides insufficient directional guidance for starting points far from the goal, making it difficult to navigate toward the target. Moreover, the screened Poisson equation already includes decay throughout free space through its screening term; absorbing obstacle boundaries introduce an additional source of attenuation. We therefore keep a Dirichlet condition at the goal but impose homogeneous Neumann (zero-flux) conditions on obstacle boundaries. The walls now act like insulation: they prevent heat from escaping through the boundary without forcing the desirability itself to vanish there. Heat can spread along a corridor without continually draining into its walls, allowing the goal’s influence to reach farther into free space. Screening still causes decay, but the additional loss through obstacles is removed. This is precisely the effect illustrated in Fig. 1 (d): compared with the absorbing Dirichlet field in Fig. 1 (c), the mixed-boundary field extends the goal’s influence much farther through the environment, preserving a stronger signal for planning along long routes. The Neumann condition also makes the value gradient parallel to smooth obstacle boundaries; therefore, gradient-based planning directs motion along walls rather than into them. This permits guidance along walls in narrow passages without the strong repulsion induced by zero-Dirichlet conditions. Under our regularity assumptions, the value field and control remain bounded at obstacles, whereas zero-Dirichlet desirability makes both diverge there (Appendix C.4 ).

We first derive dimension-general Poisson kernels and Monte Carlo weights, extending mesh-free supervision beyond three dimensions for scalability. This enables supervision generation without a volumetric configuration-space mesh. We then train PUN using noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo estimates in the weak supervision paradigm. By amortizing the PDE solution across geometries, PUN produces spatially coherent value fields that guide gradient following and local search without requiring a fully converged Monte Carlo solve for every environment. We evaluate PUN across 2D–4D environments and compare its planning success and runtime with nominal planners and stochastic controllers under execution noise. In the experiments varying the execution noise level λ \lambda , we plan a path from the current state at each control step, follow it briefly, and repeat from the updated state; we refer to this as replanning. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We formulate Poisson-based path planning as a mixed boundary-value problem, imposing a Dirichlet condition at the goal and homogeneous Neumann conditions on obstacle boundaries.

We formulate Poisson-based path planning as a mixed boundary-value problem, imposing a Dirichlet condition at the goal and homogeneous Neumann conditions on obstacle boundaries.

We introduce an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to noise-aware value fields, enabling zero-shot planning in unseen complex geometries without per-instance retraining or numerical PDE solves.

We generalize the mesh-free Monte Carlo solver WoSt beyond three dimensions by deriving the dimension-dependent Green’s function and step weights for the screened Poisson equation.

We introduce a test-time scaling strategy that evaluates reachable candidate states on a local lattice using a fixed global learned field, without retraining, improving planning success over direct gradient following in the reported 2D–4D evaluations (Tables 1 and 11 ).

On 2D application benchmarks, zero-shot WoSt-supervised FNO reaches 93.62% local-search success, up from 83.87% with gradient following on the same fields (Table 1 ). With the same local-search, FNO-based PUN achieves approximately 941 × 941\times and 58 × 58\times speedups over direct WoSt on the 2D zero-shot application benchmarks and 4D manipulator test set, respectively (Table 12 ). In 4D replanning, PUN achieves 95.00–100% success at 10.51–11.66 ms/start across the tested noise levels (Table 5 ; Fig. 1 (a)). At λ = 4 \lambda=4 , PUN is 3.29 × 3.29\times faster than RRT and 5.09 5.09 – 32.15 × 32.15\times faster than A ⋆ , Dijkstra, MPPI, and PI 2 -CMA. FNO also maintains over 90% local-search success across resolutions up to 4096 × 4096 4096\times 4096 ( 256 × 256\times as many grid points as used in training) without retraining (Fig. 1 (b)).

1. We formulate Poisson-based path planning as a mixed boundary-value problem, imposing a Dirichlet condition at the goal and homogeneous Neumann conditions on obstacle boundaries.

2. We introduce an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to noise-aware value fields, enabling zero-shot planning in unseen complex geometries without per-instance retraining or numerical PDE solves.

3. We generalize the mesh-free Monte Carlo solver WoSt beyond three dimensions by deriving the dimension-dependent Green’s function and step weights for the screened Poisson equation.

4. We introduce a test-time scaling strategy that evaluates reachable candidate states on a local lattice using a fixed global learned field, without retraining, improving planning success over direct gradient following in the reported 2D–4D evaluations (Tables 1 and 11 ).

2026-10-21.title: CoGaussian: Open-Vocabulary Gaussian-based Collaborative 3D Scene Understanding
2026-10-21.authors: Om Shivam Verma , Shaya Farahmand , Lingjun Zhao , Lu Gan
2026-10-21.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-21.abstract: Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework. CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Collaborative perception enables local agents to exchange information that may be occluded or beyond their field-of-view, improving geometric and semantic understanding of their environment, and enabling safer and more reliable decision making in autonomous driving and robot navigation. Semantic occupancy prediction (SOP) is a representative and challenging task in 3D spatial understanding, which aims to predict voxel-wise occupancy status and semantic class. Recently, 3D Gaussian-based methods [ 1 ] have been shown to be effective for SOP. The GaussianFormer family [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] represents scenes as 3D Gaussians, supervised by dense occupancy labels. VOGS-CP [ 6 ] extends GaussianFormer to collaborative SOP which communicates Gaussian primitives between neighboring agents. However, these methods are limited to predicting semantics within a closed vocabulary and heavily rely on densely annotated 3D occupancy labels that are expensive to obtain.

Vision foundation models (VFMs), such as DINO [ 7 ] and CLIP [ 8 ] have demonstrated strong open-vocabulary capabilities in 2D perception. In addition, Talk2DINO [ 9 ] and DINO.txt [ 10 ] further align 2D VFM features with natural language.
Building on the above VFMs, GaussTR [ 11 ] represents scenes as a set of sparse open-vocabulary 3D Gaussians that are predicted in a feed-forward manner and can be queried via natural language. The Gaussians are encoded with geometry and semantic information by splatting into 2D views and aligning rendered features with foundation model-derived depth [ 12 ] and semantics [ 8 , 7 ] . However, GaussTR is designed for single-agent perception and cannot leverage information that is visible only to neighboring agents.

Based on these observations, we propose CoGaussian , the first open-vocabulary multi-robot collaborative perception framework. We represent scenes as sets of sparse VFM-aligned 3D Gaussians, which also serve as the communication primitives among agents. We also explore and develop three different algorithms to aggregate and fuse information from neighboring agents. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

Open-Vocabulary Collaborative Perception: We propose CoGaussian, the first framework for open-vocabulary collaborative perception (e.g. 3D semantic occupancy prediction) in outdoor environments.

Open-Vocabulary Collaborative Perception: We propose CoGaussian, the first framework for open-vocabulary collaborative perception (e.g. 3D semantic occupancy prediction) in outdoor environments.

Multi-Robot 3D Gaussian Representation: We develop a foundation model-aligned 3D Gaussian representation for collaborative perception, along with fusion strategies to enhance information transfer among agents.

Zero-Shot Benchmarking: We evaluate CoGaussian on the Semantic-OPV2V [ 13 , 14 ] dataset in a zero-shot manner. Without any task-specific supervision, our approach achieves impressive performance for semantic occupancy prediction, highlighting the potential for open-vocabulary collaborative perception.

1. Open-Vocabulary Collaborative Perception: We propose CoGaussian, the first framework for open-vocabulary collaborative perception (e.g. 3D semantic occupancy prediction) in outdoor environments.

2. Multi-Robot 3D Gaussian Representation: We develop a foundation model-aligned 3D Gaussian representation for collaborative perception, along with fusion strategies to enhance information transfer among agents.

3. Zero-Shot Benchmarking: We evaluate CoGaussian on the Semantic-OPV2V [ 13 , 14 ] dataset in a zero-shot manner. Without any task-specific supervision, our approach achieves impressive performance for semantic occupancy prediction, highlighting the potential for open-vocabulary collaborative perception.

## II-B Joint Training

GaussTR [ 11 ] is trained per camera view , with Gaussians predicted from each camera splatted back into that view for supervision. While this approach is effective for datasets with limited camera overlap, such as in the nuScenes dataset [ 18 ] , it is suboptimal for multi-agent perception, where independent supervision fails to exploit overlapping observations across agents.
Therefore, the model is trained per scene as shown in Fig. 2 . All Gaussians predicted from cameras in a scene are aggregated and splatted into every camera in which they are visible, not only the cameras that produced them. During inference, Gaussians are predicted from each camera, aggregated, and then used by agents for downstream tasks. CoGaussian can use weights from either per-image or per-scene training. In Sec.
