2026-10-21.title: CLOSER: Evidence-Aware Active Visual Verification for Embodied Object-Goal Navigation
2026-10-21.authors: Pengying Wu , Mingye Jiang , Yunze Hu , Zhejia Wen , Kangjie Zhou , Zongru Yang , Zhe Peng , Chang Liu
2026-10-21.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-21.abstract: Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) requires an embodied agent to find an instance of a specified category in an unseen environment and stop near it. The agent typically relies on an object detector but must judge online from a limited egocentric video stream, sometimes a single frame, whether a detected candidate is the target. Detectors often confidently mistake similar objects, such as a sofa for a bed, and stopping at a false positive fails the episode. Prevailing systems also approach candidates greedily, leaving them occluded or partially observed. We present CLOSER, an evidence-aware active verification framework that treats stopping as closed-loop evidence acquisition, coupling vision–language model (VLM) verification with active perception. CLOSER fine-tunes an open-source VLM to label each view of a candidate tracked across frames as target, non-target, or uncertain, selects complementary views with an embedding-based diversity gate, and fuses their per-view probabilities with a lightweight network. If the fused judgment remains uncertain, a diffusion policy drives the agent toward the candidate using only the tracked mask and depth until the decision becomes decisive. CLOSER runs locally and plugs into existing ObjectNav systems without retraining them. On Gibson and Habitat-Matterport 3D, it raises average success rate by 3.6 points and success weighted by path length by 2.0 points, showing that verifying evidence before committing improves embodied navigation.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) is a fundamental task in embodied AI [ 1 ] in which an agent searches an unseen environment for an object of a specified target category and stops near it [ 2 , 3 ] . To find the target, the agent must explore the environment efficiently and infer where the target is likely to be located. When an object resembling the target comes into view, the agent must further judge whether it is the target. ObjectNav therefore demands both efficient exploration and reliable perception from its online egocentric video stream, and remains a challenging problem despite extensive study [ 4 ] .

To meet these demands, prevailing modular systems adopt an exploration strategy to search promising regions and an off-the-shelf object detector to recognize the observed objects [ 2 , 5 , 6 ] . Whenever a candidate for the target category is detected, the agent must decide from limited local observations whether the candidate is the target and hence whether to stop; in the worst case, only a single partial view is available. Since the episode ends once the agent stops, a wrong stop cannot be corrected, and this stopping decision has been identified as a major bottleneck of modular systems [ 7 , 8 ] . Although modern open-vocabulary detectors such as YOLO-World and Grounded-SAM [ 9 , 10 ] achieve high recall on common indoor categories, they frequently mistake semantically similar objects for the target. For example, a sofa observed from a distance may be detected as a bed (Fig. 1 ), and a stool partially occluded by a table may be detected as a chair. Such confusers are often detected with tight bounding boxes and high confidence, so raising the confidence threshold removes true targets before it removes these errors. Therefore, each detected candidate needs to be further verified before the agent commits to a stop.

To this end, recent systems introduce a closed-source vision–language model (VLM) such as GPT-4o-mini as a verifier that confirms or rejects each detected candidate [ 11 ] . Such a model provides open-world visual reasoning that the detector lacks, and can reject confusers even when the detection confidence is high. However, the verifier is accessible only through a remote API, which incurs per-query cost and latency and leaves its weights unavailable for local adaptation. A smaller open-source VLM avoids these constraints, yet its verification accuracy drops markedly on hard cases such as distant or partially occluded confusers. Moreover, existing verifiers are binary and must decide even when the current view supports neither confirmation nor rejection. Such a forced decision may stop the agent at a non-target or reject a candidate that a closer view could confirm. Recent work has proposed ternary uncertainty scores and explicit not-found outcomes [ 12 , 13 ] , but neither mechanism moves the agent to acquire more views of the candidate for verification.

In this paper, we propose CLOSER (Closed-Loop Observation Sensing for Embodied veRification), an evidence-aware active verification framework in which the agent decides whether to stop by reasoning over the visual evidence on a candidate and acting to improve it. Our key insight is that a reliable stopping decision depends not only on what the candidate appears to be but also on whether the available views suffice to identify it, and this sufficiency depends on the spatial relationship between the agent and the candidate, including its distance, viewing angle, and degree of occlusion. The agent therefore commits to a decision only when the evidence suffices and otherwise approaches the candidate to acquire more informative views (Fig. 1 ). Realizing this closed loop poses two challenges. First, the agent must learn when its evidence is insufficient, which confidence cannot reveal since distant or occluded views often yield confident predictions. Second, it must learn how to reach a more informative view without a complete map of the unseen environment.

To learn when the evidence is insufficient, CLOSER fine-tunes an open-source VLM with LoRA [ 14 ] to assess both the identity of the candidate and the sufficiency of each view. During navigation, CLOSER tracks the candidate across egocentric frames with ByteTrack [ 15 ] and caches complementary views of it, and a lightweight MLP fuses the per-view assessments of the VLM to decide whether the evidence suffices. To learn how to reach a more informative view, CLOSER imitates an expert that plans maximum-clearance paths along the Voronoi medial axis of the complete map and smooths them into Bézier trajectories, so that walls are less likely to occlude the candidate along the way. To eliminate this dependence on the map, we distill the expert trajectories into a Diffusion Transformer policy [ 16 , 17 ] that conditions only on the tracked candidate mask and depth, which encode the distance and visibility of the candidate relative to the agent. As the agent follows this policy, verification and active perception form a closed loop, in which every view cached along the trajectory refines the assessment and the approach phase ends as soon as the evidence supports a decision. CLOSER is invoked only when a candidate for the target category is detected and leaves the exploration and mapping components of existing ObjectNav systems unchanged. It can therefore be inserted into these systems as a plug-in verification layer without retraining them.

The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We propose CLOSER, a plug-in layer for existing ObjectNav systems that formulates the stopping decision as an active verification problem. Closer judges not only whether a candidate is the target but also whether its views suffice for that judgment, and it drives the agent to acquire more views by approaching the candidate when the current views are insufficient.

Since a confident prediction on a distant or occluded view can be wrong, we design the verifier in Closer to assess the sufficiency of each view in addition to the identity of the candidate. We fine-tune an open-source VLM for this assessment under a closed-source VLM teacher and train a lightweight MLP that fuses the assessments of complementary views into a single decision.

We train a map-free approach policy by distilling an expert into a Diffusion Transformer that generates a trajectory toward the candidate from its tracked mask and depth. To keep the candidate in view throughout the approach phase, the expert plans each path along the Voronoi medial axis of the free space for maximum clearance from walls and smooths the path into a Bézier trajectory.

Simulation experiments confirm that CLOSER improves ObjectNav performance. Across diverse ObjectNav systems on Gibson, HM3D v1, and HM3D v2, CLOSER improves success rate (SR), with an average gain of 3.6 points and a maximum gain of 4.9 points. CLOSER also improves success weighted by path length (SPL) by 2.0 points on average.

# II Related Work

## II-A Object-Goal Navigation and Target Verification

Existing ObjectNav methods range from end-to-end reinforcement learning, which learns continuous environment representations with multi-step look-ahead planning [ 18 ] or agent-centric relation graphs that encode object layout and target distance [ 19 ] , to modular pipelines that combine semantic mapping with goal selection [ 2 , 3 ] and zero-shot variants [ 4 ] , supported by large-scale simulators [ 20 ] . Recent methods use vision–language models to score exploration frontiers [ 6 ] or large language models to prioritize search regions [ 21 , 22 ] ; E 2 BA [ 23 ] further fuses LLM commonsense scores with geometric costs through particle filtering and uses a cascaded discriminator to decide when to backtrack. These advances concentrate on where to explore, and a separate mechanism is still required to verify whether a detected candidate is the target. For the stopping decision, DITA [ 7 ] decouples depth-based termination from the navigation policy, RATE-Nav [ 8 ] models spatial regions to trigger stopping, and ACRG [ 19 ] encodes the depth-derived agent–target distance into the policy. Classical pipelines verify candidates with detector confidence thresholds [ 2 ] , which fail under partial observability [ 24 ] . Memory [ 3 , 24 ] and blacklist mechanisms [ 25 ] improve decision consistency, SPENav [ 26 ] filters task-irrelevant objects with room-guided semantic priors, and recent systems query a closed-source VLM to verify each candidate [ 11 ] . For image goals, RSRNav [ 27 ] reasons about the spatial relationship between the goal and the current observation through direction-aware correlation and remains robust when the goal viewpoint differs from the test viewpoint. Beyond binary decisions, QAsk-Nav [ 12 ] and VLN-NF [ 13 ] introduce ternary uncertainty scores and an explicit not-found outcome, while IEVE [ 28 ] and DRIVE-Nav [ 29 ] verify potential targets by keypoint matching and cross-frame VLM inspection. However, these systems either depend on closed-source VLM APIs or do not collect further observations when the evidence on a candidate is insufficient. In CLOSER, verification runs on local hardware, and the agent approaches a candidate with insufficient evidence to acquire additional views.

## II-B Vision–Language Model Adaptation and Chain-of-Thought Reasoning

Large VLMs can be adapted by training only a small fraction of their parameters, either a lightweight query module with the image encoder and language model frozen [ 30 ] or low-rank updates such as LoRA [ 14 ] , and EverWalker [ 31 ] generates LoRA parameters on the fly from observation prototypes for lifelong navigation. Chain-of-thought supervision provides training signal beyond the final label: CL-CoTNav [ 32 ] fine-tunes a VLM on hierarchical chain-of-thought annotations so that it reasons about ObjectNav decisions, and distilling rationales from closed-source teachers into open models is now standard practice [ 33 , 34 ] . Distillation is likewise used to compress navigation models: Chen et al. [ 35 ] distill both where to look and how to move from a teacher into a student with 93% fewer parameters. However, CURE [ 36 ] shows that VLM rationales can be inconsistent with the visual evidence even when the final answer is correct, and program-based distillation [ 37 ] mitigates this inconsistency through executable verification. CLOSER adapts Qwen2.5-VL-7B with LoRA and keeps a base-model rationale only when its label is correct and a rule-based validator accepts it, so an external teacher annotates only the remaining samples (Sec. III-D3 ). Rendering novel viewpoints with 3D Gaussian Splatting also improves the viewpoint robustness of VLN agents [ 38 ] ; likewise, CLOSER renders confusers as hard negatives and refines the perceiver on its residual errors (Sec. III-D2 ).

## II-C Active Perception and Uncertainty-Driven Exploration

Active perception selects sensor placements to maximize information gain. Next-best-view (NBV) methods optimize hand-crafted metrics [ 39 ] or predict the downstream value of prospective viewpoints [ 40 , 41 ] . Uncertainty-aware methods complement view selection through conformal prediction [ 42 ] and uncertainty-driven intrinsic motivation [ 43 ] , and recent work applies them to open-vocabulary object search [ 44 ] . Diffusion models have also become expressive policy representations that capture multimodal action distributions [ 16 ] and generate navigation trajectories [ 45 ] . The approach policy of CLOSER connects these two lines without an explicit information-gain objective (Sec. III-E ). A Diffusion Transformer [ 17 ] distilled from privileged expert trajectories takes only the candidate mask and depth as input, and the verification stack decides from the newly acquired views whether the evidence suffices.

2026-10-21.title: Distributed Platoon Control for Safe and Smooth Crossing at an Unsignalized Intersection-Part I: Stability Analysis
2026-10-21.authors: Bin-Bin Hu , Shuwei Pei , Saeed Ahmed , Bayu Jayawardhana
2026-10-21.abstract:
We propose a distributed platoon controller that guarantees safe and smooth crossing of multi-vehicle systems at an unsignalized intersection. To support the stability analysis, we consider a multi-vehicle platoon maneuvering along a closed path with a single unsignalized intersection .
Unlike traditional bi-level decoupled designs on open paths, which primarily focus on intersection control while neglecting its coupling with platoon convergence, and thus hindering rigorous convergence analysis, the closed-path setting allows us to analyze the asymptotic behavior of the platoon.
The local exponential convergence analysis of the switched closed-loop system , induced by repeated vehicle switching at the intersection, is presented. Under some mild conditions on the controller gains, we show that safe intersection crossing is ensured during the transient phase and smooth crossing is achieved in steady state, where all vehicles travel at a common constant speed while avoiding collisions at the intersection. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed distributed controller is demonstrated in a high-fidelity CARLA simulator using multiple commercial vehicle models.
2026-10-21.introduction:
With advances in connected and autonomous vehicle (CAV) technologies, multi-vehicle coordination has become increasingly important in urban transportation [ 1 , 2 ] . Among cooperative scenarios, connected vehicle platooning has attracted significant attention because it enables vehicles to maintain desired inter-vehicle spacing, improving traffic efficiency, energy consumption, and safety [ 3 , 4 ] . However, urban intersections remain challenging, as vehicles from different directions must share conflict regions safely and efficiently. Frequent deceleration, acceleration, and stopping may disrupt platoon continuity, causing platoon splitting or performance degradation. Therefore, cooperative intersection control (CIC) for multi-vehicle platooning has emerged as a promising approach to improving future intelligent transportation systems [ 5 ] .

Depending on whether traffic signals are used to manage traffic at intersections, existing studies can be divided into two categories, namely, signal-based and unsignalized methods [ 6 ] .

Following the signal-based CIC research line, the seminal work [ 7 ] studied intersection control for a personal rapid transit system. Later, a isolated controller
based on max-plus models was proposed to reduce energy consumption at homogeneous intersections [ 8 ] , while a multi-agent reinforcement learning method was proposed for heterogeneous intersections by modeling intersections as basic agents [ 9 ] . However, these methods require physical traffic signals, leading to high installation and maintenance costs. This motivates unsignalized approaches with virtual infrastructure and fast computation.

Unsignalized methods have emerged as a promising alternative to signal-based control by reducing unnecessary stops through flexible vehicle coordination. Based on how decision-making, computation, and coordination responsibilities are allocated between infrastructure and vehicles, existing methods can be classified into three categories: centralized, decentralized, and distributed approaches [ 10 ] : (i) For centralized methods where vehicles obtain traffic schemes from the intersection unit, a conflict-duration graph-based framework was designed to improve safety and capacity at unsignalized intersections [ 11 ] . To reduce computational burden, an abstraction-based supervision framework was adopted in [ 12 ] . For mixed traffic, deep reinforcement learning was used to enable connected autonomous vehicles to yield right of way and optimize traffic flow [ 13 ] . For safety guarantee and performance, a polling-systems-based coordination control algorithm was proposed in [ 14 ] with rigorous upper bound.
However, these methods directly transmit acceleration commands to individual vehicles, making the system sensitive to disturbances. To improve robustness, a CIC controller was proposed in [ 6 ] , assigning each CAV a safe reference path and desired speed based on its state, onboard controller response, and origin–destination pair; (ii) For decentralized methods where vehicles distribute tasks across multiple computing nodes, a virtual platooning approach was proposed to map two-dimensional vehicle motions onto a one-dimensional virtual platoon for efficient intersection operation [ 15 ] . To handle inaccuracies and disturbances, a hybrid CIC framework was developed by integrating microscopic virtual platooning with traffic-flow regulation [ 16 ] . Later, a constraint-coupled bi-level optimization method was designed to balance performance and computational efficiency [ 17 ] .

In contrast to the centralized and decentralized methods [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] in (i)-(ii) , the distributed control policies in (iii) have also attracted considerable attention. Along this line, a distributed optimization algorithm was proposed in [ 18 ] to schedule conflict-free arrival times for trajectory planning at intersections. To minimize travel time and speed variations simultaneously, a mixed-integer nonlinear optimization method was developed in [ 19 ] to avoid near-crash conditions. Moreover, a graph-based cooperation method was proposed in [ 20 ] to formulate the conflict-free scheduling problem at unsignalized intersections, which enhances control flexibility.

However, most existing CIC methods [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] provide only limited rigorous analysis, mainly due to their bi-level decoupled designs for intersection control and platoon convergence on open paths. To facilitate stability analysis and safety guarantee, we consider a setting in which the platoon maneuvers along a closed path with a single unsignalized intersection , enabling the platoon to be analyzed as an integrated team. Compared with open-path scenarios, this closed-path setting introduces two challenges: (i) Vehicles repeatedly enter the intersection, which causes persistent coupling between intersection control and platoon convergence and invalidates decoupled optimization designs; (ii) Repeated intersection entries transform the closed-loop dynamics into a switched system, which makes the convergence analysis challenging.

To tackle these challenges, we propose a distributed controller that enables multiple vehicles to cross the intersection safely and converge to the steady-state platoon, where all vehicles travel at a common constant speed and achieve collision-free crossing.
The local exponential convergence of the switched closed-loop system , induced by repeated vehicle switching at the intersection, is rigorously analyzed. Finally, the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated.

Contribution: The contribution is summarized as follows.

We propose a distributed smooth-crossing controller that enables multiple vehicles to spontaneously form a platoon on a closed path with a single intersection;

We enable smooth constant-speed crossing without acceleration or deceleration in steady state by introducing a sensing barrier function for incoming vehicle pairs approaching the intersection;

We rigorously establish the local exponential convergence of the switched closed-loop system induced by vehicle switching at the intersection on a closed path.

The proposed algorithm is not intended to replace general-purpose intersection scheduling methods. Rather, it provides a control-theoretic model in which the interaction between intersection safety and platoon convergence remains active indefinitely, which leads to a switched closed-loop system under repeated intersection crossings. This allows the switching dynamics to be included in the rigorous convergence analysis.

2026-10-21.title: Interruption-Aware Recurrent Reinforcement Learning for UAS Navigation Under Temporary Overrides
2026-10-21.authors: Christopher Conrad , Deepak Panda , Weisi Guo , Antonios Tsourdos
2026-10-21.comment: This work has been submitted to IEEE for possible publication
2026-10-21.abstract: Safe autonomous navigation of unmanned aircraft systems (UASs) requires tactical deconfliction to address conflicts that strategic coordination cannot fully prevent. This task is challenging under partial observability, when sensor or traffic data are missing, delayed, or degraded. Geometry-based methods can offer separation assurances but face limitations in dense encounters. Recurrent reinforcement learning (RL) has therefore been proposed to learn navigation policies that integrate observation-action histories to optimise long-term safety-efficiency trade-offs. However, operational safeguards may require a remote pilot, onboard detect-and-avoid (DAA) system, or runtime assurance (RTA) mechanism to temporarily override the learned policy. A research gap remains in understanding how these interruptions affect recurrent policies when the agent regains authority. Benchmark evidence shows that interruptions make task variables less decodable from the recurrent hidden state and increase post-interruption collision risk. The findings suggest that altered recurrent context prolongs post-handback degradation through an action-observation feedback loop, in which changed actions alter the flight path and subsequent recurrent updates. To address this vulnerability, we propose three interruption-aware architectures that condition recurrent processing on interruption context through separate feature streams, dedicated interruption memory, or gated environmental features. Across simulations, all three architectures preserve more decodable task information than a standard recurrent policy. Moreover, the strongest architecture reduces post-interruption collisions by 74% and interruption-induced mission failures by 69% relative to the recurrent baseline, without degrading interruption-free performance. These results show that safe interruption does not guarantee safe handback, and support interruption-aware recurrent design for resilient UAS autonomy.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Unmanned aircraft system (UAS) traffic management (UTM) frameworks support flight planning, strategic deconfliction and information exchange for UAS navigation [ 1 , 2 ] . Nonetheless, the UAS operator or remote pilot remains responsible for flight safety, and strategic coordination cannot eliminate every conflict that develops during a flight. Aircraft may deviate from their submitted intents, surveillance information may be delayed or degraded, and non-cooperative aircraft or other hazards may be absent from networked information. Tactical deconfliction is therefore required to address emerging conflicts and complement strategic UTM services [ 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Moreover, additional safeguards are required when the tactical navigation algorithm encounters unreliable information or conditions outside its validated operating envelope. An onboard detect-and-avoid (DAA) system, runtime-assurance (RTA) mechanism or remote pilot may temporarily override nominal autonomy to resolve an emerging hazard [ 3 , 4 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 5 ] . Additionally, interruptions may arise from command-and-control (C2) link disruptions or malicious cyberphysical interference [ 10 , 11 ] . The reliability of the nominal algorithm after it regains authority, hereby referred to as handback, is therefore part of the safety problem.

Within this operational framework, tactical deconfliction has traditionally relied on geometry-based methods, including velocity-obstacle and potential-field algorithms [ 12 , 13 ] . These approaches often leverage rule-, search- or optimisation-based planning to provide predictable behaviour under explicit assumptions about aircraft dynamics, traffic behaviour and environmental conditions [ 14 , 15 ] . Advanced air mobility (AAM), however, will increase the volume, heterogeneity, and autonomy of aircraft in the airspace, creating denser and more uncertain traffic interactions [ 1 , 16 ] . These conditions make the behaviour of interacting aircraft harder to model and increase the computational cost of repeatedly solving multi-aircraft deconfliction problems online [ 14 , 15 ] .

Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a complementary approach by learning navigation policies through simulated conflict encounters [ 17 ] . It can optimise safety-efficiency trade-offs while shifting much of the computational burden to offline training [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] . However, finite sensor coverage, noise, occlusion and degraded traffic information make tactical deconfliction partially observable [ 1 , 3 ] . Recurrent RL addresses this limitation by maintaining a hidden state that summarises task-relevant history to inform current decisions [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] . Notably, Lambrechts et al. [ 24 ] show that recurrent memory encodes information correlated with beliefs over latent task variables, with more informative representations resulting in better task performance. Recurrent memory can therefore be interpreted as a learned, task-dependent information state.

Temporary overrides introduce a distinct challenge for recurrent policies. During an interruption, the policy’s proposed actions are not executed, yet its recurrent state evolves with observations generated by externally selected manoeuvres. This altered context can make task-relevant information less accessible or distort how carried information influences subsequent decisions. Consequently, an interruption that resolves an immediate hazard does not necessarily ensure safe handback.

Table I summarises existing research relevant to interrupting recurrent navigation policies. Transportation research examines transitions between automated systems and human decision-makers, focusing on improving override timing and operator readiness [ 25 , 26 , 27 ] . In UTM and other safety-critical autonomous systems, DAA and RTA research instead addresses better hazard detection, safety monitoring, and recovery behaviour [ 3 , 4 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 5 ] . Within RL, research primarily addresses the safety of learned behaviour and responsiveness to interruptions. Safe RL incorporates risk measures or safety constraints during training, whereas shielded RL masks or replaces actions that violate safety thresholds [ 29 , 30 , 31 ] . Corrigibility targets agents that accept or assist external corrections without manipulating the correcting authority [ 33 , 34 , 35 ] . Specifically, safely interruptible RL addresses how interruptions affect learning, developing algorithms that avoid seeking out or preventing future interruptions [ 32 ] .

Action-modification research provides the closest formal abstraction of the interruptions considered in this paper. Langlois and Everitt [ 37 ] introduce the modified-action Markov decision process (MAMDP), which distinguishes the action selected by a policy from that ultimately executed following external modifications. Their analysis shows that some agents ignore modifications while others adapt their behaviour to avoid modifications that reduce reward. Human-in-the-loop RL also uses human overrides as demonstrations or feedback to improve policies during training [ 36 ] .

Complementing these studies, recurrent RL has been applied to UAS navigation under partial observability [ 23 , 28 ] , while representation analysis examines which latent task variables are decodable from recurrent hidden states [ 24 , 39 ] . Influence-aware memory restricts recurrent inputs to variables relevant to unobserved environmental states, reducing interference from irrelevant features [ 38 ] . Recurrent independent mechanisms similarly organise memory into sparsely interacting modules to improve robustness to environmental changes [ 40 ] . These approaches inform the analysis of recurrent representations and the design of structured memory architectures.

Existing literature highlights why interruptions are needed, when they should be initiated, and how they affect policy learning. However, a safe interruption does not guarantee safe handback. A research gap remains in understanding how interruptions affect recurrent representations, how they influence post-handback performance, and how they should be accommodated by recurrent policies. We address this gap through the following contributions:

Interruption of recurrent UAS navigation is formulated as a handback reliability problem and modelled as a partially observable MAMDP (PO-MAMDP).

A paired evaluation framework is developed to characterise the impact of interruptions across different trigger conditions, supervisor behaviours and override durations.

Interruptions are shown to reduce task-variable decodability from the recurrent hidden state, degrade agent performance and increase post-handback collision risk.

# II Problem Formulation

## II-A Operational UTM Context

This study focuses on history-dependent tactical navigation under partial observability, as summarised in Table II . A single operator uses a nominal navigation policy to guide one UAS towards its destination while avoiding surrounding traffic and respecting operational constraints. The policy combines onboard sensor data with traffic and constraint information supplied through UTM services to generate navigation commands. 2026-10-21.title: RoboJudge: Multimodal Language Models as Judges for Embodied Video Generation
2026-10-21.authors: Siyuan Ma , Yu Qi , Cheng Ye , Ruotian Peng , Xinyi Xu , Zitiantao Lin , Zedong Cai , Yijian Huang , Weiyang Liu , Siyuan Wang , Yandong Wen
2026-10-21.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-21.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-21.abstract:
Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models,
but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task
instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used
to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on
embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap,
we introduce RoboJudge-Bench , a benchmark for evaluating
MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two
fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction
Alignment , across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10
video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands.
Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings:
general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while
specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not
consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we
construct RoboJudge-Train , comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores
and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune
a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement
learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B . Among the model judges
evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench , RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest
overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 0.719 with a statistically
significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary
baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external
benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval.
We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark
video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Recent advances in video generation have positioned generative models as a
promising foundation for embodied world models ( Li et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2025 ; Shang et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Unlike general
video generators, embodied world models must predict how the physical world
evolves under robot actions or task instructions, providing imagined rollouts
for planning and policy learning. These rollouts therefore need to be not only
visually plausible, but also physically valid and instruction-consistent,
creating a pressing need for reliable evaluation.

Evaluating embodied generated videos is particularly challenging because they
require fine-grained assessment of physical interactions and task-level
correctness, while open-ended task execution makes reference-based similarity
intrinsically unreliable. Pixel, perceptual, and representation metrics capture
visual or semantic similarity to reference trajectories ( Huynh-Thu and Ghanbari, 2008 ; Bakurov et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2018 ; Radford et al., 2021 ; Caron et al., 2021 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) , but cannot disentangle physical and task-level failures.
MLLM-based judges offer stronger multimodal reasoning ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024 ) , yet general-purpose MLLMs lack embodied-specific calibration ( Qi et al., 2026b ) .
Meanwhile, specialized video judges target general-domain quality or physical
commonsense ( He et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Bansal et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026 ) , rather than fine-grained manipulation dynamics, contact
relationships, and task completion.

To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench , a
benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied world model rollouts
along two critical axes: Physical Adherence (PA) and Instruction
Alignment (IA) . Specifically, PA covers agent consistency , scene consistency , and interaction realism ; IA covers agent match , object correctness , and goal
completion . The benchmark comprises 800 rollouts with instructions from
8 embodied source corpora and videos generated by 10 video generation models,
spanning parallel-jaw grippers, dexterous hands, and human hands across indoor
and outdoor activities. Each sample is annotated with 1–5 human ratings for
PA and IA, together with detailed rationales under a cross-review protocol.

Evaluation against 29 model-judge baselines and 8 non-MLLM metrics reveals
gaps between existing judges and human judgments. Frontier models show lower
agreement on physical adherence: GPT-5.5 ( OpenAI, 2026 ) reaches r = 0.49 r=0.49 on PA. Specialized video judges reach at most r = 0.42 r=0.42 on PA and 0.59 0.59 on IA,
while non-MLLM baselines show limited sensitivity to fine-grained physical
correctness. Failure analysis identifies cases in which existing judges overlook
interaction failures and physical hallucinations.

Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train ,
a large-scale embodied-video judge-training dataset comprising 12K videos
annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for PA and IA. We
fine-tune a 9B MLLM from Qwen3.5-9B using supervised learning followed by
reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B .
Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench , the resulting RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson r r of 0.719 compared with 0.401 for its base model. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on VideoPhy2 ( Bansal et al., 2026 ) and
Physion-Eval ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) .
We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark
video generation models using the same PA and IA criteria. These
capabilities also suggest broader downstream potential for online physical
rollout evaluation and agentic embodied video generation.
In summary, our contributions are three-fold:

1. RoboJudge-Bench . A benchmark designed for judges of embodied video
generation: 800 human-annotated rollouts from 8 corpora and 10 video generators,
spanning grippers, dexterous hands, and human hands in simulated and
real environments, rated on physical adherence and instruction alignment.

2. A systematic study of existing judges. We compare against 29 model-judge baselines and 8 non-MLLM
metrics and characterize gaps with human judgments, with failures
concentrated on fine-grained interaction errors and physical hallucinations.

3. RoboJudge-Train and RoboJudge-9B . We construct a
training dataset for embodied video judges, comprising 12K
embodied videos spanning 14 generators and real demonstrations, with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales,
together with a 9B judge fine-tuned from
Qwen3.5-9B via SFT and RL. It achieves the highest overall agreement among
the evaluated model judges and shows gains on OOD benchmarks.
As a downstream use case, we apply it to rank video generation models using
the same PA and IA criteria.
2026-10-21.related_work:
Embodied MLLM benchmarks also diagnose atomic perception, reasoning, and
planning capabilities ( Qi et al., 2026b ) .

Benchmarks for Video Generative Models. Video-generation
benchmarks have gradually moved beyond perceptual quality toward physical and
embodied evaluation. General benchmarks evaluate visual quality, text-video
alignment, and physical commonsense ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2024 ; Bansal et al., 2025 ; Bansal et al., 2026 ; Meng et al., 2025 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Qi et al., 2026a ) . Recent embodied and world-model
benchmarks further test instruction following, physical adherence, and
task-level behavior in generated rollouts ( Li et al., 2025 ; Yue et al., 2025 ; Fan et al., 2026 ; Shang et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . These benchmarks primarily
measure generated videos or generative models themselves. In contrast, our work
studies whether the judges used for embodied video evaluation are
reliable.

Video Quality Evaluation Metrics. Video evaluation metrics have also expanded in scope. Classical metrics measure
pixel-level or perceptual similarity ( Huynh-Thu and Ghanbari, 2008 ; Bakurov et al., 2022 ; Zhang et al., 2018 ) , while FVD compares video feature distributions at the
dataset level ( Unterthiner et al., 2018 ) . Learned representations such as
CLIP, DINO, and V-JEPA provide semantic or temporal features, and optical-flow
estimators such as RAFT support motion-based measures ( Radford et al., 2021 ; Caron et al., 2021 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Teed and Deng, 2020 ) . These metrics capture useful
signals, but they do not explicitly judge physical validity or task completion.
Recent MLLM-based evaluators add language-conditioned video judgments, including
VideoScore, VideoScore2, VideoPhy2, VideoCon, PhyJudge, and
WBench ( He et al., 2024 ; He et al., 2025 ; Bansal et al., 2026 ; Bansal et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2026 ; Ying et al., 2026 ) . However, they are primarily designed for
general-domain video quality, physical plausibility, or world-model evaluation,
rather than joint embodied physical adherence and instruction alignment.

Judge Model Benchmarks. A parallel line of work studies multimodal
models as judges, with an emphasis on human agreement, reliability, bias, and
calibration ( Zheng et al., 2023 ; Chiang et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2024a ; Kim et al., 2024b ; Chen et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ; Panickssery et al., 2024 ) . Existing video
judge benchmarks cover video quality, physical reasoning, preference,
feedback, and artifact judgments, but mostly in general-domain
videos ( He et al., 2025 ; Bansal et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Tang et al., 2026 ) . Physion-Eval includes egocentric human videos, and
RoboGaze studies generated robot-manipulation videos ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ) . However, they remain limited in embodiment, source, and
generator diversity, as summarized in Table 1 .

In contrast, RoboJudge-Bench tests judge reliability rather than generator quality alone, using 800 embodied videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning human hands, dexterous hands, and robot grippers. It provides paired human references for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment . RoboJudge-Train further supplies human-verified dimensional scores and model-assisted rationales for training our dedicated judge, RoboJudge-9B .

2026-10-21.title: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models
2026-10-21.authors: Yingxin Jia , Hui Geng , Wenxin Yang , Mohan Zhang
2026-10-21.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-21.comment: NeurIPS 2026 Workshop BabyVLM
2026-10-21.abstract: Vision–language models (VLMs) are exact on small sets and drift into estimation on larger ones, a profile reminiscent of children before they master counting. Children cross the barrier with epistemic actions: pointing at each item while reciting number words, moving counted items aside, partitioning the array. We give VLMs the same actions as dumb image tools with no visual intelligence of their own (a numbered tag at a coordinate, a zoom, an eraser, a grid) in a training-free agent loop. Our central claim is about measurement, not intervention: a model that counts by marking leaves a normally hidden serial procedure on the image, and the developmental principles of counting (used as measurement theory, not as a claim that VLMs are children) turn those marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: every tag is classified against point-level ground truth as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted (one-to-one correspondence), the answer is checked against the number of tags (cardinality), and order irrelevance is tested by forcing opposite traversal orders. Across 9 models, 682 images (a controlled dot-array battery; FSC-147, 8–80 objects; PixMo-Count, 2–10), and 7 harness conditions we find that (i) the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude ( R 80 R_{80} from 3 to 150 dots); (ii) as an intervention the finger mostly fails: tags help 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs (CI-solid for one), hurt imprecise pointers, and rarely beat a verbal routine or a blind point list; what the loop buys is an auditable trace, not accuracy; (iii) as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows that precise pointers read their answers off the tags, pointing precision tracks which models benefit, dense scenes fail by omission (consistent with children’s keeping-track errors), and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags; and (iv) the capacities dissociate: models follow an instructed traversal order yet often change their answer when it reverses, beyond repeat and rotation controls, and children’s regular-over-scattered advantage appears only under the routine and survives lattices that defeat a rows-times-columns shortcut.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Ask a three-year-old how many crackers are on the table and, if there are two or three, the answer is immediate and exact. Ask about twelve and the child either guesses or starts to do something: touch each cracker in turn, say “one, two, three…”, slide the counted ones aside, and announce the last word as the total ( Gelman and Gallistel, 1978 ; Fuson, 1988 ; Wynn, 1990 ) . Two systems are at work: a fast, capacity-limited individuation of up to about four items ( subitizing , Kaufman et al., 1949 ; Trick and Pylyshyn, 1994 ) and an approximate sense of magnitude ( Feigenson et al., 2004 ; Xu and Spelke, 2000 ) . Exact enumeration beyond that range is a learned procedure that recruits the hands and the space around the child: pointing keeps items and number words in one-to-one correspondence ( Alibali and DiRusso, 1999 ; Saxe, 1977 ; Graham, 1999 ) , moving items aside and scanning row by row prevent double counts and skips ( Fuson, 1988 ; Potter and Levy, 1968 ; Beckwith and Restle, 1966 ) , and partitioning turns one big count into several small ones ( van Oeffelen and Vos, 1982 ) : epistemic actions , performed not to change the world but to make a computation easier ( Kirsh and Maglio, 1994 ; Kirsh, 1995 ) .

Vision–language models (VLMs) look strikingly like the pre-procedural child: near-perfect on one to four objects, sharply worse after that, systematically under-counting dense sets, erring like noisy estimators rather than enumerators ( Testolin et al., 2025 ; Tamarapalli et al., 2025 ; Che et al., 2026 ; Budny et al., 2025 ) , with the count present in the visual features but mis-read at the output ( Pang et al., 2026 ; El-Shangiti et al., 2026 ) . VLMs have a number sense but no counting routine. The claim is not that a VLM is a child or models one, but that the developmental account of counting supplies testable hypotheses (which external scaffolds should help) and diagnostic variables (what to measure when they do not).

We therefore ask: if we give a VLM the epistemic actions that children use, does it count like a child who has learned to count, and does it fail like one? We build a training-free harness in which the model can draw a numbered tag at any image coordinate and see the tagged image, zoom into a region, grey out counted items, and overlay a coordinate grid. Every tool is a plain pixel operation with no detector, segmenter, or OCR behind it, so all perception and all decisions remain the model’s own; the harness only lends it a finger, a magnifier, and an eraser.

The deeper contribution is measurement. A model that counts by marking externalises, mark by mark, a serial procedure that is normally hidden in its activations; the developmental principles of counting give that trace a grammar, turning model-generated marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning. This is what developmentally aligned evaluation adds over a benchmark score: not whether a model counts, but which constituent capacities it has, pointing, one-to-one tracking, cardinal read-out, checking, order invariance, each measured on its own. Following the classic analyses of children’s counting ( Gelman and Gallistel, 1978 ; Gelman and Meck, 1983 ; Fuson, 1988 ) , we classify every tag as on-target, duplicate, or phantom and every object as counted or omitted against point-level ground truth, test cardinality against the tags and order irrelevance by forcing opposite traversal orders, and measure pointing precision , on a controlled dot-array battery and two photographic benchmarks, FSC-147 ( Ranjan et al., 2021 ) (8–80 dot-annotated instances) and PixMo-Count ( Deitke et al., 2025 ) (2–10).

(1) A developmentally aligned evaluation in which counting principles turn model-generated marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: each principle becomes a measurable prediction ( Table 3 ), and a wrong count decomposes into principle violations against point-level ground truth ( Section 4 ). (2) A training-free harness of dumb epistemic tools for counting, each mapped to a child strategy and a counting principle ( Section 3 ). (3) An empirical study over 9 models and 682 images with paired bootstrap uncertainty on every headline contrast ( Section 5 ), showing that the constituent capacities dissociate across models rather than forming one “counting ability” ( Table 2 ), and that the tools are diagnostic rather than therapeutic: a finger helps only models that can already point, and where it fails, the audit localises the missing prerequisite; the study costs under 153 US dollars, and all code, stimuli, and trajectories will be released.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Background

Gelman and Gallistel (1978) described counting as governed by five principles: one-to-one (each item receives exactly one tag), stable order , cardinality (the last tag names the set size), abstraction (anything can be counted), and order-irrelevance . Children acquire number-word meanings slowly ( Wynn, 1990 ; Wynn, 1992 ; Le Corre and Carey, 2007 ; Sarnecka and Carey, 2008 ; Carey, 2009 ) , and even children who know the routine make keeping-track errors on large or disorganised arrays, skipping or double counting ( Fuson, 1988 ; Gelman and Meck, 1983 ) . Accuracy improves when children point at or touch each item ( Alibali and DiRusso, 1999 ; Graham, 1999 ; Saxe, 1977 ) , when the array is regular rather than scattered ( Potter and Levy, 1968 ; Beckwith and Restle, 1966 ) , and when large sets are counted in groups ( van Oeffelen and Vos, 1982 ) . Small sets are subitized ( Kaufman et al., 1949 ; Mandler and Shebo, 1982 ) , large sets estimated by an approximate number system shared with infants and animals ( Feigenson et al., 2004 ; Dehaene, 2011 ) ; number-sensitive units emerge spontaneously in deep networks ( Stoianov and Zorzi, 2012 ; Nasr et al., 2019 ; Testolin et al., 2020 ) .

Counting benchmarks range from small sets ( Paiss et al., 2023 ; Deitke et al., 2025 ; Acharya et al., 2019 ) to dense scenes ( Ranjan et al., 2021 ) and in-the-wild or adversarial questions ( Tamarapalli et al., 2025 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . VLMs are accurate up to four or five objects and then degrade ( Testolin et al., 2025 ; Che et al., 2026 ) ; failure grows with overlap, occlusion, compositional structure, and prior-knowledge bias ( Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024 ; Pothiraj et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ; Vo et al., 2025 ) and tracks the serial demand that also slows humans ( Budny et al., 2025 ) . Remedies include count-aware training ( Paiss et al., 2023 ) , pointing supervision ( Deitke et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) , and point-then-count prompting ( Alghisi et al., 2026 ; Hou et al., 2026 ) .

Language models can call vision tools ( Gupta and Kembhavi, 2023 ; Surís et al., 2023 ; Hu et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Su et al., 2025 ) , receive marks from a segmenter ( Yang et al., 2023 ) or a coordinate scaffold ( Lei et al., 2025 ) , or zoom into regions ( Wu and Xie, 2024 ; Shen et al., 2025 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Closest to us, Autonomous Imagination ( Liu et al., 2025 ) , SketchVLM ( Collins et al., 2026 ) , point-then-count prompting ( Alghisi et al., 2026 ) , LVLM-Count ( Fetrat Qharabagh et al., 2024 ) , and ABACUS ( Mondal et al., 2026 ) let a model mark, cursor over, or tile the image, and treat the marks as an intervention or an explanation judged by task accuracy (positioning table in Table 4 ). We treat them as measurement : dumb pixel tools keep every mark the model’s own, and point-level ground truth decomposes the trace into omissions, duplicates, phantoms, and broken cardinality. The matching is standard (point-based crowd-localization metrics, Idrees et al., 2018 ; Wang et al., 2021 ; Song et al., 2021 ; TIDE’s error taxonomy, Bolya et al., 2020 ); new are the loop that makes the marks and the principle tests that read them.

2026-10-21.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines
2026-10-21.authors: Yingxin Jia , Xuanyi Li
2026-10-21.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-21.comment: ACML 2026
2026-10-21.abstract:
When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because planners, prompts, and implementation quality vary together
across systems, and the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool
contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one
audited HighwayEnv testbed (kinematic observations, discrete meta-actions, 1 1 Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We freeze the planner, encoder, and protocol, treat
the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools), and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, scripted certificate policies,
caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port
(RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory TG-Mem with five variants, a retrieval-free
consolidated rulebook, and a flat K K -step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a
property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of
ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p = 0.011 p\!=\!0.011 ) and have a negative pool-averaged effect, and even the rulebook’s apparent pool-immunity
( 0.97 0.97 to 0.98 0.98 on five pools) collapsed to 0.03 0.03 to 0.98 0.98 on five fresh draws. (2) No
retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler, which sits significantly above both memories under
paired tests. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a scripted always- SLOWER policy and
by a single 15 15 -token caution instruction (both 0.98 0.98 ), and metrics that price caution erase the
rulebook’s lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. Neither
retrieved structure nor raw in-context history solves the oracle-solvable history-necessity diagnostic. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool
comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We
release the testbed, diagnostics with certificates, the replay benchmark, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
2026-10-21.introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising decision makers for autonomous driving that
reason over scenes in natural language. A recurring finding is that they improve substantially when given
an experience memory , a store of past situations and the actions that worked, retrieved and injected
as few-shot guidance at decision time ( Wen et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024a ; Mei et al., 2024 ) . This paper asks the question those reports leave open. When does experience memory help,
and under which warmup experiences, prompt compositions, and decision cadences? Published comparisons
cannot answer this, because the memory varies together with the surrounding architecture and with
implementation quality, and the two factors we find to matter most, which experiences the warmup
pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them.

Our primary contribution is the controlled evaluation itself. We fix one planner, one encoder,
and one warm-up, freeze, and evaluate protocol, and we instrument it with controls this literature has
not used. The warmup pool becomes a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools with model-free
pool-level tests). Token-matched irrelevant-filler arms span content, dose, and a
disclaimer × \times domain factorial. Two constructed diagnostics are certified well-posed by scripted
oracles before any LLM run. Scripted non-LLM certificate policies bound what caution alone
achieves, metrics price caution rather than only collisions, and a quantified audit measures the
fidelity of the baseline ports. On this testbed we evaluate a probe suite that spans the memory
design space (§ 3 and § 4 ). At the rich end sits TG-Mem (Temporal-Graph
Memory), our episodic design. Published driving memories retrieve flat text by embedding
cosine ( Wen et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024a ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Mei et al., 2024 ) or a single-frame
grid ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , whereas TG-Mem stores episodes as small typed temporal graphs matched
by a combined structural and temporal score, a prompt-level driving instantiation of the temporal
knowledge-graph memory line ( Rasmussen et al., 2025 ; Chhikara et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) , with five variants that toggle
curation, keys, and injection. At the distilled end sits a consolidated rulebook : the same
experience compressed once into at most eight rules ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) and injected at every
decision with no retrieval. At the direct end sits a flat K K -step history baseline, and at the
content-free end a token-matched padding arm and a four-content filler suite . Each
probe is both a design under evaluation and a control for its neighbors.

The evaluation yields four findings (Figure 1 ). Each is a statement about this
testbed, HighwayEnv with kinematic observations, discrete meta-actions, a 1 1 Hz decision
cadence, and gpt-4o-mini for every decisive contrast, and each baseline statement concerns our
audited ports under this harness (§ 4 ), not the published systems. Table 1 maps each finding to the confirmatory evidence behind it.

(M1) The warmup pool acts as a lottery: the headline gains are knife-edges that resampling
reverses. Both headline gains, the diagnostic’s → 0.95 0.45\!\to\!0.95 ( p = 0.001 p{=}0.001 ) and the merge margin of + 0.15 +0.15 (significant under pairing), are properties of a particular draw. Resampled, the diagnostic
effect spans 0.95 0.95 to 0.10 0.10 , and on merge the reported pool is the best of ten disjoint pools: each
memory exceeds No-Memory in one pool of ten (exact sign test p = 0.011 p\!=\!0.011 ), sits significantly below it
in five, and has a pool-averaged effect near − 0.20 -0.20 (§ 5 ). A pool swap also flips the
flat memory’s entire disposition from aggressive to timid on the history-necessity diagnostic
(Figure 1 c), and the rulebook’s “pool-immunity,” confirmed on five pools, reversed on
five fresh draws. (M2) No retrieval design tested exceeds our token-matched fillers. Injecting content-free
tokens produces merge-safety changes comparable to the memories’. Fillers span 0.59 0.59 to 0.80 0.80 on merge against the memories’ 0.66 0.66 to 0.67 0.67 , and the strongest
filler is significantly above both under paired tests. The designs that reach the collision-only
ceiling turn the caution dial hardest, and the dial needs no memory: a scripted always- SLOWER policy and a single 15 15 -token caution instruction both score 0.98 0.98 , and the rulebook’s best cells sit
at that operating point while metrics that price caution erase its lead (§ 5.1 ). (M3) The operative ingredient dissociates (curation on merges, key precision on the
diagnostic), and representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. TG-Mem and its five
variants never robustly beat flat memory across splits. Its temporal edges, the design’s central
component, contribute at most marginally in a pool-conditional ablation. The key × \times injection × 2 2\!\times\!2 (Table S44) finds compact injection consistently harmful while the key-type attribution
flips with the pool, and even raw temporal context handed to the planner directly does not pass the
history-necessity diagnostic that memory was hypothesized to solve. (M4) Baseline implementation quality silently inverts conclusions. A subtly crippled port
halved the flat baseline and manufactured a false win for our own method. We quantify the artifact and
release the audited ports.

(i) An evaluation framework for agent experience memory, with instruments this literature
lacks: the warmup pool as a resampled random factor with model-free pool-level tests, token-matched
filler and padding arms with a disclaimer × \times domain factorial (the nearest analog is exemplar
sensitivity in in-context learning ( Lu et al., 2022 ) ), oracle-certified diagnostics, scripted
certificate policies, caution-pricing metrics, and a quantified baseline audit. (ii) A probe suite spanning the design space, all ours: TG-Mem, the first episodic
temporal-graph memory for closed-loop driving, with five variants, plus the consolidated rulebook, the
flat K K -step history baseline, and the filler instruments. (iii) Findings M1 to M4 from the first controlled closed-loop comparison of flat,
structured, temporal-graph, distilled, and history-based context (one protocol, three backbones), a
real-data-seeded replay benchmark ( 54 54 highD cut-ins), and released ports, seeds, caches, and protocols.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

No prior driving-memory paper treats the warmup pool as a random factor
(DiLu ablates pool size , never composition ( Wen et al., 2024 ) ), and none measures agent memory
against token-matched irrelevant filler, even though random documents can improve RAG
accuracy ( Cuconasu et al., 2024 ) and length alone degrades it ( Du et al., 2025 ) .

DiLu ( Wen et al., 2024 ) established the closed-loop reason, reflect, and memorize paradigm on HighwayEnv . LimSim++ ( Fu et al., 2024a ) , LeapAD ( Mei et al., 2024 ) , and
SafeDrive ( Zhou et al., 2025 ) extend it, all retrieving over flat representations, and other
driving agents with memory or reflection ( Fu et al., 2024b ; Mao et al., 2024 ) share the same
confound of joint variation. RESPOND ( Chen et al., 2026 ) , the closest prior work, retrieves a × 3 5\!\times\!3 ego-grid by pattern matching. TG-Mem adds the two axes it lacks, temporal structure and
relational retrieval, though our experiments bear out no advantage for either, and our grid port’s failed
audit rules out any claim about the published system.

Outside driving, knowledge-graph memories, some of them temporal, report strong recall and context
reductions: Zep ( Rasmussen et al., 2025 ) , Mem0 and its graph variant ( Chhikara et al., 2025 ) , A-MEM ( Xu et al., 2025 ) ,
HippoRAG ( Jiménez Gutiérrez et al., 2024 ) , and Optimus-1 ( Li et al., 2024 ) . That evidence is almost entirely open-loop QA , and mixed even there (Mem0’s graph variant trails its flat variant on single-hop and
multi-hop questions). In closed-loop control we find only two same-agent comparisons of structured
against flat memory, AriGraph ( Anokhin et al., 2025 ) and G-Memory, where flat retrieval baselines often
score below no-memory on ALFWorld ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and neither is token-matched. The known tendency of unfiltered experience accumulation to degrade
performance ( Xiong et al., 2026 ) takes a sharper form here: the pool controls the sign.

That what gets stored and injected dominates is anticipated by Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) ,
Voyager ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , Generative Agents ( Park et al., 2023 ) , and DiLu’s own curated
pool ( Wen et al., 2024 ) . ExpeL ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) distills insights
open-loop. Our rulebook is its closed-loop instantiation, a distillation control that posts the
evaluation’s best collision-only cell while its gains price as caution (§ 5.1 ).

2026-10-21.title: PanoGraphGS: Unifying Panoptic Segmentation and Hierarchical 3D Scene Graphs with Gaussian Splatting
2026-10-21.authors: Jinghan Gao , Siyu Wang , Dongyu Feng , Yiyuan Pan , Rong Xiong
2026-10-21.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-21.abstract:
3D scene graphs support language-guided navigation by organizing physical
entities and their containment and spatial relations into hierarchical maps.
Building such structured maps requires a scene representation that consistently
distinguishes semantic regions and object instances across viewpoints. To this
end, we present PanoGraphGS, a unified framework that integrates panoptic 3D
Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical 3D scene graph construction.
The framework learns semantic and instance features on shared Gaussian
geometry. Prototype-based semantic learning and association-based instance
learning produce consistent panoptic predictions across viewpoints. The learned
representation supports novel-view panoptic segmentation and direct
Gaussian-level panoptic decoding. A semantic-aware scene graph module further
recovers a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy with containment and spatial
relations. We further release NaviGS, a real-world dataset for panoramic scene
understanding. The dataset provides 3DGS, mesh, RGB, semantic, and depth data. For 3D scene graph identification, PanoGraphGS
outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in object-node accuracy
by more than 50% points on average across Replica and
NaviGS.
PanoGraphGS also achieves
state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods in 2D
panoptic segmentation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of PanoGraphGS
in both hierarchical 3D scene
understanding and 2D panoptic segmentation. The project website is available at: https://github.com/gaojh0333/PanoGraphGS .
2026-10-21.introduction:
Panoptic 3D scene reconstruction is fundamental to language-guided robotic
navigation. Successful navigation requires embodied agents to recognize
semantic categories, maintain persistent instance identities, and reason about
spatial organization in a globally consistent map. Such
tasks require reasoning over nested containment and spatial relations. A 3D
scene graph formalizes this organization by representing physical entities as
nodes and their containment and spatial relations as
edges [ 1 , 2 ] .
3D Dynamic Scene
Graphs [ 3 ] , Hydra [ 4 ] , and
HOV-SG [ 5 ] , have advanced structured spatial mapping.
However, these pipelines commonly rely on per-pixel RGB-D observations or
depth-derived geometry. Incomplete or noisy depth can degrade object-extent
estimation, cross-view association, room partitioning, and spatial-relation
inference. Moreover, existing methods typically construct scene graphs and
dense panoptic representations separately, requiring an additional stage to
associate panoptic predictions with graph entities.

These limitations motivate a unified 3D representation that preserves
geometry, semantic categories, and persistent instance identities while being
learned directly from multi-view RGB observations. 3D Gaussian Splatting
(3DGS) [ 7 ] provides such a representation through explicit,
spatially anchored Gaussian primitives and differentiable rendering.
Visibility-aware rendering lifts multi-view semantic and instance supervision
into a shared 3D field. The learned features can be rendered for novel-view
panoptic prediction or decoded directly from Gaussians for 3D entity
abstraction. Unified-Lift [ 8 ] learns Gaussian- and
object-level representations from multi-view segmentation cues. More recently,
GaussianGraph [ 9 ] extends 3DGS toward scene graph
generation by clustering Gaussian primitives and associating them with CLIP
features and spatial relations extracted from 2D foundation models. However,
its reasoning mainly focuses on object-level spatial relations and relies on
high-dimensional vision–language features for semantic association, while
clustering may discard fine-grained spatial information. Explicit
identification, matching, and hierarchical association across the
floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy remain unaddressed. Consequently, dense
panoptic prediction and hierarchical scene organization remain loosely
integrated. Establishing globally consistent panoptic predictions within a
Gaussian representation therefore presents two challenges. First,
viewpoint-dependent visibility and occlusion produce nonuniform multi-view
supervision. Second, the same physical object may receive different view-local
pseudo-instance identifiers across views, causing conflicting identity
supervision without cross-view association. Gaussian-level labels also do not
explicitly encode the floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy or its containment and
spatial relations. Recovering this structure requires joint reasoning over
Gaussian semantics, persistent instance identities, and reconstructed geometry.

To address these challenges, we propose PanoGraphGS, an end-to-end framework
that integrates panoptic 3D Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical
3D scene graph construction. PanoGraphGS jointly learns semantic and instance
features anchored to shared Gaussian geometry. The semantic branch combines
residual feature projection and category prototypes with confidence-weighted
supervision, while the instance branch associates view-local pseudo-labels with
persistent Gaussian instance identities to ensure consistent object
correspondence across views. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , the
resulting panoptic Gaussian representation supports both panoptic segmentation
and direct Gaussian-level decoding. The
semantic-aware hierarchical reasoning module combines structural semantics with
Gaussian geometry to recover the floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy
and its containment and spatial relations, enabling structured spatial queries
such as locating the bed1 in the living room on floor1 . CLIP [ 10 ] is further used to assign functional
categories to rooms. Our main contributions are:

We propose Prototype-Based Semantic Learning, which jointly optimizes 2D rendered and 3D Gaussian features in a unified semantic space, overcoming the limitation of optimizing features in only the 2D or 3D domain.

We propose Prototype-Based Semantic Learning, which jointly optimizes 2D rendered and 3D Gaussian features in a unified semantic space, overcoming the limitation of optimizing features in only the 2D or 3D domain.

We propose Association-Based Instance Learning, which associates view-local instance masks with persistent identities for cross-frame consistent panoptic prediction, with confidence-aware supervision reducing the impact of unreliable labels.

We propose a semantic-aware hierarchical 3D scene graph construction method that organizes learned panoptic Gaussians into a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy without additional training or RGB-D inputs.

We achieve state-of-the-art performance in both 2D panoptic segmentation and 3D scene graph construction.

1. We propose Prototype-Based Semantic Learning, which jointly optimizes 2D rendered and 3D Gaussian features in a unified semantic space, overcoming the limitation of optimizing features in only the 2D or 3D domain.

2. We propose Association-Based Instance Learning, which associates view-local instance masks with persistent identities for cross-frame consistent panoptic prediction, with confidence-aware supervision reducing the impact of unreliable labels.

3. We propose a semantic-aware hierarchical 3D scene graph construction method that organizes learned panoptic Gaussians into a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy without additional training or RGB-D inputs.

4. We achieve state-of-the-art performance in both 2D panoptic segmentation and 3D scene graph construction.
2026-10-21.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A 3D Gaussian Segmentation

3DGS-based segmentation has progressed from open-vocabulary semantics and instance grouping to panoptic understanding. Open-vocabulary methods embed vision–language features into 3D Gaussian primitives. LangSplat [ 11 ] learns language-aligned Gaussian features, while OpenGaussian [ 12 ] and OVGaussian [ 13 ] extend this paradigm to point-level open-vocabulary segmentation. Mask-lifting methods transfer 2D masks and instance information into Gaussian representations. Gaussian Grouping [ 14 ] learns identity-aware Gaussian features for object grouping, while Unified-Lift [ 8 ] combines Gaussian- and object-level representations with association learning for 3D instance segmentation. More recently, PLGS [ 15 ] jointly learns semantic and instance attributes from multi-view supervision, and PanoSLAM [ 16 ] integrates panoptic Gaussian learning with sequential RGB-D mapping. Similarly, PanoGS [ 17 ] combines open-vocabulary semantics with instance segmentation, while PanopticSplatting [ 18 ] introduces query-guided cross-view label refinement for panoptic segmentation. Despite these advances, existing methods mainly focus on novel-view panoptic prediction, with feature optimization restricted to either the 2D or 3D domain. In contrast, PanoGraphGS jointly optimizes 2D and 3D features, enabling both panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian-level decoding.

## II-B Hierarchical 3D Scene Graphs

Armeni et al. [ 1 ] first organize buildings, rooms, and objects into a multi-layer graph, while 3DSSG [ 2 ] learns object relations from indoor reconstructions. 3DDGS [ 3 ] integrate geometry with objects, places, and agents, Hydra [ 4 ] enables online hierarchical mapping, and HOV-SG [ 5 ] introduces an open-vocabulary floor-room-object hierarchy. GaussianGraph [ 9 ] novelly constructs structured scene graphs directly from Gaussians. However, these approaches commonly rely on per-pixel RGB-D observations for geometry and primarily focus on object-level recognition. In contrast, PanoGraphGS leverages learned semantic and instance features together with Gaussian geometry to recover a hierarchical floor-room-stuff-object scene graph with explicit containment and spatial relations without training.
