# 2 Background and Problem Formulation

## 2.1 Multimodal Agents

A multimodal agent is a goal-directed system that interacts with the environment through multimodal observations and external actions. Its observations may comprise language, images, structured states, and tool outputs. Its actions may involve language generation, GUI operations, API calls, or tool execution. At task step k k , the agent selects an action according to a k ∼ π ( ⋅ ∣ g , h k , m k ) a_{k}\sim\pi(\cdot\mid g,h_{k},m_{k}) , where g g denotes the task goal, h k h_{k} the interaction history, and m k m_{k} the persistent memory. The action a k a_{k} queries or modifies the external environment and yields a new observation o k + 1 o_{k+1} . The resulting observation is incorporated into the interaction history or persistent memory, providing context for subsequent decisions. This process forms a closed interaction loop in which the agent can adjust its behavior based on environmental feedback [ 217 , 213 , 198 , 236 , 171 , 186 ] .

## 2.2 Robotic Systems

A robotic system interacts with the environment through sensing and actuation. Its observations may comprise vision, proprioception, force, and tactile signals. Its task-level actions may be represented as skills, waypoints, trajectories, or motion commands. These actions must be grounded with respect to the robot’s embodiment and estimated state. Their execution is further subject to geometric, dynamic, safety, and control constraints [ 17 , 50 , 30 , 69 ] .

At task step k k , this grounding can be expressed as a k → Exec e u ⁡ ( t ) a_{k}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Exec}_{e}}u(t) for t ∈ [ t k , t k + 1 ) t\in[t_{k},t_{k+1}) . Here, Exec e \mathrm{Exec}_{e} denotes the execution operator conditioned on embodiment e e . The control input u ⁡ ( t ) u(t) may represent joint-position, velocity, or torque commands. This formulation also covers learned and end-to-end policies that implement the grounding process implicitly [ 14 , 13 , 12 , 21 ] .

## 2.3 Multimodal Embodied Agents

A multimodal embodied agent (MMEA) can be characterized by five PAPAV capabilities: multimodal perception, consequence anticipation, task-level planning, embodied action, and outcome verification. The system maintains task state throughout sensing and execution. Execution feedback informs subsequent decisions. These functions operate as a persistent closed loop between multimodal task processing and physical execution. Observed effects may differ from anticipated outcomes during execution. These discrepancies can prompt the agent to revise its task belief, reassess action feasibility, and adjust the remaining plan. Failure of an individual action does not necessarily imply failure of the overall task. The agent can use available evidence to assess recovery options and select an alternative action consistent with the task goal. Persistent embodied task loop: task-relevant state persists across successive rounds of physical execution, and selected actions can produce observable changes in the physical environment.

Task-level capability returns: each claimed PAPAV capability provides a documented output that can influence a subsequent task-level decision within the interaction loop.

Embodiment-grounded commitments: task decisions explicitly account for physical feasibility, execution timing, and control constraints imposed by the deployed body and operating environment.

## 2.4 PAPAV Roles in the Task Loop

Equation ( 1 ) defines five task-level roles by their outputs and uses. Perceive forms a task belief from multimodal evidence. Anticipate estimates the state changes caused by candidate interventions, and need only estimate decision-relevant consequences [ 191 ] . Plan selects and organizes actions under task, environmental, and embodiment constraints. Act grounds the selected plan into an executable intervention and reports its progress. Verify converts post-action evidence into a verdict for continuation, termination, retry, or replanning, and must inform subsequent task decisions [ 79 , 38 ] . 2026-10-22.title: Asymmetric On-Policy Distillation Learns In-Context Exploration
2026-10-22.authors: Sriyash Poddar , Yanda Bao , Jacob Krantz , Matthew Chang , Xavier Puig , Roozbeh Mottaghi , Natasha Jaques , Abhishek Gupta
2026-10-22.abstract:
Sequential decision-making under partial observability is difficult because agents must explore to infer hidden, task-relevant information before acting effectively.
Learning such information-gathering behaviors tabula rasa via online reinforcement learning is sample-inefficient, whereas offline imitation averages expert actions across hidden states and fails to learn exploration. In this work, we propose ASTEROID, a simple and effective student–teacher supervised learning framework that can learn test-time exploration. Although a privileged expert never needs to explore, we demonstrate that a history-conditioned student can learn to do so when trained with on-policy contexts: the student first collects on-policy context under partial observability, and the privileged expert provides action labels conditioned on that context. By distilling expert actions directly conditioned on the student’s on-policy history, the student learns to systematically resolve partial observability, i.e., search while uncertain and exploit once the hidden state is revealed. This enables efficient test-time exploration (similar to Bayesian posterior sampling) without incurring the impractical training-data costs of reinforcement learning. Across a diverse range of eleven different environments, including discrete exploration benchmarks, robotic manipulation, navigation, and Procgen environments, ASTEROID achieves ∼ \sim 2 × \times higher returns under fixed exploration budgets, uses up to ∼ \sim 100 × \times fewer interactions than RL baselines, and outperforms frontier models at exploration. Finally, our method transfers policies trained in simulation to vision-denied real-world robot manipulation, exhibiting efficient exploration and increasing success by + 40 % +40\% over standard distillation. Overall, it provides a simple yet surprisingly effective framework to learn efficient test-time exploration.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Sequential decision-making under partial observability is a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL) [ 34 , 53 ] . In the real world, from robotics to embodied AI, agents receive only partial, noisy observations of the environment. To act successfully, agents must first explore to uncover hidden, task-relevant information [ 31 , 79 , 42 , 74 , 46 , 71 ] . For example, a household robot searching for an object must use onboard sensing to infer likely object locations, track locations it has already searched, and adapt future exploration based on prior attempts [ 12 , 11 , 30 ] . These problems are formalized as partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) [ 34 ] .

Solving these tasks requires policies with memory [ 28 , 50 ] . Learning them from scratch via recurrent RL is sample-inefficient, since the agent must learn to gather information and exploit it at the same time [ 5 , 79 , 21 ] . One way to improve sample efficiency is to assume training-time access to a privileged expert that observes the hidden state and acts accordingly. For example, in household navigation, an oracle planner could use the full map of the training environments, which is unavailable at deployment. In practice, these teachers can be trained in fully observed tasks using RL, imitation learning, or hybrid approaches [ 78 , 75 , 60 , 27 , 52 ] . This expert can teach the student how to act once the hidden state is known, but not how to find it [ 44 ] . As a result, naively copying the expert does not teach the student to explore [ 70 ] . Interactive imitation [ 65 ] offers a natural fix by relabeling student mistakes with expert actions. However, standard approaches [ 59 ] train the student to predict the average expert action across possible hidden states, so it dithers between hypotheses instead of resolving them [ 37 , 70 ] . Other approaches propose to address the student-teacher mismatch using expensive online RL [ 74 ] , differentiable experts [ 73 ] , or offline coverage assumptions [ 42 ] .

In this work, we propose ASTEROID ( A symmetric S tudent Te acher R oll- O ut I n-context D istillation), a framework that shows that privileged experts can teach exploration through interactive imitation. The idea is simple: the student generates the history online, and the expert provides the labels. ASTEROID rolls out the current student under partial observability, producing a history of observations, actions, and rewards, then asks the expert what it would do from the state the student has reached. The expert does not explore; it only labels the student’s histories. As a result, failed searches and probes become useful context: they specify evidence accumulated so far, while the expert provides next actions given the hidden state. With on-policy history, the policy can identify inconsistent hypotheses and adapt its exploration and action distribution accordingly.

Why does this teach exploration? A partial history represents uncertainty over the hidden state. Returning to household navigation: suppose the object could be in location A A , B B , or C C . If the student searches A A and finds nothing, its history rules out A A but is still consistent with B B and C C . A privileged expert would label this history with search ( B ) when the object is at B B , and search ( C ) when it is at C C . The student therefore learns to act and explore the remaining valid actions: if it fails at A A , it samples search ( B ) or search ( C ) . If it then fails at B B , every label is search ( C ) , since only C C remains. Unlike random sampling of locations, the policy conditions on its history and never retries hypotheses it has ruled out. Across many training tasks, ambiguous histories are labeled with a distribution of potential, consistent expert trajectories. The student samples from this distribution to explore, and each new observation and feedback eliminates additional hypotheses. The key insight: the set of histories that the student needs to learn to adapt from (e.g., failing at A A , failing at B B and then moving to C C ) is entirely covered by on-policy behavior. This is in-context exploration , i.e., searching while uncertain, and exploiting once the hidden state is revealed. Additionally, we show that a curriculum over the student rollout horizon improves sample efficiency and enables longer-context adaptation (Section 5 ). Overall, ASTEROID incorporates very simple changes into standard online student-teacher distillation to enable test-time exploration behavior .

We show both empirically (Section 6 ) and theoretically (Appendix H ) that ASTEROID approximates Bayesian posterior sampling, a provably efficient exploration strategy [ 53 ] . However, posterior sampling has been hard to scale: prior approaches maintain an explicit posterior [ 3 ] or assume infinite offline data [ 42 ] , which are intractable in realistic settings. ASTEROID avoids both: it does not maintain an explicit posterior, and on-policy supervised learning avoids impractical data costs. Because it is a simple extension of student–teacher distillation, ASTEROID works with modern architectures and existing sim-to-real frameworks [ 75 ] . In summary, we make the following contributions:

We present ASTEROID, a simple student–teacher distillation framework that enables in-context exploration and test-time improvement learned solely from privileged experts.

We evaluate our method across 11 environments, including navigation in realistic household simulators and real-world robot manipulation, where it outperforms RL and supervised baselines under fixed exploration budgets while using two orders of magnitude fewer training interactions.

We show that learned policies exhibit efficient real-world exploration and, under appropriate assumptions, recover posterior sampling with error linear rather than quadratic in context length.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Student–Teacher Distillation. Learning from privileged experts arises in settings from self-driving [ 13 ] to robotic exploration [ 17 ] . Interactive imitation addresses the covariate shift that drives the learner into unseen states [ 59 ] , and prior work suggests that on-policy imitation is necessary under partial observability [ 65 ] . Our work targets this non-realizable regime, where the learner must take information-gathering actions that are not recoverable from a fully observed expert [ 63 , 40 ] . Prior approaches handle this via additional assumptions, such as differentiable experts [ 73 ] , predicting hidden information [ 38 ] , or incorporating RL with bootstrapping to induce exploration [ 74 , 70 , 61 , 37 ] . In contrast, we learn information-gathering behavior using iterative distillation of expert actions conditioned on on-policy histories, which is more sample-efficient than RL-based alternatives.

Meta Learning. Meta-RL learns adaptive exploration across task distributions using recurrent policies [ 28 , 21 , 79 , 44 ] , but requires extensive online interaction [ 5 ] , making it difficult to scale to high-dimensional, sparse-reward domains. Our approach replaces this expensive RL-based adaptation with supervised learning, making it efficient to learn long-horizon exploration. Further, unlike prior work limited to Bayes-Adaptive MDPs [ 40 , 79 , 42 ] , our method scales to POMDPs, where the policy explores within a single episode to estimate the underlying state and achieve task success.

Posterior Sampling. Posterior sampling methods [ 67 , 53 ] drive exploration by maintaining a belief over hidden parameters, acting optimally under samples from this belief, and updating it based on feedback. Despite strong empirical and theoretical results [ 10 , 53 ] , such approaches require maintaining an explicit posterior and solving for policies under sampled parameters [ 53 , 3 ] , limiting scalability to high-dimensional settings. ASTEROID does not explicitly optimize a posterior-sampling objective. Instead, posterior-sampling-like behavior emerges through iterative on-policy distillation, even in high-dimensional continuous environments (Section 6 ), and we include theoretical insights to show convergence to posterior sampling on the covered history support (Appendix H ). In Section 6 , we show that current frontier models are inefficient at performing such exploration under partial observability, motivating the need to explicitly learn such behavior.

In-Context Decision-Making. Transformers trained autoregressively on sequential data exhibit in-context learning [ 9 , 25 ] , which Decision Transformer [ 15 ] and Algorithm Distillation [ 39 ] leverage for decision-making. These works focus on using online rollouts as context to adapt behavior without external prompts. Closest to our work, Decision-Pretrained Transformer [ 42 ] learns an in-context policy that performs posterior sampling by pairing randomly generated contexts with privileged expert supervision. Such methods assume the offline dataset covers all possible interaction histories, which is intractable in high-dimensional domains. ASTEROID, instead, uses on-policy contexts, removing the coverage assumption and scaling to much harder, higher-dimensional problems (Section 6 ).

We include an extended discussion of related work in Appendix A .

2026-10-22.title: AtomicRL: Atomic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-22.authors: Likui Zhang , Zhe Zhu , Zhihao Zhan , Yibo Bai , Hanlin Wang , Dongwei Li , Bin Wang , Tianle Zhang , Xiaodan Liang , Liang Lin
2026-10-22.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-22.abstract: Vision–language–action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration. AtomicRL introduces Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses semantic-aware gating to constrain TD residuals from failed atomic subtasks from propagating across task boundaries, mitigating credit contamination while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%. These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) ( Beyer et al., 2024 ; Deitke et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) have established Vision–Language–Action (VLA) ( Intelligence et al., 2025b ; Kim et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025b ) models as a prominent paradigm for robotic manipulation. Although imitation learning (IL) from large-scale robot demonstrations enables VLA models to acquire diverse manipulation skills, its performance is inherently constrained by the coverage of the demonstration data. Reinforcement learning (RL) overcomes this limitation by directly optimizing policies with task feedback obtained through environment interaction, and recent work ( Li et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) has successfully applied RL to VLA models. However, existing VLA-RL methods still face substantial challenges in long-horizon manipulation tasks.

First, most methods rely on terminal-only success rewards. In an episode that completes the first k k subtasks but fails at subtask k + 1 k+1 , the absence of a terminal success reward causes generalized advantage estimation (GAE) to propagate failure-related temporal-difference (TD) residuals backward to t 0 t_{0} , suppressing the advantages of correctly executed actions. We refer to this as credit contamination, where useful behavior in failed trajectories is systematically devalued, with the effect worsening as the horizon grows.
Prior work ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Tan et al., 2025 ; Zhai et al., 2025 ) mitigates reward sparsity through stage-level preference optimization or subtask-level intermediate rewards, but these approaches alter reward density without resolving credit contamination.
Second, subtask mastery is uneven, with failures increasingly concentrated in a few bottleneck subtasks during later training. Uniform task sampling and fixed exploration then waste interaction budget on saturated subtasks while providing insufficient exploration for the bottlenecks.

To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, as illustrated in Fig. 1 , an RL post-training framework built around atomic task structure. Our key insight is that semantic subtasks provide a unified basis for both the propagation of learning signals and the allocation of exploration resources. AtomicRL couples Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO) with Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE), supported by a lightweight Progress–Completion Critic (PCC) that estimates atomic subtask progress and completion boundaries. PCC also provides progress estimates for constructing dense progress-based shaping rewards (PBSR).
SAPO modulates TD-residual propagation in advantage estimation with a soft gate conditioned on semantic boundaries. Within each atomic subtask, it preserves standard GAE trace decay; across subtask boundaries, it maintains propagation between successful subtasks while attenuating residuals from failed subtasks. By leaving one-step TD residuals and value bootstrapping unchanged, SAPO reduces failure interference while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and successful subtask dependencies.
BATE tracks the mastery of each subtask via a moving average of its completion rate, jointly adjusts the sampling weight of full tasks and the strength of subtask-level entropy regularization, directing interaction and exploration resources toward bottleneck subtasks.
Finally, to support physical deployment, we develop an automated Real2Sim2Real pipeline. Given a single real-world multimodal demonstration and the required auxiliary information, the pipeline reconstructs an interactive simulation environment. It connects simulation-based RL with real-robot deployment, shifting costly physical trial-and-error to parallel simulation with reproducible resets.

We conduct extensive experiments in both simulation and the real world. On LIBERO-LONG ( Liu et al., 2023 ) AtomicRL achieves success rates of 99.0% with π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} ( Intelligence et al., 2025b ) and 98.8% with OpenVLA-OFT ( Kim et al., 2025 ) , improving over PPO by 3.6% and 4.0%. On CALVIN ABC-D ( Mees et al., 2022 ) , the average completed sequence length improves from 3.56 to 4.56, while the success rate of completing full five-subtask chain improves by 9.5% over PPO.
Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further yields an average improvement of 21.3% on real-robot long-horizon tasks. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of AtomicRL for long-horizon VLA reinforcement learning. Overall, our contributions are as follows:

We introduce AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework built around atomic task structure for long-horizon robotic manipulation.

We propose SAPO to mitigate cross-subtask credit interference and BATE to adaptively direct task sampling and exploration toward bottleneck subtasks.

We develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that streamlines simulation construction and RL training for efficient real-robot deployment.

We validate the effectiveness of AtomicRL through extensive experiments conducted in both simulated environments and real-world robots.

1. We introduce AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework built around atomic task structure for long-horizon robotic manipulation.

2. We propose SAPO to mitigate cross-subtask credit interference and BATE to adaptively direct task sampling and exploration toward bottleneck subtasks.

3. We develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that streamlines simulation construction and RL training for efficient real-robot deployment.

4. We validate the effectiveness of AtomicRL through extensive experiments conducted in both simulated environments and real-world robots.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Reinforcement Learning for VLA Models

Reinforcement learning (RL) optimizes policies through environment interaction and task-level feedback. Recent work has explored both offline and online RL paradigms for VLA policies. Offline RL approaches leverage task feedback to enable continued policy improvement ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2025a ) . π 0.6 ∗ \pi_{0.6}^{*} ( Intelligence et al., 2025a ) integrates expert demonstrations, autonomous interaction data, and human corrections through advantage-conditioned learning. For scalable online training, VLA-RL ( Lu et al., 2025 ) and SimpleVLA-RL ( Li et al., 2026 ) explore frameworks for continually improving VLA policies through environment interaction, while RL4VLA ( Liu et al., 2026 ) systematically investigates how different RL algorithms affect VLA generalization. Furthermore, Flow Q-Learning ( Park et al., 2025 ) , Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025a ) and π R ​ L \pi_{RL} ( Chen et al., 2026a ) investigate online RL fine-tuning for flow-matching policies, addressing challenges in action likelihood computation and exploration.

RL for long-horizon manipulation introduces additional challenges due to sparse and delayed task feedback ( Chen et al., 2026b ; Li et al., 2025c ; Dalal et al., 2024 ) . STARE-VLA ( Xu et al., 2025 ) exploits the semantic stage structure of trajectories to perform stage-level preference optimization and reward shaping, while IG-RFT ( Su et al., 2026 ) combines trajectory-level and subtask-level rewards to provide intermediate guidance. However, dense reward shaping provides useful process guidance over long-horizon trajectories, but cannot eliminate the spurious interference caused by later-stage failures.
In contrast, AtomicRL gates the propagation of advantage signals at the semantic boundaries of atomic tasks to prevent cross-task interference from unreliable signals, while allocating the exploration budget to bottleneck atomic tasks to improve the efficiency of long-horizon RL.

## 2.2 Online Reinforcement Learning in Real World

Online reinforcement learning for real-world manipulation is constrained by interaction costs and safety risks. To reduce reliance on real-robot trial and error, some research focuses on learning action-conditioned world models and optimizing policies through imagined interactions ( Team et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025a ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Jiang et al., 2026a ) . WoVR ( Jiang et al., 2026b ) addresses prediction errors and their accumulation to improve the reliability of model-generated rollouts for VLA reinforcement fine-tuning
, while PlayWorld ( Yin et al., 2026 ) and RISE ( Yang et al., 2026b ) learn world models from autonomous robot interactions and transfers policies trained through model-based reinforcement learning to real hardware.
Although world models can effectively capture short-term dynamics, long-horizon predictions still exhibit visual distortions and action–state inconsistencies. Other studies adopt an explicit Real2Sim2Real method, combining real-scene reconstruction with physics simulation to provide interactive environments for policy optimization ( Li et al., 2025b ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . GSWorld ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) integrates Gaussian-on-Mesh assets with physics engines to support visually faithful policy training, while
RialTo ( Torne et al., 2024 ) constructs digital twins of real-world environments and uses reinforcement learning in simulation to improve policy robustness.
However, constructing environments requires coordinating scene reconstruction, physical asset preparation, and control alignment, making it complex and costly to reproduce. AtomicRL introduces an automated Real2Sim2Real pipeline that uses only a single demonstration to reconstruct a real-world manipulation scene as an interactive simulation environment for long-horizon online RL. The trained policies are then transferred to physical robots for evaluation.

2026-10-22.title: Do Earth-Trained Humanoid Controllers Walk on the Moon? Gravity, Terrain, and Soil Transfer
2026-10-22.authors: Guillem Casadesus Vila , Sri Aditya Deevi , Grace X. Gao
2026-10-22.comment: . Supplementary material () included as an ancillary file
2026-10-22.abstract: The Moon changes gravity, terrain, and soil at once. Learned locomotion has studied reduced gravity on rigid ground and granular terrain mostly at Earth gravity, but not humanoids under both, generalist-controller transfer, or the Earth cost of lunar adaptation. On a simulated Unitree G1, we train 12 policies with one recipe, varying gravity, terrain geometry, and ground contact (rigid or three-dimensional resistive force theory, 3D RFT), and including Earth-to-Moon fine-tuning and gravity randomization. We test them at both gravities on rigid ground and 3D RFT, and at their training gravity on three held-out soil models. We also test the frozen SONIC, a released generalist humanoid controller, at both gravities on rigid ground only. Gravity transfer is asymmetric. Earth-trained policies keep 0.64 to 0.75 survival at the Moon on flat rigid ground, Moon-trained and fine-tuned policies cannot stand at Earth, and SONIC survives at most 0.10 at the Moon. Rough training lifts combined-tile survival from 0.53 to 0.98 at Earth and 0.80 to 0.99 at the Moon. In 3D RFT, soil training helps on Earth sand, on tiles and for rough-trained policies also on flat sand. On the stiffer lunar soil it helps only flat-trained Earth policies at Earth and changes the survival of Moon-trained policies by at most a few hundredths. In the sampled rollouts of the held-out soil models, Moon-trained policies keep most of their rigid-ground progress on lunar regolith at the low G1 foot pressure, with per-seed progress ratios of 0.84 to 1.39 apart from one seed with a short rigid reference. A gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain has a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 ° 20\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} . Lunar results are simulation predictions conditional on the contact model and soil stiffness.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Walking on the Moon is hard for people. Suited Apollo crews often loped [ 1 ] , fell 27 times across the Apollo surface missions [ 2 ] , and paid a metabolic cost that limits how long astronauts can work outside [ 3 , 1 ] . Humanoid robots could take mundane and dangerous surface tasks off the crew [ 4 ] , and their form suits tools and interfaces designed for people, a premise of NASA’s Robonaut 2 [ 5 ] . Learned humanoid controllers now walk over rough, deformable, and sloped terrain on Earth [ 6 , 7 ] , but lunar operation changes several of these conditions at once ( Fig. 1 ). Gravity falls to 1.62 m s − 2 1.62\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-2} , craters and rocks, with measured size statistics [ 8 , 9 ] , change the available footholds, and regolith yields under contact [ 10 ] . A controller can stay upright under these changes yet make little commanded progress, and adapting it to one condition can cost performance in another.

Prior learned-locomotion studies mostly adapt one task-specific recipe to one of these conditions, reduced gravity on rigid ground [ 11 , 12 ] or granular media at Earth gravity [ 13 ] . A quadrupedal manipulator trained at lunar gravity has been tested on compliant ground contact withheld from training, with friction calibrated to a regolith simulant [ 14 ] , and a quadruped has been trained with granular contact for the lunar surface [ 15 ] . Only two of these study a humanoid, each under a single condition. To our knowledge, no study has tested a pretrained generalist humanoid controller, such as SONIC [ 16 ] , under reduced gravity, or compared fine-tuning, training from scratch, and gravity randomization for the Moon by Earth performance and compute.

We ask how much of an Earth-trained humanoid controller’s performance survives lunar gravity, terrain, and soil, and what it costs to close the gap. We train 12 G1 policies with one recipe ( Fig. 2 ). Eight are trained from scratch and cover every combination of Earth or Moon gravity, flat or rough terrain, and rigid or granular ground. The other four are two Earth-to-Moon fine-tunes and two gravity-randomized policies. Granular ground uses three-dimensional resistive force theory (3D RFT) [ 17 , 18 ] , and we call training on it soil training. The released SONIC controller is a frozen reference. Every policy faces the gravity change, so we study gravity first, then whether rough or soil training widens or narrows the remaining gap.

The contributions of this letter are:

A two-way study of gravity transfer for learned humanoid locomotion, testing 12 policies and the pretrained SONIC controller at Earth and lunar gravity, which shows that transfer is asymmetric.

An analysis of training on rough terrain and on 3D RFT soil at each gravity, on held-out terrain, slopes, and soils.

A comparison of training strategies for the Moon, namely training from scratch, fine-tuning, and gravity randomization, finding that the gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain keeps a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 ° 20\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} .

An evaluation on three soil models held out of training: the material point method (MPM) [ 19 , 20 ] , the soil contact model (SCM) [ 21 ] , and the continuous representation model (CRM) [ 22 ] .

1. A two-way study of gravity transfer for learned humanoid locomotion, testing 12 policies and the pretrained SONIC controller at Earth and lunar gravity, which shows that transfer is asymmetric.

2. An analysis of training on rough terrain and on 3D RFT soil at each gravity, on held-out terrain, slopes, and soils.

3. A comparison of training strategies for the Moon, namely training from scratch, fine-tuning, and gravity randomization, finding that the gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain keeps a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 ° 20\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} .

4. An evaluation on three soil models held out of training: the material point method (MPM) [ 19 , 20 ] , the soil contact model (SCM) [ 21 ] , and the continuous representation model (CRM) [ 22 ] .

# II Related Work

## II-A Humanoid Controllers and Adaptation

History-based policies transfer humanoid locomotion to hardware [ 6 ] , including blind walking over rough, deformable, and sloped surfaces [ 7 ] , and Unitree releases G1 velocity-tracking training and deployment code [ 23 ] . For dynamics that change at deployment, rapid motor adaptation trains a policy across randomized conditions with a module that infers them online [ 24 ] . Randomizing simulator parameters during training is the standard way to obtain such robustness [ 25 , 26 ] , whereas fine-tuning a trained network on a new condition can erase earlier skills, an effect known as catastrophic forgetting [ 27 ] . Training one policy across Earth and lunar gravity applies the same idea to the Moon.

Generalist whole-body controllers instead learn broad motor skills from human motion [ 28 , 29 ] . SONIC trains a motion-tracking controller on about 700 hours of motion capture and connects it to navigation through a real-time kinematic planner [ 16 ] . To our knowledge, none of these controllers has been evaluated under reduced gravity. Because SONIC’s references, observations, and pretraining differ from the velocity policy’s, we compare complete controllers rather than architectures.

## II-B Reduced-Gravity and Planetary Legged Locomotion

Space humanoids have so far served manipulation, teleoperation, and model-based walking rather than learned locomotion [ 5 , 30 , 31 ] . SpaceBok and SpaceHopper study hopping and attitude control under reduced gravity [ 32 , 33 ] , and Xu et al. address low-gravity jumping [ 34 ] . Arm et al. study gravity-scaled, power-optimized quadrupedal walking with a base-offload rig, evaluated on flat rigid ground [ 12 ] . Belmonte-Baeza et al. train a quadrupedal mobile manipulator at lunar gravity on rough, hilly, and cratered terrain and test it on compliant ground contact, withheld from training, with friction calibrated to a regolith simulant [ 14 ] . Vyas trains quadrupedal policies with rigid and granular lunar-regolith foot contact and finds that granular contact makes training harder, changes the gait, and raises energy use [ 15 ] . A quadruped climbed granular Mars-analog slopes of up to 25 ° 25\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} , the testbed maximum [ 35 ] . Klein and Roberts use the G1 and Unitree’s training code to compare an Earth baseline, lunar fine-tuning, and lunar training from scratch [ 11 ] . Unlike these studies, we train across gravity, terrain, and ground with one recipe and three seeds, and we test whether policies adapted for the Moon still walk on Earth.

Human walk–run transitions under reduced gravity are usually described by the Froude number [ 36 , 1 ] . At equal Froude number, however, humans in simulated reduced gravity change relative stride length by up to 67 % 67\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} [ 37 ] , so we use it to normalize speed without assuming that gaits match.

## II-C Granular Contact and Prediction Credibility

Resistive force theory (RFT) predicts local intrusion stresses in granular media [ 17 ] , and its three-dimensional form extends it to arbitrary intruder motion [ 18 ] . Choi et al. combine granular simulation with adaptive quadrupedal control and physical sand tests [ 38 ] , Chen et al. validate biped sinkage and slip on sand [ 39 ] , and Kerimoglu et al. show that foot-induced yielding and foot shape change bipedal performance on granular slopes [ 40 ] . GM-Loco trains a G1 with 3D RFT and checks the policy in MPM [ 20 ] and on basalt, dry sand, and beach sand [ 13 ] .

How granular resistance scales with gravity is unsettled. Low-velocity drag in cohesionless spheres is proportional to effective gravity over a 20-fold range [ 41 ] , whereas the penetration depth of low-velocity impacts into sand is independent of effective gravity over the tested range [ 42 ] , cone resistance on a lunar simulant is only 9 to 29 % 29\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} lower at 1/6 g than at 1 g [ 43 ] , and parabolic-flight wheel tests show that gravity acting on the soil itself changes wheel mobility at matched load [ 44 ] . Since no Earth test settles these differences for lunar regolith, we judge simulators by whether their comparisons predict real ones [ 45 ] and ask whether policy comparisons keep their sign across soil models rather than which model is correct.

2026-10-22.title: Test-Time Motion Steering for Perceptive Humanoid Fall Recovery
2026-10-22.authors: Osher Azulay , Cheng-Lin Hsieh , Stella X. Yu
2026-10-22.abstract:
Humanoid fall recovery requires selecting a motion that suits both the surrounding scene and the task. The same fallen pose can admit several ways to stand, with different routes, support transitions, and final headings. Yet reliable recovery alone does not provide control over which of these alternatives the robot executes. Steering this choice requires anticipating the physical consequences of a requested movement. We present RISE, an approach to perceptive humanoid recovery that lets task objectives steer how the robot returns to standing at inference time.
It builds on two insights: diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movements, and anticipating how these movements unfold allows recovery to be steered toward a task objective. We learn a recovery vocabulary that connects intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback. A visual diffusion planner learns from executions of this vocabulary to predict motion intent as future body states. Task costs guide this prediction toward a desired heading, rise speed, or path. The planner then generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent, allowing the requested movement to shape its execution. Simulation experiments demonstrate diverse recoveries, terrain adaptation, and test-time steering without retraining, complemented by real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1. Project page: RISE .
2026-10-22.introduction:
For a fallen humanoid, standing up is only part of recovery: the robot must also choose how to stand. Fig. shows that even the same fallen pose
admits several ways to stand, such as rolling to either side or rising
directly. The scene and next task
determine which fits: a wall can obstruct a recovery route, a step can
change the available support, and the task may require the robot to face a
particular direction. Steering lets task objectives select among feasible
recoveries, preparing the robot to continue its task.

Prior work has achieved reliable fall recovery and controllable whole-body
motion, but combining onboard perception with test-time steering remains under-explored, as Fig. 2 shows. Recovery
controllers now stand up from diverse postures and manage falls [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , and VIGOR adapts
recovery to uneven ground using egocentric depth [ 4 ] .
In these methods, the learned policy alone decides how the robot stands.
Other whole-body controllers,
including perceptive ones, are often directed through commands such as
joystick or heading inputs [ 5 , 6 ] . These
commands work well for trained behaviors, but each must be defined, with
labeled data, before training. Guided motion generation is more flexible: it
expresses task objectives as test-time costs that can be designed after
training and combined as needed [ 7 , 8 ] .
We bring this flexibility to perceptive fall recovery.

Steering fall recovery is harder than steering from an upright pose. The
robot starts from varied fallen configurations and must shift support among
its hands, knees, feet, and torso to rise, so its motor actions must adapt to
its configuration and contacts. Uneven terrain compounds the difficulty:
steps, slopes, and nearby obstacles change the available supports and routes,
so a request feasible in one scene can fail in another. Yet this is the
practical setting, as humanoids rarely operate on flat ground with clear
space. Steering here needs several feasible ways to stand from each pose, but
each recorded recovery shows only one. It also needs to anticipate how a
requested movement will unfold under changing contact with the surrounding
terrain.

We introduce RISE (Perceptive R ecovery via I ntent S t e ering),
which addresses these needs with two insights (Fig. 3 ). First, diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movement
patterns , providing several ways to stand from each pose. We compose
compatible recorded segments and adapt them to terrain, building a multimodal recovery repertoire. From the repertoire’s physical
executions, we learn a recovery vocabulary : motion latents that a
feedback decoder turns into motor actions using proprioception and egocentric
depth. Second, a planner trained on the robot’s own executions can
anticipate how recovery will unfold , so steering its predictions shapes the
executed recovery. Our visual diffusion planner
predicts this unfolding as motion intent : a sequence of
future body states. Prior planners denoise future
states jointly with actions or motion
latents [ 9 , 8 ] . Our planner is
instead state-first: task costs steer the predicted states, then motion latents
are generated conditioned on them, making the requested recovery an explicit
condition for execution.

In
simulation, RISE recovers more reliably and with lower contact forces
than prior work while offering several ways to stand from the same pose.
A single trained model follows heading, speed, and path objectives across
terrains without retraining.
Planning with egocentric depth improves recovery even when the decoder already
uses depth. The state-first design tracks these objectives more accurately than
joint generation of states and motion latents.
Real-world demonstrations show perceptive and steerable recovery.

Our contributions are threefold:

We
introduce RISE, to our knowledge the first framework for humanoid fall recovery
that combines perception with test-time steering by task objectives.

We propose a motion-matching pipeline that builds a multimodal
recovery repertoire by composing recorded motions, coarsely adapting them
to terrain, and collecting their physical executions.

We introduce a visual state-first diffusion planner that steers
predicted body states toward task objectives, then generates motion latents
conditioned on those states to realize the requested recovery.

# II Related Work

Humanoid Fall Recovery. Prior fall-recovery methods differ in how they design or learn recovery but
share one goal: returning the robot upright. Early work designed protective
falls and scripted get-up
sequences [ 10 , 11 ] . Learned controllers
extended these capabilities to safe falling [ 12 ] and to
recovery from diverse postures on real
humanoids [ 1 , 2 ] . FIRM unifies fall prevention,
impact mitigation, and recovery [ 3 ] , and VIGOR uses
egocentric depth to infer a recovery goal suited to the nearby
terrain [ 4 ] . None lets a task decide how the robot stands;
in RISE, task objectives choose the heading, speed, and path of
recovery at test time.

Steering Whole-Body Motion. To our knowledge, no prior whole-body controller offers both onboard scene
perception and test-time steering (Fig. 2 ).
Many controllers, including perceptive ones, are directed through commands
such as joystick or heading inputs [ 6 , 5 ] .
These commands work well for trained behaviors, but each command type must be
defined, and its data labeled, before training. Test-time objectives are more
flexible: they can be designed after training and combined as needed. Such
objectives already steer simulated characters, whose state and scene are known
exactly [ 7 , 9 ] . A real robot is
harder to steer: objectives act on predicted motion, but sensing, state
estimation, and mismatched dynamics [ 13 ] make the robot depart
from its plan. BeyondMimic steers a real humanoid, but on flat ground, and
notes that its guidance suits coarse-grained
objectives [ 8 ] . Fall recovery on uneven terrain demands
finer control: contact-rich movement there is hard to predict, and far fewer
motions keep the robot supported. The robot must also stand up from arbitrary
initial configurations rather than a fixed starting state, sensing its joint
configuration and pelvis orientation but not where it lies on the terrain. We
steer recovery with egocentric depth, through predictions learned from the
robot’s executed recoveries ( Sec. IV-C ).

Multimodal Recovery Data. Steering requires several feasible recoveries from the same pose and position,
which recorded recovery data rarely provides. Such data is scarce next to the
motion data behind general whole-body control and
loco-manipulation [ 6 , 14 ] . Large motion-capture
datasets include get-up demonstrations on flat
ground [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] , but because
recovery is not a focus category, they contain only a limited number.
Recovery controllers that imitate humans likewise rely on sparse
demonstrations [ 3 , 4 ] . Each recording also
shows only one way to stand from its start, since a performer can hardly fall
into the same pose twice. VIGOR aligns each demonstration to many terrains but
still pairs each starting pose with one recovery, repeating one route per
configuration in our tests ( Sec. IV-B ). Motion
graphs [ 18 ] , physics-based
augmentation [ 19 ] , and motion matching [ 20 ] broaden the skills and terrains that data covers. We use motion matching with
a different aim: composing recordings at compatible frames so that each
starting pose has several physically executable recoveries for steering
to choose among, rather than one.

State–Action Diffusion Planning. Diffusion planners that output actions differ in when actions are generated
relative to the states they realize. Diffuse-CLoC and BeyondMimic denoise
states jointly with actions or motion
latents [ 9 , 8 ] . Under guidance, the
task cost changes the states at every denoising step while the actions are
updated alongside them. The actions are therefore never conditioned on the
final steered states, and whether they realize those states depends on the
shared denoising keeping the two consistent. We hypothesize that generating
actions from the completed steered plan helps the robot follow task
objectives while still completing recovery. Decision Diffuser follows this
ordering in simulation, inferring each action from consecutive states through
inverse dynamics [ 21 ] . Our planner instead
generates motion latents conditioned on the full steered state sequence, which a
feedback decoder executes on the real robot; Sec. IV-F compares
this ordering with joint generation.

2026-10-22.authors: May Espinola , Qifan Zhang , Yu Xiang

2026-10-22.introduction:
Recent advances in frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, planning, and tool use Arena AI [2026] . In particular, recent demonstrations of GPT-6 Astra have shown impressive robot manipulation behaviors, including interpreting visual observations, generating robot actions, and correcting mistakes through closed-loop interaction Zhang et al. [2026] , Su et al. [2026] , Team et al. [2026] . NVIDIA’s Astranomy report Yang et al. [2026a] further demonstrates the potential of frontier AI models for robot manipulation through different control configurations, including direct action generation, agentic tool use, and supervision of pretrained robot policies. These results suggest that general-purpose AI models may be capable of performing robot manipulation without task-specific policy training.

Despite these promising demonstrations, an important question remains: How well do frontier AI models perform on established robot manipulation benchmarks? Existing evaluations often use different tasks, robot platforms, and control interfaces, making systematic comparisons difficult. Connecting frontier AI models to standardized benchmarks is essential for understanding their capabilities, identifying limitations, and comparing their performance with conventional robot learning approaches.

Motivated by this question, we develop a unified manipulation pipeline to evaluate frontier AI models on LIBERO-10 (also known as LIBERO-Long) Liu et al. [2023] , a subset of LIBERO-100 containing ten held-out, long-horizon manipulation tasks. LIBERO-10 has been widely adopted for evaluating robot learning methods, including generalist robot policies and vision-language-action models such as Octo Team et al. [2024] , OpenVLA Kim et al. [2024] , π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} Intelligence et al. [2025] , UniVLA Bu et al. [2025] and UniAct Zheng et al. [2025] . Built upon the open-source Inspect Robots framework Robocurve [2026] , our pipeline enables frontier AI models to interact with the simulation environment through visual observations and structured tool calls, allowing closed-loop manipulation without task-specific training or fine-tuning. We evaluate multiple frontier AI models, including GPT and Claude models, under a common protocol, exploring different reasoning modes to investigate the impact of reasoning effort on manipulation performance. Beyond task success rates, we analyze API calls, inference latency, token usage, and monetary cost to understand the tradeoffs between reasoning capabilities, manipulation performance, and efficiency.

Our work provides a standardized evaluation of frontier AI models on robot manipulation tasks, offering insights into their capabilities and limitations. By releasing our code and evaluation results, we provide reproducible, ready-to-use baselines for future research, reducing the need to repeatedly evaluate these computationally expensive models and lowering evaluation costs.

# 2  Closed-Loop Manipulation with Frontier AI Models

## 2.1  Observations and Prompt Context

Each observation contains two 256 × 256 256\times 256 RGB images, from the fixed third-person (agentview) camera and the wrist camera, together with the robot state. The robot state has 12 values: the end-effector position ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) in meters in the world frame, its orientation in the 6D rotation representation (the first two columns of the rotation matrix), the current gripper command, and the two measured finger positions. The gripper command only records whether the model last asked the gripper to open or close; the measured finger positions show where the fingers actually stopped, so the model can tell whether it closed on an object or on nothing. Each observation is sent as one message: the robot state as text, followed by the two labeled camera images. The model never sees object poses or the success signal.

The system prompt, reproduced verbatim in Figure 2 , has two parts. The first part is a generic agent instruction that is independent of the robot and the task: it explains the tool-call interface, requires exactly one tool call per turn with a short note on every motion, tells the model when to call done or give_up , and states the budget of 80 LLM calls. The second part, appended under Embodiment notes , contains the environment guidelines that we wrote for LIBERO. They describe the robot, the coordinate frame, the rotation representation, the gripper behavior, and the available sensing, followed by eight general manipulation rules. The same prompt is used for all ten tasks and all models; only the embodiment name changes with the task. The task instruction is not part of the system prompt. It is LIBERO’s original natural-language task description, which the model receives as the first user message and again at the top of every observation message. The instructions of all ten tasks are listed in Figure 5 .

Each LLM call is stateless, so every call resends the fixed context (the system prompt and the task instruction), followed by the interaction history accumulated so far. Text and images in this history are treated differently. The text history is complete: it contains the text part of every observation since the start of the episode (the task instruction and the 12 robot-state values), the model’s own tool calls and notes, and the execution feedback of each call. Images, in contrast, are kept only for the two most recent observations (the previous and current observations in Figure 1 ), i.e., at most four images per call; the images of all earlier observations are replaced by a short text placeholder. Because each call adds one observation, the length of the history is bounded by the budget of 80 LLM calls.

## 2.2  Action Interface and Execution

The model acts through three tools, one tool call per turn. Their full definitions are given in Figure 3 , and Figure 4 shows one example of each. The tool calls are generated through the native function-calling interface of each model’s API: every request includes the name, description, and argument format of each tool, and the model replies with a structured call that names one tool and gives its arguments in JSON, which the framework then executes. For instance, in one task-0 episode, Claude Opus 5.5 (high effort) returned the following move_to call, which sets all ten dimensions to rotate the gripper by 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} about the vertical axis while moving over a fallen can:

move_to(targets, note) moves the end effector to an absolute target pose (Figure 4 , left). In each call, the model outputs two arguments. targets gives target values for any subset of the ten action dimensions: the position ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) in meters in the world frame, the six entries of the 6D rotation representation, and the gripper command. note is a short explanation of what the model observes and why it chose the motion. The tool description tells the model that the end effector moves along a straight line at a fixed safe speed, that unspecified dimensions keep their current value, and that each dimension is bounded: x , y ∈ [ − 0.6 , 0.6 ] x,y\in[-0.6,0.6] m, z ∈ [ 0.42 , 1.6 ] z\in[0.42,1.6] m, rotation entries in [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , and the gripper command in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] .

move_to(targets, note) moves the end effector to an absolute target pose (Figure 4 , left). In each call, the model outputs two arguments. targets gives target values for any subset of the ten action dimensions: the position ( x , y , z ) (x,y,z) in meters in the world frame, the six entries of the 6D rotation representation, and the gripper command. note is a short explanation of what the model observes and why it chose the motion. The tool description tells the model that the end effector moves along a straight line at a fixed safe speed, that unspecified dimensions keep their current value, and that each dimension is bounded: x , y ∈ [ − 0.6 , 0.6 ] x,y\in[-0.6,0.6] m, z ∈ [ 0.42 , 1.6 ] z\in[0.42,1.6] m, rotation entries in [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] , and the gripper command in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] .

done(summary, hindsight) lets the model end the episode when it believes the task is complete (Figure 4 , middle). No action is executed, and the episode ends immediately. A done call is never scored as a success, for the following reason. LIBERO’s success checker runs after every control step, and as soon as the task is complete it ends the episode as a success (Sec. 2.3 ). The model is therefore asked for its next call only when the checker has just reported that the task is not yet complete. Since done does not move the robot, the task is still incomplete when the model calls it, so the episode counts as a failure. In other words, a done call means that the model believes it has finished when it has not.

We still provide done because the model never sees the success checker and must decide by itself when the task is finished. Without done , a model that believes it has finished would have no way to stop and would keep acting. The frequency of done calls therefore indicates how often a model mistakes an unfinished task for a finished one.

give_up(reason, hindsight) declares that the model believes the task cannot be completed, for example after repeated failed grasps or when an object or the container has been knocked out of reach (Figure 4 , right); reason explains why. As with done , no action is executed and the episode ends immediately as a failure. The framework also issues give_up on the model’s behalf when the budget of 80 LLM calls is exhausted.

Both done and give_up also require a hindsight field, in which the model states what it wishes it had known at the start of the episode, such as camera placement, controller behavior, or metric scale, written as advice for a future attempt. These notes are logged for analysis but are never fed back to the model, so every episode remains zero-shot.

The adapter (Figure 1 ) interpolates a straight-line trajectory from the current end-effector pose to the target at a fixed safe speed, producing a sequence of absolute end-effector actions at 20 Hz (about eleven actions per call on average). The number of interpolated steps is returned to the model as the tool result and kept in the interaction history. The actions are then executed one at a time: each 10-D action is converted to LIBERO’s 7-D absolute pose command by orthonormalizing the 6D rotation and converting it to axis-angle form, and LIBERO’s operational space controller (OSC) drives the Franka Panda arm for one control step.

## 2.3  Termination and Evaluation

After every control step, LIBERO’s success checker evaluates the task’s goal predicates on the current simulator state. If they are satisfied, the episode ends immediately as a success, even if actions of the current call remain. Otherwise, execution continues with the next action of the same call. When all actions of the call have been executed and the task is still incomplete, the new camera images, robot state, and execution feedback are appended to the history, and the model is queried for the next call. Algorithm 1 summarizes one episode.

An episode normally ends in one of five ways:

the success checker reports success;

the model calls done or give_up ;

the model has used all 80 LLM calls, in which case the framework issues give_up on its behalf;

the episode reaches 900 control steps; this limit is checked after every step, so it can end an episode in the middle of a call; or

the next LLM call would exceed the per-episode spending cap, which guards against runaway API cost.

An episode counts as a success only in case 1, when LIBERO’s success checker reports success; episodes that end in any other way count as failures. We report the success rate, the fraction of episodes that end in success.

2026-10-22.title: SP-HLM: Sparse-Pose-Driven Motion Generation and Whole-Body Control for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
2026-10-22.authors: Zhaohui Yang , Quanbao Lin , Chengqi Shi , Zhenglang Weng , Jicheng Lin , Boyu Chen , Tengjie Zhu , Guanzhu Ren , Jiahao Xu , Yang Feng , Xiaokang Yang , Yao Mu
2026-10-22.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires an effective interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control. Existing interfaces typically rely on a single action representation for both task intent and whole-body coordination. This may burden the high-level policy or leave one aspect underspecified. We present SP-HLM, a framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. The interface combines five task-critical body poses with a learned latent motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms. SP-VLA, a vision-language-action model, first predicts task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions using asynchronous action-chunk inference. Given these sparse targets, SP-MGM, a motion generation model trained through two-stage distillation, reconstructs coordinated full-body motion in real time. A pretrained motion encoder maps this motion to a compact latent representation. SP-GMT, a general motion tracker, then integrates the explicit sparse targets with this implicit motion prior for whole-body control. Experiments in simulation and on a real humanoid robot demonstrate improved motion tracking, whole-body coordination, and loco-manipulation success over existing approaches. Additional results and videos are available on our project page .
2026-10-22.introduction:
The motion interface between high-level task policies and whole-body control
is an important design choice in humanoid loco-manipulation [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Existing interfaces emphasize different aspects of humanoid motion. Joint-space actions [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] directly specify joint configurations, but can require the high-level policy to model whole-body coordination alongside task intent. Task-space actions provide a compact, task-grounded representation, yet sparse targets alone do not fully specify coordinated whole-body motion. Token-space actions [ 7 ] can encode reusable coordination patterns, while task-critical spatial targets may remain implicit. These trade-offs motivate an interface that combines representations of spatial intent and whole-body coordination, rather than encoding both in a single form.

We argue that task-critical spatial intent and whole-body coordination should instead be represented in complementary forms. Spatial intent remains explicit, specifying where task-relevant body parts should move, whereas whole-body coordination is encoded implicitly as a learned motion prior describing how the body should move. Following this principle, we expose only five task-critical body poses—the pelvis, two wrists, and two ankles—as explicit spatial constraints and complement them with a latent whole-body motion representation. This interface preserves direct task-space control while avoiding the need for the high-level policy to explicitly specify full-body coordination.

Following this formulation, we present SP-HLM, a humanoid loco-manipulation framework built on a sparse-pose-driven interface. At its core, SP-GMT performs whole-body control by jointly conditioning on sparse task-space targets and a learned motion latent. We pretrain a motion variational autoencoder (VAE) to encode full-body motion into a compact latent representation. This latent provides coordination information not fully specified by the sparse targets while enabling efficient policy training.

To obtain this implicit motion prior from sparse task-space targets at deployment, we introduce SP-MGM, which reconstructs coordinated full-body motion from five-point pose targets in real time. Starting from a pretrained motion generation model, SP-MGM reduces network depth and denoising steps and employs two-stage distillation to improve sparse-pose adherence and temporal consistency.

The proposed interface also reduces the burden of high-level action prediction. SP-VLA predicts only task-relevant sparse body poses and finger joint positions from multimodal observations and language instructions, without directly predicting full-body configurations. We further adopt asynchronous action-chunk inference for responsive closed-loop execution. Together, SP-VLA specifies task-space intent, SP-MGM recovers coordinated whole-body motion, and SP-GMT integrates the explicit sparse targets and implicit motion prior for whole-body control.

We separately evaluate SP-GMT, SP-MGM, and the complete SP-HLM system. SP-GMT achieves competitive motion-tracking performance against representative state-of-the-art baselines. SP-MGM improves sparse-pose adherence over the motion-generation baseline while achieving a 1.45 × \times higher generation rate. For loco-manipulation, SP-HLM achieves a 52.75% overall success rate across eight simulated tasks, outperforming the token-space and joint-space baselines. We further validate SP-HLM on four real-world tasks, demonstrating its feasibility for humanoid loco-manipulation. Our main contributions are:

We propose a sparse-pose-driven motion interface for humanoid loco-manipulation, combining five task-critical body poses with a learned motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms.

We develop SP-GMT , a whole-body tracker conditioned jointly on sparse targets and a pretrained motion representation, and SP-MGM , a real-time sparse-conditioned motion generator trained through two-stage distillation.

We present SP-HLM , a humanoid loco-manipulation framework that integrates the above two components with SP-VLA , which uses asynchronous action-chunk inference to predict task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint-position targets from multimodal inputs. The resulting system achieves higher overall success than the evaluated baselines across eight simulated tasks and is further validated on four real-world tasks.

1. We propose a sparse-pose-driven motion interface for humanoid loco-manipulation, combining five task-critical body poses with a learned motion prior to represent spatial intent and whole-body coordination in complementary forms.

2. We develop SP-GMT , a whole-body tracker conditioned jointly on sparse targets and a pretrained motion representation, and SP-MGM , a real-time sparse-conditioned motion generator trained through two-stage distillation.

3. We present SP-HLM , a humanoid loco-manipulation framework that integrates the above two components with SP-VLA , which uses asynchronous action-chunk inference to predict task-relevant sparse poses and finger joint-position targets from multimodal inputs. The resulting system achieves higher overall success than the evaluated baselines across eight simulated tasks and is further validated on four real-world tasks.

# II RELATED WORK

## II-A General Humanoid Motion Generation and Control

Recent work increasingly uses motion generation as an intermediate layer between high-level semantic commands and low-level humanoid control, typically producing dense whole-body references for downstream tracking [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Some methods formulate motion synthesis as an in-betweening problem [ 11 ] , whereas others employ generative models as online motion planners [ 12 , 13 ] . Although these approaches demonstrate the effectiveness of generative motion priors for hierarchical control, they largely rely on dense motion references rather than explicit task-space interfaces tailored to loco-manipulation.

In parallel, general motion tracking has emerged as a scalable approach to acquiring versatile whole-body control from large and diverse motion corpora [ 7 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . Recent studies improve generalization by scaling motion data and model capacity [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] , while others leverage heterogeneous motion sources or expert specialization [ 21 , 22 , 23 ] . Related efforts learn reusable behavioral representations that can be transferred to downstream control tasks [ 24 , 25 ] . Together, these advances provide increasingly general and robust motion generation and control capabilities, while the interface for conveying task-relevant whole-body intent from high-level loco-manipulation policies remains comparatively less explored.

## II-B Motion Interfaces for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation

Recent humanoid loco-manipulation systems increasingly pursue unified whole-body behaviors through vision-language-action models (VLAs) [ 1 , 5 , 4 , 26 , 27 ] , world-action models [ 28 , 29 ] , and perceptive reinforcement policies [ 2 , 30 ] . Beyond the choice of policy architecture, an important design consideration is the motion interface through which task-level intent is conveyed to whole-body execution. Existing approaches span decoupled upper- and lower-body control [ 5 , 1 ] and explicit whole-body kinematic representations [ 31 , 4 ] . While these interfaces provide direct control over robot motion, they can require the high-level policy to reason over relatively detailed body configurations. Other methods adopt more compact learned motion representations, such as motion tokens [ 28 , 32 ] , which capture reusable coordination patterns but make task-relevant spatial constraints less explicit.

Recent work also explores compact task-space interfaces based on sparse body targets or low-rate task-space trajectories, leaving the remaining whole-body coordination to downstream controllers [ 33 , 34 , 35 ] . In contrast, SP-HLM combines explicit task-space targets with a learned whole-body motion prior, providing a compact interface between task-level intent and coordinated whole-body execution.

2026-10-22.title: TARSphere: A Robot-Oriented Full-Stack Framework for Long-Horizon Embodied Agents in Evolving Physical and Social Environments
2026-10-22.authors: Yicheng Xu , Zhikai Xu , Ziyuan Chen , Yuhang Dong , Tao Zhang , Zhucun Xue , Yong Liu , Jiangning Zhang
2026-10-22.comment: . Project page: this https URL Code: this https URL
2026-10-22.abstract:
Robots must act under physical and social constraints while adapting to changes in their environment and human needs.
Existing embodied-agent systems often focus on specified goals or abstract execution into symbolic actions, limiting evaluation in an evolving world.
We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for physically and socially grounded long-horizon embodied agents.
TARSphere-Infra runs robot policies in a physics simulator with embodied NPCs and constrained dialogue.
An event-driven finite-state machine (FSM) uses completed actions and delivered information to update task states and evaluate outcomes.
TARSphere-Harness, its embodied brain harness, lets a frozen multimodal large language model (MLLM) act through multi-level executable skills, using observations, hierarchical memory, and execution feedback to revise its decisions.
On this foundation, agent-in-the-loop curation aligns task semantics, causal dependencies, and scene geometry to construct TARSphere-Bench: 360 episodes across 30 indoor scenes.
Five paired conditions assess perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding for navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks.
Our evaluation of 8 MLLMs shows that general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, while task updates and human interaction remain difficult .
Frequent collisions and falls further motivate evaluating execution safety alongside task success, even with a shared action interface and decision budget.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Robots operating in everyday environments must account for physical constraints [ 11 ] , human safety, appropriate interaction, and social norms [ 19 , 23 ] .
As the world evolves, sensory conditions, physical access, and people’s actions and needs can change during execution [ 9 , 23 , 8 ] .
Long-horizon tasks therefore require tracking world states, interpreting human intentions, and adjusting plans using execution feedback [ 34 , 4 , 9 ] ( Figure 1 ).

Vision-language-action (VLA) models [ 3 , 10 ] and world-action models (WAMs) [ 38 ] have advanced robot control,
yet they often lack the ability to adapt to dynamic and uncertain environments.
Large language models (LLMs) provide broad knowledge for reasoning yet lack the ability to perform complex, real-world tasks [ 1 , 9 , 8 ] .
This complementarity motivates embodied agents that connect reasoning to action [ 1 , 9 , 37 , 14 ] .
However, Harness VLA [ 39 ] , RoboClaw [ 13 ] , and HumanCLAW [ 14 ] focus on tasks with specified goals, leaving an evolving world with human involvement largely unexamined.
Other settings, including EmbodiedBench’s high-level tasks [ 37 ] , LoTa-Bench [ 5 ] , ALFWorld’s text environments [ 28 ] , and Embodied Agent Interface [ 12 ] , abstract physical execution into discrete symbolic actions.
GRBench [ 35 ] combines robot execution with virtual NPC dialogue, while PARTNR [ 4 ] evaluates embodied human-robot collaboration with temporal task constraints. These gaps motivate a physically and socially grounded foundation for benchmarking robotic agents in an evolving world, with task outcomes tied to execution and human interaction.

Insight. Studying embodied intelligence requires physically and socially grounded execution and tasks revealing capabilities across varied situations in a changing world ( Sections 4.2 , 4.3.2 and 4.3.4 ).

Challenge 1: Embodied execution is not symbolic [ Sections 4.2 and 4.3.4 ]. A valid action call does not guarantee successful execution: the robot must contend with contact, friction, balance, and human responses.
The agent must therefore revise decisions using physical execution feedback.

Challenge 2: The world changes during execution [ Sections 4.3.2 and 4.3.3 ]. Physical conditions, human activity, and task requirements can change while a plan unfolds.
The agent must interpret the current situation and reconsider what to do next.

Challenge 3: Evaluation must assess diverse capabilities [ Section 4.2 ]. Within this setting, evaluation must reveal how agents handle varied situations across multiple capability dimensions.
Aggregate success alone can mask different capability gaps across task families ( Section 4.2 ).

We introduce TARSphere, a robot-oriented full-stack framework for embodied agents under physical and social constraints.
TARSphere-Infra couples robot controllers with embodied NPCs in a physics simulator ( Challenge 1 ).
An event-driven FSM maintains world and task states, while TARSphere-Harness combines observations, memory, skills, and execution feedback for replanning ( Challenge 2 ).
We build TARSphere-Bench through agent-in-the-loop curation, pairing navigate-and-report and fetch-and-deliver tasks with five capability conditions: perceptual robustness, disruption adaptation, task update, human coordination, and intent understanding ( Challenge 3 ). Paired variants retain their Base scene and task family.

Across 8 MLLMs, general-purpose models can outperform embodied models, with capability gaps varying by task family ( Section 4.2 ).
Planning credit does not ensure successful execution, and collisions and falls remain common ( Sections 4.2 and 4.3.4 ).
These findings call for agents that combine general reasoning, adaptation to world changes, and safe execution ( Sections 4.2 and 4.3.2 ).

Our contributions are three-fold.

We formulate long-horizon embodied tasks under physical and social constraints, where execution outcomes and world changes continually shape the agent’s decisions.

We develop TARSphere Framework, where physical execution and interaction with embodied humans update task states and supply evaluation evidence; an embodied brain harness uses observations, memory, executable skills, and world feedback to guide model decisions.

We introduce agent-in-the-loop curation for 360 TARSphere-Bench episodes in 30 scenes and five paired capability conditions, aligning task semantics, geometry, and execution.

1. We formulate long-horizon embodied tasks under physical and social constraints, where execution outcomes and world changes continually shape the agent’s decisions.

2. We develop TARSphere Framework, where physical execution and interaction with embodied humans update task states and supply evaluation evidence; an embodied brain harness uses observations, memory, executable skills, and world feedback to guide model decisions.

3. We introduce agent-in-the-loop curation for 360 TARSphere-Bench episodes in 30 scenes and five paired capability conditions, aligning task semantics, geometry, and execution.
