# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Embodied Interactive Simulation Environments

VirtualHome [ 22 ] represents household activities as executable programs; Habitat [ 27 ] and RoboTHOR [ 6 ] support navigation and indoor interaction.
Habitat 2.0 [ 29 ] adds rearrangement, and BEHAVIOR-1K [ 11 ] broadens household activities and object-state changes.
RoboCasa [ 20 ] provides diverse kitchen scenes and composite tasks, while ManiSkill3 [ 30 ] enables GPU-parallel contact-rich manipulation.
Human participation introduces additional demands: Habitat 3.0 [ 23 ] studies social navigation and collaborative rearrangement; PARTNR [ 4 ] evaluates household collaboration under spatial, temporal, and capability constraints.
GRBench [ 35 ] combines robot execution with virtual NPC dialogue.
TARSphere couples physical robot execution, embodied NPC behavior, and changing task requirements in one event-driven environment.
Communication depends on proximity, visibility, hearing range, and human availability, while completed actions and delivered messages commit task-state changes.
Paired conditions compare adaptation and interaction within matched scenes and task families, relating capability demands to decisions, physical execution, and completion.

## 2.2 Embodied Foundation Models

SayCan [ 1 ] grounds skill selection in executable behaviors, and Code as Policies [ 15 ] generates programs combining perception, control APIs, and feedback loops.
Inner Monologue [ 9 ] uses scene descriptions, success feedback, and human interaction to revise decisions.
SayPlan [ 26 ] uses hierarchical 3D scene graphs and simulator feedback for planning, while VoxPoser [ 8 ] composes observation-grounded 3D value maps for closed-loop manipulation.
Complementary action models, including RT-2 [ 3 ] , OpenVLA [ 10 ] , and GR00T [ 2 ] , connect multimodal inputs to robot control; HY-Embodied [ 33 ] targets spatial understanding and embodied action.
TARSphere evaluates frozen multimodal models through a shared harness exposing bounded primitives, higher-level skills, hierarchical memory, and measured execution feedback.
This setting examines how model decisions respond to evolving goals, access, and human needs, alongside ablations of the perception, memory, and skill interface supporting those decisions.

## 2.3 Robotic Agent Systems and Interfaces

ROS [ 24 ] and ROS 2 [ 18 ] provide modular infrastructure for robot perception, planning, and control.
OK-Robot [ 16 ] integrates open-vocabulary perception, navigation, and manipulation for household pick-and-drop tasks.
RoboClaw [ 13 ] links data collection, policy learning, and deployment through a VLM controller orchestrating learned primitives.
ASPIRE [ 17 ] repairs control programs and accumulates reusable skills, while Zetta [ 7 ] develops runtime critics and recovery skills around a frozen policy.
To separate decisions from execution, HumanCLAW [ 14 ] studies VLM decisions through a simulated human body excluding execution-side disturbances.
TARSphere retains robot dynamics and records collisions, falls, motion residuals, and task outcomes.
Its event-driven evaluator checks evidence against the requirements active when it was produced, including authorized task revisions and recipient acceptance, supporting analysis of how physical execution, adaptation, and human interaction jointly affect completion.

2026-10-22.title: DONIC: Generalist Dexterous Bimanual Tracking Control from Human Demonstrations
2026-10-22.authors: Mingze Sun , Ziang Cao , Yuan Fei , Qiankuan Tao , Zihan Wang , Tianqi Liu , Junhao Chen , Haiwen Diao , Fangzhou Hong , Zhaoxi Chen , Ziwei Liu
2026-10-22.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-22.abstract: Despite recent progress in dexterous reference tracking, existing models focus primarily on single-hand manipulation and a limited range of interactions, leaving the bimanual dexterous behaviors common in real life unaddressed. The scarcity of contact-rich bimanual manipulation data and the increased complexity of coordinating contacts make developing a generalist bimanual tracker particularly challenging. Therefore, we present 1) DONIC , the first generalist bimanual tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, together with 2) BiHOI , a multi-view dataset of 1,575 1{,}575 sequences spanning 229 229 objects and emphasizing sustained bimanual interaction, where reconstructed interactions are retargeted into robot references. DONIC combines proximal policy optimization with behavioral cloning in a feedback loop that recycles verified successful executions into training demonstrations. An object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback while supervising each hand according to its reference contact role. Clip-Centered Advantages remove reference-dependent advantage offsets while preserving within-trajectory differences. Together, these designs enable one single policy to learn coordinated manipulation across heterogeneous references. Without fine-tuning, a single checkpoint achieves 86.79 % 86.79\% success on unseen trajectories of training objects and 57.32 % 57.32\% on held-out objects, surpassing the state-of-the-art bimanual tracking baselines by 77.36 77.36 and 45.73 45.73 percentage points.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation supports household assistance, industrial assembly, and assistive care. Unlike gripper-based manipulation, it requires precise coordination of finger motions and changing hand–object contacts to grasp, reorient, and reposition objects [ 28 , 2 , 8 , 33 ] . Generalizing across objects and behaviors is challenging, especially when human demonstrations must be retargeted to robot hands with different kinematics [ 26 , 19 , 38 ] . Simulation-ready objects [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] and synthetic trajectories [ 12 , 40 ] enable large-scale interaction data, but may not fully capture natural human manipulation. Recent trackers therefore learn from human hand–object motion [ 19 , 38 , 1 ] , yet remain largely limited to single-hand tasks. Many everyday tasks instead require asymmetric bimanual coordination: one hand stabilizes an object while the other opens, rotates, or repositions it [ 9 , 41 , 43 ] . This motivates a generalist bimanual reference tracker that learns from diverse human motion to control different objects and tasks with one policy.

Developing such a tracker poses two challenges. First, public datasets include bimanual manipulation [ 9 , 41 , 20 , 10 ] , but fully tracked hand–object sequences with sustained two-hand contact remain scarce, limiting the available coordination patterns. Second, a shared policy must learn trajectories with changing hand roles and contact timing. Hand-pose accuracy alone does not ensure successful object manipulation, while requiring both hands to satisfy contact conditions can mask one hand’s progress. Unequal clip difficulty also creates advantage offsets that can weaken updates for useful actions in harder sequences. Shared training therefore needs feedback grounded in object motion and each hand’s reference contacts, alongside advantages that preserve differences among transitions within each clip.

We address these challenges with DONIC , a generalist bimanual reference tracker, and BiHOI, a multi-view hand–object interaction dataset. BiHOI contains 1,575 1{,}575 sequences spanning 229 229 objects and 14.77 14.77 hours, captured from 32 32 calibrated RGB views. It covers symmetric manipulation and asymmetric coordination. We reconstruct both hands and the object, then retarget hand motion to robot references paired with the object trajectory. Combined with public references, BiHOI broadens the training objects and coordination patterns. DONIC learns one policy for both hands through proximal policy optimization (PPO) [ 31 ] and behavioral cloning (BC) on verified demonstrations. Trajectory-specific policies optimize screened references, while successful shared-policy executions are verified and reused. At inference, one checkpoint tracks new references without further training. Our object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback and supervises each hand’s reference contacts, including asynchronous engagement. Our Clip-Centered Advantages (CCA) subtract each clip’s mean estimated advantage before PPO updates, removing clip-dependent offsets while preserving within-clip differences. On held-out trajectories and objects from public datasets, DONIC exceeds the stronger bimanual baseline by 77.36 77.36 and 45.73 45.73 percentage points in success rate, respectively.

Our contributions are:

To our knowledge, DONIC is the first bimanual reference tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human motion datasets; a single checkpoint is evaluated on unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning.

We introduce BiHOI, a multi-view hand-object interaction dataset emphasizing coordinated bimanual manipulation, and reconstruct its recordings into robot motion references.

We propose an object-centered per-hand reward and CCA to support joint PPO training across bimanual references with different contact roles and difficulty.

On our two public-data evaluation splits, DONIC outperforms bimanual adaptations of DexTrack and Dexplore in success rate and completion, reaching 86.79 % 86.79\% and 57.32 % 57.32\% success on unseen trajectories and objects, respectively.

1. To our knowledge, DONIC is the first bimanual reference tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human motion datasets; a single checkpoint is evaluated on unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning.

2. We introduce BiHOI, a multi-view hand-object interaction dataset emphasizing coordinated bimanual manipulation, and reconstruct its recordings into robot motion references.

3. We propose an object-centered per-hand reward and CCA to support joint PPO training across bimanual references with different contact roles and difficulty.

4. On our two public-data evaluation splits, DONIC outperforms bimanual adaptations of DexTrack and Dexplore in success rate and completion, reaching 86.79 % 86.79\% and 57.32 % 57.32\% success on unseen trajectories and objects, respectively.

# 2 Related Work

Human trajectories provide motion targets, but retargeting alone cannot ensure successful contact. Sequence-specific policies commonly use reinforcement learning to correct retargeted motion. ManipTrans [ 15 ] reuses a general hand-motion imitator but learns a task-specific residual policy for interaction. DexMachina [ 23 ] learns from individual demonstrations by gradually removing virtual object assistance. CHORD [ 44 ] guides sequence-specific learning through contact-wrench matching, while ConTrack [ 17 ] trains one policy per clip with an adaptive balance between object tracking and motion fidelity. We instead learn one generalist bimanual policy that tracks diverse references without per-reference training or fine-tuning at test time.

Generalist policies share knowledge across objects, motions, or skills, predominantly in single-hand settings. UniDexGrasp++ [ 33 ] generalizes grasping across object geometries, UniCross [ 42 ] unifies multiple manipulation skills, and ArtManip [ 39 ] learns category-level articulated in-hand manipulation. For reference tracking, DexTrack [ 19 ] combines reinforcement learning with demonstrations mined by trajectory-specific controllers. Dexplore [ 38 ] expands exploration around reference motions, while AdaDexTrack [ 1 ] combines specialist distillation with online reference modulation. Bimanual tracking must coordinate complementary hand roles and contact timing. Existing work explores narrower generalization: BiDexHD [ 43 ] distills teachers into a separate trajectory-conditioned policy for each operation category and evaluates new object–tool combinations and instances within categories; PhysGraph [ 16 ] transfers task-trained policies to new tool and object geometries. We jointly train one bimanual reference tracker across operation categories and human motion datasets, and evaluate it on unseen trajectories and objects without fine-tuning.

GRAB [ 32 ] records whole-body grasping with detailed contact information, while ARCTIC [ 9 ] captures the coupled motion of two hands and articulated objects. OakInk2 [ 41 ] organizes bimanual manipulation into primitive and complex tasks, and TACO [ 20 ] covers diverse tool–action–object compositions. GigaHands [ 10 ] further expands the scale and diversity of bimanual activities with language annotations. Complementing these motion collections, H2O [ 13 ] and HOI4D [ 21 ] support egocentric interaction understanding, while HOT3D [ 3 ] and HO-Cap [ 34 ] provide recordings and annotations for hand–object reconstruction and tracking. Capture and annotation conventions differ, and human kinematics do not ensure executable robot actions. We harmonize, retarget, and screen zero-residual feasibility to form a common bimanual reference pool for joint training.

2026-10-22.title: Object- and Task-Aware Active Perception for Safe Navigation of Mobile Manipulators in Semi-Static Environments
2026-10-22.authors: Jingxing Qian , Xintong Du , Jun Yang , Siqi Zhou , Steven L. Waslander , Angela P. Schoellig
2026-10-22.abstract: Mobile manipulators must navigate safely in cluttered, partially unknown environments across logistics, manufacturing, and service applications. Semi-static changes between robot visits can lead to outdated scene knowledge and increased collision risk. We propose an active perception framework that enables a high degree-of-freedom (DoF) mobile manipulator to inspect uncertain or safety-critical regions with its hand camera during navigation. A probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view (NBV) formulation prioritizes observations near the desired path and around uncertain or potentially changing objects. The perception objective is integrated into hierarchical-task model predictive control (HTMPC), exploiting kinematic redundancy for viewpoint adjustment while preserving the higher priority of base-trajectory tracking. The system unifies navigation, map maintenance, and active perception in a closed loop. Real-world tests show improved map consistency, reduced task-dependent map entropy, and lower navigation risk than passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional simulation and real-world sequences demonstrate responses to controlled semi-static scene changes.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Mobile manipulators have gained increasing interest in a wide range of applications, including household assistance, logistics, and industrial automation. In these settings, robots are often required to execute navigation tasks across large workspaces over extended periods of time [ 1 ] . However, many deployment sites are cluttered, partially unknown, and semi-static, where objects may appear, disappear, or shift between robot visits. Clutter introduces frequent occlusions, blind corners, and narrow passages, while semi-static scene changes cause previously observed regions to become outdated. These challenges are particularly pronounced when the robot must perceive the environment through a limited field of view (FoV). In such cases, occlusions and blind spots can prevent changes from being detected until the robot is in close proximity, leaving new obstacles in previously traversable areas undetected. This can lead to delayed reactions, increased collision risk, and reduced navigation efficiency.

To operate safely and robustly in such cluttered, semi-static environments, a mobile manipulator must not only navigate toward its desired goal but also maintain an up-to-date, consistent understanding of the scene over time. However, this requirement is not well supported by most existing navigation pipelines, which typically assume a static world with an offline-constructed map for downstream planning and control [ 2 ] , or only track short-term, highly dynamic objects between consecutive frames. Recent research on long-term and semi-static mapping has made important progress toward maintaining consistent environment representations across repeated traversals [ 3 , 4 ] . By incorporating semantic and object-level reasoning, these approaches can detect scene inconsistencies and accommodate long-term changes, thereby improving map quality and robustness over time. Nevertheless, such methods remain fundamentally passive: they depend on observations collected along the robot’s nominal trajectory, and thus can only update the regions that the robot happens to observe. In cluttered environments, this is often insufficient, especially in occluded regions where up-to-date scene knowledge is most needed.

This limitation is especially critical because not all map regions affect navigation equally. Outdated knowledge in task-relevant and safety-critical regions, such as areas along the planned path, narrow passages, and blind corners, has a disproportionate impact on the robot’s ability to move safely and efficiently. As seen in Figure 6 , when the robot makes a sharp turn around the boxes, it is most important for the robot to observe the region around its navigation path behind the orange-shaded blind corner, which is not immediately observable by the fixed camera on the robot base. An outdated or incomplete map in these regions can lead to overly conservative behavior, unnecessary replanning, getting stuck, or collisions. Therefore, map maintenance is particularly valuable in regions where it improves the robot’s ability to make safe task decisions. In this work, we refer to this principle as task-awareness : observations should be prioritized according to their relevance to the robot’s current navigation task, especially when they reduce uncertainty in map regions that affect safe progress toward the goal.

Active perception provides a means to acquire these observations during task execution. Related approaches couple perception and motion planning for control and collision avoidance [ 5 , 6 ] . Next-best-view (NBV) planning has also been studied for exploration [ 7 ] , object seeking [ 8 ] , inspection [ 9 ] , pose estimation [ 10 ] , and grasping [ 11 ] . A camera mounted on the manipulator hand provides a natural mechanism for viewpoint control. However, many NBV methods target short-horizon operation in static scenes [ 12 , 13 ] or geometric completeness [ 14 , 15 ] . They generally do not jointly consider long-term scene changes, object-level map consistency, and relevance to the current navigation task.

For semi-static environments, this omission is particularly important because scene changes often occur at the level of objects: furniture may be moved, shelves may be added, or obstacles may partially block previously traversable space. A partial mismatch at the visible edge of a cabinet can indicate that the cabinet has moved, making its previously mapped region worth checking again. As a result, identifying which objects or occupied structures are likely to have changed and which of them matter more for the robot’s navigation task is critical for effective map maintenance and safe task execution. This motivates an object-aware active perception strategy in which viewpoint selection is informed by uncertainty in the maintained semi-static map, especially when such uncertainty may affect path clearance. Task awareness then determines whether this potential change matters to the next maneuver.

Moreover, because the hand camera is mounted on a manipulator, viewpoint selection cannot be treated independently from navigation. The robot must realize informative camera motions without compromising progress on its primary navigation task. We therefore use hierarchical-task model predictive control (HTMPC) as the mechanism for enforcing this priority structure and realizing the selected viewpoints through the robot’s kinematic redundancy [ 16 , 17 ] .

In this work, we aim to enable safe mobile manipulation in cluttered, semi-static environments over extended periods of time through integrated active perception and whole-body control. Specifically, we develop an object- and task-aware active perception framework that combines the planned navigation path with uncertainty in the maintained semi-static map. Our approach enables a mobile manipulator to exploit its kinematic redundancy to direct a hand camera toward uncertain, occluded, and safety-critical regions while continuing to execute its primary navigation task. By actively updating the map where it matters most, the robot can better detect and adapt to incremental scene changes and improve map consistency in task-relevant areas. We deploy the system on a real mobile manipulator and evaluate reconstruction accuracy, task-dependent map entropy, and navigation safety against passive and task- or object-unaware baselines. Figure 2 illustrates the resulting behavior in cluttered scenes. Our main contributions are as follows:

We formulate a probabilistic next-best-view (NBV) objective that uses task-dependent map entropy and path-conditioned grid weights to prioritize uncertain or potentially changing regions along the planned path.

We formulate a probabilistic next-best-view (NBV) objective that uses task-dependent map entropy and path-conditioned grid weights to prioritize uncertain or potentially changing regions along the planned path.

We introduce a hierarchical-task control framework that assigns higher priority to navigation than to active perception within a two-stage optimization problem. This allows the robot to exploit its kinematic redundancy to gather informative observations while bounding the base-tracking cost during camera-task optimization.

We demonstrate the system on a mobile manipulator with a hand camera in cluttered indoor environments. In the tested static scenes, the proposed system reduces task-dependent map entropy, improves map consistency, and lowers navigation risk compared with passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional scene-change sequences demonstrate the closed-loop map-maintenance behavior.

1. We formulate a probabilistic next-best-view (NBV) objective that uses task-dependent map entropy and path-conditioned grid weights to prioritize uncertain or potentially changing regions along the planned path.

2. We introduce a hierarchical-task control framework that assigns higher priority to navigation than to active perception within a two-stage optimization problem. This allows the robot to exploit its kinematic redundancy to gather informative observations while bounding the base-tracking cost during camera-task optimization.

3. We demonstrate the system on a mobile manipulator with a hand camera in cluttered indoor environments. In the tested static scenes, the proposed system reduces task-dependent map entropy, improves map consistency, and lowers navigation risk compared with passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional scene-change sequences demonstrate the closed-loop map-maintenance behavior.

# II Related Work

## II-A Semantic and Object-Aware Mapping

Early mapping systems rely on sparse feature points [ 18 ] or dense volumetric grids such as occupancy grids [ 19 ] and signed or Euclidean distance fields (SDFs/EDFs) [ 20 ] to construct an accurate geometric map. However, purely geometric maps lack semantic context, limiting their expressiveness in complex environments. More recent work has incorporated semantic and object-level knowledge into geometric maps. Early approaches introduced objects into mapping by using predefined CAD models [ 21 ] . Subsequent object-aware methods further decompose the scene into semantic or object submaps on-the-fly [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] , allowing higher-level reasoning about object relationships and scene structure for downstream planning tasks [ 25 , 26 ] .

Despite these advances, most semantic and object-aware mapping systems continue to prioritize geometric accuracy under a static-world assumption. When deployed over long time horizons in real-world semi-static environments, these methods can accumulate inconsistencies, leading to map corruption, degraded localization, and increased safety risks.

## II-B Change Detection in Semi-Static Environments

To relax the static-world assumption, several strategies have been proposed to handle scene dynamics. A common approach identifies potentially dynamic objects based on prior semantic knowledge and treats them as outliers [ 27 , 28 ] . While efficient, this strategy can lead to information loss and instability when large parts of the scene have changed [ 29 ] . Another strategy jointly tracks the robot and objects [ 22 , 30 , 31 ] , but typically relies on motion consistency across consecutive frames, making them less effective for semi-static environments, where changes occur between robot visits.

Detecting semi-static changes is critical for long-term autonomy, but has received less attention. Some recent approaches estimate object-level consistency based on overlap between observations and mapped objects [ 3 , 32 ] . Other approaches leverage learned representations or scene graphs to predict object changes [ 33 , 34 ] , use Bayesian formulations to propagate object consistency [ 35 , 4 ] , and jointly optimize robot state and object consistency [ 36 ] .

While these methods improve long-term map consistency, they are typically evaluated in open-loop mapping scenarios and rely on passive observations. As a result, changes occurring in occluded or task-critical regions may remain undetected until they lead to failure. An open question is how to couple probabilistic object-level change estimates with online viewpoint selection and control for safe navigation.

## II-C Active Perception in Robotics

Active perception deliberately selects sensor viewpoints to acquire observations that improve a robotic task [ 37 ] . For exploration and reconstruction, NBV planners commonly seek views that reveal unmapped space or reduce map uncertainty [ 38 , 39 ] . Naazare et al. [ 9 ] extend this principle to exploration and inspection with an arm-mounted RGB-D camera, combining information gain with coverage of user-specified regions of interest. These approaches establish the utility of movable sensors, while the choice of which regions to inspect depends on the task being performed.

For navigation, Fisher-information methods select observations that improve localization [ 40 , 14 ] . The Fisher Information Field [ 41 , 42 ] represents the information available for visual localization and supports evaluation of candidate poses during motion planning. Learning-based methods instead predict informative viewpoints from data for localization [ 13 , 12 ] or exploration [ 15 ] . Our objective uses map uncertainty and path relevance to choose observations of obstacles and free space that affect navigation.

Visibility-aware and risk-averse planners also account for sensing limitations and path-relevant uncertainty when planning motion at the cost of navigation efficiency [ 43 , 44 ] . Our focus is maintaining object-level consistency across repeated visits and realizing informative hand-camera views under a navigation-first task hierarchy.

## II-D Perception-based Mobile Manipulation

Perception-based control frameworks, in which onboard sensor data continuously inform motion planning and control, have enabled mobile manipulators to operate in changing environments for tasks such as reactive grasping and obstacle avoidance [ 45 , 46 , 47 ] .
In all these works, however, the coupling is one-directional: the robot perceives to inform control, but sensor viewpoints are determined passively by the task-driven motion rather than actively optimized.
Active perception has been explored in mobile manipulation for specific subtasks such as object recognition [ 48 ] and grasp pose detection [ 49 ] . SPIN [ 50 ] further learns coordinated perception, interaction, and navigation from onboard vision without constructing an environment map. Our setting emphasizes persistent object-map maintenance: observations acquired during navigation must reveal changes to a scene mapped on earlier visits, and the resulting map must inform subsequent motion.

Hierarchical task control offers a principled way to integrate active perception into whole-body motion planning for kinematically redundant robots. By establishing a strict order among tasks, the hierarchical task control framework leverages the robot’s redundancy such that the lower-priority tasks are solved only in the null space of higher-priority ones [ 51 , 52 ] , avoiding conflicting motions inherent in the tasks.
HTMPC instantiates this idea in a model predictive control setting through nonlinear lexicographic optimization, which enables strictly ordered sequential mobile manipulation tasks [ 16 , 17 ] .
In this work, we employ HTMPC with active perception as an explicit task in the hierarchy, secondary to the navigation task, resolving the inherent perception-control objective conflicts and creating a truly bidirectional perception-control loop: the robot plans its action based on the latest perceived map, and simultaneously optimizes its sensor placement to actively perceive the surrounding environment.
This enables safe whole-body navigation in unstructured, semi-static environments.

2026-10-22.title: HuMiT: Low-Latency Whole-Body Humanoid Teleoperation via Compact Reference Tracking
2026-10-22.authors: Liu Cao , Botian Xu , Ruoqu Chen , Jiajun Liu , Mingzhi Pei , Zihao Wang , Zhongyu Li , Mengdi Xu
2026-10-22.abstract:
Real-time whole-body humanoid teleoperation remains challenging due to the computational latency introduced by optimization-based retargeting pipelines and future-frame conditioning.
Existing motion tracking policies typically require dense reference targets including full joint positions, body-part transformations, and even future frames, which tightly couples the controller to expensive upstream modules.
In this work, we present HuMiT , a whole-body teleoperation system built on a unified tracking policy that requires only a compact reference target, consisting of root height, root velocity, and the SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints at the current frame, yet achieves competitive tracking fidelity compared to methods relying on more diverse reference states including complete joint positions, dense body-part transformations, and even future frames.
Experiments show that our policy achieves a communication-to-inference latency of ∼ \sim 20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) across different motion types.
We validate the system on a Unitree G1 humanoid, showcasing split-second reactive responses such as catching a tossed ball, as well as coordinated loco-manipulation capabilities. Project page: https://xiaohu-art.github.io/Track/ .
2026-10-22.introduction:
Humanoid robots hold unique promise for operating in human-centric environments due to their morphology that naturally matches the workspaces and tools designed for people.
Teleoperation is a practical paradigm for human-in-the-loop robot control.
It provides a scalable mechanism for collecting diverse demonstration data to train autonomous policies,
and also allows human operators to intervene in high-risk scenarios or situations where autonomous systems are likely to fail.

However, building an effective whole-body teleoperation system remains challenging. A primary issue is large teleoperation latency , which arises from two sources. First, optimization-based retargeting [ 1 ] introduces substantial per-frame delay and can suffer from numerical instability. Second, existing learning-based tracking policies rely heavily on full reference states as inputs, including complete joint positions, body-part transformations, and their velocities [ 2 , 3 ] .
Moreover, many of these methods condition the policy on future reference frames to enable anticipatory control [ 4 , 5 ] , which further exacerbates the latency problem.
A secondary challenge is limited whole-body coordination , as many approaches decouple upper- and lower-body control [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] , which is particularly restrictive for dynamic tasks.
In addition, hardware-centric solutions based on exoskeletons [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] or marker-based motion capture [ 12 , 13 ] further constrain deployment flexibility.

In this work, we investigate a simple but consequential question: does high-fidelity whole-body motion tracking truly require a full reference state at deployment? We find that a compact reference target (CRT) , consisting only of a root height, root linear and angular velocity commands, and the SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints (bilateral wrists and ankles) at the current frame, is sufficient as the deployment-time input of a unified whole-body tracking policy that achieves competitive tracking performance compared to methods relying on full reference states (i.e., complete joint positions, dense body-part states, their velocities, and future frames).
This compact reference design dramatically reduces the information that the upstream sensing module must provide, and it removes the retargeting pipeline from the online control loop entirely, resulting in significantly lower end-to-end latency.

We present HuMiT , a low-latency whole-body teleoperation system for humanoid robots.
HuMiT employs lightweight human motion sensing to produce compact reference targets, which are then tracked by a whole-body policy trained in parallel simulation.
As shown in Fig. 1 , HuMiT enables a wide range of dynamic whole-body skills that are difficult to achieve with high-latency or decoupled systems.

Our contributions are as follows:

Compact reference suffices at deployment. Through cross-method comparison and ablations under identical conditions, we show that a compact reference target matches full-reference policies.

Low-latency teleoperation system. By removing optimization-based retargeting and future-frame conditioning from the online loop, HuMiT achieves a communication-to-inference latency of ∼ \sim 20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) between operator and robot motion, while maintaining robust tracking performance.

Dynamic whole-body teleoperation for humanoids. We validate HuMiT on a Unitree G1 humanoid executing reactive catching and coordinated loco-manipulation, confirming that the unified compact-reference design supports tightly coupled whole-body control under low-latency constraints.

2. Low-latency teleoperation system. By removing optimization-based retargeting and future-frame conditioning from the online loop, HuMiT achieves a communication-to-inference latency of ∼ \sim 20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) between operator and robot motion, while maintaining robust tracking performance.

# II Related Work

## II-A Learning-Based Humanoid Whole-Body Control

Decoupled vs. unified control. Partitioning whole-body control into separate upper- and lower-body policies [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] simplifies learning but fundamentally limits movements that couple limb motion and base stability, whereas unified policies integrate all degrees of freedom, enabling true loco-manipulation at the cost of increased training complexity.

Reference target design. Among unified tracking controllers, prior methods differ in what reference information the policy observes.
BeyondMimic [ 2 ] conditions the policy on joint positions and joint velocities as reference targets.
BFM [ 3 ] augments this with body-part local positions, providing denser spatial supervision.
SONIC [ 4 ] and OmniClone [ 5 ] further extend the reference to include future frames for anticipatory control.
Despite these differences in reference richness, all of these methods share the assumption that dense reference targets are necessary for high-fidelity tracking, an assumption that remains largely unexamined.

## II-B Humanoid Teleoperation Systems

Existing teleoperation systems [ 14 ] differ mainly in their sensing modality and in the resulting end-to-end latency.

Hardware-centric sensing. Exoskeleton-based systems [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] capture the operator’s upper body while the lower body is driven by joysticks or pedals, so sensing leads to decoupled control. Optical marker-based motion capture suits [ 12 ] are accurate but expensive, require extensive calibration, and restrict the operator to a constrained workspace.

Vision-based pose estimation. Camera-based methods estimate human body pose using models such as SMPL [ 6 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] , offering greater flexibility and lower hardware cost, but the computational overhead of pose estimation followed by optimization-based retargeting makes the high-frequency, low-latency throughput required for responsive teleoperation hard to reach. HumanPlus [ 18 ] and OmniH2O [ 19 ] adopt this approach and inherit its latency limitations.

Direct extremity control. A concurrent work, ExtremControl [ 20 ] , operates directly on the SE(3) poses of six links (pelvis, torso, hands, and feet) and incorporates velocity feedforward into the PD controller, reporting latency as low as 50 ms with optical motion capture and 60 ms with a VR-based setup.
Its deployable policy, however, is distilled from a privileged teacher that observes up to 32 future reference steps, and its reference is anchored by the operator’s global pelvis and torso poses.
In contrast, HuMiT is trained in a single stage without distillation or any future-frame supervision, and replaces global pose anchoring with root height and velocity commands.

## II-C Motion Retargeting

Motion retargeting bridges the embodiment gap between the human operator and the target robot by converting captured human motion into robot-executable commands.
Classical approaches solve per-frame inverse kinematics (IK) or nonlinear optimization problems [ 21 , 1 ] to map human joint positions onto the robot’s kinematic structure.
While geometrically accurate, they introduce two practical drawbacks for teleoperation: (i) the per-frame optimization incurs non-negligible latency that accumulates in the control loop, and (ii) the numerical solvers are prone to instability (e.g., singularities, local minima), leading to jittery or infeasible reference commands.

In HuMiT, retargeting is performed offline only during training data preparation. At deployment, the tracking policy directly consumes scaled human keypoints as reference targets, completely removing retargeting from the online loop and eliminating its associated latency and instability.

2026-10-22.title: RangeNav: Task-Aligned LiDAR Range-Image Pretraining for Robot Navigation
2026-10-22.authors: Samuel Foo Enze , Manthan Patel , Fan Yang , Linus Kramer , Pascal Roth , Marco Hutter , Cesar Cadena
2026-10-22.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots operating in dense crowds and cluttered sites require 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} perception to react to surrounding hazards. While panoramic LiDAR offers full-surround coverage, learning representations within reinforcement learning (RL) is sample-inefficient under sparse rewards, and existing 3D pretrained point-cloud encoders are too memory-heavy for massively parallel RL simulation. We present RangeNav , a compact (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained entirely on synthetic data. RangeNav uses anisotropic convolutions and circular padding to handle the extreme aspect ratio and azimuthal seam of range images. We pretrain the network using a navigation-aligned objective combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and bird’s-eye-view (BEV) prediction, then freeze it for policy learning. In simulation, adding semantic and BEV supervision increases success rates over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution realistic test environments, respectively. Zero-shot real-world deployments on a Unitree B2-W quadruped demonstrate robust navigation through dense crowds, low-light settings, and construction zones where limited-field-of-view depth policies struggle. Code and models will be open-sourced.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Autonomous navigation enables mobile robots to operate in challenging real-world domains, from negotiating dense pedestrian crowds in last-mile delivery to inspecting unstructured industrial and construction sites. A major driver of recent progress in learning-based navigation has been the use of pretrained visual representations. Rather than requiring the policy to learn perception from scratch, a frozen or lightly fine-tuned encoder supplies rich geometric and semantic features. This approach has proven effective for RGB-based navigation [ 1 , 2 ] and depth image-based policies [ 3 , 4 ] .

However, both RGB and depth cameras inherit limitations. RGB features degrade under poor lighting and appearance shifts, and depth cameras return noisy or missing values beyond a few meters, in sunlight, and on reflective or textureless surfaces. Crucially, both are limited to a narrow field of view (FoV). Obstacles approaching from the side, pedestrians overtaking from behind, and routes outside the current view are simply invisible until it is too late to react. LiDAR addresses these weaknesses with 360 ∘ 360^{\circ} coverage, metric range up to tens of meters, and invariance to illumination, making it the natural sensor for the crowded, outdoor, and industrial settings that motivate this work. Yet pretrained representations for LiDAR-based navigation remain underexplored. Although point-cloud foundation models (FMs) such as Sonata [ 5 ] and Utonia [ 6 ] learn strong geometric and semantic features, their computational cost limits their use in massively parallel reinforcement learning (RL), and their effectiveness as pretraining sources for compact navigation encoders remains an open question. A navigation-ready LiDAR encoder should therefore be lightweight enough for large-scale RL, pretrained so the policy does not have to learn perception from sparse rewards, and generalizable across scenes and to the real world.

To this end, we present a compact LiDAR range-image encoder pretrained specifically for navigation. Exploiting the fixed scan pattern of spinning LiDARs, we spherically project each scan onto a 2D range image [ 7 ] . This representation is cheap to compute and batches predictably across parallel environments, but its geometry differs from a perspective image: it has many more azimuthal columns than elevation rows, and the image wraps around at the 0 ∘ / 360 ∘ 0^{\circ}/360^{\circ} seam. We account for both with a fully convolutional encoder that uses anisotropic kernels and circular convolutions along the azimuth. We pretrain the encoder on range images rendered from
TartanGround [ 8 ] with three navigation-aligned objectives: range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and BEV prediction, which preserve object semantics, obstacle boundaries, and top-down traversability information. The frozen latent representation then feeds an RL navigation policy using spatially-enhanced recurrent units (SRUs) [ 3 ] (Fig. 1 ).

In simulation, our pretraining recipe improves navigation success rate (SR) over a reconstruction-only baseline by an average of 32.03 and 23.73 percentage points (pp) in procedurally generated training and out-of-distribution test environments, respectively. Compared with the depth-based policy of [ 3 ] , our LiDAR policy achieves comparable average SR, shorter navigation times, and higher success weighted by path length (SPL), and surpasses it in crowded and densely cluttered environments, highlighting the benefits of a wider FoV. Deployed zero-shot on a Unitree B2-W robot, the policy navigates obstacle-rich environments, unlit spaces, dense crowds, and cluttered construction sites, settings in which limited-FoV depth policies struggle.

In summary, our contributions are:

A navigation-aligned pretraining recipe combining range reconstruction, semantic segmentation, and BEV prediction that significantly improves downstream navigation.

A lightweight (183k parameters) LiDAR range-image encoder with anisotropic and circular convolutions, suitable for large-scale RL.

Extensive simulation and zero-shot real-world evaluation demonstrating the advantages of LiDAR-based navigation policies over limited-FoV depth-based policies.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Work

Recent methods decouple perception learning from downstream control, reducing the perceptual burden on policy learning caused by sparse rewards [ 9 , 10 , 3 ] . Several works build upon RGB vision foundation models [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] , keeping encoders frozen or lightly fine-tuned for point-goal navigation [ 1 , 2 ] , image-goal navigation [ 9 , 14 ] , and visual affordance prediction [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] . Concurrently, representations learned directly from depth images [ 18 , 3 , 4 ] have demonstrated robust zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for navigation. While these camera-based representations highlight the benefits of pretrained perception, they are typically designed for perspective projections with dense, isotropic pixel grids. Adapting them to panoramic LiDAR range images requires accounting for the large horizontal-to-vertical aspect ratio, structured beam sparsity, and azimuthal wraparound.

Most general-purpose LiDAR encoders operate directly on irregular 3D geometry. Seminal architectures like PointNet++ [ 19 ] and MinkowskiEngine [ 20 ] consume raw point sets or sparse spatial tensors, while recent FMs such as Sonata [ 5 ] and Utonia [ 6 ] pretrain Point Transformers [ 21 ] across large-scale 3D datasets. Lightweight variants like LitePT [ 22 ] optimize hierarchical point processing to reduce overhead. However, point-based and sparse-tensor operations incur prohibitive memory and runtime costs across thousands of parallel RL environments (Sec. IV ). Projection-based approaches circumvent these costs by structuring scans into standard arrays. Notably, RangeNet++ [ 7 ] showed that spherical projection allows efficient 2D convolutions, and RangeFormer [ 23 ] further scaled range representations using vision transformers. However, these systems are optimized and benchmarked for semantic perception, and pretrained range encoders remain largely unexplored for RL navigation.

Effective pretraining preserves task-relevant information. Prior work guides visual navigation encoders with auxiliary supervision, including action and temporal-distance predictions [ 24 ] , dynamics and progress targets [ 25 ] , depth prediction and loop-closure classification [ 26 ] , and auxiliary occupancy prediction for stereo cameras [ 27 ] . While these studies show the benefit of task-aligned supervision for camera inputs, combining complementary geometric and semantic objectives for LiDAR navigation has received little attention.

2026-10-22.title: Spacetime Splines for Adaptive Robot Motions
2026-10-22.authors: Boxuan Zhang , Ante Marić , Sylvain Calinon
2026-10-22.abstract:
Movement primitives commonly represent robot motions through basis
functions indexed by time or phase. Inspired by spacetime representations employed in physics,
we propose a spline-based formulation in which spatial geometry and
temporal progression are represented within a common set of continuous variables. The proposed method jointly estimates a shared Bézier
curve, while allowing spatial and temporal model complexity to be adapted independently (e.g., demonstration-specific phase modulation). As use case, we consider an alternating optimization process that simultaneously estimates path intervals observed in partial demonstrations. Simulation experiments demonstrate accurate joint
recovery, refinement through modifications in model complexity and continuity, and improved robustness to variance in the demonstration set. Finally, we demonstrate online retiming and synchronization capabilities in a patient-turning task assisted by a robot, evaluated with a physical manikin.
2026-10-22.introduction:
To adapt and coordinate robot motions, we need to consider both spatial and temporal information. For example, human-guided demonstrations may produce recordings of different durations that can speed up or slow down in different parts of the motion. The recorded paths and sampling rates may also differ, and some recordings may contain only part of the overall motion, starting and stopping at different points of the full path.

Spline representations provide compact continuous models of robot motion [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Bézier curves provide one such representation that allows for easy modification of through geometrically-interpretable control points and favorable mathematical properties. For example, De Casteljau’s algorithm can be used as a stable method for evaluating and subdividing these curves [ 5 , 6 ] .
Temporal alignment and phase-based methods account for nonlinear timing differences or separate path geometry from timing [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] , while others learn from incomplete or partial demonstrations [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] . A common thread is that temporal and spatial aspects are encoded and
optimized separately.

Inspired by spacetime representations in physics, we propose a continuous dynamic curve representation that homogeneously encodes spatial geometry and motion timing as an augmented state space.
Figure 1 shows an example in which different phase modulations produce different spacetime curves preserving a spatial path. We consider in this paper a use case in which we jointly estimate a shared geometric path with a demonstration-specific modulation of the phase function that describes progress along that path.
We utilize and alternating optimization process that adapts path geometry by modifying spatial coordinates of the control points,
and motion timing through the temporal coordinates of the control points. This allows us to estimate path intervals in partial demonstrations of a longer motion.

The main contributions of this work are:

Spacetime dynamic curve representation: a modular continuous
spline encoding that homogeneously couples path geometry and phase, while allowing independent spatial and temporal adaptation.

Coverage estimation in partial demonstrations: joint inference of path intervals observed in partial demonstrations.

Spatial and temporal adaptation: adaptive refinement of shared Bézier geometry and demonstration-specific phase for online retiming and synchronization of robot motions.

spline encoding that homogeneously couples path geometry and phase, while allowing independent spatial and temporal adaptation.

2. Coverage estimation in partial demonstrations: joint inference of path intervals observed in partial demonstrations.

3. Spatial and temporal adaptation: adaptive refinement of shared Bézier geometry and demonstration-specific phase for online retiming and synchronization of robot motions.

# II Related Work

## II-A Spline-Based Motion Representation and Adaptive Fitting

Spline representations provide compact continuous models of robot
motion [ 3 , 4 ] , with Bézier and B-spline models offering
smoothness, explicit control-point structure, and analytical
derivatives [ 5 , 6 ] .

B-spline Movement Primitives (BMPs) [ 3 ] combine B-spline representations with movement-primitive parameterizations, while concatenated Bézier splines have been used as continuous motion encoding for distance-field and dynamical-system construction [ 4 ] . Spline parameters have also been adopted as structured action representations for policy learning [ 17 , 18 ] . In parallel, free-knot and adaptive spline methods optimize or refine knot placement according to the data, allowing representation capacity to be allocated nonuniformly [ 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] .

Our work builds on these ideas but addresses an additional structural ambiguity: reconstruction error may originate from insufficient complexity of the spatial and temporal models representing the robot motion. Including both position and velocity information in an augmented state space enables additional dynamic information to be encoded in the curve. However, this approach has limitations, discussed in [ 24 ] , which can be addressed through the use of a phase variable. We propose to adapt geometry and phase components of the joint spacetime curve in an alternating optimization scheme and evaluate candidate refinements under a common regularized objective.

## II-B Temporal Alignment and Geometry–Phase Modeling

Temporal variations are common when learning motion from multiple demonstrations. Dynamic time warping (DTW) [ 7 ] and related registration methods [ 8 ] are commonly used to align demonstrations with nonlinear timing differences. This warping process is typically used as a pre-processing step to align trajectories and requires the discretization of the curve and the tuning of hyperparameters to define the allowed distortion, which typically depends on the chosen resolution of the curve (number of discretization points) and which often only considers local warping. Our approach instead relies on a continuous time adaptation function that does not require discretization.

In functional data analysis, temporal misalignment is often treated as phase variation and separated from spatial variation. Curve registration methods estimate nonlinear transformations of the independent variable in order to align salient structures across observations [ 25 ] . Raket et al. [ 9 ] showed that excessive alignment can absorb genuine spatial variability into the estimated warping functions. This motivates joint formulations in which the complexity of the temporal transformation and the spatial representation must be balanced rather than treating alignment as an independent preprocessing step.

Recent robotics methods further separate path geometry from timing. Braglia et al. [ 10 ] proposed arc-length-based alignment using a time-independent path parameterization. Their subsequent phase-independent Dynamic Movement Primitive (DMP)
formulation further decouples the demonstrated geometric path from its
timing law, allowing execution phase to be redesigned independently for applications including human–robot co-manipulation and time-optimal motion generation [ 11 ] . TimewarpVAE [ 12 ] similarly incorporates differentiable temporal warping into representation learning.

We jointly estimate a shared geometric spline and demonstration-specific monotone phase functions, with the recovered phase remaining an explicit component of the motion representation and allowing for subsequent constraints or modifications. Each demonstration is additionally associated with an explicit coverage interval on the shared path, allowing the encoding of temporal progression and spatial coverage.

## II-C Learning from Partial Demonstrations

Some work addresses incomplete supervision, such as missing action labels or partially observed state–action information [ 13 ] . Other methods consider demonstrations that cover only part of a task. Pervez et al. [ 14 ] combined temporal synchronization with movement learning from incomplete teleoperation demonstrations. Silvério et al. [ 15 ] combined movement models learned from partial subtasks through uncertainty-aware controller fusion. Partial demonstrations have also been used to guide policy learning without requiring exact trajectory reproduction [ 16 ] .

Our setting differs in that a partial demonstration is modeled as an observation of an unknown contiguous interval of a common continuous motion. Its coverage is estimated jointly with the shared geometry and demonstration-specific phase. Complete and partial demonstrations therefore contribute to a shared representation, while spatial coverage remains separate from temporal progression.

2026-10-22.title: Robot Generalization Beyond Volume: The Diversity Path via Zero-Shot Capabilities
2026-10-22.authors: Rafael Felix
2026-10-22.abstract: General-purpose robots must handle tasks, objects and environments they were never trained on, yet zero-shot generalization remains one of the least solved problems in physical AI. In digital AI, zero-shot capability grew with the volume and, above all, the diversity of training data, much of it sourced from the crowd. Robotics instead relies on paid collection by a few well-funded teams, which yields volume without diversity. We formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, and show that more samples from the same collectors shrink the unseen region only slowly, while each new contributor can extend it. Building on this and on zero-shot learning, we propose a shared latent space for robot actions that combines multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label learning; As a scalable source of diverse data, we propose a community of developers building applications on one standard, approachable robot, Origami. We close with a testable hypothesis and an evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data.
2026-10-22.introduction:
In recent years, several reports have projected strong growth for robotics through 2050. McKinsey estimates a $370B general-purpose robotics market by 2040 [ 59 ] , Japan has set a national target of 10 million AI robots by 2040 [ 64 ] , and Morgan Stanley projects a $5T humanoid market by 2050 [ 61 ] . These projections are driven by falling hardware costs, growing AI capabilities, and adoption that starts with developers and spreads through society. However, to achieve the true return on investment in physical AI, robot generalization is a major hurdle, and existing research has not yet found scalable solutions [ 100 , 4 ] .

The idea that an individual, on a given day, arrives home with a new appliance and hands it to their home robot, which has never seen the object before, is the promise of general-purpose robotics, as illustrated in Figure 1 . A general autonomous system should be capable of inferring the new object’s affordances, selecting a suitable grasp, and completing tasks with it [ 3 , 46 ] . Current robotic systems perform poorly at this capability, known as zero-shot generalization [ 100 , 4 ] . Zero-shot generalization has been the target of extensive studies over the past decades in the field of digital AI such as computer vision [ 50 , 92 ] , large language models [ 71 , 8 ] , audio [ 70 ] and multi-modal learning [ 23 , 22 , 21 ] . We argue that it determines whether robots remain confined to controlled settings or become general-purpose economic assets.

In digital AI, zero-shot generalization has progressed as a function of the volume and diversity of data [ 16 , 23 ] . As illustrated in Figure 2 volume is the density with which each situation is represented in the latent space, and diversity is the footprint those situations cover. This mirrors a familiar result for Gaussian processes: posterior uncertainty shrinks only near observed inputs, so spreading samples across the input space reduces uncertainty far more than repeating them in one region [ 76 ] . Volume helps AI systems recognize patterns accurately, but diversity allows them to interpolate within the latent space and act on concepts they have never seen. Seminal research and industry efforts have demonstrated zero-shot capabilities in large language models (LLMs) [ 8 , 47 ] , computer vision [ 69 ] , and other fields [ 70 , 32 ] . Robotics has yet to show comparable zero-shot capability. Moreover, the problem of diversity has been largely overlooked, as industry and research efforts have prioritized demonstrations of robots performing single tasks [ 13 , 98 ] . Industrial and early-stage robots are typically deployed for a single, repetitive task, and each new task requires reprogramming or new training data [ 6 , 100 ] . A robot able to perform an array of tasks within the same facility, adapting to new parts, layouts and procedures, would amortize its cost across many functions and lower the integration cost of each new task. For instance, in a warehouse, a robot trained to pick a given type of product could take on new types of object, or develop new tasks. In elderly care, a robot that delivers meals could assist carers with preparing food, a new task with new handling demands [ 78 ] . Further examples of zero-shot settings are depicted in Figure 1 ,

In this paper, we propose a novel approach based on our prior work in zero-shot and noisy-label learning applied in physical AI. Our approach combines a crowd-sourced data collection with recent advances in zero-shot generalization, generative AI, learning from noisy labels and scalable trust and safety [ 23 , 28 , 19 ] . We argue that generalization will emerge from structured data acquisition combined with community-driven crowd-sourcing. This combination allows us to acquire large volumes of data safely, while widening the range of scenarios, objects, situations and environments far beyond what any single engineering team could cover. Unlike digital AI, robots must also transfer what they learn in simulation to the physical world, where simulation never fully matches reality, a challenge known as the sim-to-real gap [ 99 , 81 ] . A community running the same robotic platform in both simulation and reality exposes that gap at scale, and provides the tools to close it.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews how digital AI reached zero-shot behavior, what builds a latent space, how each training stage has drawn on crowd-sourced data, and how learning from imperfect data can absorb noisy contributions. Section 3 presents our approach. We first formulate zero-shot generalization in physical AI as coverage of the deployment distribution, showing why more data from the same collectors closes the gap only slowly, while each new contributor can widen it. We then describe a shared latent space for robot actions built from multi-modal alignment, generative augmentation, and noisy-label and uncertainty learning, in which safety is part of the space from pre-training onward and seen/unseen detection lets the robot hand control to a human (Section 3.2 ). Real2Sim2Real treats simulation and reality as noisy teachers of each other across a community running the same robot (Section 3.3 ), and a community of developers building on one standard, approachable robot provides the data, with a cost model for each contributed hour (Section 3.4 ). Section 4 sets out a testable hypothesis and evaluation protocol relating real-robot zero-shot success to the diversity of contributed data. Section 5 discusses limitations and open questions, and Section 6 concludes.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Zero-shot capabilities

Zero-shot capabilities are essential for online platforms such as TikTok and Instagram, where new harmful trends and content designed to evade guidelines emerge faster than training data can be collected [ 60 , 33 , 55 ] , much as a home robot meets objects it was never trained on. Beyond trust and safety, modern LLM chatbots and their applications also extend well beyond their training data [ 47 ] . Where collecting training data would be prohibitive, dangerous or unethical, zero-shot learning is, to the best of our knowledge, the most prominent set of techniques available [ 86 ] . It allows AI models to reason about unseen circumstances by associating them with prior knowledge embedded in their latent space [ 92 ] .
Over the past decades, the field has moved through three eras. Early methods described classes by hand-defined attributes, so an unseen class could be recognized from its description [ 50 ] . Deep learning replaced hand-made descriptions with learned ones, including generative models that synthesize examples of unseen classes [ 23 , 93 ] , alongside methods robust to imperfect labels [ 28 ] . The GPT era turned zero-shot from a research benchmark into everyday behavior: large language models performed new tasks from a prompt alone [ 8 ] , instruction tuning made that ability reliable across unseen tasks [ 87 ] , and human feedback aligned it with what people actually ask for [ 68 ] . Vision-language models such as CLIP extended it to images [ 69 ] , and early robot models have begun transferring this web-scale knowledge to physical actions [ 7 ] .
Despite this progress in digital AI, comparatively little research has addressed zero-shot generalization in robotics. Recent robot foundation models show impressive results on the tasks and settings they were trained for, yet their performance still drops sharply when the task or environment is genuinely new [ 100 , 4 ] . Applied directly to robots, the zero-shot toolkit of digital AI falls short, but it points to a clear pathway. Across all three eras, one principle holds: a model handles the unseen only when its latent space is rich enough to place it, solving new cases by interpolating within that space.

## 2.2 What builds a latent space

In the latent space, AI models build representations of concepts of the world. The more diverse the latent space, the more generalizable it becomes [ 49 , 80 , 16 ] . Representation quality is what learning ultimately depends on [ 5 ] , zero-shot performance tracks how well the embedding space covers unseen classes [ 92 ] , and CLIP zero-shot transfer improved as its training data grew broader [ 16 ] .

In physical AI, no single method yet controls a robot end to end; a working system layers several. Classical control and engineering handle sensing and low-level loops [ 66 ] . Reinforcement learning, trained largely in simulation, teaches basic motor skills such as balancing, reaching, and locomotion, effectively learning motor control from experience [ 75 , 74 ] . Vision-language-action (VLA) models inherit a web-scale latent space and use it to orchestrate those skills from visual and linguistic context [ 7 , 46 , 6 , 65 , 66 ] . How they connect to the body is still open: some systems map VLA outputs directly to actuators [ 6 ] , while others have the VLA call lower-level policies, so it never commands the actuators itself, which limits risk [ 3 ] . World models add a further layer: they learn a latent representation of how the world changes, so a robot can imagine several ways of completing a task, predict the outcome of each, and choose the most promising before acting [ 35 , 36 , 62 , 97 ] . The architecture of physical AI is therefore far from settled.

Despite their progress, a systematic link between these paradigms and zero-shot generalization has yet to be established: each builds a latent space, but none addresses how the diversity of that space is sourced. Furthermore, when building foundational latent spaces, two patterns are often observed: (1) pre-training models follow scaling laws for general world contextual understanding, and (2) once pre-trained, these models require expert-level annotation for supervised fine-tuning stages [ 43 , 68 ] .

## 2.3 Scaling laws and Noisy-labels from crowd-source data

Training data for AI has come from people in three distinct ways.

Community-driven data is produced by people pursuing their own goals and becomes training data as a by product, so its diversity grows with the number of people taking part [ 8 , 48 ] . Crowd-sourced data is produced by paid workers executing tasks someone else designed, which scales and offers control but reflects its designers’ choices [ 15 , 68 , 58 , 1 ] . Specialized data is produced by trained experts, in robotics mostly teleoperators on the target hardware, which matches the robot’s embodiment but is the most expensive per sample and concentrated in a few teams [ 24 , 79 ] .

Each training stage has drawn on a different form of crowd-sourcing. Pre-training, governed by scaling laws, needs volume and diversity: language models found both in text written by people all over the world as a by-product of everyday use [ 8 , 72 ] . Supervised fine-tuning needs expert, high-signal data: it came from paid annotators [ 68 ] and, increasingly, from volunteer communities [ 48 ] . Table 1 compares these sources with the workarounds robotics uses today.

These sources differ in cost, scale and diversity. Paid crowd-sourcing, from annotation micro-tasks [ 15 ] to paid robot teleoperation [ 58 ] , offers control, but its cost grows with every sample and its coverage reflects its designers. Volunteer communities scale with shared motivation. Data generated as a by-product of use, as in games with a purpose [ 85 , 14 ] , scales with the number of people who want to take part.
The common response is that robotics simply lacks data volume. We agree, but how data is collected determines what it contains: paid collection by a few teams yields volume without diversity for pre-training, and expensive, narrow expertise for fine-tuning. Language models, by contrast, sourced each stage from the crowd. A further barrier is hardware. Robots are expensive for companies to lend to collectors and expensive for annotators to buy, so collection stays concentrated in a few well-funded teams. Workarounds that avoid robots altogether, such as egocentric human video, lower the cost but introduce an embodiment gap: human hands and viewpoints differ from a robot’s, which limits how well the data transfers [ 34 , 44 ] .
Robotics relies largely on paid collection for both stages. Companies have raised substantial capital [ 25 ] , with teleoperation and egocentric data collection a major cost [ 24 , 79 , 2 ] , yet their models still need new demonstrations for each new task [ 6 , 100 ] . A notable exception is the LeRobot community, whose contributed datasets on the low-cost SO-100 arm were used to pre-train SmolVLA [ 77 , 11 ] . These open tools, however, are built for research speed: they evolve quickly, often without backward compatibility, and favor rapid experimentation over the stability needed to build reliable applications. Their community data is a by-product of writing papers, not of solving everyday problems, so it stays concentrated on the tasks researchers choose to study. Our approach differs in where contributions come from: a community of developers building applications on one stable, standard robot and platform, whose data reflects the problems they actually need to solve.

Crowd-sourced data is never clean. In classification, learning with noisy labels has developed methods that select likely-clean samples during training [ 39 , 51 ] , model noise that depends on each instance rather than on its class alone [ 91 , 28 ] , and estimate how much noise a dataset contains [ 31 , 29 ] . In robot learning, the quality of demonstrations matters as much as their quantity: policies trained on demonstrations from operators of mixed skill perform markedly worse than those trained on proficient operators alone [ 57 ] . Imitation methods have so far handled this mainly by filtering, discarding low-quality demonstrations [ 57 , 1 ] . Filtering protects performance but discards diversity, and for zero-shot generalization diversity is the scarcer resource. We therefore treat imperfect demonstrations as noisy labels to be weighted rather than discarded (Section 3.2 ).

## 2.4 Trust and Safety in Physical AI

Most robot safety work today addresses collision avoidance, joint limits, and grasp force [ 95 , 9 , 40 ] , and treats broader safe behavior as a layer added after pre-training: a foundation model is trained to act, then fine-tuned on examples of what unsafe means [ 96 , 42 ] . This leaves two questions open. First, how can a robot avoid unsafe behavior in situations for which no data can ethically or practically be collected? Second, why is safety absent from the stage where the latent space is formed? Both are zero-shot problems, and the same foundations address them. Rare or dangerous situations can be generated rather than staged, so the robot learns them without putting anyone at risk [ 94 , 42 , 22 ] . The robot should also recognize when it has left familiar ground: building on generalized zero-shot learning with domain classification, which separates seen from unseen inputs [ 18 , 22 ] , and on estimating out-of-distribution noise [ 31 ] , it can detect when a situation falls in 𝒮 unseen \mathcal{S}_{\text{unseen}} and stop or hand control to a human through teleoperation.
