2026-10-22.title: OMAR: Open-World Multi-Attribute Reasoning for Scene-Conditioned Shelf Organization
2026-10-22.authors: Benedikt Kreis , Rohit Menon , Benno Wingender , Muhammad Ehsan Ullah , Nils Dengler , Maren Bennewitz
2026-10-22.abstract:
With the advent of foundation models, robots are increasingly capable of understanding and executing explicitly specified human tasks.
Extending these capabilities to open-ended tasks, however, requires robots to infer appropriate actions from the observed scene.
Household organization exemplifies this challenge, as robots must often act without detailed instructions, predefined object vocabularies, or known object-receptacle associations.
While robots may follow instructions or learn organization preferences from demonstrations, inferring the latent organization of an occasionally changing scene and placing a novel object consistently with it remains challenging.
We propose an open-world multi-attribute reasoning pipeline that grounds unknown objects across views and constructs an instance-level 3D scene graph for placement reasoning.
First, a vision-language model proposes labels together with attributes such as content and packaging type, which are grounded through segmentation, depth, and multi-view association.
Then, an LLM reasons over this representation to infer the latent shelf organization and rank scene-consistent object placements without explicitly user-provided preferences.
The resulting placement rankings guide subsequent geometric and kinematic feasibility checks for execution.
Our experimental evaluation shows that our approach leads to improved instance mapping and placement coherence over single-view language-grounding and geometry-only baselines, enabling autonomous placement of previously unseen objects without predefined object-receptacle mappings or class-specific retraining.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Households are constantly changing environments, and their organization reflects implicit and evolving human conventions.
To effectively organize objects in such environments, service robots must act beyond explicitly specified tasks.
When storing groceries, a robot must determine where a previously unseen object belongs, even without detailed instructions or user-provided preferences.
As object locations change, predefined object vocabularies and object-receptacle mappings cannot fully specify appropriate placements.

We study scene-conditioned shelf organization, in which the robot must infer the latent organization from the observed arrangement and place a novel object consistently into it.
This task requires reasoning over multiple object attributes, including content, packaging type, edibility, and orientation.
These attributes can suggest competing placements, and their relative importance depends on the organization of the particular scene.
Category labels alone therefore provide insufficient context.
Placement reasoning requires object-level descriptions grounded in the observed shelf.
Multi-view grounding provides this object-level context by associating instances across views and revealing occluded objects.

Vision-language models (VLMs) and large language models (LLMs) offer semantic knowledge beyond predefined object sets, supporting the prediction of semantically plausible placements [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , but plausibility alone does not ensure geometric or kinematic feasibility.
Joint pick-and-place pipelines address grasp-placement compatibility through task-aware 6-DoF grasp selection and feasibility evaluation [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , but do not infer the shelf’s latent organization from semantic object attributes.
The resulting challenge is to connect grounded, scene-dependent semantic reasoning with feasibility-aware planning so that placements of unseen objects preserve the observed organization and remain executable in confined shelf spaces.

We address this gap via open-world, multi-attribute reasoning (OMAR), which places previously unseen objects consistently with the observed shelf organization.
As shown in Fig. 1 , our pipeline grounds VLM-generated object descriptions across views in an instance-level 3D scene graph, capturing content, packaging type, edibility, and orientation rather than category labels alone.
An LLM reasons jointly over these attributes and their scene-dependent relevance to infer the latent shelf organization and propose placements that preserve its coherence, without user-provided preferences, predefined object-receptacle mappings, or class-specific retraining.
These proposals guide grasp prediction and geometric and kinematic feasibility checks, linking multi-attribute shelf coherence to executable placements.
To summarize, the main contributions of our work are:

An open-world multi-attribute mapping pipeline that grounds unknown objects across views and creates an instance-level 3D scene graph for placement reasoning.

An open-world multi-attribute mapping pipeline that grounds unknown objects across views and creates an instance-level 3D scene graph for placement reasoning.

An LLM-based reasoning pipeline leveraging instance-level scene representation to infer the latent shelf organization and rank scene-consistent object placements.

Our evaluation shows that our approach leads to improved instance mapping and placement coherence over single-view language-grounding and geometry-only baselines.

1. An open-world multi-attribute mapping pipeline that grounds unknown objects across views and creates an instance-level 3D scene graph for placement reasoning.

2. An LLM-based reasoning pipeline leveraging instance-level scene representation to infer the latent shelf organization and rank scene-consistent object placements.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Classical and Learning-based P&P Approaches

Pick2Place [ 4 ] uses object-centric perspective affordances to produce task-aware 6-DoF grasps that align grasp selection with downstream placements.
Alternatively, cost-based joint pick-and-place formulations produce place-aware grasps, as demonstrated by Shanthi and Hermans [ 5 ] and, more recently, UniP [ 6 ] , which introduced a generalized placeability metric that scores object configurations based on geometric and physical stability criteria.
With a similar emphasis on physical stability, Paxton et al. [ 8 ] learn stable object placements.
Moving from individual placements to multi-step rearrangement, REAP [ 9 ] uses a heuristic learned from motion-planner feedback, reducing motion-planning queries while guiding search toward geometrically feasible actions.

Beyond physical feasibility, semantic placement planning is considered by Wingender et al. [ 10 ] , although the approach uses predefined semantic labels.
Similarly, Adeleye et al. [ 11 ] combine object recognition with semantic reasoning to select grocery storage locations in shelf environments, but operate on a closed object set without checking geometric feasibility.
These approaches thus either omit placement semantics [ 8 , 4 , 5 , 6 ] or rely on predefined object sets without considering multiple object attributes [ 10 , 11 ] .
Furthermore, some approaches [ 5 , 8 ] do not address placements into geometrically challenging confined spaces.

## II-B Foundation Model-based P&P Approaches

The generalization promise and semantic reasoning capabilities drives the increased use of foundation models in robotic manipulation.
For example, TidyBot [ 12 ] combines open-vocabulary detection using ViLD [ 13 ] with object-centric manipulation, using sparse user preferences to bootstrap personalized object rearrangements.
ContextSortLM [ 14 ] and APRICOT [ 15 ] similarly use language models to learn detailed user-specific spatial preferences for object placements.
While these approaches demonstrate the value of foundation models for semantic placement decisions, their reasoning requires user specific input.

ConceptGraphs [ 16 ] and BBQ [ 17 ] use 3D scene graphs as LLM input for language-guided object selection and relational object grounding, respectively.
These works ground language-model reasoning in observed objects and their spatial context through scene-graph representations.
Rather than grounding a user-specified object query, we reason over scene-graph attributes to infer shelf organization and rank placements of unseen objects.

Foundation models have also been applied specifically to task-oriented grasping.
GraspGPT [ 18 ] and FoundationGrasp [ 19 ] leverage semantic knowledge to bias grasp selection towards task-relevant affordances, while GraspMolmo [ 20 ] combines a multimodal foundation model with large-scale synthetic data to improve generalization.
These methods primarily reason about how an object should be grasped, rather than how it should be placed.

Conversely, several recent approaches focus on semantic placement.
AnyPlace [ 21 ] learns generalizable object-to-receptacle placements from multimodal supervision, PlaceIt3D [ 2 ] reasons about language-guided placements in real 3D scenes but without robotic embodiment, and Set It Up [ 3 ] targets functional object arrangements.
These methods produce semantically meaningful placements but only partially address geometric and kinematic constraints.

Integrated foundation-model-based systems that focus on confined spaces are LLM-Pack [ 22 ] which uses VLMs to identify grocery items and an LLM to generate human-like packing sequences.
EMPOWER [ 1 ] employs LLM agents for perception, planning, and execution, enabling multi-step object rearrangements through a set of predefined manipulation skills.
However, these systems do not explicitly couple semantic placement reasoning with the grasp-dependent geometric feasibility of executing individual placements in space-limited environments.

Our approach addresses the existing gaps by coupling open-world, foundation-model-based semantic reasoning with grasp-placement compatibility.
A persistent multi-view instance map provides a holistic and instance-consistent representation of complex scenes across viewpoints and enriches objects with detailed semantic attributes beyond category labels, enabling more informed placement decisions.
This allows to jointly consider semantic and geometric fit, reachability, and grasp feasibility across multiple shelf boards with varying clearance.

2026-10-22.title: Post-hoc Epistemic Uncertainty for Vision-Language-Action Policies
2026-10-22.authors: Johannes Keller , Albrecht M. Bloße , Adrian Lindenmeyer , Thomas Neumuth , Daniel Schneider
2026-10-22.abstract:
Vision–language–action (VLA) policies need to recognize gaps in their training knowledge to request useful demonstrations or assistance in new situations, especially when failures are costly.
Disagreement within an ensemble of independently trained policies can guide these decisions, but requires training and running multiple policies.
We propose post-hoc kernel-variance heads that estimate epistemic uncertainty from the embeddings of a single policy.
Each head computes the conditional variance of a Gaussian process conditioned on embeddings from the training demonstrations.
Fitting requires no regression targets or gradient updates and leaves the policy unchanged.
In experiments with SmolVLA on LIBERO-10, the kernel variance heads perform competitively with two-policy ensemble scores in task-level correlation with task success, in demonstration acquisition during active learning, and in referral to a stronger supervisor policy as a proxy for human assistance.
For SmolVLA, the head on the vision–language backbone reduces uncertainty-scoring time by up to approximately a factor of 50 compared with ensemble scores, while also substantially reducing setup costs.
We also show that the established evaluation protocol on LIBERO-10 primarily rewards recognition of coverage differences between tasks, while execution variability weakens assessment of within-task rankings.
Thus, controlled perturbations provide a complementary evaluation: modality-specific heads identify unfamiliar camera, instruction, or state inputs, while fused heads can detect unfamiliar combinations of individually familiar inputs.
With a supervisor proxy trained on the evaluated perturbation families, the decoder head improves within-task referral over ensemble disagreement.
These findings show that useful uncertainty estimates for adaptive robot learning can be obtained from a single policy.
Code available at https://github.com/post-hoc-vla-uncertainty/post-hoc-vla-uncertainty .
2026-10-22.introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models bring pre-trained visual and linguistic representations to robot control [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
After deployment, such a policy keeps encountering tasks, scenes and instructions that its training demonstrations cover only partially.
In tasks where failures may be costly, when facing difficulties due to insufficient training knowledge, the robot should respond adaptively by deferring tasks to seek human assistance or by requesting relevant additional training demonstrations [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
Both responses are effective only if guided by the policy’s epistemic uncertainty, that is, by how poorly its training data support a situation.
Unlike aleatoric ambiguity, epistemic uncertainty shrinks with more relevant demonstrations [ 15 , 16 ] .

Flow-based VLAs do not provide such an estimate by themselves.
This motivates dedicated methods for quantifying epistemic uncertainty in these policies.
For example, Römer et al. [14] derive velocity-field disagreement (VFD), an ensemble estimate of the divergence between flow-matching policies.
They use VFD in SAVE, an active fine-tuning procedure that they evaluate on LIBERO [ 17 ] , a simulation benchmark of language-instructed household manipulation tasks.
In each round, SAVE requests a few new demonstrations, preferring situations that VFD rates as uncertain, and then fine-tunes the policy.
In their evaluation, VFD correlates more strongly with task success than six alternative uncertainty scores, including other ensemble-based measures and entropy-based scores.
SAVE with VFD needs at least 22% fewer demonstrations than the compared acquisition strategies.
The price is an ensemble of at least two policies: every additional member must be pre-trained, fine-tuned alongside the deployed policy in every adaptation round, and integrated jointly with it whenever a score is computed.

We ask whether this ensemble is necessary to obtain comparably useful estimates of epistemic uncertainty.
Ensemble disagreement reflects differences between the predictions of independently trained policies, which can arise where the demonstrations leave their behaviour weakly constrained.
Their disagreement can therefore serve as an indirect signal of demonstration coverage.
This motivates assessing coverage directly in the embedding space of a single trained policy, using lightweight uncertainty estimation heads.
Each head reads embeddings that the policy already computes and compares a queried observation with support observations from its training demonstrations (Figure 1 ).
The approach assumes that the embeddings keep unfamiliar observations apart from familiar ones [ 18 ] , a property that we do not enforce during training.
Its practical usefulness further depends on whether unfamiliarity helps identify situations where the policy may fail or benefit from assistance or additional demonstrations.
We assess these relationships empirically across our experiments.
The measure is the posterior variance of a Gaussian process (GP) with a Gaussian kernel, conditioned on the support embeddings [ 19 ] .
It needs no regression targets and no gradient update and does not alter the policy’s predicted actions but can inform decisions such as when to request help or new demonstrations.
Fitting it post hoc to a trained policy takes one feature extraction pass over the support observations and one Cholesky factorization.
Since the heads are this cheap, several of them can be attached to different embeddings of the same policy.
Heads on modality-specific representations, such as the camera or instruction tokens, can then indicate which part of an input is unfamiliar.

We organize the study around five questions.

Does a single-policy kernel variance head match ensemble scores in calibration to task success and referral gain to a stronger supervisor on LIBERO-10? 1 1 1 Here, referral means handing the most uncertain situations to a more capable supervisor policy, which serves as a proxy for human assistance.

Does active fine-tuning with the SAVE protocol guided by kernel variance scores acquire demonstrations as effectively as ensemble scores?

How much computation does the kernel variance head save compared to ensemble scores?

Which properties of an uncertainty score do the established evaluations of Q1 reward on LIBERO?

Do kernel variance heads on different context embeddings respond selectively to perturbations of the inputs they read, and do kernel variance heads support within-task referral under such perturbations?

Post-hoc epistemic uncertainty heads that read the embeddings of a single trained VLA policy.
Instead of pre-training, fine-tuning and running a second policy, they require only one feature extraction pass over the support observations and one matrix factorization. In our experiments, this makes the heads up to about 44 times faster to set up per fine-tuning round and up to about 50 times faster to use.

A comparison on the LIBERO manipulation benchmark, in which the kernel variance heads perform comparably to uncertainty scores from a two-policy ensemble in ranking tasks by their failure rate and in selecting new training demonstrations, following the setting of prior ensemble-based work [ 14 ] .
We additionally evaluate success gain from handing uncertain situations over to a stronger policy, where the kernel variance heads again match or exceed the ensemble.
Our analysis shows that in this setting, the evaluations mainly test whether a score recognizes how well training demonstrations cover a task, which is useful in itself.
However, they test the ranking of situations within a task only weakly, because relatively large execution noise obscures reproducible differences in the outcomes.

A within-task evaluation that perturbs single input modalities and their combinations in a controlled way.
In this evaluation, our uncertainty heads detect most perturbations at least as sensitively as the ensemble scores and match or exceed them in deciding which situations within a task to hand over to a stronger policy.
Attached to the embeddings of separate input modalities, context-specific uncertainty heads also indicate which of them are unfamiliar.

2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

VLAs often fine-tune vision-language backbones on large robot datasets [ 20 ] and output actions as discrete tokens [ 1 , 2 , 4 ] or through continuous generative heads [ 3 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
Flow-matching action experts [ 21 ] , like diffusion policies [ 22 ] , sample action chunks from multimodal distributions.
On LIBERO [ 17 ] , a widely used simulation benchmark for these models, high scores may reflect memorized layouts and instructions and do not necessarily imply robustness under changed object positions, cameras, lighting or wording [ 23 , 24 ] .
This motivates evaluations that vary conditions within a task (Sections 4.4 – 4.6 ).

Epistemic uncertainty reflects limited knowledge about the true function, whereas aleatoric uncertainty reflects inherent randomness in the data and cannot be reduced by collecting more [ 15 , 16 ] .
For expressive models, epistemic uncertainty is mainly uncertainty about which of the many functions that fit the data is correct, so it is large where data sparsity leaves predictions weakly constrained [ 16 ] .
For a robot policy, it concerns which actions the training demonstrations imply in a given situation, while aleatoric uncertainty arises, for example, when demonstrators solve a task in several valid ways or when contact outcomes are stochastic.
A principled estimate may approximate the posterior over functions and measures the spread of its predictions [ 25 ] .

Weight-space methods such as deep ensembles [ 26 ] , Monte Carlo dropout [ 27 ] and Laplace approximations [ 28 , 29 ] define the prior over functions only implicitly through the weights.
In practice, ensemble members and weight-space particles often converge to similar functions [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] , mean-field variational approximations can underestimate the variance between separated data regions [ 33 ] , and the resulting spread can follow aleatoric noise more closely than data density [ 34 , 25 ] .
Depending on protocol, decisions such as referral and acquisition may only need a ranking, in which case an underestimated functional spread can still serve them if its ordering is right, although this is not guaranteed.
Even single-model entropy or confidence scores can appear to capture epistemic uncertainty [ 35 , 36 ] .
However, by design, they cannot capture the uncertainty associated with their single function.
Implicit biases of trained networks [ 36 ] or aleatoric estimates that become unreliable away from the training data [ 37 ] can nevertheless make these scores correlate with training-data coverage.
Such agreement is indirect and does not mean that the scores represent epistemic uncertainty, either separately or as an explicit component of total uncertainty.

By contrast, methods with explicit priors over functions allow predictive variance to grow with distance from the training data, with the predictive distribution reverting to the prior far from training support. Examples include GP output layers on spectrally normalized networks [ 38 , 18 ] , deep GPs [ 39 ] and functional variational Bayesian neural networks [ 40 ] .
Deterministic scores based on radial basis function prototypes, feature densities, Mahalanobis distance or nearest neighbours also use feature-space distances or densities, but do not generally define a posterior over predictive functions [ 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 ] .
In direct comparisons, such distance-aware single models match or improve upon deep ensembles in detecting unfamiliar inputs [ 41 , 42 , 45 , 25 ] .
Methods that score distances in learned representations depend on a feature space that keeps unfamiliar inputs apart from familiar ones, which feature collapse can prevent [ 18 ] .

Our uncertainty scoring head places such an explicit GP prior over functions defined on embeddings of a frozen policy, post hoc.
Spectral normalization could make these embeddings more distance-preserving, but introducing it would modify the policy and would require further retraining.
Instead, we leave the policy unchanged so that the head can be attached to any trained policy.
The head’s score, the GP conditional variance [ 19 ] , vanishes at support inputs and approaches the prior variance far from them.
Without the ridge, its square root equals the power function of kernel interpolation, which is the worst-case interpolation error over the unit sphere of the kernel’s reproducing kernel Hilbert space [ 46 , 47 ] .
It therefore measures coverage in the chosen embedding geometry without requiring output targets to fit the head.

For diffusion and flow models, epistemic uncertainty has been estimated from ensemble disagreement of denoising means (DECU) [ 48 ] , from a Gaussian approximation of the generative posterior predictive (GU) [ 49 ] , and from velocity-field disagreement (VFD) [ 14 ] .
Runtime monitors for robot policies use action-chunk entropy and embedding novelty [ 50 ] , temporal action consistency [ 51 ] , learned density estimators [ 52 ] or language-model embeddings [ 53 ] .
VLA failure detectors learn from internal features [ 54 ] , combine last-layer Mahalanobis distance with action consistency [ 55 ] , or measure action disagreement under hidden-activation perturbations of a single model [ 56 ] , and VLA confidence has been calibrated with prompt ensembles and Platt scaling [ 57 ] .
Most of these robotics methods focus on failure detection during execution.

Outside robotics, attribution methods explain an existing uncertainty estimate post hoc by its input features, through counterfactuals [ 58 , 59 ] , gradients [ 60 ] or Shapley values [ 61 ] .
Multimodal models estimate uncertainty per modality to weight their fusion [ 62 , 63 ] and use disagreement between modalities for OOD detection [ 64 ] , and a recent benchmark uses modality-specific and cross-modal perturbations to test how vision–language uncertainty scores respond to different sources of uncertainty [ 65 ] .
Our raw context kernel-variance heads assess unfamiliarity separately for each input modality by reading its representation before cross-modal mixing.
To our knowledge, this is the first use of separate coverage estimates to assess unfamiliarity in the individual input modalities of a VLA policy.
Our heads can inform decisions taken before execution, such as requesting additional training demonstrations or human assistance, and can also score observations during execution.

Early work on data selection by expected information gain or variance reduction includes MacKay [66] and Cohn et al. [67] .
Deep active learning uses Bayesian disagreement [ 68 , 69 , 70 ] or representation diversity [ 71 , 72 ] , or combines uncertainty and diversity in gradient space [ 72 ] .
GP methods use integrated variance reduction and mutual information [ 73 , 74 ] , and transductive active learning targets a specified population [ 75 ] .
Interactive imitation learning collects expert feedback on situations encountered by the learner [ 8 , 9 ] , with some methods using uncertainty or risk to decide when to query the expert [ 76 , 77 , 78 , 10 ] .
Related approaches address supervision across robot fleets [ 11 ] and learning during deployment [ 12 ] .
Data curation selects which existing demonstrations to keep [ 79 ] , whereas multi-task active fine-tuning selects which new demonstrations to collect [ 13 , 14 ] .
Of these, we build on the SAVE procedure of Römer et al. [14] , keep its rule for choosing demonstrations and replace only its uncertainty score, VFD, with the variance of our kernel heads.

Selective prediction allows a model to abstain on uncertain inputs and evaluates uncertainty scores through the trade-off between coverage (the fraction of inputs retained) and risk on the retained inputs [ 80 , 81 , 82 , 83 , 84 ] .
This trade-off does not distinguish epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty, since rejecting inherently ambiguous inputs also lowers retained risk.
Combined with the fact that many scores labelled epistemic remain entangled with aleatoric noise [ 37 , 85 , 34 , 25 ] , this creates a major evaluation limitation: improved performance can reflect sensitivity to inherent ambiguity rather than the identification of missing knowledge.
Deferral passes rejected inputs to a second decision maker, whose errors also affect combined performance.
Some evaluations of combined performance assume that an oracle correctly labels every deferred case [ 86 ] and therefore inherit the same limitation.
Learning to defer formulates the delegation decision as a learning problem [ 87 , 88 ] and has also been studied with imperfect simulated experts [ 89 ] .
Deferral also arises in robotics, where calibrated uncertainty guides requests for assistance [ 90 , 91 ] .
Our supervisor referral follows the deferral view with an imperfect expert.
Under a fixed referral budget, we pass selected conditions to a stronger policy and evaluate each ranking by the supervisor’s actual, possibly negative, performance gain on the referred conditions.
Where irreducible randomness affects both policies alike, referring a condition contributes no expected gain.
This reduces, but not eliminates, the credit a score receives for detecting ambiguity alone.
The metric primarily rewards identifying conditions for which the supervisor’s broader training coverage provides a performance advantage.

2026-10-22.title: Sufficient and Necessary Causal Explanations for the Analysis of Autonomous Systems
2026-10-22.authors: Tom Yaacov , Khen Elimelech , Hana Chockler , Moshe Y. Vardi
2026-10-22.abstract: Understanding failures of autonomous systems is challenging, particularly when their behavior depends on black-box components such as neural networks. In this work, we make a distinction between two objectives of failure analysis: reproduction, which seeks to identify conditions sufficient to reproduce an observed failure, and avoidance, which seeks to identify the changes required to prevent it. Previous work on causal explanations of system failures is based on the concept of sufficient explanations and naturally supports reproduction. Nevertheless, we observe that it does not address the problem of avoiding the failure. In this paper, we introduce and formalize the concept of necessary explanations for system analysis as the correct formalism for failure avoidance. We place necessary explanations in the framework of actual causality and show that, together with sufficient explanations, they provide a unified causal framework for addressing both objectives of failure analysis. We present an efficient approximation algorithm for generating necessary explanations based on the notion of causal responsibility. We evaluate the efficiency of our approach across multiple environments. We demonstrate the practical utility of necessary explanations for failure avoidance through counterfactual generation and show that it outperforms existing methods.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Autonomous systems rely on algorithms and digital computation to control real-world machines and achieve complex objectives autonomously [ 1 ] . As these objectives become increasingly challenging, modern systems have come to rely heavily on black-box components, such as neural networks [ 2 , 3 ] . The opacity of these components, combined with the complexity of systems and the variability of their operating environments, makes it difficult to interpret system behavior and gain insight into how decisions were made.
This difficulty has motivated the rapidly growing interest in Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), which is widely regarded as crucial for the widespread adoption of autonomous systems [ 4 , 5 ] .

Explainability becomes even more vital when failures happen. Understanding failures, known as failure analysis , is crucial for the development and debugging of systems, and it is especially challenging when systems rely on black-box components, often provided by a third party.
An explanation should help us gain insight into what affected the system behavior that led to the failure outcome. Addressing this goal requires answering two questions: (1) what counts as an explanation? (2) how to generate the right one?
Post-hoc XAI, where explanations are based on the analysis of the outcome rather than the process,
is a suitable paradigm for analyzing black-box systems, as it does not require any changes or even access to
the internals of the system, and it is the one we follow in this paper.

To position this work clearly, we first mention the underlying conceptual contribution of this paper (which we discuss in detail in Sec. IV ), with which we identify the two complementary explanation objectives: outcome avoidance , and outcome reproduction . In the first case, our concern is changing the outcome (with minimal effort), e.g., when we wish to repair the failure; the explanation should hence provide insight on which elements in the scenario should be changed (and how), in order to change the (failing) outcome.
In the second case, our concern is generating additional scenarios, in which the same (failing) outcome is maintained , e.g., as part of a debugging process; the explanation should hence provide insight on which elements in the scenario are sufficient to recreate the outcome, regardless of the rest. The two forms of explanation are complementary, but one cannot be deduced from the other.

A recent work [ 6 ] suggested using the framework of “actual causality” [ 7 , 8 ] to formally define and generate causal failure explanations (for CPSs).
According to our categorization, that work addressed the objective of failure reproduction, by focusing on the generation
of “sufficient explanations” (an established concept in actual causality). Roughly speaking, a sufficient explanation is a subset of elements
of the failure execution that is, by itself, sufficient to result in a failure, even if all other elements are changed or removed.
Such explanations are not suitable for failure avoidance, as removing or changing such a sufficient subset does not guarantee that the failure
is avoided. Intuitively, this is because multiple sufficient subsets may exist.

This work seeks to extend the foundations laid in [ 6 ] to address the objective of failure avoidance by introducing and applying the concept of “necessary explanations”. Roughly speaking, a necessary explanation is a subset of elements of the failure execution such that
removing them avoids the failure. Together, this provides, for the first time, a unified (causal) formal framework for failure analysis, allowing to address both objectives. As exact computation of such causal explanations quickly becomes intractable when the number of inputs increases [ 9 ] , we also develop a practical, scalable algorithm
for generating necessary explanations based on the notion of causal degree of responsibility [ 10 ] .

The paper contributions: (i) We suggest a conceptual categorization of the objectives of failure explanation—avoidance and reproduction—providing a basis for understanding,
comparing, and advancing work in this field. (ii) We introduce the notion of necessary explanations for autonomous system failures and discuss its application to failure avoidance. (iii) We develop a practical, scalable algorithm for generating necessary explanations and provide an experimental evaluation demonstrating its efficiency across multiple environments.
Finally, to demonstrate the superiority of this framework for explanation for failure avoidance, (iv) we provide a study comparing
with prior work on failure avoidance not based on causal reasoning. We show that our approach achieves a higher success rate, lower computation time, and better quality.
For clarity, the paper is presented (and contributions (iii) and (iv) are evaluated) using a setup of an autonomous car with a black-box neural controller, trained to avoid collisions (as in Fig. 1 ). In our evaluation, we use two autonomous driving simulators, of both high and low fidelity, showing that the benefits of our approach are simulator- and system-independent.

The rest of the paper is structured as follows.
After overviewing the related work, Sec. II provides preliminaries on the autonomous system testing model and introduces the running example. Sec. III gives a brief overview of actual causality and introduces our setup. Sec. IV introduces the conceptual framework of failure analysis. Sec. V presents our theoretical contributions, extending the framework with necessary explanations. Sec. VI presents the approximation algorithm for computing necessary explanations. The experimental performance evaluation is presented in Sec. VII . Sec. VIII demonstrates the practical utility of necessary explanations for failure avoidance, comparing it with existing work. Sec. IX concludes the paper.

Related Work: In explainable AI, actual causality has been used in various domains, such as images [ 9 ] , audio [ 12 ] , and process mining [ 13 ] . Since computing actual causes is generally hard, these approaches introduce efficient approximations [ 14 ] . Similarly to us, they treat the AI model as a black box.

Existing explainability approaches for failure reproduction include sensitivity analysis [ 15 , 16 ] , which examines neighborhoods around falsifying traces, identifying regions where a property is violated. As mentioned, actual causality has also been proposed for failure reproduction, providing a more structured, high-level alternative by identifying minimal subsets of elements that reproduce the observed failure [ 6 ] .

Failure avoidance methods focus on modifications to a failing scenario that change its outcome. Existing approaches for failure avoidance primarily generate counterfactuals , passing examples similar to the original [ 17 , 18 ] .
While counterfactuals can provide valuable insight into the observed behavior, they focus on input-output changes rather than the underlying causal mechanisms, potentially attributing importance to downstream effects and including modifications that are not necessary for avoiding the failure.
Autonomous systems work on explainability also use counterfactual attribution for root-cause analysis [ 19 ] . This approach relies on causal discovery, which infers causal relationships from data,
a fundamentally different approach from
the one we adopt in this paper, which allows reasoning within an abstract model.

2026-10-22.title: Reconstruction-Augmented Visuomotor Pre-Training of 3D-Grounded Bimanual Dexterity from RGB-Only Human Videos
2026-10-22.authors: Xingyi He , Zhiwen Qiu , Adhitya Polavaram , Yunhao Cao , Cory Fan , Julius Samwer , Saleh Kalantari , Kuan Fang
2026-10-22.abstract: We present SpatialDex, a framework that learns 3D-grounded bimanual dexterity from RGB-only human videos through reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context. From each video, we reconstruct the scene geometry and estimate the hand motion, align them at a shared video-level scale using the hand-size prior of 3D hand estimates. We retain the reconstructed geometry as both a policy input and a prediction target. The policy grounds the token grid of a pre-trained vision-language model in this geometry through gated residual fusion, is trained to predict future scene geometry alongside wrist and finger actions, and generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists. Pre-trained on 1M human-video clips and fine-tuned with a small number of robot demonstrations, SpatialDex outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 16.5 points on nine simulated dexterous tasks across two embodiments and by 38.3 points on six real-world bimanual dexterous tasks. Under a matched comparison, pre-training with reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over pre-training on hand motion alone. Project page and video: https://spatial-dex.github.io/
2026-10-22.introduction:
Bimanual dexterous manipulation requires coordination between both hands to stabilize, reorient, and transfer objects while adapting to their shapes and changing positions in the surrounding environment. Geometric representations support this coordination by capturing spatial relationships between hands and objects [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] , while pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) can provide complementary visual and semantic priors [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Learning such coordination therefore demands both spatial grounding and diverse experience of how the two hands act across objects and scene configurations. Robot demonstrations supply the former through depth sensing and executable commands, but collecting them through teleoperation is costly, which limits the range of tasks, objects, and configurations they cover.

Human videos on the web provide an alternative source of rich everyday activities and physical interactions with diverse environments at scale. However, these RGB-only recordings lack explicit scene geometry or robot-compatible action labels. Learning from these videos therefore calls for recovering the demonstrated hand motion and the scene geometry at a consistent scale and keeping them aligned across time.

Recent methods pre-train vision-language-action (VLA) models on human videos with explicit wrist and finger motion supervision, and transfer learned skills to robots through action-space alignment [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Other approaches exploit 3D cues by predicting point tracks [ 12 ] , adopting shared hand-object keypoint representations [ 13 ] , combining calibrated geometry with spatial-language and wrist-motion supervision [ 14 ] , or reconstructing hand-object interactions to synthesize robot trajectories [ 15 ] . However, recovering scene geometry at a scale consistent with the recovered hand motion from RGB-only videos remains challenging, as scale errors misalign reconstructed geometry with hand trajectories and compromise spatial supervision. Although some studies integrate geometric and visual features [ 3 ] or combine spatial and human-motion supervision [ 14 ] , their training objectives provide limited direct supervision for how fine-grained hand behavior relates to changes in the surrounding scene. How to effectively incorporate these cues into human-video pre-training therefore remains underexplored.

In this work, we present SpatialDex , a framework for pre-training 3D-grounded visuomotor policies from large-scale RGB-only human videos. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context by reconstructing scene geometry alongside hand motion and using both to supervise policy pre-training. To make reconstructed hand-object distances consistent with the demonstrated motion, we use the hand-size prior in 3D hand estimates to calibrate scene geometry with a shared scale across frames and both hands, as illustrated in Figure 1 . The reconstructed geometry then serves the policy in two roles. As an input, it is combined with the image-patch features of a pre-trained VLM through progressive dual-gated fusion, which adds spatial information while retaining the visual priors of the VLM. As a target, future scene geometry is supervised alongside wrist and finger actions, so that the policy captures spatial relationships and scene dynamics. The policy generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists, and it is fine-tuned to bimanual dexterous tasks with a small number of robot demonstrations.

In summary, the contributions of this work are threefold:

We introduce a data pipeline that aligns reconstructed scene geometry with human hand motion at a shared video-level scale, producing 1M video clips with aligned geometry and motion annotations for policy pre-training.

We develop a reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training framework that combines progressive dual-gated fusion of geometric and visual features with future geometry prediction, and generates finger motion conditioned on both wrist trajectories.

We evaluate SpatialDex on nine simulated tasks across two embodiments and six real-world tasks, reaching mean success rates of 76.3% and 81.7% compared with 59.8% and 43.3% for the state-of-the-art methods.

1. We introduce a data pipeline that aligns reconstructed scene geometry with human hand motion at a shared video-level scale, producing 1M video clips with aligned geometry and motion annotations for policy pre-training.

2. We develop a reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training framework that combines progressive dual-gated fusion of geometric and visual features with future geometry prediction, and generates finger motion conditioned on both wrist trajectories.

3. We evaluate SpatialDex on nine simulated tasks across two embodiments and six real-world tasks, reaching mean success rates of 76.3% and 81.7% compared with 59.8% and 43.3% for the state-of-the-art methods.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Work

Learning dexterous behavior from human video. Human video provides a scalable source of diverse manipulation experience [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] , but converting observed behavior into supervision for robot control requires bridging substantial embodiment and action gaps. One line of work recovers human hand motion and uses it to learn transferable action priors [ 19 ] . VITRA [ 9 ] , Being-H0.5 [ 10 ] , EgoScale [ 11 ] , and UniDex [ 20 ] demonstrate that large-scale egocentric or Internet video can provide useful supervision for dexterous policy learning. A complementary direction uses 3D points and correspondences to guide policies or transfer demonstrations across objects [ 12 , 13 , 21 , 22 ] . ARM4R [ 12 ] represents human demonstrations through 3D point trajectories, while Dexterous Point Policy [ 13 ] uses shared object–hand keypoints to connect human observations with robot actions. These approaches capture either demonstrated hand behavior or the motion of selected scene elements, but the surrounding 3D scene remains only partially represented. Unlike prior approaches that primarily recover action supervision from human videos, SpatialDex additionally reconstructs the surrounding scene and aligns it with the recovered wrist and finger actions.

Scene reconstruction and scale calibration. Recent approaches increasingly rely on metric-depth foundation models [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] to lift RGB human videos into 3D. For example, Dexterous Point Policy [ 13 ] uses monocular metric depth to lift object observations into 3D, while VideoManip [ 26 ] uses predicted metric depth as a common spatial reference for hand–object reconstruction. However, predicted metric scale can still deviate from the true physical dimensions, making scene geometry inconsistent with recovered hand motion. To reduce this mismatch, some methods introduce human-hand cues for scale calibration. VIPA-VLA [ 14 ] , for instance, rescales reconstructed geometry using depth ratios between estimated hand joints and corresponding scene points. SpatialDex instead estimates a shared video-level scale from 3D hand correspondences aggregated across frames and both hands, producing scene geometry consistently aligned with recovered wrist and finger actions for large-scale policy pre-training.

Geometry-aware visuomotor policies. Explicit geometry has long supported manipulation through point clouds [ 1 , 27 ] , voxels [ 28 ] , and rendered 3D views [ 29 , 30 ] . While effective for spatial reasoning, these geometry-centric policies typically lack the broad visual and semantic priors of pre-trained vision-language models. Recent VLA methods therefore incorporate depth-derived 3D cues into pre-trained visual representations [ 2 , 31 , 32 , 3 ] . These methods mainly treat geometry as an additional input to the policy, while the interaction between newly introduced geometric features and pre-trained visual priors is less explicitly modeled. SpatialDex instead explicitly targets this injection problem through reconstruction-augmented pre-training, using progressive geometry fusion and auxiliary forward dynamics prediction to better exploit reconstructed scene geometry.

2026-10-22.title: CausGround: Causal Interaction Grounding for Adaptive Embodied Planning
2026-10-22.authors: Yijun Shen , Diqi He , Jinbang Guo , Wanyue Zhang , Jiaming Mi , Huan Yang , Zhongyuan Wang , Zhiwei Yu , Kai Zhang
2026-10-22.abstract:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising reasoning capabilities, but deploying them for physical interaction requires reliable planning that accounts for when actions are executable and how they change the world.
These preconditions and effects are often environment-dependent and are not fully captured by MLLMs, making adaptation to new environments challenging.
Yet existing adaptation approaches either update model parameters through costly environment-specific training or rely on unstructured interaction experience that is difficult to ground and reuse.
To address this challenge, we introduce CausGround , a non-parametric causal interaction grounding framework that distills interaction experience into reusable action-centered causal knowledge.
CausGround learns from experience by identifying action preconditions and effects, and organizes them in a factorized world-state representation that jointly captures object attributes and inter-object relations.
At planning time, task-relevant causal dependencies are grounded in the current observation, supporting backward reasoning over action preconditions and forward reasoning over action effects for action selection and multi-step causal planning.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of CausGround across diverse long-horizon embodied settings spanning simulated high-level planning, interaction reasoning, and real-world robot manipulation.
Evaluated on the adapted VirtualHome and RoboCasa benchmarks, CausGround consistently improves vision-based high-level planning across MLLM backbones, improving average task success from 24.9% to 53.3% on VirtualHome and closed-loop planning success from 43.0% to 57.0% on RoboCasa.
Consistent gains are also observed on SWITCH benchmark, with average interaction reasoning accuracy improving from 25.8% to 31.9%, indicating stronger reasoning over action selection, recovery, and verification.
Moreover, real-world experiments further show that CausGround can reason backward from MLLM-interpreted goal states to derive executable high-level action sequences for sequential manipulation.
These results demonstrate that explicit action preconditions and effects provide a reusable causal grounding mechanism for long-horizon embodied planning across diverse environments without parameter updates.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Embodied agents powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated promising reasoning capabilities for high-level planning ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Driess et al., 2023 ; Feng et al., 2025b ) . Yet successful embodied interaction requires more than knowing what to do: agents must know when an action is executable and how it changes the world. Such interaction knowledge is often environment-dependent, involving available actions, object states, action preconditions, and effects ( Kim et al., 2025 ; Han et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . As illustrated in Fig. 1 , a planner may correctly infer that an object should be placed into a fridge, yet attempt the action before satisfying the precondition that the fridge be open. Such precondition violations can accumulate over long-horizon execution, leading to invalid actions, repeated attempts, and costly trial-and-error ( Raman et al., 2024 ; Zhi et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2025 ) . Effective embodied planning therefore requires agents to account for task semantics while adapting their planning to the interaction dynamics of the environment in which the task is executed.

Existing approaches still fall short in enabling efficient environment adaptation. A direct strategy is to specialize embodied agents through fine-tuning or reinforcement learning ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Zhai et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025a ) , but such parametric adaptation requires substantial environment-specific interaction data and repeated optimization, making it costly to deploy across diverse environments, particularly in real-world settings.
Non-parametric approaches instead incorporate interaction feedback or episodic memory at inference time ( Anwar et al., 2025 ) , but such experience is often retained as unstructured trajectories or task-level memories ( Ginting et al., 2025 ; Buoso et al., 2025 ) . This makes it difficult to identify which parts of an experience are causally relevant rather than incidental, reuse them across tasks, or ground them in the current visual scene.
Moreover, existing representations do not always jointly capture the fine-grained object attributes and inter-object relations required to determine whether an action’s preconditions are satisfied ( Chen et al., 2025 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) .
This raises a central question: Can interaction experience be distilled into reusable causal knowledge that tells an embodied agent both what must be true before an action and what changes as a result?

To this end, we introduce CausGround, a non-parametric causal interaction grounding framework for adaptive embodied planning. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , CausGround abstracts interaction experience into action-centered causal knowledge, representing each action through its relevant preconditions and resulting state effects. Rather than storing complete trajectories, it organizes reusable action-centered causal knowledge over a factorized world-state representation that jointly captures object attributes and inter-object relations.
At planning time, the current observation and task are grounded into the same representation to construct a task-relevant local causal graph from reusable causal knowledge. This allows the planner to reason backward over action preconditions to determine what must happen before an action becomes executable, and forward over state effects to anticipate how the world should change after execution. Composing such causal dependencies provides a structured reference for multi-step planning without updating model parameters.

We evaluate CausGround across heterogeneous long-horizon embodied settings.
In simulation, we adapt VirtualHome ( Puig et al., 2018 ) and RoboCasa ( Nasiriany et al., 2026 ) for visually grounded high-level planning and observe consistent improvements under both one-shot and closed-loop planning, including an increase in average task success from 24.9% to 53.3% on VirtualHome and from 43.0% to 57.0% under closed-loop planning on RoboCasa.
Beyond simulation, we evaluate interaction reasoning on SWITCH ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) , a real-world egocentric long-horizon interaction benchmark, where CausGround improves average accuracy from 25.8% to 31.9%.
We further validate the framework on real-robot manipulation, where CausGround reasons backward from interpreted goal states to derive executable high-level action sequences and successfully complete multi-step interactions.
Together, these results show that explicit causal interaction knowledge provides a reusable grounding substrate for long-horizon embodied reasoning across diverse environments.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate embodied interaction knowledge around action preconditions and state effects, and introduce a factorized world-state representation that jointly captures object attributes and inter-object relations, enabling interaction knowledge to be grounded in current visual observations.

We introduce CausGround, a non-parametric framework that distills interaction trajectories into reusable action-centered causal knowledge and dynamically grounds task-relevant causal dependencies for planning. This enables reasoning over both what must hold before an action and how the world changes after it without parameter updates.

We evaluate CausGround across long-horizon embodied settings spanning VirtualHome and RoboCasa simulations, the real-world egocentric SWITCH benchmark, and real-robot manipulation, demonstrating consistent gains in planning and interaction reasoning across environments and MLLM backbones.

1. We formulate embodied interaction knowledge around action preconditions and state effects, and introduce a factorized world-state representation that jointly captures object attributes and inter-object relations, enabling interaction knowledge to be grounded in current visual observations.

2. We introduce CausGround, a non-parametric framework that distills interaction trajectories into reusable action-centered causal knowledge and dynamically grounds task-relevant causal dependencies for planning. This enables reasoning over both what must hold before an action and how the world changes after it without parameter updates.

3. We evaluate CausGround across long-horizon embodied settings spanning VirtualHome and RoboCasa simulations, the real-world egocentric SWITCH benchmark, and real-robot manipulation, demonstrating consistent gains in planning and interaction reasoning across environments and MLLM backbones.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

Environment Adaptation for Embodied Agents. Embodied agents deployed in new environments often need to adjust their behavior based on newly acquired interaction experience.
Earlier approaches typically absorb environment-specific experience into model parameters through fine-tuning, imitation learning, or reinforcement learning ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Kang et al., 2025 ; Tian et al., 2026 ) .
With the growing capabilities of foundation models, recent work has increasingly explored adaptation without continual parameter updates, using execution feedback ( Wang et al., 2023 ) , past trajectories ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , or external memory ( Sohn et al., 2026 ) to provide environment-specific information during deployment.
This shifts environment adaptation from updating the model itself toward leveraging external environment knowledge. Therefore, effective adaptation depends not only on how experience is acquired and accumulated, but also on how the underlying world state is represented.

World State Representations for Embodied Planning. Existing world-state representations vary substantially in their level of abstraction.
Free-form textual representations can flexibly summarize observations and state changes, but often entangle multiple entities and dynamic properties within a shared description ( Hao et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) .
Object-centric representations reduce this entanglement by organizing state information around individual entities ( Yoneda et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) , while more factorized representations further separate each object into explicit attribute-value pairs, enabling finer-grained state tracking ( Shen et al., 2026 ; Rozanov and Rei, 2025 ) . Yet embodied interaction depends not only on the state of individual objects, but also on relations among them ( Ju et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) .
Therefore, a world-state representation for embodied planning should jointly capture fine-grained object attributes and explicit inter-object relations, providing a shared basis for grounding observations and environment-specific interaction knowledge.

Interaction-Grounded High-Level Planning. A structured world state provides a basis for grounding environment-specific knowledge, but effective planning further requires turning such knowledge into actionable guidance.
MLLM-based planners can generate actions or action sequences from current observations and task descriptions ( Lv et al., 2024 ; Feng et al., 2025b ) , leveraging strong pretrained priors to guide task completion. Before committing actions to the environment, world-model-based planners further predict action-conditioned state changes ( Li et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2026 ) and evaluate candidate trajectories through simulation or adaptive latent-space rollouts ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Yao et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) , providing lookahead for multi-step decisions.
However, while world models support reasoning about action consequences, action conditions are not always explicitly represented, which can make action proposal less reliable. Moreover, dependencies across multiple actions are typically instantiated only through rollout, requiring repeated simulation during planning. CausGround instead exposes action conditions, effects, and cross-action dependencies as explicit environment-specific knowledge that can be directly reused by the planner.

2026-10-22.title: AirPlayground: Benchmarking Aerial Navigation across Diverse Reconstructed Environments
2026-10-22.authors: Rangya Zhang , Yujing Shang , Zhuoyuan Yu , Mingsheng Li , Qingsong Yan , Chao Yan , Yuhang Zhang , Mir Feroskhan
2026-10-22.abstract: Large-scale aerial resources provide a foundation for learning navigation across diverse environments. However, existing resources remain limited in providing (1) densely sampled flight demonstrations for learning different policy formulations and (2) broad environment coverage for standardized closed-loop evaluation. To address these limitations, we introduce AirPlayground, a unified benchmark for training and evaluating aerial navigation policies across diverse environments. We first construct 94 photorealistic 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) environments spanning indoor, urban outdoor, and vegetation settings, with aligned collision geometry. Building on these environments, we develop a scene-adaptive pipeline for automated expert flight collection, yielding 94K demonstrations and 46.5M synchronized observation–state–action samples at 50 Hz. We further provide an extensible API that supports training different policy formulations on this shared corpus and evaluating them under unified protocols in the corresponding environments. We benchmark seven baselines spanning four policy paradigms across three navigation settings in seen and unseen environments, and further examine scaling behavior with ACT. Scaling ACT’s training corpus from 5 to 70 scenes raises median success rates on seen and unseen environments from 30.6 % 30.6\% and 16.8 % 16.8\% to 41.2 % 41.2\% and 29.4 % 29.4\% , respectively. Through this shared training and evaluation framework, AirPlayground supports analysis of how offline prediction errors relate to closed-loop outcomes. Our analyses highlight the roles of prediction errors, execution protocols, and scene interactions in closed-loop performance.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Learning-based aerial navigation depends on large-scale, diverse experience to generalize across environments ( Zheng et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . Acquiring experience through online interaction can be costly and difficult to scale. Offline demonstrations support scaling policy learning without environment interaction during training ( O’Neill et al., 2024 ) . Yet policies trained on demonstrations learn from expert states, whereas deployment exposes them to states shaped by their actions ( Seo et al., 2024 ) . Small errors can compound through feedback, so accurate imitation does not guarantee reliable navigation. Assessing reliability therefore requires systematic closed-loop evaluation across diverse environments, where policies must respond to the consequences of their actions.

To meet these learning and evaluation needs, aerial navigation research has produced both flight datasets and interactive environments. Large-scale datasets such as CityNav and OpenFly provide aerial trajectories for navigation and vision-language learning ( Lee et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) , substantially increasing the scale and diversity of reusable flight experience. In parallel, 3DGS-based embodied platforms make reconstructed real-world scenes available as photorealistic, geometrically grounded environments for interactive navigation ( Liu et al., 2026b ; Miao et al., 2026 ; Xia et al., 2026 ) . Recent benchmarks further combine reconstructed environments, collision-aware interaction, and flight trajectories for policy learning and evaluation ( Guo et al., 2026 ) .

Despite this progress, two limitations remain in the resources for aerial policy learning and evaluation. (i) Limited dense flight experience. Densely sampled observation–action demonstrations remain limited across diverse real-world environments. Dense supervision captures continuous flight control for learning different action representations, while coverage across scenes exposes policies to varied visual conditions and spatial structures. (ii) Limited standardized evaluation across diverse environments. Standardized closed-loop evaluation remains limited in its coverage of environments with diverse appearances and spatial structures. Indoor spaces, urban outdoor areas, and vegetation present different visibility and obstacle configurations, making evaluation across these settings important for assessing how consistently policies perform beyond a narrow set of scenes.

To address these limitations, we introduce AirPlayground, a unified benchmark for aerial navigation that pairs dense flight experience with photorealistic 3DGS reconstructions and executable geometry. AirPlayground comprises 94 reconstructed scenes spanning indoor, urban outdoor, and vegetation environments, with nearly 100K flight demonstrations and 46.5M RGB frames under 50 Hz observation–action supervision. To scale collection, we develop a scene-adaptive pipeline, reusable across reconstructed scenes, that models navigable space, samples navigation tasks, and generates expert demonstrations. We further introduce an extensible cross-policy API that adapts the shared corpus to each policy’s native representation and maps its outputs to a common control interface under unified evaluation protocols. By linking recorded trajectories to executable scene geometry, AirPlayground also enables analysis of how offline prediction errors relate to closed-loop outcomes.

Specifically, AirPlayground makes three main contributions.

(i) Dense flight experience paired with executable reconstructions of real-world environments. We pair dense flight demonstrations with photorealistic reconstructions and aligned navigation and collision geometry for policy learning and matched closed-loop execution.

(ii) A unified benchmark across navigation policy paradigms. Our extensible API supports shared-data policy training and unified closed-loop evaluation across three navigation settings, while preserving each policy’s native representations and inference structure through adapters.

(iii) Cross-policy evaluation and deployment diagnosis. We benchmark seven baselines and analyze offline predictions and closed-loop behavior. These studies show that offline accuracy alone does not fully explain deployment performance and examine how execution horizons and scene geometry affect navigation, demonstrating the benchmark’s value beyond performance comparisons.

# 2 Related Work

Prior work has expanded navigation-level supervision from constrained simulated settings toward larger urban environments, richer tasks, and broader scene coverage ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025b ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026c ) . More recent efforts scale collection through automated planning and expert trajectory generation ( Low et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Adang et al., 2025 ) . Other efforts collect fine-grained flight demonstrations for reactive control and long-horizon navigation ( Wang et al., 2025a ; Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Despite these advances, temporally dense flight demonstrations remain limited in scale and environmental coverage, constraining the continuous control experience for training diverse navigation policies.

Recent embodied-navigation research uses 3D Gaussian Splatting to reconstruct photorealistic real-world environments, providing a real-to-sim bridge for policy learning and evaluation ( Chhablani et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Low et al., 2025 ; Quach et al., 2024 ) . To support collision-aware navigation, these representations are augmented with metric geometry, collision models, and navigation structures, enabling interactive navigation across reconstructed environments ( Miao et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Xia et al., 2026 ) . Aerial benchmarks also pair 3DGS environments with geometry for collision checking and evaluation: OpenFly spans 18 scenes from multiple rendering sources, while HUGE provides four reconstructed outdoor environments ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) . These platforms establish important foundations, but broader coverage of reconstructed indoor, urban outdoor, and vegetation environments is still needed for systematic cross-scene policy evaluation.

Offline evaluation measures prediction errors against expert demonstrations, while interactive aerial benchmarks assess task success and path efficiency through closed-loop rollouts ( Xue et al., 2026 ; Lou et al., 2026 ) .
Studies in autonomous driving and robot manipulation examine this mismatch, including the predictive value of evaluation metrics and task-critical errors ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) .
This mismatch also depends on how predictions are executed: work on action-chunking policies investigates execution horizons ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) , while studies of aerial agents examine how execution mechanisms affect flight outcomes ( Xu et al., 2026 ) .
However, a systematic understanding of the offline-to-closed-loop gap in aerial navigation remains limited.
By pairing flight demonstrations with executable worlds, AirPlayground supports trajectory replay and policy evaluation in corresponding scenes, providing an experimental basis for tracing offline predictions to their closed-loop consequences.

2026-10-22.title: FlowVLA: Learning Flow-Aware Physical Completion for Quantitative Robotic Pouring
2026-10-22.authors: Liwen Yang , Yutian Zhang , Jiaqi Zhai , Li Yang , Tutian Tang , Qiwei Shan , Yancheng Bi , Qiankuan Shangguan , Yangkun Zhu , Ce Hao , Dong Wei , Qiaojun Yu , Dibo Hou
2026-10-22.abstract: During steady pouring, images and robot pose may remain nearly unchanged while transferred mass accumulates, making the return decision ambiguous for a whole-task vision–language–action (VLA) policy. We present FlowVLA, which separates motor generation from physical-completion estimation. A shared π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} action expert learns approach, pour, and return with boundary-aware supervision. A target-independent estimator fuses visual, joint, wrist-wrench, and recurrent force-belief histories to maintain an estimate of transferred mass. The controller initiates return when this estimate plus predicted residual outflow reaches the requested mass. In coffee-pot/water experiments, FlowVLA achieves 13.1 g goal-balanced mean absolute error (MacroMAE), lower than all tested VLA baselines. Across all attempts, 53.7% both complete the task and finish within ± 10 % \pm 10\% of the requested mass. The same model interpolates to held-out 150/250-g targets without retraining. Independently trained models further evaluate the formulation in three additional container–fluid settings.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models connect visual and language understanding to robot control, enabling a single policy to perform diverse manipulation tasks [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Quantitative pouring adds a requirement beyond executing the manipulation sequence: the transferred mass must match a requested amount. This matters in food preparation [ 4 ] and household drink-serving tasks [ 5 ] (Fig. 1 ). Without online electronic-scale feedback, the robot must infer how much liquid has been transferred and when to return the container upright. During steady pouring, images and robot pose can remain nearly unchanged while mass accumulates, so visually similar states may require either continued pouring or return. We call this ambiguity physical-completion aliasing . Understanding “pour 200 g” specifies the goal but does not reveal physical progress, and initiating return does not stop liquid transfer immediately.

Whole-task VLA policies typically learn completion implicitly alongside motion. Policies use force or tactile feedback to guide action generation [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] , while FM-VLA encodes force histories as memory tokens [ 9 ] . Wrist wrench is informative about liquid transfer, but it also varies with arm motion, container pose, grasp geometry, and liquid dynamics [ 4 ] . Force conditioning therefore does not by itself define the accumulated physical quantity needed for a stopping decision. Precision-pouring controllers make this quantity explicit by closing the loop on fill level [ 10 , 5 ] , source-mass loss [ 4 ] , or predicted overpour [ 11 ] . Their feedback formulations offer a useful starting point, but generally assume prescribed grasps or constrained motions. The remaining challenge is to integrate quantitative completion into a learned whole-task policy that must also grasp, transport, pour, return, and place the container.

Our insight is to treat physical completion as a persistent state separate from motor generation. FlowVLA couples a shared π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} action expert with explicit flow and mass estimation. Boundary-aware supervision distinguishes continued pouring from return at action-chunk boundaries. A recurrent force observer provides temporal belief to the action expert and a dedicated completion head, which fuses this belief with visual, joint, and wrist-wrench histories to estimate transferred mass. The physical estimators are target-independent, while the requested mass conditions the POUR prompt and completion threshold. The controller accounts for liquid transferred during return by triggering return when predicted terminal mass reaches the target. Real-robot comparisons with whole-task VLA and load-based baselines, mechanism ablations, and held-out target interpolation evaluate this formulation, alongside additional container–fluid regimes with independently trained models.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We formulate physical-completion aliasing in quantitative pouring and introduce FlowVLA, which separates motor generation from estimation of the hidden physical progress needed for quantitative stopping.

We develop boundary-aware action learning that combines multirate force observations and recurrent belief with stage-specific prompts in a shared π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} action expert. Row-wise masking and exact-return-boundary sampling jointly supervise the transition from steady pouring to return.

We design a target-independent completion module that maintains flow and accumulated mass from causal multimodal histories and predicts residual outflow, enabling return decisions based on predicted terminal mass rather than current transferred mass.

# II Related Work

## II-A Robotic Precision Pouring

Precision-pouring methods use visual feedback to estimate liquid level or volume in the receiving container and adjust the pouring trajectory [ 10 , 12 , 5 ] . Other approaches plan with simplified fluid dynamics [ 13 ] or acquire pouring skills through self-supervised trials [ 14 ] . These methods explicitly control the poured quantity, but generally assume a prescribed grasp or restricted pouring motions. Sensing at the source container offers an alternative to observing the liquid surface. Pouring by Feel estimates mass loss from proprioceptive and tactile measurements and regulates pouring with proportional–integral–derivative (PID) control [ 4 ] . RoboCAP is the closest quantity-aware reference: it accumulates capacitance-based mass estimates and predicts overpour to stop a prescribed wrist motion [ 11 ] . Flow estimation and delayed-outflow compensation also appear in industrial ladle control [ 15 , 16 ] . Like these methods, FlowVLA reasons in physical units. Unlike prescribed-motion controllers, it couples completion estimation to a learned sequence spanning grasping, transport, pouring, return, and placement.

## II-B Force-Aware and Progress-Aware Robot Policies

Diffusion Policy learns visually conditioned action sequences through denoising diffusion [ 17 ] . VLA models also condition actions on language. RT-2 transfers vision–language knowledge to robotic control [ 1 ] , while π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1 learn language-conditioned manipulation across tasks [ 2 , 3 ] . Force-aware methods add feedback about physical interaction. Reactive Diffusion Policy (RDP) combines slower visual action generation with high-rate tactile correction [ 8 ] . Within VLA models, ForceVLA incorporates six-axis wrench through a mixture of experts [ 6 ] , and TA-VLA learns from torque histories with auxiliary future-torque prediction [ 7 ] . ForceVLA2 further couples force awareness with hybrid force–position control [ 18 ] . FM-VLA is the closest temporal-force reference: it encodes force histories as memory tokens for action generation [ 9 ] . FlowVLA instead converts causal multimodal history into explicit flow and mass estimates and uses them in a terminal-mass rule, separating physical completion from action generation. Beyond physical feedback, progress-aware policies estimate the remaining task horizon or learn visual progress representations [ 19 , 20 ] . These help locate the robot within an execution sequence, but normalized progress does not specify how many grams have been transferred. FlowVLA maintains flow in g/s and mass in g across perceptually similar states, then estimates whether returning now will achieve the requested quantity. For persistent state estimation, differentiable filters and KalmanNet combine learned observations or updates with explicit state evolution [ 21 , 22 ] . Our observer integrates flow and recursively updates mass and uncertainty.
