2026-10-22.title: Toward Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI
2026-10-22.authors: Meng Luo , Zechen Bai , Shanqing Xu , Yanlin Li , Kaixin Li , Mengchen Qian , Weifeng Lu , Ran Zhang , Yingtian Zou , Ziyang Luo , Wei Chen , Hongzhan Lin
2026-10-22.abstract: 未获取到摘要
2026-10-22.introduction:
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) describes a system that improves the process by which it improves, not only its behavior. The idea goes back to I. J. Good’s speculation about machines that design better machines ( Good, 1966 ) and to self-referential learners such as the Gödel machine ( Schmidhuber, 2003 ) , and recent digital agents have begun to approach it ( Chen et al., 2026d ) . STOP ( Zelikman et al., 2024 ) applies a program that improves code to its own source, and the Darwin Gödel Machine ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) lets improved coding agents modify themselves; both judge each candidate with executable tests. Yet a system can get better at a task, and a fixed procedure can keep producing better versions of it, without anything recursive happening. RSI requires two further links (Section 2.2 ): what the system retains from earlier improvements must make its next revision better, and the improver , the component that revises the learning procedure, must in turn use what it has gained to help produce its own next improvement.

Physical RSI asks the same question of systems that learn by acting in the physical world, such as robots. Digital RSI supplies the mechanisms (language models that write reward code or controllers, archives of earlier variants, and automated experiment loops); physical RSI tests how these mechanisms use physical experience and whether they hold under physical constraints (Figure 1 ). The physical setting changes the experimental conditions in four ways (Table 1 ). First, physical outcome checks depend on sensors and task-specific verifiers, people, or learned detectors whose reliability must be established; even an automated grasp-success check can miss what it does not sense, and an error in that judgment can be reinforced and then executed on hardware. Second, every candidate costs robot time, resets, supervision, and wear, so a revision must pay off within few trials. Third, practice changes its own conditions: objects move, grippers wear, calibration drifts, and rolling back software does not repair a damaged object. Fourth, what can be improved extends beyond prompts and code to controllers, dynamics models, and the interface to a particular body. Each difference bears on the central question of RSI, whether what one round of revision teaches the improver makes the next revision better.

Consider a robot arm that keeps missing the same grasp. The failure can have several causes, and each calls for a change kept in a different place; these places organize Sections 3.1 and 3.2 . The robot’s policy , the learned controller that turns observations into motor commands, may never produce the recovery motion; an expert correction can teach it, as RECAP ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ) learns from deployment experience and corrections (Section 3.1.1 ). The robot may mistake a light touch for a stable hold because its model of contact is wrong; a world model refitted to contact data can correct the prediction and give the policy a place to practice, as in PlayWorld ( Yin et al., 2026b ) (Section 3.1.2 ). The robot may have recovered from this failure before without keeping what worked; external knowledge , such as a saved recovery or program, can be called the next time, as Zetta ( Ding et al., 2026 ) grows code-based critics and recoveries around a frozen policy in simulation (Section 3.1.3 ). Finally, the robot may keep choosing the wrong kind of repair; then the learning procedure must change: which attempts to collect, how to judge them, and how to turn them into updates (Section 3.2 ). Eureka ( Ma et al., 2024a ) rewrites reward code from simulated training results, and ENPIRE ( Xiao et al., 2026b ) lets coding agents modify the training infrastructure from robot experiments. The first three routes improve what the robot does; the fourth improves how it learns, and it is where physical RSI would begin. Recursion would further require that knowledge of why earlier repairs worked, which we call repair knowledge , improves how the next procedure revision is made. Figure 2 contrasts this route with applying a fixed training recipe to new experience.

Our central argument is that physical experience can improve task competence, the learning procedure, and the improver that revises this procedure, and that four recurring conditions, each sharpened by the physical setting, decide whether such gains carry forward. Each can fail: the new signal may not address what the learner still lacks, because sensing shows only part of a failure; the receiving component may be unable to absorb it on its body; its value may not survive later changes in behavior or hardware; or further practice may become unsafe or unaffordable. For the grasping robot, this could mean collecting more of the grasps it already makes well, refining a contact model that its controller cannot use, relying on a fix that stops working once the gripper is replaced, or practicing until the gripper wears out. A change can improve execution and still fail to help later learning: added autonomous data often yield modest gains that saturate and can even regress ( Mirchandani et al., 2025 ) .

Several research traditions supply pieces of this progression. Self-supervised grasping showed that physical outcomes alone can supervise behavior at scale, first by learning from tens of thousands of real grasp attempts ( Pinto and Gupta, 2016 ) and then through large-scale real-robot reinforcement learning (RL) with QT-Opt ( Kalashnikov et al., 2018 ) . Interactive imitation learning, as in DAgger ( Ross et al., 2011 ) and HG-DAgger ( Kelly et al., 2019 ) , showed how an expert can correct the learner in the states that the learner itself reaches. Lifelong robot learning ( Thrun and Mitchell, 1995 ) asks how knowledge gained on earlier tasks can reduce the real-world experimentation needed for later ones; model-based RL, from Dyna ( Sutton, 1990 ) and PILCO ( Deisenroth and Rasmussen, 2011 ) to Dreamer ( Hafner et al., 2020 ) , asks how recorded transitions can support practice inside a learned model; and skill-based approaches, such as options ( Sutton et al., 1999 ) and the shared RoboEarth knowledge base ( Waibel et al., 2011 ) , ask how an extended behavior can be stored and called again. Each tradition widened what one learning episode can pass on to the next.

Recent generalist and foundation-model-based systems widen both what can change and what role the change plays. RoboCat ( Bousmalis et al., 2024 ) turns a policy adapted to a new task into a source of training data for the next generalist, and SILVR ( Luo et al., 2026a ) revises a video-based planner using its own executions. In RoboCat, Eureka (in simulation), and ENPIRE, experience reaches the machinery that produces future updates (a data collector, a reward function, the training infrastructure) as well as the policy that receives them. This brings the physical problem close to the long-standing aspiration of learning to learn ( Thrun and Pratt, 1998 ) , and several reviewed systems already contain the components that a demonstration of recursion would need. The open question is how to realize that aspiration with limited trials, imperfect sensing, and a body that changes over time.

Our scope is the improvement of policies, world models, memories, skills, and the software procedures that update or use them, whenever their evidence or evaluation is connected to physical action. We discuss hardware change when it affects compatibility, maintenance, or continued experimentation. Autonomous morphology design and physical self-reconstruction are adjacent topics outside our scope.

Recent surveys cover neighboring ground (Table 2 ). Some focus on agents and embodiment: recursive self-improvement in AI systems ( Chen et al., 2026d ) , self-evolving agents ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , weights versus executable skills as stores of improvement ( Jena et al., 2026 ) , self-evolving embodied AI ( Feng et al., 2026 ) and humanoids ( Nguyen et al., 2026 ) , and levels of physical recursive self-improvement ( Zhou et al., 2026a ) . Others analyze world models for robot learning ( Hou et al., 2026 ) and manipulation ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , joint world–action models ( Lu et al., 2026b ) , actionable simulators ( Chen and Zhu, 2026 ) , verifiers for robot policies ( Wan et al., 2026 ) , and physical AI broadly ( Xiang et al., 2025 ) . Our organizing question is different: after a change has been acquired, who uses it next, and what does that use improve? Component names alone cannot answer it, because two data collectors with similar task success can yield training data of very different value; a more accurate predictor can still produce less useful training data for a policy; and the same kind of retrieved memory can change either how a program is repaired or how an outcome is judged.

The review makes three connected contributions. First, it positions RSI within robot learning by separating method paradigms and problem settings (from reinforcement learning and meta-learning to AutoML) from a ladder of claims (behavioral improvement, later-learning benefit, procedure improvement, and the two links of recursion), each defined by the comparison that would establish it. It organizes physical self-improvement along that ladder according to where experience leaves its change and which decision of the learning procedure it revises, showing that data volume and component accuracy are unreliable proxies for progress. Second, it separates mechanisms that change an improver’s knowledge or tools from evidence that the improver has improved: existing studies support the first three claims, while recursive gains still need dedicated verification. It reviews digital precedents and physical boundary cases and specifies a two-round experiment that could isolate the recursive relation, together with its controls and an estimate of its hardware cost; Table 13 records where the reviewed studies stand on each claim. Third, it names the four breakdowns above as recurring conditions ( informative feedback , usability , robustness to distribution shift , and continued practice ) and shows how each fails and which capability would restore it. Four research questions organize the review.

Section 2 lays the foundations: a primer for newcomers (Section 2.1 ), where improvement is kept, the ladder from self-improvement to recursion, the position of RSI relative to neighboring learning paradigms (Section 2.3 ), and the benchmarks and metrics used in the reviewed studies (Section 2.5 ); Figure 3 maps the review, and Appendix C collects the terms. Section 3 climbs the ladder, from improving the learner (Section 3.1 ) and the learning procedure (Section 3.2 ) to improving the improver (Section 3.3 ) and closing the recursive loop (Section 3.4 ). Section 4 turns to what current evaluation cannot yet measure, why gains stop compounding, how practice can stay safe, and which problems remain open, including the two-round test that recursion would require. \physicalaisectionaccent PAIInk

# 2 Foundations of Physical RSI

## 2.1 Learning to Act

A few groups of ideas are enough to follow the rest of the review. We introduce them with the running example of the robot that keeps missing a grasp.

A policy is the controller that maps what the robot currently observes (camera images, joint angles, force readings, and possibly a language instruction) to its next motor command; for the grasping robot, it turns a view of the object into the next movement of the arm and gripper. In the systems reviewed here, policies are usually neural networks. Generalist policies are trained on large collections of robot data spanning many tasks, as in RT-1 ( Brohan et al., 2023b ) , and sometimes many robot bodies, or embodiments , as in Octo ( Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ) . A vision-language model (VLM) reads images and text and outputs text; robot systems often use one to propose goals or to judge whether an attempt succeeded. A vision-language-action (VLA) model is a generalist policy built on a pretrained VLM, so that it reads images and an instruction and outputs actions; RT-2 ( Brohan et al., 2023a ) , OpenVLA ( Kim et al., 2024 ) , and π 0 \pi_{0} ( Black et al., 2025 ) are examples. Many recent policies output a short sequence of future actions at once, called an action chunk .

The simplest way to obtain a policy is imitation learning from demonstrations, which are often recorded while a person teleoperates the robot ( Argall et al., 2009 ) . In behavior cloning (BC), the policy is trained to reproduce the demonstrated action in each recorded situation. BC learns only from recorded situations, so its small errors can compound: if the gripper drifts slightly off the object into a state that no demonstration covers, the policy may have no good action to take. Interactive methods such as DAgger ( Ross et al., 2011 ) address this by asking an expert what to do in the situations that the learner itself reaches. In practice, a person often takes over when the robot errs, and these interventions supply corrective training data.

In reinforcement learning (RL) ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ; Kober et al., 2013 ) , the robot instead tries actions and receives a reward that scores the outcome, for example 1 for a stable grasp and 0 otherwise. On a real robot, rewards do not arrive automatically: a person, a hand-written check, or a learned reward model , such as a success detector, must judge each attempt. We call a component that supplies such judgments for learning an evaluator . Because rewards are often sparse and delayed, many methods learn a value function , or critic , that predicts how much future reward to expect; some systems use the word critic more loosely for any component, learned or hand-written, that scores behavior. The advantage of an action measures how much better it is than what the policy would typically do in the same situation. Off-policy methods can learn from experience collected by earlier versions of the policy or by other sources, which they keep in a replay buffer . On hardware, every trial costs time, supervision, wear, and a reset that returns the scene to a usable starting state, so the source of the reward and the number of available trials become central resources.

Large pretrained policies are rarely retrained from scratch. They are fine-tuned , or post-trained, on new data. A small residual policy can add corrections on top of the actions of a frozen base policy, such as a slight change to the angle at which the gripper approaches the object. Distillation trains one policy to imitate another, for example to fold a specialist’s behavior back into a generalist. When a policy learns a sequence of tasks, it can forget earlier ones, a problem studied in continual learning ( Parisi et al., 2019 ) ; replaying stored data from earlier tasks is a common protection.

A world model , or dynamics model, predicts what will happen after an action, for instance the next camera image or the next object positions ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2020 ) . The grasping robot’s contact model is one example: it predicts whether a touch will become a stable hold. A robot can use such a model to plan , by imagining the outcomes of candidate actions, or to generate imagined experience on which a policy is trained. A physics simulator is a hand-built model of this kind; a learned world model is fitted to recorded robot data and can be wrong in ways that a policy may learn to exploit.

Not every improvement is stored in network weights. A system can keep memories of earlier episodes, maintain a library of callable skills ( Sutton et al., 1999 ) , or write programs that compose perception and control functions ( Liang et al., 2023 ) . Large language models are increasingly used to write such code or to revise reward functions ( Ma et al., 2024a ) .

Results come either from simulation benchmarks or from hardware experiments on physical robots, and training in simulation before deployment on hardware is called sim-to-real transfer. Section 2.4 discusses what each setting can establish.

## 2.2 Defining Recursive Self-Improvement

We consider loops in which experience produces a retained change that affects later attempts or learning. Human demonstration, correction, reset, or approval can remain part of the loop: automation concerns who makes each decision, whereas learning concerns whether experience changes it (Table 17 in Appendix A ). A failed update can also be informative by showing where this connection breaks.

Generic pretraining without a subsequent experience–update–use comparison serves as background, as does adaptation confined to a single attempt. Rapid Motor Adaptation ( Kumar et al., 2021 ) , for example, infers current conditions from recent history without retaining the adaptation. Zeva’s interaction memory is a boundary case: it carries across retries within an episode but not across episodes or learning rounds. Simulation-only and formal studies supply enabling mechanisms, while meta-learning, AutoML, and digital agents supply precedents (Section 2.3 ); direct evidence about physical RSI must come from physical systems.

A retained change can serve four uses (Figure 4 ). It can choose or execute actions, predict outcomes or supply practice, support reuse (for example, calling a saved recovery or consulting guidance for a new program), or change how later data are collected, judged, and turned into updates. These uses are usually carried by policies, world models, external knowledge, and learning procedures, respectively (Sections 3.1 and 3.2 ). They can overlap: a policy can collect training data, a model can judge outcomes, and a memory can guide an updater. Each study is discussed mainly under the use its experiment tests, regardless of whether its authors call it self-evolving or recursively self-improving.

The learner acquires task capabilities; the learning procedure determines what experience to collect, how to judge it, and how to construct updates. An improver proposes or selects revisions of that procedure. It may be a person, a fixed rule, a search process, or a learned component, with knowledge in memory, weights, code, or prompts. Figure 2 separates the two levels: the learner improves under a fixed recipe, whereas the improver revises the recipe itself.

In the grasp example, adding a corrected grasp to the training data is a repair , an update made in response to an observed failure or limitation. The rule choosing which failed grasps need correction belongs to the learning procedure; whoever devises or changes that rule is the improver. The object being changed determines the role: an editor of task skills or data belongs to the procedure, whereas an editor of rewards, evaluators, collection rules, or update-generating training code acts as an improver.

We distinguish four claims (Table 3 ), and evidence for an earlier claim does not establish a later one. Behavioral improvement means better execution under a common task test. A later-learning benefit means that retained data, weights, models, skills, or code help a subsequent learner. Procedure improvement means that a revised collector, evaluator, editor, or updater teaches better than its earlier version. This comparison requires matched learners , which differ only in the component under test and share starting conditions, resources, and evaluation protocol (Figure 8 ).

We operationalize recursive self-improvement through two further links, which this review uses as empirical criteria for attributing a gain to recursion. First (R1), repair knowledge retained from earlier repairs must improve the improver: on new failures, its procedures must teach matched learners better than those produced by its earlier version. Second (R2), the improver, once improved, must help produce its own next improvement: given the same new repair histories, a self-revision proposed using its acquired knowledge must yield an improver that outperforms both the improver it revised and a revision of that same improver proposed with the acquired knowledge frozen. A fixed improver can repeatedly improve procedures without satisfying either link; an external designer’s growing expertise does not establish system-level recursion either. Section 3.3 develops the grasp example. A concurrent survey grades physical RSI by whether an update changes capabilities or the improvement procedure and whether its gain holds on the same or on other tasks, reserving its top level for an independently verified recursive gain ( Zhou et al., 2026a ) ; the claims here are instead defined by the comparison that would establish each. The name is shared by other concurrent work. PhysRSI-eval ( Li et al., 2026j ) applies it to agents with frozen weights that revise code, tools, and notes after each graded attempt, and Physical RSI 1.0 ( MMLab & PhysicalRSI contributors, 2026 ) names a system in which a multimodal foundation model revises the harness through which a robot acts. We read these works, like any other, by the comparisons they report; a name does not establish either link. For R1 and R2, we distinguish mechanism only , where machinery could change the improver; an uncontrolled result , consistent with a link but without a control that withholds only what was acquired; and a controlled result , which tests that contribution with matched learners and budgets (Section 4.4 ). The claim and its level of support are separate.

Two controls answer different questions. A frozen-knowledge control withholds acquired repair knowledge while retaining the improver, testing that knowledge’s contribution to the procedures produced (R1) or the self-revision proposed (R2). A fixed-improver control keeps the initial improver while the rest of the system improves. A gain over it shows that revising the improver contributes to later improvement, bearing on R2, but does not identify which acquired knowledge caused the revision.

Four conditions recur across these claims. Informative feedback distinguishes the remaining learning need. Usability means that the receiving component can represent, optimize, and execute the change. Robustness to distribution shift asks whether the change stays useful as the policy, model, task, or hardware changes, including changes caused by improvement itself. Continued practice asks whether another informative trial remains safe and affordable. These four conditions overlap and serve as diagnostic lenses rather than independently validated constructs. Section 4.2 examines their failures, and Figure 3 connects these conditions to the uses and claims above.

## 2.3 Relating RSI to Robot Learning

Reinforcement learning and meta-learning already let robots improve from experience and learn how to learn. Self-training, continual learning, and automated machine learning (AutoML) let systems learn from their own outputs, keep learning across tasks, or search for better training recipes. It is therefore fair to ask what RSI adds. These are method paradigms or problem settings, which say how an update is computed or what it must cope with, whereas the claims of Section 2.2 say what an experiment shows to have changed. An RSI system may use any of them to revise any of its components, so the categories overlap rather than exclude one another: RSI is not a further paradigm after meta-learning but a level of improvement that a system built with any of them might reach (Table 4 ).

Standard RL improves a policy under an objective and update mechanism chosen before training ( Sutton and Barto, 2018 ) . Run repeatedly on hardware, as in HIL-SERL ( Luo et al., 2025 ) and RECAP ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ) , it yields behavioral improvement, and its data or policy can supply a later-learning benefit. RL loops can also be nested inside an outer optimization over part of the learning procedure. Eureka searches over reward programs using the RL training results they produce ( Ma et al., 2024a ) , and meta-gradient RL adapts the return while the agent learns ( Xu et al., 2018 ) . LPG discovers an update rule ( Oh et al., 2020 ) , and DiscoRL learns such a rule across many agents and environments and applies it to unseen benchmarks ( Oh et al., 2025 ) . These loops target procedure improvement, while the outer search itself stays fixed. DERL ( Cheng et al., 2025 ) departs from this on text-based and mathematical reasoning tasks: it trains its reward proposer by policy gradient on the validation success of the inner policies, so the search learns from its own trials, while the rule that trains the proposer stays fixed. In the grasp example, RL that tunes the grasp under a fixed slip penalty improves behavior, whereas a search that revises the slip penalty changes the procedure; further rounds of the first kind do not become the second.

Many systems called self-improving train on their own outputs. In self-training such as Noisy Student ( Xie et al., 2020 ) , a teacher trained on labeled data labels unlabeled data, and a student trained on both becomes the next teacher. Expert Iteration ( Anthony et al., 2017 ) and STaR ( Zelikman et al., 2022 ) apply the same pattern to search and reasoning, and RoboCat ( Bousmalis et al., 2024 ) applies it to robot data collection. Each round improves behavior and helps the next learner through the data it generates, while the recipe that generates, labels or filters, and trains on the data stays fixed. When the model also judges its own outputs, as in Self-Rewarding Language Models ( Yuan et al., 2024 ) , the evaluator changes with training, but the judging prompt and the training recipe do not.

Continual, or lifelong, learning asks how a learner that meets a sequence of tasks can reuse what it learned on earlier ones ( Thrun and Mitchell, 1995 ) without forgetting them ( Parisi et al., 2019 ) . Backward and forward transfer ( Lopez-Paz and Ranzato, 2017 ) measure how learning one task changes performance on earlier and later ones. Backward transfer thus measures retention, whereas forward transfer as defined there is performance on a new task before training on it; LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023a ) , a benchmark of sequential robot manipulation tasks, instead scores forward transfer by success on each new task averaged over its training, which is closer to a later-learning benefit. Replay, regularization, and other protections against forgetting are usually chosen by designers, so continual learning defines a setting that an RSI system must also handle (Section 4.2 ) rather than a way of improving the improver.

Meta-learning trains over many tasks so that new tasks are learned faster ( Thrun and Pratt, 1998 ) , and what it learns decides which claim it can support. An initialization from which a few gradient steps solve a new task, as in MAML ( Finn et al., 2017 ) , is an acquired artifact and supports a later-learning benefit. Other methods learn part of the learning procedure: recurrent policies whose activations carry out adaptation ( Duan et al., 2016 ; Wang et al., 2016 ) , a dynamics prior that adapts online, as in GrBAL ( Nagabandi et al., 2019 ) , learned optimizers ( Andrychowicz et al., 2016 ) , and evolved or learned losses ( Houthooft et al., 2018 ; Yu et al., 2018 ; Bechtle et al., 2021 ) . When a learner guided by such a part learns better than a matched learner guided by the original, the comparison supports procedure improvement. LMPC ( Liang et al., 2024 ) is a boundary case: it fine-tunes the model that writes reward code on past teaching sessions so that later teaching needs fewer turns, but that code drives a model-predictive controller directly rather than a training run, so the gain lies in how behavior is constructed. The outer meta-training procedure that produces the part (a gradient loop, an evolutionary search, or a fine-tuning recipe) is specified by its designers and is not changed by the revisions it produces, so learning reaches the procedure but not the process that produces it.

AutoML searches over architectures, hyperparameters, and training pipelines ( Hutter et al., 2019 ) , and AutoML-Zero extends the search to learning algorithms ( Real et al., 2020 ) ; a found configuration that teaches matched learners better supports procedure improvement. Some searchers learn from their own record: the controller of neural architecture search ( Zoph and Le, 2017 ) is trained with reinforcement learning on the validation accuracy of the architectures it generates. Because it edits the learner rather than the rules for collecting, judging, or updating, it is a learned part of the procedure, like the skill editor of PRACTICE ( Bai et al., 2026 ) , and the rule that trains it stays fixed.

RSI moves the process that produces revisions inside as well, as the two links of Section 2.2 require. The requirement is self-referential, as in the Gödel machine ( Schmidhuber, 2003 ) , STOP ( Zelikman et al., 2024 ) , the Darwin Gödel Machine ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) , and Gödel Agent ( Yin et al., 2025 ) , which let the improving process act on its own code. Generalized Agent Iteration places iterative policy improvement and RSI in one formal framework, in which whether the improvement mechanism sits inside the agent separates the two, and whether the evaluation standard is grounded outside it decides whether goals can drift ( Tang et al., 2026 ) . The criterion is therefore which component changes with the revision history, not whether some outer recipe stays fixed. In the meta-learning and AutoML methods above, the component that produces revisions of the learning procedure does not change; an improver fine-tuned by a fixed recipe on its own repair histories does change and can satisfy R1, which the frozen-knowledge comparison of Section 4.4 tests. Conversely, an improver whose code changes in every round satisfies neither link if the changes come from a designer or from a search that learns nothing from earlier rounds.

## 2.4 Facing Physical Limits

Table 1 lists the terms we use to judge how closely a study is tied to physical experience. Hardware interaction connects learning directly to physical consequences, but a consequence still needs a diagnosis and a reliable judge. A binary failure label on a grasp may not distinguish pose error from slip, whereas force measurements or contact history may separate the two. Simulation, learned prediction, and formal checks represent selected consequences whose adequacy must be tested at the decision they support. Simulation is cheap and repeatable but omits some physical effects, whereas hardware captures real contact, sensing, and wear but allows few trials, so the two settings support different conclusions about cost, transfer, and the comparisons a study can afford.

Because practice changes its own conditions (Section 1 ), returning to a usable starting state may require a reset policy or human assistance; early work on autonomous real-world RL already named resets, onboard perception, and rewards without instrumentation as the ingredients that continued learning needs ( Zhu et al., 2020 ) . Moving knowledge to another robot adds a further gap, because reuse across bodies needs compatible coordinates, timing, sensing, and reachable effects. A study’s connection to physical experience is therefore a matter of degree. It depends on the success evaluation (who or what judges whether an attempt succeeded), on interaction coverage and recoverability, and on whether successive trials remain comparable. The success evaluation may rely on the same evaluator that supplied the learning signal or on one independent of it, a difference that Section 4.1 shows to matter. Table 1 contrasts these conditions with those of digital self-improvement, Section 4.3 develops their consequences for continued learning, and Table 18 in Appendix A shows what evidence each robot domain contributes.

These conditions weigh on each paradigm of Section 2.3 in a different place. Meta-learning needs a distribution of training tasks, and on hardware every sampled task costs trials, resets, and supervision; domain-adaptive meta-learning meta-trains on previously collected human and robot demonstrations, and LMPC collected its training data in simulation. Eureka and DrEureka run their reward search in simulation, where many candidates can be trained in parallel, and DrEureka then deploys the resulting policy on hardware ( Ma et al., 2024b ) . For RSI, the bottleneck shifts to revision histories: an improver learns from them, and each entry needs at least one learning round judged by physical trials, so these histories accumulate more slowly than the task samples of meta-learning or the transitions of RL, and no executable test settles whether a revision helped. Simulation, stored traces, and learned models can screen candidate revisions before hardware trials, but their adequacy for that screening is itself a claim to test (Section 4.4 ).

## 2.5 Benchmarking Self-Improvement

Most comparisons in this review run in simulation, and the benchmarks differ in what they stress (Table 5 ). LIBERO ( Liu et al., 2023a ) supplies sequential manipulation suites, and LIBERO-PRO ( Zhou et al., 2025b ) perturbs manipulated objects, initial states, task instructions, and environments to test whether behavior depends on the original cues; LIBERO-Plus ( Fei et al., 2025 ) varies seven factors, including camera viewpoint, initial robot state, and sensor noise. RoboCasa ( Nasiriany et al., 2024 ) broadens household task coverage, and RoboTwin 2.0 ( Chen et al., 2025c ) and RoboDojo ( Chen et al., 2026g ) cover bimanual manipulation. VLABench ( Zhang et al., 2025d ) and Meta-World ( Yu et al., 2019 ) supply further manipulation suites, and SIMPLER ( Li et al., 2024 ) mirrors real robot setups for policy evaluation. Navigation studies use Habitat ( Savva et al., 2019 ) and R2R-CE ( Krantz et al., 2020 ) , and household agents use EmbodiedBench ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . Except for LIBERO’s lifelong protocol, which scores transfer and forgetting along a task sequence, these suites test a system at one point in time, and a claim about improvement across rounds still needs a protocol on top that fixes what carries over between rounds and what stays held out (Section 4.2 ). A recent benchmark prototype moves in this direction: it provides no in-domain demonstrations, carries experience over between requests within a deployment, and names how quickly an agent becomes competent in a deployment as a quantity of interest ( Cai et al., 2026 ) . PhysRSI-eval ( Li et al., 2026j ) fixes what carries over between rounds, in simulation. Six model-and-configuration systems revise a persistent workspace of code, tools and notes with frozen weights, for up to 17 graded rounds on each of 18 RoboDojo tasks, and each system is scored on five axes: first-attempt score, how early gains appear, attained score, physical budget saved, and the share of first-round failures later solved. The axes need not agree: Claude Opus 5.5 attains a higher score than GPT-6.1 Sol but scores lower on gain timing and budget saved. In a six-task ablation with GPT-6 Astra, withholding all information from earlier rounds lowers success over rounds 4–6 from 15 of 36 attempts to 3 of 36.

A second group of benchmarks targets the components on which self-improvement relies. FailBench ( Navasardyan et al., 2026 ) tests success detectors on 2,197 real and simulated manipulation attempts, where the best of 13 VLM detectors reaches 0.77 balanced accuracy. CaliBench ( Sadeghi et al., 2026 ) tests whether the outcome frequencies of video world models are calibrated. MC-EvoBench ( Song et al., 2026a ) fixes the controls that a transfer claim needs, and RLE-Bench ( Ma et al., 2026 ) holds out robustness perturbations that coding agents cannot query. RoboCoach-Bench ( Lei et al., 2026 ) collects 32 simulated tasks for agents that write and revise training code. Digital benchmarks of recursive self-improvement isolate related questions. PAST-Bench ( Xue et al., 2026a ) turns retained experience on and off across ordered task sequences, and RSIBench-Data ( Meng et al., 2026a ) has agents revise training-data strategies for a fixed model. RSIGym ( Meng et al., 2026b ) measures the fraction of the remaining performance gap that agents close across benchmarks.

Hardware evaluations instead use task suites built by each study, and their budgets vary widely, from a handful of trials per task, as in PhysEvo’s 25 trials over five real tasks ( Tian et al., 2026 ) , to hundreds of evaluation episodes, as in the more than 600 pairwise episodes of RoboArena ( Atreya et al., 2025 ) . Most controlled downstream comparisons concern manipulation; navigation, locomotion, flight, and robotic laboratories support particular mechanisms without testing each condition across robot bodies (Table 18 ). Simulation results support mechanism comparisons at scale, whereas hardware results show what survives real contact, sensing, and resets (Section 2.4 ). Because tasks, trial counts, and metrics differ, results are compared within each study rather than across studies; Appendix B records the settings behind selected numbers.

Most studies report success rate, the fraction of trials that reach a task-defined goal as judged by a person, a scripted check, or a learned detector. Some give partial credit for progress through task stages, which needs a different statistical model than binary success. Others add efficiency during execution, such as cycle time in HIL-SERL ( Luo et al., 2025 ) or throughput in RECAP ( Physical Intelligence et al., 2026 ) .

Learning efficiency is reported as the time, episodes, or supervision needed to reach a level of performance. ConRFT ( Chen et al., 2025d ) reaches 96.3% average success on eight real tasks after 45–90 minutes of online fine-tuning, and VLAC ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) raises real success from about 30% to 90% within 200 episodes. ENPIRE ( Xiao et al., 2026b ) reports the time its robot fleet needs to reach a target, and LMPC ( Liang et al., 2024 ) counts chat turns per successful teaching session.

Retention asks whether earlier competence survives later learning or deployment, and a later-learning benefit on a new task is forward transfer . ACCRUE ( Kim et al., 2026 ) reports transfer as a cut in real-robot training time for later tasks, CIDER ( Li et al., 2026d ) reports forward transfer of an accumulated policy, and MC-EvoBench sets out the controls that such a claim needs.

Resource use is counted in robot hours, demonstrations, interventions, compute, or model tokens. CARD ( Sun et al., 2024 ) needs about 14K tokens per task against about 663K for Eureka, and ENPIRE’s fleet scaling shortens the time to target at lower per-robot utilization and faster-than-linear token growth; because studies count different parts of this work, their costs are not directly comparable (Section 4.1 ). \physicalaisectionaccent PAIBlue

2026-10-22.title: From Acceptance and Avoidance to Affective Viscosity: Designing Social Agents Intermediating in Human Relationships
2026-10-22.authors: Tomoko Yonezawa
2026-10-22.comment: The 2nd International Workshop on Trust and Blame in Multi-Person Multi-Agent Societies (TBSA_2nd) in HAI 2026
2026-10-22.abstract:
As social agents become embedded in human relationships, they are expected not only to provide smooth assistance but also to handle rejection, discomfort, jealousy, persistence, and other forms of social tension. This paper connects two research directions: acceptance and avoidance in response to an agent’s gaze, approach, and contact, and affective viscosity as a model of how negative affect accumulates, persists, is suppressed, and is expressed over time. We argue that avoidance should not be treated merely as a failure of interaction, but as a relational signal that indicates boundaries between humans and agents. Building on this view, affective viscosity provides a design perspective for agents that maintain, suppress, or express negative states depending on social relationships and interaction histories. We discuss several ongoing design cases, including triadic jealousy, discomfort suppression, patience timing, and spatiotemporal stickiness, and consider how these cases lead to broader questions of blame and accountable intervention. Rather than designing agents as simple scapegoats or artificial villains, we ask
how agents can intermediate in problematic social situations
while making their intervention traceable, limited, contestable, and repairable.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Social agents are often designed to be polite, helpful, and smoothly cooperative. However, agents embedded in human relationships may need to do more than maintain pleasant interaction. They may be approached or avoided, accepted or rejected, welcomed or perceived as intrusive. They may also need to express hesitation, discomfort, jealousy, or limits of patience when social tension arises. These reactions should not be treated only as breakdowns of interaction. They may indicate relational boundaries and provide important cues for how agents should intervene in social environments.

Our previous and ongoing work on acceptance and avoidance focuses on how users respond to an agent’s gaze, approach, and contact, and how such responses can be estimated and reflected in the agent’s behavior. This perspective treats avoidance not simply as a negative outcome, but as a signal that the agent has entered a boundary-sensitive region of interaction. The next step is to model how such boundary-sensitive states persist and transform over time. In particular, discomfort, jealousy, annoyance, and reluctance may accumulate, remain latent, leak through behavior, or suddenly become explicit. We refer to this temporal and relational property as affective viscosity.

This perspective also leads to questions of blame and responsibility. Once an agent detects social tension and intervenes, it may change the trajectory of the relationship. If the intervention fails, becomes annoying, or exposes a tension that participants preferred to ignore, the agent may become a target of blame. However, assigning blame to an agent should not simply mean placing an artificial scapegoat or villain in the environment. A more productive question is how to design agents whose interventions are traceable, limited, contestable, and repairable. In this sense, affective viscosity is not only a model of negative emotion, but also a basis for discussing how agents can take part in socially risky intervention.

Prior work on trust in automation and human–robot interaction has
emphasized that trust is not simply a positive attitude, but a basis
for appropriate reliance under uncertainty ( 3 , 4 ) . Reviews of trust in AI and human–automation
trust further suggest that trust depends on both system properties
and the user’s interpretation of agency, reliability, and risk ( 7 , 6 ) . However, when agents
are embedded in social relationships, the issue is not limited to
whether users rely on them. Agents may also affect interpersonal
boundaries, social norms, and the distribution of responsibility.

In socially embedded HAI, trust, blame, and responsibility may be
distributed across users, agents, developers, institutions,
bystanders, and broader social contexts. This makes it necessary to
consider not only whether an agent is trusted, but also how the
agent is treated as a social participant when it refuses, avoids,
asserts a boundary, or becomes involved in socially disruptive
interaction.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2. Acceptance and Avoidance as Relational Signals

Human acceptance and avoidance do not emerge as instantaneous
binary reactions. They are grounded in temporally developing
cognitive, affective, and bodily states. In human interaction,
discomfort toward another person’s approach, hesitation before
rejection, or the decision to continue a relationship often involves
gradual changes in attention, arousal, memory, expectation, and
interpretation. Such changes take time. Therefore, if a social agent
expresses acceptance, avoidance, discomfort, or rejection as an
immediate symbolic output, the expression may appear behaviorally
convenient but psychologically unnatural.

This view is consistent with process-oriented theories of emotion.
Scherer’s component process model treats emotion as a dynamic
process of sequential appraisal checks, rather than as a single
instantaneous output ( 8 ) . Gross’s process
model of emotion regulation also distinguishes multiple points at
which emotion can be modulated, including attention, cognition,
and response expression ( 9 ) .

This point is important for human–agent interaction. An agent that
is always accepting may appear polite, but it lacks a believable
boundary. Conversely, an agent that immediately rejects or displays
anger may break the interaction before a relationship can be
adjusted. A more natural design requires an internal process in
which negative affect accumulates, is temporarily suppressed, leaks
through external behavior, and is eventually expressed depending
on the situation. The external expression should not be identical to
the internal state. Rather, the gap between the internal state and
the displayed behavior is itself a social signal. It allows an agent to
have something like “honne” and “tatemae”: an internal state that
may differ from its outward expression, while still allowing the agent
to express rejection or avoidance according to the relationship and
the situation.

This paper extends our recent discussion of negative aversion and
real reliability, where discomfort and rejective reactions were framed
as legible self-disclosure for boundary learning and relational
repair ( 2 ) . Here, we shift the focus
from familiar reliability to trust and blame in socially risky
intermediation.

2026-10-22.title: Reading the Room: Scale-ambiguous Semantic Registration of Sparse VSLAM Maps to Floor Plans in Partially Built Environments
2026-10-22.authors: Bjorn Stragier , Emilia Szymańska , J. Micah Prendergast , Lukas Rosenberger Schmid
2026-10-22.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-22.abstract:
Many robotic construction applications, such as progress tracking, require registering a sensor trajectory to a prior 2D floor plan.
Visual capture is attractive for its low cost and availability, but aligning a visual simultaneous localization and mapping (VSLAM) map to a floor plan is difficult; VSLAM recovers geometry only up to an unknown similarity transform, the sparse point cloud is cross-modal to the symbolic floor plan, sites are only partially built during capture, and construction sites are visually repetitive, degrading map quality while removing distinctive features.
Existing methods address at most two of these challenges.
We thus introduce Reading the Room (RR), a global-local approach to register scale-ambiguous, sparse, semantic VSLAM maps to partially built floor plans.
Our key idea is to define a single robust, differentiable, class-balanced semantic-geometric energy function that governs all stages of the pipeline.
We develop two global initialization schemes, leveraging a single inaccurate user-provided correspondence if provided, or estimating the initialization globally using a cross-modal matching network.
Both schemes are designed to find initial candidates with respect to the energy function, which is then directly optimized for local refinement.
We evaluate RR on 33 sequences across three active construction sites against classical and learning-based baselines, achieving a 4.5× improvement in mean absolute trajectory error over the strongest baseline in the general unconstrained setting, which increases to 7.6× when an anchor is provided.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Autonomous robots and perception technologies have the potential to transform modern construction.
Tracking construction progress against design intent is one of the most direct levers to reduce project delays and cost overruns [ 1 ] . However, doing so requires registering a sensor trajectory captured by a robot or site operator to a prior 2D floor plan.
To this end, camera-based capture is an especially attractive sensing solution given its vast availability, low cost, weight, and energy consumption, as well as providing visual fidelity and human interpretability.
While several works investigate registering dense LiDAR-based reconstruction to floor plans [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] , the visual counterpart remains less explored.

In this work, we study the task of aligning a sparse, scale-ambiguous 3D map, as recovered by a monocular VSLAM system [ 5 , 6 ] , to the floor plan of a site under active construction.
Multiple properties compound to make this setting unusually difficult, as shown in Fig. 1 .
First, monocular VSLAM recovers geometry only up to an unknown similarity transform, since scale is not observable without auxiliary sensing.
Second, the two representations are highly cross-modal, as VSLAM outputs a sparse, noisy 3D point cloud while the floor plan is a symbolic drawing of design intent.
Third, construction sites are only partially built during capture, so large parts of the plan may not yet physically exist, making it an unreliable prior.
Lastly, such sites are often visually repetitive, consisting mostly of walls, columns, and voids, which both degrades VSLAM quality and removes the distinctive features registration typically relies on.

Existing approaches address at most one or two of these challenges.
Cross-view indoor localization methods [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] generally assume known metric scale and a fully built environment.
Methods embedding a floor plan directly into the SLAM pipeline [ 15 , 16 ] similarly assume a known, already-built environment and a metric-range sensor such as LiDAR.
Map-alignment methods such as region decomposition [ 2 ] and graph matching [ 4 ] require dense metric reconstructions a sparse VSLAM map cannot easily supply.
Recent sparse VSLAM methods instead by-pass dense reconstruction by detecting manually placed visual markers with positions marked a-priori in the floor plan [ 17 ] .
Learning-based cross-modal matchers [ 18 , 19 ] can generalize across visually dissimilar modalities [ 20 , 21 ] , but have never been evaluated on this domain.
Thus, no existing method jointly handles unknown scale, sparse representations, the cross-modality gap, and partial construction.

To close this gap, we introduce Reading the Room (RR), a global-local registration approach built around a single energy function.
We propose a robust, differentiable, class-balanced semantic-geometric objective for cross-modal registration in partially built construction sites.
We then develop a two stage approach to globally initialize and locally refine this (or any other) energy function in feature-degraded and structurally ambiguous environments.
We thoroughly evaluate RR across 3 datasets of active construction sites spanning 33 total sequences.
For practical relevance, we consider two cases, where an initial guess by a site operator is provided as well as the unconstrained global regsitration task, both of which are naturally handled by RR.
We compare RR against several classical and learning-based methods and achieve state-of-the-art performance in both tasks.
In summary, our main contributions are:

We introduce Reading the Room (RR), a novel global-local approach to register scale-ambiguous sparse VSLAM maps against partially built symbolic floor plans.

We introduce Reading the Room (RR), a novel global-local approach to register scale-ambiguous sparse VSLAM maps against partially built symbolic floor plans.

We propose a novel class-balanced semantic-geometric energy function and develop a two stage pipeline combining correspondence-free cross-modal dense feature matching or anchored initialization with local refinement to optimize this energy objective.

We thoroughly evaluate RR across 33 sequences spanning three active construction sites, showing a ≥ 4.5 × \geq 4.5\times improvement in median ATE over the most competitive baselines, providing a first effective solution to this challenging problem.

2026-10-22.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

## II-A Cross-view Localization

Cross-view localization aims to localize a query image directly against a floor plan, without a SLAM algorithm or multi-view constraints in the loop.
Early work scored predicted room-layout edges against projected floor-plan edges [ 7 ] .
Embedding-based methods such as LaLaLoc [ 8 ] and its successors [ 9 , 10 ] instead learn a shared panorama/floor-plan latent space.
More recently, methods render or predict depth and sometimes semantic rays [ 11 ] from candidate poses and compare them against observed depth [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] .
These methods rest on several assumptions we cannot make.
First, depth-ray methods require a known pixel-to-metre ratio, whereas our floor plans carry no reliable scale.
Second, we instead register a sparse map, which is easier to store, transmit, and anonymize than full single views.
Finally, all of these methods assume the built environment matches the plan closely, which may fail when large parts of a site are not yet built.

## II-B SLAM with Floor Plan Priors

A separate line of work integrates a floor plan directly as a prior into a tracking or SLAM pipeline, rather than registering a map to the plan later.
FP-Loc [ 15 ] tracks a 3D LiDAR from a known start pose against a floor plan by detecting ceiling/ground planes and matching wall features to floor-plan elements via an approximate nearest-neighbour field. Zimmerman et al. [ 16 ] extend this to global localization with a semantic map whose object-level cues resolve the structural symmetry via Monte Carlo localization. However, these methods assume a known, already-built environment and a metric-range sensor (LiDAR) that directly observes scale, neither of which holds in our setting.

## II-C Map Registration

Complementarily, map registration aims to estimate a rigid or similarity transform aligning a SLAM map to a floor plan.
Most prominently, point cloud methods such as ICP [ 22 ] align dense LiDAR scans to reference geometry.
Recent works couple this with as-planned BIM/CAD models; diS-Graphs [ 23 ] jointly optimizes pose and a non-rigid plan deformation, while Lidar2BIM [ 3 ] registers a LiDAR map to a BIM model via a Hough-transform.
However, these methods assume a metric range sensor, whereas in our case scale is an unknown the algorithm must recover.
Alternatively, if scale is unknown but the modalities match, registration can be posed as a 2D image-alignment problem. Manual-correspondence methods sidestep the transform search entirely; Lu et al. [ 24 ] use a 360-degree camera and VSLAM in construction but require several site-manager-selected tie points, while Bagh et al. [ 17 ] require physical fiducial markers that are also manually annotated on the plan.
The closest unconstrained approach is region decomposition [ 2 , 25 , 26 ] , which registers a dense occupancy grid map to a floor plan by scoring candidate region overlap.
A related graph-based work [ 4 ] matches regions with a learned graph network instead.
All of these methods require a dense or volumetric reconstruction, which in a sparse, monocular VSLAM setting cannot reliably be produced.

## II-D Cross-modal Feature Matching

An alternative to registering full maps is to match local features between two images directly, without reducing either to an occupancy grid.
Classical descriptors such as SIFT [ 27 ] remain a common choice to match keypoints via handcrafted, scale- and illumination-invariant descriptors.
Learned sparse matchers instead match detected keypoints (typically from SuperPoint [ 28 ] ) via attention, as in SuperGlue [ 29 ] and LightGlue [ 30 ] .
Detector-free dense matchers such as LoFTR [ 18 ] , its efficient variant [ 31 ] , and RoMa [ 19 ] regress correspondences over a dense grid, which tend to outperform sparse matchers precisely in the low-texture, repetitive conditions that also characterize construction sites.
All of these matchers are trained for same-modality correspondence and are not, by default, cross-modal. MatchAnything [ 20 ] and MINIMA [ 21 ] address this gap without changing the underlying architecture by fine-tuning existing matchers on large synthetic cross-modal datasets (such as optical-to-infrared or optical-to-map imagery).
Both report that dense matchers retain their advantage over sparse and semi-dense ones even after cross-modal adaptation, suggesting cross-modal generalization is largely a property of training data rather than architecture.
However, neither framework has yet considered the domain gap of sparse, unscaled VSLAM maps against a symbolic floor plan.

2026-10-22.title: Watch Your Step: Anticipated Perception for Humanoid Locomotion
2026-10-22.authors: Matthias Heyrman , Chenhao Li , Ioannis Dadiotis , Marco Hutter
2026-10-22.abstract:
Perceptive locomotion policies typically observe a dense robot-centric elevation map, although only the terrain beneath and around the next footsteps informs the control decision.
Learned encoders compress the whole visual input, leaving the policy to work out which inputs matter while learning the baseline locomotion task.
Learning both at once slows training and, without computationally expensive attention mechanisms, makes generalization to new terrain harder.
We instead remove redundant inputs from the elevation map before the policy sees it.
A lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts future footholds from proprioception and the velocity command alone, and we sample the elevation map only in small patches around these predicted footholds.
We train the prediction model alongside the locomotion policy, periodically retraining it on new policy rollouts as the robot’s gait matures.
This allows the perception to anticipate where the policy will step, while the policy learns to leverage terrain information around those steps.
With the proposed lightweight preprocessing, the policy reaches a given terrain difficulty in roughly a third of the training iterations required with the complete map.
It outperforms policies that observe the complete map where footholds are sparse, including in narrow walled corridors, and on unseen terrain, and it matches an attention-based encoder trained at several times the cost.
The policy transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid traversing various obstacles, stairs, gaps, and step-downs beyond the training distribution in both indoor and outdoor environments.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Vision is an indispensable tool when traversing unstructured terrain.
People constantly survey the ground ahead of them to plan their next steps and to adjust the trajectory of a foot in mid-air.
Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has driven significant progress in legged robot locomotion [ 1 , 2 ] .
Using high-fidelity physics simulators, modern RL algorithms with parallelized environments, and effective techniques to reduce the sim-to-real gap, humanoids can be conditioned on a robot-centric elevation map [ 3 ] to traverse rough terrain.

However, this reliance on dense environmental maps introduces fundamental limitations related to sample efficiency, redundancy, and distraction.
Only the small regions of terrain where the feet will next make contact should inform control decisions, yet policies typically sample and process the full map uniformly, even though most of it describes terrain the robot will never step on, such as cells far to the side or directly opposite the commanded velocity direction.
These irrelevant inputs make it hard to learn which regions of the map matter and can distract the policy with terrain features that have no bearing on the next step, while the larger state space makes generalization to different terrains harder and increases the computational cost of the policy.
By contrast, people tend to look at the ground approximately 1.5 seconds, i.e., 2 to 3 steps, ahead of them, focusing on their planned footholds instead of the entire surrounding scene [ 4 ] .
On more challenging terrains, this look-ahead lets them intuitively adapt a step in mid-air: if a foothold seems insecure or they notice a better spot near the original target, they shift their focus and change the step trajectory.

Existing work primarily aims to reduce redundant information from the full elevation map through learned embeddings that feed the control policy.
Typical encoders compress the full input into a latent vector [ 2 ] , scale well to complex terrains [ 5 , 6 ] , and transfer to real-world locomotion [ 7 , 8 ] .
However, encoders such as CNNs still have to learn to extract the relevant features from the full map, and thus inherit the redundancy and sample inefficiency of the visual input rather than addressing it.

Attention-based encoders, conditioned on proprioception and the elevation map, weigh terrain features to focus on possible future steps [ 9 ] , and later work extends them with local and global feature streams [ 10 , 11 ] and uncertainty-aware terrain estimates [ 10 ] .
Using egocentric depth images alongside a height scan enables an attention-based anticipatory gaze that better respects onboard compute limitations [ 12 ] .
These methods learn where to look, but nothing in the encoder structure ensures that the attended features are future footholds; the encoder has to discover the focus implicitly from the task reward.
Other depth-based methods encode the images directly [ 13 , 14 ] .
All of these methods process the entire visual input when deployed and leave it to the policy to ignore what does not matter.
Terrain outside of its next steps can therefore still distract it.

Another approach analyzes the terrain and plans where the robot’s feet should land, a long-standing body of work.
Classical methods select candidate contact regions based on kinematic reachability and terrain geometry [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] , and learning-based approaches evaluate candidate footholds based on the height map around the nominal landing position [ 19 ] or across the local map under kinematic and collision constraints [ 20 ] .
These foothold selection methods run as standalone modules that hand a target to a downstream tracking controller.
This requires strongly defined hand-crafted selection criteria for each platform, such as thresholds on the slope, roughness and curvature of a foot-sized patch, its distance to edges, and robot-specific checks of kinematic reachability and leg collision.
These criteria encode the designer’s notion of a safe foothold and must be manually retuned for a new foot geometry or gait.
The module is also not necessarily conditioned on how the downstream controller actually moves, which leaves its output liable to be inaccurate or suboptimal for the gait that executes it.

The mismatch between planner and controller is especially pertinent for modern legged locomotion controllers, which are RL policies trained in simulation to maximize a reward.
RL-based approaches can learn precise foot placement in simulation through a terrain difficulty curriculum and crafted rewards [ 21 , 22 ] and can learn to track foothold planners [ 23 , 24 ] , use them to shape rewards [ 25 ] , or track a decoupled learned planning policy [ 26 ] .
In these cases, however, the foothold serves as a tracking target or a reward that shapes the policy’s actions, not as a filter that shapes the policy’s observations.
Prior work has used predicted footholds to reward safe locomotion using privileged information acquired in simulation during training [ 14 ] , but the predictions never reach the hardware.

Filtering the elevation map around future footholds before the policy sees it raises two challenges.
First, the filter cannot observe the terrain to decide where to look, as it would inherit the overhead of the full elevation map that it is meant to remove.
It must therefore predict the footholds entirely from the robot’s own state and command, while the policy, like a person, can still adjust its trajectory to choose footholds based on the terrain it sees around each prediction.
Second, where the feet will land is a property of the gait, which the policy is still learning.
A predictor fit to an early, unsteady gait would misplace its patches once the policy improves, and a policy trained on misplaced patches may learn to distrust them.

In this paper, we propose a human-inspired, state-based sampling module that filters the elevation map before the locomotion policy receives any terrain information.
To filter the elevation map without observing it, a lightweight foothold prediction model (FPM) predicts the robot’s next two footholds from its current proprioceptive state and velocity command alone.
We treat only the terrain around these predicted footholds as relevant for locomotion and sample the elevation map in patches surrounding them.
These patches act as the exteroceptive observation of the locomotion policy, creating a state-conditioned representation of the terrain.

To ensure that the predicted footholds, and with them the sampled patches, stay up-to-date as the locomotion policy learns more difficult terrains, we co-train the FPM and the locomotion policy in an iterative training loop.
We train the locomotion policy with RL in simulation and, after a fixed number of iterations, refit the FPM in a self-supervised fashion on the footholds the current policy produces, allowing the perceptual filter to adapt as the policy converges.
We demonstrate that this approach reaches a given terrain difficulty in roughly a third of the iterations required by other methods using the complete elevation map, at a lower perception cost to the policy and across a variety of rough and sparse terrain styles.
We also show indoor and outdoor hardware experiments, where the resulting policy successfully transfers to a Unitree G1 humanoid (Fig. 1 ).

In summary, our contributions are as follows:

A self-supervised foothold prediction model (FPM) that accurately predicts the next two footholds from the current proprioceptive state and velocity command, co-trained on policy rollouts during RL training.

A human-inspired perceptive locomotion pipeline that samples the elevation map only around the footholds predicted by the FPM, with insights into its key design choices, such as the prediction horizon and the encoding of the sampled patches.

Simulation and hardware experiments, including comparisons against state-of-the-art elevation-map encoders, that demonstrate the advantages of restricting the policy’s exteroceptive input to the terrain around its next predicted footholds over the complete map.

2026-10-22.title: End-to-End Reinforcement Learning for Quadrupedal Jumping in Lunar Gravity
2026-10-22.authors: Levin Müller , Oliver Fischer , Marco Trentini , Yusuke Tanaka , Marco Hutter
2026-10-22.abstract: Legged robots can extend planetary exploration to rugged and discontinuous terrain that is inaccessible to conventional rovers. In lunar gravity, jumping further expands this mobility by enabling robots to cross obstacles and gaps that cannot be traversed by walking alone. We present a multistage reinforcement-learning approach that produces a single end-to-end control policy for commanded point-to-point jumping under lunar gravity. The resulting policy has a simple architecture and relies exclusively on mission-compatible onboard sensing, making its deployment on a real lunar mission plausible. In simulation, the learned policy performs accurate point-to-point jumps with landing errors smaller than the robot’s body size. We analyze the torque and power demands of lunar jumping and characterize performance degradation under extreme outlier events, including control-update freezes of up to 1 s 1\text{\,}\mathrm{s} during flight. Hardware transfer demonstrates that the policy can successfully execute a vertical jump under lunar-gravity offloading. Furthermore, the measured torque and power profiles are consistent with the simulation results and remain within the robot’s hardware limits.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Robotic exploration of the solar system is essential for advancing scientific understanding of planetary bodies and preparing future human missions. While orbiters and stationary landers provide valuable measurements, scientifically relevant targets require mobile surface systems to acquire local observations and interact with the terrain. As interest grows in sustained surface operations [ 1 ] , infrastructure construction [ 2 , 3 ] , and scientific access to challenging terrain, missions increasingly target sites such as permanently shadowed regions, crater walls, and lunar lava tubes – areas that remain difficult to reach with conventional mobility systems [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] . Planetary rovers have so far relied predominantly on wheeled locomotion, which provides substantial flight heritage and reliability on comparatively benign terrain, but remains limited on steep, loose, rugged, or discontinuous surfaces [ 11 ] . In contrast, recent advances in deep reinforcement learning have substantially improved the ability of legged robots to traverse rough and unstructured terrain, motivating their investigation for planetary exploration. Beyond robust walking, the morphology of legged robots also enables dynamic locomotion modes such as jumping [ 12 ] . For a lunar robot, jumping is not intended to replace walking as an energy-efficient mode of long-range traversal. Still, it can serve as a useful mobility primitive for overcoming obstacles, terrain discontinuities, slopes, and gaps that would otherwise be untraversable [ 13 ] . In low gravity, such maneuvers are especially attractive because relatively moderate launch velocities can produce extended ballistic flight phases [ 12 ] .

At the same time, lunar jumping imposes additional control and deployment challenges: the controller must demonstrate high robustness, particularly during flight and landing, to avoid crashing onto the surface. Specifically on non-redundant system architectures, FDIR may even require the ability to recover from a mid-flight system reboot. In addition, constraints in computing hardware for aerospace engineering favor the development of a low-complexity controller. Although quadrupedal jumping has been demonstrated in both terrestrial and low-gravity contexts, commanded point-to-point jumping for a quadruped in lunar gravity has not yet been sufficiently investigated. To address this gap, we develop a deployment-lean reinforcement-learning framework for commanded point-to-point jumping in lunar gravity. The key idea is to pair the governing ballistic properties of lunar flight with a multistage control scheme. This provides a versatile training framework to synthesize an end-to-end deep reinforcement learning-based jumping controller within a single multilayer perceptron control policy. The control policy maps onboard-feasible observations to joint-position targets.

Specifically, our contributions are:

We formulate commanded point-to-point jumping in lunar gravity by exploiting the ballistic flight structure to relate the target position and flight trajectory-apex height to the desired launch velocity.

We introduce an end-to-end RL framework that learns the full jumping maneuver using a single deployable control policy, while avoiding dense motion references, online trajectory generation, and policy switching.

We evaluate the resulting controller on the Magnecko [ 14 ] quadruped for jumping accuracy, recovery, and robustness to random failures.

We transfer the resulting controller to gravity offloading hardware to evaluate the sim-to-real profile of the torque and power curves.

2. We introduce an end-to-end RL framework that learns the full jumping maneuver using a single deployable control policy, while avoiding dense motion references, online trajectory generation, and policy switching.

3. We evaluate the resulting controller on the Magnecko [ 14 ] quadruped for jumping accuracy, recovery, and robustness to random failures.

4. We transfer the resulting controller to gravity offloading hardware to evaluate the sim-to-real profile of the torque and power curves.

# II RELATED WORK

Quadrupedal jumping has been achieved with trajectory optimization and online MPC tracking [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] , and with fast online trajectory generation [ 18 , 19 ] . Chignoli et al. additionally use an offline jump-feasibility classifier to select omnidirectional jumps in real time [ 20 ] . These architectures are highly complex and depend on substantial onboard computation and accurate dynamics models, which makes them ill-suited to a space-deployment setting.

Reinforcement learning (RL), by contrast, is generally more robust and cheaper at rollout time. A common strategy shapes training with a motion reference: Bellegarda et al. track optimized trajectories with a learned policy [ 21 ] , Liu et al. learn the parameters of a hand-designed foot trajectory for distance-controllable
jumps [ 22 ] , and others imitate optimized or example trajectories [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] . In low gravity, Sang and Wang combine a main-point trajectory generator with staged rewards and shared experience across tasks [ 26 ] , which Ye et al. later augment with
behavior cloning to reach higher relief [ 27 ] . While motion references improve robustness, they make controller development tedious and limit the jump to the performance of the reference; moreover, reference-based jumping has, to
our knowledge, not been transferred to low-gravity or offloaded hardware.

Other works avoid references entirely. Atanassov et al. obtain a single goal-conditioned policy spanning a wide range of jumps purely through curriculum design, though only under Earth gravity and dense velocity guidance [ 28 ] .
Hierarchical or switching controllers that pair a learned high-level policy with model-based or per-phase low-level controllers add capability but introduce additional modules and potential points of failure at deployment [ 29 , 30 ] . Closest to our setting, Xu et al. demonstrate continuous lunar pronking on a hardware-in-the-loop digital-twin testbed that pairs an offload with a tilting platform and treadmill [ 31 ] . While the latter shows promising results, continuous pronking is undesirable in a mission scenario due to the high cost of transport and unnecessary risk. We instead focus on a single jump, to be deployed only when necessary.
