2026-10-22.title: Joint-Angle Invariance of Jacobian-Based Performance Indices for Serial Robotic Manipulators
2026-10-22.authors: Yaohua Zhou , Mingdao Lin , Jiayu Song , Xixin Zhao , Haidong Huang , Jiahu Qin , Xiaocong Li
2026-10-22.comment: . Accepted at the 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS 2026)
2026-10-22.abstract: This article investigates the joint-angle invariance (JAI) of Jacobian-based performance indices for serial robotic manipulators. We identify kinematic conditions under which representative performance indices, including manipulability, stiffness, and other Jacobian-derived indices, remain independent of the first and last joint angles. This property allows a systematic reduction in the effective configuration-space dimensionality, thereby simplifying the performance evaluation. The utility of JAI is demonstrated through two application scenarios: workspace performance map construction and task layout optimization. Comparative results show that the proposed JAI-based strategy reduces computational effort and storage requirements without compromising the effectiveness.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Serial robotic manipulators have been widely deployed in manufacturing, medical, and aerospace industries due to their large workspaces, structural simplicity, and versatility. The evaluation of the motion/force transmission capabilities relies heavily on Jacobian-based performance indices. The Jacobian captures the instantaneous mapping between joint velocities and Cartesian twists, as well as between joint torques and Cartesian wrenches. On this basis, performance indices are derived to measure various aspects of robot behavior. Notable examples include the manipulability index [ 1 ] , which characterizes the motion capability, and the stiffness index [ 2 ] , which evaluates the magnitude of resistance to applied wrenches.

For decades, these performance indices have been applied in robotics. They serve as critical tools in robot design optimization, where geometric parameters are chosen to maximize dexterity or stiffness in targeted regions of the workspace. In trajectory planning, they are used to avoid singularities and maintain desirable kinematic capability. Redundancy resolution strategies frequently incorporate these indices to exploit extra degrees of freedom (DOFs) for enhancing task performance, such as maximizing manipulability. Furthermore, task layout optimization, such as selecting the placement pose of fixtures or workpieces, has been shown to benefit significantly from Jacobian-based performance analysis.

The investigation of performance distribution within the robot workspace facilitates the evaluation of its capabilities. Breitkopf [ 3 ] visualized the distribution of manipulability across the entire workspace of a serial robot. Kuang et al. [ 4 ] employed a sector space meshing method to construct the distribution of the Jacobian condition number, considering the workspace boundary. Such analyses provide valuable guidance for the design and optimization of robots. For instance, Ginnante et al. [ 5 ] utilized a task priority control algorithm to optimize task-oriented robot design, thereby enhancing the kinetostatic performance in desired regions of the workspace. In contrast, Hwang et al. [ 6 ] focused on a comprehensive dimensional synthesis based on global performance indices.

Designing trajectory optimization schemes that incorporate Jacobian-based performance indices can effectively enhance the execution capability of robotic manipulators. For redundant robots, manipulability optimization has been widely recognized as a fundamental approach to improving motion capability while avoiding singular configurations. Tan et al. [ 7 ] proposed a manipulability optimization method based on singular value analysis, which avoids the instability associated with pseudo-inverse computations. Yang et al. [ 8 ] extended the optimization beyond the velocity level and developed a manipulability maximization scheme at the acceleration level. To improve computational efficiency in redundancy resolution, Shen et al. [ 9 ] introduced a derivative propagation approach. Further advancements include the optimization of velocity/force manipulability in bilateral teleoperation of coordinated remote redundant manipulators [ 10 ] . More recently, cross-domain manipulability transfer has gained attention. For instance, Gong et al. [ 11 ] incorporated Riemannian manifold theory to achieve cross-domain mapping of human-robot manipulability ellipsoids via parallel transport. In manufacturing processes such as grinding, polishing, and milling, various stiffness-based trajectory optimization methods have been explored, with the aim of mitigating vibrations during execution [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] .

In the field of robotic manipulation and manufacturing, task layout optimization generally refers to the systematic adjustment of the workpiece pose, so as to enhance overall operational performance. Vahrenkamp et al. [ 15 ] proposed an extended manipulability measure and applied it to online grasp selection for humanoid robots. For tasks involving the manipulation of large-scale objects, Franceschi et al. [ 16 ] introduced a hierarchical optimization framework ranging from global to local levels to optimize work cell layout. In specific process applications, Jiao et al. [ 17 ] focused on robotic drilling systems, developing a redundancy optimization model that considers directional stiffness performance. In machining optimization incorporating stiffness thresholds, Liao et al. [ 18 ] concentrated on robotic milling, optimizing both the robot redundancy and workpiece setup. Regarding autonomous exploration and planning, Liu et al. [ 19 ] established an efficient exploration information system capable of continuously identifying high-manipulability configurations, thereby enabling adaptive layout decisions in unknown environments. Moreover, the adjustment of the robot base constitutes a critical aspect of task layout optimization, with typical applications including manipulator repositioning via mobile platforms for the machining of large components [ 20 ] .

Jacobian-based performance indices are widely used in robotics, while their dependence on the full joint configuration presents two challenges. First, in high-DOF systems, these indices tend to vary considerably across the joint space, resulting in high computational and visualization costs. Second, the absence of identifiable invariance properties hinders theoretical analysis and limits their applicability in efficient optimization. To address these issues, it is essential to identify structural properties that simplify analysis without loss of generality.

This study introduces joint-angle invariance (JAI)–a property exhibited by specific Jacobian-based performance indices for a class of serial robots, whereby the indices remain independent of the first and last joint angles. This invariance substantially reduces the computational burden in both performance analysis and optimization. The utility of JAI is demonstrated in two application scenarios: performance map construction and task layout optimization, and we achieve notable gains in computational efficiency in both cases.

2026-10-22.title: Mixture of Flow Matching and Particle Filter for Proprioception-Based Online Contact Estimation
2026-10-22.authors: Seo Wook Han , Min Jun Kim
2026-10-22.comment: Author accepted manuscript; (including a cover page), 21 figures, 5 tables
2026-10-22.abstract:
In this article, we propose ContactFlowFilter, a novel approach for contact estimation that determines the number of active contacts, their locations, and the associated force vectors.
We consider a robot manipulator equipped with joint torque sensors and a base force/torque sensor; such a proprioceptive-only setup presents a challenging inverse problem characterized by (i) multi-modality from non-unique solutions, (ii) temporal dependencies in state evolution, and (iii) discrete contact events involving contact addition/removal.
Existing approaches, such as particle filters (PFs) and learning-based methods, often struggle to address these challenges simultaneously.
To overcome this, ContactFlowFilter integrates a generative model into the PF framework.
The recursive structure of the PF captures temporal dependencies, while the flow matching model serves as an auxiliary proposal distribution to track multi-modal beliefs and detect contact events.
Extensive validation in both simulation and real-world experiments confirms the effectiveness of the proposed method.
In real-world settings, ContactFlowFilter achieves the lowest dissimilarity from the target distribution, with errors of only 0.36 cm and 0.88 cm for single- and dual-contact scenarios, respectively, while operating at 0.69 ms and 2.69 ms.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Contact information is crucial for robots performing physical interactions .
While collision detection [ 33 , 15 , 26 ] typically provides simple binary information (i.e., contact or no-contact), estimating a detailed contact state that includes contact location and force (e.g., 𝒓 i \bm{r}_{i} and 𝑭 i \bm{F}_{i} in Fig. 1 ) unlocks a wide range of interactive applications.
For example, such detailed contact information can transform the robot’s body into an intuitive human-robot interface, allowing users to trigger different commands by touching specific locations [ 9 , 20 ] or to control the robot by leveraging the contact state as a virtual joystick [ 6 ] .
It also supports interactive control schemes, such as constraining the contact force on the robot’s body [ 41 ] , and substituting for a dedicated force/torque (F/T) sensor used for admittance [ 28 , 27 , 31 ] or direct force control [ 22 ] .
Furthermore, this detailed estimation capability enables advanced strategies such as hybrid motion-force control under unknown forces from outside the target region [ 12 ] , safe navigation through cluttered environments where unexpected contacts can occur [ 23 , 25 , 50 ] , and whole-body manipulation of humanoid robots [ 39 , 2 , 1 ] .

In essence, all these applications rely on the ability to identify the detailed contact state, which consists of (i) the total number of contacts, (ii) their locations, and (iii) the associated force vectors.
However, accurately estimating the contact state remains a largely unsolved problem.
To address this, researchers have explored two main sensory pathways.
The first approach uses exteroceptive sensors, such as surface-mounted tactile skins [ 37 , 19 ] , to directly obtain rich contact information at the interaction region.
The second relies on proprioceptive sensors, such as joint torque sensors (JTSs) and F/T sensors [ 13 , 36 , 21 ] , to infer the contact state from the robot’s internal state.
We focus on the latter approach because these sensors are widely available and integrated into modern robotic systems.
For instance, commercially available platforms such as the Franka Emika Panda, KUKA iiwa and iisy, and Kinova Gen3 are already equipped with JTSs, while F/T sensors can be readily installed (see Fig. 1 ).

However, due to their sparse placement, proprioceptive sensors provide only indirect information about external contacts, as they capture the resulting internal joint torques and forces.
We need to solve an inverse problem that estimates the contact state that best explain these sparse, internal sensor measurements.
As shown in Fig. 1 , our objective is to estimate the contact state, which includes the contact locations on distinct links ( 𝒓 i ∈ ℝ 3 {\bm{r}}_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{3} ), the corresponding three-dimensional (3D) force vectors ( 𝑭 i ∈ ℝ 3 {\bm{F}}_{i}\!\in\!\mathbb{R}^{3} ), and the number of contacts (up to two).
By constraining our scope to scenarios with up to two point contacts, we isolate and tackle the core challenges of the contact estimation problem:

Multi-modality ( Singularity ):
The primary challenge stems from the inherent ambiguity of the inverse problem.
While the forward mapping (from contact to sensor reading) is deterministic, the inverse mapping is ambiguous; as illustrated in Fig. 2 (a), distinct contact states may correspond to identical sensor measurements.
This singularity [ 42 , 44 ] implies that the contact state might not be reliably determined from a single observation, leading to inherent uncertainty in the estimation.
Consequently, the probability distribution of possible solutions becomes multi-modal .
Due to the uncertain nature of the problem, it is more informative and important to predict the multi-modal distribution, rather than yielding a single deterministic solution.

Temporal Dependency :
Although the ambiguity of inferring contact states from single observations remains an inherent problem, it can be mitigated in specific contexts by leveraging temporal dependency .
For instance, consider the discrete state evolution depicted in Fig. 2 (b).
In this scenario, the ambiguity is significantly compounded as the number of contacts increases (e.g., when simultaneously estimating two contacts).
Nevertheless, estimating the second contact becomes more reliable by incorporating past information about the first contact [ 13 ] .
In the case of continuous evolution such as the sliding contact force shown in Fig. 2 (b), knowing the previous contact location simplifies the estimation.
Performing localization around the previous estimate improves efficiency by avoiding the need to explore the entire robot surface [ 36 ] .
Consequently, leveraging temporal dependency , specifically utilizing past estimates, provides a prior context for inferring the current state.

Contact Event Detection :
Determining the number of active contacts requires identifying discrete transitions, specifically the addition or removal of contacts (see Fig. 2 (c)).
While providing a prior context enables effective temporal tracking, its validity strictly depends on the correct discrete state; otherwise, undetected contact events cause the estimator to propagate incorrect past information.
Therefore, robust contact event detection serves as a critical prerequisite for reliable estimation of the complete contact state, including the number, location, and force.

As detailed in Section II , prior work on proprioception-based contact estimation can be broadly categorized into model-based and learning-based approaches.
The former is dominated by particle filter (PF)-based methods [ 36 , 14 , 61 , 47 , 24 ] , while the latter includes deep learning techniques, from probabilistic mapping [ 32 ] to diffusion models [ 13 ] . Each of these categories exhibits distinct strengths and weaknesses.

While PF-based approaches are well-suited for addressing temporal dependency through recursive belief updates, they often fail to handle multi-modality due to particle starvation [ 54 , 55 , 30 ] .
This well-known issue of PFs arises when the particles fail to populate high-belief regions.
In contrast, learning-based approaches excel at estimating multi-modal distributions.
For instance, to capture multi-modality, probabilistic mapping [ 32 ] evaluates probabilities for each region of a discretized state space, and generative models [ 13 ] learn the underlying data distribution.
These feed-forward approaches, however, are typically non-recursive and trained on temporally independent samples, thus lacking a native mechanism for leveraging temporal dependency .
As for contact event detection , it remains a challenge for both categories of approaches.
Although PFs recursively track contact states, they rely on hard-to-tune thresholds to identify discrete transitions.
Feed-forward learning-based methods struggle to model these discrete transitions, as their non-recursive nature inherently restricts temporal reasoning.

In this paper, we propose a novel framework called ContactFlowFilter that tackles the aforementioned challenges: our approach is built upon a recursive structure of PFs for capturing temporal dependency , while a generative model serves as an auxiliary proposal distribution to track multi-modal beliefs and detect contact events .

As depicted in Fig. 3 , ContactFlowFilter updates the contact belief by drawing particles from two complementary proposal distributions: the PF’s temporal prediction and the generative auxiliary proposal.
By preserving the PF’s recursive structure, the proposed method effectively captures temporal dependency , while the generative component complements the PF by representing multi-modal distributions.
Building upon this hybrid framework, we propose a robust method for contact event detection that augments conventional criteria by combining temporal context with generative estimates.

To formally implement the mixture of two proposal distributions, we adopt the dual-sampling concept [ 54 ] .
We first formulate the PF motion model as Gaussian sampling on the robot surface, providing a basis for integrating the generative model and deriving its importance weights.

The generative component is built upon a novel data representation designed to capture the underlying distribution of contact states.
We utilize a fixed-size array of paired contact points to represent up to two simultaneous contacts, which allows the model to infer the spatial relationships between the points.
This is supported by our proposed observation representation, where spatially aligned robot kinematics data, JTSs data, and base F/T sensor data are mapped as a sequence along the kinematic chain.
A transformer encoder then processes this sequence to extract cross-modal correlations.

To achieve real-time performance for high-fidelity temporal tracking, we employ flow matching [ 34 , 8 ] as the generative backbone, leveraging linearized probability paths for few-step inference rather than curved diffusion trajectories [ 17 , 52 , 35 ] .
We also implement a computationally efficient motion model using pre-processed mesh data [ 14 ] .

In summary, our contributions are centered on a main framework (C1) , which is realized through key technical contributions (C2, C3) :

C1) A novel hybrid framework, ContactFlowFilter , that synergistically combines a generative model and a particle filter to address the key challenges of the contact estimation problem ( multi-modality , temporal dependency , and contact event detection ) while ensuring real-time performance.
(Validated in simulation (Section VII-C ) and real-world experiments (Section VII-D and supplementary video).)

C2) A spatially aligned data representation and a transformer-based architecture tailored to extract cross-modal correlations, enabling the flow matching model to effectively learn the multi-modal distribution of contact points.
(Validated in Section VII-A .)

C3) A robust method for contact event detection that leverages a combination of distributions generated by the flow matching model and the PF.
(Validated in Section VII-B .)

We present thorough validation in both simulation and real-world settings.
Comparative experiments confirm that ContactFlowFilter achieves superior performance compared to existing methods.
To assess the estimation accuracy, we employ localization error metrics along with the defined dissimilarity based on the approximated likelihood of the time-dependent belief.
In the real-world experiment, the proposed method achieved the lowest dissimilarity to the target distribution, with localization errors of 0.36 cm \mathrm{cm} and 0.88 cm \mathrm{cm} while maintaining average execution times of 0.69 ms \mathrm{ms} and 2.69 ms \mathrm{ms} for single-contact and dual-contact scenarios, respectively.

The rest of this article is organized as follows.
Section II reviews related research, and Section III presents the preliminaries.
Section IV introduces the baseline PF framework for contact estimation, followed by a discussion of its limitations.
We then present the proposed method, ContactFlowFilter , in Section V and detail its implementation in Section VI .
Section VII demonstrates the experimental validation of the proposed method.
Finally, Section VIII concludes this article.

# II Related Work

## II-A Model-Based Approaches

The line-of-force (LoF) method is a widely adopted technique that geometrically localizes a contact and identifies the corresponding force from the external wrench [ 5 , 11 , 21 , 45 ] .
Because this geometric construction yields a single, deterministic solution based solely on the current observation, it is inherently limited to single-contact scenarios.
Although [ 21 ] demonstrates dual-contact estimation on a robot with redundant sensing (i.e., JTSs and F/T sensors at the base and end-effector), the LoF method lacks temporal reasoning; the estimation is instead enabled by the dual F/T sensor setup, which prevents the spatial mixing of forces.
Intuitively, the base F/T sensor localizes a contact along the robot’s main kinematic chain, while the end-effector F/T sensor identifies a second contact on any attached tool.

Another family of methods is based on the PF [ 38 , 36 , 14 , 61 , 59 , 3 , 47 , 24 ] .
As a recursive approach, the PF naturally incorporates temporal information, allowing it to track contact states over time.
In this framework, a set of particles, representing contact points, is updated and resampled at each time step to minimize an error metric, defined via quadratic programming (QP).
However, a well-known issue with standard PF-based algorithms is particle starvation [ 54 , 55 , 30 ] , where the greedy resampling process causes all particles to converge to a single high-belief region (even to a local minimum), which prevents the particle set from representing a multi-modal distribution.

To address the challenge of multi-modality (i.e., the singularity problem), several approaches have been proposed.
For instance, the methods in [ 42 , 44 ] employ a non-greedy strategy to narrow down contact point candidates, evaluating each using a QP-based error metric.
However, extending these approaches to scenarios with more than one contact point is not straightforward.

While such non-greedy schemes effectively handle multi-modality, both they and the LoF method rely on a static formulation that cannot capture the time-dependent characteristic of the contact estimation problem.
In contrast, the PF framework inherently supports temporal reasoning, making it a more promising foundation.
Therefore, this work focuses on advancing the PF-based approach by overcoming its own limitations.

A key limitation of existing PF-based approaches for scenarios with more than a single contact [ 36 , 14 , 61 , 47 , 24 ] is their reliance on a hard-to-tune threshold for contact event detection.
While these methods track each contact point with a dedicated particle set, managing the number of sets depends on a highly sensitive threshold.
Such dependency limits the adaptation to contact changes, leading to detection errors such as false positives or missed contacts.
To overcome this, we introduce a robust particle set management scheme that utilizes the output of flow matching, as detailed in Section V-D .

Additionally, PF-based methods are mainly distinguished by their strategies for representing and updating particles on the robot’s surface.
These include projecting particles represented in Cartesian space onto the robot surface [ 36 , 59 ] , parameterizing the surface with a single variable [ 38 , 24 ] , and using graph-based searches directly on the mesh [ 14 , 61 , 47 ] .
In Section IV-B , we introduce a highly efficient particle update method that performs Gaussian sampling directly on the robot’s surface by using pre-computed geodesic distances from the mesh data.

## II-B Learning-Based Approaches

Recently, several learning-based approaches have been proposed for contact localization [ 32 , 60 , 46 , 13 , 9 ] , which vary in their formulations.
For example, the probabilistic mapping approach in [ 32 ] treats the robot’s link surfaces as 2D images and estimates the contact probability for each region.
Other formulations include binary classification over predefined points on the robot’s surface [ 60 , 46 ] , or regression of the contact location, either as a 3D point in Cartesian space [ 9 ] or as a single 1D parameter on the robot’s surface [ 46 ] .
However, a common limitation of these approaches is that they do not estimate the contact force and inherently lack a mechanism for temporal reasoning.

Among these learning-based methods, the work most relevant to ours is the diffusion model-based approach presented in [ 13 ] .
While it employs a recursive inference scheme similar to the PF, relying on temporally independent training data forces the model to assume that the first contact point remains fixed.
It also shares the common limitation of other learning-based approaches in its inability to estimate contact force.
In contrast, by integrating the output of a generative model into the PF framework, the proposed method performs both temporal reasoning and contact force estimation, while maintaining the representational power of the generative model.
By utilizing a flow matching model, our approach further achieves significantly faster inference (15.97 ms \mathrm{ms} → \,\rightarrow\, 2.69 ms \mathrm{ms} ) while even demonstrating substantial improvements in performance.

2026-10-22.title: Preserving Operator Intent Under Actuation Constraints: Teleoperation of Manipulators with Coupled Transmissions
2026-10-22.authors: Xuhan Miao , Zijin Han , Yutong Shen , Haidong Huang , Shanliushui Gao , Lei Zhang , Xiaocong Li , Chenguang Yang
2026-10-22.comment: . Contribution to the IROS 2026 workshop "5th Sensorimotor-Augmented Teleoperation: Human-Interaction-Oriented Paradigm and Real-World Concerns"
2026-10-22.abstract: Teleoperation enables intuitive control of remote engineering robots for precision tasks. Existing direct joint-mapping methods have two limitations: independent motor saturation disrupts pitch–roll coordination in differential wrists, while fixed mappings struggle with abrupt tracking changes caused by gravitational loads and actuation constraints. We propose an actuator-constraint-aware leader–follower teleoperation method that jointly models leader gravity compensation, leader–follower joint mapping, and follower differential-wrist control. Specifically, we perform coordinated saturation in motor space according to the available gravity margin and integrate continuous angle unwrapping, feedback-state monitoring, and feasible-reference updates. This preserves the operator’s motion direction, reduces coordination distortion, and suppresses recovery transients during saturation or brief communication failures. Real-robot experiments demonstrate smoother wrist trajectories and more continuous recovery than direct mapping.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Teleoperation enables humans to operate robots in hazardous, confined, or contact-uncertain environments, and has become an important interface for remote manipulation and demonstration collection [ 1 , 2 ] . Compared with keyboards, joysticks, and vision-only interfaces, a leader manipulator directly expresses the operator’s joint motion, reducing cognitive load caused by action planning and coordinate transformation. Recent low-cost leader–follower systems support dexterous manipulation and imitation learning, but commonly rely on independent joint mapping or end-effector tracking, without explicitly modeling transmission coupling, configuration-dependent gravity, and actuator saturation [ 2 , 3 ] .

This issue is particularly pronounced in the engineering manipulator studied here. The leader and follower exchange joint angles, wrist commands, and gripper states through a custom serial protocol. The follower combines heterogeneous motors with a differential wrist, and uses proportional mapping, PID current control, gravity compensation, encoder unwrapping, and feedback timeout protection. In the existing implementation, the differential wrist drives pitch and roll through sum–difference motor commands, followed by independent motor saturation [ 4 ] . When one motor saturates, the realized pitch–roll ratio and motion direction deviate from the operator command. Moreover, the distributed treatment of gravity compensation, angle continuity, and feedback loss does not provide a unified model of the available actuation margin. Consequently, fixed mapping cannot capture configuration-dependent capability, while temporarily infeasible commands may accumulate and cause abrupt recovery motions.

We propose an actuator-constrained teleoperation method for manipulators with coupled transmissions. The method maps transmission coupling, gravity demand, actuator limits, and feedback state into a unified actuator-space model. Operator commands are then projected onto the feasible set while preserving local motion direction and pitch–roll coordination as much as possible. A continuous feasible-reference update further prevents command accumulation during saturation or short communication dropouts. The resulting design extends the existing leader–follower hardware and real-time control pipeline, while addressing motion distortion caused by coupled actuation and gravity-dependent capability.

The contributions are threefold:

We formulate the motion distortion induced by differential transmission and actuator-level saturation, and characterize how gravity compensation changes the available actuation margin.

We propose an actuator-space intent-preserving command projection that integrates gravity compensation, joint mapping, and PID current control, thereby reducing coordination distortion near saturation.

We introduce continuous feasible-reference management using encoder unwrapping and online feedback monitoring, which suppresses error accumulation and recovery transients after temporary infeasibility.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Immersive and Digital-Twin Teleoperation

Immersive teleoperation aims to reduce the cognitive gap between the operator and the remote robot by providing a spatially consistent visual or digital representation of the robot and its environment. Recent systems use virtual reality, stereoscopic feedback, or digital twins to improve viewpoint control, robot compatibility, and operator intuitiveness [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . These methods mainly improve the human–robot interface, but the generated commands are often passed to the robot through direct joint tracking or Cartesian control. Consequently, they do not explicitly address how coupled transmissions, gravity-dependent load, and motor saturation distort coordinated motions at the actuator level. Our method complements immersive interfaces with an actuator-space feasibility layer that preserves coordinated operator motion when the follower reaches its execution limits.

## II-B Learning-Based Teleoperation and Shared Autonomy

Learning-based teleoperation uses imitation learning, reinforcement learning, or learned intent recognition to reduce operator workload and support autonomous assistance. Recent work learns mode switching from human intent [ 8 ] , combines teleoperation with open-world shared control [ 6 ] , and uses large-scale teleoperated data to improve manipulation policies [ 9 ] . These methods can handle complex task-level behavior, but their performance depends on training-data coverage and learned policies do not inherently guarantee safe execution under unseen actuator constraints. Moreover, learning-based assistance may modify the operator’s command without explicitly preserving its instantaneous multi-DoF coordination. Our model-based method operates before policy execution and preserves the operator’s local motion direction under gravity and actuator saturation without requiring task-specific training data.

## II-C Optimization-Based and Constraint-Aware Robot Control

Constraint-aware control regulates robot commands according to collision, singularity, torque, velocity, or contact constraints. Existing approaches use control barrier functions [ 10 ] , Cartesian impedance and null-space projection, or quadratic programming to maintain safety and feasibility [ 11 ] . These methods provide formal or numerical constraint handling, but most impose constraints in joint or Cartesian space and treat actuator saturation as a final clipping operation. Such clipping can change the coordination ratio of coupled degrees of freedom, while accumulated infeasible references may produce abrupt recovery motions. Our method formulates the coupled differential wrist and gravity-compensated actuator margins directly in actuator space, then performs coordinated command projection and continuous feasible-reference updates to reduce motion distortion and recovery transients.

2026-10-22.title: From VLM Planners to Robotic Agents: Self-Evolving Harnesses for History-Dependent Manipulation
2026-10-22.authors: Tingwen Du , Haoyu Guo , Hanxue Zhang , Xuanxu Wang , Junting Dong , Chao Gao , Mingfei Han , Tao Lu , Mulin Yu , Chunhua Shen , Xiaojun Chang , Zhihui Li
2026-10-22.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models achieve strong performance
across embodied manipulation tasks by unifying visual understanding,
language conditioning, and action generation. However, long-horizon tasks can involve non-Markovian dependencies: successful
decisions may require retaining task progress and past interaction outcomes,
while partial observability and execution errors compound over time. Existing work has begun to address these challenges by augmenting
foundation-model policies with memory and by introducing hierarchical
architectures that separate high-level planning from low-level execution. We organize the high-level VLM as a robotic agent through an editable
harness to maintain task context and improve planning through execution
experience. We instantiate this approach as SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), with a
fixed VLA executor providing low-level control. The harness maintains and updates task context using observations and execution
feedback to guide subsequent planning. Self-evolution uses environment rollouts to propose and evaluate
harness revisions, with the selected configuration fixed before held-out
testing. On RoboMME, SERA achieves 51.38% overall success with autonomous selection,
compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. Our exploration suggests that agentic planning is a promising direction for
history-dependent robotic manipulation.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language
instructions to robot actions, providing a foundation for general-purpose
manipulation ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ) .
Long-horizon tasks, however, can require information that the current observation
does not reveal ( Koo et al., 2025 ; Dai et al., 2026 ) . For example, when a robot
must repeat an operation a specified number of times, similar images may call
for different decisions depending on how many repetitions have actually
succeeded. An earlier observation may also contain a cue that is no longer
visible. Such history-dependent decisions require preserving task-relevant
information and tracking execution outcomes over successive interactions.

Existing research provides several foundations for these capabilities.
Memory-augmented policies equip VLA models with mechanisms for retaining and
using historical information, including compact temporal representations ( Koo et al., 2025 ; Jang et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2026 ) , memory retrieval, and
recurrent state updates ( Shi et al., 2025a ; Hu et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) .
Hierarchical architectures introduce a high-level planning layer that
issues intermediate decisions to low-level executors ( Ahn et al., 2022 ; Belkhale et al., 2024 ; Duan et al., 2025 ; Sridhar et al., 2025 ) and can
incorporate environment feedback ( Huang et al., 2022 ) . Agentic systems further
organize reasoning, actions, and feedback into iterative decision processes ( Yao et al., 2022 ; Shinn et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2023 ) . Recent embodied harnesses
explore external task management ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Gu et al., 2026 ) and experience-driven adaptation ( Chen et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Ding et al., 2026 ) .
Together, these developments motivate studying how the high-level planner in a
hierarchical architecture can manage task context and make use of execution
experience.

Our focus is on two connected responsibilities of this planning process.
Within an episode, issuing a command does not establish that the intended
operation has succeeded. In the repetition example, updating progress requires
interpreting subsequent observations and feedback, while retaining information
needed for later decisions. Access to history therefore needs to be accompanied
by an explicit process for maintaining decision-relevant task context.
Across attempts, an execution record must be translated into a reusable change
to influence future planning. This raises a question: how can we support both
ongoing context management and improvements to the planning process from
execution experience? We explore an editable harness around the high-level VLM
as a common mechanism for these responsibilities. The harness organizes context
and feedback during execution, while providing an explicit object for revision
during self-evolution. This also offers a way to investigate experience reuse
when additional demonstrations and manual annotations are costly.
Figure 1 illustrates this design direction.

We present SERA (Self-Evolving Robotic Agent), which organizes a VLM as an
agent within an editable harness around a fixed VLA executor. During task
execution, the harness supports sustained context management over long horizons,
guiding the extraction, retention, and updating of task progress and execution
outcomes from observations and feedback. This context supports the
VLM’s subsequent planning.
However, a predefined harness may not anticipate all task requirements,
motivating execution-driven self-evolution to identify and repair its limitations.
Analysis and revision agents autonomously diagnose failures from execution
traces and propose candidate repairs to planning guidance, assessment
criteria, and control rules.
A verifier evaluates these candidates through environment rollouts,
providing feedback for further revision and harness selection.
This process revises the harness without manually constructing additional
demonstration datasets for supervised fine-tuning of the high-level VLM planner.
The selected harness is fixed before held-out testing, while task context
continues to be updated within each episode.

We evaluate SERA on RoboMME, a benchmark for history-dependent robotic
manipulation ( Dai et al., 2026 ) . Autonomous SERA achieves 51.38% overall
success, compared with 44.38% without self-evolution. These results support an
empirical exploration of agentic planning and the aggregate effect of
execution-driven harness revisions. Our contributions are:

An agentic planning framework that organizes a high-level VLM within an
editable harness for sustained task-context management over long horizons,
tracking task progress and execution feedback to guide a fixed VLA executor.

An agentic planning framework that organizes a high-level VLM within an
editable harness for sustained task-context management over long horizons,
tracking task progress and execution feedback to guide a fixed VLA executor.

An execution-driven self-evolution procedure that autonomously proposes
and evaluates revisions to planning guidance, assessment criteria, and
control rules from rollout feedback, without constructing an SFT dataset.

We evaluate SERA on RoboMME and achieve 51.38% overall
success. Harness self-evolution improves success by 7.00 percentage points
over the initial configuration.

2. An execution-driven self-evolution procedure that autonomously proposes
and evaluates revisions to planning guidance, assessment criteria, and
control rules from rollout feedback, without constructing an SFT dataset.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Memory-Augmented Policies

Generalist robot policies learn language-conditioned manipulation from diverse
data ( Brohan et al., 2022 ; Open X-Embodiment Collaboration, 2023 ; Octo Model Team et al., 2024 ) .
VLA models connect pretrained vision-language representations with action
learning ( Brohan et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2024 ; NVIDIA et al., 2025 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ).
Related embodied models, including PaLM-E, incorporate visual and continuous
state inputs into language models for embodied reasoning and planning ( Driess et al., 2023 ) . These developments provide a foundation for
language-conditioned manipulation, while history-dependent tasks additionally
require information beyond the current observation. Recent work has also
emphasized the importance of historical information in manipulation, with
benchmarks such as RoboMME explicitly evaluating history-dependent
behavior ( Dai et al., 2026 ) .

Memory-augmented policies incorporate such information through different
representations and update mechanisms ( Fang et al., 2025 ) . HAMLET aggregates compact moment tokens
across timesteps to condition action prediction ( Koo et al., 2025 ) .
MemoryVLA retrieves perceptual and cognitive information from a memory bank
and fuses it with current representations ( Shi et al., 2025a ) , while
ContextVLA compresses past observations into a context token for efficient
multi-frame conditioning ( Jang et al., 2025 ) . Other designs address
cross-subtask information transfer through event-triggered latent memory
in WeaveLA ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) , hierarchical experience retrieval in
ECHO ( Hu et al., 2026 ) , and temporal aggregation through frame- and
chunk-level recurrent queries in ReMem-VLA ( Li et al., 2026 ) .
These methods integrate historical information into action prediction through
compact temporal representations, memory retrieval, or recurrent updates.

## 2.2 Hierarchical Robotic Planning

Hierarchical approaches connect high-level reasoning to executable robot
behavior through intermediate decisions ( Rana et al., 2023 ; Shi et al., 2025b ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) . SayCan combines language-model
planning with affordance estimates for pretrained skills ( Ahn et al., 2022 ) , and Inner Monologue incorporates environment feedback
into subsequent planning ( Huang et al., 2022 ) . Code as Policies
expresses robot behavior as programs invoking perception and control APIs ( Liang et al., 2022 ) . Other interfaces include the spatial value
maps of VoxPoser, the relational keypoint constraints of ReKep, and the
language motions of RT-H ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Huang et al., 2024 ; Belkhale et al., 2024 ) .
RoboPARA further uses dependency graphs and resource constraints to organize
parallel dual-arm execution ( Duan et al., 2025 ) .

Memory and hierarchical planning can also be combined. MemER trains a
high-level VLM to nominate historical keyframes and predict language subtasks;
selected keyframes inform subsequent decisions, while a low-level VLA executes
the subtasks ( Sridhar et al., 2025 ) . Goal2Skill combines structured task
memory with subtask verification and replanning in a VLM–VLA hierarchy ( Liu et al., 2026 ) .

## 2.3 Agentic Embodied Systems and Self-Evolution

Research on language models and agents studies reasoning, interaction, and
feedback-driven refinement ( Madaan et al., 2023 ) . ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions
and observations ( Yao et al., 2022 ) ; Reflexion stores textual feedback for
subsequent attempts ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) ; and Voyager accumulates
reusable executable skills through interaction in Minecraft ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . Related methods improve prompts or agent code using execution
feedback ( Agrawal et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . These works provide precedents for agent loops and
experience reuse, although their evaluation settings differ from robotic
manipulation.

Recent embodied systems place these ideas around learned
executors ( Ahn et al., 2024 ) .
Harness VLA combines a frozen VLA primitive with analytic primitives and
task-specific and global memories ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) .
HarnessWAM maintains evidence-grounded task state and a task graph, and
compiles plans into capability-constrained WAM skills ( Gu et al., 2026 ) . RoboMemory combines spatial, temporal, episodic,
and semantic memories with a planner–critic loop ( Lei et al., 2025 ) .
HELM couples episodic memory with a learned state verifier and recovery control
around a frozen VLA ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) . Cortex combines task-context memory
and skill constraints in a deployment harness ( Peng et al., 2026 ) .

Execution-driven harness adaptation is also an emerging research direction.
ETA studies experience-derived strategy and skill updates subject to runtime
checks before promotion ( Chen et al., 2026 ) .
SHAPER evolves textual skills and a context-code harness using rollout
feedback and validation while keeping its planner and executor frozen ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Zetta revises runtime critics, recovery playbooks,
and executable tools from failed rollouts ( Ding et al., 2026 ) .
Within this line of work, SERA explores an editable harness for high-level
planning in history-dependent robotic manipulation. The harness supports
within-episode context management and is revised using development-stage
execution experience, with the selected version fixed before testing.

2026-10-22.title: Make it Walk: Computational Design of LEGO Walkers
2026-10-22.authors: Siqi Li , Fancheng Gao , Chi-Wing Fu , Peng Song
2026-10-22.abstract:
LEGO walkers are walking automata constructed from modular LEGO Technic bricks. They exhibit intriguing locomotion and are also highly reconfigurable through the modular
Technic bricks, making them widely applicable in education, recreation, and robotics research. However, existing LEGO walkers are designed mostly by reusing existing single-actuator walking mechanisms.
Although the locomotion is stable, their fixed walking gaits limit their adaptability and versatility. This paper presents the first computational solution capable of designing LEGO walkers that not only walk stably, but also support a variety of walking gaits.
Our idea is twofold. First, we control the foot motion trajectory of each leg mechanically via a specifically-designed gear-linkage mechanism, in which we incorporate a pair of 3D-printed non-circular gears to work with a LEGO Technic mechanism. Second, we drive each leg by an independent motor and synchronize the timings of multiple leg motions via a simple yet adaptable control algorithm, enabling stable and versatile locomotion. Importantly, we take this modeling as a foundation to co-design the morphology and control of the LEGO walkers to meet the target locomotion and appearance. Leveraging our approach, we created a variety of LEGO walkers, demonstrating various walking gaits and appearances, and fabricated some of them to show their locomotion capability in the real world.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Walking automata are mechanical systems designed to produce legged locomotion.
The LEGO Technic system provides an accessible and modular platform for rapid prototyping walking automata, namely LEGO walkers .
These walkers deliver intriguing
locomotion behaviors and have been widely used in
recreational robots [ 6 ] and robotics research.
In addition, they serve as effective STEM education tools, nurturing hands-on exploration of the gait principles and stable creeping locomotion.

Existing works create LEGO walkers largely by reusing existing linkage-based walking mechanisms such as Klann linkage [ 11 ] and Jansen’s linkage [ 10 ] ; see Figure for examples.
Once assembled, such designs are able to walk stably, driven by a single actuator.
Yet, they are specifically constrained to deliver few fixed walking gaits pre-defined in existing walking mechanisms, limiting their versatility and expressiveness.

In this work, we present a new computational solution to create LEGO walkers that can deliver a variety of walking gaits while walking stably.
This problem is non-trivial for two reasons.
First, we cannot rely on existing walking mechanisms, since they generally produce a fixed walking gait.
Hence, the first challenge asks for modeling the morphology of the LEGO walker, including which mechanical parts to use, how to connect them, and also how to actuate them.
The second challenge lies in the vast design space of our problem.
To achieve stable walking with varying gaits, we need to determine not only the geometry and layout of the mechanical parts but also the control and actuation of these parts.

To address these challenges, our key idea is to decouple the trajectory and timing control of each walking leg, simplifying the walker’s morphology and control.
At the leg level, we propose to control the foot motion trajectory of each leg mechanically via a specifically-designed gear-linkage mechanism and incorporate a pair of 3D-printed non-circular gears to work with the LEGO Technic mechanism.
In this way, we can enlarge the design space of the walking gait.
At the walker level, we propose to drive each leg by an independent motor and synchronize the timings of multiple leg motions via electronically controlling the actuation of the driving motors.
By this means, each leg is modeled with its own gear-linkage mechanism, so our LEGO walker can feature a simple and lightweight morphology for delivering stable walking with varying gaits; see Figures and for examples.

To design LEGO walkers, we
only need to specify the desired walking gait (including the foot trajectory and footfall pattern) and provide a body frame of the walker.
Then, our computational approach co-designs the morphology and control of the LEGO walker to meet the target walking gait and walker appearance.
In particular, our approach first constructs and optimizes the leg mechanism to approximate the target foot trajectory, then generates the leg layout to match the given body frame, and optimizes the control on the leg actuations for stable walking guided by the gait theory.
At the end, our approach generates all the information necessary for fabricating the LEGO walker, including
the LEGO Technic brick assemblies,
the shape of the non-circular gears for 3D printing,
the assembly instructions, and
the control for the servo motors.
We validate our approach through the design and physical realization of several LEGO-based quadruped and hexapod walkers, demonstrating the practicality and versatility of our approach.

In this work, we make the following contributions:

We exploit a new class of LEGO walkers that integrates mechanical control (for generating leg trajectories) and electrical control (for synchronizing leg motions) for realizing a variety of walking gaits, where the core is a modular and lightweight leg mechanism modeled as a five-bar linkage with two non-circular gears.

We propose an optimization-based approach, capable of efficiently co-designing the morphology and control of LEGO walkers, satisfying the target walking gait and walker appearance, while ensuring stable walking and fabricability.

1. We exploit a new class of LEGO walkers that integrates mechanical control (for generating leg trajectories) and electrical control (for synchronizing leg motions) for realizing a variety of walking gaits, where the core is a modular and lightweight leg mechanism modeled as a five-bar linkage with two non-circular gears.

2. We propose an optimization-based approach, capable of efficiently co-designing the morphology and control of LEGO walkers, satisfying the target walking gait and walker appearance, while ensuring stable walking and fabricability.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

With the advance and growing popularity of digital fabrication, the computational design and fabrication of personalized walking automata has attracted immense interest from the graphics community.
A number of computational methods have been developed to design automata that perform intriguing walking motion in mid air ,
including
mechanical characters [ 5 ] ,
mechanical figures [ 3 ] ,
linkage-based characters [ 20 ] ,
kinetic wire characters [ 24 ] , and
compliant mechanical systems [ 19 ] .

Beyond displaying walking motion, other research has explored the design of automata capable of walking stably on the ground.
Bharaj et al. [ 2 ] developed a computational tool for designing personalized walking automata, where the automata are first interactively created by users from a library of predefined template linkage mechanisms and then optimized to achieve stable walking on the ground.
Cheng et al. [ 4 ] designed a six-leg automaton with a fixed walking gait based on a composite 3D cam-follower mechanism.

A walking robot is a legged robotic system that moves across the ground, where each leg is typically built of an open kinematic chain with multiple actuated joints.
Several computational approaches have been developed for designing different kinds of walking robots, including
robotic creatures [ 15 , 9 ] and
skinned quad-robots [ 7 ] .
In particular, Zhao et al. [ 25 ] presented a computational approach called RoboGrammar for generating optimized structures of walking robots to traverse given terrains.

Although walking robots provide versatile locomotion capabilities by supporting a wide variety of walking gaits, they need a large number of actuators to drive every robot joint. Hence, they are often expensive to fabricate and complex to control. Due to low structural stiffness and relatively large joint clearance, LEGO Technic systems are rarely used for building walking robots. In this work, we study the computational design and fabrication of LEGO walkers, which are inexpensive to fabricate and easy to control, while supporting stable walking with varying gaits.

LEGO Technic is an advanced building system for creating complex and functional models built of LEGO Technic bricks such as
beams, axles, pins, and gears.
Existing research works [ 12 , 26 , 17 , 8 , 23 ] on creating LEGO models mainly focus on designing static structures with non-Technic bricks. Regarding LEGO Technic, Xu et al. [ 22 ] introduced a method to compute and construct LEGO Technic models that follow user-specified sketches.
To the best of our knowledge, we are not aware of any research work on constructing LEGO Technic walkers.

2026-10-22.title: S-Rolling: Steerable Rolling Gaits for Twistable Snake Robots in Low-Clearance Environments
2026-10-22.authors: Qingling Fan , Zhongqiang Ren
2026-10-22.abstract:
Snake robots can traverse complex environments with limbless
locomotion, but maneuvering in low-clearance environments remains challenging because a gait must maintain a small swept height while also providing planar steering.
Existing rolling gaits preserve a low swept height body configuration but generally provide limited steering, whereas steering gaits often introduce vertical undulation and require additional clearance.
With that in mind, this paper develops S-rolling, a steerable rolling gait that combines low swept height locomotion with planar maneuverability for twistable snake robots.
S-rolling is designed using an S-shaped planar backbone curve, whose head and tail segments roll with independently controlled angular velocities, producing different motion modes.
We derive its joint space gait equation, in which a central twist joint realizes the relative rotation between the two segments.
We also develop a quasi-static kinematic model relating the segment rolling speeds to the linear and angular velocities of the robot.
Real-robot experiments demonstrate the various motion modes, traversal through a 10 10 cm clearance test track, and maneuvering tasks beneath a large workpiece and a car chassis.
In these low-clearance scenarios, S-rolling successfully performs approximately 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} and 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} heading changes, whereas the baseline rolling arc gait cannot change the robot heading.
2026-10-22.introduction:
The paper is motivated by robot navigation in Low-Clearance Environments (LCE), by which we refer to expansive horizontal surfaces that have restricted vertical space (i.e., a ceiling) above them.
Examples of LCEs include the space beneath a vehicle chassis (Fig. 1 ), and navigating robots in LCEs naturally arises in applications such as exploration or inspection of vehicles or large industrial parts.
Navigating LCEs is quite challenging: on the one hand, the limited vertical space requires the robot to have a small cross section to be able to enter LCEs.
On the other hand, the robot should be easily maneuverable, such as moving back and forth and changing directions in LCEs.

Snake robots, as a class of hyper-redundant mechanisms, enjoy a small cross section and can traverse complex environments such as pipes, narrow passages, and compact spaces with limbless locomotion [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
However, due to the limited vertical space of LCEs, a snake robot must maintain a small swept height to avoid collision with the ceiling, which makes many existing gaits, cyclic motion in the shape space, for snake robots inapplicable:
To name a few, concertina gaits rely on lateral anchoring and may require sufficient contact with the surrounding walls [ 4 , 5 ] , which may not be available in LCEs.
Sidewinding can generate steerable motion, but its vertical undulation increases the swept height and may collide with the ceiling in LCEs [ 6 , 7 ] .

Possible gaits for snake robots to locomote in LCEs include rolling and rectilinear gaits, which maintain a small swept height.
However, these gaits generally provide limited steering capability [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] : the robot can only move back and forth along a straight line without changing direction, which limits its maneuverability in LCEs.

This paper is interested in enabling the snake robot to achieve steerable motion in LCEs, without losing existing gaits for the snake robot to traverse complex terrains.
To generate steerable motion in LCEs, this paper considers a so-called twistable snake robot (T-Snake) [ 12 ] and develops a new S-rolling gait for T-Snake.
T-Snake is a mechanism that can not only bend its backbone as the popular modular snake robot does [ 13 ] , which allows T-Snake to achieve any gait that regular snake robot has, but also twist about its backbone (Fig. 1 (a)), which provides new possibilities for locomotion.
Based on such T-Snake mechanism, we take the view that low swept height and planar maneuverability can be achieved simultaneously by coordinating the rolling motions of different body segments, without introducing additional vertical undulation.
With that in mind, the proposed S-rolling gait leverages an S-shaped backbone curve, which consists of two tangential circular arcs with opposite signed curvatures.
The two segments of T-Snake can roll with independently controlled angular velocities, which thus enables steerable motion in LCEs.

Designing and controlling such new gaits for T-Snake faces the fundamental challenge of coordinating the many degree of freedom (DoFs) of a snake robot to generate effective motion with real-time computation.
To address the challenge, we begin our design of S-rolling using the backbone curve approach [ 14 , 15 ] , which provides an intuitive geometric method to model and design the gait of the snake robot.
Then, we further derive the gait equations, closed-form shape space motion, of S-rolling based on the designed backbone curve, which allows light-weight and fast computation.
With the help of the S-rolling gait, we further derive a quasi-static kinematic model that relates the two segment rolling speeds to the linear and angular velocities of the robot, which allows locomotive reduction of a complicated snake robot to a simple differential drive car, for easy maneuver in practice.

To summarize, the technical contributions of this paper include: (i) the development of S-rolling gaits, which include both the design of the backbone curve and the further derivation of gait equations, and (ii) the quasi-static locomotive reduction of T-Snake as a differential-drive car based on S-rolling that enables easy maneuver in LCEs.

For verification, we conduct real-robot experiments with T-Snake hardware.
We first demonstrate forward and backward translation, clockwise and counterclockwise in-place turning.
We then evaluate the gait on a test track containing 10 10 cm clearance passages.
Finally, we demonstrate two practical tasks beneath a large workpiece and a car chassis, with clearance heights of 15 15 cm and 13 13 cm, respectively.
Compared with the rolling arc gait [ 8 ] , which cannot change the robot heading in these tasks (Fig. 1 (c)), S-rolling successfully performs approximately 90 ∘ 90^{\circ} and 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} heading changes while maintaining low-clearance locomotion.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Works

## II-A Gait Design Methods

Designing snake-robot gaits is difficult because many redundant DoFs couple shape-space motion to workspace displacement.
Central pattern generators [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] and reinforcement learning [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] improve adaptability, but often provide limited geometric interpretability.
Parameterized gait equations simplify redundant-joint control for common gaits [ 22 , 23 , 8 ] .
This approach offers low computational cost and high real-time performance.
Backbone curve methods [ 14 , 15 ] encode body shape and orientation geometrically, enabling diverse rolling and climbing gaits [ 8 , 24 , 25 ] .
We use this advantage to design S-rolling and derive its joint-space equation.

## II-B Rolling and Low-Clearance Locomotion

Rolling-based gaits are developed for transport, terrain traversal, pipe climbing, and manipulation [ 26 , 8 , 24 , 27 ] .
These existing rolling gaits typically prescribe a fixed rolling direction.
In particular, the rolling arc gait [ 8 ] , considered as the baseline in this paper, provides low swept height locomotion, but does not provide any steering capability.

The proposed gait targets low-clearance environments, which constrain the gravity direction but not the horizontal plane.
Let h z h_{z} denote the height of a narrow gap, and A c ​ d A_{cd} denote the cross-sectional diameter of the snake robot.
We define an LCE by 1 ≤ h z / A c ​ d < 2 1\leq h_{z}/A_{cd}<2 , analogous to the restricted-maneuverability criterion in [ 28 , 29 ] .

Concertina gaits [ 4 , 5 ] need lateral anchoring, while ceiling-floor anchoring consumes the available height.
Planar rolling and rectilinear gaits keep swept height low.
But steering of these gaits requires additional vertical body waves or lifting [ 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 ] .
Sidewinding steers effectively but increases swept height [ 6 , 7 ] .

2026-10-22.title: Linear Twisting Sidewinding Gaits for Twistable Snake Robot Motion Planning on Complex Terrains
2026-10-22.authors: Qingling Fan , Zhongqiang Ren
2026-10-22.abstract:
Sidewinding is an efficient gait for snake robots to locomote on various terrains, by undulating the backbone curve and shifting the contact segments along it.
However, relying solely on undulatory motion limits the locomotive capability of snake robots, and combining it with twisting motion can improve their speed and robustness.
This hypothesis has recently been verified by the rolling vector approach, which locomotes the robot like a differential-drive car.
Yet its twisting is concentrated in a short buffer segment, imposing most of the workload on the two twist joints in the middle, which can often overburden the motors and limit its locomotion.
With that in mind, this paper develops a new family of twisting sidewinding gaits that distribute the workload over the entire body with our proposed linear twisting function.
Under matched turning speed and total output power, our gaits reduce the peak output power of a single twist joint by 42%.
Real-robot experiments show that, with the reduced workload, our new gaits can locomote the robot in various terrains that the existing rolling vector approach cannot.
Besides, our new gaits can move up to 49% faster than conventional sidewinding without twisting.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Snake robots are hyper-redundant limbless robots that can traverse complex environments [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] such as sandy slopes, pipes, and compact spaces, using versatile gaits, which are cyclic motions in the shape space.
Among these gaits, sidewinding is regarded as highly efficient and robust in many terrains [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
During sidewinding, the snake keeps its body lifted except for a few static contact segments, and undulates its backbone curve both horizontally and vertically to continuously shift these segments, transporting itself using the friction at contact.

While being highly efficient and robust, sidewinding is still relatively slow to traverse even flat ground, and may get trapped on uneven terrains.
In contrast, the rolling motion of wheels is way faster on many complex terrains.
We take the view that relying solely on undulatory motion limits the locomotive capability of snake robots, and that combining it with rolling motion can improve both efficiency and robustness without losing the various gaits.
This hypothesis has been partially verified in simulation by the recent literature [ 8 ] , which considers locomotion of a twistable snake robot (T-Snake), a modular snake-robot mechanism that can not only bend but also twist about its backbone curve.
A rolling vector approach [ 8 ] is proposed to coordinate the motion of joints, which kinematically reduces the T-Snake to a differential-drive car.
This rolling vector approach twists by assigning different rolling speeds to the head and tail segments, bridged by a short buffer segment.
As a result, the twisting is concentrated within the buffer segment, and burdens the two twist joints in the middle of the body, while leaving the others almost idle (Fig. 1 (a)), which can often overload the motors in the buffer segment and limit its locomotion capability.

To coordinate the large number of joints while avoiding such uneven workload, this paper proposes a new linear twisting approach that distributes the twisting motion over the entire body.
Specifically, we let the twisting vary linearly along the backbone curve, and refer to the resulting gaits as linear twisting sidewinding (LTS).
Following the backbone curve approach [ 9 , 10 ] , this linear twisting leads to a family of gaits:
When the twisting is uniform along the whole body, the entire robot rolls like a wheel during sidewinding, which we call rolling sidewinding .
When the twisting varies along the body, different parts of the robot roll at different speeds, which turns the robot, and we call this gait twisting sidewinding .
In twisting sidewinding, the point where the rolling speed is zero acts as the turning center, and it can be placed anywhere along the body.

Since the twisting of the LTS is spread over the entire body, all twist joints share the load.
On our hardware implementation of the T-Snake, we compare the two gaits under similar angular velocities and similar total output power during in-place turning.
Under this fair comparison, the two most-loaded twist joints of the existing rolling vector approach carry 96.8 % 96.8\% of the total power, while those of our LTS carry only 45.1 % 45.1\% (Fig. 1 (b)).
The LTS reduces the peak output power of a single twist joint by 42 % 42\% , leaving a larger margin before a joint motor saturates (Fig. 1 (c)).
Besides, our LTS with evenly distributed workload enables the robot to locomote on various complex terrains.
We compare our LTS against conventional sidewinding without twisting on four types of outdoor terrains, and our LTS moves the robot faster than conventional sidewinding, reducing the traversal time by up to 49 % 49\% for a fixed travel length (Fig. 1 (d)).
Real-robot experiments also validate the translating and turning motions of the proposed gaits.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Works

The large number of redundant DoFs makes it challenging to design gaits for snake robots.
Existing methods for snake robot gait design can be classified into central pattern generators [ 11 , 12 ] , reinforcement learning [ 13 , 14 , 15 ] , parameterized gait equations [ 16 , 17 ] , and the backbone curve methods [ 9 , 18 , 19 ] .
In this paper, we leverage the geometric intuition of the backbone curve method to design and analyze linear twisting sidewinding gaits for the T-Snake.

The proposed gaits are based on the sidewinding locomotion, which is an efficient gait family for snake robots to locomote on complex terrains [ 4 , 20 , 6 , 7 ] .
Sidewinding achieves both translational and turning maneuvers in many ways.
For example, conical sidewinding enables fixed-point turning [ 4 , 21 ] , and sidewinding with the contact length control technique allows navigation on sandy slopes [ 2 ] .
Recent works [ 22 , 23 ] further improved sidewinding motions by adding artificial scales on the snake robots and modulating the spatial frequency of the vertical body wave.

Snake robots that can not only bend but also twist are designed and realized in several ways.
The first class adds the limited twisting capability to snake robots’ inner backbone, using twist joints [ 24 , 25 , 26 ] , cable-driven design [ 27 , 28 ] , and the helical spring backbone [ 29 ] .
The twisting angular range of this class of robots is limited.
Another class adds unlimited torsion to outer layers, such as the ARCSnake [ 30 ] and EELS [ 3 ] .
The inner backbones of this class of snake robots still cannot twist unlimitedly.
Different from these existing snake robots, the T-Snake mechanism considered in this paper can twist its backbone unlimitedly and meets the mechanical requirement of the proposed gaits.

2026-10-22.title: Distance Field Driven Reinforcement Learning for Reactive and Robust Collision Avoidance
2026-10-22.authors: Taiga Ikeshima , Sheila Sutjipto , Lan Wu , Francisco J. Naranjo-Campos , Taiki Ishigaki , Taisuke Kobayashi , Teresa A. Vidal-Calleja , Eiichi Yoshida
2026-10-22.comment: Accepted to 2026 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
2026-10-22.abstract: Robust and reactive collision avoidance remains a central challenge for deploying Reinforcement Learning (RL) policies on real robotic manipulators, particularly when transferring behaviours learned in simulation to the physical world. This paper presents an RL framework that integrates the Euclidean Distance Field (EDF) directly into the observation space, providing the agent with continuous geometric cues that support stable and responsive avoidance behaviours. By leveraging the rich spatial information encoded in the EDF, the method enables a streamlined reward formulation that achieves effective obstacle avoidance both with and without Artificial Potential Field guidance. The proposed approach is validated on a 7‑DoF redundant manipulator, demonstrating zero‑shot transfer from simulation to real hardware. Despite being trained exclusively with randomised static objects, the deployed policy generalizes to previously unseen real environments and exhibits robust online avoidance of dynamic obstacles. These results highlight the potential of EDF‑based representations to mitigate the sim‑to‑real gap and support reliable and real-time collision‑aware behaviour in complex and changing environments.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Generating motions that allow a robot to safely reach a target position while avoiding obstacles remains one of the fundamental challenges in mobile robotics and manipulation. As robots are increasingly deployed in cluttered, dynamic, and unstructured environments, the ability to reactively determine collision‑free actions from real‑time sensory data has become necessary for robust autonomy.
This need for reliable, responsive obstacle avoidance is especially pressing where the robot must continuously resolve its motion when presented with incomplete spatial modelling.

A classical solution to real‑time obstacle avoidance is the Artificial Potential Field (APF) method [ 1 ] , which generates control actions by combining attractive and repulsive potentials. While APF is computationally efficient and reactive, it is known to suffer from local minima and non-reachable goals in the presence of obstacles, restricting its applicability in more complex environments.
Beyond reactive-based strategies like APF, collision avoidance has also been addressed using offline motion planning by sampling-based methods such as Probabilistic Roadmaps (PRM) [ 2 ] and Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRT) [ 3 ] . While these sampling-based approaches can navigate complex spaces, they often incur significant computational overhead and lack the real-time reactivity for operating in dynamic or unmodelled environments.
As an alternative method, optimisation-based motion planning [ 4 ] has been proposed, formulating collision avoidance as a constrained optimisation problem and directly computing a trajectory.

Recent advances in machine learning have introduced alternative strategies for navigating complex environments. Deep networks can encode the structure of the environment for collision‑free trajectory prediction [ 5 ] , while Reinforcement Learning (RL) [ 6 ] has enabled robots to acquire reactive behaviours directly through interaction with their simulated environment. Hybrid frameworks seek to leverage the benefits of combining traditional methods and RL. For instance, Schneider et al. [ 7 ] integrated guidance from APFs into deep RL to mitigate the local‑minima issue inherent in classical potential fields. However, their method relies on the assumption that accurate spatial information regarding obstacle location and geometry is readily available. Xu et al. [ 8 ] proposed a hybrid architecture in which a deep RL policy produces avoidance actions that guide an APF planner online, enabling real‑time motion generation in cluttered scenes. They further extend the potential‑field formulation to account for link‑level proximity for full‑body collision avoidance. Li et al. [ 9 ] similarly combine RL with APF by learning situation‑dependent scaling factors that modulate the magnitude of the field, improving robustness in cases where standard APF formulations struggle. These works highlight the appeal of APF‑RL combinations: APFs provide structure and computational efficiency, while RL introduces adaptivity and reduces the need for manual tuning.

In practice, obtaining precise and consistent environmental information is nontrivial and remains a primary source of the sim-to-real gap for RL-based methods, as sensing and modelling can introduce noise and uncertainty that simulations fail to capture.
Policies trained entirely in simulation may behave unpredictably when deployed if real‑world perception deviates from the training assumptions. So far, depth camera images and point clouds from LiDAR have shown a relatively small sim-to-real gap, but ad-hoc tricks are still needed to bridge the gap. Although domain randomisation [ 10 ] helps by exposing the policy to varied conditions during training, reliable scene understanding remains essential for robust deployment.

To minimise these perceptual discrepancies, Euclidean Distance Fields (EDFs) have the potential to provide a robust representation for bridging the reality gap in reactive motion planning.
Unlike raw point clouds, which are susceptible to sensor noise, or traditional geometric modelling of the environment, which often results in conservative behaviour, an EDF provides a dense spatial signal representing the distance to the nearest obstacle at any given point in the workspace. For example, Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) have been utilized for manipulator collision avoidance [ 11 , 12 ] . Despite its potential usefulness for learning, to the best of our knowledge, the distance field representations have not been well exploited with RL.

An advantage of the distance field is its ability to be generated in real-time [ 13 ] . By training RL policies on EDF-informed observations, an agent can learn to navigate based on the underlying spatial structure of the environment rather than specific pixel-level features or predefined location information. In this work, we propose to exploit EDFs with RL to reduce the sim-to-real gap, as the distance gradients provided by an EDF in the real world can be mapped consistently to the idealised fields encountered during training, ensuring more predictable and robust behaviour on real hardware. Fig. 1 illustrates an example experiment for real-time collision avoidance using RL with EDF, trained in simulation and transferred to the real robot.

The contributions of this paper are then as follows:

A novel RL framework that incorporates real-time Euclidean Distance Field measurements directly into the observation space, enabling the policy to learn reactive and robust collision‑avoidance behaviours

A streamlined reward mechanism that achieves obstacle avoidance with and without APF guidance for the RL method.

Zero‑shot transfer from simulation to a 7-DoF redundant manipulator, where the deployed policy generalizes to real scenes and exhibits online avoidance of previously unseen dynamic obstacles, despite being trained only with static objects in simulation.
