# II Related work

## II-A Robot foundation models for manipulation

Modern manipulation policies are increasingly built on large
pretrained robot foundation models that map observations and language
instructions to actions [ 19 , 4 , 2 , 3 , 1 , 20 , 21 ] .
RT-1 and RT-2 [ 19 , 4 ] ,
OpenVLA [ 2 ] , and Octo [ 3 ] established this recipe for broad instruction-conditioned
manipulation, while recent generalist and humanoid systems extend it
across embodiments and physical settings [ 20 , 21 ] .
Progress has also come from more capable action interfaces, including
flow-matching action experts over continuous action
chunks [ 1 , 14 , 22 , 23 ] ,
and efficient action tokenization [ 24 , 25 ] .
In parallel, models that couple action generation with future visual
state prediction use video-generation priors to improve robustness to
unfamiliar skills and embodiments [ 5 , 6 , 26 , 27 , 28 , 29 , 30 , 31 ] .
These advances rely on increasingly large cross-embodiment datasets
for robot learning [ 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 ] .
Yet deployed policies remain bounded by training-distribution
coverage: small errors compound into out-of-distribution states, and
precision-critical subtasks can resist improvement even after many
additional teleoperation episodes [ 9 , 7 ] .
This limitation motivates post-training procedures that refine
pretrained policies through interaction with the deployment
environment.

## II-B Human-in-the-loop post-training

Human-in-the-loop learning extends imitation learning by allowing a
human to intervene on states visited by the current policy, directly
addressing covariate shift and compounding
errors [ 8 , 36 , 10 ] .
Subsequent systems improve when interventions are triggered, how mixed
demonstration and intervention data are weighted, what corrective data
are collected, or how disruptive takeover
is [ 11 , 13 , 37 , 9 , 38 , 39 , 40 , 41 , 42 , 43 , 44 ] .
Related methods extract different learning signals from interventions:
RLIF treats intervention signals as rewards for off-policy reinforcement
learning, MILE models the intervention process and uses both intervention
and non-intervention feedback, and Sirius reweights deployment data with
approximated human trust for weighted behavioral
cloning [ 45 , 46 , 13 ] .
Many interactive imitation-learning systems still update models in batches.
RoboCopilot [ 12 ] moves toward continual
fine-tuning within an interactive collection loop, but its workflow
remains round-based and the deployed policy still comes from batched
retraining.
RECAP [ 14 ] scales full-model HIL improvement with
advantage conditioning over demonstrations, rollouts, and corrections,
but it still operates through phase-based offline updates and leaves a
fully concurrent online framework as future work.

Recent systems move policy improvement closer to deployment, but each
keeps only part of the desired closed loop. RL
Token [ 15 ] performs online learning on top of a frozen
pretrained policy by training a lightweight actor-critic rather than
updating the full backbone. Value-based routes must estimate action
quality from sparse outcome feedback [ 15 , 47 , 48 , 49 ] ,
which is difficult for high-dimensional action chunks in real robots.
Hi-ORS [ 18 ] avoids a learned critic through outcome-based rejection sampling and
supervised updates, but still relies on trajectory-level outcome
supervision; ConRFT [ 50 ] instead retains a Q-function
and gates its online consistency-policy fine-tuning with human
interventions. RoboPocket [ 17 ] accelerates policy
iteration by visualizing predicted policy trajectories in AR and
collecting human corrections without executing those predictions on
the physical robot.

TIDE targets a complementary setting in which real-robot deployment
remains in the data loop, the video backbone, cross-modal adapter, and
action expert are jointly updated, and supervision is organized by
action-source provenance rather than learned values or trajectory-level
reward labels.

2026-10-22.title: DepState-JEPA: Learning Depth-Grounded State Representation for Visual Perception and Manipulation
2026-10-22.authors: Xiujian Liang , Liuyuan Na , Zehao Du , Jiacheng Xu , Weixi Song , Mingyang Sun , Xingjun Ma , Cewu Lu , Jianhua Sun
2026-10-22.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-22.abstract:
Predictive representations for robot manipulation should connect scene geometry with the state changes induced by actions. Our intuition is that understanding what an action will change starts with understanding where things are: complementary RGB and depth observations ground a common scene representation from which to infer those changes. Guided by this intuition, we introduce DepState-JEPA , a dual-stream RGB–Depth joint-embedding predictive architecture that connects spatial understanding with action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, DepState .
Built on V-JEPA 2.1, the framework uses depth both as a complementary observation stream and to ground both modalities in metric 3D space, aggregating shared information into DepState while retaining modality-private features for decoding.
Ray-conditioned readouts predict local features without target depth; after an action-conditioned transition, the same decoders predict future RGB and depth features using the predicted state and fixed initial private features.
Robot-state readouts provide recursive proprioceptive inputs; object-trajectory supervision and calibrated forward kinematics shape state learning through motion targets and joint–TCP consistency.
Comparisons show stronger RGB-encoder transfer after RGB-D adaptation, feature completion, conditioned visual forecasting, and manipulation success. Within-model ablations identify contributions from depth content, metric coordinates, and future-state matching, with additional control gains from FK regularization.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Learning visual world models enables anticipation of action outcomes ( Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Maes et al., 2026 ) .
For manipulation in real-world space, this requires relating the current spatial arrangement to
the changes an action may cause. Consider a robot reaching for a cup:
RGB reveals its appearance and context, while depth locates the cup and
gripper relative to the table in three-dimensional space. Anticipating the reach then requires
reasoning about how this arrangement will change, not merely recognizing
the cup. This raises a broader question: how can the geometry revealed by depth inform a robot’s predictions of how its actions will change the scene?

RGB JEPAs predict representations rather than pixels ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ) :
V-JEPA 2 supports action-conditioned planning ( Assran et al., 2025 ) ,
while V-JEPA 2.1 strengthens dense visual features ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) . Depth-related JEPAs offer complementary designs. LeMuMo-JEPA combines RGB
and aligned depth features within a common Transformer for multimodal
perception ( Cornelissen et al., 2026 ) .
Locate 3D’s 3D-JEPA predicts masked point-cloud features enriched by lifted
2D features, rather than maintaining separate RGB–depth streams ( Arnaud et al., 2025 ) ; JEPADepth predicts depth from RGB with auxiliary
latent supervision, rather than encoding measured depth ( Grigore & Popa, 2026 ) .
These designs target multimodal perception or geometric estimation, but do not establish a common state interface between spatial understanding and action-driven evolution. This motivates our work:

Can complementary observations ground a spatially queryable, temporally predictive shared state representation while retaining modality-private features in separate decoding paths?

To answer this question, we introduce DepState-JEPA (Fig. 1 ),
a joint-embedding predictive architecture centered on DepState ,
a depth-grounded shared latent state connecting RGB–depth observations,
spatial readout, and action-conditioned transition. Built on V-JEPA 2.1, an independent
Depth-Video branch provides complementary observations and metric
grounding for both streams. DepState aggregates shared information,
while private paths preserve modality-specific detail for decoding
rather than forming separate evolving states. This common interface
supports reading missing spatial content and forecasting representations
after robot actions.
Representation learning uses images and video; robot prediction
initializes DepState from a single RGB-D frame and evolves it under
actions and proprioception, without accessing future RGB-D images.

Specifically, visible metric depth and camera intrinsics place both streams in metric 3D
coordinates; shared–private projections and learned aggregation form
a compact, geometrically grounded DepState. Ray-conditioned readouts
query local shared features without target depth; private features
supply modality-specific decoding detail. After action-conditioned transitions,
the same decoders predict future RGB and depth features with fixed
initial private memory. Robot-state readouts supply recursive proprioception;
object-motion supervision shapes the state. Calibrated forward kinematics
couples independent joint and end-effector predictions, propagating
consistency gradients into the transition alongside direct physical supervision.

Training proceeds in two stages: 1) RGB-D adaptation learns
DepState from images and video clips via masked shared-feature completion
and dense modality-feature prediction, exploiting spatial and temporal
context. 2) Robot post-training learns
action-conditioned transitions and physical readouts using future-state
and feature targets, physical supervision, and kinematic regularization,
while RGB-D replay retains the adaptation objectives. Evaluation
(Sec. 4 ) spans
spatial understanding, multi-step forecasting, and manipulation, with
controlled ablations testing the roles of geometry, feature sharing,
and kinematic consistency.
Our contributions are threefold:

Dual-stream RGB–Depth Video JEPA framework. We introduce DepState-JEPA , which connects spatial understanding and action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, DepState . Independent RGB and depth encoders capture complementary observations, while metric depth grounds both streams in a common 3D coordinate frame.

Dual-stream RGB–Depth Video JEPA framework. We introduce DepState-JEPA , which connects spatial understanding and action-conditioned prediction through a shared latent state, DepState . Independent RGB and depth encoders capture complementary observations, while metric depth grounds both streams in a common 3D coordinate frame.

Unified DepState construction and prediction pipeline. We aggregate shared RGB–depth features into DepState, retaining private features for modality-specific decoding. Ray-conditioned readouts predict missing features without target depth and are reused after action-conditioned transitions to predict future features, with initial private memory fixed throughout rollout. Robot-state readouts supply recursive proprioception; object-trajectory supervision and joint–TCP consistency provide complementary training signals for state evolution.

Empirical gains and controlled component analysis. RGB-D adaptation improves RGB-encoder transfer; the full pipeline supports feature prediction and manipulation. Within-model ablations identify contributions from depth and metric coordinates, private decoding for visual accuracy, and future-state matching for control performance.

Independent RGB and depth encoders capture complementary observations, while metric depth grounds both streams in a common 3D coordinate frame.

# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures

Joint-embedding predictive learning uses target representations, rather than
pixels, as the objects of prediction. I-JEPA learns image representations by
predicting masked regions from visible context ( Assran et al., 2023 ) , while
V-JEPA extends this approach to spatiotemporal video features ( Bardes et al., 2024 ) . V-JEPA 2 scales video pretraining and connects learned
features to robot prediction and planning ( Assran et al., 2025 ) .
V-JEPA 2.1 further develops dense and multi-level supervision, strengthening
the spatial detail retained by video representations ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) . A complementary direction changes the unit of
prediction: Causal-JEPA masks object-level latents and infers them from
surrounding context to encourage interaction-dependent prediction ( Nam et al., 2026 ) . These approaches illustrate how prediction targets
and representation structure shape what a model learns. DepState-JEPA
extends the RGB-centric video JEPA framework along the modality axis,
introducing an independent Depth-Video stream. We retain V-JEPA 2.1’s dense
feature-learning design while making measured geometry an explicit input
to shared-state construction, complementing spatial cues learned from RGB.

## 2.2 Depth and 3D Representation Learning for JEPAs

Depth-related JEPAs differ in whether depth is predicted, used for
supervision, or encoded as geometric input.
JEPADepth combines masked latent prediction with photometric supervision
for monocular depth estimation ( Grigore & Popa, 2026 ) .
Depth-Regularized JEPA aligns RGB features with depth features during
training while retaining RGB-only inference ( Khan, 2026 ) .
Le MuMo JEPA fuses RGB and camera-aligned LiDAR depth through learnable
fusion tokens within a shared Transformer ( Cornelissen et al., 2026 ) .
3D-JEPA in Locate 3D learns masked point-cloud representations from
RGB-D-derived geometry enriched with lifted 2D foundation-model features ( Arnaud et al., 2025 ) .
SR-JEPA predicts missing-entity features in native 3D scenes at supplied
target locations ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) .
DepState-JEPA jointly encodes RGB and measured depth in independent video
streams, using visible metric depth to ground both streams in camera
coordinates. Shared–private factorization retains modality-specific
features alongside the shared state, whereas ray-conditioned readout
predicts missing content without target depth or a supplied 3D location.
The same state evolves under actions to predict future RGB-D features,
connecting geometric representation learning with spatial completion and
temporal prediction through a common interface.

## 2.3 Action-Conditioned World Models for Robotics

Latent world models support robot control by predicting how representations
change under actions. DINO-WM learns transitions over frozen DINOv2 patch
features and optimizes action sequences toward visual goals ( Zhou et al., 2024 ) ; PLDM studies JEPA-based planning from reward-free
offline trajectories ( Sobal et al., 2025 ) . V-JEPA 2 adapts pretrained video
features through action-conditioned robot post-training ( Assran et al., 2025 ) , whereas LeWorldModel jointly learns its encoder
and dynamics from pixels with a distributional regularizer ( Maes et al., 2026 ) . A related question is how physical information
should shape the representation. MCR uses proprioceptive state–action
alignment for robot representation learning ( Jiang et al., 2024 ) ;
PSG-JEPA grounds individual states and state pairs in physical quantities ( Yan et al., 2026 ) , and physically grounded JEPA combines inverse dynamics
with state alignment ( Liu et al., 2026b ) .
DepState-JEPA studies consistency among predicted physical quantities in
addition to their direct supervision. Calibrated forward kinematics
couples independent joint and end-effector readouts of the predicted state;
object motion is supervised through increment-based pose trajectories.
The kinematic constraint regularizes the depth-grounded state transition without
imposing hard guarantees of physically correct dynamics.

Concurrent work. Closely related recent preprints advance geometric
supervision and spatial prediction ( Khan, 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) ,
including geometry-conditioned video modeling ( Kim et al., 2026 ; DreamX Team et al., 2026 ) ; physical state grounding and
physics-conditioned latent dynamics ( Yan et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Liu et al., 2026b ) ;
and joint world modeling and action generation ( Lin et al., 2026 ) .
These directions complement our use of an explicit depth stream,
depth-lifted positions, and selectively shared RGB-D features for spatial,
temporal, and robot prediction.

2026-10-22.title: NavBind: Diagnosing Instruction-Action Binding at Route Forks in Navigation VLAs
2026-10-22.authors: Josh Qixuan Sun , Xiaoying Xing , Yurun Chen , Huaiyuan Weng , Wentao Zhu , Mark Crowley
2026-10-22.abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) navigation models translate visual observations and instructions into actions.
Navigation success assesses whether an agent reaches the goal.
However, reaching the goal successfully does not establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions or relies on visual cues or navigation history.
We introduce NavBind to diagnose instruction-action binding: whether changing the instruction influences the probabilistic distribution of the actions, with the navigation context fixed.
We construct 3,252 route-fork contexts by recombining route-aligned instruction segments from R2R-CE and RxR-CE.
Each context pairs full instructions that share the description of the route already traveled but specify different branches.
Both are evaluated under the same agent state and navigation history.
We compare generated local action sequences, the likelihoods of fixed reference action sequences under both instructions, and changes in visual attention and attribution.
Across the evaluated models, higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.
2026-10-22.introduction:
In vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) ( Krantz et al., 2020 ) , vision-language-action (VLA) models ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) map visual observations and instructions to actions.
Success rate measures whether an agent reaches the goal but does not establish whether it follows the instruction.
Route-fidelity metrics ( Jain et al., 2019 ) assess the similarity between the generated trajectory and the ground-truth trajectory, providing an indirect measure of instruction following.
However, these metrics still cannot establish whether the model genuinely follows the instructions , as it may instead rely on visual cues or navigation history alone.

Language interventions, i.e., changing the language instruction and observing how the local actions or navigation performance change, provide a more direct test of language dependence.
NavTrust ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) and Contrast Sets ( Anwar et al., 2025 ) rephrase instructions and assess changes in navigation performance.
However, these tests keep the intended navigation behaviour unchanged.
R2RIE-CE ( Taioli et al., 2024 ) modifies instructions by injecting direction, object, and room errors.
However, it neither ensures that the modified instructions describe feasible routes nor provides reference actions corresponding to them.
Without matching reference trajectories for the modified instructions, a behavioural change alone does not show that the model followed them.
We therefore ask not merely whether the model’s behaviour changes, but whether changing the instruction to describe another feasible route makes the model more likely to choose the corresponding actions .
We keep the agent’s state, navigation history, and completed instruction prefix fixed.
In Figure 1 , both turning left and continuing up the stairs are feasible, and the remaining instruction specifies which branch to take.
We use instruction-action binding to describe the requirement that the model assigns higher probability to the actions required by the instruction.

We introduce NavBind , a controlled diagnostic built through cross-route
recombination of route-instruction examples drawn from R2R-CE and RxR-CE.
Using fine-grained route-language alignments, we retain one example’s
completed instruction prefix and combine it with either its original suffix
or a compatible suffix from another route.
The resulting full-instruction pairs specify different executable
branches under the same replayed history and agent state, yielding
3,252 contexts with reference action sequences for both branches.

Within each fixed context, we first ask: does changing the instruction
change the action sequence the model generates?
We then ask: does the model assign higher probability to the actions
for a branch when instructed to take that branch rather than the other?
We test this by comparing the likelihood of each reference action
sequence under the two instructions.
This comparison can reveal changes in action preference even when the
generated sequence stays the same.
Finally, we examine the visual response: do attention heatmaps and
gradient-based attribution heatmaps highlight different image regions
under the two instructions?

We evaluate four navigation VLAs on NavBind : Uni-NaVid ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , StreamVLN ( Wei et al., 2025 ) , JanusVLN ( Zeng et al., 2026 ) , and FutureNav ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) .
We find that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions.
(Table 1 ).
It also shows that models respond more strongly when the instructions
contrast opposite turns than when they contrast forward movement with a turn.

Our contributions are:

We construct NavBind by recombining instruction segments
across routes into full instructions for two feasible branches.
Each pair preserves the agent state, history, and
completed instruction prefix, and provides reference action
sequences for both branches.

We diagnose instruction-action binding using generated
sequences to measure output changes, fixed-target likelihoods
to assess preferences for the instructed actions, and attention
and gradient-based attribution heatmaps to track spatial changes.

We show that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. This supports evaluating how
language affects local decisions alongside navigation success.

1. We construct NavBind by recombining instruction segments
across routes into full instructions for two feasible branches.
Each pair preserves the agent state, history, and
completed instruction prefix, and provides reference action
sequences for both branches.

2. We diagnose instruction-action binding using generated
sequences to measure output changes, fixed-target likelihoods
to assess preferences for the instructed actions, and attention
and gradient-based attribution heatmaps to track spatial changes.

3. We show that higher reported navigation success does not imply that the model more faithfully follows the instructions. This supports evaluating how
language affects local decisions alongside navigation success.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Language Diagnostics in VLN

Goal completion can obscure whether an agent followed the described route.
Stay on the Path introduced CLS and longer R4R routes ( Jain et al., 2019 ) , while LAW extended language-aligned supervision
and evaluation to VLN-CE ( Raychaudhuri et al., 2021 ) .
Modality ablations further showed that R2R agents could rely strongly on graph
structure ( Hu et al., 2019 ) . These works motivate
language-specific evaluation through task metrics, supervision, and modality
ablations.

Early diagnostics mask object, direction, and numerical cues ( Zhu et al., 2022 ) and swap directional tokens ( Hahn et al., 2023 ) .
Skill-focused evaluations append atomic instructions to truncated RxR
episodes ( Yang et al., 2023 ) and construct human-refined atomic
instructions, including same-start left/right pairs ( Wang et al., 2024 ) .
These studies evaluate agents on discrete navigation graphs and
their action tests cannot be directly applied to navigation VLAs
that execute low-level actions.

In VLN-CE, NavTrust evaluates whether agents maintain navigation performance
under instruction corruption and stylistic variation ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) .
Contrast Sets tests instruction rephrasing with unchanged navigation
goals on a physical robot ( Anwar et al., 2025 ) .
However, these tests keep the intended navigation behaviour unchanged.
R2RIE-CE injects direction, object, and room errors into
instructions to study error detection and localization ( Taioli et al., 2024 ) .
The modified instructions are not paired with matching reference
trajectories.
However, it neither ensures that the modified instructions describe feasible routes nor provides reference actions corresponding to them.
Without matching reference trajectories for the modified instructions, a behavioural change alone does not show that the model followed them.
CAST pairs generated alternative instructions with short action
branches for counterfactual training ( Glossop et al., 2026 ) , but the intended action behaviour only include a short horizon rather than a long horizon.

NavBind constructs full-instruction pairs for long-horizon navigation
by recombining original route-aligned instruction spans across source
routes.
The pairs specify different executable branches under the same
agent state, navigation history, and completed instruction prefix.
Scoring both reference action sequences under both instructions tests
whether the model’s local action preferences shift toward the
instructed branch.

## 2.2 Language-Action Coupling in VLAs

Recent work examines whether language and other multimodal signals influence
VLA action generation. VLA-Trace connects representation similarity,
attention-path knockouts, and rollout-level behavioural probes ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , while Häon et al. (2025) identify semantic
activation directions and intervene on them to steer actions. Zhang et al. (2026b) diagnose linguistic blindness in manipulation VLAs using
contradictory instructions and recalibrate attention at inference time, while Zhan et al. (2026) study robustness to linguistic perturbations and
strengthen language guidance through residual steering. These studies
establish that language and internal pathways can affect VLA actions, but their
evaluations center on manipulation and often combine diagnosis with model
modification. NavBind tests instruction-action binding in frozen navigation
VLAs: two valid route instructions share the same history but specify different
executable branches. We align behaviour with fixed-target likelihood and
visual attribution.

2026-10-22.title: SMR: Learning streaming motion retargeting for humanoids from human semantic
2026-10-22.authors: Chun Gu , Juntong Zhang , Jingyu Li , Li Zhang
2026-10-22.abstract:
Retargeting human motion to humanoids requires preserving motion semantics
while accounting for the robot’s physical constraints. Kinematic pipelines
prescribe a robot trajectory through geometric matching, without establishing
whether it can be executed under the robot’s dynamics. Prior physics-supervised
neural methods train bidirectional full-sequence models on physics-refined
kinematic trajectories, remaining tied to prescribed kinematic solutions and
requiring noncausal context. We propose SMR, a streaming neural motion
retargeter learned from semantic-conditioned physics experts. We convert human
motion into robot-aware task-space targets for body landmark positions,
orientations, and velocities. Physics experts track these targets directly in
simulation under contact, dynamics, and actuator constraints. We train a single
strictly causal Transformer on their executed state trajectories that complete
the motion and pass semantic and physical validity checks. At each incoming
frame, the student uses only current and past human observations to generate a
robot motion reference for a downstream whole-body controller. Experiments
demonstrate that semantic-conditioned
physics experts generate motion with higher semantic fidelity and physical
validity than direct optimization-based retargeting, while the resulting
streaming retargeter achieves improved closed-loop performance over kinematic
and physics-refined baselines under a common whole-body controller.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Large-scale human motion datasets such as AMASS, LAFAN1, and BONES-SEED provide
a rich source of whole-body motion for humanoid learning and control ( Mahmood et al., 2019 ; Harvey et al., 2020 ; Bones Studio, 2026 ) . Transferring these
motions to robots requires more than geometric matching because humans and
robots differ in morphology, joint structure, mass distribution, contact
mechanics, and actuation. For streaming applications such as live teleoperation,
retargeting must satisfy two requirements: preserving human motion semantics
in physically executable robot references, and generating those references from
current and past human observations.

The first requirement depends on how robot motion is generated for supervision.
Kinematic retargeting pipelines use inverse kinematics or geometric optimization
to construct robot trajectories ( Penco et al., 2018 ; Darvish et al., 2019 ; Araujo et al., 2025 ) . Although these methods
can incorporate contact and collision constraints, geometric agreement alone
does not establish dynamic executability. Using the resulting trajectories as
neural supervision can tie the learned mapping to solutions selected by the
kinematic solver. Physics-supervised methods such as NMR ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) refine these trajectories through simulated tracking, but still use the
prescribed kinematic motion as the expert’s tracking target. This motivates
specifying the motion to preserve directly through robot-aware task-space
semantics and using the resulting physical execution to generate robot
supervision.

The second requirement is causal inference from a live human stream.
NMR’s learned retargeter ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) uses bidirectional modeling over a
complete motion sequence and therefore depends on future observations. This
prevents use in a streaming setting where the reference at time t t must
be generated from observations available up to t t . The challenge is therefore
to retain the benefits of physics-based supervision while learning a causal
retargeter.

To address these challenges, we propose SMR, a streaming neural motion
retargeter learned from semantic-conditioned physics experts. We represent
human motion as robot-aware task-space targets for body landmark positions,
orientations, and velocities. The experts track these targets directly in
closed-loop simulation, using robot state and limited future semantic context
to generate motion under contact, dynamics, and actuator constraints. IK is
used only for initialization, rather than to prescribe a tracking trajectory.
We retain executed state rollouts that complete the motion and pass semantic
and physical validity checks, and use them to train a single strictly causal
Transformer. At each incoming frame, the student generates a robot motion
reference for a downstream whole-body controller using only current and past
human observations. As summarized in Table 1 ,
SMR is the only compared method combining dynamics-grounded supervision with
real-time teleoperation.

Experiments show that semantic-conditioned physics experts generate motion
with higher semantic fidelity and physical validity than direct
optimization-based retargeting. Under the same frozen whole-body controller,
SMR achieves improved closed-loop performance over kinematic and physics-refined
baselines. We further demonstrate whole-body motion execution on a physical
Unitree G1 using SMR-generated references.

Our contributions are threefold: (1) we formulate physics-based retargeting around robot-aware human semantics, allowing experts to determine the robot trajectory instead of refining a prescribed kinematic solution; (2) we distill privileged expert rollouts into a single causal retargeter that generates streaming motion references from human observations, without robot-state inputs or future frames; and (3) we demonstrate improved closed-loop performance over kinematic and physics-refined baselines under a common frozen controller, alongside whole-body motion demonstrations on a physical Unitree G1.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related work

## 2.1 Optimization-based motion retargeting

Early motion retargeting methods transferred motion between articulated
characters through constrained optimization ( Gleicher, 1998 ; Popović and Witkin, 1999 ; Tak and Ko, 2005 ) .
For humanoids, geometric methods use Cartesian objectives to accommodate
differences in morphology and joint structure ( Penco et al., 2018 ; Darvish et al., 2019 ) . Later approaches improve morphology
adaptation and geometric matching ( Araujo et al., 2025 ) , incorporate physical
constraints into data generation ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , and preserve human–object
or human–environment interactions ( Yang et al., 2025 ) . UMR further
uses learned surface correspondences to guide constrained pose matching and
contact transfer ( Cao et al., 2026 ) . Dynamics-aware methods incorporate force
equilibrium ( Rouxel et al., 2022 ) , optimal control ( Grandia et al., 2023 ) , or kinodynamic trajectory optimization ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Dhedin et al., 2026 ) . Direct Dynamic
Retargeting uses sampling-based model predictive control to optimize task-space
imitation directly in simulation, without an intermediate kinematic trajectory ( Roux et al., 2026 ) . These methods generate robot motion by optimizing input
poses or trajectories. SMR instead learns from accepted physics-expert rollouts
and generates streaming references with a causal neural model, without solving
a retargeting optimization problem at deployment.

## 2.2 Learning-based and physics-supervised retargeting

Learning-based retargeters learn cross-skeleton mappings through shared latent
spaces, skeleton-aware architectures, and paired or unpaired motion
translation ( Villegas et al., 2018 ; Aberman et al., 2020 ; Lee et al., 2023 ; Choi et al., 2020 ; Yan et al., 2023 ) . Online upper-body retargeting has
also been demonstrated using unpaired adversarial learning ( Yagi et al., 2024 ) . Physics enters these models through feasibility
constraints in Human2Humanoid ( Huang et al., 2026 ) and simulated
tracking feedback in IKMR ( Chen et al., 2025a ) . ReActor jointly adapts reference
motions and trains a tracking policy through bilevel optimization ( Müller et al., 2026 ) , while OmniTrack uses privileged simulation rollouts
to generate references for training a downstream tracking policy ( Li et al., 2026 ) . NMR is most closely related to our approach: it trains
clustered RL experts to track GMR-generated trajectories and uses their rollouts
to supervise a full-sequence neural retargeter ( Zhao et al., 2026 ) . In SMR,
experts directly track robot-aware human semantics, with IK used only for
initialization. Accepted state rollouts then supervise a human-only, strictly
causal motion-reference generator.

## 2.3 Physics-based motion tracking

Physics-based motion tracking studies how robots and simulated characters
execute reference motions under dynamics and contact constraints. DeepMimic
and PHC address this problem through reinforcement learning in simulation ( Peng et al., 2018 ; Luo et al., 2023 ) . Subsequent humanoid systems improve
sim-to-real transfer ( He et al., 2025 ) and motion diversity ( Liao et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2025b ; Han et al., 2025 ) , introduce online
dynamics adaptation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) , and scale motion tracking
through larger datasets and models ( Luo et al., 2026 ; Qi et al., 2026 ) .
MimicLite focuses on efficient training of general motion-tracking policies ( Robotparty Lab, 2026 ) . These approaches use robot-state feedback
to produce control actions, whereas SMR generates motion references from human
observations. We evaluate these references with a frozen whole-body controller
to isolate the effect of retargeting on downstream execution.

2026-10-22.title: How Representational Priors Shape Generalization in World Action Models
2026-10-22.authors: Junha Chun , Youngjoon Jeong , Taesup Kim
2026-10-22.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-22.abstract:
World action models (WAMs) are shown to substantially diverge under generalization performance based on their generative backbones.
We investigate this gap through the representational geometry that WAMs inherit from their backbones and how policy training reorganizes it.
Our central hypothesis is that a useful representational prior would structure geometry that separates nuisance information from the in-distribution manifold in advance of training as a policy.
We quantify this with nuisance orthogonality ; orthogonality of the feature under visual variation outside the empirical in-distribution manifold.
Across various image and video backbones, we show that a higher orthogonality from the representational prior is associated with stronger robustness to visual variations after WAM training, enabling policy generalization measurable prospectively for world models.
In addition, analyzing the resulting robust WAMs reveals nuisance suppression ; relative suppression of feature displacement caused by such variations and robust action generation of the policy.
Together, these findings provide a geometric perspective on how the representational prior of the world model shapes the generalization performance of WAMs.
2026-10-22.introduction:
World action models (WAMs) have recently become a major paradigm for a robotic foundation model ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Pai et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2026 ) .
They inherit the representations and rich spatiotemporal knowledge from generative backbones with scalable pretraining, predict the future with world modeling objective, and generate actions from the features from the reasoning process.
It has been shown that they improve generalization to out-of-distribution scenes by predicting how the world changes.

However, recent researches question whether the capabilities of WAMs come from explicit test-time prediction or enriched representations from the world modeling, and whether video prediction is a good representational prior or objective for world modeling.
FastWAM finds that representational gains from world modeling, rather than explicit future generation at test time, is the main contributor of WAM’s performance ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) .
Furthermore, ImageWAM shows image editors as backbones led to significant improvements to the policy generalization from edit-aware representation which contain task-relevant visual changes and is evidenced by attention maps ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) . We therefore ask:

Which geometric structure makes a backbone’s representational prior useful for WAM generalization, and how does policy adaptation transform that structure?

Understanding this question is necessary to explain why some inherited representations support stronger generalization. Inspired by the baseline WAMs and fundamental questions about their representations and performances, we start by analyzing the representational geometry of in- and out-of-distribution observations.

Throughout the paper, we introduce nuisance orthogonality , which characterized the geometric separation between feature displacement from visual variations and the empirical in-distribution manifold.
High nuisance orthogonality therefore measures a potential for disentangled representational prior which presents in the generative backbones before policy training.
We show that nuisance orthogonality is highly related to the generalization performance of WAMs, across visual variations and models, allowing prospective diagnostics of world models.
Furthermore, we present nuisance suppression after policy training, a suppressing behavior of residual displacement so that the policy can remove nuisance information, improve scene retrieval, and enable robust action generation.

Our contributions are as follows:

A geometric characterization of representational priors: Nuisance orthogonality, the fraction of feature displacement orthogonal to the empirical span of in-distribution data, quantifying whether a backbone separates action preserving visual changes from directions that distinguish clean scenes.

An evidence from nuisance orthogonality to policy robustness: Across world model comparisons, higher nuisance orthogonality is associated with stronger downstream visual robustness motivating a diagnostic for assessing world model backbones before WAM policy training.

An analysis on how representations reshape after policy adaptation: We introduce nuisance suppression to measure how representation space change after adaptation, showing that more robust policy exhibits stronger and more consistent nuisance suppression.

1. A geometric characterization of representational priors: Nuisance orthogonality, the fraction of feature displacement orthogonal to the empirical span of in-distribution data, quantifying whether a backbone separates action preserving visual changes from directions that distinguish clean scenes.

2. An evidence from nuisance orthogonality to policy robustness: Across world model comparisons, higher nuisance orthogonality is associated with stronger downstream visual robustness motivating a diagnostic for assessing world model backbones before WAM policy training.

3. An analysis on how representations reshape after policy adaptation: We introduce nuisance suppression to measure how representation space change after adaptation, showing that more robust policy exhibits stronger and more consistent nuisance suppression.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

World action models (WAMs) are emerging as a major paradigm for robot foundation models by action generation with predictive modeling of future visual observations ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Pai et al., 2025 ; NVIDIA et al., 2026 ) .
Their appeal lies in transferring spatiotemporal priors from generative pretraining to robotics control, while future prediction provides supervision linking actions to their visual consequences.
Empirical studies report improved data efficiency and generalization to unseen objects, tasks, and environments, with strong robustness under visual perturbations ( Zhang et al., 2026c ) .
Beyond direct policy execution, predictive world modeling can help test-time planning by evaluating the consequences of candidate actions ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) .

Recent work further shows that video prediction co-training is necessary to improve world representation, but explicit test-time generation contributes only to trivial improvements of downstream tasks ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) .
In addition, some offer an alternative to video generation backbones showing that pretrained image editing representations are helpful for visual generalization ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Labs, 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) .
These researches motivate examining the representational priors of generative backbones and their underlying generalization performance.
Our study investigates which geometric properties inherited from visual pretraining are related with robustness and how they reshape after policy adaptation.

Nuisance invariance and disentanglement provide a foundation for separating task information from irrelevant variation ( Achille and Soatto, 2018 ) , although unsupervised disentanglement is not identifiable without inductive biases or supervision ( Locatello et al., 2019 ) .
Related objectives remove nuisance factors adversarially ( Ganin et al., 2016 ) , separate shared from domain-specific features, or encourage orthogonality between task and nuisance representations ( Bousmalis et al., 2016 ; Sarhan et al., 2020 ) , with applications in domain adaptation and fair representation learning.

In robot manipulation, prior work has decomposed generalization failures into factors of variation and studied which properties of pretrained visual representations predict robustness to distribution shift ( Xie et al., 2023 ; Burns et al., 2023 ) .
In visual reinforcement learning, similar ideas enable transfer across visual domains and robustness to task-irrelevant distractors ( Higgins et al., 2018 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) .
More recent work disentangles nuisance factors through explicit or implicit separation in latent action pretraining ( Bu et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Jeong et al., 2026 ; Dai et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026a ) .
Our diagnostic instead measures nuisance separation in pretrained representations and relates it empirically to policy robustness.

2026-10-22.title: SimPT: An Automated Simulation Framework for Intervention-Based VLA Post-Training
2026-10-22.authors: Caicheng Wang , Zipeng Ye , Zhexuan Zhou , Zilong Huang , Xi Zhang , Yuchen Xie
2026-10-22.abstract:
Human-in-the-loop (HIL) post-training improves vision–language–action
(VLA) policies through expert corrections, but costly human supervision
and repeated real-robot evaluation limit algorithm exploration and
development. We introduce SimPT (Simulation-based Post-Training), a
simulation framework that automates intervention-based VLA post-training
by integrating policy rollouts, corrective data collection, policy
training, and standalone evaluation. To automatically determine
intervention timing and recovery strategies, we develop an Agent-Compiled
Progress Graph that tracks task progress using privileged simulator state
and retains stable snapshots during policy execution. After a rollout
fails, a CuRobo-based expert attempts recovery from these snapshots,
starting at more advanced task stages and falling back to earlier ones as
needed to generate corrective trajectories. We implement and compare four

Generalist vision–language–action (VLA) policies map visual observations
and language instructions directly to robot actions [ 1 , 2 ] . When these policies
encounter states outside the demonstration distribution, or
out-of-distribution (OOD) states, they may produce inappropriate actions [ 3 ] . Such errors can drive the robot further from the
demonstration distribution and compound over time [ 4 ] .
Human-in-the-loop (HIL) robot learning addresses this problem through expert
takeover, using corrective demonstrations to update the policy [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] . However, developing
HIL algorithms on physical robots requires substantial human effort to
collect corrections and repeated hardware use for evaluation. Environmental
variation further complicates reproducible comparisons [ 8 ] . These costs and sources of variability limit systematic
exploration and development of HIL post-training algorithms.

Simulation offers controllable scenes, repeatable trials, and scalable data
collection for developing and evaluating HIL algorithms before hardware
experiments [ 9 , 10 ] .
Platforms such as RoboTwin [ 11 ] and SIMPLER [ 8 ] support demonstration generation, policy evaluation, and
sim-to-real research, while automated HIL post-training remains comparatively
underexplored. IntervenGen extends simulation-based data generation to
corrective behavior by expanding a small set of human interventions into
synthetic recovery trajectories, but relies on human experts to determine
when and how to intervene in the initial recovery demonstrations [ 12 ] .
Automating these decisions in simulation requires selecting suitable recovery
states along a failed policy rollout and determining how an expert should
complete the task from those states. Both depend on task progress.
Vision-language models (VLMs) can monitor execution, but repeated visual
queries incur inference overhead [ 13 ] . CuRobo-based scripted
experts can execute predefined task sequences from initial states [ 14 ] , but the motion planner itself does not infer
task progress or select corrective actions for states reached by the policy.

Motivated by these challenges, we introduce SimPT , a simulation
framework that integrates policy rollouts, automated corrective data
collection, policy training, and
standalone evaluation to support the exploration and development of VLA
post-training algorithms (Fig. 1 ). To guide recovery, an agent
compiles task information into an Agent-Compiled Progress Graph .
During policy execution, the graph tracks task progress through fixed checks
on privileged simulator state and retains stable snapshots without further
agent queries. After rollout failure, SimPT attempts expert recovery from
snapshots at more advanced task stages and falls back to earlier ones as
needed. A CuRobo-based expert resumes
execution from each restored state, and successful recovery trajectories
are retained for policy post-training.

Using SimPT, we implement and compare HG-DAgger [ 6 ] ,
RECAP [ 15 ] , DPO+SFT [ 16 ] , and
FlowPRO [ 17 ] on seven RoboTwin manipulation tasks. In
independent data collections, the Progress Graph requires 75.0% fewer
recovery attempts than a fixed-interval snapshot baseline. We further use
SimPT to develop RECAP-CF-LPF, a refinement of RECAP that combines
cross-fitting (CF) and Butterworth low-pass filtering (LPF) of value
predictions. This combined refinement increases the overall
success rate from 76.50% to 79.36% in held-out simulation trials. Applied
to real-robot HIL post-training, it increases success from 72% to 96%
across 25 scenarios of an Ethernet cable-insertion task.
Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce SimPT, a simulation framework that automates the
intervention-based VLA post-training workflow to support systematic
algorithm exploration and development.

We develop the Agent-Compiled Progress Graph to track task progress
and retain stable snapshots during policy execution. After rollout failure,
expert recovery starts from more advanced task stages and falls back to
earlier ones as needed.

We compare four post-training methods on seven RoboTwin tasks
and use SimPT to develop RECAP-CF-LPF. By combining cross-fitting and
low-pass filtering, this refinement improves policy success in both
simulation and real-robot HIL post-training.

# II Related Work

## II-A Intervention-Based Robot Learning

Interactive imitation learning mitigates distribution shift by collecting
expert supervision during policy execution [ 18 ] .
DAgger aggregates expert labels on states encountered by the learner and
retrains the policy on the expanded dataset [ 4 ] .
HIL variants differ in how they allocate expert control: HG-DAgger lets a
human expert decide when to take over and return control [ 6 ] , whereas ThriftyDAgger requests assistance based on
novelty and estimated risk within an intervention budget [ 19 ] . Their behavior-cloning policy updates use
expert-labeled data [ 20 ] , without directly using the
success or failure of autonomous rollouts as learning signals.

To learn from autonomous experience as well as expert corrections, recent
VLA post-training methods incorporate reinforcement learning (RL) [ 21 ] . RECAP learns a value function to estimate future
returns, accounting for remaining task steps and failure penalties, and uses
the resulting advantages to condition policy training [ 15 ] . Noisy frame-level value estimates can
nevertheless yield misleading advantages in OOD states. STEAM addresses this
challenge by learning temporal-offset predictors from frame pairs in expert
demonstrations and conservatively combining their advantage estimates [ 22 ] . Its ensemble reduces advantage overestimation at the
cost of training and evaluating multiple predictors.

Preference optimization offers an alternative without a separately trained
value function or critic. FlowPRO adapts direct preference optimization
(DPO) [ 16 ] to flow-matching VLAs and uses a proximal
regularizer to constrain implicit reward magnitudes and mitigate reward
hacking. Its preference pairs are constructed from failed and corrective
trajectories collected through human intervention and rollback [ 17 ] . Across these approaches, corrective data collection
and repeated real-robot evaluation demand substantial expert time and
hardware resources, constraining systematic algorithm exploration.

## II-B Task Monitoring and Failure Recovery

Task monitoring connects execution feedback to failure detection and
recovery [ 23 , 24 ] . DoReMi uses VLM
queries to detect task-constraint violations and trigger replanning [ 13 ] . Language-model agents also encode task knowledge in
executable programs for robot planning and control, as demonstrated by Code
as Policies [ 25 ] , ProgPrompt [ 26 ] , and VoxPoser [ 27 ] .
Code-as-Monitor extends this idea to execution monitoring by compiling task
constraints into code that checks tracked geometric elements, reducing
reliance on repeated VLM queries [ 28 ] . AgentChord
complements monitoring with context-aware recovery branches added to task
graphs before execution, allowing detected failures to trigger prepared
corrective behaviors [ 29 ] . We instead use an
Agent-Compiled Progress Graph to guide expert recovery from stable snapshots
after terminal rollout failure, generating corrective trajectories for VLA
post-training.

## II-C Simulation for Data Generation and Policy Evaluation

Simulation supports both scalable training-data generation [ 30 , 31 ] and controlled policy evaluation [ 32 , 33 ] . RoboTwin combines generative digital
twins with task code to generate demonstrations and benchmark manipulation
policies [ 11 ] . Related benchmarks study knowledge transfer
in lifelong robot learning, as in LIBERO [ 34 ] , and unify
policy evaluation across simulation and the real world, as in RoboDojo [ 35 ] .

IntervenGen extends data generation to recovery behavior, focusing on
robustness to object pose estimation errors. It combines closed-loop policy
execution with transformed replay of human source interventions to
synthesize corrective trajectories [ 12 ] . RLinf provides
scalable infrastructure for embodied RL [ 36 ] , while its
real-world extension, USER, supports asynchronous online policy learning.
Its HG-DAgger workflow relies on human experts to determine intervention
timing and provide corrective actions [ 37 ] . Our simulation
framework supports intervention-based VLA post-training without human
takeover.

2026-10-22.title: State-Dependent Objective Coordination for End-to-End Balance and Navigation
2026-10-22.authors: Xuhao Huang , Xitao Xu , Yuxin Zheng , Yunfan Ren , Zheng Gong
2026-10-22.abstract: Traditional robotic navigation systems separate mapping, planning, and low-level control through cascaded modules, introducing computational overhead and accumulated latency. End-to-end reinforcement learning offers a compact unified policy that maps onboard observations directly to control actions. However, on inherently unstable platforms such as two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robots, navigation progress and obstacle avoidance can conflict with attitude stabilization in a strongly state-dependent manner. We propose a lightweight state-dependent objective coordination method for integrated navigation and control. A pitch-conditioned scalarization coefficient β ⁡ ( s ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \beta(s)\in[0,1] adjusts the relative contributions of balance stabilization and navigation objectives during training, without extra control hierarchies or auxiliary attitude-stabilization controllers, such as proportional–integral–derivative (PID) or linear–quadratic regulator (LQR) controllers. To support zero-shot deployment, simulation training models execution delay, action hold, asynchronous and noisy observations, and dynamics uncertainty. Gradient analysis reveals persistent directional interference and state-dependent variation in the objectives’ relative scales. Comparisons with alternative reward-weighting, constraint, training, and control-structure strategies show that PPO+ β ⁡ ( s ) \beta(s) , where PPO denotes proximal policy optimization, achieves 98% and 95% success rates with small attitude excursions on the fixed obstacle map and the randomly generated high-obstacle-density map, respectively. Zero-shot hardware experiments further demonstrate bounded attitude behavior and consistent obstacle avoidance using only onboard observations. Training and evaluation code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Real-world robot deployment increasingly requires compact control policies that satisfy multiple objectives within a single dynamical system under limited onboard computation and strict latency constraints. In strongly coupled robotic systems, these objectives may induce state-dependent conflicts, where an action that improves one objective can degrade another. Modular or hierarchical frameworks usually handle such interactions through interfaces between perception, planning, navigation, and low-level control [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . However, when multiple objectives share the same control inputs and are jointly constrained by system recoverability, interface-level coordination may lead to inconsistent or overly conservative behavior.

We study this problem on a two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robot that must maintain attitude stability while performing goal-directed obstacle-avoiding navigation. Navigation progress, obstacle avoidance, and attitude stabilization all act through the same wheel-torque commands. Near the upright state, excessive emphasis on stabilization may suppress effective navigation. At larger attitude deviations, aggressive navigation and avoidance actions may reduce recoverability and increase the risk of falling. Therefore, the appropriate balance between stabilization and navigation varies with the current attitude state.

A fixed reward coefficient applies the same objective weighting across states and therefore cannot explicitly adapt to state-dependent attitude risk. A large stabilization weight may be overly conservative near the upright state, whereas a small weight may provide insufficient stabilization as attitude risk increases. Structural alternatives, such as stage-wise training, hierarchical control, and policy composition, do not necessarily adjust this trade-off according to the current attitude state.

To address this issue, we propose state-dependent objective coordination through a state-conditioned scalarization coefficient β ⁡ ( s ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \beta(s)\in[0,1] . During training, β ⁡ ( s ) \beta(s) adjusts the relative contributions of balance stabilization and navigation progress according to the robot’s pitch magnitude. Navigation receives greater relative emphasis near the upright state, while stabilization is progressively emphasized as the pitch deviation grows. The coefficient is used only for reward construction during training. At deployment, a single end-to-end actor maps onboard observations directly to wheel torques without online reward computation, policy switching, or an auxiliary stabilizing controller.

We further incorporate deployment-relevant discrepancies into simulation training, including execution delay, action hold, asynchronous and noisy observations, and dynamics uncertainty. The resulting actor is trained in NVIDIA Isaac Sim and directly transferred to the physical robot without policy adaptation, as illustrated in Fig. 1 .

Our contributions are as follows:

We formulate simultaneous balance and obstacle-avoiding navigation as a state-dependent objective coordination problem and introduce a pitch-conditioned scalarization coefficient β ⁡ ( s ) \beta(s) for training a unified end-to-end policy.

We empirically analyze the interaction between the balance and navigation objectives through gradient direction and relative scale, and compare the proposed method with alternative reward-weighting, constraint, training, and control-structure strategies.

We demonstrate zero-shot transfer of the learned actor from simulation to a physical two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robot under matched obstacle-avoidance tasks.

1. We formulate simultaneous balance and obstacle-avoiding navigation as a state-dependent objective coordination problem and introduce a pitch-conditioned scalarization coefficient β ⁡ ( s ) \beta(s) for training a unified end-to-end policy.

2. We empirically analyze the interaction between the balance and navigation objectives through gradient direction and relative scale, and compare the proposed method with alternative reward-weighting, constraint, training, and control-structure strategies.

3. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer of the learned actor from simulation to a physical two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robot under matched obstacle-avoidance tasks.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II RELATED WORK

Strongly coupled robotic control tasks cannot always be decomposed into independent subproblems. On underactuated or inherently unstable platforms, navigation, obstacle avoidance, attitude recovery, and action smoothness share the same control inputs, such that improving one objective may compromise another. Existing robotic systems commonly organize these behaviors through modular, hierarchical, or hybrid architectures that separate perception, planning, navigation, and low-level control [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 ] . However, under strongly coupled dynamics, objective conflicts may still emerge at the action level and vary with the robot state.

In reinforcement learning, multiple objectives are typically coordinated through reward design or scalarization. Weighted sums provide a simple formulation [ 11 ] , but fixed weights do not explicitly adapt the relative objective preference to state-dependent risk. Dynamic weighting, preference adaptation, and reward scheduling have therefore been explored [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] . However, these approaches typically rely on predefined weighting strategies or external preference variables. In contrast, the coefficient in this work is analytically prescribed from the robot attitude state and is used only for training-time objective scalarization without introducing additional policy inputs or online coordination. Safe reinforcement learning further shows that objective conflicts may appear in policy-gradient directions. ESPO exploits reward–cost gradient conflicts for adaptive optimization [ 15 ] , motivating objective coordination beyond reward weights alone.

State-wise safe reinforcement learning considers instantaneous constraints associated with the current state, using safety evaluators, recovery policies, and reachability-based mechanisms [ 16 , 17 ] . These studies indicate that safety objectives should adapt to current risk rather than rely only on global penalties. Model-based safety frameworks, such as CLF–CBF–QP and CBF-constrained MPC, enforce safety constraints through optimization [ 18 , 19 ] . Although providing stronger theoretical structure, they typically require explicit dynamics, online optimization, or dedicated safety controllers.

This challenge is particularly evident in obstacle-avoiding navigation of two-wheeled inverted-pendulum robots, where navigation progress must be balanced with attitude recoverability. Prior studies have coordinated posture, mobility, and navigation through hierarchical optimization, modular planning, MPC, or learning-based control [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] . However, existing approaches typically rely on separated stabilization and navigation components. In contrast, this work addresses the state-dependent conflict between balance stabilization and obstacle-avoiding navigation through training-time objective coordination, yielding a compact unified policy suitable for direct deployment.

2026-10-22.title: Learning to Absorb Corrections: Critic-Weighted Residual Flow for Vision-Based Insertion
2026-10-22.authors: Yiqing Yuan , Zhi Li , Jinrong Yang , Mingshan Sun , Mei Yu Zhi , Yong Zhao , Liangliang Ren , Hui Cheng
2026-10-22.abstract: Vision-based insertion requires correcting alignment errors while retaining useful behavior learned from demonstrations. We present ACT–Flow, an online learning framework that couples an adaptive Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) with a conditional residual flow policy. Following anchor-guided warmup, ACT absorbs successful executed actions through behavioral cloning, while residual targets are recomputed relative to the updated prior. A chunk-level critic learns from successful and failed interactions and evaluates final composed actions. Its estimates weight generated residual candidates for flow matching, complemented by supervision from successful real executions. Candidate scoring is confined to training; deployment uses RGB observations and samples one residual per action chunk. We evaluate the framework on power-plug, USB, and key insertion, together with cable routing and needle threading. Results show a five-task mean success rate of 66% at 20,000 post-initialization interaction steps, exceeding the strongest baseline by 18 percentage points at this checkpoint. Evaluations at matched checkpoints with the residual disabled show ACT’s mean success increasing from 16% to 76%. Component ablations further support the complementary roles of behavior absorption, value weighting, and successful-action supervision.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Vision-based insertion requires a robot to correct alignment errors during execution. Inserting a power plug, USB connector, or key can fail when small position or orientation errors persist, or when the target moves after the initial approach. Demonstration-trained policies, including Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) [ 1 ] and Diffusion Policy [ 2 ] , provide effective action priors. However, limited demonstrations cannot cover every state encountered during deployment, and deviations from the training distribution can compound [ 3 ] . This motivates a policy that can both correct execution errors and incorporate successful corrections into its learned behavior.

Existing methods obtain corrective guidance from demonstrations or human intervention. DOME [ 4 ] , MILES [ 5 ] , and AutoSERL [ 6 ] use demonstrations to guide visual alignment, recovery, or automatic intervention. HIL-SERL [ 7 ] incorporates human corrections into reinforcement learning (RL), while CR-DAgger [ 8 ] learns residual policies from compliant corrections. Demonstration-guidance mechanisms depend on available reference behavior, while human corrections require operator effort. Beyond obtaining guidance, a further question is how the robot should represent corrections and retain the useful behavior they produce.

Residual adaptation provides a natural representation: a base policy supplies nominal behavior and an additional policy learns corrections [ 9 , 8 , 10 , 11 ] . FlowDAgger [ 12 ] similarly steers a frozen generative policy through its latent variables. A frozen prior provides a stable basis for adaptation, but successful corrections remain in the additional module rather than becoming part of the prior itself. The central question is: how can a robot learn effective insertion corrections from interaction and absorb successful corrected behavior into an improving action prior?

Joint prior–residual learning raises two issues. Updating the prior changes the residual needed to reproduce a successful action, making historical labels inconsistent. Critic estimates rank corrections but cannot replace observed successful actions as supervision. Learning must combine these signals while tracking the evolving prior. Retaining successful executed actions provides a stable reference: their decomposition can change as the prior improves, while their role as observed targets is preserved.

We present ACT–Flow, an online framework for vision-based insertion that coordinates an adaptive ACT prior with a conditional residual flow policy. Following anchor-guided demonstration and correction warmup, successful executed actions update ACT through behavioral cloning (BC), while residual targets are recomputed against the updated ACT to preserve consistent supervision. To combine value guidance with observed successful behavior, residual learning couples critic-weighted flow matching (FM) [ 13 ] on generated candidates with FM on successful executions. The critic learns from both outcomes and scores composed actions.

We evaluate three insertion tasks—power-plug, USB, and key insertion—plus cable routing and needle threading. Comparisons and ablations examine adaptation, behavior absorption, and residual supervision. Our contributions are:

An online learning framework for vision-based insertion connecting an ACT prior and residual flow policy through anchor-guided initialization, online correction, and successful-experience feedback.

A behavior-absorption mechanism that updates ACT from successful actions and relabels residual targets under the current prior, keeping correction supervision consistent as the base policy changes.

Critic-weighted residual flow learning that combines value-weighted fitting of generated corrections with FM supervision from successful executed actions.

Comparisons on three real-world insertion tasks and two additional manipulation tasks, supported by component ablations and diagnostics of base-policy improvement, residual contribution, and critic ranking quality.

1. An online learning framework for vision-based insertion connecting an ACT prior and residual flow policy through anchor-guided initialization, online correction, and successful-experience feedback.

2. A behavior-absorption mechanism that updates ACT from successful actions and relabels residual targets under the current prior, keeping correction supervision consistent as the base policy changes.

3. Critic-weighted residual flow learning that combines value-weighted fitting of generated corrections with FM supervision from successful executed actions.

4. Comparisons on three real-world insertion tasks and two additional manipulation tasks, supported by component ablations and diagnostics of base-policy improvement, residual contribution, and critic ranking quality.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Demonstrations and Corrective Interaction

DAgger [ 3 ] aggregates corrective supervision, while CR-DAgger [ 8 ] collects compliant corrections. MILES [ 5 ] augments a reference demonstration through self-supervised recovery, and HD-Space [ 14 ] organizes collection within overlapping atomic state–action spaces. Simulation can also supply demonstrations: Li et al. [ 15 ] use appearance-noise annealing to shape optimization for sim-to-real conveyor manipulation. SERL [ 16 ] supports practical real-world RL; HIL-SERL [ 7 ] incorporates human corrections, while AWAC [ 17 ] and RLPD [ 18 ] exploit prior data for online learning. AutoSERL [ 6 ] automates demonstration-guided intervention and recovery, and Focus-Then-Contact (FTC) [ 10 ] combines residual RL with affordance guidance and timed human intervention.

Visual task conditioning offers a complementary route to robust imitation. Vision-instructed pre-training (VIP) [ 19 ] uses future images and sparse point flows to specify targets; SAM2Grasp [ 20 ] combines object prompts with temporal tracking to disambiguate grasp trajectories. These approaches clarify task targets, while our focus is learning and absorbing corrections during interaction.

In our setting, corrective experience must support both prior improvement and residual learning. We use HD-Space’s collection principle for warmup, successful actions to update ACT, and both outcomes to train the residual-learning critic.

## II-B Residual Adaptation and Prior Updating

Residual RL [ 9 ] adds learned corrections to a nominal controller. Policy Decorator [ 21 ] refines a frozen imitation policy and evaluates composed actions. CR-DAgger [ 8 ] learns residual motions and forces from compliant supervision; FTC [ 10 ] and HiL-ResRL [ 11 ] combine frozen priors with human-guided residual RL. FlowDAgger [ 12 ] steers a frozen generative policy through latent-space corrections. In contrast, RL-100 directly fine-tunes an imitation-pretrained diffusion policy through offline and online RL [ 22 ] .

A frozen prior provides a stable residual reference but does not absorb corrections. Updating the prior permits behavior absorption, yet changes the residual required to reproduce a previously successful action. We retain executed actions as stable targets, update ACT from successful experience, and recompute residual targets against the current ACT.

## II-C Value-Guided Generative Policy Learning

Advantage-weighted regression [ 23 ] uses value-derived weights for supervised policy fitting. FM [ 13 ] provides a generative regression objective; reward-weighted fine-tuning [ 24 ] favors high-reward samples while regularizing deviation from a reference model. Flow Q-Learning [ 25 ] trains a separate one-step actor with value optimization and distillation from a behavior-cloned flow policy. PACT [ 26 ] calibrates credit assignment using intervention-derived preferences, while Max-Q [ 27 ] uses chunk-value regression to select between policy and replay actions for imitation.

Under an evolving prior, critic rankings provide value guidance but cannot replace successful-action targets. We combine critic-weighted FM on generated candidates with successful-execution FM, both referenced to the current ACT.
