2026-10-22.title: PHD-Hand: A Printable Humanoid Dexterous Hand with Linkage-Driven 3-DOA Digits
2026-10-22.authors: Neel Adwani , Muhaiminul Islam Akash , Saffia Ouali , Ethan Liu , Cong Wang
2026-10-22.comment: Submitted and Accepted at IEEE-RAS International Conference on Humanoid Robots (Humanoids 2026). . Supplementary video: this https URL
2026-10-22.abstract:
Currently, dexterous humanoid robot hands are widely considered the final hardware bottleneck that hampers generalist robots from physically assisting people at home and work.
As conventional tendon-driven designs suffer from high cost, demanding maintenance, poor reliability, and short durability, alternative linkage-driven designs have increasingly gained attention.
Despite their potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon-driven hands, integrating multiple degrees of actuation (DOA) in a single digit with linkage drivetrains is a challenge for design and fabrication.
Only a few studies have managed to present functional humanoid hands that are completely linkage-driven and have at least three DOAs per digit without compromising actuator placement and other design preferences. Our work introduces a new linkage-driven hand featuring a unique flexure hinge. Together with elastic drive rods made of spring steel, the linkage drivetrains are significantly simplified. Unlike other linkage-driven designs of similar dexterity, our design does not require many miniature moving parts. As a result, the hand can be fabricated easily with a budget 3D printer. This not only significantly lowers the barrier to entry for using and developing dexterous humanoid robot hand functions, but also allows the hands to be sized much closer to regular human hands. The design offers desirable kinematic advantages as well. A prototype is evaluated for grasping and object manipulation. In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics and control of the hand.
2026-10-22.introduction:
This paper discusses the design of linkage-driven dexterous humanoid robot hands.
With the recent breakthroughs in perception and reasoning powered by artificial intelligence (AI), replicating the dexterity of human hands is increasingly considered the last physical bottleneck that holds back the robotics industry.
Having humanoid dexterous hands not only allows robots to seamlessly handle objects in our daily lives, but also enables robot learning of hand skills directly from native human demonstration.
Other than resembling the appearance of human palm and digits 1 1 1 In human anatomy, the thumb is not a finger - i.e., a regular human hand has five digits, including one thumb and four fingers. ,
a humanoid robot hand ideally should have at least three degrees of actuation (DOA) 2 2 2 Because of the complex kinematics of dexterous robot hands, the term “degrees of freedom (DOF)” has been used to indicate quite different meanings in the literature.
Instead, we have found “degrees of actuation (DOA)” to be a more precise term. per digit.
The “ root joint ” of a digit should have two DOAs for tilting, while the “ upper two joints ’’ 3 3 3 For a finger, the root joint is an MCP joint, and the upper two joints include a PIP joint and a DIP joint.
For the thumb, the root joint is a CMC joint, and the upper two joints include an MCP joint and an IP joint.
To keep the narrative concise and friendly to a broader audience, instead of the anatomical terminology, we use the terms “root joint” and “upper two joints” in this paper. almost always flex/extend together and share a single DOA 4 4 4 The thumb actually moves differently from the fingers, though the difference is not that significant. .

A straightforward way to build such a digit is to place the actuators inside or on the digits to drive the joints “locally” with a structure similar to serial robot manipulators (e.g., [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] ).
This results in a dilemma of the digit either having weak actuation or being oversize and overweight.
It is therefore desirable to have the actuators placed off the digits, which requires additional drivetrain(s) to deliver actuation to the upper two joints.
The most common solution is to use tendon drives.
The design is largely inspired by human anatomy and has been the mainstream choice of dexterous robot hands [ 5 ] .
However, without self-healing, the complex tendon systems required for dexterity wear out and loosen up quickly, which leads to demanding maintenance and short life span [ 6 ] .
Performance of tendon-driven hands is often jeopardized by cable fraying, knot slippage, and tension drift [ 7 ] [ 8 ] .
In particular, cable rupture is the top failure mode [ 8 ] .
In addition, tendon-driven bidirectional actuation requires either two actuators per DOA (leads to sizing problems) or closed-loop tendon routing (prone to loosening and slacking) [ 9 ] .
The absence of bidirectional actuation excludes the hand from performing certain skills.

Compared to tendon-drives, rigid drivetrains do not have weaknesses mentioned above.
They also provide better precision and can bear higher load [ 10 ] .
Some designs use geared drivetrains to transmit actuation from actuators placed off the digit to the upper two joints. [ 11 ] shows a representative design in this category.
Each of its digits has a 2-DOA root joint and 1-DOA coupled upper two joints.
Actuation is transmitted to the upper two joints using a bevel gear drive coaxially located with the drive shafts of the root joint. Other than the fabrication hassle and inevitable backlash, complexity of the design results in a hand size significantly larger than human hands.

Alternatively, linkage-driven designs have the potential to avoid the weaknesses of tendon and gear-based designs [ 12 ] .
However, integrating three DOAs with linkage drivetrains in one digit (while keeping the actuators off the digit) poses a great challenge for design and fabrication.
There are only a few presentations [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] , which share similar designs and have only emerged over recent years.
Among them, the design presented in [ 13 ] is both pioneering and most ready for practical use.
It adopts a novel 5-joint linkage drivetrain to deliver actuation to the upper two joints through the root joint (Fig. 1 -a, the portion circled in red).
As impressive as the prototype and demonstration are, the nontrivial number of miniature parts (Fig. 1 -b) require serious fabrication capability and make it challenging to balance between durability, size, and cost.
The prototype in [ 13 ] has a hand length around 218 mm which is 13% larger than average male human hands.
The design is replicated in [ 14 ] and improved in [ 15 ] with hand lengths of 255 mm and 219 mm respectively.
In addition, the kinematics of the root joint and upper two joints is partially coupled, which complicates the control.
More details of these designs will be examined later in Section II with a summarizing comparison to our work.
Some other designs work around the challenge by strategically reducing the number of DOAs based on human hand synergies - e.g., [ 18 , 19 , 20 , 21 ] .
Despite being able to realize a decent variety of hand functions, the strategy does not provide the potential of advanced dexterity that the robotics community is currently wishing for.

Our work aims at developing a dexterous humanoid robot hand that

Has five digits with three DOAs per digit (two for the root joint, one for the coupled upper two joints);

Has each DOA bidirectionally actuated with a decent strength, good backdrivability, and minimal backlash;

Can be fabricated at a size very close to human hands with minimal costs using a budget 3D printer;

Has long-lasting durability and requires minimal maintenance.

This paper continues from our earlier publication [ 22 ] , which introduces the flexure design of the root joint and presents a preliminary prototype of three digits, together with strength test results.
Our prior work suffers from a series of problems, including mechanical interference, non-humanoid topology, and fabrication complications.
The new design in this paper resolves those problems and demonstrates legitimate humanoid dexterity.
In addition, this paper presents our latest findings on kinematics and control of the hand.

1. Has five digits with three DOAs per digit (two for the root joint, one for the coupled upper two joints);

2. Has each DOA bidirectionally actuated with a decent strength, good backdrivability, and minimal backlash;

3. Can be fabricated at a size very close to human hands with minimal costs using a budget 3D printer;

4. Has long-lasting durability and requires minimal maintenance.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Design and Fabrication

Figure 2 illustrates our proposed design.
The root joint is the key element.
We present a unique design in the form of a flexure hinge.
The design is inspired by stress-relieving structures commonly used to protect cable connectors.
As a single-piece anisotropic flexible structure, it provides two DOFs of tilting motion while restraining axial rotation.
It gives a wide motion range to satisfy the need of dexterity, yet does not bend sharply.
This is an important feature that allows an elastic drive rod made of spring steel to go through its center and smoothly deliver bidirectional actuation to the upper two joints without the need of complicated mechanisms and many moving parts (as opposed to the designs in [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] ).
In addition, bending of the flexure hinge does not force/require the elastic rod to move axially.
This completely decouples the drivetrain kinematics of the root joint and the upper two joints, which greatly simplifies modeling, estimation, and control.
In terms of actuation, the root joint is driven by two RC servos that connect to the root phalanx of the digit through two rigid drive rods and four ball joints.
The design evolves from the classic 2-DOF planar 5-bar mechanisms.
Note that the axial rotation of the drive rods is not constrained because of the ball joints, though it does not affect the function of the drivetrain.
The upper two joints of the digit are coupled by a cross 4-bar mechanism, which is a commonly used design.
Reported coupling ratios of the upper joints of human digits fall between 0.75 and 0.8 [ 23 ] .
We find a ratio of 0.77 optimal for our design.
The cross 4-bar mechanism is actuated by the elastic drive rod that passes through the root joint.
As of now, we have decided to make the coupling rod go from outside of the middle phalanx.
Other than minimizing mechanical interference and providing a bigger motion range, the option allows easy shaping of the coupling rod to give it certain flexibility, which helps realize the passive compliance desired in hand-object interaction [ 24 ] [ 25 ] .

Figure 3 -a shows a prototype.
The digits are modular (Fig. 3 -b), allowing easy reconfiguration of the hand topology and repair.
Thanks to the unique design, the hand can be fabricated using a budget FFF 3D printer, generic hardware (ball joints, rods, pins, and fasteners), and generic mini-scale RC servos commonly available on the market of crafting hobbies.
Because of its nontrivial shape, 3D printing of the root joint can be tricky but can still be done reliably with carefully tuned settings.
We recommend using TPU 95A filament, a 0.4 mm nozzle, a nozzle temperature of 215 °C, a bed temperature of 55 °C with an enclosure, a printing speed of 100 mm/s, a layer height of 0.15 mm, and 15% infill, with the print placed horizontally without any supports (Fig. 3 -c).
The upper two joints are made as flexible strips 3D printed with TPU.
The phalanges can be either 3D printed with PETG for higher rigidity or with TPU so that the whole digit body can be made in one single piece to
further simplify assembly.
The elastic drive rod is cut from 304 stainless spring steel wires of 0.6 mm thickness.
It is flexible enough to bend with the root joint without causing significant resistance, while is strong enough to avoid buckling when pushed.

Our literature survey has found four existing designs that are fully linkage-driven, have at least three DOAs per digit, and with all actuators placed off the digits.
Three of them are presented in research papers while the other one is a commercial product.
As detailed in Table I , the parts of our design are not only significantly fewer but also can be affordably made without industrial-level fabrication.
The advantage greatly lowers the barrier to entry for the use and development of dexterous robot hand functions.
The concise design also allows the hand to be made at a more compact size closer to regular humans.
Instead of the custom linear actuators with leadscrews used in other designs, our design uses generic RC servos.
Despite giving a raised back-palm, the choice not only simplifies fabrication but also provides a good backdrivability.

2026-10-22.title: SLoSa: Small, Low-Power, and Safe Foundation Models for Robotic Task Planning
2026-10-22.authors: Weizhe Xu , Jialiang Fan , Essien Taylor , Zijun Wang , Russell Joseph , Fanxin Kong
2026-10-22.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO)
2026-10-22.abstract:
Safe robotic task planning requires planners that can reliably achieve task goals while satisfying safety constraints.
Classical planners search over explicit symbolic task representations and can
provide formal guarantees with respect to encoded safety constraints, but require rigid input formats.
Their computational cost also increases rapidly with the search space.
In contrast, large language models (LLMs) offer flexible task interfaces and strong generalization capabilities, but they are large, power-hungry, and pre-trained with little robot-specific safety data and knowledge.
Thus, they can be difficult to deploy locally on robotic systems with limited resources.
To address these limitations, we present SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic compression and fine-tuning framework for training foundation-model-based robotic task planners with S mall size, Lo w power demand, and Sa fety awareness.
The framework first constructs a safety-aware dataset using classical planners, an advanced teacher LLM, and formal verifiers, followed by two training stages: supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning (RL) fine-tuning guided by a verification-based reward machine to enforce safety alignment. We evaluate SLoSa across four Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) domains, two household simulation environments, local edge platforms, and a desktop robotic arm.
Across the PDDL tasks, verifier-guided post-training raises the success rate of compact 4B–14B planners to 70.5–76.0%, while INT4 deployment on a Jetson Orin requires 17.85–26.41 W of average power.
Results in household simulators and on the physical robot further demonstrate the applicability of SLoSa across diverse robotic task settings.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Robotic task planning converts a high-level goal into an executable sequence of actions [ 1 ] .
In safety-critical settings, reaching the goal is not enough: every intermediate state must also satisfy requirements such as ordering, mutual exclusion, and resource constraints [ 2 , 3 ] .
A plan that eventually places an object correctly can still be unacceptable if it enters a restricted region, manipulates a fragile object in the wrong order, or violates a required inspection step.
We therefore study safety-constrained task planning : generating plans that are executable and goal-reaching while satisfying explicit trajectory-level constraints.

Classical planners offer a principled solution when a correct symbolic task specification is available.
Systems such as Fast Downward and OPTIC search over states defined by action preconditions and effects [ 4 , 5 ] ; PDDL3 expresses trajectory constraints, and tools such as VAL check a candidate plan against the formal specification [ 6 , 7 ] .
This formal structure provides an auditable safety criterion, but it comes with two practical costs.
First, tasks in complicated environments can induce exponentially growing search spaces as the number of objects and planning horizon increase, making symbolic search difficult to scale [ 8 ] .
Second, users must provide rigid symbolic inputs and carefully engineered domain specifications .
Imitation and reinforcement learning can amortize planning into compact policies [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] .
However, learned policies are commonly tied to particular task distributions, and their outputs do not inherit a formal guarantee without an explicit specification and verifier.

LLM planners offer a complementary strength: they can interpret high-level
task descriptions and directly generate candidate action
sequences [ 13 , 14 ] .
Recent systems ground language into symbolic specifications or integrate LLMs
with planners and formal verifiers [ 15 , 16 , 17 ] .
An inference-time verifier can reject an invalid plan
and prompt the model to revise it [ 18 , 19 ] .
However, this process leaves the base planner unchanged, so repeated failures
increase token usage, latency, and computation.
Moreover, general-purpose LLMs can be too large for memory- and power-limited
robot computers.
These limitations motivate a planner that combines safety-aware plan
generation, compact local inference, and flexible task interfaces.

We introduce SLoSa , a neuro-symbolic post-training framework for this combination.
Rather than keeping the verifier only in the inference loop, SLoSa uses formal feedback to change the compact planner itself.
First, SLoSa constructs behavior-changing safety-aware training data by retaining planning instances in which the supplied constraint rejects the baseline plan while a verified alternative remains feasible.
Second, compression-aware supervised fine-tuning (SFT) adapts compact, quantized LLMs using the verified plans.
Third, verifier-guided Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) refines the planner with a reward hierarchy that separates unparseable outputs, precondition violations, safety violations, goal failures, and successful plans.
At inference, SLoSa combines local plan generation with verifier feedback to enforce the supplied safety constraints while reducing the tokens spent on iterative repair.

We evaluate SLoSa using three compact open-source LLM backbones across four PDDL domains that cover manipulation, transportation, object transfer, and tool use, together with separately trained planners for safety-adapted VirtualHome and ALFWorld to evaluate the applicability of the same post-training pipeline beyond PDDL-based planning. The results show consistent improvements from safety-aware post-training
across model sizes, task domains, and input representations.
We further evaluate local inference on an NVIDIA RTX 4080 and a Jetson Orin,
and demonstrate the complete vision-grounded planning pipeline on a desktop 6-degree-of-freedom (6-DoF) robotic arm.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic post-training framework that
improves compact LLM planners through behavior-changing safety-aware data
construction, compression-aware supervised fine-tuning, and
verifier-guided GRPO.

We construct safety-constrained evaluation tasks spanning four PDDL planning domains and two adapted household simulation benchmarks, with formally verified plans and task-specific trajectory constraints.

We conduct extensive experiments across multiple model sizes, task
domains, and input representations, showing consistent improvements from
safety-aware post-training. We further validate local edge deployment,
verifier-guided inference, and physical robotic-arm execution.

1. We introduce SLoSa, a neuro-symbolic post-training framework that
improves compact LLM planners through behavior-changing safety-aware data
construction, compression-aware supervised fine-tuning, and
verifier-guided GRPO.

2. We construct safety-constrained evaluation tasks spanning four PDDL planning domains and two adapted household simulation benchmarks, with formally verified plans and task-specific trajectory constraints.

3. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple model sizes, task
domains, and input representations, showing consistent improvements from
safety-aware post-training. We further validate local edge deployment,
verifier-guided inference, and physical robotic-arm execution.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Work

Classical, learned, and neuro-symbolic task planning. Classical planners search over explicit task representations and can validate a plan against its goals and constraints [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
Their explicit semantics make failures interpretable, but formal specification construction is labor-intensive, and tasks in complicated environments can induce exponentially growing search spaces as the number of objects and the planning horizon increase [ 8 ] .
Imitation learning and reinforcement learning instead learn policies or search guidance from demonstrations and interaction [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] .
But they are generally optimized for a specific training distribution. SLoSa adopts this general direction but uses symbolic planners and validators primarily as sources of training supervision, while a compact neural model generates the initial plan at deployment.

LLM planning with formal grounding and runtime assurance. LLMs have been used to generate actions, select skills, and translate natural-language requests into planning specifications [ 13 , 14 ] .
LIMP grounds open-ended robot instructions into symbolic representations from which verifiable behaviors can be synthesized [ 15 ] , while [ 16 , 17 ] translate language into syntactically valid temporal logic for downstream motion planning.
Other systems retain a verifier in the inference loop: ISR-LLM translates natural-language tasks into PDDL and iteratively refines long-horizon plans, while the Safety Chip enforces LTL constraints around an LLM-driven agent [ 18 , 19 ] .
These approaches provide important assurance at the interface between language and execution, but a weak base planner can still require repeated generation and verification.
SLoSa instead uses formal validation during post-training to improve the first-pass plan quality of the compact planner itself.
At deployment, the resulting planner can still be paired with an ISR-style verifier and repair loop, retaining formal guarantees for validator-accepted plans while reducing regeneration tokens.

Safety post-training and compact deployment. Quantization and parameter-efficient fine-tuning reduce the memory and adaptation cost of LLMs [ 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 ] , but compression alone does not optimize satisfaction of task-level safety constraints.
SafeGen-LLM uses verified PDDL supervision to improve safety generalization across properties, domains, and input formats [ 24 ] .
SLoSa studies a complementary question: whether verifier knowledge can be transferred into small, low-power LLM planners that improve safe plan generation with lower memory use and less dependence on repeated repair.

2026-10-22.title: GGraph: A GPU-Accelerated Library for Graph-Based Robot Deployment and Learning
2026-10-22.authors: Yash Rampuria , Rohan Garg , Daniele Gammelli , Marco Pavone
2026-10-22.abstract:
Autonomous mobile robots require spatial representations that capture geometry
and semantics while staying sparse enough for planning in large, unknown
environments. Graphs provide a natural representation for this purpose and underpin both classical planning methods and a growing class of reinforcement-learning (RL) policies. However, RL
training needs hundreds to thousands of parallel environments, each constructing
and updating its own graph. Existing graph libraries are typically designed for either single-robot
deployment or fixed graphs, and CPU-based graph construction limits scalable training to only a
few dozen environments. We introduce GGraph , an open-source GPU-accelerated
graph library for both robot deployment and large-scale learning. GGraph supports real robots through ROS 2 interfaces and vectorized GPU-based policy training, with built-in support for tasks including 3-D navigation, exploration, and loop-closure integration. For single-robot operation, GGraph updates graphs in milliseconds. At scale, it enables graph-based exploration policies to train across hundreds of parallel robots, reducing wall-clock training time by one order of magnitude. Across simulation and real-world experiments, these results establish GGraph as a unified graph infrastructure for both large-scale robot learning and deployment.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Progress in mobile robotics has been driven by a small set of design tools that became shared infrastructure, including occupancy grids for planning [ 1 ] , GPU elevation mapping for locomotion [ 2 ] , OpenCV for perception [ 3 ] , PyTorch for learning [ 4 ] , and massively parallel simulators for RL [ 5 ] . Each is valuable because one implementation serves both deployment on a robot and training in simulation, so improvements on either side transfer.

Graphs have long been used for robot planning. A navigation graph stores sparse collision-free nodes connected by traversable edges, and nodes can carry frontiers, traversability, semantics or learned scores. Such graphs underpin classical exploration planners [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] and a line of learned policies that reason over the graph with Graph Neural Networks [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] . Despite this, no shared tool builds and maintains these graphs. Deployment planners construct them inside planner-specific, single-robot code. Learning pipelines rebuild them for every environment on the CPU, so a 16-worker training run spends much of its wall-clock time maintaining graphs rather than learning. GPU graph libraries [ 12 , 13 ] target fixed graphs consumed by a model, not graphs that grow and are merged and re-scored at every step of a rollout.

To address this gap, we present GGraph , a GPU-resident navigation-graph library that serves as one design tool for both deployment and learning (Fig. 1 ). GGraph takes occupancy grids or elevation maps as input. It samples collision-free waypoints, merges them incrementally into a persistent world-frame graph with stable node identities, and attaches per-node attributes through a layer system. Shortest paths, connectivity and frontiers are all available as CUDA tensors. The same implementation serves single-robot deployment through ROS 2 and policy learning across many parallel environments.

Building such a library raises some technical challenges. First, the graph changes at every step, as each observation adds a varying number of nodes and edges that must be merged into a graph already covering the explored world. Second, existing graph builders rely on sequential data structures, such as priority queues and per-node objects, that cannot run in parallel on a GPU. Third, learning requires hundreds of such graphs, each growing at a different rate, to be updated together. Fourth, on a real robot the graph must survive loop closure, which moves every node placed since the drift began. GGraph stores each graph as parallel tensors with stable node identities, so adding, merging, pruning and correcting nodes are single vectorized operations. It merges each observation with one batched nearest-neighbor assignment and one line-of-sight kernel over all candidate edges. It also reformulates graph search as edge-parallel Bellman–Ford and pointer-jumping connected components, running one robot or N N environments through the same kernels. The novel contribution of GGraph is to make the navigation graph itself a batched, GPU-resident, loop-closure-aware data structure shared by deployment and learning. To our knowledge, no other library provides this capability. Our contributions are:

An open-source GPU navigation-graph library. An
extensible layer system stores geometric, semantic and learned
attributes per node, and ROS 2 and batched interfaces let the same code
serve deployment and learning (Sec. IV-A ).

An open-source GPU navigation-graph library. An
extensible layer system stores geometric, semantic and learned
attributes per node, and ROS 2 and batched interfaces let the same code
serve deployment and learning (Sec. IV-A ).

Validation in robot deployment and policy learning. We use GGraph to build 3-D graphs from real-world sensor data, attach frontier and semantic layers, and correct the whole graph after loop closure in one vectorized pass. Used as a batched RL environment, GGraph trains graph-based exploration policies that reach the quality of prior learned policies in a fraction of the training time and outperform baselines on held-out maps, on a ground vehicle in a high-fidelity simulator, and on a real robot (Secs. V-A and V-B ).

Scalability benchmarks. Graph updates take just tens of milliseconds as graphs grow to a million nodes, and environment-step throughput scales with the number of parallel robots, reaching 27 × \times that of a SoTA baseline (Secs. V-A3 and V-B1 ).
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Representations for Navigation

Early navigation in unknown environments used 2-D occupancy grids [ 1 ] , with frontier-based exploration driving the robot toward free cells that border unexplored space [ 14 ] . Volumetric maps such as OctoMap [ 15 ] and Voxblox [ 16 ] store occupancy or distance to surfaces across a 3-D volume. Topological maps [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] keep only the places a robot can reach and the transitions between them, and scene graphs [ 20 ] organize places into a semantic hierarchy. Exploration planners combine both. GBPlanner [ 7 ] plans over local and global graphs built on a volumetric map, and TARE [ 6 ] keeps a sparse roadmap along the past trajectory with dense point-cloud data around the robot. In both, the graph sits on a dense map that the planner still queries to score exploration gain. GGraph instead makes the graph the primary representation, storing frontier, semantic and learned attributes on its nodes and using dense maps only as transient inputs, so one graph serves both classical planners and learned policies.

## II-B Graph Libraries and Ecosystems

Navigation planners mutate their graphs as the robot explores, merging local observations into a global graph in custom C++ or Python code inside each planner [ 6 , 7 , 9 ] . SWAGGER [ 21 ] builds sparse waypoint graphs from occupancy grid maps using NetworkX [ 22 ] with partial GPU support, but derives each graph from a single map rather than merging across observations. Outside navigation, GPU graph libraries serve other workloads. Graph learning frameworks such as PyTorch Geometric [ 12 ] are fully tensorized and batch graphs by stacking adjacency matrices block-diagonally, but treat each graph as a fixed model input without spatial merging, and graph analytics libraries such as cuGraph [ 13 ] run GPU analytics over graphs built from edge lists. As Table I summarizes, navigation tools are largely CPU-based and GPU libraries lack spatial merging and navigation operations. GGraph combines GPU acceleration, spatial merging, navigation and exploration operations, and batched policy learning in one library.

## II-C Learning-Based Robot Exploration

Learning-based exploration trains reinforcement learning policies to choose where a robot goes next, and graphs suit them because one graph is both the map the robot traverses and the input a graph neural network [ 23 ] reasons over. Chen et al. [ 24 ] trained graph neural network policies with DQN and A2C over a graph of past poses, landmarks and candidate frontiers for exploration under localization uncertainty. ARiADNE [ 9 ] connects uniformly distributed viewpoints into a collision-free graph and trains an attention network with soft actor-critic to pick the next neighboring viewpoint, using each node’s count of observable frontiers as a feature. Its large-scale successor [ 10 ] adds graph rarefaction and a privileged critic, and GRATE [ 11 ] uses a graph transformer encoder and Kalman-filtered waypoints. These three train in 2-D grid worlds with 16 to 32 Ray workers for one to three days, and in ARiADNE’s released code each worker builds its graph in Python on the CPU. GGraph builds and merges every environment’s graph on the GPU, so hundreds of environments step as one tensor operation, which makes on-policy methods such as PPO [ 25 ] practical, as in massively parallel locomotion learning [ 26 ] .

✓ partial support (mainly CPU based); * batched across parallel environments.

2026-10-22.title: HyperDrone: Simulation-to-Reality Transfer at Millions of Frames per Second
2026-10-22.authors: Jonas Eschmann , Giuseppe Loianno
2026-10-22.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-22.comment: Accepted at Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
2026-10-22.abstract: We present HyperDrone, an extremely fast quadrotor simulator focused on high-performance batch rendering that is more than 20 × 20\times faster than existing state-of-the-art batch quadrotor simulators. HyperDrone combines highly optimized multirotor dynamics with HyperLux, a new ray-tracing engine that supports Nvidia OptiX, Vulkan, Apple Metal and WebGPU backends that takes full advantage of modern ray-tracing hardware, capable of running both components entirely on the GPU. HyperLux renders RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow observations at configurable levels of fidelity, including reflections, realistic lighting, motion blur, anti-aliasing, and Physically Based Rendering (PBR). Even in the highest-fidelity settings, HyperLux achieves millions of Frames Per Second (FPS) on consumer-grade GPUs while rendering realistic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the merits of HyperDrone by training a vision-based yaw-control policy purely in simulation and transferring it to a real small-scale quadrotor (Crazyflie) with a camera, running completely onboard.
2026-10-22.introduction:
In recent years, imitation learning from human demonstrations has become a dominant method for advanced learning-based control of robots. This is particularly the case in the field of manipulation [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] and locomotion [ 4 , 5 ] . Conversely, for aerial vehicle autonomy, imitation learning from human demonstrations has not experienced comparable widespread adoption. In the case of quadrotors, in particular, two major trends have been imitation learning from (privileged) expert policies [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] and using pre-trained models as vision encoders [ 9 , 10 ] . The latter promise to bring broader generalization by virtue of having been pre-trained on massive amounts of real-world images collected from the internet.

Imitation learning from human demonstrations and pre-trained vision models are motivated and driven by scaling laws that were first observed in Large Language Models (LLMs) [ 11 ] . Early indications hint that similar scaling laws might exist in robot imitation learning [ 12 ] . The potential that scaling robot imitation data could bear similarly large returns as LLM scaling, has led to the formation of a large number of commercial robot imitation data creation/curation companies. These companies also bet on monopolizing forces known as the “data flywheels” [ 13 ] limiting accessibility while the capital expenditure (CAPEX) requirement for large-scale robot data collection is by itself already a major hurdle for reproducibility and progress in the community.

The alternative is training robot control policies entirely in simulation without requiring real-world data. Not only are methods fully trained on synthetic data more accessible to fellow researchers, but they are also more introspectable. Due to the lack of interpretability of deep neural networks, in general we cannot get strong guarantees for learned end-to-end controllers. The best way to reason about the behavior of the trained control policy is through introspection of the data that went into training it. For vision foundation models [ 14 , 15 , 16 , 17 ] this data is usually proprietary, hampering reproducibility, interpretability of the resulting behavior and the opportunity for independent researchers to study effects of modifying the data distribution.

To accelerate the research of vision-based aerial vehicle control we present the following contributions:

HyperDrone : An extremely fast simulator for training end-to-end visual control policies. HyperDrone consists of:

HyperLux : A fast, large-batch ray-tracing renderer for RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow perception

Highly optimized multirotor dynamics simulation

Sim2Real Transfer of a yaw-control policy trained entirely in simulation

1. HyperLux : A fast, large-batch ray-tracing renderer for RGB, depth, semantic/instance segmentation, surface normals and optical flow perception

2. Highly optimized multirotor dynamics simulation
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

In the recent past, several quadrotor simulators have been proposed and optimized for different purposes. We focus on simulating cameras and quadrotor dynamics to support visual control policies, and the main related simulators are listed in Table 1 .

A very popular simulator for this purpose has been Flightmare [ 18 ] . However, it does not support batch rendering and hence is comparatively slow. It has been measured to yield ≈ 230 \approx 230 Frames Per Second (FPS) in [ 19 ] which is prohibitively slow for reinforcement learning which usually requires millions or even billions of samples. Furthermore, it requires proprietary, licensed software to replace the default scenes.

To overcome the low rendering throughput, multiple batch-rendering-based simulators have been proposed. These cluster into Nvidia Isaac-based and Habitat-based simulators. VisFly [ 19 ] is based on a custom version of Habitat [ 23 ] for batch rendering. Habitat in turn uses OpenGL through the Magnum engine. It is the only other simulator that supports quadrotor dynamics, batch rendering and is compatible with the latest generation GPUs (Nvidia Blackwell/5000-series, released in early 2025). However, it falls short of HyperDrone when it comes to fidelity features like motion blur and anti-aliasing. Note that we leave an exhaustive performance comparison for later and only focus on qualitative features in this section.

Aerial Gym [ 20 ] is based on Isaac Gym and implements a batch raytracer mainly for depth perception and semantic segmentation. While depth perception and semantic segmentation is also supported in HyperDrone, our main focus is on RGB observations which are not supported for general 3D mesh scenes (only for simple geometric objects) by Aerial Gym. Furthermore, due to Nvidia Warp limitations, Aerial Gym does not take advantage of ray-tracing cores in modern GPUs. Additionally, Isaac Gym, which Aerial Gym builds upon, was deprecated in mid-2024 and hence Aerial Gym does not support Nvidia Blackwell GPUs (5000 series).

OmniDrones [ 21 ] follows a similar strategy by building onto Isaac Sim. Compared to Aerial Gym it does not implement its own rendering pipeline and relies on Isaac Sim for camera simulation. OmniDrones is built on Isaac Sim 4.1.0 which was released in mid-2024 and hence does not support Blackwell/5000-series GPUs, either. Since the project is not maintained anymore we do not expect this to change.

Initially, when conceptualizing HyperDrone we were planning to build it on top of Madrona [ 22 ] , an open-source batch raytracer and rasterizer that has shown promising performance. However, while investigating Madrona we found that it does not take advantage of ray-tracing hardware in RTX-series cards and that the codebase is relatively complex.

Hence, we concluded that there is a need for a new simulator that focuses on rendering performance while supporting the needs of realistic visual quadrotor simulation like motion blur, anti-aliasing and reflections. While designing HyperDrone we also keep in mind that in the future we should support rolling-shutter simulation as well, even though for now we focus on global shutter cameras.

2026-10-22.title: COWBOY: A Scalable Sim-to-Real Framework for Learning Contextual Whole-Body Manipulation
2026-10-22.authors: Jiahui Yang , Jason Jingzhou Liu , Ray Muxin Liu , Andrew E. Wang , Kenneth Shaw , Deepak Pathak , Ruslan Salakhutdinov
2026-10-22.abstract:
Mobile manipulators must adapt not only to objects, but also to the spatial context in which they appear: where to position the base, how to manipulate, and where to look while navigating surrounding scene geometry. To address this, we present COWBOY, a scalable sim-to-real framework for learning such contextual whole-body manipulation. On whole-body dexterous grasping, COWBOY transfers zero-shot to hundreds of objects and diverse in-the-wild scenes, spanning cluttered tabletops, shelves, drawers, and other unstructured settings.
Rather than learning scene adaptation directly with RL in simulation, a vectorized environment-aware whole-body controller (WBC) handles reaching in thousands of scenes by coordinating base-arm motion, collision avoidance, and active vision. Then, local RL experts are trained in local scenes for object interaction and can be reused across thousands of full-scene layouts. We distill these composed WBC–RL teachers into a single vision policy that controls the mobile base, arm, dexterous hand, and actuated camera from point-cloud observations. The resulting policy exhibits contextual whole-body behavior, automatically adapting base placement, camera viewpoint, arm trajectory, and grasp strategy to observed scene and object geometry. Videos are available at cowboy-manip.com
2026-10-22.introduction:
Humans effortlessly interact with diverse environments and objects in their daily lives. A person reaching for the same object may move very differently depending on whether it lies on an open tabletop, inside a shelf, behind clutter, or within a drawer. These behaviors rely on whole-body adaptation: people reposition their body, adjust their viewpoint, and coordinate their arms and hands to maintain visibility and avoid obstacles.

Similarly, deploying robots in everyday environments requires policies that generalize not only across objects, but also across the spatial contexts in which those objects appear. For mobile manipulators, this is further complicated by partial observability, since onboard sensors provide only an incomplete view of the scene. From this context alone, the robot must coordinate its base, arm, and camera to reach the object, maintain visibility, and avoid collisions. We refer to this scene-conditioned whole-body reasoning capability as contextual whole-body manipulation .

Reinforcement learning (RL) in simulation is a promising approach for learning
contextual whole-body manipulation as diverse training scenarios can be generated at scale. Recent sim-to-real manipulation systems have demonstrated impressive generalization across large object sets; however, they typically do not generalize across diverse environments and are often trained in a single fixed setting [ 26 , 37 ] . Training mobile manipulation policies across varied environments remains challenging because it requires global scene understanding beyond local object interactions, often over high-dimensional spatial representations. This complicates both policy conditioning and reward specification. The difficulty is exacerbated by the high-dimensional action spaces of mobile manipulators, requiring coordination of the base, arm, and perception.

To this end, we present COWBOY, a sim-to-real framework for training mobile manipulation skills across thousands of diverse environments and hundreds of objects, enabling contextual whole-body manipulation learning at scale. Our framework first proposes a vectorized, environment-aware whole-body controller (WBC) that operates across many scenes on a single GPU. Given only an end-effector goal, the WBC coordinates base-arm motion to reach the target while avoiding obstacles in the scene. It also controls an actuated neck to maintain visibility to the object.

Our WBC enables us to decompose contextual whole-body manipulation into two stages: global free-space reaching and local interaction. First, the WBC brings the end-effector near a target object while avoiding obstacles and maintaining gaze on the object. Then, for each desired manipulation behavior, we train a local RL policy
to learn interactions across hundreds of objects. Since each RL policy only needs to handle one type of local manipulation behavior, policy conditioning and reward specification become tractable. Finally, we distill both the WBC reaching behavior and the state-based local policies into a unified vision-based whole-body policy. Importantly, during distillation, we reuse each local policy by generating thousands of full-scene layouts around the local scene, enabling scalable training across diverse scenes and objects.

We demonstrate COWBOY on whole-body dexterous grasping with a mobile manipulator equipped with a 16-DoF hand and an actuated neck for active vision. COWBOY achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, robustly grasping hundreds of geometrically diverse objects across in-the-wild settings, including shelves, drawers, and cluttered tabletops. The policy generates adaptive, context-dependent behaviors, coordinating approach direction, base placement, camera viewpoint, grasp strategy, and collision-avoiding motion from the surrounding scene. Ablations validate the key design choices of our framework and show that they are critical for robust in-the-wild mobile manipulation.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Works

## 2.1 Robot Learning for Mobile Manipulation and Whole-Body Control

Mobile manipulation has largely advanced through demonstration-driven pipelines that learn coordinated base, arm, and end-effector behavior from real-world data, with advances in low-cost whole-body teleoperation [ 13 ] , open-world articulated-object interaction [ 47 ] , active perception from human demonstrations [ 48 ] , whole-body imitation from human demonstrations [ 49 , 40 ] , and scalable household data collection [ 20 ] . Although these systems achieve impressive long-horizon behavior, scaling demonstrations is difficult because each trajectory must encode scene-dependent base placement, approach direction, visibility, and obstacle avoidance.

RL end-to-end whole-body control has become popular for training fast WBC. Beyond direct visual imitation or keypoint tracking frameworks [ 2 , 52 , 46 ] , alternative paradigms leverage residual learning for task-specific manipulation [ 56 ] , adversarial motion priors for emergent mode-switching [ 27 ] , or teleoperation interfaces with real-time coordination [ 15 ] . Recent humanoid systems have further shown visual sim-to-real transfer for loco-manipulation and door opening [ 16 , 50 ] . Spin studied wheeled mobile manipulation with perception, interaction, and navigation [ 41 ] . Deep Whole-Body Control learned unified locomotion-manipulation policies for legged robots [ 12 ] . Visual Whole-Body Control extended this direction to vision-based legged loco-manipulation [ 24 ] . These works demonstrate the promise of simulation-trained whole-body control, but evaluate generalization in settings with more constrained object–environment variation than ours. N 2 M 2 [ 18 ] and Boosted Hybrid RL [ 19 ] use RL to condition base control on end-effector trajectories or 6D targets, while ReLMM focuses on autonomous real-world learning of modular navigation and grasping [ 39 ] .

## 2.2 Sim-to-Real for Manipulation

Sim-to-real RL trains closed-loop manipulation policies in simulation for real-world deployment, enabling data scales beyond physical interaction alone. OpenAI Dactyl showed sim-to-real in-hand reorientation on a Shadow Hand via domain randomization [ 31 ] . DeXtreme demonstrated agile Allegro-hand manipulation [ 14 ] . Visual Dexterity reoriented novel object shapes from depth [ 5 ] , and DexNDM improved in-hand rotation transfer with learned joint-wise dynamics [ 25 ] . Together, these works show robust object- and dynamics-level dexterity but with only the reorientation task.

Beyond in-hand reorientation, recent systems train manipulation policies from different perceptual modalities, including point clouds [ 32 , 6 , 55 , 8 ] , depth [ 26 , 7 ] , and RGB pixels [ 37 , 38 ] . DexFunc and SimToolReal extend sim-trained control to affordance-guided grasps [ 1 , 21 ] , while other work scales sim-to-real dexterity to higher-dimensional action spaces such as bimanual and humanoid manipulation [ 23 , 22 ] . These directions expand the complexity of policies trained in simulation, but are still largely evaluated in relatively fixed environments. In contrast, our framework scales visual policy training over joint object–environment variation.

ManipGen adopts a related local-policy formulation [ 7 ] , but relies on a separate inference-time motion planner. This assumption is difficult for mobile manipulation in unstructured scenes, where robust whole-body planning must operate directly from partial onboard observations. We instead distill local policies and whole-body motion generation into a single end-to-end policy for mobile manipulation, without requiring a whole-body motion planner at inference time.

## 2.3 Whole-Body Control for Mobile Manipulation

Whole-body control coordinates redundant degrees of freedom for task-space objectives like reaching, posture regulation, collision avoidance, and gaze control. QP-based differential IK libraries, such as Pink and Mink [ 4 , 54 ] , simplify composing tasks and constraints. While efficient for single-robot control, collision avoidance requires constrained solves with scene-dependent active constraints, making large-batch execution across many environments difficult.

Optimization-based WBC (e.g., PlaCo [ 10 ] , OpenSoT [ 17 ] , ARC-OPT [ 30 ] ) and MPC frameworks like OCS2 [ 11 ] handle richer constraints and dynamics. However, they introduce per-step or horizon-dependent online optimization problems that are expensive to evaluate in batch.

Reactive methods provide a different trade-off. RMPs produces expressive behavior through geometrically consistent pullbacks [ 33 ] , and geometric fabrics further compose reaching, posture regulation, collision avoidance, and gaze control as metric-weighted task-space policies [ 43 , 45 ] .
We use fabrics not because they are universally more optimal than optimization-based WBC, but because they provide a fixed reactive computation graph that can be evaluated efficiently in parallel across many simulated environments. Appendix A provides a more detailed comparison.

2026-10-22.title: One Policy, Many Styles: Where to Aggregate Preferences for Steerable Humanoid Control?
2026-10-22.authors: Ziqian Huang , Yuzhuo Chen , Shimin Zhang , Junyang He , Xinyue Annie Yang , Animesh Garg
2026-10-22.abstract: Modern robotic agents are increasingly expected to support steerable control, where a single policy can adjust its behavioral style at runtime under changing user preferences. Preference-conditioned reinforcement learning provides this interface, but conditioning alone does not ensure that a requested behavior change is strong, does not leak into unrelated behaviors, and does not compromise task performance. Our evaluation combines Preference Reward Responsiveness (PRR) with coverage and utility metrics. We use these measures to compare reward-level, advantage-level, loss-level, and PCGrad-based aggregation across two humanoid-control frameworks. No aggregation level performs best across all environments and criteria. Experiments show that aggregating objectives early produces a wider range of behavioral responses but greater unintended changes in other objectives, while aggregating them later improves control precision at some cost to responsiveness.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Robotic and embodied agents are increasingly expected to operate under changing user preferences and behavioral constraints. A household robot may need to prioritize speed in one setting, energy efficiency in another, or smooth and safe motion around humans. Rather than training separate policies for every trade-off, an ideal system should support steerable control, where behavior can be adjusted at runtime through a compact and interpretable preference interface.

Multi-objective reinforcement learning (MORL) provides a natural framework for this problem by representing behavior through multiple reward dimensions and conditioning a policy on a preference vector which specifies desired objective trade-offs ( Basaklar et al., 2023a ; Liu et al., 2025 ) . This enables one policy to expose a continuous control interface at test time, but conditioning alone does not guarantee steerability. Increasing one preference may produce little change in the intended behavior, produce unintended behaviors, or compromise the essential tasks that the robot must continue to perform.

This distinction is not captured by aggregate return or Pareto-coverage measures alone ( de las Heras Molins et al., 2026 ) .
A useful evaluation should answer three questions: Does the policy respond strongly when a preference changes? Does the change unintentionally affect other behaviors? Does the policy still perform the task reliably without more failures? We therefore formulate preference-conditioned steerability as a multidimensional evaluation problem and introduce a unified suite based on the Preference Reward Responsiveness (PRR) matrix, Self-PRR, Cross-PRR, Selectivity, and Rank Accuracy. These metrics complement standard utility measures by exposing both intended responsiveness and cross-objective leakage ( de las Heras Molins et al., 2026 ) .

pWe compare reward, advantage, and loss-level scalarization within PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) across two independently implemented humanoid-control systems, ProtoMotions ( Tessler et al., 2025 ) and MimicKit ( Peng, 2025 ) , to test whether the findings generalize across implementations. Within ProtoMotions, we additionally test PCGrad-based gradient surgery ( Yu et al., 2020 ) as a later aggregation point that resolves objective conflicts directly in gradient space. Reward-level aggregation achieves the widest controllable range in ProtoMotions, whereas later aggregation achieves higher hypervolume in fixed-direction MimicKit. Its weaker cross-objective precision persists across both frameworks, but these experiments do not isolate the cause of their different coverage rankings. A preliminary check in MetaDrive ( Li et al., 2023 ) , a driving domain, shows a broadly similar pattern.

Our contributions are:

We formulate preference-conditioned robot steerability as a multidimensional evaluation problem that separates responsiveness, monotonicity, selectivity, task preservation, and failure behavior.

We present a framework that trains preference-conditioned policies under different PPO-based aggregation strategies and evaluates their steerability using the suite above, validated across two independently implemented humanoid-control systems.

We show that the payoff from aggregating preferences early depends on the experimental setting: coverage and utility rankings differ across frameworks, while later aggregation consistently yields higher selectivity and lower cross-objective leakage.

Code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Pref-Align-RL-214C/ .
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Background and Related work

Preference-conditioned MORL trains a single policy over preference vectors so that it can represent multiple objective trade-offs at runtime ( Basaklar et al., 2023b ; Ambadkar et al., 2026 ) . Recent work applies this to humanoid control through a mixture-of-experts architecture ( Li et al., 2026a ) , but fixes a single aggregation point and does not measure cross-objective leakage. We instead study how the aggregation point affects whether changing a policy’s preference input predictably changes its behavior.

In the LLM literature, Constitutional AI shows how written principles can guide behavior through self-critique and AI feedback ( Bai et al., 2022 ) . The constitution shapes training rather than serving as a continuous runtime control. SteerLM enables runtime steering by conditioning generation on desired attribute values, while multi-objective alignment methods combine rewards or model predictions to trade off properties such as helpfulness, safety, and coding ability ( Dong et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . Recent methods extend this idea to fine-grained value priorities and efficient adaptation across a Pareto frontier of user preferences ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026b ) . Together, these works motivate an explicit interface for controlling behavior.

The level at which objective signals are combined during training can affect how well each preference controls behavior. The level at which objective signals are combined during training can affect how well each preference controls behavior. Gradient-surgery methods such as PCGrad address objective conflicts by modifying per-objective gradients before they are combined ( Yu et al., 2020 ) . Preference-conditioned MORL is usually evaluated with Pareto coverage and utility, which do not directly separate intended response from cross-objective leakage. Recent controllability work begins to expose this limitation ( de las Heras Molins et al., 2026 ) . We extend this perspective to embodied control by comparing reward, advantage, and loss-level combination and evaluating responsiveness, monotonicity, selectivity, task preservation, and failure behavior across two robot-control settings.

2026-10-22.title: Navigation Explainability for Object Avoidance with LLMs for Assistive Robots
2026-10-22.authors: Courtney Young , Yi Lian , Taery Kim , Sehoon Ha
2026-10-22.abstract:
Blind and visually impaired individuals face uncertainty when navigating unfamiliar areas. Whether a cane or a guide dog is used for navigation, this may prove to be challenging.
To mitigate this challenge, we present the Context-Aware Navigation Explanation framework that explains guide dog movements for obstacle avoidance and navigation using a large language model.
This system integrates perceptual context with planned future trajectories to generate natural-language explanations of robot movement.
We deploy the system on a Unitree Go2 platform in indoor navigation scenarios and evaluate how different explanation context configurations affect user trust and explanation satisfaction. Results show a strong positive relationship between explanation satisfaction and trust, and suggest that combining obstacle information with future trajectory leads to the most effective explanations. These findings highlight the potential of context-aware language explanations to improve transparency and trust in assistive robot navigation.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Guide dogs can substantially improve the quality of life for blind and visually impaired (BVI) individuals [ 1 , 2 ] . However, high training costs and short service lives limit access to approximately 2% of the BVI population [ 3 ] . To address this gap, researchers have developed guide robots in both wheeled and quadrupedal forms as potential assistive alternatives that can expand accessibility and complement animal guides [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Although these systems have shown promise, successful deployment in real-world environments depends not only on navigation capability, but also on whether users can understand the robot’s behavior, trust its decisions, and interact with it comfortably [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] .

Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and speech interfaces
create new opportunities for assistive navigation robots to interpret their surroundings and communicate their intent with natural language. This capability is especially important in BVI navigation, where users may not directly inspect the environment or infer why the robot is adjusting its path. However, it remains unclear which natural-language explanations are most effective in helping BVI users understand the robot’s behavior and build trust during navigation.

This study investigates how differences in robot guide dog navigation explanations affect user trust. We hypothesize that changes in the content and quality of LLM-generated comments, driven by different input context configurations, will lead to corresponding differences in trust.

We propose a context-aware navigation explanation framework (Fig. 1 ), which generates real-time natural language explanations of a robot guide dog’s navigation behavior. This framework constructs a structured textual context by integrating detected obstacle information with future waypoints from a navigation planner over a short temporal window, then provides this context to an LLM to generate explanations of the robot’s current intent. By varying the amount and type of information included in this context, we evaluate how context design influences explanation satisfaction and overall system trust through a user study.

Our results show a strong positive correlation between explanation satisfaction and trust, indicating that satisfying explanations are closely associated with increased user trust. We also observe that the condition combining obstacle information and future trajectory, with a moderate explanation frequency, generally received the highest ratings for both satisfaction and trust, outperforming both the no-future-trajectory and higher-frequency conditions. Item-level analysis further reveals that users particularly value explanations that are informative and complete to their goals.

Our contributions are as follows:

We propose a context-aware navigation explanation framework that integrates perception and future trajectory information to generate real-time natural language explanations for assistive navigation.

We propose a context-aware navigation explanation framework that integrates perception and future trajectory information to generate real-time natural language explanations for assistive navigation.

We investigate how different types and amounts of contextual information affect explanation satisfaction and user trust through a controlled user study.

We show that combining obstacle awareness with future navigation intent improves both explanation satisfaction and perceived trust compared to limited-context explanations.

We provide insights into which aspects of explanations (e.g., completeness, usefulness, informativeness) most influence user trust in assistive navigation settings.

2. We investigate how different types and amounts of contextual information affect explanation satisfaction and user trust through a controlled user study.

2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Robot Guide Dogs and Assistive Guiding for BVI Users

Robotic guidance for BVI users differs from generic mobile navigation: the system must lead safely in shared spaces while supporting a user’s situational awareness and interpretation of motion decisions, especially when behavior deviates from the user’s expectation [ 11 , 13 , 12 ] .
Early assistive systems explored a range of feedback modalities, including haptic, audio, and tactile interfaces [ 4 , 14 ] ,
highlighting trade-offs between information richness and cognitive load [ 15 , 12 ] . More recent work emphasizes real-world deployment challenges and participatory design with BVI users [ 16 , 10 ] .

Recent “robot guide dog” paradigms extend these ideas using mobile and quadruped platforms that support physical guidance and richer interaction [ 6 , 5 , 7 , 8 ] . These systems frame guiding as an integrated problem spanning navigation, physical interaction, and safety [ 7 ] . User-centered studies further highlight the importance of communication in assistive navigation: BVI users prefer semantic, personalized feedback that helps them interpret the robot’s behavior, while also emphasizing the need to manage cognitive load from excessive audio information [ 11 , 17 , 12 ] .

## II-B Trust and Communication in Assistive HRI

Trust and communication remain central barriers to adoption for assistive robots. Studies with BVI users emphasize that trust develops through consistent behavior and clear communication, and may be difficult to establish without sufficient transparency [ 17 , 13 ] . Participatory design work similarly identifies explainability and user-tailored feedback as critical requirements [ 11 , 16 , 12 ] . Across human-robot interaction (HRI), explanations have been shown to improve users’ understanding of robot behavior, though their effectiveness depends on content and delivery [ 9 , 18 ] .

Recent work studies how robots communicate intent under sensory and attention constraints [ 19 ] . Dialogue-based assistive systems such as DRAGON show how natural language can support BVI users during navigation [ 20 ] , but explaining motion decisions in real time remains an open challenge when they arise from planning constraints and dynamic scenes. At the same time, implicit communication through motion plays an important role: legible trajectories can convey intent, but may still lead to ambiguity when environmental constraints cause unexpected deviations [ 21 , 22 ] . This motivates combining motion cues with explicit explanations, particularly for assistive navigation.

## II-C Explainable Navigation

Explainable navigation aims to help users understand why a robot acts as it does and anticipate future behavior [ 23 , 24 ] . Prior work formulates explanation generation as a design problem over modality, timing, and representation [ 25 , 26 ] , while recent systems leverage vision-language models to generate real-time navigation rationales [ 27 ] . These approaches show that providing explanations can improve user preference and understanding during navigation. Other work frames explanation as resolving mismatches between user expectations and robot behavior, enabling contrastive reasoning such as explaining why one path was chosen over another [ 28 , 29 ] .

To support real-time explanations in complex environments, recent work increasingly leverages foundation models to translate perceptual inputs into grounded natural language [ 30 , 31 ] . Building on these insights, we generate real-time motion explanations conditioned on image observations and predicted future trajectories to help users understand and anticipate robot behavior.

2026-10-22.title: Learning Dynamic Games for Cooperative Iterative Tasks
2026-10-22.authors: Mark Pustilnik , Francesco Borrelli
2026-10-22.abstract: We consider cooperative and iterative tasks involving multiple agents whose interactions are modeled as a dynamic game with shared constraints. We propose a general learning framework applicable to nonlinear and nonconvex dynamic games that uses previously executed feasible trajectories to construct a sampled joint safe set and player-specific cost-to-go functions. At each time step, the agents jointly select a previously sampled terminal state and a Generalized Nash equilibrium used to reach it. A new solution is adopted only if it satisfies a cooperative acceptance rule agreed upon by the players. The framework accommodates individual non-degradation requirements and selection criteria such as weighted costs and Nash bargaining. We show that the proposed framework guarantees recursive feasibility and characterize conditions under which each player’s cost is non-increasing across iterations.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Many robotic systems repeatedly perform cooperative tasks from identical initial conditions, including payload transport and coordinated assembly using multiple manipulators. Previous executions provide trajectory data that can improve subsequent performance. Although
the agents cooperate, each may retain its own dynamics, constraints, and objective, while shared constraints couple their decisions. Dynamic games model these interactions. Learning Model Predictive Control (LMPC) exploits repeated single agent tasks by constructing terminal safe sets and cost-to-go functions from successful trajectories, enabling improvement while preserving recursive feasibility [ 1 ] . Extending this principle to dynamic games requires addressing multiple equilibria with different player trade-offs: improving one player’s cost may worsen another’s. Learning must therefore determine both how to improve previously executed trajectories and how the players agree on which new solution to adopt. In this work, we consider cooperative iterative tasks in which the players agree in advance on rules for selecting new solutions.
Cooperation does not require a common objective: each player retains its individual cost function, while candidate solutions are evaluated according to a jointly agreed criterion. Individual non-degradation can determine admissibility, while weighted costs or Nash bargaining (NB) select among admissible candidates. We propose a general learning framework for dynamic games where each agent uses previously executed feasible joint trajectories to construct a sampled joint safe set. At each time step, candidate solutions connect the current joint state to a previously visited joint state, after which the remainder of a trajectory from a previous successful iteration can be reused. Since the terminal state is selected from a finite set of previously sampled states, the learning problem naturally includes a discrete decision layer in addition to the continuous dynamic-game equilibrium computation.

The framework accommodates nonlinear dynamics and nonconvex costs and constraints, starting from an initial successful feasible trajectory. The resulting performance depends on the initial trajectory, sampled states, and candidates returned by the game solver. The contributions of this paper are:

A learning framework for cooperative iterative dynamic games with shared constraints, jointly selecting terminal occurrences and equilibrium candidates using a pre-agreed cooperative rule.

Recursive-feasibility and individual non-degradation guarantees under stated conditions, supported by an explicitly retained feasible continuation.

A nonlinear, nonconvex three-player demonstration comparing equilibrium exploration and cooperative selection under shared collision-avoidance constraints.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Work

Learning from repeated tasks has been studied through Iterative Learning Control (ILC) [ 2 , 3 ] , including robust formulations that account for non-repetitive disturbances [ 4 ] , as well as through Batch-MPC [ 5 , 6 ] . Extensions of LMPC have considered simultaneous improvement of multiple objectives [ 7 ] , decentralized multi-agent control under shared constraints [ 8 ] , and non-cooperative distributed MPC with iterative learning [ 9 ] . In games with coupled feasible sets, generalized Nash equilibria (GNEs) provide the corresponding solution concept. Normalized equilibria impose a common structure on the shared-constraint multipliers across players [ 10 , 11 ] , whereas non-normalized equilibria enlarge the set of candidate solutions by allowing more general multiplier allocations [ 12 ] . Learned terminal information has also been incorporated into generalized Nash games [ 13 ] , while cooperative criteria such as Nash bargaining can be used to compare candidate outcomes [ 14 ] .

Iterative learning exploits repeated executions to improve performance, while equilibrium selection addresses trade-offs among players. This work combines these perspectives through cooperative selection of terminal occurrences and equilibrium candidates using stored joint trajectories. Feasible continuations and player-wise acceptance support recursive feasibility and individual non-degradation, even when candidate generation is incomplete. The retained backup need not itself be an equilibrium; equilibrium selection determines which candidate trade-offs are explored.
