2026-10-22.title: Flexible Language-Guided Representation Editing for Adaptive Robot Behavior
2026-10-22.authors: Audrey Lee , Nathaniel Dennler , Ilia Sucholutsky , Andreea Bobu
2026-10-22.comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026), Austin, TX.
2026-10-22.abstract: Trajectory demonstrations show robots how to behave but not why, leaving them to guess which features of the task actually matter. Incorrect guesses produce misaligned internal representations and lead to incorrect robot behaviors. Because task features are often semantically defined, we argue that natural language is better suited for specifying features rather than relying on demonstrations. Although existing representation editing methods have proposed using language to specify new features, only allowing additive edits produces feature sets that are often over-specified or too narrowly scoped, especially in sequential editing tasks. We propose the Flexible Feature Editing Pipeline ( Flex ), which uses language models to iteratively refine a robot’s internal representation of task features from natural language corrections via three complementary operations: Add missing features, Generalize existing specific features, and Mask irrelevant features. We evaluate Flex on 2D navigation scenarios, 7DoF Franka tabletop manipulation tasks, and a real-world study using naturalistic human language corrections and real-robot demonstrations. Comparisons against single-operation and unscaffolded baselines show that all three operations are necessary in interactive scenarios, and that Flex achieves consistently higher normalized reward compared to other feature editing approaches while maintaining compact, transferable representations. Project available at https://mit-clear-lab.github.io/FLEX/ .
2026-10-22.introduction:
Imagine a scenario like in Fig. 1 , where a human asks their personal robot to bring them coffee. While the instruction seems simple, executing it well depends on the features , or measurable properties of the environment, that the robot internally uses to represent the task. For example, a user may prefer that the robot stays away from sensitive electronics or that it stays close to the table to avoid damage from spills. Unfortunately, human instructions rarely describe these features explicitly when specifying tasks, forcing the robot to guess which features matter. When the robot guesses incorrectly, the human and robot end up with misaligned representations, and the robot fails to complete the task in the way that the human desires.

A common approach to address the representation misalignment problem is to iterate between specifying features and optimizing reward, often through demonstrations [ 39 , 29 ] . However, demonstrations carry little semantic information, so the robot can only implicitly recover which features actually matter to the user. In contrast, natural language contains rich semantic content. When a user says, “Don’t spill coffee on my laptop!” their language communicates both what matters about the task (avoiding the laptop) and why that matters (preventing damage). Language contains the semantic content that demonstrations lack. We therefore propose that feature specification is better addressed through language, while demonstrations are better-suited for reward optimization once the right features are known.

Even a simple language correction contains a wealth of information when interpreted in context. However, existing methods fail to leverage this fully, either failing to update the robot’s underlying representation in a generalizable way [ 41 ] or continually adding features until representations become redundant and inefficient [ 39 ] . None of these methods account for the full space of ways a feature representation can be wrong: it may be incomplete (missing relevant features), over-specified (tracking irrelevant features), or incorrectly abstracted (tracking a feature at the wrong level of abstraction).

We propose Flex , a flexible feature editing pipeline that uses Language Models (LMs) to adapt a robot’s internal representation of task features in response to natural language corrections. As shown in Fig. 1 , when the human says “Don’t spill coffee on my laptop!”, Flex identifies the correction’s intent and applies three operations: Add introduces the laptop as a relevant obstacle, Generalize broadens the newly added feature to all electronics, and Mask removes the now-irrelevant bowl feature. This yields a feature set aligned with the human’s true intent. Unlike prior methods that support only a single operation, Flex selectively applies whichever combination of edits the user’s language correction warrants.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Reward Learning from Human Feedback. Learning from human feedback is necessary to adapt robot policies to new users and tasks [ 22 , 17 , 42 , 6 ] . Past work has proposed many feedback signals—such as demonstrations [ 16 , 51 , 4 , 48 ] , corrections [ 30 , 5 , 10 ] , rankings [ 20 , 35 , 33 ] , and other user behaviors [ 31 , 26 , 19 , 44 ] —to adapt robot behavior to user preferences. However, many of the most common forms of feedback are underspecified; for example, similar demonstrations can be consistent with many possible reward functions [ 12 , 15 , 9 ] . Resolving this ambiguity requires large amounts of data that are impractical to collect from non-expert users [ 23 , 19 ] . While past work has addressed the data efficiency problem by combining multiple types of feedback [ 31 , 18 , 24 , 36 ] , these approaches collect data and train rewards offline. We instead focus on robots that adapt at deployment time through iterative user feedback.

Specifying Trajectory Features. To make online reward learning tractable for the amount of data that can be collected at deployment time, the robot must restrict its set of reward hypotheses to a low-dimensional space, rather than attempting to learn directly from high-dimensional observations [ 7 , 13 ] . Prior work defines this space by using expressive trajectory features that are either designed by experts [ 1 , 55 , 49 , 27 ] , learned from data [ 29 , 11 , 19 , 28 , 14 , 21 ] , or generated with LMs [ 39 , 34 ] .
The problem of representation misalignment [ 12 , 47 ] arises when these feature sets do not capture what the user actually cares about, which results in the robot failing to complete the user’s desired task.
This problem motivates recent works that allow users to directly edit the feature set to align user and robot
representations [ 39 , 27 ] .
However, these prior methods support only a single type of edit: adding features [ 39 ] , removing features [ 40 ] , or generalizing the scope of features [ 3 ] .
Our work unifies these separate editing operations into a single framework, and demonstrates that all three edit types are necessary to address the full range of representational misalignment types.

Natural Language for Robot Learning. A growing body of work incorporates natural language into robot learning pipelines, using language to clarify task goals [ 41 , 56 , 46 , 8 , 52 , 50 ] , redirect ongoing behavior [ 45 , 18 , 32 ] , or update internal representations such as safety constraints [ 2 , 43 ] .
However, these approaches treat language primarily as a signal for how to perform a task, rather than which features of the environment matter [ 24 ] .
We identify that language carries unique semantic information that makes it particularly well-suited for feature editing. LMs are equipped to leverage this data because they are trained on human-generated data and have reasonable priors over shared preferences [ 54 , 3 , 38 ] , which allows them to efficiently leverage sparse natural language corrections [ 36 , 53 ] .
The iterative nature of our approach provides advantages over approaches that use language solely to specify task goals from single instances of feedback.

2026-10-22.title: inr2action: Encoding Robot Episodes as Neural Implicit Representations for Recall and Action
2026-10-22.authors: Leann Alhashishi , Christos Margadji , Sebastian William Pattinson
2026-10-22.abstract: Long-horizon robotic operation requires memory that scales with essential information rather than execution time. We present a parameter-space memory framework where each episode is stored as a separable object. A neural implicit representation is fitted to episode video from a shared, meta-learned initialization; the resulting weight delta constitutes the memory. Crucially, this delta remains a fixed size regardless of whether the episode spans a hundred or a hundred thousand frames. A learned projector maps the weight delta into token embeddings, conditioning a language model for question answering and a decoder for joint command regression, without frame retrieval at query time. On RoboMME, the language model exceeds chance across all question types, and the decoder achieves a mean R 2 R^{2} of 0.51. Replacing the delta with matched noise drops performance by 11.4 points, while random-origin weights are non-decodable, proving the meta-learned initialization is essential for embedding episode content. By representing individual experiences as fixed-size weight deltas in a common parameter space, this approach decouples memory cost from time horizon and provides a basis for scalable streaming memory.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Robots that operate over extended horizons must remember what they have observed.
When the information that determines the correct action has already left the field of view, a robot without memory can only guess.
In robotic manipulation, the evidence that resolves such a decision can lie seconds, minutes, or in long-horizon deployments hours in the past, and by then the scene itself may no longer show it: a quantity that accumulated over time, a property visible only before it was occluded, a reference fixed at the outset of the episode.
Feeding the entire observation stream back into the policy is not a general answer, as its cost scales with how long the robot has been running rather than with how much of what it saw actually needs to be remembered.
We consider such settings non-Markovian, as the information needed at time t t is distributed across the episode rather than contained in any single frame, a gap that recent benchmarks make explicit [ 1 ] .
Throughout, memory refers to a persistent representation of information that can be accessed independently of the original input that produced it.

Existing sequence models hold information in one of three places.
The first is transient activations: an LSTM’s hidden state [ 2 ] or a transformer’s key-value cache [ 3 ] compresses observed history, but the stored information is bound to the current computation, and once the forward pass ends or the context window closes it cannot be queried on its own terms.
The second is explicit external storage, from differentiable memory matrices [ 4 ] to retrieval over document collections [ 5 ] , which decouples storage capacity from model capacity at the cost of memory becoming a record that must be retrieved before reasoning can proceed.
A third and more recent paradigm encodes memory directly into parameters: Titans [ 6 ] updates a dedicated memory module’s weights during inference, and GradMem [ 7 ] performs test-time gradient descent on learnable memory tokens, both showing that gradient-based optimization at inference time can construct persistent memory for a model.
These methods, however, have been developed primarily for language sequences, and they continually update a single running memory over an incoming stream rather than representing individual experiences as separable memories.

In this work, each robot episode is encoded as its own parameter-space memory: a neural implicit representation (INR) fitted to the episode from a shared meta-learned initialization, whose weights constitute the memory.
A learned projector maps these weights into token embeddings for a language model, which answers natural-language questions about the episode, and the same tokens condition an action decoder that predicts the robot’s next joint command.
No frame is stored, reconstructed, or retrieved at query time.
We evaluate on RoboMME [ 1 ] , a benchmark of 16 non-Markovian manipulation tasks spanning temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory, and show that a memory encoded in this way is legible to a downstream model without frame re-access.
The contributions of this work are:

A formulation of episodic memory for robotics as INR weights, and a tensor-wise projector mapping them into the token space of pre-trained language backbones, yielding, to our knowledge, the first system to answer natural-language questions about a video episode from INR weights alone.

An action decoder of the same weight-tokens that regresses the robot’s optimal next joint command, extending weight-space memory from recall to action.

Matched noise and within-task controls, together with an initialization ablation, attributing both question answering and action decoding to episode content and establishing the shared meta-learned origin as the condition that renders the weights decodable.

2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related work

## II-A Neural Implicit Networks

A neural implicit representation (INR) is a neural network trained to encode a signal as a continuous function, f ⁡ ( x ) → y f(x)\to y , mapping input coordinates directly to signal values rather than storing data on a discrete grid. Once trained, the network can then reconstruct the original signal through forward passes over the learned parameters. SIREN [ 8 ] established the basic feasibility of representing perceptual signals this way: its periodic sine activations counteract the spectral bias of ReLU networks, which limits the fine detail they can represent, and yield high-fidelity reconstructions of images, objects, and audio.

Subsequent work extended what fitted parameters can hold.
NeRF [ 9 ] extended implicit representations from two dimensions into three, so that scene geometry and appearance could be recovered directly from learned parameters.
LeRF [ 10 ] built on this by distilling CLIP and DINO feature embeddings into a NeRF’s weight space, allowing open-vocabulary semantic queries over the encoded scene.

Video, being a substantially larger signal than a static image or scene, makes fitting speed a practical bottleneck for these pixel-wise architectures. NeRV [ 11 ] represents video as a function of time t t , predicting a full RGB frame from a single temporal coordinate rather than querying spatial locations one at a time, which is considerably faster to fit and reconstruct than pixel-wise INRs [ 12 ] .

Fitting cost has itself been a target, falling from hours to seconds through alternative parameterizations [ 13 , 14 ] , amortized prediction of weights in a single forward pass [ 15 ] , or meta-learned initializations that converge in a handful of gradient steps [ 16 ] , making per-instance fitting practical online rather than offline.
This literature establishes that perceptual detail, geometry, semantics, and temporal evolution can all be stored in INR parameters, but it largely treats fitted weights as a route to reconstruction and compression rather than as representations to be queried in their own right.

## II-B Weight Space Learning

Weight space learning treats the parameters of trained networks as a data modality in their own right [ 17 ] .
Functa [ 18 ] (data as a function) introduced this framing for INRs, treating each fitted function as a data point in a learned representation space, with classifiers trained directly on these resulting modulation vectors generalizing to unseen instances.
This effect depends on all fitted functions sharing a common origin, an observation grounded via the Implicit Function Theorem [ 19 ] .

A shared initialization is the standard means of supplying such an origin.
MAML [ 20 ] learns an initialization from which a few gradient updates produce task-specific parameters, which offers a way to produce fitted weights that remain comparable across instances.
COIN++ [ 21 ] applies this combination of shared initialization and fast per-instance fitting to INRs specifically by meta-learning a shared base network and representing each new signal through low-dimensional modulations fitted at inference time.
It is a close precedent for treating adaptation from a common origin as an encoding mechanism.
Gielisse et al. [ 22 ] show that meta-learned SIREN initializations combined with a transformer over the resulting weights can outperform permutation-equivariant alternatives on classification.

Once fitted weights sit in a shared coordinate system, standard learning algorithms can exploit that structure directly.
De Luigi et al. [ 23 ] show that an encoder trained over fitted INR weights for 3D shapes yields embeddings that support retrieval, clustering, and classification.
Weight-space representations have more recently begun serving as direct inputs to foundation models: LLaNA [ 24 ] projects fitted NeRF weights into the embedding space of a large language model, following the training scheme of LLaVA [ 25 ] , so that the model answers natural-language queries about a 3D scene while conditioning on weights rather than on pixels, image features, or rendered views.

## II-C Memory in Robotic Manipulation

Robot manipulation systems store interaction history in the same three places identified in Section I : as an external record, in activations, or, far more rarely, in parameters. The first is the most common and takes two forms. Symbolic approaches derive non-differentiable abstractions from the interaction history, tracking object-centric states [ 26 ] or appending past actions to the input prompt [ 27 ] , with recent systems using large vision-language models to write language-based subgoals or memory summaries [ 28 , 29 , 30 ] . Offloading memory and reasoning externally in this way is costly at inference and makes end-to-end optimization difficult. Perceptual approaches instead retain differentiable visual or multimodal features, either appended directly to the model input as context tokens [ 31 ] or cached in memory banks for later retrieval [ 32 , 33 ] . Recurrent approaches compress history into a fixed-size latent state through iterative updates, from recurrent behavior-cloning policies [ 34 ] to recent state-space models [ 35 , 36 ] . Each of these retains observations, derived features, or activation states.

2026-10-22.title: Real2Sem2Real: 3D Semantic Augmentations for Robot Learning from a Single Human RGB Demonstration
2026-10-22.authors: Matthew Strong , Ankush K. Dhawan , Julien Poffet , Giuse Pham , Jinho So , Monroe Kennedy III
2026-10-22.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-22.comment: Matthew Strong and Ankush K. Dhawan contributed equally. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-22.abstract: Human video scales easily and does not need robot hardware, but existing methods require depth sensing, overlay the robot onto 2D video, or generate data only for the demonstrated objects. We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R), a real-to-semantic-to-real pipeline that turns one monocular RGB video of a human demonstration into thousands of robot demonstrations across the semantic object instances of a category. R2Sem2R tracks the SE(3) pose of each object with DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splats, outperforming existing methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth. R2Sem2R then aligns digital cousins, each generated from one or a few photographs, to the demonstrated objects with a semantic alignment. This alignment matches whole objects and the functional regions of target objects, such as a coffee machine’s tray. R2Sem2R maps the human hand to a feasible robot grasp that extends to the cousins. Robot demonstrations are generated either in IsaacSim, for photorealistic rendering, or MuJoCo, for contact physics, and R2Sem2R can generate over 2,000 episodes in about two hours. On two real robots and four tasks, we train a vision-language-action policy on data from one human video per task, and policies trained on our data match or exceed policies trained on teleoperation across diverse object instances. The project page is available at https://real2sem2real.github.io/ .
2026-10-22.introduction:
End-to-end robot learning maps pixels to actions in closed loop and is a promising route for robots that take on everyday tasks [ 1 ] , but it is data hungry. Vision-language-action (VLA) models are pretrained on more than a million robot trajectories [ 2 ] , and Diffusion Policy [ 3 ] still needs on the order of a hundred demonstrations per task. Robot data has two costs – every trajectory requires human time, and every new object instance requires data collection on that instance, so hundreds of demonstrations of a single object will not generalize to other objects of the same type.

Teleoperation [ 4 ] is physically grounded but difficult to scale, and each alternative does not address every flaw. Demonstration augmentation [ 5 , 6 ] still starts from some teleoperation and needs privileged state or accurate 3D observations. Simulated collection [ 7 ] needs modeled assets and a human in the loop, and handheld grippers [ 8 ] require custom hardware and hundreds of demonstrations per task. Human video [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] must first be annotated with states and actions, which requires motion-capture and depth hardware [ 12 ] or for rendering the robot into inpainted 2D frames [ 13 ] , where objects cannot be moved from their motion in video. Imprecise recovered object motion compounds into drifting poses and implausible geometry (Fig. 2 ) that are insufficient for a source of data.

Real-to-sim-to-real pipelines reconstruct real objects, recover their motion from a video, and render robot demonstrations in simulation with no robot in the loop. Real2Render2Real (R2R2R) [ 14 ] showed that one smartphone scan and one RGB video suffice to fine-tune a VLA, but it augments spatially, not semantically. For example, their exact mug and coffee machine in a human demonstration must be present at deployment, and covering more objects means a scan and a demonstration for every pairing. Digital cousins [ 15 , 16 ] substitute similar simulated assets, but overall similarity does not say where a mug should rest on a new coffee machine. Humans know a mug is lifted by its handle and set on a platform. Given one human video of a mug placed on a coffee machine, why can’t a policy succeed on mugs and coffee machines it has never seen?

The first step is recovering object trajectories. The strongest pose estimators assume a depth sensor [ 17 ] , and RGB-only trackers drift or fail at initialization on textureless objects. We track each object with a DINOv3-distilled Gaussian splat [ 18 , 19 ] , optimizing its pose against feature, photometric, silhouette, and monocular depth-ranking losses from an initialization seeded on the table plane. The grasp comes from the demonstrator’s hand via HaMeR [ 20 ] , following the method in Phantom [ 13 ] .

The second step is augmentation. Beyond perturbing object poses, we add semantic and functional augmentation . Cousins are generated with MV-SAM3D [ 21 ] from one or several images (online, AI-generated, or real photos), and distilled with DINOv3 features. A semantic alignment registers each cousin to the demonstrated object, and for functional placement/motion, a weighted alignment registers each functional and target object by its region of interaction rather than its whole body, so augmentation extends beyond single-object pick-and-place.

Finally, an interactive viewer can be employed to build the simulated scene, a camera optimization matches the simulated camera to the real one without AprilTags, and parallel generation in photorealistic IsaacSim [ 22 ] , or MuJoCo [ 23 ] , generates over 2,000 episodes in about two hours, after about 25 minutes of setup, with no human in the loop. Among prior methods (Table I ), ours is the only one that transfers demonstrations across object instances from a single monocular RGB video.

We present Real2Sem2Real (R2Sem2R) , summarized in Fig. 1 . Our contributions are:

An RGB-only 4D object tracker on DINO-distilled Gaussian splats that outperforms prior methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth;

An RGB-only 4D object tracker on DINO-distilled Gaussian splats that outperforms prior methods and FoundationPose with estimated metric depth;

A semantic alignment of digital cousins for whole objects and functional placement/motion regions, producing demonstrations for every cousin pairing;

Fast, parallel generation in MuJoCo or IsaacSim, enabled by an interactive scene creation tool that ports directly to simulation; and

Nearly 2,000 real rollouts on two robots, where a VLA trained on data from one human video per task matches or outperforms two hours of teleoperation.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# II Related Work

Learning from human video. The embodiment gap must be closed before human video can supervise a policy. DexCap [ 12 ] uses motion-capture gloves and a depth camera, egocentric methods co-train with robot data [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] , and Phantom [ 13 ] overlays a rendered robot on the 2D video, tying each demonstration to its exact viewpoint and scene. VideoManip [ 25 ] , VidAct [ 26 ] , and WARPED [ 24 ] need less hardware but generate data only for the demonstrated objects in question, lacking generalization. WARPED builds a digital twin of the single object demonstrated per task and augments each demonstration tenfold, retexturing and translating the object, scaling the scene, and perturbing the camera, but never changes the object’s shape or geometry . Learning from human video also requires many demonstrations per task, 250 to 350 videos for Phantom and 30 for WARPED (Table I ), whereas R2Sem2R starts from one.

Object pose tracking. BundleSDF [ 27 ] and FoundationPose [ 17 ] track novel objects from RGB-D, so monocular pipelines substitute estimated depth, as VideoManip [ 25 ] and VidAct [ 26 ] do with MoGe-2 [ 28 ] and MoGe-3 [ 29 ] , and accuracy hinges on that estimate (Sec. IV-B ). RGB-only alternatives traditionally fit a differentiable renderer. RSRD [ 30 ] renders distilled DINO features and fails on textureless objects in our experiments, and WARPED [ 24 ] tracks a splat fitted to a SAM3D-generated mesh from a MegaPose [ 31 ] initialization, so its errors start from a generated model. We track a splat distilled from a scan of the real object, initialized upright on the table plane.

Demonstration generation. MimicGen [ 5 ] , RoboCasa [ 7 ] , and DemoGen [ 6 ] multiply teleoperated demonstrations but need privileged state or depth, or some initial teleoperation. R2R2R [ 14 ] removes both by tracking objects in RGB video and replaying them kinematically, and its followers [ 32 , 33 , 34 , 35 ] widen spatial augmentation. All vary where the demonstrated objects are, not which .

Digital cousins and category-level generation. ACDC [ 15 ] introduced digital cousins, and SimFoundry [ 16 ] , WorldComposer [ 36 ] , and RoboCousin [ 37 ] build sim-ready scenes and cousins from video, panoramas, or images, but take their trajectories from teleoperation, scripted skills, or planners, and SimFoundry registers cousins by overall geometry, which does not compute where a placed object must rest. Vision-language agents convert a recording into a simulatable twin [ 38 ] , but each conversion often runs up to an hour per scene and reproduces only one scene in non-modular fashion.
However, some methods transfer a demonstration across instances . Real2Gen [ 39 ] uses two RGB-D cameras and places the object at the center of the target, which does not extend to a tray or a peg. ShapeGen [ 40 ] collects five teleoperated RGB-D demonstrations per task, annotates contacts and keypoints, and trains a shape warping, changing only the manipulated object . AffordGen [ 41 ] transfers annotated keypoints with DINOv2 under the same assumptions. R2Sem2R removes each requirement. It starts from one monocular RGB human video with no teleoperation, annotation, or trained warping, and also varies the target object, in addition to the grasped object. Distilled feature fields [ 42 , 30 ] have helped with retrieval, segmentation, and grasp transfer, and we use DINOv3 features [ 18 ] , distilled into each cousin’s splat, to align whole objects and the contact region from the human demonstration autonomously (Sec. III-C ).

2026-10-22.title: T-WLA: Bridging Slow Vision and Fast Touch
2026-10-22.authors: Kaichen Zhou , Yuzhen Chen , Hannah Yao , Chonghe Jiang , Rao Fu , Xihang Yu , Wei Dai , Bashar Kabbarah , Haoyu Chen , Ishita Goluguri , Zhiyang Dou , Haonan Chen , Fangneng Zhan , Mengyu Wang , Wojciech Matusik , Antonio Torralba , Paul Pu Liang
2026-10-22.abstract:
In contact-rich manipulation, contact conditions can change before a visual policy updates its action plan.
Recomputing the plan through the visual policy adds latency, while tactile feedback alone does not specify how the ongoing motion should be revised for the task.
We introduce T-WLA, a world–language–action architecture that uses shared visual memory to guide both action generation and tactile correction.
At each visual update, the visual branch integrates the current image, task instruction, and retrieved history into a visual memory that conditions base-action generation.
The same memory is cached for a lightweight tactile editor, which combines it with the active action chunk and incoming touch to predict residual corrections to unexecuted actions without rerunning the visual branch.
Future-image and future-pressure prediction provide training-only supervision, encouraging the visual memory and tactile features to capture interaction dynamics relevant to action generation and correction.
We evaluate T-WLA on tactile-conditioned hand-motion prediction using EgoTouch and Tachin, and on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks.
T-WLA reduces finger-joint MPJPE by 30% relative to the strongest reported baseline and achieves an average success rate of approximately 50.0% across real-robot manipulation tasks.
Videos and codes are available at the project website . Keywords: Robot foundation models; Vision–language–action models (VLA); World-action models (WAM); Visuotactile Manipulation; Residual Action Correction.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Contact-rich manipulation refers to tasks whose success depends on precisely managing physical contact with objects or the surrounding environment ( Hogan, 2022 ; Lee et al., 2019 ) .
Tactile feedback complements vision by revealing local contact conditions that are difficult to infer from images alone ( Niu et al., 2026 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Xue et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026b ) .
For example, when inserting a plug into a socket, vision guides alignment and approach, while touch provides feedback on contact and insertion resistance.
Because these conditions can change between visual updates, tactile feedback supports rapid corrections to the ongoing motion.

Despite the importance of tactile feedback in contact-rich manipulation, many general-purpose robot policies rely primarily on vision.
Vision–language–action (VLA) models adapt pretrained vision–language backbones to predict robot actions from visual observations and language instructions ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Physical Intelligence et al., 2025 ) .
World–action models further integrate future-state prediction with action generation, linking control decisions to the anticipated evolution of the environment ( Zhang et al., 2026b ; Yuan et al., 2026 ) .
Without tactile feedback, these models must infer local contact conditions from visual cues, which may limit their response to visually subtle contact changes during precise manipulation.

Recent work incorporates tactile feedback into robot control through variable-rate expert architectures ( Niu et al., 2026 ) , residual adaptation ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , and inference-time policy steering ( Wu et al., 2026b ) . We investigate a complementary question: how can fast tactile feedback correct a slow visual policy between visual updates? Our central idea is to generate asynchronous tactile corrections conditioned on persistent visual memory. The visual branch processes RGB observations at 39.7 Hz, producing a base action chunk and a history-aware visual memory at each update. The tactile branch processes touch at 119.1 Hz, combining recent tactile context with the cached visual memory and the active action chunk to predict residual corrections to its remaining, unexecuted actions. This allows contact feedback to refine ongoing motion without waiting for the next visual update or rerunning the visual branch.

We instantiate this idea in T-WLA, a multi-rate architecture for asynchronous visual–tactile control
(Fig. 1 ).
The visual branch generates an action chunk and a history-aware visual representation, which is cached until the next visual update.
Between these updates, a lightweight tactile editor combines the cached representation with recent tactile observations to produce high-frequency residual corrections to the ongoing action chunk.
This separation allows the controller to respond to changing contact conditions without repeatedly running the visual branch.
During training, future-image and future-pressure prediction regularize the control representations, encouraging them to capture information relevant to subsequent interactions.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:

Memory-guided asynchronous control. We propose T-WLA, which uses the same history-aware visual memory to guide base-action generation and tactile correction.
A lightweight tactile editor uses this memory and the active action chunk to correct unexecuted actions between visual updates, without rerunning the visual branch.

Memory-guided asynchronous control. We propose T-WLA, which uses the same history-aware visual memory to guide base-action generation and tactile correction.
A lightweight tactile editor uses this memory and the active action chunk to correct unexecuted actions between visual updates, without rerunning the visual branch.

Predictive supervision for control. We regularize the visual memory through future-image prediction and the tactile features through both future-image and future-pressure prediction.
These auxiliary objectives complement action supervision, and their prediction heads are removed at inference.

Evaluation across hand-motion prediction and robot manipulation. Experiments on EgoTouch and Tachin show improved finger-joint prediction accuracy, while real-robot tests show that T-WLA increases mean task success from 17.0% to 50.0%. Ablations examine the contributions of tactile input, visual history, and predictive supervision.

A lightweight tactile editor uses this memory and the active action chunk to correct unexecuted actions between visual updates, without rerunning the visual branch.

2. Predictive supervision for control. We regularize the visual memory through future-image prediction and the tactile features through both future-image and future-pressure prediction.
These auxiliary objectives complement action supervision, and their prediction heads are removed at inference.

# 2 Related work

## 2.1 Memory and Action Chunk Execution

A single observation may not provide enough information to determine the next
action. Memory-based policies address this limitation by retaining information
from earlier observations; for example, MemoryVLA stores consolidated perceptual
and cognitive entries that can be queried over long horizons ( Shi et al., 2026 ) . A complementary line of work predicts temporally
extended action sequences. ACT introduced transformer-based action chunking to
reduce the effective decision horizon ( Zhao et al., 2023 ) , while generative
policies such as Diffusion Policy, RDT-1B, and π 0 \pi_{0} generate multi-step
actions with diffusion or flow-based objectives ( Chi et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025a ; Black et al., 2024a ) . Such temporal coherence can
reduce responsiveness when new observations arrive during execution ( Liu et al., 2025b ; Zeng et al., 2026 ) . Bidirectional Decoding improves
closed-loop adaptation by selecting among candidate chunks ( Liu et al., 2025b ) , while Consistency Policy and Streaming Diffusion
Policy accelerate generative action synthesis ( Prasad et al., 2024 ; Høeg et al., 2025 ) . Real-time chunking instead
explicitly accounts for inference latency when transitioning between successive
chunks ( Black et al., 2025 ) . T-WLA addresses a complementary setting: it
retains visual history across policy updates and uses high-rate tactile feedback
to revise the unexecuted portion of an active action chunk.

## 2.2 Tactile Foundation Models

Tactile representation learning aims to produce features that transfer across sensors and tasks ( Bi et al., 2026a ; Tao et al., 2026 ; Heng et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2026c ; Huang et al., 2025 ) .
Heterogeneous Tactile Transformer learns a shared model across sensor types ( Bi et al., 2026b ) , while FG-CLTP aligns tactile features with visual and language representations ( Ma et al., 2026 ) .
Other work explores transferring representations learned from human tactile recordings to dexterous robots ( Zhang et al., 2026a ) and scaling pretraining through tactile foundation models ( Team et al., 2026 ; Zhou et al., 2026b ) .
Our tactile encoder follows this direction through contrastive pretraining on synchronized tactile and hand-pose histories.
Building on tactile representations, several systems study how to incorporate touch into manipulation policies.
Multi-rate architectures allow tactile feedback to influence control between visual updates.
T-Rex assigns vision and touch to experts operating at different rates ( Niu et al., 2026 ) , while Reactive Diffusion Policy combines a slow visual diffusion policy with a fast latent tactile controller ( Xue et al., 2025 ) .
FA-RDP adapts this division to task demand ( Zhuo et al., 2026 ) , and DSWAM organizes world–action modeling into cooperating slow and fast systems ( Zhu et al., 2026 ) .
Residual adaptation provides another mechanism for incorporating touch into existing policies.
ViTaR attaches a lightweight visuotactile residual branch to a frozen backbone ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , while ResTacVLA applies residual adaptation in feature space ( Zhang et al., 2026d ) .
Tactile feedback can also guide action execution through inference-time adaptation.
FBFM introduces asynchronous feedback during flow-matching execution without additional training ( Li et al., 2026 ) , while inference-time policy steering adjusts a fixed policy using vision and touch ( Wu et al., 2026b ) .
Complementary approaches use touch as training supervision without requiring tactile input at deployment ( Gubernatorov et al., 2026 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ) .
These approaches enable tactile feedback to influence action generation and execution. In T-WLA, a cached, history-aware visual representation connects a slow visual policy to a fast tactile editor, which combines visual memory with recent touch to refine the ongoing action chunk. Predictive supervision encourages these representations to capture evolving interaction dynamics, while auxiliary predictors are used only during training and add no inference cost.

2026-10-22.title: VeriCalib: Verifiable Target-Based LiDAR-Camera Calibration
2026-10-22.authors: Xiangcheng Hu , Xieyuanli Chen , Feiyi Chen , Shengli Ren , Shiyang Chen , Guoqiang Ye , Hao Wang , Ping Tan , Steven L. Waslander , Fuchun Sun , Jin Wu
2026-10-22.abstract:
Target-based extrinsic calibration estimates the rigid transform between sensors from a few observations of a known target, and its result is commonly assessed by the root-mean-square error of the fitted residuals. However, this scalar error is computed on the same observations and therefore cannot indicate whether to accept the result, re-extract, recollect or add observations.
This paper presents VeriCalib, which formulates extrinsic calibration as a verifiable estimation problem and reports a calibration state.
The key insight is a two-level extrinsic compensation mechanism, in which the extrinsic compensates the rigid part of each observation error at the residual level, and rotation and translation compensate each other at the parameter level. Consequently, the fitted residual can reveal neither an inconsistency between the observations and the model nor whether the estimated extrinsic is reliable in every direction.
Accordingly, we assess the calibration through a structured covariance that jointly propagates the uncertainty of the camera and LiDAR board features with a known-geometry prior, and estimate its scale as a variance component from the residuals. On this covariance, we decouple rotation and translation to resolve the precision along each direction and guide data collection toward the weakest one. Since this precision presumes consistent observations, we further develop within-view and cross-view checks that examine the internal residual and the rigid discrepancy between observations, respectively, with thresholds that hold their significance level under an unknown noise level. We also extend the minimal detectable bias to the extrinsic to bound the smallest detectable fault along each direction. These criteria form a calibration state that indicates whether to accept the result or how to collect the data.
Experiments in simulation and on real-world robot platforms show that the structured covariance predicts the observed estimation scatter, and that weakest-direction acquisition meets a strict rotation requirement with up to 30 % 30\% fewer observations than D-, A-, and E-optimal designs. Under an unknown noise magnitude, the consistency checks detect faulty observations while removing few fault-free ones, unlike robust estimators with fixed thresholds. Cross-session validation further confirms a verified calibration state.
The code and datasets will be released to support the future research of verifiable state estimation. 1 1 1 https://github.com/JokerJohn/VeriCalib
2026-10-22.introduction:
Extrinsic calibration, which estimates the rigid transform
between two sensor frames, is a core problem in multi-sensor robotics perception.
Every fused measurement passes through this transform,
and its error propagates into dependent tasks as a systematic bias.
Such a bias degrades perception and planning
in autonomous driving ( Bai et al., 2022 ; Dong et al., 2023 ) ,
grasping on embodied platforms ( Fang et al., 2023 ) ,
and the trajectory and map references used for evaluation ( Hu et al., 2024 ; Hu et al., 2025a ) .
Among sensor pairs, the LiDAR-camera pair is widely adopted,
as it combines 3D geometry with 2D visual
semantics ( Lin and Zhang, 2022 ; Koide et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) .
Its extrinsic is commonly estimated from a calibration target with a known pattern,
such as a checkerboard or a circular-hole board,
which provides well-defined cross-modal
correspondences ( Mirzaei et al., 2012 ; Zhou et al., 2018a ; Beltrán et al., 2022 ; Zheng and Zhang, 2026 ; Hu, 2026 ) .

As there is no external ground truth, the calibration result is commonly assessed by the root-mean-square error (RMSE) of its fitted residuals ( Domhof et al., 2019 ; Zheng and Zhang, 2026 ) , its consistency ( Yuan et al., 2021 ) , or covariance ( Brookshire and Teller, 2012 ; Pandey et al., 2015 ; Yamada and Yaguchi, 2024 ) . Figure 1 illustrates the gap: on a set with two extraction errors, a conventional pipeline returns a residual, whereas our method identifies the inconsistent observations and reports a calibration state.
Learning-based assessments likewise return only a binary label ( Tahiraj et al., 2025 ) or a conformal interval ( Cocheteux et al., 2025 ) , and neither specifies the corrective action that a failed calibration requires. Consequently, a large residual provides no criterion
for choosing among accepting the result, re-extracting the features,
recollecting the observations, and adding observations, and even in mass-production calibration the number and placement of targets are determined empirically.

We formulate this task as the verifiable calibration problem ,
which assesses whether the estimated extrinsic satisfies given
precision and detection requirements
and determines the subsequent calibration action accordingly.
Solving this problem involves three challenges.

Independent and nominal noise modeling. Existing uncertainty-aware calibration methods ( Koo et al., 2020 ; Kümmerle and Kühner, 2020 ; Brookshire and Teller, 2012 ) model the target features as independent measurements with a nominal noise magnitude. However, the camera features on one board share the estimated board pose, the LiDAR features share the fitted board plane, and the actual noise magnitude varies across sensors and scenes. As a result, the reported precision and the test thresholds do not match the actual uncertainty, leading to overconfident acceptance or to the rejection of consistent observations.

Independent and nominal noise modeling. Existing uncertainty-aware calibration methods ( Koo et al., 2020 ; Kümmerle and Kühner, 2020 ; Brookshire and Teller, 2012 ) model the target features as independent measurements with a nominal noise magnitude. However, the camera features on one board share the estimated board pose, the LiDAR features share the fitted board plane, and the actual noise magnitude varies across sensors and scenes. As a result, the reported precision and the test thresholds do not match the actual uncertainty, leading to overconfident acceptance or to the rejection of consistent observations.

Coupled constraint analysis. Existing observability analyses of calibration ( Mirzaei et al., 2012 ; Lv et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ) verify only that the extrinsic is observable and, like degeneracy analyses in LiDAR registration ( Zhang et al., 2016 ; Tuna et al., 2024 ) , do not account for the compensation between rotation and translation. As a small rotation and a compensating translation yield nearly the same target observations, this compensation masks weakly constrained directions. Data collection is thus left without a criterion for which target pose to add and when the collected poses suffice.

Insufficient model consistency assessment. Real target observations contain gross errors such as mis-extracted features and wrong correspondences. Existing calibration methods reject them by fixed robust thresholds ( Beltrán et al., 2022 ; Zheng and Zhang, 2026 ; Wiesmann et al., 2024 ) , without a stated significance level or a bound on the smallest fault that passes undetected, which reliability analyses provide only for individual measurements ( Baarda, 1968 ; Abdul Hafez et al., 2025 ) . A faulty observation can therefore pass undetected and bias the accepted extrinsic, whereas a consistent one can be discarded.

The three analyses depend on one another, since the precision and thresholds rest on the covariance and all three presume consistent observations, whereas existing pipelines address them separately through a scalar residual. We therefore represent the observation as a unified structured measurement factor , its residual together with the covariance and the local Jacobian, and resolve the dependence by first selecting the consistent observations under a robust working scale and then evaluating the scale, the directional precision, and the detection limits on the selected set ( Sections 5.5 and 7.2 ). Figure 2 follows this procedure on the head pair, from the factor of each observation to the calibration state that feeds back into data collection.

This paper presents VeriCalib, which formulates target-based extrinsic calibration as a verifiable estimation problem on the structured measurement factor. We identify the root cause that prevents a scalar calibration residual from revealing the extrinsic state as a two-level extrinsic compensation ( Section 4 ). At the residual level, the extrinsic absorbs the rigid part of each observation error, and at the parameter level, rotation and translation compensate each other, so that neither a small residual nor an aligned projection implies an accurate extrinsic. Whereas geodetic reliability analyzes the redundancy of individual measurements ( Förstner, 1987 ) , this mechanism acts on the rigid-body extrinsic and its coupled rotation and translation, and it determines how the observations of a calibration are weighted, which target poses the calibration requires, and which faults it can detect.

Our first contribution ( Section 5 ) is a structured covariance model for target observations, on which every reported precision, threshold, and detection limit rests. Unlike independent feature covariances of nominal magnitude, its shape is derived from the measurement model of each sensor, through the shared board pose in the camera side and the shared board plane with a known-geometry prior in the LiDAR side ( Sections 5.2 and 5.3 ), and its scale is estimated from the absorbed residual components, which alone determine the estimate ( Section 5.5 ). We further quantify the precision gain of the weighted over the unweighted solver ( Theorem 1 ).

As the precision of a calibration is limited by its weakest direction, our second contribution ( Section 6 ) resolves the precision of the extrinsic by physical direction. Marginalizing the compensation between rotation and translation from the information of this covariance yields directional precisions and a weakest-direction score for selecting the next target pose ( Section 6.2 ). Its closed form for the four-hole target further shows that a common increase of the board distance leaves the rotation precision invariant ( Section 6.1 ).

Directional precision holds only for observations consistent with the model. To this end, our third contribution ( Section 7 ) is a model consistency assessment with directional detection limits. A within-view check tests the internal residual of each observation, and a cross-view check tests its agreement with the remaining observations, both at a significance level that holds under an unknown noise magnitude ( Sections 7.1 and 7.2 ). We further extend the minimal detectable bias (MDB) of geodetic reliability ( Baarda, 1968 ; Teunissen, 2018 ) from individual measurements to the directions of the extrinsic, which is, to the best of our knowledge, the first direction-resolved detection limit for target-based calibration ( Section 7.4 ). The three analyses combine into a calibration state, each value of which indicates the next calibration action ( Section 7.5 ).

The framework requires only a target-specific factor construction, which we provide for circular-hole and checkerboard targets ( Section 3.3 ). Section 2 reviews related work and Section 3 formulates the problem. Section 4 analyzes the two-level compensation, and Sections 5 , 6 and 7 develop the first three contributions in turn. Section 8 reports the experiments in simulation and on real-world data, Section 9 discusses the results and the scope of the verification,
and Section 10 concludes the paper.

1. Independent and nominal noise modeling. Existing uncertainty-aware calibration methods ( Koo et al., 2020 ; Kümmerle and Kühner, 2020 ; Brookshire and Teller, 2012 ) model the target features as independent measurements with a nominal noise magnitude. However, the camera features on one board share the estimated board pose, the LiDAR features share the fitted board plane, and the actual noise magnitude varies across sensors and scenes. As a result, the reported precision and the test thresholds do not match the actual uncertainty, leading to overconfident acceptance or to the rejection of consistent observations.

2. Coupled constraint analysis. Existing observability analyses of calibration ( Mirzaei et al., 2012 ; Lv et al., 2022 ; Yang et al., 2023 ) verify only that the extrinsic is observable and, like degeneracy analyses in LiDAR registration ( Zhang et al., 2016 ; Tuna et al., 2024 ) , do not account for the compensation between rotation and translation. As a small rotation and a compensating translation yield nearly the same target observations, this compensation masks weakly constrained directions. Data collection is thus left without a criterion for which target pose to add and when the collected poses suffice.

3. Insufficient model consistency assessment. Real target observations contain gross errors such as mis-extracted features and wrong correspondences. Existing calibration methods reject them by fixed robust thresholds ( Beltrán et al., 2022 ; Zheng and Zhang, 2026 ; Wiesmann et al., 2024 ) , without a stated significance level or a bound on the smallest fault that passes undetected, which reliability analyses provide only for individual measurements ( Baarda, 1968 ; Abdul Hafez et al., 2025 ) . A faulty observation can therefore pass undetected and bias the accepted extrinsic, whereas a consistent one can be discarded.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Target-Based Calibration

Target-based methods estimate the extrinsic from observations of a calibration object with known geometry. Planar checkerboards are the most common targets, whose plane constrains the extrinsic ( Mirzaei et al., 2012 ) and whose edges and vertices yield line and point correspondences ( Zhou et al., 2018a ) . Fiducial markers recover the board pose from a single image, and LiDARTag ( Huang et al., 2021 ) extends their detection to point clouds. Spherical targets ( Tóth et al., 2020 ; Kümmerle and Kühner, 2020 ) and circular-hole boards instead provide features that both sensors localize directly. Four-hole boards are detected by velo2cam ( Beltrán et al., 2022 ) , fitted with a rigid hole-layout template by Domhof et al. (2019) , combined with a checkerboard in JointCalib ( Yan et al., 2023 ) , and registered across mechanical and solid-state scan patterns by FAST-Calib ( Zheng and Zhang, 2026 ) . These known patterns provide a geometric prior for feature extraction and estimation ( Hu, 2026 ) , which targetless and increasingly learning-based methods do not exploit ( Pandey et al., 2015 ; Yuan et al., 2021 ; Koide et al., 2023 ; Petek et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; An et al., 2024 ) .

## 2.2 Noise and Uncertainty Modeling

The precision of an extrinsic depends on both the observation geometry and the measurement noise. Uncertainty-aware methods model the noise with analytic plane covariances ( Koo et al., 2020 ) or probabilistic spherical-target fusion ( Kümmerle and Kühner, 2020 ) , but model the target features as independent. Since all camera features on one planar target are derived from a single Perspective-n-Point (PnP) pose, independent blocks count the pose information repeatedly and understate the uncertainty along correlated directions. LiDAR mapping propagates the point noise to the parameters of a fitted plane ( Yuan et al., 2022 ) , whereas target-based calibration models each extracted LiDAR feature with an independent variance. Our previous work P 2 Calib ( Hu, 2026 ) improves these features with pattern priors, which this paper propagates into their covariance ( Section 5.3 ).

The absolute noise magnitude is rarely known. In LiDAR registration, closed-form covariances derived from white sensor noise ( Censi, 2007 ) are smaller than the errors observed on real data ( Landry et al., 2019 ) , since pose-level errors and sensor biases dominate ( Brossard et al., 2020 ; Laconte et al., 2019 ) . For the calibration result, Cramér-Rao bounds ( Brookshire and Teller, 2012 ; Pandey et al., 2015 ) and Markov chain Monte Carlo posteriors ( Yamada and Yaguchi, 2024 ) depend on assumed noise parameters, and conformal intervals ( Cocheteux et al., 2025 ) are calibrated on held-out data but lack a physical covariance structure. Geodetic adjustment recovers the magnitude from the residuals by variance component estimation ( Koch, 1999 ; Teunissen and Amiri-Simkooei, 2008 ) , which Ulrich and Hillemann (2024) applied to the observation groups of hand-eye calibration. Robot state estimation instead learns noise covariances from sensor data ( Liu et al., 2018 ) , which a single calibration session does not provide, and Hagemann et al. (2022) detect the systematic errors of camera calibration that a white-noise covariance does not represent. Most calibration methods that report a covariance adopt nominal magnitudes ( Brookshire and Teller, 2012 ) , whose error propagates into the reported precision, the MDB, and every test referred to a nominal χ 2 \chi^{2} threshold. In this paper, we assemble the covariance shape of each observation into a single cross-modal residual covariance and estimate its scale from the residuals as one global variance component ( Section 5 ).

## 2.3 Constraint Analysis

Observability analysis determines which calibration parameters are constrained by the collected data, and it has been conducted for LiDAR-camera ( Mirzaei et al., 2012 ; Fu et al., 2020 ) , LiDAR-inertial measurement unit (IMU) ( Lv et al., 2022 ) , and visual-inertial calibration ( Yang et al., 2023 ) . Several methods further select informative data segments or target poses by maximizing a scalar function of the information matrix ( Maye et al., 2016 ; Peng and Sturm, 2019 ; Lv et al., 2022 ) . However, a calibration in which all parameters are observable may still constrain certain physical directions only weakly, and a scalar criterion does not indicate which directions these are.

Direction-resolved analysis has been studied mainly in LiDAR registration, where degeneracy detection examines the spectrum of the information matrix ( Zhang et al., 2016 ; Nobili et al., 2018 ; Hinduja et al., 2019 ; Hatleskog and Alexis, 2024 ) . X-ICP ( Tuna et al., 2024 ) analyzes the rotation and translation blocks separately, whereas our previous work DCReg ( Hu et al., 2026 ) eliminates their coupling through Schur complements, which has also been adopted for visual-inertial initialization ( Xu et al., 2026 ) . These methods assume a nominal noise model and analyze registration rather than calibration. In this paper, we show that the rotation-translation compensation also arises in target-based calibration, as the parameter-level part of a two-level compensation ( Section 4 ), and form the Schur complements from the structured covariance, so that their inverses are calibrated directional precisions ( Section 6 ).

## 2.4 Consistency Assessment and Reliability

Reliability theory originates from geodetic adjustment, where Baarda’s data snooping ( Baarda, 1968 ) tests individual observations against the assumed model, and the associated MDB quantifies the smallest fault that the test detects at a specified significance level and power. Later studies formalized the distributions of these statistics ( Teunissen, 2018 ; Imparato et al., 2019 ; Zaminpardaz and Teunissen, 2025 ) , and Förstner (1987) applied the analysis to mensuration problems in computer vision, where the redundancy of each measurement determines the fraction of its error that the estimate absorbs. In robotics, integrity monitoring has quantified the localization safety of Kalman filtering ( Duenas Arana et al., 2020 ) , fixed-lag smoothing, and simultaneous localization and mapping ( Abdul Hafez et al., 2020 ; Abdul Hafez et al., 2025 ) . Brunson and Wang (2025) applied the MDB to the pre-analysis of IMU error calibration in the integration of a global navigation satellite system with an IMU. In these applications, faults are defined on individual measurements or landmarks, and no target-based calibration method reports a detectability limit along the directions of the extrinsic.

Calibration results are also checked by repeatability, agreement with a reference calibration, or visual inspection, and none of these assessments provides a threshold calibrated to the noise of the observations. Fault tests in calibration act at two levels ( Table 1 ). Within-observation tests reject a board by geometric thresholds or RANSAC on its own features ( Beltrán et al., 2022 ; Zheng and Zhang, 2026 ) , and cross-observation tests reject a board whose residual against the joint estimate exceeds a robust threshold ( Fischler and Bolles, 1981 ; Yang et al., 2020 ; Wiesmann et al., 2024 ) , although a biased observation of high leverage pulls the fit toward itself and leaves a small residual. The learned detector of Tahiraj et al. (2025) instead classifies the whole calibration without a controlled false-alarm rate. Certifiable algorithms ( Yang et al., 2021 ; Yang and Carlone, 2023 ; Wise et al., 2026 ) and globally optimal estimators of other inter-sensor misalignments ( Hu et al., 2025b ) certify the optimality of the estimate for a given model, but do not assess whether the measurements are consistent with that model.

As Table 1 shows, a covariance modeled by a prior method is independent across features and mostly of fixed or learned scale, constraints are analyzed on the coupled six degrees of freedom, and no prior method reports a detection limit, so that the three challenges are addressed by separate literatures, each assuming the noise magnitude, the nominal noise model, or the calibrated covariance that another must supply. We therefore formulate all three analyses on a single structured measurement factor ( Section 4 ).

2026-10-22.title: Learning-Enhanced Observer for Sensorless Task-Null-Space Compliant Control
2026-10-22.authors: Nuo Chen , Ya-Jun Pan , Onur Toker
2026-10-22.abstract: This paper presents a novel framework integrating a robust wrench observer with a hybrid pose and force controller for physical Human-Robot Interaction (pHRI). In pHRI tasks, robots are expected to perform task-space motions robustly while remaining compliance with human disturbance, which proposes distinct control objectives. Most existing approaches focus mainly on either robustness or compliance and rely on force sensors for real-time tracking. To address these limitations, we propose a novel framework with the following key contributions. Firstly, a neural network (NN) is trained to improve the observer performance by compensating for system friction and unmodeled dynamics. Secondly, a task-null-space decomposition is applied to separate the joint velocity and reduce the effect of the human disturbance on the observer. Finally, a hybrid pose and force controller is introduced to achieve the end-effector pose and force tracking. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework provides robust and accurate wrench estimation while maintaining reliable pose and force tracking performance. The proposed approach offers an effective solution and framework for pHRI without the need of force/torque sensor measurements which can be applied to many robotic manipulator platforms which do not have force/torque sensors.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Physical human-robot interaction (pHRI) has received increasing attention due to the need of humans and robots to share the same workspace. Compared with traditional robotic tasks, pHRI requires the robot to achieve two different objectives at the same time. On one hand, the robot should accurately complete its task, such as position, orientation, and force tracking. On the other hand, it should remain compliant when unexpected human interaction occurs to ensure safety. Therefore, an effective pHRI framework should provide accurate task execution, reliable interaction state estimation, and compliant response to human disturbances.

Force control is necessary for robotic tasks which involve physical contact with humans or the environment. In literature, commonly used force control approaches include the direct force control [ 4 ] , hybrid position and force control [ 5 , 11 ] , impedance control [ 19 ] , and admittance control [ 16 , 23 ] . The hybrid position and force control usually regulates motion and interaction force in different task directions, while the impedance and admittance control regulate the relationship between the motion and force. Some recent studies have combined these control strategies to achieve both accurate force tracking and compliant motion. Hybrid force-impedance controllers were developed to achieve force tracking during fast end-effector motions [ 14 ] and large force pulling [ 25 ] . In [ 10 ] , a framework to combine force regulation and compliant behavior within a passivity formulation is presented. In [ 29 ] , an impedance-admittance framework to improve compliance and adaptability in changing conditions is proposed. These studies have shown the effectiveness of hybrid control in different interaction tasks. However, the force regulation and compliant control often require a reliable interaction force measurements from force and torque sensors.

Access to the interaction force is an important part of pHRI. Force and torque sensors can provide direct measurements of external wrench [ 13 , 1 ] , but they often increase the hardware cost and may not be available in all robotic systems. Force/torque measurements often are noisy and need signal processing before applied to the controller. Observers provide an alternative solution by estimating end-effector wrench from robot dynamics and available joint motion [ 3 ] . Among them, momentum observers are commonly used because they do not require noisy acceleration [ 18 , 9 ] . However, the estimation accuracy may be affected by joint friction, unmodeled dynamics, and control errors [ 15 ] . To address these limitations, recent studies have applied adaptive [ 21 ] and learning-based compensation [ 17 ] to improve the estimation performance. Moreover, for redundant manipulators, external disturbances may generate joint motion that does not contribute to the task-space motion [ 27 ] . Such motion can appear in the null-space while the end-effector task remains almost unchanged [ 28 ] . However, conventional momentum observers are usually constructed using the overall joint motion, meaning that the human null-space motion may be incorrectly reflected in the task-space estimation. This issue is especially important in pHRI, where human applied disturbance cannot be fully rejected but should be handled differently from the task-related motion.

In pHRI, robustness and compliance are often treated as two independent objectives. Robust controllers are designed to reject external disturbances and maintain accurate task execution, while compliant controllers allow the robot to respond compliantly to human and/or the environment interaction. Most existing approaches mainly focus on designing different controllers and switching between them according to different states [ 2 , 26 , 8 , 31 ] , making it difficult to achieve both tracking and disturbance rejection objectives at the same time. Moreover, many studies on the pose and force control are conducted on 2D-flat surfaces [ 30 , 22 , 12 ] , limiting their applicability to real-world tasks. Motivated by these challenges, we aim to achieve the robust end-effector task performance while allowing a compliant motion under human applied disturbance. For a redundant manipulator, human interaction can be accommodated through null-space motion without changing the desired end-effector behavior. The overview of the proposed framework is illustrated in Fig. 1 . The proposed framework consists of an observer module and a hybrid controller for simultaneous task execution and compliant pHRI. The observer combines a conventional momentum observer with a task-null-space decomposition and neural-network (NN) compensation to estimate the end-effector interaction force while reducing the influence of null-space human disturbances. Based on the estimated force, the controller integrates position, orientation, and force tracking with task-space admittance and null-space compliant control to generate the commanded torque, enabling a desired robust task-space performance together with a compliant interaction with human.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

A new NN-enhanced momentum observer with task-null-space interaction decomposition is proposed for sensorless external force estimation. The NN compensates for observation errors caused by joint friction and model uncertainties. The proposed decomposition separates the estimated task-space force from null-space human interactions. Compared with the learning-based observer in [ 4 ] and [ 17 ] , this design eliminates the influence of null-space disturbances on the NN-enhanced observer.

A hybrid pose and force controller is developed by integrating the Cartesian position and orientation tracking, force regulation, task-space admittance control, and null-space compliant control. Unlike the 2D-flat surface tasks in [ 30 ] and [ 22 ] , the proposed controller enables the simultaneous position, orientation, and force tracking on a 3D-curved surface. Meanwhile, it achieves a compliant behavior to ensure both task robustness and pHRI safety at the same time instead of the need of mode switching as presented in [ 2 ] and [ 31 ] , which may cause instability.

The proposed observer-controller framework is evaluated on a 7-degree-of-freedom (DoF) Franka Emika Panda robot. Experimental results under different trajectories and interaction scenarios demonstrate an improved force estimation performance, accurate pose and force tracking, and effective compliant responses in null-space.

In summary, the proposed approach offers a new and feasible solution and framework for pHRI without the need of force/torque sensor measurements. As a result, the new framework can be applied to many robotic manipulator platforms which often do not have force/torque sensors. One example is that for underwater robotic manipulators, it is challenging to install force/torque sensors at the end-effector in the underwater environment.
