2026-10-22.title: Causal world models under physical parameter shifts
2026-10-22.authors: Chu Lin , Yi Sun
2026-10-22.abstract: World models predict how embodied systems evolve under actions, but their accuracy can degrade when physical conditions move outside the training distribution. We study two components of causal modeling: which inputs a predictor may use, and how its mechanism computes their effects. In a synthetic benchmark with shortcut features, a frozen dependency mask derived from paired interventions reduces mean out-of-distribution (OOD) RMSE from 1.769 for a fully connected predictor to 0.697, close to the generator-oracle mask (0.694). For robot link-mass extrapolation in CausalWorld, with disjoint training and test mass ranges, we develop finger-local world models in which link masses enter inertia and dynamics-bias terms through explicit affine coefficients, actions act through either a learned torque network or the known PD controller, and learned residuals capture contact-related effects. Compared with a separately trained control whose mass inputs are fixed at training means, the known-PD model turns out-of-range masses into a consistent predictive gain: median time-averaged joint R 2 R^{2} over 150-step rollouts rises from 0.609 to 0.727, with improvement in all ten task–seed runs (exact two-sided sign test, p ≈ 0.002 p\approx 0.002 ). In a shared 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent robotic world model (RWM) configuration (median joint R 2 R^{2} of 0.755–0.768 versus 0.752), whereas supplying out-of-range masses sharply degrades the MLP and recurrent predictors. These results indicate that how a physical parameter enters the dynamics mechanism determines whether its out-of-range value helps or harms prediction.
2026-10-22.introduction:
World models are used to predict the evolution of embodied systems as they execute actions [ 1 ] . Their prediction accuracy may degrade when physical conditions deviate from the training environment. Recent theory connects generalization across multi-step goals to learned predictive world models [ 2 ] . Embodied applications require these models to remain useful under changing conditions, such as when a robot handles a different payload or operates with different physical properties. Pearl’s structural causal model (SCM) framework separates structural dependencies from the functions governing those relationships [ 3 ] . This separation motivates two questions for a world model: which inputs should a predictor use, and how should its dynamics mechanism compute their effects?

Causal dynamics models, such as CDL [ 4 ] and recent structure-distribution approaches [ 5 ] , learn or estimate dependencies between current state, action, and next state, and use them to restrict irrelevant inputs to the dynamics predictor. Such constraints remove direct prediction paths from excluded shortcut inputs. However, if the OOD shift involves a true causal factor, such as a heavier robot link, the relevant dependency must remain. The computation performed after reading the shifted value is then determined by the mechanism. Input selection alone does not specify how this function should extrapolate. Recent context-aware mechanical models and structured physical world models further motivate examining how parameter information enters the dynamics mechanism [ 6 , 7 ] .

We develop a robot world-model configuration that assigns physical parameters and control inputs distinct roles: link masses enter inertia and dynamics bias through explicit affine coefficients, actions produce torque through the known PD controller, and a neural residual models contact-related effects without directly receiving robot masses. The dependencies are fixed to each finger’s local state and action, with shared object context. We compare this configuration with an MLP and mass-affine dynamics with learned torque under the same input routing. Each model is paired with a separately trained mass-information control: mass inputs are removed from the MLP or fixed at their training means in the structured models. A complementary synthetic experiment uses an intervention-derived mask to evaluate shortcut dependence. Figure 1 summarizes the robot architecture and prediction procedure.

The experiments connect dependency selection to physical parameter extrapolation. Frozen intervention-derived masks reduce mean synthetic OOD RMSE by 60.6%. In CausalWorld, supplying out-of-range link masses to an unstructured MLP or to a recurrent robotic world model sharply degrades prediction, whereas the known-PD mass-affine model improves its median time-averaged joint R 2 R^{2} over 150 steps from 0.609 for its fixed-mass-input control to 0.727. The median within-run benefit of mass information is 0.121 under the heavy-mass shift, compared with 0.009 within the training mass range. In a shared 100-step benchmark, the learned-torque model is competitive with the strongest recurrent baseline (median joint R 2 R^{2} of 0.755 with actual masses and 0.768 with fixed mass inputs, versus 0.752), and the known-PD model retains a positive mass benefit in every run.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

A mass-informed robot world-model design. We develop finger-local mass-affine dynamics with learned-torque and known-PD variants. Masses enter inertia and bias through explicit coefficients, while torque and residual networks use mass-excluded inputs. Joint integration and a separate object-state predictor generate future trajectories.

Competitive OOD prediction in a shared CausalWorld benchmark. Over a common 100-step forecast, the learned-torque model reaches median joint R 2 R^{2} of 0.755 with actual masses and 0.768 with fixed mass inputs, compared with 0.752 for the strongest tested RWM configuration, with slightly lower joint NRMSE and object-position RMSE and without using observation history. The accuracy margins are small; the larger difference lies in how the models respond to out-of-range mass inputs, which sharply degrade the MLP and recurrent predictors.

Consistent predictive benefit from out-of-range masses. Separately trained mass-information controls show that the known-PD design improves median 150-step mean joint R 2 R^{2} from 0.609 to 0.727. Actual masses improve prediction in all ten task–seed runs in both the 150-step ablation and the 100-step benchmark; the latter yields a median paired mass gain of 0.071 (exact two-sided sign test, p ≈ 0.002 p\approx 0.002 in each case).

2026-10-22.title: RoPT: Robust 6DoF Object Pose Tracking in Video
2026-10-22.authors: Yongqing Liang , Yuzhong Chen , Sihang Li , Junsuk Kim , Chase Kidder , Hui-ping Wang , Yunzhi Xu , Raihan Haque , Yubiao Zhang , Chen Feng
2026-10-22.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-22.abstract:
Accurate 6-DoF object pose tracking is essential for robotic interaction, yet conventional monocular pipelines frequently suffer from catastrophic divergence under rapid object motion.
We present RoPT, a robust tracking framework engineered to overcome this limitation by unifying visual perception, temporal kinematics, and global re-localization into a tightly coupled closed loop.
Unlike existing open-loop trackers, RoPT delivers three critical capabilities that fundamentally alter system resilience. First, the visual perception component tracks object masks to robustly handle partial and severe occlusions. Second, a kinematic factor graph regularizes frame-to-frame updates, forecasts forward pose predictions, and drives a parallel multi-hypothesis verification scheme to bypass local minima. Finally, an active re-localization module transforms the pipeline into a closed-loop system, making it failure-aware and capable of deterministic self-recovery. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework across challenging benchmarks alongside real-world robotic demonstrations, achieving significantly higher tracking survivability under rapid motion.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Robust 6DoF object pose tracking serves as a foundational pillar in modern robotics by providing the precise geometric awareness necessary for seamless human-robot collaboration and complex manipulation. 6DoF pose estimation involves determining the full rigid transformation of an object in three-dimensional space, which encompasses its translational position and rotational orientation relative to a defined coordinate frame. While recent breakthroughs in video understanding have significantly advanced 2D object localization and mask segmentation, these methods often operate purely in the image plane. Such approaches fail to provide the full spatial orientation and geometric grounding required for a robot to interact reliably with the physical world. Consequently, a critical discrepancy remains between existing video understanding frameworks and the requirements of robotic control.

The effectiveness of a tracking system depends on the two critical attributes of robustness and failure-awareness. Robustness entails the ability of an algorithm to remain accurate during high-speed motion and significant fluctuations in object appearance. Conversely, failure-awareness requires the system to actively monitor its own tracking state, dynamically quantifying uncertainty so it can flag tracking anomalies before drift compounds irrecoverably. In real-world deployments or data-driven imitation learning pipelines, losing the 6-DoF tracking of a target object is catastrophic, causing a complete breakdown in policy execution and resulting in total failure of the entire manipulation process. Despite these high stakes, conventional frame-to-frame local refinement pipelines [ 26 , 24 ] fail on both counts.
When subjected to sudden high-acceleration displacements, objects frequently shear entirely out of the local tracking crop, causing visual networks to process background clutter and become trapped in false local minima. Furthermore, because these monocular trackers operate as open-loop systems, they lack the structural capacity to detect their own divergence, leading to permanent task failure. To achieve true tracking resilience under real-world dynamics, a framework must not only anticipate motion through continuous temporal regularization but also possess a deterministic mechanism to self-heal once visual tracking breaks.

To address these challenges, we introduce RoPT, a robust 6-DoF object pose tracking framework designed specifically to bridge the gap between fragile visual perception models and the rigorous demands of dynamic robotic manipulation. While techniques such as mask-based tracking, kinematic filtering, and feature-based re-localization have been explored individually in literature, isolated components are insufficient to handle the compounding errors of high-speed physical interactions. Our primary contribution to the robot learning community lies not in a single algorithmic silver bullet, but in a meticulously engineered, closed-loop system architecture that balances accuracy, resilience, and computational efficiency. We observe that robustness against rapid, erratic object motion, a ubiquitous challenge in contact-rich tasks and teleoperation,
has received disproportionately little attention due to its inherent difficulty. RoPT explicitly tackles this by tightly integrating continuous kinematic velocity forecasting with a parallel multi-hypothesis verification scheme and a deterministic, failure-triggered self-recovery module. By intelligently routing expensive computational resources only when geometric ambiguity or catastrophic tracking loss occurs, the framework achieves near real-time performance at 18.6 FPS, ensuring it remains practical for latency-sensitive control and imitation learning pipelines.
In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

Resilience to High-Acceleration Dynamics: We propose RoPT, a closed-loop 6-DoF tracking framework that maintains unbroken trajectory consistency during rapid, erratic object motions where existing state-of-the-art trackers catastrophically diverge.

Kinematic Factor Graph-Enabled Multi-Hypothesis: We introduce a continuous temporal graph backend that drives a parallel multi-hypothesis verification scheme, allowing the system to gracefully bypass local geometric minima and severely degraded 2D masks.

Failure-Aware Active Self-Recovery: We design a deterministic re-localization module that automatically detects catastrophic tracking divergence and instantly self-heals by matching real-world observations against predictive synthetic CAD renderings.
2026-10-22.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

The integration of 6DoF object tracking has become a cornerstone for complex robotic tasks, ranging from aerial manipulation [ 20 ] to autonomous drone-based grasping [ 21 ] . Beyond basic pick-and-place, recent work has utilized high-fidelity tracking to enable visual servoing through point-tracking [ 22 ] and reactive manipulation in highly dynamic environments [ 4 , 3 ] . These frameworks also play a vital role in human-robot interaction via VR [ 1 ] and reducing uncertainty during grasping tasks [ 2 ] . Most notably, real-time tracking has facilitated high-speed capabilities, such as catching flying objects [ 31 ] and online replanning [ 19 ] .
Despite these advancements, these applications remain tethered to the accuracy of the underlying pose estimator. Existing frameworks often struggle in real-world settings characterized by rapid motion or near-field constraints, where depth information is either unavailable in web-based video data or rendered invalid by the minimum working distance of active sensors during close-range manipulation.

Existing 6DoF perception frameworks are generally categorized into static pose estimation and temporal tracking. Static estimation is further divided into image-based methods that rely on learned categorical priors [ 11 , 15 , 14 , 9 , 12 ] and model-based methods that utilize explicit 3D geometry for alignment [ 18 , 16 , 26 , 7 , 29 , 13 , 24 , 30 , 8 ] . While model-based approaches typically yield higher geometric precision by leveraging CAD-defined constraints, they mainly focus on local pose refinement and assume the pose changes between frames are small.
Our work moves beyond this assumption and provide a robust tracking framework under any object motions.

Recent large-scale foundation models has revolutionized 2D perception by providing unprecedented zero-shot generalization for segmentation and feature matching, such as EdgeTAM [ 32 ] , MAST3R [ 10 ] and VGGT [ 23 ] .
Our work bridges this gap by utilizing these foundation models as a robust perception backbone for robotic visual perception.

2026-10-22.title: Reinforcement learning for hardware acceleration and system-level optimization on FPGA and integrated-circuit platforms: A survey
2026-10-22.authors: Hamza Kheddar
2026-10-22.subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Performance (cs.PF); Robotics (cs.RO); Systems and Control (eess.SY)
2026-10-22.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for enabling adaptive, autonomous, and self-optimizing behavior in modern computing systems, particularly as applications increasingly migrate toward embedded, edge, and heterogeneous hardware platforms. Field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and integrated circuits (ICs) offer compelling advantages for RL deployment, including low latency, energy efficiency, and fine-grained architectural customization, but they also introduce unique design challenges that differ substantially from conventional CPU- and GPU- based implementations. This review presents a comprehensive survey of RL implementations on FPGA and IC platforms, with a particular emphasis on architectural design, performance measurement, and hardware–algorithm co-design. A broad body of more than one hundred studies is systematically analyzed and organized into major RL families, ranging from model-based Markov decision processes and classical value-based methods to deep RL, Actor-critic (AC), policy-gradient (PG), and multi-agent approaches. The review further categorizes existing works according to abstraction levels, hardware realization strategies, and application domains, highlighting how different RL algorithms map onto reconfigurable and fixed hardware substrates. In contrast to prior surveys that focus narrowly on specific algorithms or platforms, this work provides a unified perspective spanning both FPGA and IC implementations, encompassing acceleration techniques, reconfigurable hardware approaches, energy-aware control, and system-level optimization. Detailed comparisons are provided in terms of resource utilization, latency, throughput, power consumption, and achieved performance gains. Additionally, this review identifies recurring architectural patterns, discusses practical limitations, and outlines open research challenges and future directions for RL-driven intelligent hardware systems. By consolidating design insights, evaluation metrics, and application trends, this review aims to serve as a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners working at the intersection of RL and hardware platforms.
2026-10-22.introduction:
Recent years have witnessed a growing shift toward intelligent, autonomous decision-making embedded directly within computing systems, with increasing emphasis on assessing the real-world applicability and feasibility of algorithms that demonstrate strong performance under simulation-based evaluations. As workloads become increasingly dynamic and heterogeneous—particularly in networking and edge computing, cyber–security, robotics [ 8 ] , natural language processing, intelligent sensing, and embedded environments—traditional static control and optimization techniques, such as proportional–integral–derivative control and fixed-rule heuristic approaches [ 108 ] or meta-heuristic-based optimization methods [ 127 ] , often struggle to cope with variability in data rates, power budgets, timing constraints, and environmental conditions. These approaches are typically designed around fixed operating assumptions and lack the adaptability required to respond effectively to non-stationary workloads or unforeseen runtime disturbances.

RL ( RL ), as a core paradigm within ML ( ML ), has gained prominence in this context because it provides a principled framework for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. By continuously interacting with an environment and updating its policy based on observed rewards, an RL agent can learn to adapt its behavior online, even when system dynamics are partially unknown or change over time. This capability makes RL particularly attractive for modern computing platforms that must balance competing objectives such as performance, energy efficiency, latency, and reliability under tight operational constraints. However, translating RL from software-centric implementations to practical hardware platforms introduces significant challenges. Many RL algorithms rely on iterative updates, stochastic exploration, and memory-intensive computations that are difficult to reconcile with the strict latency, power, and determinism requirements of embedded systems. Implementations based purely on general-purpose CPU or GPU often suffer from high energy consumption, unpredictable execution timing, and limited scalability, which restrict their suitability for real-time or resource-constrained applications.

FPGA ( FPGA )s and IC provide an alternative hardware substrate that fundamentally reshapes how ML , particularly RL , can be realized in practice. FPGA provide fine-grained parallelism, customizable datapaths, and reconfigurability, allowing RL algorithms to be mapped onto hardware architectures tailored to specific workloads and constraints. IC -based realizations, including ASIC and SoC platforms, further extend these advantages by enabling deterministic execution, compact form factors, and ultra-low power operation. At the same time, these platforms impose stricter design constraints, limited flexibility after deployment, and increased development complexity compared with software-based solutions. As a result, the intersection of RL with hardware design has evolved into a multidisciplinary research area encompassing algorithm–hardware co-design [ 64 ] , hardware acceleration [ 90 , 41 , 58 ] , architectural specialization [ 25 ] , numerical precision optimization [ 5 ] , and system-level control, including digital twin–based frameworks [ 106 ] . In this emerging landscape, RL plays a dual role: it can be treated as a workload to be accelerated on hardware, and it can also serve as a control mechanism for the hardware itself, governing tasks such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, resource allocation, scheduling, partial reconfiguration, and energy management. This duality blurs the traditional boundary between learning algorithms and hardware platforms, creating new opportunities as well as new design challenges. Despite rapid progress, the existing literature on RL implementations for FPGA and IC platforms remains fragmented.

Motivated by the increasingly practical shift of RL from a purely algorithmic concept to a hardware-constrained workload, this review consolidates and structures the fast-growing body of RL implementations on FPGA and IC platforms.
In particular, this survey emphasizes real-time pattern recognition and perception-driven decision-making systems, where hardware constraints critically affect learning efficiency, latency, energy consumption, and deployment feasibility.
Instead of revisiting algorithmic fundamentals, it adopts a hardware-centric lens to clarify how design and implementation choices shape real-world realizations of RL .
The review organizes the literature into coherent categories and distills recurring design patterns, trade-offs, and limitations, thereby clarifying the current state-of-the-art and highlighting open challenges that guide future research at the intersection of RL , pattern recognition, and intelligent hardware.

Several surveys have examined the relationship between RL and reconfigurable or heterogeneous hardware, yet significant gaps remain. The survey in [ 118 ] provides an extensive overview of domain-specific RL architectures, with a primary focus on FPGA -based accelerators. However, it does not integrate IC implementations, unified abstraction layers, nor does it cover the complete spectrum of RL algorithmic families such as SARSA ( SARSA ), MC ( MC ), AC ( AC ), and PPO ( PPO ). Similarly, the work in [ 44 ] concentrates on ML applications within FPGA EDA ( EDA ) tools. While valuable, its treatment of RL is brief, lacks architectural depth, and does not relate RL methods to accelerator design or runtime optimization. The review in [ 162 ] centers on ML techniques for control and monitoring but does not address RL -driven FPGA or IC architectures, nor broader comparisons across RL categories. Additionally, the heterogeneous-chip scheduling survey in [ 99 ] identifies RL primarily as a future research direction without analyzing existing RL implementations, hardware mapping strategies, or design-flow implications. Consequently, none of these studies provide a unified RL -centric perspective that spans both FPGA and IC platforms while simultaneously comparing all major RL types, synthesizing research areas and applications, and identifying cross-cutting architectural and methodological limitations. A detailed comparison of our coverage with prior surveys is provided in Table 1 .

In contrast, the present review fills these gaps by systematically analyzing more than 120 FPGA / IC -related RL works and providing a unified and hardware-centric synthesis. The main contributions are summarized as follows:

Unified FPGA / IC perspective: consolidates RL -based realizations across reconfigurable accelerators and dedicated IC engines within a single RL -centric view.

Unified FPGA / IC perspective: consolidates RL -based realizations across reconfigurable accelerators and dedicated IC engines within a single RL -centric view.

Finally, while several RL -based FPGA / IC implementations incorporate CPU or GPU , these processors typically serve auxiliary functions—such as orchestration, environment simulation, or data management—whereas the dominant learning and inference workload is executed on FPGA , ASIC , and custom hardware engines, with general-purpose processors contributing minimally to the computational pipeline.

To ensure methodological rigor, transparency, and reproducibility, this review adopts a systematic literature search and selection strategy centered on peer-reviewed studies addressing the implementation of RL on FPGA and IC platforms. The primary search was conducted using Scopus as the main indexing engine, which provides broad coverage of major scientific publishers and digital libraries, including IEEE Xplore, Elsevier ScienceDirect, ACM Digital Library, Web of Science, Wiley, Springer, and IET Digital Library, among others. To consistently retrieve works at the intersection of RL algorithms and hardware realization, a structured Boolean query was formulated and applied across databases using title, abstract, and keyword fields. The search logic was designed to capture both classical and deep RL methods, while explicitly constraining results to hardware-oriented implementations rather than purely algorithmic or simulation-based studies. The generic query structure can be expressed as:

Selected papers =
FROM (“Title” OR “Abstract” OR “Keywords”)
SELECT (References WHERE
(RL OR DRL OR “Reinforcement Learning” OR “Deep Reinforcement Learning”) AND (FPGA OR “Field-Programmable Gate Array” OR ASIC OR IC OR SoC OR “Integrated Circuit”)) FILTER (Language = “English” AND Year BETWEEN 2015 AND 2026 AND DocumentType = (“Journal Article” OR “Conference Paper”))

The logical operators AND and OR ensure precise targeting of studies that explicitly combine RL with FPGA or IC hardware platforms. The selected time window reflects the emergence of practical RL hardware realizations, from early tabular and MDP ( MDP )-based accelerators to modern deep and AC architectures.

To balance completeness with technical focus, the retrieved studies were further screened using relevance and quality criteria. Seminal RL hardware-acceleration works were retained when they directly supported the FPGA / IC -centered taxonomy, architectural discussion, performance comparison, or application-level analysis of this review. However, earlier works already extensively covered in prior surveys were not repeated exhaustively unless they established a necessary technical baseline or motivated a later research direction. This avoids redundant historical coverage while preserving the foundational context required for the proposed survey.

Redundant studies, papers with insufficient hardware-implementation details, works lacking meaningful evaluation results, and studies only weakly related to RL -based FPGA / IC platforms were excluded. Priority was given to recent studies that provide clear implementation details and contribute to emerging directions such as energy-efficient RL acceleration, quantized RL hardware, FPGA / IC -based runtime optimization, RL -assisted synthesis, MARL ( MARL ) hardware, and application-specific deployment.

# 2 Background

## 2.1 FPGA and IC

Modern FPGA are heterogeneous fabrics composed of several tightly coupled resources rather than only a sea of logic cells. The core of the device is formed by a 2D array of CLB . Each CLB contains one or more slices , and a slice integrates LUT , FF , optional LUTRAM ( LUTRAM ), and dedicated carry logic. LUT implement arbitrary combinational functions, FF provide sequential storage, LUTRAM enables small on-chip memories close to the logic, and fast carry chains support efficient arithmetic operations such as adders and counters.

Surrounding and interleaved with the CLB array are specialized resources. Columns of BRAM offer larger, synchronous memories with configurable width and depth, used for data buffering, FIFO , and on-chip caches. Dedicated DSP ( DSP ) slices provide high-speed arithmetic units (typically multipliers, add–accumulate units, and pre/post-adders), which are essential for signal processing, ML , and other compute-intensive workloads. At the periphery of the device, I/O banks host programmable input/output blocks that interface the FPGA fabric with external signals and support various standards and voltage levels. These computation and storage blocks are connected by a rich hierarchy of routing resources. Local and global interconnect networks, including long lines and dedicated global routing (often driven by global buffers, GBs), allow signals to traverse the chip and distribute clocks and resets. Clock-management tiles, such as PLL ( PLL ) and MMCM ( MMCM ), generate and condition internal clocks, enabling frequency synthesis, phase shifting, and jitter reduction. Configuration and control logic, typically including a configuration memory interface and state machines, orchestrate device programming, partial reconfiguration, and global control signals. Together, CLB (with LUT , FF , LUTRAM , and carry logic), BRAM , DSP slices, I/O banks, global routing, clock-management, and configuration/control logic form the heterogeneous substrate on which hardware-aware RL and MDP -based techniques can operate to dynamically optimize performance, power, and resource utilization. Figure 2 (a) illustrate a typical FPGA board resources.

Unlike reconfigurable FPGA , an IC implements a fixed hardware architecture that is defined at fabrication time. Modern ASIC or SoC devices integrate multiple subsystems on a single die, including general-purpose CPU cores, hardware accelerators, on-chip memories ( SRAM ( SRAM )/read-only memory (ROM)), I/O interfaces, and analog or mixed-signal blocks. The digital logic is typically built from standard cells (gates, flip-flops, etc.) placed and routed once during design, with no post-silicon reconfiguration capability.

These IC also embed rich infrastructure for power and clock management, such as clock trees, PLL , and DVFS ( DVFS ) controllers, as well as on-chip interconnects like buses or NoC . In hardware-aware RL and MDP -based schemes, the IC is therefore treated as a fixed substrate whose tunable parameters include operating points (voltage/frequency domains), power-gating states, and scheduling or resource-allocation policies for the embedded accelerators and memories. This contrasts with FPGA , where RL may additionally control spatial reconfiguration of the logic fabric itself. Figure 2 (b) illustrate a typical IC resources.

The unified abstraction hierarchy highlights the structural similarities and key differences between FPGA and IC design flows. At the SLD ( SLD ) level, both platforms rely on high-level algorithm modeling using MATLAB, Simulink, or SystemC to explore functionality and performance. Beyond this level, DSC have increasingly emerged as an additional abstraction layer between high-level ML / RL models and low-level hardware implementation. Unlike general-purpose HLS ( HLS ) tools, which mainly translate C/C++/SystemC descriptions into hardware, DSC operate on domain-aware representations such as tensor graphs, dataflow graphs, neural-network operators, or accelerator templates. This enables compiler-level optimizations such as operator fusion, memory tiling, scheduling, quantization, and hardware-aware mapping before generating HLS code, RTL ( RTL ), or intermediate hardware descriptions. In the context of RL -based FPGA / IC systems, DSC are particularly relevant for deep RL methods such as DQN ( DQN ), PPO , and DDPG ( DDPG ), where policy/value networks, replay buffers, and learning-update pipelines introduce repeated computational patterns that can be systematically optimized.

HLS then bridges software and hardware by converting C/C++/SystemC descriptions into RTL for both technologies, although ASIC tools emphasize early power and area exploration. RTL design remains common to both flows, relying on Verilog or VHDL ( VHDL ) to define datapaths, control logic, and finite-state machines. Divergence appears at the physical level: FPGA implementation performs placement, routing, and timing closure over a fixed reconfigurable fabric, while ASIC flows involve full custom physical design, including floorplanning, clock-tree synthesis, routing, sign-off timing analysis, and DRC/LVS checks before tape-out. This unified view clarifies how RL hardware—such as MDP or QL ( QL ) accelerators—can be designed coherently for both FPGA prototyping and IC deployment. Table 2 provides a unified view of abstraction layers common to both FPGA and IC design flows, highlighting their shared stages and key distinctions.

## 2.2 Platforms and Simulators

Beyond conventional design environments such as MATLAB/Simulink, HDL Coder, and vendor-specific toolchains including AMD-Xilinx Vivado, a growing number of research-oriented simulators and platforms have been proposed to enable flexible integration of learning algorithms with hardware-aware evaluation.
These platforms aim to decouple RL agent development from low-level hardware implementation details, support rapid design-space exploration, and provide meaningful performance, energy, and latency feedback prior to physical deployment. For example, Chen et al. [ 21 ] introduced VPR-Gym , a Python-based platform built on top of the OpenAI Gym framework to enable systematic exploration of AI ( AI ) techniques for FPGA placement optimization. By decoupling learning agents from the underlying C++ implementation of the VPR toolchain, VPR-Gym lowers the barrier for integrating modern RL , evolutionary strategies, and other AI-based optimizers into the FPGA computer-aided design (CAD) flow. The platform supports multiple learning paradigms, flexible reward formulations, and parallel environment execution, making it particularly suitable for rapid experimentation and comparative evaluation of placement strategies while preserving compatibility with industrial-grade FPGA CAD tools. Beyond FPGA placement, simulation frameworks targeting emerging hardware paradigms have also been proposed. Rakka et al. [ 114 ] presented HDRLPIM, a cycle- and energy-aware simulator for hyper-dimensional RL implemented on processing-in-memory (PIM) architectures. The simulator models associative processor-based accelerators using SRAM and ReRAM technologies and focuses on accelerating inference in hyper-dimensional QL . By abstracting the hardware execution of core RL operations—such as Q-value computation and action selection—HDRLPIM enables detailed evaluation of latency, energy consumption, and energy–delay product, offering a valuable tool for early-stage design-space exploration of non-von-Neumann RL accelerators. In the context of power electronics, Xu et al. [ 150 ] proposed an FPGA -based circuit simulator designed to accelerate RL -driven power converter design. The simulator offloads time-domain circuit simulation to an FPGA accelerator deployed on cloud-based platforms, significantly reducing the training time of RL agents compared to conventional software simulators. By packaging the accelerator within an OpenAI Gym-compatible environment, the framework enables seamless integration with standard RL algorithms while allowing on-the-fly modification of circuit parameters without regenerating bitstreams. This work highlights the importance of hardware-aware simulators in making RL -based design methodologies practical for real-world engineering applications. Complementary to these simulation platforms, Canese et al. [ 14 ] presented a MATLAB/Simulink-based toolchain that automatically generates FPGA intellectual property (IP) cores for tabular QL accelerators. The framework produces synthesizable VHDL code and integrates directly with the AMD-Xilinx Vivado flow, enabling users to customize Q-table dimensions, numerical precision, and target FPGA devices. By leveraging HDL Coder, the tool reproduces established hardware architectures while significantly reducing development time and facilitating design-space exploration. Although the framework demonstrated full compatibility with existing QL accelerators, support for Intel FPGA platforms and ASIC design flows was identified as future work.

2026-10-22.title: PCLA-Bridge: A Framework for Cross-Domain Deployment of CARLA Agents
2026-10-22.authors: Masoud Jamshidiyan Tehrani , Jinhan Kim , Paolo Tonella
2026-10-22.abstract: Most high-performing end-to-end autonomous driving agents (ADAs) are developed for the CARLA Leaderboard, tightly coupling them to CARLA’s APIs, sensor layouts, coordinate systems, and internal clock. Reusing these models on real datasets, alternative simulators, or physical platforms necessitates substantial manual re-engineering. We present PCLA-Bridge, a deployable tool that runs unmodified CARLA Leaderboard agents from any sensor source to any control destination without an active CARLA server. With PCLA-Bridge handling dependency isolation, tensor marshalling, routing, and synthetic timing, integrators only need to provide a minimal interface. We validate the tool across two operational paradigms: offline replay on in-domain CARLA recordings and real-world nuScenes logs, and live closed-loop control across three diverse simulation engines: MetaDrive, AWSIM, and AlpaSim. We analyze the lightweight integration requirements for each platform, highlighting output translation (such as converting agent actions into target trajectory formats) and coordinate-frame transformations, showing that integration requires minimal glue code rather than structural changes. All eight evaluated agents execute across all three simulators without modification, confirming the reliability of PCLA-Bridge and establishing a foundation for systematic sim-to-real, cross-sim, and security testing.
2026-10-22.introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving agents (ADAs) are typically built and evaluated in a single simulator, most commonly the CARLA simulator [ 1 ] . Because these implementations assume a specific end-to-end environment, relying on native sensor tensors, routing, temporal synchronization, and coordinate conventions, a published agent becomes tightly coupled to its original execution harness. This coupling hinders code reuse, cross-environment evaluation, and any transition toward physical deployment. Currently, to run a published CARLA agent on real-world logs or within another simulator, researchers must manually re-engineer the agent.

While the PCLA framework [ 2 ] decoupled 41 Leaderboard agents from the Leaderboard codebase [ 3 ] to enable execution across diverse CARLA environments, those agents remained bound to the simulator itself. This paper offers a tool that removes that dependency. PCLA-Bridge executes unmodified agents without a CARLA server, allowing any data source to drive the agent and any control target to consume its outputs. While an earlier extended abstract introduced this concept using offline replay [ 4 ] , this paper describes a fully functional tool featuring live, closed-loop operation and documents the practical requirements for integrating new data sources.

The envisioned users are autonomous driving (AD) researchers and software engineering (SE) testers who need to evaluate a published PCLA agent on inputs that the agent’s native simulator cannot produce. These inputs may come from real-world logs, alternative simulators, adversarial perturbations, or physical vehicles. PCLA-Bridge enables this evaluation without requiring the user to modify or rewrite the agent.

As illustrated in Fig. 1 , PCLA-Bridge loads each agent in a standalone environment. The bridge then handles the complex data transformations that an integrator would otherwise need to implement manually. Specifically, it marshals external sensor readings into the exact tensor layout expected by the agent by resizing cameras and zero-filling absent modalities. It also sets the navigation route using GPS waypoints and manages a synthetic clock for agents that rely on wall time. Because both the data source (such as a simulator, a dataset log, or a physical vehicle) and the control target are entirely external, PCLA-Bridge is inherently source- and target-agnostic.

As detailed in Table I , portability is fundamentally a property of the agent rather than the bridging tool. Sensor-only agents consume physical data streams and can be ported directly to new environments. Privileged agents, however, rely on ground truth data that only the host simulator can provide, such as exact ego pose or rendered bird’s-eye view, meaning they cannot be driven by empirical sensors. Finally, a third class of systems, such as Autoware [ 5 ] , does not follow a monolithic sensor-in and control-out architecture and therefore cannot be ported using this approach.

2026-10-23.introduction:
As robots expand to perform tasks in more general, varied, and dynamic environments, their ability to manipulate quickly, reliably, and safely will increasingly depend on directly sensing and reacting to contact—that is, on tactile sensing.

However, sensors must first be customized to fit the end-effector or surface of interest. As a result, research on the use of tactile sensing is fundamentally limited by customizability: researchers must either adapt their work to sensors manufactured in fixed geometries, or they must possess sufficient design and fabrication expertise to develop custom sensors in-house. These constraints are particularly limiting when instrumenting custom-designed robot geometries or larger, irregular surfaces.

In this paper, we focus on conformal tactile skins , as they integrate distributed sensing elements into thin, flexible surfaces that can be wrapped around robot geometries, enabling fully sensorized robot bodies. However, existing tactile skins, such as FlexiTac [ 1 ] , provide only normal-force (1D) estimates and require manual redesign for each new geometry. We present a sensor design that can be easily customized to fit many robot geometries, scaled in sensing area or resolution, and used to estimate normal and shear forces (3D) over local groups of sensing elements.

Several efforts have partially addressed sensor customizability and made tactile skins more capable and accessible for the robot control and learning communities [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] .
AnySkin provides replaceable sensing surfaces but relies on a predefined electronic layout [ 2 ] , while eFlesh automates the design of a deformable sensor body but relies on separately supplied magnetometer electronics [ 3 ] . In addition to the challenges of customizing the entire sensor, existing sensors are sampled at rates ranging between 30 and 100 Hz.
Such raster scanning-based acquisition can limit the ability to resolve and respond to contacts lasting only a few milliseconds. Beyond hardware, changes in sensor geometry must also be accommodated by the software used to acquire, simulate, and process tactile observations.

To address these limitations, we introduce OpenTac , an open sensor design environment and software ecosystem for customizable, scalable tactile sensing (Fig. ). OpenTac supports the design of low-cost piezoresistive tactile skins that estimate both local normal and shear forces with millimeter-scale spatial resolution over planar and developable surfaces. Our sensor combines a flexible printed circuit board and a piezoresistive film with a structured elastomeric overlay that redistributes lateral pressure across neighboring sensing elements, allowing local shear to be decoded while retaining normal-force information. The sensing layout, electrode geometry, and mechanical overlay can be customized to the surface geometry and force range of interest.

To support this degree of customizability, OpenTac includes a full-stack ecosystem of design, simulation, and interoperability tools. OpenTac-CAD is a design tool that automatically generates sensor fabrication files from a desired geometry. Users can provide a 2D outline, select a developable surface on a 3D robot model, or specify an abstract verbal description, such as “ design a star-shaped sensor that fits inside a circle with a diameter 5 cm .”
In addition, OpenTac-CAD produces a machine-readable manifest file describing the sensor’s geometry, electrical addressing, and mechanical configuration. OpenTac-Sim provides tools to simulate the sensors and sensor-object interactions for robot manipulation tasks across any sensor design described by the manifest file. OpenTac-Transfer enables cross-sensor transfer by mapping calibrated tactile observations across sensor layouts using their physical coordinates and local surface frames. These components allow sensors with different shapes, resolutions, and electrical layouts to share acquisition and processing tools and provide a common interface for downstream control and learning.

Scaling tactile coverage also increases the number of measurements required to read the sensor. To address this, we also provide OpenTac-Xampling , an adaptive acquisition method
which operates across different sensor outlines using adaptive partial scans. For example, on a 32 × 32 32\times 32 skin, adaptive acquisition of sparse contact events reaches 1286 Hz, more than a 19 × \times increase over full-array scans (67 Hz) achieved by conventional acquisition [ 4 ] .

We evaluate all components of the OpenTac ecosystem. We use OpenTac-CAD to generate fabrication files for more than 30 sensor layouts (including robot fingers, grippers, palms, and feet), fabricate the corresponding sensors, and deploy them on four real robot embodiments.
We further evaluate the 3D force estimates against a commercial force/torque sensor.
Finally, we demonstrate that our sensor’s normal and shear force estimates enable contact-rich feedback control and manipulation policy learning.

To summarize, our main contributions are:

OpenTac: a full-stack ecosystem for automated sensor design, fabrication, simulation, cross-sensor observation mapping, and kilohertz-rate adaptive acquisition.

A customizable tactile skin that estimates normal and shear forces using a simple, scalable construction.

Evaluations spanning over 30 fabricated layouts, sensor characterization, high-speed sensing, and real-world robot control and learning, demonstrating the utility of the resulting tactile observations for contact-rich manipulation.

All OpenTac hardware, software, and firmware is available under permissive licenses, enabling replication, modification, and redistribution for research and commercial use.

2. A customizable tactile skin that estimates normal and shear forces using a simple, scalable construction.

3. Evaluations spanning over 30 fabricated layouts, sensor characterization, high-speed sensing, and real-world robot control and learning, demonstrating the utility of the resulting tactile observations for contact-rich manipulation.

# 2 Related Work

Tactile sensing hardware typically involves optical, magnetic, capacitive, and/or resistive transduction to recover contact. GelSight provides high-resolution optical contact sensing [ 5 ] , while uSkin integrates
distributed three-axis force elements [ 10 ] . GelSlim uses marker displacements and inverse finite-element modeling to estimate dense contact forces [ 14 ] , while Yan et al. use a magnetized film to decouple normal force and one shear component [ 15 ] . Mechanical structures can also encode shear into differential pressure: Sun et al. place a bump over four piezoresistive cells and infer
load direction from their relative responses [ 13 ] . OpenTac builds on this principle using a single-FPCB (flexible PCB) sensing architecture designed for automated customization and shared readout design that specifies a unified cross-sensor interface.

Early work on customizing and scaling tactile skins used modular or severable elements to cover complex
robot surfaces [ 16 , 17 ] , while later systems such as
the iCub skin, RobotSweater, and conformal tactile textiles target large-area conformable
coverage [ 12 , 18 , 19 ] . ReSkin and AnySkin decouple the replaceable magnetic interface from the electronics [ 11 , 2 ] . eFlesh automates magnetic microstructures [ 3 ] , and FlexiTac provides an open flexible pressure array [ 1 ] . Computational design tools have also produced personalized FPCB tactile gloves [ 20 ] and surface-conforming capacitive sensors for existing 3D objects [ 21 ] . Lim et al. use laser-patterned flexible circuits to integrate capacitive pressure and bending sensors with temperature and proximity modules in customizable multimodal skins [ 22 ] .
OpenTac instead starts from robot geometry and jointly generates the sensing layout, routing, connectorization, mechanical structure, and associated metadata, enabling robot-specific tactile skins.

Tactile simulation and manipulation. TACTO [ 23 ] and Taxim [ 24 ] focus on simulating the imaging process inherent in vision-based tactile sensors. DiffTactile [ 25 ] , TacEx [ 26 ] , and Taccel [ 27 ] additionally implement sensor surface deformation mechanics for robot manipulation. HydroShear further models shear and stick-slip effects for
sim-to-real learning [ 28 ] . Tactile feedback has been used in fine manipulation and shear-based control [ 29 , 30 ] . Different to prior work, OpenTac-Sim implements a simulation framework specifically for OpenTac sensors using the compiled sensor geometry and bump layout to generate normal and tangential deformation observations.

Acquisition and cross-sensor representations. High-rate tactile sensing has used event-driven hardware [ 31 , 32 ] and adaptive subsampling of dense arrays [ 33 ] . OpenTac-Xampling applies adaptive sampling across arbitrary compiled layouts using manifest-defined valid regions and neighborhoods.
Cross-sensor tactile representation learning combines aligned synthetic tactile data with real-world multimodal data to learn sensor-agnostic visuo-tactile representations [ 34 , 35 , 36 ] . 2026-10-23.abstract: We consider the offline generation of coordinated paths for N N interchangeable robots and N N goals in planar environments with polygonal obstacles. After a conformal map to a circular domain, starts and goals become the poles and zeros of a rational function R R , and the paths are the branches of its Generalized Root Locus (GRL), i.e. the streamlines of the logarithmic potential − log ⁡ R -\log R . We show that, for every phase outside a finite set of critical phases and a set of boundary phases, the induced gradient motion drives each robot to a distinct goal along pairwise disjoint paths that never reach the obstacles; the robot–goal assignment is produced by the construction, and with the gain used as a clock all robots move as the closed-loop roots of the GRL and arrive together at a prescribed time. Obstacles become streamlines through successive Milne–Thomson reflections, and for a finite number of reflections a finite test certifies safety for the potential that is actually computed. Reciprocal root-locus planning is recovered as a special case. The method is illustrated on two polygonal workspaces, 100 random instances compared with independent harmonic planning and artificial potentials, and a scene with ten robots and ten obstacles.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Coordinated motion of several robots in a cluttered environment is usually organized in two layers: an offline layer that builds feasible global paths, and an online layer that tracks them and handles finite size, actuation limits and close interactions. This paper is about the first layer. We consider N N interchangeable robots and N N goals in a planar workspace with polygonal obstacles, and look for smooth paths that are collision-free by construction; assigning robots to goals is part of the problem.

Potential-based methods encode the whole problem in a scalar field. The artificial potential field (APF) of Khatib [ 1 ] may have local minima; harmonic function methods (HFM) [ 2 ] remove them, since solutions of the Laplace equation have no interior extrema. Navigation functions [ 3 ] also exclude spurious minima, but need a map onto a sphere world, hard to build for polygonal scenes. For several robots, electrostatic analogies have been used without obstacles [ 4 ] , and root-locus (RL) constructions have produced collision-free formations [ 5 ] and single-robot paths among diffusive hazards [ 6 ] . The reciprocal root locus (RRL) [ 7 , 8 ] handles polygonal workspaces through a conformal map, but enforces obstacle avoidance by heuristic corrections, without a proof of non-penetration.

The Generalized Root Locus (GRL) bridges these lines of work. If starts and goals are the poles and zeros of a rational function R R , the GRL branches are the streamlines of the logarithmic potential − log ⁡ R -\log R [ 9 ] : integral curves of a harmonic field, as in HFM, with the branch structure of the root locus. The invariance of the stream function along the gradient motion keeps each robot on its branch, but does not say where the robots go, whether two paths can meet, or whether the obstacles are respected. This paper answers these questions:

Certified coordinated motion (Theorem 1 ). For every phase outside a finite set of critical phases and a set of boundary phases, the GRL in the workspace consists of exactly N N disjoint arcs, each joining a start to a different goal. The gradient motion converges along them, the robot–goal assignment is induced by the construction, and with the gain used as a clock the robots leave the starts together, move as the closed-loop roots of the GRL and arrive together at a prescribed time. The result holds on any bounded domain with obstacles.

Certificate for computed obstacle potentials (Proposition 3 ). Obstacles are made streamlines by successive Milne–Thomson reflections. For a finite reflection depth, the boundary residual bounds the set of excluded phases, and a finite test certifies obstacle safety for the potential that is actually computed.

RRL as a special case (Section 5.5 ). The RRL planner [ 7 , 8 ] is recovered with the same guarantees, which supplies the boundary-invariance argument that was missing.

Algorithm and experiments (Sections 6 and 7 ): the complete procedure, with the critical set verified by the argument principle, evaluated on reference examples, in a Monte Carlo comparison with independent harmonic planning and artificial potentials, and on a scene with ten robots and ten obstacles.

2026-10-23.title: DiffDreamer: Coupling World Models with Differentiable Simulation for Agile Quadrotor Control
2026-10-23.authors: Fanxing Li , Yuxiang Huang , Shengyang Wang , Fangyu Sun , Shuyu Wu , Tianbao Zhang , Dexin Zuo , Yan Yufei , Danping Zou , Wenxian Yu
2026-10-23.abstract: Tasks such as quadrotor dynamic-gate racing require agents to anticipate external motion while maintaining precise high-frequency control. World-model-based reinforcement learning (RL) provides a natural solution by learning latent dynamics for future imagination, yet it often entangles environmental evolution and the robot’s own dynamics in a single learned rollout, where model bias can affect policy optimization efficiency. We propose DiffDreamer , a differentiable reinforcement learning framework that tightly couples a learned world model with differentiable simulation for actor optimization. In one optimization step, the learned world model propagates latent states that capture external dynamics and history-dependent features, while the differentiable simulator propagates the robot’s explicit physical state. We further decompose the actor objective into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. Experiments on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing show that DiffDreamer improves training convergence over the model-free, model-based, and differentiable-RL baselines, and final performance over these baselines and classical planning and control methods. Additional experiments assess reward decomposition and the odometry-conditioned relative-state representation through ablations. We also provide proof-of-concept real-world flight experiments for validation.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Many robotic tasks require agents to anticipate external environmental evolution to achieve precise control. This structure is particularly prominent in agile aerial robotics. A representative example is dynamic-gate racing with quadrotors [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] , where the robot must predict the future motion of moving gates and generate accurate control commands to pass through narrow openings at high speed. Existing solutions [ 2 ] often address this challenge through modular pipelines that decouple prediction, planning, and control. Although such designs are interpretable and effective, they usually rely on task-specific engineering and optimize each module separately.

World-model-based reinforcement learning [ 4 , 5 ] provides an integrated alternative. By learning compact latent dynamics from interaction, methods such as Dreamer [ 4 ] can imagine future trajectories and optimize policies in latent space. However, in agile robotic control, a learned world model often has to capture both the evolution of the external environment and the robot’s high-frequency rigid-body dynamics within the same learned rollout. This entangles two sources of dynamics with different structures: the external dynamics are partially observable and history-dependent, whereas the robot’s internal dynamics are often smooth and available through physical modeling. As a result, policy optimization through purely learned rollouts may suffer from model bias and less accurate gradients for precise physical control. This motivates using differentiable simulation for the robot’s physical motion, so that the learned world model can focus on latent external dynamics.

Differentiable reinforcement learning (DiffRL) [ 6 , 7 ] offers a complementary direction. By backpropagating through a differentiable physical model, it can provide low-variance first-order gradients for policy optimization and be particularly effective for smooth robotic systems. However, differentiable RL alone typically assumes that the transition and reward structures are differentiable and explicitly available. This makes it difficult to handle partially observable external dynamics, moving targets with unknown future motion, and non-differentiable task events such as gate-crossing rewards.

To address this problem, we propose DiffDreamer, which structurally separates robot dynamics from external environment dynamics and couples their rollouts for policy optimization. DiffDreamer synchronizes latent world-model imagination with differentiable physical rollouts: under the same action, the world model updates an implicit state representing external time-varying features, while the simulator propagates the explicit robot state. The actor receives both states as input, and its objective is decomposed into a critic-driven pathway for non-differentiable task rewards and a simulator-driven pathway for differentiable motion rewards. We compare DiffDreamer with RL, trajectory planning, and model predictive control (MPC) baselines on aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing, and demonstrate its effectiveness through transfer to real quadrotor flight.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose a dual-pathway policy optimization framework that synchronizes latent imagination with differentiable physical rollouts to improve optimization accuracy and reduce the burden of learning high-frequency robot dynamics within the world model.

We conduct comprehensive experiments on two quadrotor tasks with dynamic external environments to validate the advantages of the proposed method in terms of control accuracy and predictive capabilities.

We conduct ablation studies on reward decomposition and odometry-conditioned relative-state representation to assess their contributions.

We provide proof-of-concept validation of aggressive tracking and dynamic-gate racing in real-world scenarios.

# II Related Work

## II-A Agile Quadrotor Flight and Modular Pipelines

Agile quadrotor flight, including autonomous racing, typically relies on modular pipelines for perception, state estimation, trajectory planning, and low-level control under tight real-time constraints [ 8 ] . In dynamic environments with moving targets or gates, these pipelines often use motion-prediction modules to support downstream planning and control.
Representative approaches combine learned gate perception with trajectory generation and tracking [ 1 ] , learned data abstraction with nonlinear filtering and time-optimal planning [ 9 ] , or model-predictive and time-optimal control for aggressive waypoint or gate traversal [ 10 , 11 , 12 ] .
Policy search can also tune model-predictive controllers for agile flight [ 2 ] .
Elastic Tracker combines target-motion prediction with visibility-aware spatio-temporal trajectory optimization for aerial tracking [ 13 ] .
These modular pipelines are effective and interpretable, especially when the environment structure and task objectives are well specified.
However, their modules are usually designed and optimized separately, so prediction or planning errors may propagate to downstream control.

## II-B Model-based Reinforcement Learning

Model-based reinforcement learning uses learned or known dynamics models for planning and policy optimization, supporting sample-efficient end-to-end policy learning. Model-free methods learn directly from interaction with the environment and typically require more data [ 14 , 15 ] . Classical and modern approaches have explored probabilistic dynamics and uncertainty-aware planning, such as PILCO and PETS [ 16 , 17 ] , short model-generated rollouts for value/policy learning, such as MBPO [ 18 ] , and latent dynamics for planning or imagination-based actor-critic learning, such as MuZero, Dreamer, and TD-MPC [ 19 , 4 , 5 , 20 , 21 , 22 ] .

Despite their sample efficiency, model-based methods remain sensitive to model fidelity, especially in high-accuracy and high-frequency robotic control [ 23 ] . In agile quadrotor tasks, a single learned rollout must often capture both partially observable external motion and fast rigid-body dynamics, which introduces distinct learning challenges.

2026-10-23.title: Progress Probes $P^2$: Lightweight Runtime Monitoring for Vision-Language-Action Models
2026-10-23.authors: Atiksh Bhardwaj , Edward W. Duan , Junwon Seo , Prithwish Dan , Wei-Chiu Ma , Andrea Bajscy , Preston Culbertson
2026-10-23.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models can perform diverse manipulation tasks directly from visual observations and natural language instructions, but they remain prone to mistakes and unpredictable failures. Deploying these policies without continuous human supervision will require robust runtime monitors that detect when the policy has gone off-course. Existing monitors use external foundation models, such as vision-language models (VLMs) to supervise the policy, introducing significant complexity and computational cost for monitoring at runtime. In this work, we investigate an alternate approach: can a VLA’s own internal activations provide the information needed to monitor its execution? Our method trains linear probes on policy activations from demonstrations to estimate progress, then flags executions that deviate from expected progress. In experiments with the open-source VLA π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} and across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, this approach is competitive with or outperforms VLM-based monitors in task failure detection, as well as methods which require failure data for training. These findings suggest that simple probes of VLA internals can be used to develop reliable runtime monitors, opening a path toward building policies that can act reliably and monitor their execution without external foundation models.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have made strong progress toward the goal of generalist, language-conditioned robot policies. Models such as π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 1 ] and GR00T [ 2 ] can execute diverse, multi-stage manipulation tasks across a variety of tasks and embodiment and, especially after task-specific fine-tuning, can achieve relatively high mutli-task success rates. However, even well-trained policies still experience a wide variety of failure modes, (e.g., poor language grounding [ 3 ] , deadlocks, and mistakes [ 4 ] ) which are often sudden and difficult to predict.

A natural framework for addressing such failure modes during deployment is runtime monitoring: using an external verifier or monitor to detect when the policy’s execution is straying from typical/successful deployment.
Existing approaches obtain this monitoring signal from several sources. Sentinel [ 5 ] uses an external VLM, along with an action consistency heuristic, to judge when the policy is failing to make progress on a particular task. Generalist reward models, such as Robometer [ 6 ] , learn to judge task progress from datasets of robot videos. Other methods instead use policy internals directly for failure detection. For example, SAFE [ 4 ] trains a failure classifier to predict rollout success directly from policy activations, while FIPER [ 7 ] combines an internal-based anomaly score and an uncertainty metric over actions to flag anomalous rollouts.

In this work, we investigate a different use of policy internals for runtime monitoring.

Specifically, we build on recent successes in mechanistic interpretability for VLAs [ 8 , 9 ] , which demonstrated that the activations of the VLM backbone contain easily-decodable representations of task-relevant features such as end-effector pose, object states, and task phase.
We hypothesize that a VLA’s internal activations may also encode task progress : how far the policy has progressed through a task. In successful executions, progress advances predictably over time (monotonically decreasing), while in suboptimal or failed executions, the progress probe falls behind the elapsed time. Furthermore, task progress can be learned entirely from successful executions and can be labeled without human supervision.

We study progress probes by training them on the π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} [ 1 ] VLA
using a dataset of success-only task executions. At deployment, runtime monitoring consists of taking the VLA’s internal activations (that are already computed as part of the forward pass of inference), passing them through the linear progress probe, and measuring the deviation between the current estimated task progress and the expected task progress computed from successful demonstrations. Not only does our probe-based monitor require only successful data for training, but it also runs between 5 × 5\times and 20,000 × 20,000\times faster than an external foundation-model monitor.

Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, we find that linear probes can indeed accurately predict task progress for demonstrations, and that they provide an effective signal for detecting unsuccessful policy rollouts. Our monitor achieves competitive or superior failure detection performance with both Robometer and SAFE baselines, while providing fast inference and requiring only successful demonstrations for training. This result indicates that even when VLAs fail to generate successful actions, their activations still retain information useful for detecting task progress and failure, which can be obtained using a simple linear readout. Specifically, our contributions are as follows:

We demonstrate empirically that linear probes trained over demonstration data can accurately decode task progress from π 0.5 ′ ​ s \pi_{0.5}^{\prime}s vision-language representations, across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.

We demonstrate empirically that linear probes trained over demonstration data can accurately decode task progress from π 0.5 ′ ​ s \pi_{0.5}^{\prime}s vision-language representations, across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks.

We develop a minimalist progress-based runtime monitor which uses these probes to detect deviations from expected progress at runtime, without failure data or an external VLM.

We evaluate our monitor on 6 VLABench tasks and 6 real-world manipulation tasks, achieving AUROC scores of 0.788 and 0.78 respectively, matching or exceeding competitive baselines including SAFE and Robometer.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# II Related Work

Interpretability of Robot Policies. Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the behavior of neural networks by studying their internal representations and computations.
Over the past decade, researchers in computer vision and language modeling have developed tools to understand what neurons learn and how semantic concepts and structured knowledge are encoded and used.
One particularly exciting perspective is the linear representation hypothesis [ 10 , 11 ] , which posits that high-level concepts are encoded as directions in activation space and that interventions along concept directions can steer model behavior [ 12 ] .
This allows one to connect the study of representations to their functional role and reveal behaviors not visible in model output [ 13 , 14 ] .

More recently, researchers have extended similar ideas to robotic VLAs, investigating how their internal representations encode semantic concepts [ 15 ] , motion primitives [ 16 ] , and physical and relational states [ 8 , 9 ] .
Our work contributes to this growing body of interpretability research on robotic VLAs by investigating whether linear probes trained only on successful demonstrations can extract a task progress signal from internal activations.
Beyond decoding, we further show that this signal can be turned into a lightweight runtime monitor that detects departures from expected progress, demonstrating how VLA internals can support failure detection without an external foundation model.

Runtime Monitoring of Robot Foundation Models. Learned robot policies, including VLAs, remain prone to unexpected failures during deployment, motivating techniques for monitoring policies at runtime and detecting failures as they occur. Existing runtime monitors differ primarily in the signals they use to recognize such failures. One approach is to use deviations from successful behavior, flagging observations or policy outputs that appear anomalous relative to successful executions [ 17 , 7 ] . Another is to leverage an external evaluator, such as a VLM judge [ 5 , 18 , 19 ] or a learned failure predictor [ 4 ] trained directly over policy internals. More general reward models can also serve as runtime monitors by recognizing abnormal task progression [ 6 ] . Overall, several design decisions remain open for runtime monitoring, including whether monitoring requires an external validator, whether it must be trained on failure data, and whether the policy’s own representations provide useful signals for monitoring. We study the latter hypothesis by probing these representations for task progress and detecting failures when estimated progress deviates from the progression expected during successful execution.

2026-10-23.title: Humanoid Mobility via Attention-based Contacts
2026-10-23.authors: Junzhe He , Kehan Wen , Chong Zhang , Clemens Schwarke , Zewei Zhang , Kaixian Qu , Siyuan Hu , Matthias Müller , Vladlen Koltun , Marco Hutter
2026-10-23.comment: under review
2026-10-23.abstract: Humanoid mobility over complex terrain requires accurate foot placement and coordinated whole-body motion capable of robust adaptation. Reinforcement learning (RL) policies trained without motion references generalize well across terrains, yet eliciting effective whole-body coordination through reward design and exploration alone remains challenging. In contrast, reference-based methods yield natural motions but struggle to adapt beyond the predefined trajectories in their training data. We introduce a learning framework that bridges these two approaches by using motion data strictly as a training prior. An explicit, self-supervised, attention-based contact planner predicts future body–environment contacts, while a contact-conditioned tracker translates these plans into coordinated whole-body motion. Together, they establish contact as an interface between sensory observations and control actions. This abstraction allows the policy to internalize the contact-aware structure of locomotion rather than directly replicating kinematics. Consequently, a single policy can exploit data-driven motion priors for natural whole-body coordination while retaining the flexibility to discover environment-dependent behaviors through reinforcement learning. Building on the learned contact planner and tracker, a subsequent fine-tuning stage bootstraps their acquired capabilities to explore environment variations beyond those covered by the original motion data. Operating entirely from onboard observations without any reference inputs at deployment, this framework enables versatile humanoid mobility in challenging environments.

2026-10-23.title: Echo: Coupled Action and Task Status Signal Denoising for Vision Language Action Models
2026-10-23.authors: Yufeng Liu , Bohao Fan , Juntu Zhao , Xinyi Wang , Hang Yu , Wenzhuan Luo , Yingzhi Wang , Qinghai Li , Yingdong Hu , Junliang Guo , Richard Wang , Dequan Wang , Yang Gao , Cheng Ma
2026-10-23.comment: Project page: this https URL
2026-10-23.abstract: Recognizing task completion and failure enables robots to stop upon success and initiate recovery or replanning after failure. Existing methods augment Vision Language Action (VLA) policies with task status signal prediction to support these execution decisions. However, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs. Moreover, the potential of task status signals to directly guide action generation remains underexplored. We present Echo, a framework that combines task status signal learning without frame-level progress annotations with a compact design for status prediction and action generation within a single VLA. Specifically, Echo represents task status with stop and failure signals, added as two dimensions of each action chunk and denoised together with robot actions. Their combination distinguishes ongoing execution, successful completion, and failure. To learn these signals without fine-grained progress annotations, Echo constructs successful, failed, and recovery trajectories with complementary supervision properties. To enable status signal-guided action generation, Echo controls interactions between the signals and actions and denoises the signals faster than the actions. These allow later action denoising steps to condition on cleaner status estimates while preserving accurate signal prediction. Extensive real-world manipulation experiments show that Echo accurately predicts task status and consistently improves policy performance.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Vision Language Action (VLA) models have shown strong capabilities in robotic manipulation by mapping visual observations and language instructions to robot actions ( Intelligence et al., 2025 ; Bjorck et al., 2025 ; Team et al., 2026 ) . Reliable execution also requires recognizing whether a task is ongoing, has succeeded, or has failed to determine when to continue, stop, or intervene. Existing methods predict progress, completion, or failure signals either within VLA policies or through external monitoring models ( Apanasevich et al., 2026 ; Feng et al., 2026 ) .

However, existing approaches face two limitations. First, learning and integrating these signals can require fine-grained frame-level supervision, external monitoring models, or complex architectural designs ( Pacaud et al., 2025 ; Feng et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2026 ) . Second, the predicted signals are typically used only for monitoring, leaving their potential to improve action generation underexplored ( Pacaud et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) .

We present Echo, a compact framework that jointly denoises robot actions and task status signals within a single VLA, learning the signals without frame-level progress annotations and using them to improve action generation. Echo represents task status through a stop signal (SS), indicating whether execution should terminate, and a failure signal (FS), indicating whether execution is in a failure state. Low SS indicates ongoing execution, while high SS with low FS indicates successful completion, and high SS with high FS indicates terminal failure. Within ongoing execution, elevated FS indicates a recoverable failure, as shown in Figure 1 . Echo appends SS and FS as two additional dimensions of each action chunk and denoises them together with robot actions. This formulation reuses the VLA’s visual, language, and robot-state features with little additional parameter overhead.

To learn these signals without frame-level progress annotations, Echo combines successful demonstrations, failed policy rollouts, pre-intervention failure segments, and recovery demonstrations using subtask-level prompts together with success or failure labels. Failed rollouts and pre-intervention failure segments supervise terminal and recoverable failures, respectively, while their actions are excluded from imitation. Recovery demonstrations pair similar status supervision with corrective actions at corresponding recoverable failure states, linking failure recognition to recovery behavior.

To use the learned status information during action generation, Echo controls interactions among SS, FS, and robot actions while preserving accurate and complementary signal predictions. It also introduces asynchronous denoising, denoising signal tokens faster than action tokens so that later action denoising steps condition on cleaner status estimates. When the policy recognizes a recoverable failure with low SS and elevated FS, these estimates, together with the current observations, can guide action generation toward corrective behavior learned from recovery demonstrations.

Experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate accurate task-status prediction and improved performance over action-only baselines, with larger out-of-distribution gains. Component ablations, signal interventions, and failure-data scaling analyses examine how status signals influence action generation and how different data sources contribute to prediction and execution.

Our contributions are threefold: 1) We introduce a compact task status representation that incorporates stop and failure signals into VLA action chunks with little additional parameter overhead. 2) We develop a supervision scheme that learns these signals from successful, failed, and recovery data without frame-level progress annotations. 3) We design controlled interactions and asynchronous denoising to couple status prediction with action generation.
