# 2 Related Works

Task Status Signal Modeling. Task status signals characterize task progress, completion, and failure ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026c ; Dai et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ; Liufu et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . Visual-language reward models learn execution quality through representation learning, temporal supervision, and trajectory comparisons ( Ma et al., 2023 ; Alakuijala et al., 2024 ; Ayalew et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) . When deployed as standalone evaluators, these models introduce additional evaluation alongside the control policy. Complementary approaches predict completion ( Yang et al., 2025 ) or detect failures using policy features, temporal consistency, uncertainty, and visual reasoning ( Gu et al., 2026 ; Park et al., 2026 ; Agia et al., 2024 ; Xu et al., 2025 ; Duan et al., 2024 ) . Progress can also be extracted through lightweight probes ( Bhardwaj et al., 2026 ) . Although feature-based monitoring reduces overhead, accurate signal extraction alone does not ensure action feedback. Jointly achieving reliable task status prediction and signal-guided action adjustment with low overhead remains underexplored.

Task Status Signals for Action Improvement. Task status feedback improves policies through several mechanisms. VLAC ( Zhai et al., 2025 ) uses critic tokens to estimate rewards for
online reinforcement learning, while GRAPE ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) optimizes policies using trajectory preferences; both require additional policy updates. Other methods use execution assessments to trigger backtracking, intervention, or corrective control ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Deng et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ; Lin et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . More directly, VLA-Corrector ( Pan et al., 2026 ) monitors visual dynamics deviations and applies gradient-guided corrective replanning, while ProgressVLA ( Yan et al., 2026 ) propagates progress gradients through a world model to guide action denoising. These mechanisms demonstrate the utility of execution feedback, but introduce additional policy optimization, monitoring and recovery components, or inference-time gradient computation. Preserving accurate status estimates while directly improving action generation with minimal additional training and inference overhead remains an open challenge.

2026-10-23.title: Geometry-Dependent Properties of Physically Crosslinked PPy-PVA Hydrogels Enable Tunable Iontophoretic Drug Delivery
2026-10-23.authors: Heather Jin Hee Kim , Mohsen Alishahi , Kyuin Park , Mikaila K. Roncevich , Larissa M. Shepherd , Cara M. Nunez
2026-10-23.abstract: Objective: Iontophoresis enables noninvasive transdermal drug delivery. The control of drug release, however, has largely relied on current modulation. Here, we explore geometry-driven factors, gel microstructure, and local electric fields, as alternative levers for regulating drug transport. Methods: To investigate iontophoretic drug delivery, we encapsulate bovine serum albumin (BSA) in polypyrrole-polyvinyl alcohol (PPy-PVA) hydrogels. Five distinct hydrogel geometries were fabricated to impose variation in pore architecture and electric field distribution, including Hilbert curve-based designs that use increased corner density to enhance local electric field strength. Using formulation studies, we determined the ideal PPy content, drug loading efficiency, and current density. Maximum field strength of individual hydrogel geometries was simulated via finite element analysis, and microstructures were characterized by scanning electron microscopy. Lastly, we assessed differences in the transport metrics of the hydrogel geometries through an in vitro study using a Franz diffusion cell and an artificial membrane . Results: The engineered geometries produced clearly differentiated microstructures and electric field strengths. Drug delivery studies demonstrated that iontophoresis substantially enhanced permeability compared with passive diffusion, with each geometry yielding different profiles in cumulative release, flux, and permeability. Notably, the average iontophoretic permeability was ( 3.80 ± 1.93 ) × 10 − 5 (3.80\,\pm\,1.93)\times 10^{-5} , exceeding values reported in previous studies using artificial membranes. Conclusion: This study showed that the geometry-driven fabrication of drug-loaded hydrogel can achieve different delivery characteristics in both iontophoretic and passive transport using artificial membranes . Significance: Geometry-mediated control complements existing approaches for iontophoretic drug delivery without requiring individual current-density control.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Transdermal drug delivery, the delivery of ionized drug molecules through the layers of the skin, has gained increased attention due to its minimally invasive administration, potential for reduced skin side effects, and improved patient adherence to treatment [ 1 ] . The primary challenge of transdermal drug delivery is penetrating the stratum corneum, the outermost layer of the epidermis. This layer is composed of keratinized corneocytes embedded in a dense lipid matrix and serves as a formidable barrier to most therapeutic molecules [ 2 , 3 ] . For large drug molecules or other peptide-based therapeutics, the stratum corneum significantly hinders passive delivery.

Our work focuses on iontophoresis, which applies a mild constant or pulsed current to drive ionized drug molecules across the skin via an imposed electric field [ 4 ] (Fig. 1 ). The required current density varies depending on the delivery medium and the study context (e.g., in vitro or in vivo), and has been reported in the literature to range from as low as 5 μ ​ A ​ cm − 2 \mu\mathrm{A\,cm^{-2}} to as high as 3 mA cm -2 [ 5 ] . A typical iontophoretic drug delivery system consists of a power source, a pair of electrodes serving as the anode and cathode, and a drug reservoir, which is typically a gel or solution containing the active drug placed against the skin.
Upon generation of an electric field from the applied current, charged drug molecules are repelled from the electrode of like charge and driven through the stratum corneum. The kinetics of iontophoretic delivery follow the Nernst-Planck equation [ 6 ] , where the flux is governed by both electrochemical gradients and electric field strength. Particularly, chemically or physically crosslinked hydrogel-based iontophoresis has been successfully employed to deliver a wide range of therapeutics [ 7 ] , including bovine serum albumin (BSA) [ 8 , 9 ] , lidocaine [ 10 ] , insulin [ 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 5 ] , and vaccines [ 16 ] .
Iontophoretic delivery using gels enables fine control over release kinetics by tuning parameters such as current density, waveform, and pulsing schemes [ 17 ] .
While this approach offers substantial flexibility, most strategies for controlled release have focused on modulating electrical input, whereas alternative routes, such as tailoring the gel’s permeability or structural properties, remain comparatively underexplored. To further expand the controllability of drug release, this work is motivated by the freeze-thaw process of physically crosslinked hydrogels, where gel properties are highly sensitive to geometry due to mold-induced mechanical stress. We hypothesize that mold-induced hydrogel geometry can act as an indirect mediator that modulates key transport-relevant properties of drug-loaded hydrogels, namely their porous microstructure and local electric field strength, both of which appear in the governing equations for iontophoretic transport.

In this work, we conduct an in vitro study to investigate how hydrogel geometry serves as an indirect modulator of drug release behavior by influencing both microstructure and electric field strength during freeze-thaw-induced physical crosslinking. Using bovine serum albumin (BSA) as a model drug, we investigate how geometry-driven variations in the gel affect (1) microstructure and (2) electric field distribution, and how these factors collectively govern drug release. To this end, we design five distinct hydrogel geometries using mold-defined templates with varied shapes (but consistent area) to generate a range of electric field intensities. Because freeze-thaw processing inherently couples geometry with microstructural evolution, each geometry produces a unique microstructure arising from mechanical stresses experienced during crosslinking within the mold (Section I-B4 ). The gel was formulated using a one-factor-at-a-time process across all geometries (Section III-B3 ). We then conducted a drug delivery study to assess whether transport parameters differ across gel geometries (Section II-F ). In Section III-D , we present results, which show that geometry-mediated variations in pore structure and electric-field localization influence iontophoretic transport outcomes.

The governing equations for iontophoresis are the Poisson-Nernst-Planck (PNP) equations, which couple ionic transport and electrostatics.
The Nernst-Planck equation describes the flux, J i J_{i} , of species i i as the combined result of (1) diffusion due to a concentration gradient ( − D i ∇ c i -D_{i}\nabla c_{i} ), (2) electromigration under an electric potential gradient ( z i ​ D i ​ F R ​ T c i ∇ ϕ \frac{z_{i}D_{i}F}{RT}\,c_{i}\nabla\phi ), and (3) convection driven by the fluid velocity ( c i ​ 𝐯 c_{i}\mathbf{v} ) (Eq. 1 ). In this expression, D i D_{i} is the diffusion coefficient of species i i , ∇ c i \nabla c_{i} the gradient of the concentration of species i i , z i z_{i} is the valence of species i i , F F is Faraday’s constant, R R is the universal gas constant, T T is the absolute temperature, ∇ ϕ \nabla\phi is the electric potential gradient, and 𝐯 \mathbf{v} is bulk fluid velocity vector.

Complementing this, the Poisson equation (Eq. 2 ) expresses Gauss’s law in differential form (Eq. 3 ) by relating the divergence of the electric displacement field to the local charge density, where ϕ \phi is the electric potential, ε \varepsilon is the permittivity of the medium, and ρ \rho is the charge density. Together, the equations couple ionic motion with the resulting electric field. Poisson’s law determines the electric field from charge distribution, while the Nernst-Planck equation describes how ions respond to that field.

For a planar surface, Gauss’s law (Eq. 4 ) gives the relation between the electric field, E E , and surface charge density, σ \sigma , as:

where ε n \varepsilon_{n} is the normal component of the permittivity at the surface.

Optimization of an electrode’s electric field strength is critical across a range of applications, including electroadhesion [ 18 ] and field-responsive gas sensor systems [ 19 ] . In these prior works, electrodes were deliberately engineered with regions of high charge density, such as sharp corners, edges, or areas of pronounced curvature, to generate locally intensified electric fields, thereby enhancing electroadhesive forces and improving sensor sensitivity. Following Gauss’s law (Eq. 4 ), electric-field lines converge and emerge perpendicularly from these geometrical features, resulting in pronounced field amplification near tips and edges. Such localized field enhancement is expected to play a similarly important role in influencing iontophoretic drug transport.

To exploit this electrostatic phenomenon, we employ parametrically generated Hilbert-Piano curves in our electrode geometries. Hilbert-Piano curves are a class of space-filling fractal curves characterized by recursive geometric complexity (Supplementary Fig. S1).
Hilbert-Piano curves generate a large number of corners and sharp angles, which can be harnessed to concentrate electric fields and amplify local field intensity in electrode designs [ 19 , 18 ] .

Hydrogels play a central role in iontophoretic drug delivery systems, however, the hydrogel itself must be ionically conductive. Therefore, among the available materials that enable this, we use conductive polypyrrole (PPy) as it stands out not only for its intrinsic electronic conductivity, but also its chemical stability, environmental robustness, and biocompatibility [ 20 , 21 , 22 ] . When doped, PPy supports mobile charge carriers along its conjugated backbone, making it especially attractive for electroactive drug-delivery platforms. Blending PPy with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) yields a composite hydrogel that is both mechanically resilient and ionically conductive, an ideal environment for loading macromolecules such as bovine serum albumin (BSA).

BSA is a globular protein consisting of 583 amino acids with a molecular weight of approximately 66.5 kDa [ 23 ] . BSA is frequently employed as a model macromolecular drug in transdermal and nanoparticle-based delivery studies, where it often serves as a surrogate for other large therapeutic proteins, such as insulin [ 24 , 25 ] . Because BSA shares structural and functional similarities with human serum albumin, it enables its use in pharmacokinetic modeling and drug-protein interaction research without the cost or ethical concerns associated with human-derived materials [ 26 ] . Furthermore, BSA-based nanocarriers are among the most widely investigated drug delivery platforms due to their stability, solubility, and efficient uptake into tissues [ 27 ] .

The freeze-thaw (F/T) technique is one of the most widely used physical crosslinking methods and is particularly attractive because it generates porous networks without chemical crosslinkers [ 28 ] . In this process, a precursor polymer solution is subjected to repeated cycles of F/T. These physically crosslinked regions persist upon thawing, producing a stable, semi-crystalline network [ 29 ] . During freezing, ice formation induces volumetric expansion, so gels confined in rigid molds develop significant internal stresses as the phase change progresses. In F/T hydrogels, ice crystallization and melting act as a porogen, with fluid-matrix interactions and volume changes reshaping pore size, connectivity, and network morphology. Under rigid confinement and consistent F/T conditions, these stresses and local expansions strongly govern pore nucleation, alignment, and evolution within the gel network [ 30 ] . The role of mold-induced geometric confinement in shaping microstructure, permeability, and drug delivery performance remains underexplored relative to other F/T parameters [ 31 ] .

# II Materials and Methods

## II-A Calibration and Spectral Component Separation

Most PPy nanoparticles in the gel composite are immobilized within the PVA hydrogel matrix through physical entanglement and hydrogen bonding. Nevertheless, a small fraction of unbound nanoparticles may undergo passive diffusion through the gel network. In such cases, spectral overlap can occur between PPy and BSA, as PPy exhibits a broad absorption peak spanning 250-300 nm [ 32 , 33 , 34 ] , whereas BSA displays a pronounced absorption peak near 278 nm [ 35 ] . To enable separation of their signals, we apply spectral unmixing using non-negative least squares (NNLS) regression [ 36 ] . NNLS separates overlapping signals by estimating component ratios (amplitudes) that cannot be negative. NNLS is a widely used and well-established regression technique for unmixing overlapping spectra across modalities, including ultraviolet-visible spectroscopy (UV-Vis) [ 37 , 38 ] , fluorescence [ 38 ] , and Raman spectroscopy [ 39 ] , as well as fluorescent microscopic imaging [ 40 , 41 ] . ## II-B Iontophoresis Device Design

Pyrrole, polyvinyl alcohol (PVA, Mw 89,000-98,000), hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 , 30 %), deionized (DI) water, sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), phosphate-buffered saline (PBS, 1x, pH 7.4), and bovine serum albumin (BSA) were purchased and used as received from Sigma Aldrich. DI water was used for all solution preparations. Whatman filter paper (0.45 μ \mu m pore size) was obtained from Lab Source. Silver/silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) paste for electrodes was sourced from Voltera. Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) was obtained from Dow Corning.

The polypyrrole nanoparticle (PPy-NP) solution was prepared by adding 2.9 mmol of pyrrole and 2.9 mmol of SDS to 35 mL of DI water [ 43 ] . The mixture was ultrasonicated for 30 minutes to ensure proper dispersion. Subsequently, 30.9 mmol of hydrogen peroxide was gradually introduced as the oxidizing agent. The initial solution exhibited a faint yellow tint due to the presence of pyrrole. The reaction mixture was then stirred at room temperature using a magnetic stirrer. After 20 hours of stirring, the solution turned dark green, indicating the formation of polymerized PPy, although the resulting PPy at this stage was insoluble (Supplementary Fig. S3(a)).

To obtain water-soluble PPy nanoparticles (PPy-NPs), the reaction mixture was stirred at 80 ∘ C for 3 hours, then cooled to room temperature. Almost immediately upon heating, the solution changed to a brown color, indicating the progression of the reaction. The final solution was filtered using a Whatman filter to remove particles exceeding the pore size, yielding a stable dispersion of PPy-NPs. Simultaneously, 13 wt% of polyvinyl alcohol was dissolved in DI water for 24 hours at 80 ∘ C until the solution achieved clear transparency, and cooled down to room temperature (Supplementary Fig. S3 (b)). The PPy-NP solution is then blended with the PVA solution under continuous stirring for 5 hours to ensure homogenous mixing. Upon blending, the resulting PPy-PVA mixture exhibits increased viscosity. To load BSA into the prepared PVA-PPy solution, BSA was first dissolved in PBS at a concentration of 20 mg mL -1 (Supplementary Fig. S3 (c)). This concentration was selected based on the entrapment efficiency results described in Section II-D2 , which identified the most effective drug loading conditions. The resulting BSA solution was then added to the PVA-PPy solution and stirred for 1 hour. The resulting solution is then cast into molds (Supplementary Fig. S3 (d)) corresponding to 5 electrode geometries (Section II-B3 ). The solution fills the mold’s negative space, generating three-dimensional structures with uniform height, resulting in consistent volume. The cast solution then undergoes three F/T cycles, each cycle consisting of a 24-hour freeze followed by a 24-hour thaw. This process facilitates physical crosslinking of the PVA matrix through crystallite formation. Once the gel is physically crosslinked, it is transferred to the device.

To examine how physical crosslinking across different gel geometries influences swelling-mediated microstructural patterns, local electric fields, and, ultimately, drug delivery performance, we designed five gel geometries with a fixed footprint area, but varying curvature and corner density: Plain , Circle , Interdigital , Hilbert 2nd , and Hilbert 3rd (Fig. 2 : a, b, c, d, and e, respectively). Hilbert 2nd and Hilbert 3rd geometries were directly derived from the fractal Hilbert curve [ 44 ] , while the Interdigital geometry choice was motivated by electroadhesive actuator designs that are intended to enhance electric field strength [ 18 ] . We also used Plain and Circle geometries as they are the two most commonly used electrode configurations in commercial iontophoresis systems [ 45 ] . The Circle electrode pair was defined by a boundary diameter of 23 mm, while the other geometries were constrained within a 23 mm × \times 23 mm = 529 mm 2 footprint. The cathodal electrode area (drug-loaded region) was fixed at 175.49 mm 2 , and the electrode gap between cathode and anode was maintained at 1 mm across all designs. A parametric geometry-generation pipeline was implemented in CAD software (Grasshopper) to enforce these constraints and ensure consistency across geometries.

Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) gaskets were fabricated to house the electrodes and connecting wires (Fig. 2 ). The molds for these gaskets were first 3D printed using a resin printer (Standard Resin, Saturn 4 Ultra 16K), post-cured, and subsequently heated at 80 ∘ C to remove residual monomers. PDMS (Sylgard 184, Dow Corning) was prepared by mixing the base and curing agent at a 10:0.7 weight ratio (7 wt% curing agent) and cured at 80 ∘ C for 4 hours. After cooling to room temperature, silver/silver chloride (Ag/AgCl) paste was injected into the anode side of the gasket and cured at 100 ∘ C for 10 minutes. Following electrode preparation, the prepared drug-loaded hydrogel was thawed and mounted in the cathode compartment of the device. The PDMS gasket served to minimize evaporation and maintain the structural integrity of the hydrogel during the delivery study.

## II-C Characterization of Drug-Loaded Gel

Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR) spectra were collected for four sample types: PPy, BSA solution, PPy-PVA hydrogel, and BSA-loaded PPy-PVA hydrogel (Bruker Vertex V80V Vacuum FTIR). Spectra were recorded in absorbance mode over 4000-500 cm -1 . To improve peak resolution and facilitate identification of overlapping features, second derivative spectra were computed using a Savitzky-Golay filter with a seven-point window. All spectra were processed in MATLAB 2025b, including baseline correction.

## II-D Gel Condition Enhancement for Drug Delivery

In this section, we identify the parameters affecting drug delivery performance and employ the one-factor-at-a-time method to identify promising parameters, which are then tested individually. Three samples per condition were prepared and evaluated for all characterization procedures, with the exception of scanning electron microscopy (SEM). For SEM analysis, one sample was imaged for each geometry.

We measured the electrical conductivity of PPy-PVA hydrogels using a four-probe AC method to minimize errors from electrode-gel interface resistance, which is significant in DC measurements (Fig. 3 (a)). The conductivity was evaluated as a function of PPy content. Hydrogels were synthesized at nine PPy feed ratios ranging from 10 wt% to 90 wt% in 10 wt% increments. For PVA, a 13 wt% solution was used. Each hydrogel sample had dimensions of 10 mm × \times 10 mm × \times 2 mm and was subjected to three F/T cycles. A custom test jig with a groove with a matching dimension was fabricated via 3D resin printing (Standard Resin, Saturn 4 Ultra 16K) and subsequently plasma-treated to minimize interference from residual uncured resin (Fig. 3 (a)). The test jig was wiped with isopropyl alcohol after every sample. During measurements, a sinusoidal AC signal of 300 Hz and 200 m V r ​ m ​ s V_{rms} was applied to the circuitry (Keysight 33600A Series). A series resistor, R s R_{s} , of 2.2 k Ω \mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolOhm} , was connected in line with the gel sample. The gel voltage, V g ​ e ​ l V_{gel} , was measured, and the current through the circuit was calculated as, I = V r ​ m ​ s − V g ​ e ​ l R s I=\frac{V_{rms}-V_{gel}}{R_{s}} . The bulk resistance of the gel was then obtained from, R b ​ u ​ l ​ k = V g ​ e ​ l I R_{bulk}=\frac{V_{gel}}{I} (Fig. 3 (b)). Finally, the conductivity, σ \sigma , was calculated using σ = L R b ​ u ​ l ​ k ​ A \sigma=\frac{L}{R_{bulk}A} , where A A is area, 1 cm 2 , and L L is the linear distance between the inner sensing probe, which was 5 mm (Fig. 3 (a)).

To quantify BSA loading in the PPy-PVA hydrogels, we calculated the entrapment efficiency (EE, %) as the ratio of the measured mass of encapsulated BSA to the initially loaded mass. Hydrogel samples with 10 mm × \times 10 mm × \times 2 mm were prepared with 5, 10, 20, 30, 40 concentrations (mg mL -1 ) of BSA. The samples were subjected to F/T cycles under the same conditions as used for other characterization experiments. Alongside drug-loaded gels, blank samples with the same dimensions were created and subjected to the same F/T cycles to serve as a baseline. After preparation, each sample was dissolved in 10 mL DI water and vortexed vigorously for 24 hours to ensure complete dispersion. Dissolved samples were analyzed by UV-Vis spectroscopy.

To evaluate the impact of current density on the BSA release ( Q Q , μ \mu g cm -2 ), gel samples measuring 10 mm × \times 10 mm × \times 2 mm were prepared. Current densities of 0.5 mA cm -2 , 1 mA cm -2 , and 2 mA cm -2 were applied for 30 minutes. During testing, the Ag/AgCl electrode was positioned 1 mm from the drug-loaded gel, and both the electrode and gel were housed in a PDMS gasket and mounted onto a two-compartment Franz diffusion cell (11.28 mm orifice, jacketed, PermeGear). PBS solution from the receptor compartment was sampled and analyzed using UV-Vis spectroscopy. Since the samples contained an unknown contribution of both BSA and PPy, they were processed using the pipeline described in Section II-A1 . The current density that resulted in the highest BSA release was used for the drug delivery test.

## II-E Coupled Effects of Geometry and Physical Crosslinking on Hydrogel Properties

Hydrogel geometry is defined by a negative mold template, inherently coupling microstructure and electric field distribution. We examine two key properties (microstructure and maximum electric field strength), each affected differently by the F/T driven physical crosslinking process: the microstructure of physically crosslinked hydrogels is characterized via SEM to capture fabrication effects, while electric field strength is evaluated through simulation.

Hydrogel samples with five distinct geometries were fabricated according to the established parameters. The samples underwent identical F/T cycles and were subsequently freeze-dried for 60 hours to preserve their microstructural features. For the three geometries with pronounced periodic geometry features ( Interdigital , Hilbert 2nd , Hilbert 3rd ; Fig. 2 (c)-(e)), two distinct local regions were sampled: (i) narrow cross-sections where mechanical constraint is maximal, and (ii) wider sections that experience comparatively lower constraint. In contrast, the Plain and Circle geometries (Fig. 2 (a), (b)) consist of a single bulk volume with relatively uniform cross-section. For these samples, we sectioned from the center and near the edge to capture any radial variations that may arise from differential swelling against the mold walls. Microstructural features included geometry-level median pore area and bulk porosity, as well as region-specific (local) pore area and porosity.

First, SEM was used to image gel cross-sections (Zeiss Sigma 500). Each image was manually annotated to define a region of interest (ROI) excluding peripheral gel walls that lacked discernible pores or exhibited compression artifacts. Pore areas within each ROI were quantified in ImageJ, and local porosity was calculated (MATLAB R2025b) as the pore area fraction. Bulk porosity for each geometry was then computed as the volume-weighted average of regional porosities, using normalized volume fractions extracted from the compiled ImageJ output.

To evaluate how hydrogel geometry influences the local electric-field distribution, each gel design was modeled in CAD (Grasshopper) , accounting for consistent volume, and exported as a .STEP file for import into Ansys Maxwell for finite element analysis. The five electrode geometries were then simulated under a 5 V potential difference to compute the resulting electric field strength.

## II-F Drug Delivery Experiments

A Franz diffusion cell was modified to accommodate the dimensions of the experimental devices. Custom designed adapters featured either a circular or rectangular diffusion area (Fig. 3 (b)). Each adapter was affixed to the receptor compartment with a clamp, and deviations in receptor volume introduced by the adapter were quantified and incorporated into the concentration calculations. Note that the drug-loaded gel area was kept constant at 175.49 mm 2 . The donor compartment was replaced with the test device, with the anode and cathode connected to a power supply delivering a constant current density. 2026-10-23.title: Dispersive Tree Agreements for Multi-Robot Coordination
2026-10-23.authors: Shashank A. Deshpande , Blake T. Edwards , Jonathan P. How
2026-10-23.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
2026-10-23.comment: . Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Robotics
2026-10-23.abstract:
Multi-robot coordination of nonlinear systems is naturally
formulated as joint-space optimal control subject to constraints
over groups of robots. Existing methods that approach joint
optimality remain largely centralized, offline, and confined to
collision-free motion planning, while decentralized, real-time
counterparts target safe navigation without pursuing the joint
optimum. This paper develops a decentralized, real-time planner
that approaches the joint optimum as an anytime process. We extend
a recent single-robot framework that searches dispersive trees of
forward-propagated commands for differentially flat systems to
coordinate a multi-robot team near-optimally. We first show that the inter-robot coupling can be effectively
replaced by some local constraints, under which locally grown
dispersive trees contain a near-optimal agreement. It is this
structure that the robots pursue by decentralized column
generation, negotiating rents on the shared space that guide the
search of each robot’s tree. The negotiation settles on an agreement
whose near-optimality is certified at quiescence. Our
protocol, WarpWeaver, implements this negotiation as an
asynchronous real-time loop over a receding horizon, and
demonstrates effective closure to quiesced agreements even when
real-time deadlines cut the negotiation short. In
simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time by up to 22 % 22\% against centralized offline planners on the Dynobench suite and by up to 37 % 37\% against a
decentralized real-time baseline, and nearly doubles the success
rate of a task-specific planner on graph connectivity. Hardware
experiments on six robots planning onboard demonstrate real-world
implementability.
2026-10-23.introduction:
This paper addresses the coordination of a team of robots with
differentially flat nonlinear dynamics, formulated as optimal control in the joint
space of the team subject to constraints over groups of robots.
We seek control inputs
whose cost lies near the joint optimum, via
distributed computation across the robots in real time, to
maintain robustness to changes in the individual objectives of
the robots as well as in the dynamics of the environment. Existing approaches to this problem
divide broadly into centralized, offline planners with
guarantees of asymptotic optimality, and real-time decentralized
planners that work with simplified dynamics, without pursuing
the joint optimum.

A range of centralized planners derive from multi-agent path
finding [ 1 ] and handle pairwise conflicts in a
high-level search on top of low-level single-robot planners
running model predictive control [ 2 ] ,
sampling-based planning [ 3 ] , or search over
graphs of discontinuity-bounded motion primitives [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
Sampling-based planners search the composite configuration
space of the team [ 7 , 8 ] . These planners provide
asymptotic guarantees of completeness or optimality, and focus
on motion planning with pairwise separation.

Decentralized planning, on the other hand, comes with real-time
advantages such as robustness to changes in the individual
objectives or in the environment. Decentralized trajectory
optimization involves
high-frequency replanning of safe splines around the incumbents
communicated by peer robots, while often simplifying the
robots’ dynamics [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 ] . Consensus-based
distributed optimization instead lets the robots negotiate, with
gradient-based local optimization driven by penalties on
mutual disagreement [ 15 , 16 ] .
Coordination across these methods, however, often settles in
local optima,
without pursuing the joint optimum.

In summary, real-time multi-robot coordination deals with multiple
sources of complexity. First, planning and control at the level
of a single robot must respect the nonlinear dynamics of its
control system. In addition, these
control trajectories must coordinate to satisfy various
constraints over groups of robots while evading the many local
minima of the joint problem.
Finally, the algorithm that addresses these challenges must
decentralize across the robots under limited communication and
maintain robustness to communication delays within the team.
While existing approaches handle this complexity in part, this
paper develops a decentralized framework that tackles each of its
sources in unison.

We employ dispersive forward tree search [ 17 ] ,
which finds near-optimal control inputs for differentially flat
systems, for single-robot planning and control. To solve coordination, we first show that the coupling among the
robots can be absorbed into suitable constraints on each robot
alone, so that tractably sized dispersive trees grown locally by the
robots jointly contain a near-optimal agreement. It is this structure that the
remainder of our development pursues. We formulate the selection of this
joint agreement as an integer linear program and approach its
solution by column generation [ 18 , 19 ] , in which the
dual of its linear relaxation sets rents on the shared space.
Under these rents, the search for a new column becomes a
single-robot problem that each robot solves near-optimally with
its own dispersive forward tree.
Notably, this column generation procedure is effectively
decentralized, to distribute the computational load of the
process across the robots while limiting communication within
the team to a manageable amount. We show that the resulting process implements an
anytime negotiation whose agreement is certified near-optimal
once it reaches quiescence, up to the resolution of the search and a gap that the agents compute online. This development culminates in
WarpWeaver, the real-time multi-robot planner that we propose,
which runs the negotiation asynchronously across the team over a
receding horizon and remains robust to bounded communication
delays. Our experiments thereby demonstrate that this negotiation,
driven by decentralized column generation, is a pattern well
suited to real-time multi-robot coordination, as the
agreements that it commits within real-time deadlines come close in
cost to those that it reaches when given time to quiesce.

In summary, this paper makes the following contributions.

∙ \bullet Joint optimal control as distributed
dispersive forward search. We cast a broad class of multi-robot
coordination problems as joint-space optimal control of
differentially flat nonlinear systems, and prove that suitably constrained, locally grown
dispersive forward trees contain a near-optimal agreement
( Proposition 1 ).

∙ \bullet Decentralized column generation. We
pursue this structure by decentralized column generation under
limited communication, in which rents on the shared space guide the
tree search of each robot, and prove that the negotiated agreement
is certified near-optimal at quiescence, relative to the joint
solutions robust at the search resolution
( Propositions 4 and 2 ).

∙ \bullet Real-time protocol. We develop
WarpWeaver, an asynchronous protocol that runs decentralized
column generation over a receding horizon onboard each robot, to
coordinate the team in real time under bounded communication
delays, whose agreements within real-time deadlines come
close in cost to quiesced ones.

∙ \bullet Evaluation and hardware
experiments. We benchmark WarpWeaver in simulation against
centralized offline, decentralized real-time, and task-specific
planners. It reduces total travel time by up to 22 % 22\% against
centralized offline planners on Dynobench and by up to 37 % 37\% against
a decentralized real-time baseline. Further, on a graph connectivity
task, it nearly doubles the success rate of a task-specific planner. We further deploy it on a team of six robots, each planning
onboard in real time.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III formulates the joint optimal control problem and its flat
reformulation, and Section IV reviews dispersive forward
tree search. Section V develops the decentralized
column generation scheme, its near-optimality certificate, and the
WarpWeaver protocol. Section VI presents the simulation
experiments and benchmarks, and Section VII the real-robot
experiments. We conclude in Section VIII . The proofs are
deferred to Appendix A .
2026-10-23.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Sampling and Search for Multi-Robot Motion Planning

Sampling-based planning extends to multi-robot motion planning in
the composite configuration space of the
team [ 7 , 8 ] . For geometric paths,
search over the tensor product of individual roadmaps has been
shown to be asymptotically optimal [ 8 ] , and near-optimal at
a finite sample size [ 20 ] . While it is
unclear how this decomposition carries over to robots with
continuous dynamics, kinodynamic tree search in the composite state
space has been shown to be probabilistically
complete [ 21 ] .
Decentralized implementations of composite search have also been
demonstrated, with robots replanning in turn by merit-based token
passing [ 22 ] or exchanging probability
distributions over their plans [ 23 ] .

Kinodynamic extensions of multi-agent path finding on
graphs [ 1 ] retain its two-level structure, a
high-level search that coordinates the team on top of low-level
local planners. The low-level graph search is then replaced by a range of methods spanning sampling-based tree
search [ 3 ] , model predictive
control [ 2 ] , and search over graphs of motion
primitives joined up to a bounded
discontinuity [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] .
These implementations are predominantly centralized and offline,
and guarantee solution properties ranging from probabilistic or
resolution completeness to asymptotic optimality.

## II-B Trajectory Optimization for Multi-Robot Motion Planning

Centralized trajectory optimization coordinates the team within a
single program [ 24 , 25 ] , whose size grows with the number of robots.
Scalable variants involve a discrete coordination layer, such as
priority-based search over mixed-integer programs for tracked
reference paths [ 26 ] and multi-agent path finding
over Bézier curves [ 27 ] .
Decentralized trajectory optimization segregates the program across
the robots, each of which replans a trajectory around the incumbent
commitments of its peers. These commitments enter as collision
penalties in gradient-based optimization [ 9 ] ,
or as separating constraints robust to imperfect
communication [ 10 , 11 ] .
Distributed model predictive control [ 12 , 13 ] follows a similar pattern over short horizons, with linear safe
corridors [ 14 ] preserving feasibility. These planners run in real time at scale, typically on
simplified models of the dynamics.

Instead of iterative replanning around incumbent commitments,
consensus-based distributed optimization lets the robots
negotiate. Each robot keeps local copies of the shared variables
and optimizes them under its nonlinear dynamics.
Penalties on mutual disagreement, updated by the alternating
direction method of multipliers, drive the team toward agreement
on these variables [ 15 , 16 ] .

## II-C Coordination Beyond Inter-Robot Separation

Several tasks of utility constrain groups of robots beyond pairwise
separation, such as maintaining a connected communication
network [ 28 ] or keeping robots tethered to
each other. Existing work typically addresses these
tasks by deploying dedicated mechanisms. For instance, connectivity
maintenance is commonly enforced
by potential functions that keep the algebraic connectivity of the
communication graph positive [ 28 ] , a design
that Realm [ 29 , 30 ] extends to
line-of-sight constraints derived in real time from onboard point
clouds. Our method is able to address
coordination beyond collision avoidance by specification of hard
constraints on the joint-space dynamics, as we demonstrate by
implementing connectivity maintenance in simulation and tethering
in hardware experiments.

## II-D Column Generation and Decentralized Pricing

Column generation is a canonical technique for solving large linear
programs by generating their variables on
demand [ 18 , 19 ] . Dual
prices from a restricted master program guide the search for new
columns, with a Lagrangian bound on the gap [ 31 ] and branching for integrality [ 32 ] .
This technique has been applied to
multi-agent path finding on graphs by
branch-and-cut-and-price [ 33 ] , and to multi-robot
routing over space-time positions with pricing by
resource-constrained shortest paths [ 34 ] .
Column generation has been shown to distribute effectively across
robots, with local pricing
and an exchange of columns among neighbors, for task
assignment [ 35 ] .

We formulate joint optimal control as a search over the dispersive
forward trees of the robots [ 17 ] and distribute
this search across the team via column generation, running
asynchronously in real time with a certificate of near-optimality
at quiescence, relative to the joint solutions that are robust at the search resolution.

2026-10-23.title: SCOPE: Scene-graph Construction Optimized by Plan Error-correction for Robot Long-term Planning Datasets
2026-10-23.authors: Chaoyue Li , Zeyu Gao , Yanfeng Lu , Fan Luo
2026-10-23.comment: . Accepted at IROS 2026. Project page: this https URL
2026-10-23.abstract:
Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) stands as a fundamental challenge in robotics, essential for enabling autonomous agents to execute complex, long-horizon tasks in diverse environments. While Large Language Models (LLMs) introduce a new paradigm for TAMP by leveraging extensive common sense, their inherent reasoning limitations hinder direct application, and fine-tuning strategies to enhance these capabilities are currently bottlenecked by the scarcity of high-quality datasets. Existing automated generation methods often suffer from homogeneity, limiting model generalization, and unsolvability, where hallucinated scene graphs create physical mismatches with task goals. To address these issues, we propose S cene-graph C onstruction O ptimized by P lan E rror-correction ( SCOPE ), an automated framework designed to generate diverse and executable TAMP datasets. SCOPE incorporates multi-level diversity metrics to maximize the information entropy of scenarios. Crucially, it introduces a Plan Feedback Error-correction pipeline that utilizes planner execution failures as feedback signals to retroactively rectify logical inconsistencies in scene graphs, ensuring physical feasibility. Experimental results demonstrate that SCOPE exhibits greater robustness to erroneous scene graphs and generates higher-quality data. When utilized for LLM fine-tuning, SCOPE-generated data yield a downstream TAMP model that achieves an absolute 12.33% gain in success rate over its counterpart fine-tuned with data generated by DELTA, a state-of-the-art PDDL-based planner.
More demos and information are available on https://scope-page.github.io/ .
2026-10-23.introduction:
Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) stands as a fundamental challenge in the field of robotics. Traditional approaches [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] rely primarily on rule-based designs and heuristic searches. However, these methods often lack sufficient generalization capabilities. The emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) [ 4 , 5 ] has introduced a new paradigm [ 6 , 7 ] for addressing TAMP challenges. By leveraging their extensive common sense knowledge, LLMs demonstrate significant potential in handling complex TAMP tasks in different scenarios, enhancing the universality of planning systems.

Current methods utilizing LLMs for TAMP can be broadly categorized into Symbolic Planning and Direct Planning. Symbolic Planning [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] employs the LLM as a translator that decomposes tasks based on hand-crafted rules to generate problem definitions for traditional planners. While this approach achieves a relatively high success rate, it relies heavily on manually defined domains and rules. Consequently, this paradigm exhibits limited error tolerance, making full automation difficult. Conversely, the Direct Planning methods [ 6 , 11 , 12 ] utilize the LLM directly as a planner. These methods exploit the common sense reasoning capabilities of the model and require minimal manual prior constraints, allowing users to accomplish a wide range of tasks through natural language. Nevertheless, the success rate of this approach is often limited by the inherent shortcomings of LLMs in temporal reasoning and their tendency towards hallucination. Ultimately, the performance of both paradigms is intrinsically constrained by the underlying planning capabilities of the LLMs.

Therefore, fine-tuning LLMs with extensive data serves as an effective strategy [ 13 , 14 ] to internalize planning logic and enhance temporal reasoning capabilities. A standard TAMP fine-tuning sample consists of three core elements: the scene graph describing the environmental state, the instruction defining the task goal, and the plan serving as the solution path. However, constructing TAMP datasets currently requires balancing data quality and annotation cost. Manually annotated datasets [ 15 ] offer high quality yet incur prohibitive costs, making them difficult to scale for fine-tuning needs. While data constructed using LLMs [ 16 ] offers a low-cost automated alternative, it often suffers from low quality.

This deficiency primarily manifests in two aspects. First, the generated content suffers from a lack of diversity. Due to the preference of LLMs, the scene graphs often exhibit high repetitiveness, resulting in insufficient information entropy within the dataset and limiting the generalization ability of the model. Second, the generated tasks frequently suffer from unsolvability because of the wrong scene graphs. Influenced by hallucinations, automatically generated scene graphs often contain logical flaws, such as missing key interactive objects or incorrect attributes. This mismatch between the environment and the task renders the generated problems physically unsolvable, thereby introducing a significant amount of noise into the training data.

To address these challenges, we propose S cene-graph C onstruction O ptimized by P lan E rror-correction ( SCOPE ), an automated generation framework designed specifically for constructing high-quality TAMP datasets. To mitigate the homogeneity inherent in LLM-generated content, SCOPE incorporates multi-level Diversity Metrics during the Scene Graph Construction phases. Specifically, we monitor Global Diversity to ensure a broad coverage of task types while leveraging Local Diversity to enrich fine-grained variations in object attributes and spatial relationships, thereby maximizing the information entropy of the dataset. Second, to tackle the prevalent issue of unsolvability in automatically generated data, SCOPE introduces a Plan Feedback Error-correction pipeline. This pipeline establishes a closed-loop system for generation and verification, where execution results from the planner serve as feedback signals. This process allows the system to retroactively identify and correct logical inconsistencies within the scene graph while iteratively generating feasible planning sequences, effectively solving mismatches between the environment and the task.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose SCOPE, an automated data generation framework that integrates diversity-aware generation and Plan Feedback Error-correction. By maximizing data diversity and iteratively rectifying logical inconsistencies through execution feedback, SCOPE effectively constructs highly diverse and physically executable TAMP datasets with high quality.

We investigate the impact of data quality on the end-to-end planning performance of fine-tuned LLMs through extensive experiments, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . Validated in the AI2-THOR environment, our results demonstrate that the high-quality data generated by SCOPE significantly improves the planning success rate, achieving an absolute 12.33% gain over data generated by DELTA.

1. We propose SCOPE, an automated data generation framework that integrates diversity-aware generation and Plan Feedback Error-correction. By maximizing data diversity and iteratively rectifying logical inconsistencies through execution feedback, SCOPE effectively constructs highly diverse and physically executable TAMP datasets with high quality.

2. We investigate the impact of data quality on the end-to-end planning performance of fine-tuned LLMs through extensive experiments, as illustrated in Fig. 1 . Validated in the AI2-THOR environment, our results demonstrate that the high-quality data generated by SCOPE significantly improves the planning success rate, achieving an absolute 12.33% gain over data generated by DELTA.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Task and Motion Planning with LLMs

With their remarkable capabilities in common sense reasoning and semantic understanding, LLMs have introduced a paradigm shift in solving TAMP problems. Existing approaches utilizing LLMs can be broadly categorized into two distinct streams: Symbolic Planning and Direct Planning.

In the Symbolic Planning paradigm, the LLM functions primarily as a semantic translator to bridge natural language and classical solvers. LLM+P [ 7 ] pioneered this approach by converting natural language instructions into PDDL problem definitions to leverage the optimality of external planners. To scale this approach to large environments, SayPlan [ 8 ] grounds LLMs into 3D scene graphs, utilizing semantic search to extract relevant sub-graphs and reduce the problem scope. To address long-horizon tasks, LLMGenPlan [ 17 ] investigates generalized planning, in which the LLM synthesizes generic Python policy programs for an entire class of problems within a domain and refines them through an automated debugging loop. DELTA [ 18 ] integrates LLM-based scene graph pruning and goal decomposition, breaking down complex objectives into sequences of solvable sub-problems.

Conversely, the Direct Planning paradigm utilizes the LLM directly as a planner. LLM-As-Planner [ 19 ] demonstrates the zero-shot capability of models to generate high-level action sequences based on common sense knowledge. RoCo [ 9 ] facilitates collaborative planning through dialog. CoPal [ 11 ] incorporates iterative feedback mechanisms to correct execution failures. DAG-Plan [ 20 ] proposes generating Directed Acyclic Graphs to explicitly model temporal dependencies.

Ultimately, the performance of both paradigms is intrinsically constrained by the underlying planning capabilities of the base models.

## II-B Instruction Tuning and Automated Data Generation

Instruction tuning has emerged as a pivotal paradigm for unlocking the complex reasoning and planning capabilities of LLMs [ 13 , 15 ] . However, the efficacy of this approach is intrinsically tied to the quality and diversity of the training corpora [ 21 ] . While foundational datasets such as TaskLama [ 15 ] and FLAN [ 21 ] offer high-quality examples, they rely on expensive human annotation and are inherently limited in scale. To address data scarcity, previous works have attempted to synthesize training data using LLM [ 22 ] . Although scalable, these methods often introduce noise due to LLM hallucinations, leading to mismatches between instructions and responses. To mitigate this, recent approaches leverage automated PDDL planners [ 16 , 23 ] to construct instruction tuning datasets, yielding higher logical consistency than purely LLM-generated data. However, existing PDDL-based pipelines typically produce scene graphs that are structurally simple and lack diversity, resulting in homogeneous environment configurations. Furthermore, due to persistent hallucinations in the task formulation process, these methods often fail to guarantee solvability, frequently generating invalid samples where task goals are logically incompatible with the initial environmental states.

2026-10-23.title: Point-Level Refinable Semantic Mapping for Spatial Understanding
2026-10-23.authors: Taimeng Fu , Yi Du , Zitong Zhan , Qiwei Du , Shaoshu Su , Zhipeng Zhao , Chen Wang
2026-10-23.abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for long-horizon robot autonomy, enabling robots to reason about objects, their spatial relationships, and past observations across time. However, existing object-centric semantic maps are primarily designed for static environments and rely on an append-only point integration strategy, where newly observed points are accumulated but previously integrated points are rarely reevaluated. Consequently, perception errors accumulate over time, and outdated points persist after objects move or disappear. Although recent dynamic mapping methods update object-level representations in changing scenes, they do not explicitly revise noisy or obsolete points within each object. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object representations through probabilistic point-level confidence updating. Each object point maintains a confidence score that is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: consistent observations reinforce reliable points, while inconsistent segmentation masks, depth measurements, and visibility cues suppress spurious and outdated points. Combined with object tracking and re-identification to preserve instance identities under motion and relocation, our framework enables object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated. Experiments demonstrate improved mapping accuracy over the previous method by 3.46% on Replica and 2.55% on ScanNet, show robustness in dynamic environments and under perception noise, and provide an effective spatial memory for object navigation and embodied question-answering with success rates of 82.4% and 76.7%.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Open-vocabulary 3D semantic maps have emerged as a key spatial memory representation for robot autonomy [ 1 ] by grounding open-ended semantic concepts in 3D space [ 2 ] . They enable robots to localize task-relevant objects, reason about object relationships, and maintain persistent spatial context for embodied tasks, e.g., vision-language navigation [ 3 ] and mobile manipulation [ 4 ] .

Recent open-vocabulary mapping systems [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] construct object-centric 3D semantic maps by integrating RGB-D observations with open-vocabulary perception models. However, real-world robotic deployment requires long-term operation in dynamic environments, where objects are frequently moved, removed, or rearranged. Existing methods are largely designed for static scenes and rely on an append-only point integration strategy: newly observed points are continuously added to object instances, while previously integrated points are rarely revisited or revised.

Several recent methods have extended semantic mapping to dynamic environments by detecting object changes and updating object-level map representations [ 8 , 9 , 10 ] . For example, Khronos [ 8 ] identifies changed objects through depth consistency, while OpenIN [ 9 ] and DualMap [ 10 ] associate movable objects with supporting anchors to maintain object identities. However, these approaches primarily reason about scene changes at the object or relation level, without explicitly revising noisy or outdated points within each object instance. As a result, local artifacts introduced by perception errors or stale observations can remain embedded in the object representation, degrading long-term mapping quality.

To address both dynamic environments and noisy perception, we propose an online refinable open-vocabulary semantic mapping framework that continuously refines object-centric maps over time. The key idea is to maintain a probabilistic confidence estimate for every object point, rather than treating integrated points as permanent entries. Each confidence score is updated online using multi-view temporal evidence: points consistently supported by new observations are reinforced, while those inconsistent with segmentation masks, depth measurements, or visibility cues are progressively down-weighted and eventually removed. This enables semantic maps to preserve reliable geometry while eliminating perception artifacts and outdated points caused by object motion. To maintain consistent object identities, the framework further combines 2D tracking for in-view motion with feature-based re-identification after objects leave and re-enter the field of view, as shown in Fig. 1 .

To evaluate its effectiveness as an online spatial memory for autonomous robots, we integrate the proposed semantic mapping framework into a vision-language navigation (VLN) framework [ 11 ] and evaluate it on object navigation and embodied question answering tasks in real-world environments.
The main contributions of this work are:

We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework with point-level confidence updating, enabling object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated.

We introduce a multi-view temporal update mechanism that reinforces reliable object points while suppressing spurious and outdated points caused by perception errors and object motion, improving mapping accuracy and robustness in dynamic environments.

We integrate object tracking and feature-based re-identification to preserve consistent object identities under motion and demonstrate the proposed map as an effective online spatial memory for vision-language navigation and embodied question answering.

1. We propose an online refinable semantic mapping framework with point-level confidence updating, enabling object-centric semantic maps to be continuously refined rather than monotonically accumulated.

2. We introduce a multi-view temporal update mechanism that reinforces reliable object points while suppressing spurious and outdated points caused by perception errors and object motion, improving mapping accuracy and robustness in dynamic environments.

3. We integrate object tracking and feature-based re-identification to preserve consistent object identities under motion and demonstrate the proposed map as an effective online spatial memory for vision-language navigation and embodied question answering.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Open-Vocabulary Semantic Mapping

Semantic mapping augments geometric reconstruction with object labels, instance structure, and region-level semantics for navigation and manipulation [ 2 ] . Earlier metric-semantic systems [ 12 ] rely on closed-set detectors [ 13 ] , while recent vision-language foundation models [ 14 , 15 ] enable open-vocabulary maps that can be queried with free-form language.
Building on these advances, recent works integrate open-vocabulary semantic maps with large language models (LLMs) for embodied reasoning and long-horizon planning [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] .
These approaches demonstrate the value of structured semantic memory for language-guided robotic reasoning. However, they mainly focus on semantic abstraction and typically assume that fused object points remain valid once inserted. As a result, erroneous or old points introduced by noisy perception or object motion are difficult to revise through later observations.

## II-B Dynamic Semantic Map Updating

Real robotic environments are dynamic, where task-relevant objects may be moved, removed, or re-observed at different locations.
Dynamic semantic mapping systems reason about environmental changes using geometric consistency and object relations.
Khronos [ 8 ] uses ray-casting to verify geometric changes, but its verification is primarily object-level and does not explicitly refine erroneous points within an otherwise valid instance or suppress false semantic instances using semantic inconsistency. OpenIN [ 9 ] and DualMap [ 10 ] maintain movable objects through relations to relatively stable anchors. Such relation-based updating depends on the existence of a suitable anchor and sufficiently complete re-observation of that anchor. In contrast, our method maintains each instance independently without requiring predefined object-to-anchor relations.

2026-10-23.title: Skeleton-Grounded Latent Action Model for Robot World Models
2026-10-23.authors: Qi Lv , Jiayi Lin , Yuxin Jiang , Jianzong Wang , Xiang Deng , Mike Shou Zheng
2026-10-23.comment: Project Page: this https URL
2026-10-23.abstract:
Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions.
Latent action models enable learning dynamics from videos by encoding visual transitions as proxy actions.
However, reconstruction-driven latent actions mix robot motion with object responses and other scene changes, complicating their correspondence with robot controls.
We propose SkeLAM , a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling.
SkeLAM decomposes latent actions into a kinematic component grounded by robot skeleton supervision and a residual component retaining complementary visual dynamics.
Cross-modal swap reconstruction encourages RGB-derived and skeleton-derived kinematic representations to be interchangeable during video reconstruction.
The world model incorporates both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout reduces its dependence on future-derived residual information.
A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions.
At inference, the model generates future observations from the current observation and robot actions.
On DROID, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1% compared with DreamDojo.
Motion probing supports kinematic specialization, while qualitative results demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts.
Policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Robot world models simulate how environments evolve in response to robot actions, supporting policy evaluation and model-based planning ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ) .
Accurate simulation requires modeling robot motion and resulting scene changes.
Latent action models encode visual transitions as proxy actions ( Bruce et al., 2024 ; Ye et al., 2025 ) , allowing world models to learn dynamics from large-scale videos without explicit action annotations ( Gao et al., 2026 ) .
These latent actions are learned through future-observation reconstruction, with the current observation providing visual context ( Gao et al., 2025 ; Liang et al., 2026 ) .
For action-conditioned simulation, inferred latent actions serve as supervision for mapping robot controls into the learned latent action space.

Learning this mapping is challenging since reconstruction objectives encourage latent actions to encode robot motion together with object responses and other scene changes ( Nikulin et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) .
For example, similar end-effector motions may produce different object responses under different contact states ( Gu et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) , introducing scene-dependent variation beyond robot motion into the adaptation target.
These interaction outcomes are useful for world modeling, since accurate simulation requires predicting how robot motion affects the surrounding scene.
This motivates a dedicated kinematic component for action adaptation, together with a residual component retaining complementary transition information for dynamics learning.

To this end, we propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model for controllable robot world modeling.
Robot skeletons describe robot configuration and motion while abstracting scene appearance.
Related robot world models use skeleton sequences or kinematic renderings as direct conditioning signals for generation ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wu and Gao, 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ) .
SkeLAM uses paired RGB and skeleton transitions to learn kinematic and residual components from RGB observations.
Skeleton supervision grounds the kinematic latent in robot motion, while the residual latent supplies complementary information for RGB reconstruction.
Together, the two components jointly support reconstruction, providing a dedicated target for action adaptation while retaining information for dynamics learning.
During representation learning, skeletons supervise the RGB latents, while the deployed interface uses RGB observations and robot actions.

We further introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction, which replaces the RGB kinematic latent with its paired skeleton counterpart while retaining the RGB residual.
Reconstructing the same transition under this substitution encourages compatible motion conditioning in the RGB decoder, extending cross-modal correspondence beyond alignment in latent space.
The world model learns from both components through separate conditioning pathways, while branch dropout prepares it for the zero-residual condition used at deployment.
A lightweight adapter maps robot actions to the kinematic space, and subsequent world-model fine-tuning adapts generation to these predicted conditions.
At inference, generation uses the current observation and robot actions.

To assess motion accuracy and visual fidelity, we evaluate SkeLAM on DROID ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) .
Compared with DreamDojo, SkeLAM reduces end-effector ADE by 19.5% and LPIPS by 11.1%.
Motion probing shows that the kinematic component approaches the performance of the concatenated representation with half the latent dimensions, while latent interventions and component ablations support its role in generation.
Qualitative results further demonstrate zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer in generated rollouts.
Open-loop policy evaluation shows agreement between predicted success rates and those measured in real robot executions.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model that separates the conditioning roles of robot motion and complementary visual dynamics, providing a dedicated kinematic target for robot action adaptation.

We introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction to encourage compatible RGB and skeleton motion conditioning during generation.
Combined with branch dropout, this design supports robot action conditioning through the
kinematic pathway learned from visual transitions.

Experiments on DROID demonstrate gains in motion accuracy and visual fidelity, supported by representation analyses and component ablations.
We further show zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer and agreement between predicted and measured policy success rates.

1. We propose SkeLAM, a skeleton-guided latent action model that separates the conditioning roles of robot motion and complementary visual dynamics, providing a dedicated kinematic target for robot action adaptation.

2. We introduce cross-modal swap reconstruction to encourage compatible RGB and skeleton motion conditioning during generation.
Combined with branch dropout, this design supports robot action conditioning through the
kinematic pathway learned from visual transitions.

3. Experiments on DROID demonstrate gains in motion accuracy and visual fidelity, supported by representation analyses and component ablations.
We further show zero-shot human-to-robot motion transfer and agreement between predicted and measured policy success rates.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Action-conditioned robot world models. Robot world models support interactive simulation ( Yang et al., 2024 ; Wu et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) and policy evaluation ( Zhu et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Liao et al., 2025 ) .
Visual prediction supports foresight-guided policy learning ( Lv et al., 2025a ; Cai et al., 2026a ) and multi-view data augmentation ( Wang et al., 2026 ) .
Related research addresses video procedure planning ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , temporal answer grounding ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and cloud–edge agent execution ( Huang et al., 2026 ) .
DALI-R ( Luo et al., 2026 ) reranks actions with 3D point-cloud latent predictions and task-completion scores.
Control representations include action embeddings, skeleton sequences ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Wu and Gao, 2026 ) , and kinematic renderings ( Xu et al., 2026 ) .
Recent models further incorporate spatial grounding ( Gu et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026b ) .
Separating camera and object motion also supports camera-controlled video generation ( Cheng et al., 2026b ) .

Latent action learning from videos. Latent action models encode visual transitions for world modeling ( Bruce et al., 2024 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ; Garrido et al., 2026 ) and robot policy learning ( Ye et al., 2025 ; Liang et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026a ) .
Reconstruction-based learning is sensitive to distracting dynamics and ambiguous action correspondence ( Nikulin et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) .
Olaf-World ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) aligns integrated latent actions with temporal differences in frozen video features across contexts.
LAOF ( Bu et al., 2026b ) uses agent optical flow as motion supervision to reduce sensitivity to distractors.
Shared RGB–depth features provide geometric supervision ( Govind et al., 2026 ) , alongside advances in latent representations for policy learning ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Shen et al., 2026 ; Xie et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026b ) .
LARYBench ( Nie et al., 2026 ) evaluates representations using semantic action classification and physical action regression, independently of downstream policies.
A systematic study finds that proxy metrics support coarse model selection but poorly rank downstream policy performance ( Bu et al., 2026a ) .
SkeLAM grounds its kinematic component in robot skeletons while retaining complementary visual dynamics in a separate residual.

Structured action representations. Quantized skills support autoregressive action generation ( Li et al., 2025 ) , while flow-matching policies preserve latent-action structure and align latent and physical actions through interpolation-based sampling during decoder training ( Lyu et al., 2026 ) .
Spatial and kinematic priors include voxel heatmaps ( Yang et al., 2026c ) , robot graphs with differentiable kinematics ( Lv et al., 2025b ) , and trajectories defined by endpoint positions and velocities ( Lv et al., 2026 ) .
Joint image, LiDAR, and action modeling supports autonomous-driving trajectory generation ( Cheng et al., 2026a ) .
SkeleWAM ( Sheng et al., 2026 ) jointly learns action and future-state prediction over sparse 3D robot–object skeletons.
Skel-WAM ( Cai et al., 2026b ) cotrains visual and hand-skeleton dynamics on human and robot videos, with a robot-trained action expert.
SkeLAM uses skeleton supervision to ground video-derived kinematic latents for action-conditioned video prediction.

2026-10-23.title: VecTile: A Low-Cost Flexible Tactile Array for 3-DoF Force Sensing
2026-10-23.authors: Jian Hou , Xin Zhou , Adam J. Spiers
2026-10-23.comment: . Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
2026-10-23.abstract:
Tactile sensing provides robots with contact information difficult to obtain from vision alone.
Shear force is particularly important for understanding tangential contact, guiding corrective motions, and maintaining grasp stability, yet flexible and low-cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force.
We introduce VecTile, a low-cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three-axis force sensing.
VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns.
The sensor can be fabricated in-house without specialized equipment. The complete system costs less than 35 USD for a 4 × \times 4 array.
We validate the sensing mechanism through finite element analysis and hardware experiments.
In controlled single-taxel tests over 1–5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force, VecTile achieves root-mean-square errors of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces.
A VecTile calibrated while flat retains accuracy when curved, while a five-minute manual calibration is sufficient for practical use.
Two applications demonstrate its utility. First, shear readings are sensitive enough to stop a sharp scalpel from puncturing a balloon after contact. Second, the sensor substantially improves Diffusion Policy-guided power-plug insertion. All designs and code will be released upon paper acceptance. Project website: https://jiannnh.github.io/VecTile/.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Tactile sensing gives robots a sense of touch during manipulation. It reveals force, friction, stiffness, and other properties that are difficult to infer from vision alone [ 1 , 2 ] . This information is particularly important for grasp-stability estimation [ 3 , 4 ] , object recognition [ 5 , 6 ] , and in-hand manipulation [ 7 , 8 , 9 ] .

During manipulation, the normal-force component captures only part of the contact state. While the shear components reveal the direction and magnitude of tangential loading, supporting grasp-stability assessment, friction and slip reasoning, and contact regulation [ 10 , 11 ] . Flexibility is also important because conformable tactile skins can cover non-planar and adaptive surfaces, including rounded fingers and soft grippers [ 12 , 13 ] . Because direct contact exposes tactile sensors to wear and damage, low cost and repairability are important for practical deployment [ 14 , 15 ] .

These considerations motivate tactile skins that combine 3-degree-of-freedom (DoF) force sensing, flexibility, and low cost. Existing tactile architectures, however, trade among these properties due to fabrication and integration complexities [ 2 ] : Vision-based [ 11 , 16 , 17 ] and magnetic-based [ 10 , 15 ] sensors can recover rich multi-axis contact information but are rigid, while thin capacitive [ 12 ] and piezoresistive [ 13 ] arrays more readily conform to curved surfaces yet do not provide shear force information. An easily accessible flexible tactile array providing local 3-DoF force measurements therefore remains underexplored.

We introduce VecTile (Fig. 1 ), named as such due to its capability of reading a 3-DoF force vector at each tactile pixel (taxel). VecTile is a low-cost, flexible, 6 ​ mm 6~\mathrm{mm} -thin, 4 × 4 4\times 4 tactile array (16 local 3-DoF taxels at a 10 ​ mm 10~\mathrm{mm} pitch) that combines a piezoresistive array with passive silicone nubs.

The complete sensor and readout board cost less than 35 USD (of which 25 USD is spent on an Arduino Nano that can be replaced with a lower-cost microcontroller and ADC circuit if needed). Raw frames stream at 343 Hz, and the measured end-to-end latency relative to a commercial force/torque (F/T) reference is approximately 25 ​ ms 25~\mathrm{ms} . Most conveniently, this sensor can be easily produced in-house without the need for expensive equipment or tools. At its core is a combination of a standard flexible PCB (FPC), whose fabrication can be out-sourced at low cost (we used JLCPCB’s services) and silicone parts that can be easily produced via 3D printed molds (we used PLA molds from a Bambu Lab P1S) and hobby-grade vacuum chamber (less than 150 USD).

After Section II outlining related work, Section III details the electronic design, the nub-based transduction mechanism validated via finite element analysis, as well as the fabrication process.
Section IV experimentally evaluates various nub heights and quantifies their force-reconstruction accuracy on physical sensors, resulting in a design with 0.39 ​ N 0.39~\mathrm{N} normal RMSE and 0.16 ​ N 0.16~\mathrm{N} shear RMSE with a range of 1 1 – 5 ​ N 5~\mathrm{N} normal force and up to 1.5 ​ N 1.5~\mathrm{N} shear per taxel.
We further assess performance differences between flat, convex, and concave configurations and demonstrate a practical calibration process through short manual interactions against an F/T reference.

Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of VecTile on compliant gripper fingers in two downstream tasks (Section V ). In the scalpel–balloon interaction, we show that the sensor’s shear force sensitivity allows a sharp scalpel to push against a fully blown balloon without rupturing it. A visuotactile plug-insertion task (Fig. 1 ) shows the sensor’s practicality via a learned manipulation policy under partially visual occlusion.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# II Related Work

Existing tactile sensors obtain multi-axis contact information using various forms of transduction hardware. Vision-based sensors such as GelSight [ 16 ] and DIGIT [ 17 ] use cameras to image the deformation of an elastomer surface, from which recent learning-based methods estimate a resultant 3-axis force [ 18 ] . However, their cameras, illumination, and optical paths require rigid housings, resulting in relatively bulky units with a limited sensing area. Magnetic sensors instead infer deformation from relative motion between magnets and magnetometers. eFlesh [ 10 ] and ReSkin [ 15 ] place magnetic skins over magnetometer boards to improve replaceability and customizability. However, the active electronics beneath the sensing surface complicate large-area integration and limit how freely the sensor can bend.

Thin capacitive and piezoresistive matrices can form conformable tactile skins, but simple implementations primarily measure normal pressure [ 12 , 13 ] . CoinFT recovers a six-axis wrench from capacitive layer displacement, but remains a rigid, single sensing unit rather than a distributed skin [ 19 ] .

Our VecTile design utilizes raised nubs as an alternative by mechanically converting shear into differential normal pressure. Prior works have also investigated this mechanism: Huh et al. created a rigid capacitive sensor for slip detection [ 20 ] and Yu et al. proposed a flexible piezoelectric nub array wrapped around finger sections of rubber gloves [ 21 ] . While both provide evidence for this mechanism’s high performance, neither has created a design that is particularly practical or cost effective in terms of in-house fabrication: the former requires spin coating of silicone on PCB, while the latter requires material coating, etching, and bonding.
