2026-10-23.title: Calibration-free IMU-based Relative Orientation Estimation under Dynamic Human Motion
2026-10-23.authors: Ruiyuan Li , Hassan Osman , Ajay Seth , Manon Kok
2026-10-23.comment: . Submitted to IEEE Sensors Journal
2026-10-23.abstract:
Recent magnetometer-free inertial measurement unit (IMU) methods can reduce drift in joint motion estimation using rigid-body constraints, but they typically require pre-calibrated sensor locations, assumptions of specific joint models (e.g., hinge joints) or limited motion types, or an external reference for global orientation.
Furthermore, challenges related to high-frequency impacts (e.g. at foot strikes during gait) and numerical differentiation of noisy measurements have not been explicitly addressed.
We propose an extended Kalman filter that estimates relative IMU orientation and sensor location simultaneously, requiring neither offline sensor location calibration nor a global orientation anchor.
A systematic simulation study shows that the quality of the relative orientation and the sensor location estimates depends on different motion-intensity sources: the joint center acceleration and the relative angular velocity, respectively.
A low-pass filter (LPF) is used to mitigate real-signal outliers before applying the rigid-body constraint.
When applied to the OpenSense dataset with real IMU measurements across four subjects with three lower-body joint types during walking and complex tasks including various motion types, the proposed method achieves an overall relative orientation error of 2.61 ∘ , compared with 10.40 ∘ for a baseline using offline-estimated sensor locations and 7.43 ∘ for a baseline using marker-derived sensor locations. These results show that the proposed calibration-free estimation framework handles real IMU data effectively and achieves accurate relative orientation without offline sensor location calibration.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Accurate joint kinematics estimation is fundamental to human motion tracking and reconstruction, with applications in rehabilitation, sports, and entertainment [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Inertial measurement units (IMUs) are a practical option for human motion estimation, as they are inexpensive, portable and lightweight, which allows their use outside the laboratory [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] . Joint kinematics can be estimated from single IMU (global) orientation estimates, which are commonly obtained by fusing gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer measurements [ 7 , 8 ] . However, sensor errors, e.g. due to indoor magnetic disturbances corrupting the magnetometer measurements, lead to erroneous orientation estimates.
Since joint kinematics such as joint angles are described by the relative orientation between adjacent body segments, typically the relative orientation is of most interest. Relative orientation between adjacent sensors can be estimated without the use of magnetometers [ 6 ] , which is the focus of this work. Note that our focus is on relative sensor orientation, and sensor-to-segment calibration to obtain relative segment orientation is therefore outside the scope.

Existing methods for relative orientation estimation typically rely on assumptions regarding joint type [ 9 , 10 ] , offline calibration [ 11 ] , or have primarily been validated on simulated IMU measurements [ 12 ] or real walking motions [ 11 , 13 ] , limiting their practical applicability.
In this work, we enable magnetometer-free and calibration-free 3D joint kinematic estimation using real IMU measurements during diverse human motions.

To this end, we extend the method of [ 11 ] to jointly estimate the relative sensor orientation and sensor locations online using only acceleration and angular velocity measurements, eliminating the need for offline sensor location calibration.
A systematic simulation study shows that, under sufficient joint center acceleration intensity, online sensor location estimation does not degrade orientation estimation accuracy. It further shows that orientation and sensor location estimation are primarily governed by joint center acceleration and relative angular velocity, respectively.
To improve reliability on real IMU measurements, we mitigate high-frequency measurement outliers caused by foot-strike impacts in the acceleration and numerical differentiation of angular velocity using a low-pass filter (LPF).
Finally, the proposed framework is extensively validated on the OpenSense dataset [ 14 ] , containing walking and diverse lower-body motions.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# II related work

Recent advances in inertial motion capture have moved toward magnetometer-free methods [ 6 ] . Some magnetometer-free methods focus on lower-dimensional or planar joint models [ 9 , 10 ] , whereas [ 11 ] incorporated a joint-connection model, modeling the connection of adjacent segments by a 3D joint. This enabled long-term, drift-free relative IMU orientation estimation using an extended Kalman filter (EKF) without assuming specific joint or motion types.
The approach relies on knowledge of where the sensors are placed on the body, which was determined in [ 11 ] using a separate offline calibration step [ 15 ] . In contrast, our method estimates the sensor locations online, jointly with the relative IMU orientation, removing the need for this offline calibration.

Joint relative IMU orientation and sensor location estimation has also been studied in [ 12 ] . Using the orientation of one IMU as the anchor, they estimate the global orientation of a lower-body kinematic chain and validate their method on re-simulated IMU signals synthesized from marker trajectories to reduce artifacts present in real IMU measurements. Similarly, [ 13 ] jointly estimates each IMU’s global orientation and sensor location using multiple kinematic constraints, including the joint connection model, and uses magnetometer measurements for initialization.
The results are evaluated on human gait motion and humanoid robot data. Although these methods enable online sensor location estimation, the effects of artifacts in real IMU measurements have not been systematically addressed.

Such artifacts result from impact-related transients [ 16 , 17 ] . Numerical differentiation required to evaluate the joint-connection model is highly sensitive to these artifacts [ 18 ] , potentially violating the Gaussian measurement noise assumption.
Low-pass filtering (LPF) has been shown to reduce IMU measurement errors during impulsive motion [ 19 ] . We therefore incorporate LPF into the proposed method and evaluate its effect on the joint-connection model using real IMU measurements. Inspired by the observability analysis from [ 20 ] , we further study how estimation performance varies with motion intensity, first systematically in simulation and then using real human-motion data. Additionally, we evaluate the proposed method on a broader range of human motions than the walking motions considered previously [ 13 , 12 , 11 ] .

2026-10-23.title: RGraph-Eval: Task-Grounded Scene Graphs for Evaluating Robot Video Generation
2026-10-23.authors: Aleksandr Lazarev , Sofia Zimina , Roman Kuznetsov , Tatiana Zemskova , Iaroslav Koshelev , Dmitry Yudin
2026-10-23.abstract: Generated robot videos can look convincing while depicting the wrong interaction: a different object is moved, a grasp disappears, or a placement ends outside its destination. We introduce RGraph-Eval, a reference-based framework that makes these discrepancies explicit through task-grounded temporal scene graphs. Unlike approaches that construct separate evidence representations for different evaluation dimensions, we organize task entities, interactions, and motion within a unified, interpretable scene graph representation. A foundation-model pipeline identifies manipulation roles, grounds persistent object masks, infers and verifies state transitions and action intervals, and reconstructs manipulated-object motion in three dimensions. Applying this representation to a generated video and a reference demonstration supports an interpretable RGraph-Eval score with visible-object, relation-change, and 3D path-shape components. We also introduce ShareRobot-SG, a collection of 1,000 manipulation scenes from ten ShareRobot sources annotated with the multimodal representation. Our evaluation separates graph-generation quality from agreement with human video judgments, and includes comparisons with adapted SVG2 and SG-Ego, a benchmark of three video generators. The framework connects robot-video assessment to the observable entities and interactions underlying a task, while making the graph annotations reusable beyond evaluation. Code will be publicly available at https://github.com/SashaDance/rgraph-eval .
2026-10-23.introduction:
Video generation depicts possible robot behavior from an initial observation and a language goal, supporting behavior inspection, visual demonstrations, and data generation for robot learning ( Mei et al., 2026 ) . Generated videos can serve as an additional source of training data, complementing demonstrations collected through physical interaction. Recent work explores scalable robot data synthesis with compositional world models ( Ye et al., 2026 ) and learning robotic manipulation by imitating generated videos without physical demonstrations ( Patel et al., 2026 ) . However, using generated videos as a data source requires assessing their quality: visually realistic sequences may still depict incorrect object motion, inconsistent interactions, or failed task outcomes. Evaluation should therefore assess not only visual appearance but also whether the generated behavior preserves task-relevant entities, interactions, and final states.

Consider the instruction “stack the white plate onto the red plate.” A plausible video can move the wrong plate, omit the grasp, or leave the white plate beside the red one. Such errors may occupy a small region while the background remains stable. Conversely, different speeds or intermediate motions can preserve the intended interaction. Evaluation must distinguish appearance, object identity, temporal interaction, and the achieved state.

Existing evaluators address complementary parts of this problem. General video benchmarks assess visual and temporal quality ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . Robotics and world-model benchmarks emphasize instruction following and physical consistency ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Reference-based methods compare a prediction with an observed execution ( Wei et al., 2026 ) . Learned reward models additionally approximate human preferences or task progress ( Liu et al., 2025 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; He et al., 2025 ) . These approaches provide useful assessments, but their scores need not identify which visible object or interaction accounts for a disagreement. A structural representation can supply that missing connection between an assessment and the evidence in the video.

Task-grounded temporal scene graphs connect assessment to this evidence. We call these graphs task-grounded because their entities and relations are selected with respect to the manipulation goal: they represent the robot, manipulated object, relevant supports and target, and their task-relevant interactions rather than exhaustively describing the entire scene. Nodes identify task entities, masks ground them in image regions, relations describe changing interactions, and trajectories capture motion.

Graph-based assessment depends on extraction quality: incorrect object assignments propagate through tracking, relations, and geometry, while language models may infer goal-consistent rather than observed outcomes. We address these risks through visual grounding, persistent tracking, and independent verification, and evaluate graph quality separately from human alignment.

Figure 1 summarizes the framework. We make three contributions. First, we introduce a foundation-model pipeline for annotating manipulation videos with grounded temporal graphs, including masks, states, actions, and estimated 3D motion. Second, we present ShareRobot-SG, a 1,000-scene collection spanning ten manipulation sources for studying the quality and breadth of this representation. Third, we introduce reference-based RGraph-Eval assessment with an explicit component decomposition, evaluated through human alignment, generator comparison, and component analysis.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 Evaluating Generated Videos

PSNR measures pixel-wise reconstruction error, SSIM compares local structure ( Wang et al., 2004 ) , and LPIPS measures learned perceptual distance ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) . Frame-wise appearance similarity does not explicitly assess manipulated-object identity, interaction, or task completion ( Deng et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2025 ) .

VBench evaluates appearance, consistency, and motion ( Huang et al., 2024 ) . RBench emphasizes task adherence, physical plausibility, and subject stability ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , while WorldModelBench assesses instruction following and world-model violations ( Li et al., 2025 ) . For manipulation, neither background stability nor a plausible final image establishes coherent robot–object interaction.

Human-aligned evaluators include TIQA, which learns text-quality prediction for generated images from human ratings ( Koltsov et al., 2026 ) , and VideoReward, which learns video preference dimensions ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . VideoScore2 assesses visual quality, text alignment, and physical consistency ( He et al., 2025 ) , while RoboReward estimates robotic task progress ( Lee et al., 2026 ) . Ref4D-VideoBench compares reference and generated videos across semantics, events, and other dimensions ( Wei et al., 2026 ) . We instead make grounded objects, masks, relation changes, and geometry the comparison interface.

## 2.2 Scene Graph Generation from Video

Visual Genome and Action Genome establish object–relation representations for image and video understanding ( Krishna et al., 2017 ; Ji et al., 2020 ) . Recent annotation pipelines use foundation models to extend graph generation beyond fixed object categories. SVG2 extracts large-scale spatiotemporal scene graphs from video ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . SG-Ego supports scene-based reasoning about human activities ( Pistilli et al., 2026 ) . Their broad object vocabularies make them relevant comparisons for manipulation-focused extraction.

Our pipeline combines open-vocabulary object descriptions with task roles and an explicit state–action schema. We adapt SVG2 and SG-Ego to the same manipulation setting, although these methods naturally produce broad scene-description relations, including geometric relations. Such predicates are useful for general scene understanding, but they are not sufficient to determine whether a manipulation was executed correctly. Moreover, when ground-truth-quality depth and camera geometry are available, they can be computed directly from reconstructed 3D object positions.

## 2.3 Scene Graphs in Robotics and Annotation

Scene graphs already support robotic perception, planning, and control. VeriGraph uses graph structure to verify robot plans ( Ekpo et al., 2026 ) , and Compose by Focus uses task-relevant scene graphs for skill composition ( Qi et al., 2026 ) . SG-RAPL uses a 3D scene graph to ground language-driven, hierarchical action planning for humanoid robots in warehouse environments ( Yudin et al., 2026 ) . These works establish that structured object relations have value beyond image description.

Despite these applications, datasets pairing robotic manipulation observations with explicit scene-graph annotations remain relatively scarce. SG-Bot provides a synthetic tabletop dataset with graph, depth, and segmentation annotations ( Zhai et al., 2024 ) . EmbodimentSemantic pairs real-robot observations with spatial scene graphs and provides a simulator-grounded manipulation benchmark ( Jaber and others, 2026 ) .

ShareRobot-SG augments ShareRobot manipulation videos ( Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence, 2025 ) with object identities, masks, changing relations, action timings, and estimated 3D motion.

2026-10-23.title: To Route or to Adapt? Multi-Expert Diffusion Planners in Unseen Regions
2026-10-23.authors: Yun Li , Ehsan Javanmardi , Simon Thompson , Jiachen Gong , Qunli Zhang , Zifan Zeng , Shiming Liu , Peng Wang , Yidu Zhang , Manabu Tsukada
2026-10-23.comment: Accepted to the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026). . Code and weights: this https URL
2026-10-23.abstract:
Diffusion trajectory planners with domain-specific experts
face a practical question in unseen regions: can they
rely on selecting among existing experts, or must the
planner itself adapt? We study this question using a
planner with a shared adapter and per-domain expert
adapters. Across three real-world held-out maps, none
of eight test-time routing schemes improves the
fleet-mean lateral offset over the static default,
which uses the same expert for every scene. Even an
oracle that selects the best expert for each scene
reduces the mean offset by only 0.9 0.9 m. In contrast,
reward-based fine-tuning on just 20 20 target-region
scenes yields substantially larger gains. On matched
evaluation slices, joint replay achieves a fleet-mean
offset of 6.9 6.9 m, compared with 12.4 12.4 m for the
static default. Comparisons under the same target-region
training budget show that target-region training drives
the improvement, while replaying training scenes limits
forgetting on the original ODDs. On nuPlan, fine-tuning
across training cities also improves open-loop offsets,
although closed-loop performance deteriorates.
Further diagnostics reveal that two test-time adaptation
baselines achieve low offsets by producing degenerate
trajectories. These results show the limited headroom
for selecting among existing experts and the greater
open-loop gains available from adapting the planner.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Deploying a trajectory planner in an unseen region
presents a challenge for models trained with
domain-specific experts. One approach is to select
the most suitable expert for each new scene,
reusing what the planner has already learned.
Another is to update the model using data from
the new region. The former avoids additional
training but is limited by the available experts;
the latter can change the planner’s predictions
but risks degrading performance on the original
training domains. How much can expert selection
actually achieve before adaptation becomes necessary?

We investigate this question using a reward-fine-tuned
diffusion trajectory planner [ 1 , 2 ] with a shared adapter and four
per-ODD expert adapters. The four training ODDs
are ODD-Hongo (the University of Tokyo’s Hongo
campus), ODD-Kashiwa (suburban Kashiwa),
ODD-Shalun (a controlled test site),
and ODD-Nagoya (Nagoya University campus).
The three held-out maps are Knowledge Hub
(a research campus), Ishiodai (a suburban
district), and Morikoro (an open park), all in
Aichi Prefecture, Japan.
Within the Generator–Selector framework of the
Autoware end-to-end reference
architecture [ 3 ] , we compare
methods that select among existing expert
trajectories with methods that modify the
planner’s adapter weights,
as shown in Figure 1 .

We first examine whether routing can make better
use of the existing experts. Across the three
held-out maps, none of eight routing schemes
improves the fleet-mean lateral offset over the
static default, which uses the geographically
nearest training expert (ODD-Nagoya on all three
maps). More importantly, an oracle that selects
the lowest-offset expert trajectory for each
scene improves the mean offset by only 0.9 0.9 m.
Even perfect selection among the four existing
trajectories therefore offers little additional
benefit. We next examine whether updating the
planner can overcome this limitation.
Fine-tuning the shared adapter on geometrically
perturbed training scenes improves performance
on the open-park map, while reward-based
fine-tuning with 20 20 target-region scenes
provides substantially larger gains.
On matched evaluation slices, joint replay,
which mixes target-region and training scenes
during fine-tuning, achieves a fleet-mean
offset of 6.9 6.9 m, compared with 12.4 12.4 m
for the static default. Comparisons with
other fine-tuning methods show that
target-region training drives the improvement,
while replay primarily preserves performance
on the original training ODDs.

We also examine the limits of these improvements.
On nuPlan, fine-tuning across three training
cities reduces open-loop lateral offset in each
held-out city but degrades closed-loop performance.
In addition, two test-time adaptation baselines
produce low lateral offsets by collapsing toward
nearly stationary or scene-independent trajectories.
These observations distinguish improvements
in open-loop trajectory metrics from improvements
in driving behaviour, which remain to be established
for the proposed adaptation methods.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Our planner builds on reward-based diffusion policy
training [ 1 , 2 ] , using a shared
adapter and per-ODD experts. Conformal prediction has
been applied to trajectory uncertainty [ 4 , 5 ] and semantic
uncertainty in BEV planning [ 6 ] .
Selective conformal risk control combines abstention
with calibrated prediction [ 7 ] .
We examine whether a conformal corridor can help
select among the trajectories of existing experts
when the deployment region differs from the
calibration domains.

GeCo [ 8 ] uses geographic channel
attention and contrastive imitation learning to
train a policy across regions. Drive-Anywhere [ 9 ] instead uses multimodal foundation
model representations to improve generalisation
to unseen environments. Our setting differs from
both: the planner and its domain-specific experts
are already trained, and we examine whether
geographic location can guide their selection
or weight mixing without retraining the backbone.

Related approaches include online expert selection
for trajectory prediction [ 10 ] ,
mixtures of denoising experts for robotic
manipulation [ 11 ] , and
CLIP-based LoRA retrieval for open-vocabulary
segmentation [ 12 ] .
These methods differ in their tasks and available
supervision. We evaluate both selecting among
the trajectories generated by existing experts
and combining their adapter weights.
The latter is related to model soups and
weight-space merging [ 13 , 14 ] , although our geographic mixing
weights depend on the deployment location.

The shared-plus-expert adapter structure is
related to multi-task learning with shared
representations [ 15 , 16 ] . For adaptation, we study
fine-tuning on geometrically perturbed training
scenes, related to scene augmentation for OOD
generalisation [ 17 , 18 ] and generative simulation [ 19 , 20 ] . We also fine-tune with a small
set of target-region scenes, using replay
of training scenes to limit forgetting [ 21 , 22 ] .
Separately, we evaluate test-time adaptation
baselines [ 23 , 24 ] and analyse their degenerate predictions
in App. A and
App. B .

2026-10-23.title: AstroBench: Benchmarking Free-Floating Capture and Space Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-23.authors: Zizhe Wang (1), Jia Deng (1), Xin Lu (1), Zehao Jia (1), Yi Huang (2), Yao Zhu (2) ((1) Astroup Lab, Beijing, China, (2) Harbin Institute of Technology, Beijing Research Institute)
2026-10-23.comment: . Code and assets: this https URL ; project website: this https URL
2026-10-23.abstract: Capturing a loose object inside a spacecraft requires a robot to approach a target that can translate and rotate, and whose motion changes when contact is made. These conditions motivate evaluation beyond manipulation of supported objects. We introduce AstroBench, an open benchmark for free-floating capture and space robotic manipulation with a fixed-base arm. The task suite combines four initial-motion tracks with sample-storage operations based on MELFI hardware and cap and captive-screw servicing based on the Robotic Refueling Mission. The two workcells provide nine task definitions and 29 task–target combinations. A metadata-filtered Objaverse inventory supplies 8,414 object instances for asset expansion, alongside five cabin visual contexts and versioned task instructions. We report two acquisition-focused experiments using existing checkpoints. A frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} DROID joint-position policy captures 2 of 200 static targets and 4 of 200 moving targets across twenty object identities. A cube-specific ACT policy captures 8 of 10 static targets and 6 of 10 moving targets in a separate experiment. Each experiment retains its recorded observation, action and capture configuration. The results document difficult direct transfer for the tested generalist checkpoint and successful task-specific capture behavior, while identifying concrete settings for studying motion-aware perception and contact-sensitive control. Code, task definitions and editable workcell assets are available at https://github.com/AstroUpLab/AstroBench .
2026-10-23.introduction:
Loose-object recovery, sample handling and equipment servicing are useful capabilities for robots operating inside spacecraft. A robot may need to intercept a drifting tool, transfer a sample card into a storage box, or engage a service interface with a specialized tool. Although these tasks share components with terrestrial manipulation, their physical setup changes the role of support, approach direction and contact. A free object has no table to resist an incidental push. A storage or service interface instead provides an explicit fixture, whose geometry determines where the robot can move and how the operation should be completed.

Free-floating capture offers a particularly direct way to study this difference. Even a target initialized at rest can move after the fingers touch it. A translating or rotating target adds an interception problem: the robot must align the gripper with a useful grasp configuration before that configuration moves away. The visual observation, the action prediction and the resulting contact therefore correspond to different moments of a changing scene. Capture performance depends jointly on recognizing the object, approaching it, and coordinating contact with gripper closure.

Existing robot benchmarks have established effective ways to organize language-conditioned tasks, test transfer and vary environments [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . Space Robotics Bench further develops robot-learning infrastructure for mission-relevant space environments [ 4 ] . We build on this approach by focusing on free-floating object acquisition and a small set of hardware-grounded space operations. The benchmark separates the target object, initial motion, visual context and operation goal, so that each can be recorded and varied explicitly.

AstroBench contains three task groups (Fig. 1 ). Free-floating capture uses static, drifting, tumbling and faster-tumbling initial conditions. A MELFI-inspired storage workcell supports card transfer, insertion and extraction, together with lid opening and closing. An RRM-inspired service workcell supports removal and stowage of FDV1 and SMA caps and loosening or tightening of captive screws. The hardware workcells are authored from NASA and ESA references, with identifiable moving parts, target frames and tool interfaces. The arm has a fixed base throughout; the free-floating body in the capture tasks is the target object.

This paper evaluates capture as an acquisition event: an episode succeeds when the target first satisfies the recorded capture detector. We examine two existing policy configurations. The first is a frozen π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} DROID joint-position checkpoint evaluated on twenty objects, each under static and dynamic conditions. The second is ACT trained on a local cube task, evaluated at ten positions under both conditions. The experiments document what each tested system can capture and provide concrete traces for further analysis.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we organize a space manipulation suite that combines controlled initial object motion with storage and servicing tasks derived from real hardware references. Second, we release an extensible resource comprising an 8,414-instance object inventory, five cabin visual contexts, editable workcell assets and explicit language-conditioned task specifications. Third, we report acquisition results and reproducible execution settings for a generalist-policy transfer experiment and a task-specific imitation-learning experiment. Together, these resources support study of object motion, contact formation and precise operation goals in a common task framework.

# II Related Work

Manipulation benchmarks. LIBERO organizes robot-learning problems around transfer of task knowledge [ 1 ] . CALVIN evaluates language-conditioned manipulation and long-horizon composition [ 2 ] . RoboCasa expands the diversity of everyday tasks and environments [ 3 ] . These benchmarks demonstrate the usefulness of explicit task definitions, controlled variation and executable evaluation. Table I summarizes their research emphasis. AstroBench uses those principles to structure free-floating capture and hardware-specific operations. Its object-motion tracks and fixture geometry make the physical conditions of each task explicit.

Space robot learning. Space Robotics Bench provides modular environments, procedural generation and robot-learning studies across space scenarios [ 4 ] . AstroBench concentrates on the capture of unsupported objects and manipulation at specified storage and service interfaces. We use MELFI documentation to inform sample-storage geometry [ 11 , 12 ] , and NASA’s RRM material to inform cap, fastener and tool relationships [ 13 , 15 ] . These sources ground the choice of tasks and visible hardware. The robot placement and evaluation parameters are engineering choices for the benchmark.

Visual policies. ACT predicts action chunks from images and robot state [ 5 ] . The π 0.5 \pi_{0.5} model investigates broad robotic generalization using vision, language and action [ 6 ] , and OpenPI provides model implementations and deployment configurations [ 7 ] . We use these two approaches to obtain complementary capture measurements: direct transfer of an existing DROID checkpoint, and execution of a policy trained for the cube task. The present contribution is the benchmark and its empirical characterization; no new policy architecture is introduced.

Object and environment assets. Objaverse offers a large collection of annotated 3D objects [ 8 ] . Its scale makes metadata screening practical, but an asset name does not determine whether its geometry is suitable for a particular gripper or contact model. AstroBench therefore preserves object identities, selection reasons and source attribution separately from runtime asset configuration. NASA Astrobee ISS assets supply the cabin visual contexts [ 9 , 10 ] . Task bodies and robot mounting are described independently of those surroundings.

2026-10-23.authors: Ninad Joshi , Prabhat Kumar
2026-10-23.comment: 5 figures
2026-10-23.abstract: Tilt-rotor quadcopters redirect thrust for translation without banking, but complicate modeling, state estimation, and disturbance rejection. This paper presents a simulation-based flight stack for a 2.00 kg 2.00\text{\,}\mathrm{kg} tilt-rotor quadcopter. The system uses a six-degree-of-freedom nonlinear model with first-order motor dynamics and two-axis rotor tilt, parameterized using a 3D CAD model. A cascaded PD controller commands forward and lateral tilt angles. A 14-state EKF fuses sensor data across hover, early-transition, and transition modes using a hysteretic (Schmitt-trigger) classifier to prevent covariance discontinuities. Because the proportional position loop leaves a steady-state offset under constant wind, a small bounded neural residual is added on top of the unmodified PD controller. It is trained by behavioral cloning from a teacher with privileged access to the true wind, while the deployed network never observes wind. In simulation, the EKF achieves a post-settling position root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.226 m 0.226\text{\,}\mathrm{m} (horizontal) and 0.03 m 0.03\text{\,}\mathrm{m} (vertical) and an attitude RMSE below 0.8 ° 0.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\SIUnitSymbolDegree} , and it estimates a wind velocity of ( 2.0 , − 1.2 ) ​ m / s ($2.0$,$-1.2$)\,$\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s}$ to within 0.15 m / s 0.15\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} per axis. The residual reduces steady-state station-keeping error under wind by approximately 49 % 49\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} , from 0.117 m 0.117\text{\,}\mathrm{m} to 0.060 m 0.060\text{\,}\mathrm{m} at 1.5 m / s 1.5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} and from 0.319 m 0.319\text{\,}\mathrm{m} to 0.162 m 0.162\text{\,}\mathrm{m} at an out-of-distribution 3.9 m / s 3.9\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} . The framework provides a basis for hardware-in-the-loop and flight-test studies.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have gained significant attention due to their wide range of applications in videography, agriculture, surveying, construction, education, and research. Conventional multirotor UAVs provide excellent hovering capability and maneuverability, but their rotors are fixed relative to the airframe. The vehicle is therefore underactuated, and translational motion must be produced by tilting the whole vehicle through changes in motor speed.

A tilt-rotor quadcopter adds actuation by allowing the rotor assemblies to change their orientation [ 1 ] . The thrust vector can then be redirected to generate translational force directly, rather than relying solely on changes in rotor thrust magnitude, at the cost of stronger coupling between the translational and rotational dynamics. The configuration considered in this work, the vehicle employs twelve actuator inputs: four motor inputs for rotor thrust, four actuators for tilting along the α \alpha direction, and four actuators for tilting along the β \beta direction. The nominal thrust of the four rotors is assumed to remain constant, and the required α \alpha and β \beta angles are determined from the desired trajectory. The vehicle motion is simulated using a position-based trajectory-tracking approach rather than a prescribed flight duration. The simulation continues until the vehicle reaches the final waypoint, so the completion time emerges from the vehicle dynamics and control response. A time budget terminates runs that fail to converge to a commanded waypoint.

Existing studies often employ simplified mass and inertia parameters along with simple control strategies, whereas the influence of wind and complex trajectories on the resulting dynamic response has been less extensively investigated [ 2 , 3 , 4 ] . Previous work has implemented standard PID controllers [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] .

This work instead develops a six-degree-of-freedom nonlinear dynamic model of a tilt-rotor UAV using the physical and inertial parameters obtained from its 3D CAD model, and evaluates its trajectory and attitude response. For control, it adds a neural network (NN) that acts as a small additive correction on a PD controller.
Our goal is to study whether a bounded learned correction can recover the
wind-trim offset of the proportional loop; we do not claim superiority over
integral action or disturbance observers, which are not evaluated here.

2026-10-23.title: Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion for Anticipating Navigation Retreat in Robotic Flexible Endoscopy
2026-10-23.authors: Chi Kit Ng , Tianchun Wu , Jiatan Sun , Yuming Sun , Jianru Zhang , Hongliang Ren
2026-10-23.abstract: Flexible robotic endoscopes provide access through tortuous anatomy, where friction, deformation, and wall interaction separate commanded insertion from useful distal progress. Operators interpret this mismatch and retreat to recover a navigable configuration. Recognizing the approach to that decision requires relating motor intent to distal response and the local visual scene. We introduce Multimodal Progress-Residual Fusion (MPRF), a causal model that anticipates operator retreat from commands, electromagnetic (EM) tracking, and endoscopic video. A nominal-progress model predicts the response expected in normal or successful navigation; a temporal predictor combines its EM residual with all three observed modalities. In a 150-episode colon-phantom collection, MPRF achieves 0.580 ± 0.007 0.580\pm 0.007 AUPRC across three seeds, compared with 0.511 for the strongest reduced-modality control. Complete multimodal histories provide the principal ranking advantage, while the residual adds an explicit intent–response representation with a small, uncertain increment over raw fusion. Analysis of frozen alarms relates warning timing to the behavioral label and explains the increase in event recall under a longer matching window. These results establish a basis for behavioral assistance during operator-controlled navigation.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Flexible and continuum endoscopes provide access through natural orifices and curved anatomical passages while limiting the access incision [ 1 , 2 ] . Robotic actuation adds distal dexterity, stabilizes viewpoints, and supports repeatable navigation [ 3 , 4 ] . During teleoperation, these capabilities still depend on an operator who interprets whether intended motion produces useful progress. The operator repeatedly chooses between continued insertion, orientation adjustment, and withdrawal. Recognizing an approaching change of strategy is therefore an important component of assistance alongside motion generation.

This recognition problem is particularly challenging in flexible mechanisms. Friction, backlash, distributed deformation, and changing environmental interaction separate proximal actuation from distal response [ 5 , 6 ] . A sustained insertion command produces different outcomes according to the current configuration: forward tip translation, local bending, or little observable progress. Conversely, limited displacement also accompanies deliberate inspection and viewpoint correction. Figure 1 illustrates the resulting ambiguity. Interpreting motion requires both the command that elicited it and the scene in which it occurred.

A pre-retreat cue has a specific operator-assistance role: it identifies a developing pattern associated with abandoning the current attempt. Such a cue provides a candidate trigger for inspecting the view and preparing reorientation, with action authority retained by the operator. This role fits the spectrum of shared control in medical robotics [ 7 , 8 ] . Its immediate measurable endpoint is the operator’s upcoming decision; prospective evaluation then connects cue delivery to workload, navigation efficiency, and physical interaction.

Existing approaches improve contact observability, estimate continuum state, or compare expected and measured body response [ 9 , 10 ] . Temporal video–kinematic models also predict surgical activities [ 11 ] . The research gap addressed here is a short-horizon behavioral transition during flexible-endoscope navigation: relating what the operator commands , how the tip responds , and what the camera observes to the decision to retreat. An isolated stream admits several plausible interpretations. Their temporal relationship supplies the context needed to distinguish sustained progress from an attempt approaching abandonment.

The recorded transition from manual navigation to the retreat controller provides weak behavioral supervision. This operational definition preserves the operator’s actual decision and gives a precise log index for causal training. It encompasses recovery and repositioning, with timing that reflects operator judgment. We consequently evaluate both the trained horizon and an expanded matching window for the same predictions.

MPRF makes the intent–response relationship explicit. A first stage learns nominal EM and visual increments from normal and successful navigation. The difference between expected and observed EM change becomes a progress residual. A causal recurrent model fuses this residual with the original commands, pose, and visual features so that context determines its predictive meaning.

The study contributes a log-derived formulation of retreat anticipation, a two-stage residual representation conditioned on multimodal context, and a matched evaluation that separates sensor complementarity, residual contribution, and alarm timing. Episode-level resampling quantifies the sensitivity of the principal ranking contrasts; probability traces explain how the fixed alarm rule converts scores into warnings.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Robotic Endoscopy and Operator Assistance

Continuum mechanisms accommodate curved anatomical paths through distributed deformation [ 5 , 1 ] . Robotic endoscopes combine flexible actuation with interfaces for distal steering and insertion [ 3 ] . Sensor-guided colonoscopy and autonomous endoscopic control address navigation and task execution [ 12 , 4 ] . These advances motivate assistance that also recognizes the state of an ongoing human-controlled attempt. Within the autonomy spectrum [ 7 , 8 ] , MPRF predicts a forthcoming operator transition and supplies an advisory probability. Its supervision derives directly from recorded control-state changes.

## II-B Sensing and Expected Response

Data-driven contact localization improves observability of continuum interaction [ 9 ] . Endoscopic vision also reveals transmission effects, including backlash [ 6 ] . Wang et al. compared expected and observed soft-body response for proprioception and contact detection [ 10 ] . This principle motivates our progress residual, with a different target: future operator retreat. Raw multimodal context remains essential because friction, steering, tracker variation, and successful exploration all influence an observed discrepancy. MPRF learns its behavioral interpretation from causal histories.

## II-C Multimodal Temporal Prediction

Surgical data science integrates heterogeneous procedural signals to support intervention [ 13 ] . EndoNet learns visual representations for phase and tool recognition [ 14 ] ; SV-RCNet incorporates temporal dependencies for workflow recognition [ 15 ] . Multimodal transformers combine video and robot kinematics for activity prediction [ 11 ] . Here the event is an imminent navigation-strategy change. Commands provide the intent needed to interpret EM motion, while video contextualizes the distal scene. Matched modality controls test the value of retaining each stream, and a complete raw-fusion control isolates the additional residual channel.

2026-10-23.title: Demonstration-Based Robotic Feeding Using Dynamic Movement Primitives
2026-10-23.authors: Kenzhi Iskandar Wong , Kitti Thamrongaphichartkul , Sri Harsha Turlapati , Yanshuo Lu , Kanichi Doi , Boyu Ma , Bin Zhou , Lin Yang , Ananda Sidarta , Lek Syn Lim , Arun-Kumar Kaliya-Perumal , Jianfei Yang , Domenico Campolo
2026-10-23.comment: Accepted on RAAI 2026
2026-10-23.abstract:
This paper presents a demonstration-based robotic feeding framework that
integrates human demonstration, Dynamic Movement Primitive-based motion
planning, vision-based scene perception, and robot control. A human
operator first demonstrates the scooping and feeding motions while the
position and Euler-angle orientation of the spoon are recorded using a
motion-capture system. The recorded trajectory is segmented into
scooping and feeding motions, which are encoded using separate Dynamic
Movement Primitives. Before task execution, an RGB-D camera estimates
the participant’s mouth position, while two AprilTags are used for
robot-frame registration and tray localization. The detected tray pose
is used to position the scooping motion, whereas the detected mouth
position defines the positional goal of the feeding motion. The
approach, scooping, and feeding trajectories are then executed
sequentially by a Kinova Gen3 manipulator through a ROS 2-based
framework. A real-world experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the
integrated pipeline and shows that the learned spoon motions can be
reproduced within the detected experimental scene.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Robot-assisted feeding aims to support individuals with upper-limb motor
impairments while reducing reliance on continuous caregiver assistance [ 2 , 11 ] .
A robotic feeding system must coordinate several components within a
complete task sequence, including food acquisition, utensil transport,
mouth localization, motion generation, and robot control.

Previous studies have addressed different components of robot-assisted
feeding, including end-to-end feeding systems [ 11 ] , bite-transfer trajectories
considering efficiency and user comfort [ 1 ] ,
visual and haptic sensing for inside-mouth food transfer [ 15 ] , and robust mouth perception with
physical-interaction-aware control [ 8 ] . Flexible
mealtime assistance across different activities and user preferences has
also been investigated [ 7 ] . Related robotic systems
have explored human-motion retargeting, compliant rehabilitation
control, and compliant manipulation [ 13 , 9 , 5 ] .

An important component of the feeding task is the generation of the
spoon motion. Scooping and feeding require task-specific trajectories in
which both the position and orientation of the spoon evolve throughout
the motion. Learning from demonstration provides a practical means of transferring human-demonstrated motions to robotic systems [ 12 ] , as well as task-relevant skills and interaction strategies [ 4 ] . Among the available representations, Dynamic
Movement Primitives (DMPs) are well suited for encoding demonstrated
motions as stable nonlinear dynamical systems shaped by learned forcing
terms [ 6 , 14 ] . DMP-based approaches have also been applied and extended to various manipulation tasks, including contact-rich and interaction-aware scenarios [ 17 , 18 , 10 ] .

Despite these advances, transferring demonstrated spoon motions into a
complete feeding pipeline that adapts them to the current task scene
remains a challenge. Direct replay of a demonstrated trajectory ties the
robot motion to the conditions under which the demonstration was
recorded, whereas a practical feeding system should adapt the learned
scooping and feeding motions to the current bowl and mouth locations.
This paper addresses this problem through an integrated framework that
combines human demonstration, DMP-based motion generation, RGB-D-based
mouth localization, AprilTag-based tray localization, and robotic
execution. The learned scooping motion is retargeted according to the
detected tray location, while the detected mouth position defines the
feeding goal. The scope of the present work covers offline motion
learning and task execution using scene information acquired before the
robot begins moving. Continuous mouth tracking and online adaptation,
food detection, and more complex food-manipulation tasks requiring
cutting or multiple utensils are outside the current scope.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section II introduces the DMP formulation and
learning procedure. Section III describes the
demonstration-based feeding framework, mouth perception, task
execution sequence, and robot control. Section IV presents the
experimental setup and results. Section V discusses the main findings and limitations, and Section VI concludes the paper.

2026-10-23.title: Multi-Tool Selection for Robotic Systems: Comparing Semantic Retrieval and LLM
2026-10-23.authors: Miguel Sousa , Luis Ramos Pinto , João P. Matos-Carvalho
2026-10-23.abstract:
Natural-language interfaces allow users to command robotic systems without interacting directly with mission planners or robotics middleware. Their reliable use depends on robot tool routing, defined here as the selection of the smallest complete subset of predefined executable capabilities required to satisfy a request.
This task is particularly difficult for compound instructions, where incomplete selection may omit necessary sensing or monitoring capabilities, while excessive selection may expose irrelevant tools. We compare four routing strategies: three progressively refined ChromaDB-based methods – fixed-threshold retrieval, relative-distance retrieval, and clause-aware aggregated retrieval – and a cloud-hosted 120-billion-parameter language-model baseline. The methods are evaluated on 164 manually annotated prompts organised into three complexity levels, from direct single-tool requests to compound requests requiring at least three tools. Using exact-match accuracy, completeness, precision, a completeness-weighted composite score, and routing latency, CDB-v3 achieves the best macro-average score among the retrieval-only methods, with 0.7822 0.7822 ,
compared with 0.8869 0.8869 for the large-model baseline. Although the LLM provides higher routing quality, CDB-v3 exhibits substantially lower latency and can be deployed locally without requiring cloud connectivity. These results identify
a quality–latency trade-off between direct large-model selection and clause-aware semantic retrieval for privacy-sensitive, connectivity-constrained, and resource-constrained robotic systems.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Natural-language interfaces are becoming an attractive way to interact with
robotic systems. Instead of invoking commands through mission planners,
terminals, or custom graphical interfaces, users can express requests directly
in natural language, such as “land the drone”, “start mapping the area”, or
“report the current battery level”. Large language models (LLMs) make such
interfaces increasingly practical, but a critical challenge remains: mapping a
user request to the correct robot capability or set of capabilities.

In robotics, capability selection is not merely a usability problem. A routing error may activate an incorrect process, produce misleading information, or issue an unintended command to the robot. As the number of available robot functions grows, reliable intent-to-capability matching becomes a fundamental requirement for safe and effective natural-language control. Traditionally, this decision logic is encoded through behaviour trees, state machines, launch configurations, or manually designed if–then rules that determine which robot capability should be activated under each condition. These approaches remain effective for predefined and well-structured workflows, but they become increasingly difficult to design, extend, and maintain as the number of capabilities, mission types, operating conditions, and possible user requests grows. Conversational interfaces shift part of this burden from handcrafted decision logic to runtime capability selection, making the routing layer a critical component of the overall system.

This challenge is particularly relevant in ROS-based systems, where a single robot or fleet may expose dozens of processes for navigation, mapping, monitoring, mission execution, telemetry collection, payload operation, and system management. A request may require one capability or a coordinated set of capabilities. For example, the instruction “monitor the battery and land when it drops below 25%” requires both a telemetry capability and an
actuation capability. The routing layer must therefore determine not only which capabilities are semantically relevant, but also whether several tools
must be selected to satisfy all parts of the request.

Large LLMs can perform this selection directly by receiving the complete tool catalog and reasoning over the user request. However, dependence on a cloud-hosted model may be impractical in robotic deployments with intermittent
connectivity, limited bandwidth, high communication latency, or strict
confidentiality and data-sovereignty requirements. Robot telemetry, mission
information, maps, and operational commands may be unsuitable for transmission
to external infrastructure. Even when a large model can be deployed locally,
its memory, computational, energy, and latency requirements may exceed the
resources available at the robotic edge. These constraints motivate lighter
routing mechanisms that can execute locally, while preserving as much
selection quality as possible.

This paper studies tool routing as a bounded multi-label selection problem. The router cannot invent commands or generate arbitrary executable code. Instead, it must select a subset from a fixed allowlisted catalog of 42 robot tools. We compare four implementations of this routing function: CDBv1, which uses a fixed semantic-distance threshold; CDBv2, which uses a threshold relative to the nearest result; CDBv3, which decomposes compound prompts into intent-like clauses and aggregates their retrieval results; and a cloud-hosted
120-billion-parameter LLM that performs direct selection from the complete
catalog.

The evaluation uses 164 manually annotated requests divided into three
complexity levels: 43 direct single-tool requests, 52 consequential requests
requiring exactly two tools, and 69 compound requests requiring three or more
tools. All routers are evaluated against the same ground-truth assignments
using exact-match accuracy, completeness, precision, a
completeness-weighted composite score, and routing latency.

The main contributions of this work are the formalisation of robotic tool routing as bounded multi-label capability selection, an empirical comparison of fixed-threshold, relative-distance, and clause-aware semantic retrieval under the same tool catalogue and prompt dataset, and a direct comparison between the strongest retrieval-only method and a large cloud-hosted LLM, exposing the resulting trade-off between routing quality and latency.

The results show that CDBv3 is the strongest retrieval-only strategy. Its
macro-average composite score is 0.7822 0.7822 , compared with 0.5863 0.5863 for CDBv2
and 0.3330 0.3330 for CDBv1. The 120B LLM achieves a higher score of 0.8869 0.8869 , but
CDBv3 provides substantially lower routing latency and does not require cloud
connectivity. The results therefore do not establish retrieval as a universally more accurate replacement for large-model routing. Instead, they show that clause-aware semantic retrieval is a practical local alternative when latency, connectivity, computation, privacy, or data sovereignty are primary deployment constraints.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

Tool-using language-model agents combine natural-language interpretation with calls to external functions or services. ReAct alternates reasoning, action selection, and observation, allowing an agent to update its behaviour after receiving the result of a tool invocation [ 15 ] . Toolformer
investigates whether language models can learn when to call external tools,
which tool to use, which arguments to provide, and how to incorporate the
returned result into subsequent generation [ 13 ] .
ToolLLM extends this problem to large collections of real-world APIs and
includes both single-tool and multi-tool instructions [ 11 ] .

In embodied systems, Code as Policies translates natural-language instructions
into programs composed from predefined perception and control
APIs [ 9 ] . SPINE uses language models to interpret
incomplete mission specifications and connect them to semantic planning for
ground and aerial robots [ 12 ] . These systems show that
language models can mediate between human requests and executable robotic
functions. Their principal focus, however, is task planning, policy generation,
or orchestration rather than a controlled comparison of routing mechanisms for
selecting from an allowlisted set of independently executable robot tools.

The present work treats tool selection as a separate classification and
retrieval problem. The router cannot invent arbitrary commands, modify tool
names, or directly generate shell instructions. It must return one or more
known capability definitions whose executable interfaces are specified in
advance. This restriction bounds the action space and separates probabilistic
language understanding from the robot’s execution boundary.

Dense retrieval represents queries and candidate records as vectors in a
shared embedding space, allowing semantically related items to be matched even
when they do not contain the same surface terms. Dense Passage Retrieval
demonstrated the effectiveness of learned dense representations for selecting
relevant passages from large collections [ 6 ] .
Retrieval-augmented generation subsequently combined a neural retriever with a
generative model, conditioning generation on retrieved external
records [ 8 ] . Although the present study does not use retrieval
to provide candidates to a smaller generative model, the underlying retrieval
principle is relevant: a natural-language request is compared against textual
descriptions of known capabilities, and the nearest capability records are
used to determine the routing output.

ChromaDB (CDB) is used as the implementation substrate for dense capability
retrieval [ 5 ] . Each allowlisted tool is stored with a textual
summary, description, and associated metadata. At query time, the user request
is embedded and compared with the stored capability embeddings. CDB
supports approximate nearest-neighbour search through a Hierarchical Navigable
Small World index [ 10 ] . CDB itself is not proposed as a
new routing algorithm in this work; it provides vector storage, indexing, and
similarity search. The evaluated contribution lies in the routing policies
implemented above this infrastructure, including fixed-distance filtering,
relative-distance filtering, and clause-aware aggregation.

Related retrieval-based systems have also been studied in software engineering.
Chen et al. evaluate a retrieval-augmented framework in which relevant code is
selected from a repository before being supplied to a language
model [ 4 ] . Koziolek et al. retrieve validated industrial
function blocks for inclusion in LLM-generated control
programs [ 7 ] . These works demonstrate how retrieval can
connect generative models to existing domain-specific components. In contrast,
the present work does not generate control code. It evaluates whether semantic
retrieval alone can select the predefined processes required by a robotic
request.

Agent-oriented software systems further illustrate the value of bounded tool
sets. RepairAgent plans and invokes software-analysis and validation tools
during program repair [ 3 ] , while Batole et al. use
an agent-oriented approach for locating software-design
issues [ 1 ] . SALLMA proposes separate operational and
knowledge layers for LLM-based multi-agent systems, including intent
management, orchestration, and persistent agent configuration [ 2 ] . These architectures are related to the separation
between capability descriptions, routing, and execution considered here, but
their evaluation targets software repositories or broader agent architectures
rather than real-time robotic capability selection.

The reliability of the routing boundary is important because retrieval and LLM
components introduce integration failure modes beyond model accuracy alone. A
study of open-source LLM applications with retrieval support identified
recurring functionality, efficiency, and security defects [ 14 ] . These findings support treating routing, output
validation, and process execution as explicit components rather than combining
them into an unrestricted end-to-end agent.

Previous research has established that LLMs can invoke tools, generate
policies, coordinate multi-step tasks, and use retrieved context. Less attention has been given to the narrower routing boundary between an unconstrained natural-language request and a fixed set of robot-facing processes. In particular, there is limited empirical evidence comparing different embedding-only retrieval policies with direct large-model selection under the same capability catalog, annotations, and evaluation metrics. This work addresses that gap by comparing three progressively refined retrieval methods with a 120B LLM baseline, considering both routing quality and latency.

2026-10-23.title: Revisiting Distribution Matching for State-to-Vision Policy Distillation in Laparoscopic Robotic Manipulation
2026-10-23.authors: Mingyu Sheng , Jianan Fan , Dongnan Liu , Guoyan Zheng , Ron Kikinis , Weidong Cai
2026-10-23.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
2026-10-23.abstract:
End-to-end control policies trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) have emerged as an alternative to conventional surgical robotic control approaches, with recent studies exploring state-based policies trained on privileged state observations.
However, such approaches rely on precise physical states that are difficult to obtain reliably in surgical environments.
Vision-based RL provides an alternative by learning manipulation policies directly from RGB observations, avoiding explicit state estimation and manually engineered perception pipelines while enabling policies to acquire task-relevant visual representations.
Nevertheless, obtaining vision-based policies via pure RL methods for surgical manipulation remains challenging. Thus, imitation learning (IL) becomes another solution, yet it requires a large number of expert demonstrations, which are difficult to obtain in minimally invasive surgery.
In this work, we propose a framework for state-to-vision policy distillation in laparoscopic robotic manipulation.
Specifically, a state-based policy with privileged observations is employed as the teacher, and a vision-based policy learns from RGB observations and robot proprioceptive information, which requires less expert demonstrations than IL and introduces superior performance than RL methods.
We conduct extensive experiments on various surgical manipulation tasks in the simulated environment.
Experimental results show that, in the context of laparoscopic robotic manipulation, training vision-based policies with general-purpose RL methods is challenging, whereas our proposed state-to-vision policy distillation leads to more consistent and stable performance across tasks.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Dexterous manipulation skills are critical components of surgical robotics tasks such as needle insertion, knot tying, and tissue retraction [ 1 ] .
In recent years, significant progress has been made in applying deep reinforcement learning (RL) to accomplish such complex autonomous or semi-autonomous subtasks [ 2 , 3 ] .
This progress has been largely enabled by the development of high-fidelity surgical robot simulators [ 4 , 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] .
However, a key limitation of RL-based surgical robotics lies in its reliance on privileged state information, which typically assumes accurate and noise-free access to the physical states of surgical objects, with limited integration of visual perception [ 10 ] .
This issue is particularly pronounced in fine manipulation tasks such as needle handling, where even minor deviations in object pose can lead to task failure [ 2 ] .

Recently, benchmarks have been proposed to provide a diverse set of learning-based tasks that capture varying levels of dexterity and precision required in the surgical context [ 8 ] .
Benchmarks provide standardized platforms for evaluating autonomous policies. Nevertheless, surgical manipulation tasks still remain highly challenging due to their stringent requirements for precision, robustness, and safety in constrained operating environments.

To reduce the reliance on privileged state information, vision-based policy learning provides an alternative by directly mapping visual observations to control actions [ 11 , 12 , 13 ] .
Such policies can avoid state estimation and manually engineered perception pipelines by leveraging visual information to learn task-relevant representations.
However, learning effective control policies directly from visual observations via RL remains a major hurdle in surgical robotics.
In the context of surgical manipulation tasks, the difficulty is further amplified by the severe visual sparsity of task-relevant objects.
For instance, the needle and instruments of surgical robots often occupy only a few pixels in high-resolution RGB observations, making reliable perception and localization hard to achieve.
Furthermore, the instability of RL exacerbates the training difficulty in such sparse and precision-critical settings [ 14 ] .
Imitation learning (IL) defines a stable training objective, which transforms RL into supervised learning given a large number of expert demonstrations as data labels [ 15 , 16 ] .
However, compared with general robotic manipulation tasks, such as opening bottles or folding clothes, expert demonstrations for laparoscopic manipulation tasks are much more expensive and scarce.

To facilitate vision-based policy learning under these limitations, policy distillation provides an effective approach for transferring knowledge from a state-based policy to an RGB-based policy [ 17 , 18 , 19 ] .
The state-based policy has access to privileged robot and object state information and serves as the teacher, and the RGB-based policy then learns to reproduce the teacher’s behavior from visual observations and robot proprioceptive states.
Such knowledge transfer provides guidance for learning visuomotor policies from high-dimensional visual inputs, enabling the vision-based policy to acquire effective manipulation behaviors without relying on privileged state information during execution.
However, most studies on policy distillation consider discrete action settings, such as those in Atari games, and thus the potential of policy distillation for continuous-control surgical robotic manipulation remains unexplored.

In this work, we propose a policy distillation framework for continuous-control laparoscopic robotic manipulation.
Specifically, we proposed a distribution-matching-based policy learning approach that overcomes the limitation of previous methods by Gaussian alignment. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach through both theoretical analysis and empirical validation.
We employ SurRoL [ 8 ] as the simulation environment, where a Patient Side Manipulator (PSM) executes the manipulation task while an Endoscopic Camera Manipulator (ECM) provides RGB observations.
During training, the state-based policy has access to all privileged state information, including the coordinates and orientations of all objects, and serves as the teacher for the vision-based policy.
In contrast, the vision-based policy only receives RGB observations and robot proprioceptive states, and is trained to distill the behavior of the state-based teacher without accessing privileged object states during execution.
Through theoretical analysis and empirical evaluation, we provide insights into various distribution matching objectives for policy distillation, which may serve as a useful reference for future research on vision-based policy learning in surgical robotics manipulation.
The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

We formulate state-to-vision policy distillation as a stochastic distribution matching problem, where a vision-based student policy learns to match both the action and the uncertainty of a privileged state-based teacher policy, reducing the demand for expert demonstrations and demonstrating stronger stability.

We provide a unified first- and second-order gradient analysis of commonly used distribution matching objectives, revealing their distinct gradient scaling, parameter coupling, and curvature properties for Gaussian policies.

We evaluate the proposed method across various surgical robotic manipulation tasks, and the experimental results demonstrate its stronger stability and higher success rate on complex tasks.

1. We formulate state-to-vision policy distillation as a stochastic distribution matching problem, where a vision-based student policy learns to match both the action and the uncertainty of a privileged state-based teacher policy, reducing the demand for expert demonstrations and demonstrating stronger stability.

2. We provide a unified first- and second-order gradient analysis of commonly used distribution matching objectives, revealing their distinct gradient scaling, parameter coupling, and curvature properties for Gaussian policies.

3. We evaluate the proposed method across various surgical robotic manipulation tasks, and the experimental results demonstrate its stronger stability and higher success rate on complex tasks.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Vision-Based Reinforcement Learning

Vision-based policies show greater potential for real-world applications because they can prevent the policy from becoming overly reliant on privileged states, but they are more difficult to train due to partial observability and the high dimensionality of image inputs.
To date, there have been numerous studies on how to train vision-based policies.
Asymmetric actor critic [ 20 ] leverages state-based critics to provide target values for vision-based actors, avoiding difficult vision-based critic learning. Nevertheless, asymmetric training may lead to an unbalanced model learning trajectory.
To ensure that both the actor and the critic receive image inputs, Yarats et al. [ 12 , 13 ] developed DrQ and DrQv2 for image-based RL training by introducing an augmentation technique.
Laskin et al. [ 11 ] proposed a method based on contrastive representation learning.
With sufficient expert demonstrations, imitation learning can obtain policies via supervised learning [ 15 , 16 ] ,
whereas the high demand for expert demonstrations is a limitation in the context of surgical robotic manipulation, where expert demonstrations are more expensive and scarce.
These methods all achieve great performance in humanoid robotic control, but are challenged when applied to surgical robotic manipulation.

## II-B Learning-Based Surgical Robotic Manipulation

To date, most methods focus on state-based policies, where the robotic agent is assumed to have access to the privileged states of objects [ 2 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] .
Based on state-based policies, surgical robotic manipulation is inevitably solved in two steps: perception and then manipulation.
For example, the agent acquires object states via a hand-crafted image processing pipeline and then feeds the states into the policy network to obtain the robotic actions [ 26 ] .
Such working pipelines are intuitive and simple to deploy in the real world.
Nevertheless, a pure vision-based policy is still an attractive solution because of its one-step processing and stronger robustness against noise and varying scenes.
To this end, some studies start to involve pixel-based observations [ 3 , 27 , 28 , 29 ] .
Haiderbhai et al. [ 3 ] and Gondokaryono et al. [ 28 ] trained RGB-based policies with conventional CNNs and LSTMs for basic manipulation tasks.
To deal with more complex tasks, most vision-based studies depend on additional input observations, such as depth and segmentation masks, which may require extra processing pipelines, or rely on pretrained large models, resulting in high computational costs and potential error propagation.
In this case, how to efficiently obtain a simple and effective vision-based policy remains a problem.

## II-C Policy Distillation

The concept of policy distillation was first introduced by Rusu et al. [ 18 ] , aiming to transfer the knowledge of multiple task-specific deep Q-networks to a single network.
Czarnecki et al. [ 19 ] further pointed out that the learning trajectory can oscillate once reward learning is involved in the distillation process.
Based on policy distillation, various vision-based policies for real-world manipulation tasks have been developed, by using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence or Mean Square Error (MSE) to transfer policy knowledge [ 30 , 17 , 31 ] .
In most settings, policy distillation employs one policy as the teacher and another as the student, which can largely avoid the high demand for expert demonstrations, and trains the student policy through relatively stable supervised learning.
We identify that the above properties of policy distillation are more appropriate for surgical vision-based policy training (i.e., low demand for expert demonstrations and a comparatively smooth training trajectory). Furthermore, most studies pertain to discrete action spaces, which cannot be applied to continuous-control laparoscopic robotic manipulation.
These considerations motivate our study.
