2026-10-23.title: Co^2Gen: Collaboratively Generating Task Plans for Decentralized Multi-Robot and Human Collaboration
2026-10-23.authors: Yi Loo , Siddhant Shrivastava , Minh Long Pham , Malika Meghjani
2026-10-23.abstract: Visual Language Action (VLA) models are designed to be generalist robot models that can be implemented across embodiments, tasks and environments. However, their ability to collaborate with other robots and humans remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a framework to automate the generation of multi-robot collaborative data for decentralized VLA training without requiring human teleoperation. Our framework first utilizes a decentralized collaborative planning approach to generate multi-robot collaborative robot plans in the form of an executable function. We then utilize the collaborative plan to produce collaborative demonstration data to finetune VLA models in a decentralized manner. We show that our approach produces demonstration data that when used to finetune VLA models on decentralized collaboration tasks matches the task performance of VLA models finetuned on human-teleoperated collaborative data.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Visual Language Action (VLA) models [ 11 , 3 , 2 , 6 ] unify visual perception, language understanding and low-level robot actions into a single model, enabling them to generalize across embodiments, tasks and environments. Modern VLA models pre-train on large scale human demonstration datasets [ 18 , 10 ] and utilize Supervised Finetuning (SFT) on smaller task specific datasets for task adaptation [ 11 , 21 ] . If these VLA models are to be deployed on robots in real world environments, they invariably have to operate in the vicinity or even directly collaborate and coordinate with other robots and humans. However, the modren VLA models’ ability to perform collaborative tasks with other robots or even humans in zero-shot remains underexplored.

In this paper, we show that VLA models, even when finetuned on task specific single robot demonstrations, fail to coordinate with each other on collaborative manipulation tasks as most of the pretrained data of VLA models come from non-collaborative single robot demonstration data. Hence, the VLA models fail to learn to coordinate their policy execution with one another. We then show that finetuning on demonstration data that is collected collaboratively in a multi-robot manner does improve VLA models performance on decentralized collaborative tasks. Furthermore, we extend these results to zero-shot human collaboration as well.

However, the data collection process for simultaneous multi-robot collaborative data can prove challenging due to either additional human cost for each additional robot or the lack of teleoperation interfaces to collect said demonstration data. To bridge this gap, we propose Co 2 Gen: Collaborative Plan Generation for Decentralized VLA Training for Collaborative Tasks, a framework to autonomously generate collaborative data for multi-robot systems without multi-robot collaborative demonstrations. Our key insight is that collaborative robot demonstrations require the coordination and sequencing of each individual robot’s sub-tasks to be conditioned on the successful sub-task execution and state of another robot. For example in Figure 1 , the arm on the right should only perform its sub-task of placing its cube when the cabinet is in an open position. Hence, any collaborative plan would need to sequence robot sub-tasks conditioned on both environment state and sub-tasks of other robots.

Given a collaborative task prompt and environment state, our proposed approach, Co 2 Gen, first leverages Visual Language Models (VLM) to generate a collaborative execution plan in the form of executable Pythonic function [ 22 , 14 ] . We structure the plan generation process to be decentralized, where each robot utilizes a VLM to collaboratively propose and refine the generated execution plan using a collaborative Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) process [ 25 , 19 ] . The resultant execution plans composes and calls on individual skills that are available for each robot and utilizes VLMs as a semantic verifier to check for sub-task preconditions for each robot skill execution.

We then utilize the generated collaborative execution plan to generate collaborative robot demonstration data together with a human verifier to check for task success. Finally, we finetune the VLAs on resultant demonstration data. Each robot’s VLA model is finetuned separately in a decentralized manner from its local data stream. We show that it enables VLAs to match the task execution success rate of VLAs finetuned on human teleoperated collaborative demonstrations. We further show that they also retain the match the for zero-shot human-robot collaboration across manipulation tasks. To summarize, our contributions are:

We show that VLA models fail to generalize to simple collaborative tasks even when finetuned on task specific single-robot demonstrations.

We show that VLA models fail to generalize to simple collaborative tasks even when finetuned on task specific single-robot demonstrations.

We show that collaborative robot demonstrations finetuning massively improves VLA models’ performance on collaborative tasks.

We propose Co 2 Gen, an autonomous way to produce collaborative robot data through an executable Python function that composes single robot skills into collaborative plans. The collaborative plan is also generated in a decentralized manner by utilizing a collaborative MCTS process.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# II Related Work

Foundation Models for Single and Multi-Robot Systems. Since their introduction, many works leverage the sematic reasoning capabilities of FMs for robot planning and task execution. Most notably, SayCan [ 1 ] matches language instructions with low-level robot skills through a pre-trained value function for skill selection in open ended tasks. ProgPrompt [ 22 ] and CaP [ 14 ] leverage the code writing capabilities of LLMs to generate robot policies in the form of code given access to low-level skills, code libraries and environment specifications for single robot task execution. In our work, we extend this capability to generate robot plans for collaborative tasks.

In the multi-robot context, SMART-LLM [ 9 ] utilizes a central LLM planner to perform task decomposition and allocation for a heterogeneous multi-robot system whereas LaMMA-P [ 24 ] utilizes the central LLM planner to generate PDDL problem descriptions for each robot and a PDDL planner at the task execution level. RoCo [ 16 ] utilizes multi-agent dialog to generate sub-task plain which then fed to a centralized motion planner. For our approach, we utilized multi-agent dialog to perform collaborative tree search to generate a programmatic collaborative plan that decomposes and allocates sub tasks while also coordinating sub-task sequencing by checking for sub-task pre-conditions. Each robot then executes their sub-task via a decentralized planner.

VLA models for Multi-Robot Tasks. Though initial VLA models are primarily applied to single robot tasks [ 4 , 11 , 3 ] , recent works have explored applying VLA models to multi-robot systems, primarily on the long standing problem of bi-manual manipulation [ 12 , 15 ] . These approaches utilize information sharing between arms to coordinate each of their policies. InterAct [ 13 ] uses Hierarchical Attention Encoder to facilitate information sharing between robot arm policies. TwinVLA [ 7 ] utilizes cross attention between the VLA models of both robot arms for information exchange and coordination. MolmoAct2 [ 6 ] couples an embodied-reasoning VLM backbone with a flow-matching continuous action expert to enable coordinated dual-arm manipulators. SkillVLA [ 23 ] proposes a hierarchical reasoning approach to bi-manual manipulation, where a high level VLM generates sub-tasks for each individual arm which are then passed on to low-level VLM linked to each arm’s action experts. In our work, we extend bi-manual manipulation to a true multi-robot system where each arm has a separate policy via a VLA model. To our knowledge, we are the first to explore VLA models’ ability to collaboratively execute tasks in a decentralized manner and to collaborate with humans in a zero shot manner.

Motion planning is central to robotics, and it is increasingly used to
correct the motions proposed by learned planners and policies. In both uses, constraints must hold at every
instant of the motion, not only at sampled times. To our knowledge, no
algorithm provably converges to a globally optimal motion once a
smoothness cost is combined with such constraints. We cast planning and
steering as a single continuous-time program: robots avoid one another and
static or moving obstacles, and a learned proposal is steered by keeping the
motion close to it. The program is elementary to state, yet nonconvex. We
propose GlobMP (Global Motion Planning), a gradient projection method over
piecewise-polynomial curves, on which each constraint is one polynomial per piece that must
stay nonnegative over the whole motion; it alternates cost reduction with
feasibility restoration. Under
mild assumptions, we show that, from a fine grid start, its cost approaches the global optimum as the number of polynomial pieces grows, with every constraint met to any chosen tolerance, or exactly on stable instances. We
demonstrate its superior performance over strong baselines in real and
synthetic experiments, including teams of up to 200 200 robots, multi-robot
planning on the Robotarium testbed and an extended benchmark, maze
navigation, and steering tactile-reactive policies on a bimanual humanoid.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Motion planning is a fundamental problem in robotics: it asks for a trajectory that connects a given initial state to a goal while satisfying motion constraints, such as avoiding collisions ( LaValle, 1998 ) . It underlies navigation, manipulation ( Sundaralingam & Hermans, 2019 ; Gao et al., 2024 ; Amice et al., 2024 ) ,
multi-robot coordination ( Li et al., 2021 ; Tang et al., 2025 ; Shaoul et al., 2025 ) ,
and, increasingly, the steering of learned planners and policies ( Janner et al., 2022 ; Carvalho et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Giaretta et al., 2026 ) .

Motion planners approach this problem in several ways, each with a gap.
Sampling-based planners explore many routes ( Karaman & Frazzoli, 2011 ) , yet
smoothing their waypoints can introduce collisions; optimization-based
planners improve a motion locally ( Zucker et al., 2013 ; Tedrake & the Drake Development Team, 2019 ) , with TrajOpt ( Schulman et al., 2014 ) also supporting
continuous collision checks. Constraints enforced
at sampled times do not ensure feasibility between them
( Hargraves & Paris, 1987 ; Figure 1 ). Convex-region planners search a decomposition
of free space ( Deits & Tedrake, 2015a ; Marcucci et al., 2023 ) , and semidefinite
relaxations certify a polynomial motion as globally optimal only when the
relaxation is tight ( Graesdal et al., 2026 ) . Even shortest-path complexity depends on
the geometry: polynomial-time in the real-RAM model among planar discs ( Chang et al., 2005 ) , NP-hard among polyhedra
in ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} ( Canny & Reif, 1987 ) , and still open in ℝ 3 \mathbb{R}^{3} even among disjoint unit discs or axis-aligned unit cubes ( Mitchell, 2017 ) .

Our setting is a point robot in ℝ n \mathbb{R}^{n} that travels between prescribed
boundary states around obstacles while minimizing a smoothness cost; steering a learned planner or policy is the
same problem with one added constraint that keeps the robot near its proposal. Although
elementary to state, this setting already contains the core difficulty of
avoiding collisions; to
our knowledge, no algorithm converges to its global optimum once
a derivative cost such as acceleration or snap is combined with collision
constraints on the whole time interval. We introduce GlobMP and show that, from a fine grid start, its cost approaches the
global optimum as the number of pieces grows, within any constraint tolerance or exactly on stable instances.

2026-10-23.title: CMAR-search: Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning for Object Search in Dynamic Interactive Environments
2026-10-23.authors: Kaiyao Liao , Qingfeng Li , Xinlei Zhang , Chen Chen , Qing Sun , Jianwei Niu
2026-10-23.comment: Published in ICRA 2026.
2026-10-23.abstract: Dynamic interactive object search in large-scale human environments presents substantial challenges for existing methods. Current scene representations like 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) only provide coarse-grained spatial segmentation and cannot identify functional areas such as storage or leisure areas. Without functional area understanding, existing methods are constrained to exhaustive sequential exploration at large scales, resulting in inefficient search behaviors—particularly in open-layout environments with numerous interactive objects such as drawers and cabinets. Moreover, these methods lack adaptability to environmental dynamics such as object relocations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes CMAR-search, a novel framework built upon Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning (CMAR). Our approach leverages commonsense about area functionalities and aggregates environmental memory to construct a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG), which organizes the environment into functional areas with their associated containers. Through this structured representation, CMAR enables hierarchical action planning at both macro-area and micro-container levels, empowering the system to efficiently identify and inspect semantically relevant areas for effective object search. Notably, CMAR continuously integrates real-time perception, accumulated memory, and commonsense to dynamically relocalize objects in changing environments. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that CMAR-search significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both success rate and search efficiency for object search in dynamic interactive environments.
2026-10-23.introduction:
In human-centered environments, interactive object search is a fundamental embodied AI task where a robot must locate target objects through navigation and physical interaction such as opening cabinets and drawers. This problem becomes particularly challenging in large-scale, dynamic settings that demand long-horizon reasoning and semantic understanding of spatial layouts. Current approaches typically extract environmental information into 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) that structurally represent rooms and objects [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] and utilize Large Language Models (LLMs) for high-level reasoning of robotic actions [ 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . However, as environmental complexity increases, these methods encounter several critical issues: (1) In open-layout home environments, existing scene representation methods struggle to effectively segment functional areas, making it difficult to narrow down possible object search ranges; (2) their reliance on atomic actions—such as opening only one container at a time—considerably slows down search processes when handling multiple containers; and (3) they lack robust adaptation to environmental dynamics, showing limited integration of historical memory and object commonsense for efficient object relocation, which significantly restricts their real-world applicability.

Inspired by Kahneman’s dual-system theory of cognition (System 1 for intuitive processing and System 2 for deliberate reasoning) [ 10 ] , this paper proposes a novel framework centered on Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning (CMAR). Our approach addresses the above limitations through two core innovations. First, in decision granularity, our Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG), constructed using object-functional commonsense and spatial relationships, enables LLMs to perform macro-level planning using functional areas as units. The system directs LLMs to generate comprehensive search commands for entire areas at once, significantly reducing the number of LLMs calls and mitigating error accumulation. At the micro-level, these commands are decomposed into optimized sub-steps for inspecting all containers. Our CMAR-based sequence—considering distance, semantic similarity, and risk factors—determines the optimal execution order, further enhancing search efficiency. Second, in dynamic response, the CMAR mechanism synergistically retrieves historical memory and object-functional commonsense to infer optimal search strategies. This framework allows the robot to systematically explore new environments and adapt to changes in a human-like manner, leading to significant improvements in success rate and efficiency in dynamic interactive object search tasks.

To summarize, our main contributions are as follows:

This paper proposes CMAR-search, a novel framework for dynamic interactive object search, which introduces CMAR to enable adaptation to environmental dynamics (e.g., object relocations) by synergistically leveraging real-time perception, historical memory, and commonsense, significantly improving search robustness in changing environments.

The framework constructs an F3DSG that organizes environments into functional areas with their associated containers, enabling hierarchical action planning at both macro-area and micro-container levels to efficiently identify and inspect semantically relevant areas, reducing unnecessary exploration in large-scale environments.

Extensive experiments in both simulated and real-world environments demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in success rate and efficiency for dynamic interactive object search tasks.

# II RELATED WORKS

## II-A 3DSG-based Environmental Representation

3DSG as a sparse environmental representation can abstract hierarchical, object-centric models of environments from dense perceptual data, thereby providing a powerful interface for high-level reasoning and task planning in robotics [ 4 , 5 , 11 ] . Existing research has constructed hierarchical graphs such as “building–floor–room–object” and enhanced their representational capacity by incorporating object-object relationship edges [ 12 , 13 , 14 ] , integrating Voronoi graphs for navigation support [ 15 ] , or distinguishing between static and dynamic objects [ 5 ] . There are also some methods that try to implement dynamic updates for 3DSG [ 2 , 16 ] . However, most of these methods rely on a pre-built, static scene graph representation, which inherently lacks the ability to dynamically evolve based on interactive experiences (e.g., inspecting container interiors) and fails to excavate the semantically critical layer of “functional areas” essential for task planning. In contrast, our work aims to construct a functional and dynamically updatable 3D scene graph, whose core innovation lies in leveraging LLMs to infer functional area segmentation beyond purely geometric space, thereby laying the foundation for efficient interactive object search.

## II-B LLM-driven Robotic Planning

LLMs have been widely used to generate behavioral sequences for robots, achieving remarkable progress in tabletop manipulation and vision-language navigation (VLN) tasks [ 17 , 18 ] . Some studies have attempted to apply LLMs to more challenging mobile manipulation tasks in home environments, such as generating plans through information retrieval for task matching [ 18 ] , fine-tuning LLMs to encode object relationships [ 19 ] , or iteratively pruning scene graphs [ 5 ] . MoMa-LLM [ 1 ] encodes scene graphs and instructions into natural language inputs for LLMs to generate next-step actions, enabling a certain level of interactive environmental information utilization. However, existing methods generally suffer from limited abstraction levels and single-grained instruction generation, making it difficult to adapt to the complex and diverse interactive reasoning demands in large-scale environments. This study significantly enhances the reasoning efficiency and generalization capability of LLMs in interactive tasks by introducing a hierarchically abstracted action space and structured task representation.

## II-C Object Search

Traditional object search methods include heuristic approaches based on frontier exploration [ 20 ] and reinforcement learning models [ 21 ] . With the increasing application of scene graphs, graph neural networks (GNNs) have been used to search for objects with relational constraints within graphs [ 22 ] or to cope with dynamic changes [ 23 , 24 ] . Recent studies have employed LLMs to assess semantic similarity for guiding search [ 25 , 26 ] , but these are still limited to non-interactive navigation tasks. Schmalstieg et al. [ 27 ] explicitly proposed the interactive object search task, emphasizing operations on containers to find interior objects. MoMa-LLM [ 1 ] further supports interactive search using scene graphs but lacks adaptability to environmental changes. We propose the CMAR mechanism, integrating real-time perception, historical memory, and functional commonsense, to enable efficient and robust interactive object search in dynamic environments.

2026-10-23.title: PATH: Preference-Aware Traversability Estimation for Robotic Teleoperation in Off-Road Navigation
2026-10-23.authors: Xianghao Meng , Wenshuo Wang , Cheng Shao , Lewei Feng , Qingxiao Liu , Canyu Wang , Junqiang Xi
2026-10-23.abstract: Traversability estimation is critical for ground vehicle teleoperation, yet existing methods often neglect the human operator’s preferences for speed and risk tolerance. To address this gap, we propose PATH-Net, a Preference-Aware Traversability estimation Hierarchical Network that adaptively generates preference-conditioned traversability cost maps and speed profiles for off-road teleoperation. Our framework integrates visual and geometric bird’s-eye-view features with short-term historical vehicle states through a multi-head shared-backbone architecture. Our PATH-Net infers traversability cost maps while optimizing speed recommendations by using maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning and sparse speed supervision. Our method incorporates operator preference via an asymmetric feature aggregation mechanism, splitting inference into a cost branch that prioritizes high-risk traversability regions and a speed branch that outputs preference-adjusted recommended speeds. Experiments with 15 operators across 225 teleoperated trajectories show alignment with user-specific navigation strategies, achieving modified Hausdorff distance of 0.17 ​ m 0.17\,\mathrm{m} (aggressive) and 0.15 ​ m 0.15\,\mathrm{m} (conservative). In the questionnaire assessment, participants reported lower NASA-TLX workload scores with PATH-Net recommendations than without recommendations, decreasing from 34.7 34.7 to 22.2 22.2 . These results support preference-conditioned trajectory and speed recommendation for off-road teleoperation.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) have become indispensable tools for exploration and inspection in hazardous environments, where direct human presence is impractical or unsafe (e.g., nuclear facilities, disaster zones) [ 1 ] . While teleoperation remains the dominant control paradigm for navigating complex unstructured terrain, its effectiveness is fundamentally constrained in non-line-of-sight (NLOS) scenarios. Human operators in such settings must synthesize partial information streams, limited to delayed visual feeds and coarse vehicle-state telemetry [ 2 ] , while deprived of critical physical cues like vestibular feedback and tactile vibrations that enable instinctive control in manned vehicles. This sensory mismatch induces high cognitive load, frequently manifesting as compromised depth perception and degraded situational awareness [ 3 ] , which collectively elevate the risk of erroneous maneuvering decisions. To mitigate these limitations, there is growing recognition that teleoperation frameworks must evolve beyond pure remote control toward context-aware decision-support systems capable of augmenting human perception and judgment.

Off-road traversability assessment has evolved through multimodal sensor fusion [ 4 ] . Pioneering methods primarily utilized exteroceptive geometric information (e.g., digital elevation and 3D LiDAR point clouds) to extract topographic features such as local gradients, discontinuity heights, and roughness metric [ 5 , 6 ] . While effective for structural hazards, these geometric approaches face inherent limitations when discriminating terrains with analogous structures [ 7 , 8 ] but different mechanical properties such as soft grass and solid rock. To address this, vision-based semantic segmentation emerged as a complementary solution [ 9 , 10 ] . Nevertheless, most supervised learning paradigms demand labor-intensive pixel-wise labeling, which constrains their scalability in unstructured environments [ 11 , 12 ] . Recent advances adopt self-supervision by exploiting proprioceptive signals [ 13 , 14 ] , including inertial measurements, wheel-terrain interaction forces, and suspension dynamics, as implicit traversability indicators [ 15 , 16 , 17 , 18 ] . Concurrently, visual foundation models like DINOv2 offer pre-trained feature embeddings that mitigate annotation dependency, demonstrating remarkable transferability across off-road domains [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] .

The robotic traversability prediction undergoes a paradigm shift alongside the diversification of sensory data modalities [ 22 , 23 , 14 ] . Early approaches relies on deterministic heuristics, where hand-crafted functions mapped geometric features to traversability scores [ 24 ] . Recent methods have embraced data-driven learning frameworks, evolving along three research thrusts: (i) continuous cost representations learning, (ii)navigation behavior imitation, and (iii) policy optimization from sensory observations [ 25 ] . Representation learning methods such as HDIF (How Does It Feel?) [ 15 ] and Velociraptor [ 20 ] extract traversability features from visual-geometric inputs, with some architectures additionally predicting speed constraints. Notably, these approaches address a critical limitation of classical planners by capturing terrain properties that defy pure geometric characterization. Complementarily, inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a principled framework for cost function inference. Maximum entropy IRL and its extensions treat demonstrations as outcomes of near-optimal policies, enabling the recovery of implicit cost functions that explain observed navigation behaviors. This proves particularly valuable for encoding human operator preferences and safety considerations that remain opaque to geometry-based planners [ 26 , 27 ] .

Despite these advancements, directly applying traversability assessment methods tailored for autonomous systems to teleoperated off-road vehicles has two limitations. First, they are predominantly operator-agnostic and platform-centric [ 28 , 29 ] , optimizing for single, fixed traversability metrics (e.g., energy efficiency or vibration minimization) while neglecting operator preference. Although terrain–vehicle interaction determines the physical feasibility of traversal, operators may still choose different routes and speed profiles for the same environment [ 30 , 31 ] . For instance, a route deemed optimal by algorithms may prove unacceptable to risk-averse operators due to their perceived safety differences. This misalignment between system recommendations and human judgment can erode trust [ 32 ] and trigger automation rejection [ 33 ] . Second, many approaches rely on static environmental representations, failing to incorporate dynamic vehicle-state context [ 26 ] . Vehicle motion states such as speed transients, angular kinematics, roll/pitch dynamics could influence terrain negotiation strategies for human operators. Therefore, historical motion contains complementary information beyond single-frame terrain analysis, particularly for operator’s adjustment anticipation.

In this paper, we propose PATH-Net (a Preference-Aware Traversability estimation Hierarchical Network) for robotic teleoperation, which directly learns candidates of cost functions and speed maps from operator demonstrations. Unlike traversability models that produce a single cost function, our PATH-Net leverages a questionnaire-derived preference parameter to asymmetrically aggregate these candidates, emphasizing upper-tail costs or selecting recommended speed profiles according to the operator preference. This design allows one trained model to generate aggressive, neutral, and conservative navigation advice without training separate models for various operators. This paper’s contributions are as follows:

We introduce a spatiotemporal-BEV temporal convolutional network to dynamically couple terrain perception with vehicle motion history, enabling interactive traversability prediction and yielding kinematic-specific costs and speeds.

Our multi-head network with entropy-regularized IRL unifies aggressive/conservative demonstrations through shared feature extraction and parallel prediction of cost functions and speed profiles.

We introduce a risk-aware approach that employs conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) optimization for upper-tail cost aggregation and quantile-based speed selection, enabling explicit trade-offs between risk and efficiency. A single parameter controls both the conservatism of the cost map via CVaR’s risk threshold and the recommended speed bounds via quantile selection, generating interpretable behaviors ranging from aggressive to cautious.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II formulates the teleoperation decision-support problem and provides an overview of PATH-Net. Section III presents the feature extraction, cost and speed learning, and asymmetric aggregation methods. Section IV describes the experimental platform, dataset, and evaluation protocol. Section V reports the experimental results, and Section VI concludes the paper.

# II Problem Formulation

## II-A Problem Definition

We address the problem of non-line-of-sight teleoperation for off-road navigation, where an operator controls a UGV in unstructured terrain with limited sensory feedback. In such scenarios, traversability depends not only on terrain geometry but also on operator preferences. For instance, an efficiency-preferred operator may favor shorter, faster paths, while a risk-averse operator may prioritize slower trajectories with greater obstacle clearance. To accommodate these differences, PATH-Net aims to generate recommendations that reflect both terrain traversability and the operator’s route-speed preference.

Simultaneously, a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) encodes the kinematic history, 𝐇 kin , t \mathbf{H}_{\mathrm{kin},t} . These representations are concatenated to form the joint feature map, 𝐌 feat , t \mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{feat},t} . This joint feature map feeds into a convolutional backbone with parallel prediction heads. Each head outputs candidate cost maps and speed maps. The cost map is learned via Maximum Entropy IRL to match human operator preferences, while the speed map is learned from speed supervision. These heads generate diverse candidate cost and speed maps for subsequent aggregation without explicit preference specialization.

During inference, the questionnaire-derived preference parameter ρ \rho is mapped to an aggregation level α \alpha . PATH-Net then aggregates the candidate maps asymmetrically: the cost maps use upper-tail aggregation, while the speed maps use quantile-based selection to generate preference-dependent speed bounds. The final outputs, C final C_{\mathrm{final}} and V final V_{\mathrm{final}} , guide the path planner to generate the recommended trajectory.

2026-10-23.title: OASIS: Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System for Open-Vocabulary Retrieval and Navigation in Dynamic Environments
2026-10-23.authors: Kaiyao Liao , Qingfeng Li , Chen Chen , Xiaoze Wu , Qing Sun , Jianwei Niu
2026-10-23.comment: Accepted for oral presentation at ACM Multimedia (ACM MM) 2026. including supplementary material
2026-10-23.abstract: Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes. To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Modern embodied agents face increasingly complex tasks in unstructured environments, where instructions involve rich, open-vocabulary descriptions beyond simple object categories. A user might command a robot to “find the sealed silver can on a round table” or “locate the bed with a lit lamp.” Fulfilling such requests requires a scene representation that transcends traditional geometric mapping, demanding fine-grained attribute recognition ( e.g. , color, material, state) and spatial relationship reasoning. Crucially, these capabilities must remain robust in dynamic real-world settings where objects are frequently repositioned. Consequently, the challenge has shifted from static mapping to constructing a dynamic, semantic-rich scene graph capable of supporting intricate queries and adapting to environmental changes on the fly.

However, deploying semantic maps in real-world systems still involves a practical trade-off between efficiency and reasoning capability. Dense mapping approaches ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Werby et al., 2024 ; Mirzaei et al., 2025 ) embed rich semantics into many spatial elements, providing detailed understanding but sometimes introducing clutter and distractors, while also requiring relatively high computational and memory resources. Conversely, lightweight methods ( Maggio et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) are more efficient, but may not preserve enough spatial context for complex reasoning, making it harder to distinguish visually similar objects based on their surroundings or attributes. A remaining challenge appears in dynamic environments. Although some methods address object relocalization, they often depend on repeated re-observation. During active navigation, rapid robot motion and a limited camera view can cause shifted targets to be missed, which reduces the efficiency of these scanning-based strategies.

To bridge this gap, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS) for robust open-vocabulary retrieval and dynamic object relocalization. As illustrated in Figure 1 , OASIS avoids processing redundant context globally through an on-demand retrieval strategy. Our key insight is that indoor environments are inherently structured around stable, large-scale objects ( e.g. , beds, tables, sofas), which we define as semantic anchors. Inspired by human episodic memory, OASIS constructs an anchor-centric graph rather than a dense per-pixel map, retaining only salient semantic descriptions and high-quality representative frames. During retrieval, a Large Language Model (LLM) first reasons over the semantic anchors to filter irrelevant regions, followed by on-demand Vision-Language Model (VLM) verification of the retrieved representative frames. This strategy keeps memory lightweight while preserving the ability to distinguish fine-grained visual attributes. In dynamic settings, OASIS additionally maintains transient observations along the navigation trajectory in a lightweight buffer; if a target is missing at its initial anchor, the system queries this buffer and re-verifies candidate views for reliable relocalization.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We present OASIS, an online anchor-centric scene inference system that unifies online mapping, open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments.

We propose a human-inspired episodic memory curation mechanism that uses scale-aware scoring and spatio-semantic clustering to select representative frames, yielding a multimodal anchor-centric scene graph with integrated semantic, visual, and geometric representations.

Built upon this scene graph, OASIS supports hierarchical coarse-to-fine retrieval and view-driven navigation, and introduces a Transient Visual Buffer to reliably relocalize moved objects after scene changes.

We conduct extensive simulation and real-world experiments on retrieval and navigation under static and dynamic settings, demonstrating strong performance and reliable object relocation after scene changes.

1. We present OASIS, an online anchor-centric scene inference system that unifies online mapping, open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments.

2. We propose a human-inspired episodic memory curation mechanism that uses scale-aware scoring and spatio-semantic clustering to select representative frames, yielding a multimodal anchor-centric scene graph with integrated semantic, visual, and geometric representations.

3. Built upon this scene graph, OASIS supports hierarchical coarse-to-fine retrieval and view-driven navigation, and introduces a Transient Visual Buffer to reliably relocalize moved objects after scene changes.

4. We conduct extensive simulation and real-world experiments on retrieval and navigation under static and dynamic settings, demonstrating strong performance and reliable object relocation after scene changes.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# 2. Related Work

## 2.1. Open-Vocabulary 3D Scene Understanding

Closed-set semantic mapping relies on detectors trained for fixed object categories ( Hughes et al., 2022 ; McCormac et al., 2017 ; McCormac et al., 2018 ; Rosinol et al., 2020 ) . Open-vocabulary methods instead distill features from vision-language models ( e.g. , CLIP ( Radford et al., 2021 ) ) into 3D representations. Dense mapping methods ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Werby et al., 2024 ; Mirzaei et al., 2025 ) project pixel-aligned features into 3D space, enabling fine-grained queries but incurring high computational and memory costs. Conversely, object-centric or lightweight semantic point cloud methods ( Maggio et al., 2024 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) construct sparse maps by aggregating features at the instance level. While these approaches are significantly more efficient, they often discard the surrounding visual context required for complex reasoning. Our work builds upon the efficiency of lightweight representations but augments them with an implicit storage mechanism to retain rich contextual details without the overhead of dense fields.

## 2.2. Retrieval and Reasoning on Scene Graphs

Recent advancements in open-vocabulary scene understanding have focused on reasoning about and locating objects within complex environments using foundation models.
Early approaches primarily utilized CLIP-based matching ( Tang et al., 2025 ; Takmaz et al., 2023 ; Peng et al., 2023 ; Gu et al., 2024 ) , which directly computes cosine similarity between text queries and stored visual features. While efficient for simple identification, these methods lack the capability for multi-step reasoning or handling spatial relationships.
To overcome these limitations, LLM-based methods ( Rana et al., 2023 ; Honerkamp et al., 2024 ; Linok et al., 2025 ; Yin et al., 2024 ; Werby et al., 2024 ) leverage the reasoning power of LLMs to infer potential locations or generate navigation plans based on textual abstractions of the scene. However, relying solely on text descriptions often results in the loss of critical visual details ( e.g. , object states or specific textures) necessary for precise identification.
More recently, VLM-based approaches ( Mirzaei et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ) have emerged, directly processing images to retain visual fidelity. Despite their superior understanding, these methods typically suffer from high latency and computational costs, making them less practical for real-time applications.
Our work bridges these gaps by introducing an efficient VLM-driven mechanism that operates on implicit storage, enabling detailed visual reasoning without the heavy overhead of full-image processing.

## 2.3. Object Navigation

Object navigation requires agents to locate and move towards specific target instances within an environment ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Ye et al., 2021 ; Chaplot et al., 2020 ; Luo et al., 2022 ; Ramakrishnan et al., 2022 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Zhou et al., 2023 ; Yokoyama et al., 2024 ; Dorbala et al., 2023 ; Kuang et al., 2024 ) . Traditional approaches typically rely on static semantic maps, assuming that objects remain fixed throughout the mission. These methods combine SLAM with semantic segmentation to build a persistent representation, allowing the agent to plan paths to previously observed locations.
However, real-world environments are inherently dynamic. Existing works on dynamic navigation ( Tang et al., 2025 ; Jiang et al., 2025 ) typically address this by relying on continuous fine-grained modeling and geometric matching of objects along the trajectory to update the map. This strategy faces significant challenges: navigation often involves transient observations, making it difficult to capture and update the state of small objects accurately in real-time. Furthermore, when a target is missing from its expected location, these methods often lack the active reasoning capability to deduce its whereabouts.
In contrast, our proposed method leverages subtle visual details observed along the path, enabling the system to infer the new location of displaced objects based on semantic context, even if the new location lies outside the immediate navigation trajectory.

2026-10-23.title: Know When to Escalate: Critic-Guided Adaptive Execution for Cloud-Local Embodied Agents
2026-10-23.authors: Wei Zhang , Lirong Xiang , Charles Fleming
2026-10-23.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
2026-10-23.abstract:
Recent advances in foundation-model agents have enabled increasingly capable embodied systems for long-horizon planning and interaction. However, embodied agents require fast, closed-loop decisions as they continuously perceive and act on a changing environment. Deploying strong cloud agents leaves the platform idle for seconds between consecutive actions, while lightweight local models respond quickly but are more vulnerable to errors. Existing hierarchical architectures typically assign models fixed roles, whereas conventional model routers make stateless per-request decisions.
We present CARE, a critic-guided adaptive execution framework that dynamically determines when to escalate control from a local executor to a stronger cloud model. A lightweight critic model monitors execution reliability and triggers escalation when local execution becomes unreliable; once escalated, control persists until the agent recovers, avoiding step-wise switching. To support such control transfer, a shared handoff memory maintains execution context and task-level progress across executors, enabling the model to intervene without restarting from scratch.
Across diverse embodied benchmarks, CARE improves task success by 6.3 6.3 – 18.3 18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline. CARE further approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8 28.8 – 82.6 % 82.6\% .
2026-10-23.introduction:
Executing long-horizon robotic tasks requires embodied agents to repeatedly interpret observations, select grounded actions, and update their decisions based on action outcomes. Recent advances in generative foundation models have strengthened these capabilities [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ] , enabling such models to coordinate perception, decision making, and embodied skills as general-purpose reasoning modules [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 ] . Because model inference lies directly within the perception–action loop, high inference latency can leave the agent acting on stale observations, potentially causing failure in time-sensitive interactions. To balance strong reasoning with responsive closed-loop interaction, recent hierarchical and slow–fast architectures pair powerful foundation models with lightweight local executors or specialized controllers [ 9 , 10 ] .

Despite these advances, long-horizon embodied execution remains challenging because each action affects what the agent observes and must do next. Consider an agent midway through a rearrangement task. An earlier action has displaced the target object, causing the next grasp to fail even though the resulting observation appears similar to the previous one. If the agent overlooks this feedback, it may repeat the same action, lose track of task progress, and compound earlier errors [ 9 , 11 ] . Execution difficulty also changes along the trajectory. A lightweight executor may handle routine steps well but struggle after ambiguous observations, failed actions, or deviations from the expected state. The appropriate executor may therefore change as interaction unfolds.

This challenge is particularly pronounced in cloud–local embodied systems, where execution must continuously balance model capability against interaction latency. As shown in Figure 1 , local models provide responsive interaction but may struggle in difficult states, whereas cloud models offer stronger reasoning at the cost of seconds per decision [ 2 , 10 , 1 ] . Existing hierarchical systems typically assign these models fixed planner–executor roles, implicitly assuming that the designated executor remains appropriate throughout the task. Replanning methods can revise plans or actions in response to feedback, but generally do so without reconsidering which model should execute the subsequent trajectory [ 7 , 12 , 13 ] . Per-query model routing likewise selects an executor independently for each request, without explicitly modeling how executor suitability evolves within an embodied trajectory [ 14 ] .

We present CARE , a critic-guided adaptive execution framework for cloud–local embodied agents. Rather than routing individual actions independently, CARE uses a critic model to assess whether local execution should continue under the current interaction state and selectively escalates execution to the cloud when local execution becomes unreliable. Importantly, escalation is treated as a stateful control transfer rather than a one-step model selection: cloud intervention persists through the current recovery, avoiding premature hand-backs. Once the critic supports local execution again, control returns to the local executor to recover low-latency interaction. Meanwhile, a shared handoff memory preserves observations, completed progress, and failure context across model handoffs, allowing both executors to maintain a consistent execution state. By combining critic-guided control transfer with stateful handoff memory, CARE avoids both persistent cloud invocation and myopic per-action routing while adapting execution authority to the evolving difficulty of the task.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce a new formulation of cloud–local embodied collaboration as a stateful adaptive execution problem and propose a novel critic-guided execution framework that dynamically determines when execution should be escalated and when local control can be safely resumed.

We introduce a new formulation of cloud–local embodied collaboration as a stateful adaptive execution problem and propose a novel critic-guided execution framework that dynamically determines when execution should be escalated and when local control can be safely resumed.

We develop CARE, a novel stateful execution mechanism that combines persistent cloud intervention with shared execution memory, enabling reliable control transfer while preserving execution continuity across model handoffs.

We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of CARE across three long-horizon embodied benchmarks spanning diverse observation modalities and execution interfaces. CARE improves task success by 6.3 6.3 – 18.3 18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8 28.8 – 82.6 % 82.6\% .

1. We introduce a new formulation of cloud–local embodied collaboration as a stateful adaptive execution problem and propose a novel critic-guided execution framework that dynamically determines when execution should be escalated and when local control can be safely resumed.

2. We develop CARE, a novel stateful execution mechanism that combines persistent cloud intervention with shared execution memory, enabling reliable control transfer while preserving execution continuity across model handoffs.

3. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of CARE across three long-horizon embodied benchmarks spanning diverse observation modalities and execution interfaces. CARE improves task success by 6.3 6.3 – 18.3 18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8 28.8 – 82.6 % 82.6\% .
2026-10-23.related_work:
# II Related Work

## II-A Long-horizon embodied agents

Generative foundation models are increasingly used as high-level planners for embodied agents. Early work studies text-based interactive environments [ 5 , 15 ] using explicit world knowledge [ 16 ] , reflective reasoning [ 13 , 17 ] , and plan construction [ 18 ] ; with vision-language models, planning has extended to visually grounded interaction through scene graph representations [ 19 ] , memory-augmented visual reasoning [ 20 ] , and multimodal plans that guide downstream control policies [ 8 ] . Other work trains open-source planners by reinforcement learning [ 21 ] or supervised finetuning [ 22 ] . Another parallel line of work makes interaction latency a first-class design constraint by organizing execution hierarchically, pairing a computationally intensive foundation model with faster specialized models or policies. This hierarchy is instantiated through program or skill generation [ 6 ] , intermediate representation prediction [ 23 ] , slow–fast reasoning and control [ 2 ] , and semantic guidance to downstream policies [ 24 ] , while the execution models themselves have grown more capable through large-scale vision-language-action pretraining [ 1 , 25 ] . Both lines strengthen what each model contributes, but they fix the assignment in advance: planning improves the instructions an executor receives, and hierarchy fixes which model executes them. We instead study the runtime question left open by both—which model should hold execution authority as a plan is carried out, and when that authority should change.

## II-B Embodied execution monitoring

Outside embodied settings, cascades invoke a strong model only when a weak model’s output fails a reliability check, using signals such as answer consistency [ 26 , 27 ] or few-shot self-verification [ 28 ] , while routers predict the target model before generation [ 14 ] . These methods decide over a single self-contained input: the escalated model answers once, and the decision does not affect what is asked next. Embodied execution violates both properties—control may later return to the local executor, and an incorrect action changes the state at which later decisions are made—so escalation becomes a stateful control problem rather than a routing problem. Within embodied systems, failure-recovery methods use execution feedback to diagnose failures and generate corrective plans [ 29 , 30 ] . Their primary output is an explanation or a revised plan. Our critic instead controls a different decision variable: which of two executors holds execution authority, and when that authority should change.

2026-10-23.title: Motion Retargeting with Spatiotemporal Preferences for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
2026-10-23.authors: Xiongbo Shi , Shihang Du , Zongyou Yu , Ao Zhou , Xudong Zhang , Ziyu Lin , Haodong Zhang , Junqiao Zhao , Guang Chen
2026-10-23.abstract: Human motion retargeting bridges the embodiment gap between humans and humanoid robots by converting human demonstrations into reference trajectories for whole-body control and loco-manipulation. For object-interaction tasks, successful execution depends on accurately preserving body--object relations at critical stages. However, uniform per-frame iteration budgets do not account for these localized accuracy requirements, limiting the computational efficiency of retargeting. To address this limitation, we present Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), which uses keyframes and key body parts to allocate optimization effort. Specifically, a vision-language model selects relevant motion signals and body parts, and keyframes are identified from changes in the selected signals. Based on these selections, STR assigns additional solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to the selected parts. To further improve contact fidelity, we introduce Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) to refine object-surface contact positions using an approximate object-wrench model while retaining the selected surface directions. Building on the resulting references, we develop Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL), which combines adaptive key-stage sampling with a contact reward based on target proximity and object contact forces for downstream control. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 and real-world experiments on a Unitree R1 demonstrate that STR improves geometric contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, while the resulting references improve downstream task completion across diverse object-interaction motions.

2026-10-23.title: Decision Making and Ride Comfort Evaluation Based on Lane-Change Prediction for Autonomous Vehicles
2026-10-23.authors: Mohamed Manzour , Aditya Kumar , Rubén Izquierdo , Miguel Ángel Sotelo
2026-10-23.abstract: Predicting surrounding vehicles’ lane-change intentions enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate potential hazards and respond proactively rather than relying solely on reactive maneuvers. This study investigates the benefits of integrating lane-change prediction, based on knowledge graph embeddings and Bayesian inference, into autonomous vehicle decision-making. Three driving strategies are evaluated in risky merging scenarios simulated in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal action, and prediction-based lateral action. The proposed prediction model anticipates the surrounding vehicle’s lane change approximately 3-4 seconds before its occurrence, allowing the ego vehicle to adjust its behavior accordingly. In the representative simulation records, reactive driving results in a collision accompanied by aggressive deceleration. In contrast, prediction-based longitudinal action initiates early braking to establish a safe gap, while prediction-based lateral action performs a lane change when a safe adjacent lane is available. Both predictive strategies avoid collisions in the evaluated records. Compared with reactive driving, peak deceleration before impact is reduced by 31.5% with longitudinal action and 91.0% with lateral action. Additionally, an ISO 2631-1-based horizontal vibration estimate is used to provide a ride comfort assessment. Overall, the results highlight the potential of lane-change prediction to support safer and smoother driving through proactive decision-making, with additional insights into ride comfort provided by vibration-based estimates.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Lane changes are among the most common driving maneuvers, yet unexpected lane changes can create hazardous situations, particularly when a vehicle merges into an occupied lane with limited space for braking or avoidance. Predicting such maneuvers before they begin gives an autonomous vehicle additional time to respond. However, the benefit of this anticipation depends on the driving decision taken, as different responses may have different implications for safety and ride comfort. Figure 1 illustrates a scenario in which a target vehicle approaches a slower preceding vehicle in the rightmost lane and intends to merge into the ego vehicle’s lane. Without anticipation, the ego vehicle may be unable to avoid a collision. With prediction, it can either brake to create a safe gap or change lanes when an adjacent lane is available.

While avoiding collisions is essential, the resulting vehicle motion also affects passenger comfort. Braking may introduce substantial longitudinal deceleration, whereas lateral avoidance produces acceleration in a different direction. Since discomfort depends on the magnitude, direction, and timing of vehicle motion [ 1 , 4 ] , these responses should be examined beyond their safety outcomes. This study investigates the effects of lane-change prediction on autonomous vehicle decision-making and ride comfort using an existing knowledge graph embedding and Bayesian inference framework [ 12 , 13 ] . Three driving configurations are compared in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal control, and prediction-based lateral control. Their behavior is analyzed through response timing, collision outcomes, acceleration, and jerk, while ride comfort is additionally assessed using an ISO 2631-1-based estimate of horizontal vibration.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# 2 RELATED WORK

Lane-change prediction has evolved from Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based models capturing vehicle motion and traffic context [ 15 ] to dual-Transformer architectures combining intention and trajectory prediction [ 6 ] . More recently, an interactive dynamic Bayesian network integrated with a Transformer was proposed to model vehicle interactions and jointly predict intentions and trajectories [ 8 ] . Beyond prediction, planning based on Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) has been investigated for decision-making under uncertain vehicle intentions [ 9 ] . However, avoiding a collision does not necessarily ensure a comfortable driving response, particularly when comparing braking with lane changing. Previous research has investigated the influence of longitudinal and lateral acceleration and jerk on passenger discomfort [ 4 ] .
Complementing these measures, ISO 2631-1 provides a frequency-weighted vibration assessment framework [ 10 ] , also considered in simulation-based comfort evaluation [ 7 ] . Nevertheless, the safety and comfort trade-offs between anticipatory braking and lateral avoidance in response to predicted lane changes remain insufficiently explored. To address this gap, this study compares both prediction-based strategies with reactive driving in CARLA, evaluating collision outcomes, response timing, vehicle dynamics, and ISO-based ride comfort.

2026-10-23.title: PhysibleMDM: Enforcing Inference-Time Physical Feasibility Constraints on Motion Diffusion Models via Noise Optimization
2026-10-23.authors: Maximilian Stölzle , David Müller , Agon Serifi , Ruben Grandia , Espen Knoop , Moritz Bächer
2026-10-23.abstract:
Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) can generate diverse and visually appealing human motion; yet, the resulting trajectories frequently violate physical constraints, limiting their downstream use in simulation and control. We present PhysibleMDM , a framework that promotes physical feasibility of MDM output by optimizing at inference time the diffusion noise without retraining the generative model.
We introduce a set of surrogate feasibility constraints that can be evaluated without full trajectory simulation. These constraints combine kinematic checks (e.g., ground penetration, slip, and self-collision) with dynamic feasibility tests computed via an inverse-dynamics inner loop formulated as a cone program. We solve the resulting black-box noise optimization problem using the Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Sep-CMA-ES), thereby avoiding reliance on computationally expensive and discontinuous gradients. An autoregressive scheme then chains optimized segments to synthesize long motion sequences. Across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid, PhysibleMDM reduces mean ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and ground slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%, respectively, relative to unoptimized diffusion output. Across 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot, it achieves median reductions of 89.5% in per-sequence mean acceleration-reconstruction error and 79.5% in the mean inverse-dynamics residual.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Motion Diffusion Models ( Tevet et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Kim et al., 2023 ; Rempe et al., 2026 ) currently achieve state-of-the-art performance in synthesizing human-like motion for physics-based characters and robots. These generators are typically trained on large corpora of human motion capture data and can be conditioned on various signals, including text, style, goals, and semantic tasks ( Dabral et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024a ; Huang et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . The generated motion commonly serves as a reference for Reinforcement Learning-based trackers ( Peng et al., 2018 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Serifi et al., 2024b ; Liao et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2026 ) . Errors can arise at multiple stages of this pipeline. In particular, generated motions may exhibit physical artifacts that hinder their execution. Kinematic artifacts include joint-limit violations ( Lee et al., 2025 ) , self-collisions ( Khazoom et al., 2022 ) , ground penetration ( Yuan et al., 2023 ) , undesired ground slip ( Pan et al., 2025 ) , and foot placement in non-traversable regions ( Nguyen et al., 2016 ) . Dynamic artifacts include motions requiring joint torques beyond actuator limits ( Herzog et al., 2014 ) or contact forces outside friction cones ( Grandia et al., 2021 ) , as well as trajectories inconsistent with the dynamics of unactuated coordinates, such as the floating base of a legged robot ( Herzog et al., 2014 ; Grizzle et al., 2014 ) . These artifacts degrade downstream tracking performance ( Araújo et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , as infeasible reference motions cannot be reliably tracked.

Several methods mitigate these artifacts before or during training , for example, by learning from motions tracked in physics simulation ( Wu et al., 2025 ; Watanabe et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) , or fine-tuning the generator with physics-informed objectives ( Serifi et al., 2024a ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) .
While effective in practice, these approaches can be resource-intensive, particularly when generative models and tracking policies are retrained across refinement iterations, and they do not inherently guarantee that all samples from the final diffusion model satisfy the desired physical constraints.

Inference-time optimization incorporates explicit objectives and constraints during generation without retraining the diffusion model. Common approaches steer intermediate denoising states through gradient guidance ( Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021 ; Karunratanakul et al., 2023 ) or projection onto feasible sets ( Yuan et al., 2023 ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Watanabe et al., 2026 ) . Noise optimization offers an alternative in which objectives and constraints are evaluated on fully denoised motions ( Karunratanakul et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) . Gradient-based noise optimization requires costly backpropagation through both the diffusion sampler and the physical-feasibility evaluation. Contact-rich motion further introduces non-smooth objectives and constraints for which gradients may be poorly informative ( Antonova et al., 2023 ; Paulus et al., 2026 ) . Sampling-based optimization has shown promise for optimal control of contact-rich legged locomotion ( Xue et al., 2025 ; Alvarez-Padilla et al., 2025 ; Schramm et al., 2026 ) . Recent work also applies sampling-based optimization to diffusion noise for image generation and protein design ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Tan et al., 2026 ) , but does not address the kinematic and dynamic feasibility requirements of robotic motion. Efficient gradient-free optimization of initial and posterior diffusion noise for these requirements, while retaining characteristic motion style, remains unexplored.

To address this gap, we propose PhysibleMDM, a gradient-free method that jointly optimizes initial and posterior diffusion noise at inference time. Parallel forward passes through the frozen model generate a population of motions for evaluating task objectives, kinematic constraints, and constrained inverse-dynamics residuals. These evaluations guide Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy ( Ros and Hansen, 2008 ) , whose diagonal covariance supports high-dimensional search, in iteratively refining the noise population. Noise standardization regularizes noise toward its training-time statistics to help limit deviations from the learned motion distribution. An autoregressive scheme chains optimized segments into long motion sequences.

In summary, the contributions of this paper are:

A physical-feasibility formulation for Motion Diffusion Models that combines kinematic constraints with constrained inverse-dynamics residuals, enabling inference-time refinement without a tracking controller or full trajectory simulation.

A scalable sampling-based method for high-dimensional noise optimization in Motion Diffusion Models (realized via Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy), evaluating non-smooth objectives and constraints on fully denoised motions without costly gradient computation.

A diffusion-noise optimization strategy, applicable to any pretrained MDM without architecture-specific changes, that combines joint initial and posterior noise optimization with noise standardization, balancing optimization flexibility against deviations from the model’s learned distribution and supporting motion-style retention in Motion Diffusion Models.

# 2 Related Work

Guidance and projection steer diffusion sampling by modifying intermediate denoising states or their clean-sample estimates ( Karunratanakul et al., 2023 ; Christopher et al., 2024 ; Bodmer et al., 2026 ) . Noise optimization instead evaluates objectives on fully denoised samples and adjusts the stochastic inputs, using gradients ( Karunratanakul et al., 2024 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ) or sampling-based updates ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Tan et al., 2026 ) . The latter support non-differentiable objectives without backpropagating through the denoising process. Relative to these sampling-based methods, our approach jointly optimizes initial latent and posterior noise with Sep-CMA-ES, whose diagonal covariance yields linear internal time and memory scaling with the number of noise variables ( Ros and Hansen, 2008 ) , making it suitable for this high-dimensional search.

Existing methods incorporate physics at different stages of motion generation. Before training, motion data can be refined through kinematic-constraint-aware retargeting ( Yang et al., 2026 ) or collected through simulated tracking, with the latter sometimes repeated as the generator and tracker improve over successive training rounds ( Watanabe et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . Physical objectives can also guide learning directly through dynamics-consistency losses ( Serifi et al., 2024a ; Xing et al., 2026 ) or preference-based post-training ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Other approaches introduce physics during generation: PhysDiff projects intermediate denoising states through simulated execution ( Yuan et al., 2023 ) , while CLoSD alternates motion planning and execution ( Tevet et al., 2025 ) . Alongside this choice of when to incorporate physics, methods differ in what they predict. Whereas most motion diffusion models generate kinematic state trajectories, joint state–action models also generate controls, learning both from trajectories collected with tracking controllers ( Huang et al., 2025 ; Wu et al., 2025 ) . However, incorporating physics before or during training does not ensure feasibility of individual generated samples, particularly under distribution shift. Predicting controls alongside states does not remove this limitation, since the predicted states may differ from the motion produced by executing those controls. Furthermore, approaches that use simulated tracking depend on a trained tracking controller. To address these limitations, our method evaluates kinematic constraints and constrained inverse-dynamics residuals on each fully generated motion and optimizes diffusion noise at inference time, requiring neither generator retraining nor tracking-controller rollouts.

Further related work appears in Appendix A .

protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher’s frozen

2026-10-23.title: Integrated Respiratory Sensing and Gated Control for Autonomous Needle Insertion Via CT Bore Robotic Arm
2026-10-23.authors: Emma Huang , Moira Bohley , Krishna Jamakhandi , Rebecca Fellbaum , Sophia Tang , Sean Tutton , Albert Hsiao , Alexander Norbash , Changwei Chen , Derek Chen , Ananya Rao , Lizzie Peiros , Michael C. Yip
2026-10-23.abstract: Currently, CT-guided lung biopsy is a highly manual procedure requiring patient breath-holding, iterative manual needle insertions, and repeated CT confirmation scans to accurately target a tumor. Automating this process within the CT bore—without relying on manual needle placement or patient breath-holding—has the potential to reduce procedure time, patient discomfort, and radiation exposure. In this work, we present an integrated sensing and control system capable of performing a gated needle insertion within the CT bore. The experiments demonstrate the system’s ability to track and predict patient breath cycles, perform autonomous respiratory-gated needle insertion, and detect breath cycle anomalies.

The sensing system design depends on the timing, amplitude, and direction of chest motion during breathing.
Table I summarizes reference measurements from healthy individuals [ 16 , 17 , 18 ] .
Normal breathing follows an approximately periodic but asymmetric pattern, with expiration generally lasting longer than inspiration [ 18 ] .
The chest moves in three dimensions during breathing, primarily along the dorsoventral direction, and the displacement varies across anatomical locations [ 19 ] .

Nine OptiTrack markers were placed in a 3 × 3 3\times 3 grid on each volunteer’s chest, with the upper row just below the collarbones and the lower row just above the lower edge of the ribcage.
Each volunteer breathed naturally during a 10-minute recording, and the dorsoventral component of the recorded chest motion was extracted.
Fig. 2 shows approximately periodic chest motion during normal breathing, abrupt changes during coughing and hiccups, and smaller, irregular fluctuations during talking.

The measured mean amplitude of 4.98 mm is comparable in magnitude to the reference sternum displacement of 4.33 mm.

This system must sense and react to typical and abnormal breath cycles.

The measured breathing amplitude has a mean of 4.98 mm and a standard deviation of 0.62 mm.
A lower reference amplitude is defined as the mean minus two standard

As a design criterion, the sensor should distinguish approximately 10 spatial increments across this reference displacement, giving a target spatial resolution of 0.37 mm.
For safety, signals outside the distribution must be detected quickly to prevent unintentional insertion. Examples include hiccups and sneezes, which, while rare, could occur during operation.
These events are signified by rapid thoracic motion within 35 ms and 20 ms, respectively.
The desired reaction time for these types of events would be 5 ms.

## II-B Mechanical Design

In order to accurately render the breathing profile displacement, a bench-top breathing mechanism was created as a simplified torso skin phantom which provides a platform to run breathing profiles both synthetic and real. A version of the needle driver platform from a CT-guided needle biopsy robot [ 14 ] , which will be referred to as the CT bore robot, was created and featured the sensing and actuation to isolate the functional components being designed and assess their capabilities. Finally, a separate CT-compatible version was also created to integrate with the CT bore robot.

The testbed takes in a motion profile and outputs a single-degree-of-freedom translational output to mimic the motion of the outer layer of skin around the chest.

The Breathing Mechanism is a skin phantom holder on a capstan drive which simulates the motion of breathing, shown in Fig. 3 (a). Each skin phantom is made with 00-20 silicone and secured over a 0.625” 60A durometer silicone rubber layer to replicate the compliance of the epidermis and dermis respectively with a 5 by 15 mm rectangular cube secured behind to model the stiffness the rib cage provides beneath the skin [ 20 ] . The phantom is mounted to a carriage on a linear rail which is driven with a CubeMars AK60-V3 motor using a capstan drive mechanism. The capstan drive can reproduce the 95th percentile breathing displacement (6.22 mm) and meet the velocity requirements for travel within the average breath duration (4.335s) seen in Table I .

The Needle Mechanism simulates the similar mechanism on the CT bore robot and the one degree of freedom (DOF) of the wristed end. This is shown in Fig. 3 (a). The carriage driver (1 DOF wrist) uses a capstan drive mechanism powered by a CubeMars GL60II Gimbal Motor, while the needle insertion mechanism powered by a CubeMars GL40II Gimbal Motor, providing a representation of the clutch-unclutch needle insertion mechanism on the CT bore robot.

The carriage carries two sensing systems: a VL53L4CD ToF (Time of Flight) sensor and an AS5048B Hall effect sensor detailed in Fig. 3 (a,b). The ToF sensor is used to detect distance while approaching to make initial contact with the phantom. It is placed on the front of the carriage with the sensor focal point angled to match with the needle tip and contact sensor. Once in contact with the surface the contact sensor is designed to measure real-time chest displacement. The contact sensor drives a spring-tensioned capstan drive to convert linear displacement to rotation, which is read by rotating a magnet in front of the hall effect sensor shown in green in Fig. 3 (b).

The CT-integrated needle sensing system is a compact and optimized version of the bench-top needle mechanism. The CT-integrated contact sensor mechanism, shown in Fig. 3 (c), is similarly compacted for CT-integration and designed to minimize metal components for compatibility with a CT scanner. Similarly, the ToF sensor is mounted in the front and angled to measure near the needle tip and the edge of the contact sensor.

Rather than a capstan drive, the needle driver on the CT uses a “clutch-unclutch” mechanism shown in Fig. 3 (d). This action is achieved using a Dyneema string within a Bowden cable, which, when tensioned, tightens a collar around the needle. It can be activated when desired and left inactive when the needle needs to move freely, depending on the stage of the breathing cycle. While a direct-drive motor could presumably provide cleaner dynamics and direct motion measurements, CT imaging is negatively impacted by dense metals, which can introduce artifacts and distort the scans.

The biopsy procedure proceeds through four sequential steps following the position of the robot in the CT bore [ 22 ] : (1) torso approach and contact, (2) breathing cycle sensing, (3) initial drive and dermal puncture, and (4) gated needle drive to the target depth.
