2026-10-23.title: Tactile-Based Robotic Manipulation: From Mechanics-Driven to Data-Driven Perspectives
2026-10-23.authors: Jingyi Xiang , Yixuan Wang , Wenzhen Yuan
2026-10-23.comment: . Author accepted manuscript. Posted with permission from the Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems, Volume 10; copyright 2027 the author(s), this https URL . Published version: this https URL
2026-10-23.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct access to physical interactions at the contact interface, making it a critical modality for robust and dexterous manipulation. Over the past several decades, tactile-based manipulation research has evolved from mechanics-driven approaches, which explicitly interpret tactile signals through contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning, to data-driven approaches that learn tactile representations and manipulation policies directly from data. This paper reviews the development of tactile-based manipulation from these two complementary perspectives. We first introduce the fundamentals of tactile sensing, and then review, from a mechanics-driven perspective, how those signals form manipulation-relevant state representations and subsequently influence the robot action. We then examine the recent advances in data-driven tactile manipulation, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future opportunities toward scalable, generalizable, and robust tactile-enabled robotic systems.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Manipulation is the process by which a robot physically interacts with and changes the state of objects in its environment. Because these interactions occur through contact, many manipulation-relevant quantities—including contact state, force distribution, slip, and local object geometry—can only be observed at the contact interface. Tactile sensing provides direct measurements of these interactions and therefore plays a critical role in enabling robust and dexterous manipulation.

Research on robotic tactile sensing and manipulation has existed for decades. A central question throughout this history has been how tactile signals can be transformed into actionable information for robot control. Early research largely approached this problem from a mechanics-driven perspective, seeking explicit connections between tactile measurements, description of physical interactions, and manipulation actions. For example, tactile feedback can be used to detect slip so as to secure grasp, guide insertion and assembly based on force feedback, or measure local geometry for contact alignment. Although different approaches have been proposed—including analytical models, handcrafted feature extraction, and supervised learning techniques—the common principle is the use of explicit knowledge about contact mechanics and task structure to interpret tactile signals and guide robot behavior. In this review, we collectively refer to these approaches as mechanics-driven tactile-based manipulation .

In recent years, the rapid progress of data-driven robot learning has profoundly reshaped tactile-based manipulation research. In contrast to mechanics-driven approaches, these methods typically do not require explicit modeling of intermediate physical quantities. Instead, they learn task-relevant implicit representations and action policies directly from data, often through imitation learning, reinforcement learning, or large-scale multimodal pretraining. This trend emerged alongside the remarkable success of vision-based robot learning, where end-to-end learning frameworks have demonstrated impressive performance across a wide range of manipulation tasks. Consequently, a major research direction in tactile-based manipulation has become the integration of tactile observations into learning architectures originally developed for vision. This direction is particularly promising because vision and touch provide highly complementary information: vision captures global scene context and long-range spatial relationships, while tactile sensing provides precise local measurements of contact and physical interaction. Recent advances in sensor development, scalable robot learning, and multimodal foundation models have further accelerated this trend, creating new opportunities for tactile-enabled manipulation while also introducing new challenges.

In this review, we examine tactile-based manipulation from both mechanics-driven and data-driven perspectives. We first discuss how tactile sensing captures the physics of contact and how tactile signals can be transformed into manipulation-relevant information through explicit reasoning. We then review recent advances in learning-based manipulation, including imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models that leverage tactile observations as part of large-scale multimodal learning frameworks. By bringing together these two perspectives, we aim to provide a unified understanding of how tactile information contributes to robotic manipulation, identify the connections between classical and modern approaches, and highlight the key challenges and opportunities that will shape the future of tactile-enabled robotics. Owing to the breadth of the field, we emphasize representative works that illustrate major ideas and trends rather than providing an exhaustive catalog of existing research.

# 2 TACTILE SENSING FUNDAMENTALS

## 2.1 Tactile Sensors and Signals

The first step towards tactile-based manipulation is the tactile sensors. Tactile sensors measure touch, either in the form of a single point force/torque (F/T) sensing or the distributed information over the fingertip or an area of skin. Commonly seen output signals from tactile sensors include:

Normal Force , the component of contact force perpendicular to the sensor surface. It is the most commonly measured tactile quantity.

Normal Force , the component of contact force perpendicular to the sensor surface. It is the most commonly measured tactile quantity.

Shear Force corresponds to tangential loads at the contact interface and plays a critical role in grasping and in-hand manipulation. The capability to measure shear force is much less common, but some modern tactile sensors, including magnetic [ 124 , 143 ] and vision-based designs [ 132 , 153 ] , can estimate local shear distributions.

Torque is available for F/T sensors. For distributed tactile sensors, torque can be inferred from the spatial distribution of forces.

Contact Geometry is typically achieved from the spatial distribution of the deformation or measured normal force across the sensing surface.

Vibration in tactile signals contains important information about contact dynamics and is typically generated during sliding motion. In addition to extracting temporal features of tactile signals, some tactile systems explicitly incorporate accelerometers or vibration sensors to capture high-frequency signals.

Auxiliary Modalities such as temperature and proximity. They are less commonly used in robotic manipulation and are therefore outside the scope of this review.

Over the past decades, a large number of tactile sensors have been developed [ 24 ] . They vary in characteristics such as sensitivity, spatial resolution, force range, bandwidth, robustness, and manufacturing complexity. One rough way to categorize the sensors is based on the number of their measurement units. So, there are:

F/T sensors: only one measuring unit, but can typically measure 6-axis or 3-axis forces and torque. Installed at the wrist or fingertip
. The force measurement is usually much more precise.

F/T sensors: only one measuring unit, but can typically measure 6-axis or 3-axis forces and torque. Installed at the wrist or fingertip
. The force measurement is usually much more precise.

Array-based tactile sensors: typically contain 4-100 sensing units to measure normal force with a spatial resolution of several millimeters. So a rough shape estimation is available but not precise shapes or textures.

Vision based tactile sensors: using an embedded camera to capture raw images, so the spatial resolution can be very high. The downside is the bulkiness in size. Some sensors in this category are designed to measure the surface geometry of every image pixel [ 153 , 79 ] , while others track the motion of the printed markers [ 108 , 132 ] , so their spatial resolution depends on the number of markers.

One major challenge in tactile manipulation is the strong dependency on sensor hardware. The quality and availability of tactile signals vary substantially across sensors, often requiring sensor-specific denoising and preprocessing methods, and training data when using machine learning methods. As a result, algorithms and learning models developed for one sensor frequently transfer poorly to another, and the performance of one manipulation system highly depends on the choice of sensors. We will further discuss this issue in Section 5.1 . Throughout this review, we therefore focus on reviewing manipulation methodologies based on how they are built on tactile signals rather than individual sensors.

To abstract out the implementation differences, it is useful to adopt a unified physical view of tactile sensing. Tactile sensors consist of two components: a deformable contact medium, typically made of compliant materials such as elastomers or structures filled with air or liquid, and a transducer that converts the deformation of the medium into measurable electrical signals. Transduction mechanisms may be resistive, capacitive, magnetic, piezoelectric, or optical. Based on this description, tactile sensing is fundamentally indirect: rather than measuring contact itself, sensors measure contact-induced deformation so as to infer information about the interaction. Consequently, the differences among tactile sensors can be featured by the design of the contact medium and the choice of transduction mechanism.

## 2.2 Tactile Simulation and Closing Sim-to-Real Gaps

The growing adoption of data-driven manipulation methods has created a strong demand for tactile sensor simulation. Modern learning-based approaches often require large amounts of training data, while collecting tactile data using physical robots is costly and difficult to scale. Simulation, therefore, provides an attractive alternative for generating large datasets and training manipulation models in a safe and highly parallelized manner. It also provides a good platform for quickly evaluating the design of robotic systems at low cost.

Accurately reproducing tactile sensor outputs while maintaining high simulation speed remains a long-standing challenge.
While existing technologies cannot perfectly reproduce real sensor responses, improving simulation fidelity also comes at the cost of computational complexity. Since simulation efficiency is also critical for large-scale data generation, practical tactile simulators must balance accuracy and speed. Accordingly, current efforts in tactile simulation generally follow two complementary directions: developing more accurate and efficient sensor models, and designing algorithms to mitigate the sim-to-real gap.

Unlike conventional robot simulation, tactile simulation must model both the contact mechanics between objects and the sensor, as well as the sensor transduction process that converts deformation into measurable signals. Most robotic simulators employ simplified contact models that cannot fully capture the fine-grained contact phenomena required for tactile sensing, while sensor noise, calibration errors, and manufacturing variations further complicate accurate simulation.
Existing tactile simulators roughly range from physics-based methods [ 92 , 1 , 4 , 25 ] to data-driven [ 107 , 110 , 27 ] and hybrid approaches [ 99 , 113 ] , each offering different trade-offs between fidelity, computational cost, and adaptability to individual sensors.
In some applications, particularly those that rely primarily on geometric information, the sim-to-real gap can be sufficiently small to permit zero-shot transfer or transfer with only minor calibration [ 120 , 114 ] . However, tasks involving force estimation, frictional interactions, slip detection, or dynamic contact typically require substantially more accurate modeling.

To mitigate the sim-to-real gap, one common strategy is to reduce the dimensionality of the tactile representation. Rather than relying on high-resolution raw signals, many manipulation models take input of lower-dimensional contact features such as binary contact states, contact locations, estimated contact geometry, or other task-specific abstractions [ 101 , 147 , 156 , 144 , 146 ] . These representations are often easier to simulate consistently and therefore transfer more reliably to real systems. However, this simplification may discard fine-grained tactile information that could otherwise improve manipulation performance.

When higher-fidelity tactile representations are required, researchers have explored techniques to explicitly bridge the domain gap. One approach is domain randomization, where sensor parameters, contact properties, and measurement noise are randomized during training to improve robustness to simulation errors [ 33 , 18 , 95 ] . Another approach is domain adaptation, which employs transfer learning techniques or generative models to align simulated and real tactile observations [ 23 , 131 , 59 , 80 , 165 ] . Despite these advances, reliable sim-to-real transfer remains an open challenge for tactile-based manipulation.

2026-10-23.abstract: This paper presents an integrated control framework for high-speed platooning of articulated vehicles, combining advanced longitudinal and lateral control strategies to address the challenges of safe and efficient autonomous driving. 2026-10-23.title: MPBRS: Multi-Potential-Based Reward Shaping for Unified Reward Configuration in Humanoid Locomotion
2026-10-23.authors: Van Chung Nguyen , Hung Manh La
2026-10-23.abstract: Designing and tuning reward functions remains one of the main challenges in building effective reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for humanoid locomotion. While shaping rewards can accelerate learning, naively formulated terms often conflict with the desired behavior, overfit to a specific robot, or become unstable under small weight changes. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) offers an alternative solution: shaping the reward via differences of a potential function to guide exploration without changing the optimal policy. In this paper, we study Multi-PBRS for humanoid locomotion and propose a unified reward configuration. We then evaluate the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots, requiring only robot-specific metadata (joint/link mappings and default poses) rather than per-robot reward redesign. Our experiments show that, compared to standard shaping, MPBRS provides more consistent scaling behavior and reduced tuning sensitivity across robots, making it easier to tune without altering the optimal policy.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Recently, reinforcement learning (RL) has become one of the most widely used approaches for humanoid locomotion. The use of RL for humanoid locomotion is due to its ability to learn coordinated, whole-body behaviors that are difficult to design by hand [ 1 , 2 ] . However, despite the success of RL in humanoid locomotion, its application depends heavily on the reward function design [ 1 , 2 ] . The design of the reward function greatly affects the behavior of the humanoid robot. For example, when the reward is specified in a naive way-such as a quadratic tracking error or a sparse task-success signal-the agent may learn strategies that maximize the reward while producing unintended behaviors that do not match the designer’s intent [ 3 , 4 ] . Conversely, well-shaped rewards can substantially speed up learning, whereas poorly scaled or conflicting terms can cause brittle behaviors, reward hacking, unstable training, or policies that only work for a single morphology and fail under small changes in dynamics or sensing. As a result, developers often spend significant time tuning reward terms and weights to reach an acceptable balance between training stability and behavioral quality. This tuning process is further complicated by the sensitivity of humanoid RL to hyperparameters and reward scaling, which makes it difficult to isolate the effect of individual reward terms and tune them systematically. Furthermore, the design of the reward function is severe for humanoid locomotion since it involves high-dimensional control and contact-rich dynamics with foot-ground interactions, and morphology-dependent constraints. Consequently, many locomotion pipelines rely on extensive reward design and per-robot tuning: weights are repeatedly adjusted until training stabilizes and the resulting gait appears plausible. Unfortunately, this workflow is time-consuming, hard to reproduce, and often does not transfer even between similar humanoids. A reward that works well on one robot may require significant modification on another due to differences in morphology, actuation, or physical design.

In [ 1 ] , Ng, Harada, and Russell proposed a class of shaping rewards defined by differences of a potential function that is policy-invariant in discounted MDPs. This method has appeared in many researchers because it can provide richer learning signals while leaving the baseline task objective unchanged, effectively separating task specification from convergence acceleration.

Later, several follow-up works [ 5 , 6 , 7 ] examined PBRS in RL and concluded that it leads to faster learning. However, this evidence is largely drawn from grid-worlds or other low-dimensional domains. Meanwhile, high-performing RL results in robotics-especially for legged locomotion-still depend on straightforward, manually tuned shaping rewards that provide no policy-invariance guarantees [ 8 ] .

In this paper, we examine deep RL locomotion in 3D under a unified reward design and test how multi-PBRS compares to standard shaping when deployed unchanged on nine humanoid robots. Rather than delivering large improvements in convergence rate, MPBRS primarily improves training stability and portability, showing lower sensitivity to weight selection and reward magnitude. This reduces tuning overhead and supports more consistent reuse across diverse humanoid designs.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Chapter II covers the literature review, outlining the related work and providing an overview of the method. Chapter III presents the methodology of the potential-based reward shaping used in this paper. Chapter IV provides a system overview, including the case study of nine humanoid robots and the experimental setup used in this paper. Chapter V presents the results of the method. Finally, Chapter VI concludes the paper.

# II LITERATURE REVIEW

## II-A Reward shaping for locomotion

Recently, high-performing RL locomotion systems often rely on direct reward shaping (DRS). The DRS is a dense terms that encode task-relevant objectives such as velocity tracking, uprightness, base-height regulation, and regularization penalties on energy or action changes [ 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . The DRS is attractive because they are simple to compute and do not require external demonstrations, but their effectiveness depends strongly on careful scaling and balancing of terms. In humanoid locomotion, small changes in reward weights can produce different behaviors, ranging from overly conservative gaits to unstable oscillations. The small changes in reward weight can lead to solutions that exploit a proxy objective rather than the intended task [ 13 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] .

A second common approach is imitation learning, which provides dense rewards by tracking reference signals . Imitation learning strongly encourages the robot to replicate the desired behavior. In physics-based character control, imitation and reference tracking have been particularly successful for producing coordinated whole-body motion and locomotion skills [ 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] . In robotics-oriented biped learning, iterative design pipelines often incorporate structured objectives and reference-like heuristics (e.g., posture targets, height/orientation regulation, cadence-related signals) and emphasize that reward shaping and tuning are major determinants of training stability and final gait quality [ 21 , 22 ] . While imitation learning can substantially accelerate learning, it introduces an additional design burden: the choice of reference quantities and their weights can bias solutions toward reproducing the reference rather than solving the underlying task, and these choices frequently do not transfer cleanly across morphologies [ 23 , 24 , 25 ] . This lack of portability motivates shaping methods that provide dense guidance while reducing sensitivity to hand-tuned scaling.

## II-B Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS)

Ng, Harada, and Russell [ 1 ] proposed potential-based reward shaping (PBRS), showing that shaping rewards constructed in this way preserve the set of optimal policies in discounted MDPs. This property has appealed to many researchers, as it suggests a principled separation between (i) a base reward that expresses the task objective and (ii) an auxiliary shaping signal that improves the robot’s behaviour without altering an optimal solution. Wiewiora [ 5 ] further showed that PBRS is closely related to Q Q -value initialization, providing intuition for why PBRS can speed up early learning: an informative potential effectively redistributes long-horizon value into denser step-wise feedback. Subsequent work has explored PBRS in broader settings (e.g., episodic tasks and learned or dynamic potentials) and generally reports faster convergence in low-dimensional environments such as gridworlds or classic control [ 26 , 27 ] .

For humanoid locomotion, however, the primary practical benefit of PBRS appears to differ from the common expectation of large convergence gains. Jeon et al. [ 4 ] benchmark PBRS-style shaping in humanoid locomotion and find that improvements in convergence speed can be modest, while PBRS terms are notably more robust to reward scaling than typical direct shaping. This motivates treating PBRS not only as a tool for faster learning, but as a mechanism for reducing tuning sensitivity and improving reward portability. Building on this perspective, our work evaluates a single unified multi-PBRS reward configuration reused across nine humanoid robots, with the goal of measuring how MPBRS affects robustness to scaling and the degree of per-robot reward retuning required.

2026-10-23.abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models.
A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation.
This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations.
In this paper, we introduce F uture RE presentation learning via self- D istillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step.
Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets.
We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better.
Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.
2026-10-23.introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs; Pai et al. 2025 ; Liang et al. 2025 ; Kim et al. 2026b ; Ye et al. 2026 ) have recently emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies. Built on pre-trained video diffusion models (VDMs; Wan et al. 2025 ; Ali et al. 2025 ), WAMs have shown strong generalization to unseen tasks ( Ye et al., 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) , adaptation to new robot embodiments ( Ye et al., 2026 ) , and skill transfer from human videos to robots ( Dyna Robotics, 2026 ) . Their core idea is to leverage the rich spatiotemporal priors learned from large-scale in-the-wild video datasets ( Chen et al., 2024 ; Nan et al., 2024 ) by training a model to jointly predict future frames and corresponding actions. This allows the strong generalization capabilities of pre-trained video models to extend from future video prediction to robot control.

Recent works have shown that WAMs can achieve competitive performance with a separate action decoder that generates actions conditioned on intermediate hidden states of the VDM ( Ma et al., 2026 ; Dyna Robotics, 2026 ; Qiu et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . These hidden states are obtained from a single forward pass with Gaussian noise ϵ ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝐈 ) \bm{\epsilon}\sim{\mathcal{N}}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I}) as input.
This design substantially reduces inference latency by avoiding iterative denoising with large VDM backbones, making WAMs more practical for robot control. However, because the action decoder directly leverages these hidden states, policy performance depends on how well they capture future robot-object dynamics.

In this paper, we aim to improve the control performance of the recent line of WAMs that use a single VDM forward pass for action generation.
We start by performing an analysis of how well the VDM hidden states learn meaningful information to generate actions during WAM training.
We first find that VDM hidden states generated from noise already capture information about future robot motion. Specifically, a lightweight probe trained on frozen hidden states can predict future motion primitives, with classification accuracy increasing throughout WAM training (see Figure 1(a) ).
Moreover, these hidden states become increasingly similar to those extracted from ground-truth future observations at the same VDM layer (see Figure 1(b) ).
These findings suggest that the VDM progressively learns to generate future video representations from noise.
However, a clear gap in future-motion probing accuracy remains relative to representations extracted from clean future observations, suggesting that generating sufficiently informative future representations from noise remains challenging.

Inspired by this, we propose F uture RE presentation learning via self- D istillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework for training WAMs to improve the future representations obtained from a single video denoising step for action generation; see the overview in Figure 2 .
We train the VDM through self-distillation to align representations generated from noise with those extracted from ground-truth future observations, encouraging the model to capture richer future information for predicting actions.
Specifically, FRED uses a momentum teacher, implemented as an Exponential-Moving-Average (EMA) copy of the online VDM, to extract the target representations from noisy future observations at the same intermediate layer used for action conditioning.
We further condition the VDM on a short history of observations, providing temporal context that helps the intermediate hidden states better represent future robot motion.
As a result, FRED reduces the future-motion probing performance gap to representations extracted from clean future observations and further improves structural similarity to them (see Figure 1 ). Notably, this closer alignment with representations of future observations translates into better robot control performance (see Figure 4(c) ).

To validate the generality and effectiveness of FRED, we conduct extensive experiments in diverse real-world robotic manipulation scenarios.
We first evaluate FRED on zero-shot environment generalization using a varied set of real-world manipulation tasks, including long-horizon manipulation, out-of-domain tasks, and object grounding.
Our results show that FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs in these settings, improving long-horizon performance from 61.7% to 81.7% and out-of-domain task success from 10.4% to 52.1% at the 14B scale.
We further evaluate FRED on human-to-robot skill transfer by co-training the video model on human videos without action labels, including tasks absent from robot training data.
We show that FRED significantly outperforms competing WAMs, improving task success from 19.4% to 50.0%, while achieving 97.2% instruction-following performance.
These results highlight that FRED improves future representation quality and achieves strong robot control in both zero-shot generalization and human-to-robot transfer.

We summarize the main contributions of this paper below:

We interpret the VDM in WAMs as a future representation generator that produces intermediate hidden states containing predictive information about future robot motion in a single forward pass.

We present FRED, a framework that improves future video representations generated from noise for action prediction through self-distillation using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets, and short-history conditioning for richer temporal context.

We show that FRED consistently outperforms baseline WAMs across diverse real-world manipulation settings: zero-shot environment generalization and human-to-robot skill transfer.

1. We interpret the VDM in WAMs as a future representation generator that produces intermediate hidden states containing predictive information about future robot motion in a single forward pass.

2. We present FRED, a framework that improves future video representations generated from noise for action prediction through self-distillation using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets, and short-history conditioning for richer temporal context.

3. We show that FRED consistently outperforms baseline WAMs across diverse real-world manipulation settings: zero-shot environment generalization and human-to-robot skill transfer.
2026-10-23.related_work:
# 2 Related Work

World Action Models. Prior work studies robot control via World Action Models (WAMs), which build on pre-trained video diffusion models (VDMs) and jointly model future observations and actions using robot data, allowing spatiotemporal priors from large-scale video to guide action generation ( Shen et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026a ; Kim et al., 2026b ; Ye et al., 2026 ) . These models generate plausible future visual states to support action prediction, but iterative denoising with large video backbones incurs substantial computational cost at inference time. Recent WAMs address this bottleneck by decoupling video and action generation and reducing video denoising to a single step. Within this shared design, some works predict actions without explicitly generating future videos at inference by masking access to future video features ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) or directly decoding actions from video-backbone states ( Li et al., 2026b ) .
In contrast, another line of work conditions action prediction on future video representations obtained from noise in a single video denoising step ( Pai et al., 2025 ; Ma et al., 2026 ; Qiu et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) .
Our work follows the latter design and focuses on how to train WAMs to generate more informative future representations for action generation.

Diffusion Models and Representation Learning. Prior works have shown that diffusion denoisers learn discriminative representations useful for visual recognition ( Xiang et al., 2023 ; Yang & Wang, 2023 ; Li et al., 2023 ) . More recent work improves these representations during generative training, where REPA ( Yu et al., 2025 ) aligns noisy diffusion features with clean image
representations from a pre-trained visual encoder, while SRA ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) uses lower-noise representations from the diffusion model itself as targets.
This direction has been extended to VDMs through alignment with pre-trained video representations ( Zhang et al., 2026 ; Lee et al., 2025 ; Bhowmik et al., 2026 ) , while Self-Flow ( Chefer et al., 2026 ) incorporates self-supervised representation learning directly into flow matching without an external encoder.
Our work studies representation learning in WAMs, where intermediate video representations from a single denoising step directly condition action generation. AGRA ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) adapts representation alignment to this setting by aligning these representations with features from a frozen visual encoder.
FRED instead uses representations extracted from observed future frames as distillation targets for representations generated from noise.
This improves the future video representation used by the action decoder without aligning the intermediate video features to a fixed external representation.

2026-10-23.title: TerraTransfer++: Demonstration-Free End-to-End Planner
2026-10-23.authors: Zikang Xiong , Weixin Li , Zhouchonghao Wu , Akshay Rangesh , Saarth Bonde , Grantland Hall , Chen Tang , Yihan Hu , Wei Zhan
2026-10-23.subjects: Robotics (cs.RO) ; Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
2026-10-23.abstract:
End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments.
Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail;
closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone.
Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward.
Our approach exploits this asymmetry by decoupling learning to drive and learning to plan from learning to see .
We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action Kullback-Leibler divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss.
Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on.
From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.4 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard , above every published method including DriveZero-Scale ( 57.1 57.1 ), and 95.5 95.5 PDMS on navtest , without human demonstrations.
2026-10-23.introduction:
End-to-end autonomous driving maps raw sensor inputs ( e.g. , camera
images) directly to control commands. Deep learning and large-scale driving
data have made this approach widely adopted and continuously improved across
benchmarks ( Bojarski et al., 2016 ; Codevilla et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Chitta et al., 2023 ; Dauner et al., 2024a ; Zhou et al., 2024 ) .
However, this progress relies on expensive standard pipelines that follow
either of the two routes.

The open-loop strategy draws its behavioral supervision from fleet logs:
imitation copies logged human
driving ( Codevilla et al., 2019 ; Hu et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ; Chitta et al., 2023 ) , and open-loop reinforcement
learning (RL) optimizes against logged trajectories ( Karkus et al., 2025 ) .
These logs provide millions of multi-camera
hours ( Caesar et al., 2020 ; Sun et al., 2020 ; Caesar et al., 2021 ) , yet
safety-critical events (collisions, near-misses, recoveries, etc. ) remain
vanishingly rare in natural driving: at NHTSA crash rates, a collision
occurs only once every ∼ 16 {\sim}16 k driving hours ( National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 2025 ) , so
logging a single rare event can easily cost over $1M in fleet operation
alone ( Kelkar et al., 2025 ) . Each sub-route inherits this scarcity in its
own way: imitation can only copy the actions the recorded drivers took, and
open-loop RL never sees how other vehicles would have responded to the
alternative actions it explores. Broadening interaction coverage with human
data therefore demands ever more collection and curation.

The closed-loop framework instead trains inside a photorealistic,
sensor-rendering
simulator ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2022 ; Chitta et al., 2023 ; Karkus et al., 2025 ) ,
where the policy experiences the consequences of its own actions. This
interaction, however, costs rendering and a heavy vision-backbone forward pass
at every step. Co-training multiple interacting agents multiplies these
per-step costs, so most image-based closed-loop work instead trains the ego
policy against scripted or log-replayed traffic, and the behavior
distribution stays close to the logged or hand-designed
content ( Dosovitskiy et al., 2017 ; Chen et al., 2019 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ; Wu et al., 2022 ) .
These costs confine this route to fine-tuning a pretrained imitation policy,
as in Figure 1 , rather than pretraining driving competence
from scratch.

Recently, multi-agent self-play has risen as a promising alternative to offer
the missing interaction: one shared policy controls every agent, so each
policy improvement reshapes the traffic every other agent faces, and the
interactive behavior co-evolves with the policy. Vectorized simulation makes
this co-training highly efficient, executing millions of steps per second on
commodity hardware ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2026 ; Seong et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) .
Training requires only a basic definition of driving quality as per-step
rewards: goal reaching, collision avoidance, comfort, and simple rule
compliance. These rewards specify general driving objectives rather than
separate rules for corner cases. The resulting interactions naturally produce
the collisions, recoveries, yielding, negotiation, and overtaking that logged
traffic seldom contains, all without expert trajectories or
behavior-specific rewards.

Despite its promise, however, self-play does not yield deployable end-to-end
driving policies per se , as they observe vectorized scene state rather than
raw sensors. Deploying these policies would require a two-stage perception
stack that recovers their HD-map-style inputs from images. Such a stack
demands high-quality perception, is sensitive to perception noise, and forfeits
the co-optimization of a fully differentiable end-to-end model. As a result,
it has mostly remained confined to traffic simulation rather than an
end-to-end
solution ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ; Chang et al., 2026 ; Seong et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2026 ; Konstantinidis et al., 2026 ; Ahmadi et al., 2026 ) .

In this work, we unite the strengths of self-play and end-to-end driving in a
paradigm that learns driving policies without expert demonstrations. Self-play
learns driving competence without human demonstrations but consumes vector
state; end-to-end recipes consume raw sensors but depend on human
demonstrations, whose coverage of rare interactions is the very gap identified
above. We bridge this gap by decoupling learning to drive and learning to plan from learning to see , and we never use logged
demonstration trajectories as supervision. Figure 1 contrasts its three stages with the
conventional workflow.

In the first stage, we train a policy π θ \pi_{\theta} tabula rasa through multi-agent self-play in TerraZero ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , our
vectorized driving simulator, in the spirit of
GigaFlow ( Cusumano-Towner et al., 2025 ) . One parameter set controls every agent
in every scene. The policy learns from the long-tail distribution of its own
behavior and never imitates a human trajectory. The resulting policy is a
strong planner, scoring 94.19 94.19 on nuPlan val14 and 70.87 70.87 on the
interactive long-tail InterPlan suite, above every imitation-based planner we
are aware of, and 0.632 0.632 human-similarity on WOSAC 2023, on par with the
strongest learned sim agents.

In the second stage, the policy becomes the self-play teacher, and a
trajectory teacher learns to plan from its self-play rollouts. A closed-loop
policy emits one action per step, but planning interfaces and pseudo

2026-10-23.title: Alpha: Systematic Fault Injection and Robustness Evaluation for LLM-Driven Embodied Manipulation
2026-10-23.authors: Jona Joy
2026-10-23.comment: . Code and reproduction artifacts: this https URL
2026-10-23.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, combining natural-language goal decomposition with physical execution. However, standard evaluations typically focus on end-to-end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring where and why failures occur across the perception, planning, kinematic, and actuation stack. We present Alpha, a systematic fault-injection and robustness-evaluation framework for LLM-driven embodied manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across four operational boundaries: perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable inverse-kinematics targets), and planning (planner-output corruption), alongside concurrent fault conditions. To cleanly separate environmental and physical fault vulnerabilities from planner-pipeline sensitivities, we introduce a matched evaluation methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama-3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner under identical seeds, task geometries, physics parameters, and safety-monitoring criteria across a balanced 150-episode matrix (75 episodes per planner). Across the full matrix, the Scripted Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM planner achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p = 3.01 × 10 − 4 p=3.01\times 10^{-4} ). Crucially, when excluding planner-output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p = 1.00 p=1.00 ). This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently. The aggregate performance difference is driven entirely by planner-output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the serialization and schema-validation sensitivity of the prompt-to-JSON interface rather than an intrinsic cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts to establish complete discard-bias transparency. Key limitations include a single simulated tabletop pick-and-place task, evaluation on a single local open-weight model, and n = 5 n=5 sample sizes per intensity cell.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Embodied artificial intelligence systems increasingly combine probabilistic large language model (LLM) reasoning with physical robotic execution stacks [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . In such systems, high-level task planners translate natural-language objectives and perceptual scene descriptions into structured action plans (e.g., approach, grasp, transfer, and release). While recent benchmarks have demonstrated impressive nominal task-completion rates across multi-step household and industrial manipulation tasks [ 4 , 5 ] , these evaluations overwhelmingly measure aggregate end-to-end success in nominal, unperturbed environments.

Consequently, when an embodied agent fails, existing evaluation protocols rarely localize the failure to its causal origin: did the failure stem from noisy or delayed sensor observations, physical actuator slip, kinematically infeasible joint commands, syntax errors at the serialization boundary, or flawed semantic reasoning? In real-world deployments, autonomous robots routinely encounter hardware degraded states, communication latencies, grasp disturbances, and mechanical limits [ 10 , 11 ] . Understanding how embodied LLM architectures degrade under controlled, reproducible faults is essential before these agents can be safely deployed in safety-critical human environments.

Controlled fault injection provides a principled methodology for answering these questions. In distributed software engineering and cloud infrastructure, chaos engineering and active fault injection systematically subject running systems to synthetic faults to observe failure signatures and evaluate automated containment boundaries [ 16 , 17 ] . However, translating this methodology to embodied robotic agents introduces fundamental challenges: physical simulation dynamics, closed-loop contact mechanics, non-deterministic language generation, and complex API interfaces must all be monitored synchronously without confounding the agent’s internal control logic.

Furthermore, evaluating an LLM planner in isolation leaves open a critical counterfactual question: is a given failure caused by an intrinsic limitation of the language model, or is it an unavoidable physical consequence of the injected disturbance that would equally thwart any competent controller? Without a strictly matched baseline, environmental physics failures (such as a slippery block falling out of a gripper) are easily conflated with planner cognitive failures.

To address these challenges, this paper presents Alpha , a reproducible fault-injection and robustness-evaluation harness for LLM-driven embodied manipulation in simulation. Alpha couples a modular middleware fault wrapper ( ChaosRoboticsWrapper ) with a high-rate validated safety monitor, structured telemetry logging, and an explicit counterfactual evaluation protocol. Alpha injects calibrated faults at four distinct boundaries of a manipulation pipeline: (1) sensor lag at the perception layer, (2) grip slip at the actuation layer, (3) unreachable inverse kinematics (IK) at the kinematic execution layer, and (4) planner-output corruption at the planning/serialization layer, in addition to multi-fault concurrent conditions.

To decouple environmental dynamics from planner vulnerabilities, we introduce a matched LLM-vs-Scripted-Oracle methodology . Under this protocol, an LLM agent powered by Llama-3 [ 20 ] and a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner are evaluated across an identical balanced matrix of 150 episodes (75 per planner), sharing identical random seeds, scene spawn coordinates, physical parameters, fault formulas, and safety-incident thresholds.

The primary empirical finding of this paper is that across all physical, kinematic, and perceptual perturbations (F1, F2, F3, and Concurrent F1+F2), the LLM agent and the Scripted Oracle perform identically : both achieve exactly 55.0% task success across 60 seed-matched episodes with zero discordant pairs. Physical actuator slip degrades both agents with identical monotonic decay, perceptual lag is accommodated within the grasp tolerance, and kinematic offsets prevent goal placement for both controllers. The overall difference between the two systems (64.0% Oracle vs. 44.0% LLM across the full 150-episode matrix) is driven entirely by F4 planner-output corruption, where text serialization breaks Pydantic schema validation. We show that this divergence isolates the serialization and schema-validation sensitivity of the prompt-to-JSON execution pipeline , rather than an intrinsic defect in LLM spatial or physical reasoning.

Contributions. This paper makes the following contributions:

Decoupled Fault-Injection Architecture: We present ChaosRoboticsWrapper , a modular middleware framework that injects calibrated perception, actuation, kinematic, and serialization faults into a simulated robotic manipulation pipeline without modifying the robot controller or prompt templates.

Synchronous Telemetry and Formal Safety Monitoring: We develop a 240 Hz safety-monitoring engine that enforces formal force thresholds, workspace spatial bounds, and a validated temporal deduplication window (15 simulation steps), distinguishing raw repeated contact scans from unique continuous safety incidents.

Matched Counterfactual Evaluation Methodology: We formulate a seed-matched comparative protocol pairing an open-weight LLM agent against a deterministic Scripted Oracle across 150 controlled episodes, isolating physical environmental limits from planner-specific interface sensitivities.

Empirical Robustness Characterization: We provide an empirical characterization of manipulation degradation under sensor staleness, grip constraint weakening, unreachable kinematic targets, and JSON syntax corruption, establishing that physical failure modes dominate independently of planner intelligence while interface schema parsing forms the primary point of software fragility.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III details the system architecture and safety monitoring framework. Section IV formalizes the fault taxonomy and intensity calibration. Section V describes the experimental setup and model provenance. Section VI presents the empirical results and statistical decomposition. Section VII audits historical pilot attempts for discard-bias transparency. Section VIII discusses core scientific takeaways, Section IX states threats to validity and limitations, and Section X concludes.

# II Related Work

Embodied LLM Planning and Robotics Benchmarks. The integration of large language models as high-level planners for embodied manipulation has expanded rapidly. SayCan [ 1 ] combined LLM plan generation with learned value-function affordances to constrain language outputs to physically executable behaviors. Inner Monologue [ 4 ] and Code as Policies [ 6 ] demonstrated that textual environmental feedback and direct Python code generation enable closed-loop task execution. Multimodal vision-language-action (VLA) foundation models such as PaLM-E [ 3 ] and RT-2 [ 2 ] directly map visual tokens and task instructions to continuous robot actions. Standard benchmarks in this domain (e.g., VirtualHome [ 7 ] , ALFRED [ 8 ] , and BEHAVIOR [ 9 ] ) evaluate task completion across complex multi-step sequences. However, these benchmarks evaluate agents under nominal environmental conditions and do not inject controlled component failures at intermediate execution boundaries.

Robotics Fault Injection and Middleware Reliability. Classical dependability and fault injection in robotics have a long history in safety-critical domains [ 10 , 11 ] . Researchers have investigated hardware bit-flips, sensor noise injection, and network packet loss in ROS/ROS 2 middleware architectures [ 12 , 13 ] . In industrial manipulators, fault-tolerant control architectures typically rely on analytical redundancy, threshold-based disturbance observers, and emergency joint braking [ 14 , 15 ] . Alpha extends physical fault injection to the emerging paradigm of LLM-orchestrated manipulation, bridging low-level simulation physics with modern prompt-based serialization interfaces.

Structured LLM Output, Pydantic Schema Validation, and Failure Handling. When language models are deployed in autonomous decision loops, unstructured text must be converted into strictly typed, executable representations. Tool-use frameworks and libraries such as Pydantic [ 21 ] enforce schema constraints over LLM-generated JSON payloads. However, recent empirical software engineering studies indicate that small perturbations, token dropouts, or syntax deviations frequently trigger unrecoverable JSON decoding or validation errors [ 22 ] . In this work, Alpha explicitly formalizes serialized output corruption as an operational fault class, demonstrating how schema validation acts as a rigid boundary that prevents corrupted trajectories from reaching physical joints at the cost of complete episode abortion.

Autonomous Safety Monitoring and Contact Taxonomy. In physics simulation environments such as PyBullet [ 19 ] , detecting safety violations is non-trivial: contact points, reaction impulses, and joint limits are sampled at high simulation rates (e.g., 240 Hz). Naive thresholding on raw contact points results in severe overcounting, where a single mechanical contact lasting 0.5 seconds generates over 100 violation events. Prior safety-monitoring frameworks in autonomous driving and manipulation propose temporal filtering and state-based incident clustering [ 23 , 24 ] . Alpha implements an explicit contact taxonomy with an audited deduplication window to distinguish transient contact oscillations from sustained, unique safety incidents.

Chaos Engineering in Cyber-Physical Systems. Formalized by Netflix to verify high-availability cloud microservices [ 16 , 17 ] , chaos engineering proactively introduces localized component outages to verify automated failover and system resilience. While cyber-physical systems have begun adopting chaos-testing principles for IoT and automotive communication [ 18 ] , embodied manipulation introduces continuous spatial geometry and irreversible mechanical actions (e.g., dropping a fragile object). Alpha adapts the core principles of chaos testing to robotic manipulation by defining reproducible fault hooks across perception, kinematics, actuation, and serialization.

2026-10-23.authors: Yunfei Xie , Howard H. Qian , Shiyi Lan , Kaiyu Hang , Chen Wei
2026-10-23.subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV) ; Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)

2026-10-23.abstract:
Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability.
The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) [ 20 ] suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion?
To examine this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ( S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} ), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model’s sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion.
We find that S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs).
Beyond this correlation, S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs).
With S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} , we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.
2026-10-23.introduction:
Robotic foundation models increasingly build on large pretrained vision-language models [ 4 , 3 ] , video models [ 48 ] , and world action models [ 14 , 27 , 5 ] . Yet selecting and evaluating these models remains expensive: the most reliable test is still closed-loop rollout in simulation [ 29 , 32 ] or the real world [ 1 ] , where evaluation is slow, noisy, and benchmark-dependent. This expense motivates low-cost offline proxies for robotic capability.

A natural approach is to use existing perception-side proxies, such as visual question answering scores for VLMs [ 30 , 55 ] or pixel-level video quality for world models [ 17 , 50 , 22 ] . However, these metrics measure passive perception or generation quality, not whether a representation is organized for action [ 57 , 23 , 45 , 34 ] . Two scenes may look visually different but require similar robot motions; conversely, two visually similar scenes may demand different trajectories. For robot task success, a model must produce motions of different tasks even for scenes alike. This requires aligning the visual representation with the motor representation.

This perspective connects robotics to the Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) [ 20 ] , which argues that as models of different modalities scale and solve diverse tasks, they are converging to a shared statistical model of reality in each of their own representation spaces.
For example, images and text are both projections of a common underlying reality.
As vision and language models scale,
they increasingly agree on the relative distances between data points.
We bring PRH to robotics and ask: can physical motion be viewed as another projection of the world, such that scaled embodied models better align vision and language representations with the structure of robot trajectories?

We test this prediction of PRH: the more capable an embodied model is, the more closely its sensory representations align with its motor representation. In other words, episodes nearby in sensory representation space should also be nearby in motor representation space.

We formalize this as Sensorimotor Alignment ( S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} ), a training-free metric, illustrated in Figure 1 . For each episode in a robot dataset, a model’s image and text features form its sensory representation, and the recorded end-effector trajectory forms its motor representation. We measure alignment by comparing each episode’s nearest neighbors in sensory and motor spaces. More overlap between the two neighbor sets means stronger sensorimotor alignment.

In Section 3 , we show that S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} correlates positively with downstream robot task success across model families, in simulated and real-world settings. The correlation is strong for Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) in closed-loop manipulation, indicating that models with higher sensorimotor alignment tend to perform better. S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} computed on raw Vision-Language Models (VLMs) also correlates with the success of the VLAs later fine-tuned from them, more strongly than their general visual question answering (VQA) scores do. For World Action Models (WAMs), S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} is likewise a better indicator of success than video quality metrics such as FID [ 17 ] , SSIM [ 50 ] , and PSNR [ 18 ] , and for real-robot policies, S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} computed offline correlates with physical-robot success under consistent conditions. These results suggest sensorimotor alignment reflects embodied performance better than passive perception or pixel quality.

Prior work has observed several phenomena in VLAs and WAMs only through closed-loop results, without explaining them at the representation level. We use S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} to supply that explanation, as shown in Section 4 . For example, fine-tuned VLAs often ignore the language instruction and act mainly on what they see; we find that their task success correlates with the S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} of their vision features, not their text features.

Our contributions are threefold:

Inspired by the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, we propose a new view of embodiment: stronger embodied models should align their sensory representations more closely with their motor representation. To test this, we introduce S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} , a training-free offline metric that measures alignment between sensory and motor representations.

Across model families, in simulation and on real robots, higher S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} goes with higher task success, making S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} a low-cost offline proxy for choosing models before closed-loop evaluation.

We further find that S 2 \mathrm{S}^{2} explains, at the representation level, phenomena that prior work observed only through closed-loop results, making it a diagnostic tool for understanding how design choices shape embodied models.

We make sensorimotor alignment measurable, offering a cheap, representation-level account of embodied model success that closed-loop success rates alone cannot reveal.

2026-10-23.title: Decentralized Bi-Level Optimization for Cooperative Orbital Transportation of a Rigid Payload
2026-10-23.authors: Sidhdharth D. Sikka , Revathy Ravuri , Hei Yin Jowett Chan , Tim Echtermeyer , Shaoshuai Mou
2026-10-23.subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY) ; Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-23.abstract: The rapid growth of the space economy, alongside increasing orbital congestion and debris, is driving demand for reliable on-orbit transportation of large and non-cooperative objects. Performing such transportation with a swarm of small spacecraft distributes risk and removes the single point of failure inherent to monolithic architectures, but requires solving a non-convex trajectory optimization coupling every agent’s cone-constrained thrust to the payload’s rotational dynamics. Existing approaches span decentralized control laws with asymptotic guarantees but limited constraint enforcement, and centralized and partially centralized planners that reintroduce a single point of failure. In this work, we present a decentralized bi-level framework driven by exact gradients: the problem is split into an inner convex thrust allocation and an outer search over payload torque trajectories. This decomposition yields fuel-efficient solutions quickly, without requiring full NLP convergence, and at short timescales its performance scales with the number of agents. Theoretical convergence guarantees are established, and the method is validated through extensive Monte Carlo simulation, including closed-loop recovery from in-flight faults. These properties make the framework well suited to spacecraft swarm applications.
2026-10-23.introduction:
The rapid growth of the space economy has significantly increased demand for reliable and efficient on-orbit transportation solutions, to support both commercial and scientific applications. At the same time, increasing orbital congestion and the proliferation of large debris pose growing risks to sustainable space operations. Addressing these challenges requires transportation technologies capable of safely and efficiently altering the orbit of non-cooperative objects, whose tumbling motion and the limited thrust of servicing spacecraft already make even close-proximity operations demanding [ 1 ] .

Monolithic mission architectures, with a single spacecraft performing the entire manoeuvre, are costly, risk prone, and lack redundancy. Multi-agent architectures offer a promising alternative, distributing the risk across multiple spacecraft, thereby also increasing robustness and operational flexibility through coordinated action.

While cooperative object transportation with multiple agents has been widely studied across terrestrial and aerial domains [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] , including decentralized learning-based [ 6 ] and model-predictive [ 7 ] controllers for multi-robot payload transport, its application in orbital settings is comparatively limited. Notable approaches include decentralized PD control [ 8 ] , occlusion-based heuristics [ 9 ] , back-stepping control for space manipulators [ 10 ] , and cooperative multi-satellite detumbling of tumbling targets through designed torque control laws [ 11 ] . Formation-based methods have also been proposed, such as those by Meng et al. [ 12 ] , re-framing cooperative transport as a formation tracking problem. However, these methods typically offer asymptotic guarantees with limited constraint enforcement and little attention to fuel efficiency or convergence time; factors that are critical to real-time orbital operations.

Partially centralized architectures have been explored for cooperative transportation tasks in orbit. In particular, mothership-style systems, featuring centralized planning and distributed actuation, have been proposed for missions such as asteroid exploration [ 13 ] , telescope assembly [ 14 ] , and orbital debris mitigation [ 15 ] . Most recently, cooperative transportation of passive free-flyers by pushing chaser spacecraft has been demonstrated under human-in-the-loop velocity commands, with stability and safety enforced by barrier conditions and thrust allocated by a centralized mixed-integer program [ 16 ] . While effective in many scenarios, these architectures concentrate planning or allocation in a single node and therefore remain vulnerable to single-point failures that can jeopardize overall mission success.

Fully decentralized architectures remove this vulnerability by distributing computation and decision-making across the agents, and are increasingly seen as essential as space operations scale up [ 17 , 18 ] . A mature body of distributed control delivers decentralized transport with force distribution and fault response [ 12 ] and fault-tolerant formation flying under actuator loss [ 19 , 20 , 21 ] . However, these methods guarantee asymptotic tracking or synchronization, treats thrust-direction cones and terminal boundary conditions only approximately, and optimize no mission objective such as fuel. The nearest decentralized optimizer [ 22 ] uses duality to handle collision constraints between free-flying vehicles, not an objective coupled through a shared payload. Decentralized trajectory optimization with hard constraint satisfaction therefore remains open.

This paper addresses this problem of cooperative orbital transportation involving a rigid body and N N spacecraft agents that must collaboratively manoeuvre the object from an initial state to a desired final state while minimizing total fuel. Each agent is affixed to a fixed location on the payload’s surface and can exert thrust within a constrained angular range.

A constrained optimization framework is well-suited to this problem, as it naturally incorporates relative orbital dynamics, attitude dynamics, actuation constraints, and trajectory boundary conditions. Optimization-based planning has been applied to spacecraft swarms through sequential convex programming [ 23 ] , reachable-set collision constraints [ 24 ] , and hierarchical planning over dynamic communication topologies [ 25 ] , but in centralized or hierarchical settings and for free-flying agents rather than agents rigidly coupled through a shared payload. However, the problem is inherently non-convex due to the coupling between agents’ control inputs and the rotational dynamics of the rigid body. Previous work [ 26 ] addressed this challenge using a centralized bi-level optimization approach where the overall problem was split into an inner convex problem that solved for optimal control input trajectory given a torque profile, while the outer non-convex optimisation problem used population-based heuristics to optimize the torque trajectory. This method is still susceptible to a single-point failure due to the centralised approach taken.

In this paper, we extend the previous approach to a decentralized setting, taking advantage of the multi-agent architecture and thereby removing the single point of failure. Rather than treating the outer torque search as a purely heuristic problem, we observe that the optimal value of the inner convex problem is differentiable in the torque trajectory, and that its exact gradient is available at relatively low computational cost once the inner solver has converged. The outer problem is then solved by projected gradient descent with random restarts, and decentralization acquires a precise role: each agent runs an independent restart stream from its own random seeds, so a swarm of N N agents draws N N times as many restarts per unit wall-clock and can therefore reach basins of attraction a single node would miss, and a single max-consensus round over a line-of-sight communication graph delivers the swarm-wide best trajectory to every agent. The same decentralized search is embedded in a closed-loop recovery mode that detects in-flight actuation and communication faults, detumbles the payload, identifies and removes failed agents, and replans with the survivors.

The key contributions of this paper are:

a first-order method for the outer problem of the bi-level formulation introduced in [ 26 ] , using the exact envelope-theorem gradient of the inner optimal value;

a decentralized multi-start architecture whose solution quality improves with the number of agents; and

a closed-loop fault-recovery mode, made possible by the decentralization of the architecture.

The remainder of the paper is organised as follows. Section II describes the problem of interest, its bi-level reformulation, and the equivalence of the two. Section III presents the proposed method and establishes its convergence guarantee. Section IV evaluates the method through Monte Carlo testing against sampling-based and direct-NLP baselines across cone half-angles, compute budgets, and fleet sizes, including closed-loop fault-survivability statistics, and Section V reports the results. Section VI discusses implications and future work.

2026-10-23.authors: Taekoan Yoo , Wonkyung Jung , Kyunghun Kim , Kyeongbo Kong

2026-10-23.abstract:
World action models increasingly rely on pretrained video models assumed to capture physical dynamics for prediction, planning, and action generation.
Existing evaluations assess plausibility, probe representations, or measure predictive surprise, but rarely identify which history-conditioned physical expectations conflict with observations.
We introduce PhysTrace 1 1 1 https://github.com/PhysTrace/PhysTrace , a training-free framework aligning MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations with observed video windows to temporally localize physical violations and provide interpretable descriptions without task-specific probes or classifiers.
We also introduce IntPhys2-Timing , adding violation intervals to IntPhys2.
PhysTrace achieves a Hit Rate of up to 70.7% across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and outperforms the compared methods in overall possible–impossible discrimination accuracy on IntPhys2.
Applied to reconstructed videos along the trajectories of pretrained diffusion/flow-based video models, PhysTrace reveals attribute- and noise-dependent patterns in physical violation localization, enabling interpretable physical consistency analysis across timesteps.
2026-10-23.introduction:
In robotic control, Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have rapidly advanced by leveraging semantic knowledge and generalization capabilities acquired through large-scale vision-language pretraining for robot action generation [ 28 , 8 , 49 , 15 , 20 ] . More recently, research has increasingly explored leveraging future dynamics and predictive and spatiotemporal priors acquired through video pretraining for action prediction and planning [ 16 , 23 , 45 , 39 , 19 , 3 ] . In particular, diffusion/flow-based generative video models have emerged as key pretrained backbones for these approaches, as they can directly generate future visual dynamics [ 9 , 35 , 26 , 27 ] . This growing reliance on pretrained video models makes it increasingly important to determine whether they have learned the physical dynamics required for robotic control.

To this end, various benchmarks and evaluation methods have been proposed to assess intuitive physics, physical plausibility, and motion consistency in input or generated videos [ 32 , 11 , 25 , 7 , 48 , 2 , 46 ] . In parallel, probing studies have investigated the physical information encoded within pretrained video models [ 18 , 31 , 12 , 34 ] . This line of work has also extended beyond encoder-based representation models to the intermediate denoising representations of diffusion-based video generators, showing that physics-related information can be decoded from pretrained representations. However, these approaches primarily focus on predefined physical labels, model-level preferences, or physics-related signals encoded in intermediate representations.
Even when a physical inconsistency can be detected, they provide limited insight into which history-conditioned physical expectation conflicts with the observed behavior.

More fundamentally, physical consistency is not a static visual property of individual frames, but a temporal property that emerges from changes in object identity, state, motion, and interaction across time. Sparse or short observations may therefore miss brief violations or lack the context needed to determine what should have occurred. Likewise, a single plausibility score cannot reveal where the expected and observed dynamics begin to diverge. Evaluating physical consistency thus requires continuously relating local observations to the physical expectations established by their temporal history.

Rather than probing intermediate representations, a natural alternative is to directly ask a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) to assess physical plausibility from video. However, Pixels to Principles [ 6 ] reports near-chance performance of recent MLLMs in challenging intuitive-physics settings on GRASP [ 17 ] and IntPhys 2 [ 11 ] , despite physics-related cues being recoverable from their visual representations. Similarly, QuantiPhy [ 22 ] shows that, in quantitative kinematic inference from video, multimodal models often rely on pretrained world knowledge rather than faithfully integrating visual evidence with the provided physical prior. These findings suggest that current MLLMs are unreliable as direct judges of physical validity. Instead, we use the MLLM for reasoning over temporal context to formulate expected states, while physical consistency is assessed against the corresponding video evidence.

From this perspective, we propose PhysTrace , a training-free framework that traces physical consistency in videos through history-conditioned temporal video-language alignment. As illustrated in Fig. 2 , PhysTrace uses the general contextual reasoning capability of an MLLM to formulate the state expected at the current time based on prior observations as temporal context. It then compares this expected state with the actual video observation in a shared multimodal embedding space, thereby tracing physical consistency over time.
By relating temporally separated events, this process enables temporal localization of physical violations while the jointly generated expected and observed states provide an interpretable description of which physical expectation diverges from the actual observation.
To quantitatively evaluate this temporal behavior, we construct IntPhys2-Timing by augmenting IntPhys2 [ 11 ] with violation intervals, enabling evaluation of physical violation localization in video reconstructions across generative timesteps.

In summary, we propose a training-free framework for tracing physical consistency over time through history-conditioned temporal video-language alignment, together with IntPhys2-Timing for evaluating the temporal localization of physical violations.

We propose PhysTrace , a training-free framework that localizes physical violations by temporally aligning history-conditioned expected states with video observations. Textual descriptions of both states reveal which physical expectations conflict with observations.
