# 2 Related Work

## 2.1 VLA and World-Model-Based Policies

VLA models couple pretrained vision-language representations with robot action generation, allowing large-scale multimodal knowledge to inform language-conditioned control [ 28 , 8 , 49 , 15 , 20 ] . Beyond this paradigm, recent work has explored leveraging predictive dynamics and spatiotemporal priors learned from video for robot policy learning. VPP [ 16 ] extracts predictive visual representations from a video diffusion model for action prediction without explicit future visual rollouts.

More direct approaches, including World Action Models (WAMs) and related world-model-based policies, couple future prediction with action generation or planning [ 23 , 45 , 39 , 19 , 3 ] . Video Policy [ 23 ] couples future video generation with action generation, while DreamZero [ 45 ] jointly models future world states and actions using a pretrained video diffusion backbone. EVA [ 39 ] generates future visual rollouts and uses an inverse dynamics model to derive executable actions and provide an executability signal for aligning the video world model. Cosmos Policy [ 19 ] generates actions as latent frames and predicts future states and values for model-based planning, whereas V-JEPA2-AC [ 3 ] predicts action-conditioned future states in latent space for planning. Despite their architectural differences, these approaches share the goal of exploiting predictive dynamics learned from video as priors for robot control.

## 2.2 Pretrained Video World Models as Policy Priors

Prior work has explored different classes of video models for learning representations and dynamics relevant to robot control. Self-supervised video representation models learn temporal structure without explicit robot actions. V-JEPA2 [ 3 ] follows a latent predictive objective, while VideoMAE V2 [ 38 ] learns general spatiotemporal representations through masked video reconstruction. A separate line of work develops robot-specific, action-conditioned world models. DreamDojo [ 13 ] , for example, learns interaction dynamics from large-scale human videos and is subsequently adapted to generate future visual states conditioned on robot actions.

Another line of work builds general-purpose generative video models, such as Stable Video Diffusion [ 9 ] , Wan [ 35 ] , and the Cosmos-Predict family [ 26 , 27 , 29 ] .
These diffusion/flow-based models directly generate temporally evolving visual sequences and have increasingly been repurposed as pretrained backbones for representation-based policies and WAMs [ 16 , 23 , 45 , 19 ] . Unlike latent predictive or robot-specific world models, our work focuses on this class of pretrained generative video models and examines whether their generated dynamics preserve physical consistency. Specifically, we evaluate Wan2.1, whose pretrained video backbone is adopted by DreamZero [ 45 ] , and Cosmos-Predict2, which is adapted for visuomotor control and planning in Cosmos Policy [ 19 ] .

## 2.3 Physical Understanding and Probing in Video Models

A broad range of benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate physical understanding in videos, including input-video benchmarks for intuitive physics and plausibility [ 32 , 11 , 43 , 21 ] and evaluators for physical plausibility and motion consistency in generated videos [ 25 , 7 , 48 , 2 ] . Among them, IntPhys2 [ 11 ] evaluates four intuitive-physics principles—permanence, immutability, spatio-temporal continuity, and solidity—through video-level discrimination between physically possible and impossible events.
However, it does not provide temporal annotations indicating when a physical violation occurs. To evaluate temporal localization, we introduce IntPhys2-Timing , which augments impossible videos with temporal annotations of their physical violations.

Beyond output-level evaluation, probing studies investigate whether pretrained video representations encode physics-related information [ 18 , 1 ] . Recent work compares such representations across predictive, masked-reconstruction, and diffusion-based pretraining paradigms [ 31 ] , while diffusion-specific studies decode physical plausibility from intermediate denoising representations [ 12 , 34 ] or evaluate model-native preferences through the denoising objective [ 46 ] .

Existing approaches either probe physics-related information from internal model representations or evaluate physical plausibility at the level of an entire video or video pair.
Methods such as TRAJAN [ 2 ] temporally localize motion inconsistency, while predictive violation-of-expectation (VoE) approaches [ 24 , 14 , 11 ] measure time-resolved surprise from discrepancies between predicted and observed representations. However, such surprise signals primarily quantify model-dependent prediction error and do not explicitly identify which physical expectation established by prior observations conflicts with the current observation. PhysTrace instead externalizes the history-conditioned expected state and directly aligns it with the current video observation, enabling temporally localized and interpretable physical diagnostics.

2026-10-23.title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
2026-10-23.authors: Hossein Resani , Javen Qinfeng Shi
2026-10-23.subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-23.abstract:
Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque.
We introduce Inside-JEPA which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and show that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state.
On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065–.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050–.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking.
An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels.
Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs . .621).
For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.
2026-10-23.introduction:
World models that predict in a learned latent space rather than in pixels can ignore what is unpredictable and keep what matters for acting [ 26 , 4 , 8 ] , and they now support planning from images and video [ 5 , 49 , 7 ] .
Their states, however, are opaque vectors.
A probe trained on relation labels can often read from them whether the cup is inside the bowl, but no part of the state is committed to that relation, so neither a goal nor what the model believes can be stated in those terms, although relations between objects are the natural vocabulary for both [ 46 , 21 , 47 ] .
In our real-video evaluations, these relations are geometric predicates computed from 2D entity bounding boxes, so inside denotes an image-plane proxy for containment.

A direct remedy is to build the relations into the state: for every ordered pair of entities, a small vector of soft symbols, which we call relational channels, that the predictor consumes and forecasts like the rest of the latent.
Unlike neuro-symbolic pipelines that read predicates out of a representation with supervised heads [ 24 , 46 , 31 ] , such channels sit inside the dynamics and are trained only through the world model’s own objectives, with no relation labels.
Nothing in a latent-prediction objective, however, says what they should mean.
A predictor is as well served by a static code, or by one that changes without tracking anything, as by a code for the relations: the symbol grounding problem [ 18 ] , inside a world model.
To our knowledge, no prior work has tested whether relational channels in a world model learn meaningful relationships from real videos, or which training signals help them do so.

We study this question with Inside-JEPA ( ).
Our method adds one term to the JEPA objective, an inverse-dynamics loss in which a head must recover the action from the relational channels before and after it, so that the action labels an action-conditioned world model consumes anyway must explain how its relational channels change.
To find out what grounds the channels, we compare five models that differ only in whether and where the inverse gradient enters the state and in whether its targets are shuffled ( Fig. 2 ), plus label-free and label-fraction controls.
Because post-hoc channel matching makes it easy to find meaning that is not there, each relation is matched to a single channel, and every model is also scored with its relation head replaced by a randomly initialised one, which sees the same box geometry ( Fig. 3 ).

Across a controlled 2-D world, Something-Something V2 with Something-Else boxes [ 13 , 32 ] , RH20T robot episodes [ 12 ] and objects found by an off-the-shelf detector and tracker [ 28 , 37 ] , the pattern is the same ( Fig. 4 ).
Latent prediction alone leaves the channels at or near the level of a random relation head, or below it.
Inverse dynamics grounds them: matched relational AUROC rises by .065–.103 in ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on robot episodes with end-effector actions and held-out tasks, and by .050–.061 with tracked objects on five relations; the gain is positive in all 18 settings of Fig. 4 and smallest with tracked objects on thirteen relations and with a frozen V-JEPA 2 encoder (+.016 to +.042).
What grounds them is correct action labels that the channels themselves must explain: an inverse head on the entity latents decodes the action best of all models yet barely moves the channels, and shuffled labels, two label-free objectives and labels on 5% of the pairs do not ground them.
The grounded channels are useful: given an action, their forecasts of the relations that change score almost as well as the observed future, and a readout of the 16 channels selects actions towards relational goals better than a readout of the prediction-only model’s whole latent (top-5 .425 vs . .244, frequency prior .174).

Our contributions are:

Inside-JEPA , a JEPA world model with relational channels inside its latent state, and evidence that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground those channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone ( INV-S ) or as part of the full state ( INV-Z ) ( Sec. 3 ).

A controlled account of what grounds the channels : five models that differ only in their inverse head, on two datasets with two kinds of action and with automatically found objects, scored by one-to-one matched AUROC and against a random relation head. Grounding needs an inverse head that reads the channels and correct action labels on thousands of pairs; latent prediction, shuffled labels and two label-free losses do not ground them ( Secs. 5.1 and 5.2 ).

Uses and limits of the grounded channels : action-conditioned forecasting and one-step action selection towards relational goals on Something-Else, and a measured account of where grounding stops: left/right, a distributed code, a stronger encoder and a supervised ceiling ( Secs. 5.3 and 5.4 ).

2026-10-23.related_work:
# 2 Related work

JEPAs predict target-encoder embeddings instead of pixels [ 26 , 4 , 8 ] ; V-JEPA 2 adds action conditioning and plans with it [ 5 ] ; DINO-WM and navigation world models plan in the feature space of pretrained encoders [ 49 , 7 ] ;
and model-based RL learns action-conditioned latent dynamics [ 16 , 15 , 17 ] .
All keep unstructured vector states.
We keep the JEPA objective and ask what relational channels in its state come to mean.

Interaction networks model physics over given objects and relations [ 9 ] ; C-SWM learns object-factored transitions with a contrastive loss [ 23 ] ; slot models discover objects without boxes [ 30 , 22 , 39 ] and roll them forward [ 45 ] .
Scene graphs and their spatio-temporal versions describe pairwise relations with supervised predicates [ 46 , 21 ] , and neuro-symbolic reasoners execute programs over such structure [ 31 , 47 ] .
Our relational channels are pairwise like a scene graph but trained without relation labels and part of the dynamics state; our learned-object experiments try slots, then a detector and tracker.

Latplan learns propositional states from images for classical planning [ 3 ] , and skill-to-symbol methods derive symbols from the preconditions and effects of actions [ 25 ] .
Closest to our setting, Migimatsu and Bohg ground predicate classifiers on Something-Something V2 with Something-Else boxes from action labels alone, turning each action’s hand-written PDDL pre- and post-conditions into partial labels [ 33 ] .
Our inverse loss also ties the channels to what actions do, but needs no hand-written conditions or separate classifier: it is a differentiable term in a JEPA, and its channels are tested on relation labels it never sees.
Because that method needs hand-written conditions for every action, we do not run it; our comparisons hold the architecture fixed and vary only the training signal.

Predicting the action from consecutive observations shapes features for manipulation and exploration [ 1 , 36 ] , pretrains representations for imitation [ 11 ] and labels or infers actions in unlabelled video [ 6 , 38 ] .
Recent work has also incorporated inverse dynamics into JEPA-style world models: as the sole anti-collapse regulariser [ 20 ] , as a contrastive head replacing SIGReg [ 10 ] , as a decoder of actions from latent differences [ 48 ] , or to keep them plannable when little of the frame moves [ 40 ] ; for linear systems, exact action reconstruction provably keeps every state direction reachable within the horizon [ 42 ] .
They shape the whole latent for control, as our INV-Z arm does; we use the term to give chosen channels of the state a meaning, and measure whether it does.

Concept-bottleneck models supervise concept channels directly [ 24 ] ; linear probes test what a representation encodes [ 2 ] ; and unsupervised factors are not identifiable without inductive bias or supervision [ 29 ] .
We use linear probes, never in training, to check that relational information is present and as planning readouts, and a relation-supervised version of our channels only as a ceiling.
Temporal self-supervision, arrow-of-time classification [ 34 , 44 ] and contrastive prediction [ 43 ] , provides our label-free controls; our InfoNCE control contrasts start and goal channels without the action.

2026-10-23.title: Navigating human-robot interaction challenges in private and residential aged care homes
2026-10-23.authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal , Mohammad Ali Armin , Akila Pemasiri , Harshala Gammulle , Tharindu Fernando , David Silvera-Tawil , Simon Denman
2026-10-23.subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC) ; Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
2026-10-23.comment: Author-accepted manuscript of a book chapter published online in Elsevier's Reference Module in Materials Science and Materials Engineering (2026). Scheduled for inclusion in Comprehensive Robotics for Extreme and Challenging Environments (June 2027)
2026-10-23.abstract:
This chapter explores how robotic systems and ambient intelligence can enhance care for older adults in residential aged care (RAC) homes and private homes. Although these settings differ, we frame both as extreme and challenging environments for human–robot interaction (HRI), characterised by cluttered and dynamic layouts, diverse resident needs, and limited on-site technical support. We review embodied and non-embodied systems that assist with daily living, safety monitoring, and social engagement, highlighting hybrid deployments where robots complement fixed and wearable sensors.
To ensure these technologies are usable and effective, design considerations consider the cognitive, physical, and social needs of older adults. Interaction design prioritises accessibility for older adults with low digital literacy, using robust but simple voice interfaces, small sets of non-verbal cues, accessible screen-based companions, and safe object handovers.
Privacy, trust, and acceptability are addressed via practical strategies such as on-device inference, data minimisation, visible consent controls, and transparent data handling aligned with emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and privacy regulation.
Evaluation emphasises real-world metrics including false alarms per day, time to recover from faults, staff workload, and long-term system reliability. We close by outlining open research challenges and future directions for scalable, regulation-ready deployments that support aging with dignity, safety, and independence.

2026-10-23.title: Sensitive dependence of the motion of a legged robot on granular media
2026-10-23.authors: Chen Li , Paul B. Umbanhowar , Haldun Komsuoglu , Daniel E. Koditschek , Daniel I. Goldman
2026-10-23.subjects: Biological Physics (physics.bio-ph) ; Other Condensed Matter (cond-mat.other); Soft Condensed Matter (cond-mat.soft); Robotics (cs.RO); Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM)
2026-10-23.abstract: Legged locomotion on flowing ground ( e.g. granular media) is unlike locomotion on hard ground because feet experience both solid- and fluid-like forces during surface penetration. Recent bio-inspired legged robots display speed relative to body size on hard ground comparable to high performing organisms like cockroaches but suffer significant performance loss on flowing materials like sand. In laboratory experiments we study the performance (speed) of a small (2.3 kg) six-legged robot, SandBot, as it runs on a bed of granular media (1 mm poppy seeds). For an alternating tripod gait on the granular bed, standard gait control parameters achieve speeds at best two orders of magnitude smaller than the 2 body lengths/s ( ≈ 60 \approx 60 cm/s) for motion on hard ground. However, empirical adjustment of these control parameters away from the hard ground settings, restores good performance, yielding top speeds of 30 cm/s. Robot speed depends sensitively on the packing fraction ϕ \phi and the limb frequency ω \omega , and a dramatic transition from rotary walking to slow swimming occurs when ϕ \phi becomes small enough and/or ω \omega large enough. We propose a kinematic model of the rotary walking mode based on generic features of penetration and slip of a curved limb in granular media. The model captures the dependence of robot speed on limb frequency and the transition between walking and swimming modes but highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the physics of granular media.
